case_report: A three-month-old female child was brought to our hospital due to concerns about apparent blindness. The child had a history of frequent episodes of flexor spasms accompanied by eye twitching since one and a half months of age. These episodes occurred approximately five to six times daily and were associated with drooling. According to the parents, the child did not respond to light or sound. She was the second child in a family with no consanguinity, born at full term through a normal delivery. There was no history of jaundice, fever, or convulsions in the immediate neonatal period. Upon examination, the child exhibited global developmental delay. Her head circumference was in the 10th percentile. Ophthalmic examination showed that the child did not respond to or follow bright light, and both pupils had very sluggish reactions. The anterior segments and vitreous of both eyes were normal. Fundus examination revealed bilateral optic nerve colobomas with variable-sized discrete dome-shaped pale areas with sharp borders (chorioretinal lacunae) located just nasal to the optic discs. The fovea was unaffected in both eyes.
test_results: EEG showed burst of spike, polyspike, sharp and slow-wave complexes with suppression in between, predominantly over the right hemisphere. Bilateral synchronous and symmetrical discharges were also present along with slow waves of high amplitudes that were seen more on the right hemisphere. It showed burst suppression and hypsarrhythmia pattern. CT scan of the child revealed hypogenesis of the corpus callosum with small inter-hemispheric cyst.

case_report: A 25-year-old female presented with a mass in the right thigh, which she had noticed for approximately 18 months. The patient experienced tingling sensations along the leg when the lesion was bumped, but had no other symptoms. There was no relevant past medical or family history. Physical examination revealed a small, mobile, well-defined subcutaneous mass. No other lesions were found, and a thorough examination, including assessment of nodal status, was otherwise normal.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging showed a solid, well-circumscribed, smoothly contoured ovoid mass measuring 21 mm × 11 mm × 11 mm in maximum diameter, present anteriorly to the quadriceps compartment of the right thigh at the junction of the biceps femoris and vastus lateralis, and suggesting a neurogenic tumor. The tumor was diagnosed initially on core biopsy, with subsequent excision. Macroscopically the tumor measured 20 mm in maximum dimension and was located within subcutaneous fat. The tumor had a homogeneous, yellowish, myxoid cut surface. Microscopically the tumor was thinly encapsulated and lobulated and of variable cellularity, and was composed of patternless distributions of slender spindle cells with minimally to mildly atypical vesicular nuclei and long cytoplasmic processes within delicately collagenous to focally myxoid stroma, intermingled with more cellular nodules of plump, polygonal cells with moderately pleomorphic vesicular nuclei with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli and irregular chromatin, with moderate to abundant amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm. The mitotic index was up to 2 per 10 high power fields (hpf) including markedly abnormal forms. No lymphovascular invasion or necrosis was seen. Immunohistochemically, the tumor was diffusely and strongly positive for S100 protein, SOX10, D2-40, CD56 and glial fibrillary acidic protein in both the epithelioid and spindle cell populations, with focal CD34 expression. Epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) highlighted perineurial cells in the surrounding capsule, with some cytoplasmic expression in the epithelioid cells. There was complete loss of nuclear INI1 expression in the epithelioid cells, although the spindle cells around the nodules of epithelioid cells retained INI1. The tumor was negative for HMB45, MelanA, smooth muscle actin, desmin, AE1/AE3, CD79a, CD45, and CD30.
diagnosis: Epithelioid malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor

case_report: A 13-year-old boy was admitted to our clinic from another hospital. His serum electrolytes were as follows: urea: 33 mg/dL (normal 8.4-38.4), creatinine: 0.91 mg/dL (normal 0.84-1.25), Na: 139 mmol/L (normal 135-150), K: 4.3 mmol/L (normal 3.5-5), Cl: 109 mmol/L (normal 96-110). Venous gas analysis showed pH: 7.35 (normal 7.31-7.41), HCO3 content: 20.7 mmol/L (normal 24-28), and pCO2: 38.4 mmHg (normal 41-51).
test_results: In DMSA scan, there was a huge high-grade radioactivity accumulation in anterior to the left kidney and extends through the pelvis. The left kidney can be hardly seen in the posterior images because of the radioactivity accumulation that belongs to the urinary bladder. Both kidneys accumulated the activity low grade. In left posterior oblique images, the left kidney is seen when the attenuation goes away. We took an ultrasonography (USG) image and confirmed the huge activity accumulation was the urinary bladder. In his CT, the anatomical details were better. Furthermore, dilated ureter may be seen like deviated neurogenic bladder. However, there was no ureter abnormality in USG or CT. We took Tc-99m MAG3 scintigraphy in 10 days. The concentration functions of the radioactivity of both kidneys were normal.

case_report: An 11-year-old Sudanese boy presented with frequent bleeding episodes, including bruising, nosebleeds, and gum bleeds. The most common type of hemorrhage was extensive bleeding after trauma, followed by subcutaneous bleeding. The patient had a history of delayed bleeding episodes since circumcision, which took approximately one month to stop. Repeated episodes of nosebleeds were also reported. He did not receive blood or blood product transfusions. He reported subcutaneous bleeding following trauma while playing with friends. Hemorrhage into joints also occurred after trauma, but spontaneous joint bleeding was not reported. Pain and slight swelling of muscles sometimes persisted for months. Family history revealed that all family members were normal except his mother, who had a history of severe interval bleeding episodes (heavy menstrual bleeding). The patient had no known chronic illnesses, drug allergies, or developmental abnormalities. On examination, the patient was neither jaundiced nor cyanosed, and was not dysmorphic. There was no noticeable change when checking the ear, nose, and throat. The cardiopulmonary examination was normal. The patient’s central nervous system examination showed good sensation and reflexes. He had no skin rash or organomegaly. Liver function tests and complete blood count were all normal. Viral screening for HIV, HBV, and HCV were negative.
test_results: The main abnormal investigations were as follows: fast lysis of whole blood clots and shortened euglobulin lysis time. The other tests including clotting time, prothrombin time (PT), partial thromboplastin time (PTT), and thrombin time (TT) were all within the normal values. Platelet count, bleeding time, and von Willebrand factor were also normal. Concerning the clot lysis test, the blood was collected and promptly placed in a glass test tube and incubated at 37°C. The clot was formed and retracted normally, but then underwent lysis. Following a few hours of incubation (5–8 hours with interval assessment), the clot was hardly visible, and it was just a small strand of fibrin. The fibrinogen and d-dimer concentration were within normal limits. To determine the status of fibrinolysis, euglobulin lysis time was calculated, and the result indicated shortened lysis time. We treated the patient’s plasma with a pooled normal plasma and repeated the euglobulin lysis time, which returned to normal.

case_report: A 37-year-old woman, who had just given birth via full-term spontaneous vaginal delivery, reported a 2-week duration of intensely itchy, red papules located on her abdomen, back, chest, and lower extremities, with the umbilical area unaffected. Additionally, red, dusky plaques and tense blisters were observed on both lower legs and knees, which had evolved from the papules over the past week. She had been treated with oral cephalexin and topical mupirocin, as well as topical triamcinolone, but saw no improvement. There was no warmth, pain, or pus at any site, and her extremities showed no swelling. The patient did not report any fever or chills. She also denied recent exposure to plants or irritants, and had not used any new topical products or cosmetics. Her medical history was unremarkable, with no previous skin conditions or known allergies.
test_results: Punch biopsy of the right lower extremity demonstrated intraepidermal and subcorneal vesicle formation with associated eosinophils and lymphocytes, superficial papillary dermal edema and red cell extravasation, and perivascular interstitial lymphohistiocytic inflammation. The Gram/periodic acid–Schiff with diastase special stain was negative for pathogenic organisms. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) testing for IgG, IgG4, IgM, IgA, and C3 and basement membrane BP180 NC16A antibody indirect immunofluorescence tests were negative.

case_report: In 2019, a 5-year-old girl was referred to the metabolism department in the Children's University Hospital in Damascus with a complaint of short stature, measuring 96 cm in height and weighing 13 kg. She exhibited developmental delay, stubby fingers, and distinct facial characteristics including a coarse face, facial hirsutism, bushy eyebrows, telecanthus, a flat nasal bridge, a long philtrum, low set ears, and a short neck. The patient had a history of jerking seizures and was treated with Phenobarbital and Phenytoin. Additionally, she had Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) with normal pulmonary pressure and was prescribed Digoxin. Radiographs and laboratory tests were conducted for further investigation. Spine radiographs revealed mild kyphoscoliosis and signs of osteoporosis, indicated by reduced vertebral body height and low density. Left hand radiographs showed mild acroosteolysis in the distal phalanges. Head and neck radiographs indicated an elongated sella turcica and an elevated palate. Bone densitometry using dual energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) showed a lumbar spine Z-score of −4.8 (−46%) and a bone mineral density (BMD) of 0.232 for the lumbar vertebrae. Laboratory results and the karyotype were normal. Screening for lysosomal mucopolysaccharide (MPS) enzymes returned normal results.
test_results: WES results came positive for autosomal dominant NOTCH2 gene-related disorders. The sequencing revealed a heterozygous nonsense mutation (NM_024408.3:c.6463G > T) protein change (Glu2155*), which creates a premature stop codon.

case_report: A one-year-old girl was brought to our center due to delays in neurodevelopment, bilateral hearing loss, and visual issues. Her parents are first cousins. The perinatal history was without complications. Physical examination showed normal growth parameters. She had bilateral hearing loss and was using hearing aids. The liver was palpable 6 cm below the right costal margin. Notable facial features included arched eyebrows, a broad nasal root, low set ears, downward slanting eyes, epicanthal folds, strabismus, and a myopathic face. Laboratory tests showed ALT at 101 U/L (normal range: 0–37) and AST at 53 U/L (normal range: 0–41). An ophthalmologic examination indicated septooptic dysplasia, with a pale optic disc and irregular optic disc margins. Visual evoked potentials demonstrated bilateral elongated P100 latency. Cranial MRI revealed nonspecific gliosis in the subcortical and periventricular deep white matter, and the superior margin of the sella had a mildly upward convexity. Analysis of very long chain fatty acids showed elevated C26:0, low C24:0, low C22:0, an elevated C26:0/C22:0 ratio, and highly elevated levels of phytanic acid and pristanic acid.
test_results: Molecular genetic analysis for PEX genes indicated homozygous novel IVS1-2A>G mutation in the PEX1 gene.

case_report: A 5-year-old girl exhibited increasing difficulty in walking and limb tightness. She experienced mild developmental delays, including late sitting and walking, and was unable to run or climb stairs. She showed clumsiness and frequent falls while walking. Since 8 months of age, she had seizures characterized by right lower limb jerking, which then generalized. These seizures were effectively managed with carbamazepine. The child had moderate cognitive and language impairments and was unable to attend school. Her brother displayed similar but milder symptoms. At presentation, her head circumference measured 56 cm, above the 95th percentile for her age. Mental examination revealed severe language impairment. Motor system examination indicated severe spasticity with grade 4 power in all limbs, exaggerated reflexes, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. She also had severe incoordination, a scissoring gait, and walked on her toes.
test_results: Her MRI showed temporal polar subcortical cysts.

case_report: A 30-year-old woman reported experiencing pain in her left knee, accompanied by occasional episodes of locking, for the past year. Physical examination indicated tenderness on the medial joint line and a positive McMurray's test. Standard x-ray images of the knees appeared normal. MRI of the left knee showed a bucket handle tear of the medial meniscus and a partial tear of the anterior cruciate ligament. Arthroscopic partial meniscectomy was planned based on her symptoms and MRI results. During the arthroscopic procedure, mild synovial hypertrophy was observed, and a bucket handle tear in the medial meniscus was noted, which had a brownish-black appearance. The anterior cruciate ligament was also partially torn. Additionally, the lateral meniscus and the articular cartilage over the medial femoral condyle exhibited brownish-black discoloration. Meniscectomy for the bucket handle tear of the medial meniscus was performed, and the specimen was collected.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the excised tissue showed pigmentation and degenerative changes. Ferric chloride test was also found to be positive.

case_report: A 62-year-old woman presented with a two-year history of pain in the lower left abdomen. She was admitted to the urology unit and underwent a routine eye examination. She had a 10-year history of hypertension. The patient reported no eye-related symptoms. Visual acuity was measured at 0.6 in the right eye and 0.8 in the left eye. The manifest refraction was +1.50DS/−0.75 DC×100° in the right eye and +1.00DS in the left eye. The anterior segment examination showed normal results.
test_results: Ophthalmoscopy revealed RAH located at the inferior macular fovea in the right fundus and at the subtemporal rim of the optic disc in the left fundus. Spectral domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) revealed a retinal tumour in the inner layer of the retina in the right fundus. OCT demonstrated a pre-retinal membrane and retinal tumour located in the inner layer of the retina in the left fundus. Computed tomography (CT) revealed bilateral renal angiomyolipoma, multiple hepatic angiomyolipoma and multiple pulmonary nodules. Brain CT showed extensive bilateral calcification near the cella lateralis.

case_report: A 73-year-old man with a history of controlled hypertension and progressive shortness of breath over 3 months (New York Heart Association functional class II) and recent nonproductive coughs was referred with a water-bottle heart sign on his chest X-ray, indicating pericardial effusion. Physical examinations showed normal vital signs and an oxygen saturation of 94% without supplemental oxygen. Other physical examination findings were unremarkable. The patient did not report systemic symptoms such as weight loss, fever, anorexia, or fatigue. Electrocardiography revealed atrial fibrillation rhythms and nonspecific ST-T changes. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, renal and hepatic function tests, urine analysis, coagulation profile, and inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein), were all within normal ranges. A 2D transthoracic echocardiographic examination showed severe circumferential pericardial effusion up to 25 mm anterior to the right ventricular outflow tract without right atrial and right ventricular collapse. Additionally, a large non-homogenous intrapericardial mass was visible on the anterior side of the right ventricular outflow tract without obvious compressive effects on the cardiac chambers. Other echocardiographic parameters were within normal ranges except for moderate mitral and tricuspid regurgitation. A multislice spiral thoracic CT scan with contrast was performed to assess the extension and invasion of the mass, revealing a large ill-defined non-enhancing mass. The mass was an intrapericardial lesion adjacent to the right atrium, extending toward the right ventricular outflow tract and the base of the ascending aorta. No other lesions were noted in the chest or upper abdomen, except for severe pericardial effusion. The patient was referred for thoracotomy and mass resection after consultations with a cardiac surgeon. Following general anesthesia and mid sternal thoracotomy, pericardiocentesis was performed, yielding 500 cc of bloody pericardial fluid. A large mass, 13 cm at its greatest dimension, was discovered. The mass was attached to the pericardium over the ascending aorta and the right atrium. On gross examination, the tumor was partially encapsulated, with some areas showing capsule invasion (stage IIb according to the Masaoka staging system). The tumor was brownish with a spongy solid consistency on cut surfaces, with areas of hemorrhage and necrosis. After total mass resection and pericardial biopsy, the specimen was sent to the surgical pathology department in a 10% buffered neutral formalin solution. The surgery was uncomplicated, and the patient was discharged in good general condition. His next visit was scheduled for 4 weeks later in the outpatient clinic.
test_results: The microscopic examination of the prepared sections revealed a typical mixture of epithelial cells and lymphocytes with variable proportions of the 2 components throughout the lesion. The epithelial cells possessed round-to-polygonal shapes and contained vesicular nuclei with conspicuous nucleoli. The cells formed sheets and solid nests in some areas. The intermingled lymphocytic component was composed of mature lymphocytes. Small-sized vessels were present, some surrounded by a clear space containing lymphocytes and proteinaceous material. The epithelial component was positive for Pan-CK and focally for CD5. The labeling profile of the intermingled lymphocytes was compatible with mature T lymphocyte (positive for CD3, TdT, and CD5). The proliferative activity was 70%.

case_report: The patient, a 35-year-old male, presented with a 20-year history of joint pain and limited mobility, which had worsened over the past year. He developed kyphosis at age 11. He reported pain in his palms, wrists, and elbows without rash or erythematous swelling. Over time, he experienced pain and restricted movement in his hips and ankles, particularly during squatting. He also had pain in his hips and knees, making it difficult to stand and sit. Claudication was noted, and he was treated with occasional painkillers. By age 34, he required a crutch to walk due to severe hip pain and restricted motion. Laboratory tests showed a normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate (2 mm/h) and negative HLA-B27. Hip radiographs indicated sacroiliitis. Physical examination revealed abnormal spinal curvature and limited cervical spine motion, with flexion contractures in the elbows and knees, and restricted motion in the elbows, shoulders, knees, and ankles. The Patrick test and occiput-to-wall distance test were positive. Radiological findings included reduced interarticular space in the hip joints with bilateral femoral neck aseptic necrosis, enlarged interphalangeal joints, osteosclerosis, irregular joint surface contours, and narrowed knee joint spaces. Additionally, herniated disks in the thoracolumbar spine, lumbar spine hyperplasia, and platyspondyly of the cervical spine were observed. His five family members, including parents, wife, and son, showed no signs of skeletal dysplasia.
test_results: The proband carried a frameshift mutation (c.670dupA) and a nonsense mutation (c.756C > A, p.Cys252*) in exon 4 of WISP3. The frameshift mutation (c.670dupA) was found in the paternal allele, and the nonsense mutation (c.756C > A, p.Cys252*) was found in the maternal allele. The son of the proband was found to carry the frameshift mutation (c.670dupA) inherited from his grandfather.

case_report: A 44-year-old male visited the pulmonary clinic due to unusual findings on a chest CT scan. He reported an eight-month history of coughing, fatigue, and reduced exercise tolerance. He had a history of recurrent lung infections, including a severe pneumonia episode in his 20s that required hospitalization, and possible sinusitis. He had a brief smoking history of about four years, quitting in his 20s. Imaging studies, including chest X-Ray and chest CT, revealed peri-bronchial consolidation predominantly in the upper lobes, micronodular changes, both calcified and noncalcified mediastinal adenopathy, axillary lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly. Pulmonary function tests indicated mild obstruction without improvement after bronchodilator use, with normal lung volumes and diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO). Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) showed 126 WBCs/ml, with a differential of 1% basophils, 1% eosinophils, 83% monocytes/macrophages, and 15% lymphocytes, and a CD4/CD8 ratio of 3.8. The BAL fluid culture identified Hemophilus influenza, for which antibiotics were administered. Endobronchial biopsies revealed non-necrotizing granulomas.
test_results: Serum IgG levels of 478 mg/d (normal- 695-1620) and low serum IgA levels of 55 mg/dL (normal: 70-380 mg/dl), IgM levels 57 mg/dL (normal: 60-265 mg/dl) and low H influenzae titers suggesting impaired immune response.

case_report: A 28-month-old Russian female presented with congenital left-arm swelling. She was born after 38 weeks' gestation by vaginal delivery, with a birth weight of 2.95 kg. She is the second of fraternal twins, with her twin sister showing no abnormalities. The parents reported no history of radiation exposure, and the mother had no significant illnesses during pregnancy or abnormal obstetric history. No other family members exhibited similar physical features. The patient was admitted to a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) in Russia for respiratory difficulty and underwent extensive evaluation for one month without a conclusive outcome, after which she was referred to our hospital. Upon admission, the patient was alert with stable vital signs. Her height was 94 cm (90th percentile according to the CDC growth chart) and weight was 14 kg (between the 75th–90th percentile per the CDC growth chart). She exhibited significant left-arm swelling (without pain), restricted motion, and difficulty moving the arm. The circumferences of the right and left arms were as follows: upper arm (midpoint between the tip of the olecranon process and the tip of the acromion), 14.5 cm and 22 cm; forearm (at two fingers distance from the elbow crease), 14 cm and 22.5 cm, respectively. Bioimpedance analysis (InBody S10; Biospace, Seoul, Korea) showed the amount of water and moisture ratio (i.e., extracellular fluid/total water amount) in the right upper limb to be 420 mL and 0.389%, respectively, and in the left upper limb to be 1,050 mL and 0.412%, respectively. The patient also had a dysmorphic face with a flat midface, wide-set eyes, a depressed nasal bridge, a bulbous nasal tip, and epicanthal folds. All other parts of the body appeared normal. Various rehabilitative assessment tools, with the assistance of a Russian interpreter, indicated developmental delays in gross motor skills, fine motor skills, personal-social functions, and functional activities. Routine blood tests and urinalysis were within normal limits. Total protein (6.1 g/dL) and albumin (4.0 g/dL) levels were also within normal limits.
test_results: Various diagnostic evaluations including X-ray, computed tomography (CT), angiography, lymphatic scan, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), chest CT, and abdomen ultrasonography (US) indicated lymphatic malformation of multiple organs.

case_report: A petite nine-year-old girl (somatometric features <3rd centile) was admitted with a two-month history of fever and generalized malaise, accompanied by intermittent abdominal pain, muscle pain, and throat pain at the onset. Physical examination and laboratory tests showed elevated inflammatory markers [white blood cell count 23,200/μl (neutrophils: 81%), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 117 mm/h, c-reactive protein 261 mg/L, ferritin 421 ng/ml, fibrinogen 6.21 g/L, serum amyloid A 590 mg/L], anemia (hemoglobin 9.9 g/dl), mesenteric lymphadenitis, myositis/fasciitis of the left major gluteal muscle, and corneal sediments due to uveitis. No clear source of infection was identified. The patient had two previous admissions for prolonged fever at the ages of 12 and 26 months, with elevated inflammatory markers being the only abnormal findings. At the ages of seven and eight years, she experienced episodes of arthritis that resolved on their own. Additionally, she had short-term fever episodes of unknown origin 1-2 times per year without other symptoms. Family history revealed that her father and several paternal relatives had similar symptoms. Her father experienced arthritis of small and large joints, recurrent fever episodes, and abdominal pain, and had surgeries for adhesive obstructive ileus. Similar symptoms were reported in four other paternal family members. The paternal grandfather had been treated for ankylosing spondylitis and had coronary heart disease surgery at a young age. Three out of five paternal siblings had symptoms of arthritis, serositis, and abdominal pain from a young age.
test_results: A novel heterozygous mutation in the cysteine residue located in exon 3, C73Y, as a common name (c.305G>A, p.C102Y). The same mutation was identified in five members, two of whom also carried a concomitant R92Q mutation while three members were carriers of the R92Q.
diagnosis: Tumor Necrosis Factor Receptor Associated Periodic Syndrome
Orpha_name: Tumor necrosis factor receptor 1 associated periodic syndrome

case_report: The patient is a 12-year-old girl weighing 33 kg and measuring 138 cm in height. She visited the pediatrics clinic due to facial asymmetry. Initially, she experienced a sore throat, cough, and runny nose, which were followed 2 days later by pain around the right ear and a vesicular rash on the right ear pinna and behind the ear. Facial asymmetry began 3 days after the appearance of the periauricular rash. She came to the clinic on the second day of facial paralysis. She did not report any audiovestibular symptoms such as vertigo, tinnitus, nausea, vomiting, or hearing loss. Her medical history includes a varicella infection at the age of 5. The patient exhibited Grade 4 peripheral facial paralysis based on the House-Brackmann (HB) classification. Physical examination revealed crusting vesicular lesions on the right ear pinna and in the mastoid area, with additional crusted lesions in the outer ear canal. The tympanic membrane appeared normal.
test_results: Results of the brainstem auditory evoked potential (BAEP) were normal.

case_report: A 16-year-old female presented to the orthopedic clinic with a history of diffuse back pain lasting for one year, which worsened with prolonged sitting or standing. Her vital signs included a blood pressure of 120/90 mmHg and a heart rate of 88 beats per minute. She weighed 63 kg and had a height of 160.3 cm. Physical examination revealed no abnormalities; there was no tenderness, redness, or warmth in the back, and back mobility was normal without kyphoscoliosis. The patient had a normal stature and no history of fractures. Laboratory tests showed normal liver and renal function. The 25-hydroxy-vitamin D level was 7.2 ng/mL, and the 1,25-dihydroxy-vitamin D level was 27.88 pg/mL. Calcium was 10.1 mg/dL, phosphate was 3.7 mg/dL, intact parathyroid hormone was 31.7 pg/mL, and rheumatoid factor was 5 U/mL. Thyroid-stimulating hormone was 0.484 µIU/mL, but serum free T4 was within normal limits. Bone turnover markers were also within normal limits: bone-specific alkaline phosphatase was 19.11 U/L, osteocalcin was 15.76 ng/mL, and C-terminal telopeptides of type I collagen was 0.265 ng/mL. Imaging studies, including skull X-ray, rib series, and long bones (tibia, fibula, and humerus), showed no abnormalities or sclerotic changes.
test_results: Spine X-ray showed sclerotic change of spine endplate and pelvic bone. Rugger-jersey vertebra and sandwich vertebra was shown. On whole body bone scan with Tc-99m hydroxymethylene diphosphonate (HDP) image, there was suspiciously increased uptake in vertebra. Normal uptake was observed at growth plate area. There was no evidence of increased bone turnover marker and only an axial skeleton involvement was shown on the whole body bone scan.

case_report: An 85-year-old male with a decade-long history of diabetes mellitus presented with a painful penile ulceration that had been worsening over a period of 3 months. Initially, he experienced itching of the glans, which developed into a papular lesion and subsequently into a painful ulcer. On physical examination, a single 5-cm purulent ulceration with an indurated base was observed on the glans. There were no superficial lymphadenopathies, and his overall health status was stable. Initial surgical biopsy indicated nonspecific inflammatory changes. Tests for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) were negative, and no infectious agents were identified from local samples or skin biopsy cultures. Other laboratory results, including complete blood count, plasma C-reactive protein (CRP), cytobacteriological examination of urine, and renal and liver function tests, were within normal limits. Computed tomography (CT) urography revealed no abnormalities in the urinary tract. During his hospital stay, a peripheral pustular lesion appeared on the lateral side of the glans.
test_results: Histopathology revealed a neutrophilic dermal infiltrate with focal neutrophilic vasculitis without cytocalsia.

case_report: A 39-year-old Caucasian male visited our outpatient clinic with seven painless, non-itchy papules that developed within a recent tattoo. These papules emerged approximately three weeks after the patient received a large tattoo on the front side of his right thigh. Initially, the lesions exhibited rapid growth, which later stabilized. Upon physical examination, the papules were found to be unilateral, erythematous, and dome-shaped, with sizes ranging from 4 mm to 1 cm in diameter. Five of the seven lesions were located within the red-inked area of the tattoo, while the remaining two were within the black/gray-inked area. Most of the papules had a thin crust on their surface. The patient reported no previous medical conditions and no additional symptoms. He had received multiple tattoos in the past without any issues and reported no recent sun exposure.
test_results: An excisional biopsy revealed well-circumscribed symmetric tumors with a central keratin-filled crater. The cytologic atypia was mild and the tumors were accompanied by neutrophilic microabscesses and a mixed cell infiltrate.

case_report: A 10-month-old (corrected 8-months) girl arrived at the emergency department experiencing severe diarrhea and vomiting. Her medical history included a preterm birth at 32 weeks and parental consanguinity. Physical examination showed her height, weight, and head circumference were below the 3rd percentile, but her mental and motor development were normal. The liver was palpated 2 cm below the mid-costal margin, and the spleen was 1.5 cm below the mid-costal margin. Laboratory results indicated a serum glucose level of 28 mg/dl (normal >65 mg/dl) and elevated liver function tests with alanine-aminotransferase (ALT) at 244 IU/L and aspartate-aminotransferase (AST) at 274 IU/L. Further analysis showed hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia with fasting insulin levels at 11.7 mIU/L (normal ≥2). Despite treatment with diazoxide, hypoglycemia and elevated liver function tests persisted.
test_results: Transferrin isoelectric focusing testing was performed and type I pattern was seen. Sanger sequencing revealed a homozygous known mutation (c.413T>C, p.M138T) in the MPI gene.

case_report: A 10-year-old girl was seen by a neurologist at the OPD Neurology, Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences hospital, Islamabad, for evaluation of congenital microcephaly and seizures. Her family history revealed that her 8-year-old sister exhibited similar characteristics. The patient presented with short stature, a slim body, and distinct facial features including a narrow forehead, bulging eyes, a pointed nose, fuller lips, a broad mouth, and constant drooling. An ophthalmic examination indicated reduced vision due to retinal lesions and bilateral cataracts. She demonstrated good control of her head and other body parts, recognized her parents socially, and was observed smiling. Both children experienced developmental delays, learning disabilities, repetitive behavior, absence of speech, and mood disturbances. The mother reported no viral infections or medication use during the full-term pregnancy, and the delivery was normal.
test_results: The patient had an MRI exam that showed frontal lobe disproportion, cortical simplification, and myelin dystrophy. The results of whole-exome sequencing analysis uncovered that the syndromic MCPH phenotype is due to a missense variant in exon 2 of the RTTN gene (NM_173630.4: c.57G > T(pGlu19Asp). Sanger sequencing data analysis detected the causative variant in the proband and affected sibling as biallelic, while the parents were heterozygous.

case_report: A 26-year-old male visited Tianjin Medical University General Hospital due to a painless neck lump, first noticed 6 years ago, which had recently grown rapidly. The patient experienced agitation, irritability, excessive sweating, and discomfort while swallowing. Previously, he had been diagnosed with nodular goiter by other hospitals and had intermittently taken Euthyrox® for several years. He also reported childhood hearing impairment and language learning difficulties, though clinical examination indicated normal mental and physical development. Physical examination revealed a visible grade III goiter, with an enlarged, tough thyroid without palpable nodules and a clear boundary. Laboratory tests showed a free thyroxine level of 9.99 pmol/l (normal range: 11.5–23.5 pmol/l), a free triiodothyronine level of 6.07 pmol/l (normal range: 3.5–6.5 pmol/l), and a thyroid stimulating hormone level of 2.401 μlU/ml (normal range: 0.3–5.0 μlU/ml). Thyrotrophin receptor, thyroglobulin, thyroperoxidase antibodies, carcinoembryonic antigen, thyroglobulin, and calcitonin levels were within normal ranges. A chest X-ray showed tracheal narrowing at the superior thoracic aperture, and a thyroid ultrasound revealed multiple hypoechoic signals in each lobe and isthmus of the thyroid. Cervical lymph node enlargement was also noted. Cervical computed tomography scan showed diffuse enlargement of each lobe and thickening of the thyroid isthmus, with numerous oval, low- and slightly high-density nodules in the thyroid. Electrical capacitance tomography results were consistent with signs of a nodular goiter.
test_results: The two vestibular aqueducts were enlarged, more markedly in the right aqueduct.

case_report: An 86-year-old male presented with itchy, multiple, irregularly shaped, and erythematous to brown patches on his back for a duration of 3 weeks. He reported no other systemic symptoms. His medical history included cerebral infarction, hypercholesterolemia, and prostate cancer. He was undergoing treatment with chemotherapy agents bicalutamide and triptorelin acetate for prostate cancer and had been on anticoagulant and statin therapy for several years. Laboratory tests showed unremarkable results for complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, and urinalysis. The antinuclear antibody titer was low at 1:40, and the anti-DNA titer was negative. Rheumatoid factor and thyroid function levels were within normal ranges. Tests for anti-Ro/SS-A, anti-La/SS-B, p-ANCA, c-ANCA, SmJO1, and Scl70 were negative.
test_results: A skin biopsy of the lesion revealed interstitial histiocytic infiltration in the upper and mid-reticular dermis with few eosinophils and neutrophils. Alcian blue stain at pH 2.5 revealed no mucin deposition in the interstitial infiltrate.

case_report: A 66-year-old woman with a history of post-traumatic epilepsy and hypothyroidism was brought to the emergency department following a seizure at home. She had been on phenytoin for over 40 years, but her husband noted inconsistent medication adherence and lack of recent neurologist visits. While watching television, she saw flashing lights, followed by generalized tonic stiffening with an atonic component, resulting in head trauma from hitting a table. This was followed by generalized clonic movements and urinary incontinence. The episode lasted 27 minutes and resolved without pharmacologic intervention. The patient had no memory of the event. In the emergency department, her phenytoin level was 6.3 mcg/mL (therapeutic range 10.0-20.0 mcg/mL). A head CT showed no acute intracranial abnormalities; no prior imaging was available for comparison. Lactic acid was elevated at 3.9 mmol/L. Thyroid function tests showed a high T3 uptake of 51%, low thyroid-stimulating hormone level of 0.03 mU/L, and normal T4 level. Urinalysis revealed a small amount of blood and 3+ bacteriuria, with no leukocytes or nitrates. Complete blood count, vitamin B12, folate, and chemistries were unremarkable. Blood alcohol and urine drug screenings were negative. The patient's epilepsy reportedly began in childhood, following a traumatic brain injury from a fall off a horse at ages 12-14. Seizures started a year after the accident, and she had been on phenytoin since then. Her last reported convulsive seizure with impaired awareness was 41 years ago, though it was unclear if she had focal seizures with intact awareness. There is no reported history of developmental delays. The rest of her medical history is non-contributory.
test_results: The EEG background had a clear bilateral posterior dominant rhythm of 8 to 9 Hz, with occasional multifocal spikes. Immediately after falling asleep, the EEG background changed to a continuous pattern of high-amplitude multifocal spikes and slow-wave discharges.
Orpha_name: Continuous spikes and waves during sleep

case_report: A 42-year-old male patient experienced acute epigastric pain and was admitted to multiple hospitals before being transferred for further care. Initial laboratory tests, including routine blood tests, ALP, amylase, transaminase, and creatinine, were within normal ranges. Computed tomography (CT) showed a small amount of retroperitoneal exudation around the pancreas. Treatment with a proton pump inhibitor, anisodamine, and tramadol was initiated, but symptoms recurred. Six days later, elevated alanine transaminase (118 U/L) and γ-GGT (146 U/L) levels were noted, while amylase and lipase levels remained normal. Peripancreatic exudation was observed on CT, leading to hospital admission. Creatinine levels increased gradually (89.9 μmol/l on day 6 and 93.9 μmol/l on day 7), and urinary sediment examination showed proteinuria (2+) and hematuria (0–2/μL). Nine days after onset, the patient reported abdominal colic pain and diarrhea, with new ascites detected on a plain abdominal CT scan. Enhanced CT on day 11 revealed increased ascites. By day 14, progressive oliguria developed. On day 21, the patient's condition worsened, with urine output approximately 200 ml/day, CRP level at 137 mg/L, creatinine at 275 μmol/l, albumin at 23.2 g/L, and ALP at 202 U/L. The patient was transferred to a specialized kidney disease hospital and began intermittent bedside hemodiafiltration on day 24 due to water overload and heart failure symptoms. By day 25, the patient developed a fever exceeding 39 degrees Celsius. Hemoglobin and platelet counts, initially normal, decreased to 67 g/l and 10 × 10^9/l, respectively. Pathogen detection tests, including blood culture, atypical pathogens, and G/GM test, were negative. Tests for HBV, HCV, HIV antibody, and HHV-8 PCR were negative. Polyclonal light chains in blood and urine were elevated, with serum kappa and lambda light chain levels at 170 mg/l and 208.25 mg/l, respectively (kappa/lambda ratio: 0.82). IgG and IgA levels were normal, while IgM and complement 3/4 levels were below normal. Antibodies, including ANA, RF, ANCA, and platelet-associated IgG, were undetectable. Serum VEGF and IL-6 levels were > 800 pg/ml and 11.5 ng/ml, respectively. An abdominal puncture on day 40 drained 1000 ml of ascites fluid, which contained 121 total cells, including 40 nucleated cells (34 mononuclear and 6 multinuclear). Ascites fluid analysis showed total protein at 28.0 g, albumin at 14.4 g/l, glucose at 14.96 mmol/l, and IL-6 at 1022 pg/ml. Bone marrow biopsy indicated marked hyperplasia of granulocytes and megakaryocytes, with negative reticular fiber staining. PET/CT revealed increased FDG activity in multiple lymph node regions without evidence of carcinoma. Lymph node pathology showed plasmacytosis. After ineffective antibiotic treatment with meropenem, intravenous methylprednisolone (60 mg qd) and intravenous immunoglobulin (20 g qd for 5 days) were administered on day 36. Early glucocorticoid therapy led to a significant reduction in pleural effusion and ascites, with general improvement. However, by day 46, the patient's temperature increased again, accompanied by a mild increase in bilirubin and a significant decrease in blood cells.
test_results: Histopathology showed a massive hemorrhage in the lymph nodes with a normal lymph node structure, decreased lymphoid follicles, an atrophied germinal center, a concentric circle arrangement in the partial mantle zone, the proliferation of small vessels, enlargement of the paracortical zone, and flaky or focal infiltration of mature plasma cells.

case_report: A 2-year-old boy was evaluated by a pediatric nephrologist for non-nephrotic range proteinuria. He did not exhibit hematuria, body swelling, or signs of vasculitis. His 24-year-old maternal uncle had a similar presentation 10 years prior, with a renal biopsy showing non-specific changes and a few sclerosed glomeruli, but remained asymptomatic except for proteinuria. Physical examination of the child showed no weight gain, ascites, pleural effusion, or hypertension. Blood pressure was recorded at 85/51 mmHg. Serum albumin levels were normal despite an elevated urine protein/creatinine ratio of 176 mg/mmol/l, which is within the non-nephrotic range. Urine protein electrophoresis detected trace amounts of albumin with normal globulin fractions. Urine β-2 microglobulin concentration was elevated at > 500 ng/ml (normal range < 300 ng/ml). Serum protein electrophoresis showed high-normal albumin concentration without abnormalities. The 24-hour urinary calcium was 1.58 mmol/day, and adjusted urinary calcium excretion was 0.14 mmol/kg/day (normal range < 0.06 mmol/kg/day), both of which were elevated. Serum phosphate level and fractional excretion of urinary phosphate were normal. Urinary tract ultrasound was normal and showed no evidence of nephrocalcinosis.
test_results: Both the child and his maternal uncle were found to be hemizygous for a nonsense pathogenic variant in exon 9 of the CLCN5 gene [NM_000084.4; c.1399C>T; rs797044811], which results in a stop codon at residue 467, leading to a truncated non-functional protein [NP_000075.1; p.R467X]. His mother was also confirmed to be an unaffected heterozygous carrier for the same variant.

case_report: The patient is a 20-month-old male who was referred to a clinic due to delays in motor milestones and neurological regression, first observed at 6 months of age by his parents. He was born at 39 weeks of gestation through normal vaginal delivery to consanguineous parents. The mother had good prenatal care but experienced preeclampsia in the final trimester. The patient's birth weight was 3350 g (Z-score 0SD) and head circumference was 34 cm (Z-score 0SD). Shortly after birth, he was admitted to the NICU due to a low APGAR score at 5 minutes, not crying, and possible birth asphyxia, but did not require assisted ventilation and was discharged in good condition after 2 days. Post-discharge, limb jerking movements were noticed during sleep, diagnosed as neonatal sleep myoclonus by a family physician, and resolved within a few days without treatment. He was readmitted for exaggerated neonatal jaundice with an indirect bilirubin level of 17 mg/dL, treated with phototherapy. Developmentally, he achieved neck holding at 2 months, rolling over at 4-5 months, and started crawling at 6 months. Subsequently, his motor development halted and regression began, with a gradual loss of crawling ability and use of his legs, especially the left foot. By 8 months, he could not sit even with support. His parents consulted a pediatric orthopedist and were then referred to a child neurologist. A pelvic X-ray was normal, with no contractures, joint deformities, or scoliosis. At 9 months, neurological examination revealed lower limb spasticity, hand fisting, increased deep tendon reflexes (DTR 3+) in lower limbs, and bilateral upward plantar reflex. Ophthalmic examination was normal. His weight was 8 kg (Z-score −1SD) and head circumference was 45 cm (Z-score 0SD). Biochemical and basic metabolic tests, including serum creatine phosphokinase (CPK), thyroid, liver, and kidney function tests; uric acid level; plasma amino acid chromatography (HPLC); and alpha-1, 4 glucosidase enzyme activity level measured by dried blood spot (DBS) test were within normal limits. Occupational therapy was initiated, and a follow-up visit was scheduled at 1 year old. At 12 months, his motor abilities had significantly declined; he could no longer crawl or roll over, and his lower limbs had become more spastic. He had acceptable social interactions and no significant feeding or swallowing problems, but his speech and cognitive skills progression were arrested. His weight was 8.5 kg (Z-score −1SD), height was 76 cm (Z-score 0SD), and head circumference was 46 cm (Z-score 0SD). A brain and spinal MRI were reported normal. Additional metabolic studies, including serum ammonia and lactate, metabolic screen (MS/MS), acylcarnitine, and urine organic acid profiles, were normal. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography revealed an ectopic right kidney and horseshoe kidneys. Cardiologic and ophthalmologic consultations showed no significant findings.
test_results: Whole-exome sequencing was done according to motor neurologic regression, speech, and cognitive delay; parents’ consanguinity; normal metabolic test results; and imaging study. The second brain MRI which was done at 18 months old indicated delayed myelination of subcortical white matter in addition to abnormal signals of posterior periventricular white matter. The T1-weighted sequence at the level of basal ganglia indicated no significant finding. Sagittal T1-weighted image showed mild thinning of the corpus callosum and upper vermis. Furthermore, electromyography and nerve conduction velocity studies (EMG-NCV) revealed generalized sensory polyneuropathy.

case_report: A 53-year-old Asian (Pakistani) male with a history of hypertension and ischemic heart disease for 6 years, noncompliant with medications, and a chronic smoker for 30 years, presented with a 2-day history of sudden, progressive weakness in both lower limbs. The weakness was symmetrical, ascending, and accompanied by difficulty walking and mild weakness in both upper limbs. The patient also experienced paresthesia, tingling, and intense myalgias in the lower limbs, along with dribbling of saliva and an inability to fully close the right eye. He had received the first dose of the Sinovac-CoronaVac COVID-19 vaccine 8 days before symptom onset. There was no history of respiratory or gastrointestinal illness, febrile illness, or other predisposing infectious or autoimmune disorders. A complete review of systems was unremarkable. Upon presentation, the patient was well-oriented, afebrile (36.7°C), normotensive (110/70 mm Hg), with a heart rate of 83/min, respiratory rate of 17/min, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. Physical examination revealed 3/5 power in both lower limbs, predominantly in the plantar flexor, dorsiflexor, and quadricep muscle groups, with no muscle atrophy or wasting. Deep tendon reflexes were absent in the lower limbs bilaterally. Upper limb power was 4/5 bilaterally, with normal motor examination otherwise. Sensory examination showed intact pain, touch, and vibration sensations, but mildly reduced proprioception in the lower limbs. The patient had an ataxic gait and a positive Romberg sign, with the rest of the lower limb cerebellar examination unremarkable. Upper limb deep tendon reflexes, sensory, and cerebellar examinations were normal. Cranial nerve examination revealed horizontal gaze diplopia and an inability to abduct the right eye, consistent with right-sided Abducens nerve (CN VI) palsy. Facial signs indicated right-sided lower motor neuron facial palsy, but the corneal reflex was intact. The rest of the cranial nerve examination was unremarkable, and meningeal signs were absent. Detailed chest and abdominal examinations were normal. Laboratory investigations, including complete blood count, renal, and liver function tests, were normal. A noncontrast computed tomography scan of the brain showed no acute hemorrhage. The patient received aspirin 300 mg and clopidogrel 300 mg. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed no abnormalities, and antiplatelets were discontinued.
test_results: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed elevated proteins in the CSF without pleocytosis. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography performed 10 days after the onset of symptoms showed prolonged latencies with reduced conduction velocities and prolonged F waves delineating acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy.

case_report: A 24-year-old female, 2 months postpartum following a full-term vaginal delivery, presented with sudden onset of whole-body tremors and involuntary, chaotic eye movements that continued during sleep. The patient experienced difficulty walking and had intermittent, irregular muscle contractions. Prior to these symptoms, she had a history of fever, headache, vomiting, joint pain, and muscle pain. General and systemic examinations were normal. Neurological examination showed the patient was conscious, oriented, and had normal speech. Ocular examination revealed chaotic, bilateral, multivectoral eye movements in all directions. Axial myoclonic jerks were observed, which increased when sitting or standing. The patient's gait was ataxic. No other neurological abnormalities were found. There was no history of vaccination. Laboratory investigations, including hemogram, platelet count, and peripheral blood smear, were normal. Biochemical tests showed serum bilirubin at 1.7 mg/dl, serum glutamic pyruvate transaminase at 25 Iu/L, serum alkaline phosphatase at 127 Iu/L, and serum protein at 6.6 gm% with no reverse albumin-globulin ratio. Renal function tests were normal, and thyroid examination was normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed five lymphocytes, normal protein levels, and normal sugar levels. X-ray of the chest and ultrasound of the whole abdomen were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging of the cranium was also normal.
test_results: ELISA IgM antibody for dengue virus was positive in serum.
diagnosis: Opsoclonus Myoclonus Syndrome associated with Dengue Infection

case_report: A 60-year-old woman visited the dermatology outpatient clinic with depigmentation on her neck for 3 months and itchy lesions on her elbows. The elbow lesions, which appeared mainly during summer, had been present for several years. The patient is originally from the Philippines and has no history of direct contact with tuberculosis. Her medical history includes atopy, high blood pressure, and hypothyroidism following thyroid gland resection for papillary carcinoma. She is currently on levothyroxine, olmesartan, and vitamin D. Clinically, the neck lesions showed depigmentation. On the extensor side of the elbows, there were smooth, hard, and infiltrated erythematous papules.
test_results: Histology showed a dense perivascular and interstitial lymphocytic infiltrate associated with focal histiocytic palisading around necrobiotic areas. Colloidal iron staining showed mucin deposition in the necrobiotic zones. Miller’s stain did not show elastophagocytosis. CD68 immunostaining showed the presence of histiocytes without palisade formation, but they were scattered and interstitial. There was no argument for an infectious origin on the different special stainings performed (Periodic Acid Schiff and Ziehl–Neelsen).

case_report: A 54-year-old male arrived at our department with a 2-week history of reduced vision in his right eye. He had been receiving treatment in the pulmonology department for a 6-month history of bronchial asthma and allergic rhinitis with parasinusitis. The visual issue coincided with episodes of coughing up blood. Visual acuity was measured at 20/50 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Both pupils responded normally to light and accommodation. Ocular movements, anterior segments, and intraocular pressure were normal in both eyes. There was no inflammation observed in the anterior chamber or vitreal cavity. Examination of the left eye's fundus was normal with a cup/disc ratio of 0.4, while the right eye showed pallid optic disc swelling and splinter hemorrhages at the disc margin. Goldmann perimetry indicated central scotomas in the right eye.
test_results: Fluorescein angiography showed localized filling delay and late hyperfluorescence of the right optic nerve head. In addition, localized filling delay in the peripapillary choroid was demonstrated. Laboratory evaluation revealed a hematocrit of 44.9%, and a white blood cell count of 13,600/uL with 34% eosinophilia. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 30 mm/hr and the C-reactive protein was 1.72 mg/dL. Total IgE was 323.4 IU/mL, anti-nuclear antibody was positive, and the following results were all negative: 2 IgG antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCAs, cytoplasmic-ANCA and perinuclear-ANCA), and anti dsDNA antibodies. A bone marrow biopsy showed 17.2% eosinophils (eosinophilic hyperplasia). Multiple dirty-appearing nodules in the trachea and both main bronchi were found by bronchoscopy and sections of a paraffin-embedded nodule specimen demonstrated diffuse eosinophilic infiltration of the bronchial wall.

case_report: A 69-year-old woman with chronic hepatitis B was admitted for further evaluation of a hepatic lesion identified by abdominal ultrasound during a routine health examination. She had no symptoms, and physical examination showed no notable abnormalities. Laboratory tests revealed normal results, including liver enzyme levels: white blood cell count 4,550/μL, hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 25 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 21 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 262 U/L, γ-glutamyltranspeptidase 16 U/L, and C-reactive protein 0.0 mg/dL. The patient tested positive for hepatitis B virus surface antigen and negative for hepatitis C virus antibody. Tumor markers showed elevated levels of carcinoembryonic antigen at 5.3 ng/mL (normal range: <5 ng/mL) and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9) at 39.2 U/mL (normal range: <37 U/mL). α-fetoprotein and protein induced by vitamin K antagonist II (PIVKA-II) were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a well-defined peripheral hypoechoic mass that was isoechoic and homogeneous internally. CT imaging showed a poorly enhanced tumor measuring 13 mm in diameter in the 5th segment of the liver. FDG-PET indicated slight uptake by the hepatic tumor with a maximum standard uptake value (SUV max) of 3.4, and no other sites showed FDG uptake. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and colonoscopy did not reveal any pathological findings. During exploratory laparotomy, no peritoneal dissemination was observed, and an anterior segmentectomy of the liver was performed.
test_results: Microscopy revealed that the lymph follicles varied in size and shape with germinal centers that were composed of small or large lymphoid cells and tangible body macrophages. The follicles were CD20-positive and bcl-2-negative. The interfollicular area was composed of CD3-positive small T cells. The lymphoid cells in follicles showed ordinary immunoreactivity, while the cells in the mantle zone were positive for CD5 and the cells in the germinal center were positive for CD10.
Orpha_name: Lymphoplasmacytic inflammatory pseudotumor of the liver

case_report: A 21-year-old female exhibited swelling in her left leg starting at puberty, which extended to the left flank and buttock. There was no difference in limb length and no segmental overgrowth. No venous issues were noted. The patient also had hypertrophy or edema of the left breast. Additionally, there was a skin vascular anomaly on both sides of her neck and two small telangiectasias on her left thigh.
test_results: Lymphoscintigraphy showed rerouted lymph drainage through the deep lymphatic vessels via popliteal nodes but with normal levels of transport in the nonswollen left leg and functional aplasia in the swollen right leg. Genetic analysis is being performed on DNA from skin fibroblasts. H&E staining as well as staining for lymphatic vessel markers revealed no obvious vascular alteration. 3D histology of the entire lymphatic vasculature as shown in 2D as well as 3D revealed a normal, nondilated lymphatic vessel architecture and low PROX1 expression. A very low number of valves was detectable compared with control samples. Neither cystic vascular lesion nor nonconnected vessel fragments were detected. A Podoplanin-positive lymphatic vessel, which is packed with erythrocytes, was seen. Erythrocytes, highlighted by autofluorescence, were observed within unstained blood vessels draining into the Podoplanin-positive lymphatic vessel. This indicated a potential shunting site.

case_report: A 48-year-old Chinese man presented with instability while walking for 2.5 years and dysarthria for 10 months. He was born and lived in Jilin province. In August 2012, he began experiencing gradual instability while walking, characterized by bilateral foot-dropping and a gradual cold sensation spreading from the feet to the thighs. In April 2014, he developed dysarthria and coughing while drinking water. Despite seeking treatment at another hospital, no abnormalities were detected via spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA) genetic sequencing. His symptoms progressed to include involuntary head tremors, instability while sitting, and severe muscle pain in both lower limbs. In February 2015, he was evaluated at our hospital. He reported no history of disease. His mother and older brother had similar symptoms. His mother developed symptoms at 51, with severe muscle atrophy in both lower extremities, and was bedridden for 6 months with mild dementia before passing away 5 years later. His older brother experienced symptom onset at 36 and died after 9 years. Physical examination revealed dysarthria, slightly decreased muscle strength in the lower limbs, absent lower extremity deep tendon reflexes, and postural and resting tremors in the upper extremities without myoclonus. He performed poorly on the finger-to-nose and heel-to-knee tests. Babinski and Chaddock signs were absent. He had a wide-based ataxic gait and was positive for the Romberg sign. Routine blood tests, including thyroid function, rheumatoid immune antibodies, and tumor markers, were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure was normal, but CSF protein and immunoglobulin (IgG) levels were slightly elevated. Blood and CSF tests for neuromyelitis optica (NMO)-IgG, aquaporin 4 antibodies (AQP4-Ab), and paraneoplastic antibodies were negative. SCA genetic sequencing results were also negative. Given the patient's clinical symptoms and family history, an expanded genetic screening was proposed to include over 200 additional possible mutations associated with ataxia.
test_results: A heterozygous mutation site was found at the second exonic sequence of the PRNP gene: c.305C > T (cytosine to thymine). This mutation results in an amino acid change (p.P102L, valine to leucine).

case_report: A 38-year-old Argentinean female presented with gradually worsening unsteadiness that began at age 23. She experienced significant instability and gait issues over time, characterized by short steps, hesitation when starting to walk, fear of falling, and the need to hold onto walls to prevent falls. She also reported multiple falls, dizziness, neck pain, and constipation. These symptoms have progressively impacted her mobility and daily functioning, and she now requires assistance for movement. There is no relevant medical, family, or psychosocial history, and no previous interventions were noted. Neurological examination revealed dysarthria, interrupted slow horizontal and vertical eye movements, and slow horizontal saccades. Spasticity and hyperreflexia were more pronounced in the lower extremities. Mild cervical dystonia with bradykinesia was also observed. Ataxic symptoms were more noticeable in the left upper extremity. Gait was spastic, and no cognitive abnormalities were detected. Brain MRI with and without contrast showed no significant findings.
test_results: The analysis identified two variants in CAPN1 (MIM:114220) considered as probably pathogenic Class 2. She was heterozygous for a splicing mutation in intron 16 (c.1729+1G>A) and a second splicing mutation in intron 12 (c.1353+2T>C). Carrier testing in the parents was not performed.

case_report: A 37-year-old male presented for a routine eye examination with a primary complaint of decreased vision in the right eye, for which he was using spectacles. He reported having a larger right eye since early childhood. Examination showed best corrected visual acuity of 6/9 (+1.00Dx160) in the right eye and 6/6 in the left eye. Intraocular pressures measured with Goldman applanation tonometer were 11 mmHg in the right eye and 13 mmHg in the left eye. The right cornea had a diameter of 13.5 mm, compared to 11.75 mm for the left cornea. Anterior segment examination of the right eye revealed Haab's striae in the nasal half of the cornea, which was otherwise clear. Gonioscopy of the right eye showed prominent iris processes. The anterior segment of the left eye was normal. The cup disc ratio was 0.3 for the right optic disc and 0.2 for the left optic disc. Posterior segment examination was normal. Central corneal thickness was 449 microns in the right eye and 500 microns in the left eye.
test_results: Anterior segment optical coherence tomography demonstrated the Haab's striae. Visual field testing and optical coherence tomography - retinal nerve fiber layer demonstrated defects in the right eye.

case_report: A 2-year-old male child, born from a nonconsanguineous marriage, presented with intrauterine growth retardation followed by significant postnatal growth impairment, body asymmetry, and a triangular face. He was the third preterm infant, delivered via cesarean section at 32 weeks of gestation due to maternal preeclampsia. At birth, his weight was 1140 g, length was 34 cm, and head circumference was 28 cm. He has two brothers with normal body habitus and no family history of dwarfism. Chromosome analysis was not performed due to financial constraints. Physical examination revealed a well-appearing but short and thin child with triangular facies, broad forehead, and low-set prominent ears. Additional findings included facial asymmetry with left eyelid ptosis, micrognathia, high-arched palate, downturned mouth corners, hemihypertrophy on the right side involving the lower limb, and cryptorchidism. His height was 71 cm, weight was 6450 g, and head circumference was 45 cm, all of which were below average for his age. There were no skin abnormalities such as café-au-lait macules or signs of occult spinal dysraphism. No clonus or spasticity was observed in his extremities. Basic investigations, including hormone levels, were within normal limits.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a conus medullaris at the inferior border of the L3 vertebral body and L5-S1 posterior vertebral fusion defect. Urodynamic study showed overactive detrusor and detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia.
Orpha_name: Silver-Russell syndrome due to a point mutation

case_report: A 41-year-old female presented with swelling of the left upper eyelid persisting for 6 months. Visual acuity was 10/10 in the right eye. Best corrected visual acuity in the left eye was 7/10 with refractive errors of +3.25D spherical and −3.0D astigmatism, measured using a Snellen card. Intraocular pressure was 14 mm Hg in both eyes. Palpation revealed a firm, immobile mass approximately 10 × 10 mm2 located in the midline of the left upper eyelid beneath the eyebrow. Hertel exophthalmometry showed no proptosis. Ocular motility was unrestricted in all directions for both eyes. Slit lamp biomicroscopic and dilated fundus examinations were normal in both eyes. The patient's medical history and general physical examination were unremarkable.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a well-circumscribed − 9 × 9 mm2 in size – solid mass keeping intensive contrast in the left frontobasal, subgaleal area. The tumour was located extraconally in the anterior orbit. Although there was a connection between cortical frontal osseous and solid mass, there was no bone destruction in MRI. Histopathological examination revealed diffuse infiltration of uniform, spindle-shaped cells arranged in whorls. The nuclei of the tumour cells were elongated cigar-shaped with blunted ends. There were no mitotic figures, nuclear pleomorphism and nuclear atypia. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for smooth muscle actin (SMA) and h-caldesmon, but negative for desmin and S100 protein. CD31 and CD34 immunostaining showed sparse accompanying thin-walled vascular structures. Ki67 index was 1%.

case_report: A 55-year-old male reported experiencing pain in the left loin for 4 months, intermittent fever for 1 year, and easy fatigability for 2 years. The abdominal pain was intermittent and crampy, accompanied by burning sensation during urination. Two years prior, the patient was evaluated for easy fatigability and weakness and was found to be seropositive for HIV. He started antiretroviral therapy but discontinued it after 1 month. Laboratory tests revealed anemia (hemoglobin level of 7.1 g/dl). The white blood cell count was within normal limits but showed toxic granules. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated (140 mm/1 hr). Urine microscopy indicated numerous pus cells, granular casts, and a few red blood cells. Blood tests showed elevated blood urea (55 mg/dl) and creatinine (2.4 mg/dl). Ultrasonography revealed a dilated pelvicalyceal system with calculi and a large low amplitude moving echogenic area, suggestive of pyonephrosis in a hydronephrotic kidney with urolithiasis. Computed tomography also indicated hydronephrosis with pyonephrosis. A nephro-ureterectomy was performed due to the non-functioning kidney and to eliminate the source of infection, as the patient had recurrent fevers. Pre-operative imaging did not show involvement of adjoining organs or enlarged nodes. The nephrectomy specimen revealed a large tumorous mass measuring 9 × 6 cm, replacing the entire kidney with grayish-yellow and necrotic areas. Normal renal parenchyma was not identifiable. Multiple cystic spaces with impacted calculi were observed.
test_results: A microscopic examination showed multiple basophilic colonies surrounded by neutrophilic abscesses and granulation tissue replacing most of the renal parenchyma, which showed features of chronic pyelonephritis. The colonies stained weakly positive with methanamine silver and stained positive with acid fast stain.

case_report: A 3.5-year-old boy presented with renal failure, skeletal abnormalities, and ocular issues. He was born to a 20-year-old mother and a 33-year-old father, who are not related, following an uneventful first pregnancy. Delivery was vaginal at 39 weeks of gestation. Birth measurements were: weight 3700 g (50th-75th percentile), length 57 cm (97th percentile), head circumference 36 cm (75th-97th percentile), and thorax circumference 33 cm (25-50th percentile). The Apgar score was 9 at 1 minute. Family history was unremarkable. Early neonatal records noted proteinuria, hematuria, and glycosuria, but no further evaluation was done. At 12 months, the child was treated for a urinary tract infection. At three years, he developed bronchopneumonia and was hospitalized, where elevated creatinine levels were found. He was then referred to the Pediatric Nephrology Department. Laboratory tests showed persistent proteinuria, glycosuria, hematuria, eGFR (Schwartz) of 30.56 ml/min/1.73 m2, and elevated serum levels of creatinine, uric acid, urea, total cholesterol, and triglycerides. Complete blood count, blood glucose, albumin, thyroid, and liver function tests were normal. Kidney ultrasonography revealed increased renal cortex echogenicity and decreased cortico-medullary differentiation. At 3.5 years, a clinical geneticist noted distinctive dysmorphic features: dolichocephaly, high forehead, thin hair, full cheeks, low-set prominent ears, long philtrum, microretrognathia, rhizomelic shortening of limbs, brachydactyly of toes and fingers, narrow chest, and pectus excavatum. Ophthalmological examination confirmed strabismus, nystagmus, and high hyperopia.
test_results: Cytogenetic analysis revealed a normal male karyotype (46,XY).

case_report: A 40-year-old male presented with a history of multiple swellings on his body, first noticed 8 years ago as a small lump on his left cheek. Over time, similar swellings appeared on his scalp, left axilla, back, and right thigh. These swellings were slow-growing, itchy, painless, and did not cause significant discomfort apart from cosmetic concerns, leading to a delay in seeking medical attention. In the past 6 months, he experienced intermittent low-grade fever, loss of appetite, unintentional weight loss, and progressively worsening breathlessness. He also reported numbness in both feet. He denied any history of addictions or over-the-counter drug use. On physical examination, he was tachypneic with a respiratory rate of 24/min. Multiple swellings were observed in the mentioned areas, most measuring approximately 2 × 2 cm, brownish in color, and soft and fleshy to the touch. There was no hepatosplenomegaly or significant lymphadenopathy. Auscultation revealed a diffuse polyphonic wheeze. Sensory examination showed graded loss of pain, touch, and temperature sensations from the toes to the shin, and bilateral ankle jerks were absent. Laboratory investigations indicated anemia (hemoglobin = 10.8 gm/dL) and persistent leukocytosis with a predominance of eosinophils. The absolute eosinophil count ranged from 36,000/μL to 44,000/μL. Peripheral blood smear did not show any blasts or abnormal cell lineages. Biochemical tests were normal, including renal function (serum creatinine: 0.8 mg/dL; range: 0.6–1.2). Urinalysis showed no active sediment, and stool examination was negative for ova and parasites. HIV and filarial serologies were negative. Anti-nuclear antibody (by ELISA) and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (by indirect immunofluorescence) tests were negative. Imaging studies, including chest radiograph and contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the neck, chest, and abdomen, showed no mediastinal or abdominal lymphadenopathy or mass lesions in the thorax or abdomen. Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme levels were normal. Workup for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis was negative, but serum total IgE levels were elevated (36 kU/L; normal <1.58 kU/L).
test_results: Bone marrow examination showed increased eosinophil and their precursors (16%) with normal blast cell count (1%). There were no aberrant T-cell clones. Karyotype was normal, and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) studies for BCR-ABL, JAK2, PDGFRA, PDGFRB, and FGFR1 were all negative. Histopathology of the excised lump on the left cheek showed a circumscribed lesion located in the dermis, composed of variably sized vascular spaces lined by plump endothelial cells and interstitial increase in eosinophil, lymphocyte, and plasma cells. The endothelial cells were positive for CD31.
diagnosis: Hypereosinophilic Syndrome  secondary to Angiolymphoid Hyperplasia with Eosinophilia

case_report: A 58-year-old male noticed a red papule on the lateral side of his left knee 6 months ago, which appeared without any known cause. Over time, the papule enlarged to 2*3 cm. He sought medical attention at an external facility and received a diagnosis of 'keloid.' He was treated with 'Compound Betamethasone injection 1mL topical injection' once a month for four months. Despite this treatment, the lesion expanded to an irregular plaque measuring 7*8 cm, with ulceration and crusting on the surface, and several small papules emerged around the periphery. The patient visited our hospital in May 2022, where he underwent a general examination and skin biopsy.
test_results: Histopathology of the lesions showed the following: diffuse infiltration of tumour cells in the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, partly interspersed among collagen fibres and focal infiltration of surrounding lymphocytes and large-sized tumour cells that were rich in cytoplasm, with round or irregular nuclei, obvious nucleoli, obvious heterotypes, and obvious interstitial phenomenon. The immunohistochemistry results were as follows: CD30 (+++), CD3 (+), CD4 (+), CD8 (+), CD56 (-), ALK (-), CD20 (-), and Ki-67 90% or more. PET-CT showed limited skin thickening and soft tissue mass formation with increased metabolism on the outer portion of the left knee, and increased metabolism in the bilateral inguinal lymph nodes; bone marrow cell morphology showed granular, red, and meganuclear triplet proliferative bone marrow.
diagnosis: Primary cutaneous ALK-negative anaplastic large cell lymphoma
Orpha_name: Primary cutaneous anaplastic large cell lymphoma

case_report: A 55-year-old female presented to the outpatient clinic of the oral and craniomaxillofacial surgery department with multiple painful nodules on her lip mucosa. She was in excellent general health with no history of other diseases. She reported a non-specific pressure on her lips over the preceding years but could not provide detailed history regarding her symptoms or the palpability of the nodules. She denied any history of viral infections in the oral region. External examination showed no visible changes to the lips. Oral examination revealed multiple nodules beneath the non-inflammatory mucosa of the upper and lower lip, which were painful upon palpation. Enlarged ostia were observed, secreting a clear, tenacious mucus. Local excision of the palpable masses was performed in all four quadrants of the vermilion. Upon incision, berry-like tumors were observed beneath the mucous membrane, not infiltrating the lip muscles. Post-surgical healing was uneventful. The patient returned four and five years later with recurrent painful swellings of the minor salivary glands at the same site. The physical appearance of the lesions remained consistent throughout the nearly six-year observation period.
test_results: The specimen showed multiple ductal ectasia of minor salivary glands and oncocyte metaplasia. Inflammatory reaction of the interstitium was seen and the acini showed irregular atrophia. Following local recurrence of the glandular swelling and renewed operation, a generalised chronic lymphoid sialadenitis was diagnosed with focal acute sialectasia. There were neither eosinophil granulocytes, granuloma nor cellular atypia. Stainings were done for CD45, CD138, and IgG4, and revealed lymphoplasmacellular infiltrates, mainly located in broadened interstitial spaces with some exocytosis in the ductal and acinar compartments. Immunoglobulin G subclass 4 (IgG4)-positive cells were mostly scattered, yet also showed some clustering. Nevertheless, when referring to the total (CD138-positive) plasma cell population, IgG4-positive cells accounted for 5% at the utmost. Antinuclear antibody (ANA) screening (human epithelial type 2 (HEP 2) cells) revealed a slightly evaluated titre (1:160; reference: 1:80) and a microscopically defined finely speckled reaction pattern. Furthermore, an unknown cytoplasmic fluorescence pattern was noted. The level of IgG4 was very low: 0.01 g/L (reference: 0.052–1.25 g/L). C-reactive protein was intermittently elevated (maximum 62 mg/L). Quantitative assessment of other parameters revealed normal values (ds-DNA-, U1 RNP-, Sm-, SSA-, SSB-, Scl-70-, centromere- and Jo-1-antibodies).

case_report: A 43-year-old male patient underwent allogeneic progenitor cell transplantation from an HLA-matched sibling donor and received treatment with eculizumab. The patient had previously been diagnosed with stage 4 ALK-negative anaplastic large cell lymphoma following a splenectomy due to uncontrolled splenic hemorrhage. Due to the aggressive nature of the disease, the CHOP regimen was initiated immediately after diagnosis and staging procedures. After two cycles of the CHOP regimen, no significant response was observed, leading to the initiation of the ESHAP regimen. Following two cycles of the ESHAP regimen, a short-term partial response was achieved, and allogeneic progenitor cell transplantation was performed using cells collected peripherally, with a reinfused CD34+ cell count of 5.3 × 10^6/kg. Busulfan and cyclophosphamide were used for conditioning, and cyclosporine was administered for graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis. On the 7th day post-reinfusion, the patient developed acinetobacter sepsis and was treated with a broad spectrum of antibiotics. During recovery from sepsis, the patient experienced rapid neurological and renal deterioration, presenting as stupor, a tonic-clonic epileptic seizure, severe headache, and hallucinations prior to the seizure.
test_results: The ldh level was increased dramatically up to 3200 U/L and schistocytes were detected at the peripheral blood smear (20–30/HPF). Despite being hyponormotensive during the period of sepsis, he had hypertensive episodes with a maximum of 180/100 mmHg accompanying the neurological symptoms. Cranial MRI and lumbar puncture revealed no pathological feature. CSF culture was negative and cytological analysis revealed no malignant cells. Viral analysis of CSF and blood was negative regarding CMV and EBV. His Hb level has decreased from 9.5 to 7.2 g/dL with an MCV of 96 fL and reticulocyte count of 2.49%.
