Both direct and indirect coombs tests were negative and haptoglobulin level was slightly decreased below the lower limit of normal. ADAMTS13 activity was %37 with no detectable inhibitors. All complement levels were in normal range (C3, C4, Factor H, and Factor I). Urinalysis revealed a protein concentration of 120 mg/dL.
Orpha_name: De novo thrombotic microangiopathy after kidney transplantation

case_report: A three-year-old female child, born to parents from a non-Agrawal community with a non-consanguineous marriage, presented with macrocephaly and a history of seizures during infancy, which were managed with medication. The child exhibited delayed developmental milestones, beginning to walk with support at around 15 months and without support only after two years. At three years, she still had difficulty running or walking on stairs. There was also a mild delay in social and language development; she was unable to construct phrases or sentences and had a vocabulary of 10-15 words. The birth history was unremarkable, with a normal vaginal delivery at term and no history of birth asphyxia. Family history did not indicate similar features in close relatives. General physical examination findings were normal. Routine blood tests and electrolyte levels were within normal limits. The patient was noted to have global developmental delay with seizures and was referred for further imaging.
test_results: MRI showed multiple ill-defined discrete and confluent T2 hyperintensities in subcortical and peripheral white matter with corresponding hypointensities on T1W images and no inversion on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR). No diffusion restriction or blood products were noted on DWI and GRE respectively. No abnormal post-contrast enhancement was noted. Subcortical cystic change was noted in bilateral anterior temporal region. No abnormal NAA peak was noted on spectroscopy. Deep white matter and basal ganglia were normal.

case_report: A 47-year-old woman presented with intermittent cough, shortness of breath, fever, and body temperature up to 38.5°C, accompanied by right eyelid swelling around June 17, 2017, which worsened progressively. She experienced a weight loss of approximately 9 kg. On July 5, 2017, she visited a local hospital and underwent both eyes and head computed tomography (CT) scan, which showed no significant abnormalities. Chest CT indicated pulmonary infection with a high possibility of fungal infection and a small amount of pleural effusion in the left lung. She was treated with antibiotics for about 10 days, but her symptoms did not improve. Subsequently, her symptoms worsened, and she developed a high fever with a maximum body temperature of 39.4°C. She was transferred to our hospital on July 17, 2017, with a diagnosis of “pulmonary infection.” Physical examination revealed a high body temperature of 39°C, right eyelid swelling, and a painless enlarged lymph node approximately 2 cm × 2 cm in size in the left axilla. Lung auscultation revealed coarse respiratory sounds with moist rales. There was no hepatosplenomegaly or lower limb edema. Laboratory data showed decreased leucocyte count (1.50 × 10–9/L) and hemoglobin (88 g/L), elevated aspartate transaminase (AST) (61 U/L), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) (724 U/L). The Galactomannan (GM) test was positive, while the plasma (1,3)-β-D-glucan (G) test was negative. Coagulation function, kidney function, ferritin, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were normal. Sputum culture, acid-fast staining, and blood culture ruled out an infectious origin. HIV, hepatitis, and syphilis test panels were negative. Her autoimmune workup was also negative. Reexamination of chest CT showed interstitial exudation in both lungs, mass lesions, and left pleural effusion, still suggesting fungal infection. Bronchoscopy revealed acute inflammatory changes in the bronchial mucosa. After symptomatic treatment with antibacterial, antifungal, and leucocyte-elevating agents, her systemic symptoms such as fever, cough, and eyelid swelling improved, and leucocyte count increased. Reexamination of orbital and chest CT showed no abnormalities in the orbit, but interstitial exudation of both lungs and left pleural effusion were more pronounced than in the previous CT scan. On August 4, 2017, positron emission tomography (PET)-CT images showed multiple spherical lesions and ground glass-like increased images in the lungs, with significant lower lobe involvement and mostly hypermetabolic activity; left pleural and right interlobular effusion. Biopsy of hypermetabolic nodules in the chest wall revealed difficulty in differentiating inflammation and tumor, and PCR was negative for tuberculosis in paraffin-embedded tissue. Anti-infective treatment was continued, and the patient was discharged one week later due to improvement in symptoms. However, fever returned after a brief respite and did not improve. She revisited our hospital on August 28, 2017. Reexamination of chest CT exhibited a reduced volume of multiple lesions in both lungs, and the interstitial exudation was slightly absorbed compared to before. A blood reexamination revealed a re-decrease in leucocyte count, higher levels of AST and LDH than during the first admission, and elevated blood β2 microglobulin (2549 ng/mL). A biopsy of the lung tissue showed a high number of inflammatory cell infiltrations in the pleura. Anti-infective treatment was ineffective, and her fever persisted, along with redness, swelling, heat, and pain in the right thigh. On September 1, 2017, vascular ultrasound of the right lower limb showed intermuscular venous thrombosis, multiple enlarged inguinal lymph nodes, and subcutaneous soft tissue edema with interstitial effusion on the lateral thigh.
test_results: Histopathological examination demonstrated focal rimming of individual adipocytes by infiltrating small to medium-sized atypical T lymphocytes with irregular and hyperchromatic nuclei. Immunohistochemistry exhibited positivity for CD3, CD8, granzyme B (GB), CD43, and T-cell intracellular antigen-1 (TIA-1), and negativity for CD4, CD56, CK, and CD79, Ki67 staining positive was 50%. A monoclonal rearrangement of TCR-β gene was confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

case_report: A 16-year-old female patient presented with complaints of gum bleeding. She was observed to have a thin build. The right thumb was absent, and the right forearm appeared shorter than usual. Vital signs were within normal limits. Examination of the face and skull showed underdeveloped malar eminences and zygomata, as well as an underdeveloped maxilla and mandible. The ears were noted to be low-set and rotated, with skin tags present. Intraoral examination indicated inflamed gingiva, attributed to poor oral hygiene.
test_results: Radiological examination supported the clinical findings. Ocular examination showed downward slant of palpebral fissures, ptosis of upper lids and limbal dermoid in right eye measuring around 1 × 1 cm in diameter.

case_report: A 46-year-old male presented to the Musculoskeletal Oncology Clinic at Royal Rehabilitation Center at King Hussein Medical Center with complaints of progressive right shoulder pain over an 8-month period. The pain was exacerbated by movement and accompanied by a swelling that increased in size over time. There was no history of trauma to the affected area, and no family history of neurofibromatosis type 1 or type 2. Physical examination revealed a soft tissue mass on the posterior aspect of the right shoulder, which was tender to deep palpation and firm in consistency. An x-ray examination indicated increased soft tissue intensity. Further evaluation with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with intravenous contrast showed a relatively well-defined, lobulated, superficially located large soft tissue mass measuring approximately 7 x 6 x 5 cm in the posterior aspect of the right shoulder. The mass exhibited mixed signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, with heterogeneous enhancement observed in fat-saturated post-contrast images.
test_results: Open incisional biopsy revealed spindle cells and prominent mitotic activity with rhabdomyoblastic differentiation.

case_report: A 26-year-old Chinese woman was admitted to the Affiliated Weihai Second Municipal Hospital, Qingdao University, presenting with high blood pressure and low potassium levels, along with symptoms of weakness. She had previously visited the reproductive clinic three months earlier for high blood pressure (160/110 mm Hg) and low potassium levels. Her medical history revealed that she had not experienced menstruation before the age of 18. After undergoing hormone replacement therapy (HRT), she had irregular menstruation, which ceased after stopping the HRT. She was married but had not been pregnant, and her husband was in good health. Her parents and two sisters were healthy, with normal pubertal and reproductive histories. Physical examination showed female external genitalia, immature breasts and vulva, with breast development at Tanner stage G2. She had no menstruation. Her blood pressure was recorded at 160/110 mm Hg. She was 160 cm tall, weighed 55 kg, and had a body mass index (BMI) of 21.48 kg/m2. Examination of the heart, lungs, thyroid, and abdomen showed no abnormalities. Ultrasound examination indicated immature female ovaries or uterus. CT examination revealed right adrenal proliferation and slightly less pronounced left adrenal proliferation. Laboratory tests showed normal hemoglobin and blood cell counts, as well as normal renal, liver, and thyroid function tests. Calcium and phosphate levels were normal. The patient had low levels of potassium (3.2 mmol/L), estradiol (< 18.35 mmol/L), testosterone (< 0.087 mmol/L), and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (0.764 μmol/L), while ACTH, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), and aldosterone levels were elevated.
test_results: The patient carried compound heterozygous mutations in the CYP17A1 gene: c.985–987 delinsAA (p.Tyr329LysfsX90) in exon 6, and c.1486C > T (p.Arg496Cys) in exon 8. The c.985–987 delinsAA mutation caused amino acid alterations with the tyrosine-329-Lysine (Tyr329Lysfs). The c.1486C > T mutation led to amino acid alterations with a substitution of arginine by cysteine (p.Arg496Cys). The patient's chromosome karyotype was 46,XX.
Orpha_name: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency

case_report: A 4-month-old female infant presented with widespread blisters that began at 3 months of age. Initially, the lesions appeared on the hands and feet and later spread to the scalp, face, and trunk. The parents reported recurrent episodes of coughing, respiratory distress, increased body temperature, and restlessness, during which the child's entire body would turn red. These episodes resolved spontaneously within a few hours and were exacerbated by handling the child. There was no family history of skin diseases or atopy. Physical examination showed multiple tense vesicles, bullae, erosions, and hemorrhagic crusted lesions on the face, scalp, and trunk. A positive Darier's sign was noted on the thigh. There was no evidence of organomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood cell count and biochemical profiles, were within normal limits. Serum tryptase levels were elevated above 200 IU. A chest X-ray, performed due to repeated episodes of respiratory distress, revealed reticulogranular patterns in both lung fields, with no infectious cause identified for these infiltrations.
test_results: The histological examination of a biopsy taken from the thigh revealed sub-epidermal bullae with a dense infiltration of mast cells and in the upper dermis. The toluidine blue and Giemsa stains showed that almost all of the infiltrating cells in the dermis were mast cells.

case_report: A 25-year-old female reported experiencing shortness of breath, dizziness, and overall weakness. She had a history of two recurrent pregnancy losses at 2–3 months gestation. Currently, she is 4 months pregnant. On physical examination, her blood pressure was recorded at 100/70 mmHg, her pulse rate was 94 beats per minute, and her oxygen saturation was 88%. There were no signs of cyanosis or clubbing. Cardiovascular examination revealed the apex beat located in the left 5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line, a parasternal heave, a palpable P2, and a loud S1. An ejection systolic murmur was noted in the pulmonary area. Electrocardiography showed an incomplete right bundle branch block without other significant abnormalities.
test_results: A 2D transthoracic echocardiogram showed situs solitus of the atria, AV concordance, D-loop ventricles, and ventriculoarterial concordance. There was a complete absence of interatrial septum, dilated right atrium, and right ventricle associated with morphologically normal AV valves attached at the same level at crux. There was no evidence of any ventricular septal defect or patent ductus arteriosus. There was no cleft in mitral leaflets, no mitral regurgitation, mild tricuspid regurgitation (TR), and significant pulmonary arterial hypertension measured by TR jet velocity.

case_report: An 8-year-old male with no prior health issues presented with a 2-day history of fever. He was admitted following recurrent generalized tonic-clonic seizures that escalated to refractory status epilepticus within hours. Laboratory tests revealed elevated aspartate transaminase at 406 IU/L (normal range: 10-40 IU/L) and alanine transaminase at 324 IU/L (normal range: 7-56 IU/L), while other routine tests were normal. Upon admission, the patient was intubated, and continuous infusions of pentobarbital and midazolam were administered to achieve electroencephalography suppression, resulting in hypotension that necessitated pressor support.
test_results: A lumbar puncture was performed on the day of admission, which showed slightly elevated cerebrospinal fluid protein of 48.3 mg/dL (normal 15-45 mg/dL) without pleocytosis. A meningoencephalitis panel was positive only for recent or current infection with influenza A/B by antibody enzyme immunoassay. A brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) done at this stage of his illness was read as normal, other than gadolinium enhancement of the meninges. When the patient developed dilated pupils and hypertension, computed tomography (CT) and MRI scans of the head were performed, and extensive bilateral brain lesions were seen. The CT head with and without contrast (hospital day 15) showed extensive focal and confluent areas of low density in the cerebellum and right cerebral hemisphere, including the right basal ganglia. Magnetic resonance imaging brain without contrast (hospital day 36) showed diffuse areas of edema and microhemorrhages involving bilateral cerebellar hemispheres, bilateral occipital lobes, right cerebral white matter, right basal ganglia, and left sylvian region. There was mild T2 hyperintensity and suggestion of minimal hemorrhage in both thalami. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (hospital day 36) showed markedly low N-acetylaspartate diffusely and a large lactate peak in the mid-occipital gray matter.

case_report: An 8-year-old male presented to the hospital with symptoms of dizziness, headache, and intermittent chest pain. He was found to have persistent hypertension with blood pressure readings of 160/100 (> 99th percentile). Laboratory results showed mild hypernatremia (147 mmol/L) and hypokalemia (3.1 mmol/L), while bicarbonate (23 mmol/L), blood urea nitrogen (9 mg/dL), and creatinine (0.5 mg/dL) were within normal ranges. An EKG indicated left ventricular hypertrophy, which was confirmed by an echocardiogram. The patient was admitted for further evaluation, and Pediatric Nephrology was consulted. Additional tests including thyroid function, vanillylmandelic acid, cortisol, and renal ultrasound with Dopplers were normal. Both renin and aldosterone levels were found to be low at < 0.1 ng/mL/h and < 1.6 ng/dL, respectively. Family history revealed hypertension in the patient's father, paternal grandfather, and half-brother, with early-onset hypertension noted in the father at age 13 and the half-brother at age 9.
test_results: Genetic studies were positive.

case_report: A 20-year-old woman on interferon beta-1a therapy for multiple sclerosis reported a visual field defect in the lower temporal quadrant of her left eye. Visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. Intraocular pressure measured 15 mmHg in the right eye and 17 mmHg in the left eye. Anterior segment examinations were normal bilaterally. Pupils were equal, round, and reactive to light without any relative afferent pupillary defect. Fundus examination of the left eye revealed ischemic retinal whitening in the supra-nasal area, while the right eye fundus examination was normal. The patient did not exhibit reduced visual acuity, color vision disturbances, or pain with eye movements. Interferon beta-1a treatment was discontinued after 7 weeks due to potential prothrombotic effects. The patient had increased thromboembolic risk factors, including hormonal contraception and cigarette smoking. A comprehensive laboratory work-up was conducted, including tests for connective tissue disease, vasculitis, borrelia, syphilis, HIV, HSV, CMV, and factor V Leiden mutations. Laboratory results showed borderline lupus anticoagulant, leukopenia, decreased platelet count, slightly elevated D-dimer concentration, and prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time. Further biochemical tests excluded certain conditions. Anti-cardiolipin antibodies in the IgG or IgM class, lupus anticoagulant, and antibodies against β2-glycoprotein were negative when tested again after 12 weeks. IgM and IgG antibodies against CMV were detected. Transthoracic echocardiography and carotid artery ultrasonography were unremarkable. Glatiramer acetate therapy was initiated 3 weeks after discontinuing interferon beta-1a. Two weeks into glatiramer acetate therapy, the patient experienced neurological worsening, including fever, headache, impaired consciousness, left-sided weakness, and lower limb ataxia. Lumbar puncture showed a mild elevation of cerebrospinal fluid protein, no oligoclonal bands, and a negative encephalitis panel.
test_results: Fluorescein angiography (FA) revealed BRAOs and subtle, segmental arteriolar wall hyperfluorescence (AWH) at the site of BRAO in the late phase. A repeat FA performed two weeks later showed reperfusion of the occluded arterioles and resolution of the AWH. The brain MRI showed diffuse and limited hyperintense changes in fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) and T2 sequences located periventricularly in the subcortical white matter, mainly in the frontal and parietal lobes, in the pons, in the basal ganglia and in the corpus callosum. MRI revealed also post contrast leptomeningeal enhancement. Repeated FA showed new BRAOs and AWH in both eyes.

case_report: A 43-year-old male with no notable prior medical history was found to have a metastatic ileal G2-NET at age 34. Initial findings included an approximately 3-cm ileal mass with multiple metastases in the lymph nodes, mesentery, and liver. Histological analysis of the ileal mass, which was excised via segmental ileal resection due to severe stenosis, showed infiltration from the mucous membrane to the subserous adipose tissue, a mitosis count of 1 per 10 high-power fields (HPF), a Ki67 index of about 3%, and widespread neoplastic involvement of lymphatic vessels both near and distant from the tumor. The patient began treatment with first-generation somatostatin receptor ligands (SRLs) due to the extensive spread of the disease. After nearly a decade of stable disease under SRL therapy, recent 68-Ga-DOTATOC PET and abdominal MRI scans indicated disease progression. The patient is now being considered for peptide receptor radionuclide therapy. Given the extensive disease involvement at a relatively young age, a genetic evaluation was recommended.
test_results: The analysis identified the mutation p.I119T (c.356T>C) in heterozygosity of exon 1 of CDKN1B. This mutation was identified in control databases in 152 of 279,092 alleles at a frequency of 0.0005446 (gnomAD). In-silico analysis does not predict a difference in splicing. This variant was determined to be of uncertain significance according to ACMG guidelines, 2015, and had already been reported in the literature in association with early-onset pituitary adenoma.

case_report: A female infant was delivered at 38 weeks gestation to a 35-year-old first-time mother via elective caesarean section due to a history of retinal detachment. The family history was negative for miscarriages, neurological disorders, or autoimmune diseases. The infant's birthweight was 2845 g (AGA, Z-score: −0.48 SDS), length was 52 cm (Z-score: 1.98 SDS), and head circumference was 34.5 cm (Z-score: 0.82 SDS). At birth, she exhibited hypotonia, cyanosis, and stridor, with worsening respiratory distress necessitating nasotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. Apgar scores were 4, 6, and 8 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes, respectively. Bilateral vocal cord palsy in the adduction was observed. No dysmorphic features were present. At 8 days old, she was transferred under mechanical ventilation to a tertiary pediatric hospital for further evaluation. Laryngo-tracheo-bronchoscopy showed uncoordinated vocal fold movements, allowing for extubation and spontaneous breathing. Lung function tests indicated decreased respiratory flow, particularly during inspiration. Brainstem auditory evoked potentials (BAEPs) were normal. An Endoscopic Arytenoid Latero-Abduction (EALA) was performed. Due to persistent stridor and progressive respiratory distress requiring noninvasive respiratory support, a tracheostomy was performed at 46 days old. Intraoperative laryngeal electromyography (LEMG) demonstrated reproducibility of motor evoked potentials with a train of 8 stimuli at 250 Hz at a threshold of 300mA and activation of the chordal structures by direct muscle stimulation with a train of 5 stimuli at 250 Hz, with an activation threshold at 25 mA. No spontaneous neurotonic activity was noted during LEMG, but asynchronous activity was detected during spontaneous respiration, more pronounced in the left muscles. The infant showed rapid improvement, no longer requiring respiratory support 48 hours post-surgery. She experienced feeding difficulties, with good sucking but poor swallowing, leading to breastfeeding failure and the need for nasogastric tube (NGT) feeding during the initial weeks of life. Enteral nutrition was well tolerated, with normal results from upper gastrointestinal contrast-enhanced study, gastric emptying scintigraphy, and multichannel intraluminal impedance-pH monitoring. An automated auditory brainstem response (AABR) test showed a normal bilateral response. At 3 months old, she was discharged home and able to feed from a bottle.
test_results: NGS detected the presence of the following variants in the MUSK gene (NM_005592.3): c.565C>T in exon 5, and c.2287G>A and c.2368G>A in exon 15. The c.565C>T and c.2287G>A were inherited from the mother and the c.2368G>A was inherited from the father. The c.565C>T variant causes the insertion of a premature stop codon (p.Arg189Ter) likely leading to a consequent formation of a truncated nonfunctioning protein. The c.2287G>A variant causes the aminoacidic change p.Ala763Thr (rs199507468). The c.2368G>A variant leads to the missense change p.Val790Met (rs199476083).

case_report: A 21-day-old white male was brought to the primary pediatrician due to poor feeding and failure to regain birth weight. Laboratory tests showed sodium at 106 mmol/L, potassium at 7.1 mmol/L, and glucose at 1.8 mmol/L. A 17-OH progesterone level was also measured. The infant was then transferred to a tertiary referral hospital for electrolyte imbalances. The birth history included an uneventful pregnancy and delivery, with a birth length of 51 cm (65th percentile) and a birth weight of 3.35 kg (37th percentile). Apgar scores were 8 and 9. Hyperpigmentation of the scrotum was observed at birth, and hypoglycemia was noted on the first day of life. The infant was discharged on the second day of life. The past medical history included two previous admissions for unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, with a maximum bilirubin level of 367 μmol/L, treated with phototherapy on both occasions. The parents observed progressive skin pigmentation over the first three weeks of life, which they attributed to phototherapy. Upon arrival at the hospital, the physical exam showed normal vital signs, a blood pressure of 68/33 mmHg, and a weight of 3.1 kg (7th percentile). No dysmorphic features were noted. The genital exam revealed normal male genitalia with both testes descended, and a normal phallus with the urethral meatus at the tip. The physical exam was notable for marked bronzing of the skin.
test_results: A T to C base change in the second exon was found, which substitutes proline for leucine at codon 447.

case_report: Patient 1 is a 25-year-old Egyptian male presenting with progressive vision loss, hearing impairment, and changes in facial features over recent years. He is the child of first cousin parents. Family history includes two older female siblings who died at 4 months of age from an unknown cause, a stillbirth at 7 months of gestation, a younger female sibling who died at 20 years from atrial fibrillation, two unaffected siblings, and a younger brother with similar facial changes. Additionally, a maternal cousin died at 4 years from hydrocephalus, and another sibling with mental subnormality died at 2 years; their parents were also consanguineous. Pregnancy and delivery were uneventful. At age 6, facial palsy and recurrent headaches were noted. The condition progressed with worsening hearing and vision. Examination revealed the patient was uncooperative and had communication difficulties. He was tall (183 cm, 2.0 SD above mean) with an increased arm span (191 cm) and a large head (63 cm, 4.5 SD above mean), and his weight was average. Developmental delays, delayed speech, and poor school performance were reported, but an IQ test was not feasible due to hearing and vision issues and lack of cooperation. Notable facial features included frontal bossing, high anterior hairline, prominent supraorbital ridges, proptosis, strabismus, depressed nasal root, midface hypoplasia, and prognathism. Orodental examination showed a receding premaxilla, macrognathia, thick alveolar ridge, high arched palate, irregular conical-shaped teeth, and class II occlusion. Skeletal examination revealed prominent medial clavicles and upper ribs, bilateral radial deviation of index fingers, camptodactyly of 5th fingers, broad big toes with wide spacing between the 1st and 2nd toes, clinodactyly of 4th and 5th toes, hypoplastic nails, and soft tissue syndactyly between fingers and toes. No history of bone fractures was reported, and the patient declined further bone density assessment.
test_results: X-ray studies showed diffuse thick dense cranial bones, thick calvarium, narrow skull base foramina, normal size and shape of sella turcica, hypoplastic maxilla, protruded mandible, diffuse sclerotic texture of long bones with medullary cavity expansion of metacarpals, and metatarsals and phalanges of hands and feet. MRI of the brain denoted no pituitary gland lesions with patent cavernous sinuses and inferior sagging of the infundibular recess of third ventricle. Audiogram showed bilateral profound mixed hearing loss. Eye evaluation and fundus examination revealed hypotropia, exotropia, and bilateral optic atrophy. Cytogenetic analysis by G-banding using peripheral blood leukocytes denoted normal male karyotype in all studied metaphases (46, XY).

case_report: A 38-year-old male, nephew to the proband and son of case 2, has a history of physically demanding work. He previously underwent surgeries for cleft lip and palate and for undescended testis. Despite not having a growth hormone deficiency, he received growth hormone treatment until age 13 due to short stature, but the treatment was discontinued as it did not enhance growth velocity. He experienced mild learning difficulties, particularly with spelling, during school and found physical activities challenging in his youth. He is currently not on any medication. Physical examination revealed a height of 1.62 cm (−3.0 SD) and weight of 59.7 kg (−1.7 SD). Notable features included widely spaced eyes, mild ptosis, downslanting palpebral fissures, low set ears, short philtrum, high palate, and mild dysarthria. Examination of the extremities showed brachydactyly and interdigital webbing. There was no evidence of scrotal shawl or inguinal hernia. Muscle bulk, MRC strength assessment, and general neurological examination were normal.
test_results: He also carried the c.2266dup, p.Cys756Leufs*19 variant. Muscle biopsy showed central nuclei and few COX-negative fibers. Mitochondrial enzyme activities corrected for citrate synthase activity were moderately decreased for complexes I and IV. There were no mtDNA deletions.

case_report: The patient is a 29-year-old male who was admitted with severe jaundice. His parents reported that he had experienced jaundice and itching since birth without receiving any treatment. He measures 163 cm in height and weighs 81 kg. Laboratory tests showed normal results for hemolytic anemia parameters, including hemoglobin, coagulation function, thyroid function, ceruloplasmin, and immunoglobulin. Total bilirubin was recorded at 237.8 μmol/L, with unconjugated bilirubin at 228.8 μmol/L, while other liver function parameters were within normal limits. Tests for hepatitis, Epstein–Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus were negative. A CT scan revealed a low-density liver with a normal shape, and the CT index was 50 HU, indicating fatty liver. A liver biopsy indicated bullous steatosis around the peri-central veins of the hepatic lobule, bile pigment sedimentation, and mild periportal inflammation, with a normal liver plate structure. There is no consanguinity between the patient's parents.
test_results: The genetic test results showed two suspected homozygous pathogenic mutations. One mutation was the c.1456 T > G p.Y486D homozygous mutation. Y486D is located on exon 5, changing the 1,456 thymine (T) into guanine (G) and changing residue 486 tyrosine (Tyr) into aspartic acid (Asp). His parents were c.1456 T > G p.Y486D heterozygous carriers. The other mutation was the c.211G > A p.G71R homozygous mutation. G71R is located in exon 1, mutating the 211 guanine (G) into adenine (A) and changing residue 71 from glycine (Gly) to arginine (Arg). His father was a c.211G > A p.G71R homozygous carrier without any symptoms, and his mother was a heterozygosis carrier.

case_report: A 19-year-old male with no prior health issues was admitted to a tertiary hospital presenting with sudden onset of involuntary eye movements, widespread myoclonic jerks, and mild confusion. He reported experiencing fever, chills, muscle aches, sore throat, and dizziness that began 9 days prior. Upon admission, his vital signs were stable and he was afebrile. Spontaneous eye movements were first noted by an otolaryngologist 4 days before admission, followed by the development of generalized myoclonus 2 days later. There was no history of medication use or toxin exposure. Neurological examination showed chaotic, multidirectional saccadic eye movements with large amplitudes. He exhibited moderate-to-severe myoclonic jerks affecting his head, trunk, and all four limbs both at rest and during movement. He was disoriented in both space and time and was unable to stand or sit due to severe truncal ataxia. Initial brain MRI performed on the day of admission and follow-up imaging on the 5th hospital day were normal. Electroencephalography showed no spikes or spike-and-wave components. Routine laboratory tests were normal except for elevated muscle enzymes (creatine kinase 1029 U/L, normal range 26-174 U/L). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal cell counts and protein levels, with negative results for cytology and viral markers.
test_results: Serological tests revealed no acute infections of rubella virus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, syphilis, herpes simplex virus-1 and -2, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), streptococcal infection, varicella-zoster infection, mycoplasma, or hepatitis A, B, or C. Tests for antinuclear antibodies were negative. Immunofluorescence analysis revealed that the patient's serum and CSF were negative for anti-Hu, anti-Ri, anti-Yo, and neuromyelitis optica antibodies. Contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography (CT) revealed a mediastinal mass detected, but biopsy proved this to be a benign lesion that had extensive necrosis and chronic inflammation without granuloma. Malignancy was not detected on positron-emission tomography-CT. On admission the patient had no symptoms or signs of parotitis, orchitis, or pancreatitis; however, his serum IgM antibody titer index for the mumps virus was elevated at 1.20 (negative <0.9), but he was negative for the IgG antibody. Enzyme immunoassays produced negative results for CSF IgM and IgG antibodies to the mumps virus. On the 26th hospital day his serum IgG antibody titer index to mumps virus was 1.40 (negative <0.9), and he was negative for the IgM antibody.
diagnosis: Opsoclonus-Myoclonus Syndrome associated with mumps virus infection

case_report: A 47-year-old woman was admitted to Nagoya City University Hospital, Nagoya, Japan, with a complaint of abdominal swelling persisting for 12 months. Physical examination revealed a significantly swollen and firm abdomen without tenderness. Laboratory tests showed slight anemia and a mild increase in C-reactive protein levels, with no abnormalities in tumor markers. A computed tomography (CT) scan identified two retroperitoneal masses: one measuring 26 × 15 × 29 cm, slightly enhanced, involving and displacing the right kidney, and another smaller, walnut-sized mass of low density adjacent to the larger mass. The larger mass occupied almost the entire retroperitoneal cavity. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed the larger mass had low T1 and high T2 signal intensities, while the smaller mass had high T1 signal intensity with a low signal in fat suppression, indicating it was primarily fat-containing. The larger mass appeared to be mainly composed of mucinous tissue. The patient underwent surgery under general anesthesia to remove the tumor along with the right kidney en bloc. The tumor was well-circumscribed, encapsulated, and weighed 8.5 kg. Gross examination confirmed the presence of two distinct components. The smaller component was yellowish and histopathologically consisted mainly of fat cells of varying sizes, with mature-appearing adipose tissue and scattered lipoblasts with large hyperchromatic nuclei. Immunohistochemical analysis showed strong staining for S-100 protein, indicating fat content. The larger component was white and histopathologically contained abundant mucinous mesenchyme with atypical spindle cells. There was extensive invasion into the renal parenchyma, but the surgical margin was clear. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed that the poorly differentiated cells did not express several mesenchymal markers, including S-100 protein.
test_results: The amplification of MDM2 gene was detected in the nuclei of both small and giant tumors.

case_report: A 34-year-old female presented with sparse hair, rough skin, photophobia, and hearing impairment persisting for over 30 years. At birth, she had minimal fine hair on the scalp, no eyebrows or eyelashes, rough and dark skin with pronounced lines, and exhibited photophobia by closing her eyes and crying in a well-lit room. During infancy, her parents observed a lack of auditory response and vocalization without speech. Over time, her skin roughness worsened, nails thickened with yellow substance accumulation and damage to the nail plate. Hair growth remained minimal, with no development of axillary or pubic hair. Ophthalmic examination showed vascular keratitis. She had no history of head trauma, special medication, and exhibited normal mental development, teeth, and sweating. Her parents are not consanguineous, and the condition is present in four generations of her family. Physical examination revealed sparse, thin, and short scalp hair with flaky pigmentation and granular keratins. Milky papules of 1 to 2 mm were noted around the eyes. The tongue had circular leukoplakia with white ridges and fissures. The skin was dark with dark brown patches, especially on the back and waist. Hands and feet were rough, with thickened nails and subungual hyperkeratosis, and partial nail plate damage. The first fingers and toes were short and thick.
test_results: A heterozygous mutation of c.G148A (nucleotide mutation at position 148 in the coding region from G to A) was detected in the proband GJB2 gene. First-generation sequencing tests showed that both the mother and daughter of the proband were heterozygous at this locus.

case_report: A 9-year-old boy, born to nonconsanguineous parents, was brought to the pediatric emergency department with worsening abdominal pain and fever over the past 24 hours. His medical history included recurrent episodes of fever, pharyngitis, and diarrhea since age 4, occurring in a cyclical pattern every 21 days and lasting about a week. On initial physical examination, he had a fever of 39.6°C, blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg, and a heart rate of 100 beats per minute. Abdominal tenderness and guarding were noted, particularly in the right lower quadrant. No superficial lymph nodes or hepatosplenomegaly were detected. Pulmonary and heart examinations were normal, and the rest of the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests on admission showed a total white blood cell count of 3000/mm3, an absolute neutrophil count of 340/mm3 (normal range: 1500–8000/mm3), hemoglobin level of 13 g/dl, and platelet count of 174000/L. Bleeding time and coagulation time were within normal limits. C-reactive protein was elevated at 268 mg/L (<3 mg/L), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was 420 UI/L (normal range: 200–400). A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen indicated increased bowel wall thickness of the small intestines and ascending colon at 8 mm (normal: 4 mm). Bacterial and fungal cultures showed no growth, and stool polymerase chain reaction assay was negative. Additional laboratory tests were conducted, with serology for hepatitis A, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, human immunodeficiency virus, and cytomegalovirus returning negative. Epstein–Barr virus serologic test results were consistent with previous exposure. Serologic tests for antinuclear and antinative DNA antibodies were negative.
test_results: Bone marrow aspiration examination demonstrated a maturation arrest of granulocytic cells.

case_report: A 61-year-old woman with a history of Sjogren’s syndrome noticed significant swelling and abdominal distension about one month ago, accompanied by a weight gain of approximately 6 kg. She was admitted due to renal dysfunction and abnormal urinalysis results. Previous blood tests one month earlier showed normal renal function (creatinine = 0.78 mg/dl) and no abnormalities in urinalysis. She had no prior history of renal dysfunction or abnormal urine analysis. Upon admission, her vital signs were: blood pressure 114/74 mmHg, pulse rate 94/min, body temperature 38.2 °C, height 156 cm, and weight 46 kg. She was alert and exhibited mild facial, upper and lower extremity, and abdominal edema. There was no superficial lymphadenopathy, joint pain, neurological abnormalities, or skin lesions, and heart and lung examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory findings on admission included mildly impaired renal function (creatinine = 1.07 mg/dL, eGFR = 41 mL/min/1.73 m2), urine protein 2+ [urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio (UTP/Ucr): 0.78 g/gCr], and microscopic hematuria. Antinuclear antibodies (speckled pattern) × 40 and anti-SS-A antibodies were positive. Biochemical tests revealed a low platelet count (7.2 × 104/μL) and elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) level (3.33 mg/dL). Tests for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, human immunodeficiency virus, human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), and tuberculosis infection were negative. Elevated serum IL-6 level at 14.8 pg/mL (reference value: 0.0–4.0 pg/mL) and serum VEGF at 384 pg/mL (reference value: 0.0–38.3 pg/mL) were noted. Haptoglobin levels were normal, and blood smears showed no crushed red blood cells. ADAMTS13 activity was 34%, and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) was ruled out. Computed tomography revealed generalized lymphadenopathy, pleural effusion, and ascites.
test_results: Lymphatic pathology showed lymph nodes with preserved follicular structure and plasmacytoid infiltration between the follicles. Extensive fibrosis of the bone marrow was reported. Periodic acid–Schiff staining revealed diffuse endothelial cell swelling and macrophages in the glomerulus. Periodic acid-methenamine staining showed no double contours or spike. No areas of tubular interstitium were found to be devitalized, and no inflammatory cell infiltration was observed. There was no fibrin thrombus or fibrinoid necrosis in the glomeruli or arterioles. Immunofluorescence staining showed that only IgM was deposited in the mesangial region, whereas other immunoglobulins and complement were not. Congo red stain was performed to search for renal amyloid, but the results were negative. Electron microscopy revealed endothelial cell swelling, subendothelial space enlargement, and mesangiolysis, but showed no electron-dense deposits.

case_report: An 84-year-old right-handed, white male presented with a 1-year history of changes in speech. Initially, he was diagnosed with an 'invisible stroke' by a general practitioner. However, as symptoms continued to progress, he was referred for further consultation. On initial examination, his speech was characterized by short sentences that included nouns but omitted verbs, adverbs, and adjectives.
test_results: Formal neuropsychological evaluation revealed extremely low verbal fluency, poor repetition, and mildly impaired naming ability with occasional paraphasic errors. Performance on executive function tasks was mostly within normal range with the exception of difficulty on a task of visuomotor set shifting (Trails B). Tests of memory, attention, and visuospatial functioning were normal. Other than a slight slowing of saccade initiation and upward gaze, his neurological examination was generally unremarkable and free of Parkinsonism, scoring a 2 (for a postural tremor and gait) on Part III of the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS). The results of his magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed atrophy of the midbrain, diffuse regions of the frontal lobes, and focal atrophy of the anterior pole of the left temporal lobe. A fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-positron emission tomography scan showed left temporal lobe hypometabolism.
diagnosis: Agrammatic Variant of Primary Progressive Aphasia

case_report: A 55-year-old female presented with multiple intermittently painful raised skin lesions located on the right shoulder, right chest, and right upper back. The lesions first appeared at the age of 40 years, initially involving only the right shoulder. After remaining unchanged for 5 years, the number of lesions gradually increased, extending to the upper back and chest on the same side, and were associated with severe pain, especially upon touch. Some of the skin lesions had been excised, but new lesions continued to develop. The patient had a history of menorrhagia, for which a hysterectomy was performed 10 years ago. Histopathology of the hysterectomy specimen confirmed the presence of uterine leiomyoma. There was no history of any associated systemic conditions, and no other family members were affected. General physical examination results were within normal limits. Cutaneous examination revealed multiple reddish-brown papulonodular lesions, ranging from 2 to 10 mm, distributed in a segmental pattern over the right shoulder, upper back, and chest. The lesions were firm and tender to touch, and an atrophic scar was present at the site of excision on the shoulder.
test_results: Histopathological examination of skin lesion showed well-defined benign spindle cell neoplasm composed of smooth muscle cells arranged in whorls in the dermis, confirming the diagnosis of leiomyoma. Computed tomography scan of whole abdomen showed a corticomedullary cyst involving mid pole of the right kidney measuring approximately 3.2 cm × 2.8 cm × 2.5 cm with no calcification or haemorrhage suggestive of a simple renal cyst.
Orpha_name: Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer

case_report: The patient is a 26-month-old Chinese girl, the second child of parents who are not related by blood. She was born after a normal pregnancy. There is no known family history of liver disease. The child was admitted to the hospital due to growth retardation, with a height of 83 cm (−1.67 SD). Her father's height is 176 cm (+0.54 SD) and her mother's height is 164 cm (+0.63 SD). Physical examination revealed an enlarged liver, extending 7 cm below the right costal margin. Laboratory tests indicated significantly elevated liver transaminases, increased triglycerides, and slightly reduced glucose levels.
test_results: Patient 2 inherited compound heterozygous mutations on the PYGL gene, including c.280C > T/p.R94X on exon 2 from her mother and c.1832C > T/p.A611V on exon 16 from her father. The missense mutation c.1832C > T/p.A611V is a novel mutation.

case_report: A 34-year-old woman presented with weight gain and easy bruising. She had a history of gestational diabetes diagnosed during the 25th week of pregnancy and delivered a 2,200-g female infant via cesarean section at 37 weeks. Eight months postpartum, she returned to the hospital due to amenorrhea after stopping breastfeeding, along with continued weight gain and multiple bruises. Her blood pressure was recorded at 170/106 mmHg, and her BMI was 24.6 kg/m2. Physical examination revealed a rounded face, a prominent fat deposit on the upper back, multiple bruises, and abdominal stretch marks. Laboratory tests showed elevated morning plasma cortisol and ACTH levels.
test_results: Low-dose dexamethasone suppression testing was not associated with a reduction in plasma cortisol concentration. High-dose dexamethasone suppression testing was associated with a reduction in plasma cortisol concentration. Pituitary magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 3×4×6 mm hypointense nodule on the left side of the pituitary gland.

case_report: A 12-year-old Chinese girl exhibited facial deformities present since birth, with no notable family history. Physical examination revealed an unusual unilateral wedge-shaped anterior hairline with loss of the eyebrow on the same side, increased distance between the eyes, colobomas of the medial eyelid on the same side, and a broad bifid nose. The left eye appeared nearly normal except for a slight symblepharon, but vision was limited to light perception. The right eye was normal in both appearance and vision. No gastrointestinal anomalies were detected.
test_results: Two novel stop-gain mutations in the FREM1 gene were found in the patient: heterozygous c.3939 A > C (p.Y1313X) variant at exon 23 and heterozygous c.580G > A (p.R194X) variant at exon5. The former mutation was also found in the healthy father, whereas the latter 1 was not.

case_report: A 24-year-old woman visited our out-patient clinic with a brown discoloration that started as a small spot on her left breast 11 years ago and gradually expanded. The left breast tissue did not develop during the peripubertal period. The patient reported no systemic diseases or medication use. Her family history was unremarkable. Dermatological examination showed a brown patch with irregular borders, approximately 10 cm in diameter, composed of several smaller macules on the left breast skin. Physical examination revealed that the underlying left breast tissue was significantly underdeveloped compared to the right breast tissue. Additionally, the patient had congenital underdevelopment of the right breast.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the brown patch demonstrated minimal acanthosis, papillomatosis, increase in basal layer melanin, minimal dermal fibrosis and mononuclear cell infiltration around vessels, and hypertrophy of the erector pili muscle. Immunohistochemical stains for estrogen and progesterone were negative. Positive staining with androgen was noticed in epidermis, skin appendages and stromal cells of the dermis.

case_report: A 34-year-old Korean male presented to the emergency department with persistent insomnia and progressive cognitive decline. Symptoms began 9 months prior with severe insomnia and irregular, coarse breathing during sleep. Over time, he developed excessive sweating, bilateral action tremors, and restlessness. Two months before admission, memory issues and impaired executive function were observed, along with delusions of persecution and social withdrawal. Three days before admission, he experienced gait disturbance and mild postural instability. The patient had no prior health issues and had a background in law, working as a civil servant until memory problems led to job loss. Vital signs indicated significant fluctuations in blood pressure, increased heart rate, and rapid breathing. Initial body temperature was 38.0°C, which normalized after pneumonia treatment. Neurologic examination showed disorientation, anomic aphasia with paraphasia, and a Mini-Mental State Examination score of 17/30. Additional findings included hypophonia, dysarthria, both resting and action tremors, and akathisia. His gait was ataxic with a backward tilt tendency. Cranial nerve functions, muscle volume, tone, power, and sensory functions were normal. There were no signs of rigidity or bradykinesia, and deep tendon reflexes were normoactive without pathological reflexes. Routine blood tests were normal, but both plasma and urine catecholamine levels were elevated. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal, and the patient tested negative for 14-3-3 protein.
test_results: Direct sequencing of the PRNP gene identified a heterozygous p. Asp179Asn mutation homozygous for methionine at codon 129 and for glutamate at codon 219.

case_report: A 17-month-old girl presented with vaginal bleeding for three days. She exhibited normal growth and development with no prior medical history. Physical examination showed a height of 78.5 cm (25–50 percentiles) and a weight of 10 kg (25 percentile). Pubertal stage was B3 according to the Tanner score. No café-au-lait spots were observed, and other organ examinations were normal. Pelvic ultrasonography indicated an enlarged uterus (45×12×20 mm) and ovaries (Lt. 16×23 mm and Rt. 32×14 mm) with a unilateral ovarian cyst (15×33 mm) on the left ovary. Pelvic MRI confirmed these findings and showed no abnormalities. Routine laboratory tests and serum levels of LH, FSH, DHEAS, TSH, T4, and prolactin were normal, but serum estradiol was elevated at 140 pg/ml (normal range <10 pg/ml). The patient was treated with medroxy-progesterone acetate (MPA) for three months. Follow-up showed regression of the ovarian cyst and a decrease in breast size to B2. At 3 years old, the patient was referred again due to vaginal bleeding. Her height was 100 cm (95 percentile) and weight was 15.2 kg (75 percentile). Bone age was consistent with 5 years, and the Tanner score was B3. Pelvic ultrasonography showed an enlarged uterus (17×34×54 mm) and ovaries (Lt. 11×12 mm and Rt. 37×35 mm). Results of the GnRH test at 30, 60, and 120 minutes were LH: 3 → 4.8 → 5.7 → 7.9 μu/ml and FSH: 2.9 → 16 → 16.5 → 18 μu/ml. Brain MRI showed no abnormalities. The patient received LHRH-agonist therapy for two months, which was discontinued due to spotting, increased breast size, and an inappropriate response. During follow-up, the patient experienced recurrent vaginal bleeding and bilateral ovarian cysts, and was treated with medroxy-progesterone acetate, LHRH-agonist, and cyproterone acetate.
test_results: CT scan of maxillary bone revealed a fibrous dysplasia of the right maxillary bone.

case_report: A 43-year-old woman was admitted in January 2004 with a 2-month history of fever, dry cough, and sore throat, unresponsive to antibiotic therapy. She had previously received supportive care for eosinophilia at another hospital. Physical examination revealed a 1×1 cm non-tender cervical lymph node, hepatosplenomegaly extending 3 cm below the costal border, peritonsillar exudates, and pretibial pitting edema. Auscultation of the left lower lung field revealed diffuse crackles, with no heart murmur detected. Peripheral blood counts were: hemoglobin 11.3 mg/dL, platelets 182,000/mm3, and white blood cells 20,730/mm3 (neutrophils 46%, lymphocytes 13%, monocytes 3%, eosinophils 36%, basophils 1%, and plasma cells 10%). The absolute eosinophil count was 7,462/mm3. LDH was 1,529 IU/L, serum IgE 9.5 IU/mL, and b2-microglobulin 2.70 mg/L. Cultures of sputum, blood, throat swab, and pleural fluid were negative. Tests for Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, VDRL, and HIV were negative. EBV VCR IgG antibody was positive, while IgA and IgM antibodies were negative. Multiple stool examinations for ova and parasites were negative. Tests for Clonorchis sinensis, Paragonimus westermani, and specific IgG antibodies for cysticercus, paragonimus, sparganum, clonorchis, and toxocara were negative. Electrocardiogram and echocardiogram results were normal. CD3/CD4 lymphocyte percentage was 66.1%, and CD3/CD8 lymphocyte percentage was 14.6%. The total CD3/CD4:CD3/CD8 (Helper:Suppressor) ratio was 4.53, higher than the normal reference range of 0.9-3.6. Chest X-ray showed mild pulmonary congestion and a left pleural effusion. Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen revealed diffuse hepatosplenomegaly, bilateral pleural effusions, and left paraaortic, subcarinal, and paratracheal lymphadenopathy. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy indicated a markedly increased number of eosinophils (24.8%), along with a significant number of plasma cells and lymphocytes. Cytogenetic analysis showed a normal karyotype, 46 XX. Despite empirical antibiotic treatment, the fever and sore throat persisted.
test_results: Pleural cytology demonstrated lymphocyte dominant exudates with a few atypical cells. A liver biopsy demonstrated a few atypical lymphoid cells and eosinophils in the sinusoids and the portal space. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy revealed a markedly increased number of eosinophils (24.8%), and a significant number of plasma cells and lymphocytes.
diagnosis: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma with hypereosinophilic syndrome

case_report: A 50-year-old woman was admitted for the management of widespread skin erosions that developed 15 days following the administration of the Pfizer/BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine. She had no notable medical history. Clinical examination showed extensive erosions following the rupture of blisters, predominantly affecting the trunk, back, and scalp, covering approximately 75% of the skin surface. A positive Nikolsky sign was observed. There was no involvement of mucosal surfaces.
test_results: Histological examination showed a superficial epidermal blistering process with intact basal layer and intraepidermal eosinophils. Direct immunofluorescence showed intracellular IgG and C3, and indirect immunofluorescence was positive for anti-intercellular substance antibodies.

case_report: A 42-year-old male presented with persistent left chest pain and newly developed shortness of breath during physical activity. He has no regular medications and his medical history includes multiple stab wounds to the left anterior chest 16 years ago, which required wound care and a prolonged course of antibiotics due to a superficial infection. On examination, he appeared generally healthy but had a borderline elevated heart rate and an oxygen saturation of 95% on room air. His lung sounds were equal and symmetrical, but a pansystolic murmur was noted below the level of the nipple, corresponding to a keloid scar from the stab wounds. The rest of the physical examination was normal, and a plain erect chest X-ray did not provide additional information.
test_results: PE was excluded; however, it did reveal a complex left-sided intra- and extrathoracic vascular malformation within the anteromedial segment of the left lung’s lower lobe, the lingula segment, the subdiaphragmatic space and the left chest-wall. The arterial supply derived from large tortuous vessels arising from a combination of the coeliac trunk, six posterior intercostal arteries and the left inferior phrenic artery. It then communicated with the left upper and lower lobe subsegmental pulmonary arteries, and the left lower lobe pulmonary vein. Aortic angiography was undertaken, confirming the CTPA findings and demonstrating predominant supply of the vascular malformation via the left intercostal arteries and the left inferior phrenic artery—draining into the left inferior pulmonary artery and vein.

case_report: A 52-year-old female presented with a skin eruption lasting for 3 weeks, primarily experiencing a burning sensation in the affected areas. She had been using diphenhydramine and cetirizine for relief. The patient reported unintentional weight loss but did not experience night sweats, joint pain, or pleuritic pain. Her medical history included cirrhosis and chronic pain. She had no personal history of dermatologic conditions but had a family history of psoriasis. Physical examination revealed multiple erythematous papules and pustules on the flanks, shoulders, axillae, and upper arms. The pustules were flaccid and contained fluid levels. Additionally, there were desquamated areas with geographic and serpiginous borders.
test_results: The histological report of the punch biopsies indicated superficial perivascular dermatitis and subcorneal pustules. Histological features suggesting psoriasis were not identified.

case_report: A three-year-old male presented with increased seizure frequency despite being on multiple anti-seizure medications. The patient was admitted for further evaluation. His past medical history includes epilepsy, infantile spasms, developmental delay, gastroesophageal reflux, laryngomalacia, and dysphagia. The mother reported no prenatal or neonatal complications. The child experienced infantile spasms at 11 months of age and was treated with prednisone. Clobazam was initiated for seizure prevention, but myoclonic seizures developed after two months. Adjusting the clobazam dose reduced seizure frequency. At 16 months, tonic-clonic seizures began, and a ketogenic diet was introduced, reducing seizures from 20 to 10 episodes per day. Cannabinol was added at age two, further decreasing seizures to fewer than five per day. However, seizure frequency later increased to over 10 per day. At two years and three months, levetiracetam was started without significant improvement. Three months later, zonisamide was introduced, also without significant effects. The ketogenic diet was discontinued, and the zonisamide dose was increased, reducing seizure frequency to four to five episodes per day.
test_results: A genetic test showed a mutation in the MYO5A gene of chromosome 15q21. The first mutation was already reported, and an additional test shows an additional deletion of unknown significance. 1) MYO5A, located at band 15q21. 2) Loss 18p11.32p11.31 (2.1 MB).

case_report: The patient, a 7-year-old boy, was the second child of unrelated parents. His father was Italian, and his mother was of Cuban ancestry. Both parents and his older sister were healthy. Family history included a female cousin of his mother with mild intellectual disability and a male cousin of his father with intellectual disability. During pregnancy, there was a potential miscarriage. Fetal ultrasound scans at 12 and 20 weeks of gestation showed normal growth and development. He was delivered at term by vaginal delivery. At birth, he had a head circumference of 33 cm (0.4th centile), a birth weight of 2880 grams (10th centile), a length of 49 cm (10th centile), and an APGAR score of 9/10. Postnatally, he exhibited growth restriction with height and weight consistently on or just below the 0.4th centile, and head circumference well below the 0.4th centile. He had bilateral ptosis, epicanthal folds, hypertelorism, a broad nasal bridge with anteverted nares, and posteriorly rotated ears. Examination of hands and feet showed proximally placed thumbs, bilateral single hand creases, and partial bilateral 2-3 toe syndactyly. At 19 months, neuropsychiatric assessment indicated global hypotonia and borderline psychomotor development with a Griffith’s scale value of 93. Investigations included a normal cranial ultrasound, normal electrocardiography, an echocardiogram showing a patent foramen ovale that later closed spontaneously, a pelvic and abdominal ultrasound revealing bilateral pelvic ectasia more marked on the left consistent with bifid pelvis on this side, normal spine and hip X-rays, and a normal metabolic screen including urinary mucopolysaccharides, urinary oligosaccharides, and urinary organic acids. Chromosome analysis by karyotype and array-CGH were normal. At four years old, neuropsychiatric assessment confirmed mild psychomotor delay with an intelligence quotient (IQ) of 69 assessed by the Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale. Growth parameters were weight 14 kg (3rd centile), height 103 cm (10-25th centile), and head circumference 48 cm (<3rd centile).
test_results: The molecular analysis of the DHCR7 revealed the presence of two mutations: c.521 T > C (p.Phe174Ser), inherited from the mother and c.724C > T (p.Arg242Cys), inherited from the father.

case_report: An 8-month-old male presented with respiratory distress, fever, and fatigue. He was born at term to a non-consanguineous family with no significant family history. He had previous hospital admissions for bronchitis at 3 and 6 months of age. During one of these admissions, he experienced severe neutropenia and was treated with a broad-spectrum antibiotic, with neutrophil counts returning to normal a few days later without additional treatment. Physical examination revealed no palpable lymph nodes or tonsillar tissue. Lung auscultation identified bilateral crackles and reduced breath sounds. A chest X-ray indicated bilateral infiltrates without pleural effusion. A complete blood count at 8 months of age was within normal limits.
test_results: Immunoglobulin levels were very low (IgA <10 mg/dl, IgM 12 mg/dl, and IgG 135 mg/dl). The patient had normal T- and NK-cell numbers, and profound B-cell deficiency (1%, 50 cells/μl). The lymphocyte proliferation assay was normal.

case_report: A 23-year-old woman presented with recurrent abdominal pain and chronic constipation. Her medical history includes multiple hospitalizations during childhood for similar symptoms, with no definitive conclusions reached. She has no significant past medical history and no notable personal or family history. Physical examination revealed tenderness in the right lower quadrant. Laboratory tests were within normal limits.
test_results: Abdomino-pelvic computed tomography (CT) showed a blind, dilated bowel loop filled with fecal material, directed to the right upper quadrant (RUQ) of the abdomen. This bowel loop communicated with the sigmoid colon and was located on the mesenteric side. The Gastrografin contrast study revealed a Y-shaped structure formed by the sigmoid colon and the duplicated colonic segment. Colonoscopy showed bifurcation of the colonic lumen at the sigmoid colon and the duplicated segment was filled with huge fecalomas.
diagnosis: Sigmoid colon duplication with ectopic immature renal tissue

case_report: The patient is a 10-year-old male of Moroccan descent, born to parents who are related by blood. He has a history of microcephaly and presents with short stature. Brain imaging revealed pachygyria. The patient also experiences demyelinating peripheral neuropathy and perceptive deafness. Notably, he does not exhibit any facial features typically associated with certain conditions, nor does he have skeletal symptoms or reported abnormalities in the gastrointestinal or enteric nervous systems.
test_results: Whole-exome sequencing was conducted on DNA from blood collected for diagnostic purposes. This resulted in the identification of two heterozygous missense variants in KIFBP, one in Exon 1, NM_015634.3:c.68A>G (p. Glu23Gly; Mut1; accession number: SCV000994834), and one in Exon 7, NM_015634.3:c.1279A>G (p. Ser427Gly; Mut2; accession number: SCV000994835). The variants were inherited from the parents, and have been previously reported in healthy controls (allele frequency of 0.00223 for Mut1 and 0.0000318 for Mut2 on gnomAD browser). No other likely pathogenic variants were identified in this patient.

case_report: A 12-month-old male with mild motor delay and no other significant medical history was admitted after presenting with a 4-day history of upper respiratory symptoms, 1 day of diarrhea, and worsening mental status changes. At baseline, the patient was nonverbal, unable to roll over, sit up unassisted, or pull to stand. The infant was born at 39 weeks via spontaneous vaginal delivery to a G1P1 mother. Prenatal history included severe pre-eclampsia in the third trimester and insufficient prenatal care in the second trimester. The mother initially brought him to an outside emergency room the day prior to admission for ongoing respiratory symptoms, most notably tachypnea. He was diagnosed with bronchiolitis and sent home. On the day of admission, the family returned to the hospital as the patient had worsening symptoms and was difficult to arouse. Initial laboratory findings identified a severe metabolic acidosis with pH 6.87 (normal 7.31–7.47), pCO2 21 mm Hg (normal 30–50 mm Hg), bicarbonate 3 mmol/L (normal 18.0–23.0 mmol/L), anion gap 30 mEq/L (normal 3–10 mEq/L), and markedly elevated serum ketones. Upon transfer to the pediatric intensive care unit, the patient was afebrile, tachycardic, and tachypneic with a Kussmaul breathing pattern. He was minimally responsive to stimulation, only opening his eyes or moving with painful stimuli. Repeat labs showed similar blood gas results with severe anion gap metabolic acidosis, glucose levels >200 mg/dL (normal 54–117 mg/dL), and serum beta-hydroxybutyrate greater than 4.5 mmol/L (normal 0.02–0.27 mmol/L). Additional labs included ammonia of 115 µmol/L (normal 29–59 µmol/L), leukocytosis of 35 Th/mm3 (normal 5.0–15.0 Th/mm3), and thrombocytosis of 684 Th/mm3 (normal 150–400 Th/mm3). His respiratory viral panel was positive for rhinovirus/enterovirus. His HgBA1C was 5.1% (normal < 5.7%). An EEG did not identify any seizure activity. Urine toxicology screen, salicylate levels, alcohol levels, and acetaminophen levels were all within normal ranges. The patient was not started on any feeds to limit precursors of a possibly blocked metabolic pathway (protein or fat). He was given parenteral fluids with dextrose 10% at one and a half times maintenance to help reverse the catabolic state. The fluids contained 75 mEq of sodium acetate to correct the severe acidosis. Insulin was initiated at 0.1 units/kg/h for elevated serum glucose levels in the 300–400 mg/dL range. To address the hyperammonemia, he was loaded with an enteral ammonia scavenging agent, sodium phenylbutyrate (250 mg/kg), and then received maintenance doses (150 mg/kg) every 6 hours. Co-factor supplementation with carnitine (60 mg/kg per day divided twice a day) and thiamine (50 mg) was also initiated. The patient had been started on empiric antibiotics prior to transfer, which were continued during the initial evaluation. After 36 hours on this regimen, his lab abnormalities resolved. He was subsequently transitioned to a normal calorie infant formula and transferred to acute care pediatrics, where he continued to improve. He remained on an oral ad lib diet in the general wards, which he tolerated well, although his solid food intake remained low. He was stable prior to discharge, very well-appearing, and without any significant illness symptoms. The patient was discharged home on a regular diet including formula and baby foods, puree as well as levocarnitine (30 mg/kg twice daily).
test_results: Our patient’s sequencing showed a homozygous variant c.1543A>G (p.Met515Val) in the OXCT1 gene.

case_report: A 24-year-old male presented with severe symmetrical fixed flexion deformities of both knees, accompanied by posterior subluxation of the tibia. He also exhibited severe palmar flexion deformities of both wrists, along with a combination of boutonniere and swan neck deformities in the fingers of both hands. The patient had multiple well-defined, irregular, erythematous, hyperkeratotic, scaly, and itchy plaques distributed across the body, including the lips but not the oral cavity, and hyperkeratotic nails. Three years prior, the patient experienced burning micturition with pus discharge, painless shallow ulcers on the glans penis, and a desquamatory rash that eventually spread to the entire body. He also had multiple joint pain and swelling involving the knees, ankles, back, and wrists. This episode lasted for 4–5 months and was treated symptomatically. Following the reduction of swelling, the patient developed deformities in both hands and the left knee. He was then started on methotrexate (7.5 mg/week, later increased to 15 mg/week with 15 mg/day folinic acid supplementation). The treatment resulted in the disappearance of skin lesions and a reduction in joint pain and swelling, although the previously established deformities persisted. After a symptom-free period of 9–10 months, the patient discontinued methotrexate on his own, leading to the development of a severe desquamatory rash over the entire body and severe pain and swelling in joints such as the knees, feet, ankles, shoulders, hands, and wrists. Methotrexate was restarted at 7.5 mg/week and later increased to 20 mg/week with 15 mg/day folinic acid supplementation. Subsequently, the patient developed severe bilateral symmetrical fixed flexion deformities of the knees, toes, shoulders, wrists, and finger joints. Currently, there is no involvement of the hips, elbows, sacroiliac joints, or spine, and there is no other evidence of systemic involvement.
test_results: Histopathological examination of skin biopsy showed focal hyperkeratosis and keratotic plugging, papillomatosis with elongation of rete ridges. Epidermis showed the pustule filled with acute infiltrate of neutrophils, whereas upper dermis showed focal melanin pigment incontinence and diffuse chronic inflammation.

case_report: A 52-year-old male presented with multiple growths on the face persisting for 25 years. Examination revealed multiple dome-shaped growths of varying sizes ranging from 5 mm to 2 cm, which were soft to firm in consistency, non-tender, and non-indurated. Additionally, the patient exhibited multiple brownish-black pigmentations on the hands and back. The patient reported no other significant medical history. He was moderately built, and his vital signs were within normal limits. Two lesions were excised: one from the area lateral to the left ala of the nose and another from above the right eyebrow. The excised specimen measured 1.2 × 1 × 1 cm and was brownish-black in color.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the lesion revealed cystic areas that consist of central keratinaceous material surrounded by basophilic cells resembling basal cell carcinoma. Tumor islands composed basaloid cells showing peripheral palisading arranged in solid islands, adenoid and lace-like pattern, surrounded by a moderately cellular stroma and condensation of mesenchymal cells around tumor islands in some areas. Cystic areas contain keratin surrounded by basophilic cells and proliferations from the wall of the horn cyst. Histopathological examination of the lesion on the eyebrow revealed solid areas resembling basal cell epithelioma with cribriform pattern and central melanin pigmentation. Whereas histopathological examination of the lesion on the forehead revealed central keratin filled cystic areas, lined by stratified squamous epithelium with cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and a vesicular nuclei, basal cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and a granular layer. Cord-like proliferation of basaloid cells was seen in one area of the lining.

case_report: A 17-year-old female from a rural area in the Birbhum district of West Bengal presented to the Department of Oral Pathology and Microbiology at Burdwan Dental College and Hospital with multiple missing teeth. Extraoral examination revealed no significant findings. Intraoral examination showed multiple retained deciduous teeth, several missing permanent teeth, and malocclusion. The canines and molar teeth in the upper arches had noticeable mottling and a rough, scratchy surface. Retained teeth included 52 and 65 in the upper arch, and 73, 74, 84, and 85 in the mandibular arch. Absent teeth in the maxillary arch were 11, 12, 14, 15, 17, 18, 21, 22, 24, 25, 27, and 28. Absent teeth in the mandibular arch were 32, 33, 42, 43, 34, 44, 37, and 47. There was spacing in the lower arch and open contact points involving the maxillary posterior teeth, particularly between 26 and 65.
test_results: OPG revealed the presence of multiple unerupted/retained deciduous and permanent impacted teeth along with teeth where root completions were not evident.

case_report: A 10-year-old male presented with swelling in the right cheek region persisting for 2 months, accompanied by increasing tooth mobility and frequent gum bleeding. Since the age of 4, he experienced recurrent febrile episodes with temperatures ranging from 101°F to 103°F, along with boils and furuncles on the face, and dull earache. Each episode was managed with antibiotics and antipyretics. Physical examination showed boils on the face and extensor surfaces of the hands, and significant swelling from the right malar region to the inferior border of the mandible. Intraoral examination revealed diffuse gingival enlargement, generalized tooth mobility, spontaneous gum bleeding, local factors, and mucosal ulcers in the floor of the mouth. Imaging studies (CBCT and orthopantomogram) indicated severe alveolar bone loss up to or beyond the apical third of the roots. Hematological tests showed mild anemia, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), increased C-reactive protein (CRP), and a marked decrease in absolute neutrophil count (ANC). Differential leukocyte count revealed significant lymphocytosis, neutropenia, and eosinophilia, with an absolute eosinophil count of 336 cells/mm3. The patient was referred to hematology and advised to undergo differential leukocyte counts twice weekly for 3 weeks. Urine culture identified Escherichia coli, and stool examination showed bacterial cells. Blood tests consistently showed pronounced neutropenia (10%–22%) and lymphocytosis (70%–88%). A peripheral smear showed no abnormalities. Serum immunoglobulin assessment revealed significantly elevated IgG and slightly elevated IgA levels. Liver function tests indicated increased alkaline phosphatase levels. During a subsequent febrile episode, the patient exhibited increased gingival enlargement and pus discharge from the gingival sulcus of the upper left first molar. A gingival tissue biopsy, Gram staining, and pus culture were performed. The biopsy indicated a chronic inflammatory lesion. Gram staining of the pus showed increased Gram-positive cocci in pairs and a few thick Gram-negative bacilli. Pus culture revealed normal oropharyngeal microflora. The patient was treated with 500 mg of amoxicillin TID and 500 mg of paracetamol TID for 5 days.
test_results: It reported an adequate particulate cell density and suppression of erythropoiesis and megakaryopoiesis. Myelopoiesis was grossly suppressed and maturation arrest was seen at metamyelocytic stage. Lymphopoiesis was accelerated and the bone marrow was hypoplastic.

case_report: A 77-year-old woman was admitted to Fujita Health University Hospital with complaints of difficulty swallowing and vomiting after every meal, shortness of breath, and a 5 kg weight loss over the past month. Physical examination showed conjunctival pallor, spoon-shaped nails, cracks at the corners of the mouth, and a smooth tongue with loss of normal papillae. Laboratory tests indicated microcytic hypochromic anemia with iron deficiency: red blood cell count 274 × 10^4/μl, hemoglobin 3.8 g/dl, hematocrit 28.1%, mean corpuscular volume 57.0 fl, mean cell hemoglobin 13.9 pg, mean cell hemoglobin concentration 24.4%, serum iron level 7 μg/dl, total iron binding capacity 425 μg/dl, and serum ferritin level 2.0 ng/ml. Serum liver and kidney function tests were within normal limits (serum AST 13 IU/l, serum ALT 5 IU/l, serum BUN 14.7 mg/dl, and serum creatinine 0.49 mg/dl).
test_results: A web was detected that prevented passage of the endoscope into the upper portion of the esophagus. Barium-swallow esophagography also revealed a circumferential web at the cervical esophagus.

case_report: A six-month-old female patient was admitted due to limb trembling. Genetic analysis revealed a compound heterozygous mutation: c.1004C>T (p.Ala335Val) inherited from the mother and c.698G>A (p.Arg233His) from the father. At three months of age, she exhibited a right-eye squint to the left, limb trembling with head turning to the left, upper limb stiffness, and lower limb paralysis, each episode lasting several seconds and occurring more than ten times daily. The patient can respond to sounds, track objects, and laugh but is unable to turn over or sit upright without support, showing delayed growth and development. Physical examination noted a wide eye distance, narrow eye fissures, and low ear position. Muscle strength and tension were normal, but there was bilateral knee hyperreflexia and Achilles tendon hyperreflexia.
test_results: Cranial MRI showed an enlargement of bilateral ventricles and a slightly wider extrafrontal space.

case_report: The patient is a 3-year-old female who presented to the Department of Rehabilitation for delayed language development. She is the first child of non-consanguineous Chinese parents. Her antenatal and birth history were normal. She was delivered by cesarean section with a birth weight of 3.2 kg and a length of 50 cm. At 6 months old, she exhibited hypotonia. She achieved sitting unsupported at 10 months and walking independently at 28 months. At 3 years old, her physical examination revealed a height of 95 cm (50th–75th percentile), weight of 15 kg (50th–75th percentile), and head circumference of 47.5 cm (10th–25th percentile). Dysmorphic features included bushy eyebrows, downslanted palpebral fissures, esotropia, depressed nasal bridge, and sparse teeth. She had significant speech delay, producing no meaningful words, poor eye contact, and lack of interest in her surroundings, indicating abnormal social interaction. Laboratory tests including blood counts, liver and renal function tests, thyroid profile, and metabolic screen by mass spectrometry were normal. Brain MRI showed a thin corpus callosum, a mega cisterna magna, and ventriculomegaly.
