Long-term video-EEG revealed atypical sharp waves in the right occipital and posterior temporal regions, though she had no history of seizures. Ophthalmological and hearing assessments were normal. The Gesell Developmental Diagnostic Scale indicated a developmental age of 8 months for speech. The Autistic Behavior Checklist (ABC) score was 61, and the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS) score was 36. Family history review showed no similar presentations among relatives, except for the mother who had mild symptoms. The mother graduated from middle school with poor grades, had unclear pronunciation, slightly poor language expression ability, and an intelligence test score of 85.
test_results: We identified the proband carried a heterozygous missense variant c.1343C > T, p.Ala448Val in exon 9 of CLCN4 gene (Genbank association number NM_001830). Sanger sequencing was applied to confirm the variant. Her mother was confirmed to be the carrier of the heterozygous variant. The variant co-segregation is consistent to the X-linked hereditary mode in genetics. This missense variant causes an amino acid substitution of an alanine residue with a valine residue (p.Ala448Val). Comparative amino acid sequence alignment of CLCN4 across different species revealed that the alanine at position 448 is highly conserved. The identified variant was not found in searched public databases (ExAC, gnomAD, dbSNP and 1000 Genomes Project).
diagnosis: syndromic X-linked intellectual disability  associated with a novel CLCN4 variant

case_report: A 63-year-old woman reported experiencing leg tremor and instability while standing for the past 2 years. She had a history of angina 5 years ago and briefly used a calcium antagonist, with no history of mental illness or use of psychotropic drugs. During the physical examination, continuous trembling was observed in her lower limbs when standing, which ceased when she walked, sat, lay down, or leaned against a wall. Fine ripples were noted in the quadriceps muscles while standing, with no similar movements in other body parts. There were no signs of bradykinesia, muscle rigidity, or gait disturbances. Additionally, there were no indications of supranuclear gaze palsy, cerebellar signs, autonomic dysfunction, restless legs syndrome, or cognitive dysfunction. She did not exhibit REM sleep behavioral disorder or insomnia. Alcohol had no effect on the tremor, and there was no family history of tremor or parkinsonism. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, electrolytes, glucose, renal and liver functions, vitamin B12, and thyroid function, were all within normal ranges. Chest X-ray and electroencephalogram results were noncontributory. Head MRI showed small infarctions in the cerebral white matter but was otherwise normal. Surface electromyography of the lower leg muscles revealed rhythmic spontaneous motor unit potentials at a frequency of 5–6 Hz, with a burst duration of 100 ms and an amplitude of 200–400 µV. There was a noticeable left-right difference in motor burst amplitude, with the right side showing larger amplitudes than the left. The tremors were not synchronized among different muscles and legs, and no discharges were recorded while she was supine or sitting with her feet dangling.
test_results: The SBR values were 3.31 in the right striatum and 3.50 in the left striatum.

case_report: A term male infant, weighing 3885 g (>95th percentile), was born vaginally to a 22-year-old woman. The mother reported no family history of bleeding disorders. The pregnancy proceeded without complications, and resuscitation at birth was straightforward. Initial physical examination in the newborn nursery showed no abnormalities. However, at 6 hours of age, the infant suddenly developed widespread bluish skin discoloration, became hypotensive, and exhibited significant abdominal distention. Laboratory results revealed a hemoglobin level of 5.5 g/dL and a PTT exceeding 100 seconds. The infant received a blood transfusion of 20 cc/kg of O Rh-negative packed cells. An abdominal radiograph indicated a normal bowel gas pattern but showed intestines clustered centrally, suggesting the presence of free fluid in the peritoneal cavity. A bedside abdominal ultrasound identified a ruptured splenic hematoma with a substantial amount of free fluid in the peritoneal cavity.
test_results: FVIII was <0.01 U/mL.

case_report: A newborn male, delivered vaginally at full term (40 weeks gestation) with a birth weight of 3115 grams, presented with a mass composed of several nodules located on the maxillary gingiva. The mass, which was approximately 2 cm at its largest dimension, was surgically removed. Upon examination, the cross-section of the mass appeared whitish-yellow and had a notably smooth surface.
test_results: The lesion was composed of a proliferation of large polygonal cells with demarcated cell membrane, granular cytoplasm, and small uniform nuclei. The overlying surface epithelium was not hyperplastic. These cells were negative for S100.

case_report: The patient is a 9-year-old girl who began experiencing symptoms at 3 months old. She presents with two primary clinical manifestations: (1) episodes of unilateral limb weakness, predominantly on the right side but occasionally on the left, often triggered by physical activity, occurring in clusters 5–7 days per month, and (2) episodes characterized by eye deviation to one side, immobility of limbs, and loss of consciousness, lasting from 10 minutes to several hours. Covering her eyes to induce sleep can reduce the duration of these episodes. Additionally, she shows signs of developmental delay, motor dysfunction, absence of speech, and seizures. Treatment with levetiracetam, depakene, oxcarbazepine, clonazepam, and phenobarbital has not been effective. Physical examination findings include poor comprehension and calculation abilities, dysarthria, ataxia, and a broad-based gait.
test_results: Cranial MRI revealed atrophy of the cerebellar vermis. The result of the genetic tests revealed the heterozygous mutation c.971_973delAGG (p.E324del) in ATP1A3.

case_report: A female infant was born at 39 weeks of gestation to a 25-year-old mother and a 28-year-old father, both healthy, with no consanguinity or notable family history. Prenatal monitoring revealed fetal hydrocephalus at 30 weeks of gestation. The baby was delivered via cesarean section due to fetal distress, with Apgar scores of 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. At birth, the infant weighed 3690 g, measured 49 cm in length, and had a head circumference of 37.5 cm (above the 95th percentile). She presented with flat areas of alopecia on the scalp and multiple small elevated nodules on the right side of the face. Additional findings included a nodular lesion at the outer canthus of the right eye, a reddish lesion on the bulbar conjunctiva, and aniridia of the right eye. The infant also had low-set ears and multiple soft subcutaneous masses over the back. Fundus examination revealed bilateral optic disc coloboma. Cardiovascular and respiratory system examinations were normal. The nervous system examination showed a full passive and active range of motion of the extremities, with normal reflexes and muscle tone. Radiography of the chest and skeleton showed no abnormalities.
test_results: A head computed tomography (CT) scan was performed, which demonstrated homogeneous low-density lesions in the cistern magna and right cerebellopontine angle indenting smoothly the brachium pontis. There was severe right lateral ventricular dilation. The patient underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head, which showed a lipomatus mass, measured at 25 × 12 mm, seen at the right cerebellopontine angle cistern, indenting smoothly the brachium pontis with no alteration of its signal, also with similar lesions noted in the posterior aspect of foramen magnum; cervical canal with no bleed, intact brain stem, with atrophic right cerebral hemisphere; and dilated lateral ventricle and prominent overlying subarachnoid spaces. The right periauricular cutaneous lesion was submitted to histopathological examination and showed that the dermis has rudimentary hair follicles surrounded by fibrous connective tissue interpreted by mature fat lobules. Electroencephalography (EEG) was done, which showed the presence of diffuse slow delta activity related to brain damage (encephalopathy). Ultrasound of both kidneys revealed 2 cm cortical cyst in the upper pole of the right kidney. Repeat MRI of the brain demonstrated no change. Magnetic resonance imaging angiography of the brain was normal. The MRI of the spine showed large subpialjuxtamedullary lipoma filling the entire spinal canal, which is widened, and engulfing the spinal cord. The spinal cord is tethered and is remarkably compressed at the thoracic level, displaced to the left and protruding into the left lateral foramina at the level of dorsolumbar junction. The vertebrae are of normal heights and signal, and normally aligned and the discs are unremarkable.

case_report: A 6-year-old boy was referred to a tertiary center after an incidental finding of nephrotic range proteinuria during an examination for nocturnal enuresis. Upon admission, he was normotensive, had no peripheral edemas, and his physical examination was normal. Family history indicated that his maternal uncle had proteinuria of unknown cause. The patient's past medical history was unremarkable, and he was not on any medication. He had a mild motor development delay that required temporary reflex locomotion therapy. His height and weight were in the 10th and 25th percentiles for his age, respectively. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 11.1 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin at 134 g/dL, and platelets at 272 × 10^9/L. Serum creatinine was 49 μmol/L, potassium 4.7 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24.9 mmol/L, cholesterol 5.6 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.03 mmol/L, albumin 49.8 g/L, and total protein 75 g/L. Urinalysis revealed 2+ protein, a protein to creatinine ratio of 315 mg/mmol, microalbumin to creatinine ratio of 58 mg/mmol, calcium to creatinine ratio of 0.6 mmol/mmol, 13 erythrocytes/μL, and no leukocytes. Infectious disease screening, including EBV, CMV, gonorrhea, and HIV serology, was negative. Immunology tests showed mild hypogammaglobulinemia at 5.19 g/L, with normal C3 and C4 levels at 0.73 and 0.22 g/L, respectively. Antinuclear antibodies, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and the extractable nuclear antigen panel were all negative. Renal ultrasound indicated that both kidneys were of normal size with no evidence of renal cysts, kidney stones, nephrolithiasis, or nephrocalcinosis. A percutaneous renal biopsy showed histologic features with approximately 30% of glomeruli exhibiting mild segmental mesangial hypercellularity. One glomerulus had a globally collapsed capillary tuft, and three glomeruli had segmental collapse with adhesion to Bowman's capsule. Two glomeruli were globally sclerotic, with sparse small foci of interstitial fibrosis. Electron microscopy revealed segmental capillary collapse, podocyte foot processes effacement (~70% of loops), podocyte hypertrophy, and microvillous change. Corticosteroid administration was considered but not initiated due to the absence of hypoalbuminemia and edemas. Ramipril was prescribed. Urine protein electrophoresis showed 50% low molecular weight proteinuria. Urine concentrations of renal tubular damage markers (N-acetyl β-D-glucosaminidase 192 nkat/L, alpha 1 microglobulin 279 mg/mL) were significantly increased, while albuminuria was moderately increased. Hypercalciuria was present intermittently.
test_results: The analysis revealed a known pathogenic variant c.[952C>T];[0], p.[(Arg318Cys)];[0] (rs137853263 in the dbSNP database) in the OCRL gene. No other causative variants in known FSGS-associated genes were found. Sanger sequencing of parental DNA samples confirmed the presumed inheritance of the variant. The patient's mother is a healthy carrier of the c.952C>T p.(Arg318Cys) variant, while analysis of the father's DNA was negative.

case_report: The patient is a 59-year-old female of Russian Ashkenazi Jewish descent with a family history of an unspecified disease linked to neurological symptoms and early mortality. Her clinical presentation includes bilateral facial palsy, muscle weakness, personality changes, and progressively worsening visual acuity over the past three decades. Upon referral to the Ophthalmology Division at Hospital de Clinicas in Buenos Aires, the physical examination revealed orthostatic hypotension, bilateral facial palsy, right lateral rectus palsy, and reduced sensation in the face, cornea, and limbs. Visual acuity was measured at 20/400 in the right eye and 20/200 in the left eye.
test_results: Electrophysiological studies revealed bilateral facial nerve dysfunction. On slit-lamp biomicroscopy, thin linear refractile lines were found in corneal stroma, arranged in a branching pattern spreading centripetally from the limbus. Mainly the periphery of the cornea was affected, while the center was spared.
diagnosis: Familial Amyloidosis of the Finnish Type

case_report: A 54-year-old Caucasian man visited the eye clinic with a history of blurred vision and a gritty sensation in his right eye for over six months. His Snellen visual acuity was 6/5 in both eyes. Examination showed mild redness and a stromal opacity with deep blood vessel growth in the upper part of the right cornea. There was no inflammation in the anterior chamber, and corneal sensation was normal. The left eye examination was normal. The right eye was treated with topical prednisolone acetate 0.5%. Three weeks later, the patient reported no symptoms, and the redness had resolved. The topical treatment was gradually reduced and stopped. The patient returned three months later with similar eye symptoms, along with sudden onset tinnitus in the right ear and hearing loss for three weeks. Ocular examination showed the corneal stromal opacity, with no signs of active inflammation. Blood tests revealed a high ESR (88 mm at 1 hour) as the only positive finding. All autoantibodies, including ANA, cANCA, pANCA, were negative, serum ACE levels were normal, and no antibodies were detected against treponema pallidum and borrelia burgdorfi.
test_results: An audiogram revealed bilateral sensorineural deafness.

case_report: A 51-year-old woman, nonsmoker, with no underlying diseases or suspicious case history, was admitted to the hospital due to symptoms of cough, expectoration, and worsening shortness of breath. A month prior, chest radiograph and HRCT thorax showed increased lung markings with areas of bilateral and patchy ground glass shadowing. She did not respond well to a short-term broad-spectrum antibiotic. In the month leading up to her hospital admission, her shortness of breath worsened significantly, and her exercise tolerance decreased to only a few feet at a time. Upon admission, her blood pressure was 113/69 mmHg, heart rate was 119 beats/min, respiration rate was over 30 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation was 93% with high flow oxygen (10 L/min) via nasal cannula at rest, dropping to 88% after minimal exertion. Her temperature was normal. Physical examination showed distinct respiratory distress, positive three depressions sign, and cyanosis. Pulmonary examination revealed significantly decreased breath sounds and diffuse velcro rales, with no crackles or wheezing. Cardiac examination showed a regular rhythm with no gallop or edema. There were no signs of skin rash, joint deformity, hepatosplenomegaly, or lymphadenopathy. Blood gas analysis showed Po2 of 8.54 KPa, Pco2 of 4.9 KPa, pH of 7.421, and FiO2/PaO2 ratio of 120. White blood cells and hemoglobin levels were within normal limits, with a slightly increased neutrophil percentage of 74.1%. Serologic tests for ANA, Sm, UI-NRnp, Jo-1, Scl-70, SSA, SSB, P-ANCA, RF, C-ANCA, and HIV were all negative. ECG showed sinus tachycardia.
test_results: Transbronchial lung biopsy (TBLB) showed slight proliferation of inflammatory and fibrous tissue. Her chest CT scan revealed areas of ground glass attenuation and consolidation in bilateral bases of her lungs accompanied with traction bronchiectasis. Bronchoscopy was performed and the results suggested absence of microorganism infection or tumor cell and eosinophil count was normal. Cytology and culture results for mycobacterium, fungus, and bacteria were all negative. BAL fluid test results for cytomegalovirus, chlamydia, Legionella, herpes simplex virus, and respiratory syncytial virus were negative too. Percutaneous lung biopsy was performed and the slides showed diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) associated with hyaline membrane formation, pulmonary interstitial edema, and immature collagen edema, and focal type II pneumocyte hyperplasia were also visible.

case_report: A 76-year-old Caucasian Australian woman presented over 5 years ago with urinary symptoms, including dysuria and urgency. Her past medical history included mild hypertension, and she had no history of smoking or previous hospitalizations. Imaging revealed a high-density retroperitoneal tumor with some fat density around the right inguinal canal, which was surgically resected. The tumor measured 10 cm in diameter, had a lobulated contour, and a pale whorled cut surface. Histological examination showed widespread dense fibrosis with a variable chronic inflammatory infiltrate rich in plasma cells, especially at the tumor's periphery. The tumor was hypocellular and densely fibrotic, composed mainly of bland stromal cells resembling fibroblasts. Occasionally, mildly atypical larger cells and some vacuolated cells were observed, but no diagnostic lipoblasts were identified. The fat from the right inguinal canal consisted of mature adipose tissue with extensive fat necrosis, and no lipoblasts were found. Immunohistochemistry results showed the tumor was negative for S100, CD34, cKit, desmin, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK), with no increase in IgG4-positive plasma cells. The retroperitoneal tumor was considered an inflammatory pseudotumor in the fibrosing stage (IgG4-negative variant), and the fat necrosis in the right inguinal canal was deemed benign. Five years later, the patient presented again with similar urinary symptoms, and imaging showed a retroperitoneal tumor at the previous excision site. She underwent en bloc excision with a right hemicolectomy. The excised tumor, centered in the deep mesocolon, was lobulated and 10 cm in diameter with a pale fleshy cut surface. An incomplete rim of chronic inflammation was noted, but the recurrent tumor consisted of poorly differentiated pleomorphic cells, including bizarre forms, with the morphology of a pleomorphic undifferentiated sarcoma. Despite marked pleomorphism, mitoses were infrequent (less than 1 per 10 high-power fields). Occasional vacuolated cells were present, but classic lipoblasts were not identified. Immunohistochemistry again showed the neoplastic cells were negative for S100, CD34, cKit, desmin, and ALK.
test_results: The primary tumor, the bland adipose tissue resected from the inguinal canal at the time of surgery, and the recurrent tumor all underwent FISH testing, which demonstrated MDM2 amplification in all three specimens.

case_report: A 65-year-old female with an 11-year history of a tremor-dominant condition underwent bilateral subthalamic nucleus stimulation surgery in October 2011. The procedure was performed under fluoroscopic guidance without any complications. The pulse generator was implanted in a left subclavicular pouch and secured to the underlying muscle fascia, without proximal stitches. Postoperative functional outcomes were favorable, with a reduction in the UPDRS III score from 47 to 7, allowing for a significant decrease in medication. The patient was discharged without surgical complications and advised to avoid extreme exertion and contact sports. Follow-up visits included inspection of the surgical wound, which showed no signs of skin manipulation. Four months post-surgery, the patient exhibited signs of recurrent symptoms with diminishing response to stimulation. Over the next three months, the clinical condition reverted to preoperative status, with a UPDRS III score of 43 on medication by May 2012, regardless of stimulation.
test_results: X-ray studies of the system displayed twisted extensor leads and an evident disconnection between these and the distally migrated electrode lead connections. Proximally to the slightly rotated IPG, the extensors seemed to curl, however, the electrode leads were spared. A change in electrode impedance was also identified, with persistent abnormally high readings.

case_report: A 22-year-old male patient reported a gradual onset of worsening bilateral muscle wasting and tremors in the distal upper limbs over the past 5 years. Symptoms were exacerbated by exposure to cold. Physical examination showed symmetrical muscle atrophy in the hands and forearms, along with decreased muscle strength during finger flexion, extension, and abduction, as well as wrist flexion and extension. Tendon reflexes in the affected areas were also diminished.
test_results: Electroneurophysiology and electromyography showed signs of chronic motor neuron lesion at C7, C8, and T1 myelotomes, bilaterally. Magnetic resonance images (MRI) acquired in neutral position showed loss of cervical lordosis and focal cord atrophy at C5-C6 level. MRI acquired in flexion revealed widening of the posterior epidural space. On postcontrast images, uniform enhancement of the epidural space was observed. The enhancement was reduced in the neutral position.

case_report: Case 2 involves a 34-year-old female of Greek descent. She experienced repeated pathological fractures starting at age 28. From age 30, she exhibited increasing cognitive and behavioral symptoms resembling frontotemporal changes. At age 33, her Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score was 14 out of 30, and her Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score was 8 out of 30.
test_results: Computer tomography (CT) scan revealed cerebellar atrophy, diffuse low-density areas of the brain white matter, and subependymal and basal ganglia calcifications. Brain MRI showed hyperintensities of the white matter, brain atrophy, and a thin corpus callosum.

case_report: A 50-year-old male presented with a 1-month history of epigastric pain. He had no prior history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, or alcohol consumption, but had a 20 pack-year history of smoking. Upon admission, his vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed tenderness in the epigastric region, with no other notable findings. Laboratory results were as follows: white blood cell count 6000/mm3 (normal range: 6000–10,000/mm3), hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL (normal range: 12–16 g/dL), platelet count 270,000/mm3 (normal range: 130,000–450,000/mm3), blood urea nitrogen 13.9 mg/dL (normal range: 8–23 mg/dL), creatinine 0.95 mg/dL (normal range: 0.5–1.3 mg/dL), serum albumin 4.5 g/dL (normal range: 3.0–5.0 g/dL), aspartate aminotransferase 21 U/L (normal range: 5–37 U/L), alanine aminotransferase 30 U/L (normal range: 5–40 U/L), alkaline phosphatase 124 U/L (normal range: 39–117 U/L), and lactate dehydrogenase 293 IU/L (normal range: 218–472 IU/L). Total bilirubin was 0.48 mg/dL with a direct fraction of 0.19 mg/dL (normal range: 0.2–1.2/0.05–0.3 mg/dL). Amylase was 159 U/L (normal range: 43–116 U/L) and lipase was 483 U/L (normal range: 7–60 U/L). Serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) was within normal limits. Carbohydrate antigen 19-9 was 68.75 U/mL (normal range: 0–39 U/mL). Contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic computed tomography (CT) showed a 4.7 cm enhancing mass with anterior mesenteric soft tissue infiltration in the head of the pancreas. Magnetic resonance imaging indicated a pancreatic head mass with superior mesenteric vein invasion. Contrast-enhanced neck and chest CT showed no abnormalities. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) revealed an ill-defined hypoechoic mass in the head of the pancreas. Specimens from EUS-fine needle biopsy (EUS-FNB) showed several atypical lymphoid cell clusters with a high Ki-67 index. Due to the difficulty in obtaining a definitive diagnosis from EUS-FNB, a laparoscopic surgical biopsy was performed for further histologic examination.
test_results: Hematoxylin-eosin staining showed the acini structure destruction within the pancreatic parenchyma and different-sized lymphoid follicles with reactive germinal centers around the duct. Immunohistochemical examination showed that cells were positive for the B-cell marker CD20, T-cell marker CD3, and slightly positive for IgG4. However, cells were negative for the B-cell marker Bcl-2.

case_report: A 6-year-old male presented with symptoms of easy fatigue, weakness, and swelling. Physical examination showed an increased heart rate, enlargement of the liver and spleen, and edema with a positive Godet sign. Additional findings included curly hair and thickened skin on the hands and feet. The patient is the only child in the family, and there is no consanguinity between the parents.
test_results: Echocardiography revealed biventricular dilatation, significantly decreased left ventricular function, second-degree mitral insufficiency, second-degree tricuspid insufficiency, and a thrombus 3 cm in diameter within the left ventricle. Genetic studies demonstrated a desmoplakin gene mutation.

case_report: A 63-year-old male presented with progressive muscle weakness and difficulty climbing stairs, beginning at age 39. He was born to non-consanguineous parents, had normal psychomotor development, and no family history of neuromuscular disorders. Within 12 months of symptom onset, he ceased running, developed a waddling gait, and by age 53, could no longer walk long distances. Serum CK levels were consistently elevated, ranging from 600 to 3,000 U/L (normal upper limit: 350 U/L). Cardiopulmonary examinations were unremarkable. A muscle biopsy of the vastus lateralis at age 40 showed severe fibroadipose replacement, predominance of type 2 fibers, increased fiber size variability, necrotic fibers with macrophagic invasion, numerous splitting fibers, and subsarcolemmal and intracytoplasmic vacuoles with finely granular material, but no sarcotubular aggregates. Immunohistochemistry revealed desmin and myotilin accumulations within muscle fibers and increased p62 detection compared to controls. Early-stage electromyography (EMG) and electroneurography (ENG) indicated a myopathic pattern in the quadriceps femoris. Sanger sequencing and MLPA analysis ruled out involvement of the DMD gene. The latest physical examination showed bilateral hypotrophy of the anterior thigh and gastrocnemius, winged scapula, and selective weakness in pectoral, upper, and lower limb muscles, resulting in a waddling gait and bilateral foot drop. The patient could climb stairs and stand from a seated position only with external aids. He reported recent mild upper limb weakness and right thigh myalgias, without cramps or myoglobinuria, and no dysphagia or dysphonia. The most recent CK level was 2,400 U/L. A muscle MRI scan revealed diffuse morphological changes in several upper and lower limb muscles, with severe fibroadipose degeneration in the shoulder and pelvic girdles. The pelvic girdle and thigh muscles showed relative sparing of the rectus femoris, gracilis, sartorius, and short head of biceps femoris. The medial and posterior thigh compartments were most affected, with diffuse bilateral hypotrophy, mostly symmetric. Dystrophic changes were also noted in the leg muscles, with relative sparing of the flexor hallucis longus, flexor digitorum longus, and tibialis posterior muscles. In the shoulder girdle, there was diffuse fatty degeneration, with relative sparing of the right supraspinatus, and bilateral sparing of the trapezius, infraspinatus, and pectoralis muscles. In the upper arm, the triceps brachii was most affected, followed by the deltoid muscle. Despite MRI findings, clinical examination of the upper limbs was normal, with an MRC score of 5 in all areas except for the pectoral muscles, which had an MRC score of 4 bilaterally.
test_results: A Clinical Exome Sequencing was performed at our center, revealing the presence of two heterozygous TRIM32 variants: c.1181G > A/p.(Arg394His), and c.1781G > A/p.(Ser594Asp).

case_report: A 33-year-old Caucasian male visited his general practitioner (GP) due to a progressively enlarging mass on the medial aspect of his left upper eyelid. The GP performed an incision and drainage procedure. Seven weeks later, the patient went to a tertiary hospital emergency department with wound dehiscence, purulent discharge, and an enlarging palpable mass, leading to a referral to ophthalmology. There was no history of trauma or any relevant past medical or ocular conditions apart from the incision and drainage. On examination, a 1.3 mm × 8 mm firm, non-erythematous, non-tender, tethered palpable mass was observed over the left medial canthus and upper eyelid. The palpebral aperture of the left eye was 4 mm, compared to 8 mm on the right. Visual acuity was 6/6 in the right eye and 6/12 pinhole to 6/9 in the left eye, with normal intraocular pressures in both eyes. Anterior and posterior segments examination of the eyes were normal. The patient had a full range of extraocular eye movements, no proptosis, normal color vision, and full visual fields to confrontation. Mild neuropraxia was noted in the V1 distribution, and there were no palpable cervical or pre-auricular lymph nodes. Initial incisional biopsy histopathology revealed detached squamous epithelium and underlying subepithelial stroma with areas of inflamed granulation tissue and necrotic debris, without evidence of dysplasia or invasive malignancy. Computerised tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were conducted to further characterize the lesion.
test_results: Histological findings showed a proliferation of bland spindled, stellate cells arranged in fascicles with a fibrohistiocytic appearance. Occasional mitoses were noted. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated the cells were positive for SMA and calponin. AE 1/3, C-kit, CD34, Sox10, Melan-A, desmin and H-Caldesmon were negative.

case_report: An 81-year-old male presented with significant fatigue and reported darker urine over the past two weeks. Symptoms began with moderate, self-limiting diarrhea lasting three days, without fever or abnormal stool findings, followed by progressive muscle weakness. Ten days prior to seeking medical attention, the patient fell and bruised his scalp, but clinical examination and workup showed no lasting effects from the incident. The patient had no respiratory, urinary, or digestive complaints. His wife noted that he had experienced muscle weakness after short walks since his youth, which improved after a few minutes of rest. He had never taken statins. His medical history included late-onset diabetes mellitus (managed with oral hypoglycemic drugs), mild to moderate cognitive impairment of unknown origin, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and a cholecystectomy. Current medications included tamsulosin 0.4 mg/day, vitamin D3 1000u/day, ASA 100 mg/day, vitamin B12 5000 IU/week, gliclazide 30 mg/day, memantine 10 mg/day, rivastigmine 27 mg/day, linagliptin 5 mg/day, and venlafaxine 75 mg/day. The patient had a family history of consanguineous marriages. During physical examination, he was well-oriented, with normal blood pressure (130/80 mmHg) and afebrile, and no additional noteworthy clinical findings. Four years earlier, in 2015, he had been hospitalized for myalgia with nausea, vomiting, and decreased urine output after exposure to high temperatures during a fishing trip. He arrived at the hospital with acute renal failure, signs of uremia, and rhabdomyolysis. His serum myoglobin level was 5351 ng/mL (normal range: < 72 ng/mL), and he tested positive for urine myoglobin. He was negative for anti-Leptospira and anti-Plasmodium antibodies. He underwent three hemodialysis sessions and fully recovered from renal impairment. Between 2015 and 2019, he remained asymptomatic and engaged in supervised physical activities. His creatine kinase (CK) levels were consistently above normal range. During his recent hospitalization, his workup showed elevated blood glucose and glycated hemoglobin levels, with normal renal function. He experienced another episode of rhabdomyolysis, indicated by high serum CK and plasma myoglobin (364 ng/mL) levels. Tests for viral infections, including PCR for Epstein-Barr virus, antibodies against Coxsackie A and B viruses, and enterovirus RNA in peripheral blood, were inconclusive. The patient had a history of muscle fatigue since youth, recurrent rhabdomyolysis, persistent elevation in CK levels, and a family history of consanguineous marriage.
test_results: Genetic analysis revealed a homozygous insertion at Chr11:64.525.744 T > TA in the gene PYMG causing a frameshift mutation and the introduction of a stop codon halting translation (p.Asn168*fs).

case_report: A 36-year-old female with a medical history of asthma, environmental allergies, and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) presented with a 14-year history of persistent and gradually increasing skin lesions on the palms and soles, which are asymptomatic. Her asthma and environmental allergies are managed with fluticasone propionate-salmeterol 250-50 µg/dose inhaler, one puff inhaled once daily, and levocetirizine 5 mg, one tablet taken orally once daily. GERD is controlled through dietary and lifestyle changes. Her parents are non-consanguineous. Similar skin lesions are present in her paternal grandfather, father, and three siblings. Physical examination of the skin showed multiple punctate hyperkeratotic papules, each measuring 0.3 to 0.4 cm, located on the lateral aspects of her fingers, palms, and soles. No similar lesions were observed on other parts of the body. Hair, nails, and mucous membranes appeared normal. The patient reported using a pumice stone to mechanically debride the papules on her palms and soles.
test_results: Genetic sequence analysis and deletion and duplication testing of the AAGAB gene performed on a peripheral blood sample revealed a heterozygous non-sense variant [c.370C>T (p.Arg124*)] in exon 4 of the AAGAB gene. No rare variants were found in the COL14A1 gene.

case_report: A 10-year-old Spanish girl visited the dermatologic clinic due to discoloration of the scalp and eyebrows present since birth. She was born to parents who are related by blood and has a twin sister with the same appearance. Her 13-year-old brother is healthy. The patient's medical history includes developmental delay and epilepsy characterized by tonic-clonic seizures. Additionally, she has severe neuromuscular scoliosis with perpendicular obliquity of sapropelic origin, gastro-oesophageal reflux, and is under endocrinological evaluation for early puberty. Physical examination revealed facial hypopigmentation, greyish eyebrows, and grey hair tufts. Laboratory tests returned normal results.
test_results: Hair shaft examination under light microscopy showed giant uneven melanin granules in the medullar zone. The patient was a homozygous carrier of the pathogenic variant c.5152C>T (p.Gln1718*) in the MYO5A gene NM_000259.3.

case_report: A 2-month-old female infant presented with severe dilated cardiomyopathy and was administered digitalis and diuretics. She was referred for a heart transplant. Her twin sister had passed away suddenly in the early days of life without a clear cause of death. Initial physical examination showed growth retardation due to failure to thrive, hypotonia, S3 gallop, tachypnea, and liver enlargement. An echocardiogram revealed severe left ventricular dilatation (end diastolic diameter = 45 mm) with global hypokinesis and an ejection fraction of 20%. A thoracic radiograph indicated severe cardiomegaly. No significant ventricular arrhythmias were observed. Heart failure was managed with diuretics and digitalis. Elevated urinary dicarboxylic acids were detected, and biochemical studies of fatty acid metabolism showed a normal carnitine level (24 umol/L).
test_results: The serum acylcarnitine profile showed elevated levels of C6, C8, C10, and C10.1.

case_report: A 4-year-old patient assigned as female at birth presented to the genetic outpatient clinic with ambiguous genitalia and skeletal dysplasia. The patient was delivered via cesarean section to non-consanguineous parents and had a cleft palate, which was surgically corrected at 4 months. Developmental milestones included standing at 1 year and walking at 3 years with the aid of physiotherapy. Physical examination of the head showed trigonocephaly, a prominent frontal region, almond-shaped eyes with antimongoloid slant, a flat nasal bridge, a long philtrum, retromicrognathia, and a short neck. Radiographic imaging of the head indicated vertebral fusion between C5 and C6. Limb abnormalities included prominent hips, shortening of the right lower limb, valgus knees, and rhizomelic arms. Radiographic imaging of the limbs showed femur bowing, an underdeveloped acetabulum, and femoral head. At birth, external female genitalia were noted. Abdominal ultrasonography identified ovaries, a small uterus, and a shortened vagina. Hormone analysis revealed elevated levels of testosterone, luteinizing hormone, and follicle-stimulating hormone. A peripheral blood karyotype showed 46XY with a positive SRY gene. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed Arnold–Chiari malformation type 1. The patient also had moderate bilateral conductive hearing loss, which was managed with hearing aids.
test_results: After performing WES on the mother, father, and patient, we identified 1,582 variants causing non-synonymous, stop-gain, and frameshift changes; selected those with minor allele frequency (<0.01) in various databases; filtered variants unique to the daughter and absent in the parents; and detected one nonsense heterozygote variant in the SOX9 gene of the patient. We sequenced only the SOX9 gene and confirmed the variant. The pathogenic variant was caused by a guanine to adenine change at the 344 bp (c.G344A), resulting in a tryptophan to a premature stop codon change at position 115 (p.Trp115*) of the HMG domain. The frequency of this variant was 0 in the Genome Aggregation Database and Exome Aggregation Consortium databases and was not reported in the Ensembl genome and ClinVar databases. The parents did not have the nonsense variant and were homozygous for the reference allele (G).

case_report: A 37-year-old woman reported experiencing pain in her right leg for six months and in her left leg for four weeks. The pain in the left leg was mild, whereas the pain in the right leg had progressively worsened. She had previously been treated with antibiotics for low-grade osteomyelitis based on radiographic features, but her symptoms did not improve, leading to her referral to our institution. There was no family history of similar conditions. General examination showed no abnormalities. Local examination revealed mild tenderness without significant findings. Routine blood tests were normal. A frontal radiograph of both legs showed sclerosis and cortical thickening in the diaphyses of both tibias, more pronounced on the right side. A CT scan indicated circumferential cortical thickening with nearly complete replacement of the medullary cavity. MRI findings were consistent, showing bone marrow edema and minimal adjacent soft tissue inflammation. A whole-body Tc-99 m methylene diphosphonate (MDP) bone scan revealed focal areas of increased tracer uptake in both tibial diaphyses, more prominent on the right side, with no other areas of increased uptake in the skeleton.
test_results: Biopsy from the right tibial diaphysis showed cortical thickening with packed trabeculae.
Orpha_name: Glycogen storage disease due to muscle phosphofructokinase deficiency

case_report: A 49-year-old woman was referred to the gynecological department after a tumor was identified in the lower uterine segment, extending into the cervical canal. There was no history of prior pelvic irradiation. A biopsy performed at a regional hospital described the tumor as 'mesenchymal' but did not provide a specific diagnosis. Imaging studies, including ultrasonography, CT scan, and MRI, revealed a heterogeneous mass measuring 73 mm × 49 mm × 44 mm in the lower uterine segment, infiltrating the uterine wall and cervix. These imaging methods also indicated the presence of pelvic lymphadenopathy. A subsequent biopsy of the tumor portion protruding into the cervix indicated a malignant, likely mesenchymal, tumor, though classification was challenging due to sample limitations such as necrosis and a limited amount of viable tumor cells. A CT scan of the chest showed no evidence of metastases at the time.
test_results: The RNA NGS analysis revealed a fusion transcript of the EWSR1 (exon 11; NM_013986.3) and WT1 (exon 8; NM_024424.3) genes. The fusion was detected in 3923 unique reads (65.1% of the reads spanning the breakpoint). The detected fusion maintains an open reading frame and does not create a premature termination codon.
diagnosis: Desmoplastic Small Round Cell Tumor  of the uterus

case_report: A 47-year-old female presented with chronic low back pain and right L5 radiculopathy. An MRI of the lumbar spine performed at an outside institution revealed a mass-like lesion at the right L5–S1 foramen. The patient was managed with analgesics over a 1-month period, resulting in partial symptom resolution. She later visited the emergency department due to persistent symptoms, where another MRI of the lumbar spine (T1 and T2 weighted sequences) was obtained. No contrast injection was performed as it is not part of the low back pain/radiculopathy investigation protocol in the emergency department.
test_results: It showed the previously described lesion at the right L5–S1 foramen, as well as other ipsilateral lesions in the posterior paraspinal muscles and the anterior epidural space. Most of the lesions had a mass-like appearance and low signal intensity in all MR sequences. One lesion in the posterior paravertebral muscle showed mixed signal intensity on T2 weighted sequence, defining a fluid–fluid level. All the lesions were unchanged compared with the outside scan. The CT scan confirmed the calcified nature of the lesions and also showed no contrast enhancement. It also contributed to an additional finding of interstitial lung disease, as seen in a few images at the base of the lungs in the thoracolumbar region.
diagnosis: lumbar paraspinal tumoral calcinosis secondary to limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis

case_report: A 15-year-old female presented with distal muscle pain in both forearms, bilateral ankle arthritis, and intermittent fever reaching up to 39°C, six months following a meningococcal group C vaccination containing aluminium hydroxide in the deltoid muscle. Laboratory tests indicated an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) greater than 90 mm/h, mild anaemia with haemoglobin at 11.1 g/dl, and normal creatine kinase levels below 200 U/l. Anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA) were positive at a titer of 1/320 with a mottled pattern, and the rheumatoid factor was twice the upper limit of normal. Tests for anti-extractable nuclear antigen (ENA), anti-dsDNA, and anti-citrullinated protein antibodies were negative. The patient exhibited increased C3 levels, normal C4 levels, polyclonal gammopathy with IgG at 2 g/dl, and elevated α-2-microglobulin at 3 mg/dl. The patient was administered prednisolone at a dose of 7.5 mg/day, which led to a complete resolution of symptoms and laboratory abnormalities. Twenty-two months later, nearly three years post-vaccination, the patient returned with fatigue and muscle pain, primarily in the right forearm, along with swelling and functional impairment. There was no fever or abnormal laboratory findings at this time. MRI of the right forearm showed inflammation in the superficial and deep flexor muscles, indicating myositis.
test_results: A muscle biopsy was performed in the flexor compartment of the right forearm, which showed extensive fibrosis and an inflammatory process involving the endomysium, perimysium and fascia, with macrophages.

case_report: A 5-month-old male, born at full term via cesarean section to nonconsanguineous parents, was admitted due to developmental delays. The mother had taken antiabortion medication early in the pregnancy. There was no family history of developmental delays or seizures. At 5 months, the child was unable to lift his head or roll over. Physical examination revealed wide-set eyes, a high palatal arch, polydactyly of the right little finger, and polydactyly and syndactyly of both little toes. The grandfather had polydactyly of the right hand. Chromosome analysis showed a normal male 46, XY karyotype. Brainstem auditory evoked potential (BAEP) testing indicated moderate hearing loss in the left ear. Visual-evoked potential testing showed abnormalities in the bilateral visual pathways. Brain MRI revealed high signal intensity in the bilateral parietal white matter on T2-weighted images, along with ventricular enlargement and extracerebral space widening.
test_results: Increased pyrimidine and metabolite levels in urine were detected.

case_report: A 13-month-old female presented with persistent urinary bladder infections. The child was born after a normal pregnancy, and the mother did not have diabetes. No skin abnormalities were observed on the patient's back. The patient was able to walk with parental assistance. The lower limbs appeared well-formed, although the calf muscles seemed slightly smaller than what is typical for her age.
test_results: Ultrasound images were suggestive of urinary retention. On plain abdominal X-ray, hypoplasia of the lower sacrum was observed. The S3-5 segments of the sacrum were absent. A T1-weighted sagittal magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated that the spinal cord terminated at the level of the mid L1 vertebral body and the distal cord had a typical 'drumstick' appearance. No other intradural malformations were noted on imaging. The left kidney was located between the L2 to L4 vertebral bodies, and the pelvis was occupied by a large pelvic kidney.

case_report: A 55-year-old male reported experiencing mild visual loss in his right eye over a six-month period. Examination revealed visual acuity of 20/60 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. The left eye appeared normal. In the right eye, a white, elevated lesion was observed in the temporal fundus. The lesion measured 3.9 mm in thickness and had a largest basal diameter of 5.8 mm. The peripheral part of the lesion was flat and white, while the central part was elevated with fine retinal vessels on its surface. The feeding retinal arteriole and venule showed minimal dilation. There were no signs of vitreous seeds, macular edema, or subretinal fluid.
test_results: The mass was 3.9 mm thick and its largest basal diameter was 5.8 mm, as measured by CDI. Fluorescein angiography revealed that the mass was nonfluorescent with a prominent halo of retinal hyperfluorescence in the late phase. Ultrasonography revealed that the echogenic mass displayed moderate internal reflectivity, suggesting intrinsic vascular pulsations. The patient underwent 18F-FDG PET/CT imaging, which showed no positive uptake in the other parts of the body. Immunohistochemistry results revealed Homer-Wright rosettes and occasional fleurettes, with positive neuron-specific enolase.

case_report: A 38-year-old pregnant woman, weighing 62 kg and in her fourth pregnancy (gravida 4, para 0), was admitted to the cardiology department at 22 weeks of gestation due to chest tightness and shortness of breath persisting for 3 weeks. The symptoms began 3 weeks prior and included chest tightness and shortness of breath. The patient was classified as New York Heart Association grade II for heart failure. At 25 years old, she underwent a transcatheter procedure to close a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) at a local hospital, which she reported was completely successful, followed by irregular post-operative check-ups. Between 2010 and 2020, she had three spontaneous first-trimester abortions without any pregnancy-related discomfort. There was no relevant family history. Upon admission, her vital signs were: temperature 36.2°C, heart rate 75 bpm, respiratory rate 19 breaths per minute, blood pressure 92/53 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 97% with 33% oxygen concentration. Physical examination showed mild cyanosis of the lips and a loud P2 systolic murmur between the second and fourth intercostal spaces along the left sternal border. Blood tests indicated a mildly elevated hemoglobin level of 15.3 g/dL, normal hematocrit at 44.4%, and a platelet count of 1.22 × 10^11/L. Prothrombin time was within normal limits, while partial thromboplastin time was slightly reduced at 27.6 seconds. Electrocardiography (ECG) revealed an abnormal Q wave in the high lateral border, slight ST-segment changes in the lower border, right axis deviation, and clockwise transposition. Arterial blood gas analysis showed a pH of 7.47, PCO2 of 28.2 mmHg, PO2 of 85.3 mmHg, and SaO2 of 97.4% at 21% oxygen concentration.
test_results: Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) revealed the occlusion between the descending aorta and pulmonary artery. Color Doppler echocardiography revealed a bidirectional shunt signal on both sides of the occlusion. Spectral Doppler echocardiography revealed the pressure gradient (PG) and blood velocity of the bidirectional shunt. The pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP) was estimated at 117 mmHg, and the brachial systolic pressure at 124 mmHg.

case_report: A 32-year-old Korean woman experienced visual loss in her right eye upon waking and was referred to our clinic 16 hours later. Eight years earlier, she had developed itching and tender violaceous erythematous non-elevated patches with central necrotic vesicles on the dorsum of both lower legs and feet. These skin lesions improved with treatment using colchicine 0.6 mg/day, hydroxyzine, and methylprednisolone 4 to 8 mg/day. A biopsy revealed obliterative vasculopathy. A segmental limb pressure test with a bidirectional Doppler test indicated normal blood pressures in all four extremities. She received intermittent treatment with pentoxifylline and mupirocin ointment for the skin lesions over three years. She was otherwise in good health, did not smoke, and was not taking oral contraceptives or experiencing migraines. She had one son and no history of spontaneous abortion. At the time of presentation, her visual acuity was hand motion in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed a whitish edematous retina, a cherry-red spot, and narrowing and segmentation of retinal arteries. Laboratory tests, including rheumatological tests such as anti-nuclear antibody; anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies; anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody; anti-DNA antibodies; rheumatoid factor; cryoglobulin; antithrombin activity; protein C and S activity; D-dimer; anti-beta2-glycoprotein; anticardiolipin antibody; lupus anticoagulant; prothrombin gene mutation; factor V Leiden gene mutation; and homocysteine, were all within normal limits except for slightly elevated C-reactive protein (0.62 mg/dL) and fibrinogen (425 mg/dL). Serology tests were positive for hepatitis B antigen, while other serology tests were normal. Echocardiography and Holter monitoring showed normal findings. She agreed to undergo intra-arterial thrombolysis after being informed of the potential risks and benefits.
test_results: Cerebral angiography showed severe focal vasospasm of the right internal carotid artery as soon as the catheter was placed, which was subsequently relieved by continuous intra-arterial infusion of nimodipine 5 mg. Selective angiography of the origin of the right ophthalmic artery showed no definite thrombus or steno-occlusive lesion within the ophthalmic artery. Seven hours after intra-arterial thrombolysis, retinal arterial perfusion on fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) did not improve (arm to retina time, 29 seconds; arteriovenous transit time: about 4 minutes). FFA three days after intra-arterial thrombolysis showed nearly complete restoration of retinal arterial perfusion (arm to retina time, 17 seconds; arteriovenous transit time, about 30 seconds) with the exception of the macular area (no reflow phenomenon). Six weeks after thrombolysis, her visual acuity remained hand motion and fundus photography showed severe retinal atrophy in the macula and disc pallor. Retinal perfusion was restored sparing macula on FFA and macular photoreceptor disruption was observed on optical coherence tomography.

case_report: A 29-year-old female was referred to our hospital for evaluation of cervical polyps. A hysteroscopy with fractional curettage revealed an endometrial carcinoma (grade II). The patient subsequently underwent a radical hysterectomy followed by postoperative brachytherapy in the vagina. Approximately 12 months later, during a routine clinical examination, a nodular goiter was identified, leading to a subtotal thyroidectomy. Due to intestinal complaints, a colonoscopy was performed, revealing small polyps in the sigmoid colon and rectum, from which a biopsy was taken. Histopathological investigations identified mucosal ganglioneuroma. Neurological examination showed significant dysdiadochokinesia on both sides and an ataxic uncertain gait pattern. Cerebral MRI scans revealed two infra-tentorial tumorous lesions on the left side. Due to tumor growth, a resection was performed, and histopathological examination of the excised tumor tissue showed meningioma WHO° I. Physical examination revealed macrocephaly, multiple facial papules, gingival trichilemmomas, and acral keratoses. The family history was unremarkable concerning related syndromes.
test_results: Human genetic test detected a novel germline G132F mutation in PTEN gene. This mutation occurs within exon 5, which encodes a portion of the phosphatase domain.

case_report: An 8-year-old, previously healthy, right-handed boy arrived at the emergency department with new onset horizontal binocular double vision in all directions of gaze, headache, unsteady movements, and reduced oral intake. Initially, there was no drooping of the eyelids or eyelid involvement. He had experienced vomiting and diarrhea starting ten days prior, lasting for one week, but these symptoms had resolved before his presentation. Before arriving at the hospital, he had increasing headache frequency and an episode where he fell from a couch, became stiff, and made incomprehensible sounds for 5–10 seconds. He had a six-month history of weekly frontal headaches lasting up to 30 minutes, which responded to ibuprofen and cold compresses. He did not experience aura with his headaches but did have sensitivity to light. There was no family history of migraine headaches or other neurological conditions. A review of systems showed no obvious weakness, sensory changes, speech difficulties, or swallowing issues. He had no systemic symptoms such as cough, rash, joint pains, or night sweats. An optometry exam six months prior was normal. He was not on any daily medication. On initial examination, he was alert and cooperative, afebrile with normal vital signs. His pupils were equal and reactive, visual fields were normal, and visual acuity was documented as normal. Examination of extraocular movements revealed slight left-sided inward turning of the eye. He had difficulty with the finger-to-nose test on both sides, was unsteady with poor balance, and unable to perform a tandem gait. The rest of the neurological and general examinations were unremarkable. Initial investigations, including complete blood count, electrolytes, and a CT brain scan, were normal. Over the next 24 hours, his condition evolved; he developed a severe throbbing headache affecting the whole head and had misaligned eye movements in all directions, followed by a decrease in level of consciousness. On upward gaze, downbeat vertical nystagmus was observed, and horizontal double vision was noted on bidirectional lateral eye movements. Deep tendon reflexes remained normal. Ophthalmological evaluation showed visual acuities of 20/50 in the right eye and 20/30 in the left eye, as well as convergence retraction nystagmus. Fundoscopy was normal. By 48 hours after admission, the patient had complete paralysis of eye movements.
test_results: Cerebrospinal fluid analysis (CSF) revealed 1 RBC, 0 WBC, glucose 3.0 mmol/L (normal range 2.2–3.9 mmol/L), and protein 0.14 mmol/L (normal range 0.15–0.45 g/L). CSF bacterial culture was negative. CSF viral PCR studies completed for herpes simplex virus, varicella zoster virus, enterovirus, and parechovirus were all negative. Acetylcholine receptor antibody testing was negative. A brain MRI completed 72 hours after presentation showed normal grey and white matter structures of cerebral hemispheres, as well as normal brainstem, cerebellar, and ventricular structures. An electroencephalogram (EEG) was normal for age. Nerve conduction studies (NCS) of the left upper extremity showed normal motor (ulnar nerve) and sensory (median nerve) function. No significant electrodecremental response was seen with repetitive slow frequency (2 Hz) stimulation of the left ulnar nerve during rest and after 1 minute of exercise. The patient was unable to tolerate further testing including more proximal NCS testing (e.g., face) or EMG testing. The GQ1b/GM1 antibody panel was sent and returned negative for antibodies. Campylobacter jejuni was isolated from the stool culture and further evidence of a resolving infection was confirmed with serologic markers (positive IgM and IgG).

case_report: A 54-year-old female presented to our respirology specialty clinic with a history of a small amount of blood-tinged sputum. She had experienced a chronic cough with small amounts of sputum for 10 months and had noticed intermittent blood-tinged sputum in the last few days. One week before her hospital visit, she had been seen at a local clinic and treated with antibiotics for 7 days based on simple radiographs, but her symptoms persisted. Approximately 20 years ago, she had been treated successfully for pulmonary tuberculosis and had no respiratory symptoms until 10 months ago. She had a history of spine surgery for back pain 14 years prior but no other diagnosed underlying diseases. She had no history of upper respiratory infections or pneumonias requiring antibiotics and had never been hospitalized. She had not undergone chest imaging before visiting the local clinic. The patient was a lifetime non-smoker, active, and healthy at baseline. She did not report chest pain, dyspnea, or any limitations in her activity level. On admission, her vital signs were stable, and her chest examination was clear to auscultation without wheezes, rhonchi, or rales. The rest of her physical examination was unremarkable. Spirometry revealed a forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) of 1.40 L (71% predicted), forced vital capacity (FVC) of 3.53 L (88% predicted), and an FEV1/FVC ratio of 69%. The flow-volume loop indicated mild obstruction, and lung volumes were not measured at that time.
test_results: A computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest showed multiple large air-filled cystic lesions in the right lower lobe, which measured 12.0×11.0×5.5 cm3 in aggregate and were primarily located in the right lower lobe. At its perimeter were many small, fluid-filled spaces, the largest of which measured 1.5×1.0×1.0 cm3, and there was some calcification. Moreover, an oval-shaped opacity in the distal right middle lobe bronchus was surrounded by a low attenuation in the right middle lobe and there was no clear connection between the lesion and the tracheobronchial tree. The other lung parenchyma was normal. On a flexible bronchoscopic examination, the opening of the right middle lobe bronchus was not seen and there was no endobronchial lesion.
diagnosis: Congenital Cystic Adenomatoid Malformation  with Bronchial Atresia

case_report: A 47-year-old male presented with abdominal pain persisting for 3 days. He had a history of acute appendicitis 10 years ago, for which he underwent an appendectomy. He had no history of hypertension or diabetes mellitus. The patient was an ex-smoker and a social drinker. It was noted that he consumed raw anchovies 4 days prior to the onset of symptoms. Upon admission, his vital signs were as follows: blood pressure 120/70 mm Hg, pulse rate 68/min, respiration rate 16/min, and body temperature 37℃. There were no signs of urticaria or facial angioedema. Abdominal examination revealed no splenomegaly or palpable mass, but there was epigastric and periumbilical tenderness without rebound tenderness. Digital rectal examination was unremarkable. Laboratory results showed a hemoglobin level of 14.2 g/dL, white blood cell count of 10,350/mm3 with 1.6% eosinophils, platelet count of 221,000/mm3, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 4 mm/hr. Blood chemistry results were as follows: total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 29 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase 35 IU/L, gamma glutamyl transpeptidase 68 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 138 IU/L, lactate dehydrogenase 351 IU/L, blood urea nitrogen 20.2 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, sodium 142 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, chloride 109 mmol/L, amylase 15 IU/L, lipase 32 IU/L, and C-reactive protein 0.34 mg/dL. Urinalysis results were normal.
test_results: The gastroscopic finding showed that there was a marked mucosal swelling and one thread like living worm (about 1.0 to 1.2 cm) was found penetrating the gastric mucosa in the lesser curvature of the lower body. It was withdrawn with biopsy forceps. The endoscopic ultrasonographic finding showed that there was diffuse mucosal and submucosal swelling without mass. The most affected layer was the submucosa. Its character was homogenous and relatively hypodense. The 5-layered wall structure was well preserved. The colonoscopic finding showed that there was round erythematous mucosal swelling and one thread like living structure (about 1.0 to 1.1 cm) was found penetrating the colonic mucosa in the transverse colon area. It was also withdrawn with biopsy forceps. The endoscopic ultrasonographic finding showed that there was diffuse submucosal swelling. Thickened submucosal layer showed generally homogenous echo and was not easily distinguishable from other layers.

case_report: M.A. is a 20-month-old male infant who presented with a pulsatile swelling in the anterior abdominal wall. He is the only child of a 29-year-old housewife and a 34-year-old primary school teacher in a non-consanguineous marriage. The parents occasionally consume alcohol but do not smoke. M.A. was born at term at a clinic near Yaounde with a birth weight of 3,000 grams. At birth, healthcare personnel observed a pulsatile mass on the anterior surface of the abdomen, covered with hyperpigmented skin. The mass was initially considered to be an umbilical hernia requiring no active intervention. A family friend recommended consulting our services. On physical examination, his anthropometric measurements were normal for his age (weight 12.5 kg, height 85 cm, head circumference 48 cm). A pear-shaped midline abdominal mass was noted, extending from the epigastric region to the umbilical region, measuring 20 cm in length and 12 cm in diameter, and covered by hyperpigmented skin. In the epigastric hollow, there was an oblong mass measuring 5 x 7 cm, extending into the thorax, firm to palpation, and pulsating at the rhythm of the patient’s radial pulse at a rate of 105 beats per minute. The rest of the mass had a soft consistency. On auscultation, bowel sounds were heard. Heart sounds were normal and heard over the precordium. Lung examination revealed no abnormalities. No dysmorphic features or other abnormalities were noted.
test_results: A chest X-ray has shown a slightly enlarged heart. An abdominal ultrasound revealed no intraabdominal organ abnormality. There was a herniation into the abdominal cavity through the diaphragm, containing a pulsatile mass representing a portion of the left ventricle. Echocardiography showed an alteration in the cardiac morphology. The left ventricle appeared thin and elongated, measuring 41.1 mm x 15.2 mm compared to the right ventricle, 44.6 mm x 24.3 mm. No other structural abnormality of the heart was noted and cardiac function was satisfactory.

case_report: A 38-year-old Japanese man presented with a worsening productive cough and dyspnea on exertion over the past week. His medical history included appendicitis, and he had no significant family medical history. The patient frequently engaged in house-painting and had a 20-year history of smoking one pack of cigarettes per day. On examination, his temperature was 37.6°C, blood pressure was 176/114 mmHg, pulse rate was 95/min, respiratory rate was 20/min, and SpO2 was 88% on room air. Physical examination revealed inspiratory crackles in both lung fields and clubbing of the toes. Laboratory tests showed elevated levels of aspartate aminotransferase (80 IU/L), alanine aminotransferase (52 IU/L), and lactate dehydrogenase (497 IU/L). KL-6 was significantly elevated at 27959 U/ml (normal range: <500 U/ml). Arterial blood gas analysis, with 4 L/min O2 via nasal cannula, indicated a pH of 7.52, PCO2 of 27 mmHg, and PO2 of 82 mmHg. Imaging studies, including chest X-ray and chest CT, revealed diffuse ground-glass opacity bilaterally, with a crazy-paving pattern observed on the CT scan.
test_results: Bronchoscopy yielded bronchial alveolar lavage fluid that was muddy white in appearance, containing periodic acid Schiff-positive material in cytology. Transbronchial lung biopsy showed intra-alveolar eosinophilic mucin accompanying mild interstitial inflammation. Serum granulocyte macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) autoantibodies titer was elevated to 20.9 μg/ml (normal range: <1.0 μg/ml).

case_report: A 52-year-old woman reported a progressive decline in vision in both eyes over the past two to three years. There is no family history of eye diseases, including her deceased parents. Her best-corrected visual acuities were 20/63 in the right eye and 20/50 in the left eye. Fundus examination, fluorescein angiography, and full-field electroretinography results were normal. Visual fields were complete as assessed by Goldman perimetry.
test_results: A relative central scotoma was detected in both eyes.

case_report: A 74-year-old woman presented with right ankle pain, swelling, and difficulty walking for the past month. She reported no fever, weight loss, or night sweats. Her medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Ankle plain radiography showed an osteolytic lesion. Physical examination revealed good performance status and minor swelling of the right ankle, with no other significant findings. Blood tests showed normal hemogram, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (61 mm/h), and elevated C-reactive protein (7.45 mg/dL, reference range <0-5 mg/dL). Serum calcium was elevated at 13.2 mg/dL (reference range 8.5-10.5 mg/dL), and lactate dehydrogenase was elevated at 683 U/L (reference range 230-460 U/L). Plain radiography of the right ankle indicated disruption of the fibula’s structure, consistent with an osteolytic lesion. MRI revealed complete distortion of the distal fibular metaphysis architecture by pathological tissue infiltrating the bone cortex and marrow, extending to surrounding soft tissue. Additional imaging showed multiple lesions in the lower half of the right tibia, fibula, talus, and metatarsal bones. Bone marrow biopsy and neck, chest, and abdominal CT scans were free of disease. Whole-body PET/CT scan revealed pathological uptake of 18-FDG throughout the skeleton, especially in cranial and long bones, with many lesions accompanied by soft tissue masses, particularly in the lower extremities and maxilla (SUV max: 15). Increased 18-FDG uptake was also observed in the nasal and zygomatic bones bilaterally (SUV max: 20), as well as in the cervical, iliac, and inguinal lymph nodes (SUV max: 5.5) and regionally in bone marrow. The patient underwent a biopsy of the fibula.
test_results: The histopathological examination showed diffuse infiltration of large-sized cells. Neoplastic cells expressed the B-cell associated antigens CD20, CD79a, PAX5, BCL-6, MUM-1, BCL-2 (80%), SIg/CIgM(k) and C-MYC (> 40%). The expression of CD3, CD4, CD8, CD5, CD23, CD30, CD10, CyclinD1 was negative. Additionally, in situ, hybridization for EBER was negative. The proliferation fraction, as detected by Ki-67 (MIB-1 antigen), was 90%. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) tests did not reveal rearrangement for C-MYC and BCL2 genes.
diagnosis: multifocal double expressor primary non-Hodgkin lymphoma of the bone , stage IVEA

case_report: The patient is a 12-year-old male, the youngest child of first-cousin parents, who presented with developmental delay, speech delay, ataxia, and bilateral cataracts. He was born at term via normal vaginal delivery after an uncomplicated pregnancy, with a birth weight of 3.5 kg. There were no postnatal complications. At 12 years old, his weight was 33 kg (10th to 25th percentile), height was 147 cm (25th percentile), and head circumference was 53 cm (50th to 75th percentile). The parents described him as active and cooperative. Physical examination revealed subtle dysmorphic features, including bushy eyebrows, a flat midface, and a high arched palate. He exhibited an ataxic gait, dysmetria, intention tremor, and dysdiadochokinesia. A convergent squint was noted in the left eye. Muscle tone was normal, and deep tendon reflexes were present. Pectus carinatum was observed, along with bilateral clinodactyly of the fifth fingers and flat feet. A skeletal survey was normal except for mild kyphosis in the lower thoracic spine. He could stand with support and walked with support, displaying an ataxic gait. A developmental assessment at 8 years old indicated he could form full sentences, though with poor articulation, and required assistance with dressing and feeding. At 6 years old, a pelvic ultrasound identified a left undescended testis, which was corrected via orchidopexy. He had also been diagnosed with infantile bilateral cataracts, which were surgically corrected. Brain imaging, including X-ray computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging, showed cerebellar atrophy with a dilated 4th ventricle. All other investigations were normal, and the family history was unremarkable. The patient's four living siblings were healthy, and the mother had experienced one spontaneous abortion.
test_results: The sequencing of SIL1 revealed a homozygous deletion from the 5′ untranslated region (UTR; c.-197) to exon 1 (c.90). Instead of the deleted bases, there was a homozygous insertion of one base (C) of unclear origin and 20 bases from intron 1. Both parents turned out to be heterozygous carriers of the same c.-197_90delinsCTGTACTTTCTCAGTTCACT mutation.

case_report: A 59-year-old male was brought to the emergency area after experiencing right-sided paralysis and subsequently falling into a coma. The patient's medical history was notable only for significant smoking. A brain CT scan identified a blockage in the basilar artery. The patient underwent a thrombolysis procedure followed by an embolectomy, but there was no significant clinical improvement. He was then admitted to the intensive care unit in a severe coma. Neurological examination revealed complete paralysis of all four limbs, inability to speak, spontaneous eye opening, and loss of bladder and bowel control.
test_results: A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan with T1- and T2-weighted, fluid-attenuated inversion recovery, and diffusion-weighted imaging sequences revealed ischemic lesions with perilesional subacute edema at the level of the pons, midbrain, cerebellar hemispheres, vermis, and the left occipital lobe without sign of hemorrhage. The electroencephalography (EEG) findings were within the normal range, and somatosensory evoked potentials showed the conservation of cortical components. The PET scan and SPM analysis demonstrated a significant reduction of glucose metabolism in both cerebellar hemispheres in comparison with controls. No FDG uptake abnormalities were found in basal ganglia, cingulate structures, cortical, subcortical, or infratentorial regions.

case_report: A 6-year-old girl was admitted to the Child Neuropsychiatric Unit of the University Hospital of Bari following a tonic–clonic seizure that occurred shortly after waking up. The episode involved loss of consciousness, upward eye rolling, wheezing sounds, spasms in the trunk and limbs, and urinary incontinence, all of which subsided after three to five minutes. A similar seizure had occurred approximately six months prior. She is the third child of consanguineous parents who are first cousins. Her medical history showed no issues during pregnancy, labor, or in her motor and linguistic development. She is in the first grade of primary school and has difficulties with reading and writing. During a neurological examination using Touwen’s procedures, head examination revealed swinging movements while walking and running, and slight hyperextension when focusing on objects placed in front of her, which her parents noticed early in her life. Examination of the extrinsic ocular muscles showed absent horizontal eye movements with preserved vertical gaze. Assessment of standing and walking revealed difficulty maintaining an upright position, jumping on one limb on both sides, a clumsy gait, and exaggerated synkinetic arm movements. Vestibular tests (Romberg, tandem, and star-shaped gait) and cerebellar tests (index–nose test with open and closed eyes) were not performed correctly. No other neurological deficits were observed. Blood tests, including blood count, electrolytes, creatinine, urea, glucose, bilirubin, liver enzymes, albumin, cholesterol, triglycerides, lactate dehydrogenase, creatine phosphokinase, fibrinogen, thyrotropin, free thyroxin, free triiodothyronine, and C reactive protein, were within normal ranges. An interictal electroencephalogram (EEG) showed slow and sharp waves in the parietal, temporal, and occipital regions, more pronounced on the right side during both sleep and wakefulness, with occasional diffusion. Treatment with Valproic Acid (15 mg/Kg/day) was initiated.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated hypoplasia of the brainstem, a left thalamus volume larger than the right, an enlarged fourth ventricle, an anterior and posterior midline bulbar and pontine cleft (split-pons sign), a butterfly configuration of the medulla, an occipital and parietal plagiocephaly on the right side, and a slight benign enlargement of the subarachnoid spaces in the frontotemporal area. There were no signal changes within the medulla or pons in any of the brain MRI sequences. The genetic investigation confirmed the presence of a homozygous ROBO3 variant (c.3584_3588dup, p.Ile1197TrpfsTer44), which causes a shift in the reading window and a premature termination of the protein.
diagnosis: Horizontal Gaze Palsy with Progressive Scoliosis  syndrome
Orpha_name: Horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis

case_report: A 53-year-old female with a history of arterial hypertension presented with bilateral vision blurring for 5 days. She had no prior ocular complaints or neurological or auditory symptoms. Best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/32 in the right eye (RE) and 20/100 in the left eye (LE). Slit-lamp examination showed no anterior chamber inflammation in the RE, but noted few keratic precipitates, +1 cells in the anterior chamber, and localized posterior synechiae in the LE. Ocular pressure was 14 mmHg in both eyes. There were +1 vitreous cells in both eyes and 2+ vitreous haze in the LE. Fundus examination revealed optic disc hyperemia and a shallow ERD in the posterior pole in the RE and diffuse depigmentation producing a sunset-glow appearance with some pigmentary changes in the LE. Medical history excluded ocular trauma or surgery.
test_results: Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) showed ERD with a few subretinal septa and undulations of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in the RE. Findings were unremarkable in the LE. Fluorescein angiography findings included multifocal delayed choroidal perfusion, multiple areas of pinpoint leakage, and optic disc hyperfluorescence in the RE and areas of RPE changes that were more prominent around the optic disc in the LE. Indocyanine green angiography revealed hypofluorescent dark dots in intermediate and late phases in the RE and showed no obvious abnormalities in the LE. B-scan ultrasonography showed diffuse medium-reflective choroidal thickening predominating around the optic nerve head in the RE and a normal choroidal thickness in the LE.

case_report: A 55-year-old woman with a medical history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia was transferred to the emergency room with an 11-day history of a pruritic, painful, blistering rash on the trunk, face, and extremities, without mucosal involvement. She had received naltrexone for alcohol use disorder 3 days before the rash appeared. The patient reported no other new medications, over-the-counter drugs, illicit substances, or supplements. Eleven days prior, she was admitted to another facility for fever and a perioral rash and was treated with antibiotics and steroids for one week before discharge. Two days after discharge, she presented to a second facility with a new vesiculobullous eruption and rash progression to her trunk and extremities, leading to her transfer to our facility. On examination, she was afebrile and tachycardic, with diffuse erythema, bullae, pustules, intermittent dependent pus lakes, hyperpigmented scaly plaques on the face extending to the scalp, several erythematous papules coalescing into semiannular plaques, and pronounced desquamation on the extremities. The patient had a negative Nikolsky sign, negative Asboe-Hansen sign, no palmoplantar involvement, and no oral, genital, or ocular mucosal involvement. The total body surface area involved was 40%, with 6% open. Laboratory findings included leukocytosis with a total leukocyte count of 26.78 × 10^3/mcL, neutrophilia with a total neutrophil count of 24.14 × 10^3/mcL, eosinophilia with a total eosinophil count of 0.89 × 10^3/mcL, and a negative antinuclear antibody titer.
test_results: A 4-mm punch biopsy revealed neutrophilic dermatitis with subcorneal pustules and a superficial and mid-dermal perivascular and interstitial infiltrate composed of lymphocytes, eosinophils, and scattered neutrophils. There was no evidence of epidermal necrosis or fungal elements and direct immunofluorescence was negative.

case_report: J.W., a 33-year-old male IT analyst with a history of ulcerative colitis treated with pentase and predfoam enema, was referred to the emergency department by his general practitioner due to a 1-week history of an erythematous wound on his right lateral leg that did not improve with oral flucloxacillin. Upon hospital review, a localized abscess was identified, and inflammatory markers showed a White cell count (WCC) of 13.4 and C-reactive protein (CRP) of 179.
