The patient was admitted by the orthopedic team and administered intravenous antibiotics, including benzylpenicillin, flucloxacillin, and metronidazole. Four days later, he underwent an incision and drainage procedure, which revealed blood-stained pus. Two days post-procedure, the WCC increased to 20.3 and CRP to 283. A further debridement of a 25 × 15-cm area was performed, revealing a bubbly appearance of the margins, extensive erythema, necrosis of the skin distal to the wound, discharge, and fat necrosis.
test_results: Histology confirmed inflammation with necrosis of the tissues. Histology confirmed an ulcer and abscess with acute inflammation and fibrosis and granulation tissue which extends to the margins with no vasculitis or neoplasia.

case_report: A 70-year-old male arrived at the Emergency Department with jaundice that had been present for the past month. His medical history includes colon polyps, a right hemicolectomy performed two years ago for an adenoma with low-grade dysplasia in the caecum, cholecystectomy, inguinal hernia repair, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. Upon presentation, his vital signs were within normal limits. The abdominal examination indicated reduced bowel movements. Blood biochemistry tests at admission revealed a total bilirubin concentration of 14 mg/dL (normal range 0.1–1.2) and elevated liver enzymes: aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 51 IU/L (normal range 0–32), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) at 78 IU/L (normal range 0–32), γ-glutamyltranspeptidase at 628 IU/L (normal range 10–60), and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) at 457 U/L (normal range 40–129). Chest and abdominal radiography showed no abnormalities. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a dilated biliary tree.
test_results: An esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) revealed a sizable ulcerative polypoid tumor in the ampulla of Vater. An abdominal contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan (CECT) showed cholangiectasis, a dilatated common bile duct (1.4 cm), a dilated major and accessory pancreatic duct, and an indistinct and thickened duodenum wall between the ampulla of Vater and the heterogeneous appearing head of the pancreas. Enlarged lymph nodes with necrosis were found in porta hepatis (1.9 cm) and behind the third part of the duodenum (1.3 cm). A PET scan showed a hyperactive lesion in the ampulla with a high standardized uptake value (SUV max 10.6). Macroscopic examination revealed a tumor measuring 3.1 × 1.9 cm located at the ampulla of Vater. A total of nine lymph nodes were dissected. Microscopic examination showed large, mostly uniform, oval tumor cells with irregular nuclei, finely granular chromatin, and indistinct nucleoli. The neoplastic cells showed little pleomorphism. They were composed of organoid nests or trabeculi, separated by thin fibrovascularseptae. In a few nests, tumor cells showed peripheral palisading, often with a minor component of pseudoglandular formation. The majority of those formations contained small foci of necrosis. The surface of the neoplasm was ulcerative. The neoplastic cells were infiltrating the pancreatic parenchyma. Two out of the nine dissected lymph nodes were occupied by the neoplasm. Surgical margins were clear of tumor cells. The neoplasm was characterized by the expression of synaptophysin, CD56, CK8/18, and EMA. With the marker of cell proliferation Ki67/MIB1, the percentage of positive nuclei was up to 45%.
diagnosis: Large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the ampulla of Vater
Orpha_name: Carcinoma of the ampulla of Vater

case_report: A 51-year-old female patient was admitted to the Clinic of Nephrology and Clinical Immunology. Five months earlier, she was hospitalized for type 2 acute respiratory insufficiency and elevated D-dimer levels (9730 ng/ml). A thoracic CT scan with and without contrast revealed pleural effusions on both sides (12 mm on the right, 5 mm on the left) and three ulcers on the aortic arch (up to 5 mm in diameter). During her hospital stay, she experienced sudden intense chest pain and developed heart failure progressing to cardiogenic shock. Electrocardiography indicated ST-elevated myocardial infarction (STEMI) of the anterior wall, with elevated cardiospecific enzymes (high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTnI) 20,000 ng/ml, creatin kinase MB (CK-MB) 259 IU/L). She was transferred to a reference health facility. Risk factors included arterial hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and smoking. Coronary angiography showed narrowing of the ostial segment of the left anterior descending artery (LAD). Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stent (DES) implantation in the LAD was performed. Echocardiography confirmed ischemic cardiomyopathy with an ejection fraction (EF) of 38%. The patient later experienced back pain, altered consciousness, hemodynamic instability, and differences in arterial blood pressure in the upper extremities. CT angiography revealed occlusion of the left common carotid artery (ACC), subclavian and axillary arteries, and a penetrating aortic ulcer localized infrarenal. The patient also exhibited left-sided body weakness. A head CT scan showed an acute ischemic lesion (13 mm in diameter) high parietal on the right and a chronic ischemic lesion (9 mm in diameter) on the front right. A neurologist recommended continuing dual antiplatelet therapy and proposed further imaging and immunological testing.
test_results: Doppler ultrasonography of carotid and vertebral arteries registered left occlusion, right ACC/external carotid artery (ACE) stenosis with suspected 'macaroni sign', as well as suspected left vertebral artery (AV) occlusion. MRI with MRA showed chronic (micro) ischemic frontoparietal lesions on the right, and to a lesser extent on the left; on the absence of flow in the extracranial segment of the left AV as well as multiple stenoses on the longer segment of the left internal carotid artery (ACI) as well as a stenosis by about 60-70% of the right ACI on the retreat. CT angiography of the head and neck was also performed, the following was observed: occlusion of the left ACC along its entire length, stenosis of the right and left ACI, occlusion of the left a. subclaviae, as well as moderate narrowing of the truncus brachiocephalicus and right a. subclaviae. Laboratory tests verified elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 56mm/h and a C-reactive protein (CRP) of 54 mg/L.

case_report: A 68-year-old man was referred to Kindai University in 2004 with bilateral uveitis of unknown cause. The right eye had lost vision following penetrating keratoplasty performed in 2007, with suspected Candida keratitis. The left eye exhibited mild anterior chamber inflammation, keratic precipitates, and small corneal edema, leading to refractory secondary glaucoma and bullous keratopathy, which necessitated DSAEK in 2011. Clinical findings during these periods included unilateral high intraocular pressure and corneal edema with keratic precipitates. Detection of CMV DNA in the aqueous humor after DSAEK was noted. Corneal grafting failed despite administration of 0.5% ganciclovir eye drops six times daily and 0.1% fluorometholone eye drops four times daily for over a year. After a second DSAEK in 2013, 1.0% voriconazole, 0.5% ganciclovir, and 0.1% betamethasone phosphate eye drops were administered four times daily for two years. In 2015, the patient presented with small crystalline opacities in the center of the cornea, which progressed slowly and multiplied by 2017. The patient reported visual disturbance without eye pain or foreign body sensation when the corneal opacity covered the visual axis. Gram staining of the scraped cornea revealed an unstained small oval microorganism visible by Fungiflora Y staining. Given the past episode of vision loss in the other eye due to suspected Candida keratitis, two doses of voriconazole were administered by intrastromal injection. As the treatment was ineffective, penetrating keratoplasty was performed.
test_results: A polar tube with multiple loose coils was detected in the spore-like elements of the microorganisms by TEM.

case_report: A six-year-old female child, born to consanguineous parents, presented to the dermatology outpatient clinic with beaded deposits on the eyelid margins for the past year and hoarseness of voice. According to her mother, the child had multiple discrete vesicles on the elbows and upper arms during early infancy, which lasted for 1–2 days and healed with scars. These vesicles stopped appearing after 1–2 years. The mother also noted hoarseness of voice since early infancy. The child was otherwise healthy and active, with no history of convulsions or other neurological symptoms. An older sibling did not have similar complaints. On physical examination, multiple waxy white beaded lesions were observed on both eyelid margins, and multiple pock-like scars of varying sizes were noted on the elbows, upper arms, and lower back, with no fresh vesicles. Oral cavity examination showed a tongue with almost normal consistency and appearance, a thickened frenulum with yellow-white infiltration, and multiple beaded lesions on the mucosal side of the lower lip. Indirect laryngoscopy revealed a few small beaded deposits on the epiglottis and vocal cords.
test_results: Biopsy from oral mucosa revealed deposits of periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)-positive hyaline material around capillaries and adnexal structures.

case_report: An 11-year-old boy was referred to the corneal clinic for evaluation of astigmatism and possible amblyopia in the right eye. The patient had no history of ocular trauma, including forceps delivery. The boy had been using corrective spectacles and undergoing occlusion and atropine therapy in his left eye for the past 2 years. Despite this, vision in his right eye did not improve after the 2 years of therapy. At the time of presentation, uncorrected visual acuity (UCVA) was 0.2 in the right eye and 1.2 in the left eye, while best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 0.7 in the right eye and 1.2 in the left eye. Refractive error was measured at +3.25–5.50 × 15 in the right eye and +1.25–0.75 × 5 in the left eye.
test_results: Slit-lamp examination revealed a snail-track lesion at the level of Descemet's membrane along the superotemporal cornea in the right eye. Noncontact specular microscopy revealed an endothelial cell density of 1,730 and 2,570 cells/mm2 in the right and left eyes, respectively. Central corneal thickness was measured using noncontact corneal pachymetry and was 572 µm in the right eye and 534 µm in the left eye. Corneal topography of the right eye revealed an asymmetric bow tie WTR astigmatism with superior steepening (steep K = 50.98 D × 95, flat K = 43.72 D × 5). The left eye had a mild WTR astigmatism (steep K = 46.30 D × 93, flat K = 44.76 D × 3).

case_report: The patient, a 16-year-old male, initially sought medical attention at the age of 12 due to an incidental finding of elevated creatine-kinase levels (8413 IU/L), which was confirmed upon further testing. He was born to non-consanguineous parents following a normal pregnancy and delivery, and his psychomotor development was typical. The patient was actively involved in competitive soccer and reported no symptoms other than cramps following intense physical activity. He did not experience weakness, fatigue, muscle pain, or dark urine. At 12 years old, a neurological examination revealed normal results except for mild sural pseudohypertrophy. A cardiological evaluation showed no abnormalities. At 13 years old, a muscle MRI indicated mild T2 hyperintensity in the right triceps surae.
test_results: A muscle biopsy, performed on the brachial biceps at 13 years of age, showed mild myopathic signs (few hypotrophic fibers and two necrotic fibers). The IHC study was normal, except for staining with antibodies against alpha- and gamma-sarcoglycan, which revealed a severe reduction in reactivity in many fibers. A severe (>70%), but not total, reduction in alpha-, beta-, gamma-, and delta-sarcoglycans was also confirmed by Western blot analysis with residual protein levels of 25%, 29%, 27%, and 29%, respectively, compared to control biopsies.

case_report: The patient, a 3-year-old male, was admitted to the Tomsk Genetic Clinic. Clinical examination revealed short stature, high forehead, tower head, downslanted palpebral fissures, narrow nose, micrognathia, bilateral microtia, short neck, short limbs, narrow chest, micromelia, brachydactyly, and muscular hypotonia. Developmental milestones and intellect were normal. Echocardiography showed no heart defects. Chest radiography indicated short horizontal ribs. Brain MRI revealed moderate internal hydrocephalus and enlargement of subarachnoid spaces in the frontal lobes. The patient received gastrostomy feeding for nutritional support. He was born from the second pregnancy at 34 weeks of gestation via caesarean section, with a birth weight of 1.6 kg and length of 41 cm. Prenatal ultrasonography at 20 weeks showed ventricular enlargement and intrauterine growth retardation. Postnatal complications included feeding problems, respiratory distress syndrome, and neonatal pneumonia. The patient is of Slavic descent. Family history includes Turner syndrome in a paternal cousin, bronchial asthma, and arterial hypertension in maternal relatives. The parents are nonconsanguineous. The first pregnancy ended in a miscarriage at 25 weeks of gestation, with prenatal ultrasonography at 19 weeks indicating shortened fetal long bones. The third pregnancy also ended in a miscarriage at 12 weeks of gestation.
test_results: The patient is a compound heterozygote for two mutations in the ORC6 gene: a c.2T>C transition within the initial methionine of the transcription start site (p.Met1Thr) and a splice site mutation (c.449+5G>A). The presence of these variants and inheritance from parents were confirmed. Mutations c.2T>C (p.Met1Thr) and c.449+5G>A were inherited from the father and mother, respectively.

case_report: A 3-year-old boy was admitted to our clinic after experiencing episodes of sudden loss of consciousness for over a year. During these episodes, he exhibited a global lack of muscle tone, cyanotic lips, and spontaneous recovery within 2-3 minutes. Since the onset of these episodes, he showed poor mental function, frequent crying, ingestion of a semiliquid diet, reduced appetite, and disturbed sleep. Convulsions persisted despite treatment with sodium valproate 9 mL twice daily (ineffective) and topiramate 75 mg twice daily (effective but poorly controlled). Oxazepine was added on January 5, 2021, resulting in no seizures but a rash appeared 4 weeks later, along with increased sleep. Oxazepine was discontinued on February 25, 2021, and the rash resolved. Perampanel, two tablets once daily, was added on February 26, 2021. However, the patient continued to experience episodes characterized by sudden rapid head drops, sometimes accompanied by lip smacking, slow shaking of both upper extremities, and sudden freezing. These episodes often occurred after excitement and subsided after 1 minute. At the time of admission, the patient was receiving sodium valproate 12 mL twice daily, topiramate 25 mg twice daily, and perampanel 8 mg once daily. The patient had no abnormal birth history. He had a history of delayed growth milestones, such as slow rolling over and inability to sit unassisted at 9 months, and had been diagnosed with developmental delay. At the time of admission, he could not sit unassisted, recognize people, speak, and exhibited unconscious pronunciation. The patient's parents were healthy, non-blood relatives. He was the only child in his family, and neither parent had other offspring. There was no obvious family history of developmental delay or seizures. Physical examination findings included a temperature of 37.3 °C, pulse of 102 beats/min, respiration of 24 breaths/min, and weight of 17.7 kg. The patient exhibited a clear mind, poor spirit, frequent crying, limited development, moderate nutrition, pharyngeal congestion, coarse breath sounds in both lungs, and slightly elevated muscle tension. Laboratory findings were within normal limits.
test_results: Complex heterozygous mutations were found in the patient’s ADSL gene: The splicing mutation c.154-3C>G (present in his father) and the missense mutation c.71C>T (p. Pro24Leu) (present in his mother). The missense mutation c.71C>T causes an amino acid change from proline to leucine (p. Pro24Leu). The splicing mutation c.154-3C>G was predicted to be pathogenic. Magnetic resonance imaging in July 2020 showed bilateral external frontal temporal space widening and abnormal signals around the posterior horns of both lateral ventricles, suggestive of myelin hypoplasia; follow-up examination showed similar findings. Electroencephalography performed in July 2020 revealed an abnormal electroencephalogram with slightly more medium-high amplitude in the left and right frontal regions, a few full-conduction irregular medium-high amplitude spikes, sharp slow waves, and a slow background rhythm. In July 2021, video electroencephalography revealed highly rhythmical patterns during most of the waking period and the entire sleep period. The patient exhibited multifocal slow waves, spiky slow waves, and polyspinous slow waves, with left and right asymmetry, asynchronous anterior and posterior findings, pronounced anterior activity, and an obvious sleep period.

case_report: A 7-month-old white boy presented with small, discrete, asymptomatic, yellow-red papules initially noticed on his face at 1 month of age. The papules gradually increased in number and spread to his upper trunk and upper arms over the following weeks. The child was otherwise healthy and developmentally normal, with both weight and height at the 50th percentile. His parents were not consanguineous, and the family history was unremarkable. Clinical examination revealed multiple, scattered yellow-red monomorphic papules measuring 2 to 5 mm on the face, upper trunk, and upper limbs. Mucous membranes, palms, soles, and teeth were normal. There was no organomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Neurodevelopmental and ophthalmic examinations were normal. Routine blood tests showed normal hematologic and biochemical results. Serum lipid screening (cholesterol, triglycerides, HDL, and LDL cholesterol), IgA, IgG, IgM, serum protein electrophoresis, and syphilis serology were all normal or negative. X-ray screening of the skeletal system showed no bony defects. An upper abdominal ultrasonography was normal.
test_results: Histological examination of the biopsy specimen taken from a lesion on the left shoulder showed a normal epidermis and sufficient proliferation of large, pleomorphic epitheliod histiocytic cells with large cytoplasm within the upper- and mid-dermis without epidermotropism. Mitotic figures, multinucleated giant cells and cytoplasmic lipids were absent. There was an interstitial infiltration of moderate numbers of lymphocytes and scattered eosinophils. In the immunohistochemistry analysis, the cells were stained positive for CD68, but negative for the S100 protein and CD1a.

case_report: A 3-month-old girl was observed to have whitish pupils from birth. Examination identified nuclear cataracts and aniridia in both eyes. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was measured at 12.2 mmHg in the right eye and 14.6 mmHg in the left eye using a Tono-Pen. Axial length (AL) was 15.83 mm in the right eye and 13.98 mm in the left eye, consistent with nanophthalmos. The patient underwent a right kidney resection due to a Wilms tumor, followed by cataract extraction surgery. One month post-cataract surgery, increased IOP was noted in both eyes (right eye, 21.6 mmHg; left eye, 25.8 mmHg). IOP-lowering medication was prescribed, but the parents did not administer the medication as directed and missed follow-up appointments. Six months later, the girl exhibited an enlarged cup-to-disc (C/D) ratio of 0.5. Secondary glaucoma was identified.
test_results: A CNV analysis based on WES found a Chr11:30431595–36680772 deletion.

case_report: A 4-year-old girl was admitted with a chief complaint of 'intermittent head drop' for 5 months. The primary clinical presentations included sudden downward head movements occurring one to three times daily, often after waking up. Two weeks prior to admission, the frequency increased to 5–6 times daily. The patient had a history of convulsions at 1 year and seven months, characterized by sudden loss of consciousness, unresponsiveness, upward eye movement, limb collapse, and no cyanosis, lasting approximately 10 minutes without fever. She is the second child of a non-consanguineous marriage with a normal birth history and normal physical and neurological development. At birth, her head circumference was 33 cm (15th percentile), height was 51 cm (50th percentile), and weight was 3.025 kg (50th percentile). At 5 years old, her head circumference is 49 cm (15th percentile), height is 112 cm (50th percentile), and weight is 20.5 kg (75th percentile). Neurological examination upon admission revealed clear consciousness, fluent responses, reactive pupils to light, no nystagmus, centered tongue without tremor, normal limb muscle tone, muscle strength grade 5, normal motor coordination, negative neck strength, and negative Babinski sign. Tests for imbalance, including finger–nose, rotational exercise, heel–knee–tibial, and Romberg, were normal. No abnormal neurological signs were observed. Biochemical examination showed no significant abnormalities. Brain MRI+DWI revealed abnormal signals in the bilateral paraventricular and bilateral subfrontal cortex regions. A seven-hour video-encephalography (VEEG) showed a slow background, numerous abnormal epileptiform discharges during awake and sleep stages, increased slow waves, and two monitored atonic seizures, which manifested as head drop movements. The patient was treated with 5 ml of sodium valproate orally twice daily. After 3 days, she experienced no further seizures and was discharged.
test_results: Genetic testing results showed that GFAP gene exon 1 c.262 C>T, and that the pathogenic mutations could lead to the 88th amino acid change from arginine to cysteine. The patients presented a heterozygous mutation; both parents were of the wild-type.

case_report: Patient 2, a previously healthy male, experienced swelling and pain in both wrists, along with restricted movement at 11 years and 9 months old. One month later, he was admitted to the hospital. Physical examination showed his height was 155 cm (50–75th percentile) and his weight was 35 kg (10–25th percentile). No facial abnormalities were noted, and examinations of the heart, lungs, abdomen, and neurological system were normal. Swelling and tenderness were observed in the wrist joints, particularly the left wrist, and dorsiflexion of the 4th metacarpophalangeal joints of both hands was limited. Wrist radiography indicated abnormal morphology of the carpal bones on both sides, especially the proximal carpal bones, with more severe joint destruction in the right wrist compared to the left. Laboratory tests, including ESR, CRP level, RF, anti-citrullinated protein antibody levels, HLA-B27 status, urine tests, and renal function, were normal. Bone mineral density tests indicated a reduction in bone mass. The patient was treated with naproxen, MTX, and calcium, but there was no improvement in symptoms. Subsequently, he received a 3-month course of the TNFα receptor inhibitor adalimumab at 11 years and 11 months old, which also did not alleviate symptoms. He then received two doses of the TNFα receptor inhibitor infliximab, which relieved pain and swelling in the wrists, but the range of motion (both active and passive) in the wrist joints worsened.
test_results: The gene test results revealed a de novo heterozygous mutation, NM_005461:c.161C > T (NP_005452.2: p. S54L), in MAFB. This mutation was in the highly conserved transactivation domain, which is reported to be pathogenic.
Orpha_name: Multicentric carpo-tarsal osteolysis with or without nephropathy

case_report: A 13-day-old female infant, born to parents who are related by blood, exhibited grayish discoloration of scalp and eyebrow hair since birth. The child had a history of ear discharge from the left ear for 2 days. There were no reports of fever, cough, cold, or loose stools. Birth history was normal. Physical examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory tests indicated pancytopenia. The peripheral blood smear appeared normal. Examination of the hair shaft under light microscopy did not yield conclusive results. Polarized microscopy revealed a bright hair shaft with a uniform white appearance. Bone marrow examination showed slightly hypocellular marrow without intracytoplasmic inclusions.
test_results: Genetic analysis revealed mutation in RAB27A gene.

case_report: A 12-year-old, previously healthy, Southeast Asian female arrived at the emergency room with a 2-day history of increased menstrual bleeding, mild abdominal pain, and a petechial rash. Two days before her visit, she experienced vomiting, loose stools, and a subjective fever, which had resolved by the time she reached the hospital. Her vital signs included a temperature of 38°C, blood pressure of 117/69, and a normal heart rate. Physical examination revealed petechial lesions on her face and trunk, no peripheral edema, and a normal neurologic exam. Initial laboratory results indicated severe thrombocytopenia with platelet count at 11,000/µL, hemoglobin at 11.1 g/dL, a positive direct Coombs test, and normal red blood cell morphology on peripheral blood smear. Urinalysis showed 3+ blood, 3+ protein, more than 100 red blood cells per high power field (hpf), more than 100 white blood cells per hpf, and hyaline casts. Serum creatinine was elevated at 3.6 mg/dL. Serum C3 and C4 levels were both below the detectable range (C3 < 26.3 mg/dL, C4 < 7.9 mg/dL). She had a positive antinuclear antibody with a titer of 1:640 and a positive anti-double stranded DNA antibody. Testing for antiphospholipid antibodies was negative. The patient received initial treatment with 500 mg/m2 intravenous cyclophosphamide and daily 1 g methylprednisolone infusions. Over the next 2 days, her platelet count dropped to 9,000/µL, hemoglobin decreased to a low of 6.2 g/dL, and serum creatinine increased to 5.7 mg/dL. Hemodialysis was initiated.
test_results: Her peripheral blood smear revealed new appearance of moderate schistocytes. The patient’s ADAMTS13 activity was found to be <5%, revealing severe deficiency. ADAMTS13 functional inhibitor was not detected, but ADAMTS13 antibody was detected by ELISA assay (55; reference interval <18).

case_report: A 43-year-old male presented to the Makerere University Lung Institute in Kampala after being referred from a rural tertiary hospital in Uganda. He reported a 30-year history of a productive cough that began following an episode of cough during a nationwide outbreak of whooping cough at 10 years of age. The cough had worsened over the past year, was wet, and associated with large amounts of purulent sputum, difficulty breathing, chest pain, and weight loss over the past 3 months. The chest pain was mainly left-sided and non-radiating. There was no history of hemoptysis, nasal blockage, loss of sense of smell, fever, or night sweats. The patient reported no history of loud snoring, gasping for air during sleep, or somnolence. However, he experienced palpitations, dyspnea, orthopnea, and swelling in the lower limbs and abdomen. He had multiple admissions due to worsening cough and had almost monthly unscheduled outpatient visits for the cough over the past 30 years. He had been treated with intravenous and oral medications with minimal to no improvement. At 19 years of age, he was treated for clinically diagnosed pulmonary TB (without bacteriological confirmation), but there was no improvement. He had no known allergies and denied any history of cigarette smoking and alcohol use. There was no family history of similar illness. He was a farmer until 3 years prior to presentation when his symptoms limited his physical activity. On physical examination, he appeared sickly and severely wasted (37 kg body weight, height 160.5 cm, BMI 14.4 kg/m²). He had proptosis, grade 3 digital clubbing, central and peripheral cyanosis, and pretibial edema. He was afebrile (temperature 36.9°C). There was no pallor, jaundice, lymphadenopathy, or signs of dehydration. Respiratory examination revealed mild respiratory distress with a respiratory rate of 32 breaths per minute (tachypneic). His SPO2 was 99% on room air. There were no chest deformities or asymmetry. The trachea was centrally placed. There was equal air entry bilaterally with widespread loud harsh breath sounds, bilateral crepitations, and rhonchi. Cardiovascular examination showed a thin volume pulse with a tachycardia of 108 beats per minute. Blood pressure was normal (92/70 mmHg). The apex beat was located in the 5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line. Heart sounds I and II were present, with a 3rd heart sound (gallop rhythm) and a loud second heart sound in the pulmonary area (loud P2). Abdominal examination revealed mild abdominal distension, shifting dullness (indicative of moderate ascites), and a tender hepatomegaly extending 8 cm below the costal margin with a positive hepatojugular reflux.
test_results: The chest X-ray showed dilated trachea and principal bronchi with diffuse reticulolinear and ring-like opacities involving mainly the mid and lower lung zones bilaterally. A sequential high resolution computed tomography (HRCT) scan was performed using a 128-slice multidetector CT scanner. The study was performed in full inspiration with a scan time of five seconds.

case_report: A 53-year-old male with a history of congestive heart failure and alcohol use disorder arrived at the emergency room experiencing shortness of breath, abdominal distension, orthopnea, and a 20-pound weight gain over the past two months. He mentioned undergoing a 10-liter paracentesis one year prior and denied any history of coronary artery disease. The patient reported daily alcohol consumption and active smoking. His home medications included carvedilol, furosemide, spironolactone, atorvastatin, metformin, and albuterol. Vital signs were within normal limits. Cardiac examination revealed a systolic murmur at the cardiac apex, but jugular venous pulsation was not observable due to body habitus. Pulmonary examination showed clear lungs in all fields. The abdomen was distended with a positive fluid wave, and there was no lower extremity edema. Laboratory results showed creatinine at 1 mg/dL, platelets at 33 x 10^3/mm3, INR at 1.1, albumin at 3 g/dL, bilirubin at 0.8 mg/dL, and pro-brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) greater than 5000 pg/mL. The chest X-ray was unremarkable. An abdominal ultrasound revealed moderate ascites in the suprapubic region without significant fluid pockets in the lower compartments. The IVC was distended more than 2.1 cm with less than 50% collapsibility, indicating an elevated CVP greater than 10 mmHg. In the parasternal long axis view, the left ventricle had a normal ejection fraction, while the right ventricle was severely dilated with a moderate pericardial effusion. The parasternal short-axis view showed the right ventricle larger than the left with septal flattening during diastole, indicating severe right ventricular dysfunction. Paracentesis revealed 366 x 10^3/mm3 white blood cells with 61% monocytes and macrophages. The serum-ascites albumin gradient was 1.5, and the ascites total protein was greater than 2.5 g/dL. The patient was started on IV diuresis, resulting in a 20-pound weight loss over seven days and resolution of shortness of breath and orthopnea. A transthoracic echo confirmed the findings, showing a left ventricular ejection fraction of 55%-60%, a moderately-to-severely dilated right ventricle with moderate-to-severe reduction in right ventricular systolic function, a moderately dilated right atrium, moderate pulmonary hypertension with a right ventricular systolic pressure of 60 mmHg, a dilated IVC with less than 50% collapse with respiration, and a small pericardial effusion.
test_results: The patient underwent a right heart catheterization after aggressive IV diuresis which showed a right atrial pressure of 7 mmHg, pulmonary artery pressure of 73/26 mmHg, mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) of 45 mmHg, and a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 13 mmHg, with a cardiac index of 2.7 L/min/m2 and pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) of 498 dyn·s/cm5.
diagnosis: Group 1 Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension due to Primary Pulmonary Hypertension

case_report: A 2-year-8-month-old female, vaccinated according to the national immunization program, presented with a dry cough that became wet, dyspnea, chest pain, and fever. Clinical examination revealed a conscious patient with a fever of 38.5°C, tachypnea at 45 breaths per minute, and a heart rate of approximately 100 beats per minute. Oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. The patient weighed 10 kilograms and measured 88 cm in height. Pleuropulmonary examination showed signs of respiratory distress, including intercostal, subcostal, and supraclavicular retractions, and decreased vocal resonance. Auscultation revealed absent breath sounds and tympanism in the right chest. A chest X-ray indicated a right pneumothorax, which was subsequently drained. Laboratory results showed leukocytosis at 16,000/mm3 with a neutrophil count of 8,360/mm3, hemoglobin at 7.9 g/dl, CRP at 70 mg/dl, and a sterile blood culture. The patient was treated with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, but there was minimal clinical and radiological improvement. A thoracic CT scan revealed overdistension of the right hemithorax with parenchymal air cystic lesions in the external segment of the middle lobe, a significant right hydropneumothorax causing compression on the adjacent pulmonary parenchyma, and pleural inflammation. The patient was scheduled for surgery but missed the appointment due to the COVID-19 pandemic and social distancing measures. Two months later, she presented with pyopneumothorax, which was drained, yielding 100 ml of yellow liquid with pus lumps. Bacteriological examination of the pus identified Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Klebsiella pneumoniae. A right middle lobectomy was performed, and during an open thoracotomy, a gelatinous component originating from the middle right lobe and extending to the pleura and diaphragm was found and resected.
test_results: Cytological finding confirmed macroscopically multiple fragments with polypoid cerebroid and necrotic component and rare cystic wall. Microscopically, the tumor proliferation had the double epithelial and sarcomatous component.

case_report: A 26-year-old female presented with a soft, painful swelling in the left submandibular area. The patient first noticed the swelling at the age of 12 when it was the size of a pea. It gradually grew to approximately 2.5 cm by 3 cm by the time she was 18 years old, after which the size remained stable. There was a history of frequent gum bleeding in the same region. The patient was in the first trimester of pregnancy (40 days) at the time of presentation. During follow-up visits, the size of the lesion did not change despite the hormonal changes associated with pregnancy.
test_results: A panoramic radiograph revealed a well-defined radiolucency in the left mandibular angle region with a scooped-out appearance and smooth margins, with a sharp spicule projecting inferiorly from the inferior margin. There was effacement of the posterior aspect of the inferior cortical wall of the inferior alveolar canal. Delayed-phase CECT scan revealed dilated serpentine venous channels. A T2-weighted MR image revealed a diffuse heterogeneous hyper-intense lesion without any mass formation, abutting the ramus-angle region, extending anteriorly into the left pterygomandibular space, with infiltration into the left medial pterygoid and masseter muscles and subcutaneous thickening. No abnormal signal flow voids were seen. Doppler USG revealed a venous pattern with slow flow.

case_report: A 5-year-old boy with an uneventful birth history presented with global developmental delay and mild autism. At 2 years old, he had two episodes of febrile seizures, during which EEG showed slow background waves. Upon admission, he experienced frequent generalized tonic-clonic seizures lasting 30 minutes. His occipitofrontal head circumference measured 50 cm. By age 3, he could walk without support, speak simple words, and follow basic instructions. He had difficulties with social interaction and communication. On the day of admission, he was in a coma with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of nine. Physical examination revealed no neck stiffness but a positive Babinski sign. No malformations of other organs were noted.
test_results: On admission, he suffered frequent generalized tonic-clonic seizures that lasted for 30 min, which fulfilled the diagnostic criteria of convulsive status epilepticus. Cytological and biochemical examinations of the cerebrospinal fluid were normal. Etiological tests including herpes simplex virus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, Japanese encephalitis virus, coxsackievirus, mycoplasma pneumoniae, tubercle bacillus, and fungal culture were all negative. Autoimmune encephalitis and metabolic diseases were excluded by antibody and metabolic screening. The EEG showed sharp spikes in the frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes with a slow background. Brain MRI showed cerebellar atrophy, as well as broadening of the lateral and third ventricles. Repeated EEG monitoring showed a generalized low-amplitude wave with an absent sleeping spindle. His Wechsler Intelligence Scale score was 55. A trio whole-exome sequencing test was performed on both patients.

case_report: A 15-year-old Iraqi girl presented with a fever of 39°C persisting for over two weeks. One week before admission, she experienced a sore throat, fever, and a maculopapular rash on her limbs, abdomen, palms, and back. She was initially treated with doxycycline 150 mg twice daily, but due to the ongoing fever, she was hospitalized. Upon admission, her physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory results showed a leukocyte count of 23,000/mm3 (normal range: 4000 to 10,000/mm3) with 90% neutrophils, hemoglobin level of 12.6 g/dL (normal range: 12 to 16 g/dL) with a mean corpuscular volume (MCV) of 75 fL (normal range: 77 to 91 fL), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 92 mm/hour, C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 16 mg/L (normal range: 0-1 mg/L), and serum ferritin level of 2267 ng/mL (normal range: 10 to 120 ng/mL). Electrolytes, kidney and liver functions, and coagulation profile were all within normal limits. Tests for antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, c-ANCA, p-ANCA, anticardiolipin antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, antiparietal cell antibodies, anti-smooth muscle antibodies, anti-histone antibodies, and anti-mitochondrial antibodies were negative. Serological tests for CMV, EBV, HSV, HAV, HBV, HCV, HIV, adenovirus, parainfluenza, Coxsackie, influenza, Toxoplasma, and Brucella were negative. Serology for parvovirus showed positive IgG antibodies, and Coxiella burnetii antibodies (Q-fever) were also positive. A total body computed tomography (CT) scan revealed no abnormalities except for a 16-cm enlarged spleen.
test_results: Bone marrow biopsy showed no evidence of lymphoma or any other type of malignancy. A second bone marrow biopsy revealed impressive hemophagocytosis.
diagnosis: Still's disease associated with macrophage activation syndrome

case_report: A 19-year-old white male presented with a painless mass on the right side of the scrotum, which had been present for six months. His medical history included a tonsillectomy, with no other notable events. The patient was in excellent overall health. Physical examination revealed a solid mass, approximately the size of a prune, located in the paratesticular region. Grey scale ultrasonography using a 10Mhz transducer showed a well-defined hypoechoic lesion with a homogeneous echo pattern, measuring 3 × 3 cm, situated above the testicle. MRI, performed with a 1.5 Tesla machine and a surface coil, confirmed a well-circumscribed polycyclic mass, 3.5 cm in diameter, located in the spermatic cord and separate from the testicle and epididymis. T2-weighted imaging showed the lesion had very low signal density, while T1-weighted imaging revealed intermediate signal density, similar to typical T1-weighted skeletal muscle imaging. Contrast-enhanced imaging (T1-weighted and fat-suppressed) indicated low and inhomogeneous gadolinium uptake. Laboratory tests were normal. During surgery, a firm pedunculated mass originating from the spermatic cord was identified and completely removed without affecting the remaining scrotal contents. The patient had an uneventful postoperative recovery. After 12 months of follow-up, he remains in good health with no scrotal complaints.
test_results: Microscopically, both specimens were composed of dense, collagen-rich, hyalinized, partly storiform fibrotic tissue with tiny calcifications and a low cell density of interspersed spindle-like cells and lymphofollicular infiltrates. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated positive staining results for actin, D2-40, and phosphoglucomutase 1 (PGM1). Staining results were negative for cytokeratin, calretinin, caldesmon and S-100 as well as for germ cell tumor markers Oct 3/4 and placental alkaline phosphatase (PLAP). There were diffuse to patchy infiltrates predominantly consisting of CD3+ T lymphocytes and IgG-positive plasma cells. The IgG4 staining result disclosed 10 to 15 positive cells on average per high-power field, corresponding to a proportion of approximately 40% of IgG-positive cells in evaluable hot spots. There was also considerable vascularization detected by the staining of CD31 and CD34. Venulitis was found sporadically and only in small venules. The proliferation rate was approximately 5% as demonstrated by molecular immunology Borstel-1 (MIB-1) staining.
diagnosis: Paratesticular fibrous pseudotumor with histological features of IgG4-related disease

case_report: A 49-year-old male was admitted in July 2010 due to sudden onset of weakness in the proximal muscles of his limbs, affecting both sensory and motor functions. Upon clinical examination, he exhibited muscle weakness in the proximal regions of both upper and lower limbs, accompanied by sensations of tingling and pain. The muscle stretch reflexes in his lower limbs were reduced. There were no signs of upper motor neuron involvement. Nerve conduction studies showed normal results.
test_results: Needle electromyography showed abnormal spontaneous activity and neurogenic recruitment in weak muscles. Anti-HEV IgM was detected in serum (optical density ratio >10) but not in CSF. HEV RNA was detected by real-time PCR only in serum (Ct 34).
diagnosis: Acute inflammatory polyradiculoneuropathy associated with Hepatitis E virus  infection

case_report: A nine-month-old girl was admitted to the hospital with symptoms of fever, cough, diarrhea (11-12 episodes daily), and failure to thrive. She was born at term via normal delivery with a birth weight of 3200 grams following an uneventful pregnancy. She is the second child of a non-consanguineous Turkish couple, with a healthy 5-year-old sister. Upon admission, her body weight was 4.7 kg (SD: -3.5), height was 62.5 cm (SD: -1.7), and head circumference was 39 cm (3rd percentile). Relative index was 71.2. Physical examination revealed pallor, thin and weak hair, and decreased subcutaneous adipose tissue. Auscultation detected rales in the middle zone of the left lung. Her abdomen was distended with prominent bowel loops, and she had umbilical and bilateral inguinal hernias. Dysmorphic features included hypertelorism, frontal bossing, triangular face, and retromicrognathia. She had complete head control but could not sit without support. Deep tendon reflexes were normoactive. Laboratory results showed a hemoglobin level of 9.8 g/dL, leukocyte count of 14820/mm3, and platelet count of 363000/mm3. Serum transaminases were mildly elevated with aspartate aminotransferase at 105 U/L and alanine aminotransferase at 112 U/L. Vitamin D concentration was 11.6 mg/L, alkaline phosphatase was 99 u/L, calcium was 9.03 mg/dL, phosphorus was 3.15 mg/dL, and parathyroid hormone was 60 mg/L. TORCH screen was negative, and infections from hepatotropic viruses or HIV were ruled out. Coagulation tests, renal functions, and electrolytes were normal. The patient had been hospitalized three times for bronchiolitis. Cystic fibrosis was considered due to malnutrition, recurrent bronchiolitis, and elevated liver function tests, but molecular genetic analysis of the CFTR gene was normal. Stool examination showed no reducing substances but revealed fat droplets. Tests for pathogenic bacteria or parasites were negative. Normal levels of anti-endomysial antibodies ruled out celiac disease, and basic metabolic tests including ammonia, lactate, pyruvate, blood acyl carnitine profile, amino acid analysis, urinary organic acid analysis, homocysteine, and biotinidase activity were normal. Congenital immune deficiency was ruled out, and immunoglobulin profile (IgA, IgM, IgG, IgE), CD markers (CD3, CD19, CD56), and fagotest were normal. Cholesterol and triglyceride concentrations were low with TC at 26 mg/dL and TG at 9 mg/dL. Peripheral blood smear revealed acanthocytosis. Vitamin E concentration was 0.87 mg/L, vitamin A was 71 ug/L, and vitamin D was 11.6 ug/L, all very low. Abdominal ultrasonography showed multiple small stones (<3 mm) in both kidneys, and ophthalmologic examination was normal.
test_results: MTTP gene analysis revealed a novel homozygous pathogenic variant [c.506A>T (p. D169V)].

case_report: Patient 4 is a 6-year-old boy, born at term by vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 2.2 kg (−2 to −3 SD). He cried immediately after birth and has one healthy elder brother. He was referred for evaluation with bilateral clubfeet and bilateral elbow and knee dislocations noted at birth. Developmental milestones included head holding at 5 months, rolling over at 8 months, sitting at 9 months, standing at 13 months, walking with support at 15 months, and walking without support at 2 years. At 6 years, his height was 110 cm and weight 22 kg (both normal for age). Physical examination revealed a prominent forehead, mid face hypoplasia, telecanthus, downslanting palpebral fissures, and a long philtrum. He had long cylindrical fingers with broad fingertips and mild joint laxity. Bilateral elbow and knee dislocations and clubfeet were present. There was a flexion deformity at the bilateral elbows with pterygium over the cubital fossa. Bilateral hip and wrist joints were normal. Skin, hair, and nails were normal. The cervical spine was normal. Bilateral double ossification of the calcaneum, bilateral elbow and knee dislocations, and bilateral metatarsus adductus were noted. Imaging of the hip and thoracolumbar spine was unremarkable. Echocardiography was normal. Laboratory results including complete blood count, serum calcium, serum phosphorous, alkaline phosphatase, thyroid profile, and complete urine analysis were unremarkable.
test_results: Radiographs at 4 years, 5 years and 6 years of age revealed delayed carpal ossification and showed abnormal distal phalanx of thumbs and small distal phalanges.

case_report: A 29-year-old female (G3P2 + 1) conceived naturally. On 29 November 2020, a fetal ultrasound at 30 weeks of gestation in Sichuan Provincial Maternity and Child Health Care Hospital, Chengdu, Sichuan Province, China revealed a gingival mass. No abnormalities were found in other systems. Amniocentesis karyotype and chromosome microarray analysis showed no abnormality. At 30 + 4 gestational weeks, a fetal head MRI examination showed a mass between the upper and lower lips of the fetus, measuring approximately 1.6 × 1.5 cm, with part of the edge being smooth. At 14:46 on 3 February 2021, a caesarean section was performed in Jinniu District Maternity and Child Health Hospital, Chengdu, Sichuan Province, China due to 'no desire for vaginal trial labour in patients with a scarred uterus'. The birth weight was 3650 g and the Apgar score was 10-10-10 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes. After birth, a 2 × 2 × 2 cm pink lump was observed in the lower gums, protruding from the mouth, preventing the lips from closing. The mass did not break or bleed. The rest of the newborn’s systems were normal upon examination. There was no shortness of breath, cyanosis, moaning, reduced crying and movement, fever, screaming, irritation, convulsion, or other system manifestations. The newborn with the 'gingival lump' was transferred to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit, Sichuan Provincial Maternity and Child Health Care Hospital and was fed milk via a gastric tube within 1 hour after birth. Four days after birth, blood examination showed elevated tumor markers (alpha-fetoprotein: 56080.00 IU/ml; cancer antigen 199: 42.45 U/ml) while other blood tests were normal. Two days after birth, lateral digital radiography of the head showed no obvious abnormal high-density shadow in the soft tissue in the oral cavity and in the soft tissue protruding from the oral cavity. Color ultrasound examination showed a heterogeneous low echo in the lower gingiva, slightly to the right, measuring approximately 1.9 × 1.4 × 1.6 cm, with a clear boundary, regular shape, slightly higher flake echo, and no obvious blood flow signal.
test_results: Five days after birth, an MRI scan showed that there was a round local protruding mass on the right side of the lower gingiva, with a smooth edge, approximately 1.6 × 1.8 × 1.3 cm in size (anterior and posterior diameter × left and right diameter × upper and lower diameter), with uneven signal intensity, T1WI and T2WI signals, nodular watery signal shadow in the central area of the lesion, and progressive contrast enhancement in the solid part of the lesion. No definite abnormal changes were found in the shape and signal of the adjacent structure, and no exact abnormal enhancement was seen in the enhancement. The lower gingiva was slightly to the right of the cystic-solid nodule, which was closely related to the right lower gingiva, and the remaining structure was clearly delineated. After the effect of general anaesthesia was induced, the infant was intubated through nasotracheal intubation and laid in the central position of the supine position. The gingival pedicled mass in the mandibular anterior tooth area was found, the size was approximately 2.5 × 2.5 × 2.0 cm, the surface mucosa was intact, there was no redness and swelling and the movability was moderate. The mucous membrane of the normal tissue was incised outside the lesion, then the bone surface was incised whilst carefully protecting the deciduous tooth germ, so that the lesion could be completely removed. The mass was cut open and the section was solid, showing white fibrous tissue. The results of paraffin sections of frozen tissues on 25 February 2021 suggested that the ‘gingival mass’ was a granular cell tumour. The immunohistochemical results of 3 March 2021 showed that the tumour cells were pan-cytokeratin (P-CK) (–), Smur100 (S-100) (–), neuron-specific enolase (NSE) (–), calretinin (–), CD68 (–), vimentin (+) and specially stained periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) (–).

case_report: The patient is a 32-year-old woman with a history of smoking 4–5 cigarettes a day for about 3 years in her youth, but she has since quit. During a routine medical examination for an international visa, a standard chest X-ray revealed a 30 × 30 mm rounded opacity in the mediastinum, surrounded by normal lung parenchyma and not associated with adenopathies, atelectasis, or pleural effusion. Further imaging showed a 38 × 29 × 28 mm heterogeneous solid mass attached to the pericardium and surrounded by the trunk of the pulmonary artery, with no other masses or lymph nodes detected. The patient was transferred to our hospital for a cardiothoracic assessment. Physical examination was unremarkable, with no palpable lymphadenopathy in the cervical, anterior mediastinal, supraclavicular, axillary, or inguinal regions. Bilateral breath sounds were normal, and there was no history of fatigue, generalized pruritus, night sweats, fever, weight loss, cough, dyspnea, or chest pain. Laboratory results, including tumor markers BHCG, AFP, CEA, CA19–9, and thyroglobulin, were within normal limits.
test_results: A contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography (CT) revealed a 38 × 29 × 28 mm heterogeneous solid mass. It was attached to the pericardium and surrounded by the trunk of the pulmonary artery; no other masses or lymph nodes were discovered. Pathology reported a 38 × 29 × 28 mm smooth tumor. It had a grayish external surface, few cystic areas and yellowish serous contents. The microscopic report revealed a well-defined tumor, surrounded by a thickened fibrous connective capsule with focal areas of calcification without invasion and numerous small CD5-positive lymphocytes.

case_report: A 6-year-old Black African boy visited the hospital clinic with complaints of anterior knee pain and progressive bowing of his right leg, which became noticeable over the past year following a fall while playing soccer. His parents noted that the knee pain was intermittent, occurring only during sports activities. There were no additional complaints. His birth and developmental history were normal, and his mother confirmed that he had no prior medical conditions or medication use. His fine and gross motor skills, social, emotional, and language milestones were all normal. He began walking without support at 11 months of age. Clinical examination showed no leg length discrepancy, with an upper to lower segment ratio of 1.15:1. His weight was 24 kg, height was 122 cm, and BMI was 16.1 kg/m², placing him in the 70th percentile.
test_results: Plain radiograph of right leg revealed tibia vara with medial breaking and a significant depression of the medial tibial epiphysis and metaphysis (stage IV of Langenskiӧld). The angle between the femoral and the tibial shaft (F-T angle) was 11° and the angle between femoral condyles and the tibial shaft (FC-T angle) was 72°. The angle of the medial tibial plateau depression (MTPD angle) was 80° and the Drennan metaphyseal-diaphyseal angle was 21°.

case_report: A 27-year-old male of Korean descent with a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus, major depressive disorder, and alcohol-related hepatosteatosis presented with gradually worsening pancytopenia without symptoms. Initial blood tests revealed a white blood cell (WBC) count of 2.8 x 10^3/μL, hematocrit (Hct) of 37%, and platelet count of 96 x 10^3/μL. Peripheral smear showed no significant abnormalities, and the direct Coomb’s test was negative. Bilirubin was slightly elevated, but ferritin, liver transaminases, and vitamin B12 levels were normal. The patient was advised to cease alcohol consumption and return for follow-up in a month. Subsequent lab results one month later indicated further decline in blood counts: WBCs at 1.6 x 10^3/μL, Hct at 33%, and platelets at 75 x 10^3/μL. Physical examination revealed splenomegaly, which was confirmed by ultrasonography.
test_results: A bone marrow biopsy was then performed, and the results were consistent with a trilineage dysplastic process, marked erythroplasia with a few megakaryocytes and blast cells making up less than 5% of all cells. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) revealed 10% of cells to be CD3 and CD5 positive. A CT scan of the abdomen was done in preparation for a splenectomy for diagnostic purposes, which showed worsening splenomegaly measuring approximately 24 x 20 x 9 cm, for a volume of roughly 4.3 liters. Two weeks later, a repeat CT scan of the abdomen was repeated prior to surgery which showed an increase in the size of the spleen to 28 x 21 x 19 cm. Following splenectomy, the histological examination of the spleen revealed an expanded red pulp infiltrated by a uniform population of medium-sized atypical lymphoid cells. IHC revealed these cells to stain positive for CD3 and T-cell intracytoplasmic antigen (TIA-1). IHC was negative for CD56, CD5 T-cell co-expression and CD20.

case_report: Case 2 (II-1): A 12-day-old female was admitted to the Neonatology department at Hebei Provincial Children's Hospital for half a day due to reduced milk intake and fever. She was born full-term with a birth weight of 3,200 g, following an uncomplicated pregnancy. Initially, breastfeeding was successful, but milk intake gradually decreased, and she had yellow paste-like stools with reduced frequency. Twelve days post-birth, she developed a fever after contact with a febrile individual (her mother), with a maximum temperature of 38.0°C. On the third day after birth, jaundice was noted, which persisted. Upon admission, her weight was 2,970 g (a decrease of 230 g from birth weight), she appeared in pain, had sallow and mottled skin, a distended abdomen with prominent abdominal wall veins, and palpable liver and spleen enlargement (liver 6.0 cm below the rib, 6.0 cm below the xiphoid process, spleen 4.0 cm below the rib). Laboratory findings showed significantly elevated total bilirubin, predominantly direct bilirubin and bile acids, and abnormal coagulation function. Blood metabolism screening was unremarkable, but urine 4-hydroxyphenyllactate levels were elevated. Blood culture was positive for Escherichia coli. Abdominal B-ultrasonography revealed enhanced and thickened liver parenchyma echo, strong point-like echoes in the intestinal wall, and peritoneal effusion. Brain MRI indicated left intracerebral hemorrhage with ventricular enlargement. Post-admission, the patient received anti-infective and symptomatic treatments, leading to general condition improvement, although gastrointestinal symptoms and poor weight gain persisted. Genetic metabolic diseases were considered, and further evaluation was conducted.
test_results: The patient was diagnosed by genetic testing.

case_report: The patient is a female infant born at 41 weeks gestational age to an 18-year-old mother and an 18-year-old father. The mother had routine prenatal care with no significant exposures. The pregnancy was complicated by pyelectasis and an absent cavum septum pellucidum detected on ultrasound during the second trimester. At 35 weeks, after relocating, the mother began weekly non-stress tests due to suspected fetal anomalies. A repeat ultrasound at 39 weeks and 3 days showed accelerated fetal growth with measurements indicating biparietal diameter at 40 weeks, head circumference at 40 weeks and 6 days, abdominal circumference at 39 weeks and 6 days, and femur length at 37 weeks and 1 day. There was also apparent fusion of the anterior lateral ventricles. The infant was delivered by cesarean section after a failed induction of labor with Apgar scores of 9 at both 1 and 5 minutes. The infant was large for gestational age with a birth weight of 4,165 grams (96th percentile), length of 53.3 cm (98th percentile), and head circumference of 38.5 cm (approximately 100th percentile). At birth, the infant exhibited multiple dysmorphic features including macrocephaly, fusion of the left coronal suture, facial asymmetry with a hypoplastic left supra-orbital ridge and contralateral frontal bossing, and a flat occiput. The nasal bridge was depressed with short, anteverted nares and a bulbous nasal tip deviated to the right. The right ear was smaller than the left with an irregular contour and redundant tissue. Ocular anomalies included hypertelorism, irregular contour of the eyelids, microphthalmia, and inability to open the right eye spontaneously. Ectopic eyelashes were present on the upper eyelid. A dilated fundoscopic exam revealed partial clouding of both corneas, more pronounced on the right. The palate was intact and the mandible was normal. There was pre-axial polydactyly with bilateral partial duplication of the thumbs and great toes. A single transverse palmar crease was present on the right hand. Examination of the skin revealed thickened, marbled areas of normally pigmented and hypopigmented skin on the right trunk and bilaterally on the lower extremities. The skin had an atrophic, pebbly texture with patches of abnormal hair on the extremities. The abdomen was distended but soft without palpable masses or organomegaly. The remainder of the examination, including respiratory, cardiovascular, genitourinary, and neurologic systems, was unremarkable.
test_results: Subsequent brain MRI revealed near-complete agenesis of the corpus callosum. Radiographs of the upper extremities showed pre-axial polydactyly with osseus syndactyly of the extra digit to the thumb and a short first metacarpal on the right hand; the left hand also had pre-axial polysyndactyly. Radiographs of the lower extremities showed bilateral pre-axial polydactyly. CT scan of the head showed left coronal craniosynostosis as well as multiple intrasutural bones being noted, similar to wormian bones. A SNP-oligonucleotide microarray showed 46, XX without pathogenic copy number variation. Rectal biopsies were obtained which revealed the presence of ganglion cells. Rare hypertrophic nerve bundles were also noted on biopsy. After rectal biopsy, an upper GI radiographic series with barium contrast revealed malrotation without volvulus and delayed emptying of contrast through the cecum and rectum.

case_report: In 2006, a 52-year-old female patient was admitted to a neurological department due to sudden difficulties with swallowing and speech, ophthalmoparesis with vertical and horizontal eye movement disorder, dysesthesia of the hands described as 'pins and needles' in a glove-like distribution, and generalized areflexia. Muscle strength was normal. The patient was treated with 150 g intravenous immunoglobulins, resulting in complete remission of symptoms within a few days. Over the following years, the patient consulted various healthcare providers for unspecific abdominal pain, present since childhood. Diagnostic imaging including CT, MRI, and gastroscopy were normal. In October 2017, at the age of 63, the patient was hospitalized due to generalized epileptic seizures with prolonged postictal confusion. Cerebral MRI showed no abnormalities, and therapy with levetiracetam was initiated. In December 2017, the patient was admitted to an internal medicine clinic for persistent diarrhea, abdominal pain, renal failure, and a reduced general state of health. The patient experienced further generalized epileptic seizures with postictal confusion and significantly reduced vigilance, accompanied by lactic acidosis (serum lactate 26.0 mmol/l, pH 6.863), necessitating admission to the neurological intensive care unit. A slight residual ophthalmoparesis with vertical gaze palsy and bilateral limitation of upgaze was noted. Anticonvulsive therapy with levetiracetam (3 g/day) was supplemented with lacosamide (400 mg/day). Mechanical ventilation was required due to severe metabolic acidosis and respiratory failure during an epileptic seizure (serum lactate 14.7; 10.6; 16.0 mmol/l). CSF analysis showed elevated lactate (12.01 mmol/l) and protein levels (67 mg/dl), with no signs of infection. Brain CT and MRI, as well as abdominal and thorax CT, were normal. Electroneurography indicated a slight mixed axonal-demyelinating polyneuropathy, while electromyography was normal. Besides sinus tachycardia at 140 bpm and mild pericardial effusion, no signs of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome were present. Extubation attempts failed due to another severe epileptic seizure with life-threatening lactic acidosis and hyperkalemia (lactate 26.0 mmol/l; pH 6.925; potassium 7.8 mmol/l). EEG showed an alpha rhythm with intermittent slow waves and a tendency to generalize. Follow-up cerebral MRI detected multiple fat emboli. CT-angiography of the lung revealed a pulmonary embolism. Multiple vertebral fractures, likely due to severe epileptic seizures, were confirmed by CT, and surgical fixation was performed. Intensive care therapy, including ventilation, was required for over eight weeks. Successful weaning was achieved after dilatative tracheostomy and nutrition via PEG tube. Vitamin B6 was supplemented. The patient underwent rehabilitative therapy and returned to normal life after five months, with tracheostomy and PEG tube removed. Comprehensive diagnostic evaluations for various metabolic diseases, including copper metabolism disorders, lead poisoning, and adrenoleukodystrophy, were inconspicuous.
test_results: The analysis of the amino acids in the urine, CSF and serum showed a strong abnormality with ubiquitously increased amino acids, especially proline (proline in serum 3085 μmol/l (reference 90-342 μmol/l), in urine 46,531 μmol/g Crea (reference < 100 μmol/g Crea), in CSF 104 mg/dl (reference < 6 mg/dl), Hydroxyproline in urine 1395 μmol/g Crea (reference <100)). Furthermore, vitamin-B6 was decreased with 3.3 μg/l (reference > 4.9 μg/l). The targeted genetic analyses by Sanger sequencing revealed no pathogenic variant within the PRODH-gene but identified two novel variants within the ALDH4A1-gene. In combination, both heterozygous variants within the ALDH4A1 gene could lead to a compound heterozygosity (variants in trans). Since the patient’s son had only one of the two heterozygous variants of his mother, the compound heterozygous state of both variants in our patient was proven.

case_report: The patient is a 17-year-old male born to nonconsanguineous parents, presenting with hyperpigmented, rough streaks in a broad-band Blaschko-linear distribution. These skin lesions have been present since birth and have progressively extended to large areas on the right side of his body. No other family members have similar skin lesions or any cutaneous conditions. Physical examination revealed follicular hyperkeratosis across his entire body, more pronounced in the darker skin patches. On the scalp, there was an area of scarring alopecia with perifollicular erythema and follicular hyperkeratosis, displaying a tufted-like folliculitis pattern. The patient also exhibited clinodactyly of the fifth finger on both hands, more pronounced on the left side. X-ray examination confirmed clinodactyly, with no other skeletal abnormalities observed, including normal long and pelvic bones. Cytogenetic analysis of peripheral blood lymphocytes showed a normal karyotype of 46, XY.
test_results: Histopathological examination of biopsies obtained from the hyperpigmented bands and ‘background’ skin were both characterized by hyperkeratosis with basket-woven configuration in the stratum corneum and an irregular epidermal acanthosis with papillomatosis. In the papillary and perifollicular dermis, the blood vessels were dilated and surrounded by scattered lymphocytic infiltrates. In addition, in the section obtained from the ‘background’ skin, thinned and dystrophic hair shafts could be noted. The section derived from the darker bands showed instead an orthokeratotic stratum corneum, more pronounced hair follicles clustered with an evident follicular hyperkeratosis, infundibular keratinic plugs and irregular distribution of melanin pigment in the basal cell layer.

case_report: A previously healthy 15-month-old girl presented with mild shortness of breath and fever reaching up to 38.5°C over the past four days. She did not exhibit cough or feeding difficulties, and there was no prior history of breathlessness or recurrent infections. Upon initial examination, the patient was euvolemic, with a regular heartbeat at a rate of 105 beats per minute, and normal heart sounds without murmurs. Her arterial blood pressure was 90/50 mmHg, and oxygen saturation in room air was 96%. The respiratory rate was 26 breaths per minute. Pneumonia was identified, and treatment with antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanate—90 mg/kg/day orally in two divided doses for 14 days) was initiated. Despite the antibiotic therapy, the clinical examination remained abnormal, with low-intensity vesicular breath sounds noted in the right thorax.
test_results: A chest X-ray revealed cardiac dextroposition, a small right lung, and a vascular shadow behind the heart border. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed a 4-mm ostium secundum atrial septal defect (ASD) in the fossa ovalis region, with left-to-right shunt, and right inferior pulmonary vein connected with the IVC. A computed tomography angiography scan evidenced small ostium secundum ASD (5 mm), hypoplasia of the right lung, agenesis of the right pulmonary artery, normally connected pulmonary veins, and a collateral artery arising from the abdominal aorta supplying the hypoplastic right lung. The chest computed tomography (CT) scan also showed altered bronchial segmentation with a blind-ended right bronchus to the intermediate lobe. Cardiac catheterization confirmed the diagnosis and showed systolic left pulmonary artery pressure of 34 mmHg, systolic aortic pressure of 74 mmHg, and systolic pressure of 22 mmHg at the distal collateral vessel due to stenosis at its origin. The mean pressure values at left and right atria were respectively 13 and 10 mmHg.

case_report: A 28-year-old female was admitted with recurrent shortness of breath for one year, worsening over the past three days. She had no family history of pulmonary hypertension or lung/heart diseases and did not consume alcohol, smoke, or use addictive drugs. Initial examination showed she was afebrile with a blood pressure of 121/82 mmHg, heart rate of 101 beats/min, respiratory rate of 22 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation of 92% on room air. She was classified as New York Heart Association functional class III for heart failure. Physical examination revealed clear bilateral breathing sounds, an accentuated second pulmonic heart sound, slight pitting edema in the lower limbs, and Raynaud's phenomenon in both hands. Laboratory tests, including thyroid function, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, HIV, D-dimer, C-reactive protein, rheumatic factor, antiphospholipid antibody, and anti-vasculitis antibody, were within normal ranges. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed right ventricle hypertrophy, moderate tricuspid regurgitation, mild pericardial effusion, preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (62%), and fractional shortening (36%). Right heart catheterization at rest indicated a pulmonary artery pressure of 62 mmHg, pulmonary artery wedge pressure of 10 mmHg, cardiac output by thermodilution of 2.05 L/min, and pulmonary vascular resistance of 25 Wood units. A pulmonary ventilation/perfusion scan showed no signs of thromboembolic disease, but high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) revealed a dilated pulmonary artery, slight pericardial effusion, and bilateral ground-glass nodules/opacities. Abdominal ultrasound indicated a crude and thick-walled gallbladder, hepatomegaly, seroperitoneum, and increased inner diameter of the inferior vena cava and hepatic vein, suggesting hepatic congestion. Pulmonary function tests showed moderate-to-severe mixed ventilation dysfunction. The patient also presented with dry eyes and Raynaud's phenomenon, tested positive for anti-nuclear antibody (anti-SSA, + +), and had an increased level of procalcitonin. A labial salivary gland biopsy showed lymphocyte infiltration between the salivary glands.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing identified a biallelic mutation in EIF2AK4 at c.1021 C > T (p. Gln341*). Thoracoscopic biopsy demonstrated marked venule thickening and luminal occlusion due to intimal proliferation and medial hypertrophy.
diagnosis: Pulmonary Veno-Occlusive Disease  in the context of Sjogren's syndrome

case_report: A 44-year-old woman was referred for a second opinion by her uveitis specialist. She presented with left-sided photopsias, decreased contrast sensitivity, photophobia, and scotomas, with no evident intraocular inflammation. A neuroophthalmological cause had been ruled out. Treatment included Adalimumab (Humira®, AbbVie, Chicago, IL, USA) at 40 mg every two weeks, and after six months, Mycophenolate Mofetil (Cellcept®, Genentech, San Francisco, CA, USA) at 2 g per day was added. Despite this dual immunosuppressive therapy, her condition progressed, prompting the need for a second opinion. She had a history of recurrent tonsillitis and elevated ASLO (antistreptolysin) titers on multiple occasions.
test_results: FA showed bilateral retinal vasculitis. SD-OCT showed loss and/or disruption of the photoreceptor outer segment layer. The ICGA was normal—in particular no choriocapillaris circulation voids were detected. Electrophysiological investigation detected photoreceptor dysfunction ODS with reduced amplitudes. FAF showed left hyperautofluorescence in the posterior pole and one year later the right eye was involved in a similar fashion.

case_report: A 59-year-old man arrived at the emergency department experiencing cloudy vision and difficulty moving. The patient reported that the previous night, he had wrapped a cotton pad soaked in spirit around his knees and covered them with stretch film to alleviate pain. This setup remained in place for over ten hours. The patient mentioned having knee pain for over ten years without any medical or surgical treatments. He had no chronic diseases. His family history included hypertension in his father and coronary artery disease. The patient's Glasgow coma scale (GCS) score was 15. Vital signs included arterial tension of 130/85 mmHg, heart rate of 86 bpm, respiration rate of 18/min, temperature of 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation of 98%. Physical examination noted redness on the knees. Biochemical parameters indicated a high anion gap and metabolic acidosis. Differential diagnoses such as diabetic ketoacidosis, ethanol intoxication, salicylic acid intoxication, lactic acidosis, and uremia were ruled out based on drug and ethanol abuse history, kidney function tests, and blood glucose levels.
test_results: Brain tomography and MRI results were normal with no radiological pathological findings such as brain edema or atrophy, infarctions, or hemorrhages of the putamen. On ophthalmic examination there were light perception and light reflex in both eyes. The patient had no signs or symptoms of intoxication in funduscopic examination. Macula was normal, there was not cavity or pale of the optic nerve. The visual field examination was normal.

case_report: A 48-year-old woman, generally in good health, with occasional smoking habits and no family history of breast cancer, underwent a cosmetic bilateral mastopexy augmentation at age 28. She initially received 380 cc textured-surface implants placed in the sub-glandular plane. A year later, she opted for an implant exchange to 305 cc textured implants in the same plane, along with a re-mastopexy. Three years after that, she received 210 cc Allergan Biocell®-textured round TSM implants, again with a re-mastopexy. Ten years post-surgery, she experienced pain, swelling, and discomfort in her left breast without signs of infection or trauma. Ultrasound imaging of the left breast and fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of 50 cc serous fluid were performed, and the condition was deemed benign. Both implants and the surrounding inner capsule were removed, and a left breast outer capsulectomy was performed, with uneventful healing. No pathological review was conducted due to the absence of specimens. Six years later, she reported painful swelling in the upper left breast for three months, with no recent trauma, physical activity, or infection. Ultrasound identified a 9.5 cm sub-glandular fluid collection, and 100 cc of clear serous fluid was aspirated. Cytology indicated amorphous acellular material with no signs of malignancy. The seroma recurred three weeks after drainage. An intact seroma cavity was surgically removed with an en-bloc capsulectomy containing approximately 200 cc of serous fluid. The inner surface of the capsule showed a smooth luminal surface with fibrous tissue and fibrin cords, with no signs of free silicone or silicone granulomas.
test_results: The cytology report revealed the presence of large atypical cells positive for CD30 and CD3 and negative for ALK. The bacterial cultures from the serous fluid returned negative. The pathology report on the capsule described a fibrous tissue with a fibrinous covering, small-size lymphocytes, and clusters of large, atypical, invasive cells in the fibrous tissue. These cells exhibited positivity for CD30 and CD3 and negativity for ALK.
diagnosis: Breast Implant-Associated Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma

case_report: A 1-year-old female child, firstborn of second-degree consanguineous marriage, exhibited global developmental delay and experienced three episodes of seizures. There was an earlier episode of seizures at 2 months of age that was not evaluated. There was no history indicating infection or immunodeficiency. Dermatological examination showed hypopigmentation of the skin, silver-gray hair on the scalp, eyebrows, and eyelashes, with normal iris pigmentation. Blood tests, imaging studies, and peripheral smear results were normal.
test_results: Scalp hair microscopy revealed multiple irregular large clumps of melanin in the medulla of the hair shaft.

case_report: A 19-year-old male presented with exertional shortness of breath for 2 months and sought a second opinion at Samsung Medical Center. He had been prescribed ambrisentan and sildenafil from another hospital, but the treatment response was inadequate. Laboratory tests showed a brain natriuretic peptide level of 513.9 pg/mL. Echocardiography indicated a dilated right ventricular cavity, reduced right ventricular systolic function, normal left ventricular systolic function, and an estimated right ventricular systolic peak pressure of 53.5 mm Hg. The patient walked 371 meters in a 6-minute walk test. Chest computed tomography revealed diffusely scattered ground-glass opacity nodules in both lungs and an enlarged main pulmonary artery. Lung diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide was reduced to 25% of the predicted value. Right heart catheterization demonstrated severe pulmonary arterial hypertension with a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 57 mm Hg and a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8 mm Hg. A video-assisted thoracoscopic wedge resection was performed.
test_results: Histological examination showed interstitial capillary proliferation, mild interlobular septal fibrosis, and extensive interlobular septal edema.

case_report: A 61-year-old woman with a four-year history of diabetes experienced sudden onset of widespread swelling. Initial laboratory results showed hemoglobin at 8.7 g/dL, serum creatinine at 2.8 mg/dL, albumin at 2.7 g/dL, and normal serum protein electrophoresis. Urine routine microscopy revealed protein at 3+, RBC at 2-3/HPF, WBC at 2-3/HPF, and a 24-hour urine protein level of 14.3 g/day.
test_results: On LM, there was a mesangial expansion with diffuse nodular glomerulosclerosis involving all the glomeruli. These nodules were PAS positive, silver negative, and Congo negative. IF showed strong linear staining for IgG (4+) along the tubular basement membrane and blood vessels along with smudgy mesangial staining for IgG (4+), C3 (2+), and C1q (3+). There was only trace capillary wall staining for kappa and lambda. On EM, fine powdery deposits were also seen along the lamina rara interna of the glomerular basement membrane and within the mesangium.
