Bone marrow biopsy showed mild CD138-positive plasmacytosis (15-20%) with no light chain restriction seen on immunohistochemistry.

case_report: The patient is a 25-year-old woman, the first child of healthy first cousin parents, with a height of 156 cm and a body weight of 56 kg. She reported sparse hair and absence of menstruation. Her mother's pregnancy, delivery, and feeding history were normal. Her younger brother exhibited similar symptoms, including hair loss and underdeveloped gonads. Another younger brother passed away at 7 months old, and no genetic analysis was performed. Generations I and II above the patient's parents also passed away, and genetic analysis was not conducted. During childhood, her parents observed that her hair was sparser compared to other children. During adolescence, she did not develop secondary sexual characteristics, and menarche did not occur. Previous consultations revealed abnormal blood glucose levels, intellectual disability, hearing impairment, an immature uterus and ovaries with few follicles, and a bone age delayed by 9 years. Over a year of treatment with progynova, she experienced two menstrual cycles but ceased menstruating after stopping the medication. Physical examination upon admission showed sparse hair, particularly on both temporal sides and forehead. Her face appeared aged, with a large forehead and prominent ears. Secondary sexual characteristics were underdeveloped, with no axillary or pubic hair, minimal breast development, and significant vulvar underdevelopment. Unlike some patients described in earlier literature, she and her younger brother did not exhibit extrapyramidal movements such as hearing impairment, dyskinesia with oropharyngeal swallowing disorder, or difficulty walking. Her Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores were 22 and 19, respectively, indicating mental retardation. Neurological examination showed no dysarthria, dysphagia, tremor, or abnormal muscle tension; her coordination, posture, and gait were normal; muscle strength was normal, and Babinski sign was negative. Sex hormone tests revealed low estradiol (<5 pg/ml, reference range: 12.4–233 pg/ml) and low testosterone (<0.025 pg/ml, reference range: 0.07–0.78 pg/ml) levels, with normal follicle-stimulating hormone, prolactin, and luteinizing hormone levels. Other hormone tests showed high thyroid-stimulating hormone (6.36 uIU/ml, reference range: 0.27–4.2 uIU/ml), low free thyroxine (7.39 pmol/ml, reference range: 12–22 pmol/ml), and normal free triiodothyronine levels, suggestive of subclinical hypothyroidism. She had a low insulin growth factor 1 (IGF-1) level (45.7 ng/ml, reference range: 69–200 ng/ml) and a high HbA1c level (8.8%, reference range: 3.6–6%). Her C-peptide release test results were: 0 min: 2.25 ng/ml, 30 min: 2.43 ng/ml, 60 min: 2.99 ng/ml, and 120 min: 5.58 ng/ml. A transabdominal ultrasound showed an immature uterus and small ovaries. Breast ultrasound revealed tiny gland tissue in both breasts. A hearing assessment indicated bilateral mild sensorineural deafness. A left wrist X-ray showed epiphyseal closure. An electrocardiograph (ECG) was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a small pituitary, partially empty sella, no iron deposits in the globus pallidus, and multiple intracranial white matter hyperintensities possibly of vascular origin.
test_results: The patient’s DCAF17 harbored a homozygous mutation c.1111delA, p.(Ile371Term), her younger brother had the same mutation, and her parents were heterozygous for the mutation at this site. The c.1111delA mutation is a nonsense mutation leading to a premature stop codon p.(Ile371Term).

case_report: A 12-year-old male exhibited a distinct band of red hair located over the interparietal region, which had been noticeable since birth and had become more prominent over time. The remainder of his scalp hair, as well as his eyebrows and eyelashes, were brown. There was no history of trauma to the area, no treatments administered, and no signs of scalp inflammation. The scalp beneath the red hair appeared normal. The patient had no other health conditions, and the rest of the physical examination showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Light microscopy of both the red hair and brown hair showed light and dark segments under reflected light. The latter corresponded to areas of cavitation within the hair cortex which after exposure to a 10% potassium hydroxide solution, induced disappearance of the dark areas within 5 minutes. TEM of the hairs shafts showed a circular to oval cross-section. The cuticle consisted of a cobblestone pattern with overlapping cells. The microfibers composing the cortex of the red hair shafts presented large gaps between them.
diagnosis: Isolated Patchy Heterochromia with Pili Annulati

case_report: A nine-month-old male child was brought to the pediatric outpatient department with symptoms of irritability, fever, persistent crying, and facial swelling lasting for 15 days. Upon examination, the child was found to be febrile with diffuse swelling of the lower jaw that was tender to touch. There were no signs of inflammation in the skin or subcutaneous tissue over the swelling. The systemic examination did not reveal any abnormalities. Hematological tests showed hemoglobin at 12 g/dL, total leukocyte count at 12,600 cells/cc, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate at 120 mm/h. The child was administered a course of antibiotics. Despite the treatment, the child remained symptomatic and febrile with no change in symptoms. The mother later observed a diffuse bony swelling in the upper part of the front of the chest. Clinical examination revealed diffuse thickening of the left clavicle, which was also tender.
test_results: An X-ray of the skull revealed diffuse thickening of the mandible, with increased density. An X-ray of the chest revealed unremarkable lung fields and the heart with left clavicular thickening and sclerosis, with associated overlying soft tissue swelling. 99m Tc MDP Skeletal scintigraphy revealed diffusely increased uptake in both mandibles, with a similar uptake in both clavicles, while the rest of the skeleton showed no active pathological focus.

case_report: A 3-year-old girl, born to nonconsanguineous parents, exhibited developmental delay followed by regression and seizures. She was delivered at term via vaginal delivery without perinatal complications. Her developmental milestones were significantly delayed, and she had not achieved a pincer grasp. Seizures began at 15 months of age, initially presenting as focal seizures with impaired awareness, followed by generalized tonic seizures occurring once daily. The frequency of seizures gradually increased to six episodes per day, coinciding with a regression in developmental milestones. Physical examination revealed a normal head circumference, mild facial dysmorphism characterized by a prominent forehead and antimongloid slant of the palpebral fissures. Her height and weight were appropriate for her age. Auditory response was present, but visual response was poor despite a normal fundus examination. She exhibited truncal hypotonia with normal limb tone. Muscle strength was normal, but deep tendon reflexes were sluggish, and there was mild truncal ataxia. An electroencephalogram (EEG) showed multifocal epileptiform abnormalities, predominantly bifrontal, with a lack of generalized discharges, generalized paroxysmal fast activity, or burst attenuation patterns. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed a thickened, dysmorphic corpus callosum with a knob-like outpouching from the superior edge of the anterior half of the body, lacking the normal isthmic narrowing. There was thinning of the tectal plate with inconspicuous superior and inferior colliculi. The height of the pons was reduced, and the medulla appeared elongated with a straightened pontomedullary junction. The superior cerebellar peduncle was thin, with vermian atrophy and T2, FLAIR hyperintensities in the bilateral parieto-occipital regions. Metabolic screening, including tandem mass spectrometry and urine gas chromatography, yielded negative results.
test_results: Clinical exome sequencing revealed a homozygous single base pair duplication in exon 52 of the SZT2 gene (chr1: g.43907028dup; depth: 106×) resulting in a frameshift mutation and premature truncation of the protein, 18 amino acids downstream to codon 2440 (p. Asp2440ArgfsTer18; ENST00000562955.1).

case_report: A 6-year-old boy, born to nonconsanguineous Japanese parents, was delivered at 39 weeks and 6 days gestation, weighing 3,462 g. The pregnancy and family history were unremarkable. At 22 days old, he was hospitalized for pneumonia, during which jaundice and pale-colored stools were observed. Jaundice with a normal serum gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) level (28 U/L) improved with ursodeoxycholic acid treatment. The patient exhibited proteinuria, bilateral nerve deafness, motor delay, and failure to thrive. At 7 months old, upon referral to our hospital, his liver function test and serum bilirubin levels were normal, but he experienced severe itching with a high serum total bile acid level (115.0 μmol/L). His growth has been stable without significant infections. At 2 years old, during cochlear implantation for deafness, he had persistent bleeding despite normal platelet count (584 x 103/μL), platelet morphology, and PT-INR (0.85), necessitating hematoma removal post-operation. He did not exhibit arthrogryposis.
test_results: Using targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS), compound heterozygous mutations were detected in VPS33B [NM_018668.4:c.403+2T>A in intron 6 and c.1582-9C>G in intron 20]. cDNA generated from mRNA, which was extracted from whole blood, was sequenced. It was found that c.1582-9C>G mutation disrupts splicing, which generates cDNA with an abnormal insertion of an 8-bp intronic sequence after exon 20 and results in a premature stop codon. Western blotting was then performed to confirm the effects of the mutations on protein expression. The VPS33B protein was not detected in the leukocytes of the patient using the VPS33B antibody (sc-398322, Santa Cruz), which recognizes amino acids 271–570 of VPS33B.

case_report: A 59-year-old male patient presented with extensive hair loss on the right side of the scalp, which had been progressively worsening over several years. The patient also noted the occasional presence of firmly adhering scales in the affected area. There were no reports of itching, burning, or pain. The patient had a recent history of arterial hypertension, managed with oral medication. Physical examination revealed a hairless area covering half of the occipital and nuchal scalp. Dermoscopy showed scarring alopecia with loss of adnexal structures. A full body examination identified follicular hyperkeratotic papules on both lower legs, along with comedones and cysts on the abdomen. Regional lymph nodes were not palpable. Laboratory tests, including a full blood count, liver, kidney, and thyroid function tests, as well as C-reactive protein (CRP) and an antinuclear antibody screen (ANA titer), were all within normal limits.
test_results: Biopsies of the capillitium, lower leg, and abdomen showed epidermotropism and folliculotropism of lymphocytes with destruction of hair follicles. Molecular histoanalysis revealed a T-cell receptor clone with the same rearrangement pattern at all three locations of biopsies.

case_report: A 6-year-old boy was admitted due to delayed speech, poor growth, and leg weakness. He was born at 32 weeks' gestation via cesarean section, weighing 1.8 kg. He experienced slow weight gain and constipation starting at 6 months old. By age 4, he had difficulty walking and presented with thin legs. He has two older sisters and one older brother, none of whom have similar issues. His vital signs were stable. He was notably short, measuring 95 cm and weighing 15.6 kg, both below the 3rd percentile. Laboratory tests revealed normal complete blood cell count, hypokalemia, hyperchloremia, normal serum calcium, decreased serum phosphate, and significantly elevated alkaline phosphatase. Mild metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap was noted. Urine tests indicated decreased chloride excretion, a positive urine anion gap, and significant hypercalciuria in a 24-hour urine sample. Thyroid function was normal. Levels of 25-hydroxy vitamin D and 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D were low, while parathyroid hormone levels were normal. Imaging showed diffuse osteopenia, fraying in the distal radius, and fractures in the left tibia and both fibulae. Lumbar bone mineral density was reduced. Brain MRI was normal. Brainstem auditory evoked potential indicated no significant sensorineural hearing loss, with a threshold of 20 dB bilaterally. Electromyography and nerve conduction studies showed no clear electrophysiological abnormalities.
test_results: Arterial blood gas analysis showed mild metabolic acidosis, with a normal anion gap. Urine electrolytes showed decreased chloride excretion, with a positive urine anion gap and marked hypercalciuria in 24-hour urine. A skeletal survey showed diffuse osteopenia, fraying in the distal radius and fracture of the left tibia and both fibulae. Lumbar bone mineral density was decreased in dual energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA). Kidney ultrasonography showed increased echogenecity in renal parenchyma bilaterally. Abdomen and pelvis computerized tomography showed multiple calcified nodules in both renal parenchymae and thinning of the renal cortex.

case_report: Case 1 involved a 1-year-old Japanese girl with a congenital skin lesion located on the parietal region of the scalp. The patient was in good health overall and had no notable family medical history. The lesion consisted of a group of hyperkeratotic, brownish papules accompanied by hair loss, exhibiting a cobblestone-like texture.
test_results: Trichoscopic examination revealed heavily rolled hairs within papules. Skin biopsy of the lesion revealed rolled hairs embedded in follicular plugs and a dilated hair follicle infundibulum.

case_report: A 28-year-old female reported experiencing pain and swelling in the left leg for the past 2 years. The pain and swelling began gradually. There was no history of trauma or similar conditions in her family. Physical examination revealed diffuse swelling over the proximal third of the left leg, characterized by an irregular surface and bony hard consistency, which was tender upon palpation. The skin over the swelling was thickened, with no warmth detected. Knee and ankle joint movements were normal compared to the other side. No other abnormalities were found in the rest of the body.
test_results: Plain radiographs of the left leg showed extensive, dense, irregular cortical hyperostosis, resembling dripping candle wax, extending along the medial border of shaft of the tibia from proximal third to middle third with narrowing of the medullary canal. The plain radiograph of the opposite leg and arms was found to be normal. MRI showed extensive homogenous osteoid overgrowth in the cortex which encroached into the medullary cavity. No evidence of any associated vascular malformation or soft-tissue involvement or pathological fracture identified. Bone scan and SPECT revealed increased uptake along with the extent of the lesion in the left leg. Laboratory findings of ESR, C-reactive protein, α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, calcium, phosphorus, and alkaline phosphatase were all within normal limits.

case_report: A 16-year-old female, born at full term with a birth weight of 3,398 g (90th percentile), was evaluated. The pregnancy was largely uneventful except for the maternal use of Macrodantin for a urinary tract infection. At the time of evaluation, the patient exhibited short stature (10th-25th percentile), generalized hypotonia, global developmental delays, significant hearing loss, and truncal obesity. Behavioral observations included sleep disturbances, skin picking, and toenail removal. Chromosome analyses for fragile-X syndrome and Prader-Willi syndrome were normal.
test_results: DNA sequencing identified a c.3103insC, located within the same heptameric C-tract in exon 3 of RAI1.

case_report: An 11-month-old male patient visited our pediatric department in September 2014 due to rectal prolapse and intermittent bloody stools. He exhibited a protruding reddish mass with occasional fibrous and purulent discharge from the anus. The patient was delivered via cesarean section at 38 weeks of gestation, with a birth weight of 3,890 g. He had received all scheduled vaccinations. At 10 months old, he was diagnosed with an epidermal nevus in the sacral area, confirmed through biopsy at our hospital. There was no family history of gastrointestinal polyps or carcinomas reported by the parents. The patient did not experience constipation or diarrhea, and his growth was normal. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin at 12.7 g/dL, hematocrit at 37.6%, platelets at 227,000/μL, protein at 6.8 g/dL, and albumin at 4.7 g/dL. Serum levels of tumor markers, including carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), α-fetoprotein (AFP), and CA 19-9, were within normal ranges. Thyroid function tests were normal. Plain radiographs of the abdomen and chest were normal. Abdominal and pelvic CT scans revealed multiple well-enhanced polypoid lesions, each approximately 1 cm in size, located 4 to 6 cm above the anal verge, along with enlargement of regional lymph nodes and lymph nodes in both iliac chain areas. Brain MRI showed normal findings. A barium enema study identified several polypoid lesions without stalks in the anus, while a barium swallow study indicated normal stomach and small bowel. Anorectal manometry demonstrated normal rectal and anal pressure, with a normal rectoanal inhibitory reflex.
test_results: Colonoscopy revealed variously sized polypoid lesions without stalks in the anus. Histological findings revealed reactive lymphoid hyperplasia and multiple polyps with hyperplastic crypts covered with granulation tissue, and showing dystrophic calcification.

case_report: A 13-year-old girl presented to the Department of Pedodontics and Preventive Dentistry with a primary concern of missing teeth. The patient had a history of vision loss and hearing impairment. Intraoral examination revealed pale oral mucosa and a small sequestrum on the left side of the mandible. Abdominal sonography indicated spleen enlargement measuring 16.28 × 8.6 cm with a homologous echo texture. The liver, gallbladder, and kidneys were of normal size, and no lymphadenopathy was observed. Histopathologic examination of the soft tissue attached to a malformed tooth suggested a dentigerous cyst. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin at 9 mg%, white blood cell count at 2.3 × 10^9/L, differential leukocyte count with 70% neutrophils and 30% lymphocytes. Serum chemistry results included chloride at 106 mg/L and alkaline phosphatase at 8.0 KA unit/dL.
test_results: The skull radiograph and radiograph of left mandible (oblique lateral view) showed increased bone density. The OPG showed that all permanent tooth bud remained totally or partly embedded in basal bone. Vertical growth of alveolar ridge was very limited. Where a fenestration of overlaying mucosa had occurred, a localized, progressive osteitis developed leading to soft tissue inflammation.

case_report: A 10-month-old girl with a history of tonsilopharyngitis and bilateral inborn hip dysplasia, which had shown improvement, was under the care of an orthopaedist. She was admitted to the hospital due to a one-day history of fever and positive urinary findings, including ketone bodies, proteins, leukocytes, and blood. She was born at full term following a normal pregnancy and had an uncomplicated perinatal and neonatal period. There was no history of gross hematuria or colicky abdominal pain, and she had not received any medication other than antipyretics. The family history was negative for renal and metabolic diseases, including urolithiasis and nephrocalcinosis, although genetic counseling revealed that the parents share common ancestors in the fourth generation. On physical examination, the child appeared mildly dehydrated with a body temperature of 37.6 °C. Laboratory tests showed moderate anemia (hemoglobin 93.0 g/l), leukocytosis (15x10^9/l), and moderately elevated CRP (42.6 mg/l). Serum electrolyte, urea, and creatinine levels were normal. The calcium/creatinine ratio and 24-hour calcium excretion were within the reference range. Blood gas analysis was normal with no signs of metabolic acidosis. Abdominal ultrasonography suggested the presence of a stone in the left ureter. Cystourethrography confirmed a 2 cm x 0.8 cm stone in the distal part of the left ureter with mild dilatation of the renal pelvis and ureter. At 11 months of age, the patient underwent ureterolithotomy at the University Children Hospital Bratislava.
test_results: The stone was characterised as a composite of virtually pure calcium oxalate.

case_report: A 60-year-old female presented with elevated hemoglobin levels ranging from 16 to 17 g/dL over a period of at least 13 years. She does not smoke and has no known cardiac or pulmonary conditions. There is no family history of elevated hemoglobin levels. Physical examination findings were unremarkable. Oxygen saturation was measured at 99% on room air, and carboxyhemoglobin levels were less than 1%. The P50 value was 29 mm Hg (normal range: 24-30 mm Hg). Hemoglobin electrophoresis did not reveal any high-affinity hemoglobin variants. Erythropoietin levels were recorded at 11 mU/mL (normal range: 2.6-18.5 mU/mL). Additional evaluations for potential secondary causes, including a transthoracic echocardiogram with bubble study, sleep study, pulmonary function tests, and abdominal ultrasound, showed normal results. Peripheral blood PCR testing for JAK2 mutations in exons 12 to 14 was negative. Due to the persistent elevated hemoglobin levels with no identifiable cause, further genetic testing was conducted.
test_results: EGLN1 gene sequencing revealed a heterozygous missense mutation on exon 3 at c.1132C>T, resulting in amino acid substitution p.Pro378Ser (p.P378S).
diagnosis: Isolated Erythrocytosis associated with EGLN1 gene mutation

case_report: A 25-year-old female presented with a primary concern of gum enlargement persisting for several years. The patient reported that the gum enlargement began in childhood and gradually increased to its current size. Family history indicated that her father experienced similar gum enlargement, while her mother and elder sister did not exhibit such symptoms. Extraoral examination showed the patient had strabismus, a bulbous nose, prominent maxilla and mandible, and thick lips. The patient also exhibited hypertrichosis with terminal hairs on the legs and back, as well as vellus hair on the face and other body parts. Cutaneous pigmentation was noted on the feet. Intellectual and adaptive functioning were impaired. Intraoral examination revealed fair oral hygiene with multiple carious lesions, macroglossia, a high arched palate, and a skeletal open bite. There was grade III gingival enlargement on the buccal aspect of all maxillary teeth, characterized by diffuse, noninflammatory, and nonhemorrhagic involvement of the marginal, attached, and interdental gingiva. The gingiva appeared pink with areas of physiological melanin pigmentation, rounded margins, and a leathery consistency upon palpation. The surface texture was smooth with exaggerated stippling, and the gingiva was positioned coronal to the cementoenamel junction. Pseudopockets were observed in the upper anterior region without bleeding on probing. An orthopantomogram showed no bone pathology. Hematological and biochemical tests were performed, and the results were within normal limits, indicating the patient was systemically healthy. Upon examination of her family members, her father exhibited poor oral hygiene with similar gingival enlargement in the buccal and palatal/lingual aspects of the posterior teeth in both arches, while her mother and sibling showed no symptoms.
test_results: The sequence obtained was compared with the reference genome in the database. Multiple sequence alignment using the Clustal Omega software did not show any prominent variations between the samples. Hence, nonsyndromic HGF was ruled out.

case_report: A 52-year-old woman visited the surgery outpatient department at Lok Nayak Hospital, Maulana Azad Medical College, New Delhi, with complaints of abdominal pain in the epigastric and left hypochondriac regions. The pain was dull and aching, worsened by eating, and accompanied by non-bilious vomiting, hematemesis, and melena for the past 18 months. She also experienced abdominal distension, generalized body swelling, easy fatiguability, early satiety, reduced appetite, and significant weight loss over the past six months. Physical examination revealed severe pallor, anasarca, facial puffiness, and a firm 10 x 7 cm palpable lump in the epigastric, umbilical, and left hypochondriac regions, which moved with respiration and could not be insinuated in the subcostal region. Chest auscultation indicated tachycardia with an ejection systolic murmur. Routine blood tests showed a hemoglobin level of 1.5 gm% with a peripheral smear indicating a microcytic hypochromic picture, hypoproteinemia of 3.7 g/dl, and hypoalbuminemia of 1.9 mg/dl. Other blood tests were unremarkable. Ultrasonography revealed extensive diffuse thickening of the stomach wall, with a maximum thickness of 2.7 cm and increased internal vascularity with both arterial and venous blood flow. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed gross circumferential asymmetric gastric wall thickening involving the cardia, fundus, and body (lesser curvature > greater curvature), sparing the pylorus, with homogenous enhancement and aneurysmal dilatation of the stomach and passage of contrast distally. Adjacent fat planes were maintained, and multiple small perigastric and celiac lymph nodes were present. Multiple non-enhancing nodules were diffusely scattered in the spleen. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed proliferative growth in the stomach extending into the fundus and proximal body, with a few erosions and extensive growth sparing the antrum and pylorus. Multiple biopsies were taken, and histopathology showed benign follicular hyperplasia.
test_results: Microscopic examination of multiple sections showed significant foveolar hyperplasia, tortuous glands, and a few cystically dilated foveolar glands, which were limited up to the muscle layer. Mild serosal congestion was seen. No atypia or invasion was seen.

case_report: A 46-year-old woman presented with nausea, vomiting, and generalized weakness for 2–3 weeks, accompanied by body swelling. Evaluation showed severe renal dysfunction, leading to the initiation of hemodialysis. Urine examination indicated 1+ protein and 3-4 RBCs, with a urine PCR of 2.48. She continued maintenance hemodialysis after the placement of a left-arm AV fistula. She sought renal transplantation at our hospital, with her younger brother as the prospective donor. Both siblings had a history of hearing impairment since childhood. Family history revealed hearing impairment in their father and another younger brother. Further investigations identified sensorineural hearing loss and dot and fleck retinopathy in both siblings. The brother did not exhibit proteinuria or renal dysfunction, and neither had a history of hematuria. Kidney biopsy of the patient showed nodular glomerulosclerosis with congophilic deposits in the mesangium and arterioles, displaying apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Immunofluorescence was negative, and kappa/Lambda did not show any restriction.
test_results: Genetic analysis revealed mutation in NLRP3 gene in both patient and her brother. The variant identified was c.1049 C>T p.Thr350Met.

case_report: A 34-year-old male was referred to the International Center of Immunodeficiency Diseases (ICID) in January 2011 with low levels of immunoglobulins, identified after a severe case of pneumococcal meningitis that required intensive care unit hospitalization the previous month. The patient, who had undergone splenectomy due to immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), experienced a rapid and severe progression of the disease despite prior oral penicillin treatment. In the intensive care unit, he received standard antibiotic therapy, including intravenous penicillin and ceftriaxone, as well as dexamethasone. He recovered without neurological deficits. However, persistently low serum levels of IgG (2.6 g/L, normal range 6.1 g/L - 14.9 g/L) and IgA (0.14 g/L, normal range 0.80 g/L – 3.90 g/L) were noted, while IgM levels remained normal (0.73 g/L, normal range 0.39 g/L – 2.08 g/L). The patient had been diagnosed with ITP at 11 years old in 1987, presenting with severe thrombocytopenia (3 × 10^9 cells/L), mild leukopenia (2.2 × 10^9 cells/L), and lymphadenopathy. Peripheral blood smear, bone marrow biopsy, and lymph node biopsy showed normal histology. His pediatric medical records indicated no increased frequency of bacterial infections during childhood, and no family history of immunodeficiencies or autoimmune diseases. He was treated with thrombocyte infusions and intravenous immunoglobulin (0.4 g/kg), followed by a three-week course of corticosteroids (2 mg/kg), resulting in a rapid increase in thrombocyte count. Immunoglobulin levels were not measured at that time. Due to multiple relapses of severe thrombocytopenia with each tapering of corticosteroid treatment, he underwent splenectomy in 1988. Hepato-splenomegaly was observed during the surgery, and pathological evaluation of the spleen showed hyperplasia without malignancy. In 2001, several accessory spleens were identified scintigraphically but were not removed. Over the following years, he was monitored at the University Hospital Department of Hematology, experiencing several episodes of severe thrombocytopenia with bruises and petechiae, each time responding immediately but temporarily to high-dose corticosteroid treatment. Lymph node biopsy due to persistent lymphadenopathy again showed benign hyperplasia. Due to inadequate response to repeated high-dose corticosteroid courses (100 mg daily), the patient was treated in January 2009 with four doses of Rituximab (375 mg/m2 iv.) one week apart, resulting in normalization of thrombocyte counts and a sustained response for 36 months. With stable platelet counts and being a medical doctor, his follow-ups with the Hematology Department were limited to e-mails based on biannual platelet counts. After a vacation in Mallorca in December 2010, the patient returned with an upper respiratory tract infection, diarrhea, and vomiting. He developed high fevers and confusion, leading to admission to the Department of Infectious Diseases, where pneumococcal meningitis was identified. He became unconscious within hours, requiring transfer to the Intensive Care Unit on mechanical ventilation, where he received ten days of antibiotic treatment and recovered successfully. At the ICID presentation in January 2011, it was noted that the patient had experienced multiple infections over the past two years since Rituximab treatment in January 2009, including frequent upper airway infections and gastrointestinal symptoms such as daily discomfort and diarrhea. His pediatric medical records confirmed appropriate vaccination before splenectomy and adherence to pneumococcal antibody status monitoring and re-vaccination as recommended.
test_results: At evaluation in January 2011, flow cytometry revealed a severely reduced fraction (0.1%) of isotype-switched memory B cells (CD19/20+ IgD- IgM- CD38- CD27+). Additionally, selective reductions in marginal zone-like B cells (CD19/20+ IgD + IgM + CD38- CD27+) and absence of plasmablasts (CD19+ CD20- IgD- IgM+/− CD38+ CD27+) were observed. Within the T cell compartment only minor abnormalities were demonstrated, including a major, and possibly increased fraction of 15% of CD4- CD8- double negative T cells (normal range 4–11%), a slightly decreased fraction of naïve cells among CD4 T cells, and a bias towards a terminally differentiated memory fraction among CD8 T cells.

case_report: A 37-year-old female presented with a three-year history of infertility and mild pelvic pain. She had no significant surgical, family, drug, or allergic history, and no history of malignancy. Pelvic ultrasound showed multiple fluid collections in the pelvis and free fluid in the Douglas pouch. The left ovary was surrounded by a fluid collection. Inflammatory markers, including serum C-reactive protein (CRP), were within normal limits. Cancer antigen-125 (CA-125) serum level was 77 UI/mL, while carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) and CA 19-9 levels were normal. Based on the clinical presentation, laboratory results, and ultrasound findings, further surgical intervention was performed.
test_results: Laparoscopy showed mucus deposits on the peritoneal surfaces; mucinous material covered the uterus, both ovaries, pouch of Douglas, right and left paracolic gutters, diaphragm dome, and liver surface. Uterus and both ovaries had normal morphology and size. The appendix was retro-cecal and dilated with perforated walls from which came out gelatinous material. No other abnormalities were found in the abdominopelvic cavity. Peritoneal lavage was carried out. Peritoneal biopsies and appendectomy were performed. Pathology reported a low-grade appendiceal mucinous tumor limited to the mucosa without submucosal infiltration, without vascular invasion, with perforation of the wall and deposits of periappendicular acellular mucin. Peritoneal biopsies showed deposits of mucus material with macrophages, reactive mesothelial cells in a mucus substratum without visible tumor epithelial cells. Peritoneal washing was without atypical cells.

case_report: A 10-year-old girl exhibited thickened skin on her palms and soles since early childhood. Her parents observed yellowish, thickened skin lesions around her mouth starting from her first year. She experienced difficulty walking and holding objects due to the thick and cracked skin on her soles and palms. She is the first child from a non-consanguineous marriage, and her family members, including parents and siblings, do not exhibit similar symptoms. Physical examination revealed sharply defined, yellowish, thickened plaques around the mouth and widespread thickening of the skin on the palms and soles. Similar thickened plaques were present on the outer sides of her knees and elbows. The nails on both her hands and feet were abnormally formed, while her hair appeared normal. No abnormalities were found in her oral cavity.
test_results: Skin biopsy from palm revealed massive hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and papillomatosis. Histopathology of a keratotic papule showed acanthosis, suprabasal cleft and inflammatory infiltrate in dermis.

case_report: A 32-year-old female presented with severe pain in the right temporomandibular joint (TMJ) region, right ear, limited mouth opening, and facial asymmetry. She was born at full term via spontaneous vaginal delivery without perinatal or notable postnatal issues. Her parents noticed progressive enlargement of her right cheek and differing eyelid width in the months following birth. The facial asymmetry became more pronounced over the years but has remained stable recently. No other family members are affected, and her mother reported a normal pregnancy. The enlargement extended from the midline to the preauricular region and down to the lower border of the mandible. The skin on the right side of the face appeared normal with no changes in thickness. Extraoral examination showed that the right side of the mandible was larger than the left. The outer contour of the right ear was slightly larger and differently shaped compared to the left ear. The nose was normal with no deviation, but the chin was deviated toward the right side. The lower lip on the right side appeared thicker with drooping at the corner of the mouth, and the lips on the right side were very dry. The patient reported clicking in the left TMJ, difficulty chewing, and headaches on the right side. Physical examination revealed a normal symmetric body and mental health. The mouth opening was 12 mm. Intraoral examination showed tongue asymmetry with unilateral enlargement of fungiform papillae on the right side. The teeth on the affected side appeared normal except for the maxillary right first molar, which was significantly larger than the maxillary left first molar. The lower right first molar was slightly larger than the lower left first molar. The lower dental centerline was deviated to the right, and there was a downward canting of the occlusal plane. Occlusal examination revealed unattainable central relation, early contact in both central occlusion and right lateral movement, and a discrepancy in the range of mandibular motion. The patient was referred for further evaluation.
test_results: The radiographs confirmed the clinical findings. The panoramic radiograph showed that the right condyle, ramus, condylar neck, and the body of the mandible were enlarged. There was significant deposition of bone growth on the right mandible, and the bony trabeculation alteration was observed. The size of the right inferior dental canal was normal compared to the left mandibular canal and was displaced. Crowns and roots of the right mandibular molars were larger than the contralateral mandibular molars. The roots of the lower right first and second molars were remarkably divergent. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) images of the face and skull revealed that the zygomatic and frontal bones, right mastoid process, right half of the mandible and maxilla, maxillary sinus, and associated soft tissues were enlarged. CBCT also demonstrated thickening the mucosal membrane of the right maxillary sinus. There was no obstruction in the sinus meatus. Brain computed tomography (CT) showed no abnormalities. 3D skull reconstruction CT image revealed hypertrophy of the right mandible, condyle, TMJ, zygomatic bone, petrous bone, and mastoid process. The posteroanterior radiograph revealed enlargement of right half of the mandible, maxilla, and zygoma.

case_report: Patient 1, a six-month-old boy, was admitted to the hospital in April 2014 presenting with low platelet count, lung infections, bleeding, and bruising. Due to fever, low platelet count, and upper respiratory tract infection, the patient received treatment with dexamethasone sodium phosphate and γ-globulin. Following this treatment, his platelet count increased to 164 × 10^9/L, and the respiratory infection was managed. The patient was subsequently discharged. Two months later, his platelet count dropped to 42 × 10^9/L, and he experienced recurrent infections, intermittent bleeding, and frequent eczema.
test_results: The complete blood count showed the following findings: hemoglobin (Hb), 110 g/L (120–140 g/L), white blood cell (WBC), 6.74 × 109/L (3.5–9.5 × 109/L), platelet (PLT) count, 14 × 109/L (125–350 × 109/L); and mean platelet volume (MPV), 6.9 fl (7.4–11.0 fl). Blood examination showed leukocytosis of 22.82 × 109/L with hematophagocytes in the bone marrow aspirate. The liver function test indicated the following findings: alanine transaminase (ALT), 113.5 U/L (9.0–50.0 U/L), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), 2 U/L (15.0–40.0 U/L), gamma glutamyl transferase (γ-GT), 137 U/L (10.0–60.0 U/L), triglycerides (TG), 2.67 mmol/L (0.56–1.70 mmol/L); cholesterol (CHO), 6.16 mmol/L (3.11–5.20 mmol/L).

case_report: A 44-year-old male reported experiencing generalized itching for the past 5 years. He also noted swelling and pain in both knees, ankles, and small joints of the hands, with symptoms worsening after exercise. He denied having fever or other related symptoms. There was no relevant family history. Additionally, he experienced persistent dyspepsia for the past 6 months, which did not improve with medication. Physical examination showed greasy and coarse skin with deep furrows on the forehead. Both eyelids exhibited ptosis, and there was hyperhidrosis of the palms and soles. The patient had generalized seborrheic dermatitis and multiple folliculitis on both lower limbs. Examination also revealed pandigital clubbing and bulbous deformity of all digits of the hands and feet. Routine blood and urine tests, including S. VDRL, were unremarkable.
test_results: Radiograph of both hands and wrists showed increase in soft-tissue around terminal phalanges with hypertrophy of distal tufts and periosteal thickening in all metacarpals including proximal and middle phalanges. Radiograph of both feet revealed similar changes. X-ray of both forearm showed symmetric exuberant irregular sub-periosteal bone formation with cortical thickening in both radius and ulna. There was interosseus membrane ossification in Lt fore-arm. X-ray of both tibia and fibula showed gross irregularities and intense periosteal proliferation throughout the shaft including epiphysis and resultant broadening of the epiphysis. Lateral radiograph of skull revealed normal sella turcica and hyperostosis of skull bones. Chest radiograph was found to be normal. 99mTc MDP bone scintigraphy shows diffusely increased and almost symmetrical peri-cortical uptake in the entire skeletal system prominently involving the shaft of all long bones. Upper gastro intestinal endoscopy showed hypertrophied mucosal folds involving the entire stomach and antrum. CECT abdomen revealed uniform increase in stomach wall thickness >1 cm. His skin biopsy showed thickening and packing of collagen fibres in dermis.

case_report: A 14-year-old adopted female with a history of anxiety, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) presented to her gynecologist with six months of diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal pain, shortness of breath, and intermittent fevers. She had been under the care of a pediatrician and pediatric gastroenterologist. Previous treatments included an increased dose of a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor for anxiety and omeprazole for GERD, which did not alleviate her symptoms. At the gynecologist visit, she reported new left lower quadrant pain and increased nausea. The pain was described as dull and non-radiating. Her mother reported episodes of rapid breathing during sleep. The patient denied vaginal discharge, foul odor, dysuria, hematuria, constipation, bloody diarrhea, chest pain, or recent illness. Vitals were within normal limits. Physical examination showed mild tenderness in the epigastric and left lower quadrant areas. A pregnancy test was negative, and urinalysis was unremarkable. Ultrasonography showed a normal uterus and ovaries with free fluid present. The patient was referred to the emergency department for further evaluation. In the emergency department, a portable anteroposterior chest x-ray revealed cardiomegaly with a left lower lobe infiltrate. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen/pelvis showed small-volume pelvic ascites and four-chamber cardiomegaly. An electrocardiogram indicated sinus rhythm, left axis deviation, right ventricular hypertrophy, and T-wave inversion in lateral leads. Bloodwork revealed elevated liver, cardiac, and muscle enzymes: aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 290 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) at 402 U/L, creatine kinase at 732 U/L, troponin I at 1.83, and B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) at 12,139 pg/mL. A pediatric echocardiogram showed a dilated left ventricle with reduced systolic function, moderate mitral valve insufficiency, hypertrophied right ventricle, mild tricuspid regurgitation, and global hypokinesis. Cardiac measurements indicated interventricular septum thickness diastolic (IVSTd) at 1.2 cm, left atrial dimension (LAD) at 46.5 mm, left ventricular end-diastolic diameter (LVDd) at 6.5 cm, and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) at 17.5%. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed moderate to severe left ventricular cavity dilatation and severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction with multiple regional wall motion abnormalities. The ejection fraction of the left and right ventricles were 14% and 23%, respectively. There was scarring at the basal right ventricle (RV) septum/anteroseptal to the left ventricle (LV), mid-inferior RV septum, diaphragmatic aspect of the RV, LV, and apical RV free wall, suggestive of myocardial infarctions in the distribution of all three major coronary arteries.
test_results: Genetic testing demonstrated a sequence change in the LAMP2 gene, c.815T>G in exon 6, which results in an amino acid change p.Leu272Arg.

case_report: A 14-year-old male was born following an uneventful pregnancy and delivery. His early motor development was within normal limits. At 3 years old, he began experiencing difficulties with walking and climbing stairs. By age 12, he required assistance to walk. Neurologic examination at age 13 revealed symmetrical weakness in the proximal muscles of both upper and lower limbs, reduced deep tendon reflexes, inability to walk unassisted, and mild scoliosis. He also had a mild intellectual disability necessitating special education. Serum creatine kinase (CK) levels ranged from 1891 to 5002 UI/L (normal values up to 170 UI/L). A brain MRI performed at 13 years and six months showed no abnormalities. Ophthalmologic evaluation was unremarkable. Electrocardiogram results were normal, while an echocardiogram identified a secundum atrial septal defect.
test_results: We identified the same homozygous missense mutation in POMT2.

case_report: A 42-year-old male presented with a history of progressive muscle weakness and atrophy, beginning at age 10. Initial symptoms included frequent falls, thinning of the calves, and difficulty walking long distances. Over time, he developed ankle joint contractures and worsening muscle atrophy, particularly in the lower extremities. By age 30, he required a wheelchair. In the past five years, he experienced poor fine motor skills, hand muscle atrophy, and difficulty holding objects. His intellectual abilities, initially normal, declined over time, affecting writing and numeracy skills, and he developed hearing loss after age 15. Physical examination revealed a thin body, scoliosis, and wheelchair dependence. Neurological examination showed significant reductions in memory, calculation, and executive function, with a Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score of 16. Speech was not fluent, but bilateral pupils were equal and reactive to light, facial symmetry was intact, and there was no tongue muscle atrophy. Hearing loss was noted. Mild atrophy of the bilateral scapular muscles and significant atrophy of the forearm and extremity muscles, especially the calves, were observed. Muscle strength was graded as 4 in the proximal upper extremities, 3 in the distal upper extremities, and 2 in the lower extremities. Muscle tone was low, tendon reflexes were absent, and both deep and superficial sensations were diminished. Pathological and meningeal irritation signs were negative. Neurophysiological examination indicated axonal polyneuropathy in both upper and lower limbs, with absent motor action potentials in the lower limbs and significantly reduced amplitudes in the upper limbs. Sensory nerve action potentials were absent. Electromyography showed denervation potentials and reduced motor unit potentials in affected muscles. The Charcot-Marie-Tooth Examination Score was 24. Family history revealed that the proband's brother exhibited more severe symptoms. Fourteen individuals from a four-generation Han-Chinese family were enrolled for genetic screening. Peripheral venous blood samples from three family members were collected for genetic analysis. All participants provided informed consent, and the study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Affiliated Hospital of Yangzhou University.
test_results: We performed whole exon sequencing on the proband and parents and screened for novel missense variants (NM_004208: c.931C>G: p.L311V) in AIFM1, which was validated by Sanger sequencing in the proband. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the mother of the proband (III-5) also carried the variant (NM_004208: c.931C>G: p.L311V). The variant is c.931C>G, and the protein change occurs at position 311, converting leucine to valine acid.

case_report: A 22-year-old male, born to non-consanguineous parents, reported erectile dysfunction and absence of spontaneous morning erections for six months, while maintaining normal libido. He experienced irregular bowel movements, including nocturnal diarrhea for three months, and recurrent dizziness upon standing from a lying position. Additional symptoms included occasional palpitations, gustatory sweating, reduced sweating, and tingling and numbness in both distal extremities. He had persistent eye redness and itching for six months, along with decreased tear production while crying for two years. There was no history of nausea, vomiting, difficulty swallowing, limb weakness or thinning, nasal voice, vision problems, or nasal regurgitation of food. He had no past history of seizures, shock, hypoglycemia, or major illnesses such as tuberculosis, nor similar episodes in childhood. He was not on any regular medication. His family history was unremarkable. Clinical examination revealed hyperpigmentation of the skin, particularly in the creases of the palms and soles, and buccal mucosa. Both eyes were congested. Testicular volume was normal (18 ml bilaterally), and secondary sexual characteristics were present (pubic hair Tanner stage P5, axillary hair present). His resting pulse rate was 104/min, and blood pressure was 122/84 mmHg in a supine position, with a postural drop to 90/64 mmHg upon standing, without compensatory tachycardia on repeated occasions. Neurological examination showed normal higher mental function, cranial nerves, cerebellar functions, pupillary reflex, and fundoscopy. Muscle tone was normal with no muscle wasting or fasciculations. Tendon reflexes were normal except for diminished ankle jerks bilaterally. Bilateral flexor plantar responses were noted. Decreased pinprick and vibration senses were observed distally in both hands and feet. Laboratory results showed normal complete blood count, ESR, blood urea, serum creatinine, calcium, magnesium, and liver function tests. Fasting blood glucose was 80 mg/dl, with normal serum sodium (139 meq/l) and potassium (3.8 meq/l). Serum cortisol was low at 1.8 mcg/dl (normal range 6.2-19.4), and 8 AM plasma adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH) was significantly elevated at 1871 pg/ml (normal range 7.2-63.3 pg/ml).
test_results: Synthetic ACTH (synacthen) stimulation test failed to raise the plasma cortisol-3.4 mcg/dl (normal>18). Nerve conduction velocity (NCV) study of all four limbs suggested distal motor polyneuropathy with axonopathy with features of sensorimotor neuropathy. Schirmer’s test was positive, 4mm (normal > 10mm) but tear film break-up time was normal confirming the diagnosis of alacrima. A barium swallow esophagus showed narrowing of the lower esophageal sphincter constriction with dilatation of the esophagus above suggestive of achalasia cardia. Esophageal manometry revealed mean resting LES pressure >60 and absent relaxation to wet swallows. There were simultaneous contractions to wet swallow and spontaneous esophageal body contractions confirming the diagnosis of achalasia.

case_report: A 2-month-old male infant developed pneumonia with atelectasis and exhibited increasing abdominal distension and facial puffiness. At 5 months of age, he was referred to Seoul National University Children's Hospital. His height was 67.5 cm (50-75th percentile) and his weight was 8.5 kg (50-75th percentile). Physical examination revealed hepatomegaly extending 3 cm below the costal margin. Laboratory results showed hemoglobin at 9.6 g/dL (reference range, 13-17 g/dL), white blood cell count at 8,400/µL (reference range, 4,000-10,000/µL), and platelet count at 591×10^3/µL (reference range, 130-400×10^3/µL). Liver function tests indicated elevated serum aspartate transaminase at 248 U/L (reference range, 0-40 U/L) and alanine transaminase at 109 U/L (reference range, 0-40 U/L). Fasting glucose level was 20 mg/dL (reference range, 70-110 mg/dL). Liver sonography revealed fatty liver with hepatomegaly.
test_results: A liver biopsy showed cytoplasmic ballooning with deposits of periodic acid-Schif positive and diastase-digestible materials, glycogen nuclei, macrovesicular fat globules, and portal fibrosis. SLC37A4 gene sequencing revealed a compound heterozygous mutation (p.R28H and p.W107X, which was a novel mutation).
Orpha_name: Glycogen storage disease due to glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency type Ib

case_report: An 18-week-old female infant weighing 5950 g was admitted to the hospital due to respiratory distress, cough, cyanosis, and fever that had persisted for six days. The infant was born at full term through an elective repeat cesarean section, with a birth weight of 3195 g and no congenital anomalies or delivery complications. She attained normal developmental milestones until two months of age, when decreased activity was observed. Both parents were in good health and unrelated. This child was their third offspring. Their first child was healthy, but their second child died at five months of age. The infant’s vital signs upon admission were as follows: a temperature of 38.3 °C, a heart rate of 147 beats/min, a respiratory rate of 47 breaths/min, a blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg, and an oxygen saturation of 92% on room air. Clinical examination revealed lethargy, pallor, and cyanosis. Physical characteristics included a flattened nasal bridge and a slight macroglossia. Mid-systolic murmurs were detected in cardiac auscultation. Both lungs had rales on examination. The abdomen was non-tender and soft to the touch with no signs of organ enlargement. A neurological examination revealed generalized hypotonia and absent deep tendon reflexes in all four limbs. The infant had suboptimal eye contact and poor head control. The patient was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit. Initial laboratory investigations yielded the following results: The results of the urinalysis, urine culture, and blood cultures returned negative. Positive results were obtained from the tracheal secretion cultures for the presence of Acinetobacter. The COVID-19 polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test, as well as tests for Influenza A and B, were negative. The electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia, short PR interval, high-voltage R in left precordial leads, and strain pattern in V6 suggestive of left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy. Echocardiography demonstrated biventricular severe hypertrophy, significant LV systolic-diastolic dysfunction, and high LV filling pressure. The interventricular septum measured 8 mm. The LV ejection fraction was 30–35%, and mild mitral valve and tricuspid valve regurgitations were present. Chest X-ray revealed cardiomegaly with an increased cardiothoracic ratio.
test_results: Dried blood spot testing for Alpha-1,4 glucosidase (GAA) activity using tandem mass spectrometry showed significantly reduced enzymatic activity of 0.4 µmol/L/h (reference range for normal individuals: > 2.0 µmol/L/h).

case_report: Case 2, female, 10 years and 8 months, began experiencing negative myoclonus at 8 years and 7 months old. This condition presented as multiple drops of both hands or the right hand during waking hours, with the frequency ranging from 10 to 20 drops per day. The longest period without these episodes was 2 months. No other types of episodes were observed. The condition was not well-managed with VPA.
test_results: Spike and slow wave in both parietal rolandic areas and mainly in midline areas (Cz), and SWI was 70%. The amplitudes of spikes and slow waves were lower than 50uv.
diagnosis: atypical benign epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes

case_report: An 18-year-old male with no known medical history was brought to the emergency department by a friend following a scorpion sting on the distal end of his right middle finger approximately two hours prior at his home. He reported severe aching pain radiating from the right middle finger to the right shoulder, accompanied by sweating and goosebumps across his body. He experienced two episodes of vomiting, which were non-projectile, non-bilious, non-blood-stained, and contained food particles. He received a Tetanus vaccine at a nearby hospital before being referred for further management. On initial assessment, he appeared very restless due to severe pain. His respiratory rate was 24 breaths per minute with an oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. His pulse rate was 62 beats per minute, and his blood pressure was 170/120 mm Hg measured on the right arm. He was conscious, oriented, but irritable. Pupils were equal and reactive to light bilaterally. His body temperature was 34.7 degrees Celsius, indicating hypothermia, with severe sweating and goosebumps noted all over his body. Priapism was also observed. Systemic examinations were unremarkable. Local examination of the right upper limb showed a single sting mark on the medial aspect of the distal end of the right middle finger, with swelling and tenderness extending to the wrist.
test_results: A 12-lead electrocardiogram taken showed ST segment depression in leads two, three, aVf and V3-V6 and tall T waves in V3, V4. Blood reports revealed a haemoglobin of 18.6 with a haematocrit of 53.5. The total leukocyte count was raised to 22200 (neutrophils 80, lymphocytes 15). Activated partial thromboplastin time was elevated (43.2). Cardiac markers were also elevated (CKMB 63 and Troponin I 164), with total creatine kinase of 1062 and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) of 502. A 2D electrocardiography (ECG) showed mild left ventricular apical hypokinesia, with an ejection fraction of 55%.

case_report: An eighteen-year-old female presented with missing teeth in the lower front jaw region, attributed to trauma experienced one year prior, resulting in the loss of her front teeth. There was no significant history regarding medications or family. She reported a previous surgical attempt to separate joined fingers, which led to the loss of half of her left hand's ring finger due to postsurgical infection. Her prenatal, natal, and postnatal history were unremarkable. She exhibited mild to moderate mental retardation. General examination revealed an abnormally short stature, with a height of 4 feet 6 inches and a weight of 30 kg. She had vision loss in the left eye and was using an eye prosthesis. Syndactyly was observed in the middle, ring, and little fingers of both hands. Intraoral examination showed good oral hygiene and missing right and left mandibular central incisors. Relative microdontia was noted, with crown root lengths shorter than normal by approximately 8 mm, in the mandibular right and left first molars and first premolars, as well as in the maxillary first molars bilaterally. The soft tissue and other oral mucosal structures appeared normal.
test_results: The PA view of skull was found to be normal. The orthopantomogram revealed the congenital absence of all the third molars and a generalised horizontal bone loss. Enlarged pulp chambers with respect to the maxillary right and left second molars were observed. Hand wrist X-ray revealed bony union of the middle, ring, and little fingers of both hands.

case_report: A 34-year-old male patient with a history of smoking 40 packs per year and alcohol consumption presented with polyarthralgia affecting both large and small joints for the past 3 years. He reported persistent pelvic pain, primarily in both hip joints and ankles, which intensified with long-distance walking. The pain was described as vague and rated 4 on the visual analog scale. The patient had no systemic diseases and was not on any medication. There was no history of trauma, morning stiffness, weight loss, fever, or pain, and no signs of arthritis were observed. He had a past trauma that resulted in a fracture of the right wrist. Gait and posture were normal, and pelvic inspection showed bilateral muscle bulk symmetry without scars or bruises. Physical examination revealed a normal range of motion in all joints without restriction. Musculoskeletal examination showed no synovitis except for swelling at the right Achilles tendon. Neurologic examination was normal, and sacroiliac joint tests were unremarkable. There were no signs of cutaneous connective tissue involvement. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, rheumatoid factor, serum electrolytes, alkaline phosphatase, calcium, phosphate, and thyroid function tests, were all within normal limits.
test_results: Numerous, symmetric, well defined, sclerotic lesions were identified on the shoulder, wrist, ankles, pelvis, and on the spine. The size of the lesions varied from 2 to 9 millimeters. These spots are located on spongious bone tissue, and in the inner bone cortex located bilaterally in the epiphyses and metaphyses. Computed tomography scan of the pelvis and lumbar spine has not objectified lumbar spinal stenosis. Computed tomography of the ankles has objective sclerotic foci in the tibia and calcaneum of variable size.

case_report: A one-year-nine-month-old Chinese girl presented with hearing loss and regression in speech and movement since the age of one. At five months, she responded to teasing and had good neck control. By eight months, she could flip over, responded to her name, and by nine months, she could say 'mom' and 'dad.' However, her motor development was notably delayed compared to her peers. At one year old, she could not sit or crawl independently. Over time, she lost responsiveness to her surroundings, exhibited a lack of facial expression, and had hypotonia, particularly in the upper limbs, with reduced hand agility and grasping ability. Additional symptoms included choking while drinking, swallowing difficulties, and frequent breath-holding spells lasting 1–2 minutes, starting at ten months old, with cyanotic episodes occurring about ten times a day. Her weight decreased from 10.5 kg to 8 kg after symptom onset. She was the first child of non-consanguineous parents, with previous pregnancies ending in termination. She was born at 32+6 weeks via cesarean section due to maternal pregnancy-induced hypertension, with a birth weight of 1.36 kg and normal newborn hearing screening results. At the clinic visit, her height was 77 cm, weight 8 kg, and head circumference 45 cm, all below average for her age. She had poor head control, visual fixation, and sound tracking. Physical examination revealed generalized weakness, especially in the upper extremities, limb hypotonia, weak gag reflex, absent patellar tendon reflex, and negative bilateral Babinski sign. Laboratory tests showed normal ammonia, serum lactic acid, hepatorenal function, microelements, and serum amino acids. The acylcarnitine profile indicated mild elevations in octanoyl carnitine (C8) at 0.33 μmol/L (normal range 0.01–0.30 μmol/L) and decanoyl carnitine (C10) at 0.50 μmol/L (normal range 0.01–0.35 μmol/L), with other acylcarnitine species within normal ranges. Urine organic acid analysis showed mildly elevated pyruvic and lactic acids. Brain MRI showed no contrast and visual-evoked response. Video EEG and echocardiography were normal. Electromyogram indicated neurogenic changes with fibrillation activity. Nerve conduction studies revealed denervation without sensory response in the sural and median nerves but normal motor velocities. Brainstem auditory-evoked responses indicated severe sensorineural hearing loss. Ophthalmologic examination was normal.
test_results: No variant was found in the SMN gene.

case_report: A 15-year-old female presented with a widespread skin rash at one month old and experienced acute burning and redness on the face after minimal sun exposure. At three months, she was treated for sepsis. By age four, she developed her first facial skin lesion. Over time, she exhibited increased hyperpigmentation in sun-exposed areas and significant sensitivity to light. By the age of 15, she had undergone the removal of 13 skin lesions, primarily from the face, eyes, lips, neck, upper limbs, and trunk. Six of these lesions were identified as malignant, including one squamous cell carcinoma, one basaloid squamous cell carcinoma, two basal cell carcinomas, and two carcinomas of unspecified histology. Neurological symptoms were first observed at age five. By age 11, she showed moderate skin and eye sensitivity to light, mild cognitive and motor impairments, short stature (41.6 kg and 136 cm), and a reduced head circumference (49 cm).
test_results: The histopathological findings of this lesion revealed actinic keratosis. A brain magnetic resonance imaging study was performed at 13 years old and revealed microcephaly, ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly due to parenchymal brain atrophy, and discrete/diffuse bilateral/symmetric white matter hyperintensities on T2-weighted and FLAIR images.

case_report: A 58-year-old male patient presented with abnormal serum creatine kinase (sCK) levels in August 2020. The patient first noticed abnormal sCK levels on January 29, 2019, and has since observed irregular fluctuations in these levels. His medical history includes an acute cerebral stem infarction in January 2019, resulting in mild aphasia, dysphagia, and right-sided numbness and weakness. He also has a history of acute pancreatitis, a left acetabular fracture from a car accident 18 years ago leading to left leg weakness post-surgery, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes. From January 29, 2019, to November 6, 2020, the patient received daily standard treatment with metformin (500 mg/d), amlodipine besylate (2.5 mg/d), atorvastatin (20 mg/d), and aspirin (100 mg/d). Between November 12, 2019, and December 2, 2019, atorvastatin was temporarily replaced with ezetimibe (10 mg/d) due to concerns about its impact on sCK levels, but was resumed after no significant changes were observed. Additionally, the patient underwent traditional Chinese medicine treatments, including acupuncture 3-5 times a week over 18 months and three courses of herbal medicine. Acupuncture points used included Neiguan (PC6), Shuigou (DU26), Sanyinjiao (SP6), Baihui (DU20), Yifeng (SJ17), Jianyu (LI15), and Taichong (LR3). Herbal medicines included Pinellia ternata, Magnolia officinalis, Poria cohoe, Perilla leaf, and cassia twig. Physical examinations over the past two years showed normal electrocardiogram, B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), and creatine kinase MB (CK-MB) isoenzyme tests, with no morphological changes in echocardiography. Neurological examination revealed normal tendon reflexes, grade 5 limb muscle strength, normal muscle tension and volume, and no edema or color changes. The patient's limb dysfunction symptoms improved significantly after acupuncture treatment. The patient declined further tests such as electromyogram (EMG) or muscle biopsy.
test_results: No myogenic lesion was found in both lower extremities, however, neurogenic lesion could not be excluded.
Orpha_name: Isolated asymptomatic elevation of creatine phosphokinase

case_report: A 30-month-old female patient of Afro-American descent was referred for evaluation at the age of 15 months with primary concerns of inadequate weight gain, reduced muscle tone, and enlargement of the liver and spleen. The patient was born to non-consanguineous parents. The pregnancy was complicated by low amniotic fluid levels, resulting in a C-section delivery at 36 weeks. The mother is a carrier of alpha thalassemia, but the family history was otherwise unremarkable. An abdominal MRI was conducted to investigate the hepatosplenomegaly, revealing an enlarged liver with a lobular surface indicative of cirrhosis, fluid accumulation in the abdomen, and multiple lesions consistent with dysplastic nodules. A liver biopsy performed at 16 months old showed characteristics of liver storage disease and bridging fibrosis in the portal and periportal areas (METAVIR stage F3–4). An echocardiogram at 25 months old was normal. Laboratory testing results are summarized in the report. There was no report of low blood sugar levels.
test_results: Genetic testing identified two variants in GBE1: c.1544G > A; p.(Arg515His) classified as pathogenic, and c.826G > C; p.(Ala276Pro) classified as a VUS.
Orpha_name: Glycogen storage disease due to glycogen branching enzyme deficiency

case_report: A 40-year-old woman was admitted on January 25, 2010, to the rheumatism center due to a 6-month history of worsening proximal muscle weakness, which had rapidly intensified one month prior. She had been an athlete in high school and was generally healthy until three years earlier when she experienced weight loss and fatigue, leading to a diagnosis of Graves' disease with thyrotoxicosis. At that time, her serum liver enzymes, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST), were elevated to 184 IU/mL and 94 IU/mL, respectively, without evidence of viral hepatitis. After one and a half years of methimazole treatment, her hyperthyroidism went into remission, but her liver enzyme levels continued to fluctuate within twice the upper normal range. Eighteen months before admission, she reported fatigue and weakness despite being euthyroid and was referred to a gastroenterologist for persistent mild liver enzyme elevation. Tests for hepatitis B and C were negative, and ultrasonography revealed numerous small gallstones and minor liver parenchymal calcification. She was advised to have regular follow-ups at the gastroenterology department. One year before admission, she developed weight loss and myalgia, with AST levels rising again to 187 IU/mL. A liver biopsy showed minimal porto-periportal activity and minimal portal fibrosis. Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) was positive at a titer of 1:20 with a speckled pattern, while anti-smooth muscle antibody and anti-LKM-1 antibody were negative. Prednisone and azathioprine were prescribed for her persistent liver enzyme elevation. Six months before admission, she experienced recurrent myalgia, muscle weakness, and anorexia, with fluctuating liver enzyme levels despite treatment. Three months earlier, her proximal muscle weakness became more pronounced, making it difficult for her to climb stairs. On initial examination, she appeared chronically ill, but her vital signs were normal. She could walk but had difficulty climbing stairs or raising her arms. There were no specific skin lesions. During the interview, it was noted that her two sons had been diagnosed with a condition in childhood and were bedridden. Her two brothers and parents were healthy. Her serum CK level was 2,436 IU/mL, aldolase 11.9 IU/mL, and LDH 312 IU/L. Serum TSH and free T4 were normal. ANA, anti-Jo-1 antibody, and anti-PM-SCL antibody were all negative. Chest radiography was normal. Fat suppression T2-weighted MRI of the thigh showed multiple atrophies in muscles such as the gluteus maximus, tensor fasciae latae, vastus lateralis, and hamstrings, without gadolinium enhancement. Transthoracic 2D echocardiography showed normal chamber size and good systolic function without pulmonary hypertension. A muscle biopsy of the right vastus lateralis revealed myopathic changes, including small group muscle atrophy, a few regenerating fibers, inflammatory cell infiltration, and areas resembling perifascicular atrophy. Special staining showed positive results for leukocyte common antigen (LCA) and CD 68, but rare CD 4 and CD 8, indicating macrophage-lineage inflammatory cells. Dystrophin staining showed varied patterns from normal to interrupted sarcolemmal activity. EMG-NCV study indicated short duration, small amplitude, increased insertional activity, positive sharp waves, and fibrillation, consistent with myopathy. High-dose prednisone at 1.0 mg/kg/day was administered, resulting in a good initial response with serum CK levels decreasing to near normal and muscle strength improving from grade 4 minus to grade 4 plus according to the Medical Research Council's grading system. However, the initial steroid response did not last, and her muscle weakness and fluctuating serum CK levels persisted despite continued oral prednisone. Six months after referral to our center, intravenous immunoglobulin and oral cyclosporine were tried, but no further improvement in muscle enzyme levels or weakness was observed.
test_results: We performed multiple ligation probe amplification (MLPA) analysis using the test kits SALSA P034 DMD and P035 DMD from MRC-Holland (Amsterdam, Netherland) and revealed a heterozygote deletion mutation involving exon 44 in this patient. The XCI pattern was determined by PCR analysis of a polymorphic CAG repeat in the HUMARA. After digestion with the methylation sensitive enzyme HpaII, a PCR product is obtained only from the inactive X chromosome. The PCR product was analyzed by GeneScan Software (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA). XCI was calculated as the ratio between the intensities of the PCR products of the two alleles with the smallest allele given first. The presence of skewed XCI was considered if the ratio was ≥ 35:65, and considered extremely skewed if the ratio was ≥ 20:80. The heterozygous allele of the X chromosome in non-digested sample was shown with a CAG repeat polymorphism. After DNA was digested with HpaII, the patient showed one distinct peak and one faint peak, indicating that these had a highly skewed XCI and the ratio was 19:81.
Orpha_name: Symptomatic form of muscular dystrophy of Duchenne and Becker in female carriers

case_report: In 2016, a 68-year-old woman from Penafiel, Portugal, with a history of being overweight, visited her family doctor due to low back pain and thigh aches triggered by physical activity. Her physical examination was normal. A lumbosacral spine CT scan showed L4/L5 disc protrusion and facet hypertrophy, raising questions about radicular compression. A subsequent MRI ruled out nerve compression. The pain was attributed to lumbar degenerative disease, and she was treated with a short course of low-dose non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, weight loss advice, physiotherapy, and hydro gymnastics. Despite treatment, symptoms persisted, and her family doctor could not explain the thigh ache. In 2019, she was diagnosed with dyslipidemia and prescribed atorvastatin 20 mg. Six months later, her thigh myalgias worsened, and tests showed elevated CK levels (433 U/L). Atorvastatin was discontinued, and pitavastatin 2 mg was started. After one month, myalgias persisted, and CK levels increased (1087 U/L). Pitavastatin was stopped, and two months later, although myalgias slightly improved, significant pain during physical activity remained. CK levels decreased but were still elevated (747 U/L). She was referred to Rheumatology. During her first rheumatology appointment, she reported lifelong myalgia and muscle weakness in both thighs, especially during physical activities like brisk walking, running, or jumping, which improved with short breaks. Physical examination showed no muscle weakness in upper or lower limbs and no difficulty rising from a chair. CK levels remained high (566 U/L, 480 U/L, 860 U/L), and other muscle enzymes were elevated: LDH (355 U/L, 297 U/L, 302 U/L), aldolase (13.4 U/L, 12.8 U/L, 14.3 U/L), and myoglobin (256.2 ng/mL, 185 ng/mL, 316 ng/mL). Myoglobinuria was absent, and renal function was normal. Antibody tests for inflammatory myopathies and anti-nuclear antibody were negative. Electromyography of the lower limbs showed myopathic features in the proximal muscles of the left leg and distal muscles of both legs, with no sensory abnormalities.
test_results: The results showed numerous muscular fibers with subsarcolemmal glycogen vacuolation and a negative histochemical staining for myophosphorylase. The bidirectional and direct sequencing of the PYGM gene was conducted, detecting two variants in heterozygosity: c.2083G>A p.(Gly695Arg), classified as probably pathogenic, and c.2392T>C p.(Trp798Arg), classified as pathogenic.

case_report: A 45-year-old Caucasian woman, previously in good health, presented with a progressive decrease in vision in both eyes over the past year, along with sensitivity to light and difficulty driving at night. The patient noted that her visual acuity has been deteriorating since undergoing bilateral laser vision correction (LASIK) approximately 15 months ago at another facility to address myopia. No further details were provided regarding the specifics of the laser ablation. At the time of the procedure, the patient was informed that the laser vision correction would also remove the stromal opacities. Prior to the surgery, her best corrected visual acuity was reported to be 20/25 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye.
test_results: Slit-lamp examination revealed multiple crumb-like and lattice-like opacities of the corneal stroma. Multiple foci of fine granular infiltrates at the surgical flap interface were also observed.

case_report: A 15-year-old Indian female from Western Maharashtra, born at full term from a consanguineous marriage, presented with speech difficulties and decreased hearing in both ears since birth. There was no family history of genetic disease. Her mother had a first pregnancy with premature delivery at 7 months, and the child died immediately after birth. She has two siblings who are normal. During infancy, she experienced feeding difficulties due to a high arched palate and tongue nodules. There was no history of radiation exposure, significant drug intake, trauma, or major illness during her mother's pregnancy. No history of delayed developmental milestones was noted. Vital signs included a pulse of 90/min, regular in nature, and blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg in the right arm supine position. Clinical examination revealed mild pallor, bilateral polysyndactyly with duplicated thumbs on both hands, bilateral polysyndactyly of halluces, missing central incisors, a broad nose, a high arched palate, ocular hypertelorism, low set ears, and tongue nodules. Cardiac, respiratory, abdominal, and neurological examinations were unremarkable, and intelligence was normal. The female external genitalia and secondary sexual characteristics were normal. Ophthalmic examination revealed a normal fundus. Laboratory investigations showed hemoglobin at 10.4 g%, total leukocyte count at 7900 cells/mm3, differential leukocyte count with P-79%, L-13%, E-08%, and platelets at 275,000/cumm. Peripheral smear indicated microcytic hypochromic red blood cells with anisocytosis. Liver function tests, renal function tests, and serum proteins were normal. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 20 mm/1st h. Urine examination was normal. Electrocardiogram and two-dimensional echocardiogram were normal.
test_results: An x-ray of both hands with forearms anteroposterior (AP) view revealed six metacarpals in right hand showing fusion proximally of third and fourth metacarpals. Little fingers show accessory phalanges on both sides with bilateral duplication of thumbs. An x-ray of both feet AP view revealed seven metatarsals on the right side and six metatarsals on the left side. The large great toe on the right is formed by two metatarsals.
