Pure tone audiometry revealed the mild conductive type of deafness.

case_report: A 39-year-old woman with no prior health issues arrived at the emergency department after experiencing painful swelling and discoloration in her right lower leg for 4 days. She also had gangrenous changes at the tips of her right toes. The patient had no history of hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, trauma, or illicit drug use, including oral contraceptives, but had a 10-year history of tobacco use. Upon hospital admission, the initial physical examination revealed gangrenous changes affecting the entire foot and toes below the right metatarsals. The right calf was noted to be pale, with associated pain, paresthesia, and a cold sensation. Laboratory tests indicated a platelet count of 37,000/mm3.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) of arteries of the lower extremities demonstrated diffuse vascular occlusion by thrombus in the right infra-renal aorta through the popliteal artery and also left superficial femoral artery.
Orpha_name: Severe hereditary thrombophilia due to congenital protein S deficiency

case_report: A 58-year-old female patient with a history of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and a former smoker with a ≥20 pack-year history presented with no prior episodes of thrombocytopenia or bleeding. Initial blood tests at the time of cancer diagnosis and previous tests showed no abnormalities. In 2016, chest computed tomography (CT) scans revealed a tumor in the left lung. A bronchoscopic forceps biopsy of the mass in the left bronchus identified adenocarcinoma, with no EGFR mutations detected. The patient underwent an upper lobectomy of the left lung in October 2016 and received adjuvant chemotherapy with cisplatin and vinorelbine at standard doses. After the third chemotherapy cycle, the patient developed neutropenia (neutrophil count of 780 cells/μL) and anemia (erythrocyte count of 3.35 million cells/μL, hemoglobin concentration of 10.5 mg/dL), leading to a temporary deferral of the fourth cycle. Treatment with G-CSF improved neutrophil counts, and anemia also improved after a few days. The fourth chemotherapy cycle was subsequently administered, and the first-line treatment concluded successfully. A follow-up CT scan one year later showed cancer progression with a 21 mm mass at the top of the left lung. MRI and PET-CT scans revealed metastatic lesions in the left occipital lobe of the brain, measuring 19.3 mm in diameter. In September 2018, the patient underwent stereotactic radiotherapy for brain metastasis, which yielded a positive response. Immunohistochemistry detected PD-L1 expression in 70% of tumor cells, with no ALK protein expression. The patient met the inclusion criteria for second-line immunotherapy, including reference levels of blood cell count and biochemical test results, the presence of a target tumor in the left lung, and no evidence of metastatic progression in the central nervous system. Pembrolizumab at a dose of 200 mg every three weeks was initiated in October 2018. The patient tolerated four cycles of immunotherapy without side effects.
test_results: In the beginning of 2019, before the administration of the 5th cycle of pembrolizumab, a routine blood cell count test was performed, showing a sudden decrease in platelet count to 53 000 cells/μL in EDTA-K2 sample. Two additional blood samples were drawn in sodium citrate anticoagulated probe and Thrombo-Exact (Sarstedt®) probe with magnesium salt. In both those samples, we found the platelet count at an acceptable level (223 000 cells/μL).

case_report: A 35-year-old Caucasian male was referred to the Cardiology Unit for a cardiac evaluation prior to engaging in non-competitive gym activities, as recommended by his general practitioner due to a significant family history of cardiac issues. His mother had a heart transplant for end-stage dilated cardiomyopathy, and his brother was recently diagnosed with non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy with mildly reduced ejection fraction. At the time of presentation, no family genetic or histological data were available. The patient was asymptomatic with an unremarkable medical history. Physical examination revealed no abnormalities. A 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) indicated sinus bradycardia at 50 bpm. The P-wave duration was 130 ms with a bimodal morphology in the inferior leads and a negative terminal component in V1 of 60 ms. The standard transthoracic echocardiography showed no significant abnormalities; however, strain imaging revealed segmental longitudinal strain impairment in the basal and medium segments of the interventricular septum (−7%) and a mild reduction in left ventricular global longitudinal strain (GLS; −13.9%). Both the peak atrial longitudinal strain and the peak atrial contraction strain were reduced compared to normal ranges (stratified by sex and age). A 24-hour ECG monitoring showed sinus bradycardia with a daytime mean heart rate of 56 bpm, two daytime episodes of Type 2 second-degree atrioventricular block with a maximum pause of 2.92 seconds, frequent premature ventricular complexes, and a ventricular triplet followed by a 4-minute episode of atrial fibrillation at a high ventricular rate.
test_results: The comprehensive genetic testing revealed the frame shift variant c.1367 (p.Asn456Thrfs*24) of the LMNA gene, a frame shift variant characterized by the replacement of asparagine at Position 456 for a threonine, terminating at Position 24 with a termination codon.
Orpha_name: Familial dilated cardiomyopathy with conduction defect due to LMNA mutation

case_report: A 52-year-old Caucasian male with no significant medical history presented in October 2013 with left shoulder pain lasting one week. The pain began suddenly after heavy work as a barber, was continuous during arm elevation beyond 90°, worsened at night, non-radiating, and rated 7/10 in severity. He reported no fever, arm weakness, or numbness. Clinical evaluation showed normal vital signs, no fever, and pain during anterior elevation. The acromioclavicular joint was mildly tender but non-fluctuant. Muscle strength around the shoulder, elbow, and wrist was 4/5. The age-adjusted Constant score was 87/100. Systemic examination and full laboratory tests were unremarkable except for an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (33 mm/h). Radiographs of the left shoulder showed a permeative blastic-sclerotic pattern in the humeral head without cortical thickening or periosteal reaction, and narrowing of the subacromial space. Further imaging with contrast-enhanced MRI and a 3-phase bone scan indicated possible underlying bone marrow disease. Hematological investigations were unremarkable. A fine-needle bone biopsy was nondiagnostic, showing an infiltrate with extensive crushing artifact and nonspecific immunoexpression. The patient showed significant clinical improvement with analgesics and physiotherapy and declined further investigation. In March 2016, he returned to the emergency department with sudden, intense left shoulder pain after carrying a heavy load, unable to move his arm. Clinical examination showed no fever, edema, redness, or palpable lymph nodes. He reported mild discomfort and pain with shoulder movement beyond 160° over the past three years but had not sought medical care. Radiographs revealed a pathological fracture of the humeral head at the surgical neck, with diffuse permeative sclerotic areas and signs of osteonecrosis, confirmed by MRI. The patient was admitted to the hospital and underwent an open biopsy of the humeral head.
test_results: Histologic examination revealed diffuse infiltration of the intertrabecular spaces by a neoplastic population of large, lymphoid cells with clear or pale cytoplasm and ovoid or multilobated nuclei with central nucleoli.
diagnosis: Primary osseous diffuse large B-cell non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma

case_report: A male infant was delivered full-term to a 22-year-old G1P0 Mixteco mother via cesarean section. The pregnancy was marked by pre-eclampsia, delayed prenatal care, and maternal fever. APGAR scores were 1, 4, and 5 at 1 minute, 5 minutes, and 10 minutes, respectively. At birth, the infant's measurements were: weight 3.750 kg (62.6%), length 52.0 cm (65.5%), and head circumference 34.3 cm (29.1%). Physical examination revealed a large anterior fontanelle (soft and flat), an open posterior fontanelle, upslanting palpebral fissures, almond-shaped eyes, hypertelorism, significant cranial molding, hypotonia, and a single palmar crease. Karyotyping showed 46 and XY, excluding trisomy 21. Initial laboratory tests indicated normal electrolytes, BUN, and creatinine levels. The hepatic panel results were: total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 1.9 mg/dL, AST 544 units/L, ALT 268 units/L, GGT 228 units/L, and alkaline phosphatase 481 units/L. Subsequent tests showed: total bilirubin 7.0 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 5.5 mg/dL, AST 772 units/L, ALT 313 units/L, GGT 228 units/L, and alkaline phosphatase 910 units/L. The infant exhibited jaundice on day 1, which resolved within a week. By day 15, signs of respiratory insufficiency, including intermittent tachypnea, inspiratory stridor, tracheal tugging, and laryngomalacia, were observed. Feeding difficulties were noted, with a transition from gavage to oral feeding by day 30. The infant did not pass a bilateral ABR hearing test. Further tests showed C26:0 at 8.278 umol/L, C22:0 at 19.51 µmol/L, and elevated C26/C22 and C24/C22 ratios, indicating a peroxisomal function disorder. Low red blood cell plasmalogen/fatty acid ratios were observed, suggesting a defect in plasmalogen metabolism. The infant tested positive for ALD without the ABCD1 mutation. Pompe disease and mucopolysaccharidosis I disorder were excluded based on positive alpha-glucosidase and alpha-L-iduronidase enzyme activity. Ultrasound revealed a normal liver, grade one bilateral hydronephrosis, and bilateral cysts around the lateral ventricles.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed an autosomal homozygous pathogenic variant of the PEX6 gene c.1409G>C (p.Gly470Ala).
diagnosis: Zellweger’s Syndrome  with PEX6 gene mutation

case_report: A 69-year-old female patient was transferred from a local clinic to Soonchunhyang University Bucheon Hospital in Bucheon, Korea for further evaluation of thyroid masses identified via thyroid ultrasonography. The largest mass was isoechoic, measuring approximately 0.9×1.2 cm, and appeared benign among multiple masses present in both lobes. Another smaller mass, measuring 0.7×1.0 cm, located in the lower pole of the left lobe, was hypoechoic, ill-defined, and solid.
test_results: A Ct value >33, characteristic of the wild-type sequence, was calculated in this study. The ΔCt was of the sample from the patient was 8.39, suggestive of a definite BRAF mutation. A 3-bp deletion mutation in coding nucleotides 1799 to 1801 (c.1799_1801delTGA) within the BRAF mutational hotspot region was identified. The conversion of codons 600 (GTG) and 601 (AAA) into a single codon (GAA) resulted in the insertion of a glutamic acid into the activation segment of the B-raf protein (p.V600_K601delinsE).

case_report: A 64-year-old man presented with epigastric pain that had persisted for several months. He was referred to our clinic for further treatment after an initial evaluation at a local clinic. In addition to the epigastric pain, the patient recently experienced a sensation of food getting stuck in his throat but did not report any weight loss. The patient mentioned that he had undergone a gastroscopy during a routine checkup 2 years prior, which showed no abnormalities. A current gastroscopy revealed a mass measuring approximately 3.0 × 3.0 cm, with a central irregular ulcer and a raised, reddish nodular edge without clear boundaries. This mass was located 38–40 cm from the upper incisor.
test_results: The biopsy showed sheets of small hyperchromatic cells with minimal cytoplasm and stippled chromatin. Immunochemical staining showed that the tumor cells were positive for cytokeratin, CD56, and synaptophysin and negative for chromogranin A. These examinations revealed a tumor situated in the lower esophagus along with lymph nodes suspected to be indicative of metastatic involvement within the lower paraesophageal region and the left gastric region.
diagnosis: Goblet Cell Adenocarcinoma  arising from Barrett’s esophagus

case_report: A 31-year-old female reported experiencing pain in both legs for the past year, with the pain initially starting in the right leg six months before affecting the left leg. At the time of consultation, she had ongoing pain in both legs, more pronounced on the right side. She did not report pain in any other areas. There was no history of fever, trauma, or excessive stress on the bones. Additionally, there was no family history of autoimmune diseases. Physical examination revealed no signs indicating a vascular or muscular cause for the leg pain, and there was no tenderness in the bones.
test_results: She underwent a radiograph of both legs which showed cortical thickening of the diaphyses of both tibiae. A three-phase 99mTc-MDP bone scan showed intense irregular uptake in the diaphyseal region of both tibiae in delayed static images. Increased tracer activity was also noted in blood pool images in both legs. There were no other sites of bone involvement. The patient further underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) which revealed cortical thickening with bone marrow edema in bilateral tibial diaphysis along with minimal adjacent soft tissue edema. The patient then underwent a tibial biopsy which revealed predominantly dense lamellar bone with irregular sized and spaced haversian systems. The bony lamellae were thick, sclerotic with few osteocytes.
Orpha_name: Glycogen storage disease due to muscle phosphofructokinase deficiency

case_report: A 5-year-old girl, born to parents without any known genetic relation, experienced a transverse skin 'split' on the bottom of her right third toe for 3 months, accompanied by a clear fluid discharge. Over the next month, this 'split' extended around the entire toe. Her mother reported similar occurrences on the second, fourth, and fifth toes of the right foot, with durations of 3 months, 1 year, and 2 years, respectively, which resolved before noticing a shortening of those toes. The patient had no history of travel, Raynaud phenomenon, trauma, exposure to vinyl chloride gas, skin fragility, blisters at trauma sites, joint pain, or swelling of the extremities. No family members had similar symptoms. Physical examination showed no signs of palmoplantar keratoderma, connective tissue disease, excessive hair growth, or dental or musculoskeletal issues. Examination of the feet revealed a clear boundary between normal and affected crusted skin overlying bone loss on the third toe, encircling the entire toe. This area was slightly painful with clear fluid discharge but no bone fragments. Additionally, there was a shortening of the distal phalanx of the second, fourth, and fifth toes. Sensation and peripheral pulses in the feet were normal.
test_results: X-rays of the right foot revealed complete resorption of the middle and terminal phalanx of the fifth toe, complete resorption of the terminal phalanx of the fourth toe, partial resorption of the terminal phalanx of the third toe, and partial resorption of the middle and terminal phalanx of the second toe.

case_report: A 48-year-old male patient with a history of alcohol abuse began experiencing progressive walking difficulties and tremors in both hands starting 6 years ago. The patient also exhibited dysarthria and peripheral neuropathy. Neurological examinations consistently revealed a wide-based gait, dysmetria in both upper and lower extremities, intention tremor, and dysdiadochokinesia. The worsening gait issues eventually necessitated the use of a walking aid. Brain MRI indicated mild frontoparietal atrophy and diffuse cerebellar atrophy, with no signs of Wernicke's encephalopathy. His clinical presentation was repeatedly considered to be alcohol related.
test_results: Genetic testing showed a premutation in the FMR1 gene (87 CGG triplets).

case_report: An 11-year-old male child, born from a non-consanguineous marriage, presented with difficulty in rising from a sitting position and walking for six months. According to the father, the child was healthy until one year of age when he developed lower limb weakness and was given oral medications at a private hospital. At one year old, the child could not stand with support, and by 18 months, he was unable to stand without support. The child began walking later than his peers. Antenatal, natal, and postnatal histories were unremarkable. The father reported progressive knee and chest deformities as the child grew. Currently, there is no history of pain, fever, recurrent infections, or frequent hospital admissions. The child can perform daily activities like dressing and combing hair with minimal assistance but has increasing difficulty walking and rising from a sitting position over the past six months. The parents sought further treatment at the hospital, and the child was referred to the rehabilitation and neurology departments. The child is intellectually normal. On examination, he is conscious, cooperative, and well-oriented to time, place, and person. There are no sensory or cognitive impairments, ataxia, or bladder-bowel involvement. Family history is non-contributory. Physical examination revealed pectus excavatum, increased lumbar spine curvature, genu recurvatum, diffuse muscle wasting, and lower motor neuron-type weakness in both upper and lower limbs. Deep tendon reflexes are globally attenuated (grade 1), and the Gowers sign is positive. Vital signs include a temperature of 98°F, heart rate of 90 beats/min, respiratory rate of 22/min, oxygen saturation of 97%, and random blood sugar of 80 mg/dl. Anthropometric measurements showed a height of 76 cm, weight of 7 kg, head circumference of 50 cm, and BMI of 11.77. Routine investigations were conducted, and results are provided in Table []. According to WHO classification, the weight for height and height for age were both less than -3 SD. Treatment with a syrup containing coenzyme Q10 and levocarnitine was initiated.
test_results: A homozygous deletion in exons 7 and 8 of the SMN1 gene was identified.

case_report: A 37-year-old female patient presented with an 8-month history of severe uterine abnormal bleeding following surgery for the removal of an intrauterine device. The patient subsequently developed profound anemia with a hemoglobin level of 58 g/l. Prior to admission to our hospital, she received a blood transfusion of 1200 ml for hemorrhagic anemia at the Second Hospital of Hebei Medical University. The patient also reported repeated occurrences of skin purpura since childhood. There was no history of other types of bleeding such as nosebleeds, gingival bleeding, hematemesis, or melena. Additionally, there was no personal or family history of bleeding disorders, and the patient denied any intake of medicines or herbs. Laboratory results showed white blood cell and platelet levels within normal ranges. Hemoglobin was marginally reduced to 92 g/l following the blood transfusion. Prothrombin time (PT) and international normalized ratio (INR) were normal, while activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) and bleeding time (BT) were significantly prolonged but could be corrected with a plasma transfusion. Plasma FVIII levels were markedly decreased at 4.7%, whereas vWF antigen levels were normal at 128%. Autoimmune markers, including antinuclear, anticardiolipin, antidouble stranded DNA, and extractable nuclear antigen (ENA) polypeptide antibodies, were all negative. Other coagulation tests, including platelet count and function, and fibrinogen levels, were normal.
test_results: Introns 1 and 22 were not inverted. A previously reported mutation (exon 10, c.1505T>A, p.Val502Asp), and a novel unreported missense point mutation (exon 14, c.3279G>A, p.Met1093Ile) were detected.

case_report: The patient is a 2-year and 6-month-old male, the only child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents of Sri Lankan origin. He was delivered at 35 weeks of gestation via an emergency lower segment cesarean section due to severe oligohydramnios and significant fetal growth restriction. There was no history of antenatal bleeding, fetal decelerations, or miscarriages prior to this pregnancy. His Apgar scores were 8 at 1 minute and 10 at 5 minutes. At birth, his measurements were: weight—1080 g, length—30 cm, and occipitofrontal circumference—24 cm, all significantly below the 3rd percentile on the WHO growth charts. He was admitted to the Special Care Baby Unit during the first week of life due to very low birth weight. From birth to 6 months, he underwent extensive evaluations for poor weight gain, with all recorded biochemical investigations within normal ranges. Endocrine assessments related to growth were not conducted due to financial constraints. His current growth parameters, shown in Fig. A–C, remain below the 3rd percentile. His developmental milestones have been age-appropriate since birth, with no symptoms indicative of food intolerances, metabolic, or malabsorption syndromes. Despite optimal calorie intake, his growth velocity remains constant. Physical examination revealed retrognathia, small ears, a prominent nasal root with a large nose, microdontia, and sparse scalp hair (Fig. A, B). He also has a high-pitched voice. Hypopigmented patches were observed on the upper limbs, not following Blaschko lines. Limb examination showed bilateral fifth finger clinodactyly. Echocardiography identified a small ostium secundum atrial septal defect. An abdominal ultrasound revealed markedly smaller, normally functioning kidneys, with the right kidney measuring 4.5 cm and the left kidney 3.8 cm, both below the 1st percentile for kidney length according to age. A hip radiograph showed a poorly formed narrow pelvis with a flat acetabulum.
test_results: Results revealed a pathogenic compound heterozygous frameshift variant in the PCNT gene c.5059_5060delAA | p. Asn1687fs (novel variant) and c.9535dup (p. Val3179fs). His mother and father were found to be heterozygous for the variants.
diagnosis: Microcephalic Osteodysplastic Primordial Dwarfism  Type II
Orpha_name: Microcephalic osteodysplastic primordial dwarfism type II

case_report: A 36-year-old woman with no previous pregnancies visited the hospital due to heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB). She had a history of leiomyoma, which was treated with hysteroscopic myomectomy four years ago. Following the surgery, her HMB resolved but had returned shortly before her current visit. She reported no pain during menstruation or irregularities in her menstrual cycle. Laboratory tests showed anemia with a hemoglobin level of 9.5 g/dL, but no other abnormalities were found in the blood tests related to HMB. Levels of serum LH, FSH, PRL, and E2 were within normal ranges. Pelvic examination and ultrasonography indicated a normal uterus, and color Doppler showed normal blood flow. The HMB persisted despite undergoing dilatation and curettage, and the pathological examination of the removed endometrial tissue showed normal results.
test_results: MRI revealed normal uterine size, with a long axis of 84.4 mm, short axis of 50.4 mm, and width of 65.2 mm; JZE thickness was 9.4 mm.

case_report: A 53-year-old woman was admitted to the Department of Endocrinology due to diabetic ketosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic syndrome. Her medical history included herpes meningoencephalitis from three years prior, resulting in persistent confusion, amnesia, and lack of thirst. There was no known personal or family history of autoimmune or neoplastic diseases. The patient exhibited weakness and weight loss. Physical examination showed confusion (Glasgow coma scale score: 13 to 14/15), a body mass of 73 kg, height of 1.51 m, body mass index of 32.0 kg/m2, blood pressure of 130/80 mmHg, heart rate of 100 beats/minute, respiratory rate of 18 breaths/minute, and signs of extracellular dehydration. Her body temperature was normal. Breast examination showed no abnormalities. Capillary glucose concentration was >33 mmol/L and urine sample was positive for ketones (++). Laboratory tests indicated severe hyperglycemia, hypernatremia (plasma hyperosmolarity of 393.6 mOsm/L), and mild acute renal failure. Arterial blood gas parameters were normal. A COVID-19 infection was confirmed via reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay. Chest x-ray showed no abnormalities. The patient received rehydration with intravenous isotonic saline solution, potassium supplementation, and insulin therapy, which managed her ketosis and hyperglycemia. However, hypernatremia persisted (serum sodium concentration of 148 to 158 mmol/L) along with plasma hyperosmolarity (321 to 336 mOsm/L). Urine output was 1 L/day with urine osmolarity of 139.8 mOsm/L, indicating hypotonicity. Despite high serum sodium concentration, the patient did not experience thirst (fluid intake <1 L/day), and intravenous rehydration with 5% dextrose did not normalize the hypernatremia.
test_results: Desmopressin administration reduced the serum sodium concentration and plasma osmolarity to within their normal ranges (145 mmol/L and 309 mOsm/L, respectively), and the patient’s urine osmolarity increased to 743 mOsm/L. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed large porencephalic temporo-insular lesions relating to the patient’s herpes encephalitis, but her anterior pituitary gland was normal. The posterior pituitary bright spot was present and the pituitary stalk had a median location and was thin.

case_report: A 27-year-old male with a history of hypertension (peak 170/98 mmHg) and symptomatic kidney stones for over 10 years was referred on Nov 15, 2017, following a right nephrectomy and left minimally invasive percutaneous nephrolithotomy (mini-PCNL). The patient had elevated serum creatinine (SCr) levels for more than 3 years and was scheduled for renal transplantation. On Apr 28, 2018, the patient was rehospitalized with SCr 1487 umol/L and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) 33.47 mmol/L. That night, he underwent renal transplantation with a deceased donor, including a Zero-Hour Implantation biopsy (ZHIB). Post-transplant, the patient received standard immunosuppression therapy with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), tacrolimus (Tac), and methylprednisolone (Methylpred), along with hemodialysis (HD) and hypertension treatment. Follow-up assessments included routine blood tests, blood biochemical analysis, and therapeutic drug monitoring. Despite these measures, there was minimal improvement in renal graft function. Due to delayed graft function (SCr 585 umol/L and BUN 30.07 mmol/L), a percutaneous needle core biopsy of the renal graft was performed on post-operative day 46, guided by ultrasonography (USG). The biopsy showed acute T cell-mediated rejection and extensive tubular damage, with the presence of calcium oxalate (CaOx) crystals in the allograft. Comparison with the ZHIB indicated recurrence of CaOx nephropathy in the allograft kidney.
test_results: Molecular genetic testing of the patient was carried out to identify the pathogenic variants (PV) in AGXT and GRHPR, in whom a homozygous genotype for three missense mutations in the GRHPR gene was found: first, a C to T transversion (c.295C > T) in exon 4 resulting in p.(Arg99*), nonsense PV; second, a G to A transversion (c.512G > A) in exon 6 resulting in p.(Arg171His), missense variant of uncertain significance (VUS); third, a G to A transversion (c.211G > A) in exon 2 resulting in p.(Ala71Thr), missense VUS.

case_report: A 3-year-old male presented to the emergency department with a frontal headache, eye pain, vomiting, and lethargy. Physical examination was essentially normal with no focal neurologic deficits. Imaging identified increased posterior fossa fluid. A lumbar puncture showed normal opening pressure. Eye examination was limited due to patient agitation but did not reveal any abnormal findings; his visual acuity was at least fix and follow in both eyes, and the dilated eye exam was notable for peripheral geographic chorioretinal scars in both eyes. Toxoplasmosis serology was negative, and follow-up was arranged with ophthalmology. Both neurology and neurosurgery were following on an as-needed basis. At follow-up eye examination, the patient's symptoms had resolved. His visual acuities were 2.4 cycles per centimeter (20/260) in the right eye and 6.5 cycles per centimeter (20/94) in the left eye by Teller cards, and intraocular pressure was 7 mmHg in the right eye and 8 mmHg in the left eye by iCare tonometer. Cycloplegic refraction revealed high hyperopia (+7.00 +0.50 × 090 in both eyes). On subsequent exam under anesthesia, pachymetry readings were thick at 640 μm in the right eye and 616 μm in the left eye, and the horizontal white-to-white measures were small at 10.5 mm in the right eye and 10.6 mm in the left eye. Gonioscopy showed angles open to the scleral spur in the right eye and with 2 clock-hours of angle closure in the left eye. The anterior segment examination was otherwise normal. The optic nerves in both eyes had mild pallor and cup-to-disc ratios of 0.4 in the right eye and 0.3 in the left eye respectively. As previously noted, there were chorioretinal scars in the periphery of both eyes.
test_results: A-scan ultrasound measured short axial eye lengths of 18.1 mm OD and 18.3 mm OS, a thick sclera (2.0 mm OU), and a relatively large lens (4.3 mm OD and 4.1 mm OS). CT and MRI scans also demonstrate short axial eye lengths and thick sclera.

case_report: A 56-year-old male presented to the emergency department with fatigue and shortness of breath during physical activity for the past 3 to 4 days. The patient exhibited a slow heart rate and had a blood pressure reading of 160/70 mmHg. Electrocardiography (ECG) revealed an atrial rhythm with a 2:1 atrioventricular (AV) block. The patient did not report any episodes of fainting. He was admitted and monitored in the Coronary Care Unit (CCU). Serial cardiac markers and laboratory tests were within normal limits, and no reversible cause for the AV block was identified. A chest X-ray indicated slight enlargement of the heart.
test_results: A transthoracic echocardiographic evaluation detected an apically localized systemic AV valve, a dilated left atrium, a parallel arrangement of great arteries, significant systemic AV valve insufficiency, and ejection fraction (EF) of 32%. Multi-slice CT and MR angiography revealed AV and ventricular arterial discordance with persistent left superior vena cava and situs inversus abdominalis. Selective coronary arteriography demonstrated a well-developed right coronary system.
diagnosis: Congenitally Corrected Transposition of the Great Arteries
Orpha_name: Congenitally Corrected Transposition of the Great Arteries

case_report: A 52-year-old Saudi woman visited the outpatient dermatology clinic with complaints of multiple painful bumps on her trunk and upper extremities, persisting for the past 25 years. Recently, these lesions had increased in pain, size, and number. She had a history of uterine leiomyomatosis and underwent a hysterectomy 17 years ago. Her family history included multiple cases of uterine leiomyomatosis in her mother, two sisters, and two maternal aunts. Physical examination showed several smooth, nonmobile nodules, reddish to brown in color, clustered on her right arm, left forearm, and trunk. These nodules were firm and tender to touch, with diameters ranging from 0.5 to 2 cm.
test_results: Histological analysis showed a relatively well-circumscribed dermal proliferation of intersecting fascicles of spindle cells. The cells exhibited cigar-shaped nuclei and growth in between collagen bundles. The findings were consistent with a diagnosis of benign dermal leiomyoma.
Orpha_name: Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer

case_report: A 10-year-old girl, the third child in her family, was born to nonconsanguineous parents. Her two older sisters and parents did not show any signs of distal motor weakness, sensory deficits, or abnormal electrophysiologic findings. The patient experienced delayed motor milestones, beginning to walk independently at 24 months. Throughout her childhood, she encountered difficulties with gait, clumsiness, and balance, though these issues progressed very slowly. At 10 years old, a neurologic examination showed bilateral pes cavus, scoliosis, and a broad-based gait. She exhibited severe weakness in foot eversion without any proximal muscle involvement. Sensitivity to pinprick, touch, position, and vibration was reduced, with vibration sensation being more affected than pain sensation in all limbs. Sensory ataxia and a positive Romberg sign were noted. Deep tendon reflexes were absent, and no pathologic reflexes were observed. Her CMT neuropathy score was 20.
test_results: Electrophysiologic studies were performed at 7 and 10 years of age. Sensory nerve action potentials were absent in the median, ulnar, and sural nerves. Compound muscle action potentials were severely reduced in the median nerve (range, 0.2-0.5 mV) and absent in the ulnar, peroneal, and tibial nerves. Median MNCVs were markedly reduced (range, 2.6-3.0 m/s), and distal latencies were dramatically prolonged (range, 39.6-44.8 ms). The needle electromyogram was consistent with chronic neuropathy. Light-microscopy examination of longitudinal and cross-sections of nerve fibers revealed nerve fascicles that were markedly decreased in size, diffuse subendoneurial edema, and moderately to markedly decreased numbers of myelinated fibers (MFs) of all calibers, with suggestion of onion-bulb formation and endoneurial fibrosis. The mean diameter of MFs (3.14 µm) and the percentage area of MFs (1.39%) were also lower than in age-matched controls (4.5 µm and 25.2%, respectively). Electron-microscopy examination revealed findings consistent with abnormal myelin, such as focally folded, uncompacted, or deteriorating myelin, irregular myelin thickness, or fragmented myelin structures in Schwann cells or nearby macrophages. Exomes were captured using a SeqCap EZ device (version 3.0, Roche-NimbleGen, Madison, WI, USA), and sequencing was performed using a genome analyzer (HiSeq 2000, Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA). The University of California, Santa Cruz assembly hg19 (National Center for Biotechnology Information build 37.1) was used as the reference sequence. The candidate variants considered to be causative were confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The total sequencing yield of WES was approximately 10.47 Gbp, with a 91.72% coverage rate for the targeted exon regions (≥10×). The total number of observed variants was 69,592 single-nucleotide polymorphisms, of which 349 variants were observed in CMT-relevant genes that have been reported previously. Subsequent filtering was achieved for functionally significant variants, where the functionally significant variants indicate all variants that change the amino acid, such as nonsynonymous, splicing site, stop-gain/-loss, and coding indels. Filtering isolated 25 functionally significant variants in the CMT-relevant genes. Most variants have been reported in the dbSNP137 or 1000 Genome databases, except for three variants [one in the gene encoding dynactin subunit 1 (DCTN1) and one in PRX]. Mutation in DCTN1 c.2054T>G (p.V685G) was excluded because the variant was detected in unaffected family members (father and an elder sister) as well as a healthy control by capillary sequencing. However, a pair of compound heterozygote nonsense mutations, c.1174C>T (p.R392X) and c.2035C>T (p.R679X), in exon 7 of PRX were well fitted with an autosomal-recessive inheritance model within the family, and neither was found in normal controls (n=300). The c.1174C>T and c.2035C>T mutations were inherited from the patient's mother and father, respectively.

case_report: A 25-year-old Caucasian woman with a history of elevated calcium levels since age 16 presented with concerns about the effects of elevated calcium on pregnancy outcomes. Before pregnancy, her biochemistry showed albumin-adjusted calcium at 2.61 mmol/L (reference range: 2.10–2.55 mmol/L), albumin at 44 g/L (reference range: 33–48 g/L), PTH at 33 ng/L (reference range: 10–55 ng/L), and serum phosphate at 0.99 mmol/L (reference range: 0.80–1.50 mmol/L). Her previous 25-hydroxyvitamin D level was 58.1 nmol/L (reference range: 40–110 nmol/L). The calcium to creatinine clearance ratio (CCCR) was 0.79% before pregnancy. The patient's mother also had elevated calcium levels (albumin-adjusted calcium = 2.74 mmol/L, albumin 36 g/L). During the second trimester of pregnancy, the patient's albumin-adjusted calcium was 2.59 mmol/L, albumin was 33 g/L, and her CCCR increased to 1.99%. She delivered a healthy male at 40 weeks of gestational age, who had elevated calcium levels (serum calcium = 2.79 mmol/L, reference range: 1.90–2.60 mmol/L) that persisted at two years of age. While breastfeeding, the patient's albumin-adjusted calcium was 2.53 mmol/L. She experienced two first-trimester spontaneous abortions before carrying a fourth pregnancy to term, resulting in the birth of a healthy female with elevated calcium levels (serum calcium = 2.75 mmol/L, reference range: 1.90–2.60 mmol/L) at birth.
test_results: Genetic analysis revealed a heterozygous mutation of the R716 CE gene on the calcium sensing receptor.

case_report: A 14-year-old boy visited the Department of Pediatric Dentistry at Govt Dental College and Hospital, Rajiv Gandhi Institute of Medical Sciences, Kadapa, due to tooth mobility and pain in the lower right front tooth. The patient exhibited distinctive craniofacial and dental characteristics, leading to a comprehensive examination. He is the fourth child in a family with non-consanguineous parents, born after a normal labor. His birth history was uneventful, with no known exposure to infections, drugs, or irradiation during his mother's pregnancy. There were no similar malformations in the family history. Both parents and siblings appeared normal upon clinical and radiological examination. Extraoral examination showed an abnormal head shape and contour (turribrachycephaly), depressed nasal bridge, frontal bossing, midface hypoplasia, a characteristic 'crossbow shape' of the upper lip, trapezoidal mouth shape, cephalometric dolichofacial pattern, proptosis, and exorbitism. Examination of the upper limbs revealed symmetric soft tissue syndactyly of all digits, forming a single unit with a broad fused nail, resulting in a spoon-like deformity. The lower limbs also showed symmetrical syndactyly of all toes with a broad fused single nail. The patient had delayed milestones and mild mental deficiency. Other systemic examinations were normal. Intraoral features included a high-arched palate with lateral swellings of the palatine processes on either side of the midline, resembling a 'pseudocleft'. Oral hygiene was poor, with abundant dental plaque and calculus. The gingiva was congested and showed inflammatory enlargement in relation to the anterior teeth, with several decayed teeth. Angle's pseudo class III malocclusion with severe crowding of the maxillary and mandibular anterior teeth, skeletal anterior open bite, and posterior crossbite were observed. The primary teeth were retained, with delayed and ectopic eruption of permanent teeth.
test_results: Radiographs of both hands showed complete bony syndactyly of all the digits involving the phalanges. Radiographs of right foot showed syndactyly of all phalanges with fusion of first and second metatarsals and left foot showed fusion of first and second phalanges at their distal ends along with the fusion of first and second metatarsals, the third, fourth and fifth phalanges were fused at their proximal ends. Skull radiographs revealed fused coronal sutures, turribrachycephalic skull contour and elongated flat forehead.

case_report: A 12-year-old male, born to healthy unrelated parents with no family history of skeletal lesions or nephropathy, presented with a history of joint issues beginning at 2 years and 4 months old. Initial symptoms included a painful, swollen right wrist with limited movement. Six months later, swelling and pain developed in the right 2nd-5th proximal interphalangeal joints (PIPs). He was treated for one year with leflunomide and diclofenac sodium, which alleviated swelling and pain but left significant motion restriction. Methotrexate was added to his treatment regimen for three years. Joint symptoms resolved by age 7, and treatment was discontinued due to concerns about medication side effects. Between ages 7 and 11, he experienced no joint swelling or pain, and no imaging or urine tests were conducted. At age 11, mild swelling and pain reappeared in the right elbow, right wrist, and right 2nd-5th PIPs. A few months later, the right elbow became stiff with limited motion and a flexion deformity. MRI at 11 years and 8 months showed an abnormal patchy signal in the right humeral olecranon fossa, joint cavity effusion, and synovial thickening. No X-rays of the wrists or other joints were taken as they were asymptomatic. He resumed treatment with methotrexate, naproxen, and a TNFα receptor inhibitor (etanercept) for three months without improvement. A second MRI seven months later showed progression of bone lesions, joint deformation, articular surface damage, and synovitis. The right wrist carpal bones were missing. Treatment was changed to methotrexate, sulfasalazine, and diclofenac sodium for another three months without symptomatic improvement. At 12.5 years old, the patient presented with a height between the 10-25th percentile (150 cm) and weight below the 3rd percentile (30 kg). Physical examination revealed subtle facial abnormalities (protruding forehead and micrognathia) but no temporomandibular joint abnormalities. Respiratory, cardiovascular, and abdominal examinations were normal, and cognitive function was age-appropriate. Marked angular malformation of the right elbow and ulnar deviation of both hands, more pronounced on the right, were observed. Both wrist joints and bilateral 1st-5th PIPs were swollen and painful, while shoulders, hips, knees, and spine were unaffected. Laboratory tests showed normal antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, anti-citrullinated protein antibody levels, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein; elevated IL-6 (482.59 pg/ml, normal range: 0–16.6 pg/ml) and TNF-α (12.45 pg/ml, normal range: 0–5.2 pg/ml). Radiographs of the hands revealed osteoporosis and absence of most carpal bones; narrowing of all PIPs and metacarpophalangeal joints of the right hand, and deformation of the second metacarpophalangeal joints of the right hand. The proximal part of the bilateral metacarpal was tapering. X-ray of the elbows showed deformation of the distal right humerus and proximal ulnar and radius, destruction of the ossification center, narrowing of the right elbow joint space, and soft tissue swelling around the right elbow joint. Lower extremities were unaffected, and radiographs of both feet were normal. Renal involvement began at 2 years old with proteinuria (0.06 g/day), normal renal function, and normal blood pressure, which resolved without treatment over four years. At 12.5 years old, proteinuria (0.76 g/day) was detected incidentally during a routine checkup. Blood pressure, serum creatinine, albumin, and total cholesterol levels were normal. Renal ultrasound revealed compression of the left renal vein. Captopril was administered to reduce urinary protein levels.
test_results: The trio whole-exome sequencing (WES) results revealed a de novo heterozygous missense mutation at NM_005461: c.188 C > A (NP_005452.2: p. P63G). Comparative genomics analysis revealed conservation of proline 63 in the transactivation domain of MAF bZIP transcription factor B (MAFB). According to American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) guidelines, this mutation is pathogenic.
Orpha_name: Multicentric carpo-tarsal osteolysis with or without nephropathy

case_report: An 11-year-old male presented with muscle pain, weakness, lack of appetite, and vomiting. Laboratory tests showed elevated liver enzymes (AST 144 IU/L, ALT 267 IU/L) and an ultrasound revealed an enlarged liver. He is the second child in a family of three, with healthy, unrelated parents. He was born at full term with a birth weight of 3290 grams and had a normal adaptation to life outside the womb. He was breastfed until the age of 3, and his psychomotor development and growth were normal. He had episodes of asthma in early childhood. At 1 year old, he was hospitalized for elevated liver enzymes and anemia, but no further tests were conducted. He was hospitalized again at ages 4 and 5 for wheezing and asthma exacerbations. From age 6, he experienced muscle cramps without fever, easy fatigue, and muscle pain after light exercise, sometimes accompanied by vomiting. During the latest episode, tests showed decreased free carnitine and increased acylcarnitines from short to very long-chain, along with elevated levels of glutaric, 2-ketoglutaric, ethylmalonic, and dicarboxylic acids. Elevated liver enzymes (AST 90 IU/L, ALT 143 IU/L), creatine kinase (348 IU/L), and ammonia (93 μmol/L) were also noted. The plasma amino acid profile showed significant hyperprolinemia (520.1 μmol/L) and slight hyperasparaginemia (232.8 μmol/L). Neurological examination revealed preserved consciousness, general weakness, reduced muscle strength in the lower limbs, and mild muscle wasting. Heart ultrasound showed mild concentric hypertrophy of the left ventricle, and liver ultrasound indicated diffuse hyperechogenicity consistent with steatosis. During hospitalization, he received intravenous glucose (10%, 4 mg/kg/min) and l-carnitine (100 mg/kg), leading to gradual clinical improvement. A trial with Rf (150 mg/day) normalized glutaric acid levels but other organic acids and acylcarnitines remained abnormal. Upon discharge, he was advised to reduce long-chain lipid intake and control protein intake in his diet. Oral l-carnitine supplementation and Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) were continued.
test_results: Persistent dicarboxylic aciduria and elevated ethylmalonic acid.
diagnosis: Combined isobutyryl-CoA and multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency

case_report: A 71-year-old Caucasian man was diagnosed with a malignant neoplasm in an unspecified part of the right bronchus or right lung (stage IIIB) and a malignant neoplasm in the upper lobe of the left lung and left bronchus. A wedge resection of the right lower and upper lobes was performed soon after diagnosis, revealing adenocarcinoma. The patient underwent two separate courses of radiation treatment, one targeting the left lung and another targeting the right lobe. Pembrolizumab, 200 mg administered intravenously every 3 weeks, was initiated 5 years post-diagnosis following a high (100%) expression of programmed death-ligand 1 in an adenosquamous pathology core sample. At the commencement of pembrolizumab therapy, the patient's corrected calcium level was 9.2 mg/dL (normal range: 8.5-10.2 mg/dL). He had no prior medical history or other risk factors for low calcium levels.
test_results: The patient’s corrected calcium level was 9.2 mg/dL (normal, 8.5-10.2 mg/dL) at the start of pembrolizumab therapy. The calcium level after the 13th dose of pembrolizumab was 8.1 mg/dL (normal, 8.5-10.2 mg/dL). The patient’s parathyroid hormone (PTH) and corrected calcium levels after the 18th dose of pembrolizumab were 20.4 pg/mL (normal, 14-72 pg/mL) and 7.7 mg/dL (normal, 8.5-10.2 mg/dL), respectively. After the 22nd dose, the levels were 4.3 mg/dL (normal, 14-72 pg/mL) and 6.5 (normal, 8.5-10.2 mg/dL), respectively. His PTH and calcium levels remained low. Calcium-sensing receptor gene analysis (LabCorp Specialty Testing Group) was negative for any kind of genetic mutation.

case_report: An 8-year-old girl from a rural area presented with pain in her left leg and an ulcer on the anterior aspect of her left shin, persisting for 15 days. These symptoms have been recurring over the past 4 years. The ulcer typically healed with antibiotics but reappeared after a few days. A biopsy from the ulcer indicated chronic inflammatory infiltrate. Imaging showed no signs of osteomyelitis. She received anti-tubercular therapy followed by multidrug therapy for leprosy, but the ulcer continued to recur. On physical examination, there was a 3 × 3 cm ulcer on the anterior aspect of the shin and a healed ulcer just above the current one. Sensation was intact, and there were no thickened nerves or lymphadenopathy. Her general and systemic examinations, as well as laboratory investigations, were within normal limits.
test_results: A X-ray of left leg showed no evidence of osteomyelitis however, it revealed a linear calcification ending in the ulcer. Previous X-ray also showed the same linear calcification.

case_report: A 35-year-old male from Iran reported experiencing gradual weakness in both upper and lower limbs starting at age 20. At the time of evaluation, he had difficulty standing up from a seated position and washing his hair. He did not report any sensory issues. His medical history was unremarkable. He was born to parents who were not related by blood. One of his brothers exhibited similar symptoms, while four other siblings did not. On physical examination, he exhibited a waddling gait without muscle wasting. Muscle tone was normal. Muscle strength testing revealed MRC grade 4/5 weakness in hip flexion and extension, hip adduction, and knee flexion and extension. Elbow flexion strength was MRC grade 4+/5 bilaterally. Strength in the distal upper and lower limbs, as well as facial, ocular, and neck muscles, was normal (MRC 5/5). Reflexes and sensory examination were normal. Creatine kinase (CK) levels were elevated at 1990. An MRI of the upper limbs conducted three years prior showed increased T2 signal in the teres major and long head of the triceps bilaterally, without signs of atrophy or fatty infiltration. A muscle biopsy indicated end-stage muscle disease consistent with chronic muscular dystrophy. Previous genetic tests for Becker muscular dystrophy and facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) were negative. Additionally, targeted sequencing of the fukutin-related protein (FKRP) gene yielded normal results.
test_results: Next generation sequencing (NGS) revealed homozygosity for a novel splice variant [c.294+5G>A; p.(Ala98Ins4*)] in intron 5 of the ANO5 gene. Complementary DNA studies demonstrated intron inclusion and a complete absence of normal product.
diagnosis: Limb Girdle Muscular Dystrophy  due to a novel splice variant in the ANO5 gene

case_report: Patient 2, an 8.5-year-old boy, presented with multiple ecchymosis for half a day. The patient had no abnormalities at birth and was in normal physical condition. At 2 months old, he was diagnosed with thrombocytopenia. At 5 years old, he underwent cervical lymphadenectomy, and a lymph node biopsy showed reactive hyperplasia. At 7 years old, he had a colonoscopy and polypectomy due to abdominal pain and diarrhea caused by intussusception from multiple ileocecal polyps. Upon presentation, he had multiple ecchymosis on both lower limbs, scattered petechiae on limbs and trunk, and enlarged superficial lymph nodes on both sides of the neck, with the largest measuring 2 cm x 2 cm. His height and weight were normal. Physical examination and imaging did not show significant enlargement of the liver and spleen. Blood tests revealed a low platelet count of 72 (10^9/L), a normal red blood cell count of 4.53 (10^12/L), and a slightly elevated white blood cell count of 5.55 (10^9/L). The levels of serum IgA, IgG, and IgM were slightly increased (gamma globulin infusion one week before this test), and an abnormal lymphocyte proportion in peripheral blood was detected by flow cytometry. Additionally, serum detection of CMV IgM was positive, but the concentrations of CMV and EBV DNA were less than 4.00E+02 copies/ml and 2.00E+03 copies/ml, respectively, excluding CMV and EBV infections.
test_results: Peripheral blood was drawn from the patient and his parents for trios WES.

case_report: A 19-month-old male infant underwent a routine urine test, which revealed urine protein at a level of ++ and the presence of occult blood. The 24-hour protein excretion was measured at 1340 mg/24 h. Serum albumin was recorded at 39.3 g/l. After twenty days, the patient was admitted to our hospital, where repeat testing confirmed the presence of urine protein and occult blood. The patient exhibited no additional symptoms, and other laboratory tests returned normal results. The infant's pregnancy and birth were normal and full-term. There is no family history of similar symptoms, including in the mother. Electrophoresis analysis of the urine protein identified low molecular weight proteins, specifically RBP, α1-microglobulin, and β2-microglobulin. The urine calcium to creatinine ratio was within the normal range at 0.236. A renal biopsy was not conducted.
test_results: A hemizygotic mutation (c. A815G, p.Y272C) was found in the exon of the CLCN5 gene(ChrX:49850995). The same mutation was detected in his mother.

case_report: A 13-year-old girl of Black African descent was referred to the scleroderma services of the rheumatology department at Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children NHS Foundation Trust, London for a second opinion. She had a history of extensive skin thickening and widespread joint contractures that began in infancy at 9 months old. The skin changes initially appeared on her lower limbs and spread to her arms and trunk over two years. Joint contractures were observed approximately two years after the initial skin changes. There was a history suggestive of mild Raynaud’s phenomenon, but no digital ulceration, gastrointestinal, or respiratory symptoms. She was born at term with no neonatal complications. Her past medical history included valvar and supravalvar pulmonary artery stenosis requiring serial balloon dilatation, mild developmental delay, and conductive hearing loss. Microarray-based comparative genomic hybridization was normal. There was no family history of cancer. Clinical examination showed diffusely thickened skin on her limbs and trunk, sparing her face. Her weight was 41 kg (25th centile for age) and height was 139 cm (2nd centile for age). She was normotensive at the time of review. Delayed puberty was noted, with no menarche at 13 years old. Multiple joint contractures were present, but no active arthritis. There were no signs of cutaneous telangiectasia, fingertip ulceration, or calcinosis. Mild dysmorphic features included small eyes and ears, a broad nasal tip, a long and prominent chin, bilateral clinodactyly, and mild two-three toe syndactyly. Nailfold capillaroscopy showed dilated capillary loops, tortuosity, micro-bleeding, and widespread dropout. Digital thermography indicated a cold baseline cutaneous temperature of the peripheries, with some fingers remaining cool long after a cold challenge. She tested weakly positive for antinuclear antibodies (ANA at 1:160, homogenous pattern) and negative for dsDNA antibodies, rheumatoid factor, and extranuclear antibodies. Complement function (alternate and classical pathways) was normal, as were levels of C3, C4, and C1q. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein were repeatedly within normal limits. Echocardiography revealed mild persistent pulmonary stenosis, a small left pulmonary artery, mild coarctation of the aorta, mild biventricular hypertrophy, but no evidence of pulmonary hypertension. Barium swallow was normal. A skeletal survey showed advanced bone age but no skeletal dysplasia. A skin biopsy revealed hyperkeratotic epidermis and fibrotic dermis with areas of hyalinization; adnexal structures were sparse with an absence of pilosebaceous units.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed a previously well described rare heterozygous c.1499 T > C (p.lle500Thr) class 5 variant in SMAD4. Testing for variants in other relevant genes pertinent to phenotype (including PTPN11, LMNA, and MMP14) revealed no other pathogenic variants. Parental testing confirmed this variant arose de novo in the proband.

case_report: M. J. I., a 33-year-old white female housewife with primary education, has experienced bilateral hearing loss, more pronounced in the left ear, since childhood. She also reported vision impairment starting at age 16. Her parents are not related. She has a 28-year-old sister who also has bilateral hearing loss, which is more severe than that of the patient. The clinical examination of the ears, nose, and throat was normal.
test_results: The ophthalmologic test revealed right eye visual acuity only for hand movements, and left eye visual acuity only for light perception. Retinography showed bilateral hypopigmentation of the pigmentary epithelium, which included the macula. Fluorescent retinography showed sings of diffuse atrophy of the pigmentary epithelium, including the macula. The computerized visual field perimetry revealed a nearly complete absence of response to the stimulus in the right eye; this test was not done on the left eye due to low visual acuity. Pure tone audiometry showed bilateral moderate to severe sloping sensorineural hearing loss. The otoneurological exam suggested cervical peripheral labyrinth disease.

case_report: A 14-year-old girl was referred to a genetic outpatient clinic for further evaluation of head abnormalities. Pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated; family history was negative. Psychomotor development was normal. Previously, she had been under neurological observation. At the age of 10, she experienced an episode involving facial grimace on the right side and loss of sensation in the right hand area, without disturbance of consciousness. There were also a few short sensory disturbances in the right hand without disturbance of consciousness. Physical examination showed no skin and ophthalmic changes, but subtle facial asymmetry was visible, with slight hypotrophy on the right. Discreet asymmetry of the face when smiling was observed. Neurological examination was normal. Electroencephalography (EEG) recording revealed no epileptic discharges and antiepileptic treatment was not indicated.
test_results: The MRI of the head stated the presence of meningeal angiomatosis.

case_report: The patient is a 19-year-old woman who was born with a scalp defect that healed after early conservative wound management. She has no notable medical history and no neuropsychiatric issues. Her family, including parents and brothers, do not have dermatologic or systemic problems. She first visited the clinic 10 years ago at the age of nine for a scalp lesion, which had transformed into fibrotic tissue and appeared as an atrophic alopecic patch. Over the past decade, she developed atrophic and nodular skin changes on the right side of her trunk and limbs, which became more pronounced. Additionally, syndactyly of the right fourth and fifth toes, previously unnoticed, began to affect her quality of life. Upon her return to the clinic, a comprehensive physical examination revealed multiple, well-demarcated atrophic patches primarily on the right trunk and leg. Some lesions presented as brown or yellow protruding masses with deposited and herniated fat tissue. These atrophic patches and protruding masses followed a linear pattern along Blaschko's line. Only a few atrophic patches were observed on the left leg. The syndactyly of the right fourth and fifth toes was also noted.
test_results: Examination of skin biopsy specimens from the scalp showed an irregularly thickened epidermis, atrophic dermis with upward extension of the subcutaneous tissue, and mild fibrotic changes and loss of periadnexal structures. A skin biopsy from the right calf revealed prominent dermal atrophy and extension of subcutaneous fat toward the upper dermis.

case_report: A 9-year-old girl presented with a history of gradually worsening abdominal distension, decreased urine output, and abdominal pain for 2 weeks. Two weeks prior to admission, she experienced nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain without diarrhea several hours after eating bread. She had no signs of infection such as fever, rash, or sore throat. On admission, she was afebrile and had normal vital signs. Her weight was 32.2 kg (50th to 75th percentile), and height was 140 cm (75th to 90th percentile). She had a history of allergic rhinitis. A physical examination revealed periorbital swelling, pitting edema on both legs, and abdominal distension with mild diffuse tenderness and shifting dullness. Laboratory tests on admission showed hemoglobin level, 15.4 g/dL; hematocrit, 43%; peripheral leukocyte, 13,390/µL with an eosinophil count of 840/µL (6.3%); serum total protein, 2.3 g/dL; albumin, 1.3 g/dL; calcium, 7.3 mg/dL; erythrocyte sedimentation rate, 2 mm/hr; and C-reactive protein, 0.56 mg/dL. A urinalysis was normal without proteinuria. The multiple allergen simultaneous test showed positive responses to mites (class 2) and Acarus siro (class 3), with elevation of the total immunoglobulin (Ig) E value (>200 IU/mL). Anti-CMV IgM was negative. Chest and abdominal radiographs displayed pleural effusion on both sides. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed pleural effusion and massive ascites. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen confirmed marked thickening of the small intestinal wall. A pleural fluid analysis revealed lymphocytes, 25%; polymorphonuclear neutrophils, 7%; eosinophils, 0%; protein, 152 mg/dL; glucose, 116 mg/dL; and adenosine deaminase, 2 IU/L. An abdominal paracentesis was not performed. Alpha 1 anti-trypsin excretion in the stool was elevated to 1,204 mg/dL (normal, ≤54 mg/dL).
test_results: A gastroscopic examination revealed large swollen gastric folds, erythema, erosion, and exudation in the body and fundus, although the antrum was normal. Histological findings of the gastric mucosa showed moderate infiltration of eosinophils (20 to 38 per high power field) and neutrophils in the lamina propria, mucosal edema, and dilatation of the capillaries and lymphatics.

case_report: A 28-year-old female with a history of chronic back pain, tendonitis, and joint pains presented with two episodes of vomiting blood, worsening abdominal pain, and bloody diarrhea. The patient experienced joint pain in her hands, wrists, and right knee. She reported daily use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for chronic back pain. The abdominal pain was diffuse, cramping in nature, intermittent, and radiated to the back. She reported passing a small amount of blood mixed with loose stool on the morning of admission. Additionally, she noted a red, non-itchy rash on her lower legs. She denied having fevers, sore throat, red or painful eyes, or previous bleeding episodes. Physical examination showed diffuse abdominal tenderness without rebound tenderness or rigidity. A rectal exam revealed a small amount of blood mixed with scant yellowish stool. A red, palpable purpuric rash was observed on her thighs and lower legs. Blood tests showed an elevated white cell count of 13,700/mm3, C-reactive protein (CRP) of 27.78 mg/L, and D-dimer of > 35.2 mg/L (FEU). Complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, coagulation profile, and urinalysis were normal.
test_results: Upper GI endoscopy revealed mild gastric erythema and diffuse erythematous, hemorrhagic, friable mucosa with superficial, thick, adherent white exudate seen in the second portion of the duodenum. Gastric and duodenal biopsies revealed mild reactive gastropathy (negative for Helicobacter pylori) and acute duodenitis. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan showed thickening of the duodenal wall.

case_report: The patient is a 17-year-old Caucasian male who initially exhibited prolonged jaundice during the neonatal period, with an unconjugated bilirubin level of 400 μmol/L and no signs of hemolytic anemia. He was born after an uneventful pregnancy to non-consanguineous Caucasian parents. Early in life, he was found to have elevated indirect bilirubin levels and was treated periodically with phenobarbital, which reduced his bilirubin levels to an average of 100–200 μmol/L. During childhood, he remained generally healthy. At puberty, his jaundice worsened, and bilirubin levels rose to 300–350 μmol/L, although he had no other symptoms and maintained normal growth and academic performance. Laboratory tests showed no abnormalities, and hepatitis viral markers were negative. There was no evidence of other metabolic disorders, such as organic acidurias or amino acidurias, and fatty acid profiles were normal. Imaging studies, including abdominal ultrasound and MRI, showed no abnormalities. A percutaneous liver biopsy also revealed no pathological findings. Laboratory investigations indicated isolated elevation of indirect bilirubin levels, reduced glutathione (0.89 mmol/l; reference value 1.12–1.216 mmol/l), and a glucuronide level in 24-hour urine of up to 102 mg/ml (reference value 430–600 mg/ml). The patient responded to phenobarbital treatment and showed no signs of kernicterus.
test_results: Four different variants in the UGT1A1 gene were identified in the patient: g.3664A > C (c.1352A > C, rs3755319); g.4963_4964TA[7] (c.-53_-52insTA, A(TA)7TAA, UGT1A1*28, rs8175347); g.5884G > T (c.864 + 5G > T, IVS1 + 5G > T); and g.11895_11898del (c.996+2_996+5del) (reference sequence NG_033238.1).

case_report: A 34-month-old girl, born at 42 weeks of gestation, presented with congenital central nervous system abnormalities including holoprosencephaly, schizencephaly, polymicrogyria, and agenesis of the corpus callosum. She was evaluated in the Pediatric Ophthalmology Department of Kornel Gibiński University Clinical Centre in Katowice. Additionally, epilepsy and ocular fundus lesions were noted.
test_results: A normal female karyotype 46,XX was found (GTG-banding) indicating no chromosomal rearrangement. DNA microarray was also performed to extend the diagnostic process. Since no chromosome abnormalities were detected, deletions and duplications of more than 200,000 base pairs were excluded as the cause of clinical symptoms. No pathology of the anterior segment of the eye was revealed. The patient exhibited bilateral pupillary response to light; the left pupil response was sluggish. Intraocular pressure was 10 mm Hg in both eyes; central retinal thickness was 613 µm and 588 µm in the right and left eye, respectively. Gonioscopy grading: wide angle with normal structure with single iris bridges was demonstrated (C30 r0 PTM). Fundoscopic examination revealed optic disc colobomas in both eyes, extensive chorioretinal lacunae at the posterior pole with retinal pigment epithelium regrouping, peripheral retinal pigment epithelium atrophy and retinal vessel narrowing. The electrophysiological test showed that FVEP P2 wave latency was normal (119–137 ms; normal values 96–148 ms; mean 114 ms; median 113.5 ms). The P2 amplitude after stimulation of right eye and left eye recorded from the O1 was 2.26 µV and 225 nV and from the O2 was 4.85 and 4.75 µV, respectively. B-scan ultrasonography revealed an optic disc lesion consistent with optic disk coloboma.

case_report: A 40-year-old, HIV-positive female presented with a 1-month history of an annular truncal eruption. She had been on highly active antiretroviral therapy (ART) for 1 year (efavirenz, lamivudine, and tenofovir) without trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis and had a CD4 count of 316 cells/mm3. Her rapid plasma reagin and Treponema pallidum hemagglutination assay were negative. The patient was commenced on oral steroids at 0.5 mg/kg and her ART was discontinued for a 2-week period. During this time her rash improved markedly and the prednisone was slowly tapered, but the rash recurred despite discontinuation of her ART. In addition to the presenting rash, she developed an intercurrent herpes zoster infection and was treated with antivirals. Subsequently, she began developing an erythematous rash involving the malar area, annular erythematous plaques on the trunk, specifically on the “V” of the neck, and on the upper limbs with targetoid lesions on the palms and vasculitic lesions on the limbs.
test_results: ANF was negative, and histology showed a lichenoid eruption with basal cell vacuolization and colloid bodies. Her repeat ANF remained negative with a low serum complement level C3 (0.7 g/L) and C4 (0.14 g/L) and a positive anti-Ro SSA antibody.

case_report: A 3-year-old male child, born to consanguineous parents, presented with global developmental delay, hypotonia, lower limb tremors, and poor feeding. The child had a history of recurrent fever, cold, and cough since the age of 1 year. Over the past 6 months, the parents observed increased irritability. At 2 years old, the child was able to walk with support and speak monosyllables, but subsequently, there was a regression of these learned skills.
test_results: Brain MRI studies of the proband showed moderate confluent FLAIR/T2 hyperintense signal in the periventricular and deep white matter of bilateral frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes. In addition, FLAIR/T2 hyperintense signal was noted in corpus callosum involving genu and splenium. A mild FLAIR hyperintense signal was also noted in the bilateral deep cerebellar white matter. Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood using salting out technique and was subjected to a targeted exome sequencing study. Variant filtration and prioritization analysis revealed a homozygous variant c.688T > G (p.Cys230Gly) in exon 6 of the PSAP gene (NM_002778.4). This variant has not been reported in the 1000 genomes and gnomAD databases. The in-silico prediction of the variant is damaging by SIFT, PolyPhen-2, PROVEAN, and MutationTaster. The variant was classified as likely pathogenic as per the ACMG-AMP guidelines and ClinGen framework with the following criteria—PP3 (strong) and PM2 (moderate).
diagnosis: Metachromatic Leukodystrophy  due to Sap-B deficiency

case_report: A 29-year-old female with a history of hypertension was undergoing treatment for infertility related to polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) using in-vitro fertilization (IVF). She received ovarian stimulation therapy with Follistim/Gonal-F, Menopur cetrotide/ganirelix, and leuprolide before the transvaginal egg retrieval. The patient was brought to the hospital by emergency services from an urgent care clinic, presenting with worsening chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath on exertion, cough, and bloating for six days following the procedure. Her last menstrual period was one month before admission. Initial urine pregnancy test was negative. Vital signs included a blood pressure of 147/96 mmHg, a pulse of 121 beats per minute, a temperature of 99.5 F, a respiratory rate of 22 bpm, and an oxygen saturation of 97% on room air. A chest computerized tomographic angiogram (CTA) and initial chest radiographs (CXR) were obtained. Elevated D-dimer levels were noted on admission, but CTA showed no emboli. CXR and CTA revealed a large right pleural effusion, a small left pleural effusion, and associated airspace disease suggestive of atelectasis or pneumonia. A leftward mediastinal shift was observed, likely due to the larger right-sided pleural effusion and ascites. Laboratory results from the emergency department indicated elevated serum C-reactive protein (CRP) levels. Physical examination in the medical unit revealed hirsutism, obesity, decreased breath sounds in the right lung, decreased tactile fremitus, and dullness to percussion. The patient's heart rate had increased to 133 bpm. PCOS management included metformin 500mg QD, with monitoring of hemoglobin A1C and point-of-care glucose levels. Hypertension was managed with her home dose of amlodipine 5mg QD. Ultrasound-guided thoracocentesis was performed for the right-sided pleural effusion on the day of admission, yielding 1000ml of hazy, dark, straw-colored fluid. Laboratory analysis of the pleural fluid was conducted. A pleural drainage catheter was placed for continued drainage. Post-procedure CXR showed a decreased size of the pleural effusion with mildly improved aeration of the right lung. An obstetrics and gynecology (OBGYN) consult was obtained on admission.
test_results: The right ovary contained multiple enlarged follicles and a simple cyst 3.5cm in diameter. Similarly, the left ovary had multiple enlarged follicles and a simple cyst measuring 4.3cm in diameter. A minimal amount of free fluid was present in the pelvic cul-de-sac near the uterine fundus.

case_report: A 57-year-old woman with a history of drug-refractory symptomatic hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy was referred to our institution. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with a maximum wall thickness of 12 mm and a maximum pressure gradient of 73 mmHg across the left ventricular outflow tract at rest. An abnormal structure resembling thickened chordae was observed on the lateral side of the left ventricle.
test_results: Transesophageal echocardiography and contrast-enhanced CT showed that the abnormal funicular structure at the basal septum and abnormally thickened chordae caused LVOTO.

case_report: A 9-year-old boy presented with unerupted lower front teeth. He is the first child of parents who are not related by blood, but his maternal grandparents are related by blood. The boy exhibits short stature, a large head with open fontanelles, a depressed nasal bridge with a prominent nose, larger eyes, and short, wide fingers and toes with dysplastic nails. Scoliosis is evident. Intra-orally, he has a narrow arched palate with grooving, missing upper and lower deciduous central teeth, and multiple carious teeth. The parents reported a history of fractures and mentioned a living cousin with similar features.
test_results: Radiological survey revealed evidence of generalized osteo-sclerosis, open cranial sutures, a spool-shaped vertebral body, fishtail deficiency of the anterior border of vertebral bodies, and an aplastic distal clavicle. The orthopantomogram revealed absent frontal sinuses, poorly pneumatized maxillary sinuses, an obtuse mandibular angle, and dysplastic roots of upper and lower central incisors.

case_report: The patient was a one-year-old male. His parents and elder sister, who were not related by blood, were also part of the study. The patient underwent various physical examinations and tests, including blood gas analysis, blood ammonia testing, plasma acylcarnitine profiling, urinary organic acid analysis, and brainstem auditory evoked potential (BAEP) studies. His family members only had physical examinations. The acylcarnitine profile was analyzed using liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry, and urinary organic acids were analyzed using gas chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry. Blood gas analysis was performed with an automated analyzer, and BAEP was recorded using an electromyogram device. Written informed consent for data collection and publication was obtained from the parents, and the study was approved by the Ethical Committee of Quanzhou Children’s Hospital of Fujian, adhering to HIPAA regulations. The patient, a Chinese Han boy, initially presented to the dermatology department at the age of one year with a skin rash around the periorbital and perioral areas and was treated for eczema. Three weeks later, he was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit with severe tachypnea, moaning, and heart failure. The rash had spread to his limbs, neck, and groin. Capillary blood gas analysis revealed metabolic acidosis with a pH of 6.98, a base excess of -26 mmol/L, bicarbonate level of 3.9 mmol/L, an anion gap of 25.2 mmol/L, elevated lactate of 13.1 mmol/L (normal < 2 mmol/L), and elevated ammonia of 152.0 μmol/L (normal < 47 μmol/L). Biochemical tests on admission showed low ornithine (15.99 μmol/L; normal 42–325 μmol/L) and a plasma acylcarnitine profile with low free carnitine and significant increases in C5-OH, C5-OH/C0, C5-OH/C8, C3/C2, and C3/C0. The urinary organic acid profile showed excessive excretion of 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid, acetylglycine, propionylglycine, 3-methylcrotonylglycine, methylcrotonylglycine, 3-hydroxybutyric acid, pyruvic acid, and lactic acid. Increased levels of 2-keto-3-methyl-pentanoic acid and 2-keto-isocaproic acid suggested a metabolic disorder of branched-chain amino acids. The patient was treated with biotin (20 mg bid), which led to the resolution of the skin rash and normalization of acid–base balance within five days. Subsequently, the level of C5-OH decreased, and the urinary organic acid profile showed undetectable levels of acetylglycine, propionylglycine, 3-methylcrotonylglycine, and methylcrotonylglycine. During the acute episode, a BAEP study indicated significantly prolonged wave I latency and I–V interpeak latency intervals, with increased bilateral thresholds: left at 50 dB nHL and right at 60 dB nHL, indicating bilateral hearing impairment. A cattle encephalon glycoside and ignotin injection was administered. After 43 days of biotin therapy, a repeat BAEP study showed that the bilateral thresholds had decreased to 30 dB nHL, indicating improvement in hearing.
test_results: Genetic sequencing results reveal that the patient carries the maternal missense mutation c.1522C > T (p.Arg508Trp) in exon 9 of the HLCS gene, the novel paternal 2-bp deletion c. 1006_1007delGA (p.Glu336Thrfs*15) in exon 6 of the HLCS gene, and also the novel paternal 5-bp deletion c.638_642delAACAC (p.His213Profs*4) in exon 4 of the BTD gene. Furthermore, his family’s genotypes have been confirmed at a heterozygous level by Sanger sequencing, and his healthy elder sister has been shown to carry the same mutations as his father. The p.Arg508Trp mutation has been widely reported to be pathogenic. The p.Glu336Thrfs*15 and p.His213Profs*4 mutations could not be found in the literature or the 1000 Genome, ESP6500, ExAC, or dbSNP databases and were not detected in 100 healthy individuals. The effect of these mutations on protein function is predicted to be deleterious by PROVEAN and MutationTaster. Additionally, the p.Glu336Thrfs*15 mutation resides in a conserved stretch of amino acids and leads to truncated proteins lacking the conserved domains of HLCS. When all this information is taken into account, the c.1006_1007delGA (p.Glu336Thrfs*15) mutation is considered to be deleterious and likely pathogenic.

case_report: A 25-year-old woman with no prior medical history was admitted to the emergency department after being stung on the toe by an unidentified animal while walking at night in an area known to have scorpions, near a local cemetery. Shortly after the sting, she experienced significant local pain and numbness in her entire left leg, along with multiple episodes of vomiting, heavy sweating, mild difficulty breathing, elevated blood pressure, and a rapid heart rate. Initial medical evaluation revealed a blood pressure of 220/110 mm Hg and a heart rate of 156 bpm.
test_results: The electrocardiogram showed sustained ventricular tachycardia with very fast heart rate of approximately 300 bpm associated with a right bundle branch block pattern. The electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia associated with QTc interval prolongation.
