Chest radiographs demonstrated bilateral fluffy shadows compatible with pulmonary edema and a normal cardiac area. Laboratory tests showed hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, important metabolic acidosis with lactate elevation, leukocytosis, and troponin I elevation. On the second day, echocardiography showed important depression of the left ventricular ejection fraction (30%) and severe hypokinesia in wall motion, except for the apical region, which was hyperkinetic. On the third day, the echocardiography was repeated and showed a mild depression of left ventricular ejection fraction (41%) associated with hypokinesia only in the basal segments. One month later, she was evaluated at an outpatient service and was found to be asymptomatic. Echocardiography was repeated and found to have fully normalized.
diagnosis: Cardiogenic Shock due to Scorpion Envenomation

case_report: A 55-year-old male clerk was admitted for electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) in December 2006 due to medication-resistant psychotic depression. After tapering off antidepressant medication, ECT was administered three times a week. Right unilateral stimulation was performed using a Thymatron IV ECT apparatus. During the first ECT session, general anesthesia was induced with thiopental, and muscle relaxation was achieved with succinylcholine. The patient experienced prolonged apnea for approximately 25 minutes during the awakening phase, necessitating mask ventilation.
test_results: A dibucaine number test showed an inhibition rate of 53% (normal range > 70%).

case_report: The patient is a 14-year-old boy with muscle weakness starting at age 3, born to nonconsanguineous parents and without any family history of similar issues. He had decreased fetal movements and mild developmental motor delay, including toe walking. His mental development was normal. Over time, he experienced gradual weakening of the proximal muscles in his limbs and trunk, though he could still perform daily activities independently. He had difficulty climbing stairs, jumping, running, and rising from the floor but did not have respiratory issues. Physical examination revealed hyperkeratosis pilaris on the extensor surfaces of his legs and arms. Six months prior to admission, he experienced three episodes of gross hematuria with blood clots in the urine but no fever, back pain, urinary tract infection, frequent urination, trauma, swelling, joint pain, or skin rashes. Respiratory and cardiovascular examinations were normal. Mental function and cranial nerve tests were also normal. His facial, lip, tongue, and throat muscles were unaffected. Neck muscle strength was reduced (MRC grade 3/5). Limb muscle weakness was symmetrical (MRC grade 4/5 proximally and 3–4/5 distally) with atrophy in the shoulder girdle and lower legs. Sensation was intact, and muscle stretch reflexes were absent. There were no joint contractures or muscle contractions except for ankle contractures and pes cavus. Routine blood and stool tests were normal. Urine tests showed 3823 red cells/μL and 16 red cell casts/μL, with proteinuria at 187.60 mg/day. Blood pressure and glomerular filtration rate were normal. Urine red blood cell phase analysis indicated 80% abnormal erythrocytes. Cystoscopy revealed only blood clots. Abdominal ultrasonography and contrast-enhanced CT scan were normal. Electrocardiography and echocardiography were normal. Muscle enzymes were mildly elevated (CK: 394 U/L, CK-MB: 27.14 U/L). Nerve conduction tests were normal. Needle electromyography of the biceps brachii muscle showed myopathic features with myotonic discharges and polyspike and polyphasic motor unit potentials (MUP) with early recruitment. Polyphasic MUP duration was 8.9 ms, and amplitude was 450.7uV. Muscle biopsy of the left biceps brachii showed disrupted muscle structure with fibrosis and adipose tissue infiltration. Muscle fibers varied in size, with small rounded fibers and hypertrophic myofibers. Increased central nuclei within myofibers were noted. Muscle fiber necrosis with phagocytosis and regeneration was present in small groups. Both type-I and type-II fibers were affected with fiber type grouping. NADH staining showed disorganized myofibril arrangement. Immunostaining for dystrophin (R, N, and C) was normal. Collagen VI-stain by immunohistochemistry showed no difference between the patient and control. Renal biopsy was not performed due to lack of parental consent. MRI of the thigh muscles showed slight fat infiltration and bone marrow edema of the left collum femoris.
test_results: The result of sequencing revealed a de novo heterozygous G-to-A nucleotide substitution at position 877 in exon 10 of the COL6A1 gene, leading to an amino acid change of glycine to arginine, which had been previously described as pathogenic. The same mutation was not detected in his parents.

case_report: An 11-year-old male patient was referred to our clinic due to testicular enlargement and rapid growth in height. The patient presented with testicular enlargement without obvious cause, no pubic hair, no spermatorrhea, and a small amount of beard hair for 6 months. The patient was born at 36 weeks of pregnancy via cesarean section, weighing 2.1 kg (< -3sd) and measuring 46 cm (< -1sd). There was no history of asphyxiation or resuscitation. The patient exhibited catch-up growth after birth and had no history of feeding difficulties. At 2 years old, his physical and mental development was similar to that of his peers. His non-consanguineous parents were clinically normal, with his father and mother being 170 cm and 151 cm tall, respectively. There was no family history of genetic or infectious diseases. On physical examination at 11 years of age, his weight was 52.5 kg and height was 146.1 cm. The patient had a clear mind, good spirit, normal hair, and no yellow coloring or bleeding spots on the skin. He had arched eyebrows, a protruding bridge of the nose, forward-leaning nostrils, a thin upper lip, a small amount of beard, a normal jaw, and an inconspicuous laryngeal knot. Both pupils were equal in size and responsive to light. Breath sounds in both lungs were clear, with no dry or moist rales heard. Heart sounds were strong and regular, with a heart rate of 90 bpm, and no pathological murmur was found in any valve area. The abdomen was soft, with no tenderness or rebound pain observed, and the liver and spleen were unpalpable. The big toes on both feet were widened, and the limbs were normal. Limb muscle tension was normal. Physiological reflexes were present, and pathological reflexes were not found. Bilateral testes were symmetrical, about 8-10 mL in size, without pubic hair. The patient’s liver function, kidney function, electrolytes, blood glucose, and blood lipids were normal. Insulin-like growth factor was normal. Karyotype analysis of cultured cells revealed a karyotype of 46XY. Sex hormone levels were as follows: estradiol 25 pg/mL (adult male reference value: < 20-47 pg/mL), follicle-stimulating hormone 6.62 mIU/mL (adult male reference value: 1.27-19.26 mIU/mL), luteinizing hormone 3.20 mIU/mL (adult male reference value: 1.24-8.62 mIU/mL), and testosterone 1.75 ng/mL (adult male reference value: 1.75-7.81 ng/mL). Total 25 hydroxy vitamin D was 13.79 ng/mL (reference value < 20 ng/mL vitamin D deficiency). Fasting insulin was 23.1 mU/L (reference value: 2.3-11.8 mU/L). Thyroid function was evaluated as follows: Triiodothyronine 6.84 pmol/L (reference value: 2.63-5.71 pmol/L), thyroxine 12.10 pmol/L (reference value: 9.01-19.05 pmol/L), and thyroid-stimulating hormone 1.9145 μIU/mL (reference value: 0.30-4.80 μIU/mL). The patient underwent a skeletal examination, and the results showed that the bone age was 13 years. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary gland was normal. Slight lateral curvature of the thoracic spine was observed.
test_results: Whole-exome sequencing showed that there was complex heterozygous variation of the TAF6 gene in this patient, one of which was an unreported frameshift mutation c.1052delT (p.I351Tfs*40). According to Sanger sequencing, the variation originated from the child’s mother, and the paternal gene was wild-type. The other was a missense mutation c.76A>T(p.M26L). This missense mutation showed 76 nucleotide deficiency changes from adenine to thymine, resulting in the 26 amino acids changing from methionine to leucine. According to Sanger sequencing, the variation originated from the child’s father, and the maternal gene was wild-type.

case_report: A 79-year-old right-handed male with a history of diabetes, hypertension, coronary artery disease, and chronic kidney disease underwent an EVAR procedure with a left renal stent for a juxtarenal AAA found on a CT scan. The vascular surgery operative report indicated the procedure was completed successfully via access through the bilateral femoral arteries and the left brachial artery. Post-procedure, a small contained hematoma was noted at the brachial catheter insertion site after catheter withdrawal. Two months later, the patient presented to the outpatient pain management clinic with atrophy and weakness of the left forearm and pain in the left hand. Initial examination revealed a pulsatile mass of 2–4 cm in the medial left upper arm in the antecubital fossa. Motor assessment showed bilateral biceps flexion/extension at 4/5, left finger flexion at 2/5, and left hand grip at 2/5. An ultrasound of the left upper extremity revealed a pseudoaneurysm of the left brachial artery. The patient was urgently referred to vascular surgery and underwent repair of the pseudoaneurysm the following day. Four months post-repair, the patient returned with worsened left upper extremity symptoms, including significant guarding of the left hand, allodynia to the median nerve distribution, skin changes, and contracture of the digits with notable weakness and atrophy.
test_results: An X-ray of the hand demonstrated significant osteopenia.
diagnosis: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome Type II

case_report: A 24-year-old woman reported experiencing mild headaches and occasional serous leakage from her left eye, occurring at least once a month. She also noted a small skin protrusion in the left fronto-nasal area. No specific neurological symptoms were observed. An ophthalmologic examination revealed slight conjunctival hyperemia, with no other abnormalities detected.
test_results: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) examination of the brain and the orbits, without and with the administration of Gadolinium-Based Contrast Agent (GBCA), showed the presence of three venous developmental abnormalities located in the left hemisphere. A sharply hypointense area in the Gradient Echo (GRE) T2* sequence of the subcortical white matter of the left occipital lobe was related to a cavernous hemangioma with haemosiderin deposits. No dural venous thrombosis was present. In the left intra-orbital space, at the level of the clinically visible lump of the left medial canthus, we observed a T2 hyperintense cystic irregular mass, with peripheral contrast enhancement after gadolinium administration. Moreover, swelling and subcutaneous fluid retention were present in the left frontal side of the scalp. A bone hemangioma was detected in the roof of the left orbit.

case_report: A 3.5-year-old girl was referred to a tertiary care hospital in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia for evaluation of congenital contractures on August 6, 2011. The patient's mother reported a full-term normal pregnancy with normal fetal movements. Delivery was via cesarean section due to prolonged labor. The patient was born with contractures affecting her fingers, knees, and feet. These contractures improved over time with periodic physiotherapy, particularly in her thumbs and 4th and 5th fingers, which were often flexed into the palm. The patient is reported to be cognitively intelligent, with speech and language development in the 99th percentile. She was able to crawl and stand on her knees at an early age. The patient is not on any medications, has no known allergies, and has never been hospitalized or had surgery. She is followed regularly by orthopedics for consideration of soft tissue release, particularly for current talipes more pronounced on the left side. She also has pterygium webbing of the knee joints, limiting extension. The family pedigree revealed that the parents are double first-degree cousins, and they have two girls and one boy who are healthy with no similar family history reported. Upon arrival at the hospital, physical examination showed the following: temperature 37.1°C, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, pulse rate 96 beats/min, blood pressure 110/60 mmHg, and blood oxygen saturation 96%. Weight was 9.5 kg, head circumference was 45 cm, and cranial nerve examination was unremarkable. Distinct dysmorphic facial features were noted, including a triangular face with micrognathia, prominent forehead, narrow palpebral fissures, deep-set eyes, and low-set ears. There was no tongue fasciculation. Neuromuscular assessment showed isometric strength around the shoulders and elbows, with relatively preserved strength in finger flexion. The hands showed mild deformity of the 4th and 5th fingers, with creases present and no obvious hypothenar muscle eminence. In the lower extremities, there was clear thinning of the leg muscles compared to the thighs, associated with pterygium behind both knees limiting extension. Achilles tendon shortening was more noticeable on the left side with inversion, and limited ankle dorsiflexion was observed on the right side with distal weakness. Reflexes were difficult to elicit, but responses were +1 around the knees and biceps level. Examination of the back showed subtle scoliosis, and when pulled to a sitting position, the head lagged and the patient was unable to hold her head up for long periods, though she was not very cooperative according to her parents. Complete blood count and routine chemistry profiles were within normal ranges. White blood cells and differential count (lymphocytes) study were also normal, including Human leukocyte antigen, blastogenesis normal responses, ratios, CD4/CD8 ratios, Antihuman B lymphocyte serum, and T-helper cells.
test_results: At the genomic level, an array comparative genomic hybridization using microarray was used to detect any chromosomal copy number changes on the genome which appeared normal without imbalance. Also, the patient's Karyotype was normal. The skeletal survey showed normal bone density, dextrocardia with left-sided aortic arch and stomach, and no signs of skeletal dysplasia. The anteroposterior radiographs of the pelvis showed normal articulation with slight breakage of the Shenton line. Abdominal ultrasound showed normal liver, gallbladder, spleen, and pancreas. Multiple bilateral renal cysts were observed in both right and left kidneys measuring 4.9 and 5.7 cm, respectively. Knees magnetic resonance imaging (without contrast) showed bilateral knee flexion contracture deformities of the posterior fibrotic bands/pterygia with the more posterior location of the neuron bundle. Echocardiography showed dextrocardia with situs solitus and persistent left superior vena cava to the coronary sinus. The very small patent ductus arteriosus producing right-to-left shunt and patent foramen ovale causing left-to-right shunt were confirmed. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with dextrocardia.

case_report: A 68-year-old male with no significant medical history presented to the outpatient clinic after leukocytosis was incidentally discovered. He reported intermittent night sweats and slight fatigue but was otherwise in good general health. Physical examination showed no abnormalities, including the absence of lymphadenopathy, skin lesions, or palpable enlargement of the spleen or liver. Laboratory tests indicated a white blood cell (WBC) count of 16.1 × 10^9/L, with an absolute lymphocyte count of 10.0 × 10^9/L (reference range, 0.7–5.3). Other hemogram results were normal, with a hemoglobin level of 15.7 g/dL (reference range, 13.4–17.0) and a platelet count of 173 × 10^9/L (reference range, 145–348). Electrolytes and biochemical parameters, including uric acid, bilirubin, and creatinine, were within normal limits. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was 155 U/L (reference range, 105–205). A computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no abnormalities, including the absence of lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or tumors. Examination of the peripheral blood smear revealed monotonous, small- to medium-sized lymphoid cells, which were somewhat larger than typical chronic lymphatic leukemia (CLL) cells, with round nuclei and some showing a nucleolus.
test_results: Peripheral blood flow cytometry analysis indicated an expanded population of lymphocytes, which accounted for 52% of viable WBC, showed a mature T-cell immunophenotype (positive for CD45 and pan-T antigens CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7), and of which 90% were CD4-positive. The T-cell population further expressed CD26, CD28, and CD52. Among the negative markers were CD8, CD10, CD25, CD30, CD56, CD57, cyPerforin, cyGranzyme, and cyTCL1. The aspirate smears demonstrated lymphoid cells equivalent to the circulating cells in the peripheral blood. The biopsy demonstrated a slightly hypocellular bone marrow, with subtle interstitial infiltrates of small, CD3-positive lymphoid cells without significant atypia. The T-cells accounted for about 15–20% of the total nucleated bone marrow cells, with only small, loose aggregates. The majority of the T-cells were CD4-positive, but negative for CD57, Granzyme B, terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) and CD30, and for B-cell markers CD20, PAX5, and CD79a. There was no significant increase in reticulin fibers. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based clonality tests performed on the bone marrow aspirate demonstrated monoclonal rearrangement of the T-cell receptor (TCR)-γ chain gene.

case_report: The patient is a 9-year-old girl admitted to the hospital due to recurrent rashes for 8 years and a recent relapse for 1 month. The rashes initially appeared when she was 1 year old, primarily around the mouth, anus, and extremities, and were accompanied by hair loss but no diarrhea. She had been treated at multiple hospitals for dermatitis, and laboratory tests indicated zinc deficiency. Treatment with oral zinc supplements improved the rashes without leaving scars or pigmentation, but the rashes recurred after discontinuing the supplements, often during the transition from autumn to winter. Recently, she has not been taking zinc supplements regularly. Over the past month, she developed multiple skin rashes across her body, leading to her admission to the pediatric department for further evaluation. She has no history of allergic disorders. Her family includes her parents, two half-brothers, and a half-sister, all of whom are in good health. There is no family history of dermatologic disorders or toxic exposure, and her parents are not consanguineous. Physical examination revealed large, bubble-like and exfoliated rashes, mainly around the eyes, mouth, buttocks, and limbs, some of which were broken and bleeding. Her hair was noted to be sparse, soft, and brown.
test_results: The level of serum zinc was low (0.7 μmol/L; normal range, 9.8–16.8 μmol/L).

case_report: A 2-month-old male presented with a 3-day history of cough, 2 days of rapid breathing and poor feeding, and 1 day of fever. He had intermittent fever starting from day 4 of life, accompanied by a dry, non-paroxysmal cough. The antenatal and birth history were normal, with a birth weight of 3000 g, and he was discharged on day 2 of life. During the first week, he exhibited a weak cry and reduced spontaneous movement in all four limbs. Developmentally, he did not achieve neck holding but showed regard for his mother's face, responded to sound, and followed objects. The family history revealed that he was the third child in a non-consanguineous marriage, with two male siblings who had early infantile deaths at 50 and 90 days, respectively, following a history of hypotonia. On examination, he had a heart rate of 143/min, respiratory rate of 68/min, and oxygen saturation of 50% on room air. His weight was 3.6 kg (-3 Z score), length 58 cm (0.88 Z score), and occipitofrontal circumference 36.2 cm (-2.5 Z score). Muscle weakness was noted with a frog-like posture, jug-handle deformity of the upper limbs, bilateral wrist contracture, bell-shaped chest, and poor spontaneous activity. He was awake and alert with spontaneous eye-opening, extra-ocular movements, and no ptosis or facial weakness. Tongue fasciculations and flabby skeletal muscles were present. Hypotonia was indicated by head lag when pulled to sit, dangling legs on ventral suspension, and head lying below the plane of the body on horizontal suspension. There were minimal spontaneous distal movements and no antigravity movements. Deep tendon reflexes were absent, and bilateral plantar responses were mute. Sensations were intact, and there was no nystagmus. Respiratory examination showed nasal flaring, bell-shaped chest, bilateral suprasternal, intercostal, and subcostal retractions with a seesaw breathing pattern, indicating intercostal muscle weakness. Chest auscultation revealed decreased air entry with bilateral crackles. Laboratory investigations showed normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 10.7 gm/dl, MCV 88 fl, MCHC 31 gm/dl), marginally raised creatinine (1.8 gm/dl), and creatine kinase level of 56 IU/l.
test_results: Nerve conduction study was indicative of normal sensory nerves with preferential involvement of motor nerves. Electromyography was indicative of denervation.

case_report: A 6-year-old boy with phototype IV from Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, presented to the Pediatric Dermatology Service. He exhibited infiltrated, well-defined erythematous and edematous plaques with a polycyclic pattern on his face, back, and extremities for two months, accompanied by episodes of fever. He had not taken any medication. Laboratory tests showed normal blood count values, except for an elevated eosinophil count of 7%. Serological tests for syphilis (VDRL), HIV, and bacilloscopy were negative. Serum α1-antitrypsin levels were not available.
test_results: A biopsy specimen obtained from one of the infiltrated plaques showed a neutrophilic disease with edema of the dermal papillae and dense neutrophilic dermal infiltrate. A biopsy specimen of the atrophic cutaneous areas showed decreased thickness of the reticular dermis. Acid orcein staining showed marked decrease in the number of elastic fibers in the reticular dermis. The existing fibers were shortened and fragmented, but collagen appeared normal.

case_report: A 9-day-old male infant was admitted to the hospital due to subcutaneous swellings. The prenatal history was unremarkable. The patient was delivered at home via spontaneous vaginal birth at 38 weeks of gestation, being the third child of a 26-year-old mother. The parents are second-degree relatives. On physical examination, the infant was in good general condition with normal spontaneous movements and intact reflexes, including suction, searching, catching, and Moro reflexes. The infant's weight was 2950 grams, height was 49 cm, and head circumference was 34 cm. The frontal fontanel measured 2 × 2 cm and was at a normal level. Firm nodules of varying sizes were noted under the skin across the body, with the largest measuring 1 × 1 cm. No lesions were observed on the fingers. Laboratory results showed a hemoglobin level of 19.8 g/dL, erythrocyte count of 5.98 × 10^6/mm3, leukocyte count of 12,120/mm3, and thrombocyte count of 321,000/mm3. Cholesterol and triglyceride levels were within normal limits. Liver function tests, renal function tests, and thyroid hormone levels were also within normal ranges. C-reactive protein was elevated at 26 mg/dL, and the sedimentation rate was 2 mm/h. Imaging studies, including brain MRI, thorax CT, bone survey, abdominal ultrasound, and urinary ultrasound, were normal. Superficial ultrasound revealed multiple isoechoic to hypoechoic lesions among the muscle planes, with the largest lesion measuring 13 × 10 mm. Thoracolumbar MRI showed multiple mass-like lesions with peripheral contrast retention, the largest being 1.7 × 1.4 cm, located under the skin muscle planes in the thoracolumbar regions, between extremity muscles, and in sectional regions, appearing hyperintense and hypointense on T2-weighted and T1-weighted images, respectively.
test_results: Histopathology included varying amounts of extracellular collagen and uniform spindle cells. Cell bundles were spread into adjacent tissues. Lesional cells had central elongated nuclei and vaguely fibrillar cytoplasm. The diagnostic feature was the presence of intracytoplasmic, eosinophilic spherical inclusions. The lesional cells were not nuclear atypia and mitoses. In histochemical staining, these inclusions stain the brightly purple-red rounded with mason-trichrome staining. No staining with PAS was observed. As a result of the immunohistochemical staining of the lesion biopsy, smooth muscle actin was positive; desmin, S100, and CD34 were negative.

case_report: A 58-year-old Japanese man experienced blurred vision one week after receiving the second dose of the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine (BNT162b2, Pfizer, Tokyo, Japan) in 2021. Three months later, he began to experience headache, nausea, and vertigo. An MRI scan of his head showed no abnormalities. Due to worsening blurred vision and the onset of tinnitus, he consulted an ophthalmologist and was found to have iritis and uveitis. He reported leukoderma on his head and was referred to our hospital nine months after his second vaccination. Upon examination, he had depigmentation on his bilateral forehead and forearm in multiple coalescing patches, as well as annular erythema on his bilateral upper arms. His medical history included pompholyx and atopic dermatitis. Laboratory tests revealed elevated serum levels of immunoglobulin E (IgE) at 1,561 IU/mL and thymus and activation-regulated chemokine (TARC) at 1,050 pg/mL. Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone, free T3, and free T4 levels were within normal limits. Autoantibodies, including antinuclear antibody, anti-SS-A, and anti-SS-B antibody, were negative.
test_results: Histopathological examination and immunohistochemical staining of biopsy specimens from depigmentation and annular erythema at first visit showed interface dermatitis without spongiosis in the epidermis, and diminished SOX10 + and Melan-A + melanocytes in the epidermis and melanophages in the superficial dermis.

case_report: A 16-year-old female presented with sudden onset of weakness and loss of sensation on the right side of her body. She had been in good health until six months prior, when she began experiencing occasional pain in her right forearm and discoloration of the fingers on her right hand. These symptoms led to diagnoses of tendonitis and unilateral Raynaud's phenomenon. Three weeks before the current visit, she experienced numbness in her left arm and was evaluated at another hospital where a head CT scan was normal. During the current visit, physical examination revealed a weakened right radial pulse. Neurological examination showed moderate difficulties in understanding and producing speech, slurred speech, numbness on the right side, and weakness on the right side, more pronounced in the arm and face than in the leg. The right arm showed no movement, and the right leg showed minimal movement against gravity. The initial NIH Stroke Scale score was 12. An urgent brain MRI indicated restricted diffusion in the left basal ganglia, blockage in the terminal internal carotid artery (ICA) and M1 segment, a large area of reduced blood flow in the left middle cerebral artery region, and an old infarct in the right thalamus. She underwent an emergency procedure to remove the clot in the left ICA with successful recanalization. Following this, a Doppler ultrasound of the right upper extremity was performed due to the weakened radial pulse, revealing reduced arterial waveforms consistent with a clot in the axillary artery and blockages in the brachial, radial, and ulnar arteries. The Doppler ultrasound and examination of the left upper extremity were normal. A thrombectomy of the right arm was performed, showing signs of chronic clotting, and she was started on a heparin infusion. Tests for antiphospholipid antibodies were negative, ruling out acquired severe thrombophilia syndrome.
test_results: Chest CT angiogram demonstrated bilateral C7 cervical ribs with associated high-grade stenoses of the bilateral subclavian arteries, right greater than left.

case_report: A 27-year-old male visited the outpatient clinic with complaints of bone pain, recurrent forearm fractures from minimal trauma, and a progressive increase in height. His mother's pregnancy was reported to be uneventful, but detailed information about potential virilization during pregnancy was unavailable. The patient was born via normal vaginal delivery at 39 weeks with a normal birth weight. His childhood and puberty development were reported as normal. At age 15, he experienced a right forearm fracture from minimal trauma, followed by right and left forearm fractures at ages 19 and 24, respectively. A left forearm radiograph at age 24 showed osteopenia and open epiphyses. Bone densitometry at age 26, due to bone pain, indicated osteoporosis, and alendronate 70 mg/week was prescribed. After nearly a year of treatment, due to worsening osteoporosis and continued height increase, he was referred to our center for further evaluation. Family history revealed that his parents were first-degree cousins, and he had two brothers. There was no family history of infertility, primary amenorrhea, or hirsutism, but two infant relatives had died from kidney stones. The patient was born with ambiguous genitalia. Physical examination showed blood pressure of 125/75 mmHg, pulse rate of 79/minute, height of 187 cm (mother: 155 cm, father: 176 cm, target height: 172 cm), weight of 90 kg, and body mass index of 25.7. Waist circumference was 102 cm, stroke distance 200 cm, and the upper to lower body ratio was 0.85. A eunuchoid body habitus was observed. Secondary sexual characteristics were normal, with normal penis length and thickness. Testicular volume was >20 mL. No gynecomastia, goitre, acanthosis nigricans, or acromegalic features were noted. Laboratory tests showed elevated follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) levels, normal testosterone, and undetectable estrogen. Dehydroepiandrosterone sulphate, 17 hydroxyprogesterone, parathyroid hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and free thyroxine levels were normal. Growth hormone basal level was 0.32 ng/mL, and post-glucose loading level was 0.25 ng/mL. Insulin-like growth factor-1 level was 332 ng/mL (normal range: 93-575 ng/mL). Total cholesterol and triglyceride levels were high, while serum HDL was low. Fasting blood glucose and oral glucose tolerance test results were normal. Semen analysis showed a sperm count of 56 million/mm with 40% motility. Liver ultrasonography indicated grade one hepatosteatosis. Karyotype analysis revealed a 46,XY pattern. Plain bone radiography of the left wrist and hand showed open metacarpal and phalangeal epiphyses, with a bone age estimated at 15 years. Bone densitometry indicated osteoporosis in the lumbar region (L1-L4 T score - 3.68, Z score - 3.68).
test_results: A homozygous R375H guanine-adenine (G-A) mutation was detected in the CYP19A1 gene.

case_report: A 7-month-old male presented with small papules and plaques on his right cheek, first noticed at 4 months of age. The patient had no notable medical history and had achieved all developmental milestones appropriately. Physical examination revealed erythematous grouped papules on wheal-like plaques on the right cheek. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 125,000/mm3, neutrophils at 25.3% (normal range: 40-74%), eosinophils at 9.5% (normal range: 0-7%), and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 52 IU/L. Other laboratory findings were within normal limits.
test_results: A biopsy specimen of the upper lesion of a wheal-like plaque showed a spread that infiltrated the entire dermis, with no epidermotropism. Most of the cells within the infiltrates were large, epithelioid histiocytic cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm. Lymphocytes and eosinophils were scattered among the histiocytes. Immunohistochemistry showed positive staining for CD68 in lesional cells, but negative for S-100 protein or CD1a.

case_report: A 17-year-old girl was referred by her primary care physician due to an abnormal finding on an echocardiogram from another hospital. The echocardiogram identified a 20-cm mass in the anterior mediastinum. The girl had been experiencing shortness of breath, chest discomfort, and an unusual heart murmur. She also reported fatigue and a weight loss of 6 pounds. She did not have night sweats, fevers, or chills. Based on the echocardiogram results and her clinical symptoms, she was referred to pediatric oncology. A subsequent chest CT scan showed a 20 cm × 8 cm heterogeneous tumor with areas of soft-tissue density and fat tissue. The mass was compressing her left main stem bronchus and causing increased displacement of the vessels. Over the following month, her chest discomfort worsened. She underwent surgery to remove the mass. The resected mass was irregular, ovoid, measured 22 × 16 × 5 cm, weighed 941 grams, and had a solid, lobulated, yellow-orange to pink cut surface.
test_results: A histochemical stain for oil red O confirmed that the vacuoles contained lipid. Immunohistochemical stains were negative for synaptophysin, chromogranin, inhibin and Melan A. The mass was not reactive for HepPar1, glypican-3 and AFP. Negative staining for pancytokeratin and EMA. Negative stain for HMB45. Other negative stains included S100 protein, SMA, desmin, caldesmon, myogenin, CDK4, CD34 and CD31.

case_report: A 3.8-year-old girl was referred to the Pediatric Endocrinology Department for evaluation of short stature. Initial assessment at 1.6 years old revealed symmetrical short stature with a height of 72.5 cm (−2.58 SDS), sitting height of 46.1 cm (−2.3 SDS), sitting height/height ratio of 0.63 (0 SDS), weight of 8.2 kg (−3.15 SDS), and head circumference of 46.8 cm (+0.31 SDS). She was prepubertal. Notable facial features included frontal bossing and a depressed nasal bridge. No other congenital abnormalities were observed. Subscapular skinfold measured 18.4 mm and tricipital skinfold 12.5 mm. She was born at 36 weeks and 5 days of gestation, with a birth weight of 2900 g, length of 47.7 cm, head circumference of 33 cm, and an Apgar score of 9/10. On the second day of life, she experienced severe hypoglycemia requiring glucose infusion. Her parents are not related and have normal, proportional heights: mother is 162 cm tall and father is 180 cm tall (target height 164.5 cm). There is no family history of short stature. The family originates from Northern Italy and Sicily. Laboratory evaluations showed normal blood count, creatinine, liver function, electrolytes, urine analysis, and serological screening for celiac disease. Serum basal GH levels were 11.57 ng/ml with glucose levels of 59 mg/dl, IGF-1 at 19.1 ng/ml (−2.7 SDS), and IGFBP-3 at 0.7 mcg/ml (2.0–4.5). An IGF-1 generation test with 0.033 mg/kg/day of rhGH for 4 days showed IGF-1 levels of 13.6 ng/ml (−2.6 SDS) on day 0 and 8.4 ng/ml (−2.8 SDS) on day 4, indicating GH resistance. At 3.8 years old, her height was 85.9 cm (−3.76 SDS), weight 11.9 kg (−2.42 SDS), head circumference 50 cm (0.52 SDS), and growth velocity was 5.29 cm/year (−1.80 SDS). Basal IGF-1 levels were 32 ng/ml (−2.28 SDS) and IGFBP-3 was 0.8 mcg/ml (2.0–4.5). After administering a high dose of rhGH (2.8 mg/mq/day: 1.6 mg/day for 7 days), stimulated IGF-1 levels were 62.0 ng/ml (−1.78 SDS) and IGFBP-3 was 0.9 mcg/ml (2.0–4.5).
test_results: The direct sequencing of the complete coding sequence of GHR gene revealed the presence of two heterozygous variations. The first is a missense mutation caused by the transition adenine to guanine (c.1A > G) in the first codon of exon 2. This substitution involved the translation initiation codon (Methionine) of the protein. The second variation is the substitution c.307G > A, that resulted in the replacement of the amino acid Aspartic Acid at position 103 to a residue of Asparagine (p.D103N), in exon 5 of the GHR sequence. This substitution involved the highly conserved Aspartic Acid 103.

case_report: A 60-year-old female, undergoing treatment with rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide along with esomeprazole for pulmonary tuberculosis, developed a generalized skin eruption and malaise six weeks into the treatment. She did not experience fever, joint pain, or photosensitivity. Physical examination showed multiple crusted plaques on the face, trunk, and both upper and lower limbs, including areas not exposed to sunlight. Additionally, confluent erythematous macules and multiple target lesions were observed on the palms, soles, and lower limbs. Laboratory tests including hemogram, serum biochemistry, and urinalysis were within normal limits.
test_results: Findings on skin biopsy and immunological workup are presented.

case_report: A 3-year-old male child with a history of strabismus and cleft lip was referred to our clinics due to an unusual optic disc and visual loss. During the second trimester of pregnancy, the mother developed a generalized maculopapular rash but did not experience headache, fever, conjunctivitis, arthralgia, or myalgia. She tested positive for ZIKV via RT-PCR. After birth, the child was hospitalized for 4 days in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) due to hyperbilirubinemia, which was treated with phototherapy. Previous ocular history included decreased visual acuity in the right eye (OD) and sensory exotropia diagnosed at 11 months of age. Strabismus surgery was performed following unsuccessful occlusion therapy, resulting in excellent anatomical outcomes. A complete ophthalmological exam revealed best-corrected visual acuity of 20/200 OD and 20/20 in the left eye (OS). Intraocular pressure was normal in both eyes (OU). No nystagmus was observed. Extraocular muscle movements were full, but a small angle exotropia was present OD. Pupils were equally round with an afferent pupillary defect OD. The anterior segment was unremarkable OU. Examination of the posterior segment showed a centrally excavated optic disc with associated hypopigmented glial tuft, peripapillary chorioretinal atrophy, and a radial spoke-like vascular pattern OD. No foveal reflex was present OD. The posterior segment of the left eye (OS) was unremarkable.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) were performed and were remarkable for a base of skull encephalocele and callosal dysgenesis. The pituitary gland, infundibulum and optic chiasm were not well visualized.

case_report: A 37-day-old female child, the fourth born to second-degree consanguineous parents, was admitted with seizures, lethargy, poor feeding, and failure to gain weight. She was delivered via cesarean section with a birth weight of 2.9 kg. She cried immediately after birth and had no history of respiratory distress or neonatal jaundice. Her two older siblings passed away during the newborn period with a history of seizures. The mother reported noticing an unusual odor in the child's urine at times. On examination, the child was lethargic and weighed 1.8 kg, with no lateralizing signs or neurocutaneous markers. Laboratory tests including a complete hemogram, renal parameters, liver function tests, and serum electrolytes were normal. Seizures were managed with phenobarbitone. Serum lactate, pyruvate, and ammonia levels were within normal limits. Urine screening results were negative. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed no abnormalities. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed bilateral symmetrical lesions in the posterior limb of the internal capsule, thalami, brainstem, and centrum semiovale.
test_results: Serum high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) amino acid profile showed an elevation of leucine — 4,529 (47-155), isoleucine — 286 (31-86), and valine — 575 (64-294).

case_report: A 68-year-old female patient with a history of arterial hypertension since menopause, long-standing atrial fibrillation treated with direct oral anticoagulants, obesity, and anxious–depressive syndrome was admitted to the emergency department due to fatigue, reduced physical capability, and progressive shortness of breath. On admission, her blood pressure was 171/80 mmHg and her heart rate was 45 beats per minute. Physical examination revealed no heart murmurs, fine rales at the lung bases, and no lower limb edema. The electrocardiogram showed moderate sinus bradycardia with a heart rate of 46 beats per minute. During hospitalization, episodes of rapid atrial fibrillation (110 beats per minute) and moderate to severe sinus bradycardia were observed, along with several episodes of sinus arrest resulting in pathological pauses up to 7.6 seconds, symptomatic for pre-syncope. On the fourth day, the patient underwent implantation of a dual-chamber pacemaker with passive-fixation leads. Post-implantation electrocardiogram confirmed the correct functioning of the pacemaker. The patient was discharged on the sixth day in good clinical condition.
test_results: Signs of a manipulation of the PM were evident, being the generator flipped on its major axis.

case_report: A two-month-old breastfeeding girl was brought to the emergency room after experiencing 12 days of fever and weight loss. The patient was administered 20 µg of 1-desamino[8-D-arginine]vasopressin (dDAVP) intranasally, but this did not reduce her urine output. On physical examination, the infant was found to be severely dehydrated and highly irritable, with no other clinical abnormalities noted. Her height-for-age ratio was at the 3rd percentile. Initial laboratory tests showed hypernatremia (172 mEq/ml) and low urine density (1.005). After increasing her fluid intake and following a low sodium diet, her basal sodium levels returned to the normal range. Further laboratory investigations were conducted.
test_results: A short water deprivation test was performed under a strictly controlled medical setting, but this test was stopped six hours later because of weight loss (3%). Her urinary osmolality was 263 mOsmol/kg at six hours and increased to 300 mOsmol/kg one hour after dDAVP administration (20 µg intranasally). The T1-weighted images from a brain MRI did not reveal the hyperintense signal that is normally emitted by the posterior pituitary gland.

case_report: A full-term male infant, weighing 3.9 kg, was delivered at 40 weeks gestation via normal vaginal delivery to a 38-year-old mother. The parents are third-degree relatives. No significant antenatal illness was reported, and no antenatal ultrasound was performed. The infant had Apgar scores of 8 at 1 minute and 9 at 5 minutes. On the second day of life, the infant exhibited poor feeding and lethargy. An evaluation for neonatal sepsis was conducted, and initial sepsis investigations returned normal results.
test_results: MRI showed monoventricle with rudimentary posterior interhemispheric fissure and incomplete falx cerebri. There is an absence of corpus callosum, cavum septum pellucidum, and anterior fossa midline structures, posterior fossa and both cerebellar hemispheres appear normal.

case_report: A 17-year-old male returned to the hospital for rehabilitation and was referred to the genetic clinic for evaluation of unexplained intellectual and language disabilities on July 11th, 2011. He was born at 36 weeks of gestation via vaginal delivery following an induced preterm birth due to preeclampsia and intrauterine growth retardation. His birth weight was 1,500 grams (< 3rd percentile). He spent approximately 25 days in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) for very low birth weight. Both parents were 33 years old, and he had an older healthy brother. There was no family history of neurological disease or developmental delay. The parents reported delayed walking at 18 months and noticeable language development after 3 years of age. He did not exhibit autistic features, sleep problems, hyperactivity, or oppositional behaviors. He experienced two provoked seizures: the first at 3.5 years old associated with hypoglycemia (serum glucose 38 mg/dL) and the second at 7 years old during a high fever. Physical examination at 17 years old revealed no definite dysmorphic facial features or other significant findings. He was left-handed, had a normal heart sound without murmurs, no skeletal abnormalities, and a normal neurological examination. His first neurodevelopmental evaluation at 3.5 years old indicated mild intellectual disability, low adaptive behaviors, and significant developmental language delay. His ADL functional age was 33.6 months, fine motor functional age was 30.07 months, cognitive functional age was 21.44 months on the DARBAS, receptive language age was 24 months, and expressive language age was 18-24 months on the PRES. A second neurodevelopmental evaluation at 17 years old using the Korean Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (K-WAIS) showed moderate intellectual disability with FSIQ, VIQ, and PIQ all below 45. His social maturation quotient (SQ 48.7) also indicated moderate trainable intellectual disability. He continued to exhibit developmental language delay, with a receptive language age of 5 years and an expressive language age of around 3 years. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count, chemistry panel, lipid profile, thyroid function test, and urinalysis, were all normal. Brain MRI at 17 years old showed no focal lesion and normal ventricular size. Chromosome analysis performed at another hospital revealed a blood lymphocyte karyotype of 46, XY.
test_results: Whole genome array CGH revealed a duplication on chromosome 17p11.2 including the RAI1 gene region [arr 17p11.2 (17,575,978-19,654,341) × 3]. The size was estimated at approximately 2.1 Mb with 4 probes that contained 11 RefSeq genes: RAI1, SMCR5, SREBF1, MIR33B, TOM1L2, TRIM16L, FBXW10, FAM18B, ALDH3A2, SLC47A, and ALDH3A1.

case_report: A five-month-old male presented with an 8-millimeter nodule located in the left corner of the left eye. The patient was born at full term (40 weeks’ gestational age) with no abnormalities or history of trauma at birth. The lesion was first observed when the patient was four months old. The nodule was tan-orange in color and exhibited central ulceration. Following a partial biopsy performed by a maxillofacial surgeon, the nodule increased in size and became hemorrhagic. Subsequently, the parents brought the child to the Clinic of Dermatology.
test_results: The histological evaluation revealed ulcerated cutaneous cellular proliferation, diffuse infiltrates of mononucleated cells, some of which are characterized by their reniform nuclei, foamy histiocytes and numerous Touton giant cells, admixed with eosinophils. Immunohistochemistry yielded results immunoreactive for CD68, weak focal positivity for S-100 protein, but negative for Langerin. These results confirmed that the histiocytes are non-Langerhans cells.

case_report: A 74-year-old Caucasian woman presented with fever, fatigue, and painful erythematous nodules. Her medical history included a condition diagnosed three years prior, for which she received 23 cycles of azacitidine (AZA). On initial presentation, her temperature was 101.4° F with tachycardia. Physical examination revealed conjunctival pallor, tender erythematous vesicles on her right temple and bilateral ear lobes extending to the right periocular area, and tender erythematous nodules on her buttocks. A complete blood count showed pancytopenia (white blood cell count of 2.0 x 10­9/L with an absolute neutrophil count of 1,500/mm3, hemoglobin of 8.1 g/dL, and platelet count of 16 x 109/L). She was started on antibiotics (1 gm of vancomycin and aztreonam every 12 hours) and antiviral medications (650 mg of acyclovir every eight hours). Despite treatment, she remained febrile with worsening condition and development of new erythematous plaques and nodules over her shoulders, forearms, and lower extremities.
test_results: A 5-mm x 5-mm x 6-mm punch biopsy of an erythematous nodule over her right shoulder showed subcutaneous lobular and septal infiltrates of neutrophils and scattered histiocytes with sparing of the dermis. Special stainings and tissue cultures for bacteria, mycobacteria, and fungal infections were negative. Blood cultures were negative for infection. Bone marrow biopsy did not show evidence of transformation of her MDS to acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

case_report: A 66-year-old male with a history of scleredema diabeticorum and a 20-year history of diabetes presented with an ulcer on the posterior neck. He had chronic brown hyperkeratosis with underlying induration on his central upper back and posterior neck. A few weeks prior to evaluation, he developed an enlarging, tender ulcer in the area affected by scleredema on his posterior neck. The ulcer had overhanging edges toward the center. He was treated with oral double-strength trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and topical mupirocin 2% ointment twice daily for two weeks for the ulcer, and triamcinolone 0.1% cream twice daily for the underlying scleredema. Bacterial culture of the ulcer showed skin flora. The antibiotic treatment was discontinued after four weeks. There was no improvement in the scleredema after two weeks, leading to the discontinuation of the topical triamcinolone cream. The ulcer persisted.
test_results: Microscopic examination of the posterior neck specimen showed epithelial hyperplasia and deep dermal fibrosis. The dermis contained granulation tissue and telangiectasia with chronic inflammation. Special stains were negative for bacteria, fungi, and mycobacteria. Bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial skin biopsy cultures were also negative.

case_report: A 3-month-old Chinese girl, previously in good health, experienced a week of diarrhea followed by an afebrile seizure. She was referred from a district hospital for further evaluation and treatment. Her birth history was normal, delivered at term with a birth weight of 3.72 kg (75th centile) and length of 55 cm (97th centile). Initially exclusively breastfed for one month, she was then switched to various brands of cow’s milk formula due to recurrent loose stools and excessive flatulence. On examination, she was moderately dehydrated and tachycardic. Her weight was 6.2 kg (above 75th centile) and length was 61 cm (75th centile). A ballotable right kidney was noted on examination. Initial laboratory tests revealed hyponatremia (117 mmol/L), hypochloremia (90 mmol/L), hyperkalemia (9 mmol/L), and metabolic acidosis. She received an intravenous (IV) normal saline bolus (10 ml/kg) at the district hospital and IV hydration with 5% correction over 12 hours. A lytic cocktail with calcium resonium was administered every 6 hours to correct hyperkalemia. Her electrolytes normalized after 4 days of treatment. Stool cultures for rotavirus and reducing sugar were negative. Due to the possibility of cow’s milk protein allergy, she was started on extensively hydrolyzed milk formula, which resolved the diarrhea. She had no further seizures, and her neurological examination was normal, as was an ultrasound scan of the brain. Her urine culture grew Enterobacter, and she was treated with a 7-day course of cefuroxime. An ultrasound of the kidney, ureter, and bladder (USG KUB) revealed a right duplex kidney with gross hydronephrosis and hydroureter. A micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) showed grade 5 vesicoureteric reflux on the right side.
test_results: The serum aldosterone level obtained on admission was elevated at 3700 pmol/l (normal range <1109 pmol/L) with normal 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) level (0.8 nmol/L, reference range 1.0-14.12 nmol/L). Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) stimulation test was also normal.

case_report: A 43-year-old man was admitted to the Affiliated Hangzhou First People’s Hospital of Zhejiang University School of Medicine on 4 December 2017 due to physical weakness and a lack of appetite for over a month. His medical history included hypertension for 3 years, with no known heart, kidney, hematological, or hereditary metabolic conditions. The patient had a history of consuming 450 mL of 30% alcohol daily for 20 years and had ingested 150 g of medicinal liquor containing G. segetum per day for 10 days prior to symptom onset. Physical examination showed severe scleral jaundice, palmar erythema, and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory tests indicated impaired liver function with the following results: total bilirubin, 217.6 μmol/L; direct bilirubin, 156.6 μmol/L; alanine aminotransferase, 24 U/L; aspartate transaminase, 57 U/L; albumin, 32.5 g/L; alkaline phosphatase, 168 U/L; and γ-glutamate transaminase, 430 U/L. The prothrombin time was 13.7 s (INR = 1.21). Hemogram results showed a normal white blood cell count, a low platelet count (89,000/μL), and a low hemoglobin level (11 g/dL). Ascites fluid analysis revealed transudative fluid with a total nucleated cell count of 70 × 10^6/L, an albumin level of 17.1 g/L, and a serum ascites albumin gradient exceeding 11 g/L. Tests for viral hepatitis were negative, and the immunoglobulin G level was within normal limits. No serial autoantibodies related to autoimmune liver diseases were detected.
test_results: Enhanced abdominal computed tomography (CT) disclosed hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, esophagocardial varices, an uneven density, and diffuse patchy shadows in the whole hepatic lobe. The hepatic veins were not evident on the images. Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) also revealed manifestations of cirrhosis. The liver exhibited heterogeneous enhancement, and the hepatic veins became narrow, making them not clearly visible.

case_report: A 30-year-old male patient presented with pancytopenia for 23 years and fever for 11 days. At six years of age, he experienced rapidly progressive weakness, fatigue, and pallor. He was found to have pancytopenia and was treated with cyclosporine (CsA) and stanozolol, showing a good hematological response. His symptoms improved, but his peripheral blood cell counts never reached normal levels. In 2004, he experienced a relapse 8 months after discontinuing CsA and was restarted on CsA, again showing a good response. In 2011, he had another relapse 3 months after stopping CsA and was referred to our center. On admission, he reported progressive weakness and fatigue for 1 month and high-grade fever for 11 days, with a peak body temperature of 39.7 °C and no localized signs or symptoms. He had no history of hematopoietic diseases or significant infections before the initial presentation. He had been exposed to dimethylbenzene 8 months before seeking medical attention. There was no family history of inherited, hematological, or autoimmune diseases. His height was 173 cm, and his weight was 63.5 kg. Vital signs included a body temperature of 38.7 °C, a breathing rate of 23 breaths per minute, a heart rate of 98 beats per minute, and a blood pressure of 124/82 mmHg. Physical examination revealed a pallor complexion but no other abnormalities. There were no signs of mucocutaneous hemorrhage, jaundice, or exanthemata, and no significant findings in the nervous, respiratory, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, urogenital, or musculoskeletal systems. Laboratory results on admission showed white blood cells (WBCs) at 1730/µL, absolute neutrophil count (ANC) at 270/µL, red blood cells (RBCs) at 1860000/µL, hemoglobin (Hb) at 5.4 g/dL, platelets (Plts) at 6000/µL, absolute reticulocyte count (Ret) at 7600/µL, and C-reactive protein (CRP) at 145.8 mg/L. Urine examination, coagulation profile, liver and renal function tests, lactate dehydrogenase, antinuclear antibodies, serological tests for hepatitis A, B, and C, and anti-HIV antibodies were all normal. Blood culture was sterile, and the expression of CD55 and CD59 was within normal limits.
test_results: Evaluation of BM smears from the posterior superior iliac spine revealed severe hypocellularity with severe fatty replacement, predominantly lymphocytes, with few erythrocyte and myeloid precursors as well as no megalokaryocytes or dysplasia. Peripheral blood smears confirmed the severe neutropenia without atypical blood cells. No positive cytogenetic findings were identified by culturing the BM sample.

case_report: During a routine prenatal ultrasound screening in the 11th gestational week (GW), a 39-year-old woman was found to have a fetus with a giant omphalocele containing almost the entire liver. MRI in the 30th GW confirmed a covered abdominal wall defect without associated malformations. In the 37th GW, a caesarean section was performed. At birth, the male neonate presented with a covered abdominal wall defect of 7 cm, mostly occupied by the liver. An abdominal and cardiac ultrasound ruled out major associated malformations. The boy was scheduled for a staged closure. During surgery, a mass in the left liver was noted and mistaken for a hematoma. A fascial Gore-Tex patch measuring 5 × 5 cm was applied. On the 31st postnatal day, the patient’s general condition progressively worsened. Echocardiographic examinations showed worsening of the cardiac biventricular function due to herniation of the right liver into the chest. On Day 38 of life, closure of the anterior diaphragmatic hernia through the abdominal wound was performed. After reduction of the liver and resection of the CDH sac, absence of the pericardium was noted. The diaphragmatic defect of 5 × 4 cm was closed with a Gore-Tex patch and the abdominal wall defect was covered with a Gore-Tex patch. In the following 3 weeks, staged closure was continued without much progress, mostly because of the lesion in the left liver. Work-up of this lesion by ultrasound and MRI demonstrated a 5.5 × 5.1 × 5.5 cm tumor in segment III of the liver consistent with the diagnosis of a vascular tumor. The attempted therapy with propranolol (1 mg/kg/day) was ineffective and was discontinued due to the onset of bradycardia. Finally, surgical resection of the liver tumor was decided. At surgery, the well-defined mass was completely resected. While the abdominal fascia was closed using a Gore-Tex patch of 3 × 4 cm, the skin was closed directly.
test_results: Immunohistochemical examination was positive for endothelial markers CD31 and CD34, and negative for GLUT1. The proliferation rate under 5% and the sequencing of GNA-11 mutation.

case_report: A 62-year-old Japanese man was admitted to Matsushita Memorial Hospital in January 2019 due to worsening intermittent painful spasms in his legs. The patient had been healthy until 7 weeks prior, when he began experiencing painful spasms in his right calf muscle several times daily, each lasting a few seconds. These spasms increased in frequency and duration, eventually affecting the other leg. Light touch to his legs triggered painful spasms, and he became unable to walk. Six days before admission, he was taken to another hospital's emergency room by ambulance. There, he received intravenous diazepam and oral clonazepam, but the spasms spread to his trunk muscles. Three days before transfer, he developed double vision. He was then transferred to our hospital for further evaluation and treatment. He had no recent viral illness, injury, headache, bladder or bowel issues, insomnia, night sweats, or weight loss. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. He had a 56-pack-year smoking history and drank 1 liter of beer daily. On admission, his vital signs were: temperature 36.8°C, blood pressure 118/75 mmHg, pulse 83 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. General physical examination was normal. Neurologically, he was alert, oriented, and cooperative with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of E4V5M6 and intact cognitive function. Cranial nerve examination was normal except for saccadic pursuit eye movements and horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus. There was no trismus or tongue movement limitation. Muscle tone was normal in the neck and upper limbs but spastic and stiff in the lower limbs bilaterally. Painful spasms or myoclonic jerks occurred approximately every 10 seconds in the lower trunk and legs, triggered by sudden sounds or touch, each lasting a few seconds. He also had hyperhidrosis during spasms, but no fasciculations or myokymia. Tendon reflexes were normal in the upper limbs but hyperactive in the lower limbs, with absent Babinski reflex bilaterally. Coordination and sensory examinations were normal. Blood tests showed mild anemia (Hb 11.3 g/dL) and elevated levels of aspartate aminotransferase (95 U/L), alanine aminotransferase (79 U/L), creatine kinase (1,412 U/L), and C-reactive protein (2.57 mg/dL). Other blood tests, including angiotensin-converting enzyme, thyroid hormone, soluble interleukin-2 receptor, ANA, antibodies to SS-A/Ro, SS-B/La, Tg, TPO, ANCA, and glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), were unremarkable. Thoracic MRI and whole-body CT scans did not show any tumors, such as thymoma.
test_results: A needle electromyography (EMG) examination showed rhythmic 10 Hz discharges in the right vastus lateralis at rest, but no abnormal spontaneous discharges were seen. A surface EMG examination obtained on day 4 showed simultaneous agonist-antagonist continuous muscle activity. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination obtained on day 6 revealed 26 white blood cells/μL (mononuclear cells 100%) with oligoclonal bands. The IgG index was not elevated (0.62).
diagnosis: Progressive Encephalomyelitis with Rigidity and Myoclonus
Orpha_name: Progressive Encephalomyelitis with Rigidity and Myoclonus

case_report: A 7-year-old female patient, the first child of non-consanguineous Chinese Han parents, exhibited yellow-brown woolly hair on her forehead at birth. She was healthy until the age of 4, when palmoplantar keratoderma appeared on her palms and soles, later spreading to her fingers and toes. She received irregular external ointment treatment. At age 5, she developed dysplasia of deciduous teeth, with bilateral multiple incisors and molars oligodontia and irregular dentition. At age 6, she began experiencing chest tightness, shortness of breath, and dyspnea during physical activity, which progressively worsened, limiting her ability to tolerate moderate daily activities. Prior to her visit to Shijiazhuang Great Wall Cardiovascular Hospital, she was examined at Chongqing Children’s Hospital and received treatment for dilated cardiomyopathy. The patient has a healthy 4-year-old brother, and both parents are healthy with no similar cases in the family. Physical examination revealed the patient was not in acute distress, with normal intelligence. She weighed 21kg (25–30 centile) and was 125cm tall (25–30 centile). Vital signs included a body temperature of 36.4°C, pulse of 76 beats/min, respiratory rate of 20 breaths/min, and blood pressure of 88/65mmHg. She had sparse, dark-brown, woolly hair, and agenesis of primary teeth with multiple oligodontia (7 teeth) and odontoloxia. Bilateral jugular veins were slightly dilated. Thick breath sounds were heard in both lungs without dry or wet rales. The apical beat was diffuse, with cardiac boundaries enlarged bilaterally, and apical pulsation located at the 7th intercostal space of the left axillary-front line. The heart rate was 76 beats/min with premature beats, and a grade 2/6 systolic blowing-like murmur was detected at the mitral valve auscultation area. The abdomen was flat and soft, with no tenderness. The liver was palpable 3 cm below the costal margin, and the spleen was not palpable. Striate palmoplantar keratoderma was observed on both palms, fingers, soles, halluces, and heels, with a rough and chapped surface. Leukonychia was noted on toenails. Mild edema was present in both legs, and joint movements were barrier-free.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed a homozygous missense variant c.4597C > T (p.Q1533X) in exon 6 of the DSP gene, resulting in a senseless variant of the amino acid (Glutamine) at position 1533. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed that the heart was enlarged, especially the left heart, and the ventricular systolic and diastolic functions decreased. Color Doppler echocardiography demonstrated left ventricular end-diastolic diameter was 55 mm, left atrium 28*36*56 mm, right ventricular end-diastolic diameter 29 mm, right atrial diameter 33mm, left ventricular ejection fraction 25%, global heart enlargement, partial myocardial non-compaction of the left ventricle, diffuse decrease in ventricular septum and left ventricular wall motion amplitude, mild aortic regurgitation, moderate mitral regurgitation, mild tricuspid regurgitation, pulmonary hypertension (mild), mild pulmonary artery regurgitation, the main pulmonary artery and its branches widened. The diastolic and contractile functions of the left and right ventricles all decreased.

case_report: A 13-year-old female, the youngest of five siblings, was born at term with a birth weight of 3,780 g (75–90th centile). Physical examination at birth showed a narrow chest and short extremities. She experienced severe respiratory distress immediately after birth, requiring intubation and ventilation for 2 weeks. Ophthalmic examination and abdominal ultrasound were normal. During her first year, she was hospitalized multiple times due to respiratory exacerbations during infections. Her pulmonary condition stabilized with diuretic therapy, and she required supplementary oxygen for 6 months. Diuretic therapy continued until she was 2 years old. At 10 years of age, she developed mild scoliosis and was treated with a brace. Routine follow-up at 12 years of age revealed elevated liver enzymes. Aside from obesity, there were no other abnormal signs or symptoms. The liver was palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin. Tests for EBV, CMV, hepatitis A, B, and polymerase chain reaction for hepatitis C were negative. Antismooth muscle and antireticulum autoantibodies were not detected. Abdominal ultrasonography showed normal hepatic structure, biliary tract, and portal flow pattern. As she was in good health, no further diagnostic procedures were performed at that time. Follow-up ultrasonography after 1 year showed irregularly increased parenchymatous density. The liver and spleen were not enlarged, and the abdomen was not painful on palpation.
test_results: Skeletal radiographs showed a narrow thorax with a CTR of 0.64, short ribs with bulbous ends, a typical trident appearance of the acetabular margins and apparently normal bones of arms and legs. A liver biopsy revealed inflammation of the portal triangles, predominantly eosinophilic, and mild portoportal fibrosis without involvement of the bile canaliculi. The chest radiograph showed a narrow thorax with horizontally oriented clavicles, a short sternum and a CTR of 0.54.

case_report: This is a 33-year-old woman born to consanguineous parents (second-degree relatives). She exhibited distinct physical features, including a long triangular face, low-set ears, sparse eyebrows, widely spaced eyes, and crowded teeth. She did not develop secondary sexual characteristics and experienced primary amenorrhea, leading to the initiation of hormonal therapy. Since early childhood, she has had hearing difficulties. Despite normal neurodevelopmental growth, her school performance was described as below average by her mother. She enrolled in a public university but was later asked to drop out and has since stayed home. In 2017, she began follow-ups with multiple services at our center, including dermatology, neurology, speech and language team, and audiology, in addition to gynecology. Upon examination, she presented with a dystonic gait, dysarthria, and oromandibular and cervical neck dystonia. She also had bilateral ptosis and bilateral leg swelling. Laboratory tests showed elevated thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) and low free thyroxine 4 (FT4), indicating hypothyroidism. The HbA1C was 6%, indicating a pre-diabetic state. Other results showed high follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and normal luteinizing hormone (LH), suggesting hypergonadotropic hypogonadism. An MRI scan of the brain revealed increased iron depositions in the globus pallidus bilaterally.
test_results: She was found to have a homozygous variant c.436del p. (Ala147 Hists*9) in the DCAF17 gene.

case_report: The patient is an 8-year-old Chinese boy, the only child of unrelated parents. His medical history includes recurrent upper and/or lower respiratory tract infections occurring 3-4 times per year since birth. Six months ago, he developed a painless mass measuring 2 x 2 cm on his upper lip. There was no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. HIV antibody test was negative, and the complete blood count was within normal range. Absolute lymphocyte count showed a decreased CD4+ T-cell count of approximately 1075 cells/μl with a CD4 to CD8 ratio of 0.7. The patient also had an elevated EBV-DNA copy number (5.5*10^3 copies/ml). An excisional biopsy of the mass revealed a dense infiltrate of small to medium-sized lymphoplasmacytic cells with a vaguely nodular arrangement at low power. High-power examination identified two types of neoplastic cells: small round to oval cells with scant pale cytoplasm and loosely clumped chromatin, and cells with a plasmacytoid appearance containing Dutcher bodies. Immunostaining showed that the neoplastic cells were diffusely immunoreactive for pan-B cell markers (CD79a, CD20, and CD19) with lower staining intensity in the plasmacytoid cells. The plasmacytoid cells were positive for plasma cell markers (CD38 and MUM1). The Ki-67 proliferation index was estimated to be 5-10%. EBER testing demonstrated strong and diffuse immunoreactivity in the neoplastic cells. PCR-based clonal analysis revealed clonal immunoglobulin (IG) gene rearrangement. The findings included EBV-positive EMZL, decreased CD4+ T-cell count, and a history of recurrent infections.
test_results: The analyses revealed an in-frame insert mutation in MAGT1 gene (c.828_829insAT) in the patient. The mutation was validated by conventional Sanger sequencing assay. Genetic testing of his parents indicated that the mutation was inherited from his healthy mother who was a hemizygous carrier of this variant whereas his father was wild-type. This MAGT1 variant is located in MAGT1 exon 6 with 2-nucleotide insertion between the position 828 and 829 (c.828_829insAT). It changes the alanine at codon 277 to methionine and introduces 10 erroneous amino acids followed by a premature stop codon TGA at codon 287 (p.A277M.fs*11). It leads to the production of a frameshift truncated MAGT1 protein of 287 amino acids (p.A277M.fs*11), while the wild-type protein consists of 367 amino acids.
diagnosis: XMEN disease caused by a novel hemizygous mutation in MAGT1
Orpha_name: X-linked immunodeficiency with magnesium defect, Epstein-Barr virus infection and neoplasia

case_report: A 5.5-year-old male child presented to the Department of Pediatric Dentistry for the treatment of decayed teeth. The child weighed 10 kg and had an average IQ. He was the third child born to a healthy 26-year-old mother in a consanguineous marriage, delivered by cesarean section at 36 weeks of gestation. The patient exhibited short stature and skeletal findings included mesomelic and rhizomelic limb shortening. His fingers and toes showed brachydactyly and clinodactyly with dysplastic toenails. The patient had multiple vertebral segmentation defects, including hemivertebrae, butterfly-shaped vertebrae, and wedge vertebrae, resulting in scoliosis of the spine with convexity to the right side. Rib fusion and a dysplastic sacrum were also observed. Medical records indicated the presence of micropenis with both testes in the scrotal sac. Craniofacial features included macrocephaly, frontal bossing, micrognathia, and low set ears. There were marked hypertelorism and mid-facial hypoplasia due to a depressed and flat nasal bridge along with anteverted nares. The eyes were prominent with wide and down-slanting palpebral fissures, giving an appearance of pseudo-exophthalmos due to lower eyelid deficiency. The patient had a triangular mouth with an inverted 'V' (tented) appearance. The palate was deep, narrow, and showed submucous clefting. Ankyloglossia and a bifid tongue were distinct. Dental findings included malaligned teeth with gingival hyperplasia, multiple carious teeth, and fusion of the left primary mandibular lateral incisor and primary mandibular canine. The primary maxillary right central incisor was discolored and nonvital due to trauma one year prior. The child had been under growth hormone therapy, which was later discontinued due to unsatisfactory results. The patient received injection testosterone 25 mg once a month for three months for hypoplastic genitalia, and calcium supplements were also part of the medical management. The patient was referred to the Department of Paediatric Medicine for general systemic evaluation, and routine hematologic investigations were within normal limits. According to Frankl's Behavior Rating Scale, the child's behavior was positive, and he was comfortable during dental treatment using desensitization behavior management techniques. Protective stabilization was provided with cushions around the waist and lower back due to scoliosis.
test_results: Ultrasonography of the abdomen showed the presence of 6-mm cyst in the lower pole of right kidney. Two-dimensional echo and color Doppler study showed no evidence of any congenital heart disease. Orthopantogram revealed that all the permanent teeth were present, but their root formation was found to be delayed.

case_report: A 16-year-old female from Bengal, India, born to parents in a consanguineous marriage, exhibited significant short stature. Her birth weight was 2.8 kg, though her birth length is unknown. By the age of two to three years, her parents observed a lack of height increase compared to her peers. She also experienced delayed tooth eruption. There was no family history of short stature or personal history of systemic illness. On examination, her height was 120.5 cm (<3rd centile) with a height standard deviation score (SDS) of -5.84, and her body weight was 27.10 kg (<3rd centile) with a weight SDS of -2.41, based on the WHO 2006 and IAP 2015 combined chart for girls. The mid-parental height was 141 cm. The upper-to-lower body segment ratio (US:LS) was 0.9. Physical features included a prominent forehead, depressed nasal bridge, small hands and feet, crowded teeth with caries, a high-pitched voice, and thin scalp hair. Sexual Maturity Rating (SMR) was B4P2A+. No Turner’s stigmata were observed. Bone age was assessed to be 13 years. Laboratory tests showed normal complete hemogram, kidney function, and liver function. Hormonal assays indicated normal levels of thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) at 1.6 mIU/mL (RV 0.5 to 5 mIU/mL), free thyroxine (FT4) at 0.9 ng/dL (RV 0.8 to 1.8 ng/dL), follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) at 9.0 mIU/mL (RV 2 to 12 mIU/mL, follicular phase), luteinizing hormone (LH) at 6.3 mIU/mL (RV 1.0 to 18.0 mIU/mL, follicular phase), and cortisol at 14 μg/dL (RV 5 to 25 μg/dL). However, low basal levels of IGF1 (34 ng/mL, RV 98 to 180 ng/mL) and IGFBP3 (504 ng/mL, RV 2,600 to 9,000 ng/mL) were noted. A growth hormone stimulation test with clonidine showed peak GH values exceeding 40 ng/mL. MRI of the pituitary gland revealed slight enlargement, measuring 9 mm × 13.8 mm × 9.5 mm. Ophthalmological evaluation showed no vision blurring, visual field defects, or other abnormalities.
test_results: IGF1 level measured 12 hours after the last dose of hGH remained low (20 ng/mL).

case_report: A 25-year-old woman, who has had two previous pregnancies, presented with a two-week history of lower abdominal swelling and pain. Her last menstrual period was three weeks ago. She reported a loss of appetite but did not experience cough, shortness of breath, or vaginal bleeding. Her last childbirth was two years ago, and she was not using contraception. On examination, she appeared acutely ill and in pain. Her vital signs were as follows: blood pressure 130/80 mmHg, pulse rate 108 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and temperature 37.1°C. Physical examination revealed a fourteen-week-sized, mildly tender, firm, mobile abdominopelvic mass, a bulged posterior vaginal fornix, and a normal cervix. Ultrasound imaging showed a large multiseptated adnexal mass with an internal solid component, likely originating from the left ovary. Doppler study indicated blood flow within the solid component and septum. There was also free fluid in the peritoneal cavity. A chest X-ray revealed a blunted costophrenic angle with pleural effusion. Laboratory results showed a blood group of B-negative, hematocrit of 29%, platelet count of 768,000, negative urine human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), and normal liver and renal function tests. Tumor markers included CA-125 at 189.6 U/mL and LDH at 1044 U/mL. During an exploratory laparotomy, approximately 200 mL of bloody ascitic fluid was found in the peritoneal cavity, along with a 12 × 14 cm fragile, dark mass on the left ovary attached to the uterine serosa and dome of the urinary bladder. Additionally, a 10 × 6 cm cystic mass was found on the same ovary adjacent to the fragile tumor. Hemorrhagic fluid was aspirated, and the mass was excised along with part of the bladder dome. A total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy were performed, and the bladder was repaired.
test_results: Histopathology revealed solid proliferation of round to oval pleomorphic cells exhibiting an indistinct eosinophilic cytoplasm, coarse nuclear chromatin, prominent nucleoli, abundant multinucleate giant cells, extensive necrosis, and hemorrhage. A section from the cyst structure showed a fibrous convoluted cyst wall, cavity with calcification, and luteinized stroma. Sections from the uterus, cervix, and tubes showed normal appearance. No evidence of other germ cell element was noticed.

case_report: A seven-year-old girl was referred to our clinic due to short stature and abnormal genital appearance. She was born at 37 weeks of gestation with a birth weight of 2800 grams (10-25th percentile) and a height of 47 cm (10-25th percentile). During the newborn period, multiple café-au-lait spots and spina bifida were noted. Her neuromotor development was normal. At the age of three years, she underwent surgery for a filum terminale lipoma. Family history revealed her father had similar clinical features. On physical examination, her weight was 18 kg (3-10th percentile), height was 106 cm (<3rd percentile), and head circumference was 54 cm (>97th percentile). She presented with macrocephaly, broad forehead, sparse eyebrows, depressed nasal bridge, hypertelorism, low set ears, deeply grooved philtrum, short and webbed neck, pectus excavatum, kyphoscoliosis, sacral hypertrichosis, multiple café-au-lait spots, and axillary and inguinal freckling.
