Genital examination showed abnormal external genitalia with a structure resembling a phallus measuring 3.5 cm, evaluated as Prader Stage 2. No Lisch nodules were detected via slit-lamp examination. Echocardiography results were normal. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a hamartoma.
test_results: Molecular analysis revealed a novel heterozygous c.3052_3056delTTAGT (p.L1018X) variant in the NF1 gene.

case_report: A 72-year-old female presented with a rapidly enlarging neck mass and breathing difficulties. An urgent tracheotomy was performed to secure the airway. Neck and thorax CT scans revealed an infiltrative mass originating from the right thyroid lobe, extending beyond the capsule to the hyoid bone, and occupying the third and fourth neck levels. The mass had irregular borders and contained circular calcifications. It surrounded and infiltrated the right common carotid artery, compressed the trachea, and caused airway narrowing. Multiple lymph nodes were noted in the right upper jugular area. Thorax CT showed numerous metastatic nodules in the lungs, with the largest measuring 29 mm.
test_results: The tumor consisted of proliferation favoring a malign mesenchymal tumor. The tumor cells had hyperchromatic nuclei and 10–15 mitoses/10 HPF were observed. Normal thyroid tissue was observed in none of the areas. Immunohistochemically, pan-keratin, thyroglobulin, and S100 were negative in tumor cells, whereas vimentin, desmin, and smooth muscle actin were found to be positive.

case_report: A 61-year-old male arrived at the emergency department experiencing acute pain in the right inguinal region and swelling on the same side of the scrotum for the past 24 hours. Physical examination identified a painful, solid mass on the right spermatic cord, while the testicles appeared normal. The patient did not have a fever and showed no symptoms or signs of a urinary infection. Laboratory tests, including serum levels of α-fetoprotein (AFP), human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), were within normal ranges. Imaging studies included scrotal ultrasonography (US) and a computed tomography (CT) scan. The US scan showed a solid mass on the right side near the testicles, which were normal. The CT scan revealed a solid soft-tissue mass measuring 3.6 × 3.7 × 5.8 cm originating from the right spermatic cord, along with a small calcification in the inguinal canal. Retroperitoneal and pelvic lymph nodes appeared normal. Due to increasing severe pain in the hemiscrotal area, the patient underwent emergency scrotal exploration and surgical removal of the mass.
test_results: The pathological investigation revealed a variably anaplastic spindle cell neoplasm with prominent and inflamed collagenous stroma and a high degree of cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical markers of the tumor were as follows: S-100 (−), HHF-35 (−), vimentin (+), C-kit (−), desmin (+), SMA (+), and CD 34 (+). Cytogenetic evaluation in substains showed strong and diffuse nuclear positivity for murine double minute 2 (MDM2) and cyclin-dependent kinase-4 (CDK4) consistent with translocation of these genes on the long arm of chromosome 12.
diagnosis: Dedifferentiated Paratesticular Liposarcoma with Osseous Metaplasia

case_report: A 7-day-old male infant was admitted to the neonatology department on December 30, 2020, due to reduced feeding, crying, and movement over the past 7 days. The infant was the firstborn, delivered vaginally at full term, with a birth weight of 3.75 kg. Apgar scores were 10 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes post-birth. Despite being provided an adequate amount of food, the infant exhibited low sucking power, hiccups, and occasional apnea. The mother reported no exposure to toxins, chemicals, or radiation and had regular prenatal check-ups with no abnormalities detected. The parents are not related by blood, and there is no history of past illnesses or hereditary diseases in the family. Upon admission, the following observations were made: body temperature of 36.8 ℃, heart rate of 128 beats/min, respiratory rate of 34 breaths/min, arterial blood pressure of 83/46 mmHg, and SpO2 of 95%. The skin was slightly dry with poor elasticity, and there were no rashes or ecchymosis. Breathing was irregular without obvious dyspnea, the trachea was midline, and no abnormal breath sounds were detected in both lungs. Heart and abdominal examinations were normal. Neurological examination revealed no response to stimulation, a flat and soft anterior fontanelle measuring 1.0 cm × 1.0 cm, hypotonia, and absence of primitive reflexes. A few hours post-admission, the infant experienced frequent apnea neonatorum. Arterial blood gas analysis showed a pH of 7.16 (reference range: 7.35–7.45), PCO2 of 96 mmHg (reference range: 35–45 mmHg), PO2 of 276 mmHg (reference range: 80–100 mmHg), HCO3- of 34.2 mmol/L (reference range: 21.4–27.3 mmol/L), extracellular fluid base excess of 5.5 mmol/L (reference range: -3–3 mmol/L), lactic acid of 0.9 mmol/L (reference range: 0.5–2.2 mmol/L), and blood ammonia of 100 μmol/L (reference range: 18–72 μmol/L).
test_results: Serum tandem mass spectrometry showed that the glycine concentration was 850.05 μmol/L (reference range: 130–650 μmol/L), and urine organic acid analysis showed no obvious abnormality. An electroencephalogram (EEG) showed that diffuse low-amplitude irregular 1–6 Hz δ and θ waves and low-amplitude β waves were mixed in the quiet state, and the external stimulation background did not change. The EEG activity voltage was low, which represented a moderately abnormal neonatal EEG. Head magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in the neonatal period (aged 7 d old) showed that a myelinated T1 hypersignal was not found in the hind limbs of the bilateral internal capsules or cerebellar dentate nucleus, and no abnormal corpus callosum was found. When the child was 2 mo old, re-examination of head MRI showed that the corpus callosum was smaller than it was on earlier imaging; the bilateral ventricles were full and irregular (more pronounced on the left side); the corticospinal tract, the white matter of bilateral ventricles, and the parietal lobe showed symmetrical high signal intensity on diffusion-weighted imaging; and the apparent diffusion coefficient map showed slightly low signal intensity. The proband has a variant on exon 8, position chr9:6620259G>T, NM_000170.3:c.395C>A, p.(Ser132*) and a variant on exon 18, position chr9:6556173C>T, NM_000170.3:c.2182G>A, p.(Gly728Arg).

case_report: A 26-year-old woman exhibited multiple whitish papules and plaques of varying sizes, accompanied by wrinkles on both palms following water exposure for the past year. Physical examination revealed whitish discoloration and edematous wrinkling on her palms within 5 minutes of water immersion. She had no significant family or medical history of systemic disease, and her chest X-ray results were normal.
test_results: Histopathologic findings showed orthokeratosis, hyperkeratosis and acrosyringia. She was negative in the CFTR test.

case_report: A 67-year-old female patient presented with a one-week history of a painful, red patch on the left shin, which developed superficial blisters and progressed into an ulcer with a bluish to grayish border. The lesion measured 8 cm in diameter and exhibited yellowish discharge, pain, itching, and a heating sensation. The patient had been diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) three months earlier and was undergoing systemic chemotherapy with decitabine in the hematology-oncology department. Due to immunosuppression from chemotherapy, systemic antibiotics were administered for two weeks, but the lesion showed no improvement. Blood culture and skin smear tests conducted before antibiotic treatment were negative, as was the pathergy test.
test_results: The histopathologic findings showed prominent spongiotic changes in the epidermis and dispersed neutrophilic and lymphocytic infiltration with fibrinoid necrosis in the dermis. There were no atypical cells showing mitotic activity and no evidence of infection in the microbiological culture of the tissue and immunohistochemical tests, including periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) and Grocott’s methenamine silver stain (GMS).

case_report: A 2.9-year-old boy presented with developmental language delay on February 23, 2012. He was born at 41 weeks of gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery after an uneventful pregnancy, as the first child of healthy, non-consanguineous Korean parents. His birth weight was 2,960 grams (10-25th percentile), length was 51 cm (50-75th percentile), and head circumference was 32 cm (3-10th percentile). The parents were 28 and 31 years old. There was no family history of neurological disease or developmental delay. Early infancy was marked by normal feeding and muscle tone. Development appeared typical until 3-4 months of age, but delays were noted from 12 months onward. He began walking independently at 18 months and spoke his first words at 12 months. There were no signs of autism or sleep disturbances. Behavioral issues included difficulty adapting to socially acceptable behavior in kindergarten, aggressive behavior, and picking on peers. There was no history of seizures. At the clinic visit, his weight was 12.3 kg (-1.05 SDS), height was 87.8 cm (-1.16 SDS), BMI was 15.96 kg/m2 (-0.62 SDS), and head circumference was 50 cm (-1.19 SDS). Physical examination revealed a broad forehead, brachycephaly, and a downturned upper lip, with no other dysmorphic features. Eye and oral examinations were normal. Extremities showed short fingers. He was alert and maintained good eye contact, with a normal neurological examination otherwise. At 3 years old, neurodevelopmental evaluation showed inattentive and uncooperative behavior. Cognitive function was equivalent to an 18-month-old on the Bayley Scales of Infant Development II. His social quotient was 60.6 on the social maturity scale. Language evaluation indicated expressive language at an 18-month-old level and receptive language at a 12-month-old level. Adaptive skills assessment showed activities of daily living at a 19-month-old level, fine motor skills at a 20-month-old level, and cognitive function at a 16.6-month-old level. Hearing test results were normal. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, chemistry panel, lipid profile, thyroid function test, and urinalysis, were normal. Electrocardiography and chest radiograph were normal. Brain MRI showed no abnormalities, including no ventriculomegaly.
test_results: Chromosome analysis revealed a deletion within the short arm of chromosome 7, with breakpoints of p11.2 and p11.2 at least 550-band resolution. We conducted whole genome array comparative genomic hybridization (array CGH) using commercially available array-CGH slides (MACArray Karyo 1440 BAC-chip, Macrogen, Seoul, Korea) to confirm the suspected cytogenetic findings. We found a 2.6 Mb deletion on chromosome 17p11.2. The start and stop points of this deletion were estimated at 17,083,225 and 19,654,341 (GRCh37 February 2009 assembly) with a total of 5 probes: BAC90_H16, BAC-249_G12, BAC41_D18, BAC132_L20, and BAC10_I20. The 2.57 Mb region contained 15 RefSeq (NCBI reference sequence) genes: MPRIP, PLD6, FLCN, COPS3, RAI1, SMCR5, SREBF1, MIR33B, TOM1L2, TRIM16L, FBXW10, FAM18B, ALDH3A2, SLC47A, and ALDH3A1.

case_report: A 77-year-old woman with a medical history including diabetes mellitus type 1, polymyalgia rheumatica, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and hypertension, was brought to the emergency department after a fall, without losing consciousness. Prior to this, she experienced a sore throat and lethargy for three days, accompanied by a slight cough but no fever, chills, or shortness of breath. Upon arrival, she was afebrile, without tachypnea or oxygen desaturation on room air. Lung examination revealed scattered rhonchi bilaterally. A chest radiograph showed no obvious pulmonary disease. She was admitted with an initial assessment of near syncope and mild upper respiratory infection and was treated with intravenous azithromycin, with plans for discharge within 24 to 48 hours. After 48 hours, she developed sudden shortness of breath and hypoxemia of unclear cause. A repeat chest radiograph showed acute widespread pulmonary infiltrates, a significant change from the previous study. Diuretics were administered. Despite a normal B-type natriuretic peptide level and normal echocardiogram, further evaluation was needed. High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest revealed diffuse ground glass opacities throughout the lung fields, with bilateral traction bronchiectasis.
test_results: The lungs revealed diffuse alveolar wall thickening with proliferating connective tissue, formation of hyaline membranes, and type II pneumocyte hyperplasia compatible with DAD pattern: mixed exudative and organizing phase.

case_report: A 9-year-old boy from Iran, born to unrelated healthy parents, was referred for genetic counseling. He exhibited severe mental retardation and developmental delay, unable to walk, talk, or hold his neck. Seizures began at age 4 and were managed with phenobarbital. The patient was cachectic. Physical examination revealed bilateral nystagmus, microcephaly, spastic quadriplegia, and macroorchidism. Previous chromosomal studies and molecular testing for Fragile-X were normal. Brain MRI indicated cerebral atrophy. The patient has a 15-year-old brother and a maternal uncle with similar clinical features.
test_results: Oligoarray CGH was performed for both affected offspring and the mother.

case_report: A 34-year-old Hispanic male presented with a 2-week history of drowsiness, mild headache, photopsia, and blurred vision. Initially, these symptoms affected his right eye, but within 48 hours, they became bilateral. Best-corrected visual acuity was measured at 20/25 in both eyes. External examination and biomicroscopy showed no notable findings, and intraocular pressure was slightly elevated in both eyes.
test_results: Fundus examination of the right eye revealed multiple coalescent elevated gray lesions involving the macula, extending beyond the inferior temporal vascular arcade. The left fundus presented a similarly isolated lesion located in the mid periphery temporally. Fundus autofluorescence showed these lesions as multiple hyperautofluorescent spots surrounded by a slightly hyperautofluorescent halo. On FA, these lesions appeared as multiple hyperfluorescent spots with extensive leakage and pooling of the dye involving the entire macula in the right eye and focally localized in the left eye. OCT presented with the undulation of the inner retinal surface, extensive subretinal fluid, irregularities of the RPE, and a small dome-shaped separation of the outer layers of the retina below the external limiting membrane, located slightly inferior to the center of the fovea in the right eye. This finding was confirmed in multiple slides. The left eye also showed subretinal fluid, RPE irregularities, and inner retinal surface undulation, but no separation of the outer layers of the neurosensory retina was detected. OCT-angiography was also performed, subtle irregularity of the foveal avascular zone edges at the deep retinal plexus was observed in both the eyes, and small areas of flow void were detected at the choriocapillaris.

case_report: The patient is a newborn female, the first child of a 28-year-old mother and 31-year-old father, both healthy and non-consanguineous, from Holguin, Cuba. The mother had regular prenatal medical check-ups during pregnancy and took folic acid and vitamins from the early weeks. She reported no exposure to teratogens but experienced two urinary infections treated with antibiotics during pregnancy. The patient was delivered via elective Cesarean section at 38 weeks of gestation, weighing 3100 grams and measuring 48 centimeters in length. Apgar scores were 9 at one minute and 9 at five minutes. The patient was breastfed and discharged in good health.
test_results: The NBS was performed at 48 h of extrauterine life and showed a Phe blood concentration of 213 μmol/L (3.5 mg/dL). A second screening showed a Phe blood concentration of 435 μmol/L (7 mg/dL). At 28 days old, her Phe blood concentration at confirmatory diagnosis was 321 μmol/L (5.3 mg/dL). After two follow-up determinations of Phe blood concentration, the patient presented a slight increase above the desired level.

case_report: A 4-year-old male child presented with discolored teeth. His medical history was unremarkable. The mother reported an uncomplicated, full-term pregnancy from a nonconsanguineous marriage. The child appeared well-nourished with a height of 96.25 cm. Parents noted normal mental development. The child had sparse, discolored hair and had undergone 3-4 haircuts. He had a broad forehead, prominent in lateral view, with a head circumference of 51.25 cm, within the 50th percentile. There was no splitting of the superficial layer of fingernails or toenails. Dental examination showed the eruption of all four permanent first molars. Primary teeth had been extracted due to dental abscess formation. The remaining primary teeth were opaque and yellowish-brown, with severe attrition of mandibular primary incisors and maxillary primary canines. Pulp chambers of maxillary and mandibular primary canines were visible through the thin enamel. Both posterior and anterior occlusal relationships indicated a Class III tendency. A panoramic radiograph revealed increased sclerosis of the mandibular cortical bone. The remaining primary teeth and erupted first permanent molars appeared taurodontic, with extremely thin enamel, enlarged pulp chambers with greater apico-occlusal height, and apically displaced furcation. Radiographic contrast between enamel and dentin was reduced. Root formation of the first permanent molars was incomplete, preventing an objective assessment of taurodontism. A lateral cephalogram showed increased density of the mandible, especially in the symphysis region, and the base of the skull. Frontal sinus pneumatization was not very apparent. Cephalometric analysis indicated a Class III skeletal pattern due to a retrusive maxilla (reduced SNA).
test_results: Genetic analysis reports of the child revealed a 4-bp mutation in the DLX3 gene.

case_report: A 63-year-old Caucasian male was referred to the retina service for evaluation of fundus abnormalities identified by a general ophthalmologist. The patient had a history of end-stage renal disease from a young age and had undergone two renal transplantations. He also experienced profound hearing loss. Additionally, he had a 10-year history of well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus without signs of diabetic retinopathy. His medications included immunosuppressants (azathioprine, prednisone, and cyclosporine), an antihypertensive agent (nifedipine), a statin (fluvastatin), medication for benign prostatic hyperplasia (dutasteride and tamsulosin), and oral antidiabetics (glipizide and linagliptin). An ophthalmologist had previously examined the patient at 24 years of age, noting a best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 6/6 in both eyes with no significant findings on general eye examination. Over the past 5 years, the patient experienced progressive myopia and sought advice when poor vision disqualified him from renewing his driving license. On clinical examination, BCVA was 6/24 in the right eye (6/12 with pinhole) and 6/48 in the left eye (6/15 with pinhole). The refractive error was −13 dpt/−1.50 dpt × 90 in the right eye and −10 dpt/−1.0 dpt × 100 in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was normal in both eyes. Bilateral slit lamp examination showed subtle, widespread corneal opacities, anterior lenticonus, and mild cataract. Bilateral dilated fundus evaluation revealed multiple yellowish lesions of varying sizes located along the superior vascular arcades, nasally to the optic discs, and in the temporal macular regions; the largest lesion was two-thirds of an optic disc diameter.
test_results: Fundus autofluorescence imaging exposed hyperautofluorescence corresponding to the yellow lesions. On spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) of the lesions, there was subretinal deposition of hyperreflective material at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium. Fluorescein angiography did not indicate associated leakage. Full-field electroretinography demonstrated slightly reduced photopic amplitudes. The electro-oculogram (EOG) was normal. Macular SD-OCT displayed multilayered retinoschisis located in the superotemporal macula of the left eye. Furthermore, central macular thinning and an irregular foveal contour were evident in both eyes.

case_report: A 22-year-old female with a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus for approximately 15 years visited the endocrine and metabolic diseases clinic after recording blood glucose levels between 250 to 300 mg/dL (13.88-16.65 mmol/L) at home. Urine tests were positive for ketones, prompting routine clinical biochemistry tests. The patient reported no symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, cough, chest pain, dyspnea, diarrhea, constipation, or burning urination. She mentioned experiencing pain in the proximal muscles of her upper and lower extremities since childhood, which occurred intermittently after physical exertion and subsided with rest. She felt pain when climbing stairs or lifting heavy objects, which also resolved after resting. Over the past year, her symptoms had worsened, and she had been prescribed anti-inflammatory and muscle relaxant treatments by an orthopedic surgeon. During follow-up, she received appropriate fluid replacement and intensive insulin therapy. Routine examinations revealed creatinine kinase (CK) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels of 2247 and 460 U/L, respectively. Physical examination showed no abnormalities. Neurological examination and electromyography (EMG) were conducted, revealing motor-unit action potentials characteristic of myogenesis in localized muscles, with normal myogenic conduction. A nonischemic forearm exercise test was performed, measuring ammonia, CK, and lactate levels at baseline, 1, 3, 5, and 7 minutes. Laboratory data indicated a statistically significant increase in CK levels. Although ammonia levels increased, the change was not statistically significant, and no significant increase was observed in lactic acid levels.
test_results: A homozygous c.2128_2130delTTC/p.Phe710del mutation was detected in the exons of the PYGM gene.

case_report: A 1.5-month-old male infant, born from a non-consanguineous marriage, was brought to the outpatient department with issues related to poor weight gain and feeding difficulties. The infant was admitted due to insufficient postnatal weight gain (birth weight: 2010g; admission weight: 1860g). Detailed examination revealed a noticeable deviation of the mouth's angle to the right side, absence of nasolabial folds on the left side, and lack of forehead folds on the left side during crying. The tongue deviated toward the left side. Ocular findings included incomplete closure of the left eye and a convergent squint. No limb malformations or hypotonia were observed. The infant was born at term, small for gestational age, via normal vaginal delivery. The mother had a history of using an oral drug for three consecutive days during the first trimester, likely a prostaglandin analog, without documentation. The prenatal period was otherwise uneventful, with no history of instrumental delivery or perinatal asphyxia. The immediate postnatal period was also uneventful, with no reported convulsions, repeated vomiting, or persistent crying. Examination findings indicated multiple cranial nerve palsies, including the left facial nerve (lower motor neuron type), left hypoglossal nerve, and bilateral abducens nerve.
test_results: MRI was essentially normal, excluding the possibilities of any perinatal insult, space-occupying lesion, or structural anomaly. Nerve conduction velocity (NCV) test of facial nerves done at 6 months of age showed left-sided LMN type facial palsy.

case_report: A 1-day-old male infant was transferred to our hospital due to a heart murmur and increasing levels of carbon dioxide in the blood. He was born at 36 weeks and 3 days of gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery, weighing 2700 grams. The pregnancy was uneventful, and there was no significant family history. Physical examination revealed a high prominent forehead, low-set ears, a thin upper lip, and retrognathia. No abnormalities were detected in the central nervous, digestive, or urinary systems. Upon admission, laboratory tests showed thrombocytopenia and coagulation issues: platelet count was 39 × 10^3/μL, prothrombin time-international normalized ratio (PT-INR) was 1.65, activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) was 48.8 seconds, and fibrinogen level was 168 mg/dL. Surgical procedures including aortic arch reconstruction and ductus arteriosus ligation were performed at 6 days old. On the fourth day after surgery, the patient experienced intratracheal hemorrhage and required emergency pericardial drainage for pericardial tamponade on the eleventh postoperative day. The patient also had intraventricular hemorrhage and pancytopenia, necessitating regular transfusions of platelet concentrates and red blood cells. A bone marrow test was conducted at 2 months of age to explore the cause of pancytopenia.
test_results: Genetic testing of bone marrow cells revealed a partial deletion of chromosome 11.

case_report: In February 2010, a 45-year-old white man was referred to the Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery Department of the Dental Faculty of Gazi University for further investigation and treatment of his existing lesions. His medical history was non-contributory and extraoral examination was within normal limits. The intraoral examination revealed considerable expansion at the right and left posterior vestibular area of his mandible. The overlying gingiva and mucosa in the mandible were normal without any clinical signs of inflammation. All teeth had normal vitality. There was no mandibular nerve paresthesia or facial deformation.
test_results: Orthopantomograph and computed tomography showed multiple mostly dense mixed radiodense/radiolucent lesions closely associated with the roots of the upper left lateral incisor and canine, the lower left canine, premolars, first and second molars, the lower right second premolar, first and second molars. There was no root resorption or fusion of the lesions to the involved teeth. The occlusal images revealed slight buccal expansion at the molar region on the left and right side of the mandible. Biopsy specimen of this lesion composed of benign fibro-osseous tissue containing bone which ranges from woven bone trabeculae to cementum like mineralizations. Biochemical analysis of serum alkaline phosphatase, calcium and phosphorus were shown to be within the normal limits.

case_report: A 3-year-old boy, with a Puerto Rican father and Caucasian mother, visited the ophthalmology clinic due to light sensitivity and multiple congenital anomalies. Examination revealed binocular visual acuity of 2.4 cycles per centimeter using Teller acuity cards, which is approximately equivalent to 20/360 on the Snellen scale. Cycloplegic refraction indicated myopia with astigmatism in both eyes: −3.25 + 2.25 × 090 in the right eye and −3.25 + 2.50 × 095 in the left eye. The anterior segment examination showed no abnormalities. Fundus examination showed diffuse granular pigment changes and bull’s eye maculopathy, with a corresponding bull’s eye pattern on fundus autofluorescence (FAF). Optical coherence tomography (OCT) using Bioptogen revealed loss of the ellipsoid zone at the fovea. Dental examination showed crowns on multiple molar teeth and a yellow/opaque appearance of the anterior teeth, with thinning and complete absence of enamel on some teeth. Systemic evaluation noted spastic paraplegia, developmental delay, and fatty liver. The patient required a tracheostomy for respiration and a gastrostomy tube for feeding.
test_results: Clinical whole exome sequencing revealed homozygosity for a frameshift variant in CNNM4: c.279delC (p.Phe93Leufs*31). Segregation analysis revealed that this variant was present in only the patient’s father and not mother. Subsequent analysis examining other single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) revealed paternal uniparental isodisomy (UPD) on chromosome 2p22–2q37.

case_report: An 8-year-old male patient was referred to Joana de Gusmão Hospital (HIJG) on January 27, 2021, for evaluation and specialized care. The patient presented with skin lesions predominantly in exposed areas. He is the firstborn in the family, with no consanguinity between the parents, but has first-degree relatives with similar conditions (a 3-year-old brother and a deceased paternal cousin). The patient lives in a wooden house with poor basic sanitation. At 1 year of age, facial macules appeared. At age 3, he underwent surgery and two cycles of unspecified chemotherapy for a lower lip squamous cell carcinoma with level 1 adenomegaly. At age 5, he moved to Chapecó and began monitoring by the local health team, including oncology and palliative care services. Squamous cell carcinoma was identified in the right eyelid, right malar region, nasal wing, and left eyelid, along with a basosquamous carcinoma above the lip. In 2018 and 2019, basal cell carcinoma of the skin and scalp was noted. On January 27, 2021, he was admitted to HIJG, already on vismodegib 150 mg/day, acitretin 25 mg/day, tramadol for pain, sunscreen (irregular use), and UV-protective clothing (reported as small for his size). Physical examination revealed macular lesions throughout the body, less intense in the perineum, and verrucous lesions on the face and neck. Two ulcerated scalp lesions (~3 cm in diameter), an erythematous tumor with hyperkeratosis at the apex (~1.5 cm in the helix of the right ear), and a lesion (~7 cm) on the right face were observed. Blackish lesions on the face and a macerated, bleeding lesion on the tip of the tongue were also noted. A large lesion (~8 cm in diameter) in the left orbit obscured the eyeball, causing severe vision impairment and minimal acuity in the right eye. The remainder of the physical examination was largely unchanged, except for a 1+/4+ systolic murmur on auscultation. The patient was referred for interdisciplinary assessment to a psychologist, speech therapist, dentist, nutritionist, dermatologist, palliative care center, and oncologist. Analgesia was administered as part of the care plan. A transfusion of filtered and irradiated red cell concentrate was ordered due to anemia.
test_results: The cranial and face tomography result showed that the lesion in the left orbit was invasive, with bone involvement of the lateral wall. Chest tomography showed some supine atelectasis and fibroscarring changes in the anterior segment of the upper lobe of the left lung, and upper abdominal tomography showed no changes. The MRI report described solid and expansive lesions on both hemifaces, with an aggressive aspect to the left, determining the destruction of the left zygomatic arch and part of the ipsilateral frontal bone. The histopathological report proved the existence of a melanocanthoma in the skin biopsy of the cervical region; a carcinoma in the helix of the right ear; a proliferative epithelial lesion with superficial atypia in the skin of the right temporal region; an invasive squamous cell carcinoma in the left orbital lesion; and a pyogenic granuloma in the oral mucosa of the tongue edge. Immunohistochemistry of the right helix lesion was negative for monoclonal antibodies BER-EP4 and EMA.

case_report: The patient, a 6-month-old female, was admitted due to an inability to laugh and difficulties with eye tracking. She was born at 39 weeks of gestation with an Apgar score of 1–10 points and a birth weight of 3,050 g. There was no history of asphyxia, hypoxia, resuscitation, or jaundice. Both parents are healthy and report no family history of genetic disorders. At 3 months, the parents noticed the child could not laugh but did not seek medical attention. By 6 months, the child still could not laugh and had difficulty tracking movements with her eyes. Physical examination upon admission revealed clear consciousness, normal spirit and nutrition, normal head circumference, normal complexion, mild rashes, and no head deformity. Cardiopulmonary examination was normal, with no hepatosplenomegaly or neck rigidity. Specialist examinations indicated acceptable sound tracking ability, absence of babbling, clenched fists with adducted thumbs, and lack of active grasping. The child could raise her head in the prone position, but head stability was poor when pulled up from a supine position. Limb muscle tension was increased, and the cervical correction reflex was positive (+). Slit lamp and fundus examinations were normal. The Gesell developmental schedules assessment showed all function regions were below 2 standard deviations for her age. Laboratory results included glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase/aspartate aminotransferase at 77 U/L, glutamic pyruvic transaminase/alanine aminotransferase at 57 U/L, alkaline phosphatase at 215 U/L, γ-glutamyl transferase at 50 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase at 427 U/L, and creatinine at 22.9 mol/L, indicating minor liver and kidney damage. Electrolytes and myocardial zymogram were normal. Immunoglobulin M was 2.53 g/L, complement C4 was 0.41 g/L, and α-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase was 314 U/L. Fecal routine and occult blood tests were negative. Thyroid function tests were negative. Emergency blood routine reexamination showed a lymphocyte percentage of 50.80% (normal range: 20–50%) and a lymphocyte absolute number of 4.53 × 10^9/L (normal range: 1.1–3.2 × 10^9/L). TORCH series results were negative for Toxoplasma gondii, herpes simplex virus 1 and 2, and rubella virus, but human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) DNA was significantly elevated, and anticytomegalovirus IgG was positive. Ten immune series tests (including hepatitis B surface antigen, anti-hepatitis B surface antibody, hepatitis B envelope antigen, anti-hepatitis envelope antibody, anti-hepatitis B core antibody, hepatitis B pre-S1 antigen, anti-hepatitis A antibody, anti-hepatitis C antibody, anti-human immunodeficiency virus antibody, and syphilis) were negative. Immunoglobulin and complement series were normal. Blood and urine screening by tandem mass spectrometry showed no clinical significance. An electroencephalogram recorded during sleep showed no abnormalities. Cranial MRI revealed patches of slightly longer T1 and T2 signals in the bilateral cerebral hemisphere and brain stem white matter, predominantly in the frontotemporal lobe. There was decreased white matter volume, enlarged ventricles, and widened sulci. The median line was centered, and no abnormal flow vessels were observed in the cranium. These features indicated diffuse brain atrophy and delayed myelination.
test_results: The results showed that the TREX1 gene of the child was mutated by c.137 (exon2)_c.138 (exon2) insC and c.292 (exon2)_c.293 (exon2) insA. The mother TREX1 gene c.137 (exon2)_c.138 (exon2) insC was found, but TREX1 gene c.292. (exon2)_C.293 (exon2) was normal. The father TREX1 gene c.292 (exon2)_c.293 (exon2) insA mutation was observed, whereas TREX1 gene c.137 (exon2)_c.138 (exon2) was normal. The parents of the proband were heterozygous carriers with normal phenotypes.

case_report: A 34-year-old woman presented with left back pain persisting for over 6 months, which worsened over the past 5 days. She had no notable medical or family history. Routine laboratory tests showed no abnormalities. An enhanced thoracic computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a cavitary lesion with a fluid level and a thickened wall in the left lower lobe of the lung, measuring approximately 60 mm by 45 mm by 36 mm. The thickest part of the wall was about 5.6 mm and showed significant enhancement post-contrast. The surrounding pleura was thickened and adherent. Transthoracic lung ultrasound identified a hypoechoic subpleural lesion in the left lower lobe, which was inhomogeneous with clear margins and measured approximately 24 mm by 22 mm. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) showed minimal peripheral perfusion with no central perfusion. Core biopsy of the lesion's solid components, guided by CEUS, was performed.
test_results: Histopathological analysis of the lung resection specimen indicated the chronic inflammation of the lower left lung tissue, with dysplasia glandular ducts and cystic cavities formation. The largest cystic cavity was >2 cm in diameter. The smallest one was ∼2 to 5 mm. The cyst wall was covered with ciliated columnar epithelium. Immunohistochemistry revealed CK20 +, CK7 ++, CK5/6 +, P63 +, P53 −, PD-L1 −, PDL1-NC −, TTF-1 +, NapsinA +, SMA +, S-100 −, and Desmin ++.

case_report: A 14-year-old female presented with a two-month history of itchy skin lesions located on the upper and lower extremities, thighs, and pubic area. Her system review did not reveal any other complaints or associated symptoms. Physical examination showed well-demarcated annular brownish plaques, measuring between 5cm and 7cm. The borders of these plaques were scaly and elevated, with a few pustules observed on the upper and lower extremities, thighs, and pubic area. Some lesions exhibited central clearing. There were no abnormalities noted in the hair, nails, mucosal, or genital areas. The patient was treated with terbinafine 250 mg tablets and topical miconazole cream applied twice daily for two weeks. Upon follow-up after two weeks, additional lesions were observed on the lower extremity and inner thigh, despite adherence to the prescribed treatment.
test_results: Histopathology demonstrated pustules located immediately below the stratum corneum and contained mainly polymorphonuclear leucocytes with a few eosinophils, acantholytic cells in the cavity, and spongiosis in the epidermis. Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain was negative for fungal infection.

case_report: A 23-year-old male, born from a second-degree consanguineous marriage, presented to the Dermatology and Venerology outpatient clinic with complaints of nail deterioration and absence in the third and fourth toes of both feet. Dermatological examination showed onychodystrophy, white discoloration, severe hypoplasia in the first and second toenails, and anonychia in the fourth and fifth toes. The patient was born at 39 weeks of gestation via spontaneous delivery. Additional observations included difficulty in pronunciation. ENT examination revealed an asymmetric face, bilateral epicanthus, lower set ears, high arched palate, and elongated uvula. Developmental delays were noted, particularly in motor and language milestones, with minimal delays in cognitive and social skills. Family history was unremarkable. Systemic and neurologic examinations were normal, as was the ophthalmic examination.
test_results: Investigations revealed mild bilateral sensorineural loss (right: 28/27 db, left 33/27 db) on an audiometric test. An intelligence test was carried out using the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale and an intelligence quotient (IQ) of 65 was obtained. X-ray of the foot showed on both sides with hypoplasia on the toes due to onychodystrophy. There is also adhesion in the metatarsal bones.

case_report: A 38-year-old woman experienced persistent pain in her back, right arm, and ankle joints for several months and consulted multiple orthopedic, neurological, and pain clinics. She was found to have anemia and was advised to seek further evaluation at an internal medicine clinic. Before doing so, she visited the emergency department of our hospital at 11:30 P.M. on a Friday due to severe back pain. Upon admission, laboratory results showed a slightly elevated white blood cell (WBC) count of 11,700/µL, reduced red blood cell (RBC) count of 2.21 × 10^6/µL, and low platelet (PLT) count of 42,000/µL. Additionally, elevated levels of lactate dehydrogenase (2300 U/L), P-FDP (33.8 µg/mL), and d-dimer (14.22 µg/mL) were noted. The histogram from an automated hematology analyzer (DxH 500; Beckman Coulter, CA) was abnormal. While the RBC histogram appeared normal, the PLT histogram displayed an unusually shaped peak around 20–30 fL, indicating the presence of giant PLTs or PLT aggregation. The WBC histogram showed abnormal elevations at 35 fL and around 100 fL, suggesting giant PLTs and abnormal cells, including nucleated RBCs. A peripheral blood smear was prepared, revealing blasts (4%) and a significant number of orthochromatic erythroblasts (48/100 WBCs). The patient was transferred the next day to Sendai Medical Center for further treatment.
test_results: Bone marrow was examined, and 99% of cells were blasts positive for CD10, CD19, CD24, CyCD22, CyCD79a, Cy µ, and myeloperoxidase.

case_report: A 50-year-old Caucasian male arrived at the emergency department with sudden vision loss and the presence of scotoma in his left eye (OS), without any ocular pain or discomfort. His previous ophthalmic history was clear. The patient had been treating a painful anal fissure with GTN 0.2% ointment three times daily for the past two months. He experienced headaches and dizziness after nearly every application, which were partially alleviated by common analgesics. Over the past 15 days, the pain from the fissure intensified, particularly after bowel movements, leading him to increase the ointment application to up to six times daily. In the last three days, he experienced episodes of transient postural hypotension. He was not on any other medications and reported only occasional caffeine consumption. He had no history of smoking, excessive drinking, or substance abuse. Best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 85 ETDRS letters in the right eye (OD) and 75 ETDRS letters in the left eye (OS). Intraocular pressure was normal. Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) was negative in both eyes, and Ishihara plates showed no apparent color vision deficiency. Anterior chamber examination of both eyes was unremarkable. Fundoscopic examination of the right eye (OD) showed no significant findings. Fundoscopy of the left eye (OS) revealed mild retinal venous dilatation and tortuosity with scattered blot hemorrhages. Subtle, parafoveal, whitish lesions were observed in the outer retina.
test_results: Swept-source-optical coherence tomography (SS-OCT) demonstrated diffuse, hyperreflective lesions at the level of the inner plexiform layer (IPL), inner nuclear layer (INL), and outer plexiform layer (OPL). Fundus autofluorescence did not reveal any hyper- or hypofluorescent lesions of the Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE). Optical coherence tomography-angiography (OCT-A) revealed a focal, small area of capillary dropout in the deep capillary plexus. Superficial capillary plexus, outer retina, and choriocapillaris appeared normal. Fluorescein angiography (FA) revealed normal arteriovenous transit time, masking effect due to blot hemorrhages, and early punctuate leakage in the inner retina.

case_report: A 32-year-old female presented with hyperpigmented plaques on the dorsum of her feet, predominantly on the medial aspect. Erythematous macules and plaques of irregular shape and size, varying from 0.5 cm² to 4 cm² in diameter, were observed on both lower legs. These were interspersed with follicular or non-follicular pustules, erosions, and ulcers covered with yellowish crust.
test_results: Dermoscopic examination of the acute lesions revealed multiple perifollicular white globules on intense red-violaceous background interspersed with short linear vessels. Dermoscopy of the ulcer showed yellow globules with radial white striations surrounded by brown dots and patches in polarized mode and dirty yellow scales and white globules in non-polarized mode. Raw areas revealed uniformly distributed red dots and globules with peripheral white scales in polarized dermoscopy. Dermoscopy of chronic hyperkeratotic hyperpigmented plaques presented a mixture of gray-brown pigmentation along with dirty white scales and red globules. Few resolved areas reveal whitish striations in a branching pattern with brown patches and linear red vessels on a white background. Skin biopsy from the hyperkeratotic plaque revealed psoriasiform dermatitis.

case_report: The patient is a 20-month-old boy who was admitted to XiJing Hospital due to delayed neurodevelopment and recurrent episodes of lactic acidosis. He is the first child of healthy consanguineous Chinese parents, with no notable family medical history. The child was born at full-term with normal measurements for weight, length, and head circumference. At 3 months old, he experienced bilateral eyelid clonus seizures lasting between 30 seconds to 1 minute, which were effectively managed with oral levetiracetam. At 9 months old, the patient exhibited severe lactic acidosis, failure to thrive, rapid breathing, and lethargy following two days of upper respiratory symptoms.
test_results: MRI of the patient's brain revealed abnormal signal shadows in the white matter near the triangle of the bilateral lateral ventricles. Laboratory investigations during the acute episode revealed a plasma pH of 6.96 and the plasma levels of lactate, ammonia, and glucose, and alanine and citrulline levels to be 7.95 mmol/L, 93.77 μmol/L, 6.1 mmol/L, 715 μmol/L, and 69.18 μ mol/L, respectively. The levels of lactate and ketones were also elevated in urine.

case_report: A 22-year-old male patient was referred by an orthodontist due to asymptomatic radiolucent areas observed on routine radiographs. Physical examination revealed no bulging of the mandibular cortex, no displacement, no mobility, and no loss of vitality of teeth adjacent to the affected areas. The patient did not report any local trauma. Blood tests, including serum calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, and parathyroid hormone (PTH), were all within normal limits.
test_results: Radiographic findings consisted of two unilocular radiolucent areas with a sclerotic halo that did not cause absorption of tooth roots, and that were located in the left parasymphyseal region in the mandible (measuring about 2.5 cm) and the right body of the mandible (diameter of about 2 cm). Panoramic radiographs showed that the two cysts had increased in size by about 1 cm each. There were projections between the apexes of adjacent teeth in the lesions located in the body of the mandible. Needle aspiration of the cavities was negative for fluid. Corticotomy of the cysts revealed no signs of a cystic capsule or any other type of soft tissue within the bone cavity.

case_report: Case 2 involves a 13-year-old boy, the younger sibling of the individual described in case 1. He has experienced hearing difficulty and poor vision for the past 5 years, with symptoms progressively worsening. There is no history of gross haematuria. Physical examination revealed no oedema. The heart rate was 80 beats per minute and regular. Blood pressure was measured at 90/60 mm Hg, which is below the 50th percentile for his age and height. Slit-lamp examination results were normal. The patient was found to have amblyopia.
test_results: Urine examination revealed massive proteinuria (+++) and haematuria (+++). Ultrasonography revealed a normal-sized kidney (10.7 cm × 3.4 cm on the right and 10.6 cm × 4.3 cm on the left). Renal parenchyma showed normal echogenicity but a loss of corticomedullary differentiation. Pure tone audiometry revealed bilateral moderate sensorineural hearing loss.

case_report: A 22-year-old Indian woman presented for management of misaligned teeth. She exhibited short stature, mild intellectual disability, and distinctive facial features. Her academic performance was below average, and she had a history of hearing issues since childhood. Her hair was fine, sparse, and fragile with a slightly receding hairline. Additional features included thick eyebrows, protruding ears, a pear-shaped nose with a broad nasal bridge and columella. Her lateral facial profile was concave with a retruded maxilla and a prognathic mandible. Intraoral examination revealed mild crowding of the maxillary and mandibular anterior teeth, poor oral hygiene, and a bilateral Angle’s Class III molar relationship. She also had short limbs with brachydactyly of the fingers and toes, and her wrist and interphalangeal joints were hyperextensible.
test_results: A complete skeletal survey was carried out which demonstrated multiple bony exostoses in relation to bilateral ulna, right humerus, bilateral femoral, right tibia, right iliac and left pubic bone. There were no spine abnormalities. On hand-wrist radiographs, her bone age was estimated to be 19 years. Epiphyseal fusion had been completed so no cone-shaped epiphyses were seen. Her blood biochemistry was within normal limits. Her thyroid profile was normal. An echocardiogram revealed no cardiac abnormalities. However, ultrasonography of her abdomen and pelvis revealed infantile atrophic uterus and atrophic left ovary which had led to primary amenorrhea. Karyotyping demonstrated a normal female karyotype. An orthopantomogram carried out during the skeletal survey revealed a chance finding of a well-defined multilocular radiolucency in her right hemi-mandible extending from the midline to the angle region involving almost the entire height of bone. The lesion was seen extending interdentally but without any tooth displacement or root reabsorption. The inferior alveolar nerve canal was not traceable. On clinical examination, there was no paresthesia of her lower lip. Third molars were still in root formation stage. A computed tomography (CT) scan revealed mild buccolingual expansion of the right half of her mandible. A well-demarcated, multilocular lytic lesion was seen with no cortical perforation. No air-fluid levels or enhancing component was seen. A small amount of blood-tinged cystic fluid was aspirated from the lesion.

case_report: A 12-year-old female patient was referred to our retina service due to a decrease in visual acuity in her right eye. She had a history of strabismus, hyperopia, and amblyopia in the right eye. Her mother had undergone surgery for skin cancer and maxillary cysts. The patient had multiple odontogenic cysts and scoliosis and had been previously evaluated in Neuropediatrics for macrocephaly. Her intellectual capacity was normal. Clinical examination showed visual acuity of 20/80 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Anterior segment evaluation showed no abnormalities, and intraocular pressure was normal in both eyes. Fundus examination revealed an elevated lesion in the temporal region of the macula, white-greyish in color, with associated vascular distortion, causing significant traction in the macular area.
test_results: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) scan showed disorganization of the normal retinal layers, a hyperreflective mass with hyporeflective shadowing, and epiretinal membrane, leading to high distortion of the macular region. Fluorescein angiography showed retinal vascular tortuosity with early hyperfluorescence and mild leakage after three minutes of fluorescein injection.
diagnosis: Combined Hamartoma of the Retina and Retinal Pigment Epithelium  in the context of Gorlin Syndrome
Orpha_name: Combined hamartoma of the retina and retinal pigment epithelium

case_report: A 3-year-old girl initially experienced seizures at four months old. These episodes involved hypotonia, eye rolling, and subsequent stiffening on her right side, lasting approximately 15 minutes and occurring every 2–3 weeks. Phenobarbitone was administered as an antiepileptic treatment, but the seizure pattern changed to clusters of hypotonic episodes with right eye fluttering, without achieving seizure freedom. Over the following two years, various antiepileptic medications, including Levetiracetam, Lamotrigine, Clonazepam, Phenytoin, Vigabatrin, and three courses of steroids, were tried without success. At 2.5 years old, she was on a combination of Sodium Valproate, Topiramate, and Clobazam. Her condition worsened, leading to an urgent transfer for presurgical evaluation for epilepsy surgery.
test_results: A video-EEG data recorded from 12 channels revealed continuous epileptiform sharpened activity over the left posterior quadrant. During clinical events the EEG showed fast activity over the left parietal region evolving to widespread sharp and slow waves over the left hemisphere and then evolving over both hemispheres.

case_report: A 60-year-old cachectic male presented with difficulty breathing and a persistent cough. He had a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), bronchiectasis, and bullous emphysema diagnosed about 10 years ago, for which he was treated with long-acting beta agonist, long-acting muscarinic antagonist, and inhaled corticosteroid. The patient had a 20 pack-year smoking history and frequent hospital admissions due to pulmonary tract infections. Physical examination showed decreased breath sounds bilaterally, inspiratory coarse crackles, and finger-clubbing. A chest X-ray revealed right paratracheal lucency, ill-defined opaque areas, reticular dense areas, and cystic lesions mainly in the right middle and lower lung zones. Pulmonary function tests indicated a restrictive and obstructive pattern with a forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) of 2.01 liters (53%), forced vital capacity (FVC) of 2.49 liters (59%), and FEV1/FVC ratio of 88%. Arterial blood gases indicated hypoxemia and hypercapnia with respiratory acidosis (pH 7.30; PaO2 50 mmHg; PaCO2 69 mmHg; HCO3 28.3 mmol/l; SaO2 82%). The patient was started on nasal oxygen at 2 liters/min and non-invasive mechanical ventilation (NIMV) with initial inspiratory and expiratory pressures of 15/5 mmHg, later adjusted to 20/5 mmHg, in ST (spontaneous/timed) mode due to insufficient inspiratory effort. Over the following days, oxygenation improved, showing compensated respiratory acidosis with NIMV (pH 7.38; PaO2 61 mmHg; PaCO2 55 mmHg; HCO3 27.5 mmol/l; SaO2 92%). Flexible bronchoscopy revealed diverticulum orifices on the lateral tracheal wall, tracheal and main stem bronchial enlargement, and expiratory airway collapse. Bronchial brushing was performed on the right upper lobe posterior segment and right lower lobe apical segment, followed by bronchial lavage with n-acetyl cysteine solution. Cytological examination of the collected specimens was negative for malignancy and acid-fast bacilli (AFB) staining. Common bacterial and AFB cultures were also negative.
test_results: This demonstrated abnormally dilated trachea, with bilateral main stem bronchi and two diverticula arising from the intrathoracic trachea. Bilateral cystic bronchiectasis was present predominantly in the right middle and lower lobe and mosaic attenuation was observed in lung fields bilaterally.

case_report: A 32-year-old Iranian man presented with headache and difficulty breathing at Rouhani Hospital. Initial assessment showed a systolic blood pressure of 170/100 mmHg. He had undergone an open appendectomy a week prior, with postoperative systolic blood pressures ranging from 140 to 180 mmHg. During this hospitalization, due to flu-like symptoms (muscle pain, headache, and difficulty breathing), computed tomography (CT) and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests were conducted, revealing a suspicious CT scan and a positive PCR result. An electrocardiogram (ECG) was performed due to his breathing difficulty and high blood pressure, showing diffuse ST-segment elevation, leading to an echocardiography. Further examinations indicated positive serum troponin, an ejection fraction (EF) of about 35%, and thickening of the ventricular wall and papillary muscles. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) showed moderate-to-severe systolic dysfunction and significant diastolic dysfunction in the left ventricle, with no clot detected. Persistent high blood pressure was noted during hospitalization, unresponsive to three medications. The patient also exhibited sweating, a high pulse rate, and abnormal liver function tests. He was treated with anticoagulant (heparin), antiviral therapy (remdesivir), and antibiotics (targocid and meropenem) alongside routine treatments. Four days post-admission, his condition deteriorated, and neurological examination revealed right-sided hemiplegia and dysarthria, though funduscopic examination was normal. His consciousness level gradually decreased, rendering him unable to follow commands or make meaningful eye contact, though he could move his unaffected limbs. Imaging studies (brain CT and MRI scans) indicated ischemic infarction, with some brain CT findings suggestive of cortical vein thrombosis, though brain MRI with contrast, brain images, and MR venography did not confirm this. MRI showed multiple bilateral acute ischemic changes, with more prominent lesions in the right high-parietal cortex, left temporal, and basal ganglia regions. Brain and cervical MR angiography were unremarkable. Intravenous anticoagulant therapy with heparin was initiated, but discontinued after 2 days due to hemorrhagic changes seen on imaging studies. At this stage, his systolic blood pressure was 240 mmHg. Two days later, he regained consciousness, and his weakened limbs began to recover gradually. After 6 days of high blood pressure, episodic headaches, and sustained tachycardia, further evaluations were conducted.
test_results: Urinary metanephrine (MN), normetanephrine (NMN), and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) were collected in a 24-h period and were positive.

case_report: The patient is an 11-year-old male of Caucasian origin, properly vaccinated, and born from a controlled pregnancy and normal delivery. He is the youngest of three siblings, with no family history of the same pathology. His 21-year-old brother has undergone surgery for cholesteatomas, and his 27-year-old brother has spastic paraparesis due to a sporadic mutation of SPG4. The patient presents with acroosteolysis of distal phalanges of feet and hands, generalized osteoporosis, cranial malformations, presence of Wormian bones, coarse facial features, short stature, joint hyperlaxity, recurrent respiratory infections, and musculoskeletal alterations. He was born in April 2011, with a birth weight of 4340 g, height of 54 cm, and head circumference of 36 cm. The mother, aged 44 at the time, had a height of 171.3 cm and a history of gestational diabetes treated with insulin. The father was 45 years old and 173.8 cm tall. Both parents are without relevant pathologies. Maternal grandparents are second cousins. No anomalies were observed at birth. In the first months of life, hypotonia in the lower extremities and a resting posture of the neck in flexion were noted. A delay in the closure of the posterior fontanel, dentition, and language was observed. He started walking at 9 months of age. Short distal phalanges, ribs with keeled deformity, and Wormian bones in the lambdoid suture were identified. No cardiac or auditory issues were detected initially. Growth, weight, and height were good. Physical examinations revealed osteolysis in the distal phalanges of the hands and feet with deformity, shortening of the fourth and fifth metacarpals, slight occipital prominence at the level of the parietal suture, retromicrognatia, and prominent sternum. Other findings included diastasis of the supraumbilical rectum, tubiform thorax, pectus carinatum, genu recurvatum, valgus flatfoot, joint hyperlaxity, generalized cutaneous hyperlaxity (more noticeable in the elbow), mild hypotonia, delay and alterations in dentition, atopic dermatitis, slight hypertrichosis, hard and dry hair, and abnormally populated eyebrows. Additional features included ogival palate, full and slightly drooping cheeks, wide philtrum, ocular proptosis with blue and megalocorneal sclerae. Frequent colds and respiratory infections, such as pneumonia, were noted. Cardiopulmonary and neurological evaluations were normal, as was psychomotor development. At 2 years and 6 months, the weight was 12 kg, height 89.7 cm, and head circumference 50 cm.
test_results: By direct analysis of the NOTCH2 gene, a heterozygous 18-nucleotide deletion (c.6446_6463del) was detected in the sample.

case_report: A 10-year-old girl of Indian origin presented with malformed teeth in the anterior region of both the upper and lower jaws. She is the first child of parents who are not related by blood and have normal development. Her birth was at full term with a normal delivery, and her birth weight was approximately 2.5 kg. There was no history of natal or neonatal teeth. She has a younger brother without any congenital abnormalities. Her medical history includes an atrial septal defect for which she is receiving treatment. Her psychosomatic and mental development are within normal limits. On general physical examination, the patient has a short stature with a height of 110 cm. Examination of the hands and feet showed bilateral postaxial polydactyly. In the right foot, there is polydactyly with syndactyly. The lower limbs are deformed with outward bending of the knees (genu valgum). Nails are hypoplastic, and hair is thin and sparse.
test_results: Intra-oral examination along with panoramic radiography revealed multiple missing teeth (12, 22, 31, 32, 41, 42) in mandibular and maxillary anterior region and a retained mandibular deciduous incisor (81). Maxillary central incisors (12, 21) were malformed and 21 had a deep carious labial fissure. Multiple frenulum and labiogingival frenum hypertrophy were present in maxillary and mandibular anterior region.

case_report: A 2-year-old girl was admitted with severe lymphadenopathies. She had a known condition since birth. No significant infections were noted in the initial years of life until the onset of these unexplained lymphadenopathies. A biopsy was performed, which did not show malignancy. The patient was not seen for follow-up for 8 months but returned later that year with symptoms including cough, fever, and difficulty breathing, necessitating oxygen support. Lymphadenopathies were still present in all regions. There were no signs of liver or spleen enlargement. A chest X-ray revealed mediastinal enlargement and bilateral infiltrates. Cultures from bronchoalveolar lavage were negative for bacteria, including mycobacteria. PCR tests for viruses (CMV, EBV) and mycoplasma were also negative. A routine blood sample showed slight lymphopenia.
test_results: Hypogammaglobulinemia was observed. Antibodies against the received childhood vaccinations (pneumococcus, tetanus, rubella, polio, and hepatitis B) were all negative. Revaccination with Pneumo 23 and tetanus did not lead to an increase in the antibody titers. T cell numbers were low, with a slightly diminished function. The number of CD4+CD25+FoxP3+ regulatory T cells was remarkably low. Switched memory B cells were slightly low according to the Euroclass criteria. The number of double negative T cells, vitamin B12, and Fas mediated apoptosis were normal. The interferon gamma/interleukin 23 pathway was intact. Expression of IL-12 receptor beta 1 and IFN-gamma receptor expression were analysed by flow cytometry. The production of IFN-gamma was measured after stimulation of white blood cells with phytohaemagglutinin and staphylococcal enterotoxin B. HIV screening was negative. Radiosensitivity was mildly increased. A lymph node biopsy showed signs of follicular and interfollicular hyperplasia as well as granulomas. Ziehl-Nielssen staining and IGRA (Interferon Gamma Release Assay) test were negative. PCR for CMV and EBV were negative as were cultures for bacteria. Finally, a culture from the bone marrow became positive for Mycobacterium lentiflavum.
diagnosis: Immunodeficiency in a child with Rapadilino Syndrome

case_report: A 71-year-old male presented with a 3-month history of difficulties in finding words, confusion, and weakness in the left leg. CT head revealed several ill-defined hypodense areas within the right parietal and occipital subcortical white matter. MRI of the brain showed a contrast-enhancing 3.2 cm lesion in the right occipital lobe, a 1.8 cm enhancing lesion in the right precentral gyrus, and multiple smaller enhancing lesions in the right periventricular region, accompanied by vasogenic edema but without mass effect. PET/CT indicated no evidence of systemic malignancy but identified lesions in the right posterior temporal, occipital, and parietal lobes. Susceptibility-weighted angiography (SWAN) imaging revealed a hemorrhagic component in the right occipital lobe lesion.
test_results: A needle core biopsy was obtained of the right occipital lesion. Formal pathology showed an intense inflammatory process comprised foamy macrophages and T-cells with scattered small B-cells. These cells were CD3, CD163, Iba1, and CD68 positive. B cell immunohistochemistry was scantly positive. The T-cell population was found to be composed of more CD4+ than CD8+ cells. A follow-up brain MRI after 1 month demonstrated a decrease in the size of all enhancing lesions. MRI of the total spine was without evidence of disease. CSF studies were unremarkable for autoimmune, bacterial, viral, fungal, parasitic, or inflammatory etiologies. CSF flow cytometry revealed a predominance of CD5+ T cells. Repeat MRI brain off of corticosteroids demonstrated an interval increase in size and conspicuity of all previously observed enhancing lesions. Further histological analysis demonstrated areas of macrophages/lymphocytes with markedly reactive astrocytes that showed quick transition to reactive less inflamed cortex. The lymphocytic population appeared small, but polymorphous, containing scattered plasma cells. There was marked perivascular inflammation but no fibrinoid necrosis. Flow cytometric and immunohistochemical workup failed to demonstrate a definitely clonal lymphocyte population. There was no evidence of demarcated myelin loss or a vasculitic process.
diagnosis: Supratentorial lymphocytic inflammation with parenchymal perivascular enhancement responsive to steroids

case_report: A 40-year-old woman reported a reddish, painless swelling in her left forearm that had been growing over the past three months. Subsequently, she developed multiple nodular swellings across her body. She did not experience fever or weight loss. Upon examination, her overall condition was good. She had multiple erythematous papular lesions and nodular swellings ranging from 1 to 3 cm on both legs, both arms, chest wall, abdomen, back, face, scalp, and ear lobes. Additionally, she had bilateral supraclavicular and left cervical lymphadenopathy measuring 1 cm. There was no enlargement of internal organs. Laboratory results showed hemoglobin at 116 gm/L, total white blood cell count at 9.7 × 10^9/L, platelet count at 236 × 10^9/L, and a peripheral smear revealing 42% blast cells. Renal and liver functions were within normal limits, and serum lactate dehydrogenase was elevated at 2327 U/L. A skin biopsy section revealed diffusely arranged atypical cells that were positive for LCA and negative for CD20 on immunohistochemistry.
test_results: A bone marrow aspiration showed sheets of immature cells with blue vacuolated cytoplasm, round nuclei, and 1-2 nucleoli. The abnormal cells were positive for periodic acid schiff (PAS) and nonspecific esterase (NSE) and negative for peroxidase by cytochemistry. Immunophenotyping by flow cytometry showed the abnormal cells to be positive for the myeloid markers CD33 and CD11c and negative for the myeloid markers CD13, CD14, CD61, CD64, CD117, anti-MPO, and cyCD61. The cells were also positive for the T-cell markers cyCD3, CD4, CD5, and CD7 and negative for the T-cell markers CD3, CD8, CD56, anti-Tdt, TCrgd, TCrab, and CD1a. The cells were negative for all B-cell markers CD10, CD19, CD20, and cyCD79a.
diagnosis: Mixed Phenotypic Acute Leukemia  of T/myeloid with monocytic differentiation lineage

case_report: A 14-year-old male patient presented with generalized weakness and intermittent high-grade fever for 6 months. On examination, he appeared well, was afebrile, and had pallor without mucocutaneous bleeding. There was no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. His complete blood counts (CBC) showed a hemoglobin (Hb) of 8.7 g/dl, total leucocyte count (TLC) of 1.5 × 10^9/L, and a platelet count of 38 × 10^9/L. Red cell indices revealed a hematocrit of 25.2%, mean corpuscular volume of 102.5 fl, mean corpuscular Hb of 35.3 pg, and mean corpuscular Hb concentration of 34.4 g/dl. Bone marrow examination was performed, and the marrow aspirate smears were hemodilute and pauci-particulate with very few marrow cell trails showing the presence of blast cells, mature monocytes, and cells with promonocytoid features (~10%, ~13%, and ~4% of the evaluable marrow cells, respectively). Erythroid cells exhibited megaloblastic erythropoiesis with dyserythropoiesis. There was a prominence of macrophages with hemophagocytosis. The blast cells were negative for myeloperoxidase (MPO) cytochemical staining. Bone marrow trephine biopsy was suboptimal and insufficient for opinion. Flowcytometric immunophenotyping (FCIM) was suggested for further evaluation. The patient's clinical course was uneventful except for an acute onset submandibular swelling that subsided with antibiotic therapy. Subsequent CBC after 2 weeks showed persistent pancytopenia with Hb of 10.2 g/dl, TLC of 2.3 × 10^9/L, and 21 × 10^9/L platelets. Marrow aspirate smears at this time showed hypocellular marrow cell trails with myelogram comprising 18% blasts, 10% promonocytes, 4% monocytes, 10% polymorphs, 1% metamyelocytes, 3% eosinophils, 42% lymphocytes, 4% plasma cells, and 8% erythroid precursor cells. Conventional cytogenetics revealed a normal karyotype. At subsequent presentation, the patient was maintained except for worsening anemia and thrombocytopenia, without bleeding or new clinical findings. After 3 months, he presented with high-grade fever and bone pains and consented for admission. CBC showed 6.6 g/dl Hb, 0.8 × 10^9/L leucocytes, and 3 × 10^9/L platelets. Bone marrow aspirate revealed hypocellular particles with ~68% blasts and promonocytes. ~3% blast cells showed MPO positivity. The 6-color FCIM (FACS Canto II, BD Biosciences) on bone marrow revealed significant replacement by a prominent cell population with variable CD45 expression. This abnormal cluster spanned from the blast region into the monocyte position with the bulk of the neoplastic cells falling into the medium cell size range. A small number of lymphocytes, few residual myeloid precursors, and maturing monocytic elements were also present. The leukemic cells comprised ~45% of the cells in the sample and showed homogeneously bright expression of CD33, variable expression of CD13, CD34, and displayed a complex pattern of CD14/CD64 co-expression, indicating monocytic maturation. These blast cells also showed heterogeneous expression of CD11b, CD15, CD4, and bright HLA DR. The maturing monocytic elements (comprising ~3% of cells in the sample) showed normal expression of brighter CD33, CD16, CD13, HLA DR, and CD11b.
test_results: Stress cytogenetics showed 88% chromosome breaks and rearrangements in patient's peripheral lymphocytes with mitomycin C (MMC).

case_report: A 65-year-old Asian woman was admitted to our clinic in August 2019 with symptoms including fever (38.3–39 °C), chest tightness, productive cough, and shortness of breath for one day. Her medical history includes long-term leukopenia and a previous diagnosis of MDS in 2014, for which she received supportive treatments. In 2019, she was hospitalized due to increased bone marrow blasts (10% vs 4%) and decreased megakaryocytes with small round separated nuclei. She underwent four courses of amifostine without symptom improvement. During her hospital stay, she experienced recurrent pneumonia, which was temporarily alleviated by multiple antibiotic treatments. She was administered voriconazole after her last course in July 2019. Two months later, she presented again with fever and pneumonia. Upon admission, she exhibited fever and chest pain. Blood cell count revealed lymphocytopenia and monocytopenia, with a white blood cell (WBC) count of 1800 cells/mm3, a low monocyte count of 0–0.1 cells/mm3, hemoglobin level of 7.6 g/dL, and platelet count of 17 × 10^9/L. The absolute count of B cells (CD19+) was 6×10^6/L (normal range: 50–670×10^6/L), NK cells (CD3-/CD16+56+) was 34×10^6/L (normal range: 40–1000×10^6/L), CD4+ T-cell count was 141 cells/mm3, and the CD4/CD8 ratio was 0.99. She also had splenomegaly (4.1 cm in size) and iron overload (ferritin: 2361.4 ng/mL). Tests for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-DNA and cytomegalovirus (CMV)-DNA were negative. Based on lung computed tomography (CT) scan findings, she was treated with tigecycline, ceftazidime, and voriconazole. Klebsiella pneumoniae infection was confirmed by sputum culture analysis, leading to subsequent treatments with caspofungin, posaconazole, cefoperazone, linezolid, ganciclovir, sulfamethoxazole, amphotericin B, and polymyxin. Despite these treatments, her fever and pneumonia did not significantly improve. She developed chest tightness and dyspnea, requiring continuous high-flow oxygen inhalation, and was unable to undergo bronchoscopy. Complicated by severe infection, she also developed acute heart failure. Eventually, M. kansasii infection was confirmed through sequencing of her peripheral blood specimens. She was then treated with antibiotics including ethambutol, rifabutin, and clarithromycin. Her condition significantly improved within two weeks of therapy, with a notable decrease in C-reactive protein (CRP) levels from 250.87 mg/L to near normal.
test_results: The next-generation sequencing (NGS, peripheral blood) found a heterozygous mutation in GATA2 (exon6:c.1126_1128del:p.K376del) along with U2AF1 (exon2:c.C101T:p.S34F), SETBP1 (exon4, cG2602A:pD868N, exon4:cG2608A:pG870S), ASXL1 (exon12:c.G2548T:p.E850X) as well as KMT2D, BRAF, EPPK1, and ETV6.

case_report: The patient is a 7-month-old male born to nonconsanguineous parents of Chinese Han ancestry. He was delivered at 38+2 weeks via cesarean section to a gravida 2 para 2 woman, with a birth weight of 3300 g. At 10 days old, he underwent phototherapy for neonatal jaundice. Otoacoustic emissions testing showed abnormal binaural hearing. Echocardiography identified a patent foramen ovale and tricuspid regurgitation. At 7 months, his height was 66.5 cm (−1 SD), weight was 7.8 kg (−1 SD), and head circumference was 46.5 cm (+1.5 SD). Facial features included increased interocular distance, low set ears, a protruding nose, a sharp chin, and an inverted triangular face. Limb tension was noted to be high, approximately level 1+. The patient exhibited delayed movement and developmental milestones. In a supine position, his posture was asymmetric, and he was unable to turn over. In a prone position, there was no displacement or straightening posture. Head control was poor, with evident head lag. The patient could stand briefly. The Gesell adaptive behavior development quotient (DQ) scores were as follows: adaptive behavior DQ 47, grand motor DQ 23, fine motor DQ 52, language DQ 45, and personal social behavior DQ 41.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed enlargement of the bilateral lateral ventricles and the third ventricle, with the frontal horn of the bilateral lateral ventricles and the anterior part of the body obviously deformed. The corpus callosum was slightly thin.

case_report: A 6-year-old boy was brought to our hospital due to short stature and developmental delay. He was born at full term (40 weeks) via normal delivery to non-consanguineous parents, with a birth weight of 3,130 grams (25th percentile). He is the second child in the family, and his older sister has normal development. The boy exhibited delays in speech and motor skills, beginning to walk at 20 months. He engaged in cooperative play with peers. At age 5, he received speech therapy for dysarthria. At age 6, he demonstrated borderline intellectual disability with a total intelligence quotient of 70 and a social quotient of 97, indicating near-normal social functioning. Psychological assessments noted mild hyperactivity and attention deficits, but his behavior did not align with the criteria for autistic disorder. Physical examination at 6 years and 6 months revealed short stature (109.3 cm, less than 3rd percentile), macrodontia of permanent teeth, and craniofacial features such as a triangular face, prominent forehead, epicanthal folds, anteverted nostrils, broad mouth, and prominent ears. Brain MRI results were normal. Bone X-ray findings included narrowing and elongation of both iliac wings and body, small femoral heads, small distal tibial epiphyses, tibiotalar slanting, and delayed bone age. Electroencephalographic analysis showed partial seizure activity, although no clinical seizures were observed. Chromosome analysis using Giemsa/trypsin/Leishman banding for the patient and his parents revealed a normal karyotype at the 550-band level.
test_results: Whole-genome high-resolution oligonucleotide array CGH detected a heterozygous 240-kb deletion at 16q24.3 (arr[hg19] 16q24.3(89,349,966-89,593,853)x1). Array CGH analysis of parental DNA samples by using the same platform showed no deletion or gain in the 16q24.3 region. Neither the proband nor the parents had a deletion or gain in any other region. This deletion covered ANKRD11 (including exons 2-13) and part of spastic paraplegia 7 gene (SPG7; including exons 1-5).

case_report: A female patient in her 50s (age: 50 years; weight: 54 kg; height: 174 cm) had a history of dietary management until the age of 14, after which dietary restrictions were lifted and no supplements were taken. She was consuming a normal diet without protein restriction. The patient presented at the neurological clinic with symptoms including dysarthria, pyramidal signs, intention tremor, a pathological leg-extension test, and a spastic-ataxic gait pattern. Additionally, marked ataxia was observed during the finger–nose test and heel–shin test. Sensory evoked potentials were not elicited, while electroneurography showed no signs of polyneuropathy, and MRI of the spinal cord appeared normal. Cranial MRI (fluid-attenuated inversion recovery; FLAIR) revealed periventricular white matter lesions.
test_results: Laboratory blood test results showed elevated concentrations of ornithine (204 µmol/L; 2.7 mg/dL), Phe (1816 µmol/L; 30 mg/dL) and a nutritional deficiency (vitamin D and vitamin B12).

case_report: Patient 2 is an 11-year-old boy, the second child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents. There is no family history of bone fragility or autism. He was born in the breech position at 32 weeks gestation following a pregnancy complicated by placental abruption, which caused severe abdominal pain and heavy bleeding. At birth, he weighed 1.76 kg (9th percentile) and required continuous positive airway pressure for 24 hours and phototherapy for neonatal jaundice. He was fed via a nasogastric tube for the first week of life. Throughout childhood, he failed to thrive, with height and weight below the 0.4th percentile and head circumference between the 0.4th and 2nd percentiles. Insufficient weight gain led to the insertion of a percutaneous gastrostomy for nutritional support.
