He experienced frequent infections, including bronchiolitis, pneumonia, and urinary tract infections. A micturating cystourethrogram identified bilateral vesicoureteric reflux. He consistently had hypogammaglobulinemia and lymphopenia with poor vaccine responses and received 3-weekly immunoglobulin replacement therapy. Additionally, he had bilateral optic atrophy and consistently abnormal liver function tests. The patient had severe intellectual disability, delayed speech, and gross and fine motor delays, first walking at 19 months. He exhibited significant echolalia and restricted interests and was clinically diagnosed with ASD at 6 years of age. He suffered multiple fractures of the vertebrae, metatarsals, and tibias. A bone biopsy at 7 years of age showed a high rate of bone turnover and osteopenia with marked subperiosteal bone resorption. DXA scans indicated reduced bone mineral density, although the degree of reduction was difficult to determine due to his small size. He received 3-monthly pamidronate infusions. The patient underwent numerous investigations throughout his life to understand his clinical features.
test_results: Trio WES identified that patient 2 is compound heterozygous for c.3010C>T and c.5741G>A pathogenic mutations in the NBAS gene.

case_report: A 16-year-old male patient, born at 35 weeks gestation after an uncomplicated pregnancy, presented with a head circumference of 31 cm, birth weight of 2560 g, and birth length of 45 cm. Early childhood development included axial hypotonia and increased tone in all four limbs, along with global developmental delay. Cognitive assessment indicated a borderline IQ. Behavioral issues such as aggressiveness and fits of anger were noted. The patient was of short stature, with height below the 3rd percentile. He experienced intermittent headaches and recurrent dizziness. A skull MRI at age 9 showed chronic sinusitis sphenoidalis with no other abnormalities. Ophthalmologic examination revealed strabismus and hypermetropia. Neurological examination identified symptoms of a complex movement disorder, including spasticity, slight ataxia, intermittent dystonia, and stereotypies. A video recording demonstrated these movement disorders. At the time of the recording, the patient's head circumference was 54 cm, body weight was 49.2 kg, and body length was 162.6 cm (February 1, 2023). Due to partial pituitary dysfunction, growth hormone therapy was initiated at age 10, to which the patient responded well. The patient is the only affected member in his family, which includes three unaffected siblings: two sisters and one brother.
test_results: Genetic studies were conducted according to a protocol approved by the Hungarian National Public Health Center. The patient and his parents underwent pre- and post-test genetic counseling at the Department of Medical Genetics, University of Szeged.
Orpha_name: Infantile hypotonia-oculomotor anomalies-hyperkinetic movements-developmental delay syndrome

case_report: A 14-month-old female infant was admitted to our clinic for further evaluation of her condition. She was born by elective cesarean section at 36 weeks gestational age following an uncomplicated pregnancy. Her Apgar score was 9–10. At birth, she weighed 3360 g, had a head circumference of 34 cm, and a height of 51 cm. She is the first child of non-consanguineous parents, with her mother having had two previous pregnancies that ended in abortion. The family has a middle-class income, with the father working in the rubber industry and the mother being a housewife. At the time of birth, the mother was 25 years old and the father was 29 years old. There is no familial history of hereditary or metabolic diseases in the previous two generations. The infant's growth was normal, and she reached developmental milestones until the age of 2 months. At 2 months, her parents noticed she was unable to hold her neck and gradually became lethargic. At 3 months, she experienced her first episodes of generalized tonic-clonic seizures, characterized by stiffening and rhythmic jerks in her bilateral limbs, lasting approximately 3 minutes with impaired awareness. Different dosages of sodium valproate, ranging from 20 to 30 mg, were ineffective in completely controlling the seizures. At 14 months, the child was referred to our clinic due to the absence of neck holding and frequent intractable seizures. Upon admission, physical examination revealed macrocephaly with a head circumference of 47.2 cm, height of 78 cm, and weight of 10 kg; setting sun eyes; tremor; and hypotonia. Funduscopic examination showed optic atrophy. Other cranial and peripheral nerve examinations were normal. The face was symmetric with no facial dysmorphic features. A flash visual evoked potential (FVEP), brain MRI, and electroencephalography (EEG) were ordered. The FVEP revealed bilateral abnormal P100 latencies and no obvious waves in both eyes, indicating total blindness. Brain MRI showed diffuse white matter T2 hyper-intensity and T1 hypo-intensity in the periventricular, juxtacortical, and subcortical white matter, with involvement of the posterior brain stem, putamen, bilateral thalami, and cerebellum white matter. Prominent Virchow–Robin Spaces (VRS) were also observed. EEG demonstrated diffuse slow and sharp waves.
test_results: The homozygous c.914C>A (p.Ala305Glu) variant in the ASPA gene was found.

case_report: A 79-year-old white male from Alagoas reported a two-month history of multiple asymptomatic red papules spread across the skin. Dermatological examination revealed symmetrically distributed erythematous papules, with some forming clusters, predominantly on the back and limbs. The scalp, mucous membranes, palms, and soles were unaffected. The patient exhibited no systemic symptoms, and the sensitivity of the lesions remained intact. Laboratory tests for syphilis and leprosy returned negative results.
test_results: Skin biopsy showed dense mononuclear dermal infiltrate without atypia, occupying the entire dermis, and perivascular lymphocyte clusters on the superficial dermis. Wade staining was negative. The immunohistochemical examination was positive only for CD68 and negative for CD1a, CD34 and S100.

case_report: The patient, a 12-year-old boy, the only child of healthy unrelated parents, was referred to the developmental behavior department of Shanghai Children’s Medical Center due to delayed development and growth. He was delivered via cesarean section at term with a birth weight of 2.2 kg. The boy exhibited a purple coloration after birth which improved with stimulation, but he experienced feeding difficulties, leading to admission to the neonatal intensive care unit for weight management. Feeding difficulties and developmental delays were noted during infancy. He achieved sitting at 10 months, walking at 18 months, and speaking his first sentences at 2 years old. Growth delay persisted, with a current weight of 31.5 kg (P3–10), height of 146.8 cm (P10–25), body mass index of 14.62 kg/m2 (P3–5), and occipitofrontal circumference of 52 cm (−0.14SD) according to Chinese domestic data. Mild clinodactyly of both hands and abnormal facial features, including wide-spaced eyes, a prominent nasal bridge continuing to the forehead, abnormal teething, and micrognathia, were observed. There was no history of seizures. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), EEG, chest and spine X-rays, echocardiography, and abdominal ultrasound were normal. Molecular karyotyping was also normal.
test_results: An insertion variant c.4029_4030insAA leading to frameshift mutation (p.Glu1344Lysfs*49) on NSD2 was detected. The truncating variant has been confirmed as de novo variants in the proband.

case_report: A 70-year-old white female with a 2-week history of vertigo, nausea, and bilious vomiting presented to the emergency room after experiencing 2 days of bloody diarrhea and diffuse abdominal pain, totaling 12 episodes of diarrhea. The patient reported fevers, chills, fatigue, poor oral intake, and weight loss, with no precipitating or relieving factors. She denied recent travel, sick contacts, pets, raw foods, seafood exposure, antibiotic use, coffee ground emesis, hematemesis, or tenesmus. Her medical history included hyperlipidemia, lactose intolerance, and irritable bowel syndrome with a normal colonoscopy three years prior. There was no history of colon cancer. Upon admission, the patient was afebrile at 37.1°C; pulse rate was 117 beats per minute; respirations were 26 breaths per minute; and blood pressure was 171/96. She appeared to be in some discomfort. Cardiac examination revealed sinus tachycardia without a murmur. Abdominal examination showed mild distention with diffuse tenderness and decreased bowel sounds. There was no peripheral edema. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 18,700/μL with 83% segmented neutrophils; hemoglobin of 15.9 g/dL with a mean cell volume of 91.3 fL; and platelet count of 206,000/μL. Blood chemistry revealed normal creatinine and liver function tests except for an indirect bilirubin of 1.5 mg/dL and AST of 75 U/L. LDH was elevated at 961 IU/L. Lactic acid level and lipase were within normal limits. Urine was concentrated and revealed ketones. CT scan demonstrated acute colitis in the ascending and partial transverse colon. The patient was admitted and started on ciprofloxacin and metronidazole. Blood and stool cultures were obtained. She was placed on omeprazole for gastrointestinal prophylaxis. On hospital day 2, a colonoscopy revealed multiple diverticuli, mucosal edema with friability, and ulceration from the transverse colon to the sigmoid colon. The colonoscopy was not advanced beyond the transverse colon due to patient discomfort. Random colon biopsies were obtained. Metronidazole was changed from intravenous to parental, and clear liquids were started in the morning. Colonic biopsies were consistent with ischemic colitis. CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis showed no evidence of mesenteric arterial insufficiency and improvement in wall thickening in the right and transverse colon compared to the initial CT. Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies (ASCA), antinuclear antibody (ANA), myeloperoxidase (MPO), and stool studies were negative. Stool studies were also negative for E. Coli 0157:H7, Clostridium difficile, Salmonella, Yersinia, and Campylobacter. The patient continued to improve, and her bloody diarrhea resolved. On hospital day 3, the platelet count was 76,000/μL with hemoglobin of 12.4 g/dL. On hospital day 7, the platelet count was 39,000/μL with hemoglobin of 7.8 g/dL. Neurological examination was unremarkable. Hematology consultation was obtained due to thrombocytopenia.
test_results: Schistocytes were observed on the peripheral smear and bone marrow biopsy.

case_report: A 46-year-old male from Cape Verde with a history of asthma and occupational exposure to paints and solvents presented to the emergency department with complaints of progressive shortness of breath, night sweats, fever, dry cough, and unquantified weight loss over the past year. He uses an inhaled steroid-long acting bronchodilator (ICS-LABA) daily. On examination, he was tachypneic with an oxygen saturation of 94% on room air, sweating, and febrile. Pulmonary auscultation revealed diminished breath sounds and scattered crackles. Laboratory results showed hemoglobin at 11.6 g/dL, elevated inflammatory markers with C-reactive protein at 21 mg/dL, and leukocytosis with eosinophilia at 37.4%. Viral serology and direct sputum examination did not isolate any organisms. Arterial blood gas (FiO2 21%) indicated hypoxemia with a pO2 of 62 mmHg. Lung radiography revealed bilateral opacities at the periphery of the lung fields.
test_results: The computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest revealed extensive ground-glass opacification of the lung parenchyma and consolidation with air bronchogram, bilateral and plurilobar, without cavitations. The CT also showed evidence of irregular bronchial dilatations associated with established fibrosis. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BAL) showed an eosinophilic alveolitis (total cell count of 139/mm3, with 51% eosinophils and a CD4/CD8 ratio of 1:1). Histology of the transbronchial biopsy specimen (left upper lobe) revealed a flap of loose connective tissue with scattered epithelial cells.

case_report: A 6-month-old male was referred to the Pediatric Clinic at Policlinico-Vittorio Emanuele hospital in Catania, Italy, due to drug-resistant seizures. He is the second child of healthy, unrelated Italian parents. The mother was 34 years old and the father 38 years old at the time of gestation. The patient's 3-year-old sister is healthy. Normal fetal movements were reported during gestation. At 6 months of gestation, intrauterine ultrasound revealed ventriculomegaly, absence of the corpus callosum, and intrauterine growth restriction. The mother reported no infections or substance use during pregnancy. The boy was born at 37 weeks of gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery. Birth measurements were 1800 g in weight, 45 cm in length, and 32 cm in head circumference. Apgar scores were 5 at 1 minute and 8 at 5 minutes. Post-birth, he was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit in another city hospital for facial dimorphisms, cerebral malformation, low weight, and episodes of cyanosis and bradycardia. Treatment was initiated for respiratory distress and poor feeding. During a 26-day hospitalization, various laboratory tests and genetic analyses were conducted. Routine lab results showed mild metabolic acidosis, which was corrected. No abnormal movements were noted from birth to 4 months of age, when daily episodes of slow tonic movements in the upper limbs began. General hypotonia and developmental delays, including difficulty maintaining head control and persistent slow upper limb movements, were observed by the general pediatrician. Despite these issues, the baby showed good growth improvement during this period.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed severe LIS consisting of wide-spread agyria and restricted areas of pachygyria. The EEG showed poorly organized background and the presence of spikes, mainly in the temporo–central–occipital regions. At US, colpocephaly and absence of normal cortical gyration with simplified sulci and cerebral scissors were noticed.

case_report: A 41-year-old man was referred for cardiology consultation for assessment of dextrocardia. His medical history included recurrent pneumonia during childhood and normal growth, with no cardiovascular symptoms. Physical examination revealed he was in good general condition, with clear lungs and no cardiac murmur. An ECG indicated right axis deviation without signs of right ventricular hypertrophy. Chest X-ray showed pronounced dextrocardia. Echocardiography revealed normal size and contractility of cardiac chambers, hypoplasia of the right pulmonary artery, and no signs of pulmonary hypertension or intracardiac shunt.
test_results: Computed tomography demonstrated a cardiac dextroposition, hypoplasia of the right lung and right pulmonary artery, an anomalous venous drainage of the right lung to the subphrenic inferior vena cava and aortopulmonary collateral artery.

case_report: An 18-year-old female presented with facial asymmetry that had progressively worsened over the past 5 years. She has been taking carbamazepine since the age of 4 due to childhood seizures. Physical examination revealed diffuse papulo-nodular lesions on her face and two skin macules with ragged borders on the right side of her back. The patient experienced complete hearing loss in her right ear at age 15. There is no family history of similar conditions, and her seven siblings do not exhibit any related issues. Vision test results were normal, and she reported a normal puberty process.
test_results: Review of her system showed facial asymmetry was related to poly-ostotic fibrous dysplasia after 3-dimensional computed tomography (CT). Diagnosis of sebaceous adenoma was confirmed after excisional biopsy of facial lesions. Making diagnosis of fibrous dysplasia in most cases achieved with plain radiographs and confirmed after microscopic evaluation. A 'Chinese letter' appearance in histopathology and ground glass pattern in radiography led to diagnosis of fibrous dysplasia.

case_report: A 3-year-old boy presented with a high-grade fever and jaundice. The fever had been present for 7 days, followed by the appearance of jaundice and dark urine 2 days later, which resolved after 3 days. According to the parents, there was no history of hepatotoxic drug use or maculopapular rash. On physical examination, the boy had a body temperature of 39°C and desquamation on the tips of his fingers and toes. Eye examination revealed bilateral bulbar conjunctival injection. Abdominal examination showed no hepatosplenomegaly or tenderness. Abdominal ultrasonography confirmed the absence of hepatosplenomegaly, with normal echogenicity, gallbladder, and bile ducts, and no ascites was detected. Laboratory tests indicated elevated ESR, CRP, and liver transaminases, along with hyperbilirubinemia. There were no serologic findings indicative of viral hepatitis.
test_results: Echocardiography findings were normal.

case_report: A 35-year-old male, nonsmoker, asymptomatic, with no prior history of lung diseases had a routine chest radiograph that revealed alterations. His past medical history was unremarkable, with no occupational exposures or significant family history. Physical examination showed no abnormalities. Chest X-ray indicated a diffuse and bilateral micronodular infiltrate. Serum levels of neoplastic markers and angiotensin converting enzyme were within normal limits. Pulmonary function tests were normal. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage, brushing, and transbronchial biopsies did not yield diagnostic results. High-resolution chest computed tomography (CT) scan displayed multiple, bilateral small pulmonary nodules (less than 10 mm in diameter) distributed across all pulmonary lobes and adjacent to bronchioles and medium/small vessels. There were no enlarged lymph nodes, pleural effusion, or other significant pulmonary changes. Abdominal and pelvic CT scans showed no malignant lesions. Radiological skeletal study indicated no bone involvement.
test_results: Histological examination of the nodules revealed epithelioid cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and intracytoplasmic vacuolization. The tumor cells were immunoreactive to CD34 and negative for cytokeratin.

case_report: A 17-year-old female, born from a non-consanguineous marriage, visited the dermatology outpatient department with a history of skin and joint laxity. She reported frequent bruising and gaping wounds from minor trauma, but no major hemorrhagic incidents. She was born full-term via normal delivery with no neonatal or perinatal complications. There were no similar complaints in her family history, including parents and siblings. Physical examination revealed soft, velvety, and hyperextensible skin with normal recoil. Atrophic scars resembling cigarette paper were observed on the forehead, cheeks, forearms, elbows, knees, and shins. The joints exhibited hypermobility, genu recurvatum of the knees, and hallux valgus deformity of both great toes. Gorlin's sign and reverse Namaskar sign were present. There was no evidence of ecchymosis, cyanosis, digital clubbing, jaundice, or lymphadenopathy. Fundus examination, routine blood tests, urine analysis, coagulogram, blood urea, blood sugar levels, and echocardiogram results were all within normal limits. X-rays of the spine and knee joints were normal, except for the feet, which showed hallux valgus deformity.
test_results: Histopathology with special stain for collagen and elastic fibers showed a decrease in collagen fibers with the relative increase in elastic fibers.

case_report: An 18-year-old female began experiencing twisting postures in her feet and a tip-toe gait at the age of five. These symptoms progressively worsened and extended to her neck, trunk, and limbs. Two years after the onset, she lost the ability to walk and became reliant on a wheelchair. Her perinatal history was normal, and her early development showed no abnormalities. There was no family history of similar symptoms and no known exposure to heavy metals. She had a history of iron-deficiency anemia and menorrhagia, with symptom exacerbation noted before menstruation. Neurological examination identified dysarthria and generalized dystonia affecting the face, neck, trunk, and limbs. She exhibited an open-mouthed dystonic smile and slow, writhing movements of her limbs. Deep tendon reflexes were brisk, and plantar reflexes were absent due to dystonia. Her score on the Unified Dystonia Rating Scale (UDRS; maximum score, 112) was 81. Cognitive and ophthalmic examinations, as well as sensory evaluations, were normal.
test_results: She underwent a brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at the age of seven, which showed T1 hyperintensities in the basal ganglia, brainstem, cerebellum, white matter bilaterally, and pituitary gland. At the age of 18, MRI scans performed in our hospital demonstrated a greater prominence of T1 hyperintensities. She was tested for serum Mn and the level was elevated at 222.9 µg/L (normal range < 8.0 µg/L). Reanalysis of WES data revealed compound heterozygous mutations in the N-terminal region (c.367C>T, p.Q123*) and the first transmembrane domain (c.512G>A, p.G171E) of the SLC39A14 gene (NM_015359.4, NP_056174.2). This was confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

case_report: A 54-year-old male with a history of trauma and multiple retinal surgeries in the left eye reported experiencing pain and reduced vision in the right eye for the past three months. He had undergone antituberculosis therapy for pulmonary tuberculosis 20 years ago. On examination, his best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) in the right eye was counting fingers close to the face. The left eye was noted to be phthisical. Slit lamp examination of the right eye revealed medium-sized keratic precipitates and a 2+ anterior chamber reaction. Fundus examination showed vitritis, disc hyperemia, peripapillary retinal elevation, a choroidal scar in the posterior pole, and numerous subretinal lesions, some of which were coalescing and resembling retinal necrosis. Ultrasonography indicated no significant choroidal thickening (1.6 mm). Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, peripheral blood smear, ELISA for HIV, antinuclear antibodies, serum angiotensin-converting enzyme, toxoplasmosis, VDRL, TPHA, Quantiferon TB gold test, liver function tests, serum creatinine, random blood sugars, and routine urine analysis, were all negative. Chest radiology revealed collapse of the left lung due to previous pulmonary tuberculosis. Three consecutive sputum samples tested negative for acid-fast bacilli (AFB).
test_results: Fluorescein angiography showed disc leakage, multiple hyperfluorescent lesions in the mid and late phases and vascular wall staining. The large coalescent lesions showed staining in late phases. ICG showed multiple, hypointense choroidal lesions. Spectral OCT showed intraretinal and outer retinal hyper reflective lesions. RPE undulations were seen. Cytology showed few lymphocytes and macrophages.

case_report: A 6-month-old Chinese male child was admitted with recurring episodes of low blood sugar for 6 months. His parents were healthy, not related by blood, and his family history was unremarkable. The child was first admitted to the hospital at 2 days old due to repeated cyanosis and poor reaction. His blood glucose level was 0.3 mmol/L, and he recovered after receiving glucose and glucocorticoid infusion. At 22 days old, after fasting for 4 hours for an MRI examination, he appeared pale, had a poor reaction, and reduced muscle strength. His blood glucose was 2.06 mmol/L, and he recovered after glucose infusion. Subsequently, the child showed increased muscle tension and delayed movement. At 4 months old, he experienced repeated vomiting and diarrhea for one day, and low blood sugar reappeared (blood glucose, 4 mmol/L). He also had a convulsion lasting 2–3 minutes. After intravenous glucose infusion, his blood glucose returned to normal. At 6 months old, he was admitted for a systematic examination. Physical examination showed a body weight of 6600 g (3rd percentile); body length, 76.0 cm (97th percentile); head circumference, 41.0 cm (3rd percentile); chest circumference, 43.0 cm (50th percentile). He was conscious with good mental reaction, nutrition levels, and skin elasticity. He had strabismus in both eyes, more prominent in the left eye. He was unable to use his elbows to get up from a reclining position, and when standing upright, his head tilted to one side. He could not turn over or bear his weight, leaned forward fully in the sitting position, and flexed his legs in the standing position. He was not actively conscious of grasping objects but could hold objects without changing them between hands. He could pronounce vowels but was insensitive to locating sources of sound or light. He had normal muscular strength in both upper limbs, but greater muscular strength in both lower limbs, mainly in the adductor muscles. The testes were not completely lowered into the scrotum, and the transillumination test was negative. Laboratory tests, including blood routine (platelet count, 435 × 10^9/L; hemoglobin, 107 g/L), thyroid function, biochemical tests, stool and urine routine, and blood lactic acid, were normal. A fasting test was conducted for 4 hours, and the results showed that both insulin and cortisol were within the normal range. Brain CT indicated scattered low-density shadows in the brain parenchyma and plump bilateral ventricles. Brain MRI indicated extensive abnormal signals in both cerebral hemispheres, suggestive of atrophic cystic changes caused by encephalomalacia. EEG showed multiple spikes/sharp-slow waves in the left and right occipital regions during both waking and sleep, with a 2–3 Hz increase in δ activity in the occipital region, and the dominant rhythm of the occipital region was not significant in the waking state. Echocardiography indicated patent ductus arteriosus. The Gesell Developmental Schedules showed that the gross motor skills of the patient at 4 weeks and 3 months were equivalent to those of neonates at 0 months, and the fine motor skills were equivalent to those of neonates at 0–1 month. The Gesell Intelligence Scale showed that the ability to respond to people and the environment was equivalent to that of infants at 6 weeks (Developmental Quotient [DQ] = 35 points), while the ability to respond to physical objects was equivalent to that of infants at 3 weeks (DQ = 18 points). Additionally, the patient’s gross motor skills were equivalent to that of infants at 0 weeks (DQ = 0 points); his fine motor skills were equivalent to that of infants at 2 weeks (DQ = 12 points), and the ability to communicate was equivalent to that of infants at 6 weeks (DQ = 35 points).
test_results: The results revealed the heterozygous intron mutation c.1070 + 3A > G (splicing) in the coding region of the COG1 gene that was inherited from the mother, and the heterozygous mutation c.2492 g > A (p. Arg831Gln) in exon 10 of the COG1 gene that was inherited from the father.
diagnosis: Component of oligomeric Golgi complex 1  deficiency leading to Congenital Disorder of Glycosylation type IIg

case_report: A five-year-old male child, born to non-consanguineous parents, presented with increased work of breathing and fatigue for 15 days, along with a sudden onset of palpitations and difficulty in breathing for two days. The patient had a history of a three-day stay in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) due to respiratory distress, during which he received continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) and oxygen therapy. The patient exhibited significant skeletal abnormalities in the upper limbs and underlying cardiac anomalies. He was managed accordingly and advised to follow up. His developmental history was normal, and his intelligence and scholastic performance were good. There was no significant family history of similar skeletal anomalies or heart disease. On examination, the patient was conscious, anxious, breathless, afebrile, with a heart rate of 190 beats per minute, a respiratory rate of 28 per minute with increased work of breathing, spO2 of 92 percent with oxygen, well-felt peripheral pulses, and blood pressure of 94/68 mm Hg, with no cyanosis. Skeletal examination revealed abnormal shortening and deformity in the upper limbs. The right arm measured 6 cm and was shorter than the left arm, which was 4.5 cm longer and had flexion deformity and abnormalities of the thumb and fingers in both hands. Both hands were incurved and pronated with discrepancies in bulk, posture, and digital shortening with radialization of the thumb. Cardiovascular examination showed the apex beat in the fifth intercostal space, no thrill or diastolic shock, tachycardia, and a grade 3 ejection systolic murmur in the pulmonary area. Respiratory system examination revealed bilateral equal air entry and a clear chest. Abdominal examination showed a soft abdomen with non-palpable liver and spleen. Laboratory investigations revealed Hb 12.5 gm, total leucocyte count 12000/cumm, platelet count 2.5 lakhs, SGOT 44 IU/L, SGPT 42 IU/L, ALP 112 IU/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dl, serum creatinine 0.8 mg/dl, urea 22 mg/dl, serum sodium 138 meq/l, and potassium 4.1 meq/l. The patient was stabilized with intravenous fluids, oxygenation, respiratory support, and started on frusemide and dobutamine.
test_results: ECG was done showing HR of 190 beats per minute with the absence of p-wave suggestive of supraventricular tachycardia. X-ray of the upper limb was done, which was showing a bilateral absence of radius, and hypoplastic humerus on the right side along with metacarpal abnormalities of the hands. Chest X-ray was done showing multiple small opacities present on right perihilar with mild pneumonitis. 2D echocardiography was showing ASD 7 mm with bilateral flow through the defect with dilatation of the right atrium without pulmonary hypertension. No other structural cardiac anomalies were found on the echo.

case_report: A 41-year-old male reported experiencing decreased vision, haloes, and visual distortion for the past 13 years. His brother had similar visual issues. The patient's best corrected visual acuity, with +0.50 DS / -4.50 DC ×100, was 6 / 36 in the right eye, and, with +0.50 DS / -4.00 DC ×80, was 6 / 15 in the left eye. Examination of the anterior segment was normal.
test_results: Indirect ophthalmoscopy revealed vitreous floaters, macular schisis, and diffuse RPE alterations in both eyes. Also revealed was a peripheral hole in the inferotemporal quadrant in the left eye. The total error score for the Farnsworth test was 36 in the right eye and 19 in the left eye. The test results revealed tritanomaly in the right eye and diffuse color defect in the left eye. SD-OCT imaging of both eyes showed incomplete posterior vitreous detachment, elevated foveal contours, and foveal schisis. It also showed alteration of the photoreceptor layer. Foveal thickness was 292 microns in the right eye and 490 microns in the left eye. Microperimetry showed a reduced mean retinal sensitivity of 7.7 db in the right eye and 8.2 db in the left eye, with a central dense scotoma in both eyes.

case_report: The patient is a 78-year-old right-handed female with a history of hyperlipidemia and previous smoking. She presented with dysarthria and progressive muscle weakness, which began 10 years ago. Initially, the weakness affected her lower extremities, more pronounced on the right side, and gradually led to falls and the need for a rolling walker. Over the next two years, the weakness extended to her bilateral upper extremities. She also reported muscle stiffness in the lower extremities, along with progressive dysphagia and dysarthria over the past few years. Currently, she uses a wheelchair for mobility. She denied sensory abnormalities, fluctuations in weakness, neck or back pain, shooting pain, bowel or bladder incontinence, muscle twitching, muscle pain, urine discoloration, double vision, or breathing difficulty. On examination, she had impaired shoulder shrugging bilaterally, indicating spinal accessory nerve involvement. Using the Muscle Research Grading System (MRGS), her strength was graded as 4 in bilateral upper and lower extremities proximally, 4+ distally in bilateral upper extremities, and 4- in bilateral lower extremities. Spasticity was noted in both upper and lower extremities. Deep tendon reflexes were exaggerated in the bilateral patellar, biceps, and triceps regions. Sustained ankle clonus was present bilaterally. The plantar reflex was mute, and Hoffman’s sign was positive bilaterally. Sensory and cerebellar system examinations were unremarkable.
test_results: EMG showed mild inactive chronic polyradiculopathy but was unremarkable for any lower motor neuron or sensory involvement in the upper and lower extremities. The patient’s MRI was significant for T2 and SWI sulcal hypointensities in the pre-central regions on the axial sequences bilaterally, suggestive of the 'motor band sign'.

case_report: A 44-year-old woman arrived at the emergency department with a four-day history of cough and fever. The cough was dry, and the fever reached a peak of 38.1℃, which was alleviated with oral paracetamol. She did not experience chest pain or difficulty breathing. The patient had no prior health issues and was a non-smoker. Family and social history were unremarkable. Physical examination showed normal oxygen saturation and vital signs, including pulse and respiratory rates. Her body mass index was 28 kg/m2 (height 159 cm, weight 71 kg). Scattered crepitations were heard in both lung fields. A reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction test confirmed the presence of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). Due to mild symptoms and no previous health conditions, she was advised to isolate at home following national guidelines. Ten days later, she returned to the emergency department with sharp, generalized abdominal pain, nausea, and recurrent vomiting. She had no respiratory complaints. Physical examination revealed diffuse abdominal tenderness without signs of generalized peritonitis. Laboratory tests showed normal hematological, renal, and hepatic profiles, with no elevation in inflammatory markers. Amylase levels and coagulation profile were within normal ranges. The general surgery team recommended further imaging.
test_results: The contrast-enhanced computed tomography demonstrated the presence of misty mesentery with increased density of the mesentery with fat stranding encasing the mesenteric vessels along with mesenteric adenopathy.

case_report: A 77-year-old female presented with fatigue and general joint pain. Over the past three months, her fatigue worsened daily, and systemic joint pain extended to her hands and feet two months before admission. One month before admission, her symptoms aggravated, leading to loss of appetite. One week before admission, she was unable to perform daily activities independently. She also experienced weight loss and night sweats. She had no symptoms such as rash, dry mouth, dry eye, headache, cough, chest pain, abdominal pain, vomiting, or diarrhea. Her medical history included osteoporosis and depression, for which she took 20 mg of paroxetine daily. Initial vital signs were: blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, pulse rate 77 beats/min, body temperature 35.2 °C, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. She was alert and oriented. Physical examination showed joint tenderness in her hands, shoulders, thighs, feet, and neck without swelling or erythema, and bilateral pitting edema in the lower extremities. Dry mucous membranes were noted in the oral cavity. No other neurological abnormalities or signs of pallor, icterus, or apparent chest, abdominal, or skin abnormalities were observed. Laboratory tests indicated mild inflammation with elevated C-reactive protein (CRP), mild anemia, severe hyponatremia, and hypoalbuminemia. Serum iron levels were normal, but ferritin levels were elevated. Normal cortisol secretion was confirmed. Low antidiuretic hormone levels were noted. The patient was treated with 15 mg of hydrocortisone daily. On day 7, she developed a mild fever of 37.3 °C and systemic edema with mild dyspnea. Chest radiography showed bilateral infiltration at the dull costophrenic angle. Urine analysis revealed white blood cells and organisms, with Gram staining showing Gram-negative rods and white blood cells. She was treated with furosemide (20 mg/day) and ceftriaxone (2 g/day) for one week, after which dyspnea and systemic edema resolved. On day 21, systemic joint pain persisted without inflammation in laboratory data, including non-significant CRP and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Joint ultrasonography showed no signs of inflammation. She was treated with 500 mg acetaminophen and 10 mg paroxetine daily, which partially alleviated the pain. On day 30, she developed a fever of 38.5 °C and worsening systemic edema, decreased appetite, and dry oral mucous membranes. Laboratory data showed thrombocytopenia (4.1 × 104/μL), renal dysfunction (32 mL/min/L), alkaline phosphatase (261 U/L), interleukin (IL)-6 (28.1 pg/mL), and elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 6.4 mg/dL, ESR 41 mm/h). No coagulopathy was observed, and urine analysis showed no pyuria.
test_results: Enhanced neck-to-pelvic CT revealed bilateral pleural effusion, ascites, and hepatosplenomegaly without prominent lymphadenopathy. Random skin and lip biopsies were performed to exclude intravascular lymphoma and investigate the symptoms. A lumbar puncture revealed no elevation of proteins, cells, or IL-6 in cerebrospinal fluid.

case_report: The patient is a 38-year-old male with a history of bronchial asthma managed with as-needed budesonide/formoterol, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, and chronic sinusitis, for which he had sinus surgery in August 2022. He began taking methylphenidate 3 weeks prior to his visit to the pulmonary clinic due to a recent ADHD diagnosis. His main complaint was worsening shortness of breath on exertion over the past 3 weeks, affecting his daily activities, along with a dry cough. He reported no fever, night sweats, upper respiratory tract infections, chest pain, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. He had a history of occasional vaping, which he ceased 2 months ago, and no contact with animals or birds. He works as an IT technician in a closed office environment and reported no environmental exposures. There were no symptoms indicative of connective tissue disease, skin allergies, or allergic rhinitis. He was not on any long-term medications and was taking methylphenidate 36 mg at the time of presentation. On examination, he was alert and conscious with stable hemodynamics and maintained a room air saturation of 98%. Chest examination showed no wheezing or crackles, normal heart sounds, normal jugular venous pressure, no lower limb edema, no signs of connective tissue disease, and no skin rash. During a 6-minute walk test, his oxygen saturation dropped from 95% to 87% at 300 meters. Pulmonary function tests were normal, with an FEV1 of 4.06 L (105% predictive), FVC of 4.58 L (98% predictive), FEV/FVC ratio of 88.7%, TLC of 5.3 L (78% predictive), RV of 1.19 L (63% predictive), RV/TLC ratio of 78%, and expiratory reserve volume of 2.94 L (205% predictive). Serum laboratory results showed a normal complete blood count with a white blood cell count of 8.5 (reference range 4–11 × 10^9/L) and normal differentials, normal kidney and liver function, negative sputum culture, and normal urinalysis with no casts. Nasopharyngeal viral multiplex PCR was negative, and serology for connective tissue disease and ANCA were negative. Tests for HIV, hepatitis C, and hepatitis B were negative. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 120. Stool tests for parasites and helminths were negative, and the toxicology screen was negative. The chest X-ray showed bilateral peripheral airspace opacities without mediastinal enlargement and a normal cardiac shadow.
test_results: The computed tomography (CT)/high-resolution CT scan showed multiple bilateral peripheral ground-glass attenuations with thickening of the intra- and interlobular septa. The scan also showed a mild air bronchogram. The bronchoscopy showed no gross abnormalities, while the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid had a white blood cell count with prominent macrophages at 66%, neutrophils at 5%, eosinophils at 15%, and lymphocytes at 13%. The transbronchial biopsy revealed a focal interstitial eosinophilic and histiocytic infiltrate. Numerous eosinophils and macrophages, some of which were multinucleated, were observed in the alveolar spaces.

case_report: An 8-month-old female infant, the second child of healthy unrelated Chinese parents, experienced an uneventful gestation and delivery. Her older brother was in good health. At 5 months old, she developed erythematous dermatitis on her face, neck, and buttocks. Despite treatment with topical corticosteroids and a dairy-free diet, there was no clinical improvement. Her psychomotor development was slightly delayed, although her nutritional state remained normal. Starting at 7 months, she had recurrent respiratory infections and her condition worsened despite medical treatment. She was brought to the emergency room due to lethargy and shortness of breath and was transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit. Upon admission, arterial blood gas analysis revealed severe metabolic acidosis (pH = 6.98, base deficit of -25). Biochemical tests showed elevated lactate levels (8.89 mmol/L), elevated ammonia levels (132 μmol/L), and elevated glucose levels (15.9 mmol/L).
test_results: Her urinary organic acid analysis found remarkable elevations in urinary lactate, 3-oxy-butyric acid, 3-OH-isovalerate, 3-OH-propionate, 3-methylcrotonyl glycine, and methylcitrate. In addition, urinary levels of 2-OH-sovalericacid, 2-keto-isovalericacid, 2-keto-3-methvlvaleric acid, 2-keto-isocaproic, and acetylglycine were higher than normal levels. Elevated levels of leucine and valine in blood.

case_report: A 5-month-old girl, born to parents who are related by blood, exhibited delayed neck control and generalized muscle weakness. Her birth history was unremarkable. Developmentally, she achieved cooing, social smiling, and recognition of her mother by 3 months of age, but had not yet developed neck control. She received immunizations according to the national schedule, including one dose of BCG and three doses of DPT. Physical examination revealed hypotonia in all limbs, absent deep tendon reflexes, and muscle strength rated less than 2/5 (MRC grade) in both upper and lower limbs. There were no signs of muscle fasciculation, atrophy, or hypertrophy. Laboratory investigations, including a complete blood count, serum electrolytes, liver and renal function tests, echocardiography, and Creatine phosphokinase (CPK) levels (219), were all within normal limits.
test_results: Muscle biopsy done from right vastus lateralis muscle showing extensive edema and inflammation in fascia and muscle on paraffin and cryosection sections, perivascular inflammation, with numerous Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS)-positive macrophages.

case_report: A 43-year-old woman presented in April 2021 with a 10-day history of fever and dry cough. She reported mild respiratory distress, with home-recorded peripheral capillary oxygen saturation (SpO2) levels of 88%-89%. Three days prior, she had a confirmed COVID-19 infection via reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction. Her medical history included polycystic ovarian disease, with no significant family or personal history. On examination, her blood pressure was 140/90 mmHg, pulse rate was 88 beats/min, respiratory rate was 20 breaths/min, and SpO2 was 92% on room air. Lung examination showed a bilateral decrease in air entry. Initial blood tests revealed a total leucocyte count of 11650 cells/µL (neutrophils 88%, lymphocytes 8%), C-reactive protein (CRP) of 16.44 mg/L, Pct of 9.52 ng/mL, lactate dehydrogenase of 282 IU/L, ferritin of 158 ng/mL, D-dimer of 775.84 ng/mL, interleukin-6 of 18.55 pg/mL, and slightly elevated liver enzymes. Electrolyte and renal function tests were normal. Arterial blood gas analysis showed severe hypoxia with an arterial oxygen partial pressure of 39.0 mmHg. High-resolution computed tomography (CT) of the chest indicated approximately 50% lung involvement with a CT severity index (CTSI) score of 18/25. The patient was placed on a non-rebreather mask with 15 L/min of oxygen, maintaining 100% oxygen saturation. Echocardiography showed no cardiac issues with an ejection fraction of 60%. She received chest physiotherapy and incentive spirometry. Treatment included intravenous (IV) remdesivir, IV dexamethasone, oral doxycycline, low molecular weight heparin, multivitamins, antibiotics, and appropriate nebulization. Over the next 7 days, her condition gradually improved, and her oxygen requirement decreased. A repeat chest CT on day 8 showed a CTSI score of 12/25. By day 12, she was weaned off oxygen, and all reports normalized except for the persistently elevated Pct level. She was discharged with a plan to investigate the elevated Pct level on an outpatient basis.
test_results: Ultrasonography of the neck revealed a 15.7 mm × 15 mm nodule in the left lobe of the thyroid gland. Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) confirmed a malignant epithelial neoplasm. FNAC of the left supraclavicular node confirmed metastatic carcinoma. The Ctn level was 406 pg/mL. Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) was not elevated. Positron emission tomography-CT (PET-CT) confirmed the presence of a well-defined inhomogeneously enhancing fluorodeoxyglucose-avid nodule in the left lobe of the thyroid gland measuring 18 mm × 13 mm with no evidence of distant spread.

case_report: This 11-year-old boy is the second child of healthy, unrelated parents. His father and mother were 30 and 25 years old, respectively, at the time of his birth. He was born at term, and his prenatal and perinatal history were uncomplicated, except for mild hyperbilirubinemia (15 mg/dl of total bilirubin) on day 4, which improved with phototherapy. His early psychomotor development was normal, and he completed the first and second levels of elementary school with good scores. At age eight, he experienced one episode of generalized tonic-clonic seizure, which recurred several days later. He was admitted to the hospital, and phenytoin was started, which controlled the seizures. Physical and neurological examination revealed a long and thin nose with hypoplasia of nasal alae and anteverted nostrils. Ophthalmic examination showed microphthalmos with microcornea, decreased visual acuity, and glaucoma. Hearing assessment was normal. Oral cavity examination revealed yellowish teeth with caries, smaller than normal and atypically-shaped teeth with arrested development appearance. Skeletal examination of the hands showed webbing of the skin (syndactyly) between the fourth and fifth fingers, camptodactyly, and hypoplasia of the mid phalanx of the fifth fingers. Both parents were examined and showed no similar features. His school performance gradually deteriorated after the seizure episode at age eight. One year later, he complained of a progressively worsening gait problem. Examination revealed spasticity of both legs with hyper-reflexia and extensor plantar responses. Gait examination showed spastic paraparesis.
test_results: On brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), symmetrical confluent hypersignal areas of subcortical white matter were evident with decreased signal of both basal ganglia and pachygyria. Repeated electroencephalograms (EEG) showed slow background for this age with epileptiform discharges.

case_report: A 37-year-old female arrived at the emergency room with severe abdominal pain and fever. She has experienced painful urination and blood in her urine for the past 10 months. An MRI previously revealed a mass in the abdominal wall extending into the bladder. A biopsy conducted elsewhere indicated inflammation. Initial treatment included antibiotics. A cystoscopy and transurethral bladder biopsy revealed acute and chronic inflammation of the bladder and Von Brunn nests. Cytology results showed atypical urothelial cells, leading to a referral to the urology service.
test_results: Follow up CT scan imaging demonstrated a heterogeneous ill-defined enhancing soft tissue density in the space of Retzius inseparable and compressing the anterior aspect of the urinary bladder measuring 11.3 × 4.5 × 12.8 cm with a peripherally enhancing loculated collection measuring 4.7 × 6.0 × 3.0 cm along with marked thickening of urinary bladder. A repeat percutaneous biopsy was done that again demonstrated infiltrative granulation tissue and chronic inflammation. Intraoperative frozen biopsies suggested spindle cell neoplasm, possible of urachal origin but malignancy could not be confirmed.
diagnosis: Inflammatory pseudotumor secondary to urachal cyst

case_report: A 57-year-old male presented to the emergency department 12 hours after experiencing severe chest pain and excessive sweating. The patient has a history of smoking and diabetes, with irregular blood glucose monitoring and inconsistent use of oral metformin. Upon arrival, treatment with aspirin and clopidogrel was started. Initial vital signs included a blood pressure of 157/89 mm Hg, a pulse rate of 78 beats per minute, and a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute while on a non-rebreather mask, with a pulse oximetry reading of 96%. The patient continued to experience milder chest pain.
test_results: An initial ECG obtained from a clinic when his pain had been persistent for 5 hours showed atrial fibrillation, upsloping ST-segment depression at the J point followed by peaked, positive T waves in leads V2 to V6 and slight ST-segment elevation in lead aVR, with poor R-wave progression. An 18-lead ECG was performed 8 hours after the initial ECG, showing sinus rhythm, abnormal Q waves in leads III, aVF, and V9, and T-wave inversion in leads V5 to V9. The vector of the ST-segment deviated towards the inferior and posterior wall of the left ventricle.

case_report: A 5-year-old girl with short stature and developmental delays visited Samsung Medical Center. She was born at 40 weeks gestational age by vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 3,210 g (25th–50th percentile). The patient is the only child of healthy Korean parents, with the father’s height at 182 cm and the mother’s height at 168 cm. Newborn screening for inherited metabolic disorders was normal. At 1 month old, she exhibited hypotonia and hyperlaxity of the joints. At 5 years 5 months, her height was 106 cm (SDS, -1.386), weight was 20.0 kg (SDS, 0.104), and head circumference was 50.0 cm (SDS, -0.357), based on the 2017 Korean National Growth Chart. She had facial features including a prominent forehead, hypertelorism, downward-slanting palpebral fissures, thick lips, and micrognathia. Additional findings included pectus excavatum and tapering stubby fingers. She began walking at 18 months and using 2-word sentences at 5 years. At the clinic visit, she could run independently and climb stairs but had an unstable gait and frequent falls. Her receptive language was intact, but expressive language was delayed by about 18 months with inaccurate pronunciation. The K-DST at 65 months indicated global developmental delays requiring further evaluation in all areas (gross motor, 4; fine motor, 3; cognition, 6; language, 8; sociality, 8; and self-control, 8). Laboratory tests (complete blood count, electrolytes, glucose, blood gases, hepatic and renal function tests, and urinalysis) were normal. Endocrine evaluations were also normal: triiodothyronine, 111.62 ng/dL (60–181 ng/dL); thyroid-stimulating hormone, 2.431 μIU/mL (0.64–69.27 μIU/mL); free thyroxine, 1.33 ng/dL (0.89–1.8 ng/dL); 25-hydroxyvitamin D3, 17.9 ng/mL (10–150 ng/mL); insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), 174.5 ng/mL (70.2–300.3 ng/mL); and alkaline phosphatase, 282 IU/L (142–335 IU/L). Chromosome analysis showed 46, XX. Bone age at 5 years 7 months was 2 months older than chronologic age. A skeletal survey revealed lumbar scoliosis. Echocardiography and EEG results were normal. Brain MRI showed multiple white matter lesions, mainly in the bilateral frontal lobe with a left paraventricular cyst. Dental examination found malocclusion and hypodontia (missing first molars). Ophthalmological examination revealed astigmatism. Hearing was normal.
test_results: A novel, likely pathogenic, heterozygous variant, c.326_338delinsCTCGAGAC (p.Val109Alafs*10), was identified in RPS6KA3. This variant had not been previously reported and was not found in her parents or the control databases: 1,000 genomes, Exome Variant Server, and gnomAD. The novel heterozygous variant, c.326_338delinsCTCGAGAC (p.Val109Alafs*10), is a truncated variation and is likely pathogenic according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics Standards and Guidelines.

case_report: A 37-year-old male presented with progressive difficulty in walking, characterized by rigidity and weakness in both legs, starting at age 35. He also experienced urinary urgency with incontinence and erectile dysfunction. His family history was negative for neurological or endocrinological conditions. He had normal psychomotor development without learning disabilities and did not report cognitive symptoms. Neurological examination revealed mild dysarthria, spastic paraparesis with a wide-based spastic gait, brisk deep tendon reflexes, bilateral Achilles clonus, and Babinski sign. Brain MRI showed multiple congenital brain development anomalies: agenesis of the posterior commissure, hypoplasia of the right fornix and ipsilateral mammillary body, colpocephaly, right frontal parasagittal cortical thickening, two periventricular nodular heterotopic foci in the right parietal areas, and venous drainage abnormalities in the left cerebellar hemisphere and right frontal lobe. Neuropsychological evaluation showed no abnormalities. EEG did not show any epileptiform discharges. Spinal MRI indicated spinal cord atrophy. EMG did not reveal any abnormalities. SEPs showed increased central conduction time from the right arm and left leg, with no response from the right leg. MEPs were absent in both legs. VEPs and OCT were unremarkable.
test_results: Genetic analysis revealed the presence of the hemizygous mutation c.1394-2A > G in the ABCD1 gene. Hematochemical examination disclosed normal cortisol levels with an increased adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH; 352 pg/mL, n.v. 5–60 pg/mL). VLCFA plasma levels were increased.

case_report: A 25-day-old male infant was admitted due to poor weight gain and dehydration. The infant was born at full term with a birth weight of 2.63 kg (3-10th percentile). There were no complications during the perinatal period, and the family history was unremarkable. Upon admission, the infant's height was 49 cm (3-10th percentile), weight was 2.46 kg (<3rd percentile), and head circumference was 34.5 cm (10-50th percentile). Vital signs included a blood pressure of 75/41 mmHg, pulse rate of 137/min, respiratory rate of 45/min, and body temperature of 36℃. The infant was alert, with a slightly sunken anterior fontanelle and decreased skin turgor. Physical examination showed grossly normal external genitalia and no other notable findings. Initial laboratory results were as follows: serum sodium, 122 mmol/L; serum potassium, 6.3 mmol/L; serum chloride, 91 mmol/L; blood urea nitrogen, 36 mg/dL; serum creatinine, 0.8 mg/dL; plasma renin activity, 114.1 ng/mL/hr (normal range 1-2.5); aldosterone, 9,840 pg/mL (normal range 50-194). Venous blood gas analysis indicated metabolic acidosis with a pH of 7.295, pCO2 of 41.3 mmHg, and HCO3- of 20.1 mmol/L. Spot urine analysis showed sodium at 16 mmol/L, potassium at 9.7 mmol/L, chloride at 18 mmol/L, and creatinine at 3.3 mg/dL. Neonatal screening tests indicated a normal serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone level. Renal ultrasonography revealed no abnormalities.
test_results: Genetic analysis revealed a heterozygous c.2146_2147insG (p.E716GfsX28) mutation in exon 5 of the NR3C2 gene.

case_report: The patient is a 13-year-old girl born to consanguineous parents (first-degree cousins) after a full-term pregnancy via cesarean section due to maternal hypertension, pre-eclampsia, and breech presentation, with a birth weight of 3.3 kg. Her development was reported as normal until the age of one year. At 18 months, she was referred to a pediatric neurology clinic for motor delay. Examination at that time showed no dysmorphic features or visceral enlargement. She exhibited mild motor delay, could stand with support, and had a vocabulary of up to five words. Neurologic examination revealed hypertonia in the lower extremities and increased tendon reflexes in both lower and upper limbs, with a flexor Babinski sign. Cranial nerves, sensory perception, and cerebellar function were normal. Metabolic screening, including urinary glycosaminoglycans (u-GAGs), was normal. Karyotype testing and brain MRI at age two were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid examination for protein, glucose, lactate levels, and cell count also yielded normal results. Follow-up continued in pediatric neurology and child development clinics. At age three, a second u-GAGs screening was normal. At age 11, she began experiencing recurrent convulsions, generalized hypertonia, and absences with loss of consciousness for several minutes. EEG was normal, and she responded well to valproic acid treatment. By age 12, her neurologic signs had progressed to severe spasticity, impaired dexterity, severe intellectual disability with autistic features, and incontinence. Additional findings included hearing impairment (abnormal auditory evoked potentials on both sides), joint contractures, pes cavus, and skin discoloration on the arms, hands, legs, and feet.
test_results: Parieto-occipital atrophy, including cortex atrophy, thin corpus callosum, white matter thinning and mild ventriculomegaly.

case_report: A 40-year-old woman with a history of receiving a single-chamber ICD (Current VR, St Jude Medical) for secondary prevention presented at the outpatient clinic after experiencing 6 ICD shocks. The ICD was programmed with three tachycardia zones: VF at a heart rate of 214 bpm or higher (less than 280 ms), VT-2 with a heart rate between 184 and 214 bpm (326-280 ms), and VT-1 as a monitoring zone between 120 and 183 bpm (500-326 ms). Nominal SVT discriminators were activated, while SVT criteria timeout and VT therapy timeout were deactivated. Device and lead functionality were confirmed to be intact.
test_results: The episode started with a SVT at 155 bpm, which was appropriately discriminated for 127 seconds. However, HR suddenly increased, reaching the VF zone. After the detection of 12 VF intervals, a VF episode was declared. During charging, the HR slowed, reaching the VT-1 zone. Because the HR remained in the tachycardia zone no intervals could be classified as SR and the first inappropriate ICD shock was delivered. After the ICD shock, the nominal post-shock redetection criteria require 5 beats in SR (<120 bpm or >500 ms) to finalize the episode; 6 intervals classified as VF (marked as F) are needed to redetect the tachycardia as VF (in this case programmed to be in the VT-2 or VF zone, again meeting both binning criteria). The intervals within the monitor zone can neither be classified as SR nor as VF (marked as -). After the first shock a fast redetection of VF occurred because 6 of the 11 intervals were inside the VT-2 or VF zone. The capacitors were charged again and a second inappropriate shock was delivered. After the second shock the HR slowed but remained above 120 bpm (VT-1), thus prolonging the redetection period until the relevant criteria were satisfied. Unfortunately, due to the ongoing tachycardia, the episode was not ended and every time 6 VF intervals were classified, therapy was delivered. This patient received 6 consecutive shocks, until therapy was exhausted. The total duration of the episode was 355 seconds.
diagnosis: Inappropriate ICD Shocks in a patient with Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Dysplasia

case_report: The patient was a male infant delivered via cesarean section by a 33-year-old mother with no complications. He was born to healthy, unrelated parents with no family history of metabolic disorders. He was the second child in the family, with a healthy 10-year-old sister. Born at 37 weeks and 6 days of gestation, he weighed 3500 grams and had an Apgar Score of 10 at 5 minutes. No visible malformations were observed at birth. On the 5th day of life, he was taken to a local hospital due to a 4-hour history of shortness of breath, poor responsiveness, lethargy, and weak crying. He was diagnosed with neonatal pneumonia, hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE), and neonatal hyperbilirubinemia. Supportive treatment was administered, leading to an improvement in his condition, and he was discharged on the 14th day. At 26 days old, he was transferred to the Wuhan Medical & Health Center for Women and Children due to ongoing poor responsiveness and reduced feeding since birth. Laboratory tests revealed elevated creatine kinase isoenzyme MB (CK-MB) at 116 U/L (normal range 0–24 U/L), elevated creatine kinase (CK) at 221 U/L (normal range 30–170 U/L), and low platelet count at 25 × 10^9/L (normal range 242–378 × 10^9/L).
test_results: MS/MS (UPLC-TQD, WATERS, USA) showed significantly elevated propionyl carnitine level of 10.111 uM (normal range 0.5–5 uM), and propionyl carnitine/acetyl carnitine ratio at 1.373 (normal range 0.04–0.25). Urine organic acid analysis with GC/MS showed elevated 3-hydroxypropionate (normal range 0–1.1 (u)mol/mol creatinine), propionyl glycine (normal range 0 (u)mol/mol creatinine), and methylmalonate (the normal range 0.2–3.6 (u)mol/mol creatinine).

case_report: A 19-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of hyposhosphataemic rickets. Her medical history began at the age of 2 years with a diagnosis of rickets initially attributed to vitamin D deficiency and later to Fanconi syndrome. She had no history of kidney stones, renal colic, or urinary tract infections. Her family history was unremarkable. Physical examination revealed normal blood pressure and a height of 140 cm. Laboratory tests indicated impaired kidney function with a serum creatinine level of 106 µmol/L, an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 68 ml/min/1.73 m2, and low serum phosphate at 0.73 mmol/L. Other biochemical parameters were within normal limits. Urinary metabolic assessment showed significantly elevated retinol binding protein (RBP) at 62,900 mg/l (normal range 20-40 mg/l), a urinary RBP:creatinine ratio of 25,160, increased urinary calcium with a urinary calcium:creatinine ratio (uCa:Cr) of 1 mmol/mmol (normal range 0.3–0.7 mmol/mmol), and increased phosphate excretion with a fractional excretion of phosphate (FePO4) of 48% (normal value <20%) and TmP/GFR of 0.62 mmol/l (normal range 0.84–1.23 mmol/l). Imaging studies, including computed tomography and abdominal ultrasound, revealed extensive bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis.
test_results: Her genetic testing, a next-generation sequencing (NGS) panel performed on peripheral lymphocyte DNA, revealed a heterozygous c.2152C>T variant in the CLCN5 gene (reference sequence: NM_001127899.3). Both parents’ peripheral lymphocyte DNA was tested and was negative for the aforementioned mutation, therefore the variant was classified as de novo. This variant causes substitution of the amino acid arginine with a premature stop codon p.(Arg718*). X-inactivation status was studied using polymorphic markers that are differentially methylated on the inactive and active X chromosome. The androgen receptor (AR) was studied by fluorescent polymerase chain reaction in the presence and absence of the methylation-sensitive restriction enzyme HpaII. This revealed a non-random inactivation of the maternally inherited X-chromosome.

case_report: A 17-year-old female reported experiencing a sensation of a foreign body and pain in both eyes for the past three years, with no notable medical or family history. Best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was measured at 20/40 in the right eye and 20/50 in the left eye, with a refractive error of −0.5 sphere in both eyes. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy with retroillumination revealed diffuse intra-epithelial microcystic lesions extending from limbus to limbus, along with regional haze in both corneas. Other corneal layers appeared normal. Intraocular pressure (IOP) and funduscopic examinations were within normal limits.
test_results: Confocal scan examination of both corneas disclosed scattered and well-defined round to oval hyporeflective intracytoplasmic areas measuring 6.8 to 41.4 μm in their largest diameter within the superficial corneal epithelium, diffuse hyperreflective spots in the basal epithelium, irregular and poorly-defined high contrast areas in the sub-basal epithelial region and foci of sub-epithelial fibrosis. A few hyperreflective lesions containing high contrast spots, corresponding to cell nuclei, were also present. The subepithelial nerve plexus was not visible because of the regional hyperreflectivity. No abnormal finding was noted in the rest of corneal stroma and the endothelium.

case_report: A 64-year-old male presented to the emergency department with right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, and dark urine persisting for 3 days. His medical history included hypertension and coronary bypass surgery, with no history of drug use. Physical examination revealed tenderness in the right upper quadrant and newly developed periumbilical ecchymosis, while the Murphy sign was negative. Laboratory tests showed elevated hepatic function markers (Aspartate Transaminase: 348 U/L, Alanine Aminotransferase: 231 U/L), significantly high lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels, and increased C-reactive protein (CRP) at 59 mg/L. Bilirubin levels were minimally elevated (total: 1 mg/dL, direct: 0.29 mg/dL). Urinalysis indicated 3+ protein and 2+ ketone. Initial clinical findings suggested a biliary system issue. Ultrasound imaging identified biliary stones and mild diffuse gallbladder wall thickening (4 mm) without fluid accumulation or ductal dilatation. A non-contrast CT scan showed a distended gallbladder with millimetric stones and no other significant findings. The patient was admitted with a working diagnosis of cholecystitis. Over the next 3 days, hemoglobin levels dropped from 13.9 to 8.3 g/dL, accompanied by a marked increase in creatinine, LDH, CRP, and total bilirubin levels, indicative of hemolytic anemia. Coombs test results were negative. Further imaging with abdominal MRI and magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography was performed using a 1.5 Tesla MRI machine (Avanto, Siemens, Germany) with various sequences. MRI findings showed no acute biliary pathologies but revealed markedly and diffusely low T2-weighted signal in the bilateral renal cortex compared to the medulla, consistent with hemosiderin accumulation. Prominent signal loss in the renal cortex was also noted on in-phase sequences compared to out-of-phase images.
test_results: The flow cytometry analysis of peripheral blood showed deficiency of glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored proteins (GPI-APs). The bone marrow biopsy revealed only reticulocytosis.

case_report: In January 2012, a 40-year-old man was admitted to our hospital due to shock. Three days prior to admission, he experienced symptoms resembling the flu, including nausea, general malaise, lower abdominal pain, and severe diarrhea. At a previous hospital, he received 500 ml of 5% albumin and 1,500 ml/day of saline. Three days later, his consciousness deteriorated, and he developed right hemiparesis. Upon referral to our hospital, physical examination showed a temperature of 36.0°C, blood pressure of 95/72 mm Hg, pulse rate of 160 beats/min, and respiratory rate of 25 breaths/min. His SpO2 was 100% with a 10-liter/min O2 mask. The jugular vein was collapsed, bilateral radial artery pulses were weakly palpable, and his extremities were cold. A whole-blood sample coagulated easily, indicating a state of hyperviscosity. Laboratory results showed polycythemia, hypoalbuminemia, severe leukocytosis, and elevated creatinine levels. Serum electrolytes were within normal ranges, but severe metabolic acidosis was present.
test_results: Influenza virus types A and B were shown to be positive using a rapid diagnostic kit. Pericardial effusion and a collapsed inferior vena cava were revealed in heart echocardiograph and chest computed tomography (CT) examinations. Magnetic resonance (MR) angiography showed the occlusion of the division of the left M2 segment of the middle cerebral artery (MCA). Diffusion-weighted MR imaging revealed high signal intensity in the MCA territory.

case_report: A 10-year-old male patient was admitted to our hospital due to ongoing low potassium and magnesium levels. He was born at 39+5 weeks via normal vaginal delivery, weighing 3,500 grams. His family history includes his mother having chronic hepatitis B and a cousin who had a heart transplant for unknown reasons. During pregnancy, there was an excess of amniotic fluid. At four years old, he experienced muscle cramps and stiffness and was evaluated at another hospital. His height and weight were in the 50th percentile, and his blood pressure was normal. Neurological examination was unremarkable. Laboratory and imaging results revealed severe low magnesium and potassium levels, low calcium with high urinary calcium excretion, elevated renin and aldosterone levels, and calcium deposits in both kidneys. He was treated with oral potassium and magnesium supplements, amiloride, and spironolactone for six years, but his magnesium levels remained low despite additional intravenous supplements. Genetic testing for a specific condition related to low magnesium and high urinary calcium was negative after three years of treatment. At age 10, he was transferred to our hospital for acute heart failure and was treated for acute myocarditis with veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) for 13 days. His heart function improved, though the cause of the myocarditis was not determined. After ECMO weaning, he was moved to the general ward, and our pediatric nephrology team was consulted for his chronic low potassium and magnesium levels. His height was 145 cm (50th percentile) and weight 36.5 kg (50th percentile). Laboratory results showed serum sodium at 132 mmol/L, potassium at 3.2 mmol/L, total CO2 at 20.2 mmol/L, calcium at 9.6 mg/dL, phosphorus at 5.2 mg/dL, magnesium at 1.1 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen at 6.7 mg/dL, and creatinine at 0.32 mg/dL. Urine specific gravity was 1.007 with no blood or protein present. The urine calcium to creatinine ratio was 0.9. Tubular phosphate reabsorption was 92.5%, and the transtubular potassium gradient was 14.48 despite low potassium levels. His clinical findings indicated an inherited renal tubulopathy. A detailed history revealed his prenatal history of excess amniotic fluid.
test_results: A heterozygous mutation in the CLCKNB gene was detected; c.139G>A causing p.Gly(GGG)465Glu(GAG) in exon 13.

case_report: An 8-year-old girl presented with repeated episodes of clonic seizures affecting the right upper and lower limbs, each lasting 2–5 minutes, accompanied by a prolonged postictal state. These episodes did not involve sudden loss of consciousness but were associated with bladder incontinence. The first episode occurred at age 7, with a rapid increase in seizure activity followed by a decrease in frequency to 10–15 episodes per day, along with slurred speech, cognitive delay, and abnormal gait. She was born as the second twin, cried immediately after birth, and had a normal APGAR score. There was no history of neonatal seizures, blood transfusions, neurosurgery, traumatic head injury, proven allergies, or family history of epilepsy. Initial routine electroencephalogram (EEG) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were normal. The patient was initially treated with Oxcarbazepine, followed by the addition of Valproate Sodium and Clonazepam. One month ago, she experienced paraesthesia and twitching of the right arm. She was admitted to the neurology department due to an exacerbation of focal status epilepticus and generalized seizures, which could not be controlled with antiepileptic drugs alone. Neurologic examination at admission revealed constant twitching of the right hand, intermittent stiffening of the right leg and pelvic region, right hemiparesis, and muscle power Medical Research Council (MRC) grade 3 on the right upper and lower limbs, with a full 5 on the left upper and lower limbs. Exaggerated tendon reflexes were noted on the right side. She exhibited severe global developmental delay. There were no signs of meningeal irritation, and cranial nerves were intact. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal, and PCR tests for Herpes Simplex Virus, EBV, measles, Rubella, and CMV were negative.
test_results: EEG showed slow activity with focal left frontal biphasic spikes paroxysmal discharges. MRI brain T1 revealed left hemispheric atrophy and in the left insular cortex. MRI T2 axial revealed atrophy in left Caudate and putamen nuclei.

case_report: A 21-year-old female was referred to a hematologist in 2011 for persistent elevated hemoglobin levels (Hb 172–183 g/L) noted since childhood. She had no symptoms, thromboembolic events, or family history of abnormal blood counts. She was a smoker and not on regular therapy. Blood tests showed Hb 197 g/L, Hct 0.588, RBC 6.35 x 10^12/L, MCV 9.6 fL, with normal platelet and white blood cell counts, and normal biochemistry. Pulse oximetry indicated normal oxygen saturation. Clinical examination, aside from obesity (BMI 38 kg/m2), revealed no abnormal findings. JAK2 V617F mutation was negative. Six months later, she experienced a pulmonary embolism, linked to recent oral contraceptive use and smoking. She began anticoagulation therapy and underwent a 500 mL phlebotomy due to high Hb (183 g/L), Hct (0.532), and RBC (5.91 x 10^12/L). Bone marrow cytology showed reactive changes, and JAK2 exon 12 mutation was negative. Hb electrophoresis showed HbF at 0.7%, deemed clinically irrelevant. Oxygen pressure at 50 percent Hb saturation (p50) was normal. Anticoagulation was stopped after one year. In 2015, she had extensive superficial thrombophlebitis of the left saphenous vein (RBC 6.27 x 10^12/L, Hb 175 g/L, Hct 0.523) and was treated with fondaparinux for 6 weeks. In 2017, during pregnancy, she started prophylactic low molecular weight heparin (dalteparin 7500 U/24h). At 8 weeks, she had another pulmonary embolism and deep venous thrombosis in her left calf. Blood levels were Hb 196 g/L, Hct 0.600, RBC 6.74 x 10^12/L. She underwent three phlebotomy sessions. Elevated serum EPO was noted (73.4 E/L; normal range 3.3–16.6). Anticoagulation continued throughout pregnancy and 6 weeks postpartum. She delivered a healthy boy at 38 weeks. In 2019, during her second pregnancy, she was prescribed a higher dose of dalteparin (10000 U/24 h) and phlebotomy to prevent thromboembolic complications. The pregnancy ended in the first trimester due to septic abortion. Another elevated EPO value (400 E/L) was recorded. CT of the chest and abdomen and ultrasound of the neck showed no tumors but revealed thrombosis of the inferior vena cava and right common iliac vein. Long-term anticoagulation was recommended. Echocardiography showed moderate pulmonary hypertension.
test_results: This revealed a mutation in the EPAS1 gene (c.1609G > A, pGly537Arg). The variant was confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

case_report: A 24-year-old male Caucasian presented with secondary hypertension that began at age eleven. Despite treatment with four antihypertensive medications (AT1-receptor antagonist, β-blocker, calcium channel antagonist, and doxazosin mesylate), his blood pressure remained high. Initial examination showed a blood pressure of 180/95 mmHg and a heart rate of 82 beats per minute. A 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure measurement while on treatment indicated an average blood pressure of 183/98 mmHg with a heart rate of 71 bpm, with no nocturnal dip. Other physical findings were normal. Serum electrolytes were: sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, calcium 2.7 mmol/L, inorganic phosphorus 4.1 mg/dL, and magnesium 1.97 mg/dL. Renal, liver, and thyroid tests were normal. A 24-hour urine analysis showed normal catecholamines and catecholamine metabolites. Plasma renin activity under medication was undetectable (<1 ng/L), and plasma aldosterone concentration was moderately elevated (237 ng/L), while aldosterone urine excretion was within normal limits (0.44 μg/day). MRI showed no adrenal tumor or other abnormalities. Dexamethasone suppression testing (1.5 mg/day for 5 days) normalized plasma aldosterone concentration (132 ng/L) and reduced urine excretion of 18-hydroxycorticosterone (31–4.2 μg/24 h) and 18-hydroxycortisol (1760–110 μg/24 h). Posture testing resulted in an increase in plasma aldosterone concentration to 304 ng/L, a 28% rise.
test_results: The patient's deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) produced the characteristic 3.9-kb product when the 5′ primer for 11β -hydroxlase and the 3′-primer for aldosterone synthase were used for amplification.

case_report: A 69-year-old Japanese woman, who had been practicing yoga for 30 years and working as a yoga instructor for the past 2 years, observed skin hardening on her chest for 13 months before seeking medical advice. She experienced pain during physical activity in the affected areas, and the number and size of these skin lesions gradually increased. She did not report fever, joint pain, cough, or Raynaud's phenomenon. She had no history of ingesting l-tryptophan, toxic oil products, or using statin medications. Upon initial examination, multiple areas of shiny, hardened skin and painful, orange-peel-like lesions were noted on her chest and all four limbs. There were no signs of Raynaud's phenomenon, thickened skin on the fingers, finger ulcers, or bleeding around the nails. Laboratory tests showed elevated eosinophil levels (0.71 × 10^9/l, normal <0.45 × 10^9/l), while serum creatine kinase, myoglobin, aldolase, IgG, IgA, and IgM levels were within normal ranges, and antinuclear antibodies were negative.
test_results: T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed significant hyperintense thickening of the fascia of the lower extremities. Histopathological examination of a biopsy specimen from an area of induration showed marked fibrinoid degeneration of the fascia and the neighboring muscle with mixed cellular infiltration of lymphocytes and eosinophils. Immunohistochemistry manifested predominant CD8+ lymphocytic infiltrates as well as a limited number of CD4+ lymphocytes.

case_report: A 42-year-old Caucasian male presented with a history of progressive fatigue, chills, night sweats, and unintended weight loss. Physical examination revealed left cervical lymphadenopathy.
