Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed widespread adenopathy, numerous small sclerotic lesions throughout the bones, and one small lucent lesion on the right side of the pelvis. An excisional biopsy of the cervical lymph node was performed. Histologic evaluation of the excised lymph node revealed effaced architecture with many atypical cells, including those with 'horseshoe/kidney'-shaped nuclei. The neoplastic cells were immuno-reactive for CD30, ALK (diffuse, cytoplasmic), CD2, CD4, granzyme B, and TIA-1. Many background CD68+ histiocytes were observed.
test_results: A bone marrow biopsy was performed and showed extensive disease.

case_report: A 24-year-old man with no prior medical history arrived at the Emergency Department following a traumatic fall. This incident resulted in a tibiotalar dislocation, a distal fibular fracture, a posterior malleolar fracture, and a ruptured deltoid ligament. He underwent an urgent trimalleolar open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) using a posterior approach. One month after the surgery, he began experiencing new symptoms including plantar numbness, allodynia, and dysesthesia described as a sensation similar to 'stepping on a lego,' which worsened at night. He was prescribed gabapentin 100mg three times daily and referred to pain management. Physical examination revealed a well-healing surgical wound without signs of infection, but there was noticeable swelling and erythema of the left ankle, dry and scaling skin around the distal tibial joint, reduced sensation to light touch on the medial, dorsal, and plantar surfaces of the left foot, hyperesthesia of the metatarsal heads, and decreased hair growth on the dorsal aspect of the left foot. The patient’s gabapentin dosage was increased to 300 mg three times daily. Additionally, he began physical therapy, which included contrast baths, desensitization techniques, and strengthening exercises.
test_results: At two months post-op, an electromyography (EMG) showed that both the left sural sensory nerve and left lateral plantar motor nerve had no response. Left medial plantar motor and left superficial peroneal sensory nerves showed reduced amplitude. A triple-phase bone scan of the calves, ankles, and feet showed an abnormal radiotracer uptake in all three phases in the left ankle.
diagnosis: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome Type II

case_report: A 54-year-old man presented with a sudden and worsening blurring of vision in both eyes, progressing to complete blindness over six weeks. Initially, he experienced generalized blurring and horizontal double vision before losing sight entirely. There was no associated eye pain, redness, or bulging. One week after becoming blind, he began to have frontal, throbbing headaches that worsened with straining, but without nausea or vomiting. Additionally, he reported feeling lethargic, having a reduced appetite, and losing weight. His past ocular history was unremarkable. On examination, visual acuity in both eyes was no perception of light in all quadrants. The anterior segment of both eyes appeared normal. Both pupils were dilated to 5 mm and did not respond to light. Intraocular pressure was normal in both eyes. There was left esotropia in the primary gaze with limited movement in abduction. Fundoscopy showed pale optic discs in both eyes.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) scan and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a suprasellar mass that compressed the optic chiasma and adjacent brain structures with the presence of hydrocephalus.

case_report: A 37-year-old female presented with difficulty ascending stairs, difficulty sitting and standing, and episodes of falling. Neurological examination showed 4/5 muscle strength in both proximal and distal muscles of the upper and lower limbs. Deep tendon reflexes were reduced in all extremities. Family history indicated a sibling with similar issues. Blood tests revealed elevated CK levels (534 U/L) with other parameters within normal limits. Electromyography indicated myopathy. Respiratory function tests and blood gas evaluations were normal. Cardiology assessments, including ECG and echocardiography, were normal. Personal medical history included appendectomy and inguinal hernia surgery. She and her younger brother, who had more severe symptoms, presented to the hospital simultaneously. Muscle biopsy confirmed myopathy, and she had been previously diagnosed with muscular dystrophy. Both siblings sought further evaluation as their symptoms worsened.
test_results: The alpha glycosidase enzyme level was 0.2 µmol/l/h (normal range >3.3 µmol/l/h). Genetic analysis revealed the 2 mutations of c.32-13T>G and c.896T >C.

case_report: An 83-year-old man presented with a 7-day history of red eruptions on his trunk and extremities. His medical history included bronchial asthma, hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and postoperative colon carcinoma. He had no prior history of psoriasis vulgaris. Physical examination revealed irregularly shaped red areas with scales and small pustules on the trunk and extremities. He was afebrile. Blood tests showed a white blood cell count of 12,530/μl (segment 87.8%, lymphocytes 6.7%, monocytes 4.9%, eosinophils 0.5%, and basophils 0.1%) and a C-reactive protein level of 2.2 mg/dl. Treatment was initiated with oral antihistamine and topical steroid. Four days later, the patient returned with high fever and general malaise. Examination revealed an extension and new development of red areas and pustules over the entire body, with coalescence of pustules forming lakes of pus. Blood tests showed a white blood cell count of 18,920/μl (segment 88.4%, lymphocytes 65.0%, monocytes 6.3%, eosinophils 0.2%, and basophils 0.1%) and a C-reactive protein level of 20.171 mg/dl. The patient was admitted to the hospital.
test_results: Histological examination revealed neutrophil infiltration into the upper epidermis, which formed a spongiform pustule of Kogoj. Direct immunofluorescence showed no significant deposits of immunoglobulins. Pustular fluid cultures were negative for bacteria. Mutation analysis detected no significant mutations in IL36RN and CARD14.

case_report: A 5-month-old girl presented with issues related to inadequate growth, delayed developmental milestones, and an unusually large head. She is the first child of parents who are second-degree relatives, with no complications reported during pregnancy. Physical examination revealed an enlarged head circumference, folds of skin at the inner corners of the eyes, and a small jaw. There were no signs indicative of Marfan’s syndrome or neurofibromatosis type I (NF1).
test_results: Neurosonography of child’s cranium and computed tomography (CT) brain showed ventriculomegaly with prominent cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) spaces. Screening USG spine showed bilateral symmetric elongated cystic outpouchings in the entire paraspinal regions, which were communicating with the spinal canal. A solid hyperechoic structure was seen herniating into the one of the sac at the right lumbar region, which was found to be spinal cord. Whole spine MRI showed multiple lateral CSF-intensity protrusions lined by meninges through the neural foraminal expansions involving the entire spine, which were communicating with the spinal canal, suggesting meningoceles. Dural ectasia was noted predominantly posterior to the cord in thoracolumbar region. Herniation of the conus was noted into meningeal sac through the dilated right neural foramen at L2–L3 levels. Scalloping of the posterior body of thoracic and lumbar vertebrae were also noted. MRI of the brain showed cerebellar tonsillar herniation with crowding at the level of the foramen magnum causing hydrocephalus. The corpus callosum was thinned because of the ballooned third ventricle.

case_report: A 45-year-old male experienced diarrhea for 45 days and a weight loss of 7 kg per month. Prior to these symptoms, he was in good health. Laboratory results indicated elevated C-reactive protein (6.8 mg/dL), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (80 mm/hr), white blood cell count (12.28 × 10^9/L), and platelet count (453 × 10^9/L). There was a reduction in red blood cells (4.19 × 10^12/L) and hemoglobin (12.5 g/dL), while liver function tests were normal with alanine aminotransferase at 20 IU/L and aspartate aminotransferase at 13 IU/L. A peripheral blood smear revealed normocytic normochromic anemia without immature cells. Stool examination showed no ova or parasites. The patient did not have a fever or upper gastrointestinal symptoms. Initial colonoscopy revealed multiple, irregular shallow ulcerations from the rectum to the ileocecal valve. Microscopic examination showed minimal crypt distortion with focal aggregation of normal-looking lymphocytes. Empirical oral metronidazole was prescribed. Three weeks later, the diarrhea worsened, but follow-up colonoscopy and biopsy showed no interval change. Treatment continued with intravenous antibiotics. A subsequent colonoscopy a week after starting IV antibiotics showed worsening ulcers. High-dose steroids (budenofalk) and antibiotics (salazopyrin) were prescribed. Three weeks into steroid therapy, the patient developed a fever (38.2℃) and hematochezia, with abnormal liver function tests (ALT 85 IU/L and AST 339 IU/L). Laboratory findings showed severe pancytopenia (WBC, 0.18 × 10^9/L; RBC, 1.72 × 10^12/L; platelet count, 7 × 10^9/L; and hemoglobin, 12.5 g/dL) with few atypical lymphocytes in the peripheral blood smear. The final colonoscopy showed extensive ulcerations throughout the colon with fresh blood. Pathologic findings indicated severe infiltration of small to medium-sized lymphocytes with slight atypia.
test_results: The immunohistochemical stains were positive for CD3 and CD5. In addition, we were able to rule out the possibility of both B-cell LPD by negative staining of CD20, and NK/T-cell lymphoma by negative staining of CD56.
diagnosis: Epstein-Barr Virus-associated fulminant T-cell Lymphoproliferative Disorder
Orpha_name: Systemic Epstein-Barr virus-positive T-cell lymphoproliferative disease of childhood

case_report: A 32-year-old male, with no significant past medical history, presented with a complaint of purulent fluid leakage from a scrotal fistula that had been ongoing for 6 months. Physical examination identified a productive scrotal fistula. The patient reported no symptoms of painful urination, burning sensation during urination, or presence of pus in the urine. Initial laboratory tests and urinalysis showed no abnormalities. Scrotal ultrasound indicated thickening of the scrotal skin without any fluid collection. Voiding cystourethrography results were normal, showing no strictures. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a horizontal fistula located above the corpus spongiosum, ending vertically, with no fluid collection. The patient underwent a surgical procedure through a scrotal approach, during which methylene blue was injected into the fistula, and a blind channel measuring 10.5 cm was excised from the surrounding tissues.
test_results: The fistula (the channel) was lined with transitional and pseudostratified columnar epithelium with epidermic cover at the level of its scrotal extremity.

case_report: A 44-year-old woman visited the internal medicine department due to fatigue that started four months prior. She also reported a large, painful lymph node in the left axillary region. Her medical history includes a refractory IgG warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, for which she underwent a splenectomy 10 years ago, with no subsequent relapses. Her family history includes an 8-year-old son undergoing clinical studies for lymph node enlargement and Evans syndrome. Imaging studies, including a mammogram and breast and abdominal ultrasounds, showed enlarged axillary and inguinal lymph nodes. Radiological findings indicated a BI-RADS-5 classification. An excisional biopsy of the axillary lymph node conglomerate ruled out metastatic disease. Special stains for fungi and tuberculosis were negative. Findings included a slight increase in CD8+ T cells, progressive transformation of germinal centers with reactive follicular hyperplasia, and a moderate number of lymphocytes with Epstein Barr (EBER+). Non-Hodgkin lymphoma was ruled out using a lymphoma screening tube flow cytometry with monoclonal antibodies CD19/CD45/CD3/CD8/CD4/LAMBDA/KAPPA. Laboratory results showed negative antinuclear antibodies (ANA), negative antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA)-C and ANCA-P, normal serum complement C3 and C4, IgG and IgA hypergammaglobulinemia, and slightly decreased IgM. Positive IgG anti-Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and negative IgM anti-EBV were documented, with no detectable EBV DNA in the plasma. Both HIV and pneumococcal infections were ruled out. She received the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV)-13 and pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV)-23. The T cell immunophenotype distribution in peripheral blood was normal, while the B cell immunophenotype showed a slight increase in CD21low B cells and decreased memory B cells.
test_results: A double-negative T cell flow cytometry documented 27% CD3+/αβ+/CD4-/CD8- of the total T CD3+ cells and 15% of the total lymphocytes. Clinical exome sequencing revealed a heterozygous variant in the FAS gene, exon 9, c.785T>A (p.Ile262Asn). This finding was confirmed with Sanger sequencing. The same variant was found in the patient's son.

case_report: Ms J is a 52-year-old female who received a deceased donor renal transplant in May 2006 for membranous glomerulonephritis after 6 years on haemodialysis. Post-transplant, she was initially treated with alemtuzumab due to delayed graft function and was later discharged on tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone for chronic immunosuppression. Ms J tested negative for anti-HCV in her first transplant consultation in 2004 and again 12 days before the surgery. Her pre-transplant bilirubin (0.5 mg/dL), alkaline phosphatase (94 IU/L), aspartate aminotransferase (28 IU/L), and alanine aminotransferase (14 IU/L) were within normal limits. Seven days post-transplant, her alkaline phosphatase increased to 178 IU/L. Within 6 months, her aminotransferases (AST 96 IU/L and ALT 78 IU/L) and bilirubin (1.5 mg/dL) were elevated and did not return to normal levels. Tacrolimus was replaced with cyclosporine, and a CT scan of the abdomen showed cholelithiasis and small ascites. An elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy did not improve liver chemistries, and repeated tests for chronic anti-HCV/HBV antibody serologies remained negative. Tests for abnormal anti-nuclear antibodies, anti-smooth muscle antibody, anti-mitochondrial antibody, and quantitative immunoglobulins were also negative. HCV RNA testing was not performed. Over the next 7 months, Ms J developed increasing jaundice and worsening symptomatic ascites, along with declining renal graft function and uraemia.
test_results: Transjugular liver biopsy indicated cholestasis, periportal fibrosis and acute inflammation of the bile ducts with associated regeneration, and only mild lobular inflammation. Features of HCV hepatitis were absent. HCV RNA by B-DNA was positive for 7.69 × 106 eq/mL of genotype 1a virus.
diagnosis: Fibrosing cholestatic hepatitis  related to hepatitis C virus  infection
Orpha_name: Recurrent hepatitis C virus induced liver disease in liver transplant recipients

case_report: A 13-year-old girl presented with short stature. Physical examination revealed dysmorphic facial features, a short and webbed neck, low posterior hairline, cubitus valgus, brachy- and clinodactyly, and widely spaced nipples. Multiple café-au-lait spots (>15 mm, 8 spots), axillary freckling, and relative macrocephaly were observed. Dysmorphic facial features included midfacial hypoplasia, prominent nasolabial folds, low-set and posteriorly rotated ears, hypertelorism, downslanted palpebral fissures, and low nasal root. The patient did not have any neurofibroma. Cardiovascular examination revealed no cardiac murmur and echocardiography was normal. The ocular examination did not reveal Lisch nodules. There was no sign of developmental delay, and the nervous system examination was completely normal. The patient’s pubertal stage was evaluated as Tanner stage 2. Her arm span was 124.8 cm and upper/lower ratio was 0.9, suggesting no skeletal deformity. Karyotype analysis was 46,XX. Complete blood count, routine biochemistry, and urine analysis were within normal limits. The celiac antibodies were negative and thyroid function tests were normal. Both serum insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) and IGF binding protein 3 (IGF-BP3) levels were below -3 standard deviation score (SDS). Peak GH response to L-dopa and clonidine stimulation tests were 3.9 ng/mL and 4.2 ng/mL, respectively. Other pituitary hormone levels were all within normal ranges. The size of the pituitary gland was measured as 3.5 mm in the pituitary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Cranial MRI showed a hyperintense mildly swollen appearance in T2 at the cerebral peduncles and globus pallidus. T1-weighted images also showed hyperintense lesions associated with T1 limitation; after administration of intravenous contrast substance, these lesions did not show any uptake of the contrast.
test_results: Genetic analysis of both the patient and the father revealed a truncating mutation c.7846C>T (M82814), p.Arg2616X (AAA59924) in the NF1 gene. No mutation was found in PTPN11 gene.

case_report: A thirteen-year-old female presented with limited growth in height and weight, absence of secondary sexual characteristics, primary amenorrhea, and skin hyperpigmentation. She was born at term to non-consanguineous parents with a birth weight of 1.5 kg and experienced delayed developmental milestones, including late dentition. She had clitoromegaly from birth and underwent reductive surgery at age 2. Physical examination showed a bird-like facial appearance, a pointed nose, hollow cheeks, a prominent jaw, abnormal dentition, excessive scalp and body hair, and acanthosis on the nape of the neck, axilla, elbows, and knuckles. Her skin appeared shriveled, particularly on the upper limbs and trunk. Her height was 130 cm (<3rd percentile; SDS: -3.04), weight 20 kg (<3rd percentile; SDS: -2.32), and body mass index was 11.83 kg/m2 (<3rd percentile). The mid-parental height was 147 cm (<3rd percentile; SDS: -2.28). Sexual maturity rating was prepubertal. Examination of the external genitalia revealed an enlarged but surgically altered clitoris (clitoral index: 60 mm2; normal <35 mm2).
test_results: Her karyotype was 46XX. She had fasting and post-glucose hyperglycemia, hyperinsulinemia, and an increased C-peptide level. Serum beta-hydroxybutyrate level was normal and urine ketones were negative. She had a raised serum testosterone level (0.067 nmol/L). Bone age was 13 years. Abdominal ultrasonography showed normal kidneys and Mullerian structures, a liver with heterogeneous echotexture, and polycystic ovaries with echogenic stroma. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) showed reduced total body fat (11.3%). Echocardiography showed small ostium secundum ASD. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a normal pineal gland.

case_report: A five-year-old boy with no prior health issues was referred to pediatric surgery due to testicular asymmetry. His medical and family history were unremarkable. The patient reported no symptoms such as testicular pain, swelling, or urinary issues. On physical examination, he had an appropriate weight for his age and was in good general health. Both testicles were located in the scrotum and had normal consistency. A painless nodular formation was felt at the upper pole of the left testicle, with well-defined borders and adherence to the underlying structures. No masses were palpable in the inguinal region, and no other physical abnormalities were noted. Blood tests, including lactate dehydrogenase, beta-human chorionic gonadotropin, and serum alpha-fetoprotein, were all negative.
test_results: Testicular Doppler ultrasound revealed a mass in the upper third of the left testicle with 1.5 cm in length, well-defined contours, and increased vascularity.

case_report: A 51-year-old male presented with painful swelling in the left shoulder. The pain began gradually ten months prior and progressively worsened. There was no history of trauma. The swelling increased in size over three weeks and then stabilized. Pain was triggered by activities involving shoulder elevation and abduction, but not by shoulder rotation. The patient had no significant past medical or family history. Examination revealed a firm, localized, mildly tender swelling in the antero-superior aspect of the left shoulder with overlying skin redness. The patient had nearly full range of motion with mild pain during abduction and internal rotation. Tests for biceps tendonitis, rotator cuff tear, AC joint arthritis, and instability were negative.
test_results: Radiographs demonstrated calcification around the greater tuberosity and subacromial space as well as hyperostotic lesions in the scapula blade. A CT scan revealed extensive yet well-defined ossification within the proximal deltoid muscle and hyperostotic masses dribbling from the scapular blade. An MRI scan showed a large volume of low-signal intensity calcific foci within and beneath the deltoid muscle with no intra-articular involvement or extension to the proximal humerus itself. There were also multiple areas of cortical thickening of the scapula. Tc-99m MDP bone scan revealed increased uptake in the lesions in the left shoulder, indicating high-grade osteoblastic activity. No other site of abnormal tracer activity was identified.

case_report: A 16-year-old boy was referred to a Genetic Counseling Center with concerns about general growth and developmental delay, including poor weight gain and short stature. He was born to consanguineous parents through normal vaginal delivery with APGAR scores of 9 at 1 minute, 10 at 5 minutes, and 10 at 10 minutes. At birth, his weight had a Z score of -1.7, and his head circumference had a Z score of -1.1. The parents observed cutaneous photosensitivity starting at nine months and noted intellectual disability and poor weight gain after the age of two years. The family reported mild to moderate intellectual disabilities, delays in mental milestones, learning difficulties, challenges in finding directions, and poor memory. At 16 years old, physical examination showed he is thin (20 kg, Z score: -10.47), short in stature (height of 118 cm, Z score: -6.1), and has a small chin, aged face, and sunken eyes. He also has microcephaly (Z score: -6.7) and experiences skin redness over the nose or other exposed areas following sun exposure. Additionally, he has disproportionately large ears, large hands, fine tremors, and joint contractures in both upper and lower extremities with normal muscle power. Deep tendon reflexes are mildly increased. Paraclinical tests indicated a normal male C-banded karyotype and a negative fragile X syndrome triple repeat expansion test.
test_results: Brain MRI at the age of 8 years showed demyelination and diffuse white matter changes in both cerebral hemispheres, dilated ventricular system, and slight cortical atrophy.

case_report: A 24-year-old male presented with skin lesions on his legs for three weeks, accompanied by a burning sensation. Physical examination revealed well-defined, erythematous to hyperpigmented, hyperkeratotic plaques on the dorsa of the feet and index fingers. Additionally, multiple flaccid vesicles and bullae were observed. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count and liver function tests, were normal except for slightly low serum albumin levels. The patient tested negative for hepatitis C virus, despite having a history of jaundice one month prior. Serum zinc level was measured at 54.56 μg/dL (reference range: 70–120 μg/dL).
test_results: Histopathological examination of the lesion showed hyperkeratotic epidermis with focal parakeratosis, irregular acanthosis, and elongated rete ridges. In the dermis, peri-adnexal and perivascular lymphocytic infiltration along with extravasation of red blood cells were seen.

case_report: A 46-day-old, male, full-term infant presented with ongoing jaundice, pale stools, and dark urine. He had previously been admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) for four days due to neonatal jaundice that required phototherapy. After discharge from the NICU, he was not followed up until his parents brought him back to the hospital one month later due to concerns about persistent jaundice. The infant was thriving well with good oral intake and activity. His family history included consanguineous marriage but was otherwise unremarkable. On examination, he appeared well with normal vital signs for his age. His growth parameters were within normal ranges (weight: 5.3 kg at the 63.6 percentile; length: 58 cm at the 69.7 percentile). He exhibited deep jaundice in the sclera and skin. Physical examination showed no dysmorphic features. The abdomen was soft and lax, without distention or organomegaly. Systemic examinations revealed an open anterior fontanelle (AF), normal muscle tone, strength, and reflexes, normal heart sounds (S1 and S2) with no additional sounds, equal bilateral air entry (EBAE), no bruises or skin rashes, normal male genitalia, circumcised, with bilateral descended testes. Initial laboratory workup indicated obstructive hepatic pathology, with mild transaminitis (alanine aminotransferase (ALT): 288 IU/L; aspartate aminotransferase (AST): 270 IU/L), direct hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin: 164.7 umol/L, direct bilirubin: 118.3 umol/L), elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP: 927 IU/L), normal GGT: 34 IU/L, and high alpha-fetoprotein (1832.3 ng/ml). Synthetic liver function tests for albumin and coagulation profile were within normal limits (albumin: 37 g/L; partial thromboplastin time (PTT): 37.5 seconds; prothrombin time (PT): 11.0 seconds; and international normalized ratio (INR) 1). Ultrasound examination of the abdomen showed a normal biliary system and a liver with normal size, shape, and homogeneity. Histopathological examination of the liver biopsy specimen revealed focal loss of main bile ducts, marked cholestasis with portal and peri-portal inflammation (grade 2), fibrosis (stage 1), and paucity of intrahepatic bile ducts. Intraoperative cholangiography showed a patent bile duct, no inclusion defect in the gall bladder, and no biliary system dilatation.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing revealed homozygous mutations in exon 17 of TJP2 (C.2524C >T).

case_report: A 64-year-old male presented with acute abdominal pain for 2 days. Imaging of the abdomen revealed fecal material and bowel gas in the gastrointestinal tract. Pathological examination identified focal signet-ring-like cells mixed with goblet crypt-like cells extending from the submucosal layer to the subserosal layer. There was notable perineural invasion and lymphovascular invasion. Clinical examination did not reveal any tumors in other areas. A complete right hemicolectomy was performed, which showed no residual tumor.
test_results: Immunohistochemical profiles demonstrated dual differentiation: CK7(−), CK20(+), CDX2(+), CD56(+), synaptophysin (+), and chromogranin (+) in the tumor cells.

case_report: A 62-year-old mestizo female with a history of hypertension presented with intensely itchy lesions on her upper and lower limbs for 18 months, with no identifiable trigger. Dermatological examination revealed erythematous papular plaques, some with serohemorrhagic vesicles and erosions on the limbs and back, as well as papular purpuric lesions on the lower limbs. Hard and adherent lymphadenopathies were noted in the cervical, supraclavicular, and axillary regions. Hydrochlorothiazide was discontinued after a prior skin biopsy suggested a drug-related skin eruption, but there was no improvement. Prednisone at 80mg per day was initiated, resulting in only partial control of symptoms. Laboratory tests were reviewed, and a hematology consultation was requested. An antihistamine was prescribed for pruritus control. The patient experienced periods of remission and exacerbation of the skin condition during follow-up.
test_results: The histopathologic examination showed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, papillary dermal edema with cleavage and subepidermal blisters; a moderate, lymphohistiocytic and eosinophilic diffuse dermal inflammatory infiltrate, extending to the hypodermis, besides the typical 'flame figures' in the middle and deep dermis. DIF was negative and the immunohistochemical examination ruled out neoplastic skin infiltration.

case_report: A 78-year-old woman, who has been on a regimen including low-dose corticosteroids and proton pump inhibitors for 7 years, underwent high anterior resection and partial liver resections for rectosigmoid colon cancer with multiple liver metastases (S4, S6, and S8). Preoperative serum levels of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) and carbohydrate antigen (CA19-9) were 7.9 ng/ml (normal range, ≤5.8 ng/ml) and 85.7 U/ml (normal range, 0 to 37.0 U/ml), respectively. Pathological examination revealed well-differentiated tubular adenocarcinoma, T3N1M1 with lymphatic invasion. The S4 liver lesion had a positive resection margin. Postoperatively, she received adjuvant therapy (capecitabine plus oxaliplatin) for 6 months but discontinued due to side effects. One year post-surgery, an abdominal CT showed increased ascites and suspected peritoneal dissemination (Figure A). Tumor markers were within normal range, but ascites increased, and symptoms such as nausea, emesis, and abdominal distension worsened. A contrast study indicated delayed transit through the small intestine with eventual movement into the colon. FDG PET-CT suggested peritonitis carcinomatosa with diffuse low-grade FDG uptake along the small intestinal wall (Figure B). Decompression of the small intestine and administration of octreotide were initiated, but intestinal dilatation and stasis persisted (Figure). Preoperative lab results showed anemia (hemoglobin 9.6 g/dl), mildly elevated liver enzymes (aspirate aminotransferase 43 IU/l, alanine aminotransferase 47 IU/l), and poor nutritional status (total protein 4.9 g/dl, albumin 2.9 g/dl). During laparotomy, a moderate amount of serous ascites and dilatation of the small intestine with a whitish film overlaying it were observed. The bowel was hardened with wall thickness and limited contractility, similar to findings in encapsulating peritoneal sclerosis (Figure A,B). These findings were consistent throughout the small intestine. No evidence of peritoneal dissemination or mechanical obstruction was found.
test_results: Fibrotic change in the muscle and serosal layers was observed.

case_report: A 15-year-old boy from Nepal visited the medicine out-patient department with a history of high-grade fever, anorexia, and a weight loss of 10 kg over the past 5 months. He had no specific localizing symptoms, history of travel, exposure to ill contacts, or high-risk behavior. He had been treated with oral anti-tuberculosis therapy for 3 weeks by a local physician due to persistent fever. His past medical history included fever and jaundice 3 years ago, which resolved with conservative management. The patient is the youngest of eight siblings, born to non-consanguineous parents. The family history includes the death of five siblings due to undiagnosed illnesses with prolonged fever, two of whom also had jaundice. All deceased siblings passed away between the first and third decades of life. Anti-tuberculosis therapy had been started in three of these siblings without conclusive evidence of tuberculosis. The two surviving elder siblings also had a history of undiagnosed fever with jaundice, which resolved spontaneously within a few weeks. Details of treatment regimens and investigations for the deceased siblings were unavailable. Upon admission, the patient was conscious and oriented, with a fever of 38.3°C, tachycardia (pulse rate 110/min), and hypotension (blood pressure 95/60 mmHg). His respiratory rate was 20/min with 96% oxygen saturation on room air. Physical examination revealed pallor, icterus, and hepatosplenomegaly, but no rash, clubbing, cyanosis, or edema. Initial investigations showed severe pancytopenia and abnormal liver function tests. Due to the possibility of drug-induced liver injury, anti-tuberculosis therapy was modified, and empirical antibiotics were administered according to the febrile neutropenia regimen. Blood work-up revealed hyperferritinemia (3,346 ng/mL [reference range (RR): 20–250 ng/ml]), hypertriglyceridemia (33,658.1 mg/dL [RR: <150 mg/dL]), and elevated LDH (1,748 U/L [RR: 60–170 Units/L]). Further investigations showed a high titer of EBV viral-capsid antigen (EBV-VCA) immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibody, indicating an acute EBV infection. Other infection tests revealed sterile blood and urine cultures, negative serology for brucellosis, leishmaniasis, and enteric fever, a negative tuberculin skin test, and negative viral and autoimmune markers.
test_results: A bone marrow biopsy revealed hypercellular marrow showing dense histiocytic infiltration with evidence of hemophagocytosis as well as an atypical T-cell infiltrate. 18FDG-positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET CT) scan showed hepatomegaly (22.7 cm) and splenomegaly (17.9 cm), which was metabolically active with multiple FDG-avid abdominal and pelvic nodes. There was also significant FDG uptake in the axial and appendicular skeleton and the presence of FDG-avid, hypodense, bilateral, thyroid masses.
diagnosis: Familial Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis  with Perforin Gene  Mutation and EBV-associated T-cell Lymphoproliferative Disorder of the Thyroid
Orpha_name: Hemophagocytic syndrome associated with an infection

case_report: A 19-year-old woman experienced focal impaired awareness seizures (FIAS) with an aura of olfactory hallucinations, followed by behavior arrest and prominent oroalimentary automatism. She had no history of focal to bilateral tonic–clonic seizures. Her FIAS persisted for over 2 years despite treatment with 1000 mg of levetiracetam (LEV), occurring at a frequency of one seizure per week. The Edinburgh Handedness Inventory Test indicated left language dominance (right-handed). The Wechsler Memory Scale-Revised (WMS-R) showed no memory decline, with scores of verbal memory 94, visual memory 103, general memory 96, attention/concentration 105, and delayed recall 96. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a mass lesion in the left Sylvian fissure with homogeneous hyperintensity on both T1-weighted and T2-weighted images, and no diffusion restriction on diffusion-weighted images/apparent diffusion coefficient maps. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images showed normal signal in the hippocampus. Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography indicated severe focal hypometabolism in the left anterior temporal lobe. Preoperative long-term scalp video-EEG monitoring using the 10–20 international system for 3 days did not show ictal discharges but detected interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs) at T1 and F7 electrodes with reproducibility.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the neocortical specimen of the anterior temporal lobe revealed neuronal cytoarchitectural abnormalities in the cortex.
Orpha_name: Isolated focal cortical dysplasia type I

case_report: A 50-year-old female, with a history of steroid therapy, presented with symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis that has persisted for 17 years. In 2003, the patient developed cutaneous nodules symmetrically located on the joints of the hands, ankles, shoulders, and elbows. Over the next six months, the patient experienced stiffness, joint deformities, contractures, and restricted mobility in multiple joints, including bilateral elbows, wrists, knees, ankles, feet, MCP joints, bilateral PIP joints, and MTP and DIP joints. The patient's medical history includes fever, decreased appetite, cough, and breathlessness, as well as previous surgeries for subdiaphragmatic abscess resection and ovarian cyst removal. Physical examination revealed multiple smooth nodules, ranging from 5-20 mm in diameter, on the dorsal surfaces of the palms, upper arms, MCP joints, MTP joints, and PIP and DIP joints. These nodules were symmetrically distributed, firm, freely mobile, and non-tender. Additionally, a large scar connective tissue was noted along the lateral margin of both upper arms. Prominent joint flexion contractures were observed, particularly affecting the thumb, ring, and little fingers, resulting in a claw hand appearance. No signs of Raynaud phenomenon, calcinosis, or palmoplantar thickening were observed.
test_results: The results showed dermal fibrous hyperplasia, elastic fiber disorder, excessive skin coking, irregular thickening of the spinous layer, dermal collagen fiber hyperplasia, synovial fibrous tissue hyperplasia, thickened collagen fibers, and central degeneration and necrosis of cartilage tissue with calcification. Elastica van Gieson staining showed the reduction of elastic fibers in the dermis. In immunohistochemical examination, the spindle cells were positive for vimentin, and α-SMA, but CD68, CD163, CD34, and S100 were negative. Laboratory tests indicated positive results for both rheumatoid factor (RF) and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA). Imaging studies, including X-ray and computed tomography (CT), revealed worsening joint destruction in some PIP, DIP, and MCP joints, as well as bilateral joint space stenosis in MTP, MCP, and IP joints.

case_report: A 16-year-old girl began experiencing symptoms at the age of 10, which included sensitivity to light, visual disturbances, and difficulty seeing in low light. Examination showed visual acuities of 6/4 in the right eye and 6/5 in the left eye, with refraction measurements of +0.75/−0.75 × 30 for the right eye and +1.00/−1.00 × 140 for the left eye. Fundoscopy revealed an atrophic concentric band with white punctate dots and minimal pigment extending from the vascular arcades to the mid-peripheral retina around the macula. Visual field testing indicated decreased sensitivity from 10 degrees to 40 degrees. Colour vision testing showed reduced protan thresholds and normal tritan responses. An increased autofluorescence signal was observed at the macula and extending to the nasal area. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) indicated loss of the ellipsoid zone in the area of the band, with preservation of the central retina. Electroretinography (ERG) results showed extinguished rod-specific dim flash responses and reduced and delayed responses to standard flash under both photopic and scotopic conditions. The response to the 30 Hz flicker stimulus was abnormal, but the pattern ERG was relatively well preserved. Isolated S-cone responses were not measured. There was a marked reduction to rod stimuli and 30 Hz flicker with reduced responses to standard flash.
test_results: Genetic molecular analysis showed compound heterozygosity for NR2E3 c.119−2A > C and a novel mutation c.639_640insT, p.(P214SfsX39). Segregation analysis in her parents identified the NR2E3 variant c.639_640insT, p.(P214SfsX39) in her father, and the c.119-2A > C variant in her mother.

case_report: A 21-year-old female of Tamil descent presented in July 2021 with orthostatic complaints. Laboratory tests revealed persistent moderate macrocytic anemia with an initial hemoglobin level of 82 g/L and an MCV of 99.2 fl, while other complete blood count (CBC) values were normal. A vitamin B12 deficiency was identified and treated with a cumulative 5 mg of vitamin B12 over two months. Despite treatment, her hemoglobin level decreased to 75 g/L with unchanged RBC indices, leading to a referral to the hematology department of a tertiary hospital for further evaluation. In June 2022, the patient, now 21 years old, reported progressive fatigue. She measured 145 cm in height and weighed 40 kg (BMI 19.0). Clinical examination revealed a series of congenital malformations but no organomegaly or enlarged lymph nodes. Laboratory tests confirmed macrocytic anemia with a hemoglobin level of 74 g/L and a non-regenerative anemia indicated by an absolute reticulocyte count of 18 G/L. Other CBC values were within normal limits. Ferritin, transferrin saturation, folic acid, and vitamin B12 levels were normal, but holotranscobalamin (HoloTc) was reduced at 37.4 pmol/L. Peripheral blood film evaluation showed macrocytosis without other signs related to vitamin B12 deficiency. There was no evidence of hemolysis, and erythropoietin (EPO) was elevated at >750 mU/mL. Medical records indicated that she was born after an uncomplicated pregnancy with a ventricular septal defect, a double thumb on the right side, relative macrocephaly, and a lateral cleft lip. At 10 weeks old, she was hospitalized for anemia-related heart failure, which stabilized after transfusions. Elevated erythroid adenosine deaminase (eADA) activity was noted. Her hemoglobin levels remained stable above 80 g/L, and no steroid therapy was administered. Throughout childhood and adolescence, hemoglobin levels ranged from 85–100 g/L. The ventricular septal defect closed spontaneously around age 5, with asymptomatic cardiac performance. Due to short stature (birth height 44 cm and weight 2620 g, both <10th percentile, and both falling below the third percentile in childhood), she received somatropin supplementation from age 5 7/12 to 11 7/12, resulting in a growth of 28 cm (from 98 cm to 126 cm). After stopping treatment, she reached a height of 145 cm (father 165 cm, mother 155 cm). The cleft lip was surgically corrected with good results, and the polysyndactyly does not limit her daily activities.
test_results: The BM biopsy revealed normal cellularity for her age, but a highly atypical CD4-predominant T-lymphocytosis (60% of the total cellularity), an impairment of the maturation of all three cell lines, and mild myelofibrosis (maximum MF-1). The molecular pathological examinations showed no evidence of a clonal rearrangement of TCR gamma. A PET/CT scan showed no evidence of lymphoma. The karyotype analysis was unsuccessful due to insufficient metaphases, and recurrent findings typical of a myelodysplastic syndrome were not detected in fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). In the array-CGH, a copy neutral loss of heterozygosity of the short arm of Chromosome 3 and 8 was shown. No somatic mutation was identified. A heterozygous mutation in the RPL5 gene, variant c.392dup, p.(Asn131Lysfs*6), was detected with the TWIST Comprehensive Exome (Twist Bioscience) NGS panel.

case_report: A 35-year-old man presented with a two-month history of persistent right hip pain, which worsened with walking. He had no systemic diseases and was not on regular medication. There was no history of trauma, morning stiffness, weight loss, or fever. Physical examination showed normal range of motion (ROM) in all joints, with the exception of pain at the end range of motion in the right hip. Neurological examination was normal, and no skin lesions were observed. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, rheumatoid factor, C-reactive protein, thyroid, kidney and liver function tests, serum calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, alkaline phosphatase, 25[OH] vitamin D, and parathyroid hormone levels, were all within normal limits. Imaging studies of the pelvis revealed numerous small round areas of bony sclerosis on the upper heads of the femur and acetabulum. Further imaging with computerized tomography (CT) of the pelvis confirmed multiple round sclerotic nodular lesions in both iliac wings and sacrum. Whole body bone scintigraphy showed normal findings, but incidentally detected a kidney fusion anomaly, which was confirmed by urinary system ultrasonography.
test_results: Wrist radiogram revealed multiple symmetric foci of dense radio-opaque spots in the metaphyses of distal radius and ulna, carpal bones, metacarpals and phalanges. These radio-opaque spots are also detected on shoulder radiogram.

case_report: In January 2018, a 28-year-old Korean male visited the Department of Endocrinology at Seoul National University Bundang Hospital due to findings of hypoalbuminemia, hypoproteinemia, hypocalcemia, and vitamin D deficiency during a health check-up. The patient reported no physical discomfort and had no relevant personal or family medical history. His height was 170 cm and weight was 63 kg. Physical examination showed a blood pressure of 107/70 mm Hg, pulse rate of 70 per minute, respiration rate of 18 per minute, and body temperature of 36.8℃. Cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, and neurological assessments were normal. Blood tests revealed normal complete blood counts and electrolytes, as well as normal liver and thyroid function tests. Abnormal findings included hypoproteinemia, hypoalbuminemia, moderate hypocalcemia, vitamin D deficiency, and elevated levels of parathyroid hormone (PTH) and alkaline phosphatase (ALP). Kidney function, complement, spot urine, and albuminuria tests were conducted, and the results were normal. A kidney ultrasound showed kidneys of normal size with normal parenchyma. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy results were normal, and the patient did not exhibit symptoms of protein loss such as diarrhea. Elevated PTH levels were noted, and a parathyroid scan was performed, yielding normal results. Dual energy X-ray absorptiometry indicated normal bone density with Z-scores of −1.0 (BMD 0.703 g/cm2) on the left femoral and −0.8 (BMD 0.858 g/cm2) on the spine. Serum protein electrophoresis showed low albumin concentrations and compensatory increases in non-albumin proteins, particularly in the α1 and α2 globulin fractions.
test_results: DNA sequencing revealed a novel mutation of heterozygous single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) causing C>T transition at position c.1668 C>T, p.Leu556= in the ALB gene.

case_report: A 64-year-old male with a history of smoking for 44 years, having quit 16 years ago, presented with rapidly worsening difficulty swallowing, progressing from solids to liquids over four months, accompanied by an 18 kg weight loss during this period. Initially admitted to another facility, an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed whitish plaques throughout the esophagus, and biopsies identified Candida sp. He received intravenous antifungal treatment and was hospitalized for 28 days, but his swallowing difficulties worsened, eventually leading to an inability to swallow saliva. A subsequent endoscopy showed a vegetative mass in the esophageal mucosa, preventing access to the stomach. A nasogastric feeding tube was placed at this time. Further biopsies showed no malignancy. Upon arrival at the current institution, the patient appeared significantly emaciated.
test_results: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed whitish plaques in the entire esophagus and biopsies showing Candida sp. A new endoscopy revealed growth of a vegetative mass in the mucosa and it was not possible to reach the stomach. Another endoscopy was performed showing whitish papillomatous lesions, starting just below the cricopharyngeal muscle, increasing in size and becoming exophytic, multilobular polypoid mass, narrowing the esophageal lumen. New biopsies revealed papillary squamous epithelium, consistent with esophageal squamous papilloma without atypia. A tomography was performed, showing extensive esophageal lesion with 15 cm long, from the middle segment, completely obstructing the esophageal lumen. Esophageal walls were also thickened in the upper segment, but with esophageal lumen, preserved.
Orpha_name: Squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus

case_report: A 13-year-old female, born full-term via normal vaginal delivery to non-consanguineous parents, presented with decreased scalp hair noticed since birth. She exhibited thick, dark skin on the face, upper limbs, buttocks, and lower limbs from birth, with no history of a collodion membrane. Pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. The skin lesions thickened over time. The patient experienced recurrent pustular lesions on the scalp and body, photophobia, decreased visual acuity, and decreased hearing since childhood, along with poor school performance. There was no history of tooth loss or abnormal sweating. Gait was normal, and no other congenital abnormalities or systemic diseases were found. Family history was negative for similar issues, and she had two unaffected siblings. Examination revealed sparse scalp hair with follicular atrophy and multiple folliculitis lesions. Remaining hair was thin, rough, and hypopigmented, with normal hair shaft morphology on clinical and microscopic examination. Sparse hair was also noted in the axilla and pubic regions. Ciliary and supraciliary madarosis were present. Multiple hyperpigmented and hyperkeratotic papulo-plaque lesions were observed on the scalp, neck, distal forearm, trunk, buttocks, medial thighs, and lower legs. Bilaterally symmetrical, well-defined erythematous non-blanchable, non-scaly plaques were present on both cheeks. Diffuse hyperpigmentation and hyperkeratosis were noted on the elbows, knees, and dorsa of hands and feet. Bilateral palmoplantar keratoderma with a yellowish hue, velvety texture, and prominent dermatoglyphics was observed. Oral mucosa examination was unremarkable, and no nail abnormalities were detected. The patient's intelligence quotient and stature were within the normal range. Ophthalmological examination revealed bilateral corneal neovascularization and dry eye, with no abnormalities on fluorescein angiography. Otolaryngologic assessment indicated bilateral severe mixed hearing loss for higher frequencies. Routine investigations, including complete hemogram, liver function test, renal function test, and chest X-ray, were normal.
test_results: A biopsy specimen from the lower leg showed hyperkeratosis, follicular plugging, and thickening of the granular layer.

case_report: A 45-year-old female patient reported experiencing pain in the left molar region of the lower jaw for the past month. The patient was in good overall health, and her physical examination did not reveal any notable abnormalities. An intraoral examination identified a decayed left mandibular first permanent molar and the absence of the second permanent molar, which had been extracted 2 years prior due to decay.
test_results: Intraoral periapical radiograph showed well-defined irregularly shaped sclerotic masses corresponding to the roots of first and second permanent molar teeth of left mandible. Orthopantomogram showed multiple well-defined sclerotic masses with radiolucent border in both right and left molar region of the mandible. These sclerotic masses were surrounded by a thin radiolucent border and appeared to be unattached to the root apices.

case_report: A 31-year-old female patient presented to the Department of Periodontics and Oral Implantology, Maulana Azad Institute of Dental Sciences, New Delhi, with a primary complaint of multiple loose teeth. The patient was born after a full-term, uncomplicated pregnancy, and her family history was unremarkable. She had a history of vitamin D deficiency rickets at the age of one, which was treated. Her past dental history indicated normal eruption and shedding of deciduous teeth. At the age of 27, she underwent flap surgery with bone grafting in the upper anterior region. On general examination, the patient exhibited short stature (127 cm height), a long narrow trunk, short extremities with pronounced shortening in the proximal segments, bow legs, a short mid-face and maxilla, a flattened nasal bridge, and a relatively broad forehead. Limited extension and rotation were noted at the elbow, and a thoracolumbar gibbus was present. Intraoral examination showed fair oral hygiene with a plaque score of less than 1 (Sillness and Loe, 1964). The gingiva was erythematous, soft, and bled upon probing. Full mouth probing depths, mobility, and furcation involvement were recorded. Teeth 13, 14, 21, 23, 28, 33, 35, 37, 43, 45, 46, and 48 exhibited Grade I mobility; teeth 22, 26, 34, and 47 exhibited Grade II mobility; and the upper right lateral incisor exhibited Grade III mobility. Grade II furcation involvement was noted in teeth 36, 46, and 47. Generalized mucogingival problems were present. The following teeth were missing: 15, 16, 17, 24, 25, 26, 31, 32, 41, and 42. Pathologic migration was observed. The patient had Angle's Class III malocclusion with bilateral posterior cross-bite and a narrow maxillary arch.
test_results: X-ray skull (lateral view) showed relatively broad forehead and flattening of nasal bridge, short maxilla and mid-face, and short base of skull. X-ray base of skull revealed short foramen magnum. Anteroposterior (AP) spine view showed short pedicle and short interpediculate distance. Progressive narrowing of the lumbar region with posterior scalloping due to short pedicle was seen on DL spine view. Pelvis (AP) view showed characteristic “champagne glass deformity” with squaring of iliac crests. A scanogram revealed bow legs causing genu varum deformity with tibial bowing.

case_report: A 27-year-old female, 34 weeks pregnant, presented with a worsening cough, sputum production, and rhinorrhea for one week. She had no prior medical or allergy history. Vital signs and lung sounds were normal. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 13,500/µL (polymorphonuclear cells 66.6%, lymphocytes 17.7%, eosinophils 6.6%), hemoglobin of 11.8 g/dL, and a platelet count of 224,000/µL. A chest radiograph was normal. She was given symptomatic treatment with antitussive and antihistamine drugs. Two days later, she returned with wheezing in both lower lung fields. Pulmonary function tests (PFT) with bronchodilator response showed a forced vital capacity (FVC) of 3.32 L (86% of predicted), forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) of 2.74 L (83% of predicted), and FEV1/FVC ratio of 82%. Post-bronchodilator, FEV1 increased by 9%. The average forced expiratory flow rate over the middle 50% of the FVC (FEF25-75) was 63% before and 86% after bronchodilator use, with a 35% change. She was treated with a budesonide turbuhaler, clarithromycin, montelukast, and antihistamine. Two months later, she was referred back with left upper and lower lobe consolidation on chest high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) from another hospital. She reported severe cough, thick purulent sputum, and rhinorrhea, but no fever, and had lost about 7 kg post-delivery. Lung sounds were normal without wheezing. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 8,300/µL (polymorphonuclear cells 40.1%, eosinophils 14.6%), hemoglobin of 13.3 g/dL, and a platelet count of 516,000/µL. C-reactive protein was 0.51 mg/dL, urine pneumococcal antigen test was positive, and procalcitonin was <0.05 ng/mL. Electrolytes, liver, and renal function tests were normal. A chest radiograph showed infiltration in the left lower lung field, and chest HRCT showed consolidation in the left lower lobe and nodular infiltration in the left upper lobe. Electrocardiogram and echocardiography were normal. Sputum smear and culture for routine bacteria, fungi, and mycobacteria were negative. MAST allergen test was negative, and total IgE level was within normal limits. She was treated with antibiotics for Streptococcus pneumoniae and a bronchodilator.
test_results: In bronchoscopy, there was a hard purulent mass-like secretion at left lower lobe basal segment bronchus. After removal of a bronchial cast, there was no bronchial obstructive lesion. In biopsy specimen, there was consistent with mucous plug, containing necrotic epithelial cells, some eosinophils and Charcot-Leyden crystals.

case_report: The patient is a 22-year-old woman from the Fars province in southern Iran, whose parents are first-degree cousins. She exhibited no symptoms until the age of 20. During her first pregnancy, routine laboratory tests revealed elevated liver enzymes: ALT at 147 U/L (reference range: < 31 U/L), AST at 108 U/L (reference range: < 31 U/L), and Alk-P at 350 U/L (reference range: 64–306 U/L). Additionally, her serum iron level was 227 μg/dL (reference range: 50–170 μg/dL) and PT was 14.5 seconds (reference range: 10.5–11.5 seconds). She experienced a spontaneous abortion during the first trimester. Further evaluations showed negative results for autoimmune antibodies. Subsequently, she presented with symptoms including bloody vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, weight loss, and bilateral mild mid-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography indicated cirrhosis, which was confirmed by liver biopsy as cryptogenic cirrhosis. Initial clinical evaluations suggested glycogen storage disease, and she was referred for genetic counseling where whole-exome sequencing was performed.
test_results: Elevated levels of both dihydrothymine and dihydrouracil were identified in the patient’s urine in comparison with the mean concentration observed in control group’s urine (dihydrothymine (μmol/mmol creatinine): patient = 148, controls = 1.4 ± 1.1 (n = 106), dihydrouracil (μmol/mmol creatinine): patient = 254, controls = 4.9 ± 3.2 (n = 106)).

case_report: A 26-year-old female patient with a history of preterm birth at 28 weeks and developmental delay presented with delayed milestones in walking and talking. Despite graduating from high school, she was unemployed. Motor system examination revealed normal muscle strength and tone, with no motor deficits or abnormal movements. Cranial nerve function, sensory system, and deep tendon reflexes were also normal. However, the patient exhibited dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, dysarthria, and an abnormal tandem gait. Ophthalmologic examination identified congenital esotropia. Neuropsychiatric testing indicated mild cognitive impairment with a score of 31 out of 59, and an IQ test showed mild mental retardation, with scores ranging between 55 and 70.
test_results: Cranial MRI and diffusion tensor tractography findings were almost similar to those of case 1, although residual vermis tissue was smaller in this case.

case_report: A 3-year-old Saudi male, born at term via spontaneous vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 2.7 kg, presented to the emergency department at 2 years old with a 9-day history of fever, runny nose, cough, and vomiting. He also exhibited progressive lethargy and bilateral lower limb weakness, more pronounced on the right side, over the past 3 days. Additionally, he had profuse, watery diarrhea 2 days prior to presentation. There was no history of abnormal jerky movements, drug ingestion, trauma, or contact with sick individuals. He had been prescribed oral antibiotics for 1 week without improvement. His development was appropriate for his age, with no prior neurological, visual, or cognitive deficits. His past medical history included COVID-19-induced pneumonia at 6 months and acute otitis media at 20 months. He had received all vaccinations up to one year of age without complications, including live vaccines like BCG, MMR, and varicella. The patient was the first child of a consanguineous Saudi couple. The father had been diagnosed with neuromyelitis optica and was receiving monthly rituximab therapy. There was no family history of primary immunodeficiency or known genetic disease. On examination, the patient was febrile, lethargic, and hypoactive, with no facial asymmetry or dysmorphism. Pupils were reactive bilaterally, and there were no meningeal signs. Muscle tone and strength were reduced more on the right side (2/5) compared to the left side (3/5). Deep tendon reflexes were normal in the upper limbs and left lower limb but diminished in the right lower limb. Gait assessment was not possible as the patient could not bear weight. Systemic examination was unremarkable, with no signs of neurocutaneous disease. A brain CT scan showed no gross evidence of acute brain injury. A full sepsis work-up and serologic investigation for infectious or autoimmune meningoencephalitis were unremarkable. The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for neuro-vital monitoring and further management due to progressive weakness. Broad-spectrum antimicrobial and antiviral medications (ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and acyclovir) were initiated. An urgent MRI with contrast of the brain and whole spine revealed abnormal T2-FLAIR signal intensity and mild diffusion restriction in the midbrain cerebral peduncles bilaterally with leptomeningeal enhancement. Abnormal leptomeningeal enhancement was also observed in the bilateral cerebral hemispheres in the parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes and the pre-chiasmatic segments of the optic nerves. MRI of the spine showed a long segment of abnormal T2 hyperintensity and mild heterogeneous enhancement in the cervical and thoracic spinal cords, along with smooth enhancement along the cauda equina nerve roots. The patient continued to have a fever for the first 48 hours after admission, which responded to high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) (1 g/kg of body weight once daily for 2 days). There was no improvement or further deterioration in his neurologic assessment post-IVIG administration. Neuro-ophthalmologic assessment was unremarkable. The patient was discharged home after completing 3 weeks of antimicrobial therapy. He continued physical therapy with minimal improvement in lower limb weakness. At a 3-month follow-up, developmental regression in gross and fine motor skills with difficulty in phonation was noted. Parents reported repeated episodes of choking, necessitating nasogastric tube feeding for oropharyngeal dysphagia. Neurologic examination revealed axial hypotonia and diminished deep tendon reflexes. Follow-up MRIs of the brain and whole spine showed progression of signal abnormalities in the cerebral peduncles with cavitation and cystic degeneration. New bilateral areas of abnormal T2-FLAIR hyperintensity developed in the medial thalami, globi pallidi, and dorsal pons. Cervical and thoracic spinal cord signal alterations progressed to focal areas of myelomalacia and cavitation, predominantly involving the anterior horn cells. Cauda equina nerve root enhancement persisted on follow-up MRI. A trial of biotin (10 mg daily), thiamine (300 mg daily), and riboflavin (200 mg daily) was initiated, but there was no response after 4 months of therapy.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing (WES) showed that the patient harbored a novel homozygous frameshift variant in the CIITA gene (NM_001286402.1:c.1418_1424del:p.Leu473Hisfs*15). The frameshift mutation resulted in a substitution of the leucine residue at 473 to histidine, followed by 15 novel residues and a premature stop codon. Segregation analysis by Sanger sequencing confirmed that the patient was homozygous and both parents were heterozygous for the mutation. The mutation led to a complete absence of MHC II expression in B cells.
diagnosis: autosomal recessive bare lymphocyte syndrome, type II, complementation group A
Orpha_name: Immunodeficiency by defective expression of MHC class II

case_report: A 3.5-year-old girl was referred to the Department of Pediatric Otorhinolaryngology due to a cleft palate. A comprehensive assessment revealed additional malformations. The mother's history was negative for alcohol, smoking, drug abuse, fetal infections, and drug use during pregnancy. There was no family history of congenital abnormalities or consanguinity. The child had been monitored periodically since birth by pediatricians due to various issues. She experienced feeding difficulties related to orofacial malformations, including severe mandibular retrusion, cleft palate, and tongue-tie. At 3.5 years old, clinical examination showed growth retardation with a height of 77 cm (below the 3rd percentile), weight of 8800 g (below the 3rd percentile), and a head circumference of 47 cm. Craniofacial anomalies included malar hypoplasia, severe mandibular hypoplasia with retrognathia, downward slanted palpebral fissures, a high narrow hard palate, absent soft palate, small retroplaced tongue, bilateral external auditory canal atresia, and dysplastic ears. There was no evidence of mental retardation. The arms were short with limited motion in elbow extension and flexion. The lower limbs exhibited genu varum and bilateral club feet. The patient had characteristic facial features due to hypoplastic zygomatic regions and mandibular retrusion, with no restriction of jaw movement. She had speech and feeding difficulties, attributed to velopharyngeal incompetence, cleft palate, and ankyloglossia. Ocular findings included anisophthalmia, anisocoria, coloboma, and downslanting palpebral fissures due to zygomatic hypoplasia. Additionally, dysplastic low-set ears were noted. Dental and dentoskeletal relationships were within the normal range, although the lower incisors were lingually positioned with an abnormal overbite and overlap of the upper teeth.
test_results: Radiographic hand and wrist examination provided an estimated bone age of 1.5 years. Mild cardiovascular abnormalities were seen in an echocardiogram including a small Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) and mild left ventricular dilation. Hearing level was 50 dB using an audiogram. The thyroid and genitourinary tract were normal in function according to sonography. Blood amino acid chromatography was negative.

case_report: A 59-year-old male presented with a history of progressive muscle weakness starting in his late twenties at the outpatient department of the rehabilitation center, Daejeon St. Mary's Hospital (Daejeon, Republic of Korea). He was born healthy at full-term and had no health issues during childhood and early adulthood, including completing mandatory national military training. In his late twenties, he experienced frequent falls and difficulty climbing stairs, with progressive muscle weakness primarily in the pelvic girdle and proximal legs, while the motor function of the upper extremities remained normal at that time. By the age of 38, he noticed muscle weakness in the upper extremities, a waddling gait, hyperlordosis of the lower back, and anterior pelvic tilt. His gait disturbance and muscle weakness continued to progress slowly. By the age of 55, he was unable to walk and required a wheelchair for mobility. His family history indicates a genetic background of autosomal recessive inheritance related to his muscle condition. One of his elder brothers exhibited similar symptoms and was diagnosed with progressive muscular dystrophy in his twenties. The patient is married to a healthy woman and has healthy children with no signs of muscle weakness.
test_results: The electrodiagnostic study revealed myopathy, normal values in the motor and sensory nerve conduction study, and short-amplitude muscle unit action potentials with early recruitment in needle electromyography. Quantitative electromyography also showed a myopathic pattern. In the laboratory findings, the serum creatine kinase (CK) level was elevated in 2042 IU/L.
diagnosis: Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2B  with DYSF mutation

case_report: A 59-year-old woman (patient no. 18196) presented with a history of progressive recession of the frontal hairline and loss of eyebrows since 2010. She had been intermittently treated with topical corticosteroids. Upon examination, after removing her wig, five bilateral, symmetrical rounded patches of alopecia were noted in the midline occipital, temporal, and retroauricular regions.
test_results: Dermoscopic examination revealed loss of follicular orifices with mild erythema and perifollicular scaling.
diagnosis: Lichen Planopilaris  as a Koebner phenomenon in Frontal Fibrosing Alopecia

case_report: A 77-year-old male with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension presented with itchy, scaly, erythematous patches and plaques on his face and trunk for 5 months. Initial treatment with topical corticosteroids (mometasone furoate 0.1% cream) led to a significant reduction in the rashes over a few months. The patient reported no mucosal involvement, systemic symptoms, or use of over-the-counter or herbal medications. Four months post-treatment, he developed swelling of the proximal nail folds and brittle nails on multiple fingers and toes, which later progressed to nail detachment and crusted plaques on the proximal and lateral nail folds. Subsequently, a scaly erythematous patch on the left groin evolved into an infiltrative mass without serum oozing, pus, or vesicles. Physical examination of other systems was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, as well as imaging studies such as chest X-ray and computerized tomography of the chest and whole abdomen, were all normal.
test_results: Histopathological study showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia of epidermis with eosinophilic spongiosis and intraepidermal eosinophilic microabscess. Few acantholytic cells and focal area of suprabasal separation were observed. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) study showed positive IgG and C3 at intercellular space of epidermis.

case_report: A 33-year-old male experienced diarrhea one day after consuming fried pork with chili, followed by a fever the next day with a body temperature of 40°C. Blood and fecal cultures identified Salmonella Dublin. Tests for Influenza A and B viruses, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, respiratory syncytial virus, Haemophilus influenzae, varicella-zoster virus, Legionella, Campylobacter, and SARS-CoV-2 were negative. Three days later, the patient became drowsy and exhibited progressive limb weakness, dysarthria, binocular abduction paralysis, and ataxia. A brain MRI scan showed no abnormalities. After five days, the patient was unable to lift his limbs, and these symptoms were accompanied by liver and myocardial damage. Seven days later, the patient continued to have limb weakness and dysarthria, but other indicators improved, leading to his transfer from the Intensive Care Unit to the Neurology ward. Neurological examination revealed flaccid paralysis of the limbs, absence of bilateral tendon reflexes, inability to speak, ataxia (bilateral limb paralysis limited gait assessment), and positive bilateral Babinski signs. Lumbar puncture results showed normal intracranial pressure, CSF protein levels, and CSF cell count, with no bacterial growth after a 3-day culture. Follow-up brain and cervical MRI scans were normal.
test_results: The protein content had increased by 0.86 g/L (the normal range is 0.08–0.43 g/L); the cell number was normal (the number of nucleated cells was 6, normal range 0–8; the red blood cell count was 0), CSF and serum anti-GQ1b antibody was negative, and CSF anti-MOG, anti-AQP4, and anti-MBP antibodies were all negative.

case_report: A 12-year-old male presented with intellectual disability, limited speech, axial hypotonia, and distinct facial features. He reported a one-month history of bloody urethral discharge without associated flank or urethral pain. He is the second child in his family, with an older sister who is healthy. He was born at 37 weeks of gestation via vaginal delivery, weighing 3.8 kg, measuring 51 cm in length, and with a head circumference of 34 cm. At birth, he experienced mild asphyxia, which resolved with oxygen administration. He had no feeding difficulties, persistent drooling, or poor suckling, and his initial neurological examination was normal. Developmental milestones included head control at 3 months, sitting unsupported at 8 months, creeping at 15 months, and walking at 3 years. By 6 months, he exhibited axial hypotonia, developmental delay, and mild dysmorphic features. He began cooing at 5 months and babbling at 8 months, but by 1 year, he could only say 'baba' and 'mama.' He lost the ability to speak by 18 months. At 4 years, he showed poor eye contact and aversion to strangers, and by 6 years, occasional hand wringing and automatism were noted. He had no history of hospitalization, recurrent respiratory infections, constipation, or seizures. No magnetic resonance imaging was performed, and he was not on any chronic medication. Family history revealed that his mother and sister had a confirmed genetic condition, and his maternal uncles had developmental delays and died at 8 years old. His mother and grandmother had no psychiatric symptoms. The grandmother's first husband died of gastric cancer, and she remarried, having two daughters with her second husband. One of these daughters has two children, one of whom has a similar developmental delay. Additionally, the boy's grandaunt had three children, two girls and a boy, with cognitive and developmental delays, with the boy dying at 5 years old. On admission, the patient required assistance for standing, moving, and feeding. Observed craniofacial features included a broad face, deep-set eyes, protruding ears, midface retrusion, a depressed nasal bridge, and an everted lower lip vermilion. Mild hypoplasia of the scrotal sac and rugae were noted, with both testes descended bilaterally. An intelligence assessment using the Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test indicated severe mental retardation, as he could recognize only a few pictures and words.
test_results: The aCGH performed on the patient’s genomic DNA showed Xq28 duplication with breakpoints located between positions 153273980 and 153375749 bp with a size of 563.70 kb, and duplication of chromosome 17 (17p11.2p11.1) with a size of 237.67 kb. Size variations were also observed. In addition, analysis of the proband’s clinically normal sister revealed a duplication of the same region (153273980–153375749 bp), albeit with a different size, 574.40 kb. The mother showed Xq28 duplication at the same breakpoint, with a size of 543.49 kb, whereas the father’s DNA showed no duplication. No microduplication of genes, such as IRAK1, L1CAM, FLNA, or RAB39B, was observed in the Xq28 region.

case_report: A 57-year-old Chinese female presented with irregular postmenopausal vaginal bleeding for 6 months. She has a history of colon cancer and underwent a radical colon cancer operation 20 years ago. The patient and several family members have a history of cancer. Physical examination revealed a small amount of white, odorless vaginal secretions. The cervical surface appeared smooth. The vulva was atrophic, the vagina was patent, and mucosal fold atrophy was noted. The uterus was in an anterior position with a smooth surface and good range of motion. No abnormalities were detected in the bilateral adnexal areas. Routine blood tests showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Preoperative abdominal Doppler ultrasound showed that the uterus, with a size of 3.8 cm × 3.5 cm × 3.1 cm, was located in an anterior position, the uterine cavity line was clear, the endometrial thickness was 1.1 cm, and the ultrasonic echo of the endometrium was uneven. In addition, bilateral ovaries and adnexa presented no abnormality. Color Doppler flow imaging showed no abnormal blood flow signal. Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging showed that the uterus was in an anteversion and flexion position. A mass with an equal T1 and slightly long T2 signal was found in the uterine cavity, with an unclear boundary. The tumor size was about 31 mm × 23 mm, and the display of the uterine junction was not clear. The enhanced images showed that the lesions exhibited inhomogeneous enhancement. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed that the lesions exhibited a high signal. The shape and signal of the bilateral adnexa were normal. There was no obvious abnormal signal in the bladder and rectum. No abnormality was found in bilateral iliac vessels and inguinal lymph nodes. No effusion was found in the pelvic cavity, and no obvious abnormal signal was found in pelvic wall soft tissue.

case_report: Patient 3 is a 4-year-old male, born by C-section due to fetal macrosomia. At 4 years of age, the patient exhibited motor delays, walking independently at 3 years old, and speech delays, with a vocabulary of 20–30 words. Physical examination showed mild hypotonia and a significantly ataxic gait, with frequent falls. Behavioral observations included autistic features such as behavioral outbursts in unfamiliar settings, hypersensitivity to noise, and aversion to anything touching his head. Strabismus was also noted. No seizures have been reported to date.
test_results: Brain MRI revealed abnormal increased signal in the T2 imaging in thalami, brainstem, globus pallidus, and cerebellar dentate nuclei bilaterally, as well as in deep and subcortical white matter. Whole exome sequencing identified two variants inherited in trans in ABAT: a c.168+1G > A likely pathogenic variant and heterozygous c.638T > G (p.F213C) VUS.

case_report: A 32-year-old man of Turkish origin visited University Eye Hospital Tübingen (Tübingen, Germany) due to visual impairment, blurred vision, and increasing sensitivity to light in both eyes. He reported having good visual acuity during his youth and at the time of his driving test. These symptoms had been present for several years and had recently worsened significantly. There was no known family history of eye diseases. During his initial visit in 2014, his best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was measured at 20/50 in the right eye (OD) and 20/40 in the left eye (OS). The intraocular pressure was within the normal range.
test_results: Slit-lamp examination revealed multiple dense, poorly circumscribed grey-white patchy changes in the stroma accompanied by corneal opacity. Best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/50 in the right eye (OD) and 20/40 in the left eye (OS).

case_report: A 12-year-old male was referred to our center in Damascus. His parents are not related by blood. The patient has a history of pallor and anemia. Laboratory results showed hemoglobin levels with Hb A1 at 36.2%, Hb F at 62.2%, and Hb A2 at 1.6%. His father exhibited characteristics consistent with a specific hemoglobin trait, while his mother had normal indices but with Hb A2 levels at 1.9%. The patient occasionally requires blood transfusions, whereas his parents have never needed transfusions. Hematological parameters for the patient and his parents were obtained using an automated differential cell counter. Hemoglobin analysis was conducted using a capillary electrophoresis system.
test_results: The electropherogram revealed low level of (Hb A1) 36.2%, high level of (Hb F) 62.2% and low level of (Hb A2) 1.6%. The father had the β0 Codon 5 [−CT] mutation in heterozygous state, whereas, the mother presented the β+ Hb Knossos codon 27 (G > T) mutation with δ0 codon 59 [−A] mutation both in heterozygous state, thus resulting in a low level of Hb A2 (1.9%). The Molecular analysis of the proband showed that, he had inherited the β0 codon 5 [−CT] mutation from his father, and had inherited the β+ Hb Knossos codon 27 (G > T) mutation and the δ0 codon 59 [−A] mutation from his mother, so, a low level of Hb A2 (1.6%) was also observed. The result of PCR/RFLP of the Xmn-I locus at − 158 to the G훾-globin gene indicated that, the homozygosity [TT] genotype in the proband was observed.

case_report: A 17-year-old male presented to the emergency department with fever, cough, leg pain, and swelling in both lower legs. He was born to consanguineous parents and had a history of cataract surgery at age four. Physical examination revealed Marfanoid features, cognitive impairment, rhonchi in the lower zone of the left lung, and generalized swelling in both lower extremities.
