A nasopharyngeal sample tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 via PCR. Chest CT scan showed a subpleural patchy ground-glass area in the left lower lobe. Doppler venous ultrasonography identified deep venous thrombosis in both lower extremities. Laboratory results included a lymphocyte count of 700/mm3, prothrombin time/International Normalized Ratio of 1.35 (0.8-1.2), D-dimer level of 19.5 μgFEU/mL (0-0.5 μgFEU/mL), and fibrinogen level of 699 mg/dL (193-412 mg/dL). Tests for thrombophilic conditions, including factor V Leiden mutation, protein S and antithrombin levels, and antiphospholipid antibody, were within normal limits. The patient was treated with low-molecular-weight heparin for anticoagulation.
test_results: Serum homocysteine levels were above 257 nmol/mL (0-10 nmol/mL), vitamin B12 levels were 100 pg/mL (197-771 pg/mL), and folate levels were 3.07 ng/mL, hemoglobin was 8.1 gr/dL (10.2 - 13.2 gr/dL). At the follow-up two weeks later, serum folic acid and vitamin B12 levels ​​returned to normal, and serum homocysteine levels increased to 324 nmol/mL. The methionine level in the blood amino acids was 49 µmol/L. One week later, serum homocysteine level decreased to 49 nmol/mL.
Orpha_name: Homocystinuria due to cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency

case_report: A 30-year-old woman presented with a palpable neck mass that had been present for 3 years. She exhibited no clinical symptoms. Repetitive nerve stimulation testing, serum acetylcholine receptor antibody titers, and thyroid hormone levels were all within normal limits. Ultrasonography showed a hyperechoic and hypervascular 4-cm round tumor in the left neck. Chest computed tomography (CT) identified a heterogeneous capsulated mass with smooth contour measuring 3.8 cm × 4.2 cm × 3.5 cm, located between the trachea and the left common carotid artery, and distant from the lower area of the left thyroid gland.
test_results: Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) revealed a biphasic cellular pattern composed of lymphocytes and epithelial cells, with no evidence of malignancy. Histologically, fibrous capsules and the septal wall were visible, and no evidence of extracapsular invasion was observed. On microscopic examination, the tumor was composed of a lymphocyte-poor type A area and a lymphocyte-rich type B-like area. The 2 components were separated by fibrous septa or intermittently intermingled. The type A area was composed of spindle cells and terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT)-positive immature T cells, but the type B-like area contained many TdT-positive T cells and round or polygonal tumor cells with indistinct nucleoli. Cytokeratin (CK)-19 staining showed aggregates of epithelial cells in the type A area and a dense epithelial network with many CK-19-negative lymphocytes in the type B-like area.
diagnosis: Ectopic Cervical Thymoma, Stage I, Type AB

case_report: A 36-year-old female marathon runner was brought to the emergency department (ED) by Civil Defence ambulance after collapsing at the 10 km mark. Bystanders reported that she was unresponsive, trembling, and her eyes were rolling up, but there was no limb jerking observed. Her sister, who was running ahead, mentioned that the patient had been well before the marathon and that they had traveled from Australia for the event. The patient had a history of regular running, but over shorter distances. Upon arrival at the ED, she was confused, disoriented, and attempted to get off the bed. Her vital signs included a heart rate of 120 beats/min, blood pressure of 91/48 mmHg, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. Normal saline was administered through an intravenous cannula in the left antecubital fossa. Cardiovascular and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. She could move all four limbs, and her pupils were equal and reactive to light. Extensive scarring was observed on her trunk and upper limbs, sparing the hands and upper face. Previous records indicated she had sustained deep second and third degree burns over 49% of her body five years earlier, complicated by deep vein thrombosis in the right lower limb. The cicatrised skin was rubbery, firm, dry, and shiny. Rapid evaporative cooling using wet gauze and pedestal fans at 22°C was applied. One litre of normal saline was infused via two intravenous lines. The patient became progressively calmer but remained amnesic throughout her stay in the ED.
test_results: Her rectal temperature was 41.6°C initially and dropped to 38.4°C at the emergency department. Electrolytes showed the presence of some compensated metabolic acidosis (pH 7.40); pCO2 was 28.2 mmHg, pO2 98 mmHg and serum bicarbonate 16 mmol/l. Base excess was -7.3. Her creatinine kinase levels peaked at about 2,096 U/l before trending downwards. The urine myoglobin level was noted to be a maximum of 100 UG/l.

case_report: A 70-year-old woman visited the outpatient breast clinic due to changes in the skin of her left breast. She observed skin discoloration 6 months prior, which progressively increased, prompting her to seek medical attention. Her medical history includes hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, and osteoporosis, with no previous breast health issues or surgeries. She reported no associated symptoms such as pain, new masses, nipple discharge/retraction, or lymphadenopathy. During the physical examination, her vital signs were within normal limits, and she appeared to be in no distress. The breast examination revealed a single 3 × 3 cm pink, non-tender, raised lesion on the left breast at the 12:00 position. The patient agreed to a treatment procedure and tolerated it well without any complications.
test_results: The lesion was composed of confluent sheets of large lymphoid cells, predominantly located in the mid to deep dermis with focal ulcerations of the epidermis. Cells were medium to large with a moderate amount of eosinophilic cytoplasm, and large anaplastic nuclei, some with prominent nucleoli. Tissues were highly mitotic, with 95% proliferative index determined via Ki-67 staining. Abnormal cells stained positive for CD3, CD4, CD5, BCL2, MUM1, and CD30, and negative for CD20, CD10, CD8, AE1/AE3, ALK1, Myeloperoxidase, and BCL6.
diagnosis: Primary cutaneous anaplastic large cell lymphoma
Orpha_name: Primary cutaneous anaplastic large cell lymphoma

case_report: A 44-year-old female reported experiencing a sudden decrease in vision and flashes of light in both eyes for the past 2 months. The best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) measured 6/36, N24 in the right eye and 6/6, N6 in the left eye. Examination of the anterior segment revealed no abnormalities. Fundus examination showed an annular ring of altered reflex at the posterior pole in both eyes.
test_results: Fundus autofluorescence (FAF) imaging demonstrated gradually increasing hyperautofluorescence centrifugally from the fovea corresponding to the area of altered annular reflex, with the edge having maximum hyperautofluorescence. Spectral domain optical coherence tomography (SDOCT) revealed thinning of the outer nuclear layer and loss of ellipsoid zone in both eyes, the extent corresponding to the clinically visible lesion. Fluorescein angiography (FA) and indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) revealed parafoveal hyperfluorescence evident in the early phases and persisting through all phases of the angiogram. The subfoveal choroidal thickness (SFCT) was 385 μ and 399 μ in the right and left eye, respectively. Perimetry demonstrated central scotoma in both eyes. A full-field electroretinogram (ERG) revealed reduced scotopic and photopic responses in both eyes. En-face OCTA structural analysis revealed hyper-reflective dots at the level of ellipsoid zone in the right eye in a “starry-sky” pattern and in a “torpedo-like” pattern in the left eye, corresponding to the area of ellipsoid zone loss on SDOCT.

case_report: A 17-year-old girl presented with a primary concern of retained deciduous teeth. Physical examination showed short stature, prominent frontal and parietal regions, a depressed nasal bridge, a beaked nose, underdeveloped midface, an obtuse mandibular gonial angle with relative prognathism, wrinkled skin over the fingertips, and nail abnormalities. Intraoral examination identified a deep midline antero-posterior ridge of the palate, a high arched palate, multiple retained deciduous teeth with caries, crowding, and enamel hypoplasia.
test_results: Panoramic radiograph showed multiple impacted permanent and supernumerary teeth with narrow left ramus, condyle, and condylar notch. Lateral cephalogram showed hypoplastic paranasal sinuses with relative mandibular prognathism. Handwrist radiograph showed acro-osteolysis of terminal phalanges. Three dimensional CT image revealed open fontanelles and sutures, wormian bones in the lambdoidal region.

case_report: A 31-year-old right-handed woman working in finance, with drug-resistant focal epilepsy, was evaluated for epilepsy surgery in May 2017. Her neurological examination was normal. Since the age of five, she experienced seizures starting with an acoustic illusion (hearing overlapping voices and noises in both ears), accompanied by fear and a sensation of warmth. This was followed by impaired language comprehension and expression, loss of awareness, and oroalimentary automatisms. Post-seizure, language disturbances persisted for at least 10 minutes. She continued to have weekly seizures. Prolonged video-EEG showed bilateral asynchronous anterior and mid-temporal spikes interictally. One recorded seizure with usual semiology indicated an ictal onset in the right temporal region with early contralateral spreading. Brain MRI (1.5 Tesla) was normal, while 18FDG-PET/CT showed right temporal hypometabolism, more pronounced at the temporal pole and superior temporal gyrus. Neuropsychological evaluation revealed a normal cognitive profile, except for reduced phonemic fluency, naming, and verbal memory, suggesting involvement of the dominant hemisphere. Functional MRI using a T2*-weighted gradient echo planar imaging sequence was performed with three language paradigms (comprehension, association, and fluency) administered acoustically. The patient performed the tasks efficiently and had no seizures in the 15 days before the study. Visual inspection of whole-brain activity patterns showed no BOLD hemispheric activation during auditory comprehension and association tasks, and slight activation of the right middle and inferior frontal gyrus during the fluency task. Right cerebellar activation was observed during all language tasks. Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) based fiber tracking was conducted using a probabilistic algorithm with a 'seed point-waypoint' approach. Regions of interest (ROI) were identified in common anatomical locations for anterior and posterior language regions. White matter tracts were obtained using the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus as the seed point and the anterior inferior frontal gyrus (pars triangularis and opercularis) as the waypoint. Bilateral white matter tracts connecting the inferior frontal gyrus and the superior temporal gyrus were observed, with asymmetry and a prevalence of the left-sided tract, indicating left-sided language dominance. The patient provided written informed consent for further invasive study with intracerebral electrodes.
test_results: The stereo-EEG interictal recording showed an altered background and continuous epileptiform discharges in the posterior portion of the right superior temporal gyrus, which proved to be also the location of the seizure onset. Seizures presented an early propagation to the left superior temporal gyrus that clinically coincided with the irruption of language disturbance.
Orpha_name: Isolated focal cortical dysplasia type II

case_report: A 21-year-old male with no previous history of illness presented with fever, a mild headache, body aches, joint pain, and a dry cough. These symptoms started four days prior to the presentation. It was only when he noticed a rash that he came to the hospital. He had immigrated from Asia five years prior. There was no recent international travel history. He recently returned from Tennessee five days prior to the presentation. However, he reported that he did not visit the densely forested areas. On examination, there was a maculopapular, blanching rash over the volar region of the forearm, lower leg, and over his body and neck. He reported no itching or pain over the rash. He had been taking NyQuil since the onset of the fever. Despite this, his temperature was 101°F during admission. On physical examination, his conjunctiva appeared mildly injected. Besides, there was nasal congestion and a sore throat. There was diffuse muscle tenderness and arthralgia. All other systems, including the neurological, cardiovascular, and respiratory systems, were unremarkable. Measles IgM was ordered, which came back negative.
test_results: His complete blood count (CBC) on admission showed thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and hyponatremia.

case_report: A 6-year-old girl was admitted with a history of chronic difficulty breathing over 5 years, worsening in the last 2 months. At age 1, she experienced fever followed by difficulty breathing. She was treated with prednisone and antibiotics. Over the next 5 years, she received prednisone 5 mg daily. During episodes of severe respiratory infections, occurring three to five times a year, her prednisone dosage was increased to 30 mg daily. Her physical activity became increasingly limited, and she developed clubbed fingers. Two months prior to admission, she fractured her right arm and had a high fever with respiratory distress, requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation for 8 days at a local hospital. She is the younger of two siblings and has delayed physical development, occasional vomiting, and poor appetite since age one. Her parents have no history of chronic diseases. Her height is 103 cm, weight 13.7 kg, and BMI 12.9, all below the 3rd percentile for her age. Oxygen saturation was 95% with nasal oxygen supplementation at 4 L/min. Physical examination showed respiratory distress with rapid breathing. Pulmonary auscultation was normal. The liver was palpable three finger-breadths below the right costal margin, and the spleen was palpable three finger-breadths below the left costal margin. Clubbed fingers were noted.
test_results: A chest HRCT revealed the presence of crazy paving patterns. A Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) stain of the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was confirmed positive. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed diffuse enlargement of the liver and spleen. Blood ammonia was 51 umol/L. Serum ferritin was 159.89 ng/mL. Metabolic disease screening by blood testing showed Citrulline was 199 umol/L, Arginine was 15.98 umol/L, and Citrulline/Arginine was 12.44. Urine tests showed increased Uracil. Both lower extremities and left wrist X ray showed osteoporosis. The mutation in the SLC7A7 gene included C.1387 del C and IVS4+1C>T.
diagnosis: lysinuric protein intolerance  associated with pulmonary alveolar proteinosis

case_report: In 2012, a 61-year-old female presented with difficulties in word retrieval and memory issues. Her family noted that she struggled to find words and had delayed responses to questions. Her medical history was notable only for hypertension. Neurological and physical examinations were conducted, revealing no abnormalities except for impaired delayed recall. Additional evaluations included a Korean version of the Mini-Mental State Examination (K-MMSE), brain imaging, and laboratory tests.
test_results: Brain MRI showed mild cortical atrophy. The neuropsychological test revealed impairment in general neurocognitive function, especially in language, visual and verbal memory, and recognition. Ophthalmologic testing revealed right-side homonymous hemianopsia.

case_report: A 28-year-old female patient from Argentina attended an ophthalmologic consultation. She reported never having had a pupil in her right eye (RE), which she noticed when looking in the mirror, while her left eye (LE) appeared normal. Her medical history includes phototherapy for neonatal jaundice and isolated episodes of seizures associated with febrile symptoms. She has no hereditary family history of any kind. At the time of the consultation, she expressed significant concern about her personal aesthetics due to the absence of pupils. She previously visited a hospital ophthalmologic service where an attempt to perform a laser pupilloplasty was made but was ineffective. Visual acuity testing using the Snellen chart for distant vision showed only light perception in her RE and 20/20 vision in her LE. Examination for strabismus revealed a slight exotropia.
test_results: On slit-lamp biomicroscopy examination of the RE, the peripheral cornea exhibited a whitish, arcuate, and concentric ridge parallel to the sclerocorneal limbus, with well-defined edges at the 6-to-12-hour temporal level that affected the entire corneal thickness, belonging to a posterior embryotoxon associated with a completely absent pupil. Examination with the Goldmann lens for gonioscopy revealed dysgenesis of Schwalbe’s line associated with peripheral anterior synechiae in the RE that produced traction of the iris with a marked displacement that hid the pupil, giving the characteristic appearance of pseudoacorea. The study of corneal topography with a Scheimpflug camera revealed an absence of pupil in the RE and a smaller horizontal visible iris diameter than in the LE where the parameters were normal. Optical tomography of the anterior pole shows ocular dysgenesis in the RE with the appearance of a posterior embryotoxon and adhesion bands to the peripheral processes of the iris, creating iridocorneal junction bridges.

case_report: A 3-year-old male child exhibited developmental delays and feeding challenges from birth, with no prenatal or perinatal risk factors. Family history was unremarkable, and the pregnancy was normal. He was delivered at 38 weeks gestation, weighing 3.25 kg and measuring 50 cm in height. The child did not meet age-appropriate developmental milestones. At present, his height is 89.7 cm (<3rd percentile), weight 10.5 kg, and head circumference 43.7 cm (<3rd percentile). He can sit and crawl briefly but is unable to stand or walk. He shows no response to auditory stimuli or simple verbal commands and cannot articulate simple words. Clinical features include developmental delay, small stature, open mouth with drooling, underdeveloped teeth, hypotonia, paresthesia, and behavioral issues such as hyperactivity and aggression, along with mild facial features. There is no evidence of anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, or urogenital abnormalities. The development quotient (DQ) is <20, indicating severely impaired adaptive behaviors. ECG results were normal, and brain MRI showed no abnormalities. Hearing and ophthalmological assessments were normal. Laboratory tests, including CBC, MCV, MCH, and HbA1c, were within normal ranges. Hemoglobin electrophoresis results were: alkali-resistant HB determination 0.4%, HbA2 2.4%, HbA 97.2%, with no Hb-H inclusion bodies detected. Metabolic screening via mass tandem spectrometry and gas chromatography was negative. Additional laboratory tests, including thyroid function, TORCH screen, blood ammonia, and lactate, showed no abnormalities. Despite 6 months of rehabilitation therapy, physical therapy, and speech and cognitive training, there was no significant improvement in neurological function.
test_results: Genetic screening in the proband's family for inherited diseases was recommended.

case_report: A 14-month-old female toddler with no known medical conditions presented with generalized progressive asymptomatic skin lesions that began at seven months old. Her perinatal history was uneventful, and there were no changes in her activity levels. There was no history of frequent choking during oral intake, irritability, or fever. Family history was unremarkable with no similar cases. Developmental milestones were appropriate for her age. Skin examination showed multiple scaly mottled violaceous patches on her upper and lower extremities. Lesional skin punch biopsy revealed mild perivascular dermal lymphocytic infiltration with melanin inconvenience. Laboratory tests were within normal ranges for CBC, CPK, LDH, AST, ferritin, CRP, and ESR levels. ANA and dsDNA were negative. She was prescribed moisturizer creams. A year later, at 26 months old, the scaly poikilodermatous skin patches had become more widespread. The mother reported dissatisfaction with the child's activity levels, frequent choking during oral intake, inability to stand, preference for being carried, persistent unhappiness, and irritability. The child could not sit unsupported or bear weight while standing. Other developmental milestones were appropriate except for gross motor delay. Skin examination showed generalized scaly poikilodermatous patches over the body, with mild involvement of the trunk and face. Laboratory tests showed low WBC and hemoglobin counts, and elevated CPK, LDH, ferritin, CRP, and ESR levels. ANA and dsDNA were negative.
test_results: MRI revealed the right anterior thigh and vastus lateralis subcutaneous edema.

case_report: A 22-year-old woman arrived at the emergency department with generalized weakness, vomiting, abdominal pain, constipation, a 40-lb weight loss, and severe intermittent headaches over the past 2 days. She had previously undergone evaluation over the last 3 months for episodes of fainting, abdominal pain, vomiting, and chronic constipation. In the 2 weeks before her hospitalization, her mother reported episodes of right-sided weakness and facial droop. Initial non-contrast CT scan showed a left-sided temporal cyst. An MRI revealed that this cyst had a component of diffusion restriction and subtle FLAIR hyperintensities in the bilateral parietal and occipital lobes, thought to be secondary to leptomeningeal enhancement. No cerebral edema was seen on CT imaging. While in the emergency room, she experienced a witnessed tonic-clonic seizure, which was stopped with diazepam, followed by a prolonged post-ictal period of approximately 4 hours. She developed a fever of 38.9 degrees Celsius and became increasingly encephalopathic after the seizure, leading to a lumbar puncture and empiric treatment for meningitis. Her opening pressure was >55 cm H2O with an initial CSF profile showing glucose 80 mg/dl, protein 10, WBC 10 × 109/L, and RBC 525 × 109/L. Her neurological exam at the time of lumbar puncture did not show any focal deficits. Based on her recent imaging, exam, and CSF profile, she was started on empiric treatment for encephalitis. About 18 hours after the lumbar puncture, the patient became anisocoric and reported a severe headache but had intact motor strength and sensation in both upper and lower extremities. A second emergent CT scan of the head showed downward cerebral tonsillar herniation and global edema. Following a 3% hypertonic saline bolus and admission to the neuro-intensive care unit (NICU), an external ventricular drain (EVD) was successfully placed, with an opening pressure of 58 mm Hg. The patient was intubated for airway protection as she was increasingly unable to clear secretions. Intracranial pressure (ICP) management was initiated with sedation (propofol, fentanyl), hypertonic therapy, acetazolamide 1 gm BID, and dexamethasone. Midazolam was added due to intermittent ICP spikes into the 30s. Extensive testing for autoimmune and infectious sources of her presentation was initiated and was unrevealing. It was later reported by a family member that the patient had been taking “supplements” for months leading up to admission; the toxicology team was consulted. An abdominal x-ray showed evidence of radio-opaque material, prompting further investigation for heavy metal poisoning.
test_results: A peripheral blood smear demonstrated basophilic stippling.

case_report: A 62-year-old male patient with a history of arterial hypertension and a previous surgery for a herniated lumbar disc at the L4-L5 level was referred for evaluation of neuropsychiatric symptoms. The patient had a family history of 'presenile dementia' in his mother, ALS in his older brother who passed away at 53, and behavioral symptoms in another brother. The patient exhibited a progressively worsening steppage gait starting 20 years ago and became unable to walk independently a year before admission. He also developed obsessive behavior, aggression, palilalia, and apathy. Neuropsychological evaluation indicated severe cognitive impairment with predominant frontal lobe dysfunction, scoring 2 on the MMSE and 0 on the FAB. Brain MRI revealed mild frontal lobe atrophy. EMG results showed diffuse myopathic findings and mild spontaneous activity.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed a pathogenic heterozygous missense mutation p.R159H (c.476G > A) in the VCP gene.
diagnosis: Inclusion Body Myopathy with Paget's Disease of Bone and Frontotemporal Dementia
Orpha_name: Inclusion body myopathy with Paget disease of bone and frontotemporal dementia

case_report: A 58-year-old female presented to the outpatient clinic with a 1-year history of vague abdominal pain associated with nausea and vomiting. She denied any changes in her bowel habits. Her past medical history includes Type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and hypertension. On examination, she had mild generalized abdominal tenderness without guarding or rebound tenderness. No enlargement in the lymph nodes. On laboratory analysis, a full blood work-up was done including complete blood count, electrolytes, liver function test and they were normal. The tumor markers CEA, CA19-9 and CA 125 were also normal. An ultrasound of the abdomen revealed a homogeneous hypoechoic lesion anterior to the left hepatic lobe. Color Doppler images showed internal blood flow. A subsequent abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a 4.9 × 5.5 cm well-defined, homogeneous, progressively enhancing mass anterior to the left hepatic lobe. EGD and CT colonography were done and both came back negative for synchronous lesions. The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy. The surgical exploration revealed a mass originating from the falciform ligament measuring around 6 × 6 cm that was soft in nature. There was no peritoneal metastasis. The tumor was completely resected, and the specimen was sent for further evaluation. The post-operative recovery was uneventful.
test_results: The resected mass was measured 7.0 × 6.5 × 5.0 cm and it was composed of fibrofatty tissue and peritonized surface. Microscopic examination demonstrated that the tumor is composed of cellular sheets of highly atypical pleomorphic cells. The tumor cells are hyperchromatic, some with bizarre nuclei, in a background of myxoid stroma, all consistent with high-grade sarcoma. The tumor cells were negative for CD117, DOG-1, SMA, Myogenin, Calretinin, WT-1, HMB45, SOX-10 and S100, which exclude GIST (gastrointestinal stromal tumor), smooth and skeletal muscle, mesothelial, melanocytic/malignant PECOMA and neural differentiation, respectively. The tumor cells were positive for CD99, Vimentin and CD34, which is consistent with a mesenchymal differentiation and sarcoma. In immunohistochemistry, there was loss of nuclear staining for RB1. In addition, there was lack of MDM2 amplification by FISH and lack of sarcoma-specific fusions by Sarcoma Targeted Gene Fusion Panel (SARCP) testing.

case_report: A 55-year-old male with a history of distal gastrectomy and antecolic Roux-en-Y reconstruction performed 3 years prior for gastric cancer (tub2, T1, N0, M0, pStage IA) presented with a rapidly enlarging intraabdominal mass that developed postoperatively. The patient had not received adjuvant chemotherapy and had no other significant medical or surgical history. Upon admission, his vital signs were as follows: height 167 cm, weight 49 kg, blood pressure 118/73 mm Hg, heart rate 67 beats/min, and body temperature 36.6°C. Physical examination revealed a soft and flat abdomen with a midline incision scar and a mobile, elastic, hard mass palpable on the left side. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count and serum chemistry, were within normal limits, as were tumor markers (carbohydrate antigen 19-9, carcinoembryonic antigen, α-fetoprotein, neuron-specific enolase, cytokeratin 19 fragment, and soluble interleukin-2 receptor). Abdominal contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) initially identified a small mass measuring 14 mm near the Roux-en-Y limb anastomosis 22 months prior, which had not invaded the small bowel. Retrospective observation confirmed this finding. The mass had grown from 33 mm (6 months prior) to 82 mm at the time of surgery. Preoperative CT showed the tumor measuring 82 × 75 mm, appearing to originate from the mesentery of the small intestine. 18F-2-fluoro-2-deoxyglucose positron emission tomography (PET) revealed heterogeneous enhancement with an SUVmax of 4.40 in the lower abdomen. The tumor's mobility on previous CT scans supported its mesenteric origin. No significant findings indicated metastasis or other lesions. Due to the lack of a suitable route for a percutaneous or endoscopy-assisted biopsy, resection was chosen for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes.
test_results: The tumor was located in the mesentery of the small intestine, and spindle-shaped cells resembling fibroblasts or myofibroblasts proliferated sparsely with intervening collagen fibers. Invasive proliferation into the surrounding fat tissue was observed in the marginal area of the tumor. The immunohistochemistry results were negative for desmin, α-smooth muscle actin, CD34, and c-kit. Positivity for the nuclear accumulation of β-catenin was observed.

case_report: A 12-day-old female neonate was admitted to a local hospital presenting with anorexia, lethargy, and fever. Biochemical tests revealed a fasting blood-glucose (FBG) level of 20.3 mmol/L and triglyceride (TG) level of 16.71 mmol/L. Despite treatment with antibiotics and intravenous insulin infusion, her symptoms persisted. She was subsequently transferred to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) of our hospital 4 days later. The newborn's mother had hyperthyroidism during pregnancy. The neonate was delivered naturally at 41 weeks gestational age with turbid amniotic fluid and a slightly short umbilical cord. Her APGAR scores were 7 at 1 minute and 9 at 5 minutes after birth. Her birth weight was 3260 g. She is the first child of non-consanguineous parents with no family history of hereditary diseases. Upon admission to our NICU, the patient's weight was 3490 g, height was 50 cm, and occipitofrontal circumference was 34.5 cm. Physical examination revealed a lipoatrophy phenotype and the liver was palpable 8 cm below the right middle clavicle. Laboratory tests conducted on the day of hospitalization showed a white blood cell (WBC) count of 8.36 × 10^9/L and a C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration of 13 mg/L. Blood culture was negative. Biochemical tests indicated no abnormalities in liver and kidney function, an FBG level of 17.8 mmol/L, serum sodium level of 129 mmol/L, and TG level of 42 mmol/L. The C peptide level was 4.60 nmol/L and the insulin level was 520.2 pmol/L. Thyroid function tests did not show significant abnormalities. Abdominal CT revealed liver enlargement and hepatic adipose infiltration. Cardiac ultrasound identified an atrial septal defect measuring 1.6 mm.
test_results: Genetic analysis revealed two heterozygous nonsense mutations in the patient’s BSCL2 gene [c.793C > T (p.Arg265*), c.565G > T (p.Glu189*)] inherited from the father and mother respectively. Sanger sequencing verified this conclusion.

case_report: A 14-year-old female presented with severe lower abdominal and back pain persisting for the past 3 months. The pain, colicky in nature and radiating to the back, was often accompanied by nausea and vomiting, beginning with the onset of her menstrual cycle and lasting for 5 to 7 days. She also experienced urinary retention 24 hours before admission. She had her first menstrual period at age 10 and had regular cycles every 28 days with scanty flow. Her pregnancy and birth were unremarkable, and there was no family history of congenital anomalies. She had no other health issues since birth, was not sexually active, and was not using contraceptives. A few months prior, she developed severe dysmenorrhea, leading her caretakers to consult a general practitioner, who provided symptomatic treatment with an antispasmodic agent and analgesic, resulting in brief symptom relief. She was then referred to a tertiary care center for further management. On general examination, she had mild anemia, and abdominal examination revealed a tense urinary bladder. Per vaginal examination showed a bulged hymen with obstructed hemivagina. She was afebrile with normal vital signs. Routine investigations included a complete blood count and urine routine microscopic examination (RME). Her complete blood count showed a hemoglobin level of 11.5 g/dl, white blood cell count of 6.07 x 10^3/mm^3 with normal differential counts, and a platelet count of 259 x 10^3/mm^3. Urine RME showed no signs of infection, with pus cells at 1-2/HPF, epithelial cells at 2-4/HPF, and no red blood cells.
test_results: Ultrasonography of the whole abdomen revealed the uterus to have a separate fundus, body, cervix, and vagina with mild to moderately dense endometrial collections in the right moiety of the didelphys uterus which is continuous with the large dense collection (12.5 x 6 cm) within the vagina. The left moiety of the uterus showed normal features. A non-visualized right kidney (agenesis) was also appreciated via ultrasonography. A diagnosis of didelphys uterus with hematometrocolpos with an absent right kidney was concluded. Additional imaging with a computed tomography (CT) urogram revealed an absent right kidney and ureter, along with uterine didelphys with hematocolpos and a normally excreting left kidney.

case_report: An 8-year-old male patient was referred to the ophthalmology clinic due to persistent superficial corneal opacities observed after a mild conjunctivitis episode two months prior. The conjunctivitis was treated with ofloxacin eye drops (3 mg/ml) four times daily and resolved within a week. No specific testing was performed during the acute stage of the conjunctivitis. Due to ongoing superficial corneal abnormalities in both eyes, the patient was administered hydrocortisone eye drops (3.35 mg/ml) twice daily for two weeks and once daily for one week, but no significant improvement was noted. On examination, the patient reported no ocular complaints and had no significant medical or drug history, nor any previous ocular disease except for the reported conjunctivitis. There was no relevant family history. The best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 1.0 in both eyes with the following refraction: right eye (RE) +6.0 Dsph −4.5 Dcyl axis 170° and left eye (LE) +6.0 Dsph −3.5 Dcyl axis 175°. After tropicamide cycloplegia, the refraction was RE +7.0 Dsph −4.75 Dcyl axis 170° and LE +7.0 Dsph −4.0 Dcyl axis 175°. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 14 mmHg in both eyes. Axial length measured 20.94 mm for the right eye and 21.12 mm for the left eye. Slit lamp examination revealed multiple diffuse, grayish, indistinct superficial corneal opacities extending from limbus to limbus with subepithelial haze, similar in both eyes. Fundus examination was unremarkable. Anterior segment swept source OCT (SS OCT) showed abnormalities in anterior topography and pachymetry map, with bilateral general corneal thinning. Corneal apical thickness (CAT) was 360 μm in the right eye and 365 μm in the left eye, with the thinnest portions measuring 352 μm and 350 μm, respectively, located in the inferotemporal region of both eyes. Keratometric and posterior topography maps indicated with-the-rule astigmatism (RE = 5.3 D; LE = 4.7 D). The corneal shape was prolate for both anterior and posterior surfaces. Anterior and posterior elevation maps showed a typical pattern with the apex demonstrating warm colors above the BFS (RE: 7 μm, 5 μm; LE: 9 μm, 4 μm) and a slightly elevated isthmus joining the central cornea from the temporal periphery. Right-left mirror symmetry was present. Fourier indices analysis revealed abnormalities in regular astigmatism on both surfaces and asymmetry on the anterior surface. The 6 mm keratometric and real higher-order index analysis were borderline in both eyes. The Ectasia Screening Index (ESI) was 0% in both eyes. High definition (HD) morphology scans showed discrete, diffuse hyperreflective opacities with no clearly distinguishable borders and various shapes located in the anterior cornea beneath the epithelium. Confocal microscopy, performed after topical instillation of 0.5% proparacaine hydrochloride eye drops, revealed normal epithelial layers but multiple, differently oriented dark striae starting at Bowman’s layer, prominent at depths of 90–150 μm, and less evident at increasing depths. The keratocytes and intercellular space had a granular, hyperreflective appearance throughout the stroma. Corneal endothelial morphology was not documented due to poor cooperation during the examination. Confocal microscopy indicated changes affecting the entire corneal stroma. The patient's parents were examined for possible corneal abnormalities, but no changes were found. The familial history did not reveal any significant ocular diseases or parental consanguinity.
test_results: The known homozygous, pathogenic variant c.1 A > T (p.M1?) was found following CHST6 gene analysis for our patient (proband). CHST6 gene sequencing for both parents revealed the same variant in a heterozygous state.

case_report: A 69-year-old male presented with a 1-year history of red papules and plaques accompanied by severe itching. He had a 20-year history of oral lesions. One year prior, skin lesions appeared 3 days after receiving the second dose of the COVID-19 vaccine, initially presenting as isolated papules on both lower extremities, which then rapidly coalesced and spread across the entire body. Previous treatments included compound glycyrrhizin, an antihistamine agent, tripterysium glycosides, fluticasone propionate, and fluoconodimethyl sulfoxide, all of which resulted in an unsatisfactory response. Physical examination revealed widespread red papules, edematous erythema, and multiple crusts on the scalp, face, neck, trunk, and extremities. Violet plaques with white stripes were noted on the bilateral buccal mucosa and soft palate. There were no lesions on the nails or scalp. Laboratory investigations showed eosinophilia with an eosinophil percentage of 11.4% and elevated serum total IgE levels at 150 kU/L (normal range: 0–60 kU/L).
test_results: Histopathology demonstrated intercellular epidermal edema, a subepidermal blister with an underlying sparse dermal perivascular infiltrate consisting of lymphocytes and eosinophils. DIF showed linear depositions of IgG and complement component 3 at the BMZ. Indirect immunofluorescence utilizing monkey esophagus substrate demonstrated serum anti-BMZ autoantibodies of IgG at 1:40 dilution. IgG autoantibody targeting NC16A domain of bullous pemphigoid (BP) 180 by enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) was weakly positive (12 U/ml, normal range, <9 U/ml).

case_report: A 41-year-old woman presented to the ER with a 4-week history of dizziness, nausea, and vomiting. She had a past medical history of antiphospholipid syndrome associated with spontaneous abortions but was otherwise in good health. Two weeks before admission, she underwent a CT scan of the head and an ultrasound of the deep veins in her lower extremities, which ruled out thrombosis. Upon admission, physical examination revealed pedal pitting oedemas, with the rest of the clinical examination being normal. The patient also reported excessive mucous production and involuntary weight loss. Laboratory tests showed severe hypoalbuminemia at 18.1 g/L (normal > 36.0 g/L), low total protein at 32 g/L (normal > 64 g/L), and hypogammaglobulinemia at 2.3 g/L (normal > 5.4 g/L). All other blood values were within normal limits.
test_results: A gastroscopy was performed, which revealed hyperaemic profoundly enlarged gastric folds in the body of the stomach. The histopathological assessment showed a hyperplastic mucous membrane characterized by focal erosions and chronic inflammation, but no signs of malignancy. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest and abdomen showed marked hyperemic rugal folds in the gastric body as well as hypoalbuminemia-induced thickened and oedematous colonic haustra projected into the transverse colon lumen. Infections with cytomegalovirus and Helicobacter pylori were ruled out by serological tests (anti-CMV-IgG positive and anti-CMV-IgM negative, anti-HP-IgG and anti-HP-IgM negative) and by immunohistochemistry (IHC) performed on the biopsies (no staining of inclusions or Helicobacter pylori bacteria). The histopathological examination further supported the diagnosis, with findings of marked foveolar hyperplasia with cystically dilated foveolar glands and prominent mucin production.

case_report: A 74-year-old male was admitted for evaluation and surgical intervention of a liver mass. His medical history includes a sacroabdominal rectal amputation for a rectal tumor at age 65. The excised specimen revealed a 2 cm × 2.5 cm intraluminal growth with a central ulcer. Histological examination indicated a spindle-cell tumor, with strong positivity for MIB-1, and negative surgical margins. The mitotic index was greater than 5/50 high power fields. Post-surgery, the patient opted out of adjuvant chemotherapy and adhered to regular follow-up as per guidelines. The patient has never traveled outside Japan. Nine years post-surgery, a follow-up CT scan identified a 14-mm low-density area in segment 8 of the liver, with nonhomogeneous peripheral enhancement and isodensity in the late phase. Retrospective analysis of a CT scan from six months prior showed the mass had increased in size. Laboratory results were normal except for a slightly elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 0.6 mg/dL. Tests for hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis B e-antigen, and hepatitis C virus antibody were negative. Serum levels of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9), and α-fetoprotein (AFP) were within normal limits. Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI with gadolinium ethoxybenzyl diethylenetriamine pentaacetic acid (EOB-MRI) showed the mass to be isointense in the arterial phase and completely washed out in the delayed and hepatocyte phases. Gastroscopy and colonoscopy revealed no abnormalities. FDG-PET scan demonstrated strong uptake in the liver mass with no other abnormal uptake detected.
test_results: Microscopic examination of the paraffin section of the liver ‘tumor’ showed that it was composed of fascicles of spindle cells, such as fibroblasts and myofibroblasts, accompanied by many lymphocytes, plasma cell, neutrophils, and macrophages. No mitotic cells were observed in these spindle cells. IHC studies of the spindle cells showed positive staining for smooth muscle actin (SMA) and vimentin, and negative staining for desmin, CD34, and cytokeratin AE1/3. Thus, the spindle cells were diagnosed as myofibroblasts. IHC studies of white blood cells revealed that the majority of lymphocytes expressed CD3 and some cells expressed CD20. Moreover, IHC revealed some IgG4-positive plasma cells.

case_report: A 24-year-old male patient has experienced recurrent palpitations and atypical chest pain for 5 years. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) was conducted following an echocardiogram. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 113/87 mmHg and a regular heart rate and rhythm. The thyroid was normal in size and consistency without nodules. There was no elevated jugular venous distention or lymphadenopathy. Lung auscultation was clear bilaterally. Cardiac examination showed no extra heart sounds or murmurs. Abdominal examination indicated hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. There was no peripheral oedema, and the skin had no special lesions. The patient had a history of hypoglycaemia and hepatomegaly since infancy but no family history of metabolic or cardiac disease. Electrocardiogram results showed a prolonged Q-T interval (QTc 548 ms) and non-specific ST-T changes, with no pre-excitation observed on a 24-hour Holter electrocardiogram. Laboratory tests revealed decreased early morning fasting blood glucose (3.0–4.0 mmol/L), significantly elevated creatine kinase (CK, 2210 IU/L, normal reference value: 19–226 IU/L), alanine aminotransferase (61 IU/L, normal reference value: <50 IU/L), aspartate aminotransferase (179 IU/L, normal reference value: <40 IU/L), and glutamyl transpeptidase (181 IU/L, normal reference value: <60 IU/L), indicating liver injury, but normal alkaline phosphate (110 IU/L, normal reference value: 51–160 IU/L). Abdominal ultrasound confirmed hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Echocardiography showed an increased left ventricular ejection fraction (76%), enlargement of the left atrium (37 mm), and markedly thickened interventricular septum (31–34 mm). Cardiovascular magnetic resonance demonstrated asymmetrical massive left ventricular hypertrophy with a maximal thickness of 34.6 mm in the septum. There was focal late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) in the anterior septum with increased native T1 (1421.2 ms) and extracellular volume (ECV) (38.8%) in the LGE-positive area. In the LGE-negative area, native T1 was elevated (septum, 1370.0 ms; free wall, 1317.5 ms) without an increase of ECV (septum, 22.7%; free wall, 20.9%). Myocardial oedema was indicated by an elevated T2 time of 43 ms. The patient's symptoms initially improved with metoprolol treatment but recurred shortly after.
test_results: Genetic analysis revealed a novel pathogenic homozygous nonsense variant of the AGL gene (c.4284 T > G, p.Tyr1428*).
Orpha_name: Glycogen storage disease due to glycogen debranching enzyme deficiency

case_report: The parents of a 5-month-old male patient brought him to the pediatric department with a history of mild fever, generalized body ache, swelling in both upper and lower limbs, irritability, and excessive crying for the past two weeks, along with two episodes of vomiting in the last day. There was no history of trauma, bleeding, or skin rash. The baby was born at term via normal vaginal delivery, weighed 3.2 kg at birth, was fully immunized, and exclusively breastfed. The family history was unremarkable, and there was no recent travel. During the examination, the baby was alert but irritable, weighed approximately 7.5 kg, and had a head circumference of 40 cm, both around the 50th percentile. There was no pallor, jaundice, organomegaly, or lymph node enlargement. The baby had a mild fever, but other vital signs were normal. There was mild tenderness and swelling in both upper and lower limbs without deformities. The swelling was firm, without redness or localized increased temperature, and became more prominent over the next three days while the patient remained afebrile. Blood tests showed hemoglobin at 13.5 gm%, total leukocyte count at 12000/cumm, platelet count at 2.5 lacs, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) elevated to 18 (normal range 10-15), C-reactive protein (CRP) elevated to 18 mg/dl (normal <10), and alkaline phosphatase at 250 U/L. Ultrasonography of the abdomen and parotids was normal.
test_results: Plain radiographs demonstrated soft tissue swelling with hyperostosis in bilateral tibia, left femur, left radius, and right ulna in an asymmetric fashion.

case_report: A 60-year-old woman reported experiencing pain and stiffness in the small joints of both hands for the past 2 months. She was treated with analgesics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) but saw no significant improvement. Upon consulting a specialist rheumatologist, swelling and tenderness were observed in the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints, as well as the wrists, symmetrically. Her past medical and family history were unremarkable. She denied having conditions such as psoriasis, oral ulcers, urethritis, diarrhea, Raynaud’s phenomenon, photosensitivity, and thyroid disease. Laboratory tests showed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 68 mm/h and a C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 20 mg/dl (normal values < 6). Tests for rheumatoid factor (RF), anticitrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA), and antinuclear antibodies (ANA) were negative, as were other serological tests. Based on specific criteria, she had a score of 7/10. She began treatment with methotrexate (MTX) 15 mg/week and prednisone 10 mg/day. After 2 months, she reported significant improvement, with no pain, and the stiffness and swelling of her joints had resolved. ESR and CRP levels returned to normal. The prednisone dose was gradually reduced and discontinued after 3 months, while she continued with MTX. One year after starting treatment, she was in complete clinical remission with normal acute phase reactants. The patient discussed the possibility of stopping MTX therapy with her doctor, who advised that long-term treatment and follow-up were necessary.
test_results: The radiographs showed soft tissue and cartilage calcifications affecting mostly the PIPs, MCPs, as well as the distal interphalangeal joints (DIPs) and the first carpometacarpal joint of the right hand.

case_report: A six-month-old male infant was brought to our tertiary care hospital from a medical camp due to limited movement in all four limbs since the age of five months. The infant, born to non-consanguineous parents via normal vaginal delivery at term with a birth weight of 2.8 kg, had multiple hospital admissions over the past five months for low muscle tone and recurrent infections. The mother reported decreased limb movements and the appearance of multiple black skin lesions starting at one month of age. The infant also had frequent episodes of diarrhea, requiring treatment at a local hospital. There were no similar complaints among siblings. Upon admission, the infant's vital signs were normal. Physical examination revealed contractures in the knee and elbow joints, with the knee joints having the most restricted range of motion. Hyperpigmented brownish papulonodular lesions were noted on the bony prominences of the knuckles, metacarpophalangeal joints, and toes, along with flexion contractures in the elbow and knee joints. Examination of the back showed dark brown papulonodular lesions over the sacral region and flexion contractures. Additionally, hyperpigmented fleshy lesions were observed in the perianal area. Systemic examination was unremarkable, and laboratory tests were within normal limits. Ophthalmological examination was also normal. A dermatology consultation was requested due to the presence of skin lesions.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed a reticulated epidermis with branching and fused rete ridges, mild or few keratotic hyperkeratosis, and papillomatosis. The dermis exhibited the deposition of hyaline material along with spindle cells arranged singly and in fascicles.

case_report: A five-year-old female with brown skin has had erythematous-hyperchromic plaques with slightly raised edges and an atrophic center on the face (bilateral malar areas, lower eyelids, nose, and chin) since she was one and a half years old. Similar lesions with more pronounced borders are present on the dorsal area of the left hand and the lateral side of the second digit of the right hand. Dermatologic examination revealed that the lower eyelid lesions extended to the eye mucosa, initiating ectropion growth. The left nasal lesion had a meliceric crust due to a recent impetigo process, which is currently being treated. There are no significant personal medical history details. Examination of family members showed no notable skin changes.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the material collected from the dorsal area of left hand revealed cornoid lamella and hypogranulosis.

case_report: A 27-year-old pregnant Yakut woman had an ultrasound in the second trimester, which revealed increased prenasal thickness. The combined first trimester screening indicated a moderate risk (1:465) for Trisomy 21. Genetic counseling was provided due to the ultrasound findings and the moderate risk for Trisomy 21. The family history was unremarkable at that time (in 2016). Due to the ultrasound features and moderate risk for Trisomy 21, the woman underwent an invasive prenatal procedure via placenta biopsy to assess the karyotypic status of the fetus. The karyotype was normal, showing 46,XY [11/11]. The baby was born at 39 weeks of pregnancy. From 2 months of age, the boy experienced bronchitis. At 11 months old, he exhibited clinical signs including stiffness of joints in the hands, distinctive facial features, and hepatosplenomegaly.
test_results: GT confirmed a homozygous variant of c.1492C>T (p.R498W) in the VPS33A gene in the boy; then, a heterozygous variant was identified in both parents.
Orpha_name: Mucopolysaccharidosis-like syndrome with congenital heart defects and hematopoietic disorders

case_report: Patient: Male in his 70s. Chief complaint: Growing mass in the left axilla. Past history: None. History of present illness: The patient noticed an enlarging mass in his left axilla, leading to hospital admission. Examinations: Physical examination revealed an elastic, firm, fist-sized mass in the left axilla; the mass was solid and immobile. Ultrasound examination indicated that the mass was well-defined and lobulated, with a maximum diameter of 12 cm. The internal structure of the mass was heterogeneous with mixed echogenicity; areas of high echogenicity suggested significant blood flow. Contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography showed a mass measuring 11 cm × 7 cm × 11 cm, with relatively clear borders but irregular surfaces. No indications of liver or lung metastases were found.
test_results: Histopathological examination of a biopsy specimen showed densely sheathed atypical epithelial cells with spindle-shaped nuclei and rich cytoplasm. The tumor was strongly and diffusely positive for vimentin, S-100 protein, and neuron-specific enolase. The tumor was negative for epithelial membrane antigen, cytokeratin AE1/AE3, c-kit, CD34, α-smooth muscle actin, desmin, synaptophysin, HMB-45, and calretinin.
diagnosis: epithelioid malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor

case_report: A 39-year-old woman reported experiencing decreased vision in her right eye (OD) for the past year, accompanied by watering and redness in the same eye. She observed an irregular increase in the size of her pupil in OD. There was no history of trauma or previous surgeries. She had been prescribed brimonidine and timolol maleate combination therapy for glaucoma in OD. Upon examination, her visual acuity in OD was 6/12, improving to 6/6 with pinhole, and in her left eye (OS) was 6/6. Intraocular pressure (IOP) measured with Goldmann applanation tonometry (GAT) was 22 mmHg in OD while on IOP-lowering medication and 12 mmHg in OS. Examination of OD revealed conjunctival congestion, a clear cornea, irregular anterior chamber depth, and shallowness inferiorly. The superior iris appeared stretched with a loss of its normal pattern and exhibited iridodonesis. Ectropion uveae was noted at the inferior pupillary margin, with the posterior pigment epithelium being pulled toward the angle. The pupil was irregular in shape and did not react to light.
test_results: On gonioscopy, her superior angle was open till scleral spur while nasal, inferior, and temporal angles were closed with broad-based PAS.
diagnosis: ICE syndrome with essential iris atrophy

case_report: A 45-day-old male infant, born to parents who are related by blood, was admitted with a mild fever lasting for one week. There were no reports of cough, cold, vomiting, or diarrhea. Additionally, there was no history of seizures or skin rash. Physical examination revealed a distended abdomen with mild enlargement of both the liver and spleen. Skin examination showed widespread lightening of the skin and gray hair on the scalp, eyebrows, and eyelashes. Laboratory tests indicated pancytopenia, while the peripheral blood smear appeared normal. Examination of the hair shaft under light microscopy revealed large, irregular melanin granules.
test_results: Bone marrow examination showed hypocellular marrow with hemophagocytosis.

case_report: A 55-year-old male presented with progressive weakness in both upper and lower limbs, which began at age 35. He experienced difficulty rising from a seated position and climbing stairs. His medical history was unremarkable, and there was no family history of muscle weakness. On physical examination, he exhibited a waddling gait and bilateral calf muscle wasting, while other limb muscles appeared normal in bulk. Muscle tone was normal. Muscle strength testing revealed MRC 4/5 weakness in hip flexion, hip extension, hip adduction, hip abduction, knee flexion, and right knee extension, with MRC 3/5 weakness in left knee extension. Elbow flexion and extension showed MRC 4+/5 weakness bilaterally. Distal upper and lower limb strength was normal (MRC 5/5), as were facial, ocular, and neck strength (MRC 5/5). Reflexes were reduced in both upper and lower limbs, but sensory examination was normal. Laboratory tests showed a CK level of 4,910. Electromyography (EMG) indicated myopathic motor units without abnormal spontaneous activity in the right vastus medialis, vastus lateralis, biceps femoris, and medial gastrocnemius, along with fibrillations and reduced recruitment of large motor units in the right tibialis anterior. MRI of the upper and lower limbs revealed fatty infiltration and mild atrophy in the posterior calf and thigh muscles, as well as fatty infiltration and atrophy in the pectoral, latissimus dorsi, and teres muscles. An echocardiogram showed no evidence of cardiomyopathy. The patient chose not to undergo a muscle biopsy.
test_results: Next generation sequencing revealed compound heterozygosity for two variants in the ANO5 gene; a previously reported pathogenic frameshift variant [c.191dupA; p.(Asn64fs)] in exon 5 that results in a premature stop signal and a novel missense variant [c.952G>C; p.(Ala318Pro)] in exon 10.
diagnosis: Limb Girdle Muscular Dystrophy  due to novel variants in the ANO5 gene

case_report: A 30-year-old female presented 2 months after sustaining trauma to the right ankle from a fall off a bike. Due to significant pain and swelling, she was treated conservatively and her ankle was immobilized in a below-knee splint for 8 weeks. She was instructed to avoid bearing weight on the affected limb throughout this period. Upon removal of the splint, she continued to experience severe pain and swelling and remained unable to bear weight.
test_results: A radiograph of the ankle demonstrated no evidence of any bony injury. There was no evidence of ligament injury based on magnetic resonance imaging evaluation. Follow-up radiographs demonstrated a bimalleolar fracture of the right ankle and diffuse osteoporosis involving talus calcaneum and metatarsals.

case_report: A nine-month-old girl presented with jaundice, itching, and rickets. The jaundice and itching had begun within the past month. She had been previously diagnosed with rickets and was receiving vitamin D and calcium supplements. She was born to consanguineous parents and has a healthy older sister. Her prenatal history was normal, and she was born at term with a birth weight of 2,500 grams. There is no family history of chronic liver or bowel disease. Her weight was 6.3 kg (<3rd percentile, -2.47 standard deviation score) and her height was 63 cm (<3rd percentile, -3 standard deviation score), with a normal weight-for-length ratio. Physical examination revealed scleral icterus, scars on her arms from itching, and mild liver enlargement. She did not have discolored stools or diarrhea. Abdominal ultrasound showed an enlarged liver with heterogeneous parenchyma and a normal biliary tree. Laboratory tests indicated low GGT activity, mildly elevated transaminase and bilirubin levels, and elevated serum bile acid levels (135.23 mmol/L, normal range: <10 mmol/L). There was no evidence of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, with fecal elastase levels >500 mg/g. Tests for tubulopathy and urine organic acid analysis were normal. Prothrombin time was 23.9 seconds but normalized after vitamin K supplementation. Vitamin D levels were <7 ng/ml, despite ongoing supplementation. Additional vitamins A, E, K, and ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) were started. Genetic investigation was conducted for the cause of low-GGT cholestasis. No liver biopsy was performed.
test_results: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) showed a homozygous splicing variation (c.3045+3A>T) on the MYO5B (NM_001080467) gene.
diagnosis: Normal-Gamma-Glutamyl Transferase Progressive Familial Intrahepatic Cholestasis  due to a homozygous mutation in the MYO5B gene

case_report: A 2-year-old boy with a history of frequent hospitalizations since 4 months of age presented with fever, diarrhea, and abdominal distension. His weight was in the 50th percentile, and his height was in the fifth percentile. Physical examination revealed splenomegaly extending 8 cm below the left costal margin and hepatomegaly extending 4 cm below the right costal margin, with no palpable lymphadenopathy. Laboratory findings showed pancytopenia, hypofibrinogenemia, and hyperferritinemia. Serological tests for rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, hepatitis B, human immunodeficiency virus, toxoplasmosis, visceral leishmaniosis, and autoimmune diseases were negative. Immunologic evaluation indicated normal levels of immunoglobulins (IgG, IgM, IgA, and IgE) and normal lymphocyte subset counts (CD3, CD4, CD8, CD19, and NK cells). Neutrophil function assessed by the dihydrorhodamine test was normal. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy did not reveal any hemophagocytic activity, malignancy, or infection. The patient's parents were not consanguineous, and there was no family history of similar symptoms, including in two maternal half-siblings, a 10-year-old boy, and a 13-year-old girl. The patient received empirical treatment with corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulins, and antibiotics, leading to gradual clinical and laboratory improvement over the next 3 weeks. The patient experienced recurrent similar episodes over the following year, but consistently responded to steroid treatment.
test_results: The patient had biallelic mutations in the STXBP2 gene: one pathogenic variant, c.1247-1G>C (splicing acceptor site), and one VUS, c.704G>A (p.Arg235Gln). Genetic analyses of the patient's parents showed that both were heterozygous for the STXBP2 gene; the father harbored a pathogenic mutation, c.1247-1G>C (splicing acceptor site), and the mother harbored a VUS, c.704G>A (p.Arg235Gln).

case_report: A 32-year-old male, born to non-related parents, presented with dark-colored lesions on his face, eyes, mouth, and back since childhood. The lesions were asymptomatic until the age of 12, after which they increased in size and have since remained unchanged. There is no family history of similar lesions. On skin examination, multiple ill-defined bluish-grey macules to patches were observed asymmetrically over the bilateral periorbital regions, symmetrically over the bilateral malar area extending to the temples and the forehead on the left side, and the temple region on the right. Additionally, multiple bluish-grey speckled macules to patches were noted on the bilateral lumbar, infrascapular, and left scapular areas. Examination of the oral mucosa revealed a deep blue irregular mottled patch on the hard palate, and bluish-grey pigmentation of the sclera was observed. Slit lamp examination showed marked patchy bluish-grey episcleral pigmentation in all quadrants of both eyes. Visual acuity testing, intraocular pressure measurement, and dilated fundus examination were normal. Otoscopy showed a normal tympanic membrane. Dermoscopic examination of the facial lesions revealed brownish-gray structureless areas in a patchy distribution with scattered brown dots, terminal hair with perifollicular hypopigmentation, and four dot clods. Similar findings were observed in the lesions on the back, with the addition of scaling.
test_results: Histopathologic examination of hyperpigmented macules over the back showed heavily pigmented long, slender dendritic dermal melanocytes scattered in the upper, middle, and lower dermis with increased basal layer pigmentation.
diagnosis: Naevus of Ito and Naevus of Ota

case_report: A 56-year-old woman presented with epigastric pain and an enlarged liver approximately 15 years prior to the development of a hepatic tumor. Imaging studies, including enhanced computed tomography (CT) and angiography, identified narrowing of the hepatic vein and inferior vena cava (IVC) at the confluence. She underwent IVC stent placement and was prescribed acetylsalicylic acid (100 mg/day) post-procedure. Annual follow-up included enhanced or unenhanced CT scans. Hepatitis B and C virus tests were consistently negative. The patient had no history of alcohol consumption, chronic liver disease, or family history of hepatobiliary cancer. Thirteen years post-stent placement, contrast-enhanced CT revealed a 5 mm spot-like enhancement in the peripheral region of segment 8 of the liver. At that time, alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) levels were within the normal range. During the CT scan, the patient experienced an allergic reaction to the contrast material, resulting in facial edema, which was resolved with intramuscular epinephrine and antihistamines. Subsequent follow-ups utilized unenhanced CT and ultrasonography. Over the next two years, the hepatic lesion increased to 1.6 cm in diameter on ultrasonography. Laboratory tests showed elevated AFP (70 ng/mL) and lens culinaris agglutinin-reactive fraction of AFP (AFP-L3, 85.5%), which had previously been normal. Due to the observed growth of the hepatic lesion, further imaging was deemed necessary. Given the presence of a handmade stainless-steel IVC stent, which could cause significant artifacts on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), dynamic CT with contrast material under steroid preparation was performed.
test_results: Dynamic CT revealed a well-circumscribed, low-density area (mean CT value, 42 Hounsfield unit [HU]) without pseudocapsule in the peripheral liver. The nodule showed strong homogeneous enhancement (mean CT value, 145 HU) in the arterial phase. Enhancement was prolonged to the portal phase and decreased to almost the same level as surrounding hepatic parenchyma in the equilibrium phase (mean CT values, 169 and 131 HU). Histopathological findings revealed a tumor comprising atypical cells with small, round nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm, forming ductal and alveolar structures. No mucin production was observed. The tumor showed a replacing growth pattern without a hyalinized capsule and the border with the surrounding liver was vague. On immunostaining, the atypical cells were partially positive for hepatocyte specific antigen (HSA) and positive for cytokeratin (CK) 7 and CK19. Epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) was strongly positive in the tumor, mainly localized to the apical surface of the tubules. The tumor also has the component partially positive for AFP.
diagnosis: Combined hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma with stem cell features, cholangiolocellular subtype

case_report: A 56-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with bilateral myopia (−6D). She underwent femtosecond laser-assisted cataract surgery in both eyes. The left eye surgery was completed without complications, and the right eye was operated on one month later. Preoperative slit-lamp examination showed no abnormalities. Both surgeries were performed under topical anesthesia using standard phacoemulsification techniques, with Acrysof Single Piece intraocular lenses implanted in the capsular bag. Postoperative symptoms on the first day included foreign body sensation, ache, and redness. The patient was prescribed topical Ofloxacin and Dexamethasone Sodium Phosphate eyedrops, administered four times daily for one week, with a gradual reduction in the Dexamethasone dose. Two weeks after the second surgery, the patient reported visual discomfort and bothersome glare at night in her right eye. Examination revealed an anterior chamber inflammatory reaction (3+ cell) without fibrin or hypopyon. No additional findings were noted. The Dexamethasone eyedrop dosage was increased to six times daily. The left eye examination remained unremarkable. At a follow-up visit one week later, the anterior chamber reaction had improved (1+ cell), but the right pupil was fixed and dilated (6 × 9 mm) and did not respond to pilocarpine 2%. There was diffuse iris atrophy, and pigment was observed in the inferior cornea and lens, particularly along the inferior capsulorhexis line.
test_results: Gonioscopy examination of the right eye revealed a mostly closed angle with the exception of the nasal side. In addition, peripheral anterior synechiae were seen.

case_report: A 69-year-old man with no significant prior health issues was admitted to the gastroenterology department with a one-month history of lethargy, decreased appetite, persistent vomiting, significant weight loss of six kilograms, and a dry cough. He reported no abdominal pain, haematemesis, dysphagia, changes in bowel habits, or symptoms related to cardiac, respiratory, neurological systems, or bone pain. His medical history includes an appendectomy and total hip joint replacement, and he was not on any regular medication at the time of admission. Physical examination showed he was febrile (38.8°C) and appeared cachectic, but there were no signs of chronic liver disease. Abdominal examination revealed hepatomegaly without other organomegaly, and the per rectal examination was unremarkable. Cardiopulmonary examinations were unremarkable except for bilateral pitting edema up to his ankles. Blood tests indicated anemia of chronic disease with hemoglobin at 108 g/L (normal range for males: 130 - 175 g/L), serum iron at 2 μmol/L (normal: 10 - 30 μmol/L), transferrin at 1.4 g/L (normal: 2 - 3.5 g/L), transferrin saturation at 6% (normal: 16 - 50%), and ferritin at 354 μg/L (normal: 20 - 500 μg/L). C-reactive protein was elevated at 208 mg/L (normal: < 5 mg/L), but multiple urine and blood cultures were negative for bacterial infection. Serum electrolytes and creatinine were normal at 83 μmol/L (normal: 50 - 120 μmol/L). Liver function tests were normal except for hypoalbuminemia at 28 g/L (normal: 35 - 50 g/L). Protein electrophoresis, Vitamin B12, folate, and thyroid functions were within normal limits. Chest X-ray showed interstitial infiltration at both lung bases. Lung function tests indicated restrictive lung disease with FVC at 3.33 L (73%), FEV1 at 2.49 L (72%), FEV1/FVC at 75%, and decreased diffusion capacity (DLCO at 17.81 ml/min/mmHg). Abdominal ultrasound confirmed a 19 cm hepatomegaly with normal liver texture and no mass lesions. Gastroscopy, performed due to ongoing vomiting and weight loss, revealed no significant pathology. CT of the chest showed peri-aortic tissue infiltration, thickening of the interlobular septa in both lungs, and involvement of the pulmonary vessels, pericardium, lung parenchyma, and oesophagus. CT of the abdomen showed hypo-attenuated homogenous tissue infiltration with weak contrast enhancement in the renal fossa, and symmetric bilateral infiltration of the peri-renal, anterior, and posterior para-renal spaces, giving the appearance of 'hairy kidney'. The inferior vena cava, aorta, and mesentery were also involved.
test_results: Histological examination of the tissue showed xanthomatous infiltration involving the liver, omentum and surrounding the lymph nodes. The xanthomatous process was characterized by prominent foamy histiocytes, admixed with occasional giant cells and chronic inflammatory cells. Immunohistochemical stains revealed that these cells were positive for CD68 and negative for S100 and CD1a. There was no evidence of malignancy.

case_report: A 46-year-old woman presented with an 8-year history of worsening hoarseness, which had significantly worsened over the past 2 months. Initial electronic laryngoscopies revealed laryngitis, and anti-inflammatory treatments provided partial relief. Two months ago, her hoarseness became severe, leading to episodes of aphonia. A subsequent electronic laryngoscopy identified chorditis and an endotracheal mass, along with bilateral vocal tract congestion, swelling, albuginea attachment, and mucosal erosion. The patient had previously undergone a panhysterectomy for a hysteromyoma. She has been breeding doves for the past 25 years and reported no history of smoking or alcohol consumption. Physical examination was unremarkable except for coarse breath sounds and wet rales in the lower lobe of the right lung. Laboratory tests, including blood tests, tumor markers, and sputum tests for acid-fast bacilli, were normal, except for liver function tests showing ALT at 65 U/L and globulin at 19.6 g/L. Spirometry indicated an obstructive ventilatory disturbance.
test_results: A CT scan indicated variable degrees of stenosis and calcification of the distal trachea and main bronchi, accompanied by consolidation of the inferior lobe of the right lung. A fiberbronchoscopy (FOB) showed signs of dozens of white nodules extruding into the lumen of trachea and bronchi and free from peripheral bronchial tree. Nodules like paving stones pervaded the wall, sparing the posterior aspects and possessing a rigid property. Histological examination appearances a central island of osteocytes apart from bronchial mucosa.

case_report: A 5-year-old Brazilian girl was brought to the Pediatric Dentistry Clinic at the Dental School of Araçatuba, São Paulo State University (UNESP), for a thorough assessment of her oral health. Her mother reported that the primary maxillary left teeth had erupted differently compared to her other teeth. The affected teeth exhibited a yellowish color, were prone to rapid decay, frequent fractures, and were often associated with pain and gingival swelling. During pregnancy, the mother had taken medication for high blood pressure (Enalapril®), but the pregnancy and birth were otherwise uneventful. There was no family history of dental or genetic anomalies. The child was generally healthy with no congenital or acquired diseases, although she had a urinary infection treated with Amoxicillin® in the first three days of life. Extraoral examination showed no facial asymmetry but revealed a vascular birthmark (haemangioma) on the right side of her face. Intraoral examination indicated a relatively caries-free mouth with normal occlusion, soft tissues, and developing dentition, except for the maxillary left quadrant. In this area, the central incisor and the first and second molars were missing, as well as the primary right central incisor. These teeth were reportedly extracted by a dentist six months prior to the clinic visit. The residual root of the left lateral incisor was present and recommended for extraction. The left canine had been previously restored with composite resin and was less affected compared to the other teeth. Part of the permanent left first molar appeared altered, likely due to the prior extraction of the primary second molar. This observation was made during the third appointment and was not noted at the initial visit.
test_results: The panoramic radiograph revealed the presence of primary teeth and the germs of permanent teeth, including the permanent second molars, except in the maxillary left quadrant. In the affected area, it was possible to observe the primary right central incisor, which was extracted straight away. The root of primary left lateral incisor was also present. The primary left canine presented reduced radiodensity and showed wide open apex and abnormally wide pulp chambers and canals in comparison to unaffected teeth. Germs of permanent teeth from the maxillary left quadrant and also the germ of the permanent right central incisor presented a 'ghost like' appearance, showing that this condition had crossed the midline. Dental development appeared age-appropriate. Normal thickness of enamel and dentin in primary and permanent dentitions was observed in the other quadrants, except for the permanent mandibular left first molar, which showed some alterations in its crown.

case_report: The patient, a 40-year-old male with homozygous HbSS SCD, was part of the ESCORT-HU study. He began HU treatment at 23 due to recurrent VOC episodes. By the age of 30, he had experienced seven painful crises in the previous year, each lasting more than 48 hours, and was switched to HU tablets at a dose of 25 mg/kg/day. Aside from priapism, he had no other SCD-related complications. Over the first three years of the study, his fetal hemoglobin increased from 20% to 26%, and he had no painful episodes. At 37, he had an episode of acute chest syndrome and a painful crisis requiring hospitalization and exchange transfusion. At 38, deferasirox was prescribed for iron overload but was discontinued after 20 days. Mild heart failure (left ventricular ejection fraction of 55%) was detected at 38. Severe pulmonary arterial hypertension (grade 4–5) was confirmed by right heart catheterization at 41 during hospitalization for an infection. A few months later, HU was withdrawn after 17 years due to a decrease in hemoglobin levels (8.7 to 7.0 g/dL) and platelet count (160 to 116 × 109/L). Three months later, the patient was hospitalized for fever, and the peripheral blood count showed: red blood cells: 2.55 × 10^12/L; reticulocyte count: 8.59%; hemoglobin: 7.4 g/dL; leucocyte count: 24.11 × 10^9/L; and platelet count: 45 × 10^9/L.
test_results: Examination of the bone marrow revealed hyperplasia and dyserythropoiesis of the red blood cell lineage, left-shift granulopoiesis, and also dysmegakaryopoiesis with an elevated number of megakaryocytes. There were 6% CD34+ blasts of the granulocyte lineage and also intermediate bone marrow infiltration (12–15%) by CD3+, CD2+, CD8+, CD5+, CD56+ (partially), CD7-, CD57-, TdT-, TIA-1-T lymphocytes. Cytogenetic analysis demonstrated a complex clonal abnormality including deletions of 5 q, 3 p, and 7 p, and monosomies of chromosomes 16, 17, and 18.
Orpha_name: Refractory anemia with excess blasts type 1

case_report: A 16-year-old left-handed male presented with a history of rapid jerking movements since childhood. These movements were first observed at the age of 2 and affected the head, trunk, and arms. They occurred at rest, intensified with activity, and gradually worsened over time. There was no variation in symptoms throughout the day. At age 4, his initial evaluation included a normal brain MRI and an EEG that showed central sharp waves during sleep, though he had no history of seizures. He was born after a normal pregnancy and delivery, and achieved motor milestones on time. His family history was notable, with three paternal cousins and two half-brothers on the paternal side exhibiting similar jerky movements.
