His father and paternal uncle were also affected, with some family members experiencing mild dystonia. The patient was the most severely affected in his family. At age 6, he visited a movement disorders clinic, where his personal and family history were reviewed. He did not report any issues with stiffness or abnormal posturing.
test_results: Sequencing of the SGCE gene identified a single-base deletion in exon 3 (c.285delA, p.Asp96Thrfs*36). The deletion results in a shift in the translational reading frame, yielding a truncated protein. Five symptomatic relatives were also recruited for genetic study and they were found to have the same heterozygous deletion as the proband.

case_report: A 59-year-old man was referred to our hospital due to an abnormal shadow observed on a chest X-ray during a routine medical check-up. He was asymptomatic and had no history of neuroendocrine disorders. Physical examination and laboratory tests were unremarkable. Chest CT revealed a 4.5 cm mass in the thymus. PET/CT indicated significant uptake of 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose in the mass, with an early maximum standardised uptake value (SUVmax) of 9.8. The patient underwent a total thymectomy via median sternotomy. The left pleura, which was adherent and invaded by the tumor, was also excised. The mass was confined to the thymus without spreading to the pericardium or left hilum. A radical en bloc resection and lymph node staging were completed. The surgery lasted 119 minutes, and the blood loss was 40 mL.
test_results: The tumour comprised spindle-shaped cells with a pale eosinophilic cytoplasm. Necrosis was absent, and mitotic figures were 7 per 10 high-power fields (10 HPFs). The MIB-1 index was 8.5%. Fat tissue and vascular invasion was frequently observed. Cytokeratin (AE1/AE3), CK19, CD56, synaptophysin, chromogranin, and c-kit positivity and CK7 and CK20 negativity of the tumour cells. Tumour cells arranged in the nests so-called zellballen surrounded by thin fibrovascular stroma and sustentacular cells highlighted by immunostaining for S100 protein.

case_report: A 46-year-old woman was admitted to the gynecological department of a hospital in Odessa (Ukraine) on 26 December 2016 with complaints of pain in the lower abdomen and bloody discharge from the genital tract. Clinical investigation revealed multinodular uterine myoma, adenomyosis, and cicatricial deformity of the cervix. Pelvic ultrasonography showed a 35×35 mm intramural, subserosal node at the bottom region, and a 43×40 mm subserosal node at the posterior wall of the uterus. Diagnostic laparoscopy was performed, revealing a normal omentum and a uterus measuring 7×7×8 cm, deformed by intramural and subserous myomatous nodes, along with small subserous nodes on the anterior wall. Endometrioid heterotopias were also observed. A laparoscopic supracervical hysterectomy with uterine tubes using a power morcellator, posterior colpotomy, and superficial conization of the cervix was performed. Morphological study of the removed tissues showed diffuse leiomyoma with foci of endometriosis and chronic bilateral salpingitis. After 6 months in June 2017, the patient visited the Genesis Clinic (Simferopol, Russian Federation) for a follow-up examination due to relocation. She reported mild to moderate abdominal pain and pelvic discomfort. Laboratory tests for estrogen and progesterone levels were normal, as were routine blood tests, urine tests, and blood chemistry. Ultrasonography and magnetic resonance imaging were performed, followed by diagnostic laparoscopy, which revealed neoplastic disseminate nodes of whitish-gray color, ranging from 0.5 to 1.5 cm in diameter, diffusely located on the peritoneum. No exudate or adhesive process was present.
test_results: Histological structure of biopsy material was represented by the fibrous and muscular bundles with the presence of spindle-shaped cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm. IHC study revealed a high level of cytoplasmic expression of vimentin and SMA. Also, there was a high expression of progesterone receptors (from 80% to 92%) and a low expression of estrogen receptors (from 30% to 42%). The level of Ki67 expression was low and accounted for only 5% to 8%.

case_report: A term female infant was delivered by a 39-year-old woman in a peripheral hospital after an uncomplicated third pregnancy at 41 weeks of gestational age. Delivery was assisted by vacuum extraction. Apgar scores were 8, 9, and 10 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes, respectively. The infant had a birth weight of 2920 g (8th percentile), a length of 50 cm (20th percentile), and a head circumference of 35 cm (50th percentile). Postnatal physical examination revealed grouped pustular lesions and annular erythema with central lightening, yellowish crusted plaques, or slight scaling on the skin, exclusively on the face and forehead. The rest of the skin and mucosa were unremarkable. The child was transferred to a neonatal tertiary care center, and antiviral therapy with aciclovir was initiated. Approximately six hours postnatal, the baby developed focal clonic seizures of the right arm. An electroencephalogram showed focal temporo-parieto-occipital changes over the left hemisphere with low amplitude, a slight increase in slow waves, and reduced basic activity. Intermittent short-term focal rhythmic parietal theta activity and rhythmic occipital delta activity on the left were detected, with no typical epileptic discharges. A lumbar puncture showed no signs of infection, with normal protein and white blood count, and HSV-PCR was negative. Anticonvulsive therapy with phenobarbital was initiated, but seizures were controlled only after adding phenytoin. Diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging on the third day of life revealed multiple ischemic brain areas in the distribution of the middle and posterior cerebral artery on the left side, with no evidence of sinus venous thrombosis. Thrombocytopenia (minimal 91000/μl) was present, and coagulation blood tests showed increased fibrinolysis, normal plasmatic inhibitors of coagulation, normal antithrombin III (56%) and protein S (58%), but low protein C (22%). Therapy with low molecular weight heparin was started. An echocardiogram revealed no structural abnormalities, and an electrocardiogram showed a normal PQ interval and QRS complex. Central and peripheral bleeding spots were found in the ocular fundus, likely caused by trauma during birth. Renal function tests, albumin, transaminases, bilirubin, and calcium were normal. A smear of the grouped pustular lesions on the face showed no infection with staphylococcus. A biopsy of the affected skin showed evidence of cytoid bodies compatible with an interface dermatitis.
test_results: Serological studies of the infant detected maternal HSV and varicella zoster virus (VZV) specific IgG antibodies, IgM and a HSV-PCR of a swab of a skin lesion were negative. Antinuclear antibodies (ANA), anti-U1-snRNP antibodies and anti-Sm antibodies were present, while antiphospholipid, anti-Scl 70, SSA/Ro, SSB/La, anti-Tm, anti-Jo-1 and anti-ds DNA antibodies could not be detected.

case_report: A 65-year-old male presented with a 6-month history of multiple asymptomatic nodules and tumors on the face, neck, and upper extremities, showing centrifugal growth. Initial nodules in the occipital area were treated with monochloroacetic acid and cryosurgery, leading to rapid deterioration and peripheral spreading. The patient noted facial tumors developing after minor shaving injuries, while nodules on the upper extremities appeared without any apparent trigger. He reported no constitutional symptoms and had no family history of similar lesions, dermatological conditions, or malignancies. On examination, multiple nodules and tumors were observed on the face, neck, occipital area, and upper extremities. The face had three exophytic tumors with central crateriform depressions filled with keratin masses located above the upper lip, under the lower lip, and on the left cheek, along with several smaller pink nodules on the forehead and cheeks. Lesions on the neck and occipital area exhibited annular morphology with hyperkeratotic borders and central regression. Smaller nodules with keratin plugs were present on the dorsal hands and forearms. Videodermoscopy revealed thick arborizing vessels on the tumor periphery, large comedo-like openings, central yellowish scales, white circles around keratotic plugs, ill-defined blue-grey areas, and blood spots. Histopathology of incisional and excisional biopsies from the face and upper extremities showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, preserved maturation with minimal atypia, single mitotic figures, irregular craters filled with keratin, pronounced reactive fibrosis, and dense chronic lymphohistiocytic infiltrations in the dermis.
test_results: Biopsy of the bone marrow showed megakaryocyte atypia with dense clustering and grade 3 reticulin and collagen fibrosis.

case_report: A 49-year-old male presented to the hospital with severe headaches that began at the front and later spread to the back of the head, accompanied by sensitivity to light. For the past three days, he experienced severe nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and general malaise. Upon examination, he had normal body temperature, stable vital signs, no altered consciousness, and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. His history ruled out trauma or drug intoxication. Initial clinical and laboratory evaluations led to a computed tomography scan, which showed a mass in the sellar region. Subsequent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a hemorrhagic sellar mass. Laboratory tests on the fifth day after admission indicated insufficiency in the corticotropic, thyrotropic, and gonadotropic axes. Despite MRI showing a shift in the optic chiasm, ophthalmological examination revealed only minor, non-specific visual field defects without papilledema or orthoptic abnormalities. Surgical intervention was planned but postponed due to severe acute kidney injury, with a creatinine level of 11.6 mg/dL and an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of less than 20 mL/min on the fifth day after admission. The patient, a driving instructor, reported digging out a bamboo hedge before hospitalization. Further testing on the third day after admission confirmed hantavirus infection through detection of IgM and IgG antibodies against Puumala hantavirus using immunofluorescence and line immunoassays, as well as positive polymerase chain reaction results. Specific amplification and sequencing of the partial L-Segment identified a puumalavirus circulating in the Middle Rhine region in Germany. Serological tests ruled out infections by hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, and HIV. The patient was transferred to the nephrology department and became oliguric. Due to increasing nausea and rising blood urea levels, haemodialysis was considered but kidney function began to recover, avoiding the need for renal replacement therapy. Symptomatic treatment and hormonal replacement led to increased urinary excretion by day 3 and decreased creatinine levels from day 6 onwards. No specific antiviral treatment was administered. Despite overall improvement, diuretic medication was withheld from day 5, achieving a negative fluid balance with continuous weight loss daily, but urine excretion remained high (6.25 mL/kg/h). Initially attributed to the polyuric phase of acute kidney injury recovery, persistent plasma hyperosmolality and urine hypoosmolality led to further evaluation.
test_results: Copeptin levels during thirsting (copeptin t0–4.3 pmol/l; copeptin t7–4.2 pmol/l) and response to desmopressin.
diagnosis: Central Diabetes Insipidus secondary to Hantavirus Infection

case_report: A 16-year-old female presented with increasingly frequent episodes of vertigo and nausea, accompanied by gait instability. There was no relevant family history of migraines, epilepsy, or ataxia. The patient had a history of pneumonia at 6 months old but no other significant illnesses. She was born full-term and exhibited normal physical, motor, social, language, and cognitive development. Currently, she is in her third year of high school with good academic performance but reports insufficient sleep, averaging 5 hours per night. She considers her study pressure manageable. The episodes began approximately ten years ago with transient dizziness leading to a minor fall, without any apparent trigger. She experienced blurred vision for a few seconds but no other symptoms and did not seek medical attention. Two years later, another dizziness episode resulted in a distal radius fracture, again without clear cause or additional symptoms, and no neurological consultation was sought. Over the next four years, the frequency of episodes gradually increased. By age 12, the episodes became more disruptive, occurring monthly and lasting 10-20 minutes, with symptoms including vertigo, unsteady gait, irritability, photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, vomiting, and occasionally slurred speech. Between episodes, she was asymptomatic except for a slight headache. Before each episode, she experienced a moderate headache on the left side for a few seconds without visual auras. Triggers included lack of sleep and strenuous exercise, while posture and menstruation did not appear to be factors. There were no reports of tinnitus, ear fullness, diplopia, loss of consciousness, convulsions, or upper limb dysfunction during episodes. In the months leading up to her clinic visit, the frequency of episodes increased to 2-3 times daily, each lasting 1-2 hours. Severe episodes caused lower limb weakness or visual disturbances, forcing her to sit down. She had previously tried Yangxue Qingnao granules and betahistine mesylate without improvement and discontinued the treatment. No new symptoms emerged in the four years prior to the visit, and the slight interictal headache remained unchanged. A physical examination during the interictal period revealed no significant abnormalities in the nervous system or general condition. The patient was conscious with fluent speech, normal memory, and higher cortical functions. No nystagmus was observed, and cranial nerve tests were normal. Sensory examinations for touch, pain, temperature, vibration, and position were symmetrical and normal. Muscle strength in all four limbs was graded five with moderate muscle tension. Tendon reflexes were symmetrical, and coordination tests (finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin) were accurate. Pathological reflexes were negative. Due to the family's distance from the hospital, an ictal examination was not performed, but video recordings of an episode at home showed an unsteady, broad-based gait, accurate heel-to-shin test, and no nystagmus. Laboratory tests, including hematology, biochemistry, and homocysteine levels, were normal. A lumbar puncture was not performed. Head MRI revealed multiple patchy lesions in the centrum semiovale and white matter of the bilateral frontoparietal temporal lobes, with T1 hypointensity, T2 hyperintensity, and normal diffusion-weighted imaging. The cerebellum appeared slightly atrophic. There were no significant changes compared to an MRI from one year prior. Interictal electronystagmography was normal, while electroencephalogram showed a small amount of asymmetric complex delta waves in the bilateral temporal regions without other abnormalities. Additional tests, including ECG, echocardiography, transcranial Doppler ultrasonography, and head MRI angiography, were conducted to rule out heart and cerebrovascular conditions.
test_results: A novel, heterozygous mutation in the CACNA1A gene (c.3836dupA, exon 23, and p.Y1279X) leading to a premature stop codon was discovered. Further validation of Sanger sequencing for her healthy parents revealed no mutant at the same locus, indicating the identified mutation de novo.
diagnosis: Type 2 Episodic Ataxia  and Hemiplegic Migraine  due to a novel CACNA1A mutation

case_report: A 48-year-old female presented to outpatient neurology after visiting the emergency department (ED) with worsening shortness of breath (SOB), muscle fatigue and weakness, and slurred speech. She had a history of COVID-19 diagnosed eight months prior, with current symptoms beginning eight weeks post-diagnosis. A chest x-ray in the ED revealed right hemidiaphragmatic paralysis. Brain MRI showed non-specific scattered punctate white matter hyperintensities. The patient was stabilized, discharged, and referred to outpatient neurology. Physical examination by the outpatient neurologist revealed primarily unilateral symptoms: right foot drop (3/5), right lower facial weakness, severe SOB, multiple decreased reflexes mainly on the right, fatigable right-hand grip, wide-based and right foot steppage gait, numbness and tingling in the right upper and lower extremities, and bilateral arm strength of 4/5. She could get in and out of a chair with minimal assistance. Right-hand grip strength was 1/5. Additional findings included right facial nerve palsy, intact cranial nerves II-VI and VIII-XII, negative Hoffman’s and Lhermitte's sign, and decreased tone in all four extremities. No resting, intention, or action tremors were observed; cerebellar function was intact, and no fasciculations were noted. Muscle tone was decreased in both arms and legs. Sensory examination showed decreased vibration and pinprick sensation from distal to proximal in both legs. Hypoactive reflexes were noted in the right bicep, right and left brachioradialis, right patellar, and right and left Achilles. All other reflexes were 2+/4. Laboratory tests were conducted to investigate the etiology, including IgG and IgM anti-ganglioside-monosialic acid, anti-neoplastic, anti-nuclear, and anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies, which were negative. Cerebral spinal fluid protein was mildly elevated, while creatine kinase, vitamin B12, acetylcholine receptor binding antibody, sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and thyroid-stimulating hormone were within normal ranges. Laboratory analysis showed an elevated A1C of 7.1%. A chest CT with contrast confirmed an elevated right hemidiaphragm with adjacent right basilar subsegmental atelectasis, indicating a paralyzed right hemidiaphragm.
test_results: Urgent nerve conduction and electromyography (EMG) studies showed significant distal axonal demyelinating sensorimotor polyneuropathy. The sensory nerve conduction study showed a mild slowing of the right median sensory conduction velocity. There was a mild slowing of the bilateral sural sensory conduction velocity and sensory nerve action potential with prolonged latencies. Transcarpal sensory nerve conduction testing showed that the median transcarpal speed was significantly reduced. The motor nerve conduction study revealed an abnormal distal right median motor conduction velocity with increased terminal latency. There was a severe reduction in amplitudes of the right median nerve, right ulnar, right peroneal, and right tibial latencies, with prolonged terminal latencies and very small compound muscle action potentials with marked attenuation. The right ulnar nerve also showed slowing across the elbow. There was no response in the right peroneal F-waves, and the right tibial F-waves were mildly prolonged. The right soleus H-reflex showed a mildly prolonged latency compared to the left. The needle EMG findings revealed the right flexor digitorum superficialis and tibialis anterior (TA) had significant denervation, and the right extensor digitorium communis (EDC) showed moderate denervation. The right gastrocnemius medial head indicated mild denervation. Recruitment of the right first dorsal interosseous, EDC, deltoid, TA, gastrocnemius, and vastus lateralis was moderate to low. The amplitudes of the muscles in the right lower extremity were significantly reduced. No myotonia or fasciculations were present. Repetitive nerve stimulation in the right abductor digiti minimi did not show decrement in compound muscle action potentials.
diagnosis: Multifocal Acquired Demyelinating Sensory and Motor Neuropathy
Orpha_name: Multifocal Acquired Demyelinating Sensory and Motor Neuropathy

case_report: A 3-day-old female infant presented with bilious vomiting and abdominal swelling. The baby was delivered at full term through a normal delivery, and no antenatal ultrasound was performed. Physical examination revealed a distended abdomen with a palpable large cystic mass in the lower abdomen. The anal opening appeared normal, and there was a urogenital sinus present. Additionally, postaxial polydactyly was observed in all limbs. Examinations of the eyes and cardiovascular system showed no abnormalities.
test_results: USG suggested a large hydrometrocolpos. MRI scan showed large hydrometrocolpos with atretic lower vagina and associated bilateral hydronephrosis. Genitogram revealed no communication between bladder and vagina. Echocardiography suggested a VSD with a PDA.

case_report: A 24-year-old female presented with multiple, round, bluish-purple masses on both hands and feet. The patient reported a history of these masses gradually increasing in size and number. The lesions recurred quickly and were associated with pain and difficulty walking. The patient had previously undergone several surgical excisions to alleviate pain. Physical examination revealed multiple exophytic, round, compressible bluish-purple nodules.
test_results: Radiography revealed multiple enchondromas at bilateral phalanges and the left distal ulna. Histopathological analysis of the excised mass showed that the tumor consisted of bland spindle cell proliferations and dilated, slit-like, thin-walled veins involving the superficial and deep layers of the dermis. The molecular analysis showed that both the SCH tissue and cystic blood had somatic IDH1 p.Arg132Cys mutations. The NGS revealed that IDH1 mutations were identified with allele loads of 6.46 and 2.41% in the tissue and cystic blood samples.

case_report: A 12-year-old girl presented with missing lower teeth and concerns about facial appearance, along with progressive hearing loss over the past 3 months. She reported that only a few permanent teeth had erupted, causing difficulty in chewing and eating. Her dental history included the extraction of an upper left permanent molar due to severe decay. There was no significant medical or family history. General examination showed short stature and normal intelligence. Extraoral examination noted increased distance between the eyes, prominent forehead, a broad and short skull, a flattened nasal bridge, underdeveloped cheekbones, an underdeveloped upper jaw with a protruding lower jaw, and a concave facial profile. Examination of the hands revealed underdeveloped distal phalanges, and the fourth toe was shorter than usual. The chest was narrow and cone-shaped, with mild spinal curvature abnormalities such as scoliosis and kyphosis. Palpation revealed a depression over the sagittal suture and the presence of the metopic suture of the frontal bone, and the patient could bring her shoulders together at the midline. Intraoral examination showed normal mouth opening and jaw movements, a high arched and narrow palate, an erupted upper right permanent first molar, and retained deciduous teeth.
test_results: Panoramic radiograph revealed few impacted teeth, multiple retained deciduous teeth, and underdeveloped maxillary sinuses. AP view of pelvis demonstrated a widened pubic symphysis and triradiate cartilage. Skull AP and lateral views showed the presence of multiple wormian bones with open fontanelles. Chest radiograph showed bell-shaped rib cage and hypoplastic clavicles.

case_report: A 39-year-old male patient presented with dry, scaly, red skin lesions on the hands, feet, mouth, and anus. He experienced a febrile illness with diarrhea at 8 months old, after which his hair began to fall out, leading to complete body hair loss by age five. The skin lesions on his hands and feet appeared at 18 months, followed by difficulties in walking, balance, and articulation. He was born at term via normal vaginal delivery to consanguineous parents. The patient has two siblings, one female and one male, and all family members, including parents, are healthy. Despite various treatments for acrodermatitis enteropathica, including zinc replacement since 1.5 years old, his symptoms worsened. Dermatological examination showed sharply defined, erythematous hyperkeratotic plaques around the eyes, mouth, nose, anus, scrotum, and penis. There was bilateral, mutilating keratoderma extending from the palmar surfaces to the dorsum of the hands, with flexion deformities of the digits and generalized hair loss. Nail examination revealed dystrophy and subungual hyperkeratosis, and there were dental deformities. Laboratory tests showed a platelet count of 716/microliter and the presence of the JAK2 V6117F mutation. Bone marrow examination indicated cell-rich bone marrow (80% cellularity) with markedly increased megakaryopoiesis. The patient was diagnosed with essential thrombocytosis. Serum zinc level was normal at 94 microgram/dl.
test_results: Skin biopsy taken from the dorsum of the hand revealed severe hyperkeratosis, focal parakeratosis, hypergranulosis, and acanthosis. A second biopsy taken from the perioral area revealed intracorneal pustule formation, psoriasiform acanthosis, and intense inflammatory infiltration of the papillary dermis.

case_report: A 5 year and 10-month-old girl of Afro-Caribbean descent was referred to the Paediatric Metabolic clinic for intellectual disability and speech delay. She was the only child of non-consanguineous parents, born at 37 weeks due to intrauterine growth retardation associated with reversed umbilical arterial end-diastolic flow. The pregnancy was monitored closely because of maternal systemic lupus erythematosus. The family history was unremarkable, with two healthy siblings. Parents noted concerns about low muscle tone, minimal vocalization, and delayed skill acquisition from 6 months of age. She learned to sit unsupported at 1 year, walked at 2 years, and started running by 4 years. She vocalized using single vowel and consonant sounds and had persistent feeding difficulties due to oro-pharyngeal incoordination. The patient attended a special needs school and received physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and speech and language therapy, learning to communicate using Makaton. Intermittent esotropia and myopic astigmatism were diagnosed at 1 year, and a hearing assessment at 3 years was normal. On examination, her weight was 26.7 kg (98th centile), height 119 cm (91st centile), and head circumference 52.3 cm (50th–75th centile). There were no dysmorphic features or neuro-cutaneous skin stigmata. Sparse pubic and axillary hair was noted from 4 years. She had hypotonia in all four limbs with a positive Gower sign, indicating proximal muscle weakness. Tendon reflexes were normal. Cognitive assessment using the Bayley scale (3rd edition) showed a developmental age of 23 months. Language assessment (Preschool Language Scales, Edition 5) indicated a language age equivalent to 26 months, with severe impairment in both receptive and expressive skills and moderate intellectual disability. There was no history of seizures. Metabolic work-up, including intermediary metabolism, microelements, peroxisomal and lysosomal function, glycosylation, creatine, and purine/pyrimidine metabolites, were normal. Initial genetic analysis showed normal array comparative genomic hybridization and fragile X polymerase chain reaction. Routine biochemistry revealed persistently elevated alkaline phosphatase levels (1300–1832 U/L, ref. 150–380) with normal liver function tests. Urinary cortico-sterol analysis confirmed precocious adrenarche. A wrist X-ray at 5 years and 8 months showed minimal sclerosis of the distal radial metaphysis without other radiographic features of rickets. Bone age was assessed to be 8 years and 11 months. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) neurotransmitter analysis showed low pyridoxal phosphate (8 mmol/L, ref. 10–37) and 5-methyltetrahydrofolate (5-MTHF) (66 mmol/L, ref. 72–172). Plasma pyridoxal phosphate was elevated at 190 nmol/L (ref. 15–73), while red cell and plasma folate levels were normal. CSF homovanillic acid (HVA) was raised at 611 nmol/L (ref. 71–565), indicating increased dopamine turnover. Brain MRI at 6 years was normal. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography found no neurogenic changes. Electroencephalogram (EEG) recorded during wakefulness and sleep showed a moderate, non-specific abnormality with brief (1–2 s) runs of 4-6/s spike–wave complexes over the posterior half of the head, facilitated by eye closure and possibly by photic stimulation at 16 Hz. During drowsiness, runs lasting 4–6 s were seen without clinical accompaniments. During sleep, only isolated 1–2 s bursts of spike–wave complexes were seen over the posterior half of the head, involving the mid- but not the anterior temporal electrodes.
test_results: Targeted sequence analysis identified two heterozygous variants in the PGAP2 gene: NM_001256240.2 c.103del p.(Leu35Serfs*90) and c.134A > G p.(His45Arg). The c.103del p.(Leu35Serfs*90) variant is predicted to result in a protein frame-shift and subsequent premature stop gain, is absent from the gnomAD database and has not previously been reported. The c.134A > G p.(His45Arg) variant affects a highly conserved amino acid and is absent from the gnomAD database and has not previously been reported. Analysis of the NGS read data showed these variants to be on opposite alleles (in trans). Subsequent Sanger confirmation studies confirmed the presence of these variants in the proband, and parental carrier status.

case_report: A 69-year-old woman undergoing a routine hemodialysis program three times a week for 8 years, with a history of polycystic kidney disease, chronic renal failure, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, reported chest pain and shortness of breath during one of her dialysis sessions. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 140/80 mmHg in the right upper extremity and a heart rate of 78 beats per minute, with normal heart and breath sounds. An electrocardiogram indicated sinus rhythm. Cardiac enzyme levels were within the normal range. Echocardiographic findings included left ventricular hypertrophy, dilatation of the right heart chambers, pulmonary hypertension, 2-3° tricuspid regurgitation, 1° aortic regurgitation, and minimal pericardial effusion. Blood pressure measurements showed hypertension levels in both upper extremities (150/90 mmHg) and lower levels in the lower extremities (110/70 mmHg).
test_results: The descending aorta was interrupted in a 1 cm segment starting from the subclavian arterial exit. The distal of the descending aorta was being filled with internal mammarian and paravertebral collaterals. Coronary arteries were also evaluated in CT angiography, and no critic lesions were observed.

case_report: A 42-year-old male presented with recurrent tonic-clonic movements of the limbs. Pediatric records indicate he was born to non-consanguineous parents via vaginal delivery at home, with normal development until school age. His academic performance was poor, and his IQ was assessed at 80. In his late 20s, he was admitted to the orthopedic department due to pain in both ankles. In his early 30s, he began experiencing gait disturbances and memory impairment, which progressively worsened. The patient's family members have no notable clinical findings.
test_results: Electroencephalography showed diffuse slow activity. Brain MRI showed severe brain atrophy with severe white matter hyperintensity and basal ganglia atrophy with hypointensity, but relatively preserved occipital lobes and cerebellum. Brain CT revealed bilateral calcifications in basal ganglia. Multiple bone cysts in both tali were visualized in foot radiographs, which symmetrically exhibited increased tracer uptake by bone scintigraphy. The osseous lesions on microscopy consisted of convoluted lipid membrane structures filled with amorphous lipid.

case_report: A 62-year-old female with no known comorbidities and a history of severe COVID-19 pneumonia 9 months earlier presented with complaints of dry cough and progressive breathlessness (mMRC grade I–III) for 4 months. On examination, she was in respiratory distress, and her vitals were as follows: pulse rate 120 beats per minute, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 84% on room air. Auscultation revealed fine inspiratory crackles over both interscapular, infrascapular, and infraaxillary areas. Other system examinations were unremarkable. Her arterial blood gas analysis showed hypoxemia (PaO2 61 mm Hg at FiO2 of 0.30, PF ratio 203) with an elevated alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient (112.9 mm Hg). The chest radiograph displayed bilateral alveolar opacities, more pronounced on the left side.
test_results: High-resolution CT revealed ground-glass opacities with a characteristic 'crazy paving pattern' that was more conspicuous on the left side. Bronchoalveolar lavage was milky white on gross appearance and displayed PAS and PAS-D positive amorphous proteinaceous material on cytology and special staining. Histopathological examination of the transbronchial lung biopsy showed normal lung parenchyma and granular eosinophilic amorphous PAS stain–positive material in many alveoli. Her blood samples for anti-GM-CSF antibodies were positive (12.4 µg/mL, normal range < 3.1 µg/mL).

case_report: A 50-year-old woman experienced prolonged episodes of abdominal pain over the past 20 years without any clear trigger. Despite undergoing an appendectomy during her third acute abdominal episode, she continued to experience similar symptoms. She also had a history of occasional nonpitting, nonpruritic swellings, which were not concurrent with the abdominal pain and had become infrequent in recent years. She reported allergies to penicillin and seafood. Her father and one of her two sisters had similar skin swellings but did not experience abdominal pain, while other family members did not have these issues. Physical examination and blood chemistry analysis were unremarkable. Immunologic tests showed no abnormalities except for C3 and C4 levels. A CT scan of the abdomen revealed circumferential edema of the proximal jejunal bowel with thickened mesentery and a moderate amount of ascites. Gastroscopy, colonoscopy, and capsule endoscopy identified several erythemas. Over the past 8 years, she had been treated for conditions such as appendicitis, pancreatitis, ischemic enteropathy, and irritable bowel syndrome with medications including H1-receptor antagonists, glucocorticoids, and cholinoceptor blocking drugs. Although these treatments provided temporary relief for two to three days, the frequency and severity of her episodes increased from yearly to trimestrally and then to monthly over the past two years.
test_results: The serum concentration of C1-INH demonstrated a significant reduction.

case_report: A male in his late 60s with a history of rheumatoid arthritis presented with prolonged diffuse arthritic pain, shortness of breath, chronic ageusia, weight loss, and chronic anemia requiring regular transfusions. His shortness of breath was severe enough to hinder daily activities. He had been treated with prednisone 20 mg daily, methotrexate 20 mg weekly, and periodic packed red blood cell transfusions for symptomatic anemia. Upon presentation, his vitals were unremarkable. Physical examination revealed a frail-appearing male with right-sided conjunctivitis, inspiratory wheezing, and bilateral arm hyperpigmentation with skin atrophy. Laboratory results showed leukocytosis with lymphopenia, elevated metamyelocytes, myelocytes, and promyelocytes. He also had macrocytic anemia with red blood cell morphology indicating slight micro- and macrocytosis, schistocytes, and polychromasia. Additional workup for other causes was unremarkable, including tests for leukemia, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, and paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. Autoimmune tests showed a negative antinuclear antibody but elevated thyroid peroxidase and ribonucleoprotein antibodies. Perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (P-ANCA) titer was 1:160.
test_results: Bone marrow biopsy showed a hypercellular bone marrow with vacuoles, 5% blasts, and no evidence of dyspoiesis. The next generation sequencing and fluorescence in situ hybridization for multiple genetic abnormalities in the myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) panel was negative. Flow cytometry showed left shifted myeloid maturation pattern with 4.4% myeloblasts. He tested positive for a heterozygous UBA1 mutation at p.Met41Thr.

case_report: A 21-year-old male presented to the emergency department with recurrent myalgia and cramps in the lower limbs, which had been progressing for approximately two months and worsened over the past week, particularly after soccer training sessions. The patient denied experiencing fever, anorexia, or weight loss. His personal and family medical history revealed no relevant information, and he reported no use of medications, dietary supplements, alcohol, or drugs. The patient, a student, engaged in soccer practice three times a week and participated in official matches on weekends. Despite no difficulty in performing daily activities, muscle pain from exertion significantly affected his productivity. Physical examination in the emergency department showed normal vital signs and an unremarkable neurological examination. The patient had well-developed musculature without atrophy or fasciculations, normal muscle strength, sensitivity, reflexes, and no gait disturbances. Laboratory tests indicated elevated serum CK levels (1023 IU/L) with no other abnormalities. The patient was discharged with advice to follow up with his primary care physician if symptoms persisted. One week later, due to ongoing symptoms, the patient visited primary healthcare, where further laboratory tests were conducted to investigate potential causes of myopathy, including markers of inflammation, electrolyte levels (potassium, sodium, phosphate), and thyroid function. He was prescribed analgesics and muscle relaxants and scheduled for reevaluation in eight days, with the possibility of referral to a neurology consultation for further assessment.
test_results: The laboratory investigation revealed a free T4 level of 0.16 ng/dL (normal range: 0.7-1.8 ng/dL) and a serum TSH level of 134 mU/L (normal range: 0.4-5.5 mU/mL). The anti‑thyroid peroxidase (anti‑TPO) antibody was positive. CK level was 1578 U/L (normal level: <170 U/L).

case_report: A 23-year-old Caucasian man was admitted to the hospital due to a persistent fever that did not respond to standard treatments. During the physical examination, the patient exhibited significant enlargement of the liver and spleen, along with abnormal lung sounds. Laboratory tests revealed severe pancytopenia with hemoglobin at 9.3 g/dL, platelets at 93 × 10^9 cells/L, white blood cells at 2.2 × 10^9 cells/L, neutrophils at 410 × 10^9 cells/L, and lymphocytes at 1.570 × 10^9 cells/L. Additionally, there was an increase in lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels, evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and positive anti-EBV IgM antibodies. A chest X-ray indicated diffuse pulmonary infiltrates. The patient had no prior history of immunological abnormalities.
test_results: The bone marrow was hypercellular, with numerous atypical lymphoid cells and occasional hemophagocytes (identified by positive staining for CD68/PGM1). Lymphocytes were more often small and without significant atypia; a smaller percentage was represented by larger cells. Atypical lymphocytes were CD79a-, CD3+, CD2+, CD8+ and TIA1+. The majority of lymphoid cells were positive for EBER. A monoclonal rearrangement of the TCRγ genes was revealed.
diagnosis: Systemic Epstein-Barr-virus-positive T cell lymphoproliferative disease of childhood
Orpha_name: Systemic Epstein-Barr virus-positive T-cell lymphoproliferative disease of childhood

case_report: A 90-day old male infant presented with respiratory distress. He was born preterm via cesarean section due to maternal oligohydramnios, weighing 2060 grams at birth. He is the first child of the family. The pregnancy was uneventful, and ultrasonographic examinations showed no fetal abnormalities but indicated oligohydramnios at the 35th week of gestation. The parents, who are not related, have normal body habitus (father: 75 kg, 175 cm; mother: 81 kg, 174 cm). They declined ophthalmologic and cardiac examinations. Physical examination measurements were as follows: total height 58 cm, upper segment 24.5 cm, lower segment 23.5 cm, and arm span 62 cm (upper to lower segment ratio 1.04, arm span to height ratio 1.07). His maximum weight was 4.4 kg, and his actual weight was 3.9 kg. The anterior fontanel was open (0.5 cm × 0.5 cm). Ophthalmologic examination showed no lens dislocation. Notable physical features included large ear lobes, micrognathia, dolichocephaly, redundant forehead skin, and enophthalmos. The fingers were unusually long, while the toes appeared normal. Both thumb and wrist signs were positive, and there was limited motion in the elbow joints. A deep pectus excavatum was observed. Cardiac examination revealed a grade III/VI holosystolic murmur over the left sternal border and a gallop rhythm. The abdomen was soft. Karyotype analysis showed a normal 46XY. Chest X-ray indicated cardiomegaly. Brain, abdomen, and pelvic sonographic examinations showed no abnormalities. Electrocardiography indicated right ventricular hypertrophy.
test_results: Echocardiography revealed dilated aortic root (23.8 mm, Z value ≥+3) and prolaptic mitral valve with severe regurgitation. Tricuspid valve was prolaptic and severely regurgitant. There was severe pulmonary hypertension (pressure gradient of tricuspid regurgitation = 70 mmHg), pulmonary artery dilation (27.9 mm) and an atrial septal defect (7.7 mm in diameter) through an aneurismal interatrial septum with left-to-right shunt.

case_report: A 17-year-old African American male with a history of high blood pressure presented with a 4-day history of coughing, vomiting, headache, facial swelling, and lower extremity cramping. One day before admission, he noticed decreased urine output. At the referring hospital, he was found to be hypertensive with a serum creatinine of 52 mg/dL (4597 µmol/L) and was transferred to our pediatric intensive care unit for further evaluation and treatment. The patient was born at term with no significant health problems. During routine clinic visits, his primary care physician noted high blood pressure, which was attributed to his obesity. He had no prior surgeries and was not taking any medications. There was no significant family history of renal disease, dialysis, or kidney transplant. On admission, the patient was afebrile, hypertensive with a blood pressure of 179/93 mm Hg, heart rate of 88 beats per minute, and tachypneic with a respiratory rate in the 40s but saturating at 100% on room air. His height was 180 cm, weight 115 kg, and body mass index >99%. Physical examination revealed obesity, respiratory distress with nasal flaring, bilateral periorbital edema, and bilateral lower extremity edema. Laboratory results showed azotemia with blood urea nitrogen (BUN) of 203 mg/dL and serum creatinine of 52 mg/dL, measured by enzymatic method. He had severe metabolic acidosis with bicarbonate of 10 mmol/L. Severe electrolyte imbalances included hyponatremia (126 mmol/L), hyperkalemia (6.3 mmol/L), hyperphosphatemia (10.5 mg/dL), hypocalcemia (5.3 mg/dL), and severe anemia with hemoglobin at 5.1 g/dL. Parathyroid hormone levels were elevated at 682 pg/mL (normal 11–80 pg/mL). Urine dipstick showed 3+ protein and 2+ blood, and a urine protein to creatinine ratio was elevated at 14 (normal <0.2). Serological workup including complement levels, antinuclear antibodies, antinuclear cytoplasmic antibodies, and antiphospholipid antibodies was negative. Chest X-ray was significant for cardiomegaly and pulmonary edema. Echocardiogram showed severe left ventricular hypertrophy.
test_results: Renal ultrasound revealed bilateral small, echogenic kidneys (right kidney 7.7 × 5.2 × 4.8 cm; left kidney 8.7 × 4.3 × 4.1 cm).

case_report: A 70-year-old male arrived at the emergency department in Mantua, northeast Italy, due to spontaneous bleeding from the gums. The patient reported mild fatigue and headache but did not experience any bruising or other bleeding symptoms. His medical history included well-controlled hypertension and an inguinal herniotomy performed 20 years ago without any bleeding issues. Physical examination revealed mild pallor of the skin and conjunctiva, gum bleeding, and enlarged lymph nodes at superficial locations with a maximum diameter of 2 cm.
test_results: Bone marrow biopsy detected increased cellularity (90%) that accounted for at least 40% of interstitial cellular aggregates of lymphoid, lymphoplasmacytoid and plasma cells, that at immunohistochemical analysis were positive for CD20, IgM and κ light chains but negative for CD5, CD23, D1 cyclin and lambda (λ) light chains. Immunofixation confirmed a double monoclonal component, IgM kappa (κ). Immunoglobulin assays showed serum IgG levels of 5.39 g/L (normal range, 7-16 g/L), IgA 0.11 g/L (normal range, 0.7-4 g/L), but very high IgM at 63.7 g/L (normal range, 0.4-2.3 g/L). Blood tests revealed normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 9 g/dL), with normal white cell and platelet counts. With a normal prothrombin time, the activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) was mildly prolonged (ratio, 1.29; normal range, 0.82-1.18), but its full correction with a normal plasma mixing test excluded a coagulation inhibitor. Screening for lupus anticocoagulant was also negative. Factor VIII coagulant activity (FVIII:C) was 40% (normal range, 50-150%), von Willebrand factor antigen (vWF:Ag) was 18% (normal range. 50-120%), ristocetin co-factor activity (vWF:RCo) was 29% (normal range, 50-150%), and the collagen binding activity (vWF:CB) was 37% (normal range, 50-150%). Following the observation of slightly elevated serum proteins (8.8 g/dL; normal range, 6.5-8.0 g/dL), electrophoresis showed increased concentrations in the beta (β) (2.58 g/dL; normal range, 0.6-0.9 g/dL) and gamma (γ) (2.36; normal range, 0.8-1.4 g/dL) regions, with a double spike at a concentration of 1.67 g/dL.
diagnosis: Acquired von Willebrand syndrome associated with Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia

case_report: A 79-year-old male patient was admitted with a history of hypertension for over 20 years, hypertensive nephropathy for 4 years, vomiting for 9 hours, and urinary incontinence for 5 hours. Clinical findings included hemoglobin (Hb) at 72 g/L (reference range 120–160 g/L), alanine transaminase (ALT) at 18 U/L (reference range < 23 U/L), total bilirubin (TBIL) at 7.1 μmol/L (reference range 2-21 μmol/L), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) at 382 U/L (reference range 135–215 U/L), blood urea nitrogen (BUN) at 31.47 mmol/L (reference range 3.0–9.2 mmol/L), creatinine (Cr) at 588.3 μmol/L (reference range 71–115 μmol/L), and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) activity within physiological levels. Imaging via computed tomography (CT) revealed a left frontotemporal occipital subdural hematoma, left insular hemorrhage, acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pulmonary infection, grade 3 hypertension high-risk group, hypertensive nephropathy, chronic kidney disease stage 4, and pericardial effusion. Post-admission treatments included infusion of leukocyte-reduced red blood cells (LRBCs) prepared from 600 ml of whole blood, blood pressure management, hemostasis, erythropoietin, and other supportive measures. Hemodialysis was performed once every 2–3 days, resulting in a reduction of creatinine levels to 242.6 μmol/L by the 50th day, at which point hemodialysis was discontinued.
test_results: The results of the direct antiglobulin test (DAT) for anti-IgG with a Coombs card of blood samples collected on days 2, 1, and 0 before stopping piperacillin-tazobactam administration were strongly positive (4 +). After stopping the administration of piperacillin-tazobactam, the DAT for anti-IgG results gradually weakened and turned negative until 12 days after the administration of piperacillin-tazobactam was stopped. The results of the DAT for anti-C3d with the tube method of all blood samples were negative.

case_report: A 42-year-old male patient with a history of cataract surgery in the right eye 9 years ago, resulting in a best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 1.0 (20/20) in both eyes, presented with decreased visual acuity to 0.4 (20/50) in the left eye due to a posterior polar cataract. After undergoing cataract surgery in the left eye, visual acuity improved to 0.9 (20/22) but decreased to 0.5 (20/40) one week later due to significant macular edema (retinal foveal thickness [RFT] = 460 µm). Anterior chamber inflammation measured 38.8 photons/milliseconds (ph/ms) by laser flare photometry, and the patient reported floaters due to vitreitis. Treatment included corticosteroid drops (dexamethasone 0.1% TID), oral acetazolamide (250 mg), and a sub-Tenon's injection of triamcinolone acetonide (40 mg) in the left eye. One week later, BCVA improved to 1.0 (20/20), inflammation decreased to 34.9 ph/ms, and RFT decreased to 354 µm. Two weeks later, macular edema increased to 646 µm, BCVA was 0.7 (20/32), and flare was 26.2 ph/ms. A second sub-Tenon's injection of triamcinolone acetonide (40 mg) was administered, but three weeks later, there was no functional or inflammatory improvement (BCVA = 0.5 = 20/40, flare = 25.5 ph/ms), although RFT returned to normal. Dilated fundus examination revealed posterior pole hemorrhages and a temporal-inferior peripheral yellow necrotic area in the left eye. Valacyclovir (1,000 mg TID) was initiated. Laboratory tests showed normal serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (10.6 U/L), slightly elevated lysozyme (24.2 mg/L), negative QuantiFERON® Tuberculosis test (<0.1 IU/mL), positive but non-elevated IgGs for Epstein-Barr virus (1:80), slightly elevated IgGs for varicella-zoster virus (8.0 Index), no exposure to cytomegalovirus (<1 U/mL) or herpes simplex virus (<0.5 Index), and substantially elevated IgGs for Toxoplasma gondii (300 IU/mL). Clindamycin (300 mg QID) was added to the treatment. The condition remained stable for one month. Due to the COVID-19 lockdown, the patient was seen again two months later, with BCVA at 0.3 (20/63), flare at 17.4 ph/ms, and RFT at 355 µm. Decreased visual acuity was attributed to increased vitreous opacities. Fundus examination of the left eye showed slightly reduced posterior pole hemorrhages and a stable yellowish peripheral temporal-inferior lesion. Similar, more discreet lesions were noted in the peripheral temporal superior fundus of the right eye.
test_results: Polymerase chain reaction analysis of the vitreous was negative for HSV1&2, VZV, CMV, EBV, and Toxoplasma gondii.
diagnosis: Coats-like exudative vitreoretinopathy in retinitis pigmentosa

case_report: A 71-year-old Caucasian male with a history of heart transplant 18 months prior, currently on tacrolimus and prednisone, presented with redness on the face and hair loss on the eyebrows and mustache. Physical examination revealed small spicules overlying scaly erythematous plaques on the scalp, eyebrows, chin, upper cutaneous lip, and nose.
test_results: Skin biopsy showed dilated and distorted follicles with absent hair shaft and expansion of the matrix from the inner root sheath and outer root sheath with dense keratohyalin granules.

case_report: A 4-month-old girl, the third child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents, was born via C-section at 40 weeks of gestation. Prenatal ultrasound at 28 weeks indicated intrauterine growth retardation, but the remainder of the pregnancy was uneventful. The mother had a history of two medical abortions and no history of alcohol, smoking, or drug abuse. The newborn had a birth weight of 2400 g and a length of 48 cm. Due to orofacial malformations, the infant experienced feeding difficulties and was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) for 21 days. At 4 months, the child exhibited growth retardation with a height of 55 cm (3rd percentile), weight of 4100 g (below the 3rd percentile), and a head circumference of 47 cm (normal). Cognitive development was normal. Physical examination revealed craniofacial anomalies including microretrognathia, downslanting palpebral fissures, high forehead, low-set, posteriorly rotated, and dysplastic cup-shaped ears, absence of medial lower lid eyelashes, smooth philtrum, and high arched palate. Additionally, the right thumb was absent, and there was a duplication of the right second finger. The feet showed inward rotation of the halluces. Routine hematological and biochemical tests were normal. Imaging studies, including brain ultrasound, abdominal ultrasound, and echocardiography, were normal. Radiographic examination indicated radial hypoplasia, absence of the right thumb, and duplication of the right second finger. Proximal radioulnar synostosis was not observed. Hypoplasia of the malar and mandibular bones was noted. Cytogenetic analysis showed a normal female karyotype (46,XX).
test_results: Whole exome sequencing (WES) revealed a heterozygous de novo variant c.900del, p.(Met301Cysfs*19) in the SF3B4 gene. De novo status was confirmed by parental testing.

case_report: A 5-year-old female from Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, born to non-consanguineous parents, exhibited delayed developmental milestones and distinct facial features from birth. At the age of four, she began experiencing myoclonic seizures. Physical examination revealed a triangular face, broad forehead, dental malocclusion, micrognathia, and bilateral tonsillar enlargement. Hypotonic extremities were also noted. Hearing and vision assessments showed no clinically apparent deficits.
test_results: Molecular genetic test showed duplication in the 17p11.2 region.

case_report: In 2003, a 14-year-old female was admitted to the Department of Cardiology with acute pericarditis. Her medical history indicated she was born at 39 weeks of gestation with a low birth weight and congenital pneumonia, receiving an Apgar score of 5. She had no siblings. Continuous positive airway pressure was administered during the first 24 hours of life. The patient experienced multiple hospitalizations due to upper and lower respiratory tract infections during the neonatal period, infancy, and childhood. These episodes involved respiratory failure with hypercarbia, necessitating periodic mechanical ventilation and showing signs of respiratory drive dysfunction. At admission, electrocardiography (ECG) revealed moderate hypertrophy of both ventricles. An echocardiogram confirmed right ventricular hypertrophy and detected fluid accumulation in the pericardial sac. Pulmonary hypertension was also noted, associated with right ventricular hypertrophy. Laboratory blood tests were largely normal except for elevated white blood cell count and C-reactive protein levels, indicating inflammation. Arterial gasometry results showed significant changes before and after 10 minutes of volitional hyperventilation (PO2 from 69 mmHg to 82 mmHg, hemoglobin saturation from 93.2% to 97.6%, and PCO2 from 54 to 25 mmHg). Treatment for pericarditis included antibiotics (ceftriaxone during hospitalization and cefaclor after discharge), diuretics, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, albumin transfusion, antiviral therapy, and vitamin supplements. Following successful treatment, the patient was referred to the Respiratory and Sleep Disorders Centre.
test_results: The patient was heterozygous for PARM (20/25 PARM).

case_report: A 34-year-old white male presented with a lesion on the right first digit that had been present for one year and had significantly worsened over the past six months. The lesion was described as an erythematous papule, causing local pain and bleeding after minor traumas, but without itching. The patient has a history of HIV diagnosed six years ago, with recent tests showing an undetectable viral load and a CD4 count of 718 cells/mm. His antiretroviral regimen includes tenofovir, lamivudine, lopinavir, and ritonavir. He reported no other health conditions or similar cases in his family. Dermatological examination revealed erythematous, keratotic, scaly plaques with raised ridges and an atrophic center on the dorsal surface of the right first digit. No other lesions were noted.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed a large cornoid lamella with parakeratotic cells. Hypogranulosis and dyskeratosis were observed at the base. Superficial dermis showed rare perivascular mononuclear cells.

case_report: A 38-year-old woman with a 20-year history of smoking 1 ½ packs of cigarettes per day was referred to QEII Health Science Centre in Halifax, Nova Scotia, approximately 6 years ago due to fatigue, frequent colds, and persistent elevated lymphocyte levels for over 6 months. Her past medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Physical examination revealed mild splenomegaly, with the spleen palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin. Initial complete blood cell count (CBC) indicated isolated lymphocytosis at 10.2 x 10^9/L, and peripheral blood smears showed a few atypical binucleated lymphocytes.
test_results: Flow cytometry of her peripheral blood revealed an increase in polytypic CD19+/ CD20+/ CD5-/ CD10- B cells. Serum protein electrophoresis showed elevated polyclonal IgM at 9.6 g/L.

case_report: A 27-year-old woman reported a 3-week history of a painless swelling on the right lower eyelid, with no prior trauma or signs of systemic illness. The nodule was small, firm, attached to the tarsus, and pink in color. An ocular examination revealed 20/20 visual acuity in both eyes, normal findings in the anterior and posterior segments, no proptosis, and full range of extraocular movements. Initially, a surgical plan was made to incise and curette the lesion. During the procedure, the content appeared abnormal, prompting a complete excision under local anesthesia. The content was fleshy, reddish, and bloody with a gritty texture. The excised tissue was gray-tan, soft, and measured 0.5 × 0.3 cm.
test_results: Histopathological examination of hematoxylin and eosin-stained slides revealed densely packed spindle to ovoid, unremarkable endothelial cells with newly formed slits that contain red blood cells. Immunohistochemistry study showed a positive staining of the neoplastic cells by the endothelial cell marker CD31.

case_report: A 4-hour-old male newborn exhibited a complete absence of skin over the anteromedial aspect of both lower legs since birth. The baby was delivered by a 23-year-old first-time mother through a normal vaginal delivery, with both pregnancy and delivery being uncomplicated. The mother reported no exposure to medications or radiation during pregnancy. The parents were not related, and there was no family history of similar conditions or skin diseases. The baby's Apgar scores were normal, but he was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit due to the skin lesion. The baby appeared otherwise healthy, with normal weight, length, head circumference, and vital signs. Physical examination revealed symmetrical bilateral skin absence over the anteromedial aspect of the legs, extending from the knees to the dorsal and medial plantar aspects of the feet. The lesions had sharply defined borders covered by a red, ultrathin translucent membrane, with visible vascular structures. Some nails on the fingers and toes were dystrophic. The scalp and mucous membranes were unaffected. Systemic examination was normal. After 5 days, blisters developed over the preexisting lesions, and blistering also occurred on normal skin in response to minor trauma or friction. Laboratory investigations showed normal complete blood count, electrolytes, liver and renal function tests, and negative serologic tests for infection. Ophthalmological examination, abdominal and cranial ultrasound screening, and echocardiography were all normal.
test_results: Histopathological study of the skin biopsy showed subepidermal blister formation.

case_report: A 43-year-old, right-handed male presented with left-hand weakness of three months duration. His symptoms began two years earlier with an episode of sudden-onset vertigo unrelated to head and body movements and left leg heaviness, which lasted for one day. Several months later, he experienced two episodes of dysarthria and tongue heaviness lasting for a few hours. Three months before his presentation, he started to experience left-hand weakness not affecting his work along with cognitive slowing in the form of difficulty in calculation. He was born of a non-consanguineous marriage. His only sibling, his sister, was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis at the age of 40. Her illness was progressive and did not respond to treatment. His mother, who died in her 50s, had obsessive-compulsive disorder with psychotic features. His three maternal uncles died in their 50s, two due to myocardial infarction and one due to stroke. All his three children were healthy. He denied any family history of dementia or migraine. On examination, he scored 25 in MMSE. He had intact cranial nerves, decreased power over the left upper limb (4/5), deep tendon reflexes +3 without clonus, positive Babinski, normal sensory exam, intentional tremor in the left hand, and normal regular and tandem gaits. MRI brain with and without contrast showed multiple white matter hyperintense lesions on T2 and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequence in the frontoparietal region. A few of them are irregular and show a central area of hypointensity. Symmetric confluent areas of white matter hyperintensity were seen in the peri-ventricular high parietal region extending from the subcortical to the periventricular region. No enhancing lesions were found following the administration of the contrast. CT angiography of the head and neck and echocardiogram were unremarkable. There were no oligoclonal bands in the cerebrospinal fluid. The autoimmune workup was negative.
test_results: Whole genome sequencing was positive for a NOTCH3 mutation.
diagnosis: Cerebral Autosomal Dominant Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy

case_report: A 55-year-old male reported experiencing a 13-year history of left hand 'heaviness' during running, challenges with handwriting and typing, and increasing difficulty lifting his arm above his head to wash his hair. Five years prior, he observed clumsiness in his left leg, leading to tripping and stumbling, and subsequently received an ankle foot orthosis. He did not report any issues on the right side, nor did he experience any sensory symptoms, bulbar symptoms, or bowel or bladder incontinence.
test_results: A neurological examination revealed mild left hand and distal leg weakness with foot drop, asymmetric hyperreflexia, and an extensor plantar response. He had mildly increased tone in the left lower extremity. The sensory examination was normal. He had reduced movements to opening and closing his left hand. His gait was notable for a very mild reduction of the left arm swing and a left steppage gait.

case_report: A 5-year-old male patient presented with bleeding from the gingiva in the lower left back region for one week. Clinical examination revealed a dolichocephalic head, exophthalmos, frontal bossing, hypertelorism, a depressed nasal bridge, a hypoplastic maxilla, mandibular prognathism, and partial mental disability. The patient's physical condition was poor. Oral examination showed the presence of teeth 55, 54, 53, 52, 62, 63, 64, 74, 75, 83, and 84, swollen gingiva, mobility in tooth 74, a deep palatal vault, and spacing between teeth. Medical history indicated that the patient was healthy during the first year of life but experienced intermittent nosebleeds over the past year, with blood loss of 5 to 10 cc each time. The patient had repeated chest infections, diminished vision for three years, fever, cough, and episodes of hurried breathing that subsided with treatment. Additional findings included low-set ears, a depressed nasal bridge, micrognathia, short fingers, flat feet, pigeon chest deformity, a distended abdomen, an enlarged spleen, a shifted trachea toward the left, and an elongated skull. Family history was not significant. The patient's movements were restricted due to diminished vision, as reported by family members. Blood tests showed hemoglobin at 4.3 gm, packed cell volume at 20%, reticulocyte count at 4.0%, white blood cells at 7600 cells/cu mm, polymorphs at 27%, lymphocytes at 52%, monocytes at 1%, eosinophils at 20%, coagulation time at 4 minutes, and bleeding time at 3 minutes. The patient was found to have microcytic hypochromic anemia with eosinophilia.
test_results: Radiological findings showed generalized increase in bone density (Chalky white) with narrowing of skull base. Enlarged cardia and skull. Increased radiopacity of the skeletal bone of the chest. Cervical vertebra and disk space are normal. Lungs are clear.

case_report: A twenty-four-year-old female with a lifelong history of epilepsy and cognitive impairment presented with cyclic episodes of lethargy and behavioral changes. She had a history of intrauterine toxoplasmosis infection, resulting in colpocephaly, absence of posterior hemispheric structures, bilateral parieto-occipital porencephaly, and malformation of the right frontal lobe. Partial agenesis of the corpus callosum, including an absent splenium, was also noted. Developmental delays were observed during childhood, and seizures began at age 5, with multiple seizure types including atonic and generalized tonic-clonic. Approximately two years prior to presenting to Mayo Clinic, she began experiencing episodes of hypothermia with temperatures as low as 30.5°C, systemic hypotension, lethargy, and compromised functional status, leading to hospitalization for breakthrough seizures. During these episodes, she was consistently hyponatremic. These episodes occurred monthly and resolved over one to two weeks. Over the course of two years, she was found to be thrombocytopenic, anemic, and occasionally leukopenic. These hematological changes were initially attributed to valproic acid, which was part of her antiepileptic regimen along with lamotrigine for fifteen years. Valproic acid was discontinued in January 2012, and she was switched to levetiracetam, but her blood counts continued to decline. After discontinuing levetiracetam, her seizures were managed with zonisamide, clobazam, and rufinamide, and a vagal nerve stimulator was placed. Despite these changes, her blood counts remained depressed during subsequent hospitalizations. During a recent episode of lethargy and poor responsiveness, she was admitted to her local hospital and transferred to our institution. Laboratory findings included thrombocytopenia with a platelet count of 57 × 10^9/L (normal range 150–450 × 10^9/L), anemia with a hemoglobin of 8.4 g/dL (12.0–15.5 g/dL) and reticulocytopenia at 12.7 × 10^9/L (38.1–112.6 × 10^9/L). Her white blood cell count was within normal limits at 6.7 × 10^9/L (3.5–10.5 × 10^9/L). An infectious workup, including HIV, parvovirus B19 PCR, and blood and urine cultures, was negative. Iron, vitamin B12, and folate levels were normal. D-dimer, fibrinogen, and coagulation studies did not indicate disseminated intravascular coagulation. The heparin-induced thrombocytopenia PF4 antibody was negative, and no rheumatoid factor was detected. Her peripheral smear was normal, and levels of arsenic, cadmium, mercury, and lead were within normal limits.
test_results: Bone marrow biopsy showed a slightly hypocellular marrow with a mild granulocytic hypoplasia and megakaryocytic hyperplasia. Trilineage maturation was within normal limits.

case_report: A 59-year-old male patient with a history of primary biliary cirrhosis-autoimmune hepatitis overlap syndrome and end-stage cirrhosis underwent a living donor liver transplantation (LDLT). The donor was his 56-year-old wife, with compatible blood types (O to AB) and a negative lymphocyte cross-match test. The right lobe of the liver, weighing 500 grams, was transplanted without the middle hepatic vein. The graft-to-recipient weight ratio was 0.83, and the graft made up 42% of the recipient's standard liver volume. Post-transplant, the patient was started on immunosuppressive therapy with tacrolimus (Tac), mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), and prednisolone. He had a stable immediate postoperative course and was transferred out of the intensive-care unit on postoperative day (POD) 3. Approximately 2 months post-transplant, the patient experienced a progressive increase in biliary tract enzymes and total bilirubin (T-Bil). Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography showed no biliary anastomosis stenosis, and color Doppler ultrasonography and computed tomography revealed no abnormalities. A liver biopsy on POD 77 indicated minimal portal area inflammation and slight endothelial inflammation of the central venules. At this time, the patient's platelet count was below 10×10^5/mm3, and T-Bil concentration increased to 17 mg/dl. The patient received augmented immunosuppressive therapy, including intravenous corticosteroid pulse therapy, increased MMF doses, and Tac level adjustments to maintain a whole-blood concentration of 5–10 ng/ml. A subsequent liver biopsy on POD 91 showed minimal inflammation and no bile duct injury in the portal area, with chronic inflammation and hepatocyte loss in Zone 3. The sample was negative for C4d staining. Due to difficulties in maintaining Tac levels above 10 ng/ml, the patient's calcineurin inhibitor was switched from Tac to cyclosporin A (CsA), with CsA doses adjusted to maintain a blood level of 150–200 ng/ml, and everolimus was added as a third immunosuppressive agent. Additionally, the patient received two doses of basiliximab (50 mg/day). Despite no apparent causes for thrombocytopenia, such as disseminated intravascular coagulation or thrombotic diseases, the patient's platelet count declined to approximately 5×10^5/mm3, and T-Bil concentration increased to 21.4 mg/dl.
test_results: A liver biopsy taken on POD 203 showed inflammatory cells infiltrating the liver parenchyma in zone 3, as well as marked reductions in hepatocytes and central vein obliteration. Masson’s trichrome stain showed basement membrane formation caused by fibrous tissue and sinusoidal fibrosis. By contrast, the portal area (zone 1) showed minimal inflammation.

case_report: A 70-year-old man was referred to the Movement Disorder Unit of the University of Pisa due to gait difficulties, characterized by a tendency towards left lateropulsion while walking, frequent backward/lateral falls, and difficulty standing up from a sitting position. These issues had persisted for 3 years, during which he also experienced difficulty controlling the strength of his movements. Urinary urge incontinence was noted. Additionally, his wife observed limb movements during sleep. His medical history included hypertension, anxiety-depression disorder, type 2 diabetes, and chronic constipation, with no family history of neurological disease. Neurological examination revealed an ataxic gait, spasticity in the left lower limb, and asymmetric pendular movements of the upper limbs, more pronounced on the right side. He could maintain the Romberg position but exhibited multidirectional oscillations and was unable to perform tandem gait. Trunk and limb ataxia, particularly on the left side, and adiadochokinesia of the left hand were observed. He had difficulty performing the finger-to-nose and heel-to-knee tests on the left side. Brisk symmetrical deep tendon reflexes were present with an increased reflexogenic zone in the lower limbs and the upper left limb, but the Babinski sign was absent. Mild hypokinesia was detected in all four limbs, especially in the left foot. Blood tests ruled out coeliac disease and vitamin E deficiency. Electromyography showed no lower motor neuron involvement, and sensitive and motor nerve conduction studies were normal. MRI revealed atrophy of the cerebellar hemispheres and vermis, gliotic areas in the frontoparietal white matter bilaterally, and dilated perivascular spaces at the basal ganglia level. DAT-SCAN imaging indicated bilateral nigro-striatal degeneration.
test_results: A homozygous missense variant [c.1529C > T, p.(Ala510Val)] was found in the exon 11 of the SPG7 gene.

case_report: An 8-year-old girl presented to the rheumatology outpatient clinic with a 2-year history of gradually worsening weakness in the muscles near her hips and shoulders. Initially, her parents observed that she had trouble climbing into her school bus, which progressed within a month to an inability to rise from a squatting position. Over the following month, she also struggled with tasks like combing her hair. She had previously been evaluated by the neurology team at the same hospital when her symptoms first appeared 2 years ago. At that time, she exhibited proximal muscle weakness mainly affecting her lower limbs, a waddling gait, Gower’s sign, and enlarged calf muscles. Laboratory tests showed elevated creatine phosphokinase levels (CPK, 13000 IU/ml). Genetic testing revealed a heterozygous mutation (Cys72Trp) in exon 2 of the CAV3 gene, associated with limb girdle muscular dystrophy type 1C (LGMD1C). Despite no family history of myopathy, her parents were informed about the disease prognosis and potential risks for future pregnancies, but they did not return for follow-up. Two years later, a rheumatology consultation was sought due to a persistent facial rash that had not improved with dermatological treatments. A detailed history revealed that the rash had been intermittently present for the past 2 years without immunosuppressant therapy. Currently, she has difficulty getting out of bed without assistance, indicating that the weakness has spread to her trunk muscles over the past year. Physical examination showed papular eruptions on her knuckles, elbows, and knees, along with erythematous swelling of her eyelids. There was noticeable wasting of proximal muscles, including the biceps, glutei, and shoulder girdle, with winging of the scapula when she flexed her arms forward. Muscle strength was graded 2 out of 5 in the proximal muscle groups around the shoulders and hips, and 4 out of 5 in the distal muscles. Her Manual Muscle Testing (MMT8) score was 54 out of a possible 80.
test_results: The CPK levels were elevated (1769 IU/ml). The Anti-Nuclear Antibody test was positive (4+ Homogenous, 1:100). Myositis specific antibodies were positive for anti-Mi2.

case_report: A 72-year-old woman experienced behavioural changes, unsteadiness, and frequent falls over the past year. She had started oral anticoagulant therapy two years earlier due to paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Relatives reported that over the past year, she became more listless and neglected work and domestic activities. She also exhibited hyperreligious behaviour, anxiety, loss of appetite, mild lower limb weakness, and falls. Subsequently, she experienced periods of agitation, confusion, and visual hallucinations, leading to the initiation of antipsychotic medication. Her condition worsened, resulting in the loss of her ability to walk and confinement to a wheelchair. Upon admission, she showed disorientation, apathy, apraxia, short-term memory deficit (MMSE = 7), anosmia, mild flaccid proximal paraparesis, and muscular atrophy. Patellar reflexes and plantar responses were normal. Urinary incontinence was present, but there were no signs of sensory impairment. A comprehensive workup, including vitamin levels, thyroid function, and tumour markers, was normal. A 24-hour Holter monitor test revealed no paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. EEG indicated patterns of diffuse cerebral dysfunction without epileptic activity. A full-body CT scan and a breast ultrasound were unremarkable.
test_results: A brain MRI revealed T2*-pondered hypointensities around cerebral cortex (with a bilateral frontotemporal and insular predominance) and around the brainstem suggesting deposition of iron-containing products. An angioMRI did not reveal any source of bleeding. Spinal MRI showed T2* pondered hypointensities all along the spinal cord with thecal iron accumulation between L4 and S1. There were also signs of arachnoiditis between L2 and L4. CSF analysis revealed xanthochromia, 4500 red blood cells (RBC)/μL, 61 mg/dL in proteic concentration, and normal glucose level. CSF VDRL was negative and there were no neoplastic cells.

case_report: In 2012, a 35-year-old male from Iran visited Farhud’s Genetics Clinic in Tehran with a primary concern of blindness. Clinical examinations were conducted. The patient's medical history revealed that his parents were first cousins, and he had two sisters who appeared to be healthy. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient.
test_results: The sequencing results of GRK gene exon-intron boundaries did not show any mutations in this patient, but the sequencing of the SAG gene indicated a new homozygous mutation in exon four. This mutation was a C nucleotide deletion at codon 96, location chr2:233320735, c.517delC, p.P96LfsX28. This deletion causes a frame shift mutation, and premature stop codon in exon four of SAG gene. The nucleotide sequence of the 4th exon of the SAG gene in his parents showed that they were both heterozygotes for C deletion in codon number 96 and as mentioned above, the patient was homozygote for these mutations. One of her sister was also heterozygote for this new mutation. The results of the other sister’s patient showed that she is healthy for deletion of codon No. 96 of the SAG gene mutation.

case_report: A 28-year-old African American female with a 3-year history of rheumatoid arthritis presented to the emergency department (ED) in September 2019 with a fever of 101.5 °F, chills, and right ear pain. This ED visit followed multiple hospital admissions for similar symptoms including fever, chills, and a productive cough. In July 2019, the patient was admitted with sepsis secondary to bilateral community-acquired pneumonia and was treated with doxycycline and cefuroxime, but the course was complicated by neutropenia. One week prior to the September 2019 admission, the patient visited urgent care for a persistent fever lasting 3 days and right ear pain. She was diagnosed with otitis media and started on amoxicillin. The patient also had multiple lip ulcers and was given lidocaine. Her mother, who is her health proxy, noted that the symptoms did not improve after 2 days, prompting the ED visit. The patient was admitted for sepsis secondary to right middle lobe community-acquired pneumonia and a urinary tract infection. Her medical history includes asthma, pneumonia, mild intellectual disability, and anemia. Due to her mental disability, her mother provided the review of systems. According to her mother, associated symptoms included fever, chills, fatigue, ear pain, sore throat, productive cough, abdominal pain, and myalgia. There was no recent travel or sick contacts. No nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or dizziness were noted. There is no family history of rheumatoid arthritis or recurrent infections.
