There is no history of alcohol, smoking, or recreational drug use, and the patient was not sexually active. Physical examination revealed the patient was febrile at 101.5 °F, tachycardic at 117 beats per minute with a normal rhythm, intact distal pulses, normal breath sounds bilaterally with no wheezing, bilateral tympanic membrane injection without effusion, pharyngeal erythema, lower lip ulcers, abdominal tenderness, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and no active synovitis but decreased range of motion of the right wrist. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 3.50 × 10^3/μL with an absolute neutrophil count of 25 cells/mm^3, and a platelet count of 286 × 10^3/μL. Hemoglobin was 7.6 g/dL, hematocrit was 32.4%, and mean corpuscular volume was 71.1 fL. Peripheral blood smear showed no significant abnormalities with normal reticulocytes. Blood and urine cultures showed growth of Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Tests for Streptococcus pneumoniae, Epstein–Barr virus, herpes simplex virus, and influenza A and B were negative. C-reactive protein was elevated at 19.8 mg/L, and lactic acid was 2.5 mmol/L. Chest radiography in the anterior-posterior view showed infiltrates in the middle portion of the base of the right lung. Chest computed tomography showed no evidence of pulmonary embolism. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatosplenomegaly with the spleen measuring in the upper limits of normal.
test_results: The pathological evaluation of bone marrow revealed findings of normocellular focal spicules and maturing trilineage hematopoiesis, no evidence of overt dysplasia, increased immature mononuclear cells, and left shift with very rare mature neutrophils.

case_report: A 13-month-old girl was admitted to the hospital due to developmental regression. She was born at full term with a birth weight of 3700 grams and had normal development until 12 months of age, including walking with one hand held, grasping objects with two fingers, and speaking a few meaningful words. Her family history was unremarkable. One month before hospital admission, she had a three-day fever following inactivated Japanese Encephalitis and Hepatitis A vaccinations. About two weeks post-vaccination, she lost the ability to walk and could only stand with assistance. Her oral intake decreased, and she became more irritable. Upon presentation, she was unable to sit without support, could not produce meaningful speech, and required a nasogastric tube for feeding. Nystagmus was observed, and she had poor eye contact. Neurological examination revealed spastic extremities and bilateral ankle clonus. Laboratory tests showed normal complete blood cell count, liver function tests, renal function tests, and C-reactive protein levels. Serum lactate was 2.3 mmol/L. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed lympho-dominant pleocytosis with no significant increase in protein levels (red blood cell count: 0/µL, white blood cell count: 28/µL, lymphocyte count: 24/µL, protein level: 19 mg/dL, glucose level: 55 mg/dL). Microbiological studies of the CSF were negative for infection. Brain MRI revealed leukodystrophy in the bilateral periventricular white matter (PVWM) and corpus callosum, with the subcortical white matter unaffected. Diffusion restriction was noted in the PVWM without contrast enhancement. Arylsulfatase A and beta-galactosidase activities were within normal limits.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing revealed compound heterozygous ISCA2 variants of c.166T>G, p.C56G and c.422A>C, p.Q141P, each inherited from her parents. Amino acid analysis of the stored initial serum and CSF samples showed normal serum glycine level but markedly elevated CSF glycine (112 µM/L, reference range 2.9-7.9 µM/L).

case_report: The patient, currently 9 years old, was born at term with a birth weight of 2850 grams following an uneventful pregnancy. During the early years of life, the patient exhibited sparse and rare eyebrows and eyelashes, thickened toenails, erythematous lesions on the cheeks, chin, neck, and limbs, and significant skin atrophy with areas of hypo- and hyper-pigmentation on the neck and limbs. Subsequent clinical evaluations revealed persistent and multiple erosions in trauma-exposed skin areas. Growth parameters were as follows: at age 3.5 years, weight was at the 25th percentile and height at the 15th percentile; at age 8 years, weight was at the 25th percentile, height at the 50th percentile, and cranial circumference between the 10th and 25th percentiles. The patient had no major infections and exhibited normal effort tolerance; chest examination findings were normal.
test_results: Pulmonary function test showed air trapping (RV/TLC 42.56 (160 %). CT scan revealed an interstitial pulmonary disease with air trapping in both lungs. Ventilation-perfusion scintiscan showed minimal inhomogeneity in the lungs (ventilation left 43 % versus right 58 %; perfusion left 44 % versus right 56 %). O2 saturation 98 %.

case_report: A 55-year-old female experienced unexplained pain in the dorsum of the right foot and lateral leg for over two months. The pain, which had no apparent cause, sometimes became severe enough to hinder movement of the affected limb. The patient had no notable medical history, and both personal and family histories were unremarkable. Physical examination identified a pigmented area approximately 6 cm × 6 cm on the dorsum of the right foot, with a clear boundary and tenderness upon pressure. There was also localized tenderness on the lateral side of the right leg, restricted ankle joint movement, adequate peripheral blood supply, and normal sensation. During surgery, multiple nodular masses were found around the ankle joint, with the incision surface of the masses appearing brown. Laboratory tests showed slightly low prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times, while D-dimers, blood biochemistries, and urinalysis were normal. Additional tests, including blood analysis, electrocardiogram, chest x-ray, and arterial blood gas, were also normal. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed multiple nodules and soft tissue swelling around the right ankle.
test_results: Pathological examination revealed grayish-yellow irregular tissues, with a total volume of 7 cm × 6 cm × 1.5 cm, with multiple nodules within. The largest was 2.5 cm × 1.5 cm × 1.2 cm, and the smallest was 0.8 cm × 0.7 cm × 0.5 cm. The section was grayish-white and grayish-yellow and slightly tough. Under the microscope, the tumor cells in the fibrous connective tissue were nodular and lobulated, and the tumor cells grew around blood vessels. The blood vessels consisted of small arteries and veins, capillaries, and dilated veins showing diffuse hyperplasia. With eosinophilic staining, the tumor cells appeared round or oval, uniform in size, with abundant cytoplasm and clear boundary. Necrosis and pleomorphism were absent. In the surrounding adipose tissue, a proliferation of oval cells adjacent to small vessels was observed, which was consistent with tumor cell morphology. Mast cells were scattered in the stroma. Immunohistochemistry revealed diffuse immunoreactivity for smooth muscle actin (SMA), vimentin, type IV collagen, and Bcl-2. Caldesmon was weakly positive, CD34 was partially positive, and calponin was slightly positive. The Ki-67 value-added index was about 3%. Desmin, S-100, and HMB-45 were negative.

case_report: A 58-year-old French-Canadian woman was referred to the Genetic Dyslipidemias Clinic of the Montreal Clinical Research Institute in 2023. She has a 20-year history of elevated cholesterol levels accompanied by xanthelasmas. From 2012 to 2021, she was on statin therapy, which was frequently discontinued due to elevated liver enzyme levels. Since 2021, she has been on ezetimibe monotherapy. Her medical history includes macrothrombocytopenia with platelet counts as low as 77 × 10^9/L and mean platelet volume up to 15 fL, moderate hepatic steatosis, hypothyroidism, bipolar disorder, and early-onset coronary artery disease. She reports experiencing dyspnea, chest pain with mild facial edema, and discomfort, which have intensified after starting a Mediterranean diet.
test_results: A coronary angiography performed at age 55 years showed non–flow-limiting stenosis (<30%) of the ostium of the left main coronary artery and of the second diagonal coronary artery. The first diagonal coronary artery also had significant stenosis (70%-90%).

case_report: An eight-month-old female infant, born at term to non-consanguineous parents, presented with multiple hypopigmented skin lesions on the trunk and extremities since birth. Initially, these appeared as linear erosions that healed within a few days, leaving behind hypopigmentation with hyperpigmented borders. The perinatal period was uneventful. Limb and nail abnormalities were noted from birth, and developmental milestones were delayed. The patient had a history of exomphalos minor, which was surgically corrected, and an atrial septal defect that closed spontaneously by three months of age. No similar symptoms were reported in siblings or other family members. General examination showed microcephaly, hypertelorism, megalopinna, low-set ears, a broad nasal bridge, and a pointed chin. Skin examination revealed multiple hypopigmented atrophic linear streaks and macules of varying sizes on the forehead, neck, trunk, thighs, gluteal region, genitalia, and upper and lower limbs, following the lines of Blaschko. There was syndactyly of the left foot and ectrodactyly (lobster claw deformity) of the right foot. The patient had supernumerary nipples and a few skin-colored growths over the proximal nail fold of the right middle finger and right foot. Nails were dystrophic, while hair and oral mucosa were normal. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Complete blood count and serum chemistry profile were within normal limits.
test_results: Skin biopsy on the trunk showed focal spongiosis, occasional dyskeratotic keratinocytes, mild papillary edema, and focal papillary dermal fibrosis with superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate.

case_report: The patient is a 19-year-old female from an Iranian Muslim family who presented with low back pain and multiple vertebral fragility fractures. Additional complaints included primary amenorrhea, peri-oral and acral paresthesia, blurred vision, and a foreign body sensation in the eyes. She had no signs of malabsorption. Her medical history includes hypocalcemia-induced generalized tonic-clonic seizures at age 6 due to hypoparathyroidism, for which she received calcitriol and calcium supplementation with poor compliance. At age 7, she was diagnosed with alopecia areata and also had asthma, treated with salbutamol and montelukast. At age 13.5, she was noted to be short in stature (height = 134 cm, SDS = -3.8) and was found to have growth hormone deficiency but did not pursue treatment due to financial constraints. Since age 14, she experienced chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis involving the oral cavity and nails. She reported dry eye symptoms for 2 years and was using artificial tears. She also took a course of oral acyclovir for herpes simplex keratopathy. She was not under regular medical follow-up before referral to our center. Her family history includes consanguineous marriage of her parents and the death of her sister at age 14 with symptoms including blindness due to endophthalmitis, weakness, loss of appetite, fever, nausea, and vomiting. Her other siblings are healthy. Laboratory tests showed hypoparathyroidism (calcium = 6.6 mg/dl, phosphorus = 7.8 mg/dl, iPTH = < 8 pg/ml), and she was started on calcium (3 g/day) and calcitriol (0.5 micrograms daily) supplementation, with sevelamer (800 mg three times per day) added later for phosphorus control. Physical examination revealed delayed puberty (Tanner stage 3 for breast development and stage 2 for pubic hair). Hormone replacement therapy was initiated for premature ovarian failure (FSH = 64.5 IU/l, LH = 45.6 IU/l, prolactin = 35 ng/ml). Levothyroxine (50 micrograms daily) was added for subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH = 9.3 μIU/ml, TT4 = 9.8 μgr/dl, TT3 = 166 ng/dl, antithyroid peroxidase antibody = positive). Adrenal insufficiency was ruled out by the Cosyntropin test (baseline ACTH = 60 pg/ml, baseline cortisol = 11 μgr/dl, peak cortisol = > 50 μgr/dl). Due to short stature (height = 137 cm, SDS = -4), a GH test confirmed GH deficiency (IGF1 = 66 ng/ml [NL: 198–551], clonidine test: peak GH = 2.8 mIU/l), but she did not pursue GH treatment due to financial issues. Elevated liver enzymes were noted: ALT = 108 IU/l (NL: Up to 32), AST = 84 IU/l (NL: Up to 31), and ALP = 409 IU/l (NL: 64–306). Hepatitis viral markers were negative, and serum protein electrophoresis showed elevated serum IgG. Liver biopsy indicated chronic hepatitis (modified histology activity index grading: 9, staging: 3), and she was referred to a gastroenterologist. Other tests ruled out celiac disease (anti-endomysial antibody = negative), diabetes mellitus, and B12 deficiency. Ophthalmologic consultation revealed dry eyes and keratopathy due to limbal stem cell deficiency, and she was treated with cyclosporine eye drops, vitamin A eye ointment, fluorometholone eye drops, and artificial tears, followed by inferior punctum closure. Spine x-ray showed multiple vertebral fractures and spine deformity. Bone mineral densitometry revealed osteoporosis with height-adjusted lumbar spine, femoral neck, and total hip BMD Z-Scores of -5.80, -4.07, and -2.80, respectively. Brain CT and abdominopelvic ultrasound were normal except for an infantile uterus and small ovaries.
test_results: Genetic testing was performed, which indicated the AIRE gene variations. Sequencing the whole coding region and the exon-intron borders of the AIRE gene demonstrated three variants in the patient: a homozygous mutation in intron 9 (c.1095 + 2 T > A); a homozygous single nucleotide synonymous variant in exon 10 (c.1197 T > C, rs1800521); and a homozygous single nucleotide synonymous variant in exon 14 (c.1578 T > C, rs1133779). In addition, carrier screening was carried out in both parents, which confirmed heterozygous c.1095 + 2 T > A mutation. The expression levels of the AIRE mRNA in PBMCs of the patient, her parents and her three siblings are shown in Fig. According to this figure, compared to other family members with no sign of disease, the AIRE mRNA has been upregulated in the patient with a homozygous intron 9 mutation. In silico analysis using Human Splicing Finder has suggested that c.1095 + 2 T > A variation may result in alteration of an exonic splicing enhancer (ESE) site causing potential alteration of splicing.

case_report: A 49-year-old male presented with left-sided weakness and confusion for two days. His past medical history included diabetes mellitus treated with metformin and hypertension treated with valsartan/hydrochlorothiazide and clonidine. He also had a right knee replacement one week prior to his presentation. Physical examination showed a well-appearing man, who was oriented to only place and person and was noted to have confabulations and illogical thoughts, in addition to visual and auditory hallucinations. On admission, the patient was afebrile with a blood pressure of 167/100 mm Hg, a heart rate of 134, a respiratory rate of 17 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 100% on ambient air. His initial electrocardiogram (EKG) showed sinus tachycardia. The patient was admitted for further evaluation of his encephalopathy. His initial laboratory tests were significant for a potassium of 2.7 (normal: 3.5 - 5.3 mmol/L), serum bicarbonate of 35 (normal: 22 - 31 mmol/L), blood glucose of 183 (normal: 70 - 99 mg/dl), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) of 1.28 (normal: 0.34 - 4.82 microunits/mL), and hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) of 8.1%. Further workup was done to rule out other causes of the encephalopathy which were all negative, including urine toxicology, chest x-ray, computed tomography (CT) scan, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head, and an electroencephalogram. However, given his sinus tachycardia and confusion, a pulmonary embolism was considered as a differential, which was confirmed on a CT scan of the chest and appropriate treatment was started. Despite the treatment of underlying causes, the patient remained agitated, confused, and paranoid. The patient was seen by a psychiatrist for his symptoms, who suggested an initial therapy with haloperidol, 1 mg twice daily, and lorazepam as required for agitation, along with constant observation for patient safety. Due to the lack of desired clinical improvement over the next few days, other antipsychotics, including risperidone and citalopram, were added. However, those measures failed to control his episodes of severe psychosis. The patient’s hospital stay was further complicated by uncontrolled hypertension despite being on four antihypertensive medications of different classes at their maximum doses (valsartan, hydralazine, labetalol, and amlodipine). Acute psychosis in the setting of uncontrolled hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and venous thromboembolism raised the suspicion for metabolic disorders. An endocrinologist was consulted and further workup was initiated. Serum aldosterone was 3.1 (normal: ≤ 23.2 ng/dl) and plasma renin activity was < 2.1 (normal: ≤ 33.2 pg/ml), which ruled out hyperaldosteronism. Plasma metanephrines (< 10; normal: 0 - 62 pg/ml) and normetanephrines (< 10; normal: 0 - 145 pg/ml) were within normal limits. The 24-hour metanephrines (129; normal: < 400 mcg/24 hr), normetanephrines (381; normal: < 900 mcg/24 hr), vanillylmandelic acid (3.9; normal: < 8 mg/24 hr), dopamine (189; normal: 0 - 510 mcg/24 hr), norepinephrine (124; normal: 0 - 135 mcg/24 hr), and epinephrine (9; normal: 0 - 20 mcg/24 hr) were also within normal limits.
test_results: A low-dose dexamethasone suppression test showed inappropriate suppression of plasma cortisol (plasma AM cortisol after overnight 1 mg dexamethasone was 38.4; > 1.8 mcg/dL is abnormal). His serum AM cortisol was 37.6 (normal: 6.2 - 19.4 mcg/dL). The serum ACTH was less than 5 (normal: 0 - 46 pg/ml) on two separate occasions. The 24-hour urinary cortisol was 1,116 (normal: 3.5 - 4.5 mcg/24 hr). A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast was performed to evaluate the adrenal gland which showed multiple nonspecific adrenal nodules bilaterally with the largest one ranging between 3.5 - 4.5 cm bilaterally.
diagnosis: ACTH-independent Cushing's Syndrome due to primary bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia
Orpha_name: Cushing syndrome due to bilateral macronodular adrenocortical disease

case_report: A 19-year-old female, married for 8 months, presented with a 4-month history of amenorrhea and a progressively enlarging abdominal mass. A urine pregnancy test conducted at a primary health center when she was 1 month overdue was positive, and she was registered for antenatal care. Four days prior to presentation, she experienced vaginal bleeding and abdominal distension greater than expected for her period of amenorrhea, leading to her referral to our hospital. On examination, she exhibited mild pallor with normal vital signs. Cardiovascular examination was unremarkable. Abdominal examination showed a relaxed uterus corresponding to 20 weeks' gestation, and fetal heart sounds were not detected with a stethoscope. Minimal bleeding was observed on per speculum examination.
test_results: An immediate USG was done which showed 2 separate uterine horns with left horn showing echogenic foci of 1.5 am × 1 cm size suggestive of retained products of conception. There was also a right-sided 10 cm × 10 cm × 8 cm cystic lesion. Another striking finding was the absence of the right kidney. A repeat USG showed empty left horn suggesting complete abortion. An intravenous pyelogram showed the absence of right kidney which was seconded by a magnetic resonance imaging that also reported a didelphic uterus and a right ovarian cyst.

case_report: A 56-year-old female underwent an elective outpatient colonoscopy due to a significant family history of bowel cancer, as her sister was diagnosed with colon cancer at age 36. Her medical history includes menorrhagia, hypertension, depression, and two caesarean sections. She has no known drug allergies. Her regular medications are Nebivolol 5 mg once daily, Venlafaxine 150 mg once daily, and Amlodipine/Valsartan 5/180 mg. During the colonoscopy, a prominent appendiceal orifice with edematous changes was observed. The area was extensively biopsied.
test_results: Histopathological analysis of the biopsies demonstrated some mild neutrophilic inflammation with dense lymphocytic infiltrate of the lamina propria. Cross-sectional imaging revealed a 2.4 × 2.6 cm sized mass in the caecal tip involving the proximal appendix. Gross pathology of the surgical specimen demonstrated a cream solid cut surface homogenous throughout. Microscopic evaluation of the lesion demonstrated a 22 mm encapsulated well-circumscribed spindle cell mesenchymal neoplasm arising in the cecum with low-grade morphology. The additional histopathology was reported as a well-circumscribed submucosal lesion composed mainly of bland spindle cells. There was no atypia. Immunohistochemical stains showed diffuse positivity for S100 protein and SOX10 while CD34 and EMA were negative.

case_report: A 15-year-old male experienced two instances of prolonged unresponsiveness, each lasting several hours, first at age 7 and then at age 9. Both episodes occurred while traveling by train with his family. During these events, the patient suddenly became unresponsive and exhibited cyanosis, as observed by his mother. Additionally, he vomited during the initial episode. There were no reports of visual disturbances or limb jerking during either incident.
test_results: A routine EEG in 2005 showed evidence for bilateral posterior spike and wave discharges. An EEG performed in 2012 as follow-up was normal.

case_report: A 60-year-old woman visited the dermatology clinic with a 1-month history of a mildly itchy facial rash, mainly affecting the forehead, chin, and nasolabial folds. The patient described these as small hair-like protrusions. Her medical history included an allogenic bone marrow transplant complicated by graft-versus-host disease. At the time of evaluation, her immunosuppressive regimen included Prednisone 2.5 mg daily (tapering dose) and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) 1 g twice daily. Physical examination revealed multiple skin-colored follicular papules on the forehead, nose, nasolabial folds, and chin, some of which had white spiky protrusions. No other lesions were observed.
test_results: Histopathologic examination demonstrated a dilated follicular infundibulum with keratin plugging and abnormal maturation with marked inner root sheath (IRS) differentiation. The IRS cells had prominent eosinophilic cytoplasm and numerous trichohyaline granules. There was persistence of the outer root sheath beyond the isthmus.

case_report: In January 2018, a 61-year-old woman was admitted to our Internal Medicine Unit due to the development of ascites of unknown origin. She had a history of systemic sclerosis (SSc) since 2007, characterized by limited skin involvement, diffuse telangiectasias on the face, absence of digital ulcers or calcinosis, typical scleroderma esophagopathy, and no significant pulmonary, cardiac, or renal issues. Antinuclear antibodies were detected at a titer of 1:1280 with an anti-centromere pattern. The patient was sarcopenic with a body weight of 46.6 kg and a BMI of 18 kg/m2. Various examinations were conducted to determine the cause of ascites. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) ruled out gynecological diseases, including cancer with peritoneal carcinosis, despite elevated serum Ca125 levels (163 UI/mL). The CT revealed a slight reduction in liver volume without focal lesions, an increased portal vein diameter (17 mm), paraumbilical collateral venous circulation, and an enlarged spleen. Pleural-pericardial effusion was also noted. Tests for anti-mitochondrial, anti-smooth muscle cell, and anti-LKM antibodies were negative. Measurements of IgG subclasses, ferritin, and ceruloplasmin were within normal ranges. Liver function tests, coagulation proteins, transaminases, and cholestasis indices were mostly normal. Infections with HBV, HCV, and HIV, as well as alcohol or drug abuse, were excluded. Diuretics were used to manage the ascites.
test_results: The liver biopsy showed normal architecture, no necrosis or inflammation, mild fibrosis of the portal spaces, and vacuolar degeneration of several hepatocytes.

case_report: A 74-year-old male, a retired factory worker and former smoker, presented with breathlessness, cough, and loss of weight and appetite. The patient had a history of pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) 12 years ago, which was treated successfully, and was managed for obstructive airway disease. Recently, the breathlessness worsened to Modified Medical Research Council (MMRC) grade 3, accompanied by intermittent productive cough and hemoptysis of approximately 5-10 mL per episode. Upon presentation, the patient was conscious, oriented, and afebrile, with pallor and hypoxemia, maintaining oxygen saturation at 78% on room air and 95% on 2 L of oxygen via nasal prongs. Auscultation revealed right-sided crepitation in mammary and infra-axillary areas. Laboratory investigations showed normal renal function test (RFT), liver function test (LFT), serum electrolytes, and urine analysis. Chest radiographs indicated bilateral upper zone and right middle zone inhomogeneous opacities with hyperinflated lung fields. An electrocardiograph (ECG) showed normal sinus rhythm, and two-dimensional echocardiography (2D echo) indicated mild pulmonary hypertension. Arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis suggested type 1 respiratory failure. The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) and treated with empirical antibiotics, noninvasive ventilation, and supportive care. A packed red cell transfusion was administered to correct anemia, and the patient was moved to the ward after stabilization. Further evaluation with contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) of the thorax revealed patchy consolidation in the right upper, middle, and left upper lobes, along with patchy areas of random ground glass opacities and interstitial septal thickening in the right lower lobe and left upper and lower lobes. Multiple areas of air trapping were observed in the left lung, along with a few fibrotic bands. Sputum studies were inconclusive, and fiberoptic bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was performed.
test_results: TBLB histopathological report showed patchy alveolar hemorrhage with abundant hemosiderin pigment and mild focal interstitial fibrosis.

case_report: A 30-year-old G1P1 female presented to a district general hospital with a five-month history of heavy post-partum bleeding. She reported passing large clots in the preceding few days, prompting attendance at the accident and emergency department. Her general practitioner had inserted a Mirena IUS at 12 weeks post-partum, which failed to cease the bleeding. The general practitioner then prescribed norethisterone pills one month prior to admission. The index pregnancy was normal, with no associated complications. A healthy baby was born vaginally with a ventouse and was being exclusively breastfed. There had been no reported nausea, vomiting, cough, abdominal or pelvic pain, nor loss of consciousness associated with the erratic and heavy bleeding. The patient had only partaken in sexual intercourse once in the post-partum period, with the Mirena IUS in-situ. There was no notable family history. The patient had a previous appendectomy at age 19 and a borderline smear cytology result four years previously with no treatment. The general examination was largely unremarkable, with no abdominal tenderness; however, the uterus was palpable at 12 weeks' size. Normal vulva and vagina, with some large clots and blood noted in the vaginal canal. The cervical os was closed. There were no focal neurological signs nor other signs of any potential metastatic disease. One gram of tranexamic acid was administered, which slowed the bleeding. Blood results demonstrated haemoglobin of 121 and a beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (b-hCG) of 209,566. A trans-vaginal ultrasound scan demonstrated a thickened endometrium measuring 62 mm and a large mixed echoic mass in the cavity measuring 56 × 50 × 45 mm with some vascularity. Mirena IUS in-situ, with the rest of the findings being non-remarkable. A chest x-ray (CXR) was performed and was clear. An MRI scan of the head showed normal intracranial appearances and no visible metastases. Her International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) score was 9: <40 years old (30 = 0), index pregnancy (normal = 2), time since delivery (five months = 1), b-hCG (209,566 = 4), size of tumour (>50 mm, retained products of conception (RPOC) = 2), metastases (none on CXR = 0).
test_results: Histology demonstrated macroscopically a sac weighing 40.6 g, with no obvious vesicles nor fetal parts. Microscopically, it was comprised of large areas of haemorrhage with some necrosis and viable cells. The viable cells were in the form of atypical mononuclear intermediate trophoblastic cells in sheets that were surrounded by multinucleate syncytiotrophoblast tumour cells. There was no myometrial invasion, nor were chorionic villi visualised. All cells stained strongly positive for programmed death ligand 1 (PDL1). There were some tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (CD3 and CD8 positive).

case_report: A 36-year-old man, the first-born of nonconsanguineous parents from Kerala, experienced frequent episodes of abdominal colic starting at age 24. These episodes were attributed to nephrolithiasis, and he underwent extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy for the left kidney. Chemical analysis identified calcium oxalate crystals. Over time, he developed hypertension and eventually required dialysis. There was no reported family history of similar conditions.
test_results: He was also found to be homozygous for c. 445_452delGTGCTGCT (p.L151Nfs*14) truncating mutation and mother were heterozygous for the same.

case_report: A 4-year-old female with a history of persistent seizures and significant delays in overall development and muscle tone. Pregnancy and labor were reported to be without complications. Seizures were first observed around 6–8 weeks of age. Parents described various seizure types including clonic movements of the face and eyelids with bluish discoloration, sudden body flexion and contraction, and clonic/myoclonic movements affecting the limbs. No focal motor symptoms were noted. The child exhibits severe delays in cognitive, language, and motor skills, with no new milestones achieved. Additionally, she has generalized low muscle tone. She has two healthy older sisters and two cousins with epilepsy. General physical examination revealed delayed development and weakness on the right side of the body. The rest of the physical examination was normal.
test_results: Electroencephalogram (EEG) showed left and right hemispheric sharp wave complexes as well as isolated sharp waves in the left temporo-occipital, left fronto-temporal, right temporo-parietal, and right fronto-temporal regions. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was reported to be normal.
Orpha_name: Early-onset epileptic encephalopathy and intellectual disability due to GRIN2A mutation

case_report: A 10-year-old boy presented with brownish and red spots that began 5 years ago and appeared intermittently. The red spots initially spread outward and disappeared without leaving marks, while the brownish lesions on the front of the trunk and arms persisted. He had been treated with various antifungal medications by different physicians, but these treatments were ineffective. No similar lesions were observed in other family members, and no systemic disease was identified. Dermatological examination revealed erythematous, annular plaques on the front of the chest, arms, and neck, as well as brownish hyperkeratotic plaques on the left shoulder and axillary region. No lesions were found on the palms, soles, nails, hair, teeth, or mucosa.
test_results: The histopathological examination of the hyperkeratotic plaque showed hyperkeratosis with moderate papillomatosis and acanthosis.

case_report: A thirty-nine-year-old male presented with a primary concern of a non-painful swelling in the right cheek area, present since birth. The swelling increased in size gradually until the patient was 18 years old and then stabilized. There was no relevant family history. The patient was alert and had stable vital signs. Extraoral examination revealed facial asymmetry with a diffuse swelling on the right side of the face, measuring approximately 5 × 6 cm. The swelling extended from the upper canthus of the right eye to 1 cm below the lower border of the mandible, from the nasolabial fold to the tragus of the ear. The nose and chin were deviated, and the facial midlines (nasion-gnathion) were arc-shaped. An enlarged soft tissue mass was noted involving the maxilla, mandible, and zygoma on the right side. On palpation, the swelling was hard, non-tender, and noncompressible. The skin over the swelling appeared normal with no secondary changes. Mild tenderness was noted in the right condylar region. The patient exhibited restricted temporomandibular joint (TMJ) movements and had incompetent lips with significant enlargement of both upper and lower lips on the right side. No regional lymphadenopathy was observed. Intraoral examination showed restricted mouth opening with a maximum interincisal distance of about 1 cm. Enlarged right maxillary and mandibular alveolar arches, upper and lower labial mucosa, and buccal mucosa were observed. The dorsum of the tongue appeared engorged with polypoid excrescences, giving a 'multiple pebbly' appearance due to the enlargement of fungiform papillae. There was a noticeable discrepancy in tooth size between the right and left sides, with the maxillary and mandibular right teeth being larger in labiolingual, mesiodistal, and buccopalatal dimensions. A midline shift and a downward canting of the occlusal plane were also noted.
test_results: Orthopantomogram (OPG) revealed an obvious diffuse enlargement of right side coronoid, condylar processes, lower border of mandible, inferior alveolar canal, jaws, and teeth (macrodontia). Computerized tomography (CT) scan of the face revealed enlarged right petrous part of temporal bone, pituitary fossa, maxilla, mandible, condyle, zygoma, and cranial bones. Deviation of nasal bone and chin was observed towards left side due to an obvious enlargement of overlying soft tissues on right side of the face. Bone scintigraphy revealed hyperactivity and excess bone growth on right side maxilla and mandible.

case_report: A 23-year-old woman with a lifelong history of dry skin sought consultation. She was born to healthy, unrelated parents after an uncomplicated pregnancy. At birth, her skin was red and exhibited peeling without blistering. She did not have any siblings. Brownish linear streaky pigmentation with coarse scales along Blaschko’s lines was initially observed on her entire body. Mild generalized dry skin was also noted unrelated to Blaschko’s lines, and there were several linear areas of scarring hair loss on the scalp. Erythematous plaques with pustules were occasionally observed overlying the linear pigmentation along Blaschko’s lines on the neck and extremities; these pustules usually disappeared within a week. Skin biopsy of the linear coarse scales along Blaschko’s lines on the abdomen showed thickened outer skin layers and a thickened granular layer without retention of nuclei in the outer skin layers. She did not have ocular or auditory abnormalities, but her right leg was shorter than her left leg.
test_results: Whole exome sequence analysis revealed a heterozygous 1-bp deletion (c.292delT) in exon 2 of EBP, leading to a frameshift and a subsequent premature termination codon (p.Ser98Leufs*40). Direct sequence analysis of the EBP gene revealed absence of the mutation in her parents. It was also confirmed that the deletion mutation was present in only 1 allele by direct sequencing after TA cloning. Reverse transcriptase PCR using RNA samples extracted from her blood samples showed markedly lower RNA expression levels in the patient compared with those in a healthy control.

case_report: An 11-year-old male patient with a history of recurrent fractures was born to healthy, nonconsanguineous parents with no history of fractures. The patient's prenatal history was unremarkable. He was delivered at full-term via vaginal delivery, weighing 3.4 kg at birth. His cognitive and motor development were within normal limits, and he exhibited a normal gait pattern during childhood. The patient experienced his first fracture (left humerus) at age 6 following a fall. One month prior to referral, he sustained another fracture (left distal radius). Physical examination revealed blue sclera. The patient had a normal height (146.9 cm, approximately 60th percentile), normal gait pattern, and normal muscle tone.
test_results: His L1-L4 BMD (0.514 g/cm2, z-score −1.2) and femoral neck BMD (0.531 g/cm2, z-score −2.1) were low, and a spine X-ray showed multiple thoracic vertebral compression fractures.

case_report: A 19-year-old Vietnamese female presented to the Maxillofacial Surgery Department with a periapical infection and a fistula originating from her left mandibular canine. Her medical history, gathered from both the patient and her mother, included strabismus detected at six months old and congenital cataracts diagnosed at four years old, for which she underwent lens replacement surgery. At 14 years old, she was found to have congenital cardiac conditions, including ostium secundum atrial septal defect, pulmonary artery hypertension, and severe tricuspid valve leakage. Examination of the patient's mother revealed strabismus but no radiculomegaly on her panoramic radiograph. There was no family history of genetic diseases, and the patient's two younger sisters exhibited typical development. The patient's mother experienced a fever and was hospitalized for one week at 22 weeks gestation, but no abnormalities were detected during antenatal ultrasounds. Clinically, the patient had a long and broad face, a concave facial profile, thick eyebrows, a broad and protrusive mandible, and eye abnormalities including strabismus and microphthalmia on the left side. Visual impairment was present in both eyes without secondary glaucoma. Additional features included a broad nasal tip with separation of anterior cartilage nasal and a fistula on the left chin surrounded by an inflammatory area. There were no signs of hearing impairment, protruding ears, or hypoplastic ears. The patient had normal pronunciation but exhibited intellectual disability. Physical examination revealed IV-toe camptodactyly and I-hammer toe, with no abnormalities in her hands. She had a narrow, high-arched palate, severely crowded teeth, and multiple dental caries affecting teeth 11, 12, 16, 21, 26, 32, 33, 36, 43, 46, and 47, necessitating extractions and endodontic procedures. Glossitis was also noted. Panoramic radiograph showed severe dental crowding, malposition of teeth 34 and 44, retained roots of several teeth, impacted tooth 24, radiculomegaly in lower premolars and upper right second premolar, elongated roots of lower anterior teeth, taurodontic appearance of tooth 37, and under-developed tooth 48. Elongated canines' roots with open apices were observed in all quadrants, and a periapical infection was confirmed on the left mandibular canine.
test_results: Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood. Genomic DNA was used to amplify exons 1 through 15 and the exon–intron boundaries of the BCOR gene using pairs of PCR primers. Purified PCR products were sequenced in both directions. The patient was found to be heterozygous for a novel single-base deletion within intron 11 (IVS11-2delA) of the BCOR.

case_report: A 42-year-old woman experienced progressive memory deterioration over the past six months. She had a full-term birth via normal vaginal delivery without complications or abnormal physical features and developed normally. Six months ago, she began experiencing memory loss, characterized by an inability to recall recent events, which progressively worsened. There was no history of brain injury, and her medical history was unremarkable. Her father passed away from liver cancer, and her sister, who had unexplained dementia, died at the age of 40. She has two healthy children, a boy and a girl. Neurological examination revealed significant symptoms including delayed reactions, memory loss, and horizontal nystagmus. Motor system examination showed normal muscle strength (Grade 5) and coordinated movements. Sensory system examination results were normal. Tendon reflexes in both upper and lower extremities were significantly decreased without lateralization. She completed junior high school and scored 8 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and 15 on the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE). She was found to have moderate cognitive impairment. The condition showed adult-onset, chronic progression, and primarily affected high-level brain functions, mainly presenting as cognitive impairment. Additionally, examination indicated potential involvement of the peripheral nerves, as evidenced by weakened tendon reflexes.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans demonstrated diffuse and symmetrical abnormal signals in the cerebral white matter, especially around the top of the lateral ventricle. The activity of ARSA measured in white blood cells was 14.13 nmol/17h/mg, which was significantly lower than the normal value (>58 nmol/17h/mg). Nerve conduction studies showed that the evidence of polyneuropathy was superimposed upon diffuse, uniform demyelinating, and sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Electromyography (EMG) was remarkable for fibrillations and positive waves were limited to the right musculi abductor pollicis brevis. Genetic analysis indicated that there were two heterozygous mutations in the exon region of the ARSA gene: NM_000487: c.[185_186dupCA], p.(Asp63GlnfsTer18). A duplication of CA nucleotides located in exon 1 at c.185_186 resulted in a frameshift mutation. NM_000487: c.[154G>T], p.(Gly172Cys), rs74315271. A missense mutation of ARSA in exon 3 resulted in guanine being changed into thymine at nucleotide 154, and amino acid Gly being replaced by Cys.

case_report: A 63-year-old male patient with a history of dyslipidemia, Barrett’s esophagus, and a former smoker, reported experiencing precordial oppression for 15 days. The discomfort extended to the neck and upper left limb, was moderate to severe in intensity, worsened with physical activity, and was alleviated by rest. An exertion test conducted on an outpatient basis showed precordial pain of maximum intensity. Upon admission, vital signs were: blood pressure 120/70 mmHg, heart rate 100 beats per minute, respiratory rate 12 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97%, and temperature 37 degrees Celsius. Physical examination revealed no jugular engorgement or neck masses, a rhythmic heart without murmurs or gallops, normal respiratory sounds, no abdominal masses, no lower limb edema, and no neurological deficits. Based on the exertion test findings, the patient underwent cardiac catheterization and angioplasty for trunk disease involving three major vessels. A multidisciplinary team recommended myocardial revascularization. During the pre-surgical evaluation, a mass was identified in the left inferior pulmonary lobe. The patient underwent revascularization without complications. Further studies were conducted to assess the lung mass, and the patient was considered suitable for surgical resection. He subsequently underwent a left lower lobectomy by thoracoscopy with mediastinal lymph node removal. Histopathological analysis identified a primary pulmonary adenocarcinoma, T2aN2M0, stage IIIA. The patient received chemotherapy and adjuvant radiation therapy with favorable progress. After completing the oncological therapy, a PET-CT scan revealed a metabolically active lesion at the left perihilar level and para-aortic area with a Standardized Uptake Value (SUV) of 3.5, along with diffuse pulmonary basal opacities potentially related to radiotherapy.
test_results: Rounded structures were observed, without a double-wall, corresponding to damaged red blood cells (RBC). Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS), Gomori Methenamine-Silver (GMS), and mucicarmine staining were negative but trichromic staining was positive. Immunohistochemical stains were negative for malignancy. The observed spherules showed reactivity to glycophorin.

case_report: A 42-year-old male patient with no prior medical or surgical history visited the Department of Oral Medicine and Surgery at the dental clinic due to a gingival swelling in the anterior maxilla that had persisted for the past 2 months. The patient reported no use of tobacco, alcohol, or medication, and did not experience local pain. An extra-oral examination identified swelling of the upper lip. Intra-oral examination revealed a non-tender, single polylobed nodule, sessile, measuring 3 cm in diameter, covered with bluish mucosa with purplish areas, firm in consistency, located in the anterior maxillary region extending to the vestibule. Dental examination indicated mobility of the upper central incisors, and a vitality test of the left upper central incisor was negative. Retro alveolar radiological examination showed desmodontal enlargement of the upper central incisors without other signs of bone lysis. Panoramic X-ray did not reveal any specific lesion in this area. However, a CT scan showed mitted osteolysis, improperly limited, affecting both the cancellous bone and the vestibular cortical bone in the anterosuperior region, along with destruction of the floor of the nasal cavity in some areas, with the lesion extending towards the incisive foramen. This image extended from the mesial side of tooth 12 to the distal side of tooth 21, measuring 21.7 mm horizontally. The trabecular bone surrounding teeth 11 and 21 was destroyed, giving the appearance of floating teeth. For the soft tissues, the CT scan showed thickening of the upper lip muscles extending from the right canine to the distal side of the left central incisor.
test_results: The histology showed a nodular formation among the chorion with a high cell density of lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophilic polymorphonuclears, and especially by macrophages with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. These macrophages were often clustered and showed numerous images of emperipolesis (lymphocytes and some plasma cells, intact in vacuoles in the wide cytoplasm of histiocytes). The surface squamous epithelium was normal. Immunohistochemical examination shows an intense and diffuse marking of macrophages by S100.

case_report: A 42-year-old man with no prior health problems was admitted to our hospital with acute respiratory distress and superior vena cava syndrome. The patient had a family history of cancer on his mother’s side (his mother died of colon cancer, an unlabeled lung tumor in an aunt, and lymphoma in the grandfather). He was a current smoker with a history of 10 pack years. The patient had been experiencing thoracic pain, dry cough, dyspnea, fatigue, and unintentional weight loss for a month. A thoracic CT scan revealed multiple intraparenchymal masses, voluminous mediastinal lymph nodes, and pleural effusion on the right side, as well as radiological evidence of emphysema, bullous dystrophy, and diffuse bronchial syndrome. He was admitted to the pulmonology department for further examination.
test_results: A cervical lymph node biopsy showed lymphoid material with clusters of large epithelioid cells that had a large irregular nucleus and cytoplasm that was sometimes clarified. The mitoses were numerous, and there were some foci of necrosis. On immunohistochemistry, the tumor cells were positive for EMA, SALL4, SOX2, CD99, and CD30 (low) but negative for CK, CD20, CD45, CD3, CD2, ALK, Kit, BGR1, SOX10, CD56, CD1a, and PLAP.

case_report: A six-year-old boy exhibited symptoms including sudden, jerky limb movements, inability to support his neck, functional urinary incontinence, and reliance on his mother for most daily activities. Ophthalmoscopic examination showed no visual deficits. Physical examination indicated increased muscle tone and exaggerated reflexes in both upper and lower limbs, along with a positive Babinski sign. The boy was non-verbal but appeared to have normal intellectual capacity. Family history included third-degree consanguineous parents and one sibling without any noted abnormalities. At birth, the mother observed defective suckling, which was managed with bottle feeding and weaning. Developmental milestones were normal until age two, when the boy experienced fever and seizures, initially mistaken for febrile seizures. Following this, he developed progressive spastic tetraparesis, resulting in loss of walking and talking abilities, and difficulty swallowing. The boy experienced approximately twenty seizures daily and required a semi-solid and liquid diet due to swallowing difficulties.
test_results: A brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed demyelination in the brain stem and cerebellum. A brain magnetic resonance (MR) spectroscopy revealed elevated myo-inositol and choline-containing compounds with decreased N-aspartyl aspartate in the affected white matter area, and the grey matter showed neuronal degeneration. Mutational analysis by deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) sequencing revealed a missense mutation on chromosome band 14q31.3, coding for GALC gene.

case_report: A 70-year-old woman was found to have a 10 mm mass in segment VIII of the liver during a follow-up evaluation for primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). Her social and family histories were unremarkable. She had chronic rheumatoid arthritis in addition to PBC and was on oral steroids and methotrexate. Physical examination revealed no abnormalities. Laboratory tests were negative for hepatic virus, and hepatic function was within normal limits, although the antimitochondrial antibody titer was positive. Tumor markers, including carcinoembryonic antigen, carbohydrate antigen 19-9, alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), and protein induced by vitamin K absence or antagonist II (des-gamma-carboxy prothrombin [PIVKA-II]), were within normal limits. The ICG 15 min value was 9.8%, and the Child-Pugh classification was A at 5 points. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic mass, 13.4 mm in diameter, in segment VIII of the liver. An abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a 10 mm mass that was slightly enhanced in the early phase and washed out in the late phase. On gadoxetic acid (Gd-EOB-DTPA)-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), the mass was enhanced in the arterial dominant phase and washed out in the late and hepatocyte phases. A laparoscopic-assisted S8 subsegmentectomy was planned.
test_results: The follicles were CD20 (+), CD79a (+), CD10 (+), and Bcl-2 (−), and the interfollicular area was CD3 (+) and CD5 (+).
Orpha_name: Lymphoplasmacytic inflammatory pseudotumor of the liver

case_report: A 12-year-old male patient presented with a subcutaneous nodule on the anterolateral surface of his right leg. The nodule, first noticed by the patient's family about a month prior, had been growing slowly. On physical examination, the nodule measured approximately 2 cm in diameter, had a well-defined border, and was located within the skin and subcutaneous tissue. It exhibited a bluish discoloration but was not associated with pain or ulceration. An excisional procedure was performed under local anesthesia within a week of the initial presentation. The lesion was removed with 1 to 2 cm margins, including skin and subcutaneous tissue above the fascial plane. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient's legal guardians.
test_results: In the pathological examination, the size of the tumor was measured 1.6x1.5x0.5 cm. Histologically, the tumor was representing an intralymphatic lesion composed of vascular channels and papillae with hyalinized cores. Vascular channels and papillae were lined with cluster of differentiation (CD)34-positive endothelial cells (Hobnail cells) that were projecting into the lumen. Surgical margins were free of tumor.

case_report: The patient is a 24-year-old woman who has been experiencing episodic headaches for six months and elevated blood pressure for four months. Initially, she reported headaches following insufficient sleep. Four months ago, a health examination revealed hypertension with readings up to 150/109 mmHg. She has a regular menstrual cycle. Her family history includes hypertension in her father, grandfather, and grandmother. Physical examination showed elevated blood pressure but no other abnormal signs. Laboratory tests indicated elevated serum potassium and chloride levels, decreased arterial blood pH, standard bicarbonate concentration, and normal serum creatinine and glomerular filtration rate. Plasma renin activity was suppressed, while plasma aldosterone concentration was elevated. Cortisol circadian rhythm and levels, 24-hour urinary free cortisol, adrenocorticotropin, and serum catecholamine levels were all normal. A captopril challenge test showed a 31.6% suppression of plasma aldosterone. Sex hormones, thyroid hormone, and parathyroid hormone levels were within normal ranges. MRI of the adrenal glands showed no significant abnormalities. Ultrasound of the urinary system revealed uric acid crystals in the right kidney. The patient's father has hypertension, while her mother's blood pressure is normal; neither parent was available for laboratory examination or genetic screening. Her elder brother has normal blood pressure, normal serum potassium and chlorine levels, and normal arterial blood gas analysis results.
test_results: The patient was identified with a heterozygous mutation in exon 11 of the KLHL3 gene, c.1298G > A, which led to 433rd amino acid serine to be replaced by asparagine (S433N).

case_report: A 22-year-old female, previously in good health, exhibited a blood glucose level of 241 during a 1-hour glucose tolerance test at 28 weeks of gestation, leading to a diagnosis of gestational diabetes. Prior to pregnancy, elevated glucose levels were observed in random basic metabolic panels, although they did not meet the criteria for diabetes mellitus. At the time of the abnormal oral glucose tolerance test, the patient was asymptomatic. Her medical history includes ultrasounds revealing a small multicystic dysplastic right kidney, with the left kidney showing compensatory hypertrophy and a small midpole cyst. Kidney function, monitored by nephrology, has remained stable. The family history includes polycystic kidney disease in her mother and maternal grandmother.
test_results: This panel came back positive for a pathologic mutation to HNF-1β with deletion of exons 1–9 with genomic coordinates chr17 : 36047329_36105161 (GRCh37).
diagnosis: Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young Type 5
Orpha_name: Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young Type 5

case_report: The patient is a 39-year-old woman who, at the age of 25, developed a high-grade intraductal carcinoma in the left breast. The molecular phenotype showed Ki-67 at 30%, immunohistochemistry results were ER (3+), PR (2+), and HER2neu negative (+1). A left mastectomy was performed in 2009, followed by a 5-year course of adjuvant Tamoxifen. The patient has remained free of relapse for 14 years post-diagnosis. The patient's family history is not available as she is an adopted child. In 2019, she was referred to the Familial and Hereditary Cancer Unit at Hospital Universitario 12 Octubre based on criteria for genetic counselling as per the Spanish Society of Medical Oncology (SEOM) clinical guidelines. The selection criteria for germline testing include breast cancer diagnosed before the age of 40, regardless of family history.
test_results: Genetic analysis was not informative and included the BRCA1 and BRCA2 study by NGS and MLPA.
diagnosis: Hereditary Breast and Ovarian Cancer Syndrome  with low-level constitutional mosaicism in BRCA2
Orpha_name: Hereditary breast and/or ovarian cancer syndrome

case_report: A 34-year-old gravida II para I woman, at 26 weeks and 3 days of gestation, presented with a severe and persistent occipital headache lasting one day, blurred vision, and generalized body swelling for one week. She has a 4-year-old child with her 40-year-old husband, and they are in a non-consanguineous marriage. She used injectable contraception for 2 years and had regular menstrual cycles for 6 months before this pregnancy. She received antenatal care at a local health center, including one tetanus toxoid vaccination and iron supplementation for 3 months. Screening for retroviral infection, hepatitis, and syphilis was nonreactive. She did not undergo an early gestation anatomic scan. Her past gynecologic, medical, and surgical histories were unremarkable. She is of Amhara ethnicity with no known family history of hereditary or chromosomal disorders. Upon admission, her blood pressure was 180/120 mmHg, pulse rate was 84 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 22 breaths per minute, and she was afebrile. Physical examination revealed pink conjunctiva, non-icteric sclera, a gravid uterus consistent with 24 weeks of gestation, no abdominal tenderness, no organomegaly, no signs of fluid collection in the abdomen, and a positive fetal heartbeat. There was no vaginal bleeding or discharge. She exhibited pedal and pretibial edema. Neurologically, she was conscious and oriented to person, place, and time, with a deep tendon reflex of +2 and no motor or sensory deficits. Other systemic examinations were normal. Her hypertension was managed with two doses of 5 mg intravenous hydralazine in the emergency department. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 7300 cells/micL, hemoglobin of 13.4 g/dl, and platelet count of 169,000 cells/micL. Urine protein dipstick was +2. Liver function tests indicated elevated serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase (SGPT) at 89 IU/L and serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase (SGOT) at 102 IU/L. Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) was 229 IU/L, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was 288 IU/L. Total bilirubin was 0.24 mg/dl, albumin was 3.49 g/dl, blood urea nitrogen was 12 mg/dl, and serum creatinine was 0.69 mg/dl. The oral glucose tolerance test was within normal limits.
test_results: Obstetric ultrasound showed a singleton, alive, intrauterine pregnancy with average gestational age of 26 weeks, there was a single large ventricle with partially formed midline structure, amniotic fluid index was 13.4 cm, placenta was located anteriorly at the body of the uterus, and the presentation was breech; the fetus had normal four chambers of heart with normal outflow tract.

case_report: A 62-year-old male reported experiencing tingling and numbness in the right upper and lower limbs for one month. Additionally, he described a burning pain in both upper and lower limbs for the past 10 days, which worsened when exposed to cold water. Initially, the symptoms began with tingling and numbness on the right side of the face and upper limb, eventually spreading to most of the right side of the body. Despite being evaluated and managed conservatively, there was no improvement. The patient follows a vegetarian diet. There was no history of neurological disorders such as confusion or seizures, nor other symptoms like vomiting, weakness, or fever. He also had no significant medical history, including hypertension, diabetes, or ischemic heart disease. The patient does not smoke or consume alcohol and has a moderately built physique with a body mass index of 22. On physical examination, his pulse rate was 88 beats per minute, and his blood pressure was 140/90 mmHg. Examination of the central nervous system showed an absent ankle reflex and impaired pinprick and temperature sensations, indicating peripheral neuropathy. Other neurological assessments were normal.
test_results: Peripheral smear was suggestive of macrocytosis with hypersegmented neutrophils. A nerve conduction study revealed neuropathy. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with magnetic resonance angiography and magnetic resonance venography was suggestive of acute evolving infarct in the left side of the body of the septum pellucidum and left thalamus. Magnetic resonance angiography was suggestive of normal course and calibre in the bilateral internal carotid arteries, vertebral artery, circle of Willis, and its branches. No obvious filling defects and dilatation were noted. Magnetic resonance venography revealed normal internal jugular veins and sigmoid, transverse, and superior and inferior sagittal sinuses.

case_report: A 5-year-old Chinese boy presented with beaded papules on the eyelids and atrophic scars throughout the body. At birth, his skin appeared normal, but atrophic scars developed on the neck, shoulders, and buttocks due to easy bruising and festering. Hoarseness of voice began at 2 years old, followed by gradual onset of difficulty swallowing and obstruction. By age 3, hyperplastic gums and tongue were noted. Verrucous hyperplastic lesions appeared on the fingertips at age 4. The patient did not receive regular treatment for his condition. No abnormalities in vision, epilepsy, psychosis, or dyskinesia were found, and his intelligence was comparable to his peers. The parents were non-consanguineous with no family history of similar conditions. Physical examination revealed beaded papules along the upper eyelid margin, disordered arrangement of teeth, and gingival hyperplasia. Diffuse atrophic scars covered his entire body, and brownish-yellow plaques were present on both knees.
test_results: Two previously unreported heterozygous variants in the ECM1 gene were identified. In both the proband and his father, a novel frameshift variant designated as c.317_339delTCCCTCAGGAAGCTGTCCCCCTC was identified in exon 5, resulting in a Leu106Profs*12 amino acid change that introduced a frameshift and produced an aberrant ECM1 protein. In the proband and his mother, a nonsense variant designated as c.479G>A was detected in exon 6 leading to a Trp160X amino acid change that prematurely truncated the protein by introducing a stop codon at position 160. Neither of these variants were present in DNA samples collected from 100 unaffected healthy controls.

case_report: A 59-year-old African American female with a history of hypertension, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and Raynaud's phenomenon (RP) initially presented to an outside facility with 6 months of progressive shortness of breath, dry cough, and worsening RP with digital ulceration. Imaging of her chest revealed fibrotic interstitial lung disease (ILD) with a pattern consistent with non-specific interstitial pneumonia. Right heart catheterization showed pulmonary artery pressures of 80/32 mmHg (mean 47 mmHg), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 9 mmHg, cardiac output of 4.91 L/minute, and pulmonary vascular resistance of 619 dyne·second·cm−5. She was started on sildenafil 40 mg three times daily and mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg daily and referred to our PAH clinic for further evaluation. In clinic, she exhibited progression of her pulmonary symptoms and dry gangrene. She was admitted for initiation of epoprostenol and further evaluation of her symptoms. On admission, physical examination revealed multiple gangrenous digits, a right fifth digital ulcer, accentuated P2, a 2/6 systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border, and coarse crackles bilaterally on lung auscultation. Examination of the hands was limited due to the extent of the gangrene, but her digits appeared slightly puffy without sclerodactyly or other skin involvement.
test_results: Nailfold capillaroscopy was notable for capillary dilatations and dropout in the nongangrenous digits. ANA (1 : 320 nucleolar pattern) and anti-RNAP III were positive. Pulmonary function tests showed a restrictive lung defect with an FVC of 2.15 L (64% predicted), FEV1/FVC ratio of 69%, DLCO of 7.98 mL/mmHg·sec (37% predicted), and an FVC/DLCO ratio of 1.7. Esophagram showed mild dilation and dysmotility of the distal esophagus. Cardiac MRI showed no evidence of infiltrative disease. VQ scan revealed a large unmatched perfusion defect of the left base consistent with pulmonary embolism (PE).

case_report: A 25-year-old male came for an eye examination due to a gradual decrease in visual acuity in his left eye over the past few years. The patient and his family noted that he had difficulty fixating with the left eye since early childhood. He sought medical attention hoping for improvement. There was no history of trauma, ocular surgery, or any other interventions. The family confirmed that his vision had been poor since childhood. On physical examination, the patient exhibited distinctive facial and body features. There were areas of hypopigmented hair on both forearms. Facial features included synophrys, a high nasal root, a prominent nasal root, and a white forelock of hair. Oral examination revealed a high-arched palate with dental anomalies such as microdontia, oligodontia, and conical teeth. The patient had no hearing deficits, and there was no relevant family history. Examination also showed lateral displacement of the inner canthi (dystopia canthorum). Visual acuity was 6/6 in the right eye and no light perception in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was measured at 21 mm Hg in the right eye and 41 mm Hg in the left eye. Pupil examination was normal in the right eye, while the left eye had a small constricted pupil.
test_results: Slit lamp examination of the right eye showed normal conjunctiva, sclera, and anterior chamber depth with segmental heterochromia and clear crystalline lens. Slit lamp examination of the left eye showed clear cornea, deep and quiet anterior chamber with complete iris hypochromia, a small area of iris transillumination defect and mature cataract. Gonioscopy showed an open angle without peripheral anterior synechiae and with normal angle pigmentation of the left eye. B scan of the left eye showed RD.

case_report: This report details a five-year-old Middle Eastern female born to healthy, consanguineous (first cousin) parents with no notable family history and an uneventful perinatal period. At 4 months old, she experienced generalized tonic seizures characterized by up-rolling eyes and cyanosis, each lasting 4 minutes, occurring two to three times monthly. Routine electroencephalogram (EEG) results were normal. She was prescribed levetiracetam at 6 months, after which the seizures ceased. By 1 year, she no longer required anti-seizure medication. Hip imaging during the newborn period revealed a shallow left acetabulum, and follow-up imaging at 1 year showed bilateral developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH). Her gross motor development was typical until 1 year, except for tip-toeing. At 15 months, her mother observed a regression in gross motor skills; she could no longer stand or walk independently. She later regained the ability to stand alone but not to walk unaided. At 2 years, bilateral cataracts were detected and surgically removed with intraocular lens implantation. She was referred to orthopedics and neurology. At 3 years, she was assessed by both specialties and found to have spastic diplegia, with repeated hip X-rays showing bilateral subluxed hips and acetabular dysplasia. Physical therapy, gait training, and bracing were initiated, but no improvement was noted, necessitating bilateral pelvic osteotomy and hamstring and adductor release at 4 years. Her language development was appropriate: babbling at 6 months, first words at 13 months, and two-word sentences at 2 years. Currently, she can stand alone and walk with a walker. Her speech, cognitive, and fine motor skills are age-appropriate, and she is performing well in kindergarten. Around age 5, she experienced faltering growth, dropping from the 42nd to the 2nd percentile for weight over 9 months, despite adequate caloric intake and no signs of loss or malabsorption. Her height remains between the 11th and 18th percentiles, and her head circumference is above the 85th percentile. Neurological examination revealed grade 2 spasticity in the Achilles tendon (Ashworth scale), mild weakness (4/5) in upper and lower limbs, and clonus in both ankles. She exhibited a scissoring gait with toe walking. Brain MRI, magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS), and spine MRI were normal. Basic metabolic work-up and mitochondrial genome analysis were unremarkable.
test_results: Exome sequencing (ES) analysis showed the heterozygous de novo pathogenic variant c.1438C>T (p. Arg480Cys) in the FAR1 gene.
diagnosis: Autosomal dominant fatty acyl CoA reductase 1-related syndrome

case_report: An eight-year-old boy presented with difficulty in opening his mouth. Over the past year, there was a gradual reduction in mouth opening, which had rapidly worsened in the last month. The patient was born preterm at seven months of gestation with a birth weight of 1.4 kg. His parents had a consanguineous marriage, and his mother experienced pregnancy-induced hypertension, leading to a caesarian section. At birth, the boy had contractures of the fingers, knees, and toes. He exhibited delays in both motor and speech milestones. Over the past two years, he experienced patchy hair loss and widespread dental caries. At the age of four, he underwent surgery to release knee contractures, which subsequently improved his ability to walk. His sibling, also born preterm, died on the fourth day after delivery. Upon examination, the boy had normal height and weight. Central nervous system examination showed normal memory, intelligence, and affect. Hypertonia with brisk reflexes was observed in both lower limbs, while the upper limbs exhibited mild rigidity with normal reflexes. Camptodactyly was present, along with contractures of all toes and valgus deformity. Hypopigmented macules were found on the back, buttocks, and both arms. Alopecia areata was also noted. Facial examination revealed malar hypoplasia and a retrognathic mandible. The mouth opening was measured at 20 mm, with deflection to the left during the opening. Intraoral examination showed caries affecting all deciduous posterior teeth.
test_results: Altered shape and flattening of the left condyle was notable.

case_report: A 42-year-old male reported a 6-year history of mild evening fatigue in all four limbs, followed by a gradual onset of gait imbalance and recurrent double vision. Despite these symptoms, cerebral and orbital imaging showed no abnormalities, and tests for anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies, repetitive nerve-stimulation, and single fiber electromyography were negative. Over the past 3 years, he experienced worsening limb incoordination, slurred speech, difficulty swallowing, and a 20% reduction in body weight. His family history included rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren’s syndrome, and pancreatic cancer, but no history of ataxia, myasthenia gravis, neuropathy, tremors, or dementia. His medical history included allergic asthma, high blood pressure, and left retinal macular degeneration. Upon examination at our institution, general physical findings were notable for bilateral xanthelasma, vitiligo on the dorsal fingers, and yellowish papules on both feet and the left pectoral region. Neurological examination showed acalculia (mini mental state examination score: 23/30), horizontal gaze nystagmus, normal fundoscopic and pupillary responses, slow initiation of movements, hypermetric saccades primarily in the horizontal plane, and mild bilateral neurosensorial hearing loss. Additional findings included a positive Romberg’s sign, pronounced ataxic gait, inability to perform tight-rope walking, dysdiadochokinesia, arm dysmetria, tremor, slurred speech, nasal speech, and motor impairment of the hands.
test_results: A biopsy of one of the skin papulae showed nodular infiltration of the dermis by mononuclear histiocytes (CD163+, CD68+, CD14+, CD4+, CD1a−, CD207−, S100−, phosphorylated extracellular signal-regulated kinases+). Several histiocytes showed a foamy cytoplasm. MRI of the brain revealed atrophy of the midbrain, cerebellum, superior and middle cerebellar peduncles. Hyperintense signals were observed in T2 and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences within the pons, cerebellar white matter, dentate nuclei (DN), and globi pallidi in the absence of any contrast enhancement. Both the retro-orbital space and the pituitary gland appeared normal. Susceptibility weighted imaging demonstrated paramagnetic compound accumulation in the DN, caudate nuclei, and globi pallidi. Spectroscopy MRI showed a reduction of N-acetyl aspartate in the DN and globi pallidi. Whole-body bone scintigraphy with 99technetium-methylene diphosphonate (99Tc-MDP) showed intense, abnormal radiotracer activity in the distal femurs and whole tibiae bilaterally, with additional areas of weak uptake in the ulnae, radii, right mandible, and left maxilla. This pattern of skeletal colonization was further confirmed by fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) imaging, and high resolution computed tomography (CT) of the femurs and tibiae consistently showed the presence of granulomatous lesions characterized by central demineralization and peripheral osteosclerosis. Genetic testing of the formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded skin lesion identified the V600E, GTC > GAG mutation of the BRAF gene.

case_report: An 11-year-old Chinese boy presented with significant weight loss exceeding 5 kg over six months, along with pallor, fatigue, poor appetite, and nocturnal lower limb twitching. He was born to healthy parents via vaginal delivery at full term, weighing 3.7 kg, and experienced asphyxiation and hypoxia at birth. His developmental milestones were delayed, and he had a history of cerebral palsy, hydrocephalus, and left eye strabismus. At age 3, he underwent surgery for tongue tie and slurred speech, followed by three years of language rehabilitation. There was no family history of similar conditions. Physical examination revealed normotension, cachexia (height 154 cm, weight 25 kg), slow reaction, dysarthria, and unsteady gait without nystagmus or hand tremor. Laboratory tests showed severe anemia (hemoglobin 56 g/L), mild proteinuria (24-h urinary protein quantification 0.61 g), elevated blood urea nitrogen (67.8 mmol/L), creatinine (746.70 μmol/L), and an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 7.53 ml/(min•1.73 m2). Blood tests indicated significantly elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) (1073.00 pg/ml), hypocalcemia (0.49 mmol/L), hypokalemia (2.99 mmol/L), and metabolic acidosis. Antinuclear antibody (ANA) was positive (1:320), with other autoantibodies negative. Complement 3 level was low (0.63 g/L), while complement 4 level was normal. Liver function, thyroid function, carcinoembryonic antigen, alpha-fetoprotein, hemoglobin A1c, blood glucose, thyroid ultrasound, abdominal ultrasound, cardiac ultrasound, and chest CT results were normal. Ophthalmic examination revealed myopia in both eyes and a leopard pattern under the fundus. Hearing was normal in both ears. Renal ultrasound showed two small kidneys.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed dysplasia of the cerebellar vermis and extension of the upper cerebellar feet with an MTS. Genetic analysis showed novel compound heterozygous mutations in the RPGRIP1L gene [c.1334_c.1335insT (p.L447fs*7) and c.2723G > T (p.G908V)].

case_report: A 28-year-old male presented with nonspecific pain in the left lateral thigh. The patient reported experiencing similar pain intermittently over the past 3 years, for which he occasionally used over-the-counter pain medications like paracetamol, resulting in temporary relief. There was no history of trauma to the area, fever, or other systemic symptoms. Physical examination showed normal vital signs and mild localized pain upon pressure, with no other systemic abnormalities.
test_results: X-ray showed flecks of calcification in soft tissue of the left thigh. Serum phosphate level was extremely high (9.3 mg/dL; normal range, 1.7-4.5 mg/dL).

case_report: A 17-year-old male, attending a technical school in the transportation industry, was referred to our hospital after showing abnormalities in a color perception test for employment. During elementary school, he had undergone a color perception test during a health check with no noted abnormalities. He has no family history of color vision deficiency and no other symptoms. On initial examination, his best-corrected visual acuity was 1.2, with no refractive error in either eye. A specialist in color vision conducted further tests. Using Ishihara pseudoisochromatic plates, the patient could only read the first plate. However, he passed the panel D-15 dichotomous test without errors. The 100-hue test indicated a mild color vision defect with no definite axis of error, and the anomaloscope color blindness test showed a normal match. The Standard Pseudoisochromatic Plates, part 2, test revealed two mistakes for blue–yellow differentiation and five mistakes for red–green differentiation in the right eye, and two mistakes for blue–yellow differentiation and four mistakes for red–green differentiation in the left eye, indicating no definite axis for the color vision defect. The initial examination of his fundus showed no abnormalities except for a somewhat yellowish reflex in the fovea of both eyes. Fundus autofluorescence, optical coherence tomography, and multifocal ERG were normal. Fluorescein fundus angiography also revealed no abnormalities. Color vision deficiency with no apparent retinal abnormalities is sometimes associated with retinal conditions.
test_results: Both the cone ERG and 30 Hz flicker ERG showed a good response; however, the cone ERG showed wide a-wave trough. Bright flash, mixed rod and cone ERG showed a negative type with a reduced b-wave and a disappearance of oscillatory potential. No response was recorded in the rod ERG.

case_report: A 14-year-old girl presented with a brief history of difficulty breathing and left-sided chest pain, which worsened after a suspected lower respiratory tract infection. She had experienced progressive exercise limitation and wheezing over the past three months and was initially treated with bronchodilators. On examination, she exhibited rapid breathing, oxygen saturation of 92% on room air, reduced chest expansion on the left side, tracheal deviation to the left, and absent breath sounds over the left side of the chest. A chest X-ray revealed a complete collapse of the left lung with an obstruction in the proximal left main bronchus. There was no history of foreign body aspiration.
test_results: A flexible bronchoscopy was done which showed a smooth, reddish-yellow polypoidal mass occluding the entire lumen of the left main bronchus. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest showed the endobronchial mass to be part of a large inhomogeneous lesion occupying the entire left upper lobe.
