Histological evaluation showed the presence of uniform polygonal cells with finely granular chromatin in round nuclei and a moderate amount of eosinophilic cytoplasm without any nuclear atypia, mitosis or necrosis. Immunohistochemistry showed neuroendocrine differentiation of tumour cells with cytoplasmic positivity of cytokeratin, chromogranin A and synaptophysin.

case_report: A 69-year-old female with a history of treated left breast cancer in 2012 reported experiencing gradual, progressive pain in the left side of her chest wall and breast. Mammography and ultrasound examinations of both breasts were conducted, showing BI-RADS 1 findings. Bone scintigraphy was performed, revealing asymmetrical abnormal increased tracer uptake in the bilateral fronto-parietal regions of the skull. Tracer uptake in the rest of the skeleton was within normal limits for her age.
test_results: Findings showed irregular thickening of the frontal bone inner table extending to involve the parietal bones. The midline was spared and periosteum and cortical bone were unaffected. No definite evidence of lytic or sclerotic deposits was noted.

case_report: A 64-year-old male presented to the emergency department with general malaise, fever, chills, and significant swelling on the left side of the neck and face. He has a history of left-sided microtia with complete absence of the external auditory canal since birth, type 2 diabetes managed by diet, and arterial hypertension controlled with 160 mg valsartan daily. Physical examination revealed left-sided head-and-neck edema, herpetiform-grouped vesicles around the left ear and nose, and yellowish crusts with bullae formation in the perioral region. Laboratory results showed leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 25.7 (normal range: 3.8–11.0), thrombocytopenia of 64 Gpt/L (120–340), reduced hematocrit of 0.245 L/L (0.40–0.54), hemoglobin of 5.1 mmol/L (8.6–12.1), erythrocyte count of 2.5 Tpt/L (4.6–6.2), neutrophilia of 13.8 Gpt/L (1.8–7.6), lymphopenia of 11% (20–45), increased large unstained cells at 2 Gpt/L (0–0.40), and elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) of 333 mg/L (<5). HIV tests were negative. Initial antibiotic treatment with sultamicillin was administered at 3 × 3 g/d intravenously. Due to worsening facial swelling, the patient was referred to the Ear Nose Throat department. Diagnostic ultrasound and thoracic CT were performed to rule out abscess formation. Antibiotic treatment was switched to 3 × 800 mg clindamycin/d plus aciclovir 3 × 500 mg/d. Pain management included metamizole sodium 3 × 30 gtt/d. Despite treatment, only minor clinical improvement was observed. Peripheral blood analysis noted 11% blasts. The patient experienced malodorous oozing, bullae formation, and increasing edema. Firm infiltrates were noted on the left chin and submandibular region, and skin biopsies were taken, showing nonspecific putrid inflammation. Vesicles suggested dissemination. Aciclovir dosage was increased to 10 mg/kg (3 × 1000 mg/d) intravenously. Pain management was adjusted with increasing doses of pregabalin. Thrombosis prophylaxis included subcutaneous injections of certoparin sodium 3000 I.E. anti-Xa/d. Despite these measures, the patient's condition did not improve, with CRP rising to >400 mg/L, leukocytosis of 28.4 Gpt/L, and procalcitonin increasing to 3.65 ng/mL (normal range: 0–0.5). The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit under suspicion of septicemia. Central venous access was established via a subclavian catheter. Treatment included 4.5 g piperacillin, 500 mg levofloxacin, 1000 mg acyclovir every 8 hours, and initially 100 mg prednisolone. The patient developed doughy stool, prompting a change in antibiotics to vancomycin 4 × 500 mg orally. Stool samples for Clostridium difficile were negative. Clinical improvement was noted with a reduction in vesiculation and edema.
test_results: Bone marrow analysis disclosed atypical myelopoiesis, reduced atypical erythropoiesis, and micromegakaryocytic megakaryopoiesis with 10% of bone marrow blasts. Chromosomal analysis and cytodiagnostics revealed a karyotype 46/XY and translocations t(2;12)(p13; q13) and t(6;9)(p22;q34).
diagnosis: Myelodysplastic Syndrome with Refractory Anemia and Blast Excess II
Orpha_name: Refractory anemia with excess blasts type 2

case_report: An 81-year-old woman arrived at the emergency department with complaints of mild fever and right upper quadrant abdominal pain persisting for one and a half months. She had a history of an asymptomatic hepatic cyst. On physical examination, her body temperature was 36.1°C, blood pressure was 116/77 mmHg, pulse rate was 100 beats per minute, and respiratory rate was 25 breaths per minute, with an oxygen saturation of 86% on a reserved mask at 10 liters per minute. Chest auscultation revealed bilateral crackles, and her abdomen was slightly distended. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 16,100/μl, C-reactive protein level of 14.52 mg/dl, AST level of 24 U/L, ALT level of 12 U/L, ALP level of 465 U/L, γ-GTP level of 91 U/L, total bilirubin level of 1.2 mg/dl, and direct bilirubin level of 0.4 mg/dl. Imaging of the chest and abdomen revealed bilateral lung consolidation and a large cystic lesion with air in the right hepatic lobe. She was intubated and received positive pressure ventilation, vasopressors, and antibiotics (tazobactam/piperacillin and clindamycin). Post-intubation, the PaO2/FiO2 ratio was 142 with a positive end-expiratory pressure of 7 cmH2O, indicating moderate acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).
test_results: Contrast-enhanced CT showed an increase in air in the hepatic cyst and a potential connection between the hepatic infection site and peripheral bronchus.

case_report: A 40-year-old man presented to Imam Khomeini Hospital in September 2007 with pain in the flank and abdomen, accompanied by flank tenderness. His medical history was unremarkable, with no prior radiation exposure, surgeries, or infectious diseases. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count (CBC), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and renal function tests, were within normal limits. Ultrasound imaging revealed bilateral dilatation of the pyelocalyceal system with normal renal parenchymal thickness. A conventional incremental CT scan (Toshiba X Vision, Tokyo, Japan) identified a soft tissue mass in the retroperitoneal area at the level of the fourth and fifth lumbar vertebrae. Bilateral hydronephrosis and a midline shift of the ureters were also observed. A perfusion CT scan with MDCT 64 (GE 64 Slice, Milwaukee, USA) (slice thickness: 0.6 mm, kVp: 120, mAs: 450-600, Rotation time: 0.7 s) showed no blood flow signals in the mass.
test_results: Pathological examination discovered infiltration by plasma cells, macrophages, lymphocytes and eosinophils with fibrosis.

case_report: A 51-year-old male arrived at the Emergency Department experiencing chest tightness for a duration of 5 hours. The patient has a history of hypertension, managed effectively for over a year with amlodipine and metoprolol. Upon admission, his vital signs were recorded as follows: blood pressure of 132/93 mmHg, heart rate of 97 beats per minute, and respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute. Initial troponin I levels were negative. Bedside transthoracic ultrasound revealed mild regurgitation in both the tricuspid and mitral valves, with a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 60%.
test_results: ECG showed 1- to 2-mm upsloping ST-segment depression in the precordial leads, with tall and positive symmetric T waves, loss of precordial R wave progression, and a small ST-segment elevation (0.5 mm) in lead aVR. Urgent coronary angiography showed nearly complete occlusion of the proximal LAD coronary artery.

case_report: A 42-year-old African-American female with a history of ductal carcinoma in situ treated with radiation and lumpectomy five years ago presented with a two-month history of progressively worsening left-sided abdominal pain and distension. Laboratory results indicated anemia (hemoglobin of 7.3), thrombocytopenia (platelets of 126), and leukocytosis (white blood cell count of 16.5). Additional lab results showed fibrinogen at 339 mg/dL, triglycerides at 217 mg/dL, and ferritin at 550 ng/mL. Imaging studies revealed marked splenomegaly and mild hepatomegaly. PET scan demonstrated increased uptake in the spleen and pharyngeal lymph nodes. Liver biopsy and bone marrow biopsy both showed infiltration by abnormal lymphocytes.
test_results: The flow cytometry study performed on bone marrow aspirate demonstrated 53% abnormal lymphocytes with a phenotype of CD2+ CD3− CD7+ CD5− CD4− CD8− CD56+ CD57− CD16− TCRa/b− TCRg/d−. Immunohistochemistery for CD3 performed on live core biopsy confirmed the abnormal lymphocytes are CD3 negative. Further workup including Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) and T-cell receptor (TCR) gene rearrangement studies demonstrated negative EBV infection and positive monoclonal TCR gene rearrangement.

case_report: A 7-month-old male infant from Agra, Uttar Pradesh, presented with delayed developmental milestones since birth and an increase in head size over the past 2 months following a febrile illness. The child was born vaginally at term with a birth weight of 1.25 kg, and the birth and perinatal period were uneventful. He had not achieved neck holding, social smile, or cooing. At 2 months old, he experienced a febrile illness requiring a 25-day hospital stay, during which he had multiple seizures characterized by whole-body tightening and a vacant stare. He was treated with multiple antibiotics and antiepileptic drugs and was discharged on antiepileptic medications, with no further seizures reported since discharge. Persistent flaky scalp lesions were noted despite treatment. The mother observed a gradual increase in the child's head size since the febrile episode, along with excessive irritability. There were apparent visual and auditory impairments. The child was the fourth in birth order from a non-consanguineous marriage. The first child had died at 1.5 years of age from a similar illness, the second child is a healthy 5-year-old, and the third pregnancy ended in a spontaneous abortion at 3 months of amenorrhea. On examination, the child appeared small for age with a large head, weighing 4.6 kg and measuring 62 cm in length, with a weight-for-length less than –3 standard deviation (SD). Head circumference was 48 cm, greater than +3 SD. He had short, sparse, coarse, lightly pigmented hair with seborrheic dermatitis on the scalp and a depressed nasal bridge. Neurological examination revealed irritability, lack of interaction with surroundings or parents, absence of visual fixation, and no response to auditory stimuli. Muscle tone was low in all four limbs, with symmetrical movement. Deep tendon reflexes were brisk, and plantar reflexes were upgoing. Fundus examination was normal, with no nystagmus. There was no hepatosplenomegaly, and the rest of the systemic examination was unremarkable. Hematological parameters were normal except for mild anemia with a hemoglobin level of 10.5 g/dL. Serum lactate levels were elevated. MRI of the brain performed during the febrile illness showed hyperintense signals in the subcortical and deep white matter of the bilateral temporal regions, with changes suggestive of megalencephalic leukodystrophy. Reexamination of the MRI films revealed tortuous blood vessels.
test_results: Microscopic examination of the hair revealed pili torti and monilethrix. Serum copper levels were 15.74 µg/dL. Serum ceruloplasmin levels were 7.75mg/dL.

case_report: A 59-year-old woman reported experiencing neck pain for the past 6 years. Approximately 10 months ago, she began to feel pain in her back that extended down to her lower limbs and little toes. This pain caused her to stop walking after a short distance. She also developed a fear of falling while walking. Upon physical examination, weakness was observed in the triceps, more pronounced on the left side. Additionally, weakness was noted in the hip flexors and quadriceps. All deep tendon reflexes were found to be exaggerated.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of spine showed lobulated, conglomerate and discrete IDEM tumors from D4 to L3 vertebral bodies. They were hypointense on T1W and hyperintense on T2W. A similar lesion was also seen in the posterior thecal sac at C6-C7 level. Smaller discrete lesions were seen in the rest of spine. The tumors showed homogenous contrast enhancement. Small IDEM was seen around the cervicomedullary region at C1-C2. MRI of the brain showed no tumor in cerebrum or cerebellum.

case_report: A three-year-old boy presented with a two-day history of swelling around the right eye and pain in the right leg. Clinical examination showed notable swelling of the right upper eyelid with pseudoptosis and mild proptosis, but no palpable mass was detected. The patient was referred to a specialist orbital team. A subsequent review of imaging revealed abnormal bone texture and sinus disease in the body of the sphenoid, as well as abnormal bone texture in the angle of the mandibles.
test_results: Peripheral blood film demonstrated circulating blasts. WCC was 29.4x109/L, RBC was 4.97x1012/L, Hb 125 g/L, and platelets were 319x109/L.
diagnosis: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia  with ETV6-RUNX1 fusion gene

case_report: A 23-year-old female visited the Outpatients Department of the Ophthalmiatreio Eye Hospital of Athens due to worsening vision in her right eye and experiencing flashes of light in both eyes. A thorough evaluation was conducted, including a detailed review of her ophthalmic and systemic history, assessment of corrected distance visual acuity (CDVA), and slit lamp examination of both the anterior and posterior segments. The CDVA was measured at 20/50 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Intraocular pressure readings were 14 mmHg for the right eye and 15 mmHg for the left eye. The patient reported no previous history of ophthalmic or systemic diseases. The examination of both the anterior and posterior segments revealed no abnormalities.
test_results: Visual field testing revealed a large central scotoma in the right eye and was normal in the left eye. Fluorescein angiography and indocyanine green angiography were unremarkable bilaterally. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) also revealed no macular pathology. PERG P50 amplitude was reduced in the right eye but was within normal limits in the left eye. The PVEP P100 component was of reduced amplitude and normal peak time in the right eye while responses in the left eye were recorded within normal range. Rod specific ERG (DA 0.01) was of reduced amplitude in the right eye only. Bright flash dark adapted ERGs (DA 11.0) were of normal a-wave amplitude bilaterally, while b-wave was of reduced amplitude in the right eye and subnormal in the left eye, indicating a “negative ERG” in the right eye. Photopic single flash ERGs (LA 3.0) responses were subnormal in the right eye only. Light adapted 30 Hz flicker ERG (LA 30 Hz) was delayed in the right eye but within normal limits in the left eye. EOG light rise and the Arden ratio were within normal limits bilaterally. The electrophysiological findings indicated generalized retinal dysfunction associated with macular involvement in the right eye only.

case_report: A 67-year-old Chinese man with a 5-month history of chest tightness presented with worsening shortness of breath. Ultrasonography revealed hydrothorax on the right side. Thoracentesis was performed, and the results indicated chylothorax with the following values: lactate dehydrogenase at 143.8 U/L, glucose at 5.92 mmol/L, protein at 48.7 g/L, adenosine deaminase at 8.3 U/L, positive chylous test (Sudan III staining), cholesterol at 0.8 mmol/L, triglycerides at 9.2 mmol/L, negative cultures, cell count with 98% mononuclear cells, and negative biopsy for cancer. Blood tests showed total protein at 72.4 g/L and lactate dehydrogenase at 195.4 U/L. Imaging studies, including computed tomography and positron emission tomography-computed tomography, showed extensive bony destruction of the skull, several vertebrae, multiple ribs, scapulas, and the pelvis. Tumor markers such as carbohydrate antigen (CA) 125, CA 19-9, CA 15-3, CA 72-4, carcinoembryonic antigen, squamous cell carcinoma antigen, neuron-specific enolase (NSE), alpha-fetoprotein, and prostate-specific antigen were within normal limits. Serological markers for autoimmunity, including creatine kinase-MB, rheumatoid factor, antithyroglobulin antibody, and circulating immune complexes, were within normal ranges, excluding autoimmune conditions. Markers for myocardial injury, liver function, and kidney function were normal. Indicators related to tuberculosis were normal. Laboratory tests did not show elevated inflammation markers. Thoracoscopy, gastroscopy, and colonoscopy did not reveal any signs of tumors. No significant family history was noted.
test_results: Part of the bone was replaced by lymphatic-derived endothelial cells, which were positive for D2-40 staining.

case_report: This patient is a 64-year-old man with a history of partial ileal resection at age 30 due to intestinal obstruction and partial peritonitis. He experienced repeated temporary obstructions at the anastomotic site and was admitted to various hospitals. At age 62, he was referred to our hospital with recurrent severe abdominal pain and exacerbation of his condition. The patient had no history of lung disease, occupational exposures, extraintestinal manifestations, or family history of his condition. Physical examination showed a body temperature of 39.2°C, hemoglobin oxygen saturation of 99%, and blood pressure of 100/66 mmHg. A small bowel series revealed longitudinal ulcers and strictures at the ileal anastomotic site. Colonoscopy and pathological examination of a biopsied ulcer specimen showed moderate to severe inflammatory cell infiltrates with some epithelioid granulomas in the lamina muscularis mucosae and submucosa. ADA induction therapy was initiated at 160/80/40 mg every other week, resulting in complete remission. Two years later, the patient was admitted with a rapid exacerbation of productive cough, fever up to 39.2°C, and chest radiography findings of patchy bilateral consolidation and ground glass opacities. Laboratory investigations revealed a white blood cell count of 13,800/μL, red blood cell count of 386 × 10^4/μL, hemoglobin of 10.7 g/dL, total protein of 5.3 g/dL, albumin of 2.1 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase of 58 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase of 34 IU/L, and C-reactive protein of 22.2 mg/dL. Low albuminemia was attributed to severe inflammation and loss of appetite. Tests for influenza virus types A and B, Aspergillus antigen, (1→3)-β-D-glucan, QuantiFERON, and cytomegalovirus antigenemia C-7HRP were negative. Sputum cultures isolated Streptococcus pneumoniae and α-hemolytic streptococcal species. Chest computed tomography (CT) showed patchy consolidations, ground glass opacities, and small nodular opacities, predominantly in the middle, lingula, and bilateral lower lobes. Despite antibiotic treatment with intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam and meropenem and supportive care for 14 days, respiratory symptoms did not improve and radiographic findings gradually worsened.
test_results: A transbronchial lung biopsy from a right lung lesion showed fibrous thickening of the alveolar wall and intra-alveolar buds of granulation tissue associated with fibroblasts.

case_report: Patient 2 is a 3-year-1-month-old male with delays in motor and cognitive development. He was born at full-term to a healthy mother, with a birth weight of 2.8 kg. His parents are non-consanguineous Han from Anhui Province. He achieved head control at 1 year, could turn over at 1.5 years, and could sit unsupported at 2 years. He is non-verbal but can understand simple instructions. Physical examination revealed nystagmus, hypertonia in the extremities, hypotonia in the trunk, and ankle joint contractures. Bilateral tendon reflexes were symmetrically educed, and the Babinski sign was negative. Ophthalmic examination showed esotropia and optic nerve atrophy. Serum CK levels ranged from 307 to 768 U/L. Enzyme tests related to leukodystrophy were normal, as were blood and urine metabolism screens. Karyotypic analysis showed 46, XY.
test_results: A brain MRI demonstrated frontal lobe micropolygyria, abnormal white-matter signals, and dysplasia of the brainstem and cerebellum.

case_report: A 39-year-old African-American female with no known past medical history presented to the emergency department with a sore throat, difficulty breathing during physical activity, and chest pain located behind the sternum for three days. Upon admission, she reported difficulty swallowing solid foods, a habit of eating raw corn starch for the past 16 years, a craving for ice chips over the past six months, heavy menstrual bleeding for years, and easy gum bleeding when brushing her teeth. Physical examination revealed normal vital signs, conjunctival pallor, spoon-shaped nails, a smooth tongue, and cracks at the corners of her mouth. Laboratory results showed hemoglobin/hematocrit levels of 6.3/25, a mean corpuscular volume of 56.9, a Mentzer’s index of 12.84, ferritin level of 2, iron level of 81, and a total iron-binding capacity of 481. She received a transfusion of 1 unit of packed red blood cells in the emergency department and was later administered parenteral dextran for iron deficiency. Further evaluation for the source of iron deficiency included a stool test, which was negative for blood, and a pelvic ultrasound, which revealed uterine fibroids. Hemoglobin electrophoresis was performed and found to be unremarkable, though interpretation was complicated by the recent blood transfusion.
test_results: She underwent a barium swallow which was notable for a proximal esophageal web with more than 50% luminal stenosis. She underwent EGD with esophageal dilatation which completely resolved her dysphagia with solids by discharge.

case_report: A 27-year-old male metal-mechanic worker presented with muscle pain primarily in the lower extremities, decreased sensation, subjective weakness in the lower limbs, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss. These symptoms had been intermittent over the past 2 years. He also reported difficulty swallowing and mechanical lumbar pain. Neurological examination revealed decreased muscle strength (4/5 in all muscle groups, 3/5 in lower limbs), variable decreased sensation in all four extremities, and pain upon palpation. Initial tests showed normal hemogram, electrolytes, and renal function. Liver profile indicated isolated indirect hyperbilirubinemia, prompting further tests which were normal. Metabolic profile and deficiency tests were normal. Lumbar puncture showed mild hyperproteinorrachia. Electromyography and nerve conduction tests were normal. Creatine phosphokinase levels were negative. MRI of the neuroaxis showed sacroiliitis and edema of the lumbosacral fatty plane between L3 and L5. Video swallowing test documented oropharyngeal swallowing alterations and deconditioning of orofacial musculature. Autoimmunity profile was negative for ANAs, ENAs, and ANCA. Skin and soft tissue biopsy showed negative histopathology and microbiology studies. Occupational history ruled out heavy metal intoxications. Neurological symptoms varied, leading to a psychiatric evaluation which suggested borderline intelligence and a possible functional neurological disorder. Treatment with a serotonin reuptake inhibitor and neuromodulator showed no clear improvement. During hospitalization, the patient experienced right frontotemporal pain and fever. Cerebral MRI showed right temporal myositis. Antibiotic therapy was administered. Biopsy of the left temporal muscle revealed acute and subacute vasculitis type changes and neurogenic atrophy without reinnervation, Congo red stain was negative. Further imaging and laboratory studies did not show abnormalities. Dysautonomia, proprioceptive ataxia, lumbar fatty tissue edema, and temporal myositis with neurogenic atrophy were noted. Additional studies ruled out sarcoidosis, Fabry’s disease, and amyloidosis, with normal results for 1.25 OH vitamin D, ACE, and chest tomography. Alpha galactosidase A was also normal.
test_results: The complete sequencing of the TTR gene resulted in a positive finding for the pathogenic heterozygous variant c.424G>A (p.Val142Ile) missense in the TTR gene.

case_report: A 3-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of congenital transfusion-dependent anemia. She was born at 38 weeks gestational age, small for gestational age (SGA) for length (42 cm), but of normal weight (3,260 g). Her hemoglobin (Hb) values fluctuated between 5 and 10 g/dl, requiring approximately 1 unit of concentrated red blood cells every 3 to 4 months. Erythropoietin supplementation at 500 U/kg/week and prednisone at 1 mg/kg/day did not improve the anemia. Clinical examination revealed black curly hair, no visible hand or skeletal malformations, or abnormal facial features; splenomegaly was noted and confirmed by ultrasonography (11 cm in longitudinal diameter, without signs of hepatic cirrhosis or portal hypertension). Laboratory evaluation showed borderline macrocytosis (mean corpuscular volume 95 fl, normal range for age 74–94 fl), non-compensatory reticulocyte count (56,000/μl), elevated erythropoietin levels (3,316 IU/L, normal values 3.7–31.5 IU/L), increased Hb F (5.1%, normal values < 1%) and vitamin B12 (1,263 pg/ml, normal values 190–660 pg/ml), normal iron balance, no evidence of hemolysis, and a mildly positive Direct Antiglobulin Test (DAT). Polymerase chain reaction for Parvovirus B19 DNA was negative. Erythrocyte adenosine deaminase (eADA) was increased at 8.4 U/gHb (normal values < 1.2 U/gHb). Bone marrow biopsy revealed erythroid hypoplasia, with an increased granulocyte/erythroid precursor ratio (4/1), and some degree of dyserythropoiesis. In vitro erythroid precursor growth (methyl cellulose assay) was severely impaired compared to normal controls and was not rescued after lymphodepletion of the sample. Patient bone marrow plasma did not inhibit erythroid colony formation from the marrow of a healthy donor. Sanger sequencing and the Multiple Ligand Probe Assay of genes frequently associated with Diamond Blackfan Anemia (RPS19, RPL5, RPL11, RPS17, RPS26, and RPL35a) did not reveal any single-nucleotide variants or copy number variants. The dyepoxybutane chromosomal fragility test was normal. Telomere length, assayed by flow-fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), was normal in granulocytes and unmeasurable in lymphocytes due to an insufficient number of cells. Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) analysis was attempted on multiple occasions but failed due to the insufficient quantity of nucleic acid retrieved from the patient’s lymphocytes.
test_results: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) identified two compound heterozygous mutations in the gene encoding the long non-coding RNA RMRP (ENST00000363046.1): a maternally inherited single-nucleotide rare variant, n.67G>A (rs1245480029), and a novel paternally inherited one-nucleotide insertion, n.64_65insA. Both variants map to a proximal highly conserved region of the gene.

case_report: A two-year-old boy was referred to the pediatric dermatology department for evaluation of cafè-au-lait spots present since birth. Clinical examination showed a brown, irregularly shaped patch on the right arm and a hyperpigmented patch on the left latero-cervical region with an irregular lateral border and a sharp edge on the midline. No other cutaneous features such as axillary freckling, multiple cafè-au-lait spots, or soft skin were detected, and there was no familial history of similar conditions. The child was in good general health, with growth charts, head circumference, and psychomotor development within normal ranges for his age. Diffuse deep-blue oval macules on his back and generalized hypertrichosis were noted. The mother reported chronic intermittent itch, mainly on the hands, back, arms, and legs, occasionally causing excoriated papules. No cutaneous lesions were found to justify the itch. Clinical examination and the absence of pruritus in the patient’s relatives excluded scabies. There was no personal or family history of atopy, atopic eczema, or eczematous lesions attributable to irritant contact dermatitis. Regional expanded newborn screening for inherited metabolic diseases, including aminoacidemias, organic acidemias, urea cycle defects, fatty acid oxidation disorders, biotinidase deficiency, and galactosemia, was negative. Blood examinations, including liver enzymes, creatinine, thyroid function, complete blood count, immunoglobulin E count, anti-transglutaminase antibodies, and direct bilirubin, were all normal. A negative perianal scotch tape test ruled out enterobiasis. No other cutaneous features such as vascular birthmarks, telangiectasias, ivory papules, or plaques were present. Physical examination was unremarkable, with no history of musculoskeletal and neurological problems, sensorineural hearing loss, macroglossia, facial dysmorphism, dysostosis multiplex, hepatosplenomegaly, gastrointestinal diseases, or inguinal or umbilical hernias. No behavioral, mood, or sleep disorders were detected. Urinary glycosaminoglycan (GAG) levels were normal.
test_results: The patient showed a heterozygous variant NM_152419.3: c.493C>T (p.Pro165Ser) in the exon 4 of HGSNAT (heparan-alpha-glucosaminide N-acetyltransferase) gene.

case_report: A 25-year-old male was referred to the otolaryngology department for persistent hoarseness of voice since birth, with no impact on daily activities or dietary changes. The patient did not report stridor, dysphagia, dyspnea, gastroesophageal reflux, or other related symptoms. He had a history of childhood asthma with multiple exacerbations due to recurrent upper respiratory tract infections, recurrent tonsillitis, loud snoring during sleep, and mouth breathing, for which he underwent an adenotonsillectomy. Physical examination revealed craniofacial features including deep wide-set eyes, a depressed nasal bridge, retrognathia, and postaxial polydactyly of the right hand and left foot. Family history indicated consanguinity between the parents (fourth-degree relatives), who were phenotypically normal. The patient's younger sister also exhibited similar clinical features, confirmed by genetic testing.
test_results: Fiberoptic nasopharyngolaryngoscopy (NPLS) revealed a laryngeal, pedunculated, bulging, rounded glottic mass and subglottic bulging with expiration and involuting with inspiration along with abnormal-looking epiglottis, having a separate cartilaginous framework with space in-between and bilateral mobile vocal cord. Computed tomography (CT) showed the epiglottis which was bifid and thickening with a small polyp bulging at the left aryepiglottic fold with enlargement of the ipsilateral pyriform sinus. Bifid epiglottis was observed as the cleft reaching the middle of the epiglottis did not reach the base. The biopsy showed portions of respiratory mucosa with edematous stroma containing telangiectatic blood vessels and mid-lymphoplasmacytic inflammatory cell infiltrates and no dysplasia or malignancy.

case_report: A 40-year-old male presented with yellowish discoloration, thickening, and altered curvature of the right great toe nail for the past 2 years. There was a history of mild pain on walking and application of pressure for the past 2 weeks. The patient had been treated with oral antifungals but without relief. There was no history of prior trauma. On examination, there was a markedly thickened nail plate, increased proximal transverse curvature, and yellowish band-like discoloration of the medial two-thirds of the nail. However, there was no friability of the nail plate. There were no splinter hemorrhages. The cuticle was intact. There was swelling and brownish discoloration of the medial two-thirds of the proximal nail fold. There was minimal pain on applying pressure on the medial part of the nail and nail fold. Love's pin test was negative. All other nails of the feet and hands were normal. KOH mount and culture of the nail clipping did not reveal any fungal elements. X-ray of the foot did not show any bony erosions. The patient underwent a total nail avulsion which revealed a well-defined tumor extruding from below the proximal nail fold toward the distal end of the nail bed.
test_results: Histopathology of proximal transverse section revealed a polypoid fibroepithelial tumor with a foliated pattern, acanthosis, papillomatosis and deep epithelial invaginations of multilayered basal and suprabasal cells with elongated nuclei oriented perpendicular to the basement membrane, absent granular layer with clear V-shaped clefts. At places, remnants of the keratogenous zone were visible surmounting the prekeratogenous zone. The stroma had a superficial cellular, fibrillary and vascular layer and a deep, relatively, acellular layer with denser collagen. There were numerous mast cells in the stroma. A distal longitudinal section showed a different pattern of the tumor: Glove finger-like/monodigitate pattern with marked papillomatosis and multiple thick and deep epithelial ridges. On immunohistochemical analysis, the fibrous stroma showed diffuse staining for CD34 and negative staining for CD99.

case_report: A 4-year-old girl, born at eight months via lower segment cesarean section with a birth weight of 2.5 kg, presented with short stature, speech delay, kyphosis, mild dorsolumbar scoliosis, bilateral patellar dislocation, bilateral developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), bilateral congenital talipes equinovarus, and proximal femoral focal deficiency (PFFD). At birth, club foot and bilateral hip dysplasia were noted. Developmental milestones were mildly delayed: head control at four to five months, sitting at one year, standing at 1.5 years, and walking at two years. Speech was delayed, but fine motor skills and social skills were within normal limits. At seven months, the left upper and lower limbs were observed to be shorter than the right side, and PFFD was noted. Bilateral genu valgum and a lurching gait were present since birth, with prominent bilateral medial femoral condyles and bilateral patellar dislocation. Casting for clubfoot was attempted 10–12 times without relief. At age three, she underwent bilateral distal femoral epiphysiodesis with bone staples. Physical examination revealed a prominent forehead, depressed nose, long philtrum, and thin lips. Growth measurements included a height of 80 cm (-3SD), arm span of 82 cm, and head circumference of 48 cm (3rd–50th centile). Bilateral genu valgum was noted. Speech was delayed, with the child just starting to combine words. A BERA test indicated 50% hearing loss, and she has since been using hearing aids.
test_results: A splice site homozygous change c. 4044 + 2T>C (ENST00000356083.8) was noted in the COL27A1 gene. This variant was not present in the 1000 Genomes project, GnomAD browser, and in-house exome dataset. The reference base is conserved across species and is classified as pathogenic as per American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG) guidelines. The presence of this variant was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Sequencing of parents for similar change revealed absence of this change in the father, and mother was found to be heterozygous for this change. Further investigation of proband revealed stretches of homozygosity (6.59% of genome) for the region containing COL27A1 gene as revealed by microarray analysis. The presence of the region of homozygosity (ROH) containing COL27A1 gene in this patient resulted in both copies of these genes harboring same variation (c.4044 +2T >C).

case_report: A 32-year-old female patient presented with recurring bilateral pleural effusions, coinciding with her 8-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The initial presentation of SLE included widespread arthritis, predominantly affecting the knees. Physical examination revealed pain and restricted range of motion in the affected knee, along with reduced breath sounds over both lung bases. She was treated with prednisone, hydroxychloroquine (HCQ), and methotrexate (MTX) for 3 years, which was discontinued after achieving disease stability. During the medication hiatus, she experienced intermittent lower limb pain, partially relieved by prednisone. Approximately ten months before hospitalization, she developed recurring dry cough and pronounced knee pain, and imaging revealed bilateral pleural effusions.
test_results: A computed tomography (CT) scan that revealed bilateral pleural effusions. Thoracentesis and closed thoracic drainage were performed, yielding yellowish pleural effusion (2500 ml) with benign cytology. Serological assessments revealed an ANA titer of 1/1000, anti-dsDNA antibodies at 52.14 IU/mmol (normal range: 0-12), weakly positive anti-Sm and anti-RNP antibodies, without proteinuria or hematuria. Ultrasound examinations consistently revealed significant bilateral pleural effusions. A right-sided medical thoracoscopy was performed, revealing interstitial lung inflammation with lymphoid follicular hyperplasia and pleural fibrous thickening. Immunohistochemical staining of alveolar epithelium showed positivity for CD20 and CK, ruling out malignancy. A bone marrow biopsy disclosed no anomalies, while positron emission tomography-CT (PET-CT) revealed osteoporosis.

case_report: A 49-year-old female presented with difficulty in swallowing and easy fatigability for 3 months. The swallowing difficulty was initially more pronounced with solid foods. There was no history of black stools or blood in the stool. On examination, her pulse rate was regular at 98 beats per minute, and her blood pressure was 110/80 mm Hg. She exhibited pallor and spoon-shaped nails. Systemic examination revealed no abnormalities. Laboratory results showed hemoglobin at 8.8 g/dl, total leukocyte count at 6400/μL, and platelet count at 140,000/μL. Mean corpuscular volume was 60.7 fl, mean corpuscular hemoglobin was 19.2 pg/cell, and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration was 31.8 g/dl. Serum creatinine was 0.8 mg/dl, total bilirubin was 0.8 mg/dl (direct bilirubin 0.11 mg/dl), and SGPT was 8 U/L. Fecal occult blood test was negative, and stool examination for parasites was also negative. Serum iron was 40 μg/dl, total iron binding capacity was 170 μg/dl, transferrin saturation was 10%, and serum ferritin was 15 ng/ml. Peripheral blood smear showed a microcytic hypochromic pattern. Ultrasonography of the abdomen and pelvis was normal.
test_results: Barium swallow was suggestive of a web at C5 level at anterior aspect of pharyngo-esophageal junction. Upper GI endoscopy showed a smooth, circular, whitish narrowing suggestive of a post cricoid web at the C5 vertebra-level.

case_report: A 68-year-old male, with a history of liver dysfunction due to chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection and alcoholic liver disease, was identified with a 25 mm liver mass in segment III on abdominal ultrasonography and was subsequently referred for further evaluation. The patient was on antihypertensive medication and had previously undergone open reduction and internal fixation with metal plates for a fracture in his left upper extremity. He had a history of smoking and a daily alcohol intake of 80 g for 42 years. Laboratory results were as follows: aspartate aminotransferase, 46 U/L (normal range: 10–40 U/L); alanine aminotransferase, 51 U/L (normal range: 5–45 U/L); alkaline phosphatase, 210 U/L (normal range: 100–325 U/L); and gamma-guanosine triphosphate, 27 U/L (normal range < 30 U/L). Serum AFP was 822.8 ng/mL (normal range < 10 ng/mL) and AFP-L3 was 75.2% (normal range < 35%). Levels of protein induced by vitamin K absence or antagonist II, carcinoembryonic antigen, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 were within normal limits. Serological tests indicated hepatitis B surface antigen was negative, while hepatitis B surface antibody, hepatitis B core antibody, and HCV antibody were positive. There was no anemia or elevated white blood cell count and C-reactive protein level. Coagulation profile, total protein, albumin, and bilirubin levels (both total and direct) were normal. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) revealed a 24-mm mass in segment III of the liver near the left hepatic vein, and an 8 mm mass in segment VIII. These lesions exhibited weak enhancement in the early phase and washout of the contrast in the delayed phase. The segment III lesion showed abnormal uptake on fluorine-18-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) with a high standardized uptake value of 10.9, whereas the segment VIII lesion did not exhibit this uptake pattern. Magnetic resonance imaging was not performed due to the presence of metal plates in the patient's arm.
test_results: Histopathological analysis showed that both tumors consisted of fibrous tissue infiltrated by inflammatory cells, mainly plasma cells. In immunohistopathological analysis, tumor cells were diffusely positive for CD31, and partially positive for CD68 and alpha-smooth muscle actin, whereas human serum albumin and glypican 3 were negative. There were some tumor cells positive for AFP in immunohistochemical staining.

case_report: A 13-month-old male patient was admitted to the hospital in June 2019 due to chronic diarrhea and malnutrition. The patient’s symptoms began a year prior with recurrent diarrhea and malnutrition, worsening in the last 4 hours to 10 watery bowel movements. He is the second live-born child of nonconsanguineous and healthy parents, born at 35 weeks of gestation by spontaneous vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 2.15 kg, and was hospitalized as a premature infant. The family history was negative for inherent diseases. At 1 month old, the patient experienced refractory diarrhea (10-15 watery bowel movements per day) and scattered eczema, leading to multiple hospitalizations and treatment with hydrolyzing protein formula milk and supportive care. The eczema resolved by May, but diarrhea persisted. Upon admission, the patient weighed 6.4 kg, had a head circumference of 40.5 cm, length of 70 cm, failure to thrive, and moderate-severe dehydration. Abdominal subcutaneous fat thickness was less than 4 mm, and bowel sounds were active at approximately 7 per minute. Laboratory results showed a normal eosinophil count and hemoglobin concentration; high white blood cell count (23.25 × 10^9/L); normal immunoglobulin A, IgG, and IgM levels but elevated IgE levels (1970 IU/mL); high triglyceride (3.74 mmol/L); and decreased complement C3 (0.25 g/L), complement C4 (0.1 g/L), and albumin (29.1 g/L). Endocrine tests showed normal antithyroid peroxidase (aTPO), antithyroglobulin (aTG), and thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), with high free triiodothyronine (FT3, 2.20 pmol/L) and free thyroxine (FT4, 10.49 pmol/L). Multiple urinalyses indicated proteinuria (+ to +++). Multiple stool analyses were unremarkable. The patient was allergic to eggs, peanuts, and milk. Endoscopy (gastroscope and colonoscopy) revealed duodenal anterior wall erosion, with negative immunohistochemical staining for cytomegalovirus (CMV) and in situ hybridization for EBV-encoded small RNA (EBER). Flow cytometry showed a slightly higher proportion of CD25+FOXP3+ Tregs in CD4+ T cells (13.0%).
test_results: Whole exome sequencing revealed a pathogenic site in exon 5, c.542G>A (p.Ser181Asn) mutation of the FOXP3 gene.
diagnosis: Immune Dysregulation, Polyendocrinopathy, Enteropathy, X-linked  syndrome

case_report: A 4-year-old girl presented with finger joint stiffness and short stature. She was healthy at birth but had frequent hospital admissions due to respiratory issues. Physical examination revealed a short neck, large skull, rugged facial features, short nasal bridge, wide nose, and swollen eyelids. Her fingers and toes were shorter than average, with limited movement in the distal joints due to stiffness. Auditory examination indicated slight bilateral hearing loss. Initially, her vision was normal, but after one year, she developed glaucoma with elevated intraocular pressure (right eye: 30 mm Hg; left eye: 28 mm Hg). She underwent surgery in 2019. Echocardiography performed one year later showed mitral valve prolapse. Hand radiographs revealed short, wide, and bullet-shaped phalanges in the fingers and metacarpus. Chest X-ray showed paddle-shaped widened ribs and thick, irregular clavicles.
test_results: The results of an MS/MS assay showed arylsulfatase B at 0.03 mM/h (normal range: >3.4 assay µM/h).

case_report: A 65-year-old male with a history of hypertension, diabetes, renal cell carcinoma (status-post nephrectomy), and chronic kidney disease stage IV arrived at the emergency department experiencing sudden chest pain and shortness of breath. He reported no fever, chills, or previous similar episodes. His social history included a 20 pack-year smoking history and intravenous drug use. Vital signs were as follows: blood pressure 160/95 mm Hg, pulse 90 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and temperature 37.8°C. Physical examination noted a nonobese male in acute distress with chest wall tenderness upon palpation. A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed no ischemic changes. Laboratory results indicated a creatinine level of 4.3 mg/dL, within his baseline range of 3.0-4.5 mg/dL. Other laboratory values, including troponin and brain natriuretic peptide, were within normal limits.
test_results: Urine drug screen obtained was positive for cocaine. Planar V/Q scan obtained 8 hours later revealed a large filling defect in the inferior lingula and small defects in the posterior inferior left lower lobe and posterior inferior right upper lobe characteristic for PE. Repeat V/Q scan, this time with single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) owing to improved sensitivity and specificity as well as its enhanced ability to differentiate resolving from acute perfusion defects. It revealed no filling defects.

case_report: A 66-year-old man with a history of treated esophageal adenocarcinoma underwent imaging for the evaluation of mediastinal adenopathy observed on a computed tomography/positron emission tomography scan. He reported no issues with swallowing or weight loss. His physical examination was unremarkable. Endoscopic examination showed a normal esophagus. Imaging revealed a few benign-appearing mediastinal lymph nodes. Sampling of the lymph nodes yielded benign findings. Upon withdrawing the imaging scope, a 1.7×1.5-cm hypoechoic well-defined lesion was noted in the right thyroid lobe near the common carotid artery. Internal vascularity was observed on color flow assessment. The imaging scope was advanced through the mouth into the proximal esophagus. Under imaging guidance, sampling with a 22 G needle was performed successfully and easily.
test_results: The FNA results showed colloid cells, histiocytes, Hurthle cells, follicular cells, and psammoma bodies. Intranuclear inclusions and nuclear grooving were noted. It showed a 1.4-cm heterogeneous, predominantly hypoechoic mass centered within the body of the right thyroid lobe with internal vascularity on color flow assessment. Tiny punctate echogenic foci were noted consistent with calcifications.

case_report: In May 2020, a 64-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, normal kidney function, and a previous episode of bacterial pneumonia in 2019, was admitted to the emergency room at Urbino Hospital due to persistent dyspnea and cough, unresponsive to antibiotic and steroid treatments. Upon admission, she was afebrile with a peripheral capillary oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. Chest computed tomography revealed bilateral interstitial pneumonia with ground-glass opacities affecting approximately 25% of the lung parenchyma. RT-PCR tests for SARS-CoV-2 on nasal and oropharyngeal swabs were negative. However, serological tests showed positive results for SARS-CoV-2 IgG (22.70 index) and IgM (2.47 index). Initial laboratory tests indicated a serum creatinine level of 1.8 mg/dL, urinary sediment containing 20–200 erythrocytes per count ×400, and proteinuria at 50 mg/dL. Further tests revealed positive proteinase-3-ANCA (PR3-ANCA) at 761 U/mL, with negative results for antinuclear and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies. She was subsequently transferred to the unit of emerging and immunosuppressed infectious diseases and later to the nephrology, dialysis, and renal transplantation unit. Upon admission to the nephrology unit, her serum creatinine had risen to 4.8 mg/dL, proteinuria was measured at 3.3 g/day, and the presence of erythrocytes in the urinary sediment was confirmed. Complement fractions C3 and C4 were within normal ranges, while C-reactive protein was elevated at 9.4 mg/dL. Fibrinogen was 886 mg/dL, D-dimer was 2,145 ng/mL, and IL-6 was 40.2 pg/mL. White blood cell count was 11,240/mmc, hemoglobin was 8.7 g/dL, and platelet count was 288,000/mmc. Procalcitonin was slightly elevated at 0.74 ng/mL. Immunoglobulin levels (IgG, IgA, and IgM) were normal, and no monoclonal component was detected in serum protein electrophoresis. A nasopharyngeal scrub test for Staphylococcus aureus was negative.
test_results: Light microscopy showed glomeruli with cellular crescents, some of these with segmental fibrinoid necrosis and areas of sclerosis. Tubulitis and acute tubular injury were also present. An immunohistochemical stain panel for the interstitial inflammatory infiltrate showed the presence of mixed and not specific mononuclear cells (T and B lymphocytes, plasma cells, and macrophages). The glomeruli immunofluorescence studies were negative.

case_report: A 37-year-old Moroccan woman presented with recurrent febrile episodes and abdominal pain. She had a history of sensorineural hearing loss and symmetrical hyperpigmentation with leg thickening for 20 years. During hospitalization, she experienced abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fever, fatigue, weight loss of 8 kg, and night sweats. Physical examination revealed hyperpigmented and indurated plaques on the legs, sparing the knees, camptodactyly in the fifth fingers, hallux valgus, and toe retraction. Laboratory tests showed elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) at 97 mg/L, with no cytopenia. Diabetes was diagnosed with fasting blood glucose > 1.2 g/L and HbA1c at 7.7%. Abdomino-pelvic CT scan indicated splenomegaly and diffuse infiltration in multiple regions, including retroperitoneal, periaortic, bilateral perirenal, pericardial, and right pleural effusion. Infectious causes were ruled out through various serological tests. Autoimmune markers were negative. Bone scintigraphy and PET scan showed no bone infiltration. Pan aortic MRI revealed periaortic fatty infiltration, posterior mediastinal adenomegaly, paracardiac tumor lesions, and pericardial effusion. Brain MRI showed no pituitary gland infiltration. Thoracic CT scan and cardiac ultrasound confirmed right pleural effusion and a 5-cm tumor in the right atrium wall. Muscle MRI indicated subcutaneous soft tissue infiltration with edema in the medial thighs, without muscle involvement. Skin biopsy and right video thoracoscopy with pleural and pericardial biopsy were performed. Skin histology showed fibrosis with histiocyte infiltration (CD 163+, CD 68+, CD1a−, PS100−, Langherine−, CD20−), weak IgG4 marking, and no BRAF/V600E or MEK/ERK pathway mutations. Pleural and pericardial biopsy revealed similar histology. Systemic manifestations included mediastinal, pleural, cardiac, and retroperitoneal infiltration, with histopathological findings of histiocyte infiltration (CD68+ and CD163+).
test_results: Genetic analysis using next-generation sequencing showed a homozygous mutation in the SLCA29A3 gene c.1088G>A (p.Arg363Gln).

case_report: A 16-year-old Chinese female presented with continuous and excessive tear production since childhood, with no significant change over the past decade. Over the last four years, she developed persistent swelling, mild tenderness, and a progressively enlarging local mass on the right inner canthus. The ocular skin appeared dark and dull, and excessive tearing continued. Her personal and menstrual history were normal, and there was no significant medical history in her or her parents, including carcinomas. Her mother and brother exhibited similar features, including abnormalities in hair, nails, teeth, skin, and lacrimal ducts. Clinical examination revealed stenotic puncta bilaterally covered with a membrane, preventing probing of the nasolacrimal duct. There was aplasia of both lacrimal ducts with chronic tear production and local enlargement around the lower lacrimal tubules. Mild fusion of the lower eyelids was also noted. Physical examination showed the following: (1) Skin: sweaty, pale, and without freckles; (2) Hair: brown and sparse, especially at the front of the scalp; (3) Oral cavity: conical teeth and hypodontia or oligodontia; (4) Nose and ears: small ears and a hooked nose; (5) Mammary glands: absent with bilateral hypoplastic nipples; (6) Hands: brachydactyly, most prominent in the fifth fingers, with bilateral fifth finger clinodactyly and camptodactyly; (7) Nails: discolored and irregularly shaped, with short and dystrophic nail plates and horizontal grooves along the length of the nails.
test_results: We identified a heterozygous G>T transition at cDNA position 518 of TP63 (accession number: NM_003722; exon4; OMIM number 103285). This mutation is predicted to result in amino acid substitution p. G173V.

case_report: A 16-year-old female was admitted in September 2020 with elevated blood glucose levels. She exhibited increased hunger, excessive thirst, and frequent urination over the past 7 months. In May 2020, she began treatment with 1500 mg/day metformin and 60 IU/day insulin (10 IU at breakfast, 10 IU at lunch, 10 IU at dinner, and 30 IU at bedtime) at a local hospital. Despite this, her blood sugar levels remained poorly controlled, with fasting glucose between 10-14 mmol/L and post-meal glucose between 12-18 mmol/L. Her medical history includes atrial septal defect repair in 2009 and adenotonsillar hypertrophy for 7 years. There was no family history of diabetes. Physical examination revealed normal blood pressure, a BMI of 17.5 kg/m2 (height: 155 cm, weight: 42 kg), and a waist circumference of 74 cm. She had significantly reduced subcutaneous fat in her face, hips, and limbs, with prominent calf muscles. There was no increase in fat on her back and abdomen. She had visible veins in her lower legs and darkened skin patches in her armpits. The lower edge of her liver was palpable at the level of the umbilicus. Her menstrual cycles were normal, and she did not have excessive hair growth. Laboratory tests showed a glycated hemoglobin level of 8.4% (RR: 4%-6%), alanine aminotransferase at 54 U/L (RR: < 35 U/L), aspartate aminotransferase at 84 U/L (RR: < 40 U/L), triglycerides at 6.17 mmol/L (RR: 0.6–1.84 mmol/L), total cholesterol at 3.7 mmol/L (RR: < 0.51 mmol/L), high-density lipoprotein at 0.75 mmol/L (RR: > 1.5 mmol/L), low-density lipoprotein at 1.36 mmol/L (RR: < 3.37 mmol/L), total bilirubin at 33.8 μmol/L (RR: 1.71–21 μmol/L), direct bilirubin at 10.3 μmol/L (RR: < 7.32 μmol/L), indirect bilirubin at 23.5 μmol/L (RR: < 14 μmol/L), uric acid at 412.0 μmol/L (RR: < 357 μmol/L), 24-hour urinary microalbumin at 238.4 mg/24 h (RR: < 150 mg/24 h), and thyroid-stimulating hormone at 5.46 μIU/ml (RR: 0.4–2.5 μIU/ml). An oral glucose tolerance test showed fasting glucose, insulin, and C-peptide levels of 14.25 mmol/L, 22.68 μU/mL, and 3.7 μg/L, respectively, which increased to 17.00 mmol/L, 130.60 μU/mL, and 11.06 μg/L at 120 minutes after a 75 g oral glucose load. Other hormone levels, including cortisol, growth hormone, estrogen, androgen, progesterone, luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, prolactin, pancreatic damage markers, and insulin-like growth factor-1, were normal. Abdominal CT revealed liver and spleen enlargement and fatty liver, with a liver CT value of 38.16 Hu and a spleen/liver CT intensity ratio of 0.63. The mean areas of abdominal subcutaneous and visceral fat were 28.57 cm2 and 28.78 cm2, respectively, based on CT scan measurements at the L1 vertebra level. Additionally, abdominal ultrasound showed fatty liver, with the maximum diameter of the right lobe being 17.3 cm (RR: < 14 cm). No complications such as polycystic ovary syndrome, atherosclerosis, or pancreatitis were observed.
test_results: Sequencing of genomic DNA showed that the patient had a novel, heterozygous mutation affecting the LBD of PPARγ c.929T > C (p.F310S). This mutation leads to the substitution of phenylalanine by a serine. The heterozygous mutation was not found in her brother (III-2) or parents (II-1, II-2). This pattern suggests that this mutation is a de novo mutation.

case_report: An 11-year-old male presented with asymptomatic, dark-brown, spiny, hyperkeratotic, verrucous scales and ridges covering the body since birth. The patient reported that the scales shed after scrubbing and reappear within 5-7 days. He was born at full term via normal vaginal delivery. There was no history of parental consanguinity, collodion presentation at birth, blistering, or erythroderma. No family members were affected. Physical examination revealed symmetrically distributed, generalized, thickened, verrucous, dark-brown cobblestone-like lesions. The scalp and central part of the face were spared, but the ears were involved. The axillary region, dorsum of the hands, popliteal fossa, and antecubital fossa were less affected. Severe palmoplantar keratoderma and fissuring were observed. Examination of hair, nails, teeth, mucosa, and other systems was normal.
test_results: Skin biopsy showed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and papillomatosis with thick granular layer. Perinuclear vacuolization and coarse keratohyaline granules were seen in upper spinous layers.

case_report: A 13-year-old Caucasian boy presented with reduced vision. There was no family history of consanguinity or nystagmus among family members. His past medical history was unremarkable, and he has experienced slowly progressive myopia in both eyes. His best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 0.5 (logMAR) in each eye. He had high myopia with a current refraction of -7.5SD/+1.5SC at 60 degrees in both eyes. Clinical examination revealed horizontal jerk nystagmus without significant head posture. Anterior segment examination was normal with no signs of iris transillumination. Fundus examination showed hypopigmented (blonde) fundi with visible choroidal vasculature and peripapillary atrophy, along with a mildly hypoplastic optic nerve in both eyes, which was confirmed with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and orbits. Spectral domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) showed bilateral foveal hypoplasia, grade 1, with the presence of the inner plexiform and inner nuclear layers at the fovea and a widened outer nuclear layer. Additionally, the retinal nerve fiber layer showed some thinning, but Goldmann perimetry showed no constriction of either visual field. Fundus autofluorescence showed a reduced foveal reflex but was otherwise normal.
test_results: Photopic flash and flicker responses (Light Adapted 3.0) were severely attenuated in both eyes. Isolated rod responses (Dark Adapted (DA) 0.01) were also severely attenuated bilaterally. Combined rod cone (DA 3.0) and responses to high flash (DA 10.0) demonstrated normal a-waves (for pad recording); however, b-wave was markedly attenuated giving rise to an electronegative waveform in both eyes. The proband was found to have a novel hemizygous splice-site mutation c.4294-11C>G in intron 36 of the CACNA1F gene (hg19; chrX:g.49067563G>C, NM_005183.2:c.4294-11C>G). This variant has been predicted to affect the efficiency of the splice acceptor site and lead to aberrant splicing.
diagnosis: Åland Island Eye Disease and Incomplete Congenital Stationary Night Blindness

case_report: The patient is a 47-year-old male who reported a worsening gait disorder with falls over the past 3-4 years. Neurological examination revealed cerebellar syndrome characterized by slurred speech, hypometric saccades, and an intention tremor in the right hand. The patient exhibited instability while standing, reduced postural stability, and pronounced gait ataxia. Additionally, the patient has a left-sided spastic hemiparesis resulting from a traumatic brain injury sustained at the age of 23 years. Insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus was identified when the patient was 26 years old.
test_results: Blood tests showed marked hyperferritinemia and hypoferremia with normal transferrin but decreased transferrin saturation. Serum CP and ferroxidase activity were undetectable. Serum copper was 2.1 μM (reference range 11–22 μM).

case_report: A 35-year-old woman presented with asymptomatic erythematous skin lesions on the right foot, which had been present for the past 5 years and had spread from the sole to the right great toe over the last year. The patient's and family medical history were unremarkable. Dermatologic examination revealed deep-red macules on the right sole, with purple-colored punctate persisting under diascopy. A deep-red punctate was also observed on the dorsum of the right great toe. Dermoscopy of the acral volar skin showed an erythematous parallel ridge pattern with an irregular globular component. The red bands consisted of reddish rows of dots and globules arranged in a double line, with unaffected acrosiringia openings. On the dorsum of the great toe, dermoscopy revealed small, sharply demarcated red lagoons. Blood analysis and foot x-rays were normal.
test_results: Histopathologic examination revealed multiple areas of glomerulated proliferation of dilated capillaries in the papillary dermis. The immunohistochemical stains for estrogens and progesterone receptors were negative.

case_report: A 16-year-old boy, born to parents who are not related by blood, exhibited delayed developmental and social milestones since birth. He presented with persistent bifrontal headache and vomiting for one week, and had experienced a generalized tonic-clonic seizure 1½ months prior. Two years ago, he initially presented with symptoms including irritability, fearfulness, sleep disturbances, auditory hallucinations, delusions of persecution, and suicidal attempts. During the evaluation, imaging revealed a right temporal space-occupying lesion. He was subsequently started on antipsychotic and anticonvulsant medications. Over the next two years, his follow-up was inconsistent, and he experienced minimal symptom relief. Three months ago, he discontinued all medications on his own and subsequently had a single seizure episode.
test_results: Recently, MRI showed a 1.7 cm × 1.2 cm solid cystic lesion, hyperintense on T1- and T2-weighted images, in the right medial temporal lobe within the parahippocampal gyrus, with extensive cortical dysplasia suggestive of the right mesial temporal low-grade space occupying lesion. The histopathologic examination showed small fragments of cerebral parenchyma with a diffusely permeating cortical-subcortical tumor of moderate cellularity with a fibrillary background. The tumor cells showed subpial aggregation and were arranged in sleeves around blood vessels with hyper and hypocellular areas reminiscent of a schwannoma. Prominent perivascular arrangement with pseudorosettes were seen. The tumor cells were monomorphic, elongate with spindle-shaped slender nuclei, and granular stippled chromatin. There was no evidence of necrosis, mitosis, or microvascular proliferation. The cells were immunoreactive for GFAP (clone GA 5) and S-100 (polyclonal) and were negative for synaptophysin and chromogranin. EMA (clone MC 5) showed dot positivity. MiB-1 labeling index was <1%.

case_report: A 15-year-old male presented with sudden-onset, nondisabling gait ataxia lasting for 1 month, followed by right-sided weakness, difficulty speaking, and drowsiness over the past 2 days. He had no additional symptoms affecting the central nervous system or general health. His vaccination history was inconsistent, and he had a history of viral fever with a rash at 2.5 years old. Upon admission, he was drowsy but had normal temperature and vital signs. A comprehensive physical examination revealed no abnormalities. He responded to repeated commands with one or two words and could follow single-step instructions. Examination of the eyes and cranial nerves showed no abnormalities. He exhibited right-sided paralysis (Medical Research Council Grade 2) with normal reflexes and an extensor plantar response. Mild involuntary movements were observed in the distal left extremities.
test_results: An EEG disclosed polymorphic, asynchronous 3- to 4-Hz delta activity over the entire left hemisphere, with normal background activity over the right hemisphere. Brain magnetic resonance imaging disclosed bilateral, subcortical, and posterior periventricular hyperintensities on T2-weighted, gadolinium-nonenhanced images. His cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was acellular with normal glucose and mild elevation in protein (60 mg/dL). Elevated titer of IgG antimeasles antibodies was detected in the CSF, and the CSF: serum ratio was 3.

case_report: The patient, a 25-year-old African American male, was born full-term at 41 weeks via spontaneous vaginal delivery, weighing 3.71 kg. There were no complications during pregnancy or delivery. The patient was first evaluated at age 16. His height and weight were both above the 95th percentile, and his head circumference was at the 50th percentile. Physical examination revealed that the patient appeared tall with multiple joint contractures. Notable features included dolichocephaly, shallow orbits with mild ptosis (MRD1 of 2 mm in both eyes), hypertelorism (outer canthal distance of 10 cm and inner canthal distance of 4 cm), downslanting palpebral fissures, broad-based nasal bridge, midface hypoplasia with prognathism, high-arched palate, low-set ears, and pectus carinatum. Arachnodactyly was observed with ulnar camptodactyly and severe contractures of all digits. There was a decreased range of motion in the major joints. A two-dimensional Doppler color flow echocardiogram showed normal intracardiac anatomy and left ventricular function, but a mildly dilated aortic annulus at 3 cm. At age 23, CT angiograms of the abdomen, pelvis, chest, and neck revealed mild ectasia of the left common iliac artery, aneurysmal dilation of the aortic root at 4.3 cm, cardiomegaly, bilateral apical bullous disease, dilatation of the proximal pulmonary trunk above the pulmonic valve up to 4.5 cm, and 4 mm left subluxation of C1 and C2. No other aneurysms or arterial tortuosity were found. At age 25, eye and ocular adnexal abnormalities included high myopia in both eyes, hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, bilateral ptosis, and 4 prism diopters of exophoria. Refraction measured −14.00 + 3.25 × 130 and −14.75 + 2.25 × 065 in the right and left eyes, respectively. With correction, visual acuity was 20/25 in each eye. There was no lens dislocation in either eye. Fundus examination showed tilted optic nerves and a more prominent temporal scleral crescent in both eyes. No cornea or lenticular changes were observed on slit-lamp examination. Additional medical conditions included dilated cardiomyopathy, seizure disorder, bullous lung disease, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and scoliosis. A repeat echocardiogram showed mildly decreased left ventricular systolic function, with an ejection fraction of 46.6%. Family history included myopia in his mother. Genetic testing showed a normal karyotype. The patient tested negative for Angelman syndrome, Williams syndrome, and Fragile X. Testing for Marfan and other thoracic aortic aneurysm syndromes revealed a benign FBN1 variant of uncertain significance at 15q13.1-q13.2, inherited from an unaffected parent.
test_results: Sequencing of the SKI gene revealed a c.3502G>A (p.Arg117His) novel transition in codon 1.

case_report: A 38-year-old male presented with a 5-day history of fever, accompanied by generalized weakness, fatigue, and loss of appetite. The patient also reported an increased craving for salt. Physical examination revealed pallor, mild jaundice, and pigmentation on the palms, knuckles, and oral mucosa. There was no family history of similar conditions. Upon admission, his vital signs were recorded as follows: blood pressure at 90/60 mm Hg, pulse rate at 76 beats per minute, and respiratory rate at 13 breaths per minute.
test_results: Blood tests showed low hemoglobin, platelets, and a lower limit of the normal level of White blood cell count (4500/MCL). His serum sodium was decreased, serum potassium was increased, and serum chloride was normal. Urine routine microscopy and examination revealed no abnormalities. Thyroid function tests revealed increased TSH, normal T3 and T4, and anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies were high. Cortisol levels were decreased, and adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) was increased. His CT abdomen was normal. Vitamin B12 was decreased (130 pg|mL), Anti-intrinsic factor antibody was increased (33.6 units).

case_report: A 74-year-old male presented with widespread numbness. He began experiencing significant numbness in his legs in his forties, which eventually extended above his knees. At the time of the visit, he had no sensation in his hands, fingers, and toes. His legs would involuntarily move when he lay down at night, and he experienced ankle pain while walking. He also reported cramps in his thighs, calves, and left arm, along with some hearing difficulties and tremors. Family history revealed that his daughter carried the same mutation and exhibited similar symptoms of generalized numbness. He also has two unaffected daughters and a sister who were offered genetic testing but declined. On physical examination, he lacked light touch and pinprick sensation below his knees and elbows, and had reduced vibratory sense below his knees. He was areflexic throughout. Muscle strength was 4+/5 in his hands and full in his legs. There was noticeable atrophy in both feet and hands, and he was unable to walk tandem, on toes, or on heels. He had high arches in both feet, which could not be easily brought into a neutral position.
test_results: Electromyography and nerve conduction studies showed evidence of chronic axonal neuropathy with normal nerve conduction velocities and absent sural, peroneal, and tibial responses. Sequencing of 72 neuropathy genes showed a pathogenic variant, c.431T>A (p.Val144Asp) of the SPTLC1 gene.
diagnosis: Hereditary Sensory and Autonomic Neuropathies Type I
Orpha_name: Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type 1

case_report: A 64-year-old woman had intrastromal rings implanted in the left eye in January 2013 after being identified with keratoconus in both eyes in October 2009. She had no known systemic diseases, and her 36-year-old son showed no systemic or ocular conditions. During an ophthalmological examination, her uncorrected visual acuity was 0.5 (+2) in the right eye and 0.5 (+1) in the left eye, improving to 0.63 in the right eye with the pinhole test, with no improvement in the left eye. Refractometry results were +0.50 −1.00 64° in the right eye and −0.25 −0.75 133° in the left eye. Biomicroscopy of the right eye revealed focal opacification in the inferior temporal and superior temporal corneal endothelium, anterior iridoendothelial synechiae from 4 to 6 o’clock, and superonasal corectopia. The left eye showed an intrastromal segment at 70% depth, rail tracks in the paracentral area of the corneal endothelium, and patchy endothelial opacification, with no abnormalities in the left iris. Lens and fundoscopy results were normal for both eyes. Intraocular pressure was 12 mm Hg in the right eye and 11 mm Hg in the left eye. Topography indicated a K1 (flattest meridian) of 46.6 diopters (D), a K2 (steepest meridian) of 47.3 D at 93.4°, a pachymetry apex of 557 microns, and a posterior elevation of +28 microns in the right eye. The left eye had a K1 of 48.0 D, a K2 of 48.7 D at 105.4°, pachymetry of 562 microns, and a posterior elevation of +38 microns. Specular microscopy showed a decreased endothelial cell count, polymegathism, polymorphism of the endothelial cells, and numerous vesicles. Heidelberg confocal microscopy revealed keratocytes in the posterior stroma with spindle nuclei, polymorphism, polymegathism, and giant endothelial cells, along with numerous nucleated cells in both eyes. In the left eye, a hyporeflective crater-shaped lesion and a curvilinear, hyperreflective band lesion were observed.
test_results: Genetic analysis found the initiator codon variant ZEB1 (OMIM #189909): NM_030751.6:c.1A > C (p.Met1Leu) in heterozygosity, which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing.
diagnosis: Posterior Polymorphous Corneal Dystrophy  with a novel ZEB1 gene mutation

case_report: In October 2016, a 9-year-old girl presented with nausea, vomiting, lethargy, and decreased level of consciousness at the Neurology Department of Namazi Hospital, Shiraz, southern Iran. She was the third child of healthy consanguineous parents and had a healthy brother and sister. She was delivered via cesarean section due to oligohydramnios, with a birth weight of 2700 grams and a body length of 48 cm. Physical examination revealed a short neck and trunk, pectus carinatum, and kyphosis. At five months old, growth retardation was identified during a routine check-up. Dental age was delayed compared to chronological age. A bone survey indicated delayed bone age, J-shaped sella, periarticular and diffused osteopenia, and flattening of thoracic vertebrae. At 11 months old, she developed a urinary tract infection, and a voiding cystourethrogram showed bilateral vesicoureteral reflux. However, ultrasonography and renal scintigraphy of the kidneys, ureters, and urinary bladder were normal. At age 4, urine analysis revealed proteinuria, and further tests confirmed nephrotic syndrome. At age 6, she experienced sudden onset of right upper extremity paresthesia and weakness. Brain MRI showed ischemic and hemorrhagic infarcts in the left parieto-occipital and left caudate lobe. Brain MRA revealed significant wall irregularity in both internal carotid arteries, left Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA), basilar artery, and left Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA). Cervical spine MRI was normal. Two years later, she developed slurred speech, and paresthesia and weakness extended to her lower extremities. A subsequent brain MRI revealed new acute ischemic infarction in the right temporoparietal lobe and encephalomalacia with surrounding gliosis in the left parieto-occipital lobe due to the previous infarction. Brain MRA showed complete obstruction of the right MCA from the proximal part, along with significant wall irregularity and stenosis in the basilar artery, PCA, Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA), internal carotid arteries, and vertebral arteries. Brain MRV was normal.
test_results: Analysis of SMARCAL1 gene revealed a homozygous nonsynonymous homozygous mutation c. (2459G>A). This mutation was found by direct sequencing of both sense and antisense strands of the 16 coding and 2 noncoding exons of SMARCAL1.

case_report: A 38-year-old male with no prior health issues came to the emergency department reporting shortness of breath during physical activity, widespread body weakness, fatigue, and swelling around both eyes one week after receiving the first dose of the AstraZeneca SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. He reported no contact with sick individuals and denied having fever, chills, cough, abdominal or flank pain, rectal bleeding, joint pain, nausea, vomiting, painful urination, or changes in urine volume, color, and frequency. He had no known medical conditions, family history of kidney diseases or cancers, allergies, or previous adverse reactions to vaccines. On physical examination, the patient was not in distress and showed no signs of bleeding such as bruises or petechiae. His vital signs were stable except for elevated blood pressure (169/70 mmHg). Notable findings included swelling around the eyes, a puffy face, and lower limb edema. The chest examination revealed clear lungs with equal breath sounds and normal vesicular breathing. Cardiovascular examination showed normal heart sounds (S1 and S2) without additional sounds. The abdomen was soft, non-tender, and without organ enlargement. Initial laboratory tests indicated anemia (hemoglobin: 67 g/L) with approximately 2.8% schistocytes on a peripheral blood smear, low platelet count (130 × 10^9/L), and kidney dysfunction (creatinine: 960 umol/L, BUN: 43.8 mg/dL). There was evidence of non-immune hemolysis, including low haptoglobin (<0.05), normal total and indirect bilirubin, elevated lactate dehydrogenase (658 U/L), and a negative direct antiglobulin test. Inflammatory markers included C-reactive protein (12 mg/L), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (36 mm/h), and ferritin (845 ug/L). Coagulation studies showed a prothrombin time of 11.30 seconds, partial thromboplastin time of 27.10 seconds, and an INR of 1.04. The SARS-CoV-2 PCR test from a nasopharyngeal swab was negative. Urinalysis revealed cloudy urine with amorphous crystals (+3), hematuria (RBC: 18/HPF), and proteinuria (3.97 g/L). A urine culture was negative.
test_results: A renal ultrasound showed normal echogenicity, size, shape, and perfusion with preserved corticomedullary differentiation bilaterally. There was no evidence of calculi or hydronephrosis. Genetic work up came negative for C3; complement factor B (CFB); complement factor H (CFH); complement factor H-related protein 1; complement factor I, II, and V (CFI); complement regulatory protein CD46; thrombomodulin gene (THBD); complement receptor 1 (CR1); protectin (CD59); diacylglycerol kinase e (DGKE); inverted formin 2 (INF-2); methylmalonic aciduria cobalamin deficiency) chic type with homocystinuria (MMACHC); methylmalonyl-coa mutase (MMUT); phosphatidylinositol glycan biosynthesis class A protein (PIGA); and plasminogen (PLG). Biopsy results were consistent with chronic kidney disease and features of TMA. There were glomerular fibrin thrombi with fragmented red blood cells in a background of moderate arteriosclerosis and hyalinosis, interstitial fibrosis, and tubular atrophy, and 14 out of 17 glomeruli were sclerosed. Electron microscope examination revealed endothelial thickening and cellular interposition of the glomerular basement membrane.

case_report: A 5-year-old male, born prematurely at 35 weeks and 4 days via cesarean section, is the second and last child of healthy, unrelated Dutch parents. At birth, his weight was 2,060 grams, placing him in the tenth percentile. A prenatal routine ultrasound conducted at 31 weeks gestational age revealed short extremities. Postnatally, a narrow chest was observed.
test_results: Skeletal radiographs showed a narrow thorax with short, horizontally oriented ribs and a CTR of 0.65, short iliac bones with the typical trident appearance of the acetabula and relatively short long bones of the legs.

case_report: A 68-year-old woman consulted a dermatologist due to the gradual thickening and yellowing of the nail plate on the fifth toe of her left foot over the past 2 years. She reported no history of trauma, and the lesion was not associated with pain.
