Physical examination revealed thickening of the nail plate, yellow discoloration (xanthonychia), and distal splinter hemorrhages on the nail plate of the fifth toe. Dermoscopy showed visible holes in the thickened portion of the nail plate. All other nails on both hands and feet were unaffected. The patient had no significant medical history. Two mycological samples were analyzed and returned negative results.
test_results: A nail avulsion under local anaesthesia revealed the presence of a villous tumour on the nail matrix.

case_report: An 11-year-old boy presented with ongoing right cheek pain. His family history included his father's severe hearing impairment. His medical history included allergic rhinitis and chronic sinusitis, treated until 3 months prior by an otolaryngologist. Six weeks before the current visit, he had high fever, sore throat, right cheek pain, and mild swelling. A dental checkup the day before showed no abnormalities. Clinical symptoms were consistent with streptococcal pharyngitis, and a rapid antigen test for group A streptococcal infection was positive. He was treated with amoxicillin, which improved his symptoms. However, facial pain returned within 4 weeks. Physical examination showed mild tenderness and swelling of the right cheek. Head computed tomography indicated mild mucous membrane swelling and effusion in both sinuses (left). Cefditoren pivoxil was started due to suspected recurrence of cellulitis with sinusitis. Despite this, the pain persisted, leading to another visit. Physical examination revealed right cheek tenderness in the area supplied by the second branch of the trigeminal nerve. There was marked tenderness but no hyperalgesia. No facial paralysis or oral disorders were noted. Blood tests were normal. Oral clarithromycin was administered for 1 week but did not alleviate the facial pain.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed no neurovascular compression.
diagnosis: Persistent Idiopathic Facial Pain  associated with somatoform disorder

case_report: Patient 3 is a 17-year-old male born at 39 weeks of gestation via caesarian section due to lack of progression in labor. During pregnancy, fetal hydrothorax was observed. Neonatal hyperbilirubinemia was treated with phototherapy for four days. Birth measurements were: weight 3.430 kg (50th centile), length 52 cm (75–90th centile), and OFC 33 cm (<3rd centile). From the third month, the patient experienced feeding difficulties and slow growth, with delayed dentition and closure of fontanelles. Early communication issues were noted; despite a social smile at one month, he showed little interest in people and the environment, was frequently agitated, cried inconsolably, and was intolerant to loud noises. He exhibited hypotonia and deep hyporeflexia since infancy. At 13 months, he was referred for global developmental delay with significant relational difficulties. He sat independently at 36 months, never crawled, and walked independently at eight years. Babbling started at six months, but first words were spoken at eight years. He maintained a restricted diet and had difficulties with mastication and swallowing. He suffered from meteorism and severe constipation and was toilet trained at 10 years. Sleeping difficulties began at two years and persisted through childhood. Parents reported occasional brief episodes of behavior arrest in early infancy. At 19 months, he had three focal emotional seizures progressing to bilateral tonic–clonic seizures without fever. Ictal/inter-ictal EEG recordings were normal. At four years, he had a focal motor seizure during sleep, and EEG showed continuous left spikes and waves during sleep. He was treated with anti-epileptic drugs. Behavioral abnormalities and autistic features with hand stereotypies and repetitive motor patterns were noted since infancy. At seven years, physical examination showed height 109 cm (5–10th p), weight 16.6 kg (5–10th p), and OFC 51 cm (50th p). Dysmorphic features included dolichocephaly, a square-shaped face with a broad forehead, a broad nasal bridge, deep-set eyes with long slightly down-slanting palpebral fissures, long eyelashes, bushy eyebrows with mild synophrys, flat philtrum, and thin upper lip. At age 15, he showed improved sleeping patterns, eating habits, and communication skills, though masticatory difficulties, hand stereotypies, and obsessive behavior persisted. Hyperacusis was still present but better tolerated. He attended middle school with teaching support, was quiet and attentive, and had better language comprehension, though expressive language was limited to dissyllables. General motility was not fluid, and his gait was slow and mildly ataxic. He has been seizure-free since age eight, continued on antiepileptic therapy, and EEG recordings had improved, with the last EEG being normal. Adaptive skills assessed by the VABS interview showed severe delay in socialization, communication, daily living, and motor skills.
test_results: Target sequencing of a 31 epilepsy-gene panel was performed to exclude alterations in genes (GRIN2A, SCN2A, KCNQ2, SLC6A1, SLC9A6, SYNGAP1, SHANK3, and CNTNAP2) previously associated with electrical status epilepticus during slow-wave sleep (SES).
Orpha_name: Facial dysmorphism-developmental delay-behavioral abnormalities syndrome due to WAC point mutation

case_report: A 43-year-old male from Saudi Arabia was evaluated following a detailed family history. The patient reported a history of delayed puberty and delayed development of secondary sexual characteristics, which were neither evaluated nor treated. He discontinued his education during the higher secondary stage. The patient has had sensorineural deafness since childhood and was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus approximately 21 years ago, for which he is treated with metformin 500 mg three times daily and sitagliptin 100 mg once daily. He has no history of hypothyroidism. Physical examination revealed frontal and temporal hair loss, sparse eyebrows and eyelashes, widely spaced eyeballs, and a prominent nasal bridge. Additionally, there was noticeable wasting of the facial and temporal muscles. Other aspects of the clinical examination were within normal limits. Hormonal analysis showed low levels of IGF-1, total testosterone, and free testosterone index, with FSH and LH levels that were inappropriately normal. The pituitary profile, as well as adrenal and thyroid functions, were unremarkable. Laboratory results indicated a high HbA1C and low Vitamin D levels. A 12-lead ECG was normal.
test_results: Brain MRI revealed multiple deep and subcortical discrete foci and confluent bilateral periventricular white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensity. Exaggerated susceptibility weighted imaging (SWI) sequences hypointensities were seen involving the globus pallidus, red nucleus, and substantia nigra, suggestive of age-inappropriate iron deposition. Shallow sella turcica and a small pituitary gland, along with an abnormal craniofacial ratio with a relatively small cranial cavity were also observed.

case_report: An 18-month-old female infant arrived at the emergency department following a brief episode associated with fever. She was born after an uneventful pregnancy and spontaneous vaginal delivery at 38 weeks gestation. Her motor and social developmental milestones were achieved within expected timelines, though she exhibited mild expressive speech delay, speaking only five to six words and unable to combine words at 18 months. Family history included a cousin with childhood-onset epilepsy and another cousin with febrile seizures. Upon arrival, the infant displayed lateralized eye gazing, unilateral facial twitching, and unilateral body shaking. She had a fever and upper respiratory symptoms but no signs of serious or central nervous system infection. Postictal examination was reassuring with no focal neurological signs. Extensive infectious workup returned negative results. During her hospital stay, she experienced two additional similar episodes. Due to the recurrence and specific onset characteristics, she was started on levetiracetam for a short-term course. An EEG study was normal. Brain MRI showed a borderline Chiari 1 malformation but was otherwise unremarkable, with no evidence of hippocampal sclerosis or focal cortical dysplasia.
test_results: Chromosome microarray revealed p.P54L heterozygous autosomal dominant pathogenic variant of GABRB3.
diagnosis: Generalized epilepsy with febrile seizures plus

case_report: Patient 2, a 12-year-old girl, was evaluated due to parental concerns about moderate intellectual and learning disabilities, weakness, fatigue, visual impairment, and short stature. She was born full-term to healthy parents with three other healthy children. Her birth weight was 2880 g (10–25 percentile), length was 50 cm, and Apgar score was 8/8. Postnatally, she exhibited muscle hypotonia and significant delays in motor and speech development. At the time of examination, she showed growth retardation (below the 3rd percentile), weight retardation (3–10 percentile), and microcephaly (below the 3rd percentile). Facial features included low forehead hair growth, curly hair, epicanthus, thick eyebrows, downslanted palpebral fissures, a pear-shaped nose with a prominent root, large ears, an arched palate, a short philtrum, a short neck, and clinodactyly of the fifth fingers. She also had strabismus and severe hypermetropia with astigmatism. Additional findings included kyphosis of the thoracic spine and valgus deformities of the lower extremities. Moderate intellectual disability with hyperactive disorder was noted. Her speech was limited to simple sentences with a poor vocabulary. The patient had a normal female karyotype of 46,XX.
test_results: The analysis revealed two VPS13B mutations: a 1 nt substitution in exon 26, which led to an amino acid change (chr8:g.99501805T>C ENST00000358544.6:c.3989T>C ENSP00000351346.2:p.Leu1330Pro), and a frameshift mutation (1 nt deletion) in exon 52, resulting in a truncated protein (chr8:g.99832435_99832436del ENST00000358544.6:c.9472_9473del ENSP00000351346.2:p.Ser3158Glnfs*11). Both variants were confirmed by Sanger sequencing to be present in Patient 2 and her parents.

case_report: A 39-year-old male with no significant past medical history presented to the emergency department with 3 months of unintentional weight loss and 2 days of worsening epigastric pain. On initial presentation to the outside hospital, he was afebrile, had a heart rate of 108 beats per minute, blood pressure of 80/39 mmHg, respiratory rate of 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 100% on room air. Physical examination revealed diffuse hyperpigmentation. Initial laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 10.3 × 10^9/L (reference range: 4.0–10.0 × 10^9/L), sodium level of 128 mmol/L (reference range: 136–145 mmol/L), C-reactive protein level of 3.1 mg/dL (reference range <0.30 mg/dL), B-type natriuretic peptide pro (proBNP) of 1,428.0 pg/mL (reference range <125 pg/mL), and a negative troponin. He received 4 liters of normal saline without improvement in blood pressure. Initial electrocardiogram (ECG) showed sinus tachycardia and low voltage without electrical alternans. Chest X-ray revealed increased bilateral interstitial markings without focal infiltrates. Computed Tomography Angiography (CTA) was negative for pulmonary embolus but showed a trace pericardial effusion. Initial transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) before intubation demonstrated a mild-to-moderate pericardial effusion without right atrial or ventricular collapse, mildly increased right atrial pressure as evidenced by inferior vena cava (IVC) diameter measuring <2.1 cm and collapsing <50% with a sniff. There was increased variation of mitral inflow velocities. Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) was estimated at 55–60%. The patient became progressively altered and required intubation for airway protection. Despite interventions, he was acidotic with an arterial pH of 7.04 and experienced a pulseless electrical activity arrest for 6 minutes, requiring Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support, after which return of spontaneous circulation was achieved. He subsequently required three vasopressors and was airlifted to a tertiary care center for further management. The patient arrived on norepinephrine 3 mcg/kg/min, phenylephrine 9 mcg/kg/min, and vasopressin 0.03 mcg/kg/min. Repeat TTE showed tamponade physiology with a large circumferential pericardial effusion measuring 2.6 cm and diastolic collapse of the right ventricular free wall. A left-sided pleural effusion was also noted on TTE, and a right-sided pleural effusion was noted on transesophageal echocardiography (TEE). TEE also showed mild global hypokinesis with LVEF decreased to 40–45%. The patient underwent emergent pericardiocentesis with removal of 200 mL of serosanguinous fluid, leading to improvement in hemodynamics. During the procedure in the catheterization laboratory, pressors were titrated to support perfusion. About 1 hour after pericardiocentesis, the patient had been weaned off phenylephrine but remained on norepinephrine and vasopressin. Repeat ECG continued to show low voltage.
test_results: His thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) was elevated to 30 μIU/mL (reference range: 0.27–0.42 μIU/mL) with a T3 of 67.3 ng/dL (reference range: 72–153 ng/dL) and a free T4 of 0.34 ng/dL (reference range: 0.8–1.7 ng/dL). His random cortisol was <0.05 μg/dL and his cosyntropin stimulation test revealed an elevated adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and undetectable cortisol. Further autoimmune work up was significant for an elevated antinuclear antibody (1:80, dense fine speckled), as well as an elevated thyroid peroxidase antibody and 21-hydroxylase antibody level.

case_report: A 32-year-old male reported experiencing chest pain and shortness of breath for the past 2 months. He did not have a cough, expectoration, or hemoptysis, and there was no swelling or lump in any limbs. There was no history of abdominal pain or weight loss, and the patient did not have a history of tobacco smoking or other addictions. On physical examination, his pulse rate was 92 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 20 per minute, blood pressure was 116/78 mmHg, and oxygen saturation was 95%. Chest examination indicated a dull note on percussion and absent breath sounds in the entire right hemithorax, except for the right infraclavicular area where breath sounds were normal. A chest radiograph revealed a large, nonhomogeneous opacity in the right hemithorax, denser in the middle and lower lung zones, with mild displacement of the mediastinum toward the left. Ultrasonography (USG) identified a large, heterogeneous, hypoechoic mass lesion in the right hemithorax with intratumoral vessels visible on Doppler examination. USG of the abdomen showed no evidence of abdominal mass or metastasis.
test_results: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) scan of the chest showed a large, heterogeneous mass measuring 20.8 cm × 13.6 cm × 13 cm in size in the right hemithorax. The mass was broad based toward the pleura and compressing medially onto the right lung, leading to its compressive atelectasis. However, there was no invasion of the collapsed lung, which was showing a uniform, homogeneous enhancement. The chest wall muscles also showed normal attenuation, and no erosion or lytic destruction of the ribs was seen. The mass was predominantly hypodense with an average attenuation of 10 Hounsfield units (HUs). There were small peripheral fat attenuation areas (−70–−90 HU) and few calcific foci (+650–+900 HU) within the mass. An USG-guided biopsy was performed, which showed predominantly myxoid tissue with scattered atypical cells and lipoblasts in a myxoid background. Immunohistochemistry revealed that the tumor cells were positive for S100, whereas the stroma stained well with Alcian blue, suggesting an abundant mucinous background.

case_report: An 18-year-old female with a history of asthma and bipolar depression arrived at the emergency department following an overdose involving topiramate and atomoxetine. She reported experiencing headache and fatigue, alongside suicidal thoughts. On physical examination, she was found to be somnolent, exhibited lateral nystagmus, and had an increased respiratory rate, though she was not in respiratory distress. Her QTc interval measured 508 ms. Tests for acetaminophen, aspirin, ethanol, and ketone levels returned negative results. Serum osmolality was within normal limits, and her topiramate level was 70.5 ug/mL. Although she had been reportedly taking lamotrigine, the test for it was negative.
test_results: Serum bicarbonate was 16 mmol/L, with a normal anion gap, and potassium was 3.3 mmol/L. Urine pH was 5.5. Renal function testing revealed elevated creatinine (1.02-1.23 mg/dL) from a baseline of 0.71 mg/dL and a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation.

case_report: A 62-year-old man from a rural town in Western Australia presented with muscle pain, lower back pain, and progressive muscle weakness, more pronounced in the lower limbs than the upper limbs, leading to decreased mobility and falls over the past 6 months. His exercise tolerance was reduced to 50 meters due to leg weakness and lower back pain. He began using a walking aid and was referred to a neurosurgeon for evaluation. Lumbar spine MRI (T1-weighted images) showed a heterogeneous bone marrow signal throughout the lumbar spine and pelvis. T2-weighted images revealed L5/S1 disc protrusion causing mild canal narrowing. Surgical intervention was not deemed necessary, and he was referred for further evaluation of muscle weakness and to rule out hematological malignancy. His medical history included muscle pain over the last 2 years affecting the shoulders, upper arms, forearms, back, and thighs, leading to progressive weakness in both upper and lower limbs with reduced grip strength in the left hand. He experienced shooting pains down the left forearm without morning stiffness, rash, chest pain, or shortness of breath. There was no weight loss, appetite loss, or night sweats. His medical background included type 2 diabetes managed with metformin, gliclazide, and sitagliptin; hypertension managed with olmesartan/amlodipine; and gastroesophageal reflux treated with omeprazole. He did not smoke and consumed 5–6 mid-strength beers per day. There was no history of significant medical issues during infancy or early childhood. On examination, he appeared clinically well. Blood pressure was 130/80 mm Hg, and pulse rate was 80 beats/min. He was afebrile with no palpable lymph nodes, rash, or arthritis. Muscle weakness was predominantly proximal (4/5 power in the shoulders and 3/5 power in the hips) with reduced grip strength and distal weakness in the left wrist on extension. No distal weakness in the lower limbs was noted. Reflexes were normal, and plantars were down going. Mild truncal weakness (4/5 power on neck extension) was observed without overall fatigability. Muscle atrophy was noted mainly in the proximal lower limb muscles. Complete blood count showed normal hemoglobin and platelets with a mildly elevated white cell count (11.72 g/L) including increased eosinophils (1.79 g/L). Creatine kinase (CK) was 523 U/L. Thyroid function, renal function, parathyroid hormone, vitamin B12, and folate tests were unremarkable. No paraproteins were detected, but the kappa/lambda ratio was 1.69. IgG1 and IgG4 were mildly elevated (12.20 g/L and 17.3 g/L, respectively), IgA was 6.16 g/L, IgM was normal, and IgE was elevated at 1011 kU/L. Tests for HIV, hepatitis B and C, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, antinuclear antibody, and anti-extractable nuclear antigen antibodies were negative. Myositis screen showed positive PL-12 antibody. Stool examination revealed Entamoeba coli cysts, and Strongyloides IgG was increased at 1.54. No proteinuria was detected. Further investigations using CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no interstitial lung disease or suspicious masses, and no specific changes were observed in muscle bulk. Nerve conduction study showed left ulnar compression mononeuropathy at the elbow of moderate severity and mild left-sided carpal tunnel syndrome with no evidence of left-sided C5-T1 radiculopathy. Electromyography (EMG) showed no evidence of myopathy in multiple muscles tested. Spirometry showed a restrictive pattern. The Infectious Diseases team recommended treating parasites with ivermectin. A bone marrow biopsy and aspirate showed a reactive marrow with eosinophilia and no plasmacytosis or immunophenotypical evidence of a clonal B lymphocyte population.
test_results: Histopathological findings from the left quadriceps muscle biopsy revealed chronic myopathic changes with sarcoplasmic rods and possible cores. These myopathic changes included variation in fiber shape and size, mild endomysial fibrosis, occasional ragged red fibers, and type 1 fiber predominance. The sarcoplasmic rods were seen as small, clustered dark eosinophilic sarcoplasmic inclusions on hematoxylin and eosin stain and were red on Gomori trichrome stain. No myonecrosis or inflammatory cell infiltrate was found. Electron microscopy revealed sarcoplasmic electron-dense rods in groups, continuous with the Z-lines, and arranged parallel to the long axis of the muscle fibers. Thin filaments at the periphery of the rods were noted. The rods were arranged in a lattice with a periodicity in longitudinal section of approximately 11 nm. The constituent filaments within the rods measured approximately 1 μm in length and 5.5 nm in width. No cores were seen.

case_report: Patient 1 is a 37-year-old male who first visited our clinic at the age of 8 years in 1989. His clinical records up to 1992 were not retained, but a brief summary indicated that he had nystagmus since birth. He was previously noted to have retinitis pigmentosa and hyperopia through clinical examination at the age of 7 at another clinic. Upon his first visit to our clinic, his eyes did not shift in the primary position, and hyperopia and color blindness were detected. Fundus examination was grossly normal. According to the oldest detailed clinical data from 1992, his eye position indicated orthophoria, but horizontal nystagmus was evident, and he reported photophobia. His best corrected decimal visual acuity (BCVA) was 0.2 (S + 6.5/C-3.5/170°) in the right eye and 0.1 (S + 6.0/C-2.5/10°) in the left eye. Fundus examination revealed bisymmetrical inferior focal retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) mottling (Fig. a, b; photo taken in 1993).
test_results: Bright-flash ERG showed a subnormal pattern and 30 Hz flicker ERG was non-recordable in both eyes. The area of the degenerating retina was more evident with autofluorescence imaging, which showed low fluorescence. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging showed that the outer nuclear layer (ONL), ellipsoid zone (EZ), and interdigitation zone (IZ) in the foveal lesion were preserved.

case_report: A 47-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus and active smoking was referred for evaluation of newly developed high blood pressure and swelling in the extremities. Physical examination revealed significant swelling in the lower limbs and around the eyes, along with a mild red, raised rash on the face accompanied by swelling. Her blood pressure was recorded at 140/80 mmHg, and her daily urine output was 2000 mL.
test_results: At ultrasound examination, the kidneys appeared normal. Laboratory tests showed mild renal dysfunction (serum creatinine level of 1.27 mg/dL) and full nephrotic syndrome (serum albumin 1.3 g/dL and proteinuria 6.4 g/day). Urinalysis revealed microscopic hematuria, dysmorphic red blood cells and leukocyturia. The patient had mild inflammatory syndrome and normocytic, normochromic anemia. Immunological work-up was negative, except for a high anti-C1q antibodies titer (356 IU/mL). Complement fractions were low (C3 41 mg/dL; C4 8.94 mg/dL). Tests for HBV, HCV and HIV were negative. LM identified a membranoproliferative pattern—accentuation of glomerular lobules, and extensive endocapillary and mesangial hypercellularity with occlusion of some capillary loops—accompanied by vasculitis features, e.g., fibrinoid necrosis, capillary wall rupture and cellular crescents. Lesions suggestive of diabetic nephropathy—mesangial matrix expansion, tubular basement membrane and Bowman capsule thickening, arteriolar hyalinosis and arteriosclerosis—were also seen and graded as class II diabetic nephropathy. By IF, a moderate, granular staining for IgG, IgM, C1q and C3 in the mesangium and along the glomerular capillary walls was identified, consistent with an immune-complex mediated glomerulonephritis. By EM, mesangial and subendothelial electron-dense deposits were identified in addition to severe podocyte injury with diffuse foot process effacement and diffuse glomerular basement membrane thickening.

case_report: The patient is a 2.6-year-old Chinese girl, the only child in her family, born to healthy, non-consanguineous parents. Her father has single palmar creases on both hands. During the first month of pregnancy, the mother experienced an upper respiratory tract infection and reported reduced fetal movement but did not undergo prenatal examinations. The patient was delivered at 41+2 weeks via caesarean section due to social factors, with a birth weight of 2.7 kg and normal Apgar scores. She was referred to the hospital at 2.6 years old due to developmental delay. At 1 year, she could recognize people, and by 1.5 years, she could sit. However, she is currently unable to climb or stand. Her expressive language is significantly delayed, with her first word spoken at 2.5 years. She can now make involuntary sounds of two words ('mama' and 'papa'), but her language comprehension is poor. She has chronic constipation, occurring approximately once every 10 days, without feeding difficulties or vomiting. Upon admission, her weight was 7 kg (< 3rd percentile), length 78 cm (< 3rd percentile), and head circumference 45.5 cm (< 3rd percentile), indicating significant physical retardation. Distinctive craniofacial features include slightly raised eyebrows (slight ptosis with compensatory elevated eyebrows), small eyes, slightly swollen upper eyelids, hypertelorism, sparse eyebrows and hair, low nasal bridge, small nose, shallow philtrum, small and open mouth, thin upper lip, high arched palate, intermittent sparse teeth, micrognathia, low-set and protruding ears, circular arc helix, dysplasia of auricle, crus of helix and earlobe, absence of antihelix and crus of antihelix, flat forehead and face, and scaphocephaly. She does not exhibit prominent chin, uplifted earlobes, rounded nasal tip, prominent columella, medial flaring of the eyebrows, large eyebrows, sparse eyebrows in the middle, nystagmus, strabismus, or epicanthal folds. Vision, hearing, muscular tension, navel, and extremities, including fingernails and toenails, are normal. The patient is easily irritated and prone to crying but does not display stereotypic behavior, frequent smiling, or seizures. She has bilateral indirect inguinal hernia. Electroencephalogram (EEG) and B-ultrasound of the liver, gallbladder, spleen, pancreas, and kidneys are normal. Doppler echocardiogram shows an atrial septal defect (oval fossa type). Abdominal radiology with barium enema reveals dolichosigmoid. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) indicates a small frontal lobe volume, encephalomalacia around the left ventricle, and delayed myelination in the posterior horn of both lateral ventricles.
test_results: A novel de novo 22.16 Mb duplication at 2q21.2-q24.1 including the ZEB2 and other 41 genes in OMIM-listed database, (133,460,001- 155,620,000) x3, was identified by NGS-based detection of CNVs. The results of CNV have been further validated using fq-PCR. This CNV was not found in her parents. Study of the family constellation indicated that the CNV arose de novo.

case_report: A 55-year-old female presented with a pins and needles sensation in both feet for 2 weeks. She reported experiencing fever with chills and sweating for the past month and had been evaluated for unexplained fever elsewhere. She also had insomnia for 3 weeks and felt dizzy when standing up from a lying position. Examination showed a moderately built female with a blood pressure of 130/90 while lying down, which dropped to 100/80 upon standing. Her pulse rate was 80/min, and her temperature was normal despite her feeling warm. Her Mini–Mental State Examination score was 30/30. Physical inspection revealed myokymic rippling over her left arm and periorbital area, as well as fasciculations on her tongue. Motor examination was normal, but she had hyperalgesia in both feet. Previous investigations were mostly normal except for mildly elevated transaminases. The patient had taken ayurvedic medicine for 10 days, 2 months prior, for rectal bleeding before her current symptoms began. She had no prior history of taking ayurvedic medications. Sympathetic skin response testing showed absent waveform. Electromyography (EMG) revealed persistent doublets, triplets, and neuromyotonic discharges in the deltoid, biceps, and quadriceps muscles. Urine toxicology screening for heavy metals showed elevated levels of lead (162 μg/l, normal <80 μg/l), mercury (53.37 μg/l, normal <10 μg/l), manganese (38.31 μg/l, normal <2 μg/l), and nickel (18 μg/l, normal <5.2 μg/l). Electroencephalogram results were normal.
test_results: CASPR2 antibody positive in high titer and LGI1 antibody positive in low titer.

case_report: A 25-year-old woman presented with a nodular lesion on the left side of her abdomen, persisting for 5 to 7 years. The lesion was associated with pain and discharge for the past 3-4 days. It had been slowly increasing in size. She had not received any treatment for this condition. Dermatological examination revealed a large nodular lesion measuring 5 cm in diameter on the left side of the abdomen, which was not adherent to deeper structures.
test_results: It showed calcified lesion with no evidence of malignancy. Lesion was excised and the whole specimen was again sent for histopathology which showed calcified worm.

case_report: A 9-year-old male exhibited unclear and slurred speech, drooling, inability to protrude the tongue, and difficulty swallowing since early childhood. He was delivered via emergency caesarean section due to fetal distress, with a birth weight of 2.5 kg. At 6 hours old, he experienced seizures and was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit for a week. He showed motor and cognitive delays, with speech being more affected than social and motor domains. At age 6, he had brief tonic-clonic seizures on the right side of his body with loss of consciousness, which were poorly controlled despite treatment with sodium valproate, lamotrigine, and clobazam. There was no history of trauma or surgery, and family history was unremarkable. Physical examination revealed dysarthria with a nasal twang, a half-open mouth that could not be closed voluntarily, and an inability to extend the tongue beyond the lower incisor. Hearing and comprehension were normal, and there were no structural defects of the tongue. Bilateral trigemino-facio-linguo-pharyngeal palsy was observed on voluntary control, but automatic and emotional motor functions were intact. The patient could blink, close his eyes completely while sleeping, and move his jaw and facial muscles in response to emotional stimuli like laughing or crying. There was no tongue wasting or fasciculations. Hypertonia was present in all four limbs, deep tendon reflexes were exaggerated, the jaw jerk was normal, and bilateral plantar responses were extensor.
test_results: Electroencephalography (EEG) findings consisted of focal left fronto-temporal epileptiform discharges. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain revealed bilateral fronto-temporal and parietal cortical and subcortical region encephalomalacia, with involvement of opercular region. Induced sleep EEG did not reveal any continuous spike and wave discharges.
diagnosis: Acquired bilateral opercular syndrome due to perinatal asphyxia

case_report: A male infant of Chinese descent, born at 39 weeks and 6 days of gestation with a birth weight of 3,450 grams, was evaluated on the third day after birth at the Genetics and Metabolism Department of the Obstetrics and Gynecology Hospital affiliated with Nanjing Medical University. The mother, a 28-year-old primigravida, had a normal pregnancy. Laboratory results indicated elevated C3/C2 levels, while C3 and 3-hydroxypropionate levels were nearly normal. The parents were healthy and non-consanguineous. Genomic DNA was extracted from the peripheral blood of the family members using the OMEGA Genomic DNA Extraction Kit (OMEGA Biotech, USA). Mutations were confirmed through Sanger sequencing. Data extraction, sequence alignment, and SNPs and Indels extraction were conducted using Ion Torrent Suite v3.0 software. The resulting SNPs and indels were filtered through databases such as dbSNP 137, HGMD, LOVD, and relevant literature from PubMed.
test_results: Two pathogenic mutations (c.802C>T/c.827delG) were detected in the PCCA gene. The variation rs774738181 (c.802C>T) was present on the dbSNP database. c.827delG was a frameshift mutation, leading to p.Gly276ValfsX46 mutation of amino acid sequence. According to the ACMG principle, the mutation was a highly reliable pathogenic mutant type. The protein function was predicted by SIFT and PolyPhen, and the results were all harmful. The identified pathogenic mutations and suspected pathogenic mutations were confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

case_report: A 20-month-old male patient was admitted to the pediatric neurology department with a notably large head. Historical information indicated that his head size had been larger than average since birth. He is the first child of parents who are first-degree cousins. Physical examination revealed significant developmental delay. His weight was recorded at 9kg (below the 3rd percentile), height at 75cm (below the 3rd percentile), and head circumference at 55cm (above the 97th percentile). The patient exhibited a dysmorphic facial appearance, including a flattened nasal root. Bilateral simian lines were also noted during the physical examination. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed cerebellar hypoplasia.
test_results: Sequencing analysis showed two novel missense mutations in exon 6 and exon 7 of POMGNT1 gene (c.461C>A, p.Pro154His, c.550C>T, p.His184Tyr according to NM_001243766). The proband found compound heterozygote for a paternally inherited missense variant.

case_report: A 35-year-old Caucasian, right-handed female experienced a sensation of heaviness in both upper and lower limbs, pain in both knees, and difficulty with activities such as climbing stairs, running, and jumping for a duration of 1.5 months. The patient also reported balance issues. She worked in a nursing home but was only able to work part-time due to her symptoms. Clinical examination showed normal muscle strength and tone in the arms and legs, with no signs of muscle atrophy and a normal gait. Sensitivity in the feet, particularly to touch, was decreased. Deep tendon reflexes in the lower limbs were brisk, and Babinski's sign was present on both sides. There were no symptoms involving the cranial nerves. All additional examinations, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the cerebrum and corticospinal tract, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, visual evoked potentials, and somatosensory evoked potentials, were normal. No apparent cause for the patient's symptoms was identified, and the investigation was considered complete. After two years of symptom progression, the patient was reevaluated.
test_results: The patient's plasma levels of VLCFA were measured and found to be elevated; C22 : 0 = 28 μmol (normal range 18–60 μmol), C24 : 0 = 44 μmol (normal range 16–50 μmol), C26 : 0 = 1.2 μmol (normal range 0.1 to 0.7 μmol), C24 : 0/C22 : 0 ratio = 147 (normal range 40–115), and C26 : 0/C22 : 0 ratio = 6.8 (normal range 0–3).

case_report: A 38-year-old male with a history of schizophrenia presented with two days of generalized weakness and staggered, stiff movement. The physical examination was notable only for microcephaly. Neurologic assessment showed cognitive deficits in attention and memory, orientation limited to person and place, and a spastic ataxic gait. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count, showed no abnormalities. Vital organ function tests were normal, as were levels of calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus. Tests for infectious diseases, including toxoplasmosis, were inconclusive. No additional information was available.
test_results: Extensive calcification of the cerebral hemispheres, dentate nuclei, and basal ganglia as well as bilateral frontal subcortical and corticomedullary calcifications.

case_report: A 53-year-old male with a history of liver cirrhosis and portal hypertension was admitted due to mild abdominal pain and a skin rash persisting for one month. His ongoing medications included pantoprazole, spironolactone, torsemide, and rifaximin. Physical examination identified ascites and pleural effusion. Skin examination revealed erythematous, annular, symmetrical, polycyclic plaques with peripheral pigmentation and scaling on the trunk and proximal limbs, while the face, palms, and soles were unaffected. Laboratory results indicated thrombocytopenia with a platelet count of 13 × 10^3/μL, and renal and liver function tests were within normal limits.
test_results: Skin biopsy showed hyperkeratosis and follicular plugging of epidermis, prominent vacuolization of basal cell layer, and perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate in dermis.
diagnosis: Proton Pump Inhibitor Induced Subacute Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus

case_report: A 9-month-old girl presented with features initially considered to be related to Jeune syndrome. She was conceived via in vitro fertilization (IVF) and was born at 31 weeks and 4 days gestation due to premature rupture of the membranes to a 31-year-old gravida 2, para 1 mother. The delivery was vaginal, vertex, and uncomplicated. During pregnancy, polyhydramnios was noted, and a 20-week prenatal ultrasound revealed fetal hepatosplenomegaly, ventriculomegaly, total body edema, thickened nuchal fold, and echogenic kidneys. Amniocentesis was performed for microarray, karyotype, and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) for trisomy 13, 18, and 21, all of which were normal. The Apgar scores were 6, 1, and 8 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes of life, respectively. The infant required positive-pressure ventilation for cyanosis and apnea. Initial examination showed extensive lymphedema, dysmorphic features, and hypotonia. Chest X-rays revealed a severe bell-shaped chest, handle-bar clavicles, thin ribs, and left lung atelectasis. Abdominal X-ray indicated hepatomegaly, bilateral acetabular dysplasia, and flaring of iliac wings. Initial cranial ultrasound was unremarkable except for extensive scalp edema, and a spinal ultrasound raised concerns for a tethered cord. Cardiac echocardiogram showed patent foramen ovale (PFO), patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), mild right atrial enlargement, and a mildly dilated right ventricle with normal systolic wall motion. She passed her newborn hearing test at 3 months old. She was admitted to the NICU for 3 months. On the 45th day of life, she underwent surgery for the placement of a tracheostomy for respiratory failure and a gastrostomy tube for dysphagia. Her neonatal course was further complicated by non-ketotic hypoglycemia, hyperinsulinemia, nephrotic syndrome, and MRSA bacteremia and tracheitis. An immune evaluation was performed due to her infections and was normal. After discharge, she was ventilator-dependent for another 6 months. Her neonatal problems resolved, and she started receiving Early Intervention Services: physical therapy, speech therapy, occupational therapy, and feeding therapy, with good progress. Physical exam findings included a small chin, low set/posteriorly rotated ears, narrow and bell-shaped chest, rhizomelic appearing limbs, ulnar deviation at wrists, bent 3rd finger on the left hand, hepatomegaly, contractures of extensor tendons on the dorsum of feet, mild scaphocephaly, horizontal nystagmus, intermittent R > L esotropia, hypertelorism, and a shallow coccygeal dimple. There was concern for increasing head circumference.
test_results: A brain MRI showed ventriculomegaly involving lateral and third ventricles.

case_report: A 24-year-old Chinese male presented with sore eyes and blurred vision. He weighed 45 kg and was 150 cm tall. The head was brachycephalic with prominent frontal and parietal eminences. Hair was sparse and black, limited to the posterior two-thirds of the skull. The skin was dry and peeling. Facial features included a bird-like appearance with micrognathia and limited movement in the temporo-mandibular joints. The mouth was small with thin lips and a short upper lip. The palate was highly arched, and the tongue was of normal size. He had dental prostheses in the maxillomandibular anterior teeth due to partial anodontia, with an anterior open bite and yellow posterior teeth. Facial, pubic, and axillary hair were sparse. Mild motor and mental delays were noted. Eye examination revealed no light perception in the right eye and 0.15 in the left eye, with no improvement in best-corrected visual acuity in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was 43 mmHg in the right eye and 35 mmHg in the left eye. Eyelids were lax, and eyebrows and eyelashes were sparse. There was a constant searching, pendular nystagmus in the horizontal gaze, but extraocular muscle motion was full. Bilateral microcornea was present. The right cornea was edematous, hazy, and had pannus. The patient was aphakic bilaterally without any capsular remnants, and the state of the right cornea precluded further assessment. The left anterior chamber was deep centrally. Gonioscopic examination showed an open drainage angle. The left fundus had a pale and cupped optic disc (0.8), peripapillary choroid atrophy, and chorioretinal atrophy. General laboratory studies of blood and urine were normal. No cardiovascular abnormalities were detected, with normal electrocardiography and echocardiography results. Chromosome analyses were normal. Both parents, who were non-consanguineous and unaffected, were 24 years old at the time of his birth. The prenatal course, labor, and delivery were normal. He had three normal siblings: an older sister, a younger sister, and a younger brother. The mother reported no miscarriages. The patient had two normal children. He had previously visited a local hospital, but the diagnosis and treatment were unknown. Local doctors recommended transferring to a better hospital.
test_results: Multi slice computer tomography (MSCT) reconstruction revealed a disproportion between the large cranial vault and the small facial skeleton. The facial skeleton was characterized by a marked posterosuperior positioning of the maxillomandibular complex. Mandibular deficiency was noted. The ascending ramus and body of the mandible were severely underdeveloped. The prominent deviation of nasal septum was found. Ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) showed absence of lens, and did not show normal cilliary process and suspensory ligament in both eyes. The ciliary processes were far forward and even not being viewed. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed thinned peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer. A-scan ocular ultrasonography showed increased axial length of 25.08 mm (right) and 24.68 mm (left) with normal anterior chamber depth (3.39 mm (right) and 3.14 mm (left)), while the horizontal corneal diameter was 9.5 mm (right) and 9.5 mm (left).

case_report: A 1-day-old male infant, delivered at full term via normal vaginal delivery, presented with a defect in the lower anterior abdominal wall. The infant exhibited a low-lying umbilicus and an exposed bladder plate that was intermittently soaked with urine, which was being expelled in small squirts from a tiny opening on the bladder plate. The phallus was well-formed, and the infant was also passing clear urine through the urethra with a good stream. Upon insertion of a catheter through the urethra, the tip of the catheter was not visible on the exposed bladder plate. There was no evidence of pubic diastasis on clinical examination or pelvic radiograph. Hernial orifices, testes, and anus appeared normal. Additionally, the infant had polydactyly and thirteen ribs as observed on the chest radiograph.
test_results: A renal ultrasound showed bilateral kidneys normal with a well distended bladder within. On cystoscopy, there was a smooth walled good capacity bladder showing both ureteric orifices ectopically placed, very close to the bladder neck. The left orifice was oval and gaping.

case_report: A 5-month-old girl was brought to our department due to abdominal distension. She was born at full-term via vaginal delivery and was bottle-fed. Her parents, who are not related, reported that her abdomen began to swell gradually starting at 2 months old. She had been treated intermittently at a local hospital with total parenteral nutrition (TPN) and drainage of ascitic fluid, but these measures were not effective. Her current body weight is 5.0 kg, up from a birth weight of 3.0 kg. Physical examination revealed significant abdominal distension leading to severe respiratory distress, without noticeable edema. Erythema spots (nevus flammeus) were observed on her chest, upper limbs, hypogastrium, and a large area of her back since birth. Additionally, demarcated grayish-blue hyperpigmentations (Mongolian spots) were noted on her shoulder, back, buttocks, and lower limbs, which remained unchanged and asymptomatic. Ophthalmic examination revealed bilateral blue spots on the sclera and conjunctiva. Her extremities were symmetrical with no signs of hypertrophy or atrophy in the soft tissues. Abdominal ultrasonography showed normal findings except for the presence of significant ascites. Spinal ultrasonography was performed to rule out tethered cord and showed no abnormalities in the spine. Biochemical examination results were as follows: total protein, 47.5 g/L; albumin, 30 g/L; and white cell count, 4.5 × 10^9 cells/L with 12.2% lymphocytes.
test_results: Abdominal paracentesis was performed immediately when the infant was admitted to hospital and 300 mL of straw-colored fluid was slowly aspirated. Routine analysis of the peritoneal fluid showed: Rivalta test (±); white blood cell count, 2683 × 106 cells/L; mononuclear leucocyte proportion, 90%; multinuclear cell proportion, 10%; and peritoneal fluid culture negative.

case_report: A 36-year-old woman with a history of three suicide attempts and no significant drug history arrived at the emergency department with vomiting. She had ingested approximately 40 bitter almonds one hour before admission. Vomiting began within 20 minutes and was non-hemorrhagic. Upon arrival, she was confused with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 9/15. Initial vital signs indicated tachycardia and hypertension. Physical examination showed normal skin and oral mucosal coloration. Neurological examination revealed bilateral pupil dilation, while cardiovascular and pulmonary examinations were normal. Two hours post-admission, the patient developed hypotension. Four hours after admission, she became unconscious, with a further decline in blood pressure and pulse rate. Intubation was performed, and norepinephrine was administered due to low blood pressure, leading to an increase in blood pressure and pulse rate after 30 minutes.
test_results: Venous blood gas analysis at the regional hospital disclosed severe metabolic acidosis (pH = 6.92, pO2 = 43 mm Hg, HCO3 = 8.6 mmol/L, pCO2 = 42.7 mm Hg, base excess = −25.9 mmol/L).

case_report: A 67-year-old male was admitted for treatment of sigmoid colon cancer. A contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed a homogenous enhanced nodule, 20 mm in diameter, located in the right paratracheal region, resembling an enlarged paratracheal lymph node. During an FDG-PET scan for preoperative staging of colon cancer, FDG accumulation was observed in the nodule, with a maximum standardized uptake value of 5.3. The patient exhibited no clinical symptoms, and both his personal and family medical histories were unremarkable. Blood tests showed no abnormalities except for a naturally high white blood cell count. It was decided to monitor the nodule after addressing the colon cancer. The patient underwent a laparoscopic sigmoidectomy, and no abdominal lymph node metastasis (pSM, N0/stage I) was detected. A follow-up CT scan conducted 3 months postoperatively showed no change in the nodule's diameter in the middle mediastinum. The patient subsequently underwent surgical resection of the nodule without a preoperative biopsy.
test_results: Microscopic examination showed that the specimen comprised lymphocyte-poor and lymphocyte-rich areas. In lymphocyte-poor areas, the oval- to spindle-shaped neoplastic cells were arranged in a fascicular pattern. A rosette-like structure was also present in these areas. In lymphocyte-rich areas, a diffuse proliferation of polygonal-shaped neoplastic cells with vesicular nuclei and small nucleoli was observed. A few mitotic figures were also noted. The tumor cells had invaded the capsule, but not the outside adipose tissue adjacent to the capsule. The ectopic thymic tissue foci were found adjacent to the thymoma capsule. Immunohistochemical staining showed that the thymic epithelial cells were positive for cytokeratin AE1/AE3 and negative for neuroendocrine markers including synaptophysin, CD56, and chromogranin A. In lymphocyte-rich areas, the small lymphocytes were positive for the immature T lymphocyte markers TdT, CD99, and CD1a.

case_report: A 16-year-old male patient was referred to our endocrinology unit. The patient was born at 34 weeks with a low birthweight (1610 grams) through elective caesarean section due to intrauterine growth retardation. Neonatal intensive care unit admission was required for 26 days. The patient was artificially breast-fed with weaning at 5-6 months of age, and persistent growth difficulties were noted. At one year of age, the patient was re-evaluated due to suspected muscular dystrophy. He was described as having a triangular face with a prominent forehead, antimongoloid palpebral fissures, and hollow cheeks. A pseudoathletic phenotype was observed, with muscular pseudohypertrophy and phlebomegaly due to sub-total absence of subcutaneous adipose tissue. Large hands and feet were also noted. His mother reported a voracious appetite but an inability to achieve appropriate weight gain. Blood sample measurements revealed hypercholesterolemia (232 mg/dL; reference range 94–190 mg/dL), hypertriglyceridemia (129 mg/dL; reference range 30-86 mg/dL), and hypertransaminasemia (Serum aspartate transaminase-AST 63 UI/L; reference range 8-33 mg/dL). There was no reported consanguinity or similar phenotypes in the family. Cardiac evaluation (electrocardiogram plus echocardiogram) and abdominal ultrasound performed at the time of initial assessment did not detect abnormalities. At one year of age, the patient was placed on a hypolipidic diet, which was strictly followed over the years. The patient was monitored yearly through blood analysis, cardiac evaluation, and abdominal ultrasound. No significant events were registered during follow-up, except for the detection of mild-moderate scoliosis and bilateral hydrocele, which was treated through ligation of patent processes vaginalis.
test_results: NGS analysis was conducted, and the patient was found to carry the pathogenic variant c.493-1G>C in AGPAT2 gene in a homozygous state. NGS analysis also detected a heterozygous variant located in LIPE gene c.666G>C, leading to amino acid substitution p.Trp222Cys. Segregation analysis detected the same AGPAT2 variant in both parents in a heterozygous state.

case_report: A 26-year-old female patient with no known co-morbidities presented to the ER with complaints of lower limb weakness and respiratory difficulty since morning. She had a history of domestic violence with blunt trauma to her back two days prior to admission. On examination, she was responsive with a normal sensory system, decreased power in both lower limbs (1/5), plantars were down going with depressed deep tendon reflexes. She was experiencing difficulty in breathing and was using accessory muscles of respiration. Cranial nerves were intact and there were no signs of autonomic instability. Respiratory examination revealed grade IV dyspnea and decreased, but symmetrical chest expansion. Auscultation showed decreased breath sounds bilaterally. Cardiovascular examination was unremarkable and ECG was normal. Chest X-ray and MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine were unremarkable, showing no signs of injury or compression. Echocardiography was normal. Laboratory tests including complete blood count, serum electrolytes, magnesium, urea, creatinine, random blood sugar, and coagulation profile were within normal limits except for severe hypokalemia with a serum potassium level of 1.6 mmol/L and low bicarbonate levels of 12.7 mmol/L. Arterial blood gases showed a pH of 7.23, PO2 of 130.5 mmHg, and PCO2 of 30.4 mmHg. Blood and urine cultures were sent, and empiric antibiotic (Inj. Amikacin 500 mg Q12H) was started. Serum creatine phosphokinase (CPK) was raised at 520 U/L, and creatine kinase myocardial band (CKMB) was slightly increased at 10.2 IU/L. The patient was shifted to the ICU for advanced care, with monitoring of invasive arterial blood pressure, central venous pressure, respiratory rate, arterial oxygen saturation, urine output, and temperature. Initially, non-invasive ventilation (NIV) was applied but was not tolerated, so it was converted to invasive mechanical ventilation. Intravenous potassium chloride infusion was initiated at a rate of 30-40 mEq/hr through a central venous line with hourly urine output monitoring and four-hourly serum potassium level checks. On the third day of admission, serum potassium levels improved to 3.8 mmol/L, but there was no improvement in muscle power and ventilatory efforts. The internal medicine team was involved from the first day of admission. After two days without improvement, further investigations were suggested, including an electromyogram and an MRI brain with multiple sclerosis (MS) protocol.
test_results: Thyroid function test showed increased levels of free T4, 2.31 ng/dL, low T3, 0.66 ng/ml, and low thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), 0.01 mIU/L.

case_report: A 23-year-old Asian pregnant woman presented at the Department of Neurology, Affiliated Hospital of Southwest Medical University, Luzhou, Sichuan Province, China in June 2018 with a 20-year history of headache and paroxysmal spasm of the right limb, which had worsened in the past day with severe vomiting. The patient was born with a port-wine birthmark around the left eye frame. Her symptoms included episodes of temporary right-sided hemiparesis, seizures, and migraine headaches starting around age 2, without any history of head injury. All episodes began following a cold infection. The headaches were paroxysmal, lasting several hours, and occurred 1–2 times annually. The headaches were always on the left side, associated with right hemiplegia and right limb seizures lasting for minutes. The patient did not undergo surgery to ligature malformed blood vessels. She received 2.4 g benzylpenicillin sodium intravenously every 12 hours for 3 days to treat a bacterial upper respiratory infection. Physical and neurological examinations revealed right hemiplegia (4/5). Her cognitive function was normal. Vision and intraocular pressure were normal, and the eyeballs did not appear enlarged or bulging. Routine blood biochemistry analyses showed: white blood cells, 13.20 × 10^9 cells/l; neutrophils, 11.73 × 10^9 cells/l; high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, >5 mg/l. Colour ultrasonography indicated she was 17 weeks pregnant with a single live fetus. Transcranial Doppler found normal cerebral blood flow. Dynamic electroencephalography showed an increase in slow wave activity in the bilateral frontal lobe and β-fast wave activity in the left frontal lobe.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging of brain showed hypointensity in the left occipital and temporal region on susceptibility weighted imaging; and it showed evidence of atrophy, calcification and vascular malformation in the left cerebral hemisphere. Computed tomography angiography of the brain showed vascular malformation, atrophy and calcification in the left occipital and temporal region after the caesarean section.

case_report: A 70-year-old woman arrived at the emergency ward with general abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She had a history of hypothyroidism and was on levothyroxine. Her siblings had minor thalassemia. On examination, her body temperature was 36°C, blood pressure was 80/60 mm Hg, heart rate was 100 beats/min, respiratory rate was 22 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation was 90%. The patient appeared pale. Abdominal examination showed tenderness in the right upper quadrant and a positive Murphy's sign. All other examinations were normal. Her body mass index was 23 kg/m2. The patient was admitted to the general surgery ward with an impression of acute cholecystitis, and an internal medicine consult was requested for managing hypotension and hypoglycemia.
test_results: The cortisol level was 2 μg/dL, and ACTH level was 0.2 pg/L.

case_report: A 70-year-old woman from the Karen tribe presented with non-follicular pustules on erythrodermic skin located on her trunk and extremities, which had been occurring since she was 50 years old. Nail involvement was also noted. She experienced these episodes roughly once a year. There were no identifiable environmental or dietary triggers. The skin condition was managed effectively with rotational methotrexate and oral acitretin treatment.
test_results: A skin biopsy from pustules on her abdomen showed subcorneal and spongiform pustules.

case_report: A five-year-old girl was admitted in November 2016 with symptoms of fever, cough, breathlessness, and paleness for 20 days. There was no history of recurrent lower respiratory tract infections, tuberculosis, cardiac disease, pica, chronic diarrhea, bleeding, or repeated blood transfusions. Her birth and developmental history were normal, except for severe bilateral sensorineural hearing loss diagnosed during infancy, with poor compliance to treatment. She was fully immunized for her age and followed a vegetarian diet. On examination, she was afebrile but exhibited tachycardia, tachypnea, respiratory distress, severe pallor, stunting, and signs of rickets (frontal bossing, wrist widening, and pectus carinatum). Respiratory examination revealed bilateral fine crepitations; other systems were normal. Hemoglobin was severely low at 2.3 gm/dL. Chest radiograph showed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, confirmed by HRCT of the chest. Peripheral blood smear indicated macrocytosis, anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, and dimorphic anemia. Direct and indirect Coombs tests and Sickling test were negative. Liver and renal functions, stool, and urine examinations were normal. Serum lactate dehydrogenase was elevated at 1,224 IU/L. Coagulation profile was normal. Tests for anti-HIV antibody, Anti-hepatitis C antibody, and HBsAg antigen were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed mild hepatomegaly. High anti-tissue transglutaminase (TTG) IgA antibody levels (>200 U/mL) and upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed reduced mucosal folds with scalloping in the duodenum, and duodenal biopsy showed partial villous blunting with intraepithelial lymphocytes. Initial treatments included packed cell transfusions, parenteral vitamin B12, amoxicillin with clavulanate, and dobutamine, followed by a gluten-free diet, oral iron, folic acid, vitamin B12, and calcium supplements. Compliance to treatment and diet was poor. The child was readmitted in May 2017 with similar symptoms and received similar treatment. A third admission in September 2017 showed persistent bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, despite treatment for congestive cardiac failure. Tests for tuberculosis were negative. Cardiac 2D echocardiography showed a small patent ductus arteriosus. Repeat HRCT chest revealed interstitial thickening and bilateral alveolar shadows (ground-glass opacities). Bronchoalveolar lavage showed mature bronchial cytology with a few inflammatory cells. The child was discharged with a plan for pulmonary function tests. A fourth admission in November 2017 with similar complaints led to packed cell transfusions. Gastric lavage for hemosiderophages was negative.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed an irregular expansion of the alveolar spaces with widening of the interstitium. The majority of the alveolar spaces were filled with pigment-laden macrophages. Occasional peribronchial lymphoid aggregates were seen. The pigment was confirmed to be Hemosiderin on Prussian blue staining.

case_report: A forty-three-year-old female presented with a one-day history of nausea, vomiting, and seven episodes of diarrhea accompanied by lower abdominal pain. She also experienced a two-week history of fatigue, exertional shortness of breath, and a dry cough. Additional symptoms included paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, bilateral lower limb swelling, and facial swelling. Retrospective history revealed subtle difficulties with concentration and memory. Her significant medical history included relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, with a previous autologous stem cell transplant (fludarabine and cyclophosphamide conditioning) three months earlier. She had also undergone prophylactic bilateral mastectomy and oophorectomy for a known BRCA gene mutation with a family history of breast cancer; had two uncomplicated pregnancies; endometriosis; post-traumatic stress disorder; and generalized anxiety disorder. Her medications on admission included acyclovir (CMV prophylaxis) and nebulized pentamidine (PJP prophylaxis) post-autologous stem cell transplantation, gabapentin and diazepam for generalized anxiety disorder, and Progynova for hormone replacement therapy. On examination, her temperature was 36.7 °C, blood pressure 160/95 mmHg, pulse rate 90 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97% on ambient air. The examination was largely unremarkable except for mild non-pitting edema in both ankles. Bedside urinalysis revealed mild blood and leukocytes. Initial investigations showed a newly raised creatinine of 142 μmol/L with an eGFR of 39 mL/min/1.73m2 (baseline creatinine of 80 μmol/L and eGFR 79 mL/min/1.73m2, a year earlier). Her hemoglobin was 90 g/L (baseline 103 g/L, a month prior to presentation), platelet count 82 × 109/L (baseline 164 × 109/L), and white cell count 6.5 × 109/L. Liver function tests and coagulation profile were normal. Random urine protein-to-creatinine ratio was 206.9 mg/mmol, with no dysmorphic red blood cells, casts, or crystals. On Day 3, High-Resolution Chest CT (HRCT) showed multifocal consolidation in the right lower lobe of the lung. She was initially managed with empirical antibiotics including intravenous piperacillin/tazobactam and gentamicin, and later escalated to intravenous acyclovir. Eventually, she was treated with intravenous voriconazole and meropenem, with only mild response to her symptoms. All investigations, including sputum, stool, multiple blood cultures, CMV PCR, and bronchiolar lavage, failed to culture any microorganisms. Her kidney function continued to decline to a creatinine of 266 μmol/L and eGFR of 18 mL/min/1.73m2, despite usual supportive measures. A 24-hour urinary protein excretion was 1.72 g/day, with a urine volume of 1500 mL. Autoimmune, vasculitis, and glomerulonephritis screens were all negative. From Day 4 of admission, there was a deterioration in her hemoglobin to 70 g/L, and platelet count to 67 × 109/L, with red cell fragments detected on blood film. Her haptoglobin was undetectable at < 0.08 g/L, with raised reticulocytes to 288 × 109/L, and raised LDH to 529 units/L.
test_results: A kidney biopsy showed marked mesangial expansion with mesangiolysis of the glomeruli, with some showing foci of fibrinoid necrosis and capillary thrombi. The renal arterioles showed fibrinoid necrosis and subendothelial expansion.

case_report: A 62-year-old male presented to M. S. Ramaiah Dental College and Hospital, Bangalore, with oral and skin lesions. He reported hoarseness of voice since infancy and skin lesions starting around the age of four. Over the years, he developed additional oral and skin lesions. He did not have a history of seizures, visual disturbances, photosensitivity, or respiratory obstruction, but experienced restricted tongue movement and speech difficulties. The patient chose not to undergo indirect laryngoscopy and skull X-ray. A paternal sister had similar skin lesions, while no other family members were affected. There was no history of consanguinity. Physical examination showed a generally healthy individual with oral findings including thickened lingual mucosa with nodular infiltration, dry mouth, and difficulty swallowing. The tongue was enlarged with irregular pearly white infiltration, and the upper and lower lips were thickened, scarred, and protuberant. Dental examination was normal for his age. Skin examination revealed generalized acneiform scars on the face, beaded papules on the thickened eyelid margins, and multiple 2-3 mm brownish warty papules on the dorsum of the hands and feet. Systemic examination showed no abnormalities. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits.
test_results: Oral mucosal biopsied section, stained with H and E, revealed stratified squamous hyperplastic epithelium underlined with subepithelial hyalinized stroma, suggesting reduplication of basement membrane. Connective tissue showed increased vascular channels with perivascular hyalinization. These deposits stained positive with Periodic-acid Schiff. Histopathological examination of the skin biopsy showed a superficial dermis, with deposition of PAS positive material.

case_report: A 3-month-old male infant was admitted due to inadequate weight gain and poor feeding, without episodes of vomiting or fever. He was delivered at full term with a birth weight of 3094 grams, and the pregnancy was uneventful. Family history revealed that both his grandmother and mother experienced frequent urination since childhood. The patient's older sister was reported to be healthy and did not exhibit frequent urination. The infant had not undergone a detailed examination until this admission, although his insufficient weight gain had been monitored at a local clinic starting from around 1 month of age. In the week prior to admission, his weight decreased from 4880 grams to 4770 grams, and he continued to have poor feeding.
test_results: The initial blood examination showed hypernatremia (158 mmol/L) and elevated serum chloride (125 mmol/L), uric acid (8.9 mg/dL), and blood urea nitrogen (BUN; 25 mg/dL) levels. The second blood examination, performed 20 hours after fluid therapy started, showed decreased BUN (15.1 mg/dL) but elevated natremia (161 mmol/L). Treatment with intravenous fluids over the next 2 days further elevated the serum sodium (171 mmol/L) while decreasing the uric acid (7.1 mg/dL) and BUN (13.4 mg/dL). After admission, polyuria with a urine volume of 800 to 1000 mL/d (3041-3846 mL/m2/d) was observed. On the third day of admission, a high serum ADH level (130 pg/mL), plasma osmolality of 350 mOsm/kg, and low urine osmolality of 136 mOsm/kg.

case_report: A 7-year-old male child presented with painful, discharging nodular lesions on the scalp and localized hair loss for 2 months. Examination revealed multiple alopecia patches with painful, itchy, hyperpigmented plaques ranging from 2.5 cm to 9 cm in size. Small pustules were present on the plaques, some of which were discharging pus. Cervical and nuchal lymph nodes were not palpable. Laboratory results showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 25 mm at the end of 1 hour (Wintrobe method) and a raised total leukocyte count of 14,000/cmm with polymorphonuclear leukocytosis of 78%. Urine, blood sugar level, renal function tests, and liver function tests were within normal limits. Potassium hydroxide mount of skin scrapings from the affected area did not show any fungal elements, and no fungi were grown in the fungal culture of pus. The pus culture showed growth of Klebsiella pneumoniae. The patient was treated with oral novaclox and topical T-Bact cream. After 15 days, griseofulvin and prednisolone were added to the treatment regimen. The pustules and pus discharge subsided, but the plaques persisted after 1½ months of treatment.
test_results: The epidermis was mildly acanthotic. There was follicular hyperkeratosis, plugging, and dilatation. There was perivascular, and perifollicular lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate in the dermis. The deeper dermis and subcutaneous tissue showed intense granulomatous inflammation around naked hair shafts consisting of lymphocytes, plasma cells, epithelioid cells, and multinucleate foreign body type of giant cells.

case_report: The patient was a 45-year-old white male with a history of high blood pressure managed with losartan. He had a history of alcohol and tobacco use and worked as a farmer. Since November 2015, he had been under care at Barretos Cancer Hospital for Binet stage B CLL. Three months post-diagnosis, he experienced stage B symptoms and significant lymph node enlargement. Due to the unavailability of rituximab in the public health system, he was treated with fludarabine and cyclophosphamide, completing six cycles of chemotherapy and achieving a partial response. After 8 months, his condition relapsed, and ibrutinib was recommended. Before starting the new treatment, he returned to the hospital in April 2017 with fever and oropharyngeal and skin lesions that began 2 weeks prior. He had used penicillin 3 weeks earlier for an unrelated issue. Initially, the skin lesions appeared as bullae that ruptured, leading to erosions, crusts, and hemorrhagic surfaces with bloody exudation. He also had lesions on the oral mucosa and lips, causing pain and difficulty eating. He reported minor anal bleeding episodes. Physical examination revealed lesions on the ocular, oral, and urogenital mucosae, as well as the chest, scalp, back, and palms. The oral mucosa lesions were painful erosions, and hematic crusts were noted on the lips. The skin lesions were polymorphic, including bullous erosions, ulcerations, and hemorrhagic crusts across various body areas. The Nikolsky sign was positive. The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for supportive care. Intravenous immunoglobulin was administered, and daily dressing of lesions was performed. Meropenem and fluconazole were prescribed for a potential secondary skin infection. Despite these interventions, the skin and mucosal lesions worsened, and the patient's condition deteriorated, necessitating oxygen supplementation.
test_results: The histological analysis showed keratinocyte apoptosis and acantholysis.

case_report: A 13-year-old female with a known genetic mutation (c. 756dupT, p.K253X homozygous for the LIFR gene) presented to the emergency room due to pain, redness, and corneal opacity in her right eye. The patient had been under the care of multiple medical specialties but had not previously seen an ophthalmologist. Examination revealed a low blinking frequency in both eyes and mild hyperemia in the right eye.
test_results: At the RE microscopic exploration, we observed a central corneal ulceration with positive corneal staining to fluorescein, central, and inferior opacity, and no infection signs were seen. At the LE we observed a mild punctate superficial keratitis that was positive to fluorescein staining and an inferior corneal leukoma. Additionally, low tear meniscus in both eyes. The patient presents corneal hypoesthesia.

case_report: A 2.3-year-old boy was admitted to the Department of Genetic Diseases of the Emergency Hospital for Children in Cluj, Romania, for evaluation of an enlarged liver and elevated liver enzymes. The patient was the first child of his parents, born from the second pregnancy after an initial miscarriage at 8 weeks. The parents were young and healthy, with the mother being 24 years old and the father 27 years old at the time of the child's birth. The pregnancy was uneventful, and the child was delivered vaginally at term. The newborn was healthy, measuring 56 cm in length (97th percentile) and weighing 3500 g (50th percentile). At 1 year old, the child was noted to have an enlarged liver and significantly elevated liver enzymes. The patient was referred for further evaluation. Upon admission, the child was in good general condition, with a height of 90.0 cm (50th percentile) and a weight of 16.5 kg (97th percentile). Physical examination revealed severe liver enlargement, mild muscle weakness, and mild spleen enlargement. Sonographic evaluation showed the liver size to be 4.3 times the upper normal limit (UNL) and the spleen size to be 1.3 times the UNL. Normal values were considered to be 2.5% of the patient's weight for the liver and 0.2% of the patient's weight for the spleen. Liver ultrasound also showed a slightly increased echogenic pattern. Laboratory tests revealed elevated liver enzymes: alanine transaminase (ALT) at 760 UI/L and aspartate transaminase (AST) at 767 UI/L (normal values 20–40 UI/L), and gamma-glutamyl transferase (γGT) at 333 UI/L (normal values < 20 UI/L). Viral markers for hepatitis B and C were negative. There was a moderate increase in creatine phosphokinase (CPK) at 545 UI/L (normal values 30–200 UI/L) and lactic dehydrogenase (LDH) at 780 UI/L (normal values 120–300 UI/L), indicating muscle involvement. The patient also had ketotic fasting hypoglycemia (48 mg/dL) with metabolic acidosis (pH = 7.26, BE = −12.6, HCO3 − = 12.8 mmol/L) and combined hyperlipoproteinemia, with total cholesterol at 282 mg/dL (normal values for age ≤ 170 mg/dL) and triglycerides at 300 mg/dL (normal values for age ≤ 100 mg/dL). A liver biopsy performed before referral showed enlarged hepatocytes with intracytoplasmic glycogen accumulation and stellate as well as periportal bridging fibrosis with incomplete nodular transformation. Cardiac ultrasound revealed hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy with biventricular hypertrophy on electrocardiogram (EKG).
test_results: A previously unreported heterozygous variant in exon 24 of the AGL gene was identified: c.3235C>T (p.Gln1079). This variant causes the reading frame to be interrupted by a premature stop codon. Furthermore, the mutation c.1589C>G (p.Ser) in exon 12 of the AGL gene has also been detected in a heterozygous state. No disease-causing mutation was detected in the G6PC, GBE1, or SLC37A4 genes. The results were confirmed in a second independent sample at the Institute for Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine (Mainz, Germany) by conventional sequencing of exons 12 and 24.
Orpha_name: Glycogen storage disease due to glycogen debranching enzyme deficiency

case_report: A 1-year-old female child, born to parents who are not related by blood, presented with repeated episodes of fever, abdominal swelling, and vomiting over the past 6 months. The child exhibited delayed developmental milestones and growth retardation. Physical examination revealed pallor, but vital signs were within normal limits. Skin examination identified a hypopigmented macule on the face and silvery brown hair covering the body. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 8.5 g/dl, a total leukocyte count of 3200/cu.mm, and a platelet count of 4000/cu.mm, with a normal peripheral smear. Liver enzymes were elevated to twice the normal levels. An abdominal ultrasound indicated hepatosplenomegaly. Other tests returned normal results.
test_results: Microscopic examination of hair shaft showed unevenly distributed melanin aggregates.

case_report: A 71-year-old female reported experiencing itchy lesions on the left side of her body that began 2 months prior. Upon physical examination, there were violet-colored, polygonal papules arranged along specific lines on the left side, including the left leg and arm. The patient has been on olanzapine for 2 years for schizophrenia. Examination of the mucous membranes and nails showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed orthokeratosis, wedge-shaped hypergranulosis, lichenoid band-like lymphohistiocytic infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction, eosinophil infiltration, and dyskeratotic keratinocytes.
diagnosis: Unilateral Lichen Planus following the Lines of Blaschko

case_report: A 46-year-old female presented with a one-week history of fever and symmetric polyarthritis affecting the distal upper and lower extremities, accompanied by thirty minutes of morning stiffness. She experienced nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea for one day a few days before admission. She reported no recent travel or illicit drug use. Her medical history included a seizure disorder, irritable bowel syndrome, chronic mechanical back pain, and iron deficiency anemia. Her family history was unremarkable for rheumatological conditions. On examination, she was febrile (38°C), tachycardic (130 beats per minute), and hypotensive (96/64 mmHg). Physical examination revealed effusions in her wrists, ankles, and selected metatarsophalangeal joints, while cardiopulmonary, abdominal, and dermatological examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory results showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 76 mm/hr (normal: 0–12 mm/hr) and C-reactive protein of 149 mg/L (normal: 0–8 mg/L). Mild leukocytosis was noted at 11.1 × 10^9/L (normal: 4.8–10.8 × 10^9/L). Initial blood culture and serological tests for hepatitis B and C, parvovirus B19, HIV, Lyme disease, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Neisseria gonorrhea were negative. Rheumatological tests including rheumatoid factor, anti-nuclear antibody, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, anti-dsDNA antibody, and complement levels were within normal limits. Chikungunya virus serology was not ordered due to lack of travel history. She was started on oral prednisone, which led to mild improvement in her synovitis. She was discharged on a regimen of methotrexate, sulfasalazine, and hydroxychloroquine. The next day, she returned with worsening synovitis, fever (39°C), and new lumbar spine pain. Sulfasalazine and methotrexate were discontinued due to new transaminitis (aspartate aminotransferase 105 U/L (normal: 0–37 U/L); alanine aminotransferase 114 U/L (normal: 0–55 U/L)). ESR was elevated at 124 mm/hr and C-reactive protein at 170 mg/L. Right ankle aspiration was performed, followed by a methylprednisolone injection due to severe pain. The synovial fluid sample was inadequate for gram stain, and the culture was negative. She then received intravenous methylprednisolone, 250 mg every 24 hours for 2 days without improvement.
test_results: Repeated blood culture grew Streptobacillus moniliformis in the anaerobic flask.
