case_report: A 22-year-old woman reported experiencing intense pain in both hip joints, difficulty walking, and deformities in her hands, elbows, and spine. These issues began at age 6 with pain and stiffness in her fingers. She had been treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and methotrexate 15 mg weekly for the past 2 years. Her condition worsened over time, leading to increased deformities in her fingers, elbows, spine, and hip joints. There was no similar symptomatology among her immediate family members, although there was a family history of short stature and spinal deformities on her maternal side, with limited details available. Physical examination revealed normal facial features, a height of 136 cm, an upper segment (head to pubis) of 62 cm, a lower segment (pubis to heel) of 74 cm, and an arm span of 149 cm. She exhibited mild kyphosis of the thoracic spine and lumbar list due to hip joint contracture and pelvic tilt, without structural scoliosis. Flexion deformities were noted in the distal interphalangeal joints of the hands and elbows, along with hallux valgus deformities of the great toes. Movements of both shoulders and hips were painful and restricted. She had an antalgic gait and had been bedridden for the past 3 months due to worsening hip pain. The true length of the right lower limb was 96 cm and the left was 98 cm, with a limb length discrepancy of 1 cm. Her Harris hip score was 21. Inflammatory markers, including rheumatoid factor, anticyclic citrullinated peptide, and antinuclear antibody, were negative. Bone mineral profile and thyroid function tests were normal.
test_results: Anteroposterior X-ray of the hip joint showed severe arthritic changes with a reduction of bilateral femoroacetabular joint spaces (right >left) and subchondral sclerosis. The femoral neck was short and head mushroom shaped. X-ray of the hands revealed periarticular osteoporosis, a notable narrowing of the joint spaces of proximal interphalangeal and distal interphalangeal joints, and osseous enlargement of the base of the metacarpal, proximal, and distal phalangeal bones. In the lateral vertebral radiograph of the lumbar spine, there was generalized osteopenia. Platyspondyly and hyperostosis on the posterior two-thirds of end plates giving rise to a heaped-up or hump-shaped appearance was noted. Platyspondyly and Schmorl’s nodes were also noted on the magnetic resonance imaging of the spine.
diagnosis: Spondyloepiphyseal Dysplasia Tarda with Progressive Arthropathy

case_report: A 12-year-old girl, born to healthy eastern Chinese parents after a normal pregnancy, had a birth length of 51 cm. She was referred to our hospital for further evaluation and treatment. There was no family history of endocrine or musculoskeletal issues. At the age of 6, her parents observed unequal leg lengths, and imaging showed coxa plana. By age 9, she exhibited an abnormal gait and limping, with limited rotation function in the right leg. She underwent right hip arthroplasty and resection of cartilago acetabularis at another hospital, and postoperative pathology indicated chronic synovitis. Six months post-surgery, her parents noticed a warm lump in the left femoribus internus, and her left leg's flexion-extension function was restricted. Physical examination showed a height of 138 cm, normal intellectual development, and normal hearing. She had brachydactyly, bilateral skewfoot, and lumbosacral scoliosis, with limited movement in both hips. She did not have a cleft palate, cephalofacial deformities, or respiratory insufficiency. Routine analysis ruled out common skeletal dysplasia, thyroid, growth hormone disorders, and immunopathies. Bone metabolism was found to be normal.
test_results: Radiography revealed coxa plana. Radiological documentation at the ages of 7 and 12 years revealed hip dysplasia with the following deformities: short femoral necks, flattened and irregular femoral heads, and early closure of epiphysis. Spinal radiographs at the ages of 11 and 12 years confirmed evolving scoliosis, which appeared to be structural vertebral deformity. Hand radiographs confirmed the brachydactyly and significantly flattened articular surface. The metacarpi and phalanges were mild shorten.

case_report: A 14-year-old female presented with diffuse abdominal pain, distention, and vomiting, which began suddenly three days prior to her clinic visit. There was no prior history of illness. The abdominal pain was not related to meals. Nausea and vomiting were also reported. She was admitted to the Gastroenterology Ward for further evaluation. Her past medical history was unremarkable, and her family history revealed non-consanguineous parents and a mother with epilepsy. On physical examination, she exhibited a puffy face and an enlarged thyroid gland palpable in the neck. Vital signs were normal. Lung examination was clear, and heart sounds were normal. The abdomen was distended with shifting dullness indicative of ascites, but no organomegalies were noted. Extremities were normal without edema or deformities. Her pubertal development was appropriate for her age (Stage II Pubic and III Tanner), but her bone age was 10 years, which is delayed compared to her chronological age. Routine laboratory data, including FSH and LH levels, were within normal limits. Tumor marker tests showed a significant elevation in serum CA-125 levels (105.4 u/ml), while CEA levels were normal.
test_results: Thyroid function tests revealed very marked elevation of TSH -more than 100 mu/L, T4 and T3 depicted very low levels, 0.5 mu/L for T3 and 25 mu/L for T4 respectively. Abdomino-pelvic ultrasound and CT scan showed a cystic mass with a diameter of 40×45 mm located at the left lower quadrant (LLQ) which originated from the left ovary. The uterus was pubertal size (55×21 mm) with normal endometrial echo. Moderate free fluid was present in the peritoneal cavity. Liver, gallbladder, spleen, pancreas and kidneys were normal in structure and echo.

case_report: A 3-year-old male presented with a 1-month history of weakness and elevated CPK (26,123 U/L). The patient was an only child, born via vaginal delivery at 41 weeks gestation to a 34-year-old mother who had an uneventful pregnancy and adequate prenatal care. Prenatal genetic evaluations included maternal cystic fibrosis, spinal muscular atrophy, and fragile X testing which were normal. Family history was negative for relatives with developmental delay, muscle weakness, or cardiomyopathy. Both parents originated from the same village in India and reported no known consanguinity. The patient had reached appropriate developmental milestones by 2 years of age, when he developed speech regression. Audiology and ophthalmology examinations were normal. He exhibited hand-flapping, decreased eye contact, nervousness around other children, and difficulty with transitions. He had unstable and weak knees and occasionally walked on his toes. He had markedly elevated CPK (27,209 U/L), LDH (1346 U/L) and elevated liver enzymes (AST 422 U/L, ALT 386 U/L). Kidney function was normal, and urinalysis was normal. A liver ultrasound and autoimmune hepatitis workup were negative. The neurologic evaluation was significant for a slightly wide base gait and knees intermittently unsteady, with normal tone. Reflexes and gross motor strength assessment were limited due to poor cooperation. An echocardiogram was within normal measurements. He was on the 40th and 34th percentile for his weight and height, respectively. He was non-verbal, mostly not cooperative, but consolable with his parents. He had a posteriorly rotated left ear and prominent ears with no other dysmorphic features. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. Mild calf pseudohypertrophy was noted bilaterally. When rising from a sitting position on the floor, he demonstrated a unilateral positive Gowers’ sign. An accurate assessment of strength was difficult because of poor cooperation; he appeared weak in the lower limbs with a wobbly and unstable gait. Neuropsychiatric evaluation by a developmental pediatrician revealed persistent deficits in communication with a vocabulary consisting of very few words, unintelligible speech, and frequent echolalia. Social interaction was deemed poor. He had restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviors, and stereotypic hand movements. He met the criteria for autism spectrum disorder (ASD). While he had symptoms associated with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), the patient did not meet the criteria for ADHD diagnosis.
test_results: The Comprehensive Muscular Dystrophy Panel identified homozygous pathogenic missense variants in the SGCA gene, namely c.229C>T (p.Arg77Cys).

case_report: A 24-year-old female presented with gingival enlargement. She was born as one of twin females after a full-term, uncomplicated pregnancy. Her parents, aged 32 and 34 at conception, are healthy nonconsanguineous Indian individuals. Clinical examination showed enlargement of the maxillary and mandibular gingiva, including the hard palate, partially or completely covering the crowns of maxillary posterior teeth. Multiple carious teeth were noted, along with prominent labial fullness on extraoral examination. Additional findings included mild mental retardation, hirsutism, large cartilaginous parts of the ears and nose, dysplastic fingernails, aplasia of nails on the last two toes of both feet, and pes cavus deformity. Preoperative radiographs indicated an abnormal position of maxillary posterior teeth. Examination of her twin sister, mother, and father showed no abnormalities. Radiographic examination of the foot revealed hypoplastic distal phalanges of the fourth and fifth toes. No abnormalities were found in cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal, ophthalmologic, and blood examinations. The liver was normal in size, and the spleen was not palpable. Informed consent was obtained from all participants included in the case report.
test_results: Histopathological examination of excised tissues revealed an acanthotic, nonkeratinized, stratified squamous epithelium, with elongated rete pegs. Beneath the epithelium, there were dense bundles of collagenous fibrous tissue.

case_report: An eight-year-old Saudi girl arrived at the emergency department with a one-week history of cough and worsening cyanosis. She had a history of hepatosplenomegaly since infancy, but no definitive diagnosis was made. She was previously referred to a tertiary hospital for further investigations, but her family discharged her against medical advice, resulting in an eight-year loss of follow-up. The patient was born at term via spontaneous vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 2000 grams. The mother reported a 14-day neonatal intensive care unit admission for intrauterine growth restriction, during which splenomegaly and thrombocytopenia were noted. An echocardiography performed at that time showed congenital heart disease, but no further details were available. Over the years, the patient had multiple admissions for anemia and thrombocytopenia, managed with blood and platelet transfusions. No surgeries were performed. Family history revealed non-consanguineous parents with five other healthy siblings, one of whom had minimal dysmorphism but was clinically stable. Two cousins had undergone liver transplantation for unspecified reasons. On examination, the patient appeared underweight with dysmorphic features including a triangular face, frontal bossing, small chin, thin lips, and a wide mouth. She was conscious, oriented, and not in distress. Physical examination revealed central cyanosis, grade 4 digital clubbing, dry skin, multiple spider naevi over the cheeks, and dilated neck veins. Vital signs were: heart rate 92/min; respiratory rate 25/min; blood pressure 104/69 mmHg; temperature 36.5 °C; peripheral oxygen saturation 68% sitting and 80% supine, increasing to 87% with a 10-liter oxygen mask. She weighed 19 kg (below the third centile) and was 130 cm tall (at the fifth centile). Pulmonary examination showed good breath sounds bilaterally. Cardiovascular examination revealed a systolic murmur at the aortic area with normal first and second heart sounds. The abdomen was mildly distended with non-tender, firm hepatomegaly (18 cm span) and massive splenomegaly (8 cm below the costal margin). No ascites were noted. Central nervous system examination showed an active normal gait with a Glasgow coma scale of 15/15. Laboratory studies included complete blood count (CBC), coagulation tests, liver function tests, and lipid levels. Venous blood gas analysis indicated hypocapnic alkalosis (blood pH: 7.46, PCO2: 27.8 mmHg, PO2: 77 mmHg, HCO3-: 21.8 mEq/L). Serum vitamin D 25 (OH) level was 18 ng/dL (normal range: 20-50 ng/mL). Other tests were within reference ranges, including electrolytes, renal function tests, thyroid testing, blood glucose (97 mg/dL), ammonia (66 ug/dL; reference range 31-123 ug/dL), lactate (0.9 mmol/L; reference range 0.5-2.2 mmol/L), alpha-fetoprotein (6.3 ng/mL; reference range: 1.09-8.04 ng/mL), and normal glucocerebrosidase enzyme activity. Radiological investigations included a chest x-ray showing bilateral pulmonary hyperinflation without cardiomegaly. Abdominal ultrasound revealed an enlarged liver with a markedly prominent caudate lobe, no focal lesions, and no gallbladder or biliary tract anomalies. The spleen was hypertrophied, measuring about 13 cm in length. The kidneys appeared normal. Due to the patient's uncooperativeness, liver vasculature assessment on ultrasound was not possible. Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis showed severe hepatomegaly with irregular liver contours consistent with parenchymal liver disease, a disproportionately large caudate lobe, a small hypodense focal lesion (7 mm in segment 7), and signs of portal hypertension including severe congestive splenomegaly, portosystemic shunt to the left renal vein, and minimal free fluid in the pelvis. Chest computed tomography showed unremarkable lungs. An echocardiogram was performed without notable anomalies and was followed by an agitated saline transthoracic echocardiography, which twice confirmed the presence of an arteriovenous malformation.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing identified a homozygous frameshift variant in the TALDO1 gene, c.793del, p.Gln265fs.
diagnosis: Transaldolase Deficiency  complicated by Hepatopulmonary Syndrome

case_report: An 83-year-old Caucasian male, farmer, presented with sudden onset pain and redness in his right eye. He had no history of ocular trauma or previous ocular surgery, and no relevant family history or ophthalmological conditions. He was not on any topical or systemic medication. The patient had been known to the clinic for 3 months with a hypermature cataract in the right eye and a mature cataract in the left eye. He was scheduled for cataract extraction in the left eye first, followed by the right eye. During the preoperative consultation for the left eye cataract surgery, he reported acute ocular pain and photophobia in the right eye that began a few days prior. Clinical examination showed visual acuity of light perception in the right eye and counting fingers in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was 50 mmHg in the right eye and 13 mmHg in the left eye. Slit lamp biomicroscopy of the right eye revealed circumciliary congestion, diffuse corneal edema, pseudohypopyon, complete lens opacification, and suspended white particles in the anterior chamber and pupillary area.
test_results: The ultrasonography for both eyes revealed no pathological changes except for a hyper-reflective band between the middle and posterior third of the vitreous in the right eye.

case_report: Patient 1, a boy aged 7 years and 10 months, is the first child of a healthy and consanguineous Arab couple (first-degree paternal cousins). He was born at 40 weeks gestation via natural delivery following a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios and decreased fetal movements. His birth weight was 2.8 kg (15th percentile). At birth, he exhibited bilateral generalized arthrogryposis with elbow and knee flexion contractures, right foot talipes equinovarus, left foot vertical talipes, inguinal hernia, bilateral cryptorchidism, and hypotonia. A brain MRI at 6 months of age was normal. During infancy, he experienced poor feeding, food-swallowing difficulties, and recurrent respiratory infections. Intensive physiotherapy in early life reduced upper limb arthrogryposis. Lower limb arthrogryposis and talipes were managed with serial casts and surgical interventions, enabling independent walking at 20 months. At 18 months, his growth parameters were: weight, 9 kg (3rd percentile); height, 81 cm (15th percentile); and head circumference, 46 cm (15th percentile). Observed craniofacial features included a wide forehead, bitemporal narrowing, hypertelorism, bilateral epicanthus, divergent strabismus, a small depressed nasal bridge, a small nose, a short columella, anteverted nares, a smooth and long philtrum, micrognathia, a myopathic facial appearance with facial muscle weakness, a wide and opened mouth with an everted lower lip, a high arched palate, small and anteriorly rotated ears with a smooth helix and antihelix, and anterior and uplifted ear lobules. Additional findings included generalized muscle weakness, dropped shoulders, overlapping second and third toes bilaterally, dysphagia, generalized hypotonia, and delays in motor and speech development. A Cytoscan HD SNP array reported a normal result of arr (1-22) x2, (XY) x1 but detected larger homozygous regions of 83.9 Mb (3% from the autosomal genome). Sequencing of the fukutin gene (FKTN) was normal.
test_results: WES reported a homozygous missense variant of uncertain significance in NEB, NM_001271208.1:c.11969A>C (p.(Asp3990Ala)), and a pathogenic heterozygous missense mutation in the cyclic adenosine monophosphate response element binding protein (CREBBP) gene, NM_004380.2:c.5600G>A (p.(Arg1867Gln). Both parents were confirmed as carriers of the NEB gene variant, while the CREBBP gene variant was identified in the healthy father.

case_report: A 26-month-old male was brought to a tertiary care center on October 11, 2017, for evaluation of genu varum. He was born via cesarean section at 38 weeks of gestation, weighing 3.2 kg, to non-consanguineous Korean parents. Prenatal screening tests showed no abnormalities, and there was no intrauterine growth retardation. The patient had no cardiovascular issues during infancy and exhibited age-appropriate psychomotor development. Bowed legs were noted at 12 months, coinciding with the onset of walking. Upon examination, the patient had a short stature with a height of 79.3 cm (-2.99 SDS) and a weight of 11.4 kg (-0.83 SDS). Physical examination identified significant varus deformities in both lower extremities and a waddling gait. There were no signs of craniotabes or rachitic rosary. Laboratory tests showed low serum phosphorus (2.6 mg/dL, reference range 4.1-6.2 mg/dL), elevated serum alkaline phosphatase (472 IU/L, reference range 39-117 IU/L), and normal serum calcium (9.5 mg/dL, reference range 8.0-10.5 mg/dL). Levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D (32.9 ng/mL, reference range 30-100 ng/mL) and intact parathyroid hormone (40.55 pg/mL, reference range 15.0-65.0 pg/mL) were within normal limits. The patient exhibited renal phosphate wasting, with decreased tubular resorption of phosphate (TRP; 83.3%, reference range ≥ 85%) and decreased tubular maximum reabsorption of phosphate per unit volume of glomerular filtration rate (TmP/GFR; 2.16 mg/dL, reference range 2.9-6.5 mg/dL). There was no hypercalciuria. X-ray imaging of the lower extremities revealed bilateral tibia vara with metaphyseal beaking and flaring of the proximal tibia, distal tibia, and distal femur. The patient was prescribed 250 mg of oral phosphate salts (21.9 mg/kg/day) and 0.25 mcg of calcitriol (0.02 mcg/kg/day).
test_results: We identified a homozygous nonsense pathogenic variant in exon 7 of the ENPP1 gene, c.783C>G (p.Tyr261*). Segregation analysis showed that his parents and sister were heterozygous from the same variants.

case_report: A 38-year-old male presented with swelling in the right cheek, pain, and nasal discharge persisting for 15 days. He had no history of systemic diseases. The patient had previously been examined by an otolaryngologist and was prescribed antibiotics. Due to lack of improvement, he was referred to our clinic to investigate a potential dental origin. An orthopantomography provided by the patient showed displacement of the upper third molar into the maxillary sinus due to pressure from a cyst. A computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a cystic lesion involving the bone. The cyst and the displaced third molar were surgically removed under local anesthesia (Articain 40/0.005 mg/ml). Postoperative treatment included Amoxicillin 875mg/clavulanic acid 125mg for seven days and Ibuprofen 600mg three times daily for pain management, as needed. The cystic capsule was sent for further examination, which identified it as a dentigerous cyst with inflammation. No postoperative complications were observed, and the patient remained symptom-free during a seven-month follow-up period. Follow-up orthopantomography at seven months post-surgery showed significant bone occupation in the maxillary sinus, prompting a referral for additional imaging.
test_results: This was confirmed by a biopsy carried out by a maxillofacial surgeon and by histopathological examination.

case_report: A 45-year-old Greek female, measuring 168 cm in height and weighing 62 kg, presented with a history of thrombocytopenia identified 26 years ago following the appearance of bruises and petechiae on her legs. She has no significant medical or family history, does not smoke, and denies any drug or alcohol use. She is a mother of two daughters. Laboratory findings consistently showed low platelet counts (PLT: 98,000/mm3). She tested positive for HbsAg, anti-HBc, and anti-HBe, with a normal myelogram. Follow-up tests over the years indicated stable HBV status, normal liver function tests (LFTs), and low PCR HBV DNA levels, with a maximum recorded level of 7.4 × 102 IU/ML. Additionally, AFP levels have been persistently elevated, ranging from 42 to 56 ng/ml since April 2004.
test_results: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed gastric varices type II without signs of bleeding. Repeating imaging tests such as CT, MRI scanning, Doppler ultrasound and MR angiography confirmed the absence of portal or splenic vein thrombosis. Histological evaluation of liver biopsy concluded that the overall histological findings were compatible with inactive HBV carrier state without evidence of any excess inflammation or features suggesting fibrosis or cirrhosis. Immunohistochemistry confirmed HbsAg presence and HbcAg absence. The reticulin stain was negative.

case_report: A 36-year-old male, active smoker with no significant medical history and a family history of cancer in the mother (type unknown), presented with right-sided chest pain for 3 months, worsening over the past 3 weeks. Initially, he visited the emergency department 3 months ago when the pain began and was discharged after pain relief with ibuprofen. A chest x-ray (CXR) at that time was clear. On current presentation, vital signs were normal. Physical examination revealed decreased breath sounds over the right lung; other findings were unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed platelets at 729,000/µL, international normalized ratio of 1.46, prothrombin time of 16.5 seconds, partial thromboplastin time of 38.8 seconds, and D-dimer at 995 ng/mL. The CXR indicated a large right-sided pleural effusion. A computed tomography (CT) angiogram of the chest revealed multiple right-sided extra-pleural or pleural-based masses with a large right pleural effusion, masses eroding adjacent ribs, lateral margin of the T6 vertebral body, possibly involving the adjacent neural foramen, and partially extending through intercostal spaces. A significant portion of the mass was indenting the heart and displacing it to the left, with potential cardiac invasion. The patient underwent right-sided thoracentesis. Pleural fluid cytology indicated severe mixed acute and chronic inflammation with scattered uninucleate epithelioid-type histiocytic cells and an isolated large Langhans-type multinucleated histiocytic cell, suggestive of a granulomatous inflammatory process. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and cervical/thoracic/lumbar spine and CT of the abdomen/pelvis were performed for staging. The MRI of the brain and cervical/lumbar spine were negative for metastases. The MRI of the thoracic spine showed a right paraspinal soft tissue mass with direct invasion of the right side of the T6 vertebral body. CT of the abdomen/pelvis with intravenous and oral contrast with liver protocol showed porta hepatis lymphadenopathy measuring 3.1 cm. No neurosurgical intervention was performed as there were no clinical or radiological signs of cord compression. An echocardiogram revealed a large posterior extracardiac mass compressing both atria with a small pericardial effusion, primarily along the right ventricular free wall, with diastolic invagination of the right ventricular free wall.
test_results: The pathology showed invasive poorly differentiated carcinoma and a high grade of uncertain histogenesis. Immunohistochemistry was positive for EPCAM (MOC 31), AE-1/AE-3, CAM5.2 (focally), DIM staining with p40 (negative CK5/6), synaptophysin, and CDX2 (focally) and negative for chromogranin A, CD56, CK7, CK20, TTF-1, NAPSIN A, GATA-3, S-100, SOX-10, and PAX8. Ki67 was 70%-80%, and the programmed death ligand (PDL)-1 tumor proportion score was 45%-50%.

case_report: A 15-month-old female child from Dire-Dawa, Ethiopia, presented with a regression of developmental milestones and truncal ataxia starting at 11 months of age, following a febrile illness one month prior. Initially, she was diagnosed with pneumonia during the febrile illness and showed improvement after treatment. One month later, she developed upper extremity weakness, truncal ataxia, and increasing difficulty reaching for objects. Up to 10 months of age, her growth and development were normal, but she then progressively regressed in her developmental milestones. There is no history of seizures, loss of consciousness, or prior neurological illness. She was born after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, had a normal neonatal period, and is immunized according to the EPI schedule. Physical examination revealed normal vital signs and anthropometric measurements, including a head circumference of 48 cm. No dysmorphic features were noted. Neurologic examination showed that she was conscious, with midsized, reactive pupils bilaterally. Optic disc and retina assessments were normal bilaterally, and she could move her eyes in all directions. Limb power was observed to be 3/5 in all extremities, with bilateral hyperreflexia, truncal ataxia, and dysmetria. No sensory loss was detected. Laboratory blood work results were within normal ranges.
test_results: MRI of her brain revealed diffuse white matter abnormality.

case_report: A 2-year-old boy was admitted to our center due to recurrent episodes of pneumonia, having been hospitalized three times in the past six months. The primary symptom observed was a persistent cough. The child was unable to expectorate sputum due to his young age, and there was no presence of yellow-greenish sputum during the pneumonia episodes. Additionally, there were no signs of cyanosis, respiratory distress, or jaundice. Initial chest x-ray revealed chronic inflammatory changes on the right side. Treatment with antibiotics and drug-aerosol inhalation alleviated the cough symptoms. Chest CT scans indicated multiple patchy hyperdense areas in both lungs. A 3D-CT reconstruction identified a conical cleft-like protrusion on the wall of the right main bronchus, with the end pointing downward.
test_results: Yellow secretions attached to the glottis and trachea. An abnormal opening was found at the level of the tracheal carina, and yellow secretions could be seen at the opening. The contrast medium is connected to the left hepatic duct through the esophageal hiatus, and the contrast medium sequentially fills the left intrahepatic bile duct, the right intrahepatic bile duct, the common hepatic duct, the common bile duct, the gallbladder, and the duodenum. No other biliary malformation was found. The total bile acid was found to be 306.20 μmol/L.

case_report: The patient is a 38-year-old white female with a history of severe calcific aortic stenosis and calcified mitral valve. She has experienced premature aging and has a family history of similar features. Her early development was normal. In her 20s, she noticed greying of her hair, followed by progressive fatigue and exertional dyspnea. She has been under regular cardiovascular follow-up, seeing the same cardiologist as several family members. At 35, she was referred to Mayo Clinic for management of her symptomatic valve disease. Her clinical presentation included a low BMI of 16.7, with a height of 173 cm and weight of 50 kg. An echocardiogram revealed severe aortic stenosis with a mean gradient of 51 mmHg, moderate mitral stenosis with a mean gradient of 6 mmHg, and mild-to-moderate mitral regurgitation. Preoperative CT showed extensive calcification of the aortic valve extending into the left ventricular outflow tract and the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve, with no significant coronary artery disease. She underwent mitral and aortic valve replacement, tricuspid valve repair, and patent foramen ovale closure at 35. There was no evidence of lipodystrophy, muscle weakness, or cutaneous findings. Her family history includes multiple members with similar phenotypes, including her grandmother, mother, and uncles. Her maternal grandmother passed away at 32, with an autopsy revealing heavily calcified mitral and aortic valves with friable verrucous vegetations. Genetic testing on some affected family members previously identified a variant of uncertain significance in the LMNA gene, but the patient was not included in this testing.
test_results: She subsequently underwent clinical exome sequence analysis at the age of 35 by GeneDx, which reported the same LMNA variant. This variant was initially classified as a Variant of Uncertain Significance (VUS) because it was absent from the gnomAD database (PM2_supp), and in silico predictions indicated uncertainty (REVEL 0.35). The variant was further classified as likely pathogenic, supported by segregation studies (PP1_strong, PM2_supp, PP4, and PS3_supp).

case_report: A one-year-old girl was examined by a dermatologist in 2016 due to dense yellow-orange formations on the knee joints, elbow joints, and gluteal folds. Laboratory tests revealed hypercholesterolemia with a maximum total cholesterol level of 16.0 mmol/L. Echocardiography showed no structural or hemodynamic abnormalities. Abdominal ultrasound indicated no hepatosplenomegaly or fatty liver. Thrombocytopenia was not present. Extracranial color triplex scanning of the brachiocephalic arteries was not performed. Both parents had no dyslipidemia or signs of premature coronary artery disease. Plasmapheresis was conducted but did not show marked efficiency.
test_results: Targeted sequencing revealed that the patient was homozygous for a missense variant in the ABCG8 gene rs769576789 NM_022437.3:c.1715T>C p.(Leu572Pro). These variants were confirmed by Sanger sequencing, and parents were heterozygous.

case_report: A 61-year-old Chinese male with a history of grade 1 hypertension reported experiencing right lower abdominal distention and intermittent upper abdominal pain for a duration of 4 months. Laboratory tests included serum creatinine (SCr), 24-hour 3-methyl-4-hydroxymandelic acid (VMA), adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), sex hormone screening, plasma cortisol rhythm, and renin–angiotensin II–aldosterone system (RAAS) function in both upright and recumbent positions.
test_results: Ultrasonography showed a 4.4 cm × 3.4 cm hypoechoic nodule with clear boundaries and internal cord-like hyperechoic mass in the right hilum. Contrast-enhanced CT scan showed a round soft tissue nodule shadow in the right renal hilum with clear boundaries, uneven enhancement and a filling defect in the renal vein cavity. MRI showed a 4.2 × 3.2 × 3.5 cm mass with clear boundaries, slightly high DWI signal and significantly low ADC value.
diagnosis: Leiomyosarcoma originating from the renal vein

case_report: The patient is a 9-year-old boy who was first seen at the neurology department at 6 years old. He had been previously admitted to the gastroenterology ward due to ongoing nausea and uncontrollable vomiting, with a notable weight loss of approximately 6 kg over the prior 2 months. Gastroenterological evaluations, including abdominal ultrasound, barium swallow test, and upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, showed normal results. At 40 days old, he experienced non-febrile, infrequent multifocal motor seizures with fixed upward gaze and head movements, particularly during breastfeeding. Electroencephalogram (EEG) revealed frequent abnormal scattered epileptiform discharges, and phenobarbital was prescribed, resulting in seizure control. The medication was discontinued at 16 months, and he exhibited normal physical growth and neurological development until age six. He occasionally vomited once or twice a month without a clear cause, and proton pump inhibitors provided some improvement. He was born at 38 weeks gestation via an uneventful cesarean section to a nonconsanguineous family, with a birth weight of 3,050 g (z score = 0) and head circumference of 37.0 cm (z score = 2). He was admitted for prolonged physiologic jaundice in the first 2 weeks of life, with an indirect bilirubin level of 14 mg/dL, which resolved with phototherapy. His father and uncle had head circumferences above 2 standard deviations for their age but no clinical symptoms. At 6 years old, he experienced status epilepticus with generalized atonic seizures, followed by severe occasional projectile vomiting and recurrent daily nausea, particularly in the early morning and sometimes at midnight. Seizures were managed with sodium valproate and levetiracetam. He lost 6.0 kg (from 19.0 to 13.0 kg) over the next 2 months. At his first visit at this age, he had normal developmental milestones in speech, motor skills, and cognition. His weight was 13.0 kg (z score = -1) and head circumference was 52.5 cm (z score = 2). Ophthalmic examination showed normal gaze and pupil reaction to light. There was no palatal myoclonus, but nasal tone speech was noted. He had a weak gag reflex and significant drooling. Other cranial nerve examinations were normal. Knee deep tendon reflexes were exaggerated (3+), while others were normal (2+). Plantar reflexes were bilaterally downward. Gross motor function was rated 1 out of 5 (1/5) on the Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) scale. Basic biochemical and metabolic tests, including thyroid and liver function tests, serum ammonia and lactate, urine organic acids profile, metabolic screen test (MS/MS), acylcarnitine profile, and serum amino acids chromatography (HPLC), were normal. A wrist X-ray was consistent with his chronological age.
test_results: The first MRI at the age of 6 years revealed faint bifrontal confluent deep and periventricular white matter signal changes, bilateral caudate nucleus involvement, significantly high in T2-W and low in T1-W images with garland and cystic changes around the tip of the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles, especially the left side. In addition, a hyperintensity tumefactive lesion was identified in the brain stem area around the floor of the fourth ventricle and area postrema. No restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and apparent diffusion coefficient map sequences were detected. Post-contrast T1-W images showed contrast enhancement in brain stem lesions. The repeated brain MRI at age of 8 years showed enlargement of the lesion in the area postrema extending to posterior pons and involvement of bilateral middle cerebellar peduncles and dentate nuclei. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) detected a heterozygous mutation, c.262 C > T; R88C in the exon 1 of the Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein (GFAP). Sanger sequencing confirmed that this mutation is de novo.

case_report: This three-year-old boy was born at term (38 + 5 weeks) with a birth weight of 3.75 kg to healthy Han-Chinese parents (29 years) of non-consanguineous marriage. Neither parent has a family history of genetic disease. At the age of 2 months, his parents observed he did not make eye contact. Subsequently, the boy was found to have cataracts and nystagmus and underwent binocular lens extraction. His teeth began to grow at 9 months, and caries developed at 2 years old. The auricles of both ears were small, and the contour was abnormally folded, but the hearing was normal. He also had mild speech delay and dysarthria. His intelligence and athletic ability were clearly behind his peers. He had problems with cognitive functioning, such as attention and learning. He started to stand without support at 15 months and walked without assistance at 18 months. His balance function and posture stability were also not good. Routine hematologic and biochemical tests were within the normal range except for high levels of total cholesterol (7.97 mmol/L) and low-density lipoprotein (4.94 mmol/L).
test_results: The Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at aged 2 years did not find any impairment. The X-ray at 2 years suggested knee valgus, small, irregular and cracked femoral epiphyseal ossification center.

case_report: A 47-year-old female with hypertension presented to Ochsner Medical Center Clinic seeking recommendations for managing chronic pain. Her symptoms began in 2011 with weight gain and the formation of tender lipomas in her upper and lower extremities. At that time, she experienced achy, whole-body pains lasting several days, with flare-ups occurring monthly. She had a history of steady weight gain from 180 pounds in 2006 to 217 pounds in 2011. In 2011, she underwent an excisional procedure to remove an 8x10 millimeter mass in her left upper arm, which was identified as a benign lipoma. That same year, imaging of her left and right upper arms revealed multiple well-circumscribed hyperechoic nodules bilaterally, with the largest measuring 1 cm in diameter. The final interpretation indicated multiple areas of fat necrosis. Additionally, the patient was offered participation in a trial evaluating thermogenic agents but declined.
test_results: In 2011 she had an excisional biopsy of an 8x10 millimeter mass in her left upper arm and was diagnosed with benign lipoma. That year, she also had an ultrasound of her left and right upper arms demonstrating many well circumscribed hyperechoic nodules bilaterally, with the largest measuring 1cm in diameter. The final reading was consistent with multiple fat necrosis.

case_report: A 36-year-old woman, in her third pregnancy, underwent preoperative tests at 36 weeks of gestation, including blood collection, chest X-ray, and electrocardiography, which showed no significant findings. At 37 weeks and 4 days of gestation, she had an elective caesarean section due to a previous caesarean section. The surgery lasted 34 minutes with an estimated blood loss of 1010 mL, including amniotic fluid. The patient experienced no complications during or after the surgery and was discharged 6 days later. On the 18th day postoperatively, she presented with breathing difficulty and was examined urgently. She had conceived naturally and had a favorable pregnancy progression. Her first pregnancy at 28 years ended in abortion, and her second at 30 years ended with an elective caesarean section due to fetal malpresentation. She had no significant personal or family medical history. During admission, she was 154.5 cm tall, weighed 50.0 kg (non-pregnant weight: 42.0 kg), had a body surface area of 1.46 m2, was fully conscious, with a blood pressure of 123/78 mmHg, a pulse rate of 99/min, and SpO2 of 91% on room air in a supine position. Chest auscultation revealed systolic regurgitant murmurs at Levine IV at the cardiac apex with regular heartbeats. Bilateral pedal edema was noted. The brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) level was 642.5 pg/mL (normal range: ≤ 18.4). Other blood tests were unremarkable. Chest X-ray showed a cardiothoracic ratio of 55% and bilateral pleural effusion. Electrocardiography indicated a pulse rate of 94/min, sinus rhythm, no ST-segment abnormalities, and slight right axis deviation. The ejection fraction (EF) was 44.6% in the systemic circulation ventricle, with a diffuse decrease in wall motion. The systemic circulation ventricular diameter was 49.8 mm in diastole and 41.6 mm in systole, indicating slight enlargement. Severe atrioventricular valve regurgitation was observed in the systemic circulation atrioventricular valve (tricuspid valve).
test_results: On contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography (CT), the aorta was found to have the shape of a rough adductor muscle starting from the anatomical right ventricle, and the pulmonary artery started from the anatomical left ventricle.
diagnosis: Corrected Transposition of the Great Arteries
Orpha_name: Congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries

case_report: The patient is a 2-year-old male child born to nonconsanguineous parents by Lower Segment Caesarean Section from Orissa. His birth weight was 2.8 kg, and there were no reports of neonatal jaundice, hypoxia, ischemia, or intracerebral hematomas. The child experienced seizures within the first 2 hours of delivery, presenting as both left focal and generalized tonic–clonic seizures. The frequency of seizures was approximately 8–10 episodes per day. The child was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit for 30 days, but the seizures persisted. The child received treatment with phenobarbitone, levetiracetam, diphenylhydantoin, sodium valproate, steroids, and adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH). At the age of 2 years, the child was bedbound and only making cooing sounds. He exhibited auditory startle responses and continued to have seizures about 30–40 times a day. Routine investigations yielded negative results.
test_results: Urine chromatogram showed a mild increase in succinic acid, adipic acid, and ethylmalonic acid. EEG showed diffuse delta activity. Computed tomography scan of the brain showed diffuse atrophy with relative sparing of the cerebellum.

case_report: A 5-year-old boy of Middle Eastern descent presented with skin lesions, abdominal distension, and red-colored urine. He was the second child of a first-cousin consanguineous marriage. The first child had died at birth due to cord strangulation. The patient was born at full term without antenatal care; delivery was normal, and the infant cried immediately after birth. His birth weight was 2200 g, and his head circumference was 33 cm with a wide anterior fontanel (10 × 7 cm). At birth, he exhibited poor suckling activity, reddish urine, and ecchymosis. His skin was pale without bleeding, jaundice, or fever. Physical examination revealed a parasternal soft pansystolic murmur, splenomegaly 6 cm below the costal margin (BCM), and a liver palpable 2 cm BCM. Ophthalmological examination showed bilaterally sloughing corneas, dry eyes, early lens opacity, and bilaterally hyperpigmented retinas. He was admitted to the hospital and treated with antibiotics, multiple blood transfusions, and l-thyroxine for 2–3 months without improvement. The family sought further investigations abroad. Initial tests included a complete blood count and thyroid function tests. A blood smear showed normocytic normochromic anemia; osmotic fragility test was normal; Coombs test was negative. Partial thromboplastin time (PTT), prothrombin time (PT), liver and renal function tests were normal. TORCH screen was negative; bone marrow aspiration was normal with no evidence of leukemia or myelofibrosis. Echocardiogram revealed a perimembranous ventricular septal defect (VSD). Abdominal ultrasound showed significant splenomegaly with a patent portal vein. DNA study indicated heterozygosity for alpha thalassemia. Tests ruled out Gaucher’s Disease and mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS). Ammonia and lactate levels were normal; serum ferritin level was elevated (449 mg/ml). Skeletal survey results were normal. The patient received regular blood transfusions (2–3 times per month) and an iron-chelating agent (Desferrioxamine). At 10 months, he showed increased abdominal distension and brownish-stained teeth, with persistent reddish urine. At 22 months, he developed vesiculobullous skin lesions in sun-exposed areas (face, hands, and feet), which left hypopigmented areas upon healing. At 30 months, blood transfusions were stopped due to improvement, but skin lesions progressed, and red urine and brown teeth persisted. Continued investigations showed elevated serum ferritin levels, turbid urine with more than two proteins, elevated urobilinogen levels, an RBC count of 10–12 cells/HPF, and numerous WBCs. Urine culture grew E. coli. Hemoglobin electrophoresis showed Hemoglobin AA, indicating normal adult hemoglobin. At age 5, the patient had worsening skin lesions, persistent red urine, and anemia. He came to our hospital for consultation.
test_results: Uroporphyrin I concentration = 28.1 mmol/ml (normal value range is 0–4); Coproporphyrin I concentration = 10.8 mmol/ml (normal value range is 0–6); Uroporphyrin I test in RBC = weakly positive; Heptacarboxyl porphyrin levels = 33.4 (normal value range is 0–2).

case_report: A 14-year-old male reported experiencing vision impairment in both eyes for the past 2 years. His visual acuity was measured at 20/80 in the right eye, which improved to 20/40 with a correction of −5.0 DS/−1.50 D Cyl at 180°, and 20/40 in the left eye, improving to 20/20 with a correction of −0.50 DS. There was no history of systemic illness or medication use. A diffuse slit lamp examination showed a mild papillary reaction in the palpebral conjunctiva of both eyes. The corneal examination revealed multiple subepithelial lines in a pseudovortex pattern extending from the inferior paracentral cornea, with some lines crossing the pupillary axis. These lines were more pronounced in the right eye. Additionally, isolated discrete white crumb-shaped opacities of varying sizes were observed in the anterior stroma of both corneas. The intervening corneal stroma was clear, and the peripheral cornea was unaffected. Optical section illumination confirmed the subepithelial location of the linear opacities and a slightly deeper anterior stromal location of the crumb-shaped opacities. The right eye exhibited mild corneal steeping in the inferior paracentral region, while the corneal curvature in the left eye appeared clinically normal. The corneal endothelium was normal in both eyes. Other anterior and posterior segment findings were unremarkable. The patient was the only child from a nonconsanguineous marriage. Slit lamp biomicroscopic examination of his mother and paternal grandfather showed no corneal abnormalities.
test_results: In vivo laser confocal microscopy revealed the subepithelial lesions as linear hyper-reflective “vertebra”- shaped silhouetted structures at a depth of 50–80 microns. The crumb-shaped opacities were denser, discrete, present in the region from 60 to 140 microns and more prominent in the right cornea. Spectral domain anterior segment optical coherence tomography confirmed the depth of the crumb opacities to 140 microns. Corneal topography of the right eye showed steepening in the vertical meridian which was more exaggerated in the inferior paracentral region. The maximum anterior curvature was 57.8 D around the 3 mm zone inferiorly. Optical pachymetry indicated a central corneal thickness of 450 microns. There was a significant elevation of the posterior float of the cornea. The Belin/Ambrósio Enhanced Ectasia display indicated keratoconus. Corneal topography of the left eye showed the maximum anterior curvature of 45.2 D around the 3 mm zone inferiorly and the central corneal thickness of 522 microns. Genetic analysis was performed using 5 ml of the peripheral blood. The coding sequence and splice site junctions of TGFBI (BIGH3) gene were amplified from the genomic DNA of the patient and controls, and the mutation was identified by direct DNA sequencing of the samples. One reported missense mutation p.Arg555Trp and three previously reported polymorphisms (p.Lue269Phe, p.Val327Val, and p.Phe540Phe) were observed.

case_report: A 78-year-old male arrived at the emergency room with complaints of a dry cough, fever reaching 38.5°C, and general malaise for the past month. He had previously consulted a general practitioner and was prescribed amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 7 days, which did not alleviate his symptoms. His medical history includes diabetes and arterial hypertension, managed with metformin 1000 mg twice daily and amlodipine 10 mg daily for the past 7 years. He does not consume alcohol and has a smoking history of 20 pack-years, having quit 30 years ago. He had no recent hospitalizations or medical procedures. On physical examination, he was febrile at 37.8°C and mildly lethargic but fully oriented. His arterial blood pressure was 115/75 mmHg, heart rate was 85 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation was 92%. Arterial blood gas analysis showed a partial oxygen pressure of 67 mmHg, CO2 at 32 mmHg, and a pH of 7.43. Auscultation revealed diffuse crackles over the mid- and lower-lung fields bilaterally. Laboratory tests indicated elevated white blood cell counts at 12,800 cells per μL, predominantly neutrophils at 78%, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 85 mm/h, and a C-reactive protein level of 8 mg/dL. Kidney, liver, and other biochemical parameters were within normal limits.
test_results: The patient then had a chest radiograph performed. The patient was started on antibiotics without clinical or laboratory improvement and a high-resolution CT (HRCT) scan was performed. Blood and sputum cultures were negative for bacteria and urine antigen tests for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila serogroup I were all negative. Serum immunology sent for testing of antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies were all negative. A bronchoscopy was then performed 3 days after the patient`s original admission. Apart from diffusely erythematous mucosa, no focal findings were seen on direct visualisation. BAL was performed at lingula and transbronchial lung biopsy (TBLB) was performed at the basal segments of the lower left lobe. BAL was negative for malignancy and cultures were negative for bacteria, nocardia, fungi and mycobacteria. BAL had increased cellularity, 26×106 total cells and a mixed cellularity pattern, with neutrophils accounting for 12%, eosinophils 8%, lymphocytes 16% and macrophages 64%. Perls, Oil Red O and Periodic acid–Schiff stains were all negative.

case_report: A 73-year-old male patient has had disseminated arciform and round patches since his first dermatology visit in 1999. Previous treatments included ketoconazole, topical terbinafine, ketoconazole, or ciclopirox olamine, which had no impact. During a visit in July 2011, he presented with ill-defined erythematous scaly papules and plaques on the trunk and upper limbs. Additionally, onycholysis, distal leukonychia, subungual hyperkeratosis, and onychorrexis were observed on the toenails.
test_results: A mycological examination demonstrated septate hyaline hyphae, and a positive culture for T. rubrum. Skin biopsy presented several hyphae within the stratum corneum. A subungual sample also demonstrated T. rubrum.

case_report: A 15-year-old male arrived at a local hospital experiencing fatigue, fever, abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting for several days. He mentioned having a severe viral illness about six weeks before his current symptoms. Laboratory tests in the emergency department showed low sodium levels and high thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). Other tests, including complete blood count, liver function tests, lactic acid, lipase, infectious mononucleosis screen, and creatine kinase levels, were normal. Imaging studies, including a chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasound, showed no abnormalities, and he was admitted for further care. Additional history indicated recent issues with gait stability and a change in skin color over the past few weeks. Physical examination revealed generalized pallor, a dusky gray skin tone, generalized abdominal tenderness, and tenderness in the right costovertebral angle.
test_results: Laboratory studies in the emergency department were significant for hyponatremia and an elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). Further laboratory evaluation revealed positive thyroid peroxidase antibody, elevated ACTH, cortisol levels nonresponsive to cosyntropin, and persistent hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. Direct renin level was elevated, and the aldosterone level was low. At outpatient follow-up, very long chain fatty acids were normal. The diabetes autoimmune test group was normal, but the TSH remained elevated with a normal T4. Follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone were normal, but tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A was elevated.

case_report: A 50-year-old female, working as a farmer, presented with multiple raised dark brown-purplish lesions on the lower back and both upper arms for three months. The lesions were not associated with itching or any other symptoms. She had a history of being treated for sun allergy with topical emollients by a local practitioner. A detailed skin examination showed symmetrical involvement of the distal three-fourths of both upper limbs, characterized by multiple violaceous and hyperpigmented plaques with distinctive hypopigmented borders. Similar lesions were observed on the lower back. The oral mucosa and nails were unaffected. Dermoscopic evaluation using DermLite 3N revealed fine reticulate white lines, diffuse brownish hyperpigmentation on a violaceous background. Routine blood tests were within normal limits.
test_results: Histopathological examination (4 mm punch biopsy) from one of the lesions showed a lichenoid reaction pattern characterized by degeneration of the basal layer of the epidermis and a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate obscuring the dermo-epidermal junction. There was a prominent lymphocytic infiltrate and pigmentary incontinence.

case_report: The patient, a 36-year-old male, has a height of 143 cm. He exhibited an abnormal gait starting at 1 year old, and hip dislocation was observed at that time. Significant growth delay was noted from the age of 13, and hip pain began at 25 years old, particularly after walking long distances. His vision, hearing, and cognitive functions are normal. Both parents are healthy and show no signs of skeletal or extra-skeletal abnormalities. During the initial visit, the patient's wife was pregnant. The study received approval from the Ethics Committee of Huzhou Maternity & Child Health Care Hospital, and all participants provided written informed consent.
test_results: X-ray films revealed flattened bilateral femoral heads, shortened femoral neck, flattened and narrowed articular surface of the lower femur and upper tibia.

case_report: The oldest sibling, an 8-year-old boy, presented with a best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 6/36 in the right eye and 6/24 in the left eye. There was no presence of nystagmus or squint. Examination of the anterior segment and intraocular pressure (IOP) were within normal limits. Both eyes exhibited multiple, coalescent areas of chorioretinal atrophy, sparing the posterior pole, with a scalloped appearance and well-defined borders separating these areas from normal tissue. Fluorescein angiography showed no leakage at the macula in the late phase. Central macular thickness (CMT) measured 308 μm in the right eye and 333 μm in the left eye. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed multiple hyporeflective areas extending from the outer nuclear layer to the inner nuclear layer, with multiple vertical intervening bridges of retinal tissue, indicative of foveoschisis.
test_results: Plasma ornithine level was 776.7 nmol/ml (normal 10-163 nmol/ml). Electroretinogram showed diminished rod response.
Orpha_name: Gyrate atrophy of choroid and retina

case_report: An 82-year-old Japanese man was admitted to the hospital with difficulty walking. His medical history includes angina, atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus. He experienced pain and swelling in his left hand and right toe a few days prior to admission, which progressively worsened and impaired his mobility. Similar symptoms had occurred in his right upper and lower extremities a year earlier, and he was treated with antibiotics at another hospital, but the pain and swelling persisted, leading to joint deformation. Upon admission, his vital signs were as follows: blood pressure 150/100 mmHg, heart rate 92 beats per minute, and temperature 37.0°C. He was alert and oriented. Physical examination revealed swelling in both upper eyelids, the salivary gland, the dorsum of the left hand, and both legs. He reported joint pain and had a limited range of motion. Scratches were observed on both feet. Neurological examination indicated motor weakness in the distal limbs (manual muscle testing 3/5) and decreased sensation (touch, pain, and vibration) in the dorsum of the left hand and both legs. Deep tendon reflexes in both legs were diminished. Laboratory tests showed elevated inflammatory markers (white blood cell count 13,200/μl with 72.2% neutrophils, C-reactive protein 14.37 mg/dl, sedimentation rate 34 mm/h) and high uric acid levels (9.7 mg/dl). Liver function tests (aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase, γ-glutamyltransferase, lactate dehydrogenase), renal function tests (blood urea nitrogen, creatinine), and amylase levels were within normal limits. Glycometabolism (HbA1c 5.7%), thyroid function (thyroid-stimulating hormone, free T4), creatine kinase, and gonadal hormones (testosterone 0.69 ng/ml) were also normal. Serum IgG was elevated (2417 mg/ml) with high IgG4 levels (630 mg/dl, 26.1% of total IgG), while autoimmune antibodies were negative (rheumatoid factor, anti-nuclear antibody, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, anti-topoisomerase antibody, anti-centromere antibody, anti-SS-A antibody, anti-SS-B antibody, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody). Immuno-electrophoresis indicated a chronic inflammatory pattern, and serum vascular endothelial growth factor was elevated (351 pg/ml). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed normal protein levels and no pleocytosis. Urinalysis was negative for protein, occult blood, glucose, and ketones. Blood cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus, while cerebrospinal fluid cultures were negative. Brain and spine MRI showed no abnormalities. Wrist MRI revealed synovial and myelin sheath swelling with fluid accumulation on the left side. Electromyographic (EMG) studies indicated mononeuritis multiplex. Nerve conduction studies showed absent compound muscle action potentials (CMAPs) and sensory nerve action potentials (SNAPs) in the left median and ulnar nerves, with reduced CMAP amplitudes in the right median and left lower extremities. Needle EMG demonstrated neurogenic changes during voluntary movement in the upper and lower extremities, with no denervation potential at rest. Enhanced computed tomography and gallium scintigraphy did not reveal any inflammatory lesions or malignant tumors. Lymph node echography showed reactive swellings only. Echography of the lacrimal and salivary glands revealed low echoic mass lesions, indicating swelling of the glandular tissue.
test_results: A lacrimal gland biopsy showed lymphoid follicles with a germinal center. Enzyme immunostaining with anti-IgG4 antibody revealed IgG-positive plasma cells, of which about a half were IgG4-positive, on the lymphoid follicles.

case_report: A three-week-old African American female was brought to our clinic for assessment and management of gum cysts. The child was delivered at full term through vaginal birth and had no other health issues. According to the mother, the prenatal period was uneventful, and the child was born with a mouth lesion. The mother observed that the lesion had decreased in size over the past three weeks. An intra-oral examination showed a bilobed, sessile, nodular lesion measuring approximately 1.5 cm at its largest point on the right maxillary alveolar process, near the area of the unerupted canine. The lesion's surface was smooth, pink, and non-hemorrhagic. Palpation revealed no pain, discomfort, or lymphadenopathy.
test_results: A maxillary peri-apical radiograph revealed no radiographic abnormality. Urine analysis for vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) was negative. A complete blood count with differential revealed all blood values within the normal range.

case_report: A 28-year-old Iranian Caucasian woman presented with complaints of decreased vision. Her visual acuity in both eyes was 20/25 with plano refraction. Slit lamp examination showed clear cornea and clear lens, with 1+ pigment in the vitreous. Intraocular pressure measured 18 mmHg in the right eye and 17 mmHg in the left eye. She had no history of other medical conditions or drug usage. Fundus examination revealed intraretinal crystals in the posterior pole and midperiphery, midperipheral retinal pigment epithelium and choriocapillaris atrophy, peripheral pigment clumping, and retinal scarring.
test_results: Flourescein angiography highlighted the focal geographic appearance showing transmission hyperfluorescence in the crystalline retina and choriocapillaris atrophy in the adjacent noncrystalline retina. Fullfield ERG showed severely decreased scotopic a and b-wave amplitudes. Moreover, the photopic a and b wave amplitudes were both severely attenuated. Visual field testing with program SITA fast 24 -2 was performed and showed constriction of visual field bilaterally.

case_report: A 10-year-old male child presented with his parents due to concerns about his teeth. Physical examination showed a thin build, short stature, narrow chest, and the ability to bring his shoulders together in front. He had a prominent forehead with frontal and occipital bossing, a short and broad head, underdeveloped mid-face with a depressed nasal bridge, and widely spaced eyes. Intraoral examination revealed a narrow, high-arched palate, unilateral anterior and posterior crossbite, multiple decayed and retained baby teeth.
test_results: The OPG revealed multiple impacted permanent and supernumerary teeth. Chest radiograph revealed narrow thorax with tapered width superiorly, severe hypoplastic clavicle over bilateral region. Biochemical investigations showed normal serum calcium and phosphate level, but decreased serum alkaline phosphatase level.

case_report: A 7-day-old female newborn was brought to our hospital following an abnormal screening result. She was born at full-term with a birth weight of 4380 grams. The parents reported no issues with feeding, activity levels, or crying strength. Newborn screening was conducted on her third day of life. On Day 4, the laboratory received her sample. By Day 6, results indicated a high-risk condition with GAA activity measured at 0.18 uM/h (critical cutoff < 0.5) and a ratio of 42.87 (critical cutoff acid β-glucosidase (ABG)/GAA ≥ 20). An urgent visit was arranged for Day 7. Upon examination, the newborn exhibited normal muscle power, normal reflexes, no macroglossia, but a slight decrease in facial folds.
test_results: A whole blood sampling at Day 7 revealed deficient lymphocyte GAA activity (1.33 nmol/g pro/h, normal mean 66.7). Echocardiography revealed moderate left ventricle (LV) and right ventricle (RV) hypertrophy, with a LV mass index (LVMI, measured by 2-D method) of 115.7 g/m2 (normal range < 65 g/m2). Laboratory examination revealed an elevation of pro-BNP (8738 pg/mL), CK (722 U/L), and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) (112 U/L). A chest X-ray revealed mild cardiomegaly. Mutation analysis showed heterozygous c.2024_2026del (p.N675del) and c.2040+1G>T variants in trans.
Orpha_name: Glycogen storage disease due to acid maltase deficiency, infantile onset

case_report: In October 2018, a 68-year-old man was referred to the Hematology Unit of the A.O.U. Policlinico “G. Rodolico-San Marco” in Catania with elevated white blood cell (102 × 10^9/L) and platelet (785 × 10^9/L) counts. Genetic analysis revealed the presence of two mutations on the MPL gene: V501A (c.1502T>C) and W515L (c.1544G>T). A mild splenomegaly was observed, with a longitudinal diameter of 13 cm. Clonal selection of Burst-Forming Units-Erythroid (BFU-E) and Colony-Forming Units-Granulocyte and Monocyte (CFU-GM) was performed, followed by DNA extraction and sequencing. Primary mononuclear cells (MNCs) were isolated from bone marrow samples and plated for colony-forming assays. After 12 days of incubation, 40 individual colonies (20 BFU-E and 20 CFU-GM) were analyzed. Twelve out of 20 BFU-E colonies carried the heterozygous V501A-W515L mutations, while the remaining 8 exhibited the wild-type gene. Among the 20 CFU-GM colonies, 4 were positive for the double mutation, 13 were wild-type, and 3 expressed only the W515L substitution. These findings indicate a greater heterogeneity in CFU-GM compared to BFU-E colonies and the presence of distinct clones with different genetic profiles.
test_results: The BM biopsy showed granulocyte hyperplasia and megakaryocyte clustering with moderate (grade 1) fibrosis. Sequencing data confirmed both the V501A and the W515L mutations with a VAF of 38.5% and 34.4%, respectively. The analysis also detected the KITM541L mutation (VAF 59.7%).

case_report: A 43-year-old Han Chinese male presented with a history of blue iris and open-angle glaucoma, which has led to significant optic nerve and visual field damage. The blue iris was noted at birth. At 17 years old, he was identified with juvenile open-angle glaucoma. At 18, trabeculectomy was performed on both eyes due to worsening visual field impairment and unstable intraocular pressure (IOP). Over the next 20 years, his IOP ranged from 12 to 16 mmHg without the need for antiglaucomatous medications, and the bleb function in both eyes remained effective. Recently, his best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 0.4 with −9.00 diopters (spheric) in the right eye and hand movement (HM) in the left eye. At the time of trabeculectomy 25 years ago, his BCVA was 0.8 with −6.00 diopters (spheric) in the right eye and 0.1 with −7.00 diopters (spheric) in the left eye. Anterior segment optical coherence tomography (AS-OCT) measured central corneal thickness (CCT) at 494 nm in the right eye and 499 nm in the left eye. His vision continued to deteriorate due to glaucoma progression, and five years ago, vision in the left eye decreased to hand movement, prompting the use of prostaglandin eye drops for glaucoma management. Exotropia was observed in the left eye due to low vision and disuse, along with horizontal nystagmus in both eyes. No dystopia canthorum was noted. Slit-lamp examination revealed extensive iris hypopigmentation in the left eye, sparing a section between 1 and 2 o’clock, and partial hypopigmentation in the right eye, sparing sections between 3:30 and 8:30 o’clock and between 10:30 and 12:00 o’clock. Pigmented granulations were present on the anterior lens capsule. Fundus examination showed a red, sunset-like appearance due to lack of pigmentation in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) layer, diffuse nerve fiber layer loss, and an excavated optic nerve head indicative of advanced-stage glaucoma. Gonioscopy revealed heavy trabecular meshwork pigmentation with a 45° angle between the iris and trabecular meshwork surface. Normal iris vessels were seen in the peripheral iris. AS-OCT imaging of the iris configuration showed a hyperreflective signal of the anterior border layer in the normal part of the iris, with increased light absorption causing optical shadowing and decreased visualization of the posterior pigmented epithelium. Atrophy of the pigmented anterior border layer resulted in a hyporeflective area, allowing deeper penetration of the OCT signal and exaggerating the posterior pigmented epithelium signal. The nasal and temporal portions of the iris showed mixed signals from the anterior border layer and posterior pigmented epithelium. Posterior segment OCT indicated abnormal retina with thinning of the choroidal tissue at the parafovea in the left eye. Optic nerve head (ONH) and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) analysis revealed an average RNFL thickness of 47 μm in the right eye and 49 μm in the left eye. Severe visual field defects were noted, with a mean deviation (MD) of −13.52 dB in the right eye and −27.87 dB in the left eye. Hearing tests showed no neurosensorial hearing loss. Temporal bone findings were normal on computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed no cranial abnormalities. Ocular examinations of the patient's parents revealed no abnormalities except for cataracts, and the physical and ocular examinations of the patient's son were normal.
test_results: Two mutations of EDNRB gene were recognized. The first (c.1111G>A on exon 7) leads to an amino acid change from glycine to serine at codon 371. This mutation is not found in the 1000 Genome, ESP6500, ExAC_ALL, or ExAC_EAS population databases. The second mutation (c.553G>A) leads an amino acid change from valine to methionine at codon 185. The frequency of the mutation is extremely low in the 1000 Genome, ESP6500, ExAC_ALL, and ExAC_EAS population databases. The EDNRB gene shows an AR inheritance pattern. Sequencing analysis revealed that there were two heterozygous mutations in the EDNRB gene in this patient, inherited from his mother and father, respectively. These two sites constitute a compound heterozygous variation.

case_report: A 62-year-old postmenopausal female with a medical history of diabetes, hypertension, G6PD reduced activity, and breast cancer treated with left-sided mastectomy four years ago, presented with progressive abdominal distension and pain for one year. The patient had been on prophylactic tamoxifen post-mastectomy but was non-compliant, taking it irregularly for two years. A CT scan revealed bilateral complex pelvic abdominal masses, likely ovarian, with thickening of the peritoneal reflection and nodular deposits, as well as multiple pulmonary nodules in the left lung. The patient had a total abdominal hysterectomy 17 years ago due to fibroids, but it was unclear if the ovaries were removed, and surgical records were unavailable. An ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the abdominal nodules showed linear fragments of highly hyaline stromal tissue without atypia or malignant cells. The patient subsequently underwent laparotomy for excision of the pelvic mass. During surgery, a large free mobile cyst measuring approximately 28 x 26 cm, filled with gelatinous greenish fluid, was found attached to the mesentery. Additionally, two other masses were observed: one attached to the omentum measuring 5 x 5 cm, and another attached to the mesentery measuring approximately 13 x 12 x 4 cm.
test_results: Histopathology consisted of relatively encapsulated cellular tumor composed of a fascicle of spindle-shaped cells exhibiting smooth muscle differentiation with mild pleomorphism, and the largest excised mass showed a focal moderate cytological atypia, necrosis, and mitosis (5/10 high-power field [HPF]). The histopathology report consisted of interlacing bundles of smooth muscle fibers; the cyst that was attached to the mesentery showed a focal increase in mitosis of 4-6/10 HPF and foci of degenerative atypia and no area of convincing necrosis was seen. Immunohistochemistry investigation results were positive for SMA, desmin, and estrogen receptors and negative for CD10, CD117, DOG-1, CD34, myogenin, Pan-CK, beta-catenin, and Ki6<10%. The pathology report consisted of circumscribed neoplasm composed of spindle cells arranged in a fascicular pattern with trapped bronchial tubules lined by respiratory epithelium which was positive for TTF1 and CK7. There were mitosis of 5/10 HPF, focal necrosis, focal nuclear polymorphism, and focal tumor giant cells. All resection margins were free from tumors. Immunohistochemically, the lung specimen was positive for smooth muscle actin (SMA), muscle-specific actin (MSA), desmin, and Ki67:10-12% and negative for CD34, DOG1, and C-Kit beta-catenin.
diagnosis: Disseminated Peritoneal Leiomyomatosis  with malignant transformation to Leiomyosarcoma

case_report: The patient is a 20-year-old female tennis player who reported worsening chronic foot pain. She mentioned a condition affecting her right foot that started around age thirteen, causing pain on the top of her foot, which intensified during tennis activities. The pain was exacerbated by forcefully pushing off on the right foot and making lateral direction changes. Initially, the pain was only present during tennis but had been occurring most of the time for over a year with varying intensity. The pain was described as aching and moderate in intensity, not affecting daily activities but impacting her practice. She adjusted her foot placement during practice to avoid direct pressure on the midfoot. During competitions, she did not let the pain affect her push-off but experienced severe pain afterward. Recently, she increased her practice intensity after a period of relative rest over the summer. She denied any mechanical symptoms of the foot. Over-the-counter non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medications provided little relief, but prescription carbon fiber shoe inserts and padded insole supports offered some relief. She regularly replaced her tennis shoes. She sought further options for pain relief. Her past medical history included a forearm fracture at around one year of age. Her family history was non-contributory. Socially, she enjoyed competitive tennis, performed well in school, and denied substance abuse. Review of symptoms was negative. She appeared healthy with no lower extremity color changes or edema. Ankle movements were symmetric with active eversion, inversion, dorsiflexion, and plantarflexion. Active dorsiflexion and plantarflexion of the toes showed limited range of motion in the second toe of the right foot. Passive dorsiflexion of the second toe was blocked at 30 degrees, and plantarflexion was painful at 30 degrees. There was dorsal and plantar tenderness to palpation over a bony deformity at the second metatarsophalangeal joint, but no other tenderness in the tarsal, metatarsal, or phalangeal regions. Single leg toe raise was painful on the right. She had normal arches and gait. The lower extremity neurovascular exam was normal.
test_results: X-ray of the right foot revealed second metatarsal head bony changes which included flattening of the bone, sclerosis, and fragmentation.

case_report: A girl aged seven years and eight months was referred for observation due to left peripheral facial palsy, resulting in the inability to close the left eye and drooping of the corner of the mouth. She experienced her first episode of peripheral facial nerve palsy at three years and one month old, which fully resolved after corticosteroid treatment. At three years and nine months, she was found to have pure red cell hypoplasia, presenting as severe anaemia (haemoglobin: 3.00 g/dL; red blood cells: 1,000,000/mm3) with a significant deficiency of erythroid precursors in the bone marrow, but high growth of them in culture, potentially linked to anti-EPO antibodies. The haemoglobin levels did not improve with recombinant human EPO administration but normalized following corticosteroid therapy, and the addition of autologous serum to the erythroid precursor culture inhibited EPO growth. At four years and four months, she had a second episode of left facial palsy, accompanied by an acute onset of weakness on the left side of the body. Mingazzini I and II tests were positive for the left limbs. Imaging revealed a haemorrhagic stroke in the anterior portion of the right putamen and external capsule with perilesional oedema, affecting the anterior limb of the internal capsule. Blood pressure measurements during hospitalisation showed elevated diastolic values. Three weeks later, the symptoms had completely resolved. At five years and six months, she experienced a third episode of left peripheral facial palsy.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was repeated, showing gliotic evolution of the previous haemorrhagic insult without new lesions. Laboratory tests, as well as ophthalmologic, neurologic, and otoscopic examinations and a head computed tomography (CT) scan performed were normal.

case_report: A 65-year-old white woman was referred to the facial plastic surgery clinic for evaluation of a firm prominence located between the nasal dorsum and the left medial canthal region. On palpation, the prominence felt osseous and fixed. A computerized tomography (CT) scan indicated the lesion resembled a preperiosteal cyst. In 2005, the patient underwent a cosmetic open rhinoplasty at another institution, with nasal packing removed 2 days post-procedure. She subsequently noticed the gradual development of a firm lesion on the left lateral nasal sidewall. She reported no functional complaints and denied any other nasal surgery. Her medical history was otherwise unremarkable. On examination, the lesion measured 7 mm by 6 mm, was firm, nontender, nonmobile, and felt fixed to the underlying bony nasal framework. It was located halfway between the nasal dorsum and medial canthus along the path of the presumed previous lateral osteotomy. An endoscopic intranasal exam was unremarkable. The patient found the lesion cosmetically disfiguring and requested its removal. Excision of the mass was performed under local anesthesia. An infraorbital nerve block was administered, and a 1-cm vertical incision was made at the junction of the nasal and cheek subunits, dissecting down onto the capsule of the firm lesion, which appeared bony in nature. The lesion was excised with sharp dissection and sent for permanent pathology. Closure was achieved using a 5-0 fast absorbing gut suture. The patient tolerated the procedure without complications.
test_results: The entire specimen contained aggregates of histiocytes and giant cells with foamy changes and microcystic clear spaces containing degenerated erythrocytes. Special stains were negative for fungi.

case_report: A 16-year-old girl with no significant medical history presented with unilateral hyperpigmentation that has been present for 8 months. The hyperpigmentation was not preceded by inflammation or erythema. The patient had no recent history of medication use or trauma. There were no similar cases reported in her family. The parents are not consanguineous; the father has vitiligo, and the mother has oral LP, hypothyroidism, and dyslipidemia. Physical examination revealed unilateral, whorled, ill-defined hyperpigmented macules and patches located on the left side of the neck, arm, axilla, chest, abdomen, and inner thigh, following a blaschkoid pattern.
