Nail examination showed pitting.
test_results: Histopathology findings showed superficial melanin incontinence with a very mild perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate and no lichenoid interface reaction. Dermoscopy demonstrated pigmentation with brown dots consistent with melanophages.

case_report: A 76-year-old female patient presented with a 3-year history of nonproductive coughing. She did not report any other symptoms such as sputum production, shortness of breath, or fever. The patient had no history of smoking and was not on any medication. Physical examination revealed clear breath sounds in both lungs. Routine biochemistry and hematology profiles were within normal limits. Anti-nuclear antibody was positive with a titer of 1:80 in a speckled pattern. Rheumatoid factor was measured at 30.4 IU/mL (normal range: 0.1-15 IU/mL). Other autoimmune markers were negative. Chest X-ray indicated multifocal consolidations and reticulonodular infiltrations in the peripheral regions of both lungs.
test_results: The specimen revealed dense fibrosis in the subpleura, lung parenchyme and interstitium with temporal heterogeneity. Chest HRCT also showed multifocal subpleural consolidations with reticular opacities in both lungs, predominantly in upper lungs. Architectural distorsion and traction bronchiectasis were combined. There was no definite honeycomb appearance. Small localized pneumothorax in right lung was also observed. Patient underwent bronchoalveolar lavage which showed 36% lymphocytes, 1% neutrophils, 62% macrophages, and 1% eosinophils. The CD4/CD8 ratio was 0.71.

case_report: A 33-year-old male presented with impaired vision in his right eye. He reported no headache or eye pain and had no known diseases. Routine examinations excluded rheumatic immune diseases, tuberculosis, and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome. The patient had no family history of genetic diseases, no history of pet feeding, eating raw meat, working on a farm or in a slaughterhouse, and no family history of Toxoplasma infection. His parents were not consanguineous. Slit lamp examination revealed no anterior segment abnormalities. Ophthalmoscopic examination showed vitreous hemorrhage and off-white raised retinal lesions below the right optic disc. Proliferative membranes on the lesion surfaces caused superficial retinal detachment and tortuosity and occlusion of peripheral blood vessels. A horseshoe-like tear in the temporal periphery was surrounded by retinal detachment. Best corrected visual acuity was 20/40 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye, with intraocular pressures of 14 mmHg in the right eye and 15 mmHg in the left eye. The patient underwent vitrectomy on January 5, 2022. Vitreous fluid was collected and tested negative for bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites, and other pathogens. Interleukin (IL)-10 and IL-6 levels were normal, with a slight increase in IL-8. Basic fibroblast growth factor and its receptors were present in proliferative vitreoretinopathy, proliferative membranes, and vascular endothelial cells. Increased BEGF content in vitreous fluid corresponded to the formation of proliferative film on the lesion surface. Vascular endothelial cell adhesion molecules were associated with blood-eye barrier breakdown, with moderately elevated titers indicating moderate intraocular tissue edema.
test_results: Fundus photography of the right eye showed vitreous hemorrhage and off-white elevated retinal lesions just below the optic disc, with irregular edges protruding into the vitreous cavity. Proliferative membranes observed on the surface of the lesions had resulted in superficial retinal detachment and tortuosity and occlusion of peripheral blood vessels. A horseshoe-like tear about 1 disc diameter in size was seen in the temporal peripheral retina, surrounded by a small area of retinal detachment. Optical coherence tomography revealed retinal thickening at the focal site with retinal structural disturbances indicated by areas of high and low reflectance. Color ultrasound of the right eye showed retinal thickening at the lesion, stretching and uplifting of the proliferative membrane, moderate strength patchy echo at the edge of the optic disc, and sound shadow behind the echo. Twelve days after the surgery, fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) was performed and revealed vascular lesions of about 1.5 disc diameters below the optic disc of the right eye, with surrounding pigment disorder and atrophy, twisted blood vessels below the optic disc and fluorescence leakage. Indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) showed persistently low fluorescence below the optic disc.
diagnosis: Combined Hamartoma of the Retina and Retinal Pigment Epithelium
Orpha_name: Combined Hamartoma of the Retina and Retinal Pigment Epithelium

case_report: Patient 3 (P3) is a 5-month-old female who was the first child of her mother, born via vaginal delivery at full-term (40+4 weeks) with no complications during pregnancy. She spent 2 days in the NICU post-birth due to 'ductus arteriosus' and 'newborn jaundice.' At birth, her head circumference was 34 cm (<−3SD), and her body weight was 3,150 g. At 5 months old, she presented with an unusual facial appearance, no deformities in hands and feet, no skin edema, inability to follow objects or hear, absence of midline hand movements, unstable vertical head control, transient head elevation to 45 degrees in a prone position, and inability to turn over.
test_results: The cranial MRI + DWI imaging ruled out genetic coyote encephalopathy. Multiple patchy and punctate T2, slightly high signals in bilateral radiating coronas, bilateral internal capsule hind limbs, bilateral paraventricular white matter, midbrain, protocerebrum, and dorsal protocerebrum were detected. The cerebellum was hypoplastic, and the bilateral frontotemporal subarachnoid gap was expanded. The bilateral inferior of the cerebellar hemispheres was reduced and myelin production was regressed.

case_report: A 3-year-old girl was referred for further management of recurrent outward deviation of the eye one and a half years after initial eye muscle surgery. Her eye history included a 30-prism diopter outward eye deviation noted at 15 months of age. At the first consultation, no abnormalities were detected on a detailed eye examination. After a 3-month observation period without improvement, surgery on both lateral rectus muscles was performed. The initial surgery occurred when the child was 18 months old, with no complications post-surgery. At 3 years old, the outward eye deviation returned. An eye examination showed best-corrected visual acuity of 20/20 in the right eye and 20/50 in the left eye using crowded symbols. Cycloplegic refraction was +0.5 (+0.5 at 112°) in the right eye and +1.00 (+0.5 at 70°) in the left eye. Cover-uncover testing indicated variable-angle outward deviation of the left eye. Slit-lamp examination was normal in both eyes.
test_results: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the right eye was normal whereas it revealed retinal thickening mostly of inner retinal layers in the left eye. Retinal nerve fiber, ganglion cell, and inner plexiform layers were markedly thickened and showed an associated epilesional gliotic reaction. Loss of foveal depression was also visible; however, no epiretinal membrane (ERM) was present. Foveal retinal thickness was 218μm OD compared to 500μm OS. Sub-foveal choroidal thickness measured by enhanced-depth imaging OCT was 283μm OD and 224μm OS. The “shark-teeth” sign was present on OCT sections of the fovea. Marked thickening of the outer nuclear layer was also present on OCT sections near the fovea. Fundus examination of the right eye was normal. Left eye fundus examination showed a subtle elevated greyish lesion in the papillomacular region with loss of the foveal reflex. Accompanying epiretinal gliosis was also present.
diagnosis: Combined Hamartoma of the Retina and Retinal Pigment Epithelium
Orpha_name: Combined Hamartoma of the Retina and Retinal Pigment Epithelium

case_report: A 76-year-old man arrived at the emergency department of Ramón y Cajal hospital in December 2019 with fever and a painful plaque on the back of his left hand. His medical history included hairy cell leukemia (HCL) and advanced colorectal cancer. He had undergone five cycles of chemotherapy, including oxaliplatin, 5-fluorouracyl, and leucovorin, combined with cetuximab and an anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) agent, which concluded in November 2019. He was also receiving treatment with granulocyte-colony stimulating factor (G-CSF). Physical examination showed a painful, swollen, and hemorrhagic plaque with poorly defined borders on the back of his left hand, accompanied by hemorrhagic, serosanguineous bullae. Laboratory tests were normal. He was admitted and treated with intravenous antibiotics after blood cultures were taken and surgical drainage was performed. Three days later, five new hemorrhagic plaques and bullae appeared on his legs, trunk, and opposite arm, surrounded by an intense red halo. The plaque on his left hand continued to spread to his forearm and fingers. The bullous lesions developed superficial necrosis without ulceration. These new lesions had some resemblance to other conditions. New systemic antibiotic and antifungal treatments were started. After seven days, the fever and skin lesions did not respond to systemic antibiotics, and all cultures were negative. Surgical debridement of the large plaque was performed. The specimen submitted for pathological examination was a grayish cutaneous fragment measuring 12 × 10 × 0.7 cm, with a friable consistency and a surface with superficial erosions, without ulceration.
test_results: Histological sections showed dense neutrophilic infiltrates throughout the dermis and subcutaneous fat, with massive abscess formation. The epidermis was damaged with erosions covered by purulent exudate, intra-epidermal vesicles, and exocytosis of neutrophils and erythrocytes, producing a bullous reaction. There was no evidence of vasculitis, thrombosis, or granulomas. Stains for fungi were negative. Tissue cultures for bacteria, fungi, and mycobacteria were repeatedly negative.

case_report: The patient is a 4-year-old boy who was referred to the paediatric haematology clinic due to persistent anaemia. He has a history of recurrent respiratory tract infections that required admission to the paediatric intensive care unit. The patient is the third child of parents of Arab origin, who are first cousins. He was born full-term via caesarean section with a birth weight of 3.5 kg. At 20 weeks gestation, a detailed foetal ultrasound showed both kidneys were enlarged and echogenic, with early signs of dysplasia. The same ultrasound also showed polydactyly in all four limbs. A renal ultrasound after birth confirmed that both kidneys were enlarged and bright in echogenicity, with a loss of corticomedullary differentiation. A follow-up renal ultrasound at the age of three years showed that both kidneys were normal in size, shape, echo structure, and position, with normal cortical thickness and no hydronephrosis. Family history includes a father with a rheumatic disorder and the death of an older male sibling at age 3 years, reportedly due to congenital heart disease. Physical examination revealed a giant-congenital naevus with multiple smaller nevi all over the body. Several dysmorphic features were noted, including a broad depressed nasal bridge, full cheeks, narrow bi-frontal diameter, thin lips, and low-set, small ears with deformity of the left ear pinna. Examination of the extremities showed postaxial polydactyly and central polydactyly of the left hand (7 digits), central polydactyly of the right hand (6 digits), postaxial polydactyly of both feet (6 digits each), and abnormal left palmar creases. The patient's BMI was 26.3 kg/m2, classified as overweight according to WHO standards. The patient was referred to a multidisciplinary team for further evaluation. Ophthalmological examination revealed esotropia, mild cyclo-refraction-hypermetropia with healthy optic discs, and retinal vasculature. Neurologic evaluation showed language impairment with limited vocabulary and expressions. Electroencephalography and brain MRI were unremarkable. Laboratory test results were normal.
test_results: Exome sequencing showed that he is homozygous for a variant (chr20: 10393994 T>C; c.169A>G; p.Thr57Ala) in the MMKs gene.

case_report: A 78-year-old woman with a history of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy leading to heart failure (NYHA class II) and chronic anaemia diagnosed 3 years ago, arrived at the emergency department with a 2-week history of worsening asthenia and melena. She had previously been hospitalized twice for symptomatic anaemia, necessitating red blood cell transfusions. Prior investigations, including upper and lower endoscopies and video capsule endoscopy, did not reveal an acute haemorrhagic source. Her medical history also includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (GOLD 1) related to smoking. She was on chronic medications including esomeprazole 40 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, furosemide 20 mg daily, ferrous sulphate 525 mg daily, salmeterol/fluticasone 25/50 μg twice daily, and tiotropium bromide 2.5 μg daily. Upon admission, she was found to be prostrate with pale and dehydrated skin and mucous membranes. Vital signs showed hypotension (blood pressure 95/54 mmHg) and tachycardia (heart rate 101 bpm). Cardiac examination revealed a systolic murmur with an aortic focus, grade III/VI. Laboratory results indicated severe normocytic hypochromic anaemia and a non-obstructive, non-oliguric acute kidney injury (AKIN 2) with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 27.17 ml/min/1.73 m2 according to the MDRD equation. Coagulation tests showed a prolonged activated prothrombin time (aPTT) without any coagulation factor deficiency. An upper endoscopy was conducted, but no haemorrhage was detected above the D3–D4 portion of the duodenum.
test_results: The results showed a low-output, active haemorrhage in the jejunum.

case_report: A 15-year-old male reported having poor vision in his left eye since birth. His best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was measured at 20/63 in the right eye and finger counting close to face (FCCF) in the left eye. The left eye exhibited enophthalmos and a 30° exotropia. The anterior segment appeared normal in both eyes. Examination of the right fundus revealed mild temporal dragging of the optic disc, straightening of the temporal vessels, subretinal exudations, and scarring at the periphery of the temporal retina. The left fundus showed dragging of the optic disc, a falciform retinal fold, and an abnormal retinal vascular pattern, along with pigmentation and scarring of the retina. There was no history of prematurity, and the patient's parents and four siblings were reported to be normal.
test_results: Fundus fluorescein angiography showed abrupt cessation of vasculature at the temporal retina of right eye. There was brush like anastomoses and shunts at the vascular-avascular border with mild leakage from the vessels. Left eye showed mild leakage from the disc and falciform retinal fold.

case_report: The patient is a 30-year-old unmarried male construction worker with no prior psychiatric history. He has been on a daily dose of 7.5 mg prednisolone for the past 18 years following a diagnosis of Addison's disease. Approximately four years ago, he began exhibiting continuous manic symptoms, including increased talkativeness, elevated self-esteem, overly familiar behavior, irritability, excessive spending, job irregularity, and sleep disturbances. His mother reported reckless motorbike driving and multiple falls, as well as inappropriate behavior towards girls and children in public. There were no signs of psychosis or substance abuse. Over the past year, relatives observed a decline in his physical strength. Six months ago, he had a work-related accident resulting in a fractured left forearm, which required surgical intervention. Family history includes rapidly progressing paralysis and early death in his brother and cousin at ages 9 and 12, respectively, with the latter also having received steroid supplementation. Initially, the patient was uncooperative for detailed assessment. His vital signs were normal. He displayed a jovial demeanor but became irritable at times, with increased talk and psychomotor activity. Insight and judgment were poor, while cognitive functions remained normal. Initial investigations revealed elevated serum cholesterol (267) and low-density lipoprotein (193). Hemogram, electrolytes, and blood sugar levels were normal. Liver, renal, and thyroid function tests were within normal limits. Serological tests for HIV and venereal disease research laboratory were negative. An ultrasound scan of the abdomen indicated minimal fatty infiltration of the liver.
test_results: MRI of the brain showed bilateral fairly symmetrical T2/FLAIR white matter hyperintensities involving deep white matter and periventricular region, sparing subcortical U-fibers, involving pareito-occipital region. Similar signal changes were also noted along corticospinal tracts (in brainstem, crus of midbrain, cerebral peduncle and pons), lateral thalami, splenium of corpus callosum, middle and inferior cerebellar peduncles, and dentate nuclei of cerebellum. No abnormal parenchymal enhancement was noted in the postcontrast study.

case_report: A 15-year-old female presented with a large dark-colored patch over the genital area, upper and inner thighs, and the front of the neck. The lesions began at age 5 and gradually increased in size. There is a history of first-degree consanguinity and delayed developmental milestones, with the patient starting to walk and speak at age 5. She exhibits short stature, deafness, and has not attained menarche. Local examination revealed a large hyperpigmented plaque over the groin, extending from the suprapubic region to the lower anteromedial surfaces of both thighs, including the vulva. The lesion was hyperkeratotic, hyperpigmented, slightly indurated, grayish-black, and covered with slightly coarse hair, except for the pubic, suprapubic, and upper thigh regions, which were smooth and less pigmented. The vulva was hypertrophic. Another hyperpigmented indurated plaque was observed over the thyroid region. General examination showed mental retardation, deafness, short stature, a depressed nasal bridge, muddy conjunctiva with hypertrophic and hyperpigmented caruncle of both eyes, ichthyosis, brownish hair, absence of axillary and pubic hair, mitral valve prolapse, and skeletal abnormalities including long slender digits of both limbs (notably in the great toes and middle fingers), crowding of lateral toes, hallux valgus deformity of the left great toe, and syndactyly of the left 4th and 5th toes.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, elongated rete ridges, and increased pigmentation of basal keratinocytes. Dermal picture showed proliferation of dense collagen up to the subcutaneous tissue. Van Gieson stain confirmed the dermal collagen proliferation.

case_report: A right-handed man in his 70s experienced five episodes of brief unresponsiveness over a year, all occurring at rest. While watching television, he felt an epigastric rising sensation lasting about 30 seconds, followed by a 2 to 3-minute period of unresponsiveness with gaze fixation. There were no chest symptoms, convulsions, or other auras like déjà vu, fear, or panic. Urinary incontinence was noted during these episodes. He regained full consciousness within a few minutes. These events happened while he was sitting or lying on his side, and he did not fall over. Neurological examination showed no abnormalities. Brain MRI was normal, but EEG displayed intermittent semi-rhythmic delta activity in the left temporal region. ECG showed a left bundle branch block, and subsequent Holter ECG monitoring over several days revealed a complete atrioventricular block, leading to the implantation of a permanent pacemaker. After the pacemaker was implanted, the episodes of unresponsiveness and the abdominal sensation ceased.
test_results: 99m-Technetium pyrophosphate scintigraphy illustrates myocardial uptake.

case_report: A 13-year-old female, the youngest of her siblings, presented with a complaint of painless, progressive, and bilateral enlargement of the lower face and jaws. There was no family history of similar conditions. The patient was born full-term with no abnormalities until about the age of 2 years, when bilateral symmetrical prominence of the lower face was observed. This enlargement ceased at around two and a half years of age and remained unchanged for several years. Over the past 3-4 months, her parents noted a gradual increase in size to its current state. Physical examination showed the patient to be well-built, active, and mentally alert. No abnormalities were detected in the chest, abdomen, cardiovascular, or central nervous systems. There were no signs of cutaneous pigmentation, congenital abnormalities, or endocrine disturbances. Extraoral examination revealed normal facial expression and color with no ophthalmic abnormalities. There was diffuse enlargement on both sides of the face extending to the inferior border and angle of the mandible bilaterally, roughly round in shape, hard in consistency, and with ill-defined margins. The swelling was fixed with no secondary changes, and the right side was slightly larger than the left. Palpation revealed normal skin temperature and no tenderness. A single, firm, non-tender, and mobile submandibular lymph node approximately 1 cm in diameter was palpable on the right side. Intraoral examination showed the patient in the permanent dentition stage with the absence of the mandibular left second permanent molar. There was no disturbance in occlusion or shift in the midline.
test_results: CT-axial and coronal contrast images showed symmetric expansion of the mandible with 'ground glass' appearance. Different CT-Axial sections from symphysis region, body, ramus and angle of mandible were taken. The multilocular radiolucency was found to be gradually increasing in size from body to angle of mandible. Histopathological examination revealed multinucleated giant cells (up to 10 nuclei) with interlacing bundles and whorls of spindle cells and moderate vascular stroma. It also showed an eosinophilic perivascular cuffing of collagen.

case_report: An 18-year-old female with a history of migraine headaches presented with persistent nausea, vomiting, inability to tolerate oral feeds, and significant weight loss over the past 2 months. She reported vomiting after every meal, with vomitus consisting mainly of undigested food particles and no blood. She experienced intermittent constipation but no diarrhea. Despite a good appetite, she observed substantial weight loss but could not quantify it. She had not taken any medications for her migraines, with the last flare-up occurring about a year ago. She had multiple outpatient visits for similar complaints in the last 2 months and was referred to the hospital by her primary care provider. On evaluation, her vital signs were stable. Physical examination showed dry mucous membranes, mild epigastric tenderness, and decreased bowel sounds. She was started on intravenous fluids. Laboratory tests revealed a hemoglobin level of 10.2 g/dL, hematocrit 30.2%, serum sodium 132 mEq/L, and serum potassium 3.3 mEq/L. An abdominal X-ray did not show mechanical obstruction. A Gastric Emptying Study indicated markedly delayed gastric emptying time. The patient was started on metoclopramide, which improved her symptoms, and she was discharged with instructions to taper the medication as needed. One month later, she returned with similar complaints despite metoclopramide therapy. Laboratory results were similar to the initial hospitalization, showing hemoglobin level of 10.7 g/dL, hematocrit 31.9%, serum sodium 133 mEq/L, and serum potassium 3.2 mEq/L. An abdominal X-ray showed dilated bowel segments with a high burden of stool in the colon without obvious mechanical obstruction. Over the next month, she was given various prokinetic agents, including mirtazapine, ondansetron, pyridostigmine, octreotide, and promethazine, but showed no clinical improvement. A nasojejunal feeding tube was placed for nutrition, but she experienced worsening nausea despite a slow feeding rate of 10 mL/h. Consequently, she was started on total parenteral nutrition (TPN) and transferred to a tertiary center for higher-level care. At the tertiary center, she continued on TPN and underwent extensive evaluation. Laboratory investigations were within normal limits except for mild elevation of liver enzymes. Tests for antinuclear antibody, extractable nuclear antigens panel, paraneoplastic antibody panel, and acetylcholine receptor binding antibodies were negative. A right upper quadrant ultrasound showed gallbladder sludge and normal liver architecture. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) and colonoscopy were negative. A small bowel follow-through ruled out mechanical obstruction. Magnetic resonance enterography and computed tomography angiography of the abdomen were unremarkable. A deep rectal biopsy was negative for amyloidosis. Antroduodenal manometry showed a paucity of contractile activity with very low amplitudes.
test_results: A laparoscopic full-thickness intestinal biopsy revealed decreased actin staining in the circular muscles of the muscularis propria of small intestine.

case_report: The patient, a 24-year-old male, is the first child of healthy parents with no known consanguinity. He presented with a 6-year history of worsening coordination issues while walking and involuntary, jerky movements. Neurological examination showed instability of the trunk, slurred speech, and tremors in the upper limbs that occur during intentional movements. Additionally, there was no presence of negative myoclonus, but there was stimulus-sensitive myoclonus in the arms. The patient also experienced generalized seizures.
test_results: Funduscopic examination disclosed bilateral macular cherry-red spots. The brain MRI showed mild atrophy. The patient’s genetic analysis, sequencing of the exons and intron/exon splice sites of NEU1 gene by using Sanger method, identified 2 heterozygous pathogenic variants; NM_000434:c.625delG (p.Glu209SerfsTer94) variant and NM_000434:c.928G>A (p.Asp310Asn) variant.

case_report: A 50-day-old Egyptian Caucasian girl presented with ongoing vomiting, dehydration, and altered consciousness. She was born full term, weighing 3500 grams (+1 SD) via normal vaginal delivery. Her mother, aged 26, has had three pregnancies and three births, with no family history of renal diseases. The parents are first cousins. The mother reported the death of her second child at 3 months due to fever, vomiting, and diarrhea, though no medical records are available. The first child is a healthy 4-year-old girl. The patient's symptoms began at 15 days old with persistent vomiting and dehydration, leading to a 4-day stay in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) without significant improvement. After discharge, the mother noticed increased breathing rate, prompting another medical visit. Serum ammonia was recorded at 109 μmol/L (normal < 81 μmol/L). At 45 days old, the patient's consciousness deteriorated, and suckling decreased, leading to admission to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU). On admission, her modified Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) was 12, she exhibited severe dehydration with dry mucous membranes, poor perfusion (capillary refill: 5 seconds), a temperature of 38.2°C, weight 3300 grams (-2.8 SD), and bilateral diffuse sonorous rhonchi in her chest. Laboratory results showed mild absolute neutrophilia with neutrophils at 63%, C-reactive protein (CRP) at 24 mg/dL (normal < 6), and chest X-rays were clear of pneumonic patches. Serum creatinine was 1.1 mg/dL (normal: 0.3 to 1.0), and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) was 31 mg/dL (normal: 7 to 22). The chest infection and dehydration were treated with third-generation cephalosporins and intravenous fluids. The patient exhibited failure to thrive, growth retardation, hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with respiratory alkalosis, and persistent alkaline urine (pH > 7). Urine and blood tests were conducted to further investigate the condition. She began receiving intravenous bicarbonate infusion and potassium supplementation, showing partial response.
test_results: Pelvi-abdominal ultrasound (U/S) revealed bilateral nephrocalcinosis and left renal increased medullary echogenicity.

case_report: A 10-year-old boy presented with bilateral decreased vision since the age of three. His parents were consanguineous but had normal ophthalmic examinations. Best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/160 in the right eye and 20/800 in the left eye with corrections of −12.00 and −13.00 sphere, respectively. Slitlamp biomicroscopy revealed diffuse intra-epithelial microcystic changes throughout the entire corneal epithelium. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was normal, and funduscopic examination showed pathologic myopic changes in both eyes. To improve visual acuity and anterior corneal clarity, the patient underwent automated lamellar therapeutic keratoplasty (ALTK) with a thickness of 250 μm in the left eye. The corneal button was preserved in 10% formalin and sent to the pathology laboratory. The specimen was bisected, with one half processed and embedded in paraffin wax. Sections were prepared and stained with Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) for general morphology and by PAS sequence with and without diastase to identify glycogen.
test_results: Histopathological examination disclosed a partial-thickness cornea with abnormal-appearing epithelium consisting of numerous intracytoplasmic cyst-like inclusions together with cellular swelling. The cells contained moderate amounts of PAS-positive, diastase-sensitive material consistent with glycogen. Other corneal layers were unremarkable. Transmission electron microscopic examination disclosed numerous and variable-sized vacuoles within the cytoplasm in all epithelial layers. Moderate numbers of electron-dense and membrane-bound intracytoplasmic bodies similar to lysosomes were also noted, some within the vacuoles. No abnormal findings were noted elsewhere.

case_report: A 62-year-old woman visited the chest outpatient department with a four-month history of breathlessness during physical activity. She reported no exposure to drugs or environmental inhalational agents and had no history of chest pain, palpitations, ankle swelling, syncope, or gastrointestinal symptoms. She was a nonsmoker and did not consume alcohol. There was no family history of clubbing, and she was unaware of any clubbing in her lower limb digits. Her previous medical records showed no clubbing or major illnesses. She had two children, both delivered vaginally, and reached menopause at 45 years old. On physical examination, her pulse rate was 80/min, regular, with good volume, and all peripheral pulses were palpable. Her respiratory rate was 15/min, blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg, and she was afebrile. Her SpO2 at rest was 98–100% on room air. Clubbing was observed in all toes of both feet, but not in the fingers. The ratio between the diameters at the bases of the nails and at the distal interphalangeal joints of all 10 digits of the upper and lower limbs was calculated, with the sum of individual digit ratios exceeding 10 in the lower limbs. There was no swelling or skin changes around the wrists and ankles. No features indicative of connective tissue or endocrine disorders were noted. Chest examination revealed bilateral diffuse end-inspiratory fine crepitations, predominantly at the lung bases. Abdominal and other system examinations were normal. Hemogram results showed a hemoglobin level of 12.5 gm/dL, total leucocyte count of 9400/mm3 with 61% neutrophils, 37% lymphocytes, and 2% eosinophils. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 12 mm in the first hour. Blood biochemical examination and routine urine analysis were normal. Thyroid and liver function tests were normal. Tests for connective tissue disorders, including anti-nuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor, were negative. Serological testing for human immunodeficiency virus was negative. Sputum smear for acid-fast bacilli was negative. Blood and sputum cultures were sterile.
test_results: Spirometry showed a restrictive pattern. Chest roentgenography revealed haziness in both lower zones. High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) was showing interstitial thickening and honey combing in basal regions.

case_report: A 61-year-old right-handed male presented with a 24-hour history of altered speech, double vision, facial weakness, and difficulty swallowing, following 4 days of symptoms consistent with COVID-19. His medical history included a 3-year history of Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia (WM)—MYD88 positive, IgM kappa paraproteinaemia 4g/L—and a sensory peripheral neuropathy. His neuropathy included reduced sensation in a stocking distribution bilaterally and mild gait ataxia. Examination findings included global areflexia, impaired vibration sense throughout the lower limbs, difficulty in tandem walking, and preserved limb power. He was able to walk unaided with unlimited exercise tolerance. Nerve conduction studies showed evidence of a large fibre sensory and motor peripheral neuropathy, with mild slowing and prolonged distal motor latencies but without meeting criteria for demyelination. He received four cycles of rituximab at the diagnosis of WM for the neuropathy and remained stable for over 2 years. In the 5 months prior to admission, he reported progressive symptoms of gait ataxia and new reduced grip strength. Admission vital signs were stable. Cranial nerve examination revealed right-sided ptosis, complex ophthalmoplegia, facial diplegia, poor palatal lift, tongue weakness, and dysarthria. Limb examination showed widespread mild proximal weakness, areflexia, impaired vibration throughout both legs, and proprioception loss to the ankles. A nasopharyngeal swab confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection by RT-PCR, although the chest X-ray was normal. Blood tests revealed lymphopaenia (0.96 × 10^9 L), C-reactive protein of 9 mg/ml, and normal renal function. Cold agglutinins were identified, and the total IgM level was 7.51 g/L (0.35–2.42). Further blood tests were unremarkable, including HbA1C, plasma viscosity, creatine kinase, vitamin B12, folate, thyroid stimulating hormone, anti-nuclear antibodies, complements, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, hepatitis B and C serology, HIV, acetylcholine receptor antibodies, and anti-myelin associated glycoprotein (MAG) antibodies. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed a mildly elevated protein of 0.84 g/L (<0.4) but no organism, cells, or abnormal findings on cytology. Twenty-four hours later, the patient's respiratory condition deteriorated with radiological evidence of airspace consolidation. Dexamethasone and Remdesivir were started for severe COVID-19, and he required noninvasive ventilation. Neurophysiological studies showed evidence of demyelination with motor conduction block, prolonged distal motor latencies, and reduced conduction velocities. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg), 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days, was administered. One week following IVIg treatment, there was complete resolution of ophthalmoparesis, facial diplegia, and limb weakness with improving bulbar function. Eleven days into admission, respiratory function had normalized, and the patient was discharged home.
test_results: Pre-IVIg anti-ganglioside antibody panel demonstrated IgM titres of GD1a, GD1b and Gq1b all >1000 (<500) persisting at 2-month follow-up.

case_report: A 30-year-old male reported experiencing intermittent, recurrent painful cramps affecting multiple areas over a span of 2 years. Initially, the cramps began in the right index finger and eventually spread to the entire body, including the axial muscles and jaw. These cramps often led to visible jerky movements in various body parts, particularly the extremities. Approximately 1 year after the onset of these symptoms, the patient began to experience hair loss, which progressed to complete loss of all body hair, including pubic and body hair, over a few months. Two months before the current presentation, he started having recurrent episodes of diarrhea. Physical examination revealed complete hair loss (alopecia universalis). There were no noticeable bony deformities. Generalized myokymia was observed, especially in the proximal limb muscles and the paraspinal region, with movements vigorous enough to cause limb movements even at rest. The rest of the neurological examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory tests, including hemogram, renal, and liver function tests, were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed acellular fluid with normal protein and sugar levels. The patient's creatine phosphokinase (CK) level was within normal limits (142 IU/L).
test_results: The nerve conduction study done showed decreased amplitude of right tibial nerve compound motor action potential (CMAP) from the abductor hallucis. Electromyography (EMG) done in vastus lateralis, tibialis anterior, and biceps revealed fasciculation of 10 hertz frequency and high frequency grouped fasciculation of 50-70 hertz. There were also intermittent transient high frequency (150-200 Hz) decremental discharges suggestive of neuromyotonic discharges. Continuous motor unit activity (CMUA) was seen in thoracic paraspinal muscle. On activation of vastus lateralis, tibialis anterior and biceps, broad large amplitude motor unit action potentials (MUAPs) were found to be interspersed with MUAPs of normal duration and amplitude. Sural nerve biopsy showed mild loss of myelinated fibers in each fascicle with regenerating clusters suggestive of mild axonal neuropathy. Biopsy of vastus lateralis revealed variation in fiber size with atrophic and angulated fibers with some fascicles completely collapsed due to fiber atrophy consistent with mild neurogenic atrophy. Sigmoidoscopy revealed inflamed colon and biopsy of the colon demonstrated collagenous colitis.

case_report: A 32-year-old male presented to Seoul National University Dental Hospital for evaluation and management of bilateral nodular lesions on the neck, which had been present for several months. Previously, he had visited a local plastic surgery clinic due to a large lesion and pain in the right cervical area. Records from the clinic indicated that he had undergone a drainage procedure but declined surgical removal of the lesions. The patient reported that the pain and swelling decreased following the aspiration. His medical history includes cardiac septal defect repair at 10 months of age, and he reported no family history of similar skin lesions. Panoramic radiography revealed abnormal dentition: prolonged retention and submergence of deciduous second molars on both sides of the maxilla and the right side of the mandible, multiple missing permanent teeth (including maxillary second premolars on both sides, two mandibular incisors on both sides, and one mandibular molar on the right side), and microdontia of two maxillary lateral incisors (peg lateral incisors) and two mandibular premolars.
test_results: The images revealed multiple well-defined round to ovoid, smooth or scalloped, nodular lesions with diameters ranging from 2 to 20 mm in the subcutaneous layer on both sides of the cervical region. The internal structure showed fat attenuation on the level of −110 to −100 Hounsfield units (HU) and some lobulation. Additionally, the large lesion of the right upper neck displayed peripheral enhancement with mild swelling. The epidermis of that lesion was elevated, and the adjacent platysma muscle and external jugular vein were displaced medially. The histological finding was a subcutaneous cystic lesion containing sebum-like material. At the lowest magnification (×12.5), a cavity surrounded by a thin epithelial lining that formed part of the cyst wall was observed. The middle magnification settings (×40 and ×100) showed the specimen to have a wall lined by 3 to 5 layers of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium lacking a granular layer, and many sebaceous lobules were located very close to, as well as within, the cyst wall. In addition, a wavy luminal surface and sebum-like material or keratin debris were detected. The highest magnification (×400) showed numerous lobules of pilosebaceous glands on the cyst wall. The granular layer was completely absent.

case_report: A 14-year-old male has experienced episodes involving all four limbs since the age of 7. The current episodes begin with grunting and the face turning to the right, followed by jerking movements of all four limbs, lasting a few minutes. Post-episode, the patient remains in a confused state for at least 30 minutes. At the time of presentation, he was receiving treatment with VAP 300 mg twice daily, carbamazepine 200 mg twice daily, and clonazepam 0.5 mg: 1-0-2.
test_results: EEG showed evidence for bilateral occipital spike and wave discharges.

case_report: A 66-year-old male was admitted in November 2008 with an enlarged spleen, elevated red blood cell count, and low serum erythropoietin levels. Cytogenetic analysis indicated a normal male karyotype. Molecular studies were negative for the BCR-ABL1 rearrangement but identified the JAK2V617F mutation with an allele burden of 44.9%. The patient was treated with aspirin, hydroxyurea, and phlebotomies, which were well tolerated. Six years later, an abdominal ultrasound revealed dense bilateral perinephric infiltration, confirmed by a whole-body CT scan. An F-FDG-PET scan showed increased glucose uptake in the medullary channels of both humeri and femurs. Bone marrow analysis showed no change in the grading of bone marrow fibrosis (MF-0 according to the EUMNET consensus), and cytogenetic analysis revealed a complex male karyotype: 47,XY,+9[2/20], 47,XY,add(6)(p25),+9[2/20], 46,XY[16/20].
test_results: Morphological analysis demonstrated the accumulation of foamy histiocytes that were positive for CD68 and negative for the dendritic cell markers CD1a and S100, surrounded by fibrosis and a scanty lympho-monocytic infiltrate.

case_report: The patient, a 9-year-old girl, was born with congenital absence of the nose and was raised at Guangzhou City Social Welfare Institute. Her physical and intellectual development was comparable to that of her peers. The patient exhibited congenital nasal deformities and small eyes. A detailed physical examination revealed that her visual refraction, muscle strength, and tone were all functioning normally. An MRI examination was not performed due to the patient’s preferences. There were no signs of muscular dystrophy observed.
test_results: A pathogenic heterozygous variant of SMCHD1, NC_000018.10:g.2694678G > C, NM_015295.3:c.1025G > C, NP_056110.2:p.(Trp342Ser), was identified. Sanger sequencing was further performed to validate this variant. This variant results in a change in the amino acid sequence of the ATPase active structural domain of the SMCHD1 protein, which may lead to altered ATPase activity and hence affect the characteristics of the resulting protein. It was not found in the 1,000 Genome Browser, The ExAC Browser, the Exome Variant Server and GnomAD. According to ACMG standards and guidelines, this variant was categorized as pathogenic (PM1, PM2, PS3, PP3, PP5).

case_report: A 15-year-old Asian girl presented to the emergency department with increasing pain in the right lower abdomen for 3 months. She experienced severe, colicky pain in the right lower abdomen with the onset of menstruation. The pain did not radiate and was not associated with fever, vomiting, or urinary complaints. She had no past medical or surgical history. Menarche occurred 3 months earlier, and she had a regular menstrual cycle with dysmenorrhea and cyclical abdominal pain. Analgesics from a local pharmacy provided transient symptom relief. She was born at term from an uncomplicated pregnancy and had no family history of congenital diseases. She was not sexually active and did not take contraceptive pills or hormone therapy. She belonged to a middle-class family. Developmental milestones included neck control at 4 months, sitting at 7 months, walking unsteadily from 13 months, and walking steadily from 20 months. Her weight was 33 kg, and her height was 144 cm, both below the fifth percentile for her age and sex according to the National Center for Health Statistics, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and were normal. Her parents were nonconsanguineous. On admission, she was afebrile with stable vital signs except for mild anemia (pulse 84 beats/minute, blood pressure 125/80 mmHg, anemia +, temperature 98 °F). General physical examination results were unremarkable. Abdominal examination found a tender mass on the right iliac fossa. Per rectal examination revealed a mass in the pouch of Douglas. She was admitted to the gynecology department and medicated with analgesics, omeprazole, and paracetamol for symptom relief. Routine investigations were performed. Complete blood count was within normal limits with a hemoglobin level of 11.1 g/dl and erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 62 mm/first hour. White blood cell count was 12 × 10^9/L with a differential count of 62.5% neutrophils, 29% lymphocytes, and 6.8% monocytes. Red blood cell count was 3.97 × 10^12/L. Platelet count was 431 × 10^9/L. Routine urine and microscopic examinations showed no features of infection (quantity: sufficient, color: straw, albumin, sugar, and phosphate: nil, pus cells: 4–6/high-power field [HPF], epithelial cells: 3–4/HPF, RBCs: nil). Ultrasound evaluation showed a distended endometrial cavity filled with complex fluid with low-level internal echoes and nonvisualization of the right kidney.
test_results: Pelvic MRI showed two separate endometrial stripes surrounded by endometrium and a muscular layer. The right endometrial cavity and cervix were distended with blood. The right kidney was absent. MRI finding was suggestive of uterine didelphys with right-sided hematometra resulting from obstructed hemivagina with ipsilateral agenesis of the right kidney. IVU revealed an absent or nonexcreting right kidney and normal excreting left kidney.

case_report: A 2-year-old male child, born as the third child of the family via cesarean section at the 38th gestational week with a birth weight of 2050 g (3rd percentile), presented with jaundice starting on the 5th postnatal day. Physical examination showed a mild icteric appearance with no other dysmorphic features. His height and weight were within the 50–75th percentile. Laboratory results were as follows: aspartate aminotransferase (AST): 32 U/L (5–34 U/L), alanine aminotransferase (ALT): 18 U/L (0–55 U/L), gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT): 15 U/L (12–64 U/L), alkaline phosphatase (ALP): 124 U/L (40–150 U/L), total bilirubin: 2.53 mg/dL (0.2–1 mg/dL), and direct bilirubin: 1.77 mg/dL (0–0.5 mg/dL). Whole abdominal ultrasonography showed no pathological findings.
test_results: A homozygous deletion of 340 kilobase (kb) was observed in the short arm of the 12th chromosome: arr[hg19] 12p12.2p12.1 (21,017,795–21,357,948)x0. This region involved the first 10 exons of SLCO1B1 and the final eight exons of SLCO1B3.

case_report: A 20-year-old male of Asian descent presented to our hospital in July 2020 with a 9-year history of recurrent painful ulcers on both legs, which had worsened in the past few months. The patient also had a history of recurrent draining sinuses and abscesses in the axillary and genitofemoral areas, along with severe nodular acne on the face that had been present since puberty. Dermatological examination showed papulopustules and sinus tracts in the axillary regions with purulent discharge upon palpation. On the trunk and limbs, particularly the lower extremities, there were diffuse and geographic skin ulcers with undermined margins and prominent ridged erythema.
test_results: Histological examination showed pseudo-epitheliomatous hyperplasia with epidermal neutrophilic abscess formation and intradermal granuloma formation with extensive infiltration of neutrophils. PAS and acid-fast staining were negative.

case_report: The patient, an 11-year-old female, has experienced short stature for 6 years prior to hospital admission. She is the fifth child of a nonconsanguineous couple. She was born naturally at full term with low birth weight and height and was breastfed. From the age of 5, her height has been below that of her peers. Upon admission, blood tests indicated phosphorus levels at 0.80 mmol/L (normal range: 0.96–1.62 mmol/L), 1,25-(OH)2-D at 11.39 pg/ml (normal range: 20–100 pg/ml), tubular reabsorption of phosphate (TRP) at 83.7% (normal range: 84 to 96%), and alkaline phosphatase levels at 1427.40 U/L (normal range: 45–125 U/L). Other electrolytes, thyroid hormone levels, 24-hour urine calcium levels, and the ratio of maximum rate of renal tubular reabsorption of phosphate to glomerular filtration rate (TMP/GFR) were within normal limits. Blood phosphorus tests for the patient's siblings and parents showed that one sister had low blood phosphorus and exhibited bowed legs as the only clinical sign.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing analysis showed that the proband harbored the c.1402C > T; p.R468W in the SLC34A3 gene. Sanger sequencing verified this variant in other family members. The proband’s mother and father carry a heterozygous variant of the gene, and the proband’s sister had a homozygous variant. The proband also harbored a c.3917C > T (p.A1306V) homozygous variant in the LRP5 gene. The proband’s mother and father carried a heterozygous variant in the gene, but the proband’s sister was normal.

case_report: A 36-year-old Muslim male patient, who does not consume alcohol and was born from a consanguineous marriage, visited the outpatient department with a 10-year history of progressively thickening facial skin, forming longitudinal and transverse folds. He reported visual disturbances due to drooping and thickening of his eyelids. Additionally, he experienced intermittent joint pain in his wrists, elbows, and ankles. There was no other significant medical or familial history. Physical examination revealed pronounced skin folds on the forehead, between the eyes, in the nasolabial grooves, and on the chin. The nose was notably enlarged with thickened skin folds. The skin appeared greasy with excessive seborrhea and sweating. The skin on the hands and feet was also thickened, and there was severe clubbing of all fingers and toes. Cutis verticis gyrata was absent. Both ankles were mildly swollen, and his blood pressure was within normal limits. Laboratory tests showed normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, random blood sugar, serum calcium, insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), thyroid function tests, and pepsinogen-1, with a nonreactive VDRL test. Growth hormones were normally suppressed following glucose (75 g) loading. Tests for rheumatoid factor, anticyclic citrullinated protein (anti-CCP) antibodies, and HLA-B27 were negative. Slit skin smear and skin biopsy with Fite acid stain were performed, and no acid-fast bacilli (AFB) were found on both occasions.
test_results: X-rays revealed periosteal thickening of the long bones in the diaphyses of metatarsal and metacarpals as well as along cortices of long bones. Chest X-ray shows enlarged clavicles, cardiomegaly with normal lung markings.

case_report: A 43-year-old male reported experiencing excessive thirst and urination for six months. His daily urine output ranged from 3.5 to 6 liters, with a urine specific gravity of 1.003 (normal range: 1.010–1.025). Laboratory tests showed a serum sodium level of 150.4 mmol/l (normal range: 137–147 mmol/l), urine osmolality of 146 mOsm/kg (normal range: 50–1,200 mOsm/kg), and plasma osmolality of 320 mOsm/kg (normal range: 275–305 mOsm/kg). Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) was elevated at 6.72 mU/l (normal range: 0.27–4.2 mU/l), and prolactin was 23.64 ng/ml (normal range: 4.60–21.40 ng/ml). Other pituitary hormones, testosterone, and morning cortisol levels were within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a slightly thickened pituitary stalk and a small nodule in the left pituitary gland. The patient was treated with desmopressin, leading to an improvement in symptoms.
test_results: The complete blood count (CBC) showed a white blood cell count (WBC) of 2.81 × 109/l, hemoglobin of 111 g/l, and platelet count of 34 × 109/l. His bone marrow aspirate revealed dysplasia of the erythroid lineage with 6.5% myeloblasts. Standard molecular genetic analysis showed a single mutation of CEBPA, whereas FLT3-ITD, NPM1, C-kit, IDH1, IDH2, DNMT3A, PHF6, TET2, ASXL1, and EVI1 were negative. Karyotype analysis of metaphase chromosomes was 47,XY, + 8[10]. SNP-A-based karyotyping revealed a complex karyotype that included monosomy 7, 12p-, and trisomy 8, and 4 short lesions were recognized as an absence of heterogeneity (AOH) of uncertain significance.
Orpha_name: Refractory anemia with excess blasts type 1

case_report: A 10-year-old girl visited the pediatric dental clinic with concerns about the non-eruption of a permanent tooth, accompanied by pain and swelling in the upper left posterior region. Her prenatal, birth, medical, and family history were all unremarkable. The extraoral examination showed no abnormalities. The patient was in the late mixed dentition stage. Intraoral examination revealed well-defined edematous and fibrous gingival tissue covering an expanded alveolar bone measuring 6 mm by 8 mm in the area of teeth 65 and 26. Tooth 26 was partially erupted, with only the cuspal portions visible, and displayed an irregular contour with numerous shallow furrows, pits, and grooves. The tooth was extremely tender upon percussion, and palpation of the surrounding gingiva also elicited pain. According to the patient's dental history, the upper left primary second molar had exhibited similar morphological deformities and had exfoliated two years prior.
test_results: Dental development from radiographs appeared age-appropriate and showed the normal thickness of enamel and dentine in maxillary and mandibular primary and permanent dentitions. However, 26 indicated ghost-like appearance with thin layers of enamel and dentine, short roots with wide open apex, and enlarged pulp chambers. The left maxillary primary second molar (65) had exfoliated before 2 years due to a similar defect and IOPA of the affected side shows indistinct and irregular periapical radiolucency of 26. Developmental defects in erupting 2nd premolar (25) bud were also noted in IOPA.

case_report: A 21-year-old female patient reported experiencing scotoma in both eyes. She had taken Lemsip® one day prior to the onset of symptoms for flu-like conditions. Her medical history was unremarkable. Visual acuity was measured at 6/9 in both eyes. Central visual field testing revealed scotomas that matched the areas she described.
test_results: Fundoscopy disclosed typical wedge-shaped brownish discoloration in the left macular region.

case_report: A 72-year-old female patient presented to the Dermatology outpatient clinic with itchy bumps on her neck, which had been increasing in number over the past year. Her medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, systemic arterial hypertension, end-stage kidney disease on maintenance hemodialysis, hypothyroidism, and an allergy to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Physical examination revealed multiple 2 mm diameter, skin-colored, firm papular lesions located on the posterior and lateral sides of the neck.
test_results: An incisional biopsy from the posterior region of the neck showed a slightly folded epidermis with orthokeratosis, and atrophy of the spiny layer but conserving most of its interpapillary processes; thickening of the collagen fibers was observed in the superficial and medium dermis, with no change in its orientation. Argentic staining identified a decrease in the elastic fibers and fragmentation.
diagnosis: White Fibrous Papulosis of the Neck
Orpha_name: White Fibrous Papulosis of the Neck

case_report: In March 2017, a 75-year-old male presented with a one-week history of left eye periorbital swelling, forward displacement of the eye, and swelling of the conjunctiva. CT imaging showed enlargement of the lacrimal gland and medial rectus muscle. Blood tests indicated macrocytic anemia, low white blood cell count, elevated C-reactive protein (44 mg/L), positive thyroglobulin antibody (404 U/L), and thyroid peroxidase antibody (108 U/L). IgG4 levels were elevated (2.5 g/L), while other immunologic tests were negative. Ultrasound Biomicroscopy (UBM) showed diffuse thickening of the episcleral tissue. The patient was treated with prednisone 60 mg/day, leading to improvement and reduction of symptoms within 10 days. Over the following two years, he experienced three episodes of unilateral inflammatory orbital symptoms, requiring hospitalization. Prednisone was effective in two instances, while symptoms resolved without treatment in one instance. During the second episode, right eye posterior scleritis was confirmed by a typical T-sign on ultrasound. A lacrimal gland biopsy in December 2018 showed patchy lymphocytic infiltration with small T and B lymphocytes, and IgG4 staining was negative. Between 2018 and 2021, the patient had three additional hospitalizations for recurrent fevers, fatigue, weight loss, pulmonary ground glass opacities, and one episode of laryngitis. Blood tests during this period showed worsening pancytopenia and significantly elevated C-reactive protein levels (up to 236 mg/L).
test_results: Genome sequencing revealed a mutation in the splice acceptor site.

case_report: A 27-year-old male presented with progressive swelling of the legs and abdomen over a period of 2 years. He experienced multiple episodes of upper gastrointestinal bleeding, characterized by melena. He reported no alcohol consumption and was sexually inactive. There was no history of jaundice, tuberculosis, renal disease, or similar illnesses in the family. Physical examination showed mild pallor, mild jaundice, bipedal pitting edema, and engorged neck veins. His pulse was 68 beats per minute and regular, with a blood pressure of 104/68 mmHg. Abdominal examination indicated significant ascites, moderate splenomegaly, and a firm, enlarged liver with a palpable left lobe. Cardiac examination noted a laterally shifted diffuse apical impulse, a soft first heart sound, and a pansystolic murmur indicative of tricuspid regurgitation. Routine blood tests showed hemoglobin at 8.7 g/dL, total leukocyte count at 6700/cumm (neutrophils 65%, lymphocytes 27%, monocytes 3%), and platelet count at 80,000/cumm. Liver function tests revealed bilirubin at 4 g/dL (direct fraction 2.4 g/dL), aspartate aminotransferase at 120 U/L, alanine aminotransferase at 208 U/L, serum albumin at 3.7 g/dL, and serum globulin at 4 g/dL. Renal function tests showed serum urea at 48 mg/dL and creatinine at 0.9 mg/dL. Tests for hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibody, and HIV antibodies were negative. Ascitic fluid analysis showed albumin at 2.6 g/dL (serum ascites albumin gradient: 1.1) and a total cell count of 240 cells/cumm with 70% mononuclear cells. Cytological examination for malignancy was negative. An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed moderate to large varices, which were ligated. Abdominal ultrasonography showed splenomegaly, an enlarged liver with coarse echotexture, a dilated hepatic vein, and 3+ ascites. A chest X-ray indicated cardiomegaly.
test_results: Echocardiography revealed massively dilated right atrium (RA) and RV with spontaneous echo contrast in RA. A cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed: free flow of blood between RV and RA in systole, an unduly dilated and akinetic right ventricular outflow tract, an “ironed out” RV wall without evidence of any trabeculation, and RV ejection fraction 15%. RV and RA were massively dilated with akinesia/dyskinesia of RV wall, except the apex. There was significant tricuspid regurgitation and mild pulmonary regurgitation.

case_report: The patient was delivered via cesarean section at 38 weeks of gestation with a birth weight of 3820 grams. He is the third living child of a 35-year-old mother in her fourth pregnancy. The mother's second pregnancy involved a male fetus with agenesis of the corpus callosum, congenital heart disease, and absence of the nasal bone detected on ultrasound at 24 weeks, which led to pregnancy termination without genetic tests or autopsy. Antenatal ultrasonography for the patient revealed isolated agenesis of the corpus callosum at 18 weeks of gestation, and amniocentesis showed a 46, XY karyotype. The patient did not pass stool for the first three days of life and only did so after rectal stimulation. He underwent laparotomy for intestinal biopsies and was found to have Hirschsprung disease, leading to the creation of an ileostomy. At one year old, he presented with a two-day history of fever. His weight was 8.4 kg (3rd percentile), height 74 cm (3rd percentile), and head circumference 46 cm (25th percentile). Physical examination revealed hypertelorism, uplifted earlobes with a central depression, frontal bossing, telecanthus, deeply set eyes, infraorbital fold, long lashes, broad eyebrows with a medial flare, a wide nasal bridge with a prominent and rounded nasal tip, low-hanging columella, open-mouth expression, thin 'M' shaped upper lip, prominent chin, short neck, wide-spaced nipples, overlapping toes, and pes planus. Abdominal examination showed no guarding or rebound tenderness, and he had orange-colored liquid stool in an ileostomy bag. He exhibited eye contact, a social smile, and stereotypic hand movements, and spoke three indistinguishable words. Traction response was poor, and he was hypotonic on vertical suspension. He could not sit unassisted. Deep tendon reflexes were normal, bilaterally plantar reflexes were extensor, and sustained Achilles clonus was noted. Urinalysis at admission showed pyuria. Urinary ultrasound and voiding cystourethrogram revealed grade 3 hydronephrosis affecting the right ureter.
test_results: Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated enlargement of the third and lateral ventricles, the occipital and temporal horns. There was a bilateral incomplete hippocampal inversion, enlargement of thalamus, nucleus caudate, and ACC. A heterozygous “class 2” c.646dupT (p.Cys216LeufsTer23) mutation on exon 6 of ZEB2 gene was detected.

case_report: A 15-year-old female presented with back pain and progressive scoliosis in the thoracolumbar region. She was admitted to the orthopedics department for spinal deformity correction. There was no history of motor or sensory weakness. She had a history of burns on her right palm sustained while cooking. On examination, there was dissociated sensory loss over her limbs and thorax, which she was unaware of.
test_results: The MRI image showed a descend of the tonsils below the foramen magnum.

case_report: In March 2013, a 33-year-old female presented to the nephrology department with a history of recurrent acute pyelonephritis over the past 4 years. She had no significant past medical history, including symptoms such as polyuria, polydipsia, muscular cramps, carpopedal spasms, or generalized seizures, and was not on any regular medication. Her parents, aged 56 and 53, were second cousins and reported no significant medical history. Her only sibling had died from renal failure at age 25 without a definitive cause. Physical examination showed a height of 160 cm and a weight of 55 kg, resulting in a BMI of 21.48 kg/m2. Laboratory tests indicated impaired renal function (SCr 250 μmol/L, EPI-eGFR = 21.1 ml/min/1.73m2), hypocalcemia (1.42 mmol/L), and normal serum parathyroid hormone levels (65.59 pg/ml) with normal 25OH-Vitamin D levels (26 ng/ml). Her serum magnesium level was slightly low (0.60 mmol/L), and 24-hour urinary calcium was 3.9 mmol/1.73m2. Distal renal tubular acidosis was ruled out as she had normal urine acidification (pH < 5.3) and nearly normal serum bicarbonate levels (HCO3− 22 mmol/L). Renal ultrasound showed bilateral nephrocalcinosis and parenchymal renal calculi, with the right kidney measuring 9.5 cm and the left 9.4 cm. Ophthalmologic examination was normal. Over the next 3 years, she experienced six episodes of acute urinary tract infections. During the interictal periods, she underwent four biochemical assessments. Repeated tests showed significant renal magnesium loss (fractional excretion 42.7 ± 7.4%) and hypercalciuria (urinary calcium/creatinine 0.52 ± 0.08 mol/mol). Treatment with calcitriol and calcium had limited effect on her serum calcium, while her serum magnesium levels fluctuated within the normal range (0.70–0.91 mmol/L) despite renal failure. Plain abdominal radiograph and abdominal CT scans in March 2014 and February 2016, respectively, showed worsening nephrocalcinosis and renal parenchyma atrophy. Ultimately, the patient progressed to end-stage renal disease at age 36. The gradient of GFR decline was calculated to be 4.3 ml/min per 1.73 m2/year during the follow-up period, compared to 2.1 ml/min per 1.73 m2/year in the 3 years prior, with an overall slope of decline of 2.5 ml/min per 1.73 m2/year.
test_results: A homozygous cytosine-to-guanine substitution at position 346 of the open reading frame (c.346C > G) in exon 2 of CLDN16 gene was identified. This single nucleotide alteration led to a single amino acid substitution from leucine to valine at amino acid position 116 of claudin 16 (p.Leu116Val).
Orpha_name: Primary hypomagnesemia with hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis

case_report: An 18-year-old male arrived at the emergency department with a complaint of left eye pain persisting for four days. The pain intensified with horizontal eye movement, particularly when looking to the left. There was no history of trauma or other injuries to the orbit. The patient had been treated for sinusitis prior to this visit, but his symptoms worsened. He was afebrile and had stable vital signs. Physical examination revealed painful abduction of the left eye without diplopia in that direction. Slight ptosis of the left eye was noted at the initial presentation. There was no conjunctival injection, chemosis, proptosis, foreign body, or eye discharge. Visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. Visual fields, pupillary reactions, fundoscopic examination, and the remainder of the neurologic and systemic examination were normal. Laboratory investigations, including complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, thyroid function tests, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, were all within normal limits.
test_results: Orbital and brain MRI showed enlargement with increased enhancement of the left lateral rectus muscle and the left lacrimal gland, with associated inflammatory changes in the adjacent left pre-septal soft tissues. There were also subtle inflammatory changes in the adjacent orbital fat. The cavernous sinuses were unremarkable bilaterally and no evidence of abnormality along the course of the cranial nerves.

case_report: The patient is a three-month-old male, second child of non-consanguineous parents from Eastern Sri Lanka, born at full term with a birth weight of 3 kg. He had been fed starter infant formula since birth. There was no family history of neonatal death, and his five-year-old sister was healthy. The child had normal growth until three months, weighing 4.8 kg at the time of hospital admission. He presented with fever, difficulty breathing, and irritability for one day. On examination, he appeared ill, drowsy, dehydrated, and tachypneic, with crackles in both lung fields. Other system examinations were clinically normal. He was transferred to the medical intensive care unit (MICU) of a regional tertiary care hospital. Laboratory results showed leukocytosis (WBC - 24.37 × 103/μl, N-65.8), mild anemia (hemoglobin - 10.9 g/dL), and platelets at 425x103/μl. C-reactive protein was less than 6 mg/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 20 mm/first hour. Arterial blood gas indicated severe metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation: pH - 7.0604, pO2 - 88.5 mmHg, pCO2 - 8.2 mmHg, HCO3 - 2.3 mmol/L, and base excess (BE) - 20. Ketonuria was detected. Additional findings included blood glucose of 164 mg/dL, lactate of 1.1 mmol/L, and ammonia of 145 μmol/L. Renal and liver functions were normal. A 2-D echocardiogram was normal. Tall T waves were observed in the ECG recording and confirmed by a 12-lead ECG rhythm strip. The electroencephalogram showed age-appropriate normal brain electrical activity. The patient was treated with intravenous cefotaxime and paracetamol suppositories for fever, along with correction of dehydration and acidosis. Formula milk feeding was continued. Due to worsening drowsiness and decreased consciousness, the patient was ventilated. With low oral intake, he was managed with 10% intravenous glucose-containing fluids, electrolytes, and intravenous bicarbonate. Given the initial pH of less than 7.1 (pH-7.0604) and stable hemodynamics, NaHCO3 - 0.5 mmol/kg was administered over 20 minutes, followed by continuous infusion. Bicarbonate infusion and ventilatory support were adjusted every six hours based on arterial blood gases. The patient showed biochemical and clinical improvement by Day 2, leading to the discontinuation of bicarbonate infusion on Day 3. Subsequent investigations excluded possible infective causes such as severe bronchiolitis, septicemia, meningoencephalitis, and bronchopneumonia, with negative urine and blood cultures. Lumbar puncture was not performed due to lack of parental consent. Tracheal culture and PCR revealed no organisms, leading to the cessation of intravenous antibiotics, cefotaxime and clarithromycin, after seven days. Symptomatic management was continued throughout the hospital stay.
test_results: Acylcarnitine analysis of dried blood spots revealed an elevated C5:1 (0.34 μmol/L; cut-off point 0.12) and C5-OH (2.68 μmol/L; cut-off point 0.47) levels. Urine analysis revealed very high ketones, which included grossly elevated 3 hydroxybutyric (3HB) and acetoacetic acids (AcAc) and mild elevation of 2M3HB, 2MAA, and TIG.

case_report: This case involves a 1.5-year-old Caucasian female born at 41 weeks gestation following an uncomplicated pregnancy, with APGAR scores of 6, 6, and 6. At birth, she required resuscitation involving oxygen, bag-mask ventilation, and CPAP. She was admitted to the NICU for a potential perinatal infection. Her birth weight was 3780 g (87th percentile) and head circumference was 38.5 cm (greater than 99th percentile) according to WHO 0–2 years standard growth curves. On day 14 of life, her height was 54 cm (99th percentile) using the same growth curves. At 10 months, her height was 75.3 cm (98th percentile), weight was 9500 g (73rd percentile), and head circumference was 49 cm (greater than 99th percentile) based on WHO 0–2 years standard growth curves. She exhibited axial hypotonia, which delayed her ability to walk until 17 months. At the time of reporting, she has not developed any spoken words. Brain MRI findings included decreased gyration in the frontal cortex, germinal cysts, a left porencephalic cyst, and hyperintensity in the frontal and parietal white matter. An echocardiogram revealed mild pulmonary stenosis with mild insufficiency. Dysmorphic features observed were sparse hair and eyebrows (improving over time), hypertelorism, mild retrognathism, a broad forehead, and macrocephaly. Previous genetic testing via microarray identified an 83 kb duplication of 18q21.32.
test_results: Trio WES demonstrated a de novo heterozygous variant in the ODC1 gene, c.1252C>T (p.Gln418*), which causes premature termination of the protein.

case_report: A 76-year-old male experienced recurrent episodes of right orbital inflammation, each resolving spontaneously within a week. Six months prior to these symptoms, he developed intermittent fever, recurrent chest infections, congestive heart failure, and thromboembolic events, necessitating multiple hospitalizations, including intensive care. Six months later, he presented with complete right blepharoptosis, following five days of painless swelling and redness of the right upper eyelid, and partial ophthalmoplegia affecting elevation, adduction, and abduction. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head and orbits showed no abnormalities, and the eyelid swelling resolved within a few days without treatment, leaving mild residual blepharoptosis. Two months later, he presented with severe right ophthalmoplegia, proptosis, periorbital edema, and conjunctival chemosis, with visual acuities of 20/50 in the right eye and 20/32 in the left eye, normal pupillary reactions, and no intraocular inflammation. Computed tomography of the orbits revealed soft tissue swelling in the anterior orbit, enlargement of the right lacrimal gland and extraocular muscles (notably the levator palpebrae superioris/superior rectus complex and lateral rectus), intraconal fat stranding, subtle thickening of the optic nerve sheath, enlargement of the anterior right cavernous sinus, and soft tissue changes within the superior orbital fissure and orbital apex, but no discrete collection or paranasal sinus opacification. The orbital inflammation improved significantly after one week of systemic antibiotics, but mild residual right relative proptosis (1-2 mm), moderate blepharoptosis, and slight right abduction and elevation deficits remained stable at one-year follow-up. Concurrently, he was undergoing investigations for a suspected multi-organ inflammatory disorder.
test_results: DNA analysis from bone marrow revealed a mutation in UBA1.

case_report: A 5-month-old male infant presented with progressive abdominal distension over the past one and a half months. He was the second child born to parents who are second-degree relatives. His birth weight was 2.5 kg. Both antenatal and neonatal periods were without complications. There was no history of excessive urination, increased thirst, or rapid breathing. His elder sibling, a 4-year-old male, is healthy. On examination, the infant's weight was 5.2 kg (3rd centile) and height was 63 cm (25th centile). Blood pressure was 90/60 mmHg. The infant exhibited a generalized absence of fat, including the buccal pad of fat, resulting in an 'empty cheeks' appearance. Dysmorphic features included a triangular face, low anterior hairline, depressed nose, large protruding tongue, long fingers and toes, large hands and feet, prominent veins over hands and feet, and excessive hair over thighs and legs with muscular hypertrophy. There was no acanthosis nigricans. Abdominal examination revealed a firm hepatomegaly of 9 cm and splenomegaly of 2 cm. Developmental milestones were appropriate for age, and hearing was normal. Laboratory investigations showed the following: cholesterol 119 mg/dl (114-203 mg/dl), HDL <10 mg/dl (40-60 mg/dl), LDL 34 mg/dl (<130 mg/dl), triglycerides 1391 mg/dl (29-99 mg/dl), and random blood sugar (RBS) 400 mg/dl. Frequent blood glucose monitoring indicated persistent hyperglycemia (300-415 mg/dl). Serum insulin was elevated to 44 μIU/mL (normal up to 23 μIU/mL) with a simultaneous glucose level of 300 mg/dl. Liver function tests were normal except for mild elevations in AST and ALT. Urine ketone bodies were negative. X-ray of the wrist showed normal bone age, and the echocardiogram was normal.
test_results: Liver biopsy revealed extensive steatosis involving 95% of parenchyma with marked fibrosis with a fibrotic score of 3/4.

case_report: A 48-year-old Caucasian female, working as an elementary school teacher in Minnesota, was found to have elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit levels during a kidney donor evaluation. Her hemoglobin was 19.4 g/dl and hematocrit was 57%, with normal white blood cell and platelet counts. She had a history of consistently high hemoglobin and hematocrit levels, recorded at 19.3 g/dl and 58%, respectively, twenty years earlier. Her medical history included well-managed hypertension treated with lisinopril, and she had no history of tobacco use, vascular events, or microvascular symptoms. Notably, her mother and brother also had elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit levels. Initial laboratory tests showed an erythropoietin level of 1.1 mIU/mL (normal range 2.6–18.5) and a peripheral blood JAK2 mutation screen that was wild-type for both exons 12 and 14.
test_results: EPOR mutation screen revealed a heterozygous c.1316G>A, p.(Trp439*) mutation in exon 8 that caused a premature stop codon and truncated the 70 C-terminal amino acids resulting in a gain of function.
diagnosis: Autosomal Dominant Hereditary or Familial Erythrocytosis Type 1

case_report: A 9-month-old male infant exhibited swelling on the right side of the face since birth, which had been gradually enlarging. The infant also showed early eruption of deciduous teeth. The mother reported an uneventful pregnancy and birth. Developmental milestones were within normal limits. On local examination, there was a soft, non-tender, non-compressible, ill-defined, and diffuse swelling on the right side of the face, leading to unilateral facial hypertrophy. Facial movement, eye closure, and tongue movements were normal, and the infant had a good intake of feeding. No signs of facial nerve compression were observed.
test_results: The computed tomographic (CT) scan revealed moderate-sized diffuse-lipid density lesion in the subcutaneous fat planes over right maxillary, temporal, mandibular area, and mild osseous hyperplasia. Microscopic examination showed nonencapsulated lesion containing mature adipose tissue in lobules. Diffuse infiltration of salivary gland tissue, nerve fibers, skeletal muscle fibers and lymphoid tissue were seen. Presence of fibrous tissue and vessels with thickened wall was noted. Extensive examination showed no nuclear atypia or lipoblasts.
diagnosis: Congenital Infiltrating Lipomatosis of the Face
Orpha_name: Congenital Infiltrating Lipomatosis of the Face

case_report: A 45-year-old male presented for an orthopedic consultation at a tertiary center with congenital absence of nails on all toes of the left foot. Physical examination revealed that the toes of the left foot were short and bulbous, with anonychia and syndactyly between the second and third toes. No similar abnormalities were observed in the hands or the right foot. No other skeletal anomalies were detected. Sexual development and higher motor functions were normal. No facial anomalies were noted. The patient reported a family history of similar abnormalities involving unilateral feet in his late father, uncle, and grandfather. All available family members were examined. The patient was unmarried and had an unaffected brother. There was a history of consanguineous marriage in the family. The patient's daily activities were not affected by the anomaly, and observation was chosen after explaining the condition to the patient.
test_results: Radiography revealed the absence of distal phalanx of all the toes of left foot, absence of the middle phalanx of toe 2, 3, 4 and a hypoplastic middle phalanx of little toe.
