Metetarsals were grossly normal. Radiographs of the patella and that of bilateral hands and right foot were normal.

case_report: A 10-year-old boy presented with a significant scalp defect and was admitted for plastic surgery. The surgical team observed a malodorous, tender, and secreting wound following a previous unsuccessful attempt at tissue expansion reconstruction on the scalp. Due to fever and poor general condition, the patient was transferred to the pediatric ward. Osteomyelitis was excluded, and the patient responded well to debridement and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic therapy. Additionally, the patient exhibited transverse terminal limb anomalies, including brachydactyly, cutaneous syndactyly, and hypoplastic nails. His speech development was below the expected level for his age, and he had difficulties with social interactions and school performance. Growth parameters were within normal ranges. The patient was the first child of a consanguineous Iranian family, with normal gestational age and birth weight. The mother reported frequent use of analgesics such as acetaminophen and ibuprofen for toothache during pregnancy and experienced neurotic distress due to familial conflicts. The parents did not report any family history of scalp and limb defects or cognitive impairments.
test_results: Cranial bone defect under the area of aplasia cutis congenita was obvious in skull X-ray. Upper and lower extremities X-rays confirmed bony defects in fingers. Brain imaging showed focal acrania, an extensive chronic subdural collection under the areas of bone defect and mild pachygyria. Cerebellum was intact.

case_report: An 81-year-old Thai woman with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with multiple erosions lasting 4 weeks. The patient had blisters on her hands and feet, which later spread to her trunk and face. These blisters and erosions appeared on previously unaffected skin. She also reported the loss of both big toenails. She did not have a history of fever, joint pain, sensitivity to sunlight, or any previous or current skin conditions. Her hypertension and type 2 diabetes had been managed effectively with amlodipine, enalapril, hydrochlorothiazide, and metformin for 6 years. Physical examination revealed multiple erosions on erythematous to violaceous patches and plaques located on the face, both ears, right axilla, abdomen, distal fingers, and toes, along with the absence of both toenails. Some erosions were observed on normal-appearing skin.
test_results: Histological examination demonstrated subepidermal vesicle with well-preserved dermal papilla associated with dense inflammatory cell infiltration composed of lymphocytes and numerous eosinophils in the papillary dermis. A second biopsy on the perilesional skin was done for direct immunofluorescence examination and revealed linear immunoglobulin (Ig) G and C3 deposition along the dermoepidermal junction associated with shaggy deposition of fibrinogen and colloid body of IgM. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for circulating anti-basement antibodies bullous pemphigoid (BP) 180 was positive with a titer of 72.4 (normal value 0–22) and antibody for BP230 was negative.

case_report: A 6-year-old, white, female patient with light brown hair presented with a 1-year history of difficulty in combing her hair and the presence of weak and brittle hair strands. The child exhibited age-appropriate psychomotor development and had no history of illness or hospitalization. There were no reported similar cases in the family. Dermatological examination showed thick, coarse, and brittle hair in the left occipitotemporal region. The skin and its annexes were normal.
test_results: Polarized light microscopy revealed a flattened hair shaft, twisted 180º along its axis at irregular intervals.

case_report: An 83-year-old woman with a history of atrial fibrillation, coronary artery disease, and lower lip squamous cell carcinoma initially presented with bulky bilateral lymphadenopathy, confirmed as squamous cell carcinoma via biopsy. The tumor encased the right mandible and had broken through the skin on the right side of the neck. The patient was scheduled for an elective bilateral radical neck dissection, right mandible resection, tracheostomy with a Bjork flap, and left scapular chimeric osteocutaneous free flap. On the day of surgery, she arrived at the pre-operative waiting area from home. She was afebrile and mildly tachycardic with a heart rate of 103, blood pressure of 94/62, and oxygen saturation of 97% on room air. Her metabolic equivalents were approximately 4-5. Morning laboratory results showed a WBC count of 15.6, sodium of 128, and chloride of 91. All other laboratory results were within normal limits, including an ionized calcium of 1.20 and potassium of 3.9. The patient's tumor caused dysphagia, and her preoperative sodium of 128 was related to reduced oral intake ahead of surgery. It was not deemed clinically significant enough to delay resection. Upon arrival at the OR, the patient was pre-oxygenated with a face mask, and general anesthesia was induced with 90 mg of propofol, 50 mg of 1% lidocaine, 2 mg of midazolam, and 25 mcg of fentanyl. She was paralyzed with 20 mg of rocuronium and 80 mg of succinylcholine, with rocuronium given as a precurarizing dose. Intubation was achieved in one attempt with a 6.0 endotracheal tube and was uncomplicated. She had two large-bore peripheral IVs placed for access as well as a radial arterial line for close hemodynamic monitoring and frequent blood sampling. In the first hour of surgery, the patient received several 100 mcg boluses of phenylephrine for blood pressure support as well as cefazolin and metronidazole for antibiotic prophylaxis. She was also given 4 mg of dexamethasone.
test_results: An initial arterial blood gas (ABG) revealed a pH of 7.4, partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO2) of 34, partial pressure of oxygen (pO2) of 463, bicarbonate (HCO3) of 21, and a base excess of -2.8. She was noted to be hypokalemic at 2.7 and hypocalcemic at 1.03. After the third hour, another ABG was collected, which showed mild worsening of her metabolic acidosis with pH 7.4, PCO2 31, HCO3 19, and a base excess of -4.3. Potassium remained low at 3.0 but calcium was appropriately repleted. The patient had received 2L of crystalloid and put out 2L of urine. At the fourth hour of surgery, another ABG revealed a severe drop in bicarbonate to 14, and an increasingly negative base excess of -8.6. Potassium decreased again to 2.7, even after 50 mEq of repletion, and calcium dropped to 0.96. The patient received another 2L of crystalloid and urine output remained high at 500-600 mL per hour. At hour seven, the pH remained normal at 7.37 with hyperventilation to an end-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO2) of 25, HCO3 of 14, and a base excess of -9.7. Despite 80 mEq of potassium, the patient remained mildly hypokalemic at 3.3 and hypocalcemic at 1.01. The patient received another 30 mEq of potassium, 1.5 g of calcium, and 2L of crystalloid with increasing urine output to approximately 900 mL per hour. At hour eight, the pCO2 was 20, base excess worsened to -12.0, and bicarbonate dropped to 11. Hypokalemia and hypocalcemia remained notable.

case_report: A 59-year-old Caucasian man presented with gradually worsening muscle weakness and wasting in the posterior calf muscles. Neurological examination showed normal cranial nerve function and intellectual status. Manual muscle testing indicated weakness of Medical Research Council (MRC) grade 4+ out of 5 in the posterior calf muscles and slight weakness MRC grade 5- out of 5 in the anterior calf muscles. Deep tendon reflexes were symmetrically preserved. Family history suggested an autosomal recessive trait. Serum creatine kinase levels were normal in his two children and one sibling. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) using T1-weighted turbo spin echo and short T1 inversion recovery (fat-suppressed) sequences showed selective atrophy and fatty replacement in the medial heads of the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles. Follow-up MRI two years later revealed similar changes in the adductor longus muscles. Contrast-enhanced images displayed areas of fatty degeneration alongside regions with contrast enhancement and edema in the lateral head of the gastrocnemius and the proximal part of the soleus muscles. Needle electromyography of both gastrocnemius muscles showed sparse positive sharp waves. During voluntary effort, early recruitment of short and small motor unit action potentials consistent with a myopathic pattern was observed. Nerve conduction studies showed normal sensory nerve action potentials and conduction velocities in the right median and sural nerves, as well as normal compound muscle action potential amplitudes and nerve conduction velocities in the right median and tibial nerves. Serum creatine kinase level was significantly elevated to 1700U/L (normal, less than 270U/L); lactate dehydrogenase was 264U/L (normal, less than 232U/L); alanine aminotransferase was 53U/L (normal, less than 35U/L); and aspartate aminotransferase was 67U/L (normal, less than 45U/L). Gamma-glutamyl-transpeptidase level was normal. Hematoxylin and eosin staining of serial frozen sections of the gastrocnemius muscle showed marked variation in fiber size, centrally localized nuclei, and necrotic and regenerating fibers. Moderate endomysial fibrosis and some small perivascular inflammatory infiltrates were also observed. Immunohistochemical staining with various antibodies revealed markedly reduced dysferlin immunoreactivity at muscle fiber membranes but diffusely increased in the cytoplasm of many fibers. Utrophin expression was slightly upregulated. Immunoblotting analysis did not show any significant reduction of dysferlin, dystrophin, or calpain 3.
test_results: A novel homozygous splice mutation, c.762 + 5G > T, in the ANO5 gene was identified after direct Sanger sequencing of all coding exons of ANO5. Splice prediction programs showed a loss of the splice donor site. It is suggested that exon 9 could be skipped due to the identified splice donor site mutation in intron 8.
Orpha_name: Vocal cord and pharyngeal distal myopathy

case_report: A 9-month-old boy was brought to the Department of Rehabilitation Medicine of Shenzhen Children's Hospital in August 2023 due to low muscle tension in the limbs and neck, and the inability to turn over and sit up on his own. He was the mother’s only child, delivered naturally at full-term, with a birth weight of 2,800 g. There was no history of neonatal asphyxia, convulsions, hepatitis, tuberculosis, trauma, or other infectious diseases. He had no history of food or drug allergies. His parents were young and healthy with no family history of genetic metabolic diseases. The boy was born with varus deformity and ulnar deviation of the fingers. Since his 26th day of life, he has undergone four intermittent plaster corrective operations at a hospital in Guangdong. At 70 days of age, he was treated with percutaneous loosening and Ponseti plaster fixation of the bilateral Achilles tendons for congenital equine varus foot; since then, he has worn orthopedic braces for at least 3 hours every day. At the age of 5 months, he was given an orthopedic brace at a hospital in Beijing due to finger contracture deformity. A physical examination at 9 months showed that the patient's head circumference was 44 cm and that his anterior fontanelle was unenclosed at 1.0 cm × 1.0 cm. His facial features included a broad nasal bridge, large nares, a long philtrum, and micrognathia. There were no abnormalities in eye distance or the palatal arch, and the palmprints of his hands were normal. No obvious abnormalities were found in the lungs, chest, anus, or external genitalia. However, he had a right inguinal hernia that developed when crying and spontaneously recovered. The muscles of the patient's limbs and torso were flaccid, and he had developed hypotonia. Neither the knee reflex nor the Achilles tendon reflex was elicited. He had no sleep problems, breathing problems, or problems when exercising. Thyroid function and myocardial enzymes showed no abnormalities. The results of a blood test performed on the patient were as follows: myoglobin, 37 ng/ml; creatine kinase, 171 IU/L; lactate dehydrogenase, 280 IU/L; aspartate aminotransferase, 31 IU/L; and creatine kinase–MB, 7.42 ng/ml. The patient's brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and electroencephalogram data were normal, and no characteristic lesions were found via electromyography. A color Doppler ultrasound revealed a patent foramen ovale in his heart (1.4 mm). At the age of 9 months, the child had low muscle tension in the limbs and neck, an unstable vertical head position, and could not turn over or sit up on his own. The Bailey Infant Development Scale Assessment: Intelligence revealed the patient's intelligence to be consistent with that expected at 6 months of age, and his developmental index was less than 50, indicating developmental delay. His Peabody Motor Developmental Scale (PMDS) score was low, with a gross motor development score of 62. His fine motor development was at a medium to low level.
test_results: Peripheral blood samples were collected from the child and his parents and subsequently sent to Suzhou Sai fu Medical Laboratory for testing.
diagnosis: CLIFAHDD syndrome with a novel variant in the NALCN gene

case_report: A 49-year-old male patient presented with a history of low vision following a childhood traffic accident. He underwent laser treatment in both eyes at the age of 12 and again one month prior to the current visit. Additionally, he had bilateral laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis in 2002. His medical and family histories were otherwise unremarkable. He was born full term via normal delivery. Ophthalmologic examination revealed visual acuity of 0.4 in the right eye and 0.3 in the left eye, with mild cortical lens opacities.
test_results: Fundus photography showed straightening of the temporal retinal vascular arcades and temporal dragging of the macula in both eyes. Previously applied laser spots with corresponding preretinal fibrosis were observed in the temporal periphery. FFA revealed leakage due to persistent retinal NVE in the right eye. Optical coherence tomography revealed disrupted macular contour associated with epiretinal membrane in the right macula and minimal perifoveal thinning in the left macula.

case_report: A 25-year-old female with a history of epilepsy arrived at the emergency department with fever, loss of appetite, and uncontrolled seizures over the past month. The seizures were generalized, tonic-clonic, lasting about ten minutes, and included tongue biting, fecal and urinary incontinence, and postictal confusion. These episodes occurred monthly. The fever was high grade, intermittent, and temporarily relieved by medications and cold sponging, without associated rigors or chills. The patient also experienced poor appetite and sleep. She had multiple previous hospital admissions for seizure management, but no brain imaging had been conducted. Her medical history included delayed motor, language, and cognitive development, and she had been bedridden and requiring nursing care since childhood. A skin lesion had been present on her face since birth. There was no significant surgical history. She was on anti-epileptic medications, but records were unavailable. On examination, she was drowsy, of average height and build, with a dark, pigmented skin lesion on the midline of her face, extending from the submental region to the lower lip and from the nasal bridge to the forehead. The lesion was greasy to touch. She appeared pale and dehydrated, with a temperature of 102°F, pulse of 106 bpm, and BP of 90/60 mm Hg. Her right eye had multiple raised dark pigmented lesions on the temporal sides of the optic discs, and both corneas were hazy in the periphery. She had poor oral hygiene with shallow oral ulcers. Neurologic examination showed a GCS of 6/15, supple neck, reactive pupils, and upgoing plantars. Tone and reflexes were normal, but she was aphasic, and power, sensory, and cerebellar systems could not be assessed. The rest of the systemic examination was unremarkable. A urinary catheter was in place. Laboratory results showed hemoglobin of 13.4 mg/dL, platelet count of 182,000/mcL, and white blood cell count of 13,000/mcL. Urinalysis revealed 8-10 WBCs/HPF and 1-2 RBCs/HPF. Serum electrolytes, renal function tests, and liver function tests were normal. Urine culture results were unavailable due to a laboratory error. Serum calcium was 9.9 mg/dL, and blood glucose level was 120 mg/dL. An ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis was normal. Skin histopathology was not performed due to patient preference.
test_results: An MRI of the brain with contrast showed congenital cerebral malformations with cortical dysplasia and multiple hamartomas in the medial temporal lobe, thalamus, and periventricular region on right side and cerebellar atrophy with Dandy-Walker variant.

case_report: A 42-year-old woman reported a decrease in vision in the right eye for the past 4 days. Snellen's best corrected visual acuity measured 20/40 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. She had no history of systemic conditions or recent illnesses. The anterior segment examination was unremarkable. Intraocular pressure was within normal limits. Color vision testing showed normal results. Fundus examination showed bilateral glistening retinal reflexes throughout the posterior pole extending to the equator, with a wrinkled cellophane-like appearance in the right eye.
test_results: Spectral Domain-OCT in the right eye showed abnormal internal limiting membrane (ILM) in folds, schitic spaces between ILM and nerve fiber layer, intraretinal schisis with serous detachment at macula. Left eye OCT revealed a normal fovea with an epiretinal membrane along inferior macula. Fundus fluorescein angiography in the right revealed normal early phase with hyperfluorescence and staining along vessels in late phases. It was normal in the left. Electroretinogram in the affected right eye had reduced b wave and left was normal.

case_report: A 55-year-old female with a 25-year history of diabetes mellitus and a three-year history of hypertension, both managed with medications, presented with swelling on the lateral side of her right foot for one week. The swelling began gradually in the plantar area of the right foot and increased in size, accompanied by pain during walking. The pain was throbbing in nature and did not radiate. Additional symptoms included redness, warmth, pus discharge, and generalized fever. The patient reported no history of trauma. Her medical history includes a 15-year presence of a foreign body (plastic) in the plantar area of her right foot, for which she did not seek medical attention. During a subsequent pregnancy, she experienced fever and swelling in the same area, leading to hospital admission. She underwent bedside irrigation and debridement, multiple incisions and drainage procedures in the operating room, and a three-month hospital stay. She was later referred to another hospital for a skin graft. On examination, there was swelling in the plantar area of the right foot with a 2x3 cm collection, negative fluctuation, warmth, redness, tenderness, and pitting edema on the dorsum of the foot, but no pus or blood discharge. An unhealed ulcer was noted on the lateral aspect of the sole. Neurovascular examination was normal.
test_results: The right foot X-ray revealed an accessory bone growth at the base of the fifth metatarsal bone. Ultrasound was requested to rule out deep tissue collection; the report was suggestive of a collection measuring about 3x1 cm in maximum diameter on the lateral aspect of the right foot, with no internal vascularity, and diffuse subcutaneous edema in the dorsum aspect of the right foot. A CT scan was done on the patient. It showed evidence of an accessory bone seen posterior to the proximal fifth metatarsal base with evidence of articulation point to the cuboid bone. The fracture line was seen traversing this accessory bone.

case_report: A 31-year-old woman, who has been pregnant six times and has five live births, presented with a history of 13 weeks without menstruation and a slightly elevated serum βhCG level. Pelvic examination revealed an enlarged uterus measuring approximately 10–12 weeks in size, which was non-tender, mobile, and soft. The cervix was soft, and the adnexes were free. Upon admission, her serum β-hCG level was 190 IU/ml. Ultrasound examination showed endometrial thickening of 22 millimeters (mm). Two cystic lesions measuring 26 mm × 16 mm and 18 mm × 13 mm were observed within the endometrial cavity. The patient underwent therapeutic dilation and curettage (D and C). During the procedure, the uterus was noted to be soft and contained necrotic tissue not resembling typical products of conception. Severe vaginal bleeding occurred post-procedure, which was managed with bimanual massage, oxytocin infusion, and rectal prostaglandin.
test_results: Microscopic study of the curettage specimen revealed sheets of intermediate trophoblastic cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, large nuclei, nuclear atypia, and <2 mitoses/10 high-power fields (HPF). Fibrin deposition was seen in the background. The neoplastic intermediate trophoblastic cells showed invasion to the vessel wall.

case_report: Case 4 involves a 47-year-old man who is not related to family 1. He is not on any medication and works at a protected institution due to mild intellectual disability. He has no reported difficulties with physical activities and regularly runs distances of 25–30 km. He has undergone surgery for undescended testes and multiple surgeries for bilateral inguinal hernias. On physical examination, his height was measured at 159 cm (−3.4 SD) and his weight at 64 kg (−1.1 SD). Throughout his childhood, he experienced very short stature, with his height being 4 SDs below the norm at 9 years old. His physical features include widely spaced eyes, a flat nasal bridge, low-set ears, broad hands and feet, a single transverse palmar crease, and a sandal gap bilaterally. He also has a mild shawl scrotum and has been myopic since childhood (−5.5/−5.5), though his ophthalmological evaluations are otherwise normal.
test_results: A truncating likely pathogenic variant was detected in FGD1 (c.527dup, p.Leu177Thrfs*40). His muscle biopsy showed a higher prevalence of type 1 fibers and few COX-negative fibers. Mitochondrial enzyme complexes and citrate synthase activities were normal.

case_report: A 9-year-old boy reported a gradual reduction in the ability to open his mouth over the past 6 months. He experienced difficulty eating and maintaining oral hygiene for the past year, along with a burning sensation in the mouth when consuming spicy food and reduced salivation for the past 7–8 months. The patient disclosed a history of chewing tobacco and betel nut 20–25 times daily for the past 4 years, typically keeping it in the buccal vestibule on both sides for about 3–4 minutes before swallowing. Clinical examination showed a maximum interincisal distance of 11 mm. Intraoral examination revealed blanched and inelastic labial and buccal mucosa, with vertical and circular fibrous bands palpable on both sides, including the lower lip, upper lip, buccal mucosa, and retromolar region. Blanching was also observed in the vestibular mucosa, palatal mucosa, and floor of the mouth. The tongue exhibited restricted movements.
test_results: H&E-stained section showed juxtaepithelial hyalinisation and collagen fibres were arranged in separate bundles with dense inflammatory infiltrate.

case_report: A 19-year-old male with short stature was admitted for a compulsory health screening to qualify for disability benefits from the state social insurance agency. He is a university student who reported frequent falls without apparent cause, resulting in serious injuries, including a broken arm in the previous year. Consequently, he attends school daily under his mother's supervision. He is the second child of non-consanguineous, healthy parents of Turkish descent, with a healthy elder sister. There is no family history of short stature or congenital skeletal abnormalities. The patient was born at full term via vaginal delivery without complications but was small at birth and has remained shorter than his peers throughout his growth. He walked later than his peers and was frequently exempted from sports classes due to frequent falls. Despite these issues, his cognitive development and academic performance have been adequate, and he completed high school on time with his peers. His childhood medical history is otherwise unremarkable.
test_results: Sanger sequencing showed a homozygous mutation in the patient’s CANT1 gene [c.375 G < C (p. Trp125Cys)] and the same type of heterozygous mutation in both parent’s CANT1 genes.

case_report: A 27-year-old male of Arabic descent visited the dermatology clinic with concerns about bilateral, symmetrical, hyperpigmented patches on his upper back. These patches had been present since birth, gradually increasing in size and darkening over the years, and were accompanied by the development of sparse hair on the affected areas. The patient reported no factors that relieved or worsened the condition, and there were no symptoms such as pain, itching, bleeding, or ulceration. A comprehensive review of systems, as well as the patient's medical, surgical, drug, and allergy history, revealed no abnormalities. There was no family history of skin diseases or other medical or congenital conditions, and the patient's four siblings had no similar complaints or skin issues. The patient's antenatal history included a normal vaginal delivery without complications, full-term birth, and up-to-date immunizations. The mother was healthy and did not take any medications during pregnancy. Examination of the body, hair, nails, and mucous membranes showed no abnormalities. The patient had not previously sought treatment for the lesions. On local skin examination, the hyperpigmented patches were found to be bilaterally symmetrical on the upper back, with the right patch measuring 15 × 7 cm and the left patch measuring 17 × 9 cm. Both patches were homogeneous and brown with irregular borders and blotchy hyperpigmented macules, and they were associated with sparse hair growth. The skin texture of the patches was similar to that of normal skin.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed epidermal hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and focal regular elongation of rete ridges with clubbing. There was increased basal layer pigmentation. The dermis revealed focal areas with pigment incontinence. There was no increase in smooth muscle in the dermis or hyperplasia of the hair follicles.

case_report: A 37-year-old male, with no significant past medical history, was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) due to ongoing convulsive seizures. A nasopharyngeal swab test returned positive for SARS-CoV-2. Serum analysis, head CT scan, and toxicological examination showed no abnormalities. Initial treatment and intravenous Levetiracetam infusion (3000 mg/24 h iv) were administered but did not result in clinical improvement.
test_results: EEG was performed within the first 24 h, revealing generalized SE. Subsequent EEG showed a generalized delta slowing. Continuous EEG monitoring showed persistent generalized epileptic discharges compatible with non-convulsive status epilepticus (NCSE). Contrast-enhanced Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)—negative results; serum HIV, VDRL and hepatitis virus panel—negative; CSF analysis—CSF protein concentration was 56.7 mg/dL, glucose 66.1 mg/dL, 1 mononuclear white blood cell, and CSF culture and PCR yielded negative results; serum and CSF onconeural antibody and antineuronal surface antigens antibody were found positive for anti amphiphysin antibody.

case_report: A nine-year-old female patient presented to the otorhinolaryngology department with a history of mouth breathing since childhood. The patient exhibited disarticulated speech. External examination revealed elongated facial features, acute-angled nasolabial folds, open-mouth breathing, and a receding lower jaw. Dentofacial findings included facial asymmetry with deviation to the left, an anterior open bite, a downward tongue position, crowded teeth, and a high arched palate with a receding lower jaw. Further radiological investigations were conducted based on the patient's history.
test_results: On the evaluation of cervical vertebral radiographs, an incidental finding of fusion of the body of the C2 and C3 vertebra was revealed. A CT study of paranasal sinus reported the fusion of the body of C2 and C3 vertebrae.

case_report: A 57-year-old female with a medical history including hyperlipidemia, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, depression, and hypertension was brought to the emergency department following a cardiac arrest at home. CPR was administered by her son before EMS arrived, and return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) was achieved by paramedics en route to the hospital. Initial EKG during the cardiac arrest showed ventricular fibrillation. Post-ROSC EKG revealed multiple premature ventricular contractions, a new left bundle branch block, a PR interval of 166 ms, QRS duration of 129 ms, and QTc of 535 ms. Upon arrival at the emergency department, she was intubated, a left internal jugular triple-lumen central venous catheter was placed, and she was admitted to the ICU. During her ICU stay, she experienced another episode of ventricular fibrillation with loss of pulse, requiring two additional rounds of CPR, amiodarone bolus and infusion, and one shock at 150 joules. A critical care panel revealed a potassium level of 1.7, which was corrected with a total of 260 meq of potassium administered during and after the arrest. No bicarbonate or phosphorus was given during the code or hospitalization. Subsequent EKGs showed a reduction in QTc to 450 ms after potassium replacement. Admission labs indicated critical hypokalemia, and her potassium levels fluctuated, requiring daily oral potassium supplementation of 40-80 meq per day. She was later treated with amiloride and sacubitril-valsartan to help maintain potassium levels. Point-of-care ultrasound and chest x-ray showed no cardiac tamponade or pneumothorax. CT scans of the head and cervical spine were negative for acute processes, and a CT angiogram of the chest ruled out pulmonary embolism. Her mother provided additional patient history, revealing a negative nuclear medicine cardiac stress test 10 months prior due to dyspnea on exertion. Home medications included escitalopram, aspirin, and rosuvastatin. A left heart catheterization showed nonobstructive coronary artery disease, and a cardiac MRI ruled out infiltrative cardiomyopathy. The hypokalemia was new onset, with no prior history of hypokalemia and no recent changes to home medications. There were no diuretics in her home medications, and she had no recent gastrointestinal symptoms. Admission urine electrolytes were elevated, with a positive urine anion gap and a transtubular potassium gradient (TTKG) of 9, indicating renal potassium losses. Further evaluation included a negative renal artery duplex, normal cortisol levels, and plasma aldosterone and renin levels that did not indicate primary hyperaldosteronism. An HIV test was negative, and magnesium levels remained normal throughout admission. Persistent hypokalemia required ongoing daily supplementation.
test_results: The results of these tests did not suggest any monoclonal gammopathy.

case_report: An eight-month-old male infant from a rural area, admitted to the hospital with recurrent convulsions since four months of age and recurrent respiratory difficulties since six months of age, which worsened over the past seven days and was accompanied by fever. The mother reported that the baby was not growing or developing at the same rate as other children of the same age and sex in the community. The child had been hospitalized twice before for bronchopneumonia. The infant has three brothers; the eldest is five years old, and the middle one died at fifteen days old. The family lives in a two-room mud house without a sanitary latrine, drinks water from a tube-well, and bathes in a pond. The parents are laborers with a monthly income of approximately one thousand rupees. The baby was exclusively breastfed for four months and then weaned with suji, biscuits, rice, and dal, which continue to be part of the diet. On examination, the baby was conscious but irritable, with fair complexion, chubby cheeks, light-colored sparse woolly hair that was easily pluckable. Anthropometric measurements showed a weight of 4.5 kg, length of 63 cm, head circumference of 40.5 cm, and chest circumference of 36.5 cm. There was mild pallor, and the skull, spine, and bones were normal. Vital signs included a pulse of 90/min, blood pressure of 70/50 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 55/min, and normal temperature. Central nervous system examination revealed repeated myoclonic seizures of the limbs, hypertonic limbs, hypotonic trunk, generalized muscle wasting with power grade 3/5. Examination of the respiratory system showed features of pneumonia. Other systems appeared normal.
test_results: The serum copper level was 10.25 microgram/dl. Serum ceruloplasmin level was 7.3 mg/dl. The MRI study of the brain revealed prominent bilateral extra-axial C.S.F. spaces with gliosis in both posterior parieto-occipital area with prominent left lateral ventricle and cerebellar folias. MR angiography revealed tortuosity of the cerebral vessels. EEG showed gross generalized polyspike waves. Opthalmoscopic examination showed pale optic disc. Microscopic examination of hair revealed classical sign of pili torti.

case_report: An 18-month-old boy presented with three scalp swellings that began as pea-sized lumps at 10 months of age. These swellings progressively increased in size, ulcerated, and developed purulent discharge over five days. He was the fourth child of a couple with a third-degree consanguineous marriage and was born via normal vaginal delivery following an uneventful full-term pregnancy. There was no family history of similar features. The patient exhibited delayed physical developmental milestones and dentition, along with failure to thrive and difficulty in feeding. Mental development, anthropometric measurements, and vitals were normal. Auscultation revealed a 2/6 late systolic murmur in the pulmonic valve area. Laboratory tests showed a platelet count of 820,000 cells/mm3 and anti-hepatitis C virus (HCV) antibodies. Three scalp swellings (5x6 cm; 6x7 cm; and 7x7 cm) were noted, which were soft-to-firm in consistency with central ulceration in two of them. The swellings had non-fluctuating firm edges with a positive transillumination test. Other features included ulceration, discharge, and areas of granulation tissue and necrosis. Additionally, frontal bossing was noted with a depressed nasal bridge and multiple pearly pink papules over the bridge of the nose and the neck. An oral cavity examination revealed normal mucosa with gingival hyperplasia and delayed dentition. Furthermore, nodules were noted over both ears. Over the back, a hypertrophic verrucous skin-colored plaque of 10 x 4 cm was noted extending from the lower back to the anal margin. On musculoskeletal examination, bilateral wrist contractures with subcutaneous nodules and bilateral valgus deformities at the ankle with hyperpigmentation over the malleoli were noted. Chest radiography was unremarkable. Skull radiography revealed a large soft tissue lesion in the occipito-parietal region with no underlying bone involvement. Radiography of the hip joints revealed multiple symmetrical osteolytic areas in the proximal third of the femoral shaft. Bilateral knee radiography revealed symmetrical osteolytic lesions with narrow zones of transition at the proximal tibial diaphysis and soft tissue opacities. Bilateral hand radiographs revealed extension at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and flexion at the interphalangeal joints (IPJs), flexion contractures of the third, fourth, and fifth MCP joints and IPJs. Additionally, soft tissue opacities were noted on the dorsal and ventral aspects of the wrist joints, which were suggestive of soft tissue nodules. Dermoscopic examination of pearly papules over the nose, hypertrophic verrucous plaque over the back, and pearly papules and plaques over the neck revealed pinkish-white globules with peripheral brown pigmentation. Few scattered grey dots were also seen along with a few reddish globules.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the hypertrophic verrucous plaque revealed cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP) fibroblasts with plump nuclei and bland nuclear features scattered in the abundant dense eosinophilic hyalinized stroma. Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) staining highlighted the hyalinized stroma. Excision biopsy of a scalp swelling revealed fibroblasts with bland nuclear features embedded in the acellular eosinophilic hyalinized stroma. Additionally, few scattered vascular spaces and inflammatory cells were noted. PAS staining highlighted hyalinized stroma.

case_report: A 10-year-old male child came to our pediatric outpatient department with an inability to speak since birth and seizures starting at 5 years old, characterized by generalized tonic and clonic movements. He was delivered at term via vaginal delivery to parents who are not related by blood. The pregnancy, birth, and post-birth periods were without complications. There was a delay in language development from birth, but other developmental milestones were achieved normally. Physical examination revealed no other abnormalities, and his hearing was normal. Routine blood tests, including electrolytes and liver function tests, were within normal limits. Electroencephalography showed isolated bursts of sharp waves occurring independently on either side.
test_results: Magnetic resonant imaging (MRI) of brain showed grey matter lined cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) filled clefts, in bilateral frontal regions, extending from the pial surface of brain through the white matter to ependymal surface of bodies of lateral ventricles. On the left side, the cleft was communicating with the ventricle.

case_report: A 9-year-old male presented with a progressive increase in weakness in both lower limbs, reduced grip strength in both upper limbs, and difficulty walking over the past two years. There was no history of muscle pain, trauma, fever, recent vaccination, dog bite, or respiratory or gastrointestinal infections. Physical examination revealed decreased muscle strength in the lower limbs (3/5 in the right lower limb and 2/5 in the left lower limb) and upper limbs (4/5 in both hands). There were no dermal rashes or muscle hypertrophy observed. Muscle atrophy, exaggerated tendon reflexes, and fasciculations were noted. Laboratory tests, including serum creatinine phosphokinase levels, were within normal limits. Plain computed tomography of the brain showed no significant abnormalities.
test_results: T2-weighted imaging and additional fluid attenuating inversion recovery sequence showed hyperintense signals in the posterior limb of internal capsule involving corticospinal tract (CST) which was found to extending up to midbrain. The coronal images showed classical wine glass sign.

case_report: The patient, a 14-year-old boy, is the third child of an Albanian couple with no consanguinity. He was born following an uneventful pregnancy and delivery, and exhibited normal growth and neurological development. At 2 years old, he was hospitalized for severe anemia requiring a blood transfusion, though specific details of that episode are unavailable. At 14 years and 9 months, he experienced his first episode of generalized tonic-clonic seizures with loss of consciousness, followed by dark, 'coca-cola' colored urine. Laboratory tests showed myoglobinuria, elevated transaminases (AST 4559 U/I, normal 0–40; ALT 1198 U/l, normal 0–40), and significantly elevated CPK levels (138,000 U/l, normal 0–170). Echocardiography, abdominal ultrasound, brain CT, and EEG performed at the 'Mother Teresa' University Hospital Center in Tirana showed no abnormalities. Family history includes an older brother who was diagnosed with epilepsy and rhabdomyolysis at 14 years old and died at 17 years old during a sudden status epilepticus.
test_results: Exome sequencing revealed the homozygous pathogenic variant c.1001C > T (p.Ala334Val) of gene ALDOA, classified as likely pathogenic (class 2).

case_report: A 17-year-old female was born following a normal pregnancy and delivery. Her early motor development was typical. At the age of 12, she began experiencing difficulties with stair climbing and running. A neurological examination at age 16 revealed symmetrical weakness in the proximal lower limbs, reduced deep tendon reflexes, challenges in walking on heels and toes, flat feet, and mild scoliosis. She also had a mild intellectual disability that necessitated special education. Her serum CK level was measured at 1140 UI/L (normal range up to 170 UI/L). At 16 years and six months, a brain MRI showed no abnormalities. Ophthalmologic evaluation was unremarkable, and both electrocardiogram and echocardiogram results were normal.
test_results: We identified the same homozygous missense mutation in POMT2.

case_report: A 62-year-old male with a recent history of hypothyroidism presented with progressive neurological symptoms over 3–5 months, including cranial nerve and cerebellar deficits. Initial symptoms included nausea without vomiting, poor appetite due to food smelling foul, and anorexia without significant weight loss. Over the next month, he developed disequilibrium, constipation, and increased urination. He was diagnosed with hypothyroidism by his primary physician and started on levothyroxine. Following the initiation of levothyroxine, his symptoms worsened, leading him to discontinue the medication. His condition continued to deteriorate with worsening disequilibrium, gait instability, and paresthesias affecting the top of his head, left side of his face, thumb and index finger of his left hand, and the distal sacrum. One month prior to presentation, he experienced ongoing sensory changes, diplopia, insomnia, hiccups, tinnitus in the right ear, intermittent blurred vision, and worsening gait resulting in two falls. In the days leading up to presentation, he developed a hoarse voice but had no issues with dysphagia or swallowing. He described his gait as uncoordinated, with no generalized limb weakness or sensory changes except in his left hand. He denied fevers, night sweats, headaches, vertigo, respiratory symptoms, diarrhea, or vomiting. The patient reported being generally healthy with few medical conditions and regular annual physician visits. He had a history of farming until two years prior, then transitioned to mowing lawns and more recently to building operators on electric doors. He denied significant chemical or heavy metal exposure, did not drink alcohol regularly, and did not use recreational drugs. He had been a pheasant-hunting guide for many years and was concerned about Lyme disease, for which he tested negative. Symptoms worsened over the 1–2 weeks prior to admission, leading to an evaluation by endocrinology and a non-contrast MRI of the brain, which revealed parenchymal lesions in the posterior fossa and other lesions throughout the cerebrum.
test_results: Sections contained several foci of lymphocytic infiltration in the white matter of the cerebellum with sparing of the cortex. Rare histiocytic cells with larger pale nuclei were seen within the dense infiltrates of smaller lymphocytes. There were numerous CD3-positive T-lymphocytes in the perivascular spaces, but also extending with lower density into the surrounding white matter. CD20-staining revealed occasional small B-lymphocytes with no larger CD20-positive cells or atypical cells present. The in situ hybridization for an Epstein–Barr mRNA was negative.
diagnosis: Chronic Lymphocytic Inflammation with Pontine Perivascular Enhancement Responsive to Steroids
Orpha_name: Chronic Lymphocytic Inflammation with Pontine Perivascular Enhancement Responsive to Steroids

case_report: A 32-month-old boy was admitted with two days of irritability and fever. He was born at 40 weeks gestation via normal spontaneous vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 2.9 kg to a healthy 28-year-old mother. His delivery was uneventful, but he had flexion deformity of both middle fingers and was transferred for further evaluation and physical therapies in January 2002. During early infancy, he exhibited mild general hypotonia, a weak cry, and poor sucking. He experienced six epileptic seizures since the age of 15 months despite being on anti-epileptic medications. His developmental milestones were significantly delayed; he raised his head at 7 months, sat up at 26 months, and had not yet acquired the ability to stand. Physical examination revealed a flat and mid-hypoplastic face with prognathism, narrow and upward slanting palpebral fissures with hypertelorism, low-set ears, a small nose, widely spaced incisors, a carp-like mouth, and a round back. He exhibited repeated stereotyped behavior such as hitting his chin with his palm, often associated with emotional outbursts. Upon admission, he experienced a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting approximately one hour. His vital signs were: blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, pulse rate 138 bpm, respiration rate 32 bpm, and body temperature 38.5℃. Mild throat injection was noted, but other systemic examinations were normal. Neurologic examination showed he was alert, with normal cranial nerve function, decreased muscle tone in both extremities (grade IV/IV bilaterally), and physiologic deep tendon reflexes. There was no spasticity or pathologic reflex, and sensory functions were normal with no signs of meningeal irritation. Initial laboratory results were: hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL, platelet count 374,000/µL, and white blood cell count 11,780/µL. C-reactive protein was slightly elevated at 19.0 mg/dL on admission but normalized after three days. Urinalysis was normal, and all microbiologic studies were negative. A sleep electroencephalogram showed intermittent high-amplitude slow wave discharges from the temporo-occipital area, indicating mild cerebral dysfunction. Spine radiography revealed mild scoliosis, and an echocardiogram was normal.
test_results: HbH inclusions were detected under the microscope in 1.1% of brilliant cresyl blue stained RBCs. Mutation analysis for our patient showed a point mutation on the 9th exon in the ATRX gene of thymine to cytosine so that Trp(C), the 220th amino acid, was replaced by Ser(R).

case_report: A 71-year-old female with a 3-year history of severe pain during the ingestion of solids and liquids was admitted to our Department in October 2013. The patient reported sudden and intense pain episodes, primarily localized to the left side of the pharynx, triggered by eating solid foods and drinking liquids. These episodes had been worsening in recent months, significantly impacting her daily life. A neurological examination before treatment noted mild left-sided hearing loss and painful swallowing. No symptoms or signs related to compression of the tenth and eleventh cranial nerves were observed.
test_results: Presurgical MRI examination showed a significant anomaly of the PICA course. The vessel from its origin moved cranially describing a long intracisternal route. A double anomalous contact between PICA and IX, X, and XI nerves was present: At root entry or exit zone (REZ) and along the intracisternal tract of the nerve itself.
diagnosis: Glossopharyngeal neuralgia caused by a complex neurovascular conflict

case_report: A 4-year-old girl visited the outpatient department of orthopaedic surgery at VPIMS, Lucknow in July 2013 with a painless neck deformity present since birth, specifically torticollis on the left side. There was no history of maternal fever, hypertension, drug intake, or other significant events during pregnancy. She was born full-term via normal delivery at home and cried immediately after birth. Postnatally, there was no history of high fever or trauma, and she completed her vaccination schedule. Her overall physical and mental development was normal, with milestones such as neck holding, sitting, crawling, and standing achieved on time. She began walking in the ninth month, earlier than her elder brother. She attends school and is making satisfactory progress according to her teacher. She is described as shy, intelligent, and capable of understanding and performing exercises independently. She manages all her daily activities without assistance. Until her visit, she had not been seen by any doctor. On examination, she had a good build but was short in height, with her head tilted to the left side, a low hairline, and a short neck. The distance from the tip of the ear pinna to the upper border of the trapezius was significantly shorter on the affected side compared to the healthy side. Neck flexion was possible without facial asymmetry. Mild cervicodorsal scoliosis was noted on the left side of the neck. The cervical spine showed full flexion, partial extension, and limited rotation and lateral bending. There was no tenderness in the cervical spine. The left shoulder scapula was elevated, and while the right shoulder had a normal range of movement, the left shoulder showed limited movement, particularly in abduction beyond 90 degrees. Examination of the cardiovascular, respiratory, and urinary systems revealed no abnormalities.
test_results: Radiological examination of cervical spine revealed blocked vertebrae C1, C2, C3 along with spinal bifida C6 & C7. Radiological examination of chest revealed high scapula on left side as compared with normal right shoulder joints.

case_report: A 19-month-old boy was referred to the pediatric endocrinology unit for low calcium levels and short stature. He is the third child of healthy consanguineous Turkish parents, who have two healthy boys and experienced two abortions. The family history showed no affected members. The prenatal period was normal. The child was born at term via Cesarean section with a birth weight of 3,200 g (+0.02 SDS). He experienced a convulsion due to low calcium levels on day 4 and received intravenous calcium and vitamin D supplementation. He was discharged on day 14 with phenobarbital therapy. From the age of 4 months, he was hospitalized three times for lower respiratory tract infections. At 19 months, physical examination showed his height, weight, and head circumference were at −3.1, −2.7, and +0.2 SDSs, respectively. Notable features included midface hypoplasia, swollen eyelids, down-slanting palpebral fissures, long eyelashes, long philtrum, high arched palate, low set ears, and a small jaw. Additional findings were a prominent forehead, an open anterior fontanelle (4 × 4 cm), pectus carinatum, a café-au-lait spot (4 × 3 cm) on the anterior thorax, and bowing of the femora and ulnae. Eye examination showed optic atrophy and horizontal nystagmus. There was a moderate delay in developmental milestones. Biochemical evaluation revealed serum calcium at 7.4 mg/dl (N: 9.0–11), phosphorus at 4.4 mg/dl (N: 4–6.5), ALP at 84 U/L (N: 116–450), albumin at 4.1 g/L (N: 3.5-5.5), PTH at 102.3 ng/L (N: 15–88), and 25-OH vitamin D at 27 μg/L (N: 30–100). Liver and kidney function tests, thyroid function tests, and ion levels were normal.
test_results: Skeletal survey showed diffuse osteosclerosis of the craniofacial, axial and appendicular skeletons, especially in diaphyseal areas of the long tubular bones. In the evaluation of the vertebral structures, end plate irregularities, mildly reduced height (platyspondyly) and thoracic and lumbar scoliosis were observed. Pelvic bones showed sclerosis, especially in the iliac bodies.

case_report: A 3.5-month-old male infant presented with skin lesions located on bony prominences. He is the second child from a consanguineous marriage, born at term via vaginal delivery with a birth weight of approximately 2.7 kg. Shortly after birth, the parents observed that the infant had difficulty moving his limbs and cried excessively when handled. Within a few weeks, the infant developed multiple raised brownish lesions on the knees, elbows, knuckles, and ankles. The parents also reported frequent episodes of loose stools, which were managed with oral rehydration solution (ORS) by a pediatrician. There is a family history of similar symptoms in an older sibling who passed away at 5 months due to recurrent chest infections. Physical examination revealed severe flexion contractures at both elbow and knee joints, leading to flexural intertrigo. The skin on the thighs, legs, arms, and forearms was indurated. Multiple hyperpigmented nodular lesions measuring 2-3 cm were noted on the knuckles, knees, and ankles. The scalp exhibited greasy scales and mild erythema. The abdomen was distended with prominent overlying veins, likely due to malnutrition and recurrent diarrhea. General examination showed macrocephaly, excessive facial hair, and eye discharge. Laboratory results included a hemoglobin level of 11.8 g/dl, a total leukocyte count of 6700/mm3 with a differential count of P 62%, L 35%, E 03%, and normal serum chemistry values (blood urea nitrogen: 16 mg/dl, serum creatinine: 0.7 mg/dl, SGOT: 20 IU/l, SGPT: 25 IU/l). An abdominal ultrasound did not reveal any major abnormalities.
test_results: Skin biopsy from one of the papulonodular lesions showed increased amount of amorphous eosinophilic material in the dermis on hematoxylin and eosin staining with a few ectatic blood vessels. Periodic acid Schiff (PAS) staining showed intensely eosinophilic amorphous material occupying the deeper dermis with hyperplasia of the fibroblasts. The deposited material did not stain with either Alcian blue or Masson's trichrome.

case_report: A 72-year-old male with a history of hypertension for the past 4 years reported a sudden onset of blurred vision in the left eye lasting for 4 days. His best-corrected visual acuity was measured at 6/18, N6 in the right eye, and light perception with inaccurate projection in the left eye.
test_results: Clinical examination indicated an immature senile cataract in both eyes with relative afferent pupillary defect in his left eye. Fundus examination of the right eye was within normal limits while the left eye revealed the presence of subtotal rhegmatogenous retinal detachment secondary to posterior vitreous detachment induced horseshoe tear.

case_report: A 20-year-old South Asian individual, identifying as male, visited the clinic with reports of intermittent reddish discoloration of urine over the past six months. This discoloration appeared to follow a cyclical pattern, occurring approximately once a month and lasting for three to five days each time. The patient also reported progressive breast enlargement. Two years ago, the patient was found to have hypertension and was prescribed nifedipine (60 mg/day). Physical examination revealed generalized hyperpigmentation and short stature. The patient exhibited facial hair, axillary hair, and pubic hair (Tanner stage 5), along with significant breast enlargement (Tanner stage 3). Genital examination showed normal pigmentation and rugosity, with a phallus measuring 10 cm and a single opening at its tip. The labioscrotal folds were fused bilaterally, and no testes were palpable in the labioscrotal folds or abdomen. Blood pressure was recorded at 140/80 mmHg in the right upper limb while supine. Routine blood tests indicated decreased potassium levels. The expected midparental height was calculated to be 152 cm for a male offspring and 139 cm for a female offspring, but the patient's height was 140 cm, below the third percentile. The patient had no developmental delays but had an early onset of pubic, axillary, and facial hair growth, as well as an increase in penis size, starting between seven and nine years of age. Family history revealed that the patient was born from a third-degree consanguineous marriage, with no palpable gonads at birth. Additionally, the patient's elder brother had a history of young-onset hypertension, short stature, and early puberty.
test_results: Elevated levels of adrenal hormone precursors, namely, 11-deoxycortisol and 11-deoxycorticosterone, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone was noted. Analysis revealed 44 autosomes and the presence of two X chromosomes (female genotype). Ultrasonography revealed bilateral enlarged, hyperplastic adrenal glands. Normal Mullerian structures including the uterus and two ovaries with follicles were clearly demonstrated. Also, the upper part of the vagina was clearly visualized. The uterus measured 5 x 2.7 x 2.2 cm, and both the ovaries measured 2.3 x 1.1 cm. The lower part of the vagina appeared to communicate with the posterior part of the urethra. The scrotum was empty, and no testes could be identified neither in the scrotum nor in the inguinal region. Additionally, bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis was also noted. MRI of the abdomen and pelvis corroborated the findings of adrenal gland enlargement and provided visual confirmation of the uterus and ovaries, which matched the measurements from ultrasonography. The MRI also confirmed the communication between the vagina and the posterior part of the urethra.
diagnosis: 46,XX Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia due to 11β-Hydroxylase Deficiency
Orpha_name: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency

case_report: The patient is a 30-year-old woman. She was born at full term following an uneventful pregnancy. Her parents are not related by blood. During her first year of life, her development was mostly typical, although she exhibited unstable crawling, muscular hypotonia, and nystagmus. She began speaking her first words at 1 year old and formed her first sentences by 2 years old. She started walking at 1.5 years old, but her gait and balance were noted to be abnormal. At 3 years old, her cognitive development was evaluated as normal, with the exception of mild slowness and clumsiness in fine motor skills.
test_results: Increased level of free sialic acid in the urine.

case_report: A 30-year-old female presented with blurred vision in her left eye for the past year. She had a history of glaucoma surgeries in both eyes 13 years ago, and her right eye had been blind (no light perception) for more than 10 years. Her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/100 in her left eye with a refractive error of -16.0D. The intraocular pressure (IOP) was measured at 54 mmHg in the right eye and 49 mmHg in the left eye. Examination revealed a very shallow anterior chamber in the right eye with significant lens opacity, making the retina unviewable. In the left eye, the anterior chamber was extremely narrow with a forward-bulging iris. The optic disc in the left eye appeared pale with a cup-to-disc (C/D) ratio of 0.99. Visual field testing using the Humphrey field vision test showed an extremely narrow tubular field of vision in the left eye. Due to the patient's history of glaucoma surgery, elevated IOP, small cornea, and extremely narrow anterior chamber, aggressive therapy was deemed necessary. A trabeculectomy was performed on the left eye, and atropine ointment was used to dilate the pupil. On the first postoperative day, the IOP in the left eye was reduced to 20 mmHg. The equator of the lens was visible through the dilated pupil, revealing a small, spherical lens with a slight upward dislocation. The suspensory ligaments were clearly visible under high magnification.
test_results: Anterior segment optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed a microspherophakic lens with horizontal diameter of approximately 9 mm and anteroposterior diameter of approximately 8 mm. General physical examination demonstrated short stature (145 cm) and brachydactyly.

case_report: The patient is a 14-year-old boy, the second child of healthy, nonconsanguineous Chinese parents, with a healthy older sister. He began walking at 1.5 years old, though his gait was clumsy and he frequently fell. These issues did not significantly impact his daily activities initially. His symptoms gradually worsened. By age 7, he experienced significant limb muscle weakness, making it difficult to stand from a squatting position and use chopsticks. He also developed scoliosis and pes cavus. At 14, he remains able to walk independently and feed himself with a spoon. Neurological examination showed a thin body habitus, scoliosis, and bilateral pes cavus. Severe weakness and foot eversion were observed without proximal muscle involvement. Distal muscle weakness was more pronounced (4/5 Medical Research Council score) compared to proximal muscles (5/5). Sensitivity to pinprick, touch, position, and vibration was reduced distally up to the knee and elbow, with vibration sensation more affected than pain sensation in all limbs. Sensory ataxia and a positive Romberg sign were present. Deep tendon reflexes were absent, and pathologic reflexes were negative. His gait was slightly broad-based and unsteady. Routine blood, urine, and stool tests were negative, and coagulation function and blood biochemical tests, including hepatic, renal function, glucose, lipid, and ion concentrations, were normal. Tumor biomarkers and autoimmune antibodies were negative, and serum M protein was also negative. Tests for hepatitis B and C, syphilis, and HIV were negative. Lumbar puncture showed cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure at 175 mmH2O (normal range, 80–180 mmH2O), CSF leukocytes at 1/mm3 (normal range, 0–5/mm3), and elevated CSF protein levels at 1627 mg/L (normal range, 150–450 mg/L), with a negative oligoclonal band. Chest X-ray, electrocardiogram, and transthoracic echocardiography showed no dysfunction. A cyst (1.1 × 0.8 mm) was found in the right kidney, but other organs were normal. Brain MRI was normal. Spinal MRI showed spinal scoliosis without abnormal signals. Fundus examination was normal.
test_results: Electrophysiologic examinations revealed absent compound muscle action potentials (CMAPs) in the median, ulnar, peroneal, and tibial nerves, and absent sensory nerve action potentials in the median, ulnar, and sural nerves. Motor nerve conduction velocity (NCV) and sensory nerve conduction were absent in all peripheral nerves. A needle electromyogram showed insertional activity (+), spontaneous activity (+), and severely reduced recruitment of motor unit potentials. Motor unit action potentials had a prolonged duration and increased amplitude (15.5 ms and 2793 µV, respectively, in the tibialis anterior muscle, and 9.1 ms and 1174 µV, respectively, in the first dorsal interosseous muscle). High-throughput sequencing technology identified a homozygous mutation, c.1174C>T (p.R392X), in exon 6 of PRX.

case_report: A 33-year-old female presented with a widespread vesicular rash on her trunk and extremities, consisting of 40–50 lesions at various stages of development, occurring 2 weeks after receiving a post-partum attenuated varicella vaccine. The lesions crusted and resolved within 10 days without further clinical issues. Physical examination revealed splenomegaly, which had been documented since she was 5 years old and was attributed to a past episode of infectious mononucleosis. Aside from recurrent mild upper respiratory infections, she had no significant health complaints, hospitalizations, infectious complications, or lymphadenopathy. Initial laboratory findings showed selective IgA deficiency and CD4 lymphopenia (111–118 cells/μL). She was referred to the NIH Clinical Center for further evaluation. Imaging confirmed splenomegaly (17 cm cranio-caudal length) and identified modest mesenteric and retroperitoneal adenopathy.
test_results: Flow cytometric analysis of T-cell subpopulations confirmed CD4 lymphopenia (CD4 189 cells/μL), normal numbers of CD8 T cells (383 cells/μL), and an increased proportion and absolute number of CD3+TCRαβ+CD4−CD8− double negative T cells (DNT) (4.3%, 33 cells/μL). High proportion of cycling of CD4 T-cells and DNT (Ki67 12 and 42%, respectively) as well as increased PD-1 expression in CD4 T-cells (42%) were found. The proportion and absolute number of total B cells were within normal range (CD19+: 16.4%, 75 cells/μL). Total IgG levels were moderately elevated (1,716 mg/dL), IgM were within normal range (54 mg/dL), while IgA undetectable. Bone marrow biopsy showed scattered lymphocytic aggregates with prevalence of CD8+ cells. Targeted NGS with custom target enrichment revealed a novel heterozygous missense variant in the death domain (NM_000043 c.719T>A p.M240K) of the FAS gene and was confirmed by direct Sanger sequencing. FAS-induced apoptosis was evaluated in a crosslinking assay. Apoptosis was expressed as normalized fold-change of Annexin-V expression at different concentrations of crosslinking FAS antibody. In effector memory CD4 T-cells (CD3+CD4+CD45RA−CCR7−CD27−) from healthy individuals (n = 8), an average increase of 1.93 ± 0.2-fold increase in Annexin-V expression was found with 1,000 ng/mL of crosslinking FAS antibody. At the same concentration of crosslinking FAS antibody (1,000 ng/mL), the Annexin-V expression remained unchanged in the index patient (1.06 ± 0.1-fold, n = 4). Similarly, while Annexin-V expression increased significantly in DNT TCRαβ+ T-lymphocytes of healthy individuals (1.57 ± 0.07 with 1,000 ng/mL, n = 8), it remained unchanged in the index patient (0.94 ± 0.03-fold, n = 4). Functional characterization of the novel FAS genetic variant also included FAS-induced apoptosis and sensitivity to activation-induced-cell-death (AICD) assays on T cell blasts. A significant reduction of FAS-induced apoptosis was found in T cell blasts from the index patient at all concentration of crosslinking FAS antibody: at the highest concentration (1,000 mg/mL), Annexin-V expression increased in CD4 (3.06 ± 0.2-fold, n = 6) and CD8 (2.8 ± 0.3-fold, n = 6) blasts from healthy individuals but remained substantially unchanged in CD4 (1.2 ± 0.05-fold, n = 3) and CD8 (1.2 ± 0.1-fold, n = 3) blasts from the index patient. Similarly, a significant reduction in AICD was found in T cell blasts of the index patient: the proportion of dead cells after stimulation with the highest concentration of PHA (50 μg/mL) increased in CD4 (6.8 ± 0.3-fold, n = 6) and CD8 (13.7 ± 2-fold, n = 6) blasts from healthy individuals but to a lower extent in CD4 (3.3 ± 0.25-fold, n = 3) and CD8 (8 ± 1.2-fold, n = 3) blasts from the index patient. Further immunological evaluation of the patient included measurement of plasma cytokines and showed an increased level of soluble FAS ligand (801 pg/mL, normal level < 200 pg/mL) and increased levels of Interleukin-18 (7,248 pg/mL).

case_report: A 43-year-old white male presented with recurrent sinusitis, ankle and knee arthritis, painless nodular skin lesions on extremities, and eosinophilia in 2008. His medical history includes long-standing pancytopenia and myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) diagnosed in 1996 at age 30, following complaints of spontaneous rectal bleeding and fatigue, initially attributed to haemorrhoidal disease. Six years post-MDS diagnosis, he was hospitalized with hepatosplenomegaly, erythema nodosum, retroperitoneal lymph node enlargement, and bilateral pleural effusion. Laboratory tests did not reveal any fungal, bacterial, or HIV infections. Chronic granulomatous pleuritis was identified, and he was treated empirically for tuberculosis with isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide, later switching to ethambutol due to pyrazinamide allergy. Blood tests showed pancytopenia with low monocytes (haemoglobin 7.7 g/dL; WBC 3000 cells/μL; lymphocytes 750/μL; monocytes 60/μL; platelets 95,000/μL). One year later, monocytopenia slightly improved, but thrombocytopenia worsened (WBC 1900 cells/μL; lymphocytes 475/μL; monocytes 114/μL; platelets 33,000/μL). In 2006, he developed respiratory distress, and bronchial analysis was negative for bacterial infection. He was treated with clarithromycin. In 2007, he experienced a 27% total body weight loss, night fever, night sweats, Raynaud phenomenon, left thigh superficial thrombophlebitis, and painless perimalleolar ulcers. Skin and bone marrow biopsies were performed. The ulcer biopsy showed vasculitis with eosinophils, and the bone marrow biopsy revealed myelodysplastic features and noncaseating granuloma, with negative myeloculture. In 2008, he developed hypothyroidism, recurrent sinusitis, ankle and knee swellings, and nodular skin lesions. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies and antinuclear antibodies were normal. Blood tests showed WBC 28,610/μL with marked eosinophilia (5440/μL). Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy confirmed MDS without excess blasts. After 3 months of prednisone (50 mg/day), he developed arthritis and sustained night fevers. Blood culture, arthrocentesis, and thyroid biopsy were performed, identifying Mycobacterium kansasii in the bloodstream and synovial fluid. Thyroid histopathology showed chronic and acute granulomatous inflammation. He was treated with rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, and clarithromycin for 2 years. Progressive spleen enlargement led to splenectomy in 2010, followed by portal thrombosis, treated with oral anticoagulants. Histopathology of the spleen showed granulomatous inflammation, abscesses, and central necrosis. In 2012, blood tests revealed increased WBC (39,080/μL) with eosinophilia (20,630/μL) and thrombocytosis (1,099,000/μL). The nitro blue tetrazolium test indicated a phagocytosis defect, and FIP1L1/PDGFRa rearrangement was negative. He was treated with hydroxyurea, dexamethasone, and anti-NTM therapy including moxifloxacin until 2015, when MDS refractory anaemia with excess blasts (12%) type II (RAEB II) was identified.
test_results: A heterozygous germline GATA2 (c.1061 C > T; p.T354 M) mutation was determined by Sanger sequencing of peripheral blood leukocytes.

case_report: A 56-year-old woman with a history of rheumatism reported experiencing right upper abdominal distension for the past two weeks. The distension worsened after meals and improved with rest. She denied any decrease in urine output, nausea, vomiting, fever, or chills. Physical examination findings included: temperature of 37.2 °C, blood pressure of 123/70 mmHg, heart rate of 70 beats per minute, and respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute. There was no jaundice observed. Cardiac, pulmonary, and neurologic examinations were normal. Dermatologic examination showed pigmentation on both lower extremities. Laboratory tests revealed elevated indirect bilirubin (15.2 μmol/L; reference range: 1.7–10.2 μmol/L), decreased albumin (34.8 g/L; reference range: 38–48 g/L), mild anemia with hemoglobin (97 g/L; reference range: 110–150 g/L), and elevated CA125 (39.4 U/mL; reference range: < 35 U/mL). Other tumor markers, creatinine, autoimmune markers, and serum IgG4 levels were within normal limits. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan showed a rim of soft-tissue density in the retroperitoneum extending and encasing the upper end of the bilateral ureters, leading to bilateral hydronephrosis due to ureteral obstruction. Additionally, there was an abnormally enhanced soft tissue density in the gallbladder associated with dilatation of the hilar bile duct and proximal biliary ducts. A cystic density lesion was also noted in the tail of the pancreas. Surgical intervention included abdominal adhesiolysis, cholecystectomy, partial hepatectomy, bilateral intraoperative transurethral ureteral stenting, and cyst puncture. The retroperitoneum contained white and hard fibrous tissue.
test_results: Pathologic examination showed mild chronic inflammation of fibrovascular tissue, diffuse proliferation of collagen fibers, interstitial edema, no increase in the proportion of plasma cells stained by IgG4, and no cell atypia.

case_report: A 13-year-old male patient presented with complaints of mobile teeth, bad breath, and yellowish discharge from the gums for the past 3 months. The mobility of teeth increased during chewing. His dental history indicated early loss of primary teeth around 3-4 years of age and mobility of permanent incisors and molars at 9-10 years. Skin lesions were observed on the palms and soles since the age of 3 years. He was the only affected member in his family among three siblings, with parents in a consanguineous marriage. General examination showed the patient was malnourished and anaemic, with noticeable hyperkeratosis on the phalanges of hands and feet, elbows, and knees. The bilateral submandibular and submental lymph nodes were tender and palpable. Intraoral examination revealed bright red gingiva in the upper and lower anterior regions and teeth numbers 36 and 46. The gingiva was soft and edematous in teeth numbers 12, 11, 21, 22, 23, and 24. Gingival recession was noted in the lower anterior region. There was an absence of stippling and generalized bleeding on probing. Teeth numbers 36 and 46 exhibited grade IV furcation involvement. Probing depths exceeded 10 mm in the upper and lower anterior regions and teeth numbers 36 and 46. Hard tissue examination showed 23 teeth present with teeth numbers 41, 16, and 26 missing. Inflammation, pus discharge, and grade III mobility were also observed. The patient's oral hygiene index was poor.
test_results: Since the sample showed the presence of 16s rRNA gene of A. actinomycetemcomitans, further detection of two virulence genes such as fap and lkt A was performed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). The DNA extraction from subgingival plaque sample was performed by boiling - lysis method and the supernatant were used as template for the PCR reaction. PCR products were subjected to 1.5% agarose gel electrophoresis in Tris–Borate EDTA buffer. The gel was stained with 0.5 μg/ml ethidium bromide and photographed under Biorad UV gel documentation system. A 100 bp ladder served as the molecular weight marker. The PCR reactions were performed in duplicate.

case_report: A 22-year-old Hispanic woman, previously in good health, experienced a severe headache (8 out of 10 on the pain scale) and blurred vision over the past 5 days. She visited the ophthalmology clinic due to a significant reduction in vision in her right eye more than her left, which gradually worsened over the 5-day period and began to interfere with her daily activities. She did not report any flashes of light or floaters in either eye. Visual acuity testing showed 20/70 in the right eye and 20/200 in the left eye. Intraocular pressures, as well as examinations of the conjunctivae, corneas, anterior chamber, and irises, were all normal. Upon dilation, the posterior chamber examination revealed optic nerve congestion and prepapilledema. There was also subretinal fluid beneath the maculae and around the optic nerves. She was referred to the hospital for further evaluation.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of brain with contrast revealed generalized leptomeningeal enhancement with 'sugar-coating' or 'zuckerguss pattern' in her vermis region of cerebellum. Her orbital MRI showed increased signal thickening at the posterior aspect of globes and focal enhancements. Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 150 mm H2O, glucose 58 mg/dL, protein 46 mg/dL, WBC 180 cells/μL, RBC count 25, lymphocytes 96%, neutrophils 3%, and macrophages 1%.

case_report: A 52-year-old male arrived at the emergency department after experiencing five consecutive generalized tonic-clonic seizures, marking his first seizure episode. The patient had been in good health until a week prior to admission, when he developed a mild fever and muscle aches. Shortly after his arrival at the emergency department, he had two additional generalized tonic-clonic seizures. His medical history included a diagnosis and treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis 11 years ago, but was otherwise unremarkable. Upon arrival, the patient had a mild fever (37.5°C), normal blood pressure, and a slightly elevated heart rate. After receiving 4 mg of lorazepam, a neurological examination showed the patient in a stuporous state, with normal pupillary reflexes to light, symmetrical pain response in both upper and lower limbs, and no signs of meningeal irritation or pathological reflexes.
test_results: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed a white blood cell count of five (granulocytes 40%, lymphocytes 60%), a red blood cell (RBC) count of 0, a protein level of 64 mg/dL, and a glucose level of 86 mg/dL (the synchronous serum value was 121 mg/dL) with normal opening pressure of 7 cmH2O. The CSF culture was negative, and virus antibodies for herpes simplex virus and varicella zoster virus were absent. His initial brain computed tomography (CT) and brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan were unremarkable.

case_report: A 34-year-old male with no known medical conditions presented with a 3-year history of a mass in the left orbital region. Ophthalmic examination revealed a firm, palpable mass located inferotemporally in the left orbit, with no associated skin changes. The patient's visual acuity, pupil response, anterior segment, posterior segment, and optic nerve examinations were all normal. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain and orbit, performed with and without contrast, showed a well-defined mass in the left inferotemporal orbit measuring 14 mm × 9.6 mm × 15.3 mm. The mass caused mild displacement of the globe but did not involve the globe itself, nor did it show any signs of bony invasion, remodeling, attachment to the extraocular muscles, or compression of the optic nerve.
test_results: Histopathologic examination revealed a grey-tan multinodular soft tissue. Microscopically, the tumor comprised of spindle-shaped cells embedded within the myxoid matrix. The tumor cells were arranged in a reticular growth pattern, nests, and perivascular pseudo-rosette. There was no mitotic activity, there were small cells showing eosinophilic to vacuolated cytoplasm, oval to round nuclei with inconspicuous nucleoli, revealing perivascular arrangement in some regions, and nests and cords in a myxoid background. Molecular genetic study utilizing fluorescence in situ hybridization was positive for Ewing Sarcoma Breakpoint Region 1 (EWSR1) chromosome.
diagnosis: Extraskeletal Myxoid Chondrosarcoma  of the orbit

case_report: A 43-year-old female presented with persistent generalized abdominal pain and intermittent vomiting over the past two months, unresponsive to over-the-counter medications. She also experienced multiple episodes of throbbing headaches over the past year, previously treated as migraines. Currently, she reports a worsening headache over the past week, generalized in nature, with no specific aggravating or relieving factors, accompanied by bilateral ptosis and lightheadedness. She denies any history of febrile illness, seizures, limb weakness, sensory disturbances, or other preceding illnesses. There is no personal or family history of similar conditions. She does not smoke or use substances, but occasionally consumes alcohol. On examination, she was hemodynamically stable and well-oriented to time, place, and person.
