Eye examination showed bilateral ptosis with horizontal gaze palsy and normal pupils. Fundus examination was normal, with no signs of meningeal irritation. Cranial nerve examination was normal, and neurological examination revealed ataxia. The remainder of the systemic examination was unremarkable.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed hyperintense signals in a widespread brain area. Electroencephalography (EEG) showed generalized slowing with no epileptiform activity. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed severe metabolic acidosis with a pH of 7.12. A repeat brain MRI showed hyperintense signals in bilateral basal ganglia, brain stem, and white matter. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed an elevated lactate level of 3.9 mmol/L (normal: 1.1-2.3). Muscle biopsy from the quadricep muscle exhibited reduced cytochrome oxidase (COX) activity. Her muscle deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) was extracted and analyzed for a complete mitochondrial genome, which showed no pathognomonic mutations.

case_report: A 44-year-old male was admitted to our hospital in January 2019 with the following chief complaints: involuntary movements for over 10 years, memory loss and emotional instability for 3 years, and episodes of consciousness loss with convulsions for 1.5 years. The patient initially developed involuntary movements in the extremities, which gradually spread to the mouth, tongue, face, neck, and shoulders, accompanied by abnormal postures and unstable walking. Approximately 7 years later, he experienced memory loss, emotional instability, and childish behaviors. One and a half years ago, he began having episodes of consciousness loss with convulsions lasting several minutes, occurring 1 to 2 times per month without an obvious aura. There is no reported medical history. Family history indicates that the patient's mother had mild involuntary movements. One elder brother, who died 10 years ago without a confirmed diagnosis, experienced involuntary movements and mental disorders. Another elder brother also developed mild involuntary movements, while his sister, father, and son were unaffected. Neurological examination showed slurred speech, irritation, and childish behavior. Memory, orientation, and calculations were normal. Involuntary movements were observed in the extremities, mouth, face, neck, and shoulders. The patient had an unstable posture and awkward gait. Muscle power in the extremities was normal, muscle tone was reduced, and tendon reflexes in all four limbs were diminished. Brain MRI revealed significant atrophy of the bilateral caudate nuclei and mild atrophy of the bilateral putamen. Arterial spin labeling showed reduced total cerebral perfusion and increased delayed frontobasal perfusion. Electroencephalography indicated slowing of background activity and intermittent rhythmic delta activity in all electrode recordings. Electromyography and nerve conduction studies showed neurogenic damage at the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar segments, with sensorimotor axonal damage at the cervical segment and motor axonal damage at the thoracic and lumbar segments. The patient scored 21 points on the Mini-Mental State Examination, with impaired memory performance, particularly in naming and writing ability. The Hamilton Anxiety Scale score was 4 points, indicating no anxiety, and the Hamilton Depression Scale score was 9 points, indicating mild depression. The electrocardiogram was normal, and heart Doppler ultrasound showed mild mitral regurgitation. A peripheral blood smear revealed 3% acanthocytes. The level of creatine kinase was elevated to 825 U/L (normal range: 38–174) and creatine kinase-MB was increased to 5.47 μg/L (normal range: 0–5.00).
test_results: Whole exon sequencing studies revealed a novel frameshift mutation caused by a nucleotide variation in exon 2 (452delA) in the XK gene. This deletion of nucleotide 452 A in the coding region leads to an amino acid residue conversion from Gln to Arg and early termination of the XK protein (Gln151ArgfsTer2). The proband and one of his older brothers were hemizygotes, and his mother was heterozygous. This variant occurs at a very low frequency in the population.

case_report: A 33-year-old female arrived at the emergency department with reduced vision in her left eye, hearing loss in her left ear, and numbness on the left side of her face. Her medical history includes schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, intravenous drug use, and a 30 pack-year smoking history. Physical examination revealed decreased vision in the left eye, hearing loss in the left ear, and mild difficulty with speech. The remainder of the neurological examination was normal.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed four lobulated heterogeneous enhancing masses in the left CPA, right internal auditory canal, the atrium of the left ventricle, and the left foramen of Monroe. The largest was in the CPA, measuring 2.1 x 3.5 x 3.1 cm with surrounding vasogenic edema. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and MRI total spine were negative for tumor. The tumor consisted of pleomorphic epithelial cells, frequently with vacuolated cytoplasm, arranged in a well-defined papillary pattern. The tumor cells were positive for AE1/AE3, CK7, prealbumin (transthyretin), S100, synaptophysin, and vimentin. They were negative for CEA, CK20, EMA, ER, GATA3, GFAP, Napsin A, p16, PAX8, TTF1, and WT-1. Rare scattered cells were positive for p53. The Ki67 index was visually assessed as 30%-40%.
diagnosis: Primary Choroid Plexus Carcinoma, WHO Grade III

case_report: A 17-year-old male with SCT AS pattern presented to the outpatient department with a one-month history of fever, generalized weakness, dizziness, and disturbed sleep. The patient had a previous diagnosis of SCT and nephrotic syndrome at the age of 14, with a history of hospitalization for thrombocytopenia. On examination, the patient exhibited yellowish discoloration of the eyes, pallor, and pitting edema over the lower limbs. The pediatrician recommended admission for further evaluation. Blood tests were performed, including complete blood count, kidney function test, liver function test, and direct Coombs test (DCT). The DCT was positive. Treatment with antibiotics, analgesics, antipyretics, folic acid, and hydroxyurea was initiated, but the fever and joint pain persisted. Additional assessments were initiated, given the absence of improvement in the patient's condition. Ophthalmology consultation was sought to investigate the persistent symptoms, and the examination revealed findings consistent with vitamin-A deficiency. Specifically, ocular manifestations indicative of vitamin-A deficiency were identified during the ophthalmologic assessment. Furthermore, nasal endoscopy conducted under local anesthesia identified grade-I adenoid hypertrophy as part of the comprehensive evaluation. Simultaneously, abdominal ultrasound revealed significant splenomegaly (16 cm) accompanied by mild ascites and acalculous cholecystitis. Repeat blood tests were performed to delve deeper into the diagnostic process.
test_results: The results indicated a copper excretion of 17.85 ug/24 hours.

case_report: The patient is a 17-year-old female presenting with proximal muscle weakness since early childhood. She is the second child of healthy, nonconsanguineous Russian parents. Her pregnancy and delivery were normal, with a birth weight of 3.80 kg and length of 52 cm. On the third day of life, she was hospitalized with pneumonia due to aspiration and required mechanical ventilation until 4.5 months old. This was her only episode of respiratory dysfunction. She experienced delayed motor development, holding her head up at 7 months, sitting at 16 months, walking at 21 months, and always needing support to stand. In early childhood, her mouth was slightly open when in a vertical position. Phrasal speech developed appropriately for her age. There was no history of seizures, and her vision and hearing were intact. At 9–10 years old, she developed a prominent scoliotic deformity of the spine, which was treated conservatively between ages 12 and 14. At 12 years old, she had surgery for ankle tendon retraction without general anesthesia. In recent years, her condition has slowly worsened, with marked gait disturbances, difficulty climbing stairs, and inability to rise from the floor independently. Her cognitive functions are normal, and she is currently studying at university. On examination, her height is 167 cm and weight is 62 kg. Phenotypic features include micrognathia, downturned corners of the mouth, and clinodactyly of the fifth finger of the right hand. Neurological examination revealed atrophy of the pectoral and proximal muscles, weakness in facial, neck, and limb-girdle muscles, positive Gowers’ sign, and asymmetric Trendelenburg’s gait. She also has kyphoscoliosis of the thoracic spine, lumbar hyperlordosis, and a prominent asymmetric hip position. Additionally, she has pes cavus on both sides. Leg tendon reflexes were absent, while biceps and triceps reflexes were normal. Creatine kinase levels were normal. Needle electromyography showed a myopathic pattern with no spontaneous activity.
test_results: The analysis revealed two heterozygous SNVs: c.862A>T, p.(Lys288Ter) and c.93del, p.(Lys32ArgfsTer78) in the STAC3 gene (ENST00000332782.7). The validation and segregation analyses of detected SNVs showed that each of the parents is a carrier of only one, which verifies the compound heterozygosity of SNVs in the proband. The healthy brother is a carrier of the heterozygous variant c.862A>T, p.(Lys288Ter).

case_report: A 66-year-old male with no significant past medical history presented with numbness and tingling in his bilateral lower extremities for 2 weeks, which gradually ascended to his calves and bilateral hands. Cervical spine and lumbar spine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) did not reveal any significant findings. Blood tests including thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), vitamin B12, homocysteine, methylmalonic acid, hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) were unremarkable. Electromyography (EMG) and a nerve conduction study (NCS) showed specific findings. After confirming the absence of IgA deficiency, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) was administered at a dosage of 0.4 g/kg for 5 days. The patient reported improvement in foot numbness and paresthesia 2 days after infusion. However, after 5 days, the patient experienced shortness of breath, lethargy, and generalized weakness. Upon referral to our center, the patient's vitals were stable, and the physical examination was unremarkable. Chest X-ray was unremarkable. D-dimer, B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), and troponin levels were within normal limits, and electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm.
test_results: A blood workup revealed a drop in hemoglobin (Hb) levels from 13.5 to 8.3 g/dL within 3 days. Further workup to investigate hemolysis included an elevated reticulocyte count of 13% (normal range 0.5-1.5%), elevated bilirubin at 3.5 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) at 322 U/L, low haptoglobin at < 30 mg/dL, a positive direct antiglobulin testing (DAT) with IgG+, and negative complement. A peripheral blood smear showed normochromic normocytic anemia with 3+ spherocytes. The bone marrow biopsy revealed a hypercellular bone marrow with erythroid hyperplasia and negative flow cytometry.

case_report: A 37-year-old female presented with proximal muscle weakness, tachycardia, and chest pain. Blood pressure readings indicated hypertension, and she was prescribed amlodipine and benazepril, which further increased her blood pressure. A CT scan of the abdomen showed an adrenal incidentaloma in the right adrenal gland measuring 2.1 x 1.5 x 2.5 cm. The precontract density was 5 Hounsfield units, and a 15-minute delayed washout showed 11 Hounsfield units for a 72% washout. She was referred to endocrinology and visited the clinic on March 12, 2021. Physical examination revealed an obese female (BMI of 38.86 kg/m2) in no acute distress. Her blood pressure was 144/108 mmHg, pulse was 95, and she was afebrile. Thin silvery striations were noted on the abdomen, and alopecia was observed on the crown. Other systems were unremarkable. Family history included early-onset hypertension in her brother (age: 35 years) and mother (age: 30 years). Personal history included elevated anxiety, weight gain, frontal headaches, increased thirst, easy bruising with delayed clearance, and proximal muscle weakness affecting activities like climbing stairs and lifting heavy objects. Menstrual cycles were unchanged, and there was no history of exogenous corticosteroid use. Serum biochemistries showed normal TSH, creatinine, liver function tests, and serum electrolytes. However, aldosterone was mildly elevated (23 ng/dl), potassium was mildly low (3.3 mEq/L), and ACTH and DHEA sulfate were suppressed. The aldosterone to renin ratio was elevated at 59.9 on spironolactone and 71.4 three months after discontinuing spironolactone. A workup for elevated cortisol included serum cortisol, 24-hour urine-free cortisol, salivary cortisol, and a low-dose dexamethasone suppression test, but the results were nonconfirmatory.
test_results: The results revealed an inferior vena cava (IVC) cortisol of 20, left adrenal venous (LAV) cortisol of 81, and right adrenal vein (RAV) cortisol of 1280. The results of the IVC aldosterone were 24, LAV aldosterone was 660 and RAV aldosterone was 1500.

case_report: A 16-year-old male presented with non-bilious vomiting that began 5 days after being discharged from the hospital following posterior spinal fusion for scoliosis. He was born in Korea and adopted as a baby, with no known birth or biological family medical history. His past surgeries include left congenital diaphragmatic hernia repair shortly after birth, orchiopexy for undescended testis at age 5, Ladd procedure for small bowel malrotation and obstruction at age 6, and laparotomy for small bowel volvulus with lysis of peritoneal adhesions and appendectomy at age 14. His medical history includes left lung hypoplasia, ostium secundum atrial septal defect (ASD), left pulmonary vein stenosis, and chronic asthma, managed with fluticasone proprionate/salmeterol and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole. He had no known history of renal disease, vesicoureteral reflux, urinary tract infection (UTI), or embolic disease. He was a high school junior taking advanced placement courses. His height was 170 cm (between 25th and 50th percentiles for age) and weight was 35.9 kg (below 5th percentile for age). Vital signs included an oral temperature of 36.1°C, blood pressure of 127/76 mmHg, and heart rate of 81 beats per minute. Physical examination revealed a hyperdynamic precordium and a II/VI systolic murmur. He had a midline abdominal wall scar, normal bowel sounds, and no rebound tenderness or guarding. Scoliosis and a healing incision from recent spine fusion were noted. Micrognathia was present, but no other orofacial, ocular, aural, or limb deformities were observed. Laboratory results showed normal serum electrolytes, amylase, and lipase. Chest and abdomen radiographs indicated mixed bubbly lucencies and curvilinear opacities in the left lower hemithorax, suggesting the possibility of a recurrent diaphragmatic hernia with bowel migration into the chest. Abdominopelvic CT with oral and intravenous contrast was performed due to the complexity of the patient's anatomy and surgical history. CT findings included evidence of prior left diaphragmatic hernia repair and Ladd procedure with bowel malrotation. No recurrent diaphragmatic hernia was observed; pleuroparenchymal scarring and atelectasis at the left lung base, alternating with areas of relatively well-aerated lung, explained the plain radiographic abnormalities. There were no CT findings of bowel obstruction, mass, or inflammation. Renal craniocaudal dimensions were 7.5 cm on the right and 8.7 cm on the left, both below the 5th percentile for age. Both kidneys appeared abnormal, prompting further investigation into the patient's renal status. Serum creatinine was 1.2 mg/dL (reference range: 0.6-1.1 mg/dL), and blood urea nitrogen was 13 mg/dL (reference range: 6-20 mg/dL). Estimated creatinine clearance was 99.2 mL/min/1.73 m2. Hemoglobin was 12.7 g/dL and hematocrit was 36%, both within normal ranges. Urine dip testing showed no protein seven days prior to the CT scan, but protein was present in urine (30 mg/dL) on repeat dip testing done the day after CT scanning.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the biopsy specimen revealed normal parenchymal organization but hypertrophy of glomeruli and tubules. There were very few globally sclerotic glomeruli, but many tufts contained segmental zones of perihilar sclerosis. These changes were accompanied by streaks of fibrosis, tubular atrophy, and chronic inflammation. There was no evidence of renal dysplasia, medullary nephronophthisismedullary cystic disease complex or polycystic kidney disease. Electron microscopy demonstrated minimal foot process effacement and was negative for glomerular basement membrane changes.

case_report: An 18-year-old male with no history of systemic disease experienced sudden progressive blurring in the right eye, double vision, and drooping eyelid over a period of 5 days. His right eye movement was severely limited, except for lateral gaze, and his right pupil was affected. Two weeks prior to admission, he reported numbness starting in his left big toe, which gradually extended to the entire left sole. He reported no recent illnesses or vaccinations. The patient mentioned having two previous episodes of left abducens nerve palsy and numbness in his hands over the past 4 years, which resolved each time after taking oral prednisolone 15 mg for one week. Neurological examination showed complete paralysis of the right oculomotor nerve. The right eye was positioned downward and outward. Eye movement tests indicated a complete lack of adduction, upward, and downward movement in the right eye. The right pupil measured 7 mm compared to 4 mm on the left and did not react to light, with no relative afferent pupillary defect observed. Additionally, there was weakness in left ankle dorsiflexion and generalized reduction in reflexes. Sensory examination indicated decreased pin-prick and light touch sensations on the left sole, big toe, and second toe.
test_results: NCSs showed conduction blocks in the left median, left peroneal, and left tibial nerves and slow conduction velocities in the bilateral median and left tibial nerves. F waves in the bilateral tibial, left median, left ulnar, and left peroneal nerves were absent. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed cytoalbuminologic dissociation, with a total protein concentration of 50.8 mg/dL. Neuromuscular sonography revealed segmental swelling at the bilateral median, bilateral ulnar, bilateral tibial, and right sural nerves.
diagnosis: Multifocal Acquired Demyelinating Sensory and Motor Neuropathy
Orpha_name: Multifocal Acquired Demyelinating Sensory and Motor Neuropathy

case_report: We examined a 26-year-old female patient from an Italian family, along with her healthy parents and brother, who do not share any blood relation and show no symptoms. The patient began experiencing symptoms between the ages of 11 and 14. Laboratory tests revealed creatine kinase (CK) levels fluctuating from normal to 1,500 U/L. The patient's condition progressed, initially presenting with spinal contractures leading to spinal rigidity and scapular winging. Over time, she developed postural muscle atrophy and additional proximal muscle weakness in a limb-girdle distribution pattern, eventually resulting in the loss of the ability to walk.
test_results: Muscle biopsy at age of 13 years showed Z disk aggregates and atrophic type I fibers whereas type II fibers were hypertrophic. Electromyography showed axonal neuropathy.
Orpha_name: Autosomal dominant distal axonal motor neuropathy-myofibrillar myopathy syndrome

case_report: A seven-year-old girl was seen at The Department of Neurosurgery, Yuquan Hospital, Tsinghua University (Beijing, China) with a three-year history of episodic convulsions accompanied by loss of consciousness and worsening symptoms. The seizures primarily included absence seizures and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. The main clinical presentation involved a sudden bowing motion (slightly forwards and downwards, to the left) occurring either singly or in clusters. Occasionally, the body would slowly dip to the left and then to the right while the upper and lower limbs became stiff, indicative of absence seizures. These episodes lasted for about half a minute, not exceeding one minute, before subsiding. Oral medications such as oxcarbazepine, clonazepam, topiramate, and valproate provided limited symptom control, with seizure episodes occurring 4–10 times per month. There was no prior history of difficult birth, lack of oxygen, encephalitis, or any other medical conditions. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient’s family.
test_results: Brain MRI imaging revealed a clearly visible boundary in the right parietal region of the cerebral falx and the cortex. It appeared as a wedge, with the cutting-edge pointing to the white matter of deep lesions. The T1-WI had a low signal (long T1), while the T2-WI had a high signal (long T2) and FLAIR imaging showed a high signal, with a low signal in the center. No enhancement signals were detected by enhanced scanning. A visibly widened subarachnoid cyst was observed in the left temporal pole. Video electroencephalogram (VEEG) showed 1.2–2.5 Hz sharp wave and sharp slow wave (distributing or continuously appearing), which were obvious in bilateral central and front temporal regions. The occurrence in right side was a little earlier than left side. EEG concurrently displayed the highest conductivity of the high-amplitude biphasic slow waves or irregular slow waves on the right side. The histological examination revealed that bipolar single cells in a monolayer or multilayers were centered around the cortical blood vessels in the form of ependymoma-like pseudorosettes along the vascular axis. The tumor cells were arranged in palisade-like structures in a swirling effect, giving the area of the tumor in the neural parenchyma a wide range of different cell densities. The nuclei of the tumor cells were elongated, the chromatin was finely granular, no or rare nuclear fission was present and no microvascular proliferation or necrosis was observed. There were no significantly heteromorphic neurons in the lesions. The tumor cells were positive for tumor cell glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), S-100 protein, vimentin, human leukocyte differentiation antigen 34 (CD34), epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), cluster of differentiation 99 (CD99) and D2-40. However, the cells were negative for neuron markers, such as synaptophysin (Syn) and chromaffin protein/NeuN. There was no expression of oligodendrocyte transcriptor-2 (Olig-2), epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), neurofilament (NF), CD117, nestin or microtubule-associated protein 2 (MAP2) in the tumor cells. Furthermore, there were no visible changes in the p53 expression level. The Ki-67/MIBk-1 labeling index was ~1%.

case_report: A 21-year-old woman was referred to the department of periodontology at the school of dentistry, Babol University of Medical Sciences for routine dental care. She was born to parents who were not related by blood, both of whom were clinically normal. Her mother was 22 years old and her father was 29 years old at the time of her birth. There were no pregnancy complications, and no other family members exhibited similar conditions. At birth, she presented with craniosynostosis, brachycephaly, and syndactyly of the hands and feet. The patient has mild mental retardation but demonstrates satisfactory social development and bonding skills. She has never had seizures. An extraoral examination showed a brachycephalic skull with midface hypoplasia, a flat forehead, depression of the temporal bones, proptosis, hypertelorism, a short nose with a bulbous tip and septal deviation, and a trapezoidal-shaped mouth. A lateral cephalogram indicated hypoplasia of the maxilla, giving the appearance of a class III skeletal relationship. Syndactylies were observed in the right hand’s third, fourth, and fifth digits and the left hand’s second, third, and fourth digits. Both feet exhibited fusion of all toes. Intraoral evaluation revealed poor oral hygiene with varying degrees of periodontal involvement, an arched swelling (pseudo cleft configuration), class III malocclusion, anterior open bite, posterior cross-bite, supernumerary teeth, ectopic eruption, and creamy white enamel opacities. The tongue appeared excessively large, and the maxillary arch was v-shaped.
test_results: The CT scan revealed palatal cleft and maxillary hypoplasia and nasal septum deviation.

case_report: A 32-year-old woman was referred to the endocrine clinic due to increased thirst and excessive urination. Five months prior, she had recurrent sinusitis and otitis media, along with headaches and hearing loss, which did not improve with antibiotics. During a physical examination, a granuloma was found in her left middle ear and was surgically removed. Laboratory tests showed a positive c-ANCA with a titer greater than 80 (normal is less than 20) and anti-proteinase 3 levels at 93 IU/mL (normal is less than 5). She was treated with azathioprine and high doses of corticosteroids, leading to a prompt response and remission. Due to ongoing increased thirst and excessive urination for 12 weeks, she was admitted to the endocrine clinic. She was in good general condition.
test_results: Low urine osmolality and elevated serum osmolality. A pituitary MRI revealed a sellar mass with homogeneous enhancement, thickening of the pituitary stalk and mild compression of optic chiasm.
diagnosis: Diabetes Insipidus secondary to Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis

case_report: A 59-year-old Caucasian male presented with unstable angina, necessitating percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Post-procedure, his acute chest pain improved, but he continued to experience persistent right-sided pleuritic chest pain and worsening shortness of breath for one month. A CT scan of the thorax revealed diffuse nodularity of the tracheal wall. Additionally, there was consolidation in the posterior segment of the right lower lobe (RLL) with adjacent linear opacities and a small right-sided pleural effusion. The patient did not report any fevers, chills, coughing up blood, or weight loss. He had no known history of allergies, lung disease, or recurrent respiratory tract infections. Laboratory tests showed no leucocytosis, and liver and kidney function tests were normal.
test_results: Tracheal visualization revealed multiple sessile nodules protruding into the tracheobronchial lumen extending to the proximal bronchi with sparing of the posterior membranous wall of the trachea. RLL bronchus and segmental bronchi were patent without intraluminal abnormalities.

case_report: A 5-day-old male neonate presented with widespread jaundice. He was born at term via vaginal delivery, weighing approximately 2100 g. The mother, with a history of six pregnancies and six live births, was generally healthy except for mild photosensitivity. The neonate had no history of clay-colored stools, fever, or drug administration. On admission, physical examination showed pale conjunctiva, yellowing of the sclera, generalized jaundice, a few red lesions around the eyes, and mild enlargement of the spleen. The pulse was irregular, with a heart rate of about 75 beats per minute. An electrocardiogram indicated third-degree atrioventricular block, while echocardiography revealed a patent foramen ovale without other abnormalities. Blood tests showed anemia (hemoglobin 9 g/dL) and low platelet count (80,000/mm3). A blood smear indicated erythrocyte hypochromia, anisocytosis, and poikilocytosis. The reticulocyte index, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were within normal ranges. Liver function tests were elevated: aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 760 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) at 187 U/L, alkaline phosphatase at 2045 U/L, total bilirubin at 12.4 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin at 6.2 mg/dL. Prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time were normal. TORCH titers, viral hepatitis markers, and thyroid function tests were normal. Blood and urine cultures for both mother and neonate were negative. Tests for metabolic diseases, including galactosemia, tyrosinemia, and phenylketonuria, were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed a normal-sized liver and gall bladder, no bile duct dilation, and no biliary sludge. The spleen was mildly enlarged but had a normal echo pattern. Hepatobiliary scintigraphy indicated decreased hepatic uptake with no passage through the intrahepatic bile ducts. Initially, the skin lesions were a few non-scarring red annular plaques around the eyes. Over the next few days, these lesions spread to the nasal bridge and upper cheeks, developing sharp and slightly hyperkeratotic borders.
test_results: Serologic studies of the infant and mother were positive for antinuclear antibodies (ANA; 1: 640), anti-Ro/SSA: >4 index (normal: <1 index) and anti-La/SSB antibodies: >4 index (normal: <1 index).

case_report: A 57-year-old male patient sought a second opinion regarding motor neuropathy. Ten years prior, at the age of 47, he observed muscle twitching in his calves and feet but did not experience any sensory issues in his feet. His family history includes a paternal aunt diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), which raised his concerns. He consulted a neurologist specializing in motor neuron conditions at a university center. During the examination at age 47, the patient exhibited normal muscle strength, bulk, and tone in all limbs. Sensory examination results were normal. Reflex testing showed +2 responses in the brachioradialis, biceps, triceps, patellae, and ankles, with flexor plantar reflexes.
test_results: Further testing was done at his initial presentation, including an electromyogram (EMG), which demonstrated markedly reduced response amplitudes in the tibial nerves with normal conduction velocities and prolonged F-wave latencies. The parameters in both peroneal nerves were normal, except that no F-wave latency was obtained on the right, whereas it was normal on the left. All motor parameters, including F-wave latencies, were normal in the median and ulnar nerves. Sensory nerve action potentials were normal in the median, ulnar, radial, sural and superficial peroneal nerves. No other denervation potentials were observed on needle EMG. No abnormalities were detected in sampling other muscles of the legs or his arms. An EMG was repeated and showed that sensory responses in the sural and superficial peroneal nerves were not obtained. In addition, with maximal stimulation, recording the abductor hallucis muscle, no evoked responses were obtained in either tibial nerve. There were reduced response amplitudes in both peroneal nerves with demyelinating features (prolonged distal latencies and slowing of the motor conduction velocities). Needle EMG showed fasciculation potentials with rare positive sharp waves in muscles sampled below the knees (medial gastrocnemius, tibialis anterior). Overall, the study is consistent with a demyelination length-dependent neuropathy affecting both motor and sensory fibers and with minimal secondary axonal features. Genetic analysis Following Institutional Review Board protocols and procedures, whole exome sequencing was done commercially, with a panel testing more than 80 genes established to cause neuropathy. A pathogenic variant was detected in the polynucleotide kinase-phosphatase gene, rs199919568, a splice donor variant, c.1029+2T>C in intron 11 (NM_007254.2). Mutations in this gene can cause CMT type 2, but the mode of transmission is autosomal recessive, and a second mutation was not detected. Another variant was found in the lamin A gene, c.1658_1659delAA (Q553Rfs*79), and, although mutations in this gene can cause CMT type 2B1, this is an autosomal recessive condition, and a second mutation was not identified. Two variants were detected in the SH3TC2 gene, c.3413 G>A p.(S1138N) and c.3269 C>G p.(A1090G). To investigate whether these variants were in cis or trans, a daughter agreed to participate in this study, and the results indicate that she carries only the c.3269 C>G p.(A1090G) variant. These results confirm that the variants are in trans in the patient.

case_report: A 2-year-old female child presented with sudden swelling around the right eye. Initial treatment with systemic antibiotics led to mild improvement, but a cystic swelling became noticeable in the right upper eyelid. An ultrasound using a high-resolution probe (8MHz) revealed a well-defined cyst approximately 2.5×1.5 cm in size in the lateral part of the right upper eyelid. Inside the cyst, a coiled structure with parallel echogenic walls was observed, showing continuous movement. MRI of the orbits was performed to check for any deep intraorbital extension and other abnormalities. The MRI showed a cyst in the lateral part of the upper eyelid with a hyperintense signal on coronal short-tau inversion recovery image, a hypointense signal on coronal T1 image, and rim enhancement on post-contrast T1-weighted fat-saturated images (coronal and sagittal). The cyst was confined to the upper lid. Ill-defined intermediate signal intensity was seen on STIR images within the cyst. Surgical removal of the cyst was performed through an upper lid crease incision. The cyst was found to be adherent to the levator palpebrae superioris muscle and contained a live motile worm measuring about 9 cm in length.
test_results: Histopathological examination showed a worm with thick cuticle, muscle coat, longitudinal and transverse striations and double uterus.
diagnosis: Periorbital dirofilariasis caused by Dirofilaria repens

case_report: O.E, a male neonate, was delivered to a 33-year-old para 2 female at University of Nigeria Teaching Hospital, Enugu. He was admitted to the newborn special care unit (NBSCU) 10 minutes after birth due to inability to cry at birth and multiple deformities with abnormal body posture. The mother received routine antenatal care, and the pregnancy was uneventful with only routine medications used. Prenatal ultrasonography showed no fractures or other abnormalities. Labor began spontaneously and lasted approximately 8 hours, resulting in a spontaneous vertex delivery. The Apgar score was four at 10 minutes. There was no family history of a tendency to fractures or any baby with fractures at birth. Upon examination in the NBSCU, the neonate was observed in a “frog-like position” with abnormal movement of the left thigh. He exhibited respiratory distress with acrocyanosis. Physical examination revealed blue-grey sclera, micrognathia, and a high arched palate. Musculoskeletal examination showed pectus excavatum, fixed flexion deformity of the fingers, crepitus of the right humerus and ulna, and both femurs, along with bilateral talipes equinovarus and micromelia.
test_results: Radiograph revealed fractures of the right humerus, ulna and femur with osteopenia.

case_report: A 4-year-old boy was brought to our hospital due to a respiratory tract infection, an enlarged spleen, and a low platelet count. His mother, aged 26, and father, aged 31, are both healthy and of Chinese descent, with no consanguinity. The patient has two healthy sisters. His prenatal history was normal, and he was born at term through a standard delivery, weighing 3000 g, measuring 50 cm in height, and with an occipitofrontal circumference of 36 cm. There were no congenital malformations reported in the family history. Upon admission, the patient exhibited distinct facial characteristics such as a low nasal bridge, prominent epicanthic folds, wide-set eyes, and low-set ears. Both the liver and spleen were found to be enlarged. Additionally, he presented with congenital bilateral club feet, undescended testes, and delays in speech and motor development. A routine blood test revealed an elevated white blood cell count and hypochromic anemia.
test_results: Bone marrow aspiration smear revealed trilineage myelodysplasia and decreased platelet production from megakaryocyte. Peripheral blood monocytosis > 1× 109/L (peripheral blood monocyte count: 9.2×109/L, peripheral blood lymphocyte count: 8.2×109/L). Less than 20% blasts (including promonocytes) in the blood and bone marrow. Immature granulocytes and nucleated red cells in the peripheral blood. White blood cell count > 10×109/L (peripheral white blood cell count: 23.9 × 109/L). Splenomegaly. Using WES, we detected a heterozygous missense mutation (c.34G > A, p.Gly12Ser) in the KRAS gene in DNA extracted from peripheral blood of the patient. A pathogenic deletion encompassing 7311 kb (arr[GRch37] 10q22.3q23.2 (81628905_88940359)× 1) was detected by CMA from the proband. The deleted region involved the OMIM genes, including NRG3, CDHR1, RGR, LDB3, BMPR1A, and GLUD1.

case_report: An 11-month-old male infant presented to the OPD at Lady Reading Hospital Peshawar with concerns of poor growth, progressive abdominal enlargement since 5 months of age, and developmental delays. He is the second child of a first-degree consanguineous marriage, born at 37 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 3.5 kg. His medical history includes multiple hospitalizations for recurrent chest infections. Developmental milestones were delayed: social smile at 5 months, neck holding at 6 months, and sitting with support at 7 months. After 7 months, there was a regression in milestones, including loss of neck holding, sitting, and social smile. At 8 months, he received a transfusion of packed red blood cells due to severe iron deficiency anemia. His vaccinations are up-to-date. On physical examination, the infant appeared emaciated and pale with coarse facial features, including nasal bridge depression and a prominent forehead. Congenital dermal melanocytosis was noted, more pronounced on the back. His height was 68 cm and weight was 5.3 kg, both below the 3rd percentile on the WHO growth chart. Vital signs were stable: BP 80/60 mmHg, PR 68 bpm, RR 40 breaths per minute, and temperature 98°F. He was unable to hold his neck, sit, or roll over. Abdominal examination revealed a distended abdomen with an enlarged liver palpable 5 cm below the right costal margin, with a total span of 10 cm, firm and non-tender. The spleen was palpable 8 cm below the left costal margin. Neurological examination showed regression of developmental milestones, but eye movements were normal. Other examinations, including gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, and genitourinary systems, were unremarkable. Laboratory results showed hypochromic microcytic anemia with hemoglobin of 8.0 mg/dl, mean corpuscular volume 59.5 fl, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration 31.6 g/dl, and packed cell volume 25.2%. Total leukocyte count was 9000/cm2 and platelet count was 2500000/cm2. Reticulocyte count was 2.5%. Liver function tests, serum electrolytes, random blood sugar, serum cholesterol, prothrombin time, and thyroid function tests were normal. Chest X-ray was normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatosplenomegaly. MRI of the brain revealed reduced hypointense signal in white matter bilaterally, especially in subcortical regions, and thinning of the corpus callosum.
test_results: Bone marrow aspiration revealed lipid laden foamy histiocytes. Liver biopsy showed lipid-laden foamy histiocytes.

case_report: A 10-year-old female presented with increasing difficulty in breathing and a productive cough 6 hours after arriving at Abha city, which is at an altitude of 2270 meters. The family resides in a low-altitude area at 525 meters. The patient had a history of fever, cough, and mild shortness of breath. Her medical history included recurrent pneumonia since early infancy, with extensive investigations failing to identify any specific pulmonary disease. Immune evaluations and whole-exome sequencing were negative. Previous advanced chest imaging showed diffuse air space opacities and thickened interstitium. Upon admission to the emergency room, her vital signs were: heart rate of 145 bpm, respiratory rate of 28 breaths/min, blood pressure of 110/65 mmHg, temperature of 36.5 °C, and oxygen saturation of 71% on room air. Lung examination indicated severe respiratory distress with crackles predominantly at the lung bases. Neurologically, she was fully alert with a Glasgow coma scale score of 15/15.
test_results: Chest X-ray revealed bilateral extensive heterogeneous opacities that involved both lung fields. The patient underwent echocardiography that showed a normal cardiac structure and function without evidence of pulmonary hypertension or pulmonary artery anomalies. On the fourth day of admission, the NP viral panel PCR result returned negative, and the chest X-ray revealed a complete resolution of opacities.

case_report: A 41-year-old Chinese male was admitted to the Second Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University, China, on 9 August 2015, due to a progressively unstable gait over the past 4 years. The patient reported experiencing an unstable gait, leg weakness, and involuntary forward bending of both knees starting at age 37, which had progressively worsened. During childhood, the patient exhibited involuntary limb twisting and poor movement. Over the past 2 years, he experienced a decline in memory and slow reactions, leading to an inability to work. The patient denied any history of other chronic diseases or similar family history. Upon admission, physical examination showed no change in limb muscle tone. Hoffman’s sign, Romberg sign, finger-to-nose test, and bilateral Babinski sign were negative. The patient exhibited slow alternate motions and decreased tendon reflexes in all four limbs. Muscle strength in all four limbs was graded as five. Laboratory tests revealed elevated creatine kinase at 4238U/L (standard: <171U/L), glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase at 106U/L (standard: <35U/L), and lactate dehydrogenase at 317U/L (standard: <248U/L). Blood coagulation, blood lipids, rheumatism markers, tumor markers, and glycosylated hemoglobin showed no obvious abnormalities. Muscle biopsy indicated muscle fiber degeneration. No clinical drug treatment was initiated in 2015.
test_results: The sequencing results showed that the patient carried a hemizygous c.942G>A variation in the XK gene, corresponding to the XK*N.47 allele in the International Society of Blood Transfusion (ISBT) blood group database. This variation leads to a premature stop codon at position 314 and results in an incomplete C-terminally truncated protein (p.Trp314Ter). The nucleotide sequence of the allele has been submitted to the GenBank database with the accession number OK18693. The result showed that the incomplete XK protein lacked the binding site for the Kell antigen.

case_report: A 7-month-old boy presented with a two-week history of fever and persistent crying. Parents observed a swelling on the left upper tibia. Physical examination revealed a diffuse swelling on the anteromedial aspect of the left leg at the junction of the upper and middle thirds, measuring approximately 8x3x3 cm. The skin over the swelling appeared shiny, with no visible dilated veins or pulsations. Tenderness was noted at the site of the swelling. There were no abnormal movements, deformities, or involvement of other bones.
test_results: X-ray of left tibia showed an expansile osteolytic and poorly demarcated lesion involving the metaphyseo-diaphyseal region of left upper tibia. There was no periosteal reaction. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) of left tibia was done and it showed a relatively well delineated expansile metadiaphyseal intramedullary lesion in the proximal and mid tibia measuring 4.3×1.9×1.7 cms. There was marked cortical thinning in the lateral aspect and suspicious breach. Surrounding periosteal thickening was seen with edematous changes. Grossly, the specimen looked dark brown, firm in consistency, aggregate measuring 1.5×1×1cms. Cut section showed dark brown areas. Microscopic examination of sections from bone showed a vascular neoplasm composed of interanastomosing capillary sized vessels. The cells lining the vessels were of moderate size, polygonal with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and round to oval nuclei with moderate pleomorphism. Mitotic rate was 0-1/10 high power field. Formations of lumen within the cytoplasm of cells with RBC’s inside were noted. Focal areas showed myxoid change in the stroma. The tumor was immunoreactive for factor CD34 and vimentin.

case_report: A 2-year-old girl was referred for developmental delay with specific physical characteristics, including a flat occiput and a wide mouth. She is the first child of a nonconsanguineous Chinese couple, born at full term with a birth weight of 2.9 kg. Her perinatal history was uneventful. During early infancy, she experienced hypotonia and feeding difficulties. At 1 year and 6 months, assessments indicated moderate to severe developmental delay with certain behavioral features. Baseline investigations, including brain MRI and metabolic screening, returned normal results. She did not exhibit seizures, regression, or stereotypical hand movements, but had occasional abnormal outbursts of laughter. Her head circumference was within the normal range, between the 10th and 25th percentiles. Although she displayed some behavioral characteristics, her overall clinical profile was not typical.
test_results: array CGH showed a de novo arr[Hg18] 22q13.31q13.33(45,355,784-49,522,658)x1. A terminal deletion in chromosome 22 at band q13.31 region with the size of 4.17 Mb included the SHANK3 gene.

case_report: A 41-year-old female with no prior medical history presented with sudden abdominal pain, weight loss, and painless jaundice. Upon stabilization in the emergency room, she was admitted for further evaluation. Physical examination revealed scleral icterus, but was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory results indicated liver enzyme abnormalities with alanine transaminase at 144 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase at 122 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase at 331 IU/L, along with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia at 5.4 mg/dl. Screening tests for antinuclear antibody, antimitochondrial antibody, and anti-smooth muscle antibody were negative. Total protein was slightly elevated at 9 g/dl. An immunoglobulins assay showed an increased total IgG level of 15.1 g/dl, with IgG subclass analysis revealing an elevated IgG-4 level of 155 mg/dl. Tumor marker screening for cancer antigen 19-9 was within normal limits.
test_results: The ERCP showed distal stricture in the common bile duct (CBD), which was relieved with stenting. The immunoglobulins assay showed an increase in IgG total, i.e., 15.1 g/dl, and the IgG subclass analysis showed an increase in IgG-4 level, i.e., 155 mg/dl. Imaging showed lymph node enlargement close to celiac plexus origin along with minimal calcification of the pancreatic head. It also revealed the dilatation of the biliary tree.

case_report: A 2-month-old full-term female infant was admitted with a one-month history of poor feeding and weight loss. The patient exhibited increased irritability, frequent vomiting, and a weight loss of 0.5 kg over the past month. Prior to admission, she was given oral probiotics (Bifidobacterium bifidum 0.5 g/kg/day for 7 days). Her birth and family history were unremarkable. Upon admission, her weight was 4 kg (−3 SD), and she was in poor mental and nutritional condition. Physical examination revealed a palpable mass measuring 3 cm × 4 cm in the upper left abdomen. She received 10% calcium gluconate (1 ml/kg/day IV for 4 days) and furosemide (1 mg/kg/day IV for 3 days) to manage elevated serum potassium levels, 5% sodium bicarbonate (1.5 ml/kg/day IV for 3 days) to address metabolic acidosis, and 0.9% sodium chloride (19743.75 mEq/kg/day IV) for hyponatremia. After 8 days of treatment, her diet and electrolyte levels showed improvement. At the ages of 3 and 5 months, she was hospitalized twice due to recurrent poor appetite. She was treated with hydrocortisone sodium succinate (32.62 mg/m2/day) and 9α-fludrocortisone (0.1 mg/day). The hydrocortisone sodium succinate dosage was gradually reduced, along with potassium reduction and salt supplementation. Despite these measures, serum aldosterone levels continued to fluctuate. By the age of 6 months, her overall condition improved, and both hydrocortisone sodium succinate and 9α-fludrocortisone were discontinued.
test_results: Magnetic resonance urography (MRU) illustrated posterior renal cystic lesions associated with left calyces, left hydronephrosis, and left tortuous dilation of the ureter (with distal ureteral obstruction).

case_report: A 10-month-old male of Indian descent with a history of atopic dermatitis and egg allergy presented to the outpatient clinic with rhinorrhea and decreased oral intake. His birth history was unremarkable, and immunizations were current. He was initially treated for an upper respiratory infection. Two days later, he returned with additional symptoms including diffuse facial swelling and redness, perioral skin irritation, and right-sided ear pain. Augmentin was prescribed for right-sided otitis media, and topical mupirocin was applied to crusted skin on the right side of his face and upper right perioral region. Rapid COVID-19 and Influenza A and B tests were negative. Due to concerns about a possible allergic reaction, parents were advised to administer an antihistamine and monitor the facial swelling, with instructions to return if symptoms did not improve. That evening, the patient developed a fever of 100.4 °F and was taken to the emergency department at a local children's hospital. The parents were advised to continue the current treatment regimen. Over the next 48 hours, the patient's facial swelling worsened, and he developed swelling in both extremities and widespread skin peeling. Upon returning to the emergency department, initial vital signs showed a heart rate of 137 and a blood pressure of 136/108.
test_results: A physical exam was remarkable for a blanching, peeling, erythematous rash on the face and creases of bilateral arms, legs, and groin. A positive Nikolsky sign was reported.

case_report: A 4-year-old girl was born following a normal pregnancy and delivery. Her early motor development milestones were achieved on time. At the age of 3 years, she exhibited mild cognitive impairment. Neurologic examination at this age revealed hypoactive deep tendon reflexes. She was able to walk on her toes and heels without support. She had a mild intellectual disability. Her serum CK level was measured at 1564 UI/L (normal range up to 170 UI/L). At 3 years and six months, a brain MRI showed no abnormalities. An ophthalmologic evaluation found no issues. Electrocardiogram results were normal, and an echocardiogram identified a secundum atrial septal defect.
test_results: We identified the same homozygous missense mutation in POMT2.

case_report: A 71-year-old male with a history of arterial hypertension was admitted to the infectious disease unit due to severe respiratory failure symptoms consistent with bilateral pneumonia. A nasopharyngeal swab test confirmed the presence of SARS-CoV-2. The patient was treated with non-invasive ventilation for respiratory distress. After 11 days, the patient exhibited lethargy, negative upper limbs myoclonus, and random, involuntary, rapid vertical eye movements. Kidney and liver function biomarkers, serum electrolytes, and ammonia levels were within normal ranges. Head CT scan and toxicological examination showed no abnormalities. Clinical evaluation noted myoclonic positive and negative jerks along with an altered mental status.
test_results: EEG revealed generalized epileptic discharges with bilateral frontal high amplitude delta waves. CSF protein concentration was 53.9 mg/dL, glucose 104 mg/dL, 1 mononuclear white blood cell.

case_report: A 20-year-old Malaysian woman presented with Angle Class I bimaxillary protrusion. The treatment aimed to reduce upper- and lower-lip protrusion by retracting the maxillary and mandibular anterior teeth. To create space for this retraction, four first premolars were extracted. Following the extractions, a fixed pre-adjusted appliance (0.022 inch × 0.028 inch slot) and 0.016 inch nickel titanium (Ni-Ti) archwire were placed. After initial alignment, canine retraction was started on a 018 special plus Australian wire, using an elastomeric chain applying 150 g of force. After 3 months of upper canine retraction, the right canine had moved 1 mm while the left canine had moved 3 mm. The patient noted that the extraction of the upper right premolar had been difficult and took more time.
test_results: There appeared to be a radiopacity in the socket. Another radiograph, with a cone shift technique, demonstrated a radiopacity in the socket. Detailed inspection of the radiograph revealed trabeculae-like pattern of the opacity.

case_report: A 58-year-old female presented in January 2014 with a high fever exceeding 38.5°C that had persisted for one month. Previous examinations and antibiotic treatments at local hospitals had not resolved the fever. Upon admission, the patient reported chills and had a fever reaching 38.4°C along with a nonproductive cough. Physical examination revealed tender and swollen pinnae with sparing of the lobule, while the nose and eyes appeared normal. Laboratory tests indicated a hemoglobin level of 11.1 g/dL, a total leukocyte count of 10,700/mm3, and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein levels. Serological tests for antinuclear antibody and various autoantibodies, including anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, PR3-ANCA, and MPO-ANCA, were negative. There was no tenderness in the tracheal cartilage, and chest computed tomography did not show interstitial pneumonia or tracheal stenosis. Echocardiography revealed no aortic root dilatation or aortic regurgitation. Despite the exclusion of infection and hematological malignancies, the patient exhibited redness of the bilateral auricularis.
test_results: The histological evaluation showed cellular infiltrates of lymphocytes, neutrophils, and plasma cells, especially at the cartilage-skin interface, and a reduced number of chondrocytes in areas of cartilage destruction.

case_report: A 7-year-old boy presented with behavioral issues since infancy. His early developmental history indicated he was the first child, born from an unplanned pregnancy. At 36 weeks of gestation, the mother experienced oligohydramnios, and possible congenital cardiac defects were noted in the fetus. The child was delivered preterm at 36 weeks via emergency cesarean section due to fetal bradycardia. His birth weight was 1.7 kg, he had a delayed cry, and was cyanosed at birth. Cardiac evaluation at birth identified cardiac anomalies including patent ductus arteriosus, ventricular septal defect, tricuspid regurgitation, and a left atrium to right atrium shunt. He was started on digitoxin. As he grew, he exhibited global developmental delay and was diagnosed with bilateral profound sensorineural hearing loss at 6 months of age. Over time, he continued to show delayed milestones and developed behaviors such as poor eye contact, poor social and communication skills, repetitive head rocking, hand flapping movements, and a preference for fixed routines. From the age of 3, he displayed symptoms of attention deficit hyperkinetic disorder (ADHD), including an inability to sit still for more than 2-3 minutes and difficulty engaging in activities. His insistence on routine and hyperactivity increased over the years, leading to aggressive behaviors such as hitting and biting his mother, which resulted in significant distress and a psychiatry consultation with subsequent admission to a child psychiatry inpatient unit. There was no history of head injury, seizures, frequent diarrhea and vomiting, birthmarks, or failure to thrive. Physical examination revealed a small head circumference (49 cm) and bilateral flat feet. Mental status examination showed a lack of eye contact, hyperactivity, irritable mood, frequent side-to-side head movements, and hand flapping. His intelligence quotient was evaluated to be 25.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging showed multifocal symmetrical T2/fluid attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities in B/L cerebral hemisphere. Ophthalmological examination showed evidence of pigmentary retinopathy.

case_report: A 40-year-old female presented with narrowing of vaginal and urethral orifices, moderate itching, erythema over the genital region, and chronic constipation for 5 years. In the following year, she experienced pain in the anal region, difficulty passing stools, dyspareunia, and urinary retention. For the past 6 years, she had recurring oral erosions over the gums with a burning sensation when eating spicy food. She underwent multiple cystoscopies and proctoscopies in the past 3 years for urethral and anal dilatation, which provided only partial, short-term relief. There was no history of vaginal discharge. She had a dental filling 18 years ago and was being treated for hypothyroidism. Family history was not significant. Mucocutaneous examination revealed intense erythema of the vulva and vagina, partial fusion of the labia minora and majora, and burying of the clitoris. There were a few old-healed hypo- and hyper-pigmented patches over the labia minora and clitoris. Per speculum examination was not possible due to Grade 2+ introital stenosis. The anal mucosa showed hyperpigmentation, fissuring, scaling, and marked stenosis. Examination of the oral cavity revealed violaceous plaques on the labial and lingual aspects of the maxillary and mandibular gingival surfaces. Cutaneous examination showed no violaceous or hypopigmented patches or plaques, and hair and nails were normal. All routine investigations were unremarkable.
test_results: The one from erythematous patch on labia minora revealed orthohyperkeratosis, basal vacuolization, squamatization, necrotic keratinocytes, Max Joseph spaces, and pigmentary incontinence, along with dermal lymphocytic proliferation. The second biopsy from hyperpigmented patch near clitoris showed orthohyperkeratosis, focal atrophy, pigmentary incontinence and increased fibroblastic proliferation, collagen synthesis, and lymphocytic infiltrate. The third biopsy from perianal region exhibited fibrosis, pigmentary incontinence, basal vacuolization, and necrotic keratinocytes, along with dense dermal lymphocytic infiltration.
diagnosis: Vulvo-anal lichen planus with oral mucosal involvement

case_report: A 47-day old male infant presented with respiratory distress, food intolerance, and weight loss. He was delivered at 40 weeks of gestation via cesarean section due to fetal bradycardia, with a birth weight of 2800 grams and Apgar scores of 7 and 9 at the first and fifth minutes, respectively. He is the second child in the family. The pregnancy was uneventful, and prenatal ultrasonography showed no abnormalities. The parents are first cousins. The father has a normal body habitus (85 kg, 182 cm), normal echocardiographic measurements (aortic root 2.53 cm, no mitral abnormality), and normal eye examination. The mother (75 kg, 163 cm, aortic root 1.9 cm) and the only sibling (16.5 kg, 112 cm, aortic root 1.66 cm) also have normal findings. On physical examination, the infant's total height, upper and lower segments, and arm span were 58 cm, 33 cm, 25 cm, and 64 cm, respectively (upper to lower segment ratio 1.32, arm span to height ratio 1.1). His actual and maximum weights were 3.3 kg and 4 kg, respectively. The anterior fontanel was open (2.5 cm × 3 cm). Ophthalmologic examination showed mild right strabismus without lens dislocation. Notable features included large ear lobes, enophthalmos, micrognathia, high palate, dolichocephalic skull, and redundant forehead skin. The fingers and toes were unusually long, with positive thumb and wrist signs. There was limited motion in the knee and elbow joints. Mild pectus excavatum and slight scoliosis were observed. Lung auscultation revealed rales, particularly at the bases. Cardiac examination identified a grade III/VI holosystolic murmur over the left sternal border and a gallop rhythm. The abdomen was soft with the liver palpable 2 cm below the costal margin. Bilateral inguinal hernia was present, more pronounced on the right. Blood methionine level was normal (13.4 micromol/l, normal range 6-49), as was the karyotype (46XY). Chest X-ray indicated right diaphragm eventration, confirmed by fluoroscopy. Brain sonography showed no abnormalities. Electrocardiography revealed left atrial enlargement.
test_results: Echocardiography revealed dilated aortic root (23 mm, Z value ≥+3) and prolaptic mitral valve with severe regurgitation. Tricuspid valve was prolaptic and severely regurgitant as well. There was moderate pulmonary hypertension (pressure gradient of tricuspid regurgitation = 43 mmHg).

case_report: A 7.5-year-old boy presented with progressive gait disturbance and frequent falls. He was born full-term without any pregnancy or delivery complications. His developmental milestones, including sitting up without support, walking, and speech, were all within the normal range. Family history included tremors in the grandfather. At 3.5 years old, he was first seen by a pediatric neurologist for unsteady gait and toe walking, with gait unsteadiness starting around 2.5 years old and frequent falls. Hand tremors were noted prior to the clinic visit. Examination revealed a well-developed child with a normal funduscopic exam, no cardiac murmur, normal mental status including speech, normal cranial nerves, and strength. He had 1+ deep tendon reflexes (DTRs) in both upper and lower extremities with downgoing toes. His gait was wide-based and unsteady, and he had a tremor in both hands. By 6.5 years old, he experienced more falls and worsening handwriting. Examination showed pes cavus, mild scoliosis, and absence of cardiac murmur. Neurological exam revealed trace to absent DTRs, loss of position sense, positive Romberg, downgoing toes, slowed rapid alternating movements, tremor on finger-to-nose exam, and wide-based unsteady gait. By 7 years old, he had more frequent falls and worsening handwriting. Examination showed progression in ataxia in both upper and lower limbs with a wider-based gait. DTRs were absent, and a positive Babinski sign was noted. At the last exam around 7.5 years old, he was falling more frequently, and the exam showed increased tone in the lower extremities with foot drop and steppage gait, decreased proprioception in the lower extremities, and inconsistent responses in the upper extremities. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain was normal. Laboratory tests, including quantitative immunoglobulins, alpha fetoprotein, thyroid profile, serum lactate, vitamin E levels, creatine kinase, serum amino acids, and serum acylcarnitine profile, were all normal. Echocardiogram showed global hypertrophy of both ventricles. Ophthalmological examination did not show any evidence of optic atrophy.
test_results: Mutation analysis showed one allele with a GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion of approximately 1000. Frataxin sequencing demonstrated another allele harboring a c.464G>A nucleotide change. The nucleotide change predicted an amino acid substitution of tryptophan to a premature stop codon at residue 155 (W155X).

case_report: A 5-year-old girl with no significant past ocular or systemic history presented to the Bascom Palmer Eye Institute with complaints of decreased vision in the right eye (OD) that began 2 weeks prior. Examination revealed best-corrected visual acuity of light perception in the right eye (OD) and 20/30 in the left eye (OS). The eyes were orthophoric with no limitations in extraocular motility. Pupils showed asymmetrical reactivity to light, with a significant right afferent pupillary defect. An external examination noted asymmetry in the palpebral fissures. Corneal diameters measured 13.5 mm in the right eye and 12 mm in the left eye, both of which were clear with intact Descemet's membranes.
test_results: Intraocular pressure (IOP) by Tono-Pen was 35 mmHg right eye and 22 mmHg left eye. Gonioscopy revealed grade IV angles bilaterally with indistinct features without an observed Barkan's membrane. Fundus examination revealed significant optic disk cupping in the right eye and was within normal limits in the left eye. Measurement of the circumpapillary retinal nerve fiber layers (RNFL) by SD-OCT of the right eye revealed superior and inferior RNFL thinning. An examination under anesthesia was performed, during which additional IOP measurements by Tono-Pen under both light and deep sedation. The IOP was measured to be 49 mmHg and 42 mg Hg OD, and 32 mmHg and 24 mmHg OS respectively. The axial length by A-scan ultrasound is 24.3 mm right eye and 21.3 mm left eye.

case_report: A 30-year-old Asian male, employed as a school teacher, visited the outpatient neurology department of a tertiary care hospital with a three-month history of left-sided lower back pain. Initially, the pain did not radiate and was alleviated by analgesics. Over the following month, the pain spread to the right lower extremity, increased in severity, and became unresponsive to analgesic treatment. Two weeks later, the patient developed bilateral lower limb weakness and sensory deficits in the L2 region, affecting light touch and pinprick sensations. He did not report any urinary or fecal incontinence. Vital signs were within normal limits. The patient's medical history was unremarkable, with no significant past illnesses, weight loss, or current medication use. He reported no alcohol consumption and was a non-smoker. He was admitted to the neurology ward for further evaluation, and baseline investigations including complete blood count (CBC), liver function tests (LFT), renal function tests (RFT), electrolyte levels, and vitamin B12 assessment were performed. Neurological examination revealed normal mental status and intact cranial nerve function. Motor examination showed decreased strength in the hip flexors, knee extensors, ankle dorsiflexors, and toe extensors, graded as 4/5. Sensory examination indicated impaired light touch and pinprick sensation, suggesting decreased tactile sensitivity. Deep tendon reflexes were slightly diminished, graded as 2/4, and the Babinski reflex was present bilaterally. The Hoffmann test was negative. The patient had a preserved anal reflex and no saddle paresthesia was observed. The absence of saddle paresthesia, intact anal reflex, and negative Hoffmann's sign indicated relative preservation of the sacral segments and associated nerve roots.
test_results: The MRI revealed a well-defined, enhancing intramedullary lesion at the L2 level, as well as cord enlargement and edema. The tumor exhibited hyperintensity on T2-weighted imaging and isointensity on T1-weighted imaging, with varying enhancement on contrast-enhanced imaging. The MRI also revealed evidence of compression of the spinal cord at L2.
diagnosis: intramedullary spinal myxopapillary ependymoma, grade II

case_report: A two-day-old Pakistani female infant, weighing 4.6 pounds at birth, was delivered via C-section after a full-term pregnancy. She is the second child of two siblings, born to healthy consanguineous parents. The infant was referred to the Dermatology Department at Fatima Memorial Hospital, Lahore, Pakistan, for evaluation of two skin lesions located on the central line of her abdomen above the umbilicus and on the central scalp. A focal defect with a scarred atrophic plaque and thin skin was noted in the midline of the vertex area, involving the sagittal suture. This lesion measured approximately 4 × 3 cm and was situated anterior to the occipital fontanelle. The scarred plaque exhibited a complete absence of hair and had a central hemorrhagic necrotic crust, with a small ulcerated area surrounding the crust. The abdominal skin displayed a puckered, shiny scar around the umbilicus, forming a 3 × 3 cm erythematous area with a band-like small hypertrophic scar in its center, but no ulceration was present. Normal cutaneous blood vessels were visible in the surrounding area. The mother reported no toxic exposures, serious illnesses during pregnancy, or family history of the condition. Due to hypoplastic phalanges in both fingers and toes, a complete musculoskeletal examination was planned. Physical examination revealed the absence of skin and parts of both parietal bones at the sagittal suture in the occipital fontanelle region. Additionally, hypertrophic labia minora was observed. No other symptoms were noted, and the child appeared healthy. Generalized cutis marmorata was not observed. The Moro reflex was intact, and suckling after birth was normal. An ophthalmological consultation showed normal results. The baby maintained a midline position with symmetrical body posture, normal limb movements, and normal tendon reflexes. The facial response to touch was normal. The infant was kept in a newborn nursery for observation and cardiac monitoring.
test_results: The skin and parts of both parietal bones making the sagittal suture were absent in the occipital fontanelle region. Hypertrophic labia minora was observed.

case_report: A 29-year-old white female with a history of gastroesophageal reflux disease and well-controlled diabetes mellitus presented with severe, constant, recurring epigastric pain that began three days prior to her emergency department visit. She reported recurrent epigastric pain after meals accompanied by nausea and non-bilious vomiting, which had progressively worsened. The patient had previously consulted multiple gastroenterologists and had undergone repeated esophageal duodenoscopy, which did not reveal any significant abnormalities. She also reported a weight loss of approximately 30 pounds over three years due to decreased appetite. Upon admission to the emergency room, her BMI was 32 kg/m2. Physical examination revealed dehydration, epigastric tenderness, and hyperactive bowel sounds. Other tests were unremarkable. Laboratory blood work showed anemia and mild hypokalemia. An ultrasound of the gallbladder was negative for any concerns. A chest X-ray (anteroposterior) was negative. The Hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan was unremarkable. The gastric emptying study was negative. Occult stool for blood was negative. Symptomatic management included treatment for nausea with Reglan, rehydration and electrolyte replacement with intravenous (IV) fluids, pain medications, and proton pump inhibitors. Symptomatic management initially improved her symptoms, but they returned when the treatment was tapered off.
test_results: CTA/MRA of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast was positive for compression of the celiac trunk.

case_report: A 65-year-old Asian male, who is independent in daily activities, presented in December 2018 with intermittent headache, left-sided weakness, and sensory deficits over three days. He also experienced transient double vision on downward gaze. Symptoms fluctuated throughout the day. There were no fevers, head injuries, seizures, or neck trauma. Upon admission, his vital signs included a blood pressure of 115/64 mmHg and a heart rate of 68 bpm. He remained afebrile during his stay. Physical examination revealed a new left-sided facial droop, left upper limb weakness (MRC grade 4/5), and reduced sensation to pinprick on the left side of the face, upper, and lower limbs. Both eyes had limited abduction and developed bidirectional nystagmus during abduction. Other cranial nerve examinations were normal. There were no cortical signs such as visual field loss, aphasia, dysarthria, dysphasia, or hemineglect. Muscle tone, reflexes, and Babinski's reflexes were normal bilaterally. A CT scan of the brain showed no intracranial hemorrhage or infarction. He was started on aspirin and clopidogrel. MRI of the brain showed no restricted diffusion, and neither MRA nor carotid ultrasound revealed any significant stenoses, occlusions, or aneurysms. An echocardiogram showed an ejection fraction of 57%, normal atria size, and unremarkable valves with no intracardiac thrombi or valvular vegetations. A 24-hour Holter monitor did not detect atrial fibrillation. Serum glucose, sodium, potassium, and corrected calcium levels were normal. One day after symptom onset, his headache and neurological signs resolved, with motor power returning to MRC grade 5/5, sensation restored, and nystagmus resolved. He was continued on aspirin and clopidogrel for six weeks, followed by lifelong clopidogrel. He was discharged without new or worsening neurological signs. A follow-up three months later showed no new or residual neurological deficits.
test_results: An urgent computerised tomographic (CT) scan of the brain showed no intracranial haemorrhage nor infarction. His Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) of the brain did not show any restricted diffusion to indicate an acute infarct; with neither his Magnetic Resonance Angiography (MRA) nor his carotid ultrasound showing any flow-limiting stenoses, occlusions nor aneurysms. An urgent CT angiography (CTA) from the arch of the aorta to the Circle of Willis did not reveal any dissections, aneurysms and arteriovenous malformations, nor findings consistent with temporal arteritis. No cranial infarction nor intracranial haemorrhage was seen at that time. An MRI with MRA after the complete resolution of neurological deficits did not show any restricted diffusion to indicate an acute infarct. The T2 weighted images did not show any hyperintensities suggestive of previous infarction. His MRA did not show any flow-limiting stenoses, occlusions, aneurysms or neurovascular conflicts with the trigeminal nerve.

case_report: A 24-year-old male patient presented with skin thickening on the face and scalp, and increased volume of the hands and feet since his teenage years. He also reported experiencing acne since adolescence. The patient denied any family history of similar conditions. Physical examination showed erythematous follicular papules and pustules on the face, thickened skin, and pronounced facial furrows with a pattern of cutis verticis gyrata on the forehead and scalp. Soft nodules with alopecia on their surfaces were observed on the scalp, consistent with abscessing folliculitis. The hands and feet exhibited increased volume and digital clubbing, along with increased sweating (hyperhidrosis) on the hands and feet.
test_results: The radiographs of the hands, fists, and knees showed a benign hypertrophic periosteal reaction with bone enlargement by hyperostosis, as well as densification and increase of the thickness of adjacent soft tissues.

case_report: A 16-year-old male exhibited significant weakness in the proximal muscles of all four limbs, which began at age 11 with difficulties in walking and tip-toe gait. By age 16, he demonstrated a waddling gait with tip-toe walking and genu recurvatum, covering less than 50 meters. Clinical examination revealed severe proximal muscle weakness and muscle wasting, more pronounced in the lower limbs. Muscle strength was assessed using the Medical Research Council (MRC) scale: 4+/5 for arm abduction and elbow flexion, and 2/5 for hip flexion, hip abduction, and knee extension. Achilles tendon contractures were present. Bilateral symmetrical scapular winging and axial muscle weakness were noted. Sensory examination was normal, and deep tendon reflexes were intact except for absent patellar reflexes. No abnormalities were observed in the head and neck region. Cognitive development was normal, and no cardiac abnormalities were detected. Respiratory function tests showed a vital capacity of 69%, with no dyspnea. Serum creatine kinase levels were elevated at 1385 IU/L (normal <200 IU/L). Electromyography indicated abundant spontaneous activity (fibrillations and complex repetitive, myotonic discharges at rest) and clear myogenic changes during effort. Ultrasonography revealed homogeneous muscle hyperechogenicity, especially in the quadriceps. MRI of the pelvis, upper thighs, and legs showed bilateral symmetric muscle fatty replacement without muscle edema or contrast enhancement. At age 22, upper limb weakness had progressed (deltoids, biceps MRC scale 3/5; grip strength approximately 40% of normal, around 20 kg), and walking was limited to about 50 meters with a knee orthosis for genu recurvatum, though he primarily used an electric wheelchair. A muscle biopsy of the left deltoid at age 16 showed non-grouping, atrophic, round fibers with multiple internalized nuclei. Numerous cytoplasmic autophagic vacuoles were observed, strongly positive for PAS and phosphatasic acid. Immunohistochemistry staining for p62 and TDP 43 was positive in the cytoplasmic autophagic vacuoles. Vacuolated fibers expressed MHC class I and complement C5b-9 without inflammatory infiltrates. Maltase acid activity and sequencing of the exon regions and junctions (+/-25 nt) of the LAMP2 and GAA genes were normal.
test_results: Sanger sequencing of the VMA21 gene detected hemizygous, unreported, intronic, single-nucleotide substitution c.164-20T>A (NM_001017980.4) in the last intron. This variant has never been described to our knowledge (absent from gnomAD and HGMD). Its in silico analysis predicted a loss of strength of the acceptor site located 20 bp downstream. Alamut Visual Plus (v1.6.1 from Sophia Genetics) predicted a negative impact based on four algorithm predictions (GeneSplicer: −25%; MaxEntScan: −18%; SpliceSiteFinder-like: 0%; NNSPLICE: 0%). Additionally, Splice AI predicted an acceptor loss with a score of 0.42 in a scale from 0 to 1.
diagnosis: X-linked myopathy with excessive autophagy due to a novel intronic mutation in the VMA21 gene

case_report: The patient is currently 25 years old. At age 14, proteinuria was identified during a school urinary screening. He was referred to a local hospital where a lack of right radial pulse was noted. Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) revealed stenosis of the right subclavian artery. No other arterial stenosis, including renal and bilateral iliac arteries, was observed. Chest X-ray and computed tomography showed no abnormal findings. He was treated with oral prednisolone (PSL) and aspirin. At age 16, he was referred to our hospital with proteinuria exceeding 4 g/day. He had no history of Kawasaki disease or congenital syphilis, and his family history was unremarkable. On admission, urine examination showed 50–99 red blood cells per high-power field and heavy proteinuria (3.1 g/dL). The urinary β2-microglobulin concentration was normal (218 μg/dL), with no leukocyturia or bacteriuria. Hematologic examination results included a white blood cell count of 7000/μL, a red blood cell count of 468 × 10^4/μL, a platelet count of 296 × 10^3/μL, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 85 mm/h. The C-reactive protein concentration was 0.3 mg/dL.
