Blood biochemical results included a total protein concentration of 6.6 g/dL; albumin, 3.5 g/dL; blood urea nitrogen (BUN), 28 mg/dL; creatinine, 0.85 mg/dL; cystatin C, 1.10 (normal range, 0.56 to 0.87 μg/L). Creatinine clearance (Ccr) was 70.3 mL/min/1.73 m2. Concentrations of electrolytes, immunoglobulin (Ig) G, and serum complement concentrations were normal. The serum myeloperoxidase-ANCA concentration was increased (21 ELISA units or EU; normal, ≤ 10), but proteinase-3 (PR-3) was not detected. Antinuclear antibody (ANA), anti-DNA antibody, rheumatoid arthritis hemagglutinatin antibody (RAHA), and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP), as well as anti-SS-A/Ro, anti-SS-B/La, and anti-RNA antibodies were all negative. Serum concentration of sialylated carbohydrate antigen KL-6 was normal (125 U/mL, normal range, >500). Treponema pallidum latex agglutination was negative. Neither increased serum angiotensin-converting enzyme nor chest radiologic findings were present. A renal biopsy specimen included 34 glomeruli, 10 of which showed crescents. Some circumferential crescent formation was seen. Two glomeruli showed hyalinization. Marked mononuclear cell infiltration was present in the interstitium, mainly near glomeruli. Immunofluorescence examination showed no deposition of IgG, IgA, or complement components. Therapy was initiated with PSL (including methylprednisolone pulse therapy), cyclophosphamide (2 mg/kg/day), warfarin (1 mg/day), and an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor. After about 6 months, urinary protein excretion decreased to 0.3 g/day. Follow-up renal biopsy showed decreases in mesangial proliferation, crescents, and periglomerular mononuclear cell infiltration. The PSL dose was tapered, but proteinuria recurred. PSL was increased, and cyclosporine A (CyA) was added. Considering nephrotoxicity of CyA, serum concentration of CyA was strictly kept below 100 ng/mL, but the patient’s course has continued to show repeated remissions and exacerbations. Most recently, serum creatinine was 2.2 mg/dL, and cystatin C, 2.1. Ccr was 47.6 mL/min/1.73 m2.
test_results: Audiologic testing showed thresholds of 24.3 db for the right ear and 39.5 db for the left, indicated bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Cataracts were present, being more severe in the left eye. Keratitis and uveitis were absent.

case_report: A 5-year-old female, born to parents who are first-degree relatives, presented with multiple, recurrent, painless nodules of varying sizes located on the scalp, back, ear lobules, and lower lip. These lesions were initially observed at 6 months of age and have progressively increased in size. Two nodules on the scalp were surgically removed when the child was 2 years old, but they reappeared at the same locations. The child has achieved normal developmental milestones. The family history includes one older sibling and parents who are all in good health. Physical examination revealed multiple papules and nodules of different sizes, which were soft to firm and nontender. There was no evidence of gingival hyperplasia, limb flexion contractures, significant lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly. Hematological and biochemical tests returned normal results. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of the nodules showed sparse spindle cells in a Periodic acid Schiff (PAS)-positive background.
test_results: Microscopically, there were poorly circumscribed lesions in the dermis and subcutis composed of a sparse population of uniform spindle cells embedded in an abundant homogenous eosinophilic fibrillary matrix. The matrix was PAS positive.

case_report: A 16-month-old female was referred to the orthopedic department due to bowed legs and an abnormal chest X-ray. She measured 80 cm in height (50th percentile) and weighed 9.7 kg (25th percentile). Her medical history included delayed physical development, recurrent respiratory tract infections, and episodes of otitis media. Physical examination noted prominent eyes, supraorbital hyperostosis, full cheeks, and micrognathia. Radiographic imaging revealed thoracolumbar kyphoscoliosis, anterior and posterior vertebral scalloping, humerus cortical irregularity with bowing, thin wavy ribs, pelvis hypoplasia of the pubis and ischium, bilateral coxa valga, and bilateral bowed leg deformities with normal epiphyses and metaphyses. Bone age, estimated from hand X-rays, was consistent with her chronological age of 1.5 years.
test_results: Target exome sequencing revealed a heterozygous mutation in the FLNA gene, c.3578 T > C, p.L1193P.

case_report: A 20-year-old male, the eighth child of non-consanguineous parents, was referred from the medical ward due to breathlessness. He had a history of pulmonary tuberculosis at 4 months old, which was treated with anti-tubercular medication for 1 year. Since childhood, he experienced symptoms including dry cough, dyspnea on exertion for 4 months (Modified Medical Research Council-MMRC grade 4), intermittent fever, and a history of infective exacerbation 0-1/year. He also had multiple skin pigmentation and hypersensitivity to sunlight. There was no history of chest pain. Over the past 4 months, his symptoms worsened, including dry cough, increased tremor, increased frequency of bowel movements, and intermittent fever. General examination was within normal limits. Physical examination revealed bilateral crackles, and a 6-minute walk distance could not be performed. Laboratory results showed a hemoglobin level of 13.3 g/dL and a total leukocyte count of 28,000 cells per cubic millimeter of blood, with 80% neutrophils and 10% lymphocytes. Other biochemical parameters were within normal limits. Chest radiograph indicated bilateral reticulonodular opacities. Serum immunoglobulin-E was 394. Tests for human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis C virus, and hepatitis B virus were non-reactive.
test_results: High-resolution computed tomography showed intra- and interlobular septal thickening, ill-defined ground glass opacities throughout lung parenchyma, widespread ill-defined centrilobular nodules, and scattered and patchy lobular air trapping.

case_report: A 26-year-old male civil engineer reported experiencing moderately itchy lesions predominantly on sun-exposed areas for the past 5 years. He has an average sun exposure of 3–4 hours daily. The condition worsens during the summer and improves in the winter. Initially, the rash appeared on the face and subsequently spread to the sun-exposed regions of the upper limbs and feet. There is no family history of similar complaints, no history of atopy, and no history of cheilitis or conjunctivitis. Physical examination revealed bilaterally symmetrical, multiple, discrete, lichenified papules and nodules, some with excoriations, located on the face, ear lobes, “V” region of the neck, scalp, extensor surfaces of the forearms, and the dorsa of the hands and feet.
test_results: The biopsy showed mild superficial perivascular infiltrate of lymphocytes, eosinophils with mild to moderate irregular epidermal hyperplasia, thickened granular layer with stratum corneum showing marked compact orthokeratosis and focal parakeratosis. Thickened papillary dermis with papillomatosis and thickened collagen bundles in a vertical array. The capillaries in the papillary dermis are increased in number and are thick walled.

case_report: A 14-year-old girl visited her general practitioner with a year-long history of intermittent headaches accompanied by palpitations, light-headedness, nausea, dizziness, and episodes of 'going pale' when moving from a lying to a standing position. She also reported experiencing 'tunnel vision' that preceded brief episodes of loss of consciousness. Initial examination revealed pallor, a regular resting heart rate of 80 bpm, blood pressure readings of 120/64 mmHg while sitting and 122/68 mmHg while standing, and a relative increase in heart rate that resolved upon standing. All other physical examinations were normal. Laboratory tests, echocardiogram, and MRI to exclude intracranial issues were normal. A 24-hour ambulatory electrocardiogram showed recurring intermittent sinus tachycardia that coincided with the patient's symptoms. Due to the worsening severity of her symptoms, she withdrew from extracurricular activities at school, leading to feelings of low self-esteem and worthlessness. The significant impact of her symptoms on her physical, social, and psychological well-being caused her to become reclusive and isolated, and she was diagnosed with depression by adolescent psychiatrists.
test_results: Diagnostic TTT identified an elevation in her heart rate from 80 whilst supine to 140 bpm within 10 minutes of standing in the absence of orthostatic hypotension (supine blood pressure: 114/73 mmHg; blood pressure within 10 minutes of standing: 124/82 mmHg).
Orpha_name: Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome due to NET deficiency

case_report: A 27-year-old male with no significant medical history presented with a painful furuncle in the right axillary region and moderate to high-grade fever. On the fourth day of illness, he underwent abscess aspiration at a private clinic. Post-aspiration, he experienced a brief (1 minute) loss of consciousness, attributed to a vasovagal attack, followed by repeated vomiting episodes. He was subsequently admitted to Indraprastha Apollo Hospital, New Delhi. Upon admission, he was febrile (temperature 38.4°C), had a diffuse macular erythematous rash, and exhibited slight confusion without focal neurological signs (GCS-14/15). His heart rate was 122/min, and blood pressure was 78/30 mm Hg. Clinical signs indicated dehydration, and a fluid challenge of 1 liter normal saline was administered, raising his blood pressure to 98/46 mm Hg. Local examination revealed a 1-cm diameter, circular, non-tense blister at the right axilla. He was transferred to the ICU, where central venous and arterial lines were placed, and resuscitation was conducted according to surviving sepsis guidelines. He was intubated due to septic shock and placed on mechanical ventilation. Noradrenaline at 15 μg/min and dopamine at 20 μg/kg/min were administered to maintain a mean arterial pressure of ≥65 mm Hg. Hematological investigations showed hemoglobin at 13.7 g% (11.5–16.5 g/dl), total leukocyte count of 19.8 × 10^9/l (4.0–11.0 × 10^9/l), with neutrophils at 92%, lymphocytes at 8%, and eosinophils at 2%. Plasma biochemical profile revealed serum creatinine at 1.9 mg/dl (0.8–1.1 mg/dl) and urea at 91 mg/dl (15–45 mg/dl). Arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis indicated severe metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap of 26 mEq/l, serum lactate at 4.2 mmol/l (<2 mmol/l), and ScvO2 at 58%. Serum bilirubin was 3.49 mg/dl (0.4–1.1 mg/dl), aspartate transaminase (AST) was 103 IU/dl (25–40 IU/dl), alanine transaminase (ALT) was 190 IU/dl (35–70 IU/dl), and creatine kinase (CK) was 441 U/l, indicating multiorgan dysfunction. Echocardiography showed a cardiac index of 3.44 l/min/m2, systemic vascular resistance index (SVRI) of 233.3 dynes/cm5/sec/m2, with normal left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP) and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF). His APACHE-II score was 28, and Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score was 10. An abdominal ultrasound revealed no obvious visceral abnormalities. Microbiological assays ruled out malaria and dengue.
test_results: Fluid from the blister came positive for Sta. aureus, which is sensitive to vancomycin and resistant to cloxacillin.

case_report: A 72-year-old male presented with a 4-week history of reduced appetite, fatigue, difficulty breathing, and a dry cough. His medical history includes 20 years of hyperlipidemia and type-2 diabetes mellitus, as well as coronary artery bypass grafting surgery performed in 1990. Physical examination revealed absent breath sounds on the left side. Imaging studies, including chest X-ray and chest computed tomography (CT), identified a large pleural effusion on the left side. There was no evidence of peripheral lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. The patient declined a bone marrow biopsy. Positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) did not reveal any significant findings. Echocardiography indicated an ejection fraction of 40% without pericardial effusion. To manage the pleural effusion, thoracentesis and talc pleurodesis were performed. The pleural fluid was hemorrhagic, and biochemical analysis classified it as exudate with lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels at 2386 U/L and albumin at 2.6 g/dL.
test_results: Cytomorphological and immunocytochemical analysis of the pleural fluid showed high grade malignant lymphoma.

case_report: A 66-year-old Caucasian male with a 45-pack year smoking history presented with a 6-month history of chronic cough. Two chest computed tomography (CT) scans showed persistent extensive right lower lobe consolidation. His cough improved with two courses of oral antibiotics, but there was no radiological improvement. The patient's medical history included tonsillar squamous cell carcinoma treated with tonsillectomy and chemoradiotherapy. He was awaiting a partial cystectomy for a newly diagnosed urothelial malignancy. There were no significant respiratory, autoimmune, or immunodeficiency conditions prior to presentation, nor any relevant family history. He had occupational exposure to silica and asbestos, but below recommended workplace limits. Physical examination revealed fine crackles in the right lung base, with the rest of the examination being normal. Sputum cultures and cytology were non-diagnostic. Pulmonary function tests showed moderate obstructive ventilatory impairment with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 48.5%, consistent with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The FEV1 was 1.61L (47% predicted) and FVC was 3.33L (74% predicted). There was no restriction with a TLC of 6.15L (83% predicted) and a severely reduced diffusion capacity with a DLCO of 12.4 (46% predicted). Chest CT demonstrated widespread airspace consolidation in the right lower lobe with underlying reticular shadowing and mild mediastinal and right hilar lymphadenopathy. An FDG PET scan showed mild FDG avidity in the right lower lobe and moderate avidity in bilateral mediastinal lymph nodes (SUV 6.3), with no abnormal avidity elsewhere. Bronchial washings from the right lower lobe revealed a mix of bronchial, squamous cells, and lymphocytes, with no malignant cells. A cellular differential was not obtained. Endobronchial Ultrasound/Transbronchial needle aspirate (EBUS/TBNA) of lymph node stations 4R and 7 showed lymphocytes without malignancy. Flow cytometry on the TBNA sample demonstrated polyclonal B cells with a normal kappa: lambda ratio. EBUS/TBNA and BAL were repeated on two occasions. A fine needle aspiration and core lung biopsy were also non-diagnostic. The patient was treated with 25 mg of Prednisone for one month, without radiological improvement.
test_results: Histology showed a diffuse lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate in the interstitium, perivascular and peribronchiolar spaces with occasional lymphoid aggregates. There were rare giant cells present with a few isolated poorly formed granulomas including some with central necrosis in dilated lymphatic spaces. No fungal organisms or viral inclusions were detected on special stains including for HHV8, EBV and CMV. Immunohistochemistry showed a mixed T-cell and B-cell infiltrate and no evidence of monoclonality.

case_report: A 40-year-old female visited the outpatient department with shortness of breath for 6 months, classified as NYHA II. She reported no other cardiac symptoms and was not taking any cardiac medications. Her medical history did not include any known heart disease, and her childhood was reportedly normal. There was no history of rheumatic fever or significant cardiac issues in her family. She had two pregnancies at ages 25 and 32, both without complications. On examination, she exhibited uniform central cyanosis and Grade II clubbing, with oxygen saturations of 87% (preductal) and 88% (postductal). The jugular venous pulse showed a prominent a wave. Her blood pressure was 145/90 mmHg in the right arm. Mild cardiomegaly was noted, with a right ventricular type of apex. The first heart sound was normal, and the second heart sound was widely and fixedly split, with the pulmonary component louder than the aortic component. No additional S3 or S4 sounds were heard. A grade 2/6 ejection systolic murmur was present at the pulmonary outflow. A chest radiograph revealed an enlarged cardiac silhouette, a dilated main pulmonary artery, and pulmonary plethora. A 12-lead Electrocardiogram indicated a clockwise loop, sinus rhythm, right axis deviation of the QRS vector, and enlargement of the right atrium and ventricle.
test_results: Two-dimensional echocardiography images showed large secundum atrial septal defect (ASD) with bidirectional flow. There was a small upper muscular ventricular septal defect (VSD) as well. The right ventricle (RV) was giving origin to aorta, and the left ventricle (LV) was giving origin to the PA. The left ventricular thickness (posterior wall) measured 4.2 mm. Tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE) was 22 mm. The oximetry showed almost equal saturations in the right and left ventricles with similar values in aorta and PA. Anterior ventriculogram showed morphological RV giving origin to aorta, whereas posterior ventriculogram showed morphological left ventricle giving origin to PA with confluent branches. There was a small upper muscular ventricular septal defect noted. Pulmonary angiogram showed confluent and good-sized branch pulmonary arteries with good distal arborization. LV and RV angiogram was suggestive of normal biventricular systolic function.

case_report: A 33-year-old Caucasian female arrived at the emergency department with persistent non-bloody, non-bilious vomiting and generalized fatigue for three days. She mentioned experiencing similar vomiting episodes lasting 2-3 days every two months, which were alleviated by ondansetron. Additionally, she reported numbness and tingling in her feet for the past year. There was no history of fever, dizziness, abdominal pain, diarrhea, or shortness of breath. She denied smoking or illicit drug use but had a history of heavy alcohol consumption. Her medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and rheumatoid arthritis. Her medications included amlodipine and rosuvastatin, and she had previously been treated with Humira (adalimumab) for seronegative rheumatoid arthritis, which was discontinued two years ago. She had a prior hospital admission for alcohol intoxication. Laboratory tests showed elevated ethanol levels of 1839 mg/dl, and a liver biopsy revealed steatosis. She had no significant surgical history and no recent use of steroids, NSAIDs, or antibiotics. On arrival, her vital signs were normal. She appeared mildly ill but was not in acute distress, had no resting tremors, and her abdominal examination was normal. Laboratory results showed elevated creatinine of 4.05 (baseline 0.85), blood urea nitrogen (BUN) of 48, and an anion gap of 28. She was admitted for acute kidney injury due to volume depletion and treated with IV fluids, electrolytes, and supportive care. Despite treatment, lab results indicated hypophosphatemia (1.5), hypouricemia (<0.28 mg/dl; normal range 3.5-7 mg/dl), non-anion gap hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, and hypokalemia. Urine chemistries showed proteinuria 1.6g/24hrs (normal <0.3g/24hrs), phosphaturia 12.4 mg/dl (normal 2.5-4.6 mg/dl), hyperuricosuria 32 mg/dl (normal 2.7-5.4 mg/dl), and low urinary sodium <20 mmol/l. Previous lab work indicated similar results, suggesting a chronic condition. Glycosuria with euglycemia (urine glucose 500 mg/dl with normal serum glucose), hypokalemia (2.6; 3.3; 3.4) with high urine potassium, and intermittently low bicarbonate (21; 19) were noted on different occasions. Fractional excretion of phosphorus was 15% (above 5% indicates renal phosphate wasting) after treatment of her acute kidney injury. Tests ruled out multiple myeloma, genetic diseases, fibromuscular dysplasia, metal poisoning, and Wilson's disease.
test_results: A kidney biopsy showed acute tubular injury, along with 1+ IgA mesangial deposition by immunofluorescence; no immune complexes were found on electron microscopy.

case_report: An 80-year-old woman presented with difficulty in raising her right upper limb, progressive dyskinesia, and gait disorder. She had experienced neck pain for approximately 2 years and numbness in her extremities for about a year, both of which had worsened significantly before her visit. She could walk unassisted for less than 100 meters. Muscle weakness (manual muscle testing [MMT] score: 3) was observed in the entire right upper limb, while strength in the remaining limbs was normal. Hypesthesia was noted throughout the upper and lower limbs. Deep tendon reflexes were increased bilaterally in all limbs, with positive Hoffman’s and Wartenberg’s signs. Her preoperative Japanese Orthopaedic Association (JOA) score was 8.5 points. Radiographs and cervical contrast CT revealed osteolytic lesions in C3–7. A mass extended into the spinal canal from within the vertebrae, compressing the cervical spinal cord from the right side. The mass was stained in the early contrast phase and showed an internal low-density area. MRI detected a mass with the same signal profile as bone from within the C3–7 vertebrae to outside of the vertebral bodies, compressing the cervical spinal cord from the right side at the same levels. Blood tests showed no thrombocytopenia, anemia, or coagulation abnormalities. The inflammatory response was normal. Blood cultures and various tumor markers were negative. A percutaneous vertebral biopsy showed culture negativity and no neoplastic lesions.
test_results: The resected specimen exhibited various and complex proliferating patterns of vasoforming cells in low-magnification images, with most areas showing a combination of solid and vasodilated proliferating patterns. In solid areas, numerous vascular cavities had been formed by atypical cells, including epithelioid cells with infrequent mitosis. In the periphery, irregular nodules had infiltrated into the adjacent muscular and fatty-fibrous tissue. The nodules had a slit-like structure with spindle cells. Several nodules contained epithelioid cell proliferation that clearly showed ERG, CD31, and CD34, but not D2–40, immunopositivity, which were surrounded by cells positive for the pericytic markers myo1B, CD146, and SMA. The proliferating cells were negative for markers of epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, including CAMTA1, TFE3, and FOSB. The Ki-67 labelling index was calculated as approximately 16.1% (109/678) in areas with solid components and dilated capillaries and 10.6% (83/783) in areas containing slit-like blood vessels in the solid components.

case_report: A 19-year-old male presented to Chigateri General Hospital in April 2020 with joint pain for one year and generalized weakness for 20 days. He reported progressive, painless blurring of vision over the past two months, more pronounced in the right eye. There was no history of photophobia, lachrymation, or trauma. He has been managing diabetes mellitus for six years with insulin, metformin, and pioglitazone. His parents had a third-degree consanguineous marriage, and his sibling is unaffected. A maternal cousin has similar skin lesions. His mother did not receive antenatal care and had a domicile delivery. Immunization history is inconsistent. There was no history of palpitation, lower limb swelling, syncope, reduced urine output, hypertension, congenital heart disease, kidney disease, hypothyroidism, or other illnesses. The patient appeared poorly built and undernourished. Vital signs were normal, with no pallor, icterus, cyanosis, clubbing, lymphadenopathy, or edema. His body mass index was 15.4 kg/m2, middle upper arm circumference was 16.5 cm, and head circumference was 51.5 cm. He had large prominent eyes, coarse facies, malocclusion of the teeth with hyperdontia, dermatitis neglecta with acanthosis nigricans on all sides of the neck, a fissured tongue, and enlarged tonsils. Subungual hyperkeratosis was noted in his fingernails, and acanthosis nigricans was present on the dorsum of the hand extending to the forearm. His toenails showed onychodystrophy and pincer nail. Clinically, his liver was enlarged, and the examination of all other systems was unremarkable.
test_results: Retinoscopy revealed severe proliferative diabetic retinopathy in the right eye and severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy in the left eye.

case_report: An 11-year-old boy presented with a 2-month history of increasing difficulty in breathing during physical activity. Prior to this period, he was in good health. There was no history of fever, cough, wheezing, or coughing up blood. Physical examination did not reveal any abnormalities. Chest auscultation indicated a mild increase in heart rate. There were no signs of heart failure, no heart murmurs, and no abnormal lung sounds. A chest X-ray showed widespread, fine reticulonodular opacities evenly distributed across both lung fields and an enlarged main pulmonary artery. There were no Kerley B lines or fluid accumulation in the pleural space. Electrocardiography indicated a deviation of the heart's electrical axis to the right and an enlargement of the right ventricle with changes in the ST-T segment. Echocardiography confirmed the enlargement of the right ventricle and the main pulmonary trunk. The left ventricular systolic function, mitral valve, and pulmonary veins appeared normal. The estimated pressure in the right ventricle during systole was between 90 and 100 mmHg. The right atrium was also enlarged. There was no significant medical history, including no chronic liver disease or hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia. He was subsequently referred for further imaging evaluation of the pulmonary blood vessels.
test_results: CT pulmonary angiogram was taken with arterial and venous phases, along with high-resolution CT of thorax which showed innumerable, randomly distributed tiny, and centrilobular ground-glass nodules in bilateral lung parenchyma. These nodules were measuring 6–8 mm in size. No lobar predilection was observed. The main pulmonary trunk was dilated with a luminal diameter of 3.5 cm. The right and left branches of the pulmonary artery were also enlarged with peripheral pruning of the branches. Concentric hypertrophy of the right ventricle with bulging of the interventricular septum toward the left ventricle was observed along with enlarged right atrium features suggestive of pulmonary artery hypertension. There was a small 10-mm lymph node in the right paratracheal region. There was no interstitial pulmonary fibrosis evident on imaging.

case_report: An 18-year-old Korean male presented to the Department of Dermatology at Yeungnam University Hospital on November 2, 2005, with progressively generalized pigmented lesions. He was reported to be normal at birth. Reticular hyperpigmented lesions were first noted at the age of 2 on the popliteal and antecubital fossae. These changes gradually spread to the axillae and trunk. Linear sclerosing bands appeared on both the antecubital and popliteal fossae over the years. The lesions increased in size and number over time, but the patient remained asymptomatic. His family history revealed that his father had similar symptoms and passed away in his forties due to cardiovascular disease. His younger brother also exhibited similar poikilodermatous lesions, which appeared at the age of 3 and showed progressive hyperpigmented and sclerotic changes. Physical examination showed micrognathia, clubbing of the fingers, and slim extremities compared to the trunk. Dermatologic examination revealed generalized hyperpigmented, telangiectatic, and atrophic changes, particularly pronounced in the axillae, antecubital, and popliteal fossae. Linear hyperkeratotic and sclerotic bands were observed on both the antecubital and popliteal fossae. Sclerosis of the palms and soles was also noted. Laboratory tests, including complete blood cell count, liver function test, blood coagulation test, antinuclear antibody, and urinalysis, were within normal limits or negative.
test_results: Histopathologic finding revealed increased melanin pigments in the basal layer and sclerotic changes and telangiectasia in the upper dermis. The fragmentations of elastic fibers in the dermis were noted in elastic stain.

case_report: A three-day-old female in the nursery ward was evaluated for multiple red skin lesions on the chest and left shoulder. The baby was born full-term via spontaneous vaginal delivery. Shortly after birth, the patient was found to have a low platelet count and was treated with platelet transfusion and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). Two of the patient's siblings were also born with similar skin lesions and had low platelet counts. The patient's grandmother and two aunts had similar skin lesions that remained stable since birth. The mother reported that all her previous pregnancies were complicated by low platelet counts. The patient's parents are related by blood. All affected family members have normal development and growth without systemic symptoms. On examination, the patient was vitally stable with normal growth parameters, no syndromic features, and no abnormalities in head size or limb structure. Physical examination revealed a well-defined red to rose-colored patch on the left shoulder and arm measuring 4 cm x 3 cm with irregular borders, along with multiple smaller round to oval erythematous macules and patches on the right side of the chest and over the right knee. There was no tenderness or thrill. Examination of the nails, mucous membranes, and hair was unremarkable, and the systemic examination, including eye and neurologic assessments, was normal.
test_results: Histopathologic findings showed dilated capillary venular channels in the upper dermis and no arteriovenous malformations. Ultrasound revealed dilated dermal postcapillary venule with an increase in Doppler flow compared to the adjacent dermis. There were no fistula and no arteriovenous or lymphatic malformations.

case_report: A 67-year-old woman experienced abdominal swelling and alterations in bowel movements over the past 4 months. She had previously undergone a transabdominal hysterectomy and left salpingo-oophorectomy for benign conditions 2 years earlier. Imaging studies, including colonoscopy and colonography, showed adhesions and narrowing in the sigmoid colon. An ultrasound identified a pelvic mass with a smooth surface, measuring approximately 22 cm in diameter. Laboratory tests indicated an elevated CA-125 level of 104.2 U/ml. Surgical intervention included right salpingo-oophorectomy, appendectomy, removal of the infracolic omentum, and partial resection of the sigmoid colon and small intestine.
test_results: IHC analysis revealed positive staining for Ki-67 (labeling index, 50%), neurofilament (focal+), NSE, nestin, synaptophysin (focal+), P16 and P53 but was negative for CD-99, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), octamer-binding transcription factor (OCT) 3/4, S-100, estrogen receptor (ER), paired box gene 8 (PAX-8), progesterone receptor (PR), Wilms tumor (WT)-1, creatine kinase (CK)20, CK7 and calretinin.

case_report: A 73-year-old male presented with painless decreased visual acuity, floaters, and flashes in the right eye for 2 weeks. The right eye had no history of trauma, surgery, cryotherapy, or laser photocoagulation except for an uneventful cataract surgery 15 years ago. The left eye had undergone vitrectomy with retained silicone oil to treat retinal detachment 8 months prior at another hospital. The left eye was now aphakic with retinal redetachment under the silicone oil, secondary glaucoma, and band keratopathy. His medical history included essential hypertension and hyperlipidemia. His medications included amlodipine, losartan, and simvastatin. At presentation, best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 0.6 logMAR in the right eye and counting fingers in the left eye. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 14 mmHg in the right eye and 12 mmHg in the left eye. Ocular examination of the right eye showed normal conjunctiva and sclera, clear cornea, mildly shallow anterior chamber with no cell or flare, and the eye was pseudophakic. The pupil was dilatable to 5 mm. Dilated fundus examination revealed corrugated inferior bullous retinal detachment with shifting subretinal fluid. No definite choroidal detachment or retinal break was identified with a wide-field contact lens. Optical coherence tomography (SPECTRALIS, Heidelberg Engineering, Heidelberg, Germany) of the macula showed subretinal fluid, a small juxtapapillary pigment epithelial detachment, and intraretinal cysts. Ocular B-scan ultrasonography (Aviso, Quantel Medical, Clermont-Ferrand, France) demonstrated ocular wall thickening with peripheral choroidal elevation in the right eye. No tumors were identified and no subtenon fluid collection was detected. The axial length measurement (IOL Master 500, Carl Zeiss Meditec, Jena, Germany) was 22.59 mm in the right eye and 22.94 mm in the left eye. Fluorescein angiography (FA) (SPECTRALIS, Heidelberg Engineering) showed granular hyperfluorescence at the mid-periphery and peripapillary areas with no dye leakage. Indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) (SPECTRALIS, Heidelberg Engineering) demonstrated diffuse early hypercyanescence, especially in the posterior pole and superotemporal vortex veins, persisting to the late phase in the peripapillary area. FA and ICGA showed no evidence of chorioretinal inflammation. Blood tests including complete blood count, blood chemistries, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, serological test for human immunodeficiency virus, venereal disease research laboratory test for syphilis, Treponema pallidum haemagglutination test, interferon gamma assay for tuberculosis, antinuclear antibodies test, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies test were all within normal limits. The chest x-ray showed no pulmonary infiltration. After excluding infectious etiologies, 1 mg/kg/day of oral systemic steroid was administered for 7 days without clinical response.
test_results: The ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) revealed edematous thickening of the anterior choroid and thickening of the anterior sclera measuring up to 1.26 mm.

case_report: A 14-year-old Korean male presented with a 2-year history of multiple horizontal linear lesions on the lumbar region, which were asymptomatic. His familial and personal medical histories were unremarkable, and he had not taken any significant medications, including steroids. He reported no history of trauma to the lumbar area, obesity, rapid growth, or systemic illness. He noted that hypertrophic lesions developed from atrophic bands, with the atrophic bands on the upper back appearing recently. Physical examination showed several palpable hypertrophic yellowish bands on the lower lumbar region. Lesions at the middle level of the back exhibited a transitional change, with central hypertrophic bands merging into peripheral atrophic bands. Above these, slightly atrophic shiny erythematous bands with a pinkish hue were observed. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits.
test_results: Hypertrophic collagen bundles were separated by basophilic wavy fibers in the dermis without significant epidermal changes. Irregular clumped or fragmented elastic fibers between collagen bundles in the reticular dermis. Elongated elastic fibers with splitting of ends that looked like a paintbrush were observed.

case_report: A 27-year-old woman was first seen at 31 weeks’ gestation in her second pregnancy. Twelve months earlier, her first pregnancy had ended in the 22nd gestational week with an intrauterine fetal death, which had been preceded by progressive maternal thrombocytopenia and intrauterine growth restriction. Two weeks after the fetal death, the patient experienced an ischemic stroke. Her platelet count was 40,000/µL. Testing for antiphospholipid antibodies was negative. When she became pregnant for the second time, prophylactic treatment with dalteparin was started. The pregnancy was uneventful until gestational week 30, when she had a second stroke. The dalteparin dose was increased and treatment with hydroxychloroquine was started. The patient was in overall good health but had residual facial palsy and slurred speech. Blood pressure, heart rate, and temperature were normal, and she had no edema. An ultrasound evaluation showed a viable but small-for-gestational-age fetus. Her platelet count was 92,000/µL; serum LDH was mildly increased. Hemoglobin, serum haptoglobin, serum creatinine, and liver enzymes were normal.
test_results: ADAMTS13 activity was 3.9%.

case_report: A 5-year-old girl, born to second-degree consanguineous parents, presented with sudden lethargy and altered consciousness. There was no history of fever, gastrointestinal symptoms, respiratory issues, seizures, trauma, or toxin ingestion. Developmental milestones were delayed, but the perinatal period was normal. She had a similar episode of drowsiness lasting 2 days without vomiting or fever 4 months prior. Her elder sibling is healthy. On examination, the child was drowsy, responding to painful stimuli, with intact doll’s eye reflex and reactive pupils. She moved all four limbs to painful stimuli, had preserved deep tendon reflexes, and extensor plantar responses. She was afebrile, without organomegaly, sting or bite marks, or meningeal signs. Blood pressure was normal for her age. Initial brain CT was normal, and metabolic parameters including blood sugar, urea, creatinine, electrolytes, and liver enzymes were within normal limits. She was treated with ceftriaxone, acyclovir, and hypertonic saline. CSF analysis showed no cells, normal biochemistry, and sterile culture. Due to lack of improvement in consciousness, brain MRI was performed, revealing hyperintense signals in the frontal regions bilaterally with diffusion restriction. Magnetic resonance angiography and venography were normal. CSF tests for various viruses were negative. No clinically overt seizures were observed, but an EEG showed background slowing without epileptiform discharges. Historical review did not suggest drug or toxin exposure. Blood tests revealed elevated serum ammonia (465 µg/dL) with normal lactate levels. Intravenous dextrose and sodium benzoate (250mg/kg/day) were administered, leading to improved consciousness over 2 days and a reduction in serum ammonia to 210 µg/dL. A protein-restricted diet and continued sodium benzoate were initiated.
test_results: Tandem mass spectrometry report revealed elevated levels of arginine, 480 µmol/L (<50 µmol/L).

case_report: A 17-year-old male presented to the emergency department with severe anemia, indicated by a hemoglobin level of 3.5 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 4200/μL, and a platelet count of 206,000/μL. Over the past two months, he experienced fatigue and lack of energy and was on antidepressant medication. He reported no fever, pain, unintentional weight loss, breathing difficulties, or respiratory symptoms. There were no previous bleeding episodes, dietary deficiencies, recent infections, or trauma. Physical examination revealed pallor and a rapid heart rate. Laboratory tests confirmed severe anemia (hemoglobin = 3.4 g/dL) with iron deficiency, but no hemolysis, elevated inflammatory markers, or deficiencies in folic acid or vitamin B12. Coagulation tests showed prolonged prothrombin time (14.4 seconds), activated partial thromboplastin time (27.6 seconds), low fibrinogen (86 mg/dL), and elevated D-dimer levels (10,317 ng/mL), indicating coagulation factor consumption and fibrinolysis. A contrast-enhanced thoraco-abdomen-pelvic computed tomography (CT) scan revealed an extensive hematoma from the cervical to the mediastinal, abdominal, and retroperitoneal areas, along with sternal bone lesions. An echocardiogram was normal, with no signs of pericardial effusion. The patient was admitted to intensive care, and further evaluations were conducted. The patient developed pancytopenia, with minimum leukocyte and platelet counts of 3730/μL and 74,000/μL, respectively, and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), despite multiple transfusions of red blood cells and fibrinogen. Bone marrow aspirate showed a reactive process with erythropoiesis. A right thoracoscopy revealed a moderate hemorrhagic pleural effusion and a mediastinal mass with signs of internal hemorrhage, which was biopsied.
test_results: Histology displayed a lymphatic-venous malformation. Dynamic contrast-enhancing magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed an extensive cervical, mediastinal, abdominal, and retroperitoneal lesion, with bilateral hilar, pleural, mesenteric, and perirectal involvement, with fluid signal and some foci of late enhancement. Hepatosplenomegaly and minimal abdominopelvic ascites were also present. Intranodal lymphangiography revealed delay in contrast progression and deviation to vascular malformation’s ectatic lymphatic channels at abdominal, thoracic, and cervical levels. Histology second look revealed remarkable presence of dilated lymphatic channels (podoplanin positive), confirming a lymphatic-venous malformative vascular anomaly.

case_report: A 69-year-old male patient visited our hospital on December 1, 2021, due to a dry cough and shortness of breath after activity for the past 10 years and intermittent fever for the past 3 months. In early November 2011, the patient experienced a progressive cough after catching a cold and was treated with antibiotics and cough suppressants, but no significant improvement was noted. He also had shortness of breath after intense activities, which affected his daily work but not his daily life, so he did not seek further medical consultation. In early January 2012, the symptoms worsened after another cold, accompanied by a small amount of white sputum, without fever or hemoptysis. The cough improved after treatment with antibiotics and cough suppressants at a local hospital, but shortness of breath during intense activities worsened. He returned to the local hospital, and chest computed tomography (CT) showed pulmonary fibrosis. On May 8, 2012, the patient visited our interstitial lung disease clinic. Laboratory tests, including a 17-item antinuclear antibody (ANA) profile, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) profile, and rheumatoid arthritis (RA)-related antibody profile, were all negative. Complete blood count, urine sediment, routine urine testing, and biochemical analysis were normal. Chest high-resolution CT (HRCT) showed findings consistent with usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP). Pulmonary function tests indicated mild restrictive ventilation dysfunction and moderate diffusion impairment: forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1)/forced vital capacity (FVC) was 78%; FVC/FVC% predicted was 2.81 L/74.9%; total lung capacity (TLC)/TLC% predicted was 5.09 L/86.3%; diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO)/DLCO% predicted was 3.66 mmol/min/kpa/52.9%. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid tests showed a cell count of 8.6 × 10^6/L, with 64% phagocytes, 11% neutrophils, 24% lymphocytes, and 1% eosinophils. After a global multidisciplinary discussion (MDD), he was enrolled in the INPULSIS clinical trial and took nintedanib from May 21, 2012, to June 15, 2017. During this period, he experienced intermittent diarrhea, which was relieved with smectite and berberine. When the INPULSIS ON trial concluded, he started pirfenidone (0.6 g tid) on January 13, 2018, with no significant adverse effects reported. However, since September 2019, he experienced worsening exertional shortness of breath and was unable to perform physical labor. In early September 2021, he complained of fatigue and had a fever on September 12, with a maximum temperature ranging from 37.8 to 38.7°C. His dry cough worsened, and tests for COVID-19 were negative. Repeated chest CT revealed progression of pulmonary fibrosis but no significant exudative shadows. Microbiological analysis for induced sputum, 1,3-β-D-glucan test, Widal test, Weil-Felix test, mycoplasma pneumoniae antibodies, chlamydia antibody, and Legionella antibodies were all negative. Empirical antibiotics (meropenem, ceftriaxone, moxifloxacin, and azithromycin) were ineffective. He visited our outpatient department on December 1, 2021. He had no arthralgia, dry mouth, or dry eyes. He was healthy before 2012 but had a history of smoking (10 cigarettes/day for 20 years) and quit smoking in 2008. He was a farmer with no history of occupational dust exposure. Physical examination revealed a pulse oxygen saturation of 95% while breathing air, no palpable superficial cervical lymph nodes, no clubbing of the fingers, Velcro-like crackles in both lower lungs, and no swelling in either inferior limb. Routine blood test results showed a white blood cell count of 10.4 × 10^9/L (N < 9.5), neutrophil percentage of 84.3% (N < 75%), and hemoglobin of 107 g/L (N: 120–160). Urine sediment and routine urine testing showed a red blood cell count of 80/μL with 100% abnormal morphology. The 24-hour urine protein was 0.3 g. Biochemical tests revealed serum creatinine of 147 μmol/L, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) of 9.34 mmol/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 82 mm/h (N < 15), and C-reactive protein (CRP) of 25.6 mg/L (N < 8). Serum complement analysis and quantitative analysis of IgG, IgM, and IgA were normal.
test_results: The ANA profile: ANA 1:320 (AC-4), other indicators were negative; ANCA (P-type) 1:20, and myeloperoxidase (MPO): 148 RU/mL (N < 20).

case_report: A five-year-old girl visited our outpatient department with concerns about unusual hair growth on her lower back. She had been intermittently using over-the-counter topical Eflornithine for more than a year, as advised by an unqualified practitioner. Upon examination, she exhibited no neurological deficits, and her overall clinical examination was unremarkable.
test_results: Her MRI showed a normal spinal cord and vertebral column without any anomaly.

case_report: A female infant, born at full term with a birth weight of 2,380 grams, exhibited hypotonia and a submucous cleft palate, which was surgically corrected at age 6. At 3 years old, physical examination revealed facial features such as arched eyebrows with thinning at the sides, long palpebral fissures with outward turning of the lower eyelid, long eyelashes, large prominent ears with dysplastic helices, and a depressed nasal tip. Additional findings included hypotonia, joint laxity, delayed motor development milestones, and mild cognitive impairment. Two-dimensional color-doppler echocardiography and renal ultrasound results were normal. Genetic testing of the KMT2D gene, conducted via target resequencing on the MiSeq (Illumina) platform, identified a heterozygous deletion of two bases c.16085_16086delAG, resulting in a nonsense mutation at the protein level, p.Lys5362Serfs*96. At 23 years old, she experienced intermittent tactile hypoesthesia in the feet and increasing lumbar pain.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the spine revealed the presence of a lumbar endocanalar mass extending from L3 to L4, isointense on T1 and T2 weighted images with peripheral contrast enhancement. The lesion had a maximum cranial-caudal diameter of 45 mm with diffuse compression and posterior displacement of spinal nerve roots.

case_report: A 4-month-old male was delivered urgently via caesarian section at 32 weeks of gestation. Immediate intubation was required at birth due to low oxygen levels. At 28 weeks of gestation, imaging had shown a significant defect in the ventral wall, and heart imaging had identified a combination of four specific heart abnormalities.
test_results: Fetal ultrasound revealed a large ventral wall defect. Fetal echocardiography revealed tetralogy of Fallot. Fetal MRI revealed deficiency of the central tendon/anterior diaphragm with a small portion of the liver and small bowel loops protruding into the pericardial space. Postnatal echocardiography confirmed tetralogy of Fallot. There was not significant RVOT obstruction with minimal dynamic obstruction, normal-size pulmonary valve, and pulmonary arteries.

case_report: A 23-year-old unmarried female presented with a 4-day history of headache and multiple episodes of vomiting, which had been treated with analgesics prior to her admission. Physical examination revealed an afebrile patient with signs of meningeal irritation, including neck rigidity and a positive Kernig’s sign. The patient reported no significant past medical history and no recollection of similar episodes previously. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed a clear appearance with a white cell count of 880/sq mm, predominantly lymphocytes (65%). CSF protein was measured at 62 mg/dl, and glucose at 32 mg/dl. CSF staining and culture were negative for mycobacteria and other bacterial pathogens. The patient was administered broad-spectrum antibiotics (Ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and levofloxacin) without any clinical improvement.
test_results: A CT scan done 2 days after admission revealed lobulated extra-axial hyperdense lesions in the prepontine and cerebello-medullary cisterns. The neuroparenchyma, ventricular system, and other basal cisterns were normal. Contrast-enhanced MRI was done subsequently, which showed a lobulated extra-axial lesion in the prepontine cistern extending into both cerebello-medullary cisterns. The lesion showed hyperintense signal on T1 and FLAIR images, with mildly hypointense signal on T2-weighted images. There was no evidence of restricted diffusion on DWI. Susceptibility-weighted images did not reveal any evidence of blooming within the lesion. There was no evidence of signal suppression on T1-weighted fat-suppressed images. Post-gadalonium images did not show any intralesional or peripheral rim enhancement.

case_report: A 20-year-old male presented with a 10-year history of multiple skin-colored, firm, asymptomatic papules and nodules ranging from 2 to 10 mm in size, primarily located on the face, with additional discrete lesions on the scalp, ears, and neck. The lesions were densely clustered on the central face, giving a leonine appearance. There were no associated systemic abnormalities, and routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. Similar lesions were observed in the patient's mother. Physical examination revealed no hypopigmented or hypoesthetic lesions, and nerve trunks were not thickened. The lesions were not painful.
test_results: A punch biopsy from face and scalp showed multiple nests of basaloid cells in the dermis with peripheral palisading in few nests. Some of the aggregates were containing horn cysts and showing follicular differentiation. Mitotic figures and atypical cells were not noticed in nests.

case_report: A 59-year-old male was brought to the hospital due to increasing lethargy and confusion that began early in the morning. He had reported feeling fatigued frequently over the past three months. Three days before admission, he consumed a large quantity of dog meat at a party, which led to nausea and vomiting. The following day, after eating chicken and freshwater snails, he again experienced nausea and severe vomiting. On the day of admission, he did not wake up at his usual time and displayed inappropriate behavior and drowsiness. His medical history included recurrent abdominal pain and periodic convulsions during childhood, but no seizures in adulthood. Upon examination, he was in a semi-comatose state with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 10/15, disoriented to time, place, and person. His vital signs were stable: blood pressure 150/80 mmHg, pulse rate 84/min, respiratory rate 24/min, and body temperature 36℃. Laboratory tests revealed hyperammonemia (143.8 mM), elevated liver enzymes (alanine aminotransferase 179 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 91 U/L), total bilirubin 1.91 mg/dL, and blood glucose 106 mg/dL. Blood urea nitrogen was 17.7 mg/dL, and serum creatinine was 1.01 mg/dL. Blood analysis showed mild leukocytosis (10.41 × 10^3 leukocytes/µL) with normal hemoglobin, platelet count, and clotting profile. Serum electrolytes indicated mild hypernatremia (149 mEq sodium/L), with normal potassium and chloride levels. Toxicology screen results were normal. Further tests showed no gastrointestinal bleeding, and imaging (CT and diffusion-weighted MRI) revealed no brain lesions. Abdominal CT imaging was also normal. Cerebrospinal fluid examination was normal. Despite treatment with a lactulose enema, his serum ammonia level increased to 370 mM, and he remained confused, prompting the initiation of acute hemodialysis. During hemodialysis, he experienced a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, treated with 1 mg intravenous lorazepam. Although the seizure subsided, he continued to have convulsive movements, requiring additional intravenous lorazepam. Levetiracetam was administered for nonconvulsive status epilepticus. After the initial hemodialysis session, his serum ammonia level decreased to 170 mM but later rose to 228 mM.
test_results: A plasma amino acids analysis revealed elevated ornithine (196 µM; normal 19-81 µM), decreased citrulline (3 µM; normal 19-62 µM), and elevated glutamine and lysine. Urine organic acids analysis revealed highly elevated urinary orotic acid (603.5 mg/mg creatinine) and a mild urinary uracil peak.

case_report: A 30-year-old patient, gravida 1 and para 0, delivered a boy weighing 3290 g in May 2011 following a previous delivery in 2008 of a girl weighing 2970 g. Five months post-delivery, the patient experienced metrorrhagia. Pelvic echography did not reveal any distinctive features. Beta-HCG levels were slightly elevated. An operative hysteroscopy was performed, removing 5 cc of material. Weekly beta-HCG monitoring was initiated, and the patient was placed on oestroprogestative contraception. Due to the stagnation of beta-HCG levels over 2 weeks, a subsequent operative hysteroscopy was conducted, removing 3 cc of material.
test_results: The histology demonstrated the presence of several trophoblastic viable cells or nearly pyknotic trophoblastic looking cells without signs of malignancy. The immunohistochemistry showed strongly positive tumorous staining for inhibin, partially positive staining for beta-HCG and for HPL (placental lactogenic hormone), and negative staining for p63. The Mib-1(Ki67) has reached 10–15% by locations.

case_report: A 62-year-old male patient was admitted to the hospital due to abdominal pain and abdominal distension for one month, with worsening symptoms over the past five days. The patient experienced abdominal pain around the umbilicus, which was paroxysmal and accompanied by abdominal distension, with minimal gas and stool passage. Despite these symptoms, the patient continued to eat normally. Five days prior to admission, the symptoms intensified, leading to a complete cessation of gas and stool passage. Upon visiting the hospital, an abdominal CT revealed small intestinal obstruction. Physical examination showed abdominal distention, visible intestinal loops, generalized abdominal tenderness with a focus around the umbilicus, and hyperactive bowel sounds. Laboratory results indicated a WBC count of 19.61×10^9/L, hemoglobin level of 91 g/L, and serum albumin level of 22 g/L, with other tests returning normal results. The patient had a history of good health, no previous abdominal surgeries, and no history of medication use.
test_results: The patient visited our hospital for treatment and underwent abdominal CT, which revealed small intestinal obstruction. Pathological findings included: intestinal stenosis was obtained, shallow intestinal segmental ulcer formation, mucosal erosion and inflammatory granulation tissue formation, the mucosal muscle layer disappeared, submucosal fiber hyperplasia, and longitudinal extension to the mucosal layer, causing mucosal uplift and intestinal wall stenosis. A large amount of neutrophil infiltration, and vasodilatation and congestion were observed in the serosa, but no obvious structural abnormalities were found in the muscle layer and serosa layer.

case_report: An 8-year-old female child presented with fever and vomiting for 2 days and experienced a generalized tonic-clonic seizure on the day of admission. Her mother and sibling were also admitted to the hospital with severe malaria. Vital signs indicated tachycardia and hypotension. Physical examination revealed mild pallor without icterus, cyanosis, edema, or lymphadenopathy. Respiratory, cardiovascular, and abdominal examinations were normal. Neurological examination showed drowsiness, hypertonia, hyper-reflexia, and a positive Babinski response, with no meningeal or cerebellar signs. Laboratory results included hemoglobin at 9.8 g/dL, white blood cell count at 9.8×10^3/µL, and platelets at 0.37×10^6/µL. Peripheral smear examination revealed multiple trophozoites of P. vivax and thrombocytopenia. Differential leucocyte count was 60% neutrophils, 30% lymphocytes, 3% eosinophils, and 7% monocytes. Rapid malaria antigen tests (RMAT) were positive for P. vivax. Serum biochemistry, including blood sugar, renal, and liver function tests, were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination was normal. The child received supportive care for hypotension with crystalloids and inotropes in the intensive care unit. Based on peripheral smear and RMAT results, intravenous artesunate was administered according to the guidelines of the National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme, India, for severe malaria. The child responded well and was transferred to the pediatric ward after one week. There were no neurological deficits, and repeat peripheral smears showed parasitological clearance. On day 15 of illness, the child exhibited abnormal movements, including ataxia and choreo-athetoid movements of the limbs. There were no meningeal signs or cranial nerve palsies. Deep tendon reflexes were exaggerated, and Babinski sign was present. Repeat peripheral blood smear examination did not show any malarial parasites.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of brain with contrast showed high intensity signals in subcortical, cortical, left parietal, periventricular regions and pons.
diagnosis: Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis  secondary to Plasmodium vivax infection

case_report: A 29-year-old Iranian male presented to the Dermatology Department of RAZI Skin Hospital with severe itchy skin lesions on his right lateral ankle, persisting for the past 8 years. Physical examination showed multiple keratotic papules of uniform size arranged in a linear pattern, forming verrucous plaques on the lower part of his right lateral ankle.
test_results: Pathologic evaluation revealed multiple small epidermal invagination with overlying parakeratotic cornoid lamellation and underlying, slightly tortuous, eccrine duct nearby the epidermis. Loss of granular layer and few dyskeratotic cells were evident at the base of epidermal invagination.
diagnosis: Porokeratotic Eccrine Ostial and Dermal Duct Nevus
Orpha_name: Porokeratotic Eccrine Ostial and Dermal Duct Nevus

case_report: A 28-year-old man with diabetes and a history of high blood pressure presented to the outpatient department with recurring boils and leg cellulitis. At age 20, he initially had a 4 mm yellow pustule on his scalp, for which he was given a topical salicylic acid solution. The lesion worsened, leading to multiple boils ranging from 4 mm to 40 mm on his scalp, back, and gluteal region. He was treated with high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanic acid for cellulitis, but there was no improvement. High-dose steroids were then administered, resulting in progressive improvement. However, the boils reappeared when the steroid dose was reduced, necessitating a maintenance dose until complete remission. Long-term high-dose steroid use led to hypertension, uncontrolled diabetes, tooth decay, glaucoma in the left eye, and visual impairment. The steroid dosage was gradually reduced, and these side effects were managed and treated. Eventually, the steroid effects were fully reversed, and the lesions were controlled. Eight months ago, the patient presented with a high fever and severe, non-radiating pain in the left leg, rated 8/10 in severity and worsened by movement. Physical examination showed the left leg was warm, swollen, and had a limited range of motion. Numerous pustular lesions (4 mm-70 mm) with yellow-green discharge were found on the upper and lower back, groin, and gluteal region, along with occasional scars. These lesions were tender, itchy, and ruptured. Other systems were unremarkable. Vital signs were stable with blood pressure 145/85, temperature 38.0°C, respiratory rate 18, and heart rate 90 bpm.
test_results: The laboratory examination revealed evidence of cellulitis, low IgM levels, and Hb of 11.5. Staphylococcus aureus was identified in a culture of the superficial lesion. An x-ray of the tibia and fibula showed anterior tibial soft tissue ulceration, adjacent osseous tibial shaft erosion, and periosteal reaction consistent with osteomyelitis.

case_report: A 31-year-old male with a recent diagnosis of seminomatous germ cell testicular cancer, which has spread to the pelvis and retroperitoneum (evidenced by elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase and beta-human chorionic gonadotropin levels at diagnosis; normal alpha-fetoprotein), came to the emergency department after experiencing several days of severe, worsening bifrontal headaches, nausea, and right-sided blurry vision. These symptoms began one week after starting chemotherapy with bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin. Upon examination, he was neurologically intact except for reduced visual acuity in the right temporal field.
test_results: Head CT and MRI demonstrated a 2.0×2.8×2.1-cm, expansile, heterogeneously enhancing sellar and suprasellar mass displacing the optic chiasm with evidence of internal hemorrhage.

case_report: A 49-year-old female patient with no underlying diseases visited the outpatient clinic with a chief complaint of pain around the left calf for the duration of one week, without a history of trauma. The patient reported a burning sensation localized within the left calf and discomfort while walking. Physical examination revealed prominent warmth and acute tenderness on the medial aspect of the left gastrocnemius, without fever or neuromuscular deficits. Laboratory examination indicated a mildly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 58mm/hr and C-reactive protein (CRP) of 0.81mg/dL without leucocytosis. Initially, intravenous (IV) cefazolin (2 grams every 8 hours) was administered after blood culture was performed, but no symptom resolution was evident after two days. Computed tomography (CT) angiography revealed no definite stenosis or occlusion in the blood vessels. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed high signal intensity in the medial head and distal portion of the lateral head in the left gastrocnemius muscle with subcutaneous oedema on T2-weighted images.
test_results: A muscle biopsy indicated mild lymphocytic infiltration without evidence of vasculitis.

case_report: A 16-year-old girl with Down's syndrome presented with pain, redness, and watering in her right eye for 5 months. She exhibited short stature, mental retardation, brachycephaly, mongoloid slant of eyelid fissures, and short, broad hands with a simian crease. She had a history of surgery for imperforate anus soon after birth. Karyotyping showed an additional chromosome 21. On ocular examination, her best corrected visual acuity was 20/60 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Refractive error was +3.5 diopter sphere in the right eye and +0.5 diopter sphere in the left eye. Near vision was N/12 in the right eye and N/6 in the left eye. Corneal diameters were normal in both eyes, measuring 12 mm horizontally and 11.5 mm vertically. There was no posterior embryotoxon. The right eye showed loss of iris pattern with patchy iris atrophy, 360° ectropion uveae, and multiple anterior synechiae extending to the corneal periphery. The left eye also had extensive anterior synechiae. There were no keratic precipitates or cells or flare in the anterior chamber. No Brushfield spots were observed on the iris in either eye. Iridotomies were present in both eyes from a procedure done 2 years prior. No iris nodules were seen. The pupil in the right eye was 6 mm with a sluggish direct and consensual response, while the pupil in the left eye was 3 mm and reactive. Ocular findings were normal in her parents and two siblings. The highest recorded intraocular pressure was 38 mmHg in the right eye and 18 mmHg in the left eye. The right optic disc had a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.7:1 with inferior thinning of the neuroretinal rim, and the left optic disc had a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.5:1 with a healthy neuroretinal rim.
test_results: On gonioscopy, the anterior chamber angle was totally closed, and none of the angle structures could be visualized in the RE, whereas in the LE, the angles were closed in the superior 180° because of the extensive synechiae. Pachymetry revealed central corneal thickness in the RE of 637 and 630 µm in LE. On specular microscopy, there was varying degree of pleomorphism and a lack of clear hexagonal pattern with some cells showing dark centers (disseminated ICE cells). The specular count in the RE was 1700/mm2 when compared with 3000/mm2 in the LE. A scanning electron microscopy evaluation of the trabeculectomy specimen revealed the iris tissue extending onto the trabecular meshwork with collapse of trabecular beams, thickened trabecular beams, with decreased intertrabecular spaces.

case_report: A 10-year-old girl presented with a two-year history of pus rhinorrhea, nasal obstruction, and a foul-smelling nose. Ten months prior, she developed persistent swelling and broken skin on her right cheek. Physical examination revealed a smelly purulent secretion from an abscess along with soft tissues below the right medial canthus. Nasal ventilation was poor, with secretions occupying the middle and total meatus. Several teeth had not erupted and remained sub-gingival, making it difficult to distinguish between primary and permanent teeth. Root malformations of teeth #84 and #85 and alveolar bone osteonecrosis were observed. Oral hygiene was poor, with rampant caries and gingivitis present. The patient was hospitalized for 24 days. During her stay, she received amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium (800 mg every 8 hours) for 7 days, which led to the healing of her cheek skin. Laboratory tests and a CT scan of the sinuses were performed. Laboratory findings were normal. The CT scan showed bone destruction of the right maxillary sinus wall and right nasal bone, with the maxillary sinus and anterior part of the nasal cavity filled with soft tissue density. On day 8, surgery was performed under general anesthesia, during which the right gingiva, right nasal mucosa, and right facial tissue were resected for biopsies. Histological examination revealed proliferation of granulation tissue in chronic inflammatory mucosa, with no evidence of malignancy. All examination results were inconclusive.
test_results: Radiographs showed multiple bony abnormalities involving the skull, vertebrae and limb. X-rays showed generalized sclerosis, for example: thickening and increasing Cranial plate, narrowing diploic vein, Sella turcica, increased vertebral bone density in cliff, smaller pituitary fossa, and costochondral junction widening. A typical form of “sandwich” vertebra was noted. Longitudinal striation of the long bones, extreme metaphyseal flaring, reduced bone vascularity and dense bone structure was simply found. The results of whole-exome sequencing revealed homozygous nonsense mutation c.1196C > G (p.S399X) in exon 9 of the TNFRSF11A gene in the proband. Sanger sequencing was applied to confirm the presence of this identified variant, and the same heterozygous variant was found in both the patient’s father and mother.

case_report: An 18-year-old, right-handed, Caucasian male, son of healthy and non-consanguineous parents, began experiencing frequent brief nocturnal episodes of repetitive movements in the upper and lower limbs at the age of 12, as observed by his mother. His clinical history revealed no risk factors for epilepsy and no significant family history. Neurological examination showed no abnormalities. EEG background activity was within normal limits.
test_results: Interictal electroencephalogram (EEG) showed an intermittent slow in the right occipital region and rare right frontal epileptiform discharges. The video-EEG recorded a paroxysmal arousal followed by a brief asymmetric tonic seizure during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep associated to a focal ictal EEG onset in the right frontal region. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (3.0 Tesla) showed a right paramedian inferior occipital non-enhancing lesion, characterized by cortical thickening, gray–white matter blurring and an increased T2 signal of the subcortical white matter with transmantle sign.
Orpha_name: Isolated focal cortical dysplasia type II

case_report: A 25-year-old male presented with nonspecific neck pain. An MRI scan revealed a fusiform enlargement of the cervical cord at the C2 vertebral body level, characterized by a hyperintense signal on T1-weighted images and intense contrast enhancement. The patient underwent a C2 laminectomy and excision of the lesion. During the procedure, a blackish pigmented lesion was observed on the surface of the cord, extending deep intramedullary.
test_results: Histopathology showed cells with cytoplasm rich in melanin positive for S100 and HMB-45, nuclear pleomorphism and prominent nucleoli.

case_report: A previously healthy 11-year-old girl (weight, 38.4 kg; height, 155 cm) presented with a 1-month history of cough and hemoptysis. She experienced intermittent fever but did not report dyspnea, joint pain, headache, or other symptoms. Initially treated at a local hospital for suspected infection, her symptoms improved after 7 days of anti-infection treatment starting on 10 April 2017. However, the symptoms recurred a month later, leading her to visit our outpatient department on 10 May 2017. Her parents were healthy and nonconsanguineous. Laboratory tests showed a leucocyte count of 8.1 × 10^9/L (neutrophils 52%), platelet count of 407 × 10^9/L, and hemoglobin count of 106 g/L. A chest X-ray revealed areas of abnormal density in the bilateral lower lobes of the lungs. She was treated with parenteral imipenem-cilastatin for lobar pneumonia but showed no clinical improvement. Three days later, she was admitted for further evaluation of her cough and hemoptysis. Upon admission, her blood pressure was 96/54 mmHg and body temperature was 38.5°C. Physical examination was unremarkable. Subsequent laboratory tests on 14 May showed microscopic hematuria (+++) and proteinuria (++). Renal function tests revealed BUN 4.85 mmol/L, Cr 81.6 µmol/L, UA 213.7 µmol/L, and C3 1,300 mg/L. Inflammatory markers were slightly elevated with ESR at 29 mm/h and CRP at 19 mg/L. ANA was present at a low titer (1:80) without antigen-specific antibodies. p-ANCA was positive, and MPO-ANCA was 50.9 U/ml (normal <20 U/ml). PR3 and GBM were normal on 16 May. A chest CT on 16 May showed a dense shadow in the bilateral lower lobes of the lungs, without ground-glass opacity and reticulation. Pulmonary artery CT and PPD tests were normal.
test_results: The biopsies revealed glomerular cellular and microcellular crescents. Immunofluorescence microscopy showed IgA (+) and IgG (++) deposits in the glomerular capillary loop but no C3 and C1q deposits.

case_report: A 17-month-old male patient presented with fever and seizures. On the first day, he developed fever and vomiting. Eighteen hours later, he experienced generalized tonic-clonic seizures twice every half hour, each lasting several minutes, followed by a coma. On the second day, his consciousness improved to lethargy, and no further seizures were observed. On the fourth day, the patient experienced complex partial seizures and fell into a coma again. Intravenous phenobarbital was administered without benefit, so levetiracetam was prescribed. By day 10, the fever and seizures had subsided, but the coma persisted. No relapse of symptoms occurred thereafter. The patient's previous medical and family histories were unremarkable, and his mental and motor development was normal. Upon admission, head computed tomography showed no abnormalities.
test_results: On day 4, brain MRI revealed reduced diffusion in the bilateral subcortical white matter on DWI. On day 14, brain MRI showed cortical atrophy and focal necrosis, and the reduced diffusion had disappeared; T1-weighted and T2-weighted images showed cortical atrophy and focal necrosis.
diagnosis: Acute encephalopathy with biphasic seizures and late reduced diffusion
Orpha_name: Acute encephalopathy with biphasic seizures and late reduced diffusion

case_report: A 32-year-old male presented to the emergency department with lower abdominal pain persisting for one week. The pain was described as stabbing and rated 7 out of 10 in intensity. Accompanying symptoms included fever, nausea, and vomiting. There were no changes in bowel movements or urinary symptoms. The patient's medical history included peptic ulcer disease, but no previous surgeries. He was a non-smoker and did not consume alcohol. Family history was non-contributory, and there was no history of diabetes mellitus, chronic steroid use, or immunodeficiency disorders. On physical examination, the patient appeared fatigued, with vital signs indicating a low-grade fever and tachycardia. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the lower abdomen and a palpable suprapubic mass, without any overlying skin changes. The abdomen was soft and lax, with no guarding or rigidity. Laboratory tests showed a leukocyte count of 14,200/𝜇L and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 23 mm/hr. Renal and liver function tests were within normal limits.
test_results: An abdominal ultrasound examination of the patient revealed a spheric collection with poorly defined borders. An abdominal CT scan demonstrated a soft tissue mass adjacent to the anterior abdominal wall with an upward track to the umbilicus. A cystourethrogram revealed no communication with the bladder.

case_report: An 8-year 9-month-old female presented with short stature and frequent infections. She was born at 40 weeks gestation with a birth weight of 2700 g (−1.14 SDS) to nonconsanguineous healthy Korean parents. At the time of evaluation, her height was 99.9 cm (−5.45 SDS) and weight was 16.3 kg (−2.21 SDS). The mid-parental height was 164 cm (paternal height, 178 cm; maternal height, 163 cm). The patient experienced recurrent pneumonia (1–2 times per year) and watery diarrhea. Physical examination revealed erythematous patches around the right elbow, both knees, and heels, thin hair, and no signs of breast development or other secondary sexual characteristics. Psychomotor development was normal. Karyotype was 46, XX, and bone age was 1 year and 8 months younger than chronological age. The patient has a healthy 4-year-old younger sister and had a younger brother who died at 18 months from pneumonia with neutropenia. Skeletal survey showed metaphyseal striation with irregular contour around both knees, genu varum, kyphosis, and compression fractures of both ankles and the lumbar spine. Laboratory tests revealed hemoglobin level of 11.1 g/dL (RR, 11.2–14.8 g/dL), leukocyte count of 7270/μL (RR, 3150–8630/μL), absolute neutrophil count of 5850/μL (RR, 1570–8300/μL), and absolute lymphocyte count of 930/μL (RR, 1000–4800/μL). Neutrophil ratio was 80.4% (RR, 40.6%–73.5%) and lymphocyte ratio was 56.0% (RR, 20.0%–50.8%). Serum calcium level was 9.1 mg/dL (RR, 8.6–10.2 mg/dL), phosphate level was 5.1 mg/dL (RR, 2.5–4.5 mg/dL), and alkaline phosphatase level was 99 U/L (RR, 35–104 U/L). Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels were 440 U/L (RR, 0–32 U/L) and 557 U/L (RR, 0–33 U/L), respectively. Follow-up tests 3 months later showed AST of 66 U/L and ALT of 65 U/L without treatment. IGF-1 level was low at 28.9 ng/mL (RR, 93.5–441.3 ng/mL), and GH stimulation test showed a normal response (>10 μg/L). Thyroid and adrenal function tests were normal. Skin biopsy of erythematous patches revealed scattered noncaseating granuloma with a negative acid-fast bacillus stain. Magnetic resonance imaging of the sella turcica and parasellar region was normal, with incidental findings of pansinusitis and bilateral mastoid effusion.
test_results: A WES revealed 2 variants in the RMRP gene, confirmed by Sanger sequencing, NR_003051.3:n.-22_-3dup (likely pathogenic variant) and NR_003051.3:n.171G > T (variant of uncertain significance).

case_report: A previously healthy ten-year-old boy was admitted with a four-month history of worsening cognitive abilities, involuntary muscle jerks, unsteady walking, and frequent falls. There was no history of measles, fever, or trauma. He had received a measles vaccination at nine months old. On examination, he appeared confused with intermittent lapses in consciousness and periodic muscle jerks every 5 to 6 seconds, characterized by sudden flexion of the neck, trunk, and arms. He had difficulty sitting, swallowing, drooling of saliva, slurred speech, and poor interaction with the examiner. Physical examination revealed generalized muscle stiffness, increased reflexes, and a bilateral extensor plantar response. Examination of cranial nerves, fundus, and other physical assessments were normal.
test_results: Scalp electroencephalogram showed disorganized background with generalized spike-wave discharges 2–2.5/second occupying more than 80% of tracing. Following intravenous diazepam (0.3 mg/kg) administration, transient normalization of background rhythm to 6–8/second along with intermittent, generalized high-voltage slow-wave discharges was seen, but typical periodic complexes were not seen. There was no change in the mental status of the child following diazepam. Magnetic resonance imaging of brain (fluid attenuated inversion recovery sequence) showed periventricular hyperintensities involving bilateral parieto-occipital white matter. Measles antibody titers by enzyme-immunoassay were raised in both cerebrospinal fluid and serum: 5.24 IU/mL (positive >1.1) and 5.11 IU/mL (positive >1.1), respectively.

case_report: A 20-year-old woman presented with uncontrolled hand tremor and seizure attacks. Her perinatal and infancy periods were uneventful, and early developmental milestones were normal. At the age of 10 years, she began experiencing myoclonic movements affecting her entire body. These movements gradually worsened, particularly in the upper limbs, occurring frequently each day, more severely during sleep onset and awakening, and lessening when the lights were turned off. Sudden movements, such as standing up, triggered these myoclonic movements. Persistent tremulous movements of both hands, characterized by small amplitude jerks, increased in severity as the hands approached their target, making detailed hand movements, such as using a cell phone, difficult.
