Since the age of 13 years, she was unable to run due to provoked myoclonic movements. Around that time, she also developed dysarthric speech and gait disturbance, which progressively worsened. Mild intellectual disability was noted from the age of 10 years. Neuropsychological tests at age 15 indicated mild mental retardation with a full-scale IQ of 65, verbal IQ of 61, and performance IQ of 75. She also exhibited emotional lability. Generalized tonic-clonic seizures (GTCSs) began occurring half a year after the onset of myoclonus, primarily triggered by bright lights or emotional stress, occurring once a week. She started treatment with antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) at that time. Her seizures, including myoclonic movements and GTCSs, worsened with oxcarbazepine, carbamazepine, and lamotrigine, but significantly improved, especially GTCS, with valproic acid, reducing GTCS frequency to three or four times a year. At age 20, she was admitted to the hospital due to increased GTCS frequency (twice a month). She was treated with levetiracetam (2000 mg/day), valproic acid (500 mg/day), clonazepam (0.75 mg/day), baclofen (20 mg/day), and lorazepam (1.5 mg/day). Neurologic examination revealed almost continuous tremulous movements of both hands, with relatively large amplitude myoclonic movements occurring intermittently, particularly with sudden movements, arm stretching, and hand extension. She also exhibited mild dysarthria, dysmetric limb ataxia, and truncal ataxia on tandem gait. Her 15-year-old sister had normal cognition and no neurologic symptoms. Her father had experienced several seizures following head trauma in his 30s, which ceased after three years of AED treatment. The family had no ancestors from other countries, and other family history was unremarkable. Continuous video-electroencephalography (EEG) showed intermittent generalized sharp waves with posterior emphasis, although myoclonic movements, including almost continuous small amplitude jerks, were not time-locked to EEG discharges. The background rhythm on EEG was normal with a well-regulated 10-Hz posterior dominant rhythm. Photic stimuli did not provoke electrical or clinical seizures. Brain magnetic resonance imaging and magnetic resonance spectroscopy revealed no abnormalities. Somatosensory-evoked potential and visual-evoked potential tests showed normal latencies, shapes, and amplitudes.
test_results: The patient showed only abnormally enlarged restriction fragments of 62 dodecamer repeats.

case_report: The patient, a 5-year-old Japanese female with no relevant family history, exhibited a progressively worsening gait disturbance, regression in motor development, Raynaud’s phenomenon, and a shiny appearance of the skin on the face and extremities starting at age 2. By age 5, the skin abnormalities had become more pronounced. She was referred to our hospital after a skin biopsy was performed at a previous institution. Upon presentation, she had a characteristic appearance with taut facial skin, loss of wrinkles and skin folds, puffy fingers with Raynaud’s phenomenon, and skin thickening of the distal extremities extending beyond the elbows and knees, with a modified Rodnan total skin thickness score (mRSS) of 18/51. Visible capillary hemorrhage was noted on the nail fold, along with severe abnormal capillaroscopy findings, including bleeding, giant loops, and disappearance of capillaries. Contractures in the ankle and proximal interphalangeal joints led to gait disturbance and difficulty in finger motion. There were no abnormal neurological findings, and no evidence of myositis was observed based on clinical muscle weakness, muscle-derived enzyme levels, and muscle Magnetic Resonance Imaging during the baseline intensive examination.
test_results: It revealed a fibrous thickening of the dermis, relative entrapment of an eccrine sweat glands, and thickened collagenous fiber. Chest high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) demonstrated patchy areas of ill-defined air-space opacity and consolidation predominantly involving the posterior basilar aspects of the lower lobes presenting with interstitial lung disease. Blood examination showed positive ANA (nucleolar and homogeneous nuclear staining at a serum dilution of 1:160 by indirect immunofluorescence). The patient’s serum immunoprecipitated ribosomal RNAs and a 7 − 2 RNA that was consistent with the RNA component precipitated by a reference anti-Th/To-positive serum. The immunoprecipitation-immunoblot assay probed with anti-hPOP1 and anti-PM-Scl-100 antibodies revealed that the patient’s serum contained both anti-Th/To and anti-PM-Scl antibodies.

case_report: A seven-year-old female from Libya exhibits postnatal microcephaly to -3SD, sensorineural hearing loss, and global intellectual delay with comprehension difficulties. Additional clinical features include epileptic seizures, livedo, and facial characteristics such as micro-retrognathia, malar hypoplasia, dental malocclusion, limited mouth opening, and large protruding ears. Her karyotype was normal, and both parents are healthy.
test_results: The mean coverage of the exome-wide regions was 139.09, 119.25, and 148.62 reads, corresponding to a coverage of at least 10 reads of 95.99, 95.91, and 96.08% of the exome for the patient, mother, and father, respectively. Among these pertinent variants, the only one that could explain the patient’s phenotype was the de novo synonymous variant c.702G > T (transcript NM_004247.4) in the exon 9 of EFTUD2 at position chr17:42956924 (GRCh37/hg19) in the patient. This variant replaces a GGG codon to GGT, resulting in the retention of glycine at amino acid residue 234 (p.G234G). Sanger sequencing confirmed that neither parents carried the variant. We observed in all three individuals the expected PCR product band of ~ 360 bp and an additional PCR product of ~ 280 bp in the proband only. This result suggests deletion of about 80 bp in the patient’s EFTUD2 cDNA. The sequencing of the alternative cDNA showed complete deletion of exon 9. As the exon 9 length is not a multiple of 3 (83 bp), its deletion would trigger a frameshift leading to a premature stop codon that truncates the protein c.620_702del, p.His209Aspfs*25.

case_report: An 8-month-old female child presented with a history of seizures starting at 4 days old. She was born to a first-time mother at full term through a normal vaginal delivery. The ante-partum history was unremarkable. The child appeared well and active. Developmental milestones were appropriate for her age. Head circumference measured 42.3 cm, which is within normal limits. The fontanelles were normally palpable. There were no observed craniofacial abnormalities, organomegaly, or neurocutaneous markers.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) scan (head) was normal. EEG graph included normal drowsy and sleep-state patterns, which were consistent with the age of the patient. Background EEG frequency ranged between 2 and 5 Hz with amplitude of 150-200 μV. At places, sleep markers in the form of V-waves, K-complexes, and sleep spindles were also seen. There was no epileptiform activity.

case_report: A 19-year-old male presented with hemoptysis, dyspnea, and gastrointestinal hemorrhage. He had a subcutaneous mass on the left chest wall since birth. Previous hospital admission included examination and management, revealing pleural effusion, multiple osteolytic lesions of the spine, and a splenic cystic lesion. Despite conservative therapy, symptoms persisted. Two years later, he was transferred to Gifu University Hospital for further treatment. Physical examination showed a reddish brown, soft, and nontender subcutaneous mass (10 × 8 cm) on the left chest wall without signs of inflammation.
test_results: Plain radiography and gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the chest revealed pleural effusion, an infiltrative soft-tissue mass at the left chest wall, and a retroperitoneal lesion. Laboratory data indicated mild thrombocytopenia (9.0 × 104/μL) and coagulopathy (D-dimer: 31.0 μg/ml, fibrinogen: 181 mg/dL). Colonoscopy showed bleeding and multiple dilated tortuous blood vessels running along the surface of the sigmoid colon. An open biopsy specimen of the subcutaneous lesion showed irregularly dilated endothelial cells and foci of spindle cells. In immunohistochemical study, both endothelial cells and spindle cells showed positive reactivity for CD31, D2–40, and Prox-1, identifying them as being of lymphatic origin.

case_report: A 63-year-old female presented with dorsomedial pain in her left midfoot that had persisted for two years. She experienced difficulty navigating stairs and required a single crutch for extended walking. There was no history of trauma. The patient occasionally used acetaminophen to manage the pain. Physical examination revealed prominence of the medial navicular and valgus hindfoot. Pain was noted upon palpation of the dorsomedial midfoot. Her AOFAS score was recorded as 59 out of 100.
test_results: MRI images demonstrated alteration and fragmentation of the navicular bone.

case_report: A 27-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital for episodes of limb convulsions, cognitive decline over 20 years, and tremors for 15 years. The initial convulsions occurred 20 years ago, characterized by limb rigidity, foaming at the mouth, and backward head movement, lasting approximately 3 to 5 minutes. Following these episodes, she experienced slight cognitive decline, poor learning ability, poor test results, occasional communication difficulties, and challenges in understanding her work. In March 2008, she had a relapse with similar symptoms, including limb rigidity, foaming at the mouth, and a fixed gaze, lasting 3 to 5 minutes. The frequency of these episodes increased to 3 to 4 times a month, prompting her family to seek medical attention. In September 2008, she began experiencing head and body tremors, and her voice became tense with noticeable tremors, although her daily activities were not affected. Twelve years ago, her vision began to decline, and she was diagnosed with binocular cataracts. Throughout the disease course, she did not exhibit movement retardation, abnormal posture or gait, walking instability, headache, neck pain, chest pain, chest tightness, shortness of breath, or difficulty breathing. Despite multiple consultations, a clear diagnosis was not established. She was transferred to our hospital with a classification of “pyramidal system disease.” Over the past 10 years, she experienced gradual depression, lack of happiness, tension, worry, fear, irritability, and sleep disorders, without formal diagnosis or treatment. She had no history of hypertension, coronary heart disease, diabetes, cerebral infarction, surgery, trauma, blood transfusion, hepatitis, tuberculosis, or other infectious diseases. There was no relevant family medical history. Physical examination findings included: temperature, 36.2 °C; heart rate, 88 beats/min; respiration, 18 breaths/min; blood pressure, 120/70 mm Hg; binocular uncorrected visual acuity, 0.08; emaciation; and bilateral solid masses in the Achilles tendons. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations were normal. She was conscious with fluent speech, but showed cognitive decline, limited computational ability, and reduced memory and executive function. Cranial nerve examinations were unremarkable. Limb muscle strength was grade 5 with normal muscle volume, slightly low muscle tension, body tremors, and symmetrical bilateral tendon reflexes. The right finger-nose test and heel-knee test showed instability, while the left side was normal. No deep or superficial sensory disorders were noted. Bilateral Chaddock signs were present, Babinski signs were negative, and bilateral ankle clonus was positive. She exhibited the Romberg sign with eyes open but was stable with eyes closed, and could walk in a straight line steadily. Blood lipid levels were: cholesterol, 5.28 mmol/L; low-density lipoprotein, 3.5 mmol/L; and apolipoprotein B, 1.19 g/L. Liver function tests showed: total bilirubin, 23.7 µmol/L; total bile acid, 15 µmol/L; and glycocholic acid, 4.24 µg/mL. Routine blood tests revealed: red blood cell count, 3.34 × 10^12/L; hemoglobin, 114 g/L; hematocrit, 34.6%; mean corpuscular volume, 103.5 fL; mean corpuscular hemoglobin, 34.1 pg; and potassium ion concentration, 3.15 mmol/L. Renal function, thyroid function, and antinuclear antibody levels were normal. Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale scores were 55, 55, and 51. Hamilton Anxiety Scale score was 11 and depression scale score was 18. Electrocardiography showed no abnormalities, and electroencephalography revealed a small number of slow waves at 5 to 7 Hz. Abdominal color Doppler ultrasound indicated slightly rough liver parenchyma and multiple gallbladder polypoid lesions. Head MRI showed bilateral periventricular leukoencephalopathy and straight cervical curvature. Achilles tendon MRI revealed bilateral masses at the Achilles tendons.
test_results: Detection of CYP27A1 revealed 2 heterozygous variants: c. 1214G>A (chr2-219679132, p.Arg405Gln) and c. 1420C>T (chr2-219679424, p.Arg474Trp). The father had a c. 1214G>A heterozygous variant, the mother had a c. 1420C>T heterozygous variant, and the patient’s sister had no variants.

case_report: The study received approval from the Cyprus National Bioethics Committee, and informed, written consent was obtained from all participants. The subject is a 30-year-old male weight lifter who presented with sudden onset chest and back pain. Initial assessment revealed no observable phenotypic features such as iris flocculi, livedo reticularis, or aortic valve abnormalities.
test_results: Based on echocardiography and chest CT findings the patient was diagnosed with a Type A Aortic Dissection with severe aortic valve regurgitation. Intraoperative findings showed a 70 mm diameter aortic root aneurysm with dissection extending from the sinotubular junction to the aortic root. The aortic annulus was extensively dilated and the aortic dissection extended down the origin of the left main coronary artery involving also the aortic valve commissures that resulted in severe aortic valve regurgitation. There was no evidence of involvement of the distal ascending aorta and the aortic arch. MPS results identified a frameshift deletion c.363_367del GAGTC, p.Met121Ilefs*5 in the ACTA2 gene (Genbank transcript ID: NM 001613) and a non-synonymous variant c.3234C > G, p.Ile1078Met in the MYH11 gene (Genbank transcript ID: NM 001040114).
diagnosis: Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm due to ACTA2 gene variant
Orpha_name: Familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and aortic dissection

case_report: A 20-year-old male patient had a normal birth history and developmental milestones until the age of 2. From the age of 3, he experienced delayed milestones and failure to thrive. There was no evidence of mental retardation or cognitive impairment. He did not experience seizures, gait abnormalities, bowel or bladder disturbances, or visual and hearing difficulties. At the age of 10, he underwent an appendicectomy due to acute abdominal pain, which recurred frequently. Initially, the abdominal pain occurred one or two times a week, but by the age of 16, it increased to more than 5–10 episodes a day. He also developed early satiety and postprandial vomiting, but had no difficulty swallowing. The patient experienced weight loss and progressive generalized muscle wasting, along with numbness in the extremities, which worsened when stationary. He did not develop secondary sexual characteristics or experience a growth spurt. He had a normal younger sibling and no similar family history. On examination, the patient was 147 cm tall, weighed 18 kg, with a body mass index of 8.33 kg/m2 and a body surface area of 0.92 m2. Severe generalized muscle wasting was noted, but his gait was normal. Lumbar lordosis was observed during walking. Vital signs included a pulse of 84/min and a noninvasive blood pressure of 100/60 mmHg. There were no signs of thyromegaly, organomegaly, generalized lymphadenopathy, or bone tenderness. Neurological examination revealed normal mental functions and cranial nerve examination indicated chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia with a normal fundus. Muscle strength in both upper and lower limbs was graded 4/5 on the MRC scale. Deep tendon reflexes were sluggish (1+). Sensory examination showed a loss of joint proprioception, while other sensory modalities were normal. There were no cerebellar or long tract signs. Skull examination was normal in size and shape, and spine examination showed lumbar scoliosis to the left. Cardiovascular and respiratory systems were unremarkable. Examination of the external genitalia revealed both testes descended in the scrotum with no pubic hair, a small penis with a normal external meatus and glans. Axillary hair, beard, and moustache were absent. The patient was admitted to the neurology department after experiencing a convulsion.
test_results: On gene sequencing, a frameshift mutation along with deletion of exon 4 was noted.

case_report: A 33-year-old male was admitted due to severe anemia that did not improve with hemotransfusions and increasing doses of erythropoietin. Five years prior, he was diagnosed with membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis via renal biopsy and treated with steroids and immunosuppressants. The diagnosis was based on persistent proteinuria and microhematuria. The biopsy showed membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis with glomerular sclerosis in 9 out of 16 glomeruli and mesangiocapillary global proliferation in 7 glomeruli. There was no fibrinoid necrosis, vascular thrombosis, or extracapillary proliferation. Congo red staining for amyloid was negative. Immunofluorescence revealed tiny granular deposits; semilinear membrane for IgG and, to a lesser extent, C3; negative for IgA, IgM, C1q, and κ and λ light chains. A modest accumulation of intravascular fibrinogen was noted. Initial treatment with azathioprine and mycophenolate was not tolerated, so the patient remained on steroid therapy, which led to a rapid reduction in proteinuria and disappearance of microhematuria. The following year, he developed bilateral aseptic necrosis of the femoral head. Over the past 5 years, after discontinuing steroids, his renal function gradually worsened (mean serum creatinine: 2.5 mg/dL), with proteinuria (1.5-2 g/24 h) and anemia managed with darbepoetin alfa until his recent emergency admission for severe anemia (hemoglobin: 6 g/dL) accompanied by severe asthenia and dyspnea. Prior to admission, he had not been on corticosteroids or other immunosuppressive drugs. Hemoglobin levels increased after receiving 2 units of packed red blood cells. Colonoscopy and gastroscopy showed no significant findings. Peripheral smear was negative for schistocytes, and both direct and indirect Coombs tests were negative. G6PDH levels were normal. Haptoglobin was reduced, and lactate dehydrogenase was slightly elevated, but bilirubin levels were normal. Autoimmunity tests were normal except for a persistent slight reduction in C3 over the past 6 years. Complement consumption was noted, but no additional elements were observed. Antinucleolar antibodies (jo-1, Scl 70) were evaluated. Tests for common infectious agents through serology, urine, and blood cultures were negative. The patient was administered 8000 IU of erythropoietin alfa three times a week. On the third day of admission, hemoglobin levels dropped to 7 g/dL, prompting another unit of packed red blood cells. An abdominal ultrasound showed no blood collections or significant changes, only reduced kidney size consistent with chronic kidney disease. Chest X-ray revealed bilateral bronchopneumonia in the middle lobe. After 4 days of hospitalization, the patient developed hemoptysis with bright red blood and clots when coughing, a symptom not previously observed.
test_results: Multilobar alterations extended to both lungs with ground-glass appearance and intralobular involvement, as well as intra-acinar, with thickening of the interlobular septa but without distortion and rails and interlobular fissures. The ground-glass appearance seemed to spare the sub pleural zones.

case_report: A 65-year-old female patient with a history of abdominal surgery in a regional hospital in Bahir Dar 6 months ago presented with diffuse abdominal pain, weakness, and occasional vomiting of ingested material for the past 6 months. There was no history of abnormal uterine bleeding, oral contraceptive use, or gynecologic operation. The patient provided written informed consent for the publication of this case report. Examination revealed that she appeared chronically ill, was emaciated, slightly pale, and had a long midline abdominal scar. Mild tenderness was noted throughout the abdomen on deep palpation. Laboratory investigations showed a hemoglobin level of 9.3 g/dL and a WBC count of 6,900/μL. Her blood type was O positive. Liver and renal function tests were normal, as was a chest X-ray. Ultrasound imaging identified numerous hypoechoic intra-abdominal masses of varying sizes and a large hypoechoic liver mass measuring 7.5×4.7 cm in the right lobe.
test_results: Biopsy specimens were sent to two centers, and both reported a similar finding of highly cellular interlacing bundles of proliferating smooth muscle cells not associated with nuclear atypia or mitotic figures, and there was no necrosis seen.

case_report: A 24-year-old male presented with a sudden onset of visual loss in his left eye that began a few hours prior. His medical history includes a condition for which he has been receiving cyclosporin A (2 × 150 mg) and deflazacort (1 × 30 mg) for the past 3 years. Ophthalmologic examination revealed visual acuity of 20/25 in the right eye and 20/1200 in the left eye. Slit lamp examination was notable only for mild posterior subcapsular cataracts in both eyes. Intraocular pressures, pupil examination, and extraocular muscle movements were normal bilaterally. Fundus examination of the right eye showed a healthy retina, vitreous, optic nerve head, and retinal vasculature. The left eye exhibited large preretinal, intraretinal, and subretinal hemorrhages affecting the inferior part of the macula, inferior temporal arcade, nasal and superior parts of the retina, along with edema at the optic nerve head. Vascular changes included significantly increased tortuosity and diffuse perivascular sheathing. There was no vitritis.
test_results: Fundus fluorescein angiogram (FFA) of left eye revealed delayed filling of peripheral vessels, late staining of vessels and optic nerve head together with some capillary non-perfusion areas and blocked fluorescence in hemorrhagic areas. FFA of right eye was normal.
diagnosis: Retinal vasculitis due to pyoderma gangrenosum

case_report: A 56-year-old woman reported experiencing dull aching pain, swelling, and restricted movement in her left knee for the past 10 years. The pain, which began 10 years ago, has progressively worsened. There was no history of trauma. Two years after the onset of pain, she noticed a swelling on the lateral side of her left knee joint, which gradually increased in size and was associated with a reduction in knee joint movement. Activities that involved bending the knee triggered the pain. The patient has no significant past medical or family history. Physical examination revealed swelling on the lateral aspect of the left knee, without any localized redness or increased temperature. The swelling, measuring 15×5 cm, extended from the lateral aspect of the left distal femur to the fibular head. It was bony, hard, not attached to the underlying bone, and non-tender. The range of motion in the left knee joint was limited to 0–40°, with further movement restricted. There was no evidence of neurovascular impairment in the distal part of the limb. No similar lesions were found elsewhere on the body.
test_results: Plain radiographs revealed an irregular extraosseous radiolucent mass extending to the fibular head across the lateral aspect of the left knee with no bony contact. Cortical hyperostosis covered the whole length of the fibula. This cortical hyperostosis was large, thick, undulating, or irregular.

case_report: A 4-year-old female patient presented with unusually short scalp hair, which had never been cut. Her growth and development were within normal limits. Physical examination showed short, sparse scalp hair that was fine in texture and had low overall density. The maximum hair length on the parietal scalp was 2 cm. The hairs could be easily and painlessly pulled from the scalp with gentle traction. Eyelashes, eyebrows, and body hair appeared normal. No abnormalities were found in the skin, teeth, nails, and limbs during the clinical examination. Trichoscopy revealed short, thin, and vellus hairs along with rare yellow dots. Optical and scanning electron microscopy showed normal hair shafts without ruffled cuticles or hockey stick-shaped bulbs. Structural analysis of the hair shafts using X-ray spectroscopy indicated bioelement values similar to those of normal controls. Systemic examination, serum and urine analysis, including measurements of vitamins, amino acids, and biotinidase activity, did not show any other anomalies. During the course of investigations, the patient reported photophobia and was referred to Ophthalmology. Ophthalmological consultation revealed a best-corrected visual acuity of 5/10 in both eyes. Fundus examination showed pigmentary changes in the fovea bilaterally. Optical coherence tomography indicated irregularity of the photoreceptor layer and the presence of intraretinal cysts.
test_results: It revealed a c. 830delG homozygous mutation in the CDH3 gene, leading to the synthesis of a truncated protein unable to fulfill its physiologic functions.

case_report: An 83-year-old Japanese woman with a history of hypertension and dyslipidaemia underwent on-pump CABG for angina pectoris with multi-vessel coronary artery disease. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) performed preoperatively and 1 month postoperatively revealed normal wall motion of the left ventricle and the presence of MAC, with no other abnormal findings. However, follow-up TTE performed 5 months after CABG revealed a mobile nodular mass (5.0 × 8.2 mm) in the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT). The patient was prescribed apixaban 5 mg/day in addition to the aspirin 100 mg/day that she was taking for known ischaemic heart disease. A further 1 month later, the mass had enlarged to 5.0 × 13.0 mm, and the patient was referred to our hospital for further investigation. Physical examination on admission showed a Levine 2/6 systolic murmur at the left sternal border, a regular heart rhythm of 61 b.p.m., and blood pressure of 117/71 mmHg. No remarkable symptoms were observed. The results of the laboratory study were as follows: white blood cell count 4200/μL, C-reactive protein 0.04 mg/dL, serum creatinine 0.63 mg/dL, haemoglobin A1c 6.0% (42 mmol/mol), and brain natriuretic peptide 317 pg/mL. Blood tests including thrombotic and autoimmunological parameters were unremarkable, and blood cultures were negative. Electrocardiography and chest radiography revealed no abnormalities. TTE showed no significant valvular dysfunction or wall-motion asynergy in the left ventricle, though a mobile cardiac mass was observed in the LVOT. Transoesophageal echocardiography revealed a pedunculated high-echoic mass that was adhered to the posterior commissure of the mitral valve and was dynamically swinging towards the non-coronary cusp of the aortic valve in the systolic phase. Contrast computed tomography (CT) revealed MAC along almost the entire posterior leaflet of the mitral valve and a low-density string-shaped structure at the same site as the mass shown on TTE. There were no space-occupying lesions in the thoracoabdominal CT. Cardiac cine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a low-signal intensity structure between the non-coronary cusp of the aortic valve and the posterior commissure of the mitral valve. As the mass had grown rapidly in less than 6 months, surgical resection was performed to prevent systemic embolism. The pedunculated mass was vulnerable and was resected successfully.
test_results: The histological specimen which was stained with haematoxylin and eosin consisted mainly of fibrin, including calcification and hemosiderin deposition. There were no malignant findings and no bacterial mass detected.

case_report: A 3-year-old female presented to the emergency room with sudden onset of shortness of breath and cough lasting 12 hours after arriving in Abha city. Her medical history includes a repaired right congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) at 6 months old, recurrent pneumonia, and recurrent viral-induced wheezy chest. Before the CDH repair, she had multiple severe pneumonia episodes requiring pediatric intensive care unit admission and intubation twice. Chest imaging at that time showed right lung hypoplasia with an elevated right hemidiaphragm, leading to a referral to pediatric surgery. She underwent surgical repair of the CDH with a prolonged PICU stay of 2 months and was discharged without the need for oxygen. Post-surgery, she experienced viral-induced wheezy episodes necessitating emergency room visits but no further admissions. She resides at a low altitude (70 m above sea level) and is fully immunized. On physical examination, she was in acute distress with severe hypoxia, showing an SpO2 of 40% on room air. Her heart rate was 190 beats per minute, and her blood pressure was 100/62 mmHg, which is within the normal range for her age. She weighed 11 kg, placing her in the 10th percentile for her age. Lung examination revealed bilateral diminished air entry with diffuse inspiratory crackles.
test_results: Chest X-ray (CXR) on admission (A) showed bilateral patchy opacities. Echocardiography showed normal heart function and structure without pulmonary hypertension, and this was performed on day 2 of admission. The repeated CXR after 6 h (B) revealed great improvement compared with the initial CXR. On the fifth day, the patient was discharged to their home on room air with a normal heart rate, with their CXR showing a significant improvement of patchy opacities (C).

case_report: An 18-month-old boy presented with a history of fever lasting 4 months and limb swelling. The child exhibited irritability. Blood tests revealed thrombocytopenia with platelet counts below 35,000 and elevated alkaline phosphatase levels at 1417.4 KA units (normal range: 4–11 KA units). Hemoglobin levels were significantly low at 6.9 gm %. Serum calcium and phosphorus levels were within normal limits. Physical examination identified multiple swellings on both upper and lower limbs, along with bowing of the lower limbs.
test_results: His radiological skeletal survey revealed marked periosteal new bone formation surrounding the diaphysis of long bones, but the mandible and clavicles were spared. A bone scan done with 99m Tc-MDP (methyl diphosphonate) showed diffusely increased tracer uptake in all the long bones. The bones of the axial skeleton and of hands and the feet showed normal tracer distribution. A fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG PET) scan done to assess the metabolic activity showed patchy FDG uptake in the long bones, ankle joint and anterior ends of few ribs.

case_report: A 57-year-old male from Monte Dourado, PA, Brazil, was referred for neurological evaluation in Belém, PA, Brazil, due to brachiocrural paresis that had been progressing over three years. Initially, symptoms were noted in the lower limbs, and after one year, the upper limbs also exhibited paresis, along with fasciculations and tremors in the extremities. Subsequently, the patient experienced dysarthria, dysphagia, and sexual dysfunction. Thirty years prior, he had undergone surgery for gynecomastia. Neurological examination revealed impaired gait, inability to walk on tiptoes, proximal muscle atrophy in the upper limbs, and fasciculations in both upper and lower limbs. Reflex testing showed bilateral hyporeflexia in the triceps, biceps, brachioradialis, pronator, and patellar reflexes (grade 1 on the deep tendon reflexes grading scale), with absent Achilles reflexes bilaterally (grade 0). Muscle strength was graded as 4 in the bilateral lower limbs and proximal upper limbs according to the Medical Research Council (MRC) scale. Bulbar involvement was noted with uvula deviation to the right during phonation and tongue atrophy with fasciculations. Surgical scars from the gynecomastia correction were present. In January 2015, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) imaging indicated thinning of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord with slight signal changes in C4, C5, and C6, without contrast enhancement and of nonspecific nature. Electromyography showed diffuse fasciculations in the upper limbs at rest, particularly in the triceps, extensor digitorum, and first dorsal interosseous muscles of the hand, as well as in the tibialis anterior of the lower limbs. Muscle activity was generally reduced, with few motor units displaying increased duration and amplitude. A neuroconduction study of the upper limbs revealed non-excitable sensory conduction and motor conduction with increased latencies of the median nerve bilaterally. Creatine phosphokinase (CPK) levels were elevated on two occasions: 1757 U/L in June 2015 and 1638 U/L in December 2015.
test_results: Forty-six CAG repetitions were identified.
diagnosis: X-linked spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy
Orpha_name: X-linked spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy

case_report: A previously healthy 12-year-old male was brought to the emergency department 7 days after ingesting an unknown quantity of a liquid. Post-ingestion, he experienced multiple episodes of vomiting, occasionally with bloody secretions. He appeared pale. His relatives reported no seizures. Over the past week, he had anorexia, lethargy, and general discomfort. Upon examination, he was drowsy but responsive, afebrile with a heart rate of 71/min, regular rhythm, blood pressure 100/75 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation of 95% on room air. His oral mucosa was congested and swollen, with exudative ulcerations on the tongue and swollen lips. Pupils were 2 mm bilaterally and reactive to light. Lung auscultation revealed clear lung fields. The pulse was 71 beats/min with a regular rhythm, and no extra heart sounds or murmurs were detected. On arrival, his blood pressure was 90/60 mm Hg. Vital signs were stable with a body temperature of 37.7°C, pulse 71 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and blood pressure 90/60 mm Hg. There were no neurological symptoms, organomegaly, tachycardia, or tachypnea. He received intravenous therapy, including IV fluids, antiemetic (ondansetron), and ranitidine as supportive measures. Initial laboratory tests, including complete blood count, electrolytes, liver function tests, arterial blood gas, and serum amylase, were within normal limits. The initial chest x-ray was normal. Serum urea was elevated at 212 mg/dL and creatinine at 8.6 mg/dL on admission, which normalized after three dialysis sessions. Blood and urine cultures were sterile. Other blood tests, including thyroid and liver functions, were normal. Urine examination was normal. The electrocardiogram (ECG) was normal, and 2D echocardiography showed normal cardiac chambers with a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 70%.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) manifestations, significantly abnormal results in the main laboratory test results.

case_report: A 64-year-old woman presented with mildly itchy brownish to red rashes on both lateral malleoli for 7 months. She had previously been treated for lichen simplex chronicus with various topical steroids, including 0.05% clobetasol propionate ointment and triamcinolone acetonide 10 mg/mL injection, but showed minimal improvement. There was no history of significant weight loss or trauma to the affected area. She was otherwise in good health. Physical examination showed bilateral well-defined brownish hyperkeratotic plaques with a red rim on both lateral malleoli. The scalp and nails were normal, and other physical examinations were unremarkable.
test_results: The finding revealed papillated psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia, compact hyperkeratosis, and mounds of parakeratosis with neutrophils. There were pale and vacuolated keratinocytes in the superficial epidermal layer and scattered necrotic keratinocytes. The granular layer was absent. Dense inflammatory cell infiltrate was composed mainly of lymphocytes. Extravasated erythrocytes with dilated capillaries in the papillary dermis were also observed.

case_report: A 16-month-old female was admitted to a community hospital in Puerto Rico due to cough and difficulty breathing that began one day prior. She developed acute respiratory failure with hypoxemia and was transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU). The patient is the first child of healthy, non-consanguineous Puerto Rican parents, born prematurely at 36 weeks of gestation via vaginal delivery after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Birthweight was 1.87 kg (3rd percentile) and height was 40.6 cm (<3rd percentile). At birth, she exhibited congenital hypotonia, cleft palate, abundant oral secretions, bilateral hand contractures, clitoromegaly, and talipes equinovarus feet. She was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) for 28 days due to respiratory distress and poor oral coordination. There is no family history of genetic disorders or congenital anomalies. Her past medical history includes failure to thrive, congenital talipes equinovarus, global developmental delay, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and two previous hospitalizations for bronchiolitis. She has a gastrostomy for long-term nutrition due to hypotonia, dysphagia, and poor oral coordination. Physical examination revealed generalized hypotonia, left medial eye strabismus, cleft palate, mild to moderate pectus excavatum, weak cry, tapered fingers, single palmar crease, and bilateral clubfeet. Dysmorphic facial features included bitemporal narrowing, elongated face, broad-based short philtrum, retromicrognathia, long eyelashes, and epicanthal folds. Radiographic imaging showed perihilar infiltrates, severe dextroscoliosis, and mild adenoidal hypertrophy. Polysomnography indicated severe central sleep apnea with an apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) of 35.9 events per hour. Video electroencephalography monitoring and basic laboratory and metabolic workup were normal. Following the initial sleep study, the patient received supplemental oxygen at night via a 1 liter per minute (LPM) nasal cannula. In the PICU, due to severe apneas and low arousal levels, non-invasive ventilation (NIV) with a nasal mask interface and Bi-level positive pressure was administered during sleep. Supplemental oxygen was provided to maintain saturations above 92%. Additionally, the patient received albuterol, hypertonic saline 3.5%, and chest physiotherapy every 8 hours as part of her airway clearance regimen. After 15 days on NIV with an oxygen flow rate of 1 LPM, there was progressive improvement in her motor and social milestones, with increased alertness, interaction with caretakers, and smiling frequency.
test_results: Whole-exome genetic testing subsequently resulted in a heterozygous mutation in the KCNK9 gene on chromosome 8q24.3.

case_report: This male infant was delivered at 38 weeks gestation via c-section to a 36-year-old mother. Post-birth, he required intubation due to respiratory distress, which was successfully performed on the third attempt due to a short neck. Initial attempts to place an orogastric tube were unsuccessful, raising concerns about esophageal atresia. Persistent severe respiratory distress led to his referral to our hospital. The pregnancy history indicated that the mother was not regularly monitored and was treated with alpha-methyldopa from the 6th month due to hypertension. She had three ultrasonographic examinations, all reporting the fetus as normal, but polyhydramnios was noted each time. The parents are first cousins, and their six other children are healthy. Upon admission, the infant's body weight was 2790 grams (25-50%), length was 43 cm (50%), and head circumference was 38 cm (>90%). Vital signs included a body temperature of 36.4 ˚C, heart rate of 135/minute, blood pressure of 53/14 mmHg, and oxygen saturation of 85% despite intubation and 100% oxygen. Physical examination showed a large anterior fontanel, prominent forehead, protruding eyes, hypertelorism, depressed nasal root, wide nose ridge, short neck, mild shortness in the extremities, short fingers, skin folds in the extremities, a prominent abdomen, and hypotonia. Breath sounds were decreased bilaterally, and a II/VI systolic murmur was noted under the left clavicle. An orogastric tube was successfully inserted, ruling out esophageal atresia.
test_results: A radiogram of the skeletal system showed straight femurs. Transfontanel ultrasound showed that the occipital and temporal horns of the lateral ventricles were large and the sulci were prominent. Echocardiographic examination showed a patent ductus arteriosus and pulmonary hypertension. In the genetic investigation, exons 9, 10, 13 and 15 were scanned. A heterozygous T394K mutation (changing from ACG to AAG) was detected in the exon 10.

case_report: A 59-year-old woman was noted to have unusual bone characteristics following a car accident during her college years. In high school, she was thin, not athletic, had disproportionately long lower limbs, and minimal muscle mass. She began menstruating at age 13 and continued to grow until age 17, experiencing irregular periods until she started birth control pills. Menopause occurred at age 55. She reported no fractures and considered herself generally healthy. With aging, she experienced increasing stiffness, particularly in her back, hips, and lower limbs, including her knees. She used arch supports. Arthritis symptoms were present only in her ankles, with occasional swelling after prolonged sitting. Severe neck pain over eight months improved with physical therapy. L4-L5 disc surgery alleviated back pain following a fall. There was no finger clubbing, but the proximal interphalangeal joints of her right hand were enlarged. Her dental health was good. She reported minimal hearing loss since age 50, with audiometry conducted over 10 years ago. She wore eyeglasses until undergoing successful Lasik surgery at age 40. She had been taking sulfasalazine for ulcerative colitis since age 30 and macrodantin due to leukocytes in her urine. She had not used glucocorticoids but took folic acid, other vitamins, and fish oil for colitis and sulfasalazine treatment. She sporadically took a calcium supplement for five years. Physical examination showed a height of 5 feet, 10½ inches (Z-score + 2.5), an arm span of 5 feet, 11½ inches (Z-score + 2.8), sitting height of 2 feet, 11 inches (Z-score 0), head circumference of 58 cm (∼ 90%), and weight of 181 pounds. Torus palatinus was present, and her teeth appeared well-formed. She could hear a softly ticking watch. There was no tenderness with fist percussion of her spine or femora, compression of her ribs, or gentle squeezing of her forearms. Some tenderness was noted with percussion of the pretibial regions. The distal tibias were expanded with minimal overlying soft tissue. Her feet were not flat. Fingers showed some clubbing. Crepitus (2–3+) was observed on passive flexion and extension of her knees, but not with rotation of the ankles.
test_results: A skeletal survey reportedly showed 'benign osteopathia striata.'

case_report: A 7-year-old male patient presented with normal external genitalia, a right testicle in the scrotum, and a nonpalpable left testicle. The patient underwent surgical exploration, during which a fragment presumed to be remnants of the left testicle was removed. The fragment measured approximately 6.5 cm in length and 0.7 cm in diameter, had a brownish color, and a fibroelastic consistency. No testis-like structures were observed, but there was a slight bulging and firm thickening of about 0.5 cm in the region marked with a surgical thread. The entire specimen was subjected to microscopic analysis.
test_results: The histological sections showed hypoplastic vas deferens amid venous vascular structures similar to a rudimentary pampiniform plexus. There was also nerves and skeletal muscle tissue. Areas of nodular fibrosis intermingled with some vessels, foci of hyalinization and focal dystrophic calcification could be seen. Perls´ Prussian blue stain for hemosiderin was negative.

case_report: A 67-year-old female presented with unstable walking, slurred speech, and difficulty swallowing water starting at age 65. Additional symptoms included slow reaction times, memory decline, numbness in extremities, involuntary hand shaking, and excessive salivation. She reported no issues with night terrors, urination, or defecation. Her symptoms progressively worsened, leading to several backward falls. She had a history of hypertension and was on regular anti-hypertensive medication. She denied any other long-term medication use or exposure to toxic substances. She had six years of education. Her spouse and two daughters were healthy, and her parents did not experience unstable walking before their deaths. There was no consanguineous marriage. Her second elder brother had a history of a brain tumor, while her other siblings were healthy. Neurological examination showed mild dysarthria, bradykinesia, and an ataxic gait. She had difficulty opening her eyes and limited vertical eye movement. Rigidity was more pronounced on the right side, with slight postural tremor in the upper limbs and hyperactive tendon reflexes (++++) in the extremities. Bilateral Babinski’s and Romberg’s signs were negative. A levodopa challenge test indicated a 15.8% improvement rate in the MDS-UPDRS part III score (baseline score 38) after administering 200 mg of levodopa. Neuropsychological evaluations showed cognitive impairment, with scores of 19/30 on the mini-mental state examination and 8/30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment. Cranial MRI revealed a 'hummingbird' sign of midbrain atrophy, with no significant cerebellar or pontine atrophy. The midbrain to pons ratio was 0.44 (<0.52). No significant abnormal signals were observed in susceptibility-weighted imaging, and no spinal cord atrophy was seen on thoracic spine MRI.
test_results: One allele of ATXN8OS gene had more than 131 CTA/CTG repeats which was a full penetrance mutant. Another allele of ATXN8OS gene had 26 CTA/CTG repeats.

case_report: An 8-year-old female patient was seen at the pediatric dermatology outpatient clinic of the Hospital Santa Casa of Porto Alegre with a history of widespread skin condition that started in early infancy. On examination, the patient exhibited erythematous, scaly, hyperkeratotic plaques with well-defined borders, located on the mesogastrium, cubital fossae, popliteal fossae, and inguinal and cervical regions. Additionally, there was palmoplantar hyperkeratosis and yellowish hyperkeratotic plaques on the scalp and nasal introitus. Hair, nails, and mucosa appeared normal. The patient reported no symptoms and there was no family history of similar conditions or consanguinity. Upon reassessment after one month, the plaques had expanded in area, but the polycyclic pattern was no longer present.
test_results: Skin biopsy in the extensor portion of the forearm showed acanthosis, papillomatosis, and hyperkeratosis with marked epidermolysis in the granular layer.

case_report: A 7-year-old female exhibited breast development over a four-month period, accompanied by vaginal discharge and a noticeable increase in height. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. She measured 130 cm in height (+2.24 standard deviation) and weighed 28.9 kg (+1.62 standard deviation). Physical examination showed breast development at Tanner stage 3, with no pubic or axillary hair present.
test_results: Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a solid mass at the right side of the rectouterine pouch. Serum estradiol (E2) level was 41.7 pg/mL and markedly elevated for her age while luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) were suppressed below the detection limit. On gross examination, the right ovary was occupied by a 49 × 40 × 26 mm solid and fleshy mass with a tan-yellow cut surface. Microscopically, the mass showed sheets and nests of large polygonal cells intersected by fibrous septa. The septa were concentrated by stromal cells with plump spindle nuclei that resembled theca cells. The tumor cells displayed abundant clear cytoplasm with large round nuclei and conspicuous nucleoli. They also expressed placental alkaline phosphatase, c-kit, and podoplanin. Immunohistochemistry for CD3 revealed a few T lymphocytes scattered within the nests. Further investigation was performed to immunolocalize the steroidogenic enzymes. Stromal cells were positive for steroidogenic factor 1 (SF-1), P450C17 (17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase), 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (HSD), P450arom (aromatase), 17β-HSD type 1, and steroid sulfatase but negative for 17β-HSD types 2 and 5, 5α-reductases 1 and 2, and estrone sulfotransferase.
diagnosis: Pure Dysgerminoma with Estrogen-Producing Functioning Stroma

case_report: A 40-year-old woman with no known chronic medical conditions presented with general fatigue, malaise, and recurrent headaches over the past few months. Initial laboratory tests, including a complete blood count, revealed pancytopenia, leading to a referral to the hematology clinic. Upon presentation, her vital signs included a blood pressure of 100/60 mmHg, a pulse of 75 bpm without orthostasis, and a temperature of 36.9°C. Physical examination showed a fatigued woman with pallor, but no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Other aspects of the examination were unremarkable. Initial lab results indicated hyponatremia at 132 mmol/L, with normal potassium and glucose levels, and normal kidney and liver function tests. Her hemogram showed a leukocyte count of 2.45 × 10^9/L, a neutrophil count of 0.82 × 10^9/L, a hemoglobin level of 8.7 g/dL with a mean corpuscular volume of 92.7 fL, and a platelet count of 133 × 10^9/L. Coombs testing was negative, and iron studies, reticulocyte count, vitamin B12, and folate levels were normal. A blood film was nonconclusive, and bone marrow biopsy and aspirate revealed hypocellular marrow with trilineage hypoplasia. During a follow-up visit one week later, lab results showed persistent pancytopenia, a sodium level of 116 mmol/L, and a fasting blood sugar of 50 mg/dL. The patient reported worsening fatigue. She was admitted to the hospital for further management. Additional history revealed excessive postpartum bleeding after her last normal vaginal delivery at age 36, which required a total abdominal hysterectomy and resulted in amenorrhea and failure of lactation. Detailed examination showed depigmentation of areolas and loss of pubic and axillary hair.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging of the head showed partially empty sella turcica.

case_report: The patient is an 8-month-old female born to a nonconsanguineous couple. The mother is 37 years old and of Native American descent, while the father is 30 years old and of German and Irish descent. Family history includes an older sibling with cleft palate, a paternal uncle with autism, a paternal second cousin with a congenital heart defect, and a distant paternal great-great uncle with Down syndrome and webbed/fused 4th and 5th digits of one hand. During the second trimester of a normal pregnancy, an ultrasound detected an omphalocele. A later ultrasound suggested possible syndactyly of the hands. The patient was delivered vaginally at 39 weeks with induction. Birth measurements were: weight 3.552 kg (75th percentile), length 50 cm (68th percentile), and head circumference 34.5 cm (70th percentile). Apgar scores were 9 at both one minute and five minutes. At birth, multiple congenital anomalies were observed, including a 4 cm by 3.5 cm omphalocele containing intestines but no liver. The patient had a normocephalic head with sparse hair, a small nose with hypoplastic alae, a prominent columella, small palpebral fissures, small corneas, microphthalmia, a wide anterior fontanelle, and retrognathia. Syndactyly of digits 4 and 5 and webbing of digits 3 and 4 were noted on both hands. A cardiac echocardiogram on the day of birth revealed a mild patent ductus arteriosus, mild patent foramen ovale, and a normal aorta. Feeding difficulties were noted due to the omphalocele, which was surgically corrected on day 2 of life. At 4 months, an ophthalmologic assessment showed deep anterior chambers, bilateral nasolacrimal duct obstruction, microphthalmia, 8 mm corneas, a blonde fundus, and moderate hyperopia in both eyes. At 8 months, the patient continues to experience poor feeding with self-limiting volumes but has shown improved weight gain. The patient is at the 9th percentile for weight and 12th percentile for length. Cognitive and motor developments are delayed.
test_results: Sequencing of the GJA1 gene from patient genomic DNA revealed a heterozygous missense mutation in the GJA1 gene: c.65G>A (p.G22E). Deletion/duplication analysis of the GJA1 gene using the aCGH test was negative.

case_report: A 17-year-old male arrived at urgent care with his mother, reporting headache, joint pain, muscle pain, congestion, and sore throat for three days. His vital signs were normal except for a high fever of 39.4 °C. Cepheid RT-PCR tests for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 were negative. He was sent home for supportive care. On the fifth day, he was brought to the Emergency Department by EMS after experiencing a self-limited convulsive episode at home, characterized by generalized shaking and unresponsiveness for 1-2 minutes. There was no bladder or bowel incontinence. He had no history of seizures. In the ED, he was somnolent and minimally interactive; lorazepam was administered. Physical examination showed no head trauma, meningeal signs, focal neurologic deficits, respiratory distress, cardiovascular abnormalities, rash, or mucosal lesions. A head CT scan was unremarkable. Broad-spectrum antibiotics were given intravenously. Laboratory results showed mild thrombocytosis with a platelet count of 354,000 per microliter, while the rest of the blood count was normal. Urinalysis was unremarkable. A urine drug screen was positive for cannabinoids and benzodiazepines, the latter administered in the ED. He was transferred for inpatient pediatric care. Upon admission, lumbar puncture was deferred due to the absence of fever or meningeal signs, largely unremarkable initial labs, and prior antibiotic administration. The next morning, he had a fever of 38.9 °C and experienced two successive generalized tonic-clonic seizures within 30 minutes, with the second seizure captured on EEG and terminated with lorazepam.
test_results: EEG demonstrated a 90-s generalized seizure, characterized by rhythmic high-amplitude theta-delta frequencies bifrontally that evolved into polyspike and wave discharges at a frequency of 3 Hertz, followed by diffuse postictal suppression. Lumbar puncture resulted in a traumatic tap, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis demonstrated 7,161 erythrocytes and 31 leukocytes with a 63% predominance of segmented neutrophils. Corrected leukocyte count was consistent with moderate pleocytosis of 31 white blood cells per microliter (RR 0-5 * 106 cells/uL). CSF Gram stain was negative, CSF glucose was 74 mg/dL (RR 50-80 mg/dL), and CSF protein was 57 mg/dL (RR 14-45 mg/dL). The BioFire FilmArray Meningitis/Encephalitis (ME) Panel was unanimously negative.

case_report: A 30-year-old female visited the plastic-surgery clinic with wide atrophic scars on her forehead, elbows, knees, and pretibial area that had been present since childhood. Physical examination showed skin that could be stretched more than usual, joints that moved beyond the normal range, thin and fragile scars, and a tendency to bruise easily. Eye-related features included folds of skin on the inner corners of the eyes, creases below the eyes, and an increased distance between the eyes. Laboratory tests and radiography results were normal. No vascular issues were detected, and there was no relevant family history.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing revealed that the proband carried a heterozygous pathogenic variant, c1997G > A (p.P659P), in COL5A2 gene. Sanger sequencing of COL5A2 in this patient also confirmed the presence of this variant.

case_report: A female patient aged two years and eight months presented with a three-month history of asymptomatic lesions on the abdominal region. Physical examination revealed multiple violaceous papules with hyperkeratotic surfaces, distributed along the lines of Blaschko on the abdominal region, buttocks, and right thigh. No mucosal lesions or nail changes were observed. Hepatitis C serology was negative.
test_results: Histopathological examination indicated vacuolar and lichenoid interface dermatitis with pigment incontinence.

case_report: A 16-month-old Hispanic girl was evaluated at a genetics clinic due to developmental delay and distinctive facial characteristics. She was born at full term to non-consanguineous parents, aged 29 and 30 years. Her two older sisters exhibit normal development. There is no family history of intellectual disability or similar findings, although the maternal grandmother had a baby who passed away at one week old with multiple birth defects. Developmental delay was observed at 4 months, leading to a referral for early intervention therapy. At 16 months, she exhibited whining noises, lacked eye contact, and was unable to sit upright, crawl, or rollover. She had poor eye contact and episodes of inconsolable agitation with self-mutilation. She experienced constipation, abdominal bloating, and could only tolerate pureed food. She developed a periorbital urticarial rash and tested positive for multiple food allergies. Her head circumference was at the fifth percentile, while her length was at the 25th percentile. Her ears were large, at the 95th percentile. She had two skin papules above her nipples bilaterally and one lateral to her right palpebral fissure. Facial features included mild midface hypoplasia, anteverted nares, a short thick upper lip, broad philtrum, protuberant lower lip, high palate, and widely spaced teeth. She had an abnormal hair whorl offset to the side. She exhibited prominent digit pads on the middle three fingers bilaterally, excess skin on the plantar surface of her feet, few sole creases, and a palpable soft fat pad anteromedial to the heel of both feet.
test_results: A chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) using the Affymetrix Genome-wide Human Single Nucleotide Polymorphism (SNP) Array 6.0 revealed 118 independent regions of homozygosity. These ranged from 1 Mb to 5.8 Mb and encompassed 8 % of her genome.

case_report: A 28-year-old female presented for a comprehensive eye examination in October 2019 at the Eye Clinic of the University of Campania L. Vanvitelli. She reported experiencing a gradual decrease in visual sharpness over the past few months. The patient has a history of myoclonic epilepsy accompanied by muscle weakness and significant motor impairment, which began around the age of 13.
test_results: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and Sanger sequencing analysis of NEU1 gene disclosed an already described compound heterozygosity: Leu91Arg and Gly328Ser.

case_report: The patient is a 4-year-old male, the only child in a Chinese family. The parents are not related by blood and show no clinical abnormalities. The father's height is 178 cm and the mother's height is 163 cm. There is no history of developmental delay in the family. During the pregnancy, low amniotic fluid levels were noted. The patient was born at full term (40 weeks) with a small placenta and was smaller than average for his gestational age, weighing 1,850 g (<3%), measuring 42 cm in length (<3%), and having a head circumference of 27 cm (<3%). The patient experienced mild feeding difficulties, requiring Enfamil Enfacare due to under-eating. At 24 months, his height was 75 cm (<3%) and his weight was 7,500 g (<3%), with a BMI of 10.5 (<3%). Physical examination revealed a prominent forehead, fifth-finger clinodactyly, a triangular face, micrognathia, low-set ears, delayed bone age, low muscle mass, and delayed motor and speech development. No other significant abnormalities were observed. The patient received growth hormone therapy, resulting in a 3 cm increase in height after 16 injections over 114 days.
test_results: The patient’s samples were subjected to next generation sequencing-based copy number variation assays, and WES trio testing was performed.

case_report: A 60-year-old Chinese male, a non-smoker, presented to the emergency department following a road traffic accident in September 2019. He had no known history of autoimmune or connective tissue diseases. A chest radiograph showed a well-circumscribed opacity in the right lower zone, prompting a computed tomography (CT) scan of the thorax. The CT scan revealed a mildly lobulated nodule in the superior segment of the right lower lobe, measuring 1.3 cm. The patient chose to follow up with interval CT scans of the thorax instead of undergoing a biopsy. Subsequent CT scans in August 2020 and September 2021 showed that the nodule remained stable. In April 2022, the patient reported a cough with small amounts of hemoptysis over the past two months, along with a weight loss of 5 kg during the same period. A detailed history and examination did not reveal any signs or symptoms of autoimmune or connective tissue diseases. A chest radiograph in April 2022 showed a new right hilar mass compared to previous radiographs. A CT scan of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis in May 2022 showed that the initial nodule was stable, but there was a new mass-like consolidation in the medial right lower lobe, measuring 4.4 cm × 7.2 cm. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and transbronchial lung biopsy (TBLB) under fluoroscopy of the right lower lobe was performed. No endobronchial lesions or active bleeding were observed. BAL microbiology was negative, including for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear and culture. BAL cytology showed inflammatory exudates mainly consisting of neutrophils, while TBLB histology showed bronchial tissue with lymphocytic and plasma cell-rich infiltrates with no malignancy detected. Immunohistochemistry of the lymphocytic infiltrates was inconclusive for light chain restriction due to limited lesional tissue. A repeat chest radiograph in June 2022 showed that the hilar nodular consolidation persisted.
test_results: Histology showed a micronodular lymphocytic pneumonitis pattern which involved centrilobular areas with extension into small septa and peri-septal alveolar walls. It was associated with mild ongoing alveolar cell injury, inflammation, and repair. There was no evidence of malignancy of carcinoma or lymphoma. There were no granulomas, giant histiocytes, notable capillaritis or capillary thrombi, necrotizing vasculitis, or viral cytopathy identified. The proximal acinar interstitium was diffusely expanded by mild-to-moderate lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates with evenly spaced small lymphoid aggregates and occasional follicles. No follicular colonization, lymphoepithelial lesions, or light chain restriction was identified.

case_report: A 16-year-old female presented with multiple missing teeth. She exhibited short stature and an abnormal gait. There was a familial history of similar presentations in her mother and sister. She was born to non-consanguineous parents at 8.5 months of gestation with a large and dysmorphic head. Gross motor developmental milestones were significantly delayed, while fine motor, social, adaptive, and language milestones were normal. The patient appeared well-adjusted, healthy, and intelligent. Physical examination showed short stature with normal trunk length and rhizomelic shortening of the arms and legs. Additional findings included lumbar lordosis, prominent buttocks, and short, stubby fingers with a trident hand configuration. Anthropometric measurements at age 16 revealed a height of 124 cm, weight of 42 kg, mesomelic dwarfism with an upper limb to lower limb ratio greater than 1, and an arm span of 100 cm. The head circumference was 58 cm. Vital signs were within normal limits. Systemic examination showed no other abnormalities. Extraoral examination noted brachycephaly, midfacial hypoplasia, flat nasal bridge, frontal bossing, competent lips, and a concave facial profile with a normal mandible and non-prominent chin. Intraoral examination revealed the presence of eight teeth (11, 15, 17, 21, 25, 27, 36, and 46) and hypertonic lips, with no other abnormalities in the intraoral soft tissues.
test_results: Her orthopantomogram showed the presence of impacted maxillary canines (13 and 23) and the follicles of all third molars (18, 28, 38 and 48). The lateral cephalogram revealed an enlarged calvarium with increased transverse diameter, shortening of the skull base with frontal bossing and a retruded maxilla. The mandible appeared normal. The hand-wrist radiograph showed a trident hand configuration.

case_report: A 35-year-old Moroccan man presented with intermittent left flank pain and visible blood in his urine for the past 10 years. He had a history of passing stones on two occasions and had occasionally taken ibuprofen for pain relief. Physical examination showed he was in very good general condition, afebrile, with a blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg. He experienced slight left flank pain without a palpable mass. His body mass index (BMI) was 27 kg/m2. No other abnormalities were found on complete physical examination. Blood tests revealed hemoglobin (Hb) 13.4 g/dl, white blood cells (WBC) 7500/mcL, C-reactive protein (CRP) 20 mg/L, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) 0.36 g/L, creatinine 11 mg/L, sodium 140 mEq/L, and potassium 3.8 mEq/L. Urine analysis showed pH 5, negative for glucose and proteins, leukocytes 320,000/ml, red blood cells (RBC) 10,000/ml, and no crystals. Urine culture was positive for Proteus mirabilis. Imaging studies included a kidney, ureter, and bladder (KUB) X-ray which revealed two large ureteral stones and a left renal stone. Abdominal ultrasonography (US) indicated severe hydroureteronephrosis. An intravenous pyelogram (IVP) showed no concentration and excretion at 1 hour from the left kidney, indicating it was nonfunctioning. Computed tomography urography confirmed advanced hydroureteronephrosis with two large stones in the abdominal and pelvic ureter, measuring 7×3 cm and 3×3.5 cm respectively, and another stone in the left inferior renal calyx. The stones had densities between 780 and 850 Hounsfield units (HU). Surgery was recommended.
test_results: Gross examination of the specimen (left nephroureterectomy): the left kidney measured 13×7×4 cm; the left ureter appeared dilated and measured 18×2.5 cm containing multiple stones. A cut section of the left kidney showed multiple cystic lesions in the renal parenchyma. Microscopic examination of the specimen: the renal parenchyma showed fibrosis of the glomerular, a pseudo-thyroid appearance of the tubules, and interstitial lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. There were metaplastic changes in the urothelium of the ureter with no dysplasia. No lesions of malignancy were found.

case_report: A 68-year-old male was directed to the Veterans Affairs Emergency Department by his primary care physician due to a white blood cell (WBC) count of 28 x 10^3 per microliter (µL). His medical history includes a bronchogenic cyst resection six years ago, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and past episodes of rheumatic fever and malaria over forty years ago. Over the past month, he experienced a productive cough, decreased appetite, and a weight loss of approximately 10 pounds. He reported no fever, chills, chest pain, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, or changes in bowel or urinary habits. His medications included amlodipine and atorvastatin. He had no family history of malignancy or blood disorders. He had a 42 pack-year smoking history and a history of heavy alcohol use but had been abstinent for several years, with no illicit drug use. On examination, his temperature was 98.6˚F, heart rate 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and blood pressure 150/92 mmHg. He appeared in no acute distress and had a body mass index (BMI) of 33 kg/m2. Physical examination revealed bilateral lung wheezes and splenomegaly, with no cervical, axillary, or inguinal adenopathy. Laboratory results showed a WBC count of 28.65 x 10^3 per µL, an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of 4.53 x 10^3 per µL, hemoglobin level (Hgb) of 12.9 grams per deciliter (g/dL), and a platelet count of 95 x 10^3 per µL. Electrolytes, liver function tests, and renal function were within normal limits. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest with contrast revealed a small left-sided effusion and left lower lobe atelectasis versus consolidation. The abdomen showed splenomegaly and enlarged gastro-hepatic ligament nodes. A follow-up CT of the abdomen confirmed marked splenomegaly with a spleen span of 21 cm. The patient was admitted and started on treatment for community-acquired pneumonia. Further evaluation was conducted due to weight loss, leukocytosis, splenomegaly, and adenopathy. A peripheral smear revealed lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes featuring thin cytoplasmic projections. The patient showed clinical improvement and was discharged a day after admission with plans for outpatient follow-up.
test_results: A bone marrow biopsy was performed six days after discharge. Complete blood count (CBC) done on the day of the bone marrow biopsy showed a WBC count of 39.26 x 103 per µL, ANC of 3.36 x 103 per µL, Hgb of 12.0 g/dL, and a platelet count of 113 x 103 per µL. The aspirate showed normoblastic myeloid and erythroid maturation without significant dyspoeitic features. There was no increase in blasts. Atypical lymphocytes morphologically similar to those seen on the peripheral smear were seen. The core biopsy and clot sections showed cellularity of 20-40%. A reticulin stain showed mild, focal increase in reticulin fibers (grade 1). Immunophenotyping showed B-lymphocytes that were positive for CD19, CD20, had a moderate expression of CD200, and had a bright CD11c and CD103. They were negative for expression of surface kappa and lambda light chain, CD5, CD10, CD38, CD23, and CD25. Fluorescence in situ hybridization was negative for BCR/ABL translocation. Cytogenetics detected two separate complex karyotypes involving multiple deletions, monosomy 5, and an apparent derivative of chromosome 16. Molecular studies were negative for BRAFV600E mutation.

case_report: Patient 4 is an 11-year-old boy who has exhibited pendular nystagmus and intense photophobia since he was 3 months old. His medical history is unremarkable, and there is no family history of significant ophthalmologic conditions or consanguinity. At the age of 5, his best-corrected visual acuity (VA) was 20/50 in both eyes. He had a mild hypermetropic refractive error (+1.00 in the right eye and +1.50 in the left eye). Examination revealed a 5 prism diopter exotropia in the left eye. The ocular fundus examination was completely normal. Over time, his VA has decreased. Currently, at 11 years old, his best-corrected VA is 20/200 in both eyes.
test_results: The first electrophysiological test performed at the age of 3 revealed DA adapted ERGs within normal limits, but the LA 3.0 ERG and LA 30-Hz flicker ERG were nonrecordable. These results indicated a cone dysfunction and normal rod function. Farnsworth-Munsell 100 Hue Test presented multiple errors is the 3 axes. The boy recognized plates number 1 and 14 and partially plates 5 and 7–8 plates.

case_report: A 29-year-old male from Indonesia, previously without symptoms, was brought to the emergency department (ED) from a cruise ship due to shortness of breath and atrial fibrillation. He experienced shortness of breath, chest pain that worsened with breathing, and difficulty breathing while lying down for a week. He was treated with amiodarone, furosemide, and low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) on the cruise ship before being transferred to the hospital. Upon arrival at the ED, he had a normal body temperature, a heart rate of 112 bpm, blood pressure of 107/79 mm Hg, and an oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. Physical examination showed an irregular heart rhythm, a palpable apical pulse, an S3 heart sound, a rumbling diastolic murmur with a diastolic snap when lying on the left side, reduced breath sounds in both lungs, and slight swelling in both lower legs. Laboratory results indicated a white blood cell count of 13.19 x103/L, sodium level of 133 mmol/L, potassium level of 4.2 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) of 22 mg/dL, creatinine level of 1.4 mg/dL, pro-B-type natriuretic peptide level of 1250 pg/mL, troponin level of 0.04 ng/mL, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level of 1.14 mIU/mL, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) level of 403 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) level of 75 U/L, and alanine transaminase (ALT) level of 65 U/L. The patient tested positive for COVID-19. An EKG showed atrial flutter with a variable block, and a chest X-ray revealed an enlarged heart, vascular congestion, and small amounts of fluid in both pleural cavities. He was started on antibiotics, amiodarone, intravenous furosemide, and anticoagulation with LMWH. He was admitted to the telemetry floor for management of heart failure and arrhythmia. Beta-blocker was withheld due to acute heart failure exacerbation, and he was given a loading dose of digoxin.
test_results: Echocardiography revealed left ventricular internal end-diastolic diameter (LVIDd) of 5 cm, moderately reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) 40-45%, severely dilated left atrium, moderate-severely dilated right atrium, moderate-severe AR, mild-moderate aortic stenosis (AS), moderate MS with doming of anterior mitral leaflet, severe MR, and severe TR.
diagnosis: Rheumatic heart disease with multi-valvular involvement

case_report: A 66-year-old male presented with persistent hiccups lasting several days. His medical history includes end-stage renal disease and autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), for which he has been undergoing hemodialysis for the past five years. He is on the waiting list for a kidney transplant and has regular urological check-ups. The hiccups were continuous throughout the day, interfering with his ability to eat and resulting in a weight loss of 4 kg. No specific factors were identified that could provoke or alleviate the symptoms. Initial treatment with shakuyakukanzoto, a Japanese herbal medicine, was ineffective, as was subsequent treatment with clonazepam. Further treatments with metoclopramide and hydroxyzine pamoate also failed to alleviate the hiccups, leading to the prescription of gabapentin, which provided only slight symptom relief. The patient was then referred to our department for further evaluation and management. Upon examination, his vital signs were: body temperature 36.5℃, heart rate 100 bpm, and blood pressure 200/132 mmHg. Physical examinations of the neck, chest, and abdomen showed no significant abnormalities. Laboratory tests, including serum sodium and potassium levels, did not identify the cause of the symptoms.
test_results: Abdominal computed tomography revealed that one of the liver cysts, located just below the right diaphragm, was enlarged.
diagnosis: Enlarged hepatic cyst causing persistent hiccups

case_report: A one-month-old infant, born via caesarean section at 35 weeks from a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy, weighed 2,350g and measured 46 cm at birth. The parents are Portuguese and non-consanguineous. The infant presented with a one-week history of increased dejections and vomiting, primarily post-feeding. Initial examination at a local pediatric hospital revealed severe dehydration (heart rate 160 bpm, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, prolonged capillary refill time, deeply sunken eyes, mottled extremities), failure to regain birth weight (current weight 2,340g), and marked hypotonia. The infant had a normal male phenotype with no genital anomalies or skin hyperpigmentation. Laboratory tests showed elevated plasma potassium (7.4 mmol/L, NR 3.5-5.1), low plasma sodium (126 mmol/L, NR 137-145), and metabolic acidosis (pH 7.16, pCO2 46 mmHg, HCO3− 16.4 mmol/L, Lactates 5.3 mmol/L, Anion Gap −13.6 mmol/L). Treatment with 5% dextrose and 0.45% sodium chloride, along with sodium bicarbonate infusion, was initiated, and the patient was transferred to a central medical unit. During hospitalization, the patient received hydrocortisone (2.5 mg every 6 hours) and oral NaCl supplement (0.8 mEq/kg/day), showing initial clinical and laboratory improvement. Hormonal workup revealed normal plasma levels of ACTH (11.8 pg/mL, NR < 46), cortisol (10.9 µg/dL, NR 5.0-25.0), 17-OH-progesterone (10.0 ng/mL), androstenedione (0.9 ng/mL), and DHEA-SO4 (32.5 µg/dL), with markedly elevated renin (> 500 µUI/mL) and normal aldosterone (12.4 ng/dL). Kidney ultrasound showed no abnormalities, and there were no signs of enteropathy, urinary tract infection, or obstruction. The patient was discharged with an oral 20% NaCl supplement (0.4 mL, 8 times/day after feeding) and ion-exchange resin – sodic phase (1.8g, 3 times/day). At 54 days old, during a pediatric endocrinology appointment, laboratory evaluation confirmed previous results, with a plasma potassium level of 5.95 mmol/L (NR 3.5-5.1). Therapy with fludrocortisone (0.075 mg/day, 0.018 mg/kg/day) and NaCl supplementation was added.
test_results: Genetic analysis revealed that the patient is a double-homozygous carrier of two mutations: in exon 3, codon 198 with replacement of glutamic acid for aspartic acid - c.594A > C (p.Glu198Asp), and in exon 7, codon 386 with replacement of valine for alanine - c.1157T > C (p.Val386Ala).
diagnosis: Congenital hyperreninemic hypoaldosteronism due to aldosterone synthase deficiency type I

case_report: A 5-month-old male, born at term, was seen in the Gastroenterology clinic due to poor weight gain despite being fed fortified breast milk. Initially, he did not exceed his birth weight of 3.38 kg by 4 weeks and had a history of spit-ups after each feed, but no vomiting. He had 2-3 mushy stools daily without blood, mucus, or oil droplets. Ranitidine was started, and he was switched to nondairy breast milk and hypoallergenic formula. Despite these measures, his weight continued to decline, reaching 4.41 kg, below the 0.01th percentile for his age. Prior evaluations included normal BMP, CBC, urinalysis, and abdominal radiograph. An abdominal ultrasound showed no abnormal masses, ascites, or organomegaly. Laboratory results included ALT 67 U/L, A tocopherol 1.4 mg/L, beta gamma tocopherol <1.0 mg/L, total protein 5.4 g/dL, and albumin 3.9 g/dL. Stool studies indicated increased qualitative stool fat with normal neutral fat and elastase. At 7 months, he was hospitalized for failure to thrive and increasing abdominal distention.
