Further tests showed normal stool alpha 1 antitrypsin, stool reducing substance, sweat test, TTG IgA, total IgA, and DGP IgA. Repeat stool fat test was positive, and stool calprotectin was 134 µg/g. ALT was 99 U/L and AST was 91 U/L. Nasogastric tube feeds were initiated, and formula was changed to Elecare. After discharge, he gained weight and met caloric goals via oral feeds but had persistent abdominal distention. A barium enema was normal. ALT and AST peaked at 260 U/L and 121 U/L, respectively, while GGT, total bilirubin, and direct bilirubin remained normal. The patient struggled to transition to solid foods, and an occupational therapist noted oral motor incoordination and oral sensory aversion. An upper endoscopy was performed, revealing whitish duodenal mucosa with normal villi. Duodenal biopsies showed increased intraepithelial lipid accumulation. Further tests indicated low apolipoprotein B (30 mg/dL), low high-density lipoprotein (21 mg/dL), low LDL (26 mg/dL), low total cholesterol (52 mg/dL), normal triglyceride (60 mg/dL), and normal levels of vitamins A, D, and E.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed two pathogenic variants in SAR1B: a maternally inherited SAR1B c.247 C>T (p.Arg83Ter) and a de novo SAR1B c.409 G>A (p.Asp137Asn).

case_report: A 39-year-old man presented with chronic progressive pain in his right leg and was referred to our outpatient clinic on 28 July 2013 for a whole body bone scan. He reported no history of acute trauma. Initial physical examination showed no abnormalities; both lower extremities appeared symmetrical without signs of inflammation or tenderness. There were no neurological or musculoskeletal issues observed in his legs. The range of motion for both knee and ankle joints was within normal limits for both active and passive movements. A whole body bone scan was conducted 3 hours after the injection of 20 mCi 99mTc-methylene diphosphonate using a single-photon emission computed tomography/CT gamma camera with a low energy high-resolution collimator. The scan showed widespread parenchymal uptake of the bone-seeking agent in both lung fields. Additionally, there was increased radiotracer uptake in the right proximal tibiofibular joint, likely due to an inflammatory or traumatic process. Following the pulmonary findings on the bone scan, a detailed history was taken with a focus on any pulmonary issues. The patient reported no severe pulmonary symptoms, except for some exercise intolerance. He also mentioned an abnormal chest X-ray at the age of 14. His past medical history included a subclinical pulmonary condition that was not followed up due to stable X-ray findings and lack of significant clinical symptoms.
test_results: Chest radiograph demonstrated a characteristic diffuse sand-like micronodulations throughout both lung fields. CT of the chest also showed an extensive infiltrative dense calcified micronodulations in the parenchyma of both lungs.

case_report: A 54-year-old Chinese female presented to the hospital in October 2018 with hyperthyroidism, persistent hyperkalemia, and elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels. Initial symptoms in August 2017 included palpitations, fatigue, tremor, and weight loss. Laboratory tests at that time showed elevated total thyroxine (TT4), total triiodothyronine (TT3), free thyroxine (FT4), free triiodothyronine (FT3), decreased thyrotropin (TSH), and elevated anti-TSH-receptor antibody (TRAb). Thyroid ultrasound indicated abundant blood flow. Serum potassium was 5.48 mmol/L. She was treated with thiamazole 15 mg daily, later reduced to 10 mg daily, resulting in improved thyroid function. However, serum potassium remained elevated between 5.3 and 5.8 mmol/L. In August 2018, she experienced dizziness and had a blood pressure of 167/94 mmHg. She was diagnosed with hypertension and prescribed metoprolol 25 mg twice daily, nifedipine 30 mg twice daily, and furosemide 40 mg daily. Despite good medication compliance, her blood pressure remained uncontrolled, and serum potassium levels were between 5.7 and 5.9 mmol/L. In October 2018, routine checks showed serum PTH at 123.6 pg/ml (normal < 88 pg/ml). Further tests revealed serum calcium at 2.39 mmol/L (normal 2.2–2.65 mmol/L), PTH at 108.62 pg/ml (normal < 88 pg/ml), 24-hour urinary calcium at 9.52 mmol/day (normal 5.9–6.5 mmol/day), serum potassium at 6.18 mmol/L, sodium at 139 mmol/L, chloride at 108.6 mmol/L, and total CO2 at 21.2 mmol/L. Physical examination showed blood pressure of 162/80 mmHg, BMI of 29.8 kg/m2, and an enlarged, soft thyroid. Further laboratory evaluations confirmed elevated potassium and PTH with normal to low serum calcium. Urinary calcium was normal on a second test, and arterial blood gas indicated metabolic acidosis. Biochemical bone markers showed increased bone alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and tartrate resistant acid phosphatase-5b (TRAP-5b), indicating increased bone turnover. 25-Hydroxyvitamin D was 16.04 nmol/L (normal 75–250 nmol/L). Serum creatinine was 57 µmol/L, with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 101.24 ml/min*1.73m2. Serum cortisol and ACTH were normal, plasma renin was low or normal, and aldosterone was normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed normal pancreas and adrenal gland images. The patient had no prior history of hyperkalemia and no family history of the condition. Her grandmother had hypertension. Her parents were not consanguineous. Her father died of lung cancer, her mother and brother were healthy, and she had no children.
test_results: A homozygous missense variant in the KLHL3 gene, c.328 A > G (T110A) (NM_01745.3), was identified. The variant was then verified by Sanger sequencing.
diagnosis: Pseudohypoaldosteronism type II  with a homozygous KLHL3 variant

case_report: A 63-year-old African American female arrived at the emergency room experiencing progressively worsening shortness of breath, new-onset difficulty breathing while lying down, swelling in both lower legs, and weight loss over the past month. Approximately 20 years ago, a mediastinal mass was incidentally discovered, but no further action was taken at that time, and it remained untreated due to its slow progression. Physical examination revealed rapid heart rate, labored breathing, reduced breath sounds with crackles and rhonchi in both lungs, and severe pitting edema in the lower extremities. Laboratory tests showed a brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) level of 2709 pg/mL, albumin level of 2.6 g/dL, and hemoglobin level of 9 g/dL. An initial chest X-ray identified a solid mass in the mediastinum. A chest CT scan revealed a large mass in the upper anterior mediastinum, measuring 16.4 x 12 x 15.3 cm, displacing most of the left lung tissue, exerting pressure on the heart, and encasing the ascending aorta and main pulmonary trunk. Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) showed a significantly reduced ejection fraction of 28.7%. Coronary angiogram indicated 90% narrowing of the ostial left main coronary artery and a large branch from the proximal right coronary artery (RCA) supplying the mediastinal mass. An initial plan for tumor removal via thoracotomy was halted due to a significantly increased risk of bleeding and other potential complications.
test_results: A CT-guided biopsy of the mass showed nesting of small blue cells with salt & pepper chromatin pattern, abundant vasculature, and lack of mitosis. Immunostain strongly expressed synaptophysin, chromogranin A, and cluster of differentiation (CD)56 marker. A proliferation marker, Ki-67, was less than 2% and there was no evidence of necrosis within the tumor.

case_report: A 61-year-old Western European male presented to the neurological outpatient clinic with complaints of swollen hands for 8 weeks, muscle pain related to physical activity in both upper and lower limbs for 3 months, general muscle weakness, and a hoarse voice without difficulty swallowing. Neurological examination showed mild speech difficulties, enlarged calf muscles on both sides without tenderness, reduced or absent reflexes, and decreased vibration sensation in the lower limbs. The patient also reported tingling sensations in the first three fingers and the radial side of the fourth finger of the right hand, with a positive Phalen’s sign. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations revealed no abnormalities except for mild limb edema.
test_results: CK was significantly elevated (64 µmol/l*s, normal < 3.2). Electromyography (EMG) showed spontaneous activity (positive sharp waves and fibrillation potentials) in the muscles (right tibialis anterior and left gastrocnemius muscle) but no signs of chronic denervation and no myopathic changes. Nerve conduction study showed bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome but no signs of polyneuropathy. Magnetic evoked potentials were normal. TSH was elevated up to 30.5 mU/l (normal range: 0.27–4.20 mU/l), the level of T3 was under 1.50 pmol/l (normal range 3.10–6.80 pmol/l) and the T4 level under 1.30 pmol/l (normal range 12.00–22.00 pmol/l). Anti-thyreoglobulin-antibodies were 5671.0 U/ml (normal < 60 U/ml) and anti-TSH-receptor-antibodies were 5.4 U/ml (normal < 1.8 U/ml). Myoglobin was elevated to 248 µg/l (normal range 28–72 µg/l). Blood count showed a mild normocytic, normochrome anemia. Liver enzymes were elevated (ALAT up to 1.94 µmol/l*s, normal < 0.83 µmol/l*s; ASAT up to 2.75 µmol/l*s, normal < 0.85 µmol/l*s). Renal function did not show any significant abnormalities. Cerebrospinal fluid showed cytoalbuminologic dissociation without evidence of infection. Rheumatologic parameters, hepatitis serology, lipid profile, and vitamins revealed no pathologic findings. Electrocardiogram, cardiac ultrasound and pulmonary function testing demonstrated no pathologic findings. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a muscular hypertrophy of the lower limbs but no signs of myositis or myopathy (no gadolinium enhancement, no edema, no fatty degeneration).
diagnosis: Hoffmann’s syndrome secondary to Hashimoto thyroiditis

case_report: A 38-year-old female presented with a sudden-onset dull ache in her lower back, followed by sharp pain radiating from her left gluteal region to her foot after moving a dresser. The pain increased in frequency and intensity over the following weeks, disrupting her sleep. She also experienced intermittent paresthesia and numbness in the sole of her left foot but reported no weakness or other symptoms. Nortriptyline was prescribed by her general practitioner, but it provided minimal relief despite dosage adjustments. On examination, her gait was normal, tandem walking was intact, and she could walk on tiptoes and the balls of her heels. There was no muscle wasting in her lower limbs, and Romberg's test was negative. She could perform a straight leg raise up to 90° bilaterally, with slight apprehension on the left side. Muscle power and sensation in her lower limbs were normal, reflexes were preserved, and plantar responses were flexor bilaterally. A lumbosacral X-ray showed scalloping of the left L5/S1 neural exit foramen. MRI of the spine confirmed this finding and revealed a well-circumscribed lesion within the foramen with some extraforaminal extension. High T2 signal changes within the lesion suggested recent intralesional hemorrhage, likely causing the onset and progression of her symptoms.
test_results: Histopathology sections demonstrated tumor along with fragments of the adjacent dura and nerve root. There was a mixture of spindle and epithelioid cells arranged in fascicles, sheets, and nests. These cells contained abundant intracytoplasmic pigment and had prominent nucleoli. A vaguely lobular and palisading pattern of arrangement was noted. There were also psammoma bodies which coalesced in some foci forming areas of calcification. Tumor was seen infiltrating dura with ganglion cells adjacent to it. Scattered mitotic activity was seen, including focal areas where up to five mitotic figures were identified in 10 high-power fields. No areas of necrosis were identified. Immunohistochemistry confirmed the presence of both SOX10 and HMB45 positive tumor cells and loss of PRKAR1A staining.

case_report: A 59-year-old Japanese man was transferred to our hospital due to worsening abdominal pain following initial treatment at another hospital. The patient, a fisherman and recreational diver, had previously experienced decompression sickness (DCS) twice, treated conservatively both times. He was on a daily dose of 100 mg aspirin due to a history of percutaneous cardiac intervention for angina pectoris. Recently, he had been diving to a depth of 100 feet for three consecutive days using SCUBA to search for a lost item. After surfacing, he experienced sudden abdominal and postcervical pain and visited a community hospital. Computed tomography (CT) showed a significant amount of intravenous gas throughout his body, including in the portal vein (PV), superior mesenteric vein (SMV), inferior mesenteric vein (IMV), and femoral vein (FV). He was transferred to another hospital for hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT). Upon admission, US Navy Treatment Table 6 HBOT was administered. The next day, CT findings indicated reduced intravenous gas, but pneumatosis intestinalis of the transverse colon had developed. His abdominal pain persisted and worsened. He was transferred to our hospital for further treatment. On arrival, he was oriented with vital signs: blood pressure 123/69 mmHg, pulse rate 120 bpm, and oxygen saturation 93% with 3 L/min O2. Physical examination revealed a distended and mildly hardened abdomen, strong abdominal pain, tense muscles, and tenderness, indicating peritonitis. Laboratory data showed elevated white blood cell (WBC) count (22400/μL), C-reactive protein (CRP) level, hemoconcentration, acute kidney injury, acute hepatic injury, and coagulopathy (hemoglobin [Hb] 21.4 g/dL, hematocrit [Ht] 59.9%, platelet count 134000/μL, creatinine [Cr] 3.72 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase [AST] 119 U/L, alanine aminotransferase [ALT] 127 U/L, creatine kinase [CK] 2018 U/L, CRP 17.21 mg/dL, prothrombin time [PT] 52.1%, activated partial prothrombin time [APTT] 36.6 s, D-dimer 7.3 μg/mL, and fibrin degradation production [FDP] 11.8 μg/mL). Due to kidney dysfunction, contrast-enhanced CT was avoided, and plain CT was performed, revealing pneumatosis intestinalis of the transverse colon. An exploratory laparoscopy was planned for further evaluation and treatment.
test_results: A pathological examination revealed diffuse edema, congestion, hemorrhaging, and necrotic changes in the mucosal, submucosal, and muscle layers and part of the subserosa. In some of the dilated veins, there were a few gas embolus-like oval transparent spaces, and thrombus formation was found near the peripheral side.

case_report: A 40-year-old male presented with elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) in the right eye. The patient had a history of glaucoma and had been using topical antiglaucoma medications for both eyes. The left eye had been completely blind for the past 10 years due to glaucoma. The patient was referred for persistent high IOP in the right eye despite medication use over the past year. IOP readings using Goldmann tonometry were 26 mmHg in the right eye and 36 mmHg in the left eye. The best-corrected visual acuity in the right eye was 20/80, with mild myopia noted. The left eye exhibited outward deviation.
test_results: Slit lamp examination revealed slight corneal edema, Haab’s striae, iridocorneal adhesions, and atrophy of the iris with corectopia in both eyes.

case_report: A 37-year-old female without any comorbidities presented with generalized weakness for the preceding four weeks, which worsened over the last four days, making it difficult for her to walk. She denied any history of trauma, fever, travel history, or alcohol use. On physical examination, there was no pallor, icterus, cyanosis, clubbing, or lymphadenopathy. Systemic neurological examination revealed decreased bilateral deep tendon reflexes, while the rest of the neurological examination was intact. There were no signs of meningeal irritation. The patient was able to pass urine, flatus, and stool. Initial blood test results are shown in Table. On admission, she was afebrile with a heart rate of 86 beats/minute, a respiratory rate of 16 breaths/minute, a blood pressure of 130/90, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. Various biochemical, pathological, and radiological tests were performed. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbosacral spine was unremarkable. Serum calcium, serum magnesium, and thyroid function tests were normal. Serum potassium was found to be low, and 24-hour urinary potassium was very high. Blood pH was on the lower side as per the ABG results.
test_results: Urine pH was >7.5, and fractional bicarbonate excretion was >15%.
diagnosis: Type 2 Renal Tubular Acidosis  leading to hypokalemic periodic paralysis

case_report: A 70-year-old female was admitted with primary complaints of pain and swelling in multiple joints for the past 18 months, which worsened over the last 6 months, and wounds on her fingertips for the past 2 weeks. The joint pain began gradually, affecting both small joints (wrist, interphalangeal joints) and large joints (knee, elbow, shoulder, and ankle) simultaneously. The pain was bilateral, constant, non-radiating, and associated with reduced mobility, especially at the start of movement, along with early morning stiffness, which was alleviated by medication. She also experienced bluish discoloration of her fingers when exposed to cold, which turned red and painful upon warming. Over the past 2 months, she noticed progressive tightening of her skin with reduced sweating. She reported spontaneous wounds on her fingertips without any history of trauma. General and dermatological examinations revealed dry, shiny, and smooth skin with reduced transverse creases on the back of her fingers. There was flexure contracture of the affected joints with a limited range of motion. Her face had taut, shiny skin with a loss of wrinkles, an expressionless appearance, thin lips with radial furrowing around the mouth, microstomia with a two-finger-breath mouth opening, and a pinched, beak-like nose. Nail pitting and bilateral pedal edema were observed. Her vital signs were stable. Chest examination was normal. Cardiovascular examination showed normal heart sounds without any murmurs. The abdomen was soft, non-tender, with present bowel sounds and no organomegaly. The central nervous system was grossly intact.
test_results: Her Antinuclear Antibody (ANA) titre was 3.76 (positive) and Anti-Scl-70/Anti-topoisomerase-I (3.82/++) were positive. Echocardiography performed by tissue Doppler method showed left ventricular diastolic dysfunction and mild pericardial effusion.

case_report: A 28-year-old woman came to our hospital with numbness in her left arm. Since birth, her left arm and back had been larger than the right side, and this asymmetry had increased over time, causing some functional difficulties. She experienced numbness in the left arm, which worsened when the arm was lowered. Despite being examined at various hospitals and identified with a vascular malformation, she had not received any treatment. For the past two weeks, she had severe numbness in her left arm that was not alleviated by painkillers. She often needed to lift her arm above her head to feel more comfortable. Physical examination revealed that the entire left arm and part of the left back were larger than the right side, though both arms were of equal length. The skin on the left elbow, hand, and back had a bluish tint. The affected area had multiple swollen regions of varying sizes, which were soft and easily compressible. Some hard round particles were palpable under the skin. Peripheral pulses were symmetrically palpable, and no temperature difference was noted. No abnormalities were detected in the cardiovascular system or other organs. Blood tests showed elevated D-dimer levels (> 7.65 mg/L, reference value < 0.48 mg/L), while prothrombin time (PT), prothrombin time ratios (PTr), International normalised ratio (INR) values, and platelet count were within normal ranges.
test_results: An ultrasound examination of the left arm revealed numerous subcutaneous tubular structures. These were thin-walled with an anechoic lumen, completely compressible, and colour flow was present with low velocities on Doppler ultrasound. Inside these structures were many echogenic particles with posterior acoustic shadowing consistent with phleboliths. The axillary, brachial, ulnar, and radial arteries had normal diameters, velocities, and waveforms. The accompanying deep veins did not dilate, were completely compressed, and no thrombosis was observed. The topogram film showed that the humerus, ulna, and radius on the left side were smaller than those on the right side. Multiple well-defined radiopaque lesions were distributed along the left upper limb, chest, and back. A computed tomography scan of the left arm also revealed that the diameter of the left humerus was smaller than that of the right. The arterial phase showed the axillary, brachial, ulnar, and radial arteries with normal courses and early enhancement of some veins. In the venous phase, scattered calcified round or oval particles were observed within dilated sinuous superficial veins.

case_report: Patient 1, a 43-year-old woman of Hungarian origin, has two sons: the first son is affected by a condition, while the second son, aged 10, is healthy. Her parents are reported to be unaffected but declined further DNA investigation. The woman exhibited initial symptoms in childhood, starting to walk at 15 months and consistently showing weakness compared to peers. At age 6, an examination revealed myopathic alterations. During her second pregnancy at age 30, she underwent a C-section, experienced breathing difficulties, and felt 'paralyzed'. At age 41, she had elevated creatine kinase (CK) levels and showed decreased muscle strength in the forearm and finger extensors, as well as in the back muscles. She also had proximal weakness, primarily affecting the proximal lower limb muscles. At her last examination at age 43, she was able to walk but had difficulty running. She reported frequent falls, difficulty keeping her legs elevated, or rising from the floor, and needed to use the handrail to climb stairs. She had a reduced forced vital capacity (FVC) of 57% and experienced difficulty with speech and swallowing. There was no cardiac involvement or cognitive impairment.
test_results: Electromyography (EMG) was performed at age 6 and myopathic alterations were found. At age 41, she had elevated creatine kinase (CK). She has reduced forced vital capacity (FVC) on spirometry (57%). Muscle strength graded by Medical Research Council (MRC) scale showed severe muscle weakness of triceps and deltoid (2/5), neck flexors 3/5, neck extensors 4/5, biceps 4/5, wrist extensors 4/5 and pectoralis 3/5. In lower limbs, quadriceps and ileo-psoas had 3/5 score, semitendinous and semimembranous 4/5 and tibial anterior 3/5.

case_report: A 37-year-old male presented with a history of imbalance and numbness in the hands and feet beginning at age 18. Over time, the numbness improved, but the imbalance worsened. Muscle weakness in the hands and feet increased, particularly affecting the writing hand. Speech disturbance began approximately 6-7 years ago. In the past 2-3 years, he required unilateral aid for walking due to an increased risk of falls. Similar symptoms were reported in his brother, a female and male cousin, and his niece. Neurological examination showed dysarthric speech, mild effacement of the left nasolabial fold, diffuse weakness and atrophy in the legs, and mild distal atrophy in the hands. Deep tendon reflexes were absent in both upper and lower extremities. Moderate dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia were observed. Despite using a unilateral walking aid, his gait was ataxic. Joint-position sense was impaired in the toes, and plantar reflexes were absent bilaterally. Examination also revealed mild thoracic scoliosis, pes cavus, and hammer toes. Routine hematological and biochemical investigations were normal. There were no clinical symptoms of cardiac disease, and ECG results were normal.
test_results: In the electrophysiological studies, sensory action potentials were absent in the sural, superficial peroneal, median, and ulnar nerves. Median nerve conduction velocity (NCV) was 38.7 m/s, terminal latency (TL) was 4.3 ms, and F latency was 36.5 ms. Ulnar NCV was 33.45 m/s, TL was 4 ms, and F latency was 37.3 ms. Peroneal NCV was 27.3 m/s, TL was 6.2 ms, and F latency was 68.5 ms. Tibial NCV was 25.4 m/s, TL was 6.55 ms, and F latency was 64.4 ms. Brain MRI scans revealed an image of arachnoid cyst approximately 25 mm in diameter in posterior vermian area.

case_report: A 16-year-old male presented to the Oral Medicine unit with pain and swelling in the right and left posterior mandibular region for two weeks. The patient's medical and family history were unremarkable. General examination showed frontal bossing, a wide nasal bridge, hypertelorism, and palmar and plantar pits. The facial profile was asymmetrical due to swelling on the right side of the face, with normal skin temperature over the area. Intraoral examination revealed an irregular, ill-defined swelling with bony hard consistency, expanding the lingual and buccal cortex on the right side of the mandible. Blood tests, including CBC, Hb, BT, CT, ESR, serum calcium, phosphorus, and alkaline phosphatase, were all within normal limits. A panoramic radiograph showed four well-defined radiolucencies. A chest radiograph indicated bifid ribs. Cone beam CT scan demonstrated expansion of the buccal and lingual cortical plates, perforation of the lingual cortical plate, and a horizontally impacted mandibular permanent left second molar.
test_results: The histopathologic examination of the enucleated tissue demonstrated features suggestive of a keratocystic odontogenic tumor (KCOT).

case_report: A 35-month-old boy, previously in good health, came to the emergency department with a history of low-grade fever, runny nose, and abdominal pain. There was no history of recurrent chest infections, bone pain, weight loss, or fatigue. Physical examination revealed decreased breath sounds over the posterior aspect of the left lower chest zone. A chest X-ray showed a large cystic lesion in the left lower lobe. No prior chest X-rays were available for comparison. The patient was referred to a pediatric pulmonology clinic. A chest computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a multiseptated large cystic lesion within the left lower lobe with multiple solid nodules. Enlarged lymph nodes were also observed in the left paratracheal region, with the largest lymph node measuring 10 mm. Surgical resection of the lesion was performed via left lower lobectomy through a left thoracotomy. A large cyst measuring 8 × 8 × 10 cm was found within the left lower lobe, adhering to the left hemidiaphragm, but there was no evidence of invasion into the chest wall or diaphragm.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the mass revealed multiloculated cystic and solid components containing atypical rhabdomyoblasts with diffuse cytoplasmic expression of desmin and patchy nuclear expression of myogenin. One of the excised lymph nodes showed metastatic cells.

case_report: A 17-year-old female presented with significant nearsightedness and worsening vision. She measured 147 cm in height and weighed 50.6 kg. X-ray images of her hand showed short fingers and short metacarpal bones. Initial uncorrected visual acuity (UCVA) was 2/200 in both eyes, while best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/50 (-sph 20.50 -cyl 3.00 Ax 180) in the right eye and 20/40 (-sph 16.00 -cyl 6.00 Ax 30) in the left eye. A-scan biometry indicated axial lengths of 23.65/23.30 mm for her eyes. She had undergone bilateral laser peripheral iridotomies two years prior. Despite this, her initial intraocular pressure (IOP) was 26/22 mmHg as measured by Goldmann applanation tonometry. Slit lamp examination before pupillary dilation revealed edematous corneas, extremely shallow anterior chambers, open peripheral iridectomy, and contact between the iris and cornea or lens. After pupillary dilation, IOP decreased to 22/19 mmHg due to ciliary muscle relaxation. Further slit lamp examination showed bilateral superonasal subluxation of the crystalline lens, with the lens equator and zonules visible within the pupil. Central corneal edema was noted due to the anteriorly dislocated lens touching the corneal endothelium. Specular microscopy showed decreased endothelial cell counts (743/675 cells per mm2) and hexagonality (33/0%), with increased central corneal thickness (672/712 µm) measured by ultrasonic pachymeter. Rotating Scheimpflug camera examination revealed an increased anteroposterior diameter of the lens (5200/5020 µm), a hypoplastic ciliary body, elongated and stretched zonules, and the anteriorly dislocated lens touching the central corneal endothelium. Ultrasound biomicroscopy showed a steep anterior lens curvature, angle narrowing, contact between the iris and cornea or lens, a hypoplastic ciliary body, and elongated zonules.
test_results: Chromosomal analysis revealed 46, XX, inv (15) (q13qter).
diagnosis: Weill-Marchesani Syndrome  with inversion of chromosome 15

case_report: A 55-year-old male visited the outpatient department with complaints of jaundice for 15 days, a weight loss of approximately 2 kilograms over the same period, and generalized weakness for 15 days. The patient was alert and oriented to time, place, and person. Vital signs included a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation at 98%, blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg, and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15/15. Random blood sugar was measured at 153 mg/dl. The patient reported a history of dark-colored urine. Physical examination revealed pallor, but no signs of icterus, cyanosis, clubbing, lymphadenopathy, or edema. The patient denied experiencing abdominal pain, constipation, loose stools, fever, backache, or respiratory symptoms such as cough or breathlessness. The patient had no known history of chronic conditions such as diabetes mellitus, hypertension, tuberculosis, or bronchial asthma, and no significant surgical history. Additionally, the patient was not known to have Hepatitis B or HIV. On palpation, hepatomegaly was noted.
test_results: MRCP reveals the biliary hilar butterfly-shaped infiltrating neoplastic mass lesion which causes the gross dilatation of right and left hepatic ducts resulting in dilatation of intra-hepatic biliary radicles which indicates Type IV Bismuth. USG whole abdomen reveals mild hepatomegaly with the possibility of neoplastic lesion involving biliary hilum and congestive heart defect (CHD) causing obstructive dilatation of intrahepatic biliary radicals (IHBR). CECT Grossly dilated IHBR, right and left hepatic ducts with no obvious hepatic or hilar mass lesion periductal infiltration or intraductal cholcarcinoma were observed.

case_report: A 63-year-old woman experienced a sudden onset of severe difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids, along with an inability to swallow saliva, which worsened over a week and necessitated the use of a nasogastric tube. This difficulty was accompanied by increasing hoarseness of voice, without pain during swallowing, noisy breathing, or pain in the throat or neck. Three days prior, she had developed pain in her left ear, which progressed to swelling and redness, sparing the earlobe, and did not improve with amoxicillin. She also reported mild blurred vision without eye pain or redness. She did not experience hearing loss, dizziness, headache, sensitivity to light, or other neurological symptoms. There were no general or joint symptoms, and no preceding events were noted. Her medical history included long-standing limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (SSc), positive antinuclear antibody (ANA), and negative extractable nuclear antigens (ENAs) with no specific SSc-related antibodies. She had Raynaud’s phenomenon for 10 years, sclerodactyly and puffy fingers for 7 years, gastric acid reflux, and a history of joint pain. Annual echocardiogram and lung function tests had been normal. Her current medications included hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily and losartan 25 mg once daily. Physical examination showed a red, swollen left ear, sparing the earlobe, with no tenderness over the tragus or mastoid. Neurological examination revealed right-sided palatal palsy but was otherwise normal. Laboratory tests indicated an elevated C-reactive protein level of 21 mg/L (normal range 0–5), with previously normal levels, and normal kidney and liver function tests, as well as normal urine analysis. ANA was positive (titre 1:1280), with negative ENAs and ds-DNA antibody. Tests for cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody (CCP Ab), rheumatoid factor, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) were negative. Complement levels C3 and C4 were normal. Tests for HIV, hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), Influenza A and B, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and SARS-CoV-2 were negative.
test_results: Fibreoptic nasendoscopy showed left vocal cord (VC) palsy. Computed tomography (CT), axial and coronal, scan of the head showed thickening of the left pinna. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head and neck revealed bilateral thickening enhancement of the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerve complexes, just below the jugular foramen, as well as signs of left VC palsy, with enlargement of the left laryngeal ventricle and pyriform fossa, thickening of the left aryepiglottic fold and antero-medialisation of the left arytenoid cartilage.

case_report: A 32-year-old male with a history of neurofibromatosis type 2 presented with a progressively enlarging, painless swelling on the left side of the neck over the course of one year. Physical examination revealed a soft, spherical, nonpulsatile, nontransilluminant, and nontender swelling in the left anterior triangle of the neck, which was not attached to the overlying skin or underlying structures. A computed tomography (CT) scan showed a well-defined isodense, nonenhancing mass located in the left lateral aspect of the neck. The mass was positioned medially adjacent to the left lateral wall of the trachea and the esophagus, laterally adjacent to the carotid sheath, and posteriorly adjacent to the vertebral body, with no vertebral bony defects observed. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the neck revealed that the lesion appeared hyperintense on T1, T2, and fat saturation sequences, indicating a lesion with a predominant proteinaceous or hemorrhagic component. On T2 weighted axial images, the lesion exhibited a small beak-like extension towards the esophagus. During surgery, the cyst was found to be free from all surrounding structures, including the esophagus, and contained mucoid viscous secretion. Complete excision of the cyst was performed, and the patient's postoperative recovery was uneventful.
test_results: The cyst wall was lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with underlying smooth muscle bundle fibres arranged in two layers and lymphocytes in perivascular distribution.

case_report: A 23-year-old Caucasian male, employed as a printing technician, presented with a three-month history of intense palpitations and an episode of loss of consciousness during a soccer match. Witnesses reported that the patient was taken to a nearby Basic Health Unit (BHU) within five minutes, where he was found unconscious and unresponsive, with cardiopulmonary arrest in asystole confirmed by the attending physician. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation was performed for a total of 25 minutes. The patient was subsequently transferred to the local ICU and treated with induced hypothermia (32-34ºC) for 24 hours. He achieved complete neurological recovery and was discharged after five days. The patient described experiencing palpitations triggered by intense physical exertion, lasting 30-40 minutes and resolving with rest, since the age of 14. He reported two prior episodes of loss of consciousness: one at age 18 while swimming, characterized by palpitations and a rapid recovery without mental confusion or sphincter release; and another at age 19 during a soccer game, with similar characteristics. He had no other known medical conditions or family history of sudden death. He denied alcohol consumption, smoking, and the use of illicit drugs or medications. Physical examination revealed no abnormalities, particularly in the cardiovascular system.
test_results: Sinus rhythm, 55 bpm, PR interval: 130 ms, QRS: 60 ms, QTc: 349 ms, J-point to T-wave-peak interval: 220 ms.

case_report: A 34-year-old female presented with skin lesions on both lower limbs, accompanied by intense itching for the past 15 years. The lesions showed no seasonal variation and were absent in the oral cavity. No similar lesions were reported among family members. The patient had no history of diabetes or hypertension. Physical examination revealed lichenoid papules on both shins extending to the knees, which were non-tender and had mild scaling. There was no involvement of nails or mucosal areas. Laboratory investigations returned normal results.
test_results: Skin biopsy showed subepidermal bulla filled with fibrin and RBCs. Dermis showed perivascular mixed inflammatory cell infiltrate and cyst lined by stratified squamous epithelium.

case_report: A 29-year-old Chinese male presented with swelling of the face and lower limbs. On physical examination, his height was 167 cm, weight was 54.5 kg, and blood pressure was 184/110 mmHg. He exhibited slightly swollen eyelids, mild lower limb edema, and no abnormalities in the heart, lungs, or abdomen. There were no signs of xanthoma or thickening of the Achilles tendon. Laboratory examination results are available in Table. Following admission, he was administered 55 mg/day of oral prednisone.
test_results: One week later, a renal biopsy was collected and 17 glomeruli were examined under light microscope. It was found that one glomeruli was hardened, the rest were enlarged, and the capillary loops were highly dilated. Fibrosis around glomerular balloon was also observed. There was dilation of capillary loops, and thrombotic substances were found in the lumen. There was no obvious polyhemoglobin deposition in the glomeruli. Immunofluorescence microscopy showed that immunoglobulin A (IgA) was positive. Electron microscopy results showed capillary endothelial cells with obvious vacuolar degeneration and a large number of lipid vacuolar protein substances in the cavity.

case_report: The younger sister, a 6-year-old girl with a height of 108.7 cm (-1.66 SDS), was born at 37 weeks of gestation, weighing 2,100 g (-1.61 SDS); she was small for gestational age and had microcephaly. Physical examination revealed a head circumference of 43 cm (<-3 SDS) and breast development at Tanner stage II–III. Her bone age was advanced by more than 4 years. Her predicted adult height using the BP method was less than 140 cm. She exhibited features such as a bird-shaped head, microcephaly, micrognathia, and a large beaked nose. Her karyotype was 46, XX (normal female). Endocrine tests indicated central precocious puberty and subclinical hypothyroidism. Brain MRI showed a pedunculated nonenhancing mass in the tuber cinereum extending into the suprasellar cistern. She received a depot gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist (GnRHa) and recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) treatment for 4 years and 6 months for growth impairment, along with 50 μg of levothyroxine. At 11 years old, she experienced a right-slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) after slipping on the stairs and underwent surgery for fixation of the right femur head and prophylactic screw fixation of the left capital femoral epiphysis. Post-surgery, rhGH and GnRHa treatments were discontinued, and she continued with levothyroxine. At 13 years old, she had menarche, with a height of 144.3 cm (-2.0 SDS) and a bone age of 15 years. Follow-up MRI showed no significant change in the mass size. She also exhibited mild cognitive and behavioral disorders and was scheduled for further evaluation of attention and behavioral issues. The parents were healthy and nonconsanguineous, with the mother’s height at 168 cm (+1.41 SDS) and the father’s height at 174 cm (+0.16 SDS). There was no family history of dwarfism, dysmorphic facial features, or developmental delay.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing identified 2 compound heterozygous pathogenic variants of the CEP152 gene (c.2034T>G, p. Tyr678Ter* and c.314G>A, p.Trp105Ter*). These variants were inherited from their parents, confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

case_report: A 1-month-old girl was admitted to the pediatric department due to vomiting and failure to thrive (weight, 3,320 g; −1.97 standard deviation score [SDS]). She was born at 41 weeks via vaginal delivery with appropriate measurements (weight, 3,130 g [percentile 15–50], length, 49 cm [percentile 50], head circumference, 34 cm [percentile 50]). There were no complications during the neonatal period. Her family history revealed no inherited or chronic diseases, but there was consanguinity (first cousins) between her parents. During her hospital stay, the infant appeared well and physical examination showed no significant findings. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count (CBC), kidney and liver function tests, acid-base balance, and lipid profile, were within normal ranges. Urinalysis was normal and urine culture was negative. The radioallergosorbent test for cow milk protein (CMP) was negative. Barium contrast radiography showed gastroesophageal reflux in the lower esophagus, leading to the prescription of a proton pump inhibitor and an anti-reflux formula instead of a standard formula. Vomiting episodes improved during hospitalization, resulting in weight gain (28 g/day, weight at discharge of 3,520 g). One month later, she was re-admitted due to worsening vomiting and weight loss (weight, 3,440 g; −2.91 SDS). CBC, kidney, thyroid and liver function tests, lipid profile, cobalamine, folate, and iron profile were within normal ranges. Urinalysis was normal. Immunodeficiency and metabolic diseases were ruled out. Thoracic radiography, abdominal, and transfontanelar ultrasound showed no significant findings. Considering a possible non-immunoglobulin E mediated CMP allergy, the anti-reflux formula was replaced with a hydrolyzed formula, resulting in good weight recovery (58 g/day, weight at discharge of 3,850 g). At 21 months old, the child was referred to the Pediatric Gastroenterology clinic due to feeding refusal, chronic diarrhea, abdominal distension, and weight loss. There were no reports of regurgitation, irritability, hoarseness, abdominal pain, blood or mucus in stools, or other gastrointestinal symptoms. Physical examination revealed mucocutaneous pallor, a dystrophic appearance, and abdominal distension. At this time, her weight was 9,800 g (percentile 10; −1.27 SDS) and her height was 84 cm (percentile 50; 0.01 SDS). Laboratory tests identified iron deficiency anemia (hemoglobin, 11.3 g/dL; ferritin, 8 ng/mL; iron, 16 µg/dL), elevated liver enzymes (alanine aminotransferase, 104 UI/L; aspartate aminotransferase, 80 UI/L), deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins (vitamin E, 6 µmol/L; vitamin D, 13 ng/mL; prothrombin time, 53%), and low cholesterol levels (total cholesterol, 52 mg/dL; HDL-c, 13.9 mg/dL; LDL-c, 23.9 mg/dL).
test_results: The SAR1B gene sequencing confirmed a homozigosity mutation in this gene, identifying a mutation [c.83_84delTG(p.Leu28Argfs*7)]. The intestinal biopsy performed exhibited normal villi, however the enterocytes were overloaded with fat droplets. Electron microscopic examination showed enterocytes with accumulation of lipid droplets. Fecal fat quantification confirmed steatorrhea and the essential polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) were reduced.

case_report: A 33-year-old Chinese female reported a sudden onset of a para-central large scotoma in her left eye seven days after receiving the third intramuscular dose of rabies vaccine (Rabipur, Novartis) as per the standard vaccination schedule (days 0, 3, 7, 14, and 28) following a stray cat scratch. The rabies vaccine used was an embryonated-egg vaccine. She had not received any other vaccines recently and this was the first occurrence of symptoms post-vaccination. The stray cat was not available for monitoring rabies symptoms. The patient is otherwise healthy with no significant medical history or underlying conditions. Her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/20 in both eyes, with a prescription of −9.0 D for the right eye and −8.5 D for the left eye. Ophthalmoscopic examination of the left eye did not reveal any abnormalities to account for her symptoms. During follow-up, she experienced photopsia in the left eye. Visual field testing indicated an enlarged blind spot and reduced sensitivity in the superior and nasal regions.
test_results: Fundus fluorescence angiography (FFA) and autofluorescence (AF) revealed hyperfluorescence corresponding to the area of the retina in the region of ellipsoid zone abnormalities. FFA showed right eye the normal appearances in arteriovenous phase and late phase, and early choroidal background hyperfluorescence and mild diffuse leakage of fluorescein was noted in the late phase of the left eye. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrated disruptions in the ellipsoid zone of the posterior retina. Fundus AF demonstrated multiple ill-defined spots of markedly increased AF in the posterior pole.

case_report: The subject, a 57-year-old male, presented with muscular complaints. For the past two years, he experienced persistent pain in muscles and joints, particularly in the proximal muscles of the lower extremities and the hip and knee joints on both sides. These symptoms were unresponsive to mild analgesics like paracetamol and ibuprofen and were triggered by daily physical activities, though they were also present at rest. He reported left-sided tinnitus and occasional left-sided headaches. There was no history of seizures, stroke, or stroke-like episodes, and he was not on any medication. At birth, he was noted to have bilateral ptosis. At the age of 2, he underwent orchiopexy for bilateral cryptorchidism. During his school years, he had a learning disability that affected his reading and writing abilities, leading to reduced intellectual performance. No information was available regarding his developmental milestones or any formal cognitive assessments during childhood. He attended a special needs class, completed primary school, and did not pursue further formal education, later working as an unskilled laborer. On physical examination, his height was 167 cm (−2.2 SD) and his weight was 74 kg (0 SD). He exhibited a broad nasal bridge, widely spaced eyes, a prominent forehead, and a wide philtrum. His hands were small and broad with brachydactyly and interdigital webbing. Hyperextension of the proximal interphalangeal joint and flexion of the distal interphalangeal joint were noted. He had ulnar neuropathy in the left hand following a complex arm fracture. Muscle strength assessment by the Medical Research Council (MRC) was normal. There was no shawl scrotum. Ophthalmologic evaluation showed external ophthalmoplegia and ptosis, with no signs of pigmentary retinopathy, nystagmus, or renal vessel tortuosity. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the central nervous system was normal. MRI of the lower extremities did not reveal fat replacement of muscles, atrophy, or edema. Electroneurography and electromyography, echocardiography, and creatine kinase levels were all normal.
test_results: A novel hemizygous, truncating variant was detected in exon 15 of the FGD1 gene (c.2266dup, p.Cys756Leufs*19, NM_04463.3). He also carried a rare heterozygous frameshift variant in the patatin-like phospholipase domain-containing protein 2 gene (PNPLA2); (NM_020376.4) c.798del, p.(Ala267Profs*53). Muscle biopsy showed multiple COX-negative fibers and weakly stained fibers in SDH, indicating relative mitochondrial depletion. No triglyceride droplets were seen in oil red stain. He was also found to have multiple mtDNA deletions at a higher load than expected for age (mtDNA from muscle tissue). Mitochondrial complex activities for complexes I and IV were also decreased when compared to the citrate synthase activity.

case_report: A 19-month-old boy, born in March 2015, presented with multiple brown-black skin pigmentations on the face, trunk, and right leg, along with several smaller satellite lesions. He was brought to the hospital due to repeated vomiting over a period of 4 days. Physical examination revealed a round face, full cheeks, prominent forehead, widely spaced eyes, fullness around the eyes, a short nose, and an everted lower lip. The largest pigmented area was on the leg, measuring approximately 13 cm in diameter with additional measurements of (13 × 10), (8 × 6), and (4 × 2) cm.
test_results: Enhanced MRI showed hydrocephalus. The result of 6 months post-shunt MRI revealed the presence of supratentorial ventricular dilatation, brain stem volume reduction, in addition to leptomeningeal enhancement, however, no macroscopic mass was evident. Three months later, MRI showed a mass of 3 cm diameter, in the right frontal lobe. Pathological evaluation of CNS lesion, revealed that the mass was grossly dark-red to brown with the size of (4 × 4 × 2) cm. The tumor was firmly attached to the meninges. Microscopically, the tumor cells had atypical nuclei, obvious nucleoli, an increased karyoplasmic ratio, some mitoses, and remarkable necrosis, which infiltrated the brain parenchyma, accompanied with melanin deposition. The tumor cells were positively expressing the antibodies of HMB45, Melan-A, and S100. Ki-67 was positively expressed in 30% of the cells, while P53 was negative. Cytogenetic study revealed a lack of allelic deletion of P53. NRAS mutation in the third exon (codon 61), with a wild-type BRAFV600E.

case_report: The patient is a 12-month-old male presenting with distinct facial features, hearing impairment, and bone abnormalities. He was born at 38 weeks following an uncomplicated pregnancy, with a birth weight of 2.9 kg (10th percentile) and a birth length of 45 cm (3rd percentile) according to the WHO Child Growth Standards from 2006. His facial characteristics include a prominent forehead, large ears, widely spaced eyes, downward-slanting palpebral fissures, a short nose with a broad columella, thick alae nasi and septum, and a thick, everted lower lip. His primary teeth erupted at 8 months, which is within the normal range. His hands are short and fleshy, with notably hyperextensible fingers that taper from wide to narrow, ending in small terminal phalanges and nails. There are no deformities in his foramen magnum or spinal column. At 12 months, his weight is 8.2 kg and his height is 68.2 cm (<-3.17 z score, WHO). Laboratory results indicate disturbances in bone metabolism and IGF-1α levels (Vitamin D 45.2 nmol/L, IGF-1α < 25 ng/mL). He began sitting independently at 9 months and was unable to stand without support by 12 months. His intelligence quotient (IQ) at 12 months was measured at 56 using the Gesell Developmental Schedules. He exhibits difficulty in maintaining a seated position and concentrating on tasks. His auditory brainstem response (ABR) shows a threshold greater than 85 dB, indicating a hearing impairment. MRI findings reveal dilation of the bilateral ventricles and reduced cerebral white matter.
test_results: A c.2185 C > T at chrX20173554 was detected in the proband, which can cause p.Arg729Trp mutation and RSK2 instability. Subsequent analysis did not detect the same point mutation in other family members including mother, brother. This indicated that the micromutation is new but not inherited from the mother.

case_report: A 59-year-old male patient presented with a 1-month history of difficulty breathing during severe exertion, accompanied by a worsening cough and frequent throat clearing. The patient had a history of hepatitis B and chronic atrial fibrillation. He reported that he did not smoke. Physical examination results were normal. A chest X-ray showed no significant abnormalities. Pulmonary function tests indicated mild obstructive lung disease with improvement following bronchodilator administration. Echocardiography revealed an ejection fraction of 49% and mild, widespread reduced contraction of the left ventricle.
test_results: Multiple granular lesions were seen in the trachea and bronchi. Nodular areas consisting of ossified cartilaginous tissue in the subepithelial regions, with the underlying respiratory epithelium exhibiting a characteristic pattern and no atypia.

case_report: A previously healthy 2-year-old Japanese girl, the first child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents, presented with jaundice and vomiting. Growth and development were within the normal range, and no dysmorphic features were observed. Physical examination revealed hepatomegaly and jaundice. Neurologic findings were appropriate for her age. Initial laboratory results showed serum aspartate aminotransferase at 989 U/L (normal, <30), alanine aminotransferase at 1323 U/L (<30), gamma glutamyl transferase at 136 U/L (<40), total/direct bilirubin at 6.5/4.0 mg/dL (<1.2/<0.4), and immunoglobulin G at 2098 mg/dL (500 to 1280). Prothrombin time (INR) was 1.73 (0.75 to 1.15). Initial autoantibody screening, including antinuclear antibody (ANA), anti-smooth muscle antibody (SMA), and anti-liver kidney microsomal-1 antibody (LKM-1), was negative. Other causes of liver disease such as acute viral hepatitis and metabolic conditions were excluded by appropriate investigations. Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and ultrasonography showed a visible gallbladder and hepatomegaly; no choledochal cyst, bile duct dilation, tumor, or ascites was demonstrated. The patient was treated for acute liver failure (ALF) without hepatic encephalopathy. Intravenous pulse steroid therapy with methylprednisolone (pulse mPSL; 30 mg/kg/day for 3 days) was initiated 2 days after admission. Following pulse mPSL, the patient was treated with prednisolone (PSL, 1.5 mg/kg/day) and then azathioprine (AZA; 1.2 to 2.0 mg/kg/day) was added. This combination therapy improved liver function, allowing the PSL dose to be tapered to 0.15 mg/kg/day. After pulse mPSL alleviated ALF, a liver biopsy was performed. The specimen showed active interface hepatitis and a predominance of plasma cells over lymphocytic inflammation. The patient was referred to an ophthalmologist for evaluation of possible adverse effects of long-term systemic corticosteroid treatment. Best-corrected visual acuity was no light perception in the right eye and 5/20 in the left eye, with eccentric fixation and exotropia in the right eye. Anterior slit-lamp examination had no remarkable findings. A dilated fundus examination showed vascular attenuation, optic disc pallor, and retinal pigmentary changes in both eyes. Macular optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrated marked disruption of the external limiting membrane with an ellipsoid zone in both eyes, and small foveal cysts in the left eye. Scotopic and photopic electroretinograms showed no recordable responses in either eye. Ultra-widefield fundus autofluorescence examination showed a subtle ring of excessive autofluorescence in the parafoveal regions in both eyes, and ultra-widefield OCT demonstrated diffuse thinning of both retinas with loss of outer retinal structures. Serologic tests were positive for anti-recoverin antibody and negative for anti-alpha enolase antibody. Systemic evaluation including MRI, ultrasonography, and serum tumor marker determinations such as alpha-fetoprotein, carbohydrate antigen 19-9, carcinoembryonic antigen, and squamous cell carcinoma-related antigen disclosed no underlying malignancy at the age of 3 years. Since the patient had both liver and ocular involvement, an inborn error of immunity was considered.
test_results: A 400-gene panel analysis using next-generation sequencing identified a homozygous disease-causing variant in the AIRE gene (c.415C>T, p.139*). Each parent was heterozygous for the variant. The patient’s 1-year-old sister was also homozygous for the same variant.

case_report: A 22-month-old girl presented with delayed milestone achievement. The mother's pregnancy was complicated by severe nausea and a urinary tract infection. The baby was delivered at full term via caesarean section due to breech position, with a birth weight of 1800 g. Early neonatal period was marked by feeding difficulties. Subsequently, she developed abdominal distension and multiple vomiting episodes, managed as presumptive sepsis. Physical examination revealed sparse, light-colored scalp hair and reduced muscle tone. She experienced recurrent respiratory infections necessitating frequent antibiotic treatments. At 1 year of age, she had partial head control, could reach for toys, wave bye-bye, and speak single meaningful words. At 22 months, she was evaluated for developmental delay and recurrent vomiting. Anthropometric measurements showed a weight of 6.2 kg and a length of 73 cm, both below the third percentile, with a head circumference of 49.5 cm (97th percentile). Physical examination noted frontal bossing, biparietal prominence, sparse wooly hypopigmented scalp hair, and joint hyperlaxity. She was alert, active, and interacted with her parents. Hypotonia with reduced deep tendon reflexes was also noted.
test_results: Hair microscopy had shown pili torti and trichorrhexis invaginata. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain had shown tortuous vessels with mild cerebellar and cortical atrophy. Chromosomal analysis by G-banding revealed an abnormal karyotype 46, X, t(X;13)(q21;p11)[20] in all the 20 metaphases analyzed.

case_report: A 55-year-old woman was admitted with sudden onset of inability to speak and weakness in her left arm. Her medical history includes deep vein thrombosis and lung embolus two years ago, a left-sided middle cerebral artery M2 infarction with persistent mild language difficulties nine months ago, and closure of a patent foramen ovale six months ago. She was on a daily regimen of clopidogrel 75 mg and atorvastatin 40 mg. The patient had a diagnostic laparoscopy two and a half weeks prior, which revealed a tumor in the right ovary, leading to a confirmed diagnosis of ovarian cancer. She had been receiving tinzaparin 4,500 IU daily until five days before admission. Upon admission, she exhibited difficulty breathing with stridor when lying down. Neurological examination showed inability to speak, near-total facial muscle weakness with minimal forehead movement, bilateral palate paralysis, difficulty swallowing, inability to stick out her tongue, a brisk jaw reflex, slight flexion of the left elbow, pronation of the forearm, and reduced fine motor skills in both hands. Deep tendon reflexes were heightened in both upper and lower extremities. She could follow verbal commands for limb movements and communicate through gestures. Writing ability was intact without language impairment. There was no neglect or eye movement abnormalities. She involuntarily smiled when asked to whistle, could move her tongue side to side, and had nearly normal neck movement with slightly reduced strength in forward flexion. Sensory function was intact, there was no ataxia, and her gait was normal.
test_results: The initial computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain showed substance loss from an old infarction in the left frontal operculum. CT angiography was normal. The CT perfusion scan showed increased mean transit time with corresponding reduced cerebral blood flow and slightly increased cerebral blood volume in the right frontal operculum, indicating a penumbra region.

case_report: A 45-day-old female infant, the second child of non-consanguineous parents, was brought in with a 2-week history of abdominal swelling and a skin rash. There was no notable medical history related to these symptoms. The infant's older sibling had passed away at 3 months of age from an undetermined cause. The baby's growth measurements were appropriate for her age. Physical examination revealed pallor, petechiae, an enlarged liver extending 4 cm below the right costal margin, and an enlarged spleen extending 7 cm below the left costal margin. No other systems were affected. An eye examination, including the fundus, was normal. Laboratory results showed a hemoglobin level of 6.8 gm% (normal range: 11-14 gm%), a total white blood cell count of 43,900 cells/mm3 (normal range: 5000-17,000 cells/mm3) with 30% polymorphonuclear cells, 57% lymphocytes, 3% eosinophils, and 9% monocytes. Platelet count was 30,000/mm3 (normal range: 2-4.9 × 100,000/mm3). Peripheral blood smear indicated leukoerythroblastosis, and reticulocyte count was 6% (normal range: 0.1-2.4%). Liver and kidney function tests were within normal limits. Serum calcium was 9.0 mg/dl (normal range: 8.5-10.1 mg/dl), phosphorus was 3.7 mg/dl (normal range: 2.6-4.9 mg/dl), alkaline phosphatase was 370 U/l (normal range: 54-369 U/l), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was 640 U/l (normal range: 180-435 U/l). Tests for retroviral infections and TORCH titers were negative, and cultures were sterile. An abdominal ultrasound confirmed the presence of an enlarged liver and spleen. On the third day of hospitalization, the infant developed a cough, prompting a chest X-ray.
test_results: The X-ray of the skeleton showed bone in bone appearance in femur, tibia, humerus, radius, ulna, and iliac bones.

case_report: A 48-year-old Caucasian man was admitted to the emergency ward. His medical history included an episode of depression and difficulties with reading and writing. From ages 1 to 8, he experienced recurrent episodes of seizures accompanied by vomiting and loss of consciousness, previously considered febrile seizures. Ten years prior, he was diagnosed with a peptic ulcer following episodes of mild gastrointestinal bleeding. He had intermittently excluded protein from his diet. He arrived at the emergency room at 8 a.m. with complaints of headache, backache, and ear pressure since the previous evening. He had felt nauseous and vomited multiple times during the night. Later, he developed altered sensorium, prompting his wife to bring him to the hospital. Initially, he responded monosyllabically (Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) 11) but lost consciousness within 15 minutes (GCS 8). He was afebrile with stable circulatory and respiratory systems. Neurological examination revealed motor agitation, movement in all extremities, slight miosis, saccadic eye movements, and a positive Babinski sign bilaterally. Routine blood tests, including blood cell counts, electrolytes, liver parameters, intoxication screening, glucose, and C-reactive protein (CRP), were normal. Arterial blood gases showed a lactate concentration of 2.1 mmol/L and a pH of 7.5. A brain CT scan was normal. During the first 12 hours post-admission, he remained unconscious but could breathe autonomously and was circulatory stable. A lumbar puncture showed a slight increase in lactate (3.7 mmol/L) without signs of infection or inflammation. An EEG indicated suspected encephalopathy with pronounced pathological activity but no focality, asymmetry, or epileptic activity. Broad-spectrum antibiotic and antiviral treatments were administered despite no clear signs of CNS infection. Twelve hours after admission, he experienced hematemesis and respiratory instability, leading to his transfer to the ICU, where he was anesthetized and intubated. Betamethasone was administered due to concerns about a possible inflammatory lesion in the CNS. Acute MRI, including in-flow angiography, phase-contrast angiography, and diffusion series, was normal. The following morning, 24 hours after admission, the cause of unconsciousness remained unclear. The patient's sister provided crucial information, noting that the family had considered a congenital neurological disorder due to his history of seizures, cognitive difficulties, and dyslexia since childhood. They had conducted an online search using his symptoms, which suggested a potential metabolic disorder.
test_results: Our patient’s plasma ammonia concentration was therefore analyzed and turned out to be 213 μmol/L (reference level 11–32 μmol/L).

case_report: Patient 3 is a 25-year-old female with weight and body height both below the third centile. She has experienced approximately 20 fractures and uses a wheelchair. Clinical features include shortening of the lower extremities, a barrel-shaped chest, a disproportionately large head, a triangular-shaped face, blue sclera, and dental issues. Pamidronate treatment was initiated at the age of 15 years. The patient has no family history of similar conditions and has healthy siblings.
test_results: The patient was found to harbor a novel c.1667G>T (p.Gly556Val) mutation in the COL1A2 gene. The mutation was not found in the mother by Sanger sequencing.

case_report: The patient is an 8-month-old female, the second child of consanguineous parents from a small region in Tabasco, Medellin de Madero. She has one healthy older sibling. The mother received prenatal care, including four ultrasounds and five doctor visits. The patient was delivered via C-section due to oligohydramnios, with a birth weight of 3.120 kg (Z-score: -0.25) and height of 48 cm (Z-score: -0.62), weight for length 0.52, and an Apgar score of 9. She was exclusively breastfed for 5 days before developing abdominal distension and diarrhea, which increased to 10-12 liquid stools daily. At 1 month old, she was hospitalized for 8 days due to jaundice, lethargy, and severe diarrhea. Initial emergency room evaluations, including coprological and coproparasitoscopic methods, showed no abnormalities, and fecal-reducing substances were negative. Viral infections were ruled out. Tests for antibodies IgM and IgG against CMV and EBV were negative. C-reactive protein, thyroid function test, and coagulation parameters were normal. Severe dehydration was treated with IV fluids. Metabolic screening revealed elevated blood tyrosine (6.57 mg/dl, normal <4.98 mg/dl) and alpha-fetoprotein (184 ng/ml, normal 0-20 ng/ml), but normal succinylacetone levels. Subsequent tests showed normal tyrosine (46 µmol/L, normal 26-155 µmol/L) and succinylacetone levels. An abdominal ultrasound revealed a duplex kidney collecting system, and a clubfoot was diagnosed. Breastfeeding was stopped, and a partially hydrolyzed rice protein formula was introduced. Despite improvement in jaundice, bowel movements remained unchanged, leading to a switch to an extensively hydrolyzed casein formula before discharge. The patient continued to have 10-15 bowel movements per day, resulting in severe dehydration, vomiting, anorexia, and poor weight gain, necessitating a second hospitalization at 2 months old for 80 days. During this stay, another coprological study showed an acid stool pH of 5 and positive reducing substances. The patient had anemia (hemoglobin 9.6 g/dl, hematocrit 32.2%), hyperammonemia (213 µg/dl), hypernatremia (initial sodium 145 mmol/L, increasing to 152.8 mmol/L), and hypercalcemia (8.9 mg/dl). Severe malnutrition was diagnosed, and an ultrasound indicated nephrocalcinosis. Sodium bicarbonate at 7 mEq/kg/d was started for hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, elevated urinary pH, and hypokalemia. Parenteral nutrition with IV glucose/kg/minute of 6.5 was initiated due to hypoglycemia (69 mg/dl) despite enteral formula via nasogastric tube. The patient had two previous transfusions. Erythropoietin at 2,000 IU per week and 1,000 IU twice weekly, along with iron, folic acid, and complex B vitamin supplementation, was started for anemia. A positive blood culture for Klebsiella pneumoniae was treated with meropenem.
test_results: This panel allowed the identification of the NM_000343.4 (SLC5A1):c.1667T>C (p.Leu556Pro) variant. This missense mutation replaces leucine residue by proline at position 556 of the coding region of the SLC5A1 gene (exon 14 of 15) located in the single intramembrane position of the protein. The segregation analysis by Sanger sequencing confirmed the heterozygous state of both parents, and the patient's phenotype history is highly specific for a disease with a single genetic etiology.

case_report: The patient is an 8-year-old boy, born to non-consanguineous parents via an uncomplicated cesarean section at 39 weeks, with a birth weight of 3,130g, head circumference of 32cm (p3), and APGAR scores of 9 and 10 at the 1st and 5th minutes, respectively. He was exclusively breastfed until 5 months old, at which point he experienced difficulties with the introduction of complementary foods, later identified as food texture hypersensitivity. Throughout childhood, his weight and height growth were below the 3rd percentile until the age of 4. He began walking at 1 year and 3 months. Various pediatric specialists evaluated him, noting cryptorchidism, a triangular face, down-slanted palpebral fissures, megalocornea, micrognathia, anterior open bite, generalized diastema, oral motor hypotonia, and delayed tooth eruption. Dermatological examination showed xeroderma with mild eczema in the antecubital and popliteal fossae, and minimal facial fat distribution, causing a wrinkled skin appearance when smiling. He also had oropharyngeal dysphagia, gastroesophageal reflux disease, cow milk allergy, and disaccharide intolerance. Echocardiography, total abdominal ultrasonography, audiometry, and cranial magnetic resonance imaging showed no abnormalities. Genetic testing, including karyotyping and fragile X testing, returned negative results. Comparative genomic hybridization array identified two microdeletions of unknown clinical significance: 0.073Mb in 4q31.23 and 0.101Mb in 13q12.12. Maternal chromosomal microarray analysis showed no changes, while paternal analysis identified the same 4q31.23 microdeletion as the child. Plasma amino acid chromatography at 2 years of age was negative. In 2018, genetic testing revealed a heterozygous pathogenic variant in the SMARCA2 gene (NM_003070.5:C3314G>C; chr9:2110275 [GRCh 37/Hg]) of autosomal dominant inheritance. At 2 years and 5 months, the patient was noted to have autism and intellectual disability, with difficulties in communication and social interaction, limited interest in playing and eating, deficits in functional language and non-verbal communicative behaviors, irritability and crying during environmental transitions, psychomotor agitation, food selectivity, non-functional play with objects (e.g., sticks and straws), and stereotyped motor movements (e.g., flapping and walking on tiptoe). Due to persistent target symptoms unresponsive to psychosocial approaches, risperidone was prescribed. The patient continued psychiatric follow-up until 2020, when he was lost to follow-up.
test_results: In 2018, whole exome sequencing revealed a heterozygous pathogenic variant in the SMARCA2 gene (NM_003070.5:C3314G>C; chr9:2110275 [GRCh 37/Hg]) of autosomal dominant inheritance.

case_report: A 20-year-old woman reported a 1-year history of progressively enlarging white atrophic macules located on her face and upper trunk. She had a previous diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) 3 years ago and was undergoing treatment with hydroxychloroquine sulfate. Blood tests indicated normal levels of antiphospholipid, anticardiolipin, and lupus anticoagulant antibodies, while complement levels were slightly reduced. Physical examination revealed multiple 1 to 2 cm shiny white atrophic macules on the face and upper trunk.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the back showed atrophic epidermis and marked decreases in the amount of elastic fibers in the upper dermis and mononuclear cells adhering to elastic fibers. Some thrombosis of the small vessels was observed, but there were no signs of vasculitis. Elastic staining revealed a loss of elastic fibers, which was more evident in the upper dermis.

case_report: A 7-year-old Indian girl, the second child of healthy, unrelated parents, was born at full term with a birthweight of 2000 g and a length of 46.5 cm. Since birth, she has exhibited abnormal dentition, dystrophy of all 20 nails, and light-colored, sparse curly hair. At birth, both her eyelids were partially fused, which was surgically corrected at 1 month of age. Physical examination revealed hypopigmented, sparse, curled hair, absent eyebrows in the lateral two-thirds and sparse in the medial one-third, sparse eyelashes, thin lips with a short vermillion border of the upper lip, dystrophic fingernails and toenails, abnormal dentition, and bilateral syndactyly of the fourth and fifth toes. Ophthalmological, ear-nose-throat examinations, abdominal ultrasound, echocardiogram, and G-banded karyotype were all normal. There was no history of hypohidrosis, anhidrosis, heat intolerance, cleft lip, or cleft palate. The patient demonstrated normal mental and physical development. There were no other affected family members, including the patient's parents.
test_results: The microscopy of her hair shaft showed “bubbly hair” morphology.

case_report: A 25-year-old male experienced syncope after running 10 km in 28°C outside temperature. Paramedics on-site reported an initial Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) of 3, a body temperature of 41.1°C, and a blood glucose level of 3.3 mmol/l. Cool packs were applied inguinally, and 20 g of parenteral glucose was administered. The patient reported symptoms of nausea, vomiting, and a severe headache. His medical history included an autism spectrum disorder, with no other significant findings, and he was not on any medication. Upon arrival, vital signs showed a GCS of 15, a tympanic temperature of 38.6°C, a blood pressure of 129/98 mmHg, and a heart rate of 130 beats per minute. The patient was hyperventilating with a respiratory rate of 45 breaths per minute, and peripheral oxygen saturation was 98% on ambient air. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory findings included leukocyturia and haematuria on urinalysis, with a negative drug screen. Leukocyte and erythrocyte casts, as well as bacteria, were present. Electrocardiogram and chest X-ray results were normal. After rehydration with Ringer's lactate solution, the body temperature remained between 38 and 39°C. Symptomatic therapy with ondansetron was provided. Due to the presence of leukocyte casts in the urine, ceftriaxone was administered, and paracetamol and metamizole were given to manage possible concomitant fever. The patient was admitted to the general medicine ward for further observation and rehydration.
test_results: Laboratory examinations revealed acute liver injury with ASAT 6100 U/l and ALAT 6561 U/l. The CK level elevated to a peak of 15969 U/l with a slightly improved kidney function. The virus serology for hepatitis B, C, and E as well as HIV was negative.

case_report: A 19-year-old female was referred to the Department of Medical Genetics at Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Tehran, Iran in April 2015. A tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) loading test was conducted, and she was found to be BH4-nonresponsive. Informed consent was obtained from both the patient and her parents. The study received approval from the university's Ethics Committee.
test_results: PCR-Sequencing of 13 exons of the PAH gene and their flanking intron regions was used to identify any sequence variations in the patient. The patient was compound heterozygote for two variations in exons 7 & 12. The variation, c.1223G>T (p.Arg408Leu), has not been previously reported on PAHdb, db SNP, PubMed and HGMD® Professional.

case_report: A 35-year-old woman with multiple previous pregnancies was transferred to Asan Medical Center following unusual findings on lung imaging. She had been admitted to a regional tertiary hospital 10 days earlier due to abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. During the evaluation for her abdominal symptoms, an abdominal CT scan incidentally revealed a 2.7-cm nodule in the lung. A subsequent chest CT scan identified the nodule in the basal segment of the left lower lobe, characterized by a well-defined lobule. No additional nodules or active lesions were detected in the lungs. Upon admission to Asan Medical Center, her vital signs were stable, and her physical examination showed no abnormalities. Laboratory test results were all within normal ranges.
test_results: A lung needle biopsy indicated a few atypical cells that were positive for p63 and cytokeratin in a necrotic background. In 18-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography, the nodule showed a maximum standardized uptake value of 1.6 in the basal segment of the left lower lobe indicating low metabolic activity. No other significant hypermetabolic lesions were found. The follow-up chest CT performed after 1 month indicated that the mass had enlarged to 3.3×3.0 cm. No definite evidence of lymphadenopathy was seen in the hilar mediastinum. On gross examination, an ill-defined firm mass measuring 3.2×2.5×2 cm was observed. The mass was yellowish gray, firm, and granular with necrosis and an anthracotic pigment at the cut surface. Microscopic examination indicated that the mass was well-circumscribed and had replaced the normal pulmonary parenchyma. The tumor cells had a relatively uniform, mononuclear epithelioid appearance and were arranged in nests or cords. They had eosinophilic cytoplasm and irregular nuclei with prominent nucleoli. Hyaline-like materials were observed surrounding the tumor nest. Mitoses were occasionally observed. Tumor cells had positive immunoreactivity for p63, beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG), cytokeratin, inhibin, sal-like protein 4, and placental alkaline phosphatase. Immunohistochemical staining for human placental lactogen, alpha-fetoprotein, and CD30 was negative.
diagnosis: Extrauterine Epithelioid Trophoblastic Tumor of Lung

case_report: A 40-year-old woman experienced recurrent episodes of sudden loss of consciousness without any preceding symptoms, occurring while at rest. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. A resting 12-lead ECG revealed sinus rhythm with an RsR′ pattern in lead V2, a normal QT interval, and no indications of specific patterns such as Brugada or arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy. There was no evidence of early repolarization. Both echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed normal results. Exercise testing and a flecainide challenge did not reveal any abnormalities. During her hospital stay, two brief episodes of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia (VT) were documented. The initiating premature ventricular complex (PVC) had a coupling interval of approximately 280–300 ms, and the overall PVC burden was low, with fewer than 10 occurrences in 24 hours.
test_results: Baseline intervals were normal, as were anterograde and retrograde conduction. Spontaneous PVCs were not observed. Atrial and ventricular burst pacing were performed and repeated after administration of isoprenaline (5 μg/min) without arrhythmia induction. Up to 4 ventricular extrastimuli from the right ventricular apex to 10 ms above the refractory period failed to induce arrhythmia.
