Holter monitoring revealed several episodes of nonsustained polymorphic VT initiated by stereotypical PVC with a narrow QRS, qR pattern in lead V1, and left superior axis.
Orpha_name: Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation, non Brugada type

case_report: A 20-month-old boy was admitted on April 11, 2018, with a 4-day history of fever up to 39.5°C, vomiting, and diarrhea. Asymmetrical skin lesions were noted on his limbs one day before admission. He had no prior health issues, drug allergies, recent travel, or family history of immunodeficiency. He had received age-appropriate live attenuated vaccines and showed no symptoms of discomfort. On admission, he was lethargic and febrile (39.1°C); pulse rate was 155/min, respiratory rate was 56/min, and blood pressure was normal. Physical examination revealed a bulging anterior fontanelle, equal and reactive pupils, normal limb strength, and subcostal retraction. Arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2) was 100%. Fine inspiratory rales were present on auscultation. Multiple purple necrotic lesions were visible on the abdomen and right leg. Laboratory tests showed low peripheral white blood cell count (0.26 × 10^9/L), neutropenia (0.05 × 10^9/L), eosinophils (0.01 × 10^9/L), lymphocytes (0.16 × 10^9/L), monocytes (0.04 × 10^9/L), elevated C-reactive protein (CRP, 86 mg/dL), and elevated procalcitonin (49.04 ng/mL). Intravenous ceftazidime (50 mg/kg, twice a day) was started. Four hours after admission, the patient had a seizure controlled by phenobarbital (5 mg/kg, iv). Two hours later, SaO2 decreased to 86%, and he was transferred to the pediatric ICU for mechanical ventilation. One hour after ICU admission, blood pressure was 50/30 mmHg, and heart rate was 185/min. Fluid resuscitation and inotropic support were provided. Urine output was < 0.5 mL/kg/h during the 12 hours following ICU admission, and plasma albumin was 19 g/L. Colloids, including albumin, were administered intravenously, and continuous renal replacement therapy was initiated. High fever persisted with repeated seizures. Blood, skin lesion, and stool cultures taken on admission showed P. aeruginosa sensitive to meropenem and levofloxacin but resistant to ceftazidime and piperacillin. Ceftazidime was replaced with meropenem (40 mg/kg, q8h) and levofloxacin (5 mg/kg, q12h). On Day 6, white blood cell count recovered to 4.1 × 10^9/L, and CRP was 27 mg/dL, but enterococcus was found in the cerebrospinal fluid. Meropenem and levofloxacin were replaced with vancomycin (15 mg/kg, q6h) combined with meropenem (40 mg/kg, q8h). On Day 8, the patient's body temperature normalized. On Day 9, a cranial CT scan showed diffuse brain edema. Cerebrospinal fluid examination revealed protein 5.68 g/L, glucose 2.62 mmol/L (blood glucose, 7.0 mmol/L), total cell numbers 1273 × 10^6/L, nucleated cells 1238 × 10^6/L, multinucleated cells 74%, and mononuclear cells 26%. Intravenous mannitol (5 ml/kg body weight, q4h) and oxcarbazepine (5 mg/kg body weight, q12h) were given to control intracranial edema and seizures. Over the next three days, the dose of oxcarbazepine was gradually increased to a maximum of 20 mg/kg body weight. The patient was taken off the ventilator. On Day 11, the patient experienced fever and diarrhea, and P. aeruginosa was resistant to meropenem but sensitive to levofloxacin; therefore, meropenem was replaced with levofloxacin. On Day 13, the patient was transferred back to the general ward in a light coma. On Day 15, the patient's body temperature normalized, and his diarrhea greatly improved.
test_results: A hemizygous mutation (c.262G > T) in exon 4 of the X-linked BTK gene was found.

case_report: Patient 5 is a 7-year-old girl from Vietnam. Her father experienced fractures in his forearms before the age of 10. There is no additional evidence of fractures in other family members, and there is no consanguineous marriage. The mother had a full-term pregnancy of 40 weeks with good health and no history of miscarriages. The patient's birthweight was 2.8 kg (Z score −1.18, 12th percentile). Current clinical examination shows a weight of 19 kg (Z score −1.27, 10th percentile) and a height of 115 cm (Z score −1.22, 11th percentile). She has blue sclera. The patient experienced her first fracture at the age of 2 years and has had five fractures in both tibias. Mild deformities are present in the long bones of the forearms and lower legs. She is able to move normally. The patient has not undergone bisphosphonate treatment.
test_results: Ossifications of the interosseous membrane between the ulna and radius and congenital dislocation of the radial head were present.

case_report: A 74-year-old male experienced frequent episodes of lightheadedness and sensations of nearly fainting when getting out of bed and walking. He had a history of smoking 40 packs per year and had undergone radiation and chemotherapy for nasopharyngeal cancer 6 years prior. He did not have a history of diabetes or hypertension. On examination, there were notable orthostatic changes in blood pressure, measuring 168/100 mmHg while lying down and 102/44 mmHg upon standing. The remainder of his physical examination was unremarkable. Comprehensive laboratory, cardiac, and neurological evaluations were within normal limits. His symptoms persisted despite intravenous fluid administration, and normal saline infusion exacerbated his supine hypertension.
test_results: Tilt table testing showed progressive orthostatic hypotension without a significant change in heart rate. Depressor response (hypotension and widened pulse pressure response) to a small dose of clonidine.

case_report: A 27-year-old woman at 28 weeks of pregnancy presented with a widespread, itchy rash consisting of flat, merging lesions with firm vesicles and some blisters on the arms and thighs. The skin changes first appeared at 26 weeks of pregnancy on the legs and later spread to the abdomen, arms, and back. Her medical history includes one prior abortion due to sickle cell disease, with no previous occurrence of similar skin symptoms. She had been treated with methylprednisolone cream and oral cetirizine, but the skin lesions persisted.
test_results: A cutaneous biopsy showed the presence of multiple vesicles in the dermal-epidermal junction, filled by serosity and eosinophils. In the underlying dermis, a marked edema outlined a dermal-epidermal detachment, with a dense inflammatory infiltrate (predominantly with eosinophils) extending to the dermis. Direct immunofluorescence in perilesional noninvolved skin showed linear deposits of C3 at the basement-membrane zone.

case_report: A 14-year-old male arrived at the emergency department reporting pain in his left lower extremity for 5 days, specifically in the left thigh, which had intensified despite taking pain relievers. He also experienced swelling in the thigh, difficulty walking for 2 days, and numbness for 1 day. There was no history of trauma, recent surgery, medication use, or prolonged immobilization. The patient has no family history of clotting or bleeding disorders or venous thromboembolism and denies smoking or illicit drug use. He has type 1 diabetes mellitus, diagnosed at age 10, and is managed with an insulin pump. He was diagnosed with hypertension at age 9 and is on enalapril. He was born in Jamaica via normal spontaneous vaginal delivery at term and had shoulder dystocia at birth, requiring a 10-day hospital stay with a sling applied but no other interventions. His mother reported no other birth complications. Physical examination revealed significant asymmetry between the lower extremities, with tense swelling and tenderness in the left posterior thigh and calf. There was no erythema, warmth, varicose veins, or ulcers. Peripheral pulses were palpable and equal bilaterally, and the neurological exam was normal. Initial laboratory results in the emergency room showed normal complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, prothrombin time, and activated partial thromboplastin time.
test_results: A lower extremity ultrasound showed the left common femoral, left superficial femoral, and left popliteal vein were noncompressible and demonstrated no vascular flow, with intraluminal echogenic thrombus suggestive of deep vein thrombosis of the left lower extremity. The CT showed the suprarenal IVC and the hepatic segments of the IVC were patent. There was absence of infrarenal IVC. There was an anomalous course of the external iliac veins communicating with lumbar veins. There was heterogeneous material within the left common femoral vein and left external iliac vein and hypodensity within the left lumbar vein consistent with thrombus. There were prominent azygous and hemiazygous veins. The left kidney was small in size and there was compensatory hypertrophy of the right kidney.
Orpha_name: Brain malformations-musculoskeletal abnormalities-facial dysmorphism-intellectual disability syndrome

case_report: A 14-year-old male from central India arrived at our tertiary care facility with a 2-week history of persistent headache, 5 days of projectile vomiting, and neck stiffness. He experienced a single episode of generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 10 minutes. Physical examination revealed papilledema. Systemic examination indicated right-sided hemiparesis with muscle power rated at 2/5, exaggerated deep tendon reflexes, and a positive Babinski sign.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a heterogeneously enhancing mass (6.2 × 5.2 × 4 cm), located in the left lateral ventricle extending diffusely into the ipsilateral parietooccipital region with perilesional edema with a midline shift of 6 mm. There were no signs of spinal cord involvement. Magnetic resonance (MR) spectroscopy showed reduced N-acetyl-aspartate (NAA) and increased choline, with a lactate peak suggestive of a malignant mass. Histopathological examination revealed crowded and branched papillae merging to form sheets of tumor cells disrupted by areas of necrosis with tumor cells exhibiting nuclear pleomorphism (multilobulated, multinucleated hyperchromatic nuclei). Mitoses were readily identified (15–20/10 hpf). Surrounding brain parenchyma infiltration was also noted. Immunohistochemistry showed tumor cells expressing cytokeratin (focal) and P53 (diffuse) but did not express synaptophysin, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), or epithelial membrane antigen (EMA). Also, MIB-1 nuclear labeling was increased markedly, with the index being approximately 40% in areas of highest proliferative activity.

case_report: A 7-year-old boy presented to the Pediatric Department at the University of Catania, Italy, with recurrent episodes of short-duration focal seizures that began during the night. Eight days prior to admission, the child experienced a febrile episode lasting two days with a mild temperature, which was treated with paracetamol. The family history did not reveal any specific neurological disorders, and the child had no previous neurological issues. He is the first child, and his older sister is healthy. At the time of conception, the mother was 27 years old, and the father was 29. The mother reported no infectious diseases or use of drugs or alcohol during pregnancy. Fetal movements were normal, and fetal ultrasound examination was unremarkable. The child was born at term via spontaneous delivery with a birth weight of 2,800 grams, height of 49 cm, and head circumference of 35 cm, all within normal ranges. The neonatal period was uneventful, and developmental milestones were achieved on time. The parents noted that the child frequently suffered from airway infections. Vaccinations were up to date. He attended primary school with good academic performance. Upon admission, the child was treated with intravenous midazolam (0.4 mg/kg/hour) in an attempt to control the seizures, but the seizures persisted and became more frequent despite repeated intravenous midazolam treatment. Physical examination revealed no malformations. The ear, heart, respiratory tract, and abdominal organs were normal. Neurological examination showed the child was in pain with a weak voice between seizures. Patellar reflexes were notably pronounced. Fundus examination was normal. Hematologic findings, including blood count, electrolytes, plasma and urine amino acids, thyroid function tests, organic acids, plasma purine, and total cholesterol, were normal. Tests for viral infections were negative.
test_results: The EEG recording showed the presence of spike and waves particularly evident in the fronto-temporal regions. The Brain MRI was not indicative. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showed normal color, number of cells, glucose, proteins and albumin. CSF antibodies against GABA A, GABA B, LGI1, and NMDAR were negative and CSF polymerase chain reaction analyses were negative for viral agents. A new EEG showed diffuse delta-theta background.

case_report: A 47-year-old Han woman was admitted with weakness in the right lower limb and numbness in the left lower limb for over 20 days. Initially, she experienced unexplained weakness in the right lower limb. Approximately half a day later, she noticed numbness in the left lower limb along with a cold sensation. She did not report any defecation issues. An external hospital's lumbar MRI showed intervertebral disk protrusion at the S3-4 and S4-5 levels. Despite treatment for lumbar disease, her right lower limb weakness worsened, and she had difficulty walking. Her past medical history was unremarkable. Physical examination revealed stable vital signs and normal cranial nerves. Muscle power was grade 4 in the right lower limb and grade 5 in the left lower limb, with normal muscle tone in all limbs. The knee reflex was heightened in the right lower limb. Pain sensation was diminished below the left sternal angle. Proprioception and vibration sensation were reduced in the right lower limb. The right Babinski sign was positive. Routine blood tests, hepatorenal function tests, electrolyte levels, and antinuclear antibody spectrum were normal. Serum tests for herpes, CMV, and EBV DNA were negative. The CSF cell count was 1 × 10^6/L, and the protein level was 328 mg/L. CSF smear and acid-fast staining were negative. CSF culture, OB, and AQP4 antibody tests were negative. Brain MRI results were normal.
test_results: Cervical MRI indicated hyperintense and enhanced signals in the C7-T2 region.

case_report: A two years and six months old Sri Lankan girl presented with persistently low haemoglobin, white cell count, and platelet count for two weeks following a viral illness. She was born at term to healthy, non-consanguineous parents with a birth weight of 2.58 kg, after an antenatal period complicated by pregnancy-induced hypertension in the mother. The child had a large ventricular septal defect at birth, which was surgically closed at two months. She had two previous hospital admissions for respiratory tract infections that responded to standard antibiotics. Her development and immunisations were up to date. The family was from a higher middle-class background, and she had been consuming a well-balanced diet adequate in calories and proteins. She was asymptomatic without vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, or irritability. On examination, she had mild pallor but no jaundice, cyanosis, bleeding manifestations, generalised lymphadenopathy, or oedema. Her weight was 11 kg (between −1SD to -2SD), height was 85 cm (between −1SD to -2SD), and the weight for height was between median and −1SD. She did not show features of micronutrient deficiency. Abdominal examination revealed firm splenomegaly of 2 cm without hepatomegaly or other abnormalities. The cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurological systems were clinically normal. Full blood count showed haemoglobin of 9.3 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume of 72 fL, white cell count of 1.7 × 10^9/L (neutrophils-33% and lymphocytes-62%), and platelet count of 56 × 10^9/L. The blood picture revealed a mixture of hypochromic microcytic and normochromic normocytic red cells with occasional pencil cells and macrocytes. The reticulocyte count was 1%, and the direct agglutinin test was negative. Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy revealed normocellular marrow, normoblastic erythropoiesis with occasional megaloblasts, granulopoiesis with normal maturation and <1% blasts, and normal megakaryopoiesis. There were no abnormal cells. Serum ferritin was 5.7 ng/mL (normal 15–200), serum B12 was 550 pg/mL (normal 187–883), and red blood cell folate was 355 ng/mL (normal 126–651). Abdominal ultrasonography showed mild splenomegaly with a spleen length of 8.6 cm. Venous blood gas revealed a partially compensated metabolic acidosis with a pH of 7.40 and bicarbonate of 14 mmol/L. Serum sodium was 142 mmol/L, potassium was 4 mmol/L, chloride was 105 mmol/L, and the calculated anion gap was 27 mmol/L (normal 8–16). Serum lactate was 3.1 mmol/L (normal <2), and urine was positive for ketones. Plasma ammonia, creatinine, glucose, cholesterol, and transaminases were normal. Viral studies for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and human immunodeficiency virus were negative, and antinuclear antibody and lactate dehydrogenase levels were normal. Plasma amino acid profile was normal; however, urine organic acid profile revealed marked elevations of ketotic markers (acetoacetate and 3-hydroxybutyric acid) and moderate elevation of tricarboxylic acid cycle compounds (2-ketoglutarate, aconitic acid, and citric acid) during fasting as well as the fed state.
test_results: This revealed compound heterozygous variants of the SLC7A7 gene (NM_001126105.2:c.931 A > G and NM_001126105.2:c.1095 + 6T > C).

case_report: A 61-year-old woman presented with uncontrolled diabetes despite high doses of insulin and a low body mass index (BMI: 19.4 kg/m2). She had been treated with multiple daily insulin injections (5 IU/kg/day) and 2 g/day of metformin for 30 years, starting at age 29, but consistently showed poor glycemic control. From age 35, she exhibited dyslipidemia with elevated cholesterol levels and severe hypertriglyceridemia, despite intensive lipid-lowering therapy and a restricted fat diet. She also had hypertension from age 5. Additional conditions included peripheral diabetic neuropathy, nephropathy, peripheral artery disease (intermittent claudication and a right carotid endarterectomy at age 52), and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. She reported polycystic ovarian syndrome and had never conceived. Physical examination revealed lipoatrophy in the upper and lower limbs and gluteal area, facial fat, and abdominal prominence. Other findings included phlebectasia, hirsutism, and cervical acanthosis nigricans. She was underweight with a BMI of 19.40 kg/m2 (weight: 46 kg, height: 154 cm). Initial biochemical measurements showed 10% glycated hemoglobin (HbA1C), 132 mg/dL total cholesterol (HDL-C: 25 mg/dL), and severe hypertriglyceridemia at 2,919 mg/dL. Plasma leptin concentration was nearly zero (0.43 ng/mL). An abdominal ultrasound confirmed hepatic steatosis, and transient elastography indicated liver stiffness of 18 Kpa.
test_results: The genetic analysis revealed a novel heterozygous mutation in the PPARG gene (c470A > G, p. Glu157Gly, exon3).

case_report: A 53-year-old male reported a painless, gradual decrease in vision in the left eye over the past year. The patient had previously undergone successful right eye phacoemulsification with intraocular lens implantation. Examination revealed best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 20/20 in the right eye and 20/400 in the left eye. The anterior segment of the right eye showed a clear cornea, deep anterior chamber, and pseudophakia. The left eye exhibited corneal edema, Descemet's membrane folds, and guttae. The anterior chamber of the left eye was shallow (Von Herick grade I) with 360-degree iridocorneal touch, and the lens had grade II nuclear sclerosis. Applanation tonometry measured intraocular pressure at 17 mm Hg in the right eye and 15 mm Hg in the left eye. Gonioscopy indicated open angles up to the scleral spur in the right eye, while the left eye showed iridocorneal touch with peripheral synechiae from 11 to 12 o'clock. Central corneal thickness (CCT) was 525 microns in the right eye and 698 microns in the left eye. Specular microscopy of the right eye revealed polymegathism with a cell density of 876 cells per mm², a coefficient of variation of 30.6, and hexagonality of 64%. The specular image of the left eye did not freeze. Ultrasound biomicroscopy of the left eye showed a 360-degree closed anterior chamber angle with peripheral iridocorneal touch and an anteriorly pushed lens-iris diaphragm with a convex iris configuration.
test_results: Specular microscopy of right eye showed polymegathism with cell density of 876 cells per mm2, coefficient of variation was 30.6 and hexagonality was 64% and left eye the specular image did not freeze. Histopathological analysis of the host DM showed wart like lesion with thickening of the DM.

case_report: A 48-year-old female arrived at the emergency department after experiencing a fainting episode. Her medical history includes mild mental retardation, previous tobacco use, and a past hernia repair. She was not taking any medications at home. The patient reported feeling lightheaded while cooking, leading to a brief loss of consciousness and a fall. Upon regaining consciousness, she noticed a decrease in her exercise tolerance, experiencing shortness of breath after climbing one flight of stairs. She also mentioned having heavy menstrual bleeding for the past two weeks. She did not report chest pain, palpitations, sweating, swelling in the lower extremities, difficulty breathing while lying down, or sudden nighttime shortness of breath. On examination, her heart rate was 88 beats per minute, blood pressure was 113/48 mmHg, oxygen saturation was 98% on room air, and her temperature was 98.4°F. A cardiac examination revealed a 3/6 decrescendo diastolic murmur best heard at the right sternal border with radiation to the carotids. The physical exam also noted poor dental health with multiple decayed teeth and pallor in the mucous membranes, palms, and soles. Laboratory tests indicated severe iron deficiency anemia with hemoglobin at 2.9 g/dl, hematocrit at 10.7%, mean corpuscular volume at 54 fl, ferritin at 15 ng/ml, iron at 261 µg/dl, and transferrin at 218 mg/dl. In the emergency department, she received three units of packed red blood cells. A chest X-ray showed an enlarged heart, a head CT scan ruled out hemorrhage, and an abdominal/pelvic CT scan revealed multiple myomas, which were considered the likely source of bleeding.
test_results: A transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was obtained, demonstrating a thickened aortic valve with severe aortic insufficiency. Left ventricular chamber size was normal with an ejection fraction of 65%. A transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) was performed revealing an irregularly shaped mobile echodensity (1.7 cm×1.0 cm) on the aortic valve consistent with a vegetation. Also, a root abscess was present with fistula formation between the right sinus of Valsalva and the right atrium.

case_report: A 30-year-old man with no prior health issues presented with fever, chills, weakness, coughing spells, dizziness, and shortness of breath. A chest X-ray revealed bilateral lung multifocal peripheral consolidation. Testing confirmed SARS-CoV-2, and he was diagnosed with bilateral pneumonia due to COVID-19. Blood cultures showed no growth. His vital signs remained stable, and he did not require supplemental oxygen. Laboratory findings indicated pancytopenia, macrocytic anemia, and a low reticulocyte count. Hyperferritinemia was noted with a ferritin level exceeding 100,000 ng/mL. Levels of vitamin B12, iron, folate, and haptoglobin were within normal ranges, with no signs of hemolysis. The patient had ceased alcohol consumption two years prior and had no recent illicit substance use. An ultrasound-guided bone marrow aspiration and biopsy was performed five days later to evaluate the pancytopenia. The complete blood count on the day of the bone marrow biopsy showed marked macrocytic anemia (RBC 2.23 M/cumm, Hgb 8.3 g/dL, hematocrit 24.3%, MCV 108.6 fL, MCH 37.2 pg, RDW 26.0%), moderate leukopenia (WBC 2.7 K/cumm), and moderate thrombocytopenia (45 K/cumm). The peripheral blood smear indicated leukoerythroblastosis. The bone marrow aspirate and biopsy revealed a hypercellular bone marrow (85%) with marked erythroid hyperplasia and dysplasia, marked megakaryocytic hyperplasia, 13-14% blasts, and evidence of hemophagocytosis. The patient was referred to Harbor-UCLA Medical Center for further management after testing negative for SARS-CoV-2 twice.
test_results: The smears of bone marrow aspirate contained rare spicules showing marked erythroid hyperplasia and scattered blasts, without evidence of hemophagocytosis. A 500-nucleated cell count revealed the following differential: neutrophils and precursors 18.0%, erythroid precursors 58.6%, lymphocytes 7.6%, monocyte 0.4%, eosinophils 1.0%, plasma cells 1.4%, and blasts 13.0%. Dysplastic features were noted in a few erythroid precursors and some megakaryocytes. Rare dysplastic neutrophils morphologically similar to those seen in the peripheral blood smear were also found. The Prussian blue stain performed on the bone marrow aspirate smear showed adequate stainable iron stores with many ring sideroblasts (53%, 100-cell count). A flow cytometric study performed on the bone marrow aspirate showed the blasts expressed CD34, CD38, CD45 (weak), and CD117, and were negative for T-cell markers, B-cell markers, CD14 or CD64. The bone marrow biopsy sections revealed a markedly hypercellular bone marrow (90%) with marked erythroid proliferation, and increased immature cells, most of which stained positive for CD34. CD34-positive blasts represented approximately 13% of all bone marrow nucleated cells. In addition, there are many megakaryocytes of various sizes, highlighted by CD61 stain, including several micromegakaryocytes. The reticulin stain performed on the bone marrow biopsy showed mild to moderate myelofibrosis (MF 1-2/3, WHO 2017 semiquantitative grading of bone marrow fibrosis).
Orpha_name: Refractory anemia with excess blasts type 2

case_report: An 18-year-old female student has experienced necrotic lesions and vesicles in exposed areas since the age of 5, which leave asymptomatic varioliform scars and worsen during the summer. Physical examination revealed hemorrhagic/yellow crusts and erosions on the nose and ears. The dorsal surfaces of the hands were significantly affected with hemorrhagic crusts and vesicles. Additional lesions were observed on other sun-exposed areas, including the ankles and presternal region. Laboratory tests for lupus erythematosus (ANA) and uroporphyrines were normal. There is no family history of similar cases. The use of highly protective sunscreens (SPF 45) resulted in little improvement, with new lesions appearing. Topical antibiotics were administered for secondary infection.
test_results: Light microscopy showed epidermal necrosis with lymphocytic infiltration.

case_report: A 12-year-old girl presented with a 4-month history of linear and whorled inflammatory skin lesions on her trunk, legs, and arms. She had been born with congenital erythroderma and developed thickly adherent scaling at the age of one, which persisted. She was born at term following a normal pregnancy and delivery, with no notable family history. Clinical findings included growth retardation, bilateral conductive hearing loss, and a unilateral congenital cataract in her right eye. She exhibited short stature with asymmetric limb shortening, with her right arm being shorter than her left. Dysmorphic facial features included frontal bossing, a flat nasal bridge, and a depressed nasal tip. Dermatological examination revealed brown streaky hyperkeratotic plaques with thickly adherent scaling along Blaschko's lines, as well as erythematous scaling and guttate lesions on her trunk, arms, and legs. Patchy areas of scarring alopecia were noted on the frontal and temporal regions of the scalp and lateral regions of the eyebrows. Her hair was fragile, coarse, and lusterless. Blood biochemical and serological tests, as well as whole blood counts, were within normal ranges. Dorsal and lumbosacral magnetic resonance imaging showed scoliosis deformity and height losses in the left half of the T8 vertebra and the right halves of the L3 and L4 vertebrae (tethered cord).
test_results: We identified a previously reported EBP mutation, c. 440G >A (p.R147H) in the patient.

case_report: A 7-year-old girl exhibited hyperkeratotic verrucous papules arranged in a linear pattern on the sole of her left foot. These skin changes were present since birth and did not cause any discomfort. The patient had a family history of atopic dermatitis but no notable past medical history. Previous treatments with topical antifungals and salicylic acid were ineffective. Physical examination revealed unilateral hyperkeratotic papules merging into plaques, following a linear distribution along the lateral edge of the left sole.
test_results: Histopathological analysis showed columns of parakeratosis associated with scant dyskeratotic keratinocytes in the upper granular layer reminiscent of cornoid lamellae. A deep infiltrate involving sweat ducts was absent.
Orpha_name: Porokeratotic eccrine ostial and dermal duct nevus

case_report: The patient is a male infant from a consanguineous Saudi family, consisting of two healthy parents and five children (one affected male, two healthy males, one healthy female, and one deceased female). The patient presented with severe coarctation or interrupted aortic arch, patent ductus arteriosus, ventricular septal defect, gastroesophageal reflux, and glaucoma. He received treatment at the Department of Pediatric Cardiology, King Abdulaziz Medical City, Ministry of National Guard Health Affairs, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The deceased sister exhibited similar clinical features. One male sibling and the parents were carriers of the same genetic variant, while the other two children had no genetic abnormalities.
test_results: shows the chest X-ray and echocardiograms of the index patient.

case_report: A 23-year-old female, with no other health issues, visited the dermatology clinic reporting swelling and wrinkling of the palms following brief water exposure. These symptoms appeared within minutes of contact with water and resolved on their own in approximately one hour. The patient was not taking any medications, and there was no family history of similar symptoms.
test_results: Within 1 min after water exposure and before the appearance of wrinkling, the patient's palms were examined under Wood's light. It showed unique white fluorescence. Six minutes later, the patient's palm showed wrinkling and white papules.

case_report: The patient is a 4-year-old boy born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and normal vaginal delivery. He is the first child of healthy, unrelated Chinese parents, with a noncontributory family history. His motor development was normal, but his weight was lower than average for his age. Mild skin issues were noted from the first month, including erythematous lesions on the face, neck, and buttocks, which did not improve with topical steroids. At 7 months, he was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit due to deep breathing and respiratory distress. Arterial blood gas analysis showed metabolic acidosis (pH = 7.14, base deficit of –18), and serum lactate was elevated (8.89 mmol/L). He experienced a transient increase in random blood sugar (23.68 mmol/L), while blood ammonia levels were normal. Urine tests were positive for acetone. After insulin regulation, glucose levels normalized, but metabolic acidosis persisted. Elevated levels of C-3, C5-OH, propionate, and 3-MCC were found in the acylcarnitine profile and urinary organic acid analysis. The child was then given high doses of oral biotin (30 mg/d). Three days into treatment, his dyspnea significantly improved, and metabolic acidosis was resolved. A follow-up after 2 months showed significant improvement in weight gain and skin condition. Currently, at 4 years old, he continues on biotin (5 mg/d) and has no developmental delays.
test_results: Genetic analysis revealed that the mutant allele was c.1088T > A(p. V363D). The variants c.1484T > G(p. L495∗) and c.835G > T(p. E279x) are likely pathogenic factors.

case_report: The patient is a 21-month-old girl who was seen at Myelin Disorders Clinic at Tehran University of Medical Sciences due to delays in motor and language development. She is the sixth child of consanguineous parents, born at 40 weeks gestation via an uneventful vaginal delivery, with a birth weight of 3000 g (Z-score -0.5 SD) and a head circumference of 33 cm (Z-score -0.7 SD). The mother has a history of two unexplained abortions. One sister has behavioral issues, and one brother has stuttering speech. The patient has not fully achieved normal developmental milestones. At her current age, she has acceptable social interactions, follows one-step commands, requires significant support to sit, and can make sounds, but her speech is limited to sound expressions. Her mother reported feeding and swallowing difficulties. During the last clinical examination, she had a white subconjunctival lesion on the lateral aspect of the left eye, diffuse melanosis on the back, atrophy of buttock muscles, strabismus, pendular nystagmus, truncal hypotonia, pes planus, and hyporeflexia with +1 deep tendon reflexes (DTRs). Her Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) score was 3/5. Her weight was 7 kg (less than 3rd centile, Z-score -3.8 SD) and head circumference was 43.5 cm (Z-score -2.34 SD). Basic metabolic tests, including plasma lactate level, serum ammonia, Tandem Mass Spectroscopy (MS/MS), urine organic acid analysis, and creatine kinase, were all normal.
test_results: At 16 months of age, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed delayed myelination, along with the presence of hyperintensity in the globus pallidus. Additionally, there was observed atrophy of the cerebellar hemisphere and vermis. We ended up with a novel homozygous frameshift 2 nucleotides deletion in the ATCAY gene [NM_033064.5:c.883_884del, p.(Lys295AspfsTer52)]. The identified variant was confirmed by the segregation analysis in her parents. It was classified as pathogenic based on the ACMG recommendations and considered as the cause of the disease in the proband.

case_report: A 12-year-old male with no notable birth or medical history presented with concerns about lower abdominal distention and had reduced his food intake over the past 3 months. He engaged in excessive exercise relative to his food intake. Despite significant weight loss, he expressed concerns about his abdominal size. During the initial consultation, he was observed to be very lean with a body mass index (BMI) of 11.5 kg/m2 and had a heart rate of approximately 40 beats/min, indicating sinus bradycardia. Enteral nutritional supplements were administered to improve his weight. Seven days after the first visit, he was emergently hospitalized due to disorientation. On admission, his height was 145 cm, weight was 20.9 kg (BMI: 9.9 kg/m2), and he presented with impaired consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) E3V4M6), bradycardia (heart rate ~40 beats/min), and slow breathing (respiratory rate ~10 cycles/min). Blood gas analysis and blood tests showed hypercapnia, hypoglycemia, and elevated levels of creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, and transaminases. His movements were slow but not paralytic, and his cranial nerves were intact. Due to chronic hypoglycemia and dehydration, rapid correction was avoided to prevent complications such as refeeding syndrome, heart failure, pleural effusion, and ascites. Hypoglycemia and dehydration were corrected slowly (glucose infusion rate: 0.6–1.0 mg/kg/min; water: 20 mL/kg/day). On the second day of admission, he developed further impaired consciousness (GCS E1V1M1) and low blood pressure, necessitating transfer to the intensive care unit (ICU). After correcting hypoglycemia and dehydration, his consciousness improved, and he was transferred to the general ward on the third day. On the fourth day, hepatic transaminases peaked with aspartate transaminase (AST) at 4,782 U/L and alanine transaminase (ALT) at 2,265 U/L, along with coagulopathy (prothrombin time (%): 28%). Liver support therapy, including glucose infusion and enteral nutrition, was provided, leading to gradual improvement in AST and ALT levels.
test_results: T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images showed a localized high-signal area from the cortex to the white matter of the fusiform gyrus to the parahippocampal gyrus near the left hippocampus. The cortex in high-signal lesions is thickened, the boundary between white matter and cortex is indistinct and localized, and there is no tendency for invasion into the surrounding white matter. There was no contrast enhancement.
Orpha_name: Isolated focal cortical dysplasia type II

case_report: A 17-day-old black female neonate was admitted to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) due to cholestasis with acholia. She was the first child of healthy non-consanguineous parents and had minimal prenatal care. Born at 35 weeks and 5 days, she weighed 1590g (below the third centile). Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes respectively. Jaundice appeared from the second day, and acholic stools were occasionally noted. Abdominal ultrasonography indicated a possible choledochal cyst and atresia. Hepatobiliary scintigraphy was performed but yielded inconclusive results. The patient also experienced respiratory distress requiring oxygen therapy and hypertension treated with propranolol from day 14, with a normal echocardiogram. On examination, she was small for gestational age (length 39.5cm, weight 1545g, head circumference 28.5cm, all below the third centile). Her blood pressure was elevated (118/90mmHg, above the 95th centile). She exhibited marked hypotonia, well-defined café-au-lait spots following Blaschko’s lines on her back and lower limbs, a heart murmur on cardiac auscultation, and a palpable liver edge 2.5cm below the costal margin. Laboratory findings confirmed cholestasis and abnormal liver function: total bilirubin 10.8mg/dL (normal <1mg/dL); conjugated bilirubin 9.5mg/dL (normal <0.3mg/dL); aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 211U/L (normal <34U/L); alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 623U/L (normal 12 to 78U/L); gamma-glutamyltransferase (γGT) 1219UI/L (normal <38UI/L); total cholesterol 343mg/dL (normal <190mg/dL); triglycerides 240mg/dL (normal <150mg/dL); total serum proteins, albumin, activated partial thromboplastin time, prothrombin time, and fibrinogen were normal. Further investigations excluded common causes of cholestasis (including metabolic diseases screened neonatally, α1-antitrypsin deficiency, and cystic fibrosis). Due to persistent cholestasis, a repeat abdominal ultrasonography was performed, showing no choledochal cyst and a normal biliary tree but revealing bilateral serpiginous adrenal hyperplasia.
test_results: The activating mutation c.602G> A, leading to p. Arg201 to His, was identified in mosaic.

case_report: A 63-year-old male presented with increasing abdominal swelling, weight loss, and general malaise. He had been on oral anti-diabetic medication for the past 5 years, with no other significant medical history. Upon admission, his general condition was moderate. Vital signs included a temperature of 36.8℃, heart rate of 120/min, blood pressure of 100/60 mmHg, and respiration rate of 16/min. Physical examination revealed bilateral rales, tachycardia, deeper heart sounds, and ascites without splenomegaly. No peripheral lymphadenopathy was observed. Laboratory results showed hemoglobin at 10.5 g/dL, hematocrit at 31%, leukocytes at 9,600/mm3, platelets at 210,000/mm3, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 86 mm/h. Peripheral smear indicated 60% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 30% lymphocytes, 8% monocytes, and normochromic, normocytic red blood cells. Additional lab tests revealed blood glucose at 229 mg/dL, total protein at 5.3 g/dL, and albumin at 3.2 g/dL, with normal liver and renal function tests. Hepatitis markers and anti-HIV were negative, but Epstein-Barr virus immunoglobulin G was positive. Serum protein electrophoresis was normal but showed low albumin levels. Tumor markers were negative, but cancer antigen-125 was > 500 U/mL. Chest radiography showed left pleural effusion. Echocardiography was normal except for minimal pericardial effusion. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed massive ascites, and upper gastrointestinal endoscopy identified an active gastric ulcer in the cardia, with biopsy indicating regenerative hyperplasia. Computed tomography of the thorax and abdomen showed bilateral pleural effusions and significant ascites, with no organomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Ascitic fluid analysis was exudative, and direct microscopy revealed atypical lymphomononuclear cells without tuberculous bacilli. Adenine deaminase level was < 200 U/L. Bone marrow biopsy was normal but hypocellular. During follow-up, thoracentesis and paracentesis were performed due to progressive dyspnea.
test_results: A cytological analysis of both fluid materials displayed a high grade malignant lymphoma. The immune phenotype analysis by flow cytometry was consistent with B-cell predominant NHL with kappa monoclonality.

case_report: A 17-month-old girl presented with recurrent episodes of pallid breath holding. Her mother reported a history of recurrent malodorous and black-colored stools during infancy. The patient was born to consanguineous parents with a birth weight of 2950 g (<3rd percentile) and a birth height of 48.5 cm (25th–50th percentile). She experienced respiratory failure at birth and required care in the newborn Intensive Care Unit. There was a delay in motor milestones; she achieved head control at 4 months and could sit independently at 10 months but had not yet developed the ability to walk. At the time of evaluation, her weight was 7500 g (<3rd percentile) and her height was 71 cm (<3rd percentile), indicating postnatal onset short stature. Physical examination revealed pallor, tachypnea, sinus tachycardia, and dysmorphic features such as micrognathia, narrow palpebral fissures, a flat face with a low hairline, low-set ears, full cheeks, a short neck, and pectus carinatum. Additional findings included an umbilical hernia, joint contractures, axial hypotonia, weakness of extremities with absent deep tendon reflexes, muscle stiffness, and hypertrophy of limb muscles. Laboratory tests indicated severe iron deficiency anemia (hemoglobin 6 g/dL, hematocrit 20%, mean corpuscular volume 49 fL, iron 1 µg/dL) and mildly elevated creatine kinase levels (365 U/L). Hemoglobin electrophoresis and other laboratory studies were normal. Chronic gastrointestinal bleeding was identified as the cause of the anemia. Endoscopy was halted due to respiratory arrest caused by anesthetics. Repeated fecal occult blood tests were positive. Echocardiography, abdominal ultrasonography, electroencephalography, and chromosomal analysis showed normal results. Radiological studies identified multiple skeletal deformities, including bowing of the tibias and hip dislocation.
test_results: Normal nerve conduction studies with repetitive myotonic discharges on EMG.

case_report: A 38-year-old female was transferred to the emergency department (ED) from a primary care clinic due to recurrent episodes of rhabdomyolysis. Upon arrival, she exhibited mild dyspnea, severe muscle pain, fatigue, low-grade fever, transient myoglobinuria, and continuous involuntary cramping in the lower limbs. Her medical history indicated that she had engaged in vigorous physical activity for three months, preparing for a marathon, completing approximately 40 miles weekly with three days of rest each week. No family history was disclosed. She was treated with IV analgesics, reported symptomatic improvement, and was discharged with oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for five days. The next day, she returned to the ED with worsening dyspnea at rest and a fever of 40.2°C, managed with parenteral NSAIDs. She was later admitted to the nephrology department with acute kidney injury. A review of systems revealed nasal congestion, malaise, weakness, and muscle pain predominantly in the distal muscle groups. Immunological markers including antinuclear antibodies (ANA), anti-DNA, cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasm antibodies (cANCA), and blood cultures were negative. Antibodies against atypical pathogens and respiratory viruses (Pneumoslide) were positive for immunoglobulin M (IgM) Rhinovirus. Laboratory results showed increased levels of fibrinogen and C-reactive protein associated with leukocytosis, creatine kinase (CK) levels of 90,000 IU, creatine kinase myocardial band (CK-MB) of 50 IU, peak myoglobin of 250,000 IU, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) of 2,300 U/L. The two-step serologic approach for Lyme was negative. Urinalysis showed high levels of myoglobin; urine culture was sterile. The patient’s initial serum creatinine was 5.4 mg/dL. She was initially treated with IV fluids and later required plasmapheresis and hemodialysis due to refractory acute kidney injury (AKI), cardiomyopathy volume overload, and impending respiratory insufficiency. The first hemodialysis session was performed through a temporary femoral venous catheter in the emergency department-intensive care unit (ED-ICU). At 36 hours, the patient required non-invasive ventilatory support due to worsening hypoxemic respiratory failure. Capillary blood glucose monitoring revealed only mild hypoglycemia. Renal ultrasound showed normal-sized kidneys with no abnormalities. Chest X-ray did not show pulmonary congestion, cardiomegaly, or other pathological findings. A point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) performed at the ED showed a slight enlargement of the left ventricle (LV) without organomegaly or other pathological data. An echocardiogram revealed left atrial enlargement and left ventricular eccentric hypertrophy with an LV ejection fraction of 45%. On admission, CK peaked at 90,000 U/L, which progressively declined to 200 U/L upon discharge. Serum potassium peaked at 5.4 mEq/L on day 1 with a gradual decrease. Following admission, a 10% glucose infusion was started at 2 mL/kg/hour. Fluid therapy with lactated Ringer’s (LR) was initiated 24 hours later at 80 mL/hour. The patient did not present with electrolyte disturbances prior to or after initiating fluid therapy. During the hospitalization period, five hemodialysis sessions were completed. Renal replacement therapy was discontinued on day 8 following a favorable clinical progression and gradual reduction in serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen and the normalization of urine output after experiencing the anuric and polyuric phases of AKI. The patient received 2 mL/kg/hour of 10% dextrose (200 mg/kg). A total of 16.2 L of lactated Ringer’s was administered upon the completion of therapy, with a sufficient reduction in CK values and clear clinical and renal function improvement.
test_results: Acylcarnitine analysis revealed peaks of C12:0 (lauroylcarnitine), C16:0 (palmitoylcarnitine), and C18:1 (oleoylcarnitine). Molecular genetic testing yielded a mutation with the change of the DNA nucleotide c.1342T>C (exon 4) and modification in the p.Phe448Leu protein.
Orpha_name: Carnitine palmitoyl transferase II deficiency, myopathic form

case_report: A one and a half year old girl, born to parents who are not related by blood, presented with multiple raised lesions on both cheeks that had been present for one year. These lesions were gradually increasing in number. Dermatological examination showed multiple erythematous to hyperpigmented and skin-colored papules confined to both cheeks. General and systemic examinations were normal. Her physical and mental development were appropriate for her age. Routine laboratory tests, including serum cholesterol and triglycerides, were within normal limits.
test_results: Skin biopsy from one of the papules showed a normal epidermis and sheets of foamy macrophages, a few histiocytes, and occasional eosinophils in the dermis. Immunohistochemistry of the biopsy specimen showed CD68 positivity and CD 1a negativity.

case_report: The patient is a 34-month-old right-handed Hamitic boy who experiences intermittent episodes of intense pain, warmth, and redness in both feet. These episodes last from minutes to hours and began when he was 2 years old. The symptoms are symmetrical, confined to the feet, and do not extend beyond the ankle joints. They are triggered and exacerbated by physical activity and exposure to warm temperatures, such as covering his legs with blankets, and are alleviated by cooling measures like cold water. There is no family history of similar conditions, no history of drug intake prior to the onset of symptoms, and no history of blood transfusions. The patient appears well with no signs of acute illness. Multiple physical examinations have shown normal vital signs, no pallor, jaundice, or cyanosis, and no organomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Both feet are red and warm.
test_results: A skin biopsy was performed, showing nonspecific changes in the form of numerous telangiectatic blood vessels in the capillary dermis associated with sparse perivascular mononuclear cell infiltrate and some vessels showed swelling of the endothelial lining. The intimal thickening and thrombi seen in secondary EM were lacking.

case_report: An eight-year-old boy was seen at the endocrinology clinic of the Kashan University of Medical Sciences. He weighed 15.5 kg (3.5 standard deviations below the mean) and had a height of 92 cm (7 standard deviations below the mean). At birth, he weighed 3.65 kg (50th percentile) and had a crown-to-heel length of 47 cm (10th percentile). During the neonatal period, he experienced abdominal distention and vomiting, and a biopsy confirmed Hirschsprung disease. Physical examination revealed severe short stature, disproportionate short-limbed dwarfism, short and puffy hands, and genu varum deformity. The sternum was notably prominent. Joint hyperextensibility was not observed. His scalp hair, eyebrows, and eyelashes were fair, very fine, and sparse. No nail dysplasia or dental abnormalities were found. Intellectual development was appropriate for his age, and there was no clinical evidence of immunodeficiency. He developed hypothyroidism at the age of 6 years. A 3-mm kidney stone was detected at age 3, which grew to 8 mm by age 8 and was treated with lithotripsy. Vesicoureteral reflux was identified in his voiding cystourethrogram. Complete blood count, electrolytes, and renal function tests were normal. Several urinalysis samples showed sterile pyuria, possibly related to the vesicoureteral reflux or renal stone. Microscopic stool examination showed no fat globules. The patient was evaluated for celiac disease and cystic fibrosis during infancy, both of which were negative.
test_results: Skeletal X-rays revealed typical metaphyseal dysostosis, including widening, cupping, and defective mineralization in the metaphysis of the tubular bones.

case_report: In January 2020, a 24-year-old Chinese woman presented with persistent excessive thirst and frequent urination for nearly 6 months. Six months prior, she was admitted for a headache, and MRI revealed pituitary apoplexy with a weakened signal in the posterior pituitary. She underwent transnasal transsphenoidal resection for a pituitary mass, and pathology findings indicated a pituitary adenoma. Post-surgery, she was administered methylprednisolone 40 mg once. Her cortisol levels were 143.13 μg/L (8 am), 47.12 μg/L (4 pm), and 5.93 μg/L (12 pm). ACTH levels were 33 pg/mL (8 am), 18.8 pg/mL (4 pm), and < 5 pg/mL (12 pm). A 24-hour urine cortisol level was 388 μg. Gonadotrophins and thyroid hormones were within normal ranges. She subsequently developed severe excessive thirst and frequent urination, urinating approximately every 2 hours with a total daily volume of 10 liters. She did not experience backache, hand tremors, blurred vision, lower limb puffiness, or weight loss. Laboratory results showed plasma osmolality of 301.00 mOsm/L, urine specific gravity of 1.002, potassium level of 4.17 mmol/L, and serum sodium level of 138.5 mmol/L. Initial treatment with oral desmopressin, pituitrin, and potassium chloride was ineffective. She was later started on hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) and desmopressin was gradually reduced and stopped, which alleviated her symptoms. She was discharged with HCTZ twice a day but discontinued the treatment on her own, leading to readmission for frequent urination. Physical examination revealed blood pressure of 108/71 mmHg, pulse rate of 121/min, and dry skin; the rest of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory results showed urine specific gravity of 1.002, serum sodium level of 134.3 mmol/L, and plasma osmolality of 338.00 mOsm/(kg·H2O). Urinary ultrasonography scans were normal. A water deprivation test showed an initial urine specific gravity of 1.006, plasma osmolality of 281 mOsm/L, and blood pressure of 124/72 mmHg. Two hours after AVP injection, plasma osmolality was 299.00 mOsm/(kg·H2O) with unchanged urine specific gravity.
test_results: The results suggested a heterozygous mutation in arginine vasopressin receptor type 2 (AVPR2) genes c.914dupC (p.Pro306fs).

case_report: This report concerns a ten-year-old Mauritanian female child, who was referred by the orthopedics service for assessment of fragility fractures. She was born to consanguineous parents. Congenital blindness was identified at birth. She experienced five fractures (humerus, wrist, ankle, and femur) following a fall from standing height, starting at the age of 5 years. Since the femur fracture, she has been unable to walk. Clinical examination revealed microphthalmia, corneal opacity, dorsal kyphosis, curvature of the tibias, and lower limb length discrepancy. Her weight was 15 kg and height was 117 cm, both significantly below the second percentile for her age. Neurological examination was normal. Laboratory results showed normal levels of serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, creatinine, and 25 OH vitamin D3.
test_results: Radiographs showed diffuse bone demineralization, multiple vertebral fractures, and platyspondyly. Bone mineral density (BMD) revealed a Z score of −5.5 at the spine.

case_report: This case involves a 17-year-old girl from Ardebil, Iran, who has been hospitalized four times. At birth, she appeared normal except for congenital malformations of the great toes. Her parents were not related, and there is no family history of genetic disease. She was born via normal vaginal delivery with a normal birth weight. Throughout her growth, her weight remained at the minimal normal range without high levels of physical activity. At age 11, she was first hospitalized due to the onset of reduced motor function in the shoulders, back, neck, and left knee following trauma. MRI of the right shoulder was normal, but a Tc-99 bone scan showed inflammatory response in the left shoulder and right knee, along with some changes in the left shoulder. Muscle enzyme levels were approximately 1.5 times higher than normal, while other hematologic, hormonal, and biochemical tests were normal. She was treated with low-dose ibuprofen and etidronate (200 mg) every alternate day. At age 16, she was hospitalized again with more severe symptoms, including swelling and stiffness in the right lower limb, and pain in the thigh and right leg. A chest CT scan revealed severe scoliosis, MRI showed a hyper signal lesion in the soft tissue of the lower limb muscles, and an x-ray indicated bone formation in the posterior thigh. Three months later, she was hospitalized with restrictions in the glenohumeral joints on both sides, as well as in the right hip, knee, and ankle, and the left knee. Five months later, at age 17, she was hospitalized for the fourth time due to pain behind her right thigh and was treated with medication and physiotherapy.
test_results: Sequencing showed the presence of c.617G>A heterozygous mutation in the patient and absence in her immediate relatives.

case_report: A 60-year-old female patient presented with a one-year history of gaining 15 kilograms, mainly in the face and thoraco-abdominal region, along with increased urination and thirst, and pain in the right hip. Upon admission, physical examination revealed a height of 150 centimeters, a weight of 72 kilograms, a waist circumference of 120 centimeters, and a blood pressure of 170/90 mmHg. Capillary blood glucose was measured at 2.19 g/l. The patient exhibited clinical signs consistent with hypercorticism and reported hip pain during movement, though without any restriction in the range of motion.
test_results: The hormonal balance found a urinary free cortisol (UFC) level raised to 4 times the normal, plasma adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) was at the lower limit of the normal value at 14 µg/ml (10-60). The adrenal CT scan revealed a well-defined right adrenal mass measuring 46 x 33mm, spontaneously hypodense taking the contrast product heterogeneously, the left adrenal was normal non-hypertrophic. The patient had diabetes, dyslipidemia, hyperuricemia, high blood pressure, diffuse bone demineralization complicated by aseptic necrosis of the right femoral head diagnosed on standard radiography of the hip and pelvic scan. Histological examination with complementary immunohistochemical study showed a right adrenal gland measuring 50 x 40 x 25mm, the nodules measure between 0.5 and 1.5cm, with a nodular chamois yellow appearance. Microscopic examination revealed a hyperplasia of the adrenal parenchyma with an increase in the number of spongiocytes, the complementary immunohistochemical study showed an expression of cytokeratin and chromogranin A in favor of hyperplasia.
diagnosis: ACTH-independent Cushing's syndrome due to unilateral adrenocortical hyperplasia

case_report: A 30-year-old multigravida presented to the Dermatology Department two weeks postpartum with severe itching and skin lesions that began gradually 10 days prior. She had no history of skin disorders, allergies, medication use, or fever. Physical examination revealed erythematous and edematous lesions with central erosions and isolated vesicles, predominantly on the trunk, limbs, hands, and feet. The patient received treatment with topical corticosteroid and antibiotic (betamethasone dipropionate with gentamicin), loratadine, and oral antibiotic (amoxicillin) without improvement. Her healthy male newborn (birth weight 5 kg) had a 5-minute Apgar score of 10 and no skin lesions. Laboratory tests indicated elevated levels of VZV IgG and IgM and HSV IgG and IgM antibodies. Despite a working diagnosis of chicken pox and treatment with acyclovir at a daily dose of 5 mg/kg intravenously, there was no satisfactory response. The presence of vesiculobullous lesions was noted.
test_results: Histopathological findings revealed large subepidermal blister filled with eosinophils and neutrophils, subepidermal spongiosis with perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with granulocytes and no acantholysis. DIF demonstrated linear depositions of IgG and C3 complement along the dermo-epidermal junction. IIF performed on monkey esophagus revealed linear deposits of IgG at the dermal-epidermal junction. ELISA confirmed presence of circulating IgG antibodies against BP180 in titer 1:160. Salt-split skin revealed a roof pattern of the immunofluorescence.

case_report: A 40-year-old female received her second dose of the COVID-19 vaccine 4 months prior to admission. The day after vaccination, she experienced gait imbalance and vertigo, which persisted for over a month. She consulted a primary care physician 2 days after symptom onset and was given medication for symptom management. Despite this, her symptoms continued, leading to her admission to our hospital 4 months post-vaccination. On general physical examination, she exhibited gait imbalance and kept her eyes closed most of the time. There were no petechiae, purpura, or ecchymotic lesions, and no mucosal bleeding was observed. She was febrile with a body temperature of 99.6°F, showing an increasing trend. Hemodynamic parameters were normal. Neurological assessment revealed a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14/15 (E4V5M5), normal pupil size and light reaction, normal fundus, normal deep tendon reflexes, bilateral extensor plantar response, and normal pain and temperature sensation, proprioception, vibration sensation, and cranial nerve examination. Meningeal signs were absent. Ear examination was normal, and there was no history indicative of peripheral vertigo causes. The patient did not consume alcohol and had no history of altered sensorium, personality changes, seizures, or focal neurological deficits. Laboratory investigations showed hemoglobin at 10.9 g/dl, white blood cell count at 22.76 × 103/μl (neutrophils 92.3%, lymphocytes 7.2%, basophils 0%, eosinophils 0%), platelet count at 284 × 103/μl, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) at 25 mm/h, C-reactive protein (CRP) at 32 mg/l, blood urea at 46 mg/dl, serum creatinine at 1.4 mg/dl, blood glucose at 225.23 mg/dl, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 128 U/l, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) at 96 U/l, total bilirubin at 1.2 mg/dl, total protein at 5.7 g/dl, albumin at 3.2 g/dl, serum sodium at 132 mEq/l, and serum potassium at 3.7 mEq/l. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed 10 cells (all lymphocytes), mildly elevated proteins (58 mg/dl), and normal glucose (68 mg%). Daily monitoring of platelet count showed values within normal limits. Tests for SARS-CoV-2 RNA using NAAT were negative. Peripheral smear for malaria parasite was negative, and blood culture was sterile. Serological tests for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were negative.
test_results: Development of CNS manifestations during the recovery phase of fever along with typical MRI findings.

case_report: A 52-year-old Saudi male presented with asymptomatic, hyperpigmented macules on the nose and cheeks, predominantly on the left cheek, which appeared 6 months prior. The macules were violaceous with irregular borders and lacked rolled edges. The patient had a history of significant sun exposure due to his occupation as a labor supervisor for outdoor work and was not using any sun protection. There was no history of other significant skin or mucosal lesions, systemic diseases, topical applications, or trauma. Laboratory results showed a normal blood count and liver function tests. Tests for anti-nuclear antibodies and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies were negative.
test_results: Skin biopsy showed hyperplasia of the epidermis and a band-like inflammatory infiltration. High power magnification under microscopic examination showed the presence of dyskeratosis with hypergranulosis in the epidermis, and vacuolar degeneration in the basal region. In the upper dermis, the majority of the inflammatory cells were clusters of lymphohistiocytes. Cytoid bodies and lichenoid infiltrate were seen at the epidermodermal junction.

case_report: A 58-year-old Caucasian female was referred to the Regional Coordinator Centre for Rare Disease of Udine (RCCRD) in 2010. Over the previous two years, she experienced progressive neurological symptoms including pain and weakness in the left lower leg, followed by similar symptoms in the left arm, psychomotor impairment, ataxic gait, tongue enlargement, dysarthria, and dysphagia. Her medical history included mild thrombocytopenia and splenomegaly since the age of 32, nodular skin lesions resembling prurigo nodularis since the age of 40, and chronic lymphedema of the left leg since the age of 43. Electromyography (EMG) of the legs indicated bilateral demyelinating motor neuropathy, while brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was negative. Hematological parameters revealed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 10.2 g/dl, leukocytes 3700/ul, platelets 109000/ul), and a bone marrow biopsy showed foam cells. Therapy with miglustat (300 mg/day) was initiated based on clinical and histological data. After four months of therapy, there was a regression of neurological symptoms, tongue enlargement, and left leg lymphedema, along with significant improvement in skin lesions. Upon admission to RCCRD after six months of miglustat therapy, her neurological examination was normal, skin lesions were very mild, and both tonsils were normal in size and color. EMG of the upper and lower limbs was normal. Lipid profiling revealed severe hypocholesterolemia with total cholesterol at 60 mg/dl (normal range 130-200 mg/dl), very low levels of HDL-cholesterol at 2 mg/dl (normal range 45-65 mg/dl) and apoAI at 5.19 mg/dl (normal range 110-170 mg/dl), and hypertriglyceridemia at 448 mg/dl (normal range 40-150 mg/dl).
test_results: When PCR analysis of ABCA1 gene was performed, all exons could be amplified and sequenced with the exception of exons 32, 33 and 34. This amplification generated a ~6 kb fragment from control DNA as opposed to a ~ 2.5 kb fragment from the patient’s DNA, thus indicating that the patient was homozygous for a novel ~3.5 kb deletion. By using a set of specific nucleotide primers the deletion breakpoint (i.e. the junction between intron 31 and intron 34) was characterized. The deletion was generated by a recombination between two Alu sequences (Alu-SX in intron 31 and Alu-SQ2 in intron 34 respectively). At the genomic level the mutation was designated as c.4464-486_4698 + 382 Del (Ex32_Ex34del). The RT-PCR amplification of the cDNA region spanning from exons 31 to exon 35, revealed that the genomic deletion lead to the exclusion of exons 32, 33 and 34 from the mature mRNA, with no disruption of the reading frame. The predicted translation product of this abnormal mRNA would be a protein with an in frame deletion of 77 amino acids (from residue 1489 to residue 1566 of ABCA1 protein) (p.R1489_K1566del). Cholesterol efflux was negligible in the patient’s fibroblasts, either under basal conditions or after stimulation of ABCA1 expression with 9-cis-retinoic acid and 22-hydroxycholesterol.

case_report: A 76-year-old woman was admitted in August 1992 with symptoms of fatigability, puffy face, and leg edema. In 1985, she had a right thyroid tumor. Thyroid scintigraphy using 99mTc and 123I showed a large functioning thyroid nodule in the right lobe with 123I uptake values of 37.6% at 3 hours and 40.6% at 6 hours, which suppressed the left lobe. The following year, she underwent surgery for a functioning follicular adenoma in the right lobe and nodular hyperplasia in the left lobe. The right thyroid lobe was completely removed, and half of the left lobe remained. Both before and after surgery, her free T4 and TSH levels were below normal, and she was given desiccated thyroid. Three months post-operation, her thyroid function tests indicated a hypothyroid state with T3 at 66 ng/dl, T4 at 5.3 μg/dl, F-T4 at 0.29 μg/dl, and TSH at 32.3 μU/ml. The dosage of desiccated thyroid was increased to 60 mg, resulting in a low serum TSH level. In May 1991, thyroid function tests showed normal total thyroid hormone levels, suppressed TSH, and low free T4 levels. Her medication compliance was noted to be insufficient. Upon admission in August 1992, she exhibited clinical signs of myxedema, including a puffy face and non-pitting leg edema. Physical examination revealed a body temperature of 36.5°C, a pulse rate of 72 beats per minute and regular, and blood pressure of 132/70 mmHg. Her hair and skin appeared normal, and the remaining thyroid gland was not palpable. Urinalysis, hemogram, electrolyte levels, blood urea nitrogen, blood glucose, uric acid, cholesterol, and liver function tests were all within normal limits. A chest roentgenogram showed an enlarged heart, and an electrocardiogram indicated left ventricular hypertrophy.
test_results: A significant increase in serum TSH levels did not occur after drip infusion (2mg) of TRH for 30 minutes. After repeated injection of TRH (2mg/day) for 4 consecutive days, serum TSH levels were still suppressed (maximum level: 1.45μU/ml in 120 minutes of final injection day). Growth hormone (GH), LH, FSH, prolactin (PRL) and cortisol kept almost normal responses. The pituitary MRI and CT did not show any abnormality.

case_report: A 19-year-old male presented with axial lengths of 17.48 mm in the right eye and 17.15 mm in the left eye. The horizontal corneal diameters were 10 mm in both eyes. Refraction measurements showed +20.50 D in both eyes. Best corrected visual acuity was recorded as 20/100 in the right eye and 20/200 in the left eye. The patient was orthophoric with an alternating cover test and exhibited latent nystagmus. Intraocular pressure was 20 mmHg in the right eye and 19 mmHg in the left eye. Fundoscopic examination revealed crowded optic discs, retinal pigment epithelial changes, and papillomacular retinal folds in both eyes.
test_results: OCT revealed fold of sensorial retina and B-scan ultrasound images showed thickening of the sclera and choroid in both eyes. FA showed mottled hyperfluorescence due to pigment epithelial changes and mild hypofluorescence in the fold area bilaterally.

case_report: A 13-year-old boy was brought to the emergency room in February 2019 by his mother. Six months prior, a urine dipstick test at home revealed proteinuria. At a local hospital, his total urine protein was measured at 2070 mg/day (56 mg/kg/day), with normal C3 and C4 levels and a serum albumin level of 34 g/L. A renal ultrasound showed a small right kidney measuring 4 cm. No treatment was initiated at that time. The patient was born full-term via spontaneous vaginal delivery, with no complications during pregnancy or delivery. His medical history included a previous episode of bullous lesions on the lower limbs that resolved without treatment. The family history included one sister with resolved proteinuria after steroid treatment, another sister with hearing impairment and low-grade proteinuria, and a brother with recurrent bullous lesions. The parents were first-degree relatives and asymptomatic. Upon admission, the patient was asymptomatic, vitally stable, normotensive, and had a normal physical examination with no dysmorphic features, clinical edema, active skin lesions, or changes in nails or teeth. He maintained adequate urine output. Initial blood tests showed normal blood cell counts, no leukocytosis, anemia, or thrombocytopenia. Serum albumin was 32 g/L, and total urine protein was 55 g/L. Renal function was normal with creatinine at 47 μmol/L and blood urea nitrogen at 6.3 mmol/L. Liver enzymes and C3 and C4 levels were normal. Autoimmune tests were negative for ANCA, anti-double-stranded DNA, MPO-ANCA, PR3-ANC, and hepatitis screen. Initial urine analysis showed high urine protein (>600 mg/dL) and microscopic hematuria (12 red blood cells/high power field) with 24-hour urine protein at 5.32 g/day. A renal ultrasound revealed an atrophied right kidney (4 cm) and compensatory hypertrophy of the left kidney (12 cm). A Dimercapto succinic acid renal scan indicated limited function of the right kidney (2%) and normal function of the left kidney (98%). The patient was started on an oral angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor and discharged with a follow-up plan with pediatric nephrology and genetic departments.
test_results: WGS results indicated a homozygous pathogenic variant identified in the CD151 gene (c.493C>T p.(Arg165*).
diagnosis: Autosomal recessive nephropathy with pretibial epidermolysis bullosa and deafness syndrome

case_report: A 32-year-old Caucasian woman presented to the endocrinology department with an 18-month history of right temporal headache, visual acuity reduction, amenorrhea, and galactorrhea. She also experienced fatigue, weakness, nausea, and occasional vomiting. Visual field assessment revealed left eye amaurosis, temporal hemianopsia, and lower nasal quadrantanopsia in the right eye. Hormonal tests indicated panhypopituitarism, and the patient was initiated on cortisol and T4 replacement therapy.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a 4.0 cm diameter solid lobulated lesion with sellar and suprasellar components, predominantly isointense on T1 and hypointense on T2-weighted images and extension to both the cavernous sinuses and optic chiasm. Lung biopsy via bronchoscopy confirmed a moderately differentiated neuroendocrine tumor immunohistochemically positive for chromogranin, synaptophysin, prolactin, and growth hormone. Ki-67 was positive in approximately 10% of the cells. F-18 FDG images showed a markedly increased uptake in the pituitary (SUV 33) as well as in multiple lung nodules (SUV 11.1), pancreas (SUV 6), liver lesions (SUV 10.4) and right kidney nodule (SUV 8.5). The 3D PET/CT Ga-68 DOTATATE images showed moderate uptake in large pituitary lesion (SUV 4.4) and very mild uptake in some of the lung lesions; however, no increased tracer uptake was detected in the liver, pancreas, and right kidney lesions.

case_report: A 7-year-old female presented to the pediatric neurology clinic with concerns of 'abnormal eye movements' and migraines. According to her mother, the patient has experienced episodes of eye fluttering and eyes rolling back since birth. These episodes occur at least 20 times per hour daily, including during sleep. While awake, these episodes sometimes result in a brief reduction in awareness, occasionally occurring mid-conversation, requiring reorientation. Despite these episodes, her school performance remains unaffected, although teachers have misinterpreted the eye movements. The patient has no developmental issues and performs above average academically. Migraines have been present since she could speak at around three years old, described as an 'all-over squeezing' pain with photophobia and vomiting. Additional medical issues include difficulty falling asleep, managed with melatonin, and frequent urinary incontinence. Physical examination was largely unremarkable except for recurrent episodes of eyelid myoclonia observed during the visit. Hyperventilation for 2-3 minutes induced several episodes of up to 5-second upward eye deviation absence seizures.
test_results: Her 21-channel digital video-EEG results showed a burst of frontally predominant, generalized, 3–4 Hz polyspike-and-slow wave activity during photic stimulation. No seizures were noted. Her MRI scan was unremarkable. Patient's genetic panel came back with a heterozygous PLCB1 mutation reported as likely pathogenic. She was also heterozygous for SCN1A and SCN9A mutations. Her father's genetic panel was also heterozygous for SCN1A and SCN9A mutations although he has no history of seizures. Her mother's genetic testing came back normal.

case_report: In March 2007, a 47-year-old woman with a history of bilateral optic neuritis at age 35 experienced her first seizure. One month later, she experienced a second seizure and was started on lamotrigine. She presented to our institution as an elective admission to the EMU 6 months after seizure onset. Many right temporal seizures, characterized by paresthesias over the left face and arm, were observed. The interictal EEG showed right periodic lateralized discharges.
test_results: MRI showed abnormal T2 signal in the right frontal cortex, right thalamus as well as a small area of contrast enhancement in the right temporal uncus. MR SPECT showed normal choline:creatinine ratio. CSF evaluation was significant for a mild lymphocytic pleocytosis, negative HSV and CMV PCR, and cytology negative for malignant cells.

case_report: A 45-year-old female patient visited the University of Jordan dermatology clinic with concerns about hair loss on her scalp, eyebrows, and eyelashes. She also noted white discoloration of her fingernails and more severe changes in her toenails. She mentioned having sparse hair during childhood, which progressed to significant hair loss in her twenties. There was no thickening of the skin on her palms and soles. She reported that her father, children, and some siblings experienced similar symptoms with varying degrees of severity. Family history indicated that multiple relatives were affected, showing a pattern of inheritance with diverse clinical manifestations. Blood tests were performed to check for nutritional deficiencies and thyroid function, all of which were within normal limits.
test_results: A pathogenic variant in heterozygous state was identified in the GJB6 gene; this caused a single nucleotide alteration in the gene's DNA sequence. This alteration led to the substitution of the amino acid glycine with arginine at position 11 in the gap junction protein connexin 30.

case_report: Patient 1, a 20-month-old girl, is the first child of healthy parents with no family history of intellectual disability or epilepsy. She was born via full-term cesarean section following an uneventful pregnancy. At 20 days old, she experienced a focal motor seizure. Subsequently, she exhibited clusters of epileptic spasms and generalized tonic–clonic seizures. Neurological examination showed hypotonia.
test_results: VEEG showed SBs at approximately 1 month old. Cranial MRI suggests dysgenesis of the corpus callosum and cerebellar hypoplasia at approximately 6 months old.

case_report: A 10-month-old male child presented with skeletal deformities and hypopigmented macules. He was born at term to a nonconsanguineous couple with a birth weight of 2400 g. Examination revealed hemihypotrophy of the right side of the face, resulting in an asymmetric appearance. The skin showed atrophic areas with yellowish nodules over depigmented macules following the lines of Blaschko. The child had sparse hair and oligodontia. On the right side, there were coloboma of the iris and optic disc, syndactyly of the hand, ectrodactyly of the foot, and an undescended testis. The child exhibited global developmental delay and growth below the third centile. Systemic examination was normal. Ultrasonogram of the abdomen, radiographs of long bones, and echocardiography were normal.
test_results: Histopathology of skin biopsy showed very scanty collagen with adipocytes and lobules of adipose tissue in the dermis. Dermal appendages were absent. Subsequent Sanger sequencing of PCR amplicons revealed point mutations at position c. 898G > T (p.E300*) in exon 10 (CM080503), in addition to the wild-type G nucleotide. The smaller size of the mutant peak suggested a mosaic state. Parents did not carry the mutant allele.

case_report: A 49-year-old female patient presented with numbness in her fingers that gradually extended to her entire body above the bellybutton over a period of six months. Her medical history included rapidly growing cutaneous neurofibromas on her back and left thigh over five years, which were surgically removed at a local hospital. Histological analysis confirmed these were neurofibromas with malignant characteristics. Physical examination revealed widespread café-au-lait spots, axillary and groin freckling, cutaneous neurofibromas, plexiform neurofibromas, and surgical scars on her back and left thigh. A sensory deficit was noted between the C4 level and the bellybutton. No iris hamartomas were detected, and the mammary glands were normal.
