Her mother and maternal grandmother exhibited similar features, but her daughter and sons showed no clinical signs of NF1.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging showed a relative-demarcated, heterogeneously enhanced mass lesion accompanied by perifocal edema in C5-7 level, a left-sided T11 spinous process heterogeneously enhanced mass in soft tissue, intervertebral disk hernia in L2-5 level and widespread punctum enhancing lesion in her scalp and in T11-L5 level. No evidences of optic pathway glioma and neurofibromatosis 2 (NF2) had been found in head MRI.

case_report: The patient, a 3-year-old Brazilian female, was born to healthy parents and has had recurrent episodes of fever since the first month of life. These episodes initially involved high fever lasting five days, accompanied by arthritis and dactylitis. At nine months old, she developed a diffuse painful skin eruption characterized by nodules, plaques, erythematoedematous rash, and infiltrate, similar to erythema nodosum. The child was hospitalized almost monthly; sometimes her symptoms were linked to specific infections (mono-like), while other times the infections were undefined but somewhat responsive to systemic antibiotics. At eleven months old, during another fever episode, low levels of immunoglobulin G were detected, leading to the start of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) replacement therapy. IVIG reduced the frequency of infectious episodes and hospital admissions, but the skin rash and arthritis persisted.
test_results: A biopsied skin specimen from her left leg revealed septal panniculitis.
diagnosis: Sideroblastic Anemia With Immunodeficiency, Fevers, and Development Delay  Syndrome
Orpha_name: Congenital sideroblastic anemia-B-cell immunodeficiency-periodic fever-developmental delay syndrome

case_report: A 40-year-old woman presented on May 10, 2017, with a 6-day history of fever reaching up to 38.0 °C, a non-productive cough, and shortness of breath upon exertion. She had been treated with amoxicillin (1.5 g/day) at a community clinic 3 days prior, but her symptoms persisted. She reported no hemoptysis, chest pain, or weight loss and was a nonsmoker with no family history of hematologic or lung malignancies. Upon admission, her physical examination showed a body temperature of 39.0 °C, heart rate of 103 beats per minute, blood pressure of 120/70 mmHg, and respiratory rate of 25 breaths per minute. Auscultation of the lungs did not reveal wheezes or dry rales. No other significant abnormalities were noted. Laboratory tests indicated hemoglobin at 115 g/L, red blood cell count at 3.98 × 10^12/L, and an elevated white blood cell count of 20100/mm^3 with 90% neutrophils, 4% lymphocytes, and 1% eosinophils. No atypical lymphocytes were observed in the peripheral blood. Further laboratory investigations showed elevated C-reactive protein (230.1 mg/mL; normal: < 10.0 mg/mL), procalcitonin (0.88 ng/mL; normal: < 0.10 ng/mL), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (10 mm/h; normal: < 20 mm/h). Biochemical studies revealed hypoalbuminemia (33.2 g/L; normal: 40.0-55.0 g/L), elevated alanine aminotransferase (65 U/L; normal: 7-40 U/L), aspartate transaminase (55 U/L; normal: 13-35 U/L), alkaline phosphatase (129 U/L; normal: 35-100 U/L), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) (549 U/L; normal: 114-240 U/L). Arterial blood gas analysis showed PaO2 at 60 mmHg (normal: 80-100 mmHg) and SaO2 at 90% on ambient air. Tumor biomarkers, including CEA125, CA153, and CA199, were negative. Tests for Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and respiratory syncytial virus were also negative.
test_results: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest demonstrated multiple solid nodules throughout both lungs with the largest measuring 15 mm in diameter, with poor defined boundaries in the right upper lung. No mediastinal lymphadenopathy was demonstrated.

case_report: A 9-year-old boy presented with symptoms of easy fatigability and recurrent nose and gum bleeding over a 2-month period, during which he received four blood transfusions. There was a history of easy bruising but no prolonged bleeding following circumcision at age 7. Around age 5, generalized darkening of the skin, including the palms and soles, and some whitish and dark patches on the tongue were noticed. The patient had a normal birth and developmental milestones. He is the second child in a family of six children from a monogamous, non-consanguineous marriage. There was no similar illness reported in other family members. The mother is a 30-year-old stay-at-home mother, and the father is a 35-year-old self-employed trader. The patient exhibited epistaxis from both nostrils and appeared pale with hyperpigmentation on the neck, chest, arms, palms, and soles, along with scattered hypopigmented areas. Non-scrapable white and black plaques were observed on the tongue. Dental caries and gum bleeding were present, while other mucosal surfaces in the oral cavity were normal. Both eyes had epiphoria, more pronounced in the right eye. The nails on both fingers and toes were cracked, ridged, and atrophic. Anthropometric measurements and cardiovascular and respiratory system examinations were unremarkable. Renal function tests were normal, and no skeletal anomalies were detected.
test_results: The full blood count showed haemoglobin of 56 g/L white blood cells count of 2.0 × 109/L (normal = 4 – 11 × 109/L), with an absolute neutrophil count of 1.0 × 109/L, platelet count of 23 × 109/L (normal = 150-450 × 109/L), clotting profile was normal and bone marrow biopsy revealed a hypocellular marrow.

case_report: A 10-year-old male patient presented with a 13-mm well-demarcated, dome-shaped, dark red nodule on the left ala. The nodule had been present for eight months, during which it increased in size and experienced episodes of bleeding. No prior treatment had been administered. The rest of the physical examination showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Histopathology revealed a diffuse infiltrate of spindle-shaped histiocytes in a storiform pattern, few multinucleated giant cells, scattered lymphocytes, and eosinophils. Immunohistochemical studies showed tumor cells positive for cluster of differentiation 68 (CD68) and the proliferation marker Ki-67. The lesion was negative for S-100 protein, anti-melanoma antibody (HMB45), protein Melan-A, and smooth muscle actin (SMA).

case_report: A 25-year-old female patient presented with swelling and pain in the right mandibular region for the past month. Intraoral examination showed a firm, well-defined swelling in the area of the missing tooth 46. Teeth 47 and 48 were found to be carious. The overlying mucosa appeared non-ulcerated and pink. An intraoral periapical radiograph displayed a radiolucent lesion in the 46 region, measuring approximately 9 mm in diameter with well-corticated borders. Surgical excision of the lesion was carried out. During the curettage, the lesion was observed to consist of small, gritty, and hemorrhagic fragments.
test_results: Histopathologic examination revealed proliferating fibrous connective tissue with moderate cellularity, rich vascularity and hemorrhage. Trabeculae of woven bone and cementum-like material were interspersed throughout the fibrous framework. Fragments of cellular mesenchymal tissue composed of spindle-shaped fibroblasts and collagen fibers with numerous small blood vessels were observed. The fibrous tissue was devoid of any inflammatory component.

case_report: A 5-month-old female presented with recurrent respiratory and genitourinary infections, chronic diarrhea, and hyperemic skin lesions. She was born at term with a birth weight of 3650 grams to second-degree consanguineous parents. Her medical history includes frequent and severe infections. At 10 days old, she was hospitalized for sepsis, diarrhea (7-8 times daily), extensive facial and scalp rash, respiratory distress, fever, and a urinary tract infection caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae. At 4 months, she developed a gluteal abscess from which Klebsiella pneumoniae was isolated. At 5 months, she was hospitalized for pneumonia and gastroenteritis. Upon admission to our department at 5 months, her weight was 6.5 kg (10th percentile), height was 63 cm (3rd–10th percentile), and vital signs were normal. Physical examination revealed extensive erythematous skin lesions, coarse crackles in both lung fields, and an anal fissure. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 20700/mm3 (polymorphonuclear leukocytes 35.6%, lymphocytes 54.9%, monocytes 4.7%, eosinophils 3.5%), hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL, hematocrit 28.3%, mean corpuscular volume 60.9 fL, and platelet count 577000/mm3. Biochemical parameters were within normal ranges. C-reactive protein was 2.3 mg/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 22 mm/hour. Urine analysis indicated the presence of numerous bacteria, and urine culture grew extended spectrum beta-lactamase positive E. coli. High-resolution computerized tomography showed subsegmental atelectasis in the right upper lobe apical and posterior segments. Abdominal ultrasonography was normal. Immunoglobulin levels were IgG: 537 mg/dL, IgM: 52.6 mg/dL, IgA: 25.6 mg/dL, and IgE: 26.2 IU/mL. Complement levels were C3: 130 mg/dL and C4: 25 mg/dL. Lymphocyte subgroups were within normal ranges (CD3: 65.1%, CD19: 18.6%, CD3+CD4+: 47.7%, CD3+CD8+: 13.9%, and CD3-CD16+56+: 12.5%). Naive and memory T helper cell levels were normal, and there was no elevation in TCR-gamma delta T cells.
test_results: Transplacental maternal T cell engraftment was excluded by genetic analysis (PCR). Fistulography showed a rectovaginal fistula. Colonoscopy revealed granularity of the right colon, exudative mucosal ulceration, pseudopolyps, laceration, and loss of haustration of the left colon. Histopathologic examination showed irregular architectural changes on the right colon and plasma cells in the lamina propria of the left colon.
Orpha_name: Immune dysregulation-inflammatory bowel disease-arthritis-recurrent infections syndrome

case_report: A female infant was delivered vaginally at 39 weeks of gestation to a 21-year-old mother who had not received prenatal care. Upon birth, the infant exhibited large and multiple black skin lesions. The largest lesion, measuring 21×15 cm, covered most of the back, extending from the upper back to the buttocks and wrapping around to the lower abdomen and proximal thigh. This lesion was smooth and hairless. Additionally, several hundred smaller lesions, ranging from 1 mm to 5 cm in diameter, were distributed across the body, scalp, and extremities. The infant's birth weight was 2870 grams, head circumference was 32 cm, and total body length was 49 cm. Neurological examination showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Cranial US demonstrated bilateral, multiple echogenic intra-parenchymal lesions with smooth margins. These 4-24 mm in diameter lesions were present in both temporal lobes, the basal ganglia and the white matter of the cerebellum. The brain images revealed multiple lesions. Leptomeningeal involvement was easily seen on T1W images as gyral hyperintensities, especially in the parieto-occipital sulci and subarachnoid spaces. Parenchymal involvement appeared as multiple nodular lesions involving the dentate nucleus bilaterally, the right cerebellar hemisphere peripherally, the right internal capsule, left thalamus, medial temporal lobe bilaterally, right middle cerebellar pedicle, left frontal lobe, parieto-occipital sulci and subependymal regions characterized by hyperintensities on T1W images and low signal on T2W images. The lesions were easily seen on T1W images and they did not enhance significantly. The biggest lesion was located on the left thalamus that was also easily seen on US examination. The spinal MRI was normal.

case_report: A male infant, weighing 1,780 g at birth, was delivered in a breech position via cesarean section to a 27-year-old first-time mother at 36 weeks of gestation. Prenatal ultrasound indicated low amniotic fluid and ambiguous genitalia. Apgar scores were 2 at one minute and 5 at five minutes. Due to inadequate respiratory function, he was intubated and given positive airway pressure. Physical examination revealed a small head, small jaw, a small nose with upturned nostrils, ambiguous genitalia, a cleft palate, a single transverse palmar crease, and webbing between the second and third toes on both feet. Chromosomal analysis showed a 46,XY karyotype. Echocardiography identified a large patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) and an atrial septal defect. PDA ligation was performed due to worsening heart failure. At one month old, he had difficulty feeding. Abdominal ultrasound and upper gastrointestinal series indicated hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, and a pyloromyotomy was performed. At four months old, persistent jaundice and poor growth were observed. The infant weighed 2,900 g. Physical examination showed drooping eyelids and reduced muscle tone. The liver was palpable 3 cm below the rib margin. Blood tests revealed a total bilirubin of 8.6 mg/dL, direct bilirubin of 4.7 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase of 176 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase of 86 IU/L, and gamma-glutamyl transferase of 13 IU/L. Prothrombin time was prolonged with an INR of 1.85. Elevated white blood cell count (20,000/µL) and low hemoglobin (8.8 g/dL) were noted. Tests for hepatitis A, B, and C, toxoplasma, rubella, cytomegalovirus, and herpes simplex were negative. Screening for metabolic disorders was also negative.
test_results: The serum cholesterol level was reduced (21 mg/dL) and serum 7DHC level was markedly elevated (567 µg/mL).

case_report: A 34-year-old male with advanced kidney disease due to diabetes mellitus, undergoing hemodialysis for 2 years, presented with increasing pain and darkening of the penile skin that began a month prior. He reported no fever, painful urination, urethral discharge, or recent unprotected sexual activity. Physical examination showed mild swelling and surface-level tissue death of the foreskin and glans penis. Laboratory results indicated elevated blood urea nitrogen at 100 mg/dL, serum creatinine at 12.2 mg/dL, parathyroid hormone at 400 pg/mL, and a calcium-phosphorus product of 111 mg/dL.
test_results: Plain radiographs of the pelvis demonstrated widespread vascular calcification.

case_report: A 40-month-old male patient, born via spontaneous vaginal delivery after a full-term pregnancy to a healthy 32-year-old woman and her 34-year-old first cousin. Birth measurements were: weight 3.28 kg, length 50 cm, and head circumference 34.5 cm, with APGAR scores of 9 at 5 and 10 minutes. Newborn screening tests revealed elevated methionine levels at 105 µmol/L (reference range: 11–27 µmol/L). A repeated test confirmed elevated methionine at 85 µmol/L. The patient was clinically stable with an unremarkable systemic examination. Additional metabolic tests, including homocysteine and urine tests for organic acids and methylmalonic acid, were unremarkable. Renal and liver functions were also unremarkable. At 2 months old, the patient developed irritability and a skin condition characterized by multiple scaly and erosive hyperkeratotic plaques, predominantly on the lower extremities. The patient also exhibited leukotrichia and a positive hair pull test. Zinc levels were found to be very low at 3.4 µmol/L (reference range: 9.18–18.36 µmol/L). The skin condition began to resolve after two weeks of oral zinc supplementation.
test_results: The genetic study of MAT1A (NM_000429.2) revealed a homozygous variant in c.1081G>T (p.Val361Phe).

case_report: A 29-year-old woman visited the hospital for an elective removal of a soft, movable mass situated on her right lower back. The patient reported that the mass had been causing discomfort and had been present for an extended period. During the procedure, it was observed that the mass was located within the muscle tissue.
test_results: The gross specimen was partially capsulated measuring 11.0 × 10.0 ×5.5 cm, tan-pink to brown in color with a smooth outer surface. The tumor extended into the margins of the excision. The mass consisted of mainly hypocellular, vaguely lobulated, proliferation of small ovoid to spindle cell admixed with scattered lipoblasts, in a background of abundant myxoid material and arborizing vascularity. At the periphery of the lobules, increased cellularity was noted with moderately increased cytological atypia. Mitotic activity was very rare and areas of round cell composed less than 5% of the total tumor. In many of the tumor cells, stain with p53 showed evidence of p53 overexpression. Stain with Ki-67 showed a proliferation index of 2-8%. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis was positive for detection of rearrangements of the DDIT3 (CHOP) gene at the 12q13 locus.

case_report: A 52-year-old Filipino female reported a 29-year history of recurring itchy red blisters that developed into merging nodules and plaques on her lower legs. She had previously received topical and intralesional steroid treatments, which led to partial improvement. Two of her siblings exhibited similar skin issues. Physical examination revealed multiple red to darkened prurigo-like lesions with scratch marks on both lower legs, the tops of her feet, and forearms. Nail abnormalities were observed on all toes.
test_results: Histopathological examination showed a hyperkeratosis overlying an acanthotic epidermis associated with a cell-poor subepidermal blister and fibrotic changes with abundant blood vessels on the superficial dermis. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) results showed negative findings. Genetic testing of her blood samples revealed that the proband was compound heterozygous for a nonsense and another splice-site mutation in COL7A1. In silico splicing effect prediction of COL7A1: c.7485G>A indicates that COL7A1 protein translation may be affected.

case_report: A 27-year-old man, previously healthy, has experienced two years of subcutaneous nodules distributed across his body, excluding the head, neck, hands, and feet. The nodules appeared gradually and increased in number over time. The patient reported paresthesia and significant pain that disrupted daily activities, which did not respond to analgesics or anti-inflammatory medications. There was no history of mental disorders, and the systemic review was unremarkable. The patient had no family history of obesity and did not consume alcohol or smoke. Physical examination revealed multiple soft-tissue swellings, predominantly on the trunk and upper limbs, with sparing of the face, hands, and feet. These swellings were painless upon palpation. The patient's BMI was 24 kg/m2. Neurological examination was normal, and other physical findings were unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 8 mm/h and a serum C-reactive protein level of 4 mg/L. Other laboratory results, including blood cell counts, serum electrolytes, liver function tests, serum protein electrophoresis, and lipid profiles, were within normal limits.
test_results: Skin biopsy revealed a dermal mass formed of proliferating adipocytes surrounded by fairly fibrous capsules with no atypia or mitotic figures.

case_report: A 70-year-old female patient, with a history of systemic arterial hypertension, was otherwise in good health. During routine examinations, a 4.5 cm mass was incidentally discovered in the lower third of her right kidney. At the time of discovery, the patient reported experiencing low-grade fever and weakness for approximately two weeks.
test_results: Abdominal ultrassonography (USG) showed hypoechoec mass with solid aspect and irregular limits. It was heterogeneous and exofitic, containing septation and cystic areas in its interior. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a solid mass 5.2 cm for its higher dimension located in right kidney with same hemorrhagic foci and no sign of peri-renal invasion. Pathologic examination of surgical specimen revealed a firm lesion of light brown tissue with reticulated central area and clear delimitation from the adjacent parenchyma. Microscopic evaluation showed no cellular atypical or mitotic activity. Peri-renal adipose tissue was free from neoplasic invasion.

case_report: A 12-month-old female patient with a history of recurrent pneumonia and bronchiolitis presented with respiratory distress. The parents were third cousins. Physical examination showed delayed neuromotor development and rales and rhonchi in the lungs. Laboratory results were: WBC: 2800/mm3, ALC: 300/mm3, ANC: 2500/mm3, Hb: 9.5 g/dL, UA: 1.7 mg/dL, IgG: 548 mg/dL, IgM: 17.3 mg/dL, IgA: 6.1 mg/dL, LP: CD3 76%, CD19 1.8%, CD4 59%, CD8 17%, CD3-CD16/56 20.8%, CD3+ HLA DR 75.3%, CMV viral load (DNA quantitative): 842 IU/mL. Blood culture grew coagulase-negative staphylococcus. Coronavirus and Human Bocavirus were isolated on SVP. HRCT showed bronchiectasis, nodular consolidation areas, and ground-glass opacity in the lower lobe of the right lung and the upper lobe of the left lung. Cranial MRI indicated deepened and enlarged cerebral sulci. During follow-up, fungal pneumonia and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) developed. Despite multiple antibiotic, antifungal, and antiviral treatments, the patient continued to experience resistant fever and respiratory distress and ultimately succumbed to severe respiratory failure.
test_results: A homozygous p.Arg234Ter stop codon mutation was found in the patient.

case_report: A 1-day-old newborn male, born to a 24-year-old first-time mother, was brought to our center due to multiple bone deformities and low birth weight. The baby did not cry immediately after birth but did so following oronasal suctioning and tactile stimulation. The mother reported no history of trauma or physical abuse. She had regular antenatal visits, but no prenatal anomaly scans were performed. There was no notable family history or consanguineous marriage. On examination, the baby appeared ill, though his vital signs were stable. He exhibited blue sclera without pallor or jaundice. The anterior fontanelle was level, and muscle tone was normal. The baby had a weak and poorly sustained suckling reflex. Significant bone deformities were observed in both upper and lower limbs. Systemic examination revealed no other abnormalities. The baby had a low birth weight of 2100 grams and was small for gestational age, with a length of 37 cm, below the 3rd percentile. The ponderal index was calculated to be 4. Laboratory investigations showed elevated white blood cells (17300 per mm3) with neutrophils at 80% and lymphocytes at 12%. Platelet count was 183000 per mm3. Hemoglobin was 15.9 g/dL, and the peripheral blood smear was normal. Serum calcium was 9.1 mg/dL, inorganic phosphorus 7.3 mg/dL, sodium 137 mEq/L, potassium 4.6 mEq/L, urea 30 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.6 mg/dL. The baby was severely hypoglycemic with a random blood sugar level of less than 20 mg/dL. Total bilirubin was 8.9 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin was 0.8 mg/dL.
test_results: The X-ray revealed thin gracile bones with multiple fractures including bilateral clavicles, left humeral diaphysis, bilateral lower limbs, and bilateral ribs which were marked in the left hemithorax. Diffuse osteopenic changes and marked bone deformities were seen as incurvation of the bilateral humerus and left radius and ulna.

case_report: A 41-year-old female was referred to the Michigan State University (MSU) endocrinology clinic in 2008 for elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol. She had increased facial hair for over 20 years, managed cosmetically with intermittent waxing. She attained menarche around age 13 and had regular menstrual cycles until her early 20s, when she began experiencing irregular periods and was informed she had polycystic ovarian syndrome. She has two children; the first was conceived spontaneously, and the second pregnancy required clomiphene therapy. Her medical history includes hypothyroidism following radioactive iodine treatment for a toxic thyroid nodule and depression. On physical examination, her blood pressure was 122/80 mmHg, and her body mass index (BMI) was 22.6 kg/m2, both within normal ranges. She had mildly increased facial hair on her chin and a palpable thyroid nodule in the right lobe. The remainder of the physical exam was normal, with no clinical features of Cushing’s syndrome. Laboratory evaluation showed 24-hour urinary cortisol levels at 317 mcg (normal range 3.5–45 mcg/day).
test_results: The coding regions of the human glucocorticoid receptor gene (hGR, NR3C1) were sequenced and showed no mutation. Repeated overnight and 48 h dexamethasone suppression tests (DST) failed to suppress cortisol levels and 24-h urine cortisol levels were persistently elevated at multiple times. The sampling suggested pituitary source of ACTH.

case_report: A 24-year-old woman, who plays rugby recreationally, visited the outpatient clinic in May 2017 due to pain in her right big toe. She reported no history of trauma, fever, alcohol or substance abuse, and had not used corticosteroids. Her past health was generally good, with no history of trauma to the right foot, vasculitis, Caisson Disease, or alcoholism. She was not on any medication and had no known allergies. There was no significant personal or family medical history. Physical examination showed mild swelling at the first metatarsophalangeal joint (MTPJ) and an inability to actively flex the interphalangeal joint to 0 degrees, although passive range of motion was normal. The tendons of the Flexor Hallucis Longus were intact. The clinical appearance of the feet, sensation, and local blood flow to the toes were normal. There was no significant impact on daily activities, although weight-bearing was painful. No laboratory tests were performed. X-ray images of the foot did not reveal any fractures or bony abnormalities.
test_results: MRI of the right big toe showed an abnormal linear signal within the marrow cavity of the first MTT head, along with a suspected serpiginous line with bony oedema present at the dorsal aspect of both the distal phalangeal base and proximal phalangeal head. CT scan showed no fracture line, however, did show diffuse sclerosis at the MTT head. Cartilage was grossly intact.
diagnosis: Avascular necrosis of the first metatarsal head

case_report: In 2001, a 14-year-old male presented with asymptomatic brownish black-pigmented reticulated patches over the entire body, particularly on the neck, axillary, and antecubital areas, for an unknown duration. Laboratory studies were within normal limits or negative. Histologic examination revealed an increased number of melanophages in the papillary dermis with focal hydropic changes in the basement membrane zone. The patient was lost to follow-up. In 2005, the patient returned with scaly increased darkening and lichenification on the previous lesions without any interim treatment. Skin biopsy showed interface dermatitis with band-like infiltration in the upper dermis at the epidermo-dermal junction, exocytosis, and necrotic keratinocytes. Treatment with regular follow-up was recommended, but the patient declined treatment at that time.
test_results: A skin biopsy performed on the flank area showed epidermal atrophy and lymphocytic infiltration in the upper dermis with epidermotropism of atypical lymphocytes. A CD4~CD8 double stain revealed a 1 : 1 ratio of CD4 cells to CD8 cells, and the atypical T cells were mainly CD4-CD8+. A retrospective CD4-CD8 double staining on the previous biopsy specimen also revealed a 1 : 1 ratio of CD4 cells to CD8 cells and mild epidermotropism of CD4-CD8+ lymphocytes. The results of the T-cell receptor (TCR)γ gene rearrangement analysis were positive for clonality in the affected skin lesions.

case_report: A 42-year-old Caucasian male, generally in good health, exhibited mild intermittent yellowing of the skin and eyes along with fatigue. He reported no abdominal pain, fever, itching, dark urine, pale stools, or other symptoms. He also denied the use of alcohol, tobacco, and any medications. Physical examination revealed only yellowing of the sclera, with no other notable findings. Laboratory results showed elevated bilirubin levels (total 7.97 mg/dL and direct 5.37 mg/dL) and bilirubin in the urine, with no evidence of red blood cell breakdown. Liver function tests were within normal ranges (AST 21 U/L, ALT 32 U/L, GGT 21 U/L, ALP 74 U/L, albumin 5.3 g/dL, PT 12.5 s), as was the lipid profile. An abdominal ultrasound showed no abnormalities. Tests for chronic liver diseases (viral, autoimmune, and metabolic) were negative, except for elevated serum (147.4 μg/dL) and urinary (179.9 μg/24 h) copper levels, with normal ceruloplasmin. No other criteria for Wilson's disease were met, including a negative genetic test for ATP7B gene variants. Urinary coproporphyrin analysis indicated normal total levels with a predominance of isomer I (86% of total). A genetic test revealed a heterozygous variant in the ABBC2 gene (c.1483A>G − p.Lys495Glu).
test_results: Additional molecular studies revealed a homozygous deletion of a genomic region encompassing exons 4–16 of SLCO1B3 gene (encoding OATP1B3) and all exons of SLCO1B1 (encoding OATP1B1).

case_report: A 27-year-old male presented with increased intraocular pressure (IOP) in both eyes for approximately 3 months. The patient had no significant ocular or medical history, except for a previous diagnosis of myopia and an allergy to cefradine. There was no history of systemic conditions such as hypertension, diabetes mellitus, coronary heart disease, stroke, smoking, or obesity. The patient had a myopic refractive error of -3.00 diopters in both eyes. Initial IOP measurements at Zhongshan Ophthalmic Center were 28.7 mmHg in the right eye and 31.4 mmHg in the left eye, noted as the peak IOP. Best corrected visual acuity was 1.0 in each eye, as determined by the standard Snellen chart. Routine blood tests, as well as liver and kidney function and electrolyte levels, were within normal ranges.
test_results: The result showed vertical cup disc ratio of his right eye was 0.7 and his left eye was 0.8 with localized cupping in both eyes. A localized retinal nerve fiber layer thinning corresponding to the optic disc cupping was detected by Heidelberg Spectralis optical coherence tomography in each eye, with an average retinal nerve fiber layer thickness significantly reduced at 69 µm oculus dexter and 67 µm oculus sinister. Visual field defects were detected by Humphrey Visual Field Analyzer in both eyes with the visual field mean deviation of -6.75 dB oculus dexter and -5.30 dB oculus sinister. The proband has a c.281G>A, p.Arg94His in OLFM2 inherited from his father and a c.177C>G, p.Ile59Met in SIX6 inherited from his mother, which cosegregates with the phenotype in a recessive pattern. The OLFM2 mutation had a minor allele frequency of 0.005% in the Exome Aggregation Consortium and 0.004% in the Genome Aggregation Database. The SIX6 mutation was absent in the Exome Aggregation Consortium and had a minor allele frequency of 0.0004% in the Genome Aggregation Database.

case_report: A 42-year-old Japanese woman, who has had one pregnancy and one normal vaginal delivery 13 years ago, showed an increase in uterine size during a screening. She reported recent lower abdominal pain and had been experiencing urinary incontinence and constipation for several months. During a pelvic examination, a fist-sized lump was noted in the uterus and left ovary. The vulva and vagina appeared normal. The portio was not clearly visible, making endometrial smear tests and uteroscopy unfeasible. Serum tumor markers, including carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), CA125, CA19-9, and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), were all within normal limits. Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels were not measured before the operation. An ultrasound showed a cystic mass measuring 125 × 75 mm located behind the uterus, which was interpreted as an endometrioid cyst.
test_results: The MRI showed a solid lesion extending throughout the myometrium of the lower uterine segment and an irregular large cystic lesion filling the pelvic cavity behind the uterus. The solid lesion in the uterus was hyperintense on T2-weighted images (T2WIs), isointense on T1-weighted images (T1WIs) and heterogeneously enhanced on gadolinium-diethylene triamine pentaacetic acid (DTPA)-enhanced T1WI. It appeared hyperintense in diffusion-weighted images (DWIs), with an apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) value of 0.9 × 10−3 mm2/s. The subserosal cystic lesion had an irregular wall and septum, and protruded into the solid lesion of the posterior wall like an ulceration. The contents of the cystic lesion appeared hyperintense on T2WI, T1WI, and fat suppression T1WI, and included T2WI-hypointense precipitated material. Slightly solid components were present on the inner surface of the cystic wall. There were no findings indicating adenomyosis in the myometrium of the uterus, and no abnormal findings in the endometrium and left ovary. The right ovary was not detected.

case_report: A four-year-old boy presented to the outpatient clinic with concerns of developmental delay and short stature. He was born at term to a Korean father and a Japanese mother, weighing 3.68 kg, with no perinatal complications. His initial crying and muscle tone were normal. There is no family history of developmental or neuromuscular disorders. He underwent surgery for undescended testis at 8 months old. His developmental milestones were delayed: head control at 5 months, rolling over at 9 months, walking with assistance at 17 months, and walking independently at 32 months. At age 3, he could only say 'mom' and 'dad'. His height was 87.5 cm (<3rd percentile), weight 15.3 kg (10-25th percentile), and head circumference 48.5 cm (3-50th percentile). Physical examination showed a prominent forehead, highly arched eyebrows, down-slanted palpebral fissures, a broad nasal bridge, a short upper lip, a pouting lower lip, and a grimacing smile. He also had broad thumbs and terminal broadening of the finger phalanges. Neurologic examination was normal with no focal signs. Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed an epiblepharon, but the fundus and disc were normal. Cardiac evaluation showed no abnormalities. A brain MRI at age 3 revealed multifocal lesions with increased signal intensity in the subcortical white matter of both temporal and left parietal regions, as well as periventricular deep white matter. Arnold-Chiari malformation type I was also noted. Chromosome analysis showed a normal 46, XY karyotype, and tandem mass screening revealed no abnormalities. Thyroid function tests were normal.
test_results: Mutation analysis demonstrated a CREBBP gene mutation with a C insertion in exon 31, nt 4944-4945.

case_report: A 62-year-old Japanese woman from a non-consanguineous family, whose identical twin sister had shown similar symptoms, presented with gait disturbance. No other family members showed similar disorders. Their mother had died of a malignant tumor at the age of 72, but no significant ataxia or cognitive impairment had been observed until her death. Their father had been healthy until his 90s. The patient had exhibited normal physical and neurological development. At the age of 68 years, she was admitted to a hospital due to dancing-like involuntary movements in the hands and feet. Neurological examination revealed choreic movement, saccadic eye movement, slurred speech, limb and trunk ataxia, and increased deep tendon reflexes in the upper and lower limbs. Babinski sign was negative. No superficial sensory disturbance or Romberg sign was detected. There was no evidence of bladder or rectal disturbance. Brain MRI revealed severe atrophy of the cerebellum. The cerebrum also showed diffuse atrophy and bilateral hyperintense lesions on T2WI in the basal ganglia and periventricular deep white matter. Thereafter, her condition slowly deteriorated and she demonstrated cognitive decline. At the age of 73 years, her unsteadiness worsened and she became bedridden. At the age of 76 years, she died of gallbladder cancer. General autopsy was performed, at which time the brain weighed 890 g.
test_results: Genetic analysis revealed an intermediate allele (41 and 38 CAG/CAA repeats) in TBP and a heterozygous missense mutation in STUB1 (p.P243L).

case_report: A 20-month-old boy presented with an unusual morphology of the right lower leg present since birth, along with complex preaxial polydactyly on the same side. Consent for data publication was obtained from the family. The child experienced no pain in the right leg, exhibited normal growth in height and weight, and showed no abnormalities in other body parts, including the skin, hair, and face. The mother's pregnancy and delivery were uneventful, and there were no similar conditions in other family members. Over time, the abnormalities in the right lower limb became more pronounced. At the clinic visit, the patient had not yet learned to walk but could crawl normally. Physical examination showed that the right tibia was anterolaterally angulated and approximately 8.0 cm shorter than the left tibia. The right foot was internally rotated, with restricted abduction and no dorsal extension. There was complex polydactyly on the lateral aspect of the first toe, and those toes were immobile.
test_results: Radiological examination of the right leg revealed shortening, widening and thinning of the tibial stem, slender fibula, dislocation of the ankle, complex polydactyly of the right toes, and a redundant metatarsal forming an articulation with the superfluous toes.

case_report: A 12-year-old female from Syria was referred to our center in Damascus. Her medical history includes pallor and anemia. She received erythrocyte transfusions at the age of 2 years and underwent a splenectomy at 8 years. Currently, she requires blood transfusions every 40 days. Her father exhibited characteristics consistent with a specific hematological condition, while her mother had normal blood indices with a borderline hemoglobin A2 level of 3.5%. Neither parent had splenomegaly or hepatomegaly and neither had ever received blood transfusions.
test_results: The electropherogram revealed a low level of (Hb A1) 52.6%, high level of (Hb F) 42.5% and (Hb A2) was 4.9%.

case_report: A 54-year-old Japanese woman presented to the outpatient clinic with a 20-year history of subcutaneous fat loss on her left upper limb. She has been receiving treatment for hypothyroidism for 22 years and for chronic rheumatoid arthritis for 11 years. There is no family history of similar conditions. Physical examination at the initial visit showed multifocal subcutaneous fat loss on both upper limbs, shoulders, back, abdomen, and the left lower limb.
test_results: A biopsy specimen from the right shoulder revealed a decrease in adipose tissue, a prominent increase in collagen fibers and dense infiltration of lymphocytes around the vesicles.

case_report: A 77-year-old male with a medical history including post-traumatic stress disorder, multiple cerebrovascular accidents, chronic kidney disease stage 3b, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, diabetic neuropathy, and benign prostatic hyperplasia presented with symptoms of increasing confusion, altered mental status, dystonia, tremor, and hallucinations. The family reported no history of neurological disease. The patient's daughter noted that he exhibited confusion and inappropriate speech. Upon admission for evaluation of altered mental status, the patient was alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation in the emergency department, though he exhibited shuddering while remaining neurologically intact. The patient displayed aggressive and agitated behavior and began wandering the hallways, necessitating 1:1 observation. A psychiatry consultation was requested for further evaluation.
test_results: A CT scan of the head without contrast had the impression of dense calcification of the dentate nuclei and the basal ganglia and subcortical calcification of the frontal and occipital lobes.

case_report: A 36-year-old female patient reported experiencing right ankle pain for the past four years. She had significant weight loss and began physical activity shortly before the onset of symptoms. There was no history of trauma. Initially, she was treated for synovitis with physical therapy, which did not yield significant improvement. She reported paraesthesia along the posterior and medial aspects of the ankle and foot, with symptoms worsening by the end of the day and episodes of cramping in the foot. Physical examination showed a positive dorsiflexion-eversion test that caused numbness in the foot. Tinel's sign was also positive. The range of motion in the ankle was limited due to pain, which was rated 8 on the Visual Analog Score (VAS). The patient had a preoperative score of 40 points according to the American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society (AOFAS). Bilateral electromyography (EMG) revealed abnormal neurophysiologic parameters in the adductor hallucis and adductor digiti quinti muscles compared to the asymptomatic side. Initial plain radiographs identified a significant (1.8 cm) posterior bone fragment associated with the talus.
test_results: CT scan showed the presence of an articulated accessory bone. MRI disclosed the presence of an inflammatory process, bone fragment covered with cartilage, and a degenerative synchondrosis as a consequence of posteromedial impingement.

case_report: A 51-year-old female patient, who smokes and has two children, reported experiencing visual impairment and headaches in November 2005. She has a past history of amenorrhea and galactorrhea from the age of 26 to 36. Imaging revealed a large pituitary mass. She underwent a transnasal transsphenoidal surgical procedure at another facility. The mass had extended into the cavernous sinus, preventing complete removal. Initial pathological examination identified the mass as PA. Two months later, she presented at our institution with recurring symptoms.
test_results: MRI revealed a 4.0 cm recurrent pituitary lesion, extending into the cavernous sinus, which was resected. Histology showed dense, highly cellular sheets and nests of monotonous cells with ovoid nuclei and focal clear-cell features. The tumor exhibited increased vascularity and was surrounded by fibrosis and fat necrosis. Immunohistochemical stains for Synaptophysin and CD31 were positive, and all pituitary hormones, including prolactin (PRL), were negative. Ki-67 labeling index (LI) was <3% and p53 showed rare positivity. MRI detected obstructing hydrocephalus. Cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) cytology was benign. Histology revealed sheets of neuroendocrine cells with bland nuclei, moderate cytoplasm and focal clear-cell features infiltrating fibrous tissue. The specimen also contained areas of fibrosis, fibroblasts, blood vessels, hemosiderin and focal necrosis. The tumor was morphologically and immunohistochemically similar to the previous resection. Ki-67 LI was in the range of 3 – 10%. p53 showed focal positivity. Histology was similar to the prior resection. Ki-67 LI at this time was >10%, p53 showed positivity in more than 50% of the cells. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated multiple liver lesions. The patient was also found to have multiple lung and humoral bone lesions, and abdominal lymphadenopathy. FNA was performed on a 2.0 cm liver lesion using a 22-gauge needle. Air-dried Diff-Quik stained slides were prepared. Smears showed loose clusters and microacini of monotonous moderate sized cells with mildly pleomorphic, round to oval eccentrically-placed nuclei with coarsely granular chromatin and small nucleoli. The cytoplasm was moderate in amount, clear and ill-defined or absent due to its extreme fragility. Touch imprints from concurrent core biopsy (CBx) of the liver mass showed uniform solid sheets of tumor cells. Overall, morphology was similar to the cells observed on FNA. Necrosis and mitotic activity were not observed. Immunohistochemical stains performed on CBx were positive for synaptophysin, CD31, p53 (majority of cells) and, Ki-67 LI was >10%. Immunohistochemical stains for other markers (Hepar, CK7, CK20, RCC, TTF-1) were negative.

case_report: An 11-year-old male patient was referred for evaluation of headache. His medical history includes asthma managed with olopatadine, pranlukast, carbocysteine, and inhaled salmeterol xinafate/fluticasone propionate, with no recent asthma attacks or changes in medication dosage. His birth and developmental history are normal, and there is no significant family medical history, including headaches or dysautonomia. The patient has been experiencing severe, sharp, pulsating headaches for 5 days. These headaches are strictly left-sided, located in the orbitofrontal and temporal regions, with no side shift. The pain is rated at 8 on the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS) and lasts between 2 to 20 minutes. The frequency of these pain episodes is 20-30 times per day, occurring more than 20 times during the day and 2-5 times at night. The headaches have a sudden onset and clear end, accompanied by left-sided autonomic symptoms such as conjunctival injection, lacrimation, nasal congestion, eyelid edema, and ptosis, but without facial sweating or miosis. Improvement in conjunctival injection and lacrimation is noted during interictal periods, though other cranial autonomic symptoms persist. There is no photophobia, phonophobia, allodynia, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, restlessness, or aggressive behavior. The headaches occur spontaneously without prodromal symptoms or triggers such as innocuous stimulation or exercise. During interictal periods, the patient is pain-free and able to engage in activities like playing soccer. Previous treatments with acetaminophen and 100% oxygen inhalation provided by his primary care physician were ineffective.
test_results: The patient underwent neurological examination, MRI/MRA/MRV of the head, and blood examinations, all yielding normal results. The blood examinations included biochemical, complete blood count, THS/FT3/FT4, rheumatoid factor, ss-A/ss-B, anti-nuclear antibody.

case_report: A 16-year-old male patient from Colombia, born to non-consanguineous parents, had an uncomplicated pregnancy and normal prenatal controls. He was delivered at 40 weeks gestation, weighing 3500 grams and measuring 54 cm in height, with an APGAR score of 8. Postaxial polydactyly was noted on the left hand's metacarpal, along with a prominent forehead and increased head diameter. At 8 months old, during surgery to correct the polydactyly, radiography revealed spina bifida occulta at S1 and scoliosis at the left dorsolumbar junction. A CT scan showed ventriculomegaly and non-progressive hydrocephalus. Physical and occupational therapy were administered to address axial-trunk-cervical tone and hypotonia. Auditory evoked potentials measured OD: 20 dB and OI: 30 dB, with impedanciometry indicating OD curve type C and OI curve type B, both with absent reflexes. Chromosomal analysis showed a normal karyotype of 46 XY. At 1 year old, a brain scan revealed prominent lateral ventricles, and metabolic screening returned negative results. At 2 years old, the patient underwent umbilical hernia repair and ventilatory tube surgery, which improved reflexes and balance.
test_results: An MRI of the head and neck showed alterations at the level of the posterior fossa, with absence of the vermis and horizontal disposition of the cerebellar peduncles.

case_report: A 46-year-old female with no notable medical or surgical history experienced lower limb weakness and moderate low back pain for four months. She was referred to the National Institute of Neurology and Neurosurgery Manuel Velasco Suarez for further evaluation. Physical examination revealed reduced strength in the lower limbs, with a score of 2/5 in the right pelvic limb and 3/5 proximally and 2/5 distally in the left pelvic limb according to Daniel's strength scale. Sensory examination indicated hypoesthesia in the T6 dermatome. Patellar and Achilles reflexes were minimally responsive. The patient also reported overflow incontinence and constipation with difficulty evacuating for the past month.
test_results: The thoracic region showed a hyperintense signal image in the spinal cord from T6 to T11 levels in T2 and short tau inversion recovery (STIR) sequences, which occupied more than 80% of the circumference of the spinal cord in axial sections. The image also showed enlarged perimedullary vessels in the posterior epidural region, with hyperintense signal voids in T1 and a hypointense signal in T2 sequences. We found a right perimedullary fistula type I, with a feeding artery of the radiculopial branch and a perimedullary venous drainage of the segmental artery of the right L2.

case_report: A 54-year-old Asian woman exhibited dense ribs and clavicles on chest X-ray, initially noted at age 20. By age 40, she developed a protruding chin, frontal bossing, and macrocephaly. Examination of the mandible showed bony enlargement over the anterior sides to angles without signs of inflammation. She experienced progressive bilateral visual and hearing impairments starting at ages 40 and 45, respectively. Additionally, she reported intermittent headaches, peripheral facial palsy (House Brackman Scale grade III), recurrent bilateral trigeminal neuralgia, and back pain since age 40. For pain management, she was treated with celecoxib (200 mg, twice daily), tramadol (100 mg every 6 hours), and pregabalin (75 mg, twice daily), but her pain remained significant (visual analog scale score > 4). Subsequently, she was administered oral morphine (15 mg every 4 hours) and duloxetine (60 mg daily) for severe pain and depression, which improved her pain but caused drowsiness, dizziness, and nausea, along with frequent falls. In December 2016, she attempted suicide by overdosing on sleeping pills. In March 2017, she underwent surgical decompression for spinal stenosis due to worsening back pain and progressive right arm clumsiness, resulting in significant improvement in these symptoms. Previous radiographs indicated increased thickness and hyperostosis of the calvaria and mandible, as well as progressive hyperostosis at the diaphysis of the femur and tibia, leading to narrowing of the medullary canal.
test_results: Her head computed tomography (CT) images in bone window in 2014 revealed a generalized thickening of the skull and mandible as well as a narrowing of the bilateral internal auditory canals. Dense abnormal bone was encroaching on otherwise normal inner ear structures such as the vestibule; the cochlea facial canals were compressed and could not be clearly identified; and the optic canals were narrow. Magnetic resonance (MR) images of the C-spine in 2015 revealed diffuse sclerosis with blastic changes in the visible bones and canal stenosis with cord compression from the C3 to C6 levels.

case_report: A 5-year-old female child presented with a two-month history of tense, fluid-filled lesions. Two weeks before these lesions appeared, she developed dark-colored, scaly, itchy skin lesions on her trunk and extremities. The fluid-filled lesions appeared on both normal skin and the pre-existing scaly lesions. She had an episode of chickenpox one month before the scaly skin lesions appeared. Physical examination showed multiple erythematous-to-violaceous papules and plaques, ranging in size from 0.3 mm to 5 cm, distributed over the trunk and extremities. Multiple tense bullae, some hemorrhagic, were predominantly found on the upper and lower extremities. Hyperkeratotic plaques with fissures were observed on the central aspects of both palms and soles, along with a few deep-seated vesicular lesions. There was no involvement of the oral cavity.
test_results: Histopathology of the bullous lesion revealed orthokeratosis, hypergranulosis, acanthosis, and subepidermal bulla with no acantholytic cells. Adjacent basal cells showed liquefactive degeneration with scattered mixed inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes and occasional plasma cells in the upper dermis. Apoptotic keratinocytes or civatte bodies were scattered in the epidermis. Biopsy from the papule revealed hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, acanthosis with pointed rete ridges, focal basal cell degeneration, melanin incontinence, perivascular and periappendageal inflammatory infiltrate of eosinophils, neutrophils and mononuclear cells. Direct immunofluorescence of biopsy drawn from peribullous skin revealed immunoglobulin G (IgG) and C3c deposition at BMZ and C3c deposition at appendages and vessel walls.

case_report: A 13-year-old boy presented with a two-year history of decreased visual acuity in both eyes. He had no significant medical or ocular history and was not on any medication. A brain MRI conducted a year earlier showed no abnormalities, and an electoretinogram (ERG) indicated reduced electrical activity. At the time of presentation, his best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 0.5 in both eyes, with spherical equivalents of +7.00 diopters. Slit lamp examination did not reveal any specific abnormalities. Fundus examination showed tortuous and dilated retinal vessels, serous retinal detachment, subretinal fluid at the periphery, choroidal folding, and an epiretinal membrane in both eyes. Axial lengths measured by A-scan were 18.96 mm in the right eye and 18.99 mm in the left eye.
test_results: A B-scan ultrasonogram showed thickened choroid, retinal detachment and choroidal detachment.

case_report: A 1-year-old girl was admitted to the hospital due to significant growth retardation. She was born to a nonconsanguineous couple, with the mother experiencing gestational diabetes in the third trimester. At 24+3 weeks of gestation, a color Doppler ultrasound revealed that one femur was shorter than expected for the gestational age, with a femur length to plantar length ratio of 0.81 and a proximal femur shaft-epiphysis angle greater than 116°, indicating abnormal skeletal development. Various genetic tests, including amniocentesis, high-throughput gene sequencing, prenatal screening, chromosome microarray analysis, and Sanger sequencing for the FGFR3 gene c.1138G > A variations, showed no abnormalities. By the time these results were available, the fetus was 29 weeks gestational age, and the family declined further genetic testing. The girl was delivered at 39+2 weeks via cesarean section with Apgar scores of 9, 10, and 10 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes, respectively. She was breastfed for ten months, with supplementary food introduced at 6 months. The child had a poor appetite from birth. Her birth weight was 3300 g (P55.8, Z score 0.15) and length was 48 cm (P40.5, Z score -0.24). At 6 months, her weight was 6.13 kg (P7.5, Z score -1.44), height was 59.5 cm (P0.3, Z score -2.76), and cranial circumference was 45.6 cm (P97.1, Z score 1.9). At 12 months, her weight was 7.62 kg (P9.0, Z score -1.34), length was 65.5 cm (< P0, Z score -3.33), and cranial circumference was 47.5 cm (P97.1, Z score 1.9). The ratio of crown-rump length to height was above the normal upper limit. Routine tests showed an increase in d-3-hydroxybutyric acid to 2.66 mmol/L (reference value: 0–0.27 mmol/L), while other parameters including routine blood tests, liver and kidney function, electrolytes, blood glucose, blood lactate, blood ammonia, pyruvic acid, ceruloplasmin, insulin-like growth factor-1, insulin-like growth factor-1 binding protein 3, thyroid stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, free triiodothyronine, and parathyroid hormone levels were normal. X-ray findings indicated decreased bone mineral density in the tubular bones and spinal column, thick and short humeri, and irregular metaphyses with a cup-shaped deformity. Brain cranial MRI findings were normal. The patient achieved head control at 5 months, could sit with assistance at 8 months, and began climbing at 12 months. The Gesell Developmental Schedules test indicated mild motor development delay due to malnutrition. Fetal DNA extracted from amniotic fluid and panel Sanger sequencing for FGFR3 gene c.1138G > A variations were negative.
test_results: The c.1620C > A pathogenic variations was detected in exon 12 of the proband, which is a pathogenicity variant leading to an amino acid change, p.Asn540Lys. No relevant variants were identified in the parents, whose genotypes were normal. Testing for the variant in the proband and her parents was performed by Sanger sequencing, and the variant met the criteria to be identified as a pathogenic variant, PS1 + PS2 + PS3-Supporting + PS4 + PM2-Supporting + PP3, according to the 2015 ACMG guidelines.

case_report: A 10-month-old male patient was admitted due to ongoing hepatitis and jaundice. He had no significant perinatal, familial, or past medical history, except for treatment for bronchitis at another hospital two weeks before admission. During his bronchitis treatment, elevated aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels were noted. Despite intact liver function initially, he progressed to impending hepatic failure and was referred to the hepatology department. Initial laboratory results indicated acute liver failure with AST at 194 IU/L, ALT at 69 IU/L, total bilirubin at 7.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin at 6.3 mg/dL, ammonia at 57 µg/dL, and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase at 101 IU/L. Blood gas analysis showed a normal pH of 7.40 and bicarbonate level of 25.8 mmol/L, with a slightly elevated lactate level of 2.4 mmol/L. Various evaluations, including viral, autoimmune, endocrinologic, and genetic studies for ATP7B and ABCB11, returned normal results, and imaging studies revealed no significant findings. The lactate-to-pyruvate ratio was 82.5, and a plasma amino acid assay indicated the possibility of lactic acidosis. His mental status declined, becoming drowsy with hyperammonemia, and he underwent a living donor liver transplantation on day 24 of admission. Pathological examination of the liver showed cirrhosis with significant fatty change, cholestasis, ballooning degeneration, and marked ductular proliferation, suggesting a metabolic condition. The liver transplantation was successful, and the patient was discharged with normal neurological function.
test_results: WES revealed the known compound heterozygous mutation of the POLG gene (p.Arg807His and p.Arg627Trp). EEG determined left periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges. Brain MRI showed multifocal diffusion restriction areas in the left insula, deep gray matter and bilateral perirolandic area.

case_report: A 56-year-old female experienced mild pain on the dorsomedial side of the right midfoot, which worsened with prolonged standing. Initial management included the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as diclofenac and ibuprofen. Due to ongoing discomfort, she sought further evaluation. Physical examination revealed tenderness and mild swelling over the dorsomedial area. The foot was plantigrade, with a slight reduction in the range of motion (ROM) of the ankle, while the hindfoot ROM remained normal. The American Orthopedic Foot and Ankle Score (AOFAS) was 80 out of 100. Radiographic imaging indicated minimal arthritic changes.
test_results: Alteration of the navicular bone in both T1- and T2-weighted images.

case_report: A 3-month-old male infant presented with bilateral corneal opacity present since birth and was referred from the pediatric unit for ophthalmic evaluation. The mother, aged 35 years at the time of childbirth, is HIV positive. Prenatal and natal history were otherwise unremarkable. There is no family history of similar ocular conditions or other congenital anomalies. Initial ophthalmic examination revealed a positive light pursuit and homogeneous bilateral central corneal opacity without neovascularization.
test_results: Ophthalmologic examination under general anesthesia revealed a deep anterior chamber with iris strands that crossed the anterior chamber from the iris. The lens was transparent on the edges and did not adhere to the cornea. The retina was difficult to evaluate because of central corneal opacity. The intraocular pressure measured with a Schiotz tonometer was respectively 18 mmHg and 20 mmHg in the right and left eye.

case_report: A 20-year-old woman presented with increasing difficulty in breathing during physical activity and was referred to our hospital for assessment of a mass in the mediastinum. She did not report any fever or weight loss. Physical examination and electrocardiogram results were normal. A chest X-ray showed a bulging mass opacity in the left upper hilar region. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a well-defined, lobulated, round mass compressing the main pulmonary trunk in the parasternal short axis view. Chest CT scan displayed a well-demarcated, lobulated mass measuring 7 × 4 × 4 cm with heterogeneous enhancement and a fat component located in the anterior mediastinum. The mass was compressing the main pulmonary trunk without definite invasion into the lung. The patient underwent surgical removal of the mass.
test_results: The excised mass consisted of multiple areas of mature epidermis with sebaceous glands, nests of respiratory epithelium and pancreatic tissue, and foci of mature adipose tissue.

case_report: The patient, a 4-year-old male, experienced intermittent high fevers and a mild cough for six weeks. Physical examination showed tachypnea without other respiratory symptoms, and the central nervous system examination was normal. Laboratory tests indicated hypogammaglobulinemia, elevated C-reactive protein levels, and mild pancytopenia. Sputum and blood cultures were negative for bacteria, fungi, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Additional tests, including serum fungal G test, galactomannan test, toxoplasma antibodies, cryptococcal antigens, anti-nuclear antibodies, double-stranded DNA, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and extractable nuclear antigens, were all negative. Bone marrow morphology was normal. Chest X-ray and CT scans showed diffuse lung infiltrates. The patient was treated with ganciclovir and a γ-globulin (400 mg/kg) infusion. Despite treatment, high fevers and coughing persisted, and the patient developed lethargy, slurred speech, and convulsions. A head CT scan revealed multiple low-density areas in the left frontal lobe, right temporal lobe, parietal lobe, left parietal-occipital lobe, bilateral basal ganglia, and trigone of the left lateral ventricle, with bleeding in the right temporal lobe. The patient succumbed to a pulmonary hemorrhage two weeks after admission. The patient had a history of recurrent respiratory tract infections and had been exposed to a cat since birth. Plasma DNA screening for HHV 1-8 virus infections using multiplex PCR was negative. Reverse transcription-quantitative PCR revealed an LCMV load of 7.8×105 copies/ml at admission and 2.3×106 copies/ml on the eleventh day of admission when the patient developed lethargy, slurred speech, and convulsions.
test_results: PCR amplification and sequencing results demonstrated that the proband carried both hemizygous SH2D1A c.7G>T/p.A3S and c.228T>A/p.Y76X mutations.
Orpha_name: X-linked lymphoproliferative disease due to SH2D1A deficiency

case_report: A 4-year-2-month-old boy was referred to the Endocrinology Clinic for evaluation of severe short stature. He was born at term via normal vaginal delivery to consanguineous parents. The family history included familial short stature. His weight was 13 kg (1.74th percentile), height was 85 cm (0.1 percentile), and head circumference was 47 cm (−3.3 SD) according to CDC growth charts. Vital signs included a blood pressure of 100/60 mmHg, heart rate of 85 bpm, and respiratory rate of 20 bpm. Physical examination revealed that he was conscious and oriented, with no facial dysmorphia. Notable findings included subtle short upper and lower limbs, bowing of the lower limbs, waddling gait, and hyperlordosis. Urogenital examination showed micropenis. The remainder of the physical examination was normal. Initial biochemical workup results were unremarkable. Hormonal workup indicated elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone and positive anti-tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A. Duodenal biopsies confirmed CD (Marsh type 3b). A computed tomography scan of the brain was performed due to mild microcephaly and was found to be normal.
test_results: A complete skeletal scan showed changes in the bone structure at the terminal parts of the femoral bones and no changes in the pelvis. There were no remarkable changes in the bone structure of the vertebrae.

case_report: A 55-year-old female patient experienced a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Following the seizure, she exhibited altered sensorium. Upon initial evaluation, her Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score was 7/15, and she showed right-sided hemiparesis. Due to her low GCS, she was intubated and placed on ventilator support. She has been receiving treatment for major depressive disorder for the past 5 years.
test_results: Patient underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of brain which showed a large ill-defined lesion in the left frontal lobe involving the centrum semiovale and ganglio capsular region. It was crossing the midline involving the cingulate gyrus, genu, body, and splenium of the corpus callosum with brain stem involvement. It displayed iso to hypointense in T1WI and predominantly hypreintense signal in T2WI. Postcontrast study showed patchy internal and thin rim of incomplete peripheral enhancement. There were gyral swellings with no midline shift. MR spectroscopy showed elevated choline peak in most of the regions with reduction in the NAA and tall lactate peak. MRI spine screening was normal. Repeat MRI was done after 3 days and it showed extensive progression of the lesions involving bilateral basal ganglia, brainstem till the medullary level and bilateral cerebellar peduncles. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis was done which showed normal sugar and cell count, but slight increase in protein level (68 mg/dl). Oligoclonal bands were absent. CSF culture and vasculitis work ups were negative. She was also tested for antiMOG and antiaquaporin-4 antibodies, which turned out to be negative.

case_report: A 62-year-old female experienced right-sided watery nasal discharge for 4 weeks. She noted spontaneous clear, salty nasal drainage without any preceding trauma. After two weeks, she began to have a frequent dry cough due to postnasal drip, which progressively worsened, particularly when lying down, interfering with her ability to sleep.
test_results: Sinus CT showed the lesion tissue extending from the right middle cranial fossa into sphenoid sinus through a local bone defect in the lateral wall of the right sphenoid sinus. Measurement of glucose level in nasal secretions was 4.4 mmol/L.
diagnosis: Spontaneous sphenoid sinus meningoencephalocele with cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea

case_report: A 69-year-old Caucasian woman reported new visual disturbances in her left eye, which began approximately ten weeks prior to her visit to the uveitis clinic in March 2023. She experienced new floaters and central flashing initially, followed by the development of an enlarging scotoma and progressive vision loss about four weeks later. Four weeks before the onset of these ocular symptoms, she tested positive for COVID-19 antibodies and experienced fever, congestion, and cough. She had received the COVID-19 vaccination several months before contracting the infection. Her medical history includes asthma, hypothyroidism, and headaches. There is no notable family history or prior autoimmune disease.
test_results: FAF showed peripapillary and macular hyper-autofluorescent spots in the posterior pole. These spots co-localized to punctate hyperfluorescent areas on FA, arranged in a wreath-like pattern with nearly well-defined borders. OCT examination featured disruption of the ellipsoid zone (EZ) and hyper-reflective subretinal deposits in the affected left eye.

case_report: The patient is a 10-year-old Sri Lankan girl of Sinhala ethnicity, born to healthy non-consanguineous parents with two older, healthy brothers. Her pregnancy and birth history were uneventful, and there was no family history of ophthalmological or neurological diseases. Developmental delays were noted by her parents, but no medical attention was sought. She began walking unaided at around 9 years old and has a significantly unsteady gait. Her hearing is unaffected, but speech was delayed, with her first word at 3 years old and currently speaking in 3–4-word complex sentences. Photophobia has been present since infancy. At 10 years old, her height was 132 cm (10th–25th percentile), weight was 26 kg (25th–50th percentile), and occipito-frontal circumference was 51 cm (25th–50th percentile). She had no dysmorphic features. A pigmented macule with a serpiginous border (22 cm × 10 cm) was observed on her right thigh. Neurological examination showed an ataxic gait, hypotonia, dysdiadochokinesia, intention tremor, horizontal nystagmus, and dysarthria. No pyramidal or extrapyramidal signs were present. She had bilateral pes planus. Ophthalmological examination revealed fixed and dilated pupils, bilateral partial aniridia with a scalloped edge of the irises, normal fundi, and impaired pupillary light reflexes. The cornea and lens were clear, and visual acuity was reduced (bilateral 6/30). IQ assessment indicated moderate learning disability with better verbal IQ than non-verbal IQ. Short-term memory was within normal limits, but there were deficits in long-term memory. MRI of the brain showed cerebellar hypoplasia, particularly affecting the vermis, and white matter changes. Cervical spine x-ray, echocardiogram, and ultrasound abdomen were normal.
test_results: This identified a previously described pathogenic heterozygous variant in the ITPR1 gene, namely c.7786_7788delAAG p.(Lys2596del).

case_report: A 20-year-old female with a history of low calcium levels was admitted due to unusual behavior. She was found by police to be agitated and speaking incoherently. Family members reported that she had been experiencing paranoid thoughts for the past two weeks. There was no history of psychiatric disorders, paranoid behavior, or recent use of alcohol, tobacco, or illicit substances. The patient was not on any medications or herbal supplements. A review of systems showed no additional concerns. There was no family history of psychiatric or neurological conditions on her mother's side, and information about her father's side was unavailable. Upon admission, her vital signs were normal. Physical examination showed that she was uncooperative, agitated, and had slurred speech. Neurological examination revealed brisk patellar reflexes and an unsteady gait, but was otherwise normal. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 9.5 gm/dL, serum iron of 44 µg/dL, serum ferritin of 6.9 ng/mL, and a total iron binding capacity (TIBC) over 450 µg/dL. A basic metabolic panel indicated a serum ionized calcium level of 3.7 mg/dL, potassium level of 4.4 mmol/L, and magnesium level of 1.6 mg/dL. Further evaluation of her low calcium levels revealed a parathyroid hormone (PTH) level of 11.3 pg/mL, vitamin D 25 hydroxy level of 11.8 ng/mL, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level of 0.65 µIU/mL, and free T4 level of 1.06 ng/dL. Liver function tests were normal. A urine toxicology screen was negative for substance abuse, and tests for ethanol, salicylates, acetaminophen, and tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) were all negative.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) of head showed prominent basal ganglia calcifications, with additional scattered calcifications in the periventricular and subcortical white matter.

case_report: An 11-year-old boy reported difficulty in eating and limited mouth opening for the past year. The patient described experiencing a burning sensation in the buccal mucosa when consuming spicy food during the same period. He had a habit of chewing tobacco and betel nut 15–20 times daily for the past 5 years and often kept the quid in the buccal vestibule. Clinical examination showed a maximum interincisal distance of 13 mm. Intraoral examination identified palpable fibrous bands over the labial and buccal mucosa, along with blanching of the palate, soft palate, and floor of the mouth. Tongue movements were restricted, and the uvula appeared shrunken.
test_results: Histopathological examination showed moderately hyalinised collagen in connective tissue stroma. Few areas show thickened collagen bundles. Inflammatory exudate chiefly consists of lymphocytes and plasma cells.

case_report: This case report describes a 48-year-old female with primary hyperthyroidism, initially presenting with a TSH level of 0.001 mUI/L (reference range: 0.5-4.0 mUI/L) and free thyroxine (FT4) level of 3.4 ng/dL (reference range: 0.7-2.0 ng/dL). The patient exhibited a diffuse goiter without clinical signs of thyroid orbitopathy and has been monitored since 2016. She received treatment with methimazole at doses ranging from 5 to 15 mg/day and propranolol at 40 mg/day. Despite more than 48 months of treatment with good adherence, the treatment could not be successfully discontinued, and hyperthyroidism reactivation was managed by reducing the antithyroid medication dose. Thyroid ultrasound revealed a diffuse goiter and three bilateral, solid, isoechoic thyroid nodules with increased central flow on color Doppler, regular borders, and no calcifications. Two nodules were located in the middle portion and lower pole of the right thyroid lobe, and one nodule was in the middle of the left thyroid lobe. The largest nodule in the lower right measured 1.3 × 1.1 × 0.8 cm. The patient did not exhibit exophthalmos. Due to administrative procedures, anti-TSH receptor antibody (TRAb) levels were not measured. Follow-up was interrupted due to the COVID-19 pandemic and resumed in October 2021.
test_results: Both TLs increased in size, with an entrapment index of 8% (normal value of 3.5%-5%). The parenchyma had a heterogeneous uptake with three hyper-uptake nodules, two in the right TL and one in the left TL without inhibiting the rest of the gland tissue.

case_report: A 62-year-old male presented with a history of developing a small number of papular lesions on his trunk 12 months prior. Over time, he progressively developed hundreds of elevated, brownish papular lesions across his body. These lesions were neither painful nor itchy. Some papules resolved spontaneously, but new lesions continued to appear. There were no precipitating factors and no other systemic issues. General medical examination showed no abnormalities. There was no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly on palpation. Cutaneous examination revealed a widespread papular eruption on the face, trunk, and proximal parts of the arms and legs, with the scalp, palms, and soles being spared. Mucous membranes were not involved. The individual lesions were non-confluent, hemispherical, and ranged from skin-colored to brown papules, measuring 3 to 8 mm in size; some had central umblication, resembling molluscum contagiosum. The patient reported spontaneous regression of some lesions, with focal residual hyperpigmentation at the sites of resolution. The eruption was asymptomatic. Routine hematology, biochemistry, immunoglobulin, autoantibodies, and lipid investigations were normal.
test_results: Histopathalogical study of a biopsy from representative lesion showed a normal epidermis along with dermal infiltration by histiocytic cells, having vacuolated cytoplasm at places, intermixed with inflammatory cells. Perivascular arrangement of histiocytic cells was also evident in some areas.

case_report: A ten-year-old boy presented with complaints of nasal regurgitation during eating and a desire for facial aesthetic correction. The family history was negative for cleft lip and palate. According to his mother, the patient was born after a full-term pregnancy without complications, and there was no history of maternal medication or illness during pregnancy. The patient had previously undergone repair of bilateral cleft lip at ten months old. Extraoral examination showed the premaxilla and maxillary central incisors hanging down, resulting in an unaesthetic appearance. The lower lip exhibited bilateral, paramedian small pits. Intraoral soft tissue examination revealed bilateral alveolar clefts in the premaxillary region. The maxillary arch was constricted with a high arched palate. The patient had mixed dentition with congenitally missing bilateral maxillary lateral incisors. Additionally, the patient reported recurrent respiratory tract infections, breathlessness, regurgitation of food, and a nasal twang during speech.
test_results: Radiographic examination from orthopantomograph (OPG) disclosed bilateral maxillary lateral incisor tooth germ was missing indicating hypodontia.

case_report: A 28-year-old female experienced recurrent episodes of vomiting, general discomfort, and diarrhea over a 3-year period from 2004 to 2007. She was hospitalized twice due to low sodium levels, with the lowest recorded serum sodium being 114 mEq/L. Her sodium levels returned to normal with saline treatment, and her low sodium was attributed to gastroenteritis and dehydration. In July 2007, she presented again with general discomfort and recurrent vomiting, and was admitted with a sodium level of 112 mEq/L. An endocrinology consultation revealed a low calcium level (7.8 mg/dL), low serum osmolality (247 mOsm/kg), low urine osmolality (419 mOsm/kg), low phosphorus level (2.9 mg/dL), and low parathyroid hormone level (2.9 pg/mL). A repeat urine osmolality was elevated (1026 mOsm/kg). The rest of her chemistry panel, urine sodium, cortisol, and thyroid function tests were normal. She was diagnosed with chronic SIADH and started on an oral course of demeclocycline to maintain sodium levels. An abdominal CT scan showed bilateral kidney stones without any signs of neoplastic processes. A brain MRI with gadolinium revealed a heterogeneous mass in the left nasal cavity, with high T2 and low T1 signal, without intracranial involvement. A CT scan of the sinuses showed a slow-growing mass with stippled calcifications centered at the left ostiomeatal unit and middle turbinate, extending into the left maxillary sinus and superiorly toward the cribriform plate. The patient was referred to otolaryngology for evaluation of the nasal mass. Endoscopic examination revealed a 2 cm smooth-bordered, polypoid mass at the left ostiomeatal unit extending superiorly and toward the nasal septum. An outpatient tissue biopsy of this mass indicated glial tissue, most likely glioma. Surgical removal of the tumor was recommended. During this period, the patient discovered she was 10 weeks pregnant. After consulting with the Obstetrics department, it was decided to proceed with surgical removal due to the potential risk of recurrent low sodium levels during pregnancy.
test_results: Histologic examination of hematoxylin and eosin-stained slides demonstrated a proliferation of small, hyperchromatic cells exhibiting a predominantly nested pattern, in a background of fibrillar material with prominent dystrophic calcifications and a few pseudorosettes. The tumor was immunoreactive for chromogranin, glial fibrillary acid protein, pancytokeratin, neurofilament protein, neuron-specific enolase, Neu-N, S-100, and synaptophysin.
