case_report: This nine-year-old Caucasian girl was born at 41 weeks’ gestation via induced vaginal delivery, weighing 3260g. At birth, she exhibited hypotonia and lethargy, with initial feeding difficulties requiring nasogastric tube feeding for one month. She has physical characteristics including almond-shaped eyes, down-turning corners of the mouth, small hands, and a prominent metopic suture. Additional features include gross motor delay, social delay, obsessive-compulsive behavior, and rigid thinking. Family history includes several members, including the patient's father, with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS), but none report symptoms such as cataplexy, hypnagogic hallucinations, or sleep paralysis. At age two years and 10 months, she was referred to a pediatric pulmonologist for a screening sleep study prior to growth hormone therapy. An initial overnight oximetry study showed normal results with no significant desaturations. During a follow-up, the patient's mother reported episodes where the patient would fall forward for a few seconds with eyes rolling back, appearing unresponsive but conscious. These episodes occurred three to four times per week, often triggered by laughter, typically after waking from a nap, and resolved spontaneously without post-episode sleepiness. The episodes were not associated with seizures, as there was no other motor activity, eye deviation, or stereotypy. Daytime hypersomnia was also noted, with the patient sleeping more than 12 hours per night and taking a two- to three-hour daytime nap.
test_results: The initial sleep study revealed adequate sleep efficiency, but disrupted sleep overall. Specifically, our patient did not cycle through all stages of sleep as expected; sleep fragmentation was noted, especially during the REM phase. Mild sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) was identified, consisting of four central apneas, one obstructive apnea, and three mixed apneas, particularly within REM sleep. Two obstructive, but no central, hypopneas were observed. The apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) was 1.4 events per hour. The average end-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO2) measurement was 45mmHg (maximum of 61mmHg). The average oxygen saturation (SpO2) was 95 percent (minimum of 78.7 percent). The results of the second PSG study were abnormal and suggestive of narcolepsy. Spikes were noted on electroencephalography without any seizure activity and a shortened REM sleep latency was observed. The overall degree of SDB was improved compared to the previous measurement. Abnormal respiratory events were limited to one obstructive apnea and two obstructive hypopneas with an AHI of 0.4 events per hour. The average EtCO2 was 46mmHg; the SpO2 was also improved with an average of 95 percent (minimum of 87 percent). Another follow-up PSG was done at age six years and 10 months. This PSG again showed excellent sleep efficiency and decreased REM sleep latency. However, worsening sleep disruptions were observed, with increased spontaneous arousals. SDB or obstructive sleep apnea in REM sleep (an AHI of 4.4 events per hour) were also worse than previous observations. Finally, a multiple sleep latency test (MSLT) was performed to objectively quantify the degree of sleepiness. This test consisted of five nap opportunities, given at two-hour intervals. Her MSLT results showed the following sleep latencies on five respective naps: 9min 18sec; 1min 44sec; 54sec; 6min 23sec; 3min 55sec. The overall mean sleep latency was 4min 27sec. Two SOREM periods were also noted.

case_report: A 32-year-old male of Indian descent, born to non-consanguineous parents, came to the hospital with headaches and episodic vertigo following a low-speed motor vehicle accident a week earlier, during which he struck his head but did not lose consciousness. In the preceding months, he experienced mild headaches, unsteadiness, subtle behavioral changes, and itching. His medical history includes poorly controlled childhood focal epilepsy, with a significant episode at age four involving oral ulcerations, encephalitis, and right-hand weakness. During adolescence and early adulthood, his condition improved with carbamazepine and phenytoin, which were discontinued before he moved to Australia in his mid-20s. Despite this, he continued to have episodic oral mucositis, managed with intermittent vitamin supplements (B12, folate, and nicotinamide) until six months before his current presentation. In the subsequent weeks, he exhibited rapidly worsening cognitive and behavioral disturbances, multidirectional nystagmus, ataxia, progressive myoclonic twitches affecting the face and upper limbs, and autonomic dysfunction characterized by tachycardia, urinary retention, and bowel ileus. A skin biopsy confirmed superficial perivascular dermatitis. Later, he developed severe oral mucositis and required intubation due to a threatened airway and progressive encephalopathy.
test_results: Rapid whole genome sequencing identified a homozygous variant in NAXD [Chr13(GRCh37):g.111279897A>G; NM_001242882.1:c.441+3A>G:p.?], absent in ClinVar and Genome Aggregation Databases. Studies of NAXD pre-mRNA splicing using blood RNA show a near loss of NAXD transcripts with canonical exon 4-5-6 splicing, with no reads detected by RNA-Seq and only a faint band using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). c.441+3A>G causes the skipping of exons 4 and 5 (r.244_441del;p.Ala83_Gly148del), removing 66 conserved amino acids from the carbohydrate kinase domain, or the skipping of exon 5 (r.333_441del; p.Asp112Alafs*67), inducing a frameshift encoding 66 amino acids and a premature stop codon resulting in nonsense-mediated decay. The trace levels of correctly spliced NAXD transcripts, reproducibly detected with several PCR primer pairs, support a severe deficiency, but not complete absence, of NAXD.

case_report: A 66-year-old male presented with a non-painful, slowly enlarging papule on the chin, persisting for one year. On physical examination, the lesion was firm, skin-colored, and measured 4 × 5 mm. Dermoscopy showed a whitish-pinkish homogenous area without specific features, along with prominent follicular openings and linear vessels on an erythematous background in both the lesion and surrounding sun-damaged skin. Reflectance Confocal Microscopy (RCM) revealed a honeycomb pattern with mild disarray at the epidermal level, absence of atypical cells, presence of bright inflammatory cells, and reduced epidermal thickness. The Dermoepidermal Junction (DEJ) displayed sparse rings. Additionally, there was squamous hyperplasia with irregular finger-like protrusions around the hair follicle and papillomatous hyperplasia in the hair follicle epithelium. Coarse collagen fibers were noted beneath the follicles at the dermal level.
test_results: Multiple radiate small abortive hair follicles of varying degrees of maturity around a few central dilated primary follicles filled with loose keratin were seen. The abortive hair follicles were secondary or tertiary follicles. The stroma between the follicles was cellular, vascularized with some lymphoid cells. Some of the abortive hair follicles located beneath the epidermis. The epidermis was thin and rete ridges were flattened.

case_report: A 20-year-old woman from the Northeastern region of Brazil was admitted to the Fundação de Hematologia e Hemoterapia de Pernambuco (HEMOPE) during her first pregnancy. Laboratory results showed microcytosis (mean corpuscular volume of 74 fL/red cell), hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin of 6.5 g/dL and mean corpuscular hemoglobin of 21.8 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (platelets of 11 × 10^9/L), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) of 183 U/L, reticulocyte count of 1.82%, serum iron of 38 μg/dL, and transferrin saturation of 11.8%. She experienced ecchymosis and severe hemorrhagic events in the second month of gestation. Prothrombin and activated thromboplastin time were within normal ranges. Physical examination revealed a conscious, afebrile, anicteric, and pale woman in good general condition. She was oriented, cooperative, and had no edema. Her mental status was normal, with no spinal deformity, tenderness, subcutaneous nodules, or focal neurological deficits. Motor and sensory examinations were normal. Mild petechial lesions were noted on her lower and upper limbs. Her blood pressure was 140/80 mmHg. Ultrasound examination showed a fetus in a transverse position with normal biometrics, amniotic fluid, and placenta. The fetal heart rate was 140 beats per minute, and there were no contractions. Other laboratory data showed no significant changes, and renal function was normal. She had no history of excessive alcohol consumption, tobacco use, or illicit drug use. Her family history was negative for neurological and hematologic diseases, although a cousin had thrombocytopenia and died without a definitive diagnosis. Initial clinical investigation suggested a condition based on the absence of schizocytes in peripheral blood and nonspecific myelogram findings. Bone marrow examination showed hypercellularity for erythroid (27% cellularity), granulocytic (61% cellularity), and megakaryocytic sectors with some atypical features and decreased platelet genesis. Treatment with prednisone (60 mg per day) was initiated but was ineffective, leading to immunoglobulin therapy. The patient continued to have low platelet counts (17 × 10^9/L) and severe hemorrhagic events (gingivorrhagia, epistaxis), prompting a splenectomy. One week post-surgery, she developed high blood pressure, headache, hepatic enzyme alterations, and an LDH of 1675 U/L, leading to a cesarean delivery at 27 weeks' gestation due to a clinical framework suggestive of hemolysis with elevated liver enzymes and low platelet count. The baby was born healthy with no clinical complications.
test_results: The results of ADAMTS 13 enzyme activity < 5% were received with no inhibitor present.

case_report: A 55-year-old African-American woman residing in the United States was admitted to the hospital with a four-day history of mental status changes and left-sided weakness. Her family reported unusual behavior, including aggression towards her niece. The patient mentioned that her family members were trying to harm her and reported hearing fire alarms constantly going off in her house. Her medical history included type II diabetes mellitus, hypertension, breast cancer, and hypothyroidism. She had no history of psychiatric or seizure disorders. Vital signs were stable: blood pressure was 122/62 mm Hg, respiratory rate was 14 breaths per minute, heart rate was 98 beats per minute, and temperature was 36.4ºC. On examination, she was awake, alert, and oriented only to her name. Heart, lung, and abdominal examinations were normal, as was the thyroid examination. Neurological examination showed disorientation to place and time, poor memory, agraphia, dyslexia, and an unusual form of aphasia where she could not read or write but could spell words on request. Her speech was non-fluent with marked hesitation. Pupils were equal and reactive to light. Fundoscopic examination was not possible due to bilateral cataracts. Cranial nerve and sensory examinations were normal. Muscle strength and deep tendon reflexes were normal. Complete blood count results were normal. Metabolic panel testing showed a serum glucose level of 458 mg/dl. TSH levels were elevated at 15 UIU/ml.
test_results: Microsomal antibodies was raised at 617 IU/ml.
Orpha_name: Steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis

case_report: A 17-year-old female presented to the Liver Unit with severe jaundice, pruritus accompanied by scratching-induced hematomas, and generalized weakness over the past 2 months. She also reported amenorrhea, diarrhea, and a weight loss of approximately 10 kg during this period. One week prior to the onset of pruritus, she experienced fever and cough, which were treated with clarithromycin and paracetamol, resulting in clinical improvement. She mentioned a previous episode of pruritus 2 years ago, which resolved spontaneously within a month without associated jaundice. Family history revealed that her mother and maternal aunt had undergone cholecystectomy for gallstones at ages 20 and 30, respectively. Laboratory findings on admission included total bilirubin 25.8 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 23.5 mg/dL, aspartate transaminase 121 UI/L, alanine transaminase 125 UI/L, alkaline phosphatase 334 UI/L, GGT 19 UI/L, amylase 101 UI/L, serum iron 265 µg/dL, triglycerides 286 mg/dL, total cholesterol 170 mg/dL, creatinine 0.77 mg/dL, sodium 141 mmol/L, potassium 5 mmol/L, albumin 4.2 g/dL, hemoglobin 11.3 g/dL, white blood cell count 1.242 × 10^9/L, platelets 444 × 10^9/L, international normalized ratio 0.97, partial thromboplastin time 32.5 s, fibrinogen 747 mg/dL, and serum bile acid 99.8 mmol/L. Tests for viral hepatitis A, B, C, and E were negative, as were molecular tests for intestinal pathogens in stool samples. IgM and IgG antibodies against Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) were positive, but EBV-DNA was undetectable. Autoantibodies including anti-mitochondrial, anti-nuclear, anti-smooth muscle, anti-liver/kidney microsome-1, and anti-transglutaminase were negative. Immunoglobulin levels and IgG subclasses were within normal ranges. Abdominal MRI showed no biliary obstruction or gallstones. Endoscopic ultrasonography confirmed the absence of biliary tract dilatation and anatomical obstruction.
test_results: The analysis showed compound heterozygosity for two variants in the ABCB11 gene: c.1460G>A–p.(Arg487His) and c.2599C>T–p.(Gln867*). Segregation analysis revealed biparental inheritance of the variants: the father and mother were heterozygotes for c.1460G>A and c.2599C>T, respectively. Sanger sequencing has confirmed the presence of the ABCB11 mutations.

case_report: The older brother of the proband is a 9-year-old boy without microcephaly. He began speaking after more than 12 months and exhibited unsteady walking at the age of 2 years, frequently falling down. He experienced episodes of reduced movement occurring about once or twice a month, each lasting 1–5 minutes. At 3 years old, he had episodes of binocular gaze with clear consciousness, resembling atypical absence seizures. His physical examination was unremarkable, and developmental assessment indicated mild developmental delay. Brain MRI, video EEGs, serum biochemistry values, and metabolic screening results were all normal. Sodium valproate (VPA) was administered, leading to partial alleviation of symptoms.
test_results: CSF analysis indicated hypoglycorrhachia (CSF glucose: 2.6 mmol/L; CSF/blood glucose ratio: 0.481) and gene panel sequencing indicated a pathogenic mutation in the SLC2A1 gene c.73C > T (p.Q25X).
Orpha_name: Classic glucose transporter type 1 deficiency syndrome

case_report: A 17-month-old girl was admitted with a single subcutaneous nodule on the right forearm. The nodule showed no signs of pain, swelling, or erythema and had been gradually increasing in size over the past three months. The patient, born in Shanghai, had no significant health issues previously. On physical examination, a 2.0 × 1.5 cm soft, movable, and nontender mass was found on the distal right forearm. The elbow and wrist had full-range movement. Laboratory tests revealed a peripheral white blood cell count of 7.9 × 10^9 cells/L, serum C-reactive protein (CRP) less than 1 mg/L, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 12 mm/hour, all within normal limits. A PCR test for Human herpesvirus-6 (HHV-6) DNA sequences was negative. MRI scans of the mass showed medial signal intensity on T1-weighted images (TR/TE 450/35 ms) and high signal intensity on T2-weighted images (TR/TE 2500/100 ms), with strong enhancement following gadolinium contrast injection. Fat-suppressed images also showed high signal intensity on both T1-weighted and T2-weighted images, with strong enhancement after gadolinium contrast injection.
test_results: Histologically, sections of HE stain showed a diffused infiltration of large histiocytes, lymphocytes, and plasma cells with scattered neutrophils. The histiocytes showed abundant pale eosinophilic cytoplasm and mildly atypical round vesicular nuclei. Immunohistochemical results were positive for S-100 protein, CD68, and negative for CD1a. Moreover, immunohistochemical stains for monoclonal cytokeratin 7, cytokeratin 20, epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), myeloperoxidase (MPO), calretinin, mesothelial cell, actin, desmin, human melanoma black-45 (HMB-45), melanoma, CD3, CD15, CD30, CD31, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) were all negative. Lymphocyte phagocytosis (emperipolesis) was detected.

case_report: A 66-year-old male with a history of tuberculosis experienced cough and expectoration without clear cause, dyspnea on exertion, dizziness, and tinnitus in 2014. These symptoms worsened in 2017, accompanied by significant white phlegm, shortness of breath at rest, night sweats, weight loss, and fatigue. Despite being treated for tuberculosis, there was no improvement. In 2020, chest computed tomography at a local hospital showed pneumonic lesions in both lungs, mediastinal lymph node enlargement, bilateral pleural thickening, and bronchodilation changes. A soft tissue mass was also noted in the upper right lung lobe, but the imaging features were unclear. The patient was then transferred to our hospital's respiratory department for further evaluation. A routine color Doppler ultrasound revealed a large amount of right-sided pleural effusion with a maximum anteroposterior diameter of 160 mm, potentially indicating inflammation in the right lung. Laboratory results on admission indicated inflammation (white blood cell count of 14.3 × 10^9/L and erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 75 mm/h), mild anemia (hemoglobin of 92 g/L), malnutrition (serum albumin of 26.7 g/L), and elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase (347 U/L). Serum immunoglobulin (Ig) M and λ-light chain levels were elevated to 13.4 g/L and 3.58 g/L, respectively. Serum protein electrophoresis showed a notable M-spike, indicating high monoclonal Ig levels. Immunofixation electrophoresis (IFE) revealed visible bands of IgG, IgM, IgA, and λ-light chain. This inconsistency was re-evaluated using 5% β-mercaptoethanol (β-ME) to depolymerize the serum, but the results remained unchanged, indicating large amounts of abnormal immunoglobulins in the patient's blood. The patient was then referred to the hematology department.
test_results: HE staining of the lung tissue biopsy showed a scattered adenoid structure with peripherally diffuse infiltration of B lymphocytes of different sizes. Immunohistochemical analysis was positive for cluster of differentiation (CD) 20, CD21, CD79a, Bcl-2, Bcl-6, Ki-67 (15–20%) and λ-light chain expression, but negative for CD10, CD43, cyclin D, keratin AE1/AE3, epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), thyroid transcription factor 1 (TTF-1) and κ-light chain expression. Bone marrow gene molecular testing showed that T-cell receptor (TCR)β, TCRγ and TCRδ rearrangements were negative, whereas that of immunoglobulin light chain kappa (IGK) was positive.
diagnosis: Primary Pulmonary Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue  Lymphoma

case_report: A 53-year-old African American male with a history of developmental delay, schizophrenia, and paranoia underwent an emergent exploratory laparotomy and small bowel resection followed by a primary end-to-end anastomosis due to multiple self-inflicted stab wounds. During the exploratory laparotomy, no varices were observed in the abdomen, and the liver appeared normal. On postoperative day 10, the patient developed melena and epigastric pain, and his hemoglobin level decreased from 10 g/dL to 7 g/dL. A repeat exploratory laparotomy and computed tomography angiogram (CTA) did not identify the source of the bleeding.
test_results: Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) was performed and showed a large isolated gastric varix (IGV-1) in the fundus and no esophageal varices. The IGV-1 had an area with active oozing. On interventional radiology (IR) evaluation, it was noted that the portal vein and the splenic vein were widely patent, and his portal pressures were normal with a 4 mmHg hepatic venous pressure gradient, yet there were multiple large gastric varices without active bleeding.

case_report: Patient 4 is a 34-year-old Turkish woman who has experienced arm and leg weakness and muscle atrophy since she was 15 years old. There is no family history of neuromuscular disease, and her 5 siblings do not exhibit any symptoms. She has been taking riluzole since she was 15 years old. Her symptoms have shown slow progression over time. During her most recent evaluation at age 34, she was using a wheelchair but could walk short distances with assistance. She did not have difficulty swallowing and did not need oxygen supplementation. Her weight was within normal limits.
test_results: Neurophysiological examination revealed denervation activity in all muscles and no evidence of multifocal motor neuropathy.

case_report: A 36-year-old Hindu, Indian male presented with complaints of bony pain, limping, kyphosis, a dragging sensation in the left abdomen, and ptosis of the eyelids for approximately one year. The patient has a past history of epilepsy and seizures, which have been controlled for the last twenty years. General physical examination was unremarkable. Hematological investigations revealed mild anemia, a total leukocyte count of 4,000/cumm, and platelet count of 1.5 lakhs/cumm. Peripheral smear findings indicated mild dimorphic anemia with eosinophilia.
test_results: Bone marrow examination found particulate, cellular smears M:E: 3:1. Erythropoiesis was dimorphic. Megakaryocytes seen in adequate number and function. Myelogram showed myeloblast 03%, promyelocyte 01%, myelocyte 10%, metamyelocyte 20%, plasma cell 01%, polymorphs 47%, lymphocytes10%, eosinophills 08%. In addition, B.M. showed large number of large cells 30 to 100 microns in diameter having one to multiple, centrally or eccentrically placed nuclei with pale, blue-gray cytoplasm having characteristic fibrally and striated pattern. These cells stained strongly with P.A.S staining and were Sudan Black negative.

case_report: A seven-month-old male, born at term via spontaneous vaginal delivery without complications, presented multiple times to the emergency room due to severe diarrhea episodes starting at four months of age. The patient, born to non-consanguineous parents with two healthy older siblings and no significant family history, experienced watery stools 10-15 times daily, unrelated to acute illness. Initially formula-fed, his symptoms worsened with the introduction of solid foods at six months. There was no history of vomiting, poor feeding, or recurrent infections. Development and immunizations were appropriate for his age. Physical examination revealed the patient was underweight, thin, and pale, with a weight below the third percentile and a significantly protruded abdomen, but no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. Other systems were unremarkable. Extensive diagnostic workup, including basic routine labs, sweat chloride test, anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA, food and cow milk allergy testing, and upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, showed normal results. Neutropenia was noted, potentially due to folate and vitamin B12 deficiency. Various dietary restrictions, including a gluten-free diet, were attempted without improvement.
test_results: WES identified the pathogenic heterozygous variant c.765C>G p.(Cys255Trp) in SLC5A1 (OMIM: 182380). WES also identified another heterozygous variant c.899G>A p.(Arg300His) in SLC5A1 (OMIM: 182380).

case_report: A 33-year-old woman with a 30-month history of primary infertility and a body-mass index (BMI) of 22.22 kg/m2 presented with polycystic-like ovaries identified by imaging. Her husband exhibited mild oligoastenozoospermia. Controlled ovarian stimulation was conducted using an individualized protocol with gonadotropins in a down-regulated cycle. Ovarian stimulation lasted 10 days with daily administrations of 87.5 IU recombinant FSH, totaling 875 IU, leading to the development of 20 follicles larger than 14 mm. Ovulation was triggered with 5000 IU of highly purified hCG, and 36 hours later, 20 oocytes were retrieved. Estradiol levels were measured at 4932 pg/ml on the day of oocyte maturation triggering. All embryos obtained by intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) were frozen. Four months later, a frozen embryo replacement cycle was initiated after the ovaries returned to normal size. Luteal phase support included oral administrations of 2 mg estradiol valerate twice daily. Endometrial maturation was monitored by serial imaging starting from day 12 of the natural cycle. Daily intravaginal progesterone was initiated when endometrial thickness reached 8–12 mm. Embryo transfer occurred 3 days after the first progesterone administration. Medical treatment continued until serum hCGβ testing, which was scheduled 14 days post-embryo transfer. Two consecutive positive hCGβ tests confirmed implantation. Imaging performed 4 weeks later revealed two dichorionic diamniotic gestational sacs.
test_results: Ultrasonography showed bilateral enlarged ovaries; the right ovary measured 11.78 × 6.39 cm, while the left one 9.73 × 8.14 cm. No free fluids were identified in the pelvis and abdomen, apart from a light fluid spilling in the right paracolic gutter.

case_report: A 50-year-old woman experienced progressive quadriparesis following a febrile illness. Initially, she noticed weakness in her left upper and lower limbs on the third day after the fever began. The weakness then spread to the right side the following day. Over the next few days, she developed urinary incontinence, double vision, facial weakness, slurred speech, and difficulty swallowing. Physical examination revealed bilateral 6th, 7th, 9th, and 10th cranial nerve palsies, spastic quadriparesis, exaggerated tendon reflexes, and upgoing plantar reflexes. She had a history of long-standing nodular skin lesions on her lower limbs and back, which were biopsied in 2009 and showed features of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (Mycosis fungoides). She was treated with vincristine and had no skin lesions at the time of presentation, nor was she on any immunosuppressive therapy. An MRI scan of the brain revealed a bulky pons with iso to mildly hypointense lesions on T1-weighted images, which appeared hyperintense on T2 and FLAIR images. These lesions exhibited gadolinium contrast enhancement, creating a characteristic peppering appearance in the pons. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed a protein level of 108 mg/dL and glucose level of 86 mg/dL, with 0 RBCs, 2 WBCs, no bacteria on Gram stain, and negative results for AFB smear and fungal mount. Cultures showed no growth, and cytological examination revealed no malignant cells. Tests for CNS vasculitis, including anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic auto-antibodies (ANCA), anti-SSA/Ro, anti-SSB/La, dsDNA, and anti-Sm, were negative. Infectious screening for HIV, Hepatitis A/B/C, and tuberculosis were also negative. Chest X-ray and serum ACE levels were normal.
test_results: A CT-guided stereotactic biopsy of the pontine lesion revealed a marked lymphocytic infiltrate in the white matter with perivascular predominance. The lymphocytic infiltrate was composed predominantly of T lymphocytes that were CD3 reactive and few CD20-positive B lymphocytes. A few CD68-positive histiocytes were also seen. Myelin was intact, there were no granulomas, and special stains for fungi and AFB were negative.
diagnosis: Chronic lymphocytic inflammation with pontine perivascular enhancement responsive to steroids
Orpha_name: Chronic lymphocytic inflammation with pontine perivascular enhancement responsive to steroids

case_report: A 93-year-old patient presented with low potassium levels, malnutrition, and reduced kidney function identified by a family physician. The patient had a history of multiple bowel resections over the past five years. She experienced diarrhea for approximately three months, which resolved on its own, and she had no abdominal symptoms. However, one year before admission, she developed watery diarrhea that did not significantly improve with antidiarrheal medication. Her medical history included colonic perforation, abdominal wall hernia with strangulated ileus, and resection of approximately 2.3 meters (59.1 inches) of the terminal ileum. Five years prior, she underwent surgery for strangulated ileus, resulting in the resection of the small intestine, 7 cm from the terminal ileum and 50 cm from the ligament of Treitz. Upon presentation, her vital signs were as follows: blood pressure 95/67 mmHg, heart rate 59 beats per minute, oxygen saturation 95%, and temperature 36.6 °C. Physical examination revealed normal breath sounds and heart sounds with mild systolic murmurs. The abdomen was flat and soft, Murphy’s sign was negative, and there was no costovertebral angle tenderness. Lower leg edema was noted. Blood test results were: white blood cell count 15.30 × 103/μ (neutrophils 78.3%, lymphocytes 15.5%, monocytes 5.6%, eosinophils 0.4%, basophils 0.2%), red blood cell count 3.34 × 106/μ, hemoglobin 11.3 g/dL, hematocrit 33.2%, platelet count 27.9 × 104/μ, total bilirubin 1.6 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 48 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase 37 IU/L, total protein 5.2 g/dL, albumin 2.5 g/dL, blood urea nitrogen 18.7 mg/dL, creatinine 1.13 mg/dL, sodium 143 mEq/L, potassium 1.7 mEq/L, chloride 99 mEq/L, calcium 5.0 mg/dL, phosphorus 2.8 mg/dL, magnesium 0.8 mg/dL, and estimated glomerular filtration rate 34.1 mL/min/L.
test_results: An abdominal computed tomography showed mild oedema of the colon, and no other obvious abnormalities. No obvious organic abnormalities were noted on imaging, but the bowel was shortened because of repeated bowel resections. Colonic specimens showed only nonspecific inflammatory findings. The colonoscopy did not reveal any specific findings. Stool culture and histopathological examination did not reveal the exact cause.

case_report: A 21-year-old female patient presented with malformed teeth since their eruption. The patient observed the malformation from the time of tooth eruption, with no history of sensitivity or pain. The deciduous teeth were also yellowish but to a lesser extent. Past medical history includes convulsions starting at 6 months old, treated with anticonvulsants (Tab Diamox 250 mg thrice daily) until the age of five. The patient experienced delayed developmental milestones and was hospitalized at six years old due to progressive leg deformities. At 15 years old, she sustained a fracture in her left thigh following a minor fall. Her family, including parents, brothers, and a sister, are of normal stature and in good health, with no family history of consanguinity, skeletal abnormalities, or dwarfism. The drinking water at her residence is not fluorinated. On general physical examination, the patient was of short stature with short limbs and a normal-sized trunk. There was noticeable lateral bowing of the legs with slight muscle wasting but no limitation of hip movements. Vital signs and cranial nerve assessments were normal. Head and neck examination revealed a relatively large head without prognathism, exophthalmos, or facial paralysis. Intraoral examination showed microdontia with generalized enamel pitting, yellowish discoloration, and open contacts between the teeth. The crowns appeared malformed. Full mouth intraoral periapical radiographic survey indicated generalized blunting of root apices, decreased enamel density, and reduced enamel thickness. Pulp chambers and canals appeared normal. Skull radiograph showed a thick and sclerotic skull vault with widened diploë, and lateral cephalogram indicated a hypoplastic frontal sinus with midface hypoplasia. Long bone radiographs revealed increased pelvic bone density, a previous fracture site at the subtrochanteric region of the left femur, lateral bowing and cortical thickening of the right femur with a fracture along the lateral aspect at the mid-region. There was bilateral coxa valga deformity.
test_results: Reports showed she had high serum levels of phosphorus (140 mg/dl) and alkaline phosphatase (1149 U/L). Serum alkaline phosphatase assay was carried out which was then high (346 U/L), but serum phosphorus level was normal. Biochemical analysis showed an elevated level of serum alkaline phosphatase (192 U/L).

case_report: A 17-year-old girl, born in Italy, with parents who are not related and do not have similar conditions. She is the younger sibling of another case. At birth, she presented with cleft lip and palate, facial abnormalities, foot deformities, and was described as a collodion baby. The initial examination was conducted when she was 3 years old, during which her parents reported allergic reactions affecting her eyes and sensitivity to light. Upon inspection, the palisades of Vogt and meibomian glands were absent. Conjunctival swelling, tear film instability, and a reduced tear meniscus were noted. Annual monitoring of her ocular condition showed stability up to the last visit in March 2023. At that time, mucus secretions in the eyes were observed, and some eyelashes in abnormal positions were removed. The patient uses daily ocular lubricants, anti-inflammatory eyedrops, and lipid-based tear film stabilizers.
test_results: The molecular analysis revealed the presence of the genomic variant 1568T>C (p. Leu523Pro) in exon 13 of TP63, which confirms the L523P mutation in the sterile alpha motif (SAM) domain.

case_report: A 12-year-old girl was referred to a Genetic Research Center in Yazd, Iran, in June 2008 due to short stature. She is the second child from a first cousin marriage. Her family members, including her parents and two brothers, are healthy. At birth, her mother was 23 years old and her father was 28 years old. There were no reported infections or medications during the pregnancy. Family history indicated that two maternal cousins exhibited similar signs and symptoms, with more severe features. She was born at 38 weeks of gestation via vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 1700 g (<3rd centile), a height of 44 cm (<3rd centile), and a head circumference of 32 cm (10–50 percentile). She was discharged from the hospital without complications. Her developmental milestones were normal. At nineteen weeks old, she experienced her first urinary tract infection and subsequently required repeated hospitalizations for recurrent urinary, respiratory, and gastrointestinal infections. Clinically, she presented with a slender frame, weighing 25 kg (<3rd centile), a height of 133 cm (<3rd centile), and a head circumference of 49 cm (<3rd centile). She had a long narrow face with a prominent nose, and malar and mandibular hypoplasia. There was sun-sensitive erythema on the butterfly area of the face, along with hyperpigmented and hypopigmented spots (café au lait spots) on the trunk and limbs. Telangiectasia spots were noted in some areas of the trunk. Additionally, she exhibited generalized hirsutism. Ophthalmic and otic examinations were normal except for conjunctivitis in both eyes. Her teeth were normal. Her hair was fragile and fine. No deformities were observed in her fingers, toes, or joints. The external genitalia were unremarkable. Her intelligence quotient was normal. Neurological, cardiac, and brain CT scan examinations were unremarkable. Her bone age was two years behind her chronological age. Routine biochemical tests and abdominal ultrasound were normal.
test_results: GTG-banded analysis of over 50 metaphases was abnormal. The following structural chromosome abnormalities were seen in four of the observed cells: 46, XX; chrb(1) (q42); 46, XX; chrb(X) (q21); 46, XX; chrb(7) (p22); and 46, XX; chrb(9) (q13). The final diagnosis was: 46, XX (46)/ 46, XX; chrb(1)/46, XX;chrb(X)/ 46, XX;chrb(7)/ 46, XX;chrb(9). shows a distinctive symmetrical quadriradial chromatid interchanges in one of the observed cell. Sister chromatid exchange (SCE) analysis showed a mean of 80 SCE per cell in comparison to a mean of seven per cell for the normal control.

case_report: A 20-year-old Caucasian woman, with no prior medical history, arrived at the emergency room with numbness and weakness in her left-sided limbs. Neurologic examination showed no cranial nerve deficits and 4/5 strength in the left-sided limbs. There was no evidence of cerebellar dysfunction. She was unable to localize tactile stimuli or judge the size and shape of objects. Sensations of pain, pressure, and temperature were intact. Brain computed tomography (CT) revealed a large (2.1 cm), well-defined hypodense lesion in the right parietal lobe, without surrounding edema.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) without contrast showed a hypoisointense concentric mass on T1- and hyperintense on T2-weighted images. After contrast, the lesion appeared to enhance inhomogeneously, in a pattern resembling separate, alternating enhancing rings. The subsequent proton MR spectroscopy (MRS) revealed reduction in N-acetylaspartate and an increase in choline, lipids, and lactate. Histologic examination failed to show the presence of a significant number of histiocytes, foamy macrophages, or myelin loss. It showed mild to moderate nuclear atypia, whereas Ki-67 immunostaining was positive in 1% to 2% of the nuclei.

case_report: The patient is a 14-year-old Azeri boy from a healthy, non-consanguineous couple. During pregnancy, intrauterine growth retardation was noted. He was delivered at 36 weeks via cesarean section due to lack of fetal movement, with Apgar scores of 9 and 10. At birth, his weight was 2.97 kg (50th percentile, −0.45 SD) and his cranial circumference was 33 cm (10th percentile, −0.61 SD). He began sitting at four years old and took his first unaided steps at six years old, walking with an increased lift base. At nine years old, he was referred to a medical genetic counseling center and noted to have blepharophimosis and intellectual impairment. He experienced a few episodes of loss of consciousness at six years old, but his electroencephalogram (EEG) was normal. He had a non-symptomatic large atrial septal defect (ostium secundum atrial septal defect). Physical examination at nine years old revealed an occipitofrontal circumference (OFC) of 52 cm (~50th percentile) and dysmorphic facial features including a flat occiput, triangular long face, frontal bossing, protruding tongue causing an open mouth expression, thin upper lip, sparse medial eyebrows, thin eyebrows, epicanthal folds, widely spaced upward-slanted eyes, broad nasal bridge, low-set ears, anteverted ears, short philtrum, hypertelorism, ptosis, microphthalmia, and hypoplastic teeth. He was diagnosed with cryptorchidism without renal anomalies. The patient exhibited tall stature, first (big) toe/long thumbs, and missing patella. Significant skeletal and joint X-ray findings included symmetric bilateral coxa valga, hypoplastic iliac wings, scoliosis, increased diameter of the lumbar vertebral canal, genu valgum, pes planus, and a sloping forehead with a large brain capacity. Neurologically, he presented with global developmental delay, intellectual disability, poor eye contact, hypotonia, and speech difficulties. Brain MRI showed inappropriate myelination and disturbed white matter integrity, with no evidence of corpus callosum agenesis. He lacked sphincter control. Currently, the patient is under the care of a mental disability care institute, receiving physiotherapy and speech therapy due to the inability of his parents to care for him, behavioral disturbances, and ADHD traits.
test_results: We identified a de novo heterozygous mutation of guanine to adenine NM_012330.4(KAT6B):c.3147G>A (p.Pro1049 =) using WES. Sanger sequencing subsequently confirmed this heterozygous variant identified by WES in this individual. The mutation could not be detected in the parental DNA by Sanger sequencing. The results of sequence analysis revealed that the c.3147G>A; p.P1049P transition at codon 1,049 was a synonymous mutation (p.Pro1049 =) in the exon 16 of the KAT6B gene.

case_report: A 28-year-old male reported experiencing primary subfertility and increased libido for the past 8 years. He is a healthy businessman with a body mass index (BMI) of 22.34 kg/m2. The patient exhibited normal virilization and potency. Physical examination, including assessment of the external genitalia, revealed no abnormalities. Evaluation of his partner ruled out female factor subfertility.
test_results: His seminal fluid analysis revealed azoospermia with low seminal fluid volume, a normal pH and liquefaction time. USS scan and the Doppler studies of the scrotum revealed normal testicles with no cause for azoospermia detected. His serum testosterone level was 42.15 nmol/L. Serum FSH levels were 0.56 µIU/mL. His serum LH levels, thyroid profile, serum prolactin levels and serum 9 am cortisol levels were all normal. MRI of the pituitary fossa was normal. Contrast enhanced CT scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis did not demonstrate ectopic testosterone secreting tumors.

case_report: The patient, a 22-year-old female, presented with sensory disturbances in both lower extremities and an unstable gait. She was born to non-consanguineous parents in a Korean family with no known history of hereditary disorders. Her birth history and developmental milestones were normal. Symptoms began around the age of 10 and progressively worsened. Clinical examination revealed decreased sensitivity to pain, temperature, touch, and vibration, as well as a reduced sense of position in both lower extremities. An ulcer on her left toe, which had persisted for over a year, had recently healed. The patient also showed mild distal motor weakness in her lower extremities (Medical Research Council scale 4), spasticity, and increased deep tendon reflexes in both lower extremities. Her intelligence was normal, and there were no autonomic symptoms.
test_results: A nerve conduction study indicated sensory axonal polyneuropathy more than motor, and sympathetic skin response was impaired on both the soles. A novel frameshift homozygous variation was detected in the patient’s RETREG1 gene, c.765dupT/p.Gly256TrpfsTer7. Furthermore, a single nucleotide polymorphism array (Infinium Global Screening Array-24+ v2.0, Illumina) was performed with DNA from the patient and her parents, revealing paternal uniparental isodisomy of chromosome 5.
Orpha_name: Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type 2

case_report: A six-day-old Afghan female neonate was admitted to the Neonatal Unit of the Pediatric Department due to skin lesions, bleeding, and jaundice. She was born by spontaneous vaginal delivery at 38 weeks of gestation with a birth weight of 3.5 kg to a 22-year-old multigravida mother at a tertiary hospital. The mother was in good health during pregnancy and did not receive any teratogenic drugs or radiation. The baby had no history of trauma or surgery. There was no family history of similar conditions. The parents were third-degree relatives, indicating parental consanguinity. On general physical examination, the neonate exhibited lethargy, a rectal temperature of 34.9°C, a respiratory rate of 68/min, a heart rate of 170/min, blood pressure of 50/30 mm Hg, an unpalpable radial pulse, a capillary refill time (CRT) of four seconds, cold extremities, weak primitive reflexes, yellowish skin extending to the palms and soles, pale conjunctivas, and an oxygen saturation of 74%. On local physical examination of the left leg, three skin lesions present since birth were noted. A large, blue-red-colored lesion measuring 14 cm in length and 8 cm in width was observed on the left anterolateral thigh extending to the middle of the calf. The surface of the lesions had a coarse and nodular appearance with pale-pink halos. Two smaller skin lesions with similar characteristics were seen on the dorsum of the left foot. Upon admission, bleeding was noted from a ruptured nodular telangiectasia of the large skin lesion, which had started three hours prior to hospital arrival. Blood investigations showed a hemoglobin level of 9 g/dl, a total leucocyte count of 9000/mm3 (polymorphs 45%, lymphocytes 50%, eosinophils 2%, monocytes 2%, and basophil 1%), a red blood cell count of 2.8 million/mm3 (mean corpuscular volume of 91.8 fl, mean corpuscular hemoglobin of 35.8 pg), a platelet count of 317,000/mm3, a reticulocyte count of 2%, a C-reactive protein of 0.4 mg/dl, a blood sugar level of 89 mg/dl, a total bilirubin of 16 mg/dl, indirect bilirubin of 15 mg/dl, a baby blood group of ARh positive, and a mother blood group of ARh positive. Prothrombin time, INR, activated partial thromboplastin time, alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, and thyroid and renal function tests were within normal limits. Abnormal clinical findings such as tachypnea, tachycardia, hypothermia, hypotension, a prolonged CRT, an unpalpable radial pulse, cold extremities, and a history of bleeding from the large skin lesion for three hours were noted. Initially, the patient received 35 ml of intravenous normal saline over the first 20 minutes, oxygen therapy, and a local dressing to stop the bleeding. This was followed by a 70 ml fresh blood transfusion over the next hour. After these interventions, the baby stabilized with normal vital signs and adequate breastfeeding.
test_results: The longitudinal and cross-sectional images of doppler ultrasonography demonstrated superficial fast-flow vasculature within the skin lesions.

case_report: This case report details a 70-year-old Caucasian man who exhibited neuromyotonia with notable autonomic and psychological symptoms, including insomnia, anxiety, and suicidal behavior, followed by effective treatment. In April 2014, the patient experienced pain in the crural region and legs, chills, tingling sensations, hypersensitivity to mechanical stimuli, and mild weakness in the lower limbs accompanied by slight foot-drop. These symptoms developed rapidly without an identifiable cause. By June 2014, the patient showed signs of insomnia, anxiety, confusion, auditory hallucinations, and attempted suicide by slashing his left wrist. He was briefly admitted to a psychiatric ward. The patient was later referred to a neurological clinic due to muscle weakness with significant fasciculations and myokymia.
test_results: An EMG confirmed fibrillations, positive waves, fasciculations, and multiple myokymic and neuromyotonic discharges, occasional high frequency fasciculations, doublets and multiplets. Contraction curve was reduced with unstable motor unit potentials with neurogenic changes. A motor nerve conduction study showed multiple afterdischarges with long-lasting repetitions, which prevented F-waves assessment. His blood test showed high levels of creatine kinase (CK) 12.26 (nkat/L; normal value 3.60), CK myocardial bound 0.52, but no other abnormalities. No antibodies (contactin associated protein-like 2, CASPR2; leucine-rich glioma inactivated 1 protein; contactin 2; anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase) were found in his blood or in his cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Oligoclonal protein synthesis was not confirmed. Cancer was not detected (oncological markers were negative; the results of chest X-ray, ultrasonography of abdomen, endoscopic investigation of gastrointestinal tract and urological examination were negative). His CSF showed borderline results: protein 0.40g/L and 1 mononuclear cell/1mm3.
diagnosis: Morvan’s syndrome of an autoimmune type with undetected specific antibodies

case_report: An 85-year-old woman arrived at the emergency department with rapid breathing, noisy breathing, and reduced consciousness. Her medical history included coronary artery bypass graft, tissue aortic valve replacement, heart failure, chronic left pleural effusion due to a past left empyema, rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate, total hip replacement, and thoracic compression fractures. She had a COVID-19 infection six weeks prior. Initial observations showed oxygen saturation at 99% on 15 liters of oxygen via a non-rebreather mask, a respiratory rate of 45 breaths per minute, a heart rate of 80 beats per minute, and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 7/15. Arterial blood gas analysis indicated hypercapnic respiratory failure on 60% oxygen with a pH of 7.19, pCO2 of 10.4, pO2 of 17.1, and HCO3 of 30.4. Her COVID-19 test was negative. A recent echocardiogram showed moderate-severe tricuspid regurgitation, a non-dilated left ventricle, grade 1 diastolic dysfunction, and preserved systolic function. Blood tests indicated moderately elevated infection markers, and a chest X-ray showed right lower zone consolidation.
test_results: Flexible nasendoscopy demonstrated bilaterally fixed and adducted vocal cords due to bilateral cricoarytenoid joint fixation, with a rima glottidis measurement of approximately 3 mm and evidence of paradoxical breathing.
diagnosis: Bilateral Vocal Cord Palsy Secondary to Rheumatoid Arthritis

case_report: An 80-year-old, bedridden woman with multiple comorbidities, including multiple myeloma managed with palliative therapy, thalassemia, syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone, hypertension, and dyslipidemia, presented with a 3-month history of slowly progressive skin lesions and unusual hairs on her lower extremities. Caregivers observed these skin changes following the diagnosis of multiple myeloma. There was no reported trauma to the affected areas, and no family history of similar skin lesions. The patient had been on lorazepam, oxycodone, morphine, folic acid, sodium chloride, vitamin B complex, and lactulose for over 3 years. Physical examination showed multiple brown scales with adherent centers and detached, outward-turning edges, along with numerous small black dots on the extensor areas of both lower extremities, sparing the flexural regions. Abnormal hairs were also noted in the areas with skin abnormalities. Other systems were unremarkable.
test_results: Dermoscopic examination revealed multiple dark hairs with a perfectly circular arrangement, located under a thin layer of skin. Histopathological examination revealed laminated hyperkeratosis with hypogranulosis. The specimen also contained a dilated hair follicle.

case_report: A 23-year-old otherwise-healthy young man presented with multiple elevated skin lesions on his left upper extremity and upper chest for five years. Lesions initially appeared on the left palm as multiple horny elevations and subsequently developed over the entire left upper extremity and left side of the chest in a linear fashion. The condition was stable for three years. The lesions were accompanied by mild itching. Past and family medical history were unremarkable. The patient had consulted several physicians and applied various topical medications without any benefit. Clinical examination revealed skin-colored to brownish, discrete, verrucous papules, nodules, and plaques in a linear configuration following Blaschko's lines distributed over the left forearm, arm, and the left side of the upper chest strictly respecting the midline. There were depigmented macules and scars along the lateral border of the forearm, reportedly owing to burns sustained a few months previously. There were multiple small keratotic and pitted papules linearly arranged along the medial border and central part of the palm. A few of the palmar lesions had coalesced to form plaques. Apart from these keratotic papules, numerous punctate pits were also visualized over the palm. The rest of the mucocutaneous and systemic examination was within normal limits. Routine laboratory tests, serum chemistry panel and human immunodeficiency virus serology were normal.
test_results: Histopathology showed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and papillomatosis and no dermal infiltrate. Cornoid lamella-like columns of parakeratosis were seen invaginating the epidermis. Granular layer were absent beneath these columns. Dilated acrosyringia were however not visualized in the sections examined.
diagnosis: Porokeratotic eccrine ostial and dermal duct nevus
Orpha_name: Porokeratotic eccrine ostial and dermal duct nevus

case_report: A 43-year-old female presented with a mass in the upper-lateral quadrant of her left breast, first noticed 20 days prior. Her medical history includes thyroidectomy, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes mellitus. She experienced significant breast pain over the past year, leading to multiple breast imaging studies, which showed no signs of malignancy but did reveal fibrocystic changes. Consequently, she was advised to undergo annual imaging and physical examinations. Two months after her last evaluation, she discovered a mass in the same area of her left breast. On physical examination, the mass was small, had indistinct margins, and was tender to touch. There was no active pain or nipple discharge observed.
test_results: In the sonogram, a 10 mm diameter hypoechoic mass was detected in the 12 o’clock position within the left breast. The first sonography of the lesion showed a suspicious mass and the second sonography revealed the mass is growing. Considering the position of the lesion, mammography showed no evidence of mass, but some evidence of fibroglandular condensation were obvious. Macroscopic appearances: a gray-cream tissue with the size of 2 × 1.5 × 1 cm contained a creamy nodular lesion with 1.5 cm in diameter and loose formidability. Microscopic features: the tissue was composed of fusiform fibroblastic cells with the bright ellipsoid-like nuclei, elevated nucleolus and also mitotic formations were obvious. Low cellular and high cellular zones with hyaline fibrosis and erythrocyte accumulation beside a light lymphocytic infiltration existed. Adipocytic accumulation within margins of this lesion.

case_report: An 11-year-old girl presented with multiple asymptomatic erythematous lesions on the left abdomen, initially observed by her mother at birth as multiple red pinhead-sized spots. These lesions progressively expanded, with new satellite lesions forming around the original ones as she aged. There was no family history of similar skin conditions. The patient did not exhibit any visual or neurological symptoms. A cutaneous examination showed multiple discrete and confluent punctate erythematous to violaceous macules on the left abdomen, specifically in the T8 to T10 dermatomal distribution, with normal skin in the surrounding and intervening areas. No similar lesions were found on other parts of the body. Her general physical and systemic examination revealed no abnormalities.
test_results: Skin biopsy taken from the lesion showed epidermis with basket weave hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis, and hypogranulosis. Papillary dermis showed few ectatic congested thin-walled blood vessels. A few areas showed downward growth of the rete ridges between these blood vessels. There was no epidermal acanthosis and extravasation of RBCs, inflammatory cell infiltration, and hemosiderin deposition were not seen in the dermis.

case_report: A 69-year-old Saudi man with diabetes mellitus was admitted to the Neurology Department due to a persistent headache lasting 5 days, episodic confusion, and visual disturbances. His family reported that the headache began gradually on the left side of his head, eventually becoming widespread and moderate to severe in intensity. The patient experienced nausea and had 2 episodes of vomiting. Additionally, his family observed that he frequently bumped into objects while walking. The patient also reported visual disturbances during this period. His family noted episodes of confusion and lack of responsiveness to his surroundings. There was no clear history of seizures according to the family, and his past medical history was unremarkable except for diabetes. He had a minor head trauma 3 years prior without concussion, but a scan at that time showed scattered areas of bleeding in his brain. He otherwise led a healthy life and had not required hospital visits for other medical issues. His family reported normal cognitive function, particularly as he managed his own business. Upon arrival at the emergency department, the patient was lethargic. Due to the risk of airway obstruction, the emergency physician intubated him. General examination revealed no facial phakomas. While sedated, the patient exhibited tonic eye deviation with nystagmoid-like eye movement and subtle myoclonic jerks of the distal limbs. He was administered an intravenous (IV) loading dose of phenytoin and a midazolam infusion. Despite this, he experienced several clinical seizures in the following days, necessitating further titration of midazolam infusion (up to 14 mg/hr) and the addition of IV levetiracetam for optimized antiepileptic coverage. An electroencephalogram was obtained postictal. Laboratory investigations showed peripheral blood cell count, hemoglobin, renal and liver function within reference range, and elevated blood glucose (14.7 mmol/L/264 mg/dl). Thyroid function test, parathyroid hormone, and serum vitamin B12 levels were normal. Serum folate level was not available. Screening tests for Hepatitis B antigen, Hepatitis C virus, and human immunodeficiency virus antigens and antibodies were negative. Anti-TTG immunoglobulin A (IgA) titre was elevated at 35 U (reference range up to 20 U), antiendomysial antibody screen was negative, and anti-Gliadin IgA antibody results were within reference range. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) study showed a WBC of 1, red blood cell count of 1, protein level of 36 mg/dL, and glucose level of 7.6 mmol/L. CSF tuberculosis and herpes simplex virus 1 and 2 polymerase chain reaction results were negative. A duodenal endoscopic biopsy was performed, but the specimen was not properly prepared, resulting in suboptimal histopathological examination. However, increased intraepithelial lymphocytes with normal villous architecture were noted.
test_results: His anti-TTG immunoglobulin A (IgA) titre was high at 35 U (reference range is up to 20 U). The computed tomography (CT) of the patient's brain showed bilateral scattered corticosubcortical parietooccipitotemporal calcification with no oedema or mass effect. The brain MRI with and without contrast showed diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) restriction over bilateral occipital cortex (more so over the left side) in a gyriform pattern with concordant area of apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) hypointensity. Susceptibility weighted magnetic resonance sequences (susceptibility weighted imaging [SWI], susceptibility weighted angiography [SWAN]) demonstrated hyperintensity corresponding to the area of DWI restriction. T1-weighted imaging with contrast showed no contrast uptake, and we saw no oedema or mass effect. We found no cortical atrophy or any deep cerebral vein enlargement.
diagnosis: Celiac Disease Epilepsy and Occipital Calcification Syndrome

case_report: The patient is a 3-year-old male born at 31 weeks and 6 days via spontaneous vaginal delivery following premature rupture of membranes and preterm labor. The pregnancy was marked by oligohydramnios in the third trimester and a shortened cervix at 21 weeks, which was managed with cerclage. Steroids, magnesium sulfate, and antibiotics were administered before delivery. The mother had a history of deep venous thrombosis treated with heparin and enoxaparin during pregnancy. The patient was small for gestational age, weighing 1,250 g (9th percentile), with a length of 41 cm (38th percentile) and a head circumference of 27 cm (6.5th percentile), according to Fenton preterm boy curves. Prenatal ultrasounds before 32 weeks were reportedly normal. Apgar scores were 8 and 9. He is the first child of a 38-year-old, G1P1 mother of Hispanic descent and a 56-year-old father of Caucasian descent with healthy 11-year-old fraternal twin half-siblings. There is no family history of developmental delays. Placental studies showed a singleton placenta weighing 190 g (5th percentile) with acute chorioamnionitis and eccentric cord insertion. Infectious workup was negative, including prenatal group B Streptococcus culture, prenatal maternal TORCH serologies, and urine test for cytomegalovirus. Initial head ultrasound at day 7 of life revealed echogenicity of the occipital bilateral lateral ventricles and mild ventricular dilation. Serial head ultrasounds showed persistent prominent bilateral ventricles without evidence of bleeding. Brain MRI at 5 weeks of age indicated mild ventriculomegaly, small amounts of blood product in the occipital horns bilaterally, and adequate myelination for age with no migration anomalies or congenital/structural abnormalities. He had retinopathy of prematurity with an eye exam at 1 month showing immature vascularization of zone 3 bilaterally. Hearing and newborn screens were unremarkable. He was referred to the genetics clinic for evaluation due to global developmental delay, hypotonia, plagiocephaly, and congenital torticollis. At 6 months of age (adjusted to 4 months for prematurity), he lacked full head control and was not bringing his hands together to the midline but could roll and maintain good eye contact. He exhibited truncal hypotonia and slight appendicular hypertonia, mainly in the upper extremities. At 2 years and 6 months, he remained developmentally delayed but showed progress in all four areas of development. He was pulling to stand, cruising, but not yet walking independently. He could stack 7–8 blocks and had a pincer grasp but was not yet copying a line. He had a few words, maintained good eye contact with parents, and enjoyed playing with other children. There was no history of seizures, developmental regression, or behavioral abnormalities. He also had a history of periorificial and atopic dermatitis, with similar dermatologic issues reported in his father’s childhood. At the first evaluation at 2 years and 6 months, growth parameters were weight 11 kg (2nd percentile), height 87 cm (12th percentile), and head circumference 48.5 cm (26th percentile), according to CDC growth curves for males 2–20 years and Nellhaus Boys for head circumference. He had closely spaced, deep-set eyes that were mildly hooded, mild bilateral ptosis, and downslanting palpebral fissures. He had a broad and prominent forehead and a slightly triangular face with proportionately large ears. He exhibited brachydactyly and 5th finger clinodactyly. He had slight hypotonia. There were no ectodermal findings or joint hypermobility. Prior investigations included a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) array performed on the Illumina CytoSNP-850 K platform (genome build hg19) from peripheral blood, which was normal (arr(1–22)×2,(X,Y)×1). Fragile X testing showed a normal FMR1 allele with 29 repeats.
test_results: The results of the exome trio showed a heterozygous de novo truncating variant in SIN3A, NM_015477.2: c.1015C>T (p.Gln339Ter) (genome build hg19).

case_report: A 5-year-old male, born at term, as the third child to healthy, unrelated Dutch parents. A prenatal routine ultrasound at 30 weeks gestational age indicated short humeri and femora. His birth weight was 2,615 g (tenth to 25th centile). Physical examination at birth revealed no abnormalities, and he was discharged after 1 day. At 14 months, he was evaluated due to limb shortness, a small, narrow chest, and frequent episodes of upper respiratory tract infection accompanied by respiratory distress.
test_results: Skeletal radiographs showed a hypoplastic thorax, with short, horizontally oriented ribs, elevated, horizontally oriented clavicles, CTR of 0.63, short iliac bones with the typical trident appearance of the acetabula, and shortened femoral bones.

case_report: A 56-year-old woman with a history of retinitis pigmentosa and open-angle glaucoma for 20 years presented with progressive worsening of night vision and peripheral vision in her right eye over several years. She had been myopic since childhood and had been using latanoprost nightly in both eyes for an extended period. Her medical history included hypertension, depression, and elevated cholesterol levels. On examination, her best-corrected visual acuity was hand movements in the right eye and 6/12 in the left eye, with refractive errors of -1.75 in each eye. Intraocular pressures were measured at 18 mmHg in both eyes. Anterior segment examinations were unremarkable bilaterally. She had developed bilateral posterior subcapsular cataracts ten years earlier and was now bilaterally pseudophakic with clear posterior capsulotomies. Fundoscopy showed pale optic discs and extensive peripheral chorioretinal atrophy exposing bare sclera in both eyes. Small islands of retina at each posterior pole appeared clinically normal and were sharply demarcated from the atrophic areas by a pigmented border. Visual field testing indicated almost total constriction of the right visual field and severe peripheral constriction of the left visual field. Fundal fluorescein angiography confirmed significant peripheral choroidal atrophy.
test_results: Serum ornithine was elevated at 206 umol/L (reference range 27–98 umol/L). Extensive visual electrodiagnostic testing, including electroretinography, pattern electroretinography, multifocal electroretinography, electro-oculography, visual evoked potential, average visual evoked potential, and Farnsworth–Munsell 100, showed virtually abolished responses in scotopic and photopic conditions, confirming an advanced retinal dystrophy.
Orpha_name: Gyrate atrophy of choroid and retina

case_report: A 20-year-old male presented with complaints of snoring and sleep apnea, which began two years ago. He is employed in the military, and his symptoms were causing disturbances to his colleagues in the barracks. He reported a normal daily life with no family history or personal medical history of seizures and had been previously healthy. His Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) score was 14 out of 24, indicating moderate excessive daytime sleepiness, with a particular complaint of severe morning sleepiness. There were no reports of parasomnia events or periodic limb movements during sleep. He did not report tongue biting but mentioned occasional recent enuresis. Physical examination showed no apparent abnormalities, and his body mass index (BMI) was 23.1 kg/m2.
test_results: Overnight polysomnography was performed. Sleep efficiency was 81.9%, wakefulness after sleep onset (WASO) time was 59.2 minutes (17.8%), and his arousal index was 28.7/h. Stage 1 and 2 sleep were increased; however, stage 3 and REM sleep were decreased. He experienced nine apneas and two hypopneas during PSG, each episode lasted 20–40 seconds. His apnea/hypopnea index (AHI) was 2.7/h. These apneic episodes consisted of respiratory cessation accompanied by chest and abdominal movements of the obstructive type. All hypopnea was typical hypopneas. Seven out of nine apneic episodes were accompanied by rhythmic paroxysmal discharges in the bifrontal areas on EEG; clinically, five of the episodes progressed to tonic movement of all four limbs, and two episodes showed apneas only. All that seven episodes occurred during NREM sleep (two in stage 1, four in stage 2, and the others in stage 3). The other apnea and hypopnea did not accompany tonic movement. The next night, a 16-channel video-EEG monitoring was performed to classify these events and to determine the temporal relationship of apnea onset and Ictal discharge. Ten apneic events with ictal discharges preceding the apnoea were recorded throughout the night. Ictal EEG showed paroxysmal rhythmic discharges in the range of 9 to 10Hz in the bifrontal area starting just before onset of the apneic episodes. The interictal EEG was normal, and brain MRI showed no specific abnormality. Ictal SPECT revealed increased cerebral blood perfusion in the right frontal region.
Orpha_name: Autosomal dominant nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy

case_report: A 27-year-old male presented with nausea, headache, low back pain, and elevated serum creatinine. The patient, a police officer, experienced these symptoms following a 20-m multistage shuttle run test during occupational physical training. This test involved continuous running between two lines, 20 meters apart, with increasing speed intervals. The patient had no significant medical history aside from common childhood illnesses. He consumed alcohol occasionally and did not smoke. His mother had a history of renal issues, and his grandmother had passed away from renal failure. The mother's serum uric acid concentration was consistently below 2.0 mg/dL. No laboratory data were available for other family members. The patient had previously shown low serum uric acid levels during routine checkups. On examination, he was of average build, well-nourished, but appeared uncomfortable. Physical examination revealed no significant abnormalities. Urinalysis indicated a ± dipstick test for protein and was negative for sugar. The urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio was 0.22 g/g creatinine. Laboratory results showed a serum urea nitrogen of 50.9 mg/dL (normal range: 9–21), creatinine level of 4.89 mg/dL (0.4–0.9), and an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 13.3 mL/min/1.73 m2, consistent with stage 3 AKI (KDIGO). Hematologic evaluation, biological tests including creatine phosphokinase and uric acid, and serological tests were within normal limits.
test_results: Abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan revealed no morphological abnormalities in the kidneys and urinary tracts. The serum uric acid was 0.5 mg/dL and fractional excretion of uric acid was 82%.

case_report: A 32-year-old man presented with episodes of headache and dizziness over the past month and an unusual rhythm observed in the ECG. Despite a normal clinical workup for headaches and symptomatic treatment, there was no improvement. The patient reported no cardiac symptoms such as palpitations, chest pain, dyspnea, or syncope and was able to engage in strenuous physical activities like climbing and playing football without difficulty. His past medical history and physical examination were unremarkable. Notably, his mother experienced a cerebrovascular accident at the age of 35 and received a permanent pacemaker. Additionally, his brother had a permanent pacemaker implanted at the age of 13 following several episodes of seizures.
test_results: In echocardiography, both atria were mildly enlarged and no A wave was observed in the tricuspid and mitral inflow pulse in Doppler recording. Tissue Doppler imaging also confirmed no visible atrial contracture. In a 24-hour electrocardiogram Holter monitoring, the patient’s minimum, maximum, and mean heart rates were 44, 45, and 59 bpm, respectively. The patient’s electrophysiological study revealed a wide complex QRS bradycardia (40 – 45 bpm) without any discernable P wave. Also, no potential for the right atrium could be recorded, and electrical stimulation failed to provoke atrial depolarization. There was a lack of atrial capture during high output, right atrium and coronary sinus pacing, without His potential around the His bundle. No ventricular arrhythmia could be induced during programmed ventricular stimulation.

case_report: A 4-day-old male infant was admitted to the ophthalmic department of Calcutta National Medical College and Hospital on July 15, 2006. The infant, weighing 2.7 kg, was born at 40 weeks gestation by spontaneous vaginal delivery with episiotomy to a 28-year-old second gravida. The antenatal, intranatal, and postnatal periods were uneventful. The mother reported taking only iron and vitamin supplements and had no history of X-ray exposure. The infant's previous sibling, a 2-year-old female, was healthy. There was no family history of congenital anomalies or consanguinity. On examination, the infant had bilateral partially fused eyelids. Apart from this, the infant was healthy with no other congenital abnormalities identified after a thorough pediatric assessment.
test_results: Two fine extensile bands of skin measuring about 1 mm in breadth and 3 mm in length between the upper and lower eyelid in the left eye. Similar bands, one centrally and one near the lateral canthus were detected in the right eye.

case_report: A 14-year-old girl, previously in good health, presented two weeks after an uncomplicated laparoscopic appendectomy for non-perforated acute appendicitis. She reported a gradual decrease in urinary frequency to twice daily and experienced prolonged hesitancy. Initially, her urinary stream was weak and slow, eventually becoming interrupted. Straining did not improve the stream. She had no history of urinary tract infections (UTIs) or constipation and had regular bowel movements. Two months later, following an episode of acute cystitis, she completely lost the ability to void. An indwelling Foley urinary catheter was placed, and her cystitis was treated successfully with antibiotics. Each time the catheter was removed, she required re-catheterization with urine volumes ranging from 300 to 1200 mL. She reported a loss of the urge to urinate and only felt dull pain in the suprapubic region and right iliac fossa during extreme bladder distention. She remained on an indwelling urethral urinary catheter and was referred to a tertiary center for further evaluation of her urinary retention. Clinical examination revealed normal findings, and abdominal and pelvic ultrasound scans (USS) showed no obvious pathology. A pediatric neurologist found no abnormalities, and imaging and tests including MRI of the brain and spine, electromyography (EMG) of the lower extremity, somatosensory-evoked potentials (SEP) of the tibial nerve, electroencephalogram (EEG), and lumbar puncture showed no pathology. The gynecologist noted multiple follicular cysts on both ovaries on USS but found no explanation for the urinary retention. A pediatric urologist conducted an examination under general anesthesia, including a free calibration of the urethra up to 26F, followed by normal findings on cystoscopy.
test_results: Videourodynamic study (VUDS) showed an asensitive and hypotonic bladder. The bladder filling had to be stopped at 360 mL due to the patient's discomfort. Maximum intravesical pressure achieved 11 cmH 2 O. When pulling the urodynamic catheter out of the bladder manually, the maximum urethral pressure measured was 120 cmH 2 O.

case_report: A 79-year-old Caucasian female with a medical history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, and mild renal impairment was admitted to the emergency department (ED) due to a sudden severe bifrontal headache, rated 8/10 on the pain scale. She also reported difficulties in concentration. There was no history of trauma, migraine, or other intermittent headaches. Initial neurological examination was normal. Cranial CT revealed minor microangiopathic and major macroangiopathic changes, along with strio-pallido-dentate calcifications, but no other abnormalities. Laboratory tests showed mild microcytic hypochromic anemia (Hb: 9.9 g/dl, MCV: 77 fl, MCH: 25 pg) and mildly impaired renal function (glomerular filtration rate: 48 ml/min). Metamizole (2 g/d) was administered, leading to significant improvement, and the patient was discharged. Within 24 hours, she experienced difficulty speaking and returned to the ED. Neurological examination remained normal, with no signs of aphasia or dysarthria. Hours later, the patient became delirious with partially aggressive behavior and optic hallucinations. Brain MRI showed minor microangiopathic changes, small left temporoparietal postischemic defects, bilateral strio-pallido-dentate calcifications, and minor artifacts in the left occipital region related to tentorium calcification. CSF analysis revealed moderate lymphocytic pleocytosis (48 cells/μl; total protein: 0.695 g/l; glucose: 78.0 mg/dl; lactate: 1.8 mmol/l). Broad-spectrum antimicrobial and antiviral therapy with ceftriaxone and acyclovir was initiated. Microbiological analysis of CSF showed no bacterial or fungal pathogens, and PCR tests for various viral DNAs and specific antibodies were negative. Antiepileptic therapy with valproic acid (900 mg/d) was started, but EEG showed no epileptiform discharges or abnormal background frequencies. After seven days of intravenous antimicrobial therapy, the patient's condition remained largely unchanged. Neuropsychological screening (Montreal Cognitive Assessment: 13/30 points) indicated significant cognitive deterioration. Follow-up CSF analysis again showed moderate lymphocytic pleocytosis (34 cells/μl; total protein: 0.609 g/l; glucose: 59.0 mg/dl; lactate: 1.7 mmol/l), with no pathogens detected. Antineuronal antibody analysis was normal. CSF biomarkers for dementia showed elevated tau protein (478 pg/ml, norm: <450 pg/ml) and phospho-tau protein (90 pg/ml, norm: <61 pg/ml), with a reduced Aß ratio (0.38, norm: >0.5). On the 10th day, symptoms remained mostly unchanged, and follow-up brain MRI showed progressive leptomeningeal and sulcal T2/FLAIR hyperintensities parieto-occipital on both sides and temporoparietal on the left side, along with increasing unspecific subcortical and periventricular T2-FLAIR hyperintensities. A review of the medical history revealed a similar episode of aseptic meningoencephalitis seven years prior, with notable effects from steroid therapy. Despite recommending steroid treatment, the patient's legal representatives rejected it due to previous severe neuropsychiatric symptom worsening, and the patient was discharged. Five days later, she returned to the ED with worsening neuropsychiatric symptoms, particularly visual and auditory hallucinations. Another CSF analysis showed no significant changes (lymphocytic pleocytosis: 43 cells/μl; protein: 0.457 g/l; glucose: 59 mg/dl; lactate: 1.8 mmol/l; no evidence of intrathecal IgG or IgM synthesis).
test_results: Antithyroid peroxidase antibodies (anti-TPO antibodies) were markedly increased (344 IU/l, norm: <60IU/l).
Orpha_name: Steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis

case_report: A six-year-old Saudi girl with genu valgum was referred to pediatric endocrinology for further management. She was born at full-term to consanguineous parents, with normal birth weight and length, and no post-natal complications. At the age of two, her family observed delays in speech and walking. She began walking at three years old, displaying knock knees and an unsteady gait. There is a strong family history of rickets; her father has a history of rickets, short stature, and genu varum, which was surgically corrected, while her mother is healthy. She has one healthy sister with no bone deformities. There is no other family history of rickets or metabolic bone disease. The patient was initially diagnosed with nutritional rickets. Laboratory results from the referring hospital showed low calcium (1.78 mmol/L), normal phosphate (1 mmol/L), high alkaline phosphatase (423 IU/L), and elevated parathormone (PTH) levels (200 pg/ml). Her 25-hydroxyvitamin D was low (5.3 ng/dl). Liver and renal function tests were normal. She was started on vitamin D and calcium supplements, leading to mild improvement. One year later, her labs showed calcium of 2.44 mmol/L, phosphate of 1.5 mmol/L, 25-hydroxyvitamin D of 19.32 nmol/L, and PTH of 116.70 pg/ml despite supplementation. At the age of five, her growth parameters were a height of 113 cm (39th percentile, -0.25 SD) and weight of 29.3 kg (97.64th percentile, 1.98 SD).
