Physical examination revealed no dysmorphic features, mild frontal bossing, no wrist widening, and a normal gait with mild genu valgum. Initial biochemical tests showed normal calcium (2.28 mmol/L), phosphate (1.2 mmol/L), alkaline phosphatase (234 IU/L), elevated PTH (79.2 ng/L), 25-hydroxyvitamin D (32 nmol/L), and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (82 ng/L). She was on alfacalcidol 0.5 mcg daily. Radiographs of the lower limbs revealed bilateral genu valgus deformity. A whole skeletal dysplasia panel was sent, yielding inconclusive results.
test_results: A heterozygous missense variant in CYP3A4: c.902 T > C; p.Ile301Thr in the CYP3A4 gene was discovered.

case_report: A 16-year-old female patient with a family history of cardiac conditions was hospitalized due to a SARS-CoV-2 infection, presenting mild symptoms such as rhinorrhea and dry cough. Upon admission, she was in good general condition with a temperature of 37.4 °C and SaO2 of 99% at room temperature. Her heart sounds were rhythmic, and she did not exhibit retrosternal pain, tachycardia, or tachypnea. She had stage 2 hypertension (blood pressure of 150/90 mmHg) and a heart rate of 80 beats per minute. Her ECG was normal, and she showed no signs of meningeal irritation, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15/15. Laboratory results indicated elevated levels of high-sensitive cardiac troponin I (40.8 ng/L), creatine kinase (590 U/L), N-terminal probrain natriuretic peptide (154 pg/mL), D-dimers (580 ng/mL), C-reactive protein (2 mg/dL), aspartate aminotransferase (35 U/L), alanine transaminase (50 U/L), and lactate dehydrogenase (248 U/L). Normal values were observed for leukocytes (6.37 × 10^9 cells/L), lymphocytes (2.37 × 10^9 cells/L), neutrophils (6.2 × 10^9 cells/L), platelets (360 × 10^9 cells/L), creatinine (0.56 mg/dL), sodium (135 mmol/L), and potassium (4.2 mmol/L). On the 4th day of hospitalization, dynamic ECGs revealed ventricular extrasystole, prompting a cardiologic examination. Heart ultrasound showed a slightly dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 55–60%, LV dimensions of 53/35 mm, and hypokinesia in the lower wall. Treatment included conversion enzyme inhibitors and heart MRI. During hospitalization, antiviral treatment with lopinavir/ritonavir (400/100 mg q12h for 3 days) was initiated, along with anti-inflammatory medication (paracetamol 500 mg po bd for 7 days), prophylactic enoxaparin sodium (0.4 mL qd for 8 days), antihypertensive ACE inhibitors (Ramipril 2.5 mg po qd for 3 days), and a hepatoprotective drug (Silymarin 150 mg po td for 8 days). The antiviral treatment was discontinued after 3 days as per cardiologist's advice. Post-discharge heart MRI showed no evidence of viral subacute myocarditis. Early gadolinium enhancement appeared normal, with no intracavitary thrombosis or microvascular obstruction. Late gadolinium enhancement revealed a small contrast outlet with mid-myocardial topography at the basal segments of the interventricular septum and a small focal contrast outlet at the lower point of insertion in the right ventricle on the left ventricle. T2 mapping showed T2 values of 49–50 ms, and T1 mapping indicated slightly increased T1 values without extracellular compartment expansion (T1 septal precontrast 1019 ms, ECV 24%). The LV was slightly dilated (VTDi 98 mL/m2), with systolic function at the lower limit of normal (LVEF 58%). A small area of focal mid-myocardial fibrosis was noted at the basal interventricular septum, along with non-specific focal fibrosis at the lower insertion point of the RV on the LV. The MRI confirmed slight dilation of the left ventricle with preserved bi-ventricular systolic function and a small area of mid-myocardial focal fibrosis in the basal interventricular septum.
test_results: The heterozygous mutation c.448A > C (p.Thr150Pro), in exon 2 of the LMNA gene was identified.

case_report: A 23-year-old male presented to the emergency room with a 3-month history of peripheral facial palsy, hearing loss, bilateral optic disc edema, and persistent headaches unresponsive to painkillers in recent weeks. He had been on oral prednisone for facial palsy, which initially improved his symptoms, but hearing loss and decreased visual acuity developed as the medication was tapered. Upon examination, he exhibited mild left facial palsy with lagophthalmos, severe right hearing impairment, and multiple papulovesicular lesions on his face and back. Ophthalmic examination showed best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 20/32 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. The anterior segment examination was normal, and intraocular pressure was 13 mmHg in both eyes. Fundus examination revealed mild hyperemia of both optic discs with blurred borders, without signs of vitreous or retinal inflammation. No additional neurologic signs or symptoms were observed. Baseline blood tests indicated elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) at 27 mm/h and C-reactive protein (CRP) at 33.25 mg/L. The infectious and immunological panel showed a positive Weil-Felix reaction.
test_results: The cerebral magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a cranial multineuritis involving the right II cranial nerve and III, V, VII, and VIII nerves. The audiogram showed a complete hearing loss on the right side and a normal exam on the left side. The only positive test was the Weil-Felix reaction.

case_report: A 60-year-old female experienced pain and swelling in the left second and third toes for one month, with blackening occurring over the past 20 days in 2017. She also exhibited Raynaud’s phenomenon, without limb numbness or intermittent claudication. The patient had a ten-year history of poorly managed type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and hypertension diagnosed prior to admission. Despite improved blood glucose control, the pain and gangrene worsened. She had no history of smoking, drinking, or infectious disease. Upon admission, physical examination showed gangrenous lesions on the left second and third toes with surrounding red skin but no exudation. The right index finger appeared purple, and the small finger was significantly swollen, painful, and dark violet. The left anterior tibial artery pulse was weakened, and the dorsal pedis artery was not palpable. Sensory examination with a 10g monofilament on the feet was normal, as were the knee jerk and Achilles reflexes. Laboratory tests revealed hemoglobin at 87g/L, positive hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis B core antibody, and hepatitis B e antibody, with an HBV DNA load of 6.06E+03 IU/mL. Tests for hepatitis C virus and human immunodeficiency virus were negative. The ankle-brachial index (ABI) values were 1.21 in both limbs. Color Doppler ultrasound indicated atherosclerosis and segmental occlusions in the left anterior tibial artery. Lower limb angiography showed occlusions in the left anterior tibial artery and peroneal artery, but with good collateral circulation. Blood flow in the dorsal and plantar arteries was normal. Electrophysiologic study indicated peripheral neuropathy. The patient was initially managed as DF with Wagner grade 4. After 30 days of treatment, including insulin, low-molecular-weight heparin, alprostadil, and dressing changes, the gangrene did not improve. Further immunological tests showed lower serum complement 3 and complement 4 levels. Tests for anticardiolipin antibody, anti-nuclear antibodies, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and rheumatoid factor were negative.
test_results: The serum cryoglobulin was positive. Serum electrophoresis revealed 4.9% abnormal M protein. Immunofixation electrophoresis showed polyclonal IgM, IgG bands, and kappa light chain. The pathology of the necrotic toes was leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

case_report: A 33-year-old male with a history of resolved immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) presented with acute onset of jaundice and dark urine, accompanied by a week of fevers, chills, and night sweats. Additional symptoms included malaise, loss of taste and smell, cough, and shortness of breath. This presentation occurred before the availability of SARS-CoV-2 vaccines. Initial vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory results showed a bilirubin level of 10 mg/dL, with other liver enzymes being unremarkable. The patient had leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 15 × 10^3/µL, while hemoglobin and platelet counts were normal. SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative. Physical examination revealed scleral icterus. Overnight, the patient experienced night sweats, nausea, and non-bloody, non-bilious vomiting. Bilirubin levels increased to 13 mg/dL (indirect) and 14 mg/dL (total). Hemoglobin levels dropped from 12.5 g/dL to 8.7 g/dL. The patient was administered IV dexamethasone 4 mg daily. Bone marrow biopsy indicated mild hemophagocytosis. Imaging, including an abdominal CT scan and a right upper quadrant ultrasound, showed no abnormalities in the hepatobiliary, pancreatic, or splenic regions. Hemolysis labs revealed lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) at 759 U/L, haptoglobin <10, ferritin 4903 µg/L, and a reticulocyte percentage of 2.33%. Serologic tests for hepatitis, HIV, Echovirus, and cytomegalovirus were negative. Mycoplasma IgM was positive with a titer of <770 U/L.
test_results: A repeat direct antiglobulin test (DAT) was positive for IgG, C3d. He was found to have a cold autoantibody and anti-E. His blood sample was reactive with three out of three cells in the antibody screen. This patient had a complement activating IgM, causing red blood cell (RBC) lysis.
diagnosis: Hyperhemolysis in the setting of mixed-autoimmune hemolytic anemia

case_report: A 44-year-old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus was admitted to the hospital presenting with dysuria, fevers, and abdominal pain. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 91x10^9 cells/L with a differential of 70% blasts, 11% lymphocytes, 7% neutrophils, and 7% monocytes. Hemoglobin was measured at 8.9 g/dL and platelet count at 45x10^9 cells/L. Urinalysis indicated pyuria, and urine culture grew extended spectrum beta lactamase (ESBL) Klebsiella pneumoniae. She was treated for pyelonephritis with a 7-day course of levofloxacin, which resolved her symptoms and fevers. Due to elevated peripheral blasts, a bone marrow biopsy was performed, revealing a hypercellular bone marrow with 85% blasts. Induction chemotherapy with cytarabine/idarubicin (7+3) was started. On day 6 of induction, the patient developed a neutropenic fever of 38.7 °C and, the following day, multiple tender erythematous papules and plaques with some scattered pustules appeared on the anterior chest. Over the next 2 days, the rash spread to the upper abdomen, bilateral upper limbs, neck, scalp, and ears. The patient was started on cefepime for empiric treatment of neutropenic fever. Blood and urine cultures were negative, and no source of infection was identified.
test_results: Biopsy of the rash from the anterior chest revealed neutrophilic infiltration of the dermis with upper dermis edema and scattered reactive fibroblasts. Fungal and bacterial stains and cultures were negative.

case_report: A 61-year-old female experienced a cardiac arrest at home. Her husband performed CPR until the emergency physician arrived. Upon arrival, ventricular fibrillation was addressed with defibrillation. Subsequent asystole was converted to ventricular tachycardia with norepinephrine. The addition of amiodarone resulted in a stable sinus rhythm. Upon arrival at the clinic, mask ventilation was replaced with endotracheal intubation. Mild therapeutic hypothermia was initiated and maintained for 24 hours. The patient was extubated after 48 hours.
test_results: Electrocardiogram presented a stable sinus rhythm without ST-segment deviation or channelopathies. The echocardiography showed a nearly unimpaired left ventricular contractile function. Neither a pericardial effusion nor a valvular heart defect could be found. The patient was investigated with head CT scan because of anisocoria. Cerebral hemorrhage could be excluded. A thoracic CT scan showed neither pulmonary embolism nor aortic dissection. An obstructive coronary artery disease has been excluded by a coronary angiography. A neurological examination revealed problems of temporal orientation.
Orpha_name: Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation, non Brugada type

case_report: A 36-year-old female patient was admitted to our hospital with symptoms of chronic cough, expectoration, chest tightness, and wheezing. She has never smoked. She has had chronic sinusitis since the age of 12 and began experiencing cough and purulent sputum at the age of 20. These symptoms have progressively worsened, leading to exertional dyspnea and persistent wheezing. At the age of 25, she underwent thoracotomy drainage and biopsy at a local hospital due to empyema and pleural effusion. Physical examination upon admission revealed diffuse expiratory wheezes and coarse crackles in both lungs.
test_results: Pulmonary function test showed that the ratio of the forced expiratory volume in 1 second to the forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC) was 43.39%. Blood gas analysis showed hypoxemia with an oxygen partial pressure (PaO2) of 62 mmHg and oxygenation index of 155 mmHg. Chest high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) scan showed well-defined multiple centrilobular nodules and diffuse tree-in-bud pattern. Paranasal sinus CT showed bilateral maxillary sinus inflammation.

case_report: The patient is a 15-year-old male with a history of delayed motor milestones, achieving independent sitting at 9 months and walking at 19 months. Language development was also delayed, though no formal neuropsychological assessment is available. No facial abnormalities were noted. At 2 years old, transient internal rotation of the left upper limb was observed but later resolved. Over time, the patient developed mild axial hypotonia, gait disturbances, and intentional tremor. By age 8, bilateral pyramidal signs, including unstained plantar clonus, increased tendon reflexes, and Babinski signs, were present. The most recent neurological examination at 15 years old showed asymmetrical distal dystonic posturing, spasticity, and bilateral pes cavus, with other neurological signs remaining stable. Levodopa and carbidopa therapy was initiated due to dystonic features but was discontinued due to lack of efficacy. The patient participated in a personalized physiotherapy program. A brain MRI at age 3 revealed areas of white matter hypomyelination, which remained stable through childhood and adolescence. Nerve conduction studies (NCS) and electromyography (EMG) were conducted at ages 4, 7, and 15. EMG was performed using a four-channel EMG machine with specific settings for amplification and filtering. Standard electrophysiological techniques were used to measure motor and sensory conduction velocities and amplitudes in the median, ulnar, peroneal, tibial, and sural nerves. Needle EMG of the bilateral anterior tibial, extensor indicis, and gastrocnemius muscles was also performed. Initial evaluations showed normal results, but the latest examination at age 15 indicated axonal sensory polyneuropathy in all four limbs. The patient has undergone multiple diagnostic investigations, all of which were unremarkable.
test_results: A heterozygous missense de novo variant c.1181A>G, p.(Tyr394Cys) in the MORC2 gene was identified. This variant is absent in the large reference population cohorts of the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD, n > 120,000 exomes and >15,000 genomes). The variant is predicted as damaging by used in silico tools SIFT, PolyPhen, and MutationTaster. Parental testing and recent publications identifying the same variant in other patients allowed reclassification of the variant to pathogenic. No other variants in known disease-causing genes were identified. Whole-exome data of the patient were also analyzed for secondary findings; analysis was negative.
diagnosis: Infantile-Onset Charcot–Marie–Tooth Disease due to a de novo MORC2 gene variant

case_report: A 10-month-old girl was brought to the ophthalmic emergency room at King Abdulaziz University Hospital, Riyadh, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, due to vitreous hemorrhage in the right eye. Her parents had observed an outward deviation of her right eye for the past 5 weeks. They reported no history of ocular or head trauma and no systemic disease. Ophthalmic examination revealed a right exotropia measuring 30 prism diopters. The vision in the right eye was central, steady, and unmaintained, and she resisted occlusion of the left eye. Extra-ocular muscle movements were full. Portable slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment was normal except for mild subconjunctival hemorrhage in the right eye, likely secondary to a previous examination under sedation. Fundus examination of the right eye showed old vitreous hemorrhage covering the macula. There were small saccular dilatations filled with dark blood involving the macula. Slit-lamp and fundus examination of the left eye was normal. She was admitted for further evaluation. General physical examination was normal, and blood work-up did not indicate any bleeding disorders. Brain magnetic resonance imaging was unremarkable with no evidence of subdural hemorrhage or CNS vascular malformation. Bone survey was normal.
test_results: Fundus fluorescein angiography showed delayed filling in the venous phase and lack of leakage in the late phase. Ultrasonography of the right eye showed a dome shaped lesion in the macula that measured 2.5mm in elevation, 8×9.5 mm in diameter with vitreous hemorrhage emanating from its surface. A scan revealed high regular internal reflectivity.

case_report: An 81-year-old right-handed male experienced a sudden reduction in sound volume, inability to swallow and speak, inability to move his tongue, and difficulties in chewing food. His medical history includes diabetes mellitus, hypertension, coronary artery disease, and benign prostate hypertrophy. Approximately four years ago, he had an event characterized by weakness in his right arm and leg, which fully resolved. He has not adhered to recommended antiplatelet therapy. His family history is unremarkable. Neurological examination revealed he was unable to produce voice, though his understanding of spoken and written language was intact. He communicated through signs and writing. Pupillary and corneal reflexes, as well as extraocular movements, were normal. The left nasolabial fold was absent. He could not open his mouth, protrude his tongue, show his teeth, whistle, chew, or swallow. His tongue was midline and immobile without atrophy, fibrillation, or deviation. Taste sensation was normal. Palatal, laryngeal, blink, and gag reflexes, as well as spontaneous smiling and yawning, were preserved. Muscle strength in both upper and lower limbs was 5/5. Deep tendon reflexes were normal. There was no Babinski response. Extrapyramidal, coordination, and sensory examinations were normal. Laryngoscopic examination showed no vocal cord paralysis. Laboratory tests, including liver and kidney function, complete blood count, urinalysis, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, were normal. Transthoracic echocardiogram revealed biatrial dilatation, mild calcification of the mitral and aortic valves, and mild insufficiency of both valves. Doppler ultrasonography of the carotid and vertebral arteries was unremarkable.
test_results: The magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of brain indicated right frontal opercular acute infarct with 3.3 × 2.6 cm on dimensions and bilateral chronic inferior frontal gyrus infarct.

case_report: The female patient was born at 41 weeks of gestation to a 27-year-old mother and a 41-year-old father. The pregnancy involved twin gestation with the loss of one twin in the first trimester. Amniocentesis results for karyotype and alpha-fetoprotein levels were normal. The delivery and postnatal period were uneventful. Birth weight was 3.09 kg (z-score −0.31) and length was 50.8 cm (z-score +0.26). Initial examination showed a hoarse cry, a right scapular hemangioma, and talipes equinovarus, which were managed with casting. At 2 months, the patient had tracheomalacia. Physical examination noted relative macrocephaly, frontal bossing, hypertelorism, a depressed nasal bridge, anteverted nares, mild pectus excavatum, single palmar creases, and short limbs with apparent rhizomelia and upper extremity acromelia. The knees had lateral dimples bilaterally and increased anteroposterior laxity. Mild hypotonia was also observed. Head ultrasounds at 4 and 5 months showed mild fullness of both lateral ventricles without hydrocephalus or increased intracranial pressure. During infancy and early childhood, the patient experienced poor growth, conductive hearing loss due to congenitally fused ossicles, and recurrent otitis media. She also had a bicuspid aortic valve and a persistent superior vena cava to the coronary sinus. By 3.5 years, her height was 86 cm (z-score −3.2) and weight was 11.3 kg (z-score −2.3), while head circumference was 51.5 cm (z-score +1.8). She had radial head subluxation, genu valgum, and generalized joint laxity. Visual acuity deficit and infantile glaucoma were noted, along with iris hypoplasia, an anteriorly displaced line of Schwalbe, abnormal angulation and insertion of the irises, and right-sided uveal ectropion. Eye movements and retinal examination were normal. She underwent multiple ocular surgeries, including bilateral surgical goniotomy, trabeculectomy, and implantation of an aqueous humor drainage device. Pre-surgery eye examination showed 20/60 visual acuity with no refractive defects. Intraocular pressures were 30 mm Hg bilaterally. Corneal thicknesses were 643 μm and 678 μm. Bilateral Haab striae were present. The pupils were round and centered with a prominent inferior ectropion uvea in the right eye. Gonioscopy revealed the iris inserted at the level of the scleral spur with multiple nonpigmented thin iris stromal extensions attached to a thickened Schwalbe line circumferentially.
test_results: EEG confirmed frequent epileptiform complexes over the right fronto-temporal area. MRI findings showed mild inferior transtentorial herniation of the medial right temporal/occipital lobe and associated mild deformity of the right cerebellum, mild dilation of the lateral ventricles, mild inferior displacement of the pituitary stalk and third ventricle, and several nonspecific scattered punctate foci of periventricular and subcortical T2/flair signal abnormalities.

case_report: A 43-year-old female presented with a painful solitary ulcer on the genitalia that had persisted for 1 year. The lesion initially appeared as a pustule, which then ruptured and formed the ulcer. There was no history of fever, joint pain, oral ulcers, abdominal pain, loose stool, preceding trauma, or weight loss. General physical and systemic examinations were normal. Cutaneous examination revealed a single ulcer measuring 3 cm × 4 cm with hyperpigmented irregular margins and slightly undermined edges, located on the lower part of the mons pubis extending to the upper part of the vulva. The ulcer was slightly tender, nonindurated, and the floor was covered with red granulation tissue. There was no regional lymphadenopathy. Routine blood workup, peripheral smear, urine analysis, stool examination, chest X-ray, and colonoscopy results were normal. Mantoux test, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, HIV testing, and Venereal Disease Research Laboratory tests were negative. Tissue smear for Donovan bodies was negative. At the venepuncture site, the patient developed an indurated plaque measuring 1 cm × 2 cm. Gram-stain and culture and sensitivity tests from the floor of the ulcer showed gram-negative bacilli sensitive to gentamicin. Smear for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) from the floor of the ulcer was negative.
test_results: Histopathology showed infiltration of neutrophils, lymphocytes, and plasma cells in the dermis with occasional ill-defined granulomas and giant cells. Special stains for AFB and fungus were negative.

case_report: A 73-year-old male with a history of smoking 20 cigarettes daily from age 20 to 72, who quit smoking a year ago, was referred for treatment of an abnormal pulmonary cystic space with nodules observed on CT. The patient was being treated for hypertension, angina pectoris, and chronic kidney disease. Blood tests did not indicate any pulmonary infectious diseases, including mycobacterial and fungal infections. Pulmonary function tests showed a forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) of 2.20 L and a reduced FEV1/forced vital capacity ratio (FEV1%) of 68% (<70%), indicating obstructive ventilatory disturbance likely due to smoking. Physical examinations of the chest and abdomen were unremarkable. Axial serial CT images in a lung window setting displayed a thin-walled cystic space with both exophytic and endophytic solid nodules along the cyst wall. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography showed marginal FDG uptake, with a maximum standardized uptake value of 2.6 in the lung nodule, and no evidence of extrathoracic malignancies. Following wedge resection of the cyst with nodules, an adenocarcinoma was identified intraoperatively.
test_results: Histopathology revealed complex glandular structures comprising nonciliated atypical cells resembling developing epithelium in the pseudoglandular phase of the fetal lung. Nuclear atypia with frequent mitotic figures was observed. The inner wall surfaces showed a lining of tumor cells, as well as squamous metaplasia or bronchiolization. Positive periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) and negative PAS-diastase stains revealed glycogen-rich tumor cells. Immunohistochemically, tumor cells were positive for oncofetal (SALL4 and α-fetoprotein), neuroendocrine (synaptophysin, CD56, and chromogranin A) markers. β-catenin was expressed only in the tumor cell membrane. Tumor cells were negative for thyroid transcription factor 1 and programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1). Ki-67 staining revealed increased cell proliferation.
Orpha_name: Well-differentiated fetal adenocarcinoma of the lung

case_report: A 5-year-old boy experienced a severe cough and breathing difficulties a month prior to hospitalization, for which he was treated with antibiotics and bronchodilators as an outpatient. A week before admission, he developed facial swelling, reduced urine output, and severe shortness of breath. He was admitted to the intensive care unit. Since infancy, he had recurrent bacterial respiratory infections, including adenoiditis, otitis media, obstructive bronchitis, and pneumonia. At age 1, he was noted to have generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. He underwent an adenoidectomy during his second year. Due to hepatosplenomegaly, he was monitored by a hematologist from ages 2 to 4.5. Previous lab results showed serum IgA at 0.24 g/L (0.41–2.97), IgM at 0.67 g/L (0.4–1.6), and IgG at 5.5 g/L (6–13). Alfa 1 antitrypsin was within normal limits. Tests ruled out co-natal and acquired viral infections, hemoglobinopathy, and malignancies. A peripheral lymph gland biopsy indicated reactive lymphadenitis. Pancytopenia was later identified. Clinical features included obstructive pulmonary disease, splenomegaly, generalized lymphadenopathy, and failure to thrive, with a poor appetite, especially during frequent respiratory infections. Mental status was normal. There was no family history of similar diseases. On admission, the boy was in a critical condition, afebrile, with a heart rate of 140/min, respiratory rate of 50/min, and blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg. His weight was 17 kg and height 101 cm, both below the third percentile. He had pale, acrocyanotic, and edematous skin and mucous membranes. Lymph nodes were swollen to about 2 cm in diameter. Pulmonary examination revealed inspiratory crackles and low-pitch wheezing. Cardiac examination showed a gallop rhythm without murmurs and weak peripheral pulses. Hepatosplenomegaly was present. Neurological examination was normal. Lab results indicated increased acute phase reactants, pancytopenia with a leukocyte count of 2.7 × 10^9/L, thrombocyte count of 40 × 10^9/L, Coombs positive hemolytic anemia with Hb at 64 g/L, and reticulocytes at 1.2%. Red blood cell osmotic resistance was normal, and peripheral blood smear showed fragmented red blood cells. Serum creatinine was 153 μmol/L (estimated creatinine clearance 30 mL/min/1.73 m^2), urea nitrogen was 13.0 mmol/L (0.1–7), and uric acid was 278 μmol/L (71–230). Coagulation tests (aPTT, PT, D-dimer, fibrinogen) were normal. Total serum proteins were 55.5 g/L, and albumin was 24 g/L. Liver enzymes and bilirubin were normal. Cholesterol was 7.28 mmol/L (up to 3), and triglycerides were 2.22 mmol/L (up to 0.7). Blood gas analysis showed global respiratory insufficiency. Urine analysis revealed proteinuria (5+) and microscopic hematuria. Cultures of blood, stool, and urine were negative. Tests for Coxsackie virus, Cytomegalovirus, and Hantaan virus (IgG and IgM) were negative. Renal ultrasound showed loss of corticomedullary differentiation and hyperechogenic parenchyma in both kidneys. Abdominal ultrasound confirmed hepatosplenomegaly. Chest X-ray indicated inflammation, congestive changes, and an enlarged heart shadow. Echocardiography revealed left ventricular cardiomyopathy and pulmonary hypertension.
test_results: IgA 0.16 g/L (0.41–2.97), IgG 3.3 g/L (6–13), IgM 0.13 g/L (0.4–1.6); all three classes of immunoglobulin were lowered in the three samples taken at monthly intervals.

case_report: A 56-year-old female presented with a 6-month history of progressively worsening hair loss at the frontal scalp. The patient reported mild itching of the scalp. She denied any history of trauma to the hair and had no known medical or surgical history, including thyroid or autoimmune diseases. She was not on any regular medications but had an allergy to sulphur. There was a family history of hair loss, with her mother also experiencing similar issues. On physical examination, there was noticeable thinning of the hair on both sides of the frontoparietal scalp, more pronounced on the left side. This was accompanied by reduced visible follicular openings, perifollicular scaling, and redness. Two specific areas were affected: a 12 × 2.5 cm area on the left parietal scalp and a 4 × 1.5 cm area on the right parietal scalp. The occipital and vertex regions were unaffected. There were no changes observed in the nails, oral mucosa, or skin. Systemic examination revealed no abnormalities. Laboratory tests showed normal full blood count, thyroid function, electrolytes, and liver/renal function. An anti-nuclear antibody titre was 160, but other autoimmune screenings were negative. Urine tests were negative for infection or casts, and the protein/creatinine ratio was within normal limits.
test_results: Two 4-mm punch biopsies of the left anterior scalp revealed a slight reduction of terminal hair with focal perifollicular fibrosis and occasional collections of perivascular lymphocytes. No lichenoid changes were seen. There were large numbers of syringomatous elements in the upper dermis. Further comparative biopsies were taken 2 months later, from clinically normal scalp and normal hair-bearing skin of the arm. Two 4-mm punch biopsies were taken from the scalp vertex. One scalp biopsy showed perifollicular fibrosis and no syringomatous elements, but the second biopsy from normal scalp showed a reduction in terminal hairs with perifollicular fibrosis/inflammation with extension of the lymphocytes into the follicular epithelium in the upper half of the hair follicles. This biopsy again showed no lichenoid reaction within the epidermis but compound and distorted hair follicles were present in the upper parts of the biopsy as well as syringomatous elements. The biopsy specimen of the left arm showed completely normal skin.

case_report: An 8.5-year-old female presented to the endocrinology clinic for evaluation of short stature. She was born at term to healthy consanguineous parents (first cousins). Physical examination revealed a height of 97 cm (−6.4SD), weight of 17.2 kg (−3.4SD), and Tanner stage 1. Her blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg, and her heart rate was 85 bpm. Notable physical features included a prominent forehead, flattened nasal bridge, hypertelorism, and short limbs relative to trunk length. There were no signs of goiter, hepatosplenomegaly, or skin abnormalities. Laboratory tests indicated normal thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and cortisol levels, a low level of insulin-like growth factor (IGF1), and an elevated fasting growth hormone (GH) level.
test_results: GH stimulating test with insulin (0.1 U/Kg/IV) showed high levels of GH post-stimulation. Her bone age was 5 years.

case_report: A 53-year-old woman presented with an asymptomatic cyst on her left vulva of uncertain duration. The initial clinical assessment suggested a vulvar abscess. There was no known history of generalized skin conditions with similar characteristics, and no associated lesions were found on the vulva or cervix. The family history was negative for dermatologic conditions involving multiple papules and nodules. The lesion was surgically removed and submitted for routine examination.
test_results: There were fragments of cystic epithelium with areas of hypergranulosis, acantholysis, suprabasilar clefting, and corps ronds, and grains formation.

case_report: A 46-year-old male presented with a bent spine. He reported back and neck pain starting 3 months prior, which progressed to difficulty standing upright 2 months ago, with mild relief upon rest. Concurrently, he experienced numbness in his limbs and around his lips, with symptoms worsening over time. Two weeks prior to admission, he lost the ability to maintain an upright trunk and had difficulty raising his head. He did not exhibit limb weakness, tremor, ataxia, or muscle cramps. There was no family history of similar symptoms. Neurological examination showed a bent spine and dropped head posture when standing. Neck extensor strength was 2/5, iliopsoas muscle strength was 5-/5, proximal lower limb muscle strength was 5/5, and distal muscle strength was 5/5. Deep tendon reflexes were absent. Light touch and pain sensation were impaired in the hands, feet, and around the lips, while deep sensation remained intact. Serum creatine kinase (CK) level was 568 IU/L (normal range: 25-175 IU/L).
test_results: Urinary organic acid analysis showed elevation of glutarate, 2-hydroxyglutaric acid, 3-hydroxyglutaric acid, glyceric acid, and 2-hydroxyadipic acid. Blood acylcarnitine analysis revealed a combined elevation of short- (C6), medium- (C8, C10), and long- (C14) chain acylcarnitines. Genetic screening was performed in the alpha ETF (ETFA), beta ETF (ETFB), and ETF dehydrogenase (ETFDH) genes. A common mutation C.770A>G (p.T257C) in Chinese population was identified in exon 7 of the ETFDH gene. A novel mutation 920C>G (p.S307C) was found in exon 8 of the ETFDH gene.

case_report: A 15-year-old male was admitted to Qilu Hospital (Jinan, China) with a history of recurrent fractures over the past three years, primarily due to falls or overexertion. These fractures occurred approximately every 3–4 months, mainly affecting the forearms and legs, and healed without significant delay when treated with external fixations. The patient did not report bone pain, limb and joint deformities, or muscle weakness. One year prior, the patient had undergone a six-month treatment with Caltrate and calcitriol (one tablet of each per day), during which he experienced one fracture. After discontinuing the treatment, he had two additional fractures from minor impacts over the following six months. The patient had not used other medications affecting bone metabolism, such as steroids. He had an appendectomy in 2006 for acute appendicitis and recovered well. The patient was born at full term via spontaneous vaginal delivery without complications: Birth height was 50 cm (50th percentile) and birth weight was 3,500 g (50th percentile). He was breastfed, had no delayed tooth eruption, and achieved sitting at eight months and independent walking at 16 months. At 8 and 12 months, he had episodes of nondisplaced fractures from minor impacts. His growth in height was slower than peers until age eight, but his intellectual development was normal. The parents were non-consanguineous and healthy, with no family history of bone disease. Upon admission, the patient's measurements were: Height, 162 cm (25th percentile); body weight, 52 kg (25th percentile); body mass index, 19.8 kg/m2; interphalangeal space, 158 cm; and head circumference, 58 cm. Physical examination showed normal development, well-proportioned body, normal gait, and erect posture. The patient had a triangular face and blue sclera. Intraoral examination revealed a crossbite of the anterior teeth with no discoloration or decay. Altered joint mobility and flexibility were noted. The patient was at stage IV on the Tanner scale for genital and pubic hair development. There were no signs of rib beading, skeletal deformities, hearing impairment, cardiac murmurs, or respiratory difficulty, and the neurological examination was normal. Laboratory tests showed normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate; levels of C-reactive protein, serum creatinine, alkaline phosphatase, calcium, and phosphorus; and 24-hour urinary excretion of calcium, phosphorus, and parathyroid hormone (PTH). Serum levels of osteocalcin and total type I collagen telopeptide were elevated, while the level of 25-hydroxyvitamin D was slightly decreased. Thyroid hormone, growth hormone (GH), cortisol, adrenocorticotropic hormone, and sex hormone levels were within normal ranges. Protein electrophoresis, rheumatic disease antibody, and Bence-Jones protein tests were negative.
test_results: An X-ray of the skull showed diffuse low bone density, the absence of Wormian bones and no indication of the ‘salt-and-pepper’ effect. Additional observations obtained from the X-rays included biconcavity deformities in the lower thoracic and lumbar vertebrae, a triradiate pelvis and acetabular protrusion, growth arrest recovery lines in the two knee joints and former fractures in the upper end of the fibula. Bone mineral density (BMD) was measured via dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry and low values (mean 0.633 g/cm2) for the lumbar vertebra L1–4 were observed.

case_report: A 12-month-old male infant of African descent presented with a history of global developmental delay, irregular sleep patterns, and inadequate weight gain. He is the first child of a 28-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus diagnosed at age 9. The mother began antenatal care at 16 weeks of gestation and received standard antenatal treatments including antihelminthics, antimalarial medications, hematinics, and tetanus toxoid, according to Tanzanian protocol. She tested negative for HIV, hepatitis B and C, and syphilis. The mother reported no history of TORCH infections, trauma, or chronic drug use, but had a urinary tract infection in the first trimester treated with oral cephalexin 500 mg four times daily for 5 days. No other familial genetic disorders were reported apart from insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus. Ultrasound evaluations at 16 and 36 weeks of gestation indicated a normal singleton pregnancy. Despite good glycemic control before pregnancy, the mother had poor glycemic control during pregnancy with HbA1C levels of 8.3% at 7 weeks and 7.9% at 29 weeks of gestation. Delivery occurred at 39+ weeks via emergency cesarean section due to fetal distress and breech presentation. The infant's birth weight was 2315 g with Apgar scores of 6/10 and 8/10 at 1 and 5 minutes respectively. His head circumference at birth was 38.9 cm (97th percentile). Chromosome analysis was not performed. At 6 months, the boy weighed 8.5 kg, which remained unchanged at 12 months. His head circumference at 1 year was 49.1 cm (99th percentile). Vital signs were stable, but physical examination showed a small-for-age child with conjunctival and palmar pallor. Growth parameters were below the 5th percentile, and developmental age was assessed at 2 months. He scored 4 on the Carter Neurocognitive Assessment Severity Scale. Facial features were normal, but neurological examination revealed hypotonia in all four limbs. Other systemic examinations were unremarkable. Blood tests, cardiac echocardiography, and renal ultrasound were conducted, showing normal results except for iron deficiency anemia: hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, mean corpuscular hemoglobin 21 pg/cell, mean corpuscular volume 69 fL, and red cell distribution width 15.1%.
test_results: The child also underwent MRI of his brain which revealed an incompletely formed interhemispheric fissure, a monoventricle with partially developed temporal and occipital horns, partial fusion of his frontal lobe, hypoplastic corpus callosum, and volume loss bilaterally at temporal lobes. His cerebellum and brain stem appeared normal.

case_report: A 10-year-old afrodescendant female child presented to the oral medicine service with a primary concern of painless gingival swelling, which was causing difficulty in chewing and aesthetic issues. The patient's mother reported no systemic health issues, chronic medication use, or complications during pregnancy and delivery. The gingival enlargement was first noticed at age 5 during deciduous dentition and intensified with the emergence of permanent teeth. The mother also mentioned that the child's father exhibited similar features, while she herself did not. The child's past medical history was unremarkable. Extraoral examination showed elevated lips, a pronounced open bite, and difficulty achieving a passive lip seal. Intraoral examination revealed generalized gingival enlargement covering nearly all maxillary and mandibular teeth, leading to problems with swallowing, speaking, and aesthetics. The gingival tissue had a rough texture, pink color, and fibrous consistency, with areas of melanic pigmentation and hyperemia at the gingival margins in the anterior vestibular region. In the palatal region, the enlargement extended toward the midline, partially obscuring the palate's depth. Teeth were displaced, with crowns partially or fully embedded in the fibrotic tissue. The gingiva was painless upon palpation. Hematological tests were normal, indicating no systemic involvement. A panoramic radiograph showed normal dental development, with all permanent teeth present and at appropriate developmental stages.
test_results: Microscopic examination revealed a hypocellular and hypovascular dense fibrous connective tissue, covered by intact stratified squamous epithelium exhibiting acanthosis and hyperplasia. Picro-sirius red staining reveals that the enlarged gingival tissue is primarily the result of an increased amount of collagen fiber bundles.

case_report: An 8-year-old boy with no prior health issues and a recent history of fever was admitted to the pediatric intensive-care unit (PICU) at Meyer Children's Hospital from another hospital due to a comatose state and repeated focal motor seizures. Blood and cerebrospinal fluid tests showed no significant abnormalities, and no clear infectious cause was found. Prior treatments included endorectal diazepam, intravenous benzodiazepines, phenytoin, and phenobarbital, all of which were ineffective.
test_results: Continuous video-electroencephalography (EEG) monitoring recorded right and left focal motor seizures and secondarily generalized seizures.

case_report: A 34-year-old male presented with intermittent pain in the right upper abdomen and jaundice for 1 month. The patient had no significant past medical history, including no special drug use or alcohol consumption. Elevated serum IgG4 levels were noted in the patient, his younger sister, and his daughter. Physical examination showed a darkened complexion, jaundice, abdominal distension, and positive shifting dullness, with negative rebound tenderness and Murphy signs. Laboratory tests revealed no abnormalities in hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), hepatitis C virus antibody (anti-HCV), anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA), anti-nuclear antibody (ANA), smooth muscle antibody (SMA), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), blood and urine amylase, or tumor markers. MRI of the liver indicated liver cirrhosis and mild dilatation of some intrahepatic bile ducts. MRCP showed obstructed bile ducts in the hepatic hilar region. Liver biopsy revealed fibrosis and fibrotic changes around the bile ducts, infiltration of numerous lymphocytes and mild plasma cells, cholestasis in peripheral hepatocytes, and local biliary thrombosis in the enlarged portal area. IgG immunostaining of the liver biopsy showed scattered IgG-positive plasma cells, while IgG4 immunostaining demonstrated few IgG4-positive plasma cells (1–3 cells/hpf). Initial treatment included oral steroids at 40 mg/day, which normalized serum IgG4 levels, but jaundice persisted. The patient's overall condition gradually worsened, leading to severe complications post-steroid therapy.
test_results: Irregular narrowing of the intrahepatic bile ducts, that is, a pruned-tree appearance, was observed.

case_report: A 42-year-old female patient was admitted with complaints of dizziness and chest tightness. Her family, including her parents and sibling, are healthy and of Han ethnicity from Wuhan, Hubei, China, with no known family history of genetic diseases. Her medical history includes rapidly progressive and widespread arterial tortuosity. At age 34, she had a subclavian artery aneurysm with a diameter of 10.2 mm and underwent subclavian artery stent implantation due to the aneurysm's increasing size. At age 37, she experienced an aortic dissection and received endovascular stent-graft placement. At age 40, she developed aortic root and arch aneurysms and underwent a Bentall operation (aortic root replacement) with total aortic arch replacement and elephant trunk repair surgery. Additionally, she had a first metatarsal fracture at age 38 without external force trauma. Physical examination revealed a normal stature with a height of 163 cm, no spinal deformity, and no significant craniofacial abnormalities. Laboratory results showed mild anemia with a hemoglobin concentration of 99 g/l. The patient also had a persistent skin wound on her left abdomen following the elephant trunk repair surgery.
test_results: A large aneurysm (18.1 mm × 33.1 mm) of the left subclavian artery near its origin was still visible in three-dimensional (3D) reconstructed images from computed tomography angiography (CTA) 2 years after the stent implantation. CTA revealed DeBakey type III dissecting aortic aneurysm, of which the proximal rupture was located at the level of the bilateral renal artery. The dissection ranged from the opening of the celiac trunk to the left internal iliac artery.

case_report: The patient, a 3-year-old boy, was born at term through an uneventful delivery with normal birth parameters to consanguineous Chinese parents. He was the first child in a second pregnancy, following an induced abortion due to fetal death. The grandparents of the patient were cousins. At the age of 5 months, the patient first presented with motor and cognitive delays. He was unable to attain head control, turn over, or actively grasp objects. His eyesight and hearing were normal. Paroxysmal hypertonia began at 1 month old, initially presenting as clenched fists and straightened limbs, progressing to flexion of both upper limbs, fisted hands, and straightened lower limbs. These episodes lasted for a few seconds to a few minutes and resolved spontaneously, with the patient remaining conscious throughout. Physical examination showed microcephaly, white skin, yellow hair, a slightly long face, high palatine arch, right hand penetration, small penis, and small hands and feet. Muscle strength was grade three, with paroxysmal hypertonia, negative limb deep reflexes, and bilateral symmetric flexor plantar reflex. MRI in 2017 showed ventricular broadening and left lateral fissure widening. A year later, MRI revealed symmetric hyperintensity in the bilateral basal ganglia on T2-weighted imaging, T2-FLAIR, and DWI sequences. Video electroencephalogram showed a normal background and recorded paroxysmal limb rigidity without epileptiform discharges. Liver and renal function, myocardial enzyme, and ceruloplasmin levels were normal, but metabolism screening indicated mild ketonuria and hyperlactacidemia (2.55–3.36). G-banding karyotype analysis: 46, XY. Gesell Developmental Scale results: Adaptability: DQ 26.7, DA 2.5, severe delay; Gross motor: DQ 23.7, DA 2.2, extremely severe delay; Fine motor: DQ 24.7, DA 2.3, extremely severe delay; Communication: DQ 49.5, DA 4.6, moderately delayed; personal-social skills: DQ 37.6, DA 3.5, severe delay.
test_results: We identified a de novo variant (c.116 G>A, p.S39N) in exon 2 of DNM1L. Gene variation was validated using Sanger sequencing.
diagnosis: DNM1L-related mitochondrial fission defects presenting as encephalopathy
Orpha_name: DNM1L-related encephalopathy due to mitochondrial and peroxisomal fission defect

case_report: A two-month-old male infant was referred to the pediatric gastroenterology department at Sisli Etfal Education and Research Hospital due to hepatosplenomegaly and thrombocytopenia. The patient had been hospitalized on the first day of life in the neonatal unit for poor feeding and received empirical ampicillin-gentamycin therapy following a sepsis workup. During follow-up, hypocalcemia and intracranial hemorrhage were noted. The patient was born at 38 weeks gestation after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, with a birth weight of 2600 grams and Apgar scores of 7 and 9. Parental consanguinity was noted, and two siblings had died in infancy from unknown causes. Physical examination revealed hepatomegaly (liver 4/3 cm), splenomegaly (spleen 3 cm), a bulging anterior fontanel (4×4 cm), weight of 3.4 kg (<3rd percentile), height of 44 cm (<3rd percentile), and head circumference of 38 cm (50-75 percentile). The patient appeared pale, and fundoscopic examination showed bilateral optic atrophy. Laboratory results included hemoglobin 11.4 g/dl, white blood cell count 4400 cells/mm3, and platelet count 24,000/mm3. Biochemical analysis was normal except for AST 118 U/L, LDH 1150 U/L, PTH 349 pg/mL, ALP 847 IU/L, and acid phosphatase 16.4 U/L. Peripheral blood smear showed leukoerythroblastosis. Arterial blood gas analysis was normal. Serology for toxoplasma, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes, and hepatitis virus was negative. Immunoglobulin levels (G, M, A), lymphocyte subsets, and urine and serum amino acid and organic acid analyses were normal. Tandem mass spectrometry showed no abnormalities. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed marked hepatosplenomegaly. Cranial ultrasonography showed ventriculomegaly of the lateral and third ventricles. A computed axial tomographic scan of the orbits demonstrated bilateral narrowing of the optic foramina. Bone marrow aspiration showed hypocellularity, and bone marrow culture was negative. Liver biopsy indicated extra-medullary hematopoiesis and significant ballooning of parenchymal cells.
test_results: Skeletal survey revealed diffuse sclerosis of all bones.

case_report: The patient is a 3-year-old boy of Pakistani descent, born at term following an uneventful pregnancy. His parents reported no consanguinity. During a routine analysis conducted for language delay and concerns related to autism spectrum disorder (ASD), the patient exhibited very low serum uric acid levels (<0.2 mg/dL), which were subsequently confirmed. The fractional excretion of urate was elevated (FE UA 117%), while serum creatinine was within normal limits (0.37 mg/dL). Other laboratory values, including glucose, urea, creatinine, calcium, sodium, potassium, and chloride, were all within normal ranges. An abdominal ultrasound showed no abnormalities.
test_results: A genetic study was performed on the patient and his parents.

case_report: A 3-year-old female patient visited the School of Dentistry at the local university with complaints of generalized tooth mobility and spontaneous gingival bleeding. The symptoms were first noticed by her mother when the child was 2 years old. The general health questionnaire revealed no significant conditions or medication use. The patient had seen several dentists previously, but no oral treatments had been performed. Family members, including her grandmother, mother, aunt, and cousins, also experienced tooth mobility and early exfoliation of permanent teeth, but there was no history of early loss of primary teeth in the family. Initial clinical and radiological assessments showed the absence of several deciduous teeth, which had been removed at home due to extreme mobility. The oral examination revealed mobility in several remaining teeth, clinical attachment loss, and a high accumulation of dental biofilm. A comprehensive periodontal examination was not possible at that time. The proposed treatment plan included the removal of all hopeless teeth, mechanical removal of biofilm and calculus from all teeth, and oral hygiene instructions. The patient was also referred to a medical geneticist for further investigation of any related systemic conditions. Approximately one month later, the patient returned, but only oral hygiene instruction was performed due to lack of cooperation. During a medical appointment, additional findings included leg stains, difficult-to-heal wounds, and a history of premature births in several family members. Blood tests were conducted, and all results were considered adequate.
test_results: The detailed review of family history showed that her mother, maternal grandmother, maternal aunt, several cousins, and great aunt had a history of periodontal disease, skin fragility, and poor wound healing, suggesting an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.

case_report: A 70-year-old man with a history of smoking cessation presented to our outpatient department with a one-year history of worsening shortness of breath on exertion and a persistent dry cough. During the general examination, his oxygen saturation dropped from 95% to 75% with exercise, and he exhibited Grade III clubbing. Chest auscultation revealed fine crackles at the bases of both lungs. A chest X-ray demonstrated a bilateral reticulonodular pattern along with fibrosis in the right upper lobe. Hematological and biochemical blood tests were within normal ranges.
test_results: High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of thorax showed bilateral reticular opacities with honeycombing in peripheral subpleural areas and interlobular, intralobular septal thickening with traction bronchiectasis, and few ground-glass opacities (GGOs) most marked in lower lobes. Spirometry showed severe restrictive abnormality with forced vital capacity of 0.85 L (26% of predicted). F-18 FDG PET/CT showed moderate grade F-18 FDG avid (maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) – 4.35) uptake in bilateral reticular opacities with relatively high grade F-18 FDG (SUVmax – 6–6.6) uptake in honeycombed areas. Low-grade FDG uptake was noted in the ground glass areas with multiple F-18 FDG avid (SUVmax – 8.72) mediastinal lymph nodes.

case_report: A 50-year-old male with a history of hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and heart failure presented with 4 months of progressive vision loss and lower extremity sensory changes. He reported painless bilateral vision loss, initially noticing darkening of distant objects, which progressed to dimness and darkness of his entire visual field, including near vision. Concurrently, he experienced bilateral lower extremity paresthesias that ascended from his feet to his hips. One month prior, a lumbar puncture at an outside institution showed mildly elevated protein of 61 mg/dL, normal cell count of 3/µL, and glucose 56 mg/dL. Tests for CSF oligoclonal bands, IgG index, myelin basic protein, and serum paraneoplastic panel were normal. MRI brain revealed T2/FLAIR hyperintensities involving the optic nerves and tracts. Spinal MRI showed a C1-T10 T2 hyperintense lesion involving the central and posterior cord without contrast enhancement or edema. He received methylprednisolone 1 gram daily for 5 days and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) 2 grams per kilogram divided over 5 days. Serum aquaporin-4 and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) antibodies were negative. His symptoms did not improve, leading to a referral for further evaluation. On general examination, his vital signs were normal. He was alert and oriented. Motor exam showed full strength in all extremities. Sensory exam revealed decreased sensation to light touch and vibration in his feet to about mid-shin bilaterally. Reflexes were normal. Fundoscopic exam showed mild temporal optic disc pallor bilaterally. He was admitted for expedited evaluation and additional treatment. After plasmapheresis, he reported subjective improvement in bilateral lower extremity sensation but no visual improvement. Optical computerized tomography (OCT) showed bilateral temporal retinal nerve fiber layer thinning and macular ganglion cell layer thinning. Humphrey visual field testing showed a nonspecific inferior defect in the right eye and left eye inferior hemifield defect that respected the midline. He was discharged home with outpatient low vision rehabilitation therapy and was using a walker due to balance difficulties.
test_results: Genetic testing identified a homoplasmic MT-DN1 gene mutation demonstrating a G3635A mitochondrial DNA mutation with p.Ser110Asn (S110N) variant.

case_report: A 12-year-old boy, previously in good health, was admitted to the hospital on February 12, 2016, presenting with blepharoptosis, voice hoarseness, fever, and an inability to walk and talk. These symptoms had persisted for approximately two months. Subsequently, the patient experienced severe agitation, sleepiness, dysphagia, limb weakness, and respiratory and circulatory failure. The patient passed away shortly after. He had a history of subacute ptosis at the age of 12. He was born vaginally at term with a birth weight of 3250 g and showed no developmental delays. Upon admission, his height was 156 cm and weight was 50 kg. The patient's mother had no abnormal symptoms post-birth, and there was no family history of similar conditions. Clinical examination revealed pyramidal signs, easily elicited reflexes, and extensor toe signs on both feet. Routine blood and urine tests, urinary sediment examination, routine fecal tests, and occult blood tests were normal. Arterial blood gas analysis showed a pH of 7.32, oxygen pressure of 11.3 kPa, carbon dioxide pressure of 4.9 kPa, and oxygen saturation of 99%. Arterial plasma lactate level was slightly elevated at 3 mg/dL. Ammonia and blood sugar levels were normal, as were other blood biochemistry indexes. Cytological and biochemical examination of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showed normal results, with positive antibodies to acetylcholine, presynaptic membrane receptor, and thymoma in the blood, and positive oligoclonal bands in the CSF. Antibody tests for Mycoplasma pneumoniae, herpes simplex virus, and Epstein-Barr virus were negative.
test_results: Gene sequencing analysis revealed a T-to-C transition at nucleotide 9176 of the mitochondrial ATPase 6 gene (Leu to Pro) in the patient and a heteroplasmic mutation in the patient’s mother. Electroencephalogram analysis revealed slow-waves of background activity. The brain MRI scan showed symmetrical abnormal signals in the basal ganglia, medial thalami, periaqueductal region of the midbrain and pons, and the bilateral white matter around the lateral ventricles.

case_report: A woman in her 60s was admitted to the coronary care unit (CCU) from the local accident and emergency department with a three-day history of pleuritic central chest pain that varied with position and was accompanied by intermittent palpitations. She has no history of similar episodes and denies experiencing syncope, pre-syncope, recent illness, or shortness of breath. Her medical history includes Raynaud’s phenomenon, gastroesophageal reflux, and mild sleep apnoea, for which she uses nocturnal continuous positive airway pressure. She was not on any regular medications and has no known allergies. The patient is a retired, independent, non-smoker with minimal alcohol consumption. Her mother died from aortic dissection, and one of her children has ulcerative colitis.
test_results: Her ECG on presentation showed an irregularly irregular rhythm with a lack of P waves, widespread ST-segment elevation with concave morphology, no reciprocal changes, subtle PR elevation in lead aVR, and PR depression in leads aVF and 2. During the evening of admission, the patient complained of chest pain radiating to the back during an episode of hypotension (BP 80/45). A CT aorta was performed, which excluded aortic dissection. The CT aorta showed aneurysms throughout the mesenteric vascular system. Aneurysmal coronary arteries, diffusely aneurysmal right hepatic artery, axillary aneurysms, bi-apical pulmonary fibrosis, and shallow pericardial effusion were also noted. Following this, 15 days after the initial discharge, the patient represented to the hospital with pre-syncope and shortness of breath. Her ECG at the time showed electrical alternans consistent with significant pericardial effusion. Her echocardiogram confirmed a large pericardial effusion with features of incipient cardiac tamponade. Her pericardial effusion progressed, and right ventricular collapse developed, causing haemodynamic compromise.

case_report: The patient was a 4-year-old boy, the first child of healthy parents who were related by blood. The pregnancy was uneventful, and the mother did not consume alcohol or tobacco during this period. The delivery was normal. The child's family, including parents and grandparents, were in good health. The child exhibited delayed motor and mental development, being able to sit without support at 10 months and walk without assistance at 17 months. He showed signs of exercise intolerance. From 18 months of age, the child experienced progressive weakness and ataxia. He was frequently admitted to local hospitals due to ataxia, weakness, and regression in motor skills. Metabolic acidosis was a significant feature throughout the illness. Over time, all motor abilities were lost, and by the age of 3, the child had no motor function. The child passed away from multiorgan failure at the age of 4.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed hypointensity on T1-weighted images and hyperintensity on T2-weighted images of the bilateral globus pallidus, in addition to symmetrical abnormality.

case_report: The patient is a two-year-old girl born at full term to consanguineous Saudi parents via cesarean section due to breech presentation. She has a history of poor sucking, hypotonia, bilateral ptosis, and recurrent admissions to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) for apnea. The family history is unremarkable. The clinical course began with a sudden cessation of breathing lasting more than 15 minutes, followed by a three-minute arrest. She also has a history of choking and coughing. Upon examination, the patient was afebrile, dehydrated, and pale, with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 3. Stabilization efforts were initiated, and she was intubated in the PICU. She received ketamine and intravenous midazolam and was treated for aspiration pneumonia with nebulized salbutamol, budesonide, and antibiotics. A serial workup was conducted.
test_results: WES revealed a diagnosis of a homozygous, likely pathogenic, variant in the SLC25A1 gene. The CT brain scan revealed volume loss of brain parenchyma associated with a mildly dilated ventricular system, extra-axial cerebrospinal fluid spaces, and thinning of the anterior part of the corpus callosum with the non-visualized posterior part.
diagnosis: Autosomal recessive combined D-2- and L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria

case_report: A male patient presented at the clinic at the age of 5 with nystagmus and misaligned eyes. He was born at term with a birth weight of 3655 g. Growth issues were noted after the age of 2. Serial endocrine levels were within normal ranges. There was no reported family history. Initial ophthalmologic examination showed high hyperopia with +9.0 diopters (D) in the right eye and +8.5 D in the left eye, along with high astigmatism of −3.0 D in both eyes. Best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/200 in the right eye and 20/60 in the left eye. The right eye exhibited exotropia of approximately 25 prism diopters (PD). Slit-lamp biomicroscopy showed no abnormalities, but ophthalmoscope examination revealed macular scarring in both eyes. After 5 years of spectacle correction, BCVA improved to 20/60 in the right eye and 20/30 in the left eye, and the amplitude of nystagmus decreased. The patient was followed up regularly for over 10 years. At the age of 20, he had a body height of 117.5 cm and a weight of 24.5 kg, along with bone dysplasia and facial features including a receding chin and prominent ears. High hyperopia and astigmatism persisted, with axial lengths of 20.28 mm in the right eye and 20.37 mm in the left eye.
test_results: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) confirmed an atrophic retina in the macula area.
diagnosis: variant microcephalic primordial dwarfism type II
Orpha_name: Microcephalic osteodysplastic primordial dwarfism type II

case_report: A 12-month-old girl with a history of mild motor delay was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit due to electrolyte imbalances following two weeks of fatigue and reduced oral intake, and one day of persistent nausea and vomiting. Laboratory results showed significant hypercalcemia (14.7 mg/dL), hyponatremia (129 mmol/L), hyperkalemia (6.2 mmol/L), hypochloremia (89 mmol/L), decreased bicarbonate (16 mmol/L), an anion gap of 24, elevated BUN (48 mg/dL), and elevated creatinine (0.96 mg/dL). Hyperuricemia (10.3 mg/dL) was also noted. Renal ultrasound indicated bilateral grade 3-4 medullary calcinosis. Nephrology assessment revealed an acutely elevated urine Ca/Cr ratio that later normalized, suggesting no primary renal disease. Endocrinology evaluation during hypercalcemia showed suppressed parathyroid hormone (3.3 pg/mL) with normal levels of albumin, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, magnesium, thyroid stimulating hormone, free-T4, Vitamin A, 25-hydroxy and 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D. Elevated parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP, 9.7 pmol/L) was found without an identifiable source despite extensive imaging and laboratory studies in consultation with Oncology; lactate dehydrogenase, alpha-fetoprotein, beta-human chorionic gonadotropin, and C-reactive protein were within normal limits. Abdominal MRI showed bilateral duplicated renal collecting systems, bilateral nephrocalcinosis, and no suspicious abdominal or pelvic masses. Brain and neck MRI were normal. Tests for lead toxicity and HIV were negative. The patient was treated with intravenous fluids, resolving her hypercalcemia (calcium 10.3 mg/dL) and other electrolyte abnormalities, and was discharged on day 11. Ten days later, she was readmitted for hypercalcemia (14.3 mg/dL) and treated with calcitonin (4 doses of 4 units/kg q12 hours) without success, followed by intravenous bisphosphonate therapy (1 dose 0.5 mg/kg of pamidronate) with good response. She was discharged on day 7 with a serum calcium level of 8.5 mg/dL. Medical Genetics was consulted during both admissions. Perinatal history included high-risk noninvasive prenatal screening for Turner syndrome, evaluated by karyotype via amniocentesis, revealing a normal female karyotype. The patient was born at 39 weeks gestation to a 32-year-old G1P0 woman via cesarean section for breech presentation. Pregnancy was complicated by fetal growth restriction, likely due to the mother’s bicornuate uterus. Birth weight was 2390 g (fourth percentile), birth length was 46 cm (seventh percentile), and head circumference was 32.5 cm (seventh percentile). The mother’s medical history included decreased height (61 inches, seventeenth percentile for US adult women), bilateral genu valgum, and a bicornuate uterus, with no history of hypercalcemia. At 12.5 months, physical examination showed a length of 68 cm (<third percentile, Z-score = −2.05), relative macrocephaly (44.5 cm, 33rd percentile, Z-score = −0.45), frontal bossing, depressed nasal bridge with anteverted nares and bulbous nasal tip, and everted lower vermillion border. Initial Medical Genetics evaluation included a skeletal survey and microarray, both normal. A custom calcium homeostasis gene panel with 37 genes was ordered and was nondiagnostic.
test_results: Exome sequencing revealed a maternally inherited likely pathogenic variant (c.325+1G>T) in RPS6KA3, located within intron 4 at a canonical splice site and predicted to result in a null allele.

case_report: A 19-year-old female from the Cape Verde islands presented with a history of recurrent nausea, vomiting, gastric regurgitation, diarrhea, and painful abdominal distension since the age of 5. These episodes increased in frequency and severity during late adolescence, leading to significant weight loss (approximately 15 kg) over the past year. She also reported progressive difficulty with gait, climbing stairs, and running, as well as poor performance in gymnastic classes at school. Additionally, she experienced progressive weakness in her upper limbs, affecting her ability to comb her hair, write, and use cutlery. There was no history of cognitive impairment, and her academic performance was good. She denied experiencing pain, sensory issues, or other dysautonomic symptoms. She was the second daughter of a consanguineous marriage, and her older sister had similar gastrointestinal complaints and was diagnosed with superior mesenteric artery syndrome. The patient developed cachexia with a Body Mass Index of 10.9. Neurological examination revealed mild bilateral symmetric ptosis without ocular paresis, generalized muscle weakness and atrophy (more pronounced in the lower extremities and distal segments), absent tendon reflexes, decreased nociception below the knees, and reduced vibration and position sense in toes and fingers. She required bilateral support to walk. Routine laboratory studies, including creatine kinase and thyroid hormone levels, were unremarkable. Plasma lactate level was elevated at 2.83 mM/L (normal 0.5–1). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed a 2.5-fold increase in protein content with a normal cell count and elevated lactate level (2.7 mmol/L, normal 0.88–1.4). Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed gastric aperistalsis with major dilation and ulcerative esophagitis, necessitating the use of a nasojejunal feeding tube for enteral feeding. Nerve conduction studies indicated marked demyelinating sensorimotor polyneuropathy, and needle electromyography showed a superimposed myopathic pattern in proximal muscles. A muscle biopsy of the deltoid muscle revealed nonspecific myopathic changes, including type I fiber predominance and increased variation in fiber size with small, angular muscle fibers and round hypertrophic fibers. No signs of mitochondrial dysfunction were observed. Brain MRI showed nonspecific symmetric and confluent T2-hyperintensity in the deep white matter.
test_results: Genetic screening of the TYMP gene identified two homozygous contiguous mutations (c. 1283G>A, c.1284 T>A), affecting the same codon (GGT>GAA), causing together the amino acid change p.Gly428Asp.

case_report: A male infant was delivered at 34 weeks gestation via caesarean section to a 24-year-old mother, her second pregnancy, from a non-consanguineous marriage. The pregnancy was without complications, and there was no exposure to known teratogens. An antenatal ultrasound at 28 weeks indicated oligohydramnios. The infant did not experience perinatal asphyxia. At birth, the infant weighed 1.5 kg and had a head circumference of 34 cm. Limb deformities were observed, with joint contractures affecting both flexion and extension. Joint mobility, both active and passive, was restricted, particularly in the shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints. The shoulders exhibited bilateral internal rotation, and the elbows were flexed. The infant had arachnodactyly with a wide gap between the index and middle fingers on both hands. In the lower limbs, the hips were fixed in flexion, the knees were extended, and the ankles were dorsiflexed. The left foot had a congenital talipes equinovarus deformity. Facial abnormalities included an asymmetric face, low-set ears, a high-arched palate, a short neck, and micrognathia. The muscles in both the upper and lower limbs were significantly underdeveloped. Additionally, the infant had hypospadias and bilateral inguinal hernia.
test_results: MRI head revealed dilatation of the ventricles with hypoplastic brainstem and hypoplasia of the inferior vermis and cerebellar hemispheres. Echocardiography revealed small-size ostium secundum atrial septal defect without pulmonary hypertension.

case_report: A 15-year-old female initially presented to an outside pediatric ophthalmologist with bilateral congenital cataracts, which were surgically removed at one month of age. At four months, a secondary membranous cataract was removed from the right eye. She had a heart murmur that resolved and a birthmark on her forehead. At 3.5 years old, she was started on topical 0.5% timolol and referred to the Vanderbilt University Medical Center (VUMC) glaucoma service for increased intraocular pressure (IOP) bilaterally (37 mmHg OD and 36 mmHg OS) and photophobia in the context of aphakia. Findings included bilateral early secondary glaucoma/ocular hypertension, bilateral inferior multifocal congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE) with pigmentation near the optic disc in the right eye, and a scalp hemangioma. Initial management with topical glaucoma medications controlled the IOP in the right eye, but the left eye's glaucoma remained uncontrolled despite maximal medical therapy. She underwent placement of an anterior chamber Baerveldt shunt and complete pars plana vitrectomy to prevent shunt blockage. Postoperative complications included inflammation and vitreous bands, requiring steroids, repeat pars plana vitrectomies with membranectomy, and shunt revision. The left eye stabilized, and IOP has remained controlled in both eyes since age 4.5 years with supplemental topical glaucoma medications. At age 8, she was referred to genetics due to her bilateral multifocal CHRPE, with no family history of related disorders. APC mutation testing was negative. At that time, she was in third grade and doing well. A few months later, she was seen again in the genetics clinic due to her mother's concern for a possible genetic syndrome. Her developmental history included VSD, dental anomalies (persistent baby teeth, fused baby teeth, delayed eruption of secondary teeth, and long roots), flat feet, a high-arched palate, and facial features distinct from other family members. Birth history noted a full-term, uncomplicated pregnancy, with a birth weight of 3.43 kg and length of 52.0 cm. Additional medical history included migraine headaches, recurrent otitis media with pressure equalization (PE) tube placement at 4 years of age, and tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy. Family history was documented through a 4-generation pedigree. Her younger sister had strabismus but was otherwise healthy. The mother had a history of unilateral amblyopia, and the father had hypertension and a childhood heart murmur. A maternal aunt with two sons and a daughter were all healthy. The father's mother had a colon polyp at age 28, with no further genetic testing or counseling details. The father had two maternal half-siblings, one with a history of a murmur and the other with extra teeth. Both parents were of mixed European ancestry. A complete physical examination revealed dysmorphic features, aphakic glasses, a bump on the forehead possibly representing an involuted hemangioma, high-arched palate, irregular tooth development and location, and positive clinodactyly without polydactyly.
test_results: BCOR sequencing showed a c.776C>A;p.S259X monoallelic pathogenic mutation in exon 4.

case_report: A 7-year-old girl, born to consanguineous parents, was referred for evaluation of short stature and mild developmental delay. Her family history did not reveal any similar conditions. She was born at 38 weeks following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, with a birth weight of 3 kg and a height of 52 cm, both within normal ranges. She remained healthy until 6 months of age when she began experiencing repetitive seizures without fever. Imaging at that time revealed cerebral malformations. Physical examination noted distinctive facial features including strabismus, a large forehead with high arched eyebrows, epicanthic folds, a broad nasal bridge, very thin lips, and a short neck. Her weight was 15 kg, and her height was 1.01 m, which is -4 standard deviations from the norm. The lower/superior segment ratio was 1, indicating proportional short stature. She exhibited mild developmental delay, though no formal psychological assessment was conducted, and her growth chart was unavailable. Neurological examination findings were within normal limits.
test_results: Brain CT scan showed pachygyria with an abnormally smooth surface with fewer folds and grooves, and bilateral hygroma.

case_report: A 10-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes mellitus was referred to the pediatric hematology department in May 2016. She exhibited skin hemorrhagic manifestations and occasional thrombocytopenia during diabetes assessment. Physical examination revealed periorbital petechiae and bruising on the lower limbs. Hospitalization and blood tests indicated severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count: 18 × 10^9/L, MPV: 9 fl) without significant morphological changes in the peripheral blood smear. Additional tests, including renal, hepatic, and thyroid functions, were normal, and common infections were excluded. Immunological tests showed no significant alterations except for transient positivity in antinuclear antibodies (homogeneous pattern, titer 1/640) without other clinical signs of systemic autoimmune disorder. Bone marrow examination indicated discrete cellularity with abundant megakaryocytes at various maturation stages, some showing slight dysmegakaryocytopoietic features. The patient received intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIG) (0.8 g/kg) for 2 days, methylprednisolone (20 mg/kg/day) for 3 days, and then prednisone (1 mg/kg/day), resulting in a partial response after 10 days (platelet count: 42 × 10^9/L). During follow-up, repeated peripheral blood smears did not show signs of giant platelet thrombocytopenia. Periodic treatments with IVIG and/or steroids were administered for platelet counts below 20 × 10^9/L. Due to partial response, therapy with Eltrombopag (25 mg/day) was initiated. After two weeks, the platelet count gradually increased, reaching 134 × 10^9/L after 4 months without side effects.
test_results: Sequencing analysis detected a heterozygous mutation c.2116C > G (p. Gln706Glu) in the MYH9 gene of the patient.

case_report: A 45-year-old Italian male business manager presented with psychiatric symptoms, cognitive decline, and progressively worsening renal function.
