At age 28, he experienced an isolated acute pericarditis and had been monitored for diastolic hypertension since age 43 (average pressure 140/90). At 45, he had multiple episodes of confusion, characterized by an inability to interact with his surroundings and a feeling of being slowed down. These episodes were initially considered panic attacks related to anxiety and depressive disorder. The patient also reported insomnia, visual hallucinations, sight impairment, and difficulty with complex reasoning in the preceding months. Brain CT and MRI scans with contrast medium showed no significant organic lesions, and an ophthalmologic examination was unremarkable. Psychiatric follow-up was recommended. Due to worsening depressive symptoms, he was hospitalized in a psychiatric care home for two months, where memory and attention decline were noted. These symptoms were attributed to stress and workplace demands. Concurrently, a decline in renal function was observed (serum creatinine 2.13 mg/dL, reference range 0.4–1.0 mg/dL), prompting nephrology consultation. His serum creatinine levels had been normal before age 44 (latest value from one year prior was 1.12 mg/dL). Urine exams revealed proteinuria (207 to 500 mg/24 h, reference range < 300 mg/24 h). A renal biopsy showed chronic thrombotic microangiopathy features, including extensive double contours, focal mesangial cell interposition, and early intravascular thrombi in occasional small vessels. Immunofluorescence demonstrated parietal and mesangial granular polytypic deposits with strong positivity for IgG and C1q, moderate positivity for IgM and C4, occasional protein pseudothrombi in capillary lumens, and vascular deposits with intense positivity for IgM and C3 and discrete positivity for C1q and C4, suggestive of cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis. Electron microscopy revealed electrodense deposits with vague annular and microtubular structuring. Further investigations did not support cryoglobulinemia (negative Rheumatoid factor test and HCV antibodies, no circulating cryoglobulins, no hypocomplementemia) or thrombotic microangiopathy (Platelets 156,000/µL, reference range 156,000–405,000/µL; absent schistocytes on peripheral blood smear; LDH 458 U/L, reference range 230–500 U/L; haptoglobin 93 mg/dL, reference range 40–240 mg/dL; normal levels of ADAMTS13 and complement factor H; no anti-factor H antibodies). Over time, the patient withdrew from social life and was unable to continue working. He experienced severe cognitive decline, psychomotor slowing, language impairment, and a spastic ataxic gait. Neurological examination revealed exaggerated deep tendon reflexes in all extremities, an abnormal Babinsky sign, and bilateral positive Hoffmann’s reflex. A new brain MRI showed extensive hyperintense T2 signal in subcortical white matter in bilateral temporal, occipital, and parietal areas, similar to those found in posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES). Cortical atrophy signs were also noted. Fundus oculi examination was normal. A brain PET suggested an inflammatory process in the occipital cortex bilaterally. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis and screening for autoimmune CNS diseases were negative. Due to the uncertain nature of the lesions and further worsening in MRI imaging, a brain biopsy was performed, revealing hypercellularity of the white matter due to macrophages and, to a lesser extent, small lymphocytes in a perivascular distribution. Foci of demyelination were observed, with no signs of neoplasms, vasculitis, or encephalitis. High-dose corticosteroid treatment was initiated without clinical response, and the patient was discharged with a strict follow-up program.
test_results: Genetic testing through NGS sequencing of a panel of genes associated to intracellular cobalamin disorders identified two heterozygous variants in MMACHC gene: c.220delA (p.Met74Cysfs*2) and c.395_397delGAC (p.Arg132del). The investigation showed the maternal origin of the c.220delA (p.Met74Cysfs*2) variant and confirmed that the two identified variants in the patient were in compound heterozygosity.
Orpha_name: Methylmalonic acidemia with homocystinuria, type cblC

case_report: A 22-year-old female noticed leukocoria in both eyes. Examination at another eye clinic revealed a vitreous strand in her left eye, leading to a referral to the Department of Ophthalmology at Osaka Medical College Hospital, Takatsuki-City, Japan for further evaluation and treatment. The patient had a history of strabismus diagnosed at the age of 2. She was born at full term with a birth weight of 3320 g and had no history of oxygen administration. No genetic investigations were performed. There was no family history of visual impairment.
test_results: At initial visit, the clinical findings of a slit-lamp examination revealed a shallow anterior chamber in both eyes. In her right eye and left eye, the diameter of the cornea was 8 mm and 9 mm and the axial length was 15 mm and 19 mm, respectively, and microphthalmus was observed in both eyes. In her right eye, the fundus was not visible due to a cataract, and ultrasonic B-mode examination revealed total retinal detachment. A magnetic resonance imaging scan of the patient’s head revealed no calcification in the right eye and no abnormalities in her brain. In the left eye, retrolental fibrovascular proliferation was found around the temporal side. The fundus exhibited FRD from the optic disc to the inferior-temporal side. Most of the peripapillary retinal vessels were involved in the retinal folds, and a part of the nasal retina covered-over the optic disc. In the periphery of the fundus, retinal avascular area was observed over the entire circumference, and pigmentation was also observed in a wide range on the temporal side. An oscillating nystagmus was observed in both eyes, and was found to be prominent in the left gaze and less conspicuous in the right gaze when her face was turned to the left. OCT images obtained when she was 22 years of age revealed bundle shading at the optic disc, combined with the finding that the nasal retina was overlaid on the optic disc. However, the layer structure of the surrounding retina was well preserved. On the temporal side of the optic disc, the elevated stalk of the fold protruding into the vitreous was observed at the site of the FRD, yet the upper and lower retinal layered structures were relatively well retained. However, on the temporal peripheral side, the retina was remarkable thinned, the layered structure was unclear, and the ellipsoid zone could not be clearly identified. Goldman kinetic visual field examination findings, with an isopter of V− 4, obtained when the patient was 22 years of age exhibited 50-degrees upwards, 40-degrees to the nasal side, 60-degrees downward, 75-degrees to the temporal side, and 80-degrees to the inferior-temporal side.

case_report: A 16-month-old female presented to the gastroenterology clinic with feeding difficulties. Her parents reported symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux and vomiting since she started solid foods at 6 months old. She was born at 37 weeks with a birth weight of 1665 g, following a cesarean section due to abnormal Doppler readings, oligohydramnios, intrauterine growth restriction, and a low biophysical profile. Despite poor weight gain, her systemic examination was normal. At 13 months, she underwent laryngoscopy and a modified barium swallow study, both of which were unremarkable. An esophagram performed a month later was described as “difficult and limited but normal” (Fig. A). Various feeding therapies and acid suppression therapy prescribed by her pediatrician did not significantly improve her symptoms. At 17 months, she underwent microlaryngoscopy, bronchoscopy, and upper endoscopy. The first two procedures were unremarkable, but the endoscopy revealed a benign proximal esophageal stricture with an internal diameter of approximately 4–5 mm and 1 mm in length (Fig. ). The stricture was dilated using 18 to 21 Fr bougie dilators without complications such as bleeding or perforation. On the day of the procedures, a physical exam noted new pallor, prompting a complete blood count (CBC). The CBC showed severe pancytopenia (white blood count 2.4 k/µL, hemoglobin 8 g/dL, hematocrit 23%, platelets 22 k/µL). Chart review indicated that the patient had been monitored for mild anemia and borderline thrombocytopenia since her one-year well-child exam (hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL, hematocrit 29.3%, platelets 140 k/µL). A follow-up blood count a month before presentation showed mild improvement in anemia (hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL, hematocrit 30.7%) but low platelets at 46 k/µL, initially attributed to a laboratory error due to sample clotting. Following the endoscopic procedure, the patient was discharged home, and no blood products were administered. She was urgently referred to pediatric hematology.
test_results: A bone marrow biopsy revealed megakaryocyte hypoplasia. BMF panel revealed a heterozygous pathogenic nonsense variant in the TINF2 gene, c.841C>T (p.Glu281*). Telomere analysis revealed extremely short telomeres in all lymphocytes, granulocytes, natural killer cells, all below the first percentile. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed bilateral globe thickening consistent with retinal exudate. Ophthalmology exam revealed exudative proliferative retinopathy bilaterally requiring laser photocoagulation and anti-vascular endothelial growth factor therapy.

case_report: The patient is a 31-year-old male, the first child of non-consanguineous Caucasian parents, with four younger sisters and no family history of congenital disease. During childhood, he experienced a delay in neurodevelopment, particularly in language acquisition, but his motor development was normal. He was identified with sensorineural hearing loss early on and began using hearing aids. By age 10, he had generalized epilepsy and continued to have convulsive episodes despite medication in the initial years. After age 16, he experienced a seizure-free period for several years. He was treated with valproic acid during adolescence and adulthood, and more recently with levetiracetam and lacosamide. In late adolescence, he developed severe behavioral issues and progressive cognitive decline, necessitating multiple hospitalizations for psychiatric decompensation. At age 27, during a psychiatric hospitalization for self and hetero-aggressiveness, he had generalized tonic-clonic seizures and developed severe, prolonged encephalopathy with depressed consciousness, associated with severe nosocomial pneumonia. MRI excluded non-convulsive status epilepticus and central nervous system lesions. His consciousness improved with infection resolution, but his neurological state did not fully recover. Neurological examination showed a well-awake and aware patient with limited speech and typical dysarthria of the hearing impaired. Severe dysphagia was present following the encephalopathic period, requiring percutaneous gastrostomy, which was removed within a year. He had no motor deficits but exhibited generalized increased muscle tone, especially in the lower limbs, with moderate spasticity and hyperreflexia, resulting in a spastic gait that required assistance. There was slight right-hand dystonia without functional limitation. His neurological deficits worsened during severe systemic illnesses, leading to rapid functional decline over the next five years. Investigations included normal metabolic, endocrine, and autoimmune panels; cerebral and spinal MRI showed no focal lesions or atrophy. Electromyography indicated slight axonal sensory neuropathy. Mitochondrial DNA sequencing was negative for pathological mutations. Ophthalmologic evaluation at age 29 was normal.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing revealed a hemizygous novel likely pathogenic variant in TIMM8A, c.45_61dup p.(His21Argfs*11).

case_report: A 24-year-old male reported experiencing painful, multiple, slow-growing yellowish-white swellings on the scalp. The initial swelling, which was asymptomatic, appeared 3 years ago and gradually increased in number, affecting various locations on the scalp. Upon examination, four swellings of varying sizes were observed on the scalp, with the largest measuring 2 cm × 1.5 cm and the smallest approximately 1 cm × 1 cm in diameter.
test_results: Histopathology revealed hyperkeratosis and acanthotic lining with stratified squamous epithelium. The cystic structure is identified in the dermis lined by squamous epithelium with abrupt keratinization filling full cystic structure.

case_report: An 83-year-old male presented with a 3-month history of severe, intermittent, and sharp pain lasting from a few seconds to about 1 minute, occurring daily. The pain was localized deep in the right side of the neck behind the jaw angle and at the base of the right tongue. The pain episodes were triggered and worsened by neck palpation, yawning, coughing, and swallowing, initially with solid food and later with liquids, leading to a weight loss of approximately 6–7 kg since symptom onset. The episodes began suddenly and resolved spontaneously. Over the past 3 months, the patient underwent multiple diagnostic tests and specialist consultations, including cerebral CT scans with and without contrast, a CT angiogram of the supra-aortic vessels, an MRI of the cervical spine, and consultations with two otorhinolaryngologists and a dentist, culminating in the extraction of wisdom teeth without symptom relief. The patient was referred for further evaluation due to the new onset of hoarseness. Medical history included hypertensive cardiopathy managed with dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, dyslipidemia treated with statins, diabetes managed with Metformin, a transient ischemic attack in 1996, and cervical spondylosis treated with paracetamol. On examination, the patient appeared disconsolate and in distress. Pain was constant and significantly worsened by swallowing solids and liquids, coughing, and local palpation. Signs of early malnutrition were noted. Neurological examination revealed reduced sensitivity of the palatine veil, hoarseness, and decreased pharyngeal reflex without distal neurological deficits. Vital signs were normal, with normotension, regular heart rhythm, and normal oxygen saturation. Laboratory results were within normal limits.
test_results: This allowed for the determination of a compression by a vascular structure derived from the right vertebral artery named PICA (posterior inferior cerebellar artery).
diagnosis: Glossopharyngeal Neuralgia due to Neurovascular Conflict

case_report: A seven-month-old male child presented with asymmetry in the size of the eyes, with the left eye being smaller than the right. He was born at full term to parents who are first cousins, following an uneventful pregnancy and normal vaginal delivery. Ocular examination revealed a smaller left eyelid, and upon retracting the eyelids, the socket was found to be empty. The right eye appeared normal. Systemic examination identified multiple congenital anomalies, including a head circumference of 34 cm (below the third percentile for his age), abnormalities in the external ear and fingers, hydrocele, and hypospadias. The left ear was malformed with hypoplasia of the antihelices, fusion of the helix with the tragus, and an obscured external auditory canal opening. The left hand had four normal digits and a pre-axial duplication of the thumb, while the right hand was normal. The child was unable to sit with support, potentially due to kyphosis of the thoracic vertebral column. Dental abnormalities and cognitive impairment could not be excluded.
test_results: Computed tomography scan of the orbit and brain showed absence of left eye in the bony socket with rudimentary optic nerve seen in the orbit and extending for a short distance into the cranium. There was hypoplasia of optic chiasma and aplasia of the entire visual pathway on the left side. The right side of the optic nerve was normal.

case_report: A 44-year-old female from the Agarwal family in eastern India has experienced imbalance for the past five years. This condition is accompanied by tremors in both hands during activities and while holding objects. Upon examination, she exhibited signs of cerebellar ataxia, along with postural and intentional tremors in both hands. Her father and paternal grandfather also presented with similar symptoms.
test_results: The MRI brain showed severe cerebellar atrophy with a CAG repeat length of 40 in PPP2R2B gene.

case_report: A 43-year-old woman with a 20-year history of intermittent abdominal pain, dizziness, and fatigue was admitted to our hospital in May 2018. She had a history of iron deficiency anemia since adolescence. Stool occult blood tests were positive, but gastroscopy and colonoscopy did not reveal any bleeding. Physical examination showed lower limb edema and mild abdominal tenderness around the umbilicus. Vital signs were within normal range. Her medical history included appendectomy, oophorocystectomy, and caesarean section. She reported no use of NSAIDs. Laboratory tests confirmed iron deficiency anemia (hemoglobin level 86 g/L, normal range: 130–175 g/L) and hypoalbuminemia (14.7 g/L, normal range: 35–55 g/L), with elevated C-reactive protein (30.95 mg/L, normal range: 0.08–7.6 mg/L). The fecal occult blood test was positive. Renal and liver functions, autoimmune antibodies, and T-spot tests were within normal range. Colonoscopy and gastroscopy results were normal. An abdominal CT scan showed segmentally thickened small intestinal walls. Due to the presence of a metal intrauterine device, magnetic resonance enterography was not performed. Capsule endoscopy revealed multiple circular ulcerations and stenoses.
test_results: Double balloon endoscopy (DBE) showed multiple ulcerative stenoses. Biopsy report suggested nonspecific moderate chronic inflammation, and villi became widen and shorten.

case_report: The patient is a 57-year-old Japanese male who was referred for cataract surgery due to poor vision in his left eye. He exhibited several notable clinical features including grey hair, cataracts in both eyes, persistent skin ulcers, soft tissue calcification, Achilles’ tendon calcification, and a distinctive facial appearance. His height was 163 cm and weight was 36 kg (BMI: 13.5). He had experienced grey hair and hair loss since his 20s, bilateral Achilles’ tendon pain, and skin hardening and atrophy since his 30s. In his 40s, he developed toe ulcers, osteomyelitis, and a high-pitched, coarse voice. He had a history of bladder cancer surgery at 39 years of age, followed by conditions such as hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidaemia, osteoporosis, and hypothyroidism. At the age of 40, he underwent cataract surgery in his right eye and subsequently developed glaucoma, for which he was treated with glaucoma eye drops. At the initial visit, his best-corrected visual acuity was 1.2 in the right eye and 0.02 in the left eye. The refraction was +0.50 DS / -1.00 DC × 90° in the right eye and −1.50 DS in the left eye. The axial length was 24.83 mm in the right eye and 24.82 mm in the left eye. The intraocular pressure (IOP) was 13 mmHg in the right eye and 15 mmHg in the left eye, managed with latanoprost and timolol maleate for both eyes. He had an intraocular lens (IOL) in the right eye and a cataract in the left eye.
test_results: The condition was attributed to a type 6 (c. 1105 C > T) homozygous mutation.

case_report: A 14-year-old female presented with progressive deformity in valgus of the lower limbs and muscle hypotrophy. Symptoms began at 15 months old, including gait instability, reduced range of motion in hands and arms, and impaired gross and fine motor skills. She is the second child of healthy consanguineous parents, with a mother who had three pregnancies and three births. The pregnancy was uneventful, with a vaginal delivery at 39 weeks, a birth weight of 2,600 g (5th centile), and a birth length of 45 cm (25th centile). Developmental milestones were normal, with sitting at 6 months and walking at 15 months. She has normal intelligence and good academic performance. On general examination, she appeared healthy but was wheelchair-bound. Her weight was 25 kg (3rd centile), height 132 cm (below 3rd centile), and head circumference 52 cm (16th centile). Physical examination revealed diminished sensitivity in hands, forearms, feet, and calves, scoliosis, and pes cavus. Muscle atrophy was noted, especially in the forearms and calves, with finger contractures. No dysmorphic features, vocal paresis, or breathing difficulties were observed. Reflexes were diminished in the Achilles and biceps. Muscle strength was 4/5 in hands, forearms, and shoulder girdle, and 3/5 in thighs, calves, and feet (MRC scale). Cranial nerves were intact, and no dysautonomic signs were present. Brain MRI and liver enzymes were normal. Motor and sensory nerve conduction studies showed absent responses in all explored nerves. Electromyography of the lower extremities indicated normal insertional activity in all explored muscles, abnormal spontaneous activity in the right rectus femoris, and increased amplitude with reduced recruitment in the left anterior tibialis, left gastrocnemius, and left rectus femoris. The findings were consistent with a sensory and motor neuropathy, axonal type, with signs of reinnervation, indicating a chronic and severe process.
test_results: The study identified a homozygous point mutation (c.487 C>T) in exon 4, resulting in a premature stop codon (p.Q163X).

case_report: A 38-year-old Caucasian male presented to the Ophthalmology Unit of the AUSL-IRCCS Hospital of Reggio Emilia with a progressive decrease in vision in his right eye over the past few years. He had no history of systemic or ophthalmic diseases, eye rubbing, or allergic conjunctivitis. Family members examined showed no physical or ocular abnormalities. On examination, uncorrected visual acuity was 'hand motion' in the right eye due to high-degree compound myopic astigmatism, and 20/20 unaided in the left eye. With a rigid gas permeable contact lens, visual acuity in the right eye improved to 20/40. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye revealed advanced corneal ectasia with Vogt striae and a faint apical scar. There was extensive iris atrophy with multiple transillumination defects, predominantly in the inferior quadrant. The pupil was oval, decentered super-nasally, approximately 3 mm in diameter, and poorly reactive to light. Intraocular pressure (IOP) measured by Goldman applanation tonometry was 26 mmHg in the right eye while on topical therapy with timolol 0.5%, brinzolamide 0.1%, and travoprost 0.001%. The left eye had a normal IOP of 13 mmHg.
test_results: Endothelial microscopy revealed a severely abnormal endothelium in the right eye with undefined cell morphology. The left eye presented a cell density of 2340 cell/mm2 with regular morphology. Corneal tomography confirmed the diagnosis of bilateral KC with more severe involvement of the right eye. Pachymetry map showed the thinnest point measuring 177 μm in the right eye. The left eye presented topographic signs of a forme fruste KC with a central pachymetry thickness of 549 μm. Gonioscopy revealed the presence of peripheral anterior synechiae for 360° with extensive obstruction of the trabecular meshwork in the right eye and normal open-angle in the fellow eye.

case_report: A 16-year-old female presented with epilepsy, developmental delay, and cerebellar atrophy. Muscle weakness was observed at 2 years old. At 1 year of age, she experienced clinical seizures characterized by twitching movements, staring episodes, cluster seizures, and spasms. By 18 months, there was only a partial response to anti-convulsive therapy. Global developmental delay was noted by 2 years old, with no speech development and a need for assistance with daily activities. She was vigorous as a newborn, passed her newborn disease screening, and began walking around 18 months. The patient is the second child in a non-consanguineous family; her mother was 33 years old at the time of birth. She was born at full term with normal birth parameters following a normal pregnancy with no known teratogenic exposure. There is no personal or family history of seizures. Clinical examination revealed deep-set eyes with nystagmus and a small nose with a nasal bridge.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing (WES) was performed commercially at Berrygenomics on the patient and her parents. Sequencing was performed on Illumina Novaseq 6000 (Illumina, San Diego, United States), using the Nano WES Human Exome V1.0 (Berrygenomics, Beijing, China) kit with 200 bp paired-end read, according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Sequence analysis of exon 28 and 12 of PIGN, using genomic DNA from the patient and her parents were performed by amplification of a 438 bp and 239 bp fragment containing the putative mutation identified via exome sequencing. Neuropsychological testing demonstrated moderate intellectual disability. Brain imaging showed the progression of mild global cerebral volume loss and cerebellar atrophy.

case_report: A 52-year-old male presented with a three-year history of periodic itching and widespread redness of the skin. He had been treated with various medications, including systemic and topical corticosteroids, systemic methotrexate, and antihistamines, without improvement. Physical examination revealed widespread redness of the skin with extensively infiltrated plaques, scratched itchy papules, pustules on the palms and soles, ear infiltration, swelling around the eyes, and dry skin with multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the armpit area. There was no enlargement of abdominal organs, and examinations of the central nervous, respiratory, cardiovascular, and musculoskeletal systems were normal. The patient’s eosinophil count was elevated to 3.1 × 10^9/L. No abnormal Sézary cells were found in peripheral blood in two separate samples. Tests for hepatitis, human T-lymphotropic virus type I (HTLV-I), and HIV antibodies were negative. No antinuclear or antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were detected. Stool examination for parasites was negative. Serum immunoglobulin E was elevated at 3382.
test_results: Peripheral blood immunophenotyping showed atypical T lymphocyte proliferation CD4+CD3-. T-cell receptor rearrangement studies revealed a clonal population of T lymphocytes. Skin biopsy showed nonspecific lichenoid dermatitis without epidermotropism. Inflammatory infiltrates consisted mainly of lymphocytes and eosinophils. Myelogram and bone marrow biopsy showed moderate eosinophilia without evidence of lymphoma. A lymph node biopsy demonstrated dermopathic lymphadenitis but no evidence of malignancy.

case_report: A 13-year-old boy was admitted in September 2018 due to severe respiratory distress and a global motor deficit, with the lower limbs more affected than the upper limbs. He exhibited motor regression, axial hypotonia with poor head control, muscle strength of 2–3/5 on the Medical Research Council’s scale (MRC) for the upper limbs, and 2/5 on the MRC scale for the lower limbs. There was generalized severe muscular atrophy and retractions of the elbow and knees, more pronounced in the distal segments. The patient was born from a non-consanguineous twin pregnancy at term without hypoxic events and has a healthy 19-year-old brother. In his first year, he was hypotonic with moderate motor delay, sitting after 1 year and walking without support after 2 years. He never achieved running, climbing stairs, or jumping on one foot, with the lower limbs consistently more affected than the upper limbs. At age 4, a neurological examination revealed a lack of deep tendon reflexes, tongue fasciculations, neurogenic changes on electromyography, motor deficit with the lower limbs more affected than the upper limbs, and muscular atrophy. A biopsy showed neurogenic changes. Genetic testing for 5q SMA was negative. Between ages 5 and 10, the condition progressed slowly, with severe proximal weakness, generalized muscle atrophy, swallowing dysfunction, ventilatory restriction, severe contractures, progressive scoliosis, and a lack of deep tendon reflexes. A gastrostomy was performed in 2019. After age 10, he became a wheelchair user, with significant motor regression. In March 2021, spine surgery was performed, after which muscular atrophy became extreme, and weakness was generalized. He lost head control and had limited active movements in the upper limbs. He exhibited paradoxical breathing without needing noninvasive ventilation or oxygen, had no deep tendon reflexes, and presented with dysphonia and a hoarse voice. There was retraction of the mandibular joint with limited mouth opening, subcutaneous nodules around the interphalangeal joints, with the upper limbs more affected than the lower limbs. He had no paroxysmal events such as myoclonus or seizures. Electroencephalography (EEG) showed frequent generalized slow waves lasting 1–2 seconds, rarely focalized, more on the left side, without clinical manifestations. Electroneurography (ENG) showed mildly reduced amplitude of Compound Motor Action Potential (CMAP) with an increased area due to reinnervation. Sensory Nerve Action Potential (SNAP) had normal amplitude and velocities. Electromyography (EMG) showed chronic denervation changes with very large, polyphasic motor unit potentials (MUP) and incomplete recruitment. An abdominal ultrasound showed no liver enlargement. Spinal X-ray revealed severe thoracic scoliosis (Cobb angle >100 degrees) with thoracic deformity and restrictive respiratory dysfunction.
test_results: Genetic testing identified three heterozygous mutations in the ASAH1 gene. The first identified mutation (NM_004315.5:c.458_459del) was a two-base pair deletion in position 458 of the coding region in exon 6 generating the substitution of tyrosine in position 153 of the protein to a stop codon – p.(Tyr153Ter), or p.(Tyr153*), leading to a premature stop codon and thus, to a truncated protein. The second identified mutation (NM_004315.5:c.1226T>C) was the T to C substitution of nucleotide 1226 of the coding region in exon 14, generating the substitution of isoleucine in position 409 of the protein to threonine – p.(Ile409Thr). The third identified mutation (NM_004315.5:c.35G>C) was the G to C substitution of nucleotide 35 of the coding region in exon 1, generating the substitution of arginine in position 12 of the protein to a stop codon – p.(Arg12Pro).
diagnosis: Non-5q spinal muscular atrophy caused by acid ceramidase deficiency

case_report: This 4.3 kg female newborn was delivered via cesarean section at 37 weeks of gestation to a 40-year-old Gravida 2 Para 2 Korean mother at a local obstetric clinic. Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes. Prenatal history and laboratory studies were normal, and prenatal sonograms at 35 weeks showed no abnormalities. Post-birth, the infant exhibited abdominal distension and multiple gross anomalies, leading to her transfer to a nearby university hospital. Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging revealed HMC and a transverse vaginal septum. Initial treatment included percutaneous drainage, which was removed after 2 days due to dysfunction, and ultrasound-guided transurethral aspiration of the HMC, draining 60 to 100 mL from the abdominal cyst. On her 15th day of life, she was transferred to the neonatal intensive care unit of Seoul National University Children's Hospital for further evaluation and management. Her measurements were: height 51 cm (50 to 75 percentile), weight 3,680 g (50 to 75 percentile), head circumference 36 cm (50 to 75 percentile), and abdominal circumference 35.5 cm. Physical examination noted a hairy forehead and ear, bilateral preauricular pits, highly arched palate, and soft palate cleft. Grade 1 to 2 systolic murmurs were heard on the left anterior precordium. Additional findings included a distended abdomen, right PAP, syndactyly (fourth and fifth), left foot deformity, and an anteriorly placed stenotic anus. The infant also had asymptomatic pyuria and bacteriuria, but no bacteremia or sepsis. Neonatal screening and tandem mass tests were normal. X-rays of the hand and foot showed bony fusion of the left third and fourth metacarpal bones, a dysplastic right fourth metacarpal bone and phalanx, right PAP, and a hypoplastic left foot with dysplastic left fourth and fifth metatarsal bones.
test_results: Abdominal sonography showed mild hydronephroses of both kidneys and 9.5 cm cystic mass at the suprapubic area. Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed HMC and a transverse vaginal septum. Abdominal sonography revealed HMC, uterine didelphys with a transverse vaginal septum, bilateral hydronephroureteroses, hypoplastic right kidney (2.4 cm) with ectopic location and mild rotation, and nonvisualization of both ovaries. Anterior displacement of the collapsed bladder was also noted. On non-enhanced abdominal MRI (outside film), HMC was seen as a large cystic mass with septation, transverse vaginal septum and severe hydronephroureteroses, and both ovaries were not visible. She underwent genitography and cystoscopy which confirmed HMC with a transverse vaginal septum.

case_report: A male infant was born to a 25-year-old mother at 30 weeks of gestation. The mother had presented with preterm labor, and an antenatal ultrasound at 26 weeks indicated polyhydramnios. The baby was delivered vaginally, weighing 1.2 kg. The infant did not cry immediately after birth, and attempts to perform endotracheal intubation were unsuccessful as the vocal cords were not visible, and only a single opening corresponding to the esophagus was observed. Resuscitation was continued using bag and mask ventilation, and the baby was transferred to the NICU. A second intubation attempt also failed. As the baby's condition deteriorated, an endotracheal tube was inserted into the observed opening, leading to improved oxygen saturation levels. A chest X-ray indicated severe respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), and natural bovine surfactant containing 100 mg/kg of phospholipids was administered through the endotracheal tube, resulting in improvement. This suggested a connection between the esophagus and trachea. With invasive ventilation using high-pressure support and 100% FiO2, the baby's oxygen saturation was maintained at 85%. Additionally, the baby had an imperforate anus, a structurally normal heart as shown by echocardiography, and a normal abdominal ultrasound.
test_results: A water-soluble dye was instilled through the endotracheal tube which showed the esophageal tracheal connection.

case_report: The subject of this report is a 13-year-old male. At the age of 2, his parents noticed firm masses with mild tenderness on his right hip and feet. Over time, these masses grew larger. Multiple surgeries were conducted to remove the masses from his feet and right hip. His sister experienced similar masses on her hip and feet, which were also surgically removed but reappeared after the operations. No abnormal calcification was found in their parents. The serum phosphate levels of both the father and mother were within normal ranges. Both parents were in good health and had no history of autoimmune conditions or similar issues. There was no consanguinity or genetic mixing in the family for the past three generations. During the physical examination, the subject was alert and cooperative. He exhibited a limp in his right leg. A large, firm mass with mild tenderness was present on his right hip.
test_results: The serum phosphate level for this patient was as high as 2.88 mmol·L−1 (normal range: 0.8–1.6 mmol·L−1). A plain X-ray of the pelvis revealed calcification of a soft tissue mass in the right hip. No cortical hyperostosis, diaphysitis, or periosteal apposition was observed at the femur or ankle joints. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis confirmed the findings of the plain radiography. The histopathological examination of the tumor mass revealed fibrous tissue hyperplasia within the cyst wall with calcification and giant cell reaction.

case_report: A 29-year-old female presented with worsening shortness of breath on exertion over the past 2 years. She had been employed at a bathtub factory with continuous exposure to silica and various organic solvents, including resin detergent and acetone solvent, for 2 years before seeking medical attention. She used a simple mask for dust protection at work. She had no prior medical history or medication use and no notable family medical history. She was an ex-smoker with a 10 pack-year history, having quit 1 month prior. Her shortness of breath was classified as New York Heart Association class III and was accompanied by a cough. Vital signs included a blood pressure of 110/60 mmHg, heart rate of 90 beats per minute, arterial oxygen tension (PaO2) of 60.1 mmHg, and oxygen saturation of 90.8% on room air. Physical examination revealed coarse breathing sounds with rales throughout the lung fields. Chest X-ray showed bilateral reticular nodular shadows. High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) demonstrated central-dominant, diffusely spreading ground-glass opacities sparing the subpleural parenchyma, with some cystic lesions and air-trapping in both lungs. Pulmonary function tests indicated a severely impaired diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide at 30% of the predicted value. Hemoglobin and hematocrit levels were 18.2 g/dL and 52.0%, respectively, with other complete blood counts within normal ranges. Liver and renal function tests were normal. Serological tests for human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis B virus, and hepatitis C virus were negative. Autoimmune studies, including rheumatoid factor, anti-nuclear antibody, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, and anti-cardiolipin antibody, were nonspecific. Thyroid profile and troponin I were negative. Echocardiography showed normal size and wall thickness in all four chambers, nonspecific findings on the inferior vena cava, and a right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) of 34 mmHg, with no definite evidence of right heart failure.
test_results: Lungs presented multiple, red-brown, ill-defined nodular lesion throughout the whole parenchyma. Microscopic examination of the lung wedge resection showed marked congestion and striking capillary proliferation in alveolar walls well demonstrated by reticulin staining. There was no capillary proliferation within walls of the larger vessel. There was no luminal narrowing or obliteration except small arteries showing muscular hypertrophy. There was focal fibrosis accompanied by calcifications.

case_report: Patient 7 is a 16-month-old girl experiencing seizures and significant intellectual and developmental challenges. The initial seizure type observed was generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Additionally, she developed infantile spasms. The patient exhibits severe spastic hypertonia and delays in motor skills and speech. Physical examination reveals dysmorphic features, including a high palatal arch and a smaller than average head size.
test_results: The EEG at onset showed focal and multifocal discharges with burst suppression. The brain MRI highlighted gyral simplification and delayed myelination. She is affected by a heterozygous variation on exon 4, which was found to be missense (nm_001320: c.332G > A, p.Arg111His).
Orpha_name: Hereditary fibrosing poikiloderma-tendon contractures-myopathy-pulmonary fibrosis syndrome

case_report: The patient is a 73-year-old Caucasian male who came to the emergency room with left-sided numbness and an unsteady gait. He has a history of aniridia diagnosed in childhood by an ophthalmologist. He has experienced long-term issues with balance and an abnormal gait. He also mentioned being slow to respond to commands. Neurological examination showed axial-locomotor ataxia in both lower extremities and mild dysmetria during the finger-to-nose test on both sides. Ophthalmologic examination revealed scalloped, dilated, and fixed pupils that were non-reactive to light. The exam also noted pseudophakia, aligning with his history of bilateral cataract removal surgery. Visual acuity was reduced, and the patient reported blurry vision. Mental status examination indicated a cooperative individual with normal appearance, making appropriate eye contact, and being alert and oriented to person, place, and time. The Mini Mental State Exam (MMSE) score was 27, showing normal memory and attention. Language was fluent without aphasia, and his thoughts were coherent. His family history showed no signs of ophthalmic or neurological conditions.
test_results: A CT brain without contrast showed cerebral cortical atrophy, specifically frontotemporal. CT scans also revealed mild white matter microvascular changes and cerebral volume loss. Visualization of the posterior fossa revealed an unremarkable cerebellum and brainstem. Repeat brain CT showed encephalomalacia consistent with prior infarcts in the thalamus with no posterior fossa findings. MRI scans confirmed these findings, which showed volume loss in the body of the corpus callosum suggestive of moderate cerebral atrophy but no posterior fossa findings. The typical finding of cerebellar vermis atrophy was not found in any of the CT and MRI scans.

case_report: An 18-month-old boy presented with shortness of breath and cough. He was born at 35 weeks by cesarean section to non-consanguineous healthy parents, with a birth weight of 1.8 kg (SD = −3.01) and a head circumference of 30 cm (SD = −4.66). Post-birth, he was hospitalized due to neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, neonatal hyaline membrane disease, and apnea. At 18 months, he was unable to raise his head, turn over, sit, crawl, or stand, with significant muscle tension in both limbs during attempted movements. His language development was delayed, and he could not produce meaningful words. His growth rate was slow, with a height of 65 cm at 18 months, significantly shorter than peers. He had recurrent respiratory tract infections and was hospitalized for acute severe pneumonia at 6 and 18 months. He developed bilateral inguinal hernia at 3 months and underwent bilateral high ligation of hernia at 6 months. No similar genetic family history was noted. Physical examination at 19 months showed a height of 65 cm (SD = −5.74), weight of 6.5 kg (SD = −4.36), and head circumference of 41 cm (SD = −6.45). He had thick arched eyebrows, a flat nose, swollen eyelids, exophthalmos, epicanthus, gingival hyperplasia, low-set ears, a short neck, pectus carinatum, short fingers, and stiff joints. The anterior fontanelle closed early at 9 months. Limb muscle tension was increased. No obvious hepatosplenomegaly was detected on palpation, and no murmur was heard during precordial auscultation. At birth, total bilirubin was 15.7 mg/dl, direct bilirubin was 2.4 mg/dl, and indirect bilirubin was 13.3 mg/dl. Urinary GAGs, routine blood examination, blood gas, electrolyte, blood glucose, and thyroid function were normal or negative. Anteroposterior chest X-ray showed a small chest shape and short floating ribs, with small shoulder blades and irregularly shaped bilateral proximal humeri. Pelvic X-ray showed a deep cusp of the large sciatic notch on both sides, small and shallow acetabulum on both sides, and lateral position of the bilateral femoral heads. Echocardiography indicated mild tricuspid regurgitation without thickened valves. Cerebral ultrasound showed bilateral ventricle widening.
test_results: Cranial MRI showed less white matter, smaller bilateral frontotemporal lobe, thinner corpus callosum, and delayed myelination.

case_report: A 32-year-old male presented with reduced hair density on the scalp and body since childhood. The patient reported no symptoms and had no history of developmental delays. There was no family history of similar conditions. Physical examination revealed widespread hair loss with short, brittle hairs on the scalp, especially in the occipital region. The moustache and pubic areas also exhibited short, broken hairs. The beard, axillary, and body hairs were absent. Follicular keratotic papules were observed on the occiput, nape of the neck, and extensor arms. The eyes, nails, and teeth appeared normal.
test_results: Light microscopy of hair showed beaded appearance with elliptical nodes separated by narrower internodes.

case_report: A 4-year-old female with no significant medical history presented to the emergency department with one week of fevers, headaches, muscle aches, dry cough, poor appetite, decreased urination, nausea, and vomiting. There was no history of recent travel or sick contacts, but she had received her 4-year-old vaccines one week prior during a well-child check. Vital signs showed an oral temperature of 98.2 degrees F, respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute, pulse of 185 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation of 95% on room air. She appeared ill, grunting, exhausted, and in moderate distress. Examination revealed slight pharyngeal redness, dry mucous membranes, rapid heart rate, and a faint, net-like rash on her dorsal hands. No other concerning findings were noted. Due to her rapid heart rate and dry mucous membranes, a 20 mL/kg bolus of crystalloid was administered, and she was treated with empiric cefepime. Despite two additional boluses, her heart rate did not improve. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 45,900/μL with an absolute neutrophil count of 39,000/μL. Multiple repeat laboratory samplings were required to obtain an accurate hemoglobin level due to ongoing hemolysis. Eventually, labs demonstrated normocytic anemia with hemoglobin at 10.9 g/dL, hematocrit at 30.0%, a normal reticulocyte count of 2.4%, normal platelet count of 302,000/μL, elevated bilirubin at 6.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin at 1.5 mg/dL, prerenal azotemia with blood urea nitrogen (BUN) at 34 mg/dL, creatinine at 0.69 mg/dL, prolonged prothrombin time (PT) at 33.6 seconds, elevated international normalized ratio (INR) at 2.9, and elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LD) at 3595 IU/L. The patient developed hypotension but responded to fluid resuscitation. She was transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) at an affiliated tertiary care hospital for further management. Upon arrival at the PICU, she was noted to be pale and slightly jaundiced. Haptoglobin was less than 20 mg/dL, indicating hemolysis. Fibrinogen was less than 60 mg/dL, and fresh frozen plasma was administered for coagulopathy. Urinalysis showed positive nitrites and leukocyte esterase but no bacteria, large blood with only 25–50 red blood cells (RBCs) per high-power field, and dark brown urine. Direct antiglobulin test (DAT) showed complement positivity with negative IgG. A hematology/oncology specialist recommended keeping the patient and all infused products warm. Further testing was conducted for various conditions.
test_results: The DL antibody test resulted positive on hospital day 18.

case_report: A 29-year-old male of Syrian origin presented with a painless swelling on the right side of the testicle that had been present for 12 months. Physical examination showed an enlarged right testicle that was not tender. Laboratory tests indicated that the tumor markers alpha-fetoprotein (α-FP) and beta human chorionic gonadotropin (β-HCG) were negative.
test_results: An ultrasound scan of the scrotum revealed a 7-cm hypoechoic, hypervascular and cystic mass replacing the right testis. A staging computed tomography scan was negative for lymphatic or metastatic disease. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed focal staining of a small proportion of the SCS cells with antibody to CD117 (c-KIT). Immunohistochemical stains of antibodies to PLAP, HCG, AFP, CD30, and CD68 and the myeloid markers CD34 and CD117 were all negative.

case_report: The patient, an 8-month-old girl, is the first child of a healthy non-consanguineous Chinese couple. She was born with a length of 45 cm, a birth weight of 2,450 g, and a head circumference of 31 cm, all measurements being below the 2nd percentile for her gestational age. The mother, aged 20, was 17 weeks into her second pregnancy at the time of presentation. The patient exhibited distinct facial characteristics and limb anomalies.
test_results: WES in the family trios identified a de novo frameshift variant of NIPBL (NM_133433.4: exon 5: c.448dupA: p.S150Kfs*23) in the proband, which was validated by Sanger sequencing. This mutation was predicted to have nonsense-mediated mRNA decay effect as the truncation occurred at the fifth exon of the 47 exons of NIPBL. By using reverse transcription quantitative PCR, we observed a reduction around 40% of the NIPBL mRNA in the peripheral blood leukocytes of the proband compared with the healthy mother.

case_report: A 23-year-old female patient presented in April 2012 with widespread skin lesions affecting the trunk, extremities, and scalp. She had experienced a similar episode at the age of 13, and also had a history of localized hair loss on the scalp, both of which resolved after using topical steroids. In June 2012, she developed localized hair loss on the scalp, coinciding with the complete disappearance of the skin lesions in that area.
test_results: A 3 cm patch of nonscarring hair loss was observed, and dermoscopic examination revealed perifollicular pigmentation, exclamation hairs and yellow dots.

case_report: A five-year-old boy presented to the hospital on April 17, 2006, with a history of recurrent fainting episodes. The initial episode occurred at the age of three and included seizure-like movements such as tonic-clonic activity, eyeball deviation, and loss of consciousness. These episodes recurred four times over a period of 16 months, primarily during walking or physical activity, lasting from several seconds to several minutes. Cardiac resuscitation was never needed. His medical history includes cochlear transplantation for congenital sensorineural deafness. Physical and neurological examinations showed no abnormalities. An electroencephalogram also revealed no abnormalities.
test_results: His resting 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed a markedly prolonged QTc interval of 590 ms. His ECG showed a structurally normal heart. A 24-hour ambulatory ECG showed no ventricular arrhythmia. An exercise treadmill test showed a marked QTc prolongation as the test progressed. It also revealed T wave alternans. Molecular genetic analysis revealed that the patient had compound heterozygous mutations in the KCNQ1 gene. One was a previously reported deletional mutation, c.828-830delCTC, p.S277del. The other was a novel splicing mutation, c.921G>A, p.V307V. The nucleotide c.921G is located at the end of exon 6; substitution of G to A was predicted to affect the splicing of mRNA. Reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction detected an abnormally spliced 593-bp mRNA product in which the exon 6 had been skipped.

case_report: A 27-year-old female presented with a gradually increasing swelling in the right mid-femur over the past 2-3 months at our university hospital outpatient clinic. She has a history of a genetic condition affecting bone formation, being the only affected family member. Her physical characteristics include short stature, mild kypho-scoliosis, a short neck, and mild ligamentous hyperlaxity. She denied any recent trauma or inflammatory conditions. Over the past decade, she experienced multiple fractures in the lower extremities, treated both conservatively and surgically with intramedullary nailing, without previous occurrences of significant swelling. Conventional radiographs revealed a large bony mass in the right femoral mid-shaft, characterized by irregular hypertrophic lamellar ossification with a sunburst pattern and spiculae, suggesting potential periosteal involvement. Laboratory tests indicated an elevated alkaline phosphatase level of 257 U/l. Imaging studies, including contrasted computed tomography of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis, as well as contrasted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the affected femur and scintigraphy, were conducted. MRI showed extensive irregular periosteal hypertrophic lamellar ossification with a sunray pattern, and possible infiltration of surrounding musculature and soft tissue could not be definitively excluded. Skeletal scintigraphy demonstrated significant tracer accumulation in the mid-femoral shaft, while the contrasted computed tomography scans of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis showed no additional lesions.
test_results: Histopathologic analysis of the bioptic specimen showed distinctive zones with the outer regions of callus containing edematous tissue with a loose collagenous network to the innermost region showing hypercellular trabeculae of woven bone and small cartilaginous islands without signs of malignant transformation.
diagnosis: Hyperplastic Callus Formation in Osteogenesis Imperfecta Type V

case_report: A 6-day-old male neonate, born at full term via vaginal delivery, exhibited nonbilious vomiting starting on the 2nd day of life. The infant passed a small amount of meconium but had no subsequent bowel movements. Mild upper abdominal distention was noted after feeding. The neonate was active, alert, and did not have a fever. The mother had multiple previous pregnancies and received adequate antenatal care. The birth weight was 2.8 kg, and the prenatal ultrasound showed no abnormalities. Physical examination showed no facial abnormalities, cyanosis, or pallor, but there was mild dehydration. The abdomen appeared normally full without visible peristalsis or masses.
test_results: Plain abdominal X-ray showed high intestinal obstruction and contrast follow-through showed no contrast beyond the duodenum consistent with duodenal obstruction.

case_report: An 8-month-old boy was brought to the pediatric clinic due to delays in mental and motor development. Since birth, he exhibited delayed motor milestones, including unsteady head control at 4 months. At 8 months, he was unable to roll over, sit without support, crawl, or grip items independently. He showed delayed intellectual development, could smile but not babble. The parents had a non-consanguineous marriage, and there was no relevant family history of similar conditions. Physical examination showed a head circumference of 43 cm, esotropia, hypotonia, and muscle weakness with limb muscle strength between level 3 and level 3+, predominantly affecting proximal muscles. Bilateral patellar tendon reflexes were absent, and there was no pathological Babinski’s sign. Serum creatine kinase (CK) levels were elevated at 1799 IU/L.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed cerebellar and brain stem hypoplasia with a characteristic flattening, pachygyria-polymicrogyria of frontotemporal lobes (type “cobblestone pavement”), white matter lesions, and multiple subcortical cerebellar cysts, which were typical brain changes in DGP. The gene panel testing identified a homozygous c.636C>T (p.Phe212Phe) variant in exon 7 of the POMGNT1 gene (NM_001243766) in the patient. Sanger sequencing revealed that the father had a heterozygous c.636C>T variant, but the mother had no variant at this site. Quantitative polymerase chain reaction (q-PCR) of DNA was used to identify whether there was an abnormal copy number in exon 7 of POMGNT1 in the patient. However, no abnormalities were found. Trio-based whole-exome sequencing (trio-WES) was performed to identify other variants and UPD. As a result, a possible paternal UPD on chromosome 1 of the patient was identified using trio-WES data analysis, which revealed the homozygous variant, and no other pathogenic variants were detected. Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) of the patient revealed a 120,451 kb loss of heterozygosity (LOH) on 1p36.33-p11.2 (888,658_121,339,317), encompassing POMGNT1, and a 99,319 kb LOH on 1q21.2-q44 (149,879,544_249,198,164). Thus, UPD was ascertained. RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) of peripheral blood samples was performed to determine whether splicing was affected. It was confirmed to cause the skipping of exon 7 in the POMGNT1 mRNA, resulting in a frameshift change (p.Asp179Valfs*23).

case_report: A 10-year-old boy with normal developmental history presented with a sub-acute onset of right-circumduction gait, partial vision loss, expressive aphasia, vomiting, and headache that began one month prior. There was no recent history of upper respiratory infection or vaccination. Physical examination revealed no fever, but noted right foot drop and right arm weakness, along with bilateral downward plantar reflexes. Fundoscopic examination indicated bilateral papilloedema (grade 2-3). Routine blood chemistries were within normal limits. A brain CT scan had been performed at another facility, leading to an unplanned CSF puncture. CSF analysis showed normal levels of protein, glucose, IgG index, lactate, and oligoclonal bands, with a negative AQP4 antibody. The CSF opening pressure was approximately 28 cm H2O. Bacterial and viral assessments of the CSF, as well as CSF PCR for tuberculosis, were all negative. Serum very long-chain fatty acid levels and adrenal function tests were normal.
test_results: Initial brain MRI without contrast showed bilateral abnormal high signal lesions in the subcortical and deep posterior white matter in T2-WI sequence that was almost isointense with CSF in the center, surrounded by a peripheral halo. In post contrast, T1-WI image show signal lesions with peripheral complete and incomplete ring enhancements were noted. Some cortical extension of the lesion located in the right posterior parietal lobe was remarkable.

case_report: A 31-year-old immunocompetent right-handed Russian woman with no medical or family history of MS presented to the emergency department with sudden onset of dysarthria and left central facial palsy. She reported a mild SARS-CoV2 infection 4 months prior and was not on any medication or exposed to toxins. Within the first 24 hours, her neurological symptoms rapidly worsened. Initial clinical examinations revealed left-sided hemiplegia with a left Babinski sign, complete left-sided anesthesia, anosognosia, left-sided visuospatial hemineglect, and fluctuating altered consciousness. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a large right frontal pseudo-nodular lesion, hyperintense on diffusion and T2-FLAIR sequences, gadolinium-enhanced, without surrounding edema. Extensive blood analysis showed no signs of systemic inflammation (normal white blood cell count, C-reactive protein, gammaglobulins, and sedimentation rate). Infectious and immune blood tests, including those for HIV, viral hepatitis, syphilis, Lyme disease, herpes viruses, quantiFERON-TB Gold, anti-nuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, cryoglobulins, anti-aquaporin-4, and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibodies, were all negative. AQP4 IgG and MOG-ab testing were evaluated using flow cytometry with a stable human embryonic kidney cell line overexpressing the M23 isoform of aquaporin-4. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed a normal white blood cell count (4/mm3), protein level of 45 mg/dL, and glucose level of 65 mg/dL (serum glucose 94 mg/dL) without oligoclonal bands. The kappa-free light chain index was slightly elevated (6.6), and the CSF cytokine profile showed elevated IL-10 (3.39 pg/mL) and soluble IL2-receptor (156 pg/mL), while other biomarkers did not indicate infection (IL-1β < 0.32 pg/mL, IL-6 = 4.04 pg/mL, INF-α < 2.92 pg/mL). Attempts to detect CSF infectious agents, including Gram staining, culture, and PCR for neurotrophic viruses (including SARS-CoV2), were negative. During the diagnostic work-up, she received intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g/day for three days (total 3 g) and five sessions of plasma exchange without any clinical improvement. Follow-up brain MRI showed significant growth of the frontal lesion from 1.6 cm3 on day 1 to 9.6 cm3 on day 14, with maintained gadolinium enhancement, the appearance of surrounding edema, and two additional inflammatory deep white matter hyperintensities.
test_results: The pathological analysis of the brain tissue revealed an active demyelinating process without any axonal loss, but with an important infiltrate of polyclonal lymphocytes (mostly T cells) and macrophages. No tumoral cells were found.

case_report: A 14-month-old male patient, the second child of a nonconsanguineous couple, presented to the Department of Endocrinology at San Raffaele Paediatric Medical Centre in Milan with hyperglycaemia (281 mg/dL) during an episode of viral pneumonia caused by H3N2 influenza. There is no family history of health issues. The patient was born at term via vaginal delivery, with the pregnancy noted for polyhydramnios and macrosomia (birth weight 3940 g). Clinical examination revealed fever, tachycardia, tachypnoea, fatigue, myalgia, malaise, and mild dehydration. Laboratory tests showed hyperglycaemia (202 mg/dL; 11.2 mmol/L) without ketoacidosis (pH 7.39, HCO3 19.2, BEB -5.1) and HbA1c 6.2% (45 mmol/mol). Complete blood count indicated macrocytic anaemia (Hb 7.5 g/dL; HCT 27.9%, RBC 2,450,000/L; MCV 95.1 fL; RDW 23.5) with normal levels of vitamin B12 and folate. An auditory brainstem response (ABR) examination revealed sensorineural hearing loss, while echocardiography and electrocardiogram results were normal.
test_results: Genetic analysis confirmed homozygous mutation in the SLC19A2 gene [c.1370delT with premature stop codon p. (Leu457Ter)].

case_report: A 26-day-old male newborn was referred from a regional hospital due to multiple fractures and limb deformities identified at birth. He was delivered at 39 weeks via vaginal route with breech presentation and had a birth weight of 2700 g. The pregnancy was uneventful and involved twins. Antenatal laboratory tests were normal, and three prenatal ultrasounds showed no abnormalities. There was no consanguinity or family history of short stature. A 6-year-old cousin had limb deformity, but the cause was unclear. The twin sister was healthy at birth. Upon clinical examination, the newborn's weight was 3200 g (−1 SDS), height was 47 cm (−2 SDS), and head circumference was 35 cm (+0.5 SDS). The newborn exhibited reduced mobility, frontal bossing, white sclerae, moderate respiratory distress, bowed legs, and shortened limbs.
test_results: Limbs X-rays showed multiple diaphyseal fractures of long bones, demineralization, and curved bones.

case_report: The patient is a 15-year-old female presenting with lower limb weakness and walking instability for two weeks. Her parents, aged 55 and 52, are healthy and have three children. The first child, who passed away in his early 20s, had congenital mental retardation and was unable to care for himself. The second child is the patient. She has exhibited slow motor response, poor coordination, difficulty feeding after birth, and lower intelligence compared to her peers. The third child, a 14-year-old male, shows no signs of congenital disorder and has been healthy since birth. None of the children experienced hypoxia or injury at birth. The parents reported no history of drug abuse, pregnancy infection, or use of malformation drugs during pregnancy, and no similar cases in the family. During her first visit, the patient was hospitalized for various examinations. She was awake with normal speech and comprehension. Cognitive assessment revealed mild impairments in memory and calculation, with MMSE scoring 25 points and MoCA scoring 21 points. Physical examination showed hypermyotonia and tendon hyperreflexia. Muscle strength in the lower extremities was 4/5 on the left and 4+/5 on the right. She was unable to walk in a straight line, and Romberg sign was positive. Pathological signs including Babinski sign, Chaddock sign, and Rossolimo sign were all positive.
test_results: Electromyography revealed the motor and sensory nerve conduction velocity decreased significantly in the right ulnar nerve and bilateral shin nerve, the deep sensory nerve conduction delayed in the right lower extremity by spinal somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEP). Brain and thoracic spinal cord MRI revealed white matter demyelination of both hemispheres, suggesting white matter disease. Reverse gantry of the cervical spine and scoliosis of the thoracic spine were also confirmed by the cervicothoracic combined MRI scan. Biochemical tests revealed a significant increase in homocysteine and a decrease of folic acid in the blood.

case_report: A 31-year-old pregnant woman, with a history of one previous pregnancy and one spontaneous abortion, presented at 36 weeks of gestation for an examination due to concerns about a fetal thoracic wall abnormality. Routine examinations at 13, 22, and 30 weeks of gestation had shown no issues, but an examination at 35 weeks revealed an abnormality in the fetal thoracic wall. Further examination identified a defect in the fetal thoracoabdominal wall, with partial displacement of the left ventricle and liver, along with rotation and elongation of the heart. There were also indications of intracardiac abnormalities such as tricuspid atresia, a ventricular septal defect, and pulmonary artery hypoplasia. At 39 weeks of gestation, she was admitted to the Obstetrics and Gynecology Clinic in Târgu Mure and delivered a male newborn via cesarean section. The newborn weighed 3,100 grams and had an APGAR score of 7. Physical examination revealed a defect in the superior abdominal wall, partial extrathoracic displacement of the heart, and partial herniation of the liver, all covered by a very thin layer of skin. Additionally, there was a diastasis of the sagittal suture. The newborn was intubated, and saline-soaked gauze pads were applied to the thoracoabdominal and cranial defects to maintain humidity.
test_results: Prenatal ultrasonography revealed a fetal thoracoabdominal wall defect with partial displacement of the left ventricle and the liver associated with rotation and elongation of the heart and a high index of clinical suspicion for intracardiac malformations such as tricuspid atresia, a ventricular septal defect, and pulmonary artery hypoplasia. Postnatal echocardiography confirmed the prenatal diagnosis and also showed a partial extrathoracic and extra-abdominal displacement of the heart and liver, a large ventricular septal defect, great arteries originating from the left ventricle with the aorta situated anteriorly, a posterior deviation of the outlet septum causing severe subpulmonary stenosis, hypoplasia of the pulmonary artery, and a large hourglass-shaped left ventricle secondary to narrowing of the heart at the level of its extrathoracic displacement. Thoracoabdominal CT-angiography showed complex cardiac malformations consisting of large ventricular and atrial septal defects, an increased left ventricular volume, with apical extrathoracic aneurysmal dilatation below the xiphoid process at the level of the abdominal midline, hypoplasia of the right ventricle, and a reduced caliber of the pulmonary trunk artery. Abdominal CT revealed partial transparietal herniation of the left hepatic lobe adjacent to a left ventricular diverticulum, and an increase in the size of the right adrenal gland with hyperdense contents suggesting an adrenal hematoma. Cranial CT revealed a diastasis of the sagittal suture causing subcutaneous herniation of the venous sagittal sinus.

case_report: A 4-month-old male child, born to healthy, consanguineous parents in an urban environment, was delivered via cesarean section at 37 weeks gestation due to severe intrauterine growth restriction and nonprogress labor. The child was born on September 1, 2014, to a 26-year-old healthy mother at EMMS Nazareth Hospital. Apgar scores were 9 at 1 minute and 10 at 5 minutes. Birth measurements included a weight of 1290 grams, head circumference of 31.3 cm, length of 36.3 cm, pulse of 138, breathing rate of 67/minute, blood pressure of 64/21 mmHg, and blood saturation of 96%. The newborn was admitted to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) at 1 day old due to severe asymmetric intrauterine growth restriction, fever, and jaundice. Immediate treatments included oxygen enrichment and antibiotic injections. Laboratory tests revealed hyperinsulinism (5560.4 pmol/L), neonatal hypoglycemia (24 mg/dL) and hyperglycemia (170 mg/dL), hypocholesterolemia (50 mg/dL), hypotriglyceridemia (36 mg/dL), cholestatic jaundice (direct bilirubin = 4.6 mg/dL; indirect bilirubin = 6.5 mg/dL), elevated C-Peptide (2747 pmol/L), hypokalemia (2.8 mEq/L), neonatal thrombocytopenia (as low as 38,000/microL), leucopenia (as low as 2990/microL), and anemia of prematurity. Further findings included urosepsis due to Enterobacter, right-sided hydronephrosis, and hydrocele. Imaging and clinical examinations, including chest X-rays, cranial ultrasound, and heart echocardiogram, were normal. Neurological examination showed normal plantar grasp reflex, Moro reflex, and sucking reflex. The child exhibited significant dysmorphic features such as emaciation, lipoatrophy, genitomegaly, craniofacial abnormalities with elfin facies, low birth weight, skin abnormalities, abdominal distension, hypertrichosis, and large low-set ears. Treatments administered included packed cells transfusion, platelet transfusion, antibiotic injections, and recombinant human insulin-like growth factor 1 (rh-IGF1) due to poor weight gain. The child's condition stabilized several days after admission, and he was discharged with a recommendation for follow-up in an outpatient clinic.
test_results: Both parents were carriers of a heterozygous deletion encompassing exon 14 of the insulin receptor gene (INSR) gene. The result of the child's genetic analysis was a homozygous deletion of exon 14 on the INSR gene after conducting sequencing analysis.

case_report: A newborn girl, aged 1 hour, was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit due to unusual skin appearance at birth. She is the first child of healthy, unrelated parents, born at full-term following an uncomplicated pregnancy. There were no signs of asphyxia during delivery, and her Apgar scores were 9 at 1 minute and 10 at 5 minutes. Her birth measurements were as follows: weight 2800 g, length 49 cm, head circumference 33.5 cm, and chest circumference 32 cm. Physical examination revealed her entire body covered with taut, shiny, thick yellow crusts, resembling parchment, with scales present on her trunk and upper limbs. The crusts caused double upper eyelid ectropion, eclabium, and auricle deformation. Her pulse oxygen saturation remained stable, and no abnormalities were detected in the examination of her heart, lungs, or nervous system. Peripheral blood tests showed no significant abnormalities in blood culture, blood cell analysis, C-reactive protein levels, or electrolytes. Imaging studies, including chest radiography and color ultrasonography of the heart, brain, digestive system, and urinary system, were normal.
test_results: Whole-exome sequencing showed that she had compound heterozygous mutations in the arachidonate 12-lipoxygenase, 12R type gene (ALOX12B), c.1798C > T (p.Arg600Trp) and c.1463G > A (p.Arg488His), originating from her mother and father, respectively.

case_report: A 15-year-old Azerbaijani female presented with bilateral swelling, pain, and restricted movement in the elbows, wrists, fingers, knees, and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints, along with bilateral hip joint pain. The limitation of bilateral finger movements began at 7 months of age, without noticeable swelling at that time. Swelling and pain in the elbows, knees, ankles, and toes started at age 5. She is the first child of healthy first-degree consanguineous parents and has a 13-year-old sister with similar joint issues. The patient has a history of recurrent hospitalizations over several years due to joint problems. Physical examination revealed swelling, movement limitation, and contractures in both knees, wrists, elbows, shoulders, hips, and ankles. There was also flexion limitation of the 3rd and 4th right proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints, flexion contracture of the 3rd and 4th PIP joints of the right hand, and the 4th PIP joint of the left hand. Additionally, there was bilateral overlapping toe deformity and bilateral axillary region squamous rashes. Other systemic examinations were normal.
test_results: Radiological evaluation of patient 1 was given.

case_report: The patient is a Caucasian female, born to a 32-year-old mother and 34-year-old father after a third full-term uneventful pregnancy. Her birth weight was 2700g, length 40 cm, and head circumference 35 cm. The patient has two healthy half-siblings from the mother’s first marriage. Family history analysis did not reveal previous bone disorders in other family members. The newborn exhibited short stature. Motor development was delayed; she began walking at the age of 2 years. At 3 years old, she was referred to the Ambulant Centre for Defects of Locomotor Apparatus in Prague. At that time, her height was 62 cm (-8.8 SD), upper segment/lower segment = 39.7 cm (-.5 SD)/22.3 cm (-10.1 SD), arm span 63 cm, head circumference 48.6 cm (between 25-50 centile), and weight was 8 kg. She had a genu valgum deformity and a waddling gait. Her hands and feet were relatively long. By the age of 4 years, she could walk only short distances. She developed recurrent paroxysmal attacks of impaired consciousness with muscular spasms. These seizures were linked to hypertension caused by a right dysplastic kidney. Following a right nephrectomy, her seizures ceased, and blood pressure normalized. Bracing was used to treat her severe scoliosis at the age of 4 years.
test_results: Radiographs taken between 2 and 6.5 years documented lack of ossification of the capital femoral epiphyses, severe metaphyseal changes, scoliosis convex to the left, and delayed carpal/tarsal bone age. Radiographs taken between 6.5 and 11 years of age documented progress of spinal scoliosis and increased genu valgum deformity. Ossification of the capital femoral epiphyses was absent and the carpal/tarsal bone age was delayed.

case_report: A 27-year-old female presented with a 12-year history of facial asymmetry. She had undergone multiple biopsies and cosmetic surgical procedures starting at age 17, with visible surgical scars on the right side of her face. The patient was also receiving orthodontic treatment for malocclusion. Clinical examination revealed hypertrophy of the soft tissue of the cheek and underlying bone, macrodontia, macroglossia, and malocclusion on the right side of the face. Additionally, the patient reported early eruption of permanent teeth and facial hair overgrowth on the affected side.
test_results: CBCT images showed diffuse bone enlargement in the right maxillary and mandibular alveoli, as well as the right zygomatic bone. Changes in trabecular patterns were seen in both jaws. Root resorption was seen in teeth #13, 14, 15, 16 and 46. Periodontal ligament space widening was obvious in teeth #44 and 45. Magnetic resonance images revealed fat infiltration into the right masseteric space up to the skull. Computed tomography (CT) scan images showed massive deformity in facial bones at the right side.
Orpha_name: Congenital infiltrating lipomatosis of the face

case_report: A 73-year-old male patient was sent to our hospital following the discovery of an elevated lesion in the posterior wall of the stomach during a previous examination. Upon admission, the patient was in good general health, with no signs of peripheral lymph node enlargement. Laboratory tests, including serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels, were all within normal ranges.
test_results: Gastroscopy showed a pigmented, elevated lesion, approximately 2 cm in diameter, in the posterior wall of the stomach. A biopsy was performed and histologic examination revealed sheet-like malignant cells with large nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasms containing dark brown pigment. Immunohistochemically, the tumor cells were positive for S-100 proteins and HMB-45 antibodies, and negative for pan-cytokeratin antibodies (AE1/AE3) and leukocyte common antigen.
diagnosis: Primary malignant melanoma of the stomach

case_report: A 6-year-old girl, born to parents who are second-degree relatives, presented with a history of a non-productive cough lasting 15 days, difficulty breathing while lying down, and noticeable neck pulsations. There was no history of fever. Her birth history was normal, and she has an older sister who is reportedly healthy. She exhibited mild delays in motor and language development. On examination, her growth was below the 3rd percentile for both weight and height. She exhibited both rapid heart rate and rapid breathing. Her facial features included a long and narrow face, a high nasal bridge, a broad nasal tip with separated nasal cartilages, laterally curved and thick eyebrows, a long philtrum, and a simple left ear. She had mild outward deviation of the eyes, bilateral complete coloboma, left-sided small cornea with cortical cataract, and searching nystagmus in both eyes. Vision assessment was not possible due to nystagmus. All 20 primary teeth were present, but no permanent teeth had erupted. She also had a small reducible umbilical hernia and fifth finger clinodactyly on both hands, more pronounced on the left side. Cardiac examination revealed a wide and fixed split second heart sound, a loud second heart sound, a third heart sound gallop at the apex, and a grade III/VI ejection systolic murmur over the pulmonary area. Fine crackles and wheezing were heard at the lung bases on both sides. Laboratory investigations showed hemoglobin of 11.6 g/dl, total leukocyte count of 11,300 cells/mm3, differential count of N54L33M13, and a peripheral smear indicating normocytic, normochromic anemia. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 40 mmHg, and urine examination was normal. Blood culture showed no growth. Chest X-ray revealed mild enlargement of the heart, increased blood flow in the lungs, and patchy inflammation in the left middle lung zone.
test_results: 2D-echocardiography revealed a large ostium secondum atrial septal defect (ASD), (17 mm in size) with dilated right atrium and right ventricle. The karyotype was 46, XX.

case_report: A 46-year-old male with a history of controlled essential hypertension presented with progressively worsening difficulty walking. His symptoms began 13 years prior with jerking clonic movements of his ankles that interfered with driving. Over time, his gait disturbance worsened and was associated with urinary urgency. He did not seek medical evaluation initially. Due to his symptoms and episodes of urinary incontinence, he was unable to continue his work at an automobile assembly plant. His family history includes a younger brother and a nephew (son of a maternal aunt) who both had leukodystrophy and are now deceased. Over the past 13 years, he did not develop speech difficulty, dysphagia, or limb weakness. Cognitive function remained intact until six weeks prior to presentation when intermittent forgetfulness and confusion were noted by his wife. He was referred to neurology and underwent MR imaging of the brain, which raised initial concerns. During a routine follow-up in the outpatient neurology clinic, he was acutely confused and had difficulty answering questions appropriately. He exhibited an ataxic gait and had difficulty with speech production and comprehension. Due to acute worsening, he was sent to the emergency department for immediate evaluation.
