Neurological examination revealed an agitated and confused male. Cranial nerve examination showed right-sided facial myokymia. There was no dysarthria. Pupils were equal in diameter and symmetrically reactive to light. Visual fields were intact bilaterally, and extraocular movements were intact without nystagmus. Coordination testing revealed bilateral dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing but no tremor. Non-sustained ankle clonus was present bilaterally. Muscle tone assessment showed Ashworth grade 3 spasticity in the quadriceps, hamstrings, and adductor muscle groups bilaterally, and Ashworth grade 2 spasticity in the right wrist. Babinski sign was flexor. Hyperreflexia (3+) was noted in the bilateral upper and lower extremities. Hoffman sign was positive. He exhibited a spastic gait without toe dragging or circumduction and was able to stand and ambulate without assistance.
test_results: A peroxisome profile showed elevated levels of VLCFAs. There is presence of long-chain fatty acids of the C24:0/C22:0 and C26:0/C22:0 ratios.

case_report: A 42-year-old woman presented with firm, brown-colored tumorous nodules on her bilateral lower extremities. The patient started noticing the growths after sustaining some insect bites in these areas. The dermatologist she initially visited treated her with triamcinolone injection and steroid tape. However, the patient did not respond to treatment, and the nodules did not soften or reduce in size. When she later visited our outpatient department in Nippon Medical School Hospital, the examination revealed dark brown-colored nodular lesions on bilateral knees, the right tibial region, dorsum of the left foot, the right calcaneal area, and the lateral side of the left foot. The nodules on her lower extremities manifested in one of two ways; the first type of nodule appeared very similar to keloids, but the other type was partially rounded in shape, unlike a usual keloid. Surgery along with radiation therapy was determined to be the best course of treatment. The nodules were resected under general anesthesia with subsequent administration of 18 Gy/3 fractions continuous radiation therapy.
test_results: The histopathologic examination revealed tuberous lesions in the dermis, increased wired collagen fibers, neutrophilic infiltrate with nuclear dust, and edematous endothelial cells in the small vessels.

case_report: This exceptionally tall 32-year-old white man, an only child, sought medical attention in 2007 for his skeletal condition. He was accompanied by his nonconsanguineous parents. He was born full-term via vaginal delivery, weighing 7 pounds, 13 ounces (50th percentile) and measuring 21.5 inches in length (90th percentile). He remained healthy until around age 10, when his mother observed that his ankles became pronated and he developed flat feet suddenly. His limbs grew disproportionately long, and he had difficulty running and participating in gym class. Both legs ached at night. He reported continued growth until at least age 24, reaching a height of 7 feet, and an endocrinologist ruled out acromegaly. His growth plates were reportedly open in his late 20s, but growth charts and imaging from that period were unavailable. He developed knock-knees with flexion contractures, resulting in a laborious and shuffling gait. He could walk barefoot for 10 minutes before experiencing knee and ankle pain. Pain in his feet persisted despite the use of shoe orthotics. After prolonged sitting, his ankles would swell over his shoes. Mobic (meloxicam), taken until one year prior, improved his mobility, generalized soreness, flexibility, and periodic leg, shoulder, and back pains. Ibuprofen provided almost the same relief. His mother noted finger clubbing since childhood, but cardiopulmonary evaluations, including a normal echocardiogram, did not reveal any abnormalities. At age 26, he was found to have hearing loss, and hearing aids have been beneficial since. His gait, thin body build, and clubbed fingertips have remained unchanged over the past five years. He experiences constant sinus congestion, which is worse in the morning.
test_results: Radiographs showed osteopathia striata.

case_report: A seven-year-old boy presented with a history of difficulty in night vision for the past five years. He was the older twin, born at term with normal birth history and developmental milestones. Family history was unremarkable and physical examination was normal. His best corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. The anterior segment examination was normal in both eyes. The other twin had no ocular complaints and his fundus examination was unremarkable. Dilated fundus examination of both eyes revealed a golden sheen over the posterior pole (Figure 1A,B). This sheen disappeared after 45 minutes of dark adaptation (Figure 1C,D). There was no evidence of bone-spicules pigmentation and the optic disc and arterioles were normal.
test_results: The electroretinogram (ERG) of both eyes showed the characteristic negative waveform morphology with non-recordable single flash rod response, negative-positive combined response and normal photopic response.

case_report: A 2-year-old female child, third in birth order, born to parents who are first cousins, delivered vaginally at term without complications, presented with sparse scalp hair, absent body hair, eyebrows, and eyelashes, and delayed tooth eruption. The mother reported that the child does not sweat and has had recurrent fevers since the neonatal period. Psychomotor development was normal. There was no family history of similar symptoms, except for a previous female sibling with similar complaints and a distinctive appearance, who experienced recurrent fever and chest infections during the neonatal period and died at 6 months of age. The parents' first pregnancy ended in a miscarriage at 2 months for unknown reasons. Skin examination showed smooth, normal-looking skin with normal palmoplantar skin and dermatoglyphics. The child had an aged appearance with finely wrinkled skin around the eyes, an everted lower lip, and low-set ears. Scalp hair was sparse, light-colored, and thin, with complete absence of eyelashes, eyebrows, and body hair. Oral examination revealed only two conical, widely spaced maxillary teeth and a low-arched, flat palate. Nails were normal. Systemic examination showed no abnormalities, and there was no evidence of mental retardation. Imaging of the jaw showed a lack of teeth with only two maxillary teeth and a left mandibular tooth bud. Biochemical tests were normal.
test_results: Histopathology of palmer skin from hypothenar area showed inconspicuous sweat glands.

case_report: A 48-year-old female visited the clinic for ongoing care. She had recently been discharged from hospice care due to chronic pain. Her medical history includes type 2 diabetes, Hashimoto's disease, migraines, and obesity. At the age of 40, she began experiencing episodic generalized pain with a severity of 7–10/10, lasting from minutes to days, with the longest episode lasting 32 days. These episodes were accompanied by migraines, auras, blurry vision, and photophobia. Over time, the frequency of pain episodes increased, and she noticed tender lumps around her abdomen. During one severe pain episode, she visited the emergency room. According to her husband, her lab tests were unremarkable.
test_results: A CT scan of her abdomen revealed many small masses in her subcutaneous tissue. Subsequent biopsies of the masses revealed histopathologic characteristics of lipomas.

case_report: A six-year-old right-handed male experienced the sudden onset of seizures during his first year. Despite multiple anticonvulsant treatments, including primidone, sodium valproate, lamotrigine, carbamazepine, levetiracetam, and prednisolone, his seizures remained uncontrolled. The family history showed no hearing difficulties, communication disorders, seizures, or other neurological issues. Neurological examinations conducted between seizures were normal, and there was no indication of encephalitis or neurometabolic disorders after thorough investigation. Blood glucose and lactate levels were within normal ranges, and imaging studies, including a CT head scan and an MRI scan, showed no abnormalities. By the fourth year, the patient developed a receptive and expressive language disorder, which worsened over time. Hearing tests confirmed normal hearing. By the sixth year, the patient continued to experience uncontrolled seizures and exhibited global aphasia.
test_results: The EEG showed bilateral generalized high voltage slow activity, interrupted with sharp and slow activity which was more prominent over the left hemisphere. The interictal brain perfusion SPECT in sleep state showed decreased perfusion in the left inferior frontal, left temporal, and left thalamic regions.

case_report: A 62-year-old female with a history of systemic lupus erythematosus arrived at our hospital reporting intermittent watery rectal discharge over the past few years, which had intensified in the last month. She also experienced constipation and occasional rectal bleeding. Her medical history includes a total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy performed ten years ago.
test_results: Proctoscopy revealed a pedunculated rectal polyp and grade 4 external haemorrhoid. Microscopically, the polyp consisted of irregularly spaced tubular crypts with focal dilatation, separated by hypertrophied muscularis mucosae, and granulation tissue cap. It was focally covered by squamous epithelium. Some of the glands demonstrate serrations. Weigert Van Gieson stain demonstrates elastic fibers in the lamina propria.

case_report: A 25-year-old female presented with a 12-year history of progressive walking difficulties. She had normal development until pre-adolescence. Thirteen years ago, she began experiencing tremors in both her upper and lower limbs. A year later, she developed unstable walking, inarticulate speech, and coughing when drinking fluids. Currently, her symptoms include difficulty walking, frequent falls, inability to walk independently, a wide-based gait, limb tremors, unsteady hand movements, slurred speech, and choking on liquids. She also reports palpitations and frequent hunger. Her birth history was unremarkable, with a gestational age of 39 weeks, head circumference of 34 cm, birth weight of 2.75 kg, and body length of 49 cm. Early reflexes, including rooting, sucking, grip, and embrace reflexes, were normal. Her parents are healthy and non-consanguineous, and she has a younger brother who is also healthy. Neurological examination showed severe dysarthria, horizontal nystagmus in both eyes, mildly elevated muscle tone, instability in bilateral finger-nose and heel-knee-tibia tests, and a positive Romberg sign. Cognitive assessments revealed mild intellectual disability and cognitive impairment, with scores of 9 on the mini-mental state examination, 7 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, and a failure score of 6 on the cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome scale. The patient has no vision problems, and other physical examinations were normal. Laboratory results were within normal limits.
test_results: Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) T1-weighted sequence cross-sectional image showed obvious cerebellar atrophy and T2-weighted sequence sagittal image showed obvious cerebellar atrophy, deepening sulcus widening, and enlarged cerebral cistern, suggesting cerebellar atrophy. Compound heterozygous mutations in the TPP1 gene were detected: A missense mutation c.1468G>A p.Glu490Lys (present in the father), and a missense mutation c.1417G>A p.Gly473Arg (present in the mother). The younger brother had only inherited the maternal mutation.

case_report: A 7-year-old Polynesian female child presented with a swelling in the left preauricular area that had grown over a period of 3 months. Physical examination revealed a 2 cm × 2 cm firm, elevated, non-painful mass that moved in conjunction with the mandible. No occlusal alterations or additional significant clinical findings were noted.
test_results: Imaging revealed expansion of the condylar head due to a 2 cm × 3 cm well-demarcated radiolucent lesion extending inferiorly into the ramus.
diagnosis: Simple Bone Cyst of the Mandibular Condyle

case_report: An 18-year-old male presented with repeated episodes of black stools (melena) for the past 15 days. The patient also reported minor bruising following trivial trauma. He had been taking oral iron supplements and had received occasional blood transfusions with no history of any other disease. His vital signs were normal with no fever. On physical examination, the patient was in no active distress and was sitting comfortably on the bed. No fresh bleed was noted in the rectal vault. A few petechial rashes were noted in the lower limbs. Systemic examination was significant only for pallor and tachycardia. On abdominal examination, his liver span was normal, spleen was not palpable, and there was no lymphadenopathy. Baseline investigations were ordered which included a complete blood picture and coagulation profile.
test_results: Peripheral blood film showed megakaryocytosis. RBC nuclear scan showed scintigraphic evidence of active bleeding at the region of the distal ileum and ileocecal junction.

case_report: A 35-year-old male presented with difficulty ascending stairs, frequent falls, and shortness of breath. Neurological examination showed muscle strength of 4/5 proximally and +4/5 distally in the upper limbs, and 3/5 proximally and 4/5 distally in the lower limbs. Deep tendon reflexes were reduced in all extremities. Among his seven siblings, only his older sister reported similar symptoms, while the others were asymptomatic. Laboratory tests including full blood count, biochemical tests, sedimentation rate, CRP, thyroid function tests, Vitamin B12, and Vitamin D levels were within normal ranges. The CK level was 296 U/L (reference range: 29-168 U/L). Electromyography indicated myopathy. Respiratory function tests showed reduced vital capacity. Blood gas analysis revealed a pH of 7.29, pCO2 of 62.6 mmHg, and pO2 of 36.4 mmHg. ECG and echocardiography were normal. The patient had a history of being evaluated 14 years ago for generalized weakness, with respiratory issues emerging 2 years later. He had been diagnosed with muscular dystrophy and had multiple hospital admissions for respiratory acidosis, including one elective intubation. Recently, his respiratory symptoms had worsened.
test_results: The alpha glycosidase enzyme level was 0.2 µmol/l/h (normal range >3.3 µmol/l/h). Genetic analysis revealed the two mutations of c.32-13T>G and c.896T >C.

case_report: A 5-year-old girl was referred for an initial retinal evaluation. Her ocular history included left-sided esotropia managed with patching and atropine penalization of the dominant eye. She had developmental delay, seizures, and significant hearing impairment. At four months old, she experienced severe hepatic dysfunction with elevated serum transaminases, and liver biopsy results indicated potential Alagille syndrome or a peroxisomal storage disorder. Previous evaluations showed a negative skin biopsy and no evidence of TORCH infection or renal dysfunction. Her enzyme levels improved spontaneously. The mother had a history of fetal demise at 16 weeks of gestation due to cystic hygroma. The family history was otherwise unremarkable for congenital anomalies or known genetic disorders. Physical examination at age 5 revealed epicanthal folds, upper lid ptosis, and bilateral single transverse palmar creases. She had approximately 15 degrees of residual left esotropia. Snellen visual acuity and intraocular pressure were not obtained due to poor cooperation, but the patient could fix and follow with each eye. Fundoscopic examination showed bilateral “salt and pepper” changes, a hypopigmented patch in the macula of both eyes, and bilateral nummular patches of hyperpigmentation in the periphery, without significant ocular nerve pallor or vascular attenuation. OCT revealed few cystic changes in the macula with loss of foveal depression and ellipsoid zone in the right eye.
test_results: Measurement of serum very long chain fatty acids showed elevation of C26:0 and C22:0 puritanic acid and phytanic acid. Review of an electroretinogram (ERG) obtained under anesthesia at an outside facility revealed complete extinction of scotopic and photopic responses. Chromosomal microarray testing and Usher syndrome mutation panel were unremarkable. Genetic evaluation revealed that she was homozygous for a PEX1 mutation (c.2528 G>A, p. GLY843ASB).

case_report: A 13.5-year-old male patient with nonconsanguineous parents presented with a one-month history of paroxysmal abdominal pain localized around the periumbilical and right lower quadrants. Three days prior to admission, he experienced loose stools containing mucus and blood. Laboratory tests showed normal levels of lymphocytes, neutrophils, erythrocytes, and platelets. Imaging studies, including abdominal ultrasound and CT, indicated ileocecitis and a small volume of ascites. The patient had a history of recurrent pneumonia since infancy and no history of transfusions. His sister had oral ulcers and died of severe pneumonia at four months old. Both his father and grandfather had histories of tuberculosis. Physical examination revealed normal nutritional status, tenderness around the umbilicus and right lower abdomen, and skin lesions on the soles of the left foot. There were no palpable enlarged lymph nodes or abnormal lung sounds on auscultation. Lymphocyte count was 2.63×10^3/μl. The percentage of CD3+ T lymphocytes was 83.48% (reference range: 55-83%), CD3+CD4+ T lymphocytes was 22.69% (reference range: 28-57%), CD3+CD8+ T lymphocytes was 51.50% (reference range: 10-39%), and the CD4+/CD8+ ratio was 0.44 (reference range: 0.98-1.94). The percentage of B cells was 0.17% (reference range: 6-19%), while NK cells were within normal range. Serum levels of IgM and IgA were low (IgA 0.01 g/L, reference 0.63-3.04 g/L; IgM 0.29 g/L, reference 0.50-2.48 g/L), but IgG and IgE levels were normal. Quantitative PCR showed an EBV DNA copy number of 3.83×10^3 copies/ml. Other tests, including CMV DNA PCR, T-spot, HIV antibody, various autoantibodies, tumor markers, fecal culture, and fecal Clostridium difficile gene Xpert assay, were negative. Chest CT revealed bronchiectasis in both lungs, and echocardiography showed mild aortic valve regurgitation. Colonoscopy revealed a large ulcer with yellow pus in the ascending colon. Biopsy from the ulcer showed diffuse proliferation of medium-sized lymphocytes with basophilic nuclei and prominent large nucleoli. Immunohistochemical analysis indicated the cells were positive for CD20, CD79a, MUM1, very weakly positive for CD138 and CD68, sporadically positive for CD2, CD3, and Kappa-light chain, and negative for Lambda-light chain. Ki-67 showed a proliferative fraction of 60%. EBER in situ hybridization was positive, and acid-fast staining was negative. Transplacental maternal lymphocytes were excluded by short tandem repeat analysis.
test_results: The genetic analysis demonstrated compound heterozygous mutations of DCLRE1C, including a paternally inherited splicing donor mutation (c.109 + 2T>C) in intron 1 and a maternally inherited c.1147C>T (p.R383X) nonsense mutation in exon 13 (NM_001033855.3). Sanger sequencing confirmed the carrying status of variants.
diagnosis: Atypical Severe Combined Immunodeficiency  due to a novel splice donor mutation in DCLRE1C
Orpha_name: Severe combined immunodeficiency due to DCLRE1C deficiency

case_report: The case involves a four-year-old male child of Avar nationality, born from a third pregnancy in a consanguineous marriage (parents are fourth cousins). He has two healthy older brothers, aged 11 and 6. At birth, his weight was 4000 g and length was 55 cm, with an Apgar score of 8/8. There is a family history of dyslipidemia, with elevated blood triglyceride levels in one sibling, the father, an aunt (paternal), and an uncle (paternal). None of these family members took lipid-lowering medications or had cardiovascular disease. At 1.5 years old, a routine examination revealed serum lactescence with a triglyceride level of up to 55 mmol/L (4850 mg/dL). Subsequent tests showed persistent dyslipidemia and elevated liver enzymes (ALT up to 61 U/L, AST up to 49 U/L). Ultrasound examination indicated hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and pancreatic inflammation. Despite several hospitalizations and a low-fat diet, serum lactescence and hypertriglyceridemia persisted. The patient received treatments including iron, ursodeoxycholic acid, antihistamines, interferon, and intestinal microflora stabilizers. Examination at a specialized medical center revealed no stigmas of dysembryogenesis. However, a light rash was observed on the hands, and a reddish rash resembling xanthomas was noted on the legs, with more than 10 elements in total. Whitish, rounded elements up to 5 mm in diameter, resembling xanthomas, were found on the dorsum of the hands and the area of the first finger. Single reddish elements, also resembling xanthomas, were present in the sacral region and on the inner surface of the legs.
test_results: We found an exonic variant: LPL (NM_000237.2: c.106G > A (rs1801177) p.Asp36Asn), in a heterozygous state. According to the analysis, the presence of a homozygous deletion of 13 nucleotides in size in exon 4 of the APOA5 gene (NM_052968: c.579_592delATACGCCGAGAGCC) was suggested, leading to the formation of a premature stop codon, p.Tyr194Gly*68. Subsequently, the deletion was confirmed by direct sequencing in a homozygous state in the proband and in a heterozygous state in both parents. This deletion was also found in the 11-year-old brother.

case_report: The patient is a 35-year-old male with a history of jaundice since birth, with total bilirubin (TB) levels ranging from 70–80 µmol/L. In adulthood, his TB levels increased to approximately 300 µmol/L. At the age of 31, he experienced right upper abdominal pain and severe jaundice, with TB levels rising above 500 µmol/L. He was found to have gallbladder stones and cholecystitis. Treatment with antibiotics and oral phenobarbital alleviated his pain and reduced TB to 300 µmol/L. Subsequently, he had recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, fever, and severe jaundice. In November 2019, he became lethargic and unresponsive following a fever, and later developed limb convulsions and urinary incontinence. Upon admission on November 15, 2019, liver function tests showed decreased albumin (21.5 g/L) and elevated AST (222 U/L), ALT (57 U/L), TB (417.4 µmol/L), and direct bilirubin (195 µmol/L). Neutrophil proportion was 88.1%, and blood ammonia was 112 µg/dL. The Coombs test was negative. Fasting plasma lipids, autoantibodies profile, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody were within normal limits. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis did not indicate central nervous system infection. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed gallstones, cholecystitis, and splenomegaly. Brain CT scans were normal.
test_results: Sanger sequencing of the UGT1A1 gene identified three heterozygous mutations, namely G71R (c.211G>A), R209W (c. 625C>T), and M391K (c.1172T>A). The M391K mutation has not been reported before. The PhastCons score of the mutation was 1, and the corresponding PhyloP value was 2.307, suggesting the high conservation of this amino acid.

case_report: A 37-year-old male arrived at the emergency department in October 2012, reporting worsening lower back pain over the past four months. He had no history of trauma or falls. He was unemployed, lived with his mother, and did not take any medications or supplements. He did not smoke, consume excessive alcohol, or use illegal drugs, and had never been treated with corticosteroids. He had no prior fractures and no family history of gonadal, endocrine, or bone diseases. He had experienced markedly delayed puberty and had received testosterone injections starting at age 16, which were discontinued three years later after satisfactory growth and development of secondary male sexual characteristics. He reported decreased libido for several years and absence of morning erections. On physical examination, he appeared well-nourished but in obvious distress due to pain in the lower thoracic/lumbar spine. He had an eunuchoidal body habitus with an arm span of 181 cm and a height of 174 cm. His pupils were round, equal, and reactive to light, and his visual fields were normal. His skin turgor was normal, mucous membranes were moist, and his teeth were in good condition without decay. Examination of the head and neck revealed hyposmia to several odorants. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were normal. There was no edema in the extremities, and neurological assessment was normal. Examination of the integument showed sparse pubic hair. The penile length was normal, but testicular volume was decreased (approximately 5 cm3 as measured by the Prader orchidometer). Biochemical tests revealed extremely low serum levels of luteinizing hormone (LH), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), testosterone, and estradiol. Serum creatinine, electrolytes, thyroid function tests (TSH and free T4), prolactin, cortisol, parathyroid hormone (PTH), and alkaline phosphatase activity were all within normal limits. Osteocalcin levels were elevated, and serum 25(OH) vitamin D levels were insufficient. A complete blood count showed normochromic normocytic anemia, and serum protein electrophoresis was unremarkable.
test_results: Radiographic examination of the spine disclosed diffuse osteopenia with moderate wedging of several mid-thoracic vertebrae along with severe compression fractures of T11, T12, and L1 (80%–90% vertebral height loss). There was a 10% superior endplate collapse at L5. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) scan of the skeleton reported a Z-score of −6.9 at the lumbar vertebrae (L2–L4), −3.3 at the femoral neck, and −4.1 at the total hip. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with particular attention to the hypophysis was carried out. The pituitary gland was normal except for a 2.4 × 2.6 mm left anterior pituitary cyst with no evidence of a mass effect.
diagnosis: Kallmann syndrome with severe osteoporosis due to hypogonadism
Orpha_name: Hyposmia-nasal and ocular hypoplasia-hypogonadotropic hypogonadism syndrome

case_report: A 44-year-old Japanese male presented with a range of systemic symptoms that had progressively developed since infancy. His parents were not related by blood, and there was no family history of similar conditions. The patient had experienced difficulty swallowing and speaking from around the age of 35, and hearing loss began at approximately 40 years old. Physical examinations revealed several notable findings. The patient was of short stature (149 cm) and exhibited muscle weakness in all limbs. The face showed mottled pigmentation and telangiectasia. Eyebrows and eyelashes were nearly absent, and there was incomplete eyelid closure due to skin hardening. Scalp hair was sparse, and the top of the head had been almost hairless since childhood. The trunk and limbs had dry skin, mild eczema, small pigmented spots, and skin hardening. Mild swelling of the lower limbs and a history of cellulitis were also observed. The left heel could not touch the ground due to a contracted Achilles tendon, causing the left knee to remain in a flexed position. Mild underdevelopment of the hands and feet, multiple calluses on the soles, and limited finger extension were also noted.
test_results: Histology of the non-sun-exposed skin showed epidermal atrophy and mild dermal fibrosis. Fragmented elastic fibers were clearly observed with Elastica–Masson staining. Muscle MRI findings showed severe fatty infiltration in the bilateral quadriceps muscles, erector spinae muscles, and muscles in the upper extremities. A chest CT scan revealed interstitial lung shadows, predominantly in the upper lobes. Liver cirrhosis was diagnosed based on the findings of CT and ultrasonography.
diagnosis: Hereditary Fibrosing Poikiloderma With Tendon Contractures, Myopathy, and Pulmonary Fibrosis
Orpha_name: Hereditary fibrosing poikiloderma-tendon contractures-myopathy-pulmonary fibrosis syndrome

case_report: A 26-year-old female, born to parents who are not related by blood and from a lower socioeconomic background, has had bone abnormalities in both upper limbs since birth. She exhibits polydactyly with five fingers and an absent thumb. For the past five years, she has experienced shortness of breath during physical activity, classified as class II. She has been assessed at multiple primary care facilities and later referred to a tertiary care center. There is no history of heart failure, chest pain during exertion, swelling of the legs, or paradoxical embolism. Physical examination revealed a loud first heart sound (S1), a wide and fixed split-second heart sound, and an ejection systolic murmur graded at 3/6 in the pulmonary area.
test_results: The electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm, first-degree atrioventricular (AV) block with PR of 240 ms, incomplete right bundle branch block, and diffuse reperfusion abnormalities. Chest X-ray showed cardiomegaly, prominence of the main pulmonary artery, and increased pulmonary vascularity. The transthoracic echocardiogram in the parasternal long-axis view and apical four-chamber view showed dilated right atrium, right ventricle, and 13 mm caudally shifted ostium secundum (OS-ASD) with left to right shunt.

case_report: A 56-year-old woman was identified with bilateral lung nodules on low-dose computed tomography (CT) during a routine medical check-up and was subsequently referred to our hospital. She reported no symptoms such as cough, sputum production, chest pain, or weight loss. The patient has no known underlying diseases and has a family history of liver cancer (father). She has a history of heavy smoking for 30 years. A chest radiograph revealed an abnormal shadow in the left upper lobe. CT imaging showed a solitary nodule measuring 18.9 × 17.8 mm in the left upper lobe, along with severe bronchiectasis. She was admitted to National Taiwan University Cancer Center and underwent pulmonary function testing and cardiac sonography. The pulmonary function test indicated a forced expiratory volume in the first second of 2.41 L, which is 115.2% of the predicted value. Cardiac sonography showed good left ventricular contractility with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 69.6%. A left upper lobe S1-S3 segmentectomy and dissection of groups 5, 6, and 11 lymph nodes were performed using uniportal video-assisted thoracoscopic (VATS) surgery.
test_results: The intraoperative frozen biopsy showed adenocarcinoma with inflammatory cell-rich background. The tumor was yellowish, well-defined, soft-to-elastic in texture tumor, and 21 × 15 × 14 mm in size. The pathological findings showed a complex glandular structure with frequent squamoid morules. The tumor cells have basally oriented nuclei and vacuolated cytoplasm. In addition, small foci of fibroblastic stroma are identified focally. Immunohistochemical stains showed TTF-1 positivity, CK (AE1/AE3) positivity, CDX-2 negativity, PAX8 negativity, and nuclear stain on beta-catenin. Next-generation sequencing revealed no G719X and Exon 19 deletions, S768I, T790M, and Exon 20 insertions, and L858R and L861Q EGFR mutation.
diagnosis: low-grade fetal adenocarcinoma of lung origin
Orpha_name: Well-differentiated fetal adenocarcinoma of the lung

case_report: A 37-year-old female patient presented with a 2-week history of recurrent generalized pruritic pustular eruption primarily affecting the trunk and extremities. Her past medical history included diffuse scleroderma for the past 7 years. Current medications were atenolol, valsartan, hydroxychloroquine, furosemide, and nifedipine. Dermatologic examination revealed superficial vesicles and pustules on normal skin or erythematous bases on the trunk and extremities. The face, palms, soles, and mucous membranes were unaffected. No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly was observed. Physical examination noted a “bird-like” face with a beaked nose, telangiectasia, and radial furrowing around the lips. The fingers appeared smooth, shiny, and tapered with nails curving over atrophic phalanges. Cultures of the pustules were sterile.
test_results: Microscopic examinations demonstrated acanthosis, focal parakeratosis, subcorneal pustules, and crust in the epidermis. A few acantholytic cells were identified. Focal vacuolar degeneration of the basal layer, infiltration of lymphocytes, and a few eosinophils accompanied by focal edema of papillary dermis were observed. Direct immunofluorescence examination was negative.

case_report: Case 2 involves an eight-year-old Sudanese boy born to consanguineous parents. He was delivered at full term via normal vaginal delivery, weighing 3.5 kg. The patient exhibited his first symptom at one year old. By the age of two, he experienced dysglycemia characterized by fasting hypoglycemia, postprandial hyperglycemia, and diabetes mellitus. Biochemical investigations revealed hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, and hyponatremia, along with elevated random glucose levels and reduced levels of C peptide and insulin. His dysglycemia was managed through dietary adjustments and the addition of cornstarch. The patient also presented with hepatomegaly and abnormal liver function tests. Additionally, he developed renal tubular acidosis and rickets. His height and weight were recorded at 110.30 cm and 21.4 kg, respectively. Comprehensive pituitary hormonal tests were within normal limits except for a low IGF-1 level. A GH stimulation test indicated growth hormone deficiency, leading to a daily prescription of 0.5 mg GH. The patient was also administered multiple medications to address electrolyte imbalances, including sodium bicarbonate, potassium, phosphorus, and vitamin D.
test_results: The patient’s WGS revealed a homozygous mutation (c.1093C>T in exon 9, R365X (NM_000340)) in the SLC2A2 gene. The mutation was confirmed by Sanger sequencing of DNA.

case_report: A 16-year-old female patient was referred to our pain clinic from the orthopedic department with ongoing pain and swelling in the right forearm. Her medical history includes a previous admission to a local hospital for a urinary tract infection, during which she received an infusion of 5% dextrose with 0.9% saline through an IV cannula placed on the right dorsum of the hand five months ago. Subsequently, there was extravasation of fluid into the surrounding tissue, resulting in persistent pain and swelling that progressively worsened. Initially, the general practitioner diagnosed cellulitis and treated her with analgesics and antibiotics, followed by a local incision and drainage procedure. Despite these treatments, her symptoms continued to deteriorate, leaving surgical scars. The primary care physician managed her condition conservatively for nearly five months before she presented to our hospital. Upon clinical examination, the limb was found to be tender, shiny, and swollen, with allodynia and stiff joints, but no evidence of nerve injury.
test_results: Doppler study ruled out any possibility of vascular disease. A diagnostic stellate ganglion block (SGB) improved the numerical pain rating score (0-10) from 7 to 2 with enhancement of limb mobility.

case_report: A 48-year-old female exhibited asymptomatic, widespread brownish-red papulo-macules arranged in a network-like pattern with areas of atrophy and prominent telangiectasias, primarily affecting the breasts, abdomen, back, and extremities. The upper limbs, particularly the extensor surfaces, and the front of the trunk were more severely affected compared to the lower limbs and back. The lesions initially appeared on the thighs and gradually spread to cover the entire body over a span of 10 years. The face, palms, and soles remained unaffected. Hair, nails, and mucous membranes were normal. The patient was obese, had no lymphadenopathy, and systemic examination revealed no abnormalities. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count, serum biochemistry, antinuclear antibody (ANA) test, urinalysis, and imaging studies (X-rays and computed tomography scans) of the chest, abdomen, and pelvic organs, showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Histologic features of effaced rete ridges, hydropic degeneration of basal cells, focal dense band-like infiltrate of lymphoid cells (prominently perivascular), dilated capillaries and extravasation of red blood cells, melanin incontinence and a few melanophages in the upper dermis, and no Pautrier's microabscess or atypical lymphoid cells. Immunohistochemical staining was negative for cluster of differentiation (CD) 3, CD4, and CD7 and positive for CD8.

case_report: A 4-month-old male patient was transferred to our institute due to weakness and reduced movement in the left lower extremity. He was born following an uneventful pregnancy and delivery and was in good health until one month prior to the visit when his parents observed the weakness. He had received OPV with DTaP at a local health center one month before these symptoms appeared. Initially, his parents delayed seeking appropriate medical help and took him to an orthopedics clinic where he was evaluated and treated. His family history and past medical history, including the perinatal period, were unremarkable. At the time of the report (2 years old), his body weight was 8.1 kg, length 66 cm, and head circumference 41.2 cm, with growth index measurements in the 50-90th percentile. Vital signs were unremarkable. Physical examination showed an alert mental status, and cranial nerve function tests were normal. Neurologic examination revealed significantly decreased spontaneous movement and flaccid paralysis in the left lower extremity (GI/V) with knee jerk (+/-), biceps tendon reflex (+/+), and ankle clonus (-/-). The response to painful stimuli in the left lower extremity was markedly reduced, but normal in other parts of his body. There was no history of intramuscular injection or trauma in the left buttock area. Laboratory evaluation, simple skeletal radiography, hip joint sonogram, and 3-phase bone scan were all within normal ranges. Brain and spinal MRI showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Electrodiagnostic evaluations showed normal sensory nerve action potentials and low amplitudes in left tibial and deep peroneal nerve.

case_report: A 46-year-old man, who does not smoke, reported experiencing a dry cough and increasing difficulty in breathing over the past 10 years. He has been employed in the building department of the tire industry for 26 years. Upon examination, he exhibited rapid breathing with a respiratory rate of 36 breaths per minute, clubbing of the fingers, and swelling in the lower extremities along with elevated jugular venous pressure and fine crackles heard in both lungs. Blood tests were generally normal, except for an increased red blood cell count. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed a pH of 7.33, PaO2 of 56.8 mmHg, PaCO2 of 21.5 mmHg, and HCO3 of 11.1 mmol/L, with an alveolar-arterial gradient of 67.13.
test_results: HRCT showed extensive fibrosis and ground glass pattern with mid-zone predominance with areas of honeycombing and paraseptal emphysema. Spirometry showed a restrictive abnormality with forced vital capacity (FVC) 2.95L (62%predicted), forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) –2.20 L (56% predicted) and FEV1/FVC–75%. Diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) was 6% of the predicted value. Two-dimensional echocardiography (2D-ECHO) showed PH with tricuspid regurgitation (TR) jet-estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP) of 62 mmHg with dilatation of right atrium and right ventricle.
diagnosis: Combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema  due to occupational exposure to talc

case_report: A 61-year-old man was admitted to the hospital on May 20, 2016, after experiencing syncope following physical activity. One month prior, he had episodes of chest tightness and dizziness, which subsided after resting for 3 to 5 minutes. Over the following days, his condition appeared to worsen progressively, and he occasionally experienced sudden syncope during activity, which resolved spontaneously without intervention. Upon admission, his blood pressure was recorded at 110/70 mmHg. An electrocardiogram revealed flat T waves in leads II, III, and AVF. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 11.4 × 10^9/L (reference range: 4–10 × 10^9/L), an eosinophil count of 3.1 × 10^9/L (reference range: 0.02–0.52 × 10^9/L) with eosinophils making up 38% of the total white blood cells (reference range: 0.4–8.0%). Hemoglobin was measured at 135 g/L (reference range: 120–160 g/L), and platelet count was 146 × 10^9/L (reference range: 100–300 × 10^9/L). Cardiac biomarkers included a cardiac troponin I level of 0.05 ng/mL (reference range: <0.2 ng/mL) and a B-type natriuretic peptide level of 441 pg/mL (reference range: <100 pg/mL).
test_results: Cardiac computed tomography (CT) showed right atrial (RA) enlargement, small right ventricle (RV), and small pericardial effusion. Echocardiography showed a mass in the right ventricle (RV) involving the right ventricular inflow tract (RVIT), tricuspid annulus, chordae tendineae, and papillary muscle, resulting in RVIT stenosis and restriction of the motion of the tricuspid leaflet and chordae. Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) was 66%. Contrast echocardiography showed a mass in the right ventricle and no blood perfusion within it.

case_report: A 7-year-old Chinese female patient with a history of night blindness since childhood was referred to our hospital. Her family history revealed that her parents, grandmother, and younger brother were all healthy. Written informed consent for participation in the study was obtained from the patient and her relatives, with her father signing on her behalf as she is a minor. The research protocol received approval from the Ethics Review Board of the First People's Hospital of Linping District and adhered to the Declaration of Helsinki. During the initial evaluation, her visual acuity was measured at 20/20 in both eyes. Examination of the anterior segment of the eyeball showed no noticeable abnormalities.
test_results: Ophthalmoscopic examination showed the golden metallic reflex in all areas of the fundus. After 3 hours of dark adaptation, the Mizuo phenomenon was demonstrated. The images obtained with a nonmydriatic retinal camera showed that the fundus color changed to normal. During 30 minutes of light adaptation, the golden sheen reappeared. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography showed that in the foveal area, three hyperreflective bands representing the inner segment/outer segment junction of the photoreceptors, the cone outer segment tips, and the RPE/Bruch’s membrane complex are clearly distinguished. However, in the parafoveal areas of both eyes, the boundaries of these hyperreflective bands become densely packed and indistinguishable. Electroretinographic (ERG) responses were recorded according to ISCEV guidelines with 30 min of dark adaptation. The dark-adapted scotopic response revealed the loss of a and b-wave amplitudes. Genetic testing revealed no GRK1 gene mutation in the patient and her relatives, but sequencing of the SAG gene indicated new heterozygous mutations in exon 2 and exon 6. Sequencing revealed a heterozygous change in nucleotide c.72_75+15delATCGGTGAGTGGTGCACAA in exon 2 of the SAG gene in this patient, her mother and her younger brother. This nucleotide change caused a nonsense mutation, p.S25X. A splicing alteration of nucleotide c.376-2A>C was identified in exon 6 of the SAG gene with heterozygous status in this patient and her father.

case_report: A 63-year-old male reported experiencing back pain and stiffness extending to the front of the trunk, neck, and chest. Physical examination revealed no involuntary movements, muscle wasting, fasciculations, or tremors. Neurological examination showed no abnormalities. Comprehensive investigations, including brain imaging, gastroscopy, colonoscopy, and CT scans of the chest and abdomen, yielded unremarkable results. MRI of the brain was also unremarkable, though mild degenerative changes were observed in the lumbar spine.
test_results: An autoimmune screen detected elevated anti-GAD titer of 50 U/mL. EMG showed characteristic continuous normal motor unit activity at rest in the paraspinal and shoulder girdle muscles, without myokymia or myotonic potentials.

case_report: A 33-year-old male with no significant past medical history presented with a two-day history of dystonic posturing affecting his left hand and arm. The episodes involved bending of the elbow and specific finger posturing, without any oculo-bulbar or sensory symptoms. These episodes occurred randomly throughout the day and were later found to be triggered by caffeine consumption. The duration of the episodes varied from several minutes to one instance lasting nine hours. The episodes were painful, with the patient unable to voluntarily relax the affected arm and hand. Mental clarity was maintained throughout and after the episodes, which ceased during sleep. Initially, the symptoms were confined to the left arm but later spread to the right arm, occurring independently in both arms at random intervals. The patient reported no family history of movement disorders and did not smoke, consume alcohol, or take any medications. On examination, his blood pressure was 129/79 mmHg, heart rate was 77 beats per minute, weight was 195 pounds (88.5 kilograms), height was six feet (182.9 centimeters), and body-mass index was 26.4. His speech was normal, and his gait was unremarkable. Cranial nerve examination was normal, with intact ocular motion and no nystagmus. Facial strength was symmetric and full, with no oro-buccolingual dyskinesias. Cervical musculature examination showed no cervical dystonia, and oropharyngeal examination revealed a brisk gag reflex without palatal myoclonus. Muscle strength in both upper and lower extremities was graded 5/5, and deep tendon reflexes were 2+ and symmetric. There was no spasticity, and Hoffman and finger flexor reflexes were absent bilaterally. No cogwheeling was detected at the wrist. The Babinski sign was absent with bilateral plantar strokes. Finger sequencing, finger-to-nose, and heel-to-shin maneuvers were accurate and symmetric bilaterally. During the clinic visit, an episode was observed, starting with a 90-degree flexion of the left elbow and extending to the hand. The posture involved flexion of the first, third, and fourth fingers at the metacarpophalangeal joints with extension of the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints, while the second and fifth fingers remained extended, resembling a bovine longhorn.
test_results: An electroencephalogram (EEG) did not reveal any focal epileptiform discharge. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) study of the brain with and without contrast enhancement was normal. A T1-weighted image did not reveal any metal deposition in the basal ganglia. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences did not reveal any white matter disease. Gradient-echo and susceptibility-weighted images did not reveal any hemosiderin deposits in the basal ganglia. Serum chemistries, including free and total calcium and a thyroid screen, were normal. A comprehensive paraneoplastic panel and an antiphospholipid antibody screen were also negative.

case_report: A six-week-old male with a history of tetrasomy 12p born at 35-weeks' gestation to a 39-year-old G2P1 mother presented to the neurosurgical clinic with ultrasound findings showing a low-lying conus at the end of the L4 lumbar vertebrae. The ultrasound was initially obtained by his pediatrician due to a coccygeal dimple. The patient also had MRI imaging of the brain and cervical spinal cord due to poor trunk and head control, which revealed a small amount of hemorrhage in the caudal thalamic groove and periventricular calcifications. The patient's parents did not report any bowel or bladder issues prior to the clinic visit. On examination, the patient was awake and alert, with well-approximated cranial sutures and a soft, sunken anterior fontanelle. Physical features included hypertelorism, a high forehead, and sparse hair on the temples. The patient was able to move his upper and lower extremities but exhibited mild, global hypotonia without spasticity. Additionally, a coccygeal dimple was observed within the gluteal cleft, overlying the tip of the coccyx with vellus hair. No cutaneous markers of spinal dysraphism were noted on the lumbosacral spine.
test_results: This revealed a low-lying conus medullaris terminating behind L4 without skeletal abnormality of the lumbar spine or sacrum.

case_report: A female child, aged 1 year and 4 months, was admitted for evaluation of delayed psychomotor development and to undergo surgery for exotropia. She was delivered at full term (40 weeks gestation) via cesarean section following an uneventful pregnancy. She is the first child of healthy, unrelated parents, with no notable family medical history. Upon admission, she exhibited a distinctive high-pitched cry and had a smaller than average head size (microcephaly). Motor function delays were observed, including delayed crawling. She could sit without support but was unable to stand, indicating developmental delays compared to typical milestones for her age. Neurologic examination revealed hypotonia in the left leg, while tendon reflexes and cranial nerve function were normal. At 6 months of age, an echocardiogram identified a ventricular septal defect.
test_results: Chromosome analysis revealed 46,XX,del (p15.2) one month after delivery. MRI revealed brain stem hypoplasia (most prominently in the pons), with normal cerebellum, diffuse mild atrophy of the deep white matter of both cerebral hemispheres, as well as mild thinning of the corpus callosum and mega cisterna magna. The anterior limb of the internal capsules on both sides showed reduced myelination.

case_report: A 13-month-old female patient presented with delayed development and infantile spasms that began at 6 months of age. She was born to healthy, unrelated parents at 40 weeks of gestation. Her birth weight was 3.0 kg, and her head circumference was 34 cm, both within normal ranges for her age. At 6 months, she experienced seizures characterized by flexor spasms occurring in clusters of 3–5, with each cluster containing 10–20 spasms. These seizures persisted despite treatment with antiepileptic drugs. Initially, her developmental milestones were normal, but following the onset of seizures, her development regressed to the level of a 3-month-old, with difficulties in turning and crawling at 13 months. Physical examination revealed a height of 79.7 cm, weight of 9.4 kg, and head circumference of 42 cm, indicating acquired microcephaly. MRI results were normal, while electroencephalography (EEG) showed very high voltage, disorganized slow waves with multifocal spikes. Metabolic screening tests, including tandem mass spectrometry, blood amino acids, lactic acid, pyruvic acid, and urine organic acids, were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination after a four-hour fast revealed a glucose level of 39 mg/dL, compared to a blood glucose level of 103 mg/dL, with a ratio of 0.38.
test_results: Bidirectional sequencing of the SLC2A1 gene revealed a de novo heterozygous missense variation (c.1198C>T) at codon 400 (p.Arg400Cys). Further analysis of the parents did not show the p.Arg400Cys variation, indicating that it was a de novo mutation.
Orpha_name: Classic glucose transporter type 1 deficiency syndrome

case_report: The patient is a 4-month and 9-day-old female infant who was delivered naturally and exhibited normal physical development. At 4 months of age, she experienced an episode where she tightly clenched her hands, indicative of unprovoked focal activity. The tremor in her upper limbs subsided after several seconds. Both parents are in good health and there is no consanguinity. There is no known family history of genetic conditions.
test_results: Biochemical examination indicated abnormal serum magnesium and calcium levels, alanine, and aspartate aminotransferases. A cardiac function examination revealed high levels of creatine kinase. A Doppler ultrasound showed characteristics of CHD, including atrial septal defect (ASD). An electrocardiogram (ECG) suggested sinus arrhythmia. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and electroencephalography revealed no abnormalities.
diagnosis: Hypomagnesemia, seizures, and mental retardation caused by a novel CNNM2 mutation

case_report: A nine-year-old female presented to the dermatology department with complaints of hair loss, scaling, burning sensation, pain, and itching of the scalp. She also reported the recent appearance of purple lesions on her neck and back. The patient had previously visited general practitioners over the past year and was treated with ketoconazole and selenium sulfide shampoo, but her symptoms did not improve. According to her parents, hair loss began approximately six months ago, was gradual in onset, and was confined to the vertex of the scalp. There was no history of endocrine dysfunction, autoimmune diseases, medication use, cosmetic use, or recent stressors. The patient had minimal exposure to direct sunlight and no family history of similar hair loss patterns. She did not style her hair in a way that would cause traction or strain and denied self-pulling of hair. Her dietary intake was adequate, and she had met all developmental milestones on time. On general examination, her vital signs were normal, with no evidence of pallor, jaundice, lymphadenopathy, or nail changes. The thyroid was not enlarged, and there was no evidence of systemic disease. Inspection of the scalp revealed a focal area of hair loss on the vertex, measuring approximately 6 x 5 cm with irregular borders. Dermoscopy showed perifollicular erythema and loss of follicular openings due to scarring, with no abnormal pigmentation. Additionally, two dark purple-colored polygonal patches with irregular borders were observed on the neck and back. Examination of the oral cavity was unremarkable.
test_results: The biopsy showed lymphocytic infiltration and fibroplasia of the perifollicular regions. Superficial scarring in the dermis was also detected.

case_report: A 14-year-old girl exhibited repetitive movements and complex motor tics, including head turning to the left and face touching, after visiting her brother in a psychiatric hospital. In October 2004, she became less communicative and had difficulties with peer relationships. Three months later, she was hospitalized due to worsening repetitive movements. Her birth and early development were normal, but she had delayed language development. There was no family history of psychological or neurological disorders, except for her brother. Neurological examination revealed continuous eye rolling and head turning to the left. The Romberg sign was positive, and the heel-to-shin test was impaired. She displayed an unsteady gait, involuntary movements, and difficulty speaking. Laboratory tests for serum ceruloplasmin, copper levels in serum and urine, and liver function were normal. The Kayser-Fleischer ring was not present. A lactic acid test showed a slight increase to 3.1. Other laboratory findings were unremarkable, including normal urine homovanillic acid and serum neuron-specific enolase levels. Her ability to process audio-visual information was moderately decreased. An intellectual evaluation using the Korean version of the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC) showed an IQ of 88, within the lower average range. She was treated with Aripiprazole (5 mg/day) for persistent motor tics and repetitive movements. Six days after starting the medication, there was a reduction in these symptoms, along with some improvement in social withdrawal and anxiety.
test_results: A brain MRI demonstrated atrophy of the cerebellum and extrusion folia on T2-weighted sagittal images. T1-weighted axial images revealed hyperintense changes in the globus pallidus and the substantia nigra bilaterally, while T2-weighted axial images showed hypointensity in the same area. The pantothenate kinase 2 gene (PANK2) gene mutation was negative in a genetic test.

case_report: A 14-year-old male presented with swollen gums and hearing difficulties for the past year. The patient also noted aesthetic concerns due to a prominent gum display and an inability to fully close the mouth. The medical history was clear of systemic diseases or medication use. There was no history of ear trauma or exposure to loud noises. Family history indicated that no other family members across three generations were affected. Intraoral examination showed generalized gingival overgrowth that was firm, nodular, and fibrotic, affecting the marginal, attached gingiva, and interdental papillae of all teeth without inflammation. The gingiva appeared dark due to heavy melanin pigmentation. The lower anterior teeth were barely visible as the enlargement extended to the incisal-third of the crowns. Dental examination indicated the patient was still in the mixed dentition stage. An orthopantomograph confirmed the presence of all permanent teeth with no alveolar bone loss. Periodontal probing (UNC-15 periodontal probe, Hu-Friedy, Chicago, IL) showed no clinical attachment loss or tooth mobility. The patient was referred to an ENT specialist for hearing management.
test_results: There was severe to profound right and moderately severe to severe left sensorineural hearing loss.
diagnosis: Idiopathic gingival fibromatosis with progressive hearing loss

case_report: A 13-year-old female presented to the emergency department with seizures, accompanied by a fever of 40℃, vomiting, and a serum glucose level of 58 mg/dL. She was delivered via cesarean section at 42 weeks and 1 day of gestation, with a birth weight of 3.56 kg. At 2 days old, she exhibited lethargy and a blood sugar test showed a level of 21 mg/dL, leading to a 14-day admission in the neonatal intensive care unit where she received transfusion therapy and her blood sugar levels stabilized. During this period, a thyroid function test was performed and results were within normal limits. No further follow-up was documented, and medical records for the first 13 years are unavailable. According to her parents, she received emergency treatment for febrile seizures and hypoglycemia multiple times until age 6. Her motor and language development were normal, though her academic performance was poor. Family history revealed no significant diseases, and she has a younger brother. Her father's height is 170 cm, her mother's height is 160 cm, and her midparental height is 158.5 cm. On examination, her height was 160 cm, weight was 53 kg, and BMI was 20.45 kg/m2. Sexual maturity rate was Tanner breast I and pubic hair I. Radiography of the left hand indicated a bone age of 12 years. Laboratory tests showed a total cholesterol level of 207.1 mg/dL, LDL-cholesterol level of 155 mg/dL, triglyceride level of 156 mg/dL, and HDL-cholesterol level of 38 mg/dL.
test_results: The MRI results showed ectopic neurohypophysis and an invisible pituitary stalk.
diagnosis: Combined Pituitary Hormone Deficiency  caused by Pituitary Stalk Interruption Syndrome

case_report: A 3-year-old female patient from Saudi Arabia visited the outpatient dermatology clinic at King Salman Armed Forces Hospital in August 2021 with recurrent vesicles and bullae on her hands and feet. The parents noted that the lesions initially appeared as small, pinpoint blisters that increased in size over a few days, filling with clear, watery fluid and forming non-painful vesicles and bullae. These blisters typically developed on areas subjected to mild trauma or friction, primarily on the hands and feet. Larger blisters occasionally ruptured, either spontaneously or due to physical contact, resulting in open sores. During healing, the blisters deflated and dried out, forming a crust that eventually peeled off to reveal new skin underneath. The new skin was initially pinkish and later darkened, leading to hyperpigmented spots, with no noticeable scarring. No mucosal lesions or nail involvement were reported. The patient had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery, was current with immunizations, and has four unaffected siblings aged 6, 8, 12, and 15 years. Teeth abnormalities and caries began concurrently with skin issues but did not interfere with eating. The parents first attempted to clean her teeth between the ages of one and a half and two years, which was initially very difficult but became easier by the age of three. The bullae did not affect the mucous membranes in the mouth. The patient was breastfed briefly and then bottle-fed until 24 months of age. Her food intake was normal, and she currently enjoys eating soups and drinking water, milk, and fruit juices. On examination, numerous vesicles and bullae filled with watery fluid were observed on the dorsum of the feet, not located on pressure sites, starting at the age of 3 months with periods of remission and exacerbation. No mucosal lesions or nail involvement were noted.
test_results: The patient is homozygous for DST c.3370C>T, p.(Gln1124*).
diagnosis: Epidermolysis Bullosa Simplex with Dystonin Gene Mutation
Orpha_name: Epidermolysis bullosa simplex due to BP230 deficiency

case_report: A 50-year-old Asian woman, gravida 2 para 2, arrived at the emergency department with severe lower abdominal pain lasting three days and abnormal uterine bleeding. She also experienced intermittent nausea, loss of appetite, and a three-kilogram weight loss over the past month. Additionally, she reported abnormal sweating and palpitations during the previous week. Her menstrual cycles had been irregular up to three months before presentation, followed by amenorrhea. On physical examination, her temperature was 37ºC, heart rate was 110 bpm, blood pressure was 133/82 mmHg, and she had bilateral pedal oedema. Abdominal examination revealed a pelvic mass resembling a 15-week sized uterus. Vaginal examination showed no pathological findings. Laboratory tests indicated anaemia with a haemoglobin level of 6.8 g/dl and significantly elevated serum β-hCG levels at 978,485 IU/L. Electrolytes, renal, and liver function tests were within normal limits. Thyroid function tests showed suppressed TSH levels (<0.005 µIU/mL), elevated FT3 (6.78 pg/mL), and elevated FT4 (6.05 ng/dL), while thyrotropin-receptor antibodies (TRAb) levels were negative. Thyroid ultrasound did not reveal any major structural abnormalities.
test_results: An abdomen ultrasound displayed an enlarged uterus with a 'snow-storm' appearance. A contrast abdomen CT scan confirmed the existence of a uterine mass measuring 15.6 cm × 16.3 cm × 8.2 cm. Anatomopathological examination showed chorionic villi with marked hydropic changes weighting 1038 g.

case_report: Patient 1, an 8-year and 4-month-old female, initially visited the clinic due to medial ankle pain experienced while running at school, which caused her to limp. Her mother had observed bowing in both lower extremities for several years, but it had not previously caused any limitations or pain. At the time of the visit, her height was 118.5 cm (3rd percentile; equivalent to the 50th percentile for an approximately 6.5-year-old) and her weight was 23.6 kg (22nd percentile). Patient 1 was the first-born child, delivered spontaneously at 36 weeks without complications. She had jaundice at birth, which resolved on its own without intervention. According to parental recall, her birth weight was 2.38 kg (10–25th percentile) and her length was 43 cm (3–10th percentile). She achieved all developmental milestones appropriately throughout her childhood. Physical examination during the clinic visit showed symmetric facial features with no blue discoloration of the sclerae. There were no abnormalities or asymmetries in her hair, teeth, or nails. Her upper extremities were symmetric and proportional to her head and torso. She was noted to be short in stature with significant genu varum alignment in both lower extremities, and her lower segment appeared disproportionate to her upper segment. She had a full range of motion in her hips, knees, and ankles, and there was no tenderness upon palpation.
test_results: Radiographs demonstrated bilateral metaphyseal irregularities and asymmetry within the distal femoral physes and proximal tibia physes. Asymmetric focal bulbous appearance of the medial proximal tibial physes compared to the lateral aspect was present bilaterally. Bilateral distal tibia demonstrated physeal cupping with asymmetric irregularities both medially and laterally. Long-leg standing films were obtained and demonstrated a mechanical axis propagating through the medial compartment bilaterally, right greater than left. Measurement of the patient’s alignment demonstrated a mechanical lateral distal femoral angle (mLDFA) of 87.6° and 89°, medial proximal tibial angle (MPTA) of 85.7° and 81.4°, and lateral distal tibial angle (LDTA) of 91.8° and 93.7° to the right and left lower extremities, respectively. Repeat radiographs demonstrated persistent metaphyseal changes and progression of her mechanical axis to a location medial to the medial compartment of the knees bilaterally. Alignment radiographs demonstrated mLDFA of 92.8° and 90.6°, MPTA of 80.8° and 76.8°, and MDTA of 94.5° and 96.7° to the right and left lower extremities, respectively. A skeletal dysplasia panel was performed at a commercial laboratory. This panel performed sequencing and deletion duplication analysis on 109 genes and identified a pathogenic variant in MMP13 [NM002427.3], c.619T > G (p.Trp207Gly) and a variant of uncertain significance (VUS) in MMP13, and c.539G > C (p.Gly180Ala).

case_report: A 33-year-old woman, pregnant for the first time, was referred to the obstetrics service at 34 weeks of gestation for an elective cesarean section due to the discovery of a large omphalocele with an exposed liver and bowel at 24 weeks of gestation in one of a set of dizygotic twins. The second twin appeared normal on ultrasound. The woman was also diagnosed with preeclampsia and gestational diabetes mellitus, and was treated with methyldopa (250 mg orally twice a day). There was no family history of congenital anomalies or genetic abnormalities, and no history of consanguinity. At birth, the affected male twin weighed 2,050 grams and had Apgar scores of 4 and 6 at the first and fifth minutes, respectively. The infant was cyanotic and hypotonic with low respiratory effort. Peripheral oxygen saturation was 90%, respiratory rate was 48 breaths per minute, heart rate was 158 bpm, and blood pressure was 64/32 mm Hg. Basic blood tests were normal. Physical examination revealed a large (10 × 8 cm) cephalic (epigastric) omphalocele with a significant portion of the liver visible. The omphalocele was covered with a saline-soaked gauze pad. Upon admission to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU), the baby was placed on nasal prong oxygen at 2 L/min and received antibiotics (ampicillin and amikacin). Daily dressing changes were performed.
test_results: A postnatal echocardiogram demonstrated an ostium secundum atrial septal defect (ASD), perimembranous ventricular septal defect (VSD), and moderate pulmonary stenosis. A plain chest X-ray showed an abnormal intrathoracic positioned stomach, which was confirmed with a plain X-ray of the upper intestinal tract with hydrosoluble contrast. Computerized tomography (CT) scan findings showed the absence of the sternum with the only small sternal ossification center and a close connection between the pericardial sac and the stomach wall.

case_report: The patient, a 20-year-old female, reported experiencing recurrent episodes of fainting during physical activity since she was 9 years old. She has had sensorineural hearing loss since she was 10 months old and has been using hearing aids since she was 14 months old. Blood tests revealed iron-deficiency anemia with a hemoglobin level of 92 g/L, with no apparent cause identified. Echocardiography showed no structural abnormalities. She was administered the highest tolerable dose of propranolol, which resulted in her remaining symptom-free, and her QTc interval was reduced to 496ms. Her parents showed no symptoms, had normal QTc intervals at rest (father 444ms and mother 426ms), and had normal hearing.
test_results: The 12-lead ECG showed a significantly prolonged QTc ranging from 545-576ms. A heterozygous missense variant was detected and a large deletion covering chr11:2868992–2,870,321 region in KCNQ1 was suspected in the proband by initial WES screening. The missense variant KCNQ1 c.1663 C > T was then validated by sanger sequencing and confirmed to be transmitted from the proband’s father. The suspected large deletion was further validated by MLPA, leading to the complete loss of exon 16 in KCNQ1. MLPA also detected the same large deletion in the proband’s mother.

case_report: A 37-year-old female reported experiencing severe pain in her feet during ambulation. At age 29, she began to perceive water droplets as burning sensations on her feet. Over time, her symptoms escalated to intense burning and lightning-like pain while walking, with sensations akin to having her feet scraped by sandpaper and then exposed to rubbing alcohol. The pain was so extreme that she contemplated drastic measures. Physical examination revealed significant pain in her feet, where even a light touch felt like a heavy object was dropped on her skin. She exhibited high arched feet. Sensory examination showed reduced sensation to pinprick and light touch up to the ankle, and diminished vibratory sense up to the knees. She was unable to walk on her heels, and her reflexes were absent. Muscle strength was intact throughout. Her score on the Charcot-Marie-Tooth examination was 10 out of 28.
test_results: Electromyography and nerve conduction studies showed evidence of chronic axonal neuropathy with normal nerve conduction velocities and absent sural and peroneal responses. Sequencing of 72 neuropathy genes showed a pathogenic variant, c.431T>A (p.Val144Asp) of the SPTLC1 gene.
diagnosis: Hereditary Sensory and Autonomic Neuropathies Type I
Orpha_name: Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type 1

case_report: A 20-month-old girl from a Taiwanese and Indonesian joint family presented with sudden drowsiness. Upon arrival, she exhibited failure to thrive (FTT), chilblain-like skin lesions, and dystonic posturing with peripheral spasticity. Brain computed tomography (CT) imaging showed encephalopathy with leukodystrophy. Serial laboratory tests indicated thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, positive anti-nuclear antibody (ANA), and high titers of anti-extractable nuclear antibodies (anti-ENA), including anti-Smith antibody (anti-Sm), anti-ribonucleoprotein antibody (anti-RNP), anti-Ro antibody, anti-La antibody, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), and anti-phospholipid antibody (APL). Initial treatment involved low-dose corticosteroids (~0.5 mg/kg/day) for worsening thrombocytopenia and hemolytic anemia, but this was tapered off within a month due to limited effectiveness and the development of aspiration pneumonia.
test_results: Her genetic analysis revealed homozygous TREX1 c.292_293 ins A; p.Cys99Met fs mutation. The reported allelic frequency (AF) in gnomAD is 0.007%. Sanger sequencing of the patient and her parental DNA confirmed that the TREX1 variants were inherited from both of her parents. Level of her plasma IFN-α was significantly higher than both of her parents and health control (53.56 v.s. 38.91, 37.17 and 35.74 pg/ml, respectively).

case_report: A 20-year-old healthy Thai man with myopic astigmatism attended our clinic for refractive surgery. He denied any past ophthalmic procedures. Best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/32 in the right eye (OD) with −7.25–3.75 × 15° and 20/40-1 in the left eye (OS) with −10.75–6.0 × 170°. Corneal tomography and corneal thickness were obtained with a rotating Scheimpflug camera system for anterior segment analysis. The result showed that the thickness of the thinnest point of the right and left cornea was 521 and 511 μm, respectively, and no ectatic changes were detected. Instead of undergoing laser vision correction, we recommended implantation of toric Implantable Collamer Lens (toric ICL) in both eyes owing to thin corneas. Two separate operations of ICL implantation were scheduled, starting with the right eye. Preoperatively, the slit-lamp examination was completely normal. His pupils were reactive to light, and the diameters of pupils were equal. His scotopic diameters of the right and left pupils measured with a corneal topography using PathFinder II Corneal Analysis Software were 7.0 and 6.4 mm, respectively. The anterior chamber depth (ACD) measured with scanning slit corneal topography was 3.32 mm in the right eye and 3.2 mm in the left eye. The white-to-white (WTW) distance measured with a caliper was 11.5 mm in both eyes. The preoperative intraocular pressures of the right and the left eyes were 17 and 16 mmHg, respectively. The patient did not require preoperative preventive iridotomies because of the presence of a hole at the center of the optic part of the fourth generation of ICL. The preoperative endothelial cell counts of the right and left eyes were 2728 and 2824 cells/mm2, respectively. The 12.6-mm ICLs were selected for both eyes. Before surgery, tropicamide 1% ophthalmic solution was applied until full pupillary dilatation was achieved. A viscoelastic agent was injected into the anterior chamber through a paracentesis port. The ICL was implanted in the right eye through a 2.75 mm temporal clear corneal incision. The viscoelastic agent was removed by manual irrigation with balance salt solution. One hour after uncomplicated surgery, the patient complained of mild ocular pain. The IOP of the right eye measured with an applanation tonometer elevated to 48 mmHg. The cornea was clear, and the vault of ICL was 1.5 times of central corneal thickness (CCT). A 250 mg acetazolamide tablet was given orally, and the IOP decreased to 30 mmHg within 1 hour. The patient was then prescribed 250 mg acetazolamide tablets every 6 hours before he was discharged. On the first postoperative day, IOP decreased to 15 mmHg. Visual acuity was 20/30-2 and improved to 20/25-2 with pinhole correction. Refraction showed +2.5−1.75 × 60°. Although the IOP was normal and the cornea was clear, we saw retention of viscoelastic agent in the anterior chamber, and the right pupil was 6 mm in diameter and slightly reactive to light. Although the ICL was in place with a vault 1.75 times of CCT, we decided to remove the viscoelastic agent by irrigation with balance salt solution. On the next day, the visual acuity was 20/25-1 and improved to 20/20-1 with pinhole correction. Refraction showed +1.37−2.25 × 31°, and the IOP was 13 mmHg. The right pupil still dilated 6 mm in diameter.
test_results: The right pupil remained 6 mm under slit-lamp examination and was slightly reactive to light.

case_report: A 20-year-old male presented with multiple carious and misaligned teeth. Physical examination showed downward slanting eyes, depressed zygomatic arches, sunken cheekbones, deformed external ears, coloboma of the lower eyelids with deficient eyelashes medially, a tongue-shaped extension of hair on the cheeks, and a retruded chin. There was no significant hearing loss or signs of mental retardation. Intraoral examination revealed crowding of the upper and lower anterior teeth, caries in teeth 11, 14, 15, 21, 25, 26, 27, 36, 46, and 47. Additional findings included a high arched palate, anterior open bite, and bifid uvula. Family history indicated that the patient's father had a similar condition but in a milder form.
test_results: Radiographic examination revealed underdeveloped condylar and coronoid processes, hypoplastic zygomatic arches, bilateral prominent antegonial notch on mandibular angle and short rami with resultant crowding of teeth. A noncontrast high-resolution (0.6) CT scan report of skull and face clearly demonstrated maxillofacial deformity with more prominent mandibular hypoplasia. The cranial vault and skull base appeared normal. It also revealed bilateral hypoplasia of external pinnae, marked hypoplasia/aplasia of bony external auditory canals, hypoplasia of middle ear cavity on either side with absence of ear ossicles. No paranasal sinus pathology was evident.

case_report: A three-year-old female with a history of mild receptive and expressive language delay presented to the emergency department with three days of altered mental status. Laboratory results showed elevated ammonia levels (207 mmol/L; normal <34) and a plasma amino acid panel indicated increased levels of glutamine, alanine, and methionine, along with decreased levels of citrulline, arginine, and ornithine. Elevated urine orotic acid was also noted. Cranial imaging, including MRI of the brain and brainstem, showed no abnormalities. She was discharged with sodium benzoate and a low protein diet. Subsequent gene sequencing identified a heterozygous variant c.205C>T p.Gln69* in the OTC gene. Her medication was adjusted to daily glycerol phenylbutyrate (Ravicti) and Citrulline supplementation, leading to normalized ammonia levels. One week later, the patient's father reported concerns about her vision, noting she was walking with her hands outstretched and unable to see items in front of her. Over the next two days, her vision continued to decline, with unresponsiveness to light, inability to identify people or objects, and worsening instability when walking. A pediatric ophthalmologist found no response to intense illumination with an indirect ophthalmoscope light, and slit-lamp and fundus exams were unremarkable. However, a severely depressed threat response was observed. Extraocular movements were intact, and both pupils were reactive to light, with the right reacting more sluggishly. Minimal anisocoria was noted (right > left).
test_results: MRI showed no abnormalities in the course, caliber, and signal intensity of the optic nerves. The remainder of the contents of the orbits including the lacrimal glands, vascular structures, and extraocular muscles were normal in appearance. MRI was positive for nonspecific abnormal enhancement involving the bilateral occipital lobes without pronounced associated FLAIR abnormality. MRI also demonstrated cortical enhancement involving the lingual and cuneus gyri bilaterally. There was no associated restricted diffusion or FLAIR signal abnormality in this region. However, there was mild prolongation involving the parietal gyri just superior to this region. There may have been minimal T2 prolongation involving the bilateral subcortical occipital white matter in the prior study. There was mild gyral restricted diffusion involving the left motor strip with corresponding mild T2 prolongation.
diagnosis: Transient Cortical Blindness in the context of Ornithine Transcarbamylase Deficiency

case_report: A 76-year-old Han Chinese woman, with no prior health issues, visited the clinic due to a firm, non-painful, bright red, dome-shaped nodule located on her right volar wrist.
