The nodule had grown quickly over the past 6 months. During the physical examination, a red-to-violet subcutaneous nodule with a diameter of 2 cm was observed.
test_results: A dermal proliferation was noticed with nests of small blue basaloid cells and a 'salt-and-pepper' chromatin pattern with scant cytoplasm and frequent mitotic nucleus. Cytokeratin-20 (CK20) immunohistochemical stain illustrates a typical paranuclear dot pattern. The tumor cells express synaptophysin (Syn) and epithelial membrane antigen (EMA). CD99, S-100, lymphocyte common antigen (LCA) and thyroid transcription factor 1 (TTF-1) are negative.

case_report: A 40-year-old Hispanic male presented with sudden onset of worsening horizontal double vision in the left eye, mild right-sided facial weakness, and a feeling of heaviness in the head for 48 hours. He experienced blurry vision in the left eye concurrent with the double vision. The patient also reported an unintentional weight loss of 30-40 pounds over the past six months. He noted a temporary worsening of vision upon waking, lasting up to 30 minutes before returning to the baseline level of impairment. No interventions improved his symptoms. He denied other symptoms such as fever, headaches, nausea, vomiting, neck pain or stiffness, night sweats, loss of vision, palpitations, shortness of breath, chest pain, abdominal pain, muscle weakness, sexual dysfunction, numbness, tingling, history of seizures, family history of neurological diseases, or previous episodes of vision changes. He also denied recent head trauma, contact with sick individuals, travel, and past surgeries or hospitalizations. On physical examination, he appeared well-groomed and in no distress, lying in bed with his left eye half-closed to see better with the right eye. Vital signs were stable: temperature 36.4 F, blood pressure 112/75 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, heart rate 58 beats per minute, SpO2 97% on room air, and mean arterial pressure 99 mmHg. Neurological examination revealed reduced visual acuity to 20/25 in the left eye, persistent binocular horizontal double vision in the left eye towards the lower right, and mild generalized right-sided facial weakness that resolved within 24 hours. The patient could see objects more clearly within two feet compared to those further away. Further examination showed unilateral left optic neuritis without other focal neurological deficits, including restricted ocular movement or internuclear ophthalmoplegia. A brain CT scan revealed focal hypoattenuation in the left frontal-parietal white matter with a faint peripherally enhancing rounded 1.8 cm lesion. Stroke was ruled out. The patient was hospitalized for further evaluation.
test_results: An MRI of the brain order revealed numerous T2-hyperintense white matter lesions within the subcortical periventricular deep white matter and corpus callosum with several lesions demonstrating Dawson's fingers. Also, a concentric 'bullseye' lesion was identified on T1 MRI in the left parietal lobe with surrounding edema vasogenic ring enhancement measuring 2.1 cm X 1.8 cm X 1.6 cm. On MR spectroscopy, a sequence of incomplete ring-enhancing lesions demonstrates lactate peak and increased choline non-specific. MRI of the cervical spine showed questionable high T2-signal lesions in the spinal cord at the level of C5-C6. These findings prompted conducting an oligoclonal bands panel, which revealed negative oligoclonal bands, elevated IgG of 5.30 mg/dL (vs. normal 0.0-0.7 mg/dL), and elevated protein of 66 mg/dL (vs. normal 15-60 mg/dL) in the CSF.

case_report: A 40-year-old Caucasian female with a history of hypertension presented to the outpatient clinic for evaluation of a persistent sensation of rocking and swaying that began a few hours after returning from a week-long ship cruise four months ago. The symptoms are more pronounced at bedtime when lying still and early in the morning upon awakening. The sensation is alleviated by activities involving motion, such as driving or being in a moving car. She reported no nausea, vomiting, headaches, double vision, vertigo, ringing in the ears, or hearing deficits. Her medical history includes hypertension managed with lisinopril, acid reflux, and a previous cholecystectomy. She denied tobacco use, alcohol consumption, and illicit drug use. Physical examination revealed no abnormalities, and there were no signs of depression. The patient did not experience relief from various motion sickness treatments, including meclizine, scopolamine, low-dose steroids, and Medrol.
test_results: Videonystagmography (VNG) and Vestibular Evoked Myogenic Potential (VEMP) were all normal. All her laboratory studies were negative. Radiological studies such as CT scan and MRI were negative.

case_report: A 46-year-old female reported experiencing a progressively worsening tingling sensation in her left posterior thigh and calf over the past two weeks. Neurological examination revealed motor strength of grade IV/V for left hip flexion and knee extension. The femoral nerve stretch test yielded a positive result for the left leg.
test_results: A magnetic resonance image (MRI) revealed a well-defined cystic lesion on the ventral side of the spinal cord at the T11 and T12 levels. The lesion was oval in shape and 36×15 mm in size. The spinal cord was compressed and displaced posteriorly and leftward. The lesion was hyperintense in T2-weighted images and hypointense in T1-weighted images. A histological study of the surgical specimens revealed that the cyst wall consisted of glial cells lined by a simple cuboidal to columnar epithelium. An immunohistochemical examination of the cells lining the cyst wall was positive for S-100 protein, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), and cytokeratin.

case_report: The patient is a 23-year-old male of Russian/Ukrainian origin, admitted to the State Budgetary Healthcare Institution—The Loginov Moscow Clinical Scientific Center—of Moscow Healthcare Department with complaints of significant fatigue, muscle weakness, weight loss, diarrhea (2–3 times daily, mushy consistency, small amount, no pathological impurities), and lower extremity edema. The patient was accompanied by his mother and did not establish personal or visual contact with the physician. His mother reported that these symptoms began two months ago following antibacterial therapy. The patient was born at 39 weeks of gestation from the first pregnancy, which was complicated by first trimester toxicosis. Birth weight and height were 3200 g and 53 cm, respectively. Early motor development was normal. At 2.5 years old, mental developmental regression was noted, with the absence of phrasal speech and only individual sounds and syllables being produced. Epileptic seizures began at 5 years old, occurring every 2–3 months, and were managed with valproic acid. Growth retardation was first observed at 12 years old. At 14 years old, the patient experienced severe stress and a significant decrease in appetite, leading to progressive weight loss. At 16 years old, he was hospitalized to investigate the endocrine nature of his weight loss and growth retardation (weight 26.5 kg, height 143.5 cm). X-ray examination indicated a bone age of 12.7 years. The discharge summary noted delayed physical and sexual development and cachexia (BMI 12.87 kg/m2). Brain MRI showed no structural abnormalities. At 22 years old, the patient was diagnosed with primary hypothyroidism and started on levothyroxine therapy. Adrenal and somatotropin insufficiency were excluded. Laboratory results showed an increase in alkaline phosphatase to 147 IU/L, moderate hypoglycemia to 3.7 mmol/L, and an increase in vitamin B12 to 2179 pg/mL. Various genetic tests were conducted throughout his life to identify the cause of his condition, excluding numerical and large chromosomal aberrations, abnormal methylation of the FMR1 gene promoter region, and aminoacidopathies and aminoaciduria. Six months prior to the current admission, the patient experienced a deterioration following antibiotic therapy for a urinary tract infection, with an increase in stool frequency to 5–6 times daily. Abdominal CT revealed a small bilateral hydrothorax, pronounced ascites, and increased intestinal gas. Upon admission, the patient was in severe condition, with short stature (143 cm), signs of hypogonadism, and cachexia (weight 31 kg). Consciousness was clear, but the patient was sluggish, retarded, and exhibited aggressive behavior, rejecting examination and medical interventions. No verbal contact was possible, and the patient did not follow commands. Cranial nerve examination showed normal fields of vision, full eyeball movement, convergent strabismus in the right eye, normal pupil reactions, and no nystagmus. Facial sensitivity and masticatory muscle strength were normal. Hearing and swallowing were unimpaired. Muscle tone was slightly reduced, with upper and lower extremity strength at 4/5 MRC points. Tendon reflexes were of medium agility, and no pathological symptoms were noted. Coordination tests were not performed, but purposeful movements were observed without tremor or discoordination. The patient was moved in a wheelchair by his mother. Routine EEG did not record typical epileptiform activity. Consultations with a gastroenterologist, nutritionist, and neurologist were conducted. CT revealed left-sided hydrothorax with compression atelectasis, gastrostasis, inflammatory changes in the colon walls, total lesion in the active stage, and pronounced ascites. Laboratory data showed decreased total protein (53 g/L), creatinine (39 μmol/L), and hemoglobin (8.2 g/dL), with increased presepsin (247 pg/mL). Clostridium Difficile was detected (Toxin A and B positive).
test_results: The results showed a heterozygous variant chr11: 687913G > A (c.662C > T, p.S221L) in exon 4 of the DEAF1 gene (NM_001293634.1). The identified variant is represented by a missense variant and leads to a substitution of serine for leucine at position 221 of the protein DEAF1. A segregation analysis was carried out for the identified variant c.662C > T of the DEAF1 gene in his mother, father, and sister. As a result of Sanger sequencing, the wild-type genotype (c.662C/C) was revealed in all of the relatives studied.

case_report: A 7-year-old boy from southwest China presented with blue cornea, photophobia, and poor vision since birth. At 36 days old, he underwent bilateral anti-glaucoma surgery, followed by long-term use of travoprost and brinzolamide eye drops. Despite this, intraocular pressure remained poorly controlled. The patient also had surgeries for an atrial septal defect and a sublingual cyst. Recently, his eye symptoms worsened, and his vision deteriorated significantly. Consequently, the boy and his family sought medical attention at the Affiliated Hospital of Southwest Medical University. A three-generational family pedigree is available.
test_results: Ophthalmic examination of the patient revealed similar pathological changes in both eyes. Uncorrectable poor vision (VOD 0.08, VOS 0.06) and horizontal tremors were observed. No hyperemia or edema was detected in the conjunctiva. The cornea was transparent but the sclera was pale blue. The diameter of the cornea was 14 mm and the center of the anterior chamber was deep. The aqueous humor was clear. The texture of the iris was unclear with partial depigmentation. The lamellar and incomplete disconnections of the root of the iris formed some iridocyridosis and slit-like iris holes (from 4 to 9 o’clock in the right eye, 3 to 9 o’clock in the left eye). The pupil displacement was worse in the right eye. The lens and vitreous of both eyes were slightly turbid. The optic disk was pale, with a cup to disk ratio of 0.9. The retina was ruddy with a wet-silk-like reflection, and the macula was not clear. IOP was 33 mmHg in the right eye and 20 mmHg in the left eye. Binocular B-ultrasound images showed prolongation of the axial axis (27.16 mm in the right eye, 26.56 mm in the left eye) associated with a long period of high IOP. Binocular ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) images showed deepening of the anterior chamber, anterior adhesion, and typical fracture of the iris. The optical coherence tomography (OCT) images of the binocular disk revealed a deepened binocular cup, which was enlarged due to the glaucoma damage.

case_report: Patient 6 is an 18-year-old female with significant intellectual disability, delayed motor skills, and marked muscle weakness. She began walking at the age of 4 years. Her first spoken words were at 5 years old, and she communicates using brief phrases. At 8 months old, she experienced febrile seizures and was treated with valproate for 9 years, which effectively managed the seizures.
test_results: The brain MRI showed low-lying spinal cord with adipose transformation of the Filum Terminale, colloid cyst of the third ventricle, microcephaly, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum and pons, and enlargement of the cerebrospinal fluid spaces. She showed a heterozygous missense in the frame variant on exon 2, which causes the deletion of only one amino acid (nm_001320:c.181_183del, p.Glu61del, p.Glu61del).
Orpha_name: Hereditary fibrosing poikiloderma-tendon contractures-myopathy-pulmonary fibrosis syndrome

case_report: A 16-year-old female was born at 38 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery, weighing 3.34 kg. She exhibited early onset mild developmental delay and experienced an atypical febrile seizure at 2.5 years, followed by absence seizures at 3.5 years. She achieved unsupported sitting at 8 months and began cruising at 12 months. Initial concerns arose due to speech delay, with first words spoken at 2 years. At 4 years old, physical examination revealed hypotonia and moderate delays in gross motor, fine motor, expressive language (approximately 100 words), and social skills. Laboratory results showed elevated plasma lactate levels at 4.4 mmol/L (reference range: 0.5–2.2 mmol/L) and CSF lactate levels at 3.3 mmol/L. Plasma amino acids analysis indicated increased alanine levels at 657 μmol/L (reference range: 148–475 μmol/L).
test_results: Respiratory chain analysis on muscle biopsy showed complex I and IV deficiency (complex I activity: 4.1 nmol/min/mg (ref range 17.9–56.7); complex IV activity: 0.76 nmol/min/mg (ref range 2.3–5.03)). Pathological analysis of the muscle demonstrated a greater number of type 1 than type 2 fibres with variation in fibre size diameter.

case_report: A 107-month-old Chinese girl, the second child in her family, presented with growth retardation and occasional presence of blood in stools. Her academic performance was below average. Physical examination showed growth retardation with a height of 125 cm (−2SD to −1SD) and a weight of 22 kg (−2SD to −1SD). The liver was palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin without abdominal distention. Vegetations were noted in the anus at the 6 o’clock position. Laboratory tests indicated mildly reduced fasting blood glucose (lowest 3.66 mmol/L). An adrenaline stimulation test did not show a positive effect on glycogen breakdown. Alpha-fetoprotein and liver transaminases were within normal limits. She experienced hematochezia, and an enteroscopy was performed, which yielded normal results.
test_results: Hepatic lobular structures were present, with hepatocytes arranged neatly in most of the areas. Small areas of hepatocytes were arranged in a nodular pattern. The masson staining had fibrosis observed around portal areas. PAS in hepatocytes without diastase treatment was strongly positive, while PAS obviously receded following diastase treatment. Masson staining showed more collagen fibroplasia in the distensible portal area. The Ishak score was 4 for inflammation and 3 for fibrosis. Both 2 cases inherited compound heterozygous mutations on the PYGL gene, including c.2467C>T (p.Q823X) on exon 20 (chr14:51372187) from father and c.2178-2A>C on exon 18 (chr14:51375675) from mother.

case_report: A 2-month-old male infant with diarrhea was referred to the infection department. He was born to a gravida 3, parity 3 mother at 37 weeks and 2 days via cesarean section due to a scarred uterus and intrauterine growth restriction, with a birth weight of 1800 g (<3%). The umbilical cord was short and thin, the placenta was small, and the amniotic fluid was clear. He was breastfed and had yellow-green mucus stools with 10–15 bowel movements per day. On admission, he weighed 2500 g, was unresponsive, had no positive cardiopulmonary signs, a flat abdomen, no pressure pain, liver and spleen not palpable under the ribs, and normal bowel sounds. Blood cytomegalovirus Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) results showed 2.254 × 103 copies/mL; TORCH, liver and kidney function, total lymphocyte analysis, and immunoglobulin quantification were normal. Cefotaxime sulbactam and meropenem were sequentially administered. The patient was transferred to the neonatal department at 2 months and 10 days old due to recurrent diarrhea and fever. At this time, his weight was 2830 g, his length was 49 cm, and his head circumference was 32 cm. The skin was pale and swollen, with little subcutaneous fat and thin yellow hair. Cytomegalovirus Immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibody was positive. Blood and urine cytomegalovirus PCR results were 9.801 × 104 and 5.516 × 105 copies/mL, respectively. Alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, and platelet results were 62 U/L, 136 U/L, and 46 × 109/L, respectively. Fecal calprotectin and Clostridium difficile were negative, and no abnormalities were found in the genetic metabolism screening for hematuria. Liver ultrasound showed non-uniform echogenic enhancement of liver parenchyma and visible lymph nodes in the hepatic hilum. Immunoglobulin quantification and total lymphocyte immunoassay showed no obvious abnormality. Hearing screening, eyeground check, cranial Computerized Tomography (CT), and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) tests showed no abnormalities. Gastroduodenoscopy and mucosal biopsy could not be performed due to the infant’s age and low weight. Intravenous nutritional support and powdered amino acid formula were administered. Meropenem was stopped after 3 days, and immunoglobulin (1.25 g) was infused for 3 days. Due to the presence of cytomegalovirus infection, growth retardation, liver function impairment, and diarrheal disease, the infant was given intravenous ganciclovir antiviral therapy (6 mg/kg q12h for 2 weeks, qd for 1 week), which was discontinued after 3 weeks. Post-treatment, blood cells and alanine aminotransferase normalized. Stool characteristics improved, but frequency remained high, with occasional blood. His parents and two siblings had no special appearance, no history of recurrent fever or diarrhea, and their body size and intelligence were normal. The mother’s breast milk cytomegalovirus PCR result was 2.254 × 103 copies/mL.
test_results: Whole-exome sequencing showed the presence of c.1708C > T (p.R570X; from the father) and c.3342-9T > G (from the mother) compound heterozygous variants in the TTC37 gene of the infant. c.1708C>T (p.R570X) was rated as a pathogenic variant (PVS1 + PM2_Supporting + PM3_Strong) and c.3342-9T>G was rated as a pathogenic variant (PM2_ Supporting+PM3 +PSV1 RNA).

case_report: Patient 2 is a 5-year-old boy, born at full term via cesarean section to healthy, unrelated parents. At 18 months old, he experienced a febrile seizure characterized by eye-rolling, cyanotic lips, and lapses in consciousness. These episodes occurred seven to eight times over the next three years. During this period, he also exhibited mild motor delays. He was prescribed sodium valproate in July 2018, but the medication was discontinued by his parents after two months without medical approval. Following the discontinuation, seizures continued to occur sporadically.
test_results: EEG demonstrated focal spike or polyspike and slow-wave burst on brain in sleep.

case_report: A 68-year-old man was admitted to the hospital after a fall. His medical history included sixteen years of limb ataxia and paresthesia. Over time, he experienced increasing numbness in his extremities and difficulty walking, particularly in low light, leading to falls. He also had episodes of double vision that resolved on their own. Five months prior, he experienced neurological decline that required mechanical ventilation and responded to plasmapheresis. The patient noted that citrus, dark chocolate, and significant stressors, such as surgery, worsened his neurological symptoms. He had been receiving treatment for monoclonal gammopathy of unknown significance for several years. Five days into his current hospital stay, he reported tingling in his lips, difficulty swallowing, and slurred speech. His ataxia worsened, and he developed limb weakness. Physical examination showed choreoathetoid movements in all four limbs and involuntary choreiform movements of the facial muscles and tongue. These facial movements were nonpurposeful, irregular, and arrhythmic, moving from one part of the face to another. The facial and buccolingual movements were present at rest and caused complete functional impairment. He could not protrude his tongue for more than ten seconds. Additional findings included partial bilateral ptosis, mild facial weakness, and complete ophthalmoplegia. His limbs were hypotonic and arreflexic with grade 3/5 muscle strength. He had severe proprioceptive loss at the wrists and ankles, vibration loss up to the elbows and knees, but preserved pinprick and temperature sensation. A week later, he developed acute respiratory distress requiring intubation.
test_results: Nerve conduction studies of the limbs showed absent bilateral median, ulnar, sural, and left radial sensory responses. F waves were delayed. Distal motor latencies were prolonged, with markedly reduced conduction velocities. The patient was strongly positive for antiGD1a, GD1b, GT1b, GQ1b, GD3, and suphatides.

case_report: The patient is a five-month-old male who presented with recurrent convulsions. He is the second child of Chinese parents, born at full-term via spontaneous delivery by a 31-year-old healthy mother. There is no family history of genetic disease, and the parents are nonconsanguineous. At three months old, the patient could steadily raise his head and responded well to lights and sounds. At five months, spasms were observed before sleep or upon waking, occurring in clusters with a frequency of 10–34 times per day. Following these episodes, the patient showed developmental regression, including unsteadiness in raising his head, slower reactions to human faces, and difficulty locating the source of sounds. Physical examination at five months showed normal weight (8 kg, reference range: 6.5–9.9 kg), height (67 cm, reference range: 62.3–72.6 cm), and head circumference (42 cm, reference range: 40.2–45.0 cm).
test_results: Electroencephalography (EEG) documented hypsarrhythmia. Neuropsychological development (Gesell Developmental Schedules) and the development quotient (DQ) assessment revealed development delay: total, 51.7; gross motor, 44.6; fine motor, 53.5; adaptability, 35.7; language ability, 71.4; and social ability, 53.5. At the age of eight months, brain MRI revealed a widened subdural space of the bilateral frontal and temporal lobes and a slightly expanded ventricular system.

case_report: A 2-year-old boy presented with redness and hazy vitreous in the right eye. He had undergone bilateral cataract surgeries a year prior. Surgical records and ultrasound indicated previous total cataracts and whitening of nuclei in the cortex of both eyes. One month ago, his mother reported redness and blurred vision in his right eye. Ophthalmic examination under anesthesia showed normal intraocular pressure in both eyes (11 mmHg OD and 12 mmHg OS). The right eye exhibited combined ciliary and conjunctival congestion, a generally clear cornea, absent lens, and opacified vitreous. Ultrasonography revealed multiple hyperechogenic dots in the anterior chamber and vitreous opacity, suggesting inflammation. Wild-field fundus photography showed a congested optic nerve head through the opacified vitreous. Fluorescein angiography displayed retinal capillaries and hyperfluorescent optic disc leakage at the venous phase. A single dose of combined vancomycin (1 mg/0.1 ml), ceftazidime (2.2 mg/0.1 ml), and dexamethasone (0.5 mg/0.1 ml) was injected into the vitreous cavity. The aqueous fluid was analyzed via metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), which can detect various microbes including bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites. The sequencing process involved DNA extraction, purification, library construction, and sequencing on a NextSeq 550 platform. High-quality data were generated after filtering, and human reads were removed. The remaining data were aligned to a microbial genome database, but the result was negative. Inflammatory factor analysis of the aqueous fluid showed elevated levels of VEGF (97.7 pg/ml), basic fibroblast growth factor (BFGF) (4.9 pg/ml), interleukin (IL)-6 (7524.5 pg/ml), vascular adhesion molecule (VCAM) (11066.9 pg/ml), and IL-8 (3023.1 pg/ml). A vitreous sample was collected via vitrectomy and cultured for bacteria and fungi, with T-SPOT and procalcitonin tests conducted to rule out tuberculosis and sepsis; all results were negative. The patient was generally well-developed with no systemic abnormalities. Family history was unremarkable. A systemic evaluation was performed, and urinalysis revealed proteinuria and microscopic hematuria. The patient was then transferred to the pediatric department for further evaluation.
test_results: Electron microscopic analysis of a renal biopsy showed mesangial proliferation and thickening of the glomerular basement membrane. A deletion in the X chromosome (Xq22.3: NC_000023.11:g.(107681122_107683515)del) encompassing exon 1 of COL4A5 and exons 1 and 2 of COL4A6 was found.

case_report: The patient is a 66-year-old Japanese male with a height of 161 cm, weight of 50 kg, and a body mass index of 19.3. He presented with persistent nasal discharge and fever, leading to a hospital visit where he was admitted for meningitis. Due to recurrent episodes, he was transferred to our facility. Upon admission, he was conscious, alert, and exhibited no neurological deficits except for spontaneous cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea and a stiff neck. His facial measurements showed a large distance between his bilateral eyeballs relative to his facial width, with inner and outer canthal distances of 35 mm and 9 mm, respectively, resulting in a canthal index of 38.5, indicative of ocular hypertelorism. Additionally, he had strabismus in his right eye, present since infancy. Funduscopy was not possible due to bilateral cataracts. No other anomalies were observed. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a cell count of 1167/μL (monocytes: 292, polycytes: 875), protein level of 413 mg/dL (normal range: 10 to 40), and glucose level of 45 mg/dL (normal range: 50 to 75), consistent with bacterial meningitis. A cerebrospinal fluid culture test was negative on admission.
test_results: An isodense mass protruding through a part of the ethmoid bone of his right anterior skull base was noted in the coronal section on computed tomography (CT), and a bone defect was present in the corresponding region on bone window CT. A round bone defect with a 10mm diameter was noted in the ethmoid bone of his right anterior skull base on three-dimensional CT, and an isodense mass protruding through the ethmoid bone and a partial cystic component were also observed on magnetic resonance imaging.

case_report: A male infant was delivered at 35 weeks of gestation to a 23-year-old first-time mother via caesarean section due to fetal distress and breech presentation. The mother was in good health throughout the pregnancy and did not take any medications known to cause birth defects, nor was she exposed to radiation. There was no family history of relatedness or birth defects. The baby cried immediately after birth, with Apgar scores of 9/10 and 10/10 at birth and at 1 minute, respectively. The newborn weighed 2.2 kg (between the 10th and 50th percentiles), measured 46 cm in length (50th percentile), and had an occipitofrontal circumference of 32 cm (50th percentile). At birth, the baby was observed to have a single umbilical artery, an imperforate anus, and a clubfoot with talipes equinovarus deformity in the left lower limb. No abnormalities of the craniofacial region were detected. A nasogastric tube was successfully inserted without difficulty. The systemic examination did not reveal any other abnormalities.
test_results: Plain X-ray abdomen showed dilation of the descending and rectosigmoid colon without the gas shadow in the distal rectum. Invertogram confirmed the intermediate type of anorectal malformations. The skeletal survey revealed hemi-vertebrae and block in the lumbar vertebrae, and also dislocation of the left knee joint. Ultrasonography of the abdomen showed left renal agenesis. The right kidney was normal. The karyotype in the peripheral blood revealed Y chromosomal abnormality, i.e. deletion in the long arm (Yq), while duplication in the short arm of the Y chromosome (Yp) [46, X,i (Yp): isochromosome Yp]. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis demonstrated the presence of two orange signals for SRY gene locus in the interphase and metaphase cells, indicating two copies of the SRY genes on the Y chromosome are present.

case_report: A 37-year-old male reported experiencing reduced vision in the right eye for a duration of 4 months. His overall health history was without notable issues. The best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) measured 20/60 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Upon ocular examination, the pupils were round and responded normally to light, with no relative afferent pupillary defect, and the visual axes were aligned. The anterior segment examination of both eyes showed no abnormalities. Examination of the posterior segment revealed dilated and twisted blood vessels with arteriovenous (AV) communication in both eyes, along with hard exudates in the macular area of the right eye. The AV malformations (AVMs) in the right eye were classified as grade II, while those in the left eye were classified as grade I. The peripheral regions of both eyes appeared normal.
test_results: Fluorescein fundus angiography (FFA) showed normal arm-to-retina time and rapid transit time in both the eyes, non-leaky retinal AV communications in the left eye, and late leakage in the perifoveal area in the right eye. Magnetic resonance neurogram finding included tortuous vertebral arteries in close approximation with left-side complex of cranial nerves VII and VIII and bilateral multiple tiny cavernous and capillary hemangiomas in supra- and infratentorial compartments with predominant involvement of brainstem and cerebellum. Optical coherence tomography examination showed hyporeflective lesions in the inner retinal layers of the perifoveal and peripapillary region suggestive of dilated vessels in both the eyes; hyperreflective lesions suggestive of hard exudates, intraretinal edema, and neurosensory detachment involving the fovea in the right eye; while the left eye showed no macular edema.

case_report: A 68-year-old Caucasian female with a history of splenectomy and systemic lupus erythematosus presented to the emergency department with severe generalized weakness for the past week. Nine days prior, the patient was diagnosed with COVID-19 at a local urgent care after being evaluated for a sore throat, loss of smell and taste, cough with green sputum production, and rhinorrhea. She received one dose of intramuscular steroids and was sent home with a course of azithromycin which she had completed. After this diagnosis, the patient became increasingly weak and developed aching suprapubic abdominal pain which she rated at a five out of 10 in severity. On presentation, she reported her cough had improved, and sore throat and rhinorrhea had resolved, but loss of smell and taste were still present. She also endorsed being jaundiced but denied fevers, chills, sweats, rashes, dyspnea, chest pain, lightheadedness, syncope, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or urinary symptoms. She has a past medical and surgical history that also includes prediabetes mellitus, gastroesophageal reflux disease, fibromyalgia, and appendectomy. The patient’s medications include calcium carbonate cholecalciferol 600 mg daily, clonazepam 0.5 mg every night, folic acid 1 mg every day, isosorbide mononitrate extended release 30 mg every morning, methocarbamol 750 mg every four hours as needed, and nitroglycerin 0.4 mg every five minutes as needed. The patient was not vaccinated against the COVID-19 virus and had not previously required specific treatment for her condition in the past four years. However, she did display evidence of low-grade hemolysis including an elevated reticulocyte count, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and indirect bilirubin with a hemoglobin between 10 and 11 gm/dL. Physical examination revealed a well-developed and nourished female with jaundice and mild tenderness in the suprapubic region on palpation. Mucous membranes were moist, pupils were equally round and reactive to light, extraocular movements were intact, and neck was supple with normal range of motion and no lymphadenopathy. On further examination, lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally, heart was regular rate and rhythm with no abnormal heart sounds, skin was warm and dry, abdominal sounds were present and normoactive, and abdomen was soft. The patient was alert and oriented to person, place, and time; cranial nerves II-XIII were intact; and she had a normal finger to nose exam and exhibited no lateralizing deficits. At the time of admission, chest x-ray showed no acute process.
test_results: Characteristic laboratory profile included anemia, elevated reticulocyte count with macrocytosis, low haptoglobin, elevated LDH, and direct antiglobulin test (DAT) results.

case_report: A 25-year-old female with a 15-year history of mitral stenosis and hypertension unresponsive to nicardipine, with no family or psychosocial history. During pregnancy, she experienced severe high blood pressure without proteinuria and was referred by a gynecologist. Clinical examination showed blood pressure of 190/95 mmHg in the upper limbs and 100/60 mmHg in the lower limbs, a left parasternal holosystolic murmur with posterior radiation, and weak pulses in both lower limbs. ECG indicated a coronary sinus rhythm with a heart rate of 75 beats per minute and left atrial hypertrophy.
test_results: The transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) showed an undilated left ventricle, hypertrophied (posterior wall at 13 mm), of good overall systolic and segmental function left ventricle fraction at 57%, sub-mitral membrane, with a single sub-papillary muscle, an attachment defect of the mitral valves responsible for a minimal leakage and a mitral stenosis under the tight valve (the mean gradient at 12 mmHg). Contrasting with the mitral surface, which was at 2 cm2 by planimetry 2.2 cm2 by pressure half time (PHT). Left-right shunt between the aorta and the right ventricular, outflow responsible for a maximum gradient at 164 mmHg and Vmax at 6.42 m/s suggesting a small perimembranous ventricular septal defect or aorto right ventricular fistula. Tricuspid aortic valve; left atrium dilated free of echo, Dilated coronary sinus, two non-motile rounded hyper-echogenic formations in the right atrium, measuring 21/16 mm. The second 10/16 mm suggest embryonic residue with a dilated coronary sinus. Undilated right ventricle with good systolic function, No sign of pulmonary hypertension. The suprasternal view showed the presence of coarctation of the aorta with V max at 4.43 m/s with a mean gradient at 79 mmHg and an extended speed reduction during diastole, without a patent ductus arteriosus. Trans-esophageal echocardiography (TOE) showed presence of a sub-mitral membrane, and a single papillary muscle, with attachment defect of the mitral valves responsible for a tight sub-valve mitral stenosis (mitral surface at 2 cm2 by planimetry and 2.2 cm2 by PHT, Gmoy at 12 mmHg) and minimal leakage. It showed also the presence of a left-right shunt between the aorta and the right ventricular flushing chamber responsible for a max Gradient at 164 mmHg and Vmax at 6.42 m/s: aorto RV suggested a small perimembranous ventricular septal defect. A complementary thoracic CT angiography showed an aspect of narrowed aortic arch with a diameter of 6 mm, measured 9 mm bellow the origin of the left subclavian artery, and the left superior vena cava (LSVC) was also found.

case_report: A nine-month-old female, born full-term via C-section with no medical history and a negative neonatal screen, was brought to the pediatric emergency department due to altered mental status and respiratory failure. The patient was found by her mother at home, cyanotic and unresponsive. Emergency medical services (EMS) were called, and the patient was noted to be in respiratory failure and cyanotic. Bag valve mask (BVM) oxygenation was initiated, and a notification was sent to the pediatric emergency department for a pediatric cardiac/pulmonary arrest. Upon arrival, the patient was cyanotic and ventilated with BVM by EMS personnel. The airway showed some secretions, and breath sounds were auscultated bilaterally. Pulses were immediately palpated. The patient was lethargic, moving all four extremities, and withdrawing from painful stimulation. Initial vital signs showed a blood pressure of 127/67 mmHg, heart rate of 142 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 6 breaths per minute, a saturation of 94% on 15 L non-rebreather mask briefly placed during the initial evaluation, and a temperature of 37°C. BVM was resumed once severe bradypnea was noted. The patient exhibited bilateral jerking movements, raising concern for seizure activity. Point-of-care glucose was 216 mg/dL. Lorazepam (1 mg) was administered via intravenous (IV) access, but the patient remained somnolent with bradypnea and bilateral jerking movements. Further physical examination revealed miotic pupils bilaterally. The mother reported that the patient had been playing near the clothing of the biological father, who is a known drug user. The child's weight was 8 kg at her last pediatrician visit. The patient was given 0.8 mg of intravenous naloxone. Anesthesia was prepared for possible intubation. After naloxone administration, the patient immediately sat up with a respiratory rate of 24 breaths per minute. The patient was suctioned, placed on her side, and protected her airway with preserved cough and gag reflexes. Laboratory studies, including a urine drug screen, were sent. An initial electrocardiogram (ECG) showed normal sinus rhythm at a rate of 134 beats per minute. A chest X-ray (CXR) showed no acute pathology. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the head showed no abnormalities. A standard urine drug screen returned positive for cocaine and opiates. Other significant laboratory studies included a white blood cell count of 15.59 × 103/mcL, with no elevated neutrophils and no bands. Urinalysis was unremarkable. Acetaminophen, salicylate, THC, and ethanol levels were negative. The patient was monitored in the emergency department, continued to have an intact airway, and maintained normal vitals. No further episodes of emesis occurred. Transport was arranged to a nearby hospital for pediatric intensive care. Child protective services were contacted. The patient was stable when EMS arrived for the transfer approximately 60 minutes later; however, during transport, bradypnea was noted again, and another dose of naloxone was administered. A total of two doses and 1.6 mg of naloxone were given.
test_results: Fentanyl, a send-out-of-hospital test performed by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, came back positive.

case_report: A 4-month-old female infant was brought in for treatment of bilateral radial ray deficiency. The infant had a history of complex cardiac issues, including multiple ventricular septal defects, failure of incorporation of the pulmonary veins, and tricuspid valve insufficiency, which necessitated cardiac surgery shortly after birth. Clinical examination and electrocardiogram showed no conduction abnormalities. The bilateral radial ray deficiencies were severe, characterized by bilateral short radii with radial deviation of the wrists and complete absence of both thumbs. Additionally, the infant exhibited micrognathia and clefting of the soft palate. An abdominal ultrasound showed no renal abnormalities. The parents were normal and unrelated, with no family history of congenital anomalies affecting the heart or limbs.
test_results: The infant was found to have a novel missense mutation of the TBX5 gene: c.215C>A, p.Thr72Lys (heterozygous). Both biological parents tested negative indicating that the mutation has arisen de novo.

case_report: A 36-year-old male, born of a non-consanguineous marriage, presented with swellings on the lateral side of both eyes for the past 6 months. The lesions were painless and varied in size with heat exposure. There was no history of oozing or bleeding from the lesions. Cutaneous examination revealed multiple papules and cystic nodules merging to form larger cysts bilaterally on the lateral periocular areas. The cysts were non-tender, firm, smooth-surfaced, and not attached to underlying structures. Beaded papules were observed on the upper and lower eyelid margins. The patient exhibited bird-like facies. Further examination showed generalized ichthyosis, sparing the cubital, popliteal fossae, and axillary folds. The palms and soles displayed diffuse keratoderma. Nails of the bilateral index and ring fingers were dystrophic, while other nails showed platynychia and koilonychia. All toenails were dystrophic. Oral examination revealed hypodontia, oligodontia, and a smooth red tongue with loss of filiform and fungiform papillae. A trans-illumination test of the cyst showed a diffuse red glow. Piercing a small cyst with a sharp needle resulted in the oozing of clear serous fluid. The patient reported having normal deciduous teeth, later replaced by small peg-like teeth. There was diffuse fine scaling over the scalp with sparse hair. Body hair and sweating were normal. Ophthalmologic and general systemic examinations did not reveal any abnormalities.
test_results: Skin biopsy from the periocular lesion revealed a cyst lined with smooth, thin epithelium, and few areas revealed foci of decapitation secretion. Histopathology of ichthyosis-like skin lesion revealed thinning of the epidermis and absence of granular layer consistent with ichthyosis, whereas palmar lesion revealed compact orthokeratosis and hyperkeratosis of the epidermis which was suggestive of palmoplantar keratoderma.

case_report: A 67-year-old non-smoker man with a history of non-obstructive coronary artery disease, hyperlipidemia, essential hypertension, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and subclinical hypothyroidism, and no family history of autoimmune disease, underwent permanent dual chamber pacemaker implantation for sinus node dysfunction. The patient was discharged home without any immediate procedural complications but returned to the hospital two weeks later with increasing shortness of breath and chest discomfort. Extensive testing was performed, including a left heart catheterization, which showed non-obstructive coronary artery disease. An imaging study revealed a small pericardial effusion without other abnormalities. He was discharged home on ibuprofen. A month later, he was admitted to our facility with worsening shortness of breath and a non-productive cough. He denied fever, chills, or chest pain at presentation. Physical examination showed decreased breath sounds in the right middle and lower lung fields.
test_results: A transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a small pericardial effusion without any other echocardiographic abnormalities. Chest radiograph and computerized tomography (CT) of the chest revealed a large right-sided pleural effusion and a small-moderate pericardial effusion. The pleural fluid analysis was consistent with an exudative effusion using Light’s criteria with a pleural fluid/serum protein ratio of 0.625, a pleural fluid/serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) ratio of 1.526, and a pleural fluid LDH > 2/3 upper limit of normal plasma levels. Pleural fluid pH was elevated to 8.6. Pleural fluid microbiology, including bacterial, fungal, and acid-fast bacilli cultures, were negative.

case_report: A 10-year-old boy was admitted to our hospital due to difficulties with walking and maintaining balance, trouble swallowing, mild delays in motor development, and mild learning challenges. His first hospital admission occurred at 9 months old following an unexplained episode of liver failure triggered by fever. Subsequently, he experienced several hospitalizations for fever of unknown origin, liver failure episodes, and gait disturbances during early childhood at another hospital. His parents reported a gradual increase in coordination problems and slurred speech since early childhood. Additionally, he received treatment for hypothyroidism at 1 year old in another hospital. The parents are consanguineous. On examination, the patient exhibited significant coordination issues with difficulty in performing bilateral finger-to-nose and heel-to-knee tests, trunk instability, slurred speech, and impaired vertical eye movements with increased reflexes and abnormal reflexes such as extensor plantar responses. There was no muscle atrophy or weakness observed. Eye examination revealed bilateral peripapillary atrophy. Other neurological and physical examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory tests including full blood count, serum chemistry, lipid profile, thyroid function tests, serum Vitamin E and B12 levels, alpha-fetoprotein, ceruloplasmin, serum lactate, ammonia, blood and urine amino acids, urine organic acids, and lysosomal enzyme analysis were all normal. Electrocardiogram and gene analysis for Friedreich ataxia were also normal. Brain MRI showed cerebellar atrophy. Nerve conduction studies indicated axonal neuropathy.
test_results: Novel homozygous mutation SCYL1:C. 1420C>T was identified in exon 11 of the SCYL1 gene. The mutation was also detected in both parents in heterozygous state.

case_report: A 14-month-old male child, the only child of his nonconsanguineous parents, presented with recurrent seizures starting at 6 months of age. The seizures were generalized tonic-clonic, accompanied by upward rolling of the eyes, lasting 1 to 2 minutes, and occurring four to five times daily. He was born at term via normal vaginal delivery with an average birth weight and had an uneventful perinatal period. Prior to the onset of seizures, his development was age-appropriate. Following the onset, there was a progressive regression in developmental milestones, including loss of neck control and social smile, and decreased responsiveness to surroundings. Additionally, he developed involuntary movements, primarily in the limbs, which occurred during wakefulness and subsided during sleep. There was no history of excessive vomiting, abnormal urine or body odor, loss of consciousness, fever, feeding difficulties, respiratory infections, or skin changes. On examination, the child was conscious with no facial dysmorphism. His vital signs were normal, and he was well-nourished. The Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) mark was present without any skin abnormalities. Developmental assessment indicated the absence of neck control and social smile, but the child could fixate, follow, and localize sound, though there was no babbling. Neurological examination revealed hypertonia in all four limbs, exaggerated deep tendon reflexes, and extensor plantar responses, along with dystonia in both upper and lower limbs. Other systemic examinations were unremarkable, and ophthalmological examination was normal. Psychological assessment using the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development (BSID-III) indicated cognitive abilities at approximately 2 months, gross motor skills at 3 months, and fine motor skills at 3 months. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 12 g/dL, a total leukocyte count of 10,000/cm2, and a platelet count of 450,000/cm2. Initial electroencephalograms (EEGs) showed focal discharges from the frontal and temporal areas with a seemingly normal background. However, the most recent EEG revealed bursts of epileptic discharges from the frontal and temporal regions with significant background abnormalities, including attenuation and slowing, particularly in the posterior regions. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) indicated cortical atrophy. Serum ammonia, serum lactate, urinary ketone bodies, random blood sugar (RBS), and arterial blood gas (ABG) levels were all normal. Tandem mass spectrometry (TMS), biotinidase enzyme activity, and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GCMS) results were within normal limits.
test_results: Genetic study with clinical exome sequencing revealed there was mutation on SCN8A(+) at exon 27, variant c.5615G>A (p.Arg1872Gin), zygosity heterozygous.

case_report: A 73-year-old male was referred to our department by Helios Clinic München Perlach. Upon initial presentation, the patient exhibited painless jaundice, diarrhea, and a weight loss of 5% over a period of 4 weeks, with an initial body weight of 86 kg. There were no signs of fever or abdominal pain. The patient had no history of alcohol abuse or previous liver or pancreatic diseases.
test_results: Computed tomography revealed a diffusely enlarged pancreas (“sausage-like” with loss of lobulation), hypoattenuating, with adjacent edema and a cystic lesion (60 × 80 mm) extending from the pancreatic tail. Routine laboratory analysis showed increased liver function test results (alkaline phosphatase 781 U/L; aspartate aminotransferase 320 U/L; alanine aminotransferase 698 U/L; gamma glutamyl transferase 1,441 U/L; total bilirubin 6.02 mg/dL) and an elevated serum IgG4 concentration (1,190 mg/dL; normal range 3–200).

case_report: A 23-year-old right-handed man with behavioral issues was admitted to our hospital. He was born at term via normal spontaneous delivery with a birth weight of 3200 g. He was healthy and performed well academically until the age of 19, when he began experiencing difficulty concentrating in college. After taking a leave of absence, his behavior worsened, including incidents of shoplifting and stealing a purse in public. At 21 years old, he experienced multiple episodes of unconsciousness and developed myoclonic jerks during sleep. By the age of 22, he exhibited agraphia and apraxia, such as an inability to cut paper with scissors. His parents were not related by blood, and there was no family history of neurological disorders. On physical examination, he was observed to be restless, impulsive, and easily distracted, with continuous action myoclonus in both hands. Neurological examination revealed normal findings for cranial nerves, muscle strength, deep tendon reflexes, sensation, cerebellar function, and extrapyramidal signs. He scored 46 out of 100 on the Addenbrooke’s Cognitive Examination version III (ACE-III), with subscores of 10/18 for attention and orientation, 12/26 for memory, 2/14 for fluency, 17/26 for language, and 5/16 for visuospatial skills. Electroencephalogram showed generalized intermittent 3–5-Hz spike-and-slow-wave complexes. Brain MRI indicated mild diffuse brain atrophy. N-isopropyl-p-(123I)-iodoamphetamine (IMP) single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) revealed widespread hypoperfusion in the cerebral cortices.
test_results: The whole-exome sequencing and filtering analysis of the patient and his parents identified de novo H338R mutation in the SERPINI1.
diagnosis: familial encephalopathy with neuroserpin inclusion bodies
Orpha_name: familial encephalopathy with neuroserpin inclusion bodies

case_report: A 6-year-old Chinese girl visited the clinic with complaints of night blindness and progressively worsening vision in both eyes over the past month. There was no history of consanguineous marriage or family history of eye disorders. Her best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was measured at 20/63 in the right eye and 20/100 in the left eye, with a refractive error of -7.50 diopters (D)/-2.50D×175° in the right eye and -5.00D/-2.75D×180° in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment revealed no abnormalities in either eye. Upon dilated fundus examination, multiple sharply demarcated, scallop-shaped areas of chorioretinal atrophy were observed bilaterally in the midperipheral and peripheral regions of the fundus. Fundus autofluorescence imaging showed hypo-autofluorescence corresponding to the areas of chorioretinal atrophy. Spectral domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) indicated increased central macular thickness (CMT) in both eyes, with measurements of 645 µm in the right eye and 648 µm in the left eye, along with multiple intraretinal cystic spaces. Fluorescein angiography (FA) in the late phase showed no leakage or staining in the macular area.
test_results: The plasma ornithine level was 1180µmol/L (normal range: 25–115µmol/L). Whole-exome sequencing in family trios identified two novel mutations in the OAT: (NM_000274.3): c.251 C > T p. (Ser84Phe) and c.648 + 2T > G. Heterozygosity of OAT: c.251 C > T p. (Ser84Phe) was confirmed in the patient’s father and OAT: c.648 + 2T > G was found in the patient’s mother.
Orpha_name: Gyrate atrophy of choroid and retina

case_report: A 42-year-old male patient presented with darkened patches on the gums compared to the adjacent pink gums. The increased pigmentation was asymptomatic and the patient's concern was aesthetic. He first noticed small isolated patches of hyperpigmentation on the buccal mucosa of the mandibular anterior region two years ago. These patches rapidly spread to form larger areas involving a significant portion of the mandibular arch, prompting the patient to seek dental advice due to their unsightly appearance. An isolated patch of pigmentation also appeared in the right mandibular posterior region. The lesion was not associated with pain or discomfort. The patient reported no history of smoking, smokeless tobacco use, or alcohol intake, and there was no familial history of carcinomas. Clinical examination revealed hyperpigmented lesions on the mandibular gingiva, involving the marginal, interdental, and attached gingiva from the distal aspect of tooth 32 to the distal aspect of tooth 44, including the lingual aspect of the attached gingiva in the same region. An isolated patch of pigmentation was also observed on the attached gingiva associated with a missing tooth 46. The lesion was blackish-blue with irregular raised borders, clearly demarcated from the adjacent normal gingiva, and confined within the limits of the attached gingiva. The surface appeared wrinkled, proliferative, and granular, with no evidence of bleeding. On palpation, the lesion was fibrotic and non-tender. The regional lymph nodes were not palpable. Routine blood investigations were normal, and radiographs did not reveal any significant abnormalities.
test_results: The report revealed sheets of melanin containing pleomorphic cells in the connective tissue.

case_report: A 21-year-old male student from Ivory Coast presented on February 4, 2015, with chronic headaches and excessive sleepiness. These issues began in 2009 when he was 15 years old. His medical history includes chickenpox during childhood, but no prenatal pathologies or developmental disorders were noted. He does not consume alcohol. The episodes started after his first term school exams and occurred 3 to 4 times a year. During these episodes, he would sleep for at least 24 hours over a span of 2 to 10 days, after which he would return to his usual state of alertness. During these periods of excessive sleepiness, he experienced nightmares involving cemeteries or funeral wakes, visual hallucinations related to death, cognitive difficulties, trouble concentrating while reading, and challenges in multitasking. He reported a sense of unreality, feeling disconnected from his body, and a sensation of being in a dream. Behavioral changes included increased appetite, heightened libido, and sex-oriented thoughts. Each episode lasted 9 to 10 days, followed by a return to normal alertness. Initially, the intervals between episodes were 5 to 6 months for the first four years, but they shortened to an average of four months over the past two years. Occasionally, he experienced brief periods of insomnia between episodes. Physical examination results were normal.
test_results: The electroencephalogram (EEG) has objectified potential acute in bifrontal puffs. The Cranioencephalic CT scan was normal.

case_report: A 47-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a year-long history of a rash resembling urticaria, lasting several days on her forearms, abdomen, and thighs, without signs of skin aging. The rash recurred monthly and was associated with increasing skin pigmentation, tenderness, itching, and pain similar to myalgia. A skin sample from the swollen red area on her right forearm showed widespread inflammatory cell infiltration, mainly neutrophils, throughout the dermis. There was also nuclear debris and slight leakage of red blood cells around the dermal blood vessels. Elastica-Masson staining did not show any abnormalities in elastic fibers. The skin symptoms improved with oral treatment using olopatadine, doxycycline, and cimetidine. Although the rash reappeared monthly, the treatment effectively reduced tenderness, itching, and myalgia-like pain. After three years, the patient developed a dry cough and respiratory distress during physical activity, and severe emphysema and IgA-λ MGUS were diagnosed following a detailed examination. Due to the rapid progression of emphysema, lung transplantation was considered. The patient was referred back to our department to evaluate the relationship between her emphysema and skin condition. Compared to her initial visit, her skin now showed sagging and wrinkles.
test_results: A skin biopsy from the left forearm showed neutrophil infiltration very similar to the initial biopsy, although the elastic fibres had disappeared entirely. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed diffuse IgG and IgA deposits in the dermis.

case_report: A 31-year-old woman came to the clinic with concerns about left breast deformity following a total mastectomy performed three years prior due to breast cancer. She had a delayed breast reconstruction using a pedicled latissimus dorsi flap with a tissue expander (Natrelle 133 FV, Allergan, Dublin, Ireland; 300 cc). Nine months later, the tissue expander was replaced with a silicone implant (BellaGel anatomical textured, Hansbiomed Inc., Seoul, Korea; moderate height, medium projection; 260 cc), and breast augmentation surgery (BellaGel round micro-textured; medium projection; 200 cc) was performed on the opposite breast. The patient was discharged without complications on postoperative day (POD) 4. The negative-pressure drainage was removed on POD 16 during an outpatient follow-up. Later that day, she was admitted to the emergency department with a high fever (up to 40.3°C) but showed no local infection signs such as redness or tenderness. She was diagnosed with an upper respiratory infection and discharged. On POD 18, she was urgently readmitted with a high fever (40.3°C) and low blood pressure (systolic blood pressure [SBP], 83 mmHg; diastolic blood pressure [DBP], 46 mmHg). She also experienced nausea, vomiting, chills, and myalgia. Diffuse macular erythroderma was noted on her trunk, bilateral arms, and bilateral legs. Initial lab results showed a white blood cell (WBC) count of 6.57×10^3/μL, a C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 29.42 mg/dL, elevated aspartate transaminase and alanine transaminase levels (123 IU/L and 92 IU/L), and a low platelet count (77×10^3/μL). Examination of the surgical sites revealed no significant inflammatory signs, except for slight swelling. Contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography indicated a mild complex fluid collection in her left breast. Prophylactic antibiotic treatment (intravenous [IV] vancomycin, 1 g twice a day) was initiated immediately. The following day, under general anesthesia, wound exploration with thorough irrigation using an antibiotic solution and implant change procedures in both breasts were performed. Intraoperative findings showed minimal clear fluid collection without infectious turbid discharge or necrotic tissue.
test_results: On POD 5, tissue culture from the left breast wound grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).

case_report: A 74-year-old male presented with general malaise, fatigue, and an unintentional weight loss of 40 pounds over six months. His medical history includes uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus and end-stage renal disease, for which he received a deceased donor renal transplant four years ago and is currently on immunosuppressive therapy. He also had a history of hepatitis C infection (genotype 1b) eight years ago and achieved sustained virologic response with Ledipasvir/Sofosbuvir therapy. A screening colonoscopy three years ago was normal. Physical examination revealed an ill-appearing man with temporal wasting, but no skin lesions or peripheral lymphadenopathy. Abdominal, lung, and chest examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin at 12 g/dL (Reference range: 12.6–17.4 g/dL), serum bilirubin at 0.4 mg/dL (Reference range: 0.2–1.3 mg/dL), and alkaline phosphatase at 250 U/L (Reference range: 38–126 U/L). Serum LDH and uric acid were within normal limits. CT abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast revealed multiple new ill-defined, irregular hypodense masses in the left hepatic lobe with mild rim enhancement, enlarged periportal lymph nodes, and multiple bulky celiac axis nodes. MRI of the abdomen showed an enlarged liver with a mildly nodular contour, multiple ill-defined T2 slightly hyperintense and T1 hypointense lesions with mild peripheral enhancement and central necrosis in the left and medial right hepatic lobes, and necrotic lymphadenopathy in the left supra celiac, hepatic portal, and periportal regions. An enhancing nodular mass was noted at the gastric cardia/gastroesophageal junction. CEA was within normal limits (2.3 ng/mL), while AFP and CA 19–9 were elevated to 38 ng/mL and 279 U/mL, respectively. Hepatitis C viral load was undetectable, and there was no serologic evidence of acute or chronic hepatitis B infection. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed a grossly normal esophagus, a non-malignant appearing nodule in the gastric antrum, and no masses at the gastroesophageal junction or gastric cardia as suggested by MRI. Non-bleeding duodenal ulcers without stigmata of bleeding were observed. Biopsies from the gastric nodule and duodenal ulcers were negative for malignancy.
test_results: CT-guided biopsy of the left lobe liver mass showed a poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma that stained positive for CK7 and CK20 and negative for Hepatocyte Paraffin-1 (HepPar-1). The surrounding liver parenchyma showed mild nonspecific chronic hepatitis with minimal fibrosis and absence of steatosis.

case_report: A 58-year-old female presented with destructive polyarthritis affecting the small joints of the hands, wrists, elbows, and knees for the past one and a half years. Over the last 6 months, she developed multiple papulonodules on the forearm, elbow, face, ears, and knees. These papulonodules were mildly erythematous, dome-shaped, glistening, translucent, non-pruritic, and non-tender, with sizes ranging from small papules to large pea-sized nodules. The lesions showed a tendency to group together. Numerous small papules were observed along the nail folds, forming a pattern known as the 'coral bead sign.' The surrounding skin appeared normal, and the oral mucosa was unaffected. Laboratory evaluations included a complete hemogram, ESR, lipid profile, chest X-ray, abdominal ultrasound, urinalysis, stool for occult blood, ANA, and hand X-ray. Results indicated mild normocytic normochromic anemia (Hb-9.2 g/dl), elevated ESR (55mm in the 1st hour), and increased triglyceride levels (175 mg/dl). The abdominal ultrasound revealed mild splenomegaly, the chest X-ray was normal, but the hand X-ray showed erosion in the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints.
test_results: The histopathological examination revealed well defined dermal infiltrate consisting of multinucleated giant cells and macrophages having abundant eosinophilic finely granular cytoplasm with ground glass appearance.

case_report: A 75-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia presented with 7 years of gait difficulties, 2 years of cognitive changes, and urinary incontinence. One year prior to her visit, she had a ventricular shunt placed for normal pressure hydrocephalus, which provided only slight temporary symptom relief. Upon examination, she exhibited a smooth saccadic break, mild postural and intention tremor in both upper extremities, and a magnetic gait. Her muscle tone was normal. Family members noted delusions and impairments in short-term memory, executive functions, and calculations. There was no reported family history of brain calcifications or psychiatric disorders. Previous CT head scans revealed extensive mineralization in both cerebellar hila, basal ganglia, thalamic pulvinar, and deep white matter. Serum calcium and phosphorus levels were within normal ranges.
test_results: Genetic testing confirmed a pathogenic variant of the SLC20A2 gene with the variant allele c.852del (p.lle285Sers*33). This specific mutation results in premature termination of the codon, resulting in a truncated or absent protein.

case_report: A 24-year-old male professional soccer player presented with right hypochondrium pain that had been developing over approximately three weeks. The pain began after he received a direct impact to his chest from an opponent's knee during a football match, following a jump. He experienced severe, throbbing, and shooting pain in the left lower rib cage, rated 8/10 on the visual analog scale for pain, which worsened in dorsal and lateral decubitus positions but improved when standing or seated. Two days later, he consulted the team physiotherapist and underwent conservative treatment for two weeks without improvement. During the initial evaluation, the player reported difficulty sleeping due to severe pain in the right lower rib cage near the costal-cartilage junction. The pain was reproducible with rib pressure, palpation of the costal rim of the 9th and 10th ribs, the Valsalva maneuver, and sit-up tests. No deformity or skin changes were noted. Hemodynamic parameters were normal with a blood pressure of 110/60 mm Hg and a pulse rate of 58 beats per minute. The hooking maneuver was positive, and traction on the ribs caused pain when they were pushed outward.
test_results: A diagnostic chest x-ray showed no signs of rib fracture.
Orpha_name: Microphthalmia with brain and digit anomalies

case_report: A 6-year-old boy, previously in good health, presented with fever, oral ulcers, and a maculopapular rash on the trunk and extremities, including the palms and soles, for 2 days. He had been tested for COVID-19 due to contact with a positive family member 2 weeks prior and had mild symptoms managed at home. He had a history of Ibuprofen use 2 weeks before presentation. Upon hospital admission for supportive care, he exhibited a low-grade fever and stable hemodynamic status. The skin rash progressed to violaceous targetoid lesions on the trunk and extremities with genital erosion, and the Nickolsky sign was positive. Additionally, he had mild purulent conjunctivitis, crusted lip lesions, and de-epithelization of the oral mucosa.
test_results: A 4-mm punch skin biopsy from target necrotic detached skin showed sloughed necrotic epidermis. Necrotic keratinocytes were abundant, the superficial dermis showed marked perivascular and interstitial lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrates.

case_report: The patient is a 6-year-old Caucasian female with a history of neurodevelopmental disorder, hypotonia, and minor facial anomalies. Family history is negative for intellectual disability or genetic conditions. She was born to non-consanguineous parents at 39 weeks of gestation following a pregnancy complicated by preeclampsia in the seventh month, leading to a caesarian section. Birth measurements were within normal ranges: weight 3460 g (75th percentile), length 50 cm (50–75th percentile), and head circumference 35 cm (75–90th percentile). Apgar scores were 8 at 1 minute and 9 at 5 minutes. At 6 months, clinical evaluation noted hypotonia and delayed psychomotor development. Auditory, visual, somatosensory, and motor evoked potentials were normal. A brain MRI at 9 months showed minimal gliotic changes in the bilateral occipital periventricular white matter. A follow-up MRI a year later showed improvement in the posterior periventricular signal, a low-signal stria in the supratrigonal area likely from a vascular element, and modest ectasia of the regional perivascular spaces. Neurological and neuropsychiatric evaluations during childhood indicated psychomotor delay and general developmental disorder with absence of language, social isolation, inconsistent visual engagement, autistic traits, poor participation, repetitive behaviors, unusual interest in objects, symptoms resembling attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, mild macrocrania, motor stereotypies, and broad-based walking. Cardiac evaluations at 2 and 6 years revealed a patent foramen ovale, and an abdominal ultrasound was normal. Neuropsychiatric evaluation at 5 years confirmed childhood autism and developmental delay. Peripheral blood karyotype analysis showed 46, XX (female, normal). High resolution array-CGH identified a very small 2p16.3 microdeletion (87 kb) with maternal transmission, involving parts of the NRXN1 gene, but without a clear pathogenetic role due to its size, transmission pattern, and presence in healthy family members. No mutations were found in the NRXN1 and ZEB2 genes. Methylation and MLPA tests of chromosome 15q11–13 were normal.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing of the patient and her parents was performed on genomic DNA obtained from peripheral blood leucocytes, identifying the de novo c.9244C > T; p.Pro3082Ser missense variant. According to the Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion score (CADD score 22) and according to the American College of Medical Genetics score (PS2, PM2, PP3) this variant can be considered as likely pathogenic. CADD values > 20 indicate that a variant is more likely to have deleterious effects.

case_report: A 33-year-old woman presented to the Neurology Clinic at Vali-e-Asr Hospital in Arak, Iran, with symptoms including headache, weakness, reduced appetite, fever, sweating, and an increased frequency of seizures occurring 3-4 times daily. She also experienced night sweats, fever, muscle pain, and had a history of living in a rural area with exposure to farm animals. Her medical history included consultations for infectious diseases and assessments for brucellosis and hepatitis C and B. She had a 10-year history of complex partial seizures, which had become uncontrolled a month prior to her hospital visit. Despite frequent medical consultations and increased medication doses, her condition did not improve. Before admission, she was taking 50 mg lamotrigine and 400 mg carbamazepine three times daily, along with 1 mg folic acid once daily. Upon examination, her body temperature was 37.8 °C, and she was fully alert with no neck stiffness. Routine laboratory tests showed elevated liver enzymes and a normal complete blood count.
test_results: A brain CT scan revealed hyper-dense areas in the left posterior parietal and temporal lobe together with peripheral hypo-density, hemorrhagic focus, and edema around it. An MRI indicated a suspicious lesion similar to those in hemorrhagic infarction or hematoma in the left temporal lobe and an abnormal signal in the left transverse sinus. The results of Wright's agglutination test (1/640), Coombs-Wright test (1/640), and 2ME (1/320) were positive and confirmed brucellosis.
diagnosis: Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis  complicating Neurobrucellosis

case_report: A 54-year-old Caucasian male was admitted following a rib fracture due to an accident. During his hospital stay, he developed sepsis secondary to pneumonia and exhibited elevated creatinine levels, necessitating hemodialysis. His medical history included coronary artery disease, aortic stenosis, and hypertension, with no significant surgical or family history. Physical examination revealed tachycardia, tenderness in the right lower chest, decreased breath sounds in the right lung, and skin pallor. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory findings indicated anemia with a hemoglobin level of 6.8 g/dL, haptoglobin less than 8 g/dL, and lactate dehydrogenase greater than 700 IU/L. The Coombs test was negative, and the peripheral smear showed schistocytes. Platelet counts ranged from 70,000 to 120,000/mL, and creatinine levels were elevated between 3 and 6.1 mg/dL, leading to intermittent dialysis due to acute renal failure. Additional tests showed negative results for blood cultures, Shiga toxin, methylmalonic acid levels, B12, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and light chain assays. ADAMTS13 levels were normal. Renal biopsy indicated proliferative glomerulonephritis with C3 deposits only, without IgG, and diffuse endocapillary hypercellularity with thrombi. Complement levels revealed low C3 at 86 mg/dL and normal C4 at 19 g/dL. Immunofixation was positive for C3 2± and negative for IgA, IgG, and IgM. Tests for antistreptolysin O, anti-nuclear antibody, and anti-glomerular basement membrane were negative.
test_results: Genetic studies showed heterozygous missense variant mutation in complement factor B (CFB), which increased the formation of C3 convertase.
diagnosis: Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome  due to complement factor B mutation
Orpha_name: Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome with complement gene abnormality

case_report: An 18-year-old male presented with no signs of pubertal development. The patient reported an absence of smell perception, with no issues related to hearing or involuntary movements. Family history included probable hypogonadism in two paternal uncles and one cousin. Physical examination revealed a height of 163 cm, an arm span of 172 cm, and an upper to lower segment ratio of 0.75, indicating eunuchoid body proportions. There was an absence of facial and body hair, a stretched penile length of 8 cm, and infantile testes measuring 1 ml. Neurological examination results were normal. Laboratory findings showed low testosterone levels at 115 ng/dl (normal range: 270–1030 ng/dl), low FSH levels at 0.85 mIU/ml (normal range: 0.7–11.1 mIU/ml), and low LH levels at 0.74 mIU/ml (normal range: 0.8–7.6 mIU/ml).
test_results: MRI of the brain displayed a hypoplastic olfactory bulb.

case_report: A 12-year-old girl with no prior health issues was admitted due to a sudden onset of headache, vomiting, tremors, difficulty speaking, disorientation in time and space, weakness in the lower limbs, and slightly blurred vision. Her parents reported mood changes, including alternating periods of depression and irritability, occurring a few weeks prior. During the clinical examination, she exhibited difficulty speaking, trouble maintaining an upright position with a slightly positive Romberg test, but no signs of meningeal irritation or focal neurological deficits. Her pupils were symmetrical and reacted normally to light. She experienced uncontrolled emotional outbursts, such as purposeless laughing. Initial blood tests, including complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, serum ammonia, and blood gas analysis, were all within normal limits. Cranial computed tomography (CT) showed no abnormalities. Tests for autoimmune, toxic, and infectious markers, as well as cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies for bacterial and viral infections, were negative.
test_results: Electroencephalography (EEG) showed bilateral diffuse slow wave activity, without epileptiform activity. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed hyperintense spots in white matter of frontal-parietal lobe, bilateral, more evident on the right in FLAIR sequence without enhancement of the focal lesions on T1 post contrast sequence. A mild increase of protein levels in CSF was present. High levels of antithyriod antibodies were noted, with anti-thyroglobulin (TG-Ab) 176.90 UI/mL (normal: 0-100 IU/ml) and anti-thyroid-peroxidase (TPO-Ab) 11.853.00 UI/mL (normal: 0-100 U/ml). Thyroid ultrasound: thyroid gland with subverted ecostructure with presence of hyperechogenic shoots which determine pseudo-nodular character in both lobes (marked vascularization is appreciated at color-doppler as for inflammatory alterations). CSF antithyroid antibodies were positive (TPO-Ab 28.00 IU/ml, TG-Ab 15 IU/ml).
Orpha_name: Steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis

case_report: A 40-year-old man was referred from the Department of Thoracic Surgery with visual loss noticed in the recovery room after undergoing video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS). The procedure involved a posterior segmentectomy of the right upper lobe and left lower lobe for lung masses under general anesthesia. The surgery was uneventful, lasting approximately 2 hours, with no significant fluctuations in blood pressure or notable blood loss. Histologic examination revealed malignant lymphoma and reactive hyperplasia in the surrounding lymph nodes. Post-surgery, his blood pressure, hemoglobin, glucose, and cholesterol levels were all within normal ranges. Ophthalmologic evaluation immediately after surgery showed visual acuities of hand motion in both eyes (OU). Pupils were reactive without any relative afferent pupillary defect, and eye motility was full OU. Slit lamp examination of the eyelid, anterior chamber, and fundus examination were normal.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) including diffusion weighted imaging (DWI) and angiography showed no abnormal findings.

case_report: A 30-year-old woman with no known drug allergies, toxic habits, or relevant family history experienced menarche at 12 years old and had a history of oral contraceptive use. Her medical history includes treatment for IIA diffuse large B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma at age 20 with poly-chemotherapy R-MegaCHOP and thoracic radiotherapy, resulting in complete remission without residual clinical toxicities. At age 27, she was treated for a CIN III HPV16+ cervical lesion with a simple trachelectomy. She has no personal history of thyroid disease. The patient presented with symptoms of hyperemesis, abdominal discomfort, and metrorrhagia. One month later, she consulted her general practitioner and was found to have a hard hypogastric mass measuring 19 × 20 × 18 cm, with a uterus size comparable to a 22-week pregnancy.
