No fetal heartbeat was detected. Laboratory results showed a negative urine β-hCG test, a serum β-hCG level of 2,662,000 mIU/mL, and a hemoglobin level of 11 ng/dL. Thyroid hormone profile analysis revealed undetectable TSH and a free T4 level of 1.85 ng/dL (normal range: 0.8–1.8 ng/dL). The patient was admitted for further monitoring and study. Imaging upon admission indicated possible bilateral pulmonary nodules without other alterations.
test_results: A uterine curettage was performed to obtain pathological characterization and reduce tumor volume. A radiography and CT scan were performed, showing bilateral reticular interstitial central bibasilar pulmonary infiltrates, bilateral de novo pleural effusion, and bilateral pulmonary nodules (3 in total), without signs of pulmonary thromboembolism.

case_report: A 15-year-old girl with no prior medical or surgical history presented with fever and drowsiness lasting 2 days. She had experienced fever and multiple enlarged cervical lymph nodes 2 weeks earlier and was treated with oral levofloxacin 500 mg once daily for 1 week. On examination, she was drowsy and febrile. Bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy was noted, involving the posterior cervical lymph nodes. Neurological examination revealed vertical gaze palsy and bilateral horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus. Blepharospasm was observed, and convergence was impaired in both eyes. Fundus examination was normal, and slit lamp examination showed no evidence of Kayser–Fleischer ring. No focal motor deficits were detected. Bilateral knee and ankle reflexes were sluggish with bilateral extensor plantar responses. Bilateral cerebellar signs and gait ataxia were present. Meningeal signs were also noted. Laboratory tests indicated leukopenia with a total leukocyte count of 3000 cells/cu.mm and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 20 mm/1st hour. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed glucose at 76 mg/dl, protein at 28 mg/dl, and 45 white blood cells with 100% lymphocytes. A video electroencephalogram was normal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain, both plain and contrast, revealed altered signal intensity that was hyperintense on T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences without postcontrast enhancement in the dorsal pons and midbrain. CSF tests for tuberculosis polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and Herpes simplex PCR were negative. CSF culture was sterile. CSF adenosine deaminase was 6.9 IU/L. CSF tests for Listeria, Epstein–Barr virus, Enterovirus, and Cryptococcus were negative. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays for human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis B virus, and hepatitis C virus were negative. Tests for antinuclear antibody, double-stranded DNA, and venereal disease research laboratory were negative. Serum paraneoplastic neuronal antigen and antibody profiles were negative. The Mantoux test was negative. The patient was treated with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g twice daily and intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg thrice daily for 10 days. She also received 0.5 mg clonazepam once daily and 1 mg trihexyphenidyl twice daily for 10 days for blepharospasm.
test_results: Cervical lymph node fine-needle aspiration cytology showed lymphocytes, sinus histiocytes, endocapillary buds, monocytoid cells, necrosis, karyorrhectic debris, and nodal reticulum.

case_report: A 12-year-old girl from Italy, with no notable family or prenatal history, exhibited bilateral congenital talon-valgus-pronated clubfoot at birth. From 18 months of age, she showed mild delays in neuromotor development. At her initial neurological assessment at 4 years old, findings included overall muscle weakness, pronounced hyperlordosis, a waddling gait, positive Gowers' sign, easy fatigability, knee valgus, and absence of tendon reflexes.
test_results: Electroneurography disclosed severe motor polyneuropathy with predominant axonal features, diffuse reduction of compound action muscular potentials (CMAP, values under 1.5 mV) and only slight decrement of NCV (38–43 m/s). Follow-up electrophysiological evaluations over time showed a slowly progressive reduction of motor action potential amplitude (values under 0.5 mV) with evidence of diffuse denervation activity on electromyography suggesting a neurogenic pattern. Muscle biopsy showed a normal histochemical pattern with wiped out areas on oxidative metabolism stains, while NADH staining showed the presence of predominant hypertrophic fibers, suggesting an alteration of the myofibrillar framework. Overall, the results pointed to significant neurogenic muscular atrophy. Spectrophotometric determination of OxPhos activities in muscle homogenate showed multiple defects of the respiratory chain complexes with high levels of citrate synthetase, an index of mitochondrial proliferation. In particular, these studies showed Complex I (NADH: ubiquinone oxidoreductase), Complexes II + III (succinate: cytochrome c reductase) and Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) activity to be 65, 55 and 66% of normal values, respectively. Estimation by real-time PCR showed that total mtDNA content was also lower than normal values, as was the mtDNA level in muscle (about 30% of normal control values), whereas the mtDNA/nDNA ratio in cultured skin fibroblasts was normal. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) of the family trio identified bi-allelic variants in MTMR5/SBF (NM_001365819.1); Sanger sequencing confirmed that the patient harbored the p.R763H (c.2291G > A) variant, inherited from her father, and the p.G1064E (c.3194G > A) variant, inherited from her mother.

case_report: A 25-year-old woman was admitted with frequent high-grade premature ventricular beats (17,000 per day) and repeated episodes of bidirectional non-sustained ventricular tachycardia without syncope. Clinical examination revealed bilateral symmetrical hand abnormalities, specifically camptodactyly of the fifth fingers. Breast hypoplasia with inverted nipples was also noted. Facial features included wide-set eyes, a broad nasal tip, a thin upper lip vermilion, and strabismus. Dental issues included tooth malalignment and hypoplasia affecting canines and molars. No abnormalities were found in the lower limbs. Intellectual assessment indicated mild mental retardation and learning disabilities. Family history revealed that the patient's mother passed away at age 30 due to a congenital heart defect and congestive heart failure. The maternal grandmother was unaffected, and no other relatives were available for examination. The mode of inheritance remains unclear due to limited family data.
test_results: Echocardiography revealed enlarged left ventricular dimension and local ventricular wall thinning.

case_report: A 49-year-old right-handed Caucasian man with a recent diagnosis of HIV presented with a 4-month history of progressive left-sided arm and leg weakness. The patient was diagnosed with HIV 2 months prior to this visit (CD4+ count: 270 cells/mm3) but declined to start antiretroviral therapy. At that time, he was also diagnosed with latent syphilis (rapid plasma regain [RPR] 1:32), and he received a 14-day course of intravenous penicillin. Neurological examination revealed mild cognitive impairment, left-sided spastic hemiparesis sparing the face with intact strength on the right side, impaired left-sided primary somatosensation to temperature, pinprick, and vibration at the distal joint of the great toe. Appendicular ataxia (left more prominent than right) was also observed.
test_results: Brain MRI revealed a punctate pattern with innumerable T2-FLAIR hyperintensities in the cortex, brainstem, cerebellum, subcortical, and periventricular areas. These areas also demonstrated hyperintensity on diffusion weighted imaging (DWI) and few of them revealing T2-shine through on the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) sequence. Around the periventricular region, there were areas of punctate enhancement. The right hemisphere demonstrated a higher lesion burden than the left. A hypointense rim involving the subcortical U-fibers on susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) was also observed.

case_report: A 32-year-old Hispanic woman was being managed for symptoms initially thought to be rheumatoid arthritis (RA). She had tried methotrexate and adalimumab with limited success. She presented for a second opinion due to persistent symptoms. Initially, she experienced two hours of morning stiffness and pain in her right shoulder, which gradually progressed to involve bilateral wrists, fingers, and knees. She also had skin lesions on her left elbow and the extensor aspect of bilateral fingers, previously considered xanthomas. These lesions were biopsied, but results were inconclusive. Laboratory tests showed hypercholesterolemia, and she was started on cholesterol-lowering medication. She also reported secondary amenorrhea but denied any history of inflammatory bowel disease, uveitis, preceding gastrointestinal infection, nail changes, or axial joint involvement. Physical examination revealed synovitis in her right shoulder, right knee, bilateral metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints, and bilateral proximal and distal interphalangeal (PIP and DIP) joints. Her right shoulder appeared deformed with decreased range of motion. The left elbow had a flexion contracture and limited range of motion. She also had limited range of motion in bilateral MCP, PIP, and DIP joints and was unable to make a fist in either hand. A well-circumscribed papulonodular lesion was noted on the left elbow. Nails and axial spine appeared disease-free. Laboratory studies showed a high rheumatoid factor (RF) of 56.4 IU/ml (normal < 7 IU/ml) and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 38 mm/hr. C-reactive protein (CRP) and antinuclear antibody (ANA) were normal. Anti-Sjögren’s syndrome related antigen A (anti-SS-A) antibody was elevated at 8.0 U, and anti-Sjögren’s syndrome related antigen B (anti-SS-B) antibody was elevated at 5.2 U. Other antibodies, including anti-Smith, anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA), anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), anti-topoisomerase (anti-scl-70), ribonucleoprotein (RNP), anti-Jo1, and hepatitis panel were negative. For secondary amenorrhea, she had a low estradiol level of 11 pg/ml, high follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) level of 76.6 mIU/ml, and high luteinizing hormone (LH) level of 62.8 mIU/ml, indicating premature primary ovarian failure. X-rays of her digits showed arthritis mutilans, predominantly in bilateral DIP joints, MCP, and PIP joints. MRI and x-ray of the right shoulder showed widening of the acromioclavicular joint and glenohumeral degenerative changes. Despite a clinical presentation similar to RA, some symptoms were unexplained, particularly DIP joint involvement, skin findings, and lack of response to methotrexate and adalimumab. She was given multiple biological agents, including etanercept, abatacept, and golimumab, over 12 months, but none were effective. She was also diagnosed with osteopenia and started on alendronate without symptom improvement. Due to refractory symptoms, she was referred to a quaternary center and given rituximab, which led to some improvement in synovitis in her right knee and hand joints within the first month. However, symptoms in her right shoulder persisted.
test_results: The synovial biopsy of the right shoulder joint showed evidence of histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm.

case_report: A 12-year-old Arab boy presented with multiple exfoliated teeth. His oral hygiene was relatively better with gingival enlargement around erupting teeth. Most of his permanent anterior teeth were lost with severe bone destruction around his remaining teeth. His lower molars appeared floating without any bone support. There was severe palmar plantar keratosis with keratinization of the dorsal surface of his hands.
test_results: A periodontal examination recorded a score of 4 (deep pocket) in his molars and incisors.

case_report: A 52-year-old male with a history of well-controlled hypertension was admitted due to worsening shortness of breath and difficulty breathing while lying down over a period of 2 weeks. Five days later, he experienced general fatigue, widespread joint pain, and noticed small red or purple spots on his right palm. His white blood cell count was 33,200 per microliter with 51% eosinophils (absolute eosinophil count: 16,600 per cubic millimeter). Laboratory tests showed elevated levels of CRP (11.97 mg/dL), troponin I (58.44 ng/mL), and pro-BNP (20989 pg/mL). Physical examination identified swelling in the lower limbs, wheezing at the bases of both lungs, and widespread red papules and petechiae on his palms and abdomen. Neurologic examination revealed weakness in the right limb with a severity scale of 3 out of 5.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed numerous foci of recent infarctions in bilateral cerebral and cerebellar regions. Transthoracic echocardiography showed mild left ventricle (LV) systolic dysfunction, global increased LV wall thickness (especially the posterior wall), and several fragile and floating thrombi with thin attachments to the LV wall.

case_report: The patient is a white female, born to a 21-year-old mother and 25-year-old father. A routine prenatal ultrasound at 5 months gestational age identified a fracture of the right femur. Subsequent prenatal ultrasound and radiograph at birth showed the fracture had resolved with mild symmetrical curvature of both femurs. The mother received standard prenatal care and multivitamin supplementation. Delivery was by elective cesarean section at 38 weeks gestational age due to concerns about potential fractures during vaginal delivery. The patient was born without complications, weighing 2,722 grams (27th percentile). She was initially fed formula and later transitioned to solid foods without vitamin supplementation. Postnatal weight gain was appropriate, but her linear growth was slow, with length percentiles below the 5th percentile. She met all developmental milestones on time and received all scheduled immunizations. At 3 months of age, the patient was taken to the emergency department with a 3-day history of excessive inconsolable crying, discomfort, and inadequate oral intake. Examination revealed crepitus at the left rib cage and blue sclera. X-rays showed non-displaced fractures of the 6th–8th left ribs. The parents denied any trauma, and there were no physical signs of child abuse or neurocutaneous markers of syndromic/congenital disease. During a peripheral venous blood draw, a nurse heard a cracking sound followed by crying and signs of distress. Radiographs revealed a non-displaced, transverse, right proximal ulnar fracture. The patient received in-patient therapy with analgesics and splints to the arm and made a full recovery. At 6 months of age, she presented to her primary care physician for evaluation of left lower extremity pain. Imaging was not obtained at that time.
test_results: Sequencing and copy number variation of COL1A1 and COL1A2 identified a heterozygous deletion of at least 18.5 kb, including COL1A1.

case_report: A 20-month-old female patient was brought to the Department of Pediatrics by her parents due to severe ataxia and developmental delay. The patient was born at 40 weeks of gestation via normal vaginal delivery, weighing 2,980 grams at birth. There were no notable perinatal issues or family history of neurological diseases or developmental delays. The patient exhibited significant developmental delays, unable to maintain a sitting posture independently due to severe ataxia, although she could roll over and crawl on her belly. Neurological examination revealed pronounced psychomotor delay, severe truncal ataxia, and mild axial hypotonia.
test_results: Conventional MRI of the brain showed hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis and enlargement of the fourth ventricle. Initial diffusion tensor imaging results showed that the fractional anisotropy values of the superior cerebellar peduncle and middle cerebellar peduncle decreased by two standard deviations below that of normal control values, and that the apparent diffusion coefficient values increased by two standard deviations.

case_report: A 23-day-old female infant, born at full term via caesarian section to a nonconsanguineous couple, was referred for imaging. Her birth weight was 2400 g (<3rd percentile), length was 47 cm (15th percentile), and head circumference was 32 cm (3rd percentile). Apgar scores were 8/10 at one minute and 10/10 at five minutes. Physical examination revealed multiple firm, skin-colored, finger-like appendages on the right cheek, periauricular, and mandibular areas. Additionally, a mobile, fleshy mass approximately 12 mm in size was noted on the right cheek. Ophthalmologic examination identified a fleshy mass in the right orbit, with the right eye being non-functional and the left eye appearing to have normal vision. An echocardiogram showed no structural abnormalities, and an abdominopelvic ultrasound was unremarkable. The extremities and genitalia were normal, and there were no documented seizures since birth. The patient was referred for further imaging.
test_results: Brain and orbit MRI was performed which showed colpocephaly and agenesis of the corpus callosum. Also, there were nodular subependymal heterotopias, adjacent to the right lateral ventricle. Aplasia of the vermis, hypoplasia of the right cerebellar hemisphere, and widening of the CSF space in the posterior fossa were some other findings in her brain MRI. There were also some skin lesions with exophytic appearance in the face up to 13 × 12 mm in the infraorbital area. In the orbital MRI, there was a mixed cystic solid mass measuring about 25 × 20 mm in her right orbital cavity. The orbital content was abnormal and suggestive of rudimentary orbit. The left orbit was completely normal.

case_report: A 53-year-old male presented with upper body deformity, restricted neck mobility, and muscle weakness in the shoulders and upper limbs. Physical examination revealed multiple, well-defined, round subcutaneous fat masses protruding above the skin surface. These masses were symmetrically distributed on the neck, shoulders, upper torso, and proximal upper limbs. The patient exhibited a pseudoathletic appearance, with notable fatty tissue accumulation around the neck. The patient reported a history of alcohol abuse spanning 39 years and had been diagnosed with alcohol-induced decompensated liver cirrhosis 9 months prior. Upon admission, the patient's body mass index (BMI) was calculated at 24.7 kg/m2, with a waist circumference of 81 cm. The patient was not classified as overweight or obese, and biochemical tests did not reveal any lipid or coagulation abnormalities. However, gynecomastia, limb muscle abnormalities, and hepatosplenomegaly were observed. Laboratory tests indicated hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 11 g/dL, red blood cell count 3,900 × 106/mL), neutropenia (1.3×103/µL), thrombocytopenia (100×103/µL), and mildly elevated hepatic enzymes (AST: 130 U/L, ALT: 90 U/L) and pancreatic enzymes (lipase: 170 U/L, amylase: 140 U/L). Endocrine evaluation revealed hyperestrogenism with normal testosterone levels and decreased dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEA-S) levels. The patient was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes based on an oral glucose tolerance test. Additional parameters, including insulin, C-peptide, and thyroid hormones, were within normal ranges.
test_results: The patient underwent computed tomography to visualize the structure of lesions and determine their location. The study also allowed to determine the degree of penetration of fat masses to deeper structures.

case_report: A 22-year-old female presented with a 2-year history of gradually worsening proximal muscle pain and weakness in both upper and lower limbs. Previous treatment with prednisone for two months showed no improvement. MRI of the pelvis and thighs revealed linear hypointense areas in both proximal medial femoral necks and the right ischium, indicative of insufficiency fractures. She had normal childhood development and pubertal growth, with a height of 154 cm and a weight of 57.1 kg at presentation. There was no family history of rickets, osteomalacia, or other metabolic bone diseases. Her menstrual history was unremarkable. Past medical history included a diagnosis of carnitine palmitoyl transferase 2 (CPT2) deficiency at age 14, identified during an evaluation for diffuse muscle pain and weakness. At that time, she had low serum carnitine levels, elevated serum alanine, normal lactate, and low pyruvate levels. Elevated levels of C16, C18:2, C18:1, and C18 were noted, suggesting CPT2 deficiency, although genetic testing was negative for the S113L variant. Other biochemical test results from that period were not available. Her symptoms resolved a few months after starting oral carnitine replacement therapy. Physical examination showed no kyphosis, scoliosis, vertebral tenderness, or joint hyperextensibility. There were no deformities in the lower extremities. She exhibited proximal muscle weakness with 4/5 strength in the upper and 3/5 in the lower extremities, along with tenderness in the thighs. The neurological exam was otherwise normal, and she had a waddling gait.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed a heterozygous known pathogenic missense variant in FGF23: c.527 G>A p. Arg176Gln (R176Q). Genetic screens for variants in PHEX (X-linked Hypophosphatemic Rickets) and DMP-1 (Autosomal Recessive Hypophosphatemic Rickets 1) were negative.

case_report: A 7-year and 5-month-old Chinese boy, the second child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents, presented with delayed motor development from birth. He achieved head and neck stability at 7 months, rolled over at 11 months, and walked independently at 2 years. His language development was significantly delayed. At 2 years old, he experienced his first epileptic episode, characterized by eye staring, lip cyanosis, foaming at the mouth, and limb jerks, lasting for several minutes. A four-hour sleep-deprived electroencephalogram (EEG) showed continuous spike-and-slow-waves (CSWS). Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and multiple auditory brainstem responses were normal, with no additional abnormalities detected. The seizures ceased spontaneously, and anti-epileptic treatment was initially declined by his parents. However, four months later, the seizures recurred, and valproic acid (VPA) was gradually introduced, starting at 10 mg/kg per day and increasing to 30 mg/kg per day within one month. On a dose of 30 mg/kg per day of VPA, the patient experienced no further seizures. Despite this, he remains unable to care for himself or speak, and neuropsychological testing indicates global intellectual disability and hyperactivity.
test_results: The variant c.625C > T (p.Gln209∗) of CNKSR2 was identified, that was inherited from his unaffected carrier mother. The mutation located toward the N-terminal of the gene alter the codon sequence of the no. 209 amino acid Gln into a termination codon, resulting in a truncated protein lacking the last 825 of 1034 residues, that leads to a truncated protein without the PDZ, DUF1170, PH, and C-terminal ETHV domains.
diagnosis: Houge type of X-linked syndromic mental retardation
Orpha_name: X-linked intellectual disability-hypotonia-facial dysmorphism-aggressive behavior syndrome

case_report: A 70-year-old woman, with no prior health issues, presented with yellowish papules on the sides of her neck and both antecubital fossae. These papules appeared two years ago and have remained unchanged, causing no itching or physical discomfort. The patient reported no history of prolonged sun exposure, rubbing, scratching, or cutaneous growths during pregnancy or weight gain. She was in good health, with no diabetes or hypertension, and did not exhibit fever or other systemic symptoms. Her family and medical histories were unremarkable. Dermatological examination showed multiple polygonal, flat-topped yellowish-white papules on both sides of the neck, resembling plucked chicken skin. Similar lesions were observed bilaterally on the antecubital fossae. The skin lesions were limited to these areas. Physical examination, including fundoscopy and cardiovascular assessment, revealed no abnormalities.
test_results: Histological evaluation revealed a folded epidermis with hyperkeratosis and orthokeratosis with thickening of collagen fibers in the superficial and medium dermis. Masson’s trichrome staining revealed haphazardly arranged and thickened collagen fibers in the papillary dermis. Elastic Van Gieson staining revealed normal elastic fibers in a normal pattern and quantity.
diagnosis: White Fibrous Papulosis of the Neck
Orpha_name: White Fibrous Papulosis of the Neck

case_report: The patient is a 24-year-old Caucasian female with a history of acute pancreatitis, first occurring at age 20 and complicated by superior mesenteric vein thrombosis. A second episode happened at age 21. She was diagnosed with combined dyslipidemia and initially treated with a statin and fibrate, which did not provide adequate control. Niacinic acid was added, resulting in improved control. At age 22, she was diagnosed with diabetes secondary to pancreatitis and has been on insulin therapy since then. She was referred to endocrinology, where hypercortisolism was considered but later ruled out. She discontinued these appointments shortly after. Her gynecological and obstetric history was unremarkable, with no menstrual abnormalities, hyperandrogenism, or infertility. At 7 weeks of pregnancy, she was referred to the outpatient endocrinology and obstetrics clinic for diabetes management. Physical examination showed loss of fat from the extremities and trunk, excess subcutaneous fat in the chin, and apparent muscle hypertrophy. These features had been present since early adolescence, according to the patient. No other notable clinical features were observed, such as hirsutism or acanthosis nigricans. Her diabetes therapy included insulin, with an initial total dose of 106 U/day (1.8 U/Kg/day). She was also treated with heparin and salmon oil. Statin, niacinic acid, and fenofibrate treatment had been discontinued upon pregnancy confirmation. She exhibited good glycemic control (HbA1c 4.7%, without hypoglycemia) and had triglyceride levels of 1566 mg/dL (reference value <150 mg/dL), for which she was prescribed gemfibrozil 600 mg, twice a day.
test_results: The presence of exon 8 c.1444C > T (p.Arg482Trp) heterozygote mutation in the LMNA gene was revealed.

case_report: A ten-month-old child reared as female was referred for genetic consultation and evaluation of 46,XY sex reversal and early-onset adrenal failure. The child is the first born to third-degree consanguineous parents and initially presented at 45 days old with generalized edema and tonic-clonic convulsions. Upon admission, no physical dysmorphisms were observed. The child had normal female external genitalia, and the gonads were not palpable. Laboratory results showed a random plasma glucose of 71.7 mg%, low sodium (110 mEq/L), low chloride (90 mEq/L), and high potassium (6.7 mEq/L). Baseline serum hormonal analysis was conducted, and no significant increase in hormone levels was observed following administration of 250 mg synacthen (DHEA was 3.18 mg/mL and androstenedione was less than 0.3 mg/mL). Treatment included intravenous saline, glucocorticoids, and mineralocorticoids for adrenal insufficiency.
test_results: A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen showed fatty deposits in both adrenal fossae with non-visualization of the adrenal glands. Both testes were found in the inguinal region, and there were no Mullerian structures.
Orpha_name: Congenital lipoid adrenal hyperplasia due to STAR deficency

case_report: Patient 4 is a 3-year-old girl who was born at term following an uneventful pregnancy to healthy, non-consanguineous parents. At 1 year old, she experienced her first febrile seizure, characterized by eye-rolling, cyanotic lips, unresponsiveness, and upper limb jittering. These episodes have occurred five times over the past year and a half. Additionally, she exhibits delayed language development. Brain MRI revealed slightly reduced white matter.
test_results: Her EEG demonstrated 3–4 Hz spike- and slow-wave bursts on brain in sleep and more than 10 episodes of absence were observed during the waking period.
diagnosis: Beta-propeller protein-associated neurodegeneration  due to de novo variants in WDR45

case_report: A 34-year-old woman was seen at an external hospital due to several weeks of pain in the right mandible. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count and electrolytes, showed no abnormalities. She began taking oral acetaminophen and NSAIDs, but her symptoms continued. About a year later, she visited our orthopaedic outpatient clinic with pain in her right femur. There were no indications of local infection, and laboratory tests remained unremarkable.
test_results: X-Rays revealed diffuse right mandible cancellous bone sclerosis with osteolytic lesions and extensive periosteal reaction. A mandible biopsy revealed infiltration by inflammatory cells, but no infection or malignancy. X-Rays revealed right femur osteitis (osteosclerosis with a homogenous fibrillary pattern). Technetium99 bone scan showed active right femur and right mandible uptake.

case_report: A 40-year-old man was admitted to our hospital with a sudden loss of consciousness and vomiting in early February 2010. His wife reported a two-month history of gradually worsening confusion and right side paresthesia. Upon admission, physical examination revealed agitation, high blood pressure (160/70 mmHg), and nuchal rigidity. Neurological examination was incomplete due to the patient's agitation. Laboratory results showed hemoglobin at 16 mg/dL and a leukocyte count of 17700/mcL (normal range: 4000-11000/mcL). Brain computed tomography (CT) showed no abnormalities. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed hyperintense areas in the anterior and peripheral aspects of the pons, cerebral peduncles, and left cerebellar hemisphere. Lumbar puncture (LP) results included glucose at 86 mg/dL (normal ≥ 45 mg/dL) and protein at 353 mg/dL (normal ≤ 45 mg/dL). The culture and smear of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) were negative, and the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay for Herpes simplex virus was also negative. The patient was treated with antibiotic therapy, including antifungal and anti-tuberculosis regimens. During hospitalization, his neurological and mental condition progressively worsened, presenting with vertigo, delirium, hallucinations, and cranial nerve palsies. Despite treatment, he passed away after 20 days.
test_results: Histopathological study of the brain showed focal involvement of the subarachnoid layer by neoplastic cell aggregation. Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) stained slides revealed anaplastic proliferation of spindle-shaped cells admixed with atypical giant cells arranged in fascicular and storiform patterns. These cells contained a typical hyper-chrome nuclei with moderate cytoplasms. Mitotic figures were also easily identified. The immunophenotyping studies suggested a strong positive reaction for vimentin and focally positive staining for CD68. However, tumor cells had negative reactions to cytokeratin, desmin, Melan A, leukocyte common antigen (LCA), S-100 protein, chromogranin, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), CD31 and CD99.

case_report: A 45-year-old man arrived at the emergency department with complaints of a headache localized around his left eye, which began 48 hours prior. He noted that this pain was different from his previous migraine headaches in both pattern and character. He had been unable to sleep since the onset of the pain. The headache was described as recurrent, brief, and severe lancinating pain, lasting only seconds and occurring every three to five minutes. Despite the brevity of each episode, the pain was intense enough to impair his functionality. Between episodes, he experienced complete pain relief with no residual symptoms. He reported no additional symptoms such as fever, chills, nausea, or vomiting. There were no autonomic or neurological symptoms during or between pain episodes, and he did not identify any factors that worsened or alleviated the pain. He did not experience shoulder girdle stiffness, general malaise, jaw claudication, or changes in appetite. There was no history of trauma, alcohol, or illicit drug use. His medical history included migraines, and he was not on any medications. At triage, his vital signs, visual acuity, glucose levels, and mental status were normal. Physical examination showed that he was not in distress at baseline, but experienced significant distress during pain episodes. Eye examination was normal with no conjunctival injection. Cranial nerve and peripheral neurological examinations were normal. Examination of the ears, nose, and throat was unremarkable. No headache trigger zones were identified around the mouth, ears, eyes, or scalp. There was no tenderness in the temporal region, and temporal pulsations were normal. The skin on his face and head was intact without erythema, blistering, altered sensation, or tenderness. Routine blood work, including complete blood count, glucose, electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, was within normal limits. No imaging was performed during this visit. Treatment with carbamazepine was initiated, and an outpatient ophthalmology appointment was scheduled. He was discharged with instructions to return to the emergency department if he developed a fever, worsening headache, neurological symptoms, or a rash.
test_results: An unenhanced CT scan of the head was obtained, which was normal.

case_report: A 4-month-old male presented with an acute cough, expectoration, and difficulty breathing for over 10 days. Two weeks prior, the child experienced paroxysmal cough, phlegm, difficulty breathing, runny nose, diarrhea, and cyanosis around the mouth. Symptoms persisted despite penicillin infusion at a local hospital. The patient, born full-term with a birth weight of approximately 3 kg, had an uncomplicated birth with no asphyxia or respiratory distress. He has had multiple episodes of pneumonia and diarrhea since birth, but chest imaging only indicated pulmonary infection. There is no significant personal or family medical history. On examination, the patient's body temperature was 36.5°C, heart rate 136 bpm, respiratory rate 62 breaths/min, fingertip oxygen saturation (SpO2) 86%, and body weight 7.2 kg. Cyanosis of the lips was noted, with no swollen superficial lymph nodes. Respiratory sounds were rough in both lungs, and fine moist rales were present. No abnormalities were detected in the heart, abdomen, or nervous system upon physical examination. Blood tests showed normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate, liver and kidney function, and C-reactive protein levels. The myocardial enzyme spectrum was normal except for elevated lactate dehydrogenase (704 U/L). Humoral immunity results were: Ig 14.0 g/L, IgG 0.93 g/L, IgM 0.29 g/L, IgA 0.0 g/L, complement C3 0.40 g/L, complement C4 0.11 g/L, and total IgE 1 U/mL. Lymphocyte subpopulation results were: CD3+ 95.49%, CD3+CD4+ 65.58%, CD16+CD56+ 3.58%, and CD19+ 0.03%. No pathogens were detected in blood and sputum tests.
test_results: His bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was milky white and Periodic acid–Schiff staining was positive. Genetic testing revealed that the BTK gene (located at chrX:100608340) had a hemizygous mutation (c.1751-1g>A). Genetic testing did not find gene mutations related to PAP such as surfactant protein B, surfactant protein C, ATP-binding cassette subfamily A member 3 (ABCA3), Nkx homeobox-1 gene (NKX2-1), and granulocyte-monocyte colony stimulating factor receptor genes. Chest spiral computed tomography plain scan showed a significant decrease in the transparency of both lungs, with ground glass or butterfly-shaped changes in both lungs, and a large bubble in the upper lobe of the right lung. Tracheoscopy revealed that his alveolar lavage fluid was pale milky white.
diagnosis: Pulmonary Alveolar Proteinosis  induced by X-linked Agammaglobulinemia

case_report: An 82-year-old man reported experiencing blurred vision and a pressure-like sensation in the left eye for the past year. His medical history included hypertension, glaucoma, and prostate cancer. Visual acuity, corrected to the best possible level, was 20/20 in both eyes. He successfully identified all Ishihara plates with both eyes. Pupil size was 3 mm bilaterally. A grade one relative afferent pupillary defect was noted in the left eye. Examination of the left optic disc revealed mild elevation and indistinct nasal margins, with unobscured blood vessels and no hemorrhages or exudates. Subtle macular edema, a few choroidal folds, and tortuous retinal vessels were observed in the left eye. The right optic disc appeared normal. The remainder of the neuro-ophthalmic examination was unremarkable, with no skin lesions indicative of neurofibromatosis. A central 24–2 threshold Humphrey visual field test showed normal results in both eyes. Macular optical coherence tomography indicated retinal thickening between the optic nerve head and fovea. Lumbar puncture revealed a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) opening pressure of 90 mm H2O. CSF analysis showed normal cell count and biochemistry, and cytology was negative for malignant cells.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and orbits showed enlarged CSF spaces around the normal appearing left optic nerve. There was no abnormal enhancement of the optic nerve or its sheath. Brain images demonstrated only age-related volume loss.

case_report: A 63-year-old woman with a history of high blood pressure and Waldenström macroglobulinemia presented with a single, well-defined, depressed plaque located on the thenar eminence of her left hand, which had been present for a decade. The patient reported no symptoms or history of trauma associated with the lesion. Dermoscopic examination revealed a stepped-scaly border and punctate vessels on an erythematous base, along with regularly distributed white dots.
test_results: A biopsy revealed a thinning of the stratum corneum and a slightly diminished stratum granulosum compared with the surrounding normal skin. Parakeratosis was not present, and only scattered mononuclear inflammatory elements were found in the dermis.

case_report: An 18-year-old male experienced a sudden onset of manic behavior in the summer of 2003 and was hospitalized within a few days. Prior to hospitalization, he was given chlorpromazine tablets (100 mg) twice daily for three days. Upon examination, he was found to be tall and thin, weighing 58 kg, and exhibited continuous talking, frequent singing and dancing, and was easily distracted by external stimuli. He was highly agitated, occasionally violent, and mildly dehydrated. His vital signs included a pulse rate of 90/min, blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg, and a body temperature of 98°F. On the day of admission, he received intramuscular injections of haloperidol (10 mg) and promethazine (25 mg) in the morning and required physical restraint. He slept for a few hours but developed acute neck dystonia in the evening, which was treated with another intramuscular injection of promethazine (25 mg). The following morning, he exhibited marked rigidity. Treatment was initiated with ziprasidone tablets (40 mg) twice daily and trihexyphenidyl tablets (2 mg) twice daily. By the third morning of hospitalization, he was nearly mute, showed significant rigidity, and had persistent dystonic movements affecting his trunk, neck, and limbs. His pulse rate was 106/min, blood pressure was 140/100 mmHg, body temperature was 103°F, and he was sweating profusely. He was not eating and appeared slightly drowsy. All medications were discontinued, and he was transferred to the intensive care unit.
test_results: CPK was 1450 IU/L. The next day, CPK level was 810 IU/L. His rigidity and fever resolved completely by fourth day and CPK level came to normal on the fifth day.

case_report: A 44-year-old African female with no past medical history presented with Raynaud’s phenomenon, fingertip pain and ulcerations, nail fold capillary changes, facial and back rash, skin tightness and depigmentation, joint pain, morning stiffness, and fatigue. Physical examination showed hypopigmented scarring skin lesions on the face and neck and tenderness and swelling of small joints in the hands and wrists. The laboratory results were as follows: antinuclear antibody (ANA) + (1:80, speckled), anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) antibody + (4.8 U/mL), cardiolipin IgM + (16 MPL U/mL), and smooth muscle antibody (SMA) + (1:20), and anti-Sjögren’s syndrome-related antigen A (anti-Ro/SSA) antibody −, anti-Sjögren’s syndrome type B (anti-La/SSB) antibody −, antinuclear ribonucleoprotein (anti-RNP) antibody −, anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-ds DNA) antibody −, and anti-Smith antibody −. Flow cytometry and bone marrow biopsy were negative. Steroids, mycophenolate mofetil, and hydroxychloroquine were started. After four days of steroids and immunosuppressants, the patient’s fatigue, joint pain, and fingertip pain improved during the treatment, but she developed a severe thunderclap headache with left lower extremity weakness.
test_results: The head CTA showed multifocal long segment stenosis ranging from mild to moderate in severity involving the M2 segments of the right MCA, sharp transition with reconstitution of the normal caliber of the vessel distally, focal narrowing of the A1 segment of the right ACA, focal narrowing of the P1 segment of the right PCA, and focal narrowing of the proximal left superior cerebellar artery.

case_report: A 63-year-old female with a medical history of hypothyroidism, hypertension, and ductal carcinoma in situ status post right partial mastectomy was admitted to the hospital due to melena lasting three days. She reported experiencing generalized weakness and fatigue for two weeks but denied symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, hematochezia, diarrhea, or constipation. On presentation, she exhibited orthostatic hypotension. Laboratory results revealed a hemoglobin level of 6.3 g/dl, a mean corpuscular volume of 108.7, and a red cell distribution width of 30. Vitamin B12 was measured at 135 pg/ml, iron at 12 µg/dl, and ferritin at 23.4 ng/ml, all of which were low, while folate levels were normal. She was administered one unit of packed red blood cells, resulting in an increase in hemoglobin to 7.4 g/dl. Additionally, serum gastrin levels were elevated at 1988 pg/ml, chromogranin A (CgA) levels were elevated at 300 ng/ml, and the urine 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) level was normal at 8.4 mg/ml.
test_results: EGD showed a 3 cm polypoidal, ulcerated, friable, bleeding mass lesion in the body of the stomach. EGD also showed evidence of atrophic gastritis. Gross appearance showed a 3.5 x 3.0 x 2.8 cm mass with a 0.9 x 0.8 cm base (deep resection margin). Microscopically, the mass was composed of tumor cells, which were relatively monotonous and arranged in predominantly glandular structures. The tumor cells were diffusely and strongly positive for synaptophysin and CgA on immunohistochemical studies, and the ki-67 proliferative index was less than 3%. This tumor demonstrated angioinvasion but margins are free of tumor cells. Microscopy also showed moderately severe chronic inactive gastritis, prominent foveolar hyperplasia, focal intestinal metaplasia, and superficial erosions.

case_report: A 20-year-old Chinese man reported experiencing blurred central vision in both eyes for 2 weeks. His family and social history were unremarkable. At age 7, he had been diagnosed with macular retinoschisis and choroidal neovascularization (CNV) in the left eye. Currently, his best-corrected visual acuity is 20/800 in the right eye and 20/200 in the left eye. Color vision testing indicated a subclinical deficit. Bilateral ocular motility, intraocular pressure, night vision, and anterior segment examinations were normal in both eyes. Medical records from 2008 showed spoke-like appearances in the bilateral macula and a round yellowish lesion inferior to the left macula. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed cystic changes and retinoschisis with subretinal fluid bilaterally, and fluorescein angiography (FA) showed slight macular fluorescein pooling in the late stage. Round choroidal neovascularization (CNV) was confirmed via OCT, FA, and indocyanine green angiography (ICGA). Full-field electroretinogram (ERG) was nearly normal, but the P1 response density of the multifocal electroretinogram (mfERG) in ring 1 (macular area) was abnormal. Electro-oculogram (EOG) could not be obtained due to poor compliance at age 7. Two years later, macular retinoschisis with cysts was still present, but follow-up was lost until 2021. In 2021, bilateral cystic changes in the macula and symmetric annular area of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) atrophy in the posterior pole extending nasal to the disc were observed, along with subretinal deposits. A pigmentary lesion inferior to the fovea was also noted in both eyes. Autofluorescence imaging showed hyperfluorescence corresponding to the area of RPE change. OCT displayed enlarged macular cysts with retinoschisis and subretinal fluid (SRF), as well as focal choroidal excavation (FCE). Optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) visualized inactive macular neovascularization (MNV) inferior to the right macula. ERG studies showed decreased cone and rod responses, with no negative ERG detected. The P1 response density of mfERG in ring 1 was decreased compared to 2008. EOG showed an absence of light peak with an Arden ratio less than 2.0. The fundus and EOG of the patient's parents and younger sister (aged 7 years) were normal.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing revealed the compound heterozygous sequence variations (p. [Arg47Leu; Trp287*]) in the coding sequence of the BEST1 allele.

case_report: An 82-year-old male with a history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) diagnosed five years ago, characterized by elevated white blood cell (WBC) count in complete blood count and bone marrow biopsy findings, presented with hematuria. The patient had no prior history of chemotherapy or radiotherapy. Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a 41×42 mm polypoid mass located on the anterior wall of the urinary bladder. Bone structures appeared normal on radiological examination. Urine samples were collected, and three slides were prepared using the cytocentrifuge technique. These slides were stained with May-Grünwald-Giemsa (MGG, Merck, Germany), Papanicolaou (PAP; Biostain, UK), and hematoxylin and eosin (H&E, Biostain, UK) methods.
test_results: After the examination by a light microscope, many small hyperchromatical cells similar to lymphocytes were detected, while they were mostly isolated or formed small groups. Focal cell molding was also noted in clusters. Light microscopic examination of collected samples showed small hyperchromatical tumor cell sheets invading submucosa and muscularis mucosa. Immunohistochemical analysis showed that the tumor cells expressed pancytokeratin and neuroendocrine markers such as synaptophysin and chromogranin. They were negative for cytokeratin 20 and leukocyte common antigen (LCA).
diagnosis: Small Cell Carcinoma of the Urinary Bladder
Orpha_name: Small Cell Carcinoma of the Urinary Bladder

case_report: A 10-year-old African-American female with Down syndrome was evaluated by the pulmonary service for a history of chronic daily cough and recurrent pneumonias over eight and a half years. The cough was more severe at night, when lying down, and during physical exertion. It also worsened during viral respiratory tract infections. There was a history of frequent vomiting of undigested food, which was not necessarily associated with the cough. The patient had been treated multiple times for asthma exacerbations and pneumonia, with transient clinical improvement following antibiotics, bronchodilators, and oral corticosteroids. Daily inhaled corticosteroids did not fully control the cough. Her past medical history included a small ventricular septal defect and chronic constipation. On examination, her weight was between the 75th and 90th percentile, and her height was between the 10th and 25th percentile. Chest examination was unremarkable. Chest X-rays showed predominantly patchy peribronchial air space consolidation, with more involvement of the right middle lobe. A Barium swallow study done at 5 years of age showed no frank aspiration or laryngeal penetration, and the esophagogram revealed normal esophageal anatomy with mildly delayed hypopharyngeal contraction but no contrast retention. Flexible bronchoscopy showed normal airway anatomy. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid contained 16% neutrophils, 35% lymphocytes, 35% macrophages, and 14% epithelial cells. Cultures grew only mixed flora. Lipid-laden macrophages were present with a Colombo index of 110, consistent with aspiration.
test_results: A repeat Barium swallow study showed severe esophageal dysfunction with multiple waves of tertiary contractions throughout a markedly dilated thoracic esophagus. The distal esophagus appeared tapered caudally with severe narrowing at the gastroesophageal junction. Small food particles with air bubbles were seen within the mid esophagus. Only small amount of contrast passed to the stomach. CT scan of the chest showed diffuse lung infiltrates that seemed worse on right middle lobe and left lower lobe. The esophagus was enlarged along its entire length but with no obvious tracheal compression.

case_report: A 13-year-old Asian Indian female presented with reduced vision in both eyes for the past 20 days. Two months prior, she experienced sudden onset left-sided facial palsy, treated with oral acyclovir, without further neurological evaluation. Her systemic history was unremarkable, with no similar past episodes and unknown immunization status. Central nervous system examination was normal except for mild residual effects of facial palsy. Best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 1/60 in the right eye (RE) and 3/60 in the left eye (LE). No anterior segment or vitreous inflammation was observed. Fundus examination of the RE showed whitish ground glass retinitis lesions with ill-defined edges and surrounding hemorrhages at the posterior pole. The LE exhibited an area of thinning with retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) mottling and hemorrhages in the macular area, without active retinal lesions. Mild venous dilation, areas of vascular occlusion, and a few healed lesions in the mid-peripheral region were noted. The optic nerve appeared normal and healthy. Spectral domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) of the RE revealed loss of nerve fiber layer (NFL), ganglion cell layer (GCL), and inner and outer nuclear layers, with the outer retina appearing completely distorted and thinned, showing intermittent complete loss of retinal tissue. OCT of the LE showed foveal thinning with total loss of retinal layer architecture. Fluorescein angiography (FA) of the RE indicated early blockage of background fluorescence in the area of active white lesion with irregular staining corresponding to RPE atrophy, followed by late staining of the retinitis lesions. FA of the LE showed patchy hyperfluorescence corresponding to RPE atrophic patches with blocked fluorescence due to intraretinal hemorrhages. No disc or vessel staining was observed in either eye. Systemic investigations were normal except for lymphocytosis. The patient was started on oral acyclovir (400 mg BD) and oral steroids at 1 mg/kg body weight in weekly tapering doses. At a 10-day follow-up, BCVA remained unchanged, and the lesions appeared to be healing. The patient was referred to a pediatrician for further evaluation due to the history of facial palsy, unknown immunization status, and macular necrotizing retinitis. Despite concerning ocular findings, there were no systemic symptoms or neurological signs. The pediatrician opted for observation without hospital admission. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was normal.
test_results: CSF analysis revealed an opening pressure of 8 cm of water, was acellular and negative for any infection on microbiological stains. IgG measles antibody in CSF (10.7 mg/dl) was raised with increased CSF/Serum quotient (4.48). MRI of the brain showed bilateral T2/flair hyper-intensities with gyral swellings involving parieto-occipital lobes. EEG examination revealed intermittent high voltage slow wave discharges suggestive of progressive myoclonic epilepsy.

case_report: A 45-year-old male reported experiencing muscle twitching, severe generalized burning pain, and episodic sweating in the extremities for 4 weeks. He had no history of weakness, difficulty swallowing, or speech issues. He was treated with Vicodin and muscle relaxants without relief. Physical examination revealed persistent muscle fasciculations over the deltoids, triceps, forearm, thighs, and calf muscles. There was no muscle atrophy or hypertrophy, and muscle strength was grade 4+ in all muscles. The fasciculations were asynchronous resting contractions involving both proximal and distal muscles, including visible asynchronous contractions in the abdominal muscles. The patient also reported constant burning pain in his distal extremities bilaterally. He was started on a 5-day course of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg). Despite high doses of Dilaudid and then morphine, the burning pain was only mildly relieved. After initiating IVIg, muscle fasciculations improved and eventually resolved, with only minor improvement in pain. The patient was then transitioned to oral Percocet and gabapentin, but significant pain relief was not achieved. The average pain level was rated 9/10 on the pain assessment scale.
test_results: Electromyography and nerve conduction studies revealed spontaneous activity in the form of grouped +3 discharges as well as neuromyotonic discharges in the right medial gastrocnemius and left deltoid muscles. Motor unit potentials were normal. VGKC antibody levels were elevated at 63 pmol/L (normal 0–31).

case_report: A 40-year-old woman was admitted to Chonnam University Hospital with a three-month history of severe generalized weakness and fatigue. She experienced a similar episode three years ago that resolved with bed rest. She reported no use of licorice, diuretics, laxatives, or any other medications, and had no significant nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. The patient appeared relatively well, with a height of 154 cm and a weight of 52 kg. Vital signs included a pulse rate of 98/min, blood pressure of 100/70 mmHg, and respiration rate of 18/min. The remainder of her physical examination was within normal limits. Laboratory findings showed persistent hypokalemic alkalosis with serum potassium at 2.4 mEq/L, serum bicarbonate at 32.7 mEq/L, PaO2 at 86.1 mmHg, PaCO2 at 48 mmHg, and total CO2 content at 32 mmol/L. Plasma pH was 7.44, and urine pH was 7.0. Electrocardiography indicated PR prolongation and T wave flattening. Serum sodium was 139 mEq/L, chloride 85 mEq/L, total calcium 5.1 mEq/L, ionized calcium 2.0 mEq/L, inorganic phosphorus 4.7 mg/dl, magnesium 1.6 mEq/L, uric acid 13.4 mg/dl, and serum osmolality 289 mosm/kg. Blood urea nitrogen was 44.0 mg/dl, serum creatinine 1.7 mg/dl, and creatinine clearance 35 ml/min. There were no proteinuria, hematuria, or abnormalities in the urinary sediment. Blood and serum studies revealed normal hemoglobin, hematocrit, white blood cell count, total protein, albumin, alkaline phosphatase, and transaminase levels. Twenty-four-hour urinary excretion included sodium at 183 mEq, potassium at 67 mEq, chloride at 247 mEq, calcium at 120 mg, protein at 150 mg, glucose at 30 mg, and urine volume at 2,300 cc. Urinary specific gravity was 1.010 and osmolality was 310 mosm/kg. Plasma renin activity was 48.2 ng/ml/hr and aldosterone level was 34.4 ng/dl. FENa was 2.6%, FECl was 5.7%, FEK was 55%, and FEUric acid was 8.2%. Thiazide and furosemide were not detected in her urine by high-performance liquid chromatography at the Department of Pharmacology, Chonnam University Medical School, Kwangju, Korea.
test_results: The biopsy specimen contained up to 8 glomeruli per section. Some glomeruli revealed focal and segmental glomerulosclerotic changes. Juxtaglomerular hyperplasia of varying degrees and multiple vacuolization of proximal tubule due to chronic hypokalemia were noted. The tubules, interstitium and blood vessels were entirely normal with no scarring or atrophy.

case_report: A 13-year-old boy presented with a history of a congenital, slow-growing swelling in the sacrococcygeal region. Recently, there was an increase in the size of the swelling and one episode of self-limiting inflammation over the past two months. Ultrasonography revealed a solid ovoid mass with an inhomogeneous echo structure, measuring 39 × 31 × 19.5 mm, attached to the posterior aspect of the sacrum, with no evidence of sinus tracts. Serum beta-HCG and alpha-fetoprotein levels were measured and found to be within normal limits. The patient underwent surgical removal of the mass along with the overlying skin.
test_results: The histological examination showed a neoplastic lesion characterized by several microcystic-hemorrhagic areas and some solid areas. The immunohistochemical analysis showed cells positive for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), lying in a myxoid stroma. Proliferation index evaluated with Ki-67 was 2%. The surgical margins were negative.

case_report: A 48-year-old female with a history of diabetes mellitus presented with right hip pain, inability to bear weight, and a history of multiple unprovoked fractures. Laboratory results revealed hypophosphatemia (0.26 mmol/L), low 1,25-hydroxy vitamin D (65 nmol/L), elevated FGF-23 (1,029 kRU/L), increased alkaline phosphatase level (525.0 U/L), normal serum calcium level (2.24 mmol/L), and elevated 24-hour urine phosphate (53 mmol/day). Bone mass density (BMD) assessment indicated osteopenia with multiple fractures. Ultrasonography identified a 3.2 × 2 cm2 heterogeneous hypoechoic mass with increased vascularity on the medial aspect of the left thigh. No additional bone or soft tissue masses were detected. An Octreotide scan revealed a hot lesion in the left upper thigh. The patient received empirical treatment with phosphate, calcium, and vitamin D supplements. The mass in the left upper thigh was surgically removed.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed a bland spindle cell proliferation in a background of hemangiopericytomatous-like blood vessels, multinucleated giant cells, smudgy/grungy basophilic matrix, and microcystic changes with rare mitosis (1-2/10 HPF). There was no evidence of pleomorphism, hyper-cellularity, or necrosis. The tumor cells showed positive immunoreactivity against ERG and CD56, with variables for CD68, while vimentin and CD34 were negative. Ki67 showed a very low proliferative index (<5%).

case_report: A 35-year-old first-time pregnant woman from Sorocaba, Brazil, with Sjögren syndrome and positive anti-Ro/SSA antibodies but negative anti-La/SSB antibodies, was examined at our department at 25 weeks of gestation. She was referred due to fetal bradycardia with a heart rate of 45 bpm noted since 21 weeks. Initial findings included left atrial isomerism and interventricular communication. Despite recommendations for intrauterine pacemaker placement, the patient declined. Follow-up included clinical and echocardiographic monitoring, and the mother received corticosteroids and β-adrenergic agents. She developed gestational diabetes mellitus, likely related to corticosteroid use (8 mg/day), and experienced a heart rate of 200 bpm with symptoms following terbutaline use (400 mg/day).
test_results: The first fetal echocardiogram showed an anatomically normal heart with bradycardic rhythm, ventricular HR of 40 bpm, and atrial HR of 147 bpm.

case_report: A 27-year-old male with no significant past medical history presented with flu-like symptoms associated with ejaculation. These symptoms included coughing, rhinorrhea, sneezing, and a hive-like rash on his forearms. He also experienced facial and cervical lymphadenopathy, which intensified with more frequent ejaculation. The patient reported that these symptoms began at age 18 following treatment with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a suspected case of acute epididymitis. The symptoms occurred regardless of whether ejaculation was due to masturbation or sexual intercourse. He had a history of a chlamydial infection two years prior, which was treated and confirmed resolved. Due to the severity of his symptoms, he avoided sexual activity and romantic relationships. He had been evaluated by multiple healthcare providers, including three urologists, an otolaryngologist, an infectious disease specialist, and an allergist. During his initial visit with an allergist, he was diagnosed with hay fever and underwent allergen testing, which revealed a cantaloupe allergy and sensitivity to poison ivy.
test_results: Immunoglobulin testing revealed an elevated IgE level of 257 IU/mL (normal: <99 IU/mL).

case_report: A 15-year-old female presented to Seoul National University Hospital on December 17, 2018, with a sudden onset of vision blurring in both eyes that began 8 days earlier. She had experienced transient weakness in her right arm and difficulty speaking 22 and 6 months prior, respectively, but did not seek medical attention at those times. She was not taking any medications and had no significant ophthalmic history. Upon presentation, she reported dysuria, increased frequency and urgency of urination, and gross hematuria, accompanied by a mild fever. Her blood pressure was recorded at 171/135 mmHg. She had no other health issues and no relevant family or trauma history. Her corrected visual acuity was measured at 20/50 in the right eye and 20/35 in the left eye. Ophthalmic examination showed significant optic disc swelling and macular exudates in the right eye. The left eye exhibited mild disc swelling, macular exudates, intra-arterial white plaques, a few retinal blot hemorrhages, and a white ischemic retina.
test_results: Fluorescein angiographies revealed disc and vascular leakage with decreased choroidal perfusion in both eyes, and retinal arterial occlusions with large non-perfusion area at temporal retina was observed in the left eye. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) images confirmed bilateral disc edema and showed fluid and multiple hard exudates in subretinal space and Henle’s layer at macula and peripapillary area in both eyes. Laboratory tests revealed microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with thrombocytopenia; hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, platelet 60,000/uL, haptoglobin < 7 mg/dL, with positive schistocytes (2.1/HPF). C-reactive protein was elevated (5.93 mg/dL) and complements were marginally decreased (C3/C4 80/6 mg/dL), but antinuclear antibody, anti-dsDNA, anti-SSA and anti-SSB were negative. She showed positive LA with high titers of anti-β2-GPI (IgM/IgG 225.6/140.7 IU/mL) and anticardiolipin antibodies (IgM/IgG 90.5/159.6 IU/mL). Renal ultrasonography showed acute pyelonephritis and acute kidney injury, and kidney biopsy findings were compatible with thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA). In addition, valvular dysfunction was noted in echocardiography. Brain MRI showed multiple infarction at right periventricular and subcortical area and left frontal lobe.

case_report: A 6-year-old Chinese girl visited the Department of Ophthalmology at People’s Hospital of Leshan in August 2017. Her parents noted a gradual decline in her vision and a bluish tint to the sclera. There was no family history of notable eye conditions, and no infections or abnormalities were reported during pregnancy or birth. Genetic disorders were not known in the family. A general pediatric physical examination revealed normal findings across all systems. The parents and other family members, all native Chinese, exhibited no eye abnormalities. Ophthalmological examination revealed prominently protruding corneas and a marked bluish discoloration of the sclera in both eyes.
test_results: Pentacam HR anterior segment tomography indicated that keratoconus with steepening in both eyes which have a maximum keratometric power of 54.10 D in the right eye and a maximum keratometric power of 54.40 D in the other eye. The thinnest point of cornea assessed by Pentacam, which showed that the right eye was 324 μm thickness with corneal astigmatism in topography (− 2.6D at 163 degrees) and 313 μm thickness measured in the other eye with corneal astigmatism in topography (− 2.7D at 172 degrees). The best corrected visual acuity of right eye was 80/200 and the manifest refraction was − 4.75 /− 2.25 × 180. In the left eye, the best corrected visual acuity was 60/200 with − 3.00/ -4.00 × 170. Intraocular pressure was within normal levels (10 mmHg in the both eyes). Axial length was 21.45 mm in the right eye and 21.33 mm in the left eye. Specular microscopy showed that the right eye with the density of 3,459 cells/mm2 in corneal endothelial and 3,654 cells/mm2 in the left eye.

case_report: A 2.5-year-old boy was seen at the Dentistry Department of Pediatric Dentistry Faculty, Shiraz University of Medical Sciences, in June 2011. He exhibited early loss of the mandibular primary canines and the maxillary right primary canine. Clinical examination showed absence of all maxillary and mandibular primary incisors. According to his parents, the primary incisors had not yet emerged. Extraoral examination noted lip eversion and fine hair, with normal eyebrows and eyelashes. There were no issues with heat intolerance or sweating. The toenails were observed to be spoon-shaped and underdeveloped. A panoramic view was not obtained due to the child's lack of cooperation. Examination of the parents' oral health showed normal dentition and no abnormalities in nails, scalp, hair, or eyebrows. There was no family history of similar conditions, except for a cleft palate in one of the maternal cousins.
test_results: Periapical radiography showed primary anterior germs. DNA was isolated from peripheral blood leukocyte collected in EDTA via the standard salting out method. Two coding exons, exon-intron boundaries, and part of 3’-UTR of MSX1 were polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplified, and the amplicons were subjected to mutation analysis by bidirectional direct sequencing (Bioneer, Korea). Regarding the GenBank entry AF426432, one homozygous C>T variant, 6 nucleotides 3’ of the stop codon (3’-UTR) of MSX1, was identified. While control DNA with C/T genotype was semi-digested into three fragments, the patient’s sample (T/T genotype) was not digested by the Avall enzyme.

case_report: A 13-year-old female presented with severe oral bleeding, nosebleeds, and a petechial rash. Initial blood tests showed severe thrombocytopenia (3x10^3/μL), anemia (6.2 g/dL), and lymphocytopenia (850/μL). She had been treated with oral prednisone at 1 mg/kg/day and intravenous immunoglobulin at 1 g/kg (two doses) for a previous diagnosis of idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) five months prior, without improvement. Her medical history included Raynaud's phenomenon, hair loss, joint pain, malar rash, sensitivity to sunlight, and fatigue without weight loss. Twelve months before admission, tests showed positive anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA) at a titer of 1/320 and positive anti-transglutaminase antibodies. Upon admission, she exhibited malar rash, vasculitic-type lesions on the fingers, and a purpuric rash on the feet and lower limbs. Laboratory results showed normal systemic inflammation markers. Hemolysis parameters (lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin, indirect bilirubin), renal function, and urinalysis were normal. Reticulocyte count was 3.5%, and blood smear showed no schistocytes or abnormalities in leukocytes and erythrocytes. Plasma ADAMTS-13 activity was normal (73%). Microbiological tests for bacteria, viruses (including cytomegalovirus, parvovirus B19, Epstein-Barr virus, herpes simplex virus), and fungi were negative.
test_results: positive direct antiglobulin (“Coombs”) test, positive ANA (title 1/1280), anti dsDNA (36 IU / mL), anti-Ro/SS-A and anti-La antibodies. Hypocomplementemia (C3 73.30 mg/dL; C4 9.93 mg/dL).

case_report: An 82-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus presented with a several-month history of unsteady gait and urinary incontinence. Neurological examination showed mild spasticity in the lower limbs and generalized hyperreflexia, but no Babinski sign or ankle clonus was present. There were no bulbar symptoms or signs, including dysarthria, dysphagia, or dysphonia, and tests for extrapyramidal symptoms, ocular movements, and parkinsonism were unremarkable. Her mini-mental state examination score was 25/30. A urodynamic study revealed dysfunction during the storage phases, indicating neurogenic detrusor overactivity. Brain MRI showed periventricular and deep white matter signal changes in the FLAIR image with no ventricular enlargement (Evans index = 0.26). Electrodiagnostic studies, including a nerve conduction study, needle electromyography, and evoked potentials, were conducted but showed unremarkable results except for prolonged central motor conduction time to the upper and lower limbs in motor-evoked potentials (MEPs). In the spine MRI, mild atrophy of the medulla oblongata was suspected; the ratio of the sagittal diameter of the medulla oblongata to that of the pons was 0.43. No pial FLAIR signal changes were observed, nor was the eye-spot sign in the anterior medulla oblongata. Hydromyelia in the cervicomedullary junction and signal abnormalities radiating laterally from the central canal in the middle portion of the caudal medulla oblongata were observed.
test_results: GFAP gene sequencing revealed a heterozygous missense mutation (c.197G > A, p.Arg66Gln) previously reported to be pathogenic.

case_report: A 67-year-old male experienced new-onset fatigue and lightheadedness while golfing. His heart rate at home was 34 bpm, prompting a visit to the emergency department. He reported no chest pain, fainting, or palpitations. There were no recent changes in his medications, and he had a strong history of medication adherence. His medical history included atrial fibrillation treated with ablation 8 years ago, type-one diabetes managed with an insulin pump, obstructive sleep apnea, and stage IIIb chronic kidney disease. An echocardiogram performed one month earlier showed an ejection fraction of 60–65%, mild left ventricular hypertrophy, grade one diastolic dysfunction, and no valvular disease. A recent outpatient nuclear medicine stress test was unremarkable. His medications included apixaban, amlodipine, flecainide, simvastatin, hydrochlorothiazide, lisinopril, metoprolol, and insulin, all dosed appropriately for his renal function. On arrival, his vital signs were notable for a heart rate of 24 bpm, blood pressure of 142/66 mmHg, respiratory rate of 18/min, oxygen saturation of 99% on room air, and body temperature of 36 °C. Laboratory results showed potassium 5.6 mmol/L, creatinine 2.12 mg/dL (baseline 1.7), BUN 43 mg/dL, AST 126 IU/L, ALT 147 IU/L, hemoglobin 17.1 g/dL, and initial troponin of 15 ng/L, with other results within normal limits. Electrocardiography indicated sinus bradycardia without heart block or ischemia. Chest radiography showed no active disease. Hyperkalemia was treated with insulin, dextrose, and sodium polystyrene sulfonate. Due to symptomatic bradycardia, metoprolol succinate and flecainide were withheld. Lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide were also withheld due to acute kidney injury, and intravenous fluids were administered. Over the next 24 hours, his bradycardia and hyperkalemia resolved, and he was discharged on a reduced dose of metoprolol succinate with instructions to resume flecainide three days post-discharge. The rest of his home medications remained unchanged.
test_results: EKG confirmed bradycardia at a rate of 30 with complete heart block and ventricular escape complexes.

case_report: A 39-year-old Japanese man presented with frontal lobe symptoms, including repetitive and socially inappropriate behaviors, disinhibition, and euphoria, and was admitted to a university hospital in November 2011. Over the previous 2 years, he exhibited slight memory impairment and abnormal behaviors, such as reading comics during a parent-teacher association meeting and pilfering. During hospitalization, he was placed in a secure unit within the psychiatric ward due to entering other rooms without permission and inappropriately touching female nurses. The patient’s Mini-Mental State Examination score was 23/30, and his Frontal Assessment Battery score was 12/18. Physical examination revealed brisk deep tendon reflexes in the extremities and a positive Babinski sign bilaterally, with no extrapyramidal symptoms. Blood tests showed subtle liver dysfunction with aspartate transaminase at 77 IU/L (normal range 9–37 IU/L), alanine transaminase at 176 IU/L (normal range 3–49 IU/L), iron deficiency (106 μg/dl; normal range 120–140 μg/dl), and elevated ferritin (656 ng/ml; normal range 27–211 ng/ml). Brain fluid-attenuated inversion recovery magnetic resonance imaging indicated diffuse high-intensity white matter areas and slight diffuse atrophy in the cerebral cortices without the 'eye of the tiger' sign. No abnormalities were found in the cerebrospinal fluid or on electroencephalography.
test_results: Exome sequencing identified a mutation in the TYROBP (DAP12) gene, located on chromosome 19q13.1. The mutation was a homozygous single-base deletion of 141G in exon 3 in the patient’s genomic DNA. His parents were each heterozygous for the mutation.

case_report: A 45-year-old female patient presented with multiple oval to round hypopigmented papules on her trunk and limbs. These lesions first appeared at the age of 15 and have gradually increased in number and size. Dermatological examination identified multiple oval to round hypopigmented papules, measuring 5 to 15 mm, located on the abdomen, chest, flanks, and back. The patient's medical history was unremarkable. Family history revealed similar symptoms in her father, two younger brothers, older sister, and daughter, all of whom developed these lesions during puberty. Her father had lesions on his abdomen and back, her sister on her abdomen, back, and upper extremities, her two brothers on their abdomens and backs, and her daughter on her lower abdomen. Laboratory tests, including urinalysis, liver function tests, and electrocardiogram, were normal. X-ray examinations of the hands, feet, chest, pelvis, supernumerary vertebrae, and ribs showed no anomalies. Additional laboratory evaluations for breast, thyroid, and gastrointestinal tract cancers were also normal.
test_results: A skin biopsy specimen demonstrated increased amounts of collagen in the dermis, particularly in the reticular dermis. Masson's trichrome stain revealed thickened and irregularly arranged dense fascicular bundles of collagen. Van Gieson-stained elastic bundles were decreased and fragmented.

case_report: A 14-year-old girl visited the outpatient Department of Periodontia at Government Dental College and Hospital, Ahmedabad, India, with concerns about early loss of both deciduous and permanent teeth, as well as mobility in the remaining teeth. She is the first child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents. Her deciduous teeth erupted normally but gradually fell out by the age of 4-5 years. Similarly, her permanent teeth also erupted normally but were lost prematurely. Two years ago, she experienced mobility and bleeding gums, for which she received periodontal flap surgery. After one and a half years, she had the same complaints and returned to the hospital. There is no family history of ichthyosis or palmoplantar keratodermas. The patient reported developing fissures, thickening, and flaking of the skin on her palms and soles, leading to peeling and exposing red, thin areas since the age of 3-4 years. These skin issues have had periods of exacerbation and remission since early childhood, with regular visits to a dermatologist but no improvement. She has also had recurrent systemic infections. Extra-oral examination revealed well-demarcated, yellowish, keratotic plaques on the skin of her palms and soles, extending to the dorsal surfaces. The skin on both palms and soles was peeling, leaving underlying red, shiny areas. Well-circumscribed, psoriasiform, erythematous, scaly plaques were present on the elbows and knees bilaterally, along with nail dystrophy and transverse grooving. Her fingers appeared pointed, giving a clawed appearance. Intra-oral examination showed edentulous areas between teeth 44 and 33, and teeth 11, 21, and 22 were also missing. The edentulous maxillary and mandibular ridges were covered with normal mucosa. The remaining teeth (12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 22, 24, 25, 26, 33, 34, 35, 36, 44, 45, and 46) were covered with soft deposits and a band of subgingival calculus. The gingiva was fiery red with inflammatory gingival enlargement classified as grade II according to the Iva Ingle Classification. Pathological migration was noted in teeth 12, 14, 23, 24, 33, and 34. Grade III mobility was observed in tooth 14, grade II in teeth 24, 25, 33, 34, 36, and 44, and grade I in the remaining teeth. There was grade III recession in teeth 14 and 33.
test_results: Orthopantogram showed extensive alveolar bone loss in all remaining teeth. The alveolar bone around the mobile teeth was devoid of definable lamina dura. An extensive alveolar bone loss was noted, giving the teeth 31, 41 and 43 a 'floating in air appearance.'

case_report: A 21-year-old male visited the orthopedic outpatient department with a history of left hip pain persisting for 1 year after a minor fall. The patient reported difficulty in performing heavy strenuous activities such as running, jumping, and other sports activities. Pain was noted at the terminal range of movements. The FABER test yielded a positive result. The patient was able to actively raise his leg.
test_results: Radiograph left hip revealed a radiolucent swelling along inferior part of neck with a well-defined, eccentric osteolytic lesion involving subcapital region of the left femoral neck. The lesion was oval shaped and without any calcification or periosteal reaction. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) suggested of cystic lesion involving synovial lining near head-and-neck junction of the left femur. Histopathological examination showed lobular pattern with stellate to spindle-shaped cells on the myxoid background. Few osteoclast type of giant cells were found in the periphery of the lobules. Tumor cells had oval- to spindle-shaped nucleus with surrounding densely eosinophilic cytoplasm within a myxoid background.

case_report: A 12-year-old girl presented with bleeding gums and loose teeth. Her deciduous teeth erupted normally but began shedding early at three years old, with complete shedding by six years old. She experienced dry, thickened skin and frequent skin infections. The family history indicated consanguineous marriage and similar symptoms in her younger brother.
