Intraoral examination revealed significant drifting of teeth, poor oral hygiene with heavy plaque accumulation, and red, soft, edematous gingiva that bled profusely upon probing. General examination showed symmetrical, well-defined, keratotic, and confluent plaques on the skin of the palms, soles, and elbows. The lesions on the soles extended to the lateral malleoli and Achilles' tendons. The skin was dry and rough. The nails exhibited transverse grooving and slight pitting. The patient had a history of recurrent skin infections. Examination of the feet showed loss of the medial longitudinal arches and bilateral pes planus.
test_results: Superficial palmar biopsy revealed marked hyperkeratosis with focal parakeratosis and acanthotic epidermis. OPG of the patient showed severe alveolar bone loss in relation to the existing permanent teeth. X-ray of hands revealed that the metacarpal index was 9.3, implying elongation of the metacarpals. In lateral projection of feet, the line of the first metatarsal made an angle with the midtalar line revealing that the proband had flat feet.

case_report: A 59-year-old Japanese man visited our hospital in April 2013 for a workplace medical examination. He was a former smoker (from age 20 to 26, 1 pack per day) and had no physical symptoms or family history of malignancies. The chest X-ray did not detect any abnormal shadow, but a CT scan revealed a mass with an irregular margin measuring 18 × 15 mm in diameter located in the subpleural area of S9 of the right lower lobe. No nodules were found in other lobes, and there was no swelling of regional lymph nodes. An FDG-PET scan was performed but did not show definitive FDG accumulation. Tumor markers including CEA, SLX, SCC, CYFRA, NSE, and ProGRP were all within normal ranges. In May 2013, a lung partial resection was performed using video-assisted thoracic surgery (VATS). During thoracotomy, the mass was found at the periphery of S9 of the right lower lobe with a whitely transparent surface. The mass was solid and hard upon palpation. Intra-operative pathological findings (frozen section) showed inflammatory granuloma with coagulation necrosis.
test_results: The permanent pathological examination showed occlusion of the peripheral pulmonary artery by worms and formation of a necrotic mass surrounded by reactive inflammatory cells and hemorrhage in hematoxylin–eosin stain and Elastica van Gieson stain.

case_report: A 71-year-old female with a history of osteoporosis, elevated vitamin B6 levels identified during a work health screening, and hypertension visited an outpatient endocrinology clinic. She reported experiencing generalized weakness and bone pain for the past six months. She mentioned that her bone pain, which had been present for many years, worsened following bisphosphonate therapy. The most recent episode of pain began six months ago and coincided with a denosumab injection. She reported no history of fractures, kidney stones, injuries, muscle aches, dental issues, or early tooth loss. Her family history included a mother who had a traumatic hip fracture at a young age. Physical examination revealed no abnormalities, and her vital signs were within normal limits. Muscle weakness was noted to be primarily axial, but strength testing showed 5/5 in all muscle groups without any asymmetry. No gum or dental abnormalities were observed.
test_results: The laboratory findings were significant for serum alkaline phosphatase 34 U/L (38-126) with a repeat being 22 U/L.

case_report: The first child admitted to the UDP-WA program was a 7-year-old girl with a congenital multisystem disorder. She had nearly 50 hospital inpatient admissions, 13 general anaesthetics, and more than 200 hospital outpatient visits for consultations across multiple specialist clinics. She had been presented to national and international experts, including a virtual international expert dysmorphology network. Discussions at the Expert Panel meeting included multiple specialists suggesting the possibility of various RNA processing disorders. A literature review by panel members that evening narrowed the search to a condition with a prevalence of approximately 1 in 1 million.
test_results: Compound heterozygous SKIV2L mutations were identified.

case_report: A 6-month-old male infant presented with persistent vomiting and a three-day history of cold symptoms. On physical examination, he was alert, had a fever, rapid breathing, signs of dehydration, reduced muscle tone, and a breath odor resembling acetone. He is the first child of parents who are related by blood, with no family history of similar conditions. His growth and development were normal until the recent illness. Initial laboratory tests indicated severe metabolic acidosis (pH: 7.06, bicarbonate: 8.5) and significant ketonuria. Blood glucose, electrolytes, liver enzymes, and thyroid function tests were within normal ranges. Tests for sepsis and cerebrospinal fluid analysis were negative for infections. The patient had elevated plasma lactate levels (27 and 35 mmol/L on two separate occasions) and normal blood ammonia levels.
test_results: Urine organic acids analysis by gas chromatography/mass spectrometry (GC/MS) indicated a very high level of 2-methyl-3-hydroxybutyric acid (MHB) (1335 mmol/mol creatinine) and trace amount of tiglylglycine (TG). Chromatography of plasma amino acids with HPLC method showed a slight increase of serine, glutamine, and aspartate amino acids. Brain MRI at the seventh month of life showed mild hypomyelination of white matter and the results were normal for other parameters.

case_report: A 32-year-old woman presented with partial lipodystrophy. Her parents, from nearby villages on Madere Island, Portugal, had no known consanguinity. Her medical history was unremarkable until puberty, when she experienced myalgia during exercise. Pubertal development was normal with spontaneous menarche at age 11, followed by primary oligomenorrhea with menstrual cycles of 30 to 60 days. She reported a first-trimester spontaneous miscarriage at age 27. Recently, she was treated with amitryptiline and then lamotrigine for painful peripheral neuropathy of the limbs. Physical examination revealed lipoatrophy of the four limbs, including palms and soles, but sparing the face, with contrasting truncal and abdominal subcutaneous fat accumulation. Peripheral lipoatrophy and central fat accumulation had progressively appeared since puberty. There was a notable loss of muscle mass from the limbs. Her height was 158 cm, weight 60 kg (BMI: 24 kg/m2), with waist and hip perimeters of 92 and 96 cm, respectively. Skin examination showed livedo reticularis, dry, tight, and atrophied skin, petechiae, purpuric lesions, and hyperkeratosis, predominantly in the extremities. No acanthosis nigricans or hirsutism were observed. Blood pressure was 120/70 mmHg, and cardiac examination was normal. Hair graying began at age 25, and she underwent surgical extraction of bilateral cataracts at age 26. Among her five siblings, a brother died at 44 from myocardial infarction, with reported dysmorphic features, premature cataracts, insulin-treated diabetes since age 26, and severe atherosclerosis leading to foot amputation at age 38. A 42-year-old sister died from sarcoma of the quadriceps femoris muscle. Biological investigations showed severe insulin resistance with moderate fasting hyperinsulinemia (168 pmol/L, normal < 100), reaching extremely high values after an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) (maximal value 53800 pmol/L at T60 min, then 29750 pmol/L at T120 min, normal < 520), without altered glucose tolerance. Hypertriglyceridemia was associated with low HDL-cholesterol and slightly elevated alanine transaminase (ALT) and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) levels. Sex-hormone binding globulin (SHBG) and adiponectin levels were low. Pituitary-ovarian functions and testosterone levels were normal, but serum anti-müllerian hormone (AMH) and inhibin B were undetectable, indicating decreased ovarian reserve. Pelvic and transvaginal sonography showed a normal uterus but enlarged ovaries (right: 6.2 cm2, left: 6.9 cm2, normal volume < 5.5 cm2) with follicles of 10.4 to 15.8 mm. Electrocardiogram and dipyridamole-thallium myocardial scintigraphy were normal, while doppler ultrasonography showed a mildly increased carotid intima-media thickness (0.9 mm, normal < 0.6 mm). Other investigations revealed mild sensorineural hearing loss. A whole-body MRI did not reveal any neoplasm. Peripheral lipoatrophy was quantified by skinfold thickness measurements. Whole-body dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) showed increased body fat, predominantly in the trunk area, consistent with clinical findings. Bone mineralization was normal. MRI imaging showed peripheral lipoatrophy affecting the four limbs. In the thighs, subcutaneous fat was asymmetrically distributed, with normal medial but reduced postero-lateral adipose tissue. MRI also showed severe loss of gluteal fat and increased subcutaneous and visceral abdominal fat depots. Imaging also revealed liver steatosis. Sequencing of LMNA and PPARG did not reveal any alterations.
test_results: WRN sequencing revealed homozygosity for a c.2242C>T transition in exon 19, predicting the synthesis of a p.Q748X WRN protein, truncated in its helicase domain.

case_report: A 13-year-old female patient, with no family history of cardiovascular disease, presented with a noticeable heart murmur and reduced exercise capacity. At five months old, she was identified with a complex congenital heart malformation at a local hospital, but further evaluation was not pursued due to limited medical technology and financial constraints. The patient developed normally during early childhood, and the condition was not apparent to the family until her exercise tolerance recently decreased. Physical examination revealed a height of 1.52 m, weight of 36 kg, a resting heart rate of 118 beats per minute, and an oxygen saturation level of 97%. Apical pulsation was observed in the right anterior chest, and systolic murmurs were heard.
test_results: The cardiac apex is oriented towards the right side in situs solitus. Except for the left superior vena cava, which terminates in the left atrium, the systemic and pulmonary veins drain into the respective right and left atria. The atrioventricular connections are concordant with a horizontally positioned septum. The VSD measures approximately 16 mm in diameter and is located above the mitral valve, below and to the left of the tricuspid valve, and directly below the aortic valve. Both ventricles are substantially enlarged, with the right ventricle occupying the upper right region and the left ventricle situated in the lower left quadrant, in concordance with the atrioventricular connections. An aorta is located on the right and posterior to the pulmonary trunk and primarily arises from the right ventricle. Based on the 3D model, it was observed that the ventricular septal defect (VSD) was near the aortic valve, while the tricuspid valve was distally positioned from the pulmonary valve. Further supported by the cardiac catheterization results which indicated a pulmonary resistance of 2.19 wood and a Qp/Qs ratio (pulmonary-to-systemic flow ratio) of 7.72.
diagnosis: Criss-cross heart with double outlet right ventricle

case_report: An 83-year-old woman was referred to the pneumonology department of our hospital due to increasing productive cough and haemoptysis. Over the past 30 years, she experienced dyspnoea on exertion and increased expectoration of mucoid sputum, which became purulent during infectious exacerbations, often with bloody streaked sputum. She denied fever, wheezes, chest pain, weight loss, or any symptoms indicative of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Her medical history included pulmonary fibrosis diagnosed 6 years ago in another country, left ovarian cancer treated with hysterosalpingo-oophorectomy 20 years ago, arterial hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and osteoporosis. There was no family history of respiratory disease, and she had never smoked. No history of GERD was noted in her medical records. On physical examination, her vital signs were normal, and finger clubbing was not present. Mild inspiratory crackles were noted at the lower third of both lung fields. Laboratory investigations showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 15 mm/h, C-reactive protein of 1.03 mg/L, oxygen saturation at 96% on room air, and arterial blood gases analysis with PaO2 of 77.3 mmHg, PCO2 of 41.5 mmHg, and pH of 7.45 (FiO2: 21%). Immunologic tests, including rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, C3, C4, p-ANCA, and c-ANCA, were within normal range, while antinuclear antibody (ANA) levels were mildly raised (1/160) without a characteristic immunofluorescence pattern. Pulmonary function tests (PFTs) conducted one month before admission revealed a forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) of 1.83 L (58% predicted), a forced vital capacity (FVC) of 1.95 L (55% predicted), and FEV1/FVC of 105%. Static lung volumes measurement and diffusion test were not performed due to the patient's inability to cooperate. Sputum results were negative for mycobacteria. Bronchoscopy was not performed as the patient did not consent. An old chest radiograph from 25 years ago showed widening of the trachea and main stem bronchi. These findings were confirmed by a new chest radiograph on the first day of hospitalisation, with no deterioration in tracheobronchial dilatation.
test_results: A high-resolution chest CT showed enlarged trachea and main stem bronchi (trachea with both sagittal and axial dimensions of 2.1 cm, right and left main bronchi measuring in axial dimensions 2.1 cm and 1.8 cm, respectively), extensive bronchiectasis, interstitial fibrosis of the lower lobes, and chronic pleural thickening.

case_report: The patient is a 15-month-old boy with a history of global developmental delay observed for 10 months. At 5 months old, he was unable to raise his head. An electroencephalogram was normal, but brain MRI showed slightly widened bilateral ventricles and subarachnoid space. Chromosome karyotype analysis and screening for genetic metabolic diseases revealed no abnormalities. Physiotherapy and rehabilitation training were administered but showed limited effectiveness. At 15 months, he still could not lift his head or sit unsupported, nor could he intentionally say 'mom' or 'dad.' He was born at 38 weeks and one day to a non-consanguineous couple, with a birth weight of 3.75 kg and a body length of 50 cm, appropriate for gestational age, but with an occipitofrontal head circumference of 38 cm (Z score +2.91SD). At 6 days old, he was admitted to the hospital for 12 days due to neonatal hyperbilirubinemia and pneumonia, during which low muscle tone and strength were noted. The family opted for observation without treatment due to the absence of other positive symptoms or signs. At referral, physical examination showed a body weight of 10 kg, body length of 80 cm, and head circumference of 48.5 cm (+1SD). No jaundice was observed in the skin and sclera. Notable facial features included mildly coarse facial features, hypertelorism, a tented upper lip, an exaggerated Cupid’s bow, macroglossia, an open mouth, and arched eyebrows. Lung examination revealed no stridor, crackles, or crepitus, and heart sounds were normal without murmurs. There was no abdominal distention, and the liver and spleen were non-palpable. Marked hypotonia was particularly evident in the lower limbs. Abdominal wall reflex was weak, and neither Achilles nor knee tendon reflexes were elicited. Ribbed arch valgus and pectus excavatum were observed. The palm and sole prints were deep, and horizontal wrinkles were present on both knees. The testes had not descended into the scrotum. The Gesell Developmental Schedules (GDS) analysis yielded a score of 8.9 for gross motor function, 23.7 for fine motor function, 26.6 for adaptive behavior, 26.6 for language ability, and 26.6 for social skills, indicating global developmental delay.
test_results: NGS detected a homozygous TBCK mutation c.247C > T(p.Arg83Ter) in the patient, which was a nonsense mutation located in exon 3. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the child was homozygous for this variant, and his healthy father and mother were both carriers.
diagnosis: Infantile Hypotonia with Psychomotor Retardation and Characteristic Facies type 3

case_report: A 17-year-old Korean male presented with itchy, violaceous blisters and nodules on both legs, which began at the age of 3 years. These blisters appeared following minor mechanical trauma and evolved into lichenified nodules due to repetitive scratching. Mild toenail dystrophy was also noted. No other skin or mucosal lesions were observed outside of the legs and toenails. There was no similar clinical history in either the maternal or paternal family lines. Pathological examination showed several dermal vacuoles with an intact dermo-epidermal junction, and no subepidermal blisters were detected. Transmission electron microscopy indicated prominent and diffuse vacuolar changes in the upper dermis, though it was unclear if the anchoring fibrils were significantly reduced. Two additional skin biopsies from the leg were performed, but subepidermal blisters were still not observed, and the pathological findings were consistent with the initial sample. Clinical and histologic findings remained inconclusive.
test_results: The patient harbored two variants of COL7A1: the novel missense variant c.3301C>T (p.R1101W) (NM_000094.4), derived from his father, and a known premature termination codon (PTC) variant, c.5797C>T (p.R1933*) (NM_000094.4), derived from the mother.

case_report: A 20-year-old Japanese woman presented for scoliosis treatment. She is the second-born of dichorionic diamniotic twins. She had previously visited a pediatrics division due to restricted motion in both elbow joints and clubfoot. At 3 years old, she exhibited proteinuria and was found to have focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Scoliosis became noticeable at age 12, but she did not seek treatment until she was 19. Her weight was 38.6 kg and height was 155 cm. Physical examination revealed a small forehead, hypotelorism, shortened fingers on both hands, and clubfoot. No café au lait spots or mental retardation were noted. The trunk showed an irregular waistline and rib hump indicative of scoliosis. Due to significant deformities beyond the elbow and ankle joints, muscular strength in the upper and lower limbs could not be accurately assessed. Other muscle weakness was absent, and there were no walking issues. Sensation, urination, and reflexes were normal except for hyperreflexia in the limbs and a positive Babinski reflex. Spirometry indicated a forced vital capacity (FVC) of 67.4%. Proteinuria was present, but there was no renal dysfunction or hypertension.
test_results: A MafB missense polymorphic mutation was identified. X-ray images of the limbs showed remarkable osteolysis in joints of the hand, elbow, and ankle. Computerized tomography revealed a partially narrowed vertebral arch. Magnetic resonance images showed deviation of the spinal cord.
Orpha_name: Multicentric carpo-tarsal osteolysis with or without nephropathy

case_report: An 18-year-old female patient presented with repeated episodes of gum bleeding since childhood and a history of prolonged bleeding following minor trauma. There was no history of bone pain. She had received multiple blood transfusions in the past, though specific details were unavailable. The patient was born to parents who were consanguineously married. On examination, she exhibited pallor and gum bleeding. Her vital signs were stable, and examinations of the cardiovascular, respiratory, and other systems were unremarkable. Laboratory investigations showed hemoglobin at 7 g/dl, total leukocyte count at 4200, differential count with polymorphs at 74%, lymphocytes at 23%, eosinophils at 3%, platelets at 2.1 lakhs, red blood cell (RBC) count at 2.82 lakhs, hematocrit at 19.3, mean corpuscular volume at 68.4, mean corpuscular hemoglobin at 18.4, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration at 26.9, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate at 15/32. Peripheral smear revealed microcytic hypochromic RBCs, normal white blood cell count with no immature cells, and adequate platelet count with normal size and morphology. Bleeding time was greater than 15 minutes, activated partial thromboplastin time was 27 seconds (control - 27 seconds), and prothrombin time/INR was 1. Serum fibrinogen was 200 mg/dL. The patient exhibited gum bleeding with a normal platelet count, normal platelet morphology, and prolonged bleeding time.
test_results: Clot retraction test was done, in which blood is allowed to clot in a test tube, and clot retraction noted after 24 h. It was absent, i.e., no clot retraction was seen after 24 h. Platelet aggregation was induced with ristocetin, ADP, and collagen. Absent platelet aggregation was seen with ADP; however, it was seen with ristocetin and collagen.

case_report: Mr. ABC, a 57-year-old male from a rural area with a history of chronic alcohol consumption over 35 years, consuming 400-500 ml of Mahuwa Daru daily in the evening. After being forced to stop alcohol intake by relatives, he developed tremors and sleep disturbances the next day. On the third day, he was found disoriented, unkempt, and incontinent of both feces and urine by coworkers and was subsequently admitted. General examination revealed malnourishment and thickening of the post-auricular and ulnar nerves. Vital signs were within normal limits. Mental state examination indicated disorientation. Pupillary reactions were symmetrical. There were no lateralizing deficits or signs of meningeal irritation. Laboratory tests showed normal haemogram, liver and renal function tests, and serum electrolytes. The patient was administered Inj Thiamine 100 mg and managed for withdrawal symptoms. He experienced four episodes of seizures over the first three days of admission. EEG results were normal.
test_results: MRI-Brain showed hyper intense signal intensities involving genu, body and splenium of corpus callosum on T2W and FLAIR.

case_report: A 33-year-old male with a history of congenital human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with positive anti-phospholipid antibodies (on immunosuppressive therapy), and chronic kidney disease (stage IIIb) arrived at the emergency department experiencing abdominal pain and shortness of breath. The patient has a history of lupus complications, including endomyocardial biopsy-confirmed lymphocytic myocarditis with residual dilated cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction of 35% and baseline brain natriuretic peptide of less than 40 pg/ml), right atrial thrombus (managed with warfarin), lupus nephritis, a previous cardiac arrest associated with respiratory failure of unknown origin with nonspecific bronchoalveolar lavage, and multiple intubations. Upon arrival (first day), his oxygen saturation was in the lower 70s. Vital signs indicated hypotension at 70/40 mm Hg, tachycardia at 110 bpm, and tachypnea, which improved with fluids, norepinephrine, and initial bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) ventilation followed by emergent intubation. Bedside ultrasound at presentation revealed signs of cardiogenic shock with volume overload. Laboratory results showed lactic acidosis and severe transaminitis.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) of chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed pleuropericardial effusion with ground-glass opacities, tapering of pulmonary arteries without evidence of embolism, diffuse ascites with thickening of the bowel wall with adrenal hyper-enhancement along with bilateral renal and splenic infarcts with angiogram showing significant narrowing of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA), the diminutive size of inferior mesenteric artery, tapering of bilateral renal arteries, and celiac trunk branches.

case_report: A 3-month-old male infant was brought to a tertiary center in December 2015 for evaluation of progressive cholestatic hepatitis. He was delivered vaginally at 39 weeks of gestation, weighing 3.4 kg, with no perinatal complications. Jaundice was observed approximately one week post-birth. During follow-up for prolonged jaundice at a local hospital, abdominal ultrasonography, scintigraphy, and liver biopsy were performed at around one month of age, ruling out biliary atresia. Upon admission, the infant was active with normal growth parameters: weight of 7.3 kg (85–90th percentile) and height of 62.3 cm (50–75th percentile). Physical examination revealed yellowish skin, icteric sclera, and hepatosplenomegaly. Developmental milestones were appropriate for age, including head control. Blood tests showed: white blood cell count of 10,200/mm3, hemoglobin level of 10.0 g/dL, and platelet count of 180,000/mm3. Liver function tests indicated aspartate aminotransferase/alanine aminotransferase levels of 1,599/301 IU/L, γ-glutamyltransferase (GGT) level of 22 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase level of 1,423 IU/L, total bilirubin/direct bilirubin levels of 9.3/7.0 mg/dL, prothrombin time of 2.74 INR, activated partial thromboplastin time of 74.3 seconds, protein/albumin levels of 5.0/3.1 g/dL, and cholesterol level of 54 mg/dL. Serum bile acid level was elevated to 131.4 µmol/L, and serum 25-OH vitamin D3 level was 6.7 ng/mL. Renal function and electrolyte levels were within normal ranges. Tests for toxoplasmosis, herpes, rubella, and cytomegalovirus were negative. Liver biopsy showed giant cell transformation of hepatocytes and moderate portal inflammation with periportal fibrosis. Immunohistochemical staining indicated focal decrease in bile salt export protein (BSEP) expression and absence of CD10 expression. A urine sample was collected and dried on filter paper for further analysis.
test_results: It revealed profuse urinary excretion of unusual bile acids, 3β-monohydroxy-Δ5-bile acid derivatives, which account for more than 86.5% of total bile acids apart from ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA).
Orpha_name: Congenital bile acid synthesis defect type 3

case_report: A 38-year-old Caucasian female, the second child from a non-consanguineous marriage, has a history of recurrent bronchopneumonias and middle ear infections starting at age four, leading to hearing impairment. Her older sister had hypogammaglobulinemia and died at age 10 from a severe respiratory infection. Two younger sisters are healthy with normal serum Ig levels. Both parents showed no signs of agammaglobulinemia. The patient was fully vaccinated, including live Bacille Calmette-Guerin and live-attenuated oral polio vaccines, without complications. At age fifteen, she exhibited severely decreased serum Ig levels, absence of circulating CD19+ B-cells, and lymphoid hypoplasia, leading to the initiation of Ig replacement therapy (IRT). At sixteen, she underwent an allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) from a healthy sibling donor, but engraftment failed, with no donor DNA detected and extremely low Ig levels recorded six months post-HSCT [IgG 2.5 g/L (NR 8.0-18.0 g/L), IgA 0.21 g/L (NR 0.9-4.5 g/L), IgM 0.14 g/L (NR 0.7-2.8 g/L)]. Over the next seventeen years, she continued intravenous IRT with occasional respiratory and intestinal infections treated conservatively. At age thirty-three, due to abdominal pain, frequent diarrhea, and weight loss (BMI 16.75 kg/m2), esophagogastroduodenoscopy and CT enterography were performed. Duodenum mucosa biopsy showed intraepithelial lymphocytosis with complete villous atrophy (Marsh-Oberhuber type 3c/Corazza-Villanacci grade B2). HLA analysis revealed the DQ5(1), 9(3) haplotype. A gluten-free diet was initiated, resulting in partial symptom regression. Throughout chronic care management, the patient presented with persistent leukocytosis [leukocytes 20.26x10^9/µL (NR 4-10x10^9/µL), 76.6% neutrophils (NR 40-60%)]. Immunophenotype of peripheral lymphocytes showed no circulating CD19+ B lymphocytes (NR 80-490/µL), CD3+CD4+ T lymphocytes 824 (NR 490-1640/µL), CD3+CD8+ T lymphocytes 1171 (NR 170-880/µL), and CD16+CD56+ 82 (NR 80-690/µL).
test_results: Clinical exome sequencing revealed the presence of a frameshift heterozygous variant c.441dup (p.Asp148Ter) in exon 4 of the SPI1 gene (NM_001080547). This genetic variant causes insertion of one nucleotide, which introduces a premature termination codon, leading to the truncation of the protein. The detected variant is very rare and has not been recorded in The Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD) population databases.

case_report: At the age of 16, the patient started having nighttime episodes marked by vocal sounds and movements of the hands and trunk, which were initially managed with carbamazepine. At the age of 35, these episodes returned and, even with the addition of topiramate, the frequency increased to up to three episodes per night.
test_results: VPSG recorded six episodes, lasting up to 96 s, among which three (50%) showed that asystole occurred after a mean of 19 s after the first motor activity and had a mean duration of 17 s. Two additional seizures occurred after CPM implantation, pacing the cardiac rhythm for 11 and 39 s. EEG showed a diffuse flattening of background activity, which was then followed by movement artifacts and then no longer interpretable. Brain MRI showed a lesion consistent with FCD in the left amygdala. Whole-exome sequencing revealed a pathogenic variant (c.1225delA, p.Thr409HisfsTer15) in DEPDC5.
Orpha_name: Autosomal dominant nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy

case_report: A 70-year-old male with a medical history of dilated cardiomyopathy and coronary heart disease came to the emergency department due to chest pain. He worked as a farmer and had no known exposure to asbestos. Acute cardiac issues were quickly excluded. A chest X-ray showed a right pneumothorax. A right pleural drain was inserted. Because of persistent air leaks, he subsequently had a right pulmonary apicectomy, partial pleurectomy, and talc poudrage performed via right thoracoscopy, which did not reveal any visible pleural abnormalities.
test_results: Histologic examination of pleural sections showed a single layer of epithelioid mesothelial cells (WT1+, calretinin+) with mild atypia and defective expression of BAP1, without evidence of adipose or lung tissues invasion.

case_report: A 22-year-old right-handed woman reported experiencing a global headache for 4 months, which began gradually and worsened over time. She also noted a progressive decline in vision in both eyes. She did not report any vomiting, seizures, or loss of consciousness. There were no other associated health conditions. Clinical examination of the central nervous system (CNS) showed normal higher mental functions and speech, but reduced visual acuity in both eyes. The pupils were of normal size and equally reactive to light. Examination of other cranial nerves, the sensory-motor system, and the cerebellum were all normal. Fundoscopy indicated bilateral papilledema.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan showed a lobulated heterogeneously T2-hyperintense right-sided intra-ventricular mass measuring 3 cm, which was extending up to the foramen of Monro. The squash preparation showed a cellular tumor composed of round monomorphic uniform-sized cells set in a background of fibrillary matrix of neuropils. Tumor cells displayed finely stippled granular chromatin, prominent micronucleoli and ill-defined cytoplasm. Nuclear pleomorphism, mitotic figures or necrotic debris were absent. Sections from the resected mass showed a tumor composed of monomorphic cells, with clear cytoplasm, round to oval nucleus, finely speckled chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli. Numerous arborising capillary-sized blood vessels were noted. No evidence of calcification, anisonucleosis, increased mitosis, necrosis or microvascular proliferation was seen. Immunohistochemistry displayed synaptophysin positivity in the tumor cells and neuropils, with GFAP expression restricted to the entrapped astrocytes only. MIB-1 labeling index (MIB-1LI) was <1%.

case_report: A 43-year-old male with a history of alcohol use presented with a 24-hour history of a painful rash on his torso, back, arms, and legs. He had been vomiting for the previous 48 hours, described cold extremities with difficulty walking, and reported daily use of heroin, crack cocaine, and alcohol. He also mentioned a chronic cough without shortness of breath, chest pain, or coughing up blood. Additionally, he reported being bitten by a friend's dog a week before admission. He was born in the UK and had always lived in London. On examination, he was tachycardic (HR 135) with cool extremities and a widespread non-blanching purpuric rash. He had reduced sensation and power in both lower limbs and epigastric tenderness on abdominal examination. There were no signs of deep vein thrombosis. Admission blood tests were conducted. Chest X-ray showed diffuse reticular opacity bilaterally, particularly in the mid and lower zones, similar to a previous radiograph from 2017. CT pulmonary angiography, requested due to raised d-dimer and sinus tachycardia, was negative for pulmonary emboli. Stool samples were collected for bacterial and viral PCR, as well as ova, cysts, and parasites. Sputum microscopy was requested to check for chest infection. Due to hyponatraemia and abnormal liver function tests, serology was tested for mycoplasma antibodies, and urine was tested for pneumococcal and legionella antigens. A blood-borne viral screen (HIV, hepatitis B and C) and a full vasculitis screen were conducted. Two sets of blood cultures were taken before starting co-amoxiclav for broad coverage of sepsis of unknown origin. Fibrinogen was 3.9 g/l, LDH was 2234 IU/l, and haptoglobins were 0.7 g/l. His urine dip was positive for blood and protein, so streptococcus titre, throat swab, and microscopy and culture were further requested. His vasculitic screen was negative for ANA, ANCA, ENA, Jo-1, LA, RNP, RO, Scl-70, SM, and anti-Scl. RF was mildly elevated at 26 IU/ml. C3 was 0.93 g/l, C4 was 0.44 g/l. ASO titre was negative. His HIV, hepatitis B and C, COVID status, and syphilis were negative. His legionella, mycoplasma, and pneumococcal antigens were negative. Full respiratory viral swab was negative. An ultrasound of the spleen was normal. The blood film showed toxic neutrophil changes, consistent with infection.
test_results: Two days into his admission, his blood culture was positive for Gram-negative rods in the anaerobic bottle. A further blood culture was returned positive for Gram-negative rods in the anaerobic bottle on day 3. Sixteen days after discharge, the 16S sequencing confirmed 16S rDNA. Punch biopsy results were later returned, showing: MACROSCOPIC DESCRIPTION: Skin biopsy punch right lower leg: tan punch biopsy measuring 4×4 mm and up to a depth of 5 mm. The skin surface looks crusty and peeling off probably bullae peeling off. MICROSCOPIC DESCRIPTION: Section shows a skin punch biopsy including detached fragments of necrotic epidermis and ulcer slough. There is thrombotic occlusion of small dermal vessels with erythrocyte extravasation, a neutrophilic infiltrate and necrosis of eccrine glands and hair follicles.
diagnosis: Purpura fulminans secondary to Capnocytophaga canimorsus bacteraemia

case_report: A 7-month-old male infant was admitted to the Second Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University following the detection of an intracranial lesion identified by imaging performed 12 days after birth at a local hospital. The infant was born at full-term via normal spontaneous vaginal delivery, with a birth weight of 3.8 kg and a length of 50 cm. Upon admission, physical examination indicated faltering growth, with a weight of 6.0 kg and a length of 58 cm, which are below the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for this age group (6.7–10.3 kg and 64.8–73.5 cm). Additional physical findings included left-hand polydactyly, syndactyly, and a reducible omental hernia measuring 1.5 × 1.5 cm. Flexible bronchoscopy revealed a bifid epiglottis, tracheal diverticulum, and laryngomalacia. Neurological examination showed normal muscle tone, strength, and reflexes. Hormonal evaluations for pituitary, thyroid, and cortisol levels were within normal limits. The parents reported frequent episodes of inappropriate laughter, consistent with gelastic seizures, although electroencephalography was not performed due to the patient's young age.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) and MRI scans showed a suprasellar hypothalamic lesion suggestive of a hamartoma. The intraoperative diagnosis was hamartoma.

case_report: A two-month-old boy from Iran presented with multiple congenital anomalies at a genetic center in Ahwaz. At birth, the patient had arch-like confluent eyebrows, long curly eyelashes, low anterior and posterior hairlines, a long philtrum, anteverted nares, a depressed nasal bridge, downturned corners of the mouth, thin lips, a high-arched palate, micrognathia, and low-set ears. Additional findings included microcephaly, small hands with the right hand missing one digit and the left hand having fused digits, hypertonicity, excessive body hair on the back and feet, cryptorchidism, a small penis, and a low-pitched cry. The patient was the second child of a non-consanguineous marriage, born at full term via normal delivery, with a birth weight of 3110 grams, a length of 46 cm, and a head circumference of 30 cm. Both parents showed no clinical symptoms and had no family history of deformities.
test_results: Echocardiography revealed both an atrial septal defect and a ventricular septal defect in the newborn. Results of kidney sonography were normal. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain showed subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) and intra-ventricular hemorrhage (IVH) with no sign of hydrocephalus.

case_report: A 26-year-old Colombian male with no prior medical history arrived at the emergency department with a 1-month history of dry cough, worsening shortness of breath, and difficulty breathing while lying down. His physical examination showed normal blood pressure (110/70 mmHg), but he had a fast heart rate (110 b.p.m.) and elevated jugular venous pressure. No heart murmurs or lung crackles were noted. An electrocardiogram showed generalized low voltages, and blood tests were within normal limits. A chest X-ray revealed a significantly enlarged cardiac silhouette. A computed tomography (CT) scan confirmed a large aneurysm in the ascending thoracic aorta (maximum diameter 96 mm) and a substantial pericardial effusion (maximum diameter 65 mm). The rest of the aorta and its branches appeared normal in size. A bedside echocardiogram showed signs of cardiac tamponade, and due to rapidly worsening symptoms, an emergency pericardiocentesis was performed to stabilize the patient. The pericardial fluid obtained was serosanguinous. The patient was then admitted to the intensive care unit for further stabilization. A transoesophageal echocardiogram revealed severe aortic regurgitation with a broad and dense central jet due to a large coaptation defect from the enlarged ascending aorta. Holodiastolic flow reversal in the descending aorta was observed, with an end-diastolic velocity of 40 cm/s. The estimated effective regurgitant orifice area was 1.5 cm². Left ventricular diameters and function were normal, indicating an acute or sub-acute onset. The overall clinical presentation suggested a high risk of aortic rupture. On the fourth day, the patient underwent ascending aorta replacement with a Bentall's procedure using a 25 mm CarbosealTM mechanical prosthesis and a 28 mm Dacron aortic graft. The excised tissue showed a thin aortic wall with histological evidence of medial degeneration and disorganization of elastic fibers. There were no complications during or after the surgery, and the patient was discharged from the hospital after one week.
test_results: The genetic variant c.409A > T, p.Ser137Cys, in EFEMP2 was identified in homozygous state.

case_report: A 14-day-old female neonate was brought to our department by her mother due to a skin lesion on the left thigh that had been present since birth. She was delivered vaginally at full term, as the first child, following an uncomplicated pregnancy. Her birth weight, length, and Apgar score were within normal limits. She exhibited a solitary, 5-mm, oval, firm, reddish, and eroded papule with crust on her left anterior thigh. The physical examination was otherwise normal, with no signs of hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, urinalysis, blood glucose level, liver and kidney function, chemistry profile, chest radiograph, and newborn screening tests, showed no abnormalities.
test_results: On hematoxylin and eosin-stained section of a skin biopsy from the lesion, focal erosion and crusting of the epidermis were observed, and the dermoepidermal junction was indistinct. Within the dermis, there was a dense dermal infiltrate of large and round histiocytic cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. The nuclei were of various shapes and sizes, from irregularly round to oval or kidney-shaped without atypia. Scattered lymphocytes, eosinophils, and neutrophils were also seen. Most histiocytic cells showed positive staining for S-100 and CD1a.

case_report: An 18-month-old boy was admitted for evaluation of resistant rickets. He had previously received two mega doses of vitamin D at a local hospital without any clinical or radiological improvement. Detailed history revealed failure to thrive, abdominal distension, and motor developmental delay. The boy was the first child of nonconsanguineous Hindu parents, born at term (37 weeks) via normal vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 2.5 kg, and had no significant antenatal or postnatal history. Exclusively breastfed for 2 months, he was then top-fed and started on the family diet at 12 months. Developmental milestones included social smile at 3 months, head holding at 6 months, and sitting with support at 11 months, but he could not sit without support at 18 months. Clinical examination showed weight 8 kg, head circumference 42 cm, and length 72 cm (all below the 3rd percentile). The anterior fontanel was wide open, with widening of wrist and ankle joints and genu valgum. Abdominal examination revealed hepatomegaly (10 cm), which was firm, smooth, and nontender, without other organomegaly or ascites. Nervous system examination showed generalized hypotonia, and the developmental age was approximately seven months. Other systems were normal. Investigations showed normal serum calcium (9.4 mg/dL), reduced phosphorus (2 mg/dL, normal 2.7–4.5 mg/dL), and markedly elevated serum alkaline phosphatase (1184 IU/L, normal 145–420 U/L). Potassium was normal (4.1 meq/L). Fasting blood sugar was 80 mg/dL, and two hours postprandial blood sugar was 96 mg/dL (normal 60–100 mg/dL). Thyroid profile was normal. 25(OH) D level was 42 nmol/L (normal 25–120 nmol/L), and 1, 25(OH)2D was within normal limits at 67 pmol/L (normal 48–144 pmol/L). Parathormone level was mildly elevated at 6.2 pmol/L (normal 1.1–5.5 pmol/L). Fasting insulin level was 15 mcU/mL (normal 5–20 mcU/mL). Liver function tests were normal. Serum cholesterol was 217 mg/dL (normal 45–182 mg/dL), and triglycerides were 268 mg/dL (normal 32–99 mg/dL), with normal HDL and LDL cholesterol levels. Blood urea, serum creatinine, uric acid, and lactate levels were normal. Urine biochemistry showed pH 6.2 (normal 4.5–8), specific gravity 1.026, glucosuria 2+, and albumin 2+. Arterial blood gas showed pH 7.22, HCO3- 15, BE −6.7. Wrist X-ray showed features of active rickets. Ultrasonography of the abdomen revealed hepatomegaly with normal echotexture; other organs were within normal limits.
test_results: Liver biopsy detected large pale staining hepatocytes with centrally placed nuclei giving appearance of plant cells and mosaic pattern with fibrous septa extending from portal tracts.

case_report: A 50-year-old circumcised male presented with a growth on the glans penis that had been present for 6 months. The patient had undergone circumcision for phimosis 8 months prior. Two months after the circumcision, the patient noticed a scaly lesion on the glans penis, which gradually increased in size and became dry, rough, and elevated. There was no history of trauma, localized skin conditions, or systemic diseases. The patient reported no exposure to sexually transmitted diseases (STD) and exhibited no symptoms or signs of STD. The patient's partner also had no significant illnesses. Clinical examination showed a well-defined, dry, rough, hard, mica-like scaly, verrucous, and hyperkeratotic plaque measuring 4 × 3 cm on the glans penis, around the urethral meatus. The shaft of the penis, scrotum, and inguinal area appeared normal. There was no regional lymphadenopathy. Blood tests for Venereal Disease Research Laboratory and HIV were negative. Hematological, biochemical, and radiological examinations did not reveal any abnormalities.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed skin with epidermis displaying massive hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, and pronounced epithelial hyperplasia without cellular atypia. The dermis showed mild lymphocytic infiltrate.

case_report: A 24-year-old female patient presented with progressive tremors and myoclonic episodes since 2020. She has experienced three documented generalized myoclonic seizures, each occurring upon awakening from sleep, lasting around three minutes, and followed by urinary incontinence. Additionally, she has constant myoclonic jerks affecting her daily activities. In 2021, a kidney biopsy was performed due to proteinuria of approximately 2500 mg/24 hours, but the results were inconclusive. The patient developed dysarthria, leading to further medical evaluation and hospitalization at our neurological clinic. The patient's parents are second-degree relatives. A detailed history revealed primary amenorrhea, with no menstruation without hormonal medications. Ultrasound examination showed the absence of ovarian tissue but the presence of the uterus and external female genitalia. The physical examination was unremarkable except for pes cavus deformities. A neurological exam revealed cerebellar abnormalities, including dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesis, and ataxic gait. The patient exhibited hand myoclonus while attempting to grasp an object. A contrast MRI revealed no abnormalities.
test_results: Next-generation sequencing analysis in patients identified a homozygous SCARB2:c.104del variant in the SCARB2 gene. The SCARB2 gene was affected by a frameshift mutation affecting a significant portion of both the luminal and downstream domains. This led to the development of non-functional amino acid residues in the protein sequence, starting at amino acid 45, which is asparagine (N) in the wild-type protein.

case_report: A 10-year-old girl presented with a three-week history of balance issues and urinary incontinence. She is the third child of consanguineous parents and had normal nervous development prior to symptom onset. The balance problems worsened over time, showing signs of cerebellar involvement and urinary incontinence. Previously, she had a low-grade fever and was treated for suspected viral cerebellitis before being referred due to symptom progression. Physical examination revealed the patient could not sit or walk independently, had abnormal cerebellar tests (finger to nose and tandem gait), diminished deep tendon reflexes, and bilateral Babinski sign. Brain and cervico-thoraco-lumbar magnetic resonance imaging results were normal. Lumbar puncture results were also normal (glucose=50 mg/dl, protein=30 mg/dl, white blood cell=3, red blood cell=0). Biochemical tests showed high lactate dehydrogenase (LDH=4775) and anemia (Hb=8.8 gr/dl, mean corpuscular volume=104 fL, red blood cell=2540000, platelet=163000). Abdominal sonography did not reveal organomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Bone marrow examination showed hypercellular marrow with megaloblastic changes. Peripheral blood smear indicated elevated mean corpuscular volume (MCV=104 fL) with hypersegmented neutrophils.
test_results: The serum level of vitamin B12 was found to be 70.41 pg/ml., which was significantly lower than the normal range (160-970 pg/ml). In urinalysis, 2+ proteinuria was observed with no leukocyturia and hematuria. Hypercellular marrow with megaloblastic changes was observed in bone marrow examination. Elevated mean corpuscular volume (MCV=104 fL) with hyper segmented neutrophil in peripheral blood smear was noted.

case_report: Mr. MT, a 32-year-old male, has been married for 11 years and has 5 children. He has no history of somatic or psychiatric conditions. He completed secondary school and works as a builder. He has no history of substance use except for smoking, which he quit 4 years ago. The patient was referred for psychiatric examination after consultations with urologists, neurologists, and general practitioners. A few minutes (10–15 minutes) after each ejaculation, he experiences intense fatigue, severe muscle, bone, and joint pain lasting 3–7 days. He also reports sneezing, eye redness, itching sensations throughout the body, and significant concentration difficulties. Additionally, he experiences temporary dental pain that resolves spontaneously. These symptoms occur with all forms of ejaculation, including nocturnal emission, masturbation, and vaginal ejaculation. The symptoms began at puberty (age 14) and have increased in severity and duration over time, initially lasting 3 days and now extending to 7 days, causing financial difficulties due to missed work. This has led to sexual avoidance behavior despite preserved sexual desire and normal erections. The frequency of sexual intercourse has decreased from twice a week to once a month. For the past 2 years, he has also experienced secondary premature ejaculation. On examination, the patient was in good general health, well-built, and had complete secondary sexual characteristics. His weight was 97 kg, height 180 cm, and blood pressure 120/80 mm/Hg. Clinical examinations, including neurological and urological assessments, were normal. Routine laboratory tests (CBC, renal function, blood glucose) and hormone levels (FT4, TSH, prolactin, cortisol, testosterone, DHEA) were within normal ranges.
test_results: The sperm freshly emitted from the patient was diluted to a concentration of 1: 40,000, then injected intracutaneously into the palmar surface of the left forearm, and compared to a cutaneous reaction to placebo with 0.9% intracutaneous saline. This test came back positive.

case_report: A 73-year-old male with a history of dilated cardiomyopathy and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 39%, who had a complete heart block and received a permanent pacemaker 15 years ago, later upgraded to a biventricular implantable cardioverter-defibrillator 2 years ago, presented with recurrent episodes of ventricular tachycardia and appropriate implantable cardioverter-defibrillator interventions despite being on antiarrhythmic medication with sotalol.
test_results: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed midmyocardial delayed enhancement with full-length midmyocardial scar from the basal anteroseptum to inferoseptum. Pace mapping from the AIV and SPV showed a near-perfect QRS match with stimulus-to-QRS latency for the clinical VT. The local intraseptal fractionated and late electrogram exhibited pandiastolic activation spanning the entirety of diastole during VT. Entrainment from a slightly more proximal position within the SPV showed concealed fusion with postpacing interval exactly matching VT cycle length and the S-V interval equal to the electrogram-QRS interval measured from SPd.
diagnosis: Localized intramural reentry confined within the ventricular septum in lamin cardiomyopathy
Orpha_name: Familial dilated cardiomyopathy with conduction defect due to LMNA mutation

case_report: The patient is a 40-year-old woman from Congo, married to a 43-year-old man. She has a low socioeconomic status and experienced an unsupervised pregnancy with an unknown gestational age. She reported the absence of fetal movements for two days and noted that fetal movements were infrequent throughout the pregnancy, with only one low-intensity movement per day. This was her eleventh pregnancy (G11P10L9D1), with a history of full-term spontaneous vaginal deliveries. One of her children has polydactyly, while the others are apparently healthy without obvious congenital malformations. She mentioned taking unknown tablets for malaria from an open market drugstore during the first trimester and occasionally consuming traditional alcohol made from fermented maize. She does not smoke or use traditional drugs and has no family history of diabetes. No antenatal ultrasonography or blood investigations were conducted. On examination, the patient appeared anxious but was hemodynamically stable with an arterial pressure of 120/60 mmHg, afebrile with a temperature of 36.5 °C, and had a symphysis-fundal height of 31 cm. Fetal heartbeats were absent, and the fetus was in breech presentation.
test_results: Ultrasonography revealed a unique fetus with no heartbeat and no movement. Its skull was not perfectly individualized and gave an impression of skull bones overlapping or anencephaly. The femoral length was 54.4 mm (pregnancy age estimated to be 30 weeks) with the fetus in breech presentation. The placenta and genital organs were not visualized. Oligohydramnios was seen with a viscous aspect, giving the impression of maceration.

case_report: A 14-year-old male presented with difficulty walking. Contractures of the Achilles tendon were first observed at age 1, and contractures of the elbows were noted at age 9. Physical examination revealed contractures in both ankles and elbow joints, along with limited neck flexion. The patient exhibited a mild waddling and toe gait, with weakness in the proximal upper limbs and both proximal and distal weakness in the lower limbs. Deep tendon reflexes were absent at both ankles and elbow joints. Family history indicated that the patient's maternal uncle had similar clinical features. Laboratory tests showed serum creatine kinase (CK) activity at 481 IU/L (reference range: 24-204 IU/L) and serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) level at 659 IU/L (reference range: 240-480 IU/L). Electromyography (EMG) revealed abnormal spontaneous activities, short duration low amplitude motor units, short duration polyphasic motor unit potentials (MUP), and early recruitment patterns on volition. Echocardiography indicated normal left ventricular systolic function with a dilated right atrium and right ventricle. Electrocardiogram (ECG) showed sinus arrest with junctional escape rhythm. Ambulatory ECG monitoring detected episodes of atrial fibrillation with complete atrioventricular (AV) block and junctional escape rhythm, with asystole lasting up to 4 seconds. An electrophysiologic study found no electrical signal in the upper right atrium, with junctional escape beats observed. A VVI type permanent pacemaker was implanted.
test_results: Genetic analysis revealed a mutation in exon 2 of the emerin gene by deletion of the C nucleotide at position 397 of the genomic DNA sequence.

case_report: This is a two-year-four-month-old female, born to a first-time mother. The girl was delivered at 39 weeks of gestation via Cesarean section due to placenta failure. She was born in generally good condition with an Apgar score of 9 at 1 minute after birth and exhibited features of intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR). Her birth weight was 1850 g (<3 percentile), height 44.5 cm (<3 percentile), and head circumference 31 cm (<3 percentile). From day 7, she was exclusively breastfed, resulting in gradual weight gain. By day 16, her weight was 2018 g, and she was discharged from the hospital in good condition. At three months old, she was treated at the Paediatric ENT Department for suspected hearing issues. An Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR) test performed during sleep revealed bilateral severe hearing loss, which was confirmed in a follow-up ABR test. At four months old, she received a hearing aid. During infancy, she exhibited physical developmental delays with weight and height significantly below the 3rd percentile, although her psychomotor development was normal. She could sit by eight months, stand and crawl simultaneously, and began walking at 14 months. She started talking at thirteen months old. An MRI of her central nervous system showed no abnormalities. She had low weight and height gains and displayed some distinctive physical features, including a triangular-shaped face, prominent forehead, ocular depression, and lipodystrophy at the lumbar region and around the elbows.
test_results: We have found a novel mutation in PIK3R1 -variant c.1956dupT (p.Lys653*) in exon 15 of PIK3R1. The variant has been confirmed to be de novo mutation (not present in biological parents).

case_report: A 42-year-old, gravida 3, para 2, Korean woman presented to the Department of Emergency Medicine at Samsung Medical Center in November 2014 with abdominal pain and fever. Her medical history included a myomectomy in 2010 and a total abdominal hysterectomy in 2011 due to symptomatic uterine leiomyoma. Previous medical records and pathology slides were unavailable for review. She had been experiencing abdominal pain for one month without any urinary or gynecologic symptoms. Initial vital signs were relatively stable: blood pressure 127/76 mmHg, pulse rate 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and body temperature 39.1℃. Laboratory tests showed elevated C-reactive protein (25.93 mg/dL) but no other significant abnormalities. Blood and urine cultures showed no growth of microorganisms. Imaging studies, including magnetic resonance imaging and computed tomography of the abdomino-pelvic region, revealed a 9-cm soft tissue lesion in the midline lower abdominal wall and a 6.6-cm lesion in the right pelvic cavity forming a fistula with the distal sigmoid colon. No other significant abnormalities were noted on imaging. An urgent exploratory laparotomy was performed for surgical resection. The midline lower abdominal wall mass was excised. During exploration, a perforation in the distal sigmoid colon with massive inflammatory changes and a fistula connected to the right pelvic mass were identified. This mass and the fistula were removed via the Hartmann's procedure. Additionally, three nodular lesions in the sigmoid mesentery and a 4-cm tumor in the terminal ileum were identified and excised.
test_results: Resected tumors were suspected to malignant tumors of mesenchymal origin by frozen section biopsy during surgery. Grossly, tumors were tan-yellow colored soft masses with necrotic changes. Microscopically, tumors were composed of nests and cords of epithelioid cells with moderate to marked atypia. Peri-tumoral hyaline material and geographic tumor necrosis were observed. Mitotic rate was 12 per 10 high power fields (HPFs) and Ki 67 labelling index was up to 50%. Immunohistochemically, the tumor cells were positive for β-hCG, human placental lactogen (hPL), inhibin-α, and p63.

case_report: A 4-year-old boy was admitted with complaints of hard skin for over 3 years, unclear vision, and communication difficulties for one day. He was born weighing 3 kg and appeared normal at birth but soon exhibited failure to thrive. At one month old, his skin became swollen and sclerodermatous on the trunk, and he experienced loss of scalp hair and stunted growth. Prior to admission, he had blurred vision, communication difficulties, dull eyes, and an inability to speak. Physical examination revealed distinctive facial features, including prominent eyes and scalp veins, delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle, generalized alopecia with sparse downy hairs, a narrow nasal bridge, thin lips, micrognathia, and small ear lobes. His neck was soft, Brinell's sign was negative, Klinefelter's sign was negative, Babbitt's sign was positive bilaterally, tendon reflexes were present, limb muscle strength was grade IV, muscle tension was high, and his skin was stiff with poor elasticity and extensive mottled pigmentation on the trunk. He had bilateral metacarpophalangeal joint contracture deformity, flexion deformity of both proximal knuckles, difficulty squatting, and fixed hip and knee joint contractures, with a horse-riding posture. He measured 77 cm in height (<1st percentile) and weighed 7.8 kg (<1st percentile). He was unable to speak or communicate and was too young for a detailed ophthalmic examination. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, cardiac enzymes, serum electrolytes, and lipids, were within normal limits. Electrocardiogram and ultrasonic cardiogram showed no anomalies. Radiographic examination indicated general osteoporotic changes, short and dystrophic clavicles, and distal phalanges osteolysis. Lateral skull X-ray showed cranial dysplasia, and chest X-ray revealed bilateral clavicle dysplasia and rib deformity. Carotid artery B-ultrasound showed 0.05 cm intima-media thickening in both common carotid arteries. EEG indicated moderate abnormalities with irregular delta waves. Brain MRI showed multiple abnormal signals in the bilateral frontoparietal cortex, bilateral semiovale center, and lateral ventricle, as well as in the deep frontoparietal white matter, suggesting cerebral infarction. Cranial MRA revealed bilateral internal carotid artery stenosis with basilar artery and thickening of the bilateral posterior communicating artery. A follow-up head MRI after 3 months showed bilateral paraventricular and central semiovale lacunar infarction. A follow-up head MRA after 3 months showed similar findings to the previous one.
test_results: The patient carried a c.1824C > T (p.G608G) heterozygous LMNA mutation.

case_report: A 4-year-old boy presented with bilateral cataracts and poor vision. His parents noted that his physical and mental development was typical until he was 2 years old. After that age, he began experiencing difficulties in learning and communicating. Additionally, oculo-digital sign and self-injury behaviors were observed. Ocular B-scan ultrasonography identified retinal detachment in both eyes. Surgical intervention included pars plana vitrectomy and lensectomy in the left eye. Postoperative fundus photographs showed a partially attached retina. The patient's father had physical disabilities due to poliomyelitis but no ophthalmic abnormalities. The mother had phthisis bulbi and keratopathy in the left eye with no light perception, and in the right eye, she had a dragged disk with a visual acuity of 20/125.
test_results: Genetic testing identified a homozygous deletion of exons 2 and 3 in the NDP in the patient.

case_report: A 78-year-old woman presented with widespread skin redness and was admitted to the hospital. She had a history of psoriasis vulgaris since the age of 47 and had been using over-the-counter medications for management. Her medical history included hypertension and chronic heart failure, which were being treated with acetazolamide, candesartan cilexetil, and amlodipine besylate. Family history revealed that her brother had psoriasis vulgaris, her niece had psoriatic arthritis, and her daughter had arthritis with a high anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) titer (×1,240), though no definitive diagnosis was made for her daughter. Initially, the patient was treated with 30 mg of prednisolone daily, but this was ineffective. The prednisolone dose was subsequently reduced, and she was given 150 mg of cyclosporine daily for 12 days, which showed effectiveness. The cyclosporine dose was then reduced to 100 mg daily. However, two weeks later, the patient developed a sudden fever, generalized swelling, widespread skin redness with multiple pustules, and areas filled with pus.
test_results: A skin biopsy showed infiltrates of neutrophils into the upper spinous and subcorneal layers of the epidermis which formed a Kogoj spongiform pustule.
diagnosis: Generalized Pustular Psoriasis  with a deficiency of IL-36RN

case_report: A 16-year-old female arrived at the emergency department experiencing intense, crampy abdominal pain lasting several minutes. The patient reported a weight loss of 4 kg over the past two weeks, along with recurrent episodes of nausea, hypertensive episodes, and occasional menstrual discomfort. Laboratory tests, including those for inflammation and tumor markers, returned normal results. The patient had her first menstrual period at the age of 13 and has had regular menstrual cycles since then.
test_results: B-mode ultrasound and a multimodal MRI with DWI and contrast media showed a large cystic mass extending from the left ovary to 15.4 cm. Within the thin-walled cyst were a hyperechoic solid structure of about 4.2 cm and a delicate septum. Doppler ultrasonography showed non-specific perfusion. CEUS examination visually verified early arterial accumulation of vesicles in the solid structure. A small central portion of the solid structure remained free of microbubble contrast media throughout the examination. In the quantitative analysis TTP in the solid part was 12.5 s, RT was 4.6 s, and relative PE was 79%.

case_report: A 43-year-old male presented with a 4-year history of incomplete eye closure and labial dysarthria. Over the past 3 years, he experienced increasing difficulty in gripping objects with either hand, thinning of the forearms, and painless burns on the distal upper extremities. He later developed numbness in the head, face, trunk, and upper limbs over the past year. He was previously treated with anti-Hansen's medication at another hospital. There was no history of visual or hearing impairment, positive sensory symptoms, or symptoms indicating dysautonomia. No family history of neuropathic illness was reported. Physical examination revealed healed thermal burns on both forearms, bifacial weakness, distal hypotonia, and wasting and weakness of the distal upper limbs. Sensation to touch and pin-prick was reduced over the scalp, face, trunk, upper limbs, and proximal lower limbs up to mid-thigh. Kinesthetic sensations and cerebellar function were intact. Routine laboratory tests, including hemogram, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and hepatic and renal function tests, were normal. Autoantibody profile (Euroline®, immunoblot technique), serum protein electrophoresis, serum angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) levels (20.1 U/l; reference range: 20-70 U/l), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antibody test, abdominal ultrasound, audiometry, and other conventional autonomic function tests were within normal limits. Urine tests for porphobilinogen and Bence-Jones protein were negative. Lumbar cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed normal results except for mildly elevated protein levels (cell count: 0/mm3; protein: 58 mg/dl, reference range: 20-40 mg/dl; glucose: 61 mg/dl, reference range: 40-60 mg/dl).
test_results: The serum lipid profile was abnormal with extremely low levels of HDL (5 mg/dl; ref: 35-65 mg/dl) and elevated TG (185 mg/dl; ref: 50-150 mg/dl); and normal levels of total cholesterol (149 mg/dl; ref: 110-220 mg/dl), very low density lipoprotein (VLDL) (37 mg/dl; ref: 10-40 mg/dl), and LDL (110 mg/dl; ref: 60-160 mg/dl). Serum apolipoprotein A1 was significantly reduced (<5.38 mg/dl; ref: 110-205 mg/dl). His sural nerve had been biopsied elsewhere, this was retrieved and reviewed. It showed mild depletion of small diameter myelinated fibers in small pockets in the periphery of each fascicle. In addition, there was a striking vacuolation of the Schwann cell cytoplasm indenting the nucleus. Skin biopsy revealed numerous bloated, finely vacuolated fibroblasts throughout the entire thickness of the skin, surrounding the dermal capillaries, nerve twigs, and cutaneous adnexal structures. The vacuolated granular cytoplasm was seen indenting the nucleus. These vacuoles stained with Oil Red O, confirming the presence of lipid rich material.

case_report: A 33-year-old woman with a history of seronegative rheumatoid arthritis, who was intolerant to methotrexate, sulphasalazine, and azathioprine, showed symptom improvement with etanercept treatment. Thirty-four years later, she presented with a vasculitic rash on her legs, acute kidney injury with a serum creatinine level of 211 μmol/L, haematuria, and proteinuria measuring 1.55 g/24 hours. ANCA tests returned negative.
test_results: A renal biopsy demonstrated pauci-immune focal necrotizing glomerulonephritis with moderate chronic damage.

case_report: A 47-year-old female with morbid obesity presented with a 1-year history of worsening shortness of breath. Initial imaging at an outside institution indicated more significant thromboembolic disease on the right side compared to the left. She received tPA treatment followed by anticoagulation, but her symptoms did not improve. Three months later, further CT imaging revealed a large thrombus in the right pulmonary artery and a large uterine mass, consistent with leiomyoma, without affecting the pelvic veins. Thrombophilia tests were negative, but ANA was positive at 1:640. She was referred to another center for further management. Pulmonary angiography showed bilateral thromboembolic disease, complete obstruction of the right pulmonary artery, disease in the left lower lobe, and pulmonary hypertension with a pulmonary vascular resistance of 4.4 Wood units.
test_results: The PEA specimen consisted of multiple pink- and white-tan irregular soft tissue fragments comprising mostly organizing thrombus. A few areas of prominent spindle cell proliferation were identified, accompanied by a marked inflammatory cell infiltration. The spindle cells were positive for SMA. CD3 and CD20 immunostains revealed mixed B- and T-lymphocytic population.

case_report: A 27-year-old woman (gravida 1, para 0) delivered a healthy 2715-g female infant at 40 weeks of gestation in a private hospital. The patient had no notable medical or family history and had not experienced problems during the course of her pregnancy. She developed a massive hemorrhage at the time of delivery and was transferred to our hospital for emergency treatment. The estimated total blood loss was approximately 4000 mL on admission. On admission to our hospital, the patient had a blood pressure of 110/50 mmHg and a heart rate of 140 beats/min. A complete blood count (CBC) revealed a hematocrit (HCT) level of 11.4% and a hemoglobin (Hb) level of 4.1 g/dL. We immediately started transfusion and uterotonic therapies and employed uterine embolization, which successfully stopped the bleeding. We estimated her total blood loss to be approximately 5000 mL at this point, and she received 3500 mL of fluid infusions, including 2800 mL of red blood cells, 1200 mL of fresh frozen plasma, and 400 mL of platelets by transfusion. Subsequently, her CBC recovered (HCT: 27.6% and Hb: 9.6 g/dL) and vital signs stabilized (blood pressure: 140/90 mmHg and heart rate: 100 beats/min). On day 7 postpartum, the patient’s general condition was relatively stable, with no evidence of hypotension, general fatigue, headache, failure to lactate, or hypoglycemia; therefore, we planned to discharge her on the following day. However, on day 8, the patient experienced a grand mal seizure and became comatose. Because her oxygen saturation level decreased to 60%, she was sedated and intubated. The laboratory data showed slightly low Hb (10.3 g/dL) and HCT levels (29.7%), a normal platelet count (262 × 103/μL), and low sodium (Na+, 111 mEq/L) and chloride (Cl−, 84 mEq/L) levels. Other tests were within the normal range. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pituitary gland revealed no abnormalities and intracranial hemorrhage could be ruled out. The seizure was attributed to hyponatremia, and NaCl replacement treatment was initiated to increase her Na+ levels by 10 mEq/day. The patient’s hormone levels on postpartum day 8 are shown in Table. The adrenal insufficiency was treated with hydrocortisone. A second MRI scan did not reveal lymphocytic hypophysitis, and a Gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted MRI showed a normal pituitary gland on postpartum day 15 (7 days after the seizure).
test_results: The hormone levels demonstrated low reactivity for ACTH, TSH, FSH, prolactin (PRL), and growth hormone (GH).

case_report: A 4-year-old girl was referred for genetic counseling due to developmental delays, eye abnormalities, and distinctive craniofacial features. She was born to a 29-year-old mother at 34 weeks of gestation via cesarean section. There was no consanguinity, and she has a healthy 6-year-old brother. Family history was unremarkable, and the pregnancy was uneventful. Birth measurements were: weight 1900 g (0th percentile), length 49 cm (47th percentile), and occipitofrontal circumference (OFC) 31 cm (2.4th percentile). The neonatal period was complicated by cyanosis and hypoxia shortly after birth, requiring oxygen support. She had a prolonged stay in the neonatal intensive care unit due to persistent oral feeding difficulties, necessitating nasogastric tube placement. She was discharged at 4 months of age after resuming oral feeding. Post-discharge, her weight gain was appropriate for her age. At birth, she had bilateral clubfoot, which required Achilles tendon lengthening surgery at 6 months. Post-surgery, foot abduction bracing was initiated, leading to significant improvement in foot position. The patient exhibited significant developmental delays. She began holding her head steady at 5 months, sitting independently at 27 months, and standing with support at 2 years. Currently, her speech development is severely delayed; she cannot say words but can produce some syllables with doubling. She responds to her name inconsistently and can stand independently but cannot walk. An ophthalmological evaluation at 6 months revealed bilateral microphthalmia, microcornea, iris dysplasia, pupil dislocation, and lens subluxation. Additionally, retinal dysplasia, congenital chorioretinal coloboma, and optic nerve hypoplasia were detected in the left eye. At the time of evaluation, she had decreased vision and myopia. Brain magnetic resonance imaging at 7 months showed subependymal gray matter heterotopia with nodules in the region of the trigones and occipital horns. At 2 years, the patient developed epileptic spasms. Electroencephalogram (EEG) showed modified hypsarrhythmia with an encephalopathic background pattern. She was treated with vigabatrin, resulting in full remission. Abdominal and renal ultrasound results were normal. Physical examination revealed prominent dysmorphic features, including an elongated face, full cheeks, high anterior hairline, upslanted palpebral fissures, strabismus, low-set ears, thick nasal alae, and flared nostrils. Two focal superficial hemangiomas were present on the inner thighs. Current measurements are: weight 14 kg (15th percentile), length 95 cm (10th percentile), and head circumference 48 cm (15th percentile). Basic metabolic workup, including serum lactate, ammonia, amino acids, organic acids, and total homocysteine, was normal. Lymphocyte chromosome analysis at the 550-band level showed a normal female karyotype 46,XX.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing (WES) revealed a novel heterozygous variant c.7778A>C, p.His2593Pro in the ANKRD17 (NM_032217.4). Subsequent parental segregation analysis confirmed de novo status of the detected variant.

case_report: A 38-year-old woman reported experiencing temporal visual field defects in the right eye and difficulty seeing at night since the age of 30. Her family history includes a deceased father who had blindness in at least the right eye. Examination of her fundus revealed mild bone spicule pigmentation and atrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in the midperiphery.
test_results: Marked decrease of amplitudes on electroretinography. Genotype screening with next-generation sequencing showed a novel heterozygous deletion (c.1860_1861del) of the RPGR gene. Goldmann perimetry showed a temporal scotoma in the right eye and wedge-shaped visual field restriction in both eyes.

case_report: A 22-year-old male presented with underdeveloped secondary sexual characteristics. He was born at term to non-consanguineous parents and had normal developmental milestones and age-appropriate intelligence. There was no history of seizures, vision problems, color blindness, hearing loss, or movement disorders. He had been receiving intramuscular testosterone injections for 4 years before presentation. He is the eldest of eight siblings (two brothers and six sisters) with no significant family medical history. His weight was 63 kg, height was 185 cm, and his upper to lower segment ratio was 0.7 (87 cm/98 cm). He had a high-pitched voice, normal sense of smell, no facial or axillary hair, and pubic hair at Tanner stage 3. Both testes were descended and prepubertal in size (2 ml in volume), with a stretched penile length of 7 cm. Neurological examination showed no abnormalities.
test_results: He was found to have an LH-0.69 mIU/ml (N-0.8–7.6 mIU/ml), FSH-0.77 mIU/ml (N-0.7–11.1 mIU/ml), Testosterone-103 ng/dl (N-270–1030 ng/dl). Other hormonal axes were normal and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain including the olfactory bulb was normal.

case_report: A 13-year-old girl presented with fever and abdominal pain for three months and vomiting for four days. The fever was gradual in onset, intermittent, low-grade, relieved by medication, and associated with chills, with increased intensity over the past four days. Vomiting was non-bilious, contained food particles, and was non-projectile. Abdominal pain was diffuse and relieved by vomiting, with no history of radiation. She also reported loss of appetite, weight loss, and fatigue. On general examination, the patient was alert and active, with a blood pressure of 110/70 mm Hg, pulse rate of 90 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 18 per minute, and SpO2 of 96% on room air. The body mass index was 14.3 kg/m2. A head-to-toe examination revealed pallor, muscle wasting, cachexia, and dry, lusterless skin. There was no icterus, cyanosis, digital clubbing, lymphadenopathy, or edema. A review of the systemic examination was unremarkable. Investigations showed severe anemia and leucopenia, with 14% blasts in the peripheral smear. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) were elevated, with a low reticulocyte count and a normal uric acid level. A blood culture was sent due to the fever, which was unremarkable for any active infection.
test_results: The initial bone marrow examination from right ileac crest failed and yielded hemodilute marrow. Hence, the procedure was repeated from left side. The morphologic examination of the aspirate smears revealed a few marrow particles with reduced cellularity for age with dilute cell trails. A nucleated cell differential count revealed 42% blasts. Auer rods were not seen. Megakaryocytes showed marked dyspoiesis with hypolobation and hypogranularity, micromegakaryocytes were present. Myeloperoxidase (MPO), periodic acid-Schiff (PAS), and Sudan Black B (SBB) were negative in blasts. Bone marrow biopsy showed hypocellular marrow with decreased cellularity for age. Normal hematopoiesis was markedly suppressed due to infiltration by abnormal blasts.
