They were large cells with intermediate nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio with irregular and vesicular nuclei, irregular nuclear contours, anisonucleosis with the peri-sinusoidal distribution. Intra-sinusoidal megakaryopoiesis was present, and scattered lymphoid cells and eosinophils were seen. There was grade 1 reticulin fibrosis. Immunophenotyping was performed on bone marrow aspirate with low side scatter characteristics (SSC) and moderate CD45+ events gated as blasts (3.2% of viable events) and low to intermediate SSC CD45 negative events gated as blast equivalents (89.0% of viable events). Blasts were positive for CD33 (heterogeneous, moderate), CD13 (heterogeneous, dim), CD117 (homogeneous, dim), CD34 (homogeneous, moderate), HLADR (homogeneous, bright), and CD7 (homogeneous, moderate). Blast equivalents were positive for CD41 (homogeneous, bright), CD36 (homogeneous, bright), CD34 (homogeneous, moderate), HLADR (heterogeneous, dim), CD56 (heterogeneous, moderate) and CD7 (homogeneous moderate). Normal lymphoid cells were considered as internal controls for defining the expression pattern. Conventional karyotype analysis revealed normal diploid female karyotype 46, XX in all 20 cells.
Orpha_name: Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia without Down syndrome

case_report: A 21-year-old male presented with small upper and lower permanent teeth. The patient reported that the size of his teeth remained unchanged with age. There was no relevant family or medical history, and no abnormal oral habits were noted. General physical examination results were normal. Intraoral soft tissue examination showed brown pigmented gingiva with normal contour. Hard tissue examination revealed retained deciduous teeth, atypical permanent teeth, and multiple decayed teeth. Many permanent teeth were missing, and the erupted teeth were widely spaced with yellowish brown discoloration. The enamel layer was absent, and post-eruption wear was evident. The upper central incisors had a semi-lunar shape, and the molars had flat occlusal surfaces. Severe attrition led to a collapsed bite and reduced vertical dimensions during occlusion. Panoramic radiography and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) images showed multiple findings. All teeth were affected, especially the posterior teeth. Multiple calcification nodules were present in the pulp chambers of both primary and permanent teeth; these nodules were needle-shaped in the incisors and round in the posterior teeth. The expected differential radiodensity between dentine and enamel was absent. Significant pericoronal radiolucencies with sclerotic margins were observed around non-erupted teeth. Impacted teeth had complete root formation with dilacerations and curvature. Dental follicles around unerupted teeth appeared hyperplastic. Extensive crown resorption with partial replacement by globular calcified structures was noted. Impacted permanent canines, second molars, and third molars had fully formed roots. An accessory mental foramen was seen on the right side of the mandible, and extensive bone loss was observed around the mesiobuccal root of the left maxillary first molar in volume-rendered CBCT images.
test_results: The histopathological examination of an extracted deciduous canine using light microscopy confirmed the absence of enamel and the absence of scalloping of the dentinoenamel junction. An ultrasound examination of his kidneys demonstrated multiple hyperechoic foci in the medulla of both the kidneys, suggesting bilateral nephrolithiasis. A 24-hour urine spectrophotometric analysis revealed very low citrate levels (18.9 mg/24 hours; reference range, 116-924 mg/24 hours).

case_report: A 64-year-old female presented with a painless, progressive swelling of the left lower extremity that had been ongoing for 1 year (Fig. A). The patient was obese, and her vital signs were within normal limits. She had no history of surgery or trauma affecting the inguinal or lower extremity lymphatic system. Additionally, she reported no allergies, no family history of similar conditions, and had never traveled overseas. Physical examination revealed that the left lower extremity below the inguinal line was significantly larger than the right side. Fibrotic changes and stemmer signs were noted on the affected side. There was no warmth or redness in the lower extremity. Measurements of leg circumferences taken 15 cm above the knee (AK) were 43 cm on the right and 52 cm on the left. Measurements taken 15 cm below the knee (BK) were 32.5 cm on the right and 36.5 cm on the left.
test_results: Lymphangiography revealed the presence of dermal backflow and the absence of lymph node uptake at the inguinal node.

case_report: A 10-year-old girl presented with growths in the upper and lower jaws, difficulty eating, speech impairment, and noneruption of teeth. The growths began 3 years ago and have progressively increased in size, leading to inadequate lip closure and poor aesthetics. The family and postnatal history were noncontributory, with no history of epilepsy, mental disorder, or similar conditions in the family. There was no history of consanguinity. The patient was malnourished and from a very poor family. Routine medical history and physical examination revealed no systemic disease. Extraoral examination showed a large, generalized multinodular growth covering both the maxillary and mandibular arches, causing everted lips and a convex profile. The maxillary growth was granular, mildly pigmented, and had multiple fissures, covering all maxillary anterior teeth completely. The mandibular growth was larger, extending beyond the submental region, appearing as a hanging mass attached to the mandible. The growth was multilobular, pebbled, and had a smooth surface, extending between the corners of the mouth. The mandibular anterior teeth were not visible. The growth was pink to pinkish-white in color, firm, and nontender on palpation, with no fluctuancy, compressibility, translucency, or associated bleeding. Mild pain was associated with the growth. Intraoral examination of the maxilla revealed a generalized growth of gingiva completely covering the maxillary teeth, extending from the right maxillary tuberosity to the left tuberosity region. The mass covered the anterior palatine region completely and extended bilaterally towards the midline of the palate without fusion. The anterior palatine region had a granular, mildly pigmented surface with a pinkish-white color and multiple fissures. The maxillary teeth were not visible except in the right and left posterior regions. The growth was firm and nontender on palpation, with no associated bleeding or pain. Intraoral examination of the mandible revealed a generalized growth of gingiva completely covering the mandibular teeth, extending from the right mandibular tuberosity to the left tuberosity region. The mass extended lingually bilaterally towards the midline and fused from anterior to posterior along the midline, reducing the normal tongue space and covering the floor of the mouth completely. The tongue was confined to a small space posterior to the fused mass. The mass was exuberant in the mandibular anterior region, obliterating the chin area and submental region. The mandibular teeth were not visible except in the right and left posterior regions. The growth was pink to pinkish-white in color, with a smooth and lobulated surface. The fusion line was well-demarcated along the midline. The tongue was pushed back. The mass was firm and nontender on palpation, with no associated pain or bleeding. There was no associated lymphadenopathy. A panoramic radiograph showed multiple retained primary and impacted permanent teeth, with the mandible relatively thinner in the angle region bilaterally.
test_results: Histological examination revealed a fibroconnective tissue with extensive collagen bundles. The overlying surface of the epithelium exhibited hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and elongation of rete ridges. The fibroconnective tissue consisting of densely arranged collagen fiber bundles, numerous fibroblasts, compressed blood vessels, and various degree of focal areas of chronic inflammatory cells.

case_report: An 8-year-old male patient was admitted due to seizures and developmental delay. He exhibited severe cognitive impairment and was non-ambulatory. Born at 36 weeks via spontaneous vaginal delivery to consanguineous parents, he was their first child. There was no maternal history of diabetes or exposure to teratogenic agents during pregnancy. Birth metrics such as weight, length, and head circumference were not documented. The neonatal period was uneventful, but by 4 months, significant developmental delays were noted, accompanied by irritability and feeding difficulties. At 5 months, the patient experienced frequent tonic seizures necessitating antiepileptic medication. Cerebral MRI indicated white matter lesions. Previously diagnosed with spastic cerebral palsy at another facility, his neurological assessment upon admission revealed severe cognitive impairment, microcephaly, and spasticity, with normal cranial nerve function. Increased muscle tone and hyperreflexia with bilateral positive Babinski sign were observed in both upper and lower limbs. Ophthalmologic examination was unremarkable. The patient was unable to sit, walk, or speak. No hepatosplenomegaly was detected. Laboratory tests showed normal complete blood count, serum electrolytes, liver and renal function, and thyroid function. Serological tests for toxoplasmosis, rubella, cytomegalovirus, and herpes simplex were negative. Urinary amino and organic acids and metabolic screening were normal. Cranial CT revealed calcifications in the basal ganglia and periventricular white matter. Brain MRI showed brain atrophy and white matter demyelination. Echocardiography identified cardiomyopathy.
test_results: The mutation analysis of the TREX1 gene revealed a homozygous novel mutation, p.R169H (c.506G>A).

case_report: A 33-year-old male presented with abdominal pain, vomiting, and weight loss. Blood tests indicated obstructive jaundice with total bilirubin at 17mg/dl and direct bilirubin at 12mg/dl, along with significantly elevated α-fetoprotein levels exceeding 5845. Imaging via computed tomography identified a 5cm mass at the head of the pancreas. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed an ulcerated lesion in the second part of the duodenum. Biopsies from this lesion showed infiltration of the duodenum near the Vater ampulla. Due to worsening biliary obstruction with total bilirubin rising to 30mg/dl, an exploratory laparotomy was performed, followed by a standard pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple’s procedure).
test_results: Histopathological examination of the specimen revealed cells with endodermal sinus pattern and characteristic Schiller-Duvall bodies, and cells with a reticular pattern. Immunohistochemical staining of the cancer cells was positive for PLAP, AFP, CK8.18, and galectin-3. Ki-67 was positive in 60-70% of the cells.

case_report: A 2-month-old Turkish male infant, the second child of a non-consanguineous marriage, was brought to our pediatric clinic following an afebrile seizure. The infant was delivered vaginally at 40 weeks of gestation after an uneventful pregnancy. There was no family history of hearing loss or kidney issues. Upon admission, the infant's vital signs were stable. His weight was 4470 g (25th percentile), length was 59 cm (50th percentile), and head circumference was 39 cm (50th percentile). Physical examination did not reveal any abnormalities. Laboratory tests showed low serum calcium (6.4 mg/dL; normal range, 8.8-10.3 mg/dL), high serum phosphate (7.2 mg/dL; normal range, 3.8-6.5 mg/dL), and low serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) (7 pg/mL; normal range, 20-65 pg/mL). Serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and 25-hydroxy vitamin D [25(OH)D] levels were within normal limits (388 U/L; normal range, 145-420 U/L and 22 ng/mL; normal range, 20-75 ng/mL, respectively). Urinalysis indicated trace proteinuria and haematuria. Serum creatinine (Cr) level was elevated at 1.3 mg/dL (normal range, 0.2-0.4 mg/dL), while blood urea nitrogen was normal. Persistent findings included serum Cr levels of 0.6-1.2 mg/dL, trace/(1+) proteinuria, and trace/(1+) haematuria. Other tests, including whole blood count, serum electrolytes (sodium, potassium, magnesium), liver function tests, and spot urine Ca/Cr ratio, were unremarkable. Neck ultrasonography confirmed the presence of the thymus gland. Urinary ultrasonography, diethylenetriamine-pentaacetic acid scan, echocardiography, and auditory function tests were normal.
test_results: The results showed a nonsense mutation (p. R367X; c.1099C>T). The C>T mutation at nucleotide 1099 in exon 6 of the GATA3 resulted in substitution of a termination signal instead of arginine at codon 367.
diagnosis: Hypoparathyroidism, Deafness, and Renal Dysplasia  syndrome

case_report: A 24-year-old female of Chinese descent reported experiencing recurrent swelling and pain in the chin area over the past 2 years. Her medical history includes early loss of some primary teeth before the age of 6 and an accidental leg fracture at the age of 10. Family history indicates that her mother lost several teeth at the age of 40. The patient measures 160 cm in height and weighs 39 kg, with a BMI of 15.23.
test_results: CBCT showed enamel hypoplasia in most of her residual teeth. Teeth #14 and # 31 were missing. No fistula or pus was noted. The panoramic film revealed that all the roots were short, and multiple well defined radiolucencies were shown at the apices of teeth #25, #26, #32–35, and #41–46. Furthermore, alveolar bone height reduction was observed as well. CBCT proved that most of the root lengths were shorter than normal. Skeletal radiography didn’t show any obvious changes. The laboratory examination results were unremarkable except that the serum ALP level was 35.0 U/L (normal range 45.0–125.0 U/L).

case_report: A 29-year-old man presented to the emergency department with abdominal pain and dizziness. He reported two instances of fainting during physical activity, one occurring 7 years ago and the other 25 years ago. His family history included his mother and two uncles, all of whom had permanent pacemakers implanted. On physical examination, his vital signs were as follows: blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, heart rate 49 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and temperature 36.8℃.
test_results: His ECG showed atrial flutter with variable ventricular response and bifascicular block (RBBB and LAFB). The echocardiogram showed a mild left ventricular systolic dysfunction (ejection fraction=50%), enlarged left and right atrium. On the third day of hospitalization, the 24-hour Holter showed ventricular pause up to 16 seconds during syncope. After RFCA, the ECG revealed bifascicular block (RBBB and LAFB) and marked first-degree AV block and the 24-hour Holter showed an intermittent second-degree AV block.
diagnosis: Progressive Familial Heart Block Type I

case_report: An 11-year-old Norwegian girl exhibited a persistent itchy rash that did not respond to topical and systemic steroids. She was in good overall health. Physical examination showed a rash on the central face characterized by red papules, excoriations, and crusts on a red background, along with excoriated papules on her upper extremities and chest. There was no evidence of cheilitis or conjunctivitis. Routine laboratory tests, complement factors, and autoantibodies were all normal. Porphyrin screening results were negative.
test_results: Phototesting showed reduced and normal MED for UVA and UVB, respectively. Skin biopsy showed focal para- and hyperkeratosis, mild acanthosis and a perivascular predominantly mononuclear infiltrate. Human leucocyte antigen (HLA) typing detected the DRB1*0407 subtype.

case_report: A 12-year-old boy from Saudi Arabia was admitted to Maternity and Children's Hospital - Alhassa with a history of intermittent fever that initially responded to antipyretics but later became continuous and unresponsive to both antipyretics and antibiotics. The fever was accompanied by an intermittent, non-productive cough without diurnal variation, weight loss of approximately 8 kilograms, anorexia, non-specific epigastric pain, and episodes of vomiting. There was no history of recurrent infections, bone pain, hair loss, skin rash, or family history of immunodeficiency or hematological disorders. The patient had a previous admission about a year ago for lobar pneumonia and parapneumonic effusion, which responded well to a 10-day course of antibiotics. On examination, the patient appeared ill and lethargic without pain or dyspnea, had a fever of 38.6°C, heart rate of 100 beats/min, respiratory rate of 25 breaths/min, blood pressure of 112/62 mmHg, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. The patient's weight was 22 kg, below the third percentile. There was decreased air entry in the right lower chest, while the rest of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory findings showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, microcytic hypochromic anemia, and hypoalbuminemia, with a normal hepatic and renal profile. A chest x-ray revealed infiltration of the right lower lobe. An abdominal ultrasound showed multiple liver abscesses. Blood culture was obtained, and broad-spectrum antibiotics were started to cover gram-positive and negative organisms as well as anaerobes. A computed tomographic (CT) study of the chest and abdomen showed linear atelectasis in both lungs, a solitary nodule in the left lung, and multifocal pyogenic liver abscesses. The liver abscess was drained via an ultrasound-guided procedure, and the drained pus culture showed S. aureus. The patient was treated with culture-sensitive antibiotics for 10 days.
test_results: The result was positive for the oxidative burst test and a normal immunoglobulin level.

case_report: A 52-year-old African American woman with a history of progressively worsening constipation over the past five years, unresponsive to multiple bowel regimens, presented to the Emergency Department with abdominal pain, distention, regurgitation, and intermittent vomiting for the past few weeks. She reported a weight loss of approximately 10 pounds, from 115 to 105 pounds, over the last 1–2 months. She denied recent symptoms of fevers, chills, diarrhea, blood in the stool, or black stools. She also denied any recent dietary changes or travel outside the United States. No family members had similar symptoms. Her social history included a former cigarette smoking history of 10 pack-years, and she denied alcohol or illicit drug use, as well as any drug allergies. Two months prior, she had undergone esophagogastroduodenoscopy (reported as normal) and colonoscopy (reported a dilated lumen with no mucosal lesions). On physical examination, she appeared emaciated and exhausted. She was afebrile (temperature 97.6°F) and hemodynamically stable (pulse rate 68 BPM, blood pressure 142/85 mm Hg). The abdomen was moderately distended without tenderness, guarding, or rigidity, and bowel sounds were decreased. Laboratory tests revealed hypokalemia with potassium at 3.4 mEq/L (3.5–5.0 mEq/L) and hypochloremia with chloride at 94 mEq/L (96–110 mEq/L). The complete blood count showed hemoglobin at 9.6 g/dL (12.0–15.5 g/dL), hematocrit at 29.4% (34–48%), and mean corpuscular volume at 102 fL (80–96 fL), indicating macrocytic anemia. Thyroid function tests were within normal limits. She was also found to have several vitamin deficiencies. Plain abdominal X-rays showed dilatation of the small and large bowel.
test_results: Computed tomography scan of the abdomen showed marked dilatation of the small and large bowel with air-fluid levels.
diagnosis: Chronic Intestinal Pseudo-Obstruction  in Systemic Sclerosis

case_report: A 60-year-old male patient presented with elevated calcium levels and increased parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels on routine laboratory tests, 10 years after undergoing parathyroid adenoma resection. He exhibited no clinical symptoms despite the elevated PTH. Family history revealed that his brothers had elevated parathyroid hormone levels, but there was no reported history of jaw, uterine, or renal tumors in the family. Preoperative PTH levels exceeded 600 pg/mL (reference range 7.5-53.5 pg/mL). Surgical pathology from the parathyroidectomy showed increased mitotic activity, a moderately elevated proliferative index, a focus with potential perineural involvement, cells with macronucleoli, and intralesional fibrosis. There was no evidence of metastasis or definitive vascular invasion. The final pathology indicated hypercellular parathyroid tissue with atypical features. Postoperative laboratory results showed normalized calcium and PTH levels for a decade. However, the patient's PTH levels later increased to 87.5 pg/mL and then to 118.6 pg/mL, leading to an endocrinology consultation. Renal function panels, including serum calcium levels, were normal. Further tests included a serum vitamin D level of 78.5 ng/mL and a 24-hour urine calcium of 179 mg/24 hr. Genetic evaluation revealed a mutation at CDC73 (c.376C>T(p.Arg126)).
test_results: Genetic screenings for multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) and RET mutations, which were negative. A subsequent neck ultrasound demonstrated no evidence of a parathyroid adenoma, while renal ultrasound demonstrated bilateral renal cysts.

case_report: A 47-year-old female visited for a routine dental checkup. Since birth, she had multiple discrete purple discolorations on the right side of her chin, neck, and lower limb. She reported experiencing blurred vision for the past year. General examination showed stable vital signs. Extraoral examination revealed facial asymmetry on the right side due to soft tissue hypertrophy, with numerous discrete purple lesions on the right frontal region of the face, eyelid, around the nose, chin, and lips. These lesions extended to the back of the neck and shoulder, not crossing the midline. Intraoral examination showed asymptomatic bright-red flat areas of discoloration present from birth on the right postero-lateral border of the hard palate, extending laterally 1.5 cm from the palatal aspect of the free or marginal gingiva near the 17 tooth region, medially 2 cm from the mid-palatine raphe region, posteriorly to the right posterolateral junction of the hard and soft palate, and on the right ventral surface of the floor of the mouth near the lingual aspect of the 44, 45, and 46 tooth regions. The right lateral border of the tongue was also bright red and enlarged. Similar purplish lesions were observed on the flexor and extensor aspects of the right lower limb. The skin lesions were flat, non-elevated, and purplish in color, while the oral lesions were bright red due to the presence of oxygenated blood in fine capillaries.
test_results: Fundoscopic examination of the right eye revealed 'bean-pot cupping' or 'bayoneting' of retinal vessels.

case_report: A 7-year-old male was brought to the pediatric outpatient department by his mother. He exhibited aggressive and hyperactive behavior, frequent falls from sitting and standing positions, and a loss of speech over the past five months. These symptoms progressed rapidly during the first month and then remained unchanged for the subsequent four months. Initially, he had slurred speech which worsened to difficulty in articulation. He was unable to sit or stand without support and could not express a need for food. He also had difficulty understanding and following commands. Previously, he was an active child capable of performing routine activities, with no family history of childhood seizure disorders. On general physical examination, the child had an average height and build with no dysmorphic facial features. He was restless and hyperactive in bed, restrained by his mother, with forward falling of the trunk while sitting. Vital signs were normal. Anthropometric measurements were: height 116 cm (10th-25th percentile), weight 20 kg (25th percentile), and occipitofrontal circumference (OFC) 50 cm (25th percentile). He was partly responsive to his mother with purposeless movements and no verbal response to commands. Sensory and motor examinations were normal. Cranial nerves were grossly intact. There were no cerebellar signs or nystagmus. On gait examination, he was unable to walk without support. With support, mixed movements including high stepping, jumping, and ataxic gait were observed. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory investigations, including complete blood count, renal function tests, and liver function tests, were all normal. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with contrast appeared normal.
test_results: EEG revealed abnormal findings of generalized seizure discharge with more spikes seen in bilateral frontal and temporal regions. During sleep, spike and slow-wave discharge were noted in both cerebral hemispheres in a generalized manner.

case_report: A 7-year-old female, genetically confirmed at 1 year of age to have a deletion of region 11.23 on the long arm of chromosome 7, was born at 41 weeks of gestation following a normal pregnancy. There was no notable family history of diseases or anomalies. The patient was monitored for pulmonary artery stenosis, behavioral issues, intellectual disability, Achilles tendinopathy, and early puberty. Clinical examination revealed facial features including periorbital fullness, a short nose with a bulbous tip, a long philtrum, a wide mouth, and full lips. Imaging performed at 5 years old for facial evaluation showed no significant asymmetry between the maxillary sinuses. At 7 years old, physical examination noted progressive facial asymmetry with right hypoglobus and enophthalmos, which were not observed in earlier years. The patient had no history of sinonasal complaints or recurrent upper respiratory tract infections, nor did she report visual disturbances or facial pain. At 7 years old, she developed early puberty and underwent skull base imaging to study the sellar region and began treatment with gonadotrophin releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists.
test_results: Facial MR scan revealed a hypoplastic and opacified right maxillary sinus with retraction of the maxillary sinus walls and diminished sinus volume. A CT scan showed a diminished volume of the right maxillary sinus, which was completely opacified; the CT scan also showed a lateralized uncinate process with retraction of the middle turbinate and demineralization of the sinus walls.

case_report: A 2-year-old boy with a prenatal diagnosis of a malformation uropathy was referred to the pediatric surgery department. On systemic examination, there were no palpable masses. An abdominal ultrasonography and color Doppler showed a vascular mass at the left renal hilum measuring 25 mm × 21 mm with vascular flow in the renal artery, displacing the renal vein. An angiography of the renal arteries revealed a true preostial aneurysm at the left renal artery measuring 7 mm × 12 mm. Renal scintigraphy indicated altered function in the left kidney (glomerular renal function at 29%) with normal drainage, while the right kidney showed good function (glomerular renal function at 71%). An endovascular treatment was attempted but was unsuccessful, and no vascular bypass procedure was feasible; the patient underwent a left nephrectomy. The excised specimen measured 75 mm × 50 mm × 20 mm, with a renal artery aneurysm measuring 30 mm × 35 mm. On cut section, the renal parenchyma contained a whitish area measuring 35 mm × 10 mm.
test_results: Histological examination showed an unencapsulated tumor infiltrating the renal parenchyma and involving focally the renal sinus. It consisted of a proliferation of spindle cells with scanty cytoplasm and no nuclear atypia nor mitosis. Hypocellular myxoid areas were seen around blood vessels and tubules, forming concentric 'onion skin' rings. Some intratumoral arterioles had myxoid changes of medial smooth muscle, characterizing angiodysplasia. The glomeruli showed juxtaglomerular hyperplasia. The wall of the aneurysm showed fibrosis with dystrophic calcifications. There were no nephrogenic rests. Tumor cells were diffusely immunoreactive for CD34, and there is no immunostaining with PS100, desmin, and cytokeratin.

case_report: A 14-year-old male presented with a 5-year history of a non-painful, protruding mass located in the right preauricular area. Physical examination identified a firm, dome-shaped mass measuring 1.5 cm in diameter, which was attached to the overlying skin but did not cause any skin changes. The entire mass was excised under local anesthesia. Upon gross examination, the mass appeared reddish-brown, globular, and had a stony hard consistency.
test_results: Microscopic examination showed a well-circumscribed nodular tumor with florid osseous metaplasia. The tumor was mainly comprised of shadow cell clusters and laminated trabecular bones with no basaloid components. The stroma admixed with shadow cell clusters showed extensive ossification along with osteoclast-like multinucleated giant cells. Bone marrow structures containing a few mononuclear cells and fibrofatty tissue were observed enclosed by bony trabeculae. On immunohistochemistry, these marrow cells were positive for antimyeloperoxidase antibodies.

case_report: The patient, F.A., a 2-year-old girl, was born at term via C-section with an APGAR score of 8–9 and a birth weight of 3840 g. Prenatal ultrasound revealed an enlarged 3rd ventricle. At birth, cranial and facial dysmorphisms were noted, including a shortened anteroposterior diameter, round face, small mouth, enlarged upper eyelids, retracted jaw, short neck, and short upper limbs with a unique palmar fold. At 2 months, approximately five violet nodules with a greenish hue, 5–6 mm in diameter, appeared on the lateral thorax, left forearm, left knee, and left shoulder. The family physician recommended coagulation tests and an ultrasound examination. However, 48 hours later, the infant developed seizures and was admitted to the neurosurgery department. Imaging revealed a right temporal cerebral hemorrhage with spontaneous resolution, avoiding the need for surgery. Left hemiparesis and mild hypertonus of the left body side developed, contrasting with global axial hypotonia. Motor delay was observed. Secondary epilepsy was diagnosed. The child exhibited significant delays in motor and developmental milestones, including the inability to sit, stand, or develop speech. At the current consultation, the child, aged 2, had a weight of 8 kg (−4 SD), height of 83 cm, head circumference of 46.5 cm, and a large anterior fontanelle of 3.5/5 cm. Skin and mucosa were slightly pale, with an erythematous plaque with scaling on the chin (5 cm diameter) and two hemangiomas on the right thorax and left retro-auricular area. Muscle tone was globally reduced, and subcutaneous tissue was diminished. No palpable lymph nodes were detected. Respiratory and cardiovascular examinations were normal. The abdomen was soft and mobile with an enlarged liver palpable 3 cm below the lower rib. Urine and feces passage were normal. Cranial and facial dysmorphia included low-positioned ears, high palate arch, small mouth, and mild plagiocephaly. The child was alert, with a social smile, and followed movements with symmetric facial expressions. Mobility was significantly impaired, with reduced movement patterns and low muscle tone. She could put her legs together, lift her hands to her mouth, and bring them to the median area but did not actively participate when lifted from the supine position. She could sit for a few seconds and hold her head briefly. When lifted from the axillae, she did not support her weight on her legs. When placed on her belly, she lifted and rotated her head. Reflexes were present bilaterally, with no clonus and normal dorsal flexion of the foot. Cognitive development included a social smile, laughter, and inconsistent following, but no speech development.
test_results: The PEX6 variant c.1445_1448del p. (Ala483del) was identified; this is an in-frame deletion of 3 bps in exon 6, which causes the loss of residue Ala at position 483. The second modified PEX6 variant c.166G>C p. (Ala56Pro) causes an amino acid change from Ala to Pro at position 56. Both parents were heterozygotes for the gene PEX6. Biochemical metabolic determinations needed for the peroxisome disease (VLCFA, prystanic acid, phytanic acid (3 mg/L), and serum plasmalogen showed high values for VLCFA C26 and pipecolic acid (406.9 µmol/L). There was also a modified ratio of VLCFA C24/C22 and C26/C22.

case_report: A 76-year-old woman with a 4-month history of a growth emerging from the abdominal wall visited our orthopedic outpatient department. She had previously undergone partial resection for endometrial cancer 5 years ago. Post-surgery, the skin developed keloid scars, but the recovery was uneventful with no signs of recurrence or infection. Four months before her visit, a growth appeared from the keloid scar on the abdominal wall and began to protrude outside the skin, increasing in size rapidly. Physical examination revealed a protruding lesion continuous with the keloid scar on the abdominal wall, measuring approximately 3 × 3 × 2 cm.
test_results: The needle biopsy specimen was characterized by high cellularity and marked nuclear pleomorphism and accompanied by abundant mitotic activity and a spindle cell morphology. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) 1 week later revealed a tumor measuring 5 × 4 × 3 cm protruding subcutaneously with no continuity to the abdominal cavity. Histopathological examination following hematoxylin and eosin staining revealed short pleomorphic spindle cells and polygonal cells with a storiform pattern, accompanied by abundant mitotic activity. The tumor was negative for smooth muscle actin, h-caldesmon, cytokeratin AE1/AE3, CAM5.2, and CD34.

case_report: An 8-month-old boy from China presented at 6 months of age with recurrent episodes of fever lasting 5–7 days, recurring every 3–7 days, occasionally accompanied by a slight cough. He exhibited no physical pain, movement issues, rash, or other symptoms. The infant was born at full term via normal delivery with a birth weight of 3.0 kg. His parents are not related by blood. There was a history of neonatal jaundice. Upon admission, the boy showed mild pallor without lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Blood tests revealed severe neutropenia (380–400/mm3) with a normal white blood cell count, microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 85–95 g/L), and slight thrombocytosis. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated (79 mm/h), and C-reactive protein was 39 mg/L (normal < 8 mg/L). Immunoglobulin levels and lymphocyte subsets were normal. Rheumatoid factors were negative. Antinuclear antibody was positive at a titer of 1:80, while the anti-ds DNA antibody was negative. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies showed a mild elevation in anti-MPO antibody (30.2 RU/ml) and a negative anti-PR3 antibody. Thyroid function tests were normal. Serum iron and transferrin levels were low, indicating iron-deficiency anemia. Bone marrow hemocytology showed myeloproliferation cells with a decreased proportion of myelocytes due to granulocytosis. Red blood cells were active and proliferative, with metarubricytes dominating and mature erythrocytes appearing small, hollow, and distorted. Cultures of blood and bone marrow puncture specimens for bacteria and fungi showed no growth. Viral serologic studies were negative. A lymphocyte interferon release assay was negative. Abdominal ultrasound and cardiac ultrasound scans were normal. Chest CT showed no interstitial or parenchymal infiltration. The patient did not undergo an MRI scan due to the absence of limb pain.
test_results: We isolated DNA from peripheral blood samples obtained from the patient and parents using the Gentra Puregene Blood Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). Whole exome library was captured by a SureSelect Human All Exon Kit (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Target regions were sequenced and aligned to the GRCh37/hg19 human reference sequence. Variants were annotated and filtered by TGex. Variants were classified following the ACMG/AMP standards and guidelines. Putative pathogenic variants were confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

case_report: A 20-year-old male reported experiencing multiple polymorphous vesiculobullous mucocutaneous eruptions around the lips for 7 months, which later spread to the buccal mucosa, leading to difficulty swallowing. Additionally, he developed conjunctivitis accompanied by blurred vision and atypical targetoid lesions with crusts surrounded by erythema on the trunk, extremities, prepuce, and perianal region. During this period, he experienced a weight loss of 5 kg.
test_results: Direct immunofluorescence of biopsy specimen from Skin lesion showed deposition of Immunoglobulin G (+) and C3 in the intercellular region of epidermal cells mainly in the suprabasal region. Linear deposition of IgG is also seen in dermo-epidermal junction. Computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a well defined intensely enhancing mass lesion with central necrosis in the right hemipelvis, 6 cm in size, abutting the right obturator internus muscle and displacing the urinary bladder anteriorly. Engorged vessels were seen around the mass. Histopathlogy of the mass showed oval to spindle cells in a background of vascular stroma infiltrated by lymphocytes. The cells were immunopsitive for CD21, CD35, CD23, S-100, Claustrin, CD34, CD31, S-100; Leucocyte common antigen, and Human leukocyte antigen-DR were also positive in some cells. Hyaline-vascular follicles were identified at the peripheral portion or occasionally scattered in the center of the tumor. Rich vascularity was highlighted by the CD34 immunostaining.
diagnosis: Follicular Dendritic Cell Sarcoma with Paraneoplastic Pemphigus

case_report: A 5-day-old female infant was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit due to refusal to breastfeed, poor responsiveness, weak cries, and cold extremities. Physical examination revealed the following: Weight 3100 g (SDS = −0.56), Height 49.5 cm (SDS = −0.37), Heart rate 125/min, Respiratory rate 36/min, Blood pressure 71/32 mmHg, Rectal temperature 37°C, SpO2 99%. Auscultation indicated no lung crackles or heart murmur. Palpation showed the liver edge about 2.5 cm below the costal margin, and the spleen was not palpable. The skin exhibited mild jaundice. Genital examination confirmed female characteristics. Two days later, the infant developed severe dehydration and vomiting. Biochemical laboratory tests indicated severe hyperkalemia with K+ 10.1 mmol/L, Na+ 105 mmol/L, Cl− 83 mmol/L, pH 7.31, BE(B) −10.8 mmol/L, and a trans-tubular potassium gradient (TTKG) of 4. Hormone levels were as follows: aldosterone 1.08 nmol/L (range 0.17–0.47), plasma renin activity 14.0 ug/L/h (range 0–15), ACTH 20.4 pmol/L, cortisol 687.2 nmol/L, testosterone 0.94 nmol/L, and 17-OHP 25 nmol/L. The infant was immediately given a supplement of 10% NaCl.
test_results: The clinical diagnosis was confirmed by molecular genetic testing.

case_report: A 61-year-old male reported experiencing a painful mass in the left epididymis for several months. There was no fever or history of trauma associated with the condition. Hematological parameters and urine indexes were found to be within normal limits. Urine culture showed no bacterial growth. Ultrasonography of the left epididymis identified a mass with mixed echotexture located in the epididymal tail.
test_results: Histopathology showed an epididymal mass comprising sheets of histiocytes with granular eosinophilic cytoplasm admixed with neutrophils, lymphocytes, and plasma cells. Many of the histiocytes contained small round to oval targetoid structures that were morphologically consistent with Michaelis-Gutmann bodies.

case_report: A 20-year-old female, with no history of medication use or medical conditions, presented for a dermatological examination due to the presence of two asymptomatic lesions located under her breast and in her groin fold. The lesions were annular macules, well-defined, and exhibited a violaceous or brownish color with a shiny surface. The lesions measured between 20 to 25 mm in their longest dimension. Dermoscopic evaluation revealed a pigmented pattern characterized by diffuse fine peppering or perifollicular pigmentation.
test_results: Histology revealed hyperkeratosis, atrophy of epidermis, hydropic degeneration of basal keratinocytes, and lichenoid dermal infiltrate with melanophages. Elastic fibers were diminished in upper dermis.

case_report: A 38-year-old Chinese female, the second child of a non-consanguineous marriage, presented with a 4-year history of unsteady walking and a 10-day history of slurred speech. She was healthy until the onset of these symptoms. Approximately 4 years ago, she developed an unsteady gait and occasional falls without obvious triggers. Over time, she experienced procrastination, poor memory, occasional incontinence, slow speech, slow thinking, and menometrorrhagia, but remained able to care for herself. Family members noted irregular menstrual cycles and decreased menstrual flow in recent years. Due to worsening symptoms, her siblings brought her to the local hospital. Ten days prior to hospitalization, she developed slurred speech, abdominal bloating, constipation, and required assistance to walk. She had no fever, chills, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, or diarrhea. Treatment at a local clinic did not improve her condition, and no treatment details were available. She was admitted to our hospital emergency department unconscious and transferred to the encephalopathy department. Auscultation revealed a slight wet rale in both lower lungs. Neurological examination showed hyperreflexia in the bilateral radial periosteal reflex, biceps, and triceps tendons, but weak bilateral knee and Achilles tendon reflexes. The abdominal wall reflex was absent, and bilateral pathological signs were negative. There was no neck resistance, and meningeal irritation was negative. Other neurological examinations could not be performed. The patient had no fever, but blood tests indicated infection: white blood cells (WBC) at 9.65 × 10^9/L (reference: 3.50–9.50), neutrophil percentage at 80.3% (reference: 40.0–75.0%), high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) at 69 mg/L (reference: 0–10), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) at 106 mm/h (reference: 0–20). Serum sex hormones indicated ovarian failure, with estradiol at 55 pmol/L (reference: 56–1,625). Other endocrine hormones were also abnormal, including total triiodothyronine (tT3) at 0.86 nmol/L (reference: 1.01–2.48) and prolactin at 835 mIU/L (reference: 58–412). Additional tests showed homocysteine at 22.5 μmol/L (reference: 0–15.0) and antinuclear antibody (1:100) (±). HIV antibody, HBV antibody, HCV antibody, glucose, lipids, glycosylated hemoglobin, tumor carbohydrate antigen, AMA profile, ANA profile, ANCA, anti-keratin antibody, anti-myeloperoxidase antibody, and anti-cyclic citrulline peptide antibody were all negative. Computed tomography (CT) scan confirmed peritonitis, pneumonia, and cholecystitis, which were associated with her abdominal bloating and constipation. Additional CT findings included multiple ground-glass nodules in the upper lobe of the right lung, dilated kidneys, and entire bilateral ureters. Ultrasound revealed bilateral mild hydrops, a dilated upper right kidney ureter, and minor ascites around the appendix. Cerebrospinal fluid pressure was 82 mm H2O, with WBC at 35 × 10^6/L, glucose at 5.18 mmol/L, chlorine at 113.0 mmol/L, and immunoglobulin G at 39.8 mg/L. Cerebrospinal fluid autoimmune encephalitis antibody spectrum, bacterial (aerobic and anaerobic) and fungal cultures, and second-generation gene sequencing of pathogenic microorganisms were negative. Cytological pathology was negative. The electroencephalogram was abnormal, showing multiple pathological waves, spikes, sharp waves, spike-slow waves, and mixed spike-slow waves in bilateral frontotemporal and midfrontal areas, with sharp waves also seen in the bilateral temporal, central-parietal, and occipital areas.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed extensive and symmetrical changes in bilateral cerebral hemisphere demyelination with glial hyperplasia involving the corpus callosum.
diagnosis: Late-onset leukoencephalopathy with vanishing white matter

case_report: A 56-year-old woman experienced chest tightness, chronic cough, and sputum production for three years, which did not improve with treatment at local hospitals. She was referred to our hospital. Imaging studies, including chest radiograph and CT scan, revealed multiple, relatively well-defined, multifocal peribronchiolar nodules. Her medical and social history did not reveal any contributory factors. Physical examination showed a blood pressure of 100/70 mmHg, pulse rate of 78/min, respiratory rate of 27/min, and body temperature of 36.8℃. The patient appeared well, with non-icteric sclera, a flat abdomen, and no gross abnormalities. Initial laboratory findings included a blood cell count of 5,750/mm3, hemoglobin of 12.7 g/dL, hematocrit of 37.3%, and platelet count of 298,000/mm3. Serum biochemical results were AST 20 IU/L, ALT 13 IU/L, ALP 182 IU/L, LDH 386 IU/L, total bilirubin 0.86 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.10 mg/dL, total protein 7.9 g/dL, albumin 4.0 g/dL, BUN 15 mg/dL, creatinine 0.6 mg/dL, total cholesterol 184 mg/dL, uric acid 4.9 mg/dL, Ca 9.3 mg/dL, P 4.4 mg/dL, Na 140.8 mEq/L, K 4.1 mEq/L, and Cl 108.7 mEq/L. Pulmonary function tests were within normal predicted values. Bronchoscopic examination did not reveal specific findings. Cultures for bacteria and fungi were negative, as were AFB stain, AFB culture, and M. tuberculosis PCR from bronchoscopic washing fluid. The patient was admitted for further evaluation. Follow-up chest CT showed persistent peribronchiolar nodules and consolidations in both the upper and middle lobes of the lung. An 18FDG-PET CT scan indicated mild increased uptake with peak SUVs of 1.5 at the RUL and 1.6 at the RML, and delayed views showed peak SUVs of 1.6 at the RUL and 1.2 at the RML. A percutaneous CT-guided needle aspiration biopsy of the RML consolidation area was performed, but the sample was insufficient for a diagnosis.
test_results: The gross appearance of the involved lung appeared consolidated. The microscopic findings showed that the alveolar walls rather than the air spaces were affected; they were expanded by the interstitial infiltrate. The inflammatory infiltrates were prominent around the bronchovascular bundles and formed rounded nodular aggregates around small intralobular vessels. The infiltrates consisted of predominantly small lymphocytic cells with some mixture of plasma cells and a few larger mononuclear cells. Surrounding parenchyma occasionally revealed lymphoid follicles. Immunohistochemically, the infiltrate was predominantly composed of T cells (CD45RO positive); there were only focal peribronchiolar or paraseptal collections of B cells (CD20 positive). Amplification of the immunoglobulin heavy chain gene by PCR showed a polyclonal pattern of reactivity.
diagnosis: Pulmonary Nodular Lymphoid Hyperplasia associated with Sjögren's Syndrome

case_report: A 32-year-old female patient has had abnormal serum liver enzyme levels for 15 years. Initially, these abnormalities were detected during a high school physical examination, but no symptoms of liver dysfunction were present, so no action was taken. Four years later, similar abnormalities were found during an occupational health examination, leading to her admission to a local hospital. Despite treatment with liver-protective drugs, her liver function indices did not improve. The patient did not experience any adverse effects and did not monitor her liver function indices in the following years. One month prior to her admission to our hospital, she visited a maternal and child health hospital for infertility issues, where routine examination revealed significantly abnormal liver function indices. She was then admitted to the Department of Hepatology at our hospital for further evaluation and treatment. Thirteen years ago, she underwent a splenectomy due to a ruptured spleen from a car accident and recovered well. Over ten years of marriage, she experienced continued infertility and did not take any infertility medications or oral contraceptives. One year ago, salpingography indicated partial obstruction of the fallopian tube, reducing the natural conception rate. Her spouse's fertility tests were normal, and in vitro fertilization (IVF) was recommended but not pursued due to financial constraints. The patient reported no history of alcohol intake or use of hepatotoxic drugs. Her father had surgery for intrahepatic bile duct stones and recovered well. Her mother, who passed away from a brain hemorrhage three years ago, had no history of liver disease. Her brother's liver function was normal. The patient's vital signs were stable, and physical examination showed no significant findings.
test_results: The genetic testing results revealed two novel heterozygous mutations in the ABCB4 gene: a 2950C>T; p.A984V mutation (exon 24) and a 667A>G; p.I223V mutation (exon 7). Pathological examination revealed cholestatic liver fibrosis (modified Scheuer score S2). An analysis of histological samples revealed a significant decrease in multidrug-resistant protein 3 (MDR3) protein staining compared to the levels of staining observed in samples from healthy subjects. Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed an increased hepatic interstitium and multiple patchy abnormal signal shadows in hepatic segments VII and VIII. No obstructions associated with the extrahepatic and intrahepatic bile ducts were observed following detailed examination using magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography.

case_report: In November 2014, an 80-year-old female with a history of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and positive anticyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies and rheumatoid factor was admitted to the rheumatology division for acute renal failure and painful skin lesions on her lower limbs. She was on leflunomide and low-dose prednisone (5 mg/day). Her medical history included osteoarthritis, dorsal vertebral osteoporotic fractures, arterial hypertension under treatment, and bowel diverticulosis. RA was diagnosed in August 2010, and she initially received methotrexate (15 mg/week) and low-dose prednisone, which was effective but discontinued due to alopecia. Leflunomide (20 mg/day) was then started. Laboratory tests in September 2014 showed creatinine at 0.6 mg/dL, ESR at 55 mm/hour, C-reactive protein at 3.17 mg/dL, serum total calcium at 8.72 mg/dL, 25-hydroxy vitamin D at 32.31 ng/mL, phosphorus at 4.6 mg/dL, and parathyroid hormone (PTH) at 394 pg/mL. Urine tests revealed low levels of total calcium (9.84 mg/24 hours), total phosphorus (189 mg/24 hours), and total magnesium (26.4 mg/24 hours). During admission, the patient reported rachialgia and oliguria (diuresis <500 mL/24 hours). Physical examination showed livedo reticularis and multiple painful, erythematous, necrotic skin lesions on her lower limbs. Laboratory tests revealed creatinine at 2.21 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen at 89.4 mg/dL, creatinine clearance at 41 mL/minute, ESR at 11 mm/hour, C-reactive protein at 0.29 mg/dL, potassium at 2.63 mEq/L, magnesium at 1.22 mg/dL, serum calcium at 7.7 mg/dL, serum sodium bicarbonate at 23 mEq/L, serum total phosphorus at 4.76 mg/dL, 25-hydroxy vitamin D at 21.35 ng/mL, and PTH at 531.4 pg/mL. Doppler ultrasound of the lower limbs ruled out deep vein thrombosis. Renal echography showed no parenchymal involvement. Skeletal X-ray of the lower limbs indicated diffuse vascular calcifications.
test_results: A skin biopsy of the lesions showed calcific sclerosis and microthrombi within a small artery with calcium deposition.

case_report: The patient is a four-year-old boy who experienced recurrent convulsions for two months at the age of 1 year and 7 months. His convulsions occurred in clusters, with a frequency of 14 times per day. In the neonatal stage, he exhibited hypotonia and was suspected to have floppy infant syndrome. His motor development was delayed, and despite active rehabilitation training, progress was slow. He could hold his head and sit only when supported. At 1 year and 5 months old, he showed motor function regression and was unable to hold his head up, sit, or roll over. Upon admission, he was treated with a ketogenic diet, ACTH, and various antiseizure medications, including levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, vigabatrin, clobazam, clonazepam, and pirampanide. After three days of ACTH treatment and two weeks of vigabatrin (100 mg/kg/d), nodding convulsions recurred.
test_results: Electroencephalography (EEG) documented hypsarrhythmia. Brain MRI results were normal.
diagnosis: Developmental epileptic disorder due to de novo variants of IRF2BPL

case_report: An 86-year-old Caucasian woman presented with nausea and abdominal pain. Imaging studies, including abdominal and endoscopic ultrasound and a computed tomography (CT) scan, revealed a 3 cm cystic lesion in the head of the pancreas, accompanied by a dilated pancreatic duct and regional lymphadenopathy. Ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration showed no malignant cells. The preoperative CA19-9 level was 54.1 U/mL (reference value < 27 U/mL). During surgery, a firm, cystic lesion was observed in the head of the pancreas with involvement of the superior mesenteric vein (SMV). A modification on Whipple procedure was performed, including partial resection and end-to-end anastomosis of the SMV. The postoperative course was uneventful. Ten months later, the patient showed no signs of recurrence. A gross 2.5 cm tumor of the head of the pancreas was noted.
test_results: Histopathology showed multiple small cysts covered by cubic mesothelial cells with uniform, small nuclei. Immunohistochemistry revealed a strong immunoreactivity for cytokeratin, vimentin and CK5. CD31 and CD34 immunoreactivity was not expressed by the cystic epithelium. There was no invasive growth or malignancy.

case_report: A 36-year-old male presented three months after a mild COVID-19 infection, which did not require hospitalization and was managed conservatively. He reported experiencing symptoms for one week, including fatigue, tiredness, shortness of breath, back pain, and tea-colored urine. His medical history did not include recent ingestion of fava beans or medications, and there was no family history of congenital hemolytic anemia. On clinical examination, he had a heart rate of 105 beats per minute and noticeable jaundice in the sclera. Laboratory investigations showed normocytic anemia with a hemoglobin level of 9.5 g/dL and thrombocytopenia with a platelet count of 121 × 10^9/L. Additional findings included reticulocytosis, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, and normal liver enzyme levels, with no signs of disseminated intravascular coagulation. A peripheral blood smear revealed spherocytes, polychromasia, and a few red blood cell fragments, without any agglutination or clumping of red blood cells.
test_results: Both direct and indirect Coombs tests were positive.

case_report: A 3-month-old male infant, born by cesarean section at full term to nonconsanguineous Bulgarian parents, had a normal Apgar score. The amniotic fluid was green, but there were no other signs of perinatal asphyxia. His birth weight, length, and head circumference were within normal ranges. At 3 months, he experienced feeding difficulties, including inconsolable crying after feeds and regurgitations. Movement issues such as dystonic postures and spontaneous Moro reflex were observed. Neurodevelopmental delay was noted: visual tracking of objects and faces was inconsistent; he began smiling at 3 months but then stopped and was not cooing. His 4-year-old sister had been diagnosed with dyskinetic CP, characterized by microcephaly, severe psychomotor delay, dyskinesias, and epilepsy. Physical examination at 3 months was normal except for a low growth rate in head circumference (−1.9 SD). Neurologic examination showed decreased neck muscle tone with absent head control, spasticity in the extremities, tendon hyperreflexia, and persistence of grasp reflex and automatic crawling. General movements were jerky and/or stiff, and dystonic postures were frequent. There was moderate psychomotor delay with a developmental quotient (DQ) of 35. Laboratory tests, including complete blood cell count, biochemistry, arterial blood gases, urine organic acids, plasma acylcarnitine, and amino acid profiles, were within reference ranges. Serology tests for congenital infections (Cytomegalovirus, Rubella, Toxoplasma gondii) and Epstein-Barr virus were negative. Sleep EEGs (lasting about 30 minutes with no seizure-like events) showed occasional primary generalized single spike-and-slow-wave complexes. Transfontanelle sonography revealed slightly dilated lateral ventricles and a large cyst-like cisterna magna, suggesting cerebellar hypoplasia.
test_results: A homozygous missence mutation c.919G > T (p.Ala307Ser) was found.

case_report: Patient 1 is an 11-year-old female. After birth, transient evoked otoacoustic emissions were not obtained, but an automated auditory brainstem response was obtained bilaterally. Her growth and development were normal. At age 10, she was referred for further investigations due to prolonged retention of primary teeth and delayed permanent tooth eruption.
test_results: Dental panoramic tomography (DPT) showed that all the unerupted teeth were present and had normal root development. Lateral cephalometric radiograph showed a convex profile with an open bite tendency. An audiogram revealed mild bilateral SNHL affecting the high frequencies.

case_report: The patient is a 13-year and 5-month-old boy with a congenital deformity of the left forearm. From the age of 3, his growth in height lagged behind peers, and his penis remained smaller than average for his age, with no development over the past two years. He was born with bilateral cryptorchidism and underwent bilateral orchidectomy. The patient has experienced reduced sweating since childhood, and his cognitive abilities are normal. He was delivered by caesarean section at term, with a birth weight of 3400 g and a birth length of 50 cm. He was fed artificially. His motor development was typical for his age and sex. The parents are not related by blood, and the mother had a healthy pregnancy. The father is 170 cm tall and healthy; the mother is 158 cm tall and has deformities in the distal segments of the little fingers of both hands, with no other health issues. The child's height, weight, and body mass index (BMI) are 144 cm (−2.4SD), 33.8 kg, and 16.3 kg/m2, respectively. The nipples are wide apart and retracted, the penis measures 2 cm × 1 cm, and the testicles have a volume of 1 ml. The 4th and 5th metacarpals and phalanges of the left hand are absent, as is the left ulna. The body is well-proportioned with no noticeable facial abnormalities or issues detected in the heart, lungs, or abdomen. Routine blood tests, liver function, and renal function tests are normal. The electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia. Bone age is estimated to be 11 years, based on Greulich and Pyle's radiographic atlas, while the actual age is 13 years and 5 months.
test_results: A pituitary MRI plain scan showed small adenohypophysis and the presence of Rathke's cleft cyst.

case_report: A 62-year-old Sri Lankan Sinhalese man from the North Central Province of Sri Lanka presented with generalized malaise and body weakness. He had a history of type 2 diabetes and had been using Mixtard (human insulin) for 10 years. He had also been hypertensive for 5 years and was on losartan potassium, which was discontinued 2 months prior due to low-normal blood pressure. He reported experiencing proximal muscle weakness for 1 month, making it difficult to rise from a squatting position and lift his arms above his head. He also noticed increased urination and nocturnal urination, along with worsening blood sugar control. There was no history of fever, vomiting, diarrhea, or drug abuse before the onset of symptoms. He denied any family history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, or renal disease. On examination, he was conscious and rational. His blood pressure was 110/64 mm Hg and his pulse was 76/minute. Cardiovascular and respiratory system examinations were normal. His abdomen was soft and non-tender. Neurological examination showed normal higher functions and cranial nerves. Motor system examination revealed hypotonia in all four limbs, with muscle strength of 4/5 in the lower limbs and 5/5 in the upper limbs. All reflexes were present but diminished, and the plantar reflex was bilaterally unresponsive. There was no sensory or autonomic involvement. Initial blood tests showed sodium ion (Na+) 146 mEq/L, potassium ion (K+) 1.95 mEq/L, urea 4.3 mmol/L, creatinine 0.7 mg/dl, and random blood glucose 300 mg/dl. Hemoglobin was 13.2 g/dL, white blood cell count was 5.7 × 10^6, and platelets were 240 × 10^6. Transaminases were normal, and serum albumin was 34 g/L. Severe hypokalemia was confirmed in a repeat blood sample.
test_results: Arterial blood gas revealed severe metabolic alkalosis with pH of 7.6, partial pressure of carbon dioxide (CO2) of 41 mmHg, and bicarbonate of 40.3 mmol/L.

case_report: A 40-year-old male, with a history of chronic smoking (10 pack-years) and no alcohol consumption, presented with recurrent episodes of biliary colic. There was no family history of cholelithiasis or neoplasia. He was admitted to the emergency department with severe acute pancreatitis and an initial systemic inflammatory response syndrome. His Bedside Index of Severity in Acute Pancreatitis (BISAP) score was 2, and his body mass index (BMI) was 23.6 kg/m². Physical examination revealed epigastric tenderness, but was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory results obtained 24 hours after the onset of pain indicated a blood lipase level of 30 times the upper limit of normal (ULN), no cytolysis, a slightly elevated gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) at 1.4 times ULN, and normal triglyceride and calcium levels.
test_results: Abdominal ultrasound (US) revealed images of intrahepatic micro- and macro-stones with posterior acoustic shadow and a thin-walled gallbladder (GB) with sludge, without dilatation of intra- or extra-hepatic bile ducts and a heterogeneous pancreas. Abdominal and pelvic CT at 96 hours of pain concluded that the CT severity index score (CTSI) was 10 and that GB contained sludge, without evidence of intrahepatic stones.

case_report: A one-year-old Indian boy was referred to our center at 8 months of age for evaluation due to certain physical features and developmental delays. He was born full-term with a birth weight of 3.6 kg (above the 95th percentile). He experienced transient neonatal jaundice that required phototherapy but resolved without complications. Developmental milestones were delayed; the child was unable to crawl, sit, hold objects, or produce sounds typical for his age. Family history indicated he was the third sibling, following two healthy children and two early miscarriages. There was no consanguinity or similar conditions in the family. Clinically, his weight was 10 kg (90th percentile), height 73 cm (75th percentile), and head circumference 44.5 cm (25th percentile). Dermatological examination revealed an asymmetrical face, bitemporal narrowing, prominent metopic sutures, epicanthic folds, wide mouth, sparse hair, and absent eyebrows. His skin was dry with mild hyperkeratosis, eczematous lesions on the neck and extremities, keratosis pilaris on the arms, seborrheic dermatitis on the scalp, and miliaria on the back. A vascular hemangiomatous plaque measuring 5 cm×3.5 cm was noted on the medial aspect of the right lower limb. Routine hematological tests, blood biochemistry, urinalysis, thyroid function tests, and serum zinc levels were all within normal ranges. Echocardiography indicated a small secundum atrial septal defect and patent ductus arteriosus. Abdominal ultrasound showed mild hepatosplenomegaly.
test_results: MRI scanning of the brain showed bifrontal subdural T2 hyperintense areas plus prominence of the frontotemporal subarachnoid space and corpus callosum hypoplasia. Karyotype revealed 46 XY, involving 9p11q21.2 chromosome.

case_report: A 35-year-old male with a history of an asymptomatic left hydrocele observed over several years reported an increase in the size of the hydrocele and the presence of nodularity in the scrotum over the past year. He was referred to Urology for further evaluation. Initial assessment revealed a hydrocele in the left testicle and a very firm, nodular mass located superiorly in the scrotum. The physical examination was otherwise unremarkable, with no gynecomastia and a normal right testicle.
test_results: An ultrasound of the left testicle was performed, showing a lobulated, heterogeneous left paratesticular mass measuring 4.1 x 4.7 cm with heterogeneous blood flow. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis was negative for metastatic disease. Final pathology of the gross specimen revealed a 6.6 cm tumor emanating from the testiculo-epididymal groove and invading into the base of the spermatic cord and scrotal wall. Specimen histology showed high-grade tumor cells forming papillary structures that surrounded fibrovascular cores. Lymphovascular invasion was present on histological examination, and resection margins were deemed negative in the final pathology report. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for Paired Box Gene 8 (PAX8), Wilms Tumor Protein (WT1), and Cancer Antigen 125 (CA-125).

case_report: A 29-year-old female presented to our clinic in March 2021 with a history of right-sided clavicle pain persisting for over three years. Initially, in 2018, she reported pain and palpable enlargement in the medial right clavicle. She had no significant past medical or surgical history and denied any history of osteomyelitis, trauma to the right clavicle, or autoimmune diseases. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest without contrast performed at that time revealed increased bone sclerosis in an expanded right medial clavicle, with cortical breakthrough, scalloping, and erosions. Hook-like osteophytes were also observed. There was no associated soft tissue mass or pathological fracture. A right clavicle core needle biopsy was performed, showing only lamellar trabecular bone and yielding nondiagnostic results. Upon evaluation in March 2021, the patient reported intermittent pain in the right clavicle since 2018, with monthly episodes of increased pain, often at night or during menses. These episodes involved throbbing pain radiating to the right shoulder and neck, leading to an antalgic posture. Physical examination revealed mild discomfort on palpation and bony irregularity in the right mid-clavicle, with no lymphadenomegaly. Radiographs from March 2021 showed cortical irregularity, erosions, and scalloping in the right mid-clavicle, with interval worsening compared to 2018. A whole-body bone scan in April 2021 indicated a solitary lesion in the right clavicle with significantly increased bony uptake corresponding to the area of sclerosis seen on radiography.
test_results: Pathological analysis of both specimens showed fragments of benign cortical and cancellous bone along evidence of prior remodeling with woven and lamellar reactive bone. The bone marrow analysis demonstrated hemosiderin deposits and fibrosis as well as a chronic inflammatory infiltrate. Microbiological evaluation was unremarkable.
Orpha_name: Medial condensing osteitis of the clavicle

case_report: A 71-year-old African American female visited the retina clinic due to progressively worsening blurry vision in both eyes over 40 years. She reported a significant decline in night, peripheral, and central vision over the past five years. Central visual acuity decreased from 20/60 in both eyes to 20/100 in the right eye and 20/80 in the left eye. She has no family history of retinitis pigmentosa. Her medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus without diabetic retinopathy, hypertension with hypertensive retinopathy, an episode of uveitis at age 58, and cataract extraction with intraocular lens placement in both eyes at age 59. Confrontational visual field testing showed constricted visual fields in both eyes. The anterior segment exam was unremarkable except for an irregular right pupil with a sluggish light response. Fundoscopic examination revealed confluent, demarcated areas of chorioretinal scarring with intraretinal pigment migration bands in the peripheral retina, more apparent temporally in the right eye and nasally in the left eye. The macula regions were relatively spared in both eyes. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the right eye showed flattening of the fovea with elevation of the inner retinal structures and outer plexiform layer, peripheral retinal thinning, loss of retinal structures, and choroid hyperreflectivity, indicating peripheral chorioretinal atrophy. The left eye exhibited an epiretinal membrane, mild flattening of the fovea with elevation of the inner retinal structures and outer plexiform layer, and disruption of the outer plexiform layer in the parafoveal region. The prominent area of involvement was located temporally in the right eye and nasally in the left eye.
test_results: A heterozygous c.830C>T, p.(T277M) mutation located on exon 7 of the BEST1 gene was identified.

case_report: A 47-year-old South-Indian woman with multiple childbirths presented to the nephrology department with bilateral pitting pedal edema and mild hypertension. She reported a history of taking steroids for three months due to musculoskeletal inflammation in her lower limbs. She is currently on cilnidipine 5 mg once daily for hypertension and has no other known comorbidities. There was no history of exposure to ifosfamide, ochratoxin A, or use of alternative medicine. Her family history includes a brother with ongoing kidney failure who is on continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis, though the primary kidney disease is unknown. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg, mild pallor, and bilateral mild pitting pedal edema. Blood tests showed hemoglobin at 10 gm/dL (normal range 11–14 g/dL), serum creatinine at 1.52 mg/dL (normal range 0.5–1 mg/dL), and blood urea at 46 mg/dL (normal range 7–20 mg/dL). A fasting lipid profile indicated cholesterol at 232 mg/dL (normal less than 200 mg/dL), triglycerides at 168 mg/dL (normal less than 150 mg/dL), HDL at 52 mg/dL (normal above 60 mg/dL), and LDL at 157 mg/dL (normal less than 100 mg/dL). Urinalysis showed trace proteinuria. A 2D-Echo revealed mild tricuspid regurgitation, mild pulmonary arterial hypertension, and an ejection fraction of 64%. Thyroid function tests and serum electrolyte values were within normal limits.
test_results: The renal tissue was examined under light microscopy using Hematoxylin and Eosin (H and E), periodic acid Schiff (PAS), periodic silver methenamine (PASM) and Masson's trichrome stain. Five of 28 glomeruli were globally sclerosed while the remaining glomeruli showed patent capillary loops with normal mesangial cellularity. There was no evidence of diffuse thickening of glomerular capillary loops, segmental sclerosis, endocapillary or extracapillary proliferation. The tubules showed tubular injury in the form of loss of brush borders and flattening of epithelium. Many proximal and distal convoluted tubules showed bizarre enlarged nuclei with prominent nucleoli. The interstitium showed mild lymphocytic infiltrate and focal mild fibrosis. No granuloma was seen. The interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy accounted for about 5% of the renal cortex. The interlobular arteries showed no specific lesion. Few arterioles showed similar bizarre enlarged nuclei. Immunohistochemistry staining for cytomegalovirus antigen and simian virus 40 antigen were negative. Immunofluorescence staining for IgG, IgM, IgA, C3, C1q, kappa and lambda light chains were negative. Real-time PCR for CMV and BK virus genomes were negative. Genetic analysis identified two rare, deleterious mutations in the exon 4 of which one is nonsynonymous mutation; rs745320524 (c.1356T>G, p.Asn452Lys) and the other is a stop-gain (loss of function) mutation; rs746677293 (c.1369C>T, p.Gln457X). Both the mutations were in homozygous condition and are in very close proximity. Both the mutations were also observed in the proband's affected sibling. The mutation rs746677293 (p.Gln457X) is a loss of function mutation with minor allele frequency (MAF) <0.001 (rare mutation). Because the mutation is in homozygous condition, the protein will be truncated midway, at 457th amino acid. Hence, a fully functional FAN1 protein (1017 amino acids) is absent in the patient and is a possible cause of the observed phenotype.
diagnosis: Karyomegalic Interstitial Nephritis due to a novel homozygous FAN1 mutation

case_report: The patient is a 37-year-old woman, the only child of parents who are not related by blood. Her early developmental milestones were typical. At the age of 35, she began to experience slow and slurred speech, accompanied by hand tremors. These symptoms worsened over the following year. At 37 years old, clinical examination revealed horizontal nystagmus, slow and slurred speech, increased reflexes, upper Rossolimo reflex, Jacobson-Lask reflex, instability during Romberg’s test, postural tremor, difficulty with rapid alternating movements, intention tremor, and clonus.
test_results: Brain MRI revealed leukoencephalopathy with cortical and cerebellar atrophy. Clinical Exome Sequencing (CES) analysis revealed two nucleotide variants in the VPS13D gene: a heterozygous nonsense variant c.9388C>T, p.(Arg3130Ter), and a novel heterozygous missense variant c.9679G>T, leading to amino acid substitution p.(Gly3227Trp) in the VPS13D protein. Both variants were validated by Sanger sequencing. The transposition of the c.9388C>T, p.(Arg3130Ter), and c.9679G>T, p.(Gly3227Trp) variants in the VPS13D gene was confirmed using the molecular cloning method.

case_report: An 18-year-old cis male patient of Turkish descent presented with a history of cognitive impairment and progressive gait disturbance. The patient’s family history included consanguinity of his parents, who are cousins. The mother has four healthy siblings and reported two spontaneous abortions and the premature death of two male children at 1 and 4 months, respectively, for unknown reasons. The father reported three healthy siblings and a gait disorder in his deceased father starting at age 40. The patient’s early childhood cognitive and physical development was unremarkable. Learning difficulties appeared during primary school, while physical abilities remained athletic. At age 15, he developed a slowly progressive gait disorder and calf cramps. By age 18, he required increasing help with reading, writing, and orientation due to cognitive decline. His walking distance was limited to approximately 100 meters, after which he needed to rest due to an increasing risk of falling. He had experienced several falls and reported muscle pain in the thigh and forearm muscles. His mood remained stable, although he occasionally expressed frustration due to increasing disability and social isolation. At age 18, the patient presented as cognitively slow but fully oriented. Emotional affect was blunted, with a low state of mood. Ocular examination revealed horizontal exotropia and occasional double vision. Facial tone was slightly reduced, and speech was mildly dysarthric. Motor signs included spastic paraparesis, overall bradykinesia, and intermittent dystonia of the fingers and arms. Tendon reflexes were brisk in the arms and clonic in the legs; there were positive Babinski and palmomental reflexes bilaterally. Coordination tests were ataxic. The walking pattern was spastic-ataxic with a widened base and signs of central hip muscle weakness, leading to an increased risk of falling, especially during running. The patient’s hair had a bristle-like appearance. Electromyography examinations were unremarkable.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed biparietal, spotty FLAIR-hyperintensities, hypointensity of the globus pallidus in T2w FLAIR and susceptibility-weighted imaging, pontocerebellar atrophy with widening of the fourth ventricle and decreased midbrain (361 mm2) but not pons midsagittal area (129 mm2), and thinning of the corpus callosum. AI-supported volumetry revealed atrophy of the thalamus (6.1 mL), midbrain (6.3 mL), and pons (8.9 mL), each with more than four standard deviations. The magnetic susceptibility of the globus pallidus was markedly reduced at 62 ppb, as measured by Quantitative Susceptibility Mapping (QSM). Imaging findings were stable at a 3.5-year follow-up.

case_report: The girl was delivered at term via cesarean section due to breech presentation to a 32-year-old mother and a 34-year-old father. Her birth weight was 3150 g (50th percentile), length was 49 cm (50th percentile), and cranial circumference was 35 cm (50th percentile). Apgar scores were 8 at 1 minute and 9 at 5 minutes. The perinatal period was generally normal, except for some breastfeeding difficulties. She met motor milestones on time, walking without support at 12 months. Development was typical until age 2, when motor difficulties, frequent falls, and stereotypic movements began. By age 5, moderate delays in psychomotor and language development were noted. Neurological examination showed fine and gross motor clumsiness with an unsteady gait. Social skills development was poor, with abnormal eye contact. Brain MRI and EEG tests were normal. Genetic tests, including targeted sequence analysis of all exons of MECP2 and FISH test for UBE3A/D15S10 allele deletion, were negative. Fragile X DNA test results were normal. At 6 years and 11 months, her weight was 21.5 kg (25th percentile) and height was 122.5 cm (50th percentile). She exhibited an unsteady gait, clumsiness, and diffuse hypotonia. Social skills were poor, with alternating phases of socialization and isolation. At the last evaluation at age 10, the Wechsler Intelligence Scales (WISC IV) indicated moderate intellectual disability (overall IQ = 44), with impairments in both verbal and performance abilities. Linguistic skills, particularly verbal comprehension, were relatively better, while significant difficulties were observed in visuospatial, visuoperceptive, and memory abilities.
test_results: Q banding karyotype on metaphase chromosomes revealed an apparently balanced de novo translocation between the distal q arm portion of chromosomes 1 and 22: 46,XX,t(1;22)(q43;q13.3). No 22q bands were visible on der (1). The translocation’s reciprocity was demonstrated by FISH, using the commercially available 22q subtelomeric probe, with the chromosome 22 breakpoint within the 22q subtelomeric probe, suggesting a potential disruption of SHANK3 gene.

case_report: A 72-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of progressive changes in gait and cognition.
