Initial symptoms included excessive daytime sleepiness and sudden awakenings at night with a scream and vacant stare, without associated limb movements. He experienced difficulty in buttoning clothes and had a few episodes of urinary and bowel incontinence. Over the next 6 months, his gait slowed, and he walked with short steps, leaning toward the right. He had trouble walking in a straight line and sustained multiple forward falls. He developed abnormal posturing of the left hand and had difficulty putting on a slipper with the left foot. He frequently bumped into objects. He also became increasingly apathetic and had difficulty performing simple calculations. A year into the illness, his behavior worsened, including aimless wandering, eating food quickly, and lack of self-care. His speech output progressively reduced, requiring undue effort while speaking. Later, he developed echolalia, stereotypical movements of the right hand (rubbing the head), head nodding, and truncal rocking. Examination showed right gaze preference, posturing of the left hand with intermittent levitation, stereotypies in the right hand, anterocollis, asymmetrical limb rigidity (left greater than right), left striatal toe, and oro-buccal, eyelid, and speech apraxia along with echolalia. Due to severe inattention (forward digit span 3) and perseveration, he performed poorly on cognitive examination (Addenbrooke's cognitive examination III score – 3).
test_results: MRI Brain revealed asymmetrical, right predominant frontoparietal atrophy. His serum sample tested positive for anti GABA-B receptor antibodies. 18F-Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (18F-FDG PET) revealed relative hypermetabolism in bilateral basal ganglia and mesial temporal cortices with diffuse cortical hypometabolism. There was no evidence of metabolically active disease elsewhere in the body. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed 15 cells, lymphocytic, protein of 80 mg/dl, and a normal CSF: serum glucose ratio (0.7). CSF cryptococcal antigen, VDRL, Gram stain, gene Xpert, TB-PCR, and neuronal antibody panel were negative. There was a bilateral theta range slowing on electroencephalogram (EEG). The serum sample tested negative for IgLON5 antibody.

case_report: Patient 2 is a Greek female who was first evaluated at 3 years and 11 months old. The family history provided by the parents was unremarkable. Both prenatal and postnatal periods were reported as normal. No birth measurements were available. The patient exhibited normal psychomotor development milestones, including babbling at 6–7 months and walking independently at 15 months. During the examination, it was noted that the patient spoke Greek fluently and had a good understanding of Dutch. At 3 years and 6 months of age, the patient presented with bilateral eye involvement, predominantly affecting the right eye, which necessitated enucleation, and 70% of the left eye, which was managed with chemotherapy.
test_results: The karyotype identified a pericentric inversion of chromosome 9, inv(9) (p11q13).

case_report: A 26-year-old Caucasian woman was referred to the infectious disease unit due to a pelvic inflammatory condition that necessitated multiple surgical interventions and antibiotic treatments. One of her four siblings passed away from pneumonia at 6 months old. Her medical history includes recurrent upper respiratory tract infections, skin warts, early tooth loss since childhood, and persistent genital warts since 2010. Physical examination revealed Clark nevus, periodontal disease, hepatosplenomegaly, and severe cutaneous warts on the feet and hands. Vulvar and cervical lesions induced by HPV were repeatedly treated, but cervical intraepithelial neoplasia recently developed. HIV testing was negative, and HPV genotyping identified HPV-18 and HPV-33 in the cervix and HPV-6 in the skin.
test_results: Immunophenotype analysis of PBMC showed severe B cell lymphopenia (3%) with adequate B and T cell subsets. High levels of peripheral eosinophils and appropriate neutrophil counts were found. Immunoglobulin levels were normal, and protective anti-pneumococcus IgG levels were detected after polysaccharide vaccine although they tended to decrease over time. Genetic evaluation for CXCR4, GATA2, NEMO, and CD40L revealed a wild-type status.

case_report: A 14-year-old female presented with burning pain in her feet, which extended to her hands after 2 weeks, persisting for a total of 6 weeks. Previous treatments included non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and oral steroids, which did not alleviate symptoms. Physical examination showed redness and swelling on the dorsal surfaces of the fingers, hands, and palms, with skin erosion on the palms due to continuous water immersion. There were no signs of arthritis or systemic inflammatory disorder. Laboratory results were as follows: white blood count 6550 K/μl, haemoglobin 13.4 g/dl, platelets 308 K/μl, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 18 mm/1h, C-reactive protein 0.1 mg/L, AST 11 U/L, ALT 6 U/L, CPK 27 U/L, C3 91 mg/dl, and C4 21 mg/dl. Tests for antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, β2-glycoprotein IgG and IgM, and anti-cardiolipin antibodies IgG and IgM were negative.
test_results: Genetic testing for the SCN9A gene mutation was negative.

case_report: A five-year-old boy, born to nonconsanguineous parents, is the third child in the family. The first child, a seven-year-old, is healthy and was born after a full-term pregnancy. The second pregnancy ended in intrauterine death at seven months. The fourth child, now one year old, is also healthy. During the third pregnancy, there was no significant history of viral fever, medication, or exposure to X-rays. The boy was born preterm at 32 weeks via vaginal delivery, weighing 1.8 kg, and spent seven days in the neonatal ICU. Early developmental milestones included head control at two and a half months and social smiling at three months. Limb development was normal until one year of age, after which minimal development was observed in all four limbs. By two years of age, the child was unable to walk or grasp objects due to hand and foot deformities but achieved bowel and bladder control by three years. Physical examination revealed microcephaly, a bird-like facial appearance, and an incomplete cleft of the secondary palate. The child's weight was 10 kg (expected 14–15 kg), height 91 cm (expected 100 cm), head circumference 43.5 cm (expected 48 cm), lower limb to upper limb ratio 49:52 (expected 1.3:1), and mid-arm circumference 12 cm (expected > 14 cm).
test_results: An X-ray of the upper limbs showed symmetrical ulnar bone shortening on both sides, the ulna measuring 11.7 cm (expected 13–15 cm) and radii absent from both hands. Only two carpal bones were present in the left and right hands, only one metacarpal on each side and one phalanx on the left side but none on the right. X-rays of the lower limbs showed the presence of calcaneum only, the rest of the tarsals, metatarsals, and phalanges being absent. The patella was absent bilaterally and there was symmetrical shortening of the tibia by 19 cm (Right) and 19.5 cm (Left) (expected 22.5-24 cm) and of the femur by 20 cm (expected 23–25 cm). An X-ray of the pelvis showed pubic diastasis and a vertically dislocated hip joint. An X-ray of the skull showed micrognathia.

case_report: This report details the case of a six-month-old female from Saudi Arabia, born via cesarean section at 37 weeks of gestation due to polyhydramnios and fetal distress. The mother, a 24-year-old healthy woman, was in her second pregnancy and had regular follow-ups with perinatology. Her first child had passed away at seven months old due to multiple congenital anomalies, including congenital heart disease (cardiomegaly, aneurysm of the atrial septum, isomerism) and bilateral hydronephrosis, with no conclusive diagnosis. During the current pregnancy, an ultrasound at 32 weeks gestation revealed bilateral hydronephrosis (right kidney measuring 2.7 cm, left kidney measuring 1.8 cm). Fetal biometry, anatomical scan, placenta, and amniotic fluid levels were all within normal ranges. The mother reported no exposure to teratogenic substances, medications, or radiation during the pregnancy. The parents are first-degree relatives, and there is no family history of genetic, metabolic, or inherited diseases.
test_results: Amniocentesis confirmed the genetic mutation in DIS3L2 via single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNP) of the fetus.

case_report: A 59-year-old male presented with a maculopapular pruritic rash affecting the face, trunk, and both upper and lower extremities. This was accompanied by a fever exceeding 38.5°C, periorbital edema, swelling of the lower lip, and mild cervical lymphadenopathy. The patient was undergoing treatment for multiple myeloma and had received a combination therapy consisting of bortezomib, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone (VRd). Despite the appearance of the rash 9 days after completing the first cycle of VRd therapy, the second cycle was continued and completed.
test_results: Laboratory tests revealed leukocytosis (11,900 cells/l; normal value <9,000 cells/l), eosinophilia (2,980 cells/ µl; normal < 500/ µl), monocytosis (1,190 cells/ µl; normal 90–690/µl) and atypical lymphocytes (2%). Increased serum alanine aminotransferase (61 U/l; normal 5–40 U/l), lactate dehydrogenase (342 U/l; normal 115–245 U/l), and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase (89 U/l; normal < 70 U/l), and decreased serum IgG (510 mg/dl; normal 861–1,747 mg/dl), IgM (7 mg/dl; normal 33–183 mg/dl), and IgA (15 mg/dl; normal 93–393 mg/ dl) levels were also observed. Viral reactivation was detected; titres of anti-human herpes virus-6 (HHV-6) IgG and anti-cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgG increased from <10 fold (at presentation) to ×640 fold (on day 40) and from 9.3 IU/ml (at presentation) to 17.9 IU/ml (on day 40), respectively. A biopsy was taken from an infiltrated erythema on the patient’s abdomen, and showed perivascular lymphocytic infiltration in the upper dermis and liquefaction degeneration at the dermoepidermal junction.
diagnosis: Drug-induced Hypersensitivity Syndrome/Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms
Orpha_name: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms

case_report: A 33-year-old Han man was admitted with neck pain and numbness in the right upper and lower limbs for 2 days. Two days prior, the patient experienced a cold and neck pain, particularly when turning his neck. The numbness in the right upper and lower limbs was progressive. One day prior, the patient developed weakness in the left upper and lower limbs, which did not hinder his daily activities. There were no reports of fever, headache, visual impairment, or defecation disorders. The patient's past medical history was unremarkable. Physical examination findings were as follows: Vital signs were stable. Cranial nerves were intact. Muscle strength in the left upper and lower limbs was grade 4. Muscle tone and reflexes were normal in all four limbs. There was decreased pain sensation below the level of the right clavicle, and diminished proprioception and vibration sensation in the left upper and lower limbs. The left Babinski sign was positive. Laboratory results showed normal routine blood test, hepatorenal function, electrolyte levels, and antinuclear antibody spectrum. Cancer spectrum was negative. Serum levels of herpes, Cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNA were negative. Lumbar puncture cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed a cell count of 24 × 10^6/L and a protein count of 185 mg/L. CSF smear and acid-fast staining were negative. CSF culture, oligoclonal band (OB), and aquaporin 4 (AQP4) antibody were negative. Visual evoked potential (VEP) showed normal P100 latency. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was normal.
test_results: Cervical MRI indicated abnormal swelling signals in the medulla-cervical cord long segment and enhanced signals in the C2-3 region.

case_report: A 12-year-old female patient was the fourth child of a 38-year-old mother and a 31-year-old father, both without significant family history. The pregnancy was uncomplicated with normal antenatal ultrasounds. She was delivered vaginally at 37 weeks of gestation with a birth weight of 3.500 g (50th centile), length of 57 cm (98th centile), and head circumference of 34 cm (50th centile). The neonatal period was unremarkable. Her psychomotor development was normal until 36 months, after which she began losing previously acquired milestones. She ceased speaking and lost purposeful hand skills around 44 months. She exhibited inappropriate laughing spells, reduced pain response, and episodes of hyperventilation. She began walking independently at 11 months and retained this ability. The patient was referred from the Neurology Department to the Genetics Department for refractory epilepsy. At age 3, she had an untreated febrile seizure followed by a spontaneous generalized tonic-clonic seizure. She also experienced occasional focal crises, absence seizures, and tonic seizures. She was treated daily with carbamazepine 10 mg/kg/d and clobazam 1 mg/kg without achieving seizure control. An electroencephalogram (EEG) at age 12 showed a slowing background with spikes and slow waves in the central region during wakefulness. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed dilatation of the perivascular basal space without other abnormalities. Blood amino acid chromatography, urine organic acid chromatography, hemogram, hepatic function test, and abdominal ultrasound were normal. Physical examination at age 12 showed a normal head circumference and ID. She was non-verbal, with preserved but impaired hand use due to stereotypic movements such as mouthing, washing automatisms, and involuntary clapping. She had a slight dyspraxic gait, inappropriate visual contact, hyperactivity, and hyperkeratosis on her hands and fingers secondary to self-harm.
test_results: The results demonstrated a de novo 1.28 Mb microduplication in Xp22.31 (chrX:6866889-8115153) without inherited origin. A complete sequencing of MECP2 (NM_004992.3) was performed and it showed a de novo variant c.338C>G (p.Pro113Arg). Variant functional prediction software VARSOME classified it as a damaging variant.

case_report: A 22-year-old Syrian Caucasian male university student presented to Al-Mouwasat Hospital in Damascus with a fever that had been recurring for 15 days, initially accompanied by vomiting for the first 2 days. Additional symptoms included aphthous ulcers, fatigue, increased urination, and increased thirst. There was no reported anorexia or significant weight loss. The patient had a history of low birth weight, sparse subcutaneous tissue during infancy and childhood, and anorexia during infancy. He had short stature and a high-pitched voice, which had been investigated in infancy without a definitive cause. He had undescended testis, corrected by orchiopexy at age 10. The patient experienced recurrent chest and middle ear infections and had been dealing with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) for the past 8 years. His parents are consanguineous, with his father having type 2 diabetes and his mother being hypertensive. His sister also has short stature and similar facial features. The patient was taking augmentin (amoxicillin clavulanate) 1 g (1 × 2), cefixime 400 mg (1 × 1), paracetamol (1000 mg) for fever, and omeprazole (20 mg) for GERD symptoms. He resides in a rural area and does not smoke or consume alcohol. Physical examination revealed a low weight (33 kg), short stature (146 cm), and a BMI of 15.48 kg/m2. Vital signs were normal except for a respiratory rate of 26 breaths/min. His temperature at admission was 37.5°C (axillary). Head and neck examination showed an elongated head (dolichocephaly), a prominent nose, and pallor of the conjunctiva without scleral icterus. He had lateral strabismus and amblyopia in the right eye, ectropion of the inferior eyelids in both eyes, normal pupils, clear lens and transparent media, and a normal fundus. A sun-sensitive malar butterfly rash with telangiectasias was noted on the nose and cheeks, reported to have started in infancy. He had cheilitis with peeling vesicles and an absent upper incisor. On the trunk, there were hypopigmented areas, café-au-lait lesions, and telangiectasia on the upper chest. No lymph nodes were enlarged or palpable, and there was no purpura or petechiae, but he had recurrent nosebleeds. Other systems were normal on examination, except for decreased breath sounds without crackles or wheezing. Chest X-ray showed no abnormalities, and urine microscopic and strip analysis were normal. ECG was normal. Laboratory tests revealed glucose (237 mg/dL), hemoglobin (6.4 g/dL), hematocrit (18.9%), mean corpuscular volume (85 fL), platelets (19 × 103/mL), LDH (692 IU/L), ALP (273 IU/L), C-reactive protein (145 mg/dL), and ESR (105 mm/h). White blood cell count was normal at admission. Tuberculin and QuantiFERON tests were negative. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), antinuclear antibodies (ANA), and rheumatoid factor (RF) were negative. Spirometry showed FEV1/FVC = 75%. Further investigations were conducted due to fever, nosebleeds, bicytopenia, elevated CRP and ESR, hyperglycemia, low weight, short stature, and abnormal facial features. Type I diabetes mellitus was confirmed by islet cell antibodies test. Growth hormone, testosterone, FSH, and LH levels were normal. Azoospermia was detected. Peripheral blood smear showed hypochromic microcytic anemia, anisocytosis, spherocytosis, elliptocytes, tear drop blood cells, giant platelets, and hyposegmented granulocytes. Bone marrow aspiration flow cytometry revealed an inversion of CD4/CD8 ratio and 6% myeloblasts. Bone marrow examination showed hypercellular marrow with multilineage dysplasia, including dysplastic erythroid lineage and dismegakaryopoiesis. Iron stain revealed several ringed sideroblasts. Histopathological examination and flow cytometry findings were consistent with myelodysplastic syndrome with excess blasts 1 (MDS EB1). Serum protein electrophoresis showed reduced immunoglobulins, and immunoglobulin quantification revealed low IgG (4.68 g/L) with normal IgM and IgA.
test_results: SCE was performed, and analysis of 100 cells showed an average of 73 SCE/cell, while the control showed 5 SCE per normal cell.

case_report: At 3 months old, Patient 1 experienced seizures and had a plasma lactate level of 4.95 mM (normal range < 2.2 mM). By the age of 6 years, the patient could only sit with support, exhibited babbling, and had hearing impairment, optic nerve atrophy, sleep apnea, proximal type renal tubular acidosis, and seizures managed by a ketogenic diet.
test_results: A brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) study revealed diffuse high intensity of white matter on T2-weighted images and a decreased N-acetylaspartate-to-choline (NAA/CHO) ratio and presence of a lactate signal on magnetic resonance spectrometry (MRS). A muscle biopsy revealed abnormal mitochondria, but sequencing of mitochondrial DNA revealed no pathogenic variants.

case_report: A 61-year-old female of Chinese descent first visited the eye clinic nearly 10 years ago with complaints of progressively worsening ptosis and limited eye movements in both eyes. Initial retinal examinations revealed a few depigmented spots near the superior arcade in the right eye and one spot in the inferior periphery of the left eye. These spots were consistently observed during regular follow-ups over the years. Recently, her best corrected visual acuities were recorded as 20/40 in the right eye and 20/70 in the left eye. She exhibited severe bilateral ptosis with significant restriction in extraocular movements in all directions. Both direct and consensual pupillary reactions were brisk. Anterior segment examination showed nuclear sclerosis in both eyes. Fundus examination revealed a hypopigmented patch with central hyperpigmentation below the inferior arcade in the right eye, while the left eye had no significant retinal findings. The previously noted hypopigmented spots were not observed during this visit. A cardiac assessment identified a first-degree atrioventricular block. Elevated blood sugar levels led to an endocrine referral, and she was started on oral hypoglycemic agents. The patient also reported hearing difficulties and was referred to otorhinology. A neurologic consultation was conducted to evaluate other potential neurologic conditions. Apart from elevated blood sugar, the hematological workup was unremarkable, and antiacetylcholine antibodies were negative.
test_results: Modified Gomori trichrome staining revealed the presence of ragged red fibers in the muscle specimen.

case_report: A 10-year-old female presented with a one-month history of mild, tender, itchy, and boggy swelling on the scalp. Initially, a small tender nodule appeared on the vertex and progressively enlarged to cover a larger area. This was accompanied by hair loss, easily pluckable hairs, and occasional purulent discharge. The patient previously underwent incision and drainage under local anesthesia by a surgeon who misidentified the condition as a bacterial abscess. During the procedure, the scalp tissue was very friable, resulting in a depression that could not be sutured, leading to a referral for further management. Physical examination revealed a localized area of hair loss at the vertex of the scalp (6 × 5 cm) with multiple boggy nodules and a polygonal incised ulcer (3 cm × 1.5 cm) with friable edges in the middle of the alopecia. Purulent discharge and patchy hair loss were observed at the periphery of the lesions. The left anterior cervical lymph nodes were palpable and tender.
test_results: Wood's lamp examination revealed yellow-green fluorescence over the affected area. Potassium hydroxide (KOH) wet mount was performed in hair samples and scalp scrapings, which showed multiple branching hyphae from skin lesion and ectothrix in hair follicles.

case_report: A 40-year-old female with a history of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) bacteremia and intravenous drug use presented with multiple non-healing lesions at various stages. The first lesion appeared five days prior to presentation on the left anterolateral shin below the knee, following intravenous drug use. Additional lesions were observed on the breasts and buttocks. The patient reported fevers before admission and swelling in the lower extremity around the initial lesion. She denied any trauma, insect bites, or tick exposure, as well as symptoms such as productive cough, shortness of breath, chest pain, diarrhea, dysuria, and urinary discoloration. On admission, the patient had a fever of 101.1°F but was hemodynamically stable and not in acute distress. Physical examination revealed a 10 cm cratered ulcer on the left lower extremity and purpuric eschar wounds on the right breast and buttocks. No visual changes, focal neurological deficits, abnormal lung sounds, heart murmurs, abdominal tenderness, hepatosplenomegaly, or signs of subacute bacterial endocarditis were noted. Initial laboratory results showed normal creatinine, glomerular filtration rate (GFR), leukocyte count, and platelet count, with a mildly elevated liver alkaline phosphatase level. Additional infectious work-up revealed elevated procalcitonin, normal lactic acid, and a negative respiratory viral pathogen panel. Inflammatory markers included a markedly elevated C-reactive protein, minimally elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, negative c-ANCA, and negative p-ANCA. The patient was treated with piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin. Initial blood cultures grew MRSA sensitive to tetracycline and vancomycin, with subsequent cultures showing no growth. Further workup included a positive cocaine urine toxicology and a negative sexually transmitted infections panel (rapid plasmin reagin negative, gonorrhea-chlamydia negative, HIV negative, hepatitis C antibody positive, hepatitis C RNA quantitative negative).
test_results: A skin biopsy of the right thigh revealed vessels of various sizes throughout the sampled dermis that showed luminal occlusion by fibrin thrombi without significant inflammation.

case_report: In January 2008, a 6.5-year-old boy from India with non-consanguineous parents was referred for an unclassified condition. He exhibited widespread muscle atrophy and hyperlaxity of the fingers. He began walking at 18 months but was never able to run, experienced frequent falls, significant muscle fatigue, and had difficulty climbing stairs. He also had frequent lung infections and trouble with solid foods. Creatine kinase levels were normal. A muscle biopsy in 2007 showed dystrophic changes. Genetic testing for FKRP gene mutations, prompted by irregular alpha-dystroglycan expression, returned negative results. Daily sessions of intermittent positive pressure breathing using the Alpha-200™ device (Air Liquide Medical Systems, Antony, France) began at 6.5 years old but were consistently performed only from 11.7 years old. The device was used for 30 minutes per day with a facial mask and abdominal belt, set at an inspiratory pressure of 30 cm H2O, a flow of 25 L/min, and a trigger at −1. At 7.5 years old, significant retractions of the elbows, hips, knees, and ankles were noted. No scoliosis was observed. By 8 years old, the patient lost the ability to walk. At 11.7 years old, arterialized capillary blood gases showed a partial carbon dioxide tension (PCO2) of 5.53 kPa (41.5 mmHg), a pH of 7.39, and bicarbonates of 26.7.
test_results: Whole-body muscle magnetic resonance imaging showed a typical COL6 pattern (“tigroid” or striated, with alternating bands of normal tissue and fibroadipeous infiltration). Cultured skin fibroblasts were done.

case_report: The patient is a 15-year-old girl born in Sweden after a full-term pregnancy. She is the third of four siblings from Assyrian consanguineous parents originating from Iraq. Limited interaction with the national health system was noted until she was 5 years old, when she exhibited sensorineural hearing impairment and developmental delay. Bilateral hearing aids were provided, leading to accelerated development across various domains. Her parents retrospectively reported frequent balance issues during her toddler years. At 7 years and 8 months, she was referred to a child neurologist due to a toe-walking gait. Examination revealed tight, almost spastic Achilles tendons, but no other neurological abnormalities. Brain imaging at 8 years old identified a central lesion in the mesencephalon, extending from the nucleus ruber dorsocaudally to the cerebellar peduncles. An MRI scan of her spine was normal. Following physiotherapy and the use of orthoses, her gait improved, though her motor skills remained below age-appropriate levels. At 12 years old, she exhibited bilateral muscle weakness in the peroneal muscles and absence of peripheral reflexes. By 13 years old, she showed cognitive delay, impaired gross and fine motor skills, and tremor. At 14 years old, she experienced learning difficulties and generalized muscle weakness. Her fingers were extremely flexible, her feet were in a plan valgus position, and she had balance problems. At 15 years old, she showed no signs of puberty, with growth delayed to a skeletal age of 10.7 years at a chronological age of 14. Hormonal tests indicated nonfunctioning ovaries. Ophthalmologic examination revealed no retinal changes and normal optic nerves. One younger sister also has learning difficulties.
test_results: Mutation analysis identified a homozygous mutation (c.530 T > G (p.Leu177Arg) (NM_153818.1)) in the PEX10 gene. Immunofluorescence microscopy analysis using antibodies raised against catalase, a peroxisomal matrix protein, did show abnormal peroxisomal staining but not in all cells. When cultured at 37 °C most cells revealed a normal peroxisomal staining, but in some cells a markedly reduced number of peroxisomes was observed. Culturing patient fibroblasts at 40 °C for 2 weeks resulted in a complete absence of peroxisomal staining with catalase immunofluorescence microscopy analysis. Neurography and electromyography showed sensorimotor polyneuropathy and chronic neurogenic changes in her leg muscles. Blood metabolites analysis showed her plasma levels of C26:0 were moderately increased resulting in an increased C26:0/C22:0 ratio. The C24:0/C22:0 ratio was borderline normal. Her phytanic and pristanic acid levels were significantly increased at both sampling occasions. Her erythrocyte plasmalogen levels were normal.
diagnosis: Zellweger spectrum disorder due to a novel mutation in the PEX10 gene
Orpha_name: Autosomal recessive ataxia due to PEX10 deficiency

case_report: A 46-year-old woman presented with a four-year history of progressively worsening walking difficulties, personality changes, and cognitive impairment. There were no significant family or personal medical histories, and no incidents of poisoning were reported. She has given birth to a daughter. Her symptoms began subtly and gradually worsened over time, starting with weakness in her left extremities. There was a noticeable decline in her recent memory, counting ability, and orientation. Her family observed mood swings, increased irritability, and a short temper. She did not report any issues with blurred vision or double vision. Over time, her symptoms intensified, and she developed urinary and fecal incontinence. About seven months ago, she fainted unexpectedly, leading to suspicions of head trauma. Following this incident, her neurological symptoms significantly deteriorated. Consequently, she was admitted to our hospital for further evaluation and treatment. A neurological examination revealed cerebellar ataxia, postural instability, and exaggerated tendon reflexes. She was unable to perform a tandem gait. On the Mini-Mental State Examination, she scored 15 out of 30, indicating significant impairments in time orientation, counting ability, and delayed recall. Routine lab tests of blood, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), including lactate and pyruvate levels, showed no abnormalities. Screening for endocrine, metabolic, and immunologic disorders, as well as tumor markers, returned normal or negative results. Ovarian function was not assessed due to fertility issues and financial constraints.
test_results: Brain MRI scans revealed diffuse, confluent white matter hyperintensities in the frontoparietal and periventricular regions, and the cerebellum on axial T2-weighted images. Coronal fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences showed periventricular cavitations. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) identified heterozygous variants in the EIF2B3 gene: a known pathogenic variant c.1037 T > C (p.I346T), and a variant of uncertain significance, c.22A > T (p.M8L). These were further confirmed by Sanger sequencing.
diagnosis: Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with vanishing white matter

case_report: The patient is an 11-year-old female who was born full term via forceps-assisted vaginal delivery due to cephalopelvic disproportion. At birth, she exhibited hypotonia, poor weight gain, and feeding difficulties. She required nasogastric feeding at seven months and a gastric tube was placed at one year of age. At 17 months, an antroduodenal motility study showed mild neuropathic changes in the stomach and small bowel, along with post-prandial hypo-motility, indicative of pseudo-obstruction. She experienced dysphagia with choking and gagging, and chronic constipation. Upper GI, endoscopy, and swallow study did not show paralysis or weakness of pharyngeal muscles, dysmotility, or aspiration. Her constipation was managed with motility agents and laxatives, and she gradually increased oral intake, though she still requires some nutrition via her feeding tube. She was diagnosed with congenital cataracts, necessitating bilateral intraocular lens implantation and strabismus surgery. A TORCH screen for infectious causes of congenital cataracts was negative. Early behavioral intervention began at eight months. She achieved independent sitting by two years of age and walking by three years of age. She started speaking single words at age two and simple sentences by age six. At two years of age, she was evaluated for neurological concerns, including seizures, but her routine EEG was normal, and no antiseizure medication was prescribed.
test_results: Muscle biopsy demonstrated neuropathic changes with large fiber groups consistent with denervation/re-innervation. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain demonstrated symmetric bilateral polymicrogyria of the frontal lobe involving the superior and middle frontal gyri. There was hypo-myelination of subcortical white matter associated with the dysplastic areas. No other areas of polymicrogyria were seen and otherwise the brain, ventricles, and extra-axial spaces were normal in appearance.
Orpha_name: DYNC1H1-related autosomal dominant childhood-onset proximal spinal muscular atrophy

case_report: A 17-year-old female reported a decrease in vision in both eyes since childhood, which has progressively worsened. She has experienced difficulty maintaining balance for the past two years and has had headaches localized to the frontal and temporal regions. Family history was not relevant. Best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 5/60 in both eyes. Examination of the anterior segment was normal. Fundus examination showed waxy pallor of the optic disc, attenuated arterioles, and pigmentary changes in the retina in both eyes. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) indicated foveal thinning, loss of the photoreceptor layer, and irregularities in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in both eyes. The electroretinogram (ERG) demonstrated an absence of photopic response and a reduced scotopic response, indicating cone-rod dystrophy. Visual evoked potential (VEP) testing showed prolonged latency and reduced amplitude in both eyes, indicating bilateral axonal neuropathy.
test_results: Polymerase chain reaction analysis revealed repeat CAG nucleotide expansion.

case_report: Patient 1 is a 19-year-old female, the firstborn child of healthy, consanguineous parents. She experienced delayed developmental motor milestones and did not start walking until the age of 3 years. During early childhood, she frequently fell, especially while running. At the age of 3 years, she developed an unsteady gait and slurred speech, which worsened over several years before stabilizing; the frequency of falls decreased after starting occupational therapy. At the time of examination, she could walk without assistance. She performed normally at school, and her cognitive function was normal with a Mini-Mental State Examination score of 30/30. She reported occasional muscle cramps, mainly in the calf muscles. She had no history of seizures, urinary or fecal incontinence, urinary urgency, or hearing or vision problems. A neurological examination at the age of 18 years showed an unsteady gait with moderate slurred speech. Limb examination revealed muscle wasting and high-arched feet without spasticity. Bilateral sixth nerve palsies with saccadic pursuit and horizontal nystagmus were noted. Additionally, mild rigidity after activation maneuvers, mirror movements, reduced movement, and poor coordination were observed in both upper extremities, more pronounced on the left side. Patellar reflexes were brisk, but Achilles and upper extremity deep tendon reflexes were absent. Rapid elbow extension and forearm supination did not show spasticity. Extensor plantar reflexes were present bilaterally (Babinski signs were present bilaterally).
test_results: Nerve conduction studies and needle electromyography (EMG/NCS) were consistent with axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy with some demyelinating features. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed increased thickness of retinal nerve fiber layers. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) depicted atrophy of the superior cerebellar vermis, thinning of the posterior mid-body of corpus callosum, bilateral parietal atrophy on T1-weighted images, bilateral hypointense stripes in the pons on T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences, bilateral hyperintensity of the lateral pons on coronal images on T2 sequences, and a hyperintense rim around both thalami on T2-weighted images.
diagnosis: Autosomal Recessive Spastic Ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay
Orpha_name: Autosomal Recessive Spastic Ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay

case_report: A 12-year-old female from Iraq presented to the Rheumatology Unit with joint contractures affecting both hands. She was born to first-degree cousins, had a low birthweight, delayed developmental milestones (began walking at 2.5 years), and exhibited protruding eyes since birth. She experienced recurrent intermittent fever with sweating, fatigue, and generalized body aches. At age 2, she was diagnosed with beta thalassemia minor and was on folic acid. At age 4, she developed bilateral knee joint arthritis and was treated with Methotrexate (MTX), which was later discontinued due to severe anemia. She developed painless flexion deformities in all fingers except the thumbs. In the same year, she was diagnosed with sensorineural deafness and received a hearing aid. At age 5, she underwent tonsillectomy for recurrent tonsillitis. At age 8, she developed a hyperpigmented, tender rash with hypertrichosis on the inner thighs and legs. She also developed painless foot deformities, including laterally angled heels, overlapping toes, medial deviation of the first metatarsal, and lateral deviation of the big toe. At age 10, she was prescribed antithyroid medication for 18 months for hyperthyroidism. Six months later, she experienced right hypochondriac abdominal pain, and an ultrasound revealed splenomegaly. The family declined a recommended splenectomy. She was diagnosed with diabetes and started on insulin a year later, and also diagnosed with celiac disease, for which she is on a gluten-free diet. Upon presenting to the rheumatology department, her clinical examination showed swollen cheeks, protruding eyes with corneal arcus, and dilated scleral vessels. She was malnourished and short-statured, weighing 25 kg, with a height of 135 cm, and a body mass index of 13.7 kg/m2. Multiple palpable, freely mobile lymph nodes were noted in the cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions. Hyperpigmented tender skin lesions with hypertrichosis were observed on the medial thighs and posteromedial legs. She had bilateral hallux valgus and irreducible flexion deformity of the hand and foot joints. A pansystolic murmur was heard over the mitral area, radiating to the axilla without thrill or heave. Blood tests showed hypochromic microcytic anemia (Hb 8.6 g/dl, MCV 49.7 fl), elevated acute phase reactants [erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 77 mm/h (normal, 0–20)], [C-reactive protein: 22 mg/dl (normal, 0–5)], and normal renal, liver, and thyroid function tests. The celiac auto-antibody screen was positive for Tissue Transglutaminase IgA antibody (tTG-IgA, 45 IU/ml), Tissue Transglutaminase IgG (tTG-IgA, 26.7 IU/ml), and anti-gliadin IgG, 20.5 IU/ml (normal less than 12 IU/ml). IL-6 was 17.56 pg/ml (normal, 0–7). Echocardiography showed mitral regurgitation and pulmonary stenosis. A neck ultrasound revealed multiple enlarged submandibular cervical lymph nodes on the left side, the largest measuring 13 mm with an oval shape and internal calcification.
test_results: Microscopic hyperpigmentation in the basal layer, sparse lymphoplasmacytic perivascular cells in the top layer of the dermis, and mild fibrosis.

case_report: The patient is a 9-year-old female child admitted to AVBR Hospital with an ear deformity and a short, deviated neck present since birth. She was born to parents who are not related by blood. The pregnancy was without complications, and there was no history of drug use or exposure to radiation. Her birth was uncomplicated, and there were no issues during or after delivery. She has developed normally. Her height is 119 cm, which is below the 3rd percentile for her age. On examination, her vital signs were stable. The right ear was malformed and lacked a visible vestibular canal, while the left ear had discharge. The neck was short and deviated to the right. There was kyphoscoliosis of the thoracic vertebrae. The right eye was smaller than the left and intermittently decreased in size involuntarily. Systemic examinations revealed abducens and right facial nerve palsy. An ophthalmic evaluation indicated retraction of the right eyeball.
test_results: Audiometry revealed profound hearing loss on right side and moderate sensorineural hearing loss on the left side. Brainstem evoked response audiometry was also suggestive of sensorineural hearing loss on the left side. Computed tomography (CT) spine showed fusion of the thoracic vertebrae, suggestive of Klippel–Feil deformity. CT paranasal sinuses were suggestive of the hypoplastic frontal sinus. CT brain was suggestive of right holesteatoma.

case_report: A 56-year-old woman presented with a six-month history of an asymptomatic mass featuring a central hole on the right side of the tongue, which did not respond to various topical treatments. Physical examination revealed a relatively firm pink to white nodule measuring 1.5×1.5 cm on the right side of the tongue, which was slightly tender upon palpation. No significant findings were noted in the examination of systemic physical conditions or local trauma. The lesion was biopsied, and the tissue sample was sent for further evaluation.
test_results: Pathological examination revealed a hyperplastic mucosal tissue with central invagination, which contained numerous acantholytic and dyskeratotic cells in the upper portion. The lower portion of the invagination was occupied by numerous villi, which were markedly elongated papillae, lining a single layer of basal cells. Chronic inflammation was observed in the underlying fibrotic stroma.

case_report: A 55-year-old female experienced a week-long headache, blurred vision, and sudden changes in mental status. During the examination, she responded to voice, followed commands with all four limbs, and showed mild weakness on her right side. She also had panhypopituitarism and elevated sodium levels due to diabetes insipidus. Brain CT imaging showed a suprasellar cistern and anterior interhemispheric subarachnoid hemorrhage with intraventricular hemorrhage, necessitating the placement of a right ventricular drain. A CT angiogram indicated a 3 mm right supraclinoid internal carotid artery aneurysm. Subsequent cerebral angiograms identified additional findings, including a 2 mm left middle cerebral artery bifurcation aneurysm, a left anterior choroidal artery aneurysm, and a 2 mm right paraophthalmic aneurysm, which were not linked to her symptoms. A transsphenoidal surgery was performed to remove the pituitary mass and clear the sellar hematoma. Pathology results were negative for hormonal markers. Initially, she was thought to have a pituitary adenoma with apoplexy and showed recovery within weeks without lasting neurological issues. However, six weeks later, she experienced worsening headaches and vision loss.
test_results: The brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with and without contrast demonstrated a moderately enhancing, expansive sellar mass with internal hemorrhage, extending into the suprasellar space. There was uniform enhancement throughout most of the mass, except for its most dorsal aspects which heterogeneously enhanced. There was also an invasion of the right cavernous sinus, protrusion into the sphenoid sinus, and mass effect on the optic chiasm. Additional stains showed INI1 loss in neoplastic cells, and an elevated Ki67 proliferation index.

case_report: A 38-year-old Japanese primigravida woman was referred to the hospital at 19 weeks of pregnancy due to a suspected fetal omphalocele. Her vital signs were stable with a normal blood pressure, height of 169 cm, weight of 58 kg, and a BMI of 22. She had a history of hypothyroidism managed with levothyroxine (50 μg/day), maintaining a euthyroid state. An ultrasound scan prior to referral indicated fetal omphalocele. The estimated fetal weight was 365 g (+2.0 SD), and amniotic fluid volume was 130 cm, indicating polyhydramnios. Doppler studies showed an MCA-resistance index (RI) of 0.89, MCA-peak systolic velocity (PSV) of 49.07 cm/second, and UA-impedance index (II) of 0.49. A 75 g glucose tolerance test returned normal results. The patient was advised to be admitted for observation from 28 weeks of gestation due to threatened premature delivery. She reported abdominal tightness but no breathing difficulty, with a cervical length of 15 mm. Betamethasone (12 mg per 24 hours, twice) was administered at 31 weeks of gestation to manage uterine contractions. Due to worsening pressure symptoms from polyhydramnios, transabdominal amniocentesis and amniodrainage were performed at 29.4 and 32.4 weeks, removing 1535 mL and 1126 mL of amniotic fluid, respectively, without complications. Premature rupture of the fetal membrane occurred at 35.1 weeks, leading to an emergency Cesarean section on the same day. The male infant weighed 3188 g at birth, with Apgar scores of 3 at 1 minute and 6 at 5 minutes, and a UA pH of 7.383. The infant had poor spontaneous respiration, necessitating intratracheal intubation at 9 minutes after birth and initiation of artificial ventilation. A chest X-ray at 3 hours post-birth revealed a bell-shaped chest, small in proportion to the body, and deformed ribs. The infant exhibited generalized hypotonia, a flat nasal bridge, a small jaw, and an abnormal facial appearance. The omphalocele was initially managed by protecting the umbilical hernia section with a wound retractor, allowing natural reduction of the hernial contents into the abdominal cavity. Radical surgery for the omphalocele was performed at 10 days of age. Endotracheal extubation occurred at 13 days of age, transitioning the infant to bi-level positive airway pressure. The infant gradually weaned off positive pressure, achieving spontaneous respiration with nasal oxygen. Enteral feeding began at 12 days of age, but swallowing dysfunction was noted during attempts at oral feeding. Full enteral feeding was established at 20 days of age, along with the initiation of swallowing training.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed hypermethylated IG-DMR and MEG3-DMR in the corresponding chromosome 14 imprinted regions.

case_report: Case 1 involves a full-term, 5-month-old girl conceived via in vitro fertilization, with no complications during prenatal and neonatal periods. Her family, including her twin sister, are all healthy. At 4 months, she began experiencing focal to generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Physical examination revealed one small café au lait spot on her trunk and hypotonia in her extremities. Her head circumference measured 38 cm, indicating microcephaly (OFC <-3 SD). She exhibited distinct facial characteristics such as a slightly large forehead, prominent cheeks, and long eyelashes. Comprehensive evaluations of her heart, eyes, liver, kidneys, and other organs showed no abnormalities. The patient showed signs of failure to thrive, with delayed and stagnant development. At 5 months, she was unable to lift her neck, roll over, or respond well to human faces, lights, and sounds.
test_results: The EEG showed multifocal spike waves, sharp waves, spike-slow wave complexes, and slow waves in the left posterior temporal region. The brain MRI was normal. Both blood and urine metabolic screening were normal. The auditory brainstem response and visual evoked potential tests were negative.

case_report: A 63-year-old male presented with a lesion on the right upper eyelid, persisting for 7 years. The lesion was nodular, measuring 5.0 cm × 7.0 cm, and exhibited ulceration, induration, and erythema. It extended to the lower eyelid. The patient had no light perception in the right eye, while the left eye had a visual acuity of 20/20. Intraocular pressure could not be measured in the right eye due to the lesion, but it was 18 mmHg in the left eye. Examination of the left orbit showed no abnormalities. A thorough examination of local lymph nodes and the lacrimal duct also showed no abnormalities. The patient reported no prior treatment for the lesion. He was otherwise in good systemic health with no significant family history. There was no history of trauma, and he worked as a farmer. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the orbit indicated right anterior orbital invasion without involvement of the bone or lacrimal gland.
test_results: A subsequent incisional biopsy revealed squamous cell invaginations extending from the epidermis into the dermis. The invaginations and papillary projections were lined with a bilayer epithelium: the luminal layer was composed of columnar cells with decapitation secretion and the outer layer was composed of small cuboidal cells. These cells had significant nuclear pleomorphism, prominent nucleoli, and increased mitotic activity. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated positivity for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), Cytokeratin 8/18, and a Cytokeratin cocktail of high and low density. It was negative for GCDFP-15 and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA).

case_report: A 3-year-old boy was first seen in our department in 2020 with a history of recurrent fever lasting more than 10 months. Each fever episode persisted for about 1–5 days, with intervals of approximately 15 days between episodes. The fever typically reached around 37.5ºC, occasionally spiking up to 39ºC, and was accompanied by bilateral conjunctival congestion and a rash resembling urticaria. There were no reports of fatigue, headache, nasal congestion, runny nose, sore throat, cough, asthma, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, or joint swelling and pain. Routine blood tests revealed elevated leukocyte count, neutrophil count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and serum amyloid protein (SAA) levels.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing identified a heterozygous variation of NLRP3 gene (c.784-786delinsTGG) in the coding region that resulted in amino acid substitution of arginine for tryptophan at codon 262 (p.R262W), which is a missense variation. The frequency of variation in this database is normal. Through family verification analysis, the parents of the subject had no variation at nucleotide locus 784 in the coding region, suggesting a spontaneous mutation. The mutation was validated using Sanger sequencing.

case_report: A 10-year-old girl presented with a firm swelling in the buccal vestibule of the anterior mandible. The mucosa over the swelling was intact, and the area was painful and tender. Electrical pulp testing showed no response in most of the teeth within the affected area, except for three teeth. However, these teeth were found to be vital upon follow-up. The patient's parents reported that the swelling began around 4 months ago and had caused noticeable asymmetry on the left side of the chin over the past 2 months.
test_results: A well-defined radiolucent lesion extending from posterior to the mandibular right first molar to the distal aspect of the left first premolar was evident. The scallop outline in the superior border of the lesion and displacement of the right lateral and second premolar were evident. Lamina dura of some of the teeth was totally or partly destroyed. The internal structure of the lesion on panoramic view was as multilocular appearance that included wispy, ill-defined trabeculae and in some areas of the lesion there was evidence of fine, straight septa making a tennis racket-like or step-ladder like pattern. On occlusal projection, some of the trabeculae were at right angles to the periphery. The occlusal view revealed a considerable expansion of the buccal and especially lingual cortical plates.

case_report: A 70-year-old Chinese male presented to the dermatology clinic in October 2023 with a primary concern of a skin nodule in the right groin that had appeared one year prior. Initially, the nodule was dark yellow-red and the size of a soybean, gradually enlarging to the size of a fava bean. Recently, the nodule had been rubbing against clothing, causing the surface to break and scab. The patient's medical history included red, swollen, and painful interphalangeal joints in both hands two years ago, and pain with skin swelling in the right hip joint one year ago, without morning stiffness or activity limitation. The patient had been diagnosed with 'gouty arthritis' and treated with etoricoxib, febuxostat, and flurbiprofen cataplasms, which provided some relief, although the joint pain recurred and worsened over time. The patient reported no fever, fatigue, weight loss, infectious diseases, or family history of similar conditions. Physical examination showed no palpable enlargement of superficial lymph nodes, and limb muscle strength was grade V. The cervical, thoracic, and lumbar vertebrae had physiological curvature with no pressure or tenderness in the cervical and thoracic spinous processes, no limitation in cervical spine activity, and no reduction in lumbar spine anterior flexion, posterior extension, or lateral flexion activity. Dermatologic examination revealed a hemispherical, elevated, isolated nodule in the right groin measuring 1.8 × 1.5 × 1.0 cm, dark yellow-red in color with a smooth surface, brown crusts in some areas, and clear borders. The nodule was hard, mobile, and not adherent to underlying tissue, with no tenderness. The distal interphalangeal joints of both hands were mildly swollen with limited movement and tenderness. No abnormalities were noted in other skin areas.
test_results: By skin histopathology, diffuse histiocyte infiltration was seen in the dermis, with pink histiocytes, with a uniform morphology, and eosinophilic 'hairy glass'-like multinucleated giant cells with clear borders. Immunohistochemistry revealed CD68 (diffuse +), vimentin (diffuse +), CD31 (diffuse +), LCA (CD45) (+), S-100 (−), CD1a (−), CD34 (−), and Ki-67 positivity in approximately 5%–10% of the patients.

case_report: A fifteen-year-old male presented with crowding of the upper and lower front teeth. Facial examination showed midface retrusion and evidence of surgically repaired bilateral upper cleft lip from childhood, along with small, bilateral, paramedian lower lip pits. He is the firstborn child of his parents, who have a consanguineous marriage. His mother's antenatal history was unremarkable for illnesses or drug intake during pregnancy, and no family members had cleft lip or palate. Detailed lip examination revealed bilateral lip pits, one of which was located at the base of a nipple-like elevation. These pits measured 3 mm in diameter and 5 mm in depth, with mucous secretion observed from one pit upon compression of the lower lip. Intraoral examination showed a collapsed V-shaped palate with severe crowding of the upper anterior teeth. There was obliteration of the upper labial vestibule due to adhesion of the lip to the gingiva by a thick fibrous band, which blanched upon retraction of the upper lip. The patient had a short uvula. The mandibular teeth were all present and well-aligned, but there was a short lingual frenum causing ankyloglossia. A posterior crossbite was noted, attributed to the narrow and collapsed arch. A general medical examination was conducted to check for systemic issues.
test_results: Radiographic investigations like chest radiograph, lateral cephalograph, orthopantomograph, and maxillary occlusal view were taken.

case_report: A 22-month-old girl was referred to our hospital with primary concerns of muscle stiffness and difficulty swallowing, along with challenges in head control. She was born at full term via normal vaginal delivery. At 8 months old, she could stand while holding onto something, indicating typical development. However, developmental progress halted at 13 months. Muscle stiffness and backward bending of the knees were noted when she stood while holding onto something. The patient exhibited a progressive decline in motor skills, and by 18 months, she could barely maintain a sitting position with support. At 20 months, she experienced symptoms of aspiration during swallowing and extended feeding times. Brain MRI scans taken at 15 months did not reveal delayed myelination or abnormal enhancement. The pattern of developmental regression was consistent with certain conditions affecting motor skills.
test_results: The patient underwent hexosaminidase assay in white blood cells, which showed increased hexosaminidase A (%) and decreased total hexosaminidase. The total hexosaminidase A & B and hexosaminidase A levels were 321.2 nmol/hr/mg (reference range, 620–1,000 nmol/hr/mg) and 74.3% (reference range, 55%–72%), respectively.

case_report: A 32-year-old woman presented to the ophthalmology department after experiencing sudden visual disturbance and metamorphopsia in her left eye. She had a history of hair loss on her head and painful intermittent muscle spasms in her extremities starting at a young age. The hair loss eventually spread throughout her body, and the frequency of painful spasms increased. There was no diarrhea. Muscle relaxant dantrolene (10 mg/day) was administered, which effectively improved the muscle spasms. Peripheral blood tests showed mild elevations in creatine phosphokinase (214 IU/L; normal range, 10–125 IU/L), antinuclear antibody (titer of > 1:1280; normal range, <1:20), and anti-DNA antibody (titer of 1:160; normal range, <1:5). Thyroid hormone, urinary cortisol, and blood testosterone levels were within normal ranges, and growth hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, and prolactin were normally secreted based on a challenge test. Radiographs indicated irregular metaphyses of the long bones in the extremities. Brain and spinal cord magnetic resonance imaging showed no abnormalities, and nerve conduction velocity tests via electroencephalography and electromyography were normal. Electrical stimulation of the tibial and peroneal nerves induced painful muscle spasms in the extensor muscles of the ankle joint and toe, lasting approximately one minute after the stimuli ended. At the age of 7, she was treated with intravenous immunoglobulin (130 mg/kg/day for 3 days) every 2 weeks for a total of 3 times, which reduced the frequency of painful muscle spasms to 2-3 times per month. After the 4th course, immunoglobulin therapy was reduced to once every 2 weeks, with no re-exacerbation of seizures. Antinuclear antibody titers decreased to 1:160 and anti-DNA antibody titers decreased (<1:5). At the age of 23, prednisolone (5 mg/day) was initiated to treat eosinophilic gastroenteritis when diarrhea was observed. Her family and medical histories were unremarkable. At the age of 32, she noticed sudden vision loss and metamorphopsia in her left eye and was referred to the ophthalmology department. She was on oral prednisolone (8 mg/day), methotrexate (6 mg once per week), dantrolene (100 mg/day), and baclofen (12.5 mg/day). Physical examination revealed generalized alopecia, bone abnormalities, and muscle spasms in the extremities occurring every few minutes. There were no other systemic symptoms such as oral aphthae, skin symptoms, headaches, tinnitus, hearing loss, or hypertension. Corrected visual acuity was 1.0 in the right eye and 0.07 in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was 13 mm Hg in the right eye and 23 mm Hg in the left eye. Two + cells in the anterior chamber and 1 + cell in the anterior vitreous were observed in the left eye. Extensive retinal hemorrhage, including the macula, tortuosity of the retinal arteries and veins, and swelling of the optic disc were noted.
test_results: Optical coherence tomography revealed foveal thickening due to intraretinal hemorrhage. Fluorescein angiography revealed hyperfluorescence of the optic disc and leakage from the retinal veins, suggesting not only impending CRVO associated with papillitis but also segmental periphlebitis due to uveitis in the peripheral retina.

case_report: A 16-year-old male presented for evaluation of growth delay and delayed puberty. He was born at full term to healthy, non-consanguineous Korean parents, with a birth weight of 3.0 kg (−0.30 SDS) and length of 50 cm (0.06 SDS). His father's height was 174 cm (−0.08 SDS) and his mother's height was 170 cm (1.74 SDS). At the initial visit, his height was 152.8 cm (−3.49 SDS) and weight was 42.7 kg (−2.82 SDS). Postnatal history was unremarkable except for bilateral ptosis, which was surgically corrected at age 4. He had no history of trauma or chronic illness. He reported mild hypotonia during physical exertion, frequent tiredness, and muscle weakness. His mother noted he walked alone at 15 months and had delayed language development. At age 18, cognitive and intellectual assessment showed a full-scale IQ of 75 on the Korean Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-IV, with a social quotient of 84 and intellectual ability estimated at the lower average level (80–89). Attention testing indicated decreased selective and divided attention. From school age, his height velocity decreased, and he showed no pubertal development during adolescence. His two younger brothers had normal growth and development, and there was no family history of genetic disorders. His blood pressure was 109/73 mmHg. Pubertal assessment indicated Tanner stage 2 for external genitalia (testes volume 4 mL). He exhibited dysmorphic craniofacial features, including an inverted triangular-shaped forehead, exaggerated Cupid's bow, arched eyebrows, down-slanting palpebral fissures, pterygium in the left eye with corneal opacity, mild ptosis, and a poorly expressive face. Mild hypotonia was present without other neurological symptoms. Laboratory tests for chemistry and thyroid hormone levels were normal. Serum IGF-1 was 155.3 ng/mL (normal range: 360.0–885.0 ng/mL) and IGF binding protein-3 was 1,698 ng/mL (normal range: 1,574–4,260 ng/mL). Bone age was delayed by over 2 years. Two different provocative GH tests (glucagon and L-dopa stimulation) indicated complete GHD with low peak GH levels (0.34 and 1.99 ng/mL, respectively). Gonadotropin-releasing hormone stimulation testing showed early puberty (peak LH 8.93 mIU/mL and peak FSH 12.10 mIU/mL). Testosterone level was 0.23 ng/mL. Brain MRI revealed a flattened pituitary gland and cerebrospinal fluid space herniated into the sella turcica, indicating ESS. Other pituitary hormone levels were normal. Karyotype and chromosomal microarray analysis were unremarkable.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing (WES) was performed and a heterozygous novel nonsense variant, c.4185del; p.(Met1396Ter), in ZNF462 was identified, which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. This variant resulted from the deletion of nucleotides “C” in exon 3 of ZNF462, making stop codon in the protein-coding sequence, which was expected to produce truncated protein. Segregation analysis using Sanger sequencing showed no ZNF462 variant in his mother.

case_report: A 21-year-old male patient visited the Dental outpatient department with a primary concern of reddish-white patches on his right inner cheek and palate for the past 2 months, accompanied by a burning sensation. The patient reported a history of a small swelling on the palate that initially appeared fluid-filled and later ruptured. The reddish-white lesion on the palate grew to its current size, and a similar lesion appeared around the same time on the right buccal mucosa. The patient had previously used topical antifungal therapy, which temporarily alleviated the burning sensation. He had no significant medical, dental, or familial history and maintained good oral hygiene. The patient did not have any habits of chewing or smoking but consumed spicy foods. On examination of the right buccal mucosa, a single erythematous lesion with radiating white striae was observed, measuring 4 × 2 cm at the level of the occlusal plane, extending from the area of tooth 45 to the distal aspect of tooth 47. The lesion was soft with elevated white irregular margins. On the palate, a single elevated erythematous lesion interspersed with white striae was noted, measuring 4 × 4 cm. It extended anteriorly 1 cm behind the incisive papilla, posteriorly up to the fovea palatina, laterally 5 mm below the free gingival margins of teeth 16, 17, 26, and 27, and posteriorly to 1 cm above the soft palate. The lesion did not affect the palatal rugae and incisive papilla but covered the mid-palatine raphae. It contained multiple small round erythematous projections of varying sizes surrounded by white striae. The surface was rough and non-tender on palpation. The patient had no other skin abnormalities. Basic hematological parameters were evaluated and found to be within normal limits.
test_results: Orthokeratinized stratified squamous epithelium of varying thickness with flat to elongated rete pegs. Areas of basal cell degeneration were evident. Juxta-epithelial connective tissue shows dense infiltration of chronic inflammatory cells of lymphocytes interspersed with increased capillaries. Presence of intraepithelial cleft.

case_report: A 64-year-old Asian woman presented with a 1-month history of difficulty maintaining an upright head position and forward gaze. She also experienced severe pain in her right foot due to limb ischemia associated with systemic sclerosis. Her medical history included a 30-year history of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis, with skin fibrosis confined to her hands and no involvement of her head or neck. There was no family history of neuromuscular diseases. One month prior to her visit, she developed gangrene in her right foot. Despite having Raynaud’s phenomenon and finger ulcerations, she had no prior symptoms in her foot before the onset of gangrene. The pain in her right foot was intense, requiring tramadol and NSAIDs for relief. As her foot pain intensified, she began experiencing difficulty in maintaining her head position. Physical examination showed significant weakness in her neck extensor muscles. Her neck deformity was flexible and could be easily corrected passively. There were no neurological abnormalities, including sensory disturbances or muscle weakness in her limbs.
test_results: Plain radiographs of her cervical spine revealed only mild degenerative changes and severe cervical kyphosis. Cervical magnetic resonance imaging showed no spinal canal stenosis and no abnormal signal change in the cervical paraspinal muscles. Computed tomographic angiography showed occlusion of bilateral anterior tibial arteries and peroneal arteries, and development of collaterals.

case_report: A 26-year-old female presented with red, atrophic, irregularly bordered, depressed patches on both sides of the neck that developed gradually over 5 months. She had previously been treated with topical hydrocortisone cream for two weeks without improvement. The patient also had a history of stridor and recurrent respiratory infections since childhood, hearing loss, and a nose augmentation operation 6 years ago. Dermatological examination showed red, atrophic patches on both sides of the neck and skin laxity on both sides of the trunk. Additional findings included frontal bossing, underdeveloped maxilla, a small nose with a broad, depressed nasal bridge and underdeveloped nostrils, a short philtrum, prominent eyes, and dental malocclusion. Her parents were first-degree cousins.
test_results: Punch biopsy from multiple skin lesions revealed elastin fragmentation and loss on the superficial dermis.

case_report: A 29-year-old woman attended the obstetrics clinic at Seoul National University Hospital for a prenatal screening ultrasound at 28+6 weeks of gestation. The mother had a history of hypertension but no other significant medical history. Ultrasound findings showed intrauterine growth retardation and skeletal dysplasia, with no evidence of oligohydramnios. Amniocentesis was performed at 31+1 weeks, revealing a 46, XX karyotype, and the achondroplasia gene study was negative. A female infant was delivered vaginally at 37+1 weeks of gestation. At birth, the infant did not cry immediately, and her heart rate was below 100 beats/min. Her respiratory status improved after a few minutes of positive pressure ventilation, and she was transferred to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit without the need for O2 supplementation. Apgar scores were 5 at 1 minute, 6 at 5 minutes, and 7 at 10 minutes. The infant was small for gestational age with a birth weight of 1.69 kg (<3rd percentile), birth length of 45 cm (3rd to 10th percentile), and head circumference of 29 cm (<3rd percentile). She exhibited coarse facial features, including a flat midface, broad and depressed nasal bridge, long philtrum, prominent mouth, and gingival hypertrophy. Additional features included shallow orbits, thick skin, full cheeks, and deep infraorbital creases. Skeletal abnormalities observed included claw hands, short upper extremities, arthrogryposis of both wrists, contractures of both hip and knee joints, bowing of both tibiae, and clubfeet. The infant also had thickened skin and thin, golden-colored hair. Skeletal radiographs showed dysostosis multiplex and findings similar to rickets. A skull radiograph revealed under-ossification of the calvarium, osteopenia of the mandible with loss of the lamina dura, and premature synostosis of the metopic suture. The infantogram showed diffuse and severe osteopenia of the long bones, healed fractures at multiple sites, and stippling at the tali. A wrist radiograph revealed diffuse osteopenia and diaphyseal cloaking at both humeri, with cupping of the distal metaphyses of the forearm bones. On the third day of life, total serum calcium (Ca) and phosphorus (P) levels were within normal ranges (9.5 mg/dL and 5.8 mg/dL, respectively), but alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels were markedly elevated (663 IU/L and 1,076.1 pg/mL, respectively). The serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25OHD) level was slightly low (5.5 mg/mL), while the 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25D) level was normal (25.9 pg/mL). The urinary Ca/creatinine (Cr) ratio was 0.10 (reference range, 0.03 to 0.9), and the urinary P/Cr ratio was 1.25 (reference range, 0.39 to 5.6). Maternal blood sample analysis showed normal levels of total Ca (9.0 mg/dL), phosphate (4.1 mg/dL), ALP (125 IU/L), PTH (16 pg/mL), 25OHD (10.1 ng/mL), and 1,25D (11.0 pg/mL). An echocardiogram detected a secundum atrial septal defect (2.8 mm), a small muscular ventricular septal defect (1.5 mm), and a patent ductus arteriosus (3.35 mm), with no significant valve abnormalities. Ophthalmologic examination revealed stromal hypoplasia of both irises but no blue sclera or corneal clouding. A urine mucopolysaccharidosis screening test was negative. The activities of β-D-hexosaminidase and α-N-acetylglucosaminidase were moderately decreased in leukocytes but were 5- to 10-fold higher than control levels in plasma. Examination of a placental biopsy specimen showed foamy vacuolar changes in trophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts.
test_results: GNPTAB genetic testing revealed compound heterozygosity of c.3091C>T (p.Arg1031X) and c.3456_3459dupCA AC(p.Ile1154GlnfsX3).

case_report: A 5-month-old male Indian child with a normal karyotype (46 XY) born to a 26-year-old first-time mother at full term via C-section presented with limb deformities. These included bilateral ectrodactyly of the feet, syndactyly of the right hand, and ectrodactyly of the left hand. A large protrusion was noted at the medial distal third of the right femur. The parents first brought the child to the out-patient department at the age of 3 months due to concerns about limb abnormalities. There was no detailed prenatal history available. The parents were second-degree relatives but had no significant family history. There was no history of exposure to radiation, prenatal teratogenic medications, or infections during pregnancy. The mother did not smoke or drink during pregnancy. The child was breast-fed, had a good appetite and cry, and did not have any bowel or bladder problems, changes in skin color, or cleft lip/palate.
test_results: Radiographic images showed bifid femur with fibular agenesis, absence of right 3, 4, 5 metatarsals and phalanges, absence of left 4, 5 metatarsals and phalanges of foot, left lateral X-ray showing caudal (sacrococcygeal) agenesis.

case_report: A 10-year-old male with a history of autism and ADHD visited the outpatient pediatric clinic due to a popping, clicking noise in both ears for about five months. Upon entering the room, the child eagerly approached the medical student and asked her to listen to his ears. The examiner heard a steady, rhythmic clicking noise in both ears, described as medium-to-high pitch, constant, and rhythmic, not correlating with the heartbeat. Physical examination showed normal vital signs: blood pressure 91/51 mmHg, pulse 94 beats per minute, and temperature 97.2°F. The bilateral ear canals were normal in size and shape, without discharge. Both tympanic membranes were pearly white and clear, with no perforation or scarring. The middle ears were free of effusion or infection, and hearing appeared intact. Nasal examination revealed mild congestion in both nares. The oral cavity, oropharynx, hypopharynx, and neck were grossly normal, with no palatal muscle movement observed. The jaw was non-tender with a full range of motion. Neurologic examination showed cranial nerves II-XII intact. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable. The patient and his mother noted the sound had been worsening, becoming louder, more constant, and increasingly bothersome. The clicking sound improved underwater and disappeared during sleep or when holding breath. Additional symptoms included difficulty hearing, sinus pressure, bilateral nasal congestion, and sore throat. The patient denied jaw pain, vertigo, dizziness, headache, cough, reflux, or vision changes. The mother denied any history of ear disease, trauma, head injuries, or loud noise exposure. Symptoms began after a respiratory illness in January 2021, presumed to be COVID-19, affecting the entire household. The patient was not tested for active infection or antibodies due to sensory issues. Family members recovered completely, but the patient had intermittent nasal congestion that worsened. Initially seen in the clinic three months after symptom onset, he described ear discomfort, cough, and sinus congestion. Diagnosed with acute sinusitis, he was prescribed oral amoxicillin, which he refused. Returning three weeks later with worsening sinus congestion and decreased hearing, he was started on fluticasone propionate nasal spray and referred to a pediatric ENT specialist. During the ENT visit, he described the ear discomfort as a 'clicking' noise.
test_results: A hearing test was performed, and tympanograms were obtained for both ears; all results were normal.

case_report: A 53-year-old woman presented with a two-week history of coughing and shortness of breath during physical activity. She also reported joint pain over the past year. Her medical history included hypertriglyceridemia (HTG) for eight years, with an initial triglyceride (TG) level of 436 mg/dL. She was treated with bezafibrate for the first six years, but the medication was discontinued due to muscle pain. Subsequently, she was treated with pemafibrate (0.2 mg/day) for two years. Despite treatment, her condition worsened, and her TG level reached 1,023 mg/dL one year ago, coinciding with the onset of joint pain. There were no significant lifestyle changes at that time. The patient had a smoking history of 10 cigarettes per day for 33 years (from age 20 to 53). There was no family history of HTG. At the initial visit, her vital signs were: blood pressure, 122/70 mmHg; pulse rate, 100 beats/min; respiratory rate, 18 breaths/min; oxygen saturation, 94% on room air; and temperature, 36.7°C. Despite relatively stable vital signs at rest, she was hospitalized due to post-exertional hypoxemia with an oxygen saturation of 85% on room air. Fine crackles were heard on the dorsal side of the lower lung field. Physical examination revealed eyelid edema, a blister-like rash on the flexor aspect of her fingers, and a keratotic rash on the radial side of her index finger. Although she experienced joint pain, she did not report any spontaneous or gripping muscle pain.
test_results: The patient was tested positive for antibodies against Jo-1 and aminoacyl transfer RNA synthetase. Chest radiography revealed interstitial changes. Chest computed tomography displayed reticular and frosted shadows, traction bronchiectasis, and consolidation of the dorsal surfaces of the lower lungs on both sides.

case_report: A 3-year-8-month-old boy was admitted to the hospital in January 2022 with a fever reaching 39°C, runny nose, cough, reduced appetite, and irritability. These symptoms began 5 days prior to admission. He was initially treated for an upper respiratory infection with symptomatic and antibiotic therapy, but his condition did not improve, leading to hospitalization. The patient is the first child of non-consanguineous parents and had a birth weight of 3,080 g. Vaccinations were administered according to the schedule. On the 11th day after his first measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination, he developed fever and rash, leading to hospitalization. In September 2020, he contracted COVID-19 from family members, experiencing a mild course with a cough lasting several days. Shortly after, his vision rapidly deteriorated to complete blindness. He was examined in several clinics and diagnosed with retinopathy and secondary macular dystrophy of unknown origin. During a hospitalization in November 2020, additional tests revealed acute otitis media, oral mucosal candidiasis, and elevated liver enzymes: aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 228.6 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) at 566.5 U/L, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) at 376.6 U/L. Bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, albumin, and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) levels were within normal limits. Leukocytosis of 15.7 x 10^9/L was detected, while other complete blood count (CBC) values, including platelet levels and coagulogram indexes, were within normal limits. Tests for viral hepatitis B and C, cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection, toxoplasmosis, rubella, and HIV infection were conducted. IgM and/or IgG antibodies to these pathogens were negative, except for a high titer of IgG antibodies to rubella, which could indicate past infection or post-vaccination antibodies. An immunological examination showed no significant abnormalities, except for a slightly increased level of IgG.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing (WES) detected a mutation in the AIRE gene, which was confirmed by gene sequencing. Two homozygous pathogenic variants, c.769C > T (p.Arg257 Ter), were identified in AIRE. A high titer of IgM antibodies to the Epstein-Barr virus (55.68) was observed with a normal IgG indicator to the Epstein-Barr virus, 3.66 (reference <9). On the 4th day after admission (9th day after the onset of symptoms), a positive serology result for СОVID-19 was obtained: IgM + IgA antibodies to SARS-CoV-2 were positive (64.38; reference range 6–8); positive PCR test for COVID-19 was also obtained.
