diagnosis: Virus-induced hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis  in a patient with Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy-Candidiasis-Ectodermal Dystrophy

case_report: The male patient, born to a healthy nonconsanguineous Brazilian couple (mother aged 31 and father aged 33), was 1 month old at his first clinical evaluation. He has an unaffected brother, and the mother reported no illnesses or drug exposure during the pregnancy, which was complicated by polyhydramnios and intrauterine growth retardation. The patient was delivered vaginally at 35 weeks of gestation, weighing 1.850 kg (<10th percentile), with a height of 38 cm (<10th percentile), and a head circumference of 30 cm (<10th percentile). At birth, he exhibited severe skin abnormalities, including a collodion membrane and congenital ichthyosis with taut facial skin, eclabium, ectropion, microcephaly, cryptorchidism, rudimentary flattened ears, and absence of hair on the scalp, eyebrows, and eyelashes. Upper limb malformations were present, including the absence of the right hand, bilateral shortening of the ulna with radius aplasia, fixed elbows, oligodactyly in the right hand with only the fifth digit present, and the absence of the fourth digit in the left foot. A cardiac ultrasound showed a patent foramen ovale, and cholesterol biosynthesis pathway testing results were normal. The patient and his family were evaluated at the Pontifical Catholic University of Paraná in Curitiba, Brazil, where peripheral blood samples were collected for genetic testing.
test_results: We identified a rare de novo missense variant (NM_015884:c.727C>T) in hemizygosity in the MBTPS2 gene. This variant was not present in his parents or brother. The variant was classified as likely pathogenic (PM2/PP3/PS2). Sanger sequencing validated the variant and confirmed its segregation only with the affected phenotype in the family. We also identified two novel missense variants (NM_000213:c.4217G>C and NM_001005619:c.1940C>T) in heterozygosity in the ITGB4 gene. Both variants were also classified as likely pathogenic (PM2/PS2 and PM2/PS2) and were not seen in any of the population databases consulted.

case_report: The patient is a 12-year-old girl with chronic compensated hemolysis, Gilbert syndrome, and recurrent abdominal pain. Blood count results include hemoglobin at 13 g/dL, red blood cell count at 4,020,000/mm3, Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV) at 90.3 fL, Mean Content Hemoglobin (MCH) at 32.1 pg, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) at 38.3 g/dL, reticulocytosis, and indirect hyperbilirubinemia. Abdominal ultrasound showed no gallstones, hepatomegaly, or splenomegaly. The patient is the only child of non-consanguineous Italian parents. Neonatal jaundice was treated with phototherapy. Family history includes the father experiencing jaundice in childhood, recurrent abdominal pain resolved after splenectomy at age 23, and gallstones treated with cholecystectomy. The paternal uncle also had gallbladder stones. Laboratory investigations were conducted to explore the cause of hemolysis. Peripheral blood smear revealed anisocytosis with stomatocytes (5%), ovalocytes (4%), schistocytes (3%), and rare spherocytes. The direct antiglobulin test (DAT) was negative. Electrophoresis and molecular assessment of beta and alpha-globin genes showed no structural hemoglobin alterations. Enzyme activity of red blood cell metabolism (Hexokinase, Glucose-6-phosphate isomerase, 6-Phosphofruttochinase, Glyceraldehyde phosphate dehydrogenase, Phosphoglycerate kinase, Pyruvate kinase, Glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase, Adenylate 6-Phosphogluconate dehydrogenase kinase) was normal. Family history indicated an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. Eosin-5′-maleimide binding test (EMA test) showed normal results with a value of 12% (normal test value > 11%). Osmotic resistance tests, including the glycerol lysis test (AGLT50) and the Pink test, were normal. Quantitative analysis of membrane proteins using Sodium Dodecyl Sulphate-PolyAcrylamide Gel Electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) was not altered. Ektacytometry, which evaluates erythrocyte deformability under an increasing osmotic gradient with constant shear stress, showed a left shift of the osmolarity curve.
test_results: We found in both subjects the missense variant c.1815G > A, p.Met605Ile in PIEZO1 gene (NM_001142864, CCDS54058) in heterozygous state. First, the variant segregated in the affected father. Currently, this variant is annotated neither in population databases nor in databases of known variant.
diagnosis: Dehydrated Hereditary Stomatocytosis  due to a novel PIEZO1 mutation

case_report: A 22-year-old male, who primarily uses his right hand, visited the outpatient department due to shortening and inability to extend the middle finger of his left hand. Physical examination revealed an extension lag in the middle finger, decreased grip strength, and reduced height of the middle ray. The patient had a history of minor trauma to the left hand, which was managed conservatively. Over the following six months, he experienced gradual shortening and decreased grip strength in the affected hand. Laboratory tests showed normal blood parameters, including calcium and parathormone levels.
test_results: The X-ray showed pathological fracture of third metacarpal with osteolytic lesion involving base of second metacarpal and carpal bones. Magnetic resonance imaging showed almost complete osteolysis of the 3rd metacarpal with only the base visible and fracture of the 4th metacarpal with thinning and resorption of the bone and surrounding soft tissue. It also showed pathological fracture involving capitate with patchy areas of osteolysis. Serial X-rays taken at 4 weeks, 8 weeks, 12 weeks, 18 weeks, and 6 months revealed that there was progressive concentric reduction of metacarpal shaft, first involving third then fourth metacarpal giving appearance of a sucked candy. Positron emission tomography scan was done to rule out any tumor, however, no evidence of tumor was found. Biopsy suggested myxoid areas, proliferating vessels interposed with skeletal muscle fragments with no evidence of malignancy.

case_report: A 56-year-old female was admitted for evaluation after outside imaging showed a pancreatic mass. She had been experiencing 8 months of symptomatic hypoglycemia associated with syncope and relieved by intake of carbohydrates. Medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus without medication requirement since 2018 and bariatric surgery 3 years prior. Physical exam revealed a woman with a body mass index of 29 with no obvious signs of pathologic processes; abdominal examination was negative for distention, palpable masses, and tenderness. Labs revealed mild anemia (Hct 33.9%), hypokalemia (3.4 mmol/L), and hyperglycemia (114 mg/dl). Her c-peptide and insulin levels were both elevated at 4.71 ng/ml and 27.9 μU/ml. Her HbA1c was 4.9%. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and endoscopic ultrasound were performed and showed that the gastrojejunostomy anastomosis from her prior bariatric surgery was quite large and could have been contributing to her glycemic lability. These studies were otherwise unremarkable and revealed no pancreatic masses.
test_results: Selective arterial calcium stimulation test (SACST) resulted in increased insulin secretion to four times normal levels localized to the gastroduodenal artery. In a 72-h fasting glucose test, her glucose level stayed consistently above 60.

case_report: A 30-year-old female presented with a firm, non-painful area on the right ear lobule. The back part of this skin area showed a 10-mm oval macule with a pronounced steel-blue color, beneath which a small nodule could be felt. The patient recalled a previous local inflammatory reaction caused by a silver earring 25 years ago. Dermoscopy of the macule showed blue-grey structures evenly spread over a yellow background. The lesion included three structural types: ring-like structures, short linear structures between the rings, and multiple dots. The distribution of these structures was uniform and parallel. A white, radiating area was noticeable in the center of the lesion. A cutaneous biopsy was performed on the firmer area, and a metallic piece from a silver earring was removed.
test_results: The histopathological study revealed the presence of brown-pigmented granules that had accumulated inside the dermic papillae and densely populated the interpapillary dermis over the elastic fibers and vessel walls surrounding the eccrine glands.

case_report: A 9-year-old male child reported experiencing reduced vision in the left eye for the past 3 months. Visual acuity measurements were 0.0 LogMAR in the right eye and 0.8 LogMAR in the left eye. During a general physical examination, multiple cafe-au-lait spots were observed on the back and arms. Fundus examination showed bilateral MPRAP and CHRRPE in the left eye.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging revealed bilateral acoustic neuroma. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed vitreoretinal traction in both eyes and disorganized inner retinal structures in the left eye. Fundus fluorescein angiography of MPRAP showed central hypofluorescence (blocked fluorescence) with surrounding hyperfluorescence (staining).

case_report: A 41-year-old woman arrived at the emergency department 3 months after an abortion, experiencing sudden abdominal pain for 15 hours on April 16, 2020. She reported having undergone an early induced abortion at a local hospital on January 14, 2020, and the intraoperative clearance object was not sent for pathological examination. Post-surgery, blood HCG levels were not reviewed due to severe travel difficulties related to COVID-19. She had no sexual activity for nearly 1 month. On April 25, 2020, she experienced pain leading to syncope once, accompanied by nausea and vomiting three times, with the vomit consisting of gastric content. Her menstrual history includes regular menstruation, menarche at 13 years old, a menstrual period of 5 days, a cycle of 30 days, and the last menstrual period on November 28, 2019, with normal menstrual volume and no dysmenorrhea. She is married, G4P3A1, with 2 previous vaginal births, 1 cesarean section in 2014, and 1 abortion. She has no significant past medical history, no history of alcohol or drug abuse, and no genetic history. Other hospitals considered causes for her abdominal pain and suggested further treatment at a superior hospital. She was transferred to our emergency department by ambulance. Physical examination revealed a temperature of 36.8°C, pulse of 120 beats per minute, respiration rate of 20 breaths per minute, and blood pressure of 80/50 mm Hg. She was conscious, in a passive position, with a painful expression, and had poor examination tolerance. Her abdomen was tense with tenderness throughout, positive rebound pain, and mobile turbidity. Pelvic examination showed normal vulva development, an unobstructed vagina with no abnormal secretions or odor, and no cervical lifting or swing pain. The abdominal wall was thick, the patient had poor coordination, uterine tenderness, significant tenderness in the bilateral appendage area, and no palpable mass.
test_results: Transvaginal uterine ultrasound reveals: a right intrauterine mixed mass (approximately 83 * 66 mm mixed echo mass), a possible pregnancy, and a rupture pregnancy (right pregnancy). abdominal effusion (large) and clots, maximum front and rear diameters of 95 mm, pelvic effusion, and about 20 mm deep. HCG levels in the blood were 17,452 IU/L and hemoglobin levels were 81 g/L. Postoperative pathology: (Right side attachment + uterus + left fallopian tube), excessive proliferation of trophoblast cells, visible infiltration of syncytial trophoblast cells and intermediate trophoblast cells into the uterine muscle layer, invasion of the right adnexa, along with vascular invasion, and no invasion of the left fallopian tube.

case_report: Patient 1 (T3188) is a 23-year-old male with lifelong distal limb weakness, abnormal gait, and congenital foot malformation. He was born at full term via spontaneous vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 3.1 kg. Bilateral clubfoot was noted at birth. He achieved sitting at 10 months and standing at 2 years old. At three years old, he learned to walk independently but was unstable, falling every 5–6 steps. He underwent orthotic surgeries on his feet at ages 1 and 6. Since childhood, his hands have been clumsy, particularly with fine motor tasks. At 16 years old, muscle twitching appeared in both thighs. With orthopedic shoes, he can walk slowly and unsteadily. Distal limb weakness and muscle atrophy have progressively worsened without sensory disturbances. At 23 years old, he is 180 cm tall and weighs 52 kg, with clear speech and alert cognition. Continuous tongue fasciculations are present when protruded. Neck flexion and proximal limb strength are normal (5/5), but grip strength is reduced (4/5). Muscle tone in all four limbs is normal. Fingers cannot be fully straightened, with limited interphalangeal joint extension, noticeable interosseous and thenar muscle atrophy, and postural tremor. Muscle atrophy below the knee is prominent. Foot deformity includes Achilles tendon contracture and toe varus. Tendon reflexes are brisk in all four limbs, and patellar clonus is positive on the right side. The pathological plantar reflex examination was incomplete due to poor cooperation. Ptosis, nystagmus, dysarthria, dysphagia, ataxia, muscle pain, and dyspnea are absent. Mental, psychological, and cognitive tests are normal. He has been training in a backstroke team for six years, primarily using arm strength.
test_results: The electrophysiologic showed nerve conduction velocity was normal. Compound muscle action potential (CMAP) was decreased in nervus peroneus communis (0.96 mV), median nerve (1.27 mV), and ulnar nerve (4.4 mV). The duration and amplitude of motor unit potential (MUP) and multiphase potentials were increased, without spontaneous activity, indicating extensive chronic neurogenic lesions. X-ray photography of distal extremities at the age of 23 years.
diagnosis: DCTN1-related distal hereditary motor neuropathy  plus congenital foot deformity
Orpha_name: Autosomal dominant intermediate Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type F

case_report: A 45-year-old Caucasian male presented with a three-week history of a tender, slow-growing lump in the left axillary region, accompanied by a low-grade fever ranging from 37.5°C to 38°C over the past week. The patient had a history of hypertension and was on a regimen of lacidipine 4mg/day, lisinopril 10mg/day, and hydrochlorothiazide 12.5mg/day. He smoked 30 cigarettes daily. Two years prior, he had undergone a laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass for morbid obesity, resulting in a weight loss of 112kg and a reduction in body mass index from 64.6kg/m2 to 28kg/m2. He was taking supplements including vitamins A, D, and E, vitamin B complex, calcium gluconate, cholecalciferol, and iron. There was no reported family history of lymphoproliferative or autoimmune diseases. Physical examination revealed a tender, non-mobile lymphadenopathy measuring 3×4cm in the left axillary region, with no other notable findings. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, coagulation tests, blood glucose, creatinine, uric acid, sodium, potassium, lipids, liver parameters, cytokeratin, lactate dehydrogenase, ferritin, serum C3 and C4, antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, C-reactive protein, thyroid-stimulating hormone, urine tests, and serology for herpes simplex virus 1 and 2, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, hepatitis B and C virus, toxoplasma, human herpes virus 8, parvovirus B19, human immunodeficiency virus 1, and human T-lymphotropic virus type 1, were all normal or negative. A thoracoabdominal computed tomography scan was normal except for the axillary lymphadenopathy.
test_results: A lymph node biopsy showed coagulative necrosis and frequent karyorrhexis with a lymphoplasmacytoid infiltrate. An investigation for mycobacteria was negative.

case_report: A 19-year-old female presented to the emergency room with left-sided chest pain and cough. CT imaging identified multiple pulmonary emboli in the left inferior segmental pulmonary arteries. She had no provoking factors or other complications at that time and was discharged on rivaroxaban with hemoglobin at 14.9 g/dL and platelet count at 402 per uL. Six weeks later, she returned with right lateral chest wall pain and shortness of breath. Her hemoglobin was 6.6 g/dL and platelet count was 485 per uL. The patient reported developing menorrhagia after starting rivaroxaban. CT imaging showed a new pulmonary embolism in the right lower lobe segmental pulmonary arteries and a decreased clot burden in the left inferior segmental pulmonary artery branches. She received a packed red blood cell transfusion and was started on a heparin drip. There were no signs of heart failure or hypoxia, and she was started on norethindrone for menses suppression. Further laboratory tests showed ferritin at 6.8 ng/mL, and she received an iron transfusion. She was transitioned to warfarin and followed up one month later with hemoglobin at 10.8 g/dL, ferritin at 36.1 ng/mL, iron saturation at 25%, and platelet count at 566 per uL. A hypercoagulable workup including protein C, protein S, antithrombin III, factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutations, lupus anticoagulant, cardiolipin antibodies, and beta-2 glycoprotein antibodies was unrevealing. Persistent thrombocytosis and a report that the patient’s father was being treated for a similar condition led to testing for JAK2, MPL, CALR, and JAK2 exon 12-15 mutations, which were all negative. Subsequent CSA revealed a heterozygous variant of unknown significance with the genomic change Chr1(GRCh37):g.43805172C>A, predicted to result in a single amino acid substitution of glutamine to lysine at codon 208 in exon 4 of the MPL gene. This variant had not been reported as associated with a clinical condition according to the HGMD.
test_results: Bone marrow biopsy revealed normocellular marrow with trilineage hematopoiesis and mild megakaryocytic hyperplasia without atypia nor dysplasia.

case_report: The patient is a 72-year-old male with a history of mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), previous subsegmental pulmonary embolism, atrial fibrillation post-watchman device, peripheral vascular disease post-right femoropopliteal bypass, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. He has a 60 pack-year smoking history and quit six years ago. He had no recent travel. Current medications include rivaroxaban, aspirin, duoneb, metoprolol, amiodarone, and amlodipine. Recently, he was hospitalized for right fifth toe osteomyelitis and treated with intravenous daptomycin due to a past anaphylactic reaction to vancomycin. Post-toe amputation, proximal bone cultures grew MRSA, leading to continued daptomycin treatment. An infectious disease specialist evaluated him, and he was discharged to rehab on a six-week daptomycin course via a PICC line. During rehab, he developed nausea and non-bloody diarrhea for three days, followed by subacute respiratory distress requiring up to six liters of nasal cannula oxygen. He was sent to the hospital for further evaluation. In the emergency room (ER), he exhibited mild respiratory distress with bilateral crackles, predominantly on the right side. The heart exam was unremarkable except for an irregularly irregular pulse. The lower extremity exam showed a well-healing right lower extremity surgical scar without edema. He was vitally stable on 4-6 liters of nasal cannula oxygen. ER blood work showed: Cr: 1.61 mg/dl, BUN: 20 mg/dl, cardiac BNP: 1432, INR: 1.7, Hb: 12.4 g/dl, WBC: 10.7 k/ul, absolute eosinophils count: 3.1 k/ul, absolute neutrophil count: 6.1 k/ul. Urinalysis was unremarkable. No baseline cardiac BNP was available, but baseline creatinine was normal four weeks prior. A chest X-ray revealed new opacification throughout the right lung, suggestive of unilateral pulmonary edema or pneumonia. He was started on linezolid and metronidazole for possible aspiration/healthcare-associated pneumonia and intravenous (IV) diuresis for possible pulmonary edema. He was admitted to the general medical floor. A CT scan of the chest the next day showed bilateral ground-glass opacities with right lung predominance. An echocardiogram showed normal systolic function without diastolic dysfunction. He continued on gentle IV diuresis, and daptomycin was discontinued upon admission. Respiratory support included albuterol/ipratropium treatments, supplemental oxygen for hypoxia, antibiotics for possible bacterial pneumonia, and diuretics for possible pulmonary edema.
test_results: Bronchoscopic fluid analysis showed a total WBC count of 8504/UL, with 40% neutrophils and 42% eosinophils. Bacterial/fungal cultures were negative for infection, and cytology was negative for malignant cells.
Orpha_name: Drug or radiation exposure-related interstitial lung disease

case_report: A 3-year-old female Nigerian child, the third of three siblings, born at term to a healthy non-consanguineous couple, presented with an absent left eye, a mass in the left orbital region, a cleft in the left alar nasi, and skin tags around the left eye since birth. She exhibited delayed developmental milestones, achieving neck control at 6 months, walking at 3 years, and was still unable to speak. There was no history of seizures or similar conditions in the family. Her pregnancy, birth, and neonatal periods were uneventful, although the mother consumed herbal concoctions during pregnancy. Upon examination at the Ophthalmology and Paediatric Neurosurgery clinics in Ibadan, Nigeria, she showed an appropriate social response, right horizontal nystagmus, and normal right pupillary size and light response. She had global hyperreflexia and bilateral flexor plantar response. Additional findings included nodular swellings around the left eye, multiple skin defects on the left side of the face, a tag or cyst at the left lateral canthus, a cleft in the left alar nasi, and a mass in the left orbital region with no identifiable left eyeball. Other examination findings were normal.
test_results: Cranial computerised tomography scan and magnetic resonance imaging showed a left orbital mass, left micro-ophthalmia, colpocephaly, corpus callosal agenesis, giant dysplastic tectum, anteverted midbrain, near horizontal aqueduct of Sylvius, hypoplastic left cerebellar hemisphere, vermian aplasia, large left retrocerebellar cyst communicating with the fourth ventricle. The left orbital ‘cyst’ represented remnant eye tissue surrounded by mixed density/intensity orbital mass.

case_report: A 21-month-old male child, born to a nonconsanguineous couple, exhibited developmental delay and occasional limb stiffness. He was delivered at full term with a birth weight of 3.2 kg without complications. The child had not achieved neck holding, intermittently opened his palms but had not developed a palmar grasp. He displayed stranger anxiety and responded to his name. He cooed but did not produce syllables. Hearing and vision were normal. There was no history of encephalopathy, seizures, diurnal variation of symptoms, or autonomic instability. No family history of similar issues was reported. On examination, his weight was 11.2 kg (-0.12SD), length was 92 cm (+2.76SD), and head circumference was 44.3 cm (-2.54SD). Physical features included bifrontal narrowing, abnormally shaped ear pinna, depression over the helix, high arched palate, non-paralytic convergent squint in the left eye, and pes planus. He exhibited spasticity and dystonia in all limbs. Muscle power was 3/5 (MRC grade) across all muscle groups, and deep tendon reflexes were brisk. Metabolic workup, including arterial blood gas analysis, lactate, ammonia, and tandem mass spectrometry, was normal. MRI of the brain revealed hyperintensity on T1WI and an alternating pattern of hyperintensity and hypointensity on T2WI, indicating delayed myelination. Myelination of the genu of the corpus callosum was also incomplete. Thyroid function tests showed low free T4 (0.57 ng/dl; reference range 0.89–1.76 ng/dl), low total T4 (3.30 mcg/dl; reference range 7.3–15 mcg/dl), and normal TSH (3.33 mIU/ml; reference range 0.34–5.6 mIU/ml), indicating central hypothyroidism. Further thyroid function tests revealed high free T3 (7.17 pg/ml; reference range 2.3–4.2 pg/ml) and high total T3 (2.86 ng/ml; reference range 1.05–2.69 ng/ml).
test_results: Targeted next-generation sequencing showed a missense hemizygous pathogenic variant in the SLC16A2 gene, causing the substitution of arginine for glycine (c.1468G>C/p.Gly490Arg) and confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

case_report: A 33-year-old male presented with a 14-year history of progressive shaking in the left upper limb, which later affected the right upper limb and subsequently both lower limbs after three years. The shaking was primarily action-induced, jerky, and occasionally caused the patient to drop objects. He experienced difficulty walking, initiating gait, imbalance, and falls. Additionally, he reported slurred speech without other bulbar symptoms. There was no significant family history. At the time of presentation, the patient was independent, employed, and had comprehensible speech. A video recording was made with written informed consent. Examination revealed normal cognition and normal ophthalmological findings, including visual acuity, anterior segment, and fundus examination. The patient exhibited bilateral horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus, mild cerebellar dysarthria, appendicular and axial incoordination, and an ataxic gait. There was distal predominant, action-induced, multifocal myoclonus involving all four limbs without sensory or auditory sensitivity. Tremulous movements of both lower limbs were observed upon standing, along with an ataxic gait. The remainder of the examination was normal. Routine blood tests, abdominal ultrasound, and brain MRI were normal. Electrophysiological evaluation showed giant somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEP) with N20–P25 amplitude of 14 µV (normal value < 10 µV), enhanced long loop reflexes, and frequent quasi-rhythmic bursts of less than 50 ms duration in all four limbs on surface electromyography (EMG), indicating a cortical origin of the myoclonus. Visually evoked potentials (VEP) demonstrated bilaterally prolonged P100 latencies of 112 ms in the right eye and 114 ms in the left eye (normal value 106 ± 4 ms). Electroencephalogram (EEG) and nerve conductivity study (NCS) were normal.
test_results: Clinical exome sequencing revealed a previously reported pathogenic homozygous missense variant in exon 5 of the NEU1 gene (chr6: g.31827960G> A; p.Arg294Cys; ENST 00000375631.4).

case_report: A 68-year-old Danish male experienced multiple episodes of lightheadedness and sensations of “passing out” while getting into bed or when food was administered via his gastric fistula tube. He also had sudden hypertensive episodes several times daily. His medical history included chronic kidney disease and hypertension since age 30. At age 51, he received external radiation therapy for lingual cancer. Ten years post-radiation therapy, he developed dysphagia and had several episodes of aspiration pneumonia. A modified barium swallow revealed silent aspiration, leading to the creation of a Percutaneous Endoscopic Gastrostomy (PEG). Despite no oral intake, he continued to have recurrent pneumonia and eventually underwent a tracheotomy. Concurrently, his renal function declined, necessitating hemodialysis three times a week. Since then, he experienced labile blood pressure. During dialysis, his interdialytic weight gain was controlled between 1.5–1.7 kg (2-3% of body weight) with an ultrafiltration rate of about 6.0 – 6.3 ml/hr/kg. His sodium concentration was mostly maintained between 140 to 142 mEq/L, and the diffusive sodium balance during dialysis was negative. Despite stable weight and sodium control, his blood pressure fluctuated between 80 mmHg and 240 mmHg, particularly during dialysis, and was difficult to manage with medications. His daily blood pressure was treated with Ca-channel blockers and ARBs, but the labile blood pressure remained unstable, leading to frequent fainting episodes and several occlusions of his arteriovenous fistula (AVF) due to extreme hypotension. Blood pressure drops occurred several times daily, often after PEG feeding and sometimes after lying in bed. His current medications included Droxidopa and Midodrine Hydrochloride for hypotensive episodes, but blood pressure remained difficult to control, especially during hemodialysis. The dialysate had the following ionic concentrations: 140 mEq/L of sodium, 2.0 mEq/L of potassium, 3.0 mEq/L of calcium, 1.0 mEq/L of magnesium, 113 mEq/L of chloride, and 10 mEq/L of acetate. Despite the unstable blood pressure, his heart rate remained stable, with variations of no more than 10 bpm during hemodialysis. Fifteen years after neck irradiation, he developed arm edema associated with his AVF, which was treated with Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty (PTA) due to brachial vein stenosis.
test_results: Cold pressor test showed 26 mmHg, 15 mmHg increase in sBP, dBP, respectively. Right Internal Carotid Artery (R-ICA) starting point and Left common carotid artery (L-CCA) bifurcation points Max Intima-media Thickness (IMT) was 3.41 mm homogenous iso-echoic plaque and 3.68 mm heterogenous iso-echoic plaque, respectively.

case_report: A 64-year-old male presented with painless jaundice. His medical history includes diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and gout. He has no history of surgeries or family history of cancer. Upon admission, laboratory tests indicated obstructive jaundice with the following results: total bilirubin 17.4 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 372 IU/L, carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) 3.0 ng/mL, and carbohydrate antigen 19–9 235 U/mL. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography showed focal wall thickening in the distal common bile duct and dilatation of the upstream bile duct. Positron emission tomography-computed tomography revealed a mild focal uptake (SUVmax 2.7) at the same site. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) was performed for preoperative biopsy and biliary drainage, revealing chronic inflammation with some atypical glands.
test_results: The immunohistochemical stain showed that tumor cells were positive for CK7 and p53 (weak) and negative for CK20 and CEA. The Ki-67 index was ∼20%. In immunohistochemical stains, the tumor cells were positive for CD56, synaptophysin, and chromogranin A. The Ki-67 proliferative index was ∼60%.
Orpha_name: Small cell carcinoma of the bladder

case_report: A 47-year-old female presented with a best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 20/20 in the right eye (RE) and 20/40 in the left eye (LE). She reported a recent onset of metamorphopsia in her left eye. Her family history included similar conditions in her two siblings and other paternal relatives. The anterior segment examination was normal. Fundus examination revealed pigmentary changes at the posterior pole in both eyes and a yellowish subretinal material located inferotemporal to the macula in the left eye.
test_results: The FA revealed bilateral early macular hyperfluorescence, with dye leakage in the late phases in the LE. The SD-OCT disclosed a normal-thickness retina and subfoveal detachment filled with hyperreflective material in the RE, with scattered choroidal hypertransmission. The LE was noticeable for retinal thickening, subretinal fluid, hyperreflective RPE subfoveal detachment, and hyperreflective intraretinal dots. Inferotemporally, there was subretinal fluid with hyperreflective material extending from the photoreceptors’ layer.
diagnosis: Best Macular Dystrophy  complicated by Choroidal Neovascularization

case_report: A 19-year-old unmarried nulligravid Japanese woman with no significant medical history presented to the emergency care unit of Fukaya Red Cross Hospital, Saitama, Japan, on September 23, 2007. She reported excessive vaginal bleeding following an uncertain period of amenorrhea. Upon examination, her vital signs indicated preshock: she was conscious, afebrile, with a pulse rate of 124 bpm and blood pressure of 112/62 mmHg. Laboratory tests revealed a hemoglobin concentration of 3.7 g/dL and a positive qualitative urine human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) test. Imaging studies, including ultrasonography and magnetic resonance imaging, identified a large intrauterine mass measuring 19 × 15 × 10 cm with numerous small vesicles, absence of a normal gestational sac, and no fetus. She was admitted for immediate treatment, which included fluid infusion and blood transfusion. Due to the risk of increased bleeding and potential perforation from the extremely enlarged uterus with a thin muscular wall, a cautious approach was taken regarding dilation and curettage (D&C). Despite stable vital signs, intermittent vaginal bleeding persisted. Sixteen hours post-admission, there was a sudden increase in bleeding, followed by the spontaneous expulsion of a large mass, after which the uterus contracted to the size of an orange, significantly reducing further bleeding. Subsequent suction D&C was performed to ensure complete evacuation. Her renal function, initially mildly impaired, showed gradual improvement without proteinuria or oliguria. Three days post-expulsion, she developed pruritic skin lesions, initially presenting as papules and erythemas on the dorsum of her hands and anterior chest. Initial treatment with oral antihistamines and local corticosteroids was ineffective. The lesions progressed to vesicles and bullae, eventually spreading across her entire body.
test_results: A skin biopsy revealed subepidermal blister formation. Linear complement C3 deposition was observed along the basement membrane zone on direct immunofluorescence analysis. Her serum immunoglobulin E level and anti-BP180-NC16a antibody index were very high.

case_report: A 38-year-old male presented with a non-healing ulcer over the left Achilles tendon region for four months, along with dry skin and hoarseness of voice. The patient reported normal body growth until age 12, after which there was no increase in weight and height, and premature graying of hair began. His parents were first cousins. He was diagnosed with hypothyroidism at age 18 and has been under treatment since then. At age 25, he developed cataracts in both eyes and underwent cataract surgery. He also had a history of recurrent upper respiratory infections and developed hoarseness of voice over 10 years since puberty. The patient has been married for six years but has no children. Four months ago, he developed itchy papules over the left lower leg and left foot, leading to an ulcer due to persistent itching. Clinical examination revealed an older appearance for his age, short stature, dry skin, thinning hair, tight skin with subcutaneous atrophy, pursed lips with furrowing, high arched palate, squeaky and hoarse voice, beaked nose, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, and flat feet. Physical examination also showed underdevelopment of secondary sexual characteristics with sparse facial, axillary, and pubic hair, and infantile genitalia with micropenis and decreased testicular volume. There was a well-defined tender ulcer of size 6 x 8 cm with hyperkeratotic margins over the left Achilles tendon region. The ulcer floor had pale granulation tissue and slough with serosanguinous discharge, and the surrounding skin was erythematous with eczematous changes. Ocular examination showed pseudophakia in both eyes, and slit-lamp examination revealed multiple tessellations on the fundus. Routine investigations were within normal limits. Hormone levels were normal except for elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone (26 mIU/L) and decreased total serum testosterone (135 ng/mL). Biopsy of the ulcer showed no evidence of dysplasia or malignancy. Radiographic examination of hands and feet showed no signs of osteosclerosis. Carotid Doppler indicated early atheromatous changes in the right distal common carotid artery. Semen analysis showed decreased semen volume per ejaculate and decreased total sperm count. Laryngoscopy revealed fibrosis of the cricoarytenoid and sulcus vocalis.
test_results: Genetic analysis revealed a substitution mutation with homozygous pathogenic variant c.3190 C>T in exon 26 of the WRN gene.

case_report: A 68-year-old right-handed woman with a 12-year education history experienced difficulty speaking over the past several years. She was under treatment for hypertension but had no history of hyperlipidemia, diabetes, or smoking. About seven months ago, she began making kana-dominant spelling mistakes in her mobile text messages, with more frequent errors compared to her handwriting. Upon visiting the hospital, she showed signs of apraxia in speech, eyelid opening, oculomotor, and buccofacial movements. There was a noticeable difference between her spontaneous and voluntary facial expressions. She exhibited perseveration, pathological laughing, and increased limb tendon reflexes. No lower motor neuron signs were observed in her extremities or tongue. Her Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score was 19/30, and her Frontal Assessment Battery (FAB) score was 7/18, indicating mild cognitive decline, including frontal lobe dysfunction. A detailed neuropsychological evaluation using the Western Aphasia Battery (WAB) for Japanese (shortened version) is provided in the table. Her spontaneous speech showed irregular stagnation and distortion, indicating apraxia of speech. While her comprehension of complex sentences was impaired, her single-word comprehension remained intact.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and perfusion single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) showed bilateral atrophy and decreased cerebral blood flow in the frontotemporal lobe, including the anterior operculum. Visual assessment of the dopamine transporter (DaT) scan revealed normal symmetrical uptake in the caudate and putamen region. The specific binding ratio (SBR) calculated as the ratio of striatal specific to non-specific binding was 5.27 on the right and 5.29 on the left, within normal range for this same age group. Tau PET with Florzolotau (18F) demonstrated remarkable uptake of the ligand around the brainstem, subthalamic nucleus, basal ganglia, and bilateral subcortical frontal lobe, while amyloid PET with 11C-PiB was negative by visual assessment.

case_report: A 67-year-old Indian male presented with an itchy rash on the lower back for 10 days. He also observed pigmented rashes in both axillae and the left inframammary area of his chest. He had no prior history of skin rash or drug allergies. His medical history included hypertension for the past eight years, managed with telmisartan. Three months prior, his ophthalmologist noted left head tilt associated with right eye hypertropia when his head was straightened. Eye examination revealed fatigable ptosis of both eyelids with a positive Cogan’s lid twitch sign. Single fiber electromyography indicated mild to moderate neuromuscular transmission defect without significant decremental response in repetitive nerve stimulation. Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody was negative. Magnetic resonance imaging of his brain and orbits were normal. Computed tomography of his chest did not show any thymic mass. He was started on pyridostigmine, which led to improvement in ptosis and head tilt on follow-up. Dermatological examination showed a 5 cm x 5 cm hyperpigmented, purplish patch with an irregular border at the center of his back. Several hyperpigmented linear streaks were noted in both axillae. Two erythematous macules were observed on his chest at the left inframammary region. There were no skin lesions on sun-exposed or other flexural areas. Full blood count, and renal, liver, and thyroid function tests were normal. Screening for diabetes was normal. Hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C viral serology were negative.
test_results: Microscopically, the epidermis showed mild basal vacuolation with rare apoptotic keratinocytes. There was pigmentary incontinence and a mild superficial perivascular infiltrate of lymphocytes.

case_report: A 5-year-old female presented to the outpatient clinic with complaints of rash and itching on her body, along with swelling, redness, and pain in both ankles. It was noted that itching and redness on her elbows and knees had appeared 3 weeks earlier, for which she had received treatment for allergy at another medical facility. Over the past 3 weeks, she experienced intermittent fever, during which the rash spread all over her body. Subsequently, both ankles became red and swollen. The patient was admitted for further investigation of the fever. Vital signs were recorded as follows: body temperature, 36.5°C; pulse rate, 80 bpm; respiratory rate, 17/min; and arterial blood pressure, 90/60 mmHg. Physical examination revealed rash and swelling on both ankles, along with maculopapular skin eruptions all over the body, particularly on the extremities. Laboratory results showed: white blood cell count (WBC), 10.8x10^3/uL; hemoglobin (Hb), 9.8 g/dL; platelets, 521x10^3/uL; aspartate transaminase, 21 U/L; alanine transaminase, 8 U/L; erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), 103 mm/h; C-reactive protein (CRP), 7.82 mg/dL (<0.5); ferritin, 382 ng/mL; fibrinogen, 644.92 mg/dL (200–400); D-dimer, 1.88 mg/mL (0–0.5); and prothrombin time, 14.7 s (11–14).
test_results: Malignancy was not detected, and histopathology was reported as infection or collagenase. No pathogenetic agent was detected in urine or blood cultures. Serological tests yielded negative results for mycoplasm, chlamydia, toxoplasm, rubella, and collagen tissue disease markers. Rheumatoid factor (RF) was 9.94 IU/mL (<19).

case_report: A 10-year-old girl has experienced short duration dyskinesia following sudden movements for the past 3 years. She was born at 38 weeks and 6 days of gestation via normal vaginal delivery, weighing 3,400 g. Her perinatal history was uneventful, and she exhibited normal development. At 6 months old, she had a sudden onset of staring episodes, which progressed to generalized hypotonic seizures lasting 3 minutes. Her growth and developmental milestones remained normal. EEG, neurologic examination, and brain MRI were normal. At 10 months old, after several afebrile seizures, she was treated with an antiepileptic drug (AED) for approximately 2 years, which effectively controlled her seizures. There is no family history of epilepsy or febrile seizures. However, her mother and her mother's siblings experienced similar dyskinesia after sudden movements during their school years, with normal development and no neurologic issues, febrile seizures, or epilepsy since birth. These symptoms have since resolved. At 7 years old, the patient began experiencing abnormal paroxysmal movements 5–6 times daily, including staggering while laughing and sudden collapses while walking. These symptoms persisted. Neurologic examinations and brain MRI results were normal. EEG showed bilateral CTS, with no changes during movements.
test_results: A heterozygous frameshift mutation, .649dup, was detected, resulting in p.Arg217Profs*8.
diagnosis: Paroxysmal Kinesigenic Dyskinesia  associated with a PRRT2 mutation

case_report: A 9-month-old boy, the second child of nonconsanguineous parents, exhibited repeated loss of developmental milestones. His birth and neonatal period were normal. At 4½ months, he experienced lethargy and listlessness following a minor febrile illness, resulting in the temporary loss of partial head control and social smile, which he regained by 6 months. Similar episodes of regression, each lasting 7–10 days, occurred at 7 months and 8½ months, preceded by labored breathing and mild fever. At 8 months, he had an isolated episode of apnea and cyanosis during sleep, which resolved spontaneously within minutes. Parents noted that he appeared floppy and had difficulty swallowing and chewing semisolid foods. There was no history of seizures or dystonic limb posturing. His highest achieved milestones were partial head control and social smile. Examination revealed microcephaly (head circumference = 40.5 cm; <−3 SD) and failure to thrive (Weight: 7.2 kg [at −2 SD]; Length: 67.5 cm [at −2 SD]). Cranial nerve function, vision, and hearing were normal, and the fundus was unremarkable. Both axial and appendicular muscle tone were decreased, with persistent fisting and hyporeflexia. No extrapyramidal signs were observed. Serum biochemistry showed persistent lactic acidemia with arterial lactate levels between 5.8 and 10.4 mmol/L (reference range <2.5 mmol/L). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed elevated lactate (10.5 mmol/L [reference range 1.1–2.4 mmol/L]), normal protein (14.4 mg/dl), and normal sugar (56 mg/dl). Pyruvate levels were not obtained. Serum ammonia was elevated (254 mg/dl). Blood gases indicated high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Hemogram, liver function tests, renal function tests, and blood sugar levels were normal. Endocrine evaluations, including thyroid stimulating hormone, cortisol, parathyroid, and Vitamin D levels, were normal. Tandem mass spectrometry of blood showed no abnormalities. Urine gas chromatography-mass spectrometry indicated elevated lactate. Electrocardiograph and echocardiogram results were insignificant. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was performed twice using a 1.5 tesla MRI scanner. The first MRI at 4 months was unremarkable except for mild white matter paucity. The second MRI at 9 months showed bilateral T2/fluid attenuated inverse recovery hyperintense globus pallidus and substantia nigra. Spectroscopy revealed a prominent lactate doublet and a mild decrease in the NAA:Cr ratio.
test_results: It revealed a homozygous missense mutation c.131A>G or p.H44R in exon 3 of PDHA1 gene. H44R is a known pathological mutation.
diagnosis: Thiamine Responsive Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex Deficiency

case_report: A 29-year-old female has had asymptomatic, slightly erythematous, and hypopigmented lesions resembling pityriasis versicolor on her face, neck, trunk, and extremities since the age of five. Additionally, she has multiple brownish-black, hyperkeratotic, papular plaque, wart-like lesions on the extremities. These lesions have progressively increased in number and size over time (Figure A, B). Examination of the hair, nails, mucosal membranes, and other systems, including abdominal echography and chest X-ray, revealed no abnormalities.
test_results: Histopathology of a flat wart-like lesion showed marked hyperkeratosis, mild acanthosis, and the presence of distinct homogeneous intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies in the large clear cells of the epidermis.

case_report: A 49-year-old female Korean patient presented with itching, skin rash, rhinorrhoea, sneezing, eosinophilia, and abdominal pain. There was no weight loss or diarrhea. Nine years prior, she experienced sudden cramping abdominal pain and visited a local emergency center. Severe tenderness of the entire abdomen was noted, and she was transferred to a high-grade hospital. Abdominal CT and ultrasonography suggested ovarian rupture, leading to another transfer to a university hospital. However, only ascites was observed, with no medical or surgical issues found through laparoscopy. Eosinophilia was consistently observed in laboratory findings across three hospitals. Tests for parasitic infestation were negative. Initial treatment included high-dose oral methylprednisolone (60 mg), which alleviated her abdominal pain. She continued on 2.5 mg methylprednisolone daily for 9 years but frequently experienced severe abdominal cramping pain. The patient had a history of heavy alcohol consumption and smoking half a pack of cigarettes per day for over 10 years. She had an anaphylactic reaction to contrast media 9 years ago and developed urticaria and itching after taking diazepam 4 years ago for sleep disturbance. There was no history of intestinal obstruction, colonic perforation, or surgery, and no specific family history. Due to symptoms of allergic rhinitis, chronic urticaria, eosinophilia, and unexplained abdominal pain, blood tests were conducted, including a complete blood count with differential, serum eosinophil cationic protein, serum total IgE, and specific IgE levels using a multiple allergosorbent test (MAST). Serum IgG, A, M, D, and IgG subclass levels were also checked. The MAST test evaluated specific IgEs for 41 allergens, with results below 0.35 IU/ml considered negative. A skin prick test for 53 allergens was performed, using histamine hydrochloride (10 mg/ml) as a positive control and physiologic saline as a negative control. Reactions were measured by wheal size after 15 minutes. Open food challenge tests were conducted for foods that tested positive on the skin prick tests. The patient underwent basic rheumatologic tests, including anti-nuclear antibody (ANA), anti-citrullinated peptide antibody, rheumatoid factor, and C-reactive protein. Routine stool examination and parasite antibody tests for Clonorchis sinensis, Paragonimus westermani, Cysticercosis, Sparganum, and Toxocara canis were negative. A psychiatric evaluation for sleep disturbance and mood was performed using the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-2), State–Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI), and Beck Hopelessness Scores. The clinical severity of chronic spontaneous urticaria was assessed using the Urticaria Severity Score, with a total score of 92 points. A gastroenterologist evaluated the patient for abdominal pain.
test_results: In the biopsy sample obtained by colonoscopy, mild chronic inflammation with scattered eosinophils (up to 20/high power field (HPF) in the ascending and descending biopsy samples, up to 10/HPF in the transverse colon sample and up to 25/HPF in the sigmoid colon sample) was observed.

case_report: A 13-year-old female from a small town in north-west Sicily, with a family history of childhood epilepsy in the father (responsive to carbamazepine) and migraine in the mother, and two healthy siblings. She reached psychomotor developmental milestones at the expected age. Her medical history includes sporadic migraine episodes since childhood and sleep apnea with snoring. At age 10, she experienced an episode of loss of awareness, head and eye deviation to the right, and gestural automatisms lasting a few minutes, followed by spontaneous recovery. Four months later, she had another episode during sleep, characterized by unconsciousness and bilateral clonic jerking. EEG recording soon after the seizure showed multifocal spikes and sharp waves. She was treated with levetiracetam at 750 mg daily. After 2 years without seizures, levetiracetam was gradually discontinued, but seizures recurred 3 months later, necessitating the resumption of treatment. Clinical examination revealed smaller than expected hands and feet, mild bilateral ptosis, mild bradykinesia, and clumsiness in gross motor tasks. Deep tendon reflexes were normal. No psychiatric comorbidities were observed, though her parents noted she was shy and avoided social interaction with peers. Cognitive assessment using the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children - IV showed low normal performance (total IQ score 78) with a disharmonic profile, indicating a perceptual reasoning index score of 76, working memory score of 88, verbal comprehension score of 86, and processing speed score of 82. Neuropsychological assessment indicated mild impairment in executive functions, particularly affecting attention span and visual-spatial abilities. Brain CT and MRI scans were normal. Current interictal video-EEG monitoring showed sporadic sharp waves in the occipital bilateral regions during sleep.
test_results: The sequence analysis detected two missense variants on the DDC gene of paternal (NM000790.4, c.1040G > A, p. Arg347Gln) and maternal (NM000790.4, c.1172 T > C, p. Leu391Pro) origin.

case_report: Patient III-5 is a 29-year-old male with no prior history of glaucoma or eye surgeries. He also has no history of diabetes or other metabolic disorders. During his most recent examination, his best-corrected visual acuity was measured at 20/150 in each eye individually and 20/100 when using both eyes together. Intraocular pressures were recorded at 23 mmHg in the right eye and 19 mmHg in the left eye. The patient exhibited bilateral small amplitude and high-velocity horizontal nystagmus without a relative null point and maintained orthophoria.
test_results: Slit lamp biomicroscopy of both eyes showed mild corneal pannuses, hypoplastic irides with small remnant stumps, and visually insignificant cortical cataracts. Funduscopic examination revealed bilateral foveal hypoplasia and optic nerve hypoplasia. The cup to disc ratio in the right eye was 0.1 and in the left eye was 0.3.

case_report: A 48-year-old female with no prior cardiovascular disease or family history of sudden cardiac death experienced an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. She collapsed after feeling nauseous while returning home. Her family performed cardiopulmonary resuscitation for 10 minutes until emergency medical services (EMS) arrived. She was found to be in ventricular fibrillation and received five defibrillations, intravenous amiodarone, and epinephrine before achieving return of spontaneous circulation. The patient was sedated and intubated by EMS and admitted to the catheterization lab. Troponin I levels were elevated at 0.698 ng/mL, with ST changes noted on electrocardiogram (ECG), but coronary angiography showed no significant coronary artery disease. Initial computed tomography angiography (CTA) was negative for pulmonary embolism. Substance abuse testing showed elevated benzodiazepine and sertraline levels, which the patient was taking for anxiety and depression. A 12-lead ECG showed sinus tachycardia of 115 beats per minute with normal QRS complexes (80 ms) and absence of prolonged PR or QTc intervals (180 and 443 ms by Bazzett’s formula, respectively). Leads V1, V2, and aVR demonstrated ST segment elevation, while leads II, III, and aVF demonstrated reciprocal ST segment depression. The patient underwent therapeutic hypothermia with a ZOLL Medical Thermoguard XP® catheter. Initial transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) showed decreased left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 30–35%, severe diffuse hypokinesis, normal left ventricle wall thickness, early diastolic dysfunction, and moderately decreased right ventricle function. An incidental thrombus on the hypothermia catheter was found on lower right extremity ultrasound, and low-intensity heparin was started. The patient recovered well and was extubated on day 8. Repeat TTE showed significant recovery with increased LVEF of 60–65% and normalized right ventricular function, chamber size, wall motion, and thickness. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with gadolinium enhancement confirmed normal left and right ventricle function without structural abnormalities, fibrosis, or evidence of myocardial infarction. Cardiac MRI also revealed suspected pulmonary emboli likely due to the hypothermia catheter. CTA confirmed non-occlusive pulmonary emboli in the right lower lobar pulmonary artery and right upper segmental and subsegmental pulmonary arteries. She was started on apixaban. She subsequently underwent a successful subcutaneous implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) implant with a Boston Scientific EMBLEM™ MRI subcutaneous ICD on day 19 and was discharged the day after the procedure. ECG post-ICD implant showed borderline tachycardic sinus rhythm at 97 beats per minute with normal PR and QTc intervals (140 and 413 ms by Bazzett’s formula, respectively) and persistent T-wave inversions. The patient was admitted into cardiac rehabilitation and recovered uneventfully with significant gains in exercise tolerance. Her family history revealed that the patient’s father was diagnosed with paroxysmal atrial tachycardia at age 37, and her paternal grandmother had a history of paroxysmal atrial tachycardia and heart block with a 'cardiac event' of unspecified etiology in her 50s.
test_results: Genomic DNA from a sputum sample was analyzed via Ambry Genetics’ CardioNext® targeted gene panel (Aliso Viejo, CA, USA). Testing revealed a VUS identified as a heterozygous c.2162G > A/p.R721H variant within exon 18 of the ACTN2 gene.
diagnosis: Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation associated with a novel ACTN2 missense variant
Orpha_name: Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation, non Brugada type

case_report: This report concerns a 12-month-old female who was born at term. Prenatal observations included cerebral ventricular enlargement, cerebral cysts, polyhydramnios, and a ventricular septal defect. At birth, her weight was 2750 g, placing her at the 10th percentile according to WHO growth standards for 0–2 years. Postnatally, she experienced respiratory distress, necessitating oxygen support and a four-week NICU stay before being discharged on oxygen. A brain MRI revealed cerebral ventricular enlargement, a right subependymal cyst, and vascular calcifications. Her medical history includes hypotonia, feeding difficulties, food aspiration, significant joint hypermobility, and hepatic calcifications. Notable facial features include the absence of eyelashes, sparse eyebrows, scalp alopecia except for a tuft of long and coarse hair on the central posterior scalp, an erythematous vascular marking on the posterior head, and an elongated head with a sloping forehead. At the time of reporting, she is undergoing physical, occupational, and speech therapy. She can sit upright with minimal assistance, self-feed independently, and primarily moves by rolling and compensated commando crawling.
test_results: She was diagnosed as having a de novo heterozygous variant in the ODC1 gene, c.1307_1311delinsT (p.Thr436IlefsX11), which is predicted to shift the reading frame, resulting in premature truncation of the protein. This variant is not observed in the population.
Orpha_name: Global developmental delay-alopecia-macrocephaly-facial dysmorphism-structural brain anomalies syndrome

case_report: A 66-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 3-year history of plantar keratosis, which had recently developed necrotic ulcers. The patient had no significant past medical history and was an active smoker with a 50 pack-year history. He occasionally used cannabis but did not consume cocaine or other illicit drugs. Physical examination revealed erythematous, infiltrated plaques and retiform livedoid lesions on the dorso-lateral and medial aspects of the feet, accompanied by central necrotic ulcers. Additionally, there were alopecic patches on the lower third of both legs and erythematous patches on the hands. No lymphadenopathy was observed.
test_results: Biopsy specimens taken from the lesions of the feet revealed a dense dermal lymphoid infiltrate of small cells with moderate atypical features, surrounding the eccrine glands with focal infiltration of the eccrine coils and ducts and the blood vessels. The perivascular infiltrate was granulomatous, associated with some thromboses and extravasated erythrocytes. A biopsy specimen taken from a patch of the hand showed a similar syringotropic aspect with mild folliculotropic and epidermotropic infiltrate. Immunohistochemical stainings demonstrated a predominance of T-cells with high expression of CD3+, CD5+, CD7+, CD4+, and the T-FH markers PD1+ and CXCL13. In addition, Bcl-6 (< 10%), PD-L1 (10%) and Ki67 (15%) stainings were slightly positive, while ICOS, CD10, CD20, CD23, CD25, CD30, CD56, perforin and granzyme were negative. A T-cell receptor gene rearrangement was demonstrated in skin lesions.

case_report: The patient is a 23-year-old female, height 165 cm, weight 36 kg. She exhibited developmental delay at the age of three and cognitive impairment that became noticeable during elementary school, leading to her enrollment in a special school for 12 years with below-average academic performance. At the age of 12, she experienced gait disturbance due to weakness in the right lower extremities. Her medical history includes recurrent abdominal pain, but clinical examinations, blood tests, and abdominal ultrasounds were repeatedly normal. Family history showed no evidence of cerebral, muscle, or cardiac disease, although her parents are first-degree cousins. Her parents, brother, and two sisters showed no phenotypic abnormalities. At the age of 14, a clinical neurological examination revealed startleness without hyperekplexia, social withdrawal, avoidance of eye contact, general wasting, and hyperkyphosis of the thoracic spine. Blood tests showed recurrent mild elevation of creatine-kinase. Needle electromyography results were normal in both weak and non-weak muscles. Nerve conduction studies were normal. A muscle biopsy from the left biceps muscle showed nonspecific changes. Cerebral CT scans were normal. EEG results indicated increased background slowing with diffuse, intermittent theta waves without drowsiness. Neuropsychological testing identified adjustment disorders, anxiety, depression, moderate intellectual disability, a negative self-image, and feelings of being unloved.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed the homozygous variant c.553C>T in exon 6 of the MICU1 gene.
diagnosis: Mitochondrial myopathy due to MICU1 variant c.553C>T

case_report: A 6-year-old boy presented with rhinorrhea for several months. Nasal endoscopy confirmed no anatomical anomalies, and he was diagnosed with adenoid hypertrophy and chronic sinusitis. He exhibited a triangular face, deep-set protruding eyes, low-set ears, a wide nose with a narrow nasal bridge, short philtrum, long thin lips, and clinodactyly. He was born as the first baby in a set of twins at a gestational age of 34 weeks. At birth, his body weight was 2,030 g (50th–75th percentile), height was 44 cm (25th–50th percentile), and head circumference was 32 cm (50th–75th percentile). His twin sister's body weight was 2,110 g (50th–75th percentile), height was 47 cm (75th–90th percentile), and head circumference was 32 cm (50th–75th percentile) at birth. Audiometry test at birth was normal. His parents were healthy without any diseases. His parents noted language and growth delays compared to his twin sister, and he was evaluated at another hospital around 1 year old, with normal karyotype results. At 16 months, he was diagnosed with mild delays in gross motor and language skills based on the Korean version of Denver Developmental Screening Test (DDST), scoring at 12 months for gross motor and language, and at 16 months for fine motor, personal sociability, and cognition-adaptation. His body weight, height, and head circumference were within the normal range of growth, but his growth indexes were lower than his twin sister's. At 29 months, his developmental delay had worsened: gross motor at 22 months, fine motor at 27 months, personal sociability at 24 months, language at 16 months, and cognition-adaptation at 16 months by Korean DDST. His parents reported difficulty concentrating and occasional word repetition, suggesting echolalia or a phonological disorder, and a preference for objects over people. His bone age was estimated to be 60 months, younger than his chronological age of 75 months. His height was 113 cm (10th–25th percentile), shorter than his twin sister. His growth indices and z scores, according to the 2017 Korean pediatric growth chart after birth, and his bone age are documented. The heights of his father and mother were 179 cm and 168 cm, respectively; midparental height (MPH) was 180 cm (MPH z score, 0.976). The patient's predicted adult height (PAH) was 170 cm (PAH z score, -0.77). Baseline growth hormonal tests at 6 years and 10 months showed insulin-like growth factor-I 163.04 ng/mL (reference, 58.37–212 ng/mL), insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 3 1,795 ng/mL (reference, 1,219–3,710 ng/mL). Hormonal tests at 7 years and 2 months showed thyroid-stimulating hormone 4.12 mIU/mL (reference, 0.17–4.05 mIU/mL), free T4 1.23 ng/dL (reference, 0.9–2.6 ng/dL), testosterone 0.04 ng/mL (reference, 0.03–1.0 ng/mL), dehydroepiandrosterone-sulfate 45.63 μg/dL (13–115 μg/dL), luteinizing hormone 0.84 mIU/mL (reference, 0.2–0.3 mIU/mL), and follicle-stimulating hormone 0.53 mIU/mL (0.36–3.0 mIU/mL). Language education, audiological tests, and psychiatric consultation were conducted. Speech delay was assessed as a fourth degree of articulation disorder in spoken language evaluation. Hearing tests by auditory brain stem response and otoacoustic emission were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging showed no anatomical anomalies of the brain, and no neurological defects were observed at 6 years of age. Kidney ultrasonogram was normal with no renal system anomalies. Ophthalmologic tests are planned for screening.
test_results: A novel SRCAP mutation (c.7732dupT, p.Ser2578Phefs*6 in exon 33) was identified. Validation by Sanger sequencing was also performed. The mutation was not found in any control population database, nor in his healthy parents. This is a novel variant and had not been reported previously. In this variant, the protein was terminated early. Based on the guidelines for interpretation of sequence variants by American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics, and Association for Molecular Pathology, this mutation may be considered pathogenic.

case_report: A 71-year-old male with a history of chronic kidney disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, prostate adenocarcinoma post-radiation therapy, and a 30-pack-year smoking history presented with new-onset hoarseness. Flexible nasopharyngoscopy identified left vocal cord paralysis. An MRI without contrast of the head, neck, and chest revealed a 7.9 × 5.5 × 6.7 cm mass in the left upper mediastinum, involving the origin of great vessels and displacing the trachea to the right. A PET-CT scan showed high radiotracer uptake in the mass located in the middle and anterior mediastinum, completely surrounding the great vessels at the aortic arch and thoracic inlet, with a maximum SUV of 6.2 cm. Additionally, small bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with emphysema and no pulmonary infiltrates were noted. Due to the patient's multiple medical conditions and the mass encasing the mediastinal great vessels, resection was not feasible. The patient preferred a less invasive diagnostic approach, leading to the performance of bronchoscopy with EBUS-TBNA technique without complications.
test_results: Histopathology revealed the expression of pancytokeratin and cytokeratin 7 with co-expression of CD5 on the cell’s surface.

case_report: A 77-year-old Japanese man reported experiencing mild lower abdominal pain for the past 3 years. The pain appeared spontaneously and worsened on an empty stomach and during stress, without any other symptoms. Despite the pain, the patient continued mountain climbing as a hobby. Abdominal computed tomography and upper gastrointestinal endoscopy performed at a local hospital showed normal results. The patient was treated with rebamipide and lansoprazole for abdominal pain, but the symptoms persisted. His medical history included active pulmonary tuberculosis 2 years ago and a colonic polyp removal 1 year ago. Physical examination showed a body temperature of 36.4 °C, blood pressure of 128/60 mmHg, pulse rate of 66 beats/min, respiratory rate of 15/min, and oxygen saturation of 95% on room air. No abnormalities were noted in the head, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, chest, and extremities. The abdominal region showed no tenderness during palpation, and swab testing, alcohol testing, and skin pinching were negative. Carnett’s sign was not assessed initially. Laboratory tests were within normal limits. Thoracic magnetic resonance imaging was performed due to suspected thoracic nerve pain, but no abnormalities were found. Conservative therapy was initiated for the abdominal pain. At a follow-up examination 7 days later, the symptoms had slightly improved, but the pain returned 9 days later. Repeated abdominal palpation still showed no tenderness, but three tender points were identified along the intercostal nerves Th10, Th11, and Th12 on the lower left side of the rectus abdominis muscle. The pain was present only when the abdominal wall was tensed, although no local sensory disturbances were observed.
test_results: Thirty minutes after the injections, the pain had reduced from 10/10 to 2/10 on a pain scale where 0 indicates no pain and 10 represents maximum pain. One week later, the pain at the sites where 1% lidocaine had been injected was resolved, but the pain remained on the lower left side of the navel. Hence, we injected 10 ml of 1% lidocaine into the subfascial space at the remaining painful point under US guidance, and the pain had completely resolved to 0/10 by 30 min after the injection.

case_report: A 56-year-old woman presented with a history of progressively decreasing visual acuity, recurrent corneal erosions, and mild foreign body sensation in both eyes for approximately one year. Her medical history included rheumatoid arthritis and high blood pressure. She was on methotrexate, folic acid, ibuprofen, and ramipril. The patient reported decreased vision, photosensitivity, and pain in both eyes. Slit lamp examination showed corneal erosions and numerous gray-white central granular opacities with subepithelial haziness involving the Bowman layer and the superficial stroma. The Bowman layer appeared glossy and thickened with dense gray-white granular and lattice opacities arranged in a breadcrumb-like pattern. The endothelium and Descemet’s membrane were normal. Fluorescein staining revealed epithelial irregularity. Anterior segment examination showed a central nuclear cataract and normal iris appearance in both eyes. Intraocular pressures measured by Goldmann applanation tonometer were 16 mm Hg in both eyes. Dilated fundus examination revealed a normal, healthy fundus in both eyes. The best corrected visual acuity was 6/60 in the right eye and 6/18 in the left eye. The treatment plan included one drop of lubricant drops for both eyes, four times per day.
test_results: AS-OCT finding revealed accumulation of deposits both in the Bowman layer and superficial stroma. On cross section, the deposits have a string of pearls appearance and some of them penetrate through the Bowman’s layer into the epithelium. The deeper layers of the stroma, Descemet’s membrane and the endothelium were normal. Central corneal thickness was 531 μm on the right and 533 μm on the left measured by AS-OCT. Molecular genetic analysis of all exons of TGFBI gene showed a single heterozygous nucleotide substitution, G to A at the position 418 in the exon 4. This mutation replaces amino acid arginine to histidine at codon 124 (R124H).

case_report: A 47-year-old Sri Lankan male presented with a history of gradual onset of widespread, symmetrical papular lesions primarily located on the face, ears, neck, upper trunk, forearms, and hands. The papules were closely spaced, measuring 2–3 mm in diameter, and arranged in a linear pattern. Clusters of papules were observed on the dorsa of both hands. The patient also exhibited progressive skin induration, tightness, and infiltration, with sclerodactyly and a noticeable 'doughnut sign' over the proximal interphalangeal joints due to skin infiltration. Additionally, he experienced increasing proximal muscle weakness, joint pain, shortness of breath particularly during exertion, and symptoms of regurgitation and difficulty swallowing, which were particularly bothersome at the time of examination.
test_results: A biopsy revealed papillary dermal myxoid material with fibroblastic proliferation consistent with the diagnosis of scleroderma.

case_report: A 40-year-old male presented with visual occlusion in the right eye persisting for over a month. The patient reported no additional discomforts and had an unremarkable medical history. Examination revealed best corrected visual acuity of 20/25 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Anterior segment examination of both eyes and fundus examination of the left eye showed no significant abnormalities. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication.
test_results: Fundus imaging of the right eye showed a mass-like yellowish white heterogeneous lesion of 1.5 papillary diameter above the temporal region of optic papillary. Part of the lesion was under superotemporal vascular arcade, which is grape-like bumpy in appearance and protruding from the surface of the retina. Cyst-like changes of partially abnormal dilated vessels were visible and were filled with dark red venous blood. Moreover, liquid level was observed at 1 place. The retinal blood vessels extending into the tumor from the branches of superotemporal vascular arcade are widened and dilated. Surface of the tumor was covered by a large number of yellowish white heterogeneous fibrous tissues. Morphology of retinal blood vessels around the lesion was basically normal, and local hemorrhage at the lower part of the lesion was observed. Moreover, petechial hemorrhage was scattered around the lesion, and there was no obvious lipid exudation. Fluorescein angiography (FA) indicated that fluorescein filling in the early stage was slow with hypofluorescence, and retinal angioplerosis stretching into the tumor from superotemporal vascular arcade was visible on laminar flow in the veins. This in turn widened and irregularly expanded the blood vessels in root-like shape, while the ends appeared in brush-like shape. Until the venous phase, the fluorescein in the tumor was gradually filled and appeared in flake-like, grape-cluster-like, and cap-like cluster with strong fluorescence. Quasi-circular hypofluorescence and semicircular liquid level were observed locally. No obvious fluorescein leakage was noted in the late stage of FA. Fluorescence was covered by scattered hemorrhage locally at the lower part of the lesion and around the lesion. On Enface, the whole lesion showed heterogeneous medium to highly reflective clumps, and the surface of the lesion remained uneven with moderately reflective grape-cluster-like nodular changes. Among them, several round low reflective shadows corresponding to cyst-like abnormal vessels filled with dark red venous blood appeared on the fundus images and liquid level was also visible. Superotemporal vascular arcade showed moderate reflection on the Enface image. The branch vessels penetrating into the lesion was tortuous and low reflective, which were adjacent to the low reflective cyst-like changes that are visible locally. Local glial fibrosis showed unevenly high reflection and a boat-like low reflective area in the lesion. On OCTA, nodular and grape-like cluster changes were observed on the margin of the lesion, which were moderately reflective. Superotemporal vessels and vessels inside the lesion were highly reflective. Retinal vessels tortuously expanded into the lesion from the branches of superotemporal vascular arcade, which were in root-like shape in the end and brush-like shape for small branches. Furthermore, circular low reflective areas can be observed. Some of these covered the retinal vessels below them, corresponding to the low reflective areas on the Enface, and liquid level was also visible. Boat-like area in the lesion below them also corresponded to Enface.

case_report: A 21-year-old male presented with pain and recurrent nodular swelling over the right foot for the past four years. He works as a farmer. Two years after the onset of painful swellings, there was a history of a sinus from the foot discharging pus with dark-colored granules. The patient had close contact with an active case of pulmonary tuberculosis (his wife). Following the onset of the discharge, the patient visited a local practitioner who sent the pus for culture and sensitivity testing. The patient was started on oral antibiotics based on the sensitivity results. The discharge mildly decreased with oral antibiotics but persisted, and the patient was advised to use local dressings. Due to the persistent discharging sinus, the patient eventually presented to the outpatient department of our hospital. On local examination, multiple nodular swellings were observed over the dorsum, medial, and lateral aspects of the midfoot. There was a discharging sinus over the dorsum of the midfoot, adherent to the bone, with non-undermined margins. There was diffuse tenderness in the mid and forefoot, and movements in these areas were painful and restricted. Blood investigations revealed a marginally high ESR (32) and elevated C-reactive protein levels (20 ng/dl). Plain radiographs of the foot showed multiple lytic lesions involving the metatarso-cuneiform joints and inter-tarsal joints, associated with significant osteoporosis.
test_results: The incisional biopsy was performed from the dorsal aspect of mid foot along with sinus tract excision. The incision revealed pus which was interspersed with dark black coloured granules on gross examination. A big sequestrum was removed from the tarso-metatarsal junction, with multiple black pigmented granules. The histo-pathological examination of the tissue revealed colonies comprising of dense tangled meshwork of slender hyphae interspersed with ovoid to round spore like structures. The colonies had brown pigmentation at the periphery.

case_report: A 54-year-old woman experienced a sudden onset of weakness in her right arm, leg, and face, along with slowed thinking, difficulty with calculations, urinary incontinence, child-like behavior, and significant fatigue. She was initially treated for these symptoms and her weakness improved with physical therapy. In the years before these symptoms, she reported heavy alcohol consumption. Two years later, she returned with slowed thinking, difficulty with calculations, and behavioral changes. Serum sodium and glucose levels were within normal limits during both her initial presentation and her follow-up visit. Thiamine levels were not available from her initial presentation.
test_results: MRI obtained at the time of her presentation at our clinic revealed a large anterior corpus callosum lesion along with left greater than right corona radiata white matter lesions.

case_report: A 66-year-old male, who does not consume alcohol, was admitted to the hospital experiencing severe, widespread abdominal pain. His medical history includes primary hypertension and chronic hepatitis B, diagnosed 20 years ago, which has been managed with hepatoprotective pills but no other medications. Two years prior, he was diagnosed with Laennec atrophic cirrhosis related to hepatitis. At the time of this admission, without ongoing therapy, there were no indications of decompensated cirrhosis. Physical examination showed no significant abnormalities, except for a slight contraction of the abdominal wall.
test_results: Ultrasound examination showed a 35 mm solid hepatic nodule in the sixth liver segment. Gross examination of the surgical specimen revealed a 35 mm × 30 mm × 38 mm round encapsulated tumor, surrounded by hepatic parenchyma. On cut section, the tumor had a multinodular solid aspect, was green-yellow in color, soft in consistency, and presented multiple small hemorrhagic areas.
