Under microscope, the encapsulated tumor was shown to be composed by multiple nodules separated by connective bands. Within the nodules, hepatocyte-like cells that displayed tubular or glandular-like, acinar and solid-trabecular arrangement of the tumor cells with clear component was noted. No atypical nuclei were identified; the reticulin framework was disintegrated. The tumor stroma was well vascularized, without ductular reaction or inflammatory cells. The hepatic parenchyma that was located adjacent to the connective capsule presented a pseudolobular architecture that was suggestive for cirrhosis, without signs of fatty change.

case_report: A 62-year-old male presented with a three-day history of abdominal distention, abdominal pain, bloating, and constipation. Additionally, he experienced itching and a burning skin eruption on the left side of the abdominal wall, which appeared 48 hours prior to admission. The patient did not report nausea, vomiting, or fever and was not on any medications. Upon admission, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Physical examination showed abdominal distention and a vesicular skin eruption on the left abdomen, extending to the back but not crossing the midline, involving the T7-T10 dermatomes. The abdomen was tense with a tympanitic percussion note throughout, decreased bowel sounds, and no signs of peritoneal irritation. Hematologic and biochemical tests were within normal limits.
test_results: Plain X-rays and abdominal computed tomography scan demonstrated distended small bowel loops and air-fluid levels.
diagnosis: Intestinal pseudo-obstruction secondary to herpes zoster

case_report: A 17-year-old female presented with blurred distance vision in both eyes for three years. Her best-corrected visual acuity was recorded as 6/9 in both eyes, with no changes observed over a follow-up period of one year. Examination of the anterior segment using a slit-lamp revealed no abnormalities. Optical biometry measurements showed an axial length of 21.80 mm in the right eye and 21.64 mm in the left eye.
test_results: Dilated fundus examination revealed bilateral and symmetrical, multifocal subretinal yellowish deposits in the posterior pole and upper nasal region, with peripapillary sparing. On FAF, the yellowish deposits appeared as hyper-autofluorescent spots surrounding an area of hypo-autofluorescence. The deposits showed staining in the late phase of the fluorescein angiogram. On OCT, subretinal fluid and intraretinal hyporeflective spaces (schisis) located predominantly in the outer nuclear layer (ONL) were seen along with elongated photoreceptors and hyperreflective deposits in the subretinal space bilaterally. The electroretinogram (ERG) was normal, and an absent light peak was noted on EOG.

case_report: A 10-year-old male presented with rectal prolapse and lower abdominal pain persisting for one month. The patient also reported passing blood and mucus per rectum for the past three weeks. There were no previous gastrointestinal issues before this presentation. On examination, the patient appeared well and was not in distress. Physical examination identified a full-thickness rectal prolapse with numerous polyps distributed throughout the rectum. The lowest polyp was located three centimeters from the anal verge. There was no history of melena.
test_results: A colonoscopy was performed and divulged a rectum completely infiltrated with polyps. In addition to the rectum, the aforesaid polyps were also observed along the length of the colon. Subsequent histopathological analysis revealed numerous pedunculated polyps in the colorectum and the terminal ileum. Sections of the polyps, including the multilobed forms, revealed ulcerated surface with underlying cystically dilated glands lined by columnar epithelium. The polyps were also observed to be budding and branching, admixed with adenomatous glands lined by dysplastic columnar epithelium.

case_report: A 60-year-old Caucasian woman with a family history of dyslipidemia and nephropathy was admitted in February 2001. Clinical findings included blood pressure of 160/100 mmHg, elevated lipid levels (cholesterol 372 mg/dl, LDL cholesterol 267 mg/dl, triglycerides 239 mg/dl), and creatinine levels within normal range (0.9 mg/dl) with a GFR of 63 ml/min calculated using the Cockroft and Gault formula. Laboratory results showed albumin levels at 3.15 g/dl, total protein at 5.7 g/dl, micro-hematuria, and proteinuria at 200 mg/dl with a proteinuria and/or albuminuria ratio of 2 g/g. Immunological tests including ASO, rheumatoid factor, C3-C4, VDRL, serum immuno-fixation, and serum immunoglobulin were within normal limits. Tests for HBV, HCV, and HIV were negative. The leucocyte count was normal. Physical examination did not reveal xanthelasma, corneal arc, or edema. An ultrasound showed kidneys with regular dimensions and structure.
test_results: A renal biopsy showed the presence of lipid deposits in the glomerular lumens under the optical microscope after staining with Red-O oil. The interstitium showed a diffuse fibrous edema and tubular atrophy in the areas of fibrosis with a moderate infiltration of inflammatory cells. An arteriole showed hyaline deposits. An immunofluorescence revealed the presence of deposits of IgM and C3 in the sub endothelial seat. An electronic ultrastructural analysis confirmed the presence of thrombi in the lumen of the glomerular capillary loops. ApoE typing identified the polymorphism (E2/2).

case_report: The patient is a 6-year-old girl born to non-consanguineous parents. Both pregnancy and delivery were uneventful. She achieved independent walking and speaking milestones at 19 months and had a normal head circumference. At 8 months and 1 year of age, she experienced episodes characterized by involuntary eye rolling and cyanosis of the lips. These episodes did not recur over the next two years. By the age of 4, she developed dystonia, primarily involving backward head movements, stiffness in the right lower limbs, and dorsal flexion of the big toe. Occasionally, her right arm rotated inward and could not be flexed, accompanied by crying and whole-body shaking. Initially, these episodes were mild, occurring three to eight times per month and lasting about 1 to 2 minutes each.
test_results: The EEG showed sharp waves and sharp slow waves in the right central temporal and left central region with a normal background during wake and sleep.
Orpha_name: Classic glucose transporter type 1 deficiency syndrome

case_report: A 60-year-old male experienced numbness in his face and oral cavity, which gradually extended to his scalp, neck, and shoulders. Two years later, he began having difficulty swallowing and slurred speech. Three years after the initial symptoms, he was seen at our hospital. Examination revealed reduced sensation to pinprick and light touch in all areas served by the trigeminal nerve on both sides and in the C1–C4 dermatomes. Corneal reflexes were absent. There was noticeable weakness and atrophy in the right facial muscles, along with dysarthria and tongue weakness. The gag reflex was absent. Involuntary, chorea-like movements were observed in the extremities, more pronounced on the right side, though muscle strength and reflexes in the extremities were normal. Blood and cerebrospinal fluid tests showed no abnormalities. MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord were also normal.
test_results: A blink reflex study showed delayed ipsilateral R2 (iR2) and contralateral R2 (cR2) responses bilaterally (latency of iR2 was 50.7 ms, and cR2 was not evoked on left-sided stimulation; latencies of iR2 and cR2 on right-sided stimulation were 49.9 and 42.4 ms, respectively; the upper normal limit of R2 latency is <41 ms). A nerve conduction study (NCS) showed decreased sensory nerve action potential amplitudes in the upper limbs. Needle electromyography revealed chronic denervation changes in the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Dopamine transporter SPECT revealed reduced 123I-ioflupane binding in the bilateral striata, with left-sided predominance.
diagnosis: Facial Onset Sensory and Motor Neuronopathy
Orpha_name: Facial Onset Sensory and Motor Neuronopathy

case_report: The patient is a 44-year-old male with a decade-long history of unexplained shortness of breath and chest tightness during intense exercise or when lying down, initially without affecting daily activities. In 2012, his hemoglobin (Hb) was elevated to 199 g/L (normal range: 120–160 g/L) with normal partial pressure of oxygen (PO2) in arterial blood gas analysis (ABG). Bone marrow cytology showed no abnormalities, and the JAK2V167F gene mutation test was negative. He received interferon treatment, but symptoms persisted. In 2013, his Hb was 201 g/L, ABG showed PO2 of 63 mmHg and partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PCO2) of 52 mmHg. Echocardiography, computed tomography pulmonary angiogram (CTPA), and electromyography (EMG) showed no abnormalities. Tests for α–glucosidase, β–galactosidase, cardiolipin antibody, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, hepatic and renal function were normal. His symptoms improved with the use of a non-invasive ventilator. In 2021, he was admitted again with worsened exertional dyspnea. Physical examination revealed no significant abnormalities. He had a 30-year smoking history and 13 years of hypertension. His elder sister experienced similar symptoms, and his father had died of cardiac enlargement. Admission tests showed creatine kinase-MB (CK-MB) at 5.63 ng/mL (normal range: <3.61 ng/mL), Hb at 187 g/L (normal range: 115–150 g/L), total bilirubin (TBIL) at 50.96 μmol/L (normal range: <23.00 μmol/L), and direct bilirubin (DBIL) at 11.95 μmol/L (normal range: <8.00 μmol/L). Immunoglobulin G was slightly elevated, but immunoglobulin G4 was normal, and serum anti-smooth muscle antibody was weakly positive. Pulmonary function tests showed forced vital capacity (FVC) at 1.43 L (35.4%), forced expiratory volume in the first second (FEV1) at 1.12 L (33.6%), FEV1/FVC ratio at 0.78, total lung capacity (TLC) at 2.66 L (43.7%), residual volume (RV) at 1.14 L (59.9%), and RV/TLC ratio at 0.42. ABG on room air in the supine position revealed PO2 at 49 mmHg and PCO2 at 69 mmHg, compared to standing position PO2 at 54 mmHg and PCO2 at 62 mmHg. FVC in the supine position was 0.77 L, significantly lower than the standing position at 1.43 L. Maximum inspiratory pressure was 4.90 kPa (normal range: 11.8 ± 3.63 kPa for adult males), 45.5% of the predicted value, and maximum expiratory pressure was 8.08 kPa (normal range: 13.2 ± 2.94 kPa for adult males), 58.2% of the predicted value. Diaphragmatic ultrasound showed right diaphragm mobility of 1.7 cm and left diaphragm mobility of 1.9 cm during maximum inspiration, and right diaphragm mobility of 0.5 cm and left diaphragm mobility of 0.3 cm during normal breathing (normal range: >2 cm), indicating bilateral reduced diaphragmatic activity. Reverse movement on both sides and thickened parasternal intercostal muscles were also observed. Abdominal ultrasound showed fatty liver. Echocardiography revealed no valvular regurgitation or pulmonary hypertension. Brain MRI, cervical spine MRI, and EMG of peripheral muscles showed no significant abnormalities. Muscle MRI of the thigh revealed fatty infiltration in T1-weighted imaging and short time of inversion recovery. Biceps brachii biopsy showed no abnormalities.
test_results: A heterozygous variant of TTN NM_001256850.1: c.90272C > T, NP_001243779.1: p. Pro30091Leu (also referred to as NM_001267550.2: c.95195C > T, NP_001254479.2: p. Pro31732Leu and NM_003319.4: c.68000C > T, NP_003310.4: p. Pro22667Leu) was identified in the proband. The genomic location of it is g.179410829A > G on chromosome 2 (GRCh37). Sanger sequencing of this variant also identified the proband's elder sister with similar symptoms and two asymptomatic sons as heterozygous carriers. WES indicated that he and his two sons as well as his sister carried heterozygous variation of TTN c.90272C > T, p. Pro30091Leu.
diagnosis: TTN-related hereditary myopathy with early respiratory failure
Orpha_name: Hereditary myopathy with early respiratory failure

case_report: A 30-year-old Asian male with no significant medical history reported experiencing a 1.5-year duration of progressive linear hair loss. The affected area measured 20 cm in length and 1.5 cm in width, extending along the right frontal, left parietal, and left occipital regions of the scalp. The condition was asymptomatic.
test_results: Histopathology from an incisional biopsy on the left parietal scalp revealed heavy lympho-histiocytic infiltrates over superficial and deep perivascular, peri-eccrine, and perifollicular areas, and lobular subcutaneous fat necrosis. Alcian blue stain revealed increased mucin deposition extending from the dermis to the subcutaneous tissue. The infiltrative cells in the dermis consisted mainly of CD4+T lymphocytes and CD123, the plasmacytoid dendritic cell marker, was also positive.

case_report: A 65-year-old man with congenital deafness began experiencing an unsteady gait at the age of 61. At 63, he developed bilateral upper limb clumsiness, dysmetria, and dysphagia. As his condition progressed, he became unable to walk without assistance and sought medical help. He reported a family history of gait issues in his mother and siblings. Neurological examination revealed saccadic pursuit, dysphagia, decreased muscle strength in all four limbs, areflexia, a positive Romberg test, and an ataxic gait. MRI scans of the brain and spine were normal. Nerve conduction studies indicated sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Whole exome sequencing was performed but did not yield any significant findings.
test_results: A heterozygous CAG repeat expansion (repeat number: 28 and 63) was noted in the ATX3 gene.

case_report: A 28-year-old woman underwent a laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG) in December 2014 and a laparoscopic revision to a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) in April 2015 due to passage problems from a sleeve stenosis. She was a smoker with no prior medical history. She was prescribed a multivitamin supplement and took no other medications. Post-RYGB, she recovered well but missed several follow-up appointments over 2.5 years without explanation. Three years post-RYGB, she experienced monthly colicky pain attacks in the right upper abdomen for five months, with a pain score of 9-10. Each episode lasted one to two hours, after which she was pain-free. The pain became progressive. Additionally, she had postprandial retrosternal pain with dyspepsia, including reflux, regurgitation of food, and nausea. An ultrasound of the abdomen requested by her general practitioner showed no abnormalities, including no gallstones. Physical examination revealed normal hemodynamic values (blood pressure 125/85 mmHg, heart rate 68 beats per minute, respiratory rate 12 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 99%, temperature 37.1ºC) and pressure pain in the right upper abdomen and epigastric region. Laboratory results were normal. A repeated abdominal ultrasound also showed no abnormalities. Helicobacter pylori serology was negative. An esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed abnormal mucosa of the distal esophagus, and biopsy pathology indicated Barrett’s metaplasia. Triple therapy with ranitidine, pantoprazole, and sucralfate was initiated, and the patient was enrolled in a clinical Barrett follow-up program. Initially, symptoms seemed to decrease, but one month later, she returned with progressive pain. Physical examination showed tachycardia (heart rate 104 beats per minute), a temperature of 38.2ºC, and diffuse pressure pain in the upper abdomen. Laboratory results remained normal. A CT of the abdomen showed no signs of internal herniation or other abnormalities. A diagnostic laparoscopy was performed due to severe pain, revealing no internal herniation, with the mesenteric and Peterson’s spaces closed. Other perioperative findings were normal, including the anatomy and position of the gastroenterostomy and enteroenterotomy, and no abnormalities were observed in the intestines. Subsequently, the pain attacks decreased to one to two times per hour and were posture-dependent. The pain localized more to a specific point in the right upper abdomen (Th8), and the patient reported an inability to wear tight clothing on the skin.
test_results: Physical examination showed a clear punctum maximum, and the pinch test and Carnett’s sign were positive.

case_report: A 15-year-old female presented to an outpatient clinic with a 3-day history of fever, cough, and lethargy. She had no prior medical conditions. On physical examination, she had a fever of 38.3°C, mild tachypnea, good oxygen saturation, and stable hemodynamics. Breath sounds were reduced in the left lung, with crepitation noted at the base. Laboratory tests revealed slightly elevated septic parameters, with a total white cell count of 17.6 × 10^3/μL and a platelet count of 487 × 10^3/μL, prompting the initiation of oral antibiotics. Due to persistent symptoms, she was brought to the casualty department several days later for further evaluation. Chest radiography revealed homogenous opacification of nearly the entire left hemithorax, obscuring the left heart border, aortic knuckle, and left hemidiaphragm, with a contralateral shift of the mediastinum. The right lung field was clear of any focal lesions.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) of the thorax revealed a large low-attenuation enhancing mass within the left thoracic cavity, measuring 11 × 13 × 16 cm. The mass was thought to originate from the left upper lobe, causing the collapse of the whole left lung. No intralesional hemorrhage or calcification was observed. Nonenhanced areas are seen within the mass, which likely represent necrosis. The mediastinum shifted to the right. The distal left main bronchus was narrowed, with tapering and occlusion of its segmental bronchi. The pulmonary trunk and left pulmonary artery were also narrowed but remained patent. There was no fat plane between the mass and pericardium, with evidence of pericardial and left pleural effusions. The chest wall was not affected. There was no evidence of mediastinal lymphadenopathy or liver lesions. The tissue biopsy measured 15 and 18 mm. Microscopic examination revealed tumor cells configured in hypocellular and hypercellular patterns with an area of necrosis. The hypercellular area displayed primitive cells with blastematous appearances. The shape ranged from spindled to ovoid, with focal pleomorphic to rhabdoid cells having intense eosinophilic cytoplasm. Subepithelial mesenchyme with the collection of stromal cells and overlying native ciliated columnar epithelium were observed. A focal immature chondroid element was identified. Immunohistochemistry of the stromal cells was strongly positive for vimentin and focal moderately positive for desmin. They were negative for EMA, pan-cytokeratin (AE1/AE3), S100, smooth muscle actin, and myogenin. CD99 shows focal nonspecific positivity, while TTF-1 highlights the presence of native respiratory epithelium and alveolar pneumocytes.

case_report: An 11-year-old girl was admitted with a 20-day history of a buccal abscess. She had a history of frequent infections since infancy, including pneumonia, bronchiolitis, and acute gastroenteritis. Additionally, she experienced recurrent fever and oral ulcers over the past two years, with the oral ulcers appearing every two months and resolving on their own. Two years prior, a biopsy of an oral ulcer at another hospital indicated chronic inflammation. Before her current admission, she presented with a buccal abscess and submandibular lymphadenopathy. Upon admission, a 0.3 cm oral ulcer was noted on her left inferior gingiva, along with a broad ulcerative lesion on her palate. Her complete blood count was within normal limits, and her T-cell subset was normal. Blood chemistry results were also within normal limits, except for a slightly elevated alkaline phosphatase level (125 U/L, normal range 42–98 U/L). T lymphocyte proliferative activity in response to mitogens (phytohemagglutinin and concanavalin A) was preserved. A nitrobluetetrazolium test to rule out chronic granulomatous disease was negative.
test_results: A biopsy from the buccal ulcer showed mucosal ulceration with marked inflammatory cell infiltration including eosinophils. The ulcerated mucosa was covered by fibrinopurulent exudate. The submucosa and adjacent skeletal muscle showed diffuse or patchy infiltration of mixed small, medium, and large lymphocytes. These lymphocytes were CD3+. CD30 was positive in the cytoplasmic membrane and perinuclear zone of large atypical lymphocytes. Anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) protein was negative.
Orpha_name: Systemic Epstein-Barr virus-positive T-cell lymphoproliferative disease of childhood

case_report: A 16-year-old female presented with thickened skin on the palms and soles, cracked lips, mild scaling on the buttocks, and fissures on the fingers and feet. Additionally, there were erosions on the perianal, vaginal, and nasal mucosa, along with widespread hair loss and sparse hair growth. Nail abnormalities and a hyperkeratotic plaque around the perianal area were also observed. The patient has congenital deafness, delayed speech, and developmental and learning challenges.
test_results: The skin biopsy demonstrated psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia with marked hyperkeratosis, and mild acantopapilomatosis, focal porokeratosis, hypergranulosis and superficial perivascular inflammatory infiltration. The immunostaining showed ki67 (mib-1) positive in 45% of the basal cells and CKM (AE1AE3) strongly positive in suprabasal layer.

case_report: A 21-year-old male patient presented with a slightly painful, slow-growing, and hard, fusiform swelling of the left middle finger for the last 3 months. There was no history of fever, and routine investigations revealed mild normocytic normochromic anemia and a slightly raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Radiography showed a lytic, radiolucent, lobulated lesion at the base of the middle phalanx of the left middle finger, with cortical expansion, a sclerotic rim, and septations. No calcification or periosteal reaction was observed. Tuberculin test, chest radiogram, sputum for acid-fast bacilli, and serum adenosine deaminase results were negative. Aspiration attempts of the lesion yielded inadequate material, leading to curettage. Gross pathological examination revealed fragments of a gray-white lobulated mass with a heterogeneous cut surface.
test_results: Histopathology revealed a tumor having a lobular pattern of growth of spindle shaped and stellate cells, with abundant myxoid and chondroid intercellular material. The lobules had a hypocellular center and a hypercellular periphery with scattered benign multinucleated giant cells and hemosiderin-laden macrophages. One portion of the tumor showed pleomorphic large bizarre cells with irregular-shaped nuclei and a smudgy chromatin pattern indicative of pseudomalignant features.

case_report: A 12-year-old Korean girl has experienced multiple asymptomatic hypopigmented papules for the past 9 years. These papules, mostly several millimeters in size, are located on her extremities and trunk. The lesions first appeared when she was 3 years old and have gradually increased in number over time. The papules are slightly indurated and exhibit an asymmetric distribution. There is no history of trauma or preceding inflammatory conditions in the affected areas. Additionally, there is no family history of similar skin conditions.
test_results: Histological examination showed hyperkeratotic epidermis and perivascular lymphoid infiltrate in the superficial dermis. Thickness of the layer of finely woven thin meshwork of collagen fibers usually seen in the papillary dermis was observed to increase in the upper dermis with hematoxylin-eosin staining. Elastic tissue staining showed primarily decreased and some fragmented elastic fibers in the thickened layer of collagen fibers in the upper dermis.

case_report: A 26-year-old male presented with the primary complaint of seeing floating spots in his right eye, which began the previous night. He had previously undergone laser-assisted subepithelial keratectomy for both eyes in September 2013 and had no other ophthalmological or general medical history. Upon initial examination, his corrected vision was 1.0 in both eyes. A fundus photograph revealed a whitish epiretinal scar located at the superonasal macula in the posterior pole of the right eye. Fluorescein angiography showed retinochoroiditis features, including a hypofluorescent lesion of the scar in the early phase and hypofluorescent lesions at the center of the scar with leakage at the margins in the later phase. Optical coherence tomography indicated an elevated retinal surface and posterior acoustic shadowing of the scar.
test_results: ELISA showed positive IgG reactions.

case_report: An 18-year-old male patient presented with a large left scrotal swelling that had been present since birth and progressively increased in size. The patient exhibited mental retardation and syndactyly involving the right middle and ring fingers, along with shortening of the right lower limb. Local examination of the left scrotum revealed a testicular mass measuring 8.0 × 5.0 cm, pyriform in shape, with a smooth outline. The left testis appeared normal. Scrotal ultrasound showed a well-defined hypoechoic, homogenous mass measuring 8.0 × 5.0 cm with significant vascularity at the upper part of the left testis. Abdominal ultrasonography indicated that the pancreas, spleen, kidneys, and other organs were normal, with no evidence of a communicating fibrous cord in the intraperitoneal or extraperitoneal regions. Intraoperative findings revealed a pyriform-shaped mass lesion measuring 7.0 × 3.0 cm attached to the upper pole of the left testis, which was found to be separate from the left testis.
test_results: Histopathologic examination of the mass revealed a fibrous capsule and normal splenic tissue.
diagnosis: Splenogonadal Fusion Syndrome with Limb Defects

case_report: A three-year-old Saudi girl presented on October 2, 2017, at the Emergency Room at Prince Mohammed Bin Abdulaziz Hospital, Ministry of National Guard Health Affairs, Medina, Saudi Arabia. She was brought in by her parents due to bilateral profuse non-stopping epistaxis lasting for a few hours. There was no bleeding from other orifices. The patient was conscious, alert, oriented, and calm, with normal vital signs: temperature 36.6°C, respiratory rate 24/minute, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, heart rate 110 beats/minute, and blood pressure 121/77 mmHg. She was not dysmorphic, cyanosed, or distressed. Active epistaxis was noted, along with multiple ecchymoses of varying colors and sizes on her upper and lower extremities and abdomen. There was no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Other systemic examinations were unremarkable. There was no history of trauma or drug ingestion. After vomiting a large amount of digested blood, the patient became paler and symptomatic with increased tachycardia. Her hemoglobin level dropped from 11.5 g/dl to 8 g/dl, while other complete blood count (CBC) indices remained normal. She received transfusions of packed red blood cells, fresh frozen plasma, and recombinant Factor VII to address symptomatic anemia and severe uncontrolled epistaxis. The Ear Nose and Throat team identified and cauterized multiple bleeding vessels, leading to almost complete cessation of bleeding six hours post-admission. The patient was born full-term via spontaneous vaginal delivery, with no neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission. She has no known chronic illnesses, is not on any medication, and had never received a blood transfusion before. There was a history of prolonged wound healing and profuse bleeding from minimal injuries at six months of age. Her parents are cousins, and she has two healthy siblings, with no family history of bleeding disorders. Initial bleeding-related work-up included CBC, which showed a normal platelet count, normal partial thromboplastin time (PTT), international normalized ratio (INR), normal Factor XIII, and a normal von Willebrand factor (VWF) panel. Flow cytometry results were normal. Gene sequencing for ITGA2B, ITGB3, and VWF showed no relevant variants. A platelet aggregation study (more than one reading) revealed a normal response to ristocetin and arachidonic acid but an abnormal response to collagen, adenosine diphosphate (ADP), and epinephrine. The peripheral blood smear was normal.
test_results: The results of a genetic study identified a homozygous RASGRP2 VUS c.956 C>T p. (pro 319leu).
Orpha_name: Pelizaeus-Merzbacher-like disease due to GJC2 mutation

case_report: A 36-year-old Chinese female visited the ophthalmology department of Xinjiang 474 Hospital in May 2020. She was born to parents who were fourth-degree relatives. Her family members, including parents, siblings, and two sons, underwent corneal topography, optometry, and general physical examinations, all of which showed normal results. The patient exhibited severe osteoporosis, approximately 20° scoliosis, joint hyperextensibility, anti-thyroglobulin antibodies, and elevated parathyroid hormone levels. The best corrected visual acuity was 14/20 in the right eye with a manifest refraction of 4.50/-3.75 × 5, and 12/20 in the left eye with a manifest refraction of -5.25/-3.50 × 5. Intraocular pressure was normal at 13 mmHg in both eyes. Slit lamp microscopy revealed horizontal nystagmus in both eyes, significant bluish discoloration of the sclera, and decreased central corneal transparency. High-definition optical coherence tomography (HD-OCT) indicated thinning of the entire cornea and a heterogeneous, mildly elevated stromal layer density. The posterior segment of the retina appeared normal. Pentacam anterior segment tomography showed increased corneal curvature in both eyes, with maximum keratometric power of 50.5 D in the right eye and 50.60 D in the left eye. The thinnest corneal points were 285 μm in the right eye with astigmatism (-4.4D at 174 degrees) and 280 μm in the left eye with astigmatism (-3.9 D at 11 degrees), with white to white values of 11.6 mm in the right eye and 11.7 mm in the left eye. Corneal densitometry revealed increased optical density in the 2-mm central area of the cornea, with values of 29.3 grayscale units (GSU) in the right eye and 30.6 GSU in the left eye. In vivo confocal microscopy (IVCM) showed disturbed corneal epithelial cell morphology in the central cornea zone, disordered nerve fibers under the basal cells with visible, highly reflective fibrotic structures, and a significant reduction in the number of stromal cells in the anterior cornea. The cell structure was difficult to distinguish, and highly reflective fibrotic structures were visible. The corneal stromal nerves were thicker than average, and the nuclei of the posterior stromal cells showed uneven size distribution without apparent activation. Axial length measurements were 21.25 mm in the right eye and 21.13 mm in the left eye.
test_results: A homozygous mutation in PRDM5; NM_018699.2:c.247C > T(p.Arg83Cys) was detected.

case_report: A 2-year-old male presented with a right-sided abdominal mass that had been noticeable for 1 month. Physical examination confirmed the presence of a palpable mass in the right abdomen. An ultrasonographic examination of the abdomen showed a large, well-defined, predominantly hyperechoic mass measuring 7 cm × 5.5 cm × 4 cm in the right paravertebral region, corresponding to the location of the normal kidney, with areas of hypoechogenicity. No normal kidney tissue was observed on the right side. There was no evidence of calcification, and no intravascular echogenic focus was detected on color Doppler sonography. The left kidney appeared normal in both position and echotexture. Due to financial constraints, a computed tomography scan was not performed. Pre-operative routine investigations, including serum urea, creatinine, and blood urea nitrogen, were within normal ranges. Serum alpha-fetoprotein levels were also normal. A right-sided nephrectomy was performed, and the specimen was sent for further examination.
test_results: On gross examination, the tumor measured 6.5 cm × 5 cm × 4 cm and was weighing 250 g. It was well-circumscribed and encapsulated. Cut sections presented homogenous gray-white tumor tissue, soft, and granular in the texture. Ureter and renal veins were not involved by the tumor. Microscopically multiple sections examined from different areas showed classic triphasic combination of blastemal, stromal, and epithelial cell types. The tightly packed blue cells are the blastemal elements, immature tubule in the picture is the epithelial element and spindle cells are stromal elements. The heterologous elements are predominant and composed of squamous epithelium with abundant keratin pearl formation and constitute about 75% of the area from where the sections were examined.

case_report: A 55-year-old African American female presented to the emergency department with headaches, vision loss, difficulty speaking, and unsteady movements. Her medical history included Down syndrome and a previous cerebrovascular accident with mild residual weakness in the lower extremities. She lived with her sister and managed her daily activities independently but required help with more complex tasks. Her family history was non-contributory, and she had no known allergies. She was taking aspirin and atorvastatin prior to admission. On initial examination, her blood pressure was 144/85, and other vital signs were normal. She was noted to be obese with facial features consistent with Down syndrome. Neurological examination showed left-sided facial droop, preference for looking to the right, vision loss, severe difficulty speaking, 3/5 strength in the left upper extremity, and 2/5 strength in the left lower extremity. Further neurological assessment was limited due to poor cooperation. Cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, and skin examinations were unremarkable. A CT scan of the brain showed hypodense areas in the right occipital, temporal, and parietal lobes.
test_results: Computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the head and the neck identified occlusions bilaterally at the supraclinoid internal carotid arteries and right posterior cerebral artery; there was collateral arterial flow within the right middle cerebral and anterior cerebral arteries.

case_report: A 37-year-old woman of northern European descent with a history of juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) presented to the emergency department with sudden onset of whole body pain, blurry vision, and weakness on the left side of her body. Five days earlier, she experienced a similar episode of whole body pain and chest pressure that woke her from sleep, followed by dizziness and blurry vision when getting out of bed. She had difficulty bringing a glass of water to her mouth and, despite mild improvement upon waking, continued to experience tongue weakness and speech difficulties. After a second episode, she sought medical attention. Upon arrival, she was alert and oriented but appeared anxious. She reported mental fogginess, short-term memory loss, and depression over the past year. She denied any previous motor or sensory symptoms and had no history of blurred vision. She also denied tobacco, alcohol, or drug use. Her vital signs were normal. Neurological examination revealed she was alert and oriented to person, place, time, and event. Cranial nerve assessment showed left nasolabial flattening. Motor examination revealed subtle weakness on the left side of her body, while sensation and cerebellar function were intact. No tremors or involuntary movements were observed. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory workup showed no leukocytosis. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis was normal, with negative results for gram stain, acid-fast bacilli stain, protein, glucose, bacterial culture, herpes simplex virus (HSV) 1 & 2, varicella zoster polymerase chain reaction (PCR), venereal disease research laboratory test (VDRL), and oligoclonal bands. Serum aquaporin-4 antibody titers and angiotensin-converting enzyme levels were also negative. A CT scan of the brain revealed a well-defined, hypo-dense round lesion (~1.3 cm) with a possible mild mass effect in the right corona radiata.
test_results: The brain MRI revealed the lesion had T2/flair hyperintense signal with a bullseye appearance.

case_report: Case 1 involves a 19-year-old Pakistani female born to consanguineous parents. She was delivered at term via normal vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 2.2 kg (<3rd centile). The patient exhibited her first symptom at 1.5 years old. By the age of 2 years, she developed rickets and experienced recurrent fractures. Physical examination at that time revealed a height of 100 cm (<5th percentile) and a weight of 23 kg (<5th percentile). The patient also developed renal tubular acidosis accompanied by aminoaciduria. Biochemical findings indicated dysglycemia, characterized by fasting hypoglycemia and postprandial hyperglycemia, along with low levels of C peptide. Her HbA1c level was elevated. At 17 years old, she was found to have diabetes mellitus, with negative results for all autoantibodies typically associated with type 1 diabetes and no features of insulin resistance. Treatment with insulin and a DPP4 inhibitor reduced her HbA1c level from 6.4% to 6.2%. Additionally, the patient had hepatomegaly and abnormal liver function tests. She was treated with multiple medications to address electrolyte imbalances, including sodium bicarbonate, potassium, phosphorus, and vitamin D.
test_results: The patient’s WGS revealed a novel homozygous mutation c.613-7T>G: IVS5-7T>G in intron 5 of the SLC2A2 gene (NM_000340.1), and both parents were carriers. The mutation was confirmed by Sanger sequencing of DNA. The patient’s cDNA Sanger sequencing revealed no extra nucleotides between exons 5 and 6, which means the mutation did not affect the coding region of GLUT2 protein.

case_report: A 7-year and 8-month-old girl presented with a history of recurrent cough and shortness of breath since infancy, along with a single convulsion episode. During hospitalization, she experienced four additional convulsions within two days, characterized by generalized tonic-clonic seizures lasting less than two minutes and occurring shortly after waking. There were no accompanying symptoms such as fever, vomiting, or diarrhea. Since 8 months of age, she had episodes of paroxysmal cough following colds, accompanied by cyanosis around the mouth and lips, and shortness of breath. Chest radiography showed increased pulmonary markings in both lungs. Cardiac ultrasonography revealed congenital heart disease, including patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), patent oval foramen, and pulmonary hypertension. She had been treated multiple times for severe pneumonia, congenital heart disease, heart insufficiency, and malnutrition, with symptomatic treatment providing relief. Born via cesarean section at 38 weeks, her family history was unremarkable. Upon admission, her vital signs were: temperature 37.0°C, pulse 112 bpm, respiration 29 breaths/min, blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, weight 18 kg, height 118 cm, and head circumference 50 cm. She was conscious but appeared malnourished with thin subcutaneous fat. No tonsillar swelling or cyanosis in the mouth and lips was observed. There was no edema. She exhibited slight delays in language, intelligence, and movement. Congenital mydriasis was noted, with pupils measuring 5 mm and unresponsive to light. Heart rate was 112 bpm with loud cardiac sounds and accentuated P2. A persistent machinery murmur (III/6) was heard at the left sternal border. Pulmonary respiration was coarse without rales. The abdomen was soft, with the liver palpable 1.0 cm below the ribs, having a sharp boundary and soft texture without tenderness. Neurological examination showed a soft neck, negative pathological signs, normal muscle strength and tone, and normal tendon reflexes. Appetite, sleep, urination, and defecation were normal. Blood analysis showed leukocytosis (8.58 × 10^9/L) with neutrophils predominating (68%). Hematocrit and platelet counts were normal. Procalcitonin was slightly elevated (1.42 ng/mL), and serum C-reactive protein was 33.84 mg/L (normal < 8 mg/L). Stool occult blood test was positive. Electrocardiography indicated sinus rhythm and right axis deviation. Chest X-ray revealed thickened lung textures, patchy blurred shadows, and an enlarged heart shadow with protrusion in the pulmonary artery segment, a plump right heart edge, and the left heart margin extending beyond the midline of the clavicle. Liver and renal function tests, cardiac enzymes, electrolytes, blood glucose, and organic acid levels were normal. The Wechsler Intelligence Scale score was 75. Video electroencephalogram showed background activity of 6–7 c/s with symmetric bilateral activity and no spike/sharp waves or paradoxical discharge upon flash stimulation. Cardiac ultrasonography confirmed congenital heart disease with PDA (0.68 cm diameter), left coronary arteriectasis, patent oval foramen (0.12 cm diameter), tricuspid and pulmonary regurgitation, and pulmonary hypertension. Cranial MRI and MRA indicated brain vessel stiffness and multiple aberrant signaling shadows in bilateral paraventricular regions.
test_results: A heterozygous mutation (c.536G>A) was identified in the ACTA2 gene, which resulted in generation of p.R179H. No mutations were identified in the ACTA2 gene in her parents.

case_report: A 14-year-old male presented with recurrent asthma attacks and laryngotracheitis with inspiratory stridor unresponsive to medical therapy. He has experienced asthma attacks since age 4 and laryngotracheitis for the past two years. Two months ago, chest imaging showed calcification in the tracheal cartilage and bronchi. His respiratory episodes increased in frequency after starting boarding school last year. He underwent adenoidectomy four years ago, during which intubation was difficult due to mild subglottic stenosis. The patient was born to consanguineous parents who are second-degree cousins and has three healthy siblings. He was born at term via spontaneous vaginal birth without complications. From age one, he had hoarseness, and at age 4, he began inhaler therapy. His family reported no benefit from beta-agonists like salbutamol. He received immunotherapy for four years without a reduction in attacks. He has a history of recurrent ear infections and hearing loss. Physical examination revealed mid-facial hypoplasia, a depressed nasal bridge, and palpable nodules in both ears. Respiratory examination showed bilateral diffuse wheezing, while other systems were normal. His weight was in the 50-75th percentile, and his height was in the 10-25th percentile.
test_results: Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed calcification in the tracheal cartilage and bronchi. CT revealed diffuse calcification in all laryngeal cartilages and epiglottis, thickening in the cricoid cartilage and narrowing of the airway at that level, and calcification and segmentary stenosis in the anterior and lateral walls of the trachea. There was also calcification in the main and bilateral segmentary bronchi, in bilateral external auditory meatus, auricular cartilages, and in bilateral Eustachian tubes. Biopsies were taken from the nodules in auricula, which revealed ossified cartilage tissue in fibrocollagenized connective tissue.

case_report: A 36-year-old female patient presented with multiple lesions that first appeared during childhood and have progressively increased in number and size over time. The patient reported that the lesions were painful with minimal trauma. Physical examination revealed blue-purple papules and nodules ranging from a few millimeters to nearly 2 cm in size, grouped in plaques averaging 10 cm on the epigastric and right inguinocrural regions. On the right hemithorax, the lesions exhibited a zosteriform pattern, while on the upper limbs, the lesions were sparse. The patient reported no similar cases in her family.
test_results: Histopathology revealed multiple dilated vessels in the papillary dermis, whose walls had more than one layer of small, round, uniform cells with round and central nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm, characterizing glomus cells.

case_report: An 88-year-old female was found lying down. Upon admission, she exhibited nausea, vomiting, altered mental status, and a slow heart rate. Her medical history includes essential hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, hypothyroidism, chronic renal failure (Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes G3a classification), ischemic stroke, and osteoporosis. Her medications included insulin (12 IU daily), levothyroxine (100 µg daily), losartan (50 mg twice daily), metoprolol (50 mg daily), amiodarone (200 mg daily), simvastatin (40 mg daily), metformin (500 mg twice daily), and omeprazole (20 mg daily). Initial vital signs showed a temperature of 35.6°C, blood pressure of 90/44 mmHg with a mean arterial pressure of 59 mmHg, heart rate of 45 beats per minute, oxygen saturation of 92% requiring supplementary nasal oxygen, and a regular respiratory rate. Physical examination revealed dehydrated skin, pupils equal in size and reactive to light, and confusion (Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14) without focal neurological deficits. Her extremities were cold, with livedo reticularis (Mottling score of 3), and no edema.
test_results: The initial electrocardiogram (EKG) demonstrated the presence of sinus bradycardia. Subsequently, a junctional pattern developed, accompanied by peaked T waves, mainly from V2 to V4, depression of the ST segment from V4 to V6, and diffuse nonspecific ST-segment abnormalities. QRS prolongation and ST shortening were not present. Blood tests revealed hyperlactatemia, metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia, renal dysfunction, and microcytic anemia. Myocardial injury was investigated with troponin levels which showed no elevation (14.4 pg/mL; 17.2 pg/mL). Point-of-care ultrasound revealed a bilateral A-line pattern with lung sliding, cardiac output was estimated at 1.6 L/minute, and the collapsibility index of the inferior vena cava was 24%. Urgent echocardiography was performed in the ICU and was compatible with normal biventricular systolic function with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 75% during dobutamine administration.

case_report: A 7-year-old girl with yellowish skin and eyes, the firstborn child of healthy parents (Korean father and Vietnamese mother) at 39 weeks of gestation, visited the Division of Endocrinology, Department of Pediatrics, Jeonbuk National University Hospital (Jeonju, South Korea), for evaluation of ongoing hemolytic anemia. Physical examination revealed chronic illness appearance, yellowish skin, yellowing of the sclera, enlarged liver, and enlarged spleen. The rest of the examination was normal. She was born at 38 weeks via vaginal delivery, with a birth weight of 2,300 g and an uneventful perinatal history. She was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit after birth due to lethargy and received a transfusion of packed red cells. Over time, she developed paleness and progressively bright yellow skin discoloration. There was no family history of hemolytic disease. On the date of birth, initial investigations showed a hemoglobin level of 5.3 g/dl, mean cell volume of 122.7 fl, total leukocyte count of 29,780/mm3, platelets of 159,000/mm3, and reticulocyte percentage of 60.18%. The direct Coombs test was positive. A peripheral blood smear showed a marked leucoerythroblastic reaction and atypical lymphoid cells (1%–2%). Total bilirubin level was 12.51 mg/dl (normal range, 0.2–1.2 mg/dl), with a direct bilirubin level of 0.94 mg/dl (normal range, 0–0.4 mg/dl). Aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase levels were 107 IU/l (normal range, 24–95 IU/l) and 22 IU/l (normal range, 6–40 IU/l), respectively.
test_results: Heterozygous missense mutation (NM_000518.5: c.79G>A, p.Glu27Lys; rs33950507) of the HBB was detected in both the proband and her mother. The proband and her mother were diagnosed with beta thalassemia trait.
Orpha_name: Hemolytic anemia due to red cell pyruvate kinase deficiency

case_report: In December 2000, an 8-year-old Caucasian girl experienced a sudden loss of vision in her right eye. Her visual acuity was measured at 20/200 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left. Fundus examination identified a pale, dot-like, subretinal lesion below the foveola with subretinal fluid and hemorrhage along the inferior arcade in the right eye. The left eye showed yellowish subretinal material. Fluorescein angiography revealed an area of hyperfluorescence with leakage at the center of the macula in the right eye, indicating a subretinal neovascular membrane. The left eye displayed hyperfluorescence without leakage, indicating staining of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) around and below the foveal center. Stratus optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed intra- and subretinal fluid in the macula of the right eye. Electrophysiological tests included a full-field electroretinogram with normal cone pathway responses but reduced rod responses. The electrooculogram was abnormal, with an Arden ratio of 1:1 in the right eye and 1:2 in the left. Family history and screening were unremarkable. In December 2000, a 20-G pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) was performed to remove the submacular membrane in the right eye. Three months post-surgery, her vision improved to 20/25 in the right eye. Postoperative fluorescein angiography showed staining fluorescence around the fovea without leakage. In July 2004, she returned with stable 20/25 vision in the right eye but a sudden decrease in vision in the left eye, mirroring the earlier condition of the right eye. Fluorescein angiography indicated a submacular neovascular membrane with hyperfluorescence and leakage at the foveal center, and Stratus OCT confirmed a type 2 membrane. Photodynamic therapy (PDT) with verteporfin was attempted but was unsuccessful. One month later, the subretinal membrane had expanded with additional subretinal hemorrhage. As vision continued to decline, a PPV with subretinal membrane removal was performed on the left eye. Three months post-surgery, her vision was 20/30 in the left eye with no signs of subretinal membrane. Ten years later, she reported central vision deterioration in both eyes over the previous year. Visual acuity was 20/200 in both eyes. Fundus color retinography and autofluorescence retinography showed hypoautofluorescence covering most of the posterior pole in both eyes. Spectral domain OCT revealed significant fluid accumulation with numerous cystic spaces and retinoschisis in both eyes. A multifocal electroretinogram showed decreased b waves in both eyes, more pronounced in the right eye. In early 2014, she underwent four bevacizumab injections in each eye and used dorzolamide eye drops for six months, both without success. After consultation, an experimental multimodal approach was chosen: another PPV with internal limiting membrane (ILM) removal and C3F8 gas injection in the left eye. Four weeks post-surgery, all retinal fluid had resolved, and her vision improved to 20/60. Four weeks later, intraretinal fluid reappeared at a lower level.
test_results: These tests confirmed a homozygous variation in the BEST1 gene (splice site c.768+1G>A).

case_report: A 5-year-old boy was referred to our congenital heart disease clinic for the evaluation of a heart murmur. He was born in Iran as the third child of an Afghan family with low socioeconomic status. His parents were relatives (cousins). According to their statement, his older brother had developmental delays and was born with craniosynostosis. The patient was born via normal vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 2800 g at 38 weeks of gestational age without significant complications during delivery. Regular vaccinations were given according to the national protocol. In the following months, his weight, head circumference, and height development were within an acceptable range (in the 50th percentile of the growth chart) for his age. Furthermore, he presented no neurodevelopmental delays warranting the attention of the parents or physicians. As an infant, he suffered from recurrent episodes of infectious otitis media with no hospitalization. He was limited in his normal activities, and his functional class was classified as Class II of the modified Ross classification for heart failure in children. Finally, at the age of 5 years, after an accidental auscultation of a systolic murmur, he was referred to our center for further investigation. At first glance, the boy's face looked normal, and his epicanthal folds were attributed to his race. However, closer inspection revealed facial abnormalities, including a broad nasal bridge, a sloping forehead, and maxillary hypoplasia. The boy's systemic blood pressure was 103/72 mmHg, and his peripheral oxygen saturation was estimated to be approximately 93.0% by pulse oximetry. Physical examination revealed hypoplasia and shortening of the distal phalanges (brachytelephalangism). On chest examination, bilateral wheezing was auscultated without significant rales or rhonchi, and a systolic ejection murmur was heard at the right upper sternal border, distributed to the periphery of the chest. His thyroid, liver, and kidney function tests and complete cell count revealed no significant impairment. Serum levels of calcium, phosphorus, vitamin-D, alkaline phosphatase, and parathyroid hormone were also normal. The boy's audiometry reported a lower limit of normal function, consistent with his history of recurrent otitis media.
test_results: An upright posterior-anterior chest radiograph revealed prominent tree-shaped tracheobronchial calcification that followed the course of the airway. A radiograph of the patient's fingers indicated hypoplasia in the distal phalanges. Twelve-lead electrocardiography showed right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH), which was subsequently confirmed by transthoracic echocardiography. A gradient of 62 mmHg above the level of the pulmonary valve represented peripheral pulmonary stenosis, and a moderate tricuspid regurgitation (TR) (gradient =130 mmHg) indicated pulmonary hypertension (gradient >68 mmHg) and concomitant segmental peripheral pulmonary stenosis. The inferior vena cava diameter was normal in echocardiography. MSCT angiography illustrated mild narrowing in the lobar branches of the right pulmonary artery and significant stenosis in the lobar and segmental branches of the left pulmonary artery. The diameters of the main and proximal right and left pulmonary arteries were estimated to be 14 mm, 9.3 mm, and 10 mm, respectively. The CT scan revealed RVH and diffuse calcification in the tracheobronchial tree.

case_report: The patient is a 15-year-old Caucasian female, born at 39 weeks of gestation following an uncomplicated pregnancy, and is the second child of healthy, unrelated parents. She has two unaffected brothers and one sister. The parents, brothers, and sister exhibit a normal phenotype. The family history is unremarkable. Between the ages of 5 and 7, she was identified with a specific delay in reading skills attributed to a phonological phonetic disorder. At 15 years old, she presented with amenorrhea and nonspecific abdominal pain. Standard blood biochemical tests were conducted, revealing analyte levels within the normal range. Physical examination did not reveal any notable signs. The patient has a weight of 42 kg and a height of 155 cm. No heart defects, cleft palate, or hearing loss were observed.
test_results: Ultrasound examination revealed a hypoplastic uterus (23 mm longitudinal diameter). Nuclear magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed the absence of the uterus and the upper part (2/3) of the vagina, with the presence of thin and nuanced branches of fibrosis. The rectum and bladder were normally represented. The ovaries were in place, of normal size, with small subcortical follicles. No signs of brain malformations were detected.

case_report: A one-and-a-half-year-old boy of Indian origin presented with a 1-year history of intermittent fever and progressive abdominal distension over 10 months. The fever ranged from mild to moderate. The child had been prescribed multiple antibiotics, including anti-tubercular therapy, over the past year. He received one aliquot of packed red blood cells at 6 months of age and multiple random donor platelets in the last 2 months. Family history was unremarkable. Physical examination revealed pallor and multiple petechial spots on both lower limbs. Abdominal examination showed the spleen palpable 7 cm below the left costal margin and the liver palpable 5 cm below the right costal margin. Laboratory results included hemoglobin of 3.4 mmol/L (5.5 g/dl), WBC count of 17×10^9/L, and platelet count of 3×10^9/L. Peripheral smear indicated spherocytes and numerous nucleated RBCs. Serum LDH level was 441 mg/dL, and the direct Coomb’s test was significantly positive (4+). Peripheral blood immunophenotyping showed 4.8% double negative αβ+ T cells out of total CD3+ cells. The autoimmune panel was positive for antinuclear antibody (>1:40) and high anti-dsDNA antibody (ELISA) (200 IU/ml). 2D echocardiography revealed mild pericardial effusion without valvular defects. The patient was started on steroids. After one week of steroid therapy, there was inadequate response, so IVIG (2 g/kg) was administered over 2 days. Gradual improvement in hemoglobin and platelet count was observed, and the patient became transfusion independent. During the fever workup, blood culture grew Escherichia coli, which was treated with sensitive antibiotics.
test_results: Clinical exome sequencing detected a pathogenic variant of KRAS (Gly13Cys) at exon 2.
diagnosis: Autoimmune Lymphoproliferative Syndrome  with Monogenic Lupus due to KRAS mutation

case_report: A 60-year-old Chinese male began experiencing gait difficulties and frequent falls at the age of 56. Physical examination revealed speech dysarthria, bilateral limb ataxia, dysdiadochokinesia, and postural instability. By age 59, the patient showed a preference for sweet foods. At age 60, findings included supranuclear gaze palsy, significant cognitive impairment, and apathy.
test_results: Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) 22/30, Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MOCA) 14/30. The patient scored 56 on the Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) Part III.
diagnosis: Progressive Supranuclear Palsy with predominant cerebellar ataxia

case_report: A 15-year-old Japanese boy was referred to our hospital due to rapidly worsening psychiatric and neurological symptoms. His growth and development were normal until age 11, when he began experiencing academic difficulties. At age 13, he visited a local hospital with a 6-month history of progressively worsening walking difficulties. Neurological examination showed a spastic gait and significant lower limb hyper-reflexia, but brain and spinal MRI scans were normal. His total plasma homocysteine level was 216 nmol/ml (normal range: 3.7-12.5 nmol/ml), serum folic acid was 1.7 ng/ml (normal range: 3.6-12.9 ng/ml), and serum cobalamine was 397 pg/ml (normal range: 233-914 pg/ml). Plasma concentrations of very-long-chain fatty acids were within normal limits. He was started on folic acid therapy (15 mg/day) based on a tentative diagnosis of subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord secondary to folic acid deficiency, but his gait disturbance continued to worsen. At age 15, he exhibited deficits in motivation and effort. One week later, he was admitted to a hospital with high fever, acute diarrhea, and vomiting due to viral gastroenteritis. After admission, he rapidly developed psychotic symptoms, including delusions and auditory hallucinations. His general condition improved with rehydration, and he was discharged 3 days later. However, his psychotic symptoms, including depression, delusions, hallucinations, and anorexia, worsened over the next 2 weeks. He experienced several episodes of generalized convulsions and was prescribed levetiracetam (1000 mg/day). He was repeatedly hospitalized due to dehydration from refusal to eat caused by his psychotic state or convulsions. He was treated with risperidone for a month but continued to suffer from delusions, hallucinations, and failure to eat. A brain MRI showed generalized atrophy and hyperintensity in the white matter around the posterior horns of the lateral ventricles on T2-weighted and FLAIR images. An electroencephalogram showed diffusely low-amplitude background activity without epileptic discharge. Nerve conduction study and biochemical examination, including lysosomal enzymatic activities, were normal. He became severely apathetic and bedridden within two months after the infectious gastroenteritis and was transferred to our hospital for further investigation. On admission, no abnormal facial appearance or skeletal anomalies were noted. Neurological examination revealed fluctuating levels of consciousness with confusion, delusion, and abnormal behavior. Cranial nerves were normal. Marked spasticity of the lower limbs was observed, with hyper-reflexia in both arms and legs, and sustained clonus at the ankles following sudden passive dorsiflexion of the foot. Pathological reflexes (Babinski and Chaddock signs) were negative. Serum folic acid and cobalamine levels were elevated (more than 20 ng/ml and 1120 pg/ml, respectively). Plasma amino acid analysis showed an elevated total homocysteine level (229.9 nmol/ml) and a decreased methionine level (10.9 nmol/ml; normal range: 19.2-32.7 nmol/ml). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis indicated normal values. Gas chromatographic-mass spectrometric urinary metabolome analysis revealed a markedly elevated urinary homocystine level of 19.7 mmol/mol total creatinine (normal: not detected) and undetectable urinary methionine levels (−3.0 SD). His urinary methylmalonic acid level was normal (−0.3 SD).
test_results: The results showed compound heterozygous mutations c.446_447 del GC ins TT (p.Gly149Val) and c.137G > A (p.Arg46Gln). In addition, heterozygous c. 665C > T (p.Ala222Val) polymorphism was noted.
Orpha_name: Homocystinuria due to methylene tetrahydrofolate reductase deficiency

case_report: An eleven-year-old male presented with a six-month history of headaches and one month of recurrent vomiting. He also reported numbness on the right side of his face. Upon examination, the patient was conscious and oriented, with sensory loss in the right V2 and V3 distribution of the trigeminal nerve. Fundus examination showed papilloedema. No motor deficits were observed. A noncontrast CT scan of the head revealed an isodense lesion in the right middle cranial fossa. MRI scan showed the lesion to be hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with homogeneous enhancement. The lesion was extra-axial, located in the right middle cranial fossa, and extended extracranially into the infratemporal fossa, causing a significant mass effect with midline shift. Routine hematological investigations and blood chemistry were normal. The patient underwent a right frontotemporal craniotomy with zygomatic osteotomy. Intraoperatively, the tumor was found extradurally in the right middle cranial fossa, extending through the dura into the intradural compartment in the temporal region and the posterior fossa into the cerebellopontine angle cistern. The tumor was destroying the temporal base and extending extracranially into the subtemporal region. It was highly vascular and firm, with a good plane of cleavage from the brain. The tumor was adherent to the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus but was separable. The portion of the tumor extending into the posterior fossa was excised by drilling the petrous apex. Complete excision of the intracranial part of the tumor was achieved. Due to significant bleeding during surgery, only partial decompression of the infratemporal extension of the tumor was performed. The dural defect at the middle fossa floor was repaired with temporalis fascia. The postoperative course was uneventful.
test_results: Microscopic examination showed small round cells arranged in linear fashion (Indian file pattern). At places there were spindling of cells whereas in other areas cells were arranged in microalveolar pattern. The cellular outlines were indistinct with scant amount of cytoplasm. Mitotic activity was brisk. The background stroma was hyalinising and myxoid, at places giving chondroid appearance. No rhabdomyoblasts or strap cells were seen. The tumour cells were immunopositive for desmin (diffuse), vimentin (diffuse), and smooth muscle antigen and focal for myogenin and were immunonegative for s-100, MIC2(CD 99). MIB 1 LI was 25% in the highest proliferating areas.

case_report: An 11-year-old Chinese boy was admitted to PUMCH with uncontrolled hypertension for one year. His parents noticed abnormalities in his lower extremities, described as 'X-shaped legs,' when he was three years old. He was also found to have right renal dysplasia. Laboratory tests showed low serum phosphorus levels and elevated ALP levels. He began treatment with oral phosphate solution, calcitriol, and orthopedic orthosis to address skeletal defects, but the treatment was ineffective. At the age of 10, he exhibited a need to increase the volume while watching TV, and a hearing test indicated bilateral hearing loss, more pronounced on the left side. In July 2021, he developed spinal kyphosis and a dragging, swinging gait, and underwent epiphyseal fixation for both knees. Before the surgery, his brachial blood pressure ranged from 100–110/70–80 mmHg, but it rose to 190–200/100–110 mmHg shortly after the procedure. He did not report palpitations, dizziness, or other discomforts. Blood pressure was managed with sodium nitroprusside, esmolol, and captopril, maintaining levels at 130–140/90–100 mmHg. A computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the renal artery showed a narrow right renal artery (approximately 1 mm in diameter) and right renal atrophy (right kidney size: 4.4 × 1.5 cm; left kidney size: 10.2 × 4.4 cm, as determined by renal ultrasound). The left renal artery exhibited severe stenosis in the initial and proximal sections. Renal function imaging indicated a total glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 79.0 ml/min, with the left kidney contributing 76.3 ml/min and the right kidney 2.7 ml/min. Subsequent systemic angiography revealed varying degrees of stenosis in the right internal carotid artery (C4–7 and cervical segment) and the lower segment of the abdominal aorta.
test_results: The results revealed an ENPP1 mutation (c.313 + 1G > A, c.783C > G), but no mutation was detected in the ABCC6 locus.

case_report: A 7-year-old boy presented with bilateral central opacification, photophobia, and significantly reduced vision since birth. His medical history includes childhood mental retardation and previous surgical interventions on the right eye in 2014, specifically phacoemulsification, intraocular lens (IOL) implantation, and anterior vitrectomy. Upon examination, visual acuity was counting fingers (CF) in the right eye and light perception (LP) in the left eye. Intraocular pressure measured 21 mmHg in the right eye and 23 mmHg in the left eye. The patient was uncooperative during further ophthalmic examinations. General physical examination revealed no additional findings. The boy was the first child, delivered preterm at 35 weeks with a birth weight of 2.51 kg. The Apgar score was 9, and he did not require an oxygen chamber. The mother reported no infections or medication use during pregnancy, and there was no known family history of any related conditions.
test_results: Slit lamp examination revealed bilateral nystagmus with no conjunctival congestion, diffuse corneal opacity of the right eye and central corneal opacity of the left eye, few strands of peripheral iris and irregular pupils in both eyes, normal IOL position in the right eye and cloudy lens with central adhesion to the posterior corneal surface in the left eye. B-scan ultrasound failed to show other abnormalities in either of the eyes. Hematoxylin-eosin (HE) staining revealed fibrous tissue with proliferated collagenous fiber and fibroblasts, scattered epithelial-like cells which were spindle or cuboidal, broken and degenerated lens cortex in the central focal region, absent Descemet membrane and lens capsule. Periodic Acid-Schiff staining confirmed the absence of Descemet membrane and lens capsule. Immunohistochemical staining revealed cytokeratins (CK), S-100, vimentin (VIM) and alpha-crystallin positive cells.

case_report: The patient is a 61-year-old male with a history of hypothyroidism and cervical spondylopathy. Two years ago, he began experiencing tremors in his right hand while at rest, which worsened with nervousness and was accompanied by periods of unresponsiveness. One year ago, he started having difficulties with speech and swallowing, and occasionally choked on water. Physical examination showed involuntary tremors in the right upper limb and difficulty with rapid alternating hand movements. MRI indicated mild atrophy of the cerebellum and pons. The Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score was 20/30. The Hamilton Anxiety Scale (HAMA) score was 16, indicating anxiety. The Hamilton Depression Scale (HAMD) score was 21, indicating depression. The Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia (SARA) score was 18/40. The Inventory of Non-Ataxia Signs (INAs) score was 7, with positive findings for hyperreflexia, spasticity, rigidity, chorea/dyskinesia, dystonia, resting tremor, and cognitive dysfunction.
test_results: Genetic testing of the proband showed a missense mutation in the CCDC88C gene located at 14q32.11. This mutation is c.1886G > A, so the encoded amino acid changes from arginine to glutamine.

case_report: A 3-day-old girl was born with underdevelopment of the left lower limb and skin irregularities in the lumbosacral area. She is the second child of parents who are not related by blood, with no family history of limb deformities or neurological issues. The pregnancy was spontaneous, and prenatal checkups at another hospital showed no abnormalities. The mother had no history of fertility treatments, alcohol use, or smoking. Due to a previous cesarean section, the baby was delivered via scheduled cesarean at 38 weeks and 1 day. At birth, her respiratory status was stable, and she did not need resuscitation. Apgar scores were 8 at 1 minute and 9 at 5 minutes. Her birth weight was 2920 g (+0.29 SD), height was 46 cm (−1.08 SD), and head circumference was 35.7 cm (+2.02 SD). Post-natal examination showed skin puckering in the lumbosacral region, underdevelopment, and paralysis from the left buttock to the lower extremities. On the third day of life, she was transferred to our hospital for further evaluation. Clinical examination confirmed underdevelopment (shortening and narrowing) of the left lower limb, with no spontaneous movements or tendon reflexes. Additional findings included lumbar skin dimples, curvature of the gluteal cleft, and scoliosis. Neurological examination of the right lower limb and upper limbs was normal, and there were no bladder or bowel issues. Ultrasonography showed no abnormalities in the intracranial space, such as hydrocephalus or intraventricular hemorrhage, and no congenital heart disease. Radiographs indicated fusion of the 9th and 10th ribs, spinal dysplasia from the 10th thoracic vertebra to the sacral vertebra, scoliosis, and underdevelopment of the left lower limb. Computed tomography revealed dysplasia of the left side of the spine below the 10th thoracic vertebra.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a separated spinal cord within a single dural tube below the 10th thoracic vertebra, syringomyelia of the right spinal cord, left lateral deviation of the spinal cord below the second lumbar vertebra, spinal cord tethered to the left dorsally below the third lumbar vertebra, and a subcutaneous mass contiguous to the dural tube below the fourth lumbar vertebra.

case_report: A 6-year-old girl was brought to the Emergency Room of Imam Hossein Hospital with severe respiratory distress and in a deep coma. She had experienced increased urination and thirst for two weeks prior to admission. Her weight was 20 kg and height was 110 cm, both at the 50th percentile. On examination, her Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score was 5, body temperature was 36.5°C, blood pressure was 85/45 mmHg, heart rate was 140 beats per minute, and respiratory rate was 45 breaths per minute. Her pupils were midsize and reactive to light. Blood glucose levels were extremely high, and venous blood gas analysis showed a pH of 6.72, PCO2 of 11 mmHg, and HCO3 of 1 mmol/L. Initial treatment was administered based on these laboratory findings. Within 24 hours, her GCS score improved to 9, and blood gas indices were pH 7.33, HCO3 10 mmol/L, base excess -14, and PCO2 19 mmHg. Approximately 48 hours after admission, following partial recovery from the coma, she experienced a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. She was treated with phenobarbital and phonation, and mechanical ventilation was initiated due to a GCS score of 5. The ventilator settings were: synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation, tidal volume 180 mL, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, positive-end expiratory pressure (PEEP) 4 cm H2O, and FIO2 60%. After 3 days, her consciousness improved, and the ventilator settings were adjusted to continuous positive airway pressure with pressure support of 12 cm H2O, PEEP of 5 cm H2O, and FIO2 of 50%. She was extubated on the fourth day.
test_results: Schistocytes were observed in peripheral blood smear. Fibrinogen was normal, but D-dimer test was positive.

case_report: A 53-year-old Caucasian man presented with a small, erythematous papular lesion that was superficially eroded, located on the hairy region of the chest. The patient was generally in good health, with mild hypertension managed by an ACE-inhibitor medication. No additional skin lesions were noted, and there was no reported history of Darier’s disease. Following a one-week course of topical corticosteroid-antibiotic therapy, the lesion evolved into a skin-colored, umbilicated papule featuring a central keratotic plug. Dermoscopy using Molemax II (Derma Medical Systems, Vienna, Austria) showed an eight-shaped whitish collarette encircled by light brown pigmentation. Additionally, a central white structureless area with an adjacent rosette was visible. Small rust-colored blood crusts were present in the center of the lesion, with no significant vascular pattern observed.
test_results: Histology featured a cup-shaped epidermal invagination filled with a hyperkeratotic and parakeratotic plug, containing numerous grains and corps ronds. The base of invagination consisted of hyperplastic epithelium with digitate projections (villi).

case_report: An 11-year-old boy, born to first-degree consanguineous parents, was evaluated at King Abdulaziz University Hospital (KAUH) for developmental delay, cerebral palsy, and intellectual disability. Clinical assessment and history-taking determined his developmental age to be 2 months. He was bedridden with minimal distal movements and unable to attend kindergarten or school. At 15 months, he was assessed by the pediatric metabolic team for potential metabolic conditions. He was born full-term via spontaneous vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 2.7 kg and had an uneventful neonatal period. Early developmental delay and delayed milestones were noted. Parents reported spastic and dystonic movements, initially treated with anti-epileptic medication. At 11 years, he was admitted to the emergency department with febrile seizure due to severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) bronchopneumonia. Examination revealed hypotonia, anorexia, wheezing, stridor from tracheal stenosis and laryngomalacia, and difficulty clearing sputum. The patient had underdeveloped lungs and frequent vomiting. During hospitalization, he received tegretol, levetiracetam, clonazepam, and omeprazole at 1 mg/kg/day twice daily. Additionally, he was given budesonide, salbutamol via nebulizer, and cough syrup three times daily. Due to poor oral intake, a multi-fiber drink called 'NutriniDrink' was recommended regularly.
test_results: Whole Exome Sequencing (WES) confirmed a rare pathogenic homozygous deletion variant in the SERAC1 gene. WES confirmed a frameshift variation present in exon six, which was present in the middle of the 'Armadillo-like helical (IPR011989)' domain. An initial biochemical analysis using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) revealed 3-Methylglucatonic aciduria (3-MGA-uria), with a concentration of 1400 mmol/mol creatinine along with mild elevation in lactic acid. A brain computerized tomography (CT) scan revealed significant brain atrophy and abnormal signal intensity bilaterally in the lentiform nuclei. There was no evidence of abnormal parenchymal or meningeal enhancement, or any space-occupying lesions. The patient had left-sided scoliosis and diffusely reduced bone density.

case_report: A 10-month-old girl was referred for evaluation of neurodevelopmental delay. She was the first child of consanguineous parents (second cousins), born full term by cesarean section without any birth complications. Her birth weight was 2700 grams and her head circumference was 35 cm. During the physical and neurological examination, motor development assessment revealed the ability to roll over, but head control was incomplete. Head nodding was observed. She exhibited hypotonicity and did not bear weight when held in a vertical position. Pendular bilateral nystagmus was noted since the neonatal period. There was no history of seizures.
test_results: MRI showed abnormal signal intensity in the white matter (hyperintensity in T2, FLAIR and low signal intensity in T1 weighted images). It showed an arrest of myelination and this image is compatible with a younger chronological age. Abnormal findings included diffuse hypersignal white matter in the cerebral and cerebellar white matter, genu of the corpus callosum, basal ganglia especially globus pallidus and ventrolateral thalamic nuclei. VEP showed increased latency (P100=138).

case_report: A seven-month-old female was referred by her pediatrician due to delayed motor milestones and neck stiffness. She was born through a normal delivery and exhibited no dysmorphic features. Physical examination showed involvement of the trunk, with the cervical region being the most affected. Both shoulders and both big toes also displayed deformities.
test_results: The CT scan showed extensive bony bridges extending from the neck to the posterior chest wall and scapulae.

case_report: This 80-year-old Swedish woman, born to non-consanguineous parents, experienced early-onset unsteadiness and gait difficulties during childhood, leading to a gradual loss of mobility. She required a cane by age 50, progressed to using a walker, and became wheelchair-bound by age 60. She developed scoliosis, restrictive pulmonary dysfunction, macular degeneration, and sensorineural hearing loss, necessitating hearing aids.
