Her symptoms included numbness, paresthesia with pain and discomfort in both legs, and tongue burning, which was alleviated with gabapentin. Despite these challenges, she worked part-time in an office. The patient also reported slurred speech and mild difficulty swallowing. On examination, she exhibited leg muscle wasting, foot drop, upper limb and facial muscle twitching, gaze-evoked and hypermetric saccades, mild coordination issues in the limbs, and slurred speech. Previously, side-changing nystagmus was documented in her medical records. There was no evidence of spasticity or other pyramidal signs; the limbs were flaccid, especially the legs. The Montreal Cognitive Assessment score was 26/30. Brain MRI showed atrophy in the frontal and parietal brain regions and in the cerebellar hemispheres. Electroneurography and quantitative sensory testing demonstrated severe axonal and demyelinating sensorimotor polyneuropathy involving thin sensory fibers. Electromyography showed a reduction of motor units and myokymia with spontaneous regular rhythmic discharges of motor units in triplets or quadruples in facial muscles. Myokymia activity was also recorded in the facial muscles. Vestibular assessment demonstrated very poor vestibular function compatible with bilateral vestibular areflexia: absence of caloric nystagmus or elicitation of dizziness/vertigo upon bithermal caloric irrigation. Additionally, the vHIT revealed very poor gain for the stimulation of the posterior and lateral canals and a depressed but still consistent response with stimulation of the anterior semicircular canals on both sides. The VOR gain measured with vHIT had an average of 0.29. The cVEMP did not demonstrate reproducible responses in two different trials on each side.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing detected the pathogenic homozygous mutation c.2860C > T (pArg954*, R954X) in SH3TC2.

case_report: A 32-year-old male presented with a persistent leg ulcer. He had a history of leg ulcers for 15 years, associated with superficial venous insufficiency, and had undergone two phlebectomies. His family history included his mother losing all her teeth by age 30 and a heterozygous alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency in his paternal uncle and grandmother, with no known venous insufficiency. The patient weighed 79 kg and was 1.73 m tall (BMI = 26 kg·m−2). Physical examination revealed a 6 by 9 cm ulcer on the anterior aspect of the left leg and bilateral brownish atrophic plaques on the pretibial areas resembling necrobiosis lipoidica. Distal pulses were present. The skin was thin with a visible venous pattern on the trunk. Four atrophic scars were observed on his right knee and both thighs. There was no skin hyperextensibility or joint hypermobility. The patient had periodontitis with apical root resorption and gingival recession. Laboratory tests showed normal values for total blood count, coagulation tests, renal and liver function tests, serum protein electrophoresis, and hemoglobin electrophoresis. Tests for antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, and cryoglobulinemia were negative. Karyotype and urinary amino acids chromatography were normal. Alpha-1-antitrypsin level was normal, and the patient had a homozygous wild-type genotype for the alpha-1-antitrypsin gene. Aortic and lower limb doppler ultrasound ruled out arterial disease and showed varicose veins on the internal aspect of the left leg emerging from incontinent neosaphenous and perforating veins. Large arteries appeared normal on CT-scan. Dental X-ray indicated generalized alveolar bone resorption.
test_results: Transmission electron microscopy analysis on skin biopsy revealed irregular interfibrillar spaces, collagen fibers with variable diameter, and collagen cauliflowers.

case_report: A 32-year-old G4P2212 mother was referred for a fetal echocardiogram after a routine ultrasound identified multiple congenital anomalies, including cardiac defects. The fetal ultrasound showed an abnormal nuchal cord, left renal agenesis, rocker bottom feet, and a possible omphalocele. Fetal echocardiography revealed a large atrial communication with right to left shunting, a dilated right atrium, tricuspid atresia with a hypoplastic right ventricle, and pulmonary atresia with a hypoplastic pulmonary trunk. The branch pulmonary arteries appeared confluent, and there was a moderate-sized patent ductus arteriosus with left to right flow and subsequent flow reversal in the ductus venosus. Free fetal DNA testing for trisomy 13, 18, and 21 was negative, and amniocentesis showed a normal 46XY karyotype and normal microarray. Maternal history was unremarkable with all negative serologies during pregnancy. Family history included a first cousin with tricuspid atresia who had undergone Fontan palliation. The male infant was born at 36 6/7 weeks gestational age at another institution with a birth weight of 2,150 grams. Apgar scores were 7 and 8 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. Umbilical lines were placed, and E type Prostaglandin was started before transport to our institution. The infant required intubation due to respiratory distress before transport. Upon arrival, an echocardiogram was performed, confirming the cardiac anatomy noted on the fetal echocardiogram, including the absence of the right atrioventricular connection and a thread-like pulmonary trunk. Left ventricular function was normal, and the coronary arteries had normal origin and distal course. Renal ultrasound confirmed left renal agenesis with an adequately functioning right kidney. Physical examination revealed microcephaly, low set ears with abnormal creases and posterior rotation, hypertrichosis, shawl scrotum, and micrognathia. Bilateral dimpling around the umbilicus was noted, possibly representing atypical accessory nipples. The hands showed brachydactyly, clinodactyly, broad thumbs, and hypoplastic nails bilaterally. The feet exhibited webbing of the second and third toes bilaterally, broad fifth toes, and deep set hypoplastic nails. Chest radiograph demonstrated vertebral anomalies and segmentation defects.
test_results: Sequencing of the CREBBP gene revealed a pathogenic sequence change of c.4444T > G which results in the amino acid change p. Tyr1482Asp.

case_report: A 5-year-old girl, born to second-degree consanguineous parents, exhibited multiple lentigines starting at the age of 2 years on her face, trunk, and thighs. The mother did not have obstetric follow-up during pregnancy, and the child was delivered full-term via cesarean section with normal birth weight and activity. Previous pregnancies of the mother resulted in healthy children, and there was no family history of lentigines, congenital heart diseases, learning difficulties, speech delays, or syndromic disorders. Physical examination showed the child's height at 101 cm (3rd centile) and weight at 13.9 kg (below the 3rd centile), with an occipitofrontal circumference of 52 cm. Facial features included a triangular face, slightly protruded mandible, broad nasal bridge, ocular hypertelorism, palpebral ptosis, low set ears, low posterior hairline, pectus carinatum, and scapula alata, with no other skeletal anomalies. A pan-systolic murmur was detected at birth, and an echocardiogram three days later revealed multiple ventricular septal defects (VSDs). The patient has been monitored with echocardiograms since then. At 4 months, the mother noticed the baby was quiet and unresponsive to sound stimuli. An audiogram at 7 months indicated sensorineural hearing loss, leading to a cochlear implant at 2 years. The child also experienced delayed speech and motor development, crawling at 13 months and walking at 24 months. Clinical examination at our hospital revealed multiple oval light brown macules, 2–4 mm in size, on both sun-exposed and sun-protected areas including the trunk and extremities. There was a darker lentigo, 5 mm in size, on the right knee, and a café-au-lait spot, 1 cm in size, on the left thigh. Oral and genital mucosa were unaffected.
test_results: Genetic testing showed a heterozygous mutation in PTPN11, c.836A > G, a missense variant resulting in the substitution of the tyrosine codon at amino acid position 279 with a cysteine codon (p.Tyr279Cys).

case_report: Patient 1 is a seven-year-old male, born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy from non-consanguineous parents. At birth, his weight and length were within normal ranges. He presented with bilateral clubfoot and hand contractures, including camptodactyly and ulnar deviation. At six years old, his height was 130.5 cm, arm span 129 cm, and upper to lower segment ratio was 0.89. Physical examination revealed muscular hypotrophy, dolicocephaly, blue sclerae, hypoplastic alae nasi, microretrognathia, high-arched palate, bifid uvula, mild thoracic scoliosis, pectus excavatum, pes planus, and joint hypermobility with a Beighton score of 8/9. His skin was noted to be velvety and translucent. Additionally, the patient had a history of allergic asthma and atopic dermatitis.
test_results: Echocardiogram showed bicuspid aortic valve, patent foramen ovale, mild interventricular septal hypertrophy without outflow obstruction, mild mitral valve prolapse, aortic root diameter 23 mm and ascending aorta diameter 21 mm. Magnetic Resonance Angiography (MRA) displayed tortuosity and elongation of the basilar and internal carotid arteries with kinking and coiling of these last.

case_report: Patient 31. A 16-year-old male with significant hearing loss in both ears. He utilized behind-the-ear hearing aids. Additionally, he experienced cholestatic liver disease from a young age, along with symptoms of hyperactivity and difficulty concentrating. The family history did not reveal any notable conditions. His parents, of European descent, were not related.
test_results: WES revealed a homozygous pathogenic mutation in the MARVELD2 gene (c.1331 + 2T > C, p.(?)).
diagnosis: Autosomal Recessive Nonsyndromic Hearing Loss Type 49
Orpha_name: Rare autosomal recessive non-syndromic sensorineural deafness type DFNB

case_report: A 70-year-old Japanese man with bladder cancer (cT1N0M0) visited the radiation oncology department in March 2014. He had been managing a condition with prednisolone (10 mg/day) since 2010. A chest CT scan showed ground-glass opacity in the subpleural region. Spirometry results indicated a restrictive pattern with a vital capacity of 55% and a forced expiratory volume of 1.0 at 76%. Despite being deemed fit for surgery under general anesthesia, he opted for radiotherapy instead. His medical history included spinal canal stenosis and a cataract in the left eye, but no conditions suggesting a high risk for severe radiation toxicity, such as diabetes mellitus. He exhibited no physical symptoms at the time. Radiotherapy was started, targeting the bladder and pelvic lymph node regions with a daily dose of 2 Gy. Early in the treatment, he experienced urinary tract pain and erythema in the radiation field, which intensified as the total dose increased. Treatments with alpha-blockers, loxoprofen, intravesical lidocaine, and betamethasone valerate ointment were ineffective. By the third week, he had Grade 3 urinary tract pain, Grade 3 radiation dermatitis, and frequent urination every 5 to 10 minutes. Consequently, radiotherapy was halted at 34 Gy, below the planned 60 Gy. In June 2014, he was hospitalized due to worsening proximal muscle weakness over the previous 2 weeks.
test_results: Elevated serum creatine kinase (CK, 2657 IU/L) and C-reactive protein (3.66 mg/dL) levels, myogenic changes in the left deltoid and biceps brachii on electromyography, a high signal in the proximal muscles on magnetic resonance imaging (short-TI inversion recovery), and the presence of autoantibodies against aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase (anti-ARS antibodies).

case_report: A 20-day-old female neonate was referred due to corneal opacity. The patient was born at term after an uneventful pregnancy. The right eye (OD) appeared normal, while the left eye (OS) exhibited a central corneal opacity. Intraocular pressure in both eyes was within normal limits. The anterior chamber structures of the left eye (OS) were partially visible through the clear area. Fundus examination revealed a normal appearance in both eyes, except for the superior periphery of the left eye (OS), which was difficult to observe due to the corneal opacity.
test_results: The iris stroma was adhered toward the back of the opacified area of the cornea.

case_report: A 16-year-old female patient exhibited a 10.5 × 8.0 cm grayish-depressed plaque with hypochromic areas on the lower half of her left thigh lateral. Telangiectatic vessels were observed around the periphery of the lesion, with visible veins nearby. The plaque has been present since birth, initially appearing violet and gradually becoming whitened and depressed over time. There is no difference in the length of the lower limbs.
test_results: Angioresonance showed a vascular malformation on the skin and subcutaneous tissue supplied by non-dilated intermuscular branches tributary from the popliteal artery. Precocious venous filling was found both in the region and malformation, suggesting precocious venous shunt. Dilated drainage veins have not been documented, except for a superficial drainage vein that courses along the subcutaneous cellular tissue of the anterior thigh. In addition, a thinning of the subcutaneous tissue thickness in the vascular alteration topography was also noticed, but without intramuscular or bone extension.

case_report: The Ethics Committee of Umbria Region (CEVAS) approved the study, and written informed consent was obtained from the parents of the enrolled child. The patient is a 6-year-old Moroccan boy who was born full-term after an uncomplicated pregnancy with a birth weight of 3,020 kg (−0.86 SDS) and a length of 50 cm (−0.1 SDS). He was the only child of non-consanguineous parents. His mother’s height was 148.9 cm (−2.82 SDS), and his father’s height was 172.5 cm (−0.39 SDS) with a target height of 167.2 cm (−1.13 SDS). The mother had a disharmonic short stature (sitting height/height ratio: 0.563 and arm span/height ratio: 0.953) and a forearm deformity. When the patient was first referred to the Pediatric Endocrinology Unit at the age of 2.9 years, he exhibited normal psychomotor development, his height was 86.5 cm (−1.90 SDS), his weight was 14 kg (50th percentile), and his body mass index (BMI) was 18.7 (1.38 SDS). The auxological data are expressed in SDS according to the population standard for age and gender. He was prepubertal with testes <2 mL in volume. The pubertal stage was evaluated according to the Tanner–Marshall method. The physical examination was normal with no bone deformities or dysmorphism. The bone age of hand and wrist at a chronological age of 3 years conformed to the Greulich–Pyle atlas standard for 2.4 years, and an X-ray of the wrist and forearm ruled out severe radiological deformity except for a mild bowing of the radius. The child was re-evaluated after 6 and 12 months. At 3.9 years, his height was 91.3 cm (−2.20 SDS) with a growth velocity of 5.30 cm/year (10th percentile; −1.61 SDS). The Rappold’s score was 6 with a pathological sitting height/height ratio of 0.58 (normal value, <0.55) and a BMI above the 50th percentile. His arm span/height ratio was normal (0.99 with a normal value >0.965), and other parameters were negative. Laboratory investigations revealed a normal hemoglobin value, and normal kidney and hepatic functions and excluded celiac disease and thyroid dysfunction. His endocrine evaluation revealed a peak growth hormone value of 4.5 ng/mL using arginine tests and 8.58 ng/mL using a clonidine test (normal value, >8) with a normal level of insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1; 88 ng/mL, 50th–75th percentile), which ruled out a growth hormone deficit. The child was examined again at 5.9 years old. His height was 1.99 SDS below the mean for age and sex (104.9 cm). The arm span was 101.5 cm with a non-pathological arm span/height ratio of 0.97. The sitting height was 59.9 cm with a distinctly supranormal sitting height/height ratio of 0.57.
test_results: Genomic DNA was extracted from the peripheral blood of the proband and his parents following standard procedures. No deletions were found through the MLPA analysis. The SHOX gene sequencing revealed the heterozygous missense variant c.1044 (c.1044 G>T) in exon 3. This transversion was predicted to change the inside of the homeodomain sequence from an Arginine to a Methionine in codon 118 (p.Arg118Met). This variant was found in neither the ExAC nor 1000G databases. The same variant was found in his mother.

case_report: A 10-month-old male infant, the second child of third-degree consanguineous parents, was delivered via cesarean section. The infant cried immediately after birth and exhibited multiple physical abnormalities that were advised to be corrected at an older age. At 10 months, the child had not achieved head control, had not turned over, but had begun babbling. Over the past month, relatives observed the child holding his head and intermittently crying, along with episodes of coughing and vomiting, prompting a visit to our institution. Physical examination showed a head circumference of 47 cm with frontal bossing. The child appeared obese and cheerful. Ocular hypertelorism was noted with an interpupillary distance of approximately 44 mm. There was an incomplete ridge in the upper lip, extending through the hard palate, with the lips still united. Additional findings included a flat nasal bridge, a very short philtrum, retrognathia, a small chin with severe tongue tie, bilateral equinovarus of the feet, postaxial polydactyly Type A with six fingers on both hands, and an additional small rudimentary finger attached to both little fingers and toes. Syndactyly was observed in the first toes and fingers.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging T2-weighted images showed a slightly hyperintense mass lesion extending from hypothalamus to suprasellar region measuring 1.8 cm × 2 cm. It was isointense in T1 and slightly hyper in flair images.

case_report: A 19-year-old female patient was admitted to Gachon University Gil Medical Center (Incheon, Korea) due to a history of persistent iron deficiency anemia (IDA) and recurrent gastroenteritis. She initially visited the outpatient clinic 4 years ago for recurrent gastroenteritis. Laboratory tests were normal except for IDA. She was prescribed iron tablets and scheduled for regular follow-ups, but her anemia persisted. She reported adherence to the medication regimen. An endoscopic study was recommended 3 years ago, but she declined; it was performed 3 years later. The patient had a history of mild intellectual disability identified at age 8, similar to her mother. Their intelligence quotient scores ranged from 50-75. She has one sister who is reported as normal. Physical examination showed moderate pallor and a normal oral cavity. There was no jaundice, cyanosis, edema, thyromegaly, lymphadenopathy, clubbing, or scoliosis. No dermatologic or genital abnormalities were noted. Anthropometric measurements indicated macrocephaly with a head circumference of 608 mm (average and 99th percentile occipito-frontal circumferences for 19- and 24-year-old Korean females are 552 and 585 mm, respectively), height 162.8 cm (55-75th percentile), and weight 62 kg (90-95th percentile). Her sister and mother did not have macrocephaly. Laboratory investigations showed hypochromic microcytic anemia with hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL, mean cell volume 68.8, ferritin 24.8 µg/L, and iron/total iron binding capacity ratio 6.6%. Stool occult blood test was negative. Gastrofibroscopy and colonoscopy revealed multiple polyps of varying sizes and shapes in the terminal ileum, stomach, and duodenum. Biopsies confirmed inflammatory and hyperplastic polyps. Family screening showed her sister was normal, but her mother had multiple polyps in the stomach and duodenum. The patient also had an intellectual disability and physical examination confirmed macrocephaly.
test_results: An approximate 240 kb microdeletion was detected in the 10q23.31 region. An approximate 220 kb microdeletion was detected in her mother in the 10q23.31 region.

case_report: A 52-year-old woman with a confirmed genetic mutation (TIMP3 p.Arg204Cys) visited the eye clinic due to a 3-month history of decreased vision in her right eye. Her visual acuity in the right eye had declined from 6/9 to 6/60. The left eye maintained good vision at 6/9 and showed no signs of abnormal blood vessel growth.
test_results: Funduscopy revealed a macular lesion.
diagnosis: Choroidal Neovascular Membrane  secondary to Sorsby Fundus Dystrophy

case_report: A 12-year-old male presented with a 6-day history of pain and redness in the left eye. Initial examination showed a best-corrected visual acuity of 1.0 in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination identified 2+ flare and occasional cells in the anterior chamber, while the funduscopic examination showed no inflammatory signs in the posterior segment of the left eye. The right eye showed no abnormalities. Ten days later, inflammatory findings were noted in the right eye. Both eyes exhibited conjunctival and ciliary injections, 1+ flare, 3+ cells in the anterior chamber, and mutton fat keratic precipitates. Additionally, redness and swelling of the optic disc were observed in both eyes.
test_results: Soluble IL-2R (895; normal range, < 459 U/mL) and serum β2 microglobulin (2.24; normal range, 0.8–1.8 mg/dL) showed slightly high levels, along with markedly high levels of urinary β2 microglobulin (1.85; normal range, 0.03–0.28 mg/L). T-SPOT.TB, treponema pallidum latex agglutination, and rapid plasma reagin test were all negative. Angiotensin converting enzyme was within normal limits.

case_report: A 3-year-old girl presented with a darkened and swollen right lower limb and inability to use the right side of her body following a febrile illness accompanied by a generalized body rash that began on the face and spread to the entire body. This was preceded by symptoms of coryza and bilateral reddish eye discharge. This occurred during a 2013 period of a community outbreak, and she had not been immunized. A week after skin desquamation, her mother noticed a darkened and swollen right foot, which was painful and progressive, involving the ankle within 24 hours, and the toes became blackened. The patient experienced several episodes of generalized tonic-clonic seizures. After seizure control, the mother observed that the child could not use her right upper and lower limbs. She was transferred to our hospital after initial management at a general hospital. On examination, she was not febrile; cardiac and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. All peripheral pulses were palpable except for the right posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis arteries. At that point, she had regained consciousness, with reduced power in the right upper and lower limbs (estimated power of 3/5 in both limbs); the left limbs were normal. There was increased tone in both right upper and lower limbs, and the right foot had areas of darkened and shrunken toes that were not tender, with proximal areas of tender swollen purpuric skin. She had a deranged clotting profile with an activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) of 90 seconds (normal range: 60-85 seconds) and a prothrombin time (PT) of 28 seconds (normal range: 11-15 seconds) and thrombocytopenia of 90,000/mm3 (normal range: 150,000-400,000/mm3) from the referring hospital; however, repeat tests at our hospital were normal, and there was no site of active bleeding. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was normal, and the echocardiograph was also normal.
test_results: The vascular Doppler study confirmed reduced flow in the right posterior tibial artery.

case_report: A 16-year-old girl, born to non-related parents, presented with widespread reticulate pigmentation, reduced sweating, difficulty tolerating heat, and nail abnormalities since birth. There was no notable family history. The patient exhibited normal physical, social, and mental development. Dermatological examination revealed reticulate hyperpigmentation covering the entire body, with hair showing mild pigmentary dilution and patchy brown discoloration. The pigmentation was more pronounced on the neck, chest, hands, and legs. The skin was generally dry. The dorsal aspect of the tongue showed diffuse pigmentation. Teeth were yellowish, with abnormal dentition and enamel defects. There was fusiform swelling at the proximal interphalangeal joints and flexion at the distal interphalangeal joints. Dermatoglyphics were absent on all fingers. Toenail dystrophy was observed. General and systemic examinations were normal. Laboratory tests, including complete hemogram, random blood sugar, liver function test, renal function test, and urine analysis, were within normal limits.
test_results: A biopsy specimen taken from the left side of the neck showed basket wave pattern hyperkeratosis with diffuse pigmentation of basal layer. Upper dermis showed pigment incontinence.

case_report: A 14-day-old female infant was brought to the hospital after experiencing fever and difficulty breathing for two days. She was conceived through in vitro fertilization and embryo transfer by parents who are not related by blood. She was born at full term with a birth weight suitable for her gestational age and had no notable issues during the perinatal period. There is no family history of diabetes or neurological conditions. Upon admission, the infant exhibited severe respiratory distress, elevated blood sugar levels, and metabolic acidosis. Her peripheral blood glucose was measured at 39.0 mmol/L.
test_results: Her first arterial blood gas analysis revealed the following parameters: pH 7.114, CO2 17.1 mmHg, and bicarbonate 5.2 mmol/L. Urinalysis demonstrated 4+ sugars and 4+ ketones. Her glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c) and C-peptide levels were 5.9% and 0.31 ng/mL, respectively. Serum insulin was 3.1 mIU/L. Further investigations showed negative pancreatic autoantibody, and a normal pancreas was identified by ultrasonography.

case_report: A 36-year-old woman underwent a laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG) in 2017 and a laparoscopic revision to a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) in August 2019 due to persistent gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) with reflux esophagitis. Her surgical history also includes a laparoscopic cholecystectomy in 2018. She was prescribed a multivitamin supplement and was not on any other medication. Six weeks post-surgery, she experienced severe colicky pain in the right upper abdomen multiple times. Her food intake was moderate, affected by nausea, vomiting, flatulence, and regurgitation of food despite using a proton pump inhibitor. Physical examination revealed normal hemodynamic values: heart rate of 75 beats per minute, temperature of 36.9ºC, blood pressure of 135/74 mmHg, oxygen saturation of 98%, and respiratory rate of 14 breaths per minute. Pressure pain was noted in the right upper abdomen. An esophagogastroduodenoscopy and ultrasound of the upper abdomen showed no abnormalities. Dietary treatment was initiated to address dumping syndrome and other food intolerances. Two weeks later (eight weeks postoperatively), she reported persistent, unsustainable pain lasting more than four hours in the right upper abdomen, with no flatulence, nausea, or regurgitation since dietary adjustments. Laboratory results indicated increased liver enzymes. An abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan and a magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography were performed, both showing no abnormalities. Ten weeks postoperatively, laboratory investigations returned to normal values. The abdominal complaints had lessened, and no acute pain episodes had occurred for three weeks. The patient could pinpoint the pain to a specific location directly lateral to the laparoscopic scar in the right upper abdomen, which appeared to be position-dependent. Repeated physical examination identified a clear trigger point with local sensory disturbance over a 3 cm area around the trigger point, including hyperesthesia and allodynia. The pinch test and Carnett’s sign were positive.
test_results: Afterward, she was completely pain-free for a day and a half. The lidocaine injection was repeated after two weeks. She was completely pain-free for a few days again.

case_report: A 50-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with irritability, memory issues, severe headache, and mild gait difficulty one month prior to hospital admission. Physical examination revealed left-sided pyramidal tract signs, including a Babinski reflex on the left and motor deficits in the left upper limb (4+/5 MRC) and lower limb (5-/5 MRC). Brain MRI showed a tumefactive lesion in the right frontal-parietal region (T2/FLAIR hyperintense), accompanied by perilesional edema, mass effect, and homogenous post-contrast enhancement. Additional small atypical lesions were observed in the white matter. One lesion at the left fronto-parietal junction exhibited a ring-like appearance post-gadolinium administration, while multiple other lesions showed a patchy enhancement pattern. A search for primary neoplasm via chest and abdominal CT scans was negative. Extensive serological tests to rule out common infectious (including HIV) and autoimmune factors were negative. CSF analysis indicated an increased IgG index (0.617), absence of oligoclonal bands, and was negative for various common pathogens, including JC virus (PCR).
test_results: Brain biopsy of cerebral lesion indicated the presence of foamy CD68-positive macrophages, along with dense perivascular presence of a variable numbers of T lymphocytes and a small number of B cells. No reaction with the antibody SV-40 that detects polyoma virus such as SV-40, JK, BK etc. was observed. There was no histological evidence of lymphoma or any other neoplastic process.
diagnosis: Aggressive Tumefactive Demyelination with Marburg-like Characteristics

case_report: A 15-year-old male presented with swollen gums affecting all teeth and difficulty chewing. The gum enlargement had been progressing over the past 3-4 months, accompanied by pain during chewing and brushing. The patient had a history of mental retardation and progressive hearing loss. There was no family history of similar conditions, and his parents were not related. The patient had started using gutka (smokeless tobacco) 3-4 months ago, consuming 2-3 packets daily. Extra-oral examination showed a symmetrical face with incompetent lips. Intra-oral examination revealed gingival enlargement around the upper and lower anterior teeth, involving the interdental papilla, marginal gingiva, and part of the attached gingiva. The gingiva was firm, nodular, fibrous, slightly erythematous, and exhibited grade I bleeding. Plaque and calculus covered more than half of the crown portions. Severe gingival enlargement covered the entire crown of the right maxillary posteriors, from the first premolar to the last molar, with the gingiva appearing reddish-pink and fibro-edematous. The enlargement seemed to originate near the mucogingival junction, with a flap of tissue covering the crown portion in the posterior region. This flap was partially attached to the interdental papilla, with some attached gingiva visible. The flap could be lifted to reveal significant plaque and calculus on the tooth surface. Probing indicated pseudo-pocket formation. A panoramic radiograph showed generalized horizontal alveolar bone loss in both maxillary and mandibular arches. Routine blood tests were normal. After thorough scaling and root planing, the patient was reviewed after one month, showing no regression in enlargement but reduced signs of inflammation.
test_results: The evaluation of the specimen under light microscope revealed parakeratinized stratified squamous acanthotic epithelium with long thin rete ridges extending into the connective tissue. The underlying connective tissue showed dense wavy bundles of collagen fibers containing numerous fibrocytes and fibroblasts. Some sections in the connective tissue exhibited infiltration of chronic inflammatory cells, a few scattered multinucleated giant cells, and areas of neovascularization that had red blood corpuscles within the lumen of the blood vessels.
diagnosis: Gingival fibromatosis associated with Jones syndrome

case_report: A 24-year-old woman was referred to Dong-A University Medical Center after a routine chest X-ray revealed a well-defined mass in the left lower lobe (LLL) of the lung. The patient reported a 6-month history of intermittent dry cough, with no other significant medical or family history. A chest computed tomography (CT) scan showed a lobulated, well-enhancing mass with an endobronchial protrusion in the LLL. Positron emission tomography-CT scans indicated no notable findings in other organs. The patient underwent a bronchoscopy, but a diagnosis could not be made from the biopsy. Subsequently, a left lower lobectomy with regional lymph node dissection was performed. The excised tumor was a well-defined, solid, lobulated mass measuring 3.5×2 cm, involving the bronchus of the LLL. Microscopically, the lesion was a multinodular mass composed of bland fusiform or round cells in a myxoid background with a delicate plexiform capillary vascular network. The tumor cells exhibited lipoblastic differentiation with multivacuolar and univacuolar cells. Additionally, there were areas with sheets of primitive round cells with a high nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio. Immunohistochemistry revealed that the tumor expressed vimentin and S-100 protein. All nineteen dissected regional lymph nodes were negative for metastasis.
test_results: The fluorescence in situ hybridization specific for the t(12;16)(q13; p11) using DNA damage-inducible transcript 3 (DDIT3) and fused in sarcoma (FUS) break-apart probes confirmed the presence of a reciprocal translocation involving DDIT3 and FUS genes.

case_report: A 20-year-old woman presented with nocturia, fatigue, and nausea. Her creatinine level was approximately 600 mmol/L. She had been undergoing regular peritoneal dialysis since August 2014 due to end-stage chronic renal failure (CRF) of unclear origin. Her treatment regimen included calcium acetate tablets, vitamin D drops, recombinant human thrombopoietin injection, and calcitriol soft capsules. Despite these treatments, she experienced persistent anemia, primarily attributed to malnutrition from anorexia. Over the past ten months, she developed progressive facial deformities, difficulty chewing and swallowing, and some degree of dyspnea. The facial deformities included asymmetric hyperplasia of the maxillary and mandibular bones, bimaxillary protrusion, nasal dorsum collapse, nostril valgus, and zygomatic collapse. Additionally, she experienced a 10-cm reduction in height and severe leg pain during walking. She reported no visual, hearing, or psychological issues. There was no history of past diseases or family history of CRF or hyperparathyroidism. Laboratory results showed a serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) level of 2815.07 pg/mL (normal range: 9.09-90.09 pg/mL), serum total calcium of 2.31 mmol/L (normal range: 2.25-2.75 mmol/L), serum phosphate of 2.08 mmol/L (normal range: 0.97-1.61 mmol/L), hemoglobin of 48 g/L (normal range: 120-160 g/L), and alkaline phosphatase of 2350 U/L (normal range: 50-135 U/L).
test_results: Non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scans showed thickening of the skull bone plates and diffuse mixed sclerotic and lytic changes in the mandible, maxilla, and calvaria. A distinct overgrowth of the maxillofacial bone indicated bone abnormalities and swelling, and the density of the bone marrow cavity was increased with a ground glass appearance. A neck CT scan showed a benign nodule on the right side of the thyroid with bilateral soft tissue signals behind the bilateral thyroid. A pelvic CT scan did not show any abnormal structures. 99mTc-methylene diphosphonate bone scintigraphy indicated increased radiotracer in the bilateral parietal, maxilla, and mandible. The signal on the right side of the mandible was the strongest. 99mTc-sestamibi single-photon emission CT/CT showed only one hyperplastic parathyroid gland on the left side. Ultrasound showed a 0.5 cm nodule on the left side of the thyroid (thyroid imaging reporting and data system (TI-RADS) 4A), a 1.0 cm nodule on the right side of the thyroid (TI-RADS 3), and one suspected parathyroid adenoma on the left side. Fine needle aspiration showed a left papillary thyroid carcinoma and right thyroid adenoma.

case_report: An 18-month-old Egyptian boy presented with generalized hyperpigmentation of the skin, weakness, vomiting, and recurrent convulsions. He was born to consanguineous parents after an uneventful pregnancy with a birth weight of 3450 g. He is the fourth child in the family; one sibling, who passed away at nine months, had similar hyperpigmentation, recurrent convulsions, and mental retardation. Other siblings are healthy. The mother noticed generalized darkening of the skin a few weeks after birth. The parents reported that he appeared darker than his siblings. At 10 and 11 months, he experienced two febrile generalized tonic-clonic convulsions. On examination, he could speak a few words and walk with support. His weight was in the 5th percentile, while his length and head circumference were in the 50th percentile. Blood pressure was 90/60 mmHg. He exhibited generalized symmetric deep hyperpigmentation, especially on elbows, knees, hands, feet, and buccal mucosa, along with hypotonia. No dysmorphic features were noted. Examination of external genitalia showed a normal-length penis and bilaterally palpable testes. No signs of alacrima or achalasia were observed. Other examination findings were unremarkable. Blood chemistry results: glucose, 48 mg/dL; sodium, 140 mmol/L; potassium, 4 mmol/L; chloride, 109 mmol/L; alanine transaminase, 28 IU/mL; aspartate transaminase, 30 IU/mL. Total blood count was normal. Cortisol level was 0.6 μg/dL (normal range: 2.8 to 23 μg/dL) and ACTH, 708 pg/mL (normal range: 6 to 48 pg/mL). An ACTH stimulation test did not increase cortisol levels. 17-OH progesterone level was 0.01 ng/mL (normal range: 0.03 to 0.9 ng/mL); androstenedione, 0.01 ng/mL (normal range: 0.1 to 0.17 ng/mL); dehydroepiandrosterone, 3 ng/mL (normal range: 50 to 480 ng/mL); plasma renin activity, 57 ng/mL/hour (normal range: 2.35 to 37 ng/mL/hour); aldosterone, 801 pg/mL (normal range: 50 to 900 pg/mL). Bone age, assessed via X-ray of the left hand and wrist, was equivalent to two years. Adrenal ultrasonography showed small adrenal glands: left 6 × 8 mm and right 7 × 8 mm. Brain CT was normal.
test_results: A molecular genetics study revealed normal ACTH receptor gene sequences, excluding FGD type 1, and a homozygous deletion (c. 111+1delG) in intron 3 of the MRAP gene was detected.

case_report: A 71-year-old woman experienced muscle pain and weakness in both thighs starting in 2014, with symptoms gradually worsening. She was admitted to the hospital in August 2016 for further evaluation. Physical examination showed a blood pressure of 105/65 mm Hg and a body temperature of 36.7°C. Manual muscle testing indicated muscle weakness in the neck flexor tendons (score of 2) and in the biceps, triceps, quadriceps, and iliopsoas muscles bilaterally (score of 4). Gowers’ sign was positive. Examinations of the eyes, lungs, cardiovascular system, abdomen, other neurological functions, joints, and skin were normal. The patient had no history of statin use. Laboratory tests revealed elevated serum levels of creatinine kinase (384 IU/L), aldolase (6.2 IU/L), lactate dehydrogenase (314 U/L), IgG (2603 mg/dL), IgA (721 mg/dL), and IgG4 (313 mg/dL). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated at 112 mm/h, while the C-reactive protein level was within normal range at 0.04 mg/dL. Other blood tests, including blood counts, serum electrolyte levels, creatinine, IgE, and blood glucose, were within normal limits. The anti-nuclear antibody test was positive with a titer of 1:1240, showing homogeneous and speckled patterns. Tests for antiaminoacyl-tRNA synthetase, anti-RNP, anti-dsDNA antibody, and anti-Sm antibodies were negative.
test_results: Fat-suppressed T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging showed high intensity. Needle electromyography showed spontaneous fibrillations and positive sharp waves in bilateral femoral quadriceps. Histological examination of her left quadriceps revealed mononuclear inflammatory cells that surrounded and invaded muscle fibers. Those inflammatory cells were positive for CD8, and MHC class I antigen was extensively expressed on the surface of almost all muscle fibers. Scattered necrotic and regenerating muscle fibers as well as variations in muscle fiber size were characteristic of inflammatory myopathy. Infiltration of inflammatory cells at perivascular sites and perifascicular atrophy were not observed.

case_report: A 24-year-old female presented to the Department of Orthodontics and Dentofacial Orthopaedics for the management of misaligned teeth in both the upper and lower jaws. She exhibited normal intelligence and was of tall stature. Her family history indicated that her father had a similar Class III malocclusion, but no other symptoms were noted. The patient had a birth weight of 2500 g following a normal pregnancy. She experienced episodes of cyanosis while crying, characterized by a bluish tint of the skin, lips, and fingernails, and was found to have a ventricular septal defect (VSD). This condition persisted until it was surgically repaired at the age of two years. Additionally, she had an umbilical hernia at birth, which resolved by itself by the age of 22 months with the application of adhesive tapes as advised by a pediatrician. The patient also had congenital cataracts and underwent surgery for both eyes at the ages of four and six years. There was no family history of cataracts, birth defects, genetic diseases, or cardiac anomalies. She had syndactyly of the second and third toes, while her fingers were normal. Her primary teeth eruption was delayed, beginning at 2 years and 6 months. Detailed clinical examination revealed severe dental and skeletal abnormalities. Extra-oral examination showed a long and narrow face with a concave profile and laterally curved, thick eyebrows. Intraoral examination revealed a Class III malocclusion with a negative overjet and deep overbite. The patient's dental and chronological ages did not match, as multiple retained deciduous teeth were observed, including the maxillary right lateral incisor, first and second molars, left lateral incisor, and first molar, along with root stumps of both right and left canines. In the mandibular arch, the right central incisor, lateral incisor, canine, left canine, and second molar teeth were retained. Both the maxillary right premolars and mandibular left second premolar were absent on clinical examination.
test_results: Severe dental and skeletal abnormalities were found on detailed radiographic examination. Lateral cephalometric radiograph showed skeletal Class III and high angle pattern. Posterio-anterior radiograph revealed a skeletal midline shift to the right. The panoramic radiograph showed permanent teeth with extremely long roots and open apices. The roots of maxillary canines were in relation with the inferior border of the orbits and the lower canine roots almost reached the lower border of the mandible. Permanent maxillary right first premolar was missing while second premolar was impacted with distal aggregation. The maxillary left central incisor had dilacerated root; all four third molars were congenitally missing.

case_report: This 19-year-old female was the fifth child of first-cousin parents. One sibling passed away at 20 days of age due to pneumonia and another died at the age of 4 months from kidney failure. There was also a full-term stillborn. None of these siblings were seen at our institution, and their medical records were not available. The patient was born at 36 weeks of gestational age via caesarean section, with a birth weight of 2600 g (5th–15th percentile) and a birth length of 46 cm (5th percentile). Head circumference data was not available. There were no clinical signs or laboratory findings indicating cholestasis during the neonatal period or her first 2 years of life. She exhibited global developmental delay, first noticed after 6 months of age, affecting all domains. She could not hold her head up or sit without support until she was 1 year old. She began walking with support at 6 years old and without support at 7 years old. She started speaking some words at 4 years old but could not name colors, recognize numbers or letters, and could only produce scribbles. She began using a spoon at 11 years old. At that time, her functional age according to Denver II was gross motor 12–13 months, fine motor 15–16 months, language 18–19 months, and personal/social 7 months. A formal neuropsychological assessment was not conducted. She experienced recurrent hypoglycemia associated with fasting from 6 months to 7 years of age without hyperinsulinism and was unresponsive to glucagon. At 10 months old, she had a febrile seizure without hypoglycemia, and at 9 years old, she began having focal motor seizures with impaired awareness and automatisms. These seizures were rare and controlled with carbamazepine. When admitted to our service at 10 years old, her weight was 14.5 kg (2.5th–10th percentile), height was 100 cm (<2.5th percentile), and head circumference was 52 cm (2.5th–50th percentile). She had subtle dysmorphic features, including frontal bossing, high forehead, down-slanted palpebral fissures, and dental malocclusion. She walked independently but had generalized hypotonia and severe intellectual disability, speaking only isolated words. Laboratory tests showed intermittent increases in transaminases (AST up to 319 U/L, ALT up to 360 U/L) without liver failure or hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 0.56 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.18 mg/dL). Methionine levels were elevated once (1533 μmol/L; reference 7–47 μmol/L) but normalized spontaneously (33.96 μmol/L on her last visit) without a specific diet. Proline levels were elevated (541 μmol/L; reference 59–369 μmol/L), with mildly elevated tyrosine and phenylalanine levels, and diminished levels of L-aspartate, glutamic acid, citrulline, arginine, and ornithine. Homocysteine levels were normal. Brain MRI and head and neck MRA at age 10 showed no brain lesions, but MRA revealed ectasia and tortuosity of both internal carotid and vertebral arteries, particularly in the cervical segments. Intracranial arteries were normal. Thoracoabdominal aorta CT angiography was normal. At age 12, 15 days after Achilles tendon tenotomy, she had a seizure followed by loss of language skills and right-side strength. She was admitted to another hospital and did not undergo brain imaging. Six months later, a neurological exam showed motor aphasia, right-side hemiparesis with pyramidal signs. She could walk with a hemiparetic gait. At age 13, another ischemic stroke led to left hemiparesis, secondary to occlusion/sub occlusion of the distal intracranial right internal carotid artery, as shown by brain MR/MRA. This extended to the anterior and middle cerebral arteries, causing a large infarct in the area supplied by those vessels. Previous ischemic areas were also observed in the right internal globus pallidum and genu of the internal capsule, as well as in the left midbrain, pons, cerebellar hemisphere, and medial cerebellar peduncle. Laboratory screening for thrombophilia was normal, and her methionine plasma level was normal.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing revealed a homozygous missense variant in ADK [Hg19 Chr 10:76.468.145C>T, c.980C>T ENST00000372734, p.Ala327Val].
Orpha_name: Hypermethioninemia encephalopathy due to adenosine kinase deficiency

case_report: A 44-year-old male presented with sudden, painless bilateral vision loss over a period of 3 days. He reported no history of ataxia, headache, seizures, numbness, weakness, or sphincter control issues. There was no history of upper respiratory infections or recent immunizations. The patient had a known history of diabetes and hypertension for 5 years without any end-organ complications. He did not smoke or consume alcohol. There was no family history of similar conditions or autoimmune diseases. On examination, the patient was conscious, oriented, and alert with normal vital signs, body mass index, and mini mental status examination. His vision was impaired in both eyes (finger counting). Pupil size and response to light and accommodation were normal. Fundus examination showed no abnormalities such as papilledema, pallor, or atrophy. Visual field assessment was challenging. Other cranial nerves, motor and sensory functions, cerebellar function, and gait were normal, with no evidence of long tract involvement. Visual field testing (Humphrey 30-2) revealed bilateral central scotoma. Visual evoked potential indicated prolonged p-100 latencies in both eyes, suggesting optic nerve involvement. Baseline hematologic and biochemical tests, connective tissue examination, and vitamin deficiency assessment were normal. MRI of the brain showed symmetrical, diffuse, confluent, bilateral high signal intensity on T2 and FLAIR images in the periventricular, centrum semiovale, and subcortical white matter, including optic radiation, with no diffusion restriction, pathologic enhancement, or mass effect. MRI of the orbits and entire spine was unremarkable. CT Angiography of intracranial and extracranial blood vessels was normal. CSF analysis showed normal cells, glucose, and protein levels without oligoclonal bands. The patient was treated with pulsatile steroid therapy followed by a brief course of oral steroids. Aquaporin-4 and anti-MOG serology were negative on two occasions. Upon reexamination three months later, the patient's vision had returned to normal, including visual acuity, fundus examination, visual field examination, and color vision. A repeat MRI of the brain showed persistence of the previously noted white matter abnormalities.
test_results: A variant in the MT -CO3 gene m.14790A > G p.CYTB: (Asn15Ser) was detected in a homoplasmic state (99.78% of 4861 NGS reads).

case_report: A 1-year-old boy, born at full-term with normal weight, height, and head circumference, began experiencing recurrent rashes at 8 months old. He exhibited a frostbite-like rash on the cheeks, nose tip, and auricles, which worsened in cold weather. Additionally, he had recurrent oral ulcers and a persistent cough during his first year. His growth was below average, with a height of 68.5 cm (below the third standard deviation) and a weight of 8 kg (between the second and third standard deviations). Family history included ankylosing spondylitis in his grandfather and father. Upon admission, physical examination revealed purplish-red non-indurating plaques on the cheeks, nose tip, and auricles. Laboratory tests showed a slightly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (27 mm/h) and a normal C-reactive protein level (1.92 mg/L). Immunological tests indicated elevated levels of IgG (20.1 g/L), IgA (1.2 g/L), IgE (>1140 IU/mL), and complement C4 (0.417 g/L). CD8+ T lymphocytes were increased (41.1%) and CD3-CD16+CD56+ T lymphocytes were decreased (4.1%). Antinuclear antibody titer was 1:100. The expression of IFN-regulated genes was higher in the patient's peripheral blood mononuclear cells compared to healthy controls. Renal and hepatic function tests, white blood cell and platelet counts, and lactate dehydrogenase levels were all within normal ranges. Viral and bacterial serology results were normal. Bone marrow cytology was negative. Chest HRCT revealed interstitial lung disease characterized by scattered granular and patchy densities with increased shadows.
test_results: Whole-exome sequencing revealed a heterozygous mutation in TMEM173 (c.463G > A, p.V155M).
diagnosis: STING-associated vasculopathy with onset in infancy
Orpha_name: STING-associated vasculopathy with onset in infancy

case_report: In 2010, a 41-year-old woman was referred for video electroencephalography (EEG) monitoring. She was born in Haiti to nonconsanguineous parents and had no family history of epilepsy on her maternal side. Her cognitive and motor development were normal, with no history of meningitis, encephalitis, febrile seizures, or head trauma. At age 13, she began experiencing myoclonic and generalized tonic-clonic seizures without any apparent trigger. Within a year, she was having nearly daily generalized tonic-clonic seizures and continuous low-amplitude myoclonic seizures, primarily affecting her facial muscles and extremities. The myoclonic seizures increased in frequency and amplitude with voluntary activity and emotional stress. She became wheelchair-dependent due to falls caused by activity-induced myoclonic seizures in her lower extremities. Eating and drinking were also affected by movement-induced myoclonic seizures in her hands and fingers. Her cognition remained unaffected. Due to the frequency of her seizures, she left school and later moved to Brooklyn, NY, USA, where she completed high school while using a wheelchair. She was initially treated with phenobarbital and carbamazepine, later switching phenobarbital to topiramate. At presentation, her medication regimen included carbamazepine and topiramate, each at 400 mg per day in divided doses, but these combinations were not particularly effective. Her general medical examination was normal. Neurological examination showed normal cognition and nearly continuous, localized myoclonus in the perioral region, hands, and fingers, resembling fasciculations. There was no ataxia, but she could not walk independently due to frequent, large-amplitude, activity-induced myoclonic seizures in her lower extremities. Complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, and brain MRI scan were normal. Serum testing for lysosomal storage diseases in 2012 was negative.
test_results: In 2016, the patient underwent genetic testing for mutations associated with epilepsy, which revealed a 56 dodecamer repeat in the CSTB gene.

case_report: A seven-month-old male infant, born to parents who are second-degree relatives, presented with developmental delay. The parents reported that the child did not smile or react to stimuli and was unable to eat solid food by six months. The child achieved head control at four months. The parents also noted poor weight gain and a history of neonatal seizures. The antenatal period was marked by gestational diabetes managed with insulin, and the mother had two previous early miscarriages. The child was born late pre-term via cesarean delivery with a birth weight of 3.9 kg. Post-delivery, the infant experienced respiratory distress, hypocalcemia, and hypoglycemia, necessitating a five-day stay in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU). Echocardiography in the NICU revealed a small patent ductus arteriosus, patent foramen ovale, and diabetic hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The patient is the youngest of three children, with two healthy older siblings. There is no family history of mental, developmental, or neurocutaneous disorders. Physical examination revealed several dysmorphic features, including coarse facial features, a long philtrum, a thin upper lip, a broad forehead, and long toes. Neurological examination showed hypotonia in all four limbs, with normal muscle strength and reflexes. Skin examination was unremarkable, and the patient had normal male genitalia and no organomegaly. Routine blood tests, including full blood count, liver function tests, thyroid function tests, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, and urinalysis, were all within normal limits. Karyotyping confirmed a genetically male child (46XY).
test_results: Whole exome sequencing picked up a BRAF gene mutation. The BRAF variant c1495A>G p.(Lys499Glu) causes an amino acid change from Lys to Glu at position 499.

case_report: A 28-year-old male visited the surgical clinic at Poursina Hospital Medical Center in Rasht, Iran, in September 2021. He reported experiencing pain and discharge of foul-smelling pus and blood from the umbilical region, which had begun suddenly about three weeks prior to his visit. Initially, he was prescribed clindamycin and ciprofloxacin tablets for ten days, but the discharge persisted. His past medical history was unremarkable. Physical examination revealed a deep umbilicus, a dense hairy abdomen, and a tuft of hair in the umbilical area. The umbilical region appeared erythematous and was tender to touch. Other physical examination findings were normal, and his vital signs were within normal limits. Upright chest and abdominal X-rays were performed, and the images did not show any abnormalities.
test_results: The ultrasonography report showed a hypoechoic area measuring 23 × 6 mm.

case_report: A 2-year-old boy, the second child of a 27-year-old healthy woman and a 28-year-old healthy man, both non-consanguineous, presented with an unremarkable family history. He was conceived naturally and delivered at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy, with normal fetal ultrasounds. At birth, his weight was 3650 g (75th percentile), length 52 cm (75th percentile), and head circumference 33 cm (50th percentile). Postnatally, there was noticeable increased growth of the trunk, widespread cutaneous capillary malformations, and gigantism with exadactyly of the right hand. Monthly follow-up visits showed regular weight and length growth, but subcutaneous masses and increased growth of the hand became more pronounced. His developmental milestones appeared normal.
test_results: MRI and CT scans revealed vascular malformations and vesicles within the masses noted in the trunk, with variable extension into the retroperitoneal and mediastinum regions; x-ray examination of the hands confirmed the skeletal exadactyly of the right hand; histological examination of the affected (and unaffected) tissues confirmed a mixed lymphatic-arteriovenous malformation. Skin biopsies from the affected (and unaffected contralateral) regions were obtained.

case_report: This 16-year-old Saudi male has a history of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency since birth. Three months ago, he began experiencing severe nodulocystic acne along with mild joint and bone pain. The bone pain, which started in the hip joints and extended to the knee joints, had a gradual onset, was mild in severity, increased with exercise, and decreased with rest. He reported no history of fever, cough, or weight loss, and no similar symptoms had been observed previously. There was no erythema or warmth noted on his joints. A dermatologist prescribed isotretinoin 40 mg once daily after normal laboratory results, including complete blood count, liver enzyme levels, renal function tests, thyroid function tests, lipid profile, and hemoglobin A1C. Two weeks after starting isotretinoin, he began to experience bone and joint pain along with worsening acne. A week later, he was admitted to the medical ward, unable to get out of bed or move his lower limbs, and suffering from severe generalized joint and bone pain, particularly in the sternal and clavicle bones, lower back, and lower limbs (buttocks, femur, knee, and shaft of the tibia), as well as severe acne vulgaris. The pain was progressive and significantly interfered with his daily activities. On examination, he was vitally stable (normal temperature, pulse rate, respiration rate, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation) and oriented to time, place, and person but appeared unwell and in pain. Severe tender acne conglobata was observed on his face, with multiple scattered acne scars and serous discharge with pustular yellow discharge from acne lesions. Acne vulgaris was also noted on his shoulder and back, with one pustule on his right armpit. Tender anterior chest swelling was observed at his sternomanubrial joint.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed bilateral symmetrical sacroiliitis noted with mild narrowing of the joint spaces and incidentally noted small bilateral hip joint effusions, with subtle edema along the iliolumbar ligaments also seen bilaterally. A three-phase bone scan demonstrated normal flow and blood pool images. Delayed images demonstrated homogeneous normal radiotracer uptake seen in both hip joints. The whole-body images demonstrated multiple abnormal intense radiotracer uptake in the sternum and posterior aspects involving multiple ribs (left: 1 and 5; right: 3, 6, and 11) and also both sacroiliac joints with multiple osseous lesions.

case_report: A 28-year-old female patient was referred to our Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery from a local dental clinic due to two radiolucent areas observed in the mandible. She initially visited the clinic complaining of pain in the left lower back tooth region. The patient has a history of similar lesions in the maxilla, which were surgically removed along with impacted teeth at another hospital. Previous medical records indicated the presence of these lesions associated with impacted teeth. There is no familial history of similar lesions.
test_results: X-ray computed tomography (CT) showed the previous lesions, which were associated with impacted teeth. X-rays advised from our department revealed more findings. CT revealed persisting lesions in the previously operated sites along with the lesions associated with the mandibular ramus region bilaterally. The mandibular lesions were also associated with impacted teeth. X-ray paranasal sinus (PNS) skull revealed calcification of falx cerebri, and a miniplate fixation in relation to the maxillary region was seen in both OPG and PNS view. Chest X-ray revealed bifid ribs. Cone beam computed tomography taken for the patient revealed the maxillary lesions extending almost half of the maxillary sinus with penetration of the posterior antral wall in the right side. In the left maxillary region, the lesion was localized only in the posterior antral region. Chest X-ray revealed spina bifida in relation to C-spine.

case_report: A 23-year-old male presented with a 1-month history of blurred vision and a 5-day history of worsening vision in his left eye. He was admitted for retinal detachment in the left eye. His medical history included Pierre Robin syndrome, identified in childhood based on physical examination. His parents had no similar medical history. Five years earlier, he was evaluated for a white pupil in his right eye and found to have long-standing retinal detachment and cataract. At that time, he underwent cataract phacoemulsification with intraocular lens implantation for cosmetic improvement, but retinal reattachment surgery was not performed, resulting in blindness in the right eye. Despite normal intelligence, physical examination showed short stature (71 cm), kyphoscoliosis, abdominal protrusion, shortened extremities, prominent joints, stubby and spoke-like fingers, enlarged forehead, flat nasal bridge, and cleft palate. He also had high myopia and hearing impairment. Ophthalmologic examination revealed no light perception in the right eye, with proliferative membranes in the vitreous cavity and closed-funnel retinal detachment. In the left eye, uncorrected visual acuity was hand motion with no improvement on correction. Intraocular pressure was 6 mm Hg. Slit lamp examination of the left eye showed corneal endothelial pigment deposits from 3 to 9 o'clock, inhomogeneous cataract with super-temporal partial defect, and tremor. Due to the cataract, the left fundus could not be clearly visualized. Ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) indicated anterior chamber angle narrowing, lens subluxation, and epichoroidal spaces leakage in the left eye. B-scan ultrasonography revealed retinal and choroidal detachment in the left eye.
test_results: Genetic analysis revealed a heterozygous splicing mutation in the COL2A1 gene (NM_001844), specifically exon c3489 + 1G > A, in the patient that was absent in the parents.

case_report: A female newborn of Mexican descent, the first child of a 37-year-old woman and a 34-year-old man, was delivered via emergency cesarean at 35 weeks due to premature rupture of membranes. Birth weight was 1940 g (p15), length was 43 cm (p15), and APGAR scores were 8/8. The newborn was admitted to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit for 15 days due to respiratory distress from transient neonatal tachypnea and neonatal sepsis, which was treated according to standard guidelines. No clinical signs of metabolic decompensation were observed. Blood samples for newborn screening were collected during the first month of life and analyzed using tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS), revealing elevated tyrosine levels of 15.96 mg/dL without the presence of succinylacetone. Further analysis confirmed the absence of succinylacetone. Plasma amino acid quantification via liquid chromatography MS/MS showed tyrosine levels of 21.5 mg/dL, higher than the initial newborn screening test. A therapeutic approach involving a low-tyrosine diet supplemented with ascorbic acid was initiated. A subsequent plasma amino acid quantification 2 weeks later showed a decrease in tyrosine concentration to 3.9 mg/dL, indicating a positive response to the dietary intervention. The patient's protein intake was then adjusted to maintain optimal levels.
test_results: This detected two heterozygous HPD variants, V212M and A33T.

case_report: A 46-year-old woman with a history of psoriasis presented with itching skin eruptions that differed from her psoriatic lesions and had been present for 2 years. She also reported sensitivity to sunlight. Dermatological examination revealed annular erythematous plaques with a central poikilodermatous appearance on the left upper leg and left flank. Treatments including class III-IV corticosteroids, ultraviolet B (UVB) therapy, and methotrexate were administered without effect.
test_results: Histology showed a superficial band-like lymphohistiocytic infiltrate in the upper dermis with focal presence of basal cell vacuolization. There was only slight lymphocytic atypia, and no loss of T-cell markers was noted. The MxA staining showed positivity for the endothelium and some inflammatory cells, but the epidermis and skin adnexal structures were negative.

case_report: A 14-year-old male was transferred from another hospital due to nausea, pain in both flanks, and difficulty in urination. His medical history includes frequent urinary tract infections starting at age six, constipation managed with MiraLAX, and issues with urination addressed through biofeedback and pelvic floor muscle training. At age seven, imaging showed left-sided grade 3 vesicoureteral reflux, right-sided grade 1 vesicoureteral reflux, and a possible narrowing in the membranous urethra. By age 13, a renal ultrasound indicated severe hydroureteronephrosis on both sides and an irregular bladder shape. During the current visit, he experienced bilateral flank pain and urinary retention. Laboratory results revealed acute kidney injury with a creatinine level of 3.5 mg/dl and a blood urea nitrogen (BUN) level of 29 mg/dl, compared to baseline levels of 0.6 mg/dl for creatinine and 18 mg/dl for BUN. The patient was on medications including oxybutynin, tamsulosin, and nitrofurantoin for urinary tract infection prevention. Additionally, he had a psychological history of anxiety, depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, for which he was receiving sertraline and dextroamphetamine/amphetamine, and was under the care of a psychotherapist and psychiatrist.
test_results: CT abdomen and pelvis showed bilateral hydroureteronephrosis and a thickened urinary bladder wall. MRI lumbar spine showed normal findings. CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed bilateral hydronephrosis and a thickened urinary bladder wall. Renal ultrasound showed bilateral hydronephrosis, trabeculations, irregular contour of the urinary bladder, and thickened bladder wall. Fluoroscopic VCUG showed progression of the vesicoureteral reflux to grade 4 and a trabeculated urinary bladder contour. Lumbar spine MRI evaluation was normal.

case_report: A 7-year-old girl exhibited multiple well-defined, irregular, variably sized brownish plaques with fine scales on her arms, legs, ankles, and buttocks, along with dusky red macules on her face. These skin changes first appeared at 5 months old, beginning as reddish lesions on the malar area and gradually spreading to other parts of the body. Initially, the lesions presented as red macules, which over time turned into brown-black plaques. The condition worsened during winter and showed improvement in summer. Examination revealed normal palms, soles, scalp, hair, nails, teeth, and mucosa. She is an only child with no family history of similar skin conditions. There were no indications of other systemic illnesses. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, liver and kidney function tests, and urine analysis, were all within normal limits.
test_results: Skin biopsy from posterior aspect of left leg showed orthohyperkeratosis, acanthosis with focally broadened granular layer. Upper dermis showed melanin pigment incontinence positively stained with Masson-Fontana stain, and perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate. Sequence analysis revealed patient was heterozygous for the single nucleotide mutation c.125G > C in exon 2 of the GJB3 gene (encoding connexin 31), predicted to cause a missense change in an arginine to proline in codon 42 (p.Arg42Pro).

case_report: A 5-year-old boy with a mutation in LMNA (c.1824C>T) was referred to our pediatric outpatient department. Initially, he presented with abdominal bloating and coarsening of the skin, which had spread to other parts of his body. A skin biopsy showed sclerema neonatorum. Since the age of 1, he exhibited loss of scalp hair, slow growth of fingernails and toenails, easy bruising, and visible veins over the scalp and forehead. He was born full-term by emergency cesarean section due to cephalopelvic disproportion and premature rupture of the membrane. The patient had normal intelligence and no family history of similar symptoms. General examination revealed the child to be of short stature (94.9 cm) and underweight (11.85 kg), below the 1st percentile of the Korean Child Growth Standards. Physical examination showed difficulty in flexing both shoulder and left knee joints, and a slightly flexed back at rest. Contracture was observed in the second metacarpophalangeal joints of both hands and the third proximal interphalangeal joint of his left foot. Skull lateral radiograph and panoramic radiograph showed mandibular condylar hypoplasia and micrognathia, leading to crowding of teeth. A dual-energy X-ray densitometer study revealed low Z-scores for bone marrow densities of the total body (-4.5), total body less head (-4.1), and lumbar spine (-1.9). Blood laboratory results indicated elevated total and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels. Although he had no cerebrovascular or cardiovascular events, a baseline brain MRI was performed to detect silent strokes or vascular changes and to assess risk over time.
test_results: MRA revealed segmental severe stenosis in the V2-V3 segments of the bilateral vertebral arteries (VAs) with collaterals from an enlarged anterior spinal artery and external carotid artery (ECA). Tortuosity in the cavernous segments of both ICAs was also observed without significant stenosis. There were no demonstrable brain parenchymal abnormalities.
diagnosis: Cerebrovascular disease in Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome

case_report: A 25-year-old female from São Paulo was brought to the clinic by her mother at ten months old due to the absence of hair, eyelashes, and eyebrows since birth. At one year old, she developed peeling lesions on her fingertips and dystrophic fingernails. By two years and six months, hyperkeratotic and peeling plaques appeared on her palms. At eight years old, she exhibited total hair loss and nail dystrophy. The hyperkeratotic plaques, initially on her palms, extended to the soles of her feet. Additionally, she showed distal tapering of her fingers. There were no changes in sweating, dentition, or hearing.
test_results: An anatomopathological examination performed on the scalp revealed alopecia. A radiological examination showed reduction of soft tissues in distal extremities of fingers, acquiring a triangular configuration, and bone structures of normal appearance. A biopsy revealed absence of hair follicles, but sweat glands with normal features.

case_report: A 65-year-old male with a history of diabetes mellitus presented with a painful rash on the palms lasting for 2 weeks. One week prior, he experienced fever and sore throat, which resolved after a week of oral antibiotic treatment. The patient did not report any other respiratory symptoms, abdominal pain, or joint pain. On physical examination, multiple purpuric macules and patches were observed on both palms, with more pronounced involvement on the right palm. Similar findings were noted on the right big toe. The mucous membranes were intact, and there was no enlargement of peripheral lymph nodes. The remainder of the systemic examination was unremarkable.
test_results: Biopsy showed perivascular neutrophilic infiltrate with some lymphocytes and few extravasated red blood cells. There was evidence of leukocytoclasia and scattered interstitial neutrophils.

case_report: A 12-year-old male was referred to a community pediatrician due to difficulties in interacting with peers. His childhood was otherwise normal, with no significant illnesses reported and no delay in puberty onset. He was born at 38 weeks of gestation due to maternal gestational cholestasis. Physical examination was largely unremarkable except for marked leukonychia. Basic biochemical and hematological tests revealed microcytic anemia with a hemoglobin level of 10.4 g/L (reference range: 11.5-15.0) and a mean cell volume of 61 fL (reference range: 78-100). Serum iron was low at 6 μmol/L (reference range: 14-31), total iron-binding capacity was 67 μmol/L (reference range: 54-80), iron-binding saturation was 6% (reference range: 20-55), and ferritin was elevated at 534 μg/L (reference range: 10-322). Hemoglobin electrophoresis and genetic testing for hemoglobinopathies were negative. Further evaluation included copper assessment due to elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALT). Serum copper was low at 0.7 μmol/L (reference range: 11-22) with an undetectable ceruloplasmin level of <0.02 g/L (reference range: 0.20-0.60). Urinary copper excretion was low-normal at 0.17 μmol/d (reference range: <1). A copper-65 absorption test was conducted to investigate in vivo copper metabolism. This test involved sequential analysis of plasma 65Cu/63Cu ratio by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry at various time points up to 72 hours after administration of a 3 mg oral dose of the stable copper-65 isotope. The results showed a significant early rise in plasma copper-65 (83% enrichment at 2 hours post-administration), followed by minimal incorporation of copper-65 into the plasma protein pool between 6 and 72 hours post-administration.
test_results: Next-generation DNA sequencing identified that he was homozygous for a pathogenic splicing mutation c.(1713 + delG);(c.1713 + delG) in intron 9 of the CP gene.

case_report: A 30-year-old male presented with a 7-day history of slow response and unsteady walking, as reported by his family. Clinical features included impaired calculation skills, limited language expression, unresponsiveness, difficulty climbing stairs, inability to walk in a straight line, and irritability. No other symptoms such as weakness, numbness, fever, cough, diarrhea, headache, nausea, vomiting, altered consciousness, or convulsions were observed. Skin manifestations, such as resembling staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome or a diffuse erythema with superficial erosions, desquamation, and cheilitis resembling acrodermatitis enteropathica, were not found in our patient. The patient had an unremarkable medical and developmental history, and his relatives did not exhibit similar symptoms. However, his scholastic performance was notably poor compared to his peers, having completed only the 8th grade. Neurological examination revealed delayed reaction times, impaired calculation ability, significant dysmetria on heel–knee–shin testing, and a positive Romberg test. Plasma total homocysteine was 296.90 μmol/L (normal value 0.0 ~ 15.0 μmol/L) and D-dimer was 9.38 ng/mL (normal value 0.0 ~ 0.55 ng/mL), both elevated. Auxiliary examinations, including blood routine, biochemistry, thyroid function, rheumatic immune-related antibodies, folic acid, vitamin B12 concentrations, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and autoimmune encephalitis antibody examination, all yielded normal results. Neuropsychological examination results indicated a Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score of 20, a Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score of 18, an International Cooperative Ataxia Rating Scale (ICARS) score of 41, and a Barthel Index (BI) score of 55. MRI revealed cortical atrophy and symmetric hyperintensities in the bilateral lateral cerebellar hemispheres, primarily observed on DWI.
test_results: Whole-exome sequencing, followed by Sanger sequencing for verification, identified compound heterozygous variant in the MMACHC gene: c.609G > A (p.Trp203*), a nonsense variant inherited from the patient’s mother, and c.482G > A (p.Arg161Gln), a missense variant inherited from the patient’s father. Liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry-based blood amino acid and acylcarnitine spectroscopy demonstrated significantly elevated levels of propionylcarnitine (10.53 μmol/L, normal range: 0.30–5.00 μmol/L), the propionylcarnitine to acetylcarnitine ratio (0.50, normal range: 0.02–0.20), and the propionylcarnitine to methionine ratio (0.90, normal range: 0.02–0.30). Gas chromatography mass spectrometry-based urine organic acid analysis showed a significant increase in methylmalonic acid (76.9 nmol/L, reference value, 0.00–4.00 nmol/L).
Orpha_name: Methylmalonic acidemia with homocystinuria, type cblC

case_report: A 4-year-old girl arrived at the Emergency Department of a tertiary care institute with significant fresh, red-coloured vaginal bleeding without any history of trauma or sexual assault. Physical examination showed short stature, short and stubby hands, delayed dentition, and bradycardia. The thyroid gland was not palpable. Blood tests indicated macrocytic anaemia with a normal coagulation profile.
test_results: Thyroid profile showed elevated levels of TSH (699 IU/mL, normal range 0.35 IU/mL – 4.9 IU/mL) with low levels of serum T3 (< 1 pg/mL, normal range 2.6 pg/mL – 4.8 pg/mL) and serum T4 (< 0.4 ng/dL) along with a markedly elevated level of Thyroid Peroxidase Oxidase (2152 U/mL normal range 0–60). Basal FSH was elevated; however, Luteinizing hormone (LH) and Prolactin levels were normal. Greyscale ultrasonography and colour flow Doppler imaging of the pelvis revealed a post-pubertal sized uterus, measuring 6.3 cm × 1.3 cm (length × transverse) with a tri-layered endometrium.
