A septated cystic lesion, measuring 5.7 cm × 3.7 cm, was seen in the right adnexa with no peripheral or septal colour flow. The right ovary was not separately visualised. A dominant follicle was seen in the bulky left ovary. Ultrasonography of the neck revealed bilateral hypoplastic thyroid lobes in the normal position. The right thyroid lobe measured 6.5 mm × 5.5 mm and the left lobe measured 8.8 mm × 6 mm. The isthmus was not visualised. There were no thyroid nodules or cysts. A wrist radiograph revealed ossification centres for the hamate and capitate, consistent with a bone age of 3–4 months. The appearance of the epiphysis at the distal end of the radius was consistent with a bone age of 1 year. Triquetral and lunate bone ossification centres were not seen indicating that the bone age of the child corresponded to more than 1 year but less than 4 years. A lateral radiograph of the skull revealed the presence of multiple Wormian bones and an enlarged sella. Radiographs of the pelvis and hip joints exhibited diffuse cortical thickening along the meta-diaphyseal region of both proximal femora. The lateral radiograph of the left knee was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging for the pituitary gland revealed hyperplasia of the anterior pituitary with homogeneous enhancement. The posterior pituitary was unremarkable.

case_report: A 20-year-old woman with no history of smoking presented with a round-shaped shadow in the right middle lung field on a chest X-ray during her employment medical checkup, while her chest X-ray 2 years ago showed no abnormalities. She had no symptoms and no comorbidities. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the chest revealed a lobulated solid mass in the hilum of the right lung measuring 3.5 × 3.0 cm in diameter, which was homogenously enhanced in the early phase scan without any intratumoral fat or calcification. FDG-PET showed a high accumulation of FDG in the mass with maximum standard uptake values of 7.1 and 8.4 in the early and delayed phases, respectively. The levels of all serum tumor markers of lung cancer, including carcinoembryonic antigen, cytokeratin 19 fragment, and pro-gastrin-releasing peptide, were within normal ranges.
test_results: The tumor contained branched gland ducts along with columnar epithelial cells with poor nuclear dysplasia arranged in papillary growth patterns. The mass was a solitary, white-colored, well-defined, and solid component measuring 2.9 × 2.5 cm in diameter. It consisted of abundant glands with single or double layers of nonciliated cells and bronchial structures that resembled the tubular epithelium of a fetal lung. Rounded morules of polygonal cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm were frequently observed. Nuclei and cytoplasm of the tumor cells were positive for β-catenin and negative for p53, nuclei of the tumor cells were positive for thyroid transcription factor 1, and the cytoplasm was positive for synaptophysin.
diagnosis: Well-differentiated fetal adenocarcinoma of the lung
Orpha_name: Well-differentiated fetal adenocarcinoma of the lung

case_report: A 36-year-old male presented to the outpatient department with a primary complaint of toothache in the lower right posterior quadrant persisting for the past 6 months. The patient also reported having had a mobile tooth extracted in that area. An orthopantomogram was performed, which showed a radiolucent area extending from the right second premolar (45) to the socket of the previously extracted second molar (47).
test_results: A microscopic study revealed the presence of sheets of spindle-shaped cells with features of pleomorphism and mitosis. Of these, only a strong positivity for Vimentin was observed. Further, IHC analysis using CD68 was done which showed focal positivity.

case_report: AA is a 7-year-old boy who was born via spontaneous vaginal delivery at a primary health care center following an uneventful pregnancy. On the second day of life, during an evaluation for jaundice, laboratory results revealed a cholesterol level exceeding 500 mg/dL (>5.68 mmol/L, normal <4.40 mmol/L) and a hemoglobin level of 6.7 g/dL (normal range 13.6–19.6 g/dL). Serum bilirubin and platelet count were within normal limits. The lipid profile was reassessed.
test_results: The laboratory work showed a very thick blood sample that was hyperlipidemic. The repeated lipid profile showed serum cholesterol 7.4 mmol/L (normal <4.40 mmol/L), high density lipoprotein (HDL) 1.10 mmol/L (normal >1.55 mmol/L), and triglyceride (TG) 80 mmol/L (normal <1.70 mmol/L).

case_report: An 11-month-old female infant from Italy was admitted to the hospital due to three days of fever, vomiting, and deteriorating general condition. Physical examination showed a febrile and pale child with normal neurological status. Her axillary temperature was 40°C, and capillary refill time was 2 seconds. There were no signs of respiratory or meningeal infections. The infant's weight was 10 kg (50th percentile), length was 74 cm (50th percentile), and head circumference was 44 cm (45th percentile). Growth had been linear since birth, and psychomotor milestones were achieved on time. She was born at term and breastfed until six months, following a varied and complete diet thereafter. There was no family history of consanguinity, blood disorders, or kidney diseases. Initial laboratory results showed leucocytosis (white blood cells, 11,620 × 103/µL); normochromic normocytic anemia with hemoglobin values below 2 standard deviations for age (Hb, 8.6 g/dL); normal MCV and MCH for her age (MCV 75.9 fl; MCH 24.6 pg); and a mild increase in C reactive protein (CRP, 2 mg/dL). Kidney function was normal (creatinine, 0.21 mg/dL; azotaemia, 20 mg/dL), but urine was turbid with 104 leucocytes (UCF), low-grade proteinuria (100 mg/dL), and a positive urine culture for Escherichia coli. Intravenous ceftazidime therapy was initiated for a urinary tract infection. After eight days, the infant was discharged with normal blood tests, and the anemia was considered a transient finding during an acute infection. The child missed her first follow-up visit. Seventeen months later, at 28 months old, during a routine visit, mild-moderate proteinuria with a mixed tubular-glomerular pattern was detected (187 mg/dL). A 24-hour urine sample showed an elevated proteinuria/creatininuria ratio (patient’s ratio: 2, normal values <0.2) with proteinuria (60 mg/dL) and creatininuria (30 mg/dL). Blood tests revealed macrocytosis (MCV 98.5 fl) without anemia (Hb 12.4 g/dL). Renal ultrasound showed no abnormalities in the kidneys or urinary tract. The patient also presented with oral aphthous ulcers, vulvar hyperaemia, and abnormal movements of the buccal rhyme.
test_results: Peripheral blood levels of folate and vitamin B12 showed a severe vitamin B12 deficiency (0.1 pg/mL; normal range values 180–914 pg/mL). DNA sequencing of the coding regions and of the exon–intronic junction of the AMN gene showed the presence of a novel intronic variant c.513+5G>A of AMN in compound heterozygosity with the known pathogenetic variant c.1006+34_1007-31del.

case_report: A 43-year-old male presented with tooth pain in the right lower back tooth region. Extraoral examination showed multiple nodules on the conjunctival surfaces of both upper and lower eyelids. The lips were diffusely enlarged, everted, and bumpy upon palpation. Intraoral examination revealed multiple nodules on the tip and lateral borders of the tongue, which appeared enlarged but functionally normal. Nodular masses were also observed on the buccal and labial mucosa. These nodules were asymptomatic, oval-to-round in shape, measuring 0.8 cm × 0.5 cm, with a sessile base and smooth surface. The patient had a history of thyroid carcinoma and underwent a total thyroidectomy 20 years ago. There was no family history of cancer or thyroid abnormalities. The patient reported chronic constipation since childhood. Anterior maxillary and mandibular teeth appeared protruded from the side profile view. Hard tissue examination revealed multiple root stumps in all four quadrants, and extraction with prosthetic rehabilitation was advised. A midline diastema was evident in the maxillary anterior region. General examination did not reveal cervical lymphadenopathy, café-au-lait spots, or diffuse pigmentation of neurofibroma on the trunk or extremities. Blood pressure and pulse rate were within normal limits. The patient was not currently undergoing any treatment, and previous medical records were not available. Biochemical analysis was within normal limits.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed bundles of disorganized and tortuous nerve fibers surrounded by a thickened perineurium. Numerous bundles of elongated cells with wavy dark nuclei were identified.

case_report: A 10-year-old Moroccan boy was referred to a medical genetics department for evaluation. He is the firstborn child of a healthy consanguineous couple, both originating from the Northwest of Morocco. There was no family history of sudden death, deafness, syncope, epilepsy, or any other genetic disease. The pregnancy was medically monitored, and no complications were reported. His mother had no history of drug ingestion or phytotherapy. His birth weight and length were within the normal range, and no dysmorphic signs were noted. At 6 months, he was found to have severe bilateral sensorineural hearing loss based on auditory evoked potential measurement. His first syncopal episode occurred at 24 months of age. An ECG showed a markedly prolonged QTc interval of 530 ms (corrected by Bazett’s formula) and T-wave alternans on leads V1 to V4. Echocardiography indicated a structurally normal heart. Treatment was initiated with a β-adrenergic blocker. His parents and his two younger brothers, aged 7 years and 1 year, were clinically normal. Blood samples from all family members were collected after obtaining written informed consent.
test_results: Molecular genetic testing of the entire coding region and flanking intronic regions of KCNQ1 and KCNE1 was undertaken by Sanger sequence analysis. This led to the identification of a homozygous frameshift mutation c.1343dupC (p.Glu449Argfs*14) in the index patient. Both parents and one sibling (IV-2) were heterozygous for this mutation. The youngest child of the family did not carry the frameshift mutation (IV-3).

case_report: A six-year-old male from a rural area presented with localized skin changes on the scalp, affecting the right parieto-frontal, left parieto-temporal, and occipital regions. The affected areas included three plaques measuring 8 × 6 cm, 5 × 6 cm, and 6 × 4 cm, respectively, with regular borders. The first two plaques had a red base, hair loss with hairs cut at the same level on the skin, pustules, and honey-colored and blood-stained crusts that fluctuated upon palpation and released purulent discharge. The third plaque showed diffuse hair loss and fine scaling on the surface. Additionally, there was bilateral cervical lymph node enlargement. The patient's mother reported the development of 'pustules' over the past two months, followed by hair loss. The patient had been treated with multiple topical azole medications without improvement. The patient had a history of Moebius syndrome, autism, and epilepsy, and was on risperidone for ongoing treatment. Imaging with the Fotofinder System GmbH® medicam 800HD (Columbia, MD) revealed erythema, black dots, comma hairs, broken hairs, interfollicular scaling, honey-colored crusts, pustules, and hair loss with hairs cut at the same level on the skin. Direct examination stained with chlorazol black was negative. Agar growth over four weeks on Mycosel® also yielded negative results.
test_results: A biopsy showed ulcerated skin, crusts, colonies of coccoid bacteria, an epidermis with parakeratosis, acanthosis with pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, spongiosis, and exocytosis of lymphocytes and neutrophils. In the dermis, there was a diffuse interstitial infiltrate of neutrophils, lymphocytes, and histiocytes with foreign body multinucleated giant cells, bare stems, and fragments of squamous epithelium immersed in the infiltrate. Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) staining revealed short spores and hyphae within and surrounding the hair shaft.

case_report: An 81-year-old man visited an urgent care center in Ontario, Canada, due to swelling and redness on his right thigh. The patient had been bitten by an unidentified insect five weeks earlier while traveling in Belize, and symptoms appeared at the bite site. Two weeks prior, he consulted a primary care provider and was prescribed oral cephalexin for a lesion. His symptoms initially improved with the antibiotics but returned after completing the course. The patient reported no recent fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea, and did not experience calf swelling, calf pain, shortness of breath, or coughing up blood. Upon examination, his vital signs were normal. The affected area on his right thigh was round, raised, and measured 5-10 millimeters in width, resembling a furuncle. There was no fluctuance, fluid drainage, or visible skin break.
test_results: A longitudinal sausage-shaped structure (8 x 12mm) was identified within the subcutaneous tissue which demonstrated a thin anechoic ring surrounding a hyperechoic structure with acoustic shadowing. There was no evidence of posterior acoustic enhancement. The structure was not compressible, nor did it appear to have any intrinsic movement. The lesion did not show any Doppler signal suggestive of vascular flow. Instead the structure, and continuing deep-field, demonstrated constant alternating colours of Doppler signal, giving the appearance of turbulent blood flow. This finding was consistent with a sonographic 'twinkle sign'.
diagnosis: Human myiasis caused by Dermatobia hominis
Orpha_name: Furuncular myiasis due to Dermatobia hominis

case_report: A 37-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a persistent rash on her lower eyelids for about one year. She reported no use of cosmetic products on her face. Dermatologic examination showed well-defined, red, scaly, slightly darker thin plaques on the outer sides of both lower eyelids. The lesions were asymptomatic and had grown larger during the summer. Dermatoscopic examination identified scales and perifollicular pigmentation on a red base.
test_results: Histopathology revealed parakeratosis, basal vacuolar degeneration, necrotic keratinocytes, dermal lichenoid infiltration and melanophages.

case_report: A 60-year-old Caucasian male presented to the dermatology clinic with a painful rash. Four weeks earlier, he noticed a lesion on his left wrist. Within 24 hours, a red and purple rash appeared on his left forearm, elbow, and left dorsal hand, accompanied by tingling and swelling of the affected skin. He initially sought care at an urgent care clinic and was prescribed cephalexin, but his condition did not improve. He then visited his primary care physician, who started him on a prednisone taper (40mg PO daily for four days, then 20mg PO daily for four days, then 10mg PO daily for four days) and referred him to the dermatology clinic. By the time he presented to the dermatology clinic, he had completed six days of the prednisone taper, resulting in mild symptom improvement. The patient reported no factors that alleviated or worsened his condition, no previous skin diseases, and no contact with sick individuals. He had a history of varicella infection during childhood and had not received the shingles vaccine. A review of systems showed no systemic symptoms such as malaise, fever, muscle pain, or joint pain. His medications included tamsulosin for benign prostatic hypertrophy and intermittent use of Vicodin and ibuprofen for chronic low back pain. He reported no known immunodeficiencies, occasional alcohol consumption, and a history of cigarette smoking and marijuana use. Physical examination revealed normal mood and affect, and orientation to place, person, and time. A full-body skin exam showed pink, ill-defined, irregular papules of varying sizes on the left distal forearm, and well-defined, round, violaceous papules on the dorsal and palmar aspects of the left digits two through five. No intact vesicles were observed.
test_results: Findings included small vessels with marginating neutrophils, fibrin thrombi, fibrinoid necrosis of blood vessel walls, karyorrhectic debris, and numerous extravasated red cells. Pathology also reported a vesicle with numerous necrotic keratinocytes with marked acantholysis and large red intranuclear inclusions, and a superficial and deep neutrophilic infiltrate with the destruction of vessels. The tissue samples at both sites also stained positive for VZV antigen and stained negative for herpes simplex virus (HSV) antigen.
diagnosis: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis  in the setting of herpes zoster infection

case_report: The patient is a 28-year-old Mexican male with no previous medical history who presents with widespread itchy skin lesions on the face and extremities. These lesions are characterized by merging red papules and nodules on the face and ears, resulting in a distinctive facial appearance. The condition has progressed over 18 months, with an increase in the number and size of the lesions. The patient underwent a one-year treatment regimen for multibacillary leprosy using WHO multidrug therapy, which included monthly doses of rifampicin 600 mg, clofazimine 300 mg once a month and 50 mg daily, and dapsone 100 mg daily. Despite this treatment, there was no improvement in his condition. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, blood chemistry, liver function, thyroid function tests, HIV testing, and serum protein electrophoresis, were all within normal limits or negative.
test_results: Biopsy revealed irregular proliferation of fibroblasts associated with abundant mucin deposition in the papillary dermis.

case_report: A 49-year-old woman was transferred to our emergency room from another hospital for treatment of a brain tumor. Her main complaint was visual field disturbance, and she had experienced a generalized tonic-clonic seizure a week prior. She exhibited right side homonymous hemianopsia upon visual field test, and papilledema was observed with fundoscopy. Brain CT revealed a large (diameter of 4 cm) iso-dense intra-axial ovoid mass in the left temporo-occipital area. A T2-weighted brain MRI showed that the mass contained an internal cystic region, abutted the choroid plexus, and had potentially invaded the trigone of the lateral ventricle. Gadolinium enhancement showed homogenous enhancement of the solid portion. The radiologist recommended both MR spectroscopy and a metastasis work-up. MR spectroscopy revealed a high choline peak. However, the metastasis work-up, including whole-body positron emission tomography, colonoscopy, and esophagogastroduodenoscopy, was negative for systemic primary cancer. Tumor removal was performed with a transcortical approach via the parieto-occipital junction. The resected tumor was covered with a glistening capsule and was found to be attached to the choroid plexus at the end of the removal. Intraventricular hemorrhage was observed immediately postoperation via a brain CT, and gadolinium enhanced brain MRI confirmed the gross total removal of the tumor 24 hours after the operation.
test_results: The tumor was well-encapsulated with a distinct fibrous capsule and was composed of columnar epithelial cells on fibrovascular cores. The tumor cells had prominent nuclear pleomorphism. Tumor cells were focally positive for epithelial membrane antigen and transthyretin. Tumor cells were positive for synaptophysin and negative for glial fibrillary acidic protein and vimentin. The Ki-67 index was 21.66%.

case_report: A 42-year-old female with a history of borderline hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus underwent elective endometrial ablation for treatment of menorrhagia. Postoperatively, in the recovery room, she experienced severe hypertension and pulmonary edema, with an ejection fraction of 25% observed on transthoracic echocardiography. She received treatment with nitrates and diuretics for four days and was subsequently transferred to the local cardiac intensive care unit, where she showed clinical improvement. Additionally, she reported experiencing palpitations, excessive sweating, and headaches over the past twelve months.
test_results: 24 hr urinary catecholamines were elevated (noradrenaline 5060 nmol/24 hr [nr: 50–1600], adrenaline 1349 nmol/24 h [nr: 5–122], and dopamine 1096 nmol/24 h [nr: 300–3900]). Chromogranin A was 240 u/L [nr: 0–30]. A CT abdomen revealed a 37 mm left adrenal mass.

case_report: The patient is a 7-year-old male, weighing 25 kg, born in 2016, who visited our genetics clinic due to the inability to walk independently and bilateral clubfoot persisting at the age of 7. During pregnancy, prenatal ultrasound indicated 'inward turning of the feet'. Postnatally, the lower limbs showed deformities with symptomatic clubfoot. Currently, the patient is 7 years old, still unable to walk independently, with normal intelligence but a diminished attention span. Muscular atrophy is observed bilaterally in the lower limbs, particularly in the quadriceps and calf muscles, with significant atrophy around the knee joint. Passive extension of the knee joint is restricted, and clubfoot deformity and muscle softness are evident in the feet. Muscle strength in both lower limbs is graded between 3 and 4, with the left lower limb exhibiting comparatively weaker muscle strength. This allows for crawling but limits the ability to stand on one knee, and transitioning from single-knee to standing is unattainable. Walking with corrective shoes results in internal rotation of both lower limbs, more pronounced on the right side. Walking is unstable and prone to falling, but the patient can rise directly from the ground with the support of both hands after a fall. Wearing corrective shoes, the patient cannot clear obstacles higher than 20 cm or lift both feet off the ground. Laboratory tests, including urine routines, blood routine examination, liver and renal function, and C-reactive protein testing, reveal no abnormalities. Paresis of the vocal cord has been excluded by laryngoscopy. The phenotypes of the patient’s parents are unremarkable, with no consanguinity and no reported family history of related diseases. Computed radiography (CR) images of the patient's lower limbs exhibit pelvic obliquity, bilateral knee joint valgus, and bilateral clubfoot. The bone structures of the bilateral femurs, tibias, fibulas, and hip joints showed no apparent abnormalities.
test_results: The results indicated a heterozygous missense mutation at position 805 (c.805C>T) in the 5th exon of the TRPV4 gene, leading to a substitution of arginine at position 269 with cysteine. The ACMG classification for this variant is pathogenic. This mutation was inherited from the father. Sanger sequencing was performed, confirming once again that the mutation was inherited from the father.
diagnosis: Neuronopathy, distal hereditary motor, type VIII

case_report: A 58-year-old Japanese man, who had thymoma surgically removed at the age of 54, was admitted to the emergency room due to sudden speech difficulties. His medical history was notable only for the thymoma, which was incidentally found during a health screening. Post-surgery, he had no recurrence and did not receive any further medical treatment. His family history was unremarkable. Upon admission, his vital signs were normal except for a mild fever (37.8 °C). His general condition was stable (height: 160 cm, weight: 60 kg). Brain MRI showed multiple lesions in the frontal lobes. The left cingulate lesion exhibited high-signal intensity in both DWI and ADC maps, indicating the presence of vasogenic edema. CSF examination showed no abnormalities, with normal levels of IgG and myelin basic protein. EEGs were within normal limits. Despite the MRI findings, the patient's neurological symptoms were not fully accounted for by the identified cerebral lesions. Acyclovir (10 mg/kg, three times a day) was administered, leading to a full recovery of his fever and neurological symptoms within a few days. However, one week after admission, his symptoms worsened again. Neurological examination revealed the return of motor aphasia and mild right hemiparesis.
test_results: Brain MRI demonstrated multiple lesions involving the frontal lobes. The left cingulate lesion was partly demonstrated as high-signal intensity in both DWI and ADC maps, suggesting that the lesion contains vasogenic edema. The MRI demonstrated that the lesion involving the left cingulate gyrus increased in size, and an abnormal signal intensity lesion in the left corona radiata, which was presumably the cause of his right hemiparesis, and edematous swelling of the bilateral medial temporal regions appeared. These lesions were not significantly enhanced by Gadolinium. Laboratory studies revealed that the patient’s blood cell counts and chemistry were normal. Marked hypogammaglobulinemia was present, with IgG 481 mg/dL (reference range, 870–1700 mg/dL), IgA 81 mg/dL (reference range, 110–410 mg/dL), and IgM 25 mg/dL (reference range, 33–190 mg/dL). There was a normal CD4/CD8 lymphocyte ratio of 0.70 with CD4 21.9 % and CD8 31.2 %.

case_report: An 11-year-old male presented with bilateral upper limb primary lymphedema characterized by significant swelling of the hands resembling 'boxing gloves.' Additional findings included lymphedema of the right thigh and genital area, along with widespread cutaneous lymph blisters, particularly on the trunk. Scattered red spider-like capillaries were also noted on the skin. There was no evidence of segmental overgrowth or venous issues. The erythematous telangiectasias were observed to be transient, appearing and disappearing over several weeks. A biopsy was performed on one of the erythematous telangiectasias.
test_results: No pathogenic variants were identified. H&E staining showed dilated vascular lumens, most likely lymphatic vessels. Analysis of the acquired 2D optical sections of the affected tissue biopsy showed dilated weakly PROX1-positive, strongly Podoplanin-positive vessels in the area of the papillary dermis but no cystic vascular structures. The lymphatic vessel density appeared increased compared with healthy control samples. Further detailed examination of the expression of PROX1 and Podoplanin in all optical sections revealed a uniform, nonaltered expression of Podoplanin and PROX1. The 3D reconstruction of the entire sample provided additional information on lymphatic vessels. In contrast with the lymphatic vasculature in normal skin, the visualized lymphatic vasculature did not show hierarchical organization of the vascular tree but hyperplastic, dilated lymphatic vessels in the deeper dermis. Nonconnected lumenized vessel fragments were present. In contrast with the papillary dermis, PROX1 was expressed only weakly in deeper dermis. In the lymphatic vasculature of the deeper dermis, no lymphatic valves were detected.

case_report: A 66-year-old female who had a double lung transplantation in October 2006 for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease experienced complications post-transplant, including chronic kidney disease and multiple malignancies such as squamous cell carcinoma of the skin. Due to gastrointestinal side effects, her medication was switched from tacrolimus to Cy-A. In February 2012, Everolimus was added to her treatment plan to reduce the Cy-A dosage, particularly because of the skin cancers. Seven years post-transplant, in 2014, she developed chronic lung allograft syndrome characterized by a restrictive allograft syndrome, with a 20% reduction in both FEV1 and FVC. Her lung function remained relatively stable until August 2015, when she was admitted to the hospital with generalized weakness and poor oral intake. She also experienced spontaneous epistaxis, leading to severe anemia that required blood transfusions. Upon admission, she needed 3 liters of oxygen via nasal cannula to maintain SpO2 above 88%. Lung auscultation revealed bilateral end-inspiratory crackles. Initial lab values, including everolimus level, and pulmonary functions are provided in the respective tables.
test_results: Chest X-ray was notable for bilateral diffuse coarse reticular nodular opacities along with alveolar opacities involving mid and lower lung zones. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest revealed interval development of multifocal nodular and ground glass opacities in both mid to lower lung zones.
Orpha_name: Drug or radiation exposure-related interstitial lung disease

case_report: AA is a 3 years and 3 months old girl who has experienced new onset unprovoked generalized tonic-clonic seizures occurring both during the night and day. She was started on valproate for treatment. During her initial evaluation at AUBMC, her psychomotor development was found to be normal, and both her physical and neurological examinations showed no abnormalities. The only noted risk factor was a family history of epilepsy in her maternal uncle.
test_results: A three-hour sleep deprived EEG revealed a normal awake background rhythm, and fragments of generalized spike and wave discharges. Brain MRI was normal except for a non-specific faint high FLAIR signal in the peritrigonal white matter. A repeat three-hour video/EEG recording revealed the presence of frequent, 2.5-3.5 Hz generalized, frontally predominant spike and wave discharges.

case_report: A 1-year-old male child, the second born to a third-degree consanguineously married couple, presented with milestone regression and seizures. The child had an uneventful perinatal history. Clinical symptoms began at 6 months of age with a gradual loss of previously achieved milestones. By 2 months, the child responded to sounds; by 3 months, he could hold his head, smile socially, and recognize his mother. Initially, he lost his social smile and recognition of his mother, followed by loss of neck control. By 8-9 months, he had lost all milestones. At 8 months, he developed an exaggerated startle response and, by 11 months, experienced multiple episodes of right-sided focal seizures. There was a history of a sibling who died at 18 months with similar symptoms. On examination, the child's head circumference was 44 cm (between the 3rd and 15th centile) with coarse facial features. Muscle tone was increased in all limbs with a power of 3/5 (Medical Research Council grade). Deep tendon reflexes were exaggerated with an extensor plantar response. Fundus examination revealed a cherry-red spot in the macula, and there was no hepatosplenomegaly. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed hyperintensity of the basal ganglia and hypointensity of the ventral thalami on T2-weighted sequences.
test_results: The enzyme assay in leukocytes for β hexosaminidase total (A + B) revealed 61 nmhol/h/mg. Gene testing was positive for homogenous missense substitution p. Cys534Tyr, c1601G>A, chr5:74016560G>A in exon 13 of HEXB gene.

case_report: In 1998, an 11-year-old girl noticed a gradually enlarging bump on her left calf. A biopsy identified it as rhabdomyosarcoma. She received combination chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, doxorubicin, actinomycin D, vincristine, and carboplatin, along with radiation therapy to the left calf. Initially, she responded well, but a local recurrence occurred a year later, necessitating a below-the-knee amputation at age 12. Later that year, she developed a palpable bump on her right lower ribs, which was surgically removed and identified as chondrosarcoma. Within 18 months, a local recurrence at the rib surgical site required a wider resection of the rib and adjacent lung tissue. At age 18, she developed a cyst-like lesion on her vulva, which was resected and identified as a small Stage I leiomyosarcoma. Due to her history of multiple early-onset sarcomas, she began annual MRI surveillance of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis at age 18. She remained stable until age 22, when an MRI detected a new small mass in her left kidney. A left partial nephrectomy was performed, and pathology revealed a Stage I, 0.9 cm clear cell renal carcinoma. Despite being referred for genetic counseling at age 18, she declined specific testing for TP53 mutations. Her family history included a maternal grandfather with bladder cancer at age 85, a maternal great aunt with uterine cancer around age 40, and a paternal great uncle with lung cancer at an unknown age. Her parents and brother had no cancer diagnoses. She was closely monitored by her physicians with body imaging and colonoscopy.
test_results: Testing revealed a heterozygous splice site mutation in TP53, IVS6-2A>G, and no other mutations in cancer-related genes.

case_report: A 10-year-old boy presented to the pediatric gastroenterology unit with rectal bleeding. He had experienced episodes of diarrhea, occasionally bloody, over a span of 10 years. The frequency and presence of blood in the diarrhea had increased over the past 3 months. Physical examination revealed rectal prolapse, but was otherwise unremarkable. The patient exhibited normal growth and showed no signs of bleeding disorders, significant anemia, bacterial or parasitic infections, or other systemic diseases. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, stool examination for parasites and ova, Clostridium difficile toxin, and coagulation profile, were all within normal limits.
test_results: Colonoscopy showed an ulcer 2×2.5 cm in diameter located at 6 o'clock in the rectum. Histopathological examination revealed fibromuscular hyperplasia of the lamina propria.

case_report: A 62-year-old male presented with a widespread rash that initially improved with three sessions of phototherapy but worsened after stopping due to transportation issues. One year earlier, he had an excisional lymph node biopsy that revealed small to intermediate CD4+/CD5+/CD8-/CD10- lymphocytes. Physical examination showed extensive deep pink scaly plaques covering more than 95% of the body surface area (BSA) with patchy dark brown pigmentation, significant thickening of the skin on the soles of the feet, and palpable lymph nodes in the neck and above the collarbone. The patchy brown pigmentation covered less area than the red, inflamed skin, and the patient's mostly depigmented skin was notable against his type V skin background. He also had areas of white hair, indicating depigmentation of both skin and hair. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 21.3 × 10^9/L, serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) level of 394 IU/L, and no detectable human T-lymphotropic virus HTLV-1/2 DNA.
test_results: Peripheral flow cytometry demonstrated an abnormal CD4+ population (34% of all lymphocytes, absolute count 15.5 × 109/L) with TRBC1 expression, a CD4:CD8 ratio of 33:1, and loss of CD7/CD8/CD26/CD56/CD57/CD16. A staging computed tomography (CT) scan showed extensive lymphadenopathy.

case_report: A 7.5-year-old boy was admitted to the endocrinology clinic with concerns about short stature. He was born at 40 weeks of gestation as the first child of parents who are not related by blood, following a pregnancy that included polyhydramnios. His birth weight was 3500 grams. On physical examination, his height was 103 cm (-4 standard deviations) and his weight was 16 kg (below the 3rd percentile, -1.7 standard deviations). He exhibited distinctive craniofacial features such as curly and dry hair, sparse eyebrows, a coarse facial appearance, a broad nasal tip with upturned nostrils, downslanting palpebral fissures, dysplastic ears, hyperextensible fingers, and unusual skin characteristics including dry, itchy, elastic skin, a hairy nevus on the left thigh, and congenital overlapping toes. An eye examination showed bilateral optic nerve hypoplasia, intermittent strabismus, ptosis, and mild telecanthus. Echocardiography revealed pulmonary stenosis.
test_results: A heterozygous mutation in exon 3 of the MEK1 gene, c.389A>G (p. Y130C) detected through his genetic testing.

case_report: The patient is a 19-year-old male of Northern European descent, the first child of non-consanguineous parents. He was born full term weighing 3550 g and had a two-vessel umbilical cord and a heart murmur due to a bicuspid aortic valve. A CT scan revealed an absent inferior vena cava and a continuous dominant hemiazygos vein draining into the azygos vein at the T9 vertebral level, with the azygos vein draining the right kidney. At 18 years old, his cardiac evaluation showed stable aortic dilation without significant aortic stenosis or insufficiency. He experienced two episodes of symptomatic pericarditis. As an infant, a small area of increased hair growth and pigmentation was noted in the lumbar region of his back, which expanded to his anterior thighs and shins over time. During his first year, localized swelling was observed in his scrotum, which became indurated and tense. An ultrasound at 17 months showed normal testes with echogenic material in the scrotum, particularly around the right epididymis, consistent with calcified meconium from meconium peritonitis. The scrotal mass grew, causing noticeable distension and involving the suprapubic area by age 4. A pelvic CT showed diffuse increased attenuation in the subcutaneous fat from the iliac crests to the upper thighs. An MRI at age 6 revealed bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. The patient has consistently been short for his age, with height percentiles dropping from 10-20th at 4 months to less than 3rd by 5 years, when he was diagnosed with growth hormone deficiency. He had mildly delayed bone age with no pituitary mass on imaging. A DEXA scan at age 9 showed normal bone mineral density. He had normal hearing at birth but developed significant hearing loss by 14 months, leading to bilateral cochlear implants. A brain MRI at 18 months showed enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles and bifrontal and bitemporal extra-axial fluid spaces, indicating cerebral volume loss. Arcus senilis was noted at age 4. At age 6, he was described to have a prominent forehead, normal nasal root, mild hypertelorism, ptosis, prominent eyes, and a cowlick with a whorl on the right side of his forehead. His external ears were slightly posteriorly rotated but otherwise normal. His hearing worsened by age 7, and he received his first cochlear implant a year later. He experienced abdominal pain and loose stools throughout childhood. An upper endoscopy and colonoscopy at age 11 showed partial lactase deficiency in the duodenal mucosa and lymphoid hyperplasia throughout the colon, with a normal terminal ileum biopsy. A CT enteroclysis at age 15 was unremarkable. At age 15, he developed pain and stiffness in multiple joints, particularly the ankles and knees, with proximal interphalangeal joint contractures in his 5th digits bilaterally and reduced range of motion in both ankles and knees. Left hand films showed normal mineralization with no erosions or joint space narrowing.
test_results: A deep skin punch biopsy from patient 2 showed mild epidermal hyperplasia with relatively mild basal hyperpigmentation and a striking infiltrate in the deep dermis and subcutis accompanied by edema and rare hemosiderin deposition. Cellular aggregates seen at low power included a predominance of plasma cells with prominent perivascular cuffing, in addition to other mononuclear cells. Immunohistochemical stains for kappa and lambda showed a polyclonal phenotype, although with inversion of the expected kappa:lambda ratio. Immunohistochemical staining for histiocytic markers showed diffuse staining of cells for CD68 and CD163, which were often present between the plasmacytic aggregates.

case_report: A 47-year-old male presented with chest pain and gradually worsening shortness of breath (MRC Grade III) over three months. He worked as a laborer and did not smoke, with no history of exposure to occupational or inorganic dusts. The chest pain was dull, aching, and localized to the left axillary region without radiation or relation to meals. He also had a cough with mucoid expectoration but no hemoptysis. Physical examination showed an averagely built individual with a BMI of 20, without clubbing or lymphadenopathy. Respiratory examination revealed reduced movements and breath sounds on the left side of the chest. A chest radiograph showed a uniform, homogenous opacity in the lower left chest with obliteration of the left cardiac border and a mediastinal shift to the right. A CT scan of the thorax revealed a large, well-defined, heterogeneous density mass in the anterior mediastinum with areas of necrosis, extending to the pleural surface but not infiltrating the chest wall. There was no involvement of mediastinal lymph nodes. Abdominal ultrasonography showed no organ enlargement. Routine blood tests and serum cortisol levels were normal. Fibreoptic bronchoscopy showed no abnormalities. Bronchial washings, bronchial brush biopsy, and transbronchial needle aspiration biopsy of the mass were inconclusive. A trans-thoracic tru-cut biopsy of the mass revealed small round tumor cells, but the exact histological diagnosis was uncertain. The patient underwent thoracotomy with tumor excision. Intra-operatively, a large firm mass was observed in the left mediastinum, invading the great vessels and extending to the chest wall. Debulking of the tumor was performed as complete excision was not possible due to infiltration of the great vessels and pericardium. Gross examination showed an uncapsulated, firm, pink-gray mass with a gritty cut surface and areas of necrosis. Histologically, the specimen showed sheets of pleomorphic spindle-shaped cells with an organoid growth pattern, including insulae, ribbons, festoons, and trabeculae of tumor cells. Some cellular nests were detached from surrounding fibrovascular septa, with central geographic necrosis in many areas.
test_results: Tumor cells expressing cytokeratin positivity, strong synaptophysin positivity, chromogranin A positivity and TTF-1 positivity.
diagnosis: Primary neuroendocrine carcinoma of the thymus

case_report: A 28-year-old female from Azerbaijan presented with muscle weakness and fatigue in the limbs, difficulty climbing stairs, and challenges with prolonged walking and exercise. She first noticed these issues during physical education classes at school, where she struggled with tasks that were easy for others. Since puberty, the weakness in her lower extremities has worsened. She experienced significant difficulty walking for extended periods, climbing stairs, and rising from a chair, eventually requiring support to rise from a squatting position. Neurological examination revealed decreased strength primarily in the proximal upper limbs (MRC grade 4) and more pronounced in the lower extremities (MRC grade 2–3), a positive Hoover’s sign, waddling gait, minor hypotrophy of the proximal limb muscles, and symmetrical decline of deep reflexes. Additional findings included small-amplitude nystagmus, absence of surface reflexes, a positive Babinski reflex on the right, and urinary incontinence during sneezing. Brain MRI showed active demyelination foci in the left frontal lobe. A follow-up MRI after 2 months revealed multiple (>10) rounded and elongated hyperintense foci on T2WI, FLAIR, and STIR, iso- and hypointense on T1WI, ranging from 2.5 mm to 5.8 mm in diameter, located periventricularly and subcortically in the white matter of the left temporal, parietal, and frontal lobes, predominantly in the left frontal lobe, with a decrease in the size of a previously active lesion and new lesions in the right frontal and parietal regions. Isoelectric focusing detected intrathecal synthesis of oligoclonal IgG bands (type 2) in cerebrospinal fluid. Electromyography (EMG) indicated primary muscular disease with predominant involvement of the proximal muscles of the lower extremities. Electrocardiography showed minor myocardial conduction abnormalities in the left ventricle. Biochemical analysis revealed elevated serum creatine kinase (746.81 U/l). MRI of both shins indicated muscular atrophy and fatty degeneration, and MRI of the head showed moderate tongue muscle atrophy. The MRI signal from other soft tissues was unchanged. Tandem mass spectrometry from a dried blood spot found normal alpha-1,4 glucosidase activity, excluding Pompe disease.
test_results: NGS showed homozygous Variant of Uncertain Significance (VUS) c.1855C > T (p.Pro619Ser) in TRIM32 gene and heterozygous VUS c.2300C > G (p.Thr767Arg) in KIF5A, c.2840G > A (p.Arg947Lys) in MYH2, c.1502G > C (p.Gly501Ala) in POMT1 genes. Variant c.1855C > T (p.Pro619Ser) is located in exon 2 of TRIM32 gene and caused the replacement of proline with serine at codon 619 of the TRIM32 protein (p.Pro619Ser). The proline residue is highly conserved and there is a moderate physicochemical difference between proline and serine. This variant is not present in population databases and it has not been reported in the literature in individuals with TRIM32-related conditions.
diagnosis: Sarcotubular Myopathy due to novel TRIM32 mutation

case_report: Patient 1 is a 16-year-old girl, born via normal vaginal delivery to a healthy consanguineous family, with normal growth parameters following an uneventful pregnancy and delivery. Developmental milestones were delayed, becoming noticeable by the second year. She began walking around 24 months of age after therapeutic intervention, but significant speech delay persisted. At age 7, her occipitofrontal circumference (OFC) was 48.5 cm (−2SD). At the time of examination, her OFC was 54.5 cm (50th percentile). Her nonverbal IQ was measured between 30–40, indicating severe impairment. She exhibited severe cognitive delay, with language limited to a few single words. Behavioral and social evaluations indicated severe deficits in adaptive behaviors across all domains, including communication, daily living skills, and socialization, and she was unable to perform any activities of daily living independently. She also displayed agitation and restlessness, characterized by pacing, hand-wringing, and fidgeting. Her gait was normal, with a wide base, but she required assistance to sit and pull herself up. Muscle tone was normal with no spasticity, and her neurological examination was unremarkable except for unequivocal visuospatial perception. Additionally, she had flexion contracture of the elbow and fingers without any history of trauma or immobilization.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a thin but fully formed corpus callosum.
diagnosis: Intellectual Disability due to TRAPPC9 gene mutations

case_report: A 51-year-old Caucasian male presented in August 2019 with a 10-month history of itchy papules on sun-exposed areas of his extremities. He had not received any prior treatments or dermatologic consultations for these lesions. There was no personal or family history of cancer. The patient experienced severe itching that disrupted his sleep. He reported no habitual UV-light or carcinogen exposure. The patient had a high cardiovascular risk profile, including arterial hypertension, hyperuricemia, coronary heart disease, and terminal kidney disease due to idiopathic nephropathy. He had undergone kidney transplants in 1990 and 2001, with transplant rejection episodes in 2000 and 2007. He was on peritoneal dialysis from 2007 to 2017 and had been on hemodialysis since 2017. Additionally, he carried a factor V Leiden mutation. His medications included felodipine, bisoprolol, clonidine, ramipril, urapidil, cholecalciferol, acetylsalicylic acid, allopurinol, phenprocoumon, thyroxine, iodine, fluvastatin, calcium acetate, omeprazole, and sevelamer carbonate. Clinical examination showed approximately 100 scaly and ulcerated papules and nodules, ranging from 3 to 20 mm, on sun-exposed areas of both upper and lower extremities. There were no signs of chronic actinic damage such as cutis rhomboidalis nuchae, poikiloderma, xerosis cutis, or freckling. Mucosal involvement and lymphadenopathy were not observed.
test_results: Histopathology revealed similar findings in 15 lesions: prominent keratinization, slightly enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei with abundant amounts of cytoplasm, and moderate atypia. The remainder was diagnosed as inverted verrucae vulgaris or viral papilloma.

case_report: A 15-year-old male presented with pain and limited movement in the left ring finger's metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint. The patient reported a history of trauma one year prior, where his left hand was stepped on during a football game. The patient has asthma and is on inhaled corticosteroids. He denied any numbness or tingling in the affected finger or hand. Clinical examination showed tenderness upon touch and restricted flexion at the fourth MCP joint of the left ring finger. The other fingers on the same hand had normal movement, and there were no signs of neurovascular issues. Routine blood tests were unremarkable.
test_results: A radiographic evaluation of the left hand showed lucency and a loss of height in the head of the fourth metacarpal. Additionally, radiographs showed volar subluxation of the ring finger at the fourth MCP joint. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the hand and wrist confirmed the deformity within the epiphysis of the fourth metacarpal and volar subluxation of the proximal phalanx of the fourth digit. MRI studies revealed flattening of the fourth metacarpal head with irregularities in the underlying cortex. Additional findings included subchondral marrow edema, effusion within the fourth MCP joint, and confirmed subluxation of the proximal phalanx of the fourth digit.

case_report: A 3-year-old girl, born to parents who are second-degree relatives, was presented by her mother due to concerns about sparse and fragile hair starting from the age of 1. The child had undergone repeated hair shaving every 6 months with the hope of promoting stronger and thicker hair growth, with the most recent shaving occurring 2 months before the hospital visit. Physical examination showed short, rough, lusterless, and sparse hair that was easily breakable on the scalp and eyebrows. Additionally, multiple discrete keratotic papules were observed across the scalp.
test_results: Dermoscopic examination under nonpolarized contact dermoscopy over vertex, frontal, bitemporal and occipital scalp showed regular variations in the diameter of the hair shaft with elliptical nodes separated by internodes, broken hair, and areas with very much thinned out internodes on the verge of breakage. Dermoscopy of keratotic papules over the occipital scalp revealed broken and beaded hair emerging from the surface of papules. Routine microscopic examination of hair from the scalp revealed regularly beaded hairs with constriction and fraying at the internodal junction.

case_report: A 12-year-old boy presented with back pain persisting for 2 years. His medical history includes bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and multiple joint contractures in both wrists and fingers, particularly in the proximal interphalangeal joint of the left fifth finger. He has two male cousins with similar physical features. His parents and sister do not exhibit any noticeable anomalies. Physical examination showed facial characteristics such as micrognathia, frontal bossing, a prominent supraorbital ridge, and hypertelorism. Additional findings included hypodontia, underdevelopment of the left fifth digital phalanx and great toes, and thoracic scoliosis. The intrinsic muscles of both hands were graded 2/5 on the manual muscle test, with no sensory impairment. Knee and ankle reflexes were hyperactive, and ankle clonus was present. His height was 154 cm (63.9 percentile). Whole-spine X-ray indicated thoracic scoliosis (Cobb angle of 17°) and vertebral body flattening. X-rays of the upper and lower extremities showed valgus deformity of the elbow and knee joints, along with mild bowing of the humerus and tibia bones. Skull CT revealed irregular sclerosis with hyperostosis, frontal sinus obliteration, and thickening and protrusion of the frontal bone. 3D CT of the skull demonstrated premature closure of all cranial sutures (pansynostosis). Brain and whole-spine MRI showed cerebellar tonsillar inferior herniation with extensive hydrosyringomyelia from the C1 to T12 levels and C2 spina bifida occulta. Laboratory tests, including complete blood cell count, blood chemistry, and immunochemistry, were normal. Electrodiagnostic tests, including nerve conduction study, electromyography, and somatosensory and motor-evoked potential tests, were within normal limits. Chromosomal analysis revealed a karyotype of 46,XY without anomalies, and no significant microdeletion or duplication was detected via chromosomal microarray test.
test_results: A hemizygous missense variant (c.3557C>T/p.Ser1186Leu) in FLNA (NM_001456.3) was detected. Family gene analysis revealed that his mother, aunt, and sister carried the same heterozygous FLNA variant and that his maternal male cousin had the same hemizygous FLNA variant as the proband.

case_report: A 70-year-old male presented to the emergency department with chest pain resembling angina, palpitations, and sweating. One year prior, an incidental adrenal finding on imaging measured 25 × 34 mm2. A 24-hour urine collection for catecholamines showed a urine epinephrine level of 150 μg (normal limit: <27 μg/day). A 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test resulted in a serum cortisol level of 188 nmol/l (normal limit < 50 nmol/l). He was referred to the emergency department due to chest pain, palpitations, and sweating. Cardiac catheterization revealed no significant coronary artery pathology, and he was discharged the next day. His medical history included hypertension, type II diabetes mellitus, and dyslipidemia. On current admission, the electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm, new T wave inversion in lateral and posterior leads, with no conduction abnormalities. Bedside echocardiography indicated hypokinesis in the distribution of the left anterior descending coronary artery. Urgent catheterization again showed no coronary artery pathology. A subsequent echocardiogram demonstrated normal ventricular function with moderate mitral and tricuspid regurgitation. During his stay in the coronary care unit, he experienced multiple episodes of hypertension and tachycardia, which were resistant to treatment with calcium channel blockers, beta and alpha adrenergic blockade, angiotensin receptor blockers, and furosemide.
test_results: A 36 × 34 × 22 mm3 right adrenal mass was identified. The adrenal mass had a density of 39 Hounsfield units (HU) prior to intravenous contrast injection, increasing to 74 HU following contrast injection. Plasma metanephrine was found to be 1200 pg/ml with a normal normetanephrine level of 163 pg/ml. Plasma cortisol level at 8 am, after overnight 1-mg dexamethasone suppression, was 2770 nmol/l, while level at 8 am without dexamethasone suppression was 3292 nmol/l. ACTH level was 174 pmol/l.

case_report: A 17-year-old female patient, the only child of healthy unrelated parents with no family history of recurrent or severe infections, autoimmune disease, or lymphoma, had an uncomplicated perinatal history and a normal interval for umbilical cord separation (7 days). She was fully immunized, including the conjugated pneumococcal vaccine, as well as measles, mumps, rubella, varicella, and BCG live vaccinations without adverse effects. At 8 months old, she presented with bronchiolitis and subsequently experienced recurrent respiratory tract infections (sinusitis, mastoiditis, otitis, and pharyngitis) every 1–6 months until the age of 3 years. She also developed skin abscesses (Staphylococcus aureus detected) treated with appropriate antibiotics in the hospital. From ages 3 to 5, she was hospitalized twice per year and treated empirically with intravenous antibiotics (ampicillin and/or cephalosporins). At 5 years old, she underwent adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy and received antibiotic prophylaxis for 6 months without a reduction in infections. No severe viral, mycobacterial, or fungal infections were noted. She was also diagnosed with intellectual disability within the autism spectrum. Immunological laboratory evaluation at 6 years old revealed low serum IgA, which was restored in subsequent measurements; normal IgG, IgM, and IgE; and normal serum IgG subclasses (except for IgG4, which was also restored in subsequent measurements). Peripheral blood immunophenotyping by flow cytometry showed normal counts. Circulating monocyte and neutrophil counts were normal. The dihydrorhodamine (DHR) test for phagocytic function was normal for her age. She was able to produce functional antibodies against vaccine antigens, including tetanus and diphtheria. At 7 years old, she began prophylactic subcutaneous immunoglobulin therapy, which lasted 5 years and resulted in a significant reduction of infections.
test_results: The patient was studied by genetic analysis (sequencing of genomic DNA).
Orpha_name: Immunodeficiency due to interleukin-1 receptor-associated kinase-4 deficiency

case_report: The patient is a three-month-old male born prematurely at 33 weeks gestation, presenting with a one-week history of vomiting after feedings and irritability. He was admitted due to severe anemia. The patient's mother had stopped feeding Poly-Vi-Sol with iron two weeks prior, concerned it was hard on the patient's stomach. The patient's medical history includes pancytopenia, two blood transfusions for low hemoglobin levels, microcephaly, and notable dysmorphic features at birth, such as small ears, up-slanting palpebral fissures, flat nasal bridge, and widely spaced nipples. Early blood transfusions precluded metabolic screening. The patient's mother reported no other health concerns, including bleeding or recent illnesses, and the patient's growth was within normal limits. On admission, physical examination revealed a cough, pallor, dysmorphic features, pale mucous membranes, a systolic murmur, hydrocele, and significantly delayed capillary refill. Laboratory evaluations showed reduced red blood cells at 0.53 x 10^6/uL (normal range: 3.8-5.4 x 10^6/uL), hemoglobin at 1.6 g/dL (normal range: 11.1-14.1 g/dL), and platelets at 14 g/dL (normal range: 32.7-37.3 g/dL). White blood cells were 4.88 x 10^3/uL (normal range: 6.0-17.5 x 10^3/uL) and neutrophil percentage was 3% (normal range: 18-46%). Mean corpuscular volume was 92.5 fL (normal range: 68-84 fL) and lactate levels were 2.7 mmol/L (normal range: 0.5-2.2). LDH was elevated at 544 U/L (normal 125-220 U/L). Uric acid levels were low at 2.8 mg/dL (normal 3.5-7.2 mg/dL), and a leukemia/lymphoma panel by flow cytometry did not reveal any markers. Bone marrow biopsy showed ringed sideroblasts, cytoplasmic vacuolization, dysmyelopoiesis, dyserythropoiesis, and 60% cellularity (normal range: 50%-70%). Fecal pancreatic elastase testing was normal, and 3-methylglutaconic acid was not found in the patient's urine. Three blood transfusions with 10 mL/kg of packed RBCs were conducted, raising hemoglobin levels from 1.6 g/dL to 12.1 g/dL. The patient was also started on Poly-Vi-Sol with iron. Once stabilized, the patient was discharged to await results from genetic testing.
test_results: Deletion analysis of the mitochondrial genome revealed an 80% heteroplasmic 5kb known as m.8483_13459del4977.

case_report: The patient is a 51-year-old male who sustained an injury to the lateral femur of the right lower limb 4–5 years ago. Within 2 months post-injury, local papules measuring 1–3 mm appeared and gradually merged into infiltrative plaques. Over the past year, these plaques have extended significantly. The patient was initially seen at the outpatient service of the Second Hospital (Jilin University, Changchun, China) and was treated with an oral antifungal agent, Lanmeishu (terbinafine hydrochloride) at 250 mg/day for 1.5 months, without improvement in erythema. Subsequently, the patient was transferred to another hospital for surgical removal of the lesions. Post-surgery, the patient received anti-tuberculosis treatment for 3 months (0.6 g/day rifampicin and 300 mg/day isoniazid orally; and 0.75 g/day streptomycin administered by intramuscular injection for 2 weeks, followed by twice-weekly injections). Despite this treatment, the skin lesions did not improve, and new perioral and abdominal papules and tubercles (1–3 mm) appeared. The surgical site exhibited infiltrated erythema and dark red tubercles at the edges. On November 25, 2004, the patient was re-examined at the Second Hospital, Jilin University. Physical examination revealed a generally good condition with a right inguinal lymph node measuring 5–7 mm. Routine blood, urine, and liver function tests were normal. Rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test and fungal culture of the tissues were negative. Electrocardiogram, chest X-ray, and bone marrow aspiration showed no abnormalities. Serum IgG was elevated at 27.80 g/l (normal range: 7.230–16.850 g/l), while IgA, IgM, and complement C3 and C4 levels were within normal ranges. Dermatological examination showed an 8×18 cm scar on the lateral femur of the right lower limb with infiltrated erythema, tubercles, and slight red swelling at the center and edges. The abdomen had 5–6 papules and tubercles (1–3 mm). The left lateral perioral region had dense light-red papules (1–3 mm), some of which were partially fused with clear basal infiltration.
test_results: Histopathological examination showed dense mature plasma cell-dominant inflammatory cell infiltration in the deep dermis and between part of subcutaneous tissues, and small numbers of lymphocytes and polykaryocytes. Immunopathologenetic analysis showed that the infiltrated plasma cells were CD79a and CD138 positive.

case_report: The patient is a 32-year-old woman. She was born at full term (40 weeks) with a birth weight of 3830 grams, a length of 52 cm, and a head circumference of 36 cm. Both pre- and neonatal periods were uneventful. At 7 months, she experienced her first febrile bilateral tonic-clonic seizure. Between the ages of one and two, her seizures became more frequent, occurring daily. Although the frequency of seizures decreased somewhat during her school years, she continued to experience several bilateral tonic-clonic seizures each week, and her epilepsy remained resistant to medication. Her development appeared normal for the first 12 to 15 months; she could sit independently at 7 months, used a few words by 1 year, and had appropriate hand use. She began walking at 24 months. However, between 12 and 15 months, she started losing previously acquired skills, including hand function and verbal communication, and showed decreased interest in her surroundings. She developed bruxism and hand-washing stereotypies. She could walk independently until school age but gradually required support for walking. Throughout childhood, she had significant sleep disturbances, including episodes of screaming and laughing. Her respiration remained unaffected. Clinical examination at 32 years old showed that she could walk a few meters with support, had ataxic and apraxic hand movements without hand stereotypies, and had no verbal communication but maintained intense eye contact. Her muscle tone was normal, and she had a slight scoliosis. Her epilepsy continued to be a major issue, with daily to weekly bilateral tonic-clonic seizures. Genetic analyses of MECP2 at the age of 18 were negative.
test_results: WES disclosed the variant, NG_011906.1:g.76130G > T, NM_001165963.1: c.4246 G > T, p.(Asp1416Tyr) in SCN1A. Parental testing indicated that the mutation was de novo.

case_report: A 14-year-old female presented with missing or unerupted maxillary anterior teeth. Eight years prior, she experienced trauma to the maxillary anterior region, resulting in the avulsion of several deciduous teeth and fractures of others, which were subsequently extracted. Her medical history was unremarkable, and there was no family history of dental or genetic anomalies. Examination revealed a deficient maxilla on the right side, causing facial asymmetry. In the right maxillary arch, the central incisor, lateral incisor, and canine were missing or unerupted, with the alveolar mucosa in the area enlarged and covered by fibrous tissue. Additionally, there was a rotated first premolar, an erupting second premolar, and unerupted first and second molars on the right side. On the left side of the maxillary arch, only the central incisor was missing, with all other teeth present. In the mandibular arch, all teeth were present except for the third molars, and all teeth exhibited some degree of hypoplasia. Oral hygiene was poor, with an active carious lesion on the mandibular left first molar. There was also deficient maxillary growth on the right side, indicating arch collapse.
test_results: The mandibular dentition was normal, as was the left maxillary dentition, except the central incisor. In the maxillary anterior region, the right central incisor, lateral incisor, and canine showed malformed and retarded development as compared to the age of the child. There was complete absence of the left central incisor and the right first molar. The second molar was also malformed, but it was not as severe as the other malformed teeth. The malformed teeth had thin radio-opaque contours with no distinction between the enamel and dentin, and wide pulp chambers, giving a ‘ghost-like’ appearance. The crowns of the affected unerupted teeth were surrounded by radiolucent areas, probably representing enlarged dental follicles. Only an insignificant amount of root formation, was visible radiographically.

case_report: A 25-year-old pregnant female (G2P2L1) with a full-term pregnancy was referred for an elective cesarean section due to an excess of amniotic fluid. The patient had a 3-year-old healthy boy from her previous pregnancy. Prenatal sonography indicated the presence of excess amniotic fluid. A cesarean section was performed, resulting in the delivery of a female newborn weighing 3250 grams. The newborn exhibited extreme backward bending of the head and a left club foot. Mild difficulty in breathing was observed.
test_results: Cervicothoracic X-ray revealed cervical hyperextension. Brain and thorax CT scan without contrast with coronal, sagittal and 3-dimensional reformatted images of the vertebra and chest wall were obtained. Images revealed absence of the posterior portion of the corpus callosum and prominent cerebellar cistern. Cerebellar vermis is not appreciated in the brain CT scan. Multiple bony abnormalities are visualized, composed of occipital bone defect around the foramen magnum causing a 2.5 cm widening of the foramen, hyperextended cervical spines as well as unfused posterior elements of cervical and thoracic spines, hemivertebra at T1, hypoplasia of the mandible, hypotelorism, posterior fusion of T10-T11-T12 and C5-C6-C7, bifid ribs with posterior fusion (ribs 3 and 4, and 7 and 8) and anterior fusion (ribs 5 and 6) were seen. Transthoracic echocardiogram detected ventricular septal defect (VSD) (apical), patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) and patent foramen ovale (PFO). Abdominopelvic sonography revealed small-sized kidneys for gestational age on both sides (right side was 35 × 17 mm and left side was 33 × 16 mm). Other abdominal organs were normal.

case_report: A 48-year-old female presented with a long-standing, slowly enlarging, asymptomatic mass on the lateral surface of the left auricle, near the concha. The patient did not recall any trauma at the site. The lesion was a solitary, 0.8 cm, skin-colored, dome-shaped nodule with irregular borders. It had a central small pitted umbilication and a tuft of fine hair protruding from it. On palpation, the mass was smooth, rubbery to firm, and fixed to the intertragal notch of the left auricle without involving the cartilage. The rest of the physical examination was normal, with no local lymphadenopathy or other masses detected. A wide local excision was planned at the patient's request to remove the mass. The mass was completely excised and was found to be adherent to the auricular epidermis, necessitating exposure of the auricular perichondrium. Post-excision, the wound and exposed perichondrium were covered with a split-thickness skin graft. The excised tissue was single, firm, globular, grey-white, and measured 0.6×0.5×0.5 cm.
test_results: Histopathological examination showed a dilated central cystic follicle that communicated with the overlying skin surface. The dilated follicular opening showed keratin debris and hair. The follicle was lined with squamous epithelium and surrounded by numerous smaller secondary follicles, many of which contained fragments of hair shafts along with many variables sized hair follicles exhibiting varying degree of maturation. Epidermis and dermis unremarkably showed strands of stratified squamous epithelium. Many fibroblasts was observed at the the stroma.

case_report: An 8-year-old boy was referred to the medical genetics department on February 25, 2014, due to severe global developmental delay and multiple exostoses identified through radiologic examination. He was born to healthy, non-consanguineous Korean parents after a full-term pregnancy (40 weeks) with a birth weight of 2,400 grams (<3rd percentile). There were no perinatal complications. Developmental delays were observed at 3 months of age, characterized by incomplete eye contact and poor head control. Physical examination revealed hypotonia, ptosis, nystagmus, microcephaly, and craniosynostosis. Chromosome analysis of peripheral blood showed a karyotype of 46,XY. At 8 months, he underwent expansion cranioplasty for craniosynostosis. His developmental delays became more pronounced, and by 45 months, he was unable to sit independently or speak meaningful words. He had surgery for strabismus. At 5 years old, he was assessed using the Korean-Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence (K-WPPSI), resulting in a full-scale IQ composite score of less than 30, indicating severe intellectual disability. The Social Maturity Scale (SMS) showed a social quotient (SQ) of 17.8 and a social age of 0.91 years. At 6 years old, protrusions were noted on his right wrist and knee. A skeletal survey revealed multiple exostoses throughout the long bones. The cause of these exostoses was not identified at that time. At 8 years old, the progression of multiple exostoses was observed, and a thorough re-evaluation of clinical data and radiographs from 4 months of age was conducted. Initial skull radiographs and 3D reconstructed images showed premature craniosynostosis of the coronal suture and large biparietal foramina. Brain MRI indicated cortical atrophy with mild ventriculomegaly. Due to premature craniosynostosis, he underwent expansion cranioplasty of the coronal suture at 6 months old. Follow-up skull examination at 8 years old showed persistent but reduced biparietal foramina. At 6 years old, physical examination revealed severe growth retardation with a height of 96 cm (<3rd percentile), weight of 15.7 kg (<3rd percentile), and head circumference of 45 cm (<3rd percentile). Facial features included sparse eyebrows, nystagmus, a prominent nasal bridge, hypoplastic nares, a downturned mouth, and a high-arched palate. The patient exhibited hypotonia and was unable to sit or walk independently. Review of the chart indicated diagnoses of craniosynostosis and mental retardation.
test_results: The chromosomal microarray revealed an 8.6 Mb deletion at 11p11.2p12 [arr 11p12p11.2 (Chr11:39,204,770-47,791,278)×1]. This deletion resulted in haploinsufficiency for all three genes, included EXT2, ALX4, and PHA21F.

case_report: A 36-year-old male presented to the urology department at the age of 17 for evaluation of cryptorchidism and was subsequently referred to the endocrinology department for further management. On clinical examination, the patient was in good general health, exhibited a depressed mood, and showed no signs of dysmorphism. His weight was recorded at 81 kg, height at 160 cm, and body mass index at 31.50 kg/m². The patient had well-developed facial hair and pubic hair at stage V. The genital examination revealed a 9-cm penis (-1 SD) and a small, empty, pleated scrotal bursa. Hormonal assessment indicated elevated gonadotropin levels with FSH at 54.1 mIU/mL (normal range: 1.27-19.26) and LH at 23.9 mIU/mL (normal range: 1-7), while testosterone levels were undetectable.
test_results: Cytogenetic examination revealed a 46,XY karyotype. Karyotyping confirmed the patient to be a 46,XY male with no evidence of mosaicism in the blood cells. PCR amplification of the SRY gene indicated that the patient's SRY gene was normal. The AMH assay showed a level of <0.01 ng/mL (3.1-5.3). The abdominopelvic computed tomography did not reveal the presence of intra-abdominal testicles or any other detectable anomaly. A laparoscopy was subsequently performed and returned negative.

case_report: Patient 2 is a 73-year-old Caucasian male. At the age of 72, the patient began experiencing widespread itching, which was soon followed by intense pain, stiffness, and swelling in his left foot. The pain and stiffness rapidly spread to both legs, accompanied by extremely painful muscle cramps, ultimately resulting in the patient becoming dependent on a wheelchair.
test_results: EMG testing showed a left peroneal nerve lesion and CMUA at rest. Laboratory investigations were positive for anti-amphiphysin antibodies. Pulmonary biopsy led to the diagnosis of a small-cell lung carcinoma, which had been detected by computer tomography earlier.

case_report: A 55-year-old female patient was admitted on June 30, 2021, presenting with painless gross hematuria for one week. The patient has a history of congenital varicose veins and venous valvular insufficiency in the right lower limb, and has previously undergone varicose vein dissection in the same limb. Prior venography indicated the presence of superficial varicose veins. The patient reported that the skin pigmentation of the right lower limb was altered at birth, varicose veins became noticeable at age 17, and gross hematuria began at age 30. There is no similar condition reported in her immediate family, including parents and children. Physical examination showed wine-red patchy changes on the right lower limb, significant hypertrophy of the right lower limb with varicose veins, and hemangiomatous changes with swelling in the right perineum.
test_results: The CT urography showed decreased strengthening of the right kidney, swelling of the renal cortex, thickening of the wall of the upper part of the right ureter, and no obvious occupying of the bladder. Multiple varicose venous malformations were found, mainly manifested as: The right internal iliac vein and its branch were thickened obviously; The right hip vein has increased significantly; A large number of round calcification spots (phlebiolith) in the pelvic and lower abdomen. During the operation, ureteroscopy showed diffuse multiple hemorrhagic points of renal pelvis and calyx with red clots. The bleeding points in the bladder were mainly distributed on the right side, and the left part was normal. Varicose veins were visible in the mucosa, and extensive hemorrhagic points and small hemangioma protruding from the bladder mucosa.

case_report: A 62-year-old woman with a history of hypothyroidism and osteopenia experienced shortness of breath and fatigue while on a cruise in Central America. At the ship’s infirmary, she was found to have a complete heart block. After disembarking, she was taken to a nearby hospital where a permanent pacemaker was implanted. Initial evaluations, including basic laboratory tests and a Lyme titer, were normal. Upon returning home, she initially felt better but later visited her primary care physician due to exertional shortness of breath and intermittent palpitations. Blood tests showed a normal complete blood count and basic metabolic panel, with a slight increase in inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate [ESR] and C-reactive protein [CRP]). She was referred to a cardiologist, and her pacemaker was checked, confirming it was functioning normally without any arrhythmias.
test_results: A transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) showed normal left ventricular function (ejection fraction 55%), normal valves, and a moderate circumferential pericardial effusion without evidence of tamponade physiology with the pacemaker leads well placed at the anterolateral wall of the right ventricle. TTE, this time, revealed a moderate to large pericardial effusion with impending tamponade physiology. Pericardiocentesis was performed with immediate removal of 500 ml of bloody fluid and an additional 210 ml of drainage over the next 24 hours. The fluid analysis revealed a sterile, exudative fluid. Cytology was negative for malignancy. Computed tomography (CT) angiography was performed to rule out a pulmonary embolism, which showed a small to moderate pericardial effusion and moderate left pleural effusion. Thoracentesis removed 1 l and again revealed sterile, exudative fluid. CXR demonstrated the re-accumulation of the left pleural effusion. Repeat thoracentesis was attempted demonstrating sterile, exudative fluid. This time, TTE ruled out the presence of pericardial effusion.

case_report: A 58-year-old female was admitted to the hospital due to isolated proteinuria. In 2005, she was noted to have hypertension but no proteinuria during a health checkup. On September 1, 2007, she experienced gross hematuria for one week. On September 28, 2007, she visited a clinic for proteinuria detected during a health checkup. Urinalysis at that time showed proteinuria (2+) and occult blood (±), with a urinary protein excretion of 1.7 g/day. She was referred and admitted to the hospital on January 28, 2008, for further evaluation of proteinuria. Upon admission, physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 148/96 mmHg, a regular pulse rate of 64 beats per minute, and no systemic edema. Laboratory tests showed blood urea nitrogen at 16.5 mg/dL, serum creatinine at 0.91 mg/dL, total protein at 7.6 g/dL, serum albumin at 4.6 g/dL, total cholesterol at 242 mg/dL, hemoglobin at 13.4 g/dL, white blood cell count at 3700/μL, and platelet count at 203000/μL. Serological tests indicated C-reactive protein at 0.03 mg/dL, negative results for hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C virus antibody, C3 at 114 mg/dL, C4 at 104 mg/dL, CH50 at 60 U/mL, and antinuclear antibody at ×40. Urinalysis showed proteinuria of 1.35 g/day without hematuria or cylinduria but with many transitional cells per high-power field and 0 to 3 leukocytes per high-power field. Urinary chemistry results included N-acetyl-β-D-glucosaminidase at 6.5 U/L and β2-microglobulin at 237 μg/L. Creatinine clearance was measured at 103.0 L/day.
test_results: Urinary cytology showed class V. Abdominal computed tomography with contrast media pointed out a mass in the right renal pelvis in association with pelvic dilatation and slight thinning of renal cortex.
diagnosis: Urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis

case_report: A 15-year-old female presented with a painless swelling in the neck. On physical examination, she exhibited marfanoid habitus, bilateral palpable thyroid nodules, and multiple yellowish-white, sessile, painless nodules on the tongue.
