Laboratory results showed TSH at 2.29 mU/mL (reference range 0.27–4.2 mU/mL), free T4 at 1.30 ng/dL (reference range 0.93–1.7 ng/dL), free T3 at 3.42 pg/mL (reference range 1.8–4.6 pg/mL), antithyroglobulin antibody at 15.29 IU/mL (reference range 0–115 IU/mL), parathormone at 53.95 pg/mL (reference range 15–65 pg/mL), calcitonin at 528 pg/mL (reference range 0–11.5 pg/mL), and CEA at 29.2 mcg/L (reference range 0–2.5 mcg/L).
test_results: Ultrasound imaging of the thyroid gland revealed bilateral, hyperecogenic nodules containing foci of microcalcification with the largest diameter of 23 mm. The immunohistochemical staining of tumor sections revealed diffuse positive staining with chromogranin, NSE, calcitonin, CEA, synaptophysin, and keratin. There was no staining with thyroglobulin. The deposition of amyloid which was stained with crystal violet and congo red was detected in some foci. Tests for RET protooncogene in exon 14 (ser836 polymorphism) and exon 15 (ser904 polymorphism) were positive, but exons 10, 11, 13, and 16 were negative.

case_report: A 34-year-old male presented to our hospital with mild renal dysfunction and anemia identified during an annual check-up in 2023. The previous year's check-up in 2022 showed normal renal function and no anemia. Current blood tests in 2023 indicated a creatinine level of 1.37 mg/dL and hemoglobin level of 8.5 g/dL. The patient had no notable medical history and reported fatigue as his primary symptom. Upon arrival, his vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed several mobile, non-tender, pinky-head-sized lymph nodes on both sides of the neck. No other significant abnormalities, including splenomegaly, were detected during the physical examination. Blood biochemistry tests confirmed anemia, renal dysfunction, elevated inflammation markers, and a protein-albumin discrepancy. Immunological tests showed a polyclonal increase in immunoglobulins without a shift in the κ/λ ratio. A computed tomography (CT) scan identified multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the bilateral cervical region.
test_results: Pathological results showed numerous clusters of mature plasma cells. Immunostaining showed that all immunoglobulin staining was similar (no staining for specific immunoglobulins). Additional blood tests showed elevated interleukin-6 (IL-6); 23.4 pg/mL (normal value; <7.0 pg/mL). Human herpesvirus type 8 (HHV-8) DNA quantification was below detection sensitivity.

case_report: A 3-year-old male was brought to the clinic due to uncontrolled heart failure and worsening clinical condition. The patient presented in a severely ill state, exhibiting weakness, rapid heart rate, and rapid breathing. Upon admission, physical examination revealed an enlarged liver, thickened skin on the palms and soles, and woolly hair. Chest X-ray showed significant enlargement of the heart. Electrocardiogram findings included rightward axis deviation and ventricular tachycardia with a right bundle branch block pattern. Echocardiography indicated enlarged ventricles, second-degree insufficiency of the mitral and tricuspid valves, and reduced left ventricular function with an ejection fraction of 37%. Ventricular tachycardia was managed with an amiodarone infusion, but the patient's condition did not improve. The patient passed away suddenly on the seventh day of hospitalization.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed a heterozygous plakoglobin gene mutation (Pk2157Del2TG) in the parents and a homozygous gene mutation in the patient.

case_report: A 24-year-old Indian male with no prior health issues reported experiencing intermittent fever for 9 months and coughing with blood for 6 months. His vital signs were stable. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and coagulation profiles, were normal. Tests for antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and venereal disease research laboratory were negative. A chest X-ray revealed a round opacity in the left upper lobe.
test_results: A plain and contrast computed tomography chest showed saccular aneurysmal dilatation with mural thrombosis of descending/lower lobe segmental branches of PA on either side and upper lobe segmental artery on the left side. The average size of aneurysmal dilatation was about 2.5–3.2 cm. Filling defect/thrombosis was seen in one of the segmental branches in the left lower lobe.

case_report: A 35-year-old male presented with neck swelling, generalized weakness, progressive exertional dyspnea, abdominal discomfort, reduced appetite, and weight loss for 1 year. Physical examination revealed a palpable mass in the thyroid gland region and pallor. Cardiovascular examination identified a systolic murmur. Laboratory results showed hemoglobin at 8.7 gm/dL with a normal peripheral blood count. Urea was 84 mg/dL, creatinine was 2.7 mg/dL, and alkaline phosphatase was 980 U/dL. Other liver function test parameters were not significant.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) scan showed a right-sided cervical mass in the thyroid measuring 3.7 × 2.5 cm pushing the trachea to the left. CT-guided FNAC smears from the mass were highly cellular with round to oval cells that exhibited a stippled or granular nuclear chromatin with moderate pleomorphism. Serum calcium was raised to 13.1 mg/dL. Radiographs of both hands showed osteopenia of phalanges with sub-periosteal bone resorption of middle phalanges and erosion of tufts of terminal phalanges. Skull radiograph showed osteopenia with fine osteolytic lesions scattered within calvaria (salt pepper appearance). Kidney-ureter-bladder (KUB) radiography exhibited bilateral nephrocalcinosis. Ultrasonography (USG) of the abdomen showed bilateral contracted kidneys with nephrocalcinosis, mild hepatomegaly and ascites. Serum parathormone level was found to be markedly raised, 212 pg/ mL (normal range: 12-72 pg/mL). Histopathology showed a cellular tumor divided into nodules by broad fibrous bands. The tumor cells were arranged in trabecular and pseudo-rosette pattern separated by thin blood vessels showing monomorphic round to ovoid nuclei and clear cytoplasm; brisk mitoses were present (8 per 10 hpf).

case_report: The patient is a 13-month-old male of Chinese descent who was referred for genetic evaluation due to recurrent fever. He is the only child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents with no family history of genetic diseases. Pregnancy was uncomplicated, and no abnormalities were noted at birth. At 7 months old, the patient experienced recurrent fever (8 episodes within two months) with a maximum temperature of 39.2°C and a persistent upper respiratory tract infection. A small facial rash appeared following the fever. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable, with no palpable lymph nodes. Laboratory tests revealed a significant increase in lymphocyte proportion (84.8%, normal range 40-70%) with normal morphology and total white blood cell count (9.67*10^9/L). The CD19+ B cell population was elevated (3,432 cells/μL, normal range 240-1,317 cells/μL), and NK cell proportion was decreased (3.03%). The patient received immunizations and symptomatic treatments but no special treatment. Over the next six months, periodic fever episodes continued every 8 days, lasting 2-3 days each. At 13 months old, the patient was admitted again for recurrent fever. Routine blood tests and immunological investigations showed increased lymphocyte proportion and CD19+ B-cells, with decreased hemoglobin level (90g/L, normal range 110-149g/L).
test_results: A bone marrow biopsy showed hyperplastic anemia. An IgH rearrangement experiment indicated that the patient’s B cells were polyclonal. An abdominal CT scan showed multiple mesenteric lymphadenopathies. An ultrasound examination revealed a normal spleen size and an accessory spleen at the hilum.
diagnosis: B cell expansion with NF-κB and T cell anergy  due to a novel CARD11 germline mutation

case_report: A 6-year-old boy of average height and weight came to the ER in 2003 with a history of repeated vomiting and headaches for the past month. He was a student at a local public school. His past medical history was unremarkable, his immunizations were up to date, and he had no known allergies. Family history revealed that his father and paternal uncle had a similar condition. On physical examination, he was vitally stable. Notable findings included left-sided facial nerve palsy and an unsteady gait. Following initial investigations, further imaging of the brain was performed.
test_results: The report described a solid mass arising from the right cerebellar cortex, which was isointense to the gray matter on T1-weighted images and hypo to isointense to the gray matter on T2-weighted images. Postcontrast images showed an intense enhancement, which was almost homogenous. The mass was causing effacement of the fourth ventricles with dilatation of the third and lateral ventricles. The vertical height of the lesion was 4.2 cm; AP dimension was 4 cm, and the transverse diameter was 4.8 cm. There was no evidence of intracranial hemorrhage. Gray and white matter signals of supratentorial brain were within normal limits. No midline structural defect was seen.

case_report: An 18-year-old male with a history of ulcerative colitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis, managed with mesalamine and ursodeoxycholic acid respectively, reported sudden onset of right calf pain without trauma or exertion, followed by pain in the right buttock, 18 months after starting isotretinoin for nodulocystic acne. Isotretinoin was briefly paused for three months due to abnormal liver function tests but was otherwise consistently taken. Upon arrival at the Emergency Department, his vital signs were stable. Laboratory results showed haemoglobin at 95 g/l (135–170), white cell count at 15.54 × 10^9/l (3.5–11), neutrophils at 11.48 × 10^9/l (1.7–7.5), ALT at 89 U/l (10–50), AST at 128 U/l (0–50), CRP at 55 mg/l (0–5), and CK at 3905 mg/l (39–308). Viral serology tests for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were negative. Initial treatment included analgesia, fluids, and discontinuation of isotretinoin. The patient was discharged with a follow-up scheduled for later that week. Within three days, he experienced pain in the left shoulder and weakness in both lower limbs, leading to an inability to bear weight. He returned to the hospital before the follow-up. Examination revealed reduced muscle strength in right hip flexion and extension (MRC grade 3/5), knee flexion and extension (MRC grade 4/5), and left shoulder abduction, adduction, flexion, and extension (MRC grade 4/5). Tenderness was noted over the right thigh, right buttock, and left deltoid, with no signs of erythema, rashes, or other dermatomyositis indicators. Repeat blood tests showed haemoglobin at 103 g/l (135–170), white cell count at 24.49 × 10^9/l (3.5–11), ALT at 70 U/l (−50), ALP at 156 U/l (30–130), CRP at 228 mg/l (0–5), and CK at 4331 mg/l (39–308). Immunology and myositis antibody panels were negative.
test_results: MRI demonstrated extensive inflammation of the right gluteus maximus with subcutaneous oedema. Electromyography showed patchy myopathic motor units in the upper and lower limb muscles, fibrillations and positive sharp waves in some of these muscle groups indicative of muscle membrane instability. CT pelvis demonstrated asymmetric expansion and oedema of the right gluteus maximus muscle with associated tracking of fluid into the posterior and lateral compartments of the thigh.

case_report: A 6-month-old male presented with delayed motor and mental development. He was born at full term following an uncomplicated pregnancy, with a birth weight of 3,250 g. No information was available regarding head circumference at birth. The family history was unremarkable, and the parents were fourth-degree relatives. Upon admission, his weight was 8,000 g and height was 68 cm, both within normal percentiles. His head circumference measured 40 cm, which is below the 3rd percentile. He exhibited poor head control and was unable to sit with support. The patient displayed hypertonia and hyperactive deep tendon reflexes. He was conscious but did not respond to visual or auditory stimuli. Other neurological and systemic examinations were normal. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, serum biochemical analysis, urine analysis, and thyroid function tests, were all within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography showed no abnormalities. The auditory brainstem response test did not detect the fifth wave. Karyotype analysis revealed a normal 46, XY pattern.
test_results: The magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed absence of the lateral and third ventricles. The thalami were fused and the corpus callosum was absent. The interhemispheric fissure and falx cerebri were formed. There was abnormal oriented sulcus at the vertex on the left. The posterior fossa and fourth ventricle were normal. The orbital MRI was also normal.

case_report: A 17-year-old Arabic male presented with chest and back pain for several days before admission. He reported a non-productive cough for 2 days but did not have a fever. On examination, his heart rate was 110 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 25 breaths per minute, and his temperature was 36.9°C. Chest examination revealed left basal crackles and decreased air entry. Initial laboratory investigations are detailed in Table. A chest x-ray indicated left retrocardiac and left lower lung zone opacity, suggesting left lower lobe consolidation, as shown in Figure. The patient was treated with ceftriaxone 1000 mg daily for seven days and azithromycin 500 mg daily for three days as an inpatient. Despite treatment, his condition did not improve, and he required oxygen two days after admission. He became more tachypneic and tachycardic, necessitating transfer to the medical intensive care unit where he was started on non-invasive ventilation. COVID-19 tests and all cultures were negative.
test_results: Hemoglobin electrophoresis was done.
diagnosis: Acute chest syndrome in sickle cell disease/HBE patient

case_report: A 48-year-old female patient presented with a history of slowly progressive, asymptomatic purpuric to erythematous eruptions on her left foot for 4 to 5 years. These skin lesions had initially been inspected by an internist. The patient had no significant past medical history of diabetes, hypertension, or drug or trauma history prior to the onset of her lesions. No member of her family had similar lesions. She had received hormone replacement therapy for 3 years, which was discontinued 3 months prior to the examination. She felt that the lesions progressed rapidly during the 3-year period. Laboratory data, including complete blood count, platelet aggregation tests, prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time, bleeding time, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, estrogen, progesterone, and other biochemistries, were within normal limits. She was referred to a dermatologist, and the examination revealed multiple grouped, nonblanchable, red to violaceous macules on an erythematous background extending from the left sole to the toes. On close examination with a hand lens, the blood contents of the lesions were clearly within capillary loops without evidence of hemosiderin deposition.
test_results: A skin biopsy specimen revealed hyperkeratosis and many dilated and proliferated capillaries in the papillary dermis. No significant inflammatory cell infiltration or red blood cell extravasation was seen.

case_report: A nine-year-old girl presented with complaints of forgetfulness and morning clumsiness for the past two months. The patient showed a decline in interest in daily homework and social activities, becoming reluctant to attend school. Teachers observed difficulties in learning and memorizing new lessons. The patient isolated herself from friends and showed a lack of interest in daily activities. A week after the onset of memory issues, she experienced jerking of the right arm. These jerks were unilateral, repetitive, lasted for a few seconds, and typically occurred in the morning, two to three times per day. Her consciousness remained intact with no up-rolling of eyeballs, frothing, or tongue biting. She responded to simple commands like “open your mouth” or “close your eyes.” There was no associated fever, photosensitivity, hearing loss, double vision, limb weakness, paraesthesia, or urinary incontinence. She visited multiple general practitioners and local faith healers, but the treatment did not show any improvement. Her developmental history was normal, and she attained normal milestones. The patient had four siblings, and there was a family history of epilepsy on the maternal side. There was no history of diabetes mellitus, ischemic heart disease, tuberculosis, or close contact with tuberculosis. On general physical examination, the patient had an average height and build, was lying in bed comfortably, and was oriented to time, place, and person. Higher mental function and speech were normal. The mini mental state examination (MMSE) score was 23 with no signs of meningeal irritation. Both pupils were equally reactive to light with normal extraocular muscle movement in all directions of gaze. All other cranial nerves were intact. The motor examination was normal, with a Medical Research Council (MRC) score of 5 in all limbs. Sensory examination was also normal, with standard cerebellar and sensory system findings.
test_results: The EEG showed generalized discharges of spikes and polyspikes of frequency 2-3 Hz with a normal background of alpha wave rhythm.

case_report: The patient, a 66-year-old male, experienced progressive weakness and muscle atrophy in both lower and upper extremities over a span of 20 years. Initially, he noticed bilateral calf atrophy without motor impairment, followed by weakness in the distal lower extremities five years later. Ten years ago, he began to experience weakness in his hands, starting with the right hand. He had a history of hypertension, a myocardial infarction 20 years ago treated with coronary angioplasty twice, recurrent trigeminal neuralgia, heavy smoking, and social drinking. His medications included aspirin, diltiazem, enalapril, atorvastatin, and clopidogrel. His brother had died at 64 years old from an unknown neurological disorder that caused quadriplegia and required a tracheostomy. His father died of a stroke at an old age. Neurological examination showed intact higher cognitive functions and normal cranial nerve examination except for anisocoria (3 mm on the right, 2 mm on the left) with normal light and accommodation responses. There was significant atrophy in the hand interosseous muscles, thenar eminences, calves, and feet bilaterally. Motor testing revealed bilateral weakness in finger abduction and adduction (4/5 on the MRC scale), and in the lower extremities, weakness in plantar (4/5), dorsal (3/5), flexion, inversion (4/5), and eversion (4/5) of the feet. Proximal muscles of the upper and lower extremities showed no significant weakness. Tendon reflexes were absent in all extremities, and plantar responses were not elicited bilaterally. There was no ataxia on finger-nose or heel-shin testing. Sensory examination showed hypoalgesia and reduced temperature sensation in a stocking-glove distribution, mild deficits in joint position sense in all extremities, more pronounced in the lower extremities, and severely reduced pallesthesia in both hands and abolished in both feet. The patient could not walk on heels or toes and had a steppage gait bilaterally. Motor nerve conduction studies in 2009 showed absence of compound muscle action potentials (CMAPs) in the peroneal and tibial nerves on the left side, increased distal latency (3.5 ms in the ulnar nerve to 5.7 ms in the median nerve), and decreased motor conduction velocity (18–32 m/s) in the median and ulnar nerves bilaterally. Sensory testing showed no sensory nerve action potentials in the sural, median, and ulnar nerves on the left side. Electromyography (EMG) revealed spontaneous activity and a neuropathic recruitment pattern in the anterior tibial muscles bilaterally. A second neurophysiological examination in 2014 showed increased distal latencies, decreased conduction velocities, absence or prolonged latencies of F-waves with A-waves, and proximal conduction blocks. EMG showed fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves in the tibialis anterior muscles bilaterally, with a neuropathic pattern of motor unit recruitment observed in the gastrocnemius, rectus femoris, and extensor digitorum communis muscles. Reduced motor unit recruitment was noted in the left deltoid muscle. Nerve ultrasound showed increased size of the median and ulnar nerves in the middle portion of the arm and forearm, but not in the carpal tunnel or elbow. Lumbar puncture results showed increased protein with no nucleated cells. Despite repeated administration of intravenous immune globulin, no objective improvement was observed, and the patient's condition progressively worsened, requiring the use of a cane for walking. Additionally, the patient developed parkinsonism, gait unsteadiness, and frequent falls, which did not respond to antiparkinsonian medications.
test_results: This WES analysis revealed the presence of two heterozygous pathogenic variants in the FIG4 gene (OMIM 609390), namely the known pathogenic variant c.122T>C (p.Ile41Thr), and the novel frameshift variant c.1795delC (p.His599Ilefs*24), respectively. These variants were verified by Sanger sequencing and we established that they were in different alleles by testing the patient's unaffected daughter, who harbored only the His599Ilefs*24 variant.

case_report: A 35-year-old Hispanic male arrived at the emergency department with a sudden increase in headache severity over the past four days. The headaches were widespread and not confined to any specific area of the head, and over-the-counter pain medications did not provide relief. There was no history of trauma, fever, night sweats, loss of consciousness, sensitivity to light, neck stiffness, or visual problems. His medical history included migraine headaches, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and benign essential hypertension. On physical examination, the patient had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 3T while on 15 liters of oxygen, pupils measured 2-2.5 mm bilaterally, and he was unresponsive to both verbal and painful stimuli. He exhibited paralysis in both upper and lower limbs. Vital signs were as follows: heart rate of 89 beats per minute, blood pressure of 159/78 mmHg, temperature of 37°C, respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 99% on 15 liters of oxygen. Laboratory results showed respiratory alkalosis with a blood pH of 7.54 and pCO2 of 27.5 mmHg, normal oxygenation at 159.3 mmHg, and a negative urinary toxicology screen.
test_results: A head CT scan revealed a 1.5 cm hematoma in the left thalamus with expansion into the lateral ventricle. Cerebral angiogram demonstrated complete stenosis of the left internal carotid artery (ICA) and partial stenosis of the right ICA.

case_report: A 30-year-old female presented with a 6-month history of numbness and tingling on the left side of her face accompanied by dental pain. She was administered carbamazepine, which led to partial improvement. She did not report any fever, cough, chest pain, arthritis, shortness of breath, or muscle pain. She experienced Raynaud’s phenomenon for the past 2 years. She reported paraesthesia in her left foot, followed by an acute onset of left foot drop lasting 1 week. Two weeks later, she experienced tingling, numbness, and weakness in her right foot. There was no history of proximal muscle weakness, bladder or bowel issues, or other cranial nerve involvement. Physical examination showed puffy hands with sclerodactyly. Sensory perception was reduced in the areas served by the maxillary and mandibular branches of the left trigeminal nerve, but the corneal reflex remained intact. Neurological examination indicated hypotonia in both lower limbs. Weakness was observed in the dorsiflexors, invertors, and evertors of both feet, with muscle power graded at 3/5 in the right lower limb and 2/5 in the left lower limb according to the Medical Research Council (MRC) scale. All deep tendon reflexes were normal except for the bilateral ankle reflex, which was absent. Sensation was decreased over the S1–S2 dermatomes. Vibration and proprioception senses were absent in the left leg and decreased in the right leg. Other system examinations were unremarkable.
test_results: Her electromyographic findings are consistent with axonal sensorimotor neuropathy. Right sural nerve biopsy confirmed vasculitic neuropathy. Laboratory investigations revealed positive ANA (Speckled pattern, 1:160) with anti-U1RNP antibody level 100.0 U/ml (normal <10U/ml) and negative anti-Ro/La, Sm, dsDNA and Scl-70, anti-neutrophilic cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA). Her complement levels were normal. Her routine blood test showed a total leucocyte count of 10,500/mm, platelets 520,000/cmm, raised acute phase reactants like ESR 62 mm in 1st hour and C-reactive protein value 20 mg/L (Normal < 5mg/L). Liver function, renal function test and urinalysis were normal. Her Hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis, and human immune deficiency virus (HIV) serology were negative.

case_report: The patient is a 32-year-old male with a 30-year history of jaundice. In May 2020, he experienced a loss of appetite after consuming approximately 500 mL of beer (equivalent to 20 g of ethanol). He took Chinese medicine with unknown ingredients for a week without symptom relief. Subsequently, he developed dizziness, headache, and mild neuropsychological symptoms. Laboratory tests revealed abnormal liver function with decreased albumin (23.8 g/L) and elevated aspartate aminotransferase (148 U/L), alanine aminotransferase (54 U/L), total bilirubin (411.8 µmol/L), indirect bilirubin (266.3 µmol/L), and direct bilirubin (145.5 µmol/L). A blood routine test indicated a high proportion of neutrophils (81.5%) and reduced hemoglobin (109 g/L). Prothrombin time activity was 42%, and the Coombs test was negative. Blood ammonia levels (16 µg/dL), fasting plasma lipids, autoantibodies profile, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, and immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM, and IgE) were within normal ranges. Viral hepatitis markers were negative. Imaging studies, including computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging, showed hepatosplenomegaly. Brain CT scans were normal.
test_results: Sanger sequencing of the UGT1A1 gene identified a compound heterozygous mutation in this patient, which was inherited from his mother (c.211G>A, p.G71R) and his father (c.-3279T>G; c.572C>T, p.S191F).

case_report: A 7-year-old male from Poland, born to healthy, non-consanguineous parents, was delivered at 39 weeks gestation. At birth, he was small for gestational age with a weight of 1904 grams (<3rd centile), a length of 46 cm (<3rd centile), and a head circumference (OFC) of 26 cm (6.5 cm < 3rd centile). He required two-stage bowel surgery to address a type IIIb intestinal atresia on the 2nd and 7th days of life. At 2 years old, he remained microcephalic with an OFC of 36 cm (9.5 cm < 3rd centile).
test_results: Brain MRI revealed colpocephaly.

case_report: A 41-year-old woman presented with a mass on the left upper lip and difficulty in pronunciation. The mass developed after she bit the upper lip 5 years earlier. The volume of the mass did not decrease, and the patient experienced pain. One year after the mass appeared, she visited an otolaryngologist. The mass was initially thought to be a mucocele and was aspirated, but only blood was obtained, and the size of the lesion remained unchanged. Two years after the aspiration, the mass increased in size, prompting a visit to a plastic surgeon. Ethanol was injected into the lesion twice; the first injection resulted in a slight reduction in size, but there was no change after the second injection. Two years after the second injection, she consulted a dental clinic and was subsequently referred to our department. Oral examination revealed a well-defined submucosal single nodule, approximately 30 × 20 mm in size, located in the left upper lip. The overlying mucosa was smooth with a bluish discoloration. On palpation, the nodule was elastic, firm, and mobile. Cervical lymph nodes were not palpable.
test_results: MRI revealed a relatively well-demarcated lesion in the left upper lip. The lesion showed low signal intensity on T1-weighted images; however, it had a high signal area suspecting the subacute bleeding image in the centre of tumor. The lesion showed mostly high signal intensity on T2-weighted images. Immunohistochemically, most endothelial cells lining the cavernous spaces, spindle cells within solid areas, and epithelioid cells within both areas strongly reacted with vimentin. The endothelial cells lining the cavernous spaces reacted strongly with CD34, CD 31, factor VIII, smooth muscle actin (SMA), and Wilms tumor-1 (WT-1). The spindle cells within solid areas focally reacted with CD34, CD31, SMA, and WT-1, whereas epithelioid cells were positive for SMA, WT-1 and negative for CD34, CD31. S100 protein, AE1/AE3, D2-40, and EMA were negative in endothelial cells, epithelioid cells, and spindle cells.

case_report: In June 2012, a 50-year-old man came to our hospital with an itchy papular skin rash on his lower limbs, dry mouth, a 6 kg weight loss, fatigue, weakness in the lower limbs, and difficulty with movement. Initial laboratory tests indicated elevated levels of gamma globulins, increased liver enzymes, and markers of inflammation. Physical examination revealed enlarged lymph nodes in the neck and groin areas. Further tests showed that the elevated gamma globulins were polyclonal, predominantly immunoglobulin G (IgG) at 50 g/L, with increased levels of kappa and lambda light chains. Complement proteins C3 and C4 were decreased, while beta-2 microglobulin was elevated. Serology tests for various infections and autoimmune markers, including cryoglobulin, ANA, AMA, ENA, ANCA, anti-DNA, LAC, HIV, HBV, Salmonella, Brucella, Leishmania, Parvovirus, Strongyloides Stercoralis, Bartonella, EBV, and CMV, were negative. A CT scan showed slightly enlarged lymph nodes in the mediastinum, retroperitoneum, and iliac regions. Electromyography (EMG) indicated mild sensorimotor neuropathy. PET/CT scanning, performed with 370 MBq of 18F-FDG after a 6-hour fast, revealed multiple areas of increased radiopharmaceutical uptake corresponding to lymph nodes in the Barety, aortopulmonary, subcarinal, hilar, celiac, para-aortic, right common iliac, and bilateral inguinal regions.
test_results: The inguinal lymph node biopsy revealed presence of capsular fibrosis, histiocytosis, plasma cell infiltration, and interfollicular plasmacytosis with large CD30 positive cells. Immunohistochemistry showed the prevalence of mature IgG positive plasma cells with a significant presence of IgG4 positive cells.
diagnosis: plasma cell variant of multicentric Castleman disease

case_report: A 7-year-old male presented with progressive hearing loss in the right ear, imbalance, headaches, and projectile vomiting for one month, along with episodes of transient loss of consciousness lasting about 30 minutes each. Physical examination revealed grade 4 papilledema, infranuclear facial palsy on the right side, sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear, impaired gag reflex, and cerebellar signs on the right side. MRI with gadolinium contrast identified an extra-axial lesion in the right cerebellopontine angle measuring 4×4.5×5.5 cm, isointense on T1W and hyperintense on T2W with intense contrast enhancement. The lesion extended into the internal auditory meatus along with the 7th/8th nerve complex, displacing and distorting the brainstem and fourth ventricle to the left, without hydrocephalus. The lesion was approached via a right retromastoid craniectomy. The tumor was firm, fleshy, moderately vascular, and mucinous at the lower pole with a well-defined plane of cleavage from the brainstem and cerebellum. The 7th and 8th nerves were not distinguishable from the tumor and could not be preserved during surgery. Complete excision was achieved. Postoperatively, the patient required lateral tarsorraphy to prevent corneal exposure in the right eye and was discharged on the 7th postoperative day. Three weeks later, he presented with a pseudomeningocoele at the operative site. A contrast-enhanced CT scan confirmed complete tumor excision, hydrocephalus, and subgaleal CSF collection at the surgical site. A ventriculoperitoneal shunt was placed on the left side, effectively managing the pseudomeningocoele. The patient received fractionated external beam radiotherapy (5400 cGY/30 fractions) but declined further treatment. At a 6-month follow-up, he exhibited mild ataxia but was otherwise asymptomatic. MRI of the brain showed no recurrence 6 months post-surgery.
test_results: Histopathological examination of surgical specimen showed a cellular tumor with mild to moderately pleomorphic round nuclei, coarse chromatin, and conspicuous nucleoli, with moderate to abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm with suggestion of cytoplasmic striations in places. The tumor cells were immunoreactive for desmin, vimentin, and myogenin. GFAP, synaptophysin, and neurofilament were negative.

case_report: A 13-year-old girl, previously in good health, presented with fever and painful swelling on the right side of her neck for 3 days. Initial treatment with oral clarithromycin was given based on elevated white blood cell count (11.5 × 10^3) and C-reactive protein (CRP) level (76 mg/dL). Due to lack of improvement, she sought specialist care on the 5th day of illness with worsening symptoms. Physical examination revealed tender right cervical lymphadenitis without tonsillar or pharyngeal inflammation. Small blisters (1–3 mm) were noted on the trunk. After 2 days, she developed conjunctivitis, vomiting, diarrhea, a generalized erythematous macular rash, and erythematous mucous membranes. Her pulse rate was 120/min and blood pressure was 80/60 mmHg. Laboratory findings showed neutrophil leukocytosis with elevated CRP, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), serum ferritin, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), and alanine aminotransferase (ALT). Serum procalcitonin and blood cultures were negative. Chest X-ray was normal, electrocardiogram (ECG) indicated sinus tachycardia, and a 2D transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a structurally normal heart with prominent and mildly dilated coronary arteries, without ectatic segments or aneurysms. Troponin I levels were normal.
test_results: Anti-COVID 19 IgM and IgG were positive in very high titres.
Orpha_name: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children and adults

case_report: The patient is a 26-month-old girl born to first-degree consanguineous Iranian/Turkish parents. She was born at term with a birth weight of 3200 grams and received routine vaccinations in Iran, including BCG at birth, Polio, Hepatitis B, Diphtheria, Tetanus, Haemophilus Influenza type B, Pertussis, and MMR until 18 months old, without notable adverse events. She had an older sister who passed away at 1.5 years old with diarrhea as the main symptom. At 18 months, she was hospitalized for pneumonia and otitis media with a perforated tympanic membrane and pus discharge. Her growth and development were age-appropriate, and she had no prior hospitalizations or significant infections. Shortly after discharge, she developed swelling, tenderness, and heat in her right thigh, unable to bear weight. She was readmitted for suspected acute osteomyelitis. An X-ray of the right femur indicated osteomyelitis. An open biopsy revealed Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) DNA complex in tissue sections from her right femur, confirmed by the Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra assay. A smear of skeletal canal fluid showed many acid-fast positive bacilli. Chest radiographs of the patient and her parents were evaluated; her parents had no pulmonary TB lesions, but the patient's X-ray showed a round density in the middle lobe of the right lung. They had no contact history of TB. She was treated with Isoniazid, Rifampin, Ethambutol, Pyrazinamide, and vitamin B6 for 9 months. The patient's unusual infection prompted an immunological workup. Initial laboratory data suggested further evaluation, but her parents declined. A few months later, she was referred to the hospital with fever, cough, and shortness of breath, and was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) due to severe tachypnea and respiratory distress. She received empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics covering bacteria, viruses, and fungi, but no pathogenic microorganism was isolated. Despite standard treatment, her respiratory condition worsened, leading to intubation. Laboratory results showed anemia, lymphopenia, decreased CD4+ count, and CD4/CD8 ratio, similar to previous records. Increased CD19+, CD20+, CD16+, and CD56+ cell counts were noted. Her anti-diphtheria antibody titer was below the protective level despite vaccination. She had elevated immunoglobulin (Ig) E and slightly reduced IgM levels.
test_results: The WES analysis and Sanger sequencing revealed a homozygous frameshift deletion mutation c.1512delG (p.I505Sfs*28) at exon 16 in the DOCK2 gene loci.
diagnosis: Combined Immunodeficiency due to DOCK2 gene mutation
Orpha_name: Combined immunodeficiency due to DOCK2 deficiency

case_report: A 33-year-old Sudanese male, generally in good health, visited the rheumatology clinic due to a five-year history of pain and swelling in the forefoot, specifically around the first metatarsal bone. The pain intensified with standing, walking, and exposure to cold weather, and was not effectively managed with painkillers. Two years ago, the pain episodes became more severe and lasted longer, significantly impacting his quality of life by limiting his movement and daily activities. Over time, the discomfort extended to his feet, ankles, and knee joints. The patient reported no history of fever or other inflammatory symptoms. On physical examination, he was found to be of average build (176 cm in height, 60 kg in weight, and a BMI of 19.4) with normal vital signs. Joint examination showed swelling, tenderness, warmth, and restricted movement in the metatarsal joints, particularly during dorsiflexion.
test_results: X-ray radiographs showed flattened and sclerotic changes in the distal end of metatarsal bones, especially the first one of both feet. A mild degree of flattening and erosion of the articulation surface were shown at the ankle joints. MRI demonstrated an ill-defined patchy marrow edema signal of the head of the first, third, and fourth metatarsal bones as well as the shaft of the proximal phalanx of the fourth toe with associated soft tissue edema.

case_report: A 47-year-old woman with a history of plaque psoriasis, joint pain, and neuropathy managed with gabapentin presented with a worsening ulcer on her calf. She also reported generalized weakness since her hospital stay. Physical examination revealed a large ulcer with a dusky gray border on the calf. Additionally, there were retiform purpura with central necrosis and surrounding erythema on the hip and dorsal hands. Punch biopsies (4 mm) showed characteristics of both occlusive vasculopathy and vasculitis in small vessels. Tissue cultures were sterile, but blood cultures identified Enterococcus faecalis, Klebsiella oxytoca, and Serratia marcescens. The patient received intravenous cefepime and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a central line infection, which resolved the bacteremia, although the skin findings persisted. Two weeks later, new inflammatory retiform purpura appeared on the thigh, and the ulcer remained despite several weeks of antimicrobial treatment. A repeat biopsy showed similar overlapping features of occlusive vasculopathy and vasculitis. Urinalysis indicated large hematuria and proteinuria (100 mg/dL). Laboratory tests revealed a positive qualitative serum cryoglobulin assay at 24 hours, an elevated kappa:lambda ratio (2.02) in serum free light chains, and an IgA kappa gammopathy on serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP). Quantitative cryoprecipitate analysis did not detect IgA, IgM, or IgG. RF assay was negative, and C3 and C4 levels were normal. HCV serology was negative. Subsequent bone marrow biopsy and flow cytometry of peripheral blood and bone marrow were unremarkable.
test_results: Serum cryoglobulins were identified again at 24 hours, and quantitative analysis of the cryoprecipitate demonstrated only polyclonal IgG, without any monoclonal proteins or IgA. RF was positive (18 IU/mL), and both C3 (69 mg/dL) and C4 (<8 mg/dL) levels were decreased.

case_report: A 2-month-old female infant, weighing 3.7 kg, presented with a history of breathlessness, feeding difficulty, and cyanosis. She was the second child of a non-consanguineous marriage and was born via normal vaginal delivery. There was no family history of congenital heart disease. Physical examination showed pallor, cyanosis, and dysmorphic facial features. Her heart rate was 154 beats per minute, and her respiratory rate was 60 breaths per minute. Blood pressure was measured at 75/35 mmHg, and oxygen saturation was 85% in room air. Signs of respiratory distress were present. All peripheral pulses were palpable. Cardiac auscultation revealed normal first and second heart sounds, a grade 3/6 ejection systolic murmur best heard at the left upper parasternal area, and an audible third heart sound. A chest X-ray showed an enlarged heart with a cardiothoracic ratio of 0.6 and pulmonary plethora.
test_results: The two-dimensional echocardiography, subcostal coronal views demonstrated the connection of the left-sided left atrium and the right-sided left ventricle through the mitral valve and the right-sided right atrium to be connected to the left-sided right ventricle through the tricuspid valve by anterior angulation of the transducer. It also shows the two great arteries arising from the right ventricle. 2-D and color Doppler imaging revealed the crossing of the atrioventricular connections. Short-axis views shows the right ventricle was superior and left ventricle was inferior with horizontal position of the ventricular septum. The standard 4-chamber view was not showing simultaneously all four chambers and both atrioventricular valves. Parasternal short axis view shows malposed great arteries. A large size inlet type of ventricular septal defect (bidirectional shunt) and a moderate size ostium secundum atrial septal defect (bidirectional shunt) were present. Biventricular function was normal.
diagnosis: Criss-cross heart with double outlet right ventricle

case_report: A 14-year-old boy (height = 140 cm, weight = 18 kg) from Fars province, southern Iran, born to first-cousin parents with no family history of genetic disorders, presented with failure to thrive, fatigue, generalized muscular atrophy, kyphoscoliosis, and flexion contracture of the knees and elbows. His motor symptoms began at age four with frequent falls, which worsened over time. He walked at 11 months without motor milestone delays. He had two prior admissions to the pediatric intensive care unit for pneumonia and respiratory distress. The patient exhibited nasal speech and sleep apnea and was using a BiPAP breathing machine. By age 12, scoliosis was noted, requiring bracing. Physical examination revealed cachexia and generalized muscular atrophy. Muscle power was decreased in the shoulder-girdle muscles, foot extensors, and limb muscles (4/5 MRC muscle scale). He had pes cavus and contractures in both knees and elbows, along with severe spine rigidity, with a chin-sternum distance of 15 cm. Transthoracic echocardiography showed mild pulmonary hypertension and mild tricuspid regurgitation. Pulmonary function testing indicated an FEV1 of 35% and FVC of 32% of predicted values. Serum calcium and phosphorus levels were 8.2 and 3.1 mg/dL, respectively. Elevated levels of creatine phosphokinase (CPK) (340 U/L) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) (1200 U/L) were observed. Nerve conduction study results were normal, but needle electromyography (EMG) showed myopathic changes in the deltoid, biceps, tibialis anterior, and rectus femoris muscles.
test_results: NGS data identified a novel, homozygous missense mutation in SEPN1 gene (chr1:25812784, NM_020451.2: exon:10, c. 1379 C > T, p.Ser460Phe). Sanger sequencing confirmed the identified mutation in SEPN1 in proband as homozygous (T/T). His mother, father and brother were confirmed to be heterozygous (C/T), and his sister homozygous for the wildtype allele (C/C).

case_report: A 32-year-old female presented with a recurrent lump in the right lumbar region. There were no associated urinary or bowel complaints. She had undergone surgery twice for similar lumps in a rural hospital 10 and 3 years prior. Her discharge card from the previous surgery indicated a diagnosis of lymphangioma. Case papers from the first surgery 10 years ago were not available. On physical examination, a lump in the right lumbar region just lateral to a previous paramedian incision was palpated. The rest of the abdomen was unremarkable. Ultrasonography revealed a multicystic complex mass in the right lumbar region measuring 25×8×7 cm. A computed tomography scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed a 25×10×6.5 cm well-defined, non-enhancing, lobulated, multiloculated cystic lesion in the right paracolic gutter on the lateral aspect of the ascending colon. Inferiorly, it was abutting the lateral wall of the urinary bladder. Similar morphology lesions were observed in the pouch of Douglas and mesentery. The patient underwent surgery with a retroperitoneal approach as the majority of the mass was retrocolic in position. An incision was made below and parallel to the 12th rib, extending from the posterior axillary line and going anteriorly towards the umbilicus, with the patient in the left lateral position. Initially, the retroperitoneal component of the lesion was dissected out from the kidney and ureter, and lastly from the retroperitoneal surface of the colon. During this process, the peritoneum was opened and the intraperitoneal component, including the pelvic component, was completely removed. Intraoperative findings showed a cystic multiloculated mass loosely attached to the serosal surfaces of the ascending colon, extending into the pelvis with intraperitoneal extension into the pouch of Douglas. The rest of the appendix, cecum, large and small bowel appeared grossly normal. Both ovaries and the uterus were visualized and found to be normal. The lesion was friable, so care was taken to avoid rupture and contamination of the pelvis with the cyst fluid. Complete resection of the lesion was performed.
test_results: Histopathology showed cystic spaces lined by flattened cuboidal to hobnail epithelium separated by thin fibrous septa. The lining epithelium showed strong immunopositivity for calretinin and immunonegativity for CD31.

case_report: A four-month-old male infant was brought to the pediatric emergency department with a two-day history of fever, rapid breathing, and multiple episodes of vomiting. The infant, the first child of consanguineous parents, exhibited respiratory distress, drowsiness, and severe dehydration upon arrival. Initial measurements recorded were a weight of 5.5 kg, height of 63 cm, and vital signs including a temperature of 39°C, respiratory rate of 52 breaths per minute, heart rate of 180 beats per minute, blood pressure of 75/50 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation of 95% in room air. Laboratory tests showed elevated blood glucose levels and ketoacidosis. A chest CT scan revealed a unifocal ground-glass opacity in the apical segment of the right upper lobe. A nasopharyngeal swab tested positive for SARS-COV-2 via rRT-PCR. Blood and urine cultures were negative. The infant received isotonic fluids and intravenous insulin and was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit. Vital signs, electrolytes, and blood glucose were monitored regularly. No additional treatment for COVID-19 was administered. The infant's consciousness and overall condition improved over time, and the ketoacidosis resolved after two days of treatment. Breastfeeding and subcutaneous Neutral Protamine Hagedorn (NPH) insulin were started, with an initial dose of 1.5 units at night. Blood glucose levels were monitored to adjust the insulin dosage, which was gradually increased to one unit in the morning and one and a half units at night. The fever subsided after three days, and the infant was discharged after seven days.
test_results: A homozygous missense variant was detected in the EIF2AK3 gene.

case_report: A 44-year-old female experienced an unprovoked saddle pulmonary embolism (PE) leading to pulseless electrical activity and multiple bilateral cerebral infarctions. The PE was managed with a tissue plasminogen activator, and the patient recovered with only a mild anoxic brain injury. Comprehensive cardiology evaluation, including a trans-esophageal echocardiogram, telemetry, and extended cardiac rhythm monitoring, revealed no cardiologic causes. During hospitalization, the patient was diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia, reported a history of menorrhagia, and received an iron infusion. She was referred to hematology for anticoagulation management and continued anticoagulation therapy with rivaroxaban. The patient underwent a hysterectomy for fibroids. Two years later, she returned to the hematology clinic with hemoglobin (Hgb) of 15.3 g/dL, hematocrit of 47.2%, ferritin of 469 ng/mL, and platelet count of 344 per uL. JAK2 mutational analysis and hereditary hemochromatosis (HH) mutation tests were negative. A sleep study indicated obstructive sleep apnea, and the patient began using nocturnal continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP).
test_results: Reflex testing for thrombopoietin (TPO) receptor mutations, encoded by the myeloproliferative leukemia virus (MPL) oncogene gene, exhibited a positive mutation. Chromosome sequence analysis (CSA) revealed a heterozygous variant with the genomic change Chr1(GRCh37):g.43814969_43814970delinsGG, a variant predicted to result in a single amino acid substitution of leucine for glycine at codon 502 in exon 10 of the MPL gene. A bone marrow biopsy revealed slight hypercellularity at 80% with maturing trilineage hematopoiesis and mildly increased megakaryocytes. There was no evidence of dysplasia nor the typical morphologic “staghorn megakaryocytes” seen in ET.

case_report: A 22-year-old Japanese woman was admitted for inpatient care due to high fever, oral aphthae, joint pain in both upper and lower limbs, and skin eruptions on her lower legs that had persisted for 3 days. Initial physical examination revealed a small painful ulcer in the mouth, multiple painful red and swollen plaques on the front of the lower legs, and small red pustular lesions on the back. Her body temperature exceeded 39°C, and she experienced general malaise. There was no relevant family history, including collagen diseases. Laboratory tests, including complete blood cell count and liver and kidney function tests, were within normal limits. However, serum C-reactive protein (CRP) levels were elevated at 5.6 mg/dL (normal range, 0–0.2 mg/dL). Tests for influenza Types A and B antigens using nasal aspirate samples were negative. Blood and urine cultures were negative. Serum samples were negative for IgM and IgG antibodies against herpes simplex virus and coxsackievirus A16. Serological tests indicated past infections with Epstein–Barr virus, rubella virus, and cytomegalovirus. Serum antinuclear antibodies and rheumatoid factor were negative. A skin biopsy from an erythematous area on the right lower leg showed lobular and septal panniculitis with an inflammatory infiltrate mainly composed of lymphocytes, consistent with EN. The high fever and skin eruptions improved with intravenous ampicillin hydrate 2 g/day and oral acetaminophen 800 mg/day for 3 days. She was discharged on day 4. However, she was readmitted on day 8 due to high fever, general malaise, painful swelling and redness of the ears, nose pain, and blurred vision. Blood and urine cultures remained negative. Computed tomography of the head and cerebrospinal fluid analysis were normal.
test_results: A skin biopsy obtained from erythema on the right lower leg showed lobular and septal panniculitis with an inflammatory infiltrate, predominantly composed of lymphocytes. Uveitis was diagnosed by an ophthalmologist in our hospital. Human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-B51 antigen was positive. A skin biopsy obtained from erythema on the left auricular cartilage showed a perichondrial infiltrate of lymphocytes admixed with histiocytes and neutrophils.

case_report: A 10-year-old male presented to the pediatrics emergency department with progressive abdominal distension over the past 4 years and swelling of the right cheek for 4 months, accompanied by discharge for 2 months. The lesion had been treated with drainage and aspiration of pus by his primary care physician, but it continued to discharge. The child also experienced a low-grade fever. He had oscillatory eye movements and decreased vision since the first year of life. There was no history of fractures. The child had received packed red blood cell transfusions at ages 6 and 8, with no available documentation. Developmental milestones were delayed. There was no history of jaundice, hematemesis, melena, epistaxis, gum bleeding, petechiae, easy bruising, or fits. The child was the sixth offspring of a consanguineous marriage, with no similar complaints or transfusions reported in siblings or extended family. On examination, the patient appeared pale with a draining sinus tract on his cheek below the lateral half of the right eye, frontal bossing, bilateral horizontal nystagmus, and poor dentition with carious teeth. He was underweight and short for his age, weighing 20 kg and measuring 118 cm in height. Vital signs included a heart rate of 120/min, temperature of 100 °F, blood pressure of 106/64 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 28/min, oxygen saturation of 98% on room air, and capillary refill time of less than 2 seconds. Severe pallor and a few petechial spots on the lower limbs were noted. Multiple lymph nodes were palpable bilaterally in the submandibular, preauricular, postauricular, and anterior cervical groups. Rachitic rosary was evident. Abdominal examination revealed a soft, distended, nontender abdomen with hepatosplenomegaly; the liver span was 18 cm, and the spleen tip was palpable 19 cm below the left costal margin. Detailed eye examination showed an intact visual field with reduced visual acuity and absent color vision. Pupils were equal in size and reactive to light, with no afferent pupillary defect and a normal accommodation reflex. Bilateral jerky nystagmus was present. Fundoscopy revealed bilateral optic nerve atrophy. Hearing was normal, and no other cranial nerve involvement was observed. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory investigations showed anemia and thrombocytopenia, with decreased hemoglobin and hematocrit levels. Total leukocyte count was within the normal range. Peripheral blood smear indicated normochromic red blood cells with anisocytosis, rouleaux formation, and reactive lymphocytes. Blood smear for malarial parasite was negative. Other laboratory results showed low serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D and calcium.
test_results: Chest x-ray revealed a generalized increase in bone density in the visualized clavicles, scapulae, and ribs. The diffuse osteosclerosis prompted a skeletal survey that showed periorbital sclerosis. Lateral radiograph of the skull also showed thickening of the calvarium and the visualized cervical vertebrae. Alternating radiodense and radiolucent lines were seen at the distal metaphyses of the radii and ulnae. Erlenmeyer flask deformities, characterized by reduced constriction of the diaphyses, were seen at the distal ends of the radii and the femora. A bone-within-a-bone appearance was visible in the iliac blades, in addition to a sandwich vertebrae appearance because of sclerosis of the vertebral endplates.

case_report: A 20-month-old girl presented with a progressively increasing number of multiple asymptomatic papules on the left side of the chest (C4, T1-3) and abdomen (T11, 12) that had appeared over the previous 17 months. Past medical history was unremarkable, with no sign or record of congenital defect. The patient had no family history of similar cutaneous lesions or abnormal disorders involving the central nervous system. Examination of the skin found three ipsilateral segmental plaques with hundreds of confluent papules distributed in a zosteriform pattern on the left chest and abdomen. Normal segments of skin intervened between the two zosteriform plaques. Plaques and papules had an erythematous to skin-colored tint and soft consistency. Among the numerous papules with a diameter of 2 to 4 mm, several larger (6 to 8 mm), discrete, dome-shaped papules were found. A complete inspection revealed none of the Café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, hypopigmented macules, periungual fibromas, gingival fibromas, or dental pitting. Neurological and ophthalmological examinations revealed no abnormal findings, and no laboratory abnormalities were observed. Other tests included chest X-ray, electrocardiogram, cranial X-ray, and magnetic resonance imaging. Results were within normal limits. Genetic study was not available.
test_results: Histopathologic examination showed normal epidermis and thickened collagen fibers in the dermis, with poor inflammatory elements. Masson-Trichrome staining for collagen revealed abundant proliferation of collagen fibers. Elastic staining showed decreased elastic tissues in the dermis. The histopathologic finding of a polypoid portion revealed prominent dermal dilated vessels with mild fibrosis in the upper and middle dermis, dense collagen bundles.

case_report: A 27-year-old male reported experiencing hair loss from the scalp over the past 6 months. The patient also noted itching and a slight burning sensation. The condition was progressive, affecting nearly the entire vertex area and extending to the parietal regions. Physical examination showed well-defined purplish plaques accompanied by skin atrophy.
test_results: Trichoscopy showed perifollicular scales, diminished follicular ostia and white dots. Blue-grey dots around the follicular structures were seen as a “target” pattern. Histopathology of a lesion showed infundibular hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, bandlike infiltrate of lymphocytes with sparing of interfollicular areas.

case_report: A one-day-old, afebrile male infant was admitted to the neonatal in-patient unit. He was delivered at forty weeks of gestation following an uneventful pregnancy. Upon admission, physical examination revealed pustules and erosions ranging from 1 to 5 cm in diameter on the feet, right hand, and neck. There was no involvement of mucous membranes, and the family history did not indicate any bullous skin conditions.
test_results: A positive culture of coagulase positive staphylococcus aureus from a skin swab.

case_report: A 64-year-old female presented with a painless, progressive swelling of the right lower extremity over a period of 6 months. The swelling extended from the ankle to the calf and thigh. At the initial visit, she was not obese and her vital signs were within normal limits. She had no history of alcohol consumption or smoking. There were no related risk factors such as surgical history, trauma, allergies, or family history. She had traveled to China but had no history of infection. Physical examination showed that the right lower extremity below the inguinal line was significantly larger than the left side. Fibrotic changes and stemmer signs were noted in the affected area. There was no sensation of heat or redness in the skin of the lower extremity.
test_results: The patient underwent lower extremity lymphangiography, which revealed the absence of inguinal lymph nodes. Venography showed no venous obstruction.

case_report: In 2001, a 16-year-old male presented with seizures that had been occurring for six years. These seizures were of the primary generalized tonic-clonic type, with one to two episodes every two weeks. He was treated with phenytoin and subsequently became seizure-free. Starting at age 12, he experienced a gradual and progressive decrease in vision bilaterally, without any field defects. He was born via normal delivery after prolonged labor and was noted to be a large baby. An umbilical hernia was present at birth and was surgically corrected on the second day of life. Macroglossia and prognathism were observed since birth. The neonatal period was uneventful. He had delayed developmental milestones and poor academic performance. At three years old, he exhibited frontal bossing and large hands and feet. At nine years old, he experienced a growth spurt, and by 13 years old, he reached a height of 185 cm (father aged 62 years was 165 cm tall and mother aged 50 years was 155 cm tall). There was a history of excessive sleepiness and lack of interest in activities. At seven years old, he underwent surgery for cryptorchidism. There was no family history of consanguinity, mental deficiency, gigantism, or neurofibromatoses. During the initial visit, physical examination revealed a tall boy with an occipitofrontal head circumference of 59 cm (> 98th percentile), height of 185 cm (above the 95th percentile according to the National Centre for Health Statistics Standards), and weight of 62 kg, which was appropriate for his age and height (75th percentile). He exhibited hypertelorism, megalophthalmos, macroglossia, prognathism, dental malocclusion, a large nose, prominent superciliary arches, divergent squint, a high-arched palate, and large hands and feet. There was no scoliosis. Ophthalmic examination revealed bilateral optic atrophy with visual acuity of 2/60 in the right eye and 6/60 in the left eye, along with total color blindness. The macula appeared normal, and no retinal pigmentary changes were observed. He had moderate myopia in the right eye and simple myopic astigmatism in the left eye. An anti-mongoloid slant of the left palpebral aperture was noted. Ocular tension was 14.6 mmHg in both eyes, with a palpebral aperture of 30 mm in both eyes, an intermedial canthal distance of 30 mm, and an interpupillary distance of 65 mm. Hypertelorism was evident due to the divergent squint. Exophthalmometry measured 20 mm on both sides. The patient had mental subnormality, but his speech was normal.
test_results: Binet-Kamath intelligence test showed evidence of moderate mental retardation with an IQ of 34. EEG showed evidence of recurrent generalized sharp wave discharges. MRI of the brain was normal, except for large sphenoid, frontal and ethmoidal sinuses, with extensive pneumatization. 2D-echocardiogram revealed floppy mitral valve with mild prolapse and Doppler study showed trivial mitral regurgitation.

case_report: A 43-year-old woman was referred to our clinic by a psychiatrist due to indifference to her surroundings and failure to respond to questions over the past two days. She exhibited mild impairment of consciousness, characterized by slow reactions, behavior, and mental functioning. These episodes occurred approximately 10 times per hour, each lasting between 10-20 seconds. A detailed review of her history revealed that these complaints began at age 10, occurring 2-3 times a week for about 10 seconds each. During these episodes, she would stare at a fixed point, not respond to questions, and after 10-15 seconds, resume her previous activity. Her coordination was impaired, and she was uncooperative. The patient was admitted to the hospital. Hematological tests and serum biochemical analyses were normal. Cranial MRI results were also normal.
test_results: Her EEG revealed 3-Hz diffuse spike-and-slow wave activity.

case_report: A 19-year-old female presented with notable facial, hand, and foot deformities, as well as a webbed neck. Her height and weight were within normal ranges for her age. Family history revealed that her elder sister exhibited similar facial features. Mental examination showed no abnormalities. She reported no issues related to the cardiac or respiratory systems. Physical examination findings included acrocephaly, a prominent forehead, hypertelorism, proptosis, lateral gaze of the left eye, a broad nasal root, a webbed neck, a short hairline, pectus excavatum, cutaneous syndactyly of both hands, enlarged thumbs, subluxations of distal phalanges of the hands, total syndactyly of the toes on both feet, polydactyly (6 fingers), and brachydactyly.
test_results: Radiological evaluation revealed acroephaly, flattened occiput, increase in anterior opening of maxilla, and hypoplasia, teeth crowding, ectopic teeth, tapered inferior tip of the mandibula, and pseudoprognatism. Cutaneous syndactyly of both hands, flexion deformity of all fingers, widening of distal phalanx of the thumb, and occasional subluxation of distal phalanges were detected. Cervical, and lumbar vertebras were not abnormal. Anteroposterior radiograms of both feet demonstrated total syndactyly, polydactyly (6 toes), brachydactyly of 4. digits of both feet, clinodactyly of both big toes, and occasional subluxations.

case_report: A previously healthy 13-year-old girl presented with stiffness in her hands and legs, along with an inability to relax these muscles for a duration of 2 months. These symptoms appeared suddenly and progressively worsened, impacting her daily activities. There was no history of drug use or infection. Physical examination revealed stiffness in the palmar and gastrocnemius muscles. No significant changes were noted during rest, activity, sleep, or exposure to cold. Additionally, there was atrophy of the thenar muscles and hypoactive deep tendon reflexes. Her mental status was assessed as normal. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, thyroid function tests, electrolytes, plasma copper level, ceruloplasmin, and vitamin B12 levels, were within normal ranges. Serum creatine kinase was elevated at 356 IU/L (normal range: 0–145 IU/L). Cranial and spinal magnetic resonance imaging results were normal.
test_results: EMG findings, both nerve conduction studies and motor-unit action potential (MUAP) morphology, were normal. Upper and lower extremity flexor muscles had a continuous burst of MUAP and high-frequency bizarre wave activities, complex repetitive and myokymic discharges.

case_report: A 32-year-old woman presented with nausea and vomiting for 12 hours, accompanied by dizziness and pain in the upper central region of the abdomen. Prior to hospital admission, she ingested eight Tylenol tablets, each containing 325 mg of acetaminophen, following a dispute with her husband. She reported no use of other medications, alcohol consumption, gallbladder stones, trauma, autoimmune diseases, or diabetes mellitus. Physical examination revealed a soft upper abdomen with mild tenderness. There were no signs of jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, or Murphy’s sign. Laboratory results were as follows: Hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, white blood cells 5.5 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 65%, and platelets 169 × 10^9/L. Initial biochemical tests showed aspartate aminotransferase 13 U/L (7-40 U/L), glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase 13 U/L (13-35 U/L), serum albumin 3.3 g/dL, serum amylase 990 U/L (0-96 U/L), serum lipase 49.5 U/L (13-60 U/L), and triglycerides 0.6 mmol/L (0.34-1.70 mmol/L). Two days later, blood biochemistry revealed aspartate aminotransferase 13 U/L, glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase 13 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 52 U/L (35-100 U/L), serum albumin 40.9 g/L, serum amylase 433 U/L, serum lipase 136.6 U/L, triglycerides 0.6 mmol/L, and serum creatinine 53 μmol/L (45-84 μmol/L). Tests for viral hepatitis markers (A, B, C, D, and E), antinuclear antibody Hep-2, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), peripheral-ANCA, and cytoplasmic-ANCA were negative. Serum IgG4 was 1.08 (0.03-2) g/L. Abdominal ultrasonography showed no abnormalities in the pancreas.
test_results: Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) showed that the pancreas was bulky without exudation. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) demonstrated swelling of the pancreas, especially the head of the pancreas, with fluid collection around the pancreas.

case_report: A 43-year-old male, HIV-seropositive since 1991, presented with a three-month history of swelling in the neck, shoulders, and upper back, accompanied by restricted mobility. He had been on a regimen of efavirenz, emtricitabine, and tenofovir for the past 5 years. His medical history included treatment for diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and coronary artery disease with a history of percutaneous coronary intervention. Physical examination revealed nonpitting, thickened, indurated plaques on the upper back and posterior neck. There was a redistribution of body fat characterized by truncal obesity, thin extremities, and a round face. Raynaud's phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and nailfold capillary changes were not observed. Laboratory results showed a CD4 cell count of 479/mL, hemoglobin A1C level of 9% (reference range: 4.3–5.8), serum glucose level of 209 mg/dL (reference range: 70–110), and total cholesterol level of 253 mg/dL (reference range: 128–219). The dexamethasone suppression test was normal. Antistreptolysin O titer was negative, and serum electrophoresis did not detect any paraprotein.
test_results: Skin biopsy showed thickening of the dermis with coarse broad collagen bundles in a fenestrated pattern. Deposition of acidic mucopolysaccharide between the collagen bundles was prominent and was confirmed by alcian blue staining.

case_report: A 33-year-old woman presented with a small palpebral aperture in the left eye. Her medical history includes a lensectomy for microspherophakia 15 years ago, scleral buckling for retinal detachment in the right eye 5 years ago, vitrectomy with circumferential explant 8 years ago (details not available), and epimacular membrane removal with sutureless 23G vitrectomy 4 years ago in the left eye. Best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/20 with +12D correction in the right eye and 20/60 with +14D correction in the left eye. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 18 mm Hg in the right eye and 2 mm Hg in the left eye. Examination revealed subconjunctival cysts in the inferotemporal quadrant of the left eye, with a positive Seidel test. The cysts extended from 4 to 6 o'clock adjacent to the limbus. Anterior segment optical coherence tomography (ASOCT) showed no communication with the anterior chamber. Choroidal folds and optic nerve head edema were observed in the left eye due to hypotony. Surgical exploration of the bleb revealed a linear wound parallel to the limbus at the 5 o'clock position, 3.5 mm from the limbus, corresponding to the site of inferotemporal sclerotomy. The wound was closed with a horizontal mattress suture (nylon). On the first postoperative day, IOP was 32 mm Hg. At 1 month, IOP was 14 mm Hg, and BCVA was 20/60 with no evidence of a bleb. Six months later, IOP was 2 mm Hg, and a filtering bleb was seen in the superotemporal quadrant adjacent to the limbus from 1 to 3 o'clock. The Seidel test was negative, and ASOCT through the bleb did not identify any scleral breach. Brilliant blue G dye was injected into the vitreous cavity, and the superotemporal bleb was explored, revealing a linear area of staining at 3 o'clock. Minimal fluid ooze was detected under pressure. The linear thinning was closed with a mattress suture and an autologous partial thickness scleral patch graft. Thinning was also noted in the superonasal quadrant, but there was no evidence of a leak. Eight months later, a filtering bleb was seen in the superonasal quadrant from 10 to 12 o'clock, with an IOP of 12 mm Hg.
test_results: A homozygous missense variation in exon 24 of the ASPH gene that results in the amino acid substitution of glutamine for arginine at codon 688 was detected (p. Arg688Gln).

case_report: The patient is a 4.5-year-old male who was born through a normal vaginal delivery without complications. His birth weight and length were within normal ranges, and his head circumference (HC) at birth was 31 ± 0.2 cm (7th centile). There is no history of seizures. Motor developmental delay was observed after 8 months of age, with the patient unable to roll over or sit without assistance. Speech delay and cognitive disability were noted after 1 year of age. By 4.5 years, clinical examinations revealed delayed gross motor development with no head control, axial hypotonia, profound intellectual and speech abilities, and spasticity in all four limbs. HC at the time of examination was 49 ± 0.2 cm (<− 3 SD), indicating postnatal microcephaly. Physical examination showed a soft cleft palate, downturned corners of the mouth, wide nasal bridge, relatively short nose, mild micrognathia, a mildly prominent forehead with bitemporal hollowing, bilateral low-set prominent ears, hypogenitalism with micropenis and bilateral cryptorchidism, and mild scoliosis. Notable features included hypertrichosis of the upper back. Ocular abnormalities such as cataract, nasolacrimal duct obstruction, and bilateral microphthalmia were also present.
test_results: Brain MRI showed the hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, cerebral white matter hypomyelination, cortical thickening (especially in the frontoparietal area), widened Sylvain fissure, enlarged ventricles, and hypomyelination in the white matter of the cerebellum.

case_report: A 16-year-old male patient underwent laparoscopic surgery for varicocele. His medical history included febrile seizures during early childhood, with no allergies, recurrent pneumonia, or other chronic respiratory diseases. Family history was unremarkable. Smoking habits were inquired but not disclosed. Preoperative tests, including complete blood cell count, liver and kidney function tests, and first-level coagulation studies (platelet count, prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and fibrinogen), were all normal. He was classified as ASA 1 by the American Society of Anesthesiologists, indicating a healthy patient. General anesthesia was administered using propofol (2 mg/kg) and rocuronium (0.6 mg/kg), with remifentanil (0.25 mcg/kg/min) for intubation. Anesthesia was maintained with 2% sevoflurane and remifentanil (0.25–0.125 mcg/kg/min). Sugammadex (2 mg/kg) was given before extubation (TOF ratio > 0.9). Both the surgery and extubation were uneventful, with no signs of upper airway obstruction, cough, or laryngospasm. Thirty minutes post-awakening, the patient exhibited hemoptysis, dyspnea, and acute respiratory failure. He was alert, tachypneic, and normothermic, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Initial vital signs were: pulse 80 bpm, blood pressure 90/60 mmHg, and oxygen saturation averaging 73% on room air. Arterial blood gas analysis showed: pH 7.37; pCO2 39.6 mmHg (5.27 kPa); pO2 39.5 mmHg (5.26 kPa); oxyhemoglobin (oxyHb) 73.7%; and HCO3− 23.1 mEq/L. An otorhinolaryngological evaluation with nasal and laryngeal fibro-endoscopy revealed no evidence of bleeding from the upper respiratory tract. Respiratory auscultation indicated diffuse rhonchi without other significant findings. Initial chest x-ray displayed an infiltrative opacification pattern primarily in the mid zones with apical sparing, suggestive of impaired pulmonary microcirculation.
test_results: Bronchoalveolar lavage revealed the presence of abundant blood. Direct microscopic examination showed leucocytes, macrophages and bronchial epithelial cells. Cytologic analysis of his bronchoalveolar lavage secretions described the presence of blood, 85% of alveolar macrophages and 15% of granulocytes. Chest CT scan revealed multiple dense opacities with blurred, confluent margins due to diffuse alveolar involvement in the pulmonary lobes. Toxicological urine test resulted positive for cannabinoids.

case_report: A 50-year-old female patient of Han nationality presented with a one-year history of mild shortness of breath. The symptom was notably exacerbated by strenuous physical activity but improved with rest. She reported no additional symptoms, including chest pain, abdominal pain, difficulty swallowing, vomiting, or indigestion. There was no history of trauma or surgical procedures. Physical examination revealed a significant reduction in breath sounds and an increase in bowel sounds in the left side of the chest.
test_results: Contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography (CT) and multiplanar reconstructions (MPRs) showed a notable displacement of the abdominal viscera into the left thoracic cavity and the interrupted hemidiaphragm. The atelectasis of the left lung was serious for most of the whole left thoracic cavity was filled by the atopic abdominal organs. The heart was also extruded into the right hemithorax and the right lung was partially compressed.

case_report: A 30-year-old male with a history of early onset glaucoma, multiple trabeculectomies, delayed eruption of permanent teeth, progressive hand deformities, psoriasis, recurrent kidney stones, Achilles tendinitis, tendon rupture, foot deformities, and underdeveloped toenails presented with shortness of breath during physical activity and heart palpitations. These symptoms have been present for three months and have gradually worsened. His family history includes early coronary artery disease in his mother and aortic valve replacement due to aortic stenosis at the age of 31. Physical examination revealed a grade 3/6 systolic murmur in the left second intercostal space, hallux valgus deformities in the feet, and abnormal tooth development.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed autosomal dominant IFIH1 mutation. The patient underwent an echocardiogram which revealed moderate mitral annular calcification, mild aortic stenosis with partial fusion of noncoronary and left coronary cusps, and calcified leaflets, with a peak gradient of 24.4 mm Hg and mean gradient of 13 mm Hg and peak velocity of 2.47 m/s. CT chest revealed minimal calcification of aortic arch and abdominal aorta, calcification of aortic valve, and ductus arteriosus remnant.

case_report: A 57-year-old man with a history of electrocauterization therapy for atrial fibrillation presented with a 3-year history of reduced sweating on the left side of his body. He occasionally experienced lightheadedness when standing but reported no changes in sexual or voiding functions. Physical examination showed pupils equal in size with normal light reaction, and no abnormalities in motor and sensory systems. Blood pressure and heart rate were recorded as 129/90 mm Hg and 66 beats per minute in a supine position, and 120/100 mm Hg and 72 beats per minute when standing. Imaging studies, including chest radiography, computerized tomography, and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and spinal cord, showed no abnormalities. After obtaining informed consent, qualitative assessment of TS was performed using the modified Minor's colorimetric method, and sweat rates on the forehead and extremities were continuously measured by capacitance hygrometers.
