Pharmacological focal sweat rates were assessed by intradermal injection of 0.05 mL of 5% acetylcholine. Results were compared with a control group of age- and sex-matched subjects without diabetes mellitus, neurological, or autonomic deficits, who had also provided informed consent. The TS test showed no sweating before heating. Sixty minutes after heating, the right side of the body exhibited diffuse sweating, while the left side was hypohidrotic, particularly in the upper half. The left side of the forehead remained almost anhidrotic, whereas the right side showed probable compensatory hyperhidrosis. The left side of the trunk at the T4/5 level had an area of relatively abundant sweating compared to adjacent segments. TS rates on the left side were unevenly reduced compared to the right side, showing 2%, 2%, and 87% of the right-side values for the forehead, forearm, and leg, respectively. Less pronounced reduction of sweating was observed in the ACh-S test on the left side, showing 36%, 56%, and 53% of the right-side values for the forehead, forearm, and leg, respectively. ACh-S values on the patient's forearm and leg were greater than 65% of the control group.
test_results: The tilt-table test showed similar BP reduction and no reactive increase in plasma norepinephrine (0.04 ng/mL in supine position vs. 0.09 ng/mL after 60° tilting for 6 min). The heart-to-mediastinum ratio in 123I-meta-iodobenzylguanidine cardiac scintigraphy was reduced to 1.58 on the delayed image. The TS test showed patchy or blotchy sweating without apparent laterality, and TS rates were markedly reduced on all sites examined. ACh-S was preserved on the forearms but was markedly reduced on legs.

case_report: A 62-year-old male presented in early December 2019 with a 1-week history of worsening shortness of breath and decreased exercise tolerance. He reported no chest pain, cough, or fever. His medical history includes essential hypertension, diabetes mellitus, asthma, and a past treatment for hepatitis C. He is allergic to penicillin. Family history includes deep vein thrombosis in his mother, sister, and daughter. Social history reveals a half pack per day smoking habit since his teens and a history of opioid use disorder, currently managed with methadone. On admission, his temperature was 98°F, blood pressure was 107/62 mmHg, respiratory rate was 20 breaths per minute, pulse rate was 96 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation was 96% on 3 liters of oxygen. He was not in acute distress. Cardiac examination showed normal heart sounds (S1 and S2) with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. The abdomen was soft and non-tender with no organomegaly. He had right-leg pitting edema and chronic venous skin changes in both legs, with palpable dorsalis pedis pulses bilaterally. Laboratory results included a D-dimer of 2,518 ng/ml (normal 0–243 ng/ml), troponin of 0.031 ng/ml (normal ≤0.010 ng/ml), BUN of 21 mg/dl (normal 7–18 mg/dl), creatinine of 1.3 mg/dl (normal 0.7–1.2 mg/dl), ESR of 10 mm/h (normal 0–22 mm/h), CRP of 1 mg/l (normal <4 mg/l), and ferritin of 113 ng/ml (normal 15–150 ng/ml). A chest X-ray was unremarkable, and an EKG showed T wave inversion in leads V2 to V5.
test_results: CT angiogram chest showed bilateral subsegmental pulmonary embolism and mild right-heart strain. The echocardiogram revealed no obvious valvular abnormalities, normal left-ventricle systolic function, mild right-ventricular hypertrophy, pulmonary arterial pressure 50–55 mmHg, severe right ventricular dilatation and dysfunction.

case_report: A 3-month-old male infant, the only child of a consanguineous Thai couple, initially presented at a local medical center with symptoms including upper respiratory tract infection, anemia, petechiae, mild hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy, flow cytometry, and bone marrow karyotype did not support certain conditions. At 4 to 5 months of age, the patient experienced two episodes of diarrhea, a 10% increase in circulating immature myeloid cells, and significantly elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels. Re-evaluation for myeloid leukemia was negative. At 5 months, the patient exhibited failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly, respiratory distress, and a chest X-ray showed bilateral reticulonodular infiltration indicative of pneumonia. Bronchoalveolar lavage confirmed Pneumocystis jirovecii via PCR. Persistent pancytopenia with monocytosis greater than 1000/mm3 was observed. Investigations for various conditions showed normal or slightly elevated absolute lymphocyte counts [CD3+, 7.3 K/μL (reference 2.2–6.4); CD4+, 4.2 K/μL (reference 1.6–4.6); CD8+, 3.1 K/μL (reference 0.7–2.4), CD19+, 0.6 K/μL (reference 0.5–1.5)] and normal or slightly increased immunoglobulin levels [IgA 1.19 mg/ml (reference 0.1–0.24), IgG 5.22 mg/ml (reference 4.57–8.83), and IgM 4.84 mg/ml (reference 0.27–0.93)]. Additional bone marrow studies showed a normal karyotype, no canonical RAS pathway gene mutations, and normal double negative T-cell counts. The patient received aggressive supportive treatments including blood transfusion, parenteral nutrition, enteral tube feeding for 4 weeks, and antimicrobial agents for pneumonia, resulting in temporary improvement of hematologic profiles. At 9 months, the patient developed mild diarrhea and inappropriate wide anion gap metabolic acidosis (serum TCO2 5; gap 20). Investigations for metabolic disorders showed normal acylcarnitine profile, plasma amino acids, and urinary organic acids.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing revealed a homozygous mutation at the acceptor site of intron 3 of TCN2 gene, c.428-2A > G (IVS3-2A > G; NM_000355.3). Sanger sequencing confirmed the homozygous mutation in the patient and heterozygous alleles in both parents. mRNA study demonstrated an aberrant transcript lacking exon 4.

case_report: A 15-year-old male presented to the thoracic surgery clinic with a non-tender mass on the anterior chest wall that had been slowly enlarging over a period of 2 months. Initially, the mass was thought to be a subcutaneous abscess due to its slow growth and fluctuation upon palpation. An ultrasound of the lesion also suggested a subcutaneous abscess. However, needle aspiration of the lesion did not yield any pus, ruling out infection. At a one-month follow-up, the skin over the mass turned whitish, with the periphery becoming reddish and inflamed. The patient began experiencing local pain and tenderness. The mass increased in size from 2x2 cm to 5x5 cm, extending to the middle part of the sternum. Laboratory tests were within normal limits. A CT scan showed an 8x5 cm mass in the anterior mediastinum, eroding the sternum and extending subcutaneously as an expanding necrotic area. Additionally, a 4x2 cm thymic tissue and conglomerated lymph nodes without definite borders were observed. A second percutaneous needle biopsy of the lesion did not yield any aspirate. Pathological examination of a trucut needle biopsy did not confirm malignancy. The patient was noted to have a sternal mass.
test_results: Frozen section examination showed malignancy.

case_report: A 14-month-old boy was brought to our hospital for evaluation of atypical genitalia. He is the only child of non-consanguineous parents, delivered by cesarean section following an uneventful pregnancy. Physical examination of the external genitalia showed an absence of scrotal rugae on the right side, ipsilateral cryptorchidism, and abnormal external tissue on the right side of the perineum. The right testis was palpable in the inguinal region, while the left testis was located in the scrotum with an intact midline raphe. The penile length measured 4.8 cm, which is within the normal range for his age. Examination beyond the genital area revealed a right monodactylous lower limb, normal muscle tone, and deep tendon reflexes. There were no dysmorphic facial features or other skeletal anomalies. The family history was negative for similar conditions, seizures, abnormal movements, or ataxia.
test_results: Ultrasonography showed that both testes were normal in size and echotexture. The karyotype of the boy was 46, XY. Hormonal profile showed normal prepubertal LH and FSH (0.1, 0.4 mIU/ml respectively). After ß-hCG stimulation, serum total testosterone increased from 0.03 ng/ml to 3.51 ng/ml and testosterone/dihydrotestosterone ratio was 8.54 ng/ml. Sertoli cell function was normal with inhibin-B at 158 pg/ml and anti-Müllerian hormone at 23 ng/ml. Skeletal survey showed right monodactylous lower limb (with only a big toe which had 2 phalanges) and normal spine alignment. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography excluded associated intra-abdominal anomalies including renal system abnormalities. Echocardiography showed a small muscular ventricular septal defect (VSD) that closed on follow-up. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed posterior fossa malformation in the form of dysplastic left cerebellar hemisphere with hypoplasia of its antero-superior compartment, total aplasia of its postero-inferior compartment and a small cleft traversing the inferior aspect of the right cerebellar hemisphere. Right focal epileptiform activity was detected by electroencephalogram. Audiological examination revealed bilateral normal function, and ophthalmological examination was normal.

case_report: A 15-day-old male child was brought to the hospital by his parents who had noticed a white reflex in the right eye for 4 days. On anterior segment examination, the right eye showed a vascularized whitish-yellow mass at the pupil extending behind the iris temporally. The posterior pole and the rest of the retina appeared normal. The left eye was normal. B-scan examination of the right eye revealed a moderate to high reflective mass temporally arising from the ciliary body with an attachment to the retina. Magnetic resonance imaging showed an enhancing lesion in the posterior aspect of the ciliary body projecting into the vitreous. A trans-scleral incision biopsy was performed under general anesthesia. Histopathology showed mild ciliary hyperplasia with no evidence of malignancy. At 1-month follow-up, there was an increase in the size of the mass, and after explaining poor visual prognosis to the family, the eye was enucleated.
test_results: Histopathology report showed primitive neuroepithelial cells with mitosis and necrosis arranged in cords and rosettes with areas of pigmentation.

case_report: A 39-year-old male with no significant past medical history presented with severe right groin and perineal pain for three days. He reported having normal sexual intercourse before the onset of symptoms. He had been intermittently using sildenafil 50 mg, approximately two to three times weekly, before sexual activity. He denied a history of priapism, mechanical trauma, vigorous sexual activity, drug use, or prolonged air travel. Physical examination revealed an enlarged right proximal corpora but no evidence of priapism.
test_results: Initial ultrasound imaging revealed mild asymmetric fullness of the right corpus spongiosis compared to the left. Follow-up contrasted magnetic resonance imaging revealed a diffusely enlarged appearance of the proximal portion of the right corpus cavernosum compared to the left, with hypointense T2 signal intensity and no definite T1 signal abnormality.
diagnosis: Partial Segmental Thrombosis of the Corpus Cavernosum

case_report: The patient is a 10-year-old Chinese Han male with a history of neutropenia and recurrent infections for over 9 years, and fever lasting for 1 week. He was admitted to the Pediatrics Department of the Ninth People's Hospital Shanghai Jiaotong University School of Medicine on March 5th, 2019. At 6 months old, his absolute neutrophil count (ANC) was 0.15 × 10^9/L during a respiratory tract infection. Family members reported that his ANC remained consistently below the normal reference range over the next 9 years. He experienced monthly episodes of respiratory tract infections, periodontitis, oral ulcers, tonsillitis, and perianal abscesses, which were managed with routine anti-infection treatments. Two years prior, he developed a lung abscess. At 6 years old, he was diagnosed with epilepsy. He exhibited delayed intellectual development and had not started primary school by age 10. At admission, his father and mother, aged 53, were in good health and had a consanguineous marriage. There was no family history of epilepsy or immunodeficiency. The mother had five pregnancies: one abortion, one male child who died of infection at 8 months, and two healthy elder sisters aged 31 and 29. The patient was the fifth pregnancy. On admission, his temperature was 38.4°C, and his weight was 34 kg. He appeared dispirited, had significant intellectual disability, and superficial lymphadenopathy. Multiple ulcers were present on his lower lip, and a 2 × 2 cm mass was palpable beside the anus.
test_results: Whole exon sequencing of the child and parents showed that the child was homozygous for the exon 3 c.430dupG mutation of the HAX1 gene NM-006118 (p.Val144fs) and that both parents carried the same mutation.

case_report: A 64-year-old Caucasian woman presented with ulcers on both sides of her lower legs, which had been present for approximately 1 year and developed without any external trauma. Doppler sonography showed pronounced superficial varicosis. The patient also had pre-existing type 2 diabetes and arterial hypertension, which were considered as factors affecting wound healing. Physical examination revealed two ulcers, each about 4 cm in diameter, on the right lower leg and one ulcer, 6 cm in diameter, on the left lower leg. Signs of chronic venous insufficiency, such as corona phlebectatica and symmetrical oedema after standing, were observed. The ulcers were located proximally, and there was significant itching. The skin around the wounds showed follicular-bound, pinehead-sized, erythematous maculae and papules. Similar skin changes were noted on the thighs and upper back.
test_results: Histological analyses of a representative follicle revealed a pronounced infiltration of predominantly CD3+CD4+ T helper cells gathering around the adnexal structures. CD8+ cytotoxic T cells or CD20+ B cells were detected only to a small extent. The T-cell γ receptor rearrangement revealed a biclonal peak at 198 and 227 base pairs. Similar findings were observed in specimens of the ulcers.

case_report: The patient is a 6-year-old Japanese boy born to healthy parents. His mid-parental target height was 180 cm, with his father's height at 177 cm and his mother's at 170 cm. His older brother is healthy. He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, with a birth weight of 3,055 g (−0.64 SD), length of 51.5 cm (+1.06 SD), and head circumference of 34.0 cm (+0.40 SD). At 19 months, he was referred due to an inability to walk unaided. A brain MRI at that time was normal. He entered a rehabilitation program that improved his ability to walk. His linear growth began to slow from 5 months of age. At 38 months, his height was 84.5 cm (−2.89 SD). Thyroid function tests showed TSH at 4.520 μU/mL and FT4 at 1.06 ng/dL, both within normal ranges. Baseline insulin-like growth factor I (IGF-I) was low at 18 ng/mL. A GH stimulation test showed peak GH responses to arginine at 4.60 ng/mL and to clonidine at 2.41 ng/mL. GH therapy at 0.175 mg/kg/week was started, significantly accelerating his growth velocity. At 6 years old, he presented with painful knee joints. His height was 109.5 cm (−1.04 SD), and his arm span was 111 cm. His facial features and body proportions were normal. His development in language, cognitive skills, and fine and gross motor skills was appropriate for his age, with some clumsiness in motion.
test_results: A radiograph of the knee showed mild metaphyseal dysplasia of the knee (shaved contour and marginal spur in the distal femoral metaphyses and to a lesser extent in the proximal tibial metaphyses, and mild cupping proximal fibular metaphyses). A subsequent skeletal survey revealed generalized metaphyseal dysplasia involving the hip and wrist as well as the knee. The spine showed generalized platyspondyly with irregular endplates. The posterior vertebral bodies were irregularly ossified. Brain CT of the patient showed bilateral calcifications of the basal ganglia.

case_report: A female infant was delivered via Caesarean section at 30 weeks and 5 days of gestation to a 29-year-old mother with no reported health issues. Routine antenatal ultrasound scans showed no abnormalities. The infant's birth weight was 1,545 grams, and Apgar scores were 7 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. At 3 days old, a heart murmur and enlarged heart were noted. Doppler echocardiography at 4 days old indicated a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) measuring 4 mm in diameter between the left subclavian artery and the main pulmonary artery. Two cycles of oral ibuprofen (10 mg/kg for the first dose, followed by 5 mg/kg/dose at 24-hour intervals for two additional doses) were administered but did not close the PDA. At 1 week old, small hemangiomas were observed in the left periauricular, temporal, and infraocular regions, which later grew into large facial hemangiomas affecting the left eye. Surgery was performed at 2 weeks old due to the ineffectiveness of oral ibuprofen and persistent cardiomegaly. The procedure revealed an atypical PDA originating from the left subclavian artery and entering the main pulmonary artery, which was surgically clipped. A subsequent three-dimensional cardiac CT scan and angiography confirmed the findings and identified additional cardiovascular anomalies, including a right-sided aortic arch and a tortuous left subclavian artery. Specifically, the scan showed a mirror image right-sided aortic arch with the first branch being a left innominate artery that divided into a left common carotid and subclavian artery, followed by the right common carotid artery and the right subclavian artery. The PDA from the base of the left subclavian artery was surgically clipped and did not form a vascular ring. A small collateral artery between the thoracic aorta and the left subclavian artery was also noted. Due to the large facial hemangioma, oral prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day) and topical clobetasol-17-propionate were started at 1 month old.
test_results: These showed the presence of the Dandy-Walker variant with hypoplastic cerebellar vermis and multiple intracranial hemangiomas in left cerebellopontine angle. No definite abnormalities in the intracranial large vessels were noted on the brain MRA.

case_report: A 4-year-old male child was seen at the Department of Plastic Surgery of Jinling Hospital with a congenital large swelling located on the thoracic back, right axilla, and upper limb. The child was born at term without any notable complications and is the first child of non-consanguineous parents in China. The swelling has been present since birth and has progressively increased in size. It tends to rapidly enlarge and cause discomfort following a cold. The swelling is tender and painful upon palpation, with no detectable pulse and normal skin temperature. Additionally, there is an irregular port-wine stain on the left chest near the axilla and another on the right lower part of the back. A smooth fatty-overgrowth mass is also observed on the left side of the lower back.
test_results: On the CT scan, it was observed that there was a mass present in the right upper extremity of the child. The borders of the mass were poorly defined and there were uneven internal densities with mostly fluid densities. There were also fat-density shadows present on the left side of the child's back. The right side of the thorax appeared to be extruded and deformed. The enhanced CT showed significant enhancement of the solid portion in the venous and delayed phases. Magnetic resonance imaging showed clear results: the left coronal and transverse views revealed multiple, variable-sized, thin-walled cystic long T1 and long T2 signals in the right shoulder, dorsum, and left axilla. The capsule was rich in plasma. Short T1 isotropic T2 signals were visible in the right axilla. Both T1WI and T2WI showed high signals, which were associated with hemorrhage. The enhancement scan reveals a marked improvement in the cyst wall. During the examination, a color Doppler test was performed, revealing a cystic mass encompassing both arterial and venous blood flow. Additionally, an abdominal ultrasound detected another cystic mass in the right adrenal area that subsequently disappeared during follow-up without special treatment. The adipose tissue from a mass on the child's back underwent whole exome sequencing, revealing a missense mutation c.1258T>C in the PIK3CA gene, which is absent in blood, resulting in the substitution of cysteine with arginine in position 420 of the protein crystal structure.

case_report: A 16-year-old female presented with severe abdominal pain that had been recurring for over 10 days, specifically localized to the left lower abdomen. The pain improved with rest and was not associated with chills, fever, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or hematochezia. Seven days prior to admission, a pelvic mass measuring approximately 13 × 10 cm was identified via color ultrasound at another clinic. After taking anti-inflammatory medication, her symptoms slightly improved, but the pain remained tolerable. Half a day before hospital admission, the abdominal pain intensified, accompanied by vomiting and palpitations, leading to her emergency department visit. Physical examination revealed a large abdominal mass palpable two transverse fingers above the navel, extending to the midaxillary line on both sides. The mass had a clear boundary, and compression elicited significant pain in the left lower abdomen. The uterus was not palpable. Admission color ultrasound showed no abnormalities in the uterus and ovaries but identified a cystic solid mass approximately 13 cm × 11 cm × 15 cm in front of the uterus. The cyst wall was locally thickened and uneven, with the thickest part measuring about 0.8 cm. Light bands in various directions were observed within the cyst, and the cyst fluid exhibited dense, weak light spots. The mass had a clear boundary and irregular shape, with no significant blood flow signals detected in the cyst wall or cyst. Laboratory results included a white blood cell count of 12.1 ×10^9/L, neutrophil count of 9.36 ×10^9/L, hemoglobin level of 112 g/L, and hypersensitive C-reactive protein level of 58.91 mg/L. Carbohydrate antigen 12-5 was 1033 U/mL, and the postmenopausal Rome index was 73.47%. Coagulation tests showed plasma fibrinogen at 7.12 g/L, D-dimer at 8.43 μg/mL, and fibrinogen degradation products at 27.55 μg/mL. Liver and kidney functions, as well as infectious markers, were within normal limits.
test_results: Laparoscopic examination during the operation showed that the dense adhesion of the greater omentum and intestine formed an approximately 15 cm × 15 cm fillet-like mass, purplish red, with bleeding and necrosis. The mass adheres densely to the left abdominal wall and does not move. There is dark red blood accumulation in the mass, approximately 1,000 mL. After separating the adhesive band between the mass and the left abdominal wall, there was obvious pelvic congestion, and the mass adhered to the left anterior wall of the uterus. There was no obvious abnormality in the appearance of uterus and bilateral fallopian tubes and ovaries. When exploring the greater omentum, there were nodules scattered between 1.0 cm × 0.8 cm and 4 cm × 4.5 cm in size. The nodules were tough and purplish red, and the blood touch was obvious. Postoperative pathological examination showed that malignant tumors were found in “pelvic tissue”, “greater omentum”, “mesentery of small intestine”, “abdominal wall mass”, and “anterior rectal wall mass”. The “bilateral ovarian biopsy tissue” showed ovarian cortex under the microscope, and no tumor was found. Microscopically, the tumor showed solid flake and nest distribution, infiltrative growth, round or oval tumor cells, rich cytoplasm, eosinophilia, large nucleus, deviation, vesicular chromatin, obvious nucleoli, easy mitosis, and poor adhesion of tumor cells in some areas. It can be seen that the rhabdomyoid cells with nuclear deviation and strong eosinophilic cytoplasm have necrosis. The results of immunohistochemistry showed the following: Bcl-2(-), CD34(-), CD45(LCA)(-), CK(AE1/AE3)(+), CK20(-), CK7(-), CR(calretinin)(-), Desmin(-), ERG(-), HMB45(-), INI1(-), S-100(-), SMA(-), TLE1(-), Vimentin(+), and WT1 (Wilm’s tumor)(-).

case_report: A 43-year-old woman with a notable family history of 'poor vision' presented with decreased visual acuity in her right eye over the past 6 months, without any other associated symptoms. Ophthalmologic examination revealed a best corrected visual acuity of 1/10 in the right eye and 9/10 in the left eye. Both eyes exhibited a normal pupillary light reflex and intraocular pressure. Slit-lamp biomicroscopic examination showed a clear cornea, a calm anterior segment with filamentous vitreous, and a clear lens without cataract. Funduscopy of the right eye identified a grayish lesion with irregular edges, occupying the papilla and extending into the interpapillary-macular space, with a fuzzy white macular focus. The left eye fundus displayed yellowish deposits around the macula, consistent with drusens. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated a hyperfluorescent area during the arteriovenous phase with increased fluorescence in the late phase. Macular optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed fibrosis at the focal point, macular edema, and choroidal neovascularization, along with posterior vitreous detachment (PVD). The color blind test, orbital MRI, and thoraco-abdominal CT scan were normal. Biological tests for infectious, inflammatory, or immune pathologies were also normal.
test_results: A mutation in exon 5 of the TIMP3 gene.

case_report: A 36-year-old male with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss was referred to the Department of Radiology. He is the first of two brothers born to healthy parents of Turkish descent, who are first cousins. The younger brother is healthy. There is no other family history of deafness in the extended family. At the age of 9 months, the hearing impairment was noticed. An audiologic assessment confirmed severe bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, and the loss was corrected with a hearing aid. Hearing loss has remained stable. He had no school problems and graduated from high school. On physical examination, he has no dysmorphic features. He has neither an obvious neurological difficulty nor a cognitive impairment.
test_results: Sagittal FLAIR images demonstrated corpus callosum hypogenesis. The rostrum, genu, and splenic portions of the corpus callosum were absent, and the body part was seen as a short thin line. Lateral ventricles were noted to be slightly small in caliper and slit like in coronal T2-weighted images. There were bilateral frontal parasagittal polymicrogyria. Nodular gray matter heterotopia was present in periventricular regions. In the inferior aspects of both cerebellar hemispheres, there were abnormal foliation and fissuration with loss of the normal architecture, consistent with cerebellar dysplasia.

case_report: A 22-year-old woman presented to LAMB Hospital in Parbatipur, Dinajpur, Bangladesh, in February 2010, with complaints of general weakness and shortness of breath on exertion for three weeks. She had a normal vaginal delivery at home four months prior and reported no specific medical history. Her vital signs were as follows: blood pressure 90/60 mm Hg, pulse rate 120 beats per minute, respiration rate 24 per minute, and body temperature 37.2 °C. Cardiac examination revealed a regular heartbeat without any audible murmurs. Fine rales were detected in both basal lung fields. A chest x-ray indicated an enlarged heart and bilateral pulmonary congestion. An electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia. Laboratory results included a hemoglobin level of 12.0 g/dL, a total white cell count of 8,000/mm3, and a normal platelet count of 240,000/mm3. Prothrombin time was normal at 15 seconds. Liver enzymes were mildly elevated with a serum aspartate transaminase level of 126.7 IU/L, while serum creatinine was within normal limits at 86.5 µmol/L.
test_results: Both the ventricles were enlarged and the left ventricular systolic function was depressed. The left ventricular end-diastolic dimension was 64 mm, and the ejection fraction was 17%. Intracardiac thrombi were noted in both left and right ventricles.

case_report: An 18-year-old female presented with a complaint of progressively worsening facial asymmetry, which she first noticed following a trauma approximately 5 years ago. The condition has gradually worsened to its current state. There is no relevant information from her past dental, medical, or family history. Extra-oral examination revealed significant asymmetry in the lower face, with the chin deviating to the left side and noticeable enlargement of the right side of the mandible. Intra-oral examination showed that the mandibular central incisor midline did not align with the facial midline, and an open bite was observed in the right posterior tooth region.
test_results: Panoramic radiograph revealed elongation of condyle, condylar neck, ramus and body of mandible on the right side. Horizontal dimension of the mandibular body was also larger as compared to that on the left side. The distance between the mandibular roots and the inferior alveolar nerve on the right side was more than that on the left side. CT demonstrated elongation and medial rotation of right lower border of the mandible.

case_report: A 13-year, 8-month-old Chinese Han boy was seen in the endocrinology department due to short stature observed over the past 7 years. He had a normal birth weight and length following an uneventful pregnancy. There were no reports of back or joint pain, or scoliosis. His motor and cognitive functions were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed a height of 126.4 cm (-4SD), sitting height of 70.5 cm, and weight of 22.5 kg. The boy exhibited disproportionate short stature with a relatively short trunk and barrel chest. His arm span measured 138.0 cm, exceeding his height by 11 cm. He had no dysmorphic facial features and was at Tanner stage 2. No other family members exhibited short stature, abnormal arm span, or a history of degenerative joint disease or hip joint replacement. Serum levels of insulin-like growth factor 1 and thyroid hormone were within normal ranges. Growth hormone stimulation tests (L-dopa and arginine) showed a peak growth hormone level of 22.6 ng/ml, indicating no growth hormone deficiency.
test_results: Radiographs revealed lumbosacral platyspondyly with characteristic superior and inferior humping of the vertebral bodies seen on lateral view. The pelvis was somewhat narrow, and the femoral necks were short. Osteoarthritic changes such as joint space narrowing, extensive osteophytes, were not observed in all involved joints including shoulders, wrists, and knees. His bone age (BA) was 11-year, 2-month old estimated by G-P BA assessment, extremely younger than chronological age. Targeted next-generation sequencing revealed a novel missense variant c.260A>C in the TRAPPC2 exon5 localized to ChromosomeXp22 in the proband, causing p. His87Pro mutation. His mother was found to be heterozygous for the c.260A>C substitution, confirming her carrier status, whereas the father was found to be normal.

case_report: A 34-year-old male presented with recurrent carpopedal spasms over a period of 4 years, accompanied by perioral numbness, cramps, muscle twitching, and generalized weakness. Two years ago, he was found to have hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypercalciuria, and elevated PTH levels without any AHO phenotype. He was treated with calcium and 1α-calcidiol, which led to symptomatic improvement. There was no family history of similar conditions or bone abnormalities. On examination, he was 184 cm tall and weighed 78 kg (BMI 23 kg/m2). He showed no signs of AHO phenotype but had latent tetany, indicated by positive Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs. His medications were discontinued for 7 days for re-evaluation. Laboratory investigations showed normal renal function (serum creatinine, 88.4 μmol/L), normal serum magnesium (0.86 mmol/L), normal 25(OH)D levels (137.2 nmol/L), and elevated PTH (63 pmol/L). A computed tomography scan of the brain was normal. Bone mineral density was within normal range (T score, 0.5 at L1-L4 and –0.2 at femur neck), and thyroid function tests were normal (T3 0.87 ng/mL, T4 7.59 μg/dL, TSH 2.20 mIU/L). Given the hypocalcemia with elevated PTH, further investigations were conducted. His serum was precipitated with polyethylene glycol (PEG) to detect heterophile antibodies, and the PEG precipitated serum PTH levels remained high (61.5 pmol/L).
test_results: The patient had blunted urinary cAMP response to exogenous PTH (recombinant 1-34) as compared to healthy control and patients with postoperative hypoparathyroidism. The patient had normal tubular reabsorption of phosphate and percentage fall in the ratio of maximum rate of renal tubular reabsorption of phosphate to glomerular filtration rate (TmPO4/GFR) when compared to two other subjects, indicating normal phosphaturic response.

case_report: A 52-year-old male presented with chest pain lasting one week, which worsened with shortness of breath over the past three days. His medical and family history of cardiovascular disease were unremarkable. Initial vital signs included a body temperature of 36.6°C, respiratory rate of 24 breaths/min, pulse rate of 112 beats/min, blood pressure of 111/87 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation of 90% on room air. Electrocardiogram (ECG) findings showed sinus tachycardia, T wave inversion in leads II, III, AVF, and V1 to V6, ST segment elevation in leads I and AVL, and a poor increase of R wave in the thoracic leads. Laboratory tests revealed an absolute eosinophil count of 12,920/mm3, high-sensitivity troponin (hsTn) level of 2037.7 pg/mL, brain natriuretic peptide level of 758 pg/mL, and D-dimer level of 57 μg/dL. Arterial blood gas analysis indicated hypoxemic respiratory insufficiency with a pH of 7.43, pCO2 of 26.7 mm Hg, and pO2 of 72.6 mm Hg. Coronary angiography showed no significant stenosis in the right coronary artery, left main artery, anterior descending artery, or circumflex artery. X-ray fluoroscopy indicated a bright band at the bottom of the heart, suggestive of pericardial effusion. Transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated left ventricular endomyocardial thickening and a dark area in the pericardial cavity, with anterior pericardium thickness of 1.0 cm, posterior pericardium thickness of 1.4 cm, left pericardium thickness of 1.7 cm, and apex thickness of 1.0 cm. The left ventricular systolic function was reduced with an estimated ejection fraction of about 31%. Emergency pericardiocentesis drained approximately 100 mL of yellow, cloudy fluid, and examination of the pericardial effusate showed a positive Rivalta test. Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed bilateral pleural effusion, scattered patches, and exudate in both lungs. Bilateral thoracentesis drained an additional 600 mL of yellow, cloudy fluid. Laboratory examination of the hydrothorax showed a positive Rivalta test, nucleated cell count of 9260/mm3 with 65% eosinophils, total protein of 34.9 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase of 201 IU/L, and adenosine deaminase of 4.8 U/L. On the third day, the patient developed a bright red purpura-like rash on both lower limbs, which rose above the skin, partially fused, and spread to the whole body. A second ECG indicated sinus tachycardia, pathological Q-wave formation in leads I and AVL, T-wave inversion in leads II, III, AVF, and V1-V6, and a poor increase of R wave in the thoracic leads. The patient tested negative for male tumor markers, antinuclear antibody, thyroid dysfunction, and TB infection. Causes of reactive eosinophilia such as fungal infections, parasitic infections, hypersensitivity reactions, and malignant diseases were excluded. Antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibodies were also negative. Treatment included oxygen, an anti-inflammatory agent (Piperacillin and Sulbactam, 4.5 g, every 8 hours), a diuretic (Furosemide, 40 mg, once a day), an anti-allergy medication (Loratadine, 10 mg, once a day), and a proton pump inhibitor (Omeprazole, 40 mg, once a day). On the fifth day, the patient developed gastrointestinal bleeding, and was treated with an intravenous infusion of somatostatin and omeprazole by micropump, fluid infusion, and other supportive measures.
test_results: A bone marrow examination indicated marked myelodysplastic activity and significantly increased eosinophils (42.5%). Flow cytometry showed there was no significant abnormal phenotypic cell population, and a biopsy showed that bone marrow hematopoietic cells are proliferating and active, mainly eosinophils. Examination of the peripheral blood using polymerase chain reaction indicated no abnormal expression of PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFRI or PCMI-JAK2, and no JAK2V617F point mutation.

case_report: This British Caucasian girl was 7 years old at her last review. She experienced blindness in her left eye following multiple corneal ruptures, an unsuccessful donor graft operation, and secondary glaucoma, which required repeated cyclodiode laser treatments. Her right eye had poor visual acuity (3/24 for distance, and N8 for near vision) due to severe myopia (−29 diopters) and early keratoconus. She and her non-identical twin sister were born to British parents through in vitro fertilization, delivered at 32 weeks gestation. She weighed 1.275 kg (3rd–10th centiles), and her sister weighed 1.588 kg (25th–50th centiles). Joint hypermobility was observed early in life, and a unilateral unstable hip was treated conservatively with a harness for 6 months. At 2 years old, she was prescribed spectacles for significant myopia and was noted to have blue sclerae during an ophthalmology referral. A minor accident caused a penetrating corneal injury that could not be successfully repaired as the surgical sutures tore and detached from the corneal tissue. A donor corneal graft was later applied but became dislodged and damaged during normal play activities. During the operation, the left lens was found to be lost, and a cataract was present in the right eye. The left eye developed secondary glaucoma, treated with laser therapy, resulting in no residual vision. The right eye showed progressive enlargement of the globe, increasing corneal ectasia, and worsening myopia. The patient permanently wears protective eyewear and was deemed unsuitable for a scleral contact lens. Dorsolamide/timolol (Cosopt) drops were used in both eyes, and latanoprost (Xalatan) drops in the left eye. Hearing loss was diagnosed in early childhood, and repeated ear tube insertions and adenoidectomy provided some benefit. She used bilateral hearing aids. Her developmental milestones were appropriate considering her combined sensory loss, and she received additional support in mainstream school. No other family members experienced corneal rupture, though her twin sister and younger brother both wore spectacles for strabismus and astigmatism respectively and had blue sclerae and mild joint hypermobility. Their parents had normal vision, and there was no other relevant family history.
test_results: The patient is compound heterozygous for two mutations in ZNF469 c.[5788delC];[5788dupC] (p.[Gln1930Argfs*6];[Gln1930Profs*133]). Further investigations confirmed the finding in the patient, and revealed that the mother was a heterozygous carrier for c.[5788delC], while the father was a heterozygous carrier for the c.[5788dupC].

case_report: The patient is a nine-year-old female with a known NBAS gene mutation in the variant c.2819A>C (p. His940Pro), associated with infantile liver failure syndrome type 2 (ILFS2). At four years old, she presented with a three-day history of vesicular skin rashes in the L2 dermatome of the left leg, accompanied by pain, low appetite, and ear discharge, but without swelling or redness. She is the daughter of consanguineous parents, born at full term, with an unremarkable neonatal period. She was admitted for varicella-zoster and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) ear infection and treated with intravenous acyclovir (15 mg/kg) for 10 days and intravenous vancomycin (15 mg/kg) for 14 days. Between the ages of two months and four years, she experienced multiple hospitalizations due to various infections, including viral hepatitis, urinary tract infection, Salmonella bacteremia, gastroenteritis, recurrent hepatitis, follicular tonsillitis, pneumonia, mastoiditis, and varicella-zoster infection.
test_results: Flow cytometry had shown low levels of CD56+ and CD16+ (2%) but had otherwise been normal.
Orpha_name: Autosomal recessive primary immunodeficiency with defective spontaneous natural killer cell cytotoxicity

case_report: A 47-year-old female patient presented with a red, infiltrated, solitary plaque on her shoulder, measuring 9 cm in its longest dimension. The lesion had been present for two months prior to consultation. Upon palpation, the lesion was tender and fixed to both superficial and deep tissues. The patient did not report any pain or itching.
test_results: Histological examination showed a slightly acanthotic epidermis and large vascular lobules in the full-thickness dermis. Each lobule was composed of aggregates of endothelial cells concentrically whorled along a preexisting vascular plexus. Immunohistochemistry showed positivity for CD31 and CD34, and negativity for smooth muscle actin.

case_report: A 4-year-old boy, the third child born to first cousins, visited the hepatology clinic due to jaundice following episodes of vomiting and diarrhea. He had a similar episode at the age of two that resolved on its own. Physical examination revealed progressive neurological dysfunction. His height was 95 cm (-2 SD), weight was 13 kg (-3 SD), and skull circumference was 43 cm. Notable physical features included enophthalmia, nystagmus, jaundice, and skin photosensitivity. The liver was palpable 4 cm below the costal margin, firm with a rounded border and smooth surface. The spleen was palpable 2 cm below the costal margin. Neurological examination indicated intention tremors, cerebellar ataxia, absent knee reflexes, and preserved ankle reflexes. Chest and heart examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory results showed ALT: 270 IU/L (N: 37), AST: 232 IU/L (N: 40), GGT: 183 IU/L (N: 50), total bilirubin: 3.35 mg/dl, direct bilirubin: 2.6 mg/dl, albumin: 3.2 g/dl, PT: 11.7 sec (INR: 1). Tests for HBV, HCV, and HAV were negative. Ceruloplasmin level, protein electrophoresis, and autoantibodies were within normal ranges. Abdominal ultrasonography indicated an enlarged liver with regular borders and homogeneous echotexture, with patent portal and hepatic veins. Fundus examination was normal, and a CT brain scan showed no abnormalities.
test_results: MRI brain showed deep white matter signal alteration at the forceps minor and major regions, middle cerebellar peduncles, the posterior segmental aspects of the pontine isthmus and basis pontis. Those areas exhibited bright signal on FLAIR and T2W1, consistent with dysmyelinating disease.

case_report: A premature female infant was born in October 2018 at an estimated gestational age of 32 weeks. The mother, a 28-year-old primigravida with pre-eclampsia, was admitted to the gynecology unit of Clinical Emergency County Hospital of Craiova and delivered the infant via caesarean section. The pregnancy was dated at 32 weeks based on the mother's last menstrual period. The newborn was assessed using the expanded New Ballard Score, resulting in a score of 20, consistent with a premature neonate. The Apgar Score was 8 at 1 minute and 5 at 5 minutes post-birth. The infant had spontaneous breathing at birth and was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit. Clinical examination revealed significant abdominal distention, suspected to be due to a right kidney condition based on thoracoabdominal radiograph and prenatal ultrasound findings. The infant was placed in an incubator and started on parenteral nutrition. A maternal vaginal infection with E. Coli, sensitive to ceftriaxone, was identified during labor. To prevent neonatal sepsis, the infant received ceftriaxone therapy at 50mg/kg/dose, twice daily for 7 days. Aminophylline therapy was initiated to reduce the risk of apnea. Vital parameters including ECG, respiration, blood oxygen saturation, and body temperature were monitored, along with stool and urine output. Blood pressure remained within normal values for her gestational age during the hospital stay. At 48 hours post-birth, the infant developed respiratory distress syndrome characterized by tachypnea (respiratory rate of 80/minute), xiphoid and lower chest retractions, marked nasal flaring, and grunting respiration, accompanied by desaturation on pulse oximetry. Intubation was performed using a 3mm endotracheal tube, and mechanical ventilation was initiated. A pediatric surgeon evaluated the infant and determined that a nephrectomy was necessary due to the mass effect of the kidney condition. The infant underwent right nephrectomy 5 days after birth.
test_results: Macroscopically, the resected kidney parenchyma seemed to be massively replaced by thin walled cysts that could be visualized through the capsule, and contained a serous clear fluid. Microscopy revealed dilated cysts lined by simple cuboidal or flattened epithelium, and islets of remnant kidney parenchyma separated by edematous stroma. Both proximal and distal tubules were occasionally distended, and sometimes dilated Bowman’s spaces could be noted in the glomerulus. Immunohistochemistry for CD34 revealed incomplete blood arcades which did not seem to be in contact with all the tubular elements of the parenchyma, when compared to a control age-matched kidney. Based on anti-CLA immunohistochemistry, it was next clear that there were much more inflammatory cells within the remnant parenchyma compared with the control. When we evaluated the basement membranes (based on anti-collagen IV immunohistochemistry), it was very interesting that we found discontinuous basement membranes surrounding the proximal and distal tubules, but continuous around blood vessels and the vascular glomerulus. This discontinuous pattern was also present under the epithelium lining the cysts.

case_report: A 76-year-old woman experienced sudden right lower abdominal pain and went to the emergency department. Her medical history includes hypertension, hepatitis B, and nodular goiter. She had an appendectomy during her teenage years and underwent surgery and chemotherapy for left lung cancer a decade ago. The night before admission, she had persistent, vague abdominal pain that disrupted her sleep and worsened with movement. She reported no nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, chills, fever, or night sweats. Upon admission, her vital signs were: blood pressure 154/91 mmHg, pulse rate 97 beats per minute, body temperature 37.0°C, and respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute with an oxygen saturation of 99% on room air. Physical examination revealed a stiff abdomen with rebound pain in the right lower quadrant. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 8,200/μL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 58 mm/hour, and C-reactive protein level of 1.40 mg/dL. Abdominal CT imaging indicated diffuse sclerosis and a misty appearance of the peritoneum extending from the right lower quadrant to the pelvic region, without lymphadenopathy. The patient was treated with prednisolone (40 mg) and tamoxifen, which alleviated the abdominal pain. A follow-up CT scan identified a mass in the right lower quadrant. Her cancer antigen 125 (CA-125) level was 263.1 U/mL. She was subsequently referred to the surgery department.
test_results: The biopsy revealed a carcinoma without a specific origin.

case_report: A 40-year-old woman with short stature reported experiencing painful snapping in her left wrist, which had started to lock. She had no family history of short stature and did not recall any trauma to the joint. Her height was 97 cm and weight was 39 kg. Tenderness was observed over the second compartment of the dorsal wrist. Active extension of the right wrist was restricted to 30° before locking occurred. The release of the locking was associated with severe pain when the wrist was passively pulled and flexed.
test_results: Radiographs showed shortening of the forearm bones and phalanges, widened metaphyses and irregular and small epiphyses. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed hypertrophy of the extensor carpi radialis longus (ECRL) and extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) tendons in the second compartment. The synoviums surrounding these tendons were also thickened. Genomic deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) was isolated from the patient's leukocytes. Direct sequencing of all coding exons and flanking introns in COMP identified a heterozygous missense variant (c.806A > G, p.Asp269Gly) in Exon 8.

case_report: A 69-year-old male presented with a 3-year history of left orbital inflammatory pseudotumor, periorbital swelling, excessive tearing, and pain behind the eye. He had a history of chronic sinusitis and underwent multiple sinus surgeries over a 4-year period. Clinical examination was unremarkable. Ophthalmologic examination revealed normal visual acuity, moderate left periorbital swelling without tenderness or redness, left nonaxial proptosis, lateral displacement of the globe, and severe limitation in left eye adduction. Blood tests, including a full blood count, autoimmune screen (antinuclear antibody, p-ANCA, c-ANCA, anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB antibodies, rheumatoid factor), serum chemistry profile, serum IgG, IgA, IgM, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and serum IgG4 level, were all within normal ranges. MRI indicated a moderately enhancing mass in the left medial orbit, eroding the medial orbital wall and involving the inferior and medial rectus muscles.
test_results: The histopathological appearance of the left orbital biopsy revealed heavy concentric fibrosis, polymorphous inflammatory infiltrate including plasma cells, histiocytes, lymphocytes and frequent eosinophils, featuring the 'onion-skin' like perivascular whirling pattern. There was no distinct granulomatous inflammation or necrosis. Immunohistochemistry staining showed that IgG4 staining was mainly positive and IgG4 plasma cells were ~ 40% of all the inflammatory cells.

case_report: Patient 1 is an 11-year-old girl from consanguineous parents. The primary clinical features observed include involuntary eye movements (nystagmus), sensitivity to light (photophobia), and degeneration of both rod and cone cells in the retina leading to reduced visual sharpness. Additional findings include severe obesity, dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), and episodes of bronchospasm. No other related symptoms have been documented so far.
test_results: A novel homozygous amino acid change on exon 8, c.2785G>T leading to p.(Glu929Ter), was detected by Sanger sequencing in this patient. The in silico prediction of pathogenicity through different bioinformatic tools resulted in deleterious variant scores in MutPred-LOF (0.432), SIFT (0) and PROVEAN (−3.376). According to the ACMG, this variant should be classified as pathogenic (PVS1, very strong evidence of pathogenicity).

case_report: A 5-year-old girl from Saudi Arabia presented with generalized weakness, easy fatigability, pallor, and poor oral intake. Her oxygen saturation was 97%, and she was hemodynamically stable. At birth, she was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) due to a hemoglobin (Hb) level of 4 gm/dL, for which she received a blood transfusion. Initial investigations included normal flow cytometry and molecular genetics that confirmed an α-thalassemia trait without clinical implications. The patient was lost to follow-up for 5 years and had no reported medical concerns during this period. Both parents are consanguineous with no significant medical history. The patient had no history of recurrent infections, blood transfusions, hypertension, diabetes, surgeries, or drug allergies. Her developmental history was age-appropriate, and vaccinations were up to date. On examination, she appeared pale and fatigued but not dysmorphic. Cardiac examination revealed a hemic systolic murmur at the apex. There was no organomegaly, dermatologic manifestations, skin inflammation, or vasculitis. Neurologic examination and other systems review were unremarkable. She was admitted for further investigation and supportive treatment. Initial blood work showed Hb of 3.8 gm/dL, reticulocytopenia, slightly elevated serum bilirubin, and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. A positive direct antiglobulin test (DAT++) was noted, and she received packed red blood cells (PRBCs) with good improvement. The patient was treated with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) 1 gm/kg/day for 2 days and prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day for 1 month, tapering over 2 weeks, with no apparent response. Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy indicated reduced erythropoiesis consistent with PRCA. Parvovirus and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNA by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) were not detected. The patient was kept under close follow-up while preparing for the bone marrow transplantation process. She has a human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-matched sibling donor.
test_results: Sequence analysis identified CECR1 c.714_738dup, p. (Ala247Glnfs*16) a homozygous variant and a heterozygous missense variant G6PD c.563C>T, p. (Ser188Ph).

case_report: A 17-year-old female presented with a history of difficulty participating in sports such as football and running. Over the past two years, she experienced four episodes of unconsciousness and unresponsiveness, accompanied by straightening and twitching of both lower limbs. These episodes did not involve tonic-clonic seizures in the upper limbs, eye rolling, jaw clenching, tongue biting, head or trunk distortion, or incontinence, and each episode resolved within a few minutes. Post-episode, she reported mild headaches. There is no family or personal history of autoimmune diseases, neuropsychiatric conditions, or hereditary disorders. Neurological examination revealed instability and inaccuracy in bilateral heel-knee-tibia tests. During a straight-line walking test, the patient exhibited a tendency to fall and shake. The Romberg test was positive, indicating balance issues, while tests for meningeal irritation were negative. Blood pressure readings were 106/73 mmHg while lying down and 110/70 mmHg upon standing. Laboratory tests, including C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, routine blood tests, and thyroid function, showed no abnormalities. Tests for HIV and Treponema pallidum antibodies were negative. Cognitive assessments yielded scores of 30 on the MMSE Scale, 28 on the MoCA Scale, and 95 on the ADL Scale. A 24-hour dynamic electroencephalogram showed no abnormalities.
test_results: The brain’s cerebellar atrophy is visible in the 1.5T MRI. The patient’s KCNC3 gene (located at chr19:50826942) was found to have the heterozygous mutation c.1268G > A. This mutation caused a substitution of histidine for arginine at location 423 (R423H). The variant in question has been categorized as a pathogenic variant based on the instructions provided by the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG). The family confirmation outcomes also indicate that the heterozygous mutation was inherited from the individual’s mother.

case_report: A 35-year-old female patient presented with a gradually enlarging lobulated mass over a period of 15 years. Upon local examination, the mass was observed to be lobulated, skin-colored, shiny, firm, and non-tender, located at the tip and dorsum of the nose. Systemic examination showed no significant findings. Radiological examination indicated no bony destruction or formation of a sinus tract. Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of the lobulated mass was performed using a 22-gauge needle, yielding a scant, blood-mixed aspirate. The smears were air-dried and stained with May-Grünwald-Giemsa. Cytology smears exhibited mild cellularity with cells in irregular clusters of anucleate squames, along with singly lying cells and loose clusters of sebaceous cells containing a moderate amount of pale cytoplasm and round to oval nuclei. The findings suggested the presence of a benign skin adnexal lesion.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed unremarkable epidermis and dermis showed strands of stratified squamous epithelium containing fragments of hair shafts along with many variables sized hair follicles exhibiting varying degree of maturation.

case_report: This female infant was born at 39 weeks’ gestation to a 35-year-old father and a 28-year-old mother with a history of three pregnancies, two of which resulted in miscarriages. The parents were first-degree relatives. Postnatal meconium aspiration necessitated intensive care, including positive pressure ventilation. At birth, the infant weighed 2080 g (<10th percentile), measured 46 cm in height (10-25th percentile), and had a head circumference of 32 cm (10-25th percentile). The infant exhibited widespread hyperpigmentation over the entire body, including the mucosa. Dysmorphic facial features were noted, including small, low-set ears, a flattened nasal bridge, and retrognathia. The external genitalia appeared entirely female, and no palpable gonads were detected bilaterally. On the second day of hospitalization, serum sodium was measured at 127 mEq/L and potassium at 4 mEq/L. Severe hypoglycemia was observed twice during the observation period. On the third day, adrenocorticotropic hormone levels were recorded at >1250 pg/mL (normal range: 10-60 pg/mL) and cortisol levels at 0.3 µg/dL (normal range: 1.7-14 µg/dL).
test_results: Abdominal USG revealed absence of adrenal structures bilaterally. A uterus was seen in ultrasonography and the karyogram was 46XX. Full bone scan imaging was performed and suspicious fractures were observed in the medial aspects of the bilateral femurs.

case_report: On November 29, 2018, a 52-year-old woman presented with symptoms of dry cough and chest oppression. These symptoms began two months prior to her admission. Her medical history included diabetes mellitus for six months, hypertension, and a laser ablation of vaginal polyps performed 12 years ago. Upon general examination, her body temperature was 36.4 °C, pulse rate was 112 bpm, blood pressure was 112/76 mmHg, respiratory rate was 20 per minute, and oxygen saturation was 94% on room air, improving to 98% with 3 L/min supplemental oxygen administered intranasally. Chest auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds over the right lung field. Abdominal examination identified a palpable mass in the lower abdomen. Hematology, biochemistry, and urinalysis results were unremarkable. T-spot tests were negative. Tumor marker tests indicated elevated cancer antigen-125 levels (CA-125, serum 663.3 U/mL and pleural effusion > 1000 U/mL, normal value < 35 U/mL). Serum levels of α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and other tumor markers were within normal limits. Chest computed tomography imaging showed right pleural effusions.
test_results: Ascites and a large irregular, cystsolidmixed mass (14 mm × 13 mm × 13 mm) in the right ovary were confirmed by abdominal ultrasound examination. Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging revealed a large pelvic mass with a low signal intensity on T1 sequences and a slightly high signal intensity on T2 sequences. Histopathologic examination of a pleural biopsy indicated fibrous tissue, striated muscle tissue, adipose tissue, and a few mesenchymal cells at the edge.
diagnosis: Meigs syndrome with benign ovarian thecoma

case_report: An 87-year-old woman presented with pain and an enlarged mass on her left middle finger. At the age of 76, she experienced finger pain due to a mallet finger. Radiographs at that time incidentally showed a typical enchondroma in the proximal phalanx of the left middle finger. To prevent a pathological fracture, curettage was performed under axillary nerve block. The cortex adjacent to the lesion was accessed dorsally by splitting the extensor tendon. After fenestration of the bone cortex, curettage and packing with a granular artificial bone graft made of hydroxyapatite were carried out. Several years postoperatively, the left middle finger gradually started to enlarge, with an increased growth rate in the past year. She had undergone an excision of uterine leiomyoma 30 years earlier and had no significant personal or family medical history. Physical examination revealed the following: Height, 145 cm; weight, 42 kg; and body mass index, 20.0 kg/m2. The left middle finger appeared swollen and tense, with a tumor measuring 5.5 cm × 5.5 cm × 4.5 cm, which was elastic and hard. Laboratory test results were as follows: hemoglobin, 12.1 g/dL (normal range, 11.2-14.5); total leukocyte count, 6040/μL (normal range, 3300–8800); platelet count, 240000/μL (normal range, 130000-350000); erythrocyte sedimentation rate, 49.0 mm/hour (normal range, 0.0-15.0); C-reactive protein, 0.1 mg/dL (normal range, 0.0-0.14); lactate dehydrogenase, 152 IU/L (normal range, 119-229); and alkaline phosphatase (Japan Society of Clinical Chemistry; JSCC), 207 IU/L (normal range, 115-359). Plain radiographs showed residual artificial bone graft material and an expansive osteolytic lesion in the proximal phalanx of the left middle finger.
test_results: The histological examination revealed a hypocellular area, with an abundance of hyaline cartilage matrix, and the lesion was diagnosed as an enchondroma.

case_report: A seventeen-year-old female presented with primary amenorrhea following a normal onset of puberty. Breast development began at age twelve, followed by a growth spurt two years later. Physical examination revealed normal vulvar anatomy and shaved pubic hair, with a vaginal depth of 3–4 cm. Pelvic ultrasound did not visualize the uterus or ovaries. MRI from the local hospital confirmed the absence of a normal uterus and the presence of a short vagina, with normal ovaries described in the report. The patient was referred to our center. On physical examination, she exhibited tall stature (height +1.17 SDS) and very sparse axillary and pubic hair. A specialized radiologist's review of the MRI indicated that the previously described ovaries appeared as atypical gonadal structures with a large solid part. Hormonal examination revealed elevated levels of anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) and testosterone.
test_results: Genetic diagnostics confirmed the suspicion of a 46,XY karyotype and an androgen receptor gene mutation (hemizygous variant NM_000044.2(AR):c.2594A>T, p.(Asp865Val)).

case_report: A two-year-old male child presented with an inability to walk since the age of one year. He was born to nonconsanguineous parents, with a birth weight of 2.8 kg and normal early physical and mental milestones. He was able to stand and walk at 10 months, but within the next few weeks, he was unable to walk and stand even with support. Frontal bossing and a potbelly appeared, and there was a failure to gain height. He received calcitriol 0.25 μg on alternate days and elemental calcium 1 g/day, but showed no improvement. On examination, he was irritable and had a blood pressure of 100/65 mmHg. He had no edema or pallor, and the anterior fontanelle was still open. He exhibited features such as frontal bossing, widened epiphysis at the wrist, rickety rosary, potbelly, and bowlegs. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Anthropometry showed a height of 73 cm (5th percentile), weight of 9 kg (5th percentile), and head circumference of 48 cm (between 75th and 90th percentile). Laboratory evaluation showed the following: Urine albumin-trace, sugar-nil, microscopy-no sediments; Hemoglobin 12.3 g/dl, Blood urea 21 mg/dl, serum creatinine 0.3 mg/dl, serum sodium 137 mEq/l, serum potassium 3.4 mEq/l, serum chloride 99 mEq/l, serum bicarbonate 22 mEq/l, serum calcium 8.9 mg/dl, serum phosphate 2.0 mg/dl (normal values for children: 4.5-6.5 mg/dl), serum alkaline phosphatase 3966 IU/l, and serum intact PTH 26.5 pg/ml (normal: 10-54). Arterial blood gas analysis showed pH 7.353, pCO2 27.0 mmHg, pO2 114.3 mmHg, HCO3 14.6 mmol/l, and simultaneous urine pH was 8.0. X-ray of wrists showed fraying and splaying of metaphyses of distal ulna and radius, and old healed fractures of the distal shaft of the radius. Ultrasound of the abdomen showed normal-sized kidneys with multiple hyperechoic foci within, suggestive of calcification. X-ray of the abdomen showed no evidence of calcification in the region of the kidneys.
test_results: The 24-h urine protein excretion was 542.8 mg/day, phosphate excretion was 437 mg/day, β2-microglobulin excretion was 37.6 mg/day (normal < 0.2 mg/day) and calcium excretion was 82.8 mg/day (9mg/kg/day). Examination of urine showed generalized aminoaciduria.

case_report: Patient 1, a 3-year-old boy, was born at 35 weeks’ gestation to a healthy Caucasian mother and an unknown father. At birth, he experienced perinatal asphyxia, had a birth weight of 1,750 g (P2.3–P5), and exhibited craniofacial dysmorphisms including a high forehead with very large fontanels, hypotelorism, and small orbits. He also had a unilateral inguinal hernia and presented with a sepsis-like condition characterized by intestinal pseudoobstruction, transient hypoglycemia, cholestatic hepatitis, and transient renal failure (maximum plasma creatinine 132 μmol/L and urea 11 mmol/L on day 5, normalizing by day 10). The patient has chronic diarrhea with steatorrhea and severe growth retardation, including short stature and macrocephaly relative to stature. He experiences frequent, mostly asymptomatic, short-fasting hypoglycemic episodes (with normal lactate and ketones) and postprandial hyperglycemia, which have persisted despite frequent meals. Transient hypocortisolism was noted, but hypoglycemia did not respond to specific treatment. He is currently receiving exocrine pancreatic yeast supplementation. The patient has moderate intellectual disability and neurosensorial deafness. He required several blood transfusions due to chronic microcytic hypochromic anemia, with normal ferritin, leukocytes, and platelets. Due to childhood infections such as bronchiolitis and middle ear infections with febrile rhinopharyngitis, inpatient admission was necessary for glycemic control; immune system deficiency was ruled out. His abdominal skin is notably thin, with upper collateral circulation and diastasis recti, but without liver or spleen enlargement. Brain MRI was normal in the neonatal period. At 3 years of age, MRI showed ventricular enlargement, cerebral subcortical atrophy, hyperintense periventricular lesions, hypomyelination, and a Chiari malformation type 1. A broad etiological investigation including peroxisomal function, carbohydrate-deficient transferrin, acylcarnitine profile, urinary organic acids, microarray comparative genomic hybridization (CGH), and UBR1, SBDS, and COX412 genes has been inconclusive.
test_results: Elevated urinary concentrations were found for erythritol and sedoheptulose with gas chromatography mass spectrometry (GC-MS).

case_report: The patient is a 3-month-old female, born at full term (40 weeks) with a birth weight of 2600 grams. She is the first child of healthy parents who are not related by blood. There was no history of phototherapy for jaundice. Both the newborn screening and the 1-month checkup showed no abnormalities. At 2 months old, her mother observed jaundice and pale stools, prompting a visit to a local clinic. The infant's weight gain was inadequate over the past month, remaining around 4500 grams despite being breastfed 8 to 10 times daily. Physical examination revealed icteric sclera and yellowish-brown skin. Laboratory tests indicated a total bilirubin level of 9.74 mg/dl, direct bilirubin level of 5.64 mg/dl, and a prothrombin time–international normalized ratio of 1.2. The patient was referred to our hospital following an intravenous vitamin K infusion. Upon admission, she appeared in good condition but had noticeable yellowing of the sclera and brownish skin. Her stools were creamy grayish-white. Blood tests at admission showed AST 195 U/L, ALT 43 U/L, GGT 95 U/L, albumin 3.7 g/dl, AFP 35898.7 ng/ml, total cholesterol 196 mg/dl, and triglycerides 233 mg/dl.
test_results: Genetic analysis revealed compound heterozygous variants in SLC25A13: NM_014251.3, c.674C > A(p.Ser225*), and c.1801G > T(p.Glu601*).
diagnosis: Neonatal Intrahepatic Cholestasis caused by Citrin Deficiency
Orpha_name: Neonatal Intrahepatic Cholestasis caused by Citrin Deficiency

case_report: A 3-year-old Pakistani boy was admitted with worsening chronic lung disease. He was born at full term via spontaneous vaginal delivery, weighing 3.0 kg, with no antenatal issues reported. His parents are first cousins, and there is no family history of infant death, developmental delay, or genetic disorders. During the neonatal period, he experienced jaundice, necessitating a 4-day course of phototherapy. Subsequently, he had prolonged jaundice with cholestasis, mixed hyperbilirubinemia, elevated liver enzymes, and hepatomegaly. In his first year, he frequently experienced nosebleeds and was given olive oil in the nostrils to manage the bleeding and dryness. In his second year, he had a mild COVID-19 infection that did not require hospitalization. Over the past year, he developed recurrent respiratory symptoms that led to multiple hospital admissions and were managed with antibiotics, inhaled steroids, and bronchodilators. Six months ago, he presented with cough, difficulty breathing, and low oxygen levels, necessitating admission to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) and ventilation for 2 days.
test_results: Computerized tomography (CT) of the chest showed diffuse homogenous ground glass opacity with interstitial septal thickening.
Orpha_name: Niemann-Pick disease type C, juvenile neurologic onset

case_report: A 52-year-old woman presented to the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at Kyushu University Hospital in January 2014 with recurrent erosive and ulcerated lesions on the buccal mucosa and tongue, persisting for the past 2 months. Her medical history included hypoferric anemia. Laboratory results showed a hemoglobin concentration of 11.5 g/dL, hematocrit at 35.7%, mean corpuscular volume of 91.2 fl, mean corpuscular hemoglobin of 29.5 pg, and a white blood cell count of 3280 cells/mm3 with the following differential: neutrophils at 60.5%, lymphocytes at 21.0%, eosinophils at 9.6%, and basophils at 1.0%. Serum chemistry revealed total protein at 5.5 g/dL and albumin at 3.6 g/dL, both below normal limits, while other parameters were within normal ranges. The C-reactive protein concentration was 1.11 mg/dL. Serum antibody tests were negative for Dsg1, Dsg3, HIV, HBV, and HCV antibodies. Serum immunoglobulin levels were also below normal limits, with IgG at 466 mg/dL, IgA at 71 mg/dL, and IgM at 32 mg/dL.
test_results: CT findings raised suspicions of thymoma. Pathological findings revealed WHO classification type AB thymoma.

case_report: A 64-year-old male with a history of atrial fibrillation since age 45 had severe hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) without gradient as shown by echocardiography at that time. He underwent pacemaker/ICD placement due to severe septal hypertrophy (35 mm at the time of implant) as a preventive measure against sudden cardiac death. Despite multiple electrical cardioversion attempts, he remained unresponsive to medical therapy. He experienced dyspnea and palpitations, leading to his first ablation at age 59, which was repeated at age 62 due to recurrence. Post-procedure assessments indicated restoration of left atrium electrical conduction without the return of atrial mechanical activity, as documented by imaging of the mitral inflow and at the mitral annulus. The patient presented for re-evaluation of thromboembolic risk and potential discontinuation of anticoagulation therapy following successful ablation. He was found to be in sinus rhythm and asymptomatic. Vital signs were normal: temperature 37.5 °C, heart rate 85 beats per minute, and blood pressure 126/75 mmHg. He reported no dyspnea or palpitations and had good functional capacity. Physical examination revealed regular heart sounds.
test_results: A 2D TTE showed a dilated left atrium and the presence of preserved atrial electrical activity (P wave on electrocardiogram). Pulsed-wave Doppler TTE showed the presence of E wave velocity with the absence of A wave. Tissue Doppler showed the presence of E’ wave, but the absence of A’ wave.

case_report: The patient is a 4-year-old boy with congenital complete sensorineural hearing loss, scheduled for cochlear implant fitting. Consent for genetic testing was obtained from his parents, and ethical approval was granted by the Ethics Committee of the 1st Affiliated Hospital of Kunming Medical University (Approval No: 2019L60, Date: 2019.9.2). Clinical data from key family members were gathered via questionnaires. Comprehensive examinations were conducted, covering intelligence, audiology, ophthalmology, hair, skin, limb joints, and the digestive system. The patient was born full-term with bilateral blue irises and normal inner canthi. No signs of intestinal disorders, such as severe constipation or intestinal blockage, were observed, nor were there any abnormalities or restricted mobility in the limbs. The family showed no abnormal skin or hair conditions. The patient underwent otoacoustic emission testing, acoustic immittance, auditory brain stem response (ABR), auditory steady-state responses (ASSR), temporal computed tomography (CT), and cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Hearing loss assessments included pure tone audiometry thresholds for adults and ABR thresholds for children. Audiological examination revealed failed bilateral otoacoustic emission. ABR and ASSR indicated absent responses to 100 dB nHL stimulus intensity in both ears. Temporal CT and cranial MRI results were normal. No other family members exhibited congenital hearing loss or blue irises.
test_results: One mutation, c.426G>T in exon 2, which leads to a missense mutation, was detected in SOX10 in the proband. The mutation led to a change from tryptophan to cysteine at position 142 and resulted in a change in protein function. According to multiple databases, including HGMD, ClinVar, 1000G, and ESP6500, c.426G>T (p.Trp142Cys) is a novel mutation in SOX10 that has not been previously reported.

case_report: A male newborn, born to a 29-year-old woman at 39 weeks' gestation with a birth weight of 3400 g, was transferred to our neonatal intensive care unit due to the presence of a common port wine nevus on his trunk. The mother's antenatal history was uneventful except for smoking 1-2 cigarettes per day and experiencing upper airway and urinary tract infections one week before delivery. There was no consanguinity between the parents. Physical examination revealed a common port wine stain partially covering the skin over the right arm, sternal region in the neck, right temporooccipital region, right leg, anterior and posterior parts of the left leg, and sacral region. Additional findings included a systolic murmur graded at II/VI, a hemangioma measuring 2 × 1 cm on the lower lip, hypertrophy of the left cheek, a widened first interdigital space, dystrophia in the nail of the first digit of the right foot, and bilateral hypertrophy of the first digits of the feet.
test_results: Ultrasonography (USG) of the left cheek revealed lipomatosis. Results of the abdominal and transcranial USGs and cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were unremarkable. Echocardiography demonstrated patent foramen ovale and asymmetric septal hypertrophy. Thoracic USG detected right pleural effusion.

case_report: A 14-month-old boy was brought to the Department of Pediatric Dentistry at Osaka University Dental Hospital due to early loss of primary teeth. Intraoral examinations showed that the primary mandibular bilateral incisors and the primary mandibular left lateral incisor were absent. The patient had a low serum alkaline phosphatase level of 192 IU/I. Radiological examinations of the lower extremities and hands did not reveal any metaphyseal irregularities.
test_results: Tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase gene sequencing demonstrated a heterozygous c.550C > T (p.Arg184Trp) mutation.

case_report: A 21-year-old woman presented with a solitary bluish macule on the posterior aspect of her right earlobe. She had worn earrings on her right earlobe for 10 years. Over time, the color of the posterior earlobe gradually changed to blue, resulting in a 0.7×0.7 cm bluish macule on the posterior aspect of the right earlobe.
test_results: The specimen was normal epidermis and the brown pigmentation was resulted from deposition of foreign substance on the dermal elastic and collagen fibers, and also basement membrane of eccrine sweat glands. SEM-EDS analysis of the tissue demonstrated the presence of silver.

case_report: A 26-year-old female presented to the dermatology clinic with sparse and short hair. She had normal hair at birth, but hair loss began at four months of age. Her hair length never exceeded 7 cm and varied in length. Physical examination revealed normal physical and mental development with no neurological issues. There was diffuse thinning of the scalp hair, which was sparse and fragile without signs of cicatricial alopecia. Eyebrows, eyelashes, nails, dental health, eyes, and sweat glands were normal. No other ectodermal abnormalities were noted. A pull test showed that hair easily shed with slight pulling. Family history included six cousins of both genders with similar hair characteristics. The parents were not related by blood. Laboratory investigations including blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, liver, thyroid and renal function tests, serum electrolytes, urinalysis, blood glucose, glucose tolerance test, Hb A1C, copper, zinc, and ferritin levels, as well as proteins, quantitative immunoglobulins, and amino acids, were all within normal ranges.
test_results: Trichogram of the patient's hair show multiple abnormalities: Distorted hair bulbs, ruffling and fraying of hair cortex with fracturing of hair shaft, resembling trichorrhexis nodosa. A scalp biopsy show marked decrease number of hair follicles; most of them are in anagen phase, accompanied by mild chronic predominantly lymphocytic perifollicular infiltration. Cicatricial alopecia dose not found.
diagnosis: Hereditary Hypotrichosis Simplex of the Scalp
Orpha_name: Hereditary Hypotrichosis Simplex of the Scalp

case_report: A 61-year-old male of Han ancestry was admitted to our hospital on July 15, 2020, with a 4-year history of progressively enlarging soft masses at multiple sites. The patient reported the development of soft masses over the abdomen for more than four years, with additional swellings in the mandible, back of the neck, and elbows also increasing in size during this period.
