He consumed an average of 500 mL of liquor daily for 45 years and smoked approximately 20 cigarettes per day for the same duration. The patient had a history of type 2 diabetes for over 20 years with poor glucose control and hypertension for 18 years without taking antihypertensive medication. There was no family history of similar conditions, and he denied any previous special drug use. Physical examination upon admission revealed the patient was conscious, had a body mass index of 21.0 kg/m2, and presented with subcutaneous masses in the mandible, back of the neck, abdomen, and elbows. There were no signs of moon face, paper skin, hirsutism, or purple striae. Laboratory tests showed a total cholesterol level of 92.16 mg/dL, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol level of 35.28 mg/dL, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol level of 37.44 mg/dL, triglyceride level of 20.7 mg/dL, hemoglobin A1c of 5.4%, and 24-hour urinary albumin of 343.5 mg/d. Thyroid function was within normal limits. Basal cortisol levels and results from a 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test were normal. Tests for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, human immunodeficiency virus, and syphilis were negative.
test_results: Ultrasonography showed diffuse lipomatosis and lymph node echo in the neck in January 2018. The thickest part of the mass in the neck was about 28 mm. In July 2020, ultrasonography showed that the thickest part of the mass in the neck was about 44 mm. Ultrasonography of the elbow suggested that there was a hypoechoic mass between the palmaris muscles on both sides of the elbow, with a range of about 51 mm × 15 mm × 34 mm on the left and 46 mm × 14 mm × 35 mm on the right. The boundary was clear and the internal echo was not uniform, with strong echoes of several fiber spacers, similar to the echoes of adipose tissue. Simultaneously, excessive fat deposition was suggested on the mandible and the abdominal area of the patient by ultrasonic examination. Computed tomography showed diffuse and marked fatty deposits in the subcutaneous superficial fascia space of the neck without internal lesions. A breast ultrasound examination showed that both sides of the breast had excessive fat deposition and a flaky strong echo was seen in the deep side of the areola. The left side was about 33 mm × 3 mm × 25 mm and the right side was about 44 mm × 8 mm × 31 mm. The internal lobular structure was disordered, and small hypoechoic areas were seen, but no obvious mass echo and mammary duct expansion was found.

case_report: Patient 1 is a 16-year-old male born at 40 weeks of gestation to non-consanguineous Italian parents. The mother was 25 years old and the father was 30 years old at the time of birth. The patient was delivered at term via an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. Birth weight was 3.750 kg (50–75th percentile) and length was 51 cm (75–90th percentile). Physical growth was consistent with age norms, but the patient exhibited psychomotor delay and significant language impairment. Milestones included independent sitting at seven months, walking at 16 months, babbling after 12 months, and first words after 24 months. Sphincter control was achieved around three years of age. At the age of 14, cognitive and behavioral assessments indicated moderate intellectual disability with severe expressive language impairment. The WISC-IV scale measured an IQ of 40. Speech was severely disordered, characterized by stuttering, speech dysfluency, articulation difficulties, and limited vocabulary. Neuropsychological evaluation revealed communication and executive function difficulties, short attention span, and behavioral issues including problems with verbal inhibitory control. Despite these challenges, the patient was relatively cooperative. No sleep disturbances were reported, and there was no diagnosis of autism. Feeding and gastrointestinal functions were normal. Physical examination revealed mild pectus carinatum and moderate craniofacial features including protruding supraorbital ridges, bushy eyebrows, deep-set eyes, bulbous nasal tip, short philtrum, and wide mouth. Neurological examination was largely normal, with the exception of mild global dyspraxia and fine motor skills impairment. The patient had no history of seizures, and both EEG and brain MRI results were normal.
test_results: His initial diagnostic examinations included a complete metabolic workup, conventional karyotyping, and Comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) array (40 kb resolution) as well as Fragile X testing, which were all negative.
Orpha_name: Facial dysmorphism-developmental delay-behavioral abnormalities syndrome due to WAC point mutation

case_report: An eight-year-old male patient from Morocco was referred for a medical genetics consultation due to the presence of distinctive facial features and multiple physical anomalies. He was born to a healthy consanguineous couple, with the mother aged 27 and the father aged 40. There is a family history of a sister who passed away at the age of three with similar symptoms. The pregnancy was not monitored medically but was reported to be uncomplicated. At birth, the patient weighed 2800g, measured 52cm in length, and had a head circumference of 36cm. His development appeared normal during the first month of life. At eight years old, clinical examination revealed delayed growth with a weight of 15kg (–3 standard deviation), height of 80cm (–4 standard deviation), and an Occipital Frontal Circumference of 52cm (mean). The patient exhibited joint contractures, painful diffusely thickened skin, hyperpigmentation over joints, papular and/or nodular skin lesions, and gingival hypertrophy. His cognitive development was reported to be normal.
test_results: His skin biopsy showed hyaline material accumulation in the dermis. Sequencing of the exon 13 of the CMG2 gene revealed a homozygous deletion in the exon 13 (c.1074delT; p.A359HfsX50).

case_report: A 20-year-old male, well-nourished and moderately built, visited the hospital in June 2018 due to a swelling in the right thigh that had been present for 3 months and was associated with pain. He had no notable comorbid conditions or relevant family history. The size of the swelling remained relatively stable. General and systemic examinations showed no abnormalities. On local examination, the swelling was found to be non-tender, measuring 2 x 2 cm, with well-defined edges, and the skin over it was pinchable. Routine blood tests showed normal hematological and biochemical values.
test_results: MRI of the right thigh showed evidence of a well-defined lesion of size 1 x1.2 x 1.4 cm in the anterolateral aspect of the distal end of the right thigh. It was hypointense on T1 and hyperintense on T2WI. The lesion was seen arising from the fascial sheath of the vastus lateralis muscle in the anterolateral aspect of the right thigh. All other structures were within normal radiological limits. Microscopically, the lesion showed a vague nodular and whorled pattern of spindled cells with indistinct cell margins and vesicular nuclei. There was a dense chronic inflammatory cell infiltrate comprising lymphocytes and histiocytes at the periphery of the tumor. Mitotic activity was counted as 7/10 hpf. There was no evidence of cellular pleomorphism, necrosis, or atypical mitosis. On IHC, the neoplastic cells were focally positive for CD68, EMA, and SMA. They were negative for PanCK, desmin, CD45, CD34, S100, H – caldesmon, HMB45, synaptophysin, CD21, CD23, MPO, CD1a, BCL2, CD30 and ALK. The ki67 index was 12%. FISH for EWSR1 gene rearrangement by using a break-apart probe (CytoTest Inc.) on chromosome 22q12.2 was positive.

case_report: A 40-year-old woman with a history of amblyopia from childhood, characterized by a refractive error of −11.25 diopters in the left eye and −8.25 diopters in the right eye, was found to have a visual field defect in the left eye at the age of 30. Her brother has a history of a similar condition affecting his vision.
test_results: Next-generation sequencing revealed a novel missense mutation (c.922G > C) in exon 8 of the RPGR gene. The patient also exhibited this heterozygous mutation. Electroretinography showed an extinguished pattern in the left eye and a more preserved pattern in the right eye. Her fundus showed RPE atrophy around the vascular arcade and optic nerve disc, although bone spicule pigmentation was not observed. Radial FAF was observed in the right eye, the image of her left eye showed a ring of hypo-FAF in the macular region and patchy atrophy around the vascular arcade. Wedge-shaped visual field restriction was observed in her right eye, while concentric visual field restriction and temporal islands were observed in her left eye.

case_report: A 42-year-old man from Henan Province, northern China, visited Peking University People’s Hospital in May 2018. He had a history of type 2 diabetes for 11 years and managed his condition with a diabetes-specific diet, regular exercise, and medications including metformin, acarbose, and sitagliptin over the past year. Blood tests conducted at multiple centers in February and August 2017 showed HbA1c levels of 4.3% and 4.4% using ion-exchange HPLC (TOSOH HLC-723 G8; Tosoh, Tokyo, Japan), and 5.1% in October 2017 using ion-exchange HPLC (Variant II Turbo 2.0 [VII-T 2.0], Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA). In March 2018, his home capillary measurements indicated fasting blood glucose levels between 6.8–7.7 mmol/L and 2-hour postprandial levels between 7.1–7.5 mmol/L. Despite these relatively low HbA1c levels, his blood glucose levels were higher. Blood samples were collected for hematological and serum biochemical measurements, which were all within reference ranges. His plasma glucose levels were 5.97 mmol/L fasting and 6.85 mmol/L 2 hours after breakfast while on routine hypoglycemic agents. Enzymatic testing for serum glycated albumin (Lucica GA-L; Asahi-Kasei, Tokyo, Japan) showed a normal value of 12.45% (reference range 11–16%). HbA1c was measured using ion-exchange HPLC (TOSOH HLC-723 G8; Tosoh), ion-exchange HPLC (VII-T 2.0; Bio-Rad), capillary electrophoresis (Capillarys 2 Flex Piercing [C2FP], HbA1c mode; Sebia, Lisses, France), and boronate affinity HPLC (Premier Hb 9210™; Trinity Biotech, Kansas City, MO, USA). The respective HbA1c values were 4.0% (20 mmol/mol), 3.7% (17 mmol/mol), 5.4% (36 mmol/mol), and 5.8% (40 mmol/mol). Unusual peaks were noted on the VII-T 2.0 and TOSOH G8 chromatograms, but not on the C2FP electropherogram. No abnormal migration was observed on the electropherogram using capillary electrophoresis of the Hb program. Both ion-exchange HPLC methods indicated unusual peaks.
test_results: Sanger sequencing analysis showed no HBA gene variants, and a heterozygous HBB mutation, β51(D2) Pro→His; HBB:c.155 C>A, was revealed.
Orpha_name: Hemorrhagic disease due to alpha-1-antitrypsin Pittsburgh mutation

case_report: A 77-year-old male with a history of atrial fibrillation and hypertension was referred to our hospital due to a gradual decrease in neutrophil count over the past 3 years. Laboratory results indicated mild leukopenia and severe persistent neutropenia, with no other significant abnormalities. Physical examination revealed no signs of skin rash, fever, arthritis, or splenomegaly. The patient had no family history of neutropenia or myeloid malignancies. Clinical evaluation showed no presence of lymphoedema, warts, pulmonary disease, immunodeficiency, or monocytopenia.
test_results: Bone marrow aspiration and a biopsy revealed normal cellularity without morphological dysplasia in hematological lineages. In the chromosomal analysis of bone marrow cells, 4 out of 20 analyzed cells showed the loss of chromosome Y. Specific IgM and IgG against HNA-1a and HNA-1d were detected.

case_report: The male patient, aged 5 years and 7 months, was admitted in November 2020 due to slow learning in kindergarten. He was previously hospitalized for half a month following a premature birth. The child was the third fetus and third birth of the mother, who had no abnormalities during pregnancy but underwent a cesarean section at 36 weeks due to intrauterine distress. His motor and language development were delayed compared to peers, with walking and speaking simple words not occurring until around 1.5 years of age. His vocabulary began to expand around 5 years of age after a prolonged period of stagnation. Upon admission, he could only speak four to five words in short sentences. In kindergarten, he was noted to have poor language expression and limited communication with classmates. At home, he could respond to family members and express needs with simple words, and he could share attention with them. No stereotyped behavior was observed, except for a particular obsession with Altman and interests in shaping plasticine and painting. Physical examination revealed a height of 124.5 cm (>+2SD) and a head circumference of 54 cm (>+2SD), with no unusual facial features or abnormalities in cardiopulmonary auscultation and other physical examinations. Behavioral evaluation showed normal eye contact and the ability to call his mother and ask and answer simple questions. There was no history of major physical diseases or family genetic history reported. The patient has two elder sisters: a 16-year-old with good academic performance and a 7-year-old with an average school record. Gesell development schedules (GDS) indicated scores of 47 in adaptability, 45 in large motor movement, 46 in fine motor movement, 33 in language, and 39 in personal-social development. Blood routine, thyroid function, biochemical tests, and hearing tests showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Craniocerebral magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a slightly shorter corpus callosum with a mildly thinner corpus callosum body.

case_report: The patient is a 13-year-old male, the first child of non-consanguineous parents. He was delivered at 41 weeks of gestation via caesarean section due to maternal aortic aneurism. At birth, his weight was 3250 g (10–25th centile), length was 58 cm (97th centile), and head circumference was 32 cm (<3rd centile). Apgar scores were 9 at both 1 and 5 minutes. Psychomotor developmental delay was observed at 8 months, along with poor weight gain and feeding difficulties. At 11 months, he experienced his first seizure, with subsequent episodes occurring approximately twice a month. The patient has digestive issues, including indigestion, vomiting, and frequent abdominal bloating, but no abnormalities were found upon gastroenterological examination. An abdominal ultrasound was normal, and no visual or hearing impairments were detected. He began walking at 4.5 years. At his most recent examination at 12 years old, his weight was 23 kg (<3rd centile), height was 133 cm (<3rd centile), and head circumference was 49 cm (<3rd centile), indicating microcephaly. He could speak only a few simple words. Observations included stereotypical hand movements, hyper salivation, unstable gait, and inability to focus.
test_results: A head CT showed signs of partial dysplasia of the temporal lobe. A sleep EEG showed irregular delta, alpha and theta wave polymorphic activity during sleep. An ECG revealed a partial block of the right bundle branch.

case_report: A 16-year-old male presented with a single, painless, red, raised lesion on the forehead that had been slowly increasing in size over a duration of 2 months. The patient reported a history of trauma to the same site 2 months prior. There were no reports of itching, pain, or loss of sensation in the area of the lesion. The patient's past medical history was unremarkable. Clinical examination revealed a single, firm, well-circumscribed, erythematous infiltrated plaque measuring 6 cm by 7 cm on the forehead. Sensations over the plaque were intact. No thickened nerves or feeding nerves were palpated in or around the lesion. There was no lymphadenopathy. No significant skin lesions were observed on other parts of the body. Hematological, biochemical, and radiological investigations, as well as a peripheral blood smear, were all within normal limits. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the lesion showed a hemorrhagic background with a few lymphocytes, occasional macrophages, and occasional clusters of giant cells. Ziehl–Neelsen stain was negative for acid-fast bacilli, and Gomori methenamine silver stain was negative for fungi.
test_results: Histopathological examination of a 4 mm skin biopsy showed multiple dilated and distorted hair follicles in the dermis with inflammatory infiltrate on low power magnification. On higher magnification, distortion and destruction of hair follicular structures with moderately dense infiltrate of atypical lymphocytes (larger with more cytoplasm and irregular nuclear contour) and mucin deposition was seen. Mild epidermotropism was present with haloed lymphocytes in epidermis. No Pautrier microabscess was seen. No eccrine gland infiltration was seen. Stains for mycobacteria and fungi were negative. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) showed predominance of CD4 lymphocytes around hair follicles and paucity of CD8 cells. CD4:CD8 ratio was 8:1.

case_report: A 70-year-old woman reported a 25-year history of reticulate pigmentation on the trunk and extremities. For the past 20 years, she experienced erythema and a burning sensation when exposed to sunlight. Over the last 10 years, she noticed hair loss from the scalp and eyebrows, along with a few itchy, violaceous, scaly plaques on the trunk and extremities. There was no history of muscle weakness, oral ulcers, or joint pain. Physical examination revealed brownish reticulate pigmentation distributed across the trunk and extremities, sparing the mid-face, with a few skip areas on the chest. She had scarring alopecia on the frontoparietal scalp and nonscarring alopecia on the eyebrows, axilla, and groin. Additionally, there were multiple, discrete, well-defined, 3–4 cm-sized, violaceous, scaly plaques on the trunk and forearm. The oral cavity, palms, soles, nails, and genitals appeared normal. Routine hematological and biochemical tests were within normal limits. Tests for antinuclear antibodies, anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies, muscle enzymes, 24-hour urine protein analysis, and a computed tomography scan of the chest and abdomen were all normal.
test_results: Her skin biopsy from the reticulate hyperpigmented plaque showed atrophic epidermis and multiple dilated, congested capillaries in the papillary dermis. Biopsy from the alopecic patch over the scalp revealed epidermal atrophy and papillary dermal sclerosis with pigment incontinence. A skin biopsy from violaceous plaque showed compact hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, irregular acanthosis, and mild papillary dermal fibrosis. A band-like lichenoid infiltrate was seen in the upper dermis at one end of the section. There was basal cell damage in this area with occasional necrotic keratinocytes and dermal melanophages. There were dilated capillaries in the papillary dermis. Direct immunofluorescence test was negative. Dermoscopic evaluation of the reticulate plaque over the chest showed the presence of dots and globules in a reticular pattern with the presence of atrophy and multiple telangiectasias.
diagnosis: poikiloderma due to lichen planus pigmentosus

case_report: A 4.5-year-old female was seen at the neuromuscular clinic with an unusual walking pattern. She was born at 37 weeks to non-consanguineous Asian parents, with no complications during pregnancy or delivery. She has a healthy 12-year-old sister. Her early development was normal until an upper respiratory illness at 10 months during a visit to China, after which her motor development slowed. At 16 months, she began walking but appeared unsteady, leading to occasional falls. By age 2, she exhibited toe walking and a steppage gait. At 3 years, following a viral illness, her unsteadiness increased, resulting in at least two falls per week. Her speech and language development were initially normal, but by 3.5 years, she stopped responding to her name and music, following verbal instructions, and her speech regressed. Family history was non-contributory. Her weight was at the 43rd percentile and height at the 29th percentile for her age. Physical examination revealed a cooperative child with inconsistent command following and limited verbal output. There was no scoliosis or joint hyperextensibility, and cardiac, pulmonary, and gastrointestinal exams were normal. She recognized her mother and could inconsistently point to her nose on command. Hearing tests showed inconsistencies. Extraocular movements were full with no nystagmus, and the fundus exam was normal. The rest of the cranial nerve exam was normal. Muscle bulk was typical for her age with no muscle atrophy. She had mild tightness in bilateral heel cords but normal tone elsewhere. Strength examination was limited due to cooperation, but she had difficulty with bilateral foot eversion (4-/5) and good power in other muscles. Deep tendon reflexes were absent at the ankles and knees bilaterally and were 1+ at other sites. Coordination in her upper extremities was normal, but her gait was wide-based, unstable, and had a steppage quality. Romberg’s test was negative. Electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction studies showed absent sensory responses in upper and lower extremities with sparing of the sural sensory response. There was a severe decrease in lower extremity compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitudes and a mild decrease in the upper extremity with normal distal latency and conduction velocities. The F wave was absent in the tibial nerve. EMG showed a neurogenic pattern with increased duration of voluntary motor unit potentials in the tibialis anterior and gastrocnemius muscles. Auditory brainstem response testing indicated bilateral auditory neuropathy/auditory synaptopathy, with profound hearing loss. MRI of the spine showed subtle cauda equina enhancement, while MRI of the brain, internal auditory canals, and cochleae was unremarkable. Creatine kinase, lactate, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies were normal. A comprehensive neuropathy panel and frataxin repeats testing were normal. On a follow-up visit, she was more unsteady and falling more frequently. IVIG treatment was started, and audiology assessments confirmed profound hearing loss, leading to cochlear implant candidacy evaluation. She received three initial doses of IVIG, with slight improvement in gait noted by her parents. The treatment was increased to every two weeks for three treatments, followed by every three weeks for three treatments, but no further significant improvement was observed.
test_results: WES revealed a compound heterozygous state with two variants in the TWNK gene: c. 561_563dupTGA, p.Asp188dup in exon 1 and c.1909 C > T, p.Arg637Trp in exon 5. Family studies showed that the patient inherited the p.Asp188dup variant from mother and the p.Arg637Trp variant from father. Follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) level was 15.8 mIU/ml. Ultrasound (US) of the pelvis was significant for an absence of ovarian structures.

case_report: A 20-year-old female, born in Italy, with no family history of similar conditions. She is the older sibling of another case. At birth, she exhibited a cleft palate, distinct facial features, foot abnormalities, widespread skin issues, and nail irregularities. Initial laboratory tests showed reduced levels of B and T helper lymphocytes. At one year old, she was admitted to the hospital with interstitial lung disease, along with symptoms of diarrhea, vomiting, lack of urine output, and severe dehydration.
test_results: The molecular analysis, performed at the age of 3, revealed the presence of the genomic variant 1568T>C (p. Leu523Pro) in exon 13 of TP63.

case_report: This 15-year-old Malay boy, born to non-consanguineous healthy parents, initially presented with seizures and developmental regression. He was healthy until 6 months old when he experienced a fever accompanied by a seizure. Starting at 2 years old, he began having frequent generalized tonic-clonic seizures (GTCS) without fever. His general physical and neurological examinations were normal, and his psychological examination showed good space-temporal orientation and social interaction. Motor examination indicated normal strength and muscle tone in all extremities. By 2 years and 6 months, he had approximately 10 episodes of GTCS per day, each lasting 1–2 minutes with 1-hour intervals between seizures. His seizures improved with 400 mg sodium valproate and 150 mg syrup carbamazepine, though the frequency varied from seizure-free periods to several episodes per day. His parents observed that seizures were more frequent between 5–6 am during sleep and during the day. Over time, he developed acute cerebellar ataxia, instability while walking, and regression in developmental and speech abilities, with no signs of improvement. His speech deteriorated from a few words to bubbling. EEG, CT scan, and MRI brain at 8 years old were normal. Currently, he experiences GTCS approximately 2–3 times per month, each lasting 1–2 minutes and resolving spontaneously. The doses of carbamazepine were increased to 300 mg, and topiramate 25 mg was added, but this did not reduce seizure frequency. He now has intellectual disabilities, including mental retardation, developmental delay, and autism features. At 11 years old, he was non-verbal with no verbal communication and had impairments in motor skills, social interaction, processing skills, learning, and memory. He enjoyed playing alone and was unaware of his surroundings. Repeated EEG at 11 years old showed abnormal records with background slowing for age, absence of alpha activity, and frequent bursts of epileptic discharges over both centro-parietal regions. At 15 years old, his motor skills improved with physiotherapy, and he can now walk without support. However, his social skills remain poor, with no social interaction. He does not attend school, and his medication was adjusted to carbamazepine CR 400 mg and increased topiramate doses of 37.5 mg. His chromosomal karyotype was normal (46, XY).
test_results: Mutational analysis for SCN1A revealed a novel heterozygous point mutation a c.5197 A > G transition in exon 26 of SCN1A.
diagnosis: Generalized Epilepsy with Febrile Seizure Plus

case_report: A 44-year-old woman experienced recurring pain in the right side of her lower jaw for six years. Throughout this period, she underwent various evaluations, including a biopsy of the jaw that did not reveal any abnormalities. Due to increasing pain, she received biphosphonate treatment for one year and had two local excisions of the lesion in her right jaw. After the second excision, she was free of pain for 10 days, but the pain subsequently returned. Eighteen months following her second jaw surgery, she was referred to our orthopedic outpatient clinic for assessment of pain in her left thigh bone. Laboratory tests, including ESR, CRP, and CBC, were within normal limits. X-rays of the femur revealed a single area of increased bone density with thickening of the cortex and new bone formation on the outer layer of the bone.
test_results: Technetium99 scan showed multiple locations of active uptake, including the right mandible, anterior chest wall, left pubic bone and left femur. Biopsy and cultures were negative for malignancy or infection.

case_report: A one-month-old girl was brought to the primary healthcare center for the first time. Since birth, her parents observed involuntary movements of the right eyelid occurring during breastfeeding. The parents are not related by blood, and the pregnancy was well-monitored, culminating in a ventouse delivery at 39 weeks without any complications. There is no history of birth trauma or relevant family history. The patient is exclusively breastfed and receives vitamin D supplements. Her psychomotor development and growth are appropriate for her age.
test_results: She displayed rhythmic elevation of the right eyelid occurring consistently when sucking on a pacifier, with otherwise-normal findings on physical and neurologic examinations.

case_report: A 13-year-old male patient was born to parents who are double first cousins, following an uncomplicated pregnancy and vaginal delivery. At the time of his conception, the father was 56 years old and the mother was 40 years old. There was a history of two neonatal deaths with unknown causes, two unaffected siblings, and two affected cousins. The patient exhibited early global developmental delay, progressive skeletal changes, and an abnormal gait starting at the age of two. He measured 115 cm in height (−5.6 SD) and had a head circumference of 48 cm (−4.16 SD). His weight was in the 10th percentile (36 kg), with a U/S ratio of 0.77 (normal ~0.9). Physical examination revealed coarse facial features, a low hairline, and prominent lips. He had a short trunk, short chest, broad elbow and wrist joints, and asymmetric genu valgum, more pronounced on the right side. His hands and feet were short and broad with brachydactyly of all fingers and toes, pes planus, prominent heels, and generalized hypertrichosis. An intellectual disability was noted with an IQ of 41. No abnormalities were observed in other body organs, and there were no visual or hearing impairments.
test_results: Radiological analysis of the hip joint revealed shallow acetabulum with abnormally flat and enlarged femoral head and narrow femoral neck, lace-like small iliac wings, and bilateral coxa valga.

case_report: A 47-year-old man of Swedish origin was referred to a retinal clinic with concerns regarding decreased night vision and visual field narrowing starting from 45 years of age. The patient did not report any metamorphopsias or visual impairment. His father had epiretinal membrane (ERM). There was no other family history of eye or skeletal diseases in first- or second-degree relatives. The best corrected visual acuity was 0.63 in both eyes (Snellen chart) and the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study visual acuity was 78 and 75 for the right and left eye, respectively. Examination of the anterior segment was normal with clear lenses and no corneal opacity. The vitreous was clear except for a Weiss ring in both eyes. There was blunting of the foveal contour and scattered pigmentary changes in the middle periphery, presenting as discrete bone-spicules and pigment clumping. Fundus autofluorescence showed patchy hypoautofluorescence in the middle periphery and more homogenous hyperautofluorescence peripherally in both eyes. Macula cross-section on optical coherence tomography revealed light ERM with a slightly flattened foveal profile. Changes were more pronounced in the left eye, but without clinically significant cystoid macular edema. Full field electroretinogram on an Espion apparatus with Dawson, Trick, and Litzkow electrodes showed moderate to significant amplitude reduction with both scotopic and photopic stimulation, with the rod-system being more affected than the cones. Threshold perimetry 24:2 showed peripheral restriction nasally up to 20 degrees, and Goldmann kinetic perimetry, performed later, confirmed the peripheral narrowing of the visual field.
test_results: Whole genome sequencing was performed and analyzed as previously described. Data was analyzed using a panel of 325 genes associated with retinal disease. Two variants previously reported as pathogenic were identified in GNPTG, c.347_349del and c.607dup. Segregation analysis confirmed the presence of one variant in each parent, consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance. Biochemical analyses to confirm the diagnosis were performed. The activities of the lysosomal enzymes hexosaminidase A and B, alfa-fucosidase, beta-galactosidase and beta-glucuronidase in plasma and leukocytes were determined by methods using the hydrolysis of synthetic substrates based on 4-methylumbelliferyl. The amount of 4-methylumbelliferon (4-MU) was measured using fluorometry. The activities of certain lysosomal enzymes were highly increased in plasma, compared to the average activity of three healthy age matched controls. Activities in leukocytes for the same enzymes were slightly decreased or within lower normal range when compared to locally established reference intervals based on 20 healthy adults.

case_report: A 38-year-old female presented with sudden onset of bilateral blurred vision, followed by a focal headache in the right occipital region one day before admission, which improved with analgesics. The next morning, she experienced a recurrence of blurred vision, predominantly on the left side. She also reported a sudden, severe headache after sneezing, followed by a right-sided headache with a pain score of 3 out of 10, similar to the previous day. Her medical history includes infrequent migraine attacks without aura, a smoking history of 10 pack-years, and receiving the second dose of the Moderna SARS-CoV-2 vaccine 18 days before symptom onset. On admission, a neurological examination revealed a blotchy scotoma in the left eye. Cerebral MRI showed an acute cortical ischemic lesion in the right posterior cerebral artery territory. Perimetry indicated patchy visual field deficits in the left upper quadrant. Further evaluation ruled out venous sinus thrombosis (normal D-dimer, normal venography), cerebral vasculitis, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, arterial hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, and atrial fibrillation. EEG demonstrated focal slowing and epileptiform discharges over the right occipital region.
test_results: CT angiography revealed a normal-sized right PCA, which was physiologically filled via the basilary artery.

case_report: A 4-year-old male child presented with a fever and painful skin lesions on the upper and lower limbs lasting for 12 days. The skin lesions initially appeared on the lower limbs and quickly developed into black necrotic areas. The child also had a history of joint pain. Physical examination revealed stellate brownish-black necrotic patches on both the upper and lower extremities. Hepatomegaly was noted. Laboratory investigations indicated normocytic normochromic anemia with neutrophilic leukocytosis. Elevated levels were observed in platelet count, ESR, and C-reactive protein. The septic screen showed neutrophilia.
test_results: WFT was positive for Ox-2 and Ox-19 Ag.
diagnosis: Purpura Fulminans secondary to rickettsial spotted fever group

case_report: An 8-month-old female infant, the first child of a nonconsanguineous Hungarian couple, presented with severe respiratory failure and low oxygen saturation (70%), necessitating intubation and mechanical ventilation with pressures of 16/5 cmH2O and 50% fraction of inspired oxygen. Initial chest radiograph showed bilateral diffuse reticulogranular opacity. The infant was born at term without complications and had been healthy prior to this event, with no history of immunocompromise, previous hospital admissions, or relevant family history. On physical examination, the patient appeared pale and her weight was below the 3rd percentile (6600 g on admission). Hepatomegaly and splenomegaly were observed. Polymerase chain reaction test detected Cytomegalovirus in the bronchoalveolar lavage, leading to the initiation of Valganciclovir treatment. Initial laboratory tests revealed a white blood cell count of 11.85 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein of 3.7 mg/L, procalcitonin of 0.11 µg/L, LDH of 807 U/L, and serum ferritin of 707 µg/L. HIV test was negative and lymphocyte subsets were normal. Immunoglobulin levels showed a low IgA concentration (0.57 g/L). A computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest revealed a 'crazy paving' pattern. An empirical treatment regimen of high-dose corticosteroids (5 mg/kg/day), azithromycin (10 mg/kg/day), and hydroxychloroquine (6 mg/kg/day) was administered but did not improve her respiratory status. The patient's condition rapidly worsened, requiring high ventilatory support with 100% oxygen.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing confirmed that the index patient was compound heterozygous for the maternal c.1429 + 2T > C and for the paternal c.821 A > G SLC7A7 mutations.

case_report: An 8-year-old boy from Chenzhou City, Hunan Province, China, visited Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University, China on October 29, 2020, with complaints of abnormal sensations in both feet over the past 2 years. The symptoms included a burning sensation and mild itching in both feet and ankles, which started without any clear cause. These symptoms were not alleviated by topical glucocorticoids but were relieved by soaking in iced water. Six months prior, the symptoms worsened, spreading from the ankles to the lower extremities, accompanied by burning pain, severe itching, normal skin temperature, and scattered chilblain-like skin lesions on both lower extremities. The patient had previously visited local clinics multiple times and was treated with dioxypromazine granules, zinc oxide borate borneol ointment, and naftifine ketoconazole cream, but these treatments did not provide relief. The patient was born prematurely at G2P2 and showed delayed growth and development compared to peers. He also had difficulty socializing due to skin lesions on his lower extremities. Physical examination revealed normal skin temperature and ruddy skin in both lower legs with ichthyosis and lichenification. The patient had a height of 108 cm (<−3 SD), weight of 15 kg (<−3 SD), blood pressure of 148/100 mmHg, normal heart rhythm, and a heart rate of 156 beats/min. The patient appeared poorly developed and malnourished with unintentional weight loss. Visible skin redness and swelling were noted on both lower extremities, particularly around the ankles and feet, along with ichthyosis and lichenification. The skin on both soles, heels, and between the toes was chapped and ulcerated, forming frostbite-like lesions. Two ulcer lesions were observed on the right ankle. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 13.67 × 10^9/L (Normal: 4.0–10.0 × 10^9/L), red blood cell count of 4.33 × 10^12/L (Normal: 4.2–6.0 × 10^12/L), platelet count of 474 × 10^9/L (Normal: 125–350 × 10^9/L), and neutrophils at 10.61 × 10^9/L (Normal: 1.8–6.3 × 10^9/L). Blood glucose was within the normal range. Elevated levels were noted for creatine kinase at 1,662 U/L (Normal: 26–174 U/L), lactate dehydrogenase at 597 U/L (Normal: 108–252 U/L), creatine kinase isoenzyme at 103 U/L (Normal: 0–24 U/L), and uric acid at 508 μmol/L (Normal: 120–450 μmol/L). Antinuclear antibody (ANA), rheumatoid factor (RF), and antistreptolysin O (ASO) screening results were within normal ranges.
test_results: The pathological examination showed only mild hypertrophy of the epidermis with hyperkeratosis and mild thickening of the granular layer in the skin tissue. No obvious abnormalities in the blood vessels or nerves in the dermis or subcutaneous fat were observed.

case_report: A 34-year-old male presented with left flank pain and a history of falling from a height. Physical examination revealed a large mass in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen and a non-reducing grade III varicocele on the left side. Blood pressure readings were generally normal, though elevated in some instances during routine checks. The patient also reported occasional abdominal pain, headache, sweating, nausea, weight loss, and loss of appetite. No other significant findings were noted in the patient's history or physical examination.
test_results: In ultrasound, a 100×127 mm hypoechoic mass with a central echo free region in the left adrenal and mild hydronephrosis in the left kidney was reported. In computed tomography (CT) scan, there was a 122×107 mm heterodense and lobulated soft tissue mass with central necrosis in the left supra renal region and another homogenous mass measuring 69×48 mm in the lower level of pararenal space and 30×30 mm mass in the left aorta. In magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), a 120×105×106 mm hyposignal mass in T1w and hypersignal in T2w with heterogenic lobulated margins was seen. The mass had pressure on the left kidney and pushed it down. Another 131×51×50 mm mass in left para-aortic area medial to the left kidney was also detected. Liver, spleen, pancreas and other viscera inside the abdomen and pelvis were normal. Metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scan showed multiple absorptive lesions in the liver and left lung.

case_report: A 7-year-old boy of Han ethnicity, weighing 23.5 kg, was admitted to the hospital due to recurrent episodes of joint swelling and severe pain over the past year. He had undergone two surgeries in the previous year for suppurative knee arthritis. There was no evident trauma before each episode, and no occurrences of pyoderma, acne, suppurative hidradenitis, systemic infection, or fever during the disease course. Physical examination revealed that the right knee joint was more swollen than the left, with increased skin temperature and tenderness, but no palpable fluctuation. The right knee's movement was restricted, with flexion less than 40° and extension up to 0°. Internal and external rotation of the right knee joint was slightly limited, and the floating patella test was negative. No abnormalities were detected in other limb joints. Upon admission, the total white blood cell count was elevated (11.08 × 10^9/L), predominantly neutrophils (7.89 × 10^9/L, 71.2%). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was high (73 mm/h). Liver and kidney functions were normal. C-reactive protein (CRP, 123 mg/L), procalcitonin (PCT, 0.10 ng/mL), and interleukin-6 (IL-6, 73.25 pg/mL) levels were elevated. Interleukin-1β (IL-1β, <5.0 pg/mL), interleukin-8 (IL-8, 15.6 pg/mL), and interleukin-10 (IL-10, <5.0 pg/mL) levels were within normal ranges. Rheumatoid factor (RF) antibody levels (IgG 26.08 AU/mL, IgA 4.12 AU/mL, and IgM 2.41 IU/mL) were normal. Autoimmune antibodies, including anti-keratin antibodies (AKA), antinuclear antibodies (ANA), anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) antibodies, anti-Smith antibodies, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA, including p-ANCA, c-ANCA, myeloperoxidase, and proteinase-3), were negative, as was human leucocyte antigen (HLA-B27). Articular cavity effusion was thick and turbid with a high number of nucleated cells (3+/HPF) and pus cells (1+/HPF), 98% of which were multi-nucleated cells. No bacterial growth was observed in the culture of articular cavity effusion (cultures were saved for 28 days). Blood coagulation function and viral screening (HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis) were normal. The boy underwent arthroscopic knee debridement and peri-knee abscess resection. Post-operatively, he was treated with vancomycin and rifampicin, but his arthritis continued to intermittently flare up. Further inquiry revealed that the patient’s 5-year-old brother had a similar history of arthritis in his right elbow and left ankle. The boy’s grandfather also had a history of recurrent pyoderma.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed that the patient, his brother, and his father were all heterozygous for the PSTPIP1 gene mutation, which was found in the exon region (c.36+68 G>A, c.137+47 G>C, and c.562+114C>G het).

case_report: A 64-year-old female presented for treatment of an infectious corneal ulcer. She reported daily episodes of urticaria-like rashes, fevers, and joint pain since birth. She had a history of meningitis that did not respond to antibiotics and bilateral sensorineural deafness since high school. Previous evaluations for collagen diseases at other hospitals showed no disease-specific autoantibodies. Her detailed ophthalmic history was unclear. Her family history included a son with similar symptoms treated with corticosteroids and immunosuppressants. On initial examination, a rash was observed on her body, along with a saddle nose and clubbed fingers. Inflammatory markers, including white blood cell count and C-reactive protein (CRP) level, were elevated. Visual acuity was 20/400 in the right eye and 20/22 in the left eye, with intraocular pressure at 11 mmHg in both eyes. Slit lamp biomicroscopy of the right pseudophakic eye revealed diffuse conjunctival injection, pterygium-like corneal invasion, corneal infiltrates with epithelial erosion, marked cell and flare with hypopyon in the anterior chamber, and an opening from previous laser iridectomy. The right fundus details were obscured by corneal opacity and anterior inflammation. The anterior segment of the left pseudophakic eye was normal, but fundus examination showed a pale optic disc, sheathing of the retinal arteries, and yellowish deposits in the posterior pole. The patient was treated with topical and systemic antibiotics (eyedrops containing 0.5% levofloxacin, 0.3% gatifloxacin, 0.5% cefmenoxime, and 0.3% gentamicin, and intravenous flomoxef at 2 g/day) and antifungal drugs (1% pimaricin ointment and oral itraconazole at 200 mg/day). She also received topical corticosteroid therapy (0.1% betamethasone and 0.1% fluorometholone eyedrops) for 9 months. Despite this treatment, repeated exacerbations of anterior inflammation with ulcerative keratitis continued. Microbiological investigations of corneal scrapes, virological investigations for varicella zoster, herpes simplex virus, and cytomegalovirus in the aqueous humor, and tests for HLA-B51 were all negative. During this period, the patient experienced an episode of aseptic meningitis, persistent urticaria-like rash, and elevated CRP levels.
test_results: A genetic analysis detected a heterozygous, germline p.Asp303Asn mutation in the NLRP3 gene in both the patient and her son.
diagnosis: Chronic Infantile Neurologic, Cutaneous, and Articular Syndrome

case_report: A 50-day-old male infant arrived at the emergency department with persistent loose stools since birth, fever for the past four days, and failure to thrive. The stools occurred approximately 10-12 times daily, were oily, foul-smelling, yellow to green in color, and lacked blood. There was no vomiting, but the stool frequency increased over time. The fever was low-grade, intermittent, and temporarily alleviated by antipyretics. The infant was the twelfth child of a consanguineous marriage, born full-term via caesarean section due to previous C-section scars, with a birth weight of 2 kg. There were no antenatal or postnatal complications, except for a three-day hospital admission on the 35th day of life for similar complaints, which were managed accordingly. The infant had been exclusively breastfed and achieved a social smile at six weeks. There was a history of a sibling's death at one year of age due to loose stools. On examination, the infant's body weight was 2.5 kg (<2nd percentile), body length was 49.5 cm (<1st percentile), and occipital-frontal head circumference was 35 cm (<1st percentile). The infant appeared lethargic, dehydrated, anemic, and febrile, with a distended abdomen and signs of failure to thrive. Further examination revealed an extensive perianal rash, oral ulcers, and overriding sutures. Other systemic examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed low hemoglobin levels, normal mean corpuscular volume and mean corpuscular hemoglobin, but an increased total leukocyte count. Initial management included intravenous fluids and antibiotics, which improved hydration status and reduced fever, but loose stools persisted. The clinical condition worsened with feeding. Further investigations were conducted for other potential causes of infantile diarrhea. Stool and blood cultures showed no growth. Absence of reducing substances in stool tests and normal serum electrolyte levels excluded certain conditions.
test_results: Lipid profile showed low levels of LDL, HDL and TC, whereas TG levels were within normal range.

case_report: An 18-year-old male presented with multiple masses on his back following two surgical resections performed one year prior. He reported no family history of any diseases. Four years ago, a painless swelling developed on his left scapula, and imaging showed osteochondromas with exostoses at the femur and tibia. The patient underwent resection of the back mass, and pathological examination revealed osteochondromas with abundant hyperplastic bone and cartilage, but no cartilage cap structure. Three weeks post-surgery, a mass reappeared at the incision site. A second resection was performed, after which a painful mass with redness and swelling at the drainage port recurred. No special treatment was administered. Over the next three months, the condition progressed rapidly, with similar masses appearing on the back, hip, and other areas. Upon visiting our hospital, a detailed physical examination revealed multiple bone masses of varying sizes on the back, ribs, humerus, and hip, leading to stiffness in the spine, shoulder, and hip. The patient exhibited scoliosis to the left due to the
test_results: The results demonstrated a heterozygous mutation in ACVR1 (c.617G > A; p.R206H).

case_report: A 16-year-old female presented with bleeding gums, ulcerations of the buccal mucosa, missing teeth, and difficulty swallowing. The patient's mother noted that her other child was healthy. Both pregnancies and deliveries were normal. The affected child had skin blisters starting at 3 months old, some spontaneous and others due to friction or pressure. These blisters contained clear fluid, left scars after rupturing, and occurred until the age of 1 year. Skin examination showed multiple hypopigmented and some hyperpigmented macules of varying sizes on the face, neck, trunk, and limbs. Poikilodermatous skin changes were observed. The skin was generally xerotic with significant atrophy. The palms exhibited hyperkeratosis with reduced palmar creases. The skin on the hands and neck was dry, atrophic, and photosensitive. The patient was of short stature. Hyperkeratotic plaques were present on the flexures. Scalp hair was normal in color and growth. Keratoconjunctivitis and conjunctival scarring were noted. The patient experienced frequent constipation and low urinary output. Scarring was also present on the genitalia. Scarring was evident in the soft tissues of the buccal mucosa and tongue, which showed reduced mobility and hardness due to fibrosis. Retained deciduous teeth were highly mobile. Mammeleons were still present in the permanent teeth at age 16. The gingivae were swollen and erythematous, with deep pockets and significant bleeding on minimal probing. In some areas, erythema extended to the mucogingival junction, resembling desquamative gingivitis. Xerostomia was evident, and the oral opening was restricted due to fibrosis.
test_results: The epidermis is flattened and atrophic; edema is present at the dermoepidermal junction, and the basal layer shows focal vacuolization with basal cell degeneration. Other histologic features include a prominence of dermal capillaries, pigmentary incontinence, and possibly, perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate.

case_report: A 51-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital due to recurring leg ulcerations. Eight years ago, she observed purpura on both legs, which developed into painful ulcerations. Laboratory tests showed positive results for antinuclear antibody (×320), anti-double-strand DNA antibody (342 IU/mL), and anti-cardiolipin antibody (18 U/mL). She was treated with 15 mg of prednisolone and topical therapies, including wound cleaning and ointments. The leg ulcerations gradually improved and healed with scars over approximately 3 years. She remained asymptomatic on a maintenance dose of 10 mg of prednisolone. However, the leg ulcerations recurred, and she was referred to our hospital 2 years ago. Physical examination showed swelling of the right leg with multiple small ulcers, white scars, and purpura. Methylprednisolone pulse therapy (1 g/d intravenously for 3 days) was administered along with antiplatelet medications, followed by 50 mg of prednisolone and 50 mg of azathioprine. This treatment led to immediate pain relief, and the leg ulcerations gradually improved and healed with scars in 2 months. After the ulcers healed, prednisolone was tapered, and she remained asymptomatic. However, 3 months ago, the ulcerations recurred on the right leg. Physical examination revealed swelling of the right leg with multiple ulcerations and a moth-eaten appearance. Methylprednisolone pulse therapy had little effect this time.
test_results: Skin rebiopsy revealed occlusion of superficial dermal small vessels due to fibrin thrombus. Infiltration of inflammatory cells around the dermal vessels was scarce.

case_report: Patient 1 is a 9-year-old Hispanic female born vaginally at 37 weeks gestation to non-consanguineous parents after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Postnatally, she spent 11 days in the neonatal intensive care unit due to hyperventilation, feeding difficulties, and jaundice. Motor and speech delays were observed starting at 9 months. She began pulling to stand at 1 year, cruising at 14 months, and walking at 18 months. At 4 years, she was able to put two words together, and by 9 years, she can speak in two-to-three-word phrases. She receives occupational and speech therapy and is enrolled in special education classes due to global developmental delay. At 4 years, she had a neurology evaluation following a single episode of a febrile seizure, and anti-epileptic drugs were not recommended at that time. At 6 years, she underwent surgery for bilateral strabismus, which was unsuccessful due to optic nerve hypoplasia.
test_results: A brain MRI at age 7 years demonstrated decreased volume of the bilateral anterior optic pathway. She was noted to have an abnormal EEG with continuous generalized slowing, consistent with mild encephalopathy.

case_report: A 20-month-old male patient was admitted to the hospital with severe pneumonia. During the hospital stay, elevated serum creatinine, proteinuria, and partially compensated high anion gap metabolic acidosis were identified. A renal biopsy revealed irregular thinning and thickening of the basement membrane with a fibrillated texture and a scalloped outer aspect of the glomerular capillary wall under the electron microscope. Podocyte foot processes were partially fused, vacuolized, and detached into Bowman’s space. Cell organelles in Bowman’s space contained microvilli. No visual or auditory impairments were noted. The patient has a family history of one sibling who died from pneumonia at six years old, but no data is available to confirm if it is part of a syndrome. There is no family history of hematuria or kidney disease. The parents are consanguineous. Pregnancy and child growth were normal. Two years later, the patient began regular hemodialysis due to progressing renal failure, reaching end-stage renal disease (ESRD). The patient has a history of six hospital admissions: three for pneumonia, one for an infected line, one for a clotted line, and one for hyperkalemia.
test_results: The homozygous pathogenic variant was detected in the IFT140 gene (IFTI40:NM 014714.4:c.634G>A:p.Gly212Arg: rs201188361). A hand x-ray and fundoscopic examination were performed to reveal the existence of CSE and RP. The results were positive.

case_report: A 48-year-old female presented with intermittent abdominal pain that began 3 to 4 months prior. Her medical and family history were unremarkable. Vital signs and physical examinations showed no abnormalities. Laboratory results were normal except for a hemoglobin level of 9.0 g/dL (range, 12–18 g/dL). Tumor markers were within normal ranges, with CA19-9 at < 2.00 U/mL (range, 0–37 U/mL) and carcinoembryonic antigen at 0.82 ng/mL (range: 0–5 ng/mL). Abdominal ultrasonography (US) identified a single uniformly shaped mass measuring 8.0 cm × 5.0 cm in the gallbladder lumen. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) showed a uniformly contrasted mass measuring 8.7 cm × 5.3 cm and a small area of calcification in the gallbladder. Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed an 8-cm-sized mass in the gallbladder body and fundus with uneven high signal intensity on T1-weighted imaging. T2-weighted imaging showed low signal intensity of the mass with a linear dark signal intensity within the mass, indicating hemosiderin deposition in the hematoma. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy was performed due to gallbladder stone and hematoma of unknown cause. The operation revealed gallbladder distention but no other specific findings. Post-removal examination of the gallbladder showed large amounts of hematomas and multiple small stones less than 1 cm in size within the lumen. The gallbladder wall was thickened, and a 1.6-cm-sized polypoid lesion with a smooth margin was detected at the gallbladder fundus. The operation concluded with plans to identify the nature of the polypoid lesion through a biopsy later.
test_results: Microscopy of the polypoid mass showed a zellballen appearance, wherein chief cells showed copious eosinophilic granules gathered to form cell groups separated by blood vessels and fibrous tissues. The mass was positive for synaptophysin, CD56, and chromogranin.

case_report: A 35-year-old man experienced bilateral blurred vision from a young age but did not seek ophthalmological consultation. In January 2016, during an examination for prescription glasses at Clinic A, bilateral corneal opacity was detected. He was referred to Hospital B in May 2016, where examinations noted corneal dystrophy; however, his visual acuity was good, and no treatment was prescribed. In July 2017, he returned to Hospital B due to worsening blurred vision in his left eye, and cherry-red spots were observed. No improvement was noted on follow-up, and he was referred to our hospital in September 2017. His past medical history was unremarkable, and his parents, who are not related, have no visual problems and are in good health. Initial examination findings included best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 6/5 in the right eye and 6/7.5 in the left eye. Ocular pressure was normal at 15 mm Hg in the right eye and 18 mm Hg in the left eye. Bilateral fine, grayish-white opacities were observed across the entire corneal stroma, with no anterior chamber inflammation on slit-lamp biomicroscopy. Fine opacities were noted centrally on the posterior cortex of the lens. Cherry-red spots were present in the fundi bilaterally. Swept-source optical coherence tomography (SS-OCT) revealed a thickened and hyperreflective retinal ganglion cell layer, partial slight elevation of the retinal pigment epithelium in the right eye, and a small amount of temporal subretinal fluid in the left eye. Fundus autofluorescence imaging showed hyperfluorescence around the fovea bilaterally. Fluorescein angiography revealed no clear abnormalities. Goldmann visual field perimetry indicated bilaterally decreased central sensitivity. The Humphrey visual field test showed slightly decreased overall sensitivity bilaterally. Multifocal electroretinography (ERG) was largely normal for both eyes, with slight attenuation in central responses. A detailed systemic examination revealed very mild gargoylism, exaggerated tendon reflexes bilaterally, and tandem gait suggestive of cerebellar ataxia. Hasegawa's Dementia Scale assessment was normal at 30/30. The patient had no seizures or myoclonus. Blood analyses showed lymphocyte vacuolation, and peripheral nerve conduction testing disclosed latency.
test_results: Blood enzyme-activity analyses revealed low beta-galactosidase and sialidase levels. Skin biopsy showed decreased activity for both these lysosomal enzymes in dermal fibroblasts. The homozygous mutation IVS7 + 3A>G was detected in the CTSA gene on direct sequencing with genomic DNA extracted from blood.

case_report: An 18-year-old female presented with painless jaw enlargement and loose teeth. Family history was non-contributory. She had a history of hypothyroidism since age 3 and underwent surgery for an atrial septal defect at age 4. The patient experienced anodontia from childhood, with dental development occurring post-surgery. Clinical examination revealed significant mandibular enlargement, missing permanent teeth, and wide edentulous spaces on intraoral examination. Skin lesions resembling café au lait spots were observed. Puberty was attained at age 15. Laboratory tests for serum cortisol, calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphate, parathyroid hormone, Vitamin D3, complete blood count, urine analysis, and liver function were all normal. An orthopantomogram radiograph showed tooth misalignment, distorted roots of premolars and molars, and the absence of several incisors and canines.
test_results: Whole-body bone scintigraphy with three-phase imaging of the skull and upper thorax was done by the intravenous administration of 20 mCi of technetium-99 m methylene diphosphonate (99 mTc-MDP). Tc-99 m-MDP first pass images of the skull and upper thorax MDP blood flow images of the skull and upper thorax shows a region of focal hyperperfusion in the right hemimandible corresponding to a focal region of tracer pooling in the same region of the right hemi-mandible in the blood pool images shown subsequently. In addition to this focus, the blood pool images show mildly increased tracer pooling in rest of the mandibular and maxillary regions as well. Delayed phase whole-body and static planar images showed diffuse heterogeneously increased tracer concentration involving the entire mandible and bilateral maxillary regions with evidence of bony expansion. Single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) study with low-dose CT of the skull and neck region showed diffuse heterogeneously increased tracer concentration corresponding to symmetrical, expansile, multiloculated cystic lesions with soap bubble appearance and soft-tissue component within involving the mandible and bilateral maxilla. The lesions were predominantly of medullary origin with few interspersed areas of cortical erosion and destruction as well.

case_report: A 47-year-old woman presented with asymptomatic papules on her face for 10 years, with no significant medical history. There was no history of previous inflammation, prolonged sunlight exposure, or trauma, except for occasional pimples around the mouth. No family history of similar skin conditions was noted. Dermatological examination showed multiple, nonfollicular, skin-colored, discrete papules on the mandibular regions, nose, cheeks, and forehead. The papules were soft and did not have a cystic sensation upon palpation. The skin between the papules appeared normal, and no similar eruptions were observed on her neck or axillae.
test_results: Skin biopsy revealed unremarkable changes in epidermis and slight fibrosis in the dermis on hematoxylin and eosin staining. Elastin staining (Verhoeff-Van Gieson) revealed patchy loss and prominent fragmentation of elastic fibers throughout the dermis. Focal collagen hyperplasia was found on Masson staining.

case_report: A 4-year-old girl was seen in the emergency department following minor trauma to the nose. Examination revealed no signs of traumatic injury but noted a bulbous nose and thin, short scalp hair that had never been cut. She was referred for further evaluation of dysmorphic features. She was born to young, healthy, nonconsanguineous parents and had an unremarkable medical history, aside from chronic nasal obstruction and snoring. Her growth parameters were within normal limits (weight in the 5th percentile, height in the 10th percentile, and head circumference in the 75th percentile), and her psychomotor development was appropriate. Physical examination showed a pear-shaped nose, a long philtrum, thin lips, a broad forehead, and sparse lateral eyebrows. She had a lighter skin tone compared to her family, with blue eyes and blonde hair. Her nails were soft, and the 5th toenails grew very slowly and had never been trimmed. Bilateral inward curving of the 2nd toes was observed as the only orthopedic finding. She exhibited hyperkinetic behavior during the examination. Radiographic imaging showed abnormalities in the proximal and middle phalanges of both toes and fingers. Bone age assessment indicated a delay of two and a half years compared to her chronological age. Neither her parents nor her older brother showed similar physical characteristics.
test_results: Two novel nonsense pathogenic mutations were identified in exon 4, both in heterozygosity—c.1198C>T (p.Gln400X) and c.2086C>T (p.Arg696X). None of these mutations were found in her parents.

case_report: A 39-year-old female presented with a 20-day history of intermittent headaches, projectile vomiting, and convulsions in the left arm. Her past medical history was unremarkable. Neurological examination revealed blurred vision and bilateral abduction deficits. Laboratory tests showed hypoalbuminemia (28.6 g/L, reference range 40.0–55.0 g/L), elevated blood urea nitrogen (8.99 mmol/L, reference range 2.60–7.50 mmol/L), normocytic anemia (92.0 g/L, reference range 115.0–150.0 g/L), increased fibrin degradation products (5.8 g/L, reference range 2.0–4.0 g/L), and elevated D-dimer (0.25 mg/L, reference range 0–0.5 mg/L). The estimated glomerular filtration rate was 41.49 mL/min. Non-contrast head CT revealed irregular hypodense lesions in the right frontal lobe and basal ganglia. Brain MRI with gadolinium showed a 54 × 40 × 24 mm tumefactive lesion with a garland-like enhancement pattern. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy indicated decreased N-acetyl aspartate levels, increased choline levels, and lipid peaks. Tumor resection surgery was performed.
test_results: Neuropathology showed vasculopathy with mild-to-moderate inflammatory changes. There is focal necrosis, gliosis, lumen stenosis, and lymphocytic infiltration within the vessel wall. Immunostaining was positive for GFAP, Olig2, CD3, CD20, CD68, and CD138, and negative for Ki67, P53, IDH1, PAX-5, IgG, and IgG4.
diagnosis: retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukoencephalopathy and systemic manifestations
Orpha_name: retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukoencephalopathy and systemic manifestations

case_report: The patient is a 64-year-old male with a history of smoking (20 cigarettes per day) between the ages of 20 and 25. He is currently being treated for bronchial asthma using inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting beta-agonists. His Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status score is 0. He was referred to our institution due to an abnormal shadow observed on a chest X-ray during a routine medical check-up. The patient is asymptomatic, and routine laboratory tests returned normal results. He has no history of occupational or environmental exposure to harmful agents. A computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a mass located between the anterior mediastinum and the right upper lobe of the lung, along with multiple nodular shadows along the right pleura and pleural effusion. The primary mass is situated between the mediastinum and the right lung lobe, making it challenging to determine its exact origin. A thin bronchoscope with endobronchial ultrasonography and a guide sheath was used to access the right B3biαx bronchial branch, and a biopsy was taken from within the mass. The histopathological examination did not yield any conclusive findings.
test_results: The pathology report revealed a solid tumor with malignant squamous cells and scarring tissue and positive immunostaining for p40 and CK5/6. The pathological diagnosis was non-keratinized squamous cell carcinoma. A PET/CT scan showed a primary tumor with high 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose accumulation, a maximum standardized uptake value of 10.95, and multiple nodules with a maximum standardized uptake value of 7.08 in the right lung interlobar region and pleura. The diagnosis was cancerous pleural dissemination. The tumor was negative for epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) gene mutation, anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) fusion gene, and the proto-oncogene tyrosine-protein kinase (ROS1). The degree of tumor PD-L1 (22C3) staining was low (5–10%). CT-guided biopsy of a pleural region showing high accumulation by PET-CT scan was performed. The pathology report described the presence of malignant squamous cells with areas of fibrotic tissues but without keratin. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) analysis was negative for gene abnormalities commonly observed in lung cancer, including RET fusion gene and BRAF mutation.

case_report: A 40-year-old Caucasian American man with a history of reactive arthritis, Graves’ disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, mitral valve prolapse, and Gilbert’s disease was admitted after experiencing one month of worsening jaundice, fatigue, lightheadedness, and shortness of breath during physical activity. He reported dark urine resembling raspberry iced tea and dark brown to black stools. He did not have fevers or chills but mentioned a long history of night sweats and occasional diarrhea, which he attributed to his medications. He had no history of blood transfusions, hepatitis, alcohol use, intravenous drug use, tattoos, or use of herbal medications or supplements. He had recently moved to Cleveland to care for his father, who had stage IV colon cancer. His mother had been treated with corticosteroids and eventually required splenectomy for anemia and jaundice at the age of 40. His maternal grandmother also had anemia and jaundice, though the cause was unknown to him. His medications included etanercept, metformin, pioglitazone, methimazole, niacin, and aspirin. He had discontinued pioglitazone and metformin more than a month before admission on the advice of an endocrinologist. He had been diagnosed with reactive arthritis 10 years prior and had been on etanercept for the past 8 years. His Graves’ disease had been managed with methimazole for the past 18 months. On physical examination, he appeared calm and well-nourished with noticeable scleral icterus and generalized jaundice. His vital signs were: blood pressure 130/76 mmHg, heart rate 102 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and temperature 97.7°F. There was no lymphadenopathy in the cervical, supraclavicular, epitrochlear, axillary, or inguinal regions. The thyroid gland was neither enlarged nor tender, and there were no signs of proptosis, lid-lag, or tremor. Lung examination was clear, and heart rhythm was regular without murmurs, clicks, or gallops. The abdomen was soft and non-tender, with the liver edge palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin; the spleen was not palpable. A vesiculobullous rash was observed on the plantar aspect of the right foot.
test_results: Direct antiglobulin test (DAT) was positive for anti IgG and negative for anti-C3.

case_report: A 30-year-old male arrived at the emergency department experiencing shortness of breath, coughing, production of phlegm, fever, and night sweats for approximately one month. He had previously been treated with antibacterial medication at another facility for these symptoms. Although there was an initial improvement, he returned to the emergency department due to the onset of hemoptysis, which progressively worsened over the month, reaching about 300 ccs per day. A chest X-ray initially showed an enlarged right hilus.
test_results: CT angiography of the thorax showed bilateral pulmonary embolism at segmentary branches of pulmonary arteries and pulmonary aneurysms.

case_report: A 41-year-old female visited the otolaryngology office due to a soft palate fistula. She reported a year-long history of purulent and serosanguineous nasal secretions that did not improve with multiple antibiotic treatments. Additionally, she noted a year-long change in the appearance of her external nose, resulting in a saddle nose deformity. Her medical history includes rheumatoid arthritis, managed with infliximab, and she denied any chronic allergies. During the interview, her speech was observed to have a hypernasal quality. Physical examination revealed a single hard palate oronasal fistula and a single soft palate oronasal fistula. The saddle nose deformity and dry secretions in the bilateral distal nasal canal led to further nasal evaluation using a 0-degree endoscope. Neck examination showed no palpable masses or lymphadenopathy. Nasal endoscopy identified a large midline septal perforation without hypertrophy or edema of the turbinates bilaterally. Laboratory studies were conducted, and her antinuclear antibody (ANA) titer was greater than 1:80. The cytoplasmic-antinuclear cytoplasmic antibody (c-ANCA), perinuclear-antinuclear cytoplasmic antibody (p-ANCA), antimyeloperoxidase (MPO) antibody, antiproteinase-3 (PR-3) antibody, and atypical p-ANCA titers were all negative. At a one-week follow-up, she continued to experience hypernasal speech, purulent nasal discharge, and increased difficulty swallowing. Repeat nasal endoscopy showed similar findings, with additional purulent drainage in the middle nasal meatus bilaterally. A bilateral sino-nasal fungal culture swab was performed, revealing the presence of Candida dubliniensis and Candida glabrata.
test_results: Three specimens were collected from the nasal biopsy: posterior nasal septum (5 mm x 5 mm), left inferior turbinate (5 mm x 5 mm), and right inferior turbinate (10 mm x 5 mm x 2 mm). All three specimens showed similar histological findings with a mixture of chronic inflammation with abundant plasma cells, lymphocytes, eosinophils, and histiocytes. The biopsy also contained dense fibrosis with hyalinization and accentuation around blood vessels, nerves, and areas of mucosal ulceration. Immunohistochemical staining primarily discovered cluster of differentiation 3 (CD3)-positive T-cells, CD20-positive B-cells, and IgG-positive plasma cells. No convincing signs of vasculitis were seen in the specimens. However, IgG immunostaining revealed extensive positivity in the plasma cells, while IgG4 immunostaining exhibited up to 40 IgG4 plasma cells per high-power field.

case_report: A 68-year-old male patient has been monitored for the past 12 years due to the need for blood transfusions, chelation therapy, and management of heart failure. The patient, whose parents had no known clinical conditions, was initially found to have an enlarged spleen at the age of 7. At the age of 35, the patient was further examined for symptoms of weakness and abdominal distension.
test_results: Microcytic anemia that did not require transfusion, hepatosplenomegaly, gallstones, and elevated HbF levels according to hemoglobin electrophoresis were detected. The patient’s DNA analysis showed heterozygous mutations of c.92+6T>C (rs35724775) (IVS-I-6) and c.93-21G>A (rs35004220) (IVS-I-110), as well as the 3′UTR+101G>C (+233 relative to termination codon) (rs12788013) mutation. In the additional genetic analysis, no α-globin chain mutation was found.

case_report: An 18-month-old girl presented with widespread yellowish, thickened skin lesions; fragile, thin, and dystrophic nails; and woolly hair. She had previously been treated for psoriasis at another clinic without improvement. Physical examination revealed woolly hair and thickened skin on the palms and soles. Electrocardiographic and echocardiographic examinations showed normal results, with no signs of cardiac involvement.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed a plakoglobin gene mutation.

case_report: A 22-year-old male from Thailand presented with bilateral reddish, thickened skin on the palms and soles, first noted at age 3. The affected areas did not cause pain or itching. Occasionally, the skin would peel, leading to maceration, erosion, and tenderness. After swimming or diving, white spongy lesions appeared on the palms but resolved within a few hours. The patient also reported excessive sweating on both palms and soles. Physical examination revealed symmetrical, well-defined diffuse redness and thickening of the skin on the palms and soles, extending to the dorsal hands, fingers, toes, and Achilles tendons. Similar skin changes were observed on both elbows and knees. These skin changes have remained stable since childhood and have not spread beyond the described areas. Additionally, the iodine starch test and water immersion test of the palms were positive. Other physical examination findings were normal. The patient's younger brother reportedly exhibited similar skin features and progression, though he was not available for examination.
test_results: Both patients were found to be compound heterozygous for c.796C>T (p.R266*, rs1553630472) and c.650_653delCTGT (p.S217Lfs*7) in the SERPINB7 gene. The single nucleotide substitution at the position 796 from C to T, c.796C>T (GRCh37: chr18:61471522C>T), changes amino acid arginine at residue 266 to a termination codon. The 4-base pair deletion c.650_653delCTGT (chr18:61468152_61468155delCTGT [GRCh37]; p.S217Lfs*7) causes a frameshift resulting in a change of amino acid residue 217 from serine to leucine and stop seven codons later.

case_report: A 23-year-old female presented for evaluation of primary amenorrhea. She had a previous surgical history of inguinal hernia repair at the age of 8. Her physical measurements included a weight of 62 kg, height of 160 cm, and a body mass index of 24.2 kg/m2. On physical examination, there was an absence of axillary hair, Tanner stage 3 breast development, and Tanner stage 1 pubic hair growth. Examination of the external genitalia revealed normal appearing labia majora and minora, but a short, blind vaginal pouch with a depth of 4 cm was noted.
test_results: Inguinal masses were palpable on both sides and identified in MRI as testis-like gonads located at the inguinal canal. Transvaginal ultrasonography and MRI showed the absence of a uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries. Laboratory evaluation revealed follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone and estradiol serum levels of 21.2 mIL/mL, 22.6 mIL/mL, and 46.5 pg/mL, respectively. Serum testosterone was elevated at 1,032 ng/dL, and chromosomal analysis confirmed a normal male 46, XY karyotype.

case_report: A 69-year-old Japanese female, who had been receiving 50–100 mg/day azathioprine for 10 years with a total estimated lifetime dose of 297 g, presented with dyspnea and low-grade fever during a routine outpatient clinic visit. Laboratory tests revealed severe anemia with a hemoglobin level of 7.1 g/dL, leukocytopenia with a white blood cell count of 1300/µL, and thrombocytopenia with a platelet count of 10.0 × 104/µL.
test_results: Bone marrow aspiration results revealed prominent proliferation of erythrocytes with 83% proerythroblasts. Chromosomal analysis revealed a complex karyotype abnormality, with deletion of 5q, -6, -7 and addition of 11q13. The karyotype of the patient’s leukemic cells was as follows: 45, XX, del(5) (q?), -6 add(6) (q21), -7, add(8) (p11.2), add(9) (q13), add(11) (q13), add(11) (q13), -12, add(16) (q12.1), add(16) (q24), der(19) add(19) (p13) add(19) (q13.1), +2 mar No morphological myelodysplastic changes were observed in the patient’s bone marrow cells.

case_report: A 43-year-old Thai female presented with a single, firm, red, hard plaque on the left side of her neck. The lesion was slightly itchy, not painful, and had been slowly growing over 15 months. She had no known underlying health conditions and no family history of cancer or autoimmune diseases. She did not experience fever, weight loss, joint pain, hair loss, mouth sores, or sensitivity to sunlight. There was no history of injury to the area. She did not smoke or consume alcohol. Dermatological examination showed a single, firm, red plaque on the left side of the neck and a faint red plaque with visible small blood vessels on the left side of the nose.
