Other examinations, including those of superficial lymph nodes, mucous membranes, scalp, hair, and nails, were normal. Laboratory tests revealed a hemoglobin level of 11.4 g/dL, a white blood cell count of 5300/mm3 with 59% neutrophils, 34% lymphocytes, and 5% monocytes, and a platelet count of 262,000/mm3. Liver function tests showed total bilirubin at 0.3 mg/dL, direct bilirubin at 0.1 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase at 20 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase at 16 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase at 82 IU/L, and gamma-glutamyl transferase at 16 IU/L. Renal function tests indicated blood urea nitrogen at 14 mg/dL and creatinine at 0.84 mg/dL. Urinalysis results were normal. Antinuclear antibody titer was 1:80 with a coarse speckle pattern.
test_results: Histopathology revealed normal epidermis, dense superficial and deep perivascular and periadnexal lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates with lobular lymphocytic panniculitis. In addition, thickened homogenized collagen in the lower dermis extending to the broadened fibrous septum and loss of adipocytes around eccrine structures were noted.

case_report: A 60-year-old man presented with a widespread, blistering rash. Physical examination revealed erythematous papules and vesicles, some arranged in an annular, herpetiform pattern, located on the trunk, axillae, upper extremities (including palms and fingers), buttocks, inner thighs, and toes. Additionally, ulcers were observed on the vermilion lips, tongue, and palate. Previous punch biopsies for routine histopathology and direct immunofluorescence (DIF) were performed by an external dermatologist. Initial histopathology indicated a subepidermal blister with neutrophils, while DIF showed a granular, linear band of IgG and C3 at the dermal-epidermal junction. Subsequent histopathology and DIF were consistent with another condition. The patient had tried oral dapsone without improvement and had been on prednisone 50 mg daily for over a month with ongoing symptoms. Treatment was initiated with dupilumab in addition to continuing prednisone.
test_results: IIF on salt-split skin showed strong binding of IgG and IgG4 BMZ antibodies to the dermal floor.

case_report: A 72-year-old Chinese man visited the neurology clinic with a history of progressive loss of taste over 2 years, unable to distinguish spicy, salty, or sweet flavors. One month after the onset, he experienced persistent tingling and numbness at the tip of his tongue and pain around the mouth, which affected his sleep. Gabapentin was prescribed, alleviating the pain. A year later, he developed paresthesia in his right upper limb, followed by muscle atrophy. Concurrently, he experienced excessive saliva production and headaches. One and a half years after the initial symptoms, he developed difficulty swallowing, hearing impairment, and reduced sense of smell. In the past 2 months, his swallowing difficulties worsened, and he developed speech difficulties, losing 5 kilograms of weight. He sought medical care at a local hospital. His family history was unremarkable. Cranial nerve examination showed absent corneal reflexes, reduced gag reflex, and loss of taste sensation across the entire tongue, without tongue atrophy or fasciculation. Light touch and pinprick sensations were reduced in the peri-oral area and right limb, while vibration and proprioception sensations remained normal. Neck flexion strength was graded at 4- by the Medical Research Council (MRC). Muscle atrophy was observed in the bilateral temporal and masseter muscles, as well as in the right upper limb (deltoid, biceps, and subscapularis muscles). Limb strength was normal. Deep tendon reflexes were normal in the upper limbs but brisk in the lower limbs. Bilateral palmomental reflexes were positive. There were no signs of extrapyramidal dysfunction, cerebellar ataxia, or dysautonomia. Systemic examination was unremarkable. The Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score was 30 out of 30, and the Revised Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Functional Rating Scale (ALSFRS-R) score was 43. Laboratory results, including complete blood count, creatine kinase, electrolytes, total cholesterol and triglyceride, liver function, renal function, blood sugar, HbA1c, and C-reactive protein, were all within normal ranges.
test_results: Nerve conduction study showed sensory nerve action potentials (SNAP) decreased in the right median nerve, ulnar nerve, and both superficial peroneal nerves. In needle electromyography, extensively chronic neurogenic changes were apparent in muscles of the bulbar, cervical, thoracic, and lumbosacral regions. A pulmonary function test showed that his forced vital capacity (FVC) was 59.3%. Genetic testing of the whole exome sequence was negative. Abnormal nucleotides repeat expansions of the AR or C9ORF72 genes were negative.
diagnosis: facial onset sensory and motor neuronopathy
Orpha_name: facial onset sensory and motor neuronopathy

case_report: A 15-year-old female of Indian descent was initially referred to the Genetics and Metabolism Unit at the University of Malaya Medical Centre (UMMC) at birth due to multiple skeletal abnormalities and intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR), along with distinctive facial features. She was the first child of a consanguineous marriage, with her parents being first cousins. Her mother and father were 24 and 28 years old, respectively, at the time of her birth. The maternal grandparents were third cousins. She has a younger brother who is healthy and shows no skeletal abnormalities. There is a family history of type 2 diabetes mellitus. During pregnancy, her mother had gestational diabetes mellitus with good glycemic control and no known teratogenic exposure. Serial antenatal ultrasound scans indicated oligohydramnios and intrauterine growth retardation, but there was no reduction in fetal movement. She was delivered at term via elective lower segment cesarean section due to an abnormal lie, with Apgar scores of 7 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. She was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) for 2 weeks for weight management. The patient experienced delays in gross and fine motor developmental milestones due to skeletal deformities but had normal intellectual development and attended regular school, performing averagely. She underwent multiple corrective surgeries for her lower limbs. For bilateral congenital talipes equinovarus (CTEV), she received serial casting from birth, followed by a Dennis Brown (DB) splint and shoes until 7 months old. For fixed flexion deformity of her knees, she underwent bilateral Ilizarov external fixation twice at ages 3 and 10 years. Bilateral distal femur and proximal tibia hemi-epiphysiodesis were performed at 6 years old. These surgeries enabled her to walk short distances of approximately 50–100 meters, though she experienced pain and fatigue with longer distances. An ophthalmology review at birth revealed an increased optic cup-to-disc ratio (CDR) of 0.8 with tortuous vessels bilaterally, but no increase in intraocular pressure, lens or corneal opacities, or retinal abnormalities. At age 12, she was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), presenting with polyuria, polydipsia, significant weight loss, and recurrent skin abscesses over 5 months. Serum blood glucose was 20.5 mmol/L, with no metabolic acidosis or ketosis, and a c-peptide level of 0.9 ng/mL. Autoantibodies (ICA, GADA, IA-2A, IAA) were negative. She was treated with metformin and subcutaneous insulin. Her T2DM was complicated by diabetic nephropathy, dyslipidemia, and fatty liver. She attained menarche at 14 years old but was diagnosed with primary ovarian insufficiency when her menses ceased after a few months of irregular cycles. Hormonal studies showed low estrogen levels, with high luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels. Pelvic ultrasonography showed both ovaries were normal in size. Physical examination at birth showed prenatal growth failure, with a birth weight of 1.46 kg (Z = −4.7 SD), length of 35 cm (Z = −8.1 SD), and head circumference of 26 cm (Z = −8.0 SD). Distinctive features included brachymicrocephaly, diffuse alopecia, down-slanting palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, hypoplastic nasal alae, bilateral low-set and simple ears, malar hypoplasia, and micrognathia. There was no cleft or high-arched palate. Bilateral symmetrical mesomelic shortening of the upper and lower limbs was noted, with the upper limbs more severely affected. Bilateral absent radii, an absent left thumb with a small, rudimentary right thumb, and bilateral congenital talipes equinovarus were observed. A capillary hemangioma was present at birth over the forehead and extending to the nose, which faded by toddlerhood. Hypopigmented mosaic skin lesions were noted since birth over her left cheek, chin, upper limbs, abdomen, and back, following Blaschko’s lines, becoming more prominent over time. At 15 years old, all her growth parameters remained well below the third centile. A skeletal survey at birth showed a small skull with micrognathia, short ulnae with bilateral absence of radii, fusion of the left metacarpal bones, short tibiae and fibulae bilaterally, and bilateral absence of patellae, indicating delayed skeletal maturation. The spine and pelvic bone appeared normal. Cranial MRI showed microcephaly with no intracranial structural abnormalities. The echocardiogram was normal. Nerve conduction study and electromyogram were normal despite multiple contractures. Chromosome study revealed normal results, 46, XX. A chromosome fragility test showed equivocal results with chromosome breakage detected in 4/139 (2.9%) cells analyzed. Serial complete blood counts showed no evidence of bone marrow failure. A multigene panel sequencing of 17 genes showed no pathogenic variant detected, and a chromosomal SNP microarray revealed no clinically significant copy number changes. However, extensive long stretches of homozygosity were seen, representing 5% of the genome, suggesting a possibility of an increased risk of recessive Mendelian disorders.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing detected a homozygous splice variant NC_000008.10(NM_001017420.3): c.955 + 2_955+5del (GRCh37 (chr8): g.27637786_27637789del) in the ESCO2 gene in the patient. This variant does not present nucleotide change as it is an intronic splicing variant. The frequency allele in gnomAD v2.1.1 is 0.000012 and in the South Asian population is 0.00009827. This sequence change affects a splice site in intron 4 of the ESCO2 gene. It is predicted to alter splicing and results in loss of protein function. Loss of function variants in ESCO2 are known to be pathogenic. Both her parents were heterozygous carriers. This variant was close to the highly conserved splice site. ClinVar listed this variant as likely pathogenic (Variation ID: 21252), and homozygosity was confirmed by parental testing.

case_report: A 62-year-old male visited the dermatology clinic with multiple discharging sinuses located on the neck and right axillary region, persisting for 2 months. The patient reported a gradual increase in the lesion size with minimal discharge. He denied any history of trauma, fever, weight loss, or tuberculosis. The patient mentioned that he is a retired teacher residing in California for the past decade and travels to India annually. Physical examination revealed multiple discharging sinuses on the anterior neck and right axilla, with mild erythema around the sinus openings and minimal serosanguinous discharge. Systemic examination showed no abnormalities. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, urine routine, renal function test, liver function test, viral markers (HIV, HBsAg, HCV), Mantoux test, and chest X-ray, were all within normal limits.
test_results: The skin biopsy showed normal epidermis and dermis had chronic inflammatory infiltrate comprising of lymphocytes and plasma cells along with noncaseating granulomas. A few thick-walled large round structures were seen, which were present both inside the granulomas and in the surrounding stroma. Periodic Acid Schiff (PAS) stain highlighted these structures and showed globular sporangia with some of them possessing sporangiospores.

case_report: A 59-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital in June 2021 due to a cough with white, foamy sputum, dyspnea, and fever persisting for 20 days. She had previously received antiinfective treatment with cefoperazone sodium sulbactam and meropenem for 2 weeks at a local hospital without symptom resolution. Lung auscultation revealed rales in both lungs, and her body temperature was 38.5°C. A CT scan showed severe diffuse ground-glass opacities, calcification of heart valves, and gastric mucosa. Procalcitonin (PCT) and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels were within normal ranges. She was treated empirically with ganciclovir, moxifloxacin, sulfamethoxazole, and caspofungin, along with oxygen therapy, prone positioning, and steroids. After 7 days, her body temperature ranged between 37°C and 37.5°C, but she continued to experience dyspnea and skin pain, followed by the development of herpes and petechiae. A follow-up CT scan showed persistent high-density shadows resembling calcification in the lungs.
test_results: Lung tissue biopsy showed the presence of crystalline materials with calcification and granulomatous foreign bodies in the interstitium and alveolar cavity. Skin biopsy showed purpura fulminans. The genetic test results showed that the patient and her son had a heterozygous mutation in the FBN1 gene, and sequence 4,163 of the cDNA in the coding region of exon 34 on chromosome 15 was changed from C base to T, thus changing the amino acid GCG (arginine R) to GTG (histidine H).

case_report: A 4-day-old male neonate, born full-term via vaginal delivery to a mother with six previous pregnancies. The pregnancy was without complications. The neonate exhibited bile-stained vomiting on the first day of life and did not pass meconium. Mild jaundice appeared after the second day, accompanied by progressively decreased feeding and reduced activity. The birth weight was 2.5 kg. Physical examination revealed no abnormalities except for facial features consistent with trisomy 21. The abdomen was not distended. Laboratory tests were normal except for elevated levels of indirect bilirubin.
test_results: A plain abdominal X-ray demonstrated a double bubble sign.

case_report: A 4-year-old boy has experienced slow growth and short stature over the past 2 years. Initially noted to have short stature, the child also presented with normal cognitive abilities, liver enlargement, difficulty breathing, nearsightedness, and glaucoma. His medical history is unremarkable for skin, heart, lung, liver, kidney, or eye diseases. He was born in Zhejiang Province, China, of Han nationality, as the first child of the second pregnancy, delivered via cesarean section at 40 weeks' gestation, with a birth weight of 3500 g and length of 50 cm, without any birth trauma or asphyxia. The father's height is 140 cm (< -5 SDS) and the grandfather's height is 147 cm (< -4 SDS), while the mother and grandmother are of normal height. There is no consanguinity in the family. The boy's current height is 90.5 cm (< -3 SDS) and weight is 12.5 kg (< -2 SDS). Physical examination revealed a round face, stubby nose with forward-leaning nostrils, long eyelashes, and thick lips. Laboratory tests showed no abnormalities in sex hormones, insulin-like growth factor (IGF)-1, IGF binding protein-3, thyroid function, biochemistry, trace elements, routine blood tests, routine urine tests, or growth hormone challenge tests. Imaging studies, including cardiac ultrasound, pituitary-enhanced MRI, and karyotyping (550 bands, G bands), were normal. Radiography indicated delayed bone age (2.4 years). Pelvic radiography revealed a beak-like femur head, and lumbar lateral radiograph showed lumbar lordosis. The patient, his father, and grandfather all exhibit significant familial short stature.
test_results: Whole-exome sequencing of the patient, his father and grandfather showed a mutation of the FBN1 gene (OMIM 102370) c.5183C>T (p. Ala1728Val), while whole-exome sequencing of the patient’s mother showed no abnormalities.

case_report: The patient was born to a healthy 30-year-old mother at 32+2 weeks gestation via Caesarian section due to decreased fetal heart rate. Birthweight was 1255 g (10th percentile), length was 38 cm (10th percentile), and head circumference was 28.5 cm (45th percentile). The parents are of Libyan descent and first cousins. Both parents and the patient's two older male siblings were healthy. The patient required an 8-week stay in the NICU for feeding and growth management. Aminotransferases were normal during the newborn period. Elevated aminotransferases were first observed at 23 months of age during an evaluation for failure to thrive, with AST at 358 U/L (normal: 10-45 U/L), ALT at 853 U/L (normal: 1-35 U/L), and GGT at 101 U/L (normal: 8-35 U/L). Alpha Fetoprotein levels were within normal limits for her age. Initial tests for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, cystic fibrosis, infectious, and autoimmune causes were negative, and a liver ultrasound showed no structural abnormalities. Liver biopsy was not performed. At 3 years, GGT levels normalized, but aminotransferases remained elevated, with AST at 216 U/L at 3 years and 58 U/L at 5 years, and ALT at 453 U/L at 3 years and 57 U/L at 5 years. A brain MRI at 2 years of age showed age-appropriate myelination with mildly prominent cerebral sulci, lateral, and third ventricles, indicating cerebral atrophy. There were no documented seizures. The patient had a longstanding history of bilateral upper extremity tremor and leg weakness. Ophthalmology follow-up revealed myopic astigmatism, esotropia, and hypolacrimation, with a normal dilated fundus examination. Hearing was normal. At 5 years of age, a brain MRI showed persistent mildly prominent cerebral sulci, lateral, and third ventricles.
test_results: A brain MRI at 2 years of age demonstrated age-appropriate myelination with mildly prominent cerebral sulci, lateral and third ventricles, consistent with cerebral atrophy. At 5 years of age, brain MRI demonstrated persistent mildly prominent cerebral sulci, lateral, and third ventricles.

case_report: A 21-year-old female patient with no notable medical, family, or psychological history was undergoing chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) in the hematology ward. She developed pancytopenia and neutropenic sepsis post-chemotherapy, which was managed with intravenous antibiotics (tigecycline, colistin, meropenem, and ceftazidime) and blood product transfusions as necessary. Due to low platelet counts, the patient experienced a pulmonary hemorrhage requiring intubation and extended mechanical ventilation in the medical intensive care unit (ICU). During this period, her cell counts recovered, but she continued to have sepsis characterized by persistent fever and positive sputum and blood cultures for Pseudomonas aeruginosa. While in the ICU, the patient developed multiple, well-defined, velvety, thickened, darkly pigmented papules on her thighs, external genitalia, lower abdomen, and sub-mammary flexures. These papules gradually enlarged, merged, and thickened to form hyper-pigmented infiltrated plaques. These skin lesions were associated with persistent fever, which was not fully explained by the controlled sepsis, as her hemodynamic status was stable and inflammatory markers had normalized. Her complete blood count, routine urine examination and culture, liver function test, renal function test, serum protein electrophoresis, blood sugar, and thyroid profile were all within normal limits. A routine Computed Tomography scan of her body revealed an incidental left thalamic ischemic stroke and multiple splenic infarctions. Trans-esophageal echocardiography did not provide additional information.
test_results: A skin biopsy revealed abundant amounts of dermal amorphous mucinous material separating increased thickened collagen bundles, confirmed by mucicarmine special stain. The biopsy also showed proliferation of stellate fibroblasts, and superficial and deep perivascular lympho-plasmacytic infiltrates.

case_report: A 52-year-old female with no significant past medical history presented with a 2-month history of sudden and progressive painless visual impairment in her left eye. She also reported experiencing mild frontal headaches for the past 2 years. On examination, her visual acuity was 6/6 in the right eye and limited to light perception in the left eye. A grade 3 left relative afferent pupillary defect was noted. The left anterior chamber showed a few non-granulomatous keratic precipitates and +1 cells. Dilated fundal examination revealed a large yellow-whitish intraocular mass above the optic disc with overlying vitritis. B-scan ultrasound confirmed the solid nature of the mass and its adherence to the optic disc. Systemic examination and investigations, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, angiotensin-converting enzyme titer, urine analysis, and chest X-ray, were unremarkable. Skin tuberculin test and blood serology for syphilis, borreliosis, toxoplasmosis, and human immunodeficiency virus were negative. Smear and culture of vitreous specimen did not show evidence of bacteria or fungi. Vitreous tap cytology did not reveal the presence of malignant cells. Interleukin-10 level and IgH gene rearrangement studies were inconclusive. Brain and orbital magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a cystic mass with an enhanced solid component in the left caudate nucleus and a smaller enhanced solid mass in the left eye over the optic nerve head.
test_results: Navigation-guided (Stereotactic) biopsy of caudate nucleus lesion revealed a hypercellular lesion, consisting of sheets of large cells with pleomorphic vesicular nuclei and brisk mitoses.

case_report: A previously healthy 13-year-old male presented to a hospital in Mexico with respiratory distress, reporting one week of fever and vomiting, and four days of cough and shortness of breath. Upon arrival, he was found to be hypoxemic and tachypneic, requiring high-flow nasal cannula. He was transferred to a tertiary children's hospital for further management. On admission to the pediatric intensive care unit, the patient was in respiratory failure and shock, necessitating bilevel positive airway pressure (BIPAP) and epinephrine for cardiorespiratory support. A chest radiograph showed moderate bilateral pleural effusions. Electrocardiogram revealed diffuse ST-segment elevation. Echocardiogram demonstrated a mildly reduced ejection fraction of 51% (reference range 56%–78%). Initial laboratory studies showed mild elevation in B-natriuretic peptide at 135 pg/mL (reference range 0–100 pg/mL) with a normal troponin. Complete blood count indicated mild anemia with hemoglobin at 11.7 g/dL (reference range 12.5–16.1 g/dL) and leukocytosis with neutrophilic predominance, white blood cell count at 28.5 TH/µL (reference range 4.0 to 15.5 TH/µL) and 42% bands (reference range 0%–10%). There was a marked elevation of C-reactive protein at 46.2 mg/dL (reference range 0–0.99 mg/dL), D-dimer at 1.52 µg/mL (reference range <0.4 µg/mL), and ferritin at 1932 ng/mL (reference range 6–70 ng/mL), indicating a hyperinflammatory state. Complete metabolic panel showed elevated transaminases with AST at 584 units/L (reference range 15–40 units/L) and ALT at 185 units/L (reference range 5–52 units/L), hyponatremia at 128 mmol/L (reference range 133–143 mmol/L), and acute kidney injury with BUN at 84 mg/dL (reference range 7–18 mg/dL) and creatinine at 1.3 mg/dL (reference range 0.4–1.00 mg/dL). A respiratory multiplex PCR panel from the nasopharynx was positive for respiratory syncytial virus. SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibody was positive, indicating prior COVID-19 infection. The patient was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics (ceftaroline and azithromycin), pulse-dose steroids (1 g daily), intravenous immunoglobulin G (IVIG 2 g/kg), and anakinra (100 mg BID). Despite these treatments, the patient had persistent respiratory distress. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest showed left hydropneumothorax and bilateral large pleural effusions without evidence of parenchymal lung disease. He underwent multiple tube thoracostomies and video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) for hydropneumothorax. Fluid analysis and cytology were consistent with empyema, and pleural biopsy demonstrated pleuritis. Blood and pleural cultures remained negative, but plasma microbial cell-free DNA next-generation sequencing showed 80,000 molecules per million of Streptococcus pneumoniae. Next-generation metagenomic sequencing from the pleural fluid confirmed the presence of Streptococcus pneumoniae DNA. The patient later reported a history of frequent “allergies and sinus problems,” with intermittent periods of congestion and fatigue, but no previous hospitalizations or serious infections. There was no family history of recurrent sinopulmonary infections, otitis media, cutaneous infections, or gastrointestinal infections.
test_results: Complement levels were obtained and C3 level was undetectably low, with C4 at 11 mg/dL (ref 21–51 mg/dL). Immune evaluation was notable for complement studies demonstrating low CH50 (24 units/mL; ref 31–60 units/mL) and AH50 (<10%; ref >46%), and persistently undetectable C3 and low C4. These findings are indicative of low classical and alternative complement pathway activity.

case_report: A 55-year-old male with a history of bilateral popliteal deep vein thrombosis six months prior, hypertension, and end-stage renal disease due to focal segmental glomerulonephritis experienced sudden left testicular pain during hemodialysis. The patient was undergoing a hypercoagulation evaluation for a renal transplant and had discontinued warfarin six days earlier. He also reported new left shoulder pain radiating down his left upper extremity starting the evening before the testicular pain. Scrotal ultrasound with color Doppler indicated poor blood flow within the left testicle, with bowel or fat noted superior to the left testicle. Surgical scrotal exploration revealed an ischemic left testicle without evidence of testicular torsion. The left testicle was wrapped in a warm saline-soaked laparotomy pad, and the right testicle and cord structures were found to be normal, leading to a 3-point orchidopexy. A small incision in the tunica albuginea of the left testicle revealed hemorrhagic seminiferous tubules, resulting in a left scrotal orchiectomy. The patient recovered well postoperatively and was not restarted on warfarin to complete the hypercoagulable evaluation. Microscopic examination showed interstitial hemorrhage and focal atrophy without malignancy. Three weeks later, the patient developed acute right-sided scrotal pain with associated left lower extremity pain above the knee. Scrotal ultrasound showed no blood flow, and physical examination revealed an edematous and tender right testicle. Surgical exploration found no torsion of the right spermatic cord, but the testis was indurated, necrotic, and unsalvageable, leading to a right orchiectomy. No bleeding was noted at the excised edges of the cord, suggesting arterial thrombosis. Pathologic evaluation showed benign testis with acute interstitial hemorrhage and focal atrophy. The patient was started on enoxaparin sodium, warfarin sodium, and aspirin to prevent further ischemic events. Extensive hypercoagulation evaluation by hematology revealed no objective evidence for a hypercoagulable state. Laboratory results, including C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, perinuclear and cytoplasmic ANCA, Hepatitis B surface and core antibodies, Hepatitis C virus antibodies, cryoglobulins, Protein C, and Protein S, were all within normal limits. Two weeks later, the patient was readmitted with sudden abdominal pain and new erythematous skin changes of the abdomen. Initially, a rectus sheath hematoma was suspected, but a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast showed nonspecific skin thickening, subcutaneous edema, and fat stranding throughout the anterior abdominal wall without a distinct hematoma. The abdominal skin worsened over the next few hours to a 19 × 14 cm well-demarcated livedoid patch with a central irregularly shaped area of impending necrosis measuring 9 × 12 cm that was cold to touch. The patient also developed sudden penile pain with swelling and darkening of the penile skin. Genitourinary examination revealed a dusky, swollen, and cold glans penis, with flaccid corpora cavernosa bilaterally. The patient had no tactile sensation in the glans penis, but the rest of the penis was tender to palpation. A penile artery Doppler study showed pulsatile penile artery flow and a normal penile brachial index.
test_results: The skin biopsy of the anterior abdominal wall contained thrombotic vasculopathy with leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

case_report: A 25-year-old Asian woman, gravida 2, para 1, with a history of one spontaneous abortion presented in the emergency department with symptoms of orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and leg swelling for four days. The patient was doing well until the 27th week of pregnancy when she experienced high blood pressure and visited an outpatient clinic. She was treated with nifedipine oral tablets three times a day for pre-eclampsia and gestational hypertension. Over the last four days, she developed mild respiratory symptoms, increasing leg swelling, and chest pain. She had no significant past medical problems or allergies and reported a miscarriage during her first pregnancy without any elective procedures. She denied alcohol, smoking, or illicit drug use, and there was no family history of cardiac issues. On admission, physical examination showed facial flushing, blood pressure of 150/110, tachycardia, no jugular venous distension, bibasilar crackles with decreased air entry at the bases, 3+ pitting edema of the legs, normal reflexes, and oxygen saturation of 71%. Electrocardiography revealed sinus tachycardia and poor R-wave progression. A chest X-ray indicated pulmonary edema with bilateral effusion.
test_results: Echocardiography showed global hypokinesis with severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction (ejection fraction of 35%). The dimensions recorded for chambers were: left atrium: 36 mm; aortic root: 29 mm, left ventricle end-diastolic (LVED): 53 mm; left ventricle end-systolic (LVES): 43 mm.

case_report: On 7 June 2019, a previously healthy, 4-month-old female infant was admitted with symptoms including lethargy, decreased oral intake, and a weak cry that had persisted for 7 days. Laboratory investigations showed normal blood gas analysis, serum electrolytes, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, renal function tests, and C-reactive protein levels. Cultures from blood, urine, stool, and cerebrospinal fluid were negative. Abdominal ultrasound and oropharyngoscopy results were normal. Despite receiving intravenous fluids and antibiotics, the patient's condition deteriorated. On hospital day 3, a neurology consultation noted global hypotonia, loss of head control, minimal response to pain, absence of spontaneous eye movements, ptosis, poor gag reflex, weak cry, and absent deep tendon reflexes. Extensive neurological studies were performed. Brain and spine magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography were normal. Tests for anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies, nerve conduction, and genetic markers for spinal muscular atrophy and mitochondrial disorders were negative. Metabolic workup, including serum amino acid and urine organic acid analysis, was normal. A videofluoroscopic swallowing study indicated tracheal penetration and aspiration without efforts to eject the bolus. Repetitive motor nerve stimulation showed low compound muscle action potential amplitude of the right abductor digiti minimi muscle, no decrement at low frequencies (2, 3, and 5 Hz), but a significant incremental response at high frequency (50 Hz).
test_results: The serum test was negative, but the stool test was positive for toxins A and B.

case_report: A 5-month-old female infant with a history of abdominal distension was admitted for continued treatment. The infant was born at 36 weeks of gestation with a birth weight of 2600 g and Apgar scores of 10 at 1 min and 5 min. The mother, a 25-year-old gravida three, had no relevant family history. A second-trimester ultrasound scan showed an abdominal cystic structure, moderate bilateral hydronephrosis, and an umbilical cord hernia. At 30 weeks of pregnancy, VAS was performed. Initial physical examination revealed a massively distended abdomen and hypoactive bowel sounds. The patient required urinary bladder catheterization. Exploratory laparotomy showed a segment of ileum with arrested meconium but no organic obstruction. The umbilical hernia was repositioned into the abdominal cavity. Abdominal radiography showed a dilated stomach and minimal gas in the distal bowel segments. Due to persistent oral intake intolerance, a central venous catheter was placed in the right internal jugular vein for TPN administration. The infant developed Enterococcus faecalis sepsis and was treated with antibiotics. Due to duodenal obstruction, surgery was performed 26 days after birth. Ladd's bands and abdominal adhesions were resected, and a Santulli stoma was created. Histological examination of the intestinal biopsy showed vacuolar degeneration of smooth muscle cells. Rectal biopsy revealed normal ganglion cells. Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy was performed to decompress the stomach. Urodynamic studies showed post-void residual urine, bilateral hydronephrosis, and detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia. Urologists recommended intermittent catheterization and ongoing antibiotic prophylaxis.
test_results: De novo missense mutation (c.533G>A/p.Arg178His) was identified in the ACTG2 gene in the infant.

case_report: The patient is a 13-year-old Chinese boy with a history of global developmental delay since birth. He was born at 35 weeks gestation and spent 3 weeks in an incubator. Developmental milestones were delayed: he sat unassisted at around 1 year, stood unassisted at approximately 20 months, and walked unassisted at about 2 years. At 2 years old, he could only speak one word. Brain MRI at that time showed abnormal long T2 signals in the white matter, while electroencephalography results were normal. He did not receive any rehabilitation training before starting special education at 6 years old. Currently, he can eat and use the toilet independently but speaks only monosyllabic words and has significant communication difficulties. He has reduced sleep and is excitable. There are no other reported health issues. He is the only child of nonconsanguineous parents with no significant family medical history. Physical examination revealed a weight of 28.3 kg and a height of 140.5 cm, both below the 3rd percentile, and an occipitofrontal circumference of 50 cm, within the normal range. He was conscious with a normal gait and had irregular dentition but no distinctive facial features. Patellar reflexes were normal, and Babinski signs were negative. The patient was unable to complete the hand-alternating movement test, heel-knee-tibia test, and intelligence quotient assessment due to non-cooperation. Blood tests, including ceruloplasmin, lactic acid, ammonia, and liver and kidney functions, were normal. Screening for genetic and metabolic diseases in blood and urine did not indicate any abnormalities.
test_results: A de novo heterozygous nonsense point mutation in exon 6 in SATB2, c.687C>A (p.Y229X) (NCBI reference sequence: NM_001172509.2) was detected in the proband. Direct sequencing validated the detected missense mutations. PCR was performed to amplify the exon with the detected mutation and its neighboring introns using the forward primer: 5’-TAGTTTTAAGGGAGCCAACTAGGA-3’ and the reverse primer: 5’-TCAGTTTACAGGAGAGTGACTGTTT-3’. PCR products were purified using micro concentrating centrifugal filter columns (Millipore, Bedford, MA, United States), sequenced by ABI 3730XL (Applied Biosystems, Forster City, CA, United States), and analyzed by DNASTAR software. The proband had the mutation that neither of his parents had. The detected heterozygous mutation c.687C>A (p.Y229X) is near the end of coding region for the CUTL domain and leads to a stop codon.

case_report: A 2-year-old girl exhibited delayed developmental milestones and generalized muscle weakness. She was the second child of a couple with no consanguinity, and her birth and prenatal history were uneventful. She experienced a global developmental delay, achieving head control at 8 months but not progressing to independent sitting. She could grasp objects with her palms and transfer them between hands. She recognized her parents, responded to her name, and could speak monosyllables. There was no regression in her neurological development. She had no history of seizures, feeding or breathing difficulties, or recurrent respiratory infections. Her vision and hearing were intact. The family history did not reveal any significant medical conditions. On examination, she appeared undernourished but alert. Her head circumference was within normal limits. There were no skin abnormalities, facial deformities, spinal issues, or contractures. She did not exhibit bulbar dysfunction but had horizontal nystagmus and tongue fasciculations. She showed generalized muscle hypotonia with absent muscle stretch reflexes and limited antigravity movements. There were no signs of ptosis, facial weakness, involuntary movements, or cerebellar dysfunction. Fundoscopic examination was normal. Other systemic examinations did not reveal any abnormalities. Initial laboratory tests showed normal hemogram, serum electrolytes, liver, renal, and thyroid function tests, and total creatine kinase levels (50 IU/L). Nerve conduction studies were also normal.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed cerebellar atrophy. Needle electromyography revealed a neurogenic pattern of involvement with normal insertional activity, frequent fibrillations and positive sharp waves, and very few motor unit action potentials (MUAPs), which were large, and polyphasic and reduced recruitment. The muscle biopsy showed variation in fiber size, fiber type grouping, and hypertrophied type 1 fibers suggestive of spinal muscular atrophy. There was no evidence of mitochondrial cytopathy in the biopsied muscle.

case_report: The patient, a 30-year-old Moroccan woman, was born to healthy parents with no known consanguinity and has a healthy younger sister. There were no complications during the perinatal period. At birth, her measurements were within normal limits, but neonatal hypotonia and slight delays in motor development were observed. During infancy, she experienced progressive height deficit not related to growth hormone deficiency, and she exhibited skin hyperextensibility and generalized joint hypermobility. At age 28, dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry showed low bone mineral density for her sex and age (z-score < 2 SD), and an audiometric test revealed mild neurosensorial hearing loss. Genetic analyses were not conducted. Physical examination revealed disproportionate short stature (145 cm, with a genetic target of 160 cm, standard deviation from ethnic average stature – 2, arm span/height ratio 1.09, normal value <1.05), soft, doughy, hyperextensible skin, small atrophic scars on the knees, and a single transverse palmar crease. Generalized joint hypermobility was noted with a Beighton score of 7/9. Skeletal abnormalities included scoliosis, severe hallux valgus, pes planus, low-set thumb, and clinodactyly of the 5th fingers. Generalized muscle hypotonia, facial features such as light blue sclerae, wide forehead, flat face, sparse scalp hair, and narrow mouth, as well as edema of the lower extremities, were also observed. Complications of joint hypermobility included recurrent sprains, temporomandibular joint dislocation, and chronic pain in the cervical spine, right shoulder, and ankles. Doppler ultrasound of the lower limbs confirmed edema of lymphatic origin, and lymphography was not performed at the patient's request. Common causes of secondary lymphedema, such as cancer, infection, and surgery, were ruled out. Ophthalmologic evaluation showed no refractive errors, including hypermetropia. X-rays of the forearms, left wrist, pelvis, lower limbs, feet, and spine revealed dextroscoliosis, L5 hemisacralization, L4-L5 disc space narrowing, metatarsophalangeal subluxation, pes planus, and hallux valgus. Heart ultrasound indicated normal cardiac and valve morphology and function. Cognitive development and mentation were normal.
test_results: This analysis disclosed in the patient the homozygous c.829G>T (p.Glu277*) variant; both parents and her sister were heterozygotes. All these carriers did not show any sign of the disease including short stature, muscle hypotonia, craniofacial dysmorphism, as well as hearing loss and lymphedema. The identified variant represents a very rare allele seen only twice in 122,600 samples from the genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD) with an allele frequency of 8.157e−6.

case_report: A 2-year-old female child was brought to the Department of Pediatric Dentistry by her mother due to a solid tubular overgrowth in the incisive papillary region, causing feeding and breathing difficulties. The child's medical history was unremarkable, and the mother reported a normal, uncomplicated full-term pregnancy. Intraoral examination showed a growth on the incisive papilla, located on the palatal side of the primary maxillary central incisors. This growth, initially a small nodule at birth, had progressively increased in size to 2–2.5 cm below the incisal edge of the maxillary central incisors. The lesion was a solitary, firm, painless, pedunculated growth measuring 2–2.5 cm × 0.5 cm × 0.5 cm on the incisive papilla. Examination of the surrounding soft tissues, including the oral mucosa, gingiva, tongue, and floor of the mouth, was normal. The growth was completely excised under local anesthesia, and the tissue was preserved in 10% formalin solution. Postoperative healing was uneventful, and no recurrence was observed.
test_results: Hematoxylin- and eosin-stained paraffin-based sections (5 μm thick) showed a parakeratinized stratified squamous epithelium with long and thick rete ridges. Underlining connective tissue stroma showed irregular and interlacing bundles of collagen fibers and numerous muscle fiber bundles. Plump- and spindle-shaped fibroblasts along with proliferating nerve bundles and endothelial cell-lined blood vessels underneath the epithelial surface with extravasated red blood corpuscles. Reticulin-stained slide showed the presence of immature muscle fibers whereas Masson's trichrome stain revealed collagen fibers and smooth muscles.
diagnosis: Oral Midline Subcutaneous Smooth Muscle  Hamartoma of Incisive Papilla

case_report: A previously healthy 3-year-old Caucasian male presented to the local hospital emergency department with difficulty swallowing, loss of appetite, fever, refusal to bear weight, and a vesicular rash. After initial blood tests and blood cultures, he was transferred to a central hospital due to orthopedic complaints. Blood tests revealed a total white blood cell count of 14.44 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein (CRP) of 118.2 mg/L. One day after admission, based on the evolution of the rash, he was identified with varicella, and ibuprofen was discontinued. Due to persistent refusal to bear weight and an antalgic position with the flexed right knee, hip and knee ultrasonography was performed, which did not reveal any abnormalities, and lumbar and hip plain radiography was also normal. The boy continued to have a fever around 39°C and worsening local tenderness on the proximal lateral portion of the right leg, maintaining an antalgic position. Empiric antibiotic therapy with flucloxacillin was initiated, and repeated ultrasonography showed prominence and increased echogenicity of the superior anterolateral muscular plane of the right leg, suggesting myositis. At this time, lab tests for creatine phosphokinase (CPK) and myoglobin were normal but still showed leukocytosis and high CRP.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed an extensive infectious process involving the upper half of the fibula with periosteum detachment as well as a 6.1 cm abscess involving the adjacent muscle and fascia. Streptococcus pyogenes grew in the microbiologic culture of the pus surgically obtained. Streptococcus pyogenes was also isolated from the blood culture previously collected.

case_report: A 69-year-old male observed a fist-sized mass on his left shoulder six months prior to admission. The patient did not report any fever, ulceration, night sweats, weight loss, or additional symptoms. Physical examination revealed a palpable subcutaneous mass located on the left scapula. The mass had a well-defined boundary, limited mobility, and was not notably tender.
test_results: CT revealed an irregularly shaped soft-tissue mass 7.0 × 5.4 × 2.7 cm in size in the left thoracic and dorsal muscle space, and examination of the mass revealed a clear boundary and uniform density. The examination of the bone adjacent to the mass revealed slight absorption and destruction. MRI confirmed an irregularly shaped soft-tissue mass in the left thoracic and dorsal muscle space with long T1 and T2 signaling and uniform low-signal intensity on T1WI and high-signal intensity with fat suppression on T2WI. The tumor was positive for CD117, Vim, CD56 and NSE and showed focal expression of desmin but was negative for myogenin, S-100, SYN, INSM1, CD34, STAT6, INI-1, Brachyury, ERG, TLE1, AE1/AE3, WT-1, CD99 and SMA. NGS detected a translocation of a fragment from exon 1 to 7 of EWSR1 and exon 2 to 5 of NR4A3. NGS detected a single-nucleotide variant (A to G) in exon 13 of KIT. FISH confirmed the presence of the EWSR1-NR4A3 fusion gene. FISH for EWSR1 and NR4A3 demonstrated red–green staining, indicating the EWSR1-NR4A3 fusion.

case_report: A 32-year-old male with no significant past medical history was admitted for evaluation of fatigue and shortness of breath during physical activity. Upon admission, the patient appeared pale, but vital signs were stable. Physical examination showed nail dystrophy and leukokeratosis plaques on the tongue. Hyperkeratotic and pigmented patches were observed on the back, neck, trunk, and palms. The patient reported no history of tobacco use. The skin lesions began at age 7 and have progressively worsened. The patient mentioned similar cases in his family, including his brother and maternal uncle. No mental retardation was noted. Laboratory results at admission were as follows: WBC: 2,200 cells/µl, Absolute neutrophil count: 1,500 cells/µl, hemoglobin: 8 g/dl, platelets: 65,000/µl, creatinine: 1 mg/dl, ALT: 13 U/L, and INR: 1.9.
test_results: Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy showed normocellularity with trilineage dysplastic changes, dysplastic changes in RBC lineage were characteristic.

case_report: The patient is a 7-year-old boy born to young, non-consanguineous parents after 41 weeks of gestation in an uncomplicated second pregnancy. The first pregnancy ended in a miscarriage at 10 weeks. At birth, the patient weighed 2,300 g (below the 5th percentile), measured 50 cm in height (25th-50th percentile), and had a head circumference of 32 cm (below the 5th percentile). Apgar scores were 7, 9, and 10 at 1, 3, and 5 minutes, respectively. He had congenital pneumonia. A brain ultrasound at 8 months showed wide lateral ventricles. The child exhibited axial hypotonia with distal spasticity from early on. He achieved sitting at 13 months and walking at around 3 years, though his gait was atactic. Dysmorphic features included an open mouth with a protruding tongue, wide mouth, high forehead, hypotelorism, biparietal narrowing, sparse hair in the temporal region, discrete telecanthus, bulbous nasal tip, short philtrum, proximal thumbs without the ability to grasp, first toes curved laterally, and an additional nipple on the left side. He had convergent strabismus and astigmatism. By age 7, he had not developed speech and exhibited behavioral issues such as self-injury (biting hands) and stereotypic movements. Brain MRI showed typical terminal zones of unfinished myelination posteriorly, asymmetric ventricles, and detectable Virchow–Robin spaces in the same location.
test_results: Array CGH (aCGH) taken as primary genetic testing had shown the presence of a 170-kb maternally derived deletion in 22q12.3 (32,323, 842-32,494,686)[hg18]. This deletion encompasses the LARGE1 gene.
Orpha_name: Developmental delay-facial dysmorphism syndrome due to MED13L deficiency

case_report: Patient 3 is a 42-year-old Yemeni male with a family history of deafness and small teeth, including two sisters and a maternal grandmother. His parents are first cousins, and there is consanguinity in previous generations. His two children do not exhibit any symptoms, and his wife, who is unrelated to him, has normal hearing. The patient has been profoundly deaf since birth and uses British Sign Language (BSL). He has been experiencing progressive issues with balance and disequilibrium. His medical history includes rhinitis and sinus surgery. On physical examination, he has a small preauricular skin hillock on one side, with otherwise normal external ears. His teeth are noted to be small.
test_results: CT of petrous temporal bones showed bilateral Michel’s aplasia with no visible inner ear structures or internal auditory canal (IAC), and hypoplastic deformed petrous pyramids.

case_report: A 6-year-old girl presented with a small head size and delayed developmental milestones. Her language and cognitive skills were behind, but her motor skills were age-appropriate. She was delivered by cesarean section at 36 weeks and 4 days, with good Apgar scores. Her birth weight was 1.8 kg (<1st percentile), and her head circumference at birth was 28 cm (<−3SD). Prenatal ultrasonography indicated intrauterine growth restriction. She began walking independently at 14 months. The patient has a 10-year-old brother with a normal head size and no developmental delays. Both parents have no developmental issues. Examination showed delayed speech and a head circumference of 43.5 cm (<−3SD). Her motor skills were normal, including independent walking, running, jumping, hopping, stair navigation, touching the ground, and block building. She could perform simple tasks but had difficulty with speech and could not read or write. On the Preschool Receptive-Expressive Language Scale, her language skills were equivalent to a 41-month-old. The Korean–Leiter International Performance Scale-Revised indicated a Full-Scale Intelligence Quotient of 43 (<0.1 percentile), similar to a 27-month-old. Her social maturity scale score was 35.5, and her social intelligence quotient was 76.92. Brain MRI showed simplified gyral patterns of the cerebral cortex. Laboratory tests, including organic acids, were normal. Chromosomal analysis showed a karyotype of 46, XX, inv (p12q13) with no clinical significance. Multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) for microdeletion syndrome and chromosomal microarray analysis were normal.
test_results: Genomic DNA was extracted from the peripheral blood of the child and her parents. Genomic DNA was enriched using the xGen Inherited Disease Panel. Two compound heterozygous variants were observed in the WDR62 gene: a heterozygous deletion variant in the boundary of intron 7 and exon 8 (NM_001083961.1: c.883-4_890del) and a heterozygous missense variant in exon 13 (NM_001083961.1: c.1684C>G). Sanger sequencing revealed that the parents were heterozygous carriers for each variant, occurring in trans configuration.

case_report: A nine-month-old male child presented with rapidly growing lesions on the trunk and abdomen, which began at six months of age. Previous pediatric evaluation noted first-degree malnutrition and no deficits in psychomotor development. Upon examination, the child appeared thinner and exhibited macrocephaly. The abdomen was notably large with multiple soft masses, also present on the back and thorax, with the largest lesion located on the right flank. Additionally, there were brownish, round macules on the penis, each approximately three millimeters in diameter. A general physical examination included a lipid profile, which showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Computerized tomography of the abdomen and pelvis revealed extensive lipomatosis in the right postero-lateral thorax-abdomen region at the T8 level, extending downward until the perineal region with signs of controlateral paraspinal muscle invasion starting at T12. Lesional infiltration of vertebral, retrodural and psoas muscle epidural regions of the spinal canal could also be bilaterally observed. Magnetic resonance of the thoracic column revealed lipomatous dorsal lesion associated with enlargement of the spinal canal and spinal cord compression in the low thoracic column, as well as nonenhanced lumbosacral medullary compression after contrast. Loss of approximately 1MB of the long arm of chromosome 10, the region where the PTEN gene is located, was revealed. The same alteration was confirmed in the peripheral blood of the patient.

case_report: A 9-month-old male presented with a painless, localized mass over the right shoulder, noted since birth. The patient was delivered via cesarean section following a difficult vaginal delivery. At birth, the obstetrician documented the swelling and associated it with lymphadenopathy. No additional investigations were conducted at that time. Over time, the parents observed an increase in the size of the mass and brought the patient to the emergency department for further evaluation.
test_results: X-rays of the affected shoulder were obtained and a right midshaft clavicle fracture nonunion was diagnosed. X-rays of the right shoulder demonstrated 2 distinct, separate portions of clavicle: a medial portion with a sternal attachment and a lateral portion with an acromial attachment. There was no evidence of reactive bone formation and both ends were corticated with a smooth appearance.

case_report: A 21-month-old male presented to the emergency department with respiratory symptoms. Over the past 10 months, there has been a noted increase in penile size and skin darkening. A sibling passed away 13 years ago with similar symptoms. The patient's weight was 13 kg (Z-score: 1.1, 85.3th percentile), height was 92 cm (Z-score: 2.4, 99.2th percentile), and blood pressure was 139/90 mmHg (Z-score for age-based pediatric blood pressure for systolic/diastolic pressure: 4.3/3.9, 100th percentile. Z-score equal to or greater than 95th percentile indicates hypertension). Physical examination revealed hyperpigmentation of the gums, skin, and scrotum, facial acne, and penile enlargement measuring 8.7 cm (above 90th percentile). Testicular size was prepubertal (less than 2 mL) with no pubic hair.
test_results: Laboratory tests showed serum ACTH: 507 pg/mL (normal: 5–60 pg/mL), cortisol: 44 μg/dL (normal: 55–248 μg/dL), 17α-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP): 67 nmol/L (normal: 0.3–2.5 nmol/L), DOC: 319 ng/dL (normal: 4–49 ng/dL), and androstenedione: 11 ng/mL (normal: 0.4–4.1 ng/mL).
Orpha_name: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency

case_report: The patient, a 53-year-old woman with a height of 150 cm and a weight of 55 kg, was scheduled for cyst and tooth extraction related to a jaw cyst of the right mandibular third molar. She had a history of hypertension and was on a daily dose of 2.5 mg amlodipine besylate. Preoperative examination showed no abnormalities. However, the diameter of the left and right pupils was not checked during the examination. The patient had undergone general anesthesia for tonsillectomy 10 years prior, but details were unavailable. No premedication was given. Upon admission, her blood pressure was 168/102 mmHg. Anesthesia was induced with 60 mg propofol and 0.3 μg/kg/min remifentanil after securing intravenous access. Following the administration of 35 mg rocuronium, tramazoline hydrochloride was applied to both nasal cavities using a cotton swab, and nasotracheal intubation was performed through the right nasal cavity without complications. Blood pressure immediately after intubation was 153/94 mmHg. Post-intubation, the left and right pupil diameters were found to be unequal, measuring 1 mm in the left eye and 4 mm in the right eye. The surgery was canceled to evaluate neurological symptoms, and the patient was awakened and extubated. Upon awakening, the patient exhibited no disorientation or motor dysfunction, but the pupil diameter remained unequal (2 mm in the left eye and 4 mm in the right eye). The left eye was miotic in response to light, while the right eye remained mydriatic. This condition persisted until discharge the following day. The patient was subsequently referred to the neurology department of a nearby medical university hospital for further consultation.
test_results: Head and neck magnetic resonance imaging and chest computed tomography revealed no abnormal findings.

case_report: A 54-year-old Moroccan woman with a 10-year history of a chronic condition, for which a small bowel resection was performed 9 years ago, and managed with azathioprine, presented with a 1-year history of an asymptomatic erythematous lesion on the left breast. There was no history of glucose intolerance, family history of similar lesions, cutaneous disease, or other systemic symptoms. Physical examination revealed a well-demarcated shiny orange-yellow infiltrated plaque measuring 6 cm in length on the left breast, with prominent telangiectasias and atrophic areas. No other cutaneous lesions or lymphadenopathies were noted.
test_results: Histology showed palisading non-caseating interstitial epithelioid granulomatous dermatitis with diffuse necrobiosis. Special stains [Periodic Acid–Schiff stain (PAS), Ziehl, Gram, Grocott] and microbiological and mycological investigations were negative.
diagnosis: Necrobiosis lipoidica associated with Crohn's disease

case_report: A seven-year-old girl was identified with blurred vision during a physical examination at five years old. She was prescribed glasses for amblyopia with a refraction of -14D in the right eye and -13D in the left eye. Her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/200 in the right eye and 20/100 in the left eye. The child's mother noticed misalignment in her left eye, leading to a visit to a private clinic and subsequent referral to our department due to retinal detachment in the left eye. At the initial visit, BCVA was 20/50 in the right eye and light perception in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was 17 mmHg in the right eye and 9 mmHg in the left eye. She had a total retinal detachment (grade CA) with severe proliferative vitreoretinopathy. After discussions with her family, it was decided to follow up without treatment. The timing of the retinal detachment was unclear. Her medical history included surgery for a small jaw and cleft palate, and intubation management for Pierre Robin syndrome. Family history included severe myopia in her mother and a history of laser treatment for a retinal tear during the mother's junior high school years.
test_results: An ultra-widefield fundus autofluorescence photograph revealed hyperfluorescence corresponding to radial paravascular retinal degeneration. Swept-source optical coherence tomography (SS-OCT) did not clearly show any PPVP.

case_report: A 61-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a palpable abdominal mass that had been present for 1½ years. She did not report systemic symptoms, general malaise, weight loss, flank pain, or urinary symptoms, but mentioned mild diarrhea and right periumbilical pain radiating to the right lower quadrant. Her medical history included well-controlled hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Previous colonoscopic and endoscopic evaluations were normal. Physical examination revealed a nontender, immobile mass in the right lower quadrant without peripheral lymphadenopathy. Other examination and laboratory findings were unremarkable. Computed tomography (CT) with intravenous and oral contrast of the abdomen and pelvis showed a heterogeneously enhancing, 10.2 × 6.9 × 6.3 cm solid mass in the right retroperitoneal space, displacing the inferior vena cava and right iliac vasculature. Significant deformation of adjacent retroperitoneal structures was noted, with no evidence of abdominopelvic adenopathy or intraperitoneal disease. An exploratory laparotomy revealed a large mass with notable tumor and perivascular inflammatory changes extending to the right iliac vessels and over the inferior vena cava. The mass was completely resected without the need for multiorgan resection. Blood loss during surgery was approximately 1 L. The patient underwent a complete curative resection, recovered well postoperatively, and was discharged on the seventh postoperative day. She has remained without radiologic evidence of disease recurrence during 2 years of follow-up.
test_results: The nodule consisted of lymphocytes with marked vascular proliferation and prominent hyalinization. Histopathology revealed regressively transformed germinal centers with normal B-cell distribution surrounded by hypervascular mantle zones composed predominantly of concentric rings ('onion-skinning') of small CD4-positive T lymphocytes and plasma cells. Hyalinized blood vessels perforating the follicles from the mantle zone were frequently observed. Immunostaining for CD21 demonstrated the characteristic follicular dendritic network of residual germinal centers. CD10 was weakly positive in some of the transformed germinal centers. PCR analysis of paraffin-embedded tissue targeting the T-cell receptor γ gene revealed no gene rearrangement. In situ hybridization for EBV and immunostaining for HHV-8 were negative.

case_report: A 40-year-old female patient exhibited numerous small dark and light spots symmetrically located on the backs of her hands and feet. She first observed these spots at the age of 26, and they have not caused any discomfort. Additionally, several freckle-like pigmented spots were observed on her face. She reported no other health conditions. Tests for autoimmune diseases and other laboratory results were negative. Her family history includes a nephew with similar skin lesions.
test_results: From hypochromic lesion, histology demonstrated a compact stratum corneum and discrete acanthosis. Using Fontana Masson staining, hypochromic lesion demonstrated marked decrease, with almost absence, of melanin. On the other hand, the hyperchromic lesion demonstrated an intense pigmentation.

case_report: A 19-year-old female, born at 36 weeks gestation, experienced multiple abscesses in the neck and face early in life, which were associated with Staphylococcus aureus and required frequent incision and drainage. Respiratory tract infections were not observed, and a thoracic CT scan showed no abnormalities. The patient exhibited retained dentition and mild eczema, but there were no signs of fungal nail disease or recurrent thrush.
test_results: The circulating total IgE was markedly elevated (970 IU/L, NR: 0-81 IU/L); T and B cell counts were normal but IgG was raised (18.5 gr/L). Complement C3 and C4 levels, and complement function tests were normal. There was a suboptimal response to test immunisation with Pneumovax II vaccine.
Orpha_name: Autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome due to STAT3 deficiency

case_report: A 56-year-old male presented with a backache persisting for over seven months, with increased pain for the past two weeks. Six months earlier, the patient experienced back pain without a clear cause. In October 2011, the patient visited the Affiliated Hospital of Inner Mongolia Medical University in Hohhot, China. A lumbar CT scan showed a bulging disc between the third and fourth lumbar vertebrae. The patient was treated with Chinese medicinal pills and plaster external treatment, but these were ineffective. In January 2012, two weeks before the current hospital admission, the patient experienced increased lumbar pain, weakness in both lower limbs, limited mobility, and dark brown urine. The patient then consulted The Second Affiliated Hospital of Inner Mongolia Medical College in Hohhot, China, where CT revealed specific findings. In February 2012, the patient was hospitalized in the Department of Orthopedics at the Affiliated Hospital of Inner Mongolia Medical University for further treatment. Since symptom onset, the patient had alternating episodes of diarrhea and constipation and had lost approximately 30 pounds. The patient's family history was not contributory, and physical and laboratory examinations showed no abnormalities.
test_results: A lumbar computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a lumbar disc bulging between the third and fourth lumbar vertebrae. CT revealed some specific findings. Lumbar vertebrae magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and thoracic MRI scans showed abnormal signals. The CT and MRI findings revealed multiple myeloma and multiple bone metastases. A Bence-Jones protein test and biopsy were performed, with negative results. However, the pathological diagnosis was positive.

case_report: A 9-year-old male, born at term to non-consanguineous parents, was referred to our outpatient clinic for evaluation of thickened nails that began at 6 months of age. He had a history of pinhead-sized yellowish spiny skin lesions present all over his body from birth, which gradually increased in size during his first year. There were no natal or neonatal teeth. The patient's intelligence was normal, and there were no similar complaints in the family. Physical examination revealed multiple follicular discrete papules on the face, upper chest, buttocks, elbows, knees, and flexures. All 20 nails were thickened with yellowish discoloration, increased curvature, and subungual hyperkeratosis. Focal plantar keratoderma was observed. The oral mucosa showed mucosal leucokeratosis. No abnormalities were found in the examination of the palms, otolarynx, and ophthalmology. All laboratory investigations were within normal limits. KOH mounts of toe and finger nails were negative for fungal elements.
test_results: Histopathology examination of Follicular keratotic papule showed follicular plugging, hyperkeratosis and acanthosis. A skin biopsy of sole showed marked hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, moderate hypergranulosis and minimal dermal inflammatory infiltration.

case_report: A 37-year-old woman with a history of gestational diabetes was admitted following a motor vehicle accident for evaluation of recurrent low blood sugar levels. She initially experienced a loss of consciousness due to a witnessed seizure, which improved after receiving 5% dextrose (D5W) at the accident scene. She had no memory of the event, and her initial blood glucose level was 32 mg/dL. Neurological, cardiovascular, and respiratory examinations showed no abnormalities. Upon arrival at the emergency department, she was not in status epilepticus, had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 12, and exhibited normal vital signs. Her psychomotor activity, perception, and cognitive functions were normal. During her hospital stay, she had recurrent episodes of low blood sugar, both when fasting and after meals, with glucose levels ranging from 32 to 70 mg/dL. Symptoms appeared when glucose levels fell below 50 mg/dL, requiring continuous infusions of 10% dextrose solution. Although she had gestational diabetes three years ago, she had no subsequent diagnosis of diabetes and reported no prior symptoms of low blood sugar such as weakness, sweating, pallor, tremors, confusion, tingling, or visual disturbances in the past year. She also reported no glycopenic symptoms before this hospitalization and was not taking any medications or supplements at home. Tests for insulin autoantibodies and sulfonylurea were negative, and her thyroid function tests were normal. An evaluation for adrenal insufficiency using a cosyntropin stimulation test was also normal.
test_results: A venous glucose measurement of 46 mg/dL yielded noteworthy increases in C-peptide and insulin concentrations. Additionally, there was a notable suppression of beta hydroxybutyrate levels. An abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with contrast revealed a 1.3 cm mass located at the tail of the pancreas.

case_report: A 17-year-old, nonparous girl presented with a one-month history of a noticeable pelvic mass and was found to have a left ovarian tumour in 2007 with a serum CA-125 level of 350 IU/L. Other tumour markers were not assessed due to financial constraints. During surgery, an intraoperative frozen section showed immature teratoma, and she underwent fertility-sparing surgery. A staging laparotomy with left salpingo-oophorectomy, peritoneal cytology, pelvic lymph node sampling, and infracolic omentectomy was performed. Postoperative histology indicated a mature teratoma with focal areas of immature teratoma in the left ovary. There was no evidence of malignant cell infiltration in the omentum or lymph nodes. Histology showed immature teratoma grade I, FIGO stage 1a. Despite being advised for close surveillance, she did not follow up after 6 months postoperatively. One year later, she experienced lower abdominal discomfort and sought medical advice again. Imaging showed a recurrence of the pelvic mass with a serum CA-125 level of 180 IU/L, after which she completed 6 courses of systemic chemotherapy (carboplatin-paclitaxel). Following chemotherapy, the tumour marker normalised (<35 IU/L), but the pelvic mass continued to increase in size.
test_results: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed presence of bilateral large adnexal masses with infiltration into uterus and also possibly to the sigmoid colon.

case_report: An 80-year-old female presented with posterior uveitis and retinitis pigmentosa. She had intracapsular cataract extractions 11 years ago, resulting in postoperative visual acuity around 20/200. Two years before presentation, her right eye became phthisical, and she experienced severe uveitis and vitreous hemorrhage in her left eye. She had no systemic inflammatory diseases, and a posterior uveitis workup was negative. Her family history indicated a genetic link. On examination, her visual acuity was no light perception in the right eye and light perception in the left eye. Intraocular pressures were 5 mm Hg in the right eye and 18 mm Hg in the left eye. The anterior segment examination revealed extensive iris neovascularization. The right eye was phthisical with no view to the posterior pole. Echography showed reduced axial length, small size, shell-like calcification of the choroid, and dense vitreous opacities with extensive retinal detachment. The left fundus examination revealed vitreous hemorrhage, pigmentary retinopathy, peripheral neovascularization, and fibrotic changes.
test_results: An electroretinogram of the left eye showed completely extinguished photopic and scotopic response.

case_report: A 16-year-old African American female presented with osteosarcoma in the right shoulder and received neoadjuvant therapy with methotrexate, doxorubicin, and cisplatin, followed by surgical resection. At age 17, she experienced a recurrence of sarcoma as a solitary lung mass, which was surgically resected, and she received IGF-1R antibody therapy for a year in a clinical trial. She declined genetic counseling at that time. At age 19, she noticed a lump in her right breast. A diagnostic mammogram showed a 3.1 cm solid lesion in the upper inner quadrant of the right breast. A PET-CT scan revealed a large hypermetabolic mass in the right breast with no metastases and small nonavid lymph nodes in the right axilla. A core biopsy of the right breast mass showed ER/PR/HER2 negative poorly differentiated ductal carcinoma. Due to prior anthracycline treatment, she received neoadjuvant carboplatin/paclitaxel for 6 cycles, but experienced clinical progression, leading to a right mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy (ypT3N0) and a prophylactic contralateral mastectomy. She was treated with adjuvant docetaxel/cyclophosphamide for 4 cycles. At age 20, she had recurrent triple-negative breast cancer in the right axillary lymph nodes and lungs.
test_results: BreastNext analysis found a heterozygous 5′UTR_3′UTR pathogenic mutation in the TP53 gene.

case_report: An 11-year-old girl, the second daughter of healthy non-consanguineous parents of Portuguese origin, presented with a severe vesiculo-pustular rash in the first week of life. A biopsy revealed dermis infiltration by CD68+CD163+S100–CD1a–histiocytes. At 2 months old, she developed bloody diarrhea, and endoscopic and histologic findings indicated early-onset inflammatory bowel disease, which improved with prednisolone and azathioprine. Despite this, she experienced recurrent blistering skin rashes and frequent chest infections. At 3 years old, she began having recurrent eye inflammation associated with ocular hypertension. She was treated with vinblastine, 6-mercaptopurine, methotrexate, and steroids, but her symptoms persisted, and she had more frequent infections, including acute otitis media, recurrent chronic sinusitis, recurrent pneumonia, and a pulmonary Aspergillus infection that responded to itraconazole. Cutis laxa was noted at 6 years old, and progressive sensorineural deafness was diagnosed at 7 years old, necessitating a hearing-assistive device. Immunological analysis at that age showed low IgM and IgA, absent responses to protein antigens, and low B cells with almost absent class-switched memory B cells, while T-cell proliferation responses were preserved. No auto-antibodies were detected. Whole blood stimulation assays indicated a significantly reduced production of IFN-γ and IL-17 in response to polyclonal T-cell stimulation and reduced production of IL-10 and IL-1β after LPS stimulation. However, there was a significant innate induction of IL-6 and TNFα in response to various TLR agonists, including LPS, PAM 2/3, Flagellin, and CL-097. She began prophylactic co-trimoxazole, immunoglobulin replacement, low-dose steroids (5 mg every other day), and hydroxychloroquine, which led to substantial improvement. Despite this, since the age of 10 years, she experienced several relapses of eye inflammation, skin rash, and pulmonary inflammation (interstitial pneumonitis) that only partially improved with high-dose steroids. Anakinra (IL1-receptor antagonist) and canakinumab (IL1β monoclonal antibody) were tried without effect. Recently, ruxolitinib was initiated as a bridge to hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing identified a heterozygous missense L848P mutation in the PLCG2 gene. Sanger sequencing showed that this mutation appeared de novo in the patient, while being absent from both parents and a healthy sibling.

case_report: In March 2013, Mr. A, a 25-year-old male, experienced a knee collision with his thigh while playing football, resulting in immediate pain and swelling over his upper quadriceps. Despite the injury, he continued playing. That evening, the pain intensified, preventing sleep. The next morning, he visited the university sports injury clinic, where examination revealed visible swelling without neurological or vascular issues. Initial treatment included rest, ice, and analgesia, and he was discharged with crutches. Five days later, Mr. A returned with increased swelling, bruising, and paraesthesia, leading to a referral to the emergency department. Imaging showed significant thigh swelling, and routine blood tests indicated a haemoglobin level of 80 g/L (normal range: 135 g/L–175 g/L). A CT scan estimated the haematoma volume at over 2 liters. Due to early neuropathy, he underwent an urgent fasciotomy. Post-fasciotomy, Mr. A received two units of packed red cells. Preoperative coagulation screen results showed normal PT and APTT with increased fibrinogen. Six days after fasciotomy closure, Mr. A returned with swelling and a discharging wound, which was evacuated, and additional packed red cells were transfused.
test_results: A prolonged APTT of 34 seconds (normal range 21–32 seconds). A low Factor IX of 27.2%.

case_report: A 14-day-old male infant was brought to the outpatient department by his parents due to a deformity in his left lower limb. He is the first child of non-consanguineous parents, with the mother aged 32 years and the father aged 33 years. The infant was born at full term via vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 2600 grams (above the 50th percentile). The APGAR scores were 2 at 1 minute and 6 at 5 minutes. There was no history of rash, teratogenic drug use, radiation exposure, or fever during the antenatal period. Upon inspection, the left leg was observed to be shorter and thinner compared to the right leg. The left foot was shorter due to the absence of the fourth ray, and syndactyly was noted between the second and third toes. There was no bowing or skin dimpling over the limb. Palpation revealed a normal ankle joint, but the left knee exhibited laxity under medial and lateral stress tests compared to the right knee. Examination of the right lower limb, upper limbs, face, pelvis, and spine showed no abnormalities. Systemic examination did not reveal any additional findings.
test_results: The X-ray of the lower limb showed the absence of proximal tibial epiphysis, absent talus, and absence of the fourth ray on the left side. Due to the absent left proximal tibial epiphysis, the tibia, as well as the fibula, was shorter than the normal side. The skeletal survey of the rest of the body showed the normal femora, contra-lateral leg, pelvis, and long bones of the upper limb. The ultrasonographic examination of the pelvis and abdomen was non-significant. The karyotyping was normal.
diagnosis: Fibular Aplasia, Tibial Campomelia, and Oligosyndactyly Syndrome  variant

case_report: A 9-month-old female child from Rajasthan (Marwadi community) presented with recurrent respiratory tract infections and failure to thrive. She experienced frequent hospitalizations due to rapid breathing and developed hepatosplenomegaly over the next 5 months. Various treatments were administered, including antibiotics, nebulizations, antifungal agents, systemic corticosteroids, and moist oxygen inhalation. Despite these interventions, the child remained tachypneic and continued to require oxygen support. A chest radiogram revealed hazy, diffuse bilateral alveolar infiltrates. High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) showed ground-glass opacification of the right upper lobe, indicative of alveolar proteinosis. Lung biopsy with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) staining demonstrated dilated alveoli lined by type-2 pneumocytes containing foamy macrophages, further indicating alveolar proteinosis. Liver biopsy revealed fairly well-preserved lobular architecture and cord pattern, a few lymphocytes in the portal tract, and finely vacuolated ballooned hepatocytes and Kupffer cells.
