Additional studies showed elevated plasma chitotriosidase levels and a fifty percent reduction in acid sphingomyelinase activity [3.6 nmol/hr/mg – NR: 8.0-14.5 nmol/hr/mg protein].
test_results: This has identified homozygous nonsense variant (c.141C > A) (p.Cys47Ter) in exon 2.
diagnosis: Niemann-Pick type C disease with mutations in NPC2 gene
Orpha_name: Niemann-Pick disease type C, late infantile neurologic onset

case_report: A 28-year-old female presented with elevated hemoglobin levels at 17.2 g/dL. Physical examination revealed an oxygen saturation of 100%, obesity, and a significant hemangioma on the lower extremity. Laboratory results showed a normal erythropoietin level of 14 mU/mL, and PCR testing for JAK2 mutation was negative. Additional evaluations for potential secondary causes of erythrocytosis, including a sleep study, did not yield any notable findings.
test_results: She was found to have a heterozygous missense mutation in the EGLN1 gene at c.616G>T, resulting in amino acid substitution pGly206Cys (p.G206C).
diagnosis: Isolated Erythrocytosis associated with EGLN1 gene mutation
Orpha_name: Autosomal recessive secondary polycythemia not associated with VHL gene

case_report: The patient is a 49-year-old male, with a height of 161 cm and a weight of 85 kg. He was born preterm at 34 weeks of gestation to nonconsanguineous parents. His medical history includes congenital anisocoria, developmental delay, hypoacusis, and tetra-ataxia. During childhood, he experienced general downslowing, chronic fatigue, and sicca syndrome of the eyes. He had recurrent respiratory infections, oral herpetic infections, and once experienced painless desquamation of the hands and foot soles. He worked as a hairdresser until the age of 38 and retired at 40. At 30 years old, left anterior hemiblock and right bundle-branch block were recorded. Since age 35, he had recurrent mild elevation of creatine kinase (CK), along with elevated aldolase and myoglobin levels. He also experienced recurrent electrolyte disturbances, including hypokalemia and hyponatremia, and developed hyperuricemia. At age 36, he had an episode of disorientation, impaired cognition, bradyphrenia, and secessus urinae. Clinical examination revealed bilateral ophthalmoparesis and dysarthria. MRI showed subcortical hyperintensities in a nonvascular distribution, which were hyperintense on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC). Neuropsychological testing indicated attention deficits, difficulty encoding visual contents, adjustment disorder, and depression. Following these episodes, his gait became disturbed with occasional falls due to increased ataxia. At age 37, he experienced an episode of untriggered rhabdomyolysis.
test_results: Muscle biopsy from the deltoid muscle suggested muscular dystrophy as only fat but no muscle tissue was detected. Muscle biopsy from the left lateral vastus muscle showed cytochrome-C-oxidase (COX)-negative fibers, glycogen depositions, fiber splitting, and ragged-red fibers. Electron microscopy showed abnormally shaped and structured mitochondria, megaconia, abnormal glycogen and lipid depositions, and dark bodies.

case_report: A 39-year-old male Caucasian patient presented to our outpatient clinic with a history of cardiomyopathy known since early childhood. The patient reported low exercise capacity (NYHA II), pronounced sweating, and an excessive need for sleep (about 10–11 hours per night) which had been present since he could remember. Blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg, and physical examination revealed proximal muscular hypotrophy. The ECG showed negative T waves in the left precordial leads (V4–V6) and flattened T waves in the peripheral leads. Blood tests indicated elevated creatinine kinase at 410 U/L (<170 U/L), high-sensitive troponin T at 45 pg/mL (<14 pg/mL), and a reduced white blood cell count at 2.2 * 10^9 cells/L (3.2 * 10^9–10.5 * 10^9 cells/L). The patient's medical history included early-onset heart failure and recurrent respiratory tract infections requiring antibiotics. At 4 months old, the patient experienced feeding difficulties, fatigue, pronounced sweating, and growth delay (<3rd percentile for weight and height), leading to hospitalization. Physical examination at that time showed tachypnoea and perioral cyanosis. The ECG showed negative T waves in the precordial leads, and a chest X-ray revealed cardiomegaly. An LV angiogram demonstrated a reduced LV ejection fraction (LVEF) and endomyocardial fibroelastosis. Treatment with digoxin was initiated and continued until the age of 6 when the patient's condition stabilized. At age 8, a neuropediatric assessment due to slow motor development and skeletal muscle hypotrophy revealed floppy muscle tone and positive Gower's sign. Dystrophic myopathy and polyneuropathy were ruled out by MRI, western blot analysis, and immunohistochemistry. At age 10, during an appendectomy, neutropenia was first noticed, and intermittent neutropenia was diagnosed (latest available neutrophil count 0.7 * 10^9 cells/L). After an episode of acute cardiac decompensation at age 12, heart failure therapy was reinitiated with digoxin, spironolactone, and furosemide and continued for a few years before being stopped again. The patient's condition continuously improved, allowing him to live an almost normal life, including graduating from high school and working as a bank clerk, although he remained rapidly exhausted and had an excessive need for sleep. At the time of the current presentation, no medical treatment had been given for at least 15–20 years. Family history included recurrent syncope in the patient's maternal uncle but was negative for premature heart disease or death from heart failure or infection. Echocardiography showed moderately reduced LVEF, hypertrophy, and non-compaction of the LV myocardium. Cardiac MRI revealed a dilated left ventricle with an LVEF of 41% and hypertrabeculation of the lateral and inferior wall compatible with LV non-compaction. The right ventricle was normal. Late gadolinium enhancement imaging showed diffuse fibrosis of the lateral LV wall.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed a variant (c.153C>G; p.Tyr51) of the tafazzin (TAZ) gene.

case_report: A five-year-old Bahraini male was born at term via a normal vaginal delivery following an uncomplicated pregnancy for consanguineous parents. His birth weight was 2.46 kg and he had an uneventful neonatal period. He had bilateral club feet corrected with splints. The patient was vaccinated and up to date. He experienced global developmental delay, starting to walk at 20 months and beginning to talk at two years, but was still unable to draw vertical lines. At 22 months, a sweat chloride test was conducted due to failure to thrive, resulting in 39 mmol/L (normal range less than 35 mmol/L). He had a healthy brother and sister with no family history of hepatic diseases. At two years and eight months, the patient presented with fever, vomiting, and yellowish discoloration of the skin and sclera. There was no history of hepatotoxic drugs or mushroom intake. Examination revealed jaundice and hepatomegaly. Laboratory results showed elevated L-aspartate aminotransferase (ASAT) at 2845.7 UL and L-alanine aminotransferase (ALAT) at 1250.9 UL. The patient was found to have an acute cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection. Total Immunoglobulin (Ig) levels, auto-liver antibodies, serum copper, and ceruloplasmin levels were checked. Serum and urinary copper and ceruloplasmin levels were within normal ranges. Eye examination showed no evidence of Kayser-Fleischer rings. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly with a normal biliary system. MRI did not reveal any changes in the basal ganglia. He was started on valganciclovir, ursodeoxycholic acid, and omeprazole. Despite treatment, liver function worsened. High serum immunoglobulin M (IgM) level (2.26 g/L, normal range 0.50-2.20 g/L) and equivocally positive anti-smooth muscle antibodies led to a trial of intravenous (IV) methylprednisolone. Liver biopsy was not performed due to coagulopathy. The option of liver transplantation (LT) was discussed, but as the patient's liver function improved, he was not sent for transplant. He was discharged on the mentioned medications as oral syrups. Later, his father noticed progressive difficulty in walking, leading to frequent falls and eventually complete inability to walk, associated with intention tremors. Physical examination showed an icteric child with a puffy face, lower limb edema, distended abdomen with ascites, and hepatomegaly. No signs of motor or sensory neuropathy were observed. Other systemic examinations were normal. The patient received albumin infusion with furosemide diuretic. Neurological assessment showed intact tone, power, reflexes, and gait, but he was unable to bear weight. Vitamin B12 and folate levels were normal. EEG was normal. Brain CT scan showed no evidence of acute ischemic or hemorrhagic insults, and no significant cerebellar changes were detected. MRI showed minimal periventricular white matter signal intensity, posteriorly adjacent to occipital horns of the lateral ventricle but not extending to the ventricle. Upon discharge, he was unable to walk or stand without support. One month later, he could stand and walk without support but continued to have intention tremor. The patient was admitted twice at three years and four months and at five years and one month with acute gastroenteritis episodes. During the first admission, he had recurrent high-grade fever and loose motions without an ALF episode (ALAT: 126 UL and INR: 1.1). He was hospitalized for six days for IV hydration and discharged after improvement. The second episode of acute gastroenteritis was associated with ALF (ALAT: 1714 UL and INR: 1.16). He presented with high-grade fever, diarrhea for six days, vomiting for three days, runny nose, and productive cough. No contact with sick individuals was reported. Physical examination showed he was conscious, alert, with icteric skin and sclera, and vitally stable. His abdomen was distended with hepatosplenomegaly. Other examinations were unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound showed mild hepatosplenomegaly with coarse hepatic echogenicity, mild dilation of intrahepatic duct, and mild gallbladder wall thickening, but no gallstones. He was evaluated for infectious, metabolic, and immunological etiologies, leading to a diagnosis of influenza A infection. He completed 10 days of cefotaxime antibiotic and was discharged on prednisolone, ursodeoxycholic acid, and omeprazole. On a follow-up visit, complete blood count, liver function tests, coagulation profile, and CMV titer were within normal range. Repeated ultrasound was normal.
test_results: This revealed a previously unreported autosomal recessive pathogenic non-sense variation c.895A>T (s299Ter) in exon 7 of the SCYL1 gene in a homozygous status. The length of the protein encoded by the SCYL1 gene is 808 amino acids, and the termination caused by the mutation as mentioned earlier makes a massive deletion after the K299 residue. Residues from 793 to 808 in the canonical protein sequence interact with COPB1 protein, which is deleted from the mutated allele of the current report.

case_report: A 3-year-old boy was admitted to the neurological in-patient department in April 2021 with intellectual disability, speech delay, and seizures. He was born at term via cesarean section with a birth weight of 3,200 g and a length of 48 cm. His parents, who are not related, were healthy and this was their first pregnancy. There was no history of prenatal exposure to alcohol, drugs, or medications. The boy exhibited global developmental delay from infancy, but no developmental regression was observed. He began crawling at 8 months, started teething and sitting at 1 year, and could stand independently by 1.6 years. He began walking at 2 years old with an ataxic gait. He started speaking in bi-syllables (baba and mama) at 2.3 years, but his language skills did not improve by age 3. He was unable to feed himself at 3 years old. The Gesell Developmental Scale showed a developmental quotient score of 46, and the Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scale indicated a score of 40, categorized as moderate intellectual disability. He experienced insomnia from birth, which resolved by age 4. The child had a high pain threshold and exhibited abnormal behaviors including poor eye contact, restricted and repetitive behaviors, fascination, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), irritability, aggressive behavior, and inappropriate laughter. He had recurrent respiratory tract infections, averaging once a month, and gastrointestinal infections two to three times per year. There were no facial, limb, or spinal deformities. His vision and hearing were normal, and muscle tone and strength were normal in all four limbs. His first seizure occurred at 2.9 years old, and by age 3, he had experienced five generalized tonic-clonic seizures. The child also showed poor eye contact, stereotyped behavior, fascination, intellectual disability, poor expressive speech, behavioral abnormalities, epilepsy, sleep dysfunction, and motor delay.
test_results: The results of Trio-WES revealed a de novo heterozygous missense variant (NM_021008.4: c.782G>C, p. Arg261Pro) in the fifth exon of DEAF1 gene, which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The variant was predicted to be damaging/disease-causing by PolyPhen-2 (score = 1), SIFT (score = 0.009), Provean (score = −5.29), Mutation Taster, and Mutation Assessor. The variant also affects evolutionary conserved amino acids within the DEAF1 SAND domain. According to ACMG, the missense variant was classified as “Likely Pathogenic” with PS2 + PM2_Supporting + PP3. This pathogenic variant was not reported in 1000 Genomes, ExAC, gnomAD, ClinVar Databases, and previous literature.

case_report: A 14-year-old boy remains aphonic, using sign language and handwriting short phrases to communicate. He exhibits drooling, difficulty swallowing, and impaired tongue movement. He was born after an uneventful pregnancy via vaginal delivery at 40 weeks’ gestational age. Birth weight was 3,570 g (50th percentile), length 51 cm (50th percentile), and head circumference 34.0 cm (just above 10th percentile). No resuscitation was required, and he was discharged home on the second day of life. Feeding difficulties were noted during infancy. He bottle-fed well but demonstrated slow weight gain in the first 2 years of life. He did not require nasogastric or gastric feeds. His feeding difficulties became clearer as he transitioned to solid food. He drooled excessively. If he drank liquid too quickly, it would run out of his mouth. He had no nasal regurgitation of liquid or solids. Chewing was difficult and he was unable to extrude his tongue beyond his lower lip and had no side-to-side tongue movement. He needed all food pureed or cut into small pieces. As a result of impaired tongue movements, he would use his fingers to push back a food bolus within his oropharynx permitting swallowing. Electroencephalography revealed a normal awake background, and he had no clinical seizures at any time. Gross motor delays were evident: He sat independently at 9 months old, walked at 18 months old, and rode a bicycle with training wheels at 7 years old. He was toilet trained at 3 to 4 years old and dry at night by 6 years old. Language regression was noted. Although he had 10 to 12 monosyllabic words at 18 to 24 months old, he lost all expressive language prior to his second birthday. He remains able to verbally communicate with guttural sounds but has not regained any spoken words. Despite complete aphonia, he shows continual progression in both his receptive language and augmentative communication skills. At 14 years old, he can use over 100 sign words and can use a smart tablet to spell words and use word recognition to type grammatically correct sentences. He can print, although his handwriting tends to be quite slow and deliberate. Magnetic resonance imaging brain at 5 years old demonstrated nonspecific changes in the periventricular white matter with no evidence of polymicrogyria or atrophy. He had multiple speech-language and psychological assessments between 6 and 14 years old, with key test scores summarized in . At 6 years old, his Leiter-R Global IQ was at the 5th percentile, while his Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence III performance was at the 0.1th percentile. Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder was diagnosed, which has improved with stimulant treatment. At 9 years old, a speech and language assessment confirmed single-word receptive vocabulary at a 6-year-old level, in contrast with very severe expressive language delay. At 12 years old, psychological testing using the Leiter-R confirmed the diagnosis of moderate intellectual disability. At 14 years old, the authors completed a brief, targeted neuropsychological assessment using select subtests from the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children V, the Test of Nonverbal Intelligence 3, and a French adaptation of the Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test–Revised. Results suggested nonverbal reasoning skills at a 5-year-old level, with relative sparing of receptive vocabulary and visual attention. Compared to testing at 9 years old, his receptive vocabulary raw score improved from a 6-year-old level to an 8.5 year-old level. Physical examination at 8 years old noted a head circumference of 53.8 cm (75th percentile). Subtle dysmorphic facial features were noted. He communicated by grunting and pointing with his fingers. He could print his name. Cranial nerve examination revealed normal pupillary constriction, normal fundi, and full and conjugate extraocular movements. Facial movement was full except for the inability to purse his lips when asked. Tongue bulk was slightly reduced, but no fasciculations were apparent. He was unable to move his tongue side-to-side and could not extrude his tongue. His palate was intact and his gag reflex was easily elicited. His sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength was normal. Muscle power, tone, and deep tendon reflexes were normal. Plantar responses were flexor. He showed no overt motor apraxia and could carry out motor tasks when verbally instructed. General examination was significant only for pes planus. He developed a mild S-shaped scoliosis (at 14 years old) of up to 18°. He has had normal echocardiogram, nerve conduction studies, and normal chromosomal microarray, Fragile X testing, and biochemical testing (serum creatine kinase, lactic acid, plasma amino acids, and acylcarnitine profile).
test_results: He was found to have nonsense mutations affecting his LINS alleles: c.1096G>T; p.Glu366X and c.1178T>G; p.Lys393X, the latter being paternally inherited.

case_report: A 12-year-old female presented with pain and swelling over both clavicles for a duration of 6 months. The symptoms began insidiously and simultaneously on both sides. She received treatment with analgesics from various doctors, which temporarily alleviated the pain and swelling, but the symptoms recurred a few days after stopping the medication. There was no fever, history of trauma, other swellings, polyarthralgia, or morning stiffness. She did not report loss of appetite or weight loss, nor were there any indications of throat infections or skin lesions. Her daily activities were not affected. There was no similar history in her family. Clinical examination revealed enlargement of the medial halves of both clavicles, which were non-tender and showed no local rise in temperature. The sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints were non-tender. The swellings were hard with a smooth surface and ill-defined margins. Both shoulders had a normal range of motion, and there were no distal neurovascular deficits. Systemic examination was unremarkable. X-ray imaging showed expansile sclerotic lesions on the medial halves of both clavicles. Blood tests revealed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR-90), C-reactive protein level of 0.6, and a total count of 8000. Antistreptolysin O titer (ASO) was negative. Peripheral smear, hemoglobin electrophoresis, and sickling test were normal. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide were negative. Mantoux test and sputum acid-fast bacillus (AFB) were negative. Liver function tests and renal parameters were within normal limits. Chest X-ray and ultrasonography (USG) of the abdomen showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed expansile lesions in bilateral (medial aspect) clavicles. Culture showed no growth. Histopathological examination showed mainly ossifying bone with foci of hemorrhage.
Orpha_name: Chronic nonbacterial osteomyelitis/Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis

case_report: A 57-year-old female visited the dermatology clinic with a red rash on the left forehead and ear, which had been present for two months. The rash was stable and asymptomatic. The patient had a history of allergic rhinitis, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and chronic sun exposure. She had been using betamethasone on the rash without improvement. Physical examination revealed multiple pink macules on the left forehead and similar lesions on the left ear. A culture was taken from the ear lesion, and a shave biopsy was performed on the preauricular area. Histologic examination showed perivascular and periadnexal dermatitis. Blood tests, including complete blood count (CBC), antinuclear antibody, and rheumatoid factor (RF), were mostly normal except for an elevated RF. Hydrocortisone cream 2.5% was prescribed, and a follow-up with an allergist was scheduled. At the follow-up, the patient reported no improvement and no itching. Ketoconazole 2% cream was then prescribed. One month later, with no improvement, the patient was advised to stop ketoconazole and start pimecrolimus 1% cream. Allergy testing was conducted but showed no relevant findings. The patient requested a reevaluation by dermatology due to the persistent rash. Two weeks later, the dermatologist noted no improvement and no new symptoms of burning or itching.
test_results: High-powered views of the biopsy specimen showed periadnexal inflammatory infiltrate consisting of intraepidermal mononuclear cell aggregates with enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei and irregular nuclear borders.

case_report: A 15-day-old female infant was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) due to recurrent fever, rash, and abnormal cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) parameters. The infant was delivered vaginally at 39 weeks and 3 days of gestation without complications. Membranes ruptured 19 hours before delivery. A rash appeared 12 hours post-birth, leading to her initial NICU admission. Initial lab results showed a white blood cell (WBC) count of 23.07×10^9/L (60.9% neutrophils) and a C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 23.7 mg/L. Piperacillin-tazobactam was started empirically. On day three, the infant developed a fever, and a lumbar puncture was performed. CSF analysis revealed a WBC count of 292×10^6/L, glucose concentration of 2.62 mmol/L, and protein level of 1.29 g/L. Meropenem replaced piperacillin-tazobactam, and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) was administered. By day 15, the fever and rash persisted, and CRP remained elevated, although the CSF WBC count decreased to 112×10^6/L. The patient was transferred to our hospital for further evaluation and treatment. Upon arrival, the infant was afebrile with stable cardio-respiratory function and normal neurologic status. Scattered rashes were present in the axillary region. Despite treatment with meropenem and vancomycin, the infant continued to experience a rash and recurrent fever. The CSF WBC count increased to 1719×10^6/L, and CRP, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and serum amyloid A (SAA) levels were elevated. All microbiologic tests, including blood culture, CSF culture, and metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of CSF, were negative. IgM antibodies for toxoplasmosis, cytomegalovirus (CMV), rubella, and herpes simplex virus (HSV) were negative. Hepatitis B serology was negative. Serum levels of procalcitonin (PCT), (1,3)-beta-D-glucan, alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, direct bilirubin, and coagulation tests were normal, as were antinuclear antibody results. Electrocardiogram, echocardiography, electroencephalogram, ophthalmologic evaluations, auditory evoked potentials (AEPs), and visual evoked potentials (VEPs) were normal. Cerebral MRI showed enlarged peri-cerebral spaces. Dexamethasone provided partial symptom relief.
test_results: Genetic testing showed the heterozygote mutation c.1210G>C (p.V404L) in exon 4 of the NLRP3 gene. The variant was de novo and absent from a large general population by searching publicly available population databases (including the gnomAD v2.1 data set and the 1000 Genomes data set). Therefore, this mutation was determined to be likely pathogenic according to the ACMG Standards and Guidelines.

case_report: A 20-year-old nulliparous woman presented to the Department of Uro-neurology with unexplained urinary incontinence. She experienced incontinence primarily during physical effort or exertion, which worsened during coughing episodes related to chronic sinusitis. The symptoms were severe, necessitating the use of up to 10 incontinence pads daily. Additionally, she reported urinary urgency occasionally accompanied by incontinence, and urinary frequency, needing to visit the toilet every 20 minutes during the day and waking up four times at night. There was no history of blood in the urine or painful urination, and she did not have urinary tract infections. She also experienced constipation, with bowel movements occurring once every three days and infrequent episodes of fecal incontinence. She had symptoms similar to irritable bowel syndrome, including frequent abdominal bloating that was relieved by passing stools. There was no visible urogenital prolapse.
test_results: Screening showed a normal bladder outline which was normally sited and a closed bladder neck at rest. There was evidence for detrusor overactivity during the filling phase. When lying supine, coughing did not lead to any leakage of urine. When standing, asking the patient to cough produced descent of the bladder base with opening of the bladder neck, which led to incontinence. When she was asked to cough during the filling phase, there was evidence of beaking of the bladder neck, demonstrating urethral hypermobility. The patient voided a volume of 400 mL with a maximum flow rate (Qmax) of 61 mL/s and no postvoid residual.

case_report: A 47-year-old woman presented with left lumbar pain and visible blood in her urine. Her past medical history was unremarkable. Physical examination showed pale skin without swelling in the extremities, a blood pressure of 130/80 mmHg, and a urine output of 1000 mL/day. Laboratory tests revealed elevated serum creatinine (4.29 mg/dL) and nephrotic syndrome characterized by high levels of protein in the urine (13.4 g/day) and low serum albumin (2.8 g/dL). Urinalysis indicated the presence of blood with dysmorphic red blood cells and acanthocytes. Kidney ultrasound results were normal. The patient exhibited signs of inflammation (C-reactive protein, 37.5 mg/L) and moderate, normocytic anemia. Tests for various antibodies, including antinuclear antibodies (ANA), anti-ds-DNA, anti-Ro, anti-La, anti-Sm, anti-RNP, anti-β2-glycoprotein 1, antiphospholipid, cANCA, pANCA, anti-GBM antibodies, cryoglobulins, and rheumatoid factor, were negative. Screening for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV was also negative, and serum protein electrophoresis did not show a monoclonal spike. The anti-C1q antibody level was elevated (75.8 IU/mL), and serum complement levels were significantly reduced (C3—58.4 mg/dL; C4—9.24 mg/dL).
test_results: By light microscopy (LM), the pattern was membrano-proliferative with diffuse lobular accentuation (mesangial and endocapillary hypercellularity). Additionally, fibrinoid necrosis, capillary wall rupture and extra-capillary hypercellularity were seen in over 50% of the examined glomeruli. There was also moderate tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis. In immunofluorescence (IF), the staining was moderate for IgG, IgM, C1q and C3, in the mesangium and along the glomerular capillary walls. By electron microscopy (EM), mesangial and subendothelial electron-dense deposits were identified in addition to severe endothelial injury. There was also severe podocyte injury with diffuse foot process effacement.

case_report: In 1997, a 24-year-old female patient experienced severe lower back pain. Imaging of the lumbar spine showed multiple areas of bone loss in the lumbar vertebrae. Laboratory tests were mostly normal, except for slightly reduced calcium levels, with normal parathyroid hormone levels. The patient was managed with NSAIDs and medical supervision. In May 2004, the patient noticed a growing nodule in the left thyroid lobe. A biopsy identified follicular thyroid cancer, leading to a total thyroidectomy. Histological examination confirmed both papillary and follicular thyroid cancer. Post-surgery, the patient experienced severe hypocalcemia, which was managed with calcium and salmon calcitonin by an endocrinologist. In September 2004, a large cystic mass was found on the anterior cervical surface, left of the clavicle. Ultrasound identified a 4 cm cyst, which was surgically removed and histologically identified as a lymphatic cyst. In 2007, a recurrence was observed and monitored via ultrasound. In 2008, the patient was referred for further evaluation. Clinical examination revealed a palpable mass in the lower anterior cervical region, measuring 3 cm and increasing in size. Laboratory tests showed elevated CPK (250 IU/L), high serum phosphorus (5.6 mg/dl), and low serum calcium (7.8 mg/dl). Imaging of the thoracic and cervical regions revealed a large cystic mass (12.5 × 2.2 × 2.3 cm) in the anterior mesothorax, with two additional masses, one paratracheal (2.6 × 4 cm) and one in the lower cervical region (2.4 × 2 cm), all interconnected. Imaging of the abdomen showed multiple cystic lesions in the spleen, and further imaging revealed no changes in the cystic lesions of the lumbar vertebrae, with additional similar lesions in the entire vertebral column, clavicle, and both femurs.
test_results: FNA procedure took place and the sample proved to be lymph.

case_report: A 6-day-old female infant was brought to the hospital with feeding difficulties for 6 days, along with rapid breathing and metabolic acidosis for 2 days. She was delivered at 38+5 weeks of gestation via cesarean section due to abnormal umbilical artery flow. Her birth weight was 2,400 g. The mother's blood type was O, and the infant's blood type was B. The family history revealed healthy parents and a healthy sibling, with no consanguinity. The infant showed no dysmorphic features. On the second day of life, she was admitted to the neonatal department with jaundice. Liver function tests indicated a total bilirubin level of 101.1 µmol/L, direct bilirubin level of 10.3 µmol/L, and a reticulocyte count of 10.42%. The Coombs test was negative. Phototherapy and immunoglobulin were administered, and the infant received intravenous nutrition. On the third day, a cranial ultrasound showed bilateral subependymal cystic cavities. By the fourth day, she developed rapid breathing. Blood-gas analysis revealed metabolic acidosis and a blood-ammonia level of 85.4 µmol/L. Routine blood tests showed a hemoglobin level of 77 g/L. Due to lack of improvement in acidosis and anemia, she was referred to our department. Upon admission, her vital signs were: temperature 36.2°C, heart rate 100/min, respiratory rate 70/min, and blood pressure 111/62 mm Hg. Clinical examination revealed low autonomic activity, diminished primitive reflexes, yellowish skin, muscular hypotonia, and poor peripheral blood circulation. Blood-gas analysis confirmed metabolic acidosis with a pH of 7.340, PCO2 of 19.9 mmHg, PO2 of 70.3 mmHg, HCO3− of 10.5 mmol/L, Base Excess of -13.4 mmol/L, and O2 saturation of 95.6%. The infant had anemia with a hemoglobin level of 103.6 g/L, reduced red blood cell-specific volume of 33.1%, and elevated total serum bilirubin levels of 104 µmol/L. Lactic acid levels were normal. She exhibited irregular breathing and was treated with humidified high flow nasal cannula (HHNFC), which was discontinued upon improvement. Hemolytic anemia was managed with transfusion of suspended red blood cells. Intermittent phototherapy was used to treat jaundice until the skin staining subsided. Blood-gas levels were monitored, indicating persistent metabolic acidosis, which was managed with intravenous sodium hydrogen carbonate, later transitioned to oral administration. On the 11th day of admission, blood amino acid levels and acylcarnitine spectrum analysis showed no significant abnormalities. Urine-organic acid analysis revealed a high 5-oxoproline level of 1,100 (normal range: 0–10.0).
test_results: Compound heterozygous variants in GSS were detected in the proband by performing whole-exome sequencing: A c.491G > A (p.?) variant was found in exon 5, and a c.1343_1348delTACTTC (p.L448_L449del) variant was found in exon 13. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the c.491G > A (p.?) and c.1343_1348delTACTTC (p.L448_L449del) variants were inherited from the mother and father, respectively. Her brother carried only the c.491G > A (p.?) variant.

case_report: A 9-year-old Chinese girl presented with pain in the posterior part of the left mandibular region and a nodule with pus discharge, noted one month prior to her visit. The patient exhibited normal growth without any height or developmental abnormalities. Physical examination identified a nodule with pus discharge and swelling under the left side of the chin. Applying gentle pressure to the surrounding tissue resulted in thick purulent drainage from the central punctum. Intraoral examination showed red and swollen alveolar mucosa in the region of the primary left mandibular second molar (#75), which was only partially erupted. All teeth in the mixed dentition displayed abnormal shapes, except for the bilateral permanent incisors in both the maxillary and mandibular regions, which were misaligned. The crowns of the primary canines and the primary maxillary first molars (#54 and 64) were enlarged, bulbous, and malformed with 2 or 3 cusps, resembling either fusion or germination. Tooth #64 exhibited level III mobility without any positive signs on percussion or palpation. The primary maxillary second molars (#55 and 65) and the primary right mandibular first molar (#84) were similarly enlarged with developmental grooves dividing the crowns into various lobules. Additionally, small tooth-like structures were observed around tooth #84. The first permanent molars lacked clearly defined cusps, resembling the tied end of a sausage. Teeth #75 and 85 were only partially erupted. According to her guardians, the patient's incisors began to erupt at age 4 and had never been replaced, indicating congenital absence of the primary incisors. Her parents also noted that the eruption of her primary dentition was delayed compared to normal children.
test_results: The panoramic radiograph revealed tooth-like radiopaque masses surrounded by a large radiolucent zone with a well-defined margin in the molar area of left mandibular. Radiopaque masses in the bilateral primary mandibular molar region appeared to be 4 odontoma and the germs of bilateral permanent mandibular premolars were absent. Radiologic and clinical findings were mostly consistent with a diagnosis of pericoronitis causing cutaneous sinus tracts in the left mandibular premolar region. Radiographic analysis of the abnormal molars showed taurodontism changes with larger pulp chambers, some of which were duplicated, and the root length was short compared with crown height; some were taurodont in configuration. The spiral CT images of both jaws were reconstructed and the craniofacial skeletons were normal. According to the otolaryngologic examination, the patient had distinct bilateral sensorineural hearing loss of acuity to frequencies above 1000 Hz. Her threshold was normal at low frequencies but obviously drop up to 75 dB at higher frequencies. The otolaryngologic examination confirmed her auditory structures, temporal bone, and ethmoid air cells were normal.

case_report: A 12-year-old male visited the outpatient department of a tertiary care hospital in Karachi with gynecomastia. His parents noted limited sociability and difficulties in social interactions, along with language delay and learning disabilities. He was born at 38+7 weeks gestation with a birth weight of 3,140 g, within the normal range. The parents reported a history of minor learning disabilities in one parent. There was no consanguinity in the parents' relationship, and no family history of genetic diseases. Physical examination revealed truncal obesity, a dysmorphic face with large ears and fleshy earlobes, and shortened toes. Gynecomastia and small testes were also observed. Ocular examination showed nystagmus. Cognitive assessment using standardized tests indicated intellectual disability, with a Full-Scale IQ score of 55. The Verbal Comprehension Index score was 58, Perceptual Reasoning Index score was 54, Working Memory Index score was 56, and Processing Speed Index score was 53, all in the extremely low range. Laboratory tests showed low testosterone levels (0.5 nmol/L; normal range: 9.2–31.8 nmol/L). Brain MRI revealed no structural abnormalities or signs of neuronal migration defects. Karyotype analysis confirmed a 46, XY result.
test_results: Genetic testing using next-generation sequencing (NGS) identified a pathogenic variant in the PHF6 gene. The specific variant identified in our patient was a frameshift mutation (c.569_570del), resulting in a premature termination codon (p.Glu190Aspfs*9). This variant was confirmed to be de novo, as parental genetic testing revealed no evidence of the mutation.

case_report: A 25-year-old male reported a lifelong absence of the left testis and a right-sided inguinal swelling persisting for 5 years, with recent onset of pain in the swelling over the past 2 days. Physical examination showed an empty left scrotum and an indirect inguinal hernia on the right side, with the right testis located at the root of the scrotum. The penis was well developed. The patient exhibited normal male secondary sexual characteristics. Past medical history included primary infertility. Semen analysis showed azoospermia.
test_results: Ultrasonography showed right inguinal hernia with undescended testis in the right inguinal canal and an absent testis on the left side. Surgical exploration revealed indirect sac with the right testis. While retrieving the testis, we noticed a complex mass resembling uterus-like structure, and gonad (left) with the fimbria-like structure. Both the gonads had vas deferens and vascular supply. Histopathological study proved it to be uterus and left gonad like structure proved to be testis which was atrophic without spermatogenesis. Chromosomal analysis revealed normal male genotype – 46 XY.
diagnosis: Persistent Mullerian Duct Syndrome with Transverse Testicular Ectopia

case_report: A 32-year-old female patient experienced depression, anxiety, and subtle gait disturbances during the second trimester of her first pregnancy, which was otherwise uncomplicated. Her primary complaints at the emergency department included difficulty finding words, concentrating, and a fear of falling while walking. She exhibited anxiety, hopelessness, and mildly decreased cognitive function, scoring 24 points on the Mini Mental State Examination. She was treated by the Department of Psychiatry for six months without significant improvement. After treatment, she displayed an unusual wide-based, shuffling, very slow, and highly fluctuating gait, walking in small steps and sometimes staggering severely, though she did not fall. Cerebral MRI showed confluent white matter lesions. The patient had been treated for mild hypertension since age 29 but was otherwise healthy. Her family history was negative for hereditary diseases, though incomplete due to loss of contact with her father at age 18. Ten months after symptom onset and six months post-partum, she presented with global bradykinesia, severe slowing and hesitation in fine motor skills, symmetric rigidity in all extremities without tremor, reduced spontaneous speech, slight amnestic aphasia, and ataxic dysarthria with loss of modulation. Her gait disturbances had worsened, limiting her to short distances independently, with difficulty lifting her feet without external instruction but no typical freezing behaviors. Apraxia was noted in both fine motor skills and gait. Another MRI revealed increasingly symmetrical, confluent FLAIR hyperintensities with partly restricted diffusion, but no contrast enhancement. Extensive blood and CSF analyses, along with electrophysiological tests, did not suggest a specific diagnosis, with no evidence of infectious or autoimmune causes. Marked parkinsonian features showed slight improvement with levodopa. CT demonstrated progressive leukoencephalopathy and spotty frontal calcifications.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed the presence of a heterozygous mutation (c.2541G>C) in the CSF1R gene leading to a change in the corresponding amino acid sequence (p.E847D).

case_report: A six-month-old male infant born post-term by cesarean section presented with widespread blisters on the body. The blisters began appearing one month prior, initially on the left elbow and subsequently spreading to other extremities, trunk, neck, and scalp, with the chest and back being the most affected areas. The lesions were associated with severe itching, particularly on the back, which worsened with rubbing and bathing. The parents reported no weight loss, vomiting, diarrhea, shortness of breath, or syncope. The infant was exclusively fed formula milk. No medication use was identified as an exacerbating factor. The last vaccination was administered two months ago at the age of four months. There was no family history of hematologic or dermatologic diseases, and the patient had no significant developmental, medical, drug, surgical, or social history. Physical examination revealed multiple tense vesicles and bullae primarily on the trunk. The underlying skin was diffusely thickened and erythematous with an orange peel (peau d’orange) appearance. Darier sign was not observed, but dermographism was positive on the back. The palms and soles were unaffected. Examination of hair, nails, mucosae, and general physical and systemic examination showed no abnormalities. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood cell count with differentials, C-reactive protein, liver, and renal function tests, were within normal limits.
test_results: Histological examination of the skin showed a subepidermal blister and a generalized infiltration of monomorphic granular cells concentrating within the papillary dermis with a few eosinophils. Giemsa stain was taken up by almost all infiltrating cells which confirmed the increased mast cells. Direct immunofluorescence was negative for IgG, IgA, and C3.

case_report: A 20-year-old Caucasian male presented to the emergency room with a history of allergic rhinitis and no other significant medical conditions or drug allergies. His immunizations were up to date, including four doses of the COVID-19 vaccine. He had no relevant family history and did not use drugs, tobacco, alcohol, or prescription medications. There was no contact with animals, recent travel abroad, or stays in rural areas. The patient reported experiencing retrosternal chest pain for the past three days, described as oppressive, intense, and pleuritic, with no alleviating or relieving factors. He also complained of easy fatigue with minimal exertion and overall weakness but denied fever, dyspnea, cough, gastrointestinal symptoms, or other systemic symptoms. On physical examination, the patient was hemodynamically stable with mild tachycardia (heart rate of 110 bpm). He had no fever, and cardiac auscultation revealed a regular rhythm without murmurs. An electrocardiogram (EKG) showed ST segment elevation in leads I, II, III, aVF, and V4-6. Laboratory tests indicated elevated levels of troponin I (11635 pg/mL - reference range: 13.8-17.5 pg/mL), with no other significant abnormalities in the complete blood count, renal function, electrolytes, liver enzymes, or inflammatory markers. Testing for SARS-CoV-2 was negative. Echocardiography revealed severe systolic dysfunction of the left ventricle, with a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 25%, showing diffuse and severe hypokinesis, particularly in the anterior and inferior walls. Right ventricular dysfunction and moderate pericardial effusion were also observed. Coronary angiography did not show any evidence of coronary artery disease. The patient was transferred to a cardiac intermediate care unit for further management. Within 24 hours of admission, the patient developed signs of low cardiac output and hyperlactatemia (maximum of 3 mmol), requiring norepinephrine and dobutamine support until clinical stability was achieved. Repeat echocardiography showed similar findings to the previous examination. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed the presence of myocarditis, associated with moderate pericardial effusion and bilateral pleural effusion, with greater involvement on the right side. Further laboratory evaluation revealed a decreasing trend in troponin I levels (506 pg/mL), elevated NT-proBNP (5086 pg/mL), and a gradual increase in eosinophil count on the complete blood count (1550 μL to 2900 μL - reference range: < 1000 uL). All other laboratory tests were within normal limits.
test_results: Endomyocardial biopsy showed areas of necrosis and interstitial and perivascular inflammatory infiltrates with numerous eosinophils.

case_report: A 68-year-old male from Gulmi, Nepal, presented with multiple episodes of loss of consciousness upon standing from a sitting position over the past 3 years. These episodes were rapid in onset, brief (usually less than 1 minute), and followed by spontaneous and complete recovery. He experienced dizziness and visual disturbances prior to losing consciousness, with dizziness not related to head position. Additional complaints included increased frequency of urination, nocturia, constipation, and erectile dysfunction. There was no history of unpleasant smells, fear, anxiety, or abdominal discomfort before the episodes. He also reported no aggravation by meals, increased ambient temperature, pain, the sight of blood, venipuncture, or intense emotion. During the episodes, his eyes remained open without up-rolling, frothing at the mouth, tongue biting, or fecal incontinence. Post-episode, he did not experience drowsiness, headache, muscle pain, or disorientation. He denied symptoms such as cough, chest pain, palpitations, breathlessness, vomiting, paralysis, or involuntary movements. He had a history of smoking for 15 years but quit 3 years ago and did not consume alcohol. Family history was unremarkable. Previous treatments included fludrocortisone and increased fluid intake, which did not completely alleviate the episodes. On examination, his blood pressure dropped from 130/100 mmHg while supine to 110/70 mmHg after standing for 3 minutes, with a pulse rate of 70/min that did not increase upon standing. Peripheral pulses were symmetrically palpable, and there was no evidence of carotid bruits, pallor, icterus, lymphadenopathy, clubbing, cyanosis, edema, or dehydration. Systemic examination of the respiratory, cardiovascular, and gastrointestinal systems revealed no abnormalities. Higher mental function, skull and spine, cranial nerves, motor and sensory, stance, and gait examinations were unremarkable. Skin examination showed no dryness or absence of hair, and pupillary examination was normal. Routine and other tests, including complete blood count, ESR, random blood sugar, renal function test, thyroid function test, chest X-ray, HIV I and II, VDRL, EEG, ANA, RA factor, and Extractable Nuclear Antigen panel, were normal. ECG, echocardiography, and Holter monitoring were also within normal limits. MRI of the head and EEG were performed and showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Deep breaths test showed a fall in pulse rate of <15 beats/min. Handgrip test revealed diastolic pressure of 90 mmHg before and 100 mmHg after the test. The Valsalva maneuver showed a ratio of the highest pulse rate in the preliminary rest period to the lowest pulse rate during the test to be <1.1. Carotid massage revealed a pulse rate of 92/min before and 88/min after the test.

case_report: An 8-year-old Chinese boy was admitted to the hospital due to delayed growth. He was born full-term, weighing 2.45 kg and measuring 48 cm in height. At 8 months gestational age, a fetal B-ultrasound indicated short limbs. His mother had hypothyroidism during pregnancy and was treated with levothyroxine sodium tablets, maintaining normal thyroid function for the remainder of the gestational period. His height measurements were 67 cm (–3.52SDS) at 1 year, 75 cm (-3.97SDS) at 2 years, 82 cm (-3.89SDS) at 3 years, and 84.5 cm (-5.02SDS) at 4 years. He began speaking at 14 months and walking at 16 months, with developmental milestones delayed by about 1 month compared to typical children. He is currently in grade two of primary school with good academic performance and has an appropriate vaccination status. He experienced recurrent respiratory infections until the age of 4 years. His parents reported no consanguinity. The patient has an elder brother who had intrauterine growth retardation and short limbs as indicated by fetal B-ultrasound. The brother was born full-term, weighing 2 kg and measuring 46 cm in length, but died at 50 days old, possibly due to pneumonia. Upon admission, the child had a height of 86 cm (-5.81SDS), weighed 15 kg (< P3r), and had a BMI of 15.6 kg/m2 (P25–50t). His head circumference was 51 cm, finger distance 90 cm, and sitting height 59 cm. The skin on the inner side of his upper limbs and thighs showed signs of livedo. He exhibited various facial features including zygomatic arch dysplasia, a high forehead, low anterior and posterior hairline, short and down-slanting palpebral fissures, low-set ears, a long nasal tip and columella, and a small mouth. Additionally, he had irregular teeth, short limbs, a 2 cm long webbed penis, and testicular volume of 0.5 mL.
test_results: The whole exome sequencing (WES) revealed compound heterozygous pathogenic variants in the proband’s POLE gene. One variant was a splicing variant (c.5811 + 2T > C). The other variant was defined as a nonsense variant (c.2006G > A), resulting in a truncated protein (p.W669X).

case_report: The patient, a 2-year and 4-month-old girl (F1-II-1), was born at 39 weeks of gestation to healthy, nonconsanguineous Chinese parents. Prenatal ultrasound imaging indicated shortened long bones. At birth, her measurements were as follows: length 46 cm (−2.61 SD), weight 2700 g (−1.98 SD), and head circumference 35.5 cm (1.4 SD) with a large anterior fontanel. Neonatal screening results were normal. At 5 months old, she was hospitalized for bacterial meningitis, during which hypocalcemia and hypoparathyroidism were identified. Laboratory results showed serum calcium (Ca) at 1.9 mmol/L (reference range 2.10–2.80), phosphorus (P) at 2.85 mmol/L (reference range 1.45–2.10), magnesium (Mg) at 0.55 mmol/L (reference range 0.66–1.05), and parathyroid hormone (PTH) at 4.8 pg/mL (reference range 12–88). Brain CT scans revealed calcification in the basal ganglia. Radiographs at 9 months showed cortical thickening and medullary stenosis of the lower limb bones. At 15 months, she experienced generalized convulsions due to hypocalcemia, with serum Ca at 1.31 mmol/L, P at 2.59 mmol/L, Mg at 0.59 mmol/L, and PTH at 10.8 pg/mL. At 2 years and 4 months, her height was 77 cm (−3.21 SD) and weight was 11 kg (−1.42 SD). The anterior fontanelle remained open, and she exhibited defective dentition and microdontia. Additional physical features included a prominent forehead and a depressed nasal root, with no other dysmorphic characteristics noted. She was treated with calcium, magnesium, vitamin D preparations, and calcitriol, and subsequently did not experience further seizures or signs of hypocalcemia.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing (WES) revealed a missense variant in exon 4 of FAM111A (c.1531 T>C) resulting in amino acid substitution (p.Tyr511His). None of her parents had this alteration, indicating that the variant occurred de novo.

case_report: A 21-day-old female infant was transferred to Samsung Medical Center due to difficulties in removing the endotracheal tube. The infant was delivered at 35+1 weeks of gestation via emergency cesarean section following spontaneous rupture of membranes and premature labor. Apgar scores were 2 at 1 minute and 8 at 5 minutes. At birth, the infant did not cry, exhibited cyanosis, and was lethargic. Positive pressure ventilation was ineffective, necessitating endotracheal intubation in the delivery room. Birth measurements were 2,030 g (25th percentile) for weight, 49 cm (75th-90th percentile) for length, and 35 cm (>90th percentile) for head circumference. The infant had low set ears. A large patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) was identified and surgically closed 12 days post-birth. Osteomeatal unit computed tomography (CT) was performed to investigate the cause of extubation failure, revealing bilateral choanal atresia, atresia of the left external auditory canal, and stenosis of the right auditory canal. At 35 days old, the infant underwent surgical repair of the choanae, followed by another extubation attempt. However, reintubation was required due to persistent desaturation and tachypnea. Postglottic stenosis was identified through laryngomicrosurgery. At 42 days old, a tracheostomy was performed, resulting in stabilized respiration without the need for respiratory support. Chest CT showed a left aortic arch with an aberrant origin of the right subclavian artery, and echocardiography indicated minimal left pulmonary artery hypoplasia without focal stenosis.
test_results: A c.3896T>C (p. leu1299Pro) missense mutation in exon 16 of the CHD7 gene was detected. Neither of the parents had the mutation. The amino acid residue L1299 is highly conserved across different species, and the L1299P variation does not occur in 200 control chromosomes from 100 healthy individuals.

case_report: A 2-year-old male child, the firstborn of healthy, unrelated parents, was delivered at 38 weeks of gestation with a birth weight of 2510 g, height of 48 cm, and APGAR scores of 10. During the neonatal period, generalized hypotonia was noted. The child exhibited no abnormalities in the heart and genitourinary system. He began sitting at 15 months and walking at 22 months. Early symptoms included feeding difficulties, dysphagia, gastroesophageal reflux, and constipation. The child experienced febrile seizures on two occasions. He had frequent infections of the upper and lower respiratory tract and ears. Immunological tests indicated reduced levels of IgA. Physical examination identified several dysmorphic features: short chin, high forehead, fine hair, everted prominent lower lip, epicanthus, downturned mouth, curly hair, broad nasal tip, abnormal hairline, long palpebral fissure, shortened nose, frontal bossing, strabismus, thick lower lip, facial asymmetry, hypertelorism, and full cheeks. At 16 months, his weight was 8 kg (<3rd percentile), height was 75 cm (5th percentile), and OFC was 48 cm (77th percentile). There was a noted delay in speech development, while intellectual development remained challenging to assess.
test_results: EEG analysis showed changes in the left mid-temporal area, activated by sleep.

case_report: A 19-year-old female high school student presented with abnormal liver function for 2 years and was admitted to the hospital on October 17, 2018. Initially, she was found to have elevated alkaline phosphatase and γ-GT levels during a physical examination, despite being asymptomatic. Her liver function showed slight improvement after taking liver-protective medications (Ursodeoxycholic Acid and Bicyclol) as an outpatient. However, follow-up liver function tests remained abnormal. Due to her busy schedule and lack of symptoms, she initially refused hospitalization. Upon revisiting the hospital outpatient clinic on October 17, 2018, she was admitted after liver ultrasonography indicated cirrhosis. Upon admission, she exhibited no jaundice, pruritus, asthenia, anorexia, or other discomforts. She reported no history of alcohol intake or use of hepatotoxic drugs and had no family history of liver disease. Physical examination revealed mild splenomegaly, with other findings being unremarkable. Laboratory data from October 18, 2018, showed alanine aminotransferase at 62 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase at 45 U/L, alkaline phosphatase at 300 U/L, γ-GT at 119 U/L, total bilirubin at 14.9 μmol/L, direct bilirubin at 4.7 μmol/L, and albumin at 43.9 g/L. Hepatitis virus markers (A, B, C, and E) were negative, as were antibodies against cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus. Ceruloplasmin and serum copper levels were normal, and no Kayser-Fleischer ring was observed. The qualitative urinary porphyrin test was negative. All autoimmune antibodies, including antimitochondrial, antinuclear, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, were negative. Serum α-1-antitrypsin concentration, thyroid function, coagulation function, and other laboratory results were normal. Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging showed liver cirrhosis, portal hypertension, splenomegaly, and cholestasis, with no obstructions in the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts as confirmed by magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography. A liver pathological examination revealed significantly decreased MDR3 protein staining compared to healthy individuals.
test_results: The result revealed a synonymous mutation on Exon 6 (c.504C > T; p.N168N; heterozygous) and a novel missense mutation on Exon 17 (c.2137G > A; p.V713M; heterozygous).

case_report: A four-year-old boy from a consanguineous Saudi family (first-degree cousins) exhibited generalized hypotonia starting at birth. The pregnancy was marked by reduced fetal movements. He had a sister with similar symptoms who passed away at 18 months due to respiratory infections, while his two paternal half-siblings are healthy. The patient experienced feeding difficulties, intermittent choking, and recurrent aspiration pneumonia. Significant motor developmental delays were observed early. By 21 months, he had good head control, could sit without support, and began crawling and reaching for objects. At his last clinical follow-up at 9 years old, he was walking independently but was a slow runner. He could draw a line, completely undress himself, and participated in group play without major cognitive deficits. He did not need long-term oxygen support. During examination, he was conscious and interactive. Vital signs were stable, and oxygen levels were maintained on room air. Dysmorphic features included plagiocephaly, facial diplegia, high arched palate, low set posteriorly rotated ears, mild dextro convexity scoliosis of the thoracic spine with spine rigidity. Generalized hypotonia, more pronounced in the axial muscles than the appendicular, and generalized weakness, more proximal than distal, were observed. He had a positive Gower sign without calf muscle hypertrophy. Deep tendon reflexes were absent, and joint hyperlaxity was noted in the knees, wrists, and elbows. A comprehensive neurometabolic workup, including blood lactic and pyruvic acids, ammonia, biotinidase, tandem mass spectroscopy, urine gas chromatography and mass spectroscopy, creatine kinase, and thyroid function, yielded normal results. Nerve conduction studies (NCS) were also unremarkable.
test_results: EMG of the vastus lateralis muscle showed neurogenic changes.
diagnosis: Congenital Myopathy due to MEGF10 Variants

case_report: A 53-year-old female with a history of hypertension presented with severe central abdominal pain persisting for 2 weeks. The pain was non-radiating, worsened by food intake, and partially alleviated by vomiting. She experienced vomiting three times daily, with the vomitus containing food but no blood. Additionally, she reported a decreased appetite and a significant weight loss of 12 kilograms (8%) over the past 2 months. Her surgical history included a hysterectomy performed 4 months ago for uterine fibroid. On physical examination, there was notable abdominal distension, mild diffuse tenderness, and active bowel sounds. She did not have a fever. Laboratory tests revealed microcytic anemia, but all other results were within normal limits.
test_results: Chest-Abdominal-Pelvic computed tomography (CT) revealed dilation of the distal bowel loops that contained impacted fecal material and multiple linear dense radiopaque material associated with fat stranding with suspected foreign body.

case_report: The patient, a 27-year-old Indian male, presented with recurrent episodes of high-grade intermittent fever, occipital headache, conjunctival congestion, and a rash for 17 years. The rash was migratory, non-pruritic, maculopapular, primarily affecting the chest, abdomen, and extensor aspects of the limbs, with exacerbations upon exposure to cold. He experienced 3-4 episodes per month, each lasting 2-3 days. Additionally, he had recurrent episodes of asymmetric non-deforming polyarthritis involving both axial and appendicular joints for 17 years, and a slowly progressive hearing loss over the past 10 years. Physical examination revealed short stature, short neck, conjunctival congestion, diffuse urticarial rash, clubbing, and bilateral papilledema. Other examination findings were normal. Laboratory results showed hemoglobin at 12.8 g/dl, total WBC count at 43900/μl (N 88%, L 06%, E 1%, M 05%), platelet count at 4.4 × 10^9/L, and ESR at 9 mm in 1 hour. C-reactive protein was elevated. Renal function tests, liver function tests, and urinalysis were normal. Rheumatoid factor, ANA, C and P ANCA were negative. Pure tone audiometry indicated bilateral severe sensorineural hearing loss with an average frequency loss of 65 dB in the right ear and 55 dB in the left ear, with higher frequencies more affected than lower ones. Brain imaging was normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed 11 WBCs (all lymphocytes), protein at 98 mg/dL, and sugar at 54 mg/dL. CSF gram stain, AFB stain, and culture sensitivity were negative.
test_results: Histopathological examination of urticarial lesions of skin showed normal epidermis, dermal inflammation with perivascular neutrophilic infiltration.

case_report: A 50-year-old male presented with a one-year history of a purplish nodular plaque on his right upper thigh, which had gradually increased in size over this period. He continued to develop more plaques in the groin, lower abdomen, and buttocks. Over the next 2 years, he developed a large area of cutaneous laxity in the right groin. The excess skin was surgically excised. The patient continued to develop new areas of slack skin that commenced as thickened, violaceous, and minimally scaly plaques limited to his groins, lower abdomen, and buttocks, which evolved into pendulous folds of skin. He had normal chest radiographs, pulmonary function tests, full blood count, serum angiotensin-converting enzyme, and calcium levels throughout the course of his condition.
test_results: An incisional biopsy revealed multiple non-necrotising granulomata, characterized by prominent and confluent multinucleate foreign body-type giant cells, with only sparsely admixed small lymphocytes. Subsequently, a further biopsy was taken and revealed multiple non-necrotizing epithelioid granulomata with strikingly prominent giant cells and a sparse population of small lymphocytes. No foreign material was identified. Ziehl-Neelsen and fungal stains were negative. Elastic van Gieson histochemistry confirmed widespread loss of elastin. PCR performed on a fresh skin biopsy demonstrated a clonal population of T cells.

case_report: A 17-year-old male presented with severe, throbbing pain in the left knee that had worsened over the past 72 hours, accompanied by progressive swelling over the past 48 hours. He was limping and unable to bear weight. Vital signs were stable. Physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness in the left knee, with no other abnormalities noted. The patient had no significant past medical history and was not on any regular medications. An initial X-ray showed an aggressive mixed sclerotic and lytic lesion at the lateral aspect of the proximal tibial metaphysis with aggressive periosteal reaction and surrounding soft tissue ossification. Initial treatment included analgesics such as meloxicam and cocodamol. Two days later, he visited his general practitioner due to worsening pain and swelling and was referred to the local hospital's Accident and Emergency Department. There, he was reviewed by the trauma and orthopaedic team, administered analgesia, and scheduled for an urgent outpatient CT scan of the left knee. Laboratory results are provided in Table. The CT scan revealed an aggressive bone lesion characterized by permeative bone destruction in the upper posterolateral tibial meta diaphysis extending to the subchondral location, with cortical break and an associated soft tissue mass measuring approximately 4.6 x 2.8 cm. There was an aggressive periosteal reaction in the form of Codman triangles and soft tissue ossifications. Extensive marrow oedema and marrow replacement were observed in the fibular head, suggesting further infiltration extending approximately 90 mm below the tibial plateau to the most inferior margin of the soft tissue component. This resulted in the widening of the proximal tibiofibular joint with posterior displacement of the popliteus muscle and popliteal sheath bundles. The mass approximated the tibiofibular trunk and partially overbreached the popliteus muscle.
test_results: Percutaneous biopsy revealed a malignant tumour composed of nests of epithelioid cells with eccentrically placed pleomorphic nuclei.

case_report: A 63-year-old female presented to the emergency department in December 2021 with lower back pain that started three months prior and extended to the right hip and anterior pelvis. The pain was mechanical and worsened with strenuous activities. She also reported reduced appetite, a weight loss of approximately 5 kg over three months, constipation, dyspepsia without dysphagia, and night sweats. Her medical history included a COVID-19 infection nine months earlier and diabetes mellitus for ten years. She had no history of trauma. Her medications included metoprolol 25 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, and pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily. Her mother had a history of gastric cancer. Vital signs were: blood pressure 120/80, respiratory rate 16, body temperature 37°C, and pulse rate 78. The patient appeared pale but had no skin lesions or atopic dermatitis. Physical, cardiac, respiratory, and skin examinations were normal, but abdominal examination revealed a 2–3 cm splenomegaly below the ribs. Spine examination showed tenderness at the L3 and L4 lumbar vertebrae. Laboratory results were: WBC 18,700 cu/mm (PMN 6826, LYMPH 1926, MONO 224, EOS 9724), HB 13.2 g/dl, PLT 171,000/ml, ESR 82 mm/hr, ALKP 695 IU/L, Ca 8.8 mg/dl, Wright negative, Coombs Wright negative, TSH 1.1 mIU/L, PTH 33.5 pg/mL, and PCR for COVID-19 negative. Endoscopy due to gastrointestinal symptoms and family history of malignancy showed antral gastritis, with pathological findings indicating eosinophilic gastritis. Treatment with prednisolone was initiated for hypereosinophilia and eosinophilic gastritis. Despite treatment, symptoms persisted, and an abdominopelvic ultrasound revealed splenomegaly measuring 171 mm with homogeneous parenchymal echo, but no lymphadenopathy. The patient was admitted for further evaluation.
test_results: 17% of all nucleated cells were atypical mast cells. CD117 and CD25 were reported to be positive.

case_report: A 56-year-old male was admitted to Huantai County People’s Hospital, Shandong, after experiencing episodes of fainting two to three times daily over a two-day period. He reported symptoms of headache, dizziness, sore throat, and excessive sweating before losing consciousness. Each fainting episode lasted approximately 40 to 50 seconds, and he felt weak upon regaining consciousness. The patient had a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF) for three years and had been intermittently taking oral amiodarone. Upon admission, his heart rate was 72 beats per minute with a blood pressure of 87/61 mmHg. Physical and neurological examinations revealed no significant abnormalities. Electrocardiography (ECG) showed AF rhythm, a prolonged RR interval, and a junctional escape rhythm. Transthoracic echocardiography results were normal. A 24-hour ECG Holter monitor recorded AF rhythm with the longest RR interval being 1.8 seconds. Routine blood tests, including measurements of electrolytes, glucose, liver and kidney function, thyroid function, and high-sensitivity troponin T, were all within normal limits.
test_results: Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a thickened nasopharyngeal soft tissue and posterior pharyngeal wall, bone destruction, and narrowing of the local pharyngeal crypt and eustachian tube. The diseased region (5.8 × 2.6 × 4.1 cm) was moderately enhanced after gadopentetic acid (Gd-DTPA) injection, with unclear demarcation from the surrounding structures, which conformed to the features of a tumor.

case_report: A 69-year-old female presented with a one-month history of recurrent visible blood in the urine, along with mild urgency and discomfort during urination. The patient had no prior history of trauma or infection. On physical examination, a fixed, smooth mass measuring approximately 5 cm × 4 cm was palpable in the lower abdomen without tenderness or rebound tenderness. Urine cytology showed an increased number of leukocytes, with no atypical cells or red blood cells. Computed tomography revealed an ill-defined solid mass in the anterior bladder wall. Cystoscopy showed a smooth bladder mucosa with no new growths on the surface, but a bulge was noted at the bladder dome with normal overlying urothelial mucosa. Biopsy results indicated 'chronic inflammation of the mucosa and lamina propria fibrous hyperplasia.' The patient subsequently underwent transurethral partial resection of the bladder tumor (TUR-BT). During TUR-BT, no abnormalities were seen in the bladder mucosa, but a mass was found deep in the muscle layer at the bladder dome. The biopsy post-TUR-BT did not reveal any signs of the tumor. After discussing options with the patient, who wished to preserve the bladder, a median laparotomy and bladder exploration were performed. During this procedure, a mass was found adhering to the apex of the bladder, pubic symphysis, and peritoneum, and was completely resected along with part of the bladder and peritoneum.
test_results: FISH revealed MDM2 and CDK4 amplification in the spindle cells and adipocytes of the tumor.
diagnosis: low-grade fibromatosis-like dedifferentiated liposarcoma  of the urinary bladder

case_report: A 38-year-old male with a history of chronic rhinitis, who had been using menthol nasal drops frequently for over two years, was admitted on 31 May, 2020 with symptoms of fever, cough, sputum production, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. The patient, who owned a Chinese toiletries store, reported a maximum body temperature of 38.9 °C, yellow purulent sputum, white frothy sputum, and muscle soreness in all four extremities, but no haemoptysis or skin rash. On admission, his vital signs included a body temperature of 37.0 ℃, pulse rate of 101 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 24 breaths per minute, and blood pressure of 141/98 mmHg, with no significant findings on cardiopulmonary auscultation. Laboratory tests showed a high-sensitivity C-reactive protein level of 48.6 mg/L, white blood cell count of 13.5 × 10^9/L, and absolute neutrophil count of 10.1 × 10^9/L. HIV antibody test was negative. Chest CT scan revealed multiple patchy ground glass opacities in both lungs, primarily in the inner field and along the bronchi. Blood gas analysis indicated a PO2 of 63 mmHg on room air. Cytological analysis of alveolar lavage fluid showed 54% phagocytes, 32% neutrophils, 11% lymphocytes, and extracellular lipid droplets. Gram-positive cocci were detected in alveolar lavage fluid smears. Bacterial culture, fungal culture, galactomannan detection, fungal D-glucan assay, and identification of Mycobacterium species were all negative. The patient was treated for community-acquired pneumonia with 4.5 g of piperacillin sodium and tazobactam sodium IV every 8 hours for nine days. A follow-up blood gas analysis on 5 June, 2020 showed a PO2 of 92 mmHg on room air. Symptoms of fever, chest tightness, and shortness of breath resolved, and cough and sputum production improved, leading to discharge on 9 June, 2020. The patient experienced a recurrence of fever on 19 June, 2020, with a maximum temperature of 40 °C, along with chest tightness, cough, sputum production, and shortness of breath. Laboratory tests showed a high-sensitivity C-reactive protein level of 48.6 mg/L, white blood cell count of 8.9 × 10^9/L, and absolute neutrophil count of 6.4 × 10^9/L. A repeated chest CT scan showed consolidation in the right lower lobe and progression of scattered patchy opacities in both lungs. The patient received 4.5 g of piperacillin sodium and tazobactam sodium IV twice a day for four days in the outpatient clinic but was admitted to the hospital on 23 June, 2020 due to lack of symptom improvement. Blood gas analysis showed a PO2 of 79 mmHg on room air. High-sensitivity C-reactive protein was 48.6 mg/L, white blood cell count was 8.9 × 10^9/L, and absolute neutrophil count was 6.4 × 10^9/L. Treatment included 1 g of meropenem IV every 8 hours, 600 mg of linezolid IV every 12 hours, and 200 mg of voriconazole PO every 12 hours from 23 June, 2020 for five days. A CT-guided biopsy of the right lower lobe mass on 24 June, 2020 revealed granulomatous inflammation. Symptoms of fever, cough, sputum production, and chest tightness improved, but shortness of breath worsened. On 27 June, 2020, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein was 15.2 mg/L, white blood cell count was 7.7 × 10^9/L, and absolute neutrophil count was 4.8 × 10^9/L. A repeated blood gas analysis showed a PO2 of 65 mmHg on room air. The patient was transferred to the First Affiliated Hospital, Zhejiang University, on 29 June, 2020, and treated with cefoperazone sodium and sulbactam sodium IV every 8 hours. A PET-CT scan showed patchy consolidations in the basal segment of the right lower lobe with increased FDG metabolism. Pathology slides from the CT-guided biopsy revealed chronic granulomatous inflammation with a large amount of lipids, identified as lipoid granuloma.
test_results: Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid smears were positive for acid-fast bacilli 2+. A mycobacterial DNA assay of the sputum identified Mycobacterium abscessus.
diagnosis: pulmonary nontuberculous mycobacteriosis secondary to exogenous lipoid pneumonia

case_report: A 15-year-old female presented with a 2-year history of clumsiness and frequent falls. She was hospitalized due to muscle weakness a few months before her clinic visit. She experienced increasing difficulty with activities such as standing on her toes, skipping, climbing stairs, and navigating curbs, with worsening falls. She was born full term after a normal pregnancy and had normal growth and developmental milestones. There was no family history of neuromuscular disorders. Her medical history included attention deficit disorder without hyperactivity, oppositional defiant disorder, depression, and anxiety. During hospitalization, her serum CK levels ranged from 7396 U/L to 16,102 U/L (reference range: 20-128 U/L). Blood counts, metabolic panel, and inflammatory markers were within normal limits, and there was no evidence of rhabdomyolysis. A myositis antibody panel was negative. MRI of the pelvis showed edema in the bilateral lumbar, psoas, gluteal, and quadriceps muscles. A biopsy of the left vastus lateralis muscle indicated a myopathic process with patchy, non-specific inflammation. She was treated with pulse intravenous steroids followed by oral steroids, but there was no symptomatic improvement. Upon neuromuscular evaluation, she had discontinued oral steroids without worsening of symptoms. Neurological examination revealed bilateral ankle plantarflexion weakness, inability to toe-walk, difficulty rising from a low stool, jumping, and running, and an abnormal gait with increased hip flexion. The rest of the examination was normal.
test_results: Neuropathologic examination of her muscle biopsy revealed polygonal myofiber size variation, necrosis, regeneration, and internalized nuclei in the absence of significant lymphocytic inflammation, inclusion bodies, vacuoles, ragged red fibers, or neurogenic changes. Loss of dysferlin expression was demonstrated by immunofluorescence with three different antibodies and by Western blot with normal human skeletal muscle control. Embryonic myosin heavy chain was diffusely expressed, MHC class I expression was patchy, and C5b-9 deposits were identified on muscle fiber surfaces by immunofluorescence. Next generation sequencing panel genetic testing revealed two pathogenic variants in DYSF: c.3225dup (p.Gly1076Trpfs*38) in exon 30 and c.3349-2A > G (Splice acceptor) in intron 30.

case_report: A 10-month-old boy from Nawabshah, Pakistan, born to first cousins, presented to the Pediatric department with prominent and protruding eyes accompanied by watery discharge over the past 6 months. The child exhibited agitation, disrupted sleep, uncoordinated muscle movements, and a lack of interest and concentration. During the mother's pregnancy, she did not take any folic acid, vitamins, or iron supplements, nor did she undergo any radiological investigations. She experienced no fever, seizures, or vaginal bleeding. The mother had a full-term spontaneous vaginal delivery without complications for either herself or the newborn. At birth, the child weighed 2.5 kg (2.9 percentile) and had an occipitofrontal circumference of 32.1 cm (11.5 percentile). Over the past 6 months, the child developed bilateral eye protrusion and enlargement.
test_results: The computed tomography scan (CT) without contrast revealed cystic enlargement of the fourth ventricle with an enlarged posterior fossa and hypoplasia of the cerebellar hemisphere.

case_report: A 63-year-old female patient presented with intermittent headaches in the right temporoparietal region and blurred vision for the past two years, with symptoms worsening in the last month. Nine years ago, she experienced a cranioencephalic trauma from a traffic accident, impacting the right temporal lobe, but no associated lesions were noted. A CT scan at that time showed no intracranial hematic collections.
