A recent unenhanced CT scan revealed a hypodense area in the right frontoparietal region with clear borders and a small mural hyperdense nodule.
test_results: Conventional sequences showed the lesion to be hypointense on T1-weighted sequences and hyperintense on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences, with a dominant cystic component and a small mural nodule. After intravenous administration of contrast media, enhancement of the mural nodule and of the peripheral cystic area was observed. Diffusion showed impeded movement of the water molecules in the mural nodule and facilitated diffusion in the cystic area of the lesion. When compared to the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), the cystic area showed less facilitated diffusion. MR spectroscopy showed an elevated choline peak and a decreased N-acetylaspartate peak at the mural nodule level. Furthermore, a double peak at 1.3 ppm and 1.5 ppm was observed.

case_report: A 15-year-old girl visited the outpatient department with a one-week history of watering in the right eye. She had restricted eye movements since birth. She was born to parents who are second-degree relatives, delivered at full term without complications. Developmental milestones were delayed. She began menstruating at 14 years old with regular cycles and normal secondary sexual characteristics. No family members had similar features. She underwent cleft palate repair at one year old and had a revision palatoplasty four years ago due to a postoperative palatal fistula. Physical examination revealed short stature (142 cm), a short neck, and a low posterior hairline without neck webbing. Hearing and speech were impaired, and an audiogram showed moderate sensorineural deafness. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were normal. Ocular examination indicated normal anterior and posterior segments, no squint in the primary gaze position, but limited abduction in both eyes. There was widening of the palpebral fissure on attempted abduction and globe retraction on adduction, consistent with bilateral Duane retraction syndrome. There was no upshoot or downshoot of the globe on adduction.
test_results: Plain radiography of the cervical spine showed complete fusion of the C1, C2, and C3 cervical vertebrae with incomplete fusion of the remaining cervical vertebrae. The interspinal foramina were enlarged.

case_report: A 17-year-old male with no known medical history was transferred to our facility from another hospital due to hydrocephalus and intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH). He initially experienced a headache for three days, which was alleviated with paracetamol. On the day he presented at the initial hospital, he developed a severe headache, persistent vomiting, and a decreased level of consciousness, with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 11/15. Upon arrival at our center, his physical examination revealed a GCS score of 9/15, with pupils equally reactive bilaterally and spontaneous movement in both upper and lower limbs.
test_results: Head computer tomography (CT) showed a well-defined, lobulated large mass measuring 6 cm × 5 cm × 3 cm expanding the frontal horn and body of right lateral ventricle that was mainly hyperdense with heterogeneous attenuations and areas of calcifications. The lesion demonstrated no gross enhancement of the contrast. It displaced the septum pellucidum and crossed the midline toward the left side about 3 cm. With mass effect on the frontal horn and body of left lateral ventricle, it obstructed the outflow of the ventricles resulting in obstructive hydrocephalus. The ventricular system was filled with blood which was shown as hyperdensities particularly seen in the dependent portions of occipital horns of bilateral lateral ventricles and third and fourth ventricles. Preoperative MRI of the brain showed a heterogeneous ventricular mass about 40 mm in diameter on the right lateral ventricle which is hypointense signal on both T1 and T2 with no contrast enhancement suggestive of intraventricular tumor associated with intraventricular hemorrhage mainly in the right lateral ventricle. Microscopically, the tumor was characterized by neuroepithelial tissue which was comprising of monotonous bland appearing cells showing fine chromatic nuclei and eosinophilic to clear modest cytoplasm, in a background of fibrillary matrix. These cells were seen in sheets and display a clear interface with neuropil. Ventricular lining of epithelial cells with intraventricular tumor was present in one focus. Many calcified bodies were observed. However, no necrosis or mitotic activity was noted. Well-controlled immunohistochemistry revealed diffuse expression of synaptophysin in tumor cells, which are negative for GFAP. Ki67 labeling index is <2%.

case_report: The patient, an eighteen-month-old Chinese boy, was the first child born to healthy parents following an uneventful pregnancy and delivery. His birth measurements were: weight 3 kg, height 50 cm, and head circumference 34 cm. He passed both the hearing test and newborn screening for hypothyroidism. From birth, he experienced feeding difficulties. At six months old, he exhibited global hypotonia and developmental delay, unable to hold up his head or sit. Physical examination showed hypotonia in the trunk and hypertonia in the extremities. He had an elongated face with bifrontal narrowing and a flat nose, but no dysplastic ears, pectus excavatum, scoliosis, flat feet, or lateral deviation of the great toe. Thyroid function tests revealed increased free triiodothyronine (FT3) at 9.49 pg/ml (normal range 2.00-4.40 pg/ml), decreased free thyroxine (FT4) at 0.49 pg/dl (normal range 1.00-1.70 pg/dl), and mildly increased thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) at 4.93 µIU/ml (normal range 0.27–4.20 µIU/ml). No similar symptoms were observed in other family members. Ultrasonography showed a normal thyroid gland. Brain MRI indicated delayed myelination and mild cerebral atrophy. He was treated with levothyroxine sodium for two months, but the treatment was discontinued due to lack of improvement. At twelve months old, he still could not hold up his head, sit, or stand, and exhibited severe global developmental delay, failing to reach any milestones. Physical examination again showed hypotonia in the trunk and hypertonia in the extremities, with an elongated face, bifrontal narrowing, and a flat nose. His height was 75.4 cm (-2 SD 73 cm), weight was 7 kg (-2 SD 8.2 kg), head circumference was 45 cm (-2 SD 44.2 cm), and chest circumference was 44 cm. Thyroid function tests showed increased FT3 at 8.86 pg/ml (normal range 2.66–4.82 pg/ml), decreased FT4 at 0.94 pg/dl (normal range 1.12–1.77 pg/dl), and normal TSH at 0.47 µIU/ml (normal range 0.38–7.31 µIU/ml). He was prescribed Euthyroxol with methimazole for three months, but the treatment was stopped due to no effect.
test_results: Genetic analysis revealed the presence of a novel splicing variant (NM_006517.4: c.431-2 A > G). The variant c.431-2 A > G may result in splicing change at protein level. Pedigree analysis revealed that this variant was inherited from his heterozygous healthy mother, but was not found in his maternal grandparents.

case_report: A 2-day-old male infant was brought to the Emergency Department with the complaint of not passing stool since birth. Parents observed abdominal distension on the first day of life and noted meconium in the urine. The infant was delivered at full term via normal vaginal delivery without any antenatal or postnatal complications. The mother, a third gravida with two healthy children, had normal antenatal scans and no history of premature rupture of membranes or gestational diabetes mellitus. Family history indicated a non-consanguineous marriage with no gastrointestinal anomalies, sudden infant death, or miscarriages. On physical examination, the infant weighed 2.9 kg, appeared dehydrated and lethargic, had significant abdominal distension, and lacked an anal opening. A nasogastric tube was inserted and passed effortlessly, with its position confirmed in the stomach on a radiograph.
test_results: An invertogram confirmed a high type of anorectal malformation. An abdominal radiograph showed an air-fluid level with a large bowel loop.
diagnosis: Congenital Pouch Colon associated with Imperforate Anus and Recto-Vesical Fistula
Orpha_name: Non-syndromic anorectal malformation with pouch colon

case_report: A 5-year-old girl was referred to a genetic clinic due to facial dysmorphism. She is the first child of a non-consanguineous Chinese couple, born at full term with a birth weight of 2.9 kg. Her perinatal history was unremarkable. During the neonatal period, she was noted to have dysmorphism and a cardiac murmur. An echocardiogram revealed a patent ductus arteriosus and a large secundum atrial septal defect. A total corrective operation was performed at 1 year of age. A developmental assessment at 2 years of age indicated severe developmental delay. Subsequently, she developed stereotypical hand movements, abnormal outbursts of laughter, and an ataxic gait. A brain MRI showed mild thinning of the corpus callosum. Physical examination at the genetic clinic revealed a head circumference at the 3rd percentile, with body weight and height between the 10th and 25th percentiles. Facial dysmorphism was noted, including hypertelorism, medially flared eyebrows, a mildly overhanging columella, a pointed chin, and fleshy, uplifted earlobes.
test_results: It showed a de novo pathogenic frameshift mutation ZEB2{NM_014795.2}:c.[3335delACTT];[=];p.ZEB2{NP_055610.1}:p.[Tyr1112Cysfs128][=].

case_report: A 10-year-old boy with no prior episodes of uveitis was referred to the Vitreoretinal Division of King Khaled Eye Specialist Hospital (KKESH) 2 years ago due to a sudden decrease in vision in the left eye 5 weeks before presentation. He had no history of skin rashes or arthritis. Family history was negative for uveitis, joint, or skin diseases. His past ocular history included lens aspiration and intraocular lens implantation in both eyes 6 years earlier for early-onset cataract. On examination, the best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/40 in the right eye and hand movement (HM) in the left eye. Anterior segment examination of both eyes showed quiet anterior chambers (ACs) with posterior chamber intraocular lenses and normal intraocular pressure. Fundus examination was unremarkable in the right eye and showed total rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RD) with extensive proliferative vitreoretinopathy in the left eye. Pars plana vitrectomy with 360° retinectomy and silicone oil injection was performed in the left eye for RD. Three weeks postoperatively, BCVA was 20/70 in the right eye and HM in the left eye. Biomicroscopic examination revealed 3+ AC reaction in both eyes and 4+ vitritis in the left eye with poor view to the fundus. The right eye had multiple distinct chorioretinal lesions with 1+ vitritis and peripheral focal vascular sheathing. Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) showed multiple early hypofluorescent areas, more numerous than clinically observed lesions, corresponding to hyperfluorescent areas in later frames with peripheral vascular leakage. Uveitis workup, including complete blood count, renal function tests, liver function tests, and chest computed tomography, were within normal limits. Fluorescent treponemal antibody absorbed, purified protein derivative, and tuberculosis Quantiferon Gold test results were negative. Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level was 64 U/L (reference range: 13–100 U/L) and serum lysozyme was 12.5 mg/L (reference range: 9.6–16.8 mg/L). The patient received 3 doses of 1 g intravenous (IV) methylprednisolone daily, followed by oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day with weekly tapering and oral methotrexate 15 mg weekly. Panuveitis was controlled, and choroidal lesions evolved into chorioretinal scars in the right eye but were resistant to treatment in the left eye, resulting in no light perception. Four months later, vision in the right eye further reduced to 20/125, with new macular chorioretinal lesions and diffuse subretinal fibrosis. The patient was admitted for 3 doses of IV methylprednisolone, followed by oral prednisolone on discharge, and continued on oral methotrexate.
test_results: The test result revealed nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-containing protein 2 (NOD2) gene with a heterozygous nucleotide substitution from C to T at position c.2798+158C>T in intron 8 (reference sequence NM_0022162.1).

case_report: A 69-year-old Caucasian male with a history of chronic phase CML since 1990 initially responded to interferon and omacetaxine mepesuccinate treatment, which was stopped after 14 years when imatinib mesylate (Gleevec) was introduced. One year after starting imatinib, resistance developed, and the disease progressed to an accelerated phase, leading to the prescription of dasatinib as a second-line treatment. Initial serum CK levels were normal, but a significant increase in serum CK levels (1,000–4,000 units/L) was observed following dasatinib initiation. Over the next 7 years, the patient did not exhibit musculoskeletal symptoms but experienced edema and multiple pleural effusions, known side effects of dasatinib. Two years into dasatinib therapy, the patient presented with enlarged neck nodes due to non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma and underwent chemoradiation therapy with three cycles of rituximab and CHOP regimen, achieving remission. Five years post non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma diagnosis, the patient developed gradual-onset proximal muscle weakness in the legs, reporting difficulty standing from a seated position and climbing stairs. Physical examination revealed full eye movements but bilateral weakness of the orbicularis oculi. Minimal weakness was noted in the upper limbs, specifically in the long finger flexors and flexor digitorum profundus 4 and 5. Significant quadriceps wasting was observed in the lower limbs, with sparing of the rectus femoris.
test_results: A muscle biopsy of our patient’s right vastus showed significant fibrosis, inflammation, and adipose tissue replacement of the interstitium. Inflammatory cell infiltrate was apparent in the perimysium, concentrated in the endomysium and necrotic fibers, and present to a lesser extent in his normal muscle fibers. The sampled vasculature appeared normal without evidence of vasculitis.

case_report: An 18-year-old male presented with bilateral leg swelling. Initial examination revealed lower extremity swelling, and he was referred to a vascular surgeon to evaluate for chronic venous insufficiency. Bilateral venous duplex ultrasonography showed a competent venous system with no venous reflux or obstruction. The patient reported experiencing bilateral lower limb swelling for ten years, with minimal swelling in the morning that worsened by the end of the day, accompanied by pain. The pain, rated 4 out of 10, increased with running and resolved with rest. He was asymptomatic at rest and during daily activities. He denied early morning stiffness, back pain, or a family history of related conditions. He had tried massage therapy, footwear modifications, and over-the-counter analgesics. Recently, he noticed more swollen ankles with activity-related pain. His bowel habits were regular, with no diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, or skin rashes. He did not have a cough, fever, or night sweats. There was no significant family history of autoimmune or bone diseases. Physical examination showed normal gait, bilateral ankle nonpitting edema without tenderness or increased local temperature, and present peripheral pulses. Fine tremors of the hands and sweaty palms were observed. The rest of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests indicated biochemical hyperthyroidism with free thyroxine at 16 pmol/L (8.8-14.4 pmol/L) and Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH) at 0.588 MU/L (0.65-3.70 MU/L). Complete blood count, renal panel, liver panel, serum calcium, and urine protein creatinine ratio were normal. Chest X-ray was normal. Ankle radiographs showed periosteal reaction along the medial aspects of bilateral distal tibial meta-diaphysis and soft tissue swelling around the ankles. A month later, the patient reported feeling well, with occasional ankle pain during prolonged standing and walking. Repeated TSH and free thyroxine tests were normal, as were triiodothyronine and thyroid-stimulating receptor antibody levels. Inflammatory markers were within normal limits (erythrocyte sedimentation rate [ESR] 10 mm/hour [1-10 mm/hour], C-reactive protein [CRP] 10.3 mg/L [0.2-9.1 mg/L]). Antinuclear antibody, extractable nuclear antigen (ENA) antibodies screening, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody tests were negative.
test_results: MRI of the ankles revealed erosions along the medial cortex of the distal tibial metaphysis and epiphysis with periosteal reaction and marked surrounding soft tissue edema. Bony edema was also noted within the talus, calcaneus, navicular, medial cuneiform, and base of the first metatarsal. Findings were fairly symmetrical. Increased uptake in bilateral distal tibia, calcaneum, and midfoot bones corresponding to prior MRI findings was observed on bone scan in keeping with inflammatory bone disease. No suspicious focus of increased radiotracer uptake is seen in the rest of the skeletal system. The left medial malleolus core biopsies showed compact bone, minimal intertrabecular areas with the presence of inflammatory cells. There were no granulomas, no malignant cells identified. No AFB were seen on the Ziehl-Neelsen stain and bone culture was sterile.
Orpha_name: Chronic nonbacterial osteomyelitis/Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis

case_report: A 29-year-old female was seen at Hangzhou Third People’s Hospital on October 04, 2021. She reported that 16 years ago, light brown patches appeared on her left waist and abdomen without any clear cause. These patches gradually spread to her left buttocks and lower limbs. She experienced no discomfort but felt a significant psychological impact. There was no progression of the patches, such as hardening, and she did not seek medical treatment during this time. She had no significant past medical history and no family history of similar conditions. A comprehensive physical examination revealed no abnormalities. Dermatological examination identified banded brown patches along the Blaschko lines on her left lower back, buttocks, and lower limbs, with some areas of fusion. The skin was smooth, not hard, with indistinct boundaries and mild atrophy upon palpation. Laboratory tests indicated a positive antinuclear antibody (ANA, 1:320, nucleolar type) and elevated immunoglobulin M (3.47 g/L). All other laboratory results were within normal limits.
test_results: The lesion on the left lower extremity was removed for pathological biopsy, which showed that the epidermal mutation disappeared, the pigment particles in the basal layer were obvious, numerous lymphocytes infiltrated the dermis, and the elastic fibers and collagen fibers stained normally.

case_report: A 52-year-old male presented to the emergency department with a 2-week history of positional vertigo, and a 3-day history of tinnitus, ear pressure, and hearing loss in the left ear. He reported no other neurologic symptoms. His medical history included coronary stent insertion for myocardial infarction and living-donor kidney transplantation for end-stage renal disease of unknown cause. His current medications were prednisolone 5 mg daily and mycophenolate mofetil 360 mg twice a day. Neurologic examination showed Weber lateralization to the right side, bilateral nasolabial fold blunting, and truncal ataxia. Other cranial nerves, motor, sensory, and cerebellar function tests, as well as the otoscope examination, were unremarkable.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed bilateral facial nerve enhancement (left > right) and subtle fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensity and T1 hypointensity in the left temporal white matter. CSF PCR revealed a positive result for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and negative results for mycobacteria, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, varicella zoster virus (VZV), and JCV. The result of serum JCV PCR was positive.

case_report: A 53-year-old Caucasian woman with no prior history of hypertension presented to the Primary Care Emergency Department with a one-week history of self-measured high blood pressure (up to 190/100 mmHg), muscle aches, and stiffness. A blood test revealed a serum potassium (K+) level of 1.73 mmol/L. Previous blood tests showed normal K+ levels except for a result of 3.18 mmol/L five months earlier. Treatment with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (enalapril 20 mg/24 h orally) and potassium supplements (50 KCl mEq/24 h orally) was initiated. Despite this, follow-up showed uncontrolled blood pressure and K+ levels of 2.13 mmol/L. Four weeks later, she was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) with uncontrolled hypertension (BP of 200/120 mmHg), severe hypokalemia (1.80 mmol/L), metabolic alkalosis (pH 7.52, HCO3− 43.5 mmol/L), and electrocardiogram changes including QT interval prolongation, a visible U wave, and T wave flattening. In the ICU, she required high doses of both intravenous and oral potassium (up to 176 mEq KCl/24 h). Due to initial difficulties in raising serum K+ levels despite high supplements, access to the bathroom was restricted, and a psychiatric consultation ruled out self-induced vomiting. Her blood pressure was eventually controlled with two oral medications (the calcium channel blocker amlodipine 10 mg/24 h and the peripheral vasodilator hydralazine 25 mg/8 h), and serum K+ levels were maintained at the lower limit of the normal range with oral 72 mEq/24 h of KCl. After stabilization of her hemodynamic and biochemical status, she was transferred to the hospitalization ward for further evaluation. Her family history was unremarkable for hypertension or endocrine diseases. Physical examination revealed high blood pressure but was otherwise normal, with no signs of hypercortisolism, hirsutism, or virilization. Biochemical and hormone data were collected. Plasma metanephrines, 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test, thyroid function, and other biochemical and hematological findings were normal; plasma renin activity (PRA) and aldosterone (ALD) were undetectable.
test_results: Adrenal computed tomography (CT) showed two calcifications in the right adrenal gland and two adrenal nodules suggestive of adenomas in the left adrenal gland, the largest of 12.3 × 10 × 14 mm. Both nodular adrenal lesions presented −2 (the largest) and 5.4 Hounsfield Units and absolute and relative percentages of washout at 15 min of 70% and 79%, suggestive of benign lesions. Further testing evidenced elevated DOC (35.8 ng/dl; reference range 2–15 ng/dl).
Orpha_name: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency

case_report: A 38-year-old female from Guangdong province, China, was admitted to Zhujiang Hospital, Southern Medical University in June 2016. At age 30, she experienced worsening gait balance, leading to frequent falls. She sought treatment at a local hospital, but no diagnosis was made. In December 2010, she was hospitalized at the Second Hospital Affiliated to Guangzhou Medical Hospital, where she was noted to have cerebellar atrophy, Type 2 Diabetes, and hyperlipemia. Despite treatment, her condition continued to deteriorate. By 2015, she exhibited slow cognitive decline. In 2016, she developed poor responsiveness, psychiatric symptoms, bilateral hearing loss, and intermittent convulsions in her upper limbs during sleep, particularly in the right upper limb. She was then referred to our hospital. Her parents were not consanguineous, and no other family members had neurological disorders. Physical examination revealed mild mental retardation, apathy, and limited speech. Cranial nerves were intact except for symmetric bilateral sensory hearing loss. She did not cooperate with the neurological examination, and sensory testing was not possible. Muscle strength was normal in the upper limbs but reduced in the lower limbs. Muscle tone was normal, but there were abnormal involuntary movements in the right upper limb. No pyramidal signs were observed. Cerebellar function tests showed mild abnormalities in finger-to-nose, heel-to-knee, and rapidly alternating hand movements. The Romberg test was negative. Electrocardiogram showed sinus bradycardia (average 44/min). Nerve conduction studies indicated significant slowing of motor conduction velocity in the right peroneal nerve (25.9 m/s), right median nerve (38.4 m/s), left ulnar nerve (45.5 m/s), and right ulnar nerve (35.6 m/s), with prolonged F wave latency. Sensory nerve action potentials were absent in the bilateral peroneal, sural, and left median ulnar nerves. Electroencephalogram showed mild to moderate abnormalities with basic rhythms of 7.2–10 Hz and 20–40 μV slow alpha activities, low amplitude, and irregular waves. Sporadic 14–25 Hz and 20–30 μV beta waves, as well as more frequent 4–7 Hz and 20–40 μV theta waves, were observed. Visual evoked potential showed prolonged bilateral P100 latency (Left = 101.1 mS, right = 107.0 mS) and decreased amplitude (Left = 3.24 μV, right = 1.30 μV). Brainstem auditory evoked potential showed bilateral disappearance of III-I, V-I, and V-III IPL. Brain MRI revealed diffuse cerebral and cerebellar atrophy.
test_results: Exome sequencing revealed a novel heterozygous missense variant, c 1618 T > A (p. Y540N), in exon 20 of the DNMT1.
diagnosis: hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type IE

case_report: A 21-year-old male was admitted to the anorectal department of a tertiary hospital due to acute and severe recurrent bleeding following RBL. The patient had mixed hemorrhoids and underwent RBL on July 2, 2020. Pulsatile bleeding occurred on Day 18 and Day 23 post-operation, both managed by suture hemostasis at a community hospital. This was the third bleeding episode, occurring 26 days post-RBL. Upon admission, vital signs were: body temperature 38.0 ℃, heart rate 90 bpm, blood pressure 147/75 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% with oxygen inhalation. The patient appeared weak, dizzy, and sweaty. Physical examination revealed a soft abdomen with bowel sounds at 7 times/min, without tenderness or rebound pain. Significant anorectal bleeding was noted, and the surgical wound had not healed. Laboratory results showed hemoglobin at 145 g/L and platelet count at 178 × 10^9/L. Coagulation study indicated a PT of 13.8 s and FVIII at 117%. Other tests, including leucocyte count, biochemical examination, infection markers (AIDS, syphilis, hepatitis), abdominal ultrasound, and chest X-ray, were negative. Pain was managed with a patient-controlled analgesia pump, and the patient was taken to the operating room for immediate hemostasis. Bleeding sites at 11 o'clock and 7 o'clock in the lithotomy position were controlled by suturing. Post-operatively, the patient was placed on a full liquid diet for 3 days and received human prothrombin complex concentrates for 3 days. On Day 6 post-operation, the patient developed joint pain and a sore throat, with a body temperature ranging from 38–39 ℃. Blood tests showed a neutrophil percentage of 87.6%.
test_results: Factor VII (FVII) was 40%, FIX 11%, FX 71.4%, FXII 35%, PT 16.7 s, APTT 59.2 s.

case_report: A 19-year-old female with a history of Fahr’s syndrome and epilepsy presented to Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia Medical Centre in June 2018 with a three-day history of abnormal behavior, emotional lability, paranoia, irrelevant speech, and poor sleep pattern. She exhibited gait instability and involuntary movements of her hands, predominantly on the right side. Physical examination revealed short stature, inappropriate affect, occasional smiling and crying, and non-compliance with commands. Her speech was irrelevant and slurred. Neurological examination showed no deficits or signs of meningism. There were choreoathetoid movements in her upper limbs (right more than left), resembling traditional Malay dance movements. Brain CT revealed extensive bilateral calcifications. She declined a lumbar puncture. Autoimmune screening for antinuclear antibody and anti-dsDNA was negative, and serum creatine kinase and lactate levels were normal. Her initial serum calcium was elevated at 2.65 mmol/L, with a normal intact parathyroid hormone (iPTH) level. At age 18, she had one episode of low iPTH at 1.43 pmol/L, but subsequent iPTH and calcium levels were normal. Her phosphate level was normal at 1.15 mmol/L. Her perinatal history included a seizure on the 25th day of life and a febrile seizure at 4 months. Her parents were nonconsanguineous. She had learning difficulties and was slower in reading and writing compared to peers but attended normal school until age 12. She has an older asymptomatic sister and a younger sister who is also a slow learner. At age 15, she experienced a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, followed by focal aware seizures. Antiepileptic treatment was initiated but she was noncompliant. At age 17, a neuropsychological assessment using the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children Fourth Edition (WISC-IV) showed an IQ of 46. At age 18, she presented to another center with acute psychosis, behavioral changes, urinary and bowel incontinence, and a stiff, backward walking gait. She was treated for meningoencephalitis but did not complete the treatment. She gradually returned to normal over 5-6 months and remained well until the current presentation. Serial brain imaging showed progressive, extensive bilateral intraparenchymal calcifications, mainly in the frontal and periventricular regions and the dentate nucleus. The calcifications in the deep white matter and periventricular regions were associated with confluent asymmetrical white matter hyperintensities without significant mass effect, indicating leukoencephalopathies.
test_results: Whole-genome sequencing detected two recessively inherited compound heterozygous variants, NR_033294.1 n.*9C>T and n.24C>T, in the nonprotein coding gene SNORD118.

case_report: A 5-year-old boy with consanguineous Saudi parents was referred from the neurosurgery department to the pediatric neurology clinic. At the age of 3 years, he experienced a fall from a height of 1.5 meters, resulting in repeated vomiting but no loss of consciousness, headache, or seizures. A brain CT scan revealed a linear fracture on the right frontal bone and incidental basal ganglia changes. Neurological examination showed speech and motor delays. His mother had an uneventful, full-term pregnancy, and he was delivered by cesarean section due to malposition without complications. He stayed in the well-baby nursery for 2 weeks due to jaundice. Developmental milestones included rolling over at 5 months, sitting at 8 months, and walking at 20 months. By age 3, he could say “mama,” “baba,” and 3–4 other words but could not form sentences. At age 4, he began losing previously acquired skills, including the ability to sit, and a few months later, he lost the ability to roll over or control his neck. He also lost speech and started experiencing frequent choking. His mother had a history of 2 first trimester abortions for unknown reasons. The patient had a 14-year-old sister who passed away several months prior, who had generalized developmental delay, spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy, and epilepsy. On physical examination, the patient had stable vital signs and no dysmorphic features. He exhibited good power but had hypotonia, hyperlaxity, and hyperreflexia in all four limbs.
test_results: Whole-exome sequencing test showed homozygous mutation c.91A>T p. (Arg31*) in exon 2 (of 17) of the SERAC1 gene on chromosome 16.

case_report: Patient (1) is a 3-year-old female, the second child born to first cousins. She was referred to the genetic clinic at the age of one year. At presentation, she had jaundice lasting one week. Her length was 71.5 cm (less than -4 SD), weight was 7 kg (less than -4 SD), and skull circumference was 39 cm (microcephalic). She exhibited global developmental delay, enophthalmia, characteristic physical appearance, and cutaneous photosensitivity. Abdominal examination showed an enlarged liver (8 cm below the costal margin), firm in consistency, with a rounded border and smooth surface. She had moderate ascites with bilateral shifting dullness and bilateral lower limb edema. Laboratory results were as follows: ALT was 94 IU/L (normal: 37), AST was 143 IU/L (normal: 40), total bilirubin was 5.9 mg/dl, direct bilirubin was 5 mg/dl, and albumin was 1.5 g/dl. Prothrombin time (PT) was prolonged with an INR of 1.7. Tests for Hepatitis A virus IgM, HBsAg, HBcAb IgM, hepatitis C virus antibodies, CMV, EBV, and rubella (IgG and IgM) were negative. Plasma amino acids showed a mild elevation of methionine at 1.3 mg/dl (normal < 0.8) and an elevated methionine/phenylalanine ratio of 1.41 (normal < 1.0). The acylcarnitine profile was normal. Total galactose (galactose and galactose 1-phosphate combined) was 1.7 mg/dl (normal < 15). Galactose 1-phosphate uridyl transferase was 71.2 uM (normal > 60).
test_results: DNA testing for galactosemia mutation revealed no copies of the Q188r, S135L, K285N, or L195P (classical galactosemia) or N314D (Duarte galactosemia). CT brain revealed central and cortical involutional brain changes. MRI brain revealed mild prominence of the brain sulci, fissures and basal cisterns with mildly dilated ventricular system more appreciated at the cerebellar hemispheres with mildly prominent cerebellar fissures. This is in addition to evidence of dysmyelinating process in the form of periventricular hyperintensity.

case_report: A 35-year-old Japanese female observed a small breast tumor and underwent a needle biopsy. Three months later, she noticed an egg-sized, slightly itchy erythema on her left breast, near the biopsy scar. Subsequently, two walnut-sized erythemas appeared. A topical steroid was applied but showed no effect. Over the next few months, the erythema's inflammatory reaction gradually decreased, leaving behind sclerotic plaques with slight pigmentation. A similar sclerotic plaque also developed on her right upper arm. She was referred to our hospital due to these sclerotic plaques. Physical examination revealed an oval sclerotic plaque and two small round sclerotic plaques on her left inner breast. An oval sclerotic plaque was also noted on her upper right arm. No physical findings indicative of systemic conditions such as Raynaud's phenomenon, sclerodactyly, or internal organ dysfunction were observed.
test_results: A histopathological examination of the biopsy specimen from the sclerotic lesion on the upper arm showed a thickened reticular dermis consisting of closely packed, homogenous collagen bundles. A significant number of mononuclear cells had infiltrated the lower dermis. Alpha-smooth muscle actin-positive cells had increased significantly in the lower dermis.

case_report: A 51-year-old man with a 20-year history of consuming 1.5 liters of beer daily, often accompanied by 360 mL of shochu, and a 4-year history of reduced appetite, developed slurred speech over a 3-week period. He experienced choking while drinking and difficulty swallowing food, eventually becoming unable to eat or drink, leading to his admission. His medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and previous burr-hole drainage for bilateral chronic subdural hematomas at age 44, after which he was independent in daily activities. On admission, his blood pressure was 112/79 mmHg, height was 183 cm, and weight was 48 kg. Neurological examination showed he was alert with a mini-mental status examination (MMSE) score of 22 points. He had horizontal gaze paretic nystagmus bilaterally, a flat facial expression, and bilateral weakness of the orbicularis oris. There was no weakness in the frontalis muscle or orbicularis oculi. His speech was slurred, and he had difficulty swallowing, with poor gag reflex and palate elevation. The jaw jerk reflex was brisk, and the snout reflex was positive. There was no emotional lability, tongue atrophy, or fasciculation. The tongue could protrude midline and move adequately side to side. Motor weakness was noted with scores of 4 in the distal upper limbs and 3 in the proximal lower limbs bilaterally on the Modified Medical Research Council’s manual muscle test (MMT). Bilateral finger-to-nose incoordination was present. He could not walk due to a wide-based gait with truncal instability. Deep tendon reflexes in the upper limbs were increased, and Babinski reflexes were positive bilaterally. Hoffmann reflexes and the forced grasp reflex were negative. Superficial vibratory and position senses were normal. A nerve conduction study showed no prolonged distal latencies, conduction blocks, or absent F-waves. Needle electromyography revealed normal unit potentials and no denervation potentials in the tongue, sternocleidomastoid, biceps, or quadriceps femoris.
test_results: Brain MRI demonstrated hyperintense lesions in the precentral gyrus bilaterally and in the splenium of the corpus callosum on FLAIR. Those lesions were also hyperintense on DWI, and the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map did not show significant signal changes.

case_report: A 25-year-old Ivorian male, unemployed, was seen in the Neurology Department on 9 January, 2012, for excessive sleepiness, behavioral changes, and persistent headaches. His medical history showed no prenatal issues or developmental disorders. There was no history of substance abuse or psychiatric conditions. The excessive sleepiness began on the evening of 27 June, 2008, following the national baccalaureate examination, after consuming a 66cl bottle of beer and experiencing flu-like symptoms. The sleepiness lasted approximately 18 hours and was accompanied by behavioral changes, including aggression, eccentric behavior, visual hallucinations related to death, intrusive thoughts of death, memory loss, and chronic headaches. These episodes persisted for about three weeks, after which the patient returned to his normal state. During these periods, the patient exhibited unusual overeating. Neurological examination results were normal.
test_results: The Cranioencephalic computed tomography (CT) was normal.

case_report: The patient is a 14-year-old Asian female, the first child of non-consanguineous parents, with one healthy sibling. Family history is unremarkable. She was delivered via forceps-assisted vaginal delivery at 40 weeks of gestation after 20 hours of labor, with a birth weight of 4250 grams. Post-birth, she experienced difficulty suckling for several days. Developmental delays were noted from the first few months of life. She began walking independently at 17 months and started speaking at 20 months. At the ages of four and a half and five, she experienced two episodes of hyperpyretic convulsions. At 7 years old, she began experiencing episodes characterized by absence, unconsciousness, rightward deviation of the head and eyes, backward head tilt, falls, limb convulsions, cyanosis of the lips, throat noises, lasting 2 to 4 minutes, and accompanied by headache, vomiting, and impaired consciousness. These episodes occurred 3 to 4 times per year.
test_results: Electroencephalogram (EEG) was obtained at 8 years old, which showed frequent epileptic discharge in right medial temporal lobe at awake, significantly paroxysmal epileptic discharge in bilateral lobe during sleep, and sporadic epileptic discharge in central and superior lobe during sleep. A second EEG was performed at her age of 12 and revealed epileptic discharge in occipital lobe. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) manifested signal enhancement in bilateral hippocampus on FLAIR sequence. A third EEG was performed to the child that illustrated slow waves in bilateral temporal regions, significant in left, with generalized spike-and-slow waves, multiple-spike-and-slow waves and slow waves in bilateral occipitotemporal, significant in left.

case_report: An 8-year-old girl was brought to the hospital for evaluation of short stature. She is the first child in her family, with healthy parents and two younger siblings. She was born at 41 weeks of gestation, weighing 3350 g, with a length of 51 cm and a head circumference of 32 cm. Clinical examination revealed short stature (109 cm, below 3 SD) and various dysmorphic features, including a bulbous nose tip, ocular hypertelorism, deep-set almond-shaped eyes, epicanthal folds, low-set ears, a high-arched palate, brachydactyly, clinodactyly, and scoliosis. Additional findings included delayed motor development, delayed speech, mild intellectual disability, and learning difficulties at school. A brain MRI showed hypotrophy of the corpus callosum. Ultrasound investigations revealed no signs of cardiac disease or other organ malformations. Bone age assessment via hand X-ray indicated a delay, corresponding to 6 years. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, sedimentation rate, electrolytes, thyroid function tests, insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), and insulin-like growth factor–binding protein 3 (IGFBP-3), were all within normal ranges. Karyotyping (350 bands) revealed an atypically elongated short arm of chromosome 15–46, XX, add(15)(p?).
test_results: Chromosomal microarray revealed pathogenic 38,584 kb-large 1 copy gain within chromosomal region 9p24.3p13.1. It allowed us to conclude that the extra region on chromosome 15 belonged to the short arm of chromosome 9.

case_report: A 12-year-old male from an Indian family of Dravidian origin exhibited progressive hair thinning over the past 2 years. He was born at term from a consanguineous marriage with sparse hair on the scalp, eyebrows, and eyelashes. Over time, his hair regrew as coarse and curly, but he experienced increased hair loss in the last 2 years. His natal and perinatal history were unremarkable, and his developmental milestones were achieved normally. There were no issues with sweating, and both personal and family medical histories were noncontributory. No systemic involvement was noted. On general physical examination, his vital signs were normal. The anterior hairline was receded and high. The scalp hair was coarse, dry, and wiry, standing out from the head. There was sparse hair with partial alopecia on the vertex, parietal, and occipital regions, resembling androgenetic alopecia. Eyebrows, eyelashes, and body hair were sparse. Examination of the palms, soles, and oral mucosa showed no abnormalities. Nails and teeth were normal, and systemic examination revealed no abnormalities.
test_results: Light microscopy of the hair shaft revealed darkly pigmented irregular twisting with variable diameters.

case_report: An eighteen-year-old male, born at term via vaginal delivery with normal perinatal history and typical motor and mental development, was admitted to the emergency department with progressively worsening crampy leg pain over one month, increased frequency of urination, and increased thirst for the past three weeks. He experienced an inability to move his limbs for the last three days. There was no history of rash, headache, fever, vomiting, diarrhea, weight loss, or bladder/bowel incontinence. He had not taken any drugs or herbal medicines. On examination, the patient was conscious, cooperative, and well-oriented to time, place, and person. Vital signs included a pulse of 92 per minute, blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg, and a respiratory rate of 16 per minute. Physical examination revealed bony deformities, including widening of both wrists and bilateral knock-knees. Chest, cardiovascular, and abdominal examinations were normal. Neurological examination showed normal higher mental functions and no cranial nerve deficits. Motor examination revealed hypotonia with muscle strength graded at 3/5 in both arms and 2/5 in both lower limbs. Deep tendon reflexes were depressed, and bilateral plantar responses were flexor. Laboratory investigations showed a random blood glucose level of 112 mg/dl, serum sodium of 144 mmol/liter, serum potassium of 1.3 mmol/liter, pH of 7.30, serum bicarbonate of 20.3 mmol/liter, serum chloride of 112 mmol/liter, partial pressure of oxygen at 83 mmHg, oxygen saturation of 93%, and partial pressure of carbon dioxide at 34 mmHg. Hemogram, kidney function, and liver function tests were conducted. Muscle enzyme levels were elevated, with Creatine phosphokinase (CPK) at 1823 U/liter (0-195) and Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) at 886 U/liter (100-235). Due to severe hypokalemia, the patient was immediately started on intravenous potassium chloride infusion at a rate of 30 meq/hour, along with oral potassium at a dose of 20 meq every 6 hours. Muscle weakness improved predictably after the initiation of potassium therapy, and the patient became ambulatory within 24 hours of treatment.
test_results: Abdominal ultrasonography (USG) revealed bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis. Digital abdominal X-ray revealed fine calcified foci in bilateral renal area. Skeletal survey revealed widening of both wrists and bilateral knock knees.

case_report: A 35-year-old male patient presented with itchy and enlarging plaques on the left leg and right thigh for six years. He previously received six sessions of chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide, vincristine, and prednisone) without improvement. Physical examination showed hardened erythematous-violet plaques on the left leg and right thigh, tissue laxity, and bilateral supraclavicular and left inguinal hyperchromia, along with left inguinal fibroelastic adenopathy. Laboratory tests including complete blood count, biochemistry, chest X-ray, fine-needle aspiration of the inguinal lymph node, and bone marrow biopsy showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Skin biopsies showed a dense infiltrate of small and atypical lymphocytes, present from the epidermis to the subcutaneous layer. Multinucleated giant cells permeated and phagocytosed atypical lymphocytes, a process known as the phenomenon of emperipolesis. Verhoeff's stain showed no elastic fibers inside the neoplastic infiltrate and elastophagocytosis. Immunohistochemical study demonstrated expression of neoplastic T lymphocytes (CD3+, CD4+, CD45RO+, CD8-, CD 20-, and CD30-) and CD68+ and CD1a+ multinucleated giant cells.

case_report: A 28-year-old male presented to the endocrinology outpatient clinic with complaints of impaired balance, hearing loss, and numbness in the hands. His medical history included type 1 diabetes mellitus, hypopituitarism, and short-term myoclonic jerks following head trauma. Medications included insulin aspart, insulin glargine, and carbamazepine. Family history revealed a consanguineous marriage between the parents, with no known history of similar conditions. Vital signs on admission were blood pressure 100/70 mmHg, heart rate 84 beats/min, and body temperature 36.6°C. The patient was not mentally retarded. Neurological examination showed the patient was awake, oriented, and cooperative; cranial nerves, motor strength, sensory testing, and proprioception were intact, with the exception of an ataxic gait. Physical examination revealed decreased hair in the face, axillary, and inguinal regions, small bilateral testes, and gynecomastia. Other examinations were normal. Laboratory results were as follows: leukocyte count 8.6 x 10^3/ml, hemoglobin 10.8 g/dl, MCV 99.7 fL, platelet count 119 x 10^3/ml, glucose 386 mg/dL, urea 80 mg/dL, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, sodium 161 mmol/L, potassium 4.48 mmol/L, calcium 5.68 mg/dL, phosphorus 5.7 mg/dL, albumin 4.02 g/dL, HbA1c 7.6%, TSH 1.42 mU/L, free T4 0.546 ng/dL, free T3 1.53 ng/L, iPTH 19.90 ng/dL, FSH 1.3 U/L, LH 7.67 IU/L, total testosterone 8.88 ng/dL, cortisol 10.15 mcg/dL, prolactin 8.19 mcg/L, B12 273.2 ng/L, folic acid 1.9 mcg/dL. Urine analysis showed pH 5.5, density 1014, microalbumin 0.34 mg/dL, microprotein 36.3 mg/dL, creatinine 227.61 mg/dL, serum osmolarity 394 mOsm/KgH2O, and urine osmolarity 590 mOsm/KgH2O. Abdominal ultrasonography indicated preserved size of the left kidney, right kidney long axis of 8.5 cm, minimal reduction in cortex thickness, and grade 1 increase in right kidney parenchyma echogenicity. Based on these findings, the patient was noted to have type 1 diabetes mellitus, hypopituitarism, chronic kidney disease, primary hypoparathyroidism, and megaloblastic anemia due to folic acid deficiency.
test_results: The audiogram showed a moderate mix type sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear and mild sensorineural hearing loss at increased frequencies in the right ear. Bilateral symmetrical calcifications were detected in the basal ganglia, vermis, and cerebellum in brain CT.

case_report: A 41-year-old Hispanic male arrived at the emergency department with a two-week history of worsening headaches, nausea, and vomiting. His neurological examination showed no focal deficits. An initial CT scan revealed dilatation of the right lateral ventricle. A ventriculostomy was performed to manage hydrocephalus. MRI of the brain did not show lesions on T2 and T2 FLAIR weighted sequences, but a suspected cyst was seen on the T1 with contrast sequence. CT-ventriculography was conducted, which identified the location of a single cyst and an obstruction at the foramen of Monro, as no contrast reached the third ventricle. Subsequently, the patient underwent endoscopic surgery via the ventriculostomy tract, and the ventricular lesion was removed.
test_results: Diagnosis was made on CSF sampling.

case_report: A 77-year-old male patient was admitted to Putuo District People’s Hospital in Shanghai after experiencing a fever for four days. On April 3rd, 2013, the patient had chills and fever with a maximum temperature of 39.4°C. He did not report symptoms such as cough, expectoration, sore throat, runny nose, chest tightness, chest pain, shortness of breath, or muscle and joint aches. A chest radiograph showed a fuzzy shadow in the left lower lung. The patient received intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g/day) and levofloxacin (0.5 g/day) for three days, which improved the fever. He was then admitted to Jingnan District Centre Hospital with a body temperature of 37.8°C. Blood tests revealed a leukocyte count of 5×10^9/l (neutrophils, 83.6%) and a C-reactive protein level of 192 mg/l. A chest CT scan showed a 'frosted glass' appearance in both lungs and a high-density shadow in the left lower lobe. A bronchiologram indicated inflammation and left lung consolidation. The patient had a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation for over 30 years, managed with amiodarone (0.2 g/day, orally), and hypertension for over 20 years, controlled with amlodipine (5 mg/day). He denied having diabetes, coronary heart disease, chronic bronchitis, asthma, chronic kidney disease, viral hepatitis, tuberculosis, typhoid fever, or other infectious diseases. Physical examination revealed a body temperature of 39.1°C, a pulse of 98 bpm, a respiratory rate of 22, and a blood pressure of 130/70 mmHg. The patient was alert, had regular respiration, and was cooperative during the examination. His skin and mucosa showed no rash or hemorrhagic spots, and his lip mucosa had no cyanosis. Mild pharyngeal congestion was noted, and the tonsils were not enlarged. Breath sounds were coarse bilaterally, with scattered rales in the left lung but no wheezing or pleural friction sounds. The heart rate was 98 bpm with a regular rhythm and no significant murmurs. The abdomen was soft without muscle tension, tenderness, or rebound tenderness, and no organomegaly or masses were detected. There was no edema in the lower extremities, and muscle strength and tension in all four limbs were normal. Blood gas analysis showed a pH of 7.49, PaCO2 of 38.6 mmHg, PaO2 of 52.6 mmHg, and SaO2 of 87% (without oxygen). An ECG indicated sinus rhythm, atrial premature beats, poor R wave progression in the anterior wall, and T wave changes. The patient received oxygen therapy, methylprednisolone, biapenem (0.6 g twice daily, i.v), and azithromycin (0.5 g/day, i.v) for treatment. Despite this, the patient continued to have a fever with a body temperature reaching 39.1°C and experienced distress on the second day after admission. It was noted that the patient had contact with chickens two weeks prior.
test_results: RNA was extracted from the throat-swab samples using the QIAamp Viral RNA Mini kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Specific RT-qPCR assays were performed to assess the presence of seasonal influenza viruses (H1, H3, or B), H5N1, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus and novel coronavirus. RT-qPCR assays with self-designed specific primer and probe sets were subsequently performed for the detection of H1 to H16 and N1 to N9 subtypes, in order to verify the viral subtypes.
diagnosis: Human infection with H7N9 avian influenza

case_report: The patient is a 4 years and 8-month-old Syrian Arabic girl, the sixth of seven siblings, born to healthy consanguineous parents, with a birth weight of 4 kg. She had normal psychomotor development and no significant illnesses until the age of 4 years and 2 months. At that time, her parents observed rapid weight gain (approximately 1 kg every 10 to 15 days) due to increased food intake (six to seven large meals per day). Additionally, changes in body secretions were noted, including reduced tear production when crying, decreased nasal discharge, unpleasant body odor, and reduced sweating. Other symptoms included blue cold extremities, alternating diarrhea and constipation, frequent urination, and excessive thirst. Two months after the onset of weight gain, she began experiencing nighttime urinary incontinence. Behavioral changes followed, such as mood swings, anxiety episodes, rage attacks, nervousness, aggressive behavior, recurrent fatigue, social withdrawal, prolonged sleep periods (12 hours continuously), and difficulty staying awake during the day. These issues prompted her admission to Damascus Children Hospital's endocrinal department at the age of 4.5 years for further evaluation. The family history over three generations was negative for similar symptoms, obesity, or psychiatric disorders. An older sister had died at 12 years old from acute myeloid leukemia (AML), but without any of the symptoms observed in the patient. Physical examination revealed general obesity without striae or altered skin pigmentation, no dysmorphic features, and no congenital malformations. Her weight was 25 kg (above the 97th percentile), length 110 cm (at the 90th percentile), and head circumference 52 cm. Her body mass index (BMI) was 20.1. Ophthalmic examination showed left exotropia with normal fundus and normal pupillary response. Laboratory analyses, including complete blood count (CBC), blood glucose, sodium (Na), chlorine (Cl), potassium (K), calcium (Ca), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), triglycerides (TG), cholesterol, urine density, creatinine, and urea, were all within normal limits. Hormonal levels, including thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), free thyroxine (T4), morning cortisol, adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), prolactin, growth hormone (GH), insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF1), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), and luteinizing hormone (LH), were also normal. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasound results were normal. Bone age assessment indicated a slight advancement, corresponding to 5 to 5.5 years old.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was normal; it showed no cortical atrophy. A homogenous mild enlargement of her pituitary gland was observed on both T1-weighted and T2-weighted images with normal hyperintense posterior lobe on T1-weighted images. A chest computed tomography (CT) scan demonstrated a 6 cm round mass filling most of her right lung and pushing her heart and mediastinum to the left with infiltration and consolidation of the right lower lobe of her right lung.
diagnosis: Rapid-onset Obesity with Hypothalamic dysfunction, Hypoventilation, and Autonomic Dysregulation  syndrome
Orpha_name: Rapid-onset childhood obesity-hypothalamic dysfunction-hypoventilation-autonomic dysregulation syndrome

case_report: A 26-year-old female patient came to the emergency department with complaints of malaise, headache, and right-sided cervical lymphadenopathy lasting for about eight weeks. Previous laboratory tests provided by the patient showed negative serology results for Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV), Cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV). Symptomatic treatment with mefenamic acid provided only mild relief. The patient mentioned an uncomplicated bite from her parrot four months before the onset of symptoms, with no signs of infection. Her medical history was unremarkable except for breast augmentation surgery. There was no significant family medical history, and she had not traveled outside Switzerland recently. The patient was not on any regular medication and reported no illicit drug use. On examination, she appeared in good general health with subfebrile temperatures and normal cardiopulmonary vital signs. Physical examination revealed right-sided cervical lymphadenopathy extending from the mandibular angle to the clavicle, and an enlarged lymph node was palpated on the left side ventral to the M. sternocleidomastoideus. The lymphadenopathy was tender to touch. The rest of the physical examination was normal. Laboratory tests showed a slightly elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) level at 9 mg/L and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 28 mm/h. Other laboratory results, including differential blood count, serum electrolytes, renal function tests, liver enzymes, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), were within normal limits. Serum protein electrophoresis indicated an inflammatory reaction. Additional laboratory tests, including serology, were conducted. Pharyngeal swabs were negative. Abdominal sonography revealed a slight enlargement of the spleen (12 cm). MRI indicated significant enlargement of the cervical lymph nodes. Further tests showed an elevated ANA titer at 1:320, while Anti-ds-DNA was negative.
test_results: The core needle biopsy revealed signs of a necrotizing lymphadenitis rich in histiocytes. Additional immunophenotypical and molecular analysis underpinned the reactive nature of this lesion.

case_report: The patient is an 18-year-old male, born to healthy, non-consanguineous parents with no family history of intellectual disability or skeletal issues. He was delivered via cesarean section at 40 weeks, following a pregnancy marked by poor maternal weight gain and atypical fetal movements at 8 months. At birth, his weight was 2.38 kg (3%), length 47 cm (13%), and occipitofrontal circumference (OFC) 34.5 cm (26%). Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at one and five minutes, respectively. He exhibited saggy skin but no other dysmorphic features. Postnatally, he experienced intraventricular hemorrhage and thrombocytopenia (7×10^3 cells/μl), which resolved after three platelet transfusions. Subsequently, he developed seizures, apnea with cyanosis, temperature instability, and hypoglycemia. Recurrent episodes of hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia resolved with age and the placement of a gastric tube for more frequent feedings. He had tracheomalacia, upper airway obstruction, increased respiratory secretions, frequent aspirations, and pulmonary infections from infancy. By age 7, he had a chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa respiratory infection. At 6 years, he developed proximal renal tubular acidosis (RTA), nephrocalcinosis, and nephrolithiasis, with renal stones composed of carbonate apatite and calcium oxalate. His RTA has been managed with fluid and electrolyte replacement, spironolactone, and hydrochlorothiazide. Initially controlled with phenobarbital, his seizures progressed to infantile spasms by 15 months, with adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) treatment providing transient relief. His current anticonvulsant regimen includes rufinamide, felbamate, clonazepam, and topiramate. Developmental milestones were delayed, with regression noted. He smiled and laughed by 4 months, reached for toys by 6 months, vocalized by 7 months, and could hold his head up and roll onto his side by 8 months. He achieved a pincer grasp at 18 months but lost it by 23 months. He never walked and lost many motor skills and all vocalization by 26 months. A cranial MRI at 14 years showed cystic encephalomalacia and a low parenchymal T2 signal in the right temporal and right occipital lobes. At 15 years, he was awake but not interactive, unable to sit independently or hold up his head, and withdrew from noxious stimuli. His height, weight, and OFC were 129 cm (<3%ile), 30.8 kg (<3%ile), and 50.3 cm (<3%ile), respectively. Facial features included a long, oval, asymmetric face, midface hypoplasia, down-slanting palpebral fissures, large cupped ears, smooth philtrum, high-arched palate, and prognathia. Dental enamel was hypoplastic, and secondary teeth 2, 6, 10, and 11 were absent. He had excessive drooling, sluggish pupillary reflexes, and left-sided hearing loss. He experienced frequent seizures, severe hypotonia, decreased muscle bulk, hypoactive deep tendon reflexes, kyphoscoliosis, and flexion contractures of most large and small joints. He had one prepubertal (1-2 mL) testis that was undescended but palpable in the inguinal canal and one undescended testis, Tanner stage III pubic hair, and a prepubertal phallus. His skin showed excretions of carbonate apatite, indicating calcium/phosphate dysregulation. Ophthalmologic examination revealed retinitis pigmentosa and cortical blindness. Previous skeletal issues included congenital bilateral hip dislocation and fractures of the distal fibula (2 years), right humerus (5 years), and spine (6 years). Kyphoscoliosis developed between 6 and 12 years of age.
test_results: A dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scan performed at age 15 years demonstrated a bone density of 0.341 gm/cm2 BMD (height adjusted Z-Score: -2.9) for the anteroposterior Spine (L1-L4) and 0.342 gm/cm2 bone mineral density (height adjusted Z-Score: -6.5) for the right forearm. Skeletal radiographs at 18 years revealed a 60° convex right scoliosis, gracile bones with reduced mineral density, and evidence of previous fractures.

case_report: A 17-year-old female presented for assessment of absence of menstruation and delayed onset of puberty. She had no significant medical or family history. Her physical measurements were as follows: weight 56 kg, height 168 cm, and body mass index 19.8 kg/m2. On physical examination, the patient exhibited underdeveloped breasts (Tanner stage 2) and absence of pubic hair (Tanner stage 1). The external genital examination showed normal female genitalia with an intact hymen and a vaginal depth of 5 cm.
test_results: Transabdominal ultrasonography and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a small uterus, measuring about 15 mm in length; however, neither ovaries nor testes were visible. Laboratory evaluation showed markedly elevated levels of follicle-stimulating hormone (65.08 mIU/mL) and very low estradiol levels (less than 5 pg/mL). The serum level of luteinizing hormone was 21.31 mIU/mL and that of testosterone was 3 ng/dL, which was within the normal range for women of that age. A karyotype was obtained and showed a normal male karyotype 46, XY.

case_report: A 55-year-old male presented to the neuro-ophthalmology clinic in April 2015 with a 4-month history of progressive, painless vision loss in both eyes. He denied experiencing headaches, weight loss, night sweats, or other neurological symptoms. Initial examination by an ophthalmologist 4 months prior revealed mild optic edema in the right eye. He was treated with oral prednisone (50 mg once daily) and a triamcinolone injection around the right eye (40 mg, once), which initially improved his vision. However, his vision subsequently worsened, leading to blindness in the left eye approximately 1.5 months before his current admission. Vision in the right eye also deteriorated 2 days prior to admission. At presentation, his visual acuity (VA) was 0.02 in the right eye and no light perception (NLP) in the left eye. A relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) was noted in the left eye. Fundus examination showed pallor in the bilateral temporal part of the optic disc. Visual field examination was not performed due to poor VA. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count (CBC), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and lymphocyte subpopulation, were normal, and HIV titer was negative. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed a normal white blood cell (WBC) count (3 × 10^6/L; normal range: <10 × 10^6/L) with several leukomonocytes, elevated protein levels (721 mg/L; normal range: 150–400 mg/L), and immune abnormalities. CSF immunoglobulin A (IgA) was 0.684 mg/dl (normal range: 0–0.5 mg/dl), IgG was 4.35 mg/dl (normal range: 0–3.4 mg/dl), and IgM was 0.21 mg/dl (normal range: 0–0.13 mg/dl). Orbit MRI showed thickening of the optic chiasma in T1- and T2-weighted imaging with significant homogenous enhancement using gadolinium. Brain MRI did not reveal any other lesions. The patient received intravenous steroids (1 g of methylprednisolone once daily for 3 days, followed by a taper). His right eye's VA improved from 0.02 to 0.5 after 1.5 months, but the left eye remained NLP. The visual field of the right eye showed a dense temporal hemianopic defect in remission. Four months later, the patient returned to the clinic with complaints of fatigue, somnolence, back and limb aches, slow speech, and unstable walking. His right VA had decreased to 0.25, while the left VA remained NLP. Blood tests were unremarkable. CSF analysis showed a significant increase in WBC count (35 × 10^6/L) and protein levels (2168.4 mg/L), along with elevated immunoglobulin levels (IgA 1.95 mg/dl, IgG 9.08 mg/dl, IgM 2.06 mg/dl). Orbit MRI indicated that the previously bulky optic nerve had become thinner and less intense. Brain MRI revealed multiple lesions in the periventricular area, lenticular nucleus, and thalamus, which were enhanced with gadolinium in T1- and T2-weighted imaging.
test_results: Histopathology of the specimen showed diffuse proliferation of large atypical lymphoid cells. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for CD20 in most lymphocytes and CD3 in scattered lymphocytes.
diagnosis: Primary central nervous system diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with optic nerve and chiasm infiltration

case_report: A 12-year-old male presented with corneal arcus and multiple skin lesions, with a 10-year history of xanthomas. Both parents had elevated levels of total serum cholesterol and LDL cholesterol. His elder brother passed away at the age of 7 years due to myocardial infarction. Physical examination revealed subcutaneous yellow nodules at the knuckles of his fingers, elbows, knees, and Achilles tendons, measuring up to 10 cm and partially coalescing. Additional yellow nodules of varying sizes were observed under the skin on the buttocks. The patient had no vision problems, and intraocular pressures were normal. Ocular examination showed a partial circumferential white-grey deposit consistent with corneal arcus, while the fundus examination was normal.
test_results: B-scan revealed extensive plaques and enhanced intima-media thickness of common carotid arterial wall. Laboratory studies disclosed the following values: Total serum cholesterol, 752.1 mg/dL (normal range, 110-220 mg/dL); triglyceride, 96.6 mg/dL (normal range, 50-150 mg/dL); LDL cholesterol, 661.3 mg/dL (normal range, 80-140 mg/dL). Findings were consistent with type IIa hyperlipoproteinemia. There are cytosine (C)>thymine (T) heterozygous double peaks at 97 in the second exon of LDL-R gene, which is in GenBank as a known mutation of NM_001195798.1:c. 97C>T. This mutation resulted in the change from C to T 33rd codon in E2 of LDL-R gene and, thus, glutamine became the stop codon in the corresponding amino acid (NP_001182732.1:p.Gln33X).

case_report: A 58-year-old Caucasian female was admitted to the surgical department of our hospital for acute abdominal pain accompanied by vomiting. She had undergone a cholecystectomy 12 years prior. Physical examination showed tenderness upon palpation in the right epigastrium. Ultrasonography of the abdomen identified the presence of gallstones in the common bile duct. An endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography was performed to remove three gallstones.
test_results: Color Doppler ultrasonography revealed that the diameter of the LRV had expanded to 9 mm. Computer tomography angiography revealed that the LRV was compressed when passing between the SMA and the right renal artery. The LRV lumen decreased to 1.7 × 7.8 mm at the narrowings but measured 7.5 × 17 mm directly before. The shape of the LRV at the levels of the left ovarian vein outlet and renal hilum was almost cylindrical, with average measurements of 12 × 11 mm and 13 × 11 mm, respectively. Comparatively, the lumen of the contralateral right renal vein at the level of the renal hilum and at its opening to the IVC, measured 7.5 × 7 and 7 × 7.1 mm, respectively. The course of the left ovarian vein was winding. Its lumen before opening to the LRV was 9.7 × 12 mm. Comparatively, the course of the contralateral right ovarian vein was almost straight. Its lumen before opening to right renal vein was 5.9 × 5.2 mm.

case_report: A 24-month-old male, second child of non-consanguineous parents, was born at 38 weeks gestation with Apgar scores of 9 and 10 at the first and fifth minutes, respectively. Birth weight and length were normal, and head circumference was above 2SD. The neonatal period was uneventful. The mother’s thyroid hormone levels during pregnancy showed low free T4 (8.75 pmol/L; normal 9.39 - 28.31) and normal TSH (3.17 mUI/L; normal 0.25 - 5.0). Family history includes a maternal relative with cerebral palsy and paternal relatives with sensorineural hearing loss starting around age forty. At 3 months, the patient exhibited global hypotonia and poor head control, leading to the initiation of a rehabilitation program without satisfactory improvement. By 12 months, severe hypotonia persisted, and the child had difficulty grasping objects and bringing hands to the midline. The child was active, reactive to stimuli, had good visual contact, a normal social smile, and appropriate interaction with parents. Cerebral MRI at this age showed enlargement of the subarachnoid spaces without white matter disorder. Brainstem auditory evoked potential was normal, while visual evoked potentials indicated a conduction delay in central optical pathways; fundoscopy was normal. Basic laboratory and metabolic investigations were unremarkable. At 21 months, the patient was referred to a Neuromuscular Pediatric Unit due to severe motor and cognitive delay. Examination revealed global severe hypotonia, inability to hold the head upright or sit without support, brief episodes of mild dystonic movements, hypertonic posturing of the limbs triggered by stress or stimuli, slightly increased myotatic reflex in triceps surae muscle, Babinski sign, and absent deep tendon reflexes at the Achilles tendon bilaterally. Eye contact and visual tracking were poor, and the patient was responsive to sounds but unable to speak. At 23 months, the patient developed myoclonic jerks involving neck and upper limb flexion, occurring up to three times daily. Initial treatment with sodium valproate improved these seizures, but they reappeared despite additional treatment with levetiracetam and vigabatrin. Electroencephalograms showed polyspike and wave discharges across both hemispheres with a slow background rhythm. Electromyography and neurography were normal, as was the electroretinogram. A repeat cerebral MRI at 24 months showed delayed myelination. Laboratory tests revealed elevated free T3 (4.84 nmol/L; normal 0.63-3.90), low free T4 (8.2 pmol/L; normal 9.1 - 25.0), and normal TSH (3.54 mUI/L; normal 0.3 - 4.5).
test_results: Direct sequencing of the SLC16A2 gene revealed 26 base duplication in exon 2 causing a Val254Glu substitution followed by a frame shift and a premature stop codon 24 aminoacids later (Exon 2 c.735_760dup p.Val254Glufs*24).

case_report: A 53-year-old woman was admitted in February 2007 with a pustular rash on her palms and soles. During her stay, she developed inflammation and swelling in the small joints and experienced right-sided low back pain. There was no personal or family history of psoriasis. Physical examination revealed sharply defined erythematosquamous lesions with clusters of sterile pustules on the palms and soles. Diffuse swelling and redness were observed over the right sternoclavicular, right wrist, and left ankle joints. Although there was pain upon palpation, the range of motion remained normal. The general physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory results indicated an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 120 mm/h (normal <20 mm/h) and a C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 6.44 mg/dL (normal <0.8 mg/dL). Serum tests were negative for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear factor, anti-dsDNA, anti-Ro, anti-La, and anti-Sm antibodies. HLA typing was negative for HLA-B51, 52, and 27. Biochemical screening showed no abnormalities.
test_results: A technetium-99m diphosphonate-labeled scintigram of bones revealed abnormal focal increases in tracer uptake in the right sternoclavicular and left ankle joints. X-ray of the wrist and the sternocostoclavicular region revealed soft tissue swelling. There were bone erosions on the knees, hands, ankles, and elbows. A computed tomography scan showed sclerosis of the sacroiliac joints. Skin biopsy from lesions on the left hand showed spongiosis and dyskeratotic cells in the basal layer, with infiltration of polymorphonuclear cells under the orthokeratotic epidermis. A dense dermal neutrophilic infiltrate was also present.
Orpha_name: Sterile multifocal osteomyelitis with periostitis and pustulosis

case_report: This case involves a 25-year-old phenotypic Japanese female, measuring 154.1 cm in height and weighing 48.5 kg, with no significant medical, family, or psychosocial history. She abstains from alcohol, tobacco, and drugs. At 18 years old, she was evaluated at a gynecology clinic for primary amenorrhea and was attributed the condition to her active participation in competitive track and field, leading to a diagnosis of athletic amenorrhea without further testing. She received no treatment and did not experience menstruation subsequently. The patient has not engaged in sexual intercourse. She presented to a local physician with abdominal distention and was referred to our hospital due to a suspected ovarian tumor, as a 17 cm mass was detected in the pelvis. Examination of the external genitalia showed clitoral hypertrophy and a narrowed vaginal opening. Pelvic MRI identified a pelvic mass measuring 218 × 115 × 178 mm, with both cystic and solid components. The uterus was not visualized. The cystic parts contained blood, and the solid parts showed contrast enhancement. FDG-PET/CT revealed FDG uptake in the tumor and enlarged abdominal para-aortic lymph nodes. Blood tests showed: WBC: 10.7/μL × 103; hemoglobin: 10.1 g/dL; platelets: 412/μL × 104; CRP: 18.1 mg/dL; total protein: 7.7 g/dL; albumin: 3.8 g/dL; urea nitrogen: 8 mg/dL; creatinine: 0.53 mg/dL; total bilirubin: 0.6 mg/dL; AST: 30 IU/L; ALT: 8 IU/L; FSH: 52.4 mU/mL; LH: 34.4 mU/mL; estradiol: < 10 pg/mL; progesterone: 0.66 ng/mL; and testosterone: 0.25 ng/mL. Serum alpha-fetoprotein was 2.4 ng/mL (within normal range), but serum beta-human chorionic gonadotropin was 5.86 ng/mL, lactate dehydrogenase was 4574 µg/L, and CA125 was 165 µg/mL. Urinalysis results were normal.
test_results: The karyotype was found to exhibit 45,X/46,XY mosaicism.

case_report: This case involves a 27-year-old female, the youngest sister of patient III-1. She was first admitted to the hospital at age 25 after experiencing a year-long gradual worsening of a gait disorder, leading to an increased risk of falling. Upon examination, her Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score was 25/30. Neurological assessment revealed mild weakness and increased muscle tone in her right limbs. Brain MRI showed ventricular enlargement, isolated hyperintense spots on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), and a bright asymmetrical signal on FLAIR in the left frontoparietal lobe and left lateral ventricle. She received treatment aimed at improving circulation and had a ventriculoperitoneal shunt placed at a local hospital. Despite these interventions, her gait disorder continued to worsen, and her cognitive function declined over the next year. At age 26, she was admitted to our institution with progressive gait disturbance and slight cognitive decline, with her MMSE score dropping to 18/30. Neurological examination at this time showed muscular hypertonia, ataxia of the right limbs, hyperreflexia, and ankle clonus in the right leg. Due to the ventriculoperitoneal shunt, subsequent MRI was not performed. Repeated CT scans indicated diffuse cerebral atrophy with ventricular enlargement and a small calcification near the anterior horns of the right lateral ventricles. An 18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) scan demonstrated reduced glucose uptake in the cerebral lobes, particularly in the frontal lobes.
test_results: DNA sequencing of the patient revealed a heterozygous mutation (c.2552T>C) in exon 19 of the CSF-1R gene on chromosome 5.
diagnosis: hereditary diffuse leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids
Orpha_name: Hereditary diffuse leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia

case_report: A 30-year-old woman, who does not smoke, was admitted to our hospital in August 2015 with a 4-month history of worsening lower limb weakness, difficulty walking, and visual problems. Her mother had experienced right lower limb weakness at the age of 40, followed by progressive cognitive and motor decline, and passed away at 60. Before her admission, the patient had neuropsychiatric symptoms including paraphasia and hallucinations. She had been treated with intravenous methylprednisolone for multiple sclerosis at another hospital, but her motor function continued to deteriorate, leading to frequent falls. Upon admission, her mini-mental state examination (MMSE) score was 25/30, and her Montreal cognitive assessment scale (MoCA) score was 17/30. Her activities of daily living (ADL) score was 50/100, and her Morse fall risk factors assessment scale score was 45. Her bilateral visual acuity was 0.8, muscle tone in her lower limbs was increased, and muscle strength in the lower limbs was grade 4. She exhibited a spastic and unsteady broad-based gait. Romberg’s sign, Babinski’s sign, and Chaddock’s sign were all positive. Most laboratory tests were normal or negative, including serum erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, vitamins (B1, B2, B6, B9, B12), glycosylated hemoglobin, thyroid function, serum copper, ceruloplasmin, anti-nuclear antibody, paraneoplastic antibodies, and antibodies specific for myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein, myelin-associated glycoprotein, myelin basic protein, and aquaporin-4. Tests for serum treponema pallidum antibody, rapid plasma reagin, tolulized red unheated serum test, and human immunodeficiency virus antibody were negative. Cerebrospinal fluid tests were normal, including negative oligoclonal IgG bands.
