Brain T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) MRI revealed multiple, asymmetrical, hyperintense lesions in the periventricular areas and white matter regions of the frontal and parietal lobes. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) showed small dots of diffusion restriction within the white matter lesions. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) indicated increased levels of choline (Cho) and decreased N-acetylaspartate (NAA). Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) showed corpus callosum fiber loss, while fibers in the bilateral frontal, parietal, occipital, and temporal lobes, as well as brainstem fibers, were preserved. Optic nerve MRI demonstrated bilateral optic nerve lesions. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed atrophy of the right peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer (pRNFL) in the temporal quadrant (pRNFL thickness 43–50 μm) and thinning of the left pRNFL in the temporal superior quadrant (65 μm). Average RNFL thickness in healthy controls is typically 93–108 μm. Visual-evoked potential (VEP) tests showed reduced amplitudes of bilateral P100, although latencies were normal. Bilateral intraocular pressures were normal (both 15 mmHg). Visual fields of both eyes were partially missing in different quadrants. Methylprednisolone therapy with two treatment courses (1000 mg/day for 5 days and 1000 mg/day for 3 days) did not result in improvement.
test_results: Genetic studies for leukodystrophy-related genes showed that a c.2345 G > A (p.782Arg > His) mutation in exon 18 of CSF1R was present.
diagnosis: Hereditary Diffuse Leukoencephalopathy with Axonal Spheroids
Orpha_name: Hereditary diffuse leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia

case_report: A 51-year-old Caucasian woman was admitted with purpuric papules on her lower extremities. She reported muscle pain and joint pain. Her renal function tests were within normal limits, but she exhibited hematuria and proteinuria (1.2 g/24 h). Laboratory results showed a mild reduction in C3 and a significant reduction in C4. Tests for HCV infection were negative, and cryocrit was measured at 0.5%. Bence-Jones proteinuria was not detected.
test_results: Skin biopsy showed leucytoclastic vasculitis. Renal biopsy showed membrano-proliferative glomerulonephritis. Ultrastructural examination evidenced mesangial, subendothelial and subepithelial organized electron-dense deposits characterized by arched fibrils with a diameter of 24 nm.

case_report: A 10-year-old male presented to the Center of Dental Specialties of the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul, Porto Alegre, Brazil, with a lesion located at the left labial commissure that had been present for two months. The lesion was asymptomatic and had shown rapid growth since it was first observed. Clinical examination identified a firm, red to purple nodule with a sessile base, measuring approximately 1 cm in diameter. An excisional biopsy was performed.
test_results: The microscopic examination revealed an endothelial cell proliferation in nodular arrangements with a 'cannon ball' pattern covered by oral mucosa. The formation of irregular capillary blood vessels with a slit-shaped lumen and presence of discrete inflammatory infiltrate in the underlying connective tissue were also observed.

case_report: In March 2014, a 70-year-old Chinese woman experienced recurrent watery diarrhea occurring 5 to 10 times daily, along with indigestion, malnutrition, respiratory tract infections, and weakness. Upon hospital admission, physical examination and imaging identified an anterior mediastinum space-occupying mass. The patient underwent a thymectomy. A colonoscopy performed at that time showed no abnormalities. One month after the thymectomy, she developed lymphatic tuberculosis and was treated with an anti-tuberculous regimen (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) for 10 months. Additionally, the affected lymph node was surgically removed. During follow-up, she showed a positive response to the anti-tuberculous treatment.
test_results: Computed tomography revealed an anterior mediastinum space-occupying mass that was diagnosed as a type B3 thymoma by computed tomography-guided percutaneous puncture biopsy.

case_report: A 24-year-old male presented with a progressive difficulty in walking and widespread involuntary movements that began around the age of 14. He had a history of delayed motor and cognitive development. Family history included a maternal grandfather who had epilepsy without dystonia or cognitive impairment, a mother with generalized dystonia and cognitive impairment, and a sister with epilepsy, generalized dystonia, and cognitive impairment. Neurological examination revealed generalized dystonia, predominantly affecting the neck and trunk. The patient was non-verbal but could understand and follow simple commands. No abnormal physical features were noted. Brain MRI and electroencephalogram results were normal.
test_results: Molecular genetic testing identified a variant, in heterozygosity, in the splicing acceptor site of GNAO1 gene(c.724-8G>A). The mother and sister were subsequently tested, and the same variant was identified.
diagnosis: GNAO1 variant causing dystonic cerebral palsy

case_report: A 9-year-old girl with no prior health issues reported experiencing a continuous, holocranial headache for the past month. She also had nausea and multiple episodes of vomiting over the same period. Clinical examination revealed mild bilateral papilledema. Vital signs were stable, and no focal neurological deficits were observed. Blood tests showed no abnormalities.
test_results: On magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, a well-defined globular mass with mixed intensity was noted within the third ventricle, thereby causing its distension. The tumor measured 47 mm × 59 mm × 55 mm in craniosacral and craniocaudal dimensions. Bilateral thalamic compression was noted along with upstream hydrocephalus. On T2 imaging, the mass appeared heterogeneously hyperintense, and on T1-weighted, a hyperintense area with multiple cystic areas was noted. The solid part of the lesion showed diffusion restriction. Postcontrast the tumor showed enhancement. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy revealed high choline and glycine peaks with low N-acetylaspartate peaks. On histopathology, small sheets of atypical round-/oval-/epithelial-like cells with enlarged round/oval/hyperchromatic nuclei with occasional nucleoli with definite cellular-nuclear pleomorphism were seen, and rare mitotic activity was noted. On immunohistochemistry, both synaptophysin and NSE were positive.

case_report: A 55-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of severe fatigue, diarrhea, and vomiting. In the emergency department, she experienced multiple apneic episodes necessitating intubation and ventilation. No infective or metabolic causes were identified. She had a history of bilateral action tremor in both upper and lower limbs for 7 months, diagnosed as benign essential tremor 2 years prior, and was on propranolol. Over the past 2 years, she lost 12 kg and was diagnosed with depression, exhibiting withdrawal and apathy. There was a family history of Parkinson's disease and multiple sclerosis, though details were initially sparse. During her ICU stay, she had recurrent apneic episodes and worsening tremor, leading to treatment with levetiracetam and phenytoin due to jerky limb movements and a depressed conscious level. Routine blood tests were normal except for mild reversible hyponatremia. She was transferred to the ICU at a regional neurosciences center. Brain MRI was normal, and lumbar puncture showed normal cerebrospinal fluid (white cell count <1, protein 0.17 g/L, glucose 5.4 mmol/L with paired plasma glucose 8.8 mmol/L, and negative oligoclonal bands). Electroencephalogram indicated encephalopathic features with continuous slow wave activity over the left frontotemporal region. She was treated with 3 days of intravenous methylprednisolone followed by high-dose oral prednisolone. After respiratory weaning, she was moved to ward-level care. Her encephalopathy and apneic episodes resolved during her stay, and her mood improved significantly. Examination showed slight hypomimia, normal vertical gaze, rest tremor of the right upper and lower limbs, asymmetrical postural and action tremor worse on the right, rest tremor of the tongue, mild right-sided limb rigidity, and moderate right upper limb bradykinesia. She started on co-careldopa, and at 100/25 mg three times daily, her tremor and bradykinesia improved. Overnight oximetry revealed a desaturation index of 1.7/h, with desaturation below 85% for 12 minutes and a low of 65%, indicating sleep-disordered breathing. Immunology tests were negative for various antibodies. Further family history revealed her mother had idiopathic Parkinson's disease diagnosed at 46 and died in her early 50s, and her 57-year-old brother was being treated for rapidly progressive atypical parkinsonism with erratic breathing and had recently started on CPAP.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed that the patient was heterozygous for the c.211G > A, p.(G71R) pathogenic mutation in exon 2 of the DCTN1 gene.

case_report: A 38-year-old female patient, typically experiencing mild headaches, presented with a sudden severe headache. An 11-mm mass lesion was identified in the sella turcica, leading to her referral to the neurosurgery department. The patient had given birth one year prior and was breastfeeding, so contrast-enhanced imaging was not performed to avoid potential side effects on the infant. Hydrocortisone (10 mg/day) was administered due to low levels of adrenocorticotropic hormone (09:00 h: 5.5 pg/mL, normal range: 7.2–63.3 pg/mL) and cortisol (09:00 h: 4.9 µg/dL, normal range: 7.07–19.6 µg/dL), along with hypereosinophilia (8.2%), indicating mild adrenal insufficiency. The patient's headache symptoms subsequently improved. An endocrine evaluation and contrast-enhanced imaging were planned after the cessation of breastfeeding. Five months later, the patient contracted SARS-CoV-2 despite having received the first and second doses of the vaccine 7 and 6 months earlier, respectively. She experienced a fever of 38°C and a severe headache for several days, for which acetaminophen was prescribed. The fever resolved, but a mild headache persisted. One month later, she returned to the department with a headache that had lasted for five days.
test_results: Head MRI revealed mild enlargement of the lesion and sphenoid sinus mucosal thickening. The patient was reassessed by MRI, revealing a pituitary cystic mass with a ring-shaped contrast enhancement that partially extended into the third ventricle and increased signal intensity on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI). Immunohistochemical analysis showed more than 50 immunoglobulin G4 (IgG4)-positive plasma cells per high-power field and an IgG4/IgG ratio of 30–40%.
diagnosis: Hypophysitis secondary to Rathke’s cleft cyst
Orpha_name: Pituitary deficiency due to Rathke cleft cysts

case_report: A 25-year-old male experienced gait instability for 10 years, initially presenting with mild walking instability and occasional dizziness. There was no muscle weakness or limb tremor. At age 23, he developed slurred speech, and gait disturbances became more pronounced, including frequent falls when turning quickly and difficulty running or climbing stairs. He also had mild learning difficulties, particularly in mathematics, and left school after grade 7. Additionally, he had recurring episodes of skin rash. Physical examination showed horizontal nystagmus, dysarthria, and absent tendon reflexes. He had a thin stature (weight 45 kg, height 169 cm), a small head circumference (52 cm), distinctive facial features (high eyebrow arches, deep eye sockets, abnormal tooth arrangement, and protruding jaw), skin hyperpigmentation and rash, and scoliosis. Cognitive assessment revealed an MMSE score of 19/30. Laboratory tests were negative for anti-O antibody, rheumatoid factor, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody.
test_results: Brain MRI revealed atrophy of the cerebellum and iron deposition in the globus pallidus bilaterally and substantia nigra.

case_report: A 6-year-old boy presented with lesions in both the maxilla and mandible, first observed by his parents 2 months before evaluation. There was no familial history of jaw disease. Physical examination revealed firm, non-fluctuant lesions with bilateral mandibular buccal bone expansion extending from the deciduous canine to the deciduous molar. The mucosa over the lesions was intact.
test_results: Panoramic radiography revealed a large lesion extending from the right ascending mandibular ramus to the left ascending mandibular ramus. The lesion consisted of a central heterogeneous mineralization and a thin marginal radiolucent area with a well-demarcated sclerotic border. Several tooth germs were displaced, and roots of multiple primary teeth were resorbed. The permanent molar teeth were significantly displaced, particularly the second molar, which was displaced into the ascending ramus. A CT scan confirmed thinned bony cortex of the inferior mandibular border and alveolar bone expansion near the mixed radiopaque mass. A displaced tooth germ grew into the maxillary sinus. Blood tests (serum calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, and PTH) were within normal limits. Incisional biopsies were performed in the mandibular and the maxillary lesions, and both specimens showed a similar histopathologic pattern. The lesions were mainly composed of fibrous tissue rich in fibroblasts with spherical calcifications. The mandibular lesion showed scarce areas of small spherical calcifications; by contrast, the maxillary specimen exhibited a larger amount of these calcified structures. Mutational analysis of GNAS and HRPT2 revealed no genetic abnormality in the lesions.

case_report: A 32-year-old woman with no prior medical conditions presented with primary amenorrhea and has been experiencing chronic and cyclic pelvic pain since the age of 12. The patient reported not having any gynecological history or sexual activity and had never sought medical attention before due to financial constraints and limited accessibility to healthcare. During the clinical examination, the patient had a normal physical appearance and well-developed secondary sexual characteristics. Additionally, a hard and painful pelvic mass was detected. Examination of the vulvo-perineal area revealed normal external genitalia, including well-defined labia majora, labia minora, and clitoris, but there was an absence of a vaginal opening.
test_results: Ultrasonography revealed an enlarged uterus with a significant mass occupying the uterine cavity. A pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan showed an anteverted uterus measuring 106 mm in height, 53 mm in thickness, and 122 mm in width. There was a pronounced accumulation of blood (hematometra) at the empty line of the uterus. The junctional zone appeared normal, and the myometrium was homogeneous. In addition, there were bilateral hematosalpinx and a hemorrhagic cyst in the left ovary. The cervix and vagina were not visualized.
diagnosis: Congenital cervico-vaginal aplasia with a functional uterus

case_report: An 18-day-old male infant presented with fever and redness in the umbilical region. Family history showed no hematologic malignancies, immunodeficiency syndrome, or sudden death among relatives. Maternal history included gravida 4, para 2, with two artificial abortions with the current husband, no infections, no pharmaceutical use, and no gestational hypertension. The infant was delivered vaginally at 36 weeks and five days of gestation, weighed 2456 g at birth, and had Apgar scores of eight at one minute and nine at five minutes. Post-birth, the infant was active and nursing well. At 14 days old, redness around the umbilical region was noticed, diagnosed as umbilical granuloma, and treated. At 17 days old, the infant became irritable and developed a fever of 38°C. The fever persisted, and irritability worsened, leading to an emergency outpatient consultation and subsequent admission for further examination and treatment. Admission findings: weight, 2,892 g (-0.3SD); body temperature, 37.8°C; heart rate, 140 bpm; respiratory rate, 40 breaths/min; blood pressure, 83/42 mmHg. Physical examination: flat anterior fontanelle, good facial color, no pharyngeal redness, no swollen neck lymph nodes, clear breath and heart sounds, soft abdomen with normal bowel sounds and no liver enlargement, redness and heat in the umbilical region with the umbilical cord still attached, no limb edema, capillary refill time within one second, no skin rash, and no apparent external malformations. Chest and abdominal radiographs showed no infiltrative shadows in the hilar area, no heart enlargement, but a thymus shadow was present. Laboratory findings: white blood cell count was 10,700/µL, neutrophil count was <500/µL, indicating neutropenia, and monocyte count was elevated. No reduction in other hematopoietic cells and no apparent biochemical abnormalities such as hemolysis. Immunological tests showed elevated c-reactive protein (CRP) at 4.6 mg/dL, with normal IgG, IgA, and IgM levels. Blood culture, urine quantitative culture, and skin culture peripheral to the umbilicus were performed.
test_results: Both the mother and he tested positive for anti-HNA1-a antibodies and anti-HNA1-b antibodies.

case_report: The patient is a 28.9-year-old woman, born after a full-term pregnancy from unrelated healthy parents. Maternal age was 44 years and paternal age was 40. During pregnancy, foetal movements were decreased. A caesarean section was performed due to premature rupture of the membranes. Birth weight was 2450 g. Post-delivery, the patient exhibited severe muscular hypotonia, weak cry, sleepiness, poor deep tendon reflexes, and abnormalities in thermoregulation. Feeding difficulties were observed due to a poor sucking reflex, necessitating gavage feeding. She was discharged with a diagnosis of congenital benign hypotonia. The patient experienced psychomotor delay, non-specific mild dysmorphisms, and strabismus. Karyotype analysis showed a normal 46, XX result. Neonatal screening for CH indicated normal thyroxine (T4) levels and a slightly elevated TSH (24 μU/ml), confirmed by a blood sample, but no treatment was administered. At 9 months, she was admitted to our hospital due to elevated serum TSH levels (40 μU/ml - nv <4 μU/ml) with normal FT4 (8 pg/ml – n.v. 5–12.5 pg/ml). Measurements showed a supine length of 66 cm (<10th percentile), body weight of 8 kg (<25th percentile), and head circumference of 45.5 cm (97th percentile). Thyroid ultrasound indicated the absence of the gland in the neck, while 99mTc-pertechnetate thyroid scintigraphy revealed a small, ectopic, sublingual thyroid gland. Levo-thyroxine therapy was initiated (8 μg/kg/die) and adjusted over several months, normalizing FT4 and TSH levels. Persistent hypotonia and poor response to stimuli, along with the absence of a sucking reflex in early life, led to a brain computed tomography scan at 12 months, which showed ventricular enlargement and craniosynostosis. At age three, despite being biochemically euthyroid on levo-thyroxine therapy, the patient exhibited poor physical and developmental progress, hyperphagia, weight gain, short stature, and decreased growth velocity. Physical examination revealed distinctive facial features (narrow bifrontal diameter, dolichocephaly, almond-shaped eyes, downturned mouth angles), abundant thick saliva, small hands, and feet. Severe scoliosis was diagnosed and initially treated with a corset, later requiring surgery at age 13. To evaluate growth retardation, two growth hormone (GH) stimulation tests (clonidine 0.150 mg/m2 orally and insulin tolerance test 0.1 UI/kg i.v. bolus) were performed, both indicating GH deficiency [GH peak 1.7 ng/ml and 5.6 ng/ml, respectively (nv >10 ng/ml)]. The combined test [GHRH (1 μg/kg) + Arginine (0.5 g/kg iv)] confirmed reduced GH response [GH peak 8.7 ng/ml (nv >20 ng/ml)]. Pituitary MRI showed an empty sella with a small, hypoplastic pituitary gland at its base. GH therapy was initiated at 0.24 mg/kg/week, adjusted based on IGF-1 levels and growth curve, and continued until age 12.9 years. Genetic tests were performed at age 16.
test_results: Methylation analysis and DNA polymorphism analysis of chromosome 15 confirmed the presence of UPD15.

case_report: A 70-year-old Italian woman reported a 4-year history of a bilateral, gradually expanding, papular eruption in the axillae. Physical examination revealed 2-4 mm firm, yellow-white, partly merging, nonfollicular papules symmetrically located along the posterior axillary folds. Other cutaneous folds were unaffected. The lesions were asymptomatic at the time of examination, though the patient noted initial itchiness and redness. Her medical history included a primary cutaneous follicular non-Hodgkin lymphoma in the right groin 15 years ago, treated with surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy. Additionally, a grade 1 urinary bladder carcinoma was excised one year prior. There were no reported symptoms related to the eyes, cardiovascular system, gastrointestinal system, or lungs.
test_results: A punch-biopsy of a representative papule showed dermal fibrosis at H&E staining. Verhoeff elastic tissue stain showed increase of thick, interlacing elastic fibers in the mid and deep reticular dermis. Fragmentation, calcification or phagocytosis of elastic fibers were not seen. Mild atrophy of the epidermis and edema in the papillary dermis were also evident.

case_report: A 17-year-old girl from a lower middle-class family presented with a history of recurrent constipation since early childhood. Prenatal ultrasound showed no abnormalities. Meconium was passed within 24 hours of birth, and there was no history of post-natal rectal probing. Constipation began after weaning at about 6 months of age, and she had multiple medical consultations since then. At the age of 1 year, she was diagnosed with Down's syndrome and hypothyroidism and started on thyroxin. Her constipation was managed with dietary measures and enemas. Initially, she passed stool every 2–3 days, but this interval gradually increased to 5–6 days. In later years, she did not pass stool without enema or laxatives, producing small, hard stools that sometimes became liquid after treatment. With age, she became reluctant to feed and often appeared withdrawn and sad. At 17 years old, she was referred to a pediatric surgeon for constipation management. At the time of referral, she had not passed stool for 9 days. She weighed 35 kg and was 134 cm tall. General examination revealed a flattened face, broad nasal bridge, low set ears, a large tongue frequently protruding from the mouth, a short neck, and low intellectual ability. The abdomen was slightly distended and mildly loaded with fecal matter. Abdominopelvic ultrasonography showed no presacral mass, and there were no renal or other abnormalities.
test_results: Barium enema showed a dilated colon and the lower end of the rectum was located high up with a beak-like appearance. Digital rectal examination (DRE) and examination under anesthesia revealed a thick diaphragm, about 3 cm from anal verge with a central hole, through which hard fecal matter was visible.
Orpha_name: Non-syndromic anorectal malformation with rectal stenosis

case_report: A 12-year-old boy presented with a painful swelling on his right hand that had been present for 7 months. Initially, the swelling was barely visible, bluish, and non-tender, first noticed at 6 years of age, and gradually increased in size. There was a history of trauma to the right hand while playing. He also had a history of recurrent swelling in the left arm every one to two months with skin eruptions since birth. These were treated by local physicians, but no medical records were available. There were no complaints of pain elsewhere in the body. He had a swelling excised above the right elbow 3 months ago, but the histopathology report was missing. There was no significant family history. On examination, a grayish, 5 cm diameter, firm, tender swelling was noted on the mid-palmar aspect of the right hand with thick adherent overlying skin, extending dorsally. There was a pea-sized non-tender swelling on the distal phalanx of the left index finger and another non-tender swelling on the left medial malleolus. His left upper limb was shortened and deformed. There was a scar with a 1 cm swelling above the right elbow. The spleen was enlarged, approximately 6 cm below the costal margin diagonally. Laboratory investigations revealed hemoglobin of 8.7 gm% and alkaline phosphatase levels of 310 U/l. The rest of the reports were within normal limits.
test_results: Histopathology of the swelling right hand confirmed spindle cell hemangioma. Plain radiology revealed soft tissue density swelling with multiple phleboliths involving the right palm. It resulted in widening of the 2nd inter-metacarpal space, scalloping of radial border of 3rd metacarpal and periosteal reaction along the ulnar border of 3rd metacarpal. Multifocal lytic areas with central areas of calcification were also noticed involving 6th right rib, left scapula, left proximal humerus and distal radius, left proximal and distal fibula. No evidence of periosteal reaction or soft tissue extension was noticed. CT angiography revealed large lobulated soft tissue density area, 4.9 x 4.7 cm, showing specks of calcification, representing phleboliths, noted between 2nd and 3rd metacarpal bones. There were no definite bony erosions. Findings of MRI – right wrist and hand were consistent with a benign vascular lesion. Skeletal scintigraphy done with Tc-99m labeled MDP showed increased tracer uptake over mal-aligned upper 3rd of left humerus. An expansile area of increased tracer concentration was also visualized over lower 3rd of left radius. Also increased tracer uptake was visualized at 2nd and 3rd metacarpals of right hand.

case_report: An 8-year-old girl presented with pain, swelling, and limited movement in both knees and the left ankle for over six months. She experienced stiffness in the morning but did not have a fever. No other joints were affected. During the initial examination, there were fluid accumulations in both knees and swelling in the left ankle, while other joints and systems appeared normal. There were no skin rashes or mucosal lesions observed. Initial laboratory results showed a normal complete blood count, complement levels, and immunoglobulin levels. However, RF and ANA were positive.
test_results: In MRI, chronic inflammation with synovial thickening was seen in both knees, suggesting erosive arthritis. Laboratory results revealed pancytopenia, coombs negative anemia (Hb: 9.7 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (30,000/mm3) and leukopenia (WBC count 2900/mm3) (predominant lymphopenia). F-ANA was positive (1/1280, speckled pattern), anti-dsDNA level was positive 1/80, rheumatoid factor level (RF) was 7.88 IU/mL (0–14 IU/mL), and C3 (65.7 mg/dL) and C4 (4.4 mg/dL) levels were low. Antiphospholipid antibodies (aPL) level was negative and urinalysis showed microscopic hematuria (5-10 RBC in hpf) and trace proteinuria (1+).

case_report: An 18-month-old Chinese–Malaysian girl presented with multiple red papules that first appeared at 10 months of age. These erythematous papules initially appeared on her face and later spread to the entire body, excluding the palms and soles. She was initially treated with topical corticosteroids by a private dermatologist, but her skin condition worsened and did not respond to the treatment. She is the only child of nonconsanguineous parents, who are healthy and show no signs of uveitis or arthritis. On physical examination, the child had erythematous papules covering her entire body, sparing only the palms and soles. The papules were pinhead-sized, flat-topped, and slightly scaly, mostly discrete over the body and extremities, with confluence occurring only on the face. Articular involvement was noted, with boggy synovial thickening of both ankle joints, wrists, and all fingers, which developed from the age of 12 months. No hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, or uveitis was detected.
test_results: Histologic examination of a papule showed well-circumscribed, noncaseating granulomas with sparse lymphocyte infiltrate at the periphery within the upper dermis. Genetic mutation analysis revealed a heterozygous c.1000C>T transition in exon 4 of the NOD2 gene. The mutation resulted in an arginine to tryptophan substitution at position 334, p. R334W, of the coding sequence. The mutation was not detected in the patient's parents.

case_report: A 46-year-old male patient exhibited widespread severe skin thickening since early childhood. Initially born with normal skin, he gradually developed thick, adherent scales starting from the face and spreading to other parts of the body. No family members showed similar symptoms. Examination revealed hyperkeratotic, thick, dry, adherent, mud-colored scales covering most of the body, particularly the face, scalp, and extremities, including the flexures. Some areas had porcupine-like spikes. The facial skin was notably thickened and rugose, resulting in an expressionless, masked appearance. The trunk had minimal involvement with patches of normal skin. Follicular prominence and atrophy were observed over the forearm flexures. The patient also had palmoplantar keratoderma. Hair was sparse, especially over the occipital area, due to thick scaling. Dental and nail abnormalities were present for the same duration, with most teeth absent and a peg-shaped canine. Subungual hyperkeratosis and prominent onychogryphosis were noted in most nails. No ophthalmological or skeletal abnormalities were observed, and there was no hearing loss. His complete blood count and chest X-ray results were normal.
test_results: Orthokeratotic hyperkeratosis with sparse parakeratosis, irregular acanthosis, follicular plugging, and multiple binucleated keratinocytes in the epidermis along with upper dermal lymphocytic infiltrate.

case_report: A 2-month-old female infant was brought to the Department of Dermatology with red vascular patches located on the buttocks, anus, perineum, and genitalia. She was delivered at full-term via normal spontaneous vaginal delivery, weighing 2.7 kg with a head circumference of 33.0 cm. She is the third child in her family, with no known family history of birth defects. Chromosome analysis confirmed a normal female karyotype. At birth, she had an imperforate anus with a middle-type rectovaginal fistula, a perineal skin tag, and a didelphys uterus. Surgical correction for the imperforate anus, rectovaginal fistula, and skin tag was performed on the third day after birth. At 1.5 months of age, a red vascular patch was observed around the perineal area, which was not present at birth and had increased in size. Consequently, she was referred to the Department of Dermatology at 2 months of age. Physical examination revealed a hemangioma extending from the labia major to the sacrum through the perineum on both sides.
test_results: Spinal sonography at 9 months of age showed 3.6×0.6×0.7-cm intrasacral meningocele. Echocardiography showed no abnormality in cardiac function. Brain sonography was normal.

case_report: A 3.5-year-old Sudanese girl was referred to our clinic for evaluation of poor growth and subcutaneous nodules. She was born to healthy first-degree consanguineous parents at term with a low birth weight after an uncomplicated pregnancy. At 6 weeks, her mother noticed irritability when handling the child. She was admitted with unexplained asymptomatic hypercalcemia at the age of 6 months. By 9 months, the child developed painful tissue swellings on the scapulae and small joints of the hands, with restriction of movements that progressed over time to involve her jaws, knees, elbows, ankles, skull, neck, buttocks, and perianal area. This was in addition to poor feeding, failure to thrive, and delayed gross motor milestones. Her calcium level was found to be 14.7 mg/dl (3.6 mmol/l), phosphate 4.2 mg/dl (1.3 mmol/l), alkaline phosphatase 152 μ/l, and PTH 20 pg/ml (3.6–32 pg/ml), which was treated by intravenous fluid and furosemide. She was not on vitamin D. She was then referred to a rheumatologist for the joint swellings. She received corticosteroids and methotrexate for 29 months without improvement and was thus referred to us to exclude a metabolic disorder. The patient had three other healthy siblings. Her calcium level was rechecked after admission in our unit and was 10 mg/dl (2.4 mmol/l). Examination at 6 months old showed normal physical examination with no dysmorphic features: weight 6.9 kg (25th percentile), length 61 cm (5th percentile), and head circumference 41.8 cm (10th percentile). At the age of 3 years, she had gingival hypertrophy and papules on the tip and around the nose, skull, neck, buttocks and perianal area, lower jaw, anterior and posterior part of the neck, interphalangeal joints, elbows, and ankles that led to deformities associated with tenderness and decreased range of movement. There were no overlying skin changes. Laboratory tests revealed serum calcium of 14.5 mg/dl (8.5–10.8 mg/dl), urinary calcium: creatinine 0.39 (˂ 0.2), serum phosphorus of 4.7 mg/dl equivalents to 1.5 mmol/L, PTH was 19.79 pg/ml (3.6–32 pg/ml), 25 hydroxy vitamin D level was 15 ng/ml (30–100 ng/ml), 1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D 78 pg/ml (20–54 pg/ml), urea 13 mg/dl (15–48.5 mg/dl), creatinine 0.1 mg/dl (0.31–0.47 mg/dl), sodium 140 mmol/l (136–145 mmol/l), and potassium 4.6 mmol/l (3.5–5.1 mmol/l) with normal liver function. X-rays of the limbs and skull showed subcutaneous calcifications and osteopenia.
test_results: Genetic testing confirmed a homozygous mutation in the ANTXR2 gene.

case_report: A 7-year-old female with two healthy younger siblings from non-consanguineous parents. At age 5, she began experiencing recurrent episodes of hepatitis, characterized by high-grade fever, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and weight loss. Laboratory findings showed elevated transaminases and bilirubin levels. Serological tests were negative for hepatitis viruses HBV, HCV, HAV, and HEV. During the second episode, she tested positive for IgG antibodies (IgM-negative) to antiviral capsid antigen (VCA), Epstein-Barr nuclear antigen (EBNA), and early antigen.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing (WES) identified a novel, heterozygous missense variant in exon 4 of NFAT5 (c.335C>T, p.Ser112Phe or p.Ser94Phe), at a position highly conserved across species. Family segregation analysis through Sanger sequencing confirmed the variant to be de novo. Quantification of EBV DNA by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) in plasma was persistently positive over several months (328,107 copies/ml). A hepatic biopsy showed active diffuse inflammation with lymphocytes, plasmacytes, neutrophils, and eosinophils expanding into the portal space and producing centrilobular necrosis; EBV early RNA (EBER) was positive, predominantly in CD3+CD8+ T cells. Colonoscopy revealed pancolitis with ulcers, and histopathology showed chronic active enterocolitis associated with EBV, with T-cell predominant EBER; quantification of EBV DNA in the gastrointestinal tract was above 7’000,000 copies per mL. Flow cytometry found low T cells: CD3+ 434 cells, CD4+ 294, CD8+ 98; with normal B and NK cells: CD20+ 406, CD16/56+ 420 cells. Further immunological workup revealed an impaired lymphoproliferation of phytohemagglutinin (PHA)-stimulated CD3+ T cells. Moreover, the patient lymphocyte subsets were shown to have decreased central and effector memory CD8+ T-cells, with expanded senescent CD4+ CD57+ T-cells. NK cell function was normal based on degranulation assays. In contrast, the expression of various cell surface markers was abnormal in NK cells from the patient as compared to healthy control, suggesting impaired NK cell differentiation. Flow cytometry for B cell subsets and Tregs found decreased plasmablasts, memory B cells, and low Tregs.

case_report: A 37-year-old, right-handed Japanese male, professionally engaged as a guitar player, was referred for reassessment of upper limb dystonia. He reported no family history of neurological disorders and had not been on any regular medication prior to the onset of symptoms. At 27 years old, after intensively practicing guitar for three months, he experienced difficulty in using a pick due to excessive wrist extension and intermittent tremulous finger movements in his right hand. At 29 years old, he was prescribed clonazepam (1.5 mg/day) and trihexyphenidyl (6 mg/day) for these symptoms, but the treatment was ineffective. Switching from guitar to piano temporarily alleviated the symptoms, but they later returned. Over time, the dystonia lost its task-specific nature and began to interfere with daily activities such as opening and closing screw cap bottles and brushing teeth. Five years post-onset, he faced significant challenges in playing instruments and eventually ceased his musical activities. During consultation, a neurological examination revealed normal cranial nerves, motor function, coordination, sensory function, and autonomic function, except for action-induced dystonic posturing of the right upper limb with excessive wrist extension and hyperextension of the fingers during voluntary, skilled movements. No sensory trick or diurnal variation was noted. Cognitive dysfunction, parkinsonism, pyramidal signs, and cerebellar ataxia were absent. Laboratory tests, including electrolytes, renal function tests, complete blood count, liver function tests, and urinalysis, were unremarkable. Serum copper and ceruloplasmin levels were normal. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging and dopamine transporter imaging with 123I-β-CIT single-photon emission computed tomography showed normal results.
test_results: Cerebrospinal fluid analyses revealed a significant decrease in homovanillic acid (22.6 ng/ml, normal range: 41.6–178 ng/ml), 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (9.1 ng/ml, normal range: 20.0–96.0 ng/ml), and total neopterin (2.0 pmol/ml, normal range: 9.0–20.0 pmol/ml) levels. Exome analysis and Sanger sequencing showed a novel heterozygous mutation c. 542T>G (p. Val181Gly) in the first amino acid of exon 5 in GCH1 gene.
diagnosis: Dopa-responsive dystonia  with a novel heterozygous GCH1 mutation

case_report: A female in her 60s presented to the emergency department with several days of nausea, vomiting, and loss of appetite. Her medical history included previous radiation therapy for Hodgkin lymphoma 30 years ago, hypothyroidism, and a permanent chamber pacemaker due to syncope from sinusoidal failure syndrome. A computed tomography (CT) scan showed pericardial effusion. Her vital signs were stable with a blood pressure of 105/45 mmHg, pulse rate of 99 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation of 95% on room air. Echocardiography revealed a 15-18 mm echo-free space around the heart and atrial collapse during diastole. Pericardiocentesis was performed, resulting in a reduction of the echo-free space, and the pericardial fluid was bloody. She was admitted for observation, and no further pericardial effusion accumulation was noted. Within one to two weeks, she developed progressive bilateral pleural effusions and respiratory failure requiring supplemental oxygen and orthopnea. Two thoracentesis procedures and pleural fluid analyses were conducted without a conclusive diagnosis. She was referred to our hospital for further evaluation due to worsening respiratory failure. Upon admission, she was on 2 L per minute of supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula, with a saturation level of 95%, but exhibited tachypnea at 29 breaths per minute in the supine position. Minimal exertion, such as transferring to a wheelchair, caused her oxygen saturation to drop to 70-80%. No signs of cardiac compromise were observed, including no jugular vein distension or peripheral edema. Chest X-ray and CT scans confirmed bilateral pleural effusion and minor pericardial fluid accumulation, with no lung infiltration or abdominal and pelvic abnormalities. Examination of the pleural effusion revealed serious fluid accumulation, negative results for tuberculosis using the loop-mediated isothermal amplification method, and normal adenosine-deaminase levels. Cytological analysis showed non-specific inflammatory findings with a mixture of lymphocytes, histiocytes, granulocytes, and prominent eosinophils. Complete blood count on admission showed normal eosinophil levels, and biochemistry assessments indicated normal liver and renal function, electrolyte levels, serum protein, and albumin.
test_results: One week after admission, about one month after the onset of symptoms, the complete blood count showed an eosinophil count of 2051/µL.

case_report: The patient is a 22-month-old Caucasian boy, born at 36 weeks by spontaneous vaginal delivery with normal prenatal care. At birth, he exhibited bilateral cloudy corneas without epiphora or photophobia. Initial treatment included topical dorzolamide 2% and hypertonic sodium chloride ophthalmic solution 5% before presentation at the Bascom Palmer Eye Institute. A bedside eye exam showed a central corneal opacity sparing the periphery. Extraocular findings included short extremities, brachydactyly, cleft palate, characteristic facial features, developmental delay, and pulmonary stenosis. An exam under anesthesia (EUA) was performed the same day, revealing intraocular pressures (IOP) of 32 mmHg in the right eye (OD) and 27 mmHg in the left eye (OS) using Tono-Pen XL. Bright red reflexes were observed prior to dilation in both eyes (OU). Other ocular findings included iridocorneal adhesion superiorly in the left eye (OS) and posterior capsular cataract in both eyes (OU). Due to the absence of limbal enlargement, normal axial lengths, and intact red reflexes prior to dilation, glaucoma surgery was deferred. Phenylephrine 2.5% was added for optical dilation and visual rehabilitation, and topical dorzolamide 2% was continued. Four months later, a second EUA showed IOPs of 30 mmHg OD and 35 mmHg OS by Tono-pen. The corneal opacities had enlarged centrally, but the clear peripheral cornea still maintained intact red reflexes. The irides had formed wispy attachments to the corneas in both eyes, and the view of the lens and posterior structures was suboptimal.
test_results: Genetic testing identified a homozygous pathogenic variant in B3GLCT (c. 660 + 1 G > A splice donor).

case_report: A 14-year-old male presented with swelling in his right leg accompanied by intermittent pain over the past year. The swelling in the lower leg intensified following physical activity and subsided with rest. The previous month, he sought treatment at another hospital where imaging revealed an abnormality in the right tibia, prompting him to seek further care at our facility. On physical examination, both lower limbs were of equal length, and there was no noticeable swelling or tenderness in the right lower leg. The range of motion and muscle strength in both lower limbs were found to be normal.
test_results: Plain radiography: the cortical expansive bone destruction of the anterior edge of the right upper tibia was irregular and lobulated, and the sclerotic edge could be seen. The long axis of the lesion was consistent with the tibia, with a maximum cross-sectional area of 2.1 × 1.9 cm and a length of approximately 7.5 cm, with no obvious periosteal reaction and no definite soft tissue mass. Computed tomography (CT): the lesion showed an eccentric polycystic expansive lucency area, and the bone cortex was expanded and thinned. Cortical interruption could be seen on some levels, and a small local lamellar periosteal reaction was observed in some parts. The lesion was associated with pathological fracture. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI): the lesion of the upper right tibia showed a low signal on T1-weighted imaging (T1WI), a high signal on T2-weighted imaging (T2WI), and a high signal on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI). The lesion showed significant enhancement on the postcontrast MRI scan. Pathological examination showed a small amount of hyperplastic fibrous tissue and irregular woven bone and osteoblasts, in which scattered nest-like epithelial cells were seen. The immunohistochemistry results showed Ki-67 (+1%), SATB2 (+), CK19 (1+), AE1/AE3 (1+), CK18 (−), EMA (−), P63 (1+), S-100 (−), MDM2 (2+), SMA (−), and β-catenin (2+, cytoplasm).

case_report: A 42-year-old Thai man with a history of polytoxicomania, arterial hypertension, type II diabetes mellitus, hepatic steatosis, depression, and EN presented to the emergency department following a fall the previous day. The head injury required several stitches, and the patient was discharged. Later that evening, he experienced a decline in general health, nausea, vomiting, fever, impaired vision, and facial swelling. Due to worsening symptoms, he went to the local hospital and was admitted to the internal medicine department with hypotension, tachycardia, hypoxia, and elevated kidney parameters and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels. Treatment included moxifloxacin and 100 mg of intravenous prednisolone. Two days later, he developed a mild rash with skin blisters on the back and limbs, along with a positive Nikolsky I sign, but without mucosal erosions.
test_results: The skin biopsy showed a subepidermal blister and detached epidermis with florid interface dermatitis and many necrotic keratinocytes as well as mild interstitial and perivascular superficial chronic florid inflammation, extravasation of erythrocytes and few eosinophils, edema of the dermis, and discrete pigment incontinence.

case_report: A 51-year-old male experienced intermittent right upper quadrant pain and decreased appetite over a period of 4 months. The pain was transient, nondebilitating, and not associated with food intake or bowel movements. The patient also reported worsening postprandial bloating without nausea or vomiting and a weight loss of 16 pounds in the past month due to food aversion. He consumed one to two alcoholic drinks daily and denied any history of heavier alcohol use. A CT scan of the abdomen revealed a solitary, cystic lesion measuring 5.3 × 4.4 cm in the body/tail of the pancreas. The pancreatic parenchyma, liver, gall bladder, and biliary tree appeared normal. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography showed normal pancreatic and intra/extra-hepatic bile ducts. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) did not show any communication between the pancreatic duct and the cystic lesion, and there was no ductal ectasia. The patient was referred for EUS. EUS examination using an Olympus linear array EUS scope identified a single cystic lesion measuring 6.9 × 2.4 cm in the body/tail region of the pancreas, without septae or solid components. The pancreatic parenchyma, pancreatic duct, and common bile duct were unremarkable, with the pancreatic duct measuring 1.7 mm in diameter, which is within normal limits. FNA was performed using a 22-gage Echotip needle, and due to the high viscosity of the cystic fluid, only a few drops of clear mucoid fluid were aspirated and sent for further evaluation. Due to the insufficient amount of fluid, tumor markers, amylase, and lipase levels could not be determined. A few direct smears were prepared, and the needle was rinsed in CytoRich™ fixative for Papanicolaou-stained AutoCyte Prep™.
test_results: The direct smears were hypocellular and insufficient for interpretation. Most of the cellularity was in LBC preparations showing predominantly degenerated debris with detached ciliary tufts (DTCs) and occasional preserved intact ciliated cells.
diagnosis: Ciliated foregut cyst of the pancreas

case_report: A 3-month-old male patient presented with recent microhematuria identified through urine analysis conducted for unrelated reasons. The patient was in good overall health with no additional clinical signs, symptoms, or urinary tract infection. An abdominal ultrasound revealed a solitary bladder mass. The mass was regular, predominantly hypoechogenic, and measured 1.2 × 1.5 cm. It appeared as an exophytic mass protruding into the bladder lumen, originating from the bladder trigone and overhanging the bladder neck. The ultrasound did not show any hydronephrosis or other lesions in the abdomen, neck, or head. Operative cystoscopy was performed, and the bladder wall appeared normal during exploration. Samples of the mass were obtained.
test_results: Biopsies showed a low mitotic index and uniform cells, with an eosinophil cytoplasm; no evidence of malignancy was present. Immunohistochemical stains were performed, revealing positivity for CD34. Neurofibroma and perineurioma were excluded because of negativity for S100.

case_report: A 4-year-old male, the third child in the family, was brought to the hospital due to neurodevelopmental delay. The antenatal period was uneventful, and he was delivered full term via normal vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 2.3 kg (<25th centile). Birth OFC and length are not available. At 4 months, the mother noticed poor vision, and the child was found to have bilateral cataracts, for which lens aspiration was performed. At 6 months, he began experiencing feeding difficulties and stiffness in both lower limbs. He has not achieved head control, smiles occasionally, and makes cooing sounds, with a developmental quotient of 4.16%. At 7 months, he experienced his first episode of generalized tonic-clonic convulsions, lasting a few minutes, and was started on antiepileptics. Multiple seizure episodes occurred until 2 years of age, after which seizures were controlled with optimal doses of antiepileptic drugs. On examination, the child appeared wasted and stunted, with a weight of 6.4 kg (<3rd centile), length of 86 cm (below 3rd centile), and OFC of 44 cm (at 3rd centile). He has microcephaly, plagiocephaly, low hairline, and a narrow forehead. Observations include deep-set eyes, microphthalmia, microcornea, and bilateral aphakia. The nose appears normal. Ears are low set and posteriorly placed. The oral cavity shows delayed dentition (currently only 12 teeth) with caries, a high-arched palate, and a spastic tongue. He has long fingers with bilateral simian crease and scoliosis with concavity to the left. His nipples are widely spaced, and he has bilateral undescended testes with micropenis. The left foot has an equinus deformity, and contractures are present bilaterally. The upper limbs are hypotonic, while the lower limbs are hypertonic. Deep tendon reflexes are brisk, and the pupil is atonic.
test_results: MRI showed corpus callosum agenesis and cerebral atrophy. VEPs were abnormal.

case_report: A 48-year-old Caucasian woman visited the outpatient clinic with complaints of pain and swelling in her left knee and small joints in her hands. Laboratory results indicated an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 40 mm/h and C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 28 mg/L. Rheumatoid factor (RF) was less than 20 IU/mL, and anticyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) was 94 IU/mL. Radiography revealed bone atrophy around the wrist. She was treated with prednisolone (15 mg/day) and methotrexate (15 mg/week), which led to an improvement in her symptoms and laboratory findings. Leflunomide (20 mg) was added but later discontinued due to oral ulcerations. After six months, she remained stable on 7.5 mg prednisolone daily and 15 mg methotrexate weekly. A year later, she reported fatigue and pain in both upper extremities. She did not report weight loss or low-grade fever. Her rheumatoid arthritis remained stable with the ongoing therapy. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure difference between the left (109/71 mmHg) and right arm (93/71 mmHg), a murmur over the left carotid artery, and reduced pulsations in both radial arteries. Laboratory tests showed a leukocyte count of 15 × 10^9/L, CRP of 14 mg/L, and ESR of 14 mm/h.
test_results: MRA and angiography demonstrated extensive vascular stenotic lesions. In the right truncus brachiocephalicus, an occlusion at its origin from the aortic arch was found. The right subclavian artery showed two important constrictions with a significant stenotic lesion of the proximal branch and distal a complete occlusion. The left subclavian artery was constricted in its proximal part. There was also occlusion of the left common carotid artery at its origin as well in its distal part. Both left common iliac artery and right external iliac artery showed stenotic lesions. PET scan demonstrated increased fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake along both brachial arteries.

case_report: A 4-month-old male infant, born full-term via emergency cesarean section due to fetal bradycardia, had Apgar scores of 5, 7, and 10 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes, respectively. He spent 2 days in the neonatal intensive care unit for observation. The infant is the child of first-degree related Saudi parents. At birth, his growth parameters were within normal ranges: weight 3,250 g, length 50 cm, and head circumference 36 cm. At 6 weeks old, he required inpatient care for a urinary tract infection associated with influenza. At 3 months old, during an outpatient visit, he was noted to be pale and failing to thrive despite adequate oral intake. His weight was 3,700 g, length 52 cm, and head circumference 37.5 cm, all significantly below the 3rd percentile according to World Health Organization child growth standards. Physical examination revealed an active infant without dysmorphic features but with a distended abdomen, dilated veins, hepatomegaly (liver span of 8 cm), splenomegaly (4 cm below the costal margin), loss of subcutaneous fat, and reduced muscle bulk. Laboratory and radiological evaluations showed severe microcytic anemia, hypothyroidism, elevated serum triglyceride levels, hepatosplenomegaly, osteopenia, and bilateral punctuated adrenal calcification. Echocardiography indicated normal heart function. A dried blood spot test revealed a very low level of lysosomal acid lipase.
test_results: A deletion/duplication genetic analysis by real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) confirmed the presence of homozygous deletion c.(428 + 1_967-1)_(*1_?)del in the LIPA gene (NM_000235.3; chr.10): (OMIM 613,497). The detected variant was a homozygous deletion that included, at least, the exons 9 and 10 of the LIPA gene. The enzyme assay was very low which confirms the variant pathogenicity.

case_report: A 4-year-old male presented with excessive urine output and increased frequency of urination. He reported increased thirst and fluid intake for 6 months. There was no history of trauma, autoimmune conditions, tuberculosis, joint pain, or deformity. A water deprivation test confirmed decreased random urine osmolality at 77.00 mosm/kg (normal serum osmolality: 295.00 mosm/kg). Urine specific gravity was 1.005. MRI revealed a uniformly thickened pituitary stalk with contrast enhancement, with no other cranial abnormalities. Investigations to rule out common causes for a thickened pituitary stalk in children, including chest radiograph, complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, serum electrolytes, blood sugar, and glycosylated hemoglobin, were normal. The anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) level was 0.30 pg/mL, which was subnormal. Serum human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG), acetylcholine esterase (ACE), and 1,25(OH)2 vitamin D3 levels were normal. Antinuclear antibody and antipituitary antibodies were negative. The anterior pituitary hormonal profile showed cortisol at 18.0 μg/dL, adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH) at 45.6 pg/mL, tri-iodothyronine (T3) at 142.0 μg/dL, tetra-iodothyronine (T4) at 8.2 μg/dL, thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) at 3.15 μIU/mL, growth hormone (GH) at 0.7 ng/mL, and prolactin at 27.0 ng/mL. Lumbar cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cytology was normal, and CSF ACE and HCG were negative. Despite extensive investigations, no definitive cause for the central DI and thickened infundibulum was identified, and the patient was kept under regular follow-up. Repeated neurological and ophthalmological examinations were conducted to monitor disease progression. The DI was managed with nasal desmopressin spray, resulting in immediate clinical improvement with decreased urine output and resolution of nocturnal enuresis. After 6 months, the child developed a left scalp swelling. At this time, there was no history of fever, lethargy, skin eruptions, or weight loss, and examination showed no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. A CT scan of the brain revealed two punched-out lytic lesions in the skull with associated soft tissue swelling.
test_results: Histological examination of biopsy of the skull lesion revealed the tumor to consist of malignant tumor cells arranged as plump spindles and giant multinucleate cells. Inflammatory cells including eosinophils were seen between the tumor cells. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) demonstrated the tumor cell positivity for CD1a and S-100.

case_report: A 17-year-old female, born to non-consanguineous parents, exhibited typical development. She presented to our hospital's orthopedic department with a history of psoriasis since the age of eight, managed with topical treatment. The primary complaint was mechanical pain associated with a sensation of patellar instability, mostly during physical education lessons, persisting for the last two years, without documented dislocation episodes. No additional musculoskeletal issues were reported. Clinical examination revealed bilateral hypoplastic patellae, positive apprehension on testing, an inability to perform a monopodal squat because of muscular weakness and pain, and a pressure callus on the sole combined with reduced longitudinal arches of the feet.
test_results: The radiographic analysis demonstrated an absent ischiopubic junction, bilateral patellar hypoplasia, and reduced longitudinal arches of the feet.

case_report: The patient is a 21-month-old male, firstborn, delivered via cesarean section at 38 weeks. The parents are not genetically related, and the mother reported no complications during pregnancy. The combined test at 12 weeks gestation was normal. At birth, his weight was 3600 g, height 51.5 cm, and head circumference 35.5 cm, all within normal ranges. These measurements remain normal currently. There is no family history of the disease in first-degree relatives. The patient's grandmother had six miscarriages, and a cousin has a history of seizures. At 2 months, the patient was referred to the clinic due to lack of neck control and hand tremors. Brain MRI showed generalized cerebral atrophy and diffuse white matter changes in the periventricular, subarachnoid, and juxtacortical regions, with involvement of the brain stem (posterior to the pons and midbrain), putamen, cerebellum, and bilateral thalami. Some lesions were DWI-positive, indicating acute changes. Dilated Virchow-Robin spaces were also noted. EEG results showed burst suppression, high-amplitude irregular and discordant electrical activity, including slow, sharp waves and multi-focal spikes, indicating hypsarrhythmia. The patient was treated with Liskantin 250 mg and Levebel 100 mg syrup. Echocardiography revealed a mid-muscular ventricular septal defect (VSD) after extra heart sounds were heard during auscultation. Elevated plasma ammonia (113.18 μmol/L) and alanine and aspartate aminotransferases (53 and 48 U/L, respectively) were noted. Metabolic tests were normal. Elevated CMV IgM levels (11.25 g/L, normal < 9) prompted a lumbar puncture, which showed normal cerebrospinal fluid analysis and no infection. Eye examination for chorioretinitis and auditory brainstem response test were normal.
test_results: A WES analysis revealed a novel variant (c.979C > T; p.Pro327Ser) in heparan sulfate 6-O-sulftransferase2 (HS6ST2) gene.

case_report: A 63-year-old Caucasian woman was referred from a county hospital with an initial diagnosis of CS. She presented with generalized fatigue, muscle weakness, insomnia, flushing, hypertension, stress symptoms, and psychiatric symptoms including deteriorated concentration, memory disabilities, and hypomania. Physical examination revealed hypertension, changed body constitution, moon face, supraclavicular fat, buffalo hump, hirsutism on her chin, proximal myopathy, and a weight loss of 5kg over a few months. Her medical history included breast cancer (right side) 16 years earlier, treated with surgery and radiation, and a superficial malignant melanoma on her right arm in 2000 with no recurrence. Biochemical tests showed 24-hour urine free cortisol at 1300nmol/24-hour (reference <183), no diurnal rhythm with serum cortisol levels between 600 to 1000nmol/L, and plasma ACTH levels between 30 and 45ng/L over a 24-hour period. Cortisol and ACTH levels did not suppress with either 1mg or 8mg dexamethasone suppression tests. An MRI scan of the sella turcica found no pituitary tumor. Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling with corticotrophin-releasing hormone (CRH) testing showed no central to peripheral ratio of ACTH, nor an increase in ACTH during the CRH test. Fasting CRH was normal at 3.5pmol/L (reference <5), and urine catecholamines and hydroxyindoleacetic acid were normal. Chromogranin A was slightly elevated at 8.2nmol/L (reference <6). The patient was not on any proton-pump inhibitors. A neck, thoracic, and abdominal CT scan showed a slight enlargement of the left adrenal gland with attenuation of 25 Hounsfield units. A 111In-pentetreotide-SRS scan after an injection of 166 MBq 111Indium-labeled octreotide demonstrated no uptake typical for an ectopic ACTH source. Treatment with cabergoline was initiated but quickly withdrawn due to side effects of dizziness, nausea, and uncontrollable shaking. Due to moderately elevated liver enzymes, ketoconazole 200mg twice daily was started despite the liver enzyme issue. Metapyrone (metyrapone) was also administered in increasing doses up to 2.5g, but further increases were limited by side effects including increased flushing and anxiety attacks. No clinical improvement was observed, and ketoconazole was discontinued due to further deterioration in liver enzymes. Cortisol and ACTH levels remained stable during the investigational period. Due to the deterioration of her health condition, a bilateral adrenalectomy was planned. The PET center in Uppsala, Sweden was contacted for further investigation.
test_results: An 11C-5-HTP-PET was performed showing an 8mm mass in the left lung lower lobe with focal uptake.
Orpha_name: Cushing syndrome due to ectopic ACTH secretion

case_report: A 7-year-old female patient visited the clinic for a routine eye examination. Her uncorrected vision was found to be perfect in both eyes. During the anterior segment examination, yellowish-white crystallized opacities were noted throughout the corneal stroma in both eyes. The rest of the anterior segment examination showed no abnormalities, and the fundus examination was normal in both eyes. The patient was subsequently referred to a university hospital.
test_results: Urinalysis revealed hemoglobin 1+ and protein 2+; 24-hr urine analysis results were phosphorus: 14.4 mg/dL, creatinine: 16.6 mg/dL, phosphorus: 3.73 mg/dL; and blood biochemistry test showed normal albumin, calcium, and sodium levels.

case_report: A 1-month-old male infant was brought in with a swelling located in the occipital region, which had been present since birth. The parents reported that the swelling had gradually increased in size to its current dimensions of 14 cm × 12 cm. The affected area featured dysplastic skin and was encircled by a ring of coarse hair. The lesion had a cystic appearance and contained clear fluid. It was compressible, nonpulsatile, transilluminant, and its size and tension remained unchanged regardless of the infant's position or crying.
test_results: Computed tomography scan of the head revealed a 14 cm subcutaneous mass of soft tissue density similar to the brain tissue, with no intracranial communication. The brain parenchyma appeared unremarkable.

case_report: A 16-year-old male presented with a history of limited movement in his elbows, thumbs, and great toes since early childhood. He experienced knee and ankle pain following physical activities and had minor deficits in fine motor skills. Physical examination revealed pectus excavatum, a high-narrow palate, and a bifid uvula. The patient had dental braces to address crowded teeth, crossbite, and to widen the palate. He exhibited large hands and feet, long fingers with bilateral fifth finger clinodactyly, reduced thumb flexion, and slightly medially deviated halluces bilaterally. There was an absence of skin creases over the distal interphalangeal joints of the toes, halluces, and thumbs. His mental development, growth, hearing, and male genitalia (Tanner stage 4) were within normal limits.
test_results: Radiographs revealed a bilateral radial head dislocation of the elbows and partial bilateral fusion of the thumbs' interphalangeal joint. A similar pattern was seen in the feet with a fusion of the interphalangeal joints of dig I and of the distal interphalangeal joints of dig II-V. Radiographs raised suspicion for a bilateral calcaneonavicular coalition, and the lumbar spine showed a fusion of the dorsal portions of the vertebrae L3 to S1 with reduced height of the disc L3-L4 and L4-L5.

case_report: A 27-year-old male clerk, born from a non-consanguineous marriage, visited the dermatology outpatient department with complaints of reticulate hyperpigmentation over the body, including the palms and soles, photophobia, reduced sweating, heat intolerance during summers, and nail abnormalities since birth. His family history was unremarkable. Dermatologic examination revealed reticulate hyperpigmentation covering the entire body, with hair showing mild pigmentary dilution and patchy golden brown discoloration. The pigmentation was particularly dense on the palms and soles, displaying a rain drop pattern, while the elbows, knees, and dorsal aspect of the tongue exhibited a reticulate pattern. The teeth were yellowish, with abnormal dentition and enamel defects. The skin on the dorsal aspect of the hands and feet appeared atrophic, shiny, and wrinkled, and the nails showed severe dystrophy affecting all fingers and toes. Dermatoglyphics were absent, and the skin was dry. General physical examination indicated the patient was thinly built and had pallor. Systemic examination was normal, except for an ophthalmic examination that revealed mild corneal degeneration. Other ophthalmic findings were within normal limits. Baseline investigations, including complete blood counts, liver and renal function tests, and urine analysis, were within normal limits except for a hemoglobin level of 9 g/dL. The patient's blood arsenic level was below the detection limit.
test_results: A biopsy specimen from a hyperpigmented macule on the back showed findings of epidermal atrophy, vacuolar degeneration, hyperpigmentation of the basal layer, and pigmentary incontinence. The dermis showed perivascular chronic inflammation, increased dermal fibrosis, with presence of dermal melanophages. Molecular analysis for KRT 14 gene mutation using genomic DNA from the blood of the patient was done by the method of PCR-bidirectional sequencing of exons 1, 4, and 6. It showed absence of mutation in the three exons (1, 4, and 6).

case_report: An 8-month-old female infant presented with a dusky red swelling on the right forearm. She was born at term via normal vaginal delivery to nonconsanguineous parents. The swelling began as a pinkish-red patch at 1 month old and gradually increased in size over the following 7 months. The parents observed excessive sweating and increased hair growth over the affected area. The infant's overall physical health was normal, with no history of bleeding. On examination, there was a single dusky red to violaceous, ill-defined indurated plaque covering most of the forearm, mainly on the ventral side. The lesion was nonblanchable, tender to touch, and warmer than the surrounding skin. Hyperhidrosis and hypertrichosis were noted at the margins. No other systemic abnormalities were found. Hematological and biochemical tests, including coagulation profile, were normal. A roentgenogram of the limb showed soft-tissue swelling without any bone abnormalities. An ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis was noncontributory.
test_results: The skin biopsy from the lesion on hematoxylin- and eosin-stained sections demonstrated the presence of discrete lobules or tufts of capillaries scattered in the superficial and deep dermis. The capillary lobules were highly cellular and densely packed with vascular spaces. Immunohistochemistry was positive for CD34, smooth muscle actin, and vimentin confirming its vascular origin.

case_report: A 64-year-old woman exhibited erythematous plaques with peripheral detachment and multiple erosions located in the inframammary, axillary, inguinal, dorsal, cubital, and popliteal fossa regions. The mucous membranes were unaffected. She noted a family history of similar lesions in her mother, siblings, and maternal aunts. Her medical history includes systemic hypertension, coronary artery disease, congestive heart failure, dyslipidemia, and hypothyroidism.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed acantholysis with intra-epidermal cleavage involving the entire epidermal thickness, demonstrating absence of dermal villi and eosinophils.

case_report: A 54-year-old Caucasian woman presented in September 2006 with complaints of pain, loss of function, and weakness in her right shoulder, persisting for several years. Conservative treatments, including analgesics and physiotherapy, provided minimal relief. Her primary concern was the increasing loss of function in her right shoulder. She also reported experiencing several unexplained falls but did not describe a waddling gait or hypotonia. She had osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures at thoracic levels 5 and 6, with a compensatory hyperlordosis of the lumbar spine. Following a traffic accident in 2004, she received conservative treatment for fractures of the right scapula and sternum. She occasionally experienced dysaesthesia in both hands. She mentioned progressive muscle atrophy in both shoulders and upper arms, which had been previously attributed to trauma and inactivity. Her family history, including her two sons, was negative for neurological or systemic diseases. There was no intellectual impairment or facial weakness. Clinical examination revealed no cardiac or pulmonary issues. Findings included a frozen right shoulder, significant isolated muscle atrophy of the deltoid and biceps muscles bilaterally, and a rotator cuff tear involving the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles on the right side. There were no signs of muscle impairment in the hip or thigh. Neurological examination results were normal, and gait analysis showed no waddling gait. Despite progressive muscle atrophy in both shoulders over the years, serum creatine kinase levels were only slightly elevated at 186 U/l.
test_results: The exact pattern of muscle atrophy was detected by a MRI of both shoulders which showed a fatty muscular atrophy of the delta- und biceps-muscle on both sides and a rotator cuff tear on the right. The results of the immuno-histological analysis matched a chronical myopathy with related endo-, peri- and epimysial fibrosis. Trauma and inflammation were excluded as causes. Further analysis (western blot) revealed an abnormal and reduced laminin α2 chain and an abnormal reduced α-dystroglycan.

case_report: The patient is a 53-year-old female from a family with no consanguinity, having healthy parents and older siblings. She presented with a history of progressively worsening unsteady gait, slurred speech, and uncoordinated movements for over 20 years. Neurological examination showed signs consistent with cerebellar involvement, including gaze-evoked nystagmus, saccadic pursuit with hypometric saccades, scanning speech, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and a wide-based gait. Both cranial nerve examination and mini-mental state examination were normal. Tests including nerve conduction velocity, electromyography, and electroencephalography were normal. Brain magnetic resonance imaging indicated diffuse cerebellar atrophy.
test_results: Novel heterozygous mutations were identified in exon 18 (NM_182961, c.1922del, and p. N641Mfs) and exon 31 (NM_182961, c. C3883T, and p. Q1295X), which caused frameshift and nonsense mutations (stop-gain). These mutations were confirmed using Sanger sequencing. According to the Sanger sequencing results, segregation of the novel SYNE1 variant (c.1922del, p. N641Mfs) was present in all of the patient’s family members and that of the other novel truncating variants (c. C3883T, p. Q1295X) was present in one of her older sisters (II:2).

case_report: A 40-year-old Saudi woman, who has never given birth and has no significant medical history aside from a previous myomectomy for leiomyoma (uterine fibroid), presented with a large abdominopelvic mass, tense ascites, and pleural effusion. She reported experiencing shortness of breath, palpitations, significant abdominal discomfort, bloating, and back pain. These symptoms began approximately three months prior to her visit, but she was delayed in seeking medical attention due to the COVID-19 pandemic. She is a housewife, does not smoke or consume alcohol, and has no recent travel history to areas with endemic or pandemic diseases. Laboratory investigations revealed an elevated serum CA-125 level of 492.6 U/mL (normal < 35 U/mL), while other tumor markers including LDH, CEA, CA19-9, and ALP were within normal limits.
test_results: Abdominal CT scan revealed a significant interval increase in the size of ascites, which caused a huge abdominal distention along with severe mass effects on the abdominopelvic organs, which have been displaced posteriorly. In addition, it revealed a large exophytic uterine fibroid measuring 15 × 20 × 17.5 cm. On pathology of surgical specimens, a giant uterine leiomyoma with degenerative changes, pleural and ascitic fluids was yielded negative for malignancy and diagnosed as a benign mesothelial proliferation, whereas H&E stain of the omentum excision confirmed multiple, large and irregular disorganized veins (thin-walled blood vessels) and arteries (thick-walled blood vessels), some with organized thrombi consistent with omental AVM.
diagnosis: Pseudo-Meigs’ syndrome with omental arteriovenous malformation

case_report: A 25-year-old male patient underwent surgical removal of a mediastinal mixed germ cell tumor, which included teratoma, embryonal carcinoma, and choriocarcinoma. He received four cycles of BEP (bleomycin, etoposide, and carboplatin) and two cycles of etoposide and carboplatin in 2009. Six months post-treatment, he reported experiencing easy fatigability and generalized weakness. Physical examination revealed pallor without lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or other abnormalities. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 6 g/dl, pancytopenia with a total leukocyte count of 3000/μl, and a platelet count of 20,000/μl. The peripheral blood smear did not show any abnormal cells. A subsequent bone marrow tap was dry.
test_results: The touch preparation showed few poorly preserved blasts, morphology of which was not clear. The decalcified sections of the biopsy were initially stained with hematoxylin and eosin stain and showed partial replacement of normal marrow by blasts. The blasts had scant to moderate cytoplasm with one to three prominent nucleoli, a few of them were binucleate and a few megakaryocytes showing multinucleation were also seen. On immunohistochemistry, the blasts were negative for myeloperoxidase and leukocyte common antigen, but positive for CD 61.

case_report: A 27-year-old male with no prior medical history was found by his parents with his head covered by a bag connected to a helium gas tank. Upon arrival of the emergency team, he exhibited impaired consciousness (Japan Coma Scale I-3) and hypoxemia (SpO2 90% on room air), though he was breathing spontaneously with stable hemodynamics. His SpO2 improved to 97% with oxygen administration. The duration of helium exposure and the time between the inhalation attempt and hospital arrival were unknown. At the hospital, his blood pressure was 131/73 mmHg, heart rate was 148 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 30 breaths per minute, and body temperature was 37.2°C. He had good oxygenation (SpO2 96% on room air) but was tachypneic. Due to persistently impaired consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale E4V2M4) and restlessness, he was sedated and intubated. Physical examination showed normal light reflexes, no limb paralysis, and no subcutaneous emphysema or other signs of airway injury. Blood tests revealed elevated white blood cell counts (19,910/mm3), lactate levels (3.4 mmol/L), and creatine kinase levels (2,883 U/L). Oxygenation was within normal range, and other test results were unremarkable.
test_results: His head computed tomography (CT) scan showed no obvious intracranial hemorrhage, cerebral infarction, or air migration to the brain.
Orpha_name: Neonatal hypoxic and ischemic brain injury

case_report: A 63-year-old man presented with a two-month history of widespread redness and thickening of the skin, sparing the axillary and inguinal regions. Neurological examination revealed muscle wasting in the interosseous muscles of the hands, ulnar claw deformity, tingling sensations in the hands and feet, and thickening of the ulnar and fibular nerves. There was significant swelling in the hands and feet. The patient reported no prior skin conditions or recent exposure to new medications or allergens.
test_results: Skin biopsies revealed epidermis with regular acanthosis, spongiosis and dermis with chronic epithelioid granulomatous infiltration in perivascular, periadnexial and perineural patterns. Fite-Faraco staining showed isolated and grouped acid-fast bacilli. Immunohistochemistry with anti-BCG was positive within nerves and inflammatory cells.

case_report: A 28-year-old Chinese woman presented with a history of fever and multiple pustules and subcutaneous abscesses within erythematous plaques on the medial parts of her bilateral thighs and buttocks at the age of 24 in 1996. These symptoms did not improve with various antibiotics. Laboratory results showed a mild leucocytosis of 13.0 × 10^9/L (normal range: 3.5–9.5 × 10^9/L), with 82% neutrophils, haemoglobin level of 9.5 g/dL (normal range: 11.5–15.5 g/dL), and a platelet count of 310 × 10^9/L (normal range: 100–350 × 10^9/L). C-reactive protein (CRP) was elevated at 20.2 mg/L (normal range: 0-8 mg/L), and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was significantly raised at 105 mm/1st hour (normal range: < 20 mm/1st hour). Renal and liver functions, urinalysis, and coagulation profile were within normal limits. A skin biopsy from the upper extremity showed neutrophil infiltration in the upper layer of the epidermis and dermis, forming abscesses. Multiple bacterial cultures from pustules and abscesses were negative for bacterial infection. The patient was subsequently treated with oral prednisolone (40 mg/day), cyclosporine (100 mg/day), and triptolide (60 mg/day). The prednisolone dose was gradually reduced and discontinued after six months following disease remission.
