In June 1998, she developed a rash with ulcerated pustules on the left lower extremity, which improved with asaisone (8 mg/day). Glucocorticoid treatment was stopped in February 2000. In April 2000, three months before admission, she experienced dizziness and a fainting episode, and was found to be pulseless in both upper limbs. Upon admission, physical examination revealed multiple scar-like lesions with surface shrinkage on her extremities. Neither radial nor brachial arteries were palpable, and blood pressure in both upper extremities was 0 mmHg. Lower limb pulses were normal, with blood pressure readings of 160/70 mmHg on the right side and 168/80 mmHg on the left.
test_results: The right innominate artery (subclavian artery, common carotid artery) was completely obliterated. Collateral circulation had formed. The left common carotid artery was entirely occluded. The initial segment of the left vertebral artery had stenosis, and the left vertebral artery was enlarged. No obvious abnormalities were found in the right upper extremities.

case_report: The patient is a 9-month-old twin girl of Sri Lankan descent, born to non-consanguineous parents, with a healthy twin sister. She exhibited congenital underdevelopment on the right side of her body, including limb abnormalities and a skin condition characterized by red, scaly patches extending from her neck to mid-thigh, including the upper arm. Additional findings included the absence of the right kidney and asymmetrical enlargement of the brain's ventricles, more pronounced on the left side. Notably, the patient also had underdeveloped hands with fused fingers, a feature not previously documented.
test_results: We performed whole exome sequencing and found a novel heterozygous variant (NSDHL, c.713C > A, p.Thr238Asn).
diagnosis: Congenital hemidysplasia with ichthyosiform erythroderma and limb defects  syndrome

case_report: A 3-year-old previously healthy Sri Lankan boy presented with drooping of the upper eyelids for three days and unsteady gait with sleepiness and reduced activity for two days. He did not have seizures, blurring of vision, limb weakness, swallowing or breathing difficulties, or bladder dysfunction. He was born to nonconsanguineous, healthy parents, had a normal perinatal period, and was developmentally age-appropriate. There was no recent history of vaccination, febrile illnesses, snake bite, or behavioral changes before the onset of symptoms. On examination, he was conscious and responsive with a GCS of 15/15. He had bilateral ptosis; however, his vision, eye movements, size of the pupils, pupillary light reflex, fundoscopy, and examination of other cranial nerves were normal. He walked with a broad-based ataxic gait and had dysmetria with positive finger nose test bilaterally. He did not have dysarthria, nystagmus, involuntary movements, or Romberg sign. Limb examination revealed normal tone and grade five muscle power in all four limbs and normal upper limb reflexes. The knee and ankle jerks were easily elicitable, and plantar responses were flexor bilaterally. There was no muscle fatiguability, sensory involvement, or signs of meningism. The examination of cardiovascular and respiratory systems was normal. His complete blood count, C-reactive protein, serum electrolytes, and calcium were normal, and the ESR was 22 mm/1st hour. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination revealed lymphocytic pleocytosis (polymorphs 2/mm3 and lymphocytes 20/mm3) with elevated proteins (55 mg/dL); however, the CSF was negative for oligoclonal bands. EEG and noncontrast CT brain were normal.
test_results: MRI brain revealed high signal intensities involving the subcortical white matter of parietal and occipital lobes, midbrain, cerebellar vermis, right cerebellar hemisphere, and right caudate and lentiform nuclei without diffusion restriction or contrast enhancement.

case_report: A 6.5-year-old Brazilian boy has experienced repeated episodes of widespread annular erythematous skin lesions, mainly on his face and limbs, starting from 15 days old. He has had difficulty gaining weight and has developed facial lipoatrophy, frontal bossing, and erythematous, swollen fingers. At 3 years old, he began having recurrent fevers. By the age of 5, he showed signs of lipodystrophy and fixed flexion contractures in the interphalangeal joints. He does not exhibit neurodevelopmental delays, muscle pain, or weakness.
test_results: A skin biopsy revealed a non-specific perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with dermal mucinosis. Laboratory evaluation showed microcytic anemia, elevated acute-phase reactants (ESR and CRP), hypertriglyceridemia, and elevated hepatic and muscle enzymes. A muscle biopsy revealed irregular muscle fibers (atrophic and hypertrophic), without inflammatory infiltrate.

case_report: A 58-year-old Caucasian female with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) on hemodialysis was brought to the emergency department (ED) by emergency medical services (EMS) due to concerns about an acute stroke. The patient reported that 18 hours before arrival, she experienced an inability to move her lower extremities, which rapidly progressed to include her upper extremities. She mentioned completing her last dialysis session two days prior and adhering to her scheduled hemodialysis appointments. Since her last session, her diet mainly consisted of potatoes, but she could not provide further dietary details. Her medical history includes hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Her home medications are a 90-mcg ProAir inhaler, a 160/4.5-mcg Symbicort inhaler, an insulin aspart sliding scale before meals, and 20 units of insulin glargine every other day. She did not take any of these medications the day before her symptoms began. The patient denied any trauma, recent vaccinations, infections, or use of diuretics or medications that could elevate potassium levels. Family history was non-contributory, and her social history included tobacco use. In the ED, her vital signs showed a heart rate of 49 beats per minute, a temperature of 37.9 °C, a blood pressure of 119/65 mmHg, an oxygen saturation of 100% on room air, and a respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute. Physical examination revealed an alert and responsive female who could not move her upper and lower extremities but had preserved sensation in all four extremities. There was no facial asymmetry, aphasia, dysarthria, or hemispatial neglect, and visual field testing was normal. Her National Institute of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score was eight. A rhythm strip performed by EMS upon arrival showed bradycardia with a heart rate of 49 beats per minute and a wide QRS complex. The patient was immediately given 2 g of intravenous (IV) calcium gluconate and 50 mEq IV sodium bicarbonate. A head computed tomography (CT) scan was performed and showed no signs of ischemia or intracerebral hemorrhage.
test_results: The patient’s chemistry panel revealed a sodium level of 120 mmol/L, potassium of 8.5 mmol/L, chloride of 94 mmol/L, creatinine of 5.0 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen of 43 mg/dL, and glucose level of 126 mg/dL. The complete blood count (CBC) was within normal limits. An initial 12-lead ECG performed in the ED showed a wide complex tachycardia with intraventricular conduction delay, a heart rate of 98 beats per minute, and a widened and prolonged QRS interval at 216 ms.

case_report: The patient is a 10-year-old female who was born at full term. By the age of 1 year, she was evaluated for growth failure. Current physical examination findings include short stature, a high-pitched voice, and distinct craniofacial features such as a triangular face, broad forehead, broad nasal root, and bilateral medial pseudo-strabismus due to bilateral epicanthial folds. Additional observations include abdominal distention with mild hepatosplenomegaly, pallor, swollen lymph nodes in the neck, dilated veins on the chest wall, periorbital edema, minimal pitting edema in the lower limbs, clubbed fingers, and scoliosis. The patient exhibits normal psychomotor development.
test_results: Abdominal echography confirmed the hepatosplenomegaly and revealed moderate-volume ascites, a hepatic cyst and dilated intrahepatic bile ducts. Liver biopsy revealed focal interstitial fibrosis. Endocrine evaluation of the patient revealed growth hormone (GH) deficiency and delayed bone age. Estimated bone age was ∼6.5 years by the time of evaluation. Echocardiogram findings included the following: dilated left atrium, mitral regurgitation, tricuspid regurgitation, atrial septal defect with left to right shunt and dilatation of inferior vena cava and suprahepatic veins. The ejection fraction was within the normal range (68%). X-ray images revealed normal long and pelvic bones and a characteristic J-shaped sella turcica. Urinary system abnormalities included bilateral vesicoureteral reflux that was more prominent in the right side, hydronephrosis of both kidneys and signs of chronic renal disease in the right kidney, such as poor corticomedullary differentiation and cortical atrophy that were confirmed by renal scintigraphy. Intravenous pyelogram (IVP) revealed right ureteropelvic junction obstruction and subsequent hydronephrosis. Three months after the surgery, reevaluation by renal scintigraphy revealed no improvement in the function of the right kidney.

case_report: A 10-year-old girl presented with an 8-month history of skin changes on her right upper limb. The patient was in good health overall, with no notable family medical history and an unaffected twin sister. The skin changes initially appeared as bruise-like discolorations. On physical examination, there were atrophic, non-sclerotic, and band-like hyperpigmented plaques observed on her right forearm and upper arm.
test_results: An initial punch biopsy revealed an unremarkable epidermis save for prominent melanin deposition in the basal layer. Mild inflammatory changes were also noted in the specimen with perivascular and focally interstitial lymphoid infiltrates without any obvious signs of sclerosis.

case_report: A 10-year-old female patient presented with complaints of drooping eyelids and decreased vision in both eyes for the past 2 years. Her parents also noticed impaired hearing and generalized weakness. The family history was unremarkable. A general physical exam revealed short stature. The best corrected visual acuity was 6/18 in both eyes. Extra-ocular movements were full with end gaze nystagmus. Bilateral moderate ptosis was noted with poor Bell’s phenomenon. Anterior segment examination was unremarkable. Fundus examination in both eyes showed pigmentary changes with optic disc pallor. Acetylcholine receptor antibody test was negative (<0.11 nmol/L). Electro-myography did not show evidence of neuro-muscular abnormality. Repetitive nerve stimulation study indicated post-synaptic myasthenia syndrome.
test_results: Muscle biopsy showed ragged red fibers on trichrome staining. She had right bundle branch block.

case_report: A seventeen-year-old female presented with concerns about delayed onset of menstruation. She reported no abdominal pain, cyclic pain, abdominal mass, or vaginal discharge. Additionally, she had no issues with urination, constipation, or history of surgeries. She is the younger sibling of another patient previously documented. On physical examination, her vital signs were within normal limits. Neck examination did not reveal an Adam's apple. Chest examination showed breast development at Tanner stage I and axillary hair at Tanner stage II. The abdominal examination was normal. Examination of the external genitalia showed pubic hair at Tanner stage III, a micropenis, clitoral hypertrophy, and normal vulva, major and minor labia. The vaginal canal measured 4 cm in length. A rectal exam identified only vaginal structures upon palpation. Previous laboratory tests indicated a testosterone level of 271 ng/dL, estradiol at 23.29 pg/mL, and FSH at 19.75 IU/mL. Subsequent tests showed a testosterone level of 613 ng/dL, dihydrotestosterone at 11 ng/dL, and a T/DHT ratio of 55.73.
test_results: Karyotype revealed 46 XY. Ultrasonography examination revealed testis at the right and left proximal inguinal canal, along with phallus at the anterior vulva. Uterus and adnexa were not found on abdominal ultrasonography. Pelvic Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) confirmed the structure of bilateral testes, corpus cavernosa, and bulbospongiosus muscle. Uterus and adnexa were not found on MRI.
Orpha_name: 46,XY difference of sex development due to 5-alpha-reductase 2 deficiency

case_report: A 39-year-old woman presented with gastric and pelvic masses discovered during a routine examination at a local hospital in October 2021. Enhanced CT scans of the abdomen and pelvis identified two masses: one in the fundus of the stomach and another on the right side of the pelvis. The patient sought treatment at our hospital. Physical examination was unremarkable, with no palpable abdominal masses, and her blood pressure and heart rate were 109/70 mmHg and 72 bpm, respectively. Re-examination with enhanced CT showed a soft tissue mass measuring approximately 33 mm × 54 mm in the gastric wall on the greater curvature of the gastric body, with clear boundaries and a smooth surface. A nodule measuring 26 mm × 29 mm was observed on the right anterior side of the pelvic wall, with unclear demarcation from the bladder wall. No other abnormalities were noted. The patient underwent laparoscopic surgery on October 9, 2021. During the procedure, a mass approximately 55 mm × 35 mm was found in the posterior wall of the gastric body, and a wedge resection of the stomach was performed. Several nodules suspected to be enlarged lymph nodes on the greater omentum adjacent to the mass were also excised and sent for frozen-section analysis, which revealed fibrous connective tissue. During the separation of the mass from the bladder, the patient's blood pressure rapidly increased to 180/120 mmHg. The anesthesiologist recommended pausing the operation, and continuous arterial blood pressure monitoring was initiated before resuming the procedure. An intraoperative consultation with a urologist confirmed that the mass originated from the right side of the bladder apex. Complete excision of the mass and bladder repair were performed.
test_results: The patient had a SDHB c.137G>A germline mutation.

case_report: The patient is a 17-year-old male, the only child of a healthy, nonconsanguineous couple, with an unremarkable family history. The pregnancy and full-term delivery were normal, but post-birth, he exhibited motor retardation and marasmus. He showed delayed motor development, standing at 18 months and walking at 2 years. Throughout childhood, he experienced progressive limb weakness and unsteady movements, failing physical education classes since primary school. At age 8, he began having recurrent episodes of loss of consciousness, characterized by dropping objects, lasting about 1 minute, occurring 5-6 times per year. By age 12, his weakness worsened, making stair climbing and carrying objects difficult, accompanied by myoclonic seizures in the head and slight clonic episodes in all four limbs, occurring both day and night. He also had difficulty using chopsticks and bowls, walked with faltering steps, and struggled to walk straight. At age 10, he developed inarticulate speech, with all symptoms progressively worsening. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg, height of 165 cm, and weight of 40 kg. He had normal vision and hearing but a left-bending thoracic spine. Neurological examination showed slurred speech with normal other cranial nerve functions. Muscle atrophy was noted in all four limbs, with proximal lower limb circumference at 31 cm and distal lower limb circumference at 27.5 cm. Bilateral motor power ratings were: biceps and triceps muscles at 4−/5, hand and wrist muscles at 5−/5, iliopsoas muscles at 4−/5, quadriceps femoris muscles at 5/5, biceps femoris muscle at 4+/5, and anterior tibial, gastrocnemius, and soleus muscles at 5/5. Muscle tone in all four extremities was low. The patient could not complete the heel-knee-tibia or finger-nose tests on either side and showed clumsiness in rapid alternating movements. Positive signs included beat back and Romberg signs. Deep and superficial senses were normal, tendon reflexes were weakened, and both Kernig and Brudzinski signs were negative.
test_results: Serum creatine kinase (CK) level was 431 U/L (normal range: 24–194 U/L). Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) level was 63.9 U/L (normal range: 0–35 U/L). Basal lactate in serum was elevated (>5 mmol/L, normal range: 0.7–2.1 mol/L). Results of electromyogram were consistent with myopathy.
diagnosis: Myoclonic Epilepsy with Ragged Red Fibers Syndrome

case_report: A 31-year-old female from Kanpur, UP, with a normal birth history but delayed motor milestones, presented with a 7-year history of progressive difficulty swallowing, drooping of both eyelids, and nasal-sounding speech, along with frequent respiratory tract infections. Physical examination showed bilateral ptosis, limited eye movement, and a high arched palate. There was noticeable wasting of the temporalis muscles on both sides. Speech was low in volume with a nasal quality. Systemic examination indicated generalized muscle weakness and reduced muscle tone, particularly in the proximal muscles of both the upper and lower limbs. Routine blood tests were normal, and creatine kinase (CK) levels were 168 IU/mL.
test_results: EMG revealed sharp, small duration polyphasic.

case_report: This male patient was two years and seven months old at the time of evaluation. He was the second child of a healthy, unrelated couple with no family history of birth defects or genetic disorders. He was born at 39 weeks of gestation via normal delivery. His birth weight was 4000 g (75-90th percentile), birth length was 51 cm (50th percentile), and head circumference was 37 cm (75-90th percentile). Due to respiratory failure, the patient required intubation and artificial respiration and was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU). At six months, he was seen at the Second Xiangya Hospital for developmental delay. At that time, he weighed 8000 g (75-90th percentile), had a length of 72 cm (50th percentile), and a head circumference of 43 cm (75-90th percentile). Brain MRI showed mildly reduced volume of the white matter and a thin corpus callosum. Electroencephalogram (EEG) showed no definite abnormality. Currently, his length is 79 cm (50th percentile), weight is 12 kg (50th percentile), and head circumference is 48.6 cm (75-90th percentile), indicating that his head is relatively large compared to his stature. Physical examination revealed frontal bossing, high forehead, deep-set eyes, sparse eyebrows, a flat nasal bridge, low-set ears, high-arched palate, bilateral strabismus, and pectus excavatum. He is unable to sit up or walk independently and cannot speak any meaningful words.
test_results: His psychomotor development was evaluated by the GESELL Developmental Diagnosis Scale (GDDS) and the developmental quotient (DQ) was determined to be 19. Neurological examination revealed generalized hypotonia and reduced deep tendon reflexes. Peripheral nerve conduction velocities showed no abnormalities. Conventional G-banding analyses showed no abnormalities.

case_report: A 50-year-old Chinese man with no prior illnesses presented with a one-month history of fever, headache, and vomiting. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed multiple ring-enhancing lesions of varying sizes scattered in both cerebral and cerebellar hemispheres. A computer tomographic (CT) scan of the thorax showed a 6.5 cm × 4.5 cm mass in the right upper lobe extending to the right hilum. Laboratory results indicated mild leucocytosis at 11.7 × 103/uL and a normal C-reactive protein level of 1.5 mg/L. Lumbar puncture demonstrated raised intracranial pressure of 26 cm H2O with clear cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) drainage. The CSF analysis showed an elevated cell count of 260 cells/mm3 with 90% lymphocyte predominance, low glucose at 1.9 mmol/L, and raised protein at 1.15 g/L. Initial mucicarmine and India Ink staining did not reveal any organisms. Subsequent testing detected CSF cryptococcal antigen, and CSF fungal culture grew C. gattii. Blood cryptococcal antigen was detected at a titre of 1:1280. Human immunodeficiency virus testing was negative. Bronchoscopy was performed to evaluate the right upper lobe mass. Bronchoalveolar lavage showed thick-walled fungal yeast forms with narrow-based budding, highlighted by mucicarmine special stain. Bronchoscopic biopsies revealed non-specific chronic inflammatory infiltrates in the submucosal stroma of the bronchial wall epithelium and lung parenchyma. The patient received induction anti-fungal therapy with four weeks of amphotericin B and two weeks of flucytosine, followed by maintenance therapy with oral fluconazole. Therapeutic lumbar punctures were performed to treat raised intracranial pressure. On outpatient review, brain imaging showed complete resolution of cerebral cryptococcomas at five months of therapy. CT chest performed for monitoring of the right upper lobe showed a reduction in the size of consolidation. However, at 15 months of anti-fungal therapy, new ground-glass opacities were observed in all lobes, with focal areas of crazy-paving pattern in the bilateral upper lobes. This coincided with the onset of a new cough. Differential diagnoses included drug pneumonitis, interstitial pneumonias, and new opportunistic pulmonary infections. Flexible bronchoscopy was repeated, but no new opportunistic infections were detected. Bronchoalveolar lavage returned turbid fluid, occasional alveolar macrophages were seen, and periodic acid Schiff (PAS) stains did not reveal any abnormalities or fungal elements. Transbronchial lung biopsies showed normal lung parenchyma.
test_results: Histological examination of the lung parenchyma showed intra-alveolar accumulation of foamy macrophages and airspaces containing PAS-positive amorphous eosinophilic material with strong immune positivity for surfactant A.

case_report: The patient is a 38-month-old male who was born at 39 weeks of gestation to consanguineous parents of Syrian origin. The father is 38 years old, and the mother is 35 years old, with no known genetic or chronic diseases. The patient has three healthy sisters aged 11, 10, and 6 years. He was delivered vaginally without complications, with Apgar scores of 9 at 1 minute and 10 at 5 minutes. His birth weight was 3.05 kg (6th percentile), length was 53 cm (54th percentile), and head circumference was 34 cm (6th percentile). He was admitted four times for lower respiratory tract infections, including pneumonia, bronchiolitis, and bronchitis. Additionally, he had ten upper respiratory tract infections associated with otitis media and conjunctivitis, which resolved spontaneously. He was treated for a cutaneous abscess, skin rash, impetigo, and candidal stomatitis. The patient experienced two generalized tonic-clonic seizures at one and three months of age, and one undocumented seizure at seven months of age. An EEG at seven months showed no abnormalities. Developmental delays were noted at one year of age. By 36 months, he could only say his name and a few two-word sentences. He started crawling at 15 months, walking at 26 months, running at 30 months, and walking up stairs at 36 months. Fine motor skills were delayed, with a pincer grasp developing at 24 months. Social skills, such as waving, began at 32 months. He was breastfed and given formula milk until three months, then switched to formula feeding until 26 months, after which he started a regular diet. He currently has a normal diet with no known food allergies or feeding problems. Bowel movements were once or twice a week until 24 months, then once or twice per day. Behavioral abnormalities included daily night terrors until 24 months and hyperactivity noted by family members but not clinically significant. At 32 months, his height was 95 cm (10th percentile) and weight was 14.0 kg (50th percentile). Dysmorphic features included a prominent forehead, posteriorly rotated ears, low nasal bridge, bulbous nasal tip, malar hypoplasia, deep-set eyes, macroglossia, prominent upper lip, flat philtrum, and short fingers. A brain MRI at 11 months showed normal and progressive myelination but mild loss of volume in the corpus callosum. Lab investigations at 36 months showed normal complete blood count, liver function tests, renal function tests, and a complete metabolic panel. Immunoglobulin levels were: IgA 1.28 g/L (normal 0.30–1.3 g/L), IgG 10.3 g/L (normal 3.1–15.8 g/L), and IgM 1.14 g/L (normal 0.50–2.20). An ENT evaluation at 33 months revealed no abnormalities.
test_results: The test revealed normal methylation patterns of DMR1 (H19), and the DMR2 (KCNQ1OT1) imprinting regions were observed. There were no deletions or duplications in the 11p15 region.

case_report: A term male infant was born to a 28-year-old Japanese woman after an uncomplicated pregnancy. At birth, the infant presented with skin nodules, petechiae, and right facial nerve palsy and was referred to our hospital at one day of age. Examination revealed widespread dusky red papules and nodules (0.5 cm–1.5 cm in diameter) with ecchymosis predominantly on the scalp, trunk, and distal extremities. Additionally, he had right facial nerve palsy, but there was no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. There were no dysmorphic features, and chromosome analysis on cultured peripheral blood lymphocytes and fibroblasts derived from buccal mucosa showed a normal male karyotype. Blood count on admission showed a white blood cell count of 1.63 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin level of 12.6 g/dL, and a platelet count of 3.4 × 10^9/L. A peripheral blood smear demonstrated 56% neutrophils, 4% monocytes, and 40% lymphocytes, with no blasts. The serum lactate dehydrogenase and C-reactive protein were 987 IU/L and 1.01 mg/dL, respectively. The results of the Coombs test, tests to rule out congenital infections, Toxoplasma gondii, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus type 1, and parvovirus B19 infection, and blood cultures were negative. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed multiple intracranial tumors. Cerebrospinal fluid was normal. A biopsy specimen of the skin nodule showed a diffuse infiltration of mononuclear cells with large oval nuclei. These cells stained positive for CD43, CD42b, and CD30 but negative for CD1a, CD68, CD34, CD56, CD99, and S-100.
test_results: Bone marrow aspiration revealed blasts with cytoplasmic blebs comprising 4.8% of the marrow nucleated cells. The blasts were positive for CD41 antigen on flow cytometric analysis. Cytogenetic studies of the bone marrow revealed hyperdiploid: 51, XY, +7, +8, +14, +19, +22 (10/20 cells).

case_report: An 11-year-old boy was admitted with symptoms of cough, fatigue, and weight loss (~4 kg) over a period of 4 months, and hemoptysis starting the day before admission. His past medical history was unremarkable. His mother was Spanish, and his father Dutch. The family medical history did not indicate any autoinflammatory or autoimmune diseases. Clinical examination revealed a pale appearance, but no oral or genital ulcers. Laboratory tests showed elevated inflammatory markers (ESR 59 mm/h; CRP 69 mg/L; leucocytes 12.2*10^9/L), microcytic anemia (Hemoglobin 6.2 mmol/L; MCV 65.9 fl), and normal renal function (serum creatinine 42 μmol/L; urinary protein excretion 0.1 g/24 h). Tests for tuberculin skin, pathergy, plasma lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipins, direct Coombs, angiotensin converting enzyme, ANA, and ANCA were negative. A chest X-ray indicated a broad mediastinum without pulmonary abnormalities. A CT-scan revealed an enlarged subcarinal mediastinal mass extending towards both pulmonary hili, without parenchymal disease. The patient experienced febrile episodes every afternoon (up to 39°C) and mild myalgia. A bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy and bronchial alveolar lavage was performed, but the biopsy results were inconclusive. A cervical mediastinoscopy was conducted, and histological examination of the enlarged lymph node showed a reactive pattern with numerous lymphocytes, lymphoblasts, and plasma cells, without signs of malignancy, tuberculosis, or sarcoidosis. Cultures of sputum, blood, stomach contents, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, and serology did not identify an infectious cause for the reactive lymphadenopathy. An ophthalmological evaluation revealed bilateral papilledema, with no additional symptoms of raised intracranial pressure.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging of the cerebrum showed dural venous sinus thrombosis with extensive collateral vessel formation. Physical examination revealed a cardiac murmur, due to tricuspid regurgitation, and a loud second heart sound, suggesting pulmonary hypertension. This was confirmed by cardiac catheterization. The mean pressure in the left pulmonary artery was 30 mmHg, the pulmonary wedge pressure was 13 mmHg, the cardiac index was 2 l/min/m2, and the pulmonary resistance measured 8.4 resistant units per m2, indicating moderate pulmonary hypertension. Angiography and CT-angiography showed multiple aneurysms in the medium sized arteries (pulmonary artery).

case_report: In July 2013, a 53-year-old male, Caucasian, unemployed, from Mundo Novo, State of Bahia, Brazil, visited the Stomatology Clinic at University Hospital. He reported experiencing pain, nasal obstruction, and difficulties with swallowing and throat pain. Physical examination revealed a painful, red, and easily bleeding lesion in the right nasal cavity, along with an infiltrative lesion on the hard and soft palate, and uvula. Additionally, there was an ulcerated lesion on the left eyebrow and right eye with seropurulent discharge, a small ulcer on the lower eyelid, a lesion on the lobe of the right ear, and another lesion in the malar region. The patient was admitted for the management of widespread skin lesions.
test_results: A biopsy of the palate lesions revealed a non-specific erosive chronic inflammatory process. The patient was positive for Montenegro reaction.

case_report: A nine-year-old boy arrived at the emergency department with a painful erection that began spontaneously earlier in the day and persisted for several hours. He had experienced a fever for three days prior but had no other symptoms. Upon examination, the boy was in pain with an erect penis but was otherwise in good health and developmentally appropriate for his age. He had no signs of puberty (Tanner stage one), no lymphadenopathy, ecchymosis, or jaundice, and his eye examination was normal. There were no indications of abuse, and both the patient and his mother denied any history of trauma. Laboratory tests showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 9.6 g/dl) with a normal full blood count and blood film. Additional tests indicated a prolonged prothrombin time and moderately elevated C-reactive protein, while electrolytes and other blood tests were normal. Hemoglobin electrophoresis was normal, excluding abnormal hemoglobins such as HbS, HbF, and normal HbA2. Deficiencies in folate, B12, and iron were ruled out. Penile Doppler ultrasonography showed decreased blood flow to the cavernous bodies. An abdominal ultrasound revealed some inflammatory mesenteric lymph nodes measuring between 1 and 1.3 cm in diameter. The patient received intravenous dextrose and analgesia. A surgical consultation led to an urgent aspiration and warm saline lavage of the cavernosa, which successfully relieved the priapism. The aspirated blood was dark and deoxygenated. A full coagulation study was later conducted while the patient was on analgesics, fluids, and low-molecular-weight heparin, which was subsequently switched to warfarin. The study showed mildly elevated protein C activity, normal protein S activity, normal fibrinogen degradation products, normal antithrombin III antigen, and elevated homocysteine levels.
test_results: The result revealed that factor II, factor V Leiden, and the MTHFR (1298) mutations were normal, while the MTHFR mutation (C677T) result was a homozygous mutant gene.
Orpha_name: Homocystinuria due to methylene tetrahydrofolate reductase deficiency

case_report: A 6-month-old Sudanese female infant was referred for consideration of liver transplant. She was born to second-degree consanguineous parents. The pregnancy was uncomplicated, and she was delivered at term by lower segment caesarean section weighing 2.5 kg. Jaundice was noted at birth, and phototherapy was initiated. Persistent unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia was observed, with levels ranging between 20 and 25 mg/dl and a conjugated fraction of less than 0.6 mg/dl. There was no evidence of hemolysis or liver dysfunction. The infant was exclusively breastfed and was developing appropriately for her age. At the time of referral, she was receiving home phototherapy daily. Upon admission to our hospital, she was placed on standard phototherapy for 10 to 12 hours each day. Clinical examination revealed icterus with normal systemic findings. Her weight and height were 6.9 kg and 65 cm, respectively, both at the 50th percentile. Her development and neurology were appropriate for her age. Apart from elevated unconjugated bilirubin, her full blood count, liver transaminases, coagulation profile, serum albumin, and liver imaging were unremarkable.
test_results: Molecular analysis revealed a normal wild type TATA box (A(TA)6TAA) sequence in our patient and her parents. Further analysis of the exon-intron boundaries in the patient revealed a novel homozygous 22 bp duplication (c.55_76dup) in the coding region of the Exon1. This 22 bp duplication causes a frame shift leading to a premature stop codon resulting in a truncated 62 amino acids protein. Both parents of the patient were heterozygous for the 22 bp (c.55_76dup) duplication. No mutations were detected in the other coding exons.

case_report: The patient is a 60-year-old Caucasian woman who experienced recurrent left pneumothoraces. She also presented with mild scoliosis, an increased metacarpal index, and mitral valve prolapse. Her family history includes mitral valve prolapse in both her mother and one of her daughters, and her brother has Usher's syndrome. Her parents were first cousins. Over a period of 10 years, the patient had additional pneumothoraces that required video-assisted pleurodeses and bullectomy. Serial CT scans revealed cystic lung disease, predominantly at the lung bases, and the development of mild bronchiectasis. In late 2004, during an examination by clinical geneticists, it was observed that the patient had pale, flat macules on her face and forehead, which had been present for at least 10 years.
test_results: A biopsy of a lesion from her neck confirmed the presence of a fibrofolliculoma. Germline mutation analysis of the folliculin (FLCN) gene identified a pathogenic mutation c.2052-2053 del, p.GlnfsX in exon 14.

case_report: A 7-year-old girl presented with pain in her left thigh and a limp. She had no history of trauma, disease, or surgery. The pain had persisted for 3 weeks before her visit to the outpatient clinic. The ranges of motion for her left hip were as follows: flexion at 130°, abduction at 30°, extension at 10°, internal rotation at 45°, and external rotation at 10°. The circumferences of her right and left thighs were 29.5 cm and 28.5 cm, respectively. Initial plain radiographs showed no abnormalities. A T2-weighted MRI scan of the hip joints revealed no abnormal findings except for left hip joint effusion. She was placed on bed rest for 4 weeks and advised to avoid weight bearing during this period. Despite this, her left thigh pain and limping did not improve. Ultrasonic measurements of the joint spaces (distance from the anterior cortex of the femoral neck to the front of the capsule) were 6.0 mm on the right side and 8.7 mm on the left side 4 weeks after the initial visit. Anechoic findings indicated joint effusion in the left hip joint space. T1-weighted and T2-weighted MRI scans taken 2 months after the initial visit showed a linear low-signal-intensity region at the left femoral capital epiphysis. Follow-up continued despite no abnormalities being found. The ultrasonic joint space measured 11.6 mm on the left side 2 months after the initial visit. Echoic findings indicated synovitis in the left hip joint space. A culture of the joint aspirate returned negative results. Laboratory data showed no abnormalities. The ultrasonic joint space measured 12.3 mm on the left side 3 months after the initial visit, indicating progression.
test_results: Plain radiograph showed bone resorption at the left femoral capital epiphysis 3 months after the initial visit. Bone scintigraphy findings showed a cold-in-hot pattern at the left femoral capital epiphysis.

case_report: A 22-year-old male patient, with no significant medical history, presented with a three-day history of fever, abdominal pain, and umbilical discharge without any digestive or urinary symptoms. On physical examination, the patient had a temperature of 38.9°C, purulent discharge from the umbilicus with surrounding erythema, and a tender mass at the umbilicus. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 24,000/mm3 and a C-reactive protein level of 42 mg/L. Urinalysis and renal function tests were normal. Culture of the umbilical discharge identified Klebsiella pneumoniae, while blood cultures were negative.
test_results: Abdominal ultrasonography showed echoic collection in a midline cavity within the anterior abdominal wall. Computed tomography scan showed a heterogeneous collection with calculus and gas formation communicating with the umbilicus.

case_report: A 13-year-old male student presented with a flattening of the right anterior chest wall since birth. He had no symptoms other than cosmetic concerns. He was the second child in his family, with no similar presentations or associated familial disorders reported. Physical examination showed normal growth parameters and IQ. There were no abnormal craniofacial findings. The chest wall was asymmetric with underdevelopment on the right side. The patient exhibited normal strength in the right upper limb and a full range of motion in the shoulder joint. Both limbs were symmetric with no finger anomalies. Auscultation of the chest revealed normal heart sounds, breath sounds, and respiration pattern.
test_results: Computed tomography scan revealed that the pectoralis major muscle was underdeveloped, but the pectoralis minor muscle and the anterior serratus muscle were present. Radiological examination of the chest showed no abnormalities of the ribs or heart.

case_report: On March 7, 2018, a 35-year-old Chinese female presented with a one-year history of persistent erythematous papules and infiltrative plaques on the nose without any obvious triggers. Initially, a hard nodule the size of rice grains appeared on the right alar part of the nose, which was painless and itchy. Over time, the skin lesions gradually increased in size, became thick, and spread across the entire nose. Infiltrating plaques also developed on the upper jaw. Past and family history revealed no similar diseases within the family. Since the onset of the illness, the patient’s urine, stool, and weight remained normal. Skin examination revealed diffuse erythematous papules, infiltrations, and hypertrophic plaques on the entire nose and upper jaw, with a smooth surface. Dermoscopy showed a bright red background with diffuse telangiectasia, but no obvious keratinized hair follicle structures. Laboratory examinations, including antinuclear antibody, anti-dsDNA antibody, anti-Ro, anti-La, and Borrelia, as well as direct immunofluorescence serology, yielded negative results. Blood and urine routine tests, liver and kidney function tests, chest X-ray, and ECG all showed no obvious abnormalities. Maxillary CT plain scan with enhancement revealed several findings: (1) a soft tissue nodule in the right soft palate, with multiple enlarged lymph nodes in both necks, and thickening and enhancement of nasal soft tissue; (2) right frontal sinus and ethmoid sinusitis.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the biopsy sample showed a normal epidermis and an inflammatory infiltrate consisting of dense perivascular lymphocytes, as well as lymphocytes surrounding hair follicles and sweat glands in the dermis. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated a predominance of CD4+ T cells compared to CD8+ T cells. The immunohistochemical panel further revealed positive staining for CD3, CD4, CD8, CD20, CD43, CD68, CD1a, and Ki-67 (10%), while staining for CD123, CD56, GB, PAS, and acid-fast organisms was negative. TCR gene rearrangement analysis did not show any clonal amplification peaks in the target fragment.
diagnosis: Jessner’s Lymphocytic Infiltration of the Skin
Orpha_name: Jessner lymphocytic infiltration of the skin

case_report: A 28-year-old male underwent simultaneous bilateral SMILE for myopia correction at a private clinic and presented to our clinic 2 days later with visual loss and severe ocular pain in his right eye. His medical history showed he was immunocompetent before surgery, with no history of HSV keratitis and no apparent infection risk factors. He did not use contact lenses. Upon presentation, his uncorrected distance visual acuity (UDVA) was reduced to counting fingers at 30 cm in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Ocular slit-lamp examination of the right eye revealed several white infiltrates within the interface, a central epithelial defect, keratic precipitates on the endothelium, 2+ cells in the anterior chamber, and intraocular hypertension. Lens and fundus details were not visible due to hazy media. The patient was taken to the clinic's operating room, where his right eye was irrigated with balanced saline solution, and topical moxifloxacin was administered via the stromal pocket. Corneal scrapes from the stromal pocket were collected for microscopic examination, inoculation of culture media (blood agar, chocolate agar, Sabouraud dextrose agar, and Mannitol salt agar), and gram staining.
test_results: PCR assay of corneal tissue revealed the presence of HSV DNA.

case_report: The patient is a 29-year-old woman who presented to our Hepato-Bilio-Pancreatic and Splenic Unit with a 3-month history of continuous abdominal pain in the right upper quadrant, which occasionally intensified. She also reported abdominal distension, a palpable mass in the right lower quadrant, and constipation. Her medical history includes polycystic ovary syndrome and gastritis. She has no children, experienced menarche at age 14 with regular menstrual cycles, and has been taking oral contraceptives for 13 years. She has no history of liver disease, diabetes, hypertension, or dyslipidemia, and does not smoke or use recreational drugs. Her body mass index (BMI) is 16 kg/m2. Her current medications include chlordiazepoxide + clidinium bromide and an oral contraceptive containing estradiol valerate 1–3 mg + dienogest 2–3 mg, which she has been taking for the past 5 years. An abdominal ultrasound revealed a solid nodular lesion originating in the right hepatic lobe. A CT scan confirmed a solid pedunculated nodular lesion in segment 5. An MRI with paramagnetic hepatospecific contrast showed an exophytic nodular lesion measuring 56 mm × 83 mm with a heterogeneous signal in different weightings. The lesion heterogeneously captured the contrast product mainly peripherally, with central areas of hyposignal likely due to fibrosis/hyalinization, in an otherwise normal liver. Liver function tests were normal except for a slight increase in total bilirubin (2.05 mg/dl). Other laboratory parameters, including leukocytes, hemoglobin, platelet counts, and renal function tests, were within normal ranges. Serum tumor markers (alpha-fetoprotein, CEA, and CA19-9) were normal, and serum virus markers (HBV, HCV, and HIV) were negative.
test_results: Histological examination showed a hepatocellular tumor with a peripheral area with a predominant trabecular pattern with steatosis, cholestasis, and fibrovascular septa with a lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate. In the central area, there were foci of atypical cells and necrosis. There was no vascular or perineural invasion. Immunohistochemical study showed expression of HEP-PAR-1, liver fatty acid-binding protein (LFABP), C-reactive protein (CRP), and glutamine synthetase (GS) in the neoplastic cells. The beta-catenin expression was membranous only. The tumoral cells had no expression of glypican-3 (GPC-3) and heat-shock protein 70 (HSP-70). Investigation for mutations in the CTNNB1 gene was made through the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) technique, with direct sequencing of PCR products obtained from tumoral DNA. However, no mutations were found.
diagnosis: Well-differentiated hepatocellular neoplasm with morphologic characteristics of an inflammatory adenoma

case_report: A male neonate weighing 2,020 g was delivered by a 33-year-old Chinese mother (gravida 2, para 2) via cesarean section. The parents are non-consanguineous. During the first 5 weeks of pregnancy, the mother was treated with progesterone and dydrogesterone until week 13 due to signs of abortion. At week 24, the mother developed lower limb edema, which progressed to anasarca by the end of the pregnancy. She was diagnosed with gestational diabetes at week 25, with blood sugar levels controlled through diet. By 36 weeks, an ultrasound showed oligohydramnios, a normal heart silhouette, increased cardiothoracic ratio, and small lung volume. Labor was induced at week 36 due to oligohydramnios and a 3-hour premature rupture of the fetal membrane. The placenta was grayish red with focal purple-red areas, and the umbilical cord appeared normal. The Apgar scores were 5 at 1 minute and 7 at 5 minutes. Ten minutes after birth, the neonate was admitted to the NICU for ventilation support due to tachypnea. Physical examination revealed a weak response, weak crying, hoarseness, respiratory distress, positive signs of triple concave, and anasarca. The neonate exhibited several distinct clinical features, including dysmorphic hypertelorism, down-slanting eyes, eye movement disorder, ectropion, hypophasis, thickened helix, constricted auricular rim, curled auricle and auricle cartilage, flat nasal bridge, small nostrils, and everted lips. The skin was ichthyotic and collodion-like, covering the entire body with a shiny, red, tight appearance, and was very friable. Extensive peeling was noted on the hands, feet, groin, and scrotum, exposing red tender skin. Breath sounds were clear with no rales. A continuous machinery murmur was heard at the upper left sternal edge, and a 3/6 pansystolic murmur was noted across the precordium, clearest at the left sternal edge. The abdomen was markedly distended, with the liver palpable 5 cm below the right costal margin and 6 cm below the xiphoid process, and the spleen palpable 6 cm below the left costal margin. Both organs had an extremely firm, stone-like texture. The neonate was immobile except upon stimulation, with flexion contractures at the elbow and knee joints, hypertonia, and akinesia. Myoclonic movements were observed soon after birth, with limb jitters lasting about 10 seconds. The bilateral testes were undescended, and the neonate had small microcaulia. Primitive reflexes were absent. At birth, the CBC showed a platelet count of 19,000/mm3, WBC 11,880/mm3, and hemoglobin 143 g/L. At 2 days of age, the CBC showed a platelet count of 8,000/mm3, WBC 13,170/mm3, and hemoglobin 165 g/L. Liver function tests indicated hypoproteinemia (TP 53.1 g/L, ALB 26.9 g/L), elevated enzymes (AST 123.4 U/L), and cholestasis (TBILI/DBILI 43/28 μmol/L, TBA 25 μmol/L, γ-GT 183 U/L, ALP 249 U/L), with LDH 326 U/L at birth. Peak values were TBILI 89 U/L, DBILI 69 U/L, TBA 37 μmol/L, γ-GT 773 U/L, ALP 296 U/L, LDH 1055 U/L. Initial coagulation tests showed PT 25.7 s, APTT 40.4 s, TT 26.4 s, INR 2.08, FIB 0.79 g/L. Bone marrow aspiration at 5 days of age indicated proliferous granulocytic and erythroid cells, a high lymphocyte ratio, and three megakaryocytes in the smear. Pathology of the placenta, fetal membrane, and umbilical cord showed chronic inflammation with placental villi denatured necrotic calcification focus and umbilical cord arteriovenous congestion and focal hemorrhage. Echocardiography at birth revealed normal atrium and ventricular chamber size, normal ventricular wall thickness, normal valve structure, normal aorta and pulmonary artery connection and diameter, LVEF 62%, a patent ductus arteriosus with a continuous left-to-right shunt signal, a ventricular septal defect with a small left-to-right shunt signal, moderate tricuspid regurgitation, and a pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 54 mmHg. Abdominal ultrasound showed palpable hepatosplenomegaly and cholestasis. Genital ultrasound revealed bilateral testis hydrocele. At 2 days of age, lung CT indicated a lack of air in the lungs, and brain CT revealed multiple hemorrhagic lesions in the left frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes. At 9 days of age, craniocerebral MRI disclosed a small hemorrhagic lesion in the left parietal lobe with widening of part of the external space. At 14 days of age, the neonate developed frequent tonic seizures, and EEG showed sharp waves, spike waves, and outburst suppressions with no observed sleep cycle. At 16 days of age, no hemorrhagic lesions were found in the craniocerebral MRI. At 19 days of age, echocardiography showed LVEF 63%, VSD with a small left-to-right shunt signal, and a pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 47 mmHg. At 35 days of age, echocardiography showed LVEF 60%, VSD, and a pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 38 mmHg. Cytogenetic evaluation revealed 46 XY with no copy number variation associated with clinical symptoms detected in the whole genome copy number variation analysis.
test_results: The leukocyte enzyme assay for β-glucocerebrosidase revealed an activity of 0.00 nmol/h/mg (control range: 10–25 nmol/h/mg).

case_report: A 44-year-old French male with no significant medical history presented with his first episode of acute global heart failure. He is of Caucasian phenotype and has not traveled outside the north-east region of France. The patient reported lower limb edema and new-onset dyspnea classified as New York Heart Association (NYHA) Class III. Upon admission, his vital signs were stable: blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg, heart rate was 80 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 15 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation was 96% on room air, and body temperature was 37°C. Physical examination revealed regular heart sounds and lower limb edema extending to the knees, without jugular venous distension or hepatojugular reflux. Bilateral inspiratory crackles were noted on auscultation. Electrocardiogram results were normal. Initial blood tests indicated elevated NT-pro-BNP levels at 1674 pg/mL (reference range < 300 pg/mL) and a mild inflammatory response with leukocytes at 14.3 × 10^9/L (reference range 4–10 × 10^9/L) and C-reactive protein at 15.8 mg/L (reference range < 5 mg/L). Renal function was within normal limits with creatinine at 93 µmol/L (reference range 59–104 µmol/L) and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 86 mL/min/1.73 m^2. Eosinophil count was 0.2 × 10^9/L (reference range 0.1–0.4 × 10^9/L). Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a dilated and hypokinetic left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 40%, and an atypical appearance at the left ventricular apex. No significant valvular abnormalities were detected, but elevated pressures were noted on both the right and left sides, along with dilated and hypokinetic right cavities. The pericardium appeared normal. The patient was admitted to the cardiology ward, where he received intravenous loop diuretics, resulting in early favorable clinical improvement. A coronary angiogram showed normal coronary arteries, but ventriculography revealed filling at the left ventricular apex. Haemodynamic assessment showed a dip-and-plateau pattern on the left ventricular pressure curve.
test_results: Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) showed a hypo-intense T1/T2 signal circumscribed to left ventricle apex assessed by balanced steady-state free precession sequence without immediate gadolinium enhancement but with sub-endocardial late enhancement.

case_report: A 17-year-old male, who is right-hand dominant and previously healthy, arrived at the emergency department with pain, swelling, and numbness in his left hand. Three days earlier, he had injured his left hand while playing football, though he could not recall a specific incident such as a fall or tackle. He noticed pain and swelling in his hand after the game, which worsened over the next few days. Initial imaging at an outside hospital showed no fractures or dislocations. Despite this, his pain, paresthesia, and swelling, particularly in the thenar compartment, continued to worsen. On physical examination, there was significant tenderness and swelling in the left thenar eminence and thumb, without any overlying erythema or open wounds. The patient had a severely limited range of motion in the wrist and thumb joints due to severe pain and was unable to oppose his thumb. Passive thumb motion caused significant pain, and he reported decreased sensation on the radial side of his left thumb. Sensation, capillary refill, strength, and range of motion were normal in the other fingers. Repeat radiographs in the ED again showed no bony injuries. Despite the imaging results, the patient's clinical presentation included tense swelling of the left thenar compartment, pain, decreased range of motion, and sensory deficit. Compartment pressures in the thenar compartment of the left hand were measured using a Stryker needle, with readings of 72 and 73 mm Hg, and a diastolic blood pressure of 80 mm Hg. The patient was taken to the operating room for an emergent fasciotomy. Bloodwork prior to surgery revealed pancytopenia with profound neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, and leukopenia.
test_results: Bone marrow biopsy revealed hypercellular marrow with megakaryocytes and granulocytic left shift.

case_report: A 6-year-old girl visited the pediatric nephrology outpatient clinic due to proteinuria detected during a school health screening. Physical examination showed no significant abnormalities, including in her external genitalia. Her spot urine protein/creatinine ratio (UPCR) was 1.34 g/g, and her 24-hour urine protein was 0.66 g. Renal sonography indicated increased echogenicity in both kidneys. Two months later, proteinuria persisted with a UPCR of 2.1 g/g. The patient sought a second opinion at another medical center, where a renal biopsy showed focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) in two out of seven glomeruli. The patient received several sessions of methylprednisolone (MTP) pulse therapy followed by daily oral steroids, but heavy proteinuria continued. Another renal biopsy two years later still showed FSGS (4/67 glomeruli). Over the next two years, multiple treatments were tried, including MTP pulse therapy, oral prednisolone, mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, and abatacept, but proteinuria worsened, with UPCR rising to 4.01 g/g. Regular medical treatment was stopped at age 12, and the patient began alternative herbal therapy. At age 14, she visited a gynecology clinic for a prolonged menstrual period lasting up to one month (menarche at age 12). Preliminary sonography revealed a left ovarian tumor, and she was referred to our hospital. Sonography confirmed a heterogeneous adnexal mass, and a CT scan showed a lobulated mass (maximum diameter: 10.1 cm) with cystic and solid components in the pelvis. Serum tumor markers were: CA-125, 77.96 unit/mL (normal: <35.0 unit/mL); CA-199, 57.01 unit/mL (normal: <34.0 unit/mL); alpha-fetoprotein, 94.88 ng/mL (normal: <7 ng/mL). Serum albumin was 2.2 g/dL, cholesterol 183 mg/dL, and triglyceride 133 mg/dL. The patient underwent cytoreductive left salpingo-oophorectomy one week after the CT scan. Pathology revealed a malignant mixed germ cell tumor in a gonadoblastoma of the ovary, composed of 75% dysgerminoma, 10% immature teratoma, 10% embryonal carcinoma, and 5% yolk sac tumor. Further analysis showed a chromosome karyotype of 46, XY, with the SRY gene present in PCR tests, although the patient had normal female external genitalia.
test_results: A genetic analysis that revealed a point mutation in intron 9 of the WT1 gene, c.1447 + 4 C > T.

case_report: A 22-year-old male patient was admitted to our hospital due to worsening weakness in the lower limbs over the past eight years. Initially, the patient experienced significant weakness in the distal parts of the lower limbs. Additionally, the patient had difficulty walking on toes and would easily become fatigued when walking. Over time, these symptoms progressively worsened. The patient gradually found it increasingly difficult to walk and had trouble climbing stairs. The patient reported no history of other diseases and denied any similar medical history in the family.
test_results: His creatine kinase (CK) was 6,679 U/L (reference range: 18.0-198.0 U/L). Electromyography revealed myogenic abnormal results.

case_report: In November 2021, a family brought their one-year-old boy with multiple fractures to the inpatient department of the Tomsk National Research Medical Center (TNRMC) genetics clinic. The parents, who are from different settlements and belong to the Tuva nationality, reported that they are not related and are clinically healthy. The child is the third born out of four pregnancies. The pregnancy was complicated by mild toxicosis and fetal hypoxia. At birth, the child weighed 3422 g and measured 50 cm in length, with an Apgar score of 7/8. The mother has a history of one spontaneous abortion at 10 weeks. The child's seven-year-old brother has unspecified epilepsy, while the five-year-old sister is healthy. The child first showed symptoms at three months old with a bruise on the shoulder joint. At seven months, the child experienced a closed displaced fracture of the right femur. At nine months, the child had a closed fracture of the lower third of the tibial shaft and a closed displaced fracture of the left humerus. By twelve months, the child had fractures of the 8th, 9th, and 10th ribs on the right side and a compression fracture of the L1–L3 vertebrae. During the initial examination at the TNRMC genetic clinic at 1.2 years of age, the mother reported that the child had been immobile in the right upper limb for one week. The examination revealed the child was anxious.
test_results: A non-displaced closed fracture was revealed in the upper third of the patient’s right humerus, and a closed non-displaced consolidating fracture of the right radius in the proximal section was also detected.

case_report: A healthy two-year-old white boy experienced a blunt injury to his right eye after hitting a sideboard in September 2008. He remained without symptoms until a month later when he presented to a local Casualty Department with a red and painful right eye. Upon referral to a children's hospital, he had light perception vision in his right eye and strongly resisted covering his left eye. Examination of his right eye under anesthesia showed conjunctival injection, corneal stromal haze, a significant anterior chamber reaction with fibrinous reaction and iris deposits, lens opacity, and elevated intraocular pressure of 30 mmHg. The corneal diameters were 12 mm bilaterally. Examination of the posterior segment was challenging due to significant media opacity, but the retina appeared attached. Examination of his left eye was normal. He was otherwise systemically well with no previous medical or ophthalmic history. An anterior chamber tap revealed small round cells in clumps, but the specimen was poorly preserved, preventing further evaluation. No mass lesion was seen on a magnetic resonance imaging scan of the right orbit. An ultrasound scan showed clumps of hyperechogenic material over the temporal lens surface, adjacent to but not in contact with the ciliary body, and extruding into the anterior vitreous. This was associated with a cataractous lens and the presence of cyclitic membranes. Intensive topical steroid therapy was initiated to treat the inflammation. He later underwent a right lensectomy and anterior vitrectomy in January 2009 (four months after initial presentation) and was left aphakic. Postoperatively, the intraocular pressure in his right eye became increasingly difficult to control despite the use of gutt Cosopt and Travatan. The cup-disc ratio in his right eye was noted to be 0.5 (compared to 0.1 in the left) and the right axial length was 23.6 mm (compared to 21.2 mm in the left). The angle was closed in all four quadrants, and an ectropion uvea was observed. There was no rubeosis. A limited trans-scleral cyclodiode laser was performed on the right eye two weeks later. He then underwent a right Baerveldt shunt (350 mm2) with 0.4 mg/mL Mitomycin-C in September 2009 due to further glaucoma progression, as indicated by an increase in the cup-disc ratio (0.7), axial length (25.8 mm), corneal diameter (14 mm), and intraocular pressure measurement (39 mmHg).
test_results: Ultrasound imaging revealed an irregular-surfaced mass with heterogeneous echogenicity measuring 8 mm in length by 11.3 mm in width by 5.4 mm in thickness.

case_report: A 50-year-old female patient has experienced a gradual worsening of gait disturbances since she was 37 years old. By the following year, she began to fall frequently and required mobility aids for walking. At the age of 45, she started to experience slurred speech. From the age of 46, she developed upper limb clumsiness, difficulty swallowing, and sleep disorders, and she is currently wheelchair-bound. Neurological examination showed severe ataxia affecting both the trunk and limbs, moderate horizontal nystagmus triggered by gaze, poor performance on the finger–nose test, and heel–knee–shin ataxia. Muscle strength and volume in all four limbs were normal, but muscle tone was increased. Tendon reflexes were absent, and a bilateral Babinski sign was present. The scale for the assessment and rating of ataxia (SARA) was 28/40, and the international cooperative ataxia rating scale (ICARS) was 52/100. Routine blood and urine tests were normal. The patient was born to parents who were first cousins. Her maternal and paternal grandmothers were sisters, neither of whom had any cerebellar symptoms. Her mother, now 73, began to experience slight gait unsteadiness at the age of 70 but has no issues with speech or swallowing. Her father, now 68, has a slightly unsteady gait but no slurred speech, double vision, or dysarthria. An uncle had gait problems starting in his sixth decade and passed away at 80 from unknown causes. The patient's younger brothers currently show no symptoms of ataxia.
test_results: Small and large bands were identified by DNA fragment analysis based on capillary electrophoresis on an ABI 3730XL DNA analyzer. CAG repeats of the patient were visible as 62/62, while CAG repeat sizes of her father and mother were seen as 62/18 and 65/13, respectively.

case_report: A 58-year-old male experienced a progressive decrease in vision in both eyes over a period of 2 months, along with weakness and numbness in his legs. He observed blurriness in both eyes in the morning without any associated periorbital pain or headache. There was no family history of similar conditions, and he reported no use of neurotoxic medications, smoking, or alcohol consumption. His best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/200, and color vision was 0/8 in both eyes. Fundus examination revealed temporal pallor of the optic discs bilaterally. Neurological examination indicated bilateral peripheral neuropathies, with muscle strength at level IV and paresthesia in both arms and legs. Visual field testing with an Octopus perimeter showed central scotomas in both eyes. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrated inferior-temporal retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thinning in the right eye and temporal RNFL thinning in the left eye, along with significant thinning of the ganglion cell-inner plexiform layer (GCIPL) in both eyes. Brain MRI revealed scattered T2 Flair-weighted hyperintense signals, while orbital MRI showed bilateral optic nerve atrophy without enhancement on T1-weighted imaging post-contrast. Additionally, a small pituitary tumor was noted, which was deemed irrelevant to the optic neuropathy. No spinal cord lesions were reported.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed the T12811C mutation with the heteroplasmy at the level of 98.93%.

case_report: A 6-year-old female was admitted to the orthopedics department, and a dermatological consultation was requested to evaluate non-healing, painless open sores on her left heel and lateral malleolus. Her medical history includes similar ulcers that began on the right plantar surface, tips of her fingers, and toes at the age of four. These previous ulcers resulted in spontaneous mutilation of her fingers and toes. Her history is negative for other dermatological or systemic diseases. She has achieved all developmental milestones with appropriate height and weight for her age, except for delayed teeth eruption. The patient's parents are a consanguineous couple with no relevant family history. Physical examination confirmed the presence of deep ulcers with local signs of infection and widespread necrosis, and a complete absence of teeth. Neurological examination showed decreased sensation to pain and temperature in her lower limbs. Her motor abilities were limited due to pain and edema. Angiographic evaluation with Doppler ultrasonography of her lower limbs showed no abnormalities. Assessment of other organs was completely negative. A dental consultation was sought, but no specific pathology was detected to explain her hypodontia. Her labs at admission are summarized in. A skeletal survey revealed a 1-cm lytic lesion in the body of her left radial bone.
test_results: Electro-physiologic studies showed evidence of sensory peripheral neuropathy.

case_report: A 45-year-old man presented with gradually worsening sensory issues in the lower limbs and balance problems since his early twenties. He experienced muscle pain after physical activity but did not notice any discolored urine. His walking was unsteady, especially in the dark, and he avoided sports since his early teenage years despite being able to run. In his thirties, he reported upper limb incoordination, slurred speech, worsening exercise intolerance, and fatigue. His unsteadiness led to falls up to four times a week, and he began using a walking stick at age 40. He had chronic constipation since his mid-30s and complained of erectile dysfunction without urinary symptoms. He noticed mild hearing deficits since his late 20s. His past medical history included anxiety and depression. His birth history was normal, and he met all neurodevelopmental milestones except for walking at 14 months. There was no family history of neuromuscular disease, ataxia, diabetes, or deafness. Clinical examination findings between ages 37 and 40 included dysarthric speech, upper and lower limb ataxia, broad-based gait, and positive Romberg's sign. Deep tendon reflexes were absent, and there was reduced pinprick sensation in a stocking distribution and asymmetrical loss of vibration sense. There was no eyelid ptosis, eye movements were normal, and muscle tone and power were within normal limits. Routine laboratory tests, including vitamin B12, folate, autoimmune screen, creatinine kinase, and vitamins A and E levels, were unremarkable. Serum lactate was slightly elevated at 2.7 mmol/L (normal range up to 2.2 mmol/L). Urinary thymidine and uridine levels were normal. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography at age 35 showed axonal sensory neuropathy and mild neurogenic changes in muscles. A repeat study five years later showed little progression, with reduced amplitudes in sensory nerve action potentials in all limbs and normal motor nerve function. Blood spot and plasma acylcarnitine profiles showed increased medium to long chain acylcarnitine species. He reported some improvement in exercise intolerance with riboflavin and co-enzyme Q10 supplementation. His resting 12-lead electrocardiogram and transthoracic echocardiogram were normal. MRI of the head showed mild cerebellar atrophy and a T2 hyperintensity in the right cerebellar peduncle without contrast enhancement. Ophthalmological assessment revealed pigmentary retinal changes and slight optic disc pallor. Genetic testing for trinucleotide expansions in common spinocerebellar ataxia and frataxin genes, as well as a screen of the POLG gene, showed no abnormalities. Several gene panels for Charcot Marie Tooth neuropathy type 2, autosomal dominant and recessive spinocerebellar ataxia, hereditary sensory neuropathy, and hereditary spastic paraplegia were also uninformative.
test_results: He underwent skeletal muscle biopsy of vastus lateralis at the age of 44 years.
diagnosis: MT-CO2 variant causing cerebellar ataxia and neuropathy

case_report: A 76-year-old female patient was admitted to the hospital due to a rapid decline in cognitive function over a period of 2 months. Relatives reported significant changes in her personality, including confusion and agitation. Neurological examination showed cognitive impairment with a Mini-Mental State Examination score of 19 out of 30 and a dysexecutive syndrome with poriomania, but no sensorimotor deficits were observed. Her medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), untreated pulmonary sarcoidosis, and breast cancer treated 2 years prior with breast resection, axillary dissection, local radiation, and systemic hormone therapy. Pulmonary sarcoidosis had been diagnosed 2 years earlier based on bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy, which revealed histologically non-necrotizing granuloma. Laboratory tests were largely unremarkable except for absolute lymphopenia (0.68 G/L) with otherwise normal blood cell counts. Serological tests ruled out HIV and syphilis infections. A chest X-ray identified two consolidations in the right upper lobe resembling granuloma. Cranial MRI showed diffuse, confluent, bilateral hyperintense lesions in the white matter extending from the frontal to the temporal lobes with multifocal contrast enhancement at the edges of the lesions. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed mild lymphocytic pleocytosis (24/3 cells) with a single plasma cell, a disrupted blood-brain barrier, intrathecal immunoglobulin G production, and positive oligoclonal bands.
test_results: Ultrasensitive PCR detected JC virus DNA (130 copies/mL) in CSF.

case_report: A 29-year-old male patient underwent surgery two years ago for an intradural extramedullary lesion. A midline laminectomy from T9 to T12 was performed, as indicated by radiographs, and the lesion was excised. Neurological status was evaluated using the American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) and the International Standards for Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord Injury (ISNCSCI) grading systems. The sensory, motor, and neurological levels were all determined to be T8, with an ASIA Impairment Scale (AIS) grade A. Post-surgery, the patient was placed on anti-tubercular therapy for nine months. Despite this, there was no neurological improvement, and the patient remained paraplegic, subsequently seeking rehabilitation at our center. Rehabilitation goals were established, and a structured program was initiated, including sitting, balance training, and wheelchair-assisted mobility. Bladder and bowel training were also started. During the hospital stay, the patient's sensory level, initially T8 at admission, ascended to T6 and then to T4, accompanied by truncal imbalance, which hindered balance training. A thorough neurological assessment confirmed the sensory level at T4.
test_results: An MRI of the thoracic spine with whole spine screening showed 2.5 x 2.7 x 7.3 cm of loculated fluid collection around the spinal canal extending from T9 to T12 vertebral levels involving the distal cord, conus medullaris, and cauda equina nerve roots. There was an extension of the collection into the posterior paraspinal soft tissue through the laminectomy window. Cord edema was also appreciated up to the T6 level.
diagnosis: Spinal Arachnoiditis with Dorsal Cord Herniation

case_report: The patient is a 3-year-old girl born at 37 weeks gestation via caesarean section. Her parents and elder sister are healthy with normal development. During pregnancy, the mother was referred for foetal growth restriction, microcephaly, and significant ventricular dilatation observed on ultrasonography at 28 weeks gestation. At birth, the amniotic fluid was excessive, but the placenta and umbilical cord were normal. Apgar scores were 3 and 5 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. The patient required mechanical ventilation due to an inability to breathe spontaneously. Birth measurements included a weight of 2116 g (–2.0SD), head circumference of 29.6 cm (–2.4SD), and body length of 44 cm (–1.8SD). Physical examination revealed microcephaly, microphthalmos, widely spaced eyes, and micrognathia. Truncal hypotonia with spastic tetraplegia and contractured digital joints were noted. Ophthalmologic examination showed bilateral optic nerve hypoplasia. Foetal MRI at 28 weeks and brain MRI at 6 days post-birth indicated an extremely thin cerebral parenchyma, hypoplastic brain stem, and absence of the cerebellum and corpus callosum. Tests for TORCH infections were negative, and karyotype was normal (46, XX). Post-birth, the patient experienced focal clonic seizures with occasional oxygen desaturation. Electroencephalogram revealed extremely poor background activities and focal rhythmic delta waves during seizures. Seizures were partially controlled with phenobarbital. At 1 month, a tracheotomy and tracheal separation were performed due to recurrent aspiration pneumonia, along with a gastrostomy and fundoplication. Due to pituitary agenesis, trichlormethiazide was administered for central diabetes insipidus, and hydrocortisone and levothyroxine for hypopituitarism. A ventriculoperitoneal shunt was placed at 7 months to manage head growth and assist in nursing care. At 3 years old, the patient exhibited spastic tetraplegia and lacked definite awareness of her environment.
test_results: A de novo heterozygous c.190 C>T (p.R64W) variant was identified in TUBA1A. Subsequent Sanger sequencing confirmed the presence of this variant in the patient 1 and absence in the genomes of both her parents. No potentially pathogenic variants related to malformations of cortical development were identified in any other genes in patient 1.
diagnosis: TUBA1A mutation causing severe cortical dysgenesis

case_report: A 2-year-old male patient was admitted in September 2019 due to an 'abnormal urine test found for 11 days'. Eleven days prior to admission, the patient tested positive for urine protein, with a 24-hour urine protein level of 784 mg. The patient has a history of growth retardation and delayed development, having raised his head at 6 months, sat at 10 months, walked at 1 year and 8 months, and currently, at 2 years old, has an unstable gait and can speak individual monosyllable words. The father has ankylosing spondylitis, the mother has a positive urine protein, and they are not consanguineous. The patient has a healthy sibling. On admission, physical examination showed: body temperature 36.5 ℃, respiratory rate 27 breaths/min, heart rate 115 beats/min, head circumference 45.3 cm, weight 11.2 kg (10-25th percentile), height 80 cm (below the 3rd percentile). The patient has simian lines on both hands, short and stubby fingers, and a narrow, slanted forehead. Cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable. Muscle tone was weak. Main laboratory results were normal for immune set, ANCA-related antibodies, anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies, pre-transfusion blood tests, urinary system ultrasound, electroencephalogram, and brainstem auditory evoked potentials. The patient was treated with oral levothyroxine tablets for hypothyroidism. A kidney biopsy under general anesthesia showed that 2 out of 25 glomeruli had focal segmental sclerosis. Immunofluorescence revealed no deposition of immune complexes. Electron microscopy showed diffusely fused glomerular foot processes with microvilli and no precise electron-dense deposits. The patient was diagnosed with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS). Family history revealed that many male members died prematurely from unknown causes, with one having an abnormal urine test and three others suffering from nephrotic syndrome and dying at ages 3, 5, and 8.
test_results: The LAGE3 gene on the X chromosome of the child had a classical splicing site (NM_006014.4:c.188 + 1G > A), which was rated as pathogenic according to ACMG guidelines.

case_report: A one-year-old female presented with swelling in the right inguinal region. The family history included consanguinity, with the parents being first cousins. Physical examination identified bilateral palpable gonads located in the inguinal area. The external genitalia appeared female, with a slight clitoral enlargement measuring 1.5 cm, and separate vaginal and urethral openings. Ultrasonography did not reveal any Mullerian structures, and the gonads were situated in the inguinal canal. The karyotype analysis showed 46,XY.
test_results: The test results showed that there was impairment in testosterone biosynthesis. Testosterone/dihydrotestosterone ratio was 3.6. Testosterone/androstenedione ratio was found to be 0.107. Genetic analysis showed a homozygous mutation c.761_762delAG corresponding to p.E254VfsX10 in the patient; both parents were heterozygous.
Orpha_name: 46,XY difference of sex development due to 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase 3 deficiency

case_report: A 70-year-old male was admitted for the ureteroscopic removal of ureter stones. He had been receiving glimepiride for diabetes, atorvastatin for hyperlipidemia, and aspirin, thiazide, valsartan, and carvedilol for hypertension and atrial fibrillation for several years prior to admission. The patient had previously undergone knee arthroplasty and cataract surgery without significant perioperative events. He had not taken serotonergic medications for at least 4 weeks before admission. Atrial fibrillation was well controlled before surgery. His physical status classification was American Society of Anesthesiologists class II. Spinal anesthesia was administered using hyperbaric bupivacaine (12.5 mg). The surgery lasted 40 minutes and was uneventful. Stable vital signs and alert mentality were maintained in the postanesthesia care unit for more than 30 minutes. Intravenous meperidine (25 mg) was given to relieve shivering. Five minutes after the meperidine injection, the patient reported sudden chest discomfort and difficulty breathing. Diaphoresis, agitation, and tachypnea (28 breaths/min) were observed simultaneously. Severe rigidity, tremors, and myoclonus began within 10 minutes, limited to the upper extremities due to prior spinal anesthesia. The patient soon became drowsy, confused, and uncooperative.
