Blood pressure increased from 98/65 mmHg at postoperative baseline to 199/95 mmHg, and pulse rate rose from 77 beats/min to 150 beats/min. Invasive blood pressure monitoring was initiated at the radial artery. Body temperature measured 25 minutes after meperidine injection was 39.8℃. Mental status deteriorated to stupor. Arterial blood gas analysis showed a pH of 7.436, PaCO2 of 27.2 mmHg, PaO2 of 114.6 mmHg, SaO2 of 98.4%, Na+ of 137 mEq/L, K+ of 4.46 mEq/L, and Ca2+ of 3.64 mg/dl. Esmolol (15 mg) was administered to lower the heart rate, and ipratropium bromide inhalation was started for bronchodilation. Despite supportive care, hypertension and tachycardia persisted, and body temperature increased further to 40.1℃. Esmolol infusion was started at 0.5 mg/kg/min. Despite this treatment, mental status deteriorated to semicoma. Pupils were dilated (8 mm) and unresponsive to light.
test_results: The results of the brain CT were unremarkable.

case_report: A 21-year-old male presented with an enlarged right upper limb and difficulty in function. The right arm had been larger than the left since birth, with occasional pain and swelling. These symptoms worsened when the limb was lowered. Examination revealed multiple distinct swollen areas over the entire arm and shoulder girdle, varying in size, soft, compressible, and significantly reduced in size when elevated. The right arm was shorter than the left due to overall shortening rather than localized shortening. The muscles of the arm and shoulder girdle were atrophic. The palm exhibited a bluish discoloration. No abnormalities were noted in other parts of the body. Peripheral pulses were palpable and equal in volume on both sides. The bones of the forearm and hand were underdeveloped and tender. Sensory function was intact. Muscle strength in the right upper limb was graded III to IV according to the Medical Research Council (MRC) scale. No bruits or thrills were detected, and there was no temperature difference. The elbow could fully flex but had restricted extension, fixed at 80 degrees of flexion. The cardiovascular system was normal. Blood tests showed normal results.
test_results: Radiographs showed multiple soft tissue swellings and hypotrophy of the bones of right upper limb. There were multiple well-defined radio-opaque lesions consistent with phleboliths in the affected upper limb and periscapular region. Musculoskeletal ultrasound showed multiple dilated tortuous anechoic lesions involving the upper limb and periscapular region. Echogenic lesions with shadowing suggestive of phleboliths were seen inside the anechoic lesions. The forearm muscles were thinned and replaced by these anechoic lesions. Color Doppler study showed no flow within the lesion but, while performing a Valsalva maneuver, there was sluggish flow within the lesion suggestive of dilated torturous venous channels involving the superficial venous system. The proximal part of the deep venous system appeared normal but the distal part was not visualized. The arterial system appeared normal. An MRI study showed multiple dilated veins in the superficial aspect of the right upper limb. The muscles of the limb were replaced by an abnormal signal. The triceps, biceps and deltoid were partially involved. No intra-osseous venous malformation was seen. The arteries were normal.

case_report: A five-year-old boy presented with blurred vision in the right eye since birth. There was no notable family history or significant birth history. He exhibited mild psychomotor delay. His best-corrected visual acuity was finger counting at 2 meters in the right eye and 20/30 in the left eye. Cycloplegic refraction measured +2.50 Dsph/–1.75 Dcyl × 60 in the right eye and plano in the left eye. External examination revealed latent nystagmus and dissociated vertical deviation in the right eye. Additional features included moderate ptosis in the right eye, synophrys, long and curly eyelashes, a crescent-shaped mouth with thin downturned lips, a low philtrum, and low-set ears. Anterior segment examination showed microcornea (horizontal visible corneal diameter = 9.5 mm) in the right eye, while the left eye was unremarkable. There was a relative afferent pupillary defect in the right eye.
test_results: Fundus examination revealed choroidal coloboma involving the optic disk and inferonasal peripapillary area in the right eye along with peripapillary pigment ring. Fundus examination in the left eye revealed optic disk pit with cup disk ratio of 0.3:1 and peripapillary pigment ring.

case_report: A 36-year-old male presented with subacute onset heart failure, palpitations, and atypical chest pain. His medical history included schizophrenia with a previous admission for paranoia and suicidal behavior 10 years ago, along with cardiovascular risk factors such as hypertension, smoking, dyslipidemia, and obesity (BMI 48 kg/m2). His medications included bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily, ramipril 5 mg daily, simvastatin 20 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lamotrigine 25 mg daily, risperidone 4.5 mg daily, and lorazepam 2.5 mg daily. Initial examination showed a heart rate of 150 beats per minute, blood pressure of 110/55 mmHg, and peripheral oxygen saturation of 90%. Heart sounds were rapid without murmurs, jugular venous pressure was elevated at 45°, and there were bilateral pulmonary rales and pedal edema. Electrocardiogram indicated rapid atrial flutter (150 beats per minute) and non-specific ST changes. A transesophageal echocardiogram excluded left atrial appendage thrombus, allowing for safe cardioversion with a 150 Joules synchronized shock, successfully reverting the patient to sinus rhythm. Transthoracic echocardiogram revealed extrinsic compression on the left atrium and moderate left ventricular systolic dysfunction with global hypokinesia. Coronary angiography showed no epicardial coronary disease but identified a large vascularized mass posterior to the heart, primarily supplied by an anomalous feeder branch from the left circumflex coronary artery. Contrast CT scan revealed a large mediastinal mass (61 × 53 × 33 mm) with heterogeneous arterial-phase enhancement and compression of the left atrium. The mass had poorly defined borders suggesting local invasion of the pulmonary arteries and pericardium. No other masses or suspicious ganglia were found in the thoracic, abdominal, or pelvic regions.
test_results: Hormonal analysis showed significant elevation of 24-h urinary and plasmatic normetanephrine values. A subsequent whole-body 123-MIBG scintigraphy confirmed an isolated enhanced uptake in the mediastinum.

case_report: A 53-year-old female with a history of a skin condition diagnosed at the age of 47 years presented with a sudden onset of widespread itchy vesicles and papules over her extremities and back. The eruption began on the back and quickly spread to her trunk and extremities. Upon presentation, she was in good overall health and recovering well 10 days post-operatively following a thyroid lobectomy for Grave’s disease. Physical examination revealed multiple pink-to-erythematous crusted papules, vesicles, and bullae with a few scattered pustules over the back, trunk, upper, and lower extremities. Physical examination also showed characteristic nail changes including longitudinal white and red streaks and distal V-notching. Tests excluded a concomitant viral eruption with negative swabs for herpes simplex and varicella-zoster virus. Wound cultures of deroofed vesicles grew scant staph aureus, likely from skin colonization.
test_results: A skin biopsy of an intact vesicle was performed showing prominent lymphocytic infiltrate with acantholysis and dyskeratosis, and in the area of the vesicle formation, there was a suprabasilar split with scattered eosinophils and occasional dyskeratotic cells.

case_report: A 57-year-old female with a seven-year history of difficulty breathing presented to our department in 2021. Since 2014, she had been experiencing shortness of breath and dizziness following physical activities. In 2018, she developed rashes on her neck and chest. In 2020, she was hospitalized due to difficulty breathing. Pulmonary function tests indicated type I respiratory failure and asthma. Blood tests revealed elevated red blood cell count and abnormal monoclonal protein levels. Bone marrow biopsy results were normal. She was treated for asthma and given hydroxyurea, but there was no improvement. Her breathing difficulties worsened during treatment, leading to her referral to our department. Upon admission, her oxygen saturation was 89%. Physical examination revealed dilated blood vessels on her neck, chest, and abdomen, peripheral cyanosis on the extremities, and skin pigmentation on her face and extremities. Laboratory tests confirmed elevated hemoglobin levels (181g/L) and monoclonal protein (M protein 35.4%, IgG-λ(+)). Her erythropoietin level was 209.77mIU/mL, and her TNFα level was elevated. Bone marrow biopsy showed 10.5% plasma cells. Abdominal CT showed no perinephric fluid, and chest CT indicated emphysema and possible interstitial lung disease.
test_results: First-pass pulmonary perfusion scintigraphy confirmed intrapulmonary shunting (shunt fraction 10.4%).

case_report: A 49-year-old Caucasian woman was referred to our center with a history of fibrous dysplasia in the left femur and tibia. At age 49, an attempt to excise the fibrous dysplasia from the proximal femur resulted in significant hemorrhaging, leading to her referral. Upon arrival, she reported progressive pain in her left thigh and lower leg. Physical examination revealed soft swelling in the left quadriceps region. X-rays of the left leg showed features of fibrous dysplasia in the proximal femur and tibia, including a ground glass appearance and a shepherd's crook deformity. MRI of the left leg indicated extensive fibrous dysplasia throughout the femur with expansive growth in the greater trochanter and fibrous dysplasia in the proximal tibia extending 20 cm distally from the tibial plateau. Four well-delineated, cyst-like, intra-muscular soft-tissue lesions were observed in the quadriceps region. Surgery was planned in two stages. Before each operation, angiography and embolization of the abnormal vascularization in both the femur and tibia were performed. The first operation involved intra-lesional excision of the tumor in the left proximal femur, followed by cryosurgery. A correctional osteotomy of the left hip was performed, along with homologous bone transplantation and fixation using a proximal femoral nail. Due to a weakened femoral head, the femoral neck screw was stabilized with bone cement, and allograft bone chips were used to induce bone matrix. An incisional biopsy of the soft-tissue lesions in the quadriceps muscle was also performed. Three weeks later, an intra-lesional excision of the fibrous dysplasia in the left tibia was conducted, followed by cryosurgery and implantation of a massive allograft inlay in the tibia, which was fixed with AO screws. During this procedure, the soft-tissue lesions in the quadriceps muscle were excised. Microscopic examination of the bone lesions in both the femur and tibia revealed hypocellular fibrous tissue with irregular bone formations and no cytologic atypia. One lesion contained remnants of fracture callus. The soft-tissue lesions showed a paucicellular tumor with spindle-shaped or stellate cells embedded in a loose myxoid alcian blue-positive inter-cellular matrix with sparse capillary blood vessels.
test_results: Confocal microscopy revealed a thin fibrous capsule at the tumor margin; however, at the interface with skeletal muscle, infiltration between the individual muscle fibers was evident, which is typical of intra-muscular myxomas.

case_report: The patient is a 5-year-old Japanese female, the second child of healthy parents. There is no family history of movement disorders. The patient's mother had transient hyperthyroidism during pregnancy, the patient's aunt has hyperthyroidism, and the patient's grandmother has hypothyroidism. The patient was born at term via cesarean section and admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit at 3 days old for severe respiratory distress syndrome, requiring mechanical ventilation. At 6 days old, congenital hypothyroidism was identified (thyroid-stimulating hormone 100.0 μU/mL, FT4 1.0 ng/dL), and levothyroxine treatment was started. Thyroid echography showed a normal-sized thyroid, and thyroid hormone levels normalized with levothyroxine therapy. Lung computed tomography revealed cystic fibrosis and ground-glass opacities typical of interstitial lung disease, with elevated serum KL-6. The patient received mechanical ventilation, hydrocortisone, and prednisolone for 1 month and did not undergo phototherapy during hospitalization. She was discharged from the neonatal intensive care unit at 2 months old with home oxygen therapy for chronic lung disease. The family moved closer to the hospital for developmental follow-up. The patient's height, weight, and general examination results were within normal limits, and no dysmorphic features were noted. Deep tendon reflexes and Babinski reflex were normal, but hypotonia and ataxia were present. At 12 months old, the patient showed significant incoordination and frequent falls, leading to a diagnosis of ataxic cerebral palsy, and physical therapy was initiated. Motor developmental delays were observed: rolling over at 9 months, sitting at 15 months, walking at 24 months, and speaking her first word at 30 months. As she grew older, choreic movements of the limbs, face, and tongue at rest, and dystonic posture of the upper limbs while walking were noted. Choreic and small jerking movements of the trunk, limbs, and face were observed at rest and were not exaggerated by the finger-to-nose test.
test_results: Sanger sequencing of the NKX2-1 gene led to the detection of a novel heterozygous insertion (c.915_916insC) in exon 3 that resulted in a frameshift starting at amino acid position 303 and a premature stop codon (p.Ala303ArgfsX132).

case_report: A 10-year-old Indian boy exhibited hyperpigmented and hypopigmented macules on the backs of his hands and feet. Both palms showed hyperpigmented macules. His face had freckle-like macules, though fewer in number compared to his hands and feet. Detailed examination identified melanotic macules in the axillary regions and on the buttocks. Some hyperpigmented macules were also noted on the chest and abdomen. There were no palmar pits or mucosal lesions. He was born full-term to non-consanguineous parents after an uneventful delivery. At the age of 5, his parents first observed hyperpigmented and hypopigmented areas on the backs of his feet and hands, along with small, discrete freckle-like macules on his face. There was no history of lesion darkening after sun exposure, photosensitivity, or photophobia. The lesions were asymptomatic. The boy's intelligence was normal, and systemic examination showed no abnormalities. His past medical history was unremarkable.
test_results: Biopsy from hyperpigmented macule showed melanocytes in all epidermal layers and were present in abundance in basal layer. Biopsy from hypopigmented macule showed much less melanocytes.

case_report: A 3-year-old girl, from a non-consanguineous family, was brought to our hospital due to high myopia and low vision identified during a routine check-up. Her family history showed no notable issues. Examination showed horizontal conjugate nystagmus in both eyes. The spherical equivalent was −8.25 diopters in the right eye and −8.50 diopters in the left eye, with axial lengths of 25.16 mm and 25.19 mm, respectively. Intraocular pressure and anterior segment were normal. Dilated fundus examination revealed empty vitreous, tessellate fundus, retinal pigmental changes, and punched-out macular in both eyes. OCT findings included outer segment retina atrophy, significant thinning of the retina and choroid, macular hypoplasia, and posterior staphyloma.
test_results: A homozygous COL18A1 variant, c.3810dup (p.Val1271Arg fs*27), was identified. Both parents and her older sister were heterozygous carriers.

case_report: A 20-year-old female first visited our hospital at 7 years and 8 months old, presenting with multiple-joint swelling and restricted movement for over 5 years, along with recurrent fever for 18 months. Her history of arthritis began at 2 years old with symmetrical polyarthritis affecting both knees, wrists, metacarpophalangeal joints, and proximal and distal phalangeal joints. Initially treated at a local hospital with NSAIDs and methotrexate (MTX), her symptoms persisted. At 6 years old, she experienced repeated fevers that did not respond to anti-infection and symptomatic treatments, leading to several visits to her local pediatrician and steroid treatment for several months. At 7 years old, she reported redness in both eyes without vision loss and was treated for anterior uveitis with tobramycin dexamethasone eye drops, which resolved her ocular symptoms. Her medical history also includes a squamous rash at 10 months old. At 8 years and 9 months old, she was referred to our hospital for recurrent arthritis without ocular complaints, rash, or other symptoms. Physical examination revealed swan neck deformities of all fingers, limited joint mobility, swelling of the wrists, elbows, and knees, and a positive right 4-word test. Blood tests indicated elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), with negative rheumatoid factor and human leukocyte antigen B27 (HLA-B27). Ophthalmic examination showed no abnormalities. MRI and other imaging confirmed arthritis. Treatment included Etanercept, recombinant human tumor necrosis factor-Fc (rhTNFR:Fc) at 0.8 mg/kg per week, combined with MTX and NSAIDs, resulting in some improvement in joint swelling and fever, though symptoms recurred.
test_results: The results revealed that she had a de-novo heterozygous mutation in the NOD2 gene (c.1538 T > C, p.M513T), with her parents presenting with the wild type. The M513T (1538 T/C) mutation was a heterozygous mutation and has been reported previously.

case_report: A 29-year-old female patient presented with pain in the right lower third of the face for 7 days, which was continuous and worsened with food intake, accompanied by swelling in the same area. She had been taking analgesics with mild relief. The patient also reported multiple missing teeth and yellowish discoloration of teeth since childhood. Family history indicated no consanguineous marriage of parents. She was the eldest of three children, with a younger brother having similar dental conditions and a younger sister with no such issues. On general physical examination, the patient appeared moderately built and poorly nourished. Extraoral examination showed mild swelling in the right submandibular region. Bimanual palpation confirmed a mild, oval-shaped swelling in the submandibular region, measuring approximately 1 cm × 0.5 cm, and soft in consistency. The anterior floor of the mouth was tender on palpation, with a firm area measuring 3 mm × 1.5 mm. Hard tissue examination revealed missing teeth: 11, 21, 23, 12, 13, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 41, 42, 43, 44, and 45. Crowns were present on teeth 14, 24, and 25. All teeth exhibited hypoplasia with yellowish discoloration. A mandibular occlusal radiograph showed a radiopaque area measuring 2 mm × 1.5 mm in the anterior part. A panoramic radiograph revealed reduced enamel thickness on all teeth, multiple impacted teeth, and hypoplastic enamel. Impacted teeth included 12, 15, 17, 18, 23, 28, 31, 34, 35, 38, 41, 43, 44, 45, 47, and 48. There was a loss of coronal structure in tooth 37 with well-defined periapical radiolucency, and pericoronal radiolucency was noted in teeth 38 and 48. An oval-shaped radiolucency was observed in the anterior mandible near the alveolar crest. The patient was treated with antibiotics for sialadenitis, and the sialolith was surgically removed under local anesthesia after 3 days. The postoperative course was uneventful. Due to a history of back pain, the patient was referred to a physician for further investigation.
test_results: Computed tomography revealed multiple calcifications in the kidney and ovarian cyst.

case_report: A 7-year-old girl visited the clinic with a history of short stature and hypothyroidism. She had been receiving growth hormone therapy for one year and was taking 25 μg of thyroxine daily. Her mother reported observing fatty stool in the child for the past three years, which was often loose and floated. The patient did not experience abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Her growth rate was slower than her peers, placing her below the third percentile for weight and height (−5 z-score). She was born at term with a birth weight of 2 kg, indicating she was small for gestational age. Her parents were not related and had no significant medical history. The patient lived with her parents and two healthy siblings and was in first grade with no academic issues. Physical examination showed a body weight of 11 kg and a height of 85 cm (both below the third percentile; −5 z-score). Additional findings included an upswept frontal hairline, underdeveloped alae nasi, small teeth, and a capillary hemangioma on the inner part of the left leg. No other abnormalities were noted in the systemic examination. Laboratory results indicated normal hemoglobin levels initially, but mild anemia (Hb: 96 g/L) with microcytosis developed during follow-up. Bone and renal profiles were normal, with mild elevations in alanine aminotransferase (59 U/L) and aspartate aminotransferase (93 U/L). Amylase was elevated (137 U/L), while lipase was low (5 U/L). The patient had mild hypothyroidism with a high thyroid-stimulating hormone level (8.3 mU/L) and normal free thyroxine (FT4: 18 pmol/L). After 8 weeks of levothyroxine supplementation at a daily dosage of 25 μg, TSH normalized to 4.5 mU/L. Fecal elastase level was low (≤15 μg/mL stool). Pure tone audiometry showed bilateral mild to moderately severe sensorineural hearing loss, requiring hearing aids. Echocardiography results were normal. An abdominal ultrasound revealed increased liver echogenicity, a dilated gallbladder, and a 0.9 cm splenule.
test_results: WES test revealed identical homozygous mutations in the UBR1 gene (C2075T > C; p. Ile692Thr).

case_report: A 2-month-old male infant presented with a mass in the right lower limb, noted since birth and progressively enlarging. The mass measured approximately 5 × 5 cm, with a purplish-red discoloration and surrounding tissue swelling. The infant's past medical history, personal history, and immunization status were normal. There were no episodes of cyanosis, convulsions, or bleeding postnatally. Family history was negative for congenital malformations, tumors, or hemorrhagic conditions. On examination, the infant's vital signs were stable, and he was alert. Hemorrhagic spots were noted on the upper hard palate. A 5 × 5 cm mass was present at the right knee joint, which was warm to the touch, of medium consistency, and well-defined. No abnormalities were detected in the central nervous, cardiovascular, or respiratory systems.
test_results: The blood tests showed a moderate anemia (HGB 77 g/L) and severe thrombocytopenia (PLT 18 ​× ​109/L). The coagulation function showed prolonged clotting time (PT ​> ​120 s, reference, 10.0–16.0 s; APTT 45.1 s, reference, 20.0–40.0 s; TT 31 s, reference, 14.0–21.0 s) and significantly hypofibrinogenaemia (FBG 0.541 g/L, reference, 1.8–4.0 g/L). The coagulation profile was deranged with prolonged prothrombin (international normalized ratio [INR] out of range), activated partial thromboplastin time (prolonged >120 s above control) and elevated D-dimer levels (21.29 mg/dL, reference <0.55 mg/dL). Fibrinogen levels decreased (54.1 mg/dL, reference 180–400 mg/dL). The mass showed an iso-intense signal on T1 weighted image (T1WI) and an iso-to-mild intense signal on T2 weighted image (T2WI) in the subcutaneous fat layer of the inguinal region of the right thigh. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated multiple heterogeneous intense enhancement.

case_report: Patient V-1 is an 8-year-old girl from a large French Canadian consanguineous family. She was born at 41 weeks of gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery, weighing 3320g (50th percentile). At birth, she had no limb deformities or other abnormalities, and her sclerae were white. She achieved independent sitting at 6 months of age and had normal-appearing teeth. Her first fracture, a nondisplaced fracture in the proximal right femur, occurred at 9 months of age. A skeletal survey at that time revealed three vertebral compression fractures. The areal bone mineral density Z-score for lumbar vertebrae L1 to L4 on dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry was −0.1 at 9 months of age. Following the initiation of pamidronate treatment at 9 months, no new vertebral compression fractures were noted. Throughout her life, there were no radiographic signs of rickets. However, she experienced 35 long-bone fractures and underwent bilateral femoral intramedullary rodding.
test_results: Iliac bone biopsy showed large amounts of unmineralized osteoid in bone.

case_report: The patient is a 6-year-old boy, the first child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents. His prenatal and birth history were without complications. Convulsions began at 4 months old following the administration of the pertussis vaccine. He experienced generalized and focal febrile convulsions that did not respond to phenobarbital and valproate treatments until he was 2 years old. After turning 2, he began having generalized tonic, clonic, myoclonic, and atypical absence seizures. The myoclonic seizures were triggered by light. His psychomotor development was delayed, and he exhibited hyperactive behaviors. A brain MRI showed normal results.
test_results: Electroencephalography revealed generalized spikes and polyspikes and waves with photosensitivity. Mutation analysis revealed heterozygous deletion of five nucleotides in exon 24 (E24 n.77532-535, c.4486-4490delCAAGA, p.Gln1496ArgfsX14).

case_report: A female patient in her sixties came to our department in September 2022 with sudden worsening of her condition, experiencing shortness of breath and fatigue. In December 2020, she had been found to have stage IV melanoma metastasis of the vulva, with advanced spread to para-aortic, iliac, and inguinal lymph nodes. Following the recommendation of the interdisciplinary tumor board, she underwent surgical removal of the melanoma metastasis, which was identified as BRAF-wildtype. She was then started on systemic treatment with ipilimumab, targeting CTLA-4, and nivolumab, targeting PD-1. From January to November 2021, she received four standard doses of immunotherapy (1mg/kg nivolumab and 3mg/kg ipilimumab based on a 70 kg weight) every three weeks, followed by eight doses of nivolumab (480mg per infusion) as monotherapy every four weeks. Due to disease progression in December 2021, systemic treatment with ipilimumab (3 mg/kg) and nivolumab (1mg/kg) every three weeks was resumed. At the end of February 2022, two weeks after the third dose of combined immunotherapy and thirteen months after the initial immunotherapy infusion, the patient presented with acute onset of dyspnea and fatigue. Laboratory tests showed normocytic normochromic anemia with a hemoglobin level of 7.6 g/dL, down from 11.7 g/dL four weeks earlier, and an elevated Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) level of 326 U/l. Acute bleeding and other potential causes, such as asthma, were ruled out as the source of her symptoms.
test_results: The direct antiglobulin test (DAT) was found positive, with anti-IgG (128+) and anti-C3d positive antibodies (2+). A DAT repeated at the end of March 2022 showed a decrease in anti-IgG (16+) antibodies and was found negative for anti-C3d antibodies. Reticulocyte levels, however, remained low despite the respective treatment (5.500 cells/uL after a week of treatment). A repeated DAT in August 2022 showed a further decrease in anti-IgG (8+) antibodies, but positive anti-C3d antibodies (16+).

case_report: A 22-year-old male from Lahore District presented with pallor, yellowish discoloration of the sclera for four years, and recent pain in the right hypochondrium. He has been receiving blood transfusions every six months for the past four years. The patient was referred from the surgical OPD to the hematology section for an opinion on cholecystectomy and management of persistent anemia with mild splenomegaly. He has a history of three to four transfusions in the last five years. The patient is the product of a non-consanguineous marriage and has two elder sisters who are both healthy. His complete blood count (CBC) results were obtained from a specialized laboratory at a tertiary care hospital, verified by two independent experts. Peripheral blood and reticulocyte images were also reviewed. The patient has no history of drug intake other than hematemics, including vitamin B12 and folic acid. Despite treatment, he has persistent anemia. There is no family history of thalassemia. Laboratory findings include anemia, high reticulocyte count, and mild splenomegaly. Direct and Indirect Coombs Tests were negative. Urine examination showed no free hemoglobin or RBCs. The absence of spherocytes and normal osmotic fragility test results were noted. G6PD assays were normal at 17.7 U/gHb. Electrophoresis results showed HBA 48.5%, HBF 47.2%, and HBA2 4.3%. Genetic analysis for common mutations in Pakistan, including IVSI-1, IVSI-5, IVSII-1, del 619, Fr 8–9, Fr 16, Fr 41–42, Cd 5, Cd 15, cd 30, Cap+1, IVSI-25, Fr 47–48,-88, cd 39, Hb-S, Hb-C, Hb-E, and Hb-D (Punjab), showed no mutations. Family analysis indicated indices similar to thalassemia trait in both parents, with the father showing slightly raised HbA2 on High-performance Liquid Chromatography. Molecular analysis of common Beta-Thalassemia mutations in both parents was negative. The patient was also tested for alpha thalassemia, with no alpha gene deletion or duplication found.
test_results: Mutation in this patient was identified by genetic analysis as −88(C > A)[HBB:c.-138C > A]. The patient was homozygous for the mutation. The genetic analysis of the parents showed that both parents were carriers of the same mutation −88(C > A)[HBB:c.-138C > A].
diagnosis: Thalassemia intermedia due to novel beta-globin gene mutation

case_report: A 17-year-old female with no prior health issues or developmental concerns presented with episodes of transient loss of consciousness (LOC). Twenty-nine days prior to her hospital visit, she experienced a sudden LOC at a station on her way to school, regaining consciousness within approximately 5 minutes and continuing her day normally. There were no subsequent signs of disorientation, confusion, tongue-biting, incontinence, or paralysis. She visited a community clinic the same day, but no cause was identified. Eight days before her hospital visit, she experienced brief nausea followed by another LOC lasting less than 10 minutes at the same station. Upon regaining consciousness, she had no postictal symptoms and walked home without assistance. She was referred to the hospital for further evaluation. Her medication history included monthly ibuprofen use for mild headaches and menstrual cramps. She reported no chest pain, palpitations, dyspnea, edema, weight gain, or orthostatic hypotension. Physical and neurological examinations revealed no abnormalities. Blood tests were normal. Imaging studies, including a plain chest radiograph, electrocardiogram, and echocardiogram, showed no abnormalities.
test_results: An electroencephalogram showed diffuse bilateral bursts of spike-and-wave complexes.

case_report: A 12-year-old female presented with a 15-day history of fever, abdominal pain with distension, bilious vomiting, and constipation, along with reduced urine output for the past 3 days. On physical examination, her height and weight were below the third percentile for her age, and she exhibited pallor and pedal edema. Vital signs included a heart rate of 104 beats per minute, a respiratory rate of 42 breaths per minute, and a blood pressure of 132/90 mmHg (above the 95th percentile). Abdominal examination showed distension, a dull note on percussion, and absent bowel sounds. Chest examination revealed diminished breath sounds with occasional crackles bilaterally. Cardiovascular and central nervous system examinations were unremarkable. Radiographic imaging indicated multiple air-fluid levels in the abdomen and mild bilateral pleural effusion. Laboratory results were as follows: hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL, total leukocyte count 5600/mm3, platelet count 89,000/mm3, sodium 129 mEq/L, potassium 5.8 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 76 mg/dL, serum creatinine 3.2 mg/dL, serum albumin 2.3 g/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 115 mm/h, and C-reactive protein negative. Urine analysis showed albumin 4+ with 50–70 red blood cells per high-power field and 10–15 pus cells per high-power field. Both urine and blood cultures were negative. The Mantoux test was negative, and gastric lavage for acid-fast bacilli was normal.
test_results: Ultrasound abdomen and unenhanced computed tomography (CT) scan revealed moderate ascites, diffuse bowel wall thickening of duodenum and jejunum, and pleural effusion. C3 10.1 mg/dL (normal 90–180 mg/dL), C4 3.2 mg/dL (normal 10–40 mg/dL), antinuclear antibody (ANA) 1:1000, and anti-double-strand DNA antibodies >800 IU/mL (normal <35 IU/mL).
diagnosis: Intestinal Pseudo-Obstruction secondary to Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

case_report: A 43-year-old Chinese man exhibited widespread reduced sweating since birth. He was born at term to parents who were not related by blood. At three days old, he experienced a severe fever and was treated in a county hospital. Subsequently, he experienced heat intolerance, rapid heartbeat, weakness, excessive facial sweating, and lack of sweating on the trunk and limbs after physical exertion or exposure to hot environments. These symptoms improved when he stayed in shaded areas or used cold water. Living in a subtropical climate, he adapted by sleeping on the floor and taking cold showers throughout the year. His family history showed no similar symptoms among his parents, four siblings, two sons, or daughter. His medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Physical examination showed generally dry skin with slight thickening of the skin on the palms and soles. His facial features, hair, teeth, and nails appeared normal, but he had sparse beard and underarm hair. His overall health, intelligence, neurological and eye examinations, as well as electrocardiography and abdominal ultrasound, were normal. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, urinalysis, general biochemical profile, thyroid function, and cholinesterase levels, were all within normal limits.
test_results: Iodine-starch test showed a detectable perspiration (blue-black stain) on the forehead, cheeks, chin, axillae and palms, while no sweating was observed on the trunk or extremities. Histological examination of serial sections revealed that hair follicles were sparse and sweat glands were wholly absent from the dermis and hypodermis in the left forearm and right thigh, though some eccrine and apocrine sweat glands were present in the right axilla. S-100 was expressed in the nerve terminals surrounding the acini and ducts of the eccrine sweat glands, while PGP9.5 was positive in the acini of apocrine glands and the nerve terminals surrounding the eccrine glands in the right axilla.
Orpha_name: Isolated generalized anhidrosis with normal sweat glands

case_report: A 15-year-old female presented with recent onset of tremor, seizures, and limb weakness. She is the first child of consanguineous parents and was born via normal spontaneous delivery. Her psychomotor development was typical. Symptoms began with a resting tremor in both hands at age five. By age seven, she experienced staring episodes and myoclonus, which occurred several times daily and lasted a few seconds. The myoclonus was sometimes triggered by voluntary movements. Five years ago, she started experiencing head drop attacks and multiple episodes of generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Since age ten, she has progressively developed limb weakness, particularly noticeable when climbing stairs, standing, and washing hands. On physical examination, she was cooperative and fully oriented. She exhibited a waddling gait and a positive Gower's sign, indicating proximal muscle weakness. Muscle strength was assessed using the Medical Research Council scale: neck extensor and flexor muscles scored 3/5, shoulder abductors 2/5, elbow and hand muscles 3/5 and 4/5, respectively. In the lower extremities, hip and knee muscles scored 3/5, and distal leg muscles 4/5. Mild facial muscle weakness was noted, but extra-ocular muscles were unaffected. Deep tendon reflexes in the biceps brachii, triceps brachii, brachioradialis, and Achilles were 1+, while the patellar reflex was absent. Sensory examination for small and large fibers was unremarkable. Resting tremor was observed in both hands. The patient's tongue was notably atrophic with fasciculations. Several staring episodes and myoclonus were observed during the examination. Brain MRI showed no pathological features. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, creatine phosphokinase, lactate dehydrogenase, ammonia, and thyroid, renal, and liver function tests, were all within normal ranges.
test_results: The ceramidase-activity level revealed about 30% reduction. Histo-pathological examination confirmed a neuropathic pattern with muscle atrophy of mainly type-II fibers, with concomitant denervation and reinnervation processes. The patient had frequent epileptic events during recording, with epileptic poly-myoclonus and generalized 2.5–3 Hz irregular sharp and slow wave complexes accentuated during intermittent photic stimulation (IPS). Needle-EMG demonstrated a neuropathic pattern with high amplitude and long duration motor unit action potentials (MUAPs), reduced recruitment, and spontaneous potentials such as fibrillation (Fib), positive sharp waves (PSW), and fasciculation (Fasc). These findings confirmed a chronic denervation process with ongoing regeneration compatible with anterior horn cell diseases. The genetic study revealed a homozygous mutation on ASAH-1 gene [c.173C>T (p. Thr58Met)]; the parents` genetic study revealed a heterozygous mutation.
diagnosis: Spinal Muscular Atrophy with Progressive Myoclonic Epilepsy
Orpha_name: Spinal muscular atrophy-progressive myoclonic epilepsy syndrome

case_report: A 45-year-old male presented with a low-grade fever and a fluctuant swelling on the posterior aspect of his lower left flank, persisting for the past month. The fever was remittent and low grade without chills or rigor. The patient initially noticed a small swelling in the left lower paravertebral area, which progressively increased to 15 cm × 7 cm. There was no history of local trauma to the area. The patient did not report any pain in the lumbar region or lower limbs. He had no prior diagnosis of diabetes or other chronic diseases and denied using steroids, illicit drugs, alcohol, or nicotine. He had a steady sexual partner and had not traveled recently. There was no family history of diabetes. As a farmer, he worked outdoors most of the day. He reported passing bulky, oily stools. His past medical history did not include acute emergencies requiring hospitalization. On examination, he was non-obese (BMI 19.4 kg/m2) with an axillary temperature of 38.1°C. A fluctuant, non-tender swelling was observed in the left lower paravertebral region. There was no evidence of acanthosis nigricans. A complete neurological evaluation showed no neurodeficit. Laboratory tests revealed leukocytosis (11,500/mm3), elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (130 mm), fasting plasma glucose of 186 mg/dl, postprandial plasma glucose of 294 mg/dl, and HbA1C levels of 11.0% (NGSP) [97 mmol/mol (IFCC)]. Pus aspirated from the swelling was inoculated in blood agar, MacConkey agar, Löwenstein–Jensen media (one covered with black paper for scotochromogen), and Sabouraud's dextrose agar (SDA) slants. A smear from the pus was stained using Ziehl–Neelsen (Z–N) stain for microscopic evaluation. Other baseline biochemical parameters were noncontributory.
test_results: An erect abdominal skiagram revealed linear fluffy calcifications along the pancreatic duct; destruction, collapse and wedging of third, fourth and fifth lumbar vertebral bodies, involvement of corresponding intervertebral discs, with evidence of paravertebral abscess. A screening magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of lumbar spine revealed extension of the vertebral and paravertebral suppuration through the left paraspinal muscle into subcutaneous plane posteriorly. Subsequently, an ultrasound of the abdomen was remarkable for a dilated main pancreatic duct with extensive intraductal calcifications. A post-meal serum C-peptide level was estimated to be 1.1 ng/ml. Pancreatic autoantibodies (anti-GAD 65 and anti-IA2) were negative.

case_report: The patient is a 7-year-old male from Italy, born at 37 weeks via caesarean section after a normal pregnancy. Birth measurements were: weight 3050 g (90th centile), length 54 cm (90th centile), and head circumference 36 cm (50th centile). Early life observations included hypotonia, poor feeding, and mild dysmorphic features. At one month old, he was admitted to Istituto Giannina Gaslini for bronchiolitis and pneumonia, which led to respiratory arrest requiring intubation, ventilatory support, and oxygen supplementation for two months. Chest CT scans revealed parenchymal consolidation with thick mucous secretions in the upper right lobe and bilateral hilar areas. Seizures were documented via EEG, showing abnormal areas in the temporal lobes, and phenobarbital was initiated. Metabolic screening, abdominal ultrasound, and routine blood biochemical tests were normal. Cardiac ultrasound identified an atrial septal defect that spontaneously closed at follow-up. Fundus oculi and visually evoked potentials (VEP) were normal. Due to gastroesophageal reflux and antral gastritis, PPI therapy was started, and Nissen fundoplication was performed at three years old. The patient experienced recurrent wheezing and respiratory infections, leading to respiratory insufficiency and emergency care admissions. Sweat test and genetic testing for cystic fibrosis were normal. Serum immunoglobulin levels indicated transient childhood hypogammaglobulinemia. Lymphocyte counts, lymphocyte proliferation test, tests for surfactant deficiency, and laryngotracheobronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) were normal. Nasal brushing indicated ciliary dyskinesia due to chronic inflammation. Periodic chest CT scans showed bronchial wall thickening, bronchiectasis, areas of consolidation with ground glass opacities, and air trapping, particularly in the medium and upper right lobes. Treatments included PEP-mask physiotherapy, bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroids, and anti-leukotriene agents. Physical examination revealed broad and sparse eyebrows, convergent strabismus, broad nasal bridge and hypertelorism, nose with broad columella and nares, ears with prominent helix and antihelix and large lobes, long philtrum, thin upper lip, short neck, low set posterior hairline. Skeletal evaluation showed pectus excavatum, short fingers and toes, broad thumbs and big toes, short nails, joint hyperlaxity of lower limbs, and flat feet. Neurological examination indicated mild psychomotor delay, speech delay, attention deficit, and hyperactivity. Brain MRI at four years old showed mild symmetrical enlargement of supratentorial ventricular cavities and enlargement of fronto-insular periencephalic spaces. At six years old, thoracic surgery for pectus excavatum was performed, resulting in improved respiratory dynamics and reduced frequency of respiratory infections.
test_results: Genetic testing for cystic fibrosis were normal.

case_report: This 47-year-old female patient has experienced frequent monthly nosebleeds since childhood, along with intermittent mild anemia and lifelong migraines. At age 25, she underwent her first colonoscopy due to chronic constipation and abdominal pain, though the specific findings from this procedure are not available. At age 28, an upper endoscopy revealed no polyps. Her family history includes her father and two children, all of whom have had severe nosebleeds. Additionally, her son and daughter have experienced migraines, and her father had gastrointestinal polyps with significant blood loss necessitating transfusions.
test_results: Germline genetic testing revealed a pathogenic c.1245_1248delCAGA variant in the SMAD4 gene.
diagnosis: Juvenile Polyposis Syndrome with Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia

case_report: A nine-year-old Turkish boy presented with abdominal pain and fever. He was found to have perforated appendicitis and was referred to the endocrine clinic for coexisting hyperglycemia (blood glucose level was 27.75 mmol/L). Family history revealed diabetes in multiple maternal relatives, including the patient's mother, who was on insulin therapy for diabetes mellitus diagnosed during the first trimester of pregnancy at age 24, and a maternal uncle. Two of the patient's siblings had a history of neonatal hypoglycemia of varying duration and severity. The patient, the first living child of the family, was born with a birth weight of 3750 grams (+6.6 SD) via caesarean section at 29 weeks gestation. The parents were distantly related. He experienced a hypoglycemic episode on postnatal day one (blood glucose was 1.33 mmol/L, insulin level was 22.7 µIU/mL, C-peptide 5.42 ng/mL (0.9-7.1)). Diazoxide treatment was initiated but later discontinued due to the development of pulmonary edema, and octreotide therapy was started. Hypoglycemia resolved at three months of age, and the child remained free of hypoglycemic episodes until nine years old, when he was admitted to the hospital. On admission, he was lethargic with pale and grayish skin. His height was 140 cm (0.7 SDS), weight was 35 kg (0.8 SDS), and BMI was 17.8 (0.7 SDS). Vital signs included a respiratory rate of 20 breaths/minute, heart rate of 72 beats/minute, and blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg. Physical examination revealed abdominal distention, rigidity, and rebound tenderness. An emergency appendectomy was performed. Post-operatively, hyperglycemia persisted, and subcutaneous insulin therapy was initiated. Laboratory results showed a blood glucose of 13.2 mmol/L, insulin of 8.82 µIU/mL (2.6-25), and C-peptide of 1.28 ng/mL (0.9-7.1). HbA1c was 9.1% (76 mmol/L). Islet cell, anti-insulin, and anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies were negative. Over the next two months, insulin requirements decreased until insulin treatment was withdrawn. During follow-up, HbA1c remained within the high normal range (6.2% to 6.4%) with dietary and lifestyle changes. At 11.5 years, HbA1c increased to 9.6% (81 mmol/L). His weight was 46 kg (0.9 SDS), height was 152 cm (0.8 SDS), and BMI was 19.9 (0.9 SDS). The patient and family declined to restart insulin therapy. At 12 years, HbA1c increased to 11.4% (101 mmol/L), and an oral glucose tolerance test indicated insulin-deficient diabetes mellitus.
test_results: Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral leukocytes using standard procedures and the coding regions and intron/exon boundaries of the ABCC8, KCNJ11, HNF4A and HADH genes were amplified by polymerase chain reaction. Amplicons were sequenced using the BigDye Terminator Cycle Sequencing Kit V.3.1 according to manufacturer’s instruction and reactions were analysed on an ABI 3730 Capillary sequencer. Sequences were compared with the reference sequences using Mutation Surveyor v5.0.1 software. The variant was classified using the American College of Medical Genetic and Genomics/Association for Molecular Pathology guidelines.
diagnosis: Congenital Hyperinsulinism due to a novel homozygous p.L171F ABCC8 mutation
Orpha_name: Diazoxide-resistant focal hyperinsulinism due to SUR1 deficiency

case_report: A 31-year-old male with no prior history of central nervous system infection, febrile convulsions, head trauma, or perinatal abnormalities presented with a notable familial history of his mother experiencing pre-sleep tremulous hand movements starting around age 40. At 25, he began experiencing tremulous movements in his limbs and fingers at bedtime, which gradually progressed to intermittent occurrences during the day. He initially sought medical attention and was managed observationally. At 27, the frequency of his tremulous movements increased. At 31, he experienced an unprovoked convulsive episode characterized by spontaneous left conjugate eye deviation, ipsilateral head version, and tonic-clonic seizures involving bilateral limbs, which resolved spontaneously after approximately two minutes. He was transported to a local hospital where intravenous anti-seizure medication was administered, and valproic acid therapy was initiated. The intensity of his tremulous movements mildly decreased, and he was referred to our institution for further evaluation of involuntary movements and seizures. On examination, his level of consciousness was normal, and no neurological abnormalities were observed, although irregular, fine dysrhythmic finger movements were noted during postural maintenance despite being on valproic acid (600 mg/day). Blood tests were unremarkable, and brain CT and MRI showed no structural abnormalities. Cognitive testing (Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-IV; intelligence quotient range: 94-114) indicated normal cognition.
test_results: Video EEG monitoring revealed no epileptic discharges but occasional generalized theta waves during awakeness. The long-latency somatosensory evoked potentials (SEP) test revealed augmented responses, with an N20-P25 amplitude of 8.91μV and a P25-N35 of 15.08μV, thus satisfying the criteria for giant SEP. The cortical (C)-reflex was also noted during the SEP examination.

case_report: An 86-year-old Puerto Rican woman, gravida 11, para 9, arrived at the emergency room with heavy vaginal bleeding. She mentioned that she was in her usual state of health until a few hours before, when she experienced a bloody bowel movement with bright red blood and large clots. She had been menopausal since age 52 and had no prior history of vaginal or rectal bleeding. She had avoided medical visits for many years due to a fear of hospitals. Her medical history included hypertension, for which she used herbal medicine. Obstetrically, she had 9 term uncomplicated vaginal deliveries in Puerto Rico. She mentioned an “abnormality” with her anus present since birth. Her family history included a granddaughter with an imperforate anus corrected at birth. She reported full control over her bowel movements, denied rectal incontinence, but noted occasional mixed diarrhea and constipation. She also denied any history of urinary tract infections. Upon admission, she was tachycardic with a heart rate between 94–101 beats per minute and blood pressure ranging from 164–170/84–123 mmHg. Other vital signs were normal. She appeared pale but did not exhibit shortness of breath, chest pain, or dyspnea. A rectal examination was not performed due to the complete absence of an external anal sphincter. Laboratory results showed Hb 10.7 g/dL and Hct 33.1%.
test_results: Bimanual examination revealed copious bright red blood from the introitus and normal postmenopausal uterus, cervix, and adnexae. However on speculum examination there was no identifiable extravasation of blood from the external cervical os. Further manual examination revealed a 2 cm opening in the posterior vaginal wall about 2-3 cm proximal to the introitus where the blood was coming from. This appeared to be a rectovaginal fistula noted caudal to the hymenal ring but within the vagina itself. A tagged red blood cell study demonstrated bleeding from the sigmoid colon 8–10 cm proximal to the rectum. The patient had spontaneous cessation of her bleeding until hospital day number 5 when she had a large dark bowel movement. The patient was taken for colonoscopy by the gastroenterology service where the gynecologic team assisted with introduction of a pediatric colonoscope through the fistula. Severe colonic diverticulosis without active bleeding was noted.
Orpha_name: Non-syndromic anorectal malformation with vestibular fistula

case_report: A previously healthy six-year-old Asian girl was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) at our institution after being referred from a community hospital for a hemoglobin level of 1.6 g/dL, for which she received one unit of uncrossmatched packed red blood cells (pRBCs). Approximately one week before admission, the child experienced fever, rhinorrhea, cough, and increasing fatigue. She also reported dark urine over the last three days before admission. Her past medical history was non-contributory, with no history of blood transfusion or family history of hematologic disorders. Physical examination revealed pallor and jaundice. Chest auscultation was clear with good air entry to the bases. There was no palpable lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, bruising, or petechiae. A chest x-ray showed mild peribronchial thickening consistent with mild lower respiratory tract inflammation, without evidence of pneumonia. An abdominal ultrasound indicated mild hepatomegaly. Upon presentation to our center, a complete blood count (CBC) showed: hemoglobin 2.1 g/dL (reference range (RR): 11.2–14.1 g/dL), mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 142.9 fL (RR: 77.4–92.1 fL), hematocrit 7.0% (RR: 34.3–42.6%), white blood cells (WBC) 10.29 × 10^9/L (RR: 4.23–9.99 × 10^9/L), and platelet count 178 × 10^9/L (RR: 203–431 × 10^9/L). Reticulocyte count was 173.6 × 10^9/L (RR: 42.4–70.2 × 10^9/L). Peripheral blood smear examination revealed severe anemia with marked red cell spherocytosis, agglutination, and polychromasia. No abnormalities were detected in white blood cells or platelets. Serum unconjugated bilirubin level was 35 umol/L (RR: < 7 umol/L), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was 2622 IU/L (RR: 470–900 IU/L), and haptoglobin was undetectable (RR: 7–163 mg/dL).
test_results: The polyspecific and monospecific DAT showed positivity in the presence of anti-IgG and -C3d (3+), anti-IgG (3+) and anti-C3d (4+). Eluate tested against a panel of cells demonstrated panreactivity (2+). Antibody screen was positive with cell I and II (3+). Antibody identification panel by indirect antiglobulin test (IAT) showed panagglutination of uniform strength as well as a positive autocontrol (4+). Blood grouping showed 3+ agglutination with anti-A, anti-B and 6% albumin control and 4+ agglutination with anti-D, A1-cells, and B-cells in forward and reverse grouping. Prewarming of the blood sample at 37 °C for two-hours did not inhibit any of the reactions. Testing for PCH by Donath Landsteiner was negative.

case_report: A 10-year-old Brazilian girl, the third child in her family, was born at 36 weeks of gestation with severe intrauterine growth restriction. She had an extremely low birth weight of 1500g. After resolving initial clinical complications, she was discharged from the hospital. Despite normal cognitive development during her first year, she exhibited significant and persistent failure to thrive. By the age of 1 year, she experienced recurrent diarrhea and frequent upper and lower respiratory tract infections, necessitating prophylactic antibiotics. At 3.5 years old, an abdominal mass was evaluated, leading to the identification of a WT in her left kidney. She underwent surgical removal of the mass and received neoadjuvant chemotherapy. At age 10, a physical examination revealed specific facial features (elongated face, prominent nose, prominent ears, malar hypoplasia, and thin upper vermilion), microcephaly, nose telangiectasias, hypomelanotic macules on her upper limbs, and clinodactyly of her bilateral fifth fingers. Her anthropometric measurements were all below the fifth percentile: weight 15.9kg, height 116cm, and occipital-frontal circumference 46cm (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention growth charts, National Center for Health Statistics, USA). She had also developed learning disabilities.
test_results: The results demonstrated an increased frequency of SCE, with an average of 48.5 SCE per cell. The G-band karyotype was normal (46, XX).

case_report: A 14-month-old girl was brought to our hospital due to unusual facial features observed after birth. She was the third pregnancy and second delivery of healthy, non-consanguineous parents, born full term via cesarean section due to low amniotic fluid. At birth, her weight was 2.4 kg (SD = −1.94) and her head circumference was 32 cm (SD = −2.35). Neonatal screening tests, including thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and 17α-hydroxyprogesterone, were normal. She had neonatal pneumonia at birth. Before visiting our hospital, she exhibited unstable head control, inability to lift her head when prone, inability to support her lower limb weight, decreased muscle tone and reflexes in her limbs, and difficulty laughing out loud. At 4 months old, her free thyroxine level was low (9.9 pmol/L, normal range = 11.5–22.74 pmol/L) while her TSH level was normal (3.22 nmol/L, normal range = 0.93–3.70 nmol/L). She was given 12.5 μg of levothyroxine daily. There were no similar genetic disorders in her family. Despite rehabilitation treatment, there was no significant improvement. Her parents and sister were healthy. Physical examination revealed a height of 64 cm (SD = −4.54), a weight of 7.3 kg (SD = −2.31), and a head circumference of 42 cm (SD = −3.93). She had a closed anterior fontanelle, prominent temporal regions, long eyelashes, sparse hair, upturned nostrils, a sharp beak-like mouth, low-set ears, a short neck, and fair skin. Her external genitalia appeared immature, and her wrist joints showed significant narrowing. There were no obvious deformities or contractures in her hands or fingers. Muscle tone in her limbs was decreased. Lung examination revealed harsh breath sounds without rales, and no heart murmur was detected. Hepatosplenomegaly was not present. Other examinations showed no significant abnormalities. Blood cell count, urine routine analysis, liver and kidney functions, and urinary glycosaminoglycan (GAG) screening by dimethylmethylene blue dye binding (DMB) assay were all within normal limits or negative.
test_results: The X-ray of the spine indicated slight scoliosis. At the junction of the thoracolumbar segment, the spine showed slight kyphosis. The anterior and posterior diameters of some thoracolumbar vertebrae were smaller than normal, and the anterior edge of the vertebral body presented a beak shape. The shape of the vertebral ends of the ribs was slightly narrow and that of the lateral ends was slightly wide. The shape of the acetabulum and lower edge of the iliac bone was irregular, and the shape of the femoral neck was thin. Echocardiography showed a slightly thickened aortic valve with incomplete opening and mild aortic and mitral regurgitation. Brain MRI showed less white matter, smaller frontal lobes, and a thinner corpus callosum. The Peabody Developmental Motor Scales indicated that the patient's motor development was obviously retarded. The equivalent age of the patient's reflexes, stationary, locomotion, object manipulation, grasping, and visual–motor integration was 1 month. The total score was under the 5th percentile.

case_report: A 34-year-old man with brown skin presented with multiple annular lesions that initially appeared on the upper limb and gradually spread to the lower limb, chest, back, and thighs bilaterally over the past 2 years. Dermatological examination showed that the lesions began as 1–3 mm brown papules, which slowly increased in size to 8–10 mm plaques with a keratotic ring. The lesions were asymptomatic, featuring a pale, thinned central area with a ridgelike border, and some were red, scaly, and dry. Examination of family members revealed no significant cutaneous changes. Routine laboratory tests and chest X-ray were normal, and the HIV test was unremarkable. The patient exhibited no signs or symptoms of malignancy. There was no history of radiation exposure, drug intake, or significant sun exposure. A specimen was taken from the lower limb.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed a keratin-filled epidermal invagination with a parakeratotic column, characteristic of cornoid lamella with sparse superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with focal interface change, and an absence of the granular layer below the cornoid lamella. The upper dermis and the stratum corneum have shown scattered clumps of necrotic keratinocytes with pigment dumplings.

case_report: A 12-year-old male presented with short, sparse hair on the scalp, eyebrows, and eyelashes, along with trauma-induced skin blistering first observed at 3 months of age. Hair loss was progressive, while skin blistering remained relatively constant with a slight increase during summer. The child was born to parents with no consanguinity and had an unremarkable antenatal history. Developmental milestones were normal, and no other family members exhibited similar symptoms. At 3 years old, nail deformities were noted and progressed over time. The palms and soles became rough with mild thickening. The patient exhibited decreased sweating overall but increased sweating on the palms, soles, nose, and right cheek. Cutaneous examination revealed lusterless, short, and sparse scalp hair, absent eyebrows, and sparse eyelashes. Additional findings included frontal bossing, nasal tip sweating, an erythematous plaque on the right infraorbital area, and retracted ala nasi. A bullous lesion was present on the left ankle, a fresh ruptured bulla on the left thigh, and multiple crusted erosions and hyperpigmented macules on the trunk, groins, thighs, and dorsa of hands and feet. The palms and soles showed hyperhidrosis and mild keratoderma. Dental examination showed hypodontia of the lower incisors, abnormal canines, and delayed persistence of deciduous teeth. Nails were slightly curved (koilonychia) with anonychia and dystrophy in some nails. Nikolsky's sign was negative. Routine investigations, electrocardiogram (ECG), and chest X-rays were normal.
test_results: Histopathological examination showed blister formation in stratum spinosum with occasional acantholytic cells.

case_report: A 14-year-old boy presented with multiple white, non-itchy areas on his distal extremities for two years. The lesions included whitish papules and depressed areas with central protrusion. On clinical examination, the patient, who appeared otherwise healthy, exhibited lumbar lordosis, laxity in large joints, tibia vara, high-arched palate, and dental misalignment. The skin lesions were scattered, white to skin-colored papules, less than 1 centimeter in diameter, with central protrusion, located on the dorsum of fingers, forearms, distal portion of the thighs, and calves. No lesions were found on the trunk or proximal areas of the extremities. Palms, soles, dorsum of feet, and mucosal membranes were unaffected. There were no sensory changes associated with the lesions. The patient had no history of medication use. Family history was negative. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, urinalysis, and blood chemistry (erythrocyte sedimentation rate and liver function tests), were within normal limits. Antinuclear antibody was negative. The patient had no risk factors for AIDS or syphilis, so HIV and VDRL tests were not requested. Hepatitis B surface antigens were not detected. Immunological assays for IgM, IgA, IgG, IgE, C3, and C4 levels were normal. A 0.5 centimeter induration was observed after tuberculin testing. Chest x-ray was normal.
test_results: Haematoxylin and eosin stained section showed faintly eosinophilic separated collagen fibers in the upper and mid-dermis. Verhoeff-vanGieson stained sections showed a marked decrease or in some areas total absence of elastic fibres, in both superficial and mid-dermis. Elastic fibres around the vessels in the affected areas are also fragmented and markedly decreased.

case_report: A 4-month-old male infant was brought in due to poor eye contact. The pregnancy and perinatal period were without complications. The infant exhibited an inability to fixate with his eyes and had nystagmus. An exotropia of 15 prism diopters (PD) was noted. Both slit lamp and fundus examinations revealed no significant abnormalities. Cycloplegic refraction showed +8.0 diopters spherical in both eyes.
test_results: ERG was extinguished in both eyes.

case_report: A 58-year-old woman presented in December 2018 with a mass in her right leg and a lesion in the right superficial lobe of the parotid gland. Initial fine needle aspiration of the parotid lesion indicated oncocytoma. Biopsy of the right leg mass revealed high-grade pleomorphic sarcoma, which was surgically removed, followed by adjuvant radiotherapy. A chest CT scan was performed to check for metastasis, revealing multiple large bullae in the biapical, paraseptal, and bibasilar regions. The patient had no history of smoking, intravenous drug use, or family history of pulmonary disease. In 2020, the patient reported persistent pain from the parotid lesion, leading to a parotidectomy. Microscopic examination of the removed tissue showed a solid neoplasm with a thin capsule in most areas, with cells arranged in a sheeted pattern and interspersed with delicate vessels. The neoplastic cells had abundant pale granular to eosinophilic cytoplasm and eccentric ovoid vesicular nuclei. The tumor morphology was consistent with the previous fine needle aspiration findings, where the tumor cells were negative for thyroid transcription factor 1 (TTF1), renal cell cancer (RCC) marker, and vimentin, but positive for pan-cytokeratin. Immunostains from the current tumor cells showed positivity for epithelial cell adhesion molecule BerEp4 and negativity for GATA binding protein 3 (GATA-3), tumor protein 63 (p63), and Paired box gene 8 (PAX8). The pathologic diagnosis was acinic cell carcinoma. The patient continued to be evaluated for cystic lung disease. Lymphangioleiomyomatosis was ruled out based on normal vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) levels, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency was excluded by normal AA genotype, and the autoimmune workup was negative.
test_results: A heterozygous c.117705_1177-3del intronic deletion in the FLCN gene was identified.

case_report: A 23-year-old male with no previous medical history visited the emergency department (ED) multiple times due to left arm pain, initially treated with tramadol and meloxicam. During his first ED visit, a computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast was performed because of elevated transaminases, which revealed no acute intra-abdominal issues. Despite treatment, elevated transaminases persisted in subsequent ED visits. He later returned to the ED with scleral icterus. An abdominal ultrasound indicated a small amount of sludge in the gallbladder and mild diffuse thickening of the gallbladder wall. He was admitted for further evaluation due to worsening transaminases and hyperbilirubinemia. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography showed mild dilatation of the intrahepatic bile ducts, likely related to a lesion in the head of the pancreas. Additionally, a second, larger lesion was identified in the uncinate process of the pancreas.
test_results: Examination of the direct smears and cell block preparations shows sheets of monotonous intermediate-sized cells with a starry sky appearance. Numerous tingible body macrophages are noted and account for the starry sky morphology. The neoplastic cells demonstrate round nuclei with finely clumped chromatin and several paracentral nucleoli. The mitotic rate is high with single-cell necrosis and increased apoptotic activity. Ancillary immunohistochemical staining was performed on the cell block, showing the neoplastic cells to express CD20, CD10, Bcl-6, and EBV. The Ki-67 proliferation index was >99%. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis showed abnormal results with evidence of MYC (8q24) gene rearrangement and t(8;14)(q24;q32) in 87% and 88% of cells examined, respectively. FISH analysis was negative for BCL2 (18q21) and BCL6 (3q27) gene rearrangements.

case_report: A three-year-old Caucasian female, born at eight months of gestation via C-section, was discharged from the hospital after three days. At four months old, she underwent surgery to correct craniostenosis. She could not support her own head at that time. She managed to sit with support at 12 months and without support at 18 months. She was unable to pronounce words and appeared to have hearing difficulties. She could stand with support but was unable to walk. Her gestation period was uneventful. PHYSICAL EXAM: hypertelorism, thin nose, micrognathia, global hypotonia, ligament laxity, level V muscle strength in all four limbs, myotactic hyporeflexia, normal motor coordination in both upper and lower limbs, bilateral flexion plantar skin reflex. She also had large palatine tonsils, altered helixes on the ear pinna, atresia of the external ear canal (EEC), and nasal wing hypoplasia.
test_results: BERA: Right Ear - no auditory evoked potentials with 130 dBpeSpl; Left Ear - threshold at 100 dBpeSpl. Wave morphology analysis and latency differentials I-III, III-V and I-V (11PPS): Left ear - 130 dBpeSpl, waves I, II and III of normal morphology; wave V with lower amplitude in twice that of wave I; normal latency interval. TEMPORAL BONE CT SCAN: EEC atresia all the way to the middle ears and presence of material resembling soft tissue; normal middle ears, inner ears and inner acoustic meatus; except for aeration loss of the mastoid antrum and cells and right ear tympanic cavity filled with soft tissue material.

case_report: This 10-year-old boy was referred to our clinic for severe short stature. He was the first child of parents who are first cousins. He was born small for gestational age. His developmental milestones were achieved within normal limits. He had an incomplete response to growth hormone (GH) stimulation as well as to exogenous GH therapy given for two years in another pediatric endocrinology department, and the treatment had been stopped. His physical and skeletal findings were not compatible with GH deficiency. Skeletal dysplasia was not considered at genetic evaluation at age 9, and GH therapy was recommended. GH insensitivity syndrome (GHIS) was excluded with an IGF-1 generation test. The patient’s anthropometric and physical examination findings are documented. His biochemical and hormonal results were within normal limits.
test_results: Skeletal survey of the patient showed slender long bones with diaphyseal constriction and flared metaphyses, slender ribs, thick cortex in the tibia and femur, short femoral neck, tall lumbar vertebrae, small pelvis and short iliac wings.

case_report: A 44-year-old male patient presented with a history of renal insufficiency since 1999. Despite undergoing renal transplantation, renal failure recurred after 5 years. The patient exhibited severe maxillary and mandibular deformities, dental abnormalities, and a prominent forehead. Physical examination revealed a short neck, short stature, and a barrel-like chest. A subtotal parathyroidectomy was performed in 2008. Over the past 6 months, the patient experienced two episodes of hypocalcemia accompanied by weakness, dyspnea, and neck bulging.
test_results: The scan pattern on early phase images showed radiotracer uptake in the thyroid region, as well as a focal zone of increased tracer uptake in the left lower part of the neck inferior to the thyroid. Delayed images revealed tracer washout from the neck region with a focal area of retained activity in the left lower part of the neck inferior to the thyroid. The SPECT images also proved the above findings.

case_report: A 9-year-old boy was referred to the Clinical Institute of Medical Genetics Ljubljana due to mixed sensorineural hearing loss and mild dysplastic signs. He was the first child of unrelated healthy parents, born after an uneventful pregnancy with normal birth parameters (birth weight at the 60th percentile, birth length at the 70th percentile) and an APGAR score of 9/9/10. Newborn screening tests indicated congenital hearing loss. At 13 days old, brain stem acoustic potential evaluation confirmed mixed sensorineural hearing loss. Physical examination noted nasomaxillary hypoplasia and mild hypotonia, which persisted until he was one year old. Subsequent medical examinations, including brain ultrasound, abdominal ultrasound, CT of the temporal bones, and eye examination, showed no additional abnormalities. He met all developmental milestones as expected. The family history was negative for genetic diseases, skeletal abnormalities, congenital anomalies, and hearing loss. At 9 years old, a clinical geneticist observed a high forehead, midfacial hypoplasia with mild hypertelorism, a hypoplastic nose, a depressed nasal bridge, and a long philtrum. Chromosome analysis in 2005 revealed a normal male karyotype 46, XY. In 2008, molecular genetic analysis for hearing loss, ordered by an otorhinolaryngologist, did not detect any mutations in the GJB2 and GJB6 genes, ruling out the most common cause of genetic nonsyndromic hearing loss.
test_results: array CGH showed minimum 2886 bp large deletion, spanning intron and exon 7 of ARSE gene (arr[hg19] Xp22.33(2,861,119×1,2,861,384-2,864,270×0,2,865,276×1)). Proximal breakpoint and next available microarray probe was only 265 bp away, distal next available probe was 1006 bp away.

case_report: A 54-year-old female with a history of asthma, hyperlipidemia on a statin, and type II diabetes mellitus visited the primary care clinic due to fatigue and muscle pain in her upper and lower limbs. She had a COVID-19 infection three months before the onset of these symptoms and has since received a two-dose series of the COVID-19 vaccine. The possibility of statin-induced muscle pain was considered but ruled out after discontinuing the statin did not alleviate her symptoms; instead, her condition worsened. Laboratory tests, including creatine kinase (CK), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), C-reactive protein (CRP), myoglobin, aldolase, and a thyroid panel, were conducted, and the results are provided in the Table. The patient was also evaluated by rheumatology to investigate potential autoimmune causes, with the results of the rheumatology panel summarized in the Table. Due to the persistence of her symptoms without improvement, additional testing was performed. An electromyography (EMG) was conducted, revealing no signs of focal nerve entrapment, cervical radiculopathy, brachial plexopathy, myopathy, or generalized peripheral neuropathy.
test_results: Muscle biopsy confirmed the presence of morphologic features of an acquired inflammatory myopathy with occasional rimmed vacuole-type structures, congophilic TDP-43-p62 positive intranuclear inclusions, and amyloid-like inclusions.

case_report: A 34-year-old woman, at 21 weeks of pregnancy, was admitted to the gynecology department due to abdominal pain, muscle cramps, and weakness. Her medical history included hypothyroidism. Vital signs and physical examination were within normal limits. Routine blood tests showed electrolyte imbalances: serum potassium was 2.32 mEq/l (normal range 3.5–5.1 mEq/l) and magnesium was 1.18 mEq/l (normal range 1.8–2.6 mEq/l). The patient received 80 mEq potassium chloride intravenously, which led to a gradual improvement in her symptoms. She was referred to the internal medicine department for further evaluation of the low potassium levels. The patient had no history of drug use other than iodine, folic acid, iron, and levothyroxine sodium replacement. There was no family history of renal disease, and both renal ultrasound and function tests were normal.
test_results: The results of a 24-hour urine test revealed calcium excretion 49.25 mg/day (normal range 100–250 mg/day), magnesium excretion 140.25 mg/day (73–122 mg/day), potassium excretion 82.5 mEq/day (25–125 mEq/day), sodium excretion 260 mEq/day and chloride excretion 257.5 mEq/day. Blood gas analysis showed compensated metabolic alkalosis (pH 7.439, HCO3 26 mol/l, pCO2 45 mmHg).

case_report: A 43-year-old female with severe anemia following splenectomy, previously identified as blood group A, Rh (D) negative, was referred to the Immunohematology Reference Laboratory (IRL) of the Iranian Blood Transfusion Organization (IBTO) in Tehran, Iran, for ABO/Rh(D) typing and antibody screening test, along with a request for two units of RBC for transfusion in December 2013. The patient's medical history included recurrent abortion and miscarriage with no history of blood transfusion. Her family history indicated that her parents had a consanguineous marriage, and she had four siblings, all alive without any suspected blood disorder, except for one brother who underwent splenectomy due to hereditary spherocytosis anemia. Her only previous child was a healthy fifteen-year-old boy. Coagulation and hematology parameters were within normal ranges, except for a very low hemoglobin level of 3.2 g/dL. The patient's serum plasma showed strong reactions in antibody panel cells, with 4+ macroscopic reactions at 37℃ and in the anti-human globulin phase. The auto control test result was negative. The Direct Anti-globulin Test (DAT) was positive (1+) with differential anti-IgG negative and anti-C3d positive (1+). These results indicated the presence of clinically significant alloantibodies against multiple negative antigens or a high-prevalence antigen. An antibody screening test result was negative for the patient’s brother. A home-made three-cell antigen panel (IBTO mini-panel) was used for the antibody screening procedure, where the patient's plasma was added to RBCs without papain enzyme using Low Ionic Strength Saline (LISS). The IBTO mini-3cell panel and antibody identification 11-cell kit, along with selected cells, were validated within a two-year period using commercial CE marked Diamed kits. The antibody screening test was performed twice in parallel using IBTO produced kits and Diamed kits. The results were compared, and in case of positive results, the 11-cell antibody ID panel from Diamed Company was used simultaneously with the IBTO 11-cell antibody ID panel. IBTO homemade antibody ID panel and selected cells were used to exclude and include alloantibodies. The column agglutination method with antiglobulin gel card (INVITROGEL AHG coombs-Germany) was used for the antibody screening test. The gel cards were incubated at 37 °C for 15 minutes and then centrifuged for 10 minutes. Standard tube methods (Bio-Rad AHG-Germany) were used for antibody identification and selected cell tests. Clinically significant alloantibodies were defined as those antibodies that could potentially cause RBC destruction based on reactivity at 37 °C and/or anti-human globulin (AHG) phase. The patient and her brother's extended phenotyping showed that they were negative for D, C, E, c, e RBC antigens.
