test_results: Adsorption and elution studies in Anti-human globulin (AHG, CE- Immunodiagnostika, Am Seerain 13 Germany, Eschelbronn) did not reveal the presence of D, C, E, c, e, RBC antigens in the blood obtained from both patients. We performed Rh phenotyping with two sources of antisera (Diagast 251/AV.AVINEE- 59120 Loos, France and CE- Immunodiagnostika, Am Seerain 13 Germany, Eschelbronn). Positive and negative control tests were performed for each antigen according to the manufacturer’s recommendations.

case_report: A 36-year-old male presented with swelling on the right side of the face for approximately 8-9 months. Extraoral examination showed a medium-sized, firm to hard, slightly tender swelling with ill-defined margins on the right side of the mandible. The overlying skin appeared normal. Intraoral examination revealed a firm, lobular, slightly tender central mandibular swelling in the right premolar-molar region, with expansion of both cortical plates. Egg-shell crackling was noted over some areas of the buccal cortical plates. The regional teeth were displaced and mobile, while the overlying mucosa appeared normal. An orthopantomogram (dental panoramic radiograph) showed a large, ill-defined central jaw lesion with mixed radiographic changes, marked alveolar bone destruction, resorption of the mesial root of the first molar tooth, and thinning of the lower border of the mandible.
test_results: The light microscopic features revealed the presence of a proliferated mass of cartilaginous tissue showing marked cellular and nuclear pleomorphism with nuclear hyperchromatism. A plain coronal CT scan revealed the presence of a large fairly defined osteolytic lesion showing sun-ray appearance and expansion of the cortical plates.

case_report: A 30-year-old female reported experiencing difficulty in stair walking and pain in her lower back and knee. These symptoms began at the age of 26 and progressively worsened, leading to an inability to climb stairs without using her arms for support. Physical examination revealed atrophy in both calf muscles, reduced strength in the lower extremity muscles, and an absent tendon reflex. The Gowers' sign was positive. She was unable to stand on her tip-toes but could stand on her heels. The patient reported no family history of neuromuscular disease.
test_results: The EMG revealed the myopathic changes in gastrocnemius, rectus femoris, and biceps brachii muscles. A muscle biopsy from the biceps brachii suggested a diagnosis of inflammatory myopathy. Magnetic resonance imaging of her lower leg disclosed symmetric fatty degeneration and decreased muscle volume of the posterior compartment muscles in both lower legs. The anterior and lateral compartment muscles had either a normal or a relatively normal signal intensity and morphology.

case_report: A 12-year-old Asian-Bangladeshi boy reported experiencing pain in the front of both knees for the past three months. The pain intensified during activities such as contact sports, rapid walking, running, and kneeling. Physical examination showed localized swelling and tenderness over both knees. There was no joint swelling, and the patient did not have a history of fever, malaise, weight loss, nocturnal temperature rise, or prior localized knee trauma.
test_results: X-rays documented a radiopaque, fragmented mass over the tibial prominences. Ultrasonogram unveiled a hyperechoic lesion surrounded with a hypoechoic lesion of unossified cartilage with a hypoechoic-thickened distal patellar tendon.

case_report: A 15-year-old male was admitted due to stumbling and weakness. At age 3, he developed a cough and diarrhea, followed by an abnormal and unsteady gait without an apparent cause. Partial remission was achieved after symptomatic treatment. Since then, he experienced recurrent episodes of ataxia and limb weakness following each incidence of diarrhea. His self-care, learning, and communication abilities gradually declined, accompanied by abdominal flatulence, gastrointestinal disturbance, and polyuria. Initially, these episodes occurred once or twice a year but increased in frequency, becoming constant approximately three years after onset. He received treatments with immunoglobulin and glucocorticoid on several occasions without success. At admission, he was emaciated, measuring 150 cm in height and weighing 40 kg. He was unable to walk independently or sit upright. Physical examination revealed decreased advanced mental function, dysarthria, right ptosis, nystagmus, hypomyotonia, hypesthesia, and pallhypesthesia in the limbs. The bilateral finger-nose test and heel-knee-tibia test results were unstable. He exhibited obvious scoliosis and a mild foot drop deformity. The patient was not born prematurely and had normal development prior to the onset of symptoms. His parents were not consanguineous. All basic metabolic, cerebrospinal fluid, and microbial pathogen tests were normal.
test_results: Brain MRI showed marked cerebellar atrophy in addition to signal changes in cerebral white matter. The electromyography showed a fibrillation potential and a positive sharp wave in the left biceps and tibialis anterior muscle. The voltage increased slightly but the polyphase wave increased by more than 40%. The amplitude and conduction velocity of the motor nerve was notably decreased, and the amplitude of the sensory nerve could not lead out. Reflexes of the bilateral tibial nerves were not elicited. These findings revealed neurogenic and myogenic lesions. The neurogenic lesions in question had appeared when the patient was 3 years old. The electroencephalogram showed frequent irregular slow waves with a high amplitude of 1.5–2 Hz in the whole cephalic region. An auditory brainstem response test showed a mild left sensorineural hearing loss. The ECG showed sinus arrhythmia, incomplete right bundle branch block, and electric axis right anteroclock transposition. Hematoxylin and eosin staining showed different sizes of muscle fibers. The reduced form of nicotinamide-adenine dinucleotid (NADH) and ATPase-staining showed a pathological aggregation in myofibrillary groups. Whole-exome sequencing was performed on this patient, and Sanger sequencing was applied to verify his parents. A compound heterozygous mutation of ADPRHL2 was recognized in the proband [NM_017825: c.62C>A, p.[S21*]; c.535C>T, and p.[Q179*]]. The mutations c.62C>A and c.535C>T were inherited from his father and mother, respectively.
diagnosis: Stress-Induced Childhood-Onset Neurodegeneration With Ataxia-Seizures Syndrome
Orpha_name: Autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia-epilepsy-intellectual disability syndrome due to RUBCN deficiency

case_report: A 12-year-old female presented with a primary concern of yellowish discoloration of her teeth, which she noted had been present since childhood. She also reported that her deciduous teeth exhibited similar discoloration. Clinical examination revealed mandibular prognathism, anterior open bite, generalized plaque and calculus deposits, yellowish discoloration of the teeth, and chipping of the incisal and cuspal enamel structures.
test_results: Orthopantomogram (OPG) revealed thin lining of enamel with thick dentin layer and pulp chamber. Postero-anterior (PA) view radiograph revealed unfused anterior fontanels. Lateral cephalogram indicated vertebrae in growing phase.

case_report: A 61-year-old postmenopausal woman arrived at the emergency department experiencing severe pelvic and abdominal pain that extended to her lower back, along with vomiting and diarrhea. She reported nocturia, recurrent urinary tract infections, frequent urination, and female urinary stress incontinence. Her family history included breast cancer in her maternal aunt and cousin. She was a former smoker, and her lifestyle was unremarkable concerning exercise, diet, and stress levels. Her medical history included osteopenia, and she had undergone surgery for a malignant mass in her right kidney in 2015 and a kidney stone operation in 1995. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count (CBC), comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), and urinalysis, showed no abnormalities. The patient was admitted for observation by her gynecologist. A transabdominal pelvic/kidney ultrasound did not detect stones but identified uterine fibroids, with the largest measuring 10.1 × 9.7 × 11.5 cm. By the next morning, the patient felt better, and her CBC and vital signs remained stable. Based on a previous ultrasound conducted 15 days before the emergency room visit, which visualized both ovaries, it was determined that there was a low risk of ovarian torsion, and surgical intervention was not pursued. The patient was discharged with a follow-up appointment scheduled. She returned to her obstetrician-gynecologist (OB-GYN) a few days later, reporting severe pain in her lower abdomen, right groin, right buttock, and occasional nausea. Further evaluation and additional testing were planned to reassess her symptoms.
test_results: The MRI findings revealed a solid mass measuring 10.5 × 9.5 × 11.3 cm anterior to the uterine fundus with numerous internal non-enhancing cystic spaces. The mass slightly abuts the anterior uterine fundus but appears to cause mass effect on the uterus. Immediately inferior to this 11 cm mass, a tubular cystic lesion measuring 3.2 × 5.2 × 5.3 cm was found. The uterus was also found to be anteverted, slightly anteflexed, and normal-sized. The findings also included a right ovarian cyst measuring 1.1 cm.

case_report: A 32-year-old Saudi male presented with an 8-year history of upper lip swelling, without any changes in voice or breathing difficulties. His past medical and surgical history was unremarkable. Physical examination revealed a single, firm mass on the upper lip measuring 2×1.5 cm, with no notable cervical lymph node enlargement. The remainder of the physical examination was normal. Laboratory tests indicated eosinophilia with eosinophils at 11%, and serological tests showed elevated serum IgE levels at 1064 IU/mL. Imaging studies included an MRI of the head and neck, which identified a 2×2 cm mass on the upper lip, and a CT scan of the neck, which revealed a polypoid mass measuring 2.5×2 cm attached to the epiglottis.
test_results: Histopathological examination showed multiple hyperplastic lymphoid follicles with reactive germinal centers beneath the intact stratified squamous epithelium of the epiglottis, and adjacent to the minor salivary gland of the lip. The lymphoid follicles were separated by mixed chronic inflammatory infiltrate with a large number of eosinophils along with plasma cells, small mature lymphocytes, as well as histiocytes.

case_report: A 21-year-old man presented with progressive visual loss and slow progressive ataxia since age 2. Neurological examination showed slight dysarthric speech, moderate spastic paraparesis with brisk osteotendinous reflexes, moderate dysmetria in all four limbs, and a spastic and ataxic gait without sensory disturbance. Genetic tests for various types of Friedreich ataxia and spinocerebellar ataxia were negative. Serum vitamin E levels were normal. Distance visual acuity was 4/10 in both eyes, with better near vision at 6/10 in the right eye and 8/10 in the left eye. Color vision was normal on Ishihara pseudoisochromatic plates, and computerized static visual fields were full bilaterally. Central keratoconus was noted as the cause of decreased visual acuity. Fundus examination showed a striated whitish peripapillary appearance with a normal optic disk in both eyes. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed significant thickening of the peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) and absence of the normal foveal depression in both eyes. Fluorescein and indocyanine green retinal angiography were normal. Full-field electroretinography (ERG) indicated an electronegative waveform in bright flash dark-adapted ERG, suggesting inner retinal rod system dysfunction. Photopic 30 Hz flicker ERG was mildly delayed bilaterally, with a reduction in the b:a ratio of the On− response. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed atrophy of the cerebellar vermis and symmetrical linear hypointense striations on either side of the pontine midline on T1-weighted sequences. Additionally, there was mild generalized cerebral atrophy with slight dilation of the posterior ventricles and thinning of the corpus callosum.
test_results: Genetic studies showed the presence of a homozygous point deletion (c6078) in the SACS gene.
diagnosis: Autosomal Recessive Spastic Ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay
Orpha_name: Autosomal Recessive Spastic Ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay

case_report: In March 2010, a 65-year-old woman was transferred from the National Police Hospital (NPH) to Shinchon Severance Hospital (Seoul, Korea) via the emergency room (ER) with a decreased level of consciousness. Her medical history included hypertension, diabetes mellitus for 10 years, recurrent cystitis, and degenerative arthritis. She had been on dexamethasone (5 mg, once daily) for approximately five years for her arthritis. Three weeks prior to admission, she was hospitalized at NPH due to drowsiness lasting 3 to 4 hours. On the day of admission at NPH, she had a fever (38.8℃) and dyspnea. She was treated with antibiotics (ceftriaxone and azithromycin) for 14 days. Her symptoms improved, but she continued to experience pain in the left lower quadrant of the abdomen. An abdomen-pelvis computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a mass-like lesion in the left renal area. While on ciprofloxacin, she developed a decreased level of consciousness. Upon physical examination at our hospital, her vital signs were: blood pressure 134/71 mm Hg, pulse rate 95 beats per minute, body temperature 36.4℃, and respiration rate 18 breaths per minute. She was drowsy, with clear breathing sounds and normal heart sounds without murmurs. Abdominal examination was unremarkable, and there was no peripheral edema. Laboratory results showed low sodium (Na) levels of 112 mmol/L (135.0-145.0), potassium (K) 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), chloride (Cl) 77.0 mmol/L (98-110), total CO2 21.0 mmol/L (24-30), low serum osmolality 240.0 mOsm (289.0-308.0), and normal urine osmolality 315.0 (50.0-1200). Thyroid function was normal. Morning serum cortisol levels were 7.1. Initial urinalysis showed 3-5 white blood cells/high-power field and yeast-like organisms. Brain magnetic resonance imaging and angiography with neck angiography (3D) showed no acute ischemic lesion, and chest X-ray was unremarkable. Sodium replacement therapy for hypotonic euvolemic hyponatremia was initiated. A low dose adrenocorticotropic hormone (1 µg cosynthropin) stimulation test indicated adrenal insufficiency; basal cortisol level was 8.56 µg/dL, and peak level during the test was 13.94 µg/dL. Steroid hormone (hydrocortisone sodium succinate; solucortef) was administered. By the third day after admission, her general condition, including consciousness, improved, and serum sodium levels normalized (136 mmol/L). Her steroid hormone dosage was gradually tapered to 7.5 mg (5 mg, 2.5 mg twice daily) of prednisolone acetate. However, she developed myalgia and leukocytosis (white blood cell count 13,650 µg/L [neutrophil 84.9%]). A follow-up abdomen-pelvic CT on the second day after admission showed an ill-defined inflammatory lesion with multifocal abscess pockets in the left perirenal space. The lesion appeared slightly reduced in size compared to the previous CT. Repeat urinalysis showed many white blood cells per high-power field and yeast-like organisms, confirmed as yeast in the urine culture. Intravenous antibiotic treatment (ubacillin 1,500 mg daily) was started. Colonoscopy showed no specific lesions.
test_results: The histology of the lesion showed a collection of foamy histiocytes also known as von Hansemann cells with von-kossa stain positive spheres (Michelis-Gutmann body).

case_report: A 57-year-old male, non-smoker, non-alcoholic, with no co-morbidities or significant past medical history, presented with mild, intermittent hemoptysis and a feeling of heaviness in the right chest for 4 years. Imaging revealed a right chest mass that had been increasing in size over the past 4 years. On examination, the patient was conscious, oriented, and afebrile with a respiratory rate of 16/min, pulse of 74/min, blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg, and oxygen saturation of 97% on room air. Systemic examination was unremarkable except for reduced breath sounds on the right side of the chest. Routine laboratory reports were normal. INR was 1.13 and APTT was 30.2 s with a control of 29.0 s. Chest X-ray (CXR) showed a dense, rounded pleural-based opacity in the right lower zone. Ultrasound revealed mild hepatomegaly and a right lower pleural mass without associated effusion. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest showed a non-enhancing right pleural mass with specs of calcification compressing the superior surface of the liver. One year prior, CT-guided fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) suggested an organized hematoma. About one month ago, a Trucut biopsy revealed dense fibrous tissue with marked hyalinization and inflammation, with no evidence of granuloma or malignancy. Serial CXRs showed progressive enlargement of the mass. Consequently, a diagnostic and therapeutic exploratory thoracotomy was performed, revealing a large, thick-walled hematoma in the pleural space adherent to the lung. Complete excision of the mass was carried out, and an intercostal tube (ICT) was placed. Intraoperative hemostasis was achieved with great difficulty. In the first post-operative hour, the ICT drained about 450 ml of frank blood. The patient continued to bleed through the ICT at a rate of 200–300 ml/h. Management included intravenous fluids, tranexamic acid, aprotinin, vitamin K, and activated Factor VII in a dose of 7.2 mg. Despite multiple blood and blood product transfusions, bleeding did not stop. Re-exploration thoracotomy was performed immediately. During the procedure, more than 1 L of blood was found in the pleural cavity with diffuse small oozes and no evidence of any surgical bleed. Oozes were cauterized, and complete hemostasis was ensured. After re-exploration, bleeding through the ICT significantly reduced to 50 ml/h. Bleeding gradually stopped, and the patient was extubated 48 hours after re-exploration. Histopathology of the pleural mass revealed fibrocollagenous pleural tissue with ulceration of the mesothelial lining and foci of fibrin deposition, suggestive of an organizing hematoma. There was no evidence of granuloma or malignancy. During the fourth to seventh post-operative days, the patient's general condition gradually worsened. He became progressively breathless, and his hemoglobin dropped to 6.7 g/dl. There was progressive worsening of CXR, suggestive of a collection of clots on the right side, even though the ICT was not draining anything. The hemoglobin continued to drop, and he was unable to maintain adequate oxygen saturation with high-flow oxygen, necessitating BiPAP support. He was again transfused with packed cells and blood products.
test_results: Factor VIII levels were reported to be 103% of normal (60–150), whereas Factor IX (functional) was only 24.5%. A repeat sample to another laboratory also showed only 18% Factor IX activity.

case_report: The patient is a 49-year-old male who began experiencing difficulty standing up from a sitting position at the age of 38. Over time, he noticed progressive weakness in both upper and lower limbs, which affected daily activities such as carrying a child and walking without stumbling. By the age of 49, he had significant difficulty walking unaided, climbing stairs, and standing up from both sitting and lying positions. A neurological examination at age 46 showed symmetric atrophy and weakness in the proximal muscles of the limbs. Shoulder abduction and adduction were graded 4/5 on both sides, elbow flexion and extension were also 4/5 bilaterally, while wrist and finger movements were normal. Hip flexion was graded 3/5 and hip extension 4/5 bilaterally. Knee flexion and extension were 3/5 bilaterally, and ankle plantar flexion and dorsiflexion were both 4/5 on both sides. There was notable weakness in the axial muscles, particularly the paraspinal and abdominal muscles. The patient exhibited a wide-based gait with a lordotic posture, a positive Gowers’ sign, and mild calf enlargement. Tendon reflexes, sensory examination, and cranial nerve examination were normal. Cognitive testing showed no abnormalities. Over a four-year follow-up period, muscle weakness progressed slowly, with more noticeable deterioration in the distal parts of the upper limbs and slight asymmetry, with the right side being more affected. The patient could walk a few meters unaided but primarily used walking sticks. No cognitive decline was observed. A nerve conduction study at age 46 showed no abnormalities, while needle electromyography indicated myopathic changes, more prominent in the proximal limb muscles, without spontaneous activity. His creatine kinase (CK) level was 1,237 U/L at age 46 and increased to 1,309 U/L a year later. Whole-body bone scintigraphy showed no abnormalities characteristic of Paget’s disease. Whole-body MRI revealed fatty replacement, predominantly in the right vastus intermedius and medialis, gastrocnemius and soleus in the calf, abdominal wall, and lumbar muscles. Family history indicated similar symptoms in the patient’s father and paternal uncle. The uncle experienced muscle weakness and difficulty walking from age 40 and passed away at 59. The patient’s father, now 73, began having trouble climbing stairs and frequent falls at age 60, and by age 68, he had difficulty walking and started using crutches. He also struggled to stand up from sitting and lying positions. ENMG examination of the father showed partial axonal degeneration of motor nerves in the lower limbs and myopathic patterns in all lower limb muscles, especially the quadriceps femoris, and proximal upper limb muscles. His CK level was 119 U/L.
test_results: Next-generation sequencing analysis of the proband revealed a previously reported pathogenic heterozygous variant NM_007126.5:c.277C > T (NP_009057.1:p.(Arg93Cys)) in exon 3 of the VCP gene. Segregation analysis showed that the detected variant is inherited from the affected father.
diagnosis: Hereditary Inclusion Body Myopathy with VCP Gene Variant
Orpha_name: Adult-onset distal myopathy due to VCP mutation

case_report: A 50-year-old female reported experiencing blurred vision in the right eye for a duration of 6 years. There was no notable family history or systemic issues. The best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) measured 20/200 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Examination of the anterior segment was normal in both eyes. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed large, dilated, and tortuous vessels originating from the disc, with multiple arteriovenous shunts in all quadrants and sclerosed vessels nasally featuring multiple acute-angled bends. Additionally, arterial MA with intralesional hemorrhage was observed temporal to the fovea. The fundus examination of the left eye showed no abnormalities.
test_results: OCTA showed multiple arteriovenous shunts and vessel of origin of MA with surrounding hemorrhagic shadow. Optical coherence tomography through the MA showed involvement of inner retinal layers with underlying shadowing. Fundus fluorescein angiography demonstrated hemorrhagic MA with minimal leak in the late phase, acute-angled patent blood vessel at the site of previous MA temporal to the fovea with multiple nonleaking arteriovenous shunts, nasal attenuated vessels with surrounding staining and grapevine-like creeping of capillaries around superior major blood vessels.
diagnosis: Combined Type II and III Retinal Racemose Angioma

case_report: A 44-year-old right-handed man presented with pain on the radial side of the left wrist, which had worsened over the past 10 days. The pain initially began 4 months prior during gym exercise. The patient, who is self-employed and engages in golf and weight training, had previously received physical therapy, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and two steroid injections at another clinic, which provided only temporary relief. He had no history of systemic diseases or trauma. Physical examination revealed mild swelling on the radial side of the wrist, severe tenderness near the radial styloid process, and moderate tenderness on the mid-dorsal aspect of the radio-carpal joint, which was occasionally swollen and inflamed. The patient had a positive Finkelstein's test and a limited range of motion in the left wrist, with thumb and wrist movements exacerbating the pain. Grip strength in the left wrist was 18 kg (compared to 29 kg in the right), and thumb pinch strength was 5 kg (compared to 8 kg in the right). The visual analog scale (VAS) score for pain was 10 at rest. An initial plain radiograph of the left wrist showed no abnormalities. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the left wrist from another clinic indicated mild tenosynovitis at the third extensor compartment and intersection syndrome, though these findings did not correlate with the clinical symptoms.
test_results: Wrist arthroscopy using standard portals under general anesthesia yielded the following arthroscopic findings: dorsal synovitis, scapho-lunate and lunato-triquetral instability.
diagnosis: Anomalous course and stenosing tenosynovitis of the extensor pollicis longus tendon

case_report: A 25-year-old Hispanic female presented with burning epigastric pain over the past six months. The pain was intermittent, non-radiating, triggered by meals, relieved by antacids, and associated with postprandial nausea. She denied any weight changes, scleral icterus, hoarseness, cough, dysphagia, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, hematochezia, or melena. The patient also denied frequent use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), cigarette smoking, or any history of H. pylori infection. The physical exam revealed a prominent head circumference above the 97th percentile, normal-looking facial features, mild epigastric tenderness, and multiple mobile soft tissue masses corresponding with lipomas of varying sizes. These were identified on the trunk, pelvis, and lower extremities. The patient emigrated from Mexico when she was 19 years old. She has a history of neonatal macrocephaly, developmental delay, mild learning disabilities, and multiple subcutaneous lipomas identified at three years of age. The family history was unremarkable except for a diagnosis of colorectal cancer in her maternal grandmother at the age of 52 years. None of the family members have any medical history of genetic disorders, developmental delay, or physical deformities.
test_results: A molecular diagnosis confirmed a heterozygous missense mutation in the PTEN gene. The esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) revealed numerous 3-7 mm sessile polyps located in the distal esophagus and gastric cardia. An erythematous and erosive mucosa was observed in the gastric antrum. The duodenum appeared normal. The colonoscopy identified numerous 3-9 mm sessile polyps throughout the entire colon and mild internal hemorrhoids. Histopathologic examination confirmed synchronous polyps of varying types, including inflammatory, lymphoid, and lipomas. Biopsy of the gastric mucosa identified chronic active gastritis and a positive immunohistochemical stain for H. pylori.

case_report: A 10-year-old female presented to a pediatric outpatient setting with complaints of fever, cough, and noisy breathing. She had been regularly followed by the pediatric department since the age of six years. Her medical history revealed that she was born to second-degree consanguineous parents, but all family members, including her parents, are well. She was an average-size full-term neonate, and there were no complications at birth. She presented with bloating, vomiting, and on-and-off episodes of diarrhea at 18 months of age. These symptoms persisted for a long time despite symptomatic treatment. At the age of four, she had her first of many respiratory tract infections, i.e., fever, cough, and noisy breathing. The patient was brought to the hospital to consult her speech delay and on-and-off ear infections when she was 4.5 years of age. Later, she reported difficulty in nasal breathing and corneal clouding at eight years and 10 years, respectively. Gross facial dysmorphism was noted in the form of frontal bossing, broad-based nose, large protruded tongue, puffy eyes and face, and coarse facial features. She had a short neck, small chest, distended abdomen, umbilical hernia, clubbing of fingers, and flexion of the distal first interphalangeal joint. Her skin was pale, coarse, dry, and scaly with a dusky complexion. She weighed 9 kg, and her height was 91 cm, which showed her weight:height, height:age, and weight:age ratios were below the normal range. Abdominal examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly, and there was no shifting dullness or fluid thrill. Further, bilateral corneal opacities were found. Hematological investigations showed microcytic anemia along with a mild increase in alanine transaminase (ALT), aspartate transaminase (AST), and alkaline phosphatase (ALP).
test_results: Enzyme analysis of alpha-L-iduronidase showed deficient enzyme levels, i.e., 0.3 umol/L of blood/h (normal range: 3.5-13 umol/L of blood/h). Urine tests (random/spot) showed elevated mucopolysaccharides. X-ray of the skull showed a J-shaped sella. Chest x-ray showed flattened, oar-shaped ribs (narrowed at vertebral ends and wide at sternal ends). X-ray of the spine showed prominent inferior beaking. X-ray of the forearm and hands showed angulation of the lower ends of the radius and ulna with slopping of lower surfaces towards each other, characteristic proximal tapering of metacarpal bones. Pure tone audiometry showed a bilateral moderately severe degree of conductive hearing loss and a moderate degree of sensorineural hearing loss.

case_report: A 6-year-old Asian girl was observed to have short, sparse hair on her scalp since birth. The hair has not grown beyond its current length. There is no family history of similar hair characteristics. Physical examination showed tightly coiled and curled light-colored hairs that were thinly distributed across the scalp. The skin, palms, soles, nails, and teeth appeared normal. There were no indications of cardiac issues or other systemic conditions.
test_results: Trichoscopy revealed 'crawling snake' appearance, with short wave cycles and trichoptilosis. Trichoscopy guided plucking of hair was done and a single strand was examined, which revealed kinking of the hair shaft and variation in shaft diameter.

case_report: A 14-year-old Asian boy presented with a 4-year history of episodes characterized by muscle stiffness and weakness in the lower limbs, typically occurring after sitting for approximately one hour following exercise. These episodes improved with leg shaking. There was no reported difficulty in climbing stairs or running. He was born at term via vaginal delivery to unrelated parents, with no history of decreased fetal movements or polyhydramnios. At birth, he weighed 3.4 kg and did not require active resuscitation. There were no feeding or breathing difficulties during the neonatal period, and his weaning period was uneventful. He achieved normal developmental milestones. Family history noted that his father experienced similar episodes of muscle stiffness. Physical examination showed no dysmorphism or neurocutaneous stigmata. Growth parameters were within normal limits. Gait was normal, and the Gower sign was negative. There was no evidence of calf muscle hypertrophy or limb weakness, either proximal or distal. Muscle tone, power, and deep tendon reflexes were normal in all four limbs. Laboratory results indicated an elevated creatine kinase (CK) level of 1024 IU/L (reference range: 25-200).
test_results: Electromyography (EMG) revealed myopathic changes. There was evidence of muscle membrane irritability with myotonia. Short exercise testing showed mild post-exercise potentiation for about half a minute at room temperature, followed by recovery toward normal. Cold exposure produced reduction in muscle action potential amplitude to about 50% accompanied by severe clinical weakness. It also exposed a post-exercise drop in amplitude with slight recovery, and a subsequent progressive further decrease in the action potential with serial exercises. Molecular genetic testing was negative for myotonic dystrophy and MC (CLCN1). Further testing detected a heterozygous pathogenic mutation c. 2111C > T; p.Thr704Met in the coding regions (c. 2020-2376) and (c. 4571-4838) of sodium channel type IV α subunit (SCN4A).

case_report: The patient is an 18-year-old female who was admitted to the hospital on October 19, 2021, due to abnormal behavior lasting for three days. She exhibited refusal to eat and had a glazed look in her eyes. She was delivered via cesarean section at 33 weeks gestation, weighing 3.8 kg (+1 SD) and measuring 48 cm in height (-1 SD). Her fontanel closed at the age of 5. Throughout her childhood, she was consistently shorter than her peers but had a higher body weight. She experienced occasional muscle tetany and limb numbness. Her academic performance was slightly below average. Menarche occurred at age 13, followed by irregular menstrual cycles ranging from 28 to 90 days. Her parents are healthy and non-consanguineous, and her two sisters have normal growth and development with no family history of hereditary diseases. On examination, her blood pressure was 104/78 mmHg, height was 132 cm (-5 SD), weight was 40 kg (-2 SD), waist circumference was 80 cm, and head circumference was 48 cm. Notable physical features included cheek freckles, high anterior hairline, sparse scalp hair, prominent forehead, depressed nasal bridge, low-set ears, partially absent dentition, small mandible, slightly higher mandibular arch, increased quilt hair, stubby limbs, small hands and feet, and short bilateral 4th toes. She did not have cubitus valgus, nail thickening or roughness, or scoliosis. Gynecological examination revealed breast development at Tanner stage 4 and pubic hair at Tanner stage 4. Her Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score was 28 points after symptom improvement. Laboratory results showed low levels of calcium, potassium, and magnesium, and high levels of phosphorus. Serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST) was 94 U/L (reference range: 0 to 40), alanine transaminase (ALT) was 70 U/L (reference range: 7 to 40), potassium was 2.57 mmol/L (reference range: 3.5 to 5.3), chlorine was 96.4 mmol/L (reference range: 99.0 to 110.0), corrected calcium was 1.06 mmol/L (reference range: 2.11 to 2.52), magnesium was 0.45 mmol/L (reference range: 0.75-1.02), and phosphorus was 1.86 mmol/L (reference range: 0.85 to 1.51).
test_results: Cranial computed tomography showed sporadic symmetrical calcifications in the cerebellar hemisphere, frontotemporal parietal lobe, basal ganglia, and thalamus. Thyroid ultrasonography showed a cystic-solid mixed nodule measuring approximately 2.3 mm × 1.2 mm in the right lobe. X-rays of the left knee, anteroposterior pelvis, left hand, and both feet showed a smaller right ilium compared to the contralateral side, shallow acetabular fossa on both sides, and no obvious abnormalities in the bone structure of the remaining pelvis or the structures of the sacroiliac and hip joints on either side. No abnormal density was observed in the pelvis. The phalanges of the left little finger were short, with thickening of the cortex of the tubular bone and narrowing of the medulla. The 4th and 5th metatarsal bones and the corresponding phalanges of both feet were short and small. Ultrasonography of the pelvic cavity showed an anteverted uterus measuring approximately 2.7 cm × 1.9 cm × 3.0 cm. Uniform endometrial echogenicity was observed with no obvious tumor-like structures. The endometrial thickness was approximately 0.4 cm. The bilateral ovaries were normal in size, with no obvious space-occupying lesions in the bilateral adnexal areas.

case_report: A 2-day-old premature female neonate, born at 34 weeks of gestation, weighing 1600 grams, was referred for cardiac investigation after a routine neonatal examination detected a heart murmur. The pregnancy was controlled, and the parents were healthy. There was no family history of congenital heart disease, consanguinity, or diabetes. Initially vigorous, the neonate became dehydrated, anxious, and cyanotic on the second day of life. Arterial blood gas analysis showed a pH of 7.35, partial pressure of oxygen at 29 mmHg, and partial pressure of carbon dioxide at 74 mmHg. Routine lab tests were normal, but glucose levels were consistently above 15 mmol/l. Following signs of respiratory distress, the infant received supplemental oxygen and surfactant, which increased oxygen saturation to 87%. The infant was then transferred to a tertiary medical facility for further evaluation. ECG revealed a right ventricular lift and incomplete right block. Clinical examination showed equal and full pulses in all extremities, no hepatomegaly, a normal first heart sound, a systolic murmur, a single second heart sound, and no diastolic murmur. A chest radiograph indicated an enlarged cardiac silhouette with a narrow mediastinum and increased pulmonary vasculature. Echocardiography showed concordant atrioventricular and discordant ventriculo-arterial connections, normal pulmonary and systemic venous return, a large atrial level hole with significant left-to-right shunting, normal AV valve morphology and function, and a large perimembranous and juxtapulmonary ventricular septal defect with a muscular posterior rim. Both coronary arteries arose normally. There was also a large patent arterial duct with left-to-right shunting. The infant continued on 100% inspired oxygen via a hood. By the fourth day of life, glucose levels remained above 15 mmol/l, and signs of metabolic acidosis were present. After consultation with an endocrinologist, insulin therapy was initiated, normalizing serum glucose levels. A routine abdominal ultrasound showed enlarged kidneys (9 x 4.2 cm), while liver ultrasound was normal. Routine lab analysis remained within normal ranges except for HbA1c, which was extremely high at 114 mmol/mol (12.6%), compared to the normal range of 29-42 mmol/mol (4.5-5.7%).
test_results: Genetic examination showed classic mutations in the EIF2AK3 gene–eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2α kinase 3.

case_report: The patient, a 31-year-old Caucasian male with a history of cerebral palsy, spina bifida, seizure disorder, and hydrocephalus with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt (VPS) placed since infancy, presented with fever, diffuse abdominal pain, and distension. Physical examination did not reveal any mass. A computed tomography scan showed a large localized intra-abdominal fluid collection with a rim-enhancing wall of variable thickness, in which the tip of the VPS catheter was embedded. The findings were interpreted as an infected peritoneal 'pseudocyst' associated with the VPS. The patient was started on antibiotics, and surgical excision and drainage of the intra-abdominal process were scheduled. During surgery, nodular peritoneal thickening with adhesions and pseudocyst formation was observed. Only a portion of the lesional tissue could be surgically excised. The fluid sent for culture grew Pseudomonas stutzeri. The resection specimen consisted of multiple membranous fragments lined by serosal surface, displaying multiple areas of nodular thickening. The nodules varied in size and had a firm gray-white cut surface.
test_results: Microscopic examination of sections from these nodular areas demonstrated a dense, expansile and tumefactive proliferation of medium-sized to large atypical epithelioid cells arranged predominantly in solid sheets, with focal nests and trabeculae formation. The neoplastic proliferation focally invaded the underlying adipose tissue. The neoplastic cells had pale to eosinophilic cytoplasm and vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli. Frequent mitotic figures were identified, without necrosis. Immunohistochemical studies revealed the neoplastic cells to be strongly immunoreactive for pankeratin AE1/AE3, CK7, CK5/6, and Cam5.2, with partial, strong expression of mesothelial markers, including nuclear-cytoplasmic staining for Calretinin, nuclear expression of WT-1, and D2-40 positivity. EMA showed membranous staining in the neoplastic cells. The neoplastic cells were positive for p53 and negative for MOC-31, monoclonal CEA, TTF-1, CD34, desmin, CDX2, PAX8, CD31, PLAP, S-100, CD68, PSA, CD43, CK20 and CD117.

case_report: An 8-year-old girl with a history of renal anomaly was referred to our hospital for evaluation of other organ deformities. The patient had lived in an orphanage since birth. Family and prenatal histories were not confirmed. She had undergone open-heart surgery due to a ventricular septal defect at the age of 6 months at another hospital. The patient was frequently treated for recurrent urinary tract infections. At the age of 4 years, she underwent an operation due to vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) and a single dysplastic kidney in the pelvis. On admission, the vital signs were as follows: systolic and diastolic blood pressure 118 (95th percentile) and 65 mmHg (75th–95th percentile); pulse rate 70 times/min.; respiratory rate 20 times/min.; body temperature 36.2℃. Body weight was 13.3 kg (-5.42 standard deviation score [SDS]) and height was 91.2 cm (-7.91 SDS). Physical examination revealed facial asymmetry, a short neck, external ear aplasia on the right side, and right thumb hypoplasia. She had normal female external genitalia and showed normal intellectual development. Initial blood examination results were as follows: hemoglobin, 10.7 g/dL; leukocyte, 8,020/μL; platelet count, 355×103/mm; serum total protein, 8.7 g/dL; serum albumin, 4.7 g/dL; total cholesterol, 246 mg/dL; aspartate aminotransferase, 38 IU/L; alanine aminotransferase, 21 IU/L; serum sodium, 141 mEq/L; potassium, 4.9 mEq/L; chloride, 109 mEq/L. The blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and serum creatinine were 31.9 mg/dL and 1.40 mg/dL, respectively, and the glomerular filtration rate (by calculated Schwartz formula) was 35.8 mL/min/1.73 m2. The urinalysis showed normal findings. The karyotype was normal female as 46, XX. The serum insulin-like growth factor 1 level was within the normal range as 186.0 ng/mL (normal range, 100–446 ng/mL). A growth hormone (GH) stimulation test was performed to evaluate her extremely short stature. In the levodopa provocative test, the GH levels showed an exaggerated increase from 3.98 ng/dL to 46.5 ng/dL.
test_results: The spine X-ray showed a fusion of C2–3, and C4–5 vertebrae as well as a fusion of L1–2, and L3–4 vertebrae. The costal X-ray showed that the 1st and 2nd ribs on both sides were fused. The X-ray also showed scoliosis and sacrococcygeal agenesis. Abdominal computed tomography revealed a single left dysplastic kidney, located in the pelvis, and uterine aplasia. Evaluation of the auditory system revealed sensorineural hearing loss of the right ear as well as external ear malformation.

case_report: A 40-year-old obese Caucasian woman with no significant medical history presented with a rapidly enlarging, painless mass on her left upper arm that developed over several weeks. She reported no other health issues, including no changes in appetite, weight, or night sweats. She had ceased smoking five years prior and was not on any medication. Clinical examination showed normal blood pressure and pulse. A small, fixed, non-tender subcutaneous mass approximately 2.0 cm in diameter was noted on the left upper arm. No other abnormal lesions or lymph nodes were detected upon examination of the rest of her body. The mass was surgically excised, revealing a gray-tan nodule measuring 1.2 cm within the subcutaneous fat of the left upper arm.
test_results: Pathology revealed a radically excised structure resembling a lymph node in which a tumoral process was seen, consisting of a diffuse proliferation of atypical spindle cells. Complementary immunohistochemical stains were negative for HMB-45, KL1, cytokeratin AE1/3, and SMa. There was focal positivity for S100 and Melan A. Further clinical investigation of the patient by a dermatologist, ophthalmologist, gynecologist, and surgeon revealed no lesions suspect for the primary tumor. A CT chest and abdomen and PET CT scan also showed no suspect lesions. We confirmed the signs of cellular atypia as described elsewhere, within a spindle cell proliferation with a nodular texture, covered by normal dermis and epidermis without an intraepidermal melanocytic proliferation. The tumor nodules were partially surrounded by fibrous septa and densely vascularized by a capillary network. A dense and extensive lymphatic infiltrate with no evident subcapsular sinus surrounded the spindle cell proliferation. The neoplastic cells were positive for CD99 and EMA and to a lesser extent for CD31. Some capillary vessels stained positive for desmin; however, the tumor cells did not. Other negative stains included CD34, CD30, CD35, Cd10, HHV8, S100, MITF, CD79a, CD20, CD3, CD2, and CD21. Additional molecular research showed a gene fusion mutation of EWSR1-CREB1 t(2;22)(q33;q12), while mutations in BRAF and NRAS genes could not be detected.

case_report: A 58-year-old woman experienced left temporal pain at night for the past three years, which woke her up during early morning hours. The headaches were dull and lasted about 2 hours after waking. These episodes occurred more than 15 days each month. The patient did not report symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, sensitivity to light or sound, blurred vision, flashing lights, temporary vision loss, double vision, ringing in the ears, or numbness and weakness in the limbs. There were no signs of conjunctival congestion, tearing, nasal congestion, runny nose, sweating, or drooping eyelids. The patient did not snore and had no family history of headaches. Her medical history included asthma and gastric ulcer. Upon admission, her blood pressure was normal, and no neurological deficits were noted. Laboratory tests, including hematology, electrolytes, fasting blood sugar, glycosylated hemoglobin, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, liver function, and kidney function, were all within normal ranges. A brain MRI showed no midline structural abnormalities.
test_results: The patient was awakened by a headache at approximately 5:40 am after the last REM phase. No sleep apnea-hypopnea events were observed. The oxygen saturation and blood pressure were normal.

case_report: A 4-year-old Sri Lankan boy experienced increasing difficulty in walking and unsteadiness over a two-week period. He is the first child of non-consanguineous parents with no notable family medical history. At 18 months, he was found to have anaemia with a haemoglobin level of 8.0 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume (MCV) of 57.8 fL, mean corpuscular haemoglobin of 17.6 pg, and hypochromic microcytic red blood cells (RBC) on blood film. His serum ferritin, serum iron, and haemoglobin high-performance liquid chromatography were within normal ranges. Peripheral blood film showed haemoglobin H inclusion bodies, and DNA analysis indicated a compound heterozygous state for a 3.7 kb α-globin gene deletion and triplicated α-globin genes (-α3.7/ααα). Both parents had normal complete blood counts, but the mother’s α-globin genotype revealed α-thalassaemia trait (-α3.7/αα). The patient was managed as non-transfusion dependent α-thalassaemia with haemoglobin H disease, receiving infrequent RBC transfusions and daily folic acid (1 mg). In the three months before the current presentation, his haemoglobin levels frequently dropped below 7 g/dL, necessitating monthly blood transfusions. He began losing motor developmental milestones two weeks prior to admission. At admission, his gross motor development was equivalent to that of a 9–12-month-old; he could sit unaided and stand with support but could not walk even with support. He was on a normal balanced diet including both animal and plant-based foods and had no chronic illnesses. Examination revealed low mood, poor appetite, irritability, and hypopigmented hair, all of recent onset. His weight was 11 kg (at -3SD), with a growth chart showing a 2 kg weight loss over the past six months. His height was 92 cm (between -2SD to -3SD) and BMI was 12.9 kg/m2 (between -2SD to -3SD). Multiple petechiae were present on the body. Neurological examination showed generalized hypotonia, grade 4 muscle power in the lower limbs, exaggerated knee jerk, and extensor plantar response bilaterally. The upper limbs were normal except for hypotonia. Glasgow coma scale and intellectual functions were unaffected. Other systems were normal on examination. Complete blood count revealed haemoglobin of 6.8 g/dL, white cell count of 2800/mm3 (neutrophils 9% and lymphocytes 89%), and platelets of 53,000/mm3. Blood film showed pancytopenia and persistent haemoglobin H inclusion bodies. Reticulocyte count was 0.6%, and bone marrow biopsy indicated mildly suppressed megaloblastic erythropoiesis with partial maturation arrest of RBC precursors. Granulopoietic progenitor cells were hypercellular with giant metamyelocytes.
test_results: MRI of the spine revealed symmetrical T2-weighted high signal intensity in the posterior column from cervico-medullary junction to the 12th thoracic vertebra. Axial T2-weighted images showed ‘inverted V sign’ with symmetrical bilateral hyperintense signal in posterior columns. MRI of the brain revealed multiple bilateral patchy T2-weighted high signal intensity in the centrum semiovale and deep white matter areas with mild cerebral and cerebellar atrophy. The ventricular system, extra-axial cerebrospinal fluid spaces and cerebellar folia were prominent. Subsequent investigations revealed; low serum vitamin B12 (116 pg/ml; normal 187–883 pg/ml) and RBC folate (91 µg/L; normal 126–650 µg/L) levels.

case_report: A 52-year-old male patient reported experiencing pain and swelling in the upper right anterior region for the past 8 months. The patient mentioned a history of trauma in the same area, followed by the development and gradual increase in swelling. Despite being prescribed analgesics and antibiotics by a local physician, there was no symptom relief, leading to a referral to the institute. An extraoral examination showed a diffuse swelling measuring 4.5 cm × 3.5 cm on the right side of the face (maxilla), extending anteroposteriorly from 1 cm behind the ala of the nose to the lobe of the ear and superoposteriorly occupying the mid-region of the face. The swelling, which had evolved over 8 months, was firm and painful, with no local rise in temperature. Intraoral examination revealed erythematous growth on the right side of the maxilla extending from teeth 14 to 17. Radiographic examination showed ill-defined radiolucency and significant bone loss on the right side of the maxilla, along with destruction of the lower orbital margin and root resorption of tooth 16.
test_results: Microscopic examination of hematoxylin and eosin stained histopathological revealed the presence of odontogenic epithelium in various patterns, predominantly in follicular pattern. Sheets like arrangement of the odontogenic epithelial cells were also seen with hyperchromatic nuclei and scanty cytoplasm. Few of the follicles showed stellate reticulum-like cells. There was evidence of increase in cellular atypia and mitotic activity. Connective tissue stroma was fibrocellular. The sections were stained with CK19 and were found to be positive.

case_report: The patient is a 66-year-old male who does not smoke, has normal blood pressure, and does not have diabetes. He has experienced spontaneous blistering at areas of friction since early adolescence and has a history of difficulty swallowing. Physical examination showed he was underweight and pale. Skin examination identified multiple flaccid blisters containing hemorrhagic fluid on the shins, elbows, trunk, groins, and buttocks, along with atrophic scarring. Mucosal examination revealed erosions on the hard palate and enamel defects. There was also scarring alopecia with sparse hair on the scalp and partial loss of toenails. Laboratory results indicated a hemoglobin level of 6 gm/dl, with a peripheral blood film showing hypochromic microcytic cells.
test_results: A stricture involving the upper third of the esophagus.

case_report: A 4-year-old Japanese boy presented with swelling and discomfort in both upper eyelids. The swelling was painless, but the patient experienced itchiness in the eyelids. An ophthalmic examination showed bilateral upper eyelid edema. There was no lymphadenopathy in the head or neck region. The patient had no history of atopic dermatitis, but he had excessive local reactions to insect bites and vaccinations. There was no family history of autoimmune renal disease. Urinalysis results were normal. Blood analysis revealed a white blood cell count of 8,200 /mL with a differential neutrophil count of 13%, a lymphocyte count of 55.5%, and a significantly elevated eosinophil count of 28.5%. A peripheral smear showed no abnormalities. The CD4/CD8 ratio was 1.46. Most laboratory blood tests, including electrolytes, serum creatinine, and blood urea nitrogen, were normal. The patient had an elevated aspartate aminotransferase level of 34 IU/L (normal range: 14–20 IU/L), while alanine aminotransferase activity was within the normal range at 16 IU/L (normal range: 10–40 IU/L). Lactate dehydrogenase and creatinine kinase activities were normal. The C-reactive protein level was 0.045 mg/dL, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 9 mm/h. Immunoglobulin levels of IgG, IgA, IgD, IgM, and IgG4 were within normal ranges (IgG, 1,173 mg/dL; IgA, 162 mg/dL; IgD, 9.9 mg/dL; IgM 206 mg/dL; and IgG4 9.7 mg/dL). The patient had a highly elevated serum IgE level of 14,351 IU/mL (reference range: 0–295 IU/mL). Serologic analyses for antinuclear antibody and MPO-ANCA were negative, and serum complement components C3, C4, and total complement activity were normal. Chest radiography results were normal, while magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed bilateral lacrimal gland enlargement without mass lesions in the orbit or adjacent bony erosion. Pranlukast hydrate was administered for 2 years, but follow-up treatment was suspended for 4 years as the symptoms did not improve.
test_results: An excisional biopsy via anterior orbitotomy was performed at the age of 10 years, which revealed eosinophilic hyperplastic lymphogranuloma involving the lacrimal gland. A mixture of CD3-positive and CD5-positive T-cells was found within the interfollicular regions, and CD20-positive B-cells were observed within the follicles. A relatively smaller number of IgG-positive and IgG4-positive plasma cells were also observed. There was no evidence of either vasculitis or prominent vascular endothelial cell proliferation.

case_report: A 67-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and two unruptured aneurysms, located at the anterior choroidal artery (4.5 mm) and at the posterior communicating artery (2.7 mm), underwent endovascular coil embolization. She had previously undergone cerebral angiography from the left common carotid artery (CCA) without any adverse reaction. Angiography showed no collateral circulation from the anterior and posterior circulating arteries. The coil embolization procedure began with a femoral puncture. A guidewire was inserted into the left internal carotid artery (ICA) and extended to the tortuous carotid artery. Subsequently, 8 Fr guiding catheters (Asahi Fubuki®; Asahi Intecc Co., Ltd., Aichi, Japan) were placed in the left CCA, and a 6 Fr intermediate catheter (Cerulean DD6®; Medikit Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Japan) was placed at the cervical C1 level of the ICA with some difficulty. The sharp branching angle and tortuosity of the CCA resulted in resistance to moving the distal access catheter to the ICA. During the procedure, the patient was restless and exhibited right-sided hemiparesis and aphasia. Angiography from the 6 Fr intermediate catheter showed slow anterograde cerebral flow and retrograde pooling of contrast material at the top of the 8 Fr catheter. Further down the catheter, an angiographic image showed folds of the left ICA. Angiography showed gradual improvement of the kinks of the artery. Right-sided hemiparesis and aphasia persisted for 7 minutes, after which the patient recovered from the symptoms. The 8 Fr guiding catheter was replaced with a 6 Fr catheter (Asahi Fubuki®), and the procedure continued. The aneurysm was embolized without any neurological deficits. Thirty minutes after the procedure, she again presented with right-sided hemiparesis and aphasia.
test_results: A computed tomography (CT) scan showed cortical edema of the left cerebral hemisphere and contrast agent leakage to the subarachnoid space. Diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) did not show hyperintensity.

case_report: A 54-year-old Hispanic man experienced a decline in grip strength, which was followed by weakness in his lower limbs after one year. Laboratory tests showed a CK level of 2400 IU/L. Initial treatments included prednisone and other immunosuppressive medications such as azathioprine, methotrexate, and mycophenolate mofetil. Although his CK level decreased to 450 IU/L, his condition continued to worsen. Nine years later, during an evaluation at a neuromuscular clinic, he was unable to rise from a seated position, locked his knees while walking to prevent falls, and exhibited severe weakness in his left hand and moderate weakness in his right hand. Physical examination revealed asymmetric muscle atrophy in the forearm flexors and quadriceps, with pronounced asymmetric weakness in knee extension and mild weakness in ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion.
test_results: EMG showed active denervation with significant brief, small, abundant, polyphasic motor unit potentials. A repeat muscle biopsy showed variation in muscle fiber size, endomysial fibrosis, chronic inflammatory cells with macrophages, and rimmed vacuoles with basophilic stippling.

case_report: A 32-year-old male was admitted with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) characterized by severe hypertension and elevated serum creatinine (SCr) levels for 9 years, and he has been undergoing renal dialysis for the past 4 years. Nine years ago, he experienced syncope and was found to have uraemia. He was treated with traditional Chinese medicine following this event. Renal dialysis commenced 4 years ago due to worsening kidney function, with an SCr level reaching 900 μmol/L. No kidney biopsy was performed during the progression of his kidney disease. The patient was born with multiple congenital abnormalities, including bilateral overlapping toes and unilateral dysplastic external ears. At the age of 10, he was noted to have a moderate degree of sensorineural hearing loss in one ear. The patient's family history includes similar congenital abnormalities and renal issues. His grandmother had a sixth finger malformation, unilateral dysplastic external ears, and hearing loss. His father had unilateral dysplastic external ears, hearing loss, and bilateral overlapping toes, and began dialysis at 53 years old. His aunt had unilateral dysplastic external ears, hearing loss, and unilateral preaxial polydactyly of one hand, and also began haemodialysis at 53 years old due to unexplained ESRD. His daughter was born with bilateral dysplastic external ears and unilateral hearing dysfunction initially misdiagnosed as otitis media. Upon examination, the patient's vital signs were within normal ranges: body temperature at 36.7 °C, respiratory rate at 18 breaths/min, pulse rate at 80 bpm, and blood pressure at 134/85 mmHg under antihypertensive treatment. Physical examination revealed bilateral overlapping toes and unilateral dysplastic external ears. Ophthalmic examination results were normal, and no anorectal abnormalities were detected. Laboratory analysis showed an increased SCr level of 941.9 μmol/L, high potassium level of 6.87 mmol/L, high phosphate level of 2.73 mmol/L, normal haemoglobin level of 145 g/L, and high parathyroid hormone level of 663.6 pg/mL. The patient was anuric.
test_results: Ultrasound examination revealed bilaterally small kidneys (left kidney, 52 mm × 34 mm; right kidney, 50 mm × 25 mm) with multiple 5-7 mm medullary cysts. The urinary tract was normal, and no additional abnormalities of the liver, spleen, or pancreas were detected.

case_report: A 63-year-old male experienced a cervical spinal cord injury following a suicide attempt. No abnormalities were detected within the brain. Post-recovery, he was prescribed 20 mg/day of duloxetine by a psychiatrist for depression. The patient was referred to Takatsuki Hospital for ongoing treatment, where the duloxetine dosage was increased to 60 mg/day due to persistent symptoms of decreased motivation and depression, but no significant improvement was noted. The patient also experienced numbness in his hands and feet due to the spinal cord injury and was taking loxoprofen (180 mg/day) and pregabalin (225 mg/day) as prescribed by an orthopedic surgeon. Two years later, he reported continued numbness and pain in his extremities, along with dizziness and lightheadedness. A year after that, he had difficulty walking, fell down some stairs, and sustained a compression fracture of the lumbar vertebrae, leading to his admission to Takatsuki Hospital. Approximately four years after starting outpatient treatment at Takatsuki, his gait worsened, and cognitive function declined, prompting a transfer to the National Center of Neurology and Psychiatry for further evaluation. Neurological examination showed restricted upward eye movements, significant muscle stiffness in the right upper limb, and mild signs associated with the frontal lobe.
test_results: An MRI of the brain revealed midbrain atrophy and hummingbird signs. Brain SPECT revealed decreased blood flow in the frontal lobe.

case_report: A 14-year-old male reported experiencing involuntary dystonic movements over the past two months, which are triggered by sudden activities following periods of physical rest. These movements last around 10 seconds. The frequency of these episodes ranges from about 20 times per day to once every few weeks. Both sides of his body can be affected, and there are occasional instances of spasmodic torticollis. Stress and anxiety appear to increase the likelihood of these episodes. The patient is unable to control these movements, but his consciousness remains unaffected during the episodes. He has no significant medical history and was healthy during birth and growth. There is no family history of involuntary movements, epilepsy, or related conditions. Physical examination revealed normal vital signs and a normal neurological examination. Laboratory tests, including routine serum tests, standard biochemistry profile, serum lactate concentration, and ceruloplasmin levels, were all within normal limits. Brain MRI and EEG results were also normal.
test_results: Heterozygous variants were found in POLG (NM_002693.2, Exon2, c.440G>T, p.Ser147Ile) and PLA2G6 (NM_003560.3, Exon7, c.991G>T, p.Asp331Tyr). Both mutant alleles were inherited from his asymptomatic mother. The POLG variant (c.440G>T, p.Ser147Ile) located on the exonuclease domain, one of the important functional domains of POLG1 protein, and may lead to infidelity of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) replication and proofreading errors. This variant was novel and not registered in the following genetic public database: Human Gene Mutation Database (HGMD), ESP6500, 1000 Genomes Project, ClinVar, and dbSNP. The missense PLA2G6 variant (c.991G>T, p.Asp331Tyr) has been reported in Parkinsonism patients with an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.
diagnosis: Paroxysmal Kinesigenic Dyskinesia  associated with a novel POLG variant

case_report: A 37-year-old woman with a 19-year history of pruritic dermatosis of the trunk presented with worsening symptoms. Physical examination showed arcuate, finely scaly erythematous patches covering 70% of the body surface area. Previous treatments included psoralen plus ultraviolet A (PUVA), topical tacrolimus, topical corticosteroids, and methotrexate, all of which were ineffective. Skin biopsy revealed a thickened epidermis with surface parakeratosis, discrete spongiosis, and a mononuclear infiltrate of the superficial dermis. Treatment with oral ciclosporin (5 mg/kg/day) led to partial remission after 3 months, followed by a relapse. Dupilumab (600 mg/2 weeks) was introduced, but after 2 months, there was no clinical response. The patient experienced intense pruritus, skin plaques, and palmoplantar keratosis.
test_results: Skin biopsy revealed an atypical dermal infiltrate of medium CD3+CD4+ lymphocytes with strong expression of PD1 and no expression of CD30. Blood immunophenotyping showed an aberrant CD4+ T-cell population with CD7 loss, aberrant expression of KIR3DL2 (2,738/mm3) and a CD4/CD8 ratio of 22. The same massive T-cell clone was found in her peripheral blood and in the skin.

case_report: A 71-year-old Chinese man experienced an inability to stand and was hospitalized for 35 hours due to limb weakness, predominantly on the left side. His medical history includes hypertension for over 2 years and essential tremors in both hands for 7 years. Initial assessments included a Mini-Mental State Examination score of 23 out of 30 and a Montreal Cognitive Assessment score of 16 out of 30, both indicating severe cognitive impairment. No similar clinical symptoms were reported in other family members. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination was performed, but the results are not available.
test_results: Eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions in adipocytes, sweat gland cells, fibroblasts that were ubiquitin-positive. The FMR1 gene revealed no expanded CGG premutations. The number of GGC repeats in NOTCH2NLC gene was 80.

case_report: A 71-year-old right-handed man with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and glaucoma experienced progressive stiffness in his right arm and speech difficulties over one year. He visited the emergency department due to speech issues and high blood pressure, but a brain MRI showed no signs of a stroke. Three months later, he exhibited mild guttural speech difficulties, significantly increased muscle tone in his right arm held in flexion, and difficulty extending and abducting his right-hand fingers, although arm strength remained full. Reflexes were slightly brisk in the right arm, with upgoing plantar reflexes on both sides. His gait was characterized by a slightly stooped posture, reduced right arm swing, and mild postural instability, but stride length and gait speed were normal. Orientation, naming, sensory, and cerebellar functions were intact. Previous brain and spinal MRI showed mild subcortical white matter hyperintensities more pronounced on the left, mild temporal lobe atrophy more on the left, and moderate spinal stenosis with severe bilateral C5-C7 foraminal stenosis, worse on the right. An electromyogram (EMG) of the right upper extremity and cervical paraspinal muscles was normal. He received intensive physical, occupational, and speech therapy, which led to some improvement in daily function. Three months later, his speech difficulties worsened, accompanied by right-sided facial droop and swallowing difficulties. The rigidity in his right upper extremity became more pronounced and extended to his right leg. His Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score was 15, with deficits in executive function, attention, visuospatial ability, and delayed recall that did not improve with cueing. A formal speech evaluation revealed a strained, hypernasal, and breathy vocal quality with slow, effortful, and segmented speech. He had frequent misarticulations, imprecise consonants, and produced only one syllable per breath, showing elements of both spastic and flaccid speech difficulties. He also displayed ideomotor apraxia in his right arm. A follow-up EMG of three limbs, cervical and thoracic paraspinal muscles, and tongue performed a year later showed focal denervation in the right flexor carpi radialis but no tongue denervation. A comprehensive laboratory assessment for metabolic, infectious, or inflammatory conditions was negative. A follow-up brain MRI revealed mild progression of atrophy, mainly in the left motor and pre-motor cortex and left temporal lobe.
test_results: A brain fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) scan demonstrated left hemisphere hypometabolism primarily within frontal lobe, basal ganglia, and thalamus. Hypometabolism of the left anterior temporal lobe was also noted.
diagnosis: Corticobasal Syndrome  with a novel TBK1 variant

case_report: A three-day-old female infant was observed to have an abdominal mass lesion identified during routine prenatal ultrasound screening. At 26 weeks of gestation, imaging revealed a defined mass in the right abdomen exerting pressure on the nearby small bowel loops. The infant was delivered at 39 weeks through vaginal birth, with a birth weight of 3,142 grams. There was no reported family or parental history of vascular disorders. Physical examination showed mild enlargement of the left lower limb and red lesions on the left thigh.
test_results: A follow-up MRI of the abdomen was obtained after delivery, and this showed a 6.3 cm × 2.7 cm × 5.5 cm cyst-like lesion in the upper abdomen. Some possible calcified spots with high T1WI signals and low T2WI signals were also noted within the mass. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen was consistent with an ill-defined cystic mass with small calcifications and encasement of mesenteric vessels. An MRI of the left lower extremity revealed a tubular structure at the anterior subcutis of the left lower leg that extended to the lateral thigh subcutis and into the ipsilateral gluteus muscle, connecting with vessels at the left pelvic sidewall. The tubular lesion displayed a signal void and homogeneous strong enhancement. A CT scan of the left lower extremity also revealed a vascular structure with no significant enhancement in the arterial phase but gradual contrast filling in the delayed phase. Reconstructed images revealed one engorged incompetent vessel on the lateral aspect of the left lower extremity that extended from the lower leg to the gluteal and pelvic regions. Subcutaneous soft tissue stranding and edematous change from the left thigh to calf were also noted. A biopsy of the left thigh lesion was performed and the pathology revealed capillary–lymphatic–venous malformation (CLVM).

case_report: A 2.5-year-old girl arrived at the emergency department with severe nosebleed lasting about one hour. Her medical history showed no umbilical cord bleeding at birth, but she had a tendency to bruise easily since infancy. She started having recurrent nosebleeds at 14 months old, with two to three episodes each month, each lasting 15 to 20 minutes. These episodes were previously managed at home with applied pressure and did not require medical intervention. At her 18-month well-child visit, her pediatrician advised monitoring her bleeding symptoms. At her 2-year well-child exam, laboratory tests showed normal complete blood count, platelet count, and PT/PTT. Upon arrival at the emergency department, she appeared well-nourished and playful, with normal vital signs and no fever. Examination revealed dried blood around her left nostril, a large bruise with a palpable hematoma on her lower abdomen, and several petechiae on her trunk, extremities, and face. The rest of the physical examination was normal. Due to her recurrent nosebleeds, bruising, and petechiae, consultations were made with an otolaryngologist and a pediatric hematologist. Bleeding was managed with vasoconstrictive spray and nasal packing. Laboratory tests showed normal white blood cell and platelet counts, low hemoglobin, and low ferritin levels. Coagulation studies indicated normal PT and PTT, and no evidence of Von Willebrand disease (VWF antigen, 107 IU/dL; ristocetin cofactor, 116 IU/dL; FVIII activity, 97 IU/mL).
test_results: Her platelet aggregation studies showed greatly reduced responses with all agonists except for agglutination to ristocetin. Immunophenotyping analysis using flow cytometry demonstrated reduced expression of CD41 (GPIIb) and CD61 (GPIIIa).

case_report: A 13-year-old male presented with multiple raised lesions on the face and body since 3 months of age and loss of eyebrows since his first year. The patient has a history of sensitivity to light and recurrent respiratory tract infections. He was born full-term via normal vaginal delivery to non-consanguineous parents and has been immunized according to schedule. There is no history of scalp hair loss, delayed developmental milestones, similar complaints in the family, or atopy. Physical examination showed multiple, pinpoint, skin-colored papules on the forehead, bilateral cheeks, chin, neck, chest, abdomen, back, bilateral arms, bilateral forearms, bilateral upper thighs, and gluteal region. Eyebrow hair loss was noted. Palms, soles, oral cavity, dentition, nails, and genitalia appeared normal. Ophthalmic examination indicated bilateral posterior blepharitis and sensitivity to light. Routine blood tests showed an elevated eosinophil count, while other results were within normal limits.
test_results: Skin biopsy of the spiny papules revealed features suggestive of keratosis pilaris. Dermoscopy over the eyebrows and lesions over trunk revealed keratinous plugs in the follicular orifices.
diagnosis: Ichthyosis Follicularis, Alopecia, and Photophobia  Syndrome

case_report: A 48-year-old male was admitted to Beijing YouAn Hospital with liver cirrhosis. Four months prior, an abdominal ultrasound indicated cirrhosis and splenomegaly, despite the patient experiencing no discomfort. At another hospital, he was diagnosed with diabetes and started on insulin therapy. The patient reported minimal alcohol consumption and no family history of liver diseases. Physical examination revealed skin pigmentation but no other abnormalities. Liver function tests showed elevated levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST). Serum markers for viral hepatitis and autoimmune liver diseases were negative. Plasma iron indices were abnormal: iron at 47 μmol/L, transferrin saturation at 97.9%, and ferritin levels exceeding 2000 ng/ml. HbA1c was significantly elevated, while testosterone levels were normal at 18.26 nmol/L. Pre-contrast computed tomography (CT) showed hepatomegaly with increased attenuation in the liver and spleen, splenomegaly, and formation of collateral circulation. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a typical decrease in T2-weighted signal intensity over the liver.
test_results: The findings confirmed established cirrhosis with a marked deposition of iron in the hepatocytes and biliary epithelia. The results showed that the patient (II-1) had new heterozygous mutations c.1288G > A (p.G430R)/c.960T > A (p.Y320X) in the TFR2 gene. These mutations were further confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

case_report: An 85-year-old woman reported a noticeable mass in her right submandibular triangle that had been present for 3 months. She was undergoing treatment for hypertension and seldom experienced tenderness. During the physical examination, the mass was found to be firm and mobile, not attached to the overlying skin or the floor of the mouth. No motor or sensory impairments were observed.
test_results: Dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging of the right submandibular gland showed a pattern characteristic of an MT (type-C time-intensity curve TIC). FNAC showed the presence of a necrotic-like substance behind lymphoid cells, neutrophils, and a few ductal acini.

case_report: A 2-year-old boy presented with an absence of speech, limited social interaction skills, and repetitive behaviors. He was the second child of healthy, unrelated Thai parents, with an older sister who had normal development. His birth weight was 3,600 g, and there were no complications during birth. He first stood with support at 10 months and walked without support at 27 months. He could not hold a spoon and feed himself until 45 months. He never developed verbal language skills. His growth metrics, including head circumference, were within normal ranges, but he had been overweight since the age of 2. At 10 years old, his BMI was 29.7 kg/m2 (>97th centile, Z score = 3.79). He had no hypopigmentation and had never shown signs of seizure, ataxia, or hypotonia. He typically walked on tiptoes, had poor eye contact, and exhibited repetitive behavior by constantly spinning the wheels of a toy car. He engaged in hand-flapping when happy and liked to bite objects such as clothes and drinking straws. At 5 years old, he was assessed using the Autism Diagnosis Observation Schedule (ADOS)-Module 1, scoring 4 for communication (cutoff = 4), 8 for reciprocal social interaction (cutoff = 7), and 1 for repetitive behaviors. At 10 years old, his non-verbal IQ was 42 (Stanford Binet Intelligence Scales-Fifth edition), and the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales-II indicated moderate deficits in communication, daily living skills, and socialization. Over time, his social interaction skills improved; by 11 years old, he enjoyed playing with peers and parents, although he still could not speak understandable words. Initial genetic testing for common causes of ASD showed normal karyotyping and normal CGG repeats on the FMR1 gene. An electroencephalogram (EEG) was also normal.
test_results: He was screened with the CMA at 10 years of age to look for pathogenic CNVs.

case_report: The patient, Z.A.S, a 35-year-old black African woman, housewife, seventh gravida and fourth para, with 5 living children, was admitted to the gastrointestinal surgery emergency of the University Hospital of Cocody (Abidjan, Cote D'Ivoire) on 25/05/2012 for abdominopelvic pain and an abdominal mass. Symptoms began about a year ago with progressive abdominal distension, amenorrhea, and asthenia. Abdominopelvic pain started approximately 10 days before admission, accompanied by a dry cough and difficulty breathing. On admission, she was emaciated, dyspneic, and very asthenic. Conjunctivae were slightly colored, without jaundice. There was no edema or collateral venous circulation. Vital signs were blood pressure = 10/06 Cmmhg, pulse = 120 bpm, respiratory rate = 22 cycles/min. Physical examination revealed abundant ascites and a large, diffuse, solid, mobile, and slightly painful abdominopelvic mass, with increased pain in the pelvis. The mass extended from the pelvis to the upper abdomen. Vaginal examination made it difficult to relate the mass to the uterus or annexes. Bilateral pleural effusion was also noted. Heart sounds were regular without murmurs. Chest radiograph showed bilateral hydrothorax, and abdominal CT-scan visualized two tissue masses: one abdominopelvic, multilobulated with multiple necrotic portions, measuring 233 mm × 200 mm, and the other in the pelvis, measuring 115 mm × 90 mm, compressing the bladder dome without signs of invasion.
