Both masses were independent of the uterus, kidneys, and above mesocolic organs, coexisting with abundant ascites without peritoneal nodulation. Emergency pleural paracentesis (500 mL) and ascites drainage (4.5 liters) were performed due to significant dyspnea. Microscopic and chemical analysis of both effusions indicated a transudate without malignant cells. Liver and kidney function tests were normal. Complete blood count showed anemia with hemoglobin at 7.9 g/dL. Tumor markers were measured: CEA = 4.77 ng/mL (normal < 5 ng/mL); serum CA-125 level = 1835 IU/mL (normal < 30 IU/mL); AFP = 8.1 ng/mL (normal < 20 ng/mL). ECG was normal. An exploratory laparotomy was performed on 03/06/2012, one week after admission. Intraoperatively, a midline incision revealed 2.5 liters of ascites and two large ovarian masses: a right ovarian tumor measuring 40 cm × 30 cm, multilobulated, solid, mobile, and a left ovarian tumor measuring 20 cm × 15 cm with similar characteristics, and the left adnexal in subtorsion. Both ovaries were enveloped by tumors. There were no lymphadenopathy or suspicious peritoneal carcinomatosis. The uterus, liver, gallbladder, and spleen appeared macroscopically normal. A total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy was performed. A blood transfusion of 1 liter of packed cells was administered along with analgesics. The postoperative course was uneventful, with no reconstitution of ascites, and the patient was discharged on day 12.
test_results: Histological analysis of the two surgical specimens concluded a double ovarian fibrothecoma which is a benign tumor.

case_report: A 79-year-old woman with a history of cerebral infarction in the left basal ganglia presented with headache and dizziness. Imaging showed an unruptured aneurysm on the right superior cerebellar artery (SCA). She was on aspirin (100 mg/d) and atorvastatin (40 mg/d) since the cerebral infarction, amlodipine (5 mg/d) and telmisartan (40 mg/d) for hypertension, and metformin (1700 mg/d) for type 2 diabetes mellitus. Her hypertension was previously uncontrolled but became managed with medication. The patient had no smoking history, autoimmune diseases, or allergic reactions. Cerebral angiography identified a small SCA aneurysm with a broad neck (maximum diameter 2.62 mm, neck diameter 2.73 mm) and narrowing of both anterior cerebral arteries (ACA). Due to the small size of the aneurysm, periodic brain imaging was planned. A dual antiplatelet regimen of aspirin (100 mg/d) and clopidogrel (75 mg/d) was initiated due to severe ACA stenosis. Two weeks later, the patient was hospitalized for dyspnea that began 3 days prior, accompanied by anorexia, nausea, dyspnea on exertion, and chest pain, but no cough, sputum, rhinorrhea, or chills. On admission, she was hypoxemic (room air pulse oximetry, 91%), and chest radiography showed multifocal consolidation and reticulonodular opacities in both lungs. Vital signs were: blood pressure, 136/66 mmHg; heart rate, 78 beats/min; respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min; and body temperature, 36.7 °C. Arterial blood gas analysis results were: pH, 7.422; PaCO2, 38.3 mmHg; PaO2, 57 mmHg; SaO2, 88.1% (2 L/min of oxygen via nasal prong). Laboratory tests showed: hemoglobin, 11.5 g/dL; white blood cell count, 7410 cells/μL (neutrophils, 65.1%; lymphocytes, 24.3%; monocytes, 9.0%; eosinophils, 0.9%; basophils, 0.7%); platelet count, 327,000 cells/μL; and C-reactive protein, 1.6 mg/dL. Serum biochemistry results were within normal limits: aspartate aminotransferase, 19 IU/L; alanine aminotransferase, 5 IU/L; total bilirubin, 0.7 mg/dL; alkaline phosphatase, 59 IU/L; total protein, 7.0 g/dL; albumin, 3.5 g/dL; blood urea nitrogen, 7 mg/dL; and creatinine, 0.57 mg/dL. Pulmonary function tests showed forced expiratory volume in one second and forced vital capacity were 1.02 L (predicted, 75%) and 1.07 L (predicted, 52%), respectively, and carbon monoxide diffusion capacity was 2.6 mL/mmHg/min (predicted, 19%). Congestive heart failure was ruled out with normal ultrasound cardiography and serum brain natriuretic peptide levels. Empirical antibiotics (piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 hours plus levofloxacin 75 mg every 24 hours) were administered due to chest radiography findings. Enhanced chest CT showed symmetric peribronchial ground-glass opacity (GGO), reticulation, and consolidation in both lungs. The patient developed a fever (37.8 °C) on the second day of hospitalization, and oxygen saturation could not be maintained at 5 L/min via nasal prong, necessitating high-flow nasal cannula (30 L/min; FiO2, 35%).
test_results: BAL samples revealed a clear color fluid, and no microorganisms were detected.
Orpha_name: Drug or radiation exposure-related interstitial lung disease

case_report: An 11-year-old female presented at a community outreach program in Hansposa, Sunsari with primary concerns of brown to yellowish discoloration of teeth, sensitivity, and difficulty while eating. She had experienced similar discoloration in her deciduous teeth. Her brother exhibited a similar condition, suggesting a familial pattern. Physical examination revealed a normal facial profile and normal molar occlusion. The teeth showed brown to yellowish discoloration with chipping of the cuspal enamel in the posterior teeth.
test_results: OPG revealed thin lining of enamel with thick dentin layer and pulp chamber.

case_report: A 14-year-old male patient has experienced progressive difficulty in maintaining balance since the age of 4 years. He is the first child of healthy, non-consanguineous Chinese parents with no family history of gait disorders. The patient had normal development until 4 years of age, when parents started noticing unsteady gait with frequent falls, cognitive decline, and speech difficulties. At age 7 years, he exhibited worsening ataxia with effort, dysarthria, gait disturbances, slowness, learning difficulties, exercise intolerance, and fatigue requiring rest. At age 10 years, his first neurological examination revealed significant cerebellar syndrome with gait ataxia, dysarthria, and mild cognitive and executive function decline. Physical examination showed pes cavus, but no scoliosis or other musculoskeletal deformities. Deep tendon reflexes in the lower extremities were absent, and the plantar response was flexor bilaterally. Sensations of light touch, pinprick, and vibration were absent, and the Romberg test was positive. Neurological examination indicated gait imbalance without dystonia, chorea, tremor, or dyskinesia. Extraocular range of motion was adequate in all directions, with no abnormalities on reflex saccade examination. At age 14, a trained neurologist noted mild cognitive impairment.
test_results: Nerve conduction study showed reduced nerve conduction velocities and low sensory and motor action potentials indicating sensorimotor axonal polymorphic peripheral nerve damage. The lower extremity muscles were biopsied, and histological analysis showed that the size of muscle fibers varied slightly, showing neurogenic pathological changes. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head showed atrophy of the cerebellum with no involvement of the brainstem or cerebral cortex, and low signal loss in the cerebellar dentate nucleus on sensitivity-weighted imaging (SWI). A nonsense mutation in exon 7 (c.739C >T; p.Arg247*) and a frameshift mutation in exon 6 (c.501dupG; p.Ser168Glufs*19) were identified by using WES, and they were co-segregated with the affected members.

case_report: A 77-year-old male with a medical history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and chronic right mastoiditis reported to his opticians with complaints of blurred vision and a gradual decrease in visual acuity in both eyes over three to four months. The opticians observed bilateral cataracts and noted a potential left homonymous hemianopia, leading to a referral to the ophthalmology clinic. The ophthalmologist subsequently referred him to the stroke clinic due to the suspected hemianopia. At the stroke clinic, the patient exhibited no other objective deficits except for reduced visual acuity and diminished left-sided visual perception. He was in good clinical condition and remained independent in his activities of daily living.
test_results: An MRI brain suggested T2 hyperintensity in a cortical distribution predominantly in the right occipital lobe with diffusion restriction on the diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) sequences and corresponding changes on the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map. The follow-up MRI suggested extensive 'cortical ribboning' on the DWI imaging seen as cortical hyperintensity in the right temporal, parietal, and occipital regions, especially in the visual field areas. Focal cortical ribboning was seen in the paramedian cortex in both frontal lobes. Similar changes were seen in the left occipital and temporal lobes. Corresponding ADC changes were persistent. EEG showed rhythmic, periodic sharp waves and triphasic waves. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis suggested acellular fluid with protein of 0.61 with a positive real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC).

case_report: A 71-year-old male with a history of hypertension, hemorrhoids, and glaucoma presented with symptoms of weight loss, hair loss, abdominal colic, altered taste, and diarrhea over a 4-month period. He reported no melena, hematemesis, or blood in his stools. Six months later, he experienced hypoesthesia and paresthesia in his hands and feet, without associated pain, weakness, rashes, joint swelling, or fever. His vision, speech, hearing, and smell remained unchanged. Physical examination showed no jaundice, pallor, or cachexia. The abdomen was soft and non-distended, with no palpable hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Neurological examination indicated mild motor weakness (4/5 on the MRC scale) in finger abduction, ankle dorsiflexion, and plantar flexion, more pronounced on the left side. Deep tendon reflexes were reduced in both ankles, and sensory testing showed decreased touch and temperature sensation in both hands and feet, while vibration and position sense were preserved. Gait and cerebellar function were normal. Initial hematological tests revealed normal blood counts and electrolytes, but hypoalbuminemia (5 μmol/L) without elevated liver enzymes. Thyroid function, vitamin B12, and folate levels were within normal ranges. Autoimmune tests, including antinuclear, anti-Smith, anti-smooth muscle, Ro, La, ribonuclear protein, anti-double stranded DNA, and anti-Jo1 titers, were not elevated. Hepatitis B and C serology were negative. A CT abdominal scan showed a few diverticula in the colon, while a CT colonoscopy revealed an extensive nodular appearance of the colonic mucosa and a few polyps.
test_results: Gastroscopy showed infiltrative lesions in the stomach and duodenum. Colonoscopy detected multiple strawberry-like hamartomatous polyps in the entire colon and occasional tubulovillous adenomas with low-grade dysplasia. Biopsies of the stomach, duodenum, and colon revealed regenerative and hyperplastic changes with prominent lamina propia odema and increased eosinophils. Nerve conduction study (NCS) showed asymmetrically reduced left peroneal sensory, right sural sensory, left peroneal motor, and left tibial motor amplitudes. There was significant reduction of bilateral ulnar sensory and motor amplitudes. Sympathetic skin responses were normal in all four limbs.

case_report: An eleven-year-old male presented with numerous darkly pigmented spots distributed across his entire body. These spots first appeared at age 5 and have progressively increased in number. Physical examination showed that the spots were unevenly distributed, with a higher concentration on the face and involvement of the palpebral conjunctiva. The spots varied in color from light to dark brown and were heterogeneous in size, all measuring less than 3 mm. No skeletal abnormalities or dysmorphic features were observed. The patient's family history was unremarkable, and no other systemic conditions were reported. A minimally invasive biopsy was performed on one of the spots (2 mm in diameter, all layers of the skin) under local anesthesia after obtaining consent from the patient's parents. Histological examination revealed an increased number of basal melanocytes and elongation of crests, consistent with lentigo simplex.
test_results: The molecular study identified a germline mutation in the PTPN11 mutation (Tyr279Cys, c.836A > G) in the tissue sample with a mutation frequency of 44.32%. ECG examination showed extreme right axis deviation (QRS axis: + 232°), suggesting right ventricular hypertrophy.

case_report: A 29-year-old woman began experiencing abnormal jerky movements in her upper limbs at the age of 10. These movements were action-induced and more pronounced in the morning. Two months later, she started having focal seizures with tonic postures in the left limb, which often progressed to generalized tonic-clonic seizures. The average frequency of these seizures was 2 to 5 per month, with tonic-clonic episodes lasting up to 5 minutes, followed by 30 to 60 minutes of drowsiness. The involuntary movements worsened during her menstrual period and improved for 5 to 7 days following each generalized tonic-clonic seizure. There was no improvement in myoclonus with fever, and the patient did not consume alcohol. Following the onset of myoclonus and seizures in early adolescence, she experienced progressive difficulties with gait and balance, becoming wheelchair-bound by the age of 21. Seizures were managed with valproate, and she has been seizure-free since the age of 15. Prior to visiting our outpatient clinic, she was on carbamazepine, which was ineffective. No other anti-seizure medications were used before valproate and piracetam, the latter of which was discontinued due to somnolence. Early developmental milestones were delayed; she walked without support at age three and spoke more complex phrases around age four. Her medical history includes insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, and her family history is unremarkable. By age 29, she had completed high school and recently scored 25/30 on the Mini Mental State Examination. Neurological examination showed severe generalized action myoclonus, global ataxia, and dysarthria.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing identified a missense variant c.959G > A (p.Arg320His) in KCNC1. Electroencephalogram disclosed generalized spike and spike-wave paroxysms. Brain MRI showed mild cerebellar atrophy.

case_report: A 10-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with a right-knee injury sustained while playing soccer without any direct contact. The child participates in sports noncompetitively and has no prior history of knee pain. Post-injury, he was unable to walk. Physical examination revealed tenderness and swelling over the patella. The extensor mechanism showed tenderness but no palpable gap in the patella. The patient was able to perform a straight leg raise with a 25° extension lag. His neurovascular examination was normal.
test_results: His X-ray radiographs revealed an inferior pole fragment that was minimally displaced with clear sclerotic margins. MRI showed edema and joint effusion. The MRI did not reveal articular cartilage separation of sleeve fractures.

case_report: A 37-year-old Caucasian male with no prior medical history underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy due to symptomatic biliary lithiasis. The gallbladder was found to contain gallstones and exhibited a moderately thickened wall without any apparent mucosal lesions. Additionally, a 1.3-cm lymph node was observed adjacent to the cystic duct, which was free of stones.
test_results: Histologically, the gallbladder showed hyperplastic and inflammatory changes consistent with xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis, and the cystic duct was normal. Beside benign reactive changes with B cell follicular hyperplasia, the lymph node was partially obliterated by a relatively circumscribed and vaguely nodular infiltrate of monotonous medium-sized cells with moderately abundant pale cytoplasm. No cytoplasmic granules were visible. Nuclei were round to oval with slightly irregular contours, somewhat open chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli. There were rare apoptotic bodies, few mitoses, and scattered histiocytes. By immunohistochemistry, the pale cells were positive for CD2, cytoplasmic CD3 (± ), CD7, CD56, perforin, granzyme B (± ) and T-cell intracellular antigen (TIA)-1, and negative for T-cell receptor β (TCRβ), TCRδ, CD1a, CD4, CD5, CD8, CD10, CD20, CD23, CD30, CD34, CD57, CD79a, CD123, CXCL13, ICOS, PD1, S100, and myeloperoxydase. The Ki-67 proliferation index was approximately 10%. EBV-encoded RNA (EBER) in situ hybridization (ISH) was negative. Polymerase chain reaction–based clonality analysis did not demonstrate clonal rearrangement of the TR genes (TRB and TRG). Next-generation sequencing (NGS) analysis using a panel of 26 genes designed for peripheral T-cell lymphomas disclosed a mutation involving the exon 4 of the DNMT3A gene (c.178-9C>T) with a variant allele fraction (VAF) of 46%. FISH analysis using a JAK2 break apart probe (9p24) showed a normal hybridization pattern.

case_report: A 16-year-old male presented with bilateral breast enlargement persisting for 4 years. He had a history of hypospadias, corrected surgically at 1 year of age. Physical examination revealed a height of 161 cm, weight of 57.8 kg (BMI 22.3 kg/m2), and blood pressure of 120/80 mm Hg. Pubertal development was noted as normal, with both breasts enlarged (Tanner stage III), pubic hair at Tanner stage V, and testicular volume of 15 mL (Tanner stage IV). A micropenis was also observed. Laboratory tests showed normal complete blood count, biochemistry, and urinalysis. Endocrine results included a testosterone level of 50.83 nmol/L (normal range 9.7 to 27.8), dihydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) level of 15.03 nmol/L (normal range 6.2 to 43.3), DHEA-sulfate (DHEA-S) level of 5,120 nmol/L (normal range 1,600 to 12,200), 17-hydroxyprogesterone level of 6.61 nmol/L (normal range 1.88 to 10.94), luteinizing hormone (LH) level of 11.5 IU/L (normal range 1.7 to 8.6), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) level of 5.5 IU/L (normal range 1.5 to 12.4), estradiol level of 0.191 mmol/L (normal range 0.026 to 0.147), β-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) level of <0.1 IU/L (normal range <2.6), prolactin level of 21.7 pg/L (normal range 4.0 to 15.2), free T4 level of 18.9 pmol/L (normal range 11.9 to 21.9), and thyroid-stimulating hormone level of 2.43 mIU/L (normal range 0.27 to 4.2). Ultrasound measurements showed the right testis at 4.3×2.0×2.6 cm and the left testis at 4.4×2.1×1.8 cm, with multiple microliths in both testes. The seminal vesicles and prostate glands were normal in size and echogenicity. Imaging studies, including sellar MRI and abdominal CT, revealed no significant findings. The karyotype was 46, XY.
test_results: A somatic mosaicism (c.2128G>A, [p.Glu710Lys]) in exon 4 was found.

case_report: The patient is a 13-year-old Japanese girl with no family history of renal disease or hypertension. There was no history of medication with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or RAAS inhibitors during her mother’s pregnancy. Prenatal ultrasonography identified an abdominal mass lesion in the fetus. At around 26 weeks of gestation, the mother underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which revealed fetal renal mass lesions (Fig. a). The patient was naturally delivered at full term with a birth weight of 3076 g. General laboratory examinations showed no clinical abnormalities, leading to the discharge of both mother and patient. However, the patient exhibited increasing blood pressure around 1 month after birth, which gradually progressed to hypertension. Upon admission at 6 months of age, her development was normal. Physical examination indicated normal weight and height without surface malformation. Blood pressure readings were taken multiple times, with an initial measurement of 110/80 mmHg on the first day of admission. Urinalysis showed no proteinuria, hematuria, or glycosuria. Serum sodium (138 mEq/L), potassium (4.8 mEq/L), and calcium (11.7 mg/dL) levels, as well as serum creatinine (0.25 mg/dL), were within normal ranges. Elevated plasma renin activity (17.1 ng/mL/hr; normal: 0.2–2.3 ng/mL/hr) and serum aldosterone levels (731 pg/mL; normal: 29.2–159.0 pg/mL) were noted. Brain MRI showed no signs of microvascular lesions.
test_results: MRI revealed an atrophic left kidney with multiple cysts and no sign of adrenal enlargement. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed left renal hypoplasia without scarring on the kidney surface. Renal DTPA scintigraphy with Tc-99 m dimercaptosuccinic acid revealed differential glomerular filtration rates (GFR) of 68 mL/min and 7 mL/min for the right and left kidney, respectively, suggesting that the left kidney was nonfunctional.

case_report: An 18-year-old Saudi female, a university student, presented for an intensive rehabilitation program and was referred to a genetic clinic by a rheumatologist. She had normal developmental milestones until the age of six years when her parents observed short stature compared to her siblings and the development of contraction deformities in both hands and feet. At 14 years old, she experienced bilateral hand and wrist pain and painful swelling in both knees. She traveled to Egypt for further evaluation and was prescribed methotrexate, which she took for two years before discontinuing it due to an inconclusive response. She has a history of trauma to her right hand resulting in a distal radial fracture. She was born by normal vaginal delivery to a consanguineous couple, with an uneventful delivery. Her family, including parents and siblings, had no skeletal abnormalities. She had normal and regular menstrual cycles and was taking vitamin D3 weekly. On examination, she was ambulatory with normal intelligence. Her height was 148 cm, BMI was 25.5 kg/m2, and her vital signs were normal. She exhibited dysmorphic facial features, including frontal bossing, a depressed nasal bridge, and a bullous nose. Additional physical findings included a subcutaneous nodule on the right plantar surface, black discoloration of the tongue tip, a high-arched palate, and teeth malalignment. Hand examination showed limited passive and active range of motion in both wrists in extension, with flexed and deformed metacarpophalangeal joints bilaterally. The right elbow was in a valgus position with limited supination. She had flat feet with tender navicular bones bilaterally and limited knee flexion, mainly on the right side. Chest, cardiovascular, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Higher mental, sensory, and motor functions were normal. Breast examination indicated Tanner’s stage 2 development. Laboratory tests showed normal CBC, calcium, liver, renal, thyroid, gonadotrophins, and estradiol levels, with low vitamin 25-OH D as the only abnormal finding. The electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm, and the echocardiogram indicated mitral valve prolapse. Radiographs of both hands revealed marked osteopenia, flexion deformity, and resorption. Radiographs of the feet showed bilateral flat feet with marked osteopenia, bony destruction, and resorption. Radiographs of both knees were normal. A DEXA scan showed normal bone density of the right femoral neck and osteopenia of the left femoral neck and lumbar spine. The nerve conduction study was normal, and the ultrasound pelvis showed normal ovaries and uterus.
test_results: The results showed a novel base variant of NM_004530.6(MMP2_i001): p. (Tyr244*) in the homozygous state. Parents were also tested and have been found to be carriers for the above-mentioned variant.

case_report: A 37-year-old woman presented with a two-month history of a soft tissue mass in the femoral region of the right lower extremity. Her past medical history was uneventful, and her family history showed no malignancies. Physical examination revealed a well-developed and nourished woman in no apparent discomfort. Examination of her heart, lungs, and abdomen detected no abnormalities. Palpation revealed a sharply demarcated tumor of hard consistency, fixed to the deep muscles of the medial femoral region. Laboratory findings were within normal range, except for a mild leucocytosis of 12,200 cells/μL (reference range, 4,300-11,300 cells/μL). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) detected a homogeneous hyperintense contrast-enhancing mass lesion of 9.3 cm length, located below the right inguinal ligament between the adductor and quadriceps femoris muscle compartment. The tumor showed entrapment of the femoral artery and vein, but without compression, and displayed homogeneous contrast enhancement after intravenous contrast application. Excisional biopsy of the soft tissue mass was performed and histopathological examination revealed a lymphoid tumor. A primary soft tissue tumor was ruled out. The mass lesion was closely observed for three months, and a slight decrease in size to 8.5 cm was noticed by repeated MRI studies.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed a lymphoid tumor of unknown dignity. Immunohistochemical staining with CD5 revealed CD5-positive lymphoid cells at the periphery of the abnormal follicles. Follicular dendritic cells located in the germinal centers showed positive staining for KiM4P and CD23, and numerous CD138-positive plasma cells were scattered through the interfollicular areas. Molecular testing for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) was negative. Histological examination confirmed complete tumor resection.
diagnosis: Castleman's disease, mixed hyaline vascular and plasma cell type

case_report: A 30-year-old female reported experiencing a gradual decrease in vision in both eyes over the past month. She also mentioned having difficulty seeing at night for the past five years. She was born to parents who are not related by blood and had normal developmental milestones. Her medical history indicated a gradual decline in hearing over the last ten years, despite having normal hearing at birth and during early childhood. Previous ophthalmic evaluations at the age of 15 were normal. There is no relevant family history. The best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was measured at 20/120 in both eyes. Examination of the anterior segment and intraocular pressures were normal in both eyes. Fundus examination showed clear media with bilateral arteriolar attenuation and bony spicule-like pigmentation in the mid periphery of both eyes. Additionally, waxy disc pallor and macular edema were observed in both eyes.
test_results: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed multiple hypo reflective cystoid spaces suggestive of CME in BE with the central macular thickness (CMT) of the right eye (RE) and left eye (LE) being 385 μm and 433 μm respectively. Pure tone audiometry revealed the bilateral absence of air-bone gap and an average hearing loss of 60db suggestive of moderately severe SNHL in both ears.
diagnosis: Usher syndrome type 3  with bilateral cystoid macular edema

case_report: A 59-year-old Caucasian male experienced episodes over 28 years characterized by recurrent urticaria, fever, periorbital angio-oedema, and conjunctival injection. These episodes were often preceded by nightmares, general malaise, fatigue, and anterior chest or upper abdominal pain similar to indigestion. The episodes progressed to urticaria, which was intensely itchy but not always raised or palpable, fever, periorbital angio-oedema, and occasionally gum or jaw pain. Approximately 4 to 6 hours after onset, symptoms typically led to hypotension and loss of consciousness on several occasions. Each episode lasted 3–4 days and was followed by fatigue lasting 1–2 weeks. Laboratory investigations revealed a fluctuating monoclonal immunoglobulin G (IgG) kappa paraprotein between 14 and 20 g/l, low levels of kappa free light chains on urine electrophoresis, low C4 complement levels, and C3 complement levels at the lower end of the normal range during remission. Raised C3d and elevated terminal component complex levels indicated ongoing complement activation. Other tests during remission, including C1 inhibitor levels, full blood count, renal and liver function, thyroid function, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and C-reactive protein (CRP), showed no significant abnormalities. Anti-nuclear and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were not detected. During an observed attack, investigations showed a markedly increased CRP of >250 mg/l, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia (with a nadir white cell count of 0.7 × 10^9/l, neutrophil count of 0.1 × 10^9/l, and platelet count of 28 × 10^9/l), and decreased complement C3 and C4 levels. The ESR remained within normal limits. No cryoproteins were isolated, and serial mast cell tryptase levels were not elevated during the attack. Multiple blood cultures and viral polymerase chain reaction tests did not identify any microbes. Notably, the significant laboratory abnormalities were delayed by a day after the onset of severe symptoms, particularly when corticosteroid treatment was delayed. All laboratory abnormalities returned to baseline following the attack.
test_results: Genetic testing of FEMV, TNFRSF1A, NLRP3 and MVK was undertaken, but no mutations were detected within the exons that have previously been associated with disease causing mutations in these genes.

case_report: The patient is an 11-year-old boy whom we first evaluated in the endocrine clinic at 8 years of age for obesity. The patient is the male child of nonconsanguineous Guatemalan parents and was born at 41 weeks of gestation by spontaneous vaginal delivery to a 23-year-old, gravida 2, para 1 mother. The pregnancy was not complicated by any exposure to viral infection or medications. His siblings and both parents are healthy with no family history of miscarriages, stillbirths, congenital abnormalities, or learning difficulties. He was reportedly well until the 19th day of life when he presented with projectile vomiting and was diagnosed with pyloric stenosis. Surgery was uncomplicated; however, he had recurrent surgical site infections which required multiple readmissions. In the interim, parents reported that he was able to walk at 3 years of age and had his first meaningful word (“Papa”) at 16 months. He attended special education classes and received speech, occupational, and physical therapy to address his developmental delays. He had recurrent acute otitis media managed with bilateral myringotomy. Audiologic evaluation also showed conductive hearing loss. He was evaluated by endocrinology for the first time at age 8 years and 8 months. He was referred by his pediatrician for evaluation of obesity and hyperphagia. His height was 134.1 cm (64th percentile), weight 63.5 kg (>99th percentile), and BMI 35.31 kg/m2. Examination was remarkable for facial dysmorphisms (prominent eyebrows, low set ears, midfacial retrusion, and mild prognathism) and a genital exam that showed a micropenis. He was prepubertal with 3 cc testicles bilaterally, stretched penile length measured at 3 cm (-2.5 SD for age is 2.8 cm; mean is 6.3 cm), and no hypospadias. Laboratory tests showed LH <0.005 mIU/ml (normal 0.02-0.3), FSH 0.184 mIU/ml (normal 0.26-3), and testosterone 9 ng/dL (normal 2.5-10). Brain MRI was normal. Due to the low gonadotropins associated with isolated micropenis, treatment was initiated via intramuscular testosterone cypionate injection of 50 mg given once a month for 3 months at the age of 9 years and 9 months. He had a normal response to testosterone injections with an improvement of stretched penile length to 5.5 cm (normal 6.3 ± 1.0 cm) after 4 doses. There were no noted adverse reactions to testosterone injections such as acne, fluid retention, decreased testicular size, or mood swings. At 10 years and 9 months, GnRH agonist stimulation testing showed an LH-predominant response with peak LH of 11 mIU/mL and peak FSH of 4.3 mIU/mL at 24 hours. Testosterone rose from 48 ng/dL (normal <7-130 ng/dL) at baseline to 132 ng/dL at 48 hours. hCG stimulation testing was done 1 month later for Leydig cell function assessment. shows that there was adequate testosterone biosynthesis (testosterone 300 ng/dL at 24 hours after the last dose of hCG) and no evidence of 5-alpha reductase deficiency (T:DHT 21.4; normal T:DHT <35) after the hCG stimulation test. Genetics referral was initially made at 1 year of age due to global developmental delay, nontypical dysmorphic facial features, and the history of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. There was no history of hypotonia, feeding difficulties, or seizures. Karyotype showed normal male (46, XY). Fragile X testing was normal. DNA oligonucleotide microarray study revealed a likely benign maternally inherited 563 kb duplication at 1p22.3. Rett syndrome, although rare in males, was ruled out at the age of 4 by sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis of the MECP2 gene. At 9 years of age, methylation study for Prader-Willi critical region was negative.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing (WES) revealed a heterozygous de novo pathogenic variant c.2712+1G>A in the EHMT1 gene.

case_report: A 46-year-old male with a normal birth and developmental history presented with nonprogressive postural and action tremors of the fingers for the past 20 years. He experiences stimulus-sensitive myoclonic jerks, which increase with exposure to sunlight and while watching TV. The severity of these myoclonic jerks has increased over the past year. He also has tonic-clonic seizures that occur more frequently upon early morning awakening and are well controlled with sodium valproate (1 g/day in divided doses). Additionally, he exhibits cognitive decline, including executive dysfunction and memory impairment for recent events. Physical examination showed action and postural tremors of the fingers and stimulus-sensitive myoclonic jerks. The rest of the examination was normal. MRI of the brain was normal.
test_results: EEG showed paroxysm of sharp and slow wave complexes mostly localized over posterior regions. IPS at frequencies between 10-25 Hz triggered generalized spike and wave complexes.
diagnosis: Autosomal Dominant Cortical Tremor, Myoclonus, and Epilepsy

case_report: A 10-month-old boy, second born of third-degree consanguineous parents, presented with right focal seizures. Following the seizures, the child exhibited altered sensorium and right hemiparesis. He was hospitalized and referred on the sixth day of illness. Upon admission, the child had a Glasgow coma score (pediatric) of 12 and significant pallor but was hemodynamically stable with well-palpable peripheral pulses. MRI brain confirmed an issue in the left middle cerebral artery territory. MR angiography showed a sudden cut-off in the left internal carotid artery just after its origin with complete occlusion, though dissection could not be ruled out. The intracranial left internal carotid artery and its branches were not visualized, and no significant collaterals were noted. Sonography and Doppler of neck vessels did not visualize the left internal carotid artery. Echocardiography was normal. Blood investigations revealed normocytic normochromic anemia (MCV = 94 μl) with normal platelet and total leucocyte counts. By the fourth day of hospitalization, the child developed thrombocytopenia with elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). Peripheral smear examination showed schistocytes (4%-5%) with a low reticulocyte count. Serum vitamin B12, folate, plasma homocysteine, and C3 levels were within normal limits. A gradual decline in hemoglobin levels and platelet count was observed. The child also developed facial puffiness and hypertension. Daily fresh frozen plasma transfusion was initiated, followed by Plasma Exchange (PEX). Once platelet counts improved to over 1 lac/mm3 and blood pressure normalized, the child was switched to oral steroids, which were continued for about a month and gradually tapered while monitoring the platelet count.
test_results: Exome sequencing revealed a novel homozygous nonsense variation in exon 2 of the SLC19A2 gene (chr1:169446604; G>C; Depth: 119x) that results in a stop codon and premature truncation of the protein at codon 199 (p. Ser199Ter; ENST00000236137).

case_report: A 58-year-old woman was admitted one year ago to the neurointensive care unit for sudden onset of intracerebral and subarachnoid hemorrhage in the right frontal lobe. Her medical history included tobacco use, moderate alcohol consumption, hypertension, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Surgical history included a left lumpectomy for breast cancer, amputation of the third finger on the right hand, and jaw surgery. Upon admission, her vital signs were: blood pressure 140/87 mmHg, heart rate 71 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation on ventilator 100%. She was awake, alert, but lethargic. The electrocardiogram (ECG) at admission showed normal sinus rhythm (60 bpm) and possible septal necrosis. A right craniotomy was performed for hemorrhage evacuation and clipping of a right middle cerebral artery aneurysm. Postoperatively, her neurological functions were intact. Troponin I levels increased from 0.33 to 3.55 ng/mL over the first two days, then decreased to 1.96 ng/mL on the third day post-surgery. Similar variations were observed in creatine kinase-MB fraction levels, which changed from 4.0 to 11.5 to 4.3 μmol/L. An ECG on the second day showed deep negative T waves in almost all leads and a prolonged QTc interval.
test_results: A two-dimensional (2D) transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a normal left ventricular cavity size with hyperdynamic basal motion, akinesis of midventricular segments and nearly normal apical motion. Left ventricular global systolic function was moderately decreased with left ventricular ejection fraction at 35%.

case_report: A 54-year-old Caucasian male presented with a mucocutaneous blistering eruption that had developed over three years. The eruption included tense blisters that easily ruptured, forming painful erosions. Some older erosions had healed with small atrophic scars and multiple milia cysts. The patient reported increased skin fragility, with lesions easily induced by minor injuries. The lesions were widespread, particularly affecting areas prone to repetitive trauma: palmoplantar regions, elbows, knees, and posterior trunk. Physical examination revealed onychodystrophy with partial loss of the big right toenail and moderate fibrosis of the fingers, resulting in reduced hand mobility. The patient also had multiple oral erosions. Previous medical records indicated an initial diagnosis based on direct immunofluorescence studies showing deposition of immunoglobulin G (IgG) and C3 at the DEJ in a linear pattern. A comprehensive metabolic panel was within normal limits. Tests for pemphigoid circulating antibodies (BPAG 180 and BPAG230) and antinuclear antibodies (ANA) were negative, and C3 and C4 levels were normal. An esophago-gastro-duodenoscopy revealed extensive erosions on the pharyngeal and upper-esophagus mucosa, with no stricture or stenosis detected. A colonoscopy showed no signs of inflammatory bowel disease. A thorough review of systems was entirely negative.
test_results: Direct immunofluorescence tests showed linear deposits of IgG and C3 at the DEJ. IgA tested negative. Fibrinogen was positive in the cleavage area. The 'salt-split skin' technique showed the localization of the immunoreactants, mainly IgG, along the dermal side of the artificially induced blisters at the level of lamina lucida.

case_report: Patient 2, a 7-year-old female, is the second child of consanguineous parents from Syria. She was born at full term following an uneventful pregnancy, with normal development for the first 2 years. At 2 years and 2 months, involuntary movements began in the left hand and soon spread to all four limbs. Muscle strength and mass declined, leading to loss of walking ability at 4 years, sitting ability at 5 years, and subsequently, speech. At 6 years, she experienced her first seizure and developed a severe epilepsy disorder. Clinical examination shows severe global developmental delay, myopathic facies with an open mouth and drooling, severe axial hypotonia with hypertonic limbs, and dystonic involuntary movements. Communication is limited to phonetic reading. Lactate levels were repeatedly elevated in both serum (up to 4.1 mmol/L) and CSF (up to 3.1 mmol/L).
test_results: Cranial MRI showed diffuse hyperintensities on T2-weighted imaging of the periventricular and central white matter with associated volume loss and atrophy of corpus callosum as well as T2 hyperintense defects of bilateral putamen and head of caudate nucleus. EEG revealed multifocal seizure activity.
diagnosis: Mitochondrial disease due to GFM2 variants

case_report: A 24-year-old male presented to the emergency department with complaints of sore throat, general discomfort, fever, and swelling in the neck and face, while maintaining normal consciousness. Physical examination revealed swollen and tender tonsils along with enlarged lymph nodes on both sides of the neck. Blood pressure and heart rate were within normal ranges. The patient had no history of chronic diseases, chronic medication use, or allergies. Laboratory tests indicated an elevated white blood cell count and increased levels of C-reactive protein in the serum.
test_results: An ultrasound examination demonstrates left jugular vein thrombosis. Contrast-enhanced neck Computed tomography reveals fluid and air density collections with soft tissue phlegmon formation in the anterior cervical region, in both soft tissue of the anterior mandibular ramus, peritonsillar, left parapharyngeal area, and left carotid space, and also there is left jugular vein thrombosis. The blood culture was positive for Fusobacterium necrophorum.

case_report: A 7-year-old girl presented with short stature and abnormal posture. She is the only child of healthy parents from the same village. She was born at term with a birth weight of 2.5 kg, and her perinatal period was uneventful. Her early childhood development was age appropriate, and school performance was average. There were no other family members with short stature or abnormal body posture. Her height was recorded as 95.5 cm, which was far below the 3rd percentile and the height predicted by the midparental height. The upper segment was short, and the upper-to-lower segment ratio was 0.94. Examination of the spine revealed thoracolumbar scoliosis, lumbar lordosis with a visibly small thoracic cavity, and asymmetrical rib anomalies. She did not have limb shortening, organomegaly, corneal clouding, or joint contractures. The rest of the physical examination was normal. Basic hematological and biochemical investigations, including full blood count, serum electrolytes, renal and liver function tests, serum calcium, serum inorganic phosphate, and serum alkaline phosphatase, were normal.
test_results: Skeletal survey revealed fused vertebra involving T5-T6, T9-T10, and L3-L4. Butterfly vertebrae were noted in T2, T4, T6, and T9. Thoracic cavity was small, and asymmetrical rib anomalies with posterior fusion of the left 6th and 7th ribs were noted. Spirometry results showed forced vital capacity (FVC) of 53%, forced expiratory volume in first second (FEV1) of 66%, and FEV1/FVC ratio of 102%, compatible with moderate to severe restrictive lung disease.

case_report: A 46-year-old woman was admitted to a psychiatric hospital exhibiting episodes of psychomotor agitation, disorganized and erotized behavior, delusions of persecution and self-reference, and auditory and visual hallucinations. These episodes reportedly began during her adolescence. The patient believed she could communicate with spirits and engaged in behaviors such as praying and lighting candles for them. Her family, neighbors, and friends did not share her beliefs. The patient also displayed suspiciousness and aggression, believing others spoke ill of her, and she would break objects without clear reason. During these episodes, she would close her eyes, scream, shake her head side to side, run her hands over her body, and touch her genitals repeatedly. She claimed to be in another place and time and confused hospital staff with distant relatives. Outside of these episodes, the patient showed below-average intelligence, disorientation to person, place, and time, and left hemiparesis. There were also reports of generalized tonic-clonic seizures since childhood, often accompanied by trauma, tongue biting, and sphincter incontinence, which were controlled with medication. An electroencephalography was performed and showed no alterations. A video electroencephalography was not conducted due to unavailability in the local public service. Physical examination revealed the patient was thin, disoriented in time, and cooperative. Her gait was unsteady and slow, and paresis of the left leg was noted. Heart and lung auscultation and abdominal examination showed no abnormalities. Blood count, biochemistry, and serology for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B and C were within normal limits.
test_results: A head CT scan revealed a large subarachnoid space communication with the adjacent lateral ventricle in the topography of occipital, temporal, and parietal lobes to the right.

case_report: A 28-year-old Indian male presented with multiple asymptomatic hyperpigmented macules located on the flexors, trunk, face, and extremities. The macules initially appeared on the dorsum of both hands and feet during childhood and later spread to the extensor aspects of both forearms and legs. Around the age of 22, freckle-like lesions emerged on the axillae, groin, and forehead, subsequently progressing to the upper back, flexural aspects of forearms, inner thighs, nape, and lateral neck. The interval between the involvement of the extensor and flexor aspects of the forearms was approximately 15 years, with the lesions initially appearing distally and gradually becoming more proximal. There was no family history of similar lesions. Mucocutaneous examination revealed numerous symmetrical brownish hyperpigmented macules, 1–2 mm in size, located in the axillae, groin, flexor and extensor aspects of both forearms, dorsae of hands and feet, shins, and inner thighs. The lesions on the dorsae of hands, feet, and forearms were atrophic, with a pronounced reticulate pattern on the axillae, groins, and distal areas including proximal palms. Additionally, a few darkly pigmented comedo-like papules and atrophic scars were observed on the upper back and neck. Multiple palmar pits with breaks in proximal palmar ridges were present. Multiple pitted follicular scars were noted on the bilateral malar, mandibular, and perioral regions of the face, with no prior history of acne in these areas. An accessory tragus on the left side was also noted as an incidental finding.
test_results: Histopathological examination of skin biopsy taken from nape of neck revealed circumscribed foci of epidermal proliferation in the form of elongated and confluent rete ridges, which displayed antler-like branching at places. The proliferation of rete ridges was most prominent around plugged and dilated follicular infundibula. The tips of rete pegs were hypermelanotic owing to concentrated pigment, which was also scattered within the papillary dermal macrophages. Biopsy taken from dorsal aspect of forearm revealed histopathology almost similar to that of biopsy taken from nape of neck except mild perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates.

case_report: A 6-year-old girl with no previous medical or surgical history was referred for evaluation of a painless swelling in the middle of the right clavicle, first observed by her parents during the neonatal period but never previously investigated. The swelling became more noticeable as she grew older. The pregnancy was without complications. She was born at full term to non-consanguineous parents through a spontaneous, uncomplicated vaginal delivery and exhibited normal development. There were no similar cases in the family. On physical examination, the swelling was non-tender. The range of motion in her right shoulder and the vascular and neurological examination of her right upper extremity were normal. No other abnormalities, particularly in the musculoskeletal system, were found.
test_results: A radiograph revealed a defect in the right mid-clavicular portion. Computed tomography with 3 dimensional reconstructions showed the bone gap with bulbous, well corticated borders and no callous formation.

case_report: A 6-year-old boy arrived at the Emergency Department with a 3-week history of an erythematous papulo-vesicular itchy rash located on the submandibular regions, trunk, and extremities. The patient was in good overall health, with no fever or other general symptoms. There were no identifiable triggers such as infections, medications, vaccines, or food allergies. His past medical and family history were unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed normal results for complete blood count (white blood cells 5.4 × 10^9/L with 27.5% neutrophils and 47.9% lymphocytes, hemoglobin 12.2 g/dl, and platelets 323,000/mmc), serum electrolytes, glucose, kidney and liver function, C-reactive protein, coagulation parameters, and standard urinalysis. A SARS-CoV-2 antigen test from a nasopharyngeal swab was negative. Topical steroids were administered. Serologic tests for antibodies against viruses (cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, PVB-19) and bacteria (Mycoplasma) were ordered, along with a dermatological evaluation. One week later, the patient returned with an extensive painful scaly papulo-erythematous rash, including some ulcerated and necrotic lesions on the trunk, limbs, and flexures. A slight fever (37.8 °C) was noted, but no other systemic symptoms were present. Antibiotic therapy (amoxicillin–clavulanate 50 mg/kg per day) was prescribed, and topical steroid use continued. Due to worsening fever, the child was admitted to the Pediatric Department of the “Vittore Buzzi” Children’s Hospital in Milan, Italy. A multidisciplinary care plan involving the Pediatric Dermatology Unit at Fondazione IRCCS Ca’ Granda Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico in Milan, Italy, was implemented. Repeated tests showed normal results for complete blood count, alkaline phosphatase, lactate dehydrogenase, creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, glucose, creatinine kinase, and urinalysis. Plasma amino acid levels were also normal. Elevated levels of C-reactive protein (34.8 mg/dl, normal ≤ 10), aspartate aminotransferase (102 U/L, normal 11–34), alanine transaminase (93 U/L, normal ≤ 49), and bilirubin (total 1.35 mg/dl, normal < 1.2; direct 0.53 mg/dl, normal ≤ 0.3) were recorded. Antibiotic therapy was continued. Due to a persistently high fever (> 40 °C), systemic corticosteroid treatment (prednisone 25 mg/kg) was administered, resulting in the patient becoming afebrile and showing progressive improvement of the skin lesions without new lesions appearing. Anti-PVB-19 Immunoglobulin M was detected, while serologies for Mycoplasma, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein–Barr virus were negative. Five days after admission, most lesions had cleared, and the child was discharged. Methotrexate (7.5 mg/week) was initiated, with a positive response.
test_results: A skin biopsy revealed a “PLEVA-like” morphologic pattern, including features of acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, and moderate spongiosis of the epidermis, with edema and hemorrhage of the papillary dermis. Adjoining, a few granulocytes and an abundant lymphoid infiltrate were documented, the latter featuring epidermotropism in a pagetoid fashion and extending throughout the dermis in a perivascular and periadnexal configuration, with scant tropism for follicular and eccrine structures. Morphologically, lymphoid cells were medium- to large-sized and slightly pleomorphic, with admixed a minor component of larger blasts. Immunohistochemistry showed an activated, CD8 + cytotoxic, partially defective T-cell phenotype (CD2-/+, CD3+, CD5-, CD7-/+, CD4-, CD8+, perforin+, CD56-, TCR-delta-), with moderate to intense CD30-positivity on 60–70% of the cells. Polymerase chain reaction for T-cell receptor gamma (TCRG) chain clonality assessment documented a monoclonal peak.

case_report: A 27-year-old female patient, G4P3, 3 months postpartum, presented with recent biliary colic and clinical cholestasis. The patient also reported unexplored pruritus during the third trimester of pregnancy and had a premature delivery at 32 weeks of amenorrhea. Clinical examination showed a BMI of 29.3 kg/m² and tenderness in the right hypochondrium. Laboratory results indicated cytolysis with aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 2 times the upper limit of normal (ULN) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) at 3.8 times ULN. Cholestasis was noted with total bilirubin at 20 mg/l, direct bilirubin at 17 mg/l, gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) at 13 times ULN, and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) at 1.6 times ULN. Tests for Hepatitis B and C were negative, and protein electrophoresis and IgG4 levels were normal.
test_results: Abdominal US showed multiple hyperechoic intrahepatic 'comet-tail' spots, sludge in the MBD that was not dilated, and gallstones. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography showed a dilated MBD at 9 mm with homogeneous contents, and edema of the papilla.

case_report: A 36-month-old female patient, born through assisted fertilization, was the first child of healthy, unrelated parents. During a routine second trimester ultrasound, ventriculomegaly and agenesis of the corpus callosum were observed. An encephalic MRI at 30 weeks of gestation showed mild ventriculomegaly on the left side and marked ventriculomegaly on the right side, along with agenesis of the corpus callosum. No other malformations were noted. The pregnancy was complicated by hemorrhages, managed with bed rest and appropriate therapy, leading to a scheduled cesarean delivery at 38 weeks and 3 days. At birth, the patient had a weight of 3500 g (75–90th percentile), length of 50 cm (75th percentile), and an occipital frontal circumference of 33.5 cm (50th percentile). Physical examination revealed mild dysmorphic features including scaphocephaly with asymmetry of the splanchnocranium, prominent forehead, deep-set eyes, large prominent ears with prominent antihelices, broad nose, high-arched palate, short frenum, abundant nuchal fold, clinodactyly of the fourth toe on both feet, and short metatarsals. The characteristic palmar and plantar creases were absent. Echocardiography indicated patency of the foramen ovale/small atrial defect with a mild left-to-right shunt and mild dilation of the right sections, with normal biventricular global systolic function. Abdominal ultrasound, ocular evaluation, audiological screening (TEOAE), and EEG did not reveal any congenital anomalies of the internal organs. Initial developmental assessment showed cervico-axial hypotonia and hypertonia in all four limbs. No history of epileptic seizures was reported.
test_results: The finding of a female karyotype with mosaicism for chromosome trisomy 8: '47, XX, +8[3]/46, XX [22] was detected.

case_report: A 77-year-old male arrived at the emergency department with a one-week history of increasing bilateral neck swelling and restricted neck movement. Prior to the neck swelling, he experienced a week of cough, fever reaching 104°F, painful swallowing, nausea, vomiting, and difficulty swallowing. He was previously treated with Tamiflu for a presumptive flu diagnosis at an urgent care clinic, but his symptoms did not improve. The patient also reported shortness of breath and pain in the right shoulder and upper chest. He denied any other symptoms. His medical history included well-controlled, insulin-dependent type II diabetes mellitus and coronary artery disease. He had a history of heavy smoking, having quit 20 years ago after a 50 pack-year history. On examination, the patient appeared well-developed but ill and uncomfortable. The right neck and sternoclavicular areas were red, firm, swollen, and tender. The right pectoral region was also red, firm, and had deep fluctuance upon palpation. The left neck was tender to touch without skin changes and had no palpable masses. A trans-nasal flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy showed no masses or lesions in the nasopharynx, nasal cavity, oropharynx, larynx, or hypopharynx. Initial laboratory results showed a leukocyte count of 37,000/mcL (normal range 3400-10,400/mcL) and blood glucose levels between 153 and 199 mg/dL (normal range 60-100 mg/dL). The patient's most recent hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) level was 6.8% (normal value <5.7%).
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) imaging revealed a 7.4 cm peripherally enhancing right sternocleidomastoid (SCM) abscess, a 10.5 cm right pectoralis major muscles abscess, and a 9.2 cm hypodense fluid collection found in the anterior mediastinum and retrosternal space.
diagnosis: Bacterial Pyomyositis due to Bacteroides fragilis

case_report: A 1-year-old male child presented to the ophthalmology outpatient department with unusual eye appearance since birth. He was delivered full-term without complications to non-consanguineous parents. At birth, both eyes were slightly protruding with abnormal eyelids and intermittent bleeding. The eye protrusion persisted until 3 months of age and has remained unchanged since. The child began experiencing tonic-clonic seizures after 3 months of age, which have decreased in frequency, with the most recent episode occurring 2 days prior to presentation. He had an increased head circumference at birth, which has not progressed. Upon examination, the child exhibited abnormally protruding eyes with coloboma in the middle third of the right upper eyelid and the medial half of the left upper eyelid, along with an abnormal skin fold below the malformed left eyelid. A skin tag was noted at the outer canthus of the right eye. The conjunctiva on the right side appeared slightly cystic, and both the conjunctiva and cornea were keratinized due to exposure. No other ocular abnormalities such as orbital cysts or microphthalmia were observed. The child also had frontal bossing, a depressed nasal bridge, and slight tongue protrusion. There were focal patches of alopecia with dermal hypoplasia on the scalp. Hyperpigmented patches were present on the right side of the chest, abdomen, and back, extending slightly to the nape and right arm. Developmental milestones were delayed. A comprehensive general and systemic examination revealed no abnormalities except for decreased muscle strength. Baseline investigations were normal, and an abdominal ultrasound identified a complex splenic cyst measuring 6 mm.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging of the head showed aplasia of cerebellar vermis with enlarged superior vermian cistern. There was subependymal grey matter heterotopia of the postero-inferior aspect of the atrium of right lateral ventricle. An axial cut shows the abnormal appearance of the cortex, with a polymicrogyric pattern posteriorly in right posterior parietal and right occipital region. A small arachnoid space posteriorly at the level of infratentorial compartment was seen.

case_report: A 24-year-old male student presented with asymptomatic lesions in light-exposed areas for two years, which have progressively increased in number. He used oral and topical antifungals without improvement. He has a history of systemic lupus erythematosus for 11 years and underwent a kidney transplant due to renal failure secondary to lupus nephritis 6 years ago. He is currently on immunosuppressant treatment with sirolimus 1mg twice daily, mycophenolate sodium 360mg daily, and prednisone 10mg daily. There is no history of consanguinity or affected relatives. Physical examination revealed numerous erythematous papules and macules resembling pityriasis versicolor on the face, neck, V-shaped neckline, forearms, and abdomen.
test_results: Histologic examination of the skin biopsy from abdomen revealed vacuolated cells in the upper epidermis with a bubbly, bluish cytoplasm, thickened granular layer and mild perivascular infiltrate in the superficial dermis.

case_report: A 14-year-old male with a family history of neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), born to nonconsanguineous parents, presented with a noticeable hollow area on the back of his scalp since birth, for which he had been under regular follow-up with a local physician. At the age of 14, he began experiencing symptoms, including vomiting predominantly after meals, which had been occurring for 2–3 years and had increased in frequency to about four times per week at the time of presentation. There were no reports of headaches, seizures, speech difficulties, weakness, gait disturbances, visual disturbances, limb weakness, facial deviation, hearing loss, or difficulty swallowing. Physical examination revealed wrist hyperflexibility and multiple café au lait spots on the chest, abdomen, and back, with the largest measuring 2 by 1 cm. Slit-lamp examination identified Lisch nodules. A bony defect was observed in the midline of the posterior parieto-occipital region. The patient's father had multiple neurofibromas and café au lait spots, and the grandmother had multiple neurofibromas across her body.
test_results: The patient was evaluated radiologically with magnetic resonance imaging of brain and found to have large posterior fossa arachnoid cyst with hypoplastic vermis and posterior superior calvarial defect with focal hyperintensity involving left globus pallidus. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) showed torcular lambdoid inversion due to abnormally high tentorium. CT head showed a bony defect in the midline in parieto-occipital region. Cerebral Angiograms showed a normal outline and branching pattern of the rest of all major arteries including the internal cerebral artery, anterior cerebral artery, middle cerebral artery, posterior cerebral artery, and vertebrobasilar system. No evidence of any steno-occlusive lesions or aneurysms/ectasia were seen. No abnormal blush or early draining veins was seen. There was an elevation of torcula and straight sinus with splaying of the transverse sinuses, suspended from the high torcula, giving an inverted Y-shaped appearance. The Vein of Galen was minimally elongated. A distinct avascular zone was seen in the posterior fossa, posterior to the elevated lateral sinuses. There was herniation of the vasculature through the calvarial effect in the occipital region into the scalp.

case_report: A previously healthy 30-year-old woman arrived at the emergency department with a 1-week history of increasing confusion, changes in personality, vertigo, and episodes resembling strokes, including temporary loss of speech. Clinical examination showed fine motor impairment in the left hand, bilateral pyramidal signs, and deficits in memory, attention, and executive functions. Due to the patient's agitation, only a brief imaging protocol was conducted, including diffusion-weighted, T2, and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences.
test_results: A brief magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) protocol (diffusion-weighted, T2 and fluid attenuated inversion recovery [FLAIR] sequences) was performed, revealing multiple supra- and infratentorial punctate diffusion-restricted lesions as well as FLAIR-hyperintense white matter lesions without evidence of restricted diffusion. In addition, the central corpus callosum revealed round (snowball), linear (spoke), and 'hanging' (icicles) T2 and FLAIR-hyperintense lesions.

case_report: The patient is a 51-year-old woman who presented with swelling of the extremities and bilateral ptosis on March 8, 2010. She reported exertional dyspnea and weakness. She married at the age of 25 and subsequently developed drooping of her eyes, with the left eye more affected than the right. These symptoms persisted and gradually worsened over the past 10 years. Approximately 8 years ago, she underwent a ptosis repair operation at a local clinic, but her symptoms did not improve. She denied any history of loss of consciousness, headache, dysphagia, dysarthria, and myalgia. There was no family history of similar symptoms and no history of trauma. She also had no previous history of diabetes or hypertension. On physical examination, her height was 151 cm and weight was 48 kg. Initial vital signs included a blood pressure of 140/80 mmHg, a pulse rate of 68 beats/min, and a respiratory rate of 20/min. She appeared lethargic with facial puffiness and no goiter. Lung and heart examinations were unremarkable. All extremities showed pitting edema. She had marked bilateral ptosis, but external ocular movements were normal. Other cranial nerve examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory findings included a total leucocyte count of 4.75 × 10^3/µL with 61.6% polymorphs, hemoglobin level of 9.0 g/dL, random blood glucose of 124 mg/dL, serum sodium of 130 mM/L, potassium of 3.7 mM/L, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) of 13 mg/dL, creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL, aspartate transaminase (AST) of 81 IU/L, alanine transaminase (ALT) of 29 IU/L, total bilirubin of 0.93 mg/dL, creatine kinase (CK) of 1,195 IU/L (normal reference: 20-180 IU/L), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) of 517 IU/L (normal reference: 101-218 IU/L), total cholesterol of 256 mg/dL, triglyceride of 121 mg/dL, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) of 40 mg/dL, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) of 196 mg/dL. Urinalysis was negative for blood and protein using a dipstick. Thyroid function tests showed serum T3 of 0.195 ng/mL (normal reference: 0.86-2.02 ng/mL), free T4 of 0.08 ng/dL (normal reference: 0.93-1.705 ng/dL), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) of 2.08 µIU/mL (normal reference: 0.27-4.2 µIU/mL), antimicrosomal antibody of 17 IU/mL (normal reference: 0-34 IU/mL), and antithyroglobulin antibody of 20.1 IU/mL (normal reference: 0-114 IU/mL). The acetylcholine receptor binding antibody test was negative. Further history revealed that at the age of 26, the patient delivered her daughter and experienced massive postpartum vaginal bleeding, after which she did not resume menses. Basal hormone levels were as follows: serum cortisol of 4.03 µg/dL, adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) of 29.64 pg/mL, growth hormone (GH) of 0.06 ng/mL, IGF-1 of 25 ng/mL (normal reference: 71-263 ng/mL), prolactin of 1.59 ng/mL, luteinizing hormone (LH) of 1.49 IU/L, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) of 4.91 IU/L, E2 of 17.29 pg/mL, and testosterone of 0.02 ng/mL.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a finding of an empty sella turcica and there was no evidence of an intracranial mass, hemorrhage and aneurysm. The combined pituitary stimulation test, including the insulin tolerance test, the thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) stimulation test and the gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) stimulation test showed panhypopituitarism.

case_report: A 16-year-old boy of mixed Dutch and Moroccan descent presented with a 2-month history of weight gain, distended abdomen, acne, and elevated blood pressure. Physical examination revealed a rounded face, excessive hair growth, and skin darkening. His blood pressure was recorded at 142/88 mmHg. A non-tender mass was felt in the upper right quadrant of his abdomen. Laboratory tests indicated a white blood cell count of 17.9×10^9/L and platelet count of 431×10^9/L. Electrolytes, creatinine, and glucose levels were within normal ranges. Plasma gamma-glutamyltransferase concentration was slightly elevated at 145 U/L. Endocrine tests showed plasma ACTH and cortisol concentrations of 285 ng/L and 785 nmol/L, respectively. The patient's high blood pressure was managed with a calcium antagonist, and ketoconazole was given to reduce steroid hormone production.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a large mass in his liver segments 4 to 8, without evidence of distant metastases. Core needle biopsy showed irregular fields of epithelial cell nests in a desmoplastic stroma, and dissociation of cells, yielding to pseudovascular spaces. Cells varied from epithelioid to spindle shaped. Immunohistochemistry was positive for cytokeratin 19, anticytokeratin, neural cell adhesion molecule, smooth muscle actin (SMA) and ACTH. No mitoses and no distinctive cellular atypia were found. Stromal cells were SMA-positive. A small cell desmoplastic tumor was ruled out by negative reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction for the Ewing sarcoma-related gene fusion product and Wilms’ tumor-related gene. Low-grade HCC with neuroendocrine features was suggested. However, the spindle-shaped epithelial cells and the lack of eosinophilic cells did not fit with that. On cut surface, a rather sharply demarcated multinodular mass of 19.5 cm with multiple small calcifications was found. Histology confirmed an epithelial tumor. The size of the epithelial fields decreased and the degree of desmoplasia increased towards the center of the tumor. Psammomatous calcifications were found within and near irregular nests of predominantly spindle-shaped epithelial cells. The nests showed necrosis and cystic changes. Ossification was seen between epithelial cells. Nests of tumor cells were infiltrating the adjacent liver with entrapment of bile ducts and cords of hepatocytes. Few mitoses were seen.
diagnosis: calcifying nested stromal–epithelial tumor  of the liver

case_report: A 14-year-old girl presented with a 3-week history of gradually worsening breathlessness and raised skin lesions on her hands, elbows, and ankles, which had been increasing in size over the past 3 years. Her pulse rate was 92/min, and her blood pressure was 120/70 mm Hg. Auscultation revealed an ejection systolic murmur in the high basal areas. Electrocardiography (ECG) indicated left ventricular hypertrophy and non-progression of the R wave in leads V1-V4. An echocardiogram (ECHO) showed severe left ventricular failure and severe aortic stenosis. Coronal and axial plain CT images revealed aortic annulus calcifications causing aortic stenosis. Axial CT coronary angiography demonstrated wall irregularity with eccentric non-calcified plaques in the ascending thoracic aorta, arch, and descending thoracic aorta. The skin lesions initially appeared on the right elbow and later spread to the dorsum of the right hand and both feet. These lesions were skin-colored with a slight yellowish hue, firm, non-tender nodules approximately 1 cm × 1 cm in size, located on the dorsolateral aspect of both feet and the right elbow, as well as the dorsum of the right hand. Hyperpigmented patches were observed over the web spaces of the right hand, which were reported by the patient as sites of healed nodular lesions. The patient did not report any history of headache, vertigo, hearing loss, seizures, blurring of vision, or learning disability.
test_results: Her fasting lipid profile revealed elevated total cholesterol (690 mg/dl), low-density lipoprotein (LDL) levels (510 mg/dl) and triglyceride levels (350 mg/dl). Skin biopsy from the nodular lesion revealed scattered foamy macrophages in the upper dermis and cholesterol clefts.

case_report: A six-month-old boy was brought to the emergency department at Children’s Hospital in Taif due to vomiting and increased urine output for 3 days. His mother was 23 years old at the time of his birth, and he was born healthy at full term via Lower Segment Cesarean Section to consanguineous parents (second-degree). His birth weight was 2.5 kg. The postnatal period was uneventful. On examination, the child exhibited severe dehydration and Kussmaul breathing. His temperature was 37.6 °C, heart rate was 155 bpm, respiratory rate was 60 rpm, and blood pressure was 88/57 mmHg. His weight was 7 kg (10-25th percentile) and length 64 cm (third percentile). No dysmorphic features were noted. His abdomen was soft, not distended, and there was no organomegaly. The genitourinary examination showed bilateral descended testicles. Ultrasound revealed structurally normal pancreas and kidneys. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory investigations showed severe metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap. Venous blood gas results were PH 7.0, HCO3 6.6, and base deficit 24. Complete blood counts, renal panel, and liver function tests were normal. Urinary ketones and glucose were positive +3, Random Blood Sugar was 30 mmol/L, and hemoglobin A1C was 16.3% (reference range: below 5.7%). Glutamic acid decarboxylase-65 antibody and insulinoma-associated antibody were negative; fasting C-peptide was 0.7 ng/mL (reference range: 1-3 ng/mL). The patient was treated according to the protocol for severe metabolic acidosis, which included normalizing fluid-volume status, hyperglycemia, electrolytes, and ketoacidosis. Intravenous insulin was later changed to subcutaneous insulin. The family history revealed that the mother and her twin sister developed diabetes mellitus at 3 months of age and are on insulin. The twin sister was thought to be identical, but no studies were performed to confirm this. The father had normal fasting blood glucose levels.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing (WES) revealed a heterozygous mutation in INS 326G>A (p.C109Y) and a heterozygous mutation in PKHD1.

case_report: An eight-month-old female infant arrived at the emergency department with a swollen abdomen. She had been experiencing worsening chronic constipation over the past two months, having bowel movements only once a week with hard, non-bloody stools. This was accompanied by frequent vomiting of food content. Attempts to alleviate symptoms with stool softeners and changes in formula milk were unsuccessful. There was no history of ingesting foreign objects. Her parents reported no previous medical or surgical issues for the infant. She had passed meconium within the first 24 hours after birth. On examination, her vital signs were normal. The abdomen was soft, lax, non-tender, and moderately distended, with palpable bowel distension. Examination of her back showed no discoloration, abnormal hair growth, or visible deformities. Her lower limbs moved freely with normal muscle tone. A per rectal examination revealed a stenotic anus without a gush of stools upon finger withdrawal.
test_results: PUT/kidney, ureter, and bladder (KUB) X-ray revealed a distended large colon by air and fecal matter with two air-fluid levels at the ascending and descending parts of the large bowel. A fluoroscopic barium enema showed a stenotic short segment at the distal rectum with a significantly distended sigmoid colon. CT pelvis without contrast showed a megacolon with a high position of the rectal pouch above the level of puborectalis muscle at the level of S2/S3. A puborectalis muscle cyst is seen with thickened walls measuring around 1×0.5 cm. MRI impressive of presacral lipoma-myelomeningocele. Biopsy of the presacral mass confirmed a mature teratoma.

case_report: A 76-year-old Japanese woman presented to the outpatient clinic with an ulcerated, infiltrated plaque on the left side of her right leg. She had a history of receiving narrow band UVB irradiation treatment for parapsoriasis en plaque over the past 4 years. During the initial physical examination, an ulcerated, infiltrated plaque was observed within scaly erythema and atrophic lesions on the right lower leg.
test_results: A biopsy specimen from the right lower leg revealed a dense perivascular infiltrate of atypical lymphoid in the upper dermis reaching into the subcutaneous tissue. Immunohistochemical staining revealed that these atypical lymphocytes, which were distributed throughout the dermis, were positive for CD3, CD8, CD30, granulysin and CCR4 and negative for CD4, CD7, and CD56. In addition, substantial numbers of CCL17 producing cells were detected at the center of the infiltrate, whereas CCL22 producing cells were not detected.

case_report: A 14-month-old female child was brought to the Pediatric Department of Union Hospital by her parents due to short limbs. She had a healthy birth history. At 3 months old, she could sit up with assistance and had normal head control. At 14 months, her communication and locomotive abilities were appropriate for her age. Physical examination revealed shorter limbs with redundant skin folds compared to her trunk. Her measurements were 73 cm in height (<50th percentile), 12 kg in weight (98th percentile), and a head circumference of 46 cm (50th percentile).
test_results: On radiological examination, the infant had a broad and irregular metaphyseal plate, with normal epiphyses. She also presented with a broad pelvis. The broadened pelvis revealed slightly flattened acetabula, and marginally widened ilia and epiphyseal plates. Vertebral X-ray revealed flattened vertebrae (platyspondyly). A hand radiograph revealed apparent ossification delay considering her age. Gene sequencing confirmed gene mutation on exon 15 of the TRPV4 gene with a heterozygous missense mutation (c.2396C > T), but no mutation was present in her parents.

case_report: A 4-year-old female born to healthy consanguineous parents from the Kurdish ethnic group was referred to Tehran Hope Generation Foundation Genetic Diagnosis Center in October 2021. The patient had a history of pneumonia, cardiomyopathy, growth retardation, peripheral edema, and distinctive craniofacial features, but no mental retardation. Cardiovascular evaluation using Magnetic Resonance study indicated constrictive pericarditis. A CT scan of the thorax revealed cardiomegaly, pericardial thickness, hepatomegaly, and mosaic lung attenuation. Molecular evaluation for Familial Mediterranean fever had been previously conducted, and no mutation was found in the related gene. Informed consent and consent for publishing the study results were obtained from the parents. The Medical Ethics Committee of the Hope Generation Foundation approved this study (Code No: IR.SBMU. MSP.REC.1396.792).
test_results: A homozygous G>A splice site variant (TRIM37; c.370-1G>A) was detected in the patient. This variant destroys the canonical splice acceptor site in intron 5 of TRIM37 gene, in which loss of function is a known mechanism of the disease. Segregation analysis in family members confirmed the cosegregation of the variant with the phenotype.

case_report: A 58-year-old woman experienced her first generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Physical examination revealed mild left pyramidal hemiparesis with upper motor neuron signs. Brain MRI showed a 16-mm right parafalcine, extra-axial lesion with homogenous contrast enhancement and surrounding vasogenic edema in the adjacent parietal and posterior frontal white matter. The lesion appeared extra-axial with a narrow dural base. Initial body CT identified pretracheal and precarinal lymphadenopathy, but no primary lesion was found elsewhere. The patient had a history of a benign breast lesion. She underwent a parasagittal craniotomy and Simpson grade-two excision of the tumor, with a small residual component left due to adherence to the superior sagittal sinus wall. Post-surgery, she recovered well without neurological deficits. Histological examination showed neoplastic cells with moderately pleomorphic nuclei, predominantly spindle-shaped, with occasional plump and polygonal forms and eosinophilic cytoplasm.
