The cells were arranged in a fascicular pattern within variable amounts of myxoid stroma, exhibiting a low mitotic rate (4/10 HPFs) and no necrosis. A well-developed and prominent peripheral lymphoid cuff was noted. Immunohistochemically, the tumor cells were positive for desmin, ALK1, vimentin, and EMA. No final diagnosis was suggested based on these findings. The differential diagnosis included atypical meningioma and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT). Due to difficulties in resolving the differential diagnosis, the case was referred for international consultation, which concluded that the lesion had meningioma characteristics.
test_results: The analysis confirmed the disruption of the EWSR1 gene at 22q12 and the disruption of the CREB1 gene at 2q33, without disruption of the ATF gene at 12q13.
diagnosis: Myxoid Variant of Angiomatoid Fibrous Histiocytoma

case_report: A 42-year-old Thai man was referred to the Oral Medicine Clinic, Faculty of Dentistry, Chulalongkorn University, Thailand for the evaluation of mouth ulcers. The lesions had been present for over six months and were previously identified as gingivitis. His medical history includes hypertension and diabetes mellitus for one year. He had been taking atenolol at 50mg per day for one year and enalapril at 10mg per day for one week. He was managing his diabetes with a controlled diet. He did not smoke or drink, and his medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Extra-oral examination (skin, genitalia, eyes) showed no abnormalities. Intra-oral examination revealed generalized erythema, desquamation, and multiple large ulcers on the gingival mucosa covered with yellowish slough tissue. Multiple disrupted bullae were observed on the labial mucosa, buccal mucosa, and ventral surface of the tongue. The patient experienced severe pain from these lesions, which hindered proper oral hygiene. Blood test results were within normal ranges for complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, creatinine, and liver function tests (aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase). The patient had been using chlorhexidine mouthwash improperly by rinsing for longer than 10 minutes. At the first visit, he was advised to discontinue the use of chlorhexidine mouthwash and was given diphenhydramine elixir mouthwash for pain relief. This change resulted in pain relief after one week, but the oral lesions remained unchanged.
test_results: H&E staining showed an ulcerated parakeratinized stratified squamous epithelium overlying fibrovascular connective tissue. The underlying connective tissue was edematous, and was infiltrated by acute and chronic inflammatory cells, including neutrophils, eosinophils, plasma cells, and lymphocytes. Direct immunofluorescence showed the deposition of IgG, IgA, and C3 in a homogeneous linear pattern at the dermoepidermal junction.

case_report: A 75-year-old white female, carrier of the BRCA2 gene mutation, presented with a family history of three daughters diagnosed with breast cancer, all BRCA2 positive. She had no other significant issues. Genetic testing confirmed the BRCA2 gene mutation. The patient was informed about the increased risks of breast and ovarian cancers. For breast cancer risk management, she opted for screening mammograms every three years. After thorough discussion and counseling, she was advised that the best option to minimize ovarian cancer risk would be laparoscopic removal of the ovaries and fallopian tubes. The patient was reviewed in the clinic prior to her elective procedure. Her medical history included hypertension, osteoarthritis, seborrheic dermatitis, and a past hepatitis A infection in 1970. Surgical history included laparoscopic sterilization and left knee replacement. Medications included lansoprazole, amlodipine, and antihistamines, with no known allergies. She had four previous normal vaginal deliveries and was current with cervical screenings, the last being negative. Her BMI was 32, and routine blood tests including urea and electrolytes, full blood count, and coagulation profile were normal. She underwent an elective laparoscopic bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy without intraoperative complications. A small retroverted uterus was noted, and both tubes and ovaries appeared normal. The course of the ureter was identified on both sides. The left ovary, adherent to the left pelvic side wall, was mobilized before removal. An electrothermal bipolar tissue sealing device was used, and the specimen was delivered with a laparoscopic bag. The tubes and ovaries were sent in the same container for histological examination. Blood loss was minimal. The patient had an uneventful recovery and was discharged home the same day. Histopathology reported that one fallopian tube showed elements of a STIC with negative p53 staining and a Ki67 index of at least 30%, with no evidence of invasive malignancy. The other tube and both ovaries were normal. The patient's case and histology results were discussed in a regional multidisciplinary meeting (MDT).
test_results: The CT thorax, abdomen, and pelvis showed tiny omental nodules in the left anterior hemipelvis. The soft tissue stranding in the parametrium was thought to be post-surgical changes.

case_report: A 52-year-old European male from Spain, born to non-consanguineous parents, provided written informed consent for the publication of identifiable data. The patient exhibited significant muscle weakness, defective dental enamel, multiple dental caries and root canals, and brittle nails. There was no evidence of dystrophy. He had congenital pes cavus of the right foot and congenital hammer toes affecting the fourth and fifth digits. The patient also had arthrosis, generalized muscle pain, muscle atrophy with involuntary muscle jerks, and severe fatigue following physical activity. Photosensitivity was noted, with erythema and skin peeling after sun exposure, though no oral ulcers, cold sores, arthritis, or Raynaud’s phenomenon were reported. Skin rashes worsened during the summer, accompanied by solar urticaria and dermographism (erythema). Each episode was associated with digestive symptoms, including a tendency towards diarrhea, and a worsening of muscle weakness. Morning muscle pain, which improved with exercise, was reported, along with muscle stiffness, fatigue, pain in the peripheral forearms and legs, and muscle contractures that had progressed over the past year. Despite regular physical activity (walking 1 hour daily, Pilates), the patient experienced muscle mass loss and intense muscle pain after exercise. He reported being in good physical condition but experienced extreme exhaustion after 1 hour of exercise. Nighttime muscle pain, which improved with short walks, was also noted. The patient experienced involuntary muscle jerks in the arms during exercise, pain in both wrists with functional impairment, and spontaneous resolution of these symptoms. Examination of skeletal muscle revealed preserved architecture without increased endomysial connective tissue or adipose infiltration.
test_results: A skeletal muscle biopsy showed discrete variability in muscle fibre size, with the presence of fibres with multiple internalised nuclei (approximately 8%). We observed no necrotic or regenerative fibres and no structural disorders (vacuoles or inclusions). Through ATPase techniques, we determined that the fibre type distribution was normal. With oxidative techniques, we observed a few COX-negative fibres with sorbitol dehydrogenase overexpression (approximately 3%), as well as NADH-TR alterations. We observed no inflammatory infiltrates and no alterations using the histochemical technique for phosphorylase and myoadenylate deaminase. He presented high creatine kinase levels and pseudomyotonia, which was observed on an electromyogram.

case_report: A 36-year-old woman (gravida 3, para 3) sought medical evaluation for an ovarian mass. Ten years prior, during her first pregnancy, she was identified with a 6-cm ovarian mass on the right side at a different medical facility. Current pelvic examination identified a firm, non-tender mass in the right adnexal region. Vaginal ultrasound and pelvic CT scan confirmed the presence of a 6-cm solid ovarian mass. MRI indicated a 61-mm solid mass with heterogeneous low signal intensity in the pelvic area. Serum tumor markers, including carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), CA125, CA19–9, squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG), and alpha fetoprotein (AFP), were all within normal limits.
test_results: Laparoscopic observation revealed that the tumor in the Douglas pouch protruded from the right ovary without adhesion. Intraoperative cytology of ascitic fluid was negative. In paraffin sections, the tumor cells were spindle shaped and arranged in intersecting bundles. They had ill-defined cytoplasmic borders and spindled to ovoid hyperchromatic nuclei with a moderate mitotic rate (10 per 10 HPF) but without significant nuclear atypia. On immunohistochemistry, vimentin, progesterone receptor (PR), CD10, CD56 and Wilms tumor gene (WT-1) were positive, alpha-inhibin was focally positive, and pan cytokeratin (AE1/AE3), estrogen receptor (ER), calretinin and epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) were negative. Ki-67 index was 8.7 %.
diagnosis: Mitotically Active Cellular Fibroma  of the ovary

case_report: An 82-year-old woman presented with widespread skin redness, scattered invasive red patches, nodules, and tumors on her face, trunk, and extremities. Blood analysis showed a white blood cell count of 14,730/µL (reference range, 3.3–8.6 × 10^3/µL), with 28% abnormal cells featuring cerebriform nuclei, a hemoglobin level of 12.2 g/dL (11.6–14.8 g/dL), and a platelet count of 311 × 10^3/µL (158–348 × 10^3/µL). Lactate dehydrogenase levels were 362 IU/L (124–224 IU/L) and soluble interleukin-2 receptor levels were 2,139 U/mL (122–496 U/mL). A serologic test for human T-cell leukemia virus type 1 was negative. Computed tomography showed no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Skin biopsy from a tumor on the left arm revealed infiltration of abnormal lymphocytes with medium- to large-sized nuclei containing convolutions in the superficial dermis. Immunohistochemical staining of the skin biopsy showed abnormal lymphocytes expressing CD3 and CD4, but not CD7, CD8, CD20, or CD30. Approximately 30% of leukocytes in the blood were morphologically abnormal, with a small percentage expressing CD4, and the CD4:CD8 ratio was 1.7 as analyzed by conventional two-color flow cytometry. Further phenotypical analysis by multicolor flow cytometry indicated that among CD3+ T cells, 84.0% were CD4–CD8–, 10.8% were CD4+CD8–, and 4.8% were CD4–CD8+. CD4+CD8– T cells expressed CD7 and/or CD26 similar to normal helper T cells, whereas CD4–CD8– T cells had reduced CD7 expression and lacked CD26 expression.
test_results: Both PB and skin samples showed a clonal peak in Vβ + Jβ1/2 and Dβ + Jβ1/2, and the size of those PCR products was completely matched between both specimens as 273 bp in Vβ + Jβ1/2 and 296 bp in Dβ + Jβ1/2.

case_report: A 64-year-old female visited her general practitioner with a three-year history of swelling in the right frontal region of the skull. Over the last year, the swelling had grown larger. Upon referral to the neurosurgery clinic, a physical examination identified a sessile, non-tender mass measuring approximately 4.3 x 1.6 cm. The skin covering the mass was intact and exhibited normal hair growth. The patient did not report any headaches or exhibit any focal neurological signs or symptoms. An initial skull X-ray indicated the presence of a bony growth, and bone scintigraphy results were normal.
test_results: A CT scan of the head showed a sclerotic thickened area of the right frontal bone with no significant mass effect on the underlying cerebrum. No brain or meningeal enhancement was noted on the scans. Review of the scans by a second radiologist confirmed an area of sclerosis and non-destructive expansion of the right frontal bone. Histologically the sample contained fragments of mature bone, whereby some of the bone marrow spaces were replaced by a spindle cell tumour forming lobules and whorls. It was composed of cells with oval nuclei, some nuclear pseudoinclusions, eosinophilic cytoplasm and indistinct cytoplasmic borders. Mitotic figures were not present.

case_report: A 17-month-old girl was brought to the endocrinology clinic with a history of poor growth since weaning at 6 months old. She was born at 38 weeks from a healthy pregnancy, the first child of non-consanguineous parents. Her birth weight was 2.8 kg (−0.46 SD), length was 48 cm (−0.21 SD), and head circumference was 33 cm (−0.33 SD). The perinatal period was uneventful. She exhibited normal growth and motor development until 7 months old, when she was unable to sit. Due to progressive motor skill delays and the onset of trunk and limb hypotonia, she was hospitalized at 15 months old. Neurological evaluation confirmed hypotonia with hypotrophic muscles; cranial nerve function and tendon reflexes were normal. Tests including complete blood count, thyroid function, lactate/pyruvate ratio, celiac disease screening, electromyography, nerve conduction studies, and brain MRI were normal. No causes of hypotonia were identified, and she was discharged with a diagnosis of 'hypotonic syndrome and motor delay'. At 17 months old, she weighed 7.8 kg (−2.2 SD) and was 68.5 cm long (−4.08 SD). She had a large anterior fontanelle, normal primary dentition, but exhibited rachitic bracelet, rachitic rosary, and coxa vara. Laboratory results showed hypophosphatemia (1.3 mg/dL), increased alkaline phosphatase activity (1173 U/L), and normocalcemia (9.2 mg/dL). Levels of 1,25-dihydroxy-vitamin D were normal (25 pg/mL), 25-hydroxy-vitamin D was 17 ng/mL, and parathormone (PTH) was slightly elevated (96 pg/mL). Decreased tubular phosphate reabsorption (69%) was observed without hypercalciuria. Skeletal X-ray revealed rib end expansion ('rachitic rosary'), cupping and fraying of the metaphyseal regions, diffusely reduced bone mineralization with periosteal reaction, and multiple fractures in various stages of healing. Body MRI ruled out tumor-induced osteomalacia.
test_results: The next-generation sequencing (NGS) showed a de novo heterozygous variant c.536G>A (NM_020638.3:c.536G>A) in exon 3 of the FGF23 gene.

case_report: The patient, a previously healthy 14-month-old boy (weight: 12 kg, height: 77 cm), presented with a five-day history of fever and irritability, along with a three-day history of skin rash prior to admission. The erythematous rash initially appeared on the trunk and upper limbs, later spreading to the hands and feet, and was accompanied by swelling of the extremities. Changes in the lips and tongue were also noted. During this period, he was treated with azithromycin and acetaminophen. His father, who was the COVID-19 index case, had close household contact with the patient and exhibited a cough before being diagnosed with COVID-19, seven days before the child's symptoms began. Upon admission to Bu-Ali Sina Hospital in Sari, Iran, in April 2020, the patient appeared irritable and ill. Physical examination showed a fever of 38.8°C, respiratory rate of 32 bpm, pulse rate of 120 bpm, and blood pressure of 84/42 mmHg. The patient had cracked and erythematous lips, a strawberry tongue, and bilateral nonpurulent conjunctivitis. A generalized erythematous maculopapular rash was observed on the skin, along with edema in the upper and lower extremities. No significant cervical lymphadenopathy was detected. Heart, lung, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Initial laboratory tests revealed leukocytosis, neutrophilia, anemia, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), elevated C-reactive protein (CRP), and increased liver transaminase levels. The real-time reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) assay for COVID-19 was negative in the nasopharyngeal specimen. Serum albumin was decreased (2.3 g/dL), and serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D was 33 ng/mL (within normal range). Kidney function, coagulation tests, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels were normal, and the initial chest X-ray was unremarkable. On the second day, echocardiography was performed, and chest sonography revealed minimal (5 mm) right-sided pleural effusion.
test_results: The serum immunoglobulin M antibody for COVID-19 reported positive (1.20), and the immunoglobulin G antibody was negative (0.37).
diagnosis: Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children  associated with COVID-19
Orpha_name: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children and adults

case_report: A 5-year-old male child presented to the dental outpatient department with decayed upper and lower front and back teeth. The child was born to nonconsanguineous parents during the mother's first pregnancy. At birth, the mother was 30 years old and the father was 33 years old. The pregnancy was complicated by preeclampsia and concluded with a lower segment cesarean section. At birth, the child experienced perinatal asphyxia, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, and did not cry immediately. The birth weight was 2.4 kg and height was 106 cm. The child had persistent thrombocytopenia and required an 11-day stay in the neonatal intensive care unit. Postnatally, the child frequently suffered from upper respiratory tract infections. At the age of 5, physical examination revealed microcephaly, alar facies, blue sclera, upslanting eyes, overhanging columella, prominent cup-shaped ears, reduced mouth opening, protruding tongue, triangular-shaped face with a small chin, and fifth finger clinodactyly. Additionally, the child exhibited noticeable speech delay, behavioral inhibition, difficulty adapting to new situations, and occasionally spoke loudly with hyperactive behavior.
test_results: Moderate hearing loss was seen with respect to the right and left ears. Ophthalmology evaluation was found normal. The 2D echo analysis has shown small atrioseptal defects.

case_report: A five-year-old boy, born to consanguineous parents of Arab ethnicity, was delivered at term via spontaneous vaginal delivery without requiring NICU admission. The family history includes liver disease in his uncles, with one uncle passing away at 11 years old and another undergoing a liver transplant and passing away at 30 years old. The specific disease affecting his uncles is unknown to his parents. At three years old, the boy presented with abdominal distention and cough, leading to a hospital visit where he was found to have Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and hepatosplenomegaly. He was subsequently seen at our hospital for follow-up in a pediatric gastroenterologist clinic. Physical examination revealed no dysmorphic features, normal developmental status, clear chest, liver palpable 4 cm below the costal margin, spleen palpable 4 cm below the costal margin, no ascites, no itching, and normal stool passage. Laboratory tests showed elevated liver enzymes, with a complete blood count (CBC) nearly within normal limits. Bone marrow examination indicated hypercellular marrow with trilineage hyperplasia and prominent juvenile megakaryocytes. Abdominal ultrasound confirmed hepatosplenomegaly with a normal patent portal vein measuring 9 mm. Symptomatic treatment for EBV was provided. During follow-up, the patient exhibited bi-cytopenia, persistent elevated liver enzymes, and hepatosplenomegaly. Further tests revealed normal high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), negative hepatic serology, normal brucella titer, EBV PCR at 1110 copies/ml, positive Immunoglobulin G (IgG), negative Immunoglobulin M (IgM), ferritin at 29 microgram/L (normal range 10.3-55), alfa fetoprotein at 1.3 ug/L (normal range 0.8-4.5), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) at 179 mmol/L (normal range 140-304), and negative results for smooth muscle antibody, liver kidney microsomes antibody, and malarial parasite.
test_results: The genetic study identified the homozygous pathogenic variant c.2906G>A in the ABCB4 gene.

case_report: An 18-year-old female patient presented with bleeding gums and swelling on the right side of the lower jaw for 6 months. The swelling, initially the size of a peanut, grew slowly to its current size. There was no associated pain. The patient also reported progressive hearing loss over 2 years and a history of multiple bone fractures, up to thirty, occurring spontaneously from minor injuries since childhood. Medical and family histories were noncontributory. Clinical examination revealed a short, stout appearance with bowing of the upper and lower limbs. Extraoral examination showed unilateral facial asymmetry. Intraorally, a bony prominence of the mandible extending from tooth 43 to the mesial aspect of tooth 47, measuring approximately 2 cm × 1 cm, was observed. The swelling was well-circumscribed, nontender, and hard in consistency, with slightly erythematous mucosa over it. Lymph nodes were not palpable. An orthopantomogram showed a mixed radiopaque and radiolucent lesion with a ground glass appearance, a deformed left condylar region, impacted tooth 33, missing tooth 45, over-retained tooth 85, and accentuated pulp spaces in teeth 17, 25, 26, 27, 28, 36, 37, 46, and 47. A skull radiograph revealed bone expansion and lytic areas in the skull vault and mandible. A lumbar spine radiograph, including the pelvis, showed scoliosis, bone expansion in the pelvic region, and osteolytic and sclerotic areas. Serum calcium and phosphorus levels were within normal limits, but alkaline phosphatase was elevated at 182 U/L.
test_results: Histopathological features showed irregular interconnecting trabeculae with prominent basophilic lines arranged irregularly, which are lined by active osteoblasts and few osteoclasts. Resorbed bone and marrow spaces were seen to be replaced by fibrovascular connective tissue.

case_report: A 17-year-old male presented with painful and tender diffuse erythema and swelling, accompanied by a necrotic lesion on the scrotum for three days. One week prior to these symptoms, he had visited the emergency room with fever and sore throat and was prescribed oral amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid. Physical examination revealed a well-demarcated necrotic lesion approximately 2 cm in size on the anterior scrotum. The lesion was confined to the scrotum, and there was no crepitus in the inflamed tissues. The patient reported no history of local trauma, sexual activity, or other predisposing factors. Laboratory tests showed neutrophilic leukocytosis with a count of 16,430×10^6/L (normal <10,000×10^6/L), elevated C-reactive protein at 70.1 mg/L (normal <5.0 mg/L), and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 32 mm/h (normal <15 mm/h). Scrotal ultrasonography indicated edematous skin thickening and increased vascularity. Blood cultures, urine cultures, and bacterial cultures of the skin were all negative. Serological tests for syphilis and Rickettsia tsutsugamushi antibodies were also negative. Evaluation for sexually transmitted diseases yielded no specific findings.
test_results: The skin biopsy of the scrotal ulcer showed epidermal necrosis and dermal neutrophilic infiltration.
diagnosis: Juvenile Gangrenous Vasculitis of the Scrotum

case_report: The third child in the family, a 10-year-old boy, exhibits clinical features similar to those of his two older cousins. His current height is 111 cm (Z-score -3.7) and his weight is 33 kg (Z-score -0.4). Developmental milestones were delayed, and multiple compression fractures were noted at 9 months of age. At 18 months, he experienced his first femoral fracture, and generalized osteopenia was identified. Since then, he has had multiple additional fractures. Physical examination showed a low posterior hairline, a short and webbed neck, low-set ears, a shield chest, and long fingers and toes. His sclerae and teeth appear normal.
test_results: Radiographs revealed moderate thoracic kyphosis and platyspondyly.

case_report: The patient is a 5-year-old Moroccan boy, the youngest of three siblings, with no consanguinity in the family. His parents and older sister are healthy and have no history of epilepsy. The patient exhibited neonatal hypotonia and psychomotor delay, and at 2 years old, he was unable to sit with head support. He began experiencing daily generalized seizures at 8 months old, which were treated with sodium valproate but showed no improvement. Clinical examination revealed stature and weight below the 3rd percentile, microcephaly at -2SD, severe hypotonia, and no facial dysmorphia or nystagmus. A CT scan was normal, but an EEG showed abnormal waves in the right fronto-temporal region. An MRI was not available. Five cousins and two maternal uncles also had epilepsy. Four of these relatives died at ages four, seven, three, and two years, respectively, and all had neonatal hypotonia, psychomotor delay, and epilepsy starting at 6 months old.
test_results: A total of 188,043 variants were detected. The WES data covered all exons of known X-Linked Epilepsy related genes, and no known pathogenic mutations were identified in these genes. Nevertheless, we identified a single hemizygous base substitution in coding exon3, c.251C > A of the PLP1 gene (based on GRCh37/hg19, and transcript ID NM_000533), resulting in substitution of alanine by an aspartic acid at amino acid 84. This mutation was found in hemizygous state in the propositus V-4 and in his cousin V-7. Sanger sequencing confirmed this mutation in hemizygous state in the affected subjects (V-9, V-10) and in heterozygous state in the obligatory carrier mothers, showing co-segregation of the mutation with the disease phenotype. The non-affected IV-12 was wild type for this mutation. Mutation c.251C > A (p.Ala84Asp) located within exon 3, results in changes of a non-polar alanine to a charged aspartic acid at position 84.

case_report: A 48-year-old female with myopia presented with recurrent floaters and reduced vision in her right eye. Her symptoms began in 2007. She had no systemic symptoms, history of ocular trauma, or previous tuberculosis infection. The condition was managed with intermittent focal laser treatment due to inefficacy and poor tolerance of general steroid treatment. In November 2015, she was admitted with vitreous hemorrhage in her right eye. At presentation, her best corrected visual acuity was 0.5 in the right eye and 0.9 in the left eye, with a spherical myopic correction of -3.75. Intraocular pressure measured 15 mmHg in both eyes using applanation tonometry. External and slit-lamp examinations of the anterior segment were normal. Fundus examination was performed after pharmaceutical mydriasis with 1% tropicamide and 10% phenylephrine hydrochloride ophthalmic solution. The left eye fundus was normal. After the vitreous hemorrhage resolved, fundus examination of the right eye revealed retinal neovascularization, fibrovascular proliferation, peripheral non-perfusion, collaterals, vascular sheathing, and peripheral branch retinal vein occlusion.
test_results: Fluorescein angiography revealed peripheral non-perfusion and retinal neovascularization with leakage in the right eye and was normal for the left eye.

case_report: An 18-year-old female presented with a primary concern of forwardly positioned teeth in the upper front region of the jaw. Family history indicated similar features in her father and grandmother. Extraoral examination showed an upward slant of the eye openings with sparse eyelashes on the lower eyelids. There was underdevelopment of the cheekbones and a small lower jaw. The upper jaw appeared to be protruding, giving the face a distinctive appearance. Intraoral examination found a narrow, high-arched palate. The upper front teeth were angled forward with spacing between the upper and lower front teeth. Root remnants were observed in the positions of teeth 26, 36, and 46. There was generalized gum recession and grade I tooth mobility.
test_results: Radiographs revealed prominent antigonial notch, short ramus, hypoplasia of the mandible, proclined upper anteriors, hypoplasia of zygomatic bone, and maxillary sinus.

case_report: A 30-year-old male reported experiencing involuntary neck movements starting at age 12 and involuntary movements in both upper limbs beginning at age 18. The neck movements were intermittent, nonrhythmic, and horizontal with rotational jerks to the left, worsening with stress and anxiety but improving with sensory tricks. He also had intermittent, brief, jerky, shock-like movements in the neck and both hands (more pronounced on the right side) with abnormal posturing during activities like writing and holding objects, which impaired his ability to perform fine motor tasks. These movements were triggered by somatosensory and auditory stimuli and did not show diurnal fluctuations or paroxysms. There was no relevant family history. Physical examination revealed no oculocutaneous telangiectasia. The patient exhibited cervical dystonia characterized by left rotacollis with right laterocollis and neck myoclonus. The upper extremities showed asymmetric dystonic posturing of both hands along with myoclonic jerks. Eye movement examination revealed slow vertical saccades and hypometric horizontal saccades without oculomotor apraxia. Gait ataxia and cerebellar signs were notably absent. Routine blood tests, including hemogram and biochemistry, were normal. There was no Kayser-Fleischer ring, and serum ceruloplasmin and 24-hour urinary copper levels were normal. Abdominal-pelvic ultrasonography and brain MRI were normal. Genetic tests for DYT 1, 11, and SCA 1, 3 were negative.
test_results: Clinical whole-exome sequencing showed a homozygous missense mutation (c. 9156G > C; p.Trp3052Cys) in exon 63 of ATM gene on chromosome 11q22. His serum AFP levels were high at 317.2 ng/ml (normal <10 ng/ml).

case_report: A 60-year-old female with no history of psychiatric issues or chronic medical conditions presented with persistent sadness, loss of interest in daily activities, decreased sleep and appetite, easy fatigability, ruminative thoughts, anxiety symptoms, and death wishes for the past 18 months. She had no history of traumatic brain injury or substance use. She was prescribed escitalopram 5 mg and clonazepam 0.5 mg per day, with the escitalopram dose increased to 10 mg/day after one week. After one month, she reported significant improvement in depressive symptoms and normalized sleep patterns. Nine months later, she began experiencing tremors, body weakness, backward falls, dizziness, muscle tightness, difficulty opening her mouth, slurred speech, and swallowing difficulties. She also developed forgetfulness and inattention, which progressively worsened. On mental state examination, she was alert and oriented with a blunt affect. Her Mini-Mental Status Examination score was 18. Neurological examination revealed bilateral resting tremors, mild cogwheel rigidity, decreased arm swing, postural instability, dysphagia, dysarthria, jaw dystonia, and vertical gaze deficit with slow saccades. Laboratory tests including thyroid, kidney, and liver function tests, complete blood count, and blood sugar levels were normal.
test_results: MRI brain revealed cerebral and midbrain atrophy.

case_report: The patient is a 17-year-old male who first exhibited muscle weakness at 5 years old. He was born at full term with no significant prenatal issues aside from mild gestational diabetes. His early developmental milestones were typical, except for a delay in walking independently until 19 months. At 5 years old, he had trouble climbing stairs, running, and hopping. There is no family history of neuromuscular disorders. Physical examination showed calf hypertrophy and greater weakness in the proximal lower extremities compared to distal (hip flexion, extension, and abduction at 3/5; knee extension, knee flexion, ankle dorsiflexion, and ankle plantarflexion at 4/5 bilaterally). He used a modified Gowers sign to rise from the floor and exhibited decreased pelvic stability during gait, with reduced speed and quality of movement while running. Laboratory tests revealed elevated creatine kinase levels (7583 IU/L; normal range 4 to 88 IU/L). Brain MRI was normal. Genetic analysis for DMD gene deletions and duplications was inconclusive. A muscle biopsy of the vastus lateralis showed histopathological features consistent with a dystrophic process, including fiber size variation due to atrophic and hypertrophic fibers, endomysial fibrosis, and increased internal nuclei. Immunostaining indicated reduced alpha-dystroglycan staining with normal staining for dystrophin, emerin, merosin, beta-dystroglycan, and sarcoglycans. Western blotting confirmed hypoglycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan.
test_results: FKRP gene sequencing showed a heterozygous pathogenic c.826C>A (p.L276I) variant in exon 4 of the patient's FKRP gene. The testing also detected two novel insertions on the other allele; a single nucleotide insertion (c.948_949insC) and an eighteen nucleotide duplication (c.999_1017dup18), resulting in a premature translation termination codon at position 389 (p.E389*). Parental testing demonstrated that the mother carried c.826C>A, while the father carried the insertion/duplication, confirming an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.
diagnosis: Limb-Girdle Muscular Dystrophy R9  due to a novel complex insertion/duplication variant in FKRP gene

case_report: A 55-year-old male with a 10-year history of diabetes mellitus type II presented with skin changes in both thighs and legs that began 2 years after his diabetes diagnosis. The skin lesions were nonpitting, erythematous, and poorly defined, with significant thickening and a peau d’orange appearance. Three years before these skin changes, the patient experienced numbness and pain in both legs, primarily in the distal regions, which worsened after the skin changes appeared, making walking nearly impossible without assistance. Concurrently, he had frequent episodes of shortness of breath and a nonproductive cough, leading to multiple hospital admissions. Physical examination revealed moderate sensory loss (touch, pain, position, and vibration) in a symmetrical stock and glove distribution, along with moderate generalized tendon hyporeflexia (2 minus). The skin lesions were most noticeable on the superior and anterior aspects of both thighs, characterized by erythema, hyperpigmentation, and a corrugated, peau d’orange texture.
test_results: Skin biopsy revealed the ballooning and swelling of collagen bundles with few scattered lymphocytes. Protein electrophoresis showed increased gamma globulin polyclonal bands. MRI of thighs revealed diffuse thickening of the skin with subcutaneous edema surrounding the muscles and entering the intermuscular compartment.

case_report: A 12-year-old girl with no prior health issues presented with elevated serum creatinine (1.17 mg/dl), low phosphate levels (2.7 mg/dl), low uric acid levels (2.0 mg/dl), and increased ferritin (279 ng/ml). These findings were noted over a 4-week period during which she experienced fatigue, loss of appetite, abdominal pain, vomiting, and weight loss. These symptoms began following a brief febrile respiratory illness treated with ibuprofen. She had two negative SARS-CoV-2 antigen tests at home during the first and sixth days of respiratory symptoms. Her primary care pediatrician monitored her for several weeks, confirming ongoing weight loss of up to 12.5 kg and normal urine output. After 8 weeks, she tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 via PCR (> 8 log10 RNA copies/ml of Omicron variant; cutoff > 3 log10 RNA copies/ml) due to mild dysphonia. She had received two doses of the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine 4 and 5 months before presentation. Upon referral to our tertiary care center at 10 weeks, the previously noted abnormalities were confirmed, along with normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.3 g/dl), elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (89 mm/hour), glycosuria, and significantly increased urinary beta-2-microglobulin (55,740 mcg/l). Serological tests showed no recent infections with Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, hepatitis B or C, or HIV. Antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 were not tested at this time.
test_results: Presence of an interstitial inflammatory infiltrate with lymphocyte predominance, with abundant eosinophils and plasma cells, tubulitis, and negative immunohistochemistry staining for SARS-CoV-2.

case_report: A 46-year-old man with no prior health issues arrived at the emergency department after experiencing a cough and high-grade fever for two days. On the day of his visit, he developed sudden shortness of breath while at rest. He had been smoking cigarettes for the past four months, initially two to three on weekends and recently three to four daily. He had no history of asthma, atopy, or illicit drug use and reported no exposure to animals, birds, livestock, chemical fumes, or recent travel. Upon admission, his vital signs were: blood pressure 110/88 mm Hg, pulse 100/min, and respiratory rate 18/min. His oxygen saturation was 75% on room air, improving to 91% with 10 L of oxygen via nasal cannula. Lung auscultation revealed bilateral coarse crackles, while the rest of the physical examination was normal, with no rash, lymphadenopathy, or pallor. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 8500/μL with 78% neutrophils and 4% eosinophils. Serum C-reactive protein (CRP) was 32.36 mg/dL, pro-calcitonin was 0.70 ng/mL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 64 mm/hour. Renal function and urinalysis were normal. Chest radiograph indicated diffuse bilateral infiltrates, and chest computed tomography revealed patchy bilateral opacifications and bilateral pleural effusions. He was treated with intravenous antibiotics, ceftriaxone and azithromycin, and oral prednisone 50 mg once daily. By the second day in the hospital, his condition improved with reduced oxygen needs. Infectious tests for pneumonia, including Legionella antigen, Streptococcus antigen, and blood cultures, were negative. By the third day, his eosinophil count had risen to 9%, peaking at 35% by day six. Despite a persistent dry cough, he remained clinically stable, and a repeat chest radiograph showed significant improvement. His IgE levels were normal, and tests for auto-immune antibodies (ANA, ANCA), hypersensitivity pneumonitis panel, and fungal infections (beta-D-glucan, Aspergillus, Coccidioides) were negative. An echocardiogram showed normal left ventricular function with an ejection fraction of 50% and normal estimated pulmonary artery pressure.
test_results: Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid cytology showed an eosinophil count of 12%.

case_report: A 61-year-old woman was discovered in a confused state on her floor by paramedics after neighbors reported not seeing her for five days. Upon arrival at the emergency department (ED), paramedics noted no unusual circumstances at her residence but mentioned she had been behaving oddly at a neighborhood party five days earlier. The patient was unable to provide information due to her altered mental status. Initial vital signs in the ED were a temperature of 36.6°C, pulse of 94/min, respiratory rate of 18/min, blood pressure of 134/59, and O2 saturation of 96% on 4 L O2 via nasal cannula. Medications found at her home included rosuvastatin, nadolol, an albuterol inhaler, citalopram, and a lidocaine patch. Her medical history, confirmed by her daughter, included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, asthma, bipolar disorder, and chronic back pain. She had undergone a partial gastrectomy for a peptic ulcer eight years ago and had been sober from alcohol for five years. Physical examination revealed a lethargic, uncooperative patient with incoherent speech, who only withdrew her right upper extremity from noxious stimuli. She exhibited icteric sclera, mild jaundice, and dry mucus membranes. No topical medication patches were present. Stool was negative for occult blood, and chest and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. There was no nystagmus, and the remainder of the neurologic examination was limited by her inability to participate. A CT-head scan showed no acute abnormalities. Hematologic studies showed a white blood cell count of 3,600/mm3, platelet count of 138,000/mm3, and hemoglobin level of 15.5 g/dL. Electrolytes were normal except for a blood urea nitrogen (BUN) of 53 mg/dL (normal 7–20 mg/dL). Initial creatinine level was 0.7 mg/dL, and GFR was 90. Other lab results included a lactate of 2.7 mmol/L (0.4–2.2 mmol/L), an INR of 3.07, a troponin T of 0.04 ng/mL (normal <0.01 ng/mL), and a creatine kinase of 531 U/L (24–170 U/L). Serum toxicology levels were normal, with acetone present but less than 10, and an acetaminophen (APAP) level of 3 mg/L (10–20 mg/L).
test_results: Transaminase levels were initially delayed and returned one hour later with elevation of the aspartate aminotransferase (AST) level up to 1240 U/L (0–34 U/L), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) to 1450 U/L (0–34 U/L), and alkaline phosphatase (AP) of 238 U/L (30–130 U/L). Direct and indirect bilirubin levels were 5.8 mg/dL (<0.2 mg/dL) and 9.3 mg/dL (<1.2 mg/dL), respectively.
diagnosis: Acute liver failure due to toxic acetaminophen ingestion

case_report: A four-and-a-half-year-old male presented for evaluation of a painless expansile lesion in the left maxillary region. The patient exhibited no other symptoms and had an unremarkable medical history. Clinical examination showed mild facial asymmetry due to increased fullness of the left upper lip and cheek. There was ipsilateral erythema, increased facial hair, and a scar in the nasolabial area. Intraoral examination revealed buccolingual expansion of the left maxillary arch with gingival overgrowth noted since the age of 3. The left maxillary primary molars showed delayed eruption. The gingiva near the primary canine was thickened, red, and edematous. The patient maintained good oral hygiene and reported delayed eruption of primary teeth in the left maxillary quadrant, particularly in the canine and molar regions. The left maxillary alveolus was widened with gingival hyperplasia. A panoramic radiograph showed delayed or absent eruption of teeth and enlargement of the left maxilla.
test_results: CBCT demonstrated evidence of a left maxillary alveolar expansile lesion with a dystrophic appearance. The cortical plates were well maintained. Trabeculation appeared to be ill defined, and generally oriented along the y-axis. The left maxillary alveolus demonstrated several missing posterior secondary teeth. There was significant expansion of the left maxilla with involvement of the maxillary sinus along the inferior aspect. The nasal fossa was slightly displaced and remodeled on the left side. Hypoplasia of the left maxillary antrum was observed with the cortical margins being intact. The sinus was partly pneumatized with minimal alveolar extensions. No frank evidence of mucosal thickening or intrasinus fluid was observed. No deviation of the nasal septum was noted. The ostiomeatal complex appeared to be within normal limits. Histopathologic examination of the decalcified hard tissue revealed mostly woven bone with fibrous stroma, while some areas contained peculiar woven bone without fibrous stroma. Osteoblasts and osteoclasts were not identified. Resting and reversal lines were noted.

case_report: A 15-year-old female presented to the orthopedic clinic with a lateral curvature of the spine. Examination revealed asymmetry in shoulder height, spinal deformity, and low back pain that began two years prior. The patient had no significant past medical interventions. She was generally healthy with no history of diabetes, hypertension, coronary heart disease, hepatitis, tuberculosis, other infectious diseases, surgeries, trauma, blood transfusions, allergies, or deviations from the vaccination schedule. Her height was 166 cm, weight 30 kg, and body mass index 10.89. Physical examination identified several distinct features: square shoulders, slender tubular bones, scoliosis, and a small pelvis. Endocrine function and cognitive abilities were normal. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia, anterior mitral valve prolapse, and mild tricuspid valve insufficiency. Pulmonary function tests indicated restrictive ventilation dysfunction with maximum voluntary ventilation exceeding 70%. Blood samples were collected in EDTA tubes after obtaining informed consent from the patient's guardians, and genomic DNA was extracted from whole blood using standard procedures.
test_results: Sequencing analysis revealed that the patient's parents were heterozygous carriers, with the father carrying the c.5683+1G>C variant and the mother carrying the c.3341G>A variant. In this case, the heterozygous variants in OBSL1 (NM_015311) were c.5683+1G>C (Splice-3) and c.3341G>A (p.Trp1114Ter). X-rays showing the slender long tubular bones, thoracic scoliosis, tall vertebral bodies and small pelvis. Computed tomography (CT) showed thoracic scoliosis and tall vertebral bodies.

case_report: A 9.6-month-old girl was admitted to Children’s Hospital Soochow University in May 2018 due to a recurrent cough lasting over half a month, which worsened with shortness of breath and difficulty breathing for three days. She had a history of pneumonia at birth and growth retardation. She was delivered by cesarean section at 35 + 2 weeks. Her parents were healthy. Her twin sister passed away in April 2018 from a lung infection following surgery for atrial septal defect and ventricular septal defect. The patient weighed 9 kg, had a height of 65 cm, and a body mass index of 21.3. She exhibited shortness of breath and difficulty breathing. Blue-purple plaques were observed on her right face, buccal mucosa, oral tongue, and palate. Her bilateral pupils were fixed and dilated with a diameter of 5 mm. Crackles and wheezing rales were noted in both lungs. A grade II/6 murmur was heard along the left sternal margin. No clubbing of the digits was observed. Routine blood tests showed a white blood cell count of 8.17 × 10^9/L, and the C-reactive protein level was normal. Examination of nasopharyngeal secretions was positive for respiratory syncytial virus and negative for sputum culture. Chest high-resolution computed tomography showed inhomogeneous lung transparency, significant exudative lesions, and marked thickening of lung fissures. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging revealed abnormal signals in the centrum ovale majus and bilateral periventricular regions. Abdominal ultrasonography indicated the presence of gallstones. Initial echocardiography showed a patent foramen ovale, but the diameter of the pulmonary artery increased during follow-up. Bronchoscopy revealed redness and edema of the bronchial mucous membranes with phlegm spots and bronchomalacia.
test_results: The patient underwent genetic analysis and the ACTA2 c.536G>A (p.R179H) heterozygous mutation was found.

case_report: The patient is a 4-year-old girl born to healthy consanguineous parents, with a healthy younger sister. Prenatal ultrasound indicated short limbs. At birth, she weighed 2660 g (-1.6 SD), measured 46 cm in length (-1.4 SD), and had an occipitofrontal circumference (OFC) of 34 cm (±0 SD). Her Apgar score was 8/10. Neonatal examination identified complete bilateral cleft lip and palate, a large anterior fontanel, hypertelorism, and a coccygeal dimple. She exhibited disproportionate short stature and facial features such as dolichocephaly, a round face, a small nose with upturned nostrils, and a long, smooth philtrum. Limb abnormalities included short proximal segments and brachydactyly with bilateral clinodactyly of the fifth finger. Transfontanel ultrasound revealed quadri-ventricular hydrocephaly and microcephaly due to agenesis and atrophy of the corpus callosum. Ophthalmologic examination showed bilateral central corneal opacity without buphthalmos or congenital glaucoma. The patient also presented with sexual ambiguity, characterized by hyperpigmented labia majora with a pseudo-scrotal appearance, but no clitoral hypertrophy, and two distinct urethral and vaginal orifices. Abdominal ultrasound indicated a morphologically normal uterus and renal pyelo-calicial dilation on the left side. Chromosome analysis on lymphocytes showed a normal 46, XX karyotype. At 4 years old, the patient weighed 11 kg (-2 SD), measured 78 cm in length (-3 SD), and had an OFC of 47 cm, with no delayed psychomotor development.
test_results: Sequencing of the 15 coding exons and flanking introns boundaries of the B3GALTL gene showed that the patient is B3GALTL mutation-negative. In addition, screening of the three intragenic SNP(s) which are described to be associated with B3GALTL gene mutations showed that the patient is heterozygous for two SNP (rs9315120, rs877103) and homozygous for the rs877104 one.

case_report: A 20-year-old woman, primigravida, was transferred to our hospital due to breathing difficulty 4 days after delivering a stillborn at 24 weeks of gestation. She was intubated in the emergency department for respiratory distress and moved to the critical care unit. There was no significant past medical or genetic history for the patient or her family, and no complications such as preeclampsia, gestational diabetes, or infections were reported during pregnancy. On examination, her Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) was E4M6Vt. Her temperature was 101°F, pulse was 122 beats per minute, and blood pressure was 118/78 mm Hg. No rash was observed. Systemic examination revealed bilateral crepitations. A chest X-ray (posteroanterior view) showed bilateral infiltrates, and an echocardiogram indicated poor left ventricular systolic function without right atrium or right ventricle dilatation. The patient was treated for pneumonia, sepsis, acute kidney injury (AKI), and peripartum cardiomyopathy. Her hemodynamics and cardiopulmonary-renal functions improved, but she continued to have a high-grade fever. On the fifth day of admission, she exhibited gross muscle weakness in all four limbs, predominantly in the proximal muscles, and had dark-colored urine. Laboratory tests showed positive urine myoglobin, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 47 mm/hour, serum creatine phosphokinase (CPK) levels of 109,200 U/L, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels of 460 U/L. Thyroid function tests were normal. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) was ruled out based on clinical criteria, negative antinuclear antibody (ANA), and negative anti-dsDNA antibody. Despite initial treatment for rhabdomyolysis, including hemodialysis and supportive measures, there was no significant recovery. Further investigation was prompted by the proximal muscle weakness and elevated CPK levels.
test_results: Muscle biopsy from the left thigh muscle showed an inflammatory reaction as evident by endomysial infiltration with lymphocytes along with few necrotic muscle fibers. Electromyography (EMG) showed myopathic pattern, i.e., polyphasic motor unit potential of decreased amplitude and duration recorded predominantly in proximal muscles of bilateral upper limbs and lower limbs. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of cervical spine showed diffuse edema within the neck and shoulder girdle muscles on both sides.

case_report: An 8-month-old female presented with jaundice and pale stools. Blood tests showed elevated liver enzymes (AST/ALT: 254/161 U/L) and bilirubin levels (total: 5.6 mg/dL) without coagulopathy. Imaging studies, including abdominal CT and MRI, identified a large hypervascular mass originating from the hepatoduodenal ligament (HDL). The patient was referred for obstructive jaundice due to this mass. On the second day of hospitalization, an exploratory laparotomy was performed, revealing no tumor-like lesions in the upper abdomen. The HDL was found to be edematous, firm, and prone to bleeding, indicating acute inflammation. Due to the risk of damaging the bile duct, hepatic artery, and portal vein, en bloc surgical excision was not performed. Instead, a liver biopsy and sampling of the HDL and lymphoid tissue near the gallbladder neck were conducted, but these did not yield definitive results. Oral corticosteroid treatment was initiated, but jaundice persisted (total/direct bilirubin: 9.1/6.6 mg/dL) and liver enzyme levels increased (AST/ALT: 322/260 U/L). The intrahepatic bile duct dilatation worsened, and the gallbladder became enlarged and palpable. Concern for spontaneous gallbladder rupture led to a biopsy and cholecystectomy on postoperative day 32. The HDL had become softer and less edematous but still bled easily, indicating subacute inflammation. No obvious lesions were found in the abdominal cavity. Intraoperative cholecystography showed complete obstruction of the cystic duct (CD), and intraoperative intrahepatic cholangiography revealed narrowing of the bile duct near the CD junction along the HDL. Due to the difficulty in obtaining clear lesions, a cholecystectomy with distal CD resection, liver biopsy, and sampling of no. 12b lymphoid tissue were performed. To address severe obstructive jaundice, a hepaticojejunostomy in a Roux-en-Y configuration was performed, connecting the jejunum to the ventral wall of the common hepatic duct.
test_results: Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated that the spindle cells were positive for CD31, CD34, and ERG, partially positive for D2-40 and Prox1, and negative for GLUT1.

case_report: A 6-year-old boy presented with intermittent low-grade fever and frontal headache over the past month. Recently, he developed right-sided torticollis without any neurological deficits. There was no history of ear discharge, toothache, or head trauma. The child was conscious, and examinations of the ear, neck, and spine were normal. Central nervous system examination showed normal higher mental functions, with palsy of the right third cranial nerve and bilateral sixth cranial nerve. Motor and sensory systems were normal, and there were no meningeal signs. Laboratory investigations revealed normal hemoglobin and leukocyte count; C-reactive protein (CRP) was positive, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was elevated at 34 mm/1st hour. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination was normal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and spine was also normal. On the third day of hospitalization, the patient experienced deterioration with seizures, altered sensorium, quadriparesis, and left upper motor neuron seventh nerve palsy. The patient was started on pulse intravenous methylprednisolone.
test_results: Repeat MRI-angiography (MRA) of the brain revealed block in the terminal right internal carotid artery (ICA), left ICA, and bilateral posterior communicating artery (PCA) suggestive of vasculitis with normal brain parenchyma and normal meninges. Repeat MRA of the brain revealed resolution of thrombosis and of thickening of the left ICA and bilateral PCA as compared to initial scan but persistent thrombosis of the right ICA. The digital subtraction angiography of cranial vessels reported complete obliteration of right ICA distal to carotid bifurcation with good collateral formation; rest of brain vasculature was normal.
diagnosis: medium vessel primary angiitis of the central nervous system
Orpha_name: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system

case_report: A 46-year-old married female presented with multiple, asymptomatic, reddish-brown lesions located in the axillae, mammary area, lower abdomen, perineum, and upper inner thighs for the past 2 years. Initially, the lesions were small and pea-sized, but they gradually increased in size and number. General examination showed no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Cutaneous examination revealed multiple well-defined erythematous to brown-colored succulent-looking papulo-plaque lesions in the aforementioned areas, ranging from 0.5 to 10 cm in diameter. Lesions were present in both areolar and periareolar regions bilaterally. The vulva exhibited mainly papular lesions, while the medial thighs showed a predominance of plaques with atrophy. The plaques had erythematous, firm, elevated borders with crusting and scarring in some areas. Multiple discrete lesions were also observed around the plaques. Initially, the patient was treated with antibiotics and topical benzoyl peroxide 5%, but the lesions did not regress. After 2 weeks, oral isotretinoin at a dose of 1 mg/kg was administered for an additional 2 weeks, but there was still no regression of the lesions, and new lesions continued to appear.
test_results: A biopsy revealed acanthosis, parakeratosis, mature polyclonal plasma cells with small uniformly sized nuclei present up to the deep dermis and fibrosis. Immunohistochemical examination revealed a polyclonal staining pattern with kappa to lambda ratio of 3:1, with CD138 being positive. Serum protein electrophoresis revealed polyclonality with levels of IgG as 2300 mg/dL, IgA as 762 mg/dL, IgM as 486 mg/dL, and IgE as 980 mg/dL. Bone marrow examination revealed a normocellular marrow with normal myeloid to erythroid ratio and plasma cells being 4% of marrow cellularity.

case_report: Patient information: A 33-year-old male presented with progressive swelling and pain in the lower abdomen for one month, predominantly on the left side. The patient had a history of an undescended left testis. Clinical assessment: A palpable mass was detected in the hypogastric region on the left side, which was slightly tender upon palpation. The left scrotal sac was empty, while the right testis and epididymis were normal. Imaging assessment: Ultrasound revealed a well-defined iso-hyperechoic solid mass measuring 75 x 67 x 66 mm in the hypogastric region on the left side, with multiple hypo-anechoic areas indicating necrosis. No calcification was observed within the mass. Color Doppler imaging showed minimal peripheral vascularity. Other abdominal organs appeared normal. Scrotal ultrasound did not visualize the left testis in the left scrotal sac, while the right testis and epididymis were normal. A CT scan identified a well-defined lobulated solid mass with soft tissue attenuation (HU +15 to +32) measuring 75 x 67 x 66 mm in the hypogastric region on the left side, located in the supra-vesical area. Post-contrast imaging showed heterogeneous enhancement with a non-enhancing necrotic area. The left testis was not visualized in the left scrotal sac, consistent with the history of an undescended testis. The right testis was normal, and no abdominal lymphadenopathy was observed.
test_results: On the gross cut specimen, the mass revealed a well-circumscribed nodular neoplasm. On microscopy, the nodules were comprised of sheets of polygonal cells with well-defined cell borders, large squares of nuclei, vesicular chromatin, prominent eosinophilic nucleoli, and a moderate amount of vacuolated cytoplasm. The nodules were separated by thin fibrous bands. The stroma showed interspersed perivascular aggregates of lymphocytes. On immunohistochemistry, tumor cells expressed SALL-4, OCT-4, and CD-117. Epididymis and vas deferens seen in the cut section were uninvolved by the tumor.

case_report: An 11-year-old male presented with moderate sensorineural hearing loss on the right side and mixed, profound hearing loss on the left side. There was no reported family history of hearing loss. Physical examination revealed a pre-auricular pit on the left side. The patient was using a conventional binaural behind-the-ear hearing aid.
test_results: He had bilateral inner ear malformations revealed by CT scan and left side congenital cholesteatoma. WES revealed a heterozygous de novo SIX1 pathogenic missense mutation (c.386A > C, p.(Tyr129Ser)). Follow-up was completed with renal ultrasonography, which was normal.

case_report: A 74-year-old Chinese Han male presented with a six-month history of widespread itching and a one-month history of blistering on the trunk. Prior to these symptoms, he was in good health as confirmed by annual physical exams. He had no chronic illnesses and was not on any regular medication. He had been treated with oral prednisone 50 mg for six days without improvement in the skin condition. Physical examination revealed numerous erosions and blisters on the trunk with a mosaic-like pattern, and the Nikolsky sign was negative. Blood count, liver function, and renal function tests conducted three days before the hospital visit were within normal limits.
test_results: Skin biopsy revealed a subepidermal blister with lymphocytes and eosinophils infiltrating into the superficial layer of the dermis. Perilesional skin direct immunofluorescence (DIF) revealed linear deposition of IgG, IgA, and C3 at the dermo-epidermal junction. Indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) studies on salt-split skin demonstrated deposits of IgG, IgA, and C3 autoantibodies on the dermal side of the dermo-epidermal separation.

case_report: A 46-year-old woman with a history of carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) and cervical intervertebral disc degeneration was referred for progressive left upper extremity weakness. The patient was 10 weeks post-carpal tunnel release on her left side, which did not alleviate her symptoms. She reported a 1.5-year history of left upper extremity weakness, impacting her ability to work as a hairstylist. There was no familial history of neurological disease. An EMG/NCS performed in October 2020 showed moderate-to-severe left CTS, mild right CTS, and mild cervical radiculopathy. Physical examination revealed bilateral hyperreflexia in upper and lower extremities (3+ biceps, brachioradialis, triceps, patellar, and Achilles), bilateral positive Hoffman sign, and bilateral upper and lower extremity weakness (deltoid 3/5 bilateral, biceps: Right 4/5, left 3/5, triceps: Right 4/5, left 3/5, wrist extensors: Left 4/5, wrist flexors: Left 4/5, hand intrinsic: Left 3/5, tibialis anterior: Right 4/5, left 4/5, extensor hallucis longus: Right 4/5, left 4/5). No sensation loss was noted. Cervical MRI showed degenerative disc disease at C5-6, C6-7, and a C6-7-disc herniation causing moderate bilateral foraminal stenosis, more pronounced on the left. The patient was referred to neurology for further evaluation.
test_results: Repeat EMG in May 2021 demonstrated widespread denervation in both upper extremities, more significant on the patient’s left side than her right. Repeat EMG, including lower extremities, was abnormal as well.

case_report: A 12-year-old boy presented with multiple, asymptomatic light-colored lesions over the flexor aspect of the upper extremities, chest, axilla, and forehead for 6 months. Some lesions resolved spontaneously, leaving behind postinflammatory hyperpigmentation. The patient reported no use of cosmetic products, no excessive sun exposure, and no mechanical trauma. There was no family history of similar lesions. Physical examination showed discrete, symmetrically distributed, 1–2 mm sized, dome-shaped, pale yellow follicular papules on the flexor aspect of both upper extremities, the axilla, chest, and a single lesion on the forehead. Oral, genital, and nail examinations were normal.
test_results: A skin punch biopsy from the papule showed a mid-dermal cyst, lined by thinly stretched epithelium and had a corrugated lining. Granular layer was absent. Abundant lamellated keratin and several vellus hair shafts were present within the cyst. On serial sections, there were no sebaceous glands noted adjacent to or within the cell wall.

case_report: The infant was admitted to the newborn intensive care unit at 6 days old for evaluation of a persistent metabolic condition. He was born after an uncomplicated full-term pregnancy to a healthy mother, with no consanguinity between the parents. Birth weight was 3100 g. The family has one healthy 4-year-old daughter. Initial physical examination at birth was normal, and the infant was breastfed. On the second day of life, he developed jaundice and rapid breathing. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed severe metabolic acidosis, and he was treated with intravenous sodium bicarbonate. Despite treatment, his condition did not improve, leading to his referral to our hospital. Upon admission, his vital signs were: temperature 37.4°C, heart rate 160/min, respiratory rate 34/min, and blood pressure 78/39 mmHg. He appeared lethargic, but the rest of the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests indicated severe metabolic acidosis without lactic acidosis or ketoacidosis. Blood ammonia was 106.0 μmol/L, and liver and renal function tests were normal. The patient had hemolytic anemia with increasing indirect hyperbilirubinemia, and his hemoglobin was 53 g/L. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) activity was normal. Blood metabolic screening and plasma amino acid chromatography showed elevated glutamic acid levels. Urine gas chromatography/mass spectrometry revealed significant excretion of 5-oxoproline. On the second day after admission (Day of Life #7), the infant developed difficulty breathing, cyanosis, and required mechanical ventilation. He underwent blood exchange due to hyperbilirubinemia and received packed red blood cell transfusions. The infant experienced several seizure episodes and was treated with intravenous sodium bicarbonate to manage his metabolic acidosis. He was eventually weaned from mechanical ventilation.
test_results: Sequencing of the GSS gene revealed one previously unreported mutation. There was a heterozygous duplication of G at nucleotide 738 of the exon 8, which results in a frame shift from serine at 247. The mutation of c.738dupG; p.S247fs was also detected in his asymptomatic father’s DNA sample. “Next-generation” DNA sequencing also showed a possible repetitive sequence in exon 3 of GSS gene. qRT-PCR results confirmed that the repetitive sequence in exon 3 of GSS gene (chr20:33530733-33530809) was inherited from his mother. These two novel heterozygous mutations were inherited from either parents.

case_report: A 45-day-old infant with female-appearing genitalia was admitted due to recurrent vomiting, poor feeding, and cholestasis. The infant, born to consanguineous parents, had a birth weight of 3300 grams. Symptoms began on the third day of life with recurrent vomiting and poor intake, resulting in poor weight gain. Parents reported intermittent clay-colored stools, which turned completely acholic a few days before admission. There was no similar presentation or family history of liver or endocrine issues. Physical examination revealed a length of 50 cm (<5th percentile), weight of 3000 g (<5th percentile), and head circumference of 36.5 cm (5–10th percentile). The infant had a weak pulse with a heart rate of approximately 130 beats per minute and a blood pressure of 50/40 mmHg at admission. The patient exhibited pallor, decreased subcutaneous fat, and appeared severely dehydrated with jaundiced sclerae and skin. External genitalia appeared normal female type. The patient was admitted to the PICU, and blood was drawn for necessary laboratory tests. Initial resuscitation included rehydration therapy and correction of blood glucose and electrolyte abnormalities. Broad-spectrum antibiotics were administered due to the patient's ill appearance. Sepsis workups, including blood and urine cultures, were performed, both of which later returned negative. Considering the cholestasis presentation, further investigations were conducted, including tyrosine level, serum and urine amino acid chromatography, urinary organic acid profile, and NH3 and lactate levels, all of which were within normal range. Serum alpha1 antitrypsin concentration was mildly increased. Markers for hepatitis and TORCH infections were negative. Laboratory tests showed serum sodium at 102 meq/lit and serum potassium at 9 meq/lit. Total bilirubin was 13.9 mg/dl, and direct bilirubin was 5.4 mg/dl. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 7. Thyroid function tests were normal, and serum glucose levels were lower than normal but without significant difference. Other laboratory findings are shown in the report. Buccal smear was negative for bar body.
test_results: Chromosome study showed 46XY pattern. Abdominal sonography showed both adrenals hypertrophic but otherwise normal. Pelvic sonography revealed the testicles in the inguinal canal, moreover, a uterus was not detected in pelvis.
Orpha_name: Congenital lipoid adrenal hyperplasia due to STAR deficency

case_report: A 10-year-old girl was admitted with a history of convulsion followed by unconsciousness since day one. She had been hospitalized six months prior for a similar episode, during which a lumbar puncture was performed. Although the cerebrospinal fluid analysis did not confirm tuberculous meningitis, antitubercular chemotherapy was initiated and continued, which the patient adhered to until the current admission. The patient was referred to dermatologists for evaluation of her unusual skin and hair color. On examination, the patient was deeply comatose with generalized hypotonia; there was no focal neurological deficit. Cutaneous examination revealed a diffuse bronze-tan of her photo-exposed body parts like face, neck, and extremities along with scattered freckles. Hair showed a silvery shine. Her parents were consanguineously married. According to them, the patient’s intelligence was normal and she was a fourth standard student. She and her six-year-old younger sister had this type of skin and hair color since early childhood, which was progressive and had not been observed in any other family member. The younger sibling did not suffer from any neurological abnormality till that age.
test_results: CT scan of the brain revealed diffuse cerebral edema. Few hairs were plucked from patient′s scalp and examined under microscope, which revealed irregular clumps of melanin along the hair shaft. A skin biopsy was done from the forearm; H and E stained histopathological section showed irregular-sized melanin granules dispersed along the basal layer of epidermis.

case_report: A 35-year-old man, in good general health, presented with erosive crusted plaques on his scalp 9 months following a hair transplant procedure for long-standing male-pattern hair loss. He experienced a mild burning sensation but no pain, itching, or foul odor, and had not used any medications like topical minoxidil prior to the appearance of the lesions. Despite treatment with both topical and systemic antibiotics, the lesions progressively enlarged. Upon referral, physical examination revealed a large ulcerative plaque with crusts on the parietal region of the scalp. The rest of the skin examination was normal, showing no signs of blistering disorders or psoriasis. There was no lymphadenopathy in the head and neck region. Bacterial and fungal cultures were negative. Routine blood tests were normal except for elevated inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein). Tests for autoantibodies (antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, thyroglobulin, and microsomal antibodies) were negative. Serum immunoglobulin levels, anti-desmoglein 1 and 3, and anti-BP180 antibodies were within normal ranges. Systemic examinations, including chest X-ray, abdominal sonogram, and computed tomography, showed no evidence of internal malignancy or infectious focus.
test_results: A Histopathological examination of a 3-mm punch biopsy showed a dense, mainly perifollicular, dermal infiltrate of neutrophils and lymphocytes. There was no evidence of malignancy or vasculitis. Direct Immunofluorescence findings were negative. Special staining for fungi was negative.
diagnosis: Erosive Pustular Dermatosis  of the scalp
Orpha_name: Erosive pustular dermatosis of the scalp

case_report: The first case involves a 5-year-old Japanese girl presenting with recurrent red plaques and scales located on the abdomen, buttock, labia, popliteal fossa, and foot. These skin lesions first appeared when she was 3 years old and are confined to the right side of her body. Her family history is unremarkable. Her father is 50 years old and her mother is 43 years old.
test_results: A skin biopsy from the patient revealed a dilapidated brick wall appearance of basal cells with suprabasal clefts and acantholytic cells.

case_report: A 23-year-old male with a history of multiple gunshot wounds to the abdomen, which necessitated a complete small bowel resection and chronic total parenteral nutrition (TPN) support via a Hickman catheter since age 17, presented in June 1996 with generalized swelling and low-grade fevers. Urine analysis showed 2+ blood without casts and a 24-hour urine collection indicated 2.0 grams of protein. Serum chemistry revealed a creatinine level of 1.9 mg/dL (estimated glomerular filtration rate of 50 mL/min/1.73 m2), blood urea nitrogen (BUN) of 37 mg/dL, and albumin of 2 gm/dL. Baseline creatinine levels were not available. Routine serology tests, including those for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), rapid plasma reagin (RPR), antinuclear antibody (ANA), and hepatitis B and C, were all negative. Complement studies showed a C3 level of 68 mg/dL (reference range 90–180 mg/dL), a C4 level of 19 mg/dL (reference range 16–47 mg/dL), and total complement levels (CH50) of less than 28 mg/dL (reference range 60–90 mg/dL). An echocardiogram revealed no vegetations. Blood cultures were positive for coagulase-negative staphylococcus. Kidney ultrasound showed the right kidney measuring 10.6 cm and the left kidney measuring 10.8 cm, with no structural abnormalities or evidence of obstruction.
test_results: Light microscopy revealed 15 glomeruli showing a lobular pattern with mesangial hypercellularity, a moderate number of capillary wall double contours, and leukocytes within capillary lumina. Three glomeruli had segmental crescents. There were interstitial inflammation and edema, associated with acute tubular cell injury. Immunofluorescence microscopy disclosed five glomeruli staining for IgM (3+), C3 (3+), and kappa (trace to 1+) and lambda (trace) light chains along capillary walls in a granular pattern and peripheral distribution. Mesangial regions were stained for IgM (1 to 2+), C1q (trace), C3 (1+), and kappa (trace) and lambda (trace) light chains in a granular pattern. Electron microscopy of three glomeruli revealed small subendothelial and few mesangial electron dense deposits. There were no tubuloreticular structures in the cytoplasm of any cells.

case_report: The patient is a 15-month-old boy admitted due to poor growth and appetite. He was born full-term at 40 weeks and 3 days, with a birth weight of 2.3 kg, head circumference of 31 cm, and body length of 50 cm. There was no history of neonatal asphyxia. He showed resistance to complementary foods. At 6 months, he underwent surgery for polydactylism. He experienced repeated eczema-like rashes and scattered bleeding points on his body. He did not have recurrent respiratory or digestive tract infections since birth. There was no family history of malignant tumors. His vaccination history includes completed doses of BCG, hepatitis B, polio, DPT, meningococcal polysaccharide (Group A), and measles vaccines. He had not received any vaccinations in the 5 months prior to admission. Physical examination revealed a weight of 7.4 kg (−3 SD), height of 72 cm (−2 SD), head circumference of 40.2 cm (−3 SD, microcephaly), six primary teeth, and normal facial features. Psychomotor development was normal. The liver and spleen were not enlarged. Blood tests showed low white blood cell count (2.41 × 10^9/L), neutrophil count (1.40 × 10^9/L), hemoglobin (87 g/L), and platelet count (7 × 10^9/L). Bone marrow smear indicated active hyperplasia, granulocyte hyperplasia with maturity disorder, decreased lymphocyte proportion, active erythrocyte proliferation, and active megakaryocyte proliferation with low platelet production. Immunoglobulin tests before gamma globulin infusion showed elevated IgG (18.7 g/L, normal range 4.7–12.3), with normal IgA and IgM. Two months later, IgG remained elevated (22.1 g/L), while IgG4 was normal (0.477 g/L, normal range 0.08-1.4). Lymphocyte immunophenotyping performed twice showed significantly reduced T lymphocytes, especially CD4+ T cells, after corticosteroid treatment. Serological tests for rubella virus, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasma, herpes simplex virus, human parvovirus B19, and Epstein-Barr virus revealed positive rubella virus antibody IgG and IgM, and CMV-IgG, with negative results for other viral antibodies. Ophthalmic fundus examination showed rubella virus retinal vasculitis in both eyes, with no lens opacity, clear optic disc, orange color, no bulge, C/D ratio of approximately 0.3, dark retina, scattered white punctate exudation foci, no hemorrhage, small and slightly tonic retinal artery, white sheath on some arteries, and positive 30-cm red globe test. Initial management included intravenous gamma globulin (1 g/kg, three doses), platelet transfusion (2 U), dexamethasone (0.2 mg/kg for 4 days), and oral prednisone acetate (0.2 mg/kg for 3 days, then 0.1 mg/kg for 1 week). Despite treatment, platelet count did not increase. Autoimmune-related antibody tests, including direct anti-human globulin test, were positive (4+). Platelet-specific and histocompatibility (HLA) antibodies were also positive. Thyroid-stimulating hormone level was high, with normal thyroxine.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing revealed two heterozygous variants of the LIG4 gene: c.833G > T (p.R278L) and c.1271_1275del (p.K424Rfs*20). Family verification results showed that these two variants were inherited from the mother and father respectively (both heterozygous).

case_report: A 47-year-old woman was admitted to the emergency unit on June 4, 2021. She reported receiving the first dose of the AZD1222, AstraZeneca vaccine for COVID-19, 18 days before admission. Twelve hours post-vaccination, she experienced chills, headache, retroocular pain, neck pain, tiredness, nausea, stomach pain, and shortness of breath. These symptoms initially improved with symptomatic medications but later worsened. She developed mild weakness in the lower limbs, which progressed over five days to the point where she could no longer stand. Upon admission, she was conscious with no cognitive deficits. Physical examination revealed motor weakness (grade 2 in the lower limbs and grade 3 in the upper limbs), hyporeflexia, bilateral Babinski's sign, mild hypoesthesia in the lower limbs without a notable sensory level, preserved coordination, and intact cranial nerve function. She also had urinary retention, necessitating bladder catheterization. Routine blood tests showed no hydroelectrolytic, metabolic, or systemic inflammatory abnormalities.
test_results: A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) study on neuroaxis showed extensive spinal cord demyelination. This lesion was hyperintense in T2 sequence and extended from the C6 cervical level to the medullary cone. It was mildly tumefactive with no gadolinium enhancement. Brain MRI was unremarkable regarding any inflammatory process. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed a pleocytosis of 205 cells/mm³ with predominance of lymphocytes (88%), and also eosinophils (7%), neutrophils (4%), and monocytes (1%). There were increased protein levels (56.7 mg/dL) and normal levels of glucose (56 mg/dL) and chlorine (125 mEq/L). Isoelectric focusing of CSF protein and serum showed identical oligoclonal IgG bands (OCB) in both (type 4 pattern).

case_report: A 15-year-old boy, born from the third pregnancy of unrelated, young, and healthy parents, presented as a hypotrophic infant with intrauterine growth retardation and asphyxia.
