At birth, he exhibited complex phenotypic dysmorphic features. The patient's phenotype includes multiple facial and skeletal abnormalities: midface retrusion, prominent forehead, frontal bossing, shallow orbits, downslanted palpebral fissures, narrow nasal bridge, large filtrum, micrognathia, small hands with short metacarpal bones and short distal phalanges of fingers resulting in brachydactyly, knee flexion contracture, pseudoarthrosis, calcaneovalgus deformity, thoracic scoliosis, lumbar hyperlordosis, coxa valga, skeletal dysplasia, pectus carinatum, generalized hypotonia, global developmental delay, cognitive impairment, complete lack of adipose tissue with resulting pseudohypertrophy of muscles, bilateral cataracts, and a progeroid facial appearance. Additionally, the patient has an extremely short stature, with a body weight of 15 kg and a height of 100 cm.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) scan of cranio-cervical junction revealed bifid arch of the atlas as a part of skeletal disorders. Additional preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a critical stenosis of cranio-cervical junction with concomitant myelopathy.

case_report: A 5-year-old male presented with a history of complex medical issues, including retinal dystrophy, acute-onset renal failure, and joint pain. He was born at term via induced vaginal delivery from a 38-year-old mother, with a birth weight of 3543 g and a length of 48 cm. The pregnancy was normal with no known teratogenic exposures. He is the fourth child of a non-consanguineous couple of northern European ancestry. Both parents and all older siblings (two males and one female) are reported healthy. The extended family history includes a paternal family history of type 1 diabetes, a paternal grandmother with alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, and a maternal cousin with hearing loss and retinitis pigmentosa of unknown etiology. The patient reached developmental milestones on time, with mild difficulties in visual tracking and speech articulation. At 3 years of age, he was referred to an ophthalmologist for nyctalopia, high myopia, and continued poor visual tracking.
test_results: Fundus exams and electroretinograms (ERG) revealed a rod-cone dystrophy in both eyes with mottling of the retinal pigmentary epithelium and dystrophy of the internal limiting membrane. The fundus photos show non-specific subretinal hypopigmentation consistent with early onset retinal degeneration typical of rod-cone dystrophies. The retinal vasculature appeared attenuated in both eyes. There was no relative afferent pupillary defect and no nystagmus. His high myopia was progressive. At 5 years of age, his refraction was −4.5 and −6.75 diopters in the right and left eyes, respectively. By the age of 8 years old, his best-corrected visual acuity was 20/50 OD and 20/50 OS with glasses and his refraction had increased to −10.25 +2.75 ×106 OD and −11.00 +1.50 ×61 OS. The ERG testing demonstrated reduced cone function under photopic conditions with reduced a-wave implicit time and amplitudes and slowed implicit times for the b-wave. Under scotopic testing, both a-waves and b-waves showed slower implicit time and diminished amplitudes. The a-wave was substantially delayed, and there were reduced incremental increases in a-wave and b-wave. A renal biopsy of the diseased kidney confirmed the cause of renal failure: histological analyses showed diffuse severe tubulointerstitial fibrosis with tubular atrophy and only focal non-atrophic tubules. Half of the 14 glomeruli examined were obsolescent. The remaining glomeruli appeared partially collapsed and some had segmental capsular adhesion and scarring. Non-obsolescent glomeruli had periglomerular fibrosis with an onion skin-like appearance, as evidenced by Masson’s trichrome staining. The tubulointerstitium contained a patchy infiltrate of lymphocytes, and eosinophils were present focally. Periodic acid-Schiff stain (PAS) showed that non-atrophic tubules had segmentally thick and thin tubular basement membranes and segmental duplication. Electron microscopy also showed tubular basement membranes that were focally thick or thin. Arteries were normal and arterioles had mild sclerosis. Except for some segmental entrapment, glomeruli were negative for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and C1q by direct immunofluorescence. An X-ray bone age study of the hand showed cone-shaped epiphyses of all phalanges with shortened metacarpals and otherwise normal bone age. The lower proximal phalanges were short with cup-shaped metaphyses, and the metatarsals were also short. Imaging of the knees was normal; however, radiographs of the lower extremities showed bilateral coxa vara, abnormal femoral metaphyses, and sclerotic changes along the metaphyseal side of the femoral growth plate. There was broadening of the femoral necks and mild bowing of the femoral diaphysis.

case_report: A 28-year-old woman from Porto Alegre presented with widespread skin pigmentary changes and photosensitivity since childhood, along with skin and mucous membrane fragility. No similar cases were reported in her family. Physical examination of the skin showed significant atrophy on the back of the hands and feet, with a few scattered erosions and resolving blisters. There was extensive dyschromia on the limbs and trunk, and a loss of dermatoglyphics on her fingers. Oral examination revealed erosive stomatitis. The patient also reported inflammation in the esophagus, vagina, and anus, which led to stricture formation and required surgical correction.
test_results: A skin biopsy showed disruption of dermal collagen bundles and a focal reduction in elastic fibers. Two heterozygous mutations were identified: the change c.328C>T results in the creation of a nonsense mutation, p.Arg110X and the insertion c.866insGG leads to a frameshift and a premature termination codon 7 amino acids downstream, p.Ala289GlufsX7.

case_report: A 30-year-old female presented for genetic counseling. At 19 years old, she began clinical evaluations for general pain and chronic fatigue. She exhibited generalized joint hypermobility with a Beighton score of 9/9 and recurrent joint dislocations, particularly in the shoulders, wrists, and knees. She reported a tendency to bruise easily and prolonged bleeding. She also experienced postural hypotension, but autonomic dysfunction was ruled out. She did not have blue sclera, dental abnormalities, or visual defects. An audiological examination indicated mild high-frequency hearing loss. At 26 years old, an MRI scan of the brain was performed due to recurrent headaches, which showed no pathological findings. An ultrasound of the neck vessels revealed kinking of the right carotid artery. A cardiac ultrasound identified mild valve insufficiency. At 24 years old, after laparoscopic removal of multiple ovarian cysts, she developed an enlarged hypertrophic scar at the laparoscope entry site. Her height was 160 cm (>25th percentile), and she had no signs of recent or old bone fractures. At 28 years old, a dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) scan showed early onset osteopenia with lumbar and femur neck Z scores of -2.1. Levels of calcium, phosphorus, parathyroid hormone, and alkaline phosphatase were normal, while 25-(OH)-vitamin D was low at 15.2 ng/mL (deficiency: <20 ng/mL). She was born via eutocic delivery, weighing 4,100 g and measuring 51 cm in length. Her psychomotor development was normal with no hypotonia or motor delay. She reported having joint hypermobility and flat feet since childhood.
test_results: The biochemical analysis of collagen revealed alterations in the production and secretion of type I collagen. On SDS-PAGE, in the patient fibroblasts both α1(I) and α2(I) chains in the medium fraction as well as in the cell layer presented as overmodified bands with a slower migration and a broader appearance compared to controls. Furthermore, the cell layer from the patient fibroblasts presented an additional broad α'1(I) band that migrates above the overmodified α1(I) band and appears to be intracellularly retained.

case_report: A 48-year-old woman has experienced bilateral occipital pain exclusively at night for the past four months. This pain wakes her at 11 pm after she falls asleep at 8 pm and occurs nightly. The pain is described as pressing and intense, lasting up to three hours, and is accompanied by nausea but not by photophobia, phonophobia, or autonomic symptoms. Treatment with meloxicam 7.5 mg and diclofenac 75 mg nightly was ineffective. She has no history of sleep apnea. Her past medical history includes hypertension managed with lisinopril 10 mg daily. On examination, her blood pressure is 113/75 mmHg, and her pulse is 83 beats per minute. She is 5 feet 4 inches tall, weighs 123 pounds, and has a body mass index (BMI) of 21.1. Neurological examination shows full ocular motion, symmetric-reactive pupils, and normal accommodation. Ophthalmological examination reveals no papilledema. Ptosis is absent. The rest of the cranial nerve and neurological examinations are normal. There is no occipital tenderness over the occipital groove, and neck extension or rotation does not provoke occipital pain along the course of the occipital nerve.
test_results: An MRI examination of the brain was normal, ruling out a structural lesion of the brain.

case_report: An 8-year-old boy was referred to the Pediatrics Neurologic Clinic in Mashhad, Iran, due to developmental delay and seizure episodes that began 6 years ago. He is the second child of healthy parents who are not related, with no family history of seizures or mental retardation. He was born at term via vaginal delivery with a normal APGAR score and birth weight. He had neonatal jaundice and underwent phototherapy. His parents noticed developmental delays when he was 2 years old. He was hospitalized for tonic-clonic seizures and was treated with valproate sodium. He achieved independent walking at 4 years old. At 6 years old, he was referred to the Children Neurology Department in Mashhad for hyperactivity and was treated with risperidone. Physical examination revealed mandibular prognathism, strabismus, and an unusual laughing facial expression. His head circumference was 51 cm. His gait was unsteady, but muscle tone, strength, and deep tendon reflexes were normal. Joint range of motion was also normal. He had a speech disability, could walk independently but could not run, had limited communicative abilities, and suffered from severe mental retardation. Laboratory findings were normal. Brain MRI and CBC tests were normal. Thyroid function tests indicated hypothyroidism, which has been managed with levothyroxine since he was 2 years old. Despite various pharmacologic treatments, seizure episodes have persisted since he was 2 years old.
test_results: Abnormal methylation pattern of the SRNP region (Maternal imprinting defects or deletion) was detected.

case_report: A 68-year-old female patient presented with lesions on the palms that had been present for 30 years. There was no reported history of trauma or local infection. Dermatological examination revealed two reddish plaques, each measuring approximately 5x5mm on the right palm and 5x10mm on the left palm. These lesions were circumscribed, nummular, and depressed, symmetrically located over the thenar regions. The soles were unaffected. The general clinical examination did not reveal any significant findings.
test_results: Direct mycological examination was performed with negative results. Histopathological aspects of skin biopsy showed a focus of sharp decrease in the stratum corneum thickness, mild acanthosis and no change in the basal layer.

case_report: A 13-month-old boy was brought to our hospital with severe heart failure and dilated cardiomyopathy (CMP), to assess the need for cardiac transplantation. He was born at full term with a birth weight of 3.0 kg. He has no siblings and no family history of CMP or sudden death. At 6 months old, he was admitted to another hospital due to lethargy, rapid breathing with respiratory distress, and a mild fever. Rhinovirus was detected from a nasopharyngeal swab. Chest radiography showed significant heart enlargement with pulmonary edema, and an echocardiogram revealed a dilated left ventricle (LV) (LV end-diastolic diameter of 38.6 mm) with a 30% ejection fraction (EF) and moderate mitral regurgitation (MR). The patient was treated with digoxin, furosemide, spironolactone, and captopril and was discharged after stabilization. At 13 months old, his body weight was 7.8 kg (< 3rd percentile) and height was 72.5 cm (< 3rd percentile). He could walk unaided and say 'mama' and 'papa'. Physical examination revealed a grade II/VI regurgitant systolic murmur at the apex. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 2740/µL with an absolute neutrophil count of 438/µL. Serum troponin I was 1.597 ng/mL (reference range: 0–0.3 ng/mL) and lactate was 3.8 mmol/L (reference range: 0.7–2.5 mmol/L). Serum electrolytes, glucose, liver function tests, creatine kinase (CK), and CK-MB levels were normal. The B-type natriuretic peptide level was 765 pg/mL. Urine organic acid analysis showed elevated levels of 3-methylglutaconic acid at 58.4 mmol/mol creatinine (reference range: 0–19 mmol/mol creatinine) and 3-methyglutaric acid at 7.5 mmol/mol creatinine (reference range: not detected). Chest X-ray revealed significant heart enlargement with pulmonary edema, and electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy. Echocardiography showed a dilated and hypertrophied spherical LV (LV end-diastolic diameter of 37.7 mm; z score: +4.6) with 23% EF, moderate MR, prominent endomyocardial trabeculations, LV non-compacted/compacted end-diastolic ratio of 2.3, color Doppler flow within the deep intertrabecular recesses, and no prominent papillary muscle, confirming the presence of dilated CMP with LV non-compaction.
test_results: Gene sequence analysis revealed a hemizygous in-frame deletion of 9 amino acids within exon 10 of the TAZ gene, c.725_751del (p.Pro242_Glu250del). The variant was not detected in the patient's mother, indicating that it was a de novo mutation.

case_report: A nineteen-year-old female presented with a primary concern of delayed onset of menstruation. She reported no abdominal pain, cyclic pain, abdominal mass, or vaginal discharge. Additionally, she did not experience any issues with urination, constipation, or have a history of surgical procedures. Her two younger sisters reported similar concerns. Physical examination indicated normal vital signs. Neck examination showed no presence of an Adam's apple. Chest examination revealed breast development at Tanner stage I and axillary hair at Tanner stage II. The abdominal examination was normal. External genital examination showed pubic hair development at Tanner stage III, a 2 cm mass on the anterior vulva resembling a phallus, and normal major and minor labia. The vaginal canal measured 1.5 cm in length. A rectal exam identified only vaginal structures upon palpation. Previous laboratory tests indicated reduced estradiol levels (26.35 pg/mL) and significantly elevated Follicle Stimulating Hormone (FSH) levels (28.94 IU/mL). Blood tests showed normal male testosterone levels (674.4 ng/dL), dihydrotestosterone (14 ng/dL), and a Testosterone/Dihydrotestosterone (T/DHT) ratio of 48.17.
test_results: Karyotype revealed 46 XY. Ultrasonography (USG) revealed testis at the right and left proximal inguinal canal, along with phallus at the anterior vulva. Uterus and adnexa were not present on abdominal USG. Pelvic Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) confirmed the structure of bilateral testes, corpus cavernosa, and bulbospongiosus muscle. Uterus and adnexa were not found on MRI.
Orpha_name: 46,XY difference of sex development due to 5-alpha-reductase 2 deficiency

case_report: A 12-year-old male, born to nonconsanguineous parents, presented with a history of delayed cry and normal motor development but never learned to run. From the age of 6 years, he experienced pain and stiffness in both legs while walking fast, particularly in the calf and thigh regions, which improved with rest. He did not experience buckling or cramps. He also had difficulty climbing stairs due to stiffness and difficulty shifting the pelvis. He reported difficulty opening his jaw since childhood. Over time, he developed a flexed posture of both elbows, became slowly stooped, and noticed a prominent chin. His cognitive functions are normal. Examination revealed a short-statured boy (height: 145 cm, arm span: 148 cm, upper segment: 70 cm, lower segment: 75 cm). His palpebral fissure was narrow at rest (6 mm gap between upper and lower eyelids) and became narrower when attempting to close and open. The patient showed no fatigability. He had bushy eyelashes, a flat forehead, a receding chin, a pursed mouth, a high arched palate, and a pinched upturned nose. There was a visible spasm in the facial muscles, malocclusion, a short neck with neck extensor contractures, mild kyphosis in the thoracolumbar region, bilateral flat feet, and hallux valgus. His gait showed externally rotated ankles causing a wide base pelvis with en bloc movement and a left hip tilt. His calf muscles were prominent, and there was transient percussion myotonia in the left thenar muscles. Tone, power, reflexes, and sensations were normal in all groups. Routine blood chemistry, thyroid function tests, liver and renal function tests, serum lactate, and ammonia levels were within normal ranges. His creatine kinase was 294 units. Cardiac evaluation was normal. Tandem mass spectroscopy for metabolic diseases was normal. X-ray of the pelvis and hip was normal. Nerve conduction studies, both motor and sensory, were normal.
test_results: Needle electromyography was done at 2 sites, right biceps and right quadriceps. The insertional activity and spontaneous activity were abundant and persistent. This consisted of discharges with variation in amplitude and frequency. Mild needle displacement produced bursts of activity which was associated with dive-bomber sound. When the needle was kept still, the spontaneous discharges continued. Motor unit potential could not be measured properly. There were complex repetitive discharges with uniform morphology. The baseline never became silent. Muscle biopsy was done from the left biceps. Paraffin and cryosections showed skeletal muscle tissue with preserved fascicular architecture. The fibers were polygonal with few atrophic and angulated fibers. Focal grouped nuclei and regenerating fibers were seen. Modified Gomori's trichrome stain did not reveal any abnormality. Succinyl dehydrogenase, nicotinamide adenine dehydrogenase, ATPase at pH 9.4 and 4.6 showed type 1 and type 2 grouping. These features were suggestive of denervation with re-innervation.

case_report: A two-year-old boy was referred to our department due to a distal diaphyseal fracture of the left femur. He is the first child of non-consanguineous parents. At birth, his weight, length, and occipital-frontal circumference were around the 25th percentile. His mother, a 26-year-old primagravida, had no history of spontaneous abortions, stillbirths, or neonatal mortalities and was married to a 27-year-old unrelated man. At birth, the child had plagiocephaly and was treated with a cranial band (Care band), which he wore for 23 hours per day until he was one year old. No skull radiographs were taken at that time. His development included motor delay, but other developmental skills were within the normal range. There was no history of visual, auditory, or other neurological symptoms, nor was there any history of anorexia, weight loss, or muscular hypotonia. Examination at the age of two years showed a pleasant boy with mild and unnoticeable facial features, including frontal bossing and slight facial asymmetry with incomplete auricular folding. There were no signs of leontiasis ossea, Cushingoid facies, macrocephaly, retarded growth, or muscular hypotonia. Neurological, ophthalmological, and auditory evaluations were normal, with no history of seizures or non-motor developmental delay. Audiometric evaluation ruled out peripheral hearing loss. Ophthalmological examination showed normal vision with no strabismus or other eye issues. Musculo-skeletal examination revealed relative ligamentous hyperlaxity with patellar instability and thoraco-lumbar scoliosis of 32 degrees.
test_results: A lateral skull radiograph showed marked cranial osteosclerosis and hyperostosis; the facial bones and base of the skull were severely hyperostosed. An anteroposterior skull radiograph showed facial bone hyperostosis. An anteroposterior radiograph of the thorax showed thick, broad and sclerosed ribs; the medial two-thirds of the clavicles were hyperostosed; thoraco-lumbar scoliosis of 32 degrees was present secondary to hemivertebrae along T8-10, and only 11 ribs were present. Anteroposterior radiographs of the pelvis and the femora revealed diaphyseal hyperostosis associated with distal diaphyseal fracture of the left femur and a stress/fatigue fracture of the mid-diaphysis of the right femur. An anteroposterior hand radiograph showed diaphyseal widening associated with hyperostosis and dysplastic terminal phalanges (increased cortex of the tubular bones). Axial reformatted CT scans revealed bilateral narrowing of the optic canal.

case_report: A 45-year-old female was referred to the Combined Care in Systemic Sclerosis (CCISS) programme at Leiden University Medical Center (LUMC) for a second opinion due to severe dyspnea. She had a history of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (SSc) diagnosed in 2017, characterized by Raynaud’s phenomenon, skin thickening on the fingers and face, abnormal nailfold videocapillaroscopy with dilatations and hemorrhages, and the presence of anticentromere antibodies. The patient reported rapidly worsening dyspnea and decreased exercise tolerance over the past 8 months, despite being on mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) for 4 months. MMF was initiated by her rheumatologist for skin involvement and progressive dyspnea. Her medications also included hydrochlorothiazide, enalapril for hypertension, and nifedipine for Raynaud’s phenomenon. Clinical examination revealed shortness of breath with minimal exertion, pitting scars, a modified Rodnan Skin Score (mRSS) of 3/51, calcinosis, and telangiectasia on her fingers. Pulmonary auscultation was normal, and peripheral edema was noted around the ankles. Oxygen saturation in ambient air at rest was 97%. She exhibited sinus tachycardia at rest (116/min) with a normal blood pressure (110/79 mmHg). Electrocardiography confirmed sinus tachycardia without arrhythmias or conduction abnormalities. The six-minute walk test (6-MWT) showed a maximal walking distance of 123 meters, with an initial SpO2 of 97% and heart rate of 115/min; SpO2 dropped to 82% after 1 minute of walking, restored to 100% with oxygen supplementation at rest, but dropped again to 84% upon resumption, leading to test termination. Laboratory tests including erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) (29 mm/h), N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) (32.0 ng/L), creatine kinase (CK) (58 U/L), and troponin T (4 ng/L) were within normal ranges. Pulmonary function tests showed normal spirometry but a decreased diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO; 38% of predicted). Transthoracic echocardiography indicated no diastolic dysfunction, a maximum tricuspid incompetence (TI) gradient of 19 mmHg, and a decreased left ventricular ejection fraction (45%) with diffuse hypokinesia. No direct or indirect signs of pulmonary hypertension were observed. Previous high-resolution chest tomography (HRCT) did not show interstitial lung disease (ILD). A repeated HRCT in our clinic revealed centrilobular ground glass opacifications (partially confluent), some septal lines, and enlarged mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes. Computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the thorax excluded pulmonary embolisms but showed pulmonary artery dilatation, lymphadenopathy, mild dilatation of the right ventricle and right atrium, and some septal flattening. A ventilation/perfusion scan did not reveal any perfusion or ventilation defects. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing showed a VO2max of 56% of predicted and an increase in AaDO2 from 5.5 kPa at rest to 9.9 kPa during exercise. Contrast echocardiography was normal, excluding cardiac-level shunting as a cause of hypoxemia on minimal exertion. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was not performed due to the patient's morbid obesity (BMI = 43).
test_results: This revealed a pulmonary artery pressure (PAP) of 56/27 mmHg with a mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) of 39 mmHg, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) was 13 mmHg, cardiac output (CO) 8 L/min, cardiac index value 3.3 L/min/m2, right atrial pressure (RAP) 10 mmHg and PVR was 3.3 Wood Units.

case_report: A 13-month-old male infant was admitted with a history of acute gastroenteritis and significant delays in gross motor and speech development. He is the first child of healthy, unrelated Sinhalese parents, with the mother being 23 years old and the father 21 years old. At 9 months, the mother observed abnormal movements of the head and upper limbs, described as generalized extensor spasms. These events, which occurred in clusters and were associated with sleep deprivation, began at that age. The spasms, lasting 1 to 2 seconds each and recurring in clusters of 10 to 20 events over 3 to 5 minutes, evolved by 14 months into flexor-type spasms. The child subsequently experienced generalized tonic-clonic convulsions, often triggered by low-grade fever, resulting in multiple hospital admissions. The source of the recurrent fever was not identified. Seizures were initially unresponsive to valproic acid (30mg/kg/day) alone for one month and in combination with carbamazepine (5mg/kg/day) for two weeks. However, a combination of valproic acid and clonazepam (0.5mg/kg/day), after discontinuing carbamazepine, effectively controlled the seizures, and the child remained seizure-free for four months. No early side effects of the medications were observed during follow-up. Physical examination revealed marked hypotonia, deep-set eyes, a wide mouth with a protruding tongue, and a pointed nose. The child has fair skin with a hypopigmented patch on the left anterior thigh. He characteristically holds his hands up and exhibits uncoordinated, jerky arm movements. He tends to sit with a rounded back, suggesting scoliosis, and has episodes of inappropriate laughter. His teeth had not erupted, and he showed significant developmental delays across all areas. At 13 months, his developmental milestones were comparable to those of a 7 to 8-month-old child. Monosyllabic babbling began at 12 months.
test_results: Microdeletion testing by multiplex ligation probe amplification (MLPA) showed the presence of a deletion involving all the probes for the 15q11.2 region.

case_report: A 13-year-old female presented with reddish, raised, asymptomatic lesions on both hands and feet for the past five months. Initially, these lentil-sized lesions appeared on the right index finger and gradually increased in size and number, eventually forming larger plaques. Similar lesions subsequently appeared on other fingers and the soles. There was no personal or family history of oral ulcers, joint pains, photosensitivity, frothy urine, or systemic complaints such as chest pain, abdominal pain, or breathlessness. Physical examination revealed multiple erythematous and edematous papular lesions on the hands and feet. These lesions were discoid, erythematous, scaly, and atrophic, forming papules to plaques on the ventral and lateral aspects of the fingers and feet. Lesions on the palms and soles were tender to touch. The dorsal aspect of the hands had multiple hyperpigmented macules indicative of postinflammatory hyperpigmentation. Bilateral concha exhibited violaceous discoid plaques measuring 1 × 1 cm. The nails on both hands showed ragged cuticles. There was no significant lymphadenopathy, and all mucosae were normal. Hematological investigations were normal except for anemia (Hb-10.9g/dL) and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (30 mm in the first hour). Biochemical tests for hepatic and renal functions, serum proteins, urine examination, and chest radiograph were normal. VDRL was non-reactive, and rheumatoid factor was negative.
test_results: Anti-nuclear antibody test was positive with a speckled pattern of immunofluorescence, and the titer being 1:160. These antibodies were identified as anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, anti-Ro52, anti-histone and anti-nucleosomal antibodies. Histopathology from the lesion over the finger showed focal basal cell vacuolization of the epidermis and moderate perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate in the dermis. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) of lesional skin showed IgM and C3 deposition along the basement membrane zone.

case_report: A 70-year-old woman experienced recurrent episodes of painful bruising on her back, abdomen, and all four extremities over a period of 5 years. She reported that these bruises appeared after scratching her skin to alleviate itching. She had a 5-year history of chronic neurodermatitis, which did not include any bleeding symptoms such as melena, hematuria, or menorrhagia. The neurodermatitis typically recurred every 4-6 months with severe itching at the affected sites, with the most recent episode occurring approximately 3 months prior. Itching symptoms were alleviated by oral antihistamines or corticosteroids, but the bruising remained unchanged. During physical examination, scattered bruises of varying sizes were observed. These lesions were tender but showed no signs of bleeding, ulceration, or scarring. Noticeable excoriation was present, particularly on the trunk. Laboratory tests indicated normal complete blood cell count, platelet count, and coagulation panels. No autoimmune abnormalities were detected that could account for the lesions. Skin punch biopsies of the lesions showed minimal superficial perivenular lymphocytic infiltration.
test_results: The patient developed a painful ecchymotic reaction on the washed red blood cell (RBC) and whole blood injection site, while no reaction was observed on the plasma and normal saline injection site.

case_report: A 25-year-old male of Hispanic and Caucasian descent with no significant past medical history arrived at our emergency department from another facility due to sudden paralysis beginning in both lower limbs. He mentioned having received an intraarticular corticosteroid injection in his right knee less than 24 hours before his symptoms began. He also consumed a high carbohydrate meal within five hours before the onset of symptoms. The weakness in his lower limbs spread to his trunk and both upper limbs. By the time of our evaluation, the patient had no symptoms following intravenous correction of low potassium levels at the other facility. At that facility, his vital signs were normal. Physical examination revealed paralysis in his limbs, but his sensation remained intact.
test_results: Initial labs were remarkable for severe hypokalemia of 1.9 mmol/L (rr 3.6-5.2) and TSH less than 0.01 (rr 0.42-5.47). Pertinent lab values during his hospital admission include elevated free thyroxine (T4) level at 3.73 ng/dL (rr 0.59-1.17), elevated TSH binding inhibitory immunoglobulin 8.60 IU/L (rr 0.00-1.75), glycated hemoglobin 5.6 (rr 4.5-6.2), urine glucose 1,000 mg/dL, urine ketones 5 mg/dL, and urine blood 2+. Imaging reported junctional rhythm with 48 ventricular rates on EKG, no radiographic evidence of acute cardiopulmonary process on Chest X-ray one-view, and no evidence of acute intracranial abnormality or hemorrhage on computed tomography (CT) head without contrast. A thyroid ultrasound showed heterogeneous vascular thyroid with no discrete mass or lesion.

case_report: A 35-year-old female presented with skin eruptions on the body for the past 12–13 years, accompanied by malodor from the affected areas for the past 5–6 years. She had been using herbal medication intermittently without improvement. The eruptions were preceded by severe itching. There was no change in the condition during pregnancy. The rash became itchy and infected during summer. There were no associated systemic complaints. The condition is progressive. Her parents and first-degree cousins were unaffected. Her 12-year-old daughter had similar lesions, but her parents and siblings were not affected. The daughter did not accompany her mother to the outpatient department. The patient exhibited greyish warty plaques on the forehead, anterior scalp, post- and pre-auricular areas, external ear, neck, nasolabial fold, dorsal surface of the hands, legs, and soles. The nails showed V-shaped scalloping at the free margins with longitudinal ridges parallel to the long axis, and the distal ends were broken. Significant subungual keratosis was noted on the right hand. Crusted coalescing plaques were present on the dorsal surface of the hands and legs. Hyperkeratotic areas with malodor were observed on the plantar surfaces, with similar nail changes in the toes. The oral mucosa appeared normal. The anterior scalp had discrete papules with a rough and spiny surface. Oral examination revealed caries, gingivitis, and poor oral hygiene, with no changes related to the skin condition. No lesions were observed on other parts of the body. Blood counts, sugar, urea, creatinine, and electrolytes were all within normal ranges.
test_results: Microscopic examination of the lesions shows hyperkeratosis along with central keratin plug. At places, the overlying epithelium shows acantholysis that results in formation of a suprabasilar cleft. In addition, the epithelial rete ridges associated with the lesions appear narrow and elongated. Examination of epithelium under higher magnification reveals varying numbers of dyskeratotic cells referred as corps ronds (round bodies) or grains. The underlying connective tissue is fibrocellular, composed of collagen fibers, fibroblasts, blood vessels and mild chronic inflammatory cell infiltrate.

case_report: An 8-year-old male from Cameroon presented at the Grace Community Health and Development Association outreach unit with progressive muscle contractures and weakness in the lower limbs, upper limbs, and trunk muscles over a period of 4 months. Initially, the weakness and contractures began in the lower limbs and within a month extended to the upper limbs and trunk muscles. This was characterized by flexural deformity of the elbow and ankle. The patient progressively experienced difficulty in walking or standing without support, poor head and waist control, and difficulty swallowing. There were no seizures, cognitive impairment, visual or auditory impairment, and no bladder or bowel dysfunction. A district hospital initially considered poliomyelitis, but stool samples tested negative for polio. His birth history was uneventful, with standing without support at 7 months and walking at 12 months. Other developmental milestones were normal, and he had normal motor and mental functions before the onset of symptoms. There was no history of measles, HIV, trauma, or hospitalization. He was fully vaccinated according to national guidelines. There was no family history of paralytic disease or mental impairment. Both parents are alive and well. On physical examination, the patient was conscious, afebrile, with no facial dimorphic features. Pupillary size and reflexes were normal. There was no ptosis or facial weakness. There was wasting of the upper limb, scapular, and spinal muscles, and contractures of the elbows and ankles. There was no calf hypertrophy or pseudohypertrophy. Muscle power was 4/5 in both upper and lower limbs. There was weakness in the cervical, lumbar, and pelvic muscles, evident by poor head control and swaying movements of the waist. Hypertonia was noted in the muscles of the arm and calf, with the upper limbs in a semi-flexed position. Sensitivity to touch, pain, temperature, vibration, and proprioception were preserved. Tendon and cutaneous reflexes were normal. He was unable to stand or walk without support. Gowers sign was absent. Cardiorespiratory examination revealed an irregularly irregular tachycardia with a heart rate of 122 beats per minute. There was no palpable abdominal mass or hepatosplenomegaly. The rest of the physical examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory investigations showed a serum creatine kinase (CK) level of 350 IU/l, hemoglobin count of 13 g/dl, white blood cell count of 8700 cells/µl, and a normal metabolic profile.
test_results: Hemoxylin–eosin stain muscle biopsy analysis revealed non-specific variation of muscle fibres diameter. Atrial tachycardia was evident on electrocardiography (ECG).

case_report: This 17-year-old boy is the first child of cousin parents once removed. The second and third children, a boy and girl, died at 1 year and 5 days of age, respectively, of unrelated causes. He was admitted for the evaluation of his muscular weakness. Pregnancy, delivery at term, and neonatal adaptation were uneventful; his weight was 3,000 grams but length and head circumference were not recorded. He developed hyperbilirubinemia during the first week after birth which required blood transfusion. Severe hypotonia was noticed since birth and kyphoscoliosis developed during the first months of life. Due to muscular weakness, he had to be bottle-fed with a large-holed teat. Gross motor development milestones were delayed. He could stand without support at 2 years and started to walk at 2.5 years. He also had speech delay and could say his first words at the age of 20 months. He went to school for 5 years but did not continue because of his motor disabilities. Although intelligence has not been formally evaluated, based on his relative good performance at school, there is no indication of mental retardation. He had a history of rupture of the ocular globe at age 15 years after his father's elbow accidentally hit his face, and of multiple dislocations of both wrists and ankles. On physical examination at the age of 17, his height, weight, and head circumference were 165 cm, 70 kg, and 55 cm, respectively. He had down-slanting palpebral fissures, microcornea (9 mm in diameter), ptosis, prosthetic left eye, and slightly bluish sclera. The skin was soft, with multiple scars on knees due to poor healing, and with hyperkeratosis follicularis. He also had hypermobile joints; however, hyperelasticity of the skin was not prominent. Generalized hypotonia was noted and muscle strength was decreased. Muscle force was estimated to be 3–4 (active movement against gravity and some movement against resistance); however, reflexes and muscle bulk were normal. Skeletal survey revealed osteopenia, kyphoscoliosis, and platyspondyly of L3 as well as distraction of the symphysis pubis and protrusio acetabuli, and downward slanting and thinning of the ribs. Bone mineral density (Norland XR-36) was normal in spine (0.991 mg/cm2) and hip (0.991 mg/cm2) but decreased in the femur (0.810 mg/cm2 which is 1.2 SD below the age-matched reference). Creatine phosphokinase, electromyogram, and nerve conduction velocity were normal. Urine samples from the patient and parents were analyzed for urinary pyridinolines. The ratio of urinary total pyridinolines, lysyl pyridinoline to hydroxylysyl pyridinoline, in the patient was 7.1 and slightly increased (0.25 and 0.23) in the father and the mother, respectively. Electrophoretic mobility of the α- and β-collagen chains of the various collagen types produced by cultured fibroblasts was faster than normal, indicating that the lysyl residues were not hydroxylated and that there were no galactosyl and glucosyl-galactosyl residues attached.
test_results: Mutation analysis on DNA of the patient showed a novel homozygous non-sense mutation in exon 12 of the PLOD1 gene at position 1302 of the cDNA sequence (c.1302 C>G) which leads to a premature stop at amino acid position 434 (p.Y434X). The parents were both heterozygous for the same mutation.

case_report: A three-year-old boy exhibited progressive hair loss on the scalp, eyebrows, and eyelashes starting at six months of age, along with significantly reduced growth. The child's prenatal history was unremarkable, and he was born to parents who are third-degree relatives. Physical examination revealed an aged appearance with prominent eyes, sparse hair with alopecia patches, and visible scalp veins. He had a beaked nose and a receded chin. His voice was high-pitched, and his growth measurements were below the third percentile. Dental and genital examinations were normal, and his intelligence was appropriate for his age. His hands were short and clawed, with thickened and hardened skin over the knuckles and racquet-shaped nails. The ribs were prominent, and the anterior fontanelle remained open. There was mottled pigmentation and sclerodermatous changes on the trunk and lower limbs, with the knees being prominent and a slight valgus deformity in the lower limbs. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits, but the serum lipid profile indicated a decrease in high-density lipoproteins (HDL).
test_results: X-ray of the chest showed a pyriform thorax, overcrowding of proximal ribs, and short clavicle with pointed lateral ends. X-ray of the skull showed diastasis of the sutures and prognathism. X-rays of hands and feet showed acro-osteolysis of phalanges and tarsals.

case_report: A 35-year-old female patient visited the medical outpatient department with a 6-month history of palpitations and chest pain. The palpitations were paroxysmal, lasted a few minutes, resolved on their own, and were not triggered by exertion or other factors. The chest pain was retro-sternal, intermittent, not related to exertion, and also resolved spontaneously. The frequency of these complaints increased three weeks before the visit. There was no significant past medical history. She was born from a non-consanguineous marriage and has an elder brother. There was no significant family medical history. She never attained menarche. Physical examination revealed dolicocephaly, arachnodactyly, a high arched palate, tall stature (Height 165 cm), an arm span (176 cm) greater than her height, a reduced upper to lower body segment ratio (0.83), and positive wrist and thumb signs. She had underdeveloped rudimentary breasts (Tanner stage 2), sparse pubic hair (Tanner stage 1), and absent axillary hair. Her external genitalia were normal. Vital signs were normal. Cardiovascular examination showed a mid-systolic click with a late systolic murmur; other systems were essentially normal. Blood tests revealed a normal hemogram, normal blood glucose, renal function tests, liver function tests, and serum electrolytes. An ultrasonogram of the abdomen and pelvis showed an atrophic uterus and streak ovaries. Echocardiogram (ECHO/Doppler) indicated prolapse of the anterior mitral leaflet, mitral regurgitation, and normal left ventricular systolic function. Further evaluation for primary amenorrhea showed low levels of estrogen (Estradiol-10 pg/mL; normal 15-200 pg/mL), serum testosterone (0.16 pg/mL, normal 0.6-6.8 pg/mL), and progesterone (0.56 ng/mL). Elevated levels of gonadotropins were noted, with follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) at 101.3 IU/L and luteinizing hormone (LH) at 31.6 IU/L. Serum prolactin (12 ng/mL, normal 0-20 ng/mL) and thyroid function tests (Free T4-9.2 mcg/dL, normal 4.6 to 11.2 mcg/dL; TSH-3.49 mU/L, normal 0.4-5.0 mU/L) were normal. Karyotype analysis showed 46 XX.
test_results: Audiometric evidence of mild bilateral sensorineural deafness.

case_report: A 59-year-old female arrived at the emergency department in February 2021 with altered mental status and blurred vision. Her medical history included aortic valve replacement and ascending aortic aneurysm repair in 2017, which was complicated by a periaortic abscess. In January 2021, she had another aortic valve replacement and ascending aortic aneurysm repair, during which amikacin beads were placed around the new graft. She was on a treatment regimen of azithromycin, ethambutol, rifampin, and amikacin. Upon initial examination, a dilated fundus exam revealed numerous yellow placoid circular lesions scattered throughout the macula and peripheral retina in both eyes, accompanied by vitritis. A brain MRI showed no acute infectious lesions. Her infectious workup was largely unremarkable except for a positive toxoplasma IgM, leading to the addition of sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim to her treatment regimen. She was subsequently discharged to a skilled nursing facility.
test_results: Head computed tomography (CT) showed new numerous scattered round foci of hyperdensity throughout the cerebrum and brainstem. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) macula showed parafoveal cystoid macular edema (CME) bilaterally.

case_report: A 14-year-old male, the first child of healthy non-consanguineous Chinese parents, exhibited significant short stature (< -4.1 SD). His gross and fine motor skills were within normal limits, and his bone age was determined to be 12 years. On the language scale, his overall performance was 80, which is below the average range (86%). His expressive language skills were normal, but his receptive language skills were impaired, with scaled scores of 10 and 5, respectively. Additionally, he experienced sleep disturbances, including insomnia, difficulty falling asleep, abnormal sleep duration, excessive daytime sleepiness, and disrupted circadian rhythms.
test_results: An IGF-1 level of 113 ng/ml (reference range 49–283), an IGF-BP3 level of 2.89 μg/ml (reference range 1.0–4.7), and a peak GH level of 12.65 ng/ml, ruling out the GH deficiency.
Orpha_name: Kleefstra syndrome due to a point mutation

case_report: A 12-year-old girl presented with a sudden onset of recurrent intrusive thoughts over the past month, compelling her to repeat or stop certain behaviors to prevent perceived dangers, such as self-harm or running into the street. She ceased eating, necessitating frequent emergency room visits for intravenous fluid administration. She engaged in repetitive dressing and undressing for approximately one hour, repeated hand washing for about one hour, crossed her hands, scratched the wall, and exhibited crying episodes with fears of self-harm or running into the street. She lives with her mother, and her father passed away two years ago due to a medical illness. There is no family history of mental illness. She was performing well in school but had frequent absences in the month prior to presentation. Her pregnancy, birth, and early development were unremarkable. During the initial visit, the family denied any prior medical illnesses. She was treated with SSRIs and cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). Due to the acute onset and severity of her symptoms, she was reevaluated in follow-up. She reported recurrent tonsillitis in the year before presentation, with the last infection occurring just before the onset of her symptoms. Her tonsillitis was severe enough that a tonsillectomy was recommended six months prior. The intrusive thoughts were accompanied by separation anxiety, forgetfulness, and abnormal sensations (tingling) in her palms and feet, leading her to repeatedly wear her shoes. Additional symptoms included anxiety and sensory abnormalities.
test_results: Lab results showed ASO = around 1,200 (normal < 200). Throat culture results came out, which showed mixed normal flora.
diagnosis: Pediatric Autoimmune Neuropsychiatric Disorders Associated with Streptococcal Infections

case_report: A 46-year-old female patient presented with abdominal distention and constipation for approximately six months. Clinical examination showed abdominal distention and ascites. Lower abdominal MR imaging revealed the left ovary measured 5.5 cm x 3.5 cm, with solid areas containing central cystic parts and peripheral contrast enhancement. An intraabdominal omental cake appearance was noted. Upper and lower GI endoscopies showed no pathological lesions. PET-CT imaging indicated increased FDG uptake at the left adnexal site (SUVmax: 15.4) and in the abdominopelvic regions, consistent with peritonitis carcinomatosis. Laboratory results showed serum LDH level at 404 U/L (normal < 250 U/L), serum albumin at 3.9 g/dl (normal 3.5-5 g/dl), and serum CA-125 at 1375.2 U/ml (normal < 35 U/ml). Levels of CA 19-9, CA 15-3, carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) were within normal limits. During a diagnostic laparoscopy, approximately 3 L of ascites and peritonitis carcinomatosis were observed. The left ovary measured approximately 6 cm x 4 cm, while the right ovary appeared normal. A wedge biopsy of the left ovary, along with omental and peritoneal biopsies, was performed. Ascitic fluid was collected for cytological examination, which was positive for malignancy. The ovarian, omental, and peritoneal tissues were reported as entirely tumoral. Tumoral infiltration consisted of uniform, medium-sized, round lymphocytic cells with round nuclei, rough chromatin structure, multiple nucleoli, narrow cytoplasm, and frequent mitosis.
test_results: The conducted histochemical studies revealed staining of the tumor cells with LCA, CD20, CD10, CD79a, Vimentin, Bcl6 (poor focally), MUM1 (poor focally), and CD43 (poor focally). Ki-67 index was determined to be 95%. The pathological diagnosis was reported as a high-grade non-Hodgkin’s B-cell lymphoma.

case_report: A three-year-old Japanese boy with a history of nephrotic syndrome (NS) was brought to the hospital due to difficulty walking since the morning. He had been on oral prednisolone (PDN) treatment for a year without achieving complete remission. The total PDN intake was 3480 mg, equivalent to 230 mg/kg of body weight, with a maximum daily dose of 30 mg (2 mg/kg of body weight). The consideration to start immunosuppressants was discussed, but the family opted to continue treatment at the community hospital due to distance constraints. On the day of presentation, the boy was reluctant to have his left upper thigh touched and had been crying incessantly. There was no relevant family history, and his birth and developmental history were normal. He had no recent infections, trauma, or surgeries, and his vaccinations were up to date. Upon arrival, his vital signs were stable, and he had no fever. His height and weight were within normal limits. Physical examination showed no redness or swelling of the left upper thigh, but he refused to stand or walk. There was no evident pain on palpation of the left thigh and hip joint, but he avoided bending his left hip joint. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count and basic metabolic panel, were unremarkable. Total protein and albumin levels were normal. Urine analysis showed elevated protein levels at 200 mg/dL (normally negative) without hematuria or bacteriuria, and the urine protein/creatinine ratio was 0.73 g/gCre (normally ≤0.15 g/gCre, ≥2.0 g/gCre in NS). These results indicated that NS was not recurrent but had not achieved complete remission. C-reactive protein levels were within normal limits.
test_results: A pelvic X-ray scan showed asymmetrical femoral heads and thinning of the left femoral head. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging revealed low intensity in the left femoral head on the T2-weighted image and high and low mixed intensities in the left femoral head on the fat-suppressed T2-weighted image. Deformation of the left femoral head was suspected, and a small amount of synovial fluid was present. The epiphysial nucleus of the right femoral head was also small for his age.

case_report: A 12-month-old Japanese boy, the second child in his family with a healthy older sister, had normal growth and development. Newborn screenings using tandem mass spectrometry showed no abnormalities. He experienced a fever, upper respiratory symptoms, and reduced oral intake. After 7 days of fever, he was admitted to the hospital due to rapid breathing and cyanosis. A rapid test detected Influenza A. Laboratory results showed mild hyperammonemia (173 μg/dL), elevated aspartate aminotransferase (AST; 461 IU/L) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT; 142 IU/L) levels, and severe metabolic acidosis (pH 6.985, pCO2 13.8 mmHg, HCO3 3.2 mmol/L, BE −26.5 mmol/L; and anion gap, 30.5 mmol/L). Creatine kinase, lactic acid, and pyruvic acid levels were normal. Hypoglycemia was not present (9.39 mmol/L) before glucose infusion began. The free fatty acid (FFA) level was elevated (1.31 mmol/L), while acetoacetic acid was low (0.04 mmol/L) and 3-hydroxybutyrate was mildly elevated (0.154 mmol/L). Physical examination showed significant hepatomegaly.
test_results: Abdominal computed tomography (CT) revealed severe fatty liver and hepatomegaly without splenomegaly. A brain MRI performed on day 10 revealed no abnormality.

case_report: A 66-year-old female with a medical history including asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) overlap syndrome, allergic rhinitis, hypothyroidism, type II diabetes mellitus, a past unprovoked deep venous thrombosis, anxiety/bipolar disorder, and back pain presented with persistent exertional shortness of breath. Five years ago, a transthoracic echocardiogram indicated stage 2 left ventricular diastolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 63%. She had two recent hospital admissions for similar symptoms, treated as COPD exacerbations with antibiotics and steroids. On this occasion, she was hemodynamically stable. Physical examination revealed positive jugular venous pulsations and normal heart sounds without heaves, rubs, or murmurs. Laboratory results showed leukocytosis, potentially influenced by a recent steroid course for COPD, and eosinophilia at 0.99 k/microL (normal <0.46 k/microL). Previous lab results indicated intermittent eosinophil elevation, with a peak of 1.13 k/microL. Brain natriuretic peptide was elevated at 3,197 pg/mL (normal < 100 pg/mL). A chest X-ray was normal, and an EKG showed no ischemic changes but noted a known left bundle branch block.
test_results: MRI showed rim of subendocardial delayed enhancement involving the apical segments and extending into the mid-walls. It corresponded to low subendocardial signals within these territories on cine images. A well-defined area of low signal intensity, consistent with thrombus on tissue characterization, was also seen along with mitral valve regurgitation. Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was done showing preserved EF with moderate mitral regurgitation. A flat filling defect was seen in the cardiac apex with the use of definity contrast.

case_report: An 18-year-old male presented with multiple painless skin swellings located on the right cheek, chin, eyelid, and suprapubic region. The swelling on the right cheek had been recurring for 4 years. The patient had a history of recurrent cardiac swellings in the left atrium and right ventricle, for which he had undergone surgery twice. He also experienced a cerebrovascular accident. There was no notable family history. On physical examination, the swelling on the right cheek measured 15 x 8 x 6 cm, was firm, non-tender, mobile, and not attached to underlying structures. The overlying skin was nodular and had areas of ulceration. The swellings on the right eyelid, chin, and suprapubic region measured 0.5 cm, 2.0 cm, and 3.5 cm, respectively. Additionally, there was a small pigmented lesion on the inner canthus of the right eye, multiple pigmented macules on the left shin, and several nevi on the legs and back. The patient also had vitiligo on the prepuce. Endocrine evaluation showed elevated adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) levels at 48.5 pg/mL.
test_results: The aspirate was thick, viscous, stringy, and gelatinous. The smears were paucicellular and revealed abundant myxoid material in the background which stained magenta with Giemsa and pale blue green with Papanicolaou stain. It was admixed with hypocellular fragments of spindle and stellate cells with oval to spindle nuclei having evenly dispersed, fine chromatin, thin nuclear membrane, and inconspicuous nucleoli. Focal mild nuclear pleomorphism was noted. Mitosis and necrosis were absent. Few fragments showed thin delicate vascular cores. Epithelial structures were not seen. There were no cytologic features of malignancy. On gross examination, the cheek mass measured 15 cm × 13 cm × 6 cm. Overlying skin was focally ulcerated. On cut-surface, it was well-circumscribed, nodular, solid, gelatinous with few cystic and hemorrhagic areas. Microscopic examination revealed a tumor in the dermis and subcutaneous plane which was composed of multiple hypocellular nodules with abundant myxoid stroma and spindle to stellate cells within it. Focally, increased cellularity was seen. The cells had bland nuclear morphology and lacked cytological atypia. Mitosis and necrosis were absent. Focal areas of capillary proliferation, epithelial proliferation, and cystic changes were also seen. The eyelid lesion also showed similar morphology.
diagnosis: Multiple cutaneous myxomas in Carney complex

case_report: A 6-year-old female with no notable past medical or family history arrived in cardiac arrest, potentially due to hypoxia from persistent seizures. Upon arrival at the emergency department, she was found to have a fever of unknown cause and duration. Following admission, she experienced frequent electroclinical seizures. Infectious and metabolic evaluations returned negative results. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed no pleocytosis, with a mildly elevated protein level of 76 mg/dL (reference range: 15-45 mg/dL) and a glucose level of 70 mg/dL (reference range: 60-80 mg/dL).
test_results: Her EEG was markedly abnormal showing frequent high amplitude generalized spike and slow wave discharges alternating with short periods of suppression. The brain MRI was positive for symmetric T2 lesions in thalami and mild restricted diffusion in bilateral hippocampus. An epilepsy panel showed a missense mutation (c.1350A>T; p.Leu450Phe) of uncertain significance in RANBP2 gene (NM_006267.4).
diagnosis: Acute Necrotizing Encephalopathy  associated with RANBP2 mutation

case_report: The patient, a female aged 1 year and 3 months, was referred due to severe growth issues. She was born from a first pregnancy, with nonconsanguineous parents who had normal growth. There was a threat of miscarriage at 27 weeks. Delivery occurred at 38 weeks and 5 days via cesarean section. At birth, the patient had severe respiratory failure, requiring ventilator support for five days and respiratory support for five months. Pulmonary hypertension was noted. Birth measurements were: weight 1490 g (Z-score −4.50), length 40 cm (Z-score −4.54), head circumference 32.5 cm (Z-score −2.59), and chest circumference 24 cm. Physical features included a hydrocephalic head, short palpebral fissures, ocular and nipple hypertelorism, depressed nasal bridge, epicanthus, microstomy, high-arched palate, hypoplastic low-set ears, short neck, low hairline, and arachnodactyly. The patient had a progeroid appearance with underdeveloped subcutaneous fat. Genital examination showed hypoplasia of the labia majora and hypertrophied clitoris. The liver extended 3 cm below the right costal arch and 1 cm below the left costal arch. Motor activity was reduced. At 9 months, the patient’s condition was severe but conscious and active. She weighed 3.3 kg (Z-score −6.54), was 54 cm tall (Z-score −6.61), and had a BMI of 11.32 (Z-score −4.67). Head circumference was 43.5 cm (Z-score −0.76), and chest circumference was 30 cm. Physical development was extremely low and disharmonic. Observations included pseudohydrocephalus, high forehead, triangular face, exophthalmos, narrow nasal dorsum, smooth philtrum, microgenia, microtia, and arachnodactyly. Skin was clean and dry, with cyanosis of the face and upper trunk when crying. Subcutaneous fat was underdeveloped, and the chest was barrel-shaped. Hepatomegaly was present. The child could not support her head but attempted to turn from prone to supine. She showed interest in toys and babbled with syllable chains. X-ray indicated delayed bone age (less than three months vs actual age of 9 months) and sparse bone structure. Valgus deformity of the knee joints was noted. Data on the patella were not provided due to transparency in X-ray scans of young children, and ultrasonography was not performed. EEG showed no epileptiform or focal pathological activity. Echocardiography revealed no heart defects but noted a patent foramen ovale and diagonal trabecula in the left ventricular cavity. At 1 year and 3 months, the patient had a height of 58 cm (Z-score −7.06), weight of 4 kg (Z-score −6.44), and head circumference of 45 cm (Z-score −0.5). Observations included a hydrocephalic head, high forehead, triangular face, exophthalmos, narrow nasal dorsum, microgenia, microtia, severe hypotrophy, and alopecia areas on the head. Subcutaneous fat was not developed. The patient did not sit independently or support herself steadily on her feet but could stand with support. She played with toys, held objects, collected pyramids, and transferred small objects. At 1 year and 11 months, short stature (63 cm, Z-score −7.04) and growth retardation (5 kg, Z-score −6.16) were noted. Clinical examination revealed dysmorphic facial features and microtia. Absent patella was noted by palpation. Cytogenetic testing showed a karyotype of 46, XX. A study of the LMNA gene showed no pathogenic changes.
test_results: Clinical exome sequencing was ordered, identifying two variants in the CDC6 gene. Parental examination revealed that they were heterozygous carriers of relevant changes in the nucleotide sequence. Neither variant had been registered in either the GnomAD database (v.2.1.1), the clinical databases (Clinvar, HGMD Professional (v.2021.1)), or the database of variants obtained by exome sequencing (WES, CES) in the Research Center for Medical Genetics – RuExac (1337 samples). The exon 3 nucleotide sequence variant of the CDC6 gene (chr17:38447363C>T) results in a premature translation termination site (p.(Gln78Ter), NM_001254.3). A variant in exon 3 of the CDC6 gene (chr17:38447361A>G), resulting in a missense replacement of (p.(Lys77Arg), NM_001254.3), is classified as a variant with uncertain clinical significance (ACMG: PM2, PM3).

case_report: A 50-year-old female reported experiencing vision loss in her right eye, along with ocular pain, headache, nausea, and vomiting. Initial intraocular pressure (IOP) measurements were 55 mmHg in the right eye and 11 mmHg in the left eye. Corneal edema obscured the fundus view. She had no notable history of systemic or ocular diseases and was not on any medication. She underwent trabeculectomy in the right eye, which normalized the IOP and cleared the cornea. Despite this, her visual acuity remained poor, leading to a referral to our glaucoma clinic. Upon current examination, visual acuity was 20/500 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye, with IOPs of 16.0 mmHg and 11.3 mmHg, respectively. Slit lamp examination showed a clear cornea and an anterior chamber free of cells or flare in the right eye. The pupil diameter was 4 mm with extensive posterior synechia and no light response. A diffuse superior subconjunctival filtering bleb and a peripheral iridotomy at 9 o'clock were noted.
test_results: Ultrawide-field fundus photography showed grayish retinochoroidal atrophy and osteocyte-like pigment clumping lesions along the retinal veins and peripapillary preretinal hemorrhage in the right eye, without any signs of inflammatory responses of the retina and vitreous body. Early fluorescein fundus angiography (FFA) of the right eye revealed transmitted hyperfluorescence consistent with retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) atrophy with more extensive areas of choriocapillaris atrophy and late FFA showed weak fluorescence and delay in venous filling in the atrophic areas. Macular spectral domain optical coherence tomography showed outer retinal thinning and preretinal hemorrhage at the macula in the right eye. Electroretinogram and Electro-oculography suggested generalized decrease in photopic and scotopic amplitude in B-wave and A-wave in the right eye. Retinal nerve fiber layer thickness of nasal quadrant was thinner than normal limits in the right eye showed by optical coherence tomography. Ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) showed shallow anterior chamber depth (ACD) (1.64 mm), complete circumferential closure of the anterior chamber angle and a peripheral iridotomy in the right eye.

case_report: A 30-year-old Jamaican-American male presented with one month of bilateral foot pain and ulcerations, with severe pain on the bottom of his left foot. He was active-duty military and a former professional athlete with no significant past medical history. He reported numbness on the plantar surface of both feet, which progressed to pain, worse at night and unrelieved by compression and over-the-counter pain medications. Physical examination revealed intact vibratory sensation in the lower extremities, extreme tenderness to palpation on the left foot, decreased dorsiflexion and plantar flexion of both feet, and decreased sensation on the plantar surface of the left foot. After a trial of compression stockings, ibuprofen, and acetaminophen, he presented to the emergency department with worsening foot pain. D-dimer was elevated, and bilateral lower extremity ultrasound was negative for deep vein thrombosis (DVT). He was referred to a vascular clinic, where he had a normal ankle-brachial index of 0.96 on the right and 0.98 on the left. He was then referred to dermatology and neurology for further evaluation. Dermatology started him on a topical steroid cream. At the neurology evaluation, his pain had significantly worsened, and he required a wheelchair due to inability to ambulate. There was no improvement in pain or skin lesions despite the prescribed treatments. Electromyography (EMG) showed severe diffuse axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy affecting the bilateral lower extremities. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed mild degenerative disc disease with mild bilateral neural foraminal narrowing at L5-S1 and no significant spinal canal narrowing. Neurology referred him to rheumatology, hematology, and a second dermatologist. Laboratory evaluation showed elevated C3 and C4 complement levels at 177 mg/dL (82-167 mg/dL) and 51 mg/dL (12-38 mg/dL), respectively. Complement CH50 was elevated at >60 U/mL (>41 U/mL). Anti-nuclear antibody test was positive at a 1:160 ratio in a speckled pattern. Cardiolipin antibody IgM was elevated at 22 MPL/mL (0-12 MPL/mL). Other tests, including HIV, hepatitis A/B/C panel, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) panel, serum protein electrophoresis, kappa and lambda free light chains panel, and serum electrolytes, were negative.
test_results: Ulcerated epidermis with neutrophilic abscess, small vessels with fibroid necrosis of the vessel wall, and pigment-laden macrophages. No evidence of a fungal infection. Perivascular inflammation with inflammatory cells within the vessel walls. Intravascular thrombosis and eosinophilic fibrinous exudate within the vessel walls. Overlying, nonulcerated, epidermis is relatively unremarkable and uninvolved. Vessels away from the ulcer demonstrated intravascular thrombosis with some eosinophilic exudate within the vascular walls. Neovascularization noted. No intravascular hyaline deposits. Extensive hemosiderin noted on the iron stain. CD31 and ERG immunohistochemistry highlighted vascular endothelium. Immunofluorescence showed IgM in the superficial, mid-dermal, and deep dermal blood vessels. C3 was 2+ clumps in the superficial, mid-dermal, and deep dermal blood vessels. Fibrinogen was 2+ in the superficial walls, mid-dermal, and deep dermal blood vessels. IgG, IgG4, and IgA were all negative.

case_report: A 13-year-old Hindu male child, the fourth born to a consanguineously married couple, presented with spasms in the upper and lower limbs. These episodes have been occurring frequently since he was 5 years old. He underwent surgery for developmental bilateral cataract at the age of 6 years. Upon admission, he exhibited carpopedal spasm, and his vital signs were within normal limits. His weight was 29 kg (<5th centile), height 132 cm (<5th centile), and head circumference 49 cm (<3rd centile). Physical examination revealed facial features such as a long face, prominent forehead, bilateral drooping eyelids, a preauricular tag on the right side, bilateral pseudophakia with secondary posterior capsular opacification, a beaked nose, a depressed nasal bridge, a long philtrum, a high arched palate, maloccluded teeth, micrognathia, and microcephaly. Latent tetany signs, including Trousseau sign and Chvostek sign, were positive. An intelligent quotient assessment indicated mild mental retardation. Other system examinations were normal. One of his sisters also had surgery for developmental cataract at the age of 4 years and exhibited delayed social and personal development and similar facial features but no signs of tetany or latent tetany. Both parents and the other two siblings were phenotypically normal. Laboratory investigations showed normal blood counts and peripheral smear. Serum calcium was 6.8 mg/dl, serum phosphorus 7.1 mg/dl, serum magnesium 2.2 mg/dl, serum albumin 3.2 g/dl, alkaline phosphatase 124 U/L, and intact PTH was 5.46 pg/ml (N = 15-65 pg/ml). Blood urea, blood sugar, serum creatinine, and electrolytes were normal. Urine chromatography was normal, and urinary pH was 8. Urine tests for sugar and ketones were negative. Chest X-ray, humerus X-ray, and abdominal ultrasound were normal.
test_results: Computerized tomographic (CT) scan of the head showed bilateral globus pallidus calcification.

case_report: Patient 9 is a 69-year-old Japanese woman. She experienced recurrent dislocation of the right shoulder starting at age 6, which she managed by self-repositioning into adulthood. She frequently had subcutaneous hematomas. At age 58, she developed a diaphragmatic hernia (hiatal hernia) that was surgically treated, followed by an abdominal hernia. She had a pulmonary embolism after surgery for gallstones. At age 65, she noticed vaginal prolapse with associated difficulties in defecation and urination. She was referred at age 69 for genetic evaluation in view of surgery for progressive vaginal prolapse. Physical examination revealed brachydactyly with excessive skin and toe deformities, but no generalized joint hypermobility. The hiatal and abdominal hernias were also noted to be progressive. After this referral, she developed a small bowel perforation that healed spontaneously.
test_results: Standard NGS panel analysis detected a heterozygous frameshift variant c.9271dup,p.(Gln3091Profs*31) in exon 27, which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Modified NGS panel analysis using long PCR-amplified product detected a heterozygous TNXA-derived 120-bp deletion in exon 35–intron 35 (c.11435_11524 + 30del), c.12150C>G,p.(Arg4050 = ) and c.12174C>Gp.(Cys4058Trp) in exon 40, c.12204 + 39dup and c.12204 + 43T>G in intron 40, and c.12628-52A>G in intron 43. MLPA showed the one-copy loss of exon 35 in TNXB and a one-copy loss of CYP21A2 (type 1 TNXB/TNXA fusion gene). Long-PCR using primers TNXB-ex26-F and TNXB-ex35-R confirmed the presence of the frameshift variant in exon 27.

case_report: A 36-year-old woman with a history of atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, and dust mite hypersensitivity presented with a sudden appearance of tender red papules and nodules with central ulcerations on both upper and lower extremities, including feet and hands. This was accompanied by swelling, high-grade fever, and general discomfort following 4 weeks of subcutaneous allergen immunotherapy. Physical examination revealed no numbness, loss of sensation, or muscle weakness.
test_results: Skin biopsy demonstrated mixed inflammation of parasitized foamy histiocytes, plasma cells, and lymphocytes following neurovascular structures with a few neutrophils at the subcutis. Clusters of acid-fast bacilli within histiocytes resembling 'globi' were observed on Fite stain and Acid-fast bacillus stain. Acid-fast bacillus culture of the skin biopsy for 8 weeks was negative. Polymerase chain reaction confirmed M. leprae detection with no drug-resistant mutation genes detected.
diagnosis: Lepromatous leprosy with erythema nodosum leprosum

case_report: A 21-year-old male exhibited multiple asymptomatic skin lesions characterized by areas of both reduced and increased pigmentation on the extremities, which have been present since he was 1 year old. The palms and soles were unaffected. There was no notable family history of similar skin conditions, and no other significant medical history was reported.
test_results: Biopsy from the hypopigmented macules showed decreased melanin pigmentation whereas biopsy from the hyperpigmented macules showed increased focal melanin in the basal layer.

case_report: The patient was born at an outside hospital at 41 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery to a 20-year-old G2P2. Birth weight was 3991 g and head circumference was 36 cm (both values above the 95th percentile). The pregnancy and delivery were reportedly without complication. The infant was transferred to our institution on the fourth day of life for further management of a vascular skin lesion and upper extremity enlargement and edema. There was a family history of vascular birthmarks, with the patient's mother having several pink macules on her trunk and extremities, and an older sibling exhibiting a port wine stain. The neonate was hemodynamically stable. On physical examination, there were blanching salmon-colored macules extending over the left cheek, left ear, chin, and across the left neck. Darker, pink/violaceous lesions were observed over the left temporal and occipital scalp. A pink patch extended over most of the right upper extremity, intermingled with areas that appeared more violaceous. The entire right upper extremity was enlarged and tensely edematous. The right arm measured 17 cm in length, 1 cm longer than the left, and the right lower arm circumference measured 14.5 cm, 3.5 cm greater than the left. Axillary, brachial, and radial pulses were bounding. At the initial and subsequent examinations, the baby was noted to move the right arm only minimally as compared with the left. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. There was no laboratory evidence of coagulopathy or platelet consumption. Prenatal screening ultrasound was reportedly normal. An echocardiogram performed at the referring institution on the first day of life was also reportedly normal. Ultrasound performed on the fourth day of life revealed massive dilation of the right subclavian, axillary, and brachial artery as well as a dilated deep venous system. The diameter of the brachial artery was 5 mm. Spectral Doppler analysis of the affected arteries demonstrated a low resistance waveform. There was arterialization of the waveforms obtained from the adjacent draining veins. There was increased vascularity of the forearm. Additionally, the musculature appeared homogeneously hyperechoic; however, there was no discrete mass. An MRI of the right upper extremity and chest obtained on the seventh day revealed the aneurysmal vessels, extending from the origin of the right subclavian artery to the right brachial artery. Time-resolved post-contrast magnetic resonance angiography showed near-simultaneous enhancement of the right upper extremity arteries and draining dilated veins. There was abnormally high T2 signal in the musculature, though no mass was identified. An MRI brain scan and a chest radiograph were both normal. A postnatal echocardiogram was interpreted as mild right ventricular hypertrophy with normal biventricular function. The superior vena cava return to the right atrium appeared increased, consistent with increased flow. The right subclavian artery was markedly dilated. These findings are consistent with high-grade arteriovenous shunting in the right arm, with resultant massive dilatation of arteries and veins with evidence of increased cardiac output.
test_results: Sequencing of the RASA-1 coding region revealed a single mutation (c.2603 + 1 G > A one copy).

case_report: This report concerns a 28-month-old girl who was born at 38 weeks and 4 days of an uneventful pregnancy to nonconsanguineous healthy parents. Her birth weight was 3700 g. She displayed head control and the ability to roll over at 3 and 4 months of age, respectively. Beyond that, she displayed no social smile or communication at 3 months of age. Upon admission at 4 months of age, she began to develop a series of seizures occurring 3–4 times a day. Shortly thereafter, she experienced developmental regression, losing the ability to control her head and roll over, and continued to show no social smile or eye contact. She did not respond to sound or light and exhibited hypotonia of the extremities. Four small café au lait spots, each 0.2–0.3 centimeters in size, were found on her arms and legs, without any neurofibromas. Her head circumference was within the normal range. No specific facial features were noted. Investigations of other organs (heart, eye, liver, kidney, etc.) were negative.
test_results: EEG suggested hypsarrhythmia patterns. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed mild delayed myelination.

case_report: A 13-year-old female was referred to the Paediatric Clinic of Dr. Georgi Stranski University Hospital, Pleven, for an evaluation of severe obesity. She was delivered naturally at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy with a birth weight of 3.9 kg and a birth length of 51 cm. Routine local national newborn screening was conducted and showed no evidence of congenital diseases. Normal early physical and psychomotor development were evident. Familial history included second-degree relatives with autoimmune diseases of the thyroid gland and a father with a metabolic syndrome (abdominal obesity, hypertension, and insulin resistance). The patient had been overweight since early-school age with a significant increase in weight over the last year and an improper diet, involving the daily consumption of large amounts of carbohydrates and fat-rich foods. She reported menarche at the age of 11, with secondary amenorrhea for the last 3 months. Her school performance had worsened over the past year. For the last couple of months, she had been suffering from severely limited mobility due to progressively increasing pains in the lumbar area, hip joints, and lower limbs. Due to the pain symptoms, the girl was referred for consultation to a paediatric neurologist in an outpatient setting, who referred her to a paediatric endocrinologist for obesity assessment. At admission, the girl was in an impaired general condition. A “mask-like face” with rough facial features, thick lips, and macroglossia was notable on physical examination. She had very dry skin with acanthosis nigricans on the neck, axillae, and arms. Abnormal fatty tissue distribution with increased accumulation in the abdominal area was observed. No hyperplasia of the thyroid gland and no abnormalities in the respiratory and cardiovascular systems were evident. She was in the fifth Tanner stage of pubertal development.
