The patient experienced difficulties in rising from a lying or sitting position, inability to get up from a crouching position, and severe difficulty climbing up and down stairs. Pain on palpation bilateral around the spine at the lumbar vertebrae level was present. Lasègue’s sign and Patrick’s tests were bilaterally positive. Significant symmetrical pseudohypertrophy of the lower legs, flat feet, and pathological walk were noted. She had decreased knee and Achilles reflexes with preserved sensitivity. The patient responded slightly slower than normal during the interview and the whole physical examination. The anthropometric measurements showed evidence of short stature and severe obesity: a height of 141 cm (−2.83 SDS), a weight of 77 kg (+1.91 SDS), a BMI of 38.7 kg/m2 (+2.88 SDS), and a waist circumference of 110 cm. The laboratory tests showed elevated levels of liver enzymes, cholesterol, and triglycerides, as well as substantially increased creatine kinase. Furthermore, insulin resistance with impaired glucose tolerance and without diabetic levels of blood glucose during oral glucose tolerance test was determined. The laboratory results and the clinical presentation evidenced the presence of metabolic syndrome, with our patient fulfilling three of all four criteria for its diagnosis (abdominal obesity, dyslipidaemia with elevated triglycerides and reduced HDL, and impaired glucose tolerance). The hormonal evaluation evidenced severe autoimmune hypothyroidism. The ultrasound scan showed a hypoechogenic, non-homogeneous-structured, and normal-sized thyroid gland, as well as normal structures and sizes of the liver and the spleen.
test_results: The EMG showed evidence of myogenic impairment of the lower limbs. The CT scan showed no evidence of anatomical impairments. No deletions and duplications in dystrophin gene were found.

case_report: A 57-year-old African American woman with a history of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (Gold Criteria 2), controlled Hypertension on hydrochlorothiazide, Human Immunodeficiency Virus on antiretroviral therapy (CD4 count of 700, viral load of 1,200), peptic ulcer disease, chronic back pain, and tobacco-use disorder presented to the emergency department with a four-day history of non-bilious, non-bloody vomiting, nausea, and diarrhea. She reported 4–5 episodes of vomiting and 3 episodes of watery, non-bloody diarrhea. She denied pain, fever, chills, shortness of breath, chest pain, and urinary changes. She attributed her gastrointestinal symptoms to food poisoning and took antacids without relief, staying hydrated with water and sports drinks. She later recalled mild chest pain that improved without identifiable triggers. Initial EKG showed normal sinus rhythm with global T wave inversions. Repeat labs revealed an initial troponin of 0.9 (normal 0.0–0.04), elevated D-Dimer of 900 (normal 220–500 ng/mL), and proBNP of 8800 (normal < 125 pg/mL). CTA was negative for pulmonary embolism. She was started on a heparin drip due to her history of gastrointestinal bleeding. On admission, she was hemodynamically stable. On the second day, she developed worsened shortness of breath and sharp, non-radiating, left-sided chest pain under her sternum and left breast, rated 8/10 in severity. The pain was described as a sharp pressure with no exacerbating or alleviating factors. She developed mild tachycardia (HR 102) but remained otherwise stable. She was uncomfortable but without diaphoresis. The pain was not reproducible with palpation. Cardiac auscultation revealed normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and she had bilateral vesicular breath sounds. There was no peripheral leg edema. Urine toxicology was positive for fentanyl, methadone, and cannabinoids. The patient had several risk factors for coronary artery disease, including hypertension, smoking, and HIV, but had no previous diagnosis of coronary artery disease. She reported limited exercise capacity since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, experiencing mild fatigue and shortness of breath over the past six months. She reported no other recent medical complications or illnesses.
test_results: Echo revealed left ventricular ejection fraction of 25–35%, left ventricle apical hypokinesis and mild apical ballooning. Coronary angiogram procedure was performed and was found to have left ventricular estimated ejection fraction of <30% with apical akinesis.

case_report: A 68-year-old female patient was admitted to the hospital due to ocular muscle weakness for 10 days. The patient experienced bilateral blepharoptosis and diplopia with symptoms worsening in the evening, and mild weakness of bilateral upper limbs. She developed edematous erythema on the face, which gradually spread to the neck, chest, and back. The patient had a history of hypertension for more than 10 years, with a systolic blood pressure of up to 160 mm Hg in the past, and was on long-term oral administration of nifedipine controlled-release tablets 30 mg once daily. A mediastinal mass was found one year ago, considered to be a thymic tumor. She denied any history of hepatitis, tuberculosis, diabetes, cerebrovascular disease, mental illness, trauma, blood transfusion, food or drug allergy, and denied any family history of genetic diseases or tumors. No smoking or alcohol habits. Specialist examination revealed edematous erythema on the forehead and bilateral upper eyelids, “V”-shaped erythema in front of the neck, and “shawl sign” on the shoulders and back. Bilateral eyelids were markedly drooping and covered about 50% of the eyeball with diplopia. Muscle strength was grade IV in both upper limbs and grade V in both lower limbs, with normal muscle tone and no significant muscle tenderness throughout the body. Laboratory analyses revealed creatine kinase isoenzyme 115 U/L (reference range, 0–24 U/L), aspartate aminotransferase 90 U/L (reference range, 13–35 U/L), and lactate dehydrogenase 604 U/L (reference range, 120–250 U/L). Antinuclear antibody was positive and showed a nuclear granular pattern with a titer of 1:320. Chest computed tomography revealed an anterior mediastinal mass considered to be a thymic tumor. Additionally, there are multiple nodules in bilateral lungs and multiple lymph nodes in the mediastinum, considered metastases of the thymic tumor. Hepatobiliary, pancreatic, splenic, and abdominopelvic ultrasound showed multiple slightly hypoechoic lesions in the liver, also considered metastases of the thymic tumor.
test_results: Electromyography showed electrophysiological findings of myogenic changes in the examined muscles, mainly in the proximal muscles, and compression of the bilateral median nerve wrists. Biopsy of the proximal muscle of the left upper limb revealed no significant swelling or degeneration of the muscle tissue and no significant inflammatory cell infiltration in the muscle interstitium. Neostigmine test was negative. Myasthenia gravis antibodies were also negative.

case_report: A six-year-old Chinese Han girl presented with a three-year history of strabismus in the right eye. Her visual acuity was OD:HM (hand motions); OS: 0.6, and refraction was: OD: − 6.00 DS (spherical lens) − 1.75 DC (cylindrical lens) × 90 < 0.05; OS: + 0.75DC (cylindrical lens) × 100 = 1.0. Intraocular pressure measured via a non-contact tonometer was OD: 17 mmHg; OS: 18 mmHg. Slit lamp examination showed normal sclera, conjunctiva, and cornea in the right eye, but the lens was opacified and dislocated without an ectopic pupil in the anterior segment. The lens was white, opacified, and displaced to the temporal area. The posterior segment of the right eye and the left eye appeared normal under slit-lamp biomicroscopy and direct ophthalmoscopy. The patient was tall and thin, with a height of 125 cm (75th-90th percentile), weight of 17.5 kg (approximately 10th percentile), and a BMI of 11.2 kg/m2. Comprehensive physical examination upon admission showed temperature at 36.7 °C, heart rate at 80 beats/minute, respiratory rate at 20 breaths/minute, and blood pressure at 80/52 mmHg. Lung and heart auscultation were normal, and abdominal palpation revealed no significant findings. Neurological examination, including cranial nerve assessment, motor and sensory system examination, tendon reflexes, and pathological signs, were all normal. Arm-span measurement, wrist and thumb sign, and other skeletal features were negative. The score of the physical examination was 0 in the systemic calculator of the revised Ghent criteria. Ocular examinations included corneal endothelium analysis, corneal topography analysis, IOL Master biometry, A-B ultrasonography, and macular optical coherence tomography. Corneal endothelium analysis showed an average endothelial cell density of 3285.6/mm2 in the right eye and 3234.8/mm2 in the left eye. Corneal topography analysis determined total corneal astigmatism of 1.4D in the right eye and 1.3D in the left eye, both with-the-rule astigmatism. Axial length was 21.39 mm (OD) and 22.20 mm (OS) as measured by IOL Master, and 21.78 mm (OD) and 22.38 mm (OS) as detected via A ultrasonography. B ultrasonography and macular optical coherence tomography detected no abnormalities. Echocardiography revealed an aortic root internal diameter of 20 mm, with a Z score of 2 (< 3). Laboratory investigations upon admission showed normal values: WBC at 9.29 × 109/L, RBC at 4.74 × 1012/L, HGB at 133 g/L, PLT at 307 × 109/L, NEU% at 0.622, and Hct at 0.394. Liver function tests showed TBiL at 7.6 µmol/L, ALB at 45 g/L, ALT at 9 U/L, AST at 35 U/L, and ALP at 206 U/L. Renal function parameters included urea at 3.74 mmol/L, Cr at 24 µmol/L, and UA at 196 µmol/L. Urinalysis revealed no protein, glucose, or occult blood. Electrolytes, coagulation function, and infectious disease investigations were normal. A comprehensive medical history from her parents revealed normal prenatal and developmental conditions. The mother had an uneventful prenatal period without specific illnesses, medication use, or exposure to harmful substances. The child was born at full term (38 weeks + 4 days) through a normal delivery, with a birth weight of 3050 g, length of 50 cm, chest circumference of 30 cm, and head circumference of 32 cm. The Apgar score was 10. There was no history of systemic illnesses, surgeries, or prolonged medication use. The child grew up in a typical working-class family, with no history of exposure to radioactive or other harmful substances. The parents are not relatives, and none of her family members, including her elder sisters and younger brother, had ocular abnormalities during childhood. The patient achieved age-appropriate developmental milestones, including rolling over at 3 months, sitting at 6 months, crawling at 9 months, walking and basic speech at 1 year and 1 month, attending kindergarten at 2 and a half years, and starting first grade at 6 years with average academic performance. Her family observed frequent falls during her initial attempts at walking, concomitant with the identification of strabismus.
test_results: Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood samples using MagPure Tissue&Blood DNA LQ Kit (Magen, Beijing, China) following the manufacturer’s instructions, then 200 ng genomic DNA of each individual was sheared by Biorupter (Diagenode, Belgium) to acquire 150–200 bp fragments. The ends of DNA fragment were repaired and Illumina Adaptor was added (Fast Library Prep Kit, iGeneTech, Beijing, China). After sequencing library were constructed, the whole exons were captured with AIExome Enrichment Kit V1 (iGeneTech, Beijing, China) and sequenced on Illumina platform (Illumina, San Diego, CA) with with 150 base paired-end reads. Raw reads were filtered to remove low quality reads by using FastQC. Then clean reads were mapped to the reference genome GRCh37 by using Bwa. After removing duplications, SNV and InDel were called and annotated by using GATK. CNVkit was used to call the large copy number variations (CNVs) and the parameters were as default. To identify large copy number variations (CNVs), part of the sequencing library was sequenced directly and each sample yielded 1G Raw data. CNVs were called by using CNVseq and the control was the health parents.
diagnosis: Isolated Ectopia Lentis due to ADAMTSL4 Mutation

case_report: A 14-month-old male of Asian and Caucasian descent presented with an 8-month history of recurrent cough, rapid breathing, and low blood oxygen levels, necessitating multiple hospital admissions. He was born full-term with an uncomplicated neonatal period and was of average size for gestational age. Early infancy was notable only for mild eczema, and he received all routine vaccinations. Family history was negative for significant medical or genetic conditions. He lived with both parents and was not on any medications. At 6 months of age, he presented with a 2-week history of dry cough and low oxygen levels, as detected by a home monitoring device (SpO2: 83–91%) at night. Physical examination revealed rapid breathing, subcostal retractions, decreased breath sounds, mild scattered wheezes, and bilateral crackles, without fever. He was treated with antibiotics for bronchiolitis and pneumonia. Despite treatment, he was hospitalized twice for ongoing symptoms of rapid breathing and low oxygen levels, both day and night. He received supplemental oxygen, albuterol, and oral and inhaled steroids. Chest x-ray showed a patchy opacity in the right mid-lung field. Respiratory viral panels were negative, and echocardiogram was normal. Persistent rapid breathing, retractions, and crackles were noted on examination outside of acute respiratory illnesses, with continued reports of nighttime low oxygen levels. A sleep study revealed obstructive sleep apnea (Apnea Hypopnea Index of 5.5) and episodes of persistent low oxygen levels below SpO2 90%. He was referred to a pediatric pulmonologist. Repeat chest x-ray showed patchy ill-defined perihilar opacities. Sweat chloride test and immune work-up were normal. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was normal.
test_results: The high-resolution CT scan showed areas of mosaic attenuation and geographic ground-glass opacities in a predominant perihilar distribution.

case_report: A 60-year-old male presented with back pain and was found to have an uncomplicated Stanford type B acute aortic dissection. During hospitalization, a contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed a 55-mm aortic root dilatation. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed severe aortic regurgitation with a vena contracta of 6 mm and a pressure halt time of 430 ms. Holodiastolic flow reversal was noted in the abdominal aorta. There was no evidence of cusp degeneration or mitral valve insufficiency. Post-discharge, follow-up CT confirmed the stability of the false lumen, leading to the scheduling of elective surgery for the aortic root. The patient's medical history includes hypertension, dyslipidemia, hyperuricemia, sleep apnea, and vasospastic angina, which developed 11 months prior. The patient is 183 cm tall, weighs 83.0 kg, and has no notable family history.
test_results: Among the tested genes, unreported heterozygous 8-base duplication mutation in the SMAD3 MH2 domain (c.742_749dup, p. Gln252ThrfsTer7) and likely benign heterozygous missense mutation in FBN2 (c.3518C > G, p. Thr1173Ser) were detected. The SMAD3 mutation causes frameshift, and premature termination codon can be formed.

case_report: A 58-year-old woman presented with uncontrolled hypertension and fluid collections around both kidneys. She had been experiencing indigestion and bloating for about 6 months. Her hypertension had been worsening over the past 2-3 years. An abdominal ultrasound 2 months prior revealed large cystic structures around both kidneys, a dilated common bile duct (1.2 cm), a liver hemangioma, and non-obstructing gallstones. During her initial visit, she reported nausea. Her medical history included hyperlipidemia, diffuse non-obstructive coronary artery disease diagnosed 3 years earlier, congestive heart failure with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 40%, a past thyroidectomy for a nodule, carpal tunnel surgery on the left hand, and a 30 pack-year smoking history. Her family history included hypertension and diabetes in a sibling and pulmonary embolism in her mother. Physical examination showed she was in no apparent distress with a heart rate of 87 b.p.m, respiratory rate of 16/min, and blood pressure of 158/108 mmHg. She was afebrile with an oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. Cardiovascular and respiratory exams were normal. Abdominal exam revealed bilateral flank fullness without tenderness. She had vitiligo spots and numerous skin telangiectasias on the upper chest, abdomen, base of the neck, arms, and thighs. Her medications included levothyroxine 112 μg, nifedipine XL 30 mg, hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) 25 mg, and niacin 500 mg daily. Laboratory data showed blood urea nitrogen 7.85 mmol/L (11 mg/dL), creatinine 88.4 μmol/L (1.0 mg/dL), sodium 142 mmol/L, potassium 2.9 mmol/L, bicarbonate 30 mmol/L, calcium 2.025 mmol/L (8.1 mg/dL), total protein 73 g/L (7.3 g/dL), albumin 27 g/L (2.7 g/dL), alkaline phosphatase 119 U/L, and normal liver enzymes, amylase, and lipase. Hemoglobin was 16.6 g/dL, hematocrit 51.7%, with normal white blood cells and platelets. JAK2 mutation was negative. Erythropoietin level was 134 mU/mL. Uric acid was 321.2 μmol/L (5.4 mg/dL), intact parathyroid hormone 237 ng/L (pg/mL), 25-hydroxy Vit D 36.4 nmol/L (14.6 ng/mL), aldosterone 0.125 nmol/L (4.5 ng/dL), renin 33.65 μmol/mL/h (1.42 mg/mL/h), and sedimentation rate 24 mm/h. ANA, c-ANCA, and p-ANCA were undetected. Urinalysis was unremarkable, and the random urine protein/creatinine ratio was 1.1 g/g. Arterial blood gas showed pH 7.45, pCO2 36 mmHg, PO2 87 mmHg, O2 saturation 91.5% on room air, and an A-a gradient of 17.3 mmHg. HCTZ was discontinued, nifedipine XL was increased to 60 mg, and lisinopril 10 mg and potassium chloride 20 mEq daily were added. CT-guided aspiration of the perinephric fluid collections revealed multiple septations, with 1000 mL of clear fluid aspirated from the right side and 650 mL from the left. Cell count showed WBC 56/mm3, red blood cells 60/mm3, lymphocytes 94%, and monocytes 6%. Chemical analysis showed albumin <10 g/L (<1.0 g/dL), creatinine 61.9 μmol/L (0.7 mg/dL), lactate dehydrogenase 34 U/L, and protein 3 g/L (0.3 g/dL). Cytology revealed a small number of lymphocytes, no epithelial or malignant cells. Renal parenchyma expanded following the procedure, but a repeat CT scan 24 hours later showed reaccumulation of the cysts bilaterally. She subsequently underwent bilateral laparoscopic decortication of perinephric cysts. Post-procedure, her blood pressure improved, and her medications were appropriately reduced.
test_results: A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed bilateral perinephric fluid collections compressing both the kidneys. Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation studies revealed 14 g/L (1.4 g/dL) of IgA-lambda monoclonal protein. Free serum kappa (k) was 4.6 mg/L and lambda (l) was 52.3 mg/L with the k/l ratio of 0.09. Urine protein electrophoresis showed a monoclonal band of IgA. Bone marrow biopsy revealed 10% plasma cells, hypocellular marrow with erythroid hyperplasia and absent iron stores.

case_report: A 20-year-old male with diabetes mellitus type 1 presented to the emergency department with sudden onset of speech difficulties, tongue deviation, left facial weakness, and numbness in the left hand, which developed over approximately 3 hours. He reported poor sleep, slight nausea, and mildly elevated blood glucose levels (183 mg/dl on home testing) before the symptoms began. He did not report any recent fevers, travel, or strenuous physical activity. By the time he arrived, his numbness had started to improve. On examination, his vital signs were normal. Physical examination revealed speech difficulties and subtle left facial weakness consistent with an upper motor neuron pattern. Muscle strength was normal in all extremities except for ankle dorsiflexion, which was graded at 4-/5 and appeared to be his baseline. There was decreased sensation in the left upper extremity, mainly in the medial forearm, but not following any specific peripheral nerve distribution. Reflexes were diminished in the upper extremities and absent in the lower extremities on both sides. The intrinsic muscles of the feet appeared atrophic, with hammer toes and high arches. The plantar reflex was absent bilaterally. Laboratory tests, including serum electrolytes, renal function, liver function tests, complete blood count with differential, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein, were all within normal limits.
test_results: MRI of the brain showed symmetric, nonenhancing areas of restricted diffusion in the corona radiata bilaterally, also seen on T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences, without edema or mass effect. Intracranial MR angiography was normal. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography demonstrated low amplitude sensory and motor responses with sensory conduction velocities in the 38- to 46-m/s range and motor conduction velocities in the 37- to 54-m/s range. Distal latencies and F-waves were also variably prolonged. Genetic testing confirmed a T467G (Leu156Arg) hemizygous disease-associated mutation in the gene for Cx2 (GJB1).

case_report: A 15-year-old female from Nigeria was brought to the emergency room in an unconscious state by her mother, with her aunt providing additional information. She had been well until three days prior when she experienced a frontal headache, which was initially treated with acetaminophen. The headache worsened, leading to unconsciousness and subsequent ER admission. There was no reported history of fever, neck pain, stiffness, jaundice, skin eruptions, fatigue, confusion, or dizziness. A few hours after admission, she experienced a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting five minutes. On examination, her Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score was 6/15. She appeared pale with cold, clammy extremities, was severely dehydrated, afebrile with a temperature of 36.7°C, had a heart rate of 101 beats per minute, blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg, respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 99% on room air. No jaundice or enlarged lymph nodes were observed. Kernig’s and Budzinski’s signs were negative, and her pupils were equal and reactive. Abdominal examination showed hepatomegaly without tenderness or other organ enlargement. A urethral catheter was inserted for urine monitoring, which drained coke-colored urine indicative of hemoglobinuria. Other physical examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory results showed anemia with a hemoglobin level of 7.4 g/dL, hematocrit of 21.6%, white blood cell count of 3.85 with a neutrophil count of 83.7%, lymphopenia of 12.5%, platelet count of 63,000, and elevated procalcitonin at 3.46 ng/mL.
test_results: The peripheral blood smear for malaria parasite was positive for P. falciparum and P. vivax. The urine was positive for hematuria and leukocytes. Abdominopelvic ultrasound revealed hepatosplenomegaly and ascites. CSF analysis and a computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain were unremarkable.

case_report: A 14-year-old male reported experiencing pain in the bones of both lower legs and upper forearms, as well as discomfort at the left corner of the mouth and the occipital region. Additionally, he had episodes of low-grade intermittent fever. These symptoms had been present for a total of five years. Laboratory results showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 40 mm/h and a C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 24 mg/L.
test_results: Radiographs of bilateral tibia showed osteosclerotic lesions and periosteal reaction. MRI showed bone marrow edema in diaphyses and metaphyses of distal tibia and femur bilaterally, and in left mandible. Tc99m-MDP bone scan revealed increased uptake in the same areas. Bone biopsy showed no evidence of granuloma, malignancy, or histiocytes.
Orpha_name: Chronic nonbacterial osteomyelitis/Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis

case_report: The patient is a 22-month-old girl born at 39 weeks' gestation with a birth weight of 2484 g (−1.5 SD), a length of 44.5 cm (−2.3 SD), and an OFC of 31 cm (−1.6 SD). Her parents are healthy. During the neonatal period, she exhibited microcephaly and low anal atresia. She has a severe neurodevelopmental delay, demonstrated by her ability to lift her head and roll over at 10 months but inability to sit up independently at 2 years of age. At 18 months, her physical examination revealed a height of 70.0 cm (−3.3 SD), a weight of 7.0 kg (−2.6 SD), and an OFC of 38 cm (−6.0 SD), indicating growth retardation and microcephaly. Additional features include strabismus, telecanthus, a broad nasal bridge, low-set ears, and mitral regurgitation.
test_results: MRI of her brain at 9 months of age revealed apparent hypoplasia of the pons and corpus callosum, proportional atrophy/hypoplasia of the cerebellum with a dilated subarachnoid space beneath the cerebellum.

case_report: A 7-year-old girl exhibited outward deviation of the eyes and restricted eye movements. Her parents observed that she had a divergent squint from birth. She had to turn her head to view objects on either side. Examination revealed vision of 6/9 in each eye with a refractive error of −1.50 DS in both eyes. The anterior segment and fundus appeared normal. Moderate drooping of the upper eyelids was noted in both eyes, with the presence of a lid crease in each eye.
test_results: Ocular examination revealed the presence of 70 PD of exotropia (on modified Krimsky test), with preference for right eye fixation though she could hold fixation well with each eye. Ocular movements revealed marked limitation of abduction (−4 on a scale of −4 to + 4) and adduction (−4 on a scale of −4 to + 4) in each eye, while elevation and depression were present. There was no demonstrable fusion or stereopsis.

case_report: The subject, a 27-year-old female from France, was evaluated for both auditory and visual functions. Historical records indicate a profound bilateral hearing loss identified at nine months old. She was born prior to the national neonatal universal hearing screening program. Concerns about her hearing were noted by her mother at four months old. Despite significant hearing loss, she used behind-the-ear hearing aids throughout her life, which allowed her to perceive environmental sounds. She utilized total communication methods and could understand speech through lip reading and cued speech. Speech therapy and schooling helped her learn speech language, though her speech intelligibility remained poor. She could not use oral communication with strangers in daily life, relying instead on sign language or written language. She achieved independent walking at two years old. The patient reported difficulties with night vision before the age of 10 and experienced frequent clumsiness and self-injury. At 27 years old, her visual acuity was measured at 7/10 in both eyes. Her visual field was significantly restricted, with a complete loss of peripheral vision, limited to the central 10-15 degrees as assessed by Goldmann field.
test_results: The audiometric assessment confirmed a bilateral symmetric profound group three hearing loss on pure tone audiometry according to the 02/1bis recommendation of the Bureau International d’Audiophonologie (BIAP). The vestibular assessment showed a bilateral areflexia in high and low frequencies (video head impulse test, rotational chair, and caloric videonystagmography). The vestibular score obtained from the computerized dynamic posturography sensory organization test was null; the visual score was decreased. Infrared reflectance imaging detected retinal vessel attenuation and pigmentary changes along the vascular arcades. On blue light autofluorescence imaging, cystic foveal lesions were hyper-autofluorescent, and outer retinal atrophy appeared as small hypo-autofluorescent areas in the mid-peripheral retina. A typical annular perifoveal ring was also observed in both eyes. Spectral domain optical coherence tomography disclosed cystic foveal lesions and remaining foveal ellipsoid zone. Outside the fovea, the outer nuclear layer, the ellipsoid zone, and the interdigitation zone lines disappeared. On full-field electroretinogram, rod and cones responses were severely reduced.

case_report: A 55-year-old male presented with a recurring, itchy rash on the scalp, forehead, face, and neck for the past seven years. Initially, the rash appeared as linearly distributed papules on the right side of the forehead and remained stable for about five years without symptoms, leading to no medical consultation. Over time, the rash spread in a linear pattern to the right side of the face, neck, and scalp, as well as the left side of the forehead and neck. The patient reported itching and noted that the lesions worsened with sun exposure. Hair loss was observed in the affected scalp areas. There was no family history of similar lesions. Physical examination revealed hyperkeratotic, skin-colored to hyperpigmented papules, both grouped and scattered, arranged in a linear pattern on the right forehead, right cheek, and left forehead. Some lesions had a violaceous hue but lacked whitish streaks on the surface. A similar pattern was observed on the right side of the neck. The lesions were not associated with erythema or scaling. Additional examination of the scalp revealed a few hyperkeratotic papulonodular eruptions on the vertex, with surrounding skin showing pigmented macules and slight atrophy, along with hair loss. Nail and oral mucosa examinations were normal.
test_results: The histopathological examination revealed a circumscribed area of hyperkeratosis with acantholytic dyskeratosis and suprabasal cleft formation. Within the focus, the epidermis showed scattered acantholytic dyskeratotic cells (corps ronds). The stratum corneum showed an array of parakeratotic dyskeratotic cells (grains). The underlying dermis showed sparse superficial perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate.

case_report: A 17-year-old male presented with multiple papules and nodules with necrosis on the trunk and limbs, persisting for one month. Initially, no visible red papules or nodules were present on the torso and limbs. Over time, papules and nodules measuring 0.8×0.4 cm appeared, increased in number, developed ulcerated, crusted surfaces, and were slightly itchy but painless. The patient was initially treated with compound indomethacin tincture and mometasone furoate cream twice daily for two weeks with poor results. Subsequently, at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi’an Jiaotong University, the patient was treated with clarithromycin (0.5 g orally once daily for one week) and corticosteroid cream (twice daily for two weeks). Throughout the disease course, the patient maintained normal spirit, food intake, night rest, and urinary function, with no significant changes in body weight. At age two, the patient experienced urticaria with severe itch, which subsided after treatment with calamine lotion. Similar urticarial lesions recurred every two years in summer or autumn, relieved by astemizole and calamine lotion. The patient's grandfather had psoriasis, with no other known genetic disorders in the family. Physical examination showed stable vital signs and no palpable enlargement of superficial lymph nodes. The examination revealed large red papules and nodules, 0.2–1.0 cm in diameter, scattered on the trunk and limbs, some with necrosis, ulceration, black crusts in the center, and white scales on the surface. Old lesions appeared as atrophic scars of various sizes with different degrees of pigmentation. The lesions were hard and non-tender upon palpation.
test_results: Histopathological examination showed that the patient had hyperkeratosis of the epidermis, dyskeratosis, acanthosis and dermal edema. In addition, dense, band-like lymphocytic infiltration was observed and a large number of atypical lymphocytes had infiltrated into the epidermis. The papillary layer of the dermis showed evident edema. Red blood cells appeared to be undergoing extravasation. Scattered malignant lymph cells infiltrated into the mid-dermis. Certain lymphocytes showed nuclear invagination with cerebriform nuclei. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated that this case was cluster of differentiation (CD)3-, CD4- and T-cell intracellular antigen-1 (TIA-1)-positive. The Ki67-positive rate was 70% and CD45RO was partially positive. In addition, the case was CD5-, CD8-, CD20- and CD30-negative and a small amount of CD79a was observed.

case_report: A one-day-old male infant, born at term with a birth weight of 3.1 kg, presented with no significant prenatal history and an uncomplicated delivery. Since birth, the infant had not passed stool and exhibited increased bilious vomiting and abdominal swelling. The anus was observed to be in a normal position with well-developed gluteal muscles and skin folds. The genital examination showed normally developed male genitalia with no visible signs of a fistula. The urine was clear and free from meconium contamination. A catheter could not be inserted more than half an inch into the anal opening. Imaging studies, including an echocardiogram, renal ultrasound, and vertebral X-ray, showed normal results with no indications of VACTERL association. An abdominal X-ray revealed multiple dilated bowel loops, including an S-shaped dilated loop of bowel extending downward toward the pelvis, indicative of the sigmoid colon.
test_results: Lower gastrointestinal fluoroscopy showed no contrast passage through the rectum, and the catheter tip met resistance at half an inch from the anal orifice.
diagnosis: Rectal atresia type 1b with a mucosal web
Orpha_name: Non-syndromic anorectal malformation with rectal atresia

case_report: A 26-year-old Japanese male experienced severe headache and nausea for about 3 weeks. He had a previous episode that involved convulsion-like symptoms. Imaging revealed a cystic nodular lesion approximately 60 mm in diameter in the left parietal lobe of the cerebrum. Medication was given, leading to symptom relief. However, 12 days later, his symptoms worsened, and he was admitted to the emergency department at the University of Miyazaki Hospital.
test_results: MRI showed a mass of 70 × 53 × 57 mm in the left temporoparietal lobe. A solid element with slight hypointensity on T1-weighted and hyperintensity on T2-weighted images along the dura mater was noted. Cystic changes were likely associated with the sanguineous fluid. A peritumoral band with hyperintensity on T2-weighted image was observed at the periphery of the lesion, suggesting an extra-axial lesion. A dural tail sign was also noted on the gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted image. The lesion appeared to be focally infiltrative to the brain surface, but no apparent connection to the ventricle was observed.

case_report: A 12-year-old male presented with decayed teeth in the upper and lower anterior regions. His early childhood was normal for the first two years, after which he experienced a lack of growth in height and weight, hair loss from the scalp and eyebrows, skin stretching, and difficulty standing or walking. Despite these physical changes, his mental development remained typical. He is currently receiving treatment for acute hepatitis. Two years prior, he visited the hospital for dental caries in the maxillary anterior but was uncooperative, so no treatment was administered. He is the second child of a nonconsanguineous marriage, with a normal sibling and no similar complaints in other family members. On examination, he appeared thin, poorly nourished, short-statured, with an abnormal gait, thin atrophic skin, loss of subcutaneous fat around the extremities, and skin that was coarse, stretched, shiny, and thickened. His chest showed a pectus carinatum structure. Systemic examination noted impaired vision, slurred speech, memory loss, breathlessness, palpitations, and restricted joint movements, making it difficult for him to stand or walk. Extraoral examination revealed mild frontal bossing, a beaked nose, protruding eyes, a high-pitched voice, and hypoplastic maxilla and mandible with a mild mid-facial deformity. Mouth opening was restricted (interincisal distance of 21 mm), and lateral movements of the temporomandibular joint were also limited. Intraoral examination showed teeth of normal size relative to the small jaw, fractured crown at tooth 11, root stumps at teeth 12, 15, 16, 21, and 22, and dental caries at teeth 13, 14, 23, 24, 25, 31, 32, 41, 42, and 45. A high arched palate and partial anodontia were also observed.
test_results: Biochemical investigations showed increased serum cholesterol which was 228 mg% and increased urinary excretion of hyaluronic acid. OPG revealed hypoplastic maxilla, hypoplastic mandible with infantile angle, and multiple missing teeth. The morphology of the condyle appeared to be altered.

case_report: An 8-year-old boy, born to healthy parents with no consanguinity, presented with various craniofacial, oral, and digital abnormalities. His antenatal and birth history were unremarkable, with a birth weight of 2500 g and a length of 50 cm. There was no family history of congenital malformations, mental illness, skeletal anomalies, or miscarriages. Abnormal facial features and missing toes were observed at birth, and hearing impairment was identified later. Developmental milestones were delayed, with the patient beginning to walk at two and a half years old. A cochlear implant was placed at 2 years and 9 months to address the hearing deficit. At 8 years old, he visited the dental department due to multiple missing teeth. Examination revealed dyscephaly with frontal bossing, mild malar and mandibular hypoplasia, hypertelorism, a broad nasal root, down-slanting palpebral fissures, macrostomia, low-set ears, choanal atresia, hypoplastic alae nasi, a long philtrum, and a thin-pinched nose. Digital anomalies included the absence of the third, fourth, and fifth toes and syndactyly in the left foot, while other limbs appeared normal. His intelligence quotient (IQ) was measured between 45-50, and he exhibited a poor response to his surroundings. Intraoral examination showed a high palatal vault, oligodontia, enamel hypoplasia, high frenal attachment in the maxilla, and ankyloglossia.
test_results: Panoramic radiograph showed multiple missing permanent teeth including maxillary and mandibular lateral incisors and canines. Tooth germs for all the permanent second and third molars were absent. The anteroposterior (AP) skull view revealed dyscephaly with frontal prominence. Foot-ankle radiograph revealed agenesis of third, fourth and fifth toes and syndactyly involving the first and second toes with complete soft tissue fusion without bony fusion.

case_report: A 60-year-old Caucasian female patient presented with a three-month history of actinic keratosis on the right chest, confirmed by biopsy. She was prescribed Imiquimod 5% cream for topical application, five times per week. After two weeks of treatment, the patient developed fever, diarrhea, myalgia, and fatigue, along with exulceration of the initial lesion and the appearance of erythematous papulosquamous lesions on the scalp, face, and trunk. The treatment was subsequently discontinued. Laboratory tests showed no abnormalities. Despite the use of topical corticosteroids and oral antihistamines, the skin eruption worsened, spreading in a craniocaudal direction and the lesions began to merge. Prednisone was initiated at a dose of 40 mg per day.
test_results: Psoriasiform hyperplasia of the epidermis, hyperparakeratosis alternated with orthokeratosis, areas of hypogranulosis, moderate superficial perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate, and foci of acantholytic dyskeratosis were observed.

case_report: A 55-year-old Japanese male presented with speech difficulties and coordination issues affecting the eyes, trunk, and limbs, progressively worsening over the past 4 years. His parents were consanguineous. Imaging studies, including a chest CT scan and brain MRI angiography, showed no abnormalities. A 123I IMP-SPECT scan did not reveal reduced circulation in the cerebellum, but stereotactic surface projections indicated slightly reduced circulation in the frontal and temporal lobes. Physical examination revealed loose, sagging skin over most of his body. Fundoscopy showed peripapillary atrophy of the retina without other changes such as angioid streaks or peau d’orange.
test_results: Laboratory data found coagulation abnormalities with a prothrombin time of 27.7 seconds (normal, 10–11 seconds), a prothrombin time-international normalized ratio of 4.07 (normal, 1.0), and an activated partial thromboplastin time of 49.7 seconds (normal, 30–40 seconds); low vitamin K-associated coagulation factors activities with factor II, 17%; factor VII, 6%; factor IX, 23%; and factor X, 12%; and urine abnormalities with protein, 2+; sugar, 2+; and occult blood, 2+.

case_report: A 31-year-old G1P0 woman experienced polyhydramnios at 22 weeks with an amniotic fluid volume of 11.5 cm. This condition led to the preterm birth of a male infant at 29 weeks. The newborn weighed 1480 g (P85), measured 38.5 cm in length (P50), and had a head circumference of 26.5 cm (P61). Immediately after birth, the infant exhibited polyuria with an average output of 5.8 ml/kg.h, followed by dehydration and a rapid weight loss of 25% by the fourth day. Persistent hyponatremia, hypokalemia, and hypochloremia were observed with Na+ at 129 mmol/L, K+ at 2.95 mmol/L, and Cl− at 94 mmol/L, necessitating intravenous fluids and supplemental electrolytes. Elevated renin and angiotensin levels were recorded (PRA1 > 12 ng/ml/h, AT-II1 > 800 pg/ml). Severe hypercalciuria was identified with a urine calcium:creatinine ratio of 1147.8 mg/g Cr, leading to medullary nephrocalcinosis. Metabolic alkalosis developed with a maximal pH of 7.521, BE of 7.8 mmol/L, and HCO3− of 31.1 mmol/L. Blood magnesium levels remained normal. Hearing tests via Otoacoustic emissions (OAE) and Auditory brainstem response (ABR) were passed. There was no family history of similar symptoms. The infant received parenteral nutrition with Na+ (up to 4 mmol/kg) and K+ (up to 4.4 mmol/kg) until 21 days after birth, followed by oral 15% KCl solution (2 ml, three times daily, gradually reduced after 3 weeks) and spironolactone (2 mg/d) for about 1 month. Symptoms gradually improved, with neonatal polyuria normalizing within 4 days and metabolic alkalosis resolving after 1 month. By 2 months, serum electrolytes were stable without oral supplements, and renin and angiotensin levels normalized (PRA1 0.79 ng/ml/h, AT-II1 82.33 pg/ml). Kidney ultrasound showed improvement in medullary nephrocalcinosis. At a corrected gestational age of 42 weeks, the infant weighed 3890 g (P40), measured 53 cm in length (P51), and had a head circumference of 35.5 cm (P53). Follow-up evaluations were conducted every 12 months. At 4 years old, the child's height was 106.4 cm, and weight was 15.8 kg. Complete blood tests and kidney function tests were normal (Hgb 122 g/L, Na 138 mmol/L, K 4.0 mmol/L, Cl 103 mmol/L, creatinine 31 μmol/L). Kidney ultrasound revealed normal size and structure.
test_results: On analysis of MAGED2 gene, a variation(c.1598C > T, p.Ala533Val) detected by Next generation sequencing was confirmed by Sanger sequencing analyses. This patient is hemizygous and his mother was a heterozygous carrier.
diagnosis: Transient antenatal Bartter’s syndrome due to a novel MAGED2 variant

case_report: A 30-year-old Vietnamese female presented with fatigue, muscle weakness, memory loss, unintentional weight gain, hair loss, and amenorrhea. She has a history of microprolactinoma identified on a recent pituitary MRI, which was treated with cabergoline. A follow-up pituitary MRI was normal, leading to the discontinuation of cabergoline. She is not on any medications and has no known allergies. Her family history includes diabetes and coronary artery disease, and she has not undergone any surgeries. Physical examination showed a blood pressure of 132/80 with other vital signs within normal limits. Notable findings included facial acne, hirsutism, a round face, lipodystrophy, central obesity, and muscle wasting in the lower extremities. There was no evidence of thyromegaly. Heart auscultation revealed normal sounds without murmurs, and lung auscultation showed normal breath sounds. The abdomen was distended and nontender with thick purple striae. She also had ecchymosis and striae on the upper extremities. Laboratory results showed a morning cortisol level of 53.6 mcg/dL (reference range: 4.3-22.4 mcg/dL) and ACTH level of 147 pg/mL (reference range: 0-46 pg/mL). Midnight salivary cortisol was 2.54 mcg/dL (reference range: <0.09 mcg/dL) and 24-hour urine cortisol was 4405 mcg/24h (reference range: 4-55 mcg/24h). Corticotropin releasing factor was 1.9 pg/mL (reference range: <10 pg/mL). White cell count was 13 x10^9/L (reference range: 4.0-10.0 x10^9/L) and TSH was 0.05 mIU/L (reference range: 0.55-4.78 mIU/L) with a normal free T4 of 1.1 ng/dL (reference range: 0.9-1.8 ng/dL). Serum potassium was 3.3 mmol/L (reference range: 3.5-4.5 mmol/L). Glycosylated hemoglobin was 6.4%, and insulin-like growth factor was within normal limits. Prolactin, luteinizing hormone, and follicular stimulating hormone levels were normal. Other laboratory tests, including electrolytes, renal function, and blood counts, were normal. A low-dose 1mg and high-dose 8mg dexamethasone suppression test did not suppress cortisol levels. Review of her brain MRI from Vietnam and post-treatment with cabergoline by a neuroradiologist did not show a microprolactinoma. Screening for multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndrome was negative.
test_results: A chest x-ray identified two left upper lobe lung masses. A computed tomography (CT) guided lung biopsy confirmed well-differentiated NET. The lung biopsy stained positive for synaptophysin, chromogranin, and pancytokeratin. The Ki-67 proliferation index was low <2%. Positron emission tomography showed hypermetabolic activity within the lung masses, left hilum, and mediastinal lymph nodes. Hypermetabolic activity in the right anterior second rib was evident. Mild metabolic activity in the medial limb of the left adrenal gland was present. Octreotide scan showed increased radiotracer uptake within the lung masses and corresponding lymph nodes.
diagnosis: Cushing Syndrome secondary to primary neuroendocrine lung carcinoma
Orpha_name: Cushing syndrome due to ectopic ACTH secretion

case_report: A 5-year-old girl with no notable past medical history presented with ongoing right ear discharge and a polyp in the external auditory canal. Imaging showed congestion in the middle ear cavities and bone loss in the petrous bone. Tissue analysis indicated inflammatory changes. Symptoms worsened, including severe ear infection, increasing facial paralysis, swelling behind the ear, and new neurological signs.
test_results: Initial computed tomography (CT) scan revealed congestion of the middle ear cavities with osteolysis of the petrous bone. The CT scan revealed a significant osteolysis of the petrous bone, mastoid and temporal bone with homolateral meningeal and cerebral extension. Histologically, the tumor was composed of spindle cell proliferation with an alternation of hypocellular zones and cellular zones associated with haemangiopericytic and nodular architecture. Tumor cells have elongated or round nuclei with fine chromatin and small nucleolus. Mitosis figures are rare. Polymorphic inflammatory reaction rich in giant cells was observed. At the immunohistochemistry, tumor cells were positive for smooth muscle actin (SMA) and negative for Desmin, Myogenin, CD34 and anaplastic lymphoma kinase ALK.

case_report: A 60-year-old male with a five-year history of elevated red blood cell count presented to our department in 2020. Over the past five years, he had been treated with hydroxyurea and phlebotomy, which provided moderate relief but frequent recurrence of symptoms. In 2019, he tested positive for IgA-κ. Upon admission, his oxygen saturation was 94%. Physical examination revealed telangiectasis on his face, chest, and back, as well as skin pigmentation on his face and lips. Blood tests showed elevated red blood cell count (RBC 7.13×10^12/L, HGB 151g/L). Laboratory results indicated increased erythropoietin level (676.16 mIU/mL) and monoclonal protein presence (M protein 5.10g/L, IgA-κ(+)). Additionally, elevated levels of IL-6, IL-8, and TNFα were observed.
test_results: A bone marrow biopsy showed 1.5% of plasma cells. Enhanced computed tomography (CT) revealed moderate amount of perinephric fluid and small amount of abdominal and pelvic fluid. Doppler bubble test indicated intrapulmonary shunt, while the result of lung perfusion scintigraphy (LPS) with Tc-99m MAA was unremarkable.

case_report: A 10-year-old female was referred by a urologist for evaluation of hypertension. Her right kidney, which was smaller in size, was removed four months prior. On the day of admission, her brachial blood pressure was recorded at 190/90 mmHg. A Doppler ultrasound study revealed a parvus-tardus pattern in the left kidney without any evidence of stenosis, extending to the aorta. Examination of the abdominal aorta showed a stenotic region just after the emergence of the celiac artery from the aorta.
test_results: CT angiography demonstrated a 20.3 mm aortic stenosis zone that started just after the emergence of celiac artery. Both left renal artery and inferior mesenteric artery originated from the stenotic region. The origin of the left renal artery had a 3.7 mm diameter without any stenosis through its length.

case_report: A 57-year-old male presented for a dermatological examination of two adjacent pigmented lesions located on the glans and the inner foreskin. These lesions had been present for an extended period and exhibited slow growth over the years. The lesions were well-defined, oval-shaped pigmented macules with a color range from brown to black and a smooth surface. They appeared as two symmetrical nevi in relation to the coronal sulcus. Dermoscopic analysis revealed a pattern with large globules in the central area and a peripheral pigment network. Confocal microscopy showed various dendritic cells in the epidermis, indicating cellular activity. Two incisional biopsies were performed at both anatomical sites to exclude malignancy and consider conservative treatment.
test_results: The histological examination of the samples revealed similar microscopic features in both samples, showing an intradermal melanocytic proliferation with congenital features and a minimal junctional component. Melanocytes were arranged in nests in the upper dermis while splaying between dermal collagen bundles in the reticular dermis. Stromal melanin deposits were more abundant in the upper part of the lesion, as were dermal melanophages. Melanocytic aggregates protruding within a vascular channel with an empty and dilated lumen lined by flattened endothelial cells were also observed. Immunohistochemical analysis using antibodies for Melanoma Marker HMB45 and Microphthalmia Transcription Factor confirmed that the neoformation was of melanocytic origin.

case_report: A 38-year-old male was admitted to the Neurology Department at the Hillel Yaffe Medical Center with a severe headache lasting two days, accompanied by dizziness and confusion. Physical and neurological examinations were unremarkable. Brain CT scan results were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a protein level of 110 mg/dL, glucose level of 66 mg/dL, presence of 2 lymphocytes, and negative results for oligoclonal bands. EEG indicated slight symmetric slowing of background activity. The patient received IV acyclovir treatment. Two days post-admission, persistent bradycardia with P wave changes on EKG was observed, lasting approximately two weeks. Cardiac transesophageal echocardiography showed normal results. Three days after admission, mild right-sided neurological signs were observed, including slight speech disturbance and reduced fluency. Brain CT angiography was normal. Five days later, the patient reported blurred vision in the right eye. Fundoscopy did not reveal arterial wall plaques. Visual field examination identified a small central scotoma in the right eye, and ocular coherence tomography showed inner retinal layer edema below the fovea.
test_results: Fluorescein angiography of the right eye disclosed central retinal artery branch occlusion.

case_report: A 5-year-old Korean boy presented with blisters and erosions on the palms and soles. These symptoms had been recurring since infancy following minimal mechanical trauma. Physical examination revealed several bullae vesicles with crusts and erosions on both soles, as well as a vesicle on the fingertip. The oral mucosa was unaffected. All affected areas were limited to sites prone to trauma. Similar occurrences were noted in the family history, involving his younger sister and father.
test_results: A skin biopsy revealed a large intraepidermal vesicle in the suprabasal layer with scanty inflammation of the dermal portion. Mutational analysis of the patient and parental DNA showed a thymine-to-cytosine transition mutation in codon 608 of exon 2 in the KRT5 gene in the patient and his father only. Identical digestion patterns were observed for the patient and his father in an RFLP analysis with Pst I, but the patterns differed for his mother and the control group.

case_report: A 56-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a fever of unknown origin, accompanied by chest and lumbar pain persisting for the past four months. She also experienced intermittent episodes of nausea and vomiting. Her medical history includes arterial hypertension, obesity, and a previous episode of deep vein thrombosis in the lower limbs. During the physical examination, her heart rate was recorded at 104 beats per minute, and her blood pressure was 160/84 mmHg in the right arm and 164/86 mmHg in the left arm. Thoracic auscultation revealed no significant findings, and the radial, humeral, femoral, and pedal pulses were normal. Laboratory tests indicated a glomerular sedimentation rate of 53 IU/L and a C-reactive protein level of 22.6 IU/L. The complete blood count showed no abnormalities. Additionally, the metabolic profile, syphilis (VDRL) test, and immunological profile, including tests for lupus, ANCA, and IgG4, were all within normal limits.
test_results: This study showed a concentric hypo attenuated and thicked lesion of 1.2 cm at the proximal ascending thoracic aorta and dense tissue with scant enhancement surrounding the aorta compatible with peri aortitis extending from the ascending aorta, aortic arch, subclavian, and infrarenal aorta to the common iliac arteries. Transesophageal echocardiography showed diffuse wall thickening from the proximal ascending aorta to the proximal third of the descending aorta (maximum thickness of 15 mm). The circumferential involvement was evidenced in the tri-planar image of the thoracic aorta. Mild aortic regurgitation was found. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), in the T1 sequence showed a thickened ascending aorta wall (13mm) with a hypointense signal and enhancement of the descending aortic wall after administration of intravenous contrast and in the T2 sequence, evidenced a hyperintense area circumferential to the aorta, extending from the ascending aorta, the aortic arch, and the descending aorta, compatible with an inflammatory process.

case_report: A 76-year-old woman with a medical history of an ovarian dermoid cyst removed at age 39 underwent a routine abdominal ultrasound at age 73. The ultrasound revealed an approximately 3-cm mass in the pancreas. A follow-up CT scan identified a 3.2-cm solid and partially hypervascular mass located in the pancreatic uncinate process.
test_results: The diagnosis of NET was supported by enhanced uptake at 68-Ga-DOTATOC PET and confirmed through endoscopic ultrasound biopsy. Histological examination of the mass documented 'three different foci of G1-NET of the pancreatic head (according to WHO 2010), respectively, 2.9, 0.6, and 0.5 cm; Ki67: 1%–2%; mitotic index: <1 mitosis/10 HPF; angioinvasion present, no necrosis or neural invasion detected; and no lymph nodes involved'. The analysis showed a missense heterozygous variant in exon 2 of CDKN1B (c.482C>G, p.S161C). It is present in population databases (rs373917399, ExAC 0.04%) and has an allele count higher than expected for a pathogenic variant. The Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD) reported an allele frequency of 0.00014.

case_report: The patient is a 17-year-old blind female who visited the sleep medicine clinic with a history of four years of insomnia that did not respond to treatment. During the initial visit, she reported no issues with falling asleep but frequently woke up during the night and could not go back to sleep. Her sleep problems varied over months, with periods of no disturbance alternating with worsening sleep. She had tried various treatments including melatonin (both immediate and sustained release), eszopiclone, zolpidem, sublingual vitamin B12, clonidine, trazodone, valerian root, and gabapentin, which were either temporarily effective or ineffective. At the initial evaluation, her medications included naproxen, topiramate, and magnesium for migraines, along with 5 mg immediate release melatonin and 100 to 300 mg gabapentin for insomnia. Socially, she attended high school full time, maintained a consistent routine with a bedtime of 10 PM and wake time of 6 AM on both weekdays and weekends, and was not employed outside of school. She reported a long-standing urge to move her legs, which worsened at night, improved with movement, and kept her awake several nights a week. She was taking 100 to 300 mg gabapentin nightly for this issue, which helped intermittently, but she still experienced the urge to move her legs some nights, waking her up after initially falling asleep. Higher doses of gabapentin were not tolerated due to residual daytime sleepiness. Magnesium was also tried for this condition but was ineffective. She had a history of heavy menstrual periods starting at age 12 but no diagnosis of anemia. The patient had bilateral retinoblastoma diagnosed at one year of age, treated with bilateral enucleation. At age 13, polysomnography showed a wake time after sleep onset of 83 minutes and a sleep efficiency of 76 percent. The periodic limb movement index was elevated at 12/hour, with an associated arousal index of 8/hour and a connection to nocturnal awakenings. Respiratory parameters were normal, with no signs of central or obstructive sleep apnea.
test_results: Over the 14-day recording period, the patient exhibited a pattern of progressively delayed bed times followed by a compensatory night of going to bed early.

case_report: A 47-year-old Caucasian woman was admitted to our Rheumatology Unit with a 6-month history of progressively appearing tender, ill-defined hard swellings on the right leg and abdominal wall, accompanied by severe erythema in the overlying skin and intermittent fever up to 39°C, unresponsive to antipyretics and antibiotics. During admission, the patient exhibited fever up to 39°C, multiple tender erythematous swellings on the abdominal wall and right leg, and several palpable lymphadenopathies in the abdomen, neck, and right groin. She reported no drug abuse, recent travel, or use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Laboratory tests showed microcytic hypochromic anemia with hemoglobin at 9.8 gm/dL, mean corpuscular volume at 69 fl, and leucopenia with neutropenia (WBCs 1.3 × 10^3/L; N 48.3%, L 43.8%, M 3.8%, E 0.4%, B 2.2%). Thrombocytopenia (up to 67,000/µL) was briefly observed during recovery. Elevated liver enzymes were noted: alanine transaminase (ALT) at 104 IU/L (normal range, 2-40), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 91 IU/L (normal range, 2-40), with an AST/ALT ratio < 1, and gamma GT at 67 IU/L (normal range, 7-38). The serum lipid profile showed slightly high levels of triglycerides, total cholesterol, and low-density lipoprotein. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 17 mm/h, and C reactive protein (CRP) was 0.05 mg/dL. Immunoglobulin assay revealed high levels of IgM at 443 mg/dL (normal range, 40-230) and IgE at 857 mg/dL (normal range, 2-200). Complement 3, complement 4, cryoglobulin levels, serum lipase, serum amylase, α-1 antitrypsin, procalcitonin, haptoglobin, creatine phosphokinase, creatinine, azotemia, serum glucose concentration, bilirubin and bilirubin fraction, serum corrected calcium, and alkaline phosphatase were within normal ranges. Antithrombin was mildly elevated at 165% (normal range, 70-130). Severe hypofibrinogenemia at 40 mg/dL (normal range, 200-450) and high levels of D-dimer at 23,701 µg/mL (normal range, 0-500) were detected. A 24-hour urinary sample showed moderate proteinuria (1.6 gm/24 h). Elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) at 500 IU/L (normal range, 40-250) and beta-2 microglobulin at 7.34 µg/mL (normal range, 0.8-2.7) were observed. Partial thromboplastin time (PTT) was shorter, while prothrombin time and iron profile were normal. Albumin level was 3.2 gm/dL. Hypergammaglobulinemia (23.78%) was noted by protein electrophoresis. Serum and urine immunofixation were negative for free light chains. TORCH screening, tuberculosis screening, Coxsackie IgM, Brucella IgG and IgM, Borrelia IgG and IgM, and Parvovirus B19 were negative. Antinuclear antibodies, lupus anticoagulant screening, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, cryoglobulin, and antiphospholipid antibodies were negative. Viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, metabolic factors, in-born or hereditary disorders (Wilson disease, lipodystrophy), drug and toxin associations with high liver enzymes, excessive alcohol consumption, obesity, and diabetes mellitus were excluded. Sonography and computed tomographic scans of the neck, chest, and abdomen revealed mild hepatosplenomegaly, widespread lymphadenopathy, and left pleural effusion. Echocardiography detected a small pericardial effusion with normal ejection fraction and preserved systolic function. The endocrine and genital organs and the breast showed no clinical abnormalities.
test_results: Surgical skin sample showed lobular panniculitis with a lymph-histiocytic and neutrophilic infiltrates with necrosis of adipocytes. Bone marrow biopsy displayed a discrete hypercellular bone marrow with an increase of megakaryocytic proliferation and low grade of dysmorphia of myeloid cells. A widespread boost of stromal fibers was noticed at silver impregnation. The marrow changes were reactive and did not reflect a myelodysplastic syndrome. Axillary lymph-node biopsy confirmed a reactive lymphadenopathy. The liver biopsy evidenced a macro-vesicular steatosis with hepatocytes ballooning. Spotty necrosis, scattered mixed neutrophilic-lymphocytic inflammation, Mallory hyaline, and perisinusoidal fibrosis were absent.

case_report: A 64-year-old male presented with severe left facial pain. His medical history includes a stomach ulcer and arterial hypertension, managed with omeprazole 20 mg orally every 12 hours and torasemide 10 mg orally every 24 hours, respectively. Three years ago, he was treated for trigeminal neuralgia with carbamazepine 200 mg orally every 8 hours and pregabalin 75 mg orally every 8 hours. Over the past four months, the intensity and frequency of his pain increased, significantly impacting his daily life. The patient appeared in poor general condition and exhibited signs of depression. Twenty days prior, he began taking indomethacin 25 mg orally every 12 hours but discontinued it due to lack of improvement. The pain was described as electric and stabbing, rated 10/10 on the visual analog scale (VAS), and located in the orbital, periorbital, frontal, and upper maxillary regions on the left side of the face. The pain occurred spontaneously and was also triggered by activities such as speaking, chewing, swallowing, sneezing, shaving, and light contact with the left side of the face. He experienced 20 to 100 attacks per day, with a recent increase in frequency affecting his sleep. Continuous mild discomfort was noted between attacks. During the visit, a pain episode was observed, accompanied by conjunctival injection and tearing of the left eye.
test_results: The neurological evaluation and magnetic resonance imaging scan showed no anomalies.

case_report: A 3-year-old boy, born to non-consanguineous parents of Chinese/Malaysian ethnicity, presented at 2 months of age with acute respiratory distress requiring mechanical ventilation. An X-ray showed interstitial pneumonitis. Bronchoalveolar lavage identified Pneumocystis jirovecii via PCR and immunofluorescence. He was treated with co-trimoxazole and fully recovered. Immunological evaluation at that time showed normal immunoglobulin levels, with CD4+ and CD8+ lymphopenia. The CD8+ count normalized quickly, but CD4+ lymphopenia persisted until 5 months of age. CD19+ B cell and NK cell numbers were normal, although B cell numbers increased and remained high (2.5–6.0 × 10^9/L, reference range 0.2–2.1 × 10^9/L). T cell immunophenotyping showed no abnormalities. Mitogen-specific T-cell blastogenesis with phytohemagglutinin (PHA) was preserved; however, T-cell stimulation with anti-CD3 in early life was absent, and stimulation with anti-CD3/anti-CD28 at 9 months of age was reduced threefold compared to a control sample. At 7 months, he exhibited global developmental delay and was hypertonic floppy with normal deep tendon reflexes and a normal brain MRI. These features improved slowly with intensive support from physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and dieticians. He experienced failure to thrive with frequent vomiting, necessitating a gastrostomy at 10 months of age. Endoscopy showed a thickened pyloric antrum. He developed erythematous papules and vesicles on his limbs. Skin biopsy revealed superficial subcorneal neutrophil microabscess formation with superficial and deep dermal and subcutaneous neutrophilia. Neutrophils were also present in a sweat duct lumen. There was no evidence of vasculitis, although interstitial leukocytoclasis was present. The acral papules resolved around 9 months, while his extremities showed a livedo racemosa pattern. At presentation, he had elevated inflammatory markers, which normalized during routine follow-up (CRP < 3 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate < 14 mm/h). The patient was managed with prophylactic co-trimoxazole and immunoglobulin replacement as a primary immunodeficiency. He did not experience further significant infections. Co-trimoxazole was stopped at 2 years of age, and immunoglobulin replacement was stopped at 21 months of age, after which he remained infection-free. He underwent routine immunization and showed adequate post-vaccination serological responses. At 33 months, he experienced a pulmonary hypertensive crisis episode characterized by hypoxia following minor stimulation. Electrocardiogram suggested right ventricular hypertrophy, confirmed by echocardiogram, which showed suprasystemic pulmonary hypertension and a pressure-loaded right ventricle. A cardiac echocardiogram at 21 months was normal. High-resolution computed tomography of the chest was abandoned due to hypertensive crises on stimulation. He was started on sildenafil, a pulmonary-specific vasodilator.
test_results: This identified a novel de novo missense variant c.852G>T in exon 7 of 8 in the gene TMEM173, encoding p.Arg284Ser in the protein STING. The variant was confirmed by Sanger sequencing, and is not present in the Exac database. In silico analysis predicted the mutation to be pathogenic based on; the physiochemical difference between arginine and serine (Grantham score 110); SIFT prediction (deleterious), PolyPhen (probably damaging), CADD (scaled = 26.7), mutation taster (disease causing), and Provean (deleterious).
diagnosis: Atypical STING-Associated Vasculopathy with Onset in Infancy
Orpha_name: STING-associated vasculopathy with onset in infancy

case_report: The patient is a 6-month-old male child born to a non-consanguineous, phenotypically normal couple. He was delivered at 39 weeks of gestation via cesarean section with a birth weight of 2,820 grams. At 6 months, his weight was 5.6 kg (<3rd percentile), his height was 63 cm (<3rd percentile), and his head circumference was 46 cm (90th percentile). The patient exhibited poor growth and developmental delays, including the absence of social smiling and maternal recognition by 12 months of age. Mild dysmorphic features were noted. Echocardiography, electromyography, hematological and biochemical tests for renal and liver function were normal, and screening for inborn errors of metabolism showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Conventional cytogenetic analysis of the proband revealed an abnormal male karyotype, 46,XY,der(11)t(1;11)(q41;p15.5). The array CGH for the proband revealed that the breakpoint of a contiguous duplication on the long arm of chromosome 1 was located in 1q41 band. We also observed two BAC clone deletions on the short arm (11p15.5) of chromosome 11. FISH analysis confirmed the breakpoint of a contiguous duplication on the long arm of chromosome 1 was located between BAC_4527 and BAC_7952. The skipped duplication pattern by the array CGH around at 1q43 region was proved to be false by FISH with 1q43 probe. The deletion of 11p15.5 predicted by the array CGH was also confirmed by FISH.

case_report: A 23-month-old girl was admitted to the hospital with a history of jaundice lasting over a year. She was born at 30 weeks of gestation and has distinct facial features, including double pointed ears, a slightly protruding jaw, and hollow eyes. Since the age of 6 months, elevated levels of total serum bilirubin (TB), direct bilirubin (DB), and total bile acid (TBA) have been noted (Table). Upon hospitalization, her weight was 9.8 kg (P12) and her height was 76 cm (P0). Physical examination revealed mild jaundice of the skin, moderate jaundice of the sclera, and pruritus. The liver was palpable 4.5 cm below the right costal margin, and the spleen was palpable 2 cm below the left costal margin. No abnormalities were detected in the lungs and heart.
test_results: Hepatobiliary radionuclide imaging showed biliary obstruction. Ultrasound indicated hepatomegaly. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) was normal.

case_report: A 30-year-old woman presented with diarrhea and sudden upper abdominal pain. She had no known personal or family history of cancer and no previous medical interventions. An ultrasound examination identified a highly echogenic lesion in liver segment VI. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan of the abdomen revealed a 12 cm x 9 cm pericholecystic fluid collection and irregular thickening of the gallbladder wall. The patient underwent an open surgical procedure, including cholecystectomy and resection of liver segments V and VI. Gross examination of the liver resection showed a 13.5 cm tumor-forming lesion with an irregular, grey surface, exhibiting areas of crumbling, suppuration, and induration near the gallbladder. The gallbladder measured 6.7 cm in length, had a wall thickness of up to 3 cm, and contained yellow concretions.
test_results: Histological examination revealed a highly pleomorphic, highly proliferative, overtly malignant tumor with hyperchromasia, atypical mitotic figures, eosinophilic cytoplasm, and prominent nucleoli. Geographic necrosis, multinucleated tumor giant cells and abundant neutrophilic infiltrate were present. The tumor infiltrated the gallbladder wall and adjacent adipose tissue, as well as the liver. The gallbladder epithelium displayed atypia with an increased nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio, hyperchromasia, and loss of nuclear polarity, characteristic of high-grade biliary intraepithelial neoplasia. Focal gland formation was observed. Immunohistochemistry revealed positivity for cytokeratin 8 and vimentin. Immunohistochemical stains against TTF-1, HepPar1, PAX8, OCT3/4, CEA, BerEp4, estrogen receptor, cytokeratins 7 and 20, as well as CDX2 and ErbB2 were negative. Ki-67-proliferation rate was over 95 %. PBRM1- and SMARCA2-expression were lost in the carcinoma but retained in the associated high-grade biliary intraepithelial neoplasia. SMARCA4, SMARCB1 (INI-1), and ARID1A were retained. PDL-1 was strongly expressed in 80 % of tumor cells as well as in some inflammatory cells. Next-generation-sequencing detected a KRAS mutation (p.Gly12Asp; allele frequency 29,5 %), a deleterious splice-site mutation in the POLE-gene (NM_006231:c.4729-1G > A; allele frequency 7,3 %) and a TP53 splice site mutation (allele frequency 17,9 %). A variant of unknown significance in the SMARCA4-gene (NM_003072:p.Leu1063Val; allele frequency 14,5 %) was discovered. PBRM1 and ARID1B mutations were detected. The mutations were verified using another NGS panel (Illumina TruSight Tumor 500-Panel) using two different tumor areas.
diagnosis: SWI/SNF-deficient undifferentiated/rhabdoid carcinoma of the gallbladder

case_report: A 23-year-old woman from Spain presented in September 2007 with elevated serum ferritin levels. At the age of 15, she had noted changes in hepatic enzyme levels. Laboratory results showed values for liver transaminases (Aspartate transaminase (AST) and Alanine transaminase (ALT)), serum ferritin, serum iron, transferrin saturation, and hepcidin, as detailed in the accompanying table. Tests ruled out Hepatitis B and C infections. Genetic analysis revealed a homozygous HFE H63D variation, with no additional genetic changes found in the HFE, HFE2, HAMP, or SLC40A1 genes. There was no reported family history of iron-related disorders, although her father had passed away due to a hepatic viral condition.
test_results: Liver biopsy revealed massive iron deposition in the liver parenchyma with moderate fibrosis. The hepatic iron concentration measured by quantitative Magnetic Resonance Imaging was of 267 μmol/g dry weight.

case_report: A 2-year-old male patient underwent surgery at the Department of Orthopaedics, Tianjin Paediatric Hospital. The right hand and left foot exhibited specific characteristics, and there was skin webbing between the 3rd and 4th fingers of the left hand. Among four other affected family members (great-grandmother, granduncle, grandfather, and father), variations in physical presentation were observed. Their hands showed similar characteristics. None of the affected individuals displayed craniofacial abnormalities.
test_results: A novel autosomal dominant heterozygous GLI3 variant, NC_000007.14(NM_000168.5):c.1622C > T; p.(Thr541Met), located in exon 11, was identified by Sanger sequencing of the patient’s gDNA sample. His father and grandfather are heterozygous for the mutation, and his great-grandmother has passed away. This variant was predicted to be most likely damaging, with a score of 1 (sensitivity: 0; specificity: 1) by Polyphen 2. Moreover, it is forecast to affect protein function, with a score of 0.00 according to SIFT. The GLI3 variant is highly conserved in the evolution of various species.

case_report: The patient, a 12-month-old boy, was the third child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents. He had two healthy sisters aged 5 and 4 years. Born at 35 weeks of gestational age via vaginal delivery without asphyxia, his birth weight was 2342 g (0.0 SD), length 45.2 cm (0.0 SD), and head circumference 33.4 cm (1.2 SD). The placental weight was 850 g. From birth, the patient experienced oliguria, and by the 5th day, his serum creatinine level was elevated to 2.63 mg/dl. Hypoalbuminemia (2.1 g/dl) and proteinuria (3+ on dipstick) were detected. He was transferred to our hospital at 6 days old. Upon admission, he was alert with stable vital signs: respiratory rate 37/min, heart rate 149/min, and blood pressure 84/54 mmHg. Bilateral microcoria and nystagmus were observed. His body posture and voluntary movements were normal, with normal muscular tone and brisk deep tendon reflexes. Laboratory tests showed an increased urine protein/creatinine ratio of 95.1 mg/mg Cre. Renal ultrasonography revealed hyperechoic signals in both kidneys with unclear cortico-medullary structures. Continuous hemodiafiltration was initiated at 7 days old and replaced by peritoneal dialysis from 12 days old. He became anuric and continued peritoneal dialysis thereafter. These therapies allowed him to survive the first 12 months. At 6 months, recurrent vomiting led to a diagnosis of intestinal malrotation, which was surgically corrected. However, vomiting persisted due to gastroesophageal reflux. Duodenal tube feeding was introduced but provided insufficient nutrition for weight gain over the 12-month follow-up. Tulobuterol (0.2 mg/day) was administered orally from 12 months, resulting in the cessation of vomiting and subsequent weight gain, reaching 5300 g (+300 g) in the last month. Thyroid function tests showed serum thyroid stimulating hormone at 2.70 μIU/mL and free thyroxine at 1.48 ng/dL, which remained stable. Neurological assessments indicated that he began gazing at and following objects from 2 months old, but generalized muscle weakness and hypotonia became evident from 3 months old. At 12 months, his developmental quotient score was less than 20, equivalent to that of a 2-3 month-old infant. He could not control his neck, roll over, or sit unaided. Electrocardiography showed normal sinus rhythm, a normal axis, and a corrected QT interval of 356 msec. The coefficient of variation in electrocardiographic R-R intervals was 13.5%, within the normal range. Echocardiography showed balanced four chambers and normal left-heart function with an ejection fraction of 82.9%.
test_results: Whole-exome sequencing followed by the Sanger method showed that the patient harbored a compound heterozygous mutations in exon 14 (NM_002292.3:c.1648C > T:p.Arg550X) and exon 27 (NM_002292.3:c.4519C > T:p.Glu1507X) in the LAMB2 gene. An inheritance analysis demonstrated that his father and mother carried the heterozygous mutations in exon 14 (NM_002292.3:c.4519C > T:p.Glu1507X) and exon 27 (NM_002292.3:c.4519C > T:p.Glu1507X), respectively.

case_report: A two-month-old male with a history of pyloric stenosis treated with pyloromyotomy presented to the gastroenterology clinic with failure to thrive, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and stridor. He was delivered via cesarean section in a breech position at 40 weeks gestation, with a birth weight of 6 lbs 13 oz and no postnatal complications. In the clinic, he appeared underweight and had difficulty breathing, with subcostal retractions and tracheal tugging. His respiratory rate exceeded 60, and his weight was below the first percentile for his age. He was transferred to the emergency department for further evaluation by gastroenterology, surgery, pulmonology, and ENT specialists. An upper gastrointestinal series revealed gastric outlet obstruction. The patient underwent a pyloroplasty. A brain MRI showed corpus callosum hypoplasia and cortical malformations in the frontal-parietal lobes, indicative of pachygyria.
