Over the next two months, the patient was monitored and returned to the clinic at four months of age for a follow-up after the pyloroplasty. The family reported poor developmental progress, particularly due to significant hypotonia. Physical therapy and feeding therapy were initiated. The patient had difficulty feeding by mouth due to hypotonia and inability to support his head, consistent with oropharyngeal motor dysfunction. In addition to failure to thrive, global developmental delay, and hypotonia, the patient exhibited ichthyosis and roving eye movements on examination.
test_results: The patient’s genetic report yielded a region of homozygosity (13.7 Mb) at 2p25.2p24.2(4951900_18695114).

case_report: A 34-year-old male of Chinese descent presented to the outpatient department on January 7, 2015, with complaints of dry eyes. He had a history of a skin condition diagnosed at 8 months old. There was no immediate family history of this condition, but similar skin findings were noted in his maternal grandmother’s brother. The patient did not have a history of wearing contact lenses. His uncorrected visual acuity was 10/20 in the right eye and 16/20 in the left eye, with a best corrected visual acuity of 20/20 in both eyes. Refractometric measurements were -0.50DS–0.75DC × 60 for the right eye and -1.00DC × 75 for the left eye. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy showed multiple, tiny, pleomorphic, greyish or brownish opacities located anterior to the Descemet membrane in the posterior stroma of both eyes. These opacities were diffusely distributed across the cornea, sparing a 2–3 mm transparent perilimbal zone. No significant abnormalities were observed in the anterior segment and the fundus. Corneal thickness was measured at 528 micrometers in the right eye and 522 micrometers in the left eye using Oculyzer™.
test_results: IVCM of the corneal layers revealed a normal epithelium layer. IVCM showed that the cell morphology and density of the keratocytes were normal in the anterior and mid stroma. Multiple hyperreflective particles (2.0–2.5 μm in diameter) were seen dispersedly outside the keratocytes in the anterior stroma (at the depth of 70–164 μm). The enlarged keratocytes were in an activated state with diffuse hyperreflectivity in the posterior stroma (at the depth of 321–494 μm). The polygonal or claw-like shaped keratocytes were interconnected in a net, with regularly distributed hyperreflective particles (2.0–3.4 μm in diameter) inside. The endothelial cells exhibited normal cell morphology with a cell density of 3,347 and 3,095 cells/mm2 in the right and left eyes, respectively. PCR results demonstrated that the patient had a complete deletion in spanning Exon1-Exon10 and flanking sequences DXS1139-DXS22S1 of STS gene.
diagnosis: Pre-Descemet corneal dystrophy associated with X-linked ichthyosis

case_report: A 26-year-old male from South India reported a 4-year history of hair loss on the scalp, shoulder, and pubic region. He also noted small pigmented lesions on the abdomen, trunk, thighs, and forearm, accompanied by moderate itching and mild scaling on the scalp. The patient experienced severe anxiety related to his skin condition. Previous treatments included topical and systemic steroids and isotretinoin, which provided limited relief. Physical examination revealed an 8×8 cm area of scarring alopecia on the parietal scalp with a few residual tufts of normal hair and minimal scaling. Non-scarring alopecia was observed in the pubic region and on the shoulder. Multiple follicular-oriented papules were present on the abdomen, trunk, thighs, and forearm. Routine investigations, including hemogram, blood sugar, renal and liver function tests, and thyroid function tests, were within normal limits.
test_results: A biopsy from the scalp revealed features of scarring alopecia with dermis replaced by fibrous tissue with perifollicular and junctional lichenoid infiltrate.

case_report: An 87-year-old Caucasian male was referred to our center by a dermatologist after a punch biopsy of a penile lesion. The patient reported a 6-month history of an enlarging lesion on the shaft of his penis, which had been treated with topical agents and antibiotics. Despite treatment, the lesion prompted referral for wide excision. The patient had a similar lesion at the same location 10 years earlier, which was excised by his general practitioner, but no histology report was available. He had no other lumps elsewhere in his body and no family history of similar conditions. His medical history included ischemic heart disease, Alzheimer's disease, and venous ulcers. Examination revealed a 2.5 cm erythematous, fleshy, exophytic plaque at the base of the shaft of the penis, with a satellite lesion proximal to it. There was no palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy. The patient underwent a wide local excision of the penile and satellite lesions. Frozen-section examination was not performed. The scrotal skin was advanced, and primary closure was performed. The foreskin was retracted to achieve a tension-free closure. The specimen measured 30 × 50 × 50 mm. Light microscopy showed intraepithelial proliferation of large, pale cells, predominantly located in the basal and parabasal layers of the epithelium, with margins apparently clear.
test_results: Immunohistochemical stains showed specific staining characteristics with strong positivity for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), the cytokeratin (CK) CK7, CAM 5.6 and HER2 protein over expression. CK20 staining was negative. Immunohistochemical staining also revealed that there were occasional cells in proximity to the margins.

case_report: A 59-year-old woman presented with abdominal distension, fatigue, and skin ecchymosis on 12 April 2022. She reported experiencing asthenia and abdominal distension 1 month prior, followed by jaundice and skin ecchymoses 1 week later. She had no other medical or family history and no history of drug use. Laboratory tests at a local hospital indicated anemia, thrombocytopenia, prolonged prothrombin time, hypofibrinogenemia, and hyperbilirubinemia. A fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) scan showed diffuse hepatomegaly and splenomegaly with a slight increase in FDG uptake, without other metabolic abnormalities or intracranial lesions. Despite receiving a blood transfusion and other treatments, her condition worsened. Physical examination revealed diffuse hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and ecchymoses without cutaneous hemangioma or neurological disorders. Additional blood tests and imaging were conducted upon her referral to our hospital.
test_results: The MRI showed hepatosplenomegaly with numerous variable-sized nodules in the whole liver and spleen, which showed hypointensity on T1-weighted images and hyperintensity on T2-weighted images and inhomogeneous enhancement in diffusion MRI. Peripheral blood samples were used to perform whole exome sequencing (WES, The Beijing Genomics Institute, Shenzhen), and the results showed compound heterozygous variants of the CTC1 gene with a missense mutation, c.3074C>T (p.Ala1025Val) (exon 19), and a splicing site mutation, c.435+9A>C (IVS3).
diagnosis: Diffuse hepatic and splenic hemangiomatosis with Kasabach–Merritt syndrome

case_report: The patient is a 9-year-old Caucasian male, born at 39 weeks gestation following an uncomplicated pregnancy. At birth, his height was 52 cm (87th percentile), weight was 3170 g (36th percentile), and head circumference was 34 cm (greater than 36th percentile) according to WHO 0–2 years standard growth curves. At age 9, his height was 134 cm (42nd percentile), weight was 26,400 g (23rd percentile), and head circumference was 54.4 cm (90th percentile) based on CDC 2–18 years standard growth curves. He achieved independent walking at 25 months, spoke his first words at 3 years, and was toilet trained at 9 years. By 4.5 years, he could form 3–4-word sentences but had limited verbal capacity. He has an intellectual disability with an IQ of 55 and exhibits behavioral concerns such as stubbornness, though he has good social skills. His medical history includes hypotonia, ataxia, significant constipation, keratosis pilaris on the upper and lower limbs and cheeks, significantly reduced sweating, and reduced sensitivity to pain. Dysmorphic facial features include sparse eyebrows and eyelashes, sparse scalp hair in early childhood with current hair being shaggy and dry, broad forehead, elongated face, low anterior hairline, infraorbital fold, hypertelorism, narrow nasal bridge, thick and anteverted nasal alae, low columella insertion, deep and short philtrum, everted lower and tented upper lip vermillion, prominent maxillary central secondary incisor teeth, diastema of the upper and lower central incisors, prominent and pointed chin, and large earlobes. Other notable physical characteristics include hypertrichosis on the back, pectus carinatum superior with excavatum inferior, winged scapulae, bilateral cubitus valgus, long fingers with broad terminal phalanges, and bilateral genu varum. He has a history of a previous nondiagnostic chromosomal microarray.
test_results: Brain MRI identified hypoplastic chiasma, tractus opticus, and a small pituitary gland. He was identified to have a de novo heterozygous variant in the ODC1 gene, c.1242-2A>G, (IVS11-2A>G) that is predicted to destroy a canonical splice acceptor site in intron 11.

case_report: A 16-year-old male with no prior health issues presented with severe pain, stiffness, and muscle twitching in both lower extremities for over a month. The pain, which was burning and non-radiating, began gradually and became continuous within days. It increased with walking short distances and was not alleviated by rest or prescribed pain medications. The stiffness was more pronounced below the knees than in the thighs. He also experienced pain on touch and sensitivity to cold, which worsened his discomfort, described as a wavy sensation in the extremities. The patient reported episodic twitching throughout the body, particularly in the calves, chest, and around the mouth, which intensified with movement. There were no issues with urinary or fecal incontinence, seizures, speech, or vision. His medical, surgical, and family history were unremarkable. Sleep was disrupted due to calf pain and nocturia. On admission, he was restless and in significant discomfort but alert and oriented. Vital signs included a pulse of 114 BPM, BP of 155/100 mmHg, and a respiratory rate of 20/minute. Muscle strength was normal in the upper extremities and lower extremities above the knee but slightly reduced below the knee bilaterally. Reflexes were active in the brachioradialis, biceps, triceps, and ankle but diminished at the knee. Plantar reflexes were absent bilaterally. Muscle bulk was symmetrical, and tone was normal. He reported decreased pin-prick sensation in the toes and fingers of both lower extremities, but joint position sense was intact. Coordination and cranial nerves two through twelve were normal, with no nystagmus or tremors observed. The patient had an antalgic gait. Physical examination revealed desquamating, blanchable erythema on both feet. There were no signs of jaundice, edema, organ enlargement, or lymph node enlargement. Abdominal, respiratory, and cardiovascular examinations were normal.
test_results: Concentric single fiber electromyography (EMG) showed neuromyotonic discharges that were irregular and continuous with triplets and multiplets having high intra-burst frequencies of 30 to 250 Hertz (Hz) interposed between normal motor unit potentials (MUPs) of electrical silence and reduced recruitment. Nerve conduction study (NCS) showed mild neuropathy. Assay for anti-neuronal antibodies (anti-voltage-gated potassium antibodies) was positive.

case_report: A 12-year-old girl presented with a painful abdominal mass. Imaging of the abdomen showed a large cystic mass with calcified tissues and fat in the pelvic region. Laboratory tests indicated normal serum tumor marker levels (alfa-fetoprotein [AFP]: 11.25 ng/mL, beta-human chorionic gonadotropin [beta-HCG]: <0.10 mg/mL). Serum CA125 levels were not assessed. A left salpingo-oophorectomy was carried out. No malignant cells were found in the ascites, even though the tumor had previously ruptured. Complete resection was achieved, and the pathological examination identified the mass as a grade 1 immature teratoma. No further chemotherapy or radiotherapy was administered.
test_results: Abdominal computed tomography (CT) revealed a large cystic mass containing calcified tissues and fat in the pelvic cavity. Four months after the operation, abdominal CT revealed multiple multinodular tumors with a maximum diameter of 9.0 cm in the pelvis, which contained calcified and fatty tissue. Open biopsy was used to obtain a specimen for histological evaluation, which supported a diagnosis of grade 3 immature teratoma with substantial primitive neuroepithelium. After the ICE chemotherapy, positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) revealed abnormal accumulation in the lower abdomen and pelvis.

case_report: A four-year-old boy was referred to the Division of Pediatric Ophthalmology at the Wilmer Eye Institute, Baltimore, Maryland for bilateral partial lens dislocation. Two months earlier, the patient had failed a vision screening at school and was referred for further evaluation. The child did not report any visual symptoms; however, the family observed that he would sit very close to the television and focus closely on toys. He had no history of trauma, developmental issues, or hearing deficits. Genetic screening at birth was normal. The family history was negative for ocular problems other than myopia in his mother. On initial ophthalmic examination, uncorrected visual acuity was 20/100 in the right eye and 20/250 in the left eye. Pupils were equally round and reactive to light, and intraocular pressure was normal by palpation. The child had no measurable stereopsis and suppression of his left eye on Worth 4-dot test. He was orthophoric at all distances. Examination revealed iridodenesis in both eyes and partially dislocated lenses; inferonasally in the right eye and inferiorly in the left eye. Cycloplegic refractive error was −14.50DS + 3.75DC x 005° in the right eye and −19.00 DS + 6.00 DC x 065° in the left eye. During a later examination under anesthesia, the macula in both eyes were within normal limits. Retinal vessels were normal without attenuation in both eyes. Peripheral exam was unremarkable in both eyes. Pachymetry measurements were 575 microns in the right eye and 584 microns in the left eye. Axial length was 21.83 mm in the right eye and 21.12 mm in the left eye. He was prescribed glasses and referred for a genetics evaluation. General physical examination found no evidence of any musculoskeletal features. Echocardiography revealed normal aortic dimensions. Genetic testing showed negative sequencing for deletion or duplication of fibrillin-1 (FBN-1) and cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS).
test_results: Slit-lamp examination was notable for iridodenesis in both eyes and partially dislocated lenses; inferonasally in the right eye and inferiorly in the left eye. Genetic testing showed negative sequencing for deletion or duplication of fibrillin-1 (FBN-1) and cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS). Echocardiography revealed normal aortic dimensions.
diagnosis: Isolated ectopia lentis with partial anterior dislocation and pupillary block

case_report: A 30-year-old female presented with 39 weeks and 6 days of amenorrhea and 6 hours of irregular abdominal pain. The abdominal pain occurred at intervals of 15 to 30 minutes and lasted for 30 seconds. She was admitted to the obstetric department of our hospital as an emergency case. The patient denied a history of other diseases and a family history of hereditary diseases. Measurements of fundal height, abdominal circumference, fetal heart rate, and external pelvis were normal. The fetus was in the Left Occiput Anterior (LOA) position. No dystocia of the head was noted. An internal examination revealed no abnormalities. The patient was admitted to the operating room as an emergency due to intrauterine distress before her laboratory results were available. Intraoperatively, laboratory tests showed the following: white blood cell count was 11.3 × 10^9/L, prothrombin time (PT) was 33.7 seconds, international prothrombin standard was 2.79, partial thromboplastin time was 60.4 seconds, partial thromboplastin ratio was 2.06, PT was 45.2 seconds, prothrombin activity was 22%, antithrombin was 17%, fibrinogen assay was 0.6 g/L, fibrin (pro) degradation product was 116.4 μg/mL, uric acid was 615 μmol/L, creatinine was 172 μmol/L, glutathione aminotransferase was 705 U/L, glutathione aminotransferase was 323 U/L, total bilirubin was 89.51 μmol/L, direct bilirubin was 70.25 μmol/L, and indirect bilirubin was 19.26 μmol/L. Ultrasound examination showed ascites and a bright liver. Obstetric three-dimensional color ultrasound showed the following: the fetal position was cephalic, the fetal heart rate was 171 bpm, fetal movements were palpable, the biparietal diameter was 9.1 cm, the head circumference was 32.0 cm, the abdominal circumference was 33.1 cm, femoral length was 6.8 cm, the placenta was in the fundus with a maturity of II, the amniotic index was 17.41 cm, umbilical artery S/D was 2.4, and the placental entrance and inferior border were indistinct. The results of the non-stress test after admission showed a non-responsive type, a flat baseline, no fetal movements, and no fetal heart fluctuations.
test_results: Genotype analysis identified a homozygous mutation in fibrinogen alpha chain gene (FGA) (p.R350H).

case_report: A 26-year-old male arrived at the hospital reporting a high-grade intermittent fever with chills for two days and a sudden onset of progressive weakness for one day. The fever was not associated with vomiting, diarrhea, or other systemic symptoms. A local doctor had previously treated him after a complete blood count screen showed Plasmodium vivax malaria (trophozoites in blood smear) and thrombocytopenia (platelets 56,000/mm3). He was prescribed cefixime 200mg orally twice a day and artesunate 200mg orally once a day for one day. The following day, he experienced a gradual progression of lower limb weakness, resulting in an inability to stand or walk. He reported no recent vaccinations, use of diuretics, trauma, or seizures. There was no history of similar weakness in the past or in his family. He also denied any use of alcohol, tobacco, or recreational drugs. He works as a driver and resides in an urban area. He had no prior history of malaria. On physical examination, his pulse was 74/min, regular; blood pressure was 124/70 mm Hg, and abdominal examination showed mild splenomegaly. Cardiac examination was unremarkable. Neurological examination revealed bilateral lower limb flaccid paralysis (grade I power) with absent knee and ankle reflexes, and absent bilateral plantar reflexes. Muscle tone in the lower limbs was reduced without muscle tenderness. Sensations in the lower limbs were intact. Upper limb power was 5/5 with no sensory deficits. Cranial nerves examination was normal.
test_results: The results revealed a potassium value of 1.47 mEq/L. The ECG showed flattened T waves and the presence of U waves.

case_report: A 38-year-old pregnant woman, in her 24th week of gestation, arrived at the emergency room experiencing drowsiness and severe epigastric pain that extended to her back, accompanied by bilious vomiting. She has a history of hypertriglyceridemia diagnosed at age 20 and has intermittently taken 600 mg gemfibrozil three times daily. She has had four episodes of pancreatitis, the first at age 28 and the most recent during the 16th week of her current pregnancy. Three episodes were associated with elevated triglyceride levels, reaching up to 7,500 mg/dL, and one episode was related to biliary issues, for which she had a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. There is no history of alcohol use or relevant family history. On admission, her vital signs were: weight 60 kg, height 158 cm, temperature 37.2°C, blood pressure 70/40 mm Hg, heart rate 136 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute. Physical examination showed marked pallor, reduced vesicular breath sounds at the lung bases, and epigastric pain without signs of peritoneal irritation. Laboratory tests indicated lipemic serum with the following results: leukocyte count 7,200 cells/mm3 (neutrophils 70%, band cells 15%), hemoglobin 13.3 g/dL, platelet count 161,000 cells/mm3, serum glucose 160 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1 mg/dL, ALT 126 U/L, AST 100 U/L, amylase 365 U/L, lipase 305 U/L, C-reactive protein 20.5 mg/L, albumin 3.2 g/dL, sodium 152 mEq/L, potassium 4.6 mEq/L, corrected serum calcium 6.2 mg/dL, HDL cholesterol 34 mg/dL, LDL cholesterol 28 mg/dL, triglycerides 1,130 mg/dL, and apolipoprotein B (apoB) 48.7 mg/dL (reference value 55–125 mg/dL).
test_results: An abdominal ultrasound revealed decreased pancreatic echogenicity and a heterogeneous lesion 9 × 7 cm in size in the tail of the pancreas. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed signs of acute pancreatitis. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan with contrast identified hepatosplenomegaly and pancreatic necrosis. Histological analysis confirmed the lipid etiology.

case_report: A 32-year-old Japanese male presented with fever, joint pain, and pain in the buttocks. His birth history was normal. He had a medical history of bronchial asthma and gastric ulcer, with no history of constipation. Upon admission, his body temperature was 40.0°C. Abdominal examination revealed no tenderness, distention, or palpable masses. Neurological examination showed no abnormalities. Anal examination indicated normal location and tone. Digital rectal examination revealed mild rectal narrowing with localized warmth and tenderness in the posterior rectal wall. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 18,000 cells/μL and C-reactive protein level of 26.11 mg/dL. Urine analysis results were normal.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) showed a scimitar-shaped deformity of his sacrum. An 8cm presacral mass containing air displaced his rectum ventrally and appeared to continue to his spinal canal through the anterior wall of his sacrum. Sigmoidoscopy showed extramural compression on the posterior of his rectum.
diagnosis: Currarino syndrome  with a presacral abscess

case_report: A 2-year-old girl presented with high spiking fever, a rash characterized by flat, non-itchy salmon-pink macules and papules that coincided with the fever, and arthritis. Laboratory findings included leukocytosis with neutrophilia, thrombocytosis, elevated CRP and ESR, anemia, hyperferritinemia, and increased LDH. Systemic corticosteroids were administered with a positive effect. Two months later, upon tapering the corticosteroids, a mass lesion developed on the right anterior chest wall accompanied by axillary lymphadenopathy. Imaging revealed destruction of the 5th right rib with periosteal reaction and an extraosseous mass lesion measuring 25 × 48 × 56 mm under the pectoralis major muscle, with areas of contrast uptake. Two surgeries were performed. Specific infections and malignancy were excluded. Morphological examination showed chronic bone inflammation with lymphocyte and plasma cell infiltration, a small number of neutrophils, and bone sclerosis. Further imaging confirmed rib osteosclerosis. Despite antibiotic treatment, the fever and rash persisted, indicating poor efficacy. Episodic corticosteroid injections reduced the fever and rash. After 5 months, the patient was admitted to the immunology and allergology department, where she again exhibited fever, rash, leukocytosis, neutrophilia, thrombocytosis, and elevated CRP. Antibiotics were reintroduced due to possible immunodeficiency, but her condition deteriorated. She developed a persistent non-spiking fever, rash, and macrophage activation syndrome with the following laboratory results: WBC 4.6 × 10^9/L, platelets 135 × 10^9/L, Hb 66 g/L, CRP 59 mg/L, AST 105 U/L, LDH 1,263 U/L, ferritin 260 ng/ml, D-dimer 2,486 ng/ml (normal value < 500), and fibrinogen 1.4 g/L. Immune deficiency was ruled out, and whole exome sequencing did not reveal any relevant findings.
test_results: Whole-body MRI, chest, and abdominal CT revealed axillar, abdominal, mesenteric, inguinal lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, joint effusion, and 5th rib osteosclerosis. There were no lung infiltrates.
diagnosis: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis with Systemic Onset

case_report: A 3-year-old girl exhibited a consistent difference in the height of her eyelid openings since birth. She had no notable medical or family history, and her birth was normal and at full term. An eye examination showed right eye recession with retraction of both the upper and lower eyelids and inward turning of the eyelid. Eye movement was normal. Retinoscopy indicated refractive errors of +4.50 in the right eye and -1.25-1.00×180° in the left eye, with best-corrected visual acuities of 20/400 in the right eye and 20/30 in the left eye. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy results were normal, and examination of the back of the eye revealed an elevated right optic disc with blurred edges.
test_results: Magnetic resonance (MR) imaging findings revealed infiltrative enhancement of the right orbital connective/adipose tissue. The right recti muscles exhibited increased volume with enhancement. The posterior aspect of the right eyeball was flattened in the forward direction.

case_report: A 22-month-old male child with a history of infantile spasms, developmental delay, and seizures presented to the emergency department with an increased frequency and change in character of seizures over the past 2 days. Previously, the seizures lasted for a few seconds and involved staring episodes and limping. Recently, the seizures have been lasting about 1 minute and involve falling to the floor, abnormal jerking movements, incontinence, and upward rolling of the eyes. There was no history of trauma, fever, rashes, vomiting, diarrhea, upper respiratory tract infections, or drug exposure. There was no family history of seizures or neurocutaneous disorders. On physical examination, the patient weighed 12.3 kg, had a blood pressure of 110/63 mm Hg, a pulse rate of 116/min, a temperature of 98.9 F, an SpO2 of 100% on room air, and a respiratory rate of 23/min. No skin features indicative of neurocutaneous disorders were observed. Systemic examination findings were unremarkable. Baseline investigations and metabolic profile results were within normal limits. The patient received a bolus dose of levetiracetam (20 mg/kg) in the emergency department, and no seizure activity was noted under nursing observation. The patient was started on topiramate 30 mg twice a day, clonazepam 0.25 mg twice a day, injectable lorazepam as needed for seizure activity, and acetaminophen as needed.
test_results: An electroencephalogram (EEG) was performed, which showed poor regional organization and lack of a posterior dominant rhythm as well as continuous epileptiform activity in the right occipital-temporal-parietal region. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed asymmetric enlargement of the right cerebral hemisphere with hypermyelination, mild ventriculomegaly, and displaced posterior falx.

case_report: A 16-year-old male presented with gynecomastia and sparse facial hair. He was born at term with a birth weight of 3000 grams. His medical history includes surgeries for bilateral cryptorchidism and penoscrotal hypospadias at ages one and two years, respectively. There was no parental consanguinity. Family history indicated male relatives on the maternal side with similar clinical features, including gynecomastia, hypospadias, sparse facial hair, and infertility. On physical examination, the patient weighed 94 kg (2.84 SD) and was 170 cm (-0.56 SD) tall. His external genitalia appeared phenotypically male with pubic hair Tanner stage IV, a penis measuring 8 cm in length and 2.5 cm in diameter, penoscrotal hypospadias, and a bifid scrotum with both testes palpable at 2 mL. He had normal axillary hair and gynecomastia consistent with Tanner stage III breast development. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Hormone levels were as follows: follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) 42.8 mIU/mL (normal: 1.5-12.4 mIU/mL), luteinizing hormone (LH) 37.4 mIU/mL (normal: 1.7-8.6 mIU/mL), total testosterone (T) 419 ng/dL (normal: 180-763 ng/dL), estradiol 30.5 pg/mL (normal: 7.6-42 pg/mL), beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) 0.73 mIU/mL (normal: 0-2 mIU/mL), and alpha-fetoprotein 2.78 ng/mL (normal: 0-7 ng/mL). Scrotal ultrasound showed both testes were atrophic, measuring 28x10x17 mm (left) and 12x14x27 mm (right). Chromosome analysis revealed a 46,XY karyotype.
test_results: DNA sequence analysis revealed a novel mutation hemizygous p.T576I (c.1727C>T) in the AR gene.

case_report: A 2-year-old Brazilian boy, born to non-consanguineous parents, exhibited persistent violaceous skin lesions and recurrent fever starting at 10 days old. Laboratory tests revealed elevated acute-phase reactants (CRP and ESR) and liver enzymes (200–400 U/L). Imaging showed sparse liver calcifications and cerebellar vermis hypoplasia. Skin biopsies indicated neutrophilic dermatosis. The patient was treated with oral prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day), but fever and skin lesions reappeared during dose reduction. Chronic systemic corticosteroid use led to complications such as hirsutism, truncal obesity, and poor growth. Colchicine and dapsone were ineffective in alleviating symptoms. Genetic screening with a primary immunodeficiency targeted gene panel did not yield conclusive results.
test_results: WES revealed two novel PSMB10 variants (c.40_42del and p.Phe14del) and a third novel PSMB10 splice site variant (c.710 + 1G>C).

case_report: A 3-month-old male infant was brought to the pediatrics department due to persistent rapid breathing and weight loss. The child was born at full term in 2011 without any immediate respiratory issues post-birth. The parents are second-degree relatives. The infant had been experiencing breathing difficulties and required oxygen support for the past three weeks. He had a sibling who passed away at 3 months old due to respiratory complications. On physical examination, the infant weighed 4.5 kg and measured 58 cm in height. His heart rate was recorded at 130 beats per minute, and his respiratory rate was 60 breaths per minute. The infant exhibited peripheral cyanosis and intercostal retractions. Auscultation revealed fine inspiratory crackles throughout the chest. His transcutaneous oxygen saturation was 80% on room air, and he required an oxygen flow of 8 L/min to maintain saturation levels above 92%. There was no enlargement of the liver or spleen. Laboratory tests indicated low total protein levels at 54 g/L and albumin at 20 g/L, while liver enzymes, renal function, and full blood count were within normal ranges. Inflammatory markers were slightly elevated. Arterial blood gas measurements on oxygen showed a pH of 7.38, Pco2 of 4.81 KPa, and Po2 of 8.53 KPa. A chest X-ray displayed diffuse alveolar infiltration with an air bronchogram. A chest CT scan revealed diffuse interstitial and alveolar infiltration. Echocardiography results were normal. Tests for respiratory fungal, viral, and bacterial pathogens, as well as HIV, were negative.
test_results: Macroscopic appearance and light microscopy of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid stained with PAS showed extracellular positive proteinaceous material and lipid-laden macrophages. The aspirated fluid was reported to be clear and a silver stain was negative for Pneumocystis jiroveci.

case_report: A 15-year-old male presented with gradually worsening bilateral leg weakness, which had been noticeable since he started school. His birth and early developmental history were normal, and he achieved motor milestones on time. He was unable to run and had difficulty climbing stairs since childhood. At the time of presentation, he also had trouble rising from a chair. Physical examination showed widespread muscle atrophy, particularly in the lower limbs. Muscle strength testing revealed significant weakness in the proximal leg muscles, with mild weakness in the upper limbs and distal legs. Deep tendon reflexes were intact, and there was no facial weakness or skeletal abnormalities. Serum creatine kinase levels were normal (106 U/L). Needle electromyography showed active myopathic patterns in the limb muscles. Spine X-rays confirmed the absence of scoliosis. Muscle CT scans and pulmonary function tests were normal. Family history revealed that the patient's mother had developmental delays from infancy and mild, stable proximal leg weakness, with difficulty climbing stairs and running. The patient's older sister also had mild, stable proximal leg weakness and developmental delays. The mother exhibited mild proximal leg muscle weakness without facial or upper-limb involvement. No family members had a history of surgeries requiring general anesthesia.
test_results: Muscle biopsy samples taken from the biceps brachii in the proband revealed many peripheral cores with unclear borders in the muscle fibers that were devoid of enzyme activities on nicotinamide dehydrogenase-tetrazolium reductase (NADH-TR) and cytochrome C oxidase (COX) staining. Almost all cores were singular within a muscle fiber, with two cores present in only a few fibers. In addition, all of the muscle fibers were type 1 fibers. Electron microscopy revealed misalignment of myofibrils in the core region compared with those within intact fibers. This genetic analysis revealed a novel heterozygous mutation [c.14590T>C (p.Tyr4864His)] in exon 101.

case_report: A 72-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 58-year history of numerous small, reddish and brownish, keratotic papules. These papules initially appeared on her lower limbs and later spread to her upper limbs and trunk. Her medical history was unremarkable for other skin or systemic conditions, except for a well-differentiated cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma in situ on her leg, which was excised two years prior. Dermoscopic examination of one lesion revealed brownish structureless areas with a brownish pseudo-reticular pattern on an erythematous base, scattered lacunae-like ectatic vessels, and hyperkeratosis with fine superficial desquamation.
test_results: Histopathology of a lesion on the trunk showed a compact, thick lamellar hyperkeratosis with focal parakeratosis overlying an atrophic epidermis associated with a dense, lichenoid infiltrate of small lymphocytes in the superficial dermis with focal accentuation in the papillomatous areas. Some melanophages, focal basal vacuolization with scattered areas of exocytosis, were also present. Immunohistochemical studies showed a similar proportion of CD4 and CD8T-lymphocytes with sparse to absent CD20 cells.

case_report: A 15-year-old female of Guatemalan descent presented with reduced central vision, involuntary eye movements, and sensitivity to light. Visual acuity testing showed Snellen BCVA at a distance of 20/250 in the right eye and 20/200 in the left eye. Auto-refraction indicated myopic refraction with astigmatism: −2.75 + 2.25 × 103 in the right eye and −3.00 + 3.00 × 076 in the left eye. She exhibited high frequency, low amplitude horizontal nystagmus and maintained normal eye alignment. The anterior segment examination was normal, while the fundus examination revealed bull’s eye maculopathy and granular pigment changes in the peripheral retina. Spectral domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) showed loss of the ellipsoid zone in the fovea, and fundus autofluorescence (FAF) displayed a bull’s eye pattern of hyper- and hypo-autofluorescence. Farnsworth D15 color vision testing indicated multiple axis errors with an achromatic pattern. Goldmann visual field testing demonstrated loss of the I1e isopter in both eyes, with preservation of the I4e and V4e isopters. Scotopic electroretinography (ERG) showed reduced amplitudes (~50%) and mildly delayed implicit times, while photopic bright flash and flicker ERG responses were not recordable. Dental examination and radiographs (bitewings, anterior and posterior periapical radiographs, and panoramic radiograph) revealed fully restored dentition with crowns on all molar teeth and composite restorations on the anterior teeth. Some teeth (20, 23, 26, 29) had slightly enlarged pulp chambers, while others appeared normal for her age. Clinically, the enamel was thin or absent on non-restored surfaces. Periapical and bitewing radiographs showed isolated residual enamel on non-restored and under-restored surfaces. No other systemic abnormalities were observed.
test_results: A 581 gene panel from Molecular Vision Lab (MVL Panel v1) revealed a homozygous CNNM4 c.706C > T (p.Arg236Trp) variant with one copy inherited from each parent.

case_report: A 5-year-old Saudi girl of Arabian origin was seen at King Abdulaziz Medical City, King Fahad National Guard Hospital’s dermatology clinic with a history of skin lesions on her left hand and left foot. Her parents noted that these lesions had been present since birth and had progressively spread and become more noticeable over time. The child also had a history of excessive sweating, limited to her left hand and left foot. There was no history of significant sun exposure or trauma, and no family members had similar skin lesions. Previous treatment with topical calcipotriol showed no improvement. Physical examination revealed multiple yellowish, thickened papules that merged into wart-like plaques, arranged in a linear pattern along the edges of her left hand and foot. On her left hand, the lesions were located on the palmar surface, extending from the thenar eminence to the base of her fourth finger. On her left foot, the lesions were found on the lateral side and the fifth toe.
test_results: Histological examination of a 4mm punch biopsy specimen taken from a papule on her left foot revealed hyperkeratosis and acanthosis. The special staining for elastic fibers (Verhoeff’s-Van Gieson stain) showed fragmentation and a reduced number of elastic fibers causing significant thinning of the dermis.

case_report: A 27-year-old male patient presented with lightheadedness and a high fever. His family history included gait problems in his grandmother, aunt, uncle, and mother starting in their 40s. Three years prior, his mother was found to have a p.Leu272Ser variant in the SPAST gene. The patient experienced spasticity in the legs at age 16, became unable to run and noticed urinary incontinence at age 18, and had difficulty walking without assistance by age 20. Concurrently, he became apathetic and mute, leading to college dropout and social isolation. Physical examination showed a temperature of 39.4°C, pulse of 129 beats/minute, breath rate of 26 times/minute, blood pressure of 73/51 mmHg, and deep pressure ulcers with black necrotic tissue and abscess formation on the sacral and bilateral greater trochanter regions. Neurological examination revealed alertness but apathy, dysarthria, intact cranial nerves except for dysarthria, inability to sit without assistance, hypertonia in all extremities, severe contractures in hip, knee, and ankle joints, muscle strength of 3 or 4/5 in upper extremities and 1/5 in lower extremities, mild oscillation and dysmetria in the finger-nose-finger test, severely decreased sensation in bilateral lower extremities, hyperactive muscle stretch reflexes with knee and ankle clonus, and extensor plantar responses. The patient also had urinary and fecal incontinence. Laboratory tests indicated a severe inflammatory response with elevated procalcitonin and hypoalbuminemia. Cultures from blood and skin and soft tissue grew Proteus mirabilis, sensitive to beta-lactams. Treatment included infusion, norepinephrine, meropenem, and surgical debridement of necrotic tissue. Nine months later, the patient developed septic arthritis of the left hip joint, requiring two arthrotomies with drainage and curettage. Over the next 13 months, ulcers on the sacral and bilateral greater trochanter regions became scar tissues, and the left hip joint showed bony ankylosis. Small, recurrent ulcers in the same areas were intractable. During this period, his cognitive function declined further, and he became unresponsive to three of eight external stimuli.
test_results: At the age of 27, a brain MRI showed symmetric lesions with a high signal in the posterior deep white matter on T2-weighted imaging (T2WI) and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) imaging. A repeat brain MRI showed a posterior cerebral white matter lesion enlargement and slight enhancement with a gadolinium contrast agent at the margins of the white matter lesion. Additional laboratory tests showed elevated adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), low cortisol, and elevated C26/C22 ratio of VLCFA. We identified a heterozygous or hemizygous variant in exon 1 of the ABCD1 gene (NM_000033.4:c.892G>A {p.Gly298Ser}) in the patient and his grandmother, aunt, uncle (patient 2), and mother.

case_report: The patient is a 31-year-old African-American, left-handed female with a recent history of hypertension. She experienced left-handed clumsiness, particularly in her left index finger and thumb, along with an episode of slurred speech and left-sided facial numbness lasting between 30 minutes to 1 hour. Initially evaluated at a local hospital, she had an abnormal EKG showing T wave inversions in leads V2–V4 and left ventricular hypertrophy. The patient declined admission and was admitted to our institution 10 days later. Her symptoms improved two days post-episode, but she continued to have difficulty with fine motor tasks such as typing. During her stay, her oxygen saturation was maintained at 95-96%. An MRI of the brain revealed a subacute infarct in the right precentral gyrus, affecting the hand knob area, which correlated with her left hand weakness. Transthoracic echocardiography showed moderate left ventricular hypertrophy without regional wall motion abnormalities, a mildly dilated left atrium, and an increased mitral valve E point to ventricular septal separation. The visually estimated ejection fraction was 45–50%. There was no evidence of right-to-left shunting on an agitated saline bubble contrast study performed in the right arm. Chest radiography indicated abnormal soft tissue densities along the right paratracheal region extending to the right main stem bronchus and along the right cardiomediastinal margin, which was further evaluated.
test_results: CT imaging demonstrated persistence of the left superior vena cava draining into the left atrium without visualization of a coronary sinus. Cardiac venous drainage is seen directly into the inferior vena cava via the great cardiac vein. Subtle high attenuation contrast extends deep into the interventricular septum. Cardiac MR demonstrated concentric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, with relative sparing of the apical chamber. Left ventricular systolic function was moderately reduced with a calculated ejection fraction of 36%. The persistent left superior vena cava drained into the left atrium resulting in a right to left shunt with a Qp/Qs = 0.694.
Orpha_name: Combined immunodeficiency due to partial RAG1 deficiency

case_report: An 86-year-old Black female presented with a 1-month history of generalized muscle weakness, dyspnea on minimal exertion, lack of energy, apathy, loss of appetite, and depressed mood, coinciding with the recent death of her son. She also experienced episodes of diarrhea and weight loss, losing approximately 5 kg during this period. The patient had a history of anemia of unknown cause diagnosed 6 years prior, for which she had received a blood transfusion but no erythropoietin treatment. She had no history of neoplasia. Her medical history included diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, and over 30 years of arterial hypertension, for which she was under clinical treatment. She also had coronary heart disease and had undergone myocardial revascularization 7 years earlier. Her medications included metformin, gliclazide, levothyroxine, enalapril, amlodipine, cilostazol, and sertraline. She had a 30-year history of smoking hand-rolled cigarettes. Physical examination at admission showed normal respiration, pallor, poor general health status, and a body weight of 46 kg. Vital signs included a heart rate of 72 bpm, respiratory rate of 20 breaths/minute, and blood pressure of 134/56 mmHg. There was no edema, jugular stasis, or peripheral lymph node enlargement. Endoscopy revealed oral candidiasis. Pulmonary auscultation was normal, while cardiac auscultation revealed rhythmic heart sounds with aortic and mitral systolic murmur. The abdomen was normal with no organomegaly on palpation. Neurological examination was unremarkable. During her hospital stay, the patient experienced loss of appetite, frequent nausea, diarrhea, and hematochezia. Despite low food intake, there was no additional weight loss. Sigmoidoscopy revealed moderate proctitis with signs of bleeding, and a rectal biopsy showed mild inflammatory infiltrate composed of lymphomononuclear cells in the superficial layer of the colonic mucosa, with reactive intestinal crypts. Laboratory tests revealed normocytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and leukoerythroblastic reaction. Urinalysis showed mild proteinuria with hyaline and granular casts. Serology for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C was negative. Serum levels of vitamin B12, folic acid, and iron were normal, as were tumor markers carcinoembryonic antigen, cancer antigen 125, and cancer antigen 19-9. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed erosive antral gastritis. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed mild splenomegaly and an atheromatous aorta. A CT scan of the chest revealed an atheromatous aorta, normal lung parenchyma, and no lymph node enlargement. An echocardiogram showed mild left ventricular hypertrophy, inferior wall hypokinesia, mitral insufficiency, and aortic stenosis. There was a progressive decrease in leukocyte and platelet counts (which dropped to 1,100 and 5,000 cells/mm³, respectively), accompanied by worsening renal function.
test_results: BM biopsy revealed extensive infiltration of the BM by aggregates of large, atypical cells (approximately 70%), consistent with cells of the erythroid lineage (positive for glycophorin A and partially positive for CD117); other findings included extensive areas of necrosis, numerous mitotic figures, and markedly reduced BM reserve.

case_report: A 69-year-old Japanese female was admitted to our hospital due to an increase in both the number and size of thyroid tumors observed during routine thyroid ultrasonography (US). On physical examination, she appeared well-nourished and was not in acute distress. There were no signs of heart failure. A soft mass was palpable in the thyroid gland. The patient's serum CEA level was slightly elevated at 5.1 ng/mL. Free T3 and free T4 levels were within normal ranges, but the TSH level was elevated at 4.56 μIU/mL. Full blood count, blood chemistry, and serum thyroglobulin levels were normal. The patient had been on thiamazole for 25 years for hyperthyroidism and had undergone surgery 10 years prior to remove a left atrial myxoma. Multiple thyroid nodules were noted at that time.
test_results: Thyroid scintigraphy revealed an increased focal uptake of 99mTc in the same lesions in the left lobe, being consistent with toxic multinodular goiter. Genetic studies found no mutation in the PRKAR1A gene. Aspiration cytology revealed the nodules to be class III.

case_report: A 25-year-old female presented with symptoms including heat intolerance, palpitations, weight gain, and goiter. Laboratory tests revealed FT4 levels at 24.46 pmol/L (normal range: 9.01–19.05), FT3 levels at 7.31 pmol/L (normal range: 2.63–5.70), and TSH levels at 8.63 mIU/L (normal range: 0.35–4.94). Radioiodine uptake was measured at 21.95% at 3 hours (normal range: 10–30%) and 41.5% at 24 hours (normal range: 25–60%). TSH levels increased from 4.50 to 34.40 mIU/L 15 minutes after an intravenous bolus of thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH). Administration of liothyronine (L-T3) reduced TSH levels from 4.61 mIU/L to 0.21 mIU/L. Pituitary MRI showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Gene sequencing identified a heterozygous Y321C substitution mutation in exon 9 of the THRB gene.
Orpha_name: Resistance to thyroid hormone due to a mutation in thyroid hormone receptor beta

case_report: A 79-year-old male with a history of non-ischemic cardiomyopathy with an ejection fraction of 30-35%, previous automatic implantable cardioverter defibrillator placement, and paroxysmal atrial tachycardia, who is also a BRCA1 carrier, experienced chronic left knee pain 30 years ago. He consulted an orthopedic specialist and received intra-articular injections of glucosamine and chondroitin for osteoarthritis. Despite multiple injections, his pain persisted. Synovial fluid aspiration was performed, yielding 100 mL of blood. Due to the lack of symptom improvement, he underwent left knee replacement surgery, which resulted in significant knee bleeding postoperatively.
test_results: Prothrombin time of 55 seconds (normal: 26-35.3 seconds). FXI activity of 35% (normal: 60-150%). Other laboratory values, including prothrombin time, international normalized ratio (1.1 [normal: 0.8-1.2]) and PT% (85% [normal: 80-120%]) were within normal limits.

case_report: The subject is a 69-year-old male. His father experienced kidney failure of unknown cause, and his mother passed away at 92 years old. Neither parent exhibited ptosis, hearing impairment, or muscle issues. He has a healthy 68-year-old brother and two healthy sons, aged 33 and 37 years. The patient achieved normal motor milestones during childhood, completed military service at 20 years old, and has maintained an active lifestyle. He has no history of migraines, visual or hearing impairments, or cardiac or cognitive issues. At 55 years old, he began to experience gradually worsening bilateral ptosis and limitations in both horizontal and vertical eye movements. By 65 years old, he had developed complete horizontal ophthalmoplegia, no upward gaze, and limited downward gaze. He has undergone bilateral surgery for ptosis. A comprehensive neurological examination was otherwise normal, except for a slight bilateral sensorineural hearing impairment, which is considered to be cochlear in origin. Cardiac evaluations, including ECG and 24-hour Holter monitoring, were normal.
test_results: Brain MRI showed slight atrophy of the mesencephalon, pedunculus cerebelli superior, and frontotemporal parts of the brain.
diagnosis: Autosomal Recessive Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia  due to POLG mutation

case_report: A 49-year-old female presented with a pink to purple dome-shaped papule on the third digit of her right foot, which was asymptomatic. She has a history of actinic keratoses but no other dermatological issues. Her family history includes colon cancer, prostate cancer, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease, and diabetes. There is no family history of breast or ovarian cancer.
test_results: The sample proved to be a primarily dermal melanocytic proliferation, with a low proliferative index as determined by Ki67 staining. The lesion contained nests and strands of atypical epithelioid melanocytes surrounded by lymphocytes and pigmented macrophages. The lesion stained positive for MART-1, however, BAP1 staining was negative.
diagnosis: BAPoma with epithelioid atypia and rare mitoses

case_report: A 41-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of periorbital angioedema and widespread skin lesions unresponsive to standard treatments. Vital signs were within normal limits. Dermatological examination revealed numerous closely-set, monomorphous, waxy papules and plaques with a succulent appearance, symmetrically distributed over the face, neck, trunk, thighs, forearms, and hands. The papules were arranged linearly. The scalp was affected, but mucous membranes were not. The glabella exhibited pronounced facial folds with horizontal and longitudinal furrowing. Some lesions on the trunk and thighs had a central depression with an elevated rim, resembling a “doughnut sign.” Finger flexion was restricted. Other systemic examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including hemogram, urine routine examination, serum biochemistry, serum electrophoresis, and thyroid function tests, were normal. Urine Bence–Jones protein was negative. Tests for ANA, RA, and HIV were negative. Imaging studies, including chest X-ray, skeletal radiological survey, and abdominal ultrasonogram, showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Histopathological examination of a representative lesion from the thigh stained with hematoxylin and eosin showed normal epidermis and separation of collagen fibres in the upper and mid reticular dermis. Alcian blue staining demonstrated intradermal mucin deposition.

case_report: A 59-year-old postmenopausal female with a 40 pack-year smoking history and a known history of presumed uterine myoma three years prior, presented to the emergency room with progressively worsening dyspnea on exertion, dry cough, and discomfort over the right hemithorax during deep inspiration. She reported no weight loss or fever but noted an increase in abdominal girth over the past two years without seeking medical consultation. Physical examination revealed slight tachypnea without accessory muscle use and a room air SpO2 of 90%. Other vital signs were within normal limits. Auscultation showed absent breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the lower half of the right hemithorax. The abdomen appeared globular, and a firm, smooth, slightly tender mass was palpated extending from the right hypochondrium to the pelvic area. No signs of ascites were observed.
test_results: Serum CA-125 was higher than 1000 IU/ml. The pleural fluid was a pale yellow exudate (fluid protein/serum protein ratio = 0.6) with pleural CA-125 level = 738 UI/ml. The cytology was negative for malignancy. A 21-cm right adnexal solid mass with smooth and pearly appearance and another 3-cm mass in the left ovary were noted and removed. The intraoperative pathologies of both masses were suggestive of ovarian fibroma, later confirmed by the examination of the whole piece.

case_report: A 40-year-old woman, previously in good health, was referred by an ophthalmologist due to anisocoria, characterized by a small right pupil and a dilated left pupil. She had no ocular symptoms and initially visited the ophthalmologist for conjunctivitis. She reported a flu-like illness lasting about three months, which occurred five months prior to the eye examination and resolved without treatment. She did not experience any vision problems and could read without difficulty. She denied symptoms such as fever, fatigue, dizziness, rapid heartbeat, fainting, recurrent vomiting, dry mouth, nasal congestion, dry eyes, constipation, or bladder issues. She also did not report abnormal sweating or intolerance to temperature changes. Her general physical examination was normal, with a blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg and a pulse of 65 beats per minute, both in supine and standing positions. Neurological examination revealed a generalized absence of muscle stretch reflexes, confirmed by several neurologists, with no reflexes in the lower and upper extremities. Plantar reflexes were flexor, and there was no Romberg sign, weakness, or sensory ataxia. Sensory examination for touch, pin prick, and cold was normal, as was the position sense of the toes and fingers. She could perceive vibration from a tuning fork (256 Hz) in both upper and lower extremities. Eye movements were normal. The right pupil measured 1.5 mm, had an oval shape, and did not respond to light; the left pupil measured about 6 mm and had a very poor light response. The left pupil's light response was segmentary, with a slight response in the right superior segment. Both pupils had poor accommodation responses, though the left pupil remained slightly more miotic after accommodation. The pupils contracted briskly with a 0.125% pilocarpine solution. Brain and cervical cord MRI results were normal. A five-minute ECG strip in DII showed an almost fixed heart rate.
test_results: The HRV was ostensibly decreased in the time domain in the supine and standing position and also during rhythmic breathing. The SD was markedly decreased, as were also the maximum/minimum ratio, the range, and the variation coefficient. The analysis of the HRV in the frequency domain, in the three conditions, showed a decrease in the absolute power of LF and HF. The increase in SBV was due to the decrease of both the LF and the HF, although the HF was most severely decreased.

case_report: A 24-year-old male has experienced sensitivity to light since birth. There is no reported family history of color vision issues or retinal disorders. At 8 months old, the patient was found to have myopia with a refractive error of −5.50 D in the right eye and −6.50 D in the left eye, along with astigmatism and nystagmus, but no strabismus. Corrective glasses were prescribed at 1 year old. By the age of 3, his parents noticed he had difficulty distinguishing colors. At 4 years old, occlusion therapy was attempted in both eyes for 2 months to address amblyopia but was not successful. At 6 years old, his best-corrected visual acuity was measured at 20/200 using Snellen charts. Magnetic resonance imaging showed no brain injuries. Both visual evoked potential flash and B-scan ultrasonography results were normal for both eyes. At 11 years old, his visual acuity was measured at 20/250.
test_results: Subnormal amplitudes under scotopic conditions and extinct responses under photopic conditions were observed in both eyes. Mutation screening revealed absence of the LCR and promoter regions of both OPN1LW and OPN1MW genes – indicative for a large deletion – but presence of the 3′ parts of the OPN1MW gene, namely exons 4, 5 and 6.

case_report: A 6-year-old boy visited a dermatological clinic due to painful, chronic wounds on his extremities, particularly on his feet. His parents, who are not related, have a healthy older daughter. Early symptoms observed soon after birth included thrombocytopenia, hypochromic microcytic anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and frequent infections. Subsequently, he developed severe diarrhea, which has been partially managed with steroid therapy. Initial skin manifestations appeared around three weeks after birth, presenting as papules and livid spots that evolved into lesions resembling livido racemosa on the extremities and face, which later ulcerated. Histopathological examination of the intact periphery of one ulcer showed multiple thrombotic cutaneous vessels with fibrinoid degeneration of the vessel walls, minimal inflammatory cells, extravasated erythrocytes, hyperplastic epidermis with signs of degeneration and parakeratotic cornification, and fibrotic dermal connective tissue. Gastrointestinal tissue samples showed similarities to Crohn’s disease. The patient received antibiotics and immunosuppressive drugs, followed by rituximab as an immunomodulatory therapy, which resulted in immunoglobulin deficiency.
test_results: The patient shows a homozygous mutation in the PEPD gene (mutation c.1342G<A;p.Gly448Arg) detected by exome sequencing after urine analysis had revealed massive imidodipeptiduria.

case_report: An 8-day-old male infant underwent an evaluation for choanal atresia under general anesthesia. Anesthesia was induced and maintained with sevoflurane at 7-8%. Following intubation, 2 μg of remifentanil was administered. No muscle relaxants were used. The anesthesia lasted for 35 minutes without any complications. One week later, the patient was scheduled for the application of bilateral nasopharyngeal tubes under general anesthesia with sevoflurane. This procedure also concluded without any issues. During follow-up, the patient's temperature rose to 42.5°C, heart rate increased to 250 beats per minute, and respiratory distress was observed. Laboratory results showed creatinine phosphokinase levels of 929 IU/L and elevated potassium levels.
test_results: Blood gas analysis revealed hypoxemia (SO2 < 85%), respiratory acidosis (PaCO2 > 60 mm Hg) and metabolic acidosis (base deficit > 10 mEq/L).

case_report: A 2-year-old girl, the second child of healthy and unrelated Chinese parents, was born at 39 weeks of gestation by cesarean section with a birth weight of 2840 g. The mother had gestational diabetes mellitus. The patient has a healthy 20-year-old brother, and there is no family history of heart disease, epilepsy, or other neurological disorders. Nineteen hours post-delivery, the patient was admitted to the neonatal unit due to repeated vomiting and digestive tract bleeding, managed with fasting and thrombin. Meconium passage was timely, but abdominal distension was noted from 4 days after birth and persisted. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a dilated bowel and bowel gas. Abdominal distension recurred over the next 2 years, leading to mechanical ileus at 1 year of age, which improved with fasting, gastrointestinal decompression, and glycerin enema. At 5 months, the patient was found to have an atrial septal defect (18 × 23 × 22 mm) and pulmonary arterial hypertension (42 mmHg). Atrial septal defect closure surgery was performed at 5 months, followed by treatment with digoxin (0.1 mg/kg.d), spironolactone (2.4 mg/kg.d), and hydrochlorothiazide (0.8 mg/kg.d). Post-surgery, the patient experienced recurrent pneumonia and was admitted to the ICU for heart failure 6 months later, with a left ventricular ejection fraction dropping to 22% at its lowest. One year after ICU discharge, the left ventricular ejection fraction ranged from 47 to 55%. At 9 months, the patient experienced epileptic spasms with hypsarrhythmia several times a day and was treated with topiramate (TPM; maximum dosage of 5 mg/kg.d), valproate (VPA; maximum dosage of 24 mg/kg.d), and cocktail therapy. No seizures were observed between 13 and 19 months with combined TPM, VPA, and cocktail therapy, which included vitamin B1 50 mg/d, vitamin B2 100 mg/d, vitamin C 200 mg/d, vitamin E 100 mg/d, L-carnitine 1000 mg/d, and coenzyme Q10 100 mg/d. Seizures returned at 19 months, occurring several times a day, and did not improve with levetiracetam (LEV; maximum dosage of 20 mg/kg.d), vigabatrin (VGB; maximum dosage of 160 mg/kg.d), nitrazepam (NZP; maximum dosage of 0.07 mg/kg.d), and clobazam (CLB; maximum dosage of 0.27 mg/kg.d). Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ATCH, 1.5 IU/kg) was added to the combined levetiracetam, vigabatrin, and cocktail therapy for 2 weeks at 1 year and 10 months, followed by prednisone, which was gradually reduced and withdrawn over 1 month, reducing seizure frequency to twice per week. From 1 year of age, the patient experienced sleep disturbances, characterized by light sleep, frequent crying during sleep, and difficulty being soothed. Dysmorphic features included a high-arched palate, frontal bossing, a congenital preauricular fistula, a tented mouth, a broad nasal root, a flat nasal bridge, and tongue protrusion. Brain MRI at 1 year showed cerebral atrophy, enlargement of the supratentorial ventricles, thinned corpus callosum, and delayed myelination. Hearing loss was confirmed by otoacoustic emissions testing at 1 year, following a failed newborn hearing screening. Chromosomal microarray analysis and mitochondrial genetic testing for the proband were normal, as were prenatal karyotype analysis results from a cord blood sample.
test_results: Trio-based WES revealed that the POGZ gene had a de novo heterozygous frameshift mutation [NM_015100.4:c.2746delA (p.Thr916ProfsTer12)], which was not found in current population databases (dbSNP, GnomAD, and ExAC). According to the guidelines of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) and the Association of Molecular Pathology (AMP), the variant identified in the present case is considered pathogenic.

case_report: An 18-year-old male patient presented with a three-year history of chest tightness and shortness of breath, which worsened significantly one week prior to admission. Symptoms included increased chest tightness, inability to lie supine, and anuria. Previous evaluations at a hospital in Beijing noted chest tightness, a small pericardial effusion, and chronic bilateral lung inflammation with interstitial changes. During that hospitalization, the patient experienced a cerebral infarction, which showed slight improvement after treatment. The patient reported no family history of genetic disorders or similar conditions. Physical examination revealed hypotension with a blood pressure of 92/62 mmHg. The patient showed normal development, intelligence, consciousness, and retinal features. Initial limb muscle strength was graded as level 5, but at the final hospitalization, muscle strength in the right upper limb was grade 4, and muscle strength in the left lower, left upper, and right lower limbs was grade 1. No electromyography, skeletal muscle MRI, or pathological examination was performed. Resting electrocardiography showed atrial/ventricular premature beats and ventricular blocks without pre-excitation. Laboratory tests indicated elevated high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T (0.187 ng/mL) and N-terminal pro-B-type brain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP; 6,554 pg/mL). Liver function tests showed elevated levels of creatine kinase (1075 U/L, 1545 U/L, and 936 U/L), creatine kinase-MB (63 U/L, 61 U/L, and 58 U/L), lactate dehydrogenase (728 U/L), alanine transpeptidase (206 U/L), and aspartate aminotransferase (273 U/L). Elevated troponin T and myocardial enzyme levels were noted, indicating secondary myocardial damage.
test_results: Left ventricular centripetal and right ventricular hypertrophy were observed on transthoracic echocardiography (ventricular septal thickness, 20-31 mm; lateral wall thickness, 26 mm). Tissue Doppler imaging revealed increased end-diastolic filling pressure, with an E value of 70 cm/s, a ventricular septum e′ value of 3 cm/s, and a lateral wall e′ value of 4 cm/s. The patient underwent coronary computed tomography (CT) angiography with maximum intensity projection, excluding acute coronary syndrome, which revealed the patency of the lumen of the coronary trunk and its branches. A cardiac MRI (CMRI) was performed, which revealed bilateral ventricular hypertrophy, severe trabecularization of the biventricular wall, and minor pericardial effusion. Myocardial strain analyses of the entire left ventricle, as well as each segment, were performed. The 16-segment bullseye diagram and longitudinal strain map revealed varying degrees of strain reduction in each segment of the patient’s left ventricle, indicating myocardial injury. The ventricular myocardium exhibited substantial late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) on MRI, sparing the mid-basal septum but involving the apex.
diagnosis: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy secondary to deficiency in lysosome-associated membrane protein-2
Orpha_name: Glycogen storage disease due to LAMP-2 deficiency

case_report: The patient, a 22-year-old male from a family with no consanguinity, has healthy parents and an older sister. At age 15, he began experiencing cognitive difficulties, particularly with studying. By age 20, he exhibited a spastic-ataxic gait and developed slurred speech. Neurological examinations showed signs of cerebellar ataxia, increased muscle tension in the lower limbs, hyperreflexia in both upper and lower limbs, positive pathological reflexes, and ankle clonus, while muscle strength and volume remained normal.
test_results: MRI of the brain showed diffuse cerebellar atrophy. NCS demonstrated normal sensory nerve conduction and motor nerve conduction. Needle EMG revealed very little or no spontaneous activity in multiple muscles (musculus quadratus labii inferioris, sternocleidomastoid, paravertebral muscle, biceps, abductor digiti minimi, tibialis anterior muscle). Large amplitude, long duration motor unit potentials, as well as reduced recruitment were shown in these muscles.

case_report: A 29-year-old male (height, 1.82 m; weight, 60 kg), the second child of healthy non-consanguineous Chinese parents, came to the clinic with complaints of difficult voiding, painful urination, and a weak urinary stream. His older brother exhibited similar symptoms, including difficult voiding and generalized skin lesions. At 27 years old, the patient experienced difficult voiding with frequent and painful urination and was treated for a urethral infection at a local hospital. Anti-infective therapy provided partial relief. Over the next two years, he experienced intermittent frequent, urgent, and painful urination with a tapering urinary stream. Despite taking oral anti-infective drugs, his symptoms of progressive difficult voiding and occasional hematuria persisted. He was admitted to the Second Hospital of Shanxi Medical University for further evaluation and treatment. Physical examination revealed normal skin on the penis and scrotum, and no abnormalities at the external urethral orifice. The patient had mechanically induced blistering on his left knee since birth, and sparse blistering on his fingers, feet, and lower extremities. These blisters healed with scarring, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and atrophy. Nail dystrophies developed in early infancy, resulting in the loss of all fingernails and toenails during childhood. The patient had sparse hair with progressive loss of body and axillary hair in adulthood. Enamel hypoplasia and pitting were also noted. No pyloric atresia or signs of digestive tract obstruction were observed. Physical examination showed severe atrophy of the distal joints, large areas of skin exfoliation, and ulcerations on some parts of the skin. The patient had various degrees of scarring and hyperpigmentation on the corners of his mouth, fingers, feet, and extremities, especially the knees. He had no history of trauma or surgical procedures. Over the past two years, he experienced a tapered urinary stream and progressive difficult voiding.
test_results: Whole-exome sequencing was performed, and a novel homozygous LAMB3 mutation was found. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the novel mutation (chr1:209801489-209801496, NM_000228.2, c.1172_1179delinsTGTGTGTGCAAGGAG) in exon 11 of LAMB3 was homozygous in the patient and his older brother, with a predicted coding sequence change of p.P391Lfs*23. Bases 1172-1179 of LAMB3 were lost and TGTGTGTGCAAGGAG was inserted in this position, which led to a transition from proline to leucine on the 391st amino acid, resulting in a frameshift and truncated protein. Retrograde urethrography was performed. Iohexol was injected into the bladder through the external urethral orifice and observation and filming were performed simultaneously. Stricture at the cavernous urethra (∼8.5 cm long) and an inflated bulbar urethra were found. Furthermore, color ultrasound showed urinary retention and a slightly larger than normal prostate with a size of about 4.9*3.5*3.4 cm.
diagnosis: Junctional Epidermolysis Bullosa  associated with a novel homozygous LAMB3 mutation

case_report: A 27-year-old male presented with a swelling in the lower lip persisting for 6 months. The patient reported that the swelling had periods of growth and reduction during this time. No additional symptoms were noted. Physical examination revealed a sub-mucosal nodular swelling on the inner aspect of the lower lip near tooth 33. The swelling matched the color of the surrounding mucosa and measured approximately 0.7 × 0.7 cm. Upon palpation, the swelling was firm, sessile, and non-tender. The lesion was subsequently excised. The excised specimen was greyish-white, firm, and measured 1 × 0.6 × 0.5 cm.
test_results: A well-circumscribed lesion composed of thin-walled cavernous vessels lined by flat endothelial cells was seen in the deeper connective tissue stroma. These cavernous spaces were filled with red blood cells and thrombi. In between the cavernous spaces, cellular areas composed of proliferating bland spindle cells were seen. A few vacuolated endothelial cells were also seen in between. Numerous plump endothelial cells showing lumina formation were noted. Mitosis and atypia were not observed. Immunohistochemical stains for vascular markers CD31 and CD34 were positive for the endothelial cells, whereas the spindle cells were negative.

case_report: A 46-year-old man, who primarily uses his right hand, experienced painful catching of the right thumb for a duration of 3 months. The patient reported no history of trauma to the hand. During the physical examination, a nodule was observed in the flexor pollicis longus (FPL) along with triggering. X-ray imaging showed no abnormalities. An injection of 1 milliliter of a 1:1 solution of triamcinolone (40 mg/mL) and bupivacaine 0.5% was administered into the right thumb flexor tendon sheath at the level of the metacarpal head. After three months, a second injection into the flexor sheath was performed due to the recurrence of symptoms three weeks earlier. The patient did not experience relief from the second injection and was scheduled for A1 pulley release. On the day of the scheduled procedure, the patient reported a recent sudden inability to actively extend the thumb interphalangeal (IP) joint and exhibited tenderness over the anatomic snuffbox. The patient again confirmed no recent trauma.
test_results: Physical examination confirmed loss of active thumb IP extension with no tenodesis effect and no evidence of scars or laceration on the hand.
diagnosis: Spontaneous Atraumatic Extensor Pollicis Longus Rupture

case_report: A 22-year-old woman exhibited swelling of the left lower limb/hindquarter, left upper limb, and left side of the face since birth. There was no evidence of excessive tissue growth or venous issues. Additionally, a skin vascular lesion was observed on the left side of the chest, along with persistent red telangiectasia on the left thigh. These conditions remained unchanged and grew proportionally with her.
test_results: Lower limb lymphoscintigraphy revealed reduced lymph node uptake of tracer in the left groin but otherwise normal-looking lymph drainage pathways in both legs. No pathogenic variants were identified in a panel of 22 genes known to be associated with lymphatic problems. H&E staining as well as staining for lymphatic vessel markers revealed no obvious vascular alteration. A normal lymph vessel network with weak PROX1 expression was shown. A very low number of lymphatic valves was detectable. No cystic vascular lesions or dilated vessels were detected. Podoplanin-positive lymphatic vessels packed with red blood cells were observed, indicating that the telangiectasias represented lymphatic vessels containing blood, hence their red color.

case_report: A 16-month-old boy was transferred from an outside hospital due to a high fever and skin rash. He was born at 40 weeks of gestation via normal vaginal delivery, weighing 3670 g. His medical history includes atopic dermatitis and a resolved episode of suspected viral meningitis at 100 days old. He received age-appropriate vaccinations without adverse events. His development in language and motor skills was normal. On admission, his weight was 11.5 kg (50th–75th percentile) and height was 81.9 cm (50th–75th percentile). He had a high fever of up to 40°C for 3 days. Physical examination revealed hand and foot swelling. Initial laboratory results showed normal complete blood count (CBC), blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine (Cr), and serum albumin levels, but elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) at 10.37 mg/dL. He was initially treated with intravenous cefotaxime. By the third day, he developed perioral ecchymosis and mild coagulopathy with a prothrombin time (PT) international normalized ratio (INR) of 1.30, activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) of 67.0 seconds, and D-dimer > 1000 ng/mL. Blood culture and respiratory viral polymerase chain reaction (PCR) did not identify any pathogens. He also developed oliguria (0.5 cc/kg/h), persistent high fever, and swollen extremities. He was transferred to our hospital on the sixth day of fever. On arrival, his vital signs were: blood pressure 149/91 mm Hg, pulse 189 bpm, and body temperature 38.2°C. He appeared acutely ill with generalized edema, oral ulcers, and multiple purpura, including perioral ecchymosis. Blood tests showed bicytopenia with hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL, platelet count 120,000/μL, and white blood cell (WBC) count 7200/μL (70.7% neutrophils, 15.8% lymphocytes, 4.8% eosinophils). Other findings included CRP 11.14 mg/dL, BUN/Cr 3 mg/dL / 0.17 mg/dL, albumin 2.3 mg/dL, PT INR 1.22, aPTT 47.8 seconds, fibrinogen 372 mg/dL, D-dimer 5.82 μg/mL, and fibrin degradation product 33 μg/mL. Cerebrospinal fluid profile and urinalysis were unremarkable. He was treated with intravenous vancomycin (60 mg/kg/day) and meropenem (60 mg/kg/day) as empiric antibiotics, but repeated cultures showed no pathogens. On the third day, new ecchymosis around his right ear and forehead developed, and high fever persisted. Peripheral blood smear, bone marrow examination, and bone scan showed no specific abnormalities. Immunoglobulin (Ig) levels were: IgG 969 mg/dL, IgM 242 mg/dL, IgA 74.3 mg/dL, and IgE 1679 kU/L. Complement fractions C3, C4, and CH50 were low at 80.0 mg/dL, 6.7 mg/dL, and 13.3 U/mL, respectively. Antinuclear antibody (ANA) was positive at 1:320 with homogenous fluorescence, and anti-double stranded (anti-ds) DNA antibody was positive at 10.8 IU/mL. Tests for other autoantibodies were negative. Two weeks later, leukopenia and worsening thrombocytopenia developed, along with persistent fever. Complement fractions decreased further to 37.9 mg/dL of C3, < 1.5 mg/dL of C4, and under 10.0 U/mL of CH50. ANA titer increased to 1:1280, and anti-ds DNA antibody level increased to 84.4 IU/mL. Lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibody were positive. Naproxen was started on the 30th day of fever, and the fever subsided by the 32nd day. Steroid therapy (methylprednisolone, 2 mg/kg/day) was initiated. Anti-ds DNA antibody level and complement fractions improved, and fever did not recur. Steroid dose was reduced to 1.0 mg/kg/day after one week and to 0.5 mg/kg/day two weeks later. Fever returned, and anti-ds DNA antibody titer increased, prompting an increase in steroid dose to 1.0 mg/kg/day, which resolved the fever. One week later, fever, hand and foot swelling, and proteinuria (Urine Protein/Creatinine ratio of 0.484 mg/mg) reappeared. Renal biopsy confirmed lupus nephritis (focal lupus nephritis, class III). Transthoracic echocardiography showed vegetation in the tricuspid valve. He was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone (1.0 g/m2) for 3 days, followed by cyclophosphamide (500 mg/m2). Steroid (deflazacort), mycophenolate mofetil, and cyclosporin were used for treatment, and the condition was well controlled.
test_results: Partial exome sequencing for 4813 OMIM genes was performed in his peripheral leukocytes. One heterozygous missense variant, c.5536A>G (p.Lys1846Glu), was found, which was inherited from his father.
