This variant was confirmed using in silico prediction tools, such as PolyPhen-2 (score 1.00) and SIFT (score 0.00). Multiple ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) analysis (P385-A2, MRC Holland, Amsterdam, the Netherlands) was done in the peripheral leukocytes of both the patient and his parents, which revealed a heterozygous deletion of exon 1 to 8 in the patient and his mother.
Orpha_name: Combined immunodeficiency due to DOCK8 deficiency

case_report: A 46-year-old male with a history of asymptomatic hyperuricemia and small psoriatic plaques on the lower limbs (resolved without treatment 10 years ago) began hypouricemic therapy due to persistently high uric acid levels over three years (8.4 mg%, 8.7 mg%, and 9.4 mg%). The patient had no known muscle, renal, or hepatic diseases and consumed fewer than 5 units of alcohol per week. He reported progressive muscle weakness and myalgia in the lower limbs over three weeks, starting six weeks after initiating hypouricemic treatment and prophylactic gout flare prevention. The treatment regimen included allopurinol, starting at 100 mg/day and increasing by 100 mg/day every two weeks to a maximum of 300 mg/day, along with 0.5 mg/day of colchicine. Mild diarrhea occurred three days after starting the medication but resolved spontaneously. By the third week, the patient experienced progressive myalgia, and by the fifth week, progressive weakness, difficulty climbing stairs, and general malaise prompted him to discontinue the medication and seek medical evaluation. He also reported tenderness and contractures in the thighs and calves, as well as dark urine by the third week, although urine analysis was not performed. Physical examination showed proximal muscle weakness in the limbs (4/5 on the Research Medical Council grading system) and tenderness in the thighs and calves, with intact sensory system, coordination, and reflexes. Biochemical evaluation revealed a five-fold increase in creatinine kinase (CK) to 1101 U/L (normal: 30-200 U/L). Hepatic enzymes were within normal limits, with alanine aminotransferase (ALT) at 33 U/L (normal: 0-55 U/L) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) slightly elevated at 37 U/L (normal: 5-34 U/L). Uric acid levels decreased to 5.5 mg/dL (previously 9.4 mg/dL before treatment). Creatinine was normal at 0.99 mg/dL, and no other biochemical or hematological abnormalities were noted.
test_results: On ENG testing, sensitive and motor nerve conduction studies, late F-responses and H-reflex were normal. After EMG evaluation of unilateral right biceps brachii and bilateral quadriceps, bilateral medial gastrocnemius and bilateral biceps femoris, increased insertional activity and spontaneous activity such as fibrillations, positive sharp waves, high-frequency myotonic discharges, and myopathic motor unit action potentials (MUAPs) of small amplitude and duration and increased polyphasic index were observed. On biceps brachii and quadriceps muscles, at maximal effort, an interferential pattern with reduced amplitudes was observed. Motor unit action potentials showed a decrease in mean duration (36% and 39% decreased for both quadriceps and 17% decreased for biceps brachii), and their polyphasic index was also increased. Some MUAPs showed satellite potentials.

case_report: A 39-year-old Caucasian woman, 30 weeks pregnant, presented with shortness of breath, cough, and fever. She exhibited severe low blood oxygen levels. Laboratory testing confirmed an influenza B infection. Despite treatment with oseltamivir and amoxicillin-clavulanate, her low oxygen levels and low carbon dioxide levels persisted. Imaging studies, including a CT pulmonary angiogram and a ventilation/perfusion lung scan, did not show any evidence of pulmonary embolism. After an elective caesarean delivery at 33 weeks, she continued to require supplemental oxygen due to persistent low oxygen levels. Her medical history included arterial hypertension and hypothyroidism during the current pregnancy. Family history noted the early death of a sister. She reported no chest pain, fainting, coughing up blood, or smoking history. Physical examination revealed slight shortness of breath and low oxygen levels (oxygen saturation at 99% with 4 L/min supplemental oxygen). Bibasilar lung crackles were present, but there was no peripheral edema or changes in skin, fingers, or nails. Initial tests showed severe low oxygen levels (PaO2 59 mmHg with FiO2 21%) and low carbon dioxide levels, with a good response to oxygen therapy. Biochemical and autoimmunity studies were normal. Chest radiography showed no pleural or pulmonary abnormalities. Pulmonary function tests indicated normal spirometry volumes but a low diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) at 56.9%. High-resolution CT scans ruled out lung parenchymal involvement. A transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) showed a non-dilated right ventricle and a tricuspid regurgitation velocity gradient of 3.0 m/s. A bubble study ruled out intracardiac or intrapulmonary shunts.
test_results: A right heart catheterization (RHC) revealed severe resting hypoxaemia (SaO2 86%) and mild, pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension (PH), partially reversible with 100% O2. Genetic testing identified a pathogenic heterozygous variant in BMRP2 gene [c.647dup p.(Val217Serfs*3)].

case_report: A 14-year-old Greek male, born to healthy non-consanguineous parents, at term and without perinatal complications, was evaluated for uncontrolled epilepsy. He experienced generalized motor seizures starting at 3.5 months of age, which were eventually managed with anticonvulsants. He exhibited developmental delays, achieving head control at 4.5 months and walking at 19 months with a broad-based unsteady gait. He was noted to have ataxic cerebral palsy. Additionally, he had delayed speech and generalized learning difficulties in school. Tubulopathy was identified at the age of 8 years, and he was initially treated for Bartter syndrome. His treatment included potassium gluconate, magnesium, spironolactone, and indomethacin. At the same age, sensorineural deafness was detected, and he began using a hearing aid. During his teenage years, he experienced infrequent secondarily generalized focal motor seizures that did not respond to several medication changes. At 14 years old, he was a pleasant, cooperative teenager with mild intellectual disability. His cranial nerve examination (II–XII) was normal, and he had normal muscle strength in the upper and lower extremities. He exhibited mild spastic hypertonia in the lower limbs, increased deep tendon reflexes, and bilateral Babinski signs. There was mildly decreased superficial sensation in the lower extremities, but no disturbance of position sensation or vibration. Romberg sign was absent. His gait was broad-based and slow, and he was unable to walk in tandem. Examination for cerebellar signs showed no tremor or dysmetria, but rapid alternating movements were slow and uncoordinated, resulting in dysdiadochokinesis. Wakefulness and sleep electroencephalogram (EEG) showed slow background rhythms without epileptiform activity. Brain computed tomography (CT) and MRI were normal. Nerve conduction studies revealed mild abnormalities on two occasions without significant differences between the tests. The motor conduction velocities on the second measurement were 41.3 m/s for the right median nerve, 38.2 m/s for the right peroneal nerve, and 40.8 m/s for the left peroneal nerve. The sensory conduction velocities were 38.6 m/s for the right median nerve, 42.9 m/s for the right ulnar nerve, and 42.3 m/s for the right sural nerve. No other abnormalities were noted in these electrophysiological studies. Laboratory tests showed normal serum vitamin E, B12, folic acid, and plasma very-long-chain fatty acid (VLCFA) levels. The patient's epilepsy was fully controlled with topiramate and carbamazepine. At follow-up, the ataxia and spasticity remained stable, with independent home ambulation and the need for support in the community. Episodic weakness occurred on multiple occasions without evidence of electrolyte disturbance or clinically overt seizures, and this responded to adjustment of the anticonvulsants. Overall, his condition was consistent with a static disorder of movement, with activity limitations, also associated with intellectual disability and epilepsy.
test_results: The patient was heterozygous for two KCNJ10 mutations: a missense mutation (p.R65C) and a duplication (p.F119GfsX25) that creates a premature truncation of the protein. Both mutations are likely damaging. The missense mutation p.R65C has been listed as disease causing in various databases including OMIM. Prediction software agrees. The truncating frameshift mutation p.F119GfsX25 is noted to be most likely damaging. Prediction software agrees.

case_report: A 7-month-old male presented to the emergency department with a mass in the left anterior chest and a fever lasting 2 days. The patient experienced delayed umbilical cord separation at 6 weeks old. He had been vaccinated according to the Japanese national immunization program without adverse reactions, receiving Bacille Calmette-Guérin vaccine, three doses of 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine, hepatitis B vaccine, and pentavalent rotavirus vaccine. The patient was born to non-consanguineous parents and showed normal growth. Family history included two maternal uncles who died at 4 and 7 months old, with the older uncle having persistent refractory diarrhea. The maternal grandmother reported that both uncles had hypogammaglobulinemia, but their medical records were unavailable. Physical examination revealed a body temperature of 38.2°C, heart rate of 181 beats/min, respiratory rate of 48 breaths/min, oxygen saturation of 98% in room air, and blood pressure of 123/77 mm Hg. The patient appeared well. Examination of the left anterior chest wall showed a firm, non-fluctuant subcutaneous mass, 5 cm in diameter, with overlying skin redness and no tenderness. The patient had dry skin and features of ectodermal dysplasia, including sparse hair and eyebrows, a depressed nasal bridge, no deciduous teeth eruption, and decreased sweating as indicated by a starch-iodine test. Laboratory results showed an elevated white blood cell count (25,000/μL with 38% polymorphonuclear neutrophils and 55% lymphocytes) and C-reactive protein concentration (7.5 mg/dL). Serum immunoglobulin levels were IgG 87 mg/dL (reference range: 300-700 mg/dL), IgG1 41.5 mg/dL (136.9-497.8 mg/dL), IgG2 22.4 mg/dL (42.3-159.6 mg/dL), IgA 10 mg/dL (9-55 mg/dL), IgM 148 mg/dL (51-188 mg/dL), and IgE <5.0 IU/mL (≤20 IU/mL). Specific antibodies for hepatitis B virus and pertussis-toxin were not detectable despite previous vaccination. Complement components were normal. B lymphocytes were present in peripheral blood (CD19+ cells: 17%). Chest X-ray showed normal lung and left rib findings. Computed tomography of the chest revealed a mass approximately 2.7 cm in diameter with poor internal contrast, extending contiguously from a focal osteolytic lesion of the left seventh rib.
test_results: Flow cytometric analysis of peripheral blood revealed normal expression of CD40 ligand and decreased NEMO expression in CD3+ cells and CD14+ cells. Analysis of the IKBKG gene by long-range PCR and the Sanger sequence revealed a novel in-frame deletion of a codon (c.262_264delGAG), which resulted in one amino acid microdeletion (∆E88) in exon 3.
diagnosis: X-Linked Anhidrotic Ectodermal Dysplasia with Immunodeficiency

case_report: The patient is a 13-year-old female, born to a 37-year-old mother and a 38-year-old father. She was delivered vaginally at 41 weeks of gestation with a birth weight of 2.6 kg (-1.6 SDS). She has a healthy brother, and there is no family history of short stature, mental retardation, or genetic disorders. Her father's height is 178 cm (1.2 SDS) and her mother's height is 161 cm (0.5 SDS). At 5 months old, she underwent PDA ligation for a patent ductus arteriosus. Her early developmental milestones were delayed. During preschool, she exhibited learning disabilities, delayed motor development, and impaired social interactions. She was nonverbal in preschool and was noted to have selective mutism at 5 years old. At 6 years old, a psychological test estimated her intelligence quotient at 64 and her mental age at 5.5 years. Her height consistently remained below the third percentile. At 8 years old, she was evaluated for short stature. Physical examination revealed a height of 115.5 cm (-2.1 SDS) and a weight of 26.0 kg (0 SDS). Notable physical features included a short neck, prognathism, blepharophimosis, clinodactyly, and a shield chest. Endocrinological tests indicated normal insulin-like growth factor-1 levels and thyroid function. Chromosome analysis results were normal (46,XX), and no pathological findings were identified in the mutation analysis of the PTPN11 gene. Brain MRI results were normal. Skull radiographs showed a thickened calvarium and prognathism. Hand radiographs revealed clinodactyly with bone age appropriate for chronological age. Whole-spine radiographs indicated large vertebral pedicles and mild scoliosis.
test_results: Clinical exome sequencing revealed a c.1498A>G (p.Ile500Val) variant in the SMAD4 gene, confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Familial genotyping confirmed the variant as a de novo variant.

case_report: A 53-year-old male presented with an 8-month history of walking difficulties and upper-limb proximal weakness. His medical history included essential tremor, bipolar disorder, asthma, and diverticular disease. Neurological examination revealed mild proximal weakness in the upper limbs and mild weakness in the lower limbs, predominantly on the right side, with muscle hypotrophy observed in the intrinsic hand muscles and the right calf. Bulbar function remained intact. Deep tendon reflexes were brisk in all limbs, accompanied by bilateral Hoffman and Babinski signs. Spasticity was not observed. There was no reported family history of the condition.
test_results: Electrophysiological studies showed active denervation and reinnervation potentials in three body regions. Increased central motor conduction time with increased latency and reduced amplitude was observed in the right upper limb as measured by transcranial MEPs. MRI T2-weighted images showed hypointensity of the bilateral motor cortex and FLAIR hyperintensity of the left cortico-spinal bundle. MRI tractography revealed reduced FA values in the cortico-spinal tract acquisitions. 18FDG-PET showed areas of hypermetabolism affecting both cerebellar hemispheres, with a prevalence in the right lobe.

case_report: The family tree is depicted in Fig. a. The primary subject (II-1) is a 28-year-old female presenting with significant hearing loss without any additional syndromic features. Audiometric evaluation revealed bilateral hearing loss across all frequencies, with a greater impact on middle to high frequencies, as indicated by pure tone audiometry (PTA). The pure tone averages at 500 Hz, 1000 Hz, and 2000 Hz were recorded at 97 dB HL in both ears (refer to Fig. b). Impedance audiometry showed a typical A-type tympanogram for each ear. Imaging studies, including temporal bone computerized tomography (TBCT) and magnetic resonance imaging-inner ear hydrography (MRI-IEH), did not reveal any notable abnormalities in the middle or inner ear. The subject (II-1) did not exhibit any additional symptoms such as vestibular disorders (e.g., dizziness, vertigo), optic issues (e.g., blurred or distorted vision, eye pain), developmental anomalies, or intellectual disability. According to family information, II-1 had congenital hearing loss with no significant progression over the years. No hearing loss or related symptoms were reported in the subject's parents (I-1 and I-2) or sibling (II-2). The parents had a consanguineous marriage. There is no history of hearing loss in the last three generations of the family.
test_results: A promising variant within LOXHD1 (c. c.5948C > T; p.S1983F) was identified after rigorous filters. It was co-segregated and validated in this family by Sanger sequencing. Although homogeneous MT-RNR1: m.827A > G was identified in the proband, her asymptomatic brother and mother also carried this variant.

case_report: A four-month-old male infant born in October 2001, the only child of consanguineous parents, was admitted to the intensive care unit with septic shock, bilateral suppurative otitis media, thrush, and diaper area candidiasis. Three days before admission, he developed a fever that partially responded to acetaminophen. Physical examination showed tachycardia, weak peripheral perfusion, significant weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, abundant mucous discharge from both tympanic ducts, erythematosquamous cutaneous lesions on the thoracic wall, thrush, and diaper area dermatitis. Blood pressure stabilized after rapid intravenous fluid infusion and red blood cell transfusion. Intravenous cefotaxime and cloxacillin were administered. Laboratory tests revealed leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance (> 40 x 10^3/mm^3) that persisted despite antibiotic treatment. Chest radiography showed mild, bilateral, symmetrical interstitial infiltrates. Urine and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cytochemistry were normal. Blood, urine, and CSF cultures were sterile. Culturing of otic discharge showed Haemophilus influenzae type B and coagulase-negative Staphylococcus. Antibiotic treatment continued for 14 days with a good clinical response. The patient's past medical history included uncomplicated fetal development, full-term eutocic delivery, and a birth weight of 3,400 grams. He experienced respiratory depression and sepsis of unknown origin at birth, treated empirically with broad-spectrum antibiotics. His umbilical cord detached at 21 days of age, and since day 23, he had recurrent episodes of bilateral non-purulent otitis media resistant to regular antibiotic treatment. He was readmitted at two months old for bronchopneumonia and mucoid suppurative otitis media. During that hospital stay, he was treated for cellulitis originating at venipuncture sites, affecting his entire arm, with intravenous penicillin and cloxacillin, resulting in a good outcome. Based on recurrent infections and physical findings, tests for human immunodeficiency virus, complement components, and quantitative immunoglobulin isotypes A, G, M, and E were performed. Determinations of CD4, CD8, and the CD4/CD8 ratio were normal. Further analyses for CD18 and CD11, as well as bone imaging and a bone marrow biopsy, were conducted.
test_results: Flow cytometry analysis detected that the CD11 and CD18 levels were low.

case_report: A 58-year-old man presented with a two-month history of sudden-onset central scotomas in both eyes. Initially, he experienced headaches, fevers, chills, and muscle aches for five days, and tested negative for COVID-19 on two occasions. His electrocardiogram, chest x-ray, and head computed tomography performed in the emergency room were normal. There was no significant medical or family history. Examination revealed best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 20/20 in the right eye and 20/100 in the left eye. The anterior segment examination was normal in both eyes. Bilateral plaque-like yellowish macular lesions were noted.
test_results: Fluorescein angiography (FA) revealed early-phase macular hyperfluorescent staining that intensified in the late phases. Indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) showed persistent macular hypofluorescence in both eyes. The foveal centered SS-OCT B-scans showed bilateral focal deposits on the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and disruption of the outer photoreceptor bands. The CC structural images displayed some focal defects. The CC flow images showed more obvious foci with loss of perfusion. The density of CC FDs within a 5 mm circle centered on the fovea were 12.52% in the right eye and 14.64% in the left eye.

case_report: A 48-year-old woman with uterine fibroids received her first subcutaneous injection of leuprorelin acetate, a GnRH agonist, at a dose of 1.88 mg on the third day of her menstrual cycle. Four weeks later, she received a second dose of the same medication. Six weeks after the initial injection, she experienced difficulty breathing and consulted her previous physician. A plain chest radiograph indicated a suspected large pleural effusion, leading to her referral to our hospital for further evaluation. Her surgical history included a laparoscopic myomectomy performed nine years earlier. The patient did not have a history of smoking. Her father had a notable family history of colon cancer. During her initial visit, her vital signs were as follows: blood pressure 138/87 mmHg, pulse 86 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and temperature 36.7°C. Physical examination revealed no pulmonary vessel murmurs, abdominal vascular murmurs, or other significant findings. Laboratory tests showed no signs of inflammation and no elevated lung cancer tumor markers, with most other results within normal limits. A plain chest radiograph demonstrated widespread decreased permeability of the right lung fields, indicative of a large pleural effusion.
test_results: Contrast-enhanced CT at the first visit showed a massive right-sided pleural effusion. Giant uterine fibroids and ascites were suspected in Douglas’s pouch. The pleural effusion was exudative based on Light’s criteria. No malignancy was observed. On magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis, degenerative uterine fibroids were considered.

case_report: Patient B is a 41-year-old woman residing in a rural area of upper Austria. At the age of 35, she was evaluated for primary immunodeficiency following her first episode of pneumonia. She has experienced recurrent bacterial bronchitis over the past four years, with no known risk factors such as allergies or smoking. She has two healthy children, a nine-year-old son and a six-year-old daughter.
test_results: IgA-, IgM- and IgG2-IgG3-IgG4 subclass deficiency (serum IgG, mg/dl [normal range]: 940 [790–1700]; serum IgG2, mg/dl [normal range]: 51 [150–600]; serum IgG3, mg/dl [normal range]: 5 [20–100]; serum IgG4, mg/dl [normal range]: <7 [8–120]; serum IgA, mg/dl [normal range]: <6 [76–450]; serum IgM, mg/dl [normal range]:29 [90–350]) with normal levels of IgG1 and antibody deficiency against bacterial polysaccharides.
Orpha_name: Combined immunodeficiency due to partial RAG1 deficiency

case_report: A 4-year-old girl, with no previous history of eczema or psoriasis, exhibited a 4-week history of widespread erythematous scaly rash that began on her face and scalp and quickly extended to her torso and limbs. Additionally, she had distinct, red-orange, waxy plaques on her palms and soles. Her growth and psychomotor development were within normal limits.
test_results: Histopathology showed basket-like hyperkeratosis, diffuse orthokeratosis and spotted parakeratosis, and a dermal superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltration.

case_report: A 58-year-old woman with a history of newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus and a previous right liver hepatectomy in 1998 presented in September 2020 to the emergency department. She reported experiencing multiple episodes of watery, non-bloody diarrhea, up to 20 loose bowel movements per day, over the past five months, along with a weight loss of 10 kgs. The patient did not report any nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain. Physical examination showed no signs of dehydration. Laboratory results indicated a potassium level of 1.9 mmol/l, anicteric cholestasis, and normal levels of albumin and hemoglobin. The clinical presentation was very similar to her condition 22 years ago.
test_results: The plasma VIP level was 451 pmol/l (upper limit 40 pmol). An abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan was performed revealing four hepatic lesions of segments I, III, IV and the sectional slice. The lesions were spontaneously hypodense, intensely enhancing after injection of contrast product in the arterial phase with a wash out in the portal phase. The lesions were hyperintense on T2- and diffusion weighted MRI, enhancing in the arterial phase with a wash out in the portal and late phases. Ultrasound-guided liver biopsy of the lesions was performed revealing a tumor cell proliferation with glandular architecture. The tumor cells were small, round and monotonous with “salt and pepper” nuclear chromatin. Immunohistochemical staining revealed that tumor cells were diffusely positive for neuroendocrine markers (synaptophysin, chromogranin A and CD56).

case_report: A 57-year-old woman presented to Seoul St. Mary’s Hospital with intermittent right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain. She had previously been treated at another hospital for right flank pain and a right ureter stone. A computed tomography (CT) scan from the other hospital indicated chronic calculous cholecystitis. Upon examination, her abdomen showed no gross abnormalities, and she had no ongoing symptoms such as pain, dyspepsia, or flank pain. Murphy signs, abdomen tenderness, and rebound tenderness were all negative. Laboratory tests revealed slight elevations in total bilirubin (1.79 mg/dL) and direct bilirubin (1.41 mg/dL), while aspartate aminotransferase (AST) was 13 U/L and alanine transaminase (ALT) was 10 U/L. Serological tests for hepatitis B and C and autoimmune markers were negative. A contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan showed no significant abnormalities in the liver, but did confirm chronic calculous cholecystitis and the presence of a few renal cysts. An elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy was planned due to the chronic calculous cholecystitis. During the procedure, 'black liver' with no nodularity was observed. The laparoscopic cholecystectomy was successfully completed without complications.
test_results: The biopsy revealed coarse, dark brown granules in centrilobular hepatocytes via hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. No signs of hemosiderin or ferritin were noted with Prussian blue staining. No signs of fibrosis were observed in the liver parenchyma with Masson trichrome staining. In the ABCC2 mutation study, a missense mutation in exon 18 was discovered: arginine in gene position 768 was substituted with tryptophan (R768W).

case_report: A 2.4-year-old Russian boy presented with psychomotor and speech disabilities. The primary concerns included poor speech development, limited comprehension of addressed speech, and a lack of age-appropriate skills. He was born from the fourth pregnancy and third childbirth, with one prior abortion. He has a healthy brother and sister, though a sibling’s blood sample was not available. The pregnancy was complicated by maternal subclinical hypothyroidism. The boy was delivered via emergency childbirth at 37 weeks of gestation, weighing 2910 grams and measuring 49 cm in length, with Apgar scores of 7 and 8. His early development was marked by delays in motor milestones: he could hold his head in the prone position at 4 months, sit without assistance at 1 year, and walk with support at 1.3 years. Biochemical tests were normal except for hypoglycemia. The leucocyte karyotype and methylation-specific PCR of the FMR1 gene promoter were normal. Functional tests showed no focal or generalized pathological activity and no significant interhemispheric asymmetry. No specific forms of activity were observed.
test_results: A brain MRI revealed high signal diffuse areas in the subcortical regions against the background of incomplete myelination.

case_report: A 32-year-old man with no prior health issues came to the hospital with left-sided chest pain that worsened with breathing. Imaging revealed multiple blood clots in both lungs. After being assessed by hematology and finding no abnormalities in blood clotting tests, he was discharged with oral blood thinners. During this hospital stay, his serum albumin level was 2.0 g/dL. Six months after completing the blood thinner treatment, a follow-up CT scan of the pulmonary arteries showed a significant reduction in the blood clots. A few months later, he returned to the hospital with chest pain, and another CT scan showed an increase in blood clots, leading to the placement of an inferior vena cava (IVC) filter. During a follow-up visit, his primary care physician noted signs of nephrotic syndrome, including multiple urine tests showing protein levels between 300 to over 600 mg/dL, serum albumin levels ranging from 1.1 to 2.1 g/dL, hemoglobin A1c of 5.3%, and LDL cholesterol of 292 mg/dL. He was urgently referred to a kidney specialist, but before the appointment, he developed swelling in all four limbs and his face, prompting another emergency room visit. Initial tests showed an albumin level of 0.8 g/dL, a CT scan of the pulmonary arteries revealed multiple blood clots in the lower lobes of both lungs, and a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed blood clots in both renal veins. He was started on a heparin drip, assessed by interventional radiology, and underwent a procedure to remove the blood clots from both renal veins. The urine protein/creatinine ratio indicated 11 g of protein in the urine, confirming nephrotic syndrome.
test_results: The patient was seropositive for anti-phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) antibody.

case_report: A 69-year-old Caucasian man presented with an itchy papular rash on his torso and extremities, which did not respond to local treatments with antibiotics and steroids. The skin lesions first appeared 4 years ago and worsened with heat and increased sweating. Multiple biopsies in the past identified multiple cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas, which were subsequently excised. Apart from his skin issues, the patient's medical history was otherwise unremarkable, and there was no relevant family history. He did not exhibit B symptoms, initial blood tests were normal, and skin cancer screening showed no abnormalities. Physical examination showed erythematous, focally eroded papules on his back, neckline, and lower extremities, fine-lamellar scaling on the extremities, and erythematous plaques on his left hand. Dermoscopy revealed yellow crypts with white halos in a radiating pattern.
test_results: Histopathologically, acanthosis, focal acantholytic dyskeratosis, and parakeratosis as well as a superficial, perivascular, lymphohistiocytic infiltrate was seen.

case_report: An 18-month-old female, who had recently undergone resection of a GAF, was referred for genetic counseling. She is the only child of healthy parents with no consanguinity. The patient's father had myelinated retinal nerve fiber persistence. A paternal uncle had multiple myeloma. The paternal grandfather passed away from Hodgkin lymphoma at 47 years old, and the maternal grandmother was diagnosed with colonic diverticular disease and one hyperplastic intestinal polyp at 60 years old. A paternal aunt of the patient's mother had colon cancer at 60 years old. The patient was born after 39 weeks of gestation. From birth, she exhibited asymmetric frontal and occipital bossing. At 9 months old, a paraspinal, non-tender, slightly mobile, nodular lesion was noted. An ultrasound revealed a 3 × 0.5-cm fusiform mass in the subcutaneous adipose tissue, without deep infiltration and vascularization. An additional subcentimetric lesion was palpable in the subcutis of the posterior neck. Surgical excision of the paraspinal lesion was performed, revealing a poorly circumscribed, rubbery white mass. Histologically, the lesion showed hypocellular sheets of haphazardly arranged collagen bands with a few interspersed spindle cells, clear cracks between collagen fibers, and rare capillary-sized vessels. An infiltrative pattern was present at the periphery with entrapment of fat and nerve fibers. Immunohistochemistry showed spindle cells positive for vimentin, CD34, and nuclear beta-catenin but negative for muscle-specific actin, smooth muscle actin, and desmin. MRI and ultrasound examinations of the neck identified the small lesion as an additional fibroma. At clinical examination at 18 months old, the child showed normal growth parameters and cranium circumference. A subtle nodular lesion below the surgical scar was still noticeable. A subcutaneous elliptical lesion involving the right frontal bone, slightly mobile, was also observed. The remainder of the physical examination did not reveal any other skin lesions or clinically evident bone abnormalities. Dental and oral examinations were normal. Retinal examination showed no signs of congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE).
test_results: The analysis identified the heterozygous variant c.4391_4394del, p.(Glu1464Valfs*8) of the APC gene (NM_000038.4).

case_report: A 23-year-old male from middle Europe experienced recurring, painful erosions in the urethral outlet area for approximately 4 years. He had a history of congenital hypospadias in the urethral area and was under regular urological examination. Due to the persistence of mucosal lesions, he was referred to the Dermatology department. Clinical examination revealed an ulcer in the urethral outlet area and a few erosions on the gingiva, resembling mild gingivitis. The gingival lesions did not affect his daily activities. He was otherwise in good health and not on any medication. Tests for sexually transmitted disorders were negative.
test_results: The indirect immunofluorescence on salt split skin showed epidermal IgG reactivity at blister roof. An isolated positive BP230 ELISA at 85 U/ml was identified, while NC16A BP180 ELISA was negative. The analysis from a biopsy of unaffected buccal mucosa revealed IgG and C3 deposition at the dermal-epidermal junction in the direct immunofluorescence. Immunoblotting analysis using human epidermal extract as substrate showed IgG immunoreactivity with BP230 and slightly also collagen VII. IgA autoantibodies did not react in any analysis. Histological examination taken from buccal mucosa yielded a hyperplastic, non-keratinizing, mucosal epithelium without cleavage. No inflammatory infiltrate was detectable in the dermis nor evidence for PAS-positive fungal elements were identified.

case_report: A 10-month-old girl was referred to pediatric gastroenterology due to prolonged jaundice lasting three months, accompanied by tea-colored urine and poor weight gain. She also had a history of unexplained low calcium levels and mild developmental delay, with no history of fever, skin rash, or changes in stool color. She was born full-term via cesarean section with an uncomplicated neonatal period. The parents are first-degree cousins, and there is no family history of liver or metabolic diseases. She was not on any medications. Physical examination showed her head circumference, weight, and length were below the third percentile. She appeared deeply jaundiced and had dysmorphic features, including a prominent forehead, deep-set eyes, small nose, and low-set ears. Her abdomen was soft with mild hepatosplenomegaly and ascites. A cardiac examination revealed an ejection systolic murmur. The rest of the systemic examination was unremarkable. Fundus examination showed a reddish area at the center of the macula surrounded by retinal opacification, consistent with cherry-red spots on the maculae of both eyes. Laboratory tests were performed, and abdominal ultrasonography indicated fullness of the pelvicalyceal system without organomegaly or other abnormalities. Brain MRI showed diffuse abnormal white matter signal intensity. The patient was admitted to the hospital for further investigation. Biliary obstruction, autoimmune, and infectious diseases were excluded. An extensive workup for causes of the cherry-red spot was conducted, ruling out Tay Sach’s disease, Sandhoff disease, gangliosidosis, metachromatic leukodystrophy, Niemann Pick disease, Farber’s disease, Goldberg’s syndrome, Gaucher’s disease, and Hurler’s syndrome.
test_results: A whole-exome sequencing (WES) test identified a homozygous pathogenic variant in the ATP8B1 gene.

case_report: The patient is a 28-year-old male with a history of asthma and smoking. He experienced progressive shortness of breath, fevers, chills, and sweats for 4 months. A computed tomography (CT) scan revealed bilateral geographic distributions of ground glass opacities with interspersed interlobular septal thickening. He reported a productive cough with clear-to-white phlegm. He took a short course of amoxicillin-clavulanate without symptom improvement. His shortness of breath worsened significantly after 4 months, and he also developed hemoptysis. Upon admission to an outside hospital, an initial CT chest scan showed multifocal areas of ground glass opacity in the upper and lower lobes with relative sparing of the periphery. No organic antigen exposure was identified in his history. Infectious disease markers for respiratory viruses, HIV, mycobacteria, and fungi were negative. Autoimmune and inflammatory markers (including ESR, CRP, ANA, ANCA, RF, and complement levels) were negative.
test_results: Bronchoscopy with BAL revealed a milky fluid that was PAS positive.

case_report: A 28-year-old Hindu unmarried woman presented with thickened skin on her palms and soles since infancy. Initially, at 3 months of age, small erythematous pinpoint papules with asymptomatic exfoliation appeared on both palms. Concurrently, erythematous scaly plaques developed on both cubital fossae and the dorsal aspects of both hands and feet. Over time, the skin on her palms and soles became thick, waxy, and yellow, with a loss of dermatoglyphics. There was also a gradual tightening of the skin over her fingers and toes. On examination, additional findings included hyperhidrosis of the palms and soles, macerated interdigital spaces with erosions emitting a foul smell, fissures in the palms and soles, conical tapering of the distal digits, minimal digital constriction in the little finger of the left hand, and mild flexion deformity of the fingers. Erythematous scaly plaques with sharp margins were present over the bilateral cubital fossae. The oral mucosa and perioral skin appeared normal. There was no history of ocular involvement, hearing impairment, dental abnormalities, or atopy. Hair and systemic examination were unremarkable. There was a history of consanguinity, with the father and mother being first-degree relatives, but neither had similar complaints. None of the siblings or other relatives had similar complaints.
test_results: Histopathology of palmar skin showed compact hyperkeratosis, sparse superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with epidermal hyperplasia. The granular layer was thickened. The papillary dermis was thickened and showed thickened bundles of collagen in vertical arrays.

case_report: A three-year-old Moroccan boy was admitted to the neuropediatrics department at Hassan II University Hospital in Fez, Morocco, due to psychomotor retardation and absence of language. He is the youngest of three siblings from a non-consanguineous marriage; his mother is 39 years old, and his father is 45 years old. He was born at term with a birth weight of 3900g following an uneventful pregnancy and delivery, with no complications noted post-birth. At 11 months, he was unable to sit without support. He achieved independent sitting by one year and walking by two years but could not climb stairs or run. His language development was limited to repetitive syllables. A maternal uncle had an undiagnosed intellectual development disorder and died at 17 years old due to an accident. Pediatric examination revealed signs of social interaction impairment, mild autistic spectrum features, and manual stereotypies. Physical examination showed axial hypotonia and trunk ataxia, with no dysmorphic features observed. Cerebral MRI indicated a discrete T2 hypersignal and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) of the right parietal subcortical white matter and a myelination defect. EEG results were normal. Tests for Angelman syndrome and metabolic diseases were negative, and karyotype analysis was normal. Informed parental consent for genetic testing was obtained.
test_results: Exome sequencing identified a variation leading to a nonsense (STOP) mutation c.3912C>G (p.Tyr1304Ter) of the grin2b gene in a heterozygous state in the patient. This finding was further validated using Sanger sequencing, which confirmed the presence of the c.3912C>G (p.Tyr1304Ter) mutation. The segregation study conducted revealed that this mutation was de novo, meaning it was not inherited from either of the parents. The identified variant, c.3912C>G (p.Tyr1304Ter), has not been previously reported in the GnomAD database. According to the criteria of the ACMG, this variant is considered pathogenic based on multiple lines of evidence, including the presence of strong pathogenicity criteria (PVS1) and supporting moderate criteria such as strong conservation (PM2), absence from population databases (PP3), and in silico predictions (PS2, PP5). Various bioinformatics tools collectively predicted the mutation to be deleterious.

case_report: An 8-year-old boy with no prior health issues was brought to the pediatric rheumatology center at Kerman University in Southeast Iran due to a gait disturbance and limping on his left lower extremity. These symptoms began three weeks before his visit, with no history of trauma or intense physical activity. Approximately one week before he refused to walk, he had a mild respiratory tract infection characterized by low-grade fever and cough. He had previously seen an orthopedist, but no condition was identified at that time. Upon his first visit to our clinic, he was afebrile. A thorough examination was conducted, revealing an antalgic gait on the left side due to difficulty in weight-bearing. Physical examination showed pain and restricted movement in flexion, internal, and external rotation of the left hip, along with a positive FABER Test. There were no signs of other contributing factors such as organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, skin lesions, or neurological deficits. Laboratory tests showed a White Blood Cell (WBC) count of 9109 /L, an Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC) of 3.2 109 /L, an Absolute Lymphocyte Count (ALC) of 109 /L, a platelet count of 312,000/µL, and a hemoglobin level of 15.5 g/dl. The Erythrocyte Sediment Rate (ESR) was 3mm/h, and the C-Reactive Protein (CRP) level was 3.5 mg/L.
test_results: The tests indicated a high IgM level of 3.4 (with a 1.1 cut off) in the first test, and a high IgG level of 3.8 (with a 1.1 cut off) in the second test, which was performed one week later. He underwent hip joints ultrasound study with a result of 7mm effusion in left side. Finally, Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) showed a moderate joint effusion at his left hip articulation and a minimal joint effusion at his right hip joint.

case_report: A 7-day-old Italian male infant presented with a dark, irregular, and raised skin lesion measuring 8 × 11 cm on the back. He was delivered full-term via cesarean section with a birth weight of 3200 g. The infant appeared healthy with no signs of lymphadenopathy or organomegaly and had an Apgar score of 10. The mother, aged 30, was healthy and did not receive any pharmacological treatments during pregnancy. There were no unusual skin lesions observed on the mother. Prenatal ultrasound one month before delivery indicated a possible angiomatous lesion. There was no known family history of melanoma. The infant has two healthy brothers. At 7 days old, he was evaluated at the Department of Dermatology of Federico II of Naples due to the clinical characteristics of the skin lesion.
test_results: A careful dermoscopic examination was performed, which revealed irregular pigmentation, atypical pigment network, irregular dots and globules, irregular streaks, and a wide blue-whitish veil. On the seventh and fourteenth days of life, 4 biopsy specimens of the flat and the raised areas were taken. The specimens were fixed in formalin and sent for histologic analysis. All specimens demonstrated similar histologic features. There was a dermic component characterized by a solid growth pattern with deep melanocytic nodules showing a high hypercellularity with no significant atypia. The melanocytes were densely packed and uniform in nature exhibiting a small nucleus, sometimes with fine nucleoli. Nuclear pleomorphism was not seen. The immunohistochemical stains showed a strong positivity for S-100 protein and ki67, while the HMB-45 staining was negative.
diagnosis: Giant Congenital Nevus with Proliferative Dermic Nodules

case_report: A 30-year-old female from Southern India presented with fever, multiple episodes of vomiting, and cough with expectoration for 5 days. She was initially treated with oral antibiotics (amoxicillin/clavulanic acid 625 mg twice daily), but continued to experience fever spikes (mild to moderate grade with Tmax of 102.6℉). Upon admission to a local hospital, she was found to have elevated blood pressure (200/110 mm Hg) and moderate thrombocytopenia (60,000/mm3). She was managed with intravenous fluids and antihypertensive medications (labetalol 2 mg/min intravenous infusion). During this period, she developed sudden visual disturbances and a decrease in sensorium. A CT scan of the brain showed ill-defined areas of parenchymal edema in the left parieto-temporal lobe white matter, left ganglio-capsular, and left hippocampal regions. MRI of the brain revealed ill-defined T2/FLAIR hyperintense signals in the left parieto-temporal region, multiple small foci of restricted diffusion in the left frontoparietal, parasagittal region, multiple small patchy FLAIR hyperintense lesions in bilateral frontoparietal subcortical white matter, left thalamus, bilateral basal ganglion, splenium of the corpus callosum on the left side, and bilateral perioptic space widening with partial empty sella. She was treated with anti-epileptics (levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily), antihypertensive medications (labetalol 100 mg twice daily oral), and glucocorticoids (methylprednisolone 500 mg intravenously for 1 day). She was then transferred to our hospital for further management. Her past medical history included an aborted twin pregnancy and gestational hypertension three years prior. She had no other known comorbidities. Family and psychosocial histories were unremarkable. Physical examination revealed pallor, tachycardia, and elevated blood pressure (190/100). She was drowsy but arousable with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14/15 (E3V5M6). Neurological examination showed bilateral extensor plantar response, while cranial nerves, motor, sensory, and other deep tendon reflexes were normal. Baseline blood investigations indicated anemia (Hemoglobin—8.2 g/dl), moderate thrombocytopenia (platelet count—51,000/mm3), and mild hypokalemia (serum K+—3.1 meq/l). Blood and urine cultures were sent, and she was started on empirical antibiotics (ceftriaxone 2 g twice daily intravenous and oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily), antihypertensives (labetalol 2 mg/min infusion followed by 100 mg twice daily oral), and anti-epileptics (levetiracetam 500 mg orally twice daily). Infective workup was negative for Dengue, malarial parasite (quantitative buffy coat test), H1N1 polymerase chain reaction test, and Scrub typhus IgM enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay test. A guarded lumbar puncture was performed, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis (CSF) was non-contributory (CSF was colorless, clear, no red blood cells or white blood cells, Glucose was 64 mg/dl, protein was 41.1 mg/dl, GeneXpert MTB/RIF assay, Herpes simplex virus 1 & 2 real-time polymerase chain reaction test were negative, and CSF culture did not show any significant growth). Blood and urine cultures did not show any significant growth. Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome workup was negative.
test_results: Antinuclear antibody by indirect immunofluorescence assay was positive (1:40 dilution, Intensity—4+, pattern nuclear coarse speckled). Extractable nuclear antigen antibodies profile was positive for Sm/RNP and negative for Sm.

case_report: A 29-year-old female presented with recurrent episodes of slurred speech and right limb weakness lasting 1-3 hours, which began abruptly at 5 a.m. on the day prior to admission. These episodes occurred three times before progressing to persistent speech difficulties and complete paralysis of the right limbs by 1 p.m. on the day of admission. Brain computed tomography (CT) performed in the emergency department showed no abnormalities. The patient was transferred to the neurology department for further treatment. Past medical history includes a cesarean section under lumbar anesthesia 21 days prior to admission, resulting in the birth of a healthy baby girl. Seven years earlier, she experienced similar transient symptoms of slurred speech and right limb weakness approximately half a month after another cesarean section, which resolved completely. At that time, brain CT was normal, and no brain MRI was conducted. Family history includes the death of her mother over 10 years ago from an undetermined cause, a healthy father who declined further genetic investigations, and no siblings. Neurological examination revealed dysarthria, tongue deviation to the right, right upper and lower limb weakness with muscle strength MRC grade 1, absent deep tendon reflexes in all limbs, positive bilateral Babinski sign, bilateral pes cavus, no significant muscle atrophy, and sensory impairment. Routine hematological, biochemical, immunological, and thyroid function tests were normal, as were laboratory results for lactate, vitamin B12, and very long chain fatty acids. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) after admission showed diffuse abnormal signals in the corpus callosum, posterior limbs of bilateral internal capsule, and centrum semiovale.
test_results: We confirmed a c.622G>A (p.Glu208Lys) mutation in the GJB1 gene.

case_report: A 45-year-old female visited the Endocrinology clinic due to weight gain. She reported increased appetite and excessive thirst. Her medical history included hypertension, high cholesterol, obesity, sleep apnea, peripheral vascular disease, and a mood disorder. She had a history of mild cognitive impairment since childhood. She began menstruating at age 13 and had regular cycles. She resided in a group home and had no marital or parental history. Her height was 4 feet 11 inches, and her body mass index (BMI) was 40. Physical examination noted short stature, facial features including a prominent forehead, upslanted eyes, a flat nasal bridge, and a thin upper lip. Examination of her extremities showed short 4th and 5th metacarpal and metatarsal bones on both sides. Blood tests revealed normal levels of calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone (PTH), cortisol, thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), free thyroxine (FT4), follicle stimulating hormone (FSH), and luteinizing hormone (LH).
test_results: Karyotype test showed terminal deletion of the long q-arm of one chromosome 2 in all analyzed cells-46, XX, del (2)(q37.1).

case_report: A 66-year-old male presented with left nasal congestion, left periorbital swelling, and mild proptosis that began one month ago. Imaging revealed notable soft tissue edema with a hyperdense area around the orbital cavity, opacification of the maxillary sinus, and involvement of the left frontal sinus. Endoscopic sinus surgery was performed, and the specimen was collected for further examination.
test_results: Microscopic examination showed diffuse interstitial infiltration of mononuclear cells with a high N/C ratio containing hyperchromatic nuclei with disruption of glandular structures. In immunohistochemical staining, these cells showed immunoreactivity for LCA, MPO, CD117, and CD68 and negativity for CD34, CD10, CD20, CD23, CD5, CD2, CD7, CD56, CD7, CD138, CD99, and cytokeratin. Subsequent bone marrow aspiration and biopsy showed trilineage hematopoiesis with no increase in blast count.

case_report: Case 1 involves a 21.5-year-old woman from Chile, born to healthy parents of average height, who exhibited extremely low birth size and poor growth after birth. Clinical observations include a small head size, bilateral hip discomfort, a prominent forehead, deep-set eyes, underdeveloped nostrils, a smooth area between the nose and upper lip, a thin upper lip, light skin with café au lait spots, joint hypermobility, broad hands and feet with wide thumbs and big toes, and broad upper legs. Radiographic imaging revealed short finger bones, cone-shaped growth plates at the ends of the distal finger bones, an extra growth plate in the middle bone of the second finger, and a curved fifth finger with a bone age of 7.9 years compared to a chronological age of 8.7 years. The femoral necks were asymmetrical with abnormal remodeling, shortening, and deformity. Endocrine evaluations showed temporarily elevated serum IGF-I, increased plasma insulin levels, and a normal growth hormone response to clonidine. Breast development occurred relatively early, but the onset of menstruation was delayed and followed by infrequent menstrual periods. Hair progressively became dry, sparse, and brittle, with increased sensitivity of the scalp. Treatment with recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) and a GnRH analogue from ages 10.1 to 11.6 resulted in a slight increase in height standard deviation score but was stopped due to poor growth response and the development of dark, thickened skin patches and high blood pressure. From the age of 18, the patient has experienced significant muscle cramps affecting the limbs, abdominal muscles, tongue, and jaw.
test_results: The electromyography (EMG) needle triggered painful vastus lateralis spasms, leading to prolonged continuous muscle activity.
diagnosis: Syndromic severe insulin resistance with muscle cramps due to biallelic POC1A variants
Orpha_name: Acanthosis nigricans-insulin resistance-muscle cramps-acral enlargement syndrome

case_report: A 32-month-old Egyptian girl was referred to the pediatric endocrinology unit for evaluation of poor growth. She is the second-born female child to consanguineous Egyptian parents, with one normal sibling. She was born at term via normal vaginal delivery in a private hospital and cried immediately at birth. Her birth weight was 1.5 kg and length was 35 cm. At 12 days old, she experienced multifocal seizures, and hypocalcemia was detected. Serum parathormone (PTH) level was not checked due to lack of facilities. The seizures were managed with intravenous calcium infusions. Subsequently, she required calcium and alfacalcidol to maintain calcium levels and has been on calcium and vitamin D supplements since then. At one year old, her weight was 4.800 kg and height was 48 cm. Despite a good appetite, she was not thriving well. There was no history of recurrent infections or previous hospital admissions. On examination, she was found to be severely growth retarded with normal mentality. Her weight was 7 kg, height 60 cm, and head circumference 38 cm (all far below the third percentile). The upper segment to lower ratio was normal. Dysmorphic features included microcephaly, deep-set eyes, peaked nose, thin lips, micrognathia, low set ears, and a depressed nasal bridge. Systemic examination, including the cardiovascular system, was within normal limits. Ophthalmic examination did not reveal any abnormalities. Investigations showed normal hemogram, liver, renal function, and urine analysis. She had low total calcium (7.4 mg/dL, normal range 8.5-10.5 mg/dL), low ionized calcium (3.3 mg/dL, normal range 4.5-5.6 mg/dL), raised serum phosphate (8.2 mg/dL, normal range 2.4-4.1 mg/dL), raised alkaline phosphatase (344 U/L, normal range 30-95 U/L), and low intact PTH (6.2 pg/mL, normal range 12-72 pg/mL). Abdominal ultrasound was normal. Radiograph of long bones showed cortical thickening with medullary stenosis, and skull X-ray revealed absent diploic space in the skull bones. Computed tomographic scan of the brain was normal. Cytogenetic and fluorescent in situ hybridization studies were normal.
test_results: The diagnosis was confirmed genetically by detection of homozygous deletion of 12 bp (155-166 del) in exon 3 of the tubulin specific chaperone E gene (TBCE gene). The parents were heterozygous carriers of this mutation.

case_report: A two-and-a-half-year-old Caucasian girl presented with vomiting of blood. No other symptoms were reported. She was observed to be very small, with growth measurements below the 3rd percentile. She appeared pale but was very alert, active, and playful. Abdominal examination showed prominent superficial veins and an enlarged spleen measuring 6 cm from the costal margin. Other systemic examinations were normal. Her stool tested positive for occult blood, but her complete blood count, coagulation profile, extended clotting study, and thrombophilia screen were all within normal limits. A Meckel's abdominal scan was normal. Repeated liver function tests were within normal limits. The patient was born by emergency lower segment Cesarean section at 33 weeks' gestation due to fetal distress. Her parents are non-consanguineous Caucasians. At birth, her mother was 34 years old, a non-smoker, and a non-alcoholic, and was taking prophylthyouracil for a hyperactive thyroid. During pregnancy, the mother had pregnancy-induced hypertension, and fetal growth was regularly monitored due to suspected growth restriction. Ultrasound confirmed restricted growth, and Doppler ultrasound showed absent end diastolic flow. There was no oligo- or polyhydramnios. Antenatal screenings for TORCH, HIV, Treponema, and Hepatitis were normal. The patient was born in good condition with Apgar scores of 9 at one minute and 10 at five minutes. Her birth weight was 1250 g, below the 3rd percentile for her age and sex. She had an imperforate anus with a rectovaginal fistula, a heart murmur, and subsequent echocardiography confirmed a perimembranous ventricular septal defect and a persistent foramen ovale. An X-ray of her spine showed hemivertebrae in the sacrococcygeal region. Surgical correction of the imperforate anus and rectovaginal fistula was performed within the first few days of life. She spent four weeks in the neonatal unit before being discharged home. She was doing well at home until she presented at two and a half years of age with vomiting of blood. Her growth trajectory has consistently remained below the 3rd percentile.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of her liver, using a gadolinium contrast agent, confirmed splenomegaly with gastric, retroperitoneal and splenic varices. The portal vein was thready with collateral vessels involving both left and right portal veins. There was no evidence of intrahepatic duct dilation in the gadolinium-enhanced MRI scan of the liver.

case_report: An 8-year-old female patient presented with multiple brownish-black spots on her face and body, which began appearing at age four and increased in number over time. She also exhibited congenital deaf-mutism and growth retardation. There was no known family history of similar conditions. Physical examination revealed numerous brownish-black macules of varying shapes and sizes, ranging from 1 mm to 5 mm in diameter, distributed across the face, chest, back, upper and lower extremities, and palms and soles. Café-au-lait macules measuring 2 × 3 cm2 were observed on the back. Distinct facial features included wide-set eyes, a flat nasal bridge, and a protruding lower jaw. Dental anomalies such as discrepancies in the dental arch, gaps between teeth, and missing teeth were noted. Additional findings included a protruding chest, scoliosis, and winged scapula. The patient had a height of 105 cm and a weight of 15 kg. Radiologic and laboratory evaluations showed abnormal or absent dental roots in some positions and uterine underdevelopment on abdominal ultrasound, consistent with findings in peers of the same age.
test_results: Genetic analysis revealed a PTPN11 gene mutation (c.836A > G, p.Tyr279Cys).

case_report: A 32-day-old female infant presented with a 4-day history of watery diarrhea and fever, experiencing 12-13 episodes of watery stools without mucus or blood in the last 24 hours. There was no history of vomiting, loss of appetite, poor feeding, or respiratory issues. She had been in contact with a confirmed COVID-19 case 4 weeks prior, but no other family members exhibited similar symptoms. The infant was breastfed since birth, born from a nonconsanguineous marriage, and was the second child. Her birth weight was 2700 grams (3–10 percentiles), and she was not premature. Upon admission, she appeared toxic, tachypneic, and irritable with a temperature of 38.4°C (axillary), a pulse rate of 140 beats/minute, a respiratory rate of 30 beats/minute, and blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg. Her weight, height, and head circumference were normal for her age. Physical examination revealed tenting skin turgor, sunken eyes, and a soft fontanelle, while other physical findings were unremarkable. Reflexes and development were normal. She was hospitalized, and empirical antibiotic therapy with ampicillin, cefotaxime, zinc gluconate, and intravenous fluid therapy were initiated. Initial laboratory investigations showed leukocytosis, neutrophilia, and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, ammonia, and D-dimer levels. Venous blood gas analysis indicated metabolic acidosis (pH: 7.22, HCO3−: 11.5 meq/L). Blood sugar and liver function tests were normal. Rehydration therapy and sodium bicarbonate were administered to correct acidemia. Urine analysis and stool exam were normal, with urine negative for glucose, acid ammine, ketone, lactate, and reducing substances. By the end of the first day, her fever improved, but diarrhea persisted. On the second day, venous blood gas analysis still showed metabolic acidosis (pH: 7.26, HCO3−: 11.5 meq/L) with a normal anion gap (11 meq/L). Spiral chest computed tomography (CT) and echocardiography were normal. Abdominopelvic ultrasonography was performed to exclude anatomical abnormalities of the urinary system and was normal. Urine and stool cultures were negative, while blood culture was positive for Klebsiella pneumoniae, leading to the prescription of amikacin. Nasopharyngeal real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) was positive for SARS-CoV-2, and COVID-19 immunoglobulin M (IgM) was elevated (4.5 U).
test_results: Venous blood gas (VBG) showed metabolic acidosis (pH: 7.22, HCO3−: 11.5 meq/L). On the second day, VBG revealed metabolic acidosis (pH: 7.26, HCO3−: 11.5 meq/L) with a normal anion gap (11 meq/L). On the fourth day, VBG still showed hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis (pH: 7.21, HCO3−: 15 meq/L, chloride: 115 meq/L). Urine pH was 6.5, with a sodium level of 105 mEq/L and specific gravity of 1.012. Urine anion gap was positive.

case_report: A 7-year-old girl with distinct facial features and short stature visited our hospital. She was born via cesarean section at 36 weeks of gestation without perinatal complications; her birth weight was 2.7 kg (25th–50th percentile). She is the second child of nonconsanguineous, healthy parents. Her midparental height was 160 cm (father's height, 180 cm; mother's height, 153 cm). Her elder brother exhibited normal growth and psychomotor development. There was no family history of genetic diseases. At initial presentation, the patient’s height was 105.8 cm (-3.54 standard deviation score [SDS]); her weight was 16.3 kg (-2.45 SDS), and her head circumference was 51 cm (-0.3 SDS). Her bone age was 4.5 years. She had dysmorphic facial features, including a small, triangular face with deep-set eyes, a broad and bulbous nose, a short philtrum, and thin lips, as well as hand anomalies such as clinodactyly and a short thumb with clubbing. X-rays revealed middle phalange dysplasia and genu varum. The patient's fine motor and gross motor development were appropriate for her chronological age. She demonstrated severe intellectual disabilities as well as obsessive-compulsive and aggressive behaviors. The patient attended a special-education school and had been receiving rehabilitation treatment for the previous 2 years. Electroencephalogram, brain magnetic resonance imaging, echocardiography, and ultrasound of the kidneys were normal. Chromosome analysis indicated a 46, XX karyotype. Ophthalmological examination revealed strabismus and mild diplopia. Results of blood biochemical and urine studies were within the normal ranges. Thyroid function test results were also normal. Serum insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) and IGF-binding protein 3 levels were 223.1 ng/mL (normal range, 26–320 ng/mL) and 2481.1 ng/mL (normal range, 2,188–4,996 ng/mL), respectively. The GH peak levels provoked by insulin and L-dopa were 44.30 ng/mL and 6.07 ng/mL, respectively.
test_results: A heterozygous c.7330C > T (p.Arg2444*) mutation in SRCAP was identified.

case_report: A 60-year-old female underwent cone beam computed tomography to evaluate implant insertion sites. Clinical examination revealed mild facial asymmetry and a deviation of the nasal septum to the left. The patient had no symptoms, with normal visual acuity, unaffected extraocular movements, no double vision, and no signs of rhinitis. The patient reported experiencing recurrent and frequent sinusitis and difficulty breathing over the past 5 years. An otolaryngologist identified nasal septum deviation as the primary cause of the patient's respiratory issues. There was no history of facial trauma, systemic infection, cranial malformation, or tumor.
test_results: Computed tomography performed in the axial, sagittal, and coronal planes revealed a hypoplastic opacified left maxillary sinus with thinning and depression of the orbital floor and posterolateral sinus wall. The uncinate process appeared lateralized and adherent to the lamina papyracea, blocking the osteomeatal complex drainage.

case_report: A 4-year-old boy with stage IV neuroblastoma underwent four cycles of chemotherapy, including high-dose chemotherapy with busulfan and melphalan, followed by autologous peripheral blood stem cell transplantation with autologous bone marrow supplementation. After eight additional cycles of chemotherapy with temozolomide and irinotecan, which resulted in stable disease, the patient received preparative conditioning with fludarabine (150 mg/m2), melphalan (140 mg/m2), and 12 Gy of TBI for subsequent allogeneic CBT. For GVHD prophylaxis, the patient was administered tacrolimus and a short-term course of methotrexate. Engraftment occurred on day 17. The patient developed grade 3 GVHD, managed by increasing the prednisolone dose, and was discharged on day 85. Proton beam therapy (39.6 Gy) was administered from days 121 to 150 post-transplantation for a right supra-mediastinum tumor with residual I123-MIBG accumulation in the right adrenal gland. The patient remained healthy with no evidence of GVHD until presenting at the hospital with a productive cough on day 159. A rapid antigen test for RSV was positive, as his older brother had similar cold symptoms. His respiratory symptoms worsened, and he returned to the hospital on day 194 with dyspnea and intercostal retractions. Upon admission, he was given 0.7-1.0 mg/kg of prednisolone, which did not improve his respiratory condition.
test_results: Thoracoscopic lung biopsy on day 244 revealed diffuse intra-alveolar hemorrhage and edema on hematoxylin-eosin (HE)-stained samples. Elastica van Gieson staining revealed diffuse obstructive lesions due to fibrocellular components with plump endothelial cells in the pre-septal pulmonary veins and venules. While pulmonary muscular arteries and arterioles showed mild medial hypertrophy and focal intimal thickening (Heath-Edwards Grade 2), severe stenosis with concentric intimal fibrosis or plexiform lesions was present. Echocardiography showed an elevated tricuspid regurgitation peak velocity of 4.1 m/s and an interventricular septum close to the isobaric. Chest computed tomography on day 231 revealed infiltration, ground-glass opacity, and septal thickening in the bilateral lung fields along with right pleural effusion.

case_report: A 21-month-old Korean boy, previously in good health, exhibited seizure and vomiting following a 6-day period of febrile respiratory illness. The patient had no prior history of neurological conditions, and his developmental milestones were appropriate for his age. Neurological examination showed a drowsy mental state, small pupils, and slow pupil reflexes. Laboratory tests identified the presence of parainfluenza virus and bocavirus through real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Other laboratory results, including cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, did not reveal any specific abnormalities.
test_results: Initial brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed T2 hyperintensity in both the cerebral hemispheres, involving the white matter and corpus callosum with multifocal areas of diffusion restriction with surrounding vasogenic edema. Petechial hemorrhages were detected on susceptibility-weighted images (SWIs). Lesions showed high signal intensity with high apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) values at the center of the lesion, middle-low ADC value area, and outermost high ADC value area. Lesions did not show enhancement after gadolinium administration. Both the basal ganglia and thalami were spared. Follow-up MR images obtained 19 days after initial presentation showed resolution of diffusion restriction in both the cerebral hemispheres. Brain MRI showed symmetrical and bilateral T2 hyperintensity involving the thalami, caudate nuclei, basal ganglia, and brain stem with diffusion restriction and petechial hemorrhage and similar ADC characteristics to the initial MR examination. The lesions showed faint enhancement after gadolinium administration.
diagnosis: Familial Acute Necrotizing Encephalopathy  with RANBP2 mutation

case_report: A 5-year-old female child, born to non-consanguineous parents, visited the orthopedic outpatient clinic due to an inability to bend both knees since birth, affecting her ability to squat and sit cross-legged. She exhibited a stiff knee gait and could walk unassisted but required help to run and climb stairs. Her developmental milestones were normal, and she performed fairly in school. She had speech difficulties, resulting in a mumbling voice, and faced challenges in social interactions, dental hygiene, and feeding. Despite these issues, she could dress herself, brush her teeth, transfer, and eat independently but needed help with bathing and toilet activities. Her antenatal history was unremarkable. She was born full-term via vaginal breech delivery with a birth weight of 2.2 kg. She was diagnosed with bilateral CTEV and genu recurvatum, for which she underwent weekly stretching, manipulation, and casting for about 2 years. She had two younger brothers; the youngest had similar symptoms at birth and passed away at 5 months due to respiratory distress. The mother experienced a spontaneous abortion during her fourth pregnancy at 4 months gestation. There was no family history of similar complaints or primary neurological/muscular disorders. On examination, the patient weighed 10.4 kg, had a height of 98 cm, and a head circumference of 42 cm. She exhibited short stature, a mask-like face, bilateral ptosis, microstomia, pursed lips, a high arched palate, and absent skin creases at the elbows, knees, and wrists. She had a clasped thumb deformity, preventing voluntary extension and abduction of both thumbs. Her knee flexion was limited to 20°. Additional findings included pectus excavatum, scoliosis of the thoracolumbar spine with left convexity, and increased right trunk-arm distance. She had broad and wide heels bilaterally. Ophthalmological examination showed poor power of the bilateral levator palpebrae superioris muscle and hypermetropia, corrected to +2.50 D in the right eye and +3.00 D in the left eye. Features such as webbed neck, H-V dimpled chin, mal-occluded teeth, and hearing loss were absent. Routine hematological tests, including serum creatine phosphokinase levels, were normal.
test_results: Electromyography studies of the bilateral tibialis anterior and the abductor pollicis brevis reported a normal insertional activity, no positive sharp waves, fibrillation, and myotonic discharge. The lateral radiographic view of the skull showed a copper-beaten appearance. Her pelvis with bilateral hips showed the following changes in the right hip-decreased femoral epiphysis height, horizontal proximal femoral physis, and coxa breva. Her lateral radiographic view of the bilateral knee showed genu recurvatum. A skeletal survey showed the delayed appearance of the ossific nucleus of the proximal fibular epiphysis, medial epicondyle of humerus and patella. However, radiographs of the thoracolumbar spine showed no wedging or hemivertebrae or any other structural scoliotic changes.

case_report: A 2-year-old female child presents with multiple heart defects and decreased visual acuity noted by her parents. There is no significant family history other than first-degree consanguinity through the parents. A previous cardiology consultation showed coarctation of the aortic arch, abnormalities of the left subclavian artery originating from the right aortic arch, and tetralogy of Fallot. She underwent successful corrective surgery shortly after birth. On examination, the patient exhibits intellectual impairment, hearing loss, and mild global hypotonia. The patient can fix and follow objects with both eyes. Pupils are equal and react normally to light and accommodation. There is a horizontal jerk nystagmus on lateral gaze and a 30 prismatic diopters alternating esotropia in primary gaze. Ocular motility is otherwise unremarkable. Fundus examination shows the presence of an optic nerve coloboma and associated chorioretinal coloboma in both eyes. The patient has dysmorphic pinnae with the upper portion being larger than the lower, as well as an absence of the antihelix, giving them a cup-shaped appearance. She has severe bilateral hearing loss and there are no other evident cranial nerve abnormalities. She has overall good mobility of her extremities, although with a mild degree of hypotonia. The patient showed no genitourinary abnormalities on previous pediatric evaluation. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows some degree of cortical underdevelopment predominantly in the frontal lobe region, as well as bilateral choanal atresia and hypoplasia of the semicircular canals. Electroretinography shows an overall decrease in scotopic and photopic responses.
test_results: This genetic test shows that the patient carries the heterozygous nonsense mutation c.6217C>T (p.Gln2073*) in exon 31 of the CHD7 gene. This mutation implies a nucleotide exchange from C to T at position c.6217C in exon 31 of the CHD7 gene, leading to a premature stop codon (p.Gln2073*), and subsequently probably either to a degradation of the mRNA or to a truncation of the CHD7 protein.

case_report: A 15-year-old male presented with swelling on the right side of the face, which had been gradually increasing in size. The swelling was accompanied by episodes of nosebleeds. The onset of the swelling was gradual. There was no relevant medical or family history, nor any history of trauma. Physical examination revealed significant facial asymmetry with a well-defined swelling measuring approximately 8 × 5 cm on the right cheek. Eye movements were restricted, resulting in a decreased width of the palpebral fissure, though visual acuity remained unaffected. Intraorally, a well-defined, non-ulcerated, pinkish-red swelling was observed, extending from the upper right canine to the maxillary tuberosity, causing obliteration of the maxillary vestibule. On palpation, the swelling was non-tender, slightly lobulated, and bony hard in consistency. It was non-pulsatile and non-compressible. The swelling was associated with grade II mobility of the teeth from the canine to the second molar on the right side.
test_results: An OPG showed lytic lesion with focal areas of opacification in right maxilla and nasal cavity. In addition, septal deviation with lateral nasal wall erosion, opacification of right maxillary sinus and loss of lamina dura with displacement of roots of first and second premolars were also noted. It showed an expansile lytic lesion of maxilla and nasal cavity involving the alveolus and hard palate with erosive borders. Posterolateral and anterolateral walls of the right maxillary sinus showed cortical break and extension into the infratemporal, temporal, buccal and facial tissues. Cortical breach was observed in the superior and medial walls of the sinus. The hematoxylin and eosin stained section showed infiltration of proliferating lesional cells with varying amount of reactive fibro-osseous proliferation. The tumor cells were in the form of aggregates of round darkly staining cells showing vacuolated cytoplasm and uniform nuclei with evenly dispersed chromatin. The tumor cells showed membrane positivity for CD 99 and were negative for Pan Cytokeratin, leukocyte common antigen, desmin and synaptophysin.

case_report: A 7-year-old female child with developmental delay was born following a normal pregnancy, labor, and delivery. There were no maternal infections or illnesses detected during the pregnancy or perinatal period. At birth, the child exhibited ocular anomalies, specifically bilateral corneal opacifications. The infant did not display symptoms such as tearing, blepharospasm, photophobia, drainage, or ocular redness. Ophthalmologic examination revealed a visual acuity of FC/20 cm in the right eye and FC/10 cm in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was normal in both eyes. Horizontal nystagmus and congenital cataract were observed in both eyes. The central retina could not be clearly examined due to severe corneal opacity.
test_results: Slit-lamp examination revealed bilateral central corneal opacities which covered the iris and pupils. High-frequency UBM and AS-OCT both showed a shallow anterior chamber with multiple areas of iridocorneal adhesions and no corneal lenticular touch in each eye. The B-type ultrasound scan performed on the patient revealed no masses, vitreous debris, or retinal detachment in either eye.

case_report: A 22-year-old male with a history of relapsed Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL) presented with impaired renal function. HL was initially diagnosed in 2007 and treated with chemotherapy (adriamycin, bleomycin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine), achieving complete remission for 7 years before relapse. Six months prior to the relapse, renal function tests were normal. Upon evaluation, serum creatinine was 2.1 mg/dl (eGFR CKD-EPI 43.4 ml/min/1.73 m2) and right hydroureteronephrosis (HUN) was observed. No obstructive lesions were found, and the cause of HUN was unclear. A double J (DJ) stent was placed on the right side, reducing creatinine to 1.8 mg/dl within a week. Due to the aggressive nature of the malignancy, chemotherapy was initiated before GFR normalization. The patient received three cycles of chemotherapy with ifosfamide (IFO), carboplatin, and etoposide (cumulative IFO dose: 18 g), achieving complete remission. Serum creatinine remained at 1.8 mg/dl during chemotherapy. The DJ stent was removed after complete resolution of HUN.
