One week later, serum creatinine increased to 2.4 mg/dl, and imaging showed reappearance of HUN. A retrograde pyelogram revealed no filling defects, and a DJ stent was reinserted. Follow-up imaging one week later showed complete resolution of HUN. Serum creatinine decreased to 1.9 mg/dl (eGFR CKD-EPI 46 ml/min/1.73 m2) and remained stable for the next 2 months. A repeat abdominal ultrasound showed normal-sized kidneys with the DJ stent in place and no HUN. The patient also exhibited signs of partial Fanconi's syndrome.
test_results: Kidney biopsy showed normal glomerular morphology, moderate interstitial inflammation composed of mainly lymphocytes and tubular atrophy amounting to 30–35% of the core. The proximal tubular epithelial cells showed markedly enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei with irregular margins. Immunohistochemistry for cytomegalovirus (CMV) and SV 40 were negative. The Ki 67 index was low.

case_report: A 35-year-old male with no prior health issues presented on 29th September 2022 with a severe and persistent cough lasting four days. He had tested positive for COVID-19 by PCR on 19th September 2022. Initially, he experienced mild upper respiratory symptoms for three days and recovered with home isolation. However, in the four days leading up to his admission, his cough worsened and persisted throughout the day, becoming more pronounced with exertion and accompanied by minimal sputum production. He did not have fever or headache and reported no wheezing or difficulty breathing. His bowel and bladder functions were normal. Due to the continuous nature of his cough, he was admitted for further evaluation and management. Upon general examination, a low-grade fever was observed. Respiratory examination revealed harsh breath sounds, while other systemic examinations were normal. Initial laboratory tests, including complete blood count, c-reactive protein, and kidney and liver function tests, were normal. The patient received treatment with IV antibiotics, nebulization, cough suppressants, and proton pump inhibitors. On the morning of 1st October 2022, the third day of his hospital stay, he reported frequent urination with large volumes of clear urine and eight to ten episodes of nocturia the previous night. His fasting blood sugar was 91 mg/dl and HbA1c was 5.1%, excluding diabetes mellitus. History ruled out primary polydipsia and head trauma.
test_results: A 24-hour urine volume of 4.2 liters, 24-hour urine osmolality of 256.6 mOsm/kg (normal reference: 500 to 800 mOsm/kg), 24-hour urinary sodium of 252 mmol, and 24-hour urinary chloride was 281.4 mmol. Serum osmolality was 285.7 mOsm/kg (normal reference: 275-295 mOsm/kg) and spot urine sodium was 90 mmol/L (normal 20-230 mmol/L). His 24-hour urine potassium, creatinine, urea nitrogen, and glucose along with his pituitary hormones (ACTH, cortisol, and thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH)) were in the normal range.

case_report: A 17-year-old Asian male presented with recurrent episodes of mild jaundice over the past few weeks. He also experienced generalized abdominal pain, primarily in the upper right quadrant. He reported no fever, nausea, vomiting, or recent medication intake. Physical examination showed a pale yellow skin tone, dark yellow urine, and brown stool. His past medical history was notable for intermittent abdominal pain and jaundice two years prior, during which laboratory tests revealed elevated conjugated bilirubin levels. The patient did not follow up as his symptoms resolved spontaneously. He has a family history of similar symptoms and elevated conjugated bilirubin levels. Current vital signs were normal. Laboratory tests indicated a total bilirubin level of 61 µmol/L, direct conjugated bilirubin of 40 µmol/L, aspartate aminotransferase of 28 U/L, alkaline phosphatase of 160 U/L, and a reticulocyte count of 1.5%. Serological tests for hepatitis A and B were negative. An ultrasound scan showed a normal liver with no biliary obstruction or organ enlargement. Other liver function tests were within normal limits.
test_results: A liver biopsy revealed melanin pigment inside the liver parenchyma, leading to the liver turning black.

case_report: A 2-year-old boy, born prematurely, with a history of failure to thrive and global developmental delay, presented for evaluation. His birth weight was 1.106 kg. He required respiratory support (oxygen via nasal cannula) in the neonatal intensive care unit and was discharged at 7 weeks. He was under ophthalmology care for retinopathy of prematurity and at 8 months was observed to have esotropia and horizontal jerk nystagmus that decreased with convergence. Eye patching was prescribed, leading to some improvement in esotropia, but at 19 months, new-onset vertical nystagmus was noted. At 2 years of age, he could say approximately two to three words, had no two-word phrases, and could not walk independently. On examination, his head circumference was at the 0.4 percentile (Z=−2.59), height at the 0.46 percentile (Z=−2.61), and weight at less than the 0.01 percentile (Z=−3.73). He had plagiocephaly with sagittal suture prominence but was otherwise nondysmorphic. Vertical and horizontal nystagmus were present. Neurological examination revealed truncal and peripheral hypotonia, decreased muscle mass, and brisk reflexes. Laboratory tests including serum creatine kinase, blood lactate, pyruvate, ammonia, acylcarnitine profile, plasma amino acids, and urine organic acids were normal.
test_results: A brain MRI completed at 21 months was notable for bilaterally symmetrical increase in signal intensity on T2- and T2 FLAIR (fluid attenuated inversion recovery)-weighted sequences in the dorsal medulla, periaqueductal gray matter, substantia nigra, medial hypothalamus, and habenular nuclei. There were two asymmetric foci in the subcortical white matter of the cerebellar hemispheres. There was no surrounding edema and no abnormal contrast enhancement. Repeat brain MRI at 3 years 3 months showed substantially increased signal intensity and extent of involvement at the same sites, with no edema, no mass effect, and no abnormal contrast enhancement at any site. No new sites of involvement were identified. The remaining portions of the brain showed no abnormality. Brain MR spectroscopy at short TE was normal within the right thalamus and left subcortical white matter. Chromosomal microarray revealed no pathogenic copy number variation, but absence of heterozygosity of unknown clinical significance totaling 32.2 Mb was detected.
diagnosis: Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency due to recessive pathogenic variants in MCAT

case_report: A 32-year-old male of Pakistani ethnicity presented with a 20-year history of night blindness. His vision was normal during childhood but progressively worsened over time. There was no history of pain, redness, discharge, or photophobia. The patient had previously undergone bilateral cataract extraction and later developed cloudy vision due to lens capsule opacification, for which yttrium aluminum garnet (YAG) capsulotomy was performed. The patient was congenitally deaf, leading to deaf-mutism, and had delayed developmental milestones up to 18 months of age. He also experienced balance issues and required support to walk. Family history revealed that his mother had bilateral hearing loss and poor vision since childhood. Her medical records indicated profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and retinal pigment epithelium changes. Her visual acuity was 2/60 in both eyes. The patient's father was phenotypically normal. Consanguineous marriages were noted in the family history, with both grandparents being phenotypically normal. One paternal uncle had decreased vision and complete sensorineural hearing loss. Clinical examination of the patient revealed a visual acuity of 6/9 in both eyes with no improvement by pinhole. Extraocular movements were normal, and there was no relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). Slit-lamp examination showed clear cornea and sclera, with bilateral pseudophakia. Intraocular pressure was normal. Ophthalmoscopy revealed a pale optic disc, attenuated blood vessels, and bony spicules in the fundus.
test_results: Electroretinography revealed reduced electrical activity of the retina indicating that photoreceptors were not functioning properly. Pure tone audiometry was performed indicating profound sensory neural hearing loss (SNHL) in both ears represented by values below 90dB on graph.

case_report: A ten-month-old Hispanic girl was brought to the pediatric otolaryngology clinic due to an observed asymmetry in her face. The mother reported noticing an uneven movement of the lower lip since birth, which became more evident when the child smiled or cried. The rest of the facial movements were symmetrical. The child was born at full term without any complications, and the mother had no medical issues. Both the child's past medical history and family history were unremarkable. During the physical examination, the child appeared well and showed no signs of respiratory distress. The otologic, nasal, and oral cavity examinations were all normal. The face appeared symmetrical when at rest. However, there was an inward deviation of the right lower lip when the child smiled. The function of the facial nerve, assessed through frowning, forehead wrinkling, eye closure, nasolabial fold depth, and tearing, was symmetrical. The neurodevelopmental examination was normal.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging of the temporal bones and internal auditory canals were within normal limits. Echocardiogram did not show cardiac abnormality. Auditory brainstem response test showed no abnormality.
diagnosis: Congenital Unilateral Hypoplasia of Depressor Anguli Oris
Orpha_name: Congenital Unilateral Hypoplasia of Depressor Anguli Oris

case_report: A white female patient, aged 11, presented with 'small lumps on the left wrist since the age of two'. Dermatological examination showed erythematous-violaceous papules on the left wrist, which became less noticeable during the vitropression test. The condition has persisted for 9 years without any changes in clinical features, local symptoms, or history of trauma.
test_results: The histopathological exam revealed an integral epidermis without atypia; and, in the dermis, inflammatory infiltrate of superficial and deep, perivascular location, around the pilo-erector muscles, hair follicles, eccrine glands and nerves. The infiltrate was made up of lymphocytes, some histiocytes, a moderate number of plasmocytes and small basophilic granulations in the cytoplasmas of the histiocytic cells. Infiltration was noticed in the hypodermal lobules. The search for alcohol-acid resistant bacilli using the Ziehl-Neelsen staining procedure culminated in a negative result. The histopathological exam revealed the same histopathological pattern as before. The immunohistochemical study of the biopsy material revealed histological characteristics of dermal lymphoid proliferation of small, perivascular and adnexal, T and B lymphocytes, with a low proliferative index.

case_report: On November 17, 2011, a 44-year-old male underwent cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) to address a two-vessel disease involving blockages in the left anterior descending and right coronary arteries. The patient had a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus, but no prior history of excessive thirst, frequent urination, or head injury. Additionally, there was no family history of frequent urination. Upon admission, his blood pressure was 127/66 mmHg and his heart rate was 79 beats per minute. The coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) operation lasted 6 hours, with CPB time of 115 minutes and aortic cross-clamp time of 69 minutes. The myocardium was protected using cold cardioplegia. There were no episodes of low blood pressure or other major complications during the operation. Intra-operative mean blood pressure was maintained between 75 mmHg and 90 mmHg. One hour post-operation, the patient's urine output increased to approximately 1,000 mL per hour. His mental status remained normal, and there were no signs of neurological deficits. Serum creatinine levels showed a slight increase from 1.15 mg/dL to 1.3 mg/dL. Serum glucose and sodium concentrations were 137 mg/dL and 140 mEq/L, respectively. The urine specific gravity was 1.020, and the urine tested negative for protein, glucose, and occult blood. Other laboratory results showed no significant changes compared to pre-operative data. The patient did not receive over-hydration with hypertonic solutions or large amounts of diuretics during the operation. On the first post-operative day, the patient's urine output continued at a rate of up to 1,050 mL per hour, and he was referred to the nephrology clinic. Clinical and laboratory findings revealed a serum osmolality of 333 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality of 80 mOsm/kg, and serum sodium of 155 mEq/L.
test_results: 10 mcg of a desmopressin nasal spray was administered for a desmopressin stimulation test without water deprivation. His urine output declined dramatically to 125 mL/hr 30 min after desmopressin use. At 60 min after nasal desmopressin administration, urine osmolality increased to 518 mOsm/kg and urine output declined from 1,050 mL/hr to 80 mL/hr. An increase in urine osmolality of more than 100% was measured by the desmopressin stimulation test.

case_report: A 59-year-old female (blood type: O, Rh positive) presented with a space-occupying lesion in liver segment V. A transarterial embolization was performed on 29 August 2018. In October 2018, the patient began taking sorafenib, which was discontinued in July 2019 due to dizziness, skin ulcers, and other symptoms. A CT scan in September 2019 showed enlargement of the liver lesions. Radiation therapy was administered on 29 September 2019 with a prescribed dose of PTV5400cGy/18f and a dose rate of 0.6–1 Gy/min over seven sessions. Following radiotherapy, Piggyback LT was performed on 13 October 2019. The patient had a history of hepatitis B and received entecavir once. HBV serology results were: HBsAg 113.23 IU/mL (ref: 0–0.05), anti-HBs 0 mIU/mL (ref: 0–10), HBeAg 0.08 PEI µ/mL (ref: 0–0.5), anti-HBe >4.4 PEI µ/mL (ref: 0–0.2), and anti-HBc 8.26 PEI µ/mL (ref: 0–0.9). Tests for HIV, hepatitis A, and hepatitis C were negative. The donor was a 21-year-old male (blood type: O, Rh positive) who had brain death from a car accident. The HLA class-I and class-II phenotypes of the donor were A11, A30; B13; DR11, DR15; DQ6, and DQ7, while those of the recipient were A2, A11; B13, B46; DR14, DR15; DQ5, and DQ6. Blood products used during the transplant were irradiated and filtered. Post-transplant, the patient developed acute renal failure and a hematoma around the liver. She received intravenous hepatitis B immunoglobulin and immunosuppressive drugs, including steroids and tacrolimus, starting on postoperative day (POD)-1. The target tacrolimus blood level was ~10 ng/mL. After continuous hemodialysis and intermittent infusion of fresh frozen plasma, leukocyte-depleted red blood cells, and other blood products, active abdominal bleeding ceased and renal function improved. Pathological analysis confirmed HCC with ~90% tumor necrosis. On POD-10, liver function improved, with AST, ALT, GGT, and ALP levels returning to normal. The patient experienced regular fevers of 37–39°C, peaking at 23:00 h daily, and rising PCT levels to 10.3 ng/mL (ref: 0–0.05). On POD-13, serum PCT levels dropped to 3 ng/mL, blood cultures were negative, and tests for cytomegalovirus and Epstein–Barr virus were negative, but the fever persisted, and red spots appeared on the chest without itching, and the Nikolsky sign was negative. On POD-17, tacrolimus was replaced with sirolimus, and mycophenolate mofetil was added for immune suppression. On POD-18, sputum culture indicated Acinetobacter baumannii and MRSA infections. On POD-19, the rash progressed to erythematous macules and papules, spreading to the limbs, palms, neck, and face. Oral examination revealed white ulcers on the buccal mucosa and lips, and severe bone marrow suppression was noted, with a WBC count of 0.86 × 10^9/L (ref: 3.5–9.5), PLT count of 35 × 10^9/L (ref: 125–350), and HGB level of 70 g/L (ref: 130–175). The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit. A dermatologist suggested the rash might be a drug-related adverse reaction and recommended gamma globulin (2500 mg, 3 days). On POD-29, the patient's abdominal incision split and was resutured. On POD-32, bone marrow aspiration was performed. The bone marrow pathology report showed no special lesions in granulocytes, red blood cells, or megakaryocytes, and no macrophages phagocytosing neutrophils or platelets. Bone marrow cell morphology examination indicated active proliferation of bone marrow cells, reduced megakaryocyte production, and decreased platelet levels.
test_results: Skin biopsy specimens exhibited epidermal dyskeratosis, basic vacuolization, and lymphocytic infiltrates. FISH analysis of the peripheral blood followed by flow cytometry detected 3% donor lymphocytes.

case_report: A 56-year-old male experienced isolated paresthesias, weakness, and cramps in the right upper limb over three months. He had no prior health issues and was active in sports such as cycling, running, cross-country skiing, and bow-shooting. Neurological examination showed isolated distal muscle weakness in the right upper limb (MRC 3), normal muscle strength in the left upper limb (MRC 5), generalized hyporeflexia, and bilateral pes cavus with normal muscle strength (MRC 5). Vibration sense was reduced in the lower limbs (ankle 4/8, toe 2/8). Slightly reduced pin prick and thermal sensation were noted. The patient could walk on heels and tiptoes. Mild ataxia was observed when standing with eyes closed (positive Romberg sign). Over the next six months, chronic progression of muscle weakness was noted. The right upper limb showed increased distal weakness (wrist extensors MRC 3, finger extensors MRC 1, wrist and finger flexors MRC 3, intrinsic hand muscles MRC 3). The left upper limb also developed mild weakness and paresthesia (wrist extensors MRC 5, finger extensors MRC 3, wrist and finger flexors MRC 4, intrinsic hand muscles MRC 4). The patient had difficulty with fine motor tasks such as buttoning clothes, unscrewing bottle caps, and turning door-knobs. No weakness was observed in the proximal upper limb muscles (MRC 5). Muscle strength in the lower limbs remained normal (MRC 5).
test_results: Nerve conduction studies (NCS) were consistent with moderate primary demyelinating sensory-motor polyneuropathy of the upper limbs with partial conduction blocks in some nerves (median, ulnar) and severe sensory-motor polyneuropathy of the lower limbs. Compound muscle action potentials (CMAPs) showed prolonged distal motor latencies, reduced nerve conduction velocities and low amplitudes with prolonged minimal F wave latencies. Sensory nerve action potentials (SNAPs) in the upper limbs showed prolonged distal latencies, reduced velocities and low amplitudes. SNAPs in lower limbs were absent. Needle electromyography revealed a severe chronic denervation syndrome with sporadic spontaneous activity in upper limb muscles (biceps brachii, deltoideus, extensor digitorum communis, interosseus dorsalis primus, and abductor pollicis). Genetic testing for CMT1A and HNPP yielded negative results. The LITAF/SIMPLE bidirectional sequencing of the proband’s sample showed a G > C transversion in exon 4 at position 348 (c.348G > C/p.Trp116Cys) present in the heterozygous state. This novel, missense variant of LITAF had not been previously reported elsewhere and was scored as pathogenic by Predict Protein Open (Effect of Protein Mutations) software and other predictive software programs (GERP, MetaSVM, PolyPhen 2 and MutationTaster). Furthermore, the mutation was scored as 'pathogenic' by the ACMG criteria (PS1 + PM2 + PM5 + PP1 + PP2 + PP3 + PP4). No other plausible, causative candidate variants were found in the proband’s genetic material by WES. WES results were verified by the amplicon deep sequencing (ADS) method. PCR amplicons (545 bp long) were generated using specific primers (forward: actggtgttccttccccttt, reverse: tcgtttgaacctgagcagtg). The amplicons were prepared for sequencing using a Nextera XT kit (Illumina) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Libraries were paired-end (2 × 100 bp) sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq1500. The results were visualized on the Integrative Genomics Viewer and analysed for the presence of the particular variant in proband. The ADS verification resulted in obtaining coverage > 6000 × in all cases. The missense variant c.348G > C of LITAF was also identified in family members I.2 and III.7 which correlated with autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. Genetic analysis did not confirm the missense variant in healthy family members (father I.1, proband´s brother II.2, other son III.6).

case_report: A 55-year-old Korean female with a history of hypothyroidism presented with chronic intermittent bloody diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, and weight loss over a period of 2 months. Additional symptoms included hair loss and loss of finger and toenails, as well as a diminished sense of taste. Physical examination revealed onychodystrophy and loss of finger and toenails, along with bilateral symmetric edema in the lower extremities. Laboratory results showed an albumin level of 1.2 g/dL, an INR of 1.4, and a hematocrit of 24.3, with normal liver function and serum chemistries. Stool culture and tests for ova and parasites were negative.
test_results: EGD revealed extensive gastro-duodenitis with gastric biopsy showing edema and marked mucosal hyperplasia and small bowel biopsy showing inflammation and blunting of the villi. On colonoscopy, innumerous polyps were seen scattered throughout the colon. It also showed 45 cm big polyp in a sigmoid colon. Biopsy showed polyps to be inflammatory with adenomatous change.

case_report: A 26-year-old Asian male construction worker was brought to the emergency department due to weakness in both lower limbs. His medical history included aseptic meningitis over a decade ago, with no lasting effects. He reported experiencing muscle cramps in the right shoulder radiating to the back for a week and had visited a traditional medicine practitioner the day before. He received non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and another unknown injection, which alleviated the cramps before he went to sleep. The next morning, he woke up with acute weakness in his legs, struggled to stand, and fell, causing bruises on his upper limbs. Upon arrival at the emergency department, his tympanic membrane temperature was 38.1°C, with normal blood pressure and no other vital sign abnormalities. He did not report any loss of consciousness, pain in limbs or trunk, respiratory symptoms, vomiting, diarrhea, or excessive sweating. He did not regularly consume alcohol or smoke. His family history included hypertension and diabetes mellitus in his grandparents, with no known conditions related to muscle weakness or hypokalemia. The patient was alert, mentally stable, and appeared well-nourished. Physical examination revealed reduced muscle strength in both lower limbs, primarily proximal, initially rated at 2/5 and later progressing to 1/5. Deep tendon reflexes in the knees and sensation in the lower limbs were normal, and upper limb muscle strength was unaffected. No Babinski sign was observed on either side.
test_results: Blood tests were normal, except for white blood cells (10,800/μL), potassium (1.7 mEq/L), and creatine phosphokinase (178 U/L). Urinalysis was normal. Electrocardiogram showed a flattened T wave and exhibited U waves in the precordial leads V1–V3.

case_report: A twenty-one-year-old female reported experiencing painful nodule-like lesions on her scalp for ten days. She had previously been treated with antibiotics, which did not result in improvement. The patient did not exhibit proximal lymphadenopathy, fever, or other systemic symptoms. Her medical history was unremarkable for physical or psychological conditions. She resides in an urban area in Hama, Syria, with a medium socioeconomic status. Prior to the appearance of the lesions, she recalled being bitten by insects during a visit to a cattle farm in a rural area east of Hama.
test_results: On examination, two ulcer-like and foul-smelling lesions filled with moving larvae covered by her thick hair were visible to the naked eye on the parietal region. The lesions ranged from 3 to 4 cm in diameter. There was no erythema or edema surrounding the lesions.

case_report: A 25-year-old female presented to our department following a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, with no prior history of seizures. Brain MRI scans revealed a strongly enhancing cortical mass measuring approximately 3×2×2 cm, accompanied by peri-lesional edema and lacking a definite dural tail sign. Due to the seizure activity caused by the mass, total surgical resection was chosen as the primary treatment. A right fronto-parietal craniotomy was performed, achieving gross total removal of the mass. The mass was well-demarcated, encapsulated, and separated from the right fronto-parietal cortex without adhesion to the dura mater. It was highly vascularized, friable, and solid, with minimal adhesions to the arachnoid membrane and no invasion into the brain parenchyma. The mass was thoroughly aspirated using a cavitron ultrasonic surgical aspirator, achieving gross total removal without injury to the surrounding area. Post-surgery, the patient experienced no further seizures, and postoperative MRI scans showed no evidence of residual mass.
test_results: The tumor had a clear cell feature. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining showed a sheet of uniform cells with round nuclei, finely dispersed chromatin, clear cytoplasm, discrete cytoplasmic borders, rare mitosis, no necrosis. The epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) was positive with a dot-like pattern, GFAP and Olig2 were focal positive, and L1CAM was strongly positive. Analysis of 1p/19q codeletion fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) showed no deletion with polysomy. Ki-67 labeling index was 14.3%, S-100 was positive, vimentin was positive, and IDH1 gene mutation was not detected.

case_report: History of present illness: A 21-month-old male was brought to the emergency department by his mother due to abnormal movements for one month. These episodes were described as tilting of the head to the left side, left gaze deviation, and fencer posturing toward the left for a few seconds with clusters up to two to three minutes. Additionally, the mother reported that the child had sudden, jerky, purposeless movements in the upper extremities. A video electroencephalogram (EEG) showed epileptic spasms, tonic-clonic seizures, and multifocal epileptiform discharges; findings consistent with epileptic encephalopathy and infantile spasms. Past medical history: The newborn hearing screening was abnormal, suggestive of auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder. On the fifth day of birth, the patient presented respiratory distress, spasticity, hypertonia, and abnormal body movements. Physical exam: Table shows the initial physical exam of the patient on admission to the hospital. Blood tests: All the results were normal, except for an elevated lactic acid (3.5 mmol/L) and a lactic acid/pyruvate ratio of 19. For this reason, an organic urine analysis was ordered, and the results showed markedly elevated levels of lactic, 3-hydroxybutyric, acetoacetic, 4-hydroxyphenyl acetic, and 4 hydroxyphenyl pyruvic acids. A peracetic acid test (PPA) was done, and it showed that methionine, valine, tyrosine, and citrulline were elevated. Magnetic resonance imaging: Prominent lateral ventricles, with apparent multiple septations mainly anteriorly. There were multiple periventricular/subependymal cysts in the caudothalamic grooves next to the temporal posterior and frontal horns and body of the lateral ventricles. Figure shows the main MRI findings of the case. Electroencephalogram: A 24-hours electroencephalogram (EEG) study during sleep showed shifting slow and occasional sharp waves occurring independently over both temporal regions. These findings indicate potentially epileptogenic dysfunction.
test_results: The abnormal chromosomal microarray test showed multiple areas of homozygosity totally approximately 398 MB. Final rapid whole-genome sequencing showed a homozygous c. 2630A>G (p. Gln877Arg) variant in the PC gen.

case_report: An 11-year-old Colombian girl was born at 38 weeks of gestation without complications. Her parents were non-consanguineous, aged 32 and 44 years at her birth. Her birth weight was 2625 g (3rd−10th percentile) and height was 49 cm (50th−75th percentile). No facial or phenotypic abnormalities were noted at birth. At 16 months and 3 years, she had pupilloplasty for coloboma repair. Her family history was unremarkable. At 8 years, she had surgery on her right eyelid. A year later, an ophthalmologic exam revealed right eye microphthalmia with an irregular pupil, inferonasal coloboma, iridectomized iris, and soft-tissue protrusion at the superolateral pouch with dermoid fat herniation. The left eye had an irregular pupil with iris atrophy. Audiometric testing showed mild-to-moderate sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear (PTA 44dB) and normal hearing in the left ear (PTA 10dB). Radiographic bone age was estimated at 6 years. Cardiac echocardiography showed a normal ejection fraction (76%). Renal ultrasonography indicated ectasia of the left renal sinus. Renal scintigraphy revealed bilateral postinfectious scarring with preserved parenchymal function, a dilated left renal sinus, renal sinus ectasia with interruption, and a probable duplex calyx system; renal function was 56% in the right kidney and 44% in the left. Spinal radiography showed a lumbar curvature to the right with slightly increased lumbar lordosis. At 11 years, the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children IV (WISC-IV) was administered, resulting in a total IQ score of 67; verbal comprehension score was 81 (average), perceptual reasoning score was 75 (low), working memory score was 68 (deficient), and information processing speed score was 62 (deficient). Her height was 133 cm (4th percentile), weight was 40 kg (66th percentile), and head circumference was 52 cm (22nd percentile). Physical examination revealed bilateral iris coloboma, right microphthalmia, inverse epicanthus, elongated palpebral fissures inclined upwards, eversion of the lateral portion of the lower eyelid, anteverted nostrils, short columella, long philtrum, and normal ear position. Acanthosis nigricans was present in the neck and armpits, and she had overdeveloped breast tissue. Cardiopulmonary auscultation was normal. Her abdomen had an enlarged panniculus adiposus and was soft and depressible without mass or organomegaly. Extremity examination showed persistent digital pads and a Beighton score of 4/6. Neurologically, she was alert and cooperative.
test_results: This genetic panel detected an intronic KMT2D variant (KMT2D NM_003482.3:c.511–2A>T) in a heterozygous state. This variant was located in the fourth intron’s acceptor site, which would produce an alteration in the splice between the fourth and fifth exon. Sanger sequencing using an ABI 3500 sequencer (Applied Biosystems, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) was then performed and confirmed the results. This variant has not been annotated in databases, such as Clinvar, ExAC, 1000 genomes and HGMD. Furthermore, it presents a DANN score of 0.9917. Besides, a segregation study was performed and showed a negative result in the parents, demonstrating that the patient’s variant was de novo.

case_report: A 13-year-old boy, previously healthy, experienced a tonic-clonic seizure. Electroencephalography (EEG) showed generalized spike-wave discharges, and sodium valproate was started. At presentation, his weight was 45 kg, height 160 cm (Z-score −0.6 and −0.4, respectively), and body mass index (BMI) was 17.6 kg/m2 (Z-score 0.5). Clinical examination and cognitive development were normal. Within six months, he was on sodium valproate, perampanel, and clonazepam due to increasing seizures and myoclonus. Six months later, he exhibited fasting hyperglycemia (6.8 mmol/L), postprandial hyperglycemia (11.1–13.8 mmol/L), and glycosuria without ketonuria. His past medical history was unremarkable, and he had no family history of diabetes mellitus. His condition worsened with severe neurological issues, including gait ataxia, loss of autonomous ambulation, dysarthria, and cognitive deterioration with significant speech difficulties. Glucose metabolism evaluation showed fasting hyperglycemia (6.8 mmol/L), glycosuria, negative ketonemia and ketonuria, and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) of 7.5%. Insulin secretion was preserved (15.7 mU/L, C peptide 0.93 nmol/L, fasting levels) with a HOMA-IR index of 4.76, indicating insulin resistance. He did not show clinical signs of insulin resistance, and his lipid profile and hepatic function were normal. Pancreatic autoimmune markers (ICA, GAD65, IAA, ZnT8) were negative. Testing for monogenic diabetes showed no mutations in known genes (GCK, HNF1A, HNF4A, HNF1B, ABCC8, KCNJ11, and INS). A basal-prandial insulin regimen was started, achieving a normal glycemic profile with a low total daily dose of insulin (0.25 μ/kg/d). Six months later, he was on 0.2 μ/kg/d of long-acting insulin analog with an excellent glycemic profile (HbA1c 6%). Autoimmune marker testing remained negative, and the same insulin regimen was continued.
test_results: An axillary skin biopsy was taken accordingly and revealing LBs within apocrine myoepithelium. Genetic testing displayed a homozygous mutation NHLRC1 c.386C > A, p.Pro129His.

case_report: In 2008, a 13-year-old boy was referred to the Department of Oral Pathology at Government Dental College and Hospital, Aurangabad, Maharashtra, with a complaint of progressive deformity on the left side of his face for the past 5 to 6 years. Physical examination revealed facial asymmetry characterized by significant underdevelopment of the left side of the face, deviation of the lips and nose toward the left, and sunken appearance of the left eye region. A large linear dark scar was observed on the left side of the mandibular mentum region, extending upward to involve the lips and left ala of the nose, creating a noticeable depression. The upper and lower lips had notching, exposing the anterior teeth on the left side. Alopecia was noted in the medial region of the left eyebrow. Hyperpigmented patches were present on the skin of the affected area. Additionally, the left ear was slightly smaller compared to the right ear. Intraoral examination showed unilateral atrophy of the tongue papillae on the left side. There was an over-retained maxillary left deciduous canine with a palatally erupted permanent canine, causing crowding in the left maxillary arch. The occlusion was disturbed with the midline shifted to the left side, and there was underdevelopment of the maxillary anterior teeth.
test_results: Radiographically, an abnormal root development was seen with maxillary left premolars. The over-retained root pieces of deciduous mandibular second molar of left side were seen on mesial and distal side of roots of second premolar. The overall eruption pattern of teeth on left side was retarded as compared to that of right side. The mandible showed decreased vertical height of ramus along with loss of gonial angle prominence on the affected side.

case_report: A previously healthy and developmentally normal 12-month-old male presented to the emergency department with febrile status epilepticus characterized by bilateral tonic-clonic movements and upward eye deviation. Control of initial seizures required administration of fosphenytoin, levetiracetam, and phenobarbital, and the patient was intubated for airway protection. Continuous EEG monitoring revealed diffuse high voltage delta slowing of the background and intermittent generalized and multifocal onset electrographic seizures without clinical changes. Seizure frequency was approximately 3 times per day, with durations ranging from 10 minutes to 2 hours. A midazolam drip was added to the treatment regimen. The last seizure occurred on day 7, and the midazolam drip was discontinued on day 9. The patient experienced cardiogenic shock, suspected to be due to myocardial inflammation, necessitating the use of 2 vasopressors, which were discontinued by day 6. Family history included febrile seizures on both maternal and paternal sides, and epilepsy in the maternal grandmother. The patient had mild flu-like symptoms one month prior and known COVID exposure, with a positive COVID IgG result. Laboratory findings indicated inflammation, elevated troponin and BNP levels, anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed normal coronary arteries and no depression in ejection fraction. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal. Genetic testing revealed variants of uncertain significance in SCN1A, PCDH19, RELN, CACNA1H, and MTOR, inherited from either parent, neither of whom had epilepsy. Additional metabolic evaluations, including urine organic acids, serum amino acids, and ammonia, were reassuring. Serum anti-NMDA receptor, anti-NMO, and anti-voltage gated K channel antibodies were negative. Infectious testing, including blood culture, urine culture, CSF culture, and respiratory viral panel, was negative. CSF HSV PCR, stool enterovirus, and serum parvovirus tests were negative. The patient was empirically treated for tickborne illnesses and later treated for Citrobacter tracheitis starting on day 10 of hospitalization. Initial MRI brain on day 3 was normal.
test_results: Repeat MRI brain on day 10 showed symmetric restricted diffusion throughout both gray and white matter, specifically the bilateral frontal and medial temporal lobes, bilateral cingulate gyri, superior parietal lobes, basal ganglia, thalami, and internal capsules. Areas of restricted diffusion had an ADC correlate with associated T2 FLAIR hyperintensities. There was no contrast enhancement or SWI dropout visualized. MRA and MRV were unremarkable. MRI Spectroscopy showed decreased neuronal integrity with reduced N-acetylaspartate peaks.
Orpha_name: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children and adults

case_report: A 55-year-old female patient with phototype III reported the appearance of skin lesions starting at age 5, which progressively increased until age 18. Similar lesions were observed in three of her siblings during their childhood. The parents were not consanguineous. Dermatological examination revealed fixed, finely scaly, symmetric erythematous keratotic plaques located on the dorsum of the hands, interphalangeal pads, wrists, elbows, groin, and feet. The plaques were notably thicker on the elbows, and a well-defined, brownish hyperpigmentation halo was present in the inguinal region.
test_results: A biopsy of the dorsum of the right foot revealed discrete papillomatosis and acanthosis, orthokeratotic hyperkeratosis in a basket-weave pattern and maintenance of the granular layer.

case_report: The patient is a 5-year-old Italian girl with a history of good health and regular vaccinations. Her family history is unremarkable. She was admitted to the emergency room at Ferrara’s Hospital due to foot pain that began three days prior following a minor trauma, accompanied by an abnormal gait with extended lower limbs. Physical examination revealed ecchymosis at the ankles and reduced mobility of the left tibiotarsic joint. No other significant findings were noted. The child had a recent episode of feverish gastroenteritis 3–4 weeks before this admission. She was discharged with a prescription for anti-inflammatory therapy (Ibuprofen) every 8 hours for 5 days and advised to rest. However, at home, she experienced night-time joint pain initially in the feet, which later spread to the dorsal spine, hands, and wrists. Ecchymosis was also noted on the wrists. She developed a fever with a maximum temperature of 38.9 °C. Due to rapid worsening of her condition, she was readmitted to the emergency room. Upon admission, her axillary temperature was 38.9 °C, and she was in pain, walking with extended lower limbs. Physical examination showed joint pain upon touch with bilateral functional limitation in the tibiotarsic joints, knees, wrists, elbows, and left metacarpophalangeal joints, as well as in the flexion of the left hand-interphalangeal joints. Pain was also triggered by movement of the cervical and dorsal spine. Cardio-respiratory examination, as well as the pharynx and mucous membranes, appeared normal, with no adenomegaly or hepatosplenomegaly observed. The skin was normal, without nodules or rash.
test_results: Blood tests revealed high grade leucocytosis (leukocyte count 19,070/μL, 82.4% neutrophils), predominantly neutrophilia, with elevated inflammation indexes (ESR 56 mm, CRP 130.5 mg/l). Further laboratory tests revealed Antinuclear Antibodies positivity (1:160, dotted score), Rheumatic Factor negativity, and confirmed the increased level of markers of inflammation: leucocytosis with neutrophilia (leukocyte count 20,030/μL, 82% neutrophils), thrombocytosis (772 platelets × 103/μl), and increased ESR, CRP, alpha2globulin and ferritin (ESR 65 mm, CRP 164 mg/l, alpha2globulin 17.8%, ferritin 267 ng/ml). The electrocardiogram was normal, while the echocardiogram was suggestive of serositis: pericardial effusion in the absence of signs of hemodynamic repercussion.

case_report: The patient is a 9-year-old girl who was referred to the Genetics Clinic due to mild learning difficulties. She was born at term via Cesarean section due to pelvi-fetal disproportion after an uneventful pregnancy. At birth, her weight was 2.3 kg (−2.38 SD) and her length was 46 cm (−2.07 SD). Occipitofrontal head circumference (OHC) at birth was not recorded. Initially, her development was within normal range, but increasing learning difficulties were noted during primary school. She is currently at her expected grade with educational support. On physical examination, her weight was 21.4 kg (−1.74 SD), her length was 119 cm (−3.15 SD on Spain 2000 growth chart), and her OHC was 48.7 cm (−2.9 SD). She had a thickened and low hanging columella. Her hands and feet, including thumbs and halluces, appeared normal. The patient's mother, aged 42, had a short stature of 141 cm (−3.87 SD) and a proportionately small OHC of 49 cm (−4 SD). She had experienced learning difficulties but obtained a Secondary School Certificate and is currently employed as a supermarket check-out worker. Her general health is good. She is a single mother of two children: the patient and a healthy 7-year-old boy. The mother had slightly posteriorly rotated ears, a prominent nose with a high nasal bridge, a low hanging columella, and a talon cusp at an upper incisor. Her thumbs were short and broad but not angulated, and her halluces were normal. The patient's maternal aunt and grandmother also had short stature and proportionate OHC but normal intelligence and normal hands and feet. The grandmother's height was 142.1 cm (−3.5 SD) and her OHC was 52.5 cm (−1.9 SD). The maternal grandfather died at age 50 from liver disease. Previous assessments of the patient included a hand X-ray for bone age, which was consistent with her chronological age, and endocrine tests that showed normal levels of growth hormone in two stimulation tests. A brain MRI scan revealed a pineal cyst measuring 9 × 9 × 5 mm with no other anomalies. Clinical data, samples, and photographs were obtained after written informed consent. This work has been approved by the Committee for Ethics in Clinical Research in La Rioja (CEICLAR).
test_results: Panel-based next generation sequencing (NGS) of CREBBP and EP300 genes was carried out. Libraries encompassing exons and introns of CREBBP and EP300 genes were prepared using the SureSelectXT2 Custom kit (Agilent) and sequenced to generate 150 bp single reads. The resulting reads were mapped to the human genome hg19 using BWA (version 0.7.12). Sequence variants were called using the Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK) version 3.3 and called variants were annotated with Annovar. ExAC browser of Broad Institute, 1000 Genomes database and dbSNP138, as well as, the Human Gene Mutation Database (HGMD), Leiden Open Variation Database (LOVD) and ClinVar databases were checked to assess the presence/absence of detected alterations in variations repositories.
diagnosis: Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome  associated with a novel EP300 variant
Orpha_name: Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome due to EP300 haploinsufficiency

case_report: A 10-year-old male child presented with a 1-month history of irritability, restlessness, and increased anxiety upon separation from his parents. The symptoms began abruptly, with the child refusing to play with his sister and other neighborhood children. He demanded constant presence of his parents and siblings, crying if they did not comply. The behavior escalated within 2 days, causing him to cry at the thought of separation and, on one occasion, scratch his face in anger, resulting in abrasions. These symptoms were most pronounced between 1 to 5 pm daily, with no clear exacerbating or relieving factors. For the rest of the day, he appeared slightly anxious but did not exhibit severe separation anxiety. The parents observed that he struggled to complete tasks at home, such as helping with chores, and his handwriting had deteriorated, making it difficult to complete homework. Over the next 4-5 days, his anxious behavior persisted despite the presence of his parents. He was prescribed oral escitalopram (5 mg) and clonazepam (0.25 mg bid) by a psychiatrist, but there was no improvement after 15 days of treatment. There was no recent stressor identified in the child's life at home or school. The parents reported that he had stopped attending school for 5 days before the onset of symptoms and had a mild fever during that period, which resolved without medication. His birth and developmental history were normal, and he had no history of school refusal, truancy, academic failures, or bullying. Physical examination showed healed scar marks on his face from self-inflicted scratches. Systemic examination was normal. Mental state examination revealed anxiety and irritability, with the child clinging to his parents and resisting separation throughout the interview.
test_results: His ASO titers were elevated (800 IU/ml).
diagnosis: Pediatric Autoimmune Neuropsychiatric Disorders Associated with Streptococcal Infections

case_report: A 17-year-old female reported experiencing fatigue for 2 years, predominantly affecting the lower limbs. She noted difficulty with squatting and climbing stairs, while walking and upper limb activities remained unaffected. Over the past 3 months, her symptoms worsened, leading to frequent tripping and requiring assistance to climb stairs. An MRI of the brain and knee joints was conducted at a primary hospital. The brain MRI was normal, but the knee MRI revealed a small amount of effusion in the right knee cavity and atrophy of the right thigh and calf muscles. No treatment was administered. Her family, including her parents and a 14-year-old brother, did not exhibit similar symptoms. She had normal developmental milestones and no significant past medical history except for esotropia since childhood. Neurological examination indicated weakness in both upper and lower limbs, with both proximal and distal muscles involved, and the left side being slightly more affected than the right. There was noticeable atrophy in the bilateral thenar and hypothenar regions, along with bilateral esotropia and facial weakness. Ptosis, diplopia, and bulbar features were absent. Laboratory tests showed normal serum CK levels. Electromyography indicated myogenic damage with normal nerve conduction velocity. Electrocardiogram, cardiac ultrasonography, and lung function tests were normal. MRI of the lower limb muscles showed fatty infiltration and muscle atrophy, with the most significant involvement in the posterior muscles.
test_results: A heterozygous mutation NM_058246:c.236-1_240delGGTGGA of the DNAJB6 gene was identified within exon 5 of DNAJB6 by genetic testing. The mutational site was confirmed by Sanger sequencing, and this site was normal in her parents.
diagnosis: Juvenile-Onset Proximal–Distal Myopathy associated with a novel splice-site mutation in DNAJB6

case_report: A 25-month-old Korean male was admitted for treatment of nasal congestion. The patient was notably tall for his age (95.2 cm, 97th percentile) and weighed 17.5 kg (97th percentile). He had a disproportionately large head with a circumference of 52 cm. Physical examination revealed significant facial deformities, including a large forehead, prominent cheekbones, and maxillary enlargement. Nasal endoscopy indicated nasal cavity obstruction due to hypertrophy of both inferior turbinates. Both tonsils were enlarged (grade II), and adenoid hypertrophy (grade III) was observed on the skull lateral view. Laboratory tests showed a highly elevated serum alkaline phosphatase concentration of 1,082 IU/L (normal range: 50-150 IU/L) and a total hydroxyproline urinary excretion rate of 330 mmoL/24 hr, which was slightly above normal. Other laboratory results were within normal limits. Plain radiographs of the skull revealed thickening and sclerotic changes in the facial bone and skull vault, along with unformed paranasal sinuses. The chest radiograph appeared normal. The lower extremities showed slight anterior bowing of the femora, reduced mineralization, loss of normal trabeculation, and coarse strand-like bone trabeculation. CT scans of the skull confirmed thickening of the facial bone and skull vault, and non-development of the paranasal sinuses, while the ethmoid sinuses appeared normal. There was also thickening of the nasal septum and both inferior conchae, leading to narrowing of the nasal cavities. Bone scans indicated increased radiotracer uptake in the facial bones and skull base, suggesting a high rate of bone turnover. To alleviate nasal symptoms, the patient underwent a submucosal partial inferior turbinectomy and an adenotonsillectomy.
test_results: Histological examination of the inferior nasal concha showed an extremely thin cortex and an abnormal spongiosa. There were increased cellularity with irregularly arranged cement lines, loose fibrovascular tissue within the intertrabecular space. The trabeculae were lined with active osteoblasts and osteoclasts, numerous osteoclasts, and an increase in osteoblastic bone formation.

case_report: The patient is a 23-year-old Italian male, first child of non-consanguineous parents, born at term via caesarean delivery after a normal pregnancy. He has a healthy younger brother. He began walking at 18 months but experienced persistent walking difficulties and frequent falls. Parents noted easy fatigability from early childhood. At 7 years old, a neurological examination revealed bilateral ptosis without ophthalmoparesis, muscle hypotonia and wasting, and absent deep tendon reflexes. There was no evident weakness, but significant exercise intolerance was observed. No cognitive impairment or other central nervous system involvement was detected. Brain nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and EEG results were normal.
test_results: Electromyography showed myopathic changes in all tested muscles. Creatine kinase (CK) level was slightly increased (about 300 U/L; normal values, n.v.:<180), lactate acid was high in blood (4.6 mmol/L; n.v.: 0.4–2.2).
diagnosis: Mitochondrial Myopathy due to a novel de novo dominant mutation in ISCU
Orpha_name: Hereditary myopathy with lactic acidosis due to ISCU deficiency

case_report: A four-month-old male infant (gestational age 40 weeks and 5 days, birth weight 3.86 kg) with a history of bilateral hydroceles presented to the emergency department for abdominal bloating. The abdominal ultrasound revealed a large volume of fluid in the abdominal cavity, and an X-ray of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder indicated bowel displacement consistent with the presence of fluid. Additionally, a chest X-ray showed reduced lung volumes with mild central lung collapse, and a liver ultrasound demonstrated forward blood flow in the portal vein and reduced pulsatility in the hepatic veins. An ultrasound of the iliac veins and inferior vena cava (IVC) excluded the presence of venous thromboembolism, and an echocardiogram showed normal heart function.
test_results: Paracentesis showed triglyceride levels >4,000 mg/dL consistent with a chylous aspirate.

case_report: A 25-year-old man presented to the emergency department with sudden onset of nausea, vomiting, slight mental disability, and abdominal pain. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and gastrointestinal examinations were unremarkable. Neurological examinations of cranial nerves and limbs were normal. The patient appeared clinically dehydrated. Initial laboratory results showed a BUN level of 35 mg/dL, creatinine level of 3.17 mg/dL, calcium level of 8.6 mg/dL, and moderate metabolic acidosis with a pH of 7.30. Urinalysis indicated hematuria [++++], leukocyturia [++], and proteinuria [+]. Urine sediment analysis revealed numerous red blood cell casts, white blood cell casts, a few granular casts, and epithelial cell casts. Renal ultrasound demonstrated normal-sized kidneys without hydronephrosis. The fractional excretion of sodium (FeNa) was 4%. The patient was admitted to the nephrology department, and intravenous fluid therapy was initiated due to dehydration. Kidney function tests and blood gases were monitored daily. The patient's condition remained stable until the 3rd day, when anuria developed, creatinine level rose to 13.5 mg/dL, and blood gas analysis showed a pH of 7.19 with high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Urgent venovenous hemodialysis was performed for two hours via a jugular hemodialysis catheter.
test_results: Pathological examination of the kidney specimen revealed tubular injury with oxalate crystals.

case_report: A 10-year-old female presented with irritable behavior and communication difficulties. The child had normal development until the age of 5 years. She is the offspring of a consanguineous marriage, with her father being her mother's maternal uncle. She was born at full term via normal vaginal delivery, with no maternal infections or complications at birth. She achieved age-appropriate motor and language milestones until 5 years old, was toilet trained, and could control her bowels and bladder. She attended school, learned to recite poems and stories, and could bathe herself with supervision. At 4 years old, she experienced a severe upper respiratory tract infection, resulting in fever and cough for 6 months and pleural effusion, which required fluid drainage. Due to financial constraints, her parents could not follow the prescribed medication regimen and follow-ups. Subsequently, she had recurrent severe fevers and was treated by an unqualified health worker. She stopped attending school and lost previously acquired communication skills, such as speaking in sentences and calling family members by name. She became self-absorbed in play, exhibited increased anger and irritability, and would hit or bite when disturbed. She ceased playing with friends, stopped asking for food, and would cry when hungry. She neglected personal hygiene, picked up sticks and stones from the floor, and put them in her mouth. She also experienced disrupted sleep, crying at night without apparent reason, and lost toilet training, passing stools and urine in her clothes. The patient was brought to Mamata General Hospital to the Psychiatric OP with these complaints.
test_results: Computerized tomography of brain showed marked reduction of brain volume with less sulci and gyri and enlarged ventricles. IQ test revealed that the patient has an IQ of 37.5.

case_report: An 18-year-old girl, the first daughter of non-consanguineous Caucasian parents, was first referred to our unit at the age of 12 with ongoing episodes of recurrent fever. At one month of age, she was hospitalized for suspected sepsis. Since then, she had experienced recurrent episodes characterized by high fevers, accompanied by oral ulcers, cervical lymphadenopathies, pharyngitis, and occasionally polyarthralgia. Initially, these episodes occurred monthly and then at variable intervals, between one to six months, lasting for three to seven days with spontaneous resolution. She was otherwise asymptomatic, with normal inflammatory markers between flares, and presented adequate growth and neurodevelopment. Family history was unremarkable. After excluding unusual infectious, malignant, and autoimmune etiologies, the patient was treated with a one to two day course of prednisolone with a favorable response. At the age of five, she underwent a tonsillectomy without any improvement. At the age of 12, she presented de novo genital ulcers during a new febrile episode and was referred to our pediatric rheumatology unit. Upon reviewing the history over the years, during attacks, the patient often presented a urticariform rash and abdominal pain with diarrhea; chest pain occurred rarely. Despite an improvement with steroids, the attack was not abruptly halted by it and low fevers persisted for a few days. It was also clear that immunizations and viral infections triggered febrile attacks. Combined with the early onset of episodes (clearly before 12 months), an extensive investigation during an asymptomatic period revealed normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and serum amyloid A (SAA). Serum immunoglobulins, including IgA, were in the normal range for age, except for a high IgD: IgA 163 mg/dL (N: 85-211) and IgD 60 mg/dL (N: <14 mg/dL). During attacks, laboratory findings showed elevated ESR, CRP, and SAA, reflecting an acute systemic inflammatory process. IgA and IgD were also elevated: IgA 371 mg/dL (N: 85-211) and IgD 77.4 mg/dL (N: <14 mg/dL). High UAV excretion was also detected: 31.9 µmol/mmol creatinine (N <0.3). Additional investigations were non-contributory.
test_results: DNA analysis of the MVK gene identified two pathogenic variants in heterozygosity, c.79-2A>G and c.1129G>A (p.Val377Ile). Genetic screening carried out on the parents confirmed that the detected variants were in compound heterozygosity in the daughter.

case_report: A two-month-old male infant from a mixed family (Romanian mother and Syrian father) was admitted to the Pediatrics Department of the 'Grigore Alexandrescu' Emergency Hospital for Children in Bucharest due to feeding difficulties and growth failure. During pregnancy, intrauterine growth restriction, oligohydramnios, and ventriculomegaly were identified. The mother was monitored for these conditions, and ventriculomegaly was noted in the second trimester. First trimester screening for aneuploidy and preeclampsia showed low risk. A fetal MRI was performed, and there was suspicion of a cleft palate. The parents chose to continue the pregnancy. At 38 weeks, the infant was delivered via cesarean section due to intrauterine growth restriction. Birth measurements were: weight 2260 g (−2.4 SD, <p1%), length 43 cm (−3.5 SD, <p1%), and head circumference 30 cm (−3.5 SD, <p1%). Apgar scores were nine at 1 minute and ten at 5 minutes. Postnatal examination showed dysmorphic facial features (hypertelorism, microphthalmia, mongoloid palpebral fissures, microretrognathia, and long philtrum), membranous partial cleft palate, low-set ears, and prominent occiput. Additional findings included umbilical and inguinal hernia, syndactyly of the third and fourth toes, fifth digit clinodactyly, floating testicles, axial hypotonia, and limb hypertonia. The infant was fed a special milk formula for premature infants but had poor intake (300 mL daily), resulting in suboptimal weight gain (600 g in six weeks). At two months old, the infant weighed 2710 g (Z score −3.12) and exhibited facial dysmorphism (hypertelorism, microphthalmia, eyelid ptosis, mongoloid slant, bilateral blepharophimosis, anteverted nostrils, long philtrum, micrognathia, and low-set dysplastic posteriorly rotated ears) and other anomalies (presacral fossa, cleft palate, clinodactyly of the fifth finger of both hands, abnormally implanted toes, and syndactyly of the third and fourth toes of the left foot). Umbilical and right inguinoscrotal hernias were also noted. Neurologic examination showed global developmental delay. A cerebral CT scan revealed asymmetric lateral ventricles. Cardiological evaluation identified an atrial septal defect with a small left-to-right shunt without hemodynamic impact. Ophthalmologic examination diagnosed severe bilateral eyelid ptosis requiring surgical treatment and hypermetropia needing postoperative optical correction. Blood samples for microarray testing were taken, and results showed no significant copy number variations. Tube feeding was initially recommended, with prior bottle feeding to stimulate the swallowing reflex. The patient was discharged with a nasogastric tube and continued a physical therapy program.
test_results: WES identified the pathogenic variant c.5602C > T (p.Arg1868Trp) in the CREBBP gene.

case_report: A 75-year-old Caucasian male with a prolonged history of retinal changes was evaluated in the clinic. He initially presented in 1985 with pigmentary changes at the macula observed by his optician. At that time, his best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 6/9 in the right eye and 6/6 in the left eye. Fundoscopy revealed pigmentary changes and drusen, which were more clearly visible on intravenous fundus fluorescein angiography (IVFA). No choroidal neovascular membrane (CNVM) was detected in any images. Multiple subsequent IVFA examinations showed no active leak. His retinal appearance was monitored without any conclusive findings or available treatment. Ten years later, ongoing review identified raised intraocular pressure and optic disc changes, leading to the initiation of treatment for glaucoma. In 2001, the patient was found to have hypertension (186/110 mmHg) and retinal examination showed cotton wool spots and hemorrhages, consistent with hypertensive retinopathy. Elevated serum urea and creatinine levels were also noted. Following bilateral cataract surgery in 2003, complicated by posterior capsule rupture in the left eye, the patient achieved a BCVA of 6/36 in each eye. Due to inadequate control of intraocular pressure, a left-sided trabeculectomy was performed in 2005. At age 64, the patient's urea and creatinine levels were recorded as 20.5 mmol/L (normal 2.8–7.2 mmol/L) and 474 umol/L (normal 60-105 umol/L), respectively, leading to the initiation of regular hemodialysis for end-stage renal failure. In 2009, he underwent dual renal transplant and started systemic immunosuppression (Tacrolimus 3 mg/day). Both transplanted kidneys failed within a year, requiring bilateral nephrostomies. In June 2010, at age 69, he was referred back to Ophthalmology with a vision of 52 ETDRS letters in the right eye and 35 letters in the left eye. Bilateral changes at the maculae were noted, with a small area of possible sub-retinal fluid. Comparison between the IVFA in 1985 and the IVFA at re-referral showed a significant increase in the number and distribution of drusen, but no vascular leakage. Poor vision in the left eye was attributed to advanced glaucoma and significant macular changes. The patient was monitored for 5 years with repeated imaging. In 2015, imaging demonstrated an increasing sub-foveal space. A loading phase of intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) was initiated with Ranibizumab 0.5 mg. After no response to six injections, treatment was switched to Aflibercept 2 mg with three further monthly doses, but again, no improvement was observed, and treatment was ceased. A systematic review of his previous notes and images was performed as part of a retinal multi-disciplinary team.
test_results: The fundus examination demonstrated multiple subretinal drusenoid deposits, mainly at the posterior pole. OCT images demonstrated that the deposits were in Bruch’s membrane, with an intact Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE). Autofluorescence imaging demonstrated large areas of increased and decreased autofluorescence involving the macula and spreading inferiorly. OCT continued to demonstrate subfoveal hyporeflective areas. Pale optic discs were noted bilaterally. Wide angle (102°) infra-red imaging demonstrates the limitation of the retinal disease to the posterior pole, involving the macula, crossing the vascular arcades and including the nasal peri-papillary region.

case_report: A 28-year-old woman, who has never been pregnant and is not sexually active, presented to the emergency department with severe pain in the abdominopelvic region. She reported experiencing abdominal pain for approximately two weeks, which had intensified to an unbearable level the day before admission. She also noted a decrease in appetite but did not experience nausea or vomiting. Her bowel movements had been normal prior to this episode. Her last menstrual period occurred 13 days prior to admission. Additionally, she reported a foul-smelling vaginal discharge. She did not have any urinary symptoms such as painful urination or increased frequency, nor did she have gastrointestinal symptoms like constipation or difficulty passing gas. She had no history of medical illnesses, surgeries, allergies, or notable family medical history. Upon admission, her vital signs were: systolic blood pressure of 90 mmHg, diastolic blood pressure of 60 mmHg, heart rate of 110 beats per minute, and body temperature of 38.2°C. Laboratory tests revealed an elevated white blood cell count (WBC 16.1 × 10^9/L and neutrophils 14.1 × 10^9/L) and increased C-reactive protein (33 mg/L). Hemoglobin levels, as well as renal and liver function tests, were within normal ranges. Physical examination of the abdomen showed tenderness with guarding and rebound tenderness, indicative of an acute abdomen. Abdominopelvic ultrasound imaging revealed a normal-sized uterus with a homogeneous myometrium and an endometrial thickness of 9 mm. The right ovary appeared normal, but the left fallopian tube and left ovary were not visualized. A complex cystic and solid pelvic mass measuring 6x7 cm was observed in the left adnexa, extending towards the cul-de-sac.
test_results: There was a complex adnexal mass sized 5x5 cm on left adnexa with conspicuous air-fluid levels supporting tubo-ovarian abscess. The sigmoid colon wall was edematous due to inflammation and beside it in the mesenteric area there was a solid mass measured 41x23mm including air-fluid levels.
diagnosis: adenocarcinoma of familial adenomatous polyposis  of the sigmoid colon

case_report: A male infant was delivered via Cesarean section due to breech presentation and respiratory distress at 36 weeks and 2 days of gestation. The mother, a 19-year-old primigravida, did not have any antenatal evaluations and presented to the hospital at the onset of labor. A prenatal ultrasound revealed polyhydramnios and short-limbed dwarfism. There was no history of substance abuse, and both parents were healthy with no family history of congenital abnormalities. At birth, the infant's heart rate was 52 beats per minute, and body temperature was 36.7℃. Apgar scores were 1 at both 1 and 5 minutes. The infant appeared cyanotic. Arterial blood gas analysis showed: pH 7.08, PaO2 44.7 mmHg, PaCO2 61.1 mmHg, HCO3 13.9 mmol/L, and oxygen saturation was 75% despite oxygen therapy via face mask. The infant was intubated, resuscitated, and transferred to the neonatal intensive care unit. An infantogram indicated a small thoracic cage and signs consistent with respiratory distress syndrome, including inadequate lung inspiration. Surfactant replacement therapy and mechanical ventilation in assist-control mode were administered, stabilizing the infant's respiratory and hemodynamic status. Initial laboratory findings included WBC 24,760/mm3 (neutrophils 47%, lymphocytes 38%), hemoglobin 17.7 g/dL, hematocrit 54.8%, platelets 239,000/mm3, serum Na 135 mmol/L, K 4.5 mmol/L, AST/ALT 59/14 IU/L, BUN/Cr 11.6/0.7 mg/dL, and non-reactive CRP. Birth weight was 2,740 g (25-50th percentile), height was 39 cm (<5th percentile), head circumference was 39.5 cm (>90th percentile), thoracic circumference was 27 cm, and abdominal circumference was 30 cm. Physical examination revealed a large head with a prominent forehead, midfacial hypoplasia, narrow thorax, very short limbs, short neck, and protuberant abdomen. Radiographs showed a large calvaria with a small cranial base, thinning and flattening of vertebral bodies, short ribs, hypoplasia of pelvic bones, and small curved long bones resembling a telephone receiver.
test_results: The baby carried R248C mutation. Nucleotide sequence analysis of cDNA revealed a C to T transition at nucleotide 742 (C742T) in one allele of the FGFR3 gene. This heterozygous 742C→T (R248C) mutation in the FGFR3 leading to an Arg248Cys (CGC→TGC) substitution.

case_report: A 50-year-old female patient reported a one-week history of reduced vision in her left eye. She had been managing seropositive rheumatoid arthritis for 15 years with methotrexate and deflazacort. Due to inadequate response, she began a regimen of 25 mg per week of etanercept 8 months prior to her current presentation. Upon examination, her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 0.8 in the right eye and 0.1 in the left eye. No cells were observed in the anterior chamber of either eye. Funduscopic examination revealed granular infiltration at the temporal macula in the right eye and the foveal area in the left eye. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography indicated a swollen ellipsoid zone and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) irregularities in the right eye, and an ellipsoid zone disruption and RPE irregularity in the left eye. Fundus autofluorescence displayed parafoveal granular hyperautofluorescence in both eyes. After various blood tests returned negative results, she was started on oral prednisolone for noninfectious uveitis. One month post-treatment, she experienced mild improvement, but two months later, her vision in the right eye deteriorated to 0.1. Compared to the initial visit, the swollen ellipsoid zone area had extended under the fovea, and new subRPE yellow-white deposits appeared in the inferotemporal area. Additionally, mild vitreous opacity with haziness was observed in the right eye.
test_results: Vitreous cytology revealed atypical mononuclear cells with positive CD20 immunostaining. PCR of the vitreous fluid was negative for herpes and cytomegalovirus.

case_report: A 3-year and 4-month-old girl was admitted to Quanzhou Children’s Hospital on July 14, 2021, after experiencing three convulsions in one day. The convulsions on the day of admission included symptoms such as eyes staring to the right, mouth tilting to the right, clonic twitching of the right limbs, and loss of consciousness. Each episode lasted approximately 20 minutes and was alleviated with diazepam, without any fever or vomiting. At birth, the child weighed 3.3 kg and measured 50 cm in height. Postnatal intellectual and motor development was delayed. At 3 months, she could track with her eyes and respond to voices. By 5 months, she could hold her head up steadily, turn over to the prone position, and vocalize “eee, eee, eee, eee.” At 7 months, she could reach out to grab objects. Near her first birthday, she could turn over freely, but by 13 months, she was still unable to sit, crawl, or stand alone; she could transfer objects between hands and make “babbling” sounds. She underwent short-term rehabilitation training. By 3 years and 4 months, she still could not sit, crawl, or stand alone; she could transfer objects between hands and say “papa, mama, nana.” The child is the third child and the second birth (the first resulted in abortion), delivered vaginally at 39 weeks and 4 days of gestation. The parents reported no history of intrauterine hypoxia or birth asphyxia. The mother, aged 43, was healthy during pregnancy, did not take any medication, and had no history of poisoning. The family, including the parents and an older brother, had no history of epilepsy or psychomotor retardation. On examination, the child’s head circumference was 47 cm, height 95 cm, and weight 12 kg. She had no distinctive facial features, was conscious and in good spirits, with no café-au-lait spots or depigmentation on the skin, no neck stiffness, clear breath sounds in both lungs, and no dry or wet rales. Her heart rate was 116 bpm with a regular rhythm, strong heart sounds, and no murmurs. The abdomen was soft with no palpable masses, and the liver and spleen were not palpable. Limb muscle strength could not be assessed, but muscle tone was increased. Bilateral ankle joint contractures were present, knee tendon reflexes were active and symmetrical, and the Brudzinski sign was negative bilaterally.
test_results: Genetic testing with trio whole exome sequencing (April 29, 2019) showed the following: (1) Chromosomal aneuploidy; the chromosome composition was 46, XX, and the number of chromosomes was normal; and (2) Chromosome microdeletion or microduplication was negative. No clinically identifiable pathogenic copy number variations were found within the scope of this assay.

case_report: A 42-year-old female, currently monitored by genetics and neurology teams, has been taking lamotrigine 50 mg/day for two years and clonazepam 1 mg/day. She reported a lesion on the right temporal region that has been present for six months, characterized by progressive, painless growth, without itching or any history of insect bite at the site. Physical examination revealed a circular plaque with well-defined edges, measuring 1.2 cm in diameter, and a smooth surface located on the right temporal region. Dermoscopic examination using contact polarized light without immersion showed a salmon-colored background, slight flaking, and white dots interspersed with groups of rosettes approximately 0.2 mm in size, all oriented in the same direction. A 4-mm punch biopsy was performed on the center of the lesion.
test_results: Histological examination showed an atypical lymphoid proliferation, with intense lymphocytic infiltrate filling the papillary and superficial reticular dermis, notably in its upper portion, with a predominance of small lymphocytes with irregular nuclei and increased volume. The immunohistochemical examination revealed a predominance of T lymphocytes reactive with CD3, CD4, and a lower expression of CD8; B lymphocytes were detected in part of the infiltrate and there was no immunoexpression of CD30.

case_report: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman with two children presented to the gynecological unit at the National Hospital of Sri Lanka, Colombo, with progressive hair loss and male-pattern hair distribution over the past year. She also reported lower abdominal pain for the past four months. There were no changes in body weight or appetite, and no postmenopausal bleeding or vaginal discharge. She had been managing hypertension for the past year and a half with regular treatment, maintaining good blood pressure control. At age 44, she underwent hemithyroidectomy for a cold nodule, which histology identified as a follicular adenoma, and she has been on L-thyroxine 50 μg daily since then. Physical examination revealed alopecia, frontal balding, and hirsutism on the face, chin, upper back, chest, and upper and lower abdomen, with a modified Ferriman and Gallwey score of 14. Clitoromegaly was also noted. Respiratory and cardiovascular examinations were normal. Pelvic examination identified a solid right ovarian mass measuring 5 cm, confirmed by pelvic ultrasound, which showed a solid mass with an intact capsule. The uterus and the other ovary appeared normal, with no free fluid detected. Liver and other abdominal organs were normal. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed a well-defined solid tumor measuring 5.5 × 3 × 6 cm in the right adnexal region. Other pelvic structures and the suprarenal glands were normal.
test_results: Histological examination of sections from the right ovarian mass stained with haematoxyline and eosine revealed cell nets comprising uniform cells with round bland nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm. Mitotic figures were sparse. They were surrounded by a proliferation of elongated spindle cells with bland nuclei. The capsule of the mass was intact. The other ovary, uterus, cervix, and the omentum were normal. The endometrium was nonreactive with atrophic changes.

case_report: A 6-year-old boy was examined in the Emergency Department due to acute abdominal pain, intense nausea, and a mild fever of 37.5°C. The clinical history indicated six similar episodes over the past 13 months, some managed at home and others requiring brief hospitalization. During the first episode, he had a white blood count of 22,000 (88% neutrophils) and underwent an appendicectomy. Previous medical records showed that amylase levels were evaluated twice and found to be slightly elevated (twice the normal value), but no further investigations were conducted due to rapid recovery and complete resolution of abdominal pain. Upon examination, the boy appeared to be in distress, with knees drawn up to his chest, experiencing epigastric pain radiating to his back, which started post-prandially. He also had moderate abdominal distension, but all vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory results revealed serum amylase at 1373 U/L (normal value 0-95 U/L), lipase at 1050 U/L (normal value 13-60 U/L), C-reactive protein (CRP) at 95 mg/L (normal value 0-10 mg/L), and erythrosedimentation rate (ESR) at 74 mm/h (normal value 0-20 mm/h). The child received intravenous (i.v.) fluids and 20 mg of proton pump inhibitor (PPI) i.v. An abdominal sonogram showed increased pancreatic volume with diffuse edema, while the gallbladder appeared normal. The following day, laboratory tests showed decreased values: amylase at 650 U/L, lipase at 350 U/L, and CRP at 30 mg/L. Intravenous fluids were administered for four days, after which amylase, lipase, CRP, and ESR returned close to normal values, and a liquid light meal was given with good results. After seven days of hospitalization, with normal laboratory tests and no abdominal pain, the child was discharged on a hypolipidic diet, 20 mg PPI daily, and pancreatic enzyme supplementation (10,000 U × 6/day) orally for two more weeks. Comprehensive evaluations excluded blunt trauma, metabolic, infectious, drug, and systemic causes. Further laboratory tests showed normal calcium, glucose, and triglycerides levels, and negative antibodies for Mumps, Cytomegalovirus, Coxsackie B, and Herpes Simplex virus. Secretin-stimulated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pancreas was scheduled as an outpatient to exclude any anatomical abnormalities. At follow-up visits, the child maintained stable body weight, appeared in good health, and had no further episodes of abdominal pain while adhering to a strictly controlled hypolipidic diet.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed normal SPINK1 and CTRC genes, a novel heterozygous variation, c.541A > G (p.S181G), in exon 4 of PRSS1 gene was revealed.
