The patient also showed the classic p.F508del mutation, in a heterozygous state, in the CFTR gene. Both mutations were absent in the patient's father but present in his clinically healthy mother.

case_report: A 24-year-old male visited the dermatology outpatient department with lifelong thickening of the skin on his palms and soles, which had progressively spread to the backs of his hands and feet over the past 5 years. He reported recurrent blistering and painful cracks on his palms. For the past 6 months, he had hyperpigmented, raised, scaly plaques on the extensor surfaces of both knees and elbows. Additionally, he experienced redness and mildly painful fissures at the corners of his mouth for the same duration. He had no other systemic issues and no family history of similar symptoms. On physical examination, there was widespread thickening of the skin on the palms and soles, extending to the backs of the hands and feet, with irregular, poorly defined borders and prominent knuckle pads. The skin on the palms and soles appeared thick, waxy, yellowish, and emitted an unpleasant odor, with a loss of normal skin patterns. There were multiple erosions and fissures of varying sizes on both palms, and pitted keratolysis on the soles. The fingers exhibited a pseudosclerodermatous appearance, with some showing conical tapering and digital constrictions at various points, along with mild flexion deformity. The nails were thickened and hypercurved, with dystrophic changes noted in both great toenails. The patient also had multiple hyperkeratotic, scaly, irregular, and poorly defined plaques on the extensor surfaces of both elbows and knees. Additionally, the lower lip was dry, erythematous, and thickened, with angular cheilitis.
test_results: Histopathology of palmar skin showed lining of stratified squamous epithelium with hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, and acanthosis. Superficial dermis shows mild perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates.

case_report: A 16-year-old girl was referred to our hospital for gallbladder surgery due to gallstones. Her face and lips appeared bluish, but she did not exhibit rapid breathing or difficulty breathing. There was no history of heart or lung disease, nor exposure to drugs or chemicals. Physical examination showed no clubbing of fingers and toes and no enlargement of organs. Chest auscultation was normal. Her mother and two brothers also had similar bluish discoloration. Additionally, many maternal family members had a lifelong history of bluish discoloration. Her younger brother had previously undergone stone removal from the common bile duct. Peripheral arterial oxygen saturation (SpO2) on pulse oximetry was 35% at room air and did not improve with oxygen administration. The arterial blood of the patient, her mother, and her older brother was dark chocolaty in color, similar to venous blood. However, the patient's arterial blood gas analysis showed normal values: arterial partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2) of 115 mm Hg, arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2) of 34.5 mm Hg, and arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2) of 92.9%. Laboratory tests indicated hemolytic anemia. Peripheral blood smear showed variations in red blood cell size and shape, and an increased number of immature red blood cells. Chest X-ray, electrocardiogram, and echocardiogram results were normal. Pulmonary disease was ruled out by chest CT and pulmonary function tests. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity was normal. The blood methemoglobin concentration was 13.0% (normal range, 0–1.5%). Hemoglobin electrophoresis at alkaline pH showed increased fetal hemoglobin (5.7%) and an abnormal band (10.5%) between fetal hemoglobin and hemoglobin A2.
test_results: This revealed a heterozygous point mutation of HBB gene (c277C>T, p.His93Tyr).

case_report: A 9-year-old boy was admitted with painful subcutaneous soft tissue masses with calcifications on the right toes and posterior chest wall. He had a history of repeated convulsive episodes starting at 2 months old. Physical examination revealed short stature (120 cm, 3rd percentile), round face, brachydactyly with short metacarpals, and subcutaneous ossifications on the 2nd toe tip and 1st web space of the right foot and the left lower posterior chest wall. His weight was 30 kg (50th percentile), indicating a normal body mass index (20.83 kg/m2, 85th-90th percentile). He was the first child of nonconsanguineous Korean parents and was born at full term by cesarean section with a birth weight of 3.3 kg. Family history showed that his maternal grandmother had short stature, round face, obesity, and brachydactyly. His mother had short stature, and two of her siblings had short stature, round face, and obesity. Further family investigation was not possible due to loss of contact after his parents' divorce. Laboratory tests showed hypocalcemia (4.2 mg/dL; normal range, 8.8-10.8 mg/dL), hyperphosphatemia (8.9 mg/dL; normal range, 3.7-5.6 mg/dL), and elevated serum PTH (146.5 pg/mL; normal range, 9-65 pg/mL). Elevated plasma thyroid-stimulating hormone (6.978 µIU/mL; normal range, 0.5-4.8 µIU/mL), follicle-stimulating hormone (5.6 µIU/mL; normal range, 0.26-3.0 µIU/mL), and luteinizing hormone (1.2 µIU/mL; normal range, 0.02-0.3 µIU/mL) were also noted. Urinary phosphorous and cyclic adenosine monophosphate response after infusion of synthetic human PTH (teriparatide acetate) was attenuated (Ellsworth-Howard test). Cranial computed tomography scan showed bilateral calcifications in the basal ganglia. His intelligence scale (Korean Educational Development Institute - Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children) indicated mild mental retardation (intelligence quotient, 67).
test_results: Sequencing of the amplified GNAS genomic DNA fragments revealed a heterozygous nonsense mutation within exon 11 (c.637 C>T). The C>T transversion results in an amino acid substitution from Gln to stop codon at codon 213 (p.Gln213*).

case_report: The patient is a 1-year-old male. At 2 months old, red plaques developed on the left side of the jaw and the upper chest. Physical examination showed firm, red plaques with increased skin temperature but no pain. Family history was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed no significant abnormalities in routine blood and coagulation profiles, and there were no signs of the Kasabach–Merritt phenomenon.
test_results: B-ultrasonography showed a patchy hyperechoic area in the chest wall, approximately 0.6 cm thick, with unclear boundaries abundant blood flow signals, and vascular echoes. The diameter of the thicker blood vessels was approximately 0.16cm. MRI indicated a thickening of the anterior chest wall epidermis, a slightly longer T2 signal on the fat suppression sequence consistent with T1, and a slightly longer T2 signal cloud shadow in the subcutaneous tissue of the left anterior margin of the mandible. Histological examination of a biopsy sample from the plaques identified blood vessels in a tufted or plexiform distribution, CD31(+), CD34(+), D2-40(-), and GLUT-1(-).

case_report: A four-year-old male from a Punjabi Muslim background was brought to the emergency room at the Indus Hospital and Health Network, Karachi, due to worsening hoarseness of voice. The child initially spoke normally until the age of two, after which hoarseness developed and progressed to difficulty breathing. There was no history of fever, tonsillitis, or sinusitis. The child has a history of recurrent paronychia and bleeding. Over the past 1.5 years, he developed multiple small vesicular lesions, primarily on the ears and nose, which ruptured and bled easily. In recent weeks, he experienced multiple episodes of spontaneous nosebleeds without any history of nose-picking or trauma. These nosebleeds were minor and resolved on their own. There was no history of prolonged bleeding post-circumcision, hemarthrosis, or easy bruising. He is the third child from a consanguineous marriage, but no other family members, including siblings, have similar complaints. On examination, the child had a hoarse voice with inspiratory stridor, intermittent subcostal and suprasternal recessions, and bilateral equal air entry. The throat was clear with no apparent obstruction. Multiple ulcerations were observed on both ears and the right nostril, along with erosions of multiple toenails. Several nails had fallen off. No active bleeding, blisters, bruising, hemarthrosis, conjunctivitis, deformed teeth, or oral ulcers were noted. The patient was admitted to the Pediatrics unit under the Otolaryngology service.
test_results: Histopathological evaluation showed fibro-collagenous tissue with ulceration, dense acute and chronic inflammation, granulation tissue formation with separately lying superficial strips of hyperplastic stratified squamous epithelium.

case_report: A 7-year-old girl presented with intellectual disability and a history of tic disorders for four years. She was born to nonconsanguineous parents with no notable family history. Her birth measurements were within normal limits. Motor and language developmental milestones were delayed; at 9 months, she could not turn, crawl, or sit independently. Clinical and neurological examination showed hypotonia, reduced movements, funnel chest, and hyperextended knees. Audiometric evaluation indicated bilateral hearing impairment. She was unable to walk or speak single words until age 2 and underwent intensive speech training with slow improvement. At age 3, she developed involuntary bursts of screaming, eye blinking, facial grimacing, and shoulder shrugging (Video S1). Initial treatment with risperidone showed no significant improvement. Aripiprazole and clonazepam were added, providing short-term relief of motor tics. Over the following years, she developed attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and self-injurious behavior (SIB), characterized by inattention, hyperactivity, cleaning rituals, rage attacks, picking at finger skin until bleeding, and repetitive slapping on the head (Video S1). She attended a special education school due to learning difficulties. Physical examination revealed a dysmorphic craniofacial appearance, including brachycephaly, broad forehead, arched eyebrows, epicanthal folds, midface retrusion, low-set ears with thickened helices, everted lower lip, and tented upper lip, as well as hyperextended knees (Fig. A). Frequent insuppressible motor and vocal tics were observed. The patient could only answer a few simple questions with slurred speech. Routine laboratory tests, including metabolic and genetic screening (whole-exome sequencing), were unremarkable. Brain MRI showed periventricular white matter hyperintensities (Fig. B).
test_results: The patient demonstrated a de novo 320-kb deletion in the 9q34.3 region (chr9:140721998–141,041,998) encompassing the EHMT1 gene.

case_report: A 22-year-old male patient reported experiencing facial redness and itching for two months. Over time, he developed multiple red patches on his face, accompanied by mild itching. The patient had previously visited another hospital, where a fungal microscopy examination was performed and found to be negative. He received various treatments, including moisturizing and anti-itch capsules, ebastine tablets, dichlorphenamide suspension, multiple injections of compound betamethasone sodium phosphate, and topical applications of dermadex cream, terbinafine cream, and hydrocortisone cream. Despite these treatments, the facial skin lesions persisted. Upon presenting to our hospital, further evaluation was conducted.
test_results: Pathological examination of the skin lesions demonstrated excessive keratinization, patchy mixed inflammatory cell infiltration in the superficial dermis, dense infiltration of lymphocytes, and numerous eosinophils around some hair follicles and sebaceous glands, with partial destruction of structures. Direct immunofluorescence and azan staining yielded negative results. Dermoscopic examination showed unclear boundaries of the lesion, irregular patches or clusters of red blood vessels on the dark red base, a few white scales on top, and follicular keratosis. The RCM examination of the facial area revealed hyperkeratosis and an abundant inflammatory infiltrate in the superficial dermis, composed of numerous sparse hyper-reflective cells. Furthermore, a hyper-reflective inflammatory infiltrate was observed around specific hair follicles and sebaceous glands. Laboratory and auxiliary examinations showed negative results for syphilis antibody, HIV antibody, antinuclear antibody, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody. The patient’s white blood cell count was 11.6 × 10^9/L, with an absolute neutrophil count of 7.81 × 10^9/L and an absolute monocyte count of 0.61 × 10^9/L. Liver and kidney function tests were found to be within the normal range.

case_report: A 45-year-old male patient was referred for examination of whitish lesions in the mouth. The patient reported that these oral lesions, along with thickened nails and callosities on the palms and soles, had been present since the age of 10. These conditions appeared spontaneously and had gradually worsened over time. The soles were particularly affected, causing discomfort and pain while walking. Excessive sweating of the soles and palms was also noted. The whitish plaques in the mouth were asymptomatic. The patient was born to non-consanguineous parents, and his dental and medical histories were non-contributory. Family history indicated that his father, brother, and son had similar conditions but declined clinical examination. The patient reported no tissue-abusing or parafunctional habits. General examination showed that the patient was moderately built and nourished for his age, with an altered gait. The nails were extremely hard, thickened, opaque brown, lusterless, and the free edges were raised by thick horny masses of subungual keratosis. Palmoplantar keratosis was more pronounced on pressure areas and elbows. All vital signs were within normal limits. Extraoral examination revealed no abnormalities. Solitary right and left submandibular lymph nodes were palpable, 1 cm × 1 cm, mobile, and firm. Intraoral examination showed a full complement of teeth. The labial mucosa, ventral surface of the tongue, floor of the mouth, vestibular mucosa, and oropharynx revealed no abnormalities. Leukokeratosis, characterized by diffuse whitish, non-tender, and non-scrapable plaque-like lesions, was present on both right and left buccal mucosae, the left retromolar region, the dorsal aspect of the tongue, the hard and soft palate, and the gingivae. Bilateral angular cheilosis was also observed. Routine investigations, including a complete hemogram, urine analysis, and fasting blood sugar, were within normal limits. Potassium hydroxide examination of nail clippings and fungal culture of the nails were negative. A biopsy from a palmar lesion indicated palmoplantar keratoderma.
test_results: Histopathological features were suggestive of oral leukokeratosis.

case_report: A 10-year-old male exhibited nystagmus and bilateral subcapsular cataracts. Additional findings included aniridia and macular hypoplasia. The best-corrected visual acuity measured 0.1 in the right eye and 0.15 in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was recorded at 13.3 mmHg in the right eye and 14.2 mmHg in the left eye. Axial length was 15.55 mm in the right eye and 15.42 mm in the left eye. Systemic examinations revealed hypospadias, with no other abnormalities detected.
test_results: A CNV analysis based on WES found a deletion of Chr11:31784908–33773171.

case_report: A 3-year-old boy was brought in with abdominal pain and a progressively enlarging bulge in the right side of his abdomen, first observed by his mother seven days prior on February 12, 2009. Biochemical tests showed no significant abnormalities. Serum levels of AFP, CA19-9, CA125, and CEA were within normal ranges.
test_results: A physical exam revealed a mildly tender mass in the right hypochondrium extending to the epigastrium; however, two lesions were found after a dynamic computed tomography. The primary lesion (8.5 × 4.3 cm) was located in the head of the pancreas and partly herniated into the abdominal wall. While the secondary lesion (1.8 × 2.1 cm) was in the left abdomen near the spleen and the tail of pancreas, and well demarcated from the surrounding structures, and no calcifications were evident within them. They all showed well-defined margins and inhomogeneous attenuation due to the presence of cystic and solid areas, in the venous phase and the delayed phase, a continuous enhancement was observed with a parenchyma density that was higher than that of the arterial phase. In addition, a large and distorted vascular shadow inside of the tumors in the arterial phase in the primary lesion. There was no radiological evidence of nodal or distant metastases; however, there was a local infiltration of the adjacent abdominal muscle that required a laparotomy. Surgery revealed the primary lesion was firmly adhered to the adjacent omental and abdominal muscle; in addition, a local infiltration of the liver and stomach were also noted. The head of the pancreas was compressed and could be separated from the tumor due to well-defined margins. The bile duct, portal vein, and the inferior vena cava were also compressed but patent. The gross specimen showed a resected mass measuring 8 × 4 × 4 cm that was well circumscribed and solid with areas of necrosis and hemorrhaging. No calcifications were evident within the mass. The secondary lesion was also adhered to the adjacent omentum and spleen; however, it was well demarcated from the surrounding structures with no evidence of originating from the pancreas. A histopathological analysis revealed a resected mass measuring 3 × 4 × 3 cm, which was well encapsulated by omentum with no calcifications within the mass. The surgical resection was difficult due to the extensive nature of the tumor, but the two lesions were completely resected without the pancreas being damaged.

case_report: A four-month-old male was transferred to Sheba Medical Center for evaluation due to poor growth, multiple fractures, intermittent diarrhea, and distinct physical features. The patient was born to an Arab-Muslim couple who were double first-degree cousins. During the third trimester of pregnancy, poor growth was observed. He was delivered via cesarean section at term with a birth weight of 1.7 kg, classified as small for gestational age, and was hospitalized for two weeks due to clavicle and arm fractures, despite an uneventful labor. At three months old, he was readmitted for pneumonia and was found to have multiple fractures and low albumin levels. Upon physical examination at four months old, the patient appeared cachectic and edematous, with a weight of 3.9 kg (−4.6 Z score) and a head circumference of 32.5 cm (−6.3 Z score). Dysmorphic features included epicanthal folds, hyperpigmentation over the metacarpophalangeal joints in both hands, over both medial malleoli, and lower limb contractures. The patient was extremely irritable and sensitive to touch. Blood tests revealed a normal complete blood count, low albumin levels (2.0 g/dL, normal range 3.5–5.0 g/dL), and normal electrolytes and lipid panel. Urine analysis showed no proteinuria, while stool alpha-1-anti-trypsin was elevated (90 mg/dL; normal <20mg/dL).
test_results: A skeletal X-ray demonstrated multiple fractures originating at different ages and osteopenia. An abdominal X-ray showed markedly distended bowels. An esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) showed thickened duodenal folds with small white papules. Haematoxylin and eosin (H & E) stains demonstrated blunting of villi and edema of the lamina propria, suggestive of intestinal lymphangiectasia. D2-40 stain for lymphatic vessels confirmed the presence of intestinal lymphangiectasia. A skin biopsy demonstrated dermal fibrosis, increased number of fibroblasts and hyalinization of the collagen.
diagnosis: Hyaline Fibromatosis Syndrome with Protein Losing Enteropathy

case_report: A 6-month-old male infant, previously in good health, was admitted due to jaundice, dark-colored urine, and reduced oral intake. He had a history of ten days of upper respiratory tract infection without fever, for which he was treated with clarithromycin and dexamethasone syrup for cough relief. There is no family history of blood disorders. Physical examination revealed significant pallor and yellowing of the sclera, with no enlargement of the liver or spleen and no abnormal lymph nodes. His blood pressure was normal, heart rate was 150 beats per minute (slightly elevated for his age), and he exhibited no rapid breathing.
test_results: Investigations revealed, on complete blood count (CBC), severe anemia with hemoglobin 4.5 g/dL (11–13 g/dL), MCV 120 fl (70–86 fl), platelets 80,000/mm3 (150,000–450,000/mm3) and high reticulocyte percentage (65%)(normal value < 1%). White count and differential were normal. The peripheral blood smear showed anisopoikilocytosis, macrocytosis, no hypochromia, polychromatophilia, numerous nucleated red blood cells, few spherocytes were present and schistocytes were absent. His biochemical studies showed increased indirect bilirubin (1.18 mg/dL) (normal value < 1mg/dL), decreased haptoglobin (0.02 g/L) (0.2–0.03 g/L), increased LDH (1323 U/L) (normal value < 280U/L), normal creatinine (0.23 mg/dL) (normal value < 1 mg/dL), normal folate and vitamin B12 levels. The immunohematological studies showed positive direct antiglobulin testing (DAT) using polyspecific antiglobulins (anti-IgG and anti-C3d) and positive DAT using the specific anti-IgG monoclonal antiglobulin. The indirect antiglobulin testing (IAT) was also positive and all cross matched blood units were incompatible. The titer of the autoantibody was very high (>1/40,960) with a strength of +4 and did not decrease until four months after the event. Immunoglobulins (IgG, IgM, and IgA) quantitation was normal. Antinuclear antibodies profile and rheumatic factor were also negative. Viral serology (Epstein-Barr virus, human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis B and C viruses, adenoviruses.) was all normal except for CMV, which was positive—IgM titer was very high (nine times the upper limit) and the IgG titer was slightly above the upper limit. CMV PCR was also positive.
diagnosis: Infantile Cytomegalovirus-Associated Severe Warm Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia
Orpha_name: Severe disseminated cytomegalovirus infection in immunocompetent patients

case_report: A 29-year-old male with Fitzpatrick Skin Type V and no significant past medical history presented with a benign nevus on the foot. During the examination, hyperpigmentation was noted on the hands and feet. Physical examination revealed stellate hyperpigmented atrophic macules. The patient reported these lesions had been present since childhood, initially appearing on the hands and feet and remaining stable since then. Family history indicated a sister with similar skin findings on the hands. The patient also reported similar lesions on his genitals and denied any hypopigmentation, itching, pain, or bleeding from the lesions. Cutaneous examination showed hyperpigmented lesions with palmar pitting and breaks in the dermatoglyphs, bilateral clinodactyly of the 5th fingers, and inferior gingival hyperplasia with teeth crowding, characterized by thickened gum tissue and limited space for teeth growth.
test_results: X-ray imaging of the hands displayed mild congenital foreshortening of the fifth finger middle phalanges bilaterally with the remodeling of the distal heads having slight shallow and radially oriented surface articulation of the head of the middle phalanges causing slight radial angulation of the distal phalanges bilaterally. Skin biopsy of the dorsal hand revealed a focus of epidermal atrophy with elongation of the rete ridges and basilar hyperpigmentation.

case_report: An 18-year-old Asian male reported a decline in vision in both eyes over the past 6 years. His medical history included delayed puberty. At age 16, he experienced worsening balance and difficulty walking. At age 12, he first noticed a gradual loss of vision and sensitivity to light in both eyes. His best-corrected visual acuity was 20/200 in both eyes. There was no drooping of the eyelids, and eye movements were complete with vertical and horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus. The anterior segment examination was unremarkable. Ophthalmoscopy revealed extensive atrophic changes in the retinal pigment epithelium and choriocapillaris in the posterior pole and midperiphery of both eyes, with visible choroidal vessels in some areas. Pigment clumps were observed without a bone spicule pattern. The retinal vessels and optic disc appeared normal. An Ishihara test showed significant color discrimination issues. Perimetry indicated a ring scotoma from 10 to 60 degrees from the fixation points in both eyes. On general examination, the patient was 176 cm tall and weighed 64 kg. He exhibited normal male secondary sex characteristics and had normal intelligence. His gait was wide-based and ataxic, and Romberg's sign was absent. Laboratory tests, including plasma and urine amino acids, phytanic acid, and lipid plasma levels, were normal. There was no family history of similar conditions.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed diffuse atrophy of the cerebellar hemispheres. Fluorescein angiography showed hypofluorescence with large, visible choroidal vessels in areas showing retinal pigment epithelial and choriocapillaris atrophy. Indocyanine green angiography showed normal fluorescence of the retinal arteries and ground-glass fluorescence of the choriocapillaris. Optical coherence tomography showed retinal thinning, blunting of the foveal pit, and disappearance of the outer nuclear layer. The foveal center measured 204 µm in the right eye and 174 µm in the left. An electroretinographic examination showed subnormal photopic and scotopic responses bilaterally. The photopic responses to both high-intensity white flash and 30-Hz flicker stimuli showed 20 and 40% reductions from the mean b-wave amplitude, respectively. The dark-adapted scotopic responses to high- and low-intensity flash stimuli showed prolonged implicit times. Electroretinographic oscillatory potentials were absent. Hormone studies were consistent with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

case_report: A 36-year-old male presented with jaundice and abdominal pain for 5 days. The patient experienced cold-like symptoms 5 days prior to hospital admission, followed by severe jaundice and persistent, non-radiating pain in the middle abdomen. Additional symptoms included nausea, chest tightness, muscle weakness, and loss of appetite. On the second day of hospitalization, the patient experienced significant upper abdominal pain with rebound tenderness. Physical examination revealed no palpable superficial lymph nodes. The abdomen was soft with mild tenderness in the upper region, but no rebound tenderness. The liver was palpable below the right costal margin, while the spleen was not palpable. Laboratory results showed: (1) White blood cells 4.60 × 10^9/L (neutrophils 84.7%, lymphocytes 10.3%, no abnormal cells detected), red blood cells 3.87 × 10^12/L, platelets 64 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 140 g/L; (2) Total bilirubin 340.5 µmol/L, direct bilirubin 281.0 µmol/L, aspartate aminotransferase 1163 U/L, glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase 1765 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase 1253 IU/L, total bile acid 109.4 µmol/L; (3) Prothrombin time 27.2 s, activated partial thromboplastin time 43.8 s, fibrinogen 1.36 g/L, thrombin time 26.4 s. CT scans indicated hepatosplenomegaly, splenic parenchymal and perisplenic hemorrhage with the largest hematoma measuring 9.5 cm × 4.3 cm, ascites, and enlarged peritoneal lymph nodes. Splenic rupture was identified via CT scans. An immediate splenectomy was performed, and a liver biopsy was conducted. Macroscopically, a liver tissue sample measuring 1.5 cm × 0.8 cm × 0.6 cm was grey-brown with a smooth capsule. The spleen, measuring 19.0 cm × 12.5 cm × 7.0 cm and weighing 870.0 grams, was completely removed. The splenic hilum capsule was absent, with numerous blood clots observed. A large subcapsular hematoma was noted upon slicing the spleen. Microscopically, the liver's normal structure was partially damaged, with many monomorphic medium-sized cells infiltrating portal areas and sinusoids, displaying thin to moderate pale or amphophilic cytoplasm, irregular nuclei, slightly condensed chromatin, and inconspicuous nucleoli. Mitotic figures and apoptosis were prominent. Spleen sections showed red pulp expansion with relative white pulp depletion. Neoplastic cells were present in the red pulp cords and sinuses, as well as around the splenic arteriolar sheath. The morphology and size of these cells were similar to those infiltrating the liver. Necrosis and blood vessel infiltration were also observed in the spleen.
test_results: Immunohistochemically, the neoplastic cells were CD3ε+, CD56+, CD16+, CD43+, Granzyme B+, TIA-1+, CD20-, CD2-, CD5-, CD7-, CD4-, CD8- and CD123-. The proliferation index was approximately 90%, assessed by Ki-67 staining and the result of EBER-ISH showed positive for most of the abnormal cells. No obvious band of cloned TCR-γ gene rearrangement was detected by the Polymerase Chain Reaction heteroduplex analysis (PCR-HA) and polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE).

case_report: A 73-year-old male with a history of chronic kidney disease stage II, benign prostatic hypertrophy, and dyslipidemia was referred to the hematology clinic. The patient had a SARS-CoV-2 infection in November 2020, which initially did not require hospitalization. Two weeks later, he was hospitalized for worsening shortness of breath and hypoxia. Laboratory results showed no anemia or thrombocytopenia, a normal aPTT of 32 seconds (normal range 24-40 seconds), and an elevated D-dimer of 2.12 µg/mL (normal range <0.5 µg/mL). A bilateral lower extremity ultrasound was negative for deep vein thrombosis (DVT). A computed tomography angiogram (CTA) of the lungs revealed scattered bilateral lower lobes lobar and segmental pulmonary emboli. The patient was started on a heparin drip, later transitioning to apixaban, and was discharged two days later. Further tests showed negative lupus anticoagulant and antiphospholipid assays. At discharge, his medications included vitamins, aspirin, apixaban, and tamsulosin. Initially, he reported no side effects from anticoagulant use. Four months later, he presented to the emergency room with a large spontaneous ecchymosis on the left thigh. Evaluation showed minimal swelling of the left lower extremity, and a duplex ultrasound found no evidence of DVT. He was discharged with a referral to the hematology clinic. At the clinic, he was hemodynamically stable with partial resolution of the left thigh ecchymosis, a new large ecchymosis on the left arm, bruises on his abdomen and lower back, and a spontaneous right conjunctival hemorrhage. He was advised to stop taking aspirin and apixaban. Laboratory studies showed an INR of 1.0 and an aPTT of 105 seconds. A CTA scan of the lungs was negative for pulmonary embolism. On follow-up, he had a new right lower extremity ecchymosis. Further testing showed a negative autoimmune panel, a negative hepatitis panel, and a negative CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Labs showed normal factors IX and XI activity and normal von Willebrand factor antigen. A mixing study did not correct the elevated aPTT, indicating the presence of an inhibitor.
test_results: Factor VIII activity of <1% (normal range 56-141) and Bethesda assay of 70.4 Bethesda units (BU).

case_report: A 60-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a sub-acute onset of dizziness and near-fainting episodes. Initial examination showed significant bradycardia and a blood pressure reading of 167/92 mmHg. Auscultation revealed a pan-systolic murmur. There were no signs of fluid accumulation in the lungs or extremities. A twelve-lead electrocardiogram indicated complete heart block with a narrow QRS escape rhythm at 30 beats per minute. Focused bedside echocardiography showed preserved biventricular systolic function without regional wall motion abnormalities and mild-to-moderate mitral regurgitation. Blood tests, including full blood count, urea and electrolytes, bone profile, and thyroid function tests, were within normal limits. High-sensitivity Troponin-I was 6.4 ng/L (reference range <19.8), and C-reactive protein was 2 mg/L (reference range 0–10). The patient received an urgent dual-chamber pacemaker implantation. The right atrial lead was secured to the right atrial appendage, and the right ventricular lead was positioned at the mid-apical septum. The device was set to DDD mode with a basic rate of 60 beats per minute.
test_results: Detailed transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) performed 1 day post-pacing revealed normal LV volumes, mild septal dyssynchrony consistent with RV pacing, and LV ejection fraction (LVEF) of 63%. There was minor focal posterior mitral annular calcification with slight doming and thickening of the anterior MV leaflet and a mildly restricted posterior leaflet. The mean MV gradient was 1 mmHg. Colour flow imaging revealed a central jet of moderate MR with an effective regurgitant orifice area of 0.31 cm2. The early-diastolic mitral annular diameter was 3.0 cm, and the left atrium was moderately dilated. RV size and function were normal. Overall right heart parameters suggested a low probability of pulmonary hypertension.

case_report: A 17-year-old male presented with a neck mass and mild neck pain, which had started a month prior and progressively worsened. The patient also experienced palpitations and sweating. Physical examination revealed a neck mass on the left side of the thyroid, while the right lobe appeared normal. The pulse rate was recorded at 100 beats per minute, and a weak tremor was noted. Neck ultrasound identified a heterogeneous solid mass in the left thyroid lobe, causing displacement of neck vessels and the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Multiple lymphadenopathies were observed in the anterior triangle on the same side, with the largest measuring 12 mm in diameter. Thyroid function tests indicated thyrotoxicosis (T4 = 18.3, T3 = 265, TSH < 0.1). Anti-TPO was negative, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was mildly elevated at 38. Other biochemical tests, including calcium, phosphorus, and complete blood count (CBC), were within normal limits. Thyroid radioisotope imaging with TC99 showed decreased and nonhomogeneous uptake.
test_results: Thyroid biopsy showed an inflammatory process. Sonoguided biopsy showed infiltration of mononuclear cells and fibrosis. In neck MRI, a hypodense thyroid mass and involvement of surrounding soft tissue and left SCM muscle was found. Open biopsy showed a white-to-gray mass with involvement of surrounding tissue and muscles. Pathology exam showed infiltration of thyroid parenchyma by mononuclear cells, fibrosis, destruction, and involvement of SCM muscle. Thyroid tissue was not seen.

case_report: A 41-year-old Muslim man from South Africa presented with widespread patchy skin discoloration. He was born to parents who are second-degree relatives. He reported the onset of gradually increasing widespread darkening of the skin starting from his trunk, followed by patchy lightening and loss of skin color from the age of 6 years, affecting his entire body. Recently, he observed a few light-colored spots on his forehead and balding scalp. Skin examination showed widespread net-like dark pigmentation covering the entire body, sparing the palms, soles, backs of hands, feet, face, and a small area on the chest which retained his original skin color. The light-colored spots were well-defined, varied in size from 4 mm to about 2 cm in diameter. Scattered dark, rough papules were noted on the extremities and proximal inner arms near the armpits, which had been present for the past 4 years. All skin changes were asymptomatic with no blistering, ulceration, thinning, mixed skin changes, scaling, or oozing. Palms, soles, mucous membranes, hair, and nails appeared normal. The patient reported no sensitivity to sunlight, systemic issues, inflammatory skin conditions, or growth delays.
test_results: A 3-mm punch biopsy revealed amorphous pink masses of amyloid in the papillary dermis.

case_report: A 14-year-old girl with fair skin and dark hair presented with shiny, beaded, and easily breakable hair since the age of four. The hair condition was primarily a cosmetic concern for the patient and her family. There was no history of trauma, shedding, or hair loss. The patient's parents were not related by blood. The mother had experienced similar hair characteristics during her childhood and adolescence, which improved with age. Other family members were not available for examination. The axillary and pubic hair appeared normal. During the examination, a light pull test resulted in a few broken hairs.
test_results: Transmitted light microscopy revealed periodic dark bands in the hair shaft, which diminished toward to the end of hair. Under light microscopy, the hair samples within normal medium were then embedded in 10% aqueous potassium hydroxide. The dark bands disappeared after 6 minutes and homogeneous color along hair shaft was achieved. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) of the hair samples demonstrated various sizes of multiple cavities within cuticular and cortical cells and indentations adjacent to these cavities. Scanning electron microscopic examination (SEM) provided observations of various severe cuticular damages corresponding to the localizations of cavities.
diagnosis: Pili annulati with fragility and weathered structure

case_report: The child was enrolled in the Baby Clinic of Araçatuba Dental School program for preventive dental care at 11 months of age, and this clinical case report is being presented when the child is 4 years old. The child's mother mentioned during the anamnesis procedure that her child had been undergoing regular medical check-ups since birth. The pregnancy was planned by the parents, and the mother received prenatal care.
test_results: An ultrasound examination performed during the fifth week of gestation showed a gastrointestinal malformation of the fetus. A subsequent morphologic ultrasound examination revealed the following findings: gastrointestinal abnormality, enlarged kidneys, and a low amount of amniotic liquid.

case_report: An 8-year-old boy was admitted in July 2015 with sudden onset of slurred speech and limb weakness lasting for one day. His family history included relatives with claw feet. His previous medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Upon admission, physical examination showed normal body temperature and blood pressure, lethargy, slurred speech, and a positive bilateral Babinski sign. Lumbar puncture revealed increased cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure of 200 mm H2O with normal white blood cell count and protein levels. Serum tests were positive for Anti-Mycoplasma pneumoniae immunoglobulin M (IgM) and negative for various other pathogens. Brain MRI indicated symmetrical abnormal signal intensity in the paraventricular white matter and the splenium of the corpus callosum. He received intravenous mannitol and ribavirin and fully recovered, being discharged one week later. In July 2018, he was readmitted with limb weakness, slurred speech, and facial asymmetry for one day. Physical examination showed blood pressure of 116/82 mmHg, shortness of breath, left hypophysis, shallow nasolabial sulcus on the left side, facial asymmetry, decreased muscle strength (4/5) in all limbs, and a probable positive Babinski sign. Laboratory tests showed normal white blood cell count, liver, kidney, and coagulation function parameters, as well as normal blood electrolytes, hemoglobin, C-reactive protein, thyroid hormone, and myocardial enzyme levels. Blood gas analysis, routine CSF analysis, CSF protein level, CSF culture, and sputum smear were unremarkable. Echocardiography, intracranial vascular ultrasonography, brain and chest CT, electroencephalography, and cervical and thoracic spine MRI showed no significant abnormalities. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI revealed abnormal signals in the bilateral centrum semiovale and corona radiata. Platelet count was slightly elevated at 323 × 10^9/L. He was treated with antiviral and symptomatic therapies and fully recovered. In April 2021, he was admitted again with a one-day history of perioral numbness. Physical examination showed blood pressure of 126/79 mmHg, left peripheral facial paralysis, tongue deviation to the left, bilateral frontal and maxillary sinus tenderness, mild atrophy of the left thenar muscle, bilateral claw foot, decreased muscle strength in foot dorsiflexion (4/5), and absence of tendon reflexes. Brain CT suggested low-density areas in the corpus callosum. MRI showed more pronounced abnormal signals in the bilateral centrum semiovale, corona radiata, and corpus callosum compared to previous scans. Brain magnetic resonance angiography was unremarkable. Needle electromyography and nerve conduction velocity studies indicated motor and sensory nerve demyelination with axonal damage, primarily in the distal peripheral nerves. CSF cell count was normal, but protein levels were elevated (480 mg/L, reference range: < 450 mg/L). CSF antibodies for autoimmune encephalitis were negative. He was treated with antibiotics, immunotherapy (IV dexamethasone), oral vitamins B1 and B12, and fluid replacement, leading to symptom resolution. Follow-up MRI three months post-discharge showed improvement in abnormal signal intensity in the bilateral basal ganglia, paraventricular white matter, and corpus callosum. Brain perfusion imaging was normal.
test_results: Whole exon sequencing showed a heterozygous mutation in the alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 (AARS1) gene [c.2093C > T(p.Ser698Phe)].

case_report: A 28-year-old female presented with short stature, recurrent abdominal pain, and neck pain since her teenage years. She has not experienced menarche. There is no family history of similar conditions. Physical examination showed facial asymmetry, a short neck, a high arched palate, scoliosis, and a height of 146 cm. Her secondary sexual characteristics were well developed, classified as Tanner stage A2P5 B5. Other examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including haemogram, biochemical, and hormonal analyses, were within normal limits.
test_results: X-ray spine showed a fusion of C2–C3, C4–C5–C6 vertebrae, hemivertebrae, scoliosis of thoracic vertebrae and cervical rib. Ultrasound of the abdomen showed bilateral normal gonads, non-visualization of uterus and fallopian tubes; both kidneys (right—9.9 × 3.46 cm, left—3.7 × 1.74 cm) were ectopic lying in the paralumbar region. The intravenous pyelogram showed non-functional left kidney.

case_report: Patient 3 was a 3-day-old male, the first child of nonconsanguineous parents. He was delivered at full term via normal spontaneous vaginal delivery. The patient was admitted to the hospital due to a temporary convulsion. Neurological examination revealed no apparent abnormalities, and muscle tone was within normal limits. There was no significant family history or reported exposure to infectious agents. Blood-gas analysis showed metabolic acidosis along with respiratory alkalosis.
test_results: Elevated pyrimidines and metabolites in urine were detected.

case_report: A 13-month-old male presented with short stature. He was born at 40 weeks gestation with a birth height of 46 cm (−2.04 SDS) and a birth weight of 3040 g (−0.55 SDS) to healthy, nonconsanguineous Korean parents. He has a younger male sibling of normal height. At the time of the visit, his height was 61.4 cm (−6.47 SDS) and weight was 6.1 kg (−3.35 SDS). The mid-parental height was 176 cm (paternal height: 180 cm, maternal height: 159 cm). He had no history of recurrent infections or congenital megacolon. Physical examination revealed no joint hypermobility, facial anomalies, hypodontia, hypotrichosis, or hepatosplenomegaly. A single Mongolian spot was noted on the posterior lower trunk. He exhibited rhizomelic short stature, brachydactyly, bowing of the tibia, genu varum, short feet, and kyphosis. Developmental milestones were normal. Radiographic findings included subtle cupping and widening at the metaphysis of both metacarpal bones, phalanges, and ulnae, bilateral acetabulum dysplasia, femur shortening (rhizomelia), and brachy-phalanges. Chest X-ray showed a normal thymus. Complete blood count was normal except for a low neutrophil ratio of 35.0% (RR: 41.5%–73.5%) and a high lymphocyte ratio of 54.0% (RR: 19.9%–49.2%). Electrolytes, renal function, liver enzymes, and alkaline phosphatase were within normal ranges. Thyroid and adrenal function tests, as well as insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) levels, were normal. Sella MRI and 2D echocardiography were also normal. At 7 years and 4 months, he returned with progressive delayed growth, measuring 87 cm in height (−7.21 SDS) and weighing 13.5 kg (−2.65 SDS).
test_results: The WES results revealed 2 variants in the RMRP gene (NR 003051.3:n.-22-3dup and NR 003051.3:n.196C > T). The patient’s father and male sibling have also been confirmed to carry the NR 003051.3:n.-22 -3dup, a known pathogenic variant, while the patient’s mother carries the NR 003051.3:n.196C > T, a known pathogenic variant. Consequently, these 2 variants were confirmed to be compound heterozygous.
diagnosis: Metaphyseal Dysplasia with Hypotrichosis and Recurrent Infections

case_report: A 56-year-old Caucasian male with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease presented with an 8-month history of bilateral upper extremity action tremor. The patient reported gait instability, three falls in the past year, urinary retention and urgency, and difficulty with navigation while driving. Physical examination showed mild left-sided dysmetria, brisk reflexes throughout, and a bilateral upgoing plantar response. Brain MRI revealed periventricular white matter hyperintensities and a left frontal juxtacortical hyperintensity, with no abnormalities in the brainstem. Cervical spine MRI showed high-grade stenosis at C5-C6 and a hyperintensity at C4. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed 3 white blood cells per mm3, 0 red blood cells per mm3, protein level of 56 mg/dL, glucose level of 65 mg/dL, and more than 5 oligoclonal bands (OCBs) restricted to CSF. The IgG index was elevated at 0.83, but the IgG synthesis rate was normal at 7.6 mg/d. A follow-up MRI of the brain and cervical spine 6 months later showed no change in lesions and no new gadolinium-enhancing lesions. Additional lab tests for vitamin B12, vitamin B1, vitamin E, copper, zinc, thyroid stimulating hormone, hepatitis B, ANA, ANCA, and tissue transglutaminase were normal or negative. A paraneoplastic panel from serum and CSF, including amphiphysin, ANNA-1, CASPR2, CRMP5, DPPX, Gad65, IgLON5, LGI1, and NMDA, was negative. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no malignancy. The patient was treated with high-dose steroids (1,200 mg prednisone daily for 5 days), but his condition continued to worsen with increased ataxia and more frequent falls. A second lumbar puncture performed 3 months later identified 17 OCBs restricted to CSF. A second autoimmune panel from serum and CSF was negative. The patient was discharged to a rehabilitation facility without improvement. Upon return to the clinic, he exhibited more pronounced ataxia and new symptoms suggestive of rapid eye movement behavior disorder (RBD). He was referred to the movement disorder clinic for further evaluation. Screening vitals showed a drop in systolic blood pressure of 32 mmHg, although he denied symptomatic orthostasis.
test_results: 123I-Ioflupane single photon emission tomography (SPECT) imaging revealed reduced tracer uptake over the right putamen, indicative of nigrostriatal degeneration. Imaging of cardiac innervation with SPECT and [123I]metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) demonstrated preserved sympathetic postganglionic neurons.

case_report: An 11-year-old male patient was referred to the ENT department on 10 July 2019, at the age of 2, for evaluation of hearing issues. He was born to healthy, non-consanguineous parents after a normal pregnancy at 36 weeks of gestation, with a birth weight of 3200 g and an Apgar score of 9, and had a good postnatal adaptation. The patient had a history of psychomotor regression and dystonic movements, and a brain MRI revealed diffuse cerebral atrophy. A psychomotor evaluation at the age of 2 years indicated a global developmental delay with a mental age of approximately 7 months: 12 months for receptive language, 6 months for expressive language, 5 months for motor development, and 3 months for affective behavior. For the assessment of profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, several tests were conducted: Distortion Product Acoustic Otoemissions (no distortion product between 750—8000 Hz), Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry (evoked auditory response absent bilaterally at maximum intensity of 90 dB nHL), Auditory Steady State Response Tests (no evoked auditory response at 100 dB nHL on all tested frequencies—500, 1000, 2000, and 4000 Hz), and a Tympanogram (normal middle ear pressure and mobility, acoustic reflexes present bilaterally only at 46 Hz and 100 dB). Cochlear implantation was performed in 2014 (at the age of 3 years and 10 months) with good functional results.
test_results: WES identified a homozygous variant in the SUCLG1 gene.
diagnosis: autosomal recessive mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome type 9
Orpha_name: Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome, myopathic form

case_report: A four-year-old New Zealand European/Māori girl was admitted to the hospital after experiencing five days of fatigue, neck and abdominal pain, vomiting, and headache. On examination, her Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score was 15, and she exhibited signs of meningism without any focal neurological deficits. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) parameters were within normal limits, though the opening pressure was not recorded. Electrolytes and random glucose levels were normal. Her symptoms gradually improved, and she was discharged after five days. However, she returned the next day with vomiting, confusion, and double vision. The patient was drowsy but responsive to commands, afebrile, and persistently tachycardic, with normal blood pressure. Cranial nerve examination revealed a right abducens nerve palsy and papilloedema. Her visual fields were intact, and the rest of her neurological examination was normal. A glucose level of 1.9 mmol/L was noted, with an elevated beta-hydroxybutyrate level of 6.1 mmol/L. A full hypoglycaemia screen identified hypocortisolaemia < 30 nmol/L. An ACTH level was < 1 pmol/L. Growth hormone/IGF-1 and thyroid hormone levels were normal. Neuroimaging (CT head and MR brain) showed features consistent with pseudotumour cerebri. There was no evidence of dural or cavernous sinus thrombosis, Chiari malformation, or a space-occupying lesion. Her CSF opening pressure was elevated at 30-40 cmH2O, which was reduced to 20 cmH2O during the procedure. A short Synacthen test performed two days later showed a post-Synacthen cortisol of 257 nmol/L. A repeat ACTH level was < 1 pmol/L. Central ACTH suppression due to prolonged exogenous glucocorticoid administration was excluded. The patient was started on acetazolamide 12.5 mg/kg/dose BD and maintenance steroid replacement (hydrocortisone 10 mg/m2/day cortisol equivalence). Her symptoms and right abducens nerve palsy improved. A short Synacthen test was repeated one month later, after the hydrocortisone had been ceased for two weeks, and showed a pre-Synacthen cortisol of 5 nmol/L rising to a peak of 14 nmol/L. Acetazolamide was discontinued two months later, at least two weeks after the patient’s papilloedema had resolved. However, the patient returned with double vision, subtle recurrence of her right abducens palsy, and mild papilloedema one month later. A repeat MR brain was normal, and opening pressure under sedation was 26 cmH2O. Due to her symptoms, she was recommenced on low-dose acetazolamide. Further work-up included serum immunoglobulins, revealing panhypogammaglobinaemia (IgG 1.9 g/L, IgA 0.11 g/L, IgM 0.29 g/L). Specific questioning revealed a history of frequent mild upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs) between one and three years of age, and one episode of Campylobacter jejuni gastroenteritis. There was no other history or evidence of heightened infection susceptibility or autoimmunity. Further immune evaluation showed significant switched memory B cell lymphopenia (< 1.0%), with preserved T, B, and NK cell proportions, and absent antibody responses to toxoid and conjugate vaccines, indicating impaired B cell differentiation and function.
test_results: Next-generation-sequencing gene panel testing confirmed the presence of a nonsense mutation in the NFKB2 gene (NM_001077494.3 c.2557C > T, p.Arg853*).

case_report: A 42-year-old male with a history of hepatic cirrhosis due to chronic hepatitis B infection presented with multiple hypopigmented patches on his limbs for one year and on his trunk and back for six months. The patches on the limbs were associated with tingling and numbness. He also reported generalized weakness for six months and intermittent fever for one month. He denied abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, weight loss, joint pain, yellowish discoloration of skin or sclera, or bleeding. His medical history included hepatitis B infection diagnosed and treated four years ago with oral tenofovir. Physical examination confirmed multiple well-defined hypopigmented macules and patches on the chest, abdomen, back, and bilateral upper and lower limbs. There were also multiple well-defined hypopigmented plaques with raised borders on the back and bilateral upper and lower limbs, displaying an inverted saucer appearance, pseudopods, and satellite lesions. Neurological examination showed reduced sensation of pain and fine touch over the hypopigmented patches on the bilateral lower limbs. The left ulnar nerve, left infraorbital nerve, and left and right greater auricular nerves were thickened and non-tender to palpation. Deep tendon reflexes of the triceps, supinator, and lower limbs were reduced. Cardiovascular, pulmonary, and gastrointestinal examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory tests indicated hypoalbuminemia, elevated serum transaminases, and reactive hepatitis B surface antigen with a quantitative viral load PCR of 5256 IU/ml. Abdominal ultrasonography showed altered liver echotexture with surface irregularity, normal hepatic doppler, and splenomegaly with splenic vein enlargement. An esophagoduodenoscopy revealed grade III esophageal varices with mild portal hypertensive gastropathy. Nerve conduction studies indicated asymmetrical axonal peripheral neuropathy involving bilateral lower limbs (sensory > motor).
test_results: A split skin biopsy from one of the lesions over the right thigh revealed diffuse infiltration of foamy macrophages surrounded by lymphocytes and plasma cells with poorly defined granulomas infiltrating the blood vessels and sweat glands. Modified Ziehl Nielsen staining of the split skin smear revealed acid-fast bacilli (Grade 3).

case_report: A 59-year-old woman visited the endocrinology outpatient department for a routine diabetes mellitus follow-up after 6 months. She had been managing diabetes for the past 5 years with oral antidiabetic medications. Her primary concern was a non-itchy red rash on both legs that had appeared 10 days prior. She reported no other symptoms and had no significant medical history, surgical history, or allergies. On examination, her vital signs were normal. She weighed 70 kg, stood 160 cm tall, and had a body mass index of 27.3 kg/m2. General examination noted the presence of acanthosis nigricans. The anterior aspect of both legs, specifically over the shins, displayed a reddish-brown papular rash with erythematous spreading borders. The rash was tender, non-blanching, and had reddish flakes. There were no signs of atrophy or ulceration, and sensations over the lesions were intact. Systemic examination was unremarkable, with no evidence of diabetic retinopathy or neuropathy. Vibration perception thresholds (VPT) over both feet were 9/15 and 10/18, indicating no neuropathy. Her blood sugar levels were elevated: fasting at 250 mg/dl and postprandial at 320 mg/dl, with a glycated hemoglobin (HbA1C) of 9.8%. Other blood tests, as well as renal and hepatic parameters, were within normal limits. Urine microalbuminuria was measured at 25 mg/dl.
test_results: Biopsy of the lesions over leg revealed sandwich-like horizontal layers of necrobiotic collagen alternating with inflammatory cell infiltrate of lymphocytes, histiocytes, multinucleated giant cells and plasma cells. These changes involved the full thickness of the dermis sparing the subcutis.

case_report: A 16-year-old male from Guatemala presented with reduced central vision and sensitivity to light. Visual acuity testing showed Snellen BCVA at a distance of 20/200 in the right eye and 20/160 in the left eye, with a manifest refraction of +1.00 + 4.50×109 and – 0.25 + 4.25×069, respectively. The patient exhibited mild end-gaze nystagmus and was orthophoric. The anterior segment examination was normal. Fundus examination revealed bull’s eye maculopathy, perivascular and segmental pigment deposition in the inferior retina, and mild vascular attenuation. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) indicated loss of the ellipsoid zone in the fovea. Fundus autofluorescence (FAF) imaging showed a hypofluorescent area corresponding to regions of retinal atrophy and pigment deposition. Color vision testing using Farnsworth D15 revealed multiple axis errors. Goldmann visual fields demonstrated superior constriction and central loss of the I1e isopter, corresponding to the inferior retinal changes. Scotopic electroretinography (ERG) showed mildly reduced amplitudes and delayed implicit times, while photopic bright flash and flicker ERG were extinguished. Dental examination noted crowns on multiple teeth and a lack of enamel. No other systemic abnormalities were observed.
test_results: Molecular Vision Lab NGS Retinal Dystrophy SmartPanel v11 (281 genes) revealed a homozygous CNNM4 c.706C > T (p.Arg236Trp) variant with one copy inherited from each parent.

case_report: A 2.5-year-old male child, apparently healthy but underweight, with a body mass index (BMI) of 17.7 (12.2 pounds, 22.5 inches) presented to the pediatric developmental wellness clinic at The Children’s Hospital, Lahore, Pakistan, with the complaints of complete hearing loss since birth and aphasia. The orientation of the patient could not be assessed due to the aphasia, although he was alert. The patient was afebrile with a heart rate of 85 bpm, blood pressure of 110/85 mmHg, and respiratory rate of 18/min. Upon a physical examination, the patient had blue homochromatic irises with a normal visual response, coarse hair texture, pallor of nails, and a slightly broad high nasal root. Segmental depigmentation was seen affecting the forehead and left forearm. The patient's mother reported the presence of a white hair patch (poliosis) in the frontal hair distribution since birth, which diminished upon cutting the hair. A delay in achieving multiple milestones, including neck holding, crawling, sitting, and walking were also reported. The mother had an uneventful natal history with two healthy daughters without the presence of any similar symptoms in them. Past medical history included episodes of bilious vomiting, failure to thrive, and multiple bouts of severe constipation at the age of six months. On imaging, a diagnosis of Hirschsprung's disease was made and confirmed with a rectal biopsy. Later, an end-colostomy at the level of the descending colon was made. The patient had a positive family history of similar symptoms present in the father and paternal aunt but without the history of Hirschsprung’s disease and hearing deficits.
test_results: An auditory brainstem response showed a bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. A DNA sample from the boy was used as a template for a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to amplify exon 2 of gene SOX10. The resulting product was subsequently sequenced, employing standard methods on an ABI PRISM 377 DNA sequencer. This patient was found to have a novel truncating mutation of the SOX10 gene, on 22q13.

case_report: The patient is a 68-year-old male presenting with axonal and demyelinating polyneuropathy, sensorineural hearing loss, chronic lymphoedema, angiokeratoma corporis diffusum, and bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome. He manages his polyneuropathy with simple analgesia as needed. His parents are healthy and do not exhibit any notable phenotypical features. He is the fourth of five siblings; a deceased sister exhibited some similar features, but his brothers do not have any known conditions. Physical examination revealed coarse facial features and bilateral symmetrical massive lymphoedema. The skin displayed a thickened, nodular surface with brownish pigmentation. Multiple millimetre-sized reddish papules were observed on the abdomen, groin, and inner aspects of both arms, which dermatoscopy identified as red lacunae. Echocardiography indicated moderate cardiomegaly, while chest x-ray, EKG, and urine tests (including urine sediment) were within normal limits. The patient has blood group A. His intelligence quotient (IQ) is slightly below average, with a normal verbal IQ but slightly reduced performance IQ.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed angiokeratomas underlying superficial (upper dermis) vascular ectasia and epidermal hyperplasia (acanthosis and/or hyperkeratosis).

case_report: A 9-year-1-month-old girl visited the Genetic Endocrinology Clinic with concerns about intellectual development and short stature. Her height was 123 cm (-2 SD), corresponding to a height age of 7 years. She weighed 23 kg (-1.3 SD) with a body mass index of 15.2 (25th-50th percentile). Her father's height was 168 cm and her mother's height was 157 cm, giving her a familial target height of 156 cm (-0.85 SD). She was delivered via caesarean section post-term without asphyxia. At birth, she weighed 4.25 kg and measured 50 cm in length. Severe developmental delays were noted during her toddler years; she began walking independently at three years old and could speak a few simple words by five years old. She exhibited distinct facial features, including a coarse face, sparse hair, narrow forehead, ptosis, deep-set eyes, broad nasal tip, short nose, malformed teeth, and large ears with moderately sized earlobes. She had tapering fingers and bilaterally curved fifth fingers, flat feet, and fourth toes shorter than the fifth. Extensive hyperpigmentation was observed, particularly on the lower limbs. No secondary sexual characteristics were present; breast and pubic hair were at Tanner stage B1 and P1, respectively. Thyroid and liver function tests were normal, but she had a complete deficiency of growth hormone. Her stature was below the 3rd percentile, and her bone age was 7 years and 10 months. Recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) injections were started at 0.036 mg/kg/day, but treatment was stopped after three weeks due to edema in both lower extremities. Ultrasonography revealed fused kidneys at the lower end (horseshoe kidney). Brain MRI showed periventricular leukomalacia and hyaline compartment formation, with a thinner pituitary compared to peers, though no definitive measurement was taken. Her karyotype was 46,XX, and chromosomal microarray did not show pathogenic variants. Her mother showed no obvious symptoms based on family reports, though no formal evaluation was conducted. Clinical data were collected at Shanghai Children’s Medical Center in 2012, with written consent from the patient's parents.
test_results: Genomic DNA was extracted from ethylene diamine tetra acetic acid-treated peripheral blood. Library preparation was performed on the proband with xGen Exome research panel v1.0. The captured DNA fragments were subsequently sequenced by HiSeq 4000. The pattern of X-chromosome inactivation in our patient and her mother was evaluated by assays of differential methylation in the genes between the active and the inactive chromosome X based on methylation-specific polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

case_report: An 18-year-old male exhibited widespread erosions and blisters since birth. Physical examination showed extensive erythematous blistering and erosions, along with hyperpigmented patches on the trunk and limbs. Additionally, there were multiple small blisters in the oral cavity, palmoplantar keratoderma, and dystrophy affecting all 20 nails. The patient did not display muscle weakness, hoarseness, ocular lesions, or other extracutaneous symptoms. Both parents, one aged 43 years and the other of unknown age, did not present with any blisters, erosions, or nail abnormalities.
test_results: TEM of a skin biopsy revealed vesicles in basal cells accompanied by hypoplastic hemidesmosomes. Immunofluorescence studies showed near-complete absence of plectin at the dermoepidermal junction. WES of case 2 found 2 PLEC mutations, c.956T>C (p.Leu319Pro) and a previously unreported c.2807G>A (p.Trp936Ter) in exon 22. Sanger sequencing also revealed c.2807G>A in his father. The presence of c.956T>C could not be confirmed in her mother, due to lack of a maternal DNA sample.
Orpha_name: Autosomal recessive generalized epidermolysis bullosa simplex

case_report: A 12-year-old boy from Saudi Arabia visited Pediatric Dentistry Clinics at Riyadh Dental Center and was later followed up at the Pediatric Dentistry Clinics, College of Dentistry, King Saud University. Written informed consent for the use of his records for educational purposes was obtained from his father. The patient reported severe spontaneous pain in the lower side of his mouth for three days. He had a history of dental fillings and extractions. He is the fourth of five siblings and presented with multiple congenital malformations. These included abnormalities of the index and middle fingers on both hands, syndactyly between the third and fourth toes of his left foot, and a deformed second toe on the right foot with a surgical scar. His parents are not related, and there was no family history of similar conditions. The patient's mother had a history of long-term acetazolamide treatment and experienced five first-trimester spontaneous abortions. During her pregnancy with the patient, she continued acetazolamide treatment (1,000 mg/day) and took folic acid under medical supervision. The boy was born full-term via spontaneous vaginal delivery, measuring 48.5 cm in height and weighing 2,270 g, with bilateral missing fingers and toes. The mother continued acetazolamide treatment while lactating for 1.5 years and stopped the medication during her subsequent pregnancy, resulting in the birth of a normal neonate. The 12-year-old boy showed no major dysmorphic features, had normal skin, hair, and nails, and exhibited good intelligence and behavior. Intraoral examination revealed mixed dentition with retained primary lower central incisors, hypocalcified permanent upper incisors, and multiple carious teeth. The tongue, floor of the mouth, upper lip, and hard and soft palate were normal.
test_results: A panoramic radiograph examination showed oligodontia of 16 permanent teeth.

case_report: A 21-year-old East-Asian female visited the clinic with complaints of peripheral vision loss and difficulty seeing at night. Her medical history includes congenital hearing loss, for which she underwent cochlear implant surgery during early childhood. She was born to healthy parents who are not related by blood and has no significant family medical history. She has a brother who is unaffected and does not smoke or drink. Upon examination, her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/50 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left eye. Initial color fundus images showed mild attenuation of retinal vessels and bone spicule pigment deposits in the mid-periphery of both eyes. Fundus autofluorescence (FAF) images revealed an abnormal parafoveal hyperautofluorescence (hyper-AF) ring, surrounded by hypo-AF spots in both eyes. Spectral domain-optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) images indicated preservation of the external limiting membrane (ELM) and inner segment ellipsoid (ISe) band only in the foveal region. There was a significant reduction in outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness in the parafoveal and perifoveal areas, indicating extensive photoreceptor degeneration. Cystoid macular edema was noted in the inner nuclear layer. The alignment of FAF and SD-OCT images showed that the outer border of the hyper-AF ring coincided with the point of ELM disruption. Full-field electroretinogram (ffERG) tests showed an absence of rod response, combined rod-cone response, cone response, and 30 Hz flicker response in both eyes since the initial presentation.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing (WES) revealed a previously unseen homozygous variant, c.60_61del in the PCDH15 gene (NM_001384140.1), which is predicted to create a stop codon (p.Phe21Ter) after the 20th amino acid. The variant was further confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

case_report: A 5-year-old boy visited the dentist due to unusual dental development. He was born to a 40-year-old mother, G2P2, at full term following a normal pregnancy. At birth, his skin was intensely red, and vesicles appeared shortly after. These vesicles evolved into verrucous lesions within a few weeks, which gradually cleared, leaving linear pigmentation. During the physical examination, the boy was found to be overweight and exhibited cognitive impairment. Hyperpigmented lines were observed along Blaschko’s lines on his trunk and limbs, and hypopigmented atrophic streaks were noted on his upper limbs. Additional findings included alopecia and strabismus. His parents were not related by blood, and his 25-year-old older brother was healthy. There was no family history of similar conditions.
test_results: The soft tissue was normal and only 14 primary teeth were present. First and second mandibular left primary molar teeth (K,L) were absent and in the maxilla, right first primary molar, right primary central incisor, left primary lateral incisor and left second primary molar (B,E,G,J) were missing. Some of both mandibular and maxillary anterior teeth were conical and in the radiograph, the primary teeth roots were normal. The first right mandibular permanent molar (30) showed a delayed development compared to their maxillary counterparts. The teeth were normal and there was only occlusal caries in the first right primary mandibular molar tooth (S) which was treated by amalgam. The child’s dental health was normal and with good occlusion. The interdental spaces were visible due to some missing teeth, sub-mucosal cleft palate and the conical condition of some other teeth. No hypoplasia or hypocalcification were seen on the teeth. Radiography revealed 13 un-erupted permanent teeth, including six mandibular anterior teeth (22,23,24,25,26 and 27)), first right premolar (28) and molar (30), four maxillary incisors and first left molar (6,7,8,9,10,11 and 14).

case_report: Patient 6 is a 59-year-old woman of Chinese descent, whose parents are cousins. She experienced shoulder dislocation at age 1, frequent bruising, recurrent dislocations of the hip and finger joints, and repeated episodes of anal prolapse during her preschool years. In elementary school, she developed knee dislocation while sitting on her heels. During the delivery of her second child and surgeries for appendicitis and breast cancer, she experienced significant bleeding. At age 49, she was referred to a genetics clinic due to bruisability, mild skin hyperextensibility, and recurrent dislocations. She had multiple bruises, including on the soles of her feet, and reported significant swelling after insect bites. She experienced dislocations of the fingers, toes, and shoulders. Cardiac ultrasonography showed no abnormalities in wall motion, mitral valves, or aortic root dilation. She had generalized and wandering pain, sometimes unrelated to joint dislocation or other physical symptoms, which was successfully treated with duloxetine. At age 58, she developed an anal laceration and rectal hematoma requiring emergency surgery. At age 59, she presented with wrinkled palms, skin hyperextensibility, translucency, bruisability, hypermobile finger joints, mildly atrophic thighs, pes planus, and moderate calluses on the soles.
test_results: Modified NGS panel analysis using long PCR-amplified product detected homozygous c.12150C>G,p.(Arg4050 = ) and c.12174C>G,p.(Cys4058Trp) variants in exon 40. MLPA showed a normal copy of TNXB and CYP21A2. Western blot analysis showed complete absence of sTNX.

case_report: The patient is an 8-year and 2-month-old male. He was delivered at full term via cesarean section, weighing 3,200 grams (−0.3 SD) and measuring 50 cm in length (−0.2 SD). Both parents are healthy and unrelated. Developmental milestones were delayed: head control was achieved at 10 months, sitting at 12 months, standing at 24 months, walking at 38 months, and combining two words at 24 months. Clinical features include hypotonia, amblyopia, astigmatism, teeth hypoplasia, and distinct facial characteristics such as hypertelorism, a broad forehead, a long philtrum, upslanting palpebral fissures, a hypoplastic columella and ala nasi, a thin upper lip, a high-arched palate, epicanthic folds, and micrognathia. Additionally, he has brachydactyly and a simian crease on his right hand. At the age of 6 years and 2 months, he presented to the Endocrinology clinic with a height of 102 cm (−3.6 SD) and a weight of 16.8 kg (−2.2 SD), based on the 2009 growth reference standards for urban Chinese males aged 0 to 18 years.
test_results: Electroencephalogram was abnormal, showing sharp waves and sharp slow complex waves on bilateral forehead and central region. Urine and plasma amino acid testing revealed hyperlactatemia. Growth hormone provocative tests revealed that the peak growth hormone levels responding to two provocative tests (clonidine 5 µg/kg, orally, and arginine 0.5 g/kg, intravenously) were 5.60 ng/ml. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan showed widened sulci and lateral ventricles and reduced volume of white matter. No signs of hypoplastic corpus callosum, delayed myelination, or simplified gyral pattern.

case_report: A 44-year-old woman presented with a new, slightly elevated red rash on the right side of her chest that appeared in the spring. Physical examination showed an edematous, red to pink erythematous, non-tender plaque on the right side of her chest. There were no surface changes observed. No other similar lesions were found.
test_results: A skin biopsy was obtained for histopathologic analysis.

case_report: A 43-year-old male presented with pain in the right lower abdominal cavity and was found to have appendicitis. A preoperative plain CT scan showed a well-defined mass, measuring up to 40 mm in length, located at the left obturator fossa and in contact with the left lateral wall of the rectum. The patient underwent a laparoscopic appendectomy and a biopsy of the mass through the retroperitoneal approach.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the biopsy specimen revealed it consisted of spindle tumor cells STAT6 (+), CD34 (+), DOG1 (−), cKIT (−), S100 (−), Desmin (−), CDK4 (−), PAX8 (−), and Ki67 positivity < 1% by immunohistochemistry.

case_report: A 48-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital with complaints of symmetrical and diffuse erythema and hyperkeratosis on her palms and soles, present since infancy. She also reported flexion contractures in her hands and feet, which significantly impacted her daily activities. These conditions have progressively worsened over time. Physical examination revealed yellowish, waxy, and thick hyperkeratosis on both her hands and feet, with a distinct erythematous border. Additionally, her skin lesions appeared atrophic and sclerotic, primarily due to the long-term flexion contractures of her fingers and toes. After obtaining informed consent from the patient and her parents, peripheral blood samples were collected from the patient and her parents.
test_results: Sanger sequencing presented that this patient is an identical homozygous missense mutation c.256 G>A (p.G86R) and her parents are heterozygous carriers.

case_report: The patient is a 53-year-old white female who began experiencing tremors at the age of 52 following a right total hip arthroplasty. Post-surgery, she experienced nausea from her pain medication and was on promethazine for several months when she first noticed a hand tremor. The tremor quickly progressed to widespread abnormal choreiform movements affecting her upper extremities and torso. Concurrently, she experienced difficulty with speech and extreme sensitivity to light, which preceded the development of blepharospasm. She had difficulty focusing without any noticeable decrease in visual acuity and described difficulty focusing on visual stimuli in open spaces, which accentuated her abnormal body movements. Examination revealed a tendency toward phasic, left torticollis, hypertrophy, and tightness of the strap muscles, which was becoming painful. The patient exhibited mixed, generalized hyperkinesias and cervical dystonia, as well as abnormal posturing within her phalanges and left hand, indicative of multi-focal dystonia. She performed movements such as clapping her hands, which were considered complex motor tics. Her gait was slow with small steps, and she frequently grimaced, reporting that she had “cracked several teeth” due to orofacial dystonia. Motor speech examination provoked accelerated, uncontrolled upper extremity movements, and tongue protrusion revealed motor impersistence. The patient also showed slowed processing speed, dissociation of knowledge from action, and echopraxia. At the time, she was taking clonazepam, carbidopa/levodopa, trazodone, naproxen, and hydrochlorothiazide with some benefit. Initial workup for secondary causes of dystonia included complete blood count (CBC) with peripheral smear (no acanthocytes seen), normal sedimentation rate, vitamin B12, methylmalonic acid, electrolytes, ammonia, ceruloplasmin, copper, liver function tests, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), paraneoplastic profile, tests of connective tissue disorders, sera rapid plasma reagin (RPR), negative anti-thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies, and tissue transglutaminase antibodies. Genetic testing for Huntington’s disease was normal. The patient’s family history was unremarkable, and additional family members did not participate in the research study. The patient had no history of diplopia, oscillopsia, or previous ophthalmologic disease processes. Neuro-ophthalmologic examination revealed normal visual acuity and color vision, constant bilateral forcible eyelid closure, and bilateral upward deviation of the eyes consistent with physiologic Bell’s phenomenon. Ocular motility was full with lateral gaze intact, and occasional esotropia with constriction of the pupils was noted. There was no nystagmus.
