Cranial nerves V and VII were intact except for occasional abnormal facial movements and frequent eye closure. The patient’s voice was hypophonic, with high-pitch and strained stuttering speech, repeating consonants at the beginning of some sentences and elongated vowel sounds. She understood what was said to her and was able to communicate her ideas despite challenges with speech, exhibiting echopraxia. She also had several episodes of spontaneous crying. The patient exhibited moderate dysarthria with features compatible with hyperkinetic dysarthria. Her receptive and expressive language skills were unimpaired, but her writing legibility and reading from a computer screen were affected due to uncontrolled upper extremity movements and visual sensitivity. EEG was moderately abnormal due to excessive myogenic activity, with tremor and jerks not associated with epileptiform activity. Background activity was predominantly around 7 Hz, intermixed with symmetrical and reactive beta activity, thought to be due to medication effect. The background activity was mainly in the theta frequency band, possibly representing medication effect or organic pathology such as encephalopathy.
test_results: The patient was found to have a c.702C > G, p.C234W missense variant in exon 7 (of 27 total exons) in the ANO3 gene that falls within the cytoplasmic N-terminus. This variant was not found in the patient’s mother and testing was not performed on the patient’s father who is deceased. For this gene, 100% of the coding region was covered at a minimum of 10× by the XomeDx test (GeneDX). The c.702C > G variant in the ANO3 gene has not been observed in approximately 6500 individuals of European and African American ancestry in the NHLBI Exome Sequencing Project or in over 60,000 individuals in ExAC. No other variants were reported in the clinical sequencing report and mitochondrial DNA sequencing revealed a m.8999 T > C p.V158A variant of uncertain significance in MT-ATP6 that was homoplasmic in both the proband and her 85-year-old mother.
diagnosis: DYT24  associated with a novel ANO3 variant

case_report: An 83-year-old male presented with a non-healing ulcer on his scalp, which appeared four months ago at the site of a previous actinic keratosis lesion following cryotherapy. The ulcer is painless, non-itchy, and has been enlarging over the past four months, accompanied by a yellowish foul-smelling discharge. The patient did not associate the ulcer's progression with sun exposure and has not used sunscreen or protective clothing for his scalp. He has no other skin ulcers and no history of such. His medical history includes ischemic heart disease, depression, melanoma, and vitiligo. He underwent coronary artery bypass grafting in 1997 and angioplasty in 2019. The melanoma on his forehead was surgically excised four years ago. He developed vitiligo 20 years ago and has not pursued treatment for it. His current medications are 75 mg of aspirin, 35 mg of trimetazidine, 10 mg of rosuvastatin, and 25 mg of quetiapine daily. He has no known allergies and no significant social or travel history. On physical examination, he was vitally stable. The scalp examination revealed a 6 cm by 8 cm erosion on the vertex, with an erythematous floor and yellow-green foul-smelling exudate in an area of androgenic alopecia. Additional skin findings included an erythematous patch with gritty scales on the right forehead, a hypopigmented macule on the left forehead (previous melanoma excision site), and extensive vitiligo (universal type). Systemic examination and examination of the nails and mucosae showed no abnormalities.
test_results: The skin biopsy showed ulceration, acute inflammation involving the superficial and deep dermis, solar elastosis, and no evidence of malignancy. The wound culture showed a heavy growth of Klebsiella oxytoca and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and both organisms were susceptible to all antibiotics.
diagnosis: Erosive Pustular Dermatosis of the Scalp
Orpha_name: Erosive Pustular Dermatosis of the Scalp

case_report: A 16-year-old male from Cape Town, South Africa, presented with dental pain due to a severely decayed tooth. He is the only child of parents who are not related by blood and has no notable family medical history. His medical history includes gastrointestinal and eye issues, which are currently being managed. He experiences progressive vision blurring, eye itching, and dryness. He also has recurring episodes of diarrhea, abdominal cramps, constipation, and allergic rhinitis. He shows signs of mouth-breathing and has a vertical maxillary excess with an excessively gummy smile. His dental examination revealed a Class III malocclusion with a protrusive lower jaw and prominent chin. He has prominent ears and thick, arched eyebrows. Both his upper and lower jaw ridges are bulbous, with the upper ridge being more affected, especially on the palatal side, creating a narrow, deep palate appearance. His gums are pale, thick, and smooth with mild pigmentation on the attached gums of the lower jaw. The upper central incisors have not erupted. The visible teeth are severely worn, small, and spaced apart. The lower incisors are barrel-shaped, and the only erupted permanent molar is also severely decayed. The erupted teeth have smooth enamel surfaces. Imaging shows underdeveloped maxillary sinuses and pneumatised frontal sinuses. The lower nasal turbinates are enlarged. There is thinning of the cortical outline of both jaw joints. The decayed molar was extracted. Generalized shortening of tooth roots, especially in certain teeth, was observed. The roots of the upper central incisors are severely curved. The follicles around the lower molar teeth are enlarged and irregularly shaped.
test_results: A pathogenic variant of FAM20A was identified. Nephrocalcinosis was present.

case_report: A 2.5-month-old male infant exhibited symptoms including poor appetite, soft limbs, reduced activity, frequent crying, and easy arousal over a period of 2 months. His height measured 60.0 cm, placing him in the 25th to 50th percentile, and his weight was 5 kg, placing him in the 10th percentile. Clinical examination noted underweight status, low muscle tone, and an enlarged anterior fontanelle. Laboratory tests showed low serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity and elevated serum calcium levels. Other biochemical parameters, including serum phosphate, intact parathyroid hormone (i-PTH), 25 hydroxyvitamin D3 [25(OH)D3], and the urinary calcium to creatinine ratio (Ca/Cr), were within normal limits.
test_results: The X-ray of chest and lower limb long bones demonstrated the decreased bone density of the metaphysis of long bones, distal ribs, and the margin of the irregular bones, the increased distance between epiphysis and metaphysis. Abdominal ultrasound examinations showed calcium deposits in the bilateral renal medulla.

case_report: A 32-year-old male farmer presented with recurrent swelling on the right side of the maxilla, persisting for six years. He had previously undergone surgery for a condition affecting the maxilla. The swelling extended through the skin and into the right nostril. Intraorally, the left maxilla was absent, and the teeth in the right maxilla were mobile, indicating involvement of the entire maxilla. Preoperative incisional biopsy results indicated a mixed type condition affecting the maxilla. A posteroanterior chest radiograph showed no signs of metastasis. The patient underwent right hemi-maxillectomy with excision of the involved soft tissue after baseline investigations. The postoperative histopathology results were consistent with the preoperative findings. The entire specimen was sent for further histological examination.
test_results: The histopathology result showed a highly cellular tumor growing in nests with anastomosing cords and a papillary configuration comprising cells with round to slightly irregular nuclei, a coarse to vascular chromatin pattern, and prominent nucleoli. The cells exhibited peripheral palisading surrounded by stellate reticulum-like connective tissue in areas. Other areas showed highly atypical cells with markedly pleomorphic nuclei and abundant mitoses. The fibroconnective stroma had areas of necrosis. The resection margins were also involved.

case_report: The patient is a 3-year-and-11-month-old female, the second child of healthy parents with a healthy 10-year-old elder brother. She was delivered via full-term cesarean section with a birth weight of 3300 g and a head circumference larger than the normal range. She exhibited hand deformities, including flexed hands and outward-tilting fingers that could not be extended. At 5 months, she was unable to look up or turn over. Following rehabilitation training, she could walk with support and say simple words like 'Mom' and 'Dad.' Rehabilitation training was discontinued thereafter. By age 3, she could walk and run independently but still only spoke a few simple words. Currently, her height is in the 97th percentile for her age group, and her weight exceeds the 97th percentile for children of the same age. She has experienced regression in language development and is unable to engage in routine communication. Her facial features include a protruding forehead, a head circumference of 57 cm, oblique cleft eyes, widely spaced eyes, a long mandibular tip, and hair thinning in both temporal areas. Except for the thumbs, the other four fingers on both hands are excessively outward, and her palms lack palm prints. The first seizure occurred at 3-and-a-half years old, characterized by cyanotic lips, dyspnea, stiffness, and fever, resolving spontaneously after 2–3 minutes.
test_results: De novo heterozygous variant was found by WES in trios: NSD1 (NM_022455.5), c.6095G > A, p.TRP2032*. EEG showed abnormal discharges in occipital area. MRI displayed that the ventricle was slightly larger.

case_report: A 3-year-old boy was referred for further evaluation of micropenis, penoscrotal hypospadias, and a history of operated unilateral cryptorchidism. His perinatal history includes maternal administration of progesterone from 12 weeks of gestation due to placental detachment, followed by intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR). Amniocentesis showed a normal 46, XY karyotype. Due to persistent IUGR and fetal circulation redistribution, a cesarean section was performed at 33 weeks and 2 days of gestation (birth weight: 1130 g, birth length: 38 cm, head circumference: 28 cm). The newborn was hospitalized in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit for one month. Apart from external genitalia deformities and right-sided cryptorchidism, the infant was normal at discharge. Right orchidopexy was performed at nine months of age. At presentation, somatometric characteristics were within the normal range (height: 91 cm, weight: 12.5 kg, 10th to 25th percentile). Examination of the external genitalia revealed a microphallus (length 2 cm) with penoscrotal hypospadias; the right testis was palpable in the scrotum, while the left testis was not detected. The rest of the physical examination was consistent with a prepubertal boy. Abdominal ultrasound identified the left testis at the inner ring of the inguinal canal. MRI of the hypothalamus-pituitary gland showed no abnormalities in the sellar region. Basal concentrations of testosterone and gonadotropins were within the prepubertal range. A GnRH stimulation test showed a normal prepubertal response.
test_results: An hCG stimulation test was performed, showing a T/Δ4 ratio >0.8, T/DHT ratio < 20, and a ΔΤ > 100 ng/dl.

case_report: A 75-year-old male experienced a sudden onset of weakness in his left upper and lower limbs. His medical history indicates he was born at full term without any trauma or hypoxia. A hemangioma was observed on the right side of his neck since birth. Routine laboratory tests showed no abnormalities. Neuropsychological assessment results were within normal limits.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed multiple posterior fossa anomalies including agenesis of the cerebellar vermis with hydrocephalus and hypoplasia of the right cerebellar vermis. Multiple complex cerebrovascular anomalies were noted as follows: narrowing of supraglenoid portion of the left internal carotid artery (ICA), bending of bilateral vertebral arteries, and narrowing of the basilar artery with calcification. Cerebral aneurysm was seen in the terminal portion of the left ICA. There was a complete absence of the right ICA from the origin with corresponding absence of the left bony carotid canal. Anomalous aortic arch anatomy was also seen. The left subclavian artery arose from the medial wall of the aortic arch, more proximal than expected. Bilateral common carotid arteries arose from the distal side of the left subclavian artery. The right subclavian artery had an aberrant course, with its proximal portion making a U-shaped bend. Single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) demonstrated reduced cerebral blood flow (CBF) in the border zones between the middle and posterior cerebral artery territories of the right hemisphere.

case_report: A three-day-old male neonate arrived at the pediatric ER with a one-day history of lethargy, reluctance to feed, and respiratory distress. He was born at 39 weeks’ gestation via a normal spontaneous vaginal delivery at home to parents in a consanguineous marriage. The mother reported no antenatal visits, and the delivery was uneventful. The patient had three male siblings who died in the early neonatal period with similar symptoms, though the cause of death was unknown. Upon arrival, the child was noted to be plethoric and macrosomic, weighing 4 kilograms (90th percentile), with normal length and head circumference. Physical examination revealed a sick, jaundiced, and drowsy neonate with the following vital signs: temperature 37°C, respiratory rate 62 breaths per minute, pulse 140 beats per minute, oxygen saturation 94%, and capillary blood sugar 22 mg/dL. Abdominal palpation showed a firm, non-tender, enlarged liver extending 5 cm below the costal margin, with no other palpable viscera. Neurological examination indicated poor neonatal reflexes. Respiratory examination showed tachypnea, subcostal recessions, and bilateral equal air entry. The rest of the physical examination was normal. The patient was admitted to the NICU, and baseline investigations were conducted. Complete blood counts and renal function tests were within normal ranges. Liver function tests showed conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (direct bilirubin = 61.5 μmol/L), mildly elevated liver enzymes (ALT = 106 U/L), and a deranged coagulation profile (INR = 1.8). Laboratory evaluation revealed hypoglycemia (blood sugar level = 18 mg/dL; 0.999 mmol/L) and a high anion gap metabolic acidosis (anion gap = 24). Blood samples taken during hypoglycemia were tested for insulin levels and serum ketones. The first voided urine during the hypoglycemic episode was tested for glucose, ketones, and reducing substances. An intravenous bolus of 10% dextrose at 2 mL/kg was administered to correct hypoglycemia. Vitamin K was given to address the raised INR. Intravenous antibiotics were started empirically. Despite these measures, hypoglycemia and reluctance to feed persisted, necessitating intravenous administration of 10% dextrose at 60 mL/kg/day. The glucose infusion rate was eventually increased to 17 mg/kg/min to maintain blood sugar levels. Critical samples taken during hypoglycemia showed negative serum ketones and a serum insulin level of 5 μU/mL (34.7 pmol/L). Urine samples were negative for ketones and reducing sugar. Oral diazoxide was initiated at 5 mg/kg/day and later increased to 15 mg/kg/day to manage hyperinsulinemia.
test_results: Urine samples for organic acid chromatography yielded two peaks of succinyl acetoacetate.

case_report: A 70-year-old male, 167 cm in height and weighing 64 kg, was admitted for a left pneumothorax. He had previously undergone surgical treatment for a right pneumothorax four times, with general anesthesia for these procedures being uneventful. Preoperative blood tests were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed significant subcutaneous emphysema from the upper trunk to the neck, without dyspnea. He was scheduled for thoracoscopic pulmorrhaphy. Preoperative vital signs included blood pressure of 127/90 (99) mmHg, heart rate of 107 beats per minute, and axillary temperature of 36.9°C. Anesthesia was induced using propofol (90 mg), fentanyl (100 μg), and rocuronium (70 mg). A 37 French double-lumen tracheal tube was used for intubation. No masseter spasm or limb rigidity was observed during induction. General anesthesia was maintained with 2% sevoflurane inhalation and intravenous remifentanil at 0.25–0.35 μg/kg/min, with muscle relaxation achieved using rocuronium. Mechanical ventilation was employed. After anesthesia induction, an arterial line was placed. Body temperature was 37.9°C 16 minutes post-induction, with an end-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO2) of 42 mmHg. Surgery commenced without issues. During the procedure, ETCO2 ranged from 47 to 50 mmHg, likely due to single-lung ventilation. The surgery concluded successfully after 2.5 hours. Body temperature at the end of surgery was 38.1°C. Just before extubation, ETCO2 was 47 mmHg under spontaneous breathing. Post-extubation, the patient exhibited an agonal breathing pattern with inspiratory and expiratory wheezing. Due to persistent subcutaneous emphysema in the neck, reintubation was performed. However, bronco fiber scope examination of the subglottic respiratory tract did not confirm the initial concern.
test_results: The arterial blood gas analysis showed a pH of 7.27, a PaCO2 of 48.0 mmHg, a PaO2 of 277.2 mmHg, and a base excess of −5.2 mmol/L.

case_report: An 11-year-old male presented to a tertiary care hospital with a history of progressively increasing seizure frequency since infancy. The patient exhibited delayed developmental milestones and right-sided hemiparesis. Seizures were predominantly right-sided, complex partial in nature, and resistant to medical treatment over the past ten years. The child was born at term through a normal vaginal delivery to parents who are not related by blood. There is no family history of neurological conditions.
test_results: Non-contrast computed tomography (CT) of head showed diffuse enlargement of left cerebral hemisphere with midline shift towards right while the right cerebral hemisphere was normal. T2W magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) images showed diffuse gyral thickening involving the left cerebral cortex causing midline shift and scalloping of inner table of left calvarium. White matter in both cerebral hemispheres show normal myelination. Linear hyperintensities involving the subcortical U fibers of left fronto-parietal region were seen on the fluid attenuation inversion recovery image. Post-gadolinium T1W image in axial plane showed no abnormal enhancement. Tc-99m ECD brain perfusion SPECT revealed diffusely decreased tracer uptake in the left cerebral hemisphere, with normal uptake in the right hemisphere.

case_report: A 36-year-old African American woman came to the emergency department with lower extremity weakness, urinary and stool retention, and a burning sensation on her abdominal skin. She had type II diabetes mellitus and a history of RBC transfusion related to the treatment of HELLP syndrome several years prior. Physical examination showed decreased strength in the lower extremities, reduced sensation to temperature and pin prick below dermatome T5, preserved proprioception, and no cranial nerve involvement. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory results indicated an Hb of 9.5 g/dL (previously 13.1 g/dL), a hematocrit of 27.9% (previously 38.3%), a white blood cell count of 3.8 × 10^9/L, and a platelet count of 131,000 × 10^9/L. Serum glucose was 168 mg/dL, and HbA1c was 5.7%. MRI of the thoracic and lumbar spine showed a bilateral, symmetric, non-enhancing central spinal cord signal abnormality from T6 - 7 through T9 - 10, suggestive of spinal cord infarction.
test_results: Hb electrophoresis testing demonstrated 71.4% HbS, 19.0% HbA, 6.3% HbA2, and 3.7% HbF.

case_report: A 20-year-old male nonsmoker began employment at a beryllium production plant on 12 March 1979. Initial chest radiograph and pulmonary function tests were normal, with a forced vital capacity (FVC) of 6.34 L (120% predicted) and a carbon monoxide diffusing capacity (DLCO) of 39.5 mL/min/mmHg (119% predicted). After working in the ceramics and alloy fabrication departments with normal routine pulmonary function tests, he was transferred on 31 December 1979 to the metal production department to operate the reduction furnace. On 12 January 1980, he reported a new rash on both forearms and was seen multiple times for this issue over the next month. On 29 March 1980, he complained of shortness of breath, chest pain, and a non-productive cough that had started several weeks earlier, along with a weight loss of 2.7 kg over the preceding month. Pulmonary function testing showed a significant decrease in FVC to 3.41 L (64% predicted) and DLCO to 8.9 mL/min/mmHg (27% predicted). The chest radiograph remained normal. On 1 April 1980, a company physician noted scattered rales on chest examination and restricted him from further work. During this work restriction, he was treated with antibiotics and antitussives. His FVC reached a low of 2.84 L (54% predicted) on 4 April 1980, but improved over the next month to 4.90 L (90% predicted), with DLCO improving to 31.2 mL/min/mmHg (94% predicted). By the end of April, his weight returned to baseline and his cough resolved. On 28 April 1980, he resumed work in the metal production department, intermittently operating the reduction furnace. In July and August, he was seen multiple times for rash and skin ulcers on the wrist and hand. In early September, he reported a productive cough and his FVC had decreased to 4.63 L (88% predicted). By 11 October 1980, he had lost 7.7 kg and reported a worsening cough and exertional dyspnea. His FVC was 4.33 L (83% predicted) with a DLCO of 24.8 mL/min/mmHg (78% predicted). The chest radiograph was normal. Over the next several months, he continued to work despite persistent symptoms. Repeat pulmonary function testing on 2 December 1980 showed further declines in FVC to 3.61 L (68% predicted) and DLCO to 20.0 mL/min/mmHg (62% predicted). On 2 February 1981, his FVC had decreased further to 2.83 L (52% predicted).
test_results: A BeLPT drawn on 21 October 1980 was normal (stimulation index of 1.4). That test and a repeat drawn on 17 March 1981 were abnormal (stimulation indices of 9.2 and 11.4, respectively). In early April, BAL at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) revealed 47% lymphocytes. A transbronchial biopsy performed at the NIH on 3 January 1983 revealed peribronchial noncaseating granulomas. Fungal stains of the tissue were negative.

case_report: A 35-year-old woman presented to the Endocrinology clinic with a 2-year history of bilateral frontal episodic headaches and amenorrhea. She had previously visited a Gynecology clinic for amenorrhea 6 months before her current admission. Initial laboratory tests showed elevated prolactin levels at 125 ng/mL (normal range: 4.8–23.3 ng/mL). Imaging of the pituitary region revealed a macroadenoma in the sella measuring 13×10×12 mm. She was prescribed cabergoline 0.5 mg twice a week. Despite this treatment, she was referred to the Endocrinology clinic 6 months later due to ongoing amenorrhea and low gonadotropin levels. Her personal and family medical histories were unremarkable, with no evidence of autoimmune disease. Physical examination showed normal temperature, blood pressure, body mass index, pulse, and respiratory rates, and her visual field was completely normal.
test_results: Pituitary MRI showed a macroadenoma in the sella measuring 13×10×12 mm. Her pituitary function profile revealed panhypopituitarism and a 13×11×12 mm sized sellar mass with diffuse enhancement which sustained toward the infundibulum and dura was observed on the gadolinium-enhanced pituitary MRI. On both T1- and T2-weighted imaging, the lesion demonstrated heterogenous intensity. Intraoperatively, thick yellowish fluid draining from the lesion was observed. Histological examination revealed that the resected lesion was infiltrated with dominantly lymphoplasmacytic cells, foamy histiocytes, and only a small focus of cholesterol clefts and multinucleated giant cells. It also showed fibrosis whereas no granuloma or epithelioid cell was observed. Immunohistochemically, these inflammatory cells were CD68, CD3, CD20, and CD138 positive. Immunostaining using pancytokeratin and epithelial membrane antigen immunostains were negative.
diagnosis: Xanthomatous Hypophysitis secondary to a ruptured Rathke’s Cleft Cyst
Orpha_name: Pituitary deficiency due to Rathke cleft cysts

case_report: In June 2009, a 60-year-old male patient presented with anemia, thrombocytopenia, weight loss, and fever. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 7 × 10^9/l, with 64.5% neutrophils, 24.6% lymphocytes, 4.2% monocytes, 1% eosinophils, 1% basophils, and 4.6% blasts. The red blood cell count was 3.38 × 10^6/cmm, hemoglobin level was 8.3 g/dl, platelet count was 49 × 10^9/l, and LDH value was 571 U/l. Physical examination revealed splenomegaly.
test_results: Bone marrow was hypercellular with 19% blast cells. Dysplastic changes in bone marrow included cytoplasmic hypogranulation of neutrophils, erythroblasts and micromegakaryocytes. Karyotyping showed a mosaic and biclonal karyotype with 45, XY, -4, der(6)t(4;6)(?;?), der(8)t(4;8)(?;?), t(13;16)(?;?)/45, XY, der(7)t(7;13)(?;?),-13. Dual-color-FISH using WCP and CEP probes specific for chromosomes 4, 6, 7, 8, 13 and 16 confirmed the translocation seen in GTG-banding. Application of subtelomeric probes for 7pter and 7qter revealed two signals of subtelomeric 7qter on both homologous chromosomes 7 and one signal of subtelomeric 7pter on intact chromosome 7. Thus, subtelomeric region 7pter was deleted on the derivative chromosome 7. Applying an RB1-specific probe showed one signal only on the normal chromosome 13 in both clones. The analysis using MCB probes specific for individual chromosome involved in translocation, determined the breakpoint location and the final karyotype was found to be with 45, XY, -4, der(6)t(4;6)(p15.1;p21.3), der(8)t(4;8)(q31.2;q22), t(13;16)(q21.3;p11.2)[]/45, XY, der(7)t(7;13)(p22.2~22.3;q21.3),-13. Immunophenotyping of peripheral blood characterized the neutrophiles which showed abnormal side scatter pattern, as well as abnormal intensity staining patterns for CD11b(63%), CD11c(59.3%), CD10(17.4%), CD13(44%), CD15(59.3%), CD16(46%) and CD33(20.4%). The majority of monocytes were HLADr+ (4.2%). Lymphocyte subsets percentages were low.
diagnosis: Myelodysplastic Syndrome , Refractory Anemia with Excess of Blasts

case_report: The patient, a female aged 6 months and 14 days, was admitted to our hospital in Yunnan Province in 2019 with general developmental delay, visual dysplasia, ventricular septal defect, and frequent nodding. Clinical data were collected from the patient and her family, and comprehensive physical and intelligence assessments were conducted. Imaging studies included computed tomography (CT) of the temporal bone and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the skull. The patient was delivered by cesarean section at 38 weeks and 6 days of gestation, with a birth weight of 3,100 grams. The mother reported no abnormal pregnancy history or perinatal complications. The patient had delayed psychomotor development, poor head stability, limited ability to turn over, and difficulty grasping objects. Her visual tracking was less than 90°, and she had poor auditory tracking. She often sucked her fingers and exhibited a tense facial expression when transitioning from lying to sitting. She occasionally showed double oblique vision. Despite good spirits and sleep, she had a poor appetite, frequent indigestion, and vomiting before 6 months, which improved thereafter. Family members noted frequent nodding behavior without signs of epileptic seizures. The patient's elder sister and parents were healthy, with no similar family medical history. Physical examination revealed stable vital signs, a head circumference of 41 cm, a flat and soft anterior fontanelle, and unique head and facial features such as a prominent forehead, yellowish hair, wider eye distance, scant eyebrows, light complexion, and bilateral auricle abnormalities. Both pupils were equal and round, and the skin was dry and prone to eczema. There were no abnormalities in the pharynx, neck, heart, lungs, or abdomen. The extremities showed normal muscle volume but reduced muscle tone, with present knee reflexes. The patient had limited hand flexibility and midline movement, could assume a prone position with elbow support, and could sit independently for a short time. She could support her weight on her legs but could not jump. Blood biochemical indices, thyroid function, and vitamin D levels were normal in July 2020. The electroencephalogram was normal. Chromosomal karyotyping showed 46, XX. Heart ultrasonography revealed a ventricular septal defect and pseudomonal tumor formation. Hip joint radiography showed bilateral hip dysplasia. Brain MRI indicated a slightly wider extracerebral space in the bilateral frontotemporal region, with no other abnormalities. Auditory brain stem response tests showed well-differentiated click waveforms at 70 dBnHL in both ears, with normal intervals and latencies. The response threshold was 20 dBnHL in the right ear and 25 dBnHL in the left ear. Developmental assessments showed delays in motor skills, personal-social interaction, language, hand-eye coordination, and performance. Fundus examination revealed retinal exudation around the right eye and no abnormalities in the left eye. A follow-up fundus examination in August 2020 showed no abnormalities in either eye.
test_results: The patient had a novel heterozygous mutation in exon 3 of the coding region of PPP1CB (CHR2-29001861), and the nucleotide 371 changed from A to G (C. 371A → G), resulting in the mutation of the amino acid at the 124th position from histidine to arginine (p.H124R). Sanger sequencing verified that the child's parents did not carry the mutation at the site, which was a spontaneous mutation. The mutation is classified as 'class 2 - possibly pathogenic.' The missense mutation c.371A>G was predicted to result in a histidine to arginine substitution at codon 124.
Orpha_name: Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair

case_report: A 22-year-old male arrived at a primary care hospital with complaints of pain and tightness in the left upper abdomen and shortness of breath lasting two days. He had a history of recurrent mild to moderate breathlessness, for which he received symptomatic treatment from local physicians. Due to his lower income and daily wage work, he had not undergone detailed evaluation previously. During the current visit, imaging showed an air-fluid level in the left hemithorax. A left-sided intercostal drain (ICD) was inserted, draining serosanguinous fluid. As symptoms persisted, a second ICD was placed, which drained blood-stained fluid. Temporary relief of respiratory symptoms was noted for a day, followed by low-grade fever and pleuritic chest pain, leading to his referral to our hospital. In the two days before admission, he reported inability to pass stool or flatus and experienced several episodes of non-bilious vomiting. No referral note was available, limiting further clinical details and treatment history. On examination, he was febrile but hemodynamically stable. Two left ICDs were present, draining turbid, foul-smelling contents. Air entry was reduced on the left side, with imaging showing abdominal viscera and fluid in the left hemithorax. Abdominal tenderness with guarding and rigidity was noted, along with moderate respiratory distress indicated by the use of intercostal muscles and subphrenic recession. Bowel sounds were absent. His pulse rate was 122 per minute, and blood pressure was 90 mm Hg systolic, improving to 110/80 mm Hg after fluid resuscitation. Respiratory rate was 34–36 per minute, and pulse oximetry saturation was 92–94%. Blood tests were unremarkable. Blood gas analysis revealed mild hypoxemia (paO2 72 mm Hg on 35% oxygen) and mild metabolic acidosis, with a pH of 7.31 and serum bicarbonate of 18 mmoles/liter.
test_results: A chest radiograph revealed an air fluid level in the left hemithorax. Air entry was decreased on the left side of the lung, which was radiologically found to be due to the presence of abdominal viscera and fluid in the left hemithorax. A chest radiograph revealed an air-fluid level in the left hemithorax with two ICDs in situ. The right lung field was normal.

case_report: A 27-year-old male presented with gradually worsening weakness in his lower limbs and a progressive inability to walk. He had a normal birth and developmental history, walking at around 1 year of age. He was active in sports, particularly soccer, until age 9. After a brief flu-like illness, he began experiencing lower limb weakness, which progressively worsened. By age 15, he could still run slowly, but by age 21, he could no longer run. He used a wheelchair starting at age 25. At age 18, he was diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and began treatment with Dexedrine. He was also morbidly obese and developed obstructive sleep apnea, for which he used a BiPAP machine. He occasionally experienced muscle cramps and stiffness but had no sensory loss in the lower limbs, no fine motor issues in his hands, no bowel or bladder incontinence, no diabetes, and no scoliosis. At age 27, physical examination revealed distal lower limb weakness with MRC grade 4/5 strength in the tibialis anterior, gastrocnemii, foot eversion, right foot inversion, and right toe dorsiflexion/plantar flexion. Sensory examination showed a mild decrease in vibration sensation in the toes, but other sensory modalities were normal. Deep tendon reflexes were brisk in the lower limbs with sustained clonus at both ankles. Bilateral Babinski signs and a brisk brachioradialis reflex on the left were noted. Hoffman's sign was absent, and the jaw jerk reflex was normal. Increased muscle tone and spasticity were observed in both legs. Laboratory tests including Vitamin B-12, folic acid, ceruloplasmin, homocysteine, vitamin E, arylsulfatase A, methylmalonic acid, peroxisomal panel, VDRL, HTLV-1, and thyroid function were all normal. Brain and spine MRI scans were normal. Electrodiagnostic testing indicated an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Family history was notable for a mother with possible “Charcot Marie Tooth Disease” and a sister with walking difficulties attributed to a past polio infection.
test_results: Genetic testing results for the KIF5A gene showed a heterozygous missense mutation (c.611G>A;p.Arg204Gln).

case_report: A 7-year-old boy presented with suppressed TSH levels, normal FT4 levels, and elevated FT3 levels, discovered incidentally during treatment with carbamazepine for partial complex seizures. These findings persisted even after discontinuing carbamazepine two years later. During this period, he experienced a significant increase in height, moving from the 75th percentile to the 95th percentile, without entering puberty. At 9 years old, he reported symptoms of fatigue, sweating, and heart palpitations, along with increased emotionality and anxiety. He denied experiencing diarrhea, heat intolerance, or weight loss. The patient had a notable family history of hyperthyroidism, including his father, paternal grandfather, aunt, uncles, and maternal grandmother. On physical examination, he appeared slightly anxious and fidgety, was sweaty, and exhibited fine tremors. There was no goiter or exophthalmos. His eyes showed mild weakness in convergence and slight conjunctival injection. His pulse rate was 88/min, and his blood pressure was 100/70 mm/Hg, which is appropriate for his age. His height was in the 91st percentile, surpassing his mid-parental height (50th percentile), his weight was in the 78th percentile, and his BMI was in the 54th percentile, within the healthy range. Laboratory investigations revealed negative TRAb, antithyroglobulin antibodies, and antithyroid peroxidase antibodies, with a normal urinary iodine level of 185 µg/L. A bone age X-ray indicated an accelerated bone age of 10.5 years.
test_results: Thyroid scan revealed a mildly enlarged thyroid gland with uniform technetium uptake in both lobes, which was highly normal at 4% [normal:1–5%] at 20 minutes.
diagnosis: Non-autoimmune hyperthyroidism due to a novel TSHR gene mutation
Orpha_name: Familial hyperthyroidism due to mutations in TSH receptor

case_report: In June 2009, C.M., a 48-year-old female, experienced a motorcycle accident resulting in a fracture of the middle third of the right clavicle, multiple rib fractures, and an ipsilateral hemithorax, with the first and second ribs remaining intact. The patient received conservative treatment using a figure-of-eight bandage. Approximately four months post-injury, radiographic imaging showed fragment displacement and lack of consolidation. The patient had a history of opiate and alcohol abuse, heavy smoking, psychopharmacological treatment for depressive syndrome, and tested positive for HCV. Physical examination revealed no vascular or nerve deficits in the right upper limb, and no central or peripheral neurological disorders were observed. Despite being informed about non-surgical options, the patient opted for surgical intervention. An open reduction internal fixation was performed, and the fracture was stabilized with a plate. The post-operative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged two days later. One week post-surgery, the patient reported numbness and tingling in the fingers of her right hand near the ulnar nerve. The vascular Adson test was normal, and peripheral pulses were palpable and symmetrical. Two weeks post-surgery, numbness and tingling extended to the median nerve area, with muscle strength in the flexor carpi radialis, opponens pollicis, and interossei muscles reduced to 4/5. Three weeks post-surgery, radial nerve deficits appeared, including weakness in the carpi ulnaris extensor and further reduction in interossei muscle strength to 3/5. Bone-tendon reflexes were sluggish in the upper right limb but normal in the upper left and lower limbs.
test_results: We noted the almost complete denervation on the extensor digitorum muscles, right flexors of the fingers and right first interosseous neurogenic damage with denervation activity on other muscles.

case_report: A 15-year-old male presented with developmental delay, hypoventilation syndrome requiring BiPAP during sleep, persistent epilepsy, involuntary movements, static encephalopathy, muscle stiffness, and cortical visual impairment. Previous genetic testing, including epilepsy and seizure disorder gene panel, mitochondrial genome sequencing, and ES trio, did not yield conclusive results. The initial ES was conducted five years ago when the patient was 10 years old.
test_results: This identified a heterozygous variant in CACNA1E, NM_001205293.1:c.1054G > A (p.Gly352Arg).

case_report: A 2-year-old male presented with a progressively enlarging, well-defined swelling on the left side of the mandible over the past year. The parents reported no pain associated with the swelling, although the child cried when it was touched. Physical examination revealed a firm to hard, well-circumscribed, mildly tender swelling measuring 4 cm × 2.5 cm on the left side of the mandible. A computed tomography scan of the head and neck showed a soft tissue mass with bone erosion in the same area. The imaging report indicated a neoplastic soft tissue lesion involving the underlying bone. The patient's blood count and other hematological and biochemical parameters were within normal limits.
test_results: Histological examination of the specimen showed mononuclear blast-like cells arranged in sheets with thin intervening fibrous septa. The cells were of intermediate size and composed of round to oval nuclei with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and prominent nucleoli and scanty basophilic cytoplasm. Immunohistochemical stain of the paraffin-embedded tissue sections showed that the blast cells were positive for CD45, CD68 and lysozyme and negative for CD3, CD20, CD99, terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT), myeloperoxidase (MPO) and CD138.

case_report: A female neonate, one day old, was delivered by elective Cesarean section at 39 weeks and 4 days. This was the first pregnancy for a healthy mother. The infant's birth weight was 2660 grams, birth length was 48 centimeters, and head circumference was 34 centimeters. There were no prenatal complications or relevant family history. Shortly after birth, the neonate required insufflation and showed immediate recovery. Physical examination showed shortening and anterolateral bowing of the left lower limb at the distal third of the tibia, with overlying soft tissue dimpling and oligosyndactyly of both feet. The left foot had three toes (missing the fourth and fifth rays), and the right foot had four toes (missing the fifth ray). The upper limbs were normal, and there were no facial dysmorphisms or other anomalies. Hip ultrasound indicated no congenital hip dysplasia.
test_results: Radiographic examination revealed hypoplasia of the left fibula, absence of two rays left and one ray on the right foot, and anterolateral bowing and shortening of the left tibia.

case_report: A 34-year-old nulligravid Caucasian woman with a history of infertility due to bilateral tubal occlusion and oligoovulation underwent an in vitro fertilization (IVF) cycle using a Gonadotropin Releasing Hormone agonist (GnRH-a) long protocol. Following down-regulation with leuprolide acetate, controlled ovarian hyperstimulation (COH) was conducted with recombinant Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (rFSH) at a daily dose of 225 IU for eleven days. Ovulation was induced with recombinant human Chorionic Gonadotrophin (rhCG) (250 mcg s.c.) when three follicles reached 17 mm in diameter. On the trigger day, estradiol levels were 27,496 pmol/L. Ultrasound-guided transvaginal follicular aspiration was performed 35 hours post-rhCG administration, retrieving eight mature oocytes. Biochemical evaluations of hematocrit, coagulation, serum albumin, liver, and renal functions were within normal ranges. The patient was asymptomatic, and two day-3 embryos were transferred. Luteal phase support was provided with vaginal progesterone at 200 mg twice daily. Twelve days post-embryo transfer, the patient developed nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dyspnea, and oliguria. Physical examination showed paleness, dehydration, abdominal tension, and lung hypoventilation, with normal temperature, blood pressure, pulse rate, and oxygen saturation. The patient's weight was 86.5 kg. Transvaginal sonography indicated ovarian enlargement (left ovary 84 × 63 mm, right ovary 79 × 61 mm) and significant ascites. Blood analysis showed hemoconcentration (hematocrit 46.1%, white blood cells 19,010/ml, platelets 855,000/ml), hyperkalemia (5.1 mmol/l), and hypoproteinemia (total protein 59 g/l, albumin 27 g/l). Renal and hepatic functions were normal. Serum b-hCG was 182 U/L. The patient was admitted to the hospital and received continuous monitoring and supportive therapy, including oral and intravenous hydration, colloid fluids, crystalloid fluids, human albumin infusion, and prophylactic low molecular weight heparin. Fluid intake and urine output were recorded daily. Despite conservative treatment, symptoms worsened, with increased dyspnea and abdominal tension, and weight increased to 87.5 kg. After four days, the patient experienced dyspnea, tachycardia, and sweating, and was treated with oxygen, furosemide (10 mg/day), and cabergoline (0.5 mg/day), and underwent abdominal paracentesis. The patient was transferred to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) due to mild hydropericardium and moderate pleural effusion. Cabergoline therapy was discontinued due to severe asthenia. In the ICU, the patient received parenteral nutrition, continuous dopamine infusion (3 γ/kg/min), intravenous hydration, and plasma expanders. Paracentesis was repeated, and albumin therapy was initiated for ascites and mild pleural and pericardial effusions. As respiratory and abdominal symptoms worsened, beta-hCG levels were 1057 U/L. Ultrasound showed a single gestational sac with a fetus at 5 weeks of gestation. Laboratory tests indicated reduced hemoconcentration (hematocrit 41.5%, white blood cells 13,000/ml, platelets 385,000/ml) but increased aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels (0.67 ukat/l and 1.17 ukat/l, respectively). Over the next 15 days, ovarian size, ascites, and pleural and pericardial effusions gradually reduced, and the patient was transferred to the Obstetric Unit. A new transvaginal ultrasound revealed two gestational sacs, one with a fetus at 6 weeks of gestational age and the other a blighted ovum, along with reduced ascites and ovarian volume.
test_results: Hepatic ultrasound scan showed a slightly inhomogeneous liver structure, dense bile and non-dilated bile ducts.

case_report: A 32-year-old healthy Mexican couple, with no consanguinity, sought antenatal genetic counseling after the birth of a male infant. The infant was born full-term weighing 3200 grams and passed away one month after birth, presenting with a specific clinical profile. The couple reported no significant past medical history and originated from different states in Mexico. They were unaware of any family history of similar conditions. Neither parent exhibited any symptoms or risk factors. There were no previous complications related to reproductive health or other medical issues, and no laboratory or imaging studies were conducted.
test_results: Elevated serum propionyl carnitine. Elevated urine organic acids concentrations: methyl citrate, 3-hydroxypropionate, 2-hydroxyisovaleric, 3-hydroxybutyric, 3-hydroxy propionic.

case_report: A newborn girl, delivered at full term, was observed to have a collodion membrane covering her skin immediately after birth and was subsequently referred to the outpatient dermatology clinic at Tottori University Hospital in Tottori, Japan. There was no relevant family history, and her parents were not related by blood. On physical examination, the infant's entire body was enveloped in a semi-transparent, shiny membrane resembling cellophane, with noticeable fissures in the inguinal region. Bilateral eyelid ectropion was also present. No other congenital anomalies were identified.
test_results: Histopathology of a biopsied specimen taken from the abdomen at 7 days of age showed compact ortho-hyperkeratosis and a normal granular layer at the light microscopic level. The dermis showed minimum superficial perivascular infiltration of inflammatory cells. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) revealed bamboo-shaped crystalloid structures, so-called cholesterol clefts, inside some of the corneocytes. A hypoplastic marginal band of corneocytes was seen. In keratinocytes of the granular layer, keratohyalin granules were decreased in number and were small, and vacuolated lamellar granules were seen occasionally. Compound heterozygous mutations were detected in the TGM1 gene (c.671dupT [p.R225Pfs*14] and c.919C>T [p.R307W]).

case_report: A 73-year-old woman reported experiencing severe sensitivity to light, pain, and redness in her left eye for two months. She had been treated with topical antibiotics and antifungals by a local eye specialist. She had a history of cataract surgery in her right eye 10 years prior but no history of trauma to either eye. Upon examination at our facility, her vision in the right eye was 20/70, and light perception in the left eye was uncertain. The conjunctiva was congested. A 2.2 mm × 2.2 mm round deep infiltrate extended to the anterior chamber, surrounded by a cellular reaction. There were overlying scars and several satellite scars around the main lesion. An epithelial defect measuring 2.3 mm × 4.2 mm was located just inferomedial to the infiltrate. Intraocular pressure was elevated as determined by palpation. Further assessment was limited due to the patient's symptoms. B-scan imaging revealed an echo-free vitreous, posterior vitreous detachment, and significant optic nerve head cupping. An anterior chamber wash was performed under peribulbar anesthesia with a 2.8 mm limbal incision at the 12 o'clock position. Using a classical Simcoe cannula, the infiltrate was aspirated along with a 2 mm × 2 mm oval, yellow mass, which resembled the nucleus of a cataractous lens. A separate membrane was also identified and removed. Smear and culture tests were negative for any organisms.
test_results: Histopathologic examination of the excised mass showed the structure of a lens with disrupted fibres, devoid of capsule, and epithelium. The lens was surrounded by inflammatory cells consisting of neutrophils, lymphocytes, and macrophages. There were few multinucleated giant cells engulfing the lenticular fibre.

case_report: An 83-year-old woman initially experienced numbness around the right corner of her mouth, which eventually spread to all areas served by the three branches of the bilateral trigeminal nerves. She was prescribed carbamazepine, but the treatment did not alleviate her symptoms. Over time, she developed progressive difficulty with speech and salivation, as well as challenges in moving food into her pharynx. A neurological examination conducted two years after symptom onset revealed paresthesia across her entire face and decreased sensation to pinprick and light touch in the left maxillary nerve region. Corneal reflexes were reduced on both sides. The patient exhibited dysarthria, mild facial weakness, and tongue weakness, with an absent gag reflex. Limb muscle strength was normal, but tendon reflexes were brisk globally, accompanied by bilateral extensor plantar responses. The patient had a distinctive eating method: after chewing food, she used a mirror in her left hand to locate the food inside her mouth and then used chopsticks in her right hand to move the food bolus into her pharynx, indicating reduced sensory perception in the oral cavity. Laboratory tests revealed mild hypothyroidism (TSH 7.23 μIU/ml, f-T4 0.87 ng/dl) with positive antithyroglobulin antibody (193.5 IU/ml) and antithyroid peroxidase antibody (≥600 IU/ml). Other autoantibodies tested were negative, except for a positive antinuclear antibody (1:1,280 titer).
test_results: Blink reflex studies showed prolonged R1 response on the right side (13.6 ms; upper normal limit of R1 latency is <13.0 ms) and prolonged bilateral iR2 and cR2 responses (latencies of iR2 and cR2 were 40.1 and 52.7 ms for left-sided stimulation and 49.9 and 42.4 ms for right-sided stimulation, respectively). An NCS was unremarkable.
diagnosis: Facial Onset Sensory and Motor Neuronopathy
Orpha_name: Facial Onset Sensory and Motor Neuronopathy

case_report: A 30-year-old obese Caucasian female presented to the emergency department with fatigue persisting for three months. She reported recent episodes of dizziness, lightheadedness, and shortness of breath during physical activity. Additionally, she experienced diffuse, relapsing-remitting lower abdominal pain over the same period. The patient had initially consulted her obstetrician-gynecologist, who referred her to the emergency department for further evaluation of anemia based on lab results. She denied nausea, vomiting, constipation, diarrhea, melena, dysphagia, or recent weight loss. However, she admitted to occasionally seeing blood in her stools, which she noted as typical for her. She was admitted for further evaluation and red blood cell transfusion. Physical examination revealed mild tenderness upon palpation of the abdomen, with no abdominal guarding, rebound tenderness, or palpable masses. Mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation was observed on her upper and lower lips, with no other significant skin lesions or physical findings. The patient had a history of hospitalization at five years old due to uncontrollable vomiting, during which she was evaluated for her condition. There was no family history of similar conditions, cancers, or gastrointestinal issues. Genetic screening at 24 years old during her first pregnancy confirmed a mutation, although her son's genetic test was negative for the same mutation. Upon presentation, the patient was afebrile with a blood pressure of 147/86 mmHg and a pulse of 109 bpm. Laboratory results showed low levels of red blood cells, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and mean corpuscular volume, with high total iron-binding capacity and low iron saturation percentage. Fecal occult blood testing was positive. Hemoglobin and hematocrit levels were monitored every 12 hours. The patient received two units of packed red blood cells and an iron infusion. Gastroenterology was consulted.
test_results: An esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) revealed hundreds of polyps in the proximal body of the stomach, with the largest measuring 3 mm. Antral inflammation was also noted. The duodenal bulb and second portion of the duodenum revealed no abnormalities. Antral and gastric biopsies were negative for Helicobacter pylori.

case_report: The patient was a 3730 g male neonate born at 37 1/7 weeks gestational age to a 30-year-old G5P2022 mother. Prenatal care began in the second trimester, with maternal history notable for tobacco use, prior opioid use, and pregnancy complicated by fetal hydrops. Post-delivery, the infant required oxygen support with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). APGAR scores were 1 at 1 minute, 7 at 5 minutes, and 9 at 10 minutes. The patient was transferred to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) due to ongoing respiratory support needs on CPAP. In the NICU, the patient exhibited anasarca and a holosystolic murmur. Blood pressure readings were in the 110s/70s mmHg range, peaking at 131/91 mmHg over two days. Initial blood work, including complete blood count, bilirubin levels, and chemistry panel, was unremarkable. Renal ultrasound showed moderately echogenic kidneys with markedly elevated left main renal artery velocities. Echocardiogram findings included mild-to-moderate mitral insufficiency, mild left ventricular hypertrophy, normal left ventricular systolic function, and questionable stenosis of the celiac trunk. The patient presented with signs of volume overload.
test_results: A computed tomography (CT) scan and angiography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were performed, showing narrowing of the aorta in the thoracic region to distal iliac and renal arteries, as well as stenosis of the celiac trunk and superior mesenteric artery.

case_report: A 16-year-old male experienced a sudden onset of limb weakness, followed by numbness and stiffness, along with palpitations. He was admitted in January 2018 due to these symptoms persisting for two years. Initially, two years ago, the patient had a sudden onset of limb weakness without an obvious cause, followed by numbness and stiffness, and palpitations. Examination at a local hospital revealed low potassium levels, which improved after potassium supplementation. However, the symptoms recurred two months ago following exposure to cold, leading to his admission for further treatment. The patient reported no other medical conditions and there was no history of consanguineous marriage in his family over three generations. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Shanxi Provincial People’s Hospital, Taiyuan, China, and informed consent was obtained from the proband and his family members. Physical examination showed a normal-sized thyroid gland and no obvious abnormalities in the heart and lungs. Blood analysis results were: potassium, 2.64 mmol/L; sodium, 133.10 mmol/L; chlorine, 96.20 mmol/L; magnesium, 0.510 mmol/L; triglycerides, 1.64 mmol/L; blood pH, 7.35; standard bicarbonate, 25.60 mmol/L; and total carbon dioxide, 20.00 mmol/L. Urine analysis showed: calcium, 0.12 mmol/24 h; magnesium, 2.200 mmol/24 h; phosphorus, 2.19 mmol/24 h; with concurrent blood potassium at 3.05 mmol/L and magnesium at 0.562 mmol/L. Circadian and pulsatile secretion of adrenocorticotropic hormone and cortisol were normal. Baseline renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system test results were: Angiotensin I (37 °C), 49.94 μg/L; Angiotensin I (4 °C), 6.87 μg/L; aldosterone, 149.05 ng/L; renin activity, 31.87 UG/L per hour, and aldosterone/renin activity ratio of 0.47. The average 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure was 105/71 mmHg. Imaging studies, including X-ray chest film, abdominal ultrasound, thyroid ultrasound, bilateral kidney and renal vascular ultrasound, adrenal ultrasound, and adrenal thin-slice computed tomography, showed no abnormalities. Electrocardiogram indicated sinus tachycardia at 105 beats per minute.
test_results: WES identified a total of 214137288 reads, among which 99.83% could be mapped to the human reference genome, and the duplicate reads accounted for 11.81%. The mean depth was 282X. A total of 67537 mutations were identified by bioinformatics analysis, including 55184 SNPs and 12353 INDELs. After dbSNP annotation, 94% of the SNPs were annotated in dbSNP, while only 35% of the INDELs could be annotated in dbSNP. Mutations in SLC12A3, CLCNKB, and HNF1B3 genes were filtered based on the following conditions: (1) The variant is located on an exon; (2) The variation does not belong to synonymous mutation; and (3) Population frequency is greater than 0.001. After filtering, only one missense heterozygous mutation in the SLC12A3 gene was left. Its population frequency was unknown. Most mutation prediction software such as Polyphen2 HDIV, SIFT, and FATHMM predicted it as a harmful mutation.

case_report: A female child aged 3 years and 5 months presented with progressive swelling and deformity of her small and large joints, first noted 6 months prior. She also experienced poor weight gain since age one year. Initially, the interphalangeal joints and the left and right metacarpal joints were affected. The symptoms gradually extended to the wrist, elbow, and knee joints, leading to restricted movement in these areas. The patient was born via normal vaginal delivery to a non-consanguineous couple, with an uneventful antenatal period. At birth, she had bilateral congenital talipes equinovarus deformity, which was corrected with a plaster cast. Her developmental milestones were age-appropriate until she experienced regression of motor milestones due to lower limb joint involvement. She has a healthy younger brother. Anthropometric measurements showed a weight of 8 kg (<5 SD), height of 75.5 cm (<3 SD), and head circumference of 44.6 cm (<3 SD) based on Indian population reference values. Physical examination revealed mildly coarse facial features, increased body hair on the back and extremities, a hairy nevus over the left ear, and breast enlargement. Ophthalmologic, ENT, and dental examinations were unremarkable. There was swelling over the dorsum of the right hand and wrist, as well as swelling and fixed flexion deformity of the left metacarpophalangeal joint and both knees. Additionally, the patient exhibited flexion deformity in all fingers at the distal interphalangeal joints. The skin on the hands and knuckles was hyperpigmented. Subcutaneous nodules were present on the dorsum of both elbow joints and the third and fourth fingers on the right side.
test_results: The X-rays showed loss of bone mineralization of the involved joints, decrease in joint space and resorption of phalanges. Cortical thinning and expansion of the phalangeal and metacarpal bones was a distinct finding. The rest of the skeleton showed a lesser degree of osteopenia. The results showed a novel base variant of MMP2:c.538G>A (p.D180N) in the homozygous state in the patient. The parents carried the variant in the heterozygous state. The sibling showed no mutation.

case_report: A 41-year-old female presented with multiple raised lesions over the body for the past two years. The lesions initially appeared on both forearms and gradually spread to the lower limbs and back. There was no family history of similar complaints or any seasonal variation. The patient had a history of pulmonary tuberculosis several years ago and received antitubercular therapy. Physical examination revealed multiple hyperpigmented, hyperkeratotic papules and plaques on the flexor aspect of both forearms, the extensor surfaces of both legs, and the dorsum of the feet. A few discrete hyperkeratotic and hyperpigmented papules were also noted on the back. There were no changes observed in the nails or oral cavity.
test_results: Histopathology showed hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, acanthosis, and papillomatosis, the latter associated with circumscribed elevation of the epidermis (church spires) and elongation of rete ridges. The dermis showed a mild inflammatory infiltrate.

case_report: An 18-year-old male high school wrestler with no significant past medical history presented to the emergency department due to cramping pain in the right leg. The pain began one day after wrestling, with no reported trauma or penetrating injury to the area. In the emergency department, the patient had a fever of 101.9°F and exhibited weakness in the right leg. Physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness over the lateral right leg. The patient was admitted, and imaging studies including X-ray and CT scan of the right leg were performed. Laboratory results showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 25 (normal range: 1–20) and a C-reactive protein level of 13 (normal range: <0.5). The X-ray was negative, while the CT scan indicated slight edema involving the right gluteus minimus muscle.
test_results: MRI results exhibited mild soft tissue edema in between the right iliac bone and the right gluteus minimus muscle, which extended laterally to the superficial aspect of the right proximal rectus femoris muscle and inferiorly to the superficial and deep portion of the gluteus medius muscle at its greater trochanteric insertion. The MRI report suggested myositis of the right gluteus minimus muscle. Additionally, MRI showed reactive bone marrow edema of the right iliac bone, abutting the right gluteus minimus muscle. Two blood cultures were sent which came back positive for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus or MSSA.

case_report: Patient 7 (PA-7) is a 6-year and 5-month-old boy with a history of intermittent claudication lasting over 5 years. His body weight is 22 kg, placing him in the 25th to 50th percentile. Clinical examination revealed claudication, swelling, and tenderness in the knee joint. Laboratory results showed decreased serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels, elevated serum phosphorus (P) levels, and normal serum calcium (Ca) and intact parathyroid hormone (i-PTH) levels.
test_results: The X-ray of knees showed the multiple bone destruction at the metaphysis and epiphysis of both knees, accompanied by soft tissue swelling. The X-ray of the pelvis showed the small low-density shadow in the bilateral ischia. The X-ray scans of his hands and ankle joints showed no abnormal signs.

case_report: A female child, aged 1 year and 10 months, was referred for evaluation due to growth delay and lack of speech. She was delivered at 41 weeks of gestation with a birth weight of 2950 grams. At birth, she exhibited congenital aniridia, cataracts, and macular hypoplasia. The genitourinary system appeared normal. Upon referral at 1 year and 10 months, her height was 74.4 cm (−2.8SD) and her weight was 8.5 kg (−3.3SD), both below the expected range for her age. Her motor and cognitive development were assessed to be equivalent to that of a 10-month-old. At 2 years and 1 month, she developed bilateral renal tumors, which were surgically removed. Pathological examination identified the tumors as Wilms tumors. The renal tumors showed a positive response to standard chemotherapy regimens. She remained well-nourished and free of tumor recurrence for over 4 years following chemotherapy.
test_results: The G-band test revealed the karyotype of 46,XX,del(11)(p11.2p14). An array-comparative genome hybridization analysis found the 14.5-Mb deletion at 11p14.3p12. The minimal segment of deletion were defined as arr[GRCh37] 11p14.3p12(24,792,569_39,222,929)×1. The deleted region was located at the chromosomal band, 11p14.3p12. The deleted interval involved 50 genes in the adjacent loci, including PAX6 and WT1. The heterozygous deletions of WT1 and BDNF were validated with FISH and qPCR analyses.

case_report: A 17-year-old male presented with a 6-day history of skin rash and a 4-day history of high fever, with the highest recorded temperature being 40.5°C. The patient also reported sore throats and knee pain during movement. He did not recall any history of obvious inducement, including the use of suspect drugs. Despite receiving empirical treatment with ceftriaxone sodium for injection and loratadine tablets for two days, there was no significant improvement in his symptoms. Physical examination showed generalized small pustules on an erythematous base distributed over the trunk, extremities, and flexures. There were no lesions observed on the oral mucosa or genital skin. The patient was otherwise in good health and reported no family history of psoriasis.
test_results: Histopathology of a skin biopsy specimen showed subcorneal neutrophilic pustule and edema, as well as peripheral infiltration of neutrophils and lymphocytes in the superficial dermis.

case_report: A 20-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of weakness and clumsiness in his right extremities. His medical history was unremarkable for perinatal issues, and there was no family history of neurodegenerative diseases. He reported no learning difficulties in university courses and no history of psychiatric illness. Physical examination revealed no visible body asymmetry, and limb circumference differences were minimal (10 cm below the elbow: right 24 cm, left 25 cm; 10 cm below the knee: right 35 cm, left 35 cm). Dystonic postures were observed in the proximal interphalangeal joints of the right hand when both arms were outstretched, with hyperextension of the thumb and flexion of the little finger. Neurological examination showed subtle weakness in the right limbs, hyperreflexia, and pathologic reflexes. Repetitive limb movements were slow with decremental responses in the right hand and foot. Mild rigidity was noted in the right extremities without resting or postural tremor. Gait analysis indicated decreased right arm swing, but base and stride were normal. The Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS)-Part III motor score was 8/108. Laboratory tests, including serum copper, ceruloplasmin, iron, ferritin, manganese, and 24-hour urine copper levels, were all within normal limits. Cognitive function assessment was normal, scoring 30/30 on both the Mini-Mental State Examination and the Korean Version of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed remarkable subcortical and brainstem hemiatrophy in the left basal ganglia, thalamus, midbrain, and pons. In addition, hypointense signals were observed on T2-weighted images and T2*-weighted (T2*W) gradient-echo (GRE) sequences in the left globus pallidus and substantia nigra. These lesions were isointense on computed tomography scans and T1-weighted images, and hypointense on diffusion-weighted imaging sequences. [18F] N-(3-fluoropropyl)-2β-carbon ethoxy-3β-(4-iodophenyl) nortropane (18F-FP-CIT) positron emission tomography (PET) scans revealed normal levels of dopamine transporters (DATs) in the bilateral basal ganglia.

case_report: A 33-year-old Caucasian male presented for nephrology consultation due to proteinuria ranging from 3.2 to 5.7 g/day and chronic renal failure with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 69 mL/min/1.73 m². Kidney biopsy confirmed AA amyloidosis. Upon admission, the patient reported chronic fatigue but no other symptoms. His family medical history was not relevant. His medical history included arterial hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and normocytic anemia. Physical examination was unremarkable except for a post-appendicitis scar in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen. Laboratory tests showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 47 mm/h (reference range: 0–12 mm/h), C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 61.17 mg/L (reference range: up to 9 mg/L), and serum amyloid A (SAA) level of 60.9 mg/L (reference range: up to 6.4 mg/L). Tests for anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA), anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), and rheumatoid factor were negative. Blood and urine cultures were also negative. The patient's medical history revealed recurrent episodes of abdominal pain with fever up to 40°C, upper respiratory tract symptoms (pharyngitis, tonsillitis), and joint pain in the elbows, knees, and wrists, along with elevated inflammatory markers since the age of 7. These episodes occurred irregularly, at least twice a year, with fever lasting 7–10 days and abdominal pain lasting 10–14 days. He was hospitalized multiple times for suspected infections, chronic endocarditis, lambliasis with cholangitis, or connective tissue diseases. An appendectomy was performed at age 14 due to abdominal pain. Inflammatory bowel disease and chronic pancreatitis were ruled out. Despite extensive investigations, the cause of recurrent fevers remained unidentified. During adolescence, acute episodes ceased, but chronic low-grade fever and fatigue persisted. At age 28, the patient was found to have proteinuria, impaired kidney function, and arterial hypertension. Kidney biopsy confirmed AA amyloidosis. Treatment with colchicine 0.5 mg twice a day led to a temporary improvement in ESR and CRP levels, but increasing the dose to 0.5 mg three times a day was not tolerated due to diarrhea. Genetic tests for FMF did not reveal any known pathogenic variants in exons 2, 3, and 10 of the MEFV gene.
test_results: The genetic diagnostic work-up was continued by next-generation sequencing (NGS).
diagnosis: Tumor Necrosis Factor Receptor-Associated Periodic Syndrome
Orpha_name: Tumor necrosis factor receptor 1 associated periodic syndrome

case_report: A 14-year-old male presented with a low platelet count, mild enlargement of the liver, enlarged spleen, and fluid accumulation in the abdomen detectable only via ultrasound. Since the age of 7, he experienced repeated episodes of blood in the urine, with negative results from urologic examinations, and frequent occurrences of bruising after minor injuries or spontaneously. A bone marrow biopsy was performed, which ruled out primary hematological disorders. Blood tests showed ALT levels at 54 U/L (normal value <40) and AST levels at 53 U/L (normal value <40). Various potential causes of liver disease, including alcohol, drugs, viral infections, autoimmune conditions, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, celiac disease, and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis/non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, were excluded.
test_results: Abdominal RM and CT scan showed asymmetrical hepatomegaly, inhomogeneous liver parenchymal enhancement after i.v. contrast injection, subcapsular hepatic venous collaterals, enlargement of the caudate lobe. The hepatic veins were patent and a flow was detectable at Doppler ultrasound. A liver biopsy showed sinusoidal congestion and atrophy of the hepatocytes lamina especially in the peri-venous area.

case_report: The patient is a 27-year-old male with a history of chronic renal insufficiency lasting over 9 years. Nine years ago, imaging showed reduced kidney volume. Blood and urine tests from one year ago indicated a serum creatinine level of 459 µmol/L, hemoglobin at 119 g/L, and urine protein at ++. The patient has had hypertension for over a year and has been undergoing regular hemodialysis and antihypertensive treatment. Physical examination noted the presence of external ear tags, overlapping toes, normal X-rays of hands and feet, and a posterior thoracic process.
test_results: Renal ultrasound showed reduced renal volume with multiple cysts in both kidneys. Pure tone electroaudiometry suggested conductive hearing loss.

case_report: A 26-year-old pregnant woman (gravida 1, para 0), with no significant medical history and a non-smoker, was admitted to the Emergency Department at 31 weeks gestational age, approximately 1 hour after exposure to an indoor boiler explosion. Upon arrival, she had been ventilated with 100% oxygen for the previous hour, and her carboxyhemoglobin (CO-Hb) level was 5.3%. An emergent cesarean section was performed due to fetal distress and 2nd degree burns covering 80% of her body. Her vital signs included a blood pressure of 140/110 mmHg, heart rate of 105 bpm, and oxygen saturation of 96%. At birth, the newborn had a heart rate below 60 bpm, was hypotonic, and showed no crying or spontaneous breathing, with bright red skin discoloration. Airway aspiration was followed by mask ventilation with 100% oxygen for approximately 30 seconds. Due to persistent absence of spontaneous breathing and a heart rate below 100 bpm, endotracheal intubation and cardiopulmonary resuscitation were performed, achieving adequate heart rate and respiration after intravenous epinephrine administration. Apgar scores were 3 at 1 minute, 4 at 5 minutes, and 6 at 10 minutes. The infant's arterial cord gas results were: pH = 7.29, PCO2 = 47 mmHg, pO2 = 25 mmHg, bicarbonate = 22.6 mmol/L, lactate = 2.6 mmol/L, and carboxyhemoglobin = 4.0%. The newborn was transferred to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) on mechanical ventilation with 100% oxygen. Over the following days, serial blood gas analyses showed a gradual reduction in CO-Hb values, reaching complete normalization by the 8th day of life, at which point the baby was extubated and continued on non-invasive respiratory support for 10 days. Laboratory data were unremarkable, and the hospital stay was uneventful. Serial cranial ultrasound revealed bilateral persistent non-homogeneous periventricular hyperechogenicity.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed a supratentorial pattern of confluent punctate white matter lesions in the deep and periventricular white matter associated with infratentorial small foci of hemorrhagic injury in the cerebellum.
Orpha_name: Neonatal hypoxic and ischemic brain injury

case_report: A 62-year-old female with no chronic medical conditions and only taking an over-the-counter multivitamin tablet was found to have abnormal liver function tests during an annual wellness visit. The laboratory results showed aspartate transaminase at 63 U/L, alanine aminotransferase at 78 U/L, alkaline phosphatase at 301 U/L, total bilirubin at 0.5 µmol/L, direct bilirubin at 0.3 µmol/L, and indirect bilirubin at 0.2 µmol/L. The patient was asymptomatic, with no abdominal pain, jaundice, nausea, vomiting, postprandial epigastric pain, intermittent nausea, bloating, or belching. Vital signs included a blood pressure of 138/84 mmHg, heart rate of 60/min, respiratory rate of 18/min, body temperature of 98.0 °F, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. Physical examination revealed a soft abdomen without palpable masses, tenderness, rigidity, or guarding. Imaging with computerized tomography showed dilated intrahepatic bile ducts.
test_results: Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) showed two large lamellated gallstones within the neck and proximal body of the gallbladder. The large stone in the neck of the gallbladder was compressing the intrahepatic biliary duct. The wall of the bladder was thickened and irregular. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) visualized a filling defect at the proximal extrahepatic biliary tree with mild intrahepatic bile duct dilation.

case_report: A 40-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital due to generalized convulsions. She had delivered her first child 3 weeks prior and had no symptoms until the onset of seizures. She had no previous medical history, including conditions related to pregnancy complications, and no family history of blood clotting disorders. The seizures were generalized and ceased on their own after 2 minutes. She reported no headaches, and there was no evidence of papilledema. Upon admission, her vital signs were as follows: blood pressure was 138/88 mmHg, heart rate was 126 beats per minute, and body temperature was 37 °C. No neurological deficits were observed. A CT scan showed intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) in the left temporoparietal lobe. Given her age and lack of hypertension history, further imaging with CT-digital subtraction angiography (CT-DSA) was conducted to check for aneurysms, arteriovenous malformations (AVM), and sinus thrombosis, none of which were found.
test_results: The PS activity was low at 37 %. The PS amount was found to be normal; however, the PS activity was still below normal.
Orpha_name: Severe hereditary thrombophilia due to congenital protein S deficiency

case_report: A 17-year-old male presented with gradually worsening bilateral swelling of the feet over the past 2 months and increasing abdominal distension over the past month. On physical examination, his pulse was 84 beats per minute and irregularly irregular. His blood pressure was 106/68 mm Hg. He exhibited bilateral pedal edema extending to the middle third of the shin, moderate ascites, and a liver edge palpable one finger breadth below the right costal margin. Jugular venous pressure was not proportionate to the pedal edema and ascites, was non-pulsatile, and there was no cyanosis. A median sternotomy scar was noted. Cardiac examination revealed an enlarged heart and a diffuse apical impulse. The respiratory examination was normal. The parents reported a history of heart surgery under general anesthesia at the age of 2 years due to heart failure, after which he was discharged in 2 weeks and remained asymptomatic. There was no history of cyanosis. The family lost follow-up after the procedure. Routine investigations showed hemoglobin at 9.7 g/dL, total leukocyte count at 9,700/µL (neutrophils 68%, lymphocytes 28%, monocytes 4%), and platelet count at 120,000/µL. Bilirubin was 2.2 mg/dL (direct fraction 1.1 mg/dL), aspartate aminotransferase was 124 U/L, alanine aminotransferase was 168 U/L, serum albumin was 3.3 g/dL, and serum globulin was 3.9 g/dL. Serum urea was 44 mg/dL and creatinine was 1.5 mg/dL. Tests for hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibody, and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antibodies were negative. Electrocardiogram (ECG) showed atrial fibrillation with a controlled ventricular rate and diminished QRS complexes. Chest X-ray indicated situs solitus, levocardia, and cardiomegaly.
test_results: Echocardiography showed gross dilatation of the right atrium and ventricle, severely depressed right ventricle (RV) function with good left ventricle (LV) function. A large thrombus was seen in RV, attached to the free wall in multiple views. Inferior vena cava (IVC) was dilated to 28 mm with minimal respiratory variations.
