The interatrial and interventricular septum was intact. RV outflow tract was free from thrombus. Patent bidirectional cavopulmonary anastomosis was seen in suprasternal view. Subcostal saggital views and coronal view were not possible due to narrow subcostal angle. Cardiac CT showed grossly dilated right atrium (RA) and RV. Large RV free wall thrombus was seen measuring 10 × 4.5 mm. Superior vena cava (SVC) to right pulmonary artery shunt was patent. The interatrial septum was intact.

case_report: A 16-year-old individual, raised as female, born from a nonconsanguineous marriage, visited our clinic with concerns about genital ambiguity and absence of menstruation, along with a lack of secondary sexual characteristics. The patient had undergone reduction clitoroplasty and vaginoplasty on 22/03/2000. There was no history of crisis episodes or cyclical abdominal pain. The patient was on a regimen of 5 mg prednisolone, previously identified as having congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH). There was no recent change in sexual identity. Other aspects of past medical history, family history, antenatal history, perinatal history, and developmental history were not significant. Previous evaluations revealed a small uterus on ultrasonography (USG) but no gonads were detected. Physical examination showed that anthropometric measurements were appropriate for age, and blood pressure was within normal limits. General and systemic examinations were normal, with no signs of Turner's syndrome. Genital examination showed a single perineal opening, a phallic length of 5 cm with a well-formed glans, and a well-formed scrotal sac. Prader staging was 3/5. Sexual maturity rating was A0P1B2. The mucosa above the perineal opening was pink. Routine biochemical and hematological tests were normal.
test_results: A karyotype analysis revealed 46XY karyotype. MRI pelvis revealed uterus didelphys with obstructed right moiety and bilateral ovarian-like structures. Histopathological examination revealed presence of testicular tissue showing atrophic seminiferous tubules with hyperplasia of Leydig cells. Epididymal tissue and an epididymal cyst are also present. However, no ovarian tissue was seen.

case_report: An 8-month-old female was brought to the Dermatologic Unit due to the presence of multiple café-au-lait macules (CALMs) observed since birth. Her medical history was unremarkable, and her growth and development were appropriate for her age. Physical examination revealed multiple CALMs, with 7 being larger than 5 mm. No additional clinical features such as Lisch nodules, axillary or inguinal freckles, neurofibromas, or gliomas were observed. The family history was notable: the patient's mother, grandfather, and two aunts also had multiple CALMs. Specifically, the mother had more than 6 café-au-lait spots larger than 15 mm. The youngest aunt had inguinal freckles and experienced benign epilepsy and mild learning disabilities during childhood, which resolved with age. The patient's mother and her family were previously examined and found to have macrocephaly but no Lisch nodules or neurofibromas. None of the family members have developed any known complications. CALMs are common in healthy newborns and children, but the presence of multiple macules, large segmental lesions, or associations with other anomalies should be noted. In this case, the family history indicated an autosomal dominant pattern due to the presence of café-au-lait spots in every generation. CALMs are often the first sign of certain conditions, and other manifestations may become evident with age. Neither the child nor the family members exhibited nevus anemicus or juvenile xanthogranuloma. Other conditions presenting with CALMs were considered but excluded based on the absence of associated manifestations such as endocrinopathies, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, lentigines, electrocardiography conduction abnormalities, ocular hypertelorism, pulmonary stenosis, abnormal genitalia, retarded growth, and sensorineural deafness.
test_results: The diagnosis in our patient, her mother, the grandfather and in the youngest aunt was confirmed by the finding of a pathogenic mutation, resulting in a stop codon, in the SPRED1 gene (c.973C > T; p.Arg325*).

case_report: Patient III:7, a 74-year-old female, presented with a 2-year history of imbalance, particularly noticeable in low-light conditions, followed by symptoms affecting the distal nerves and severe coughing episodes. She reported no issues with facial sensation, speech, or swallowing. Physical examination showed weak downbeat nystagmus when looking to the side. Eye movement tracking was disrupted in all directions, and saccades were slightly undershot. The VVOR was abnormal, and the HIT was positive bilaterally. Reflexes were reduced throughout, with absent ankle jerks. Sensory examination revealed a loss of light touch and pinprick sensation in both upper and lower limbs, along with impaired proprioception at the wrists and ankles. Finger-to-nose coordination was slightly impaired in the upper limbs. The patient exhibited a broad-based ataxic gait and a positive Romberg's sign. Laboratory investigations, including cerebellar screening, blood tests, and genetic tests, returned normal results. Autonomic function tests were also normal.
test_results: Bilateral vestibular hypofunction was confirmed on caloric and rotational test. EMG/NCS confirmed axonal sensory neuronopathy with absent sensory nerve action potentials. MRI brain showed fissural prominence within the superior cerebellar vermis. A cervical spine MRI showed a slender lower cervical/upper thoracic cord with flattening of the posterior surface and faint signal change dorsally, compatible with dorsal root ganglionopathy.
diagnosis: Cerebellar Ataxia with Neuropathy and Vestibular Areflexia Syndrome
Orpha_name: Cerebellar ataxia with neuropathy and bilateral vestibular areflexia syndrome

case_report: A young man in his early twenties presented with severe anaemia and a large mass on the left side of his abdomen. He was afebrile and exhibited normal growth patterns. His parents were both healthy. The patient had a history of multiple blood transfusions over the past 3-4 years. Clinical examination revealed severe pallor, mild icterus, an enlarged liver extending 3 cm below the right costal margin, and an enlarged spleen extending 10 cm below the left costal margin towards the umbilicus. A peripheral blood smear showed microcytic hypochromic red blood cells with multiple target cells, teardrop-shaped cells, and red blood cells with basophilic stippling. Tests for Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium falciparum malaria, as well as antibodies for Leishmania donovani using an immunochromatographic RK-39 strip, were negative. The patient's mean corpuscular volume was 66 fL (reference range 82-90); serum ferritin was 1200 ng/mL (reference range up to 236), and serum iron was 76.7 mg/dL (reference range 60-160).
test_results: Hb A, Hb A2, Hb F, and Hb E levels were found to be 6.6%, 6.5%, 29.4%, and 57.5%, respectively, by capillary zone electrophoresis (CZE).

case_report: This 18-month-old male toddler was born at term to healthy, non-consanguineous parents from Kerala, India. The pregnancy and delivery were without complications, and his birth weight was 2.9 kg. He has no siblings; the mother had one previous spontaneous abortion. His paternal grandmother experienced severe menorrhagia requiring multiple transfusions, but the rest of the family history is unremarkable. Born in the United Arab Emirates, he received the BCG vaccine (0.05 mL, intradermal injection in the upper left arm) at birth. His postnatal period included a delayed umbilical cord separation of about 3 weeks. At 2 months, he presented with a petechial rash on his arms and seborrheic dermatitis on his scalp. From 8 months of age, he had recurrent severe nosebleeds, leading to multiple blood counts. He had 10 hospital admissions since birth: six for severe epistaxis, two for marked leukocytosis, one for a bone marrow procedure, and one for a significant skin rash resembling eczema. His management included two red cell transfusions over four months, three platelet transfusions, and short-term use of tranexamic acid. He was never febrile, with temperatures ≤37.2°C. Blood cultures taken during episodes of marked leukocytosis grew Micrococcus luteus and Staphylococcus haemolyticus, considered skin flora contaminants. Physical examination revealed dry skin, bruises (petechiae and purpura), and a few scars. He was uncircumcised, with growth and development appropriate for his age. Persistent leukocytosis prompted further investigations. His white blood cell differential counts showed persistent marked leukocytosis, mainly lymphocytosis, monocytosis, and eosinophilia, with frequent 'left shift' (neutrophil bands, metamyelocytes, and myelocytes). A chest radiograph showed a notably prominent thymus, described as a 'round opacity at the mediastinum.' Abdominal ultrasound and echocardiogram findings were normal. Serum ferritin was ≤20 μg/L, and C-reactive protein (CRP) was ≤1.8 mg/L. Serum immunoglobulins (IgA, IgG, and IgM) were normal. At 9 months, his lymphocyte subset was: CD3 T cells [11,002/μL (41%), reference values (10th−90th centiles) = 1,900–5,900], CD4 T cells [6,423/μL (24%), reference values = 1,400–4,300], CD8 T cells [3,785/μL (14%), reference values = 500–1,700], CD19 B cells [14,206/μL (53%), reference values = 610–2,600], and NK cells (426/μL, 2%). Bone marrow examination was normal, with adequate megakaryocytes of normal morphology. Leukocyte RNA was negative for leukemia fusion gene transcripts. Hemostatic evaluation due to severe epistaxis showed normal platelet counts and secondary hemostasis parameters (aPTT, PT, INR, TT, and serum fibrinogen). Platelet function screen showed prolonged collagen-epinephrine and collagen-ADP closure times >300 s (normal, ≤164 s). Von Willebrand factor (vWF) antigen was 59.6% (normal, 50–200) and activity 46.7% (normal, 50–200), consistent with his blood group 'O.' Platelet aggregation studies revealed severely impaired aggregation in response to all agonists, indicating a defect in the inside-out activation of integrin αIIbβ3. Spontaneous platelet aggregation was not present. Flow cytometry showed normal expression of leukocyte receptors CD11a, CD11b, CD11c, and CD18, and normal expression (99%) of platelet receptors CD41, CD61, CD42a, and CD42b.
test_results: Two novel compound heterozygous variants were found: (1) Non-sense (stop-gain, resulting in a truncated product) NM_178443.2(FERMT3):c.1800G>A, p.Trp600* (inherited from the mother), and (2) Non-stop (stop-loss, resulting in an elongated polypeptide) NM_178443.2(FERMT3):c.2001del p.*668Glufs*106 (inherited from the father). The non-sense variant FERMT3:p.Trp600* leads to a premature truncation of the protein and the loss of 68 residues from the C-terminal. This truncation results in the loss of two α-helices and a β-sheet, comprising of three β-strands. The Trp600* variation shortens the F3 subdomain of FERMT3. The F3 subdomain is a part of the integrin-binding pocket of FERMT3 and this variation is, therefore, expected to inhibit the ability of FERMT3 to bind to integrins. The p.*668Glufs*106 non-stop variant results in an extended polypeptide with an additional 105 amino acids, a 16% extension to the wild-type sequence. Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) searches did not identify any homologous sequences or structures. Secondary structure prediction with PSIPRED indicated that this region could potentially harbor six α-helices. While secondary structures have been predicted in the extended sequence of p.*668Glufs*106, it is unclear if this extended part will cooperatively fold to produce a functional domain. Nonetheless, even if it does, its close proximity to the integrin-binding pocket of the F3 subdomain, located near the C-terminal of the protein, is likely to disrupt its ability to bind to integrins.

case_report: A 34-year-old woman with no prior health issues presented to our department in February 2010, reporting a 25-day history of headache and double vision. Physical examination identified partial paralysis of the left abducens nerve. No other systemic symptoms or signs were observed. Blood tests conducted at the time of admission showed normal biochemical, pituitary hormonal, and hematological parameters.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed an irregular intrasellar mass with suprasellar and parasellar extension. Relatively low intensity on T1-weighted images and iso-intensity on T2-weighted images, with nonuniform enhanced characteristics were found. Computed tomography (CT) scanning of the brain showed diffuse and irregular bony destruction of the sellar area. A bone scan showed sellar hypermetabolic lesion and proliferative changes throughout the skeleton. λ Serum light chain (3.3 g/L, reference 0.9–2.1 g/L) was high, and the ratio of k/λ serum light chain was 0.55, below the reference range (1.47–2.95). Urine test of Bence-Jones proteins was positive. Serum beta-2 microglobulin level was high (9.97 mg/L, reference 1.28–1.95 mg/L).
diagnosis: Sellar Solitary Plasmacytoma Progressing to Multiple Myeloma

case_report: A 24-year-old Chinese female was admitted in July 2015 with severe speech and swallowing difficulties, prominent lower lip concavity, and walking difficulties. In 2006, she exhibited an abnormal right leg posture while running, which she was unaware of until informed by her father. By 2012, she experienced right leg spasms during sleep and significant gait disturbance. In April 2015, she began dragging her right leg with involuntary inversion of the right ankle and showed slowness of movement. In May 2015, she had an acute onset of severe speech and swallowing difficulties, followed by drooling, prominent lower lip concavity, and dystonic right hand postures several days later. These symptoms slightly progressed over a week and then stabilized, with frequent fluctuations over the following week. Depression and anxiety exacerbated her symptoms. The patient had global developmental delay since early childhood with no preceding illness or drug use. There was no family history of similar conditions. Her mother died of cerebrovascular disease at 30 years old. On examination, she had prominent lower lip inversion and severe hypokinesia of the tongue, rendering her anarthric. Muscle strength was normal. She exhibited cogwheel rigidity in her right arm and both legs, particularly the right leg, and markedly slow movements, including finger and feet tapping. Deep tendon reflexes in the legs were hyperactive, and bilateral ankle clonus was present with more than three cloni. The right foot showed a positive Babinski sign, while the left was suspiciously positive. Laboratory tests and routine cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies were normal. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) indicated reduced white matter integrity of the corticospinal tract in the frontal lobe and subpontine plane. Genetic tests for spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA) and hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) were negative.
test_results: Next-generation sequencing of the patient revealed a heterozygous nucleotide substitution (c.829G > A) in ATP1A3 gene in exon 8 of chromosome 19, resulting in an amino acid substitution of glutamic acid (E) to lysine (K) at codon position 277 (p.E277K).

case_report: A 37-year-old female patient of Han Chinese descent presented with a three-year history of involuntary tremors affecting both hands and head, which began simultaneously. The tremors have progressively worsened but remain confined to the hands and head. The tremors are exacerbated by stress or anxiety and persist in the supine position. Alcohol intake does not alleviate the tremors. The patient sought medical attention due to the impact on her daily activities. Neurological examination revealed a mild postural tremor in the fingers, mild intention tremors in both hands during the finger-to-nose maneuver, and mild dysmetria on the left. A horizontal head tremor was noted, which was irregular and accompanied by slight torticollis with the head tilting to the right. There were no tremors in the mandible or protruded tongue, and the head tremor persisted when supine. Rapid alternating movement tests were normal. Dysmetria was observed during the initial phase of the finger-nose-finger maneuver on both sides. There were no signs of dysarthria. Ocular assessments showed normal saccades and pursuit movements. There were no indications of bradykinesia, muscle rigidity, or hyperreflexia. Babinski signs were absent, and there was no muscular weakness, sensory abnormalities, or bladder or bowel disturbances. A brain MRI showed no cerebellar or cerebral atrophy or other structural abnormalities. Comprehensive laboratory evaluations, including thyroid function tests and serum levels of ceruloplasmin, ferritin, and vitamin B12, were within normal limits. The patient's medical history revealed a familial pattern of tremor, with her father, grandmother, and aunt experiencing similar symptoms of head and hand tremors. The patient's father died in a motor vehicle accident in his forties, while the other family members lived into their seventies. None of these individuals received a formal medical diagnosis or treatment, and their symptoms were largely restricted to hand and head tremors. There were no reports of other features such as gait impairment, dysarthria, bradykinesia, behavioral or psychiatric disturbances, or urinary abnormalities.
test_results: Whole genome sequencing data revealed a CAG repeat expansion in the PPP2R2B gene. Subsequent sanger sequencing with capillary electrophoresis confirmed a repeat count of 74, falling within the range of full penetrance.

case_report: A 27-year-old unmarried woman, with no history of diabetes, visited the outpatient department with symptoms of increased urination and thirst for 1 month, and multiple episodes of vomiting and fever with mild shortness of breath for 3 days. On examination, her body mass index (BMI) was 14.22 kg/m2, pulse rate was 115 beats per minute, and blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg when lying down and 80/50 mmHg when standing. She showed signs of dehydration and had a fruity odor to her breath. Pallor was noted, but there was no edema, and jugular venous pressure (JVP) was normal. Gastrointestinal examination revealed mild splenomegaly, while other systems appeared normal. Initial laboratory tests showed a fasting blood sugar level of 494 mg/dl, postprandial blood sugar level of 568 mg/dl, glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) at 18.7%, and strongly positive urinary ketones. Serum creatinine was 0.6 mg/dl. Arterial blood gas analysis indicated acidosis with a pH of 7.29, pCO2 of 33 mmHg, pO2 of 90 mmHg, and HCO3 of 15 mEq/l. Total leukocyte count was 21,000/mm3 with a left shift, hemoglobin was 9 g/dl, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 65 mm at the end of the first hour. Chest X-ray showed consolidation in the left lung. Anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (anti-GAD) antibody was positive. She was treated according to the standard protocol for diabetic ketoacidosis and given antibiotics. Her condition gradually stabilized after initial treatment. However, on the 5th day of admission, she began experiencing abdominal pain, abdominal distension, and swelling of the feet. Physical examination revealed hepatomegaly, increased splenomegaly, ascites, and pedal edema. Further investigations showed abnormal liver function tests: total protein 7.1 g/dl, serum albumin 2.7 g/dl, total bilirubin 1.1 mg/dl (indirect 0.8 mg/dl), aspartate transaminase (AST) 147 U/l, alanine transaminase (ALT) 99 U/l, serum alkaline phosphatase 1431 U/l, and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT) 1075 U/l. Tests for hepatitis B and C were negative. Echocardiography, 24-hour urinary albumin, and thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) levels were normal.
test_results: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) scan of the abdomen showed nodular liver surface with attenuated hepatic veins and proximal inferior vena cava (intrahepatic and suprahepatic regions) with intrahepatic collaterals, dilated portal vein, splenic vein, dilated mesenteric venous channels, splenomegaly, and moderate ascites, indicating hepatic parenchymal changes with portal hypertension and compromised hepatic venous outflow.

case_report: A female newborn, delivered at 36 weeks gestation to a 26-year-old first-time mother via spontaneous vaginal delivery, had a birth weight of 2800 g (50th percentile) and Apgar scores of 4, 6, and 7 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes respectively. The pregnancy was uneventful, and the parents were healthy with no family history of gastrointestinal disease. The amniotic fluid was stained with thick meconium, necessitating tracheal suctioning and positive pressure ventilation during resuscitation. After stabilization, she was transferred to the neonatal intensive care unit on nasal continuous positive airway pressure. Physical examination revealed marked pallor. Laboratory results showed normocytic normochromic anemia with hemoglobin at 10.6 g/dL and hematocrit at 31.9%. C-reactive protein, kidney function tests, and serum electrolyte levels were normal. There were no signs of hemolysis or fetomaternal hemorrhage. Histopathological examination of the placenta indicated chorioamnionitis. She received intravenous antibiotics and a blood transfusion. She stabilized with no respiratory distress and was breathing spontaneously. On day two, oral feeding was initiated with both breast and formula milk. Less than 24 hours later, she exhibited irritability, lethargy, severe dehydration, and a 25% body weight loss, despite adequate urine output. Investigations revealed hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis (pH 7.18; HCO3 12.3 mmol/L; base excess –14.9 mmol/L; Cl- 129 mmol/L) due to hypernatremic dehydration (Na+ 155 mmol/L). Glucose and lactate levels were normal, and sepsis workup was negative. Loose, watery, bloodless stools with mucus were observed. She was kept nil per os, received volume expansion with normal saline, and started on fluid and sodium bicarbonate replacement therapy. Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) was initiated via a central venous line, on which she became dependent. Attempts at oral feeding resulted in weight loss, hyponatremia, and metabolic acidosis. Urinary catheterization revealed that the profuse diarrhea had been misinterpreted as urine. Diarrhea persisted despite fasting, with stool output up to 120 ml/kg/day, necessitating intravenous fluid replacement. High sodium requirements were noted, up to 10 mmol/kg/day. Stool reducing substance was negative, fecal pH was 8, and stool Na+ concentration was high (83 mmol/L). The fecal ion gap [Stool osmolality – 2 × (stool Na+ + stool K+)] was <50, indicating a secretory diarrhea pattern. On day 19, octreotide was initiated without improvement. The patient developed cholestasis and catheter-related sepsis. Extensive investigations, including repeated blood, stool, and urine cultures, metabolic screening, immunoreactive trypsinogen levels, renal, hepatic, and endocrinological testing, specific serum cow milk IgE levels, and tests for immunodeficiency and autoimmune enteropathy, were all normal. Cerebral, abdominal, cardiac, and renal ultrasounds were also normal. An endoscopy with duodenal biopsy performed on day 12 revealed unspecific inflammatory enteropathy.
test_results: DNA sequencing revealed compound heterozygous mutations of MYO5B gene.

case_report: A 48-year-old woman presented with atrial fibrillation and no history of arterial hypertension, obesity, endocrine disorders, or diastolic cardiac dysfunction. Echocardiography confirmed normal cardiac structure with no signs of hypertrophy or cardiac dilation. Holter monitoring revealed a prolonged QT interval (490–560 ms), cardiac conduction defects including SA and AV block type II, and episodes of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia. Familial history reported multiple cases of congenital cardiac defects and sudden cardiac death, as well as a Brugada-like ECG pattern in the proband’s son.
test_results: Genetic screening identified mutation R518C in CACNA1C gene (NM_001129830: c.C1552T), which is considered to be pathogenic.

case_report: A 33-year-old male experienced the onset of symptoms at age 6, including reduced visual acuity, sensitivity to light, and changes in color vision. Over the years, his best-corrected visual acuity (BVCA) declined to 1.00 LogMAR in both eyes and has remained stable for the past six years. His refractive error was measured at −4.25 sph −2.00 cyl/180° in the right eye and −4.50 sph −1.50 cyl/30° in the left eye. Fundus examination revealed a normal optic disk, foveal atrophy, and peripheral retinopathy with a 'salt and pepper' appearance. Fundus autofluorescence showed a dark central area indicating the absence of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) surrounded by an unusual hyperfluorescent perifoveal ring in both eyes. Infrared retinography confirmed foveal atrophy. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging demonstrated a significant reduction in foveal thickness along with disruption of the photoreceptor layer. The Goldmann visual field test indicated a central scotoma with mild peripheral constriction.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed that the proband carried the unpublished nonsense variant p.(Leu13*) in homozygous state. The variant generates a premature stop codon after 13 amino acids and is likely to cause mRNA-mediated decay or protein degradation.

case_report: A 48-year-old man with a history of HIV infection for 13 years presented with tense oral blisters and painful ulcerations lasting for 15 days. He had no history of skin or genital erosions. The patient showed no symptoms related to HIV and had never used antiretroviral therapy. His most recent CD4 count was 1970/mL. He was not taking any prescription or alternative medicines. Over the past 2 years, he experienced 7 episodes of intense pain and burning in the buccal mucosa, including the current episode of bullous lesions. Oral examination revealed a few well-defined erosions in the mouth and a small blister. Mild conjunctivitis and symblepharon formation were observed in the left eye. Nikolsky sign on the buccal mucosa was positive.
test_results: The histopathologic exam of perilesional tissue showed on a subepidermal blister with an inflammatory infiltrate in the upper dermis composed of lymphocytes and eosinophilic leucocytes.

case_report: A 30-year-old woman has been documented with elevated muscle and liver enzymes since the age of 10, without any muscle weakness. At the age of 18, examinations of muscle and skin samples showed an unusual buildup of intracellular lipid droplets in muscle fibers, especially in type I fibers, and in skin fibroblasts.
test_results: At the age of 18, the first muscle and skin biopsies revealed abnormal accumulation of intracellular LDs in muscle fibers, in particular in type I fibers, and in skin fibroblasts. Sequencing analysis revealed a retrotransposon insertion in exon 3 of PNPLA2 gene leading to the complete loss of PNPLA2 mRNA synthesis. A calves MRI performed in 2015 showed lipid accumulation. GSGC test performed in 2020 confirmed progressive myopathy: Walking 10 meters = 10 seconds, score 2 (for mild waddling); Climbing stairs = 13 steps up = 8.10 seconds, 13 step down = 6.40 seconds, score 1 (does not need assistance); Raising from seated floor position with no hands = 2.76 seconds, score 4 (left hand on left thigh); Getting up from chair = 0.61 seconds (< less than 1 second), score 1 (normal). A new MRI at the age of 27 displayed muscle atrophy as well as tissue substitution in the following muscles: bilateral in tensor fascia-lateral, bilateral in gluteus muscles, in vastus lateralis of the thigh and partially in sartorius, bilaterally in femoral biceps, and bilaterally in semimembranosus. Moreover, fat tissue replacement of deltoid and biceps muscles in the right upper extremity was also observed.
diagnosis: Neutral Lipid Storage Disease with Myopathy

case_report: A 51-year-old male patient reported experiencing moderate and constant pain in the right scapular region, extending to the back. In 2009, the cause of these symptoms was not determined. In September 2014, the patient began to experience cervical pain that worsened with movement and radiated to his upper limbs. After three months, the symptoms progressed to include weakness and fine motor impairment in his arms, leading to his admission to the clinical neurology ward. Initial investigations focused on infectious causes. Clinical, laboratory, and pathological evaluations ruled out tuberculosis, cryptococcosis, Lyme's disease, syphilis, AIDS, lupus, vasculitis, bacterial meningitis, neoplasms, and sarcoidosis.
test_results: A fusiform intradural extramedullary mass in the posterior region of the vertebral canal, extending from C2 to T1 levels, showing marked hypointensity on T2/short tau inversion recovery weighted images; hypointensity on T1-weighted images; and linear peripheral enhancement after contrast administration. The mass was causing compression of the spinal cord, and the space of cerebrospinal fluid was decreased between C2 and T1. Histological analysis showed a nonspecific chronic inflammatory process in dense fibrous tissue, negative for the IgG4 antibody test.

case_report: A 13-year-old girl presented with difficulty breathing, subcutaneous nodules, and joint pain over the past three months. The joint pain, which developed gradually, affected her knees, ankles, elbows, wrists, and fingers bilaterally, more on the right side, and worsened over time, impacting her daily activities. The pain was severe at night and early morning, causing her to miss school. Initially, she responded to Ibuprofen, but later it became ineffective. The pain was accompanied by swelling and redness around the joints. Two months after the onset of joint pain, her mother noticed small, round, non-tender, skin-colored subcutaneous nodules on her elbows and arms. Subsequently, the patient began experiencing chest pain and difficulty breathing with exertion, which worsened when lying down. She had a history of an upper respiratory tract infection and high fever (39-40ºC) two weeks before the joint pain, which lasted a week and improved with antipyretics. She visited multiple healthcare facilities before being referred to our hospital. Over the last three months, she experienced joint pain, subcutaneous nodules, and exertional dyspnea. She was admitted for management and further investigation. There was no recent history of palpitations, rash, coughing up blood, mood swings, or abnormal movements. On physical examination, she appeared in pain, with a temperature of 37ºC. Her respiratory rate was 28/min, heart rate was 129/min, and blood pressure was 126/70 mmHg. She measured 153 cm in height, weighed 81 kg, and had a BMI of 35. Cardiovascular examination revealed a grade 3 holosystolic murmur with the highest intensity at the apex. She exhibited an antalgic gait and had subcutaneous nodules on the extensor surface of the right elbow and interphalangeal joints, with no signs of arthritis.
test_results: A complete blood count revealed hemoglobin = 11.0 g/dL, white cell count = 13,4*1000 uL, platelets = 483*1000 uL. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) = 120 mm/hr, C reactive protein (CRP) was 2.3 mg/dl. Elevated titers of anti-streptolysin O titer (ASO) (832 IU/ml). Echocardiography revealed severe mitral regurgitation (MR), mild aortic regurgitation (AR), and diffuse mild pericardial effusion.

case_report: The patient is a 10-month-old boy, the only child of healthy, unrelated Korean parents. He was delivered at 38 weeks of gestation via cesarean section. He presented to the developmental rehabilitation clinic with general developmental delay. Physical examination revealed several dysmorphic features: congenital blepharophimosis, epicanthus inversus, micrognathia, flat and broad nasal bridge, bulbous nasal tip, high-arched palate, small mouth, and overriding toes. His body weight was 8.7 kg (SD, −0.95 kg), height was 73.4 cm (SD, +0.13 cm), and head circumference was 43 cm (SD, −1.9 cm) at 10 months of age. Both testes were undescended, and bilateral orchiopexy was performed. A frontal image of the patient was analyzed using the CLINIC application of the Face2Gene platform, highlighting features such as blepharophimosis, epicanthus inversus, micrognathia, thin upper lip, thin lip vermilion, flat broad nasal bridge, and bulbous nose. A developmental assessment using the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development at 10 months indicated an overall developmental age of 5–6 months. An echocardiogram revealed an atrial septal defect secundum (8 mm) with a left-to-right shunt. Brain MRI showed infantile CSF space widening in the bilateral frontotemporal regions.
test_results: A novel heterozygous frameshift deletion, c.4911_4921del p (Val1638AlafsTer27), in KAT6B was identified on the basis of the reference sequence NM_012,330.3 and was classified as a pathogenic variant.

case_report: A 24-year-old male presented with a history of gradually worsening tremors in both hands and the head, along with increasing difficulty in walking over more than 10 years. Initially, he noticed a reduced speed of writing despite being able to hold the pen properly, with tremors worsening during voluntary actions and improving at rest. Walking imbalance was first observed on uneven ground and progressively led to repeated falls even on smooth surfaces, requiring support for walking at the time of hospital presentation. He also reported slipping slippers with awareness. He experienced difficulty speaking fluently but had no issues with chewing or swallowing. There were no complaints of upper limb weakness, sensory loss, bladder or bowel disturbances, or visual problems. There was no history of cognitive decline, seizures, or myoclonic jerks. Similar symptoms were reported in his younger brother with a similar progression, while his parents were unaffected. There was no history of consanguineous marriage in the family. On examination, the patient was vitally stable, with normal findings in cardiac, respiratory, and gastrointestinal systems. The central nervous system examination revealed spastic weakness in the lower limbs, impaired deep sensation in the distal toes of both feet, and the presence of cerebellar signs.
test_results: MRI brain showed T2/FLAIR hyperintense signal changes in deep white matter. Genetic testing done for GAA repeats in the frataxin gene on chromosome 9 for Friedreich’s ataxia was negative.
diagnosis: Early-onset cerebellar ataxia with retained reflexes
Orpha_name: Early-onset cerebellar ataxia with retained tendon reflexes

case_report: A 57-year-old Japanese woman presented with a 1-year history of a solitary erythematous plaque on the left leg. She had been treated with topical corticosteroid for a year without any improvement. The physical examination revealed a solitary erythematous plaque with a scaly surface measuring 17 × 14 mm in diameter. The dermoscopic examination demonstrated dotted and glomerular vessels with a homogenous pinkish background and whitish scaly areas. At the periphery of the lesion, there is a whitish negative network. The glomerular vessels are less prominent and the negative network is broader and more obscure. The whitish scaly areas are also less conspicuous.
test_results: The histopathological examination of an excisional biopsy disclosed massive band-like infiltrates of atypical lymphocytes with prominent epidermotropism within a hyperplastic epidermis. Atypical lymphocytes were positively stained with CD3 and predominantly with CD8, but negative with CD4, CD20, CD30, and CD79a.

case_report: A 13-year-old boy, previously healthy except for a one-year history of psoriasis, was found to have an enlarged right tonsil during an orthodontic procedure. Physical examination revealed a significantly enlarged right tonsil with a multinodular appearance and purulent exudate. Mild splenomegaly was detected through palpation and confirmed by computed tomography (CT). No palpable superficial lymph nodes were noted. Laboratory tests showed no significant abnormalities. A tonsillectomy was subsequently performed.
test_results: Histological examination revealed a diffuse proliferation of monomorphic, medium-sized cells that partially effaced the architecture. The cells resembled hematopoietic blasts, with finely dispersed chromatin, moderate vacuolated cytoplasm, medium-large sized round nuclei and indistinct nucleoli. Mitotic figures were easily found. Neither angiodestruction nor necrosis was observed. Immunohistochemical studies showed positive immunoreactivity of the cells for CD45, CD43, tryptase, CD117, CD56 and negative immunoreactivity for CD34, TdT, CD10, CD20, CD3, PAX5, CD68(KP1), MPO, CD30, CD2, CD7, CD25, TIA1, GranzymeB, CD123, CD235 and CD61. The Ki67 labelling index of the cells was greater than 60%. In situ hybridization for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) encoding RNA (EBER) was negative. BM trephine biopsy showed the normal architecture was almost completely replaced by atypical cells that shared similar immunohistochemical and molecular characteristics with the blasts in tonsils but shared differentiating features with immature MCs, such as medium-sized oval or spindle shaped nuclei. The BM aspirate smears were also found to consist of an excess of atypical blasts with basophilic cytoplasm containing varying numbers of metachromatic granules, accounting for 69.5% of all nucleated BM cells. Auer rods were absent. These atypical cells were positive for HLA-DR, CD56, CD33, CD117, BDCA-1, CD9, CD69, CD11c, and CD11b but were negative for CD34, CD123, CD25, CD2 and MPO by flow cytometry. Chromosome analysis of BM showed an abnormal karyotype of 47, XY, + 5, t (1; 9) with an equivocal translocation involving chromosomes 1 and 9. None of the 41 leukemia-related fusion genes we detected by real-time PCR were positive. The peripheral blood smear showed up to 16% abnormal cells, which were confirmed by flow cytometry to be of similar immunophenotype as those in BM. Involvement of multiple lymph nodes, the right scapula and lung was also detected by PET-CT, and the involvement of lymph nodes was confirmed by biopsy. Sequencing of exon 8 (p. 412–448), exon 9 (p. 449–513), exon 11 (p. 549–591), exon 13 (p. 628–663), and exon 17 (p. 788–828) of the KIT gene revealed no detectable mutation, including the most frequently detected KIT D816V mutation.
diagnosis: leukemic variant of mast cell leukemia

case_report: A 23-day-old full-term female infant, the first child of a third-degree consanguineous marriage, was admitted with a history of multiple bullous lesions starting from day 5 of life. These lesions began on the right upper arm and spread to the neck, upper limb, and groin over the next 10 days, without responding to local treatment. The infant was exclusively breastfed and gaining adequate weight. The umbilical cord separated on day 10 of life. There was no history of fever or decreased feeding. Pregnancy and delivery were uneventful, and there had been no previous abortions. On examination, multiple necrotic ulcerative skin lesions with an erythematous base were observed on the neck, right elbow, groin, and left thigh, along with evolving bullous and papular skin lesions on the chest and trunk. There was no pus discharge from these lesions. Laboratory investigations showed hemoglobin at 8.5 g/dl, total leukocyte count at 85,800/mm3, absolute neutrophil count at 66,066/mm3, band forms at 11%, and platelets at 102,000/mm3. The peripheral smear indicated anisopoikilocytosis and toxic granules. Quantitative C-reactive protein was 85 mg/L, and cerebrospinal fluid values were within normal limits. A chest X-ray suggested right paracardiac pneumonia. Ultrasonography showed no collections in subdiaphragmatic, pelvic, or other sites. Blood culture revealed Acinetobacter species, and a wound swab revealed Proteus vulgaris. The infant was started on antibiotics according to sensitivity results. Screening tests for primary immunodeficiency included quantification of immunoglobulin levels (IgM, IgG, IgE, and IgA), CH50 levels, and nitroblue tetrazolium test, all of which were normal.
test_results: None of the neutrophils in the infant were positive for CD18, CD11a and CD11c with normal levels noted in both parents.

case_report: A 63-year-old Uighur woman presented with a red eye and decreased vision in the right eye for 4 days. The patient visited a primary hospital and received systemic and topical antibiotics for seven days before being referred to our hospital. On admission, she had weak light perception in the right eye, intraocular pressure (IOP) was 65 mmHg, and slit-lamp examination revealed swelling of the eyelids and notable injection of the conjunctiva. The entire cornea was cloudy and edematous, whereas the aqueous humor was milky turbid. No details regarding the iris, pupil, lens, or fundus were visible in the right eye. For the left eye, there were no significant positive findings except for a moderate nucleus, best corrected vision acuity of 20/25, and IOP of 19 mmHg. An ocular B-scan revealed mild vitreous opacity and the absence of other abnormalities in both eyes. The corneal endothelial count was 2448/mm2 in the left eye, and no data were available for the right eye. She received intravenous mannitol, cartels and alphagan eye drops to control the IOP, tobradex, and pranopulin eyedrops were also applied to alleviate the ocular inflammation, the cornea’s edema was slightly reduced.
test_results: Milky aqueous liquid was collected for cytological examination, which confirmed the presence of lens protein-laden macrophages.

case_report: A 13-year-old girl presented with a history of bilateral forearm deformity starting from the age of 5 to 6 years. There was no reported joint pain in the hands, wrist trauma, or similar conditions in the family. The patient was moderately built and significantly shorter than average for her age, with a height of 130 cm (below the 3rd percentile). Measurements included an upper segment of 69 cm, a lower segment of 61 cm, a weight of 35 kg, and a body mass index of 20.71 kg/m2. The arm-to-forearm ratio was 1.78, indicating mesomelia. Secondary sexual characteristics were assessed as Tanner-Whitehouse stage B4 (breast), P4 (pubic hair), and A3 (axillary hair). Her elder brother and parents had normal height and no hand deformities. Laboratory investigations revealed a hemoglobin level of 12.5 g/dl, normal liver and renal function tests, calcium level of 9.0 mg/dl, alkaline phosphatase level of 260 IU, and phosphorus level of 3.5 mg/dl.
test_results: X-ray bilateral wrist showed malformed medial radial epiphysis with dorsal and ulnar shift and with increased length of phalanges.

case_report: A 13-year-old boy presented with difficulty in walking, neck pain, and multiple swellings along with deformities in both upper and lower extremities. Family members reported a gradual onset of multiple swellings starting at age 6, initially appearing in the right hand and progressively worsening. There was no relevant family or treatment history. Examination revealed multiple swellings of varying sizes and shapes on the upper and lower limbs. The patient exhibited a significant shortening of the left lower limb and walked with a short limb, non-assisted gait. Palpation indicated that the swellings were bony hard. Swellings were also observed over the hip, knee, ankle, and feet bilaterally. The left lower limb showed a 2 cm shortening below the trochanter. Chest examination revealed similar swellings over the 6th, 7th, 8th, and 9th ribs bilaterally at the costochondral junction anteriorly. A thoracolumbar scoliosis with right convexity was noted. Movements were restricted in all major peripheral joints (shoulder, knee, elbow, wrist, hip, ankle, hand, and foot) and the cervical spine arc of motion was limited. Pain was present at the extremes of flexion and extension, but there was no tenderness over the cervical spine.
test_results: Plain radiographs showed multiple eccentric, expansile geographic lesions with stippled calcification in the metaphyseal region of the appendicular skeleton and ribs. Computed tomography (CT) revealed similar lesions in the right arch of C1 and C2 with no canal compromise. Histopathological examination of core biopsy revealed hypercellular tumor composed of chondrocytes with mild anisonucleosis with peripheral rim of osteoid deposition suggestive of enchondroma.

case_report: A 51-year-old female reported experiencing fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus in the left ear over a period of 2 years. These symptoms varied throughout the day and were not influenced by posture. The patient did not experience dizziness or vertigo. Additionally, she had morning headaches that resolved within 2 hours of waking up. Physical examination showed a normal otoscopy. The patient underwent three courses of systemic steroids (methylprednisolone: starting at 1 mg per kilogram per day with a descending dosage), which temporarily alleviated the symptoms. However, the symptoms recurred after stopping the steroid treatment. She also received three cycles of intratympanic steroids (0.7 mL methylprednisolone), with symptom improvement noted during the second cycle, coinciding with the initiation of treatment with hydrochlorothiazide/amiloride hydrochloride. Multiple audiometries indicated moderate sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear at low frequencies.
test_results: A hyperintense left cerebellar focal lesion of 19 × 17 × 19 mm on T2-weighted imaging, arising from the junction of the left cerebellar hemisphere, the lateral left wall of the fourth ventricle, and the cerebella vermis. The lesion partially obliterated the Foramen of Luschka, without signs of obstruction. No enhancement with intravenous contrast or vasogenic edema was described.

case_report: A 27-year-old pregnant woman, over four months into her pregnancy, was admitted for genetic counseling and prenatal assessment. She was born at full-term through vaginal delivery after an uneventful pregnancy. Her older sister is healthy. She started walking independently at 18 months. Over time, she experienced worsening symptoms. By age 11, she required assistance to walk, and by age 15, she could no longer stand or walk on her own. At age 22, she began experiencing slow speech, slurred pronunciation, and occasional choking on food. Neurological examination showed proximal muscle strength in the upper limbs as V+/V, and in the lower limbs as I/II. She was unable to straighten her knee, and her lower extremity tendons were hyper-reflexive, with a positive Babinski sign. She had normal intellectual function and no cerebellar, sensory, or autonomic dysfunctions. Routine laboratory tests were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging indicated thoracic spinal cord atrophy. Genomic DNA was extracted from her peripheral blood, and single-nucleotide polymorphism array and karyotyping were performed and verified as normal.
test_results: Finally, only two candidate variants of the SPAST gene (c.1496G>A, p.Arg499His) and NEFH gene (c.289G>T, p.Glu97) were identified in the proband. We then investigated the presence of mutations in the SPAST and NEFH genes in the patient's paternal relatives via Sanger sequencing. This variant had the same amino acid changes as the known pathogenic variant. SPAST mutation is a de novo mutation. This SPAST mutation was not found in the East Asian Population Everyman Database (ExAC) or Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD). The Mutation Taster, Polyphen 2, and SIFT software programs predicted that this SPAST variant as disease-causing, probably damaging, and deleterious. This mutation was located in a conservative site and was present in the functional domain of the AAA + ATPase domain, which is essential for the function and activity of enzymes and is a hotspot of pathogenic variants. Taken together, we identified the ACMG criteria for this mutation as PS1, PM1, PM2, PM6, and PP3, indicating that this variant is pathogenic. Sanger sequencing reconfirmed the presence of the p.Glu97∗ mutation in the NEFH gene, which was heterozygous in four paternal relatives. According to the ACMG guidelines, the c.289G>T mutation in the NEFH gene is a significant unknown mutation site that is associated with autosomal dominant diseases (CMT disease, axonal, type 2CC). Moreover, this variation was not found in ExAC. In gnomAD, the frequency of this variation was 1.81646E − 05; accordingly, PM2 was assigned.

case_report: A 53-year-old male forester and farmer was admitted with a prolonged fever reaching up to 39°C, abdominal pain, diarrhea without vomiting, productive cough, and an 8 kg weight loss. Symptoms began three weeks prior with epigastric pain followed by fever and chills. Initial medical attention was sought at one of the emergency departments of a non-academic tertiary hospital in lower Austria, where he was given supportive measures for viral gastroenteritis and advised to follow up with his general practitioner (GP). Two weeks later, symptoms persisted, and he developed a productive cough and reported an 8 kg weight loss. A chest x-ray, advised by his GP, showed no abnormalities. The patient returned to the hospital, this time to the gastroenterology emergency unit, where he was admitted for further investigation and treatment. His medical history included mild Helicobacter-associated gastritis treated a few months earlier and some previous respiratory infections. He was a non-smoker with low to moderate alcohol consumption and had not traveled outside Europe recently, with past visits to Greece in 2017 and Croatia in 2016. He reported no recent contact with wild animals or slaughter activities but had been working in the forest for the past six weeks without any known tick bites or injuries. On admission, he was neither septic nor jaundiced, with no lymphadenopathy or rash. Heart and lung examinations were normal, and abdominal examination revealed hyperactive bowel sounds. Heart rate and blood pressure were within normal limits. Laboratory results showed elevated leukocyte count (13/nL), platelet count (560/nL), and C-reactive protein (12 mg/dL). Other notable results included gamma-glutamyl transferase (gamma GT) at 108 U/L and bilirubin at 1.5 mg/dL, with other liver and kidney function tests within normal limits, as was procalcitonin. A chest x-ray revealed a discrete pulmonary infiltrate in the right upper lobe without hilar enlargement. Blood cultures were drawn, and serum was sent to a reference laboratory for antibody testing for various infections. PCR tests excluded infections with Rickettsia spp. and Coxiella burnetti, and tuberculosis was ruled out by a negative interferon gamma release assay.
test_results: The antibody titre was 1:80 in the agglutination assay which was classified as negative and the ELISA was positive for IgG (52,6 U/mL, positive cutoff > 15 U/mL) and IgM (145,3 U/mL, positive cutoff > 15 U/mL). The agglutination assay was positive at the titre of 1:640. The ELISA results changed to 91 U/mL for IgG and 322 U/mL for IgM.

case_report: A 53-year-old Chinese male presented with systemic symmetrical dermatitis persisting for over 6 months. Previous treatments with antihistamines and topical steroid creams were ineffective, and the patient experienced significant nocturnal pruritus. Prior laboratory tests showed no abnormalities. The patient had a history of allergic rhinitis and long-term exposure to chemical substances due to his occupation as an engineer. His children had a history of allergic dermatitis. Initial laboratory results revealed a total serum immunoglobulin E (IgE) level of 604.61 KU/L, a leukocyte count of 3.7 × 10^9/L with 35.50% lymphocytes, 41.40% neutrophils, 8.3% monocytes, 14.50% eosinophils, hemoglobin of 144 g/L, and a platelet count of 155 × 10^9/L. The patient was treated with antihistamines, Tripterygium wilfordii, and oral prednisone (20 mg/d). After 1.5 months, the patient reported relief from itching and a reduction in rash, although new rashes continued to develop. Upon re-evaluation, laboratory results showed a leukocyte count of 8.0 × 10^9/L with 46.70% lymphocytes, 21.90% neutrophils, 15.40% monocytes, hemoglobin of 134 g/L, and a platelet count of 190 × 10^9/L.
test_results: A peripheral blood smear showed the normal total leukocyte count with 33% blasts, and Auer corpuscles can be seen in certain cells. The bone marrow smear indicated the active granulocyte proliferation, the original granulocyte type I + II accounting for 50.4% with the Auer corpuscles in cells and the promyelocyte accounting for 0.8%. No chromosomal abnormalities or fusion genes were detected. Immunohistochemistry of the skin biopsy showed hyperplasia of lymphoid tissue, CD34(−), CD117(−), MPO (+), CD43(++), CD20(±), CD3(+), and Ki-67(+ scattered).

case_report: A 50-year-old male with a 10-year history of diabetes presented with poorly controlled blood sugar levels and cataract. Notable physical features included coarse facial characteristics, frontal bossing, congenital left facial nerve palsy with facial synkinesia, syndactyly of the left 3rd and 4th fingers, a short right 4th finger, and hypoplastic nails. The patient was born to parents who were consanguineously married. Additionally, his elder brother's granddaughter had undergone surgery for syndactyly. Examination of other family members was not possible.
test_results: Radiographs showed dense skull, pelvis, lumbar spine, and fingers.

case_report: A 40-year-old Chinese Han-ethnic man exhibited swelling in the ankles and eyelids, proteinuria with a urinary protein excretion of 3.92 g/24 h, and elevated blood pressure for one month. His father had passed away at the age of 60 years due to nephrotic syndrome. Laboratory tests indicated the absence of monoclonal gammopathy in both serum and urine. The patient had low albumin levels (31.0 g/L), normal serum creatinine (69.30 μmol/L), and reduced plasma HDL levels (0.50 mmol/L). Physical examination did not reveal macroglossia or skin bleeding, but abdominal ultrasonography showed an enlarged liver (15.7 cm) and spleen (13.7 cm). Electrocardiogram findings included sinus bradycardia, high voltage in the left ventricle, and flat T waves, while the echocardiogram results were normal.
test_results: The renal biopsy showed there were 55 glomeruli in the specimen for light microscopy (LM), and extensive amyloid deposits exclusively in the glomeruli were identified, which produced the apple-green birefringence of Congo red staining under polarized light. No amyloid deposit was identified in the tubulointerstitium and vascular walls. Routine IF examination showed negative staining for immunoglobulins, complements, and light chains (κ, λ). EM demonstrated randomly arranged fibrils with a diameter of 8–12 nm deposited in mesangium and subendothelial area. The IHC typing of renal amyloid initially using an incomplete panel of antibodies directed against light chains (κ, λ), amyloid A, and fibrinogen Aα chain was performed, and a preliminary diagnosis of probably AFib was considered according to the weak positive staining of fibrinogen Aα and its characteristic feature of exclusive glomerular amyloid deposition. Then we have performed a detailed IHC study using 8 types of the common systemic amyloid precursors. It showed a strong and uniform positive staining for ApoA-I, and weak, spotty staining for fibrinogen Aα, in the glomerular amyloid deposits in case 1. The IHC for lysozyme, transthyretin, Lect2, or AA were all negative. Double IF labeling for ApoA-I and fibrinogen Aα chain showed a strong and even staining for ApoA-I, but uneven staining for fibrinogen Aα chain in the glomerular amyloid deposits. The coexistence of ApoA-I and fibrinogen Aα chain in the majority of amyloid deposits was observed in the merged image, which suggested a mixed type of both ApoA-I and fibrinogen Aα chain in this patient. We have performed the LMD/MS analysis according to the previous method. It showed large spectra of Apolipoprotein E protein and serum Amyloid P component ranging from 27 to 118, which are common constituents of amyloid. The most abundant peptides detected was ApoA-I with 424 spectra, 36 unique peptides for 79.78% coverage of ApoA-I, but the content of fibrinogen Aα chain was quite a few with only 20 spectra, 15 unique peptides for 26.55% coverage of fibrinogen Aα. Genetic analysis showed a heterozygous mutation in c.220 T > C substitution in the APOA1 gene, leading to the replacement of tryptophan by arginine at residue 74 (p. Trp74Arg). No gene mutation of fibrinogen Aα chain was detected in this patient.

case_report: A 73-year-old male was admitted on September 21, 2015, presenting with recurrent fatigue over the past year. His medical history includes type 2 diabetes diagnosed 18 years ago and chronic kidney disease diagnosed 4 years ago. He has been taking compound α-keto acid (2520 mg three times daily, containing approximately 600 mg of calcium) for the past 4 years. Six years ago, he was found to have osteoporosis and has since been on Caltrate D (600 mg calcium) and Alphacalcidol (0.5 μg) daily. The onset of fatigue began one year ago.
test_results: Laboratory tests showed serum calcium elevated to 3.41 mmol/L. After stopping Caltrate D and Alphacalcidol, it fluctuated between 2.24 and 2.93 mmol/L. Two months ago, he felt fatigue again and was referred to endocrinology department. Laboratory tests showed elevated serum calcium level (3.03 mmol). No other clinical significant changes were found in thyroid function, blood gas analysis, immunologic test, protein electrophoresis, tumor markers, ACTH, and plasma total cortisol levels. We then comprehensively reviewed his laboratory reports in recent years. We found his serum calcium began to raise at the end of 2013, as indicated by suppressed PTH (serum calcium 2.67 mmol/L, PTH 0.76 pmol/L), and then raised up to 3.41 mmol/L in 2014. After calcium and vitamin D restriction, his serum calcium fluctuated between 2.24 and 2.93 mmol/L, and PTH were consistently suppressed (from 0.79 to 0.82 pmol/L). Further evaluation showed that his urine calcium output decreased (1.63–2.51, reference value 2.5–7.5 mmol/24 hours) when serum calcium increased. Meanwhile, his serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D, bALP, and CTX were all in low levels. No specific signs were found by DEXA, chest and abdominal computed tomography, and bone scintigraphy.

case_report: A 63-year-old woman reported difficulty walking that began 5 years prior. Within a year, she experienced recurrent unprovoked falls. After 3 years, she was unable to walk independently. Treatment with levodopa/carbidopa (750 mg/75 mg) showed no effect. Initial examination revealed normal cognition with mild bradyphrenia and slurred speech. Horizontal and vertical eye movements were normal, but there was impaired convergence and horizontal square wave jerks (SWJs). There were no signs of nuchal dystonia, limb tremor, rigidity, spasticity, or limb ataxia. Additionally, there were no indications of peripheral sensory or motor neuropathy. However, she exhibited severe posture and gait disorders. She had a broad-based stance and a tendency to fall backward with eye closure, and she actually fell during the pull backward test if not supported by the examiner. Her gait was wide-based and short-stepped with reduced trunk rotation. Despite the instability, there was no freezing of gait.
test_results: The atrophy of the midbrain and superior cerebellar peduncles was seen on MRI images. Mild striatal dopamine deficiency was found on dopamine transporter imaging. Elevated 18F-PM-PBB3 binding, implying regional accumulation of tau fibrils, was observed in the brainstem, subthalamic nucleus, and basal ganglia by PET scanning.

case_report: A 55-year-old female presented with brownish macules and papules located on the neck, inframammary area, lower abdomen, and thighs, which have been present for a year. These skin lesions exhibited a positive Darier's sign. The patient experienced occasional episodes of epigastric pain, sweating, dizziness, diarrhea, and headache. There was no history of hospitalization for severe allergic reactions or drug allergies. Dermoscopy revealed a pigment network and a light-brownish blot. Laboratory tests including complete blood count, liver function tests, kidney function tests, and tryptase levels were all within normal ranges. Abdominal ultrasonography also showed normal results.
test_results: A biopsy taken from an abdominal lesion showed hyperpigmentation of the basal layer and dermal grouping of lymphocytes and mast cells around vessels.

case_report: A 52-year-old Chinese man was admitted to the hospital following two cerebral infarctions. The initial cause for hospitalization was a sudden onset of speech disorder. Physical examination revealed symptoms similar to Broca’s aphasia. Laboratory tests showed a coagulation disorder, with a decrease in plasma fibrinogen levels as measured by the Clauss method, an increase in fibrinogen plasma concentration detected by ELISA, and prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and thrombin time (TT). Brain imaging revealed ischemic changes in multiple brain regions. The patient was treated with aspirin, clopidogrel, and atorvastatin. While short-term treatment improved his speech disorder, it did not prevent the recurrence of cerebral infarction. A subsequent ischemic stroke resulted in mild aphasia and weakness in the right upper extremity.
test_results: Coagulation tests indicated a coagulation disorder, which was characterized by a decrease in the plasma level of Fib as determined by the Clauss method, an increase in Fib plasma concentration as detected by ELISA, and prolongation of PT and TT. Genetic testing identified a rare heterozygous missense variant FGG c.952G>A (rs267606810) in the patient and his asymptomatic sister, both of whom exhibited the same alterations in Fib, characterized by reduced functional levels (Clauss method) but increased antigenic protein (ELISA assay).

case_report: A 58-year-old white male presented with numerous warty growths on his hands and feet. These lesions began appearing at the age of eight and have progressively increased in size over time. The patient has a history of an unspecified arrhythmia but is not on any medication. Family history indicates that the patient's father had similar skin lesions. Dermatological examination revealed multiple brownish, flat-topped warty plaques on the hands and feet, along with nail dystrophy.
test_results: Biopsy of the lesions revealed irregular epithelial hyperplasia, hyperkeratosis and papillomatosis.

case_report: A 14-year-old male, weighing 45 kg, was transferred to our clinic for further evaluation after being found to have pericardial effusion at a provincial hospital. Initial symptoms included fever and left shoulder pain. Physical examination revealed a reduction in the intensity of cardiac sounds and an elevated heart rate. Notably, the patient did not exhibit arthralgia or abdominal pain at any point during the clinical course. Three weeks before this event, the patient had an upper respiratory tract infection, which was treated with ibuprofen.
test_results: Echocardiography revealed a moderate pericardial effusion and a mild bilateral pleural effusion. Biological investigations showed the white blood cell count was 19,670/µL, the neutrophils count was 16.8/µL, the lymphocytes count was 810/µL, and there were high levels of inflammatory markers in the plasma tests: the C-reactive protein (CRP) level was 131 mg/L, the erythrocytes sedimentation rate (ESR) was 72 mm/h, the rheumatoid factor was positive (20UI/mL, normal value, NV < 14 UI/mL), and the ferritin level was high at 380.3 ng/mL (NV = 14–152 ng/mL). The complement fractions (C3, C4) were normal; autoantibodies were not detected; and the Quantiferon TB Gold, tuberculin skin test, and antibody work-up for common viral infections were all negative. An immunogram showed hypoIgG (652 mg/dL, NV 720–1700 mg/dL). Echocardiography revealed a circumferential pericardial effusion of 9–15 mm. Furthermore, a left pleural effusion was associated. The ECG showed PR segment depression and ST elevation in the inferior leads. In addition to a negative antinuclear antibodies (ANAs) profile, a Sanger sequencing for the MEFV gene was performed without any mutations identified. Biological investigations showed an elevated interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) level in the patient’s blood, with a 10 pg/mL recorded value (normal values < 5 pg/mL). Next-generation sequencing (NGS) performed by the Invitae Corporation, San Francisco, USA, revealed a previously unreported de novo missense mutation in the NLRP12 gene (c.1264G > A).
diagnosis: Autoinflammatory Recurrent Pericarditis Associated with a New NLRP12 Mutation

case_report: A Mexican newborn female, the second child of healthy 24-year-old parents with no family history of multiple congenital anomalies or mental retardation syndromes, was born at 37 weeks of pregnancy via cesarean section following an uneventful pregnancy. Apgar scores were 4 and 7, with a birth weight of 3265 grams, length of 49 cm, and occipitofrontal circumference (OFC) of 34 cm, all within the 50th percentile. Clinical examination revealed micrognathia, low-set ears, a short neck and thorax, and abdominal distention. A significant thoracolumbar defect measuring 7 x 9 x 4.5 cm, divided by a septum, was noted along with a congenital hemangioma. The hemangioma was greyish in color with raised edges, surrounded by a pale halo and multiple tiny telangiectasias, consistent with a rapidly involuting congenital hemangioma. No genital or limb anomalies were observed.
test_results: Radiographic findings included: narrow thorax, right hemithorax with incomplete synostosis of posterior costal arches, asymmetry and decreased intercostal space of ribs 1-7, agenesis of ribs 8-9 and 11-12, left hemithorax with asymmetry of ribs 1-2, asymmetry and decreased intercostal space of ribs 3-5, incomplete synostosis of posterior costal arches of ribs 4-5, significant increase in the intercostal space between ribs 5-6, and agenesis of ribs 8-12. Moreover, T7-T8 block vertebrae, T9-T10 hemivertebrae, irregular morphology of T6 and T11-T12, L1 hemivertebra, and thoracolumbar scoliosis were detected. A MRI revealed cerebellar displacement with tonsillar herniation of 12mm below the foramen magnum, and a thoracolumbar meningomyelocele from T6 to L3 with septate cystic lesions.

case_report: A female infant was delivered at 41 weeks to a 21-year-old G2P1T1 Mixteco mother via vaginal delivery, which was complicated by late decelerations and a tight nuchal cord. APGAR scores were 3 at 1 minute and 6 at 5 and 10 minutes. At birth, the infant's weight was 2.915 kg (5.8%), length was 51.5 cm (43.6%), and head circumference was 32.5 cm (2.6%). The infant was symmetrically small for gestational age and exhibited multiple congenital anomalies including persistent pupillary membrane, dysmorphic facial features, nocturnal lagophthalmos, microcephaly, and large fontanelles. Additional findings included absence of bilateral red reflex, nonreactive unequal light reflex, microtia, exophthalmos, high arched palate, redundant neck skin, large abdomen, and inverted feet. Laboratory tests showed hexacosanoic acid (C26:0) at 7.58 µmol/L, docosanoic acid (C22:0) at 12.79 µmol/L, and tetracosanoic acid (C24:0) at 22.27 µmol/L, with elevated C26/C22 and C24/C22 ratios. Electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and creatinine levels were normal. The hepatic panel revealed total bilirubin at 1.7 mg/dL, direct bilirubin at 2.5 mg/dL, aspartate transaminase (AST) at 557 units/L, alanine transaminase (ALT) at 215 units/L, gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) at 120 units/L, and alkaline phosphatases at 430 units/L. The infant presented with jaundice on day one, which resolved within a few weeks, and respiratory insufficiency initially thought to be due to transient tachypnea of the newborn (TTN), later considered to be due to hypotonia, respiratory muscle weakness, and inadequate respiratory drive. On day 2, total parenteral nutrition (TPN) was discontinued and feeds were initiated. An eye examination showed findings consistent with Axenfeld-Reiger syndrome. The infant tested positive for adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD) without the ABCD1 mutation. Enzyme activity tests for alpha-glucosidase and alpha-L-iduronidase were positive, ruling out lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency (Pompe disease) and mucopolysaccharidosis I disorder. A chest X-ray indicated a mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette, consistent with TTN and cardiomegaly. Ultrasound revealed a large atrial septal defect and patent ductus arteriosus with a bi-directional shunt, along with normal liver, gallbladder, and biliary findings. A brain ultrasound showed small bilateral third ventricle cysts.
test_results: Genetic testing confirmed a pathogenic homozygous variant of undetermined significance in PEX6 c.1409G>C (p.Gly470Ala).

case_report: A 42-year-old African American woman with a history of hypertension, morbid obesity, and obstructive sleep apnea arrived at the emergency department with a 12-hour history of left-sided abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Her current medications included hydrochlorothiazide, acetaminophen, ibuprofen, and lisinopril. She is married, has three children, and has no history of smoking, alcohol consumption, or illicit drug use. She had traveled to Ghana for 5 days, one month prior to her visit, and reported no symptoms during or after the trip until the onset of her current symptoms. She took her first dose of lisinopril 5 mg 12 hours before her symptoms began and had no prior use of ACE inhibitors or angiotensin II receptor antagonists. Upon arrival, she described crampy abdominal pain radiating to the left side, which was constant but varied in intensity. She also experienced persistent nausea and one episode of vomiting. She had one normal bowel movement within 24 hours of presentation and denied recent diarrhea, constipation, or contact with sick individuals. Her vital signs included a blood pressure of 187/122, pulse of 81, temperature of 36.7°C, respirations of 20, and an O2 saturation of 100% on room air. Physical examination revealed an uncomfortable patient, occasionally sitting up and writhing in bed with her eyes closed. Abdominal examination showed tenderness in the left epigastric area and left mid-abdomen, with mild left suprapubic tenderness, hyperactive bowel sounds, but no rebound tenderness or significant guarding. In the emergency department, she received intravenous fluids, pain relief, and anti-nausea medications. Laboratory results showed an unremarkable complete blood count. Her C1 esterase inhibitor functional assay and C4 concentration were within normal limits. Stool studies were negative for infectious diseases.
test_results: CT of the abdomen showed segmented target-like enhancement of a dilated loop of ileum with relatively high attenuation ascites.
diagnosis: Isolated intestinal type angioedema due to ACE-inhibitor therapy

case_report: A 14-year-old male was admitted due to severe vomiting and frequent episodes of tonsillitis. Physical examination revealed yellowing of the sclera and skin. According to his father, the patient had exhibited jaundice since birth. The father also reported that the patient's 18-year-old paternal cousin and the grandparents of both affected individuals exhibited similar symptoms. Additionally, the patient's parents are first cousins. Both the patient and his cousin had normal developmental milestones and performed well academically. Further clinical examination was conducted, and the patient's hematological report was normal.
test_results: Total serum bilirubin was 16.1 mg/dL (unconjugated bilirubin 15.6 mg/dL), aspartate aminotransferase 18 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 19 U/L, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 14 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 16.4 U/L. The patient was negative for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and anti-hepatitis C virus (HCV) antibody. The ultrasonography indicated normal liver with no biliary obstruction and raised serum bilirubin with liver function tests (LFTs) in the physiological range.

case_report: In April 2017, a 49-year-old man was admitted to our hospital due to an unsteady walk and speech difficulties for the past year. In October 2016, a cervical spine issue was considered for his walking instability. Brain MRI showed no significant abnormalities (Fig. a-f), while cervical MRI revealed a cervical disc herniation with spinal cord compression (Fig. g-h). He underwent cervical discectomy with cervical interbody fusion cage and plate-screw fixation (Fig. i), but his postoperative gait instability persisted. He had no history of smoking or drinking. His mother became paralyzed at age 50 and was bedridden until her death a few years later. His brother experienced an unsteady gait around age 46. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 133/74 mm Hg, clear consciousness, vague speech, impaired cognition (Mini-Mental State Examination score=19/30), decreased muscle strength in both lower extremities (4/5), and cerebellar ataxic gait; no other positive signs were noted. Laboratory analysis in 2017 showed normal complete blood count, urinalysis, and routine stool examination (Table). Serum creatinine, myocardial enzyme, electrolyte, C-reactive protein, thyroid-stimulating hormone, fasting blood glucose, glycosylated hemoglobin, and vitamin B12 levels were normal. Fibrinogen level was slightly low (1.95 g/L) and direct bilirubin level was slightly elevated (3.8 μmol/L). Antinuclear, thyroperoxidase, and thyroglobulin antibodies were negative. Urinary system and abdominal ultrasonography showed no significant abnormalities. Chest radiograph and brain computed tomography scan (Fig. j) showed no significant abnormalities. Routine tests and biochemistry indicators of cerebrospinal fluid were normal. The treatment plan included improving cerebrocirculation with intravenous vinpocetine (20 mg/d) and oral butylphthalide (0.6 g/d), as well as cerebrometabolism with oxiracetam (4 g/d); symptomatic treatment was also provided. His symptoms showed no significant improvement, and he was discharged on day 9 with a modified Rankin Scale score of 2.
test_results: He had a heterozygous mutation in exon 2 of the PRNP gene, positioned on chromosome 20. Specifically, he had a missense mutation of substitution of cytosine with thymine at gene loci 305, which caused proline-to-leucine substitution (P102L) on the protein polypeptide chain.

case_report: A 20-year-old male presented with fever and shortness of breath that began the previous night. He was not taking any medications, including over-the-counter drugs, Chinese herbal medicines, or supplements. He had no history of dust inhalation and did not keep pets. He had started smoking 20 cigarettes of HC per day 6 months prior and increased to 40 cigarettes a day 2 weeks before hospitalization by purchasing a second device for smoking HC. Physical examination revealed fine crackles in both sides of the posterior chest, with no wheezes, skin eruptions, or arthritis. Chest radiograph showed bilateral opacities, and high-resolution computed tomography of the chest revealed bilateral infiltrations, smooth interlobular septal thickening, and pleural effusion. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 15,690/mm3, with 88% neutrophils, 7% lymphocytes, and 1% eosinophils. Routine blood chemistry tests were within normal range, except for C-reactive protein levels of 10.12 IU/L mg/dL. Immunoglobulin E levels were within normal range. Arterial blood gas analysis, performed with the patient breathing 10 L oxygen via a non-rebreathing mask, showed PaO2 at 90.3 Torr, PaCO2 at 38.0 Torr, and pH at 7.412. The BAL returns were not increasingly haemorrhagic.
test_results: The cells recovered from the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) were 8.6 × 105/mL, which comprised 60% eosinophils, 20% lymphocytes, 15% macrophages, and 5% neutrophils. Microorganisms including fungi were not identified in the BALF culture.

case_report: A 27-year-old woman presented with a submucosal mass located in the right soft palate, which did not cause any symptoms. A plain CT scan revealed a soft tissue nodule approximately 1.5 cm in diameter in the right side of the soft palate. The lesion exhibited significant and uniform enhancement after the administration of contrast material. There was no indication of bone invasion or enlarged cervical lymph nodes. The patient received a wide local excision.
test_results: Microscopic examination revealed hypercellular, haphazard spindle cell proliferation with a small amount of nuclear atypia, abundant capillary vessels and invasion of mucinous gland. The specimen showed intense positive staining for CD34 and vimentin, partial positive staining for Bcl-2, CD99, EMA and SMA, weak positive staining for S-100, but negative for desmin.
diagnosis: Solitary Fibrous Tumor  with malignant characteristics

case_report: A 7-year-old boy visited the outpatient department due to pain in the right knee and difficulty standing from a sitting position. The patient had no symptoms 22 months prior. The pain was localized to the front of the right knee and occurred during activities such as climbing stairs, long-distance walking, running, and athletic activities. The symptoms sometimes lasted for several hours and caused difficulty sleeping at night. There was no history of trauma. The child was otherwise healthy with normal development. Routine blood tests were normal. Swelling was observed over the right knee, which was slightly warmer compared to the other knee. Extreme flexion of the right knee was restricted and painful. Patellar mobility was normal without any dislocation on either side. The hip examination was normal.
test_results: Radiologically, the irregularity, fragmentation, and sclerosis were seen in the right patella.
diagnosis: Osteochondrosis of primary center of patella

case_report: A thirteen-year-old female patient was admitted to the emergency department of another medical center one week ago due to respiratory distress and cyanosis. Her condition worsened, leading to pneumonia and respiratory failure, and she was subsequently referred to our hospital for increasing respiratory distress. Upon admission to our intensive care unit (ICU), the patient was drowsy, exhibited shallow breathing, and was cyanotic. Blood gas analysis revealed respiratory acidosis. She was intubated and placed on assisted ventilation. The patient's medical history indicated that her parents were unrelated and healthy, she was born at term weighing 3500 grams, and she had two healthy siblings. At age 3, she began overeating and rapidly gained weight, leading to multiple referrals to different medical centers. She had her first menstruation at age 12. Records from another hospital at age 10 showed her body weight was 51 kg, relative body mass index (RBMI) was 166%, BMI was 31.62 kg/m2, height was 127 cm, and height standard deviation score (SDS) was -3.04. She appeared obese and was at Tanner Stage 2 of puberty. Acanthosis nigricans was noted in the axilla and neck, and coldness in hands and feet suggestive of Raynaud phenomenon was observed.
