Other system findings were normal. Previous records indicated hypernatremia and a diagnosis of diabetes insipidus (DI) without polyuria and polydipsia. No medication for DI was given, but levothyroxine was started for primary hypothyroidism. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was normal, but bromocriptine was initiated for hyperprolactinemia. Metformin was prescribed for euglycemic hyperinsulinism noted in the oral glucose tolerance test. The patient also had cold hands and feet with discoloration, especially in the cold, consistent with Raynaud phenomenon. Obesity remained uncontrolled during follow-up. Two years before admission, her school performance declined, with decreased concentration and drowsiness becoming more evident in the past 10 days. Upon admission to our ICU, her body temperature was 39.2 ˚C, heart rate was 117/min, blood pressure was 105/60 mmHg, body weight was 69 kg, height was 145 cm (height SDS -2.28), BMI was 32.82 kg/m2, and RBMI was 159%. She had a round plethoric face, buffalo neck, and umbilical hernia. Mild acanthosis nigricans was present in the neck and armpits. Pubertal stage was at Tanner Stage 4, and other system examinations were normal. During follow-up, her condition improved, and she was extubated on the 10th day of hospitalization. Post-extubation, acidosis resolved, but PCO2 levels remained high. Acute phase reactants were negative, but fever persisted without an identifiable cause. Blood and tracheal aspirate cultures were negative. Fever continued during and after ICU stay, suspected to be of central origin. Complete blood count, renal, and hepatic function tests were normal, but hypernatremia was detected (Na: 151 mmol/L). Urine density ranged between 1015 and 1017, serum osmolality was normal, and no polyuria was observed. Megaloblastic changes were found in her peripheral blood smear, and vitamin B12 deficiency was detected. She was referred to our Pediatric Endocrinology Department for reevaluation. Some laboratory results included normal serum ACTH (21.01 pg/mL) and cortisol (14.07 µg/dL) levels, excluding Cushing’s syndrome. Prolactin levels were moderately high. Serum insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) was 32.4 ng/mL (-7.92 SD) and IGF binding protein-3 (IGFBP-3) was 1500 ng/mL (-6.54 SD). GH stimulation test showed inadequate GH response (L-DOPA-induced peak GH response: 0.08 ng/mL), consistent with GH deficiency. Left hand-wrist X-ray indicated closed epiphysis and bone age of 15 years. Metformin was discontinued due to normal blood glucose and insulin levels. The patient had secondary amenorrhea, and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism was identified in laboratory and imaging tests, leading to the initiation of sex hormone replacement therapy. Cranial MRI revealed cerebral atrophy secondary to dilation in the second, third, and lateral ventricles, with a normal-appearing pituitary gland.
test_results: Genetic analysis was performed and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) test was negative for Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS).
Orpha_name: Rapid-onset childhood obesity-hypothalamic dysfunction-hypoventilation-autonomic dysregulation syndrome

case_report: A 13-year-old girl has experienced recurrent infections since infancy. Key events in her medical history are as follows: At 45 days old, she had an exaggerated wound at the BCG vaccine site on her right deltoid, treated with antibiotics and wound care. At 14 months, she had bilateral enlarged cervical nodes with constitutional symptoms for one month, an ESR of 130 mm/hr, and fine needle aspiration (FNA) from her lymph nodes revealed caseous necrosis. Her HIV test was negative, and she was treated with first-line anti-TB drugs (2RHZE/4RH). At 3 years old, she presented with a cough and fever for 3 weeks, generalized lymphadenopathy, and left posterior lung field crepitation. Laboratory results showed leukocytosis with a left shift and raised ESR. Chest X-ray revealed left paratracheal and basal ill-defined opacity. Tests for malaria, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were negative. Gene expert MTB/RIF test and acid-fast staining from gastric aspirate did not show Mycobacterium Tuberculosis, but FNA from lymph nodes showed caseous necrosis. She was treated again with first-line anti-TB (2RHZE/4RH). At 4 years and 3 months, she had right lower extremity pain, limping, and swelling over her head. Physical examination revealed boggy swelling over her scalp, multiple enlarged cervical lymph nodes, and anterior chest wall swelling at two sites. ESR was 124 mm/hr. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepato-splenomegaly and multiple enlarged iliac groups of lymph nodes bilaterally. FNA from the chest wall abscess and lymph nodes suggested features of tuberculosis. She was treated with second-line anti-TB drugs for 2 years. At 7 years and 9 months, she presented with right-side limping, loss of appetite, weight loss, fever, and occasional cough. Physical examination showed boggy swellings over her scalp, acne-like rashes on the back, trunk, and arms, and shortening of the right lower limb with limited range of movement. MRI showed lumbosacral multifocal osteomyelitis, unilateral sacroiliac arthritis with adjacent epidural abscess, and lytic lesions over the left femoral head and neck. Skull X-ray was normal. CRP and parathyroid hormone were within normal limits. Rheumatoid factor (RF) and antinuclear antibody (ANA) were negative. FNAC from the scalp lesion showed caseous granulomatous inflammation, and a biopsy from the skin lesion suggested lupus vulgaris. She was treated with anti-TB for the fourth time (2RHZE/10RH). Despite treatment, indurated plaque skin lesions became cauliform-like, and the boggy scalp lesion became crusted; another skin biopsy suggested juvenile xanthogranuloma. Other blood tests and ophthalmologic evaluation were normal, and she completed her anti-TB course. At 11 years and 3 months, she developed right flank pain with swelling, low-grade fever, and existing scalp and skin lesions. Vital signs were stable, with abdominal tenderness and limited range of movement of the right hip joint. She had a yellowish-crusted plaque with an indurated erythematous background on the right side of the anterior scalp and forehead, and a well-demarcated skin-colored indurated plaque with a fine scale on the right side of the cheek, chin, chest, and abdomen. Abdominal ultrasound and MRI suggested right-side unilateral sacroiliac arthritis with adjacent paraspinal abscess. ESR was raised with leukocytosis and anemia. FNAC from lymph nodes showed a granulomatous lesion with caseous necrosis.
test_results: Blood PCR showed the Mycobacterium Tuberculosis complex.
diagnosis: Mendelian Susceptibility to Mycobacterial Diseases  due to autosomal dominant interferon gamma receptor 1  defect
Orpha_name: Autosomal dominant mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial diseases due to partial IFNgammaR1 deficiency

case_report: A 35-year-old female patient presented with multiple pruritic follicular keratotic and spinous papules initially over the wrists and forearms, gradually spreading to the whole body, excluding the face, palms, and soles over the past 10 years. This was followed by the development of hyperkeratotic violaceous itchy plaques over the malar area of the face, accompanied by madrosis and scarring alopecia of the scalp over the past 4 years. The scalp exhibited multiple dilated follicular orifices plugged with keratotic debris, marked perifollicular violaceous hyperpigmentation, and complete hair loss. Axillary and pubic hair were sparse with a history of recurrent episodic shedding over the last 3 years. Violaceous pigmentation was observed over the buccal and gingival mucosae, along with melanonychia in the fingernails. There was no history of photosensitivity or similar complaints in the family. Routine investigations, including viral markers for hepatitis B and C and serum antinuclear antibody levels, were normal.
test_results: Histopathological examination of hyperkeratotic alopecic plaque on scalp showed dilated follicular infundibula, with basket-weave hyperkeratosis in upper portion and compact hyperkeratotic plug in lower portion. Epithelium lining the follicular infundibulum showed marked hypergranulosis along with presence of vacuolar degeneration and apoptotic keratinocytes. Moderately dense perifollicular lymphocytic inflammation, lichenoid interface dermatitis and loss of sebaceous glands with follicular scarring. Biopsy from the follicular papules on body also revealed similar histopathological features.

case_report: An 11-year-old girl presented with shortened index, middle, and little fingers on both hands. Her overall growth and development were consistent with general Chinese standards. There were no reported abnormalities during prenatal development or birth. No family history of shortened fingers was noted. Examination of the hands showed that the thumb, index, middle, and little fingers were short, while the ring finger appeared normal and was the longest. The proximal phalanx of the index and middle fingers on both hands deviated towards the ulnar side, and the distal phalanx of the left little finger deviated towards the radial side. The feet were unaffected. Joint range of motion was normal, and no other skeletal or non-skeletal abnormalities were observed. Written informed consent for the publication of this report and any identifying images or data was obtained from the patient and her parents.
test_results: Radiographs showed shortening of the 1st and 3rd metacarpals, 2nd and 5th middle phalanges, and 3rd proximal phalanges on both sides. Fibrous connections may be observed in the 1st metacarpophalangeal joint and between the 3rd middle phalanx and a corn-like element. The patient showed a slightly shortened 1st metacarpal, the length ratio of which to the 4th metacarpal was 0.74, and the 4th metacarpal was shorter than its predicted length (4th:2nd = 0.804 for this patient). Gene sequencing confirmed a gene mutation in the region coding the potential propeptide domain of the GDF5 protein, with deletion of one base in the coding region 349G (c.349delG) on chromosome 20. This mutation resulted in termination of translation after translating six amino acids from codon 117 (p.A117fs*6).

case_report: A 55-year-old woman was referred to the neurologist due to worsening cognitive issues, including forgetfulness and reduced concentration over the past year. In the week leading up to her admission, she experienced significant headaches along with auditory and visual hallucinations. Upon admission, she exhibited aphasia, particularly with word-finding difficulties. She was disoriented and demonstrated impaired memory and visuospatial abilities. There were no signs of pyramidal or extrapyramidal involvement, myoclonic jerks, or cerebellar symptoms.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed hyperintensity of the white matter, but no atrophy or abnormalities in the basal ganglia. The 14-3-3 test in cerebrospinal fluid was positive. An electroencephalogram (EEG) showed generalized slowing with a typical pattern of periodic synchronous wave complexes.

case_report: A 4-year-old female child presented with blue eyes and absence of tear and nasal secretion production since birth. She was also unable to hear or speak since birth. There was no redness of eyes, photophobia, or blepharospasm. She was born from a nonconsanguineous marriage, following an uneventful pregnancy and full-term normal vaginal delivery. There was no history of drug usage, both topical and oral. Maternal history was unremarkable, and the child had received complete immunizations appropriate for her age. Family history was unremarkable. On examination, she responded to light. Retinoscopy under atropinization showed +6 DS in the right eye and +4 DS in the left eye. Gross and anterior-segment examinations revealed a white forelock that was dyed, synophrys, a slightly flat nasal bridge, large eyelashes, tongue tie, smooth philtrum, and inadequate tear meniscus (<0.5 cm). Her interpupillary distance was 5 cm and inter innercanthal distance was 2.5 cm, indicating no telecanthus. Schirmer's type 1 test showed 7 mm and 6 mm wetting in the right and left eyes, respectively (moderate-grade dry eyes). There was no tear dribbling when crying. Blinking rate was approximately 15 times per minute. Corneal sensation was normal. There was no corneal opacity, poliosis, hypopigmented patches on the body, dry mouth, or limb abnormalities. Both eyes had brilliantly blue irises. The pupils were of normal size and reacted normally to light both directly and consensually. Fundus examination revealed normal-sized discs in both eyes, a cup-disc ratio of 0.3 with peripapillary hyperpigmentation, and diffuse retinal hypopigmentation, exposing the choroidal vasculature.
test_results: Ear, nose, and throat evaluation by otoacoustic emission revealed abnormality up to the level of outer hair cells. Auditory steady-state response showed profound hearing loss. Brainstem-evoked response audiometry showed bilateral profound hearing loss. Impedence audiometry demonstrated bilateral A-type waves with absent reflex, and free-field audiometry showed bilateral moderate-to-severe hearing loss. Magnetic resonance imaging orbit revealed no lacrimal gland dysgenesis, but there was associated vestibular and cochlear dysplasia.

case_report: In June 2016, a 34-year-old woman from Hunan Province in South China visited our hospital with notable weakness throughout her body, muscle wasting, bilateral facial muscle paralysis, reduced voice volume, difficulty swallowing, and occasional twitching of facial muscles. These symptoms began in 2007 following the birth of her first child and progressively worsened, especially after the birth of her second child in 2011. Initially, she was diagnosed with gastritis at local hospitals. By 2012, she experienced increased difficulty swallowing and speaking.
test_results: The result showed extensive neurogenic damage, supported by reduced amplitude on musculus facialis, all limb muscles, and the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

case_report: A 21-month-old male exhibited reduced muscle tone and overall developmental delay. At this age, he could sit with support, did not speak but understood the word 'no' and could wave to say goodbye. He experienced occasional upward eye movements, head drops, hand twitching, and episodes of staring. Continuous EEG monitoring showed an abnormal slow background with multi-focal spike and wave activity, but no electrographic changes were associated with the abnormal movements. Brain MRI at 9 months revealed delayed myelination and a mild increase in T2 signal in the bilateral thalamus. CSF studies for neurotransmitters (excluding GABA) and amino acids were normal. Whole exome sequencing identified compound heterozygous variants of uncertain significance (VUS) in the ABAT gene (c.454C > T, p.P152S and c.1393G > C, p.G465R).
test_results: CSF GABA elevated at 247 nmol/L (normal range 17–67 nmol/L).

case_report: A 14-year-old boy, born to non-consanguineous parents with a normal perinatal history and typical motor and language development, presented with a history of walking imbalance starting at age 6. This imbalance began gradually and worsened over 3-4 years before stabilizing. He could play with peers and had no issues with upper limb coordination, speech, head tremors, abnormal limb posturing, myoclonus, or seizures. His 6-year-old younger brother was asymptomatic, and there were no similar complaints in other family members. Systemic examination was normal, with no signs of oculocutaneous telangiectasia, cataracts, tendon xanthomas, scoliosis, or high arched feet. Neurological examination revealed normal cognition and speech, normal fundus examination, and normal visual acuity and fields. There was no external ophthalmoplegia. Vertical and horizontal saccades were normal in latency and velocity but were hypometric. He exhibited horizontal and vertical saccadic pursuits. Other cranial nerves were intact. Motor examination showed hypotonia and hyporeflexia in the limbs, with muscle power graded at 5/5 in both upper and lower limbs. Sensory examination was normal. Mild incoordination was noted in finger-nose and knee-heel tests on both sides. Tandem gait was impaired, and his gait was slightly wide-based and ataxic. Romberg’s sign was negative, and plantar response was flexor. Mild finger dystonia was observed in both outstretched hands, along with mild fidgetiness while sitting. Laboratory tests, including complete blood counts, renal, hepatic, and thyroid functions, fasting lipid profile, serum total creatine phosphokinase, serum alpha fetoprotein, immunoglobulins G, A, and M, and vitamin E levels, were all normal. Imaging studies, including chest X-ray and ultrasonography of the abdomen and pelvis, were normal. Nerve conduction study results were also normal.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed pan cerebellar atrophy. Clinical exome sequencing showed compound heterozygous variants in the MRE11 gene. A heterozygous 5′ splice site proximal variation in intron 4 of the MRE11 gene that affects the positions 4 to 7 nucleotides downstream of donor splice site of exon 4 (c.314+4_314+7 del) was detected.

case_report: A previously healthy 3-year-old fully immunized male presented with upper respiratory tract symptoms, fever, cough, increased work of breathing, and fatigue. The symptoms began 6 days prior to presentation and progressively worsened. Initial evaluation at the outside hospital included chest and abdominal X-ray, a complete blood count, a comprehensive metabolic panel, and blood and urine cultures. Chest X-ray showed right lower lobe pneumonia with small parapneumonic pleural effusion, while abdominal X-ray showed similar lower right airspace disease and hepatomegaly. Complete blood count was remarkable for leukopenia with left shift, anemia, and mild thrombocytopenia (white blood cell = 1.6 × 10^3 units/µL with 38% bands, hemoglobin = 10.2 mg/dL, and platelets = 196 × 10^3 units/µL). Comprehensive metabolic panel showed mild transaminitis (aspartate transaminase = 107 U/L, alanine transaminase = 152 U/L) and elevated blood urea nitrogen (53 mg/dL). He was started on ceftriaxone (CTX) and vancomycin and transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit for close monitoring, where he was intubated due to respiratory status and escalated to cefepime and vancomycin. Laboratory evaluation revealed worsening microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (nadir of 4.0 g/dL), worsening thrombocytopenia (nadir 3000/µL), and acute kidney injury with creatinine trending up (peak = 2.1 mg/dL).
test_results: The initial blood culture grew penicillin susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae. Elevated lactate dehydrogenase (peak = 17 935 units/L), decreased haptoglobin (<8.0 mg/dL), and presence of schistocytes on peripheral smear.
diagnosis: Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome  caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae pneumonia

case_report: A 2-year-and-6-month-old Yemeni girl, initially diagnosed with neonatal diabetes at 20 days old and on intensive insulin therapy, presented with chronic diarrhea and liver dysfunction. She was born at term with a birth weight of 2000 g and had an unremarkable perinatal history from healthy consanguineous parents. At 18 months, she developed chronic diarrhea with greasy, frequent stools. At 22 months, she was admitted with diabetic ketoacidosis and acute liver dysfunction, which resolved spontaneously. She had three previous hospital admissions for diabetic ketoacidosis. At 2 years and 6 months, she was admitted to King Abdul-Aziz Hospital with neonatal diabetes, chronic diarrhea with dehydration, and liver dysfunction. During her stay, she continued to have loose, greasy, pale stools. Her development was appropriate for her age. Physical examination showed her height and weight at the 3rd percentile, normocephalic head, no facial dysmorphism, normal eye exam, and hepatomegaly with a span of 10 cm without splenomegaly. No skeletal deformities were noted. Initial laboratory tests indicated microcytic hypochromic anemia with Hb 9.2 g/dl (normal range 10.9–13.8 g/dl), normal blood gas, normal kidney function, normal C-peptide levels, negative diabetes-associated autoantibodies, and uncontrolled glycemic control with an HbA1C of 11%. She had primary hypothyroidism with TSH 9.5 μIU/L (normal range 0.27–4.2 μIU/L) and FT4 13 pmol/L (normal range 12–22 pmol/L). She was given 25 mcg of l-thyroxine daily. Common causes of chronic diarrhea were investigated and excluded. Stool fecal elastase was not tested due to unavailability. Liver function tests showed AST 166 U/L (normal range 15–37 U/L), ALT 107 U/L (normal range 12–78 U/L), total bilirubin 3 Umol/L (normal range 0–17 Umol/L), and a normal coagulation profile. Viral infection, autoimmune hepatitis, and metabolic problems were excluded. Abdominal ultrasound revealed diffuse coarse hepatomegaly (10.6 cm) and a small hyperechoic pancreas. Genomic DNA was extracted from her peripheral blood sample using a standard method. A skeletal survey of the skull, ribs, spine, pelvis, and long bones (humerus and femur) showed no evidence of bone anomalies.
test_results: Exome sequencing analysis identified that the patient harbored a novel biallelic frameshift variant (c.137_del GCCTCGGGGCGGCCGCTGCTCCCACCTCAGCGACG, p.Gly46AlafsTER19 [AHAE1] in the EIF2AK3 gene (OMIM # 60432). Genomic DNA from the specimen was enriched for the complete coding regions and splice junctions of the genes on the used panel. The products were sequenced using an Illumina Miseq instrument with 2 × 150 paired-end reads. The sequence was aligned to reference sequences based on the human genome build GRCh37/UCSC hg 19. Capillary sequencing was used to confirm relevant variants with clinical or uncertain significance. All sequence alterations were described according to the Human Genome Variation Society (HGVS). Data analysis was performed using gene-specific filtering sequencing analysis.

case_report: A 54-year-old male presented with increasing sharp pain in the right upper back, which began two weeks prior following a flu vaccination in the right shoulder. The pain was localized without radiation and had no specific triggers or alleviating factors. It was accompanied by a localized sensation of warmth and occasional chills. The patient reported no prior trauma, fever, cough, weakness, numbness, or pain elsewhere. His medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, morbid obesity (BMI of 44 kg/m2), and depression. He was non-compliant with his diet and medications. Upon presentation, he was afebrile but later developed a fever with a temperature of 102°F. His blood pressure was 137/75 mm Hg, and his pulse rate was 113 beats per minute. Physical examination revealed a large indurated area on the right upper back extending to the back of the neck, measuring approximately 25 cm × 20 cm, with a 3 cm × 4 cm × 3 cm area of fluctuation, erythema, and tenderness. Laboratory results showed leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 26,000/μL, lactic acidosis with a serum lactic acid level of 2.4 mmol/L (normal 0.5–1.9 mmol/L) and serum bicarbonate of 16 mmol/L (normal 22–32 mmol/L), and poorly controlled diabetes with a serum glucose level of 291 mg/dL (normal 74–118 mg/dL) and hemoglobin A1C of 10.3% (normal 4.8%–5.6%). Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 104 mm/hr (normal 0–20 mm/hr), C-reactive protein was 345.7 mg/L (normal 0–4.9 mg/L), thyroid stimulating hormone level was 1.360 μIU/mL (normal 0.450–4.50 uIU/mL), and free thyroxine level was 5.1 μg/dL (normal 4.5–12 ug/dL). Serum protein electrophoresis showed a normal pattern with no monoclonal protein, and antistreptolysin O titer was negative. Chest imaging revealed bullous changes in the upper lobes of the lung, a large area of soft tissue density in the subcutaneous tissue of the right upper back, and an enlarged right trapezius muscle. The patient was started on broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and underwent incision and drainage in the operating room. The deep-seated abscess was drained and cultured, yielding Staphylococcus lugdunensis sensitive to methicillin, leading to the initiation of intravenous Nafcillin.
test_results: A skin biopsy taken from the back showed fibroadipose tissue and skeletal muscle with focal acute and chronic inflammation with granulation tissue.

case_report: The patient is a 3-year-old male child, the youngest of three siblings, born to non-consanguineous parents with no family history of neuropsychiatric disorders or congenital malformations. The pregnancy was uncomplicated, and he was delivered vaginally at term with a birth weight of 3,200 grams. At birth, he exhibited cyanosis and delayed crying. The parents first noticed abnormalities in his eyes, and clinical examination confirmed bilateral coloboma involving the iris and retina. An echocardiography was performed and found to be normal. At 5 days old, he was hospitalized due to involuntary movements in the face and upper limbs accompanied by hypotonia and was treated for hypoglycemia attributed to poor feeding. At 27 days old, he developed tonic-clonic seizures and was hospitalized again, presenting with poor feeding, vomiting, floppiness, and cold limbs. He received intravenous antibiotics and seizure control was achieved with phenobarbitone 20 mg, sodium valproate 200 mg syrups, and intravenous benzodiazepines at maximum dosages for his weight. Physical examination revealed dysmorphic facial features including flat occiput, low set ears, arched eyebrows, long eyelashes, bilateral coloboma, hypertelorism with downslanting palpebral fissures, bulbous nasal tip, wide mouth with downturned corners, smooth philtrum, tented thin upper lip, and thin upper vermilion. Additional findings included muscular hypotonia, clinodactyly of the little fingers, a well-defined hypopigmented plaque on the umbilicus, and lichenified skin on the soles of both feet. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography showed bilateral cryptorchidism but was otherwise normal. Electroencephalogram indicated a hypsarrhythmic pattern, suggestive of generalized epilepsy. Brain MRI revealed mild cerebral atrophy, mild thinning of the corpus callosum, and mild bilateral retinal coloboma. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was inconclusive. Based on MRI and CSF analysis results, antibiotics were discontinued, and treatment focused on brain atrophy with epilepsy. After one week of hospitalization, he was discharged on the same antiepileptic syrups. At 6 months old, his parents observed back arching dystonia, chewing, twitching movements, uncontrolled laughing, giggling, and grimacing. By 1 year old, his seizures were controlled with levetiracetam syrup 100 mg twice daily, though his family remained concerned about his prognosis.
test_results: The whole exome sequence analysis revealed a heterozygous c.607C > T (p. Arg203Trp) mutation in PACS1 gene (NM_018026.3).

case_report: An 18-year-old male was admitted to Seoul National University Children's Hospital presenting with chest discomfort, nausea, and shortness of breath at rest. The patient had no known family history of significant muscle disease. At 3 years old, he was first examined due to enlarged calves, and blood tests at that time showed elevated serum creatine kinase levels (6,378 U/L). The patient remained ambulant with mild proximal muscle weakness and could ascend stairs without holding the railing one by one at the age of 18. Upon admission, his blood pressure was 118/61 mmHg, and his pulse rate was 105 beats per minute, regular, with no audible heart murmur or rales. A manual muscle test indicated minimal weakness (4/5 or more) in the lower proximal muscles, and he reported no difficulties when standing from a squatting position.
test_results: Analysis of the dystrophin-encoding gene by multiplex polymerase chain reaction showed a deletion of exons 45 to 49. The electromyogram showed myopathic changes, consisting of small polyphasic potentials. The biceps muscle biopsy revealed dystrophic features.

case_report: Patient 5 is a 47-year-old Japanese woman who underwent surgery for congenital cataract. She has a history of easy bruising and recurrent dislocations since childhood. At age 43, she experienced recurrent intestinal perforation associated with multiple diverticula of the intestine. She has chronic heart failure with mitral valve regurgitation, generalized joint hypermobility (Beighton score 6/9), recurrent dislocations, skin hyperextensibility, redundancy, and bruisability, conjunctival bruisability, generalized pain, and gastrointestinal symptoms including vomiting and diarrhea with intractable abdominal pain after eating. Her mother exhibits bruisable skin, joint hypermobility with recurrent dislocations, pes planus, hallux valgus, and lower extremity edema. Her father and sister do not present any relevant features.
test_results: Standard NGS panel analysis detected a heterozygous frameshift variant c.6948del,p.(Asp2317Thrfs*53) in exon 20. Modified NGS panel analysis using long PCR-amplified product detected a heterozygous TNXA-derived 120-bp deletion in exon 35–intron 35 (c.11435_11524 + 30del), c.12150C>G,p.(Arg4050 = ) and c.12174C>G,p.(Cys4058Trp) in exon 40, c.12204 + 39dup and c.12204 + 43T>G in intron 40, and c.12628-52A>G in intron 43. MLPA showed the one-copy loss of exon 35 in TNXB and a one copy loss of CYP21A2. Sanger sequencing and MLPA analysis were performed on her parents, which revealed the heterozygous frameshift variant in her mother and the one-copy loss of exon 35 in TNXB and CYP21A2 in her father. Western blot analysis and nano-LC/MS/MS detection showed complete absence of sTNX in Patient 5. The mean sTNX concentration by nano-LC/MS/MS was 25 ± 2 ng/mL (22.1% of normal) in her father, 41 ± 1 ng/mL (36.3% of normal) in her mother, and 113 ± 10 ng/mL in the normal control. Her sister was found to have the one-copy loss of exon 35 in TNXB and CYP21A2, and a mean sTNX concentration of 33 ± 1 ng/mL (29.2% of normal).

case_report: A 15-year-old phenotypically female adolescent was evaluated for delayed puberty and proteinuria. There was no family history of kidney disease or delayed puberty. The patient exhibited slow growth starting 3 years prior, with less than 2 cm of growth per year, delayed breast development, and absence of pubic or axillary hair. Intellectual development was normal, and the patient experienced no other discomfort. At age 14, the patient sought medical attention for lack of menstruation and growth retardation. Laboratory tests showed a growth hormone (GH) level of 0.31 ng/mL (Normal range (NR) 0.02–5.42), insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) at 56.8 ng/mL (NR 220.00–972.00), urine albumin (+++), estimated glomerular filtration rate of 56.77 mL/min/1.73 m2, and creatinine at 184 umol/L. Bone age was determined to be approximately 10.3 years (less than 3rd percentile). A growth hormone stimulation test with arginine and insulin showed peak GH levels of 7.77 ng/mL and 7.01 ng/mL, respectively. The patient declined growth hormone therapy. Later that year, the patient was admitted to the nephrology department with systemic edema, lower back pain, and proteinuria. Laboratory studies indicated nephrotic syndrome with hypoalbuminemia (23.1 g/L), hyperlipidemia (total cholesterol, 9.74 mmol/L), and massive proteinuria (urine albumin (+++)) without hematuria. A renal biopsy showed focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS). After 1 year of steroid therapy without resolution of heavy proteinuria, the patient was transferred for further assessment. Physical examination revealed a height of 136 cm (age-specific height < -3SD), BMI of 17.84 kg/m2, and a waist circumference of 64 cm. Notable facial features included prominent ears and a saddle nose. Both breasts were undeveloped with minimal areola pigmentation, and there was no armpit or pubic hair. The vulva appeared female with a visible vaginal opening, no clitoris enlargement, and no posterior lip fusion (Tanner stage 1). The estimated glomerular filtration rate was 22.64 mL/min/1.73 m2, creatinine was 262 umol/L, blood albumin was 29.0 g/L, urine albumin was (++++) and urine protein quantification was 5.40 g/24 h. Tests for anti–glomerular basement membrane, antinuclear antibody, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, complement C3, C4, antistreptolysin-O, and immunoglobulins were negative. The parathyroid hormone (PTH) level was 81.98 pmol/L (NR 1.6–6.9) and 25-hydroxy-vitamin D was 15.8 nmol/L (NR 47.7–144).
test_results: A reported variation in the WT1 gene, NM_024426.6:c.1447+4C>T, was detected in this patient. The variation was located in intron 9, which was predicted to destroy the natural splice donor site and led to abnormal gene splicing.

case_report: A three-year-old girl presented with severe abdominal pain, food refusal, constipation, and fever over the past seven days. She was born following a normal pregnancy and delivery, with non-consanguineous parents, and had a birth weight of 3130 g. Clinical examination revealed telecanthus, a prominent nasal bridge, a short philtrum, small hands, an anteriorized anus, severe psychomotor delay, absence of expressive language, and dysphagia. The main symptoms included persistent, inconsolable crying, abdominal distension, and mild fever. Blood tests showed moderate leukocytosis and abnormal electrolyte values. Urine cultures identified Escherichia (E.) coli pyelonephritis as the cause of fever and elevated white blood cell count. Antibiotic therapy was initiated, leading to the resolution of fever and leukocytosis. Despite the resolution of the urinary tract infection and normalization of blood values, the patient continued to experience abdominal bloating, severe agitation, constipation, and food refusal. Persistent crying due to abdominal distension was noted throughout the day.
test_results: Transabdominal ultrasound revealed fluid between the intestinal loops. Abdominal X-ray showed severe colic distension, causing diaphragmatic elevation.

case_report: A 60-year-old male was referred to the Omuta National Hospital due to symptoms including bradykinesia, resting tremor in the upper extremities, small stepped gait, and impaired postural reflex. He had a 5-year history of depression. At the age of 58, he exhibited a mask-like face, rigidity in the neck and limbs, stooped posture, and a tendency to lean backwards. His maternal aunt had been admitted to the hospital at 48 years of age with similar symptoms, including hypoventilation and dysphagia, severe cognitive impairment, and was tube fed. At the age of 63, the patient experienced frequent falls and difficulty in breathing while walking. He was admitted to Omuta National Hospital for further evaluation.
test_results: He was found to carry the p.F52L mutation in the DCTN1 gene (c.156T>G). The VF image obtained at the age of 63 years indicated pharyngeal retention of the bolus, and a few swallows were required for its passage into the esophagus. There was no penetration or aspiration. The tongue pressure was measured using a handy probe (JM-TPM; JMS, Tokyo, Japan) and the obtained value of 29.3 kPa was within the normal range. Manofluorography was performed with VF, and manometry using a four-channel solid-state catheter placed transnasally (UniTip Catheter; Unisensor AG, Attikon, Switzerland) did not show any decrease in pressure at the hypopharynx or upper esophageal sphincter (UES) while swallowing of a slice of jelly. The values of maximum pressure at the hypopharynx and UES while swallowing a jelly were 802.5 and 303 mm Hg, respectively. Both the duration of pharyngeal contractions and the intervals from the beginning of the pharyngeal contraction to the end of UES relaxation were approximately 0.5 s and not prolonged.

case_report: A 51-year-old female presented with a three-month history of an enlarging gingival mass on the right side of the mandible. Examination of the head and neck showed no facial asymmetry, cervical lymphadenopathy, or trismus. The patient reported no pain, sensory changes, or bleeding related to the lesion. The right mandibular second and third molars were super-erupted and grossly mobile, but not painful upon palpation. The gingival lesion was exophytic and covered with a yellowish pseudomembrane. There was slight cortical expansion at the buccal vestibule. An incisional biopsy of the gingival lesion was performed by an outside dental provider before the patient was referred for further care. Imaging studies, including a panoramic radiograph and maxillofacial computed tomography (CT) without contrast, were conducted upon admission. These studies revealed an ill-defined radiolucent lesion involving the right mandibular angle, extending through the lingual cortex and encompassing the entire bucco-lingual width of the right mandibular angle. The right mandibular second and third molars appeared super-erupted with a teeth-floating-in-air appearance, and the outlines of the mandibular canal were obscured by the intraosseous lesion.
test_results: Histopathological exam of the mandibular biopsy showed scattered spindle and stellate cells with hyperchromatic nuclei distributed in a mucous matrix. Mildly atypical and mitotic figures were seen, while necrosis was not present. Immunohistochemistry showed that the tumor cells were positive for vimentin. Vascular CD31 stain showed the characteristic thin-walled and curvilinear vasculature. The labeling index of Ki-67 was about 30%. The tumor cells were negative for CK, S-100, P63, HHF-35.

case_report: A 57-year-old male, a farmer, visited the dermatology outpatient department with a large plaque extending from below the right elbow to the extensor aspect of the forearm. The lesion began as an asymptomatic nodule on normal-looking skin and expanded over the past year through peripheral spreading and central healing. Nodular ulcerated margins were observed on the proximal and distal aspects in an arciform pattern. The whitish intervening scar was crossed by narrow strips of normal-looking skin. The patient had previously been treated with antitubercular medications without any improvement. General survey, systemic examination, and routine laboratory tests showed no abnormalities. Chest X-ray results were normal. Both the Mantoux test and HIV screening were negative.
test_results: Histopathological examination of a skin biopsy specimen from the raised margin revealed a huge pitcher like crater extending symmetrically across the upper dermis surrounded by epidermis on all sides. A keratin plug is seen at the bottom of the crater with a dense mixed inflammatory cell infiltrate in the dermis immediately adjacent to the crater. No cellular atypia or involvement of the deep dermis is seen.

case_report: A 58-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease and coronary bypass surgery in 2005 presented with sclerodactyly and digital pitting scars on multiple fingers, along with palmar and facial telangiectasias, and tightness of the lips and skin around the neck. Capillaroscopy showed capillary nailfold dropout. He also had gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Over the years, the sclerodactyly worsened; in 2011, he developed exertional dyspnea and was found to have pulmonary fibrosis. Testing for antinuclear antibodies (ANA) by indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) using Hep2 cells showed a clumpy nucleolar and coilin body staining pattern in interphase cells at a dilution of 1:640, and a 34-kDa band on Western blotting, indicating reactivity to fibrillarin. Tests for rheumatoid factor, antibodies for double-stranded DNA, RNP, Smith, Scl-70, centromere, SS-A, SS-B, Jo-1, and cyclic citrullinated peptide were negative, and serum complement levels were normal. His condition remained stable without immune modulators until 2014 when he developed pulmonary hypertension and was started on hydroxychloroquine. In 2015, he developed photosensitive erythematous lesions on the upper trunk and neck. These lesions were succulent, non-scaly pink elevated plaques on the trunk, resembling a livedo reticularis-like pattern.
test_results: Biopsy of the lesion of the left lower back showed a superficial and deep periadnexal and perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate without follicular plugging or interface changes in the dermal-epidermal junction. Mucin deposits were present. Direct immunofluorescence showed focal granular deposits of IgM, C3, and C5b-9 more pronounced at the adnexal than epidermal basement membrane and the lower third of the skin strata.

case_report: A 3-year-old Caucasian girl was brought to the outpatient stomatology clinic at the São José dos Campos Dental School, UNESP, due to delayed eruption of some teeth and significant atrophy of the left posterior inferior alveolar border. During the review of her medical, dental, and familial history, the mother mentioned the presence of maculae on various parts of the child's body. Physical examination confirmed the presence of bilateral, slate-brown maculae in the axillary region, on the back, and in the hypochondrium and groin. The mother also reported that the child had experienced seizures at around one month old, during which small blisters appeared that followed the same path as the current maculae. These blisters were initially treated with topical acyclovir but did not resolve satisfactorily. After about a month, the blisters subsided, and maculae developed in those areas, persisting until the clinic visit. Despite these findings, pediatricians considered the girl's physical and intellectual development to be normal, although she exhibited mild strabismus.
test_results: The X-ray revealed the absence of some deciduous and permanent tooth germs in the third quadrant (74, 75, 34, 35), as well as the lack of tooth 62 and of various permanent tooth germs at other sites.

case_report: This male infant, born at 41 weeks of gestation to a 30-year-old mother in good health, was delivered via normal spontaneous vaginal delivery in November 2009. His birth weight was 3,140 grams. There were no complications during pregnancy, no family history of congenital anomalies, and no maternal drug exposure during pregnancy. The baby had APGAR scores of 7 and 5 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. Due to progressive respiratory difficulties and hypoxia, he required positive pressure ventilation with intubation. After stabilization, he was transferred to our hospital for further evaluation and management. Initial physical examination and laboratory findings were unremarkable. He received surfactant replacement therapy for acute respiratory failure. Multiple extubation attempts over the next few days were unsuccessful due to recurrent apnea and hypercarbia. On the second day of life, the patient exhibited a distended abdomen and was unable to pass meconium without rectal stimulation. A gastrografin contrast enema study revealed multiple meconium plugs in the colon. Meconium was passed, and abdominal distension was relieved following the contrast study. On the sixth day of life, the patient showed sustained abdominal distension with poor bowel movement. A barium contrast enema study indicated a transition zone in the rectosigmoid colon.
test_results: The diagnosis was confirmed by rectal suction biopsy with acetylcholinesterase immunohistochemistry. In patient, a mutant band was found. Direct sequencing revealed expanded alleles containing polyalanine 26 repeats in exon 3 of the PHOX2B gene.

case_report: A full-term male neonate, born via caesarean delivery at 39 weeks of gestation to a 21-year-old mother (gravida 1, para 1), was conceived through ICSI. A prenatal sonogram at 32 weeks gestation identified polyhydramnios and a well-defined hyperechoic mass measuring 4.5×3 cm on the left lateral side of the face and neck, featuring a central cystic area. Upon initial physical examination, the neonate exhibited normal growth parameters. Notable findings included linear, well-demarcated, raised, yellowish, fleshy, and hairless plaques with a velvety surface on the left side of the forehead, parietal region of the scalp, face, chin, lower lip, and left ear, with a smaller lesion on the right side of the face. A similar but less distinct lesion was observed over the midline of the back at the lumbar and sacral regions, as well as the scrotum. Additionally, a black nodule was present over the medial canthus of the right eye. No other skin manifestations such as cafe-au-lait spots or hypo- or hyper-pigmentation lesions were observed. The infant appeared healthy with no apparent neurological deficits on physical examination.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of his brain revealed an extra-axial CSF signal intensity lesion in the left side of the posterior fossa and the cistern magna suggesting arachnoid cyst with mild left cerebellar hypoplasia. Ophthalmologic examination showed bilateral posterior polar cataract. Histopathology showed thick hyperplastic epidermis with underlying large immature sebaceous lobules and free cut margins with no evidence of cellular atypia.

case_report: An 11-day-old female infant from Saudi Arabia was referred for further evaluation and management. She was born preterm at 36 weeks through natural spontaneous vaginal delivery, with an APGAR score of 9 and a birth weight of 2.3 kg. The parents were non-consanguineous. On physical examination, the infant was stable on room air and tolerated oral feeding with moderate suckling. Her weight was 2.23 kg and her height was 42 cm. Notable physical features included low-set ears, a depressed nasal bridge, and frontal bossing. A fundoscopic exam revealed a hazy view. Both arms and thighs were short with flexion contractures at the knees. The Moro reflex was weak and unequal. There were no convulsions or abnormal movements observed. Skin examination showed no abnormal lesions, pallor, jaundice, or cyanosis. Cardiac, chest, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Echocardiography identified a small atrial septal defect (ASD) with a left to right shunt. Cranial ultrasound with Doppler study showed normal findings. A skeletal survey indicated significant shortening of both humeri with mild metaphyseal flaring of the distal humeri and discrete punctate cartilaginous calcifications at the proximal and distal humeri. Both femurs were shortened with metaphyseal flaring and discrete punctate cartilaginous calcifications at the distal and proximal femurs. Ultrasound of both hip joints suggested developmental hip dysplasia (DDH) with heterogeneous femoral heads and multiple stippled calcifications. Orthopedic consultation confirmed fetal dysplasia with subluxated hips (DDH type 2), with femoral heads superiorly displaced from the labrum. Complete blood count and inflammatory markers were unremarkable. Blood and throat cultures were negative. The metabolic screen for inborn errors of metabolism was negative. Blood chemistry tests were normal.
test_results: Genetic testing results were positive for LDLR and PEX7 genes.

case_report: An 18-month-old Syrian female was admitted with acute abdominal pain, multiple episodes of non-bilious, non-bloody vomiting, and red diarrhea. She had no prior hospitalizations or significant medical history, and her family history was unremarkable. On admission, her vital signs were within normal limits, and physical examination did not show any unusual pigmented lesions. Abdominal examination revealed generalized tenderness, reduced bowel sounds, and a possible palpable mass in the epigastric region. Blood tests showed a hemoglobin level of 9.4 g/dL (normal range: 12-16 g/dL) and a mean cell volume of 63.2 fL (normal range: 72-100 fL), while other laboratory results were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography displayed 'target and pseudo-kidney' signs. The patient underwent laparotomy, which revealed palpable masses in the jejunum. Enterotomy exposed multiple polyps on the mucosal surface, and a small bowel resection of approximately 15 cm with end-to-end anastomosis was performed. The post-operative course was uneventful.
test_results: Histopathologic study was conducted on the resected portion, which consisted of a 15-cm specimen from the small bowel containing more than 100 pedunculated polyps on mucosal surface ranging from 1 to 2.5 cm in diameter. Microscopic examination of polyps showed proliferation of papillary and glandular formations lined by hyperplastic epithelial cells. Stroma was rich in smooth muscle fiber arising from the muscularis mucosae and infiltrated with patchy mononuclear inflammatory cell infiltrate. Neither adenomatous change nor malignancy was observed.

case_report: A 19-year-old male, the eldest of four siblings, was diagnosed with diabetes mellitus type 1 at the age of 10. He presented with complaints of decreased vision. Examination revealed a visual acuity of 20/400 in the right eye, which improved to 20/300 after refraction, and 3/200 in the left eye, which improved to 20/400 after refraction. The pupils were mydriatic with a reduced light reflex. The right optic nerve head exhibited a cup to disc ratio of 0.45 and severe pallor, along with microhemorrhages in the macular area. The left optic nerve head showed a cup to disc ratio of 0.25 and severe pallor.
test_results: Goldmann Kinetic Perimetry (GKP) showed concentric reduction of 20 to 30 degrees mainly at the nasal sector of the visual field as well as an enlarged blind spot. Retinal fluorangiography (FAG) was normal in both eyes. Audiometric studies showed low-frequency hearing loss. Dental examination showed enamel hypoplasia and abnormal teeth color.

case_report: A 33-year-old male patient reported swelling on the right side of the lower jaw for 6 months. The swelling appeared suddenly and gradually increased in size. Extraoral examination showed a diffuse swelling on the right side of the mandible, extending from the ala-tragus line to the lower border of the mandible superoinferiorly, and from 1 inch behind the corner of the mouth to the angle of the mandible anterioposteriorly. The swelling was firm with no local temperature increase. The right submandibular lymph nodes were palpable, tender, and mobile. Intraoral examination showed obliteration of the right lower buccal vestibule. Radiographic examination revealed a well-defined unilocular radiolucency with sclerotic borders on the right side of the posterior body and ramus of the mandible, extending superiorly to the sigmoid notch with involvement of the coronoid process and inferiorly thinning the lower border of the mandible. Root resorption was noted in teeth 46 and 47. Fine needle aspiration cytology showed no significant findings. The patient underwent an incisional biopsy at a private clinic, which resulted in a histopathology report of Basaloid Squamous Cell Carcinoma (BSCC). A hemimandibulectomy was planned, and the right submandibular gland along with lymph nodes were removed and sent for histopathological examination.
test_results: Microscopic examination revealed odontogenic epithelium arranged in variegated pattern predominantly plexiform and with few areas of follicular pattern. Sheets and nests of basoloid cells with peripheral palisading was evident. The cells showed hyperchromatic nucleoli and stippling with lack of cytoplasm. Few follicles exhibited stellate reticulum like areas along with squamous metaplasia and microcystic change. Marked cellular atypia with increased mitotic activity was seen. Stroma was minimal with moderate fibrous tissue component. Submandibular glands and lymphnodes were free of tumor infiltration. Reactive changes like prominent germinal center and sinus histocytosis were seen in the lymphnodes. Periodic Acid Schiff (PAS) special stain was performed, showed negative expression for mucin in the microcystic space. Immunohistochemistry showed an immunoreactivity for cytokeratin (CK) 19.

case_report: A 40-year-old male presented with abdominal pressure and an ultrasound revealing an adrenal mass and uterus. He is the youngest child of nonconsanguineous parents. His brother passed away at age 5 from an unknown cause, while his sisters are married with children. Raised as a boy, there was no noted genital ambiguity at birth. His medical history includes precocious puberty at age 6 and an evaluation for nonpalpable testes at age 15. He identifies as male. Physical examination showed short stature (height = 152 cm), normal blood pressure, a 15-cm abdominal mass in the left upper quadrant, pubic hair Tanner score of 5, empty scrotum, hypospadias, a stretched penis size of 7 cm, and no gynecomastia. Biochemical tests indicated normal serum potassium, creatinine, and cortisol levels. Total testosterone was 9.1 ng/mL (normal range: 3-12 ng/mL for males and 0.1-0.7 ng/mL for females). Levels of 17-Hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP), dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS), and androstenedione were elevated.
test_results: Genetic analysis showed 46XX karyotype and compound heterozygous mutation in the CYP21A2 gene (I2G/R356W). Ultrasonography, CT scan, and MRI of the abdomen and pelvis revealed left adrenal mass of 16.4 × 11.4 × 18.4 cm, right adrenal hyperplasia, uterine hypoplasia, and prostatic hypoplasia containing two calcifications. Gonads were not visualized.
diagnosis: classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia  due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency
Orpha_name: Classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency

case_report: A 58-year-old female with a history of epilepsy since childhood, hypercholesterolemia, and obesity was taking phenobarbital 100 mg/day and atorvastatin 10 mg/day. She worked in a factory until the age of 45. She was referred to the outpatient clinic due to speech difficulties and balance issues while walking. She is the older sister of another patient. Neurological examination revealed moderate speech difficulties related to cerebellar function, fragmented eye movements during smooth pursuit, difficulty with eye movement coordination, dystonia in the upper right limb, and balance issues while walking, making tandem walking impossible but she could walk without assistance. Sensory examination was normal and osteotendinous reflexes were intact. Blood tests indicated elevated alpha-fetoprotein and cholesterol levels, and the EEG showed no epileptic activity. A neuropsychological evaluation indicated mild cognitive impairment across multiple domains. The patient declined brain MRI, CT, and electromyography, but the neurological examination did not reveal signs of polyneuropathy.
test_results: Two compound heterozygous mutations in the PNKP gene were found (c.1029+2T>C and c.1221_1223del).

case_report: A 71-year-old male with a history of calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease presented with altered taste, abdominal discomfort, and significant weight loss. He experienced changes in taste and tongue appearance, followed by alterations in nail appearance and hair loss, leading to decreased appetite and a 45-pound weight loss. There was no family history of autoimmune disease, colonic polyps, or malignancy. Physical examination revealed hair loss, geographic tongue, nail dystrophy, and hyperpigmentation on both arms. Laboratory tests showed normal results for complete blood count, electrolytes, creatinine (0.7 mg/dL), urinalysis, liver function tests, albumin, folate, vitamin B12, zinc, vitamin D, copper, selenium, vitamin E, celiac antibodies, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, antinuclear antibody, extractable nuclear antigen panel, serum protein electrophoresis, and free light chains. Prealbumin was measured at 15.9 mg/dL (reference range 18–36).
test_results: Three months prior to presentation, a colonoscopy revealed diverticulosis, an anal fissure, and a small tubulovillous adenoma in the rectum. Upper endoscopy showed erythema, congestive gastropathy, gastric polyps, and nodular, diffusely polypoid appearing small bowel with fissuring and scalloping. Biopsies showed severely edematous, atrophic stroma with glandular loss and dilated/cystic glands, and inflammation with mononuclear and eosinophil infiltrate. Immunohistochemical stain was negative for Helicobacter organisms. Video capsule endoscopy revealed nodular mucosa throughout the small bowel and denuded intestinal villi.

case_report: A 10-year-old female from a rural area in Kendrapada district, Odisha, presented to the pediatrics outpatient department with intermittent abdominal pain, anal itching, and restlessness at night for the past 2-3 weeks. Physical examination revealed no notable findings. Blood and urine tests showed no abnormalities. Her height was recorded at 130 cm and her weight at 29 kg.
test_results: Examination of the stool samples revealed spherical eggs 70 µm in diameter, yellow-colored, thick-shelled eggs that contained six central hooklets but no polar filaments. Further confirmation was done by examination of another stool sample by the concentration method. Again, the same findings were noted.

case_report: A 35-year-old man presented with hyperkeratotic papules on the anterior neck at Gangnam Severance Hospital. These papules initially appeared 2 years prior and gradually increased in number. The skin lesions expanded peripherally with some central clearing over time. The patient reported that the lesions developed following a skin injury. Previous treatments with topical antifungal and topical steroid were ineffective. The patient's medical and family history was negative for any connective tissue diseases. Physical examination revealed multiple crusted erythematous papules, ranging from 2 to 5 mm in size, arranged in an annular and serpiginous pattern. A potassium hydroxide preparation from the skin lesion was negative for fungal elements.
test_results: A punch biopsy specimen revealed focal epidermal hyperplasia with the formation of a narrow vertical transepidermal channel containing nuclear debris and eosinophilic degenerated elastic fibers. The amount and thickness of the elastic fibers in the papillary dermis had increased markedly. It looked like entering the canals toward the outside of the skin. The papillary dermis and superficial reticular dermis were infiltrated by numerous inflammatory cells, including lymphocytes and histiocytes. Verhoeff-van Gieson staining showed a markedly increased number of altered elastic fibers forming dense clumps in the upper dermis. Gomori methenamine silver stain and D-PAS stain were both negative for fungal elements.

case_report: A 36-year-old Caucasian male was referred to a retina specialist for a left eye condition. He experienced flashes of light, reduced visual acuity, and a black spot in his left eye over the last day, along with intermittent blurry vision in the left eye over the past month. The patient reported no trauma or changes in his right eye. His medical history includes stage 1 hypertension, mild hyperlipidemia, and idiopathic large joint pain. He denied symptoms such as dyspnea, fever, chest pain, and weight loss. He has never received the tuberculosis vaccine. His ocular history, aside from myopia, was unremarkable. Current medications include chlorthalidone, atorvastatin, and lisinopril. Family history was noncontributory. Best corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye. Confrontation to visual fields, extraocular motility, and pupils were normal. A slit-lamp examination showed a normal anterior segment in both eyes with intraocular pressures of 14 in the right eye and 17 in the left eye. Fundoscopic examination revealed flat, sharp, and pink discs with a normal vitreous in both eyes. The right eye retina was normal, while the left eye showed a superior non-foveal area with a sludged blood column, hemorrhage, sclerotic vessels from a previous condition, vascular sheathing in the periphery, and no neovascularization.
test_results: Fluorescein angiography (FA) revealed filling defects in the superotemporal arcade and an old extramacular BRVO. The fundoscopic examination showed flat, sharp, and pink discs with a normal vitreous in both eyes. The right eye retina contained no abnormalities, while the left eye included a superior non-foveal BRAO with a sludged blood column, hemorrhage, sclerotic vessels from an old BRVO, vascular sheathing far in the periphery, and no neovascularization. A fundoscopic examination and Optos ultra-widefield imaging confirmed a new nasal BRAO in his right eye. Fundus imaging and FA of the left eye demonstrated well-circumscribed areas of ischemia with leakage of retinal vessels at the margin between the perfused and ischemic retina.

case_report: A 9-year-old girl with fair skin visited the Pediatric Dental Clinic at 'Universidade Veiga de Almeida,' accompanied by her guardian, due to concerns about misaligned teeth. Consent was obtained for this case report. Her medical history indicated a normal birth with no systemic issues or other significant findings. The extraoral clinical examination showed no abnormalities. Her dental history included previous dental visits for prophylaxis and fluoride application. A thorough intraoral clinical examination revealed that she was in the mixed dentition stage, with the absence of three first permanent molars, a deviation from the midline, bilateral posterior crossbite, and a deep palate.
test_results: The following tooth absences were confirmed: elements 16, 26, and 46 and the tooth germs of element 15 and all the permanent second molars.

case_report: A 22-year-old female student visited the orthopedic outpatient department with complaints of gradually developing neck and left shoulder pain that radiated to her hand. She also experienced paresthesia and intermittent numbness throughout her forearm and hand, particularly around the ulnar border. For approximately one month, she noticed intermittent weakness and heaviness in her limb, along with clumsiness in her left hand, especially after performing overhead activities. Initially, these symptoms were mild, but over the past two weeks, their intensity increased, prompting her to seek medical attention. There was no history of trauma to her neck, shoulder, or left upper limb. She did not report headaches, nocturnal pain, cold intolerance, Raynaud's phenomena, cyanosis, edema, or limb claudication. The shoulder maintained a rounded contour, though some muscle wasting was observed. There was no supraclavicular fullness. Wasting of the hypothenar eminence was noted, and the left hand appeared paler compared to the right. Neurological examination revealed decreased motor power (grade 2/5 on the Medical Research Council scale) in the 4th palmar interossei muscles (T1 root of the brachial plexus) and decreased vibration sense in the left ring and little fingers (C8 root of the brachial plexus), with intact proprioception. Applying thumb pressure for 30 seconds in the supraclavicular fossa in the supracoracoid region elicited radiating paresthesia in the forearm and hand, mainly affecting the ring and little fingers. The patient was unable to complete the Roos test due to radiating paresthesia in the same region. Upper limb tension test and costoclavicular maneuver also elicited radiating paresthesia in the ring and little fingers. Adson's, Wright's, Halstead, and Cyarix release tests were negative. Further clinical examination did not reveal any glenohumeral, subacromial, or cervical disc pathology. Peripheral nerve provocation tests for radial, median, and ulnar nerves were negative.
test_results: The nerve conduction study showed prolonged F-wave latency in the left ulnar and median motor nerves but normal compound muscle action potential amplitude. Decreased medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve (MABCN) sensory neural action potential amplitude with prolonged MABCN sensory latency (2.6 ms) was noted on MABCN conduction study. Needle electromyography showed abnormal spontaneous activities and long-duration motor unit potentials in the left first dorsal interossei and abductor pollicis brevis muscles. Abnormal spontaneous activity was not present in the left shoulder and arm (deltoid, biceps and triceps) and cervical paravertebral muscles.
diagnosis: Neurogenic Thoracic Outlet Syndrome associated with Clavicular Duplication

case_report: A 19-year-old man visited our outpatient clinic in 2011. Since the age of 2 years, he had been seen by multiple dermatologists in other clinics. He experienced pruritic sub-erythroderma with extensive skin peeling and scaling since birth, with symptoms worsening in winter. He also had complaints of atopic dermatitis and hay fever. His hair, teeth, and nails appeared normal. Routine laboratory tests were normal, except for elevated IgE levels (2222 kU/L; normal, <100). Hair shaft analysis did not show trichorrhexis invaginata. Over the years, the patient was treated with topical moisturizing agents, local corticosteroids, and a prolonged course of low-dose isotretinoin; only the latter provided slight improvement according to the patient. His non-consanguineous parents of Lithuanian and Russian Jewish descent did not exhibit any skin symptoms. Initially, the patient reported that his parents had no history of obvious hair loss.
test_results: No pathogenic mutations were detected.
diagnosis: Mutations in the CDSN gene causing peeling skin disease and hypotrichosis simplex of the scalp

case_report: A 79-year-old female arrived at the emergency department after a road traffic accident. She reported feeling weak while driving but was uninjured due to wearing a seatbelt. Her medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, dyslipidaemia, constipation, hypertension, and she had quit smoking two months prior. Her medications were Lercanidipine 10 mg, Aspirin 75 mg, Ezetimibe/Simvastatin 10 mg/20 mg, Lactulose as needed, and Indacaterol/Glycopyrronium 85mcg/43mcg. She had visited her GP multiple times over the past two months due to general weakness and lethargy. She was noted to be hypertensive, requiring increased doses of antihypertensive medications. Laboratory tests from her GP showed hypokalaemia, and she was started on oral potassium supplements. Upon initial assessment, she was hypertensive with a blood pressure of 180/69. She had a slim build (BMI of 20.2 kg/m2) with no cushingoid features, and her clinical examination was unremarkable with no traumatic injury. ECG showed sinus rhythm with left axis deviation, left bundle-branch block, and QT prolongation of 502 ms. Laboratory results revealed severe hypokalaemia (K 2.2 mmol/l), normal renal function (Urea 3.4 mmol/L, Creatinine 54 ummol/L, Na 143 mmol/L), normal serum magnesium (Mg 0.79 mmol/L) with metabolic alkalosis (pH 7.53, PCO2 5.4 (40.3 mmHg), PO2 7.1 (53.3 mmHg), HCO3 34). Spot urinary potassium was 22 mmol/l. Chest x-ray showed mild cardiomegaly with no active lung disease. CT Brain showed no acute findings. She was managed with aggressive potassium replacement, requiring 80 mmol i.v. potassium chloride (KCl) daily for four days (total 240 mmol i.v. KCl) to achieve a serum potassium level above 3.5 mmol/L. Her systolic blood pressure settled below 150 mmHg. On day five of her admission, she developed a hypertensive emergency (BP 239/114 mmHg) with acute pulmonary oedema, necessitating admission to the intensive care unit (ICU).
test_results: Plasma renin and serum aldosterone taken day three of admission were both suppressed [Plasma renin 4.4 pg/ml(< 20 pg/ml), Serum Aldosterone < 26 pg/ml (42–209 pg/ml)].
diagnosis: Acquired apparent mineralocorticoid excess secondary to excessive liquorice ingestion

case_report: A 6-year-old Chinese boy presented to the stomatology department with a primary concern of dental caries, which had been noted since he was 4 years old and had progressively worsened. The patient had a history of intracranial decompression surgery at 1 year old due to hydrocephalus, followed by posterior cranial vault distraction at 2 years old. At 3 years old, he underwent a ventriculoperitoneal shunt operation for hydrocephalus, and at 4 years old, cranial vault remodeling was performed. He was born full-term via cesarean delivery after an uneventful pregnancy, with a birth height of 48 cm and weight of 2.35 kg, alongside his fraternal twin sister who had a birth height of 48 cm and weight of 1.8 kg. Family history over three generations was negative for similar conditions, and his twin sister had no medical issues. Physical examination revealed normal height (108 cm) and weight (20.4 kg) for his age. Hands and feet appeared clinically normal. Extraoral examination showed a prominent forehead, eyelid ptosis, ocular proptosis, shallow eye sockets, hypertelorism, midface hypoplasia, and a retrusive upper lip with a protrusive lower lip. Intraoral examination indicated early mixed dentition with all deciduous canines and molars present in both the maxillary and mandibular arches. The eruption chronology and status were appropriate for his age. Oral hygiene was poor, with scattered pigmentation on the teeth. Permanent teeth 36 and 46, along with deciduous teeth 54, 55, 65, 74, 75, and 85, were mostly decayed. Eruptive permanent teeth 11, 21, 36, and 46 exhibited enamel hypomineralization. The maxillary arch was constricted, and there was an anterior cross bite and open bite.
test_results: Sanger sequencing showed that the pathogenic variant c.1026C>G (p.Cys342Trp) was present on the FGFR2 gene for the patient.

case_report: A 69-year-old woman (weight: 85 kg, height: 162 cm, body mass index: 32.4 kg/m2) was admitted for an ambulatory abdominal MRI to characterize a polypoid lesion in the gastric antrum. During the pre-procedure bedside assessment, she reported having type 2 diabetes managed with lifestyle changes and depression treated with venlafaxine 75 mg/day. She also used continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) at night, prescribed by a pulmonologist. Her surgical history included the removal of benign chest tumors without complications, and she reported no allergies. Fasting times were adhered to as per guidelines. Physical examination revealed a mini-sternotomy scar but was otherwise unremarkable. The patient was scheduled for a morning MRI slot typically reserved for pediatric cases, necessitating the presence of an anesthesiologist. Initially, the MRI was planned without sedation or anesthesia, but due to the patient's claustrophobia, anesthesia was requested. An MRI-compatible anesthesia workstation was available in the MRI room. The patient was monitored according to American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) standards. General anesthesia was induced with 80 mg of propofol and maintained with sevoflurane (MAC 0.7-1.0) using a circle-absorber breathing circuit and a facemask. Spontaneous ventilation was maintained throughout the procedure. Vital signs were monitored externally with wireless MRI-compatible devices. At the end of the procedure, after discontinuation of sevoflurane, the patient, although conscious, showed poor ventilatory dynamics, was unable to fully open her eyes or speak, and required assisted ventilation with a bag-valve-mask device.
test_results: Arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis presented type 2 respiratory insufficiency, but the patient had normal SpO2 with assisted ventilation with a bag-valve-mask device with 100% oxygen.
diagnosis: Myasthenic Crisis  in a patient with Generalized Myasthenia Gravis

case_report: A 46-year-old woman from Ghana with a 4-year history of hypertension, who had not been adhering to her treatment, arrived at the hospital with weakness on her right side. She first noticed the weakness upon waking up in the morning, which prevented her from moving her right upper and lower limbs and made it difficult for her to get out of bed. She was able to move her left limbs without any issues. She did not experience slurred speech, difficulty swallowing, headaches, seizures, loss of consciousness, or loss of sensation. Additionally, there were no issues with bladder or bowel function. She reported no diarrhea, vomiting, heat intolerance, or excessive sweating. There was no history of laxative or diuretic use before the onset of the weakness. She did not engage in strenuous physical activity or consume a high carbohydrate diet the night before. There was no personal or family history of stroke or muscle weakness. At a health center, her blood pressure was recorded at 172/130 mmHg, and she was given 30 mg of nifedipine orally before being referred to our hospital for further care. Upon physical examination, she had a temperature of 36.7°C, was not jaundiced, not pale, and showed no signs of respiratory distress. Her pulse was regular at 94 beats per minute, and her blood pressure was 165/120 mmHg. She was alert, awake, and oriented to time, place, and person. Her neck was supple, and Kernig’s sign was negative. Neurological assessment revealed muscle power of 3/5 in the right upper limb and 2/5 in the right lower limb, with reduced tone and deep tendon reflexes, and a flexor plantar response. Sensation was intact, and cranial nerve examination was normal. Laboratory tests showed normal full blood count, renal and liver function tests, lipid profile, fasting blood sugar (5.8 mmol/L), and negative HIV status. A plain CT scan of the brain was normal, and a subsequent contrast-enhanced CT scan did not show any space-occupying lesions. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain was not performed due to financial constraints and limited availability in the region.
test_results: Further laboratory workup demonstrated reduced serum potassium level of 2.6 mmol/L.

case_report: A 75-year-old Japanese man visited our clinic with his wife due to observed memory issues and stuttering. He had a history of atrial fibrillation managed with a pacemaker and controlled diabetes. His family medical history was unremarkable. During the medical interview, his speech was effortful and stuttered, but there were no obvious inconsistent speech sound errors. Various cognitive and neuropsychological tests were conducted at baseline, 6 months, 1 year, and 2 years. These included the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), cognitive subscale of the Alzheimer’s Disease Assessment Scale Japanese version (ADAS-cog), frontal assessment battery, digit span of the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale–Third Edition (WAIS-III), logical memory subtests I and II of the Wechsler Memory Scale–Revised (WMS-R), copy and delayed recall of the Rey-Osterrieth complex figure test (ROCFT), and the Japanese reading test. The Neuropsychiatric Inventory (NPI) was conducted twice through interviews with his wife at 6 months and 2 years. The Japanese Raven’s Coloured Progressive Matrices (RCPM) was performed 6 months after baseline, scoring 26 out of 36, indicating nonverbal cognitive impairment. The Japanese Standard Language Test of Aphasia (SLTA) was administered at all four time points, showing worsening scores over 2 years in auditory comprehension, naming, verbal explanation, verbal fluency, reading comprehension, writing, dictation, and arithmetic operations. Scores for auditory comprehension of words, word repetition, reading aloud Kana letters and words, and reading comprehension of Kanji and Kana words remained stable with no errors. The SLTA results indicated impaired comprehension of complex sentences, while single word comprehension and object knowledge were preserved. His speech content during the SLTA subtest of verbal explanation of Manga showed progression in agrammatism.
test_results: The MRI results showed global cerebral atrophy, which progressed during the 2 years. PiB-PET and THK5351 PET indicated pathologic amyloid-β and tau protein deposition. 123I-IMP SPECT imaging showed significant regional hypoperfusion dominantly in the left hemisphere, particularly in the bilateral parietal and temporal association cortex, the precuneus, the posterior cingulate cortex, the frontal association cortex, and the occipital lobe. Pathologic amyloid-β and tau protein deposition progressed during the 2 years, and hypoperfusion also progressed during this period. The finding of 18F-2-fluoro-2-deoxy-d-glucose (FDG) PET at baseline was almost the same as that of 123I-IMP SPECT, with glucose uptake decreased dominantly in the left hemisphere, particularly in the bilateral parietal and temporal association cortex, the precuneus, the posterior cingulate cortex, the frontal association cortex, and the occipital lobe. There were no remarkable findings on either [123I] FP-CIT SPECT (DaTscans), which was performed twice.
diagnosis: non-fluent variant primary progressive aphasia  with definite Alzheimer's disease

case_report: Two weeks after experiencing a throat infection, a previously healthy 16-year-old girl suddenly developed widespread involuntary movements. In a matter of days, her condition deteriorated to the point where she was bedridden, unable to stand or walk without help, and required a naso-gastric tube for feeding. Upon initial examination, notable clinical findings included an absence of spontaneous speech, generalized involuntary movements, and a significant reduction in muscle tone, rendering her unable to sit up in bed. Muscle strength and deep tendon reflexes were found to be normal. No other abnormal signs were detected.
test_results: Antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer was elevated (300 U, normal value <200). Anti-DNase B titer was elevated (300 units/mL, normal <170 units/mL).

case_report: A 13-year-old Chinese girl was admitted to our hospital 3 years and 8 months ago with symptoms including reduced facial expression, unclear speech, and choking cough when drinking water for 3 months. These symptoms remained consistent without significant changes. She did not exhibit notable limb weakness. The patient had a history of epilepsy, managed effectively with carbamazepine (12 mg/kg) for over 10 years. Genetic testing identified a heterozygous frameshift variant [NM_145239: c.641dupC (p. Arg217Profs*8)] and a heterozygous nonsense variant [c.1011C>T, p.Gly337Gly] in the PRRT2 gene, inherited from her mother and father, respectively. Her primary motor milestones were normal. Physical examination revealed weakness in muscles innervated by multiple cranial nerves, specifically the 5th, 7th, 9th, 10th, and 12th nerves, while limb muscle strength was normal. Bilateral knee tendon reflexes were normal, and the Babinski sign was negative. Her intelligence was assessed as normal. She had previously received IVIG at a local hospital without improvement.
test_results: We performed a neostigmine (0.03 mg/kg) test, which was positive. Nerve repetitive electrical stimulation (facial nerve and left median nerve) showed attenuation > 10%, not only in the facial nerve but also in the median nerve, indicating generalized neuromuscular junction involvement. Acetylcholine receptor antibody was positive (value of AchR Ab was 0.987, reference range <0.625). MuSK antibody was also positive (value of MuSK Ab was 0.697, reference range <0.493).

case_report: DM is a 5-year-old male who first visited the Yale-New Haven Pediatric Clinic between the ages of 2 and 3 years old with delayed gross motor milestones and difficulty getting into a standing position. There was no family history of neurologic, developmental, or muscle diseases, and no evidence of consanguinity. His pregnancy and birth history were normal. Physical examination revealed prominent calves and forearms, an awkward gait, and poor running ability. He arose from the floor in a slow, stiff manner, but without the classical Gower’s sign.
