He could jump, climb stairs, and get into a chair without difficulty. Muscle strength was good, tone was normal, reflexes were brisk, and flexor plantar responses were present. Sensation, fine motor skills, vision, hearing, and cranial nerves were intact. CK level was 175 (24-195). A muscle biopsy showed scattered areas of atrophic and hypotrophic fibers with a relative increase in endomysial connective tissue on H & E staining, and a predominance of type 2 fibers on ATPase staining. Hypotrophic fibers were either type 1 or type 2, with occasional hypertrophic/hypercontracted fibers being predominantly type 2. By the age of 4 years and 6 months, it was noted that he “gets stiffer after immobility but can walk it off.” Cold temperatures did not seem to affect these symptoms. Physical exam showed muscle prominence and grip myotonia followed by transient weakness. Eyelid myotonia was not clearly observed.
test_results: An EMG showed multiple runs of spontaneous positive wave discharges that varied in both frequency and amplitude and lasted approximately 2 to 5 seconds each. CLCN1 DNA sequencing showed a homozygous transversion in nucleotide position 936 (codon 312) of C to G, resulting in an amino acid change of serine to arginine.

case_report: The fourth child in the family, a girl, was born at term to a 28-year-old mother and a 32-year-old father. At birth, her length was 53 cm (+0.7 SD) and her weight was 4000 g (+1.3 SD). Early developmental concerns included recurrent constipation, a noticeable urine odor, growth delays, and developmental delays. She began walking independently at 2.5 years, albeit with some stepping issues, and started speaking more clearly by age 3. Around age 3, she experienced recurrent fractures following minor traumas, which were managed with casts and pins. At age 4, she was treated with bisphosphonates via pamidronate infusions, leading to improved bone mineral density and reduced fracture frequency, although compression fractures remained unchanged. This treatment was stopped after 5 months due to limited drug availability and reduced fracture recurrence. At age 6, a routine eye examination revealed bilateral cataracts, which were treated with cataract extraction, posterior chamber intraocular lens implantation, and anterior vitrectomy in both eyes.
test_results: A review of a skeletal survey performed throughout the years to assess the recurrent fractures revealed thinning of the occipital bone; multilevel flattening and biconcave compression of the vertebra mostly flattened at L1/L5; a scoliosis; a left coxa valga; a non-displaced transverse fracture of the mid diaphysis of the left radius and ulna that was stabilized with pins; healed spiral fractures of the mid third of the diaphysis on the left and right femurs with residual angulation and mild bowing of the left femur; comminuted fracture of the distal third of the diaphysis of the left femur with displacement; and bone demineralization and horizontal sclerotic stripes on both tibia and fibula. Assessment of bone density showed a Z-score of −4.88. Eye examination revealed the presence of thin cornea. Color vision by Ishihara plates was normal OU. Pupils were equal, round, and reactive with no afferent pupillary defect OU. Intraocular pressure was normal (13 mmHg) OU. Cover-uncover test showed a 20 prism diopters exotropia at near and distance with no pattern, alternating fixation, and horizontal nystagmus. Ductions and versions showed limited elevation, depression, and adduction of the right eye (OD), and full motility in the left eye (OS). Anterior segment exam showed a clear conjunctiva, white sclera, clear thin corneas (central corneal thickness of 346 µm OD and 343 µm OS; average central corneal thickness for age 343 µm is around 555 µm) with normal horizontal diameter (white-to-white, 10.87 mm OD and 11.83 Mm OS), deep and quiet anterior chamber OU, normal irides, PCIOL in place OU. Funduscopic exam showed a clear vitreous OU, optic discs with large cups but healthy rims, normal vasculature, and normal macula and periphery. A brain MRI was performed but did not yield any remarkable findings.

case_report: A 47-year-old female presented with lumbosacral bone pain for 2 months, which progressively extended to the chest and backbone. An MRI scan revealed extensive lesions in the 3rd, 4th, and 5th lumbar vertebrae, bilateral femoral bones, and pubic bones. Physical examination showed pallid lips and conjunctiva, a hard, smooth, painless, and mildly enlarged spleen about 3 centimeters below the subcostal margin, and tenderness in the spine, bilateral ribs, and sternum. Laboratory tests indicated pancytopenia with red blood cell counts at 3.08 × 10^12/L, hemoglobin at 89 g/L, white blood cell counts at 7.18 × 10^9/L (neutrophils 57.8%, lymphocytes 30.1%, monocytes 10.7%), and platelets at 54 × 10^9/L. Biochemistry tests showed elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase at 492.0 U/L and β2-microglobulin at 4797.0 ng/ml. Serum immunoglobulin and complement levels were within normal ranges, and serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation electrophoresis were normal. Whole body bone emission computed tomography (ECT) indicated activated metabolism in the bilateral humerus, sternum, ribs, thoracic vertebrae, lumbar vertebrae, pelvis, and bilateral proximal femur. Bone marrow examination did not support the initial diagnosis. Bone marrow aspiration smear revealed a small number of unidentified cells in a hypoplastic background without abnormal cells. Bone marrow biopsy showed hypoplastic marrow with regional proliferation of immature cells and fibrosis. Immunohistochemistry of the bone marrow indicated that the diffused neoplastic cells were positive for CD56, CD34, CD117, CD3, CD20, CD79a, CD68 and negative for CD45, CD138, cytokeratin pan, epithelial membrane antigen, chromophilic A, and Synaptophysin.
test_results: It was found the soft tissue in the left nasal cavity and maxilla with bone destruction, mild splenomegaly with slightly enhanced uptake. Fiberoptic pharyngorhinoscopy found a polypoid, grayish-red and fragile tumor with a smooth surface and bleeding tendency on the left posterior pharyngeal wall. Biopsy of this tumor showed flaky or striated cancer cells distributed among fibers and collagen with similarly small size and a rounded or irregular shape, abundant or few cytoplasm with distributed vacuoles under the cell membrane with prominences, hyperchromatic nuclear and differently dyed nucleolus. The grid-like nerve fibers distributed among the tumor cells. The immunohistochemistry tests proved that the cancer cells is positive for CD56 (+), S-100 protein (S-100) (partial +), Ki 67 (+85%), CD57 (+), and negative for glial fibrillary acidic protein, CgA, P40, human melanoma black, CD20, CD3, Syn, T-cell intracellular antigen-1, Growth factor receptor-binding protein, CD43, CD30, cytokeratin pan, neuron-specific enolase and CD138.

case_report: A 9-year-old female patient, who showed no clinical symptoms, was referred to pediatric cardiology due to an irregular heart rate observed during a routine well-child visit. An initial electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed a prolonged QTc interval and episodes of non-sustained bidirectional ventricular tachycardia. She was subsequently admitted for further evaluation. There was no family history of arrhythmogenic disorders, congenital heart disease, or sudden death. The patient's mother and maternal grandmother had syndactyly. Physical examination showed short stature, low set ears, mild micrognathia, wide spaced eyes, and dental abnormalities. Additionally, the patient had left iris heterochromia, with one half of the iris blue and the other half green. Vital signs, including heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation, were appropriate for her age. Cardiovascular examination revealed an irregular pulse rate with normal first and second heart sounds, and no additional cardiac sounds, murmurs, rubs, or gallops were detected. Examinations of the respiratory, abdominal, and neurologic systems were unremarkable. Initial investigations included a baseline ECG showing a prolonged QTc of 485 ms and bidirectional ventricular tachycardia on ECG and Holter monitoring, with a ventricular ectopy burden of 40%. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count with differential, a comprehensive metabolic panel, cardiac enzymes (troponin and CK-MB), and thyroid function tests, were within normal limits. Exercise stress testing did not show a significant increase in ectopy from baseline at higher heart rates. Transthoracic echocardiogram and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging indicated a structurally normal heart with no signs of ventricular dysfunction.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed a de novo mutation in the KCNJ2 gene, D71N. In addition, the CPVT panel showed a G552W mutation in the SCN5A gene determined as a variation of uncertain significance (VUS).

case_report: A 40-year-old male arrived at an outside hospital with 3 days of ongoing shortness of breath, a dry cough, chills, and sweating. He reported intermittent, non-radiating, burning chest pain and an unpleasant taste in his mouth but denied having a fever. His medical history included a pulmonary embolism 8 years ago after returning from military deployment in Afghanistan. He had stopped taking Warfarin but had been using Ibuprofen, 1,600 mg orally twice daily for the past 48 hours. He was a former smoker who had resumed smoking within the last week after more than a year of abstinence. He had been released from prison approximately a year before admission and was working as a construction worker. He had no recent travel history, pets, or sick contacts at home. Upon admission, his vital signs showed a temperature of 38.2°C, heart rate of 123 beats per minute, blood pressure of 123/88 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 94%. He was 186 centimeters tall and weighed 110 kilograms. Physical examination revealed reduced breath sounds on both sides, but he was not in respiratory distress or wheezing. There was no lymphadenopathy, calf tenderness, or rash. The patient was alert and oriented but appeared anxious. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 15.4 × 10^9/L with 84% segmented neutrophils, 8% lymphocytes, 7% monocytes, and 1% eosinophils. The complete metabolic panel and D-dimer were normal. Chest X-ray showed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, and chest CT revealed widespread mixed ground-glass and solid airspace opacities mainly in the middle lung zones without signs of pulmonary emboli. The patient was started on Piperacillin/Tazobactam, Vancomycin, Azithromycin, Micafungin, and Bactrim. Over the next 12 hours, he developed refractory hypoxemia and was placed on a non-rebreather mask, then high-flow nasal cannula, and eventually required emergency intubation. Post-intubation arterial blood gas showed a pH of 7.20, PCO2 of 54, PO2 of 60, and bicarbonate of 20.8. Ventilator settings included a positive end-expiratory pressure of 22 cm H2O, 100% fraction of inhaled oxygen, peak inspiratory pressure of 44 cm H2O, tidal volume of 860 mL, and respiratory rate of 28 breaths per minute. The PaO2/FiO2 ratio was 65. Due to severe hypotension and acute hypoxic respiratory failure, the patient was transferred to a tertiary care facility for emergent V-V ECMO. Cannulation of the right internal jugular vein with a 31 French dual lumen cannula was performed at the bedside. Immediate improvement in pulse oximetry was observed with an ECMO blood flow of 4.6 liters per minute, 100% fraction of membrane lung oxygen, sweep gas flow of 5 L/minute, and 3,800 rotations per minute. The patient was administered stress dose Hydrocortisone, 50 mg IV every 6 hours, due to distributive shock presumed to be secondary to adrenal insufficiency, along with Norepinephrine at 0.3 micrograms per kilogram per minute and Vasopressin at 2.4 units per hour. Upon transfer, the white blood cell count was 38.4 × 10^9/L, though a cell differential was not performed at that time.
test_results: Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was performed 1 day later and notable for copious amounts of thin, green liquid without evidence of pus, bilaterally. Cellular analysis revealed a total nucleated cell count of 380 cells/mL with marked eosinophilia at 21% eosinophils (absolute cell count, 80 cells/mL), 4% neutrophils (15 cells/mL), 38% lymphocytes (144 cells/mL), 1% basophils (4 cells/mL), 6% macrophages (23 cells/mL), and 30% alveolar pneumocytes and bronchial cells (114 cells/mL).

case_report: A 54-year-old man with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia was admitted to the hospital due to abdominal pain and vomiting. Physical examination showed abdominal bloating without peritoneal irritation. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) identified local thickening of the small bowel wall. Conservative treatment was administered, which was effective, and the patient was discharged 10 days later after resuming oral intake. A few days post-discharge, the patient experienced a recurrence of abdominal symptoms and was readmitted. Blood tests indicated a mild inflammatory reaction and dehydration. The white blood cell count was 8200/μl, with 62.3% neutrophils, 28.3% lymphocytes, 0.7% eosinophils, 0.5% basophils, and 8.3% monocytes. Additional laboratory results were: hemoglobin 14.5 g/dl, platelets 265,000/μl, CEA 7.5 ng/ml, CA19-9 4.5 U/ml, and sIL-2R 313 U/ml. An ileus tube was inserted, and a small bowel series showed severe obstruction in the jejunum with upstream dilatation. CT confirmed that the thickening of the jejunal wall was still causing obstruction. A laparoscopic exploratory examination was performed, revealing a hard mass at the stenotic site, leading to small bowel resection with mesenteric lymph node dissection. The surgical procedure involved partial resection of the jejunum with 10-cm margins from the tumor on both sides and removal of seven mesenteric lymph nodes, none of which showed signs of metastasis. Macroscopic examination of the resected specimen revealed a tumor approximately 60 mm in diameter causing stenosis of the entire jejunal circumference.
test_results: Histologically, hematoxylin and eosin (HE) staining showed diffuse infiltration and expansion of immature, atypical cells but without tissue destruction. Immunochemical staining revealed that the cells were positive for myeloperoxidase (MPO) and CD34 and negative for CD20 (L26), CD3, CD30 (Ki1), CK (AE1/AE3), CK (MNF116), desmin, CD56, HMB-45, and S-100-protein.

case_report: The patient is a one-year-old girl, born from a consanguineous marriage. She was brought to the hospital at 10 months of age due to hypotrophy and delayed growth. Initial observations revealed steatorrhea (11.54 g/24 hours) and episodes of diarrhea. Physical examination showed a weight of 3700 g and a height standard deviation score of −4.8 SDS. Laboratory results indicated ASAT levels of 169 IU/L (normal <38 IU/L) and ALAT levels of 214 IU/L (normal <41 IU/L). Gammaglutaryl transferase was within normal limits at 16 IU/L, while alkaline phosphatase was elevated at 179 IU/L (normal 40–150 IU/L). Calcemia and total protein levels were normal. Lipid profile at the time of hospitalization showed CT: 1.3 mmol/l, TG: 0.35 mmol/l, and HDL-C: 0.9 mmol/l. Vitamin levels were 430 μg/l for vitamin A (normal 444–945 μg/l) and undetectable for vitamin E (<1 μmol/l, normal 16–35 μmol/l).
test_results: Acanthocytosis was revealed on peripheral blood smear.

case_report: An 11-year-old Caucasian male presented with congenital, bilateral, erythematous scaly skin lesions on his neck. He was born full-term from an induction ovulation pregnancy via natural delivery. At birth, multiple anomalies were observed. A high-resolution karyotype showed a normal male karyotype of 46, XY. There was no family history of deafness, renal diseases, branchial fistula, or craniofacial anomalies. Craniofacial anomalies included bilateral cleft lip, low-set ears, a broad nasal bridge, microphthalmia-associated ocular disorganization, primary vitreous hyperplasia in the right eye, and a cataract in the left eye. The patient had congenital hearing impairment and craniofacial anomalies at birth, along with ocular anomalies. At 2 years old, he underwent corrective surgery for the lip palate and experienced a seizure, but his cognitive and developmental milestones were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed erythematous scaly lesions on both sides of the neck and peri- and supra-auricular areas, along with hyperpigmented scar-like lesions on the anterior neck. He had malformed low-set ears bilaterally and a broad, flat nasal bridge. The rest of the skin examination was normal. Ocular sonography with a 12 MHz probe showed complex dysplasia and incomplete development of the left eyeball's anatomical structure, consistent with persistent primary vitreous hyperplasia. The axial length of the eyeball was smaller than normal, with an anteroposterior measurement of 11 mm, consistent with microphthalmia. At 10 years old, he underwent cataract surgery on the right eye and had nasolacrimal stenosis in the right eye. Brain MRI revealed prominent left parieto-frontal cortical sulci, fissure, and basal cistern. Renal ultrasound of the left kidney showed multiple cystic lesions, indicating nonfunctionality. No urinary anomalies were found in the right kidney at birth. Audiometric examinations at 1 year old showed bilateral severe-to-profound sensorineural hearing loss with hearing levels of 75–80 dB. A chest X-ray identified a normal thymic shadow. Scalp examination revealed poliosis (<10 white hairs), and oral examination showed small bilateral canine teeth. Nail examination was normal. Laboratory values at birth were within normal ranges, except for elevated serum creatinine and potassium levels.
test_results: Histological examinations of skin abnormalities revealed that the normal epidermal squamous tissue was replaced by a ciliated respiratory epithelium, and in the upper dermis, an aggregate of lymphocytes reminiscent of a branchial cleft cyst was present.

case_report: A 22-year-old woman with no prior health issues presented with abdominal pain, jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools that had progressively worsened over the past week. She reported no weight loss and was only taking oral contraceptives. She denied alcohol consumption, smoking, and drug use. Laboratory tests revealed elevated bilirubin levels (total bilirubin: 12.3 mg/dL, direct bilirubin: 10 mg/dL), increased gamma-glutamyltransferase (165 U/L), and elevated liver enzymes (aspartate aminotransferase: 408 U/L, alanine aminotransferase: 277 U/L). Liver function tests were within normal limits. Serological tests for hepatitis A, B, C, and HIV were negative, as were IgM serologies for cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and herpes simplex virus. An abdominal ultrasound showed a diffuse micronodular liver pattern. Further tests included autoimmune markers, urinary copper, serum ceruloplasmin, serum ferritin, transferrin saturation index, and upper abdominal magnetic resonance imaging. Results indicated a positive antinuclear factor (1:640, homogeneous nuclear pattern) and hypergammaglobulinemia (2.16 g/dL) on protein electrophoresis. Tests for anti-smooth muscle, anti-mitochondrial antibody, and liver-kidney microsomal antibody type 1 were negative.
test_results: Magnetic resonance cholangiography showed a reduced-sized liver suggestive of cirrhosis and multiple focal areas of strictures of the intrahepatic bile ducts, with associated dilations. The patient underwent an ultrasound-guided liver biopsy, which showed periportal necroinflammatory activity, plasmocyte infiltration, and advanced fibrosis.
diagnosis: Primary sclerosing cholangitis and autoimmune hepatitis overlap syndrome
Orpha_name: Primary biliary cholangitis/primary sclerosing cholangitis and autoimmune hepatitis overlap syndrome

case_report: A 47-year-old female arrived at the emergency department experiencing shortness of breath and chest pain. Her medical history did not reveal any significant issues. During the physical examination, her arterial blood pressure was recorded at 125/70 mmHg, heart rate at 86 beats per minute, and respiratory rate at 16 breaths per minute. Both cardiac and pulmonary auscultation were normal. Laboratory tests showed normal cardiac enzymes, biochemical analysis, and complete blood count, with the exception of elevated eosinophil levels. A posterior-anterior chest radiograph indicated a normal pulmonary appearance, but a hyperdense mass with regular contours, measuring 5 cm in diameter, was observed in the apical aspect of the left ventricle. Electrocardiographic (ECG) findings were normal.
test_results: A transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) showed a cystic mass lesion located in the pericardium adjacent to the left ventricle. Her CT showed a 5 x 6 cm cystic lesion with well-defined borders in the pericardium adjacent to the left ventricle. On MRI, a cystic lesion adjacent to the posterior aspect of the left ventricle was observed; the lesion was hyperintense on axial T2-weighted images, hypointense on axial and coronal T1-weighted images, and did not show contrast enhancement on postcontrast coronal T1-weighted images. The diagnosis was verified by an indirect hemagglutination test.

case_report: A 16-month-old boy presented with early development of pubic hair, acne, and rapid growth, first noticed at 12 months. He was born at 37+2 weeks via cesarean section, weighing 2.45 kg (-1.7 SDS). He is the first of fraternal twins, with a healthy twin sister. Family history includes early puberty and short stature in both the grandfather (148 cm) and father (158 cm). Physical examination revealed a height of 83 cm (+1.2 SDS) and weight of 14.3 kg (+2.8 SDS). Testicular volume was 2 mL bilaterally, with pubic hair development corresponding to Tanner stage II. Stretched penile length was 7 cm (>2 SDS). The patient had an oily face with acneiform eruptions, but no dysmorphic features, gynecomastia, or palpable abdominal masses. No cafe-au-lait spots or hyperpigmentation were observed. Bone age, assessed by the Greulich-Pyle method, was advanced to 4 years. Laboratory results showed very high serum testosterone (5.74 ng/mL; normal <0.05 ng/mL), suppressed LH (<0.07 mIU/mL; normal 0.02–0.15 mIU/mL), normal FSH (0.56 mIU/mL; normal 0.38–1.11 mIU/mL), slightly elevated α-fetoprotein (14.1 ng/mL; normal 0–10 ng/mL), and normal β-human chorionic gonadotropin (<0.2 mIU/mL; normal <5 mIU/mL). Levels of adrenocorticotropic hormone (25.4 pg/mL; normal 10–60 pg/mL), cortisol (10.44 μug/dL; normal 3–21 μug/dL), 17-hydroxyprogesterone (1.96 ng/mL; normal 0.03–9 ng/mL), androstenedione (<0.3 ng/mL; normal 0.08-0.5 ng/mL), and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (19.1 μg/dL; normal 5–57 μg/dL) were within normal ranges. A gonadotropin-releasing hormone stimulation test showed peak LH and FSH levels of 0.52 and 6.69 mIU/mL, respectively. Imaging studies, including brain MRI and ultrasonography of the scrotum and adrenal gland, were normal.
test_results: Mutation analysis of the LHCGR gene identified a heterozygous mutation, c.1730 C>T (p.Thr577Ileu). Familial genotyping confirmed a normal genotype from the mother, but the same pathogenic variant of LHCGR was identified from the father.

case_report: A 35-year-old Japanese woman was referred to the hospital for evaluation of low serum ALP detected during an annual medical checkup. Her serum ALP levels had not been previously measured. She reported mild muscle and bone pain in both lower limbs since childhood, which did not interfere with her daily activities. Her physical activity level was normal. She had no history of rickets, fractures, or dental issues, including premature loss of primary teeth, but had developmental dysplasia of the hip during infancy. She was not on any medication or supplements before admission and had no history of smoking, alcohol abuse, or illicit drug use. She had no known allergies. She has been employed in the clothing industry for about 10 years and lives with her parents in Japan. Her mother had breast cancer, and her older sister had Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. Her father had no major illnesses, and her parents had no history of fractures. On initial examination, her vital signs were: body temperature 37.0 °C, blood pressure 115/80 mmHg, pulse 101 beats/min, height 150.3 cm, and body weight 44 kg (BMI 19.6 kg/m2). Examination revealed spontaneous pain in the right femur and left crus without tenderness or pain on percussion. There were no signs of anemia or jaundice, and the thyroid was not palpable. Chest and abdominal examinations were normal. Neurological examinations, including muscle strength, deep tendon reflexes, and sensory tests, were normal except for spontaneous pain in both legs, and no skin lesions were observed. Initial laboratory tests showed a normal complete blood count (hematocrit 41.4%, hemoglobin 13.8 g/dl, red cell count 4.91 × 10^6/mm3, white cell count 6600/mm3, and platelet count 308 × 10^3/mm3). Serum ALP was significantly low at 13 U/L, serum iron was low at 40 μg/dl, and serum phosphorus was slightly elevated at 4.3 mg/dl, while serum calcium was normal at 10.2 mg/dl. Inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein 0.02 mg/dl), liver function tests (albumin 4.9 g/dl, total bilirubin 0.3 mg/dl, aspartate aminotransferase 13 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 6 U/L), renal function tests (blood urea nitrogen 8 mg/dl, serum creatinine 0.61 mg/dl), electrolytes (sodium 139 mEq/L, potassium 4.3 mEq/L, chloride 103 mEq/L), thyroid-stimulating hormone (2.35 μU/ml), and free thyroxine (1.59 ng/dl) were within normal ranges. X-rays of the limbs showed mild lateral bowing of both femurs, while X-rays of the cervical and lumbar spine showed no scoliosis. Orthopantomography was normal. Bone mineral density (BMD) measurements of the lumbar spine and femoral neck after one year indicated osteoporosis below the expected range for age (young adult mean [YAM] 87%, T-score −1.1, Z-score −1.1 in lumbar vertebra; YAM 68%, T-score −2.5, Z-score −2.2 in femoral neck). Abdominal ultrasonography revealed numerous microcalcifications in both kidneys. Additional blood chemistry tests and urinalysis were performed based on reduced BMD. Bone metabolic markers were within normal limits: tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase-5b 213 mU/dl (reference 120–420 mU/dl), undercarboxylated osteocalcin 2.14 ng/ml (reference < 4.5 ng/ml), and type I procollagen N-terminal propeptide 33.2 ng/ml (reference 16.8–70.1 ng/ml). However, bone-specific ALP was low at 1.0 μg/L (reference 2.9–14.5 μg/L) for her age. Urine analysis showed elevated phosphoethanolamine at 727.8 μmol/g Cr (reference 7–70 μmol/g Cr). Serum ALP of the patient’s mother was low at 86 U/L.
test_results: The patient underwent genetic testing, which revealed two mutations in tissue-nonspecific ALPL (exon 9, c.979T>C [p.Phe327Leu] and exon 11, c.1559delT).

case_report: A 74-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital presenting with widespread swelling and visible blood in the urine. Physical examination revealed mucocutaneous paleness, elevated blood pressure (199/73 mmHg), and generalized swelling. Laboratory tests indicated acute kidney failure with serum creatinine at 1.8 mg/dL and urea at 183 mg/dL, along with low levels of total protein and albumin, and anemia. Serum analysis identified monoclonal IgG-λ. The patient exhibited nephrotic range proteinuria (5.26 g per 24 hours) with Bence Jones protein and hematuria (30–50 red blood cells per field). Bone marrow aspiration showed 9% plasma cells, and cryoglobulins were negative.
test_results: Renal biopsy revealed glomeruli with mesangial expansion and immune deposits distributed in the mesangium and in the peripheral capillary walls in a subendothelial pattern. These deposits were strongly periodic-acid-schiff positive. Immunohistochemistry techniques were negative for detecting kappa and lambda light chains and Congo red staining was also negative. In the ultrastructural study, there were localized fibrillar deposits of an approximate diameter of 27 nm in the mesangium and capillary walls. On the other hand, irregular and discontinuous thickening of glomerular basement membranes because of an electron-dense and homogeneous deposit was observed. Serological study showed normal immunoglobulin and C4 levels but reduced C3. Immunofixation of serum identified IgG-λ monoclonal gammapathy with residual IgG-κ. C3NeF haemolytic assay was performed and resulted negative. Complement FH measurement by Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) revealed reduced levels of this protein and anti-FH autoantibodies were detected in the patient's serum and in the patient's purified IgG fraction. Anti-FH activity was confirmed by western blot analysis and another reactivity of the IgG fraction was observed. The light chain isotype of the autoantibody was determined by ELISA, and the anti-FH activity was associated mainly with monoclonal IgG-λ. A competition ELISA with immobilized FH pre-incubated with various anti-FH antibodies indicated that the autoantibody binds to SCRs 1–4 of FH. Another ELISA assay showed that the patient's IgG binds to recombinant factor H-like protein 1 (CFHL1), a splicing variant of FH which comprises SCRs 1–7 of the molecule. This was confirmed by western blot analysis of the patient's IgG. In the presence of FH and patient's IgG, an absence of C3b degradation by FI was observed. Another serum protein recognized by the patient's IgG was plasminogen, identified by mass spectrometry from a Coomassie stained-gel band, after 8% sodium dodecyl sulphate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS–PAGE). Anti-plasminogen activity was then tested in the purified IgG and in patient's serum by ELISA and western blot.

case_report: A 2-day-old female infant exhibited difficulties with feeding, frequent hiccups, and shallow respiration. She was delivered at full term via vaginal birth and was initially in good health. During pregnancy, the mother observed increased fetal movements starting at 20 weeks, but the pregnancy was otherwise normal. After being discharged from the hospital, the mother noticed the baby had frequent hiccups from the first day at home. Upon examination, the infant was found to be hypotonic with shallow breathing and experienced frequent apneic episodes, necessitating ventilatory support. The infant also developed frequent myoclonic jerks, which were managed effectively with phenobarbitone. The clinical findings included significant hypotonia, myoclonic jerks, and frequent hiccups.
test_results: The plasma glycine level was 1751 (normal range: 200–600 µmol/l), CSF glycine level of 416 (normal range: 0–10 µmol/l), and CSF/plasma glycine ratio of 0.238. The computed tomography (CT) head scan did not show any obvious abnormalities. EEG showed burst suppression pattern.

case_report: A 13-year-old female presented to the outpatient department of a tertiary care hospital in Karachi with a two-day history of sudden onset of restless, abnormal movements. These movements initially appeared in both upper limbs, then spread to the trunk on the same day, and eventually involved both lower limbs by the second day. The patient's mother noted that these movements interfered with daily activities such as bathing, picking up utensils, and eating. No abnormal movements were observed during sleep. The patient had a history of sore throat and fever three weeks prior, which resolved on its own. General physical examination was normal. The patient was alert and oriented to place and time but appeared anxious and restless with involuntary movements while lying down. Vital signs were recorded as heart rate 92/min, respiratory rate 22/min, afebrile, and blood pressure 105/80 mmHg. Mild anemia was noted. Examination revealed unclear speech, difficulty walking, generalized hypotonia, and irregular muscle contractions and relaxations, including pronation of the forearm on an outstretched hand above her head, known as 'Milkmaid's sign.'
test_results: Her laboratory investigations showed hemoglobin (Hb) levels: 11.7 mg/dL (normal range: 12.0-15.5), hematocrit (HCT) level: 40.5% (normal range: 37%-48%), total leukocyte count (TLC): 7600 IU/L (normal range: 130,000-400,000), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 55 mm 1st hour (normal: <20), antistreptolysin O (ASO titer): 584 (normal: 166 Todd units), electrocardiogram (ECG) and echocardiogram were with normal PR interval of 0.12 s.

case_report: A 64-year-old Korean male presented with a 2-week history of cough and sputum. He had a history of smoking but no significant past medical or surgical history. A chest radiograph showed a large intrathoracic mass with pleural effusion on the left side. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest revealed a well-defined mass approximately 13.0 cm in size with internal necrosis, located in the left mid-to-lower hemithorax. The mass was attached to both the left pleura and left lung, making it difficult to determine its exact origin. PET-CT imaging showed a hypermetabolic mass in the left thoracic region and multiple hypermetabolic lymph nodes in the left internal mammary, left supraclavicular, and right retrocrural regions, indicating potential metastasis. A biopsy was performed via video-assisted thoracic surgery. Microscopically, the tumor exhibited proliferation of monotonous spindle cells with immunohistochemical expression of epithelial membrane antigen, B-cell leukemia/lymphoma 2, and transducin-like enhancer of split 1 (TLE1). The pathological differential diagnoses for the biopsy included various types of sarcomas and malignant tumors. Surgery was scheduled, and a left lower lobe lobectomy with resection of the chest wall (including ribs 8-10), diaphragm, and mediastinal lymphadenectomy was performed. Multiple pleural seeding nodules were observed during the operation. The surgical specimens were examined, revealing a 13.7-cm well-defined whitish mass involving the lung parenchyma, chest wall, and diaphragm, with internal geographic necrosis and hemorrhage. Microscopically, the tumor was predominantly composed of spindle cells arranged in long fascicular growth or herringbone pattern, with a minor epithelial component. The spindle cells formed dense cellular sheets and fascicles with uniform spindle cells, ovoid vesicular nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli, and sparse eosinophilic cytoplasm. The epithelial component, located at the periphery of the mass, formed solid nests and cords with occasional small glandular lumina and scattered intercellular slits. The epithelial cells were polygonal or cuboidal with ovoid vesicular nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli, and abundant palely eosinophilic cytoplasm. Areas of gradual transition between the two components were present. The tumor also showed coagulative necrosis and increased mitotic activity (35 mitoses per 10 high-power fields). Lymphatic invasions were noted at the tumor-normal lung parenchyma border. Metastases were found in three lymph nodes (two left lower paratracheal and one ipsilateral peribronchial). The metastatic tumor cells in the lymph nodes exhibited epithelial cell proliferation in a micropapillary pattern and solid nests, resembling metastatic carcinoma. The lymph nodes were initially examined via frozen section, and the pathologist identified them as “metastatic carcinoma.” In the permanent specimen, the metastatic tumor cells in the lymph nodes differed morphologically from those in the main mass. The main mass's epithelial component was less differentiated, forming solid nests with occasional intercellular slits and cords, while the lymph node tumor cells formed well-structured micropapillary patterns and solid nests. No additional abnormal lesions were found in the lung parenchyma upon thorough inspection. The other hypermetabolic lymph nodes on PET-CT were not resected, so their status remains unknown. Immunohistochemically, both spindle cell and epithelial cell components showed strong nuclear staining with TLE1, and some areas displayed weak cytoplasmic staining for pan-cytokeratin. TTF1 immunostaining was negative in both the main mass and lymph node.
test_results: Real-time polymerase chain reaction confirmed the presence of SS18 (SYT)-SSX translocation.

case_report: A 44-year-old Caucasian male presented with multiple asymptomatic papules on both shins and the tops of his feet, persisting for over a year. Physical examination showed numerous whitish papules, each measuring between 0.2 to 0.3 cm, which appeared adherent to the skin and were not easily removed by scratching. These wart-like lesions were initially noticed on the tops of the feet and gradually increased in number and size. Similar lesions spread to the front of the legs, while the tops of the hands remained unaffected. There were no punctate keratoses on the palms or soles, and no nail involvement was noted. The patient reported no personal or family history of skin conditions such as multiple warts or other related diseases.
test_results: Biopsy specimens showed marked hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and papillomatosis, with an increased granular layer. The epidermis looked like a 'church spire'. There were no signs of parakeratosis, acantholysis, dyskeratosis, or vacuolization of epidermis.

case_report: A 68-year-old male, who had coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) surgery 3 months prior, was admitted due to a sudden increase in difficulty breathing, swelling in both legs, and low oxygen saturation (82%) on room air. His medical history includes an inferior wall non-ST elevation myocardial infarction, type II diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. He underwent three-vessel CABG following his myocardial infarction. Pre-operative assessments, including imaging and catheterization, showed no signs of pulmonary hypertension, and pulmonary function tests did not indicate significant lung disease. Upon admission, an electrocardiogram revealed a new incomplete right bundle branch block and inverted T waves in leads V1–6. Laboratory tests showed a troponin T level of 0.032 ng/mL.
test_results: Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a dilated and hypokinetic right ventricle with a ‘D-shaped’ left ventricle and elevated systolic pulmonary artery pressure (62 mmHg). Right heart catheterization confirmed severe PH with a mean pulmonary arterial pressure of 38 mmHg (66/24 mmHg absolute), right atrial mean pressure 17 mmHg, RV systolic pressure 70/5 mmHg, and cardiac output 5 L/s, with peripheral vascular resistance 5.4 Wood units, pulmonary wedge pressure 11 mmHg, and the left ventricular end-diastolic pressure 12 mmHg.

case_report: The patient is a 5-year-old girl born at term via normal vaginal delivery after an uneventful pregnancy to a healthy mother, with no neonatal complications. She is fully vaccinated according to the Saudi national vaccine schedule, and there is no family history of medical or surgical diseases. Her developmental milestones were achieved at the expected times. She has a history of uncontrolled bronchial asthma with frequent exacerbations and was on Salbutamol and Flixotide inhalers without regular follow-up. One month prior to her presentation in March 2018, she developed a fever lasting one week, which responded to antipyretics. The fever was accompanied by throat pain and difficulty swallowing. She was treated with antipyretics and oral antibiotics for three days for acute tonsillitis and then discharged. Two days later, she remained febrile with no symptom improvement, became hypoactive, and had decreased appetite and oral intake. At another hospital, blood investigations revealed pancytopenia, and she was admitted for IV antibiotics and further workups. Two days post-admission, she developed respiratory distress and was moved to isolation in the pediatric intensive care unit with community-acquired pneumonia. She received oxygen supplementation via a face mask and frequent nebulizations, stayed in the pediatric intensive care unit for three days, and showed improvement in her respiratory status. She was then transferred to the pediatric medical ward to complete a seven-day course of IV antibiotics. Her Complete Blood Count (CBC) persistently showed pancytopenia without improvement. She was discharged in good general health with a follow-up scheduled in the hematology clinic after two weeks. At follow-up, she appeared pale with a poor appetite but no change in activity. Her CBC showed WBC: 2.6 K/µL, Hb: 8 gm/dL, Platelet: 79 × 103/uL. Her parents opted not to proceed with further diagnostic procedures and sought another medical opinion. One week later, she developed a fever after contact with a febrile person and was evaluated at the emergency department of Qatif Central Hospital, Qatif, Eastern Province, KSA. Physical examination revealed normal vital signs and growth parameters in the 50th percentile for height and head circumference and the 25th percentile for weight, with a good body build and no dysmorphic features. She appeared pale but was not jaundiced or cyanosed. Examination showed congested tonsils without exudate, no lymphadenopathy, mild hepatomegaly, and an ejection systolic murmur. Other parts of the examination were unremarkable.
test_results: The result showed: marked hypocellularity of 25% with no megakaryocytes, granulocyte 41%, erythroid precursors 51%, lymphocytes 8%, no abnormal cellular collection seen, and no evidence of myelodysplastic syndrome or malignancy.

case_report: A nine-year-old girl presented with difficulty breathing, easy fatigue, and skin lesions. She had a history of occasional nosebleeds and weakness for 20 days prior to admission, along with symptoms resembling a common cold, particularly a cough, in the last two days. Her medical history revealed that the skin condition began at around 4 months old, characterized by desquamative, crusted, and non-itchy lesions on the soles of both feet. A dermatologist noted similar lesions in two of her cousins, indicating a genetic transmission of the rash, and advised no treatment was necessary. Up to the age of 8, she experienced occasional fatigue, for which anemia correction was suggested. Physical examination revealed respiratory distress and widespread skin lesions. Vital signs indicated rapid breathing, increased heart rate, normal blood pressure, and normal temperature. The lesions were located on the trunk, fingers, toes, and especially on the palms and soles. They were crusted, yellowish, peeling, and did not bleed when scratched. The lips appeared dry, brittle, and bled easily upon gentle palpation. A holosystolic murmur was audible at the apex, radiating to the axillary region, along with a gallop rhythm. The liver was palpable 3 to 4 centimeters below the rib edge, with no other organ enlargement. No clubbing or other significant findings were noted. A chest X-ray revealed an enlarged heart.
test_results: On echocardiography, the left ventricle was dilated and had a non-compaction pattern with its ratio to the compacted compartment more than 1.4/1. The M-mode displayed a decreased ejection fraction and an increased E point septal separation (EPSS). Also the color doppler mode showed mild to moderate mitral regurgitation.

case_report: A man in his late 40s visited the outpatient department due to weakness in his lower limbs. He first noticed this symptom at age 12 when he struggled to keep up with his peers while running, and it gradually worsened over time. Despite being able to walk, he had trouble climbing stairs. His family history revealed that his male siblings and maternal uncle, aged between 40 and 60 years, experienced similar muscle weakness. He had no intellectual impairment. Physical examination showed a waddling gait, enlarged calf muscles, and wasting of the quadriceps and gluteal muscles, resulting in pseudohypertrophy of the calf muscles. Knee jerks indicated weak quadriceps contractions (grade 1) upon tapping, and ankle jerks were absent. The patient used his arms to rise from the ground, demonstrating a positive Gower’s sign. Laboratory results showed a total leukocyte count of 5.7 cells/109 (reference range: 4.5-11), with neutrophils at 62% and a hemoglobin level of 11 gm/dl. Creatine kinase level was 1148 U/L (reference range: 22-172 U/L).
test_results: A molecular genetic test (multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification [MLPA]) showed duplication of exon 2 in the dystrophin gene.

case_report: A 35-day old male infant was admitted with a 3-day history of diarrhea and multiple episodes of projectile, non-bilious, non-blood-stained vomiting, accompanied by reduced urinary output. There was no fever or irritability. The infant was born at 41+4 weeks of gestation via elective cesarean section due to postdated pregnancy, with a birth weight of 3.1 kg. He cried immediately after birth and has been exclusively breastfed. Antenatal scans were normal, maternal serology was non-reactive, and there were no family genetic diseases or sepsis risk factors. On examination, the infant appeared lethargic with sunken eyes, dry oral mucosa, and a depressed anterior fontanelle. Vitals were normal. Respiratory, cardiovascular, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Blood pressure was 90/50 mm Hg (above 50th centile). The infant's weight was 3.0 kg (z score -2.78), length 55 cm (z score -0.67), and head circumference 37 cm (z score 1.78). Physical examination revealed normal male genitalia with pigmentation darker than the infant's skin tone. Laboratory investigations showed negative septic screening and abnormal electrolyte levels: serum Na+ was 116 meq/l, K+ was 6.1 meq/l, urea was 33 mg/dl, and creatinine was 0.5 mg/dl. Random blood sugar was 75 mg/dl. Initial blood gas analysis indicated: pH 7.42 (7.35-7.45), Pco2 23.5 (35-45), HCO3 15.6 mmol/L (22-28 mmol/L), Base excess -9 mmol/L (-4.0 to +4.0 mmol/L), and lactate 2.8 mmol/L (<2 mmol/L). Liver function tests were normal. Both ECG and ultrasonography findings were normal, ruling out pyloric stenosis.
test_results: 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) was positive 405ng/ml (<22.0 ng/ml).
diagnosis: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia with Salt Wasting Crisis
Orpha_name: Classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency, salt wasting form

case_report: This 2-year-old girl is the second daughter of healthy parents with no known consanguinity. There is no family history of neurological or inherited diseases. She was delivered at term via cesarean section following an uneventful pregnancy. Her Apgar score was 9 at 5 minutes. Birth measurements were as follows: weight 3560 grams (50–75%), length 49.5 cm (25–50%), and head circumference 35 cm (50–75%). The neonatal period and early months of life were unremarkable. At approximately 7 months old, cyanosis was noted in her extremities and lips. Psychomotor delay was evident as she did not achieve head control or vocalization milestones. By 1 year of age, she exhibited alternating squints and abnormal head posturing. At 14 months, a neurological examination showed alternating squint, tetraparesis with appendicular spasticity and axial hypotonia, psychomotor delay with poor social eye contact, lack of vocalization, and incomplete head control. The Griffiths Developmental Scale indicated a mental age of 6 months. Brain MRI revealed a complex malformative condition with features partially resembling PCH. During sedation for the MRI, the patient experienced desaturation to 82–83%, with minimal improvement upon oxygen supplementation.
test_results: Blood gas analysis indicated a MetHb of 20%.
diagnosis: CYB5R3-related recessive hereditary methemoglobinemia type II

case_report: A 21-year-old male with a history of depression and no other medical conditions arrived at the emergency department with a decreased level of consciousness following an overdose of amitriptyline. The patient had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of three, necessitating intubation and admission to the intensive care unit. Initial laboratory results indicated lactic acidosis, negative troponin levels, and normal kidney and liver functions. Arterial blood gas analysis showed metabolic acidosis (pH 7.2) with respiratory compensation. Electrocardiogram findings included a wide complex tachycardia with a ventricular rate of 146 bpm, a QRS duration of 118 milliseconds, and a prolonged QTc of 576 milliseconds with nonspecific ST-T wave changes. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a preserved ejection fraction of 65% and no wall segment motion abnormalities. The patient received intravenous fluids and intravenous sodium bicarbonate, aiming for a pH of 7.5-7.55. By the second day of admission, the patient's condition improved, allowing for the removal of mechanical ventilation. The QRS complex and QTc intervals began to shorten. However, cardiac troponin I levels increased, peaking at 4.08 µg/L. The patient developed a fever with a maximum temperature of 312.1 K, an elevated white blood cell count of 13.2 x 10^9/L (without peripheral eosinophilia), and an elevated brain natriuretic peptide level of 399 pg/ml. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein were elevated at 46 mm/hr and 18 mg/L, respectively. The patient reported ingesting 41 amitriptyline 50 mg tablets and denied recent flu-like symptoms or exposure to sick contacts. A viral panel was negative for common viruses, including coxsackie and adenovirus. The patient's only prescribed medication was amitriptyline, and he did not regularly use over-the-counter medications. Amitriptyline levels were not measured, but the ingestion was confirmed through a tablet count of his prescription bottle. The cardiology service was consulted.
test_results: Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) revealed a moderately dilated left ventricle with mildly reduced EF at 45%, subtle enhancement of the basal inferolateral epicardium on delayed enhancement images, non-territorial scattered areas of edema within the myocardium, and moderate pericardial effusion. CMR was negative for coronary artery stenosis or an anomalous coronary artery origin.

case_report: The patient is a 43-year-old Latin-American man with a degree-level education. He sought medical consultation due to a two-year history of progressive forgetfulness, mental confusion, disorientation, difficulty finding the right words, and mood changes, transitioning from shyness to outgoing behavior. He lost his job due to poor performance and experienced social rejection because of his new personality traits. Additionally, he reported sleep disturbances, apathy, and anxiety symptoms. Initial treatments for major depression and type II bipolar disorder were ineffective. Physical examination was normal, including pulmonary and cardiac auscultation (normal echocardiogram), except for multiple skin blemishes on the trunk. These blemishes, which neither he nor his wife considered abnormal, were distributed across his trunk and belly and changed rapidly under finger pressure. Neuropsychological tests revealed a score of 23 on the Mini-Mental Status Examination and 15 on the MOCA test. He scored 30 on the HAM-D scale and 20 on the Hamilton anxiety scale. The patient was assessed as CDR 1 and FAST stage 5, indicating moderate disease. Overall, he showed moderate-to-severe cognitive decline, including issues with declarative memory, attention, language, and executive function, along with significant emotional disturbances. No further neurological signs were observed. There were no reports of stroke-like episodes, and there was no family history of livedo reticularis, stroke, vasculitis, or related conditions. Laboratory findings showed undetermined anticardiolipin antibodies and a weak presence of lupic anticoagulant. Tests for venereal disease, HIV, hepatitis B and C, protein C and protein S, C-reactive protein, sedimentation rate, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear factor, and other rheumatic tests were all normal.
test_results: The brain MRI showed multiple areas of signal changes on cortico-subcortical transition and in the deep periventricular white matter with gadolinium enhancement, consistent with brain ischemia. Imaging also disclosed diffuse cerebral atrophy disproportionate for his age. Brain Perfusion with 99mTc - ECD brain SPECT showed accentuated diffuse hypoperfusion in parietal and frontal areas. Cerebral angiography revealed slowed distal blood flow of cerebral arteries with decreased vessel diameter and parietal irregularities suggestive of vasculitis. The venous phase was normal, and there was no vascular malformation. The anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arteries in their respective distal segments showed segmental lesions with reduced caliber associated with tortuosity and slowed flow, characterizing a late blush in the territory of the watershed zone.

case_report: A 51-year-old male from Barbados visited the Ocular Genetics clinic in April 2018. He reported a long-standing history of night blindness starting around the age of 9 to 10 years, accompanied by reduced peripheral vision, with symptoms gradually worsening over time. He also experienced hearing loss beginning 4 years ago, chronic dry skin, and recent intermittent tingling sensations in his upper and lower extremities. He did not report any balance issues or loss of smell. His medical history included non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, high cholesterol, and erectile dysfunction. His current medications were candesartan, amlodipine, rosuvastatin, low-dose aspirin, and metformin. He had no history of smoking or known medication allergies, and there was no significant family history of ocular disease. On examination, his spectacle-corrected Snellen visual acuity was 20/80 + 2 in the right eye and 20/50 + 2 in the left eye, with no improvement using pinhole correction. His refractive error was −2.75 + 2.00 × 135 in the right eye and −1.50 + 1.25 × 043 in the left eye, with a +2.50 reading addition in both eyes. His pupils were equal and reactive to light and accommodation, with no relative afferent pupillary defect. Slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment showed mild posterior subcapsular lens changes in the right eye and anterior vitreous cells in both eyes. Examination of the posterior segment revealed significant retinopathy in both eyes, with diffuse retinal pigment epithelial degeneration, mid-peripheral pigment clumps, and retinal arteriolar narrowing. The optic discs appeared normal without significant pallor, and there were no signs of diabetic retinopathy. Spectral domain optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed extensive outer retinal degeneration, with attenuation of the outer nuclear layer, ellipsoid zone, and retinal pigment epithelium, along with scattered outer retinal tubulations and bilateral epiretinal membranes. Blue-peak fundus autofluorescence indicated small regions of increased autofluorescence in the fovea with scalloped borders, while the rest of the retina showed decreased autofluorescence consistent with extensive retinal pigment epithelial degeneration. An octopus visual field test confirmed significant peripheral field constriction, with approximately 30° of residual field in each eye using the V4e target. A full field electroretinogram (ffERG) performed in 2015 using DTL electrodes and ISCEV standard parameters showed extinguished rod-driven responses and cone-driven bright flash. The 30 Hz flicker response was severely diminished, with an amplitude of 2.2 μV (normal 68-118 μV) and implicit time of 37.5 ms (normal 25-29.8 ms) in the right eye, and an amplitude of 2.1 μV (normal 68-118 μV) and implicit time of 47.0 ms (normal 25-29.8 ms) in the left eye.
test_results: The patient was found to have homozygous frameshift variants in PHYH (c.57_67dup [p.Gly23Alafs*8]).

case_report: A 66-year-old Chinese Singaporean man presented with a 1-week history of left calf pain. Examination revealed tenderness and visible swelling in the left calf, with a larger circumferential diameter compared to the right (40 cm vs. 37 cm). No neurovascular deficits were noted in the left lower limb. Laboratory results showed haemoglobin at 14.8 g/dL, white blood cell count at 13,760/mm3, and platelet count at 275,000/mm3. Serum creatinine kinase was elevated at 2,570 U/L, but there was no biochemical evidence of acute kidney injury. C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, and D-dimer levels were within normal limits. Plain radiography of the left tibia and fibula showed no fractures or signs of acute osteomyelitis. The patient was treated for left leg compartment syndrome and underwent fasciotomy and tibialis anterior resection. Intraoperatively, 80% of the left tibialis anterior muscle was found to be gangrenous, while the rest of the anterior compartment muscles were less than 50% gangrenous. The other compartments (deep and superficial posterior, lateral) appeared healthy. Histology of the biopsied muscle showed features of focal ischaemic change. Postoperatively, the patient was transferred for a short course of rehabilitation. Two weeks later, he developed acute bilateral hip pain, which MRI revealed to be bilateral undisplaced acetabular fractures. The patient reported progressive, episodic stiffness and spasms in the lower back and bilateral lower limbs over the past 2 months, similar to his initial left calf pain. There was no history of diabetes mellitus, autoimmune diseases, or family history of similar symptoms. The stiffness and spasms were triggered by sudden movements but not by noise or emotional upset. Affected areas felt tight and hard, and palpation of the lower limbs sometimes induced more intense spasms. Examination also noted non-fatiguable, limited abduction of extraocular movements bilaterally without diplopia. There was no myoclonus, encephalopathy, or signs of parkinsonism. Bilateral hip flexion was limited due to pain, but reflexes were normal in both upper and lower limbs. Cranial nerves and motor and sensory functions were intact. MRI of the brain and spine showed mild degenerative disc disease. Routine nerve conduction studies of the upper and lower limbs were normal.
test_results: Electromyography of the lower limbs showed continuous motor unit activity at rest in spite of voluntary relaxation. Serum was tested for anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibody and eventually returned positive with a value of >300 U/mL.

case_report: A 76-year-old black woman with a history of arterial hypertension and depressive syndrome, regularly taking furosemide 20 mg daily, olmesartan 20 mg combined with hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg daily, and mirtazapine 30 mg daily, experienced episodes of watery diarrhea and weight loss over two years. These episodes alternated with periods of normal bowel movements and weight restoration. One severe episode resulted in hospitalization due to hypoalbuminemia (1.7 g/dL) and associated anasarca. A CT scan of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis showed no significant findings. Upper and lower endoscopy appeared normal, with no biopsies taken. Viral serologies for HIV, HBV, and HCV were negative. Thyrotropin receptor antibodies were positive, but the patient remained euthyroid. Other autoimmune tests, including the coeliac disease panel (negative anti-transglutaminase, anti-gliadin, and anti-endomysium, normal IgA levels) and anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae, were negative. Fecal elastase was normal, and stool tests showed no undigested fats or fibers, indicating normal pancreatic function. Bacteriologic and parasitological stool cultures were inconclusive, and Clostridioides difficile toxin was negative. Fecal calprotectin was significantly elevated (1805 mg/Kg; normal < 50 mg/kg). Renal protein wasting was ruled out. The patient started a tailored nutritional plan (not gluten-free) and showed a positive clinical response with good oral feeding tolerance and normalization of stool consistency. She was discharged to the outpatient clinic and remained stable for 7 months. Subsequently, she experienced a recurrence with profuse watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, and emesis, without fever. Upon readmission, she was severely dehydrated with acute kidney insufficiency (creatinine 7.5 mg/dL), severe metabolic acidemia (pH 7.10; bicarbonate 6.3 mEqs/L), and hypokalemia (potassium 2.5 mEqs/L). In the ICU, she received fluid resuscitation and parenteral nutritional support without the need for vasopressors, ventilatory assistance, or renal replacement therapy. After 3 days, she was moved to the intermediate care unit and then to the general ward, showing slow but positive clinical improvement. Despite poor oral feeding tolerance, even with a customized meal plan, there was a gradual improvement in stool consistency and a decrease in bowel movement frequency.
test_results: The gastric mucosa was atrophic with diffuse edema and loss of the large curvature folding. A similar appearance with remarkable loss of the normal folds was observed in the duodenum. Colon and ileum biopsies were taken. Anatomopathological examination upon microscopic examination, the antral gastric mucosa biopsy showed severe lymphoplasmacytic inflammatory infiltration with increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. Helicobacter pylori microorganisms and collagen deposits were not identified. Duodenal mucosa biopsies disclosed moderate villous atrophy without crypt hyperplasia, superficial epithelium detachment, increased lymphoplasmacytic inflammatory infiltration, and mild to moderate collagen subepithelial deposits with a thickness of 6–7 µ. Terminal ileum mucosa biopsies showed morphological alterations similar to the ones described in the duodenum. Masson trichrome stain confirmed collagen subepithelial deposits. Epithelioid granulomas were not identified. Colon mucosa biopsies revealed a mild cryptic architectural distortion, normal superficial and glandular mucus activity, and heavy lymphoplasmacytic inflammatory infiltration of the lamina propria with eosinophilia and subepithelial collagen deposits. No intraepithelial lymphocytosis was observed.

case_report: A 64-year-old female with a history of rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren's syndrome, and osteoporosis, who had not been seen by rheumatology for some time, visited the family medicine clinic for a routine examination. The physical examination revealed hyperpigmented lesions on both anterior shins with sparse purpura and bilateral ulnar deviation of the metatarsophalangeal joints. Routine laboratory tests showed known leukopenia, newly identified normocytic anemia, new renal failure (with a baseline creatinine of 0.8 mg/dl two years earlier), hypercalcemia, and new hypothyroidism. She was referred to hematology, where further tests revealed an IgM kappa monoclonal gammopathy based on serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP). A bone marrow biopsy did not show any lymphoproliferative process. Her anemia progressively worsened, requiring occasional transfusions. A urine dipstick test indicated nephrotic-range proteinuria. Given her overall presentation and medical history, these findings were notable.
test_results: Kidney biopsy showed proliferative glomerulonephritis and vasculitis with IgM kappa deposition.

case_report: A two-day-old male infant, delivered at full term via vaginal delivery, was brought to the pediatric emergency department due to increasing abdominal distention and absence of stool passage since birth. Symptoms worsened following feedings. Birth history was unremarkable. Initially, vital signs were normal, but the infant later exhibited mild respiratory distress, mottled skin, and signs of dehydration after episodes of vomiting. Physical examination showed a distended abdomen with visible peristalsis. Rectal examination found no meconium staining, although the anal opening was in the normal position. Laboratory tests were within normal limits. An abdominal radiograph displayed dilated, gas-filled bowel loops in the abdominal cavity and a lack of gas in the rectal area, with no evidence of free intraperitoneal air or calcifications.
test_results: It showed a small-caliber rectum and sigmoid colon (microcolon) with a preserved rectosigmoid ratio of 2:1. A round, contrast-filled, blind-ended pouch-like structure was depicted distally at the junction of the sigmoid along with a descending colon with no flow of contrast into the proximal colon.

case_report: A 6-year-old girl arrived at the pediatric emergency department with primary complaints of hematemesis and hematochezia. Her mother observed blood in her stool three days prior, followed by episodes of vomiting blood, with symptoms worsening significantly. The child was born at 34 weeks gestation via cesarean section, presenting with intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), and required a one-month stay in the neonatal intensive care unit. She underwent laser photocoagulation treatment for vision loss in her left eye. At 6 months old, she experienced convulsions.
test_results: The cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed diffuse symmetric calcifications, changes suggesting hemorrhage, dilated lateral ventricles, septated cystic lesions in the area extending from the roof of the third ventricle to the lateral ventricle and also hemorrhage in the globe in left orbit.

case_report: A 41-year-old woman visited an outpatient clinic due to repeated episodes of nausea and vomiting after consuming fruits, sucrose, or foods containing fructose. She reported a lifelong aversion to sweets. She was breastfed until 12 months old. Her mother attempted to introduce fruits, but she refused them. At the age of three, after being made to eat fruits, she experienced nausea, vomiting, and visual disturbances. She continued to avoid sweets thereafter. In adulthood, after consuming a small amount of a beverage, she experienced nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, followed by cold sweats and faintness two hours later. There was no family history of liver or genetic diseases, and other family members did not exhibit similar symptoms. Her height was 160 cm (50th percentile), and her weight was 50.2 kg (25th to 50th percentile). Physical examination was normal, with no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. Laboratory findings were within normal limits: white blood cell count 8,460/mm3 (neutrophil 64%, lymphocytes 30.5%, monocyte 4.8%, eosinophil 0.5%, basophil 0.2%), hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, platelet count 261,000 /mm3, calcium 8.8 mg/dL, phosphorus 3.5 mg/dL, glucose 96 mg/dL, uric acid 3.0 mg/dL, total cholesterol 180 mg/dL, total protein 7.5 g/dL, albumin 4.5 g/dL, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 61 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase 19 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase 16 IU/L, blood urea nitrogen 12 mg/dL, creatinine 0.49 mg/dL, prothrombin time 0.97 INR, activated partial thrombin time 30.1 seconds, and no abnormalities in urinalysis. Liver ultrasonography indicated normal size, shape, and echotexture without focal lesions.
test_results: The patient showed known heterozygous pathogenic nonsense (c.178C>T, p.Arg60Ter) variant and known pathogenic frameshift (c.360_363delCAAA, p.Asn120LysfsTer32) variant.

case_report: A 49-year-old African American female with a history of chronic allergic rhinitis, fibroids, and normocytic anemia came to the emergency room with chest pain lasting 10 days. The pain was sharp, rated four out of 10, located mid-sternally, non-radiating, and worsened with deep breaths and movements. She also experienced malaise, chills, fatigue, and reported a subjective fever for a week, along with right-sided sinus pressure and nosebleeds. She performed nasal irrigation four times daily after experiencing nasal congestion and nosebleeds. After three days of nasal irrigation, she noted worsening fatigue and subjective fevers. Upon arrival at the emergency room, she had intermittent fever episodes with a peak temperature of 103.1°F, managed with acetaminophen. She remained afebrile during her hospital stay after starting antibiotics. In the emergency department, she had sinus tachycardia at 110 beats per minute, which improved after fluid resuscitation with lactated ringers. Her electrocardiogram (EKG) showed sinus tachycardia at 106 beats per minute, ventricular premature complexes, and right bundle branch block (RBBB). There was no previous EKG available for comparison. A chest x-ray showed no active disease, pneumothorax, or pleural effusion. A complete blood count revealed leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 15.5 x103/µL (normal 4.0 - 12.5 x103/µL) and an absolute neutrophil count of 12.55 x103/µL (normal 1.7-7.0 x103/µL). Blood biochemistry showed a c-reactive protein level of 85.2 mg/L (normal less than 3.0 mg/L), serum lactate level of 0.9 mmol/L (normal 0.5-2.0 mmol/L), and high sensitivity troponins max of 453 pg/mL (normal 2-15 pg/mL). She tested negative for COVID-19 by nasal swab and RTPCR, had an unremarkable urinalysis, and tested negative for all substances on urine drug screening. She was admitted to the hospitalist service. Two peripheral blood cultures were taken from different sites before starting empirical antibiotic treatment with vancomycin and cefepime. The blood cultures tested positive in four out of four bottles for S. mitis after 24 hours. A CT scan of the sinuses with contrast was ordered due to concern of sinus abscess and showed narrowing of the right ostiomeatal. A transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was unremarkable except for trace mitral valve regurgitation. On physical examination the day after her TTE, she developed a Janeway lesion on her left thumb and had swelling and pain in her left ankle. An x-ray of her left ankle showed a small effusion and overlying soft tissue swelling. The ankle effusion and Janeway lesion were attributed to septic emboli.
test_results: The patient underwent a TEE, which demonstrated a mobile echo density of 5mm by 3mm attached to the atrial side of the anterior mitral valve leaflet with thickening of the anterior mitral leaflet tip as well as moderate mitral valve regurgitation.

case_report: On July 8, 2022, a 23-year-old female patient presented with fever and diarrhea. Physical examination revealed an enlarged spleen extending 3 cm below the left costal margin. She reported no previous history of diseases, and her family history showed no consanguineous marriages. Blood tests indicated leukocytosis (WBC: 18 × 10^9/L, reference: 3.50–9.50 × 10^9/L), thrombocytopenia (PLT: 39 × 10^9/L, reference: 125–350 × 10^9/L), elevated ultrasensitive CRP (288.5 mg/L, reference: <10 mg/L), and increased PCT (42.6 ng/ml, reference: <0.5 ng/ml). Biochemical tests showed elevated ALT (59 U/L, reference: 0–40 U/L), AST (72 U/L, reference: 0–40 U/L), TBIL (26 µmol/L, reference: 0–23 µmol/L), DBIL (11.7 µmol/L, reference: 0–4 µmol/L), TBA (119.1 µmol/L, reference: 0–10 µmol/L), SCr (241 µmol/L, reference: 21–75 µmol/L), and decreased ALB (29 g/L, reference: 40–55 g/L). Serum liver fibrosis indicators were elevated: HA (502 ng/ml, reference: <100 ng/mL), PCIII (33.2 ng/ml, reference: <30 ng/ml), and IV-C (41.2 ng/ml, reference: <30 ng/ml). Serum tumor markers were high: CA19-9 (>1200 U/ml, reference: <39 U/ml) and CA125 (80.8 U/ml, reference: <39 U/ml). Serologic tests for viral hepatitis, autoantibodies, and platelet antibodies were negative. Serum IgM and IgG levels were normal. Serum ceruloplasmin levels and 24-hour urinary copper levels were normal, and ophthalmological examination showed no KF ring. Serum-ferritin, serum-iron, and serum-total iron binding capacity were within normal ranges. Blood culture was positive for KP, and stool culture was positive for Candida albicans. CT imaging showed slight striate shadow in the lower lobes of both lungs, slight enlargement of the liver’s left lobe, mild dilation of the intrahepatic bile ducts, splenomegaly, esophageal and gastric fundus varices, and numerous tiny cysts in both kidneys. MRI revealed dilated intrahepatic and common bile ducts. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed gastric fundus varices without red signs. PET/CT findings indicated a slightly enlarged liver with mild dilatation of the intrahepatic bile ducts, hyperplastic lymph nodes around the portal vein, and a giant spleen with no increase in FDG metabolism.
test_results: The pathological findings of the liver biopsy showed several portal tracts are interconnected by bridging fibrous septa, which contained intensive proliferation of the bile ducts without inflammatory cell infiltrates, some of the bile ducts contained bile plugs. Immunohistochemical CK7, CK8/18, and CK19 staining in the liver tissue showed massive hyperplasia of irregular bile ducts and cystic dilatation of bile ducts. Whole-exome sequencing identified compound heterozygous variants in the PKHD1 gene: two missense substitutions c.3860T > G (p. V1287G) and c.9059T > C (p. L3020P). Both variants were confirmed by Sanger sequencing in the patient and her parents, with c.3860T > G variant paternally inherited, and c.9059T > C variant maternally inherited. In-silico analysis predicted the c. 3860T > G/p. V1287G variant as unknown clinical significance and the c. 9059T > C/p. L3020P variant as deleterious.
diagnosis: Congenital Hepatic Fibrosis  complicated with biliary sepsis

case_report: An 8-month-old female child with motor delay presented with a history of left-sided weakness following a fall from a walker at ground level. There were no other signs of traumatic brain injury such as loss of consciousness, vomiting, or convulsions. She was the firstborn to a non-consanguineously married couple with a normal birth history. She attained neck control at 5 months of age but was still not sitting with support, while cognitive and language milestones were normal. Upon admission, she was conscious, oriented to her mother and surroundings, had normal vital signs and anthropometric measurements, and showed no external injuries. She exhibited reduced movement in the left upper and lower limbs with variable muscle tone and brisk deep tendon reflexes on the same side. Intermittent dystonic posturing of the left lower limb was observed. There was no cranial nerve palsy, no neurocutaneous markers, and the fundus examination was normal. A comprehensive workup was conducted. Her complete blood count, bleeding time, PT, APTT, INR, serum calcium, serum homocysteine, protein C, protein S, antithrombin III, hemoglobin electrophoresis, parathyroid hormone, lipid profile, arterial blood gas, lactate, ammonia, plasma tandem mass spectrometry, and urine gas chromatography-mass spectrometry were all normal. Additionally, echocardiogram results were normal, and tests for HIV, TORCH titres, and lupus anticoagulant were negative.
test_results: MRI of the brain showed calcification of right basal ganglia and no evidence of infarct. CT of the brain showed multiple linear calcifications in bilateral basal ganglia predominantly involving caudate nuclei.
Orpha_name: Hereditary arterial and articular multiple calcification syndrome

case_report: A 13-year-old Korean male presented with a two-year history of painless protrusion of the left eye and facial swelling. Ophthalmologic examination revealed an uncorrected visual acuity of 0.5 in both eyes. Intraocular pressure was 19 mmHg bilaterally, measured by applanation tonometry. External eye examination, including eyelids and lacrimal glands, showed left conjunctival redness and proptosis without any visible or palpable mass. The light reflex was normal in both eyes, and there was no optic nerve dysfunction. Ocular motility was within normal range bilaterally, with no discomfort, painful eye movement, or double vision. Hertel exophthalmometry indicated a 3-mm proptosis of the left eye, with measurements of 17 mm for the right eye and 20 mm for the left eye. Fundoscopic examination was normal in both eyes. Preoperative facial CT identified a soft tissue mass involving the left masseter muscle, left temporalis muscle, and left medial pterygoid muscle. Preoperative facial MRI with gadolinium enhancement showed a 1.5×1.5 cm2 homogeneous mass with high signal intensity on T2-weighted images and relatively well-defined margins, adjacent to the left masseter muscle, left temporalis muscle, and left medial pterygoid muscle. Additionally, there was exophthalmos of the left eye with diffuse thickening of the left extraocular muscles, while the right eye appeared normal. Blood tests revealed peripheral eosinophilia of approximately 26%, but IgE levels were not measured.
test_results: The histologic examination of the incisional biopsy showed abnormal vascular proliferation with marked eosinophilic infiltration in hypertrophied collagenous tissue.

case_report: A 12-year-old girl was admitted to the pediatric endocrinology department due to excessive hair growth on her body, which had become noticeable over the past year. She was born to non-consanguineous parents who are healthy. Her birth weight was normal, and her past medical history is unremarkable. Physical examination revealed severe hirsutism with a Modified Ferriman-Gallwey Score of 30, an acneiform rash on her face, and severe acanthosis nigricans in the axilla, neck, and antecubital area. Her blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg. She measured 156.5 cm in height (70th percentile), weighed 68.4 kg (99th percentile), and had a body mass index of 27.9 kg/m2 (98th percentile) at the time of admission. Her pubertal development was at Tanner stage 4, and her bone age was assessed to be 13.5 years. There was no history of spontaneous menarche. Laboratory tests showed elevated fasting insulin levels with normal fasting glucose. Glycohemoglobin (HbA1c) levels and oral glucose tolerance test results indicated a pre-diabetic state with significant hyperinsulinemia. Despite the severe hyperinsulinemia, her triglyceride, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) levels were normal, and ultrasonographic evaluation showed no hepatosteatosis. Gonadotropin levels indicated luteinizing hormone dominance with increased testosterone levels. Ultrasonographic evaluation also revealed a polycystic ovary appearance.
test_results: DNA Sanger Sequence analyses of all coding exons of INSR showed that a novel, homozygous mutation, NM_000208.4 c.779 T>G (p.Leu260Arg) was present in exon 3.

case_report: Family 1406 is a consanguineous family from Colombia. The proband, a 21-year-old male, first presented with an unusual stiff-legged gait at about one year of age. His pediatrician found no concerning features in his developmental history or examination at that time. As he grew, his parents observed that he would not bend his knees when jumping, and his gait would occasionally become stiff-legged. A neurologist noted good reflexes and no weakness. Over time, his symptoms worsened. He participated in soccer and other sports but was slower than his peers. He reported no difficulty initiating movements; however, after running for several yards, he experienced sudden muscle stiffness in his legs, requiring him to stop and rest. After a brief rest, he could resume running without difficulty. The stiffness was not accompanied by pain or weakness but worsened with cold exposure. He also experienced difficulty releasing a lacrosse or hockey stick after gripping it for a length of time and reported jaw stiffness with prolonged chewing, without choking or dysphagia. Neither parent had muscle symptoms. At 16 years, physical examination showed eyelid, hand, and foot myotonia with mild percussion myotonia at the thenar eminences and the extensor digitorum communis.
