At 20 years, physical examination showed eyelid myotonia and mild grip myotonia, with no percussion myotonia. Strength was normal in all extremities, with no muscle hypertrophy or atrophy and no heel cord contractures. Electrocardiogram and echocardiogram were normal. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography (EMG) at 12 years were normal. An EMG at 16 years showed normal sensory and motor nerve conduction studies, with fibrillation potentials noted on needle examination in the left extensor digitorum communis, without frank myotonic discharges. Muscle biopsy revealed excess fiber size variability, increased centralized nuclei, mild fiber type grouping, and focal myofibrillar disarray.
test_results: Clinical genetic testing showed no pathogenic mutations in CLCN1 and SCN4A.
diagnosis: Pathogenic mutation in ATP2A1 associated with paramyotonia congenita

case_report: A 31-year-old male presented with daily vertigo exacerbated by sudden head movements, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and balance difficulties in confined spaces. His medical history included meningitis at age 2, with no family history of vertigo, epilepsy, hearing loss, or familial cancer syndromes. He did not report headaches. Neurological and audiometric examinations revealed perceptive high tone loss in the right ear of unknown origin. An MRI examination of the cerebellum and cerebellopontine angle six months later was normal. The patient was advised to perform home exercises to alleviate symptoms. Three years later, he reported a persistent balance disorder, with initial vertigo symptoms resolved. He also experienced decreased lateral visual field perception for fast-approaching objects. Neurological examination showed bilateral horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze, subnormal tandem gait for his age, difficulty standing still with closed eyes, and a positive Dix-Hallpike test with a right-side predilection. Audiometric evaluation confirmed persistent perceptive high tone loss in the right ear.
test_results: A subsequent MRI examination focused on the cerebellum and cerebellopontine angle half a year later (time point B) was normal. A follow-up MRI examination, including thin slices through the cerebellum and cerebellopontine angle and series after contrast administration, again showed no pathology.

case_report: Patient 6 (PA-6) is a 3-month-old girl measuring 54.0 cm and weighing 3.7 kg, both below the 3rd percentile. She has experienced feeding difficulties and has not gained weight over the past 2 months. Clinical examination revealed underweight status, developmental delay, and an enlarged anterior fontanelle. Laboratory results showed decreased serum ALP and i-PTH levels, elevated serum calcium and urinary calcium/creatinine ratio, with normal serum phosphorus and 25(OH)D3 levels.
test_results: The X-ray of the chest demonstrated the thin ribs and the uneven decreased bone density of the ribs. The X-ray of both lower extremities showed the lightly curved tibia, the blurred metaphysis, and the uneven decreased bone density. Abdominal ultrasound examinations showed diffuse calcium deposits in the medulla of both kidneys.

case_report: A 39-year-old Caucasian woman presented with palpitations and a two-week history of increasing fatigue, shortness of breath, and abdominal pain with distension. Her medical history included hypothyroidism managed with thyroid replacement therapy and amenorrhea since age 20, which had not been investigated. Family history noted a first cousin who died suddenly at 20 years old from 'cardiac arrest.' Both parents were in good health, with no family history of iron overload or liver disease. The patient, an unmarried teacher, had never smoked, rarely consumed alcohol, and had no history of illicit drug use. Physical examination revealed mild jaundice and an irregular cardiac rhythm. The abdomen was diffusely tender with hepatomegaly, but no splenomegaly or evident ascites. An electrocardiogram indicated atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, and an echocardiogram showed globally decreased left ventricular systolic function with an estimated ejection fraction of 26%. The patient was admitted to the cardiovascular intensive care unit for heart failure management, heart rate control, and initiation of anticoagulation therapy. Hematologic findings included a hemoglobin concentration of 13 g/dL, platelet count of 100 K/mm3, and leucocyte count of 9.7 K/mm3. Blood chemistries revealed total bilirubin 2.6 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 1.1 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 1476 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 702 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 139 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase 52 U/L, albumin 4.1 g/dL, and lactate dehydrogenase 968 U/L. Peripheral blood smear review showed no evidence of hemolysis. Coagulation studies indicated a prothrombin time of 20 sec and an international normalized ratio (INR) of 2.1. Additional tests showed thyroid-stimulating hormone 40 uIU/mL (normal 0.27–4.2), free thyroxine 1.05 ng/dL (normal 0.93–1.7), thyroid peroxidase autoantibody (anti-TPO) 1586 IU/mL (normal < 2), follicle-stimulating hormone 0.3 mIU/mL (normal 3.5–12.5 mIU/mL), and luteinizing hormone 0.1 mIU/mL (normal 2.4–12.6 mIU/mL). Abdominal ultrasound revealed an enlarged liver with diffusely increased echogenicity, minimal ascites, and a normal-sized spleen. Doppler findings were consistent with congestive heart failure. Tests for viral hepatitis and autoimmune serologies were negative. Alpha 1-antitrypsin and ceruloplasmin levels were normal. Iron studies showed a transferrin saturation of 100% and ferritin of 116,070 ng/mL (normal 22–322 ng/mL).
test_results: Transjugular liver biopsy showed cirrhosis with 4+ iron deposition in hepatocytes and in biliary epithelium, as well as focal centrilobular necrosis. Amplification of the HFE2 gene by polymerase chain reaction with genotyping by direct sequencing disclosed that the patient was homozygous for the HFE2 Gly320Val mutation.

case_report: A 32-year-old male presented with progressive left upper quadrant pain, worsening fatigue, and night sweats. Over the past year, he experienced weight loss and constant night sweats requiring multiple changes of clothes. He also reported early satiety and decreased oral intake due to abdominal pain. Physical examination revealed clear breath sounds bilaterally, a regular heart rhythm, and significant diffuse lymphadenopathy of the anterior and posterior cervical chain bilaterally, which were non-tender. The abdominal examination showed significant tenderness to light touch in the left upper quadrant with a palpable spleen estimated 10 cm below the left costal margin. Vital signs were: temperature 100.8°F, pulse 98 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and blood pressure 99/63 mmHg. Initial labs are presented in Table. A review of his medical history revealed a previous hospital admission one year prior for abdominal pain with similar symptoms. CT imaging at that time showed severe splenomegaly, multiple enlarged upper abdominal retroperitoneal lymph nodes, and right supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. During that admission, a right cervical core needle biopsy revealed a reactive lymph node. He received three treatments of radiation therapy for splenomegaly. Further workup showed negative results for HIV, toxoplasmosis, ANA, Mantoux test, cytomegalovirus, and hepatitis A, B, and C. Epstein-Barr virus IgG was positive. IgG, IgA, and IgM were within normal limits. Interleukin 6 (IL-6) was 26.2 pg/mL (normal values = 0.0-13.0 pg/mL). Repeat abdominal and chest CT with contrast showed marked splenomegaly, measuring approximately 16.7 cm, with multiple hypoattenuating lesions in the spleen and numerous focal lesions in the left upper quadrant, periportal, and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. CT of the chest showed no cardiopulmonary process, mediastinal mass, or lung nodules. CT of the neck showed supraclavicular and cervical adenopathy, most pronounced on the right.
test_results: The results were pertinent for an enlarged lymph node with atypical lymphoid cells. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) and flow cytometry immunophenotyping were also performed which demonstrated CD20 positivity with a subset showing positivity for CD45. CD30 and CD15 were also tested and were unremarkable. In addition, paired box 5, epithelial membrane antigen, B-cell lymphoma 6, and multiple myeloma 1 were not observed.

case_report: A 66-year-old male experienced episodic limb weakness starting at age 2, affecting both lower limbs and occasionally both upper and lower limbs. Prolonged walking often triggered these episodes, and seizures occurred once or twice a month. Over time, he developed persistent muscle weakness, making activities like running, squatting, standing up, and lifting his arms difficult. Throughout his life, he had multiple hospital visits where his creatine kinase (CK) levels ranged from 600 to 1,000 U/L. Muscle biopsies from his calf, shoulder, and back at ages 13, 20, and 26 showed no abnormalities. At age 26, he underwent genetic testing, but results were inconclusive. Electrophysiologic examination of the iliopsoas, gluteus maximus, and lumbar paraspinal muscles 25 years ago indicated myopathy. Treatment with coenzyme Q10 was ineffective. He had all his teeth extracted due to intubation difficulties during vocal cord polyp surgery and was found quadriplegic after general anesthesia 10 years ago. Cervical spine MRI showed no abnormalities. Recently, he experienced worsening limb weakness, particularly in the morning, and fell, unable to stand, leading to an emergency department visit. Physical examination revealed amyotrophy in the proximal extremities (Medical Research Council Grade 4), decreased tendon reflexes, and negative bilateral pathological signs. Electrocardiogram showed U-wave inversion, and a 24-hour dynamic electrocardiogram recorded 245 premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) out of 91,847 heartbeats. EMG examination showed narrow and irregular waves without fibrillation. Blood tests indicated a potassium level of 2.9 mmol/L (normal: 3.5–5.5 mmol/L), CK level of 1,600 U/L, lactic acid level of 2.8, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) level of 224 U/L.
test_results: Genetic analysis identified a heterozygous c.220A > G mutation in the exon 2 region of chromosome 17 of the KCNJ2 gene. This mutation resulted in the substitution of alanine with threonine at amino acid 74 (p.T74A). A long-term exercise test indicated a significant decrease in the compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitude of the right little finger abductor muscle, measuring 74.4% lower than the baseline and a 66% reduction in the area.

case_report: A 15-year-old male presented with pain and swelling in the left knee and right ankle. These joint symptoms began a year prior and progressively limited his mobility. Additional chronic complaints included fatigue, persistent fever, and morning stiffness. The patient exhibited delayed mental and neurological development. Physical examination revealed weight and height below the third percentile, mild microcephaly, high arch palate, fish mouth, cervical lymphadenopathy, lack of sexual maturation, hypotonia, increased patellar deep tendon reflexes, deformity of the lower limbs (thick and floppy), and decreased range of motion in both knees. His medical history included chronic intermittent fever since infancy. Magnetic resonance imaging without contrast showed severe joint effusion. Ophthalmologic examination indicated corneal nerve enlargement and signs of past iritis and uveitis. Laboratory findings included elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (65 mm/h; normal = 0-22), positive C-reactive protein (35 mg/L; normal: 0-3), semiclear urine without proteinuria, and lower than normal levels of serum luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, and testosterone, while serum growth hormone levels were within the normal range. Antinuclear antibody and anticyclic citrullinated peptide tests were negative.
test_results: Genetic studies based on Sanger-based PCR-sequencing of the entire coding region (including splicing sites) showed a heterozygous variant NM_001243133: c.785G>A (NP_001230062: p.Arg262Gln) in Exon 3 of NLRP3 gene. The variant is absent in population databases (ExAC, 1000G, etc).
diagnosis: Chronic Infantile Neurological Cutaneous and Articular  Syndrome

case_report: A three-month-old female infant was presented to the emergency department with lethargy. The infant experienced five episodes of vomiting and exhibited seizure-like activity, characterized by upward rolling of the eyes, jerky movements of the left hand, and a fixed gaze lasting for 30 seconds. Following these episodes, the infant became floppy and unresponsive. Capillary blood glucose measurement indicated a low glucose level of 22 mg/dL.
test_results: Further testing revealed hyponatremia (123 mEq/L; normal: 136 to 146 mEq/L, hyperkalemia (5.9 mEq/L; normal: 3.5 to 5 mEq/L), and hypoglycemia (22 mg/dL; normal: greater than 50 mg/dL), as well as increased renin activity, increased adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) (712 pg/mL; normal: 25-100 pg/mL), and high dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) (3,600 nmol/L; normal: 256 ± 200 nmol/L), low aldosterone (2 ng/dL; normal: 5 to 30 ng/dL), and low cortisol, and a high 17 hydroxyprogesterone levels (130 nmol/L; normal: 3.2 ± 1.5 nmol/L). Ultrasound of the abdomen showed normal kidneys with normal corticomedullary demarcation and a normal adrenal gland.
diagnosis: Salt-Wasting Form of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia
Orpha_name: Classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency, salt wasting form

case_report: A 21-year-old male patient was admitted with a blood pressure that increased from 134/92 mmHg to 162/112 mmHg over a year, without any medications. Symptoms such as perspiration, headache, and facial pallor were absent, except for persistent hyperhidrosis occurring for approximately 5 years. Abdominal ultrasound and double lower limb arteriovenous ultrasound showed no abnormalities. He was administered betaxolol 25 mg twice daily (from 4 to 2 weeks prior to surgery), nifedipine sustained-release tablets 30 mg once daily (from 4 to 3 weeks prior to surgery), and cefuroxime 0.25 g twice daily (for prevention of incision infection). A minimally invasive thoracotomy was performed to resect the cardiac mass. He was then transferred for further treatment. Upon physical examination, his blood pressure fluctuated within 130–140/80–90 mmHg, body mass index (BMI) was 20.34 kg/m2, and heart rate was 100–110 beats per minute. The blood pressure in the lower extremities exceeded that in the upper extremities. All pulses were palpable without vascular murmurs. Blood levels of norepinephrine, dopamine, methoxy norepinephrine, and urinary norepinephrine were evaluated. Cardiac troponin I was 0.000 ng/mL, myoglobin was 9.560 ng/mL, and creatine kinase MB was 0.595 ng/mL. Computed tomography scanning of the kidneys, adrenal glands, and renal arteries was normal. During hospitalization (3 weeks prior to surgery), the patient experienced severe substernal pain related to breathing, which worsened in the supine position, slightly improved after sitting up, and was relieved after morphine 3 mg injection. Oral nifedipine sustained-release tablets were withdrawn, and symptoms improved with terazosin 2 mg once daily. His blood pressure ranged from 110–140/80–90 mmHg and heart rate was 100–110 beats per minute. For surgery preparation, a high-sodium diet was started 2 weeks before the operation, terazosin was gradually increased from 2 mg twice daily (from 2 to 1 week prior to surgery) to 2 mg three times daily (from 1 week prior to surgery), and betaxolol was increased to 25 mg three times daily (from 2 weeks prior to surgery). His blood pressure was then controlled to 100–121/56–77 mmHg and heart rate was 80–100 beats per minute. Hydroxyethyl starch 500 mL daily and 0.9% saline 500 mL daily were administered intravenously for 3 days before the operation.
test_results: A mass was observed in the right heart (possibly in the pericardial space) via echocardiography, with an anteroposterior diameter of the left atrium (LA) of 33 mm, a left ventricular end-diastolic anteroposterior diameter (LV) of 52 mm, and a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 65%. Cardiac computed tomography (CT) revealed an abnormal density shadow with rich blood supply in the right atrioventricular sulcus. Positron emission tomography (PET) CT presented an abnormal glucose concentration in the mass. Echocardiography presented LA 33 mm, LV 53 mm, LVEF 65%, and a solid mass in the pericardial space (39 mm × 35 mm × 39 mm). Somatostatin receptor imaging revealed abnormalities in the right atrioventricular sulcus. Coronary angiography revealed a blood supply of the mass from the right coronary artery.

case_report: A 2-year-old girl was observed to have difficulty seeing in low light conditions and experienced hearing loss. Vision assessment revealed a visual acuity of 20/2700 in the right eye and 20/960 in the left eye using Teller acuity cards. Cycloplegic refraction indicated hypermetropia of +7.50D in both eyes. Fundus examination showed mottling of the peripheral retinal pigment epithelium, pale optic discs, narrow arterioles, and a generally normal macula.
test_results: A full field ERG showed no response from either scotopic or photopic stimuli. The SD-OCT showed preserved retinal layers at the fovea, with the loss of the outer layers of the retina with increasing distance from the fovea. The photoreceptor layers were completely lost 2–3 mm away from the fovea and the outer plexiform layer was lost further into the mid-peripheral retina.

case_report: An 86-year-old female with no significant past medical history presented with a headache persisting for 1 year. The headache occurred exclusively at night, starting around 12 a.m., waking her up and lasting for 2–3 hours. She rated the headache severity between 4 and 7 on a scale of 1 to 10. The headache was unilateral, primarily around the right orbital region, occasionally involving the auricular area, and was described as a dull aching, non-pulsating pain without radiation. Sometimes, the headache was accompanied by right-sided rhinorrhea. There was no conjunctival injection, tearing, nausea, vomiting, or sensitivity to light or sound. She reported uninterrupted sleep before the onset of these headache episodes. There were no indications of obstructive sleep apnea or other sleep-related disorders. She had no history of migraines, recurrent headaches, seizures, neuralgias, or other neurological conditions. Family history was unremarkable. Despite multiple medical consultations, her symptoms persisted. On examination, she appeared well at rest with a regular heart rate of 70 beats/min, blood pressure of 142/68 mmHg, and clear lung fields. Ophthalmoscopy was normal, and temporal arteries were pulsatile and non-tender. The neurological examination was unremarkable. Oxygen saturation was 97% on room air. Hematological and biochemical investigations, including full blood count, blood picture, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, fasting blood glucose, lipid profile, and liver profile, were normal. Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) was 20 mm per first hour, and C-reactive protein level was 7 mg/L (normal 0.08–3.1 mg/L).
test_results: Gadolinium enhanced MRI brain was unremarkable except for mild cerebral atrophy and volume loss compatible with age.

case_report: A 52-year-old female presented to the emergency department with symptoms including night sweats, scaly skin, rash, acrocyanosis, and multiple swellings on the left side of her neck, which had been progressively increasing in size over the past three to four months. These swellings were mobile, non-tender, and firm. Her medical history included hypothyroidism, antiphospholipid syndrome, and cerebral venous thrombosis for the past six years, as well as hypertension and diabetes mellitus for the past year and a half. She also experienced wasting and deformity of the hands, weakness in the proximal muscles of the upper limbs, and weakness and paresthesia in the distal portions of both lower limbs, which had been gradually worsening over six months. Physical examination showed desquamated skin rashes with multiple skin lesions. Examination of the neck revealed enlarged left supraclavicular, anterior cervical, left cervical, right axillary, bilateral occipital, and submandibular lymph nodes. Abdominal examination indicated an enlarged liver (20 cm span) with signs of ascites and a protuberant stomach. Ophthalmic examination confirmed papilledema, and neurologic evaluation revealed mild paresthesia and tetraparesis. Bilateral claw hands were also observed.
test_results: Serum protein electrophoresis confirmed the presence of IgG lambda monoclonal protein. A biopsy of the left cervical lymph node confirmed the diagnosis of Castleman disease, the hyaline vascular type, without evidence of malignancy. Nerve conduction studies revealed polyneuropathy in all limbs (nerve conduction velocity: <33 m/s). An FDG PET-CT scan indicated sclerotic foci in some thoracic and lumbar vertebrae along with bilateral pleural and pericardial effusion.

case_report: A twelve-year-old boy visited a pediatrician because of sudden difficulty in walking. Three days prior to his visit, he had received the H1N1 vaccine at school. Two days after the vaccination, he reported to his mother that he was having trouble walking. His medical history was unremarkable. During the neurological examination, no significant abnormalities were found except for mild, fluctuating motor weakness in both legs. It was observed that while walking, his knees would buckle, but not to the extent that he would fall.
test_results: Routine laboratory results were within the normal limits. Thoracic MRI and nerve conduction study (NCS) were normal.

case_report: A 31-year-old woman visited the Rheumatology Clinic with a 6-month history of pain and swelling in her hands. Over the past year, she also experienced frequent nasal ulcers. She did not report any fever or general health decline. She has a history of epilepsy diagnosed at age 12, characterized by partial seizures, and has been on carbamazepine (300 mg twice daily) for 18 years with effective control of her condition. An attempt to discontinue the medication 15 years ago led to the recurrence of seizures, so the treatment was continued. Physical examination revealed normal cardiac and pulmonary auscultation, but arthritis was noted in the carpal, metacarpophalangeal, and proximal interphalangeal joints. There were no skin lesions, organ enlargement, or swollen lymph nodes. Laboratory results showed a hemoglobin level of 11.5 g/dL and a hematocrit of 32.5%. White blood cell count, differential count, and platelet numbers were normal. Liver and kidney function tests, thyroid hormone levels, and hepatitis B and C serology were all normal. The rheumatoid factor test was negative.
test_results: The antinuclear antibodies (ANA) were positive to a titer of 1/1280 (homogeneous pattern), and positive anti-nucleosome antibodies. The rest of the antibodies were negative, including anti-dsDNA, anti-histones, anti-Sm, anti-RNP, anti-Scl70, anti-PMScl, anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB, anti-Jo1, anti-centromere, anti-PCNA, anti-ribosomal P, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), and anticardiolipin IgM/IgGs. The complement levels were low, with a C3 of 62 mg/dL (normal: 90–180) and a C4 of 6 mg/dL (normal: 10–40).

case_report: A 58-year-old male presented with abdominal cramps and chronic diarrhea persisting for 3 months, accompanied by an unintentional weight loss of approximately 10 kg. His medical history includes Sjogren syndrome and lupus nephritis for 22 years, treated with various immunosuppressive agents such as mycophenolate mofetil, rituximab, and tacrolimus (4 mg/d) for the past 2 years. Additionally, he has been on prednisolone (7.5 mg/d), hydroxychloroquine (200 mg/d), losartan (150 mg/d), and erythropoietin (4000 IU/SC three times a week). The patient reported no recurrent infections, malnutrition, or other medical conditions. Laboratory findings showed normochromic, normocytic anemia (Hb: 8.6 g/dL), elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR: 39 mm/h), and increased creatinine levels (Cr: 1.3 mg/dL). Tacrolimus level was measured at 6.4 ng/mL. Liver function tests and thyroid function tests were within normal limits. Stool and blood cultures, ova and parasite testing, and Clostridium difficile toxin assay all returned negative results. Colonoscopy identified multiple small polyps in the rectum (two removed with jumbo forceps), mucosal inflammation, and a cobblestone appearance in the sigmoid and cecum, while the rest of the colon appeared normal. CT enterography indicated normal ileal and jejunal loops with normal wall thickness.
test_results: Histopathological examination of cecal mucosa and rectal polyps revealed crypt distortion, irregularity, and superficial erosions, and infiltration of numerous foamy epithelioid histiocytes, eosinophils, lymphoplasma cells, neutrophils, and occasional giant cells in the lamina propria. Foamy epithelioid histiocytes showed numerous PAS-positive granules in the cytoplasm. MG bodies were rarely seen. Microthrombi were also noted in the capillaries.

case_report: A 26-year-old Hispanic male with no significant past medical history presented to the emergency department due to an inability to move his lower limbs. The patient reported being asymptomatic the previous day. He mentioned waking up at 03:00 AM feeling slightly weak in his lower extremities but was able to walk to the restroom and back to bed. A few hours later, he found himself unable to move his legs. The patient denied any recent viral infections, ingestion of canned foods, past or family history of renal disease, exposure to paint fumes, spinal cord injury, tick bites, or previous episodes of paralysis. On arrival, the patient was afebrile with a pulse of 100, respiratory rate of 14/min, and blood pressure of 150/67 mm Hg. Physical examination revealed that the patient was alert and oriented, with sweating, exophthalmos, and warm extremities. Neurological examination showed 0/5 motor strength in the proximal lower extremities and 2/5 motor strength in the proximal upper limbs, with normal sensation. Laboratory results indicated serum potassium at 1.2 MeQ/L (normal range 3.5-5.1), magnesium at 0.9 mg/dl (normal range 1.2-2.2), calcium at 8.6 mg/dl (normal range 8.7-10.6), and phosphorus at 1.9 mg/dl (normal range 2.7-4.5). EKG findings showed significant U waves. The patient exhibited tachycardia, hypomagnesemia, and hypophosphatemia.
test_results: Thyroid function tests: free T4 - 6.57 ng/ml (0.60-1.60), TSH - 0.05 IU/ml (0.34-5.60), free T3 - 8.78 pg/ml (2.5-3.9).

case_report: A 7-year-old female presented to the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at Ondokuz Mayıs University, Faculty of Dentistry with complaints related to chewing function. The patient's medical history included chronic renal insufficiency and hypertension, managed with peritoneal dialysis five times daily. Extraoral examination showed no abnormalities. Intraoral examination indicated poor oral hygiene with plaque deposits in all quadrants. Caries were noted only on the maxillary left first primary molar. The patient was in the mixed dentition stage, with the first permanent molars exhibiting abnormal occlusal morphology. Additionally, the patient had class 2 malocclusion and an anterior open bite.
test_results: There was a radiolucent cystic lesion at right maxilla, first permanent molars and incisors were erupted, and the root development was incomplete. The permanent second molars were unerupted and had no root formation, while the other unerupted permanent teeth had short, blunted, and malformed roots with obliterated pulp chambers, and bone below the teeth showed well-defined margins.

case_report: A 60-year-old man with no significant past medical history came to the emergency department with a three-day history of fevers, headaches, and a painful skin rash. He reported having rhinorrhea, headaches, and a sore throat a week prior to his visit. Three days before his hospital visit, he developed painful round violaceous papules on his right ankle, which appeared shortly after his fever began. These papules grew larger and merged into more extensive lesions, spreading from his right ankle to his right thigh, abdomen, lower chest, and left lower extremity. Additionally, he experienced swelling primarily on the dorsal aspect of his hands. On physical examination, his vital signs were normal except for a temperature of 38.6°C. Palpable purpura was noted above the medial malleolus, with a chord-like purpuric lesion on the medial thigh extending upwards from the malleolar lesion. Closer inspection of the initial lesion revealed wine-colored vesicles with a purpuric base. Bilateral dorsal hand edema was also observed. The remainder of his examination was unremarkable. His complete blood cell counts and chemistries were normal. Inflammatory markers were elevated, with a C-reactive protein of 147 mg/L (normal value <8 mg/L) and a sedimentation rate of 51 mm (normal value <15 mm). Immunoglobulin A was 509 mg/dL (normal value 82-460 mg/dL). Further tests, including urine toxicology (negative for levamisole and cocaine), blood cultures, gonorrhea, chlamydia, viral hepatitis serologies, antinuclear antibodies, complements, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), cryoglobulins, and rheumatoid factor, were negative.
test_results: There was a perivascular inflammatory infiltration of neutrophils, lymphocytes, histiocytes, and eosinophils. Perivascular neutrophilic nuclear fragmentation was appreciated. Extravasated erythrocytes and nuclear dust were present in the dermis. Direct immunofluorescence revealed interstitial dermal fibrinogen deposition. IgG, IgA, IgM, and C3 were non-contributory. No pathological microorganism was found.

case_report: An 8-month-old Tibetan boy presented with skin eruptions on the face and anogenital regions, which began around 4 months after birth. The patient also experienced diarrhea, hair loss, and irritability. There was no family history of consanguineous marriage. Physical examination showed well-defined redness and crusting on the neck, the inner side of the lower limbs, and around the mouth, eyes, genital, and anal areas. Laboratory tests were normal except for a reduced serum zinc level of 28.44 μmol/L (normal range: 33.5–84.54 μmol/L). Serum alkaline phosphatase levels were not measured.
test_results: Sanger sequencing of SLC39A4 revealed that the patient was compound heterozygous for maternal c.1462_1474 + 1del AGACTGAGCCCAGG in exon 9 and intron 9 and paternal c.1110insG in exon 6. Both variants have been reported to be pathogenic.

case_report: A 16-year-old female, previously monitored by the psychosomatic medicine department for borderline personality disorder, exhibited elevated plasma calcium levels, relatively low plasma phosphate (Pi) levels, and relatively high plasma intact parathyroid hormone (PTHi) levels during follow-up. Her height and weight were recorded at 154 cm and 53.5 kg, respectively. Despite being asymptomatic, she was referred to another department in June for further evaluation of her hypercalcemia. At the time of referral, her plasma calcium was 11.5 mg/dL (normal range: 8.8–10.1), plasma Pi was 3.1 mg/dL (normal range: 2.7–4.6), and PTHi was 51 pg/mL (normal range: 10–65). Her 1,25-OH vitamin D was elevated at 59.7 (normal range: 20.0–60.0), while 25-OH vitamin D was low at 9 (normal range: < 25). Thyroid echography and 99mTc-MIBI scintigraphy showed no abnormalities in the parathyroid glands. Her 24-hour urinary calcium excretion was 100 mg/day (normal range: 100–300), and her calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio (CCCR) was below 0.01 (first measurement: 0.0053, second measurement: 0.0059; normal range: > 0.01). Her 24-hour urinary Pi excretion was 0.58 g/day (normal range: 0.5–1.0), and tubular reabsorption of phosphate was 89.9% (normal range: 80–94). Her TmP/GFR was consistent with her plasma Pi levels, indicating normal renal function. Additionally, her brother and father also had elevated calcium levels.
test_results: A pathogenic CASR mutation (CASR: NM_000388.4: exon2: c.164C > T: p. Pro55Leu) was noted in her father (I-1), brother (II-1), and the proband (II-3), but no mutation in GNA11 and AP2S1 was identified.

case_report: A 56-year-old man with a history of smoking was referred to the Urology department after ultrasound detected masses in the bladder and left kidney during an evaluation for hematuria and left flank pain. Physical examination revealed no significant findings. Laboratory tests, including complete blood cell count and blood chemistries, as well as renal function tests, were within normal limits. Urine analysis showed the presence of hematuria. Cystoscopy identified a 2-cm papillary lesion on the left lateral aspect of the bladder. A contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed significant tissue densification in the renal sinus, with marked thickening of the urothelium, causing deformity of the renal pelvis and calyces, especially in the middle and lower regions, along with some heterogeneity of the renal parenchyma, highly suggestive of a renal tumor.
test_results: Atypical lymphoid proliferation was observed, showing plasmacytoid differentiation. The neoplasm was positive for immunoglobulin light chain kappa and for CD20, but negative for CD3, CD5, CD10, Bcl-6, Bcl-2, CD23, cyclin D1, and CD38.

case_report: A 33-year-old male presented with intermittent vision loss in his left eye, which began suddenly one month prior. He reported a one-year history of skin darkening, fatigue, impotence, and weight loss. Physical examination revealed hyperpigmentation on his face, chest, abdomen, back, limbs, areolas, and armpits. He had a history of trauma leading to a ten-day coma. He did not smoke, and his family history was unremarkable. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination showed splenomegaly, scattered warts, a lump in the left breast, and palpable lymph nodes in the axillary area. Laboratory tests revealed thrombocytosis (PLT 329×10^9/L), polycythemia (RBC 5.76×10^12/L), hyperuricemia (UA 476μmol/L), dyslipidemia (TG 2.88mmol/L, HDL-c 0.59mmol/L), hyperphosphatemia (phosphorous 1.64mmol/L), and microalbuminuria (UAER 85mg/24h). Serum autoimmune antibodies and tumor markers were negative. Hormonal tests showed elevated serum thyroglobulin antibody (TGAb 14.85IU/mL), follicular stimulating hormone (FSH 5.90IU/L), and prolactin (PRL 23.68ug/L), with normal levels of FT3, FT4, TSH, estrogen, progestogen, and testosterone. An ACTH-stimulation test indicated primary adrenocortical insufficiency (24-hour urinary free cortisol, before/after ACTH stimulation 91.70ug/100.06ug) with a normal diurnal cortisol rhythm. A 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) and insulin releasing test (IRT) showed a delayed peak of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion at 120 minutes, though glucose tolerance was normal. Sonography confirmed splenomegaly, gynecomastia, and enlarged axillary lymph nodes. CT-angiography revealed occlusion of the left internal carotid artery and absence of the left intra-cranial internal carotid artery. Brain MRI showed multifocal infarction beside the left lateral ventricle. Skeletal radiographic survey and CT scan identified multifocal sclerotic bone lesions in the thoracolumbar vertebrae and pelvis. Neurologic examination and nerve conduction studies indicated distal sensorimotor polyneuropathies in the limbs. Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy showed no evidence of plasma-cell dyscrasia, and Bence Jones protein was negative in the urine. Immunofixation electrophoresis did not detect monoclonal protein in the serum and urine.
test_results: The presence of monoclonal protein (λ-light chain in the γ region) was detected.

case_report: A term female neonate was delivered spontaneously at BDTH Kaduna to a 25-year-old mother with two previous live births. The APGAR scores were 6 at the 1st minute and 7 at the 5th minute. The parents initially left the hospital with the baby but returned 14 hours later due to the baby's inability to suck and worsening breathing difficulties. The mother had received antenatal care and took both orthodox and herbal medications, with no exposure to known teratogens. She had no history of hypertension or diabetes, and there was no family history of congenital abnormalities. A 3rd-trimester ultrasound indicated polyhydramnios but no fetal abnormalities. The father, a 40-year-old businessman, had no consanguineous relationship with the mother. Upon examination, the neonate exhibited severe dyspnea with chest wall recessions, nasal flaring, tachypnea, and central cyanosis. Dysmorphic features included macrocephaly, frontal bossing, sutural diastasis, a depressed nasal bridge, and low-set ears. Additional abnormalities were very short upper and lower limbs with multiple excessive skin folds, short and stubby digits (brachydactyly), a narrow chest, and a protuberant abdomen. The head was not trilobed. Anthropometric measurements were: weight 2.5 kg, length 38 cm (upper segment 27 cm, lower segment 11 cm, US:LS ratio 2.45), occipitofrontal circumference (OFC) 40 cm, and chest circumference (CC) 27 cm, with an OFC:CC ratio of 1.5.
test_results: The radiological findings included macrocephaly with craniofacial disproportion, narrow chest with flattened ribs, poorly aerated lung fields, shortening of the long bones with telephone-handle appearance of the humerus and femur bilaterally, and widening of vertebral bodies with reduced heights.

case_report: A 29-year-old Saudi woman, who is G4T2P0A1L2 at 21 weeks of gestation, presented with no medical illnesses or previous surgeries. She is a housewife, has never smoked or consumed alcohol, and has not traveled to any endemic or pandemic regions recently. She was referred due to findings from an antenatal ultrasound conducted at another hospital, which showed multiple fetal anomalies. Her obstetrical history includes two normal term vaginal deliveries and one unexplained first-trimester miscarriage. She is married to her first-degree cousin, who works in a governmental institute, and there is no family history of genetic or congenital anomalies. This pregnancy occurred spontaneously, with no history of illicit drug use, infection, or radiation exposure. An initial early antenatal scan suggested possible fetal diaphragmatic hernia, but further validation was not possible at the maternal-fetal medicine unit due to the lack of sonographic specialists. At her first antenatal visit at 21 weeks + 0 day of gestation, an anatomy scan showed a single viable fetus with an estimated fetal weight on the 50th percentile and normal biometry measurements.
test_results: The results of her anatomy scan revealed a single viable fetus with estimated fetal weight (EFW) on 50th percentile with normal biometry measurements. Further detailed anatomy scan findings revealed a male fetus with both kidneys appearing small in size, hyperechoic dysplastic, both ureters were dilated, urinary bladder looked abnormal in shape with thickened bladder wall, and umbilical cord at fetal insertion side appeared thickened. In addition, the diaphragm was seen clearly separating the chest from the abdominal compartments with no evidence of diaphragmatic hernia. Both feet were clubbed and open hands were seen with no other anomalies or any soft marker seen. Another follow-up scan revealed a single viable fetus, cephalic in presentation, anhydramnios with normal head and femoral length biometry. Unfortunately, the abdominal circumference (AC) was not taken due to the extremely distended abdominal wall that prevented any further visualization by ultrasound. The right kidney measured 3.4 × 1.1 cm with a small cyst, the left kidney measured 2.9 × 1.3 cm with bilateral hugely dilated ureter and urinary bladder (mega cyst). TORCH screen test results were non-reactive. Amniocentesis was performed and showed normal chromosomal results. A fetal echocardiogram allowed for limited examination due to anhydramnios; however, no obvious cardiac anomalies were noted. Lungs appeared compressed due to severely distended abdomen from the progressively enlarged urinary system, otherwise no other abnormal findings noted.

case_report: A 63-year-old, right-handed, Caucasian male was referred for further evaluation of a movement disorder occurring in the context of a rheumatic condition. Three years prior to evaluation at our center, he developed an unsteady gait. Imaging of the cervical spine revealed mild compression at the C3 to C4 levels, and he subsequently underwent anterior fusion of C3 to C4. Despite the surgical intervention, his gait continued to deteriorate. During a neurological assessment, bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity were observed without the presence of a resting tremor. Treatment with l-dopa (600 mg, 3 times daily) did not result in any improvement.
test_results: MRI revealed prominent medullary, pontine, and cerebellar atrophy.
diagnosis: Multiple System Atrophy of the Parkinsonian type

case_report: The patient is an 8-year-old girl born to non-consanguineous French parents. She presented with psychomotor retardation and absence of the olfactory bulb. Genetic testing, including an array and fragile X syndrome testing, returned negative results. Sequencing of the EHTM1 gene was also normal. Clinical features include hypertelorism, plagiocephaly, upwardly sloping labial commissures, large incisors, and short fingers, particularly the fifth digit. The neonatal period was notable for failure to thrive and gastric reflux requiring treatment. Developmental milestones were delayed; she sat at 14 months and walked independently at 2 years and 6 months. Her first words appeared at around 1 year of age, but at 8 years old, she still exhibits severe language delay. Behavioral observations include frustration intolerance, emotional immaturity, anger outbursts, poor safety awareness, and concentration difficulties. She has a history of recurrent ear, nose, and throat infections, as well as recurrent left lumbar tumefaction of unknown cause, which may suggest a vascular malformation. Her growth parameters show a height following the -1SD trajectory and a head circumference at 2SD.
test_results: An ID gene panel found a variant c.6152dupC de novo in ANKRD11.

case_report: A 14-year-old male patient, born to healthy parents with no known consanguinity, showed normal early motor development. At 7 years old, he was moved to a remedial school and started seeing a psychiatrist for mild cognitive deficits. By the age of 8, he developed a slowly progressing gait disturbance. At 12 years old, he began experiencing headaches, leg pain, and occasional episodes of reduced visual acuity.
test_results: Brain MRI revealed diffuse signal elevation in T2WI in the corticospinal and sensory pathways of the brainstem and spinal cord, as well as in the cerebellum. Electroneuromyography (ENMG) demonstrated a moderate axonal-demyelinating polyneuropathy.
diagnosis: Leukoencephalopathy with Brainstem and Spinal Cord Involvement and Lactate Elevation
Orpha_name: Leukoencephalopathy with brain stem and spinal cord involvement-high lactate syndrome

case_report: A 47-year-old female patient came to our clinic reporting reduced vision in her left eye. Her best corrected visual acuity was measured at 1.0 in the right eye and 0.8 partial in the left eye (Snellen). Examination of the anterior segment using a slit-lamp and measurement of intraocular pressures showed normal results.
test_results: Fundoscopic examination revealed angioid streaks in both eyes, and subretinal fluid in the foveal area and subretinal hemorrhage inferonasal to the fovea in the left eye. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed subfoveal fluid in the left eye. FFA showed bilateral angioid streaks and comet lesions, as well as CNV in the left eye.

case_report: A 47-year-old male agriculturalist visited the dermatology outpatient department with complaints of itchy, reddish, raised lesions on the forearms, which progressively spread to the trunk, lower limbs, and face over the past 7 months. There was no involvement of mucosal areas or other systemic symptoms. The patient had a history of atopic eczema during childhood and reported adverse reactions to ibuprofen and diclofenac. Previous treatment with oral antihistamines and topical steroids by a general practitioner showed no improvement. Physical examination revealed multiple well-defined, erythematous, follicle-based papules with minimal scaling, some of which coalesced into plaques on the chest, back, lower limbs, and face. There were no pustules, but a few excoriations were noted. No lymphadenopathy was observed. Blood tests indicated peripheral eosinophilia with 25% eosinophils (normal < 6%) on differential WBC count and an absolute eosinophil count of 2990/mcL (normal <350 cells/mcL). Serum IgE level was 1873 IU/ml (normal <100 IU/ml). VDRL test and KOH fungal smear were negative. Renal function test, liver function test, urine routine examination, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and antinuclear antibodies were within normal limits.
test_results: Lesional skin biopsy showed broad acanthosis with orthokeratosis with a perivascular, perineural, and periappendageal infiltrate of eosinophils and lymphocytes in the dermis. Epidermis showed mild spongiosis but micropustules containing neutrophils/eosinophils were not seen. Follicles showed reticular degeneration with exocytosis of eosinophils and lymphocytes into the follicular epithelium.

case_report: A 3-year-old Saudi girl presented with a history of slowly growing, unruly scalp hair since early childhood. The patient has black hair that can be easily and painlessly pulled out with minor traction or combing. Her mother reported that the patient always had short hair and never needed a haircut. There is no consanguinity between the parents, and no similar condition is observed in her 3 older brothers, who have easily combable hair that requires regular haircuts. Clinical examination revealed no systemic abnormalities, with normal nails, teeth, and skin. There were no complete alopecic areas in zones subjected to rubbing or traction, but the hair pull test was positive.
test_results: The light microscopic examination of the plucked hairs revealed misshapen anagen bulbs and ruffled appearance of the cuticles.

case_report: A 13-month-old girl exhibited hair fragility and hair loss starting at 3 months of age. The mother experienced first trimester vaginal bleeding but had an otherwise uncomplicated antenatal history. The girl was born at term to non-consanguineous parents. At birth, she was covered in a collodion membrane, which shed after 2 weeks. There was no indication of photosensitivity, and sweating was normal. Physical examination noted a prematurely aged appearance, frontal bossing, sparse scalp hair, a knotted area on the right scalp, absent eyebrows, brittle finger and toe nails with onychoschizia, and normal sweating. The skin displayed mild xerosis with eczema on the trunk.
test_results: Light microscopy of haircuts showed trichorrhexis nodosa, trichoschisis. On polarized microscopy, the hair shafts exhibited light and dark banding in a tiger-tail pattern.

case_report: A 60-year-old Caucasian male of British origin was admitted in September 2007 due to sudden onset of difficulty speaking and swallowing. He had been diagnosed with diabetes mellitus and hyperlipidemia three months prior and was started on gliclazide, ramipril, and aspirin. Simvastatin was also prescribed but discontinued after the patient developed proximal muscle weakness, muscle pain, and an elevated creatine kinase (CK) level of 2599 U/L (normal: <200 U/L), which resolved after stopping the medication. Gliclazide, ramipril, and aspirin were continued. On examination, mild difficulty speaking was noted, but no other significant findings were observed. Routine blood tests, including hematology, biochemistry, thyroid function, and creatine kinase, were within normal limits. Serum cholesterol was 6.1 mmol/L, and random blood glucose was 11.2 mmol/L. A brain CT scan showed no obvious infarct. The patient was started on dipyridamole and atorvastatin four days after admission. Over the next few days, the patient remained stable with mild difficulty speaking and swallowing, tolerating soft food. One week after admission, the patient's difficulty speaking and swallowing worsened, and new symptoms of bilateral fatigable drooping eyelids, double vision, and fatigable weakness in neck flexion and shoulder abduction were observed. A planned cranial MRI was subsequently cancelled.
test_results: Edrophonium testing demonstrated a dramatic transient improvement in his dysarthria.

case_report: A 9-year-old male patient of African descent presented to the emergency department with a three-day history of inability to speak. His father reported a sudden onset of symptoms, including decreased level of consciousness and excessive sleepiness. Prior to these symptoms, the patient experienced a severe headache, described as excruciating. Initially, he was treated at a nearby clinic with analgesics and antibiotics for presumed upper respiratory tract infections due to features suggestive of tonsillitis. On examination at the emergency department, the child appeared well-nourished but ill-looking and semiconscious with a Glasgow Coma Score of E4V1M5 = 10. He had a nasogastric tube in place, a patent and protected airway, and equally reactive pupils. Motor function was 3/5 in the upper limbs and 2/5 in the lower limbs. The patient exhibited opisthotonos posture and a positive Kernig's sign. Due to the decreased level of consciousness, a full cranial nerve assessment was challenging, but the gag reflex was normal, indicating airway protection. Hematological and biochemical investigations were unremarkable, except for elevated serum transaminases: ALT 56.3 U/L (normal range 1–50 U/L) and AST 139.2 U/L (normal range 1–50 U/L). Screening for dengue, malaria, SARS-CoV-2, and HIV was negative. Other viral serology tests were not available. Brain computed tomography (CT) scan showed evidence of cerebral edema, precluding lumbar puncture. The patient received hypertonic saline (150 mL of 3% sodium chloride), antibiotics, and antiviral medications as empirical treatment. Despite initial therapy, the patient's condition did not improve by the third day.
test_results: Brain MRI showed bilateral thalami involvement with hyperintensity on flair images with central hemorrhagic transformation. The putamen and central white matter showed restricted diffusion.

case_report: Case 6 (P6) involves a 12-year-old girl, the first child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents of Belgian origin. During pregnancy, reduced fetal movements were noted. Postnatally, she was found to have a muscular ventricular septum defect (VSD), which closed spontaneously. By 18 months, developmental delay was observed, accompanied by hypotonia and delayed motor development. Physical examination revealed slight facial dysmorphism, joint hypermobility, and skin laxity. Her fingers were long and thin. At age 5, she was identified with an autism spectrum disorder and mild mental retardation, with an IQ of 52. Brain MRI indicated multiple small white matter lesions. She experienced rapid bone maturation and early puberty, attributed to being overweight.
test_results: Capillary zone electrophoresis (CZE) of serum showed a type 2 transferrin pattern with an increase of trisialotransferrin (representing 31 to 41% of the transferrin isoforms, normal range: 1–8%). Isoelectrofocusing of serum transferrin (sTF-IEF) confirmed these results.

case_report: A 77-year-old male with a history of hypertension and coronary artery disease, treated with a stent 3 years ago, presented with acute pain in the lower left quadrant (LLQ) of the abdomen. His medications included Aspirin, Famotidine, Metoprolol, Niacin, and Pravastatin. Over the past 2–3 months, he experienced increasing abdominal distension, a palpable mass in the mid to lower left abdomen, and a sensation akin to a pulled muscle. He reported indigestion with burping, constipation, nausea, loss of appetite, unintentional weight loss of 16 pounds, and night sweats. Two days before admission, he felt a sharp, localized pain in the LLQ, which was progressively more painful, especially upon palpation, and rated the pain as 7 out of 10 in severity. He also noted intermittent tea-colored urine over the past few months. He denied fever, chills, contact with sick individuals, recent travel, vomiting, diarrhea, swollen glands, or lumps, and had no history of atrial fibrillation, clotting incidents, or bleeding. Physical examination revealed a palpable mass across the abdomen extending into the LLQ with significant tenderness. There was no hepatomegaly or other notable findings. Initial laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 6.1 x 10^3 cells/mcL, hemoglobin of 11.6 g/dL, hematocrit of 36.6%, platelet count of 87 x 10^3 cells/mcL, sodium of 135 mEq/L, potassium of 4.2 mEq/L, and creatinine of 0.98 μmol/L. A CT angiogram (CTA) revealed massive splenomegaly with a large infarct in the anterior inferior pole of the spleen, a 2.2 x 4.5 cm subcarinal mass suggestive of lymphadenopathy, and left and right hilar adenopathy with an enlarged pretracheal lymph node ranging from 1 to 2.1 cm in diameter. The patient was started on IV heparin in the emergency department. A hypercoagulable workup was negative for antinuclear antibody (ANA), Factor V Leiden, and thrombin mutations. Beta-2 microglobulin was elevated at 6.04 mcg/mL (Normal: <2.51 mcg/mL), homocysteine was elevated at 19.4 μmol/L (Normal: <11.4 μmol/L), protein C levels were normal at 79% (Normal: 70–180%), protein S levels were low at 29% (Normal: 70–150%), cardiolipin IgM antibody was elevated at 54 MPL (Normal: <12 MPL), haptoglobin was low at <30 mg/dL (Normal: 30–300 mg/dL), dRVVT screen was high at 46 seconds (Normal: <45 seconds), and LDH was high at 477 IU/L (Normal: 98–225 IU/L). An abdominal ultrasound of hepatic and splenic vessels was negative for emboli. CTA was negative for cardioembolic thrombi. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiograms were negative for a cardioembolic source of the infarct. A peripheral blood smear showed mild pancytopenia with atypical lymphocytes.
test_results: Flow cytometry of the aspirate showed 110:1 kappa B cell population in 8.3% of the cells. The flow cytometry results showed the abnormal B cells expressing CD45+, CD5-, CD10-, CD11b-, CD11C±, CD19+, CD20+, CD22+, CD23-, CD38-, CD103-, FMC7+, HLA-DR+, kappa+.

case_report: A man in his late 70s experienced shortness of breath during physical activity 5 months ago. A computed tomography (CT) scan revealed moderate emphysema, a nodule in the right lower lobe of the lung, and a mass in the upper lateral part of the right breast. Positron emission tomography (PET) showed accumulation of 18F-FDG in the nodule in the right lower lobe of the lung and the mass in the right breast with maximum standardized uptake values of 4.23 and 3.11, respectively. The nodule in the right lower lobe was classified as T1bN0M0, Stage IA2 lung cancer. Due to respiratory dysfunction and other conditions (bipolar affective disorder), the decision was made to follow up without treatment. The patient visited our hospital 1 month ago for further examination of the right breast mass. Breast ultrasonography revealed a well-defined tumor lesion with a slightly heterogeneous internal echo and no enhancement of the posterior echo. Color Doppler showed some internal blood flow. T1-weighted gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a 2.2 cm smooth-edged mass with an early contrast-enhanced margin in the upper lateral region of the right breast. In the late contrast-enhanced phase, the entire mass was stained and the contrast agent was pooled. T2-weighted images displayed high intensity throughout the mass.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the biopsy specimen showed irregularly dilated and anastomosed reticulated vessels and hobnail-like endothelial cells. There was a partial area in which poorly dilated vessels were compactly arranged in alveolar nests. A characteristic reticular pattern and hobnail-like endothelial cells were observed. The rate of MIB-1 proliferation was 40% in parts of the alveolar area but < 1% overall.

case_report: A 14-year-old Chinese boy, the second child of nonconsanguineous parents, was admitted due to foamy urine and lower extremity edema persisting for one year. His family, including his parents and older brother, had no history of short stature or renal disease. He was born at 38+3 weeks gestation with a birth weight of 2.6 kg via cesarean section due to oligohydramnios and decreased fetal movement. He experienced frequent protracted diarrhea before the age of 3, and his weight was 8.3 kg, below the 3rd percentile for his age. Physical examination revealed developmental delay (weight 37.0 kg, 3rd percentile), short stature (height 137 cm, below the 3rd percentile), and characteristic facial features such as a triangular face and a broad nasal bridge with a rounded tip. Additional findings included swollen eyelids, a short neck, a barrel-shaped chest, a protruding abdomen, and two areas of jock itch on his inner thighs. His teeth were small and widely spaced, and his legs formed an X shape when walking. Laboratory tests showed lymphopenia (1.04 × 10^9/L, 16.7%, reference: 1.1–3.2 × 10^9/L, 20%–50%), confirmed by flow cytometry with significantly decreased CD4+ T-cells (208/μL, 14.57%, reference: 550–1440/μL, 27%–51%) and CD4+/CD8+ T-cells (0.55/μL, reference: 0.71–2.78/μL). Massive proteinuria (9.31 g) was detected in a 24-hour proteinuria quantification, which did not improve with treatment. Blood biochemistry revealed hypoproteinemia with low total protein (47.3 g/L, reference: 60–85 g/L) and albumin (24.9 g/L, reference: 35–55 g/L), along with dyslipidemia characterized by high total cholesterol (7.87 mmol/L, reference: <5.2 mmol/L) and low-density lipoprotein (4.27 mmol/L, reference: <3.61 mmol/L). Urea nitrogen, creatinine, and glucose levels were within normal ranges. Endocrine evaluation showed subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH 8.75 μIU/mL, reference: 0.27–4.2 μIU/mL), hypocalcemia (serum calcium 1.91 mmol/L, reference: 2.0–2.7 mmol/L), and secondary hyperparathyroidism (PTH 178.1 μIU/mL, reference: 15–68.3 μIU/mL) due to insufficient 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 (11 ng/μL, reference: 30–100 ng/μL). Cortisol, ACTH, and sex hormones (FSH, LH, estradiol, prolactin, and progesterone) were normal. Growth hormone provocation test showed peak secretion of growth hormone at 40,308 pg/mL at 30 minutes post-medication, with a normal IGF-1 level (298 ng/mL, reference: 220–972 ng/mL). Elevated levels of CRP (15.2 mg/L, reference: 0–10 mg/L), PCT (0.061 ng/mL, reference: 0–0.046 ng/mL), and ESR (39 mm/hour, reference: 0–15 mm/hour) were noted. Hepatitis infection was not detected, and autoimmune markers (ANA, ANCA, dsDNA) were negative. Radiological examination of the hand indicated a bone age of 14.3 years, consistent with his chronological age. Osteoporosis was observed in both feet and ankles via X-ray bone densitometry, but vertebrae, pelvis, and femoral head features were not available. A renal biopsy, performed with parental consent, revealed FSGS and mild mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing (WES) revealed two compound heterozygous missense mutations in the SMARCAL1 gene. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the two missense variants, c.1933C>T (p.R645C) and c.2479G>A (p.V827M), in the SMARCAL1 gene were inherited from his parents.

case_report: A 32-year-old male patient reported experiencing decreased strength in his left hand, particularly noticeable when holding a frying pan over the past few months. There was no pain or weakness in other muscles. The patient had undergone two surgeries on his left middle finger at ages 10 and 18 for macrodactyly. Neurological examination revealed reduced touch sensitivity in the left middle finger. Strength was normal in a neutral position. Electroneurography indicated mild carpal tunnel syndrome without signs of axonal damage to the radial nerve. When the left arm was abducted, there was slight weakness in pronation, radial deviation, and elevation of the left hand. Occasional fasciculations were noted in the left brachioradial muscle.
test_results: MRI of the left brachial plexus showed an accessory muscle, attached to the medial aspect of the first rib and superior border of the scapula near the base of the coracoid process. The muscle caused a significant narrowing of the costoclavicular space. No regular subclavius muscle could been identified on either side.
diagnosis: Neurogenic Thoracic Outlet Syndrome  due to Subclavius Posticus Muscle

case_report: A 29-year-old gravida 1 woman presented at 6 weeks and 2 days of gestational age for prenatal care. She had a history of liver toxicity episodes in 2009 and 2014, which were associated with oral contraceptive pills. During these episodes, she underwent extensive infectious and autoimmune testing, including for acute and chronic hepatitis A, hepatitis E, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and human herpesvirus, all of which were negative. A liver biopsy in 2014 indicated possible drug-induced cholestasis. At the start of her pregnancy, she experienced pruritus, dark urine, and pale stool. She was monitored monthly by the hospital's maternal critical care team due to elevated liver enzymes and initial TSBA levels of 215 μmol/L at 8 weeks and 3 days of gestation. Hepatology experts managed her care, starting her on ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) 300 mg three times daily, later increased to 600 mg twice daily in her first trimester. She reported mild symptom improvement after starting UDCA. Her liver enzymes, which showed a mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic pattern, improved with UDCA treatment. Monitoring during her pregnancy included liver profile and bile acid checks every 2 to 4 weeks, weekly bilirubin checks, serial growth ultrasounds every 4 weeks, and nonstress tests twice weekly starting at 32 weeks of gestation. Delivery was planned via induction of labor at 36 to 37 weeks, depending on maternal and fetal status. Growth ultrasounds were normal, with the last one at 32 weeks of gestation. Due to increasing TSBA levels, her UDCA dose was increased to 600 mg three times daily (15 mg/kg/day). Induction of labor was scheduled at 36 weeks with administration of 2 doses of betamethasone prior. Upon presenting for betamethasone, she had a reactive nonstress test and received her first dose, followed by a second dose the next day. At 36 weeks and 0 days, she arrived for induction of labor, reporting contractions and leakage of yellow-brown fluid, with decreased fetal movement. Her cervix was 4 cm dilated with no evidence of prelabor preterm rupture of the membrane. No fetal heart tones were detected, and fetal death was confirmed by two healthcare providers. She was induced with oxytocin and vaginally delivered a male newborn a few hours later. The newborn had normal anatomy.
test_results: The patient underwent genetic testing after delivery, and her result showed a heterozygous variant of ABCB11.

case_report: A 12-year-old boy of Middle-Eastern origin presented to the outpatient department with left flank pain, painful urination, fever (up to 38.5ºC), persistent vomiting, and severe dehydration for four days. Physical examination revealed tenderness at the left pleuro-vertebral angle and a palpable bladder. An unusual facial expression with smiling was also observed. The patient reported urgency and urge incontinence. Upon admission, his white blood cell count was elevated (14.5 Χ 10^9/L, granulocytes 85%), electrolytes were low (Na: 135, K: 3.1), while red blood cell count and hemoglobin concentration were normal (Hct: 37.5%, Hb: 12.5mg/dL, RBC: 4.26M/μL). Serum creatinine was within normal limits. The patient had a history of constipation, bedwetting, and recurrent urinary tract infections. Treatment included intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, intravenous fluids, and oral paracetamol for pain relief. Over the next four days, his fever persisted above 37ºC, with spikes up to 38.5ºC in the evenings. Voiding symptoms also continued. An abdominal ultrasound on the fourth day of hospitalization showed dilatation of the renal pelvis and initial ureter on the left side and slight thickening of the bladder wall. The terminal ureters were visible on both sides. A post-urination ultrasound of the bladder revealed a residual urine volume of up to 140 cc. Clinical and laboratory improvements were noted two days after the placement of a 14 Ch Foley catheter.
test_results: Urodynamic evaluation (pressure-flow study) revealed detrusor-sphincter discoordination. The filling phase revealed both phasic and final type detrusor overactivity and urine leakage. The flow phase was characterized by increased detrusor pressure and low flow (pdet.max 89 cm H2O, pdetQmax 67 cm H2O, and maximum flow (Qmax) value 7 ml/sec). EMG activity of the pelvic floor was significantly increased. Voiding cystourethrography showed a narrowing of the urethra at the level of the external sphincter and left vesicoureteral reflux. Cystoscopy revealed bladder trabeculation, but an anatomic urethral obstruction was not noticed.

case_report: A 59-year-old Caucasian woman with a history of chronic hypertension managed with amlodipine presented to the emergency department with multiple ecchymoses and abdominal pain, which had been worsening over several days. She reported no history of trauma, abnormal bleeding, familial bleeding disorders, or use of anticoagulant medications. The previous month, she had a diffuse maculopapular rash, and a skin biopsy revealed leucocytoclastic vasculitis, leading to a diagnosis of urticarial vasculitis. There was no renal or pulmonary involvement, and the aetiological assessment was negative. She was treated with prednisolone for 3 weeks, resulting in a rapid and favorable outcome. On examination, she was in good general condition with a blood pressure of 123/60 mmHg, a pulse of 85 beats per minute, and a temperature of 37°C. A large subcutaneous haematoma was noted on the entire left upper limb, a superficial haematoma on the right calf, and numerous ecchymoses around both ankles. She denied any nasal or gastrointestinal bleeding. The patient also reported pain in the left iliac area without signs of psoitis. There was no adenopathy, and her spleen was nonpalpable.
test_results: A complete blood count (CBC) revealed a haemoglobin (Hb) level of 8.8 g/dl, and a platelet count of 540 G. A coagulation profile showed a prolonged APTT of 107 seconds, a normal prothrombin time (PT) and a normal international normalized ratio. The results of the FVIII assay were low at 1% (N: 70–100) and inhibitor levels were elevated at 16 Bethesda units (BU). An abdominal CT scan showed a large haematoma on the left psoas measuring 47×12 mm.

case_report: A 5-week-old female was transferred to our institution with a 6-day history of fever reaching 103°F and multifocal cellulitis not responding to three days of vancomycin, cefotaxime, and acyclovir. The patient was born after an uncomplicated pregnancy to healthy parents, with the father having a history of familial hematuria. She exhibited no facial dysmorphism and was developmentally appropriate for her age. Recently, she had nasal congestion followed by fever and skin findings. Upon admission, she had an erythematous plaque several centimeters in size around the umbilicus and similar plaques periorbitally (more prominent on the right) and at sites of skin trauma. Laboratory results showed anemia (Hg/Hct of 11.8/35 × 103/μL), elevated white count (18.2 × 103/μL; 47% segments, 4% bands, 29% lymphocytes, 11% monocytes, and 1% eosinophils), thrombocytosis (platelets = 694 × 103/μL), and elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) (11.2 mg/L). A wound culture from the periumbilical plaque grew pan-sensitive Streptococcus aeruginosa, but five sets of blood cultures, three cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cultures, and CSF polymerase chain reaction for enterovirus, HSV-1, 2, and six were negative, despite evidence of aseptic meningitis. RSV and influenza tests were also negative. Cefotaxime was discontinued and meropenem was started. The patient developed respiratory distress requiring high flow oxygen via nasal cannula and had pulmonary infiltrates on chest radiography. Radiologic workup showed mild hepatomegaly. Her anemia worsened, necessitating a transfusion (Hg/Hct nadir of 7.2/21.4 × 103/μL). Dermatology consultation three days after transfer suggested Sweet Syndrome and recommended a biopsy. The biopsy, performed two days later, showed a neutrophilic and histiocytic infiltrate consistent with Sweet-like syndrome, though there was some hesitancy due to the lack of significant dermal edema and presence of histiocytes. Systemic steroids were recommended. However, due to concerns about atypical Kawasaki's disease, high-dose aspirin and IVIG with low-potency topical steroids for skin lesions were administered. Despite this, the patient remained febrile with rising ESR and CRP. Oral steroids were then started, to which the fever responded quickly. The patient remained afebrile with no recurrence of skin lesions, though atrophic scarring was noted on the dorsal hands at the sites of the plaques. The patient became extremely irritable, leading to the cessation of systemic steroids. Anakinra was trialed, and the patient remained afebrile while on it, but developed a positive Purified Protein Derivative (PPD), necessitating the cessation of Anakinra and treatment with isoniazid. The patient experienced a similar but less severe flare of fever and skin lesions.
test_results: The patient was found to have heterozygous V377I and R388X mutations in the MVK gene.
diagnosis: Mevalonate Kinase Deficiency , encompassing Hyperimmunoglobulinemia D Syndrome

case_report: In May 2013, a 9-year-old female experienced a sudden loss of balance at home accompanied by some tremor. Over the past 3 months, she had occasional seizure-like movements early in the morning. For the past 6 months, she also reported dizziness and difficulty waking up in the morning, with symptoms resolving after eating. This led to increased food intake and a weight gain of 10 kg over the previous year. She was not on any prescription medications at the time of evaluation. On the day of her hospital visit, she experienced a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 5 minutes early in the morning. Physical examination showed a well-nourished girl with normal vital signs, weighing 41 kg with a BMI of 22.5 kg/m2. She reported dizziness, occasional palpitations, weakness, hunger, and sweating. Her abdomen was soft and non-tender without palpable masses or organomegaly. Neurologic examinations were normal. Serum glucose level at the emergency department was 34 mg/dL. Laboratory results showed elevated insulin at 142.7 uIU/mL and elevated C-peptide at 5.88 ng/mL. Serum PTH level was 15 pg/mL (normal range, 11–62 pg/mL), serum IGF-1 was 298 ng/mL (normal range, 78–517 ng/mL), serum prolactin level was 7.5 ng/mL (normal range, 2.7-19.7 ng/mL), and serum calcium level was 9.3 mg/dL (normal range, 8.8-10.8 mg/dL). She received intravenous glucose, which promptly resolved her symptoms. Further evaluations were conducted to investigate causes of hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia.
test_results: Magnetic resonance study of the pancreas revealed a 1.3 × 1.5 cm nodule with high signal intensity on T2 weighted images, which appeared as a well circumscribed mass at the head of the pancreas and with hyposignal intensity on T1 weighted images. The insulin levels for the 8 samples were 127.1, 126.7, 115.2, 118.4, 251.6, 129.8, 458.6, and 199.4 uIU/mL, with the highest levels in the portal vein. Histopathological evaluation of the pancreatic mass was consistent with insulinoma, specifically, a well differentiated pancreatic insulinoma with a grandular growth pattern and a fibrous stroma.

case_report: A 12-week-old male infant presented with difficulty breathing and grunting. He was born full-term but small for gestational age, weighing 2381 grams. The maternal history was unremarkable. The infant had been generally well for the first few months, with occasional constipation reported by the parents. The father was a beekeeper, and the family used honey instead of sugar. At the emergency department, the infant was found to be severely malnourished, experiencing low oxygen levels, and had reduced muscle tone. He also had a weak cry and no reflexes in the lower limbs. He was placed on a high-flow nasal cannula. A chest x-ray showed an elevated right hemidiaphragm. A head ultrasound and a limited swallow study were normal. Tests for upper respiratory viral infections, SARS-CoV-2, and blood cultures were negative. The newborn screening was normal. The infant was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit and placed on bilevel positive airway pressure. Due to the history of honey exposure, the Infant Botulism Treatment and Prevention Program recommended administering Botulism Immunoglobulin Intravenous and sending a stool sample to the Center for Disease Control and Prevention. Neurology and Genetics consultations were obtained. Neurology recommended an MRI of the brain and spine, which showed levocurvature and dextrocurvature of the thoracic and lumbar areas. Genetics recommended a comprehensive metabolic and genetic workup, including plasma amino acids, urine organic acids, lactate, pyruvate, acylcarnitine profile, carnitine profile, serum creatinine kinase level, and Prader Willi methylation studies. After receiving Botulism Immunoglobulin Intravenous, the infant's lower limbs showed increased reactivity to stimuli, and deep tendon reflexes improved. He was switched from bilevel positive airway pressure to high-flow nasal cannula and transferred to the pediatric floor. However, on the fourth day, he became hypotensive and had difficulty breathing again, requiring transfer back to the pediatric intensive care unit and placement on bilevel positive airway pressure. He became bradycardic and required cardiopulmonary resuscitation, intubation, and an epinephrine dose before stabilizing. He remained intubated for three weeks. All initial metabolic and genetic tests were negative, and stool botulism testing was also negative.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing testing revealed biallelic mutations in the immunoglobulin mu deoxyribonucleic acid-binding protein 2 (IGHMBP2) gene.
diagnosis: Spinal Muscular Atrophy with Respiratory Distress Type 1
Orpha_name: Spinal Muscular Atrophy with Respiratory Distress Type 1

case_report: The 24-year-old Japanese female patient was born at 36 weeks and 6 days of gestational age by Cesarean section due to fetal distress. At birth, her body weight was 2,100 g and her height was 44 cm. She exhibited multiple physical anomalies including choanal atresia, cleft palate, micrognathia, a hypoplastic cupped auricle with atresia of the external auditory meatus, and right facial nerve palsy. Echocardiography showed no structural heart abnormalities, and eye examinations revealed no coloboma or abnormalities in the iris, retina, choroid, or optic disk. Chromosome analysis indicated a normal karyotype (46, XX). She required mechanical ventilation for respiratory distress for 2 weeks, followed by the use of an oropharyngeal tube until she was 7 months old. Surgical correction of choanal atresia was performed at age 1 year. She had tooth hypoplasia with malalignment, entropion of the right upper eyelid, and an epicanthal fold of the left eye, which were surgically treated at age 11 years. At age 11 years, she presented with severe short stature (111.5 cm, -5.87 standard deviation), deafness, right facial nerve palsy, cleft palate, malformation of the auricle with atresia of the external auditory meatus, and bilateral hypoplastic nipples. Computed tomography showed hypoplasia of the pancreatic body and tail, severe uterine hypoplasia with the presence of both ovaries, bilateral atresia of the external auditory meatus, hypoplasia of the right vestibular aqueduct, bilateral hypoplasia of the long limb of incus, and bilateral agenesis of stapes and the posterior semicircular canal. Laboratory tests revealed primary hypoparathyroidism [calcium 6.8 mg/dL (reference range: 8.6–11.0 mg/dL), phosphorus 7.1 mg/dL (reference range: 2.5–4.5 mg/dL), and intact parathyroid hormone 20.0 pg/mL (reference range: 10–65 pg/mL)], low serum levels of insulin-like growth factor 1 [14.1 ng/mL (reference range: 175–638 ng/mL)], and suspected mild primary hypothyroidism [free thyroxine 0.9 ng/dL (reference range: 1.1–1.9 ng/dL), free triiodothyronine 3.1 pg/mL (reference range: 2.3–4.7 pg/mL), and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) 5.52 μU/mL (reference range: 0.48–4.82 μU/mL)]. The triple stimulation test (insulin, luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone, and thyrotropin-releasing hormone) indicated complete growth hormone (GH) deficiency (peak GH response to insulin and arginine: 1.6 and 2.1 ng/mL, respectively; cut-off point to define severe GH deficiency: <3 ng/mL), hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (peak luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone response: 0.1 and 1.0 mIU/mL, respectively), mild primary hypothyroidism [peak TSH: 44.62 μIU/mL (reference < 35 μIU/mL)], and subclinical hyperprolactinemia [peak prolactin: 110.6 ng/mL (reference < 70 ng/mL)]. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed an empty sella. The oral glucose tolerance test revealed borderline diabetes with impaired insulin secretion. The patient began treatment with levothyroxine, alfacalcidol, and GH. Her growth velocity significantly improved after starting GH therapy. Seven months after starting GH therapy, a repeated oral glucose tolerance test showed borderline diabetes with impaired insulin secretion [insulinogenic index: 0.09 (reference: 1.34 ± 0.66)] without insulin resistance [Homeostasis Model Assessment insulin Resistance (HOMA-R): 0.2 (reference: < 1.6)]. Serum C-peptide levels were low [0.4 ng/mL (reference range: 1.1–3.3 ng/mL)], but fasting blood glucose and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) were normal, at 102 mg/dL (reference: <126) and 5.3% (reference range: 4.3–5.8%), respectively. Approximately 3 years after starting GH therapy, the patient developed diabetes mellitus, with elevated fasting blood glucose (301 mg/dL) and HbA1c (9.9%), low C-peptide levels (1.7 ng/mL), and negative anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies. She started insulin therapy. She underwent plastic surgery to correct the malformation of the auricle five times from age 14 years and began estrogen replacement therapy at age 15 years.
test_results: Comprehensive DNA sequencing using the TruSight One sequencing panel revealed a novel heterozygous mutation, c.10690 C > G (p.L3564V), in KMT2D. The mutation was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. It was absent from both of her parents, suggesting that it was de novo, and was not found in the public databases. It was predicted to be damaging by PolyPhen-2 and SIFT prediction tools.
