case_report: A 60-year-old woman presented with cough and difficulty breathing to the Pulmonary Department in April 2000. Imaging studies, including chest radiography and computed tomography (CT), identified a large mass in the anterior mediastinum, which was surgically removed via thoracotomy. The tumor was found to be a well-capsulated lymphocytic thymoma upon histopathological examination. Initial routine hematological tests showed no abnormalities. Sixteen months post-operation, the patient developed a non-productive cough and high fever. Follow-up chest radiography and CT showed no recurrence of the thymoma. Routine hematologic tests at this time revealed the following: hemoglobin (Hb) 5.9 g/dL, hematocrit (Hct) 16.9%, white blood cell count (WBC) 0.8×10^9/L, absolute neutrophil count 0.2×10^9/L, and platelet count 86×10^9/L. There was no recent exposure to chemicals or drugs, and serological tests for hepatitis A, B, C, parvovirus, and HIV were negative. Serology for cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus indicated previous exposure.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the bone marrow disclosed extremely low marrow cellularity with increased fatty areas.

case_report: A preterm female neonate weighing 2420 g was born to a 23-year-old G2P1L1 mother at 36 weeks of gestation by emergency cesarean section due to preterm labor, previous cesarean birth, and fetal distress. There was no history of maternal fever or rupture of membranes. Prenatal care was limited, and an antenatal scan at 19 weeks of gestation was normal. Both parents had a normal phenotype, and there was no history of consanguinity. The first sibling, a 3-year-old male, had appropriate growth and development for his age. Amniotic fluid was clear. The baby required resuscitation at birth. Apgar scores were 3, 5, and 8 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes of age, respectively. The baby developed respiratory distress shortly after birth and was referred to our unit. At 4 hours of age, the baby was admitted with severe respiratory distress. Arterial blood gas on admission showed severe mixed acidosis with a pH of 6.95, PCO2 of 101 mmHg, PaO2 of 52 mmHg, HCO3 of 12.9 mmol/L, and BE of –15.1 mmol/L. On examination, the baby appeared dull, with a temperature of 35.6°C, heart rate of 158/min, capillary refill time of 4–5 seconds, respiratory rate of 78/min, subcostal retractions, audible grunt, and SpO2 of 81%. Anthropometric measurements were: weight 2420 g (37th percentile), length 41 cm (2nd percentile), and head circumference 37 cm (100th percentile). Physical features included flat facies, macrocephaly, large anterior fontanel (5 × 4.5 cm), depressed nasal bridge, micrognathia, low set ears, short neck, small chest, short limbs with bowing, and bilateral clubfeet. The baby was intubated and started on conventional ventilation.
test_results: Infantogram showed small thoracic cage, slender thin ribs, 10 pairs of ribs, hypoplastic scapulae, bowed tibiae, femora and ulnae, short fibulae, short and flat vertebrae, and small iliac wings.

case_report: A 21-year-old woman exhibited skin darkening starting at 6 months old, which progressively spread to cover her entire body over 2-3 years. She also experienced progressive thickening of the skin on her palms and soles. There was diffuse thinning of scalp hair, which never grew longer than the lower end of her neck, and poorly developed pubic and axillary hair. She had no history of photophobia or other eye issues, and her hearing and sweating were normal. There was no family history of similar issues. She was born via normal vaginal delivery to a second gravida mother and has two healthy siblings. Clinical and microscopic examination showed normal hair shaft morphology. Generalized reticulate hyperpigmentation was observed, along with short, diffusely thinning scalp hair. Nails appeared dystrophic, and there was hyperkeratosis on the palms and soles, with poorly developed dermatoglyphics. Oral mucosa and teeth were normal, and there was no ocular or auditory involvement. Her intelligence quotient and stature were within the normal range, and there was no delay in the development of secondary sexual characteristics. Routine investigations, including a complete hemogram, liver function test, renal function test, and chest radiography, were normal.
test_results: Histopathology revealed basal layer degeneration and absence of skin adenexa and melanophages in dermis and interface dermatitis.

case_report: A 30-year-old female patient was admitted to the pulmonary department due to dyspnea and a dry cough, without chest pain, hemoptysis, fever, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. Her symptoms were stable, and she had not received any medication prior to admission. A chest X-ray from a local hospital showed pleural effusion on the right side. In 2006, she underwent a modified radical mastectomy to remove a breast mass on her right chest. The biopsy confirmed poorly-differentiated invasive ductal carcinoma with axillary lymph node involvement, and she subsequently received adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Her father had a history of liver cancer. The rest of her personal history, social history, and review of systems were unremarkable. Physical examination revealed decreased vocal fremitus and dullness on percussion on the right thorax. No enlarged superficial lymph nodes were palpated, and laboratory tests showed normal carcino-embryonic antigen (CEA) levels. An ultrasonic examination of the abdomen and pelvic cavity showed no signs of metastasis. High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) results indicated pleural effusion on the right side without residual mass, enlarged hilar lymph nodes, or pleural lesions. Laboratory tests of pleural effusion samples revealed erythrocytes and leukocytes, and the fluid was exudative. Cytological examination reported a large number of lymphocytes without atypical or carcinomatous cells. Thoracoscopy revealed scattered greyish nodes of various sizes on the costal pleura, presenting as exophytic masses with indistinct borders and a tendency to fuse. The pulmonary and diaphragmatic pleura were free from infiltration. A recheck of the chest X-ray was consistent with the HRCT scan.
test_results: Histological and immunological examination of biopsy specimen pictured disarranged, jagged, blood vessels of thin walls and slit-like fissures were prevailing. At higher magnification the vessels’ walls were lined with highly nuclei/cytoplasm ratioed endothelial cells with minimal cytological atypia and mitosis. Atypical cells protruding into lumina mimicking 'hobnail' appearance or endothelial papillae was absent as well as their invasion into adjacent tissues. Infiltration of lymphocytes was also rare. Combined with immunohistochemical staining positive for CD31, CD34, D2-40 and negative for CrebB-2, GCDFP-15, CEA, CA15-3, S-100, Ki-67 and myogenin.

case_report: A 65-year-old African-American man with a history of end-stage renal disease since 2018, type II diabetes, hypertension, arteriovenous malformations, coronary artery disease, deep vein thrombosis, and a pulmonary embolism in 2007, underwent a heart transplant in 2018 following a myocardial infarction in 2017. He experienced hematochezia and melena for approximately one year and presented with chronic anemia with episodic acuity for one month. His medications included tacrolimus post-heart transplant, warfarin for coagulopathy, and monthly long-acting octreotide injections for recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding. One month prior to the current presentation, he visited the emergency department with recurrent shortness of breath, hematochezia, melena, delirium, and a hemoglobin level of 4 g/dL (normal range: 13.0–17.0 g/dL), necessitating blood transfusions. He had been noncompliant with hemodialysis. Additional laboratory results showed platelets at 76 K/uL (normal range: 165–366 K/uL), creatinine at 15.53 mg/dL (normal range: 0.70–1.30 mg/dL), and an INR of 1.1. The patient received urgent dialysis. Post-transfusion, he was initially normotensive but later became hypotensive and tachycardic.
test_results: The video enteroscopy showed numerous vascular ectasias. Capsule endoscopy confirmed vascular ectasias with superficial dilated venules/capillaries, located throughout the small bowel.

case_report: A one-month-old female infant presented with limb shortening, elevated calcium levels in the blood, and epilepsy. She was delivered at 39 weeks of gestation via Caesarean section, weighing 2070 g, as the first child of consanguineous parents. Prenatal ultrasound and family medical history were unremarkable. The APGAR scores were 7 at 1 minute and 10 at 5 minutes post-birth. On the first day of life, metabolic acidosis and seizures were noted, and intubation was attempted due to respiratory failure. The infant was referred to our hospital for uncontrolled myoclonic seizures despite treatment with phenobarbital and phenytoin. At one month old, physical examination revealed a weight of 2470 g (<3rd percentile), height of 50.5 cm (3rd-10th percentile), and head circumference of 35.5 cm (10th-50th percentile). Observations included a flattened facial appearance, broad forehead, flattened nasal bridge, bilateral low-set ears, short neck, narrow thorax, shortening of the left arm with dimples on the knees, hepatomegaly palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin, and a 2/6 systolic murmur. Radiographs of the skull and long bones showed distorted trabeculation, reduced mineralization, metaphyseal irregularities, cupping, diaphyseal shortening, and shortness of the right humerus, ulna, and radius. No craniosynostosis was observed. Echocardiography identified an ostium secundum atrial septal defect. Renal ultrasonography indicated medullary hyperechogenicity consistent with medullary nephrocalcinosis. Ophthalmologic examination, cranial MRI, and EEG were normal. Blood serum tests showed calcium at 14.5 mg/dL (N: 8.8-10.2), phosphorus at 7.1 mg/dL (N: 4.5-5.5), ALP at 1 IU/L (N<70), magnesium at 1.8 mg/dL (N: 1.7-2.55), PTH at 5.5 pg/mL (N: 15-65), and 25-hydroxy vitamin D3 at 49.5 ng/mL (cut-off for deficiency <20). Urinary calcium excretion was elevated with a calcium/creatinine ratio of 0.64. Complete blood count and routine biochemistry tests for renal, liver, thyroid functions, immunoglobulins, tandem mass spectrometry, urinary and plasma amino acid analysis, and urinary organic acid analysis were all within normal limits. Seizures, previously unresponsive to antiepileptic therapy, were controlled with pyridoxine (vitamin B6) administration (100 mg/day initial, 50 mg/day maintenance dose, PO). Intravenous hydration with saline and furosemide was initiated to manage hypercalcemia, along with dietary calcium restriction. This treatment had minimal impact on calcium levels, which were 13.8 mg/dL on the third hospital day. Hypercalcemia was resistant to other treatments, including prednisolone (2 mg/kg/d). Normocalcemia was achieved with a single dose of calcitonin (4 U/kg/d). Chromosome analysis of peripheral leukocytes using high-resolution binding technique showed a normal 46,XX karyotype.
test_results: A homozygous p.267_268delHF (c.799_804delCACTTC) mutation was detected in ALPL gene. The parents were also heterozygous for the new mutation. Genomic DNA of both parents and the index patient was screened for mutations in ALPL gene, and Sanger-sequencing revealed a novel homozygous mutation, p.267_268delHF (c.799_804delCACTTC), in the index patient. This alteration was not annotated in National Center for Biotechnology Information or the human gene mutation database, and both parents were heterozygous carriers for this novel mutation in ALPL gene.

case_report: A 25-year-old female visited the outpatient department with a swelling on the right side of her neck that had been present for two years. Initially, the swelling was a small 0.5×0.5cm mass, which gradually increased to approximately 4×3cm. The patient occasionally experienced pain associated with the swelling, which became more noticeable when she stood up after bending forward for 10-15 seconds. She also reported intermittent numbness on the right side of her head and right upper limb. Four years ago, the patient had a traumatic incident involving throttling to the neck. On physical examination, a soft, non-tender, and mobile mass measuring 4×3cm was observed in the right posterior triangle of the neck when the patient bent forward for two minutes and then stood up. The swelling was not attached to the underlying muscle or skin, and there was no pulsation over it. No enlarged lymph nodes were palpable in the rest of the neck. Routine laboratory blood tests were conducted and results were within normal limits.
test_results: Ultrasound with color Doppler showed a well-defined, anechoic (echo-free) collection with multiple thin septae in the right cervical region, along the anterior aspect of the right external jugular vein, measuring approximately 28×20mm. The multiple tubular anechoic spaces within the lesion exhibited venous flow on color and spectral Doppler imaging. The lesion was located lateral to the right sternocleidomastoid muscle and was connected to the external jugular vein. The lesion was compressible and showed no evidence of thrombosis. It increased in size when pressure was applied to the proximal part of the right external jugular vein and when the patient bent forward. CT with angiography revealed a well-defined oval lesion with iso- to hypodense attenuation (40-45 HUI) in the subcutaneous plane of the right lower cervical region, along the anterior aspect of the right external jugular vein. The lesion measured approximately 35×28×20mm, was inseparable from the external jugular vein on the posterior aspect, and showed contrast intravasation from the vein during the early venous phase. Subsequent delayed scans showed gradual contrast filling and homogeneous enhancement of the lesion after six minutes. The lesion was causing indentation and displacement of adjacent structures, including the sternocleidomastoid muscle and tributaries of the right external jugular vein, leading to a contour bulge on the skin surface. There was no evidence of calcification.
diagnosis: Slow-flow venous malformation involving the right external jugular vein

case_report: A 59-year-old African-Caribbean man reported experiencing neck pain, hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, and breathing issues for two months. He had a rapidly enlarging anterior neck swelling. Physical examination identified an enlarged, hard, and immobile goitre that was very tender upon touch. The trachea was shifted to the left side, and there was no cervical lymph node enlargement. Fibre-optic laryngeal examination indicated reduced movement of the right vocal cord. Blood tests revealed normal blood cell count, calcium levels, and thyroid function tests, with negative thyroid peroxidase autoantibodies and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 95 mm/hr. A CT scan of the neck and thoracic outlet showed a large enhancing thyroid mass, primarily affecting the right lobe, causing tracheal deviation to the left, with no cervical lymph node enlargement.
test_results: Histopathology showed an admixture of fibrous tissue with focal collagen hyalinization and inflammatory infiltrate rich in lymphocytes and plasma cells. Occasional giant cells were present with atrophic thyroid follicles.

case_report: A 36-year-old Caucasian female presented for evaluation of maculopathy. Her medical history included dialysis-dependent end-stage renal disease (ESRD) and hypertension, along with hypertensive retinopathy. On examination, her visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes, and intraocular pressure was 16 mmHg bilaterally. The anterior segment examination was unremarkable. A dilated eye exam revealed macular retinal pigment epithelial changes, Siegrist lines, and Elschnig spots in both eyes. Humphrey visual fields (HVF) showed good reliability and indicated enlarged blind spots in both eyes. Family history was unremarkable for renal disease. Dilated eye exams of her parents, uncle, and daughter showed normal optic nerve structure. Both parents had age-related macular degeneration and had undergone laser treatment for retinal breaks. Her mother and maternal uncle received anti-vascular endothelial growth factor therapy for choroidal neovascularization. Her son and four grandchildren were healthy.
test_results: Genomic sequencing confirmed a heterozygous nonsense PAX2 mutation (C > G p. (Tyr73*) at position 219 in exon 3). Genetic testing revealed that both parents did not have the PAX2 mutation (C > G p. (Tyr73*) at position 219 in exon 3).

case_report: A 23-year-old female with no prior health issues presented with renal insufficiency and proteinuria. She exhibited normal growth and development and had no family history of renal disease. Physical examination findings included a height of 170 cm, weight of 50 kg, body temperature of 36.2°C, pulse rate of 96 beats/min, respiration rate of 20 breaths/min, and blood pressure of 127/85 mmHg. Laboratory tests showed microhematuria and minimal proteinuria. Urinary microprotein analysis indicated a significant increase in urinary microalbumin and urinary transferrin. Biochemistry results revealed a creatinine level of 144 μmol/L and a glomerular filtration rate of 44.2 mL/min/1.73 m2. Other biochemical indices were either slightly altered or within normal ranges. Ultrasound imaging of the kidneys showed enhanced cortical echogenicity, good blood flow in both kidneys, a cyst in the left kidney, and kidney sizes of 9.6 × 3.7 × 3.5 cm (left) and 9.4 × 3.5 × 3.6 cm (right). Electrocardiogram, cardiac Doppler ultrasound, and lung computed tomography did not show any significant abnormalities.
test_results: Renal biopsy revealed a significantly reduced number of glomeruli as compared to normal, glomerular hypertrophy (~300 μm in diameter), segmental sclerosis with adhesions and podocyte proliferation, proliferation of mesangial cells and mesangial matrix, and deposition of electron-dense material (C3 and IgM) visible in the mesangial region.

case_report: A 40-year-old man was admitted to the gastroenterology department due to difficulty swallowing solids for the past two months. He has had blisters on his body since he was six months old, and his sister has similar symptoms. At age four, he began experiencing occasional heartburn, and five years later, he first noticed difficulty swallowing, which was episodic. At age 19, his swallowing difficulties worsened, leading him to consume mostly liquids and soft foods, though the discomfort was not constant. He also had episodes of mild esophageal bleeding. In 1997, he underwent an endoscopic esophageal dilatation for a narrowing located approximately 18 cm from the incisors, which improved his swallowing. A barium swallow test a year later showed esophageal constriction at the same level. In 2014, he experienced hematochezia and hypogastric pain; tissue samples from a colonoscopy showed nonspecific inflammatory infiltration in the ascending colon and terminal ileum. Three years ago, he had hemoptysis, but a CT scan did not confirm bleeding. Two months prior to admission, he was evaluated in the cardiology unit for chest pain and elevated troponin I levels; an electrocardiogram was normal, and he declined further cardiological procedures. On admission, he did not report chest pain. Physical examination showed he was comfortable, afebrile, with a pulse of 90 beats per minute, blood pressure of 125/90 mmHg, respiratory rate of 19 per minute, and a BMI of 24.7 kg/m2. He had blisters, skin reddening, and crust formation on his limbs, contractures and limited movement in his hand joints, and loss of finger and toenails. The apex of his tongue and left palatine arch had superficial ulcerations. Laboratory tests during his hospital stay were normal. A CT scan of the chest and abdomen revealed esophageal wall thickening up to 7 mm from the fourth cervical vertebra to the fourth thoracic vertebra.
test_results: A barium swallow test revealed a narrowing of upper esophageal lumen to 7 mm along the length of 4 cm together with two diverticula on the right side not emptying of contrast. During swallowing other two diverticula appeared which were emptying of contrast. A barium swallow test also showed a noticeable weakening of the esophageal mucous membrane.

case_report: A 46-year-old male government official presented with an 8-month history of involuntary movements during sleep and a 3-month history of slow responses and unsteady walking. He reported feeling depressed without a known cause 8 months prior, coinciding with the onset of nighttime involuntary movements such as kicking and grasping, along with snoring and sleep apnea. Diazepam was ineffective. He experienced excessive sweating, temperature fluctuations (maximum 37.2°C, minimum 35.0°C after nimesulide), and severe constipation. Four months ago, he was diagnosed with mild depression at a mental health center without auxiliary examinations or treatment. Three months ago, his family observed a 20 kg weight loss, choking while drinking, slow responses, visual hallucinations, and unsteady walking. He frequently fell out of bed due to substantial movements and had fragmented sleep due to gasping and sleep apnea. He eventually spoke less, appeared blunt, and had a shuffling gait. He had no relevant medical history and denied trauma, prior blood transfusions, intravenous drug use, and alcohol abuse. He was the fourth family member to exhibit similar symptoms, with the other three dying within a year of onset. Eight months after symptom onset, he was brought to the hospital. The patient appeared dull and easily fell into 'sleep,' awakening in horror due to involuntary movements or snoring. General examination was normal. Vital signs: Temperature 36.5°C, respiratory rate 20/min, blood pressure (lying) 165/109 mm Hg, pulse 115; blood pressure (standing) 150/100 mm Hg, pulse 110. Weight 77 kg, height 178 cm. Severe cognitive impairments were noted, particularly in orientation, attention, calculation, delayed memory, and visuospatial function (Mini-Mental State Examination score 15/30, Montreal Cognitive Assessment score 9/30). He had slurred speech and dysarthria. Cranial nerves I-VIII and XI-XII were normal; CN IX and X showed slow bilateral gag reflex and limited symmetrical elevation of the soft palate. Muscle tone was normal, and muscle strength was 5/5. Spontaneous and evoked myoclonus were present. Reflexes: bilateral biceps and triceps 3/4, bilateral patellar and Achilles 4/4. Hoffman and Babinski signs were absent. Frontal lobe signs (palmomental and grasp) were not elicited. Sensations (touch, pin, vibratory, proprioception) were normal. Romberg test was negative. Coordination tests (finger/nose, heel/knee/shin) were inaccurate, and rapid alternating movements were clumsy. Arm swing was absent, with bradykinesia and postural instability. Temperature monitoring showed fluctuations from 36.0°C to 37.8°C and loss of circadian rhythm. Blood pressure monitoring indicated steady high blood pressure (~150/100 mm Hg) and loss of dipper-type rhythm, with a heart rate fluctuating around 100 beats per minute. Dynamic electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with multifocal ventricular premature beats. Blood tests (routine, coagulation, liver/kidney function, electrolytes, myocardial enzyme, blood ammonia, homocysteine, folic acid, VitB12, microelements, thyroid function/antibodies, rheumatism biomarkers, infection-related antibodies, tumor markers) were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid examination (intracranial pressure 200 mmH2O, cell count 1, glucose, chloride, protein, acetic acid, IgA, IgM, IgG, oligoclonal bands, PCR for JC virus, EB virus, HSV-I virus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis) was normal, and 14-3-3 protein was negative. Autoimmune encephalopathy-related antibodies and paraneoplastic syndrome-related antibodies in blood and CSF were detected but showed no abnormalities. Routine urinalysis and fecal analysis were normal. Hormone secretion tests indicated abnormal rhythmicity of prolactin and growth hormone.
test_results: Genetic analysis found that the patient harbored a D178N/129M haplotype mutation in PRNP (a GAC→AAC homozygous mutation at codon 178 and a methionine polymorphism at codon 129). Polysomnogram (PSG) demonstrated the patient's obvious deprivation of total sleep time; neither spindle nor slow wave sleep was detected during his “fragmented sleep,” even when he showed snoring, mentalis relaxation, sleep apnea, and hyoxemia. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed atrophy of the frontal and temporal. Extensive θ activity and scattered slow waves are recorded in an electroencephalogram (EEG).

case_report: An 11-year-old male presented with liver enlargement and significantly elevated transaminase levels. He initially sought medical attention due to unexplained nausea lasting six months. Initial examinations confirmed liver enlargement and elevated transaminase levels. The patient then took Chinese medicinal herbs for two months, which led to symptom improvement, although follow-up showed persistent liver enlargement. His primary complaint was mild upper right abdominal discomfort. The patient had no prior health issues, and potential causes of liver injury such as infection, autoimmune disease, alcohol use, or exposure to other chemicals were ruled out. Physical examination revealed a height of 130 cm, weight of 31 kg, dental dysplasia, and ligamentous laxity at the metacarpophalangeal joint. Palpation exposed superficial abdominal veins, and the liver edge was palpable 8 cm below the costal margin and 7 cm below the xiphoid process. Blood tests showed elevated aminotransferase levels (aspartate aminotransferase 77 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 102.7 U/L). An abdominal noncontrast CT scan indicated significant liver enlargement. Tests for infectious agents such as hepatitis virus, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and parasites were negative. Autoimmune antibody tests were also negative. Screening for abnormal copper and iron metabolism showed normal biomarker levels. During hospitalization, the patient exhibited a slightly low fasting blood glucose level within the normal range (3.69 mmol/L) and elevated blood triglyceride level (2.17 mmol/L). Repeated tests confirmed these findings, indicating abnormal glucose metabolism.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the biopsy sample with periodic acid-Schiff staining showed massive accumulation of glycogen in the hepatic tissue. Analysis of the patient's genetic sequences revealed a mutation; the cytosine at nucleotide position 133 in the PHKA2 gene on the X-chromosome was replaced by thymidine (c.133C>T), resulting in a change from arginine (Arg) to tryptophan (Trp) at amino acid position 45 in the PhK protein. The patient's mother was also found to carry the c.133C>T mutation in PHKA2.

case_report: An 81-year-old female with a history of hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage IIIa, hyperlipidemia, anxiety, and eczema visited her Primary Care Provider (PCP) after four Emergency Room (ER) visits due to abdominal pain, nausea, and a single episode of bloody diarrhea. During these ER visits, she underwent abdominal X-rays and both non-contrast and contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT scans. No definitive cause for her symptoms was identified. Two weeks later, at the follow-up with her PCP, she continued to experience left lower quadrant abdominal pain, which varied in intensity and seemed to improve slightly with bowel movements. She also reported intermittent loose stools. She had no recent antibiotic use, no known exposure to infectious illnesses, and no personal or family history of inflammatory bowel disease or malabsorption. She had not experienced these symptoms before and had no recent changes in diet or food intolerance. The only recent change in her medication was the addition of losartan for hypertension, which was started five weeks before the onset of symptoms. Throughout these visits, she remained afebrile and had no signs or laboratory findings indicative of a systemic infection. Her physical examination was generally unremarkable, except for mild tenderness in the left lower quadrant.
test_results: Mucosal thickening and submucosal edema of the transverse, descending, and sigmoid colon were noted.

case_report: A 1-month-old male infant was evaluated for growth issues and feeding difficulties. He was born at 36 weeks following a pregnancy complicated by SARS-CoV-2 infection in the third trimester and gestational diabetes managed with a specific diet. There were no notable familial or antenatal issues. The parents reported no familial connections. At birth, the infant did not experience asphyxiation or jaundice, and his birth weight was 2,580 g. Three days later, he was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit due to dehydration and skin changes. Laboratory tests showed hypernatremia (186 mmol/L), which was managed with water replacement. A dermatological evaluation noted desquamative erythroderma and later seborrheic dermatitis. He was discharged at 2 weeks old with normal sodium levels and breastfeeding instructions. Two weeks after discharge, he was admitted to our pediatric center in Catania, Italy. Upon admission, the infant exhibited widespread erythroderma, extensive skin flaking, and crusty areas with alopecia on the scalp. The subcutaneous tissue was underdeveloped, and muscle mass was hypotrophic and hypotonic. Physical examination findings included rhythmic heart sounds with a systolic murmur (2/6), a flat and normally shaped abdomen that was soft and painless, normal sensory responses with valid crying, normal osteotendinous reflexes, and axial and appendicular hypotonia. His weight was 2,670 g. Routine tests indicated a positive polymerase chain reaction result, consistent with systemic infections. Skin swabs identified Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Treatment with Merrem and Teicoplanin was initiated, resulting in a good response. A follow-up dermatological consultation described abundant lamellar desquamation and skin features suggestive of circumflex linear ichthyosis. Video-dermatoscopic examination of the scalp showed invaginated trichuriasis.
test_results: Genetic analyses revealed the mutation c.238dup (p.Ala80fs) in homozygosis of SPINK5, localized on chromosome 5q32. Genetic analysis in the parents revealed the same mutation in heterozygosis in both.

case_report: A 23-year-old male patient was referred to our tertiary academic center due to a defect affecting one side of his face. The patient had an adenotonsillectomy at 6 years old, and numbness began on the left side of his face 3 months post-surgery. Initially, the operating physician reported no issues. However, the numbness increased, and over the next 2 years, there was noticeable shrinkage and weakness on the left side of the face. Ten years post-surgery, the symptoms worsened, but the patient could not seek medical attention due to socioeconomic reasons. Upon physical examination at our center, there was atrophy of the cutaneous and subcutaneous fat tissue on the left side of the face, phthisis of the left ocular bulb, corneal atrophy, left zygomatic atrophy, and facial asymmetry. Hemiglossal atrophy and increased fissure size on the left side of the tongue were also observed. Maxillary atrophy caused the left upper teeth to be displaced upward and backward. The patient had no dermal lesions or extremity involvement. There was no relevant family history. The patient had autologous fat injections at ages 14 and 16, but the atrophy persisted. Serological tests showed no antibodies, and sedimentation and core reactive protein levels were normal, indicating no inflammatory disease involvement.
test_results: Computed tomography revealed no apparent neurodegeneration. The computed tomographic images revealed a decrease in left retroorbital fat tissue and atrophy of the ocular bulb. The left temporal muscle was atrophic compared with the right temporal muscle. Magnetic resonance angiography revealed no vascular abnormalities of the internal and external carotid arteries or of their branches.

case_report: A 21-year-old man with no history of smoking or significant past medical issues presented with a persistent cough. Imaging identified a lobular, heterogeneous, enhancing mass in the right lower lung. Physical examination showed no abnormalities. Computed tomography of the thorax during preoperative evaluation confirmed no additional localizations. The mass was surgically excised, and a lobectomy was performed. The tumor was multinodular, firm, and encased in a thin, fibrous pseudo-capsule, measuring up to 6 cm at its largest dimension. It was endobronchial with extension into the underlying lung parenchyma and had no attachment to the visceral pleura. The cut surface displayed a whorled white-tan appearance with focal myxoid and hemorrhagic changes. The surgical margin was clear of tumors. Microscopically, the tumor was well-circumscribed and exhibited low to moderate cellularity. It consisted of bland spindle cells arranged in crisscrossing fascicles within a hyaline to myxoid stroma, which varied in different areas of the tumor. The tumor cells had scant, wispy cytoplasm, uniform elongated nuclei with finely clumped chromatin, and small, inconspicuous nucleoli. There was minimal mitotic activity. Epithelioid cells were present in some areas. A network of branching capillary-sized blood vessels was observed. In certain regions, cellularity increased against a fibrous background, with abrupt transitions between fibrous and myxoid areas. The pleura was free of tumors. Five pedicular lymph nodes were removed and found to be reactive.
test_results: The neoplastic cells showed immunoreactivity for CD99 and MUC4 with a strong and diffuse expression of this antigen. They were negative for CK, SMA, EMA, H-caldesmon, Desmin, STAT6, MDM2, CD34, hormonal receptors, ALK (5A4, P80), and PS100. Cytogenetic and Molecular Genetic study showed the absence of SS18/SYT gene rearrangement.

case_report: A 7-year-old boy presented with seizures and asymmetrical overgrowth affecting the right side of his body. He is the third child of parents from a nonconsanguineous marriage, with an uneventful antenatal and perinatal history. Progressive enlargement of the right foot and plantar surfaces was observed from 3 to 4 months of age. Subsequently, overgrowth was also noted in the right half of the face and gluteal region. The patient experienced unprovoked seizures starting at 1½ months old, initially affecting the left side and later becoming generalized. He was started on antiepileptic medication, but adherence was poor, leading to recurrent seizures. Developmental milestones were appropriate for his age. Clinical examination revealed normal anthropometric measurements and intelligence. Head and face examination showed dolichocephaly, frontal bossing, hypertrophy of the right half of the face including the cheek and tongue, and hyperpigmented lesions on the right cheek and neck. There was hypertrophy of the right buttock and hyperpigmented lesions in the right gluteal region. Foot examination revealed macrodactyly of the great, second, and third toes with splaying, and hypertrophy of the plantar surfaces with increased rugosity. Laboratory investigations indicated normal blood counts, renal, and liver function tests.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging brain showed right hemimegalencephaly with dysplasia with white matter abnormalities. Electroencephalogram was abnormal showing generalized epileptiform discharges.

case_report: A 12-year-old Syrian girl was brought to Damascus University’s Children’s Hospital due to frequent episodes of pneumonia and bronchitis. Her mother reported that the child had never produced tears when crying since birth and had widespread pigmentation, particularly on the cheeks and genitals. The child also experienced repeated vomiting of both solid and liquid foods and had asthma. The mother noted that a cousin exhibited similar symptoms. Physical examination revealed the child was fatigued and had pigmentation on her lips, nose, and under the right eye. She showed signs of growth failure with a weight of 25.5 kg and a height of 133 cm. The child had difficulty breathing with a respiratory rate of 40–45 breaths per minute, substernal intercostal retractions, pigmentation on the genitals, digital clubbing, and thickened skin on the palms and soles. Neurological examination results were normal, and her psychomotor development was also normal. Blood tests showed sodium at 136 mmol/l, creatinine at 0.6 mg/dl, and urea at 21 mg/dl. Immunoglobulin levels were within normal ranges.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) scan of the thorax showed massive dilation of the esophagus and bilateral pulmonary infiltration. Barium swallow test showed massive dilation in the esophagus associated with a tightening in the lower esophageal sphincter (bird beak sign). Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed severe dilation in the esophageal lumen with a contraction in the lower esophageal sphincter that continues to the stomach.

case_report: A 16-year-old female presented with pain in the lower left back region of the jaw for the past 2 weeks. Physical examination revealed short stature, prominent forehead and parietal regions, a flattened nasal bridge, a beaked nose, underdeveloped midface, and palpable anterior and posterior fontanels. The patient had stubby hands with wrinkled skin over the fingertips and crested nails. She reported a history of leg fractures occurring three times due to minor trauma. There was a positive history of consanguinity between her parents and similar clinical features were noted in her maternal aunt. Intraoral examination showed a complete set of permanent teeth in both arches, a constricted maxilla with a grooved palate causing crowding, and irregularly placed teeth in the mandibular arch. Radiographic examination revealed an over-retained tooth 55, dental caries involving the pulp in tooth 37, and dental caries involving the pulp with significant destruction of the clinical crown in tooth 46.
test_results: Hand wrist radiograph showed hypoplasia/absence of terminal tuft of the thumb and index finger, also known as acroosteolysis. Increased bone density was also noted. X-ray of the skull (water's view) showed non-pneumatized frontal sinuses, hypoplastic maxillary sinuses bilaterally, and hypoplastic mandible with obtuse mandibular angle. Orthopantomogram and lateral cephalogram showed elongation of condyle and hypoplasia of coronoid process.

case_report: Patient III:6, a 78-year-old female, presented with a decade-long history of gradually worsening imbalance, numbness in the extremities, and dysesthesia. In the past year, she reported experiencing difficulty swallowing and occasional coughing. Examination of eye movements showed an abnormal vestibulo-ocular reflex with head impulse test revealing corrective saccades to the left. Pursuit movements were moderately disrupted, consistent with her age. Sensory examination indicated a loss of pinprick sensation in both upper and lower extremities. Ankle reflexes were absent. She exhibited an ataxic gait and had a mildly positive Romberg's sign.
test_results: Bithermal caloric testing and rotational test showed significant bilateral reduction of vestibular function. Video-HIT showed consistent abnormal catch up saccades bilaterally. EMG/NCS confirmed a sensory neuronopathy. MRI brain revealed an incidental frontal cavernoma and mild global atrophy.
Orpha_name: Cerebellar ataxia with neuropathy and bilateral vestibular areflexia syndrome

case_report: A 52-year-old woman presented with thickened skin on her palms and soles, a condition that started in her childhood. She also reported changes in one of her toes that began a few years ago. She is part of a family with five generations affected by similar symptoms. Her mother had a finger amputated due to the progression of the same condition. On physical examination, there was widespread thickening of the skin on the palms and soles, with constrictive bands observed on the fifth toe of the left foot. Additionally, there was generalized scaling of the skin, but no hearing loss was noted.
test_results: Anatomopathological examination of the palmar region found hyperkeratosis with orthokeratosis and parakeratosis.

case_report: The patient is a 7-year-old male. Clinical findings include atresia of the choanae, which was surgically treated, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and micropenis, managed with luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone analogue therapy, and a bicuspid aortic valve. There is asymmetry of the buccal rhyme when crying and smiling due to hypoplasia of the left mouth corner depressor. The patient exhibits motor impediment and mild craniofacial dysmorphisms, such as slightly low implanted pinnae, a prominent nasal root, hypoplastic nasal wings, mid-facial hypoplasia, and a high and narrow palate. Corrective lenses are used for myopia. An ENT evaluation documented very slight bilateral conductive hearing loss. Re-evaluation of CT radiograms taken at birth indicated 'inner ear dysplasia'.
test_results: A c.5607+17A>G heterozygous variant in intron 27 (NM_017780.4) was identified. Trio segregation analysis showed that the c.5607+17A>G variant occurred de novo in this patient.

case_report: A 53-year-old patient with stage IV melanoma was admitted to the hospital presenting with generalized paresthesia, stiffness in both hands, a sensation of throat obstruction, and mild dizziness. The patient had metastases in the liver, spleen, lung, and bones, but not in the brain. Four weeks prior, treatment with nivolumab 1 mg/kg and ipilimumab 3 mg/kg had commenced, with two doses administered before presentation. The patient reported a significant worsening of symptoms over the past few days. Medical history included arterial hypertension managed with valsartan and bisoprolol, and intermittent stomach complaints treated with pantoprazole. There were no known autoimmune disorders before starting nivolumab and ipilimumab. Serologies for hepatitis B and C virus were negative, and serum levels of TSH and free T4 were within normal limits. Upon presentation, vital signs were normal. Physical examination was unremarkable, with negative Chovestek’s and Trousseau’s signs. ECG revealed a prolonged corrected QT interval (493 ms).
test_results: Laboratory testing revealed hypocalcemia (calcium 1,35 mmol/l [normal range 2.10–2.65], albumin 38 g/l [normal range 35–52], ionized calcium 0,7 mmol/l [normal range 1,15-1,3]), marginal hypomagnesemia (0,69 mmol/l [normal range 0,70-1,00]) and hyperphosphatemia (1,75 mmol/l [normal range 0,8-1,5]. Intact parathyroid hormone (iPTH) level was inadequately low (7,2 pg/ml [normal range 15–65]), 25-hydroxy vitamin D3 level was just above normal range (121 nmol/l [normal range 13.2–118]), venous blood gas showed normal pH of 7.418.

case_report: A 12-year-old female patient, 161 cm tall and weighing 32 kg, with idiopathic scoliosis in the thoracic vertebra, presented for a posterior fusion operation. She had no significant medical history and was not on any medication. Preoperative blood tests were within normal limits, and a simple chest X-ray showed no abnormalities other than idiopathic scoliosis. X-rays of the vertebrae revealed severe scoliosis from the fifth thoracic vertebra to the first lumbar vertebra. Prior to anesthesia, atropine 0.3 mg was administered. Initial pulse oximetry was 100%, and blood pressure was 120/79 mmHg. Anesthesia induction included propofol 50 mg and succinylcholine 40 mg, followed by catheterization. Anesthesia was maintained with N2O 2 L/min, O2 2 L/min, desflurane 5%, and atracurium 15 mg. Allen's test was performed to check collateral circulation in the left hand before anesthesia induction, and arterial pressure was measured by inserting a 22 G catheter into the left radial artery. Central venous pressure was 10 mmHg when a monitoring catheter was inserted into the right internal jugular vein. The patient was positioned prone for surgery, with shoulder joints abducted at 120° and elbow joints flexed at 70°, while the neck was kept in a neutral position. After repositioning, blood pressure was 100/60 mmHg, and central venous pressure remained at 10 mmHg. However, systolic blood pressure dropped from 90 to 40 mmHg during the insertion of an introducer needle after skin incision and muscle dissection. No significant bleeding was observed in the operative field despite a blood loss of about 500 ml. To compensate for the volume loss, 6% hydroxyethyl starch (HES) 500 ml was administered, urine output was 90 ml, and central venous pressure was maintained at approximately 9 mmHg. The systolic blood pressure was restored to 90 mmHg when the operation was paused but dropped back to 40 mmHg when resumed. Despite the drop in arterial pressure, no bleeding was found in the operative field. The surgeon applied compressing force to the surgical region, resulting in a similar drop in systolic blood pressure, but central venous pressure remained around 9 mmHg. Blood pressure was measured in the right upper arm using an automated noninvasive device, showing no change when compressing force was applied to the vertebrae. A monitoring catheter was then inserted into the right radial artery. Repeated compressing caused a drop in left radial arterial pressure, but the right radial artery pressure remained stable. The blood pressure in the left radial artery decreased with pressing force applied to the surgical site, but pulse oximetry on the left middle finger remained at 100%, and no other abnormalities were observed. The surgery was completed without further incidents, and the patient was repositioned from prone to supine for awakening. After repositioning, the left radial artery pressure returned to a level similar to the right, with a systolic blood pressure difference of within 5 mmHg between the two limbs. The total surgery duration was 3 hours and 50 minutes, and anesthesia lasted 5 hours and 15 minutes. The patient was transported to the postanesthetic recovery unit after awakening.
test_results: Roos' test revealed a decrease in vascular tone and paleness in the left upper limb. An Angio Computed Tomography found that the first rib and the clavicle compressed the right subclavian artery at the same position as in the operation.

case_report: A 15-year-old Chinese male presented with a one-week history of headache and vomiting. Ophthalmic examination showed no abnormalities, and there were no neurological symptoms or short stature observed. The patient exhibited sudden and severe symptoms, including hypertension and severe kidney failure. His blood pressure was recorded at 170/123 mmHg, and serum creatinine was measured at 1,026.2 μmol/L. There were no prior symptoms reported. The patient's parents were first cousins, and his older brother had died from an undiagnosed kidney disease at the age of 8, without a kidney biopsy. The patient was admitted to the medical center on 21 May 2021. Ultrasonography revealed small kidneys with diffuse lesions (85–90 mm in diameter) in both kidneys, without cystic enlargement. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 67 g/L and a urinary protein level of 1.05 g/24 h. Chest computed tomography results were normal. Additional laboratory investigations included tests for hepatitis B virus surface antigen, antinuclear antibodies, anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies, anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, all of which were negative. The patient commenced hemodialysis treatment.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing was performed to further investigate the cause of his illness, and segregation was validated via Sanger sequencing in him and his family.

case_report: The patient is a 35-year-old male from Hebei province in northern China, of Han ethnicity, born to consanguineous parents. He was delivered normally after a full-term pregnancy, with birth weight and length within normal ranges. Initial symptoms began at age 6 with deformities in the interphalangeal joints of the fingers, followed by gradual involvement of the hips, knees, and wrists. Local hospitals prescribed glucocorticoids, which were ineffective. By age 16, he required crutches due to lower extremity arthritis. At age 26, he experienced progressive pain with numbness radiating down his left leg and right thigh. At age 34, he began to have mild difficulty with urination, and his leg pain worsened, leading to immobility. Treatments with tramadol, physical therapy, and spine injections were ineffective. He has a younger brother with similar symptoms and mild neurological impairment. Upon admission, the patient's height was 162 cm and weight was 72.5 kg. His visual analogue scale (VAS) score was 9. He had no behavioral difficulties or intellectual development issues. Physical examination revealed multiple malformations of major limb joints, particularly in the knees and hands, and obvious amyotrophy of both lower limbs. Cervical and lumbar movements were limited with compensatory kyphosis. Muscular strength in all four limbs was normal. Dysesthesia was noted in the posterolateral left calf, dorsolateral left foot, and perineal area. Bilateral knee-jerk and ankle reflexes were hypo-induced. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (13 mm/h) and C-reactive protein level (2 mg/L) were within normal ranges. Tests for rheumatoid factors were negative.
test_results: Spinal x-rays showed flat and osteoporotic vertebral bodies. Pedicles were short, and end plates were irregular. Bone bridges were seen at many levels. Kyphosis was detected in both the cervical and upper thoracic spine. Magnetic resonance imaging showed multilevel Schmorl nodes. Multilevel disc herniation and hypertrophic ligamentum flavum caused lumbar canal stenosis from L2 to S1.

case_report: A 50-year-old female visited the dermatology clinic due to a rash on her right upper chest that had persisted for about one month. She had previously been seen at an urgent care center and was given doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, oral diphenhydramine, and topical 1% hydrocortisone cream. The patient did not recall any tick bite in the affected area. Despite the treatment, the rash continued to grow. On examination, the rash appeared as a 3 cm erythematous plaque with central clearing, without any scaling, vesicles, or pustules. The rest of her skin was clear. Western blot testing of serum was negative for immunoglobulin (Ig) M and IgG antibodies. A complete metabolic panel showed normal results. A complete blood count with differential indicated slight elevations in hemoglobin, hematocrit, and RBC indices, which were attributed to her smoking and alcohol intake history. Lupus autoantibody profile results were negative. At a follow-up visit three weeks later, the original lesion remained unchanged, but new red urticarial papules, each less than 1 cm, had appeared on her left arm and thigh.
test_results: All the specimens exhibited superficial and deep perivascular, interstitial, and periappendageal lymphocytic infiltrates. There was a faint bluish hue of the matrix indicative of mucin deposition. Epidermal changes were minimal with a slight thickening of the basement membrane. Colloidal iron stain demonstrated increased superficial and deep dermal mucin deposits. DIF revealed a band of IgG deposits along the dermo-epidermal junction. No other immunoreactants were found.

case_report: A 62-year-old female presented with unintentional, involuntary, irregular, non-patterned movements, behavioral changes, and progressive cognitive decline over the past three years. These movements were not associated with posturing. According to her husband's history, the patient had no complaints for three years and had been in good health until then. She has been experiencing uncontrolled jerking movements in her arms and legs, which have worsened over time. These movements are more noticeable during periods of stress or excitement and tend to improve during rest. Additionally, he has observed that she has become increasingly forgetful, struggling with everyday tasks, and exhibiting emotional instability. There is no history of substance abuse or any significant past medical history. Her father experienced similar symptoms at the age of 50. She has two siblings who are asymptomatic at present. No other significant neurological conditions are reported within the family. On physical examination, she appeared restless and demonstrated irregular, choreiform movements involving her face, trunk, and extremities. These movements are involuntary, purposeless, and involve rapid, jerky motions. She also displayed mild bradykinesia, slowed finger tapping, and diminished facial expressiveness. The observed movements exhibited a small range of motion, mostly impacting the extremities, facial region, and tongue. There was no associated imbalance or weakness of the limbs. Cognitive assessment reveals difficulties with attention, executive functions, and memory. However, no focal neurological deficits were noted. All her laboratory investigations were unremarkable.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) brain showed head of bilateral caudate nuclei mild atrophy with ex-vacuo mild dilatation of frontal horns of lateral ventricles with a frontal horn width to intercaudate distance ratio (FH/CC) of 1.6, mildly decreased, and an intercaudate distance to inner table width ratio (CC/IT) of 0.24, mildly increased. Associated with age-related diffuse brain parenchyma, mild atrophy with bilateral frontal CSF spaces, sulci, ventricular system, basal cisterns, posterior fossa CSF spaces, and cerebellar foliae appeared prominent. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain shows head of bilateral caudate nuclei mild atrophy with ex-vacuo mild dilatation of frontal horns of lateral ventricles with an FH/CC of 1.6, mildly decreased, and a CC/IT of 0.24, mildly increased. Associated with age-related diffuse brain parenchyma, mild atrophy with bilateral frontal CSF spaces, sulci, ventricular system, basal cisterns, posterior fossa CSF spaces, and cerebellar foliae appeared prominent.

case_report: The patient is a 43-year-old male. At the age of 7, a chest X-ray revealed an enlarged heart. He experienced his first episode of ventricular tachycardia (VT) at 31 years old and was subsequently referred for intensive treatment, including catheter ablation. Following an unsuccessful catheter ablation, an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) was placed, and he was started on medical treatment including amiodarone. Over the past decade, the frequency of appropriate ICD therapies for ventricular tachyarrhythmias increased, leading to a referral for repeat catheter ablation. Despite being haemodynamically stable and asymptomatic during arrhythmias, his admission vital signs were: blood pressure 140/84 mmHg, pulse rate 68/min, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Clinical examination indicated predominantly right-sided heart failure, with jugular venous distention and pitting edema in the lower extremities. Blood tests showed no electrolyte imbalances but a high serum B-type natriuretic peptide level of 336 pg/mL (normal <18.4 pg/mL). The baseline electrocardiogram (ECG) showed normal sinus rhythm with large P waves, an rsr’ QRS complex in leads V1–4, and right-axis deviation. A chest X-ray demonstrated an enlarged cardiac silhouette with a prominent right ventricle contour, without severe pulmonary edema.
test_results: Electrocardiogram-gated multi-detector computed tomography (MDCT) depicted a remarkable RV and right atrial dilatation, and the localized coexistence of a severely thin RV wall and partial defects of the RV muscular wall. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed severe RV dilatation (RV dimension was 72 mm) resulting in D-shaped left ventricle. Left ventricular ejection fraction was 35%.

case_report: A 26-year-old male with a history of ankylosing spondylitis (Human Leukocyte Antigen B27 gene) and previous circumcision reported experiencing recurrent painful nocturnal erections over the past year. Despite consultations with multiple urologists and the use of oral analgesics, there was no relief. The frequency of these painful nocturnal erections increased from once per week to three times per week. Each episode lasted about 5 minutes, causing severe pain that woke him from sleep and negatively impacted his sleep quality and overall well-being. The patient noted that the nocturnal erections were more intense and painful compared to those occurring while awake. There was no history of priapism, sexually transmitted diseases, or genital trauma. Family history was negative for neurofibromatosis. Physical examination revealed four palpable lumps on the dorsum of the stretched penis. Two superficial nodules were located on the distal shaft, and one deep nodule was found at both the mid shaft and the base of the penis. These nodules were firm and measured 0.5 cm or less in diameter. The mid shaft nodule was tender upon palpation and corresponded with the site of painful nocturnal erections. The penis appeared otherwise normal with no curvature during erection and no palpable lymph nodes in the femoral or inguinal regions. No nodules or café-au-lait spots were observed on the rest of the body.
test_results: Physical examination and interval ultrasound imaging demonstrated an increase in the number of nodules from four to five with further growth of the existing nodules. The right intracavernosal nodule increased from 4 mm to 7 mm in diameter.

case_report: A 25-year-old female in her third trimester of pregnancy presented with episodes of headache, palpitations, sweating, and elevated blood pressure reaching 230/130 mmHg for three weeks. She had no prior history of hypertension, and her physical examination showed no abnormalities. Initial evaluation for hypertension ruled out pre-eclampsia. Biochemical tests revealed significantly high levels of urine catecholamines: Dopamine 607 μg/24 hours (reference range 65 - 400), Norepinephrine 978 μg/24 hours (reference range 15 - 80), Metanephrine 108 μg/24 hours (reference range 24 - 96), Normetanephrine 4067 μg/24 hours (reference range 75 - 375), and Vanillyl mandelic acid 13.6 mg/24 hours (reference range 2 - 7). Epinephrine level was 0.8 μg/24 hours (reference range 0.0-20.0). Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) identified a 28 × 19 mm mass near the left adrenal gland. The patient was started on phenoxybenzamine (10 mg, twice a day). Six weeks after an uneventful Cesarean Section delivery, she underwent a left laparoscopic adrenalectomy. Histopathological examination revealed normal adrenal tissue and brown fat in the juxta-adrenal mass. Despite the surgery, her symptoms persisted.
test_results: On PET-CT, a large hyper-metabolic soft tissue mass measuring 4.5 × 2.7 × 3.9 cm in the region of posterior mediastinum near the left atrium was noted. On Steady State Free Precession (SSFP) breath-hold cine MRI, the epicenter of the hypo-intense soft tissue mass was noted to be in the posterior mediastinum with no apparent fat plane between the lesion and the posterior wall of the left atrium. The mass caused smooth extrinsic compression of left atrial wall and demonstrated typical low signal on T1-weighted spin-echo and high signal on T2-weighted dark blood turbo spin-echo images. During administration of gadopentetate dimeglumine, T1-weighted inversion recovery gradient-echo myocardial perfusion imaging was performed which demonstrated heterogeneous dynamic contrast filling of the mass. Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) CMR demonstrated peripheral rim enhancement of the mass with central dark signal suggestive of central tissue necrosis.

case_report: A 25-year-old female patient presented with a 2-month history of gradual, painless, progressive reduction in vision along with floaters in the left eye. She had been treated with systemic and topical steroids for pan uveitis with disc edema at a primary health care center and was referred. Her history revealed that 8 months earlier she had undergone right eye pars plana lensectomy and vitrectomy (PPL + PPV) with intravitreal antibiotics at a different center for suspected metastatic endophthalmitis secondary to postpartum abscess. Culture reports were not available. There was no visual improvement following surgery, and she had developed phthisical changes. On examination, best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was no light perception in the right eye, while the left eye had counting fingers (CF) close to the face with accurate light projection. In the left eye, apart from fine keratic precipitates, a 3+ cellular reaction was noted in both the anterior chamber (AC) and vitreous. Lens and intraocular pressure were normal. Fundus examination showed a hyperemic disc with blurred disc margins and tortuous dilated vessels, associated with serous retinal detachment with shifting fluid.
test_results: Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) showed multiple tiny pinhead-sized hyperfluorescent spots in the superior half of the retina with an inferior serous retinal detachment. Late phase showed disc hyperfluorescence with blurring of margins.

case_report: A 14-year-old girl presented with mobile and irregularly positioned teeth. General examination revealed a convex profile, competent lips, a normally developed maxilla, and a slightly underdeveloped mandible in the sagittal plane. Intraoral examination showed crowns and gingiva appearing normal, with no signs of gingivitis or periodontitis. Clinical examination indicated grade II mobility in the maxillary and mandibular incisors and molars, along with missing maxillary and mandibular right lateral teeth. Crowding was observed in the maxillary and mandibular anterior regions. The patient's medical history indicated no general health issues. Examination of the patient's parents and siblings showed no similar conditions or familial history of such issues.
test_results: Panoramic radiograph showed normal appearance of crown, rudimentary root formation with all teeth except maxillary right canine and mandibular right first premolar. Obliterated pulp chambers were found with most of the teeth.

case_report: A 61-year-old female of Puerto Rican descent was assessed in Medical Genetics for multiple chronic pain conditions. She had previously consulted with Family Practice, Gastroenterology, Pain Medicine, Neurology, Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, Gynecology, and Ophthalmology departments. The patient experienced episodes of facial pain and had a preliminary diagnosis of Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome, which is characterized by facial weakness, facial and lip swelling, and tongue furrowing. She reported similar symptoms in other family members. A detailed family history revealed similar facial pain episodes in her mother and four of seven siblings, with symptom onset ranging from 18 to 52 years. The patient experienced pain on both sides of her body, above and below the waist, including the posterior cervical region. The most severe pain was in the neck, shoulders, upper extremities, entire back, buttock area, and lower extremities. Heating pads provided some relief, and she preferred a room temperature of 27°C (80°F). Pain triggers included stressful events, defecation, and cold temperatures. She had two severe facial pain episodes resulting in hospitalization at ages 52 and 61. The first episode included a severe headache lasting 3 days, right facial swelling, right eye weakness, and forehead paralysis. The second episode involved a global thunderclap headache, left orbital eye pain, left facial paralysis with decreased sensation, and right-sided ptosis, along with facial swelling and weakness. MR and CT brain imaging were unremarkable. Facial pain occurred several times daily, triggered by cold, smiling, brushing teeth, and chewing, but not by touching the face or food. Pain was described as electrical, shooting down the right mandible, followed by a pulling sensation in the right cheek and eye. Pain intensity was typically 5/10 but could reach 10/10, accompanied by dripping lacrimation in the right eye without facial flushing or sweating. Lacrimation worsened when eating, but she did not describe gustatory sweating. Facial pain lasted for several hours, and she avoided eating cold foods and eating in public. Sinus congestion previously triggered pain, mostly resolved after three sinus operations. She denied tear secretion and flushing as pain triggers. She often experienced rectal pain during defecation, starting around age 45 and progressively worsening, with pain severity described as worse than childbirth (10/10) and lasting for hours. She denied seizures but had several syncope events as an adult. She reported “fibromyalgia attacks” occurring about twice a month after stressful events and cold temperatures, affecting the entire body with achy and dull pain lasting for several days. She was diagnosed with fibromyalgia at age 56 by Family Medicine using the American College of Rheumatology 1990 criteria. The patient completed the Neuropathic Pain Scale, describing constant intense, sharp, deep, and often cold pain, with an intensity of 5/10 in the coccyx and lower back. She reported episodic sharp pain (10/10) in the neck, legs, and back, with coccyx pain radiating to her left leg or both legs, lasting for hours. She also described cold pain (8/10) in her feet, even on warm days. Additionally, she completed a small nerve fiber questionnaire, reporting persistent constipation, dry eyes, occasional diarrhea, and excessive sweating. She denied urination problems, dry mouth, dizziness upon standing, palpitations, hot flashes, sensitive skin, burning feet, sheet intolerance, or restless legs. She did not have severe burning pain in the distal limbs or pain triggered by warmth. EMG performed at ages 55 and 56 for Bell's palsy evaluation showed unremarkable results initially, with later findings of mononeuropathy at the wrist.
test_results: WES analysis detected a pathogenic heterozygous c.2159T>A (p.I720K) mutation in the SCN9A gene.

case_report: The patient is a 39-year-old male who began experiencing muscle weakness at the age of six. He has had monthly episodes of muscle weakness, which worsen with intense physical exertion and are associated with febrile symptoms, limiting his physical activity. The severity of these episodes varies, ranging from mild to moderate weakness to complete paralysis. During childhood, no potassium alterations were documented during these episodes. Despite the periodic nature of these episodes, the patient did not experience any delays in motor development and achieved all developmental milestones without difficulty. In adulthood, the episodes became more severe and were triggered by moderate physical exercise. No other triggers, such as drugs or anesthetic events, were identified. Many episodes required short-term hospitalizations lasting two to three days. During these hospitalizations, electrocardiograms, brain MRI, and toxic profiles were normal. Additional tests, including renal and thyroid function, hepatic function, screening for Pompe disease, and levels of lactic acid and pyruvate, were also within normal limits. During the most recent episode, mild to moderately increased CPK levels (ranging from 209 to 873 U/L) and potassium levels up to 5.3 mEq/L were observed in blood samples taken during the weakness and paralysis episodes. An electromyography study using multiMUP (multimotor unit potential) showed no abnormalities. Preliminary findings suggested muscle fiber disease. The patient reported no significant personal medical history but mentioned that a paternal great-uncle died at age 50 due to a condition associated with motor impairment, though no specific diagnosis was provided. On physical examination, the patient exhibited proximal muscle weakness in all four extremities, with 4+/5 strength in shoulder abductors and adductors, elbow flexors, and extenders, and 4/5 strength in hip flexors and extenders, as well as knee flexors. Other muscle groups were within normal limits. The patient also showed hyporeflexia in all four limbs, normal muscle tone, and gastrocnemius hypertrophy. A muscle biopsy performed at age sixteen showed isolated muscle necrosis with reparative changes. A second biopsy in adulthood revealed denervation changes, regenerating fibers, increased lipid deposition, and intracytoplasmic glycogen deposits. An NGS genetic panel, including the PYGM, PGAM1, PFKM, and LDHA genes for glycogen storage disease, showed no alterations.
test_results: The panel demonstrated a missense variant in SCN4A c.4483A > G (p.Ile1495Val.).

case_report: A five-year-old girl was admitted to the neurology department with a history of progressive hearing loss over the past seven months. Initial signs of hearing impairment were noted at the age of three. Auditory brainstem response (ABR) and auditory steady-state response (ASSR) tests indicated auditory neuropathy, leading to the use of hearing aids. Over the last five months, she exhibited bilateral ptosis, facial paralysis, drooling, and drooping of the right eyelid and mouth corner, with no worsening at night. Her medical records indicated no developmental delays. She is the first child of healthy parents who are consanguineously married. Her weight is 21.5 kg, height 114.5 cm, and head circumference 53.5 cm. Electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction velocity (NCV) tests were normal. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, ESR, CRP, blood urea, creatinine, ALT, AST, thyroid profile, serum levels of calcium, pyruvate, lactate, ammonia, and CPK, were all within normal ranges. Blood gases were also normal. Anti-MuSK antibodies tested negative, and AChR binding antibody was at the upper limit of the normal range. The patient did not respond to pyridostigmine at a dose of 120 mg/day, divided into four parts. Brain MRI with gadolinium contrast was normal. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, obtained via lumbar puncture, showed normal sugar, protein, cytology, and culture, with no malignant cells detected. Thoracic CT and thoracic and cervical MRI results were normal.
test_results: Co-Segregation analysis confirmed that the patient was mutated homozygous for the c.1036C>T (p.Pro346Ser) variant of the SLC52A3 gene. Her parents were relative and were both heterozygous carriers for this variant.

case_report: A 32-year-old male presented with difficulties in color vision, specifically an inability to perceive colors, which had been progressively worsening over the past five years and had become more severe in the last two years. His medical history includes a diagnosis of antibody-negative diabetes mellitus at the age of 27. During the examination, his visual acuity was measured at 20/20 in both eyes for distance vision. He could identify only 1 out of 12 Ishihara plates with both eyes. His pupils were symmetrical but reacted sluggishly to light, with no afferent pupillary defects observed. Fundoscopy showed temporal optic disc pallor in both eyes. Ocular movements were normal, and the remainder of the neurological examination was unremarkable. MRI of the brain and orbits with gadolinium contrast indicated mild thinning of the optic nerves bilaterally. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) showed thinning to 54 μm in the right eye and 52 μm in the left eye. Humphrey visual field (HVF) testing did not demonstrate a clear pattern of visual field loss. Laboratory tests, including assessments for toxic substances (copper, heavy metals), metabolic factors (Vitamins B1, B3, B6, B9, B12, E), and infectious agents (RPR, quantiferon gold), were all unremarkable.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed the homozygous variant WFS1 c.1672C>T:p.R558C.

case_report: A 39-year-old woman with a history of elevated cholesterol levels reported experiencing fatigue and a sensation of heaviness in both legs. She led a sedentary lifestyle, maintained a balanced diet, and did not have any gastrointestinal complaints. Her physical measurements were as follows: weight 56 kg, height 170 cm, body mass index 19 kg/m2, waist circumference 73 cm, and blood pressure 13/10 KPa. She was born to healthy, non-consanguineous parents and had normal developmental milestones. There was no family history of early cardiovascular disease, and she had no personal history of hypertension, chronic kidney, or liver diseases. Her medical history included hospitalizations for a miscarriage at age 28 and a cesarean section delivery of a healthy male at age 30. Her family history included the premature death of a brother at one week of age for unknown reasons. Laboratory tests revealed elevated total cholesterol (321 mg/dL), LDL cholesterol (161 mg/dL), and HDL cholesterol (118 mg/dL), with normal triglyceride levels. Serum apolipoprotein-A was 291 mg/dL (normal range 115 mg/dL-210 mg/dL) and apolipoprotein-B was 145 mg/dL (normal range 55 mg/dL-135 mg/dL). Additional laboratory tests, including blood count, liver and kidney function, coagulation tests, autoimmunity assays, PCR, and urine dipstick, were normal. Thyroid function tests indicated subclinical hypothyroidism. Albumin level measured by nephelometric method was critically low at 0.2 g/dL (normal range 3.4 g/dL-5 g/dL), and total bilirubin was undetectable. Calcium level was 7.5 mg/dL (normal range 8.5 mg/dL-10.1 mg/dL), total protein was 5.8 g/dL (normal range 6.4 g/dL-8.2 g/dL), and pre-albumin was 0.46 g/L (normal range 0.2 g/L-0.4 g/L). Serum protein electrophoresis showed minimal serum albumin (1.6%, normal range 55.8%-66.1%) with increased levels of other serum protein fractions, including transferrin (607 mg/dL, normal range 200 mg/dL-360 mg/dL), alpha 1-antitrypsin (2.56 g/L, normal range 0.9 g/L-2.0 g/L), and complement C4 (0.46 g/L, normal range 0.10 g/L-0.40 g/L). These findings prompted further investigation into the patient's low albumin levels. Proteinuria was ruled out by normal spot urine albumin/creatinine ratio and total protein/creatinine ratio. Other potential secondary causes of low albumin, such as inflammation and insufficient liver synthesis, were excluded by normal laboratory tests and abdominal ultrasonography, which only showed mild hepatic steatosis. Other family members (parents, brother, and son) had albumin levels near the upper limit of the normal range.
test_results: The patient is homozygous for a CA deletion near the 3′ end of exon 12, at nucleotide positions c. 1614-1615. The subsequent frame-shift should give rise to a predicted translation product of 516 amino acid residues instead of the 585 found in the mature protein (p.Leu540Phefs*2), in which the sequence Cys(538)-Thr-Leu-Ser has been changed to Cys(538)-Thr-Phe-Stop.

case_report: A 13-year-old boy with black hair exhibited a patch of hair thinning that remained unchanged over time. This condition began when he was 5 years old. His parents reported having normal hair and scalp, and there was no family history of hair disease. Physical examination revealed a patch of hair thinning on the frontal scalp without any scalp lesions. The hair within this patch could be easily pulled out with gentle traction. No abnormalities such as brittleness or lack of luster were noted in the hair shafts. The hair pull test was negative on other areas of the scalp. Other physical examinations, including those of the nails and teeth, showed no abnormalities.
test_results: The trichogram showed 88% of abnormal anagen hairs, 10% of telogen hairs, and 2% of broken hairs. Under microscopy, naked anagen hair bulbs with ruffling of the hair cuticle were observed.

case_report: A 26-year-old Korean female presented with skin lesions on the right side of her neck, trunk, leg, and foot, which had been present since birth. Her family members, including her parents and brother, did not exhibit similar symptoms. She had scoliosis and a discrepancy in leg length, with her right leg being 3.5 cm shorter than her left. She had previously undergone tooth extraction due to an uneven number of teeth on either side of her jaw. Physical examination revealed brownish papules and patches with slight depression following Blaschko's lines on the right side of her neck, trunk, leg, and foot. Additionally, plantar pitting and linear atrophoderma with hyperpigmentation were observed on her right foot. The right great toenail showed onychogryphosis. No neurological abnormalities were detected.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the papule showed multiple anastomosing strands of basaloid cell proliferation with keratin material from the follicular infundibulum. Some of these cells were connected to the epidermis, and the surrounding stroma was relatively scant and loose. Histopathological examination of the specimen from the ankle showed basal hyperpigmentation and mild basaloid cell proliferation with peripheral palisading in the superficial dermis. The radiograph confirmed scoliosis, with a Cobb angle of 37° and shortening of the right leg. NGS analysis could not identify mutations in the Sonic hedgehog pathway genes including the patched-1 (PTCH1). The smoothened (SMO) was not examined.

case_report: A 45-year-old Caucasian female with a history of thyroid cancer post-thyroidectomy presented to the emergency department with a maximum temperature of 103.7°F, shortness of breath, and midsternal chest pain. Her symptoms included fever, chills, sore throat, light-headedness, loss of appetite, malaise, shortness of breath, and chest pain. Two weeks prior to admission, she was treated for a sore throat and tender lymphadenopathy with Azithromycin and steroids, which were later switched to oral clindamycin due to lack of symptom improvement. Clindamycin was discontinued after three days due to gastrointestinal side effects. Upon admission, she was septic, febrile (39.4°C), tachycardic with a heart rate of 137, tachypneic with a respiratory rate of 37, and hypotensive with a blood pressure of 77/44, requiring brief use of pressors. She was hypoxic with an oxygen saturation of 86% on room air. Physical examination revealed respiratory distress, dry mucous membranes, tender right cervical lymphadenopathy extending 10 cm posteriorly, and decreased bilateral breath sounds. Heart sounds were normal with no murmurs. Laboratory findings showed no leukocytosis but a significant elevation in procalcitonin (22.7), elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 33.4), and a lactate level of 5.4. Initial COVID-19 test was negative. Imaging showed bilateral pleural effusion with atelectasis and bilateral patchy densities on chest X-ray. Blood cultures were drawn, and the patient was started on intravenous ceftriaxone, metronidazole, and azithromycin for severe sepsis. A CT neck without contrast was obtained and did not show any abscess or thrombosis.
test_results: CT neck with contrast showed marked right neck soft tissue infection with extensive phlegmon, adenopathy, abscess and septic thrombosis of the right internal jugular vein, subclavian and left cephalic vein thrombosis.

case_report: A 10-year-old boy was referred for neurodevelopmental assessment at 24 months due to global developmental delay, particularly affecting language, and poor growth in height and weight.
