He is the first child of healthy, unrelated parents. The pregnancy had minimal supervision, and he was born at 39 weeks and 5 days with a birth weight of 2220 grams. There was no significant medical history. His growth metrics remained below the 5th percentile. He began kindergarten at two and a half years old, with parents noting delayed psychomotor development. Milestones included head control at six months, sitting at 12 months, crawling at 20 months, and walking at two years. He exhibited severe intellectual disability and significant language delay, unable to speak any words by age five, though he appeared to understand well. At 25 months, developmental assessments indicated delays across all areas, equivalent to 12 to 18 months. He received early intervention, educational support, occupational and speech therapy, and psychomotor rehabilitation. The Griffiths Scale evaluation showed a general quotient of 41.04 at four years and 38.3 at five years, with consistent delays across various areas. At five years, he presented with short stature, cervicothoracic kyphosis, small feet, broad toes, and nonspecific facial features including slightly low-set ears and a prominent lower lip. He also had a symmetric intention tremor during manipulation. Metabolic analyses, cranioencephalic MRI, and visual and auditory assessments showed no abnormalities. Molecular analysis for Fragile X syndrome and array-CGH were normal.
test_results: Exome sequencing with analysis of copy number variations (CNV) identified a 300bp deletion involving the CUL4B gene. This deletion was confirmed by quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR).

case_report: An 11-year-old male presented with a history of nonspecific skin hyperpigmentation on the left shoulder and axilla, short stature (139.5 cm, 5.1%, Z = −1.63 based on CDC length-for-age data), and scoliosis. Physical examination revealed a bulbous nose, prominent ears, a thin upper lip, and a long philtrum. His hair was fine and sparse, and his eyebrows were thick with lateral thinning. Similar skin lesions were observed in his otherwise healthy mother. These features were not present in his fraternal twin brother or other full and half siblings.
test_results: X-ray imaging revealed the presence of cone-shaped epiphyses at the phalanges.

case_report: The patient is a 5-year-old girl from Bihar, India, born to nonconsanguineous parents with a normal perinatal period. She remained healthy until 40 months of age when she experienced acute onset lethargy and confusion following an upper respiratory tract infection, which resolved spontaneously over 5 days. During recovery, she exhibited rapid involuntary eye movements, tremulous hand and finger movements, and an unsteady gait. The gait instability gradually improved, and she regained the ability to walk without falling. Over the next 3 months, she had two episodes of febrile illness with transient increases in gait unsteadiness. At 48 months, she experienced febrile encephalopathy with seizures and was bedridden for 10 days before returning to baseline. She was then started on oral valproic acid. At 54 months, she developed slowly progressive hearing loss. At 60 months, she presented with the ability to walk without support, speak in two-word sentences, dress and undress, and feed herself. There was no history of visual impairment or similar illnesses in her family. Examination at 60 months revealed normal anthropometry, left convergent squint, horizontal nystagmus, bilateral pale optic discs, hypotonia, areflexia, and perioral and appendicular dyskinesia (intermittent spontaneous jerky movements of fingers, toes, limbs, and lips). Cerebellar examination showed gait incoordination (gait ataxia), truncal hypotonia, intentional tremors, positive finger-nose test, dysdiadochokinesia, and incoordinated slurred speech (scanning speech). Pes cavus was not present.
test_results: A targeted sequencing of ATP1A3 gene revealed a pathogenic heterozygous missense variant in exon 18 (c.2491G>A, p.E831K).

case_report: A two-month-old male infant was admitted with symptoms including fever, poor oral intake, lethargy, and cloudy urine. Initial urinalysis conducted in the outpatient department revealed numerous white blood cells in the urine. There was no family history of genetic, hepatic, or renal diseases. His past medical history was unremarkable. On physical examination, the patient appeared acutely ill and slightly lethargic but otherwise normal. He had a high fever exceeding 38℃, with no hepatosplenomegaly or costovertebral angle tenderness detected. There was no jaundice, and his abdomen was normal without signs of portal hypertension such as ascites or distended abdominal veins. Edema and oliguria were not present. His weight was 6.3 kg, placing him above the 95th percentile for his age. Laboratory results showed a hemoglobin level of 9.2 g/dL, leukocyte count of 4420/µL, platelet count of 388,000/µL, total serum bilirubin of 0.4 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin level of 0.2 mg/dL. Serum alanine aminotransferase was 26 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase was 10 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase was 274 U/L, total protein was 4.5 g/dL, and albumin was 3.2 g/dL. Blood urea nitrogen was 10.9 mg/dL and creatinine was 0.4 mg/dL.
test_results: Abdominal ultrasonography (US) revealed a large kidney (Length; Rt - 8.63 cm, Lt - 8.31 cm) with increased cortical echoes and multiple small cysts in the medulla and cortex of both kidneys. Dilatation of intrahepatic and common bile ducts were noted. The DMSA scan revealed a split renal function of 51.8% on the right and 48.2% on the left kidney. The MAG3 diuretics renogram showed a decrease in both the flow and function of both kidneys. Abdominal MRI showed large, multicystic dysplastic kidneys, fusiform dilatation of the common bile duct, and small, round, and tubular dilatation of the intrahepatic bile ducts. Needle biopsy of the liver revealed fibrotic changes.
diagnosis: Caroli's syndrome with Autosomal Recessive Polycystic Kidney Disease

case_report: A 64-year-old female presented with a 1-month history of itchy crust formation. She had no prior history of autoimmune disease or malignancy. The patient had been receiving subcutaneous bee-venom acupuncture twice a week for 2 months at an oriental medicine hospital for back pain. The exact concentration or full contents of the bee-venom acupuncture were not known. A month after beginning the bee-venom therapy, skin lesions began to appear, leading her to discontinue the therapy. Physical examination showed itchy, red, erosive, and crusted patches and plaques on the scalp and trunk, which were not located at the acupuncture sites. The oral mucosa was unaffected. Laboratory tests indicated no presence of bee-venom-specific immunoglobulin E (IgE) or wasp-venom-specific IgE in her serum. A Tzanck smear from a trunk lesion showed negative results.
test_results: A punch-biopsy specimen from the trunk revealed intraepidermal acantholysis just below the stratum corneum containing neutrophils and lymphocytes. In the dermis, perivascular infiltration of lymphocytes and histiocytes was observed. A direct immunofluorescence study showed immunoglobulin G (IgG) and complement 3 deposition in the intercellular space of keratinocytes. An indirect immunofluorescence study revealed IgG deposition in the intercellular space at a 1:160 dilution.

case_report: A 58-year-old African American male attended a hepatology clinic for a routine liver ultrasound due to a history of hepatitis C. The patient reported mild, intermittent upper abdominal pain, which was consistent with his history of gastroesophageal reflux disease. He did not experience weight loss, changes in appetite or bowel habits, jaundice, or general malaise. His medical history included hyperlipidemia, peptic ulcer disease, and hepatitis C (antibody positive, PCR negative). Physical examination and laboratory studies were unremarkable. An abdominal ultrasound revealed a well-defined mass measuring 3.4 × 2.9 cm in the head of the pancreas. A subsequent computed tomography (CT) scan confirmed an enhancing mass in the same location. No signs of disease outside the pancreas were detected. Tumor-associated antigen levels (CEA, CA 19-9, and CA-125) were within normal ranges. An endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) guided needle biopsy was performed, but the pathological findings were inconclusive. Due to ongoing concerns, a diagnostic laparoscopy was conducted, followed by a surgical procedure. The patient recovered well and was discharged on the 15th postoperative day. He is currently under close outpatient surveillance without additional treatment.
test_results: Microscopic examination revealed that all were hyperplastic lymph nodes. The remaining surgical margins were negative. This lymphoid lesion within the pancreatic head showed marked vascular proliferation and hyalinization of germinal centers. Involuted germinal centers were surrounded by concentric rings of small lymphocytes. i.e. 'onion-skinning' penetrated by hyalinized vessels. Moreover, the interfollicular zones were rich in plasma cells and hyalinized vasculature. Distribution of T and B cell markers (CD20, CD3, CD45) was normal and markers indicative of lymphoid malignancies (i.e. CD30, CD15, CD5, CD10, BCL-2) did not show evidence of such entities. PCR analysis of paraffin-embedded tissue revealed no clonal rearrangement of the immunoglobulin heavy chain or T-cell receptor gamma and beta chain genes. MALT1 (18q21) clonal rearrangement by FISH was negative.

case_report: A 59-year-old Caucasian woman presented for a cardiological examination due to experiencing palpitations over the past two years. Her medical history included treatment for Hodgkin’s lymphoma with chest radiation and splenectomy at the age of 30. She was a non-smoker and did not use illicit drugs. Physical examination showed a slightly accelerated pulse, but other vital signs and findings were unremarkable. An electrocardiogram indicated sinus tachycardia. Echocardiography identified a 2 × 3 cm mass in the inferior wall of the left atrium without other cardiac abnormalities. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging described the mass as highly vascularized and infiltrating the inferior wall of the left atrium. The mass was best delineated on cardiac magnetic resonance cine images. On T1- and T2-weighted images, the mass appeared isointense and hyperintense to myocardium, respectively. Gadolinium infusion showed positive contrast uptake on first-pass perfusion and strong, heterogeneous delayed hyperenhancement. A computed tomography angiogram of the thorax showed no metastasis. The patient was referred to a tertiary center for surgical treatment. Following sternotomy and initiation of cardiopulmonary bypass with bicaval cannulation, the tumor was exposed via left atriotomy and macroscopically excised. A partial resection of the posterior wall of the left atrium was then reconstructed with bovine pericardium. The postoperative course was uneventful except for a single episode of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and the patient was promptly discharged.
test_results: Histopathological analysis of the tumour revealed heterogeneous pattern of epithelioid, stromal, vasogenic, and spindled cells, as well as hyaline matrix. The proliferation rate was moderate (1/10 high-power fields, Ki-67 proliferation index 20%). Cardiac myxoma and local recurrence of Hodgkin’s disease were excluded with negative calretinin and specific immunohistochemistry (CD30, CD15, and Pax5), respectively. The partial expression of endothelial markers (CD31 and ERG) pointed to a vascular tumour. The WWTR1-CAMTA1 fusion, specific of the epithelioid type of hemangioendothelioma (HE), was negative.

case_report: A 12-year-old male patient presented with multiple congenitally missing permanent teeth in both the upper and lower jaws. The patient reported forwardly placed upper front teeth. Medical history indicated no systemic diseases or syndromes. Family history revealed that the maternal grandfather, mother, and maternal uncle also had missing teeth, which was confirmed through clinical and radiographic examination. Extraoral examination showed no developmental anomalies. Intraoral examination revealed retained mandibular primary anterior teeth, with symmetrical spacing in the anterior region of both the maxillary and mandibular arches. Oral hygiene was poor, with localized gingivitis observed in the lower anterior region. Retained teeth 75 and 84 were present, with pulpal involvement of tooth 75 confirmed. Macrodontia was noted in relation to tooth 46. A tooth was considered developmentally missing if it was not observed clinically or radiographically and there was no history of extraction.
test_results: Radiographically it was confirmed that 31, 32, 33, 35, 37, 38, and 41, 42, 43, 44, 45, 48, 85 were missing.

case_report: A 48-day-old full-term male infant was admitted with growth retardation and persistent vomiting for over a month. The parents were nonconsanguineous, and the pregnancy and delivery were uneventful. Post-birth, the infant exhibited dark skin, failure to thrive, poor appetite, vomiting gastric contents without bile or coffee grounds, occasional diarrhea without mucus or blood. He was previously treated with reduced glutathione, creatine phosphate, calcium gluconate, hydrocortisone, and metformin for 9 days at another hospital without improvement. The infant had no seizures, screaming, or abdominal distension during this period. Upon admission, his birth weight was 3300 g, current weight was 3500 g (< 3rd percentile), and length was 61 cm (90th percentile). Physical examination revealed the infant was awake and dehydrated, with hyperpigmented skin and reduced elasticity, and absence of subcutaneous fat. The neck was supple, and no facial dysmorphism was noted. Lung examination was clear, heart rate was regular with no murmurs, and the abdomen was non-tender without organomegaly. Genital examination showed penis scrotal hyperpigmentation and a thickened penis, with normal testicle volume (1 ml each). Neurologic examination was normal. Laboratory tests showed serum potassium at 5.9 mmol/L (normal: 3.5-5.5), sodium at 132 mmol/L (normal: 135-145), ALT at 141.1 U/L (normal: 0-40), AST at 88.8 U/L (normal: 0-40), ALP at 50.7 U/L (normal: 147.7-309.3), CK at 1586 U/L (normal: 16.5-211.5), CK-MB at 168 U/L (normal: 16.5-211.5), α-HBDH at 314 U/L (normal: 75.5-211.5), LDH-MB at 76 U/L (normal: 30-120), and LDH at 413 U/L (normal: 67-394.1). Chest and abdomen radiography showed no significant findings. Ultrasound cardiography revealed Patent Foramen Ovale. Abdominal and urinary ultrasound indicated hepatomegaly and bilateral renal enlargement. Hydrocortisone (5 mg IV every 8 hours) and fludrocortisone (0.1 mg orally per day) were administered. Glutathione and sodium fructose diphosphate were given for liver function and myocardial abnormalities. Over the next 3 weeks, the infant's appetite improved, dehydration symptoms reduced, and weight increased by 0.5 kg. Follow-up laboratory tests showed sodium at 130 mmol/L (normal: 135-145), potassium at 5.1 mmol/L (normal: 3.5-5.5), ALT at 62.8 U/L (normal: 0-40), AST at 53.3 U/L (normal: 0-40), ALP at 147.2 U/L (normal: 147.7-309.3), CK at 621 U/L (normal: 16.5-211.5), CK-MB at 97 U/L (normal: 15-80), LDH at 367.4 U/L (normal: 67-394.1), LDH-MB at 64.9 U/L (normal: 30-120), α-HBDH at 255.2 U/L (normal: 75.5-211.5), and 17-α-OHP at 0.48 ng/L (normal: 0-1.54). No lipid metabolism test was performed during hospitalization. Adrenal function tests showed no significant abnormalities. The patient was discharged on day 23 with continued oral treatment of reduced doses of cortisone acetate, fludrocortisone, and sodium supplementation. At a follow-up visit one week post-discharge, the infant's weight increased to 4.3 kg, but an outpatient electrolyte test revealed elevated serum potassium (6.7 mmol/L) and decreased serum sodium (132 mmol/L). The infant was readmitted due to unclear cause of elevated serum potassium. Examination showed poor response, stable vital signs, persistent skin hyperpigmentation, and genital enlargement. Lipid metabolism analysis revealed Apo-A at 1.67 g/L (normal: 1-1.6), Apo-B at 0.6 g/L (normal: 0.6-1.1), total cholesterol at 4.51 mmol/L (normal: 3.12-5.2), and triglycerides at 12.01 mmol/L (normal: 0.8-1.8). The 17-α-OHP value remained within normal limits.
test_results: The urine was positive for glycerol, which reached 3129.2 umol/mmol (normally negative).

case_report: A 13-year-old boy with no prior health issues was brought to the emergency department by his mother due to right-sided throat pain lasting for 5 days. The pain extended to his right ear and down the right side of his neck, worsening with swallowing and neck movements. His mother noted a tactile fever for the same duration but no change in his voice. The patient had seen his pediatrician 2 days earlier and was given amoxicillin. Despite this, the throat pain had intensified. Upon arrival at the emergency department, his temperature was 37.8°C, which increased to 38.1°C an hour later. He showed no signs of distress. Examination of the heart, lungs, abdomen, and skin was normal. Head examination showed normal tympanic membranes and external auditory canals on both sides, with no mastoid tenderness or swelling. The oropharynx was nonerythematous without exudates, and the uvula was midline. The neck was supple with enlarged, tender lymph nodes in the right anterior cervical chain. A complete blood count revealed a white blood cell count of 9,400 cells/mcL with 69% neutrophils. Serum electrolytes were within normal limits, and urinalysis showed no signs of infection.
test_results: An opacification of the right IJ vein was seen extending from the jugular foramen to the common jugular confluence, suspicious for high-grade partial occlusion.

case_report: A 13-year-old male patient presented with pain on the right side of the face, right-sided headache, and painful jaw opening for the past 5 months. The patient had a history of extraction of the maxillary deciduous second molar 5 months ago, reportedly without local anesthesia. Following the extraction, the patient experienced continuous pain on the right side of the face. Two months post-extraction, a brownish patch developed on the right cheek. The patient also reported difficulty in mouth opening for the past 3 months and reduced oral intake, leading to a weight loss of 4–5 kg. Various treatments, including analgesics, muscle relaxants, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and mouth washes, were prescribed by multiple local dentists and general medical practitioners, but there was no improvement in symptoms. The patient exhibited tense cooperative behavior upon presentation (Frankl's behavior rating: negative). Extraoral examination showed hyperpigmentation over the right cheek, with a brown pigmented lesion measuring approximately 4 cm × 3 cm, without sinus tract opening or pus discharge. Tenderness was noted over the right parotid and masseteric regions. Examination of the TMJ revealed no abnormalities. No definite trigger zones were identified. Intraoral examination showed permanent dentition, generalized extrinsic stains, chronic generalized marginal gingivitis, and an Ellis Class II fracture of tooth 21. Tooth 15 had erupted with no associated soft or hard tissue abnormalities detected intraorally. The orthopantomogram showed no discernible dental anomalies.
test_results: No sonological abnormality was detected on the ultrasound. The Department of Neurology provisionally diagnosed him to be suffering from pathology of the maxillary division of trigeminal nerve secondary to the dental extraction.
diagnosis: Chronic Atypical Facial Pain, Psychogenic in Origin

case_report: The patient is a 55-year-old Caucasian female with a medical history that includes type 2 diabetes, depression, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and chronic pancreatitis. She has been monitored in the Gastroenterology Clinic for several years due to intermittent epigastric abdominal pain, nausea, nonbloody vomiting, and chronic diarrhea. Despite extensive testing, the cause of her symptoms remained unclear. Initial esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) and endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) revealed erythematous gastropathy and duodenopathy, along with pancreatic parenchymal and ductal changes indicative of chronic pancreatitis, but no pancreatic masses were detected on EUS. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) was unremarkable. Gastric biopsies showed chronic gastritis, and tests for H. pylori were negative. She experienced recurrent abdominal pain and was hospitalized multiple times, with the pain thought to be related to GERD and acute on chronic pancreatitis. A HIDA scan indicated biliary dyskinesia with an ejection fraction of 8% following cholecystokinin infusion, leading to a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. She was prescribed pancreatic enzyme supplements and proton pump inhibitors (PPI), which initially provided mild symptom relief. However, she was hospitalized again several months post-cholecystectomy for similar symptoms. A repeat EGD revealed a nonbleeding, deep ulceration at the gastroesophageal junction (LA Grade D), diffuse erythematous mucosa throughout the stomach, and a 2 cm deeply cratered ulcer in the second portion of the duodenum (D2). Gastric and duodenal biopsies indicated severe, active chronic gastritis and duodenitis without malignancy.
test_results: Serum gastrin level was moderately elevated at 762 pg/mL while on PPI therapy, and chromogranin A was also elevated at 164 ng/mL. Serum gastrin level was then reevaluated after temporarily discontinuing PPI therapy several months later, and this time it was significantly elevated at 1,639 pg/mL. She subsequently had a SRS scan performed, which revealed two small lesions within the gastrinoma triangle.

case_report: A 9-year-old boy presented for dental treatment of broken upper incisors that had occurred 2 weeks prior. His medical history included surgical removal of bilateral congenital cataracts and replacement with intraocular lens implants. He was under regular follow-up with an ophthalmologist for glaucoma management. Family history was noncontributory. Extraoral examination showed facial dysmorphism, anteverted pinnae with increased fold in both ears, and ocular abnormalities. Intraoral examination revealed mixed dentition, poor oral hygiene with a Simplified Oral Hygiene Index score of 3.2, and class III skeletal and molar relationship with bilateral posterior crossbite and anterior open bite. The patient had decayed, missing, and filled teeth with deft scores of 3 and 12. Teeth 11 and 21 had uncomplicated crown fractures (Ellis Class II) and were clinically asymptomatic. Teeth 55, 64, 65, 75, 74, 84, and 85 were grossly decayed. All first permanent molars had a central extra cusp, and all cusps were rounded with shortened cuspal height, resembling mulberry molars. The central supernumerary cusps in teeth 46 and 36 were destroyed by occlusal dental caries. The axial surfaces of the crowns of permanent and primary molars converged toward the occlusal surface, making the occlusal table narrow and resembling a lotus flower. The incisors were tapering and screwdriver-shaped with notched incisal edges, giving them an appearance similar to Hutchinson's incisors.
test_results: Panoramic radiograph revealed features of pulpal anomalies and taurodontism. It also revealed abnormal crown morphology of unerupted second permanent molars and premolars with tapered proximal surface. Findings of intraoral periapical radiograph and vitality test of 11 and 21 were within normal limits. Blood serological investigation to rule out congenital syphilis was negative. Evaluation of intelligence quotient (IQ) showed signs of mild intellectual impairment with an IQ score of 70.

case_report: A 36-year-old woman visited the dermatology department due to an asymptomatic red plaque on her forehead that had been present for two months. The patient was otherwise in good health with no systemic symptoms, and her medical and pharmacological history was unremarkable. Dermoscopic examination showed an irregular vascular pattern with irregular linear vessels, some of which were serpiginous and of consistent caliber, set against a pink-red background with perifollicular white areas resembling scars.
test_results: Incisional biopsy displayed the presence of a diffuse and homogeneous pan-dermal infiltrate of mast cells, with some perivascular and peri-adnexal lymphocytes and plasma cells in the upper dermis.

case_report: A 35-year-old female presented with deposits on teeth persisting for the past 6-7 months. The patient also reported experiencing intermittent mild pain in the lower back region for the past three months, which worsened with daily activities and was alleviated by rest, with pain radiating to both lower limbs. The patient had no history of fractures or swellings elsewhere in the body and no history of trauma or fractures in any other part of the body. General examination showed short stature and a thin build with normal skin and gait. Pallor was observed in the palpebral conjunctiva, nails, and palms. Extraoral examination revealed hypertelorism, exophthalmos, a depressed nasal bridge, a broad face, and a prognathic mandible. Intraoral examination showed generalized gingival inflammation, generalized shallow pockets, and gingival recession with the lower anterior teeth. No caries, mobility, attrition, or abrasion were noted in any of the teeth.
test_results: Panoramic radiograph showed signs of early periodontitis with generalised mild to moderate bone loss around teeth. Generalised marked increase in the bone density, lack of distinct lamina dura, and altered trabecular pattern were noted in both jaws; the trabeculae were coarse, dense, and increased in number. Right side of the mandible showed obliteration of the inferior alveolar canal, and cotton wool appearance of the trabeculae was noted at the right angle of the mandible. Left side of the mandible was comparatively less affected, showing an increase in bone density but no cotton wool appearance and no frank obliteration of the inferior alveolar canal. The trabeculae were dense in both sides of the maxilla, the zygomatic complex appeared hyper dense on both the sides, and the maxillary sinus was hypoplastic bilaterally. Further radiographic examination revealed increased bone density of all the bones of the skull, face, and the cervical spine. These views revealed thickening of the cortical boundaries of all the bones with obliteration of the marrow spaces. Lateral skull view revealed thickening of the inner and outer cortical tables and widening of the diploic space. The base of the skull appeared highly radiodense with loss of trabecular pattern, and there was hypoplasia of foramen magnum, and other foramina were obliterated. The nasal cavity and the sinuses were also hypoplastic showing high areas of radiodensity. Anteroposterior view of cervical spine showed increased radiodensity in all the cervical vertebrae. Whole body radiographic survey showed a generalised increase in the bone density throughout the thoracic cage and both clavicular bones with normal heart shadow and normal lung fields. Radiograph of the lumbar spine showed sclerosis at all the levels and “bone-in-bone appearance.” Normal spinous processes, normal height, and morphology of the individual vertebrae were noted. Radiograph of the pelvis showed expanding osteosclerosis of the pelvic bone and the iliac wings. Radiograph of the hip joint showed generalised sclerosis of the pelvic rami and the femur bone. Radiograph of the humerus showed dense sclerosis of the humerus and scapula and “funnel-like appearance” in the humerus. Radiograph of radius and ulna showed increased radiodensity in all the bones, smoothening of the bone surfaces, and cylindrical metacarpals. Hematologic investigations showed Hb of 10.8 g/dL, white blood cells 6.5 k/uL, and platelet count 130 k/uL, and ESR was in the normal range. Red cell indices and iron profile were normal. Peripheral smear showed normocytic and normochromic anemia. Renal function and serum electrolytes were within normal limits. Liver function tests were normal, and serum calcium was 8.9 mg/dL, and serum phosphorus was 3.0 mg/dL.

case_report: A fifteen-year-old female presented with primary amenorrhea. Her medical history indicated the onset of thelarche at age 10 and pubarche at age 11. There was no notable family history, and her parents were not consanguineous. Physical examination showed a weight of 55.2 kg (0.25 SD for age and sex), height of 165.5 cm (0.95 SD), and a body mass index of 20.1 kg/m2 (0.10 SD). Her external genitalia were fully female, with breast development and pubic hair at Tanner stage V. The remainder of the physical examination was normal, with no somatic abnormalities, clitoral enlargement, or signs of virilization. Laboratory results showed normal biochemistry. Hormone levels were as follows: follicle stimulating hormone, 121 mIU/mL (normal, 0.3-10); luteinizing hormone, 13 mIU/mL (normal, 0.3-31); estradiol, 66 pg/mL (normal, 15-350); total testosterone, <20 ng/dL (normal, 15-181); prolactin, 5.3 ng/mL (normal, 1.9-25); beta human chorionic gonadotropin, <1 mIU/mL (normal, 0-10); adrenocorticotropic hormone, 50.3 pg/mL (normal, 0-46); and cortisol, 14 µg/dL (normal, 5-25). Bone age assessment indicated an age of 13.5 years based on the Greulich & Pyle method. Pelvic ultrasound showed a right gonad volume of 1.4 cm3 and a left gonad volume of 2.4 cm3, with a uterus measuring 60x25x23 mm and an endometrial thickness of 7 mm. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed smaller than normal gonads, a normally sized uterus, and no evidence of a tumor.
test_results: Chromosome analysis revealed a 46,XY karyotype (30 metaphase cells counted). SRY gene expression was confirmed by multiplex polymerase chain reaction. Direct sequencing on genomic DNA did not reveal a mutation in the SRY, SF1 and Wilms’ tumor 1 (WT1) genes.

case_report: A 10-year-old Chinese boy was born to a healthy mother with no family history of genetic diseases. His mother and father were 35 and 36 years old, respectively, at the time of his birth. Prenatal ultrasound indicated intrauterine growth retardation and polyhydramnios. He was delivered by Caesarean section at full term with a birth weight of 2350 g (3rd centile). The birth height was not recorded. The patient experienced developmental delay and neonatal hypotonia, with delayed milestones, feeding difficulties, and weak sucking and crying during the first several months of life. At age five, his complete blood count and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels were normal, but his serum growth hormone (GH) level was very low (0.97 ng/ml). A growth hormone provocative test showed a peak value of 2.66 ng/ml, and he was found to have growth hormone deficiency (GHD). At age six, he began to gain weight with a growth rate of 2-3 cm per year, and his bone age was delayed (corresponding to the age of 2 years). Currently, he presents with intellectual disability, language delay, learning difficulties, attention deficit, and minimal communication with peers. Physical examination at age 9 years and 9 months revealed a height of 118.3 cm (−6.0SD), a weight of 27 kg (−1.5SD) (BMI = 19.3 kg/m²), and an occipitofrontal circumference (OFC) of 52 cm (50–75th percentile). He had small hands (13.5 cm) and small feet (18.5 cm). Physical features included short stature, truncal obesity, short neck, thoracic-lumbar scoliosis, lordosis, kyphosis, small hands and feet, fifth finger clinodactyly, buffalo hump, barrel chest, body asymmetry, right-sided cryptorchidism, and abnormal skin pigmentation. Craniofacial features included ocular hypertelorism, narrow palpebral fissures, high arched palate, and a depressed nasal bridge. The right and left testes measured 1.7*0.8*1.0 cm and 1.7*0.9*1.1 cm, respectively. The penis measured 4.0*1.5 cm without pubic hair. No signs of precocious puberty were observed. ECG examination showed sinus cardiac arrhythmia, and brain MRI was normal. Recent assessment using the Chinese Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (C-WISC) showed a verbal scale IQ of 35 (severe), a performance scale IQ of 55 (mild), and a full-scale IQ of 38 (severe). Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices (RSPM) indicated an intelligence percentile rank of 6%. Motor development was close to normal. The boy started growth hormone (GH) therapy at age 9 years and 9 months, resulting in a growth of 4.9 cm (from 118.3 to 123.2 cm (−5.0SD)) and a weight gain of 5 kg (from 27 to 32 kg (−0.5SD)) during the first five months.
test_results: G-banding was performed on metaphase chromosomes of cultured peripheral blood lymphocytes of the family trio. FISH was directly conducted on interphases chromosomes 14 of peripheral blood lymphocytes with probe specific for the region 14q11.2 on the patient. Genomic profiling were performed on blood, hyperpigmented and normal skin samples of the patient and his parents’ blood samples using Illumina Human CytoSNP 12 BeadChip array. The SNP array data was analyzed with GenomeStudio and KaryoStudio software.
diagnosis: Maternal uniparental disomy 14 and mosaic trisomy 14
Orpha_name: Temple syndrome due to maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 14

case_report: A 54-year-old Caucasian male presented with abdominal pain and bloating, for which he had been using nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). His medical history includes hypertension, Raynaud’s syndrome, rectal cancer in remission post-surgical resection and radiation therapy, and ongoing radiation-induced cystitis. Two months prior, he was diagnosed with strongly positive anti-RNA polymerase III systemic sclerosis following the onset of dysphagia and was prescribed methotrexate (MTX) up to a dose of 20 mg weekly. He had not taken MTX for 14 days due to feeling unwell. Examination revealed a small bladder rupture attributed to cystitis, which did not necessitate surgical intervention. During the bladder evaluation, abnormal serum sodium and creatinine levels were detected, leading to further cardiac assessment.
test_results: A transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a severely reduced left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction of 10%. A coronary catheterization demonstrated no significant coronary disease. A cardiac biopsy showed cardiac necrosis without evidence of inflammation or fibrosis.

case_report: A 13-year-old male with a history of cyclic vomiting syndrome, severe obesity, developmental delay, autism spectrum disorder, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder arrived at the pediatric emergency department with a one-day history of fever reaching 103°F and non-bloody, non-bilious vomiting without diarrhea. His home medications included clonidine and guanfacine. Upon evaluation, he was afebrile with a heart rate of 103 beats per minute, blood pressure of 148/64 mmHg, and peripheral oxygen saturation of 88% in ambient air. He exhibited intermittent retching and reported tenderness upon palpation of the epigastrium. Laboratory results revealed a white blood cell count of 13.2 K/uL (reference range: 3.8-9.8 K/uL), creatinine of 0.7 mg/dL (reference range: 0.3-0.8 mg/dL), and normal serum electrolytes, liver enzymes, and lipase. Dipstick urinalysis from a clean-catch specimen showed large blood, protein >300 mg/dL, ketones, specific gravity of >1.030, and normal pH. Urine nitrates and leukocytes were negative. A chest radiograph indicated a right lower lobe airspace opacity consistent with pneumonia. Nasal PCR testing for influenza A and B was negative. The patient was admitted for treatment of community-acquired pneumonia. During the hospital stay, he experienced intermittent elevated blood pressures, with systolic readings reaching 170-180 mmHg. Repeat urinalysis with microscopy revealed 10-25 red blood cells per high-powered field and a protein/creatinine ratio of 0.28 (reference range: <0.2). Urine calcium-to-creatinine ratio and C3/C4 complement levels were normal. A renal bladder ultrasound with Doppler showed normal appearance, size, and vascular flow of both kidneys. He was discharged with a seven-day course of amoxicillin/clavulanate for community-acquired pneumonia and referred to an outpatient nephrology clinic for persistent hematuria and hypertension. He was readmitted two days later with worsening respiratory symptoms. Repeat workup showed stable mild normocytic anemia (hemoglobin level of 11.4 g/dL; reference range: 13.0-16.0 g/dL) and a nasopharyngeal PCR positive for Mycoplasma pneumoniae. He was treated with azithromycin. Microscopic hematuria with large blood on urinalysis persisted. Levels of anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), markers of hemolysis, and creatinine kinase were normal. Outpatient nephrology evaluation two months later showed persistent microscopic hematuria and elevated blood pressure, with systolic readings in the 99th percentile for age. Family history included hematuria and proteinuria in the patient's father and identical twin brother, isolated hematuria during pregnancy in the mother, and frequent nephrolithiasis in the father. Given this family history and ongoing microscopic hematuria, a gene panel was sent to evaluate for hereditary nephritis. The patient was found to have a variant of uncertain significance in the COL4A5 gene.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing confirmed this variant in the patient, his twin brother, and his mother.

case_report: A three-day-old male neonate, born at 31 weeks with a birth weight of 1500 grams, to a 29-year-old first-time mother via normal spontaneous vaginal delivery. A prenatal 20-week ultrasound indicated potential kidney abnormalities, and at 30 weeks gestation, the scan revealed low amniotic fluid levels. There is no known family history of kidney issues. The patient initially required oscillator ventilation, transitioned to a conventional ventilator by day three, and was on continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) by day 15. Physical examination showed no signs of edema. On day seven, laboratory results were as follows: serum creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 21 mg/dL, sodium 145 mmol/L, and potassium 3.5 mmol/L.
test_results: Renal ultrasound after birth showed normal-sized kidneys, with the right measuring 4.2 cm and the left measuring 4.9 cm; however, it showed bilateral mild pelviectasis and cysts, mostly on the left.

case_report: A 3-year-old girl was admitted to our hospital presenting with congenital torticollis and asymmetry of the face, skull, and trunk. She was delivered normally following an uncomplicated pregnancy, and there was no notable parental history. Early in life, she exhibited balance issues and a decline in fine-motor skills. Due to the abnormal shape of her head, craniosynostosis was initially considered. Progressive asymmetry of the skull and face led to further imaging. Clinical examination revealed a narrow, posteriorly crooked skull with facial asymmetry, left-sided hypoplasia, and hypotony in the trunk and extremities. Her facial expressions were limited. There was a noticeable deviation of the facial axis in an anticlockwise direction. A slight prominence was observed in the region of the mastoid process, suggesting tension in the muscle insertion area. Examination of the neck musculature showed no tension or spasms in the left sternocleidomastoid or trapezius muscles, and passive neck movement ranges were unrestricted. Radiological examination of the spine showed no cervical anomalies, including those of the atlas, dens, and junction. Ultrasound imaging of the neck musculature indicated that the left sternocleidomastoid muscle was 2 mm thinner compared to the right side. Repeated assessments of her intellectual status were normal for her age. Ophthalmologic and neurologic examinations did not reveal any signs of trochlear palsy as a cause of the torticollis.
test_results: A 3D-CT was performed, revealing a closure of the sagittal suture without typical scaphocephalic skull form, with no abnormalities at lambdoid sutures. A brain-MRI revealed partial fusion of the cerebellar hemispheres with no other cerebellar anomalies.

case_report: A 60-year-old male presented with progressive difficulty seeing in low light. He had previously undergone cataract surgery in both eyes and hand surgery due to chronic pain. Examination revealed shortened fourth and fifth metatarsal bones. Ophthalmic evaluation showed best corrected visual acuity of 0.18 in the right eye and 1.3 in the left eye. Refraction was +0.75 +0.50 x 10˚ in the right eye and +0.75 +0.72 x 25˚ in the left eye. Both eyes had artificial lenses. Fundus examination revealed pale optic nerves, narrowed arterioles, paravenous retinal pigment epithelium hyperplasia, a 'salt-and-pepper' appearance around the macula, and mid-peripheral bony spicules. Macular optical coherence tomography indicated macular thickness of 254 micrometers in the right eye and 188 micrometers in the left eye, with total macular volume of 9.1 mm³ and 6.8 mm³, respectively. Imaging showed loss of the foveal pit and several retinal layers, with more severe findings in the left eye. Visual field testing showed a mean deviation of -30.51 dB in the right eye and -30.74 dB in the left eye, with pattern standard deviation of +4.43 dB and +5.04 dB, respectively. Full-field electroretinogram results indicated non-recordable scotopic responses and diminished photopic responses in both eyes. Audiologic studies revealed mild hearing loss from 4 to 6 KHz in the right ear and mild to moderate hearing loss from 3 to 8 KHz in the left ear.
test_results: Gene sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis using next-generation sequencing (NGS) were positive for a Variable of Uncertain Significance as a heterozygous mutation in the PHYH gene of the variant c.290G>A (p.Gly97Glu).

case_report: A 10-year-old male presented with fever and arrhythmia. He was the first child of his parents, born via caesarean section at 40 weeks of gestation with a birth weight of 3900 g and a height of 50 cm. There was no history of asphyxia or birth trauma. The patient exhibited skin hyperpigmentation from birth and had a history of frequent infections. At one year old, an atrial septal defect was identified through ultrasonography, and atrioseptopexy was performed. The patient has intellectual disability and is non-verbal. Pre-admission blood glucose levels were not available, and it is unknown if he experienced prolonged neonatal hypoglycemia. His parents are non-consanguineous and show no recognizable abnormalities. On examination, the patient had a tall stature with a height of 162 cm (+3.5 SD) and a weight of 48 kg. Skin pigmentation was noted across the body, particularly on the penis and the joints of the fingers and toes. His heart rate was 140 beats per minute with arrhythmia. Testicular volume was approximately 10 ml, and the penis measured 12 cm in length and 9 cm in circumference. No armpit or pubic hair was observed. Laboratory tests showed low plasma cortisol levels and elevated plasma ACTH. Thyroid hormone and androgen levels were low, while glucose, electrolytes, and renin levels were within normal ranges.
test_results: The proband is homozygotic for c.712C>T/p.H238Y in MC2R. Variants come from both parents. No phenotype relevant to CNV was found.

case_report: A 57-year-old Hispanic male presented for retinal evaluation due to a progressive decline in central vision in both eyes over 7 months, more pronounced in the right eye. He reported difficulty reading, watching TV, and experiencing bilateral light sensitivity. He denied any new visual distortions, floaters, flashing lights, head or eye trauma, prior eye surgeries, or a history of strabismus or amblyopia. His ophthalmic history was notable only for poor night vision since childhood. Family history was negative for retinal diseases, and his children and grandchildren reported no night vision issues. His general medical history included well-controlled hypertension managed with lisinopril. On examination, visual acuity was counting fingers at 4 feet in the right eye and 3 feet in the left eye. Anterior segment examination, pupillary reflexes, and extraocular movements were normal. Dilated fundus examination and ultra-wide-field confocal scanning laser ophthalmoscopy revealed significant macular atrophy in both eyes with 3+ diffuse, fine, yellow flecks. Green wavelength fundus autofluorescence showed bull's eye maculopathy and hyperautofluorescent perifoveal rings bilaterally. Optical coherence tomography indicated foveal atrophy of the outer retina extending from the ellipsoid layer to the outer plexiform layer, with scattered hyper-reflective lesions in the peripheral macula corresponding to the flecks observed on fundoscopy. Visual field testing was unreliable due to high fixation losses bilaterally. Full-field ERG and multifocal ERG showed severely diminished responses in both eyes to scotopic flash, photopic flash, and 30 Hz flicker stimulation conditions, indicating severe electroretinal dysfunction of both rod and cone systems, with greater impairment of rod function. Multifocal ERG results indicated severe electroretinal dysfunction of the cone system within the central 30 degrees surrounding the fovea.
test_results: Our patient was heterozygous for two variants in the RDH5 gene: a known pathogenic variant, c.160C > T (p.Arg54), and a novel variant of presumed pathogenicity, c.814_815del (p.Leu272Aspfs63).
diagnosis: Fundus Albipunctatus  associated with a novel pathogenic variant in the RDH5 gene

case_report: This case involves a 2-month-old male infant, born to parents without a consanguineous relationship. During the prenatal period, polyhydramnios was noted at the 7th month of gestation, and the mother received progesterone injections due to vaginal bleeding. The infant was delivered at full term without complications. At 10 days old, the mother observed focal motor seizures, which progressively increased in frequency and severity. At 2 months old, the infant was brought to our hospital. He had not achieved developmental milestones appropriate for his age. Physical examination revealed hypotonia, lack of visual tracking, complete head lag, truncal hypotonia, and brisk reflexes. Video electroencephalography (VEEG) indicated potentially epileptiform interictal abnormalities in the right central region. Three electroclinical and two electrographic events were recorded, indicating focal seizures originating from the right central area. A 3T MRI of the brain showed no structural abnormalities. Antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) were optimized, including levetiracetam (26 mg/kg/day), clobazam (0.94 mg/kg/day), phenobarbitone (4.5 mg/kg/day), sodium valproate (42 mg/kg/day), lacosamide (4.25 mg/kg/day), and topiramate (5.3 mg/kg/day), resulting in a temporary reduction in seizure frequency. A follow-up VEEG recorded multifocal interictal epileptiform abnormalities and frequent focal seizures with a migrating pattern originating from multiple foci.
test_results: Next-generation sequencing identified a heterozygous missense variation in exon 24 of the KCNT1 gene (chr9:138671275; G>G/A; Depth: 136x) that results in the amino acid substitution of Threonine for Alanine at codon 934 (p. Ala934Thr; ENST00000371757).
diagnosis: KCNT1-related malignant migrating focal seizures of infancy
Orpha_name: Malignant migrating focal seizures of infancy

case_report: The patient, a 16-year-old male, is the first child of healthy parents with no family history of genetic diseases. He was born at term following a normal pregnancy and neonatal period. At 9 months, developmental delays were noted, leading to CGH array testing with non-specific results. Extended endocrine-metabolic screening identified primary hypothyroidism, and levothyroxine treatment was initiated. Psycho-motor rehabilitation was provided, resulting in autonomous walking at 16 months, spontaneous language at around 3 years, and sphincter control by 4 years. At 5 years, he underwent two surgeries for bilateral vesicoureteral reflux. At age 12, a routine abdominal ultrasound revealed hyperechoic and heterogeneous liver parenchyma, though liver function tests (LFTs) were normal. Four years later, a follow-up ultrasound showed increased liver abnormalities indicative of advanced chronic liver involvement, prompting referral to a Pediatric Hepatology Center. Upon admission, the patient was asymptomatic with a body mass index of 16.6 (<3°). Clinical examination revealed a long-limbed habitus, ligamentous hyperlaxity, arachnodactyly, bilateral flat foot, and mild splenomegaly. Facial features included a low hairline, thick horizontal eyebrows, downward eyelids, low-set extroverted ears, a thin arched upper lip, a fleshy extroverted lower lip, small teeth, and dental diastemas. Extensive laboratory, radiological, and clinical investigations ruled out common causes of chronic liver disease (CLD). LFTs were normal, and a full blood count showed mild thrombocytopenia due to hypersplenism. Abdominal doppler ultrasound and MRI confirmed chronic liver involvement with hepatic parenchymal micro- and macronodular transformation and splenomegaly. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy ruled out esophageal varices but indicated mild portal hypertension-related gastropathy. Echocardiography and ophthalmology reviews were normal, and a psychological evaluation revealed a non-verbal IQ of 63. Liver biopsy histology showed micro- and macronodular cirrhosis with disturbed architecture, veno-venous fibrotic septa, slight inflammatory lymphomonocyte infiltrate, and clusters of optically empty cells intermixed with atrophic hepatocytes. Immunohistochemical analysis identified these cells as Ito perisinusoidal cells in a setting of s.c. spongiotic pericytoma.
test_results: The genetic test showed a heterozygous de novo frameshift variant c.5751_5754delAGTT in the SON gene.
diagnosis: ZTTK syndrome due to a heterozygous variant of the SON gene
Orpha_name: Brain malformations-musculoskeletal abnormalities-facial dysmorphism-intellectual disability syndrome

case_report: A 10-month-old male presented with skin peeling confined to the hands and feet, first observed at 2 months of age. The condition was noted to worsen with exposure to heat and humidity, but not due to mechanical trauma. The patient was born following a normal pregnancy and delivery, with non-consanguineous parents and no relevant family history. Physical examination revealed erythematous erosions with peripheral desquamation on both palms and soles, along with a flaccid blister on the right-hand finger. Mycological tests on the palms and soles returned negative results. The mother declined a skin biopsy from the edge of a fresh blister for further examination.
test_results: In the index patient, we detected two heterozygous TGM5 mutations: c.2T>C, p.M1T in exon 1 and c.337G>T, p.G113C in exon 3. The father is a heterozygous carrier of the mutation c.2T>C, p.M1T and the mother is a heterozygous carrier of the mutation c.337G>T, p.G113C. No other mutations were disclosed in the analyzed regions.

case_report: A 16-year-old male presented with an asymmetrical chest appearance, with the left side appearing flatter than the right. The patient reported no chest pain or movement restrictions. There was no history of prior surgeries or congenital anomalies in the family. Physical examination revealed a flat left anterior chest wall and absence of the anterior axillary fold on the left side. The left upper extremity appeared normal with no significant differences in length or circumference compared to the right side. Sensations of pain and touch were intact, and biceps and triceps reflexes were normoactive. A chest skiagram showed normal bones in the chest wall and upper extremities, but increased radiolucency on the left side.
test_results: Computed tomography of thorax revealed absence of muscular shadow on the left anterior chest wall because of absence of pectoralis major muscle.

case_report: The subject is a 15-year-old female who was delivered at full-term by parents who are not related by blood. Her birth weight was 2.2 kg, placing her in the 3rd percentile. She exhibited excessive hair growth starting at the age of 5 years. From the age of 13 years, she experienced the development of secondary sexual characteristics and rapid growth, but she has not yet had her first menstrual period. Her body mass index (BMI) is 18.4 kg/m2.
test_results: Plasma glucose during a 5-h oral glucose tolerance test was 7.2, 17.1, 18.6, 14.2, 12.9 and 6.8 mmol/L at 0, 1-h, 2-h, 3-h, 4-h and 5-h time-points. Simultaneous measurements of serum insulin were 96.1, 256.8, >300, >300, >300 and 258.9 μU/mL. The patient's glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) was 6.8%. Ultrasound showed polycystic ovaries. Her serum testosterone was 0.97 ng/mL.

case_report: An 8-month-old male from the Philippines was brought to the plastic surgery clinic by his mother for a second opinion regarding the absence of the third toe on his left foot since birth. He is the fourth child in the family, with no similar conditions reported among relatives. His weight is 8 kg, placing him at the 15th percentile, and his length is 65.5 cm, placing him at the 3rd percentile on growth charts. The patient is receiving 400 international units of cholecalciferol (Vitamin D3) orally each day. Vaccination records indicate he is current with his immunizations. There is no known family history of similar conditions and no known allergies. His past medical history includes a fever lasting one day and a skin rash lasting two days at 6 months of age, without associated symptoms such as cough, runny nose, sore throat, difficulty breathing, vomiting, or diarrhea. This episode was suggestive of hand, foot, and mouth disease. He has no history of surgeries. Physical examination revealed a hypoplastic left third toe with no visible digit or toenail. The rest of the digits on his hands and right foot appeared normal. The hypoplastic left third toe was nontender, with no redness, swelling, discharge, or cysts.
test_results: Foot X-ray confirms hypoplastic left third toe with no visualization of middle and distal phalanges.

case_report: A 45-year-old male patient (weight: 47.5 kg, height: 158 cm, body surface area: 1.46 m²) was admitted to the hospital on July 31, 2021, presenting with recurrent fever reaching up to 40°C for over two months and generalized rashes with uneven surfaces and itching. The patient had previously received anti-allergy treatment for a 'drug rash' at a local hospital without improvement. One week prior to admission, the patient experienced noticeable shortness of breath and more frequent rash outbreaks. Upon admission, physical examination revealed a pale complexion, poor general condition, cachexia, hepatosplenomegaly, dark erythema, and papules of varying sizes on both palms. Multiple enlarged lymph nodes were palpable on both sides of the neck, supraclavicular, and inguinal regions, with the largest node measuring 2.0 cm × 2.0 cm on the right side of the neck. Initial laboratory results on July 31, 2021, indicated complete hemocytopenia, elevated inflammatory markers, and increased lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). Serum ferritin levels were elevated to 1519.25 ng/mL (reference range: 21.80–274.66 ng/mL) on August 21.
test_results: Subsequent hybrid imaging with 2-deoxy-2-[18F]fluoro-D-glucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (2-[18F]FDG PET/CT) revealed generalized and multiple enlargements of the lymph nodes, hepatosplenomegaly, and bilateral tonsillomegaly—with augmented glucose metabolism throughout the body. Laboratory results showed an increase in sIL-2R to 11,340 U/mL, and NK cell activity of 3.0%, indicating diminished NK cell activity.
diagnosis: Primary Histiocytic Sarcoma  with Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis
Orpha_name: Acquired hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis associated with malignant disease

case_report: A 68-year-old male patient, who was diagnosed with ADPKD at the age of 57, received a kidney transplant in 2012. The donor was a 60-year-old female who had passed away due to cerebral hemorrhage, and the cold ischemic time was 15 hours. The HLA mismatch was 4. The patient received immunosuppression treatment that included two intravenous doses of basiliximab (20 mg), a tapering dose of methylprednisolone down to 5 mg daily, mycophenolate, and tacrolimus for maintenance. The clinical course was marked by prolonged delayed graft function with oligo-anuria. A biopsy performed 10 days post-transplant revealed acute tubular necrosis. A subsequent biopsy did not contain glomeruli.
test_results: The renal biopsy specimen demonstrated arteriolar thrombi, occlusion of glomerular capillaries by amorphous material, fragmented red blood cells in glomeruli. No signs of hemolytic uremic syndrome were detected.
Orpha_name: De novo thrombotic microangiopathy after kidney transplantation

case_report: A 56-year-old male arrived at the Emergency Department with sudden onset of headache, right-hand clumsiness, and numbness on the right side of his face, which began a few days prior. His medical history includes hypertension managed with carvedilol, lisinopril, barnidipine, and moxonidine, chronic renal insufficiency, eczema, and three previous episodes of bacterial pneumonia. He also takes acetylsalicylic acid 100 mg and simvastatin 20 mg daily. On physical examination, his body temperature was 35.9°C, pulse rate was 94/min, and blood pressure was 162/95 mmHg. Neurological examination showed reduced sensitivity in the right side of the face, not limited to a trigeminal nerve dermatome, decreased strength and coordination in the right hand, weak tendon reflexes, and normal plantar reflexes. The patient could walk and stand normally but exhibited mental slowness and apraxia. Laboratory tests indicated elevated C-reactive protein (151 mg/L), mild anemia, and moderate hypereosinophilia (3.5 × 10^3/mm^3). Cardiac troponins I were slightly elevated (3.41 μg/L) with normal creatine kinase-MB levels. Coagulation screening, including anticardiolipin and lupus anticoagulant, showed no abnormalities. Brain MRI revealed several small areas of diffusion restriction in both cerebral hemispheres and a single lesion in the left cerebellar hemisphere, corresponding to border-zone infarctions. Extensive cardiac evaluations, including ECG, 48-hour cardiac rhythm monitoring, transthoracic and transoesophageal echocardiography, cardiac MRI, and CT angiography of the thoracic aorta, were negative for potential cardioembolic sources. No microembolic signals were detected on transcranial Doppler monitoring. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal. The patient had no history of allergic disease. Repetitive coproculture and tests for antibodies against strongyloides, filariae, and toxocara were negative. Imaging studies, including CT thorax, CT abdomen, whole-body PET with [18F]-fluoroglucose, and lymphocyte immunophenotyping, did not suggest lymphoma. There was no history of asthma, no granulomatous skin lesions, and ANCAs were negative. Angiotensin-converting enzyme, ANA, and rheumatoid factor tests were also negative. The patient had elevated IgE serum levels (8770 kIU/L). Bone marrow biopsy showed no signs of myeloproliferative disorders, with a normal karyotype (46, XY) and no PDGFRB rearrangement detected by FISH analysis. The FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion gene was not found.
test_results: A T-cell receptor rearrangement was detected by PCR on peripheral blood and bone marrow.

case_report: A 9-year-old male presented with a shorter left leg and skin abnormalities on the same side. His family history showed no notable conditions. The skin issues began when he was 3 years old. Dermatological examination identified multiple whitish papules on the left lower and upper eyelids. Segmentally located skin-colored or brownish papules were observed on the left side of the presternal area and left shoulder, accompanied by localized increased hair growth. Similar papules were found on the left thigh, arranged in a pattern following the lines of Blaschko. Imaging showed a 14 mm shortening of the left lower limb.
test_results: The histopathological examination of a papule on the left presternal area showed features consistent with a basaloid follicular hamartoma. This MRI demonstrated a mild enlargement of the left hemisphere with minimal displacement of the midline and moderate enlargement of the ipsilateral ventricle especially in the frontal horn. The frontal horn of the left lateral ventricle was anteriorly and superiorly extending. An abnormal gyral pattern with slightly flat and thick cortex consistent with coarse polymicrogyria was also present in the left frontal lobe. No signal abnormality was detected in the white matter. Bilateral small temporal arachnoid cysts were observed. Extraparenchymal abnormalities such as olfactory nerve enlargement or abnormal dilated venous channels were not seen. No asymmetric enlargement was noted in the cerebellum or in the brainstem. The cerebellar folia were normal.

case_report: The patient is a 23-year-old male with a four-year history of walking difficulties and frequent falls. He also experiences clumsiness in his arms and hands and has had speech difficulties for the past six months. He was born to consanguineous parents via successful vaginal delivery with normal birth parameters. He left school at age 14 due to learning difficulties. At age 18, during a routine examination before military service, he was found to have gynecomastia and small testicles. Physical examination revealed eunuchoid body proportions, short stature, gynecomastia, poor facial hair growth, and generalized jaundice. Neurological examination showed dysarthria and severe ataxia, making walking impossible without assistance. He exhibited appendicular dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia, particularly in the lower extremities, slightly generalized chorea while talking, hypomimia, mild bradykinesia, slight dystonia in the left hand, and brisk deep tendon reflexes in the lower extremities. Eye examination revealed fragmented pursuit eye movements with slow hypometric saccades, vertical gaze palsy, and square wave jerks in horizontal pursuit. Psychiatric examination showed regressed speech, a smaller appearance compared to peers, no delirium, no suicidal or homicidal thoughts, and no euthymic perception deviation. An IQ test indicated borderline mental capacity, with a Kent EGY intelligence test verbal performance score of 85.71. He was unable to obtain a calculable score on the Porteus maze test.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed progressive cerebellar, vermian, and cerebral cortical atrophy, and periventricular confluent white matter hyperintensities in 2022 compared to 2018. Mild mesencephalic atrophy is similar in both dates. Basal ganglia hyperintense lesions began to appear in 2022. Pituitary MRI showed a normal pituitary gland height (4 mm) for his age. Testicular atrophy detected on ultrasound (right testis 12 × 6 × 15mm, 0.56 ml, left 10 × 4.5 × 14 mm, 0.32 ml). In the X-ray evaluation of his hands at 24, it was noted that the growth plate of the distal radius, which normally starts at the age of 17 to 19 and should fuse at the most at the age of 20, did not fuse.

case_report: A 17-year-old male from Turkey was evaluated in a pediatric genetics clinic. He is the second child of consanguineous parents, with the first child having passed away due to an unspecified congenital heart defect. At one month old, he was found to have tetralogy of Fallot and pulmonary atresia (muscular atresia) with underdevelopment of the main pulmonary artery but well-developed confluent branch pulmonary arteries supplied by a patent ductus arteriosus. No coronary abnormalities were noted, and he underwent corrective surgery. Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) testing for the 22q11.2 deletion syndrome was negative, and no further genetic evaluation was conducted. The patient exhibited slow growth and mild intellectual disability, which were considered secondary to his cardiac condition. Physical measurements included a height of 149.4 cm (−3.92 SD), weight of 38.2 kg (−4.43 SD), and head circumference of 48 cm (−6.34 SD). Dysmorphic features observed included a long narrow face, bulbous nose, sparse lateral eyebrows, and strabismus.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing analysis revealed a frameshift hemizygous X chromosome variant inherited from an unaffected heterozygous mother at the gene, PQBP1 (NM_001167989: p. Arg153fs).

case_report: A 12-year-old boy from the Northwest Gondar Amhara regional state presented with left flank swelling for the past 3 months. Three days prior to admission, he began experiencing pain in the left flank, accompanied by high-grade fever, chills, rigor, and vomiting. He did not report any urinary or respiratory symptoms. His maternal pregnancy course and medical history were unremarkable, and he was born at a health center. His past medical history was also unremarkable. He has seven siblings, none of whom exhibited similar symptoms. His mother had no history of radiation exposure, use of traditional medicine, or chemotherapy during pregnancy. No dysmorphisms were observed in his general appearance. Vital signs were as follows: pulse rate 142 beats/min, respiratory rate 33 breaths/min, temperature 38.5 °C, and blood pressure 105/65 mmHg. Anthropometric measurements indicated severe stunting. Abdominal examination revealed a distended abdomen, asymmetry with bulging on the left flank, a visible horizontal line, an upward umbilical slit, and absent rectus abdominis muscles. The abdomen was soft with a tender cystic mass on the left flank, measuring 13 × 11 cm, palpable bimanually. Both testes were undescended. The patient also had scoliosis and developmental dysplasia of the hips with a waddling gait. Urinary analysis showed many red blood cells and positive leukocyte esterase. Renal function tests were normal with a creatinine level of 0.72 mg/dl and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) of 44 mg/dl. Hemoglobin was normal at 12.7 gm/dl, and electrolyte levels were normal.
test_results: Ultrasound showed a large cystic mass in his left kidney area with echo debris. His right kidney had normal echo texture and size. An X-ray of his hips showed bilateral developmental dysplasia of the hip. His left kidney is cystic and enlarged; there is no parenchyma tissue, both testes are intraperitoneal just below the kidneys, tortuous left renal vein, enlarged bladder reaching above umbilicus, and left megaureter.

case_report: DF, a 64-year-old right-handed male IT technician, began experiencing progressive changes in behavior and emotional stability at the age of 61. Over the next two years, these issues extended to other cognitive areas such as memory and language, with noticeable difficulties in word finding. Additionally, there was an increase in behavioral issues, including excessive oral tendencies and significantly inappropriate actions.
test_results: MRI indicated clear bilateral frontotemporal involution with left frontal predominance.

case_report: In early October 2012, a 66-year-old male presented with a 5-day history of an itchy rash initially on his lower limbs, which gradually spread to cover most of his body. There was no involvement of mucosal areas or other systemic symptoms. His medical history included hypertension managed with irbesartan. Physical examination revealed scaly, annular, erythematous-violaceous maculopapules on the palms and soles. Lesions in pressure areas exhibited a palpable purpuric macular appearance.
test_results: Histopathology revealed eosinophilic exocytosis and infundibular spongiosis with eosinophilic and neutrophilic micropustules. In the dermis, an inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes, eosinophils and neutrophils with perivascular and interstitial distribution was observed.

case_report: The patient is a 76-year-old Caucasian female with a history of unexplained elevated calcium levels and mild bone density reduction. She was initially evaluated for osteoporosis and mentioned a family history of elevated calcium levels. She also noted that she had not consulted a physician until the age of 60. Laboratory tests revealed a corrected serum calcium level of 12.2 mg/dL (reference range: 8.6-10.0 mg/dL). Follow-up tests one month later showed a corrected serum calcium level of 11.6 mg/dL, elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) at 136 pg/mL (reference range: 15-65 pg/mL), low serum phosphorus at 2.3 mg/dL (reference range: 2.5-4.9 mg/dL), and undetectable 24-hour urinary calcium at less than 17 mg/24 h (reference range: 100-300 mg/24 h). Imaging with a nuclear medicine sestamibi SPECT parathyroid scan showed no signs of parathyroid adenoma.
test_results: CASR gene sequencing revealed a heterozygous sequence change with a c.2039G>A mutation in exon 7 of the CASR.

case_report: A six-month-old female infant was admitted to our hospital with a seizure disorder and pancytopenia. She is the first child of healthy, non-related parents. Her perinatal and neonatal periods were uneventful except for mild jaundice during the first month. At birth, her body weight was 2950 grams and head circumference was 34 cm. Her growth and development were normal until four months of age, when she began to show neuro-developmental regression, lacking tonic neck reflex and displaying attention deficit. She experienced seizure attacks characterized by sucking and eye movements 10 days before hospitalization and was treated with phenobarbital and phenytoin at another center. She was referred to our center due to increased seizure frequency and pancytopenia. Upon admission, she was lethargic and pale, with a body weight of 6500 grams (10th percentile for age) and a head circumference of 42 cm (50th percentile for age). Physical examination revealed hepatomegaly, but the spleen was not palpable. She was febrile with an axillary temperature of 38.5°C. Complete blood count (CBC) showed pancytopenia: white blood cell (WBC) count of 1100/µL, polymorphonuclear (PMN) cells at 34%, red blood cell (RBC) count of 2870000/µL, hemoglobin (Hb) level of 8.8 g/dl, mean corpuscular volume (MCV) of 91 fl, mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) of 30 pg, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) of 33 g/dl, platelet count of 125000/µL, and reticulocyte count of 1.4%. Other chemical laboratory tests, including blood sugar, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, sodium, potassium, phosphorus, calcium, liver function tests, triglycerides, cholesterol, and lactate dehydrogenase, were normal on the first day of admission. Arterial blood gas, serum lactate and pyruvate, serum and urine amino acid chromatography, TORCH study, thyroid function tests, serum folate, and serum B12 levels were normal. Treatment with anticonvulsant drugs and antibiotics continued. She experienced status epilepticus and loss of consciousness two days after hospitalization, which was controlled by midazolam. Brain computed tomography scan showed marked brain atrophy, and visual evoked potential indicated bilateral cortical blindness. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was within normal range. Electroencephalography showed slow background activity. Abdominal sonography revealed mild hepatomegaly, and skeletal survey reported mild osteopenia. CBC performed seven days after hospitalization still showed bicytopenia: WBC of 1600/µL, RBC of 2270000/µL, Hb of 7.2 g/dl, MCV of 95 fl, MCH of 31 pg, MCHC of 33 g/dl, and platelet count of 190000/µL. Bone marrow aspiration revealed a cellular marrow with marked vacuolization of erythroid and myeloid precursors. The bone marrow cell differentiation and percentage of different developmental stages were as follows: myeloid/erythroid ratio of 3/1, myeloblasts at 2%, promyelocytes at 15%, myelocytes at 20%, metamyelocytes at 15%, bands at 10%, and PMNs at 8%. Iron staining of bone marrow showed markedly ring sideroblasts, with 22% of ring sideroblasts. The patient received a 100 cc packed cell transfusion and Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) at 5 µg/kg/day subcutaneously. On the 15th day after hospitalization, CBC results were as follows: WBC of 4100/µL, PMNs at 22%, lymphocytes at 78%, Hb of 8.2 g/dl, and platelet count of 234000/µL. Blood transfusion was repeated.
test_results: Study on mitochondrial DNA from peripheral blood sample of the patient indicated mtDNA deletion (8.5 kb deletion, 39.5% mtDNA deletion and 60.5% wild type).

case_report: A 7-month-old boy, the first child of a healthy nonconsanguineous couple, was born after an uneventful pregnancy via spontaneous vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 3450 g (Median- + 1SD). He presented with bilateral cataracts from birth and underwent surgery at 3 months of age, but his visual acuity remained poor. At 7 months, he was unable to roll over, crawl, or sit without support. Upon admission for proteinuria, physical examination revealed a weight of 11 kg (+ 2SD- + 3SD), height of 76 cm (+ 2SD- + 3SD), sparse hair, chubby cheeks, bilateral nystagmus, visual impairment, hypotonia, and absence of deep tendon reflexes. Laboratory findings showed hypercalciuria, mild proteinuria, β2-microglobulinuria, metabolic acidosis, elevated lactate dehydrogenase, and hypovitaminosis D. The estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) using the Schwartz formula was 137 mL/min/1.73 m2. Ultrasound examination indicated normal size and shape of the kidneys (left kidney: 6.5 × 2.5 cm, right kidney: 6.0 × 2.5 cm). MRI of the brain revealed severe ventriculomegaly, white matter shrinkage, leukoaraiosis, cerebellar hypoplasia, and a large cistern magna cyst. Electroencephalography results were normal. Psychomotor development evaluation could not be completed due to poor vision. Histological examination of a renal biopsy sample showed mild mesangial proliferation, mild focal mononuclear cell infiltration, and interstitial focal fibrosis, with no tubular lesions such as atrophy, necrosis, dilatation, or protein casts detected.
test_results: Whole-exome sequencing, with Sanger sequencing validation, indicated a hemizygous c.2257-2A > T DNA variant in OCRL intron 20 (NM_000276.3), a novel splicing variant.

case_report: A 65-year-old female was found to have a mass in the right kidney during a physical examination. Laboratory results showed elevated C-reactive protein at 53.4 mg/L (normal value < 8 mg/L), increased gamma globulin at 22 g/L (normal value 0.4–3.45 g/L), and an accelerated erythrocyte sedimentation rate at 33 mm/hour (normal value 0–20 mm/hour). No other clinical abnormalities were noted.
test_results: Plain CT showed a homogeneous isodensity mass in the upper portion of the right kidney with unclear boundary and the average CT value was approximately 40 HU. Enhanced CT demonstrated mild enhancement in the cortical phase, and the CT values of the 3 phases were about 42 HU, 57 HU and 53 HU, respectively. MRI showed that the mass was slightly low signal on T1 and T2, and the signal was uniform. The diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) showed slightly high signal and the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) value (b = 800) is about 1.0. The mass was slightly enhanced in the arterial phase and increased in the venous phase and delayed phase. The size of the mass was 3.7 cm × 2.9 cm × 2.8 cm. The cell H&E staining sections under the microscope showed that the lesions were backgrounded by a large number of spindle cells, and diffuse infiltration of lymphocytes and plasma cells was scattered throughout the lesion. Immunohistochemical results showed Vimentin, SMA, CD3, CD20, CD21, CD38, CD68, CD138, LCA positive, anaplastic lymphoma kinase1, Desmin negative, Ki67 5%.
diagnosis: Renal Inflammatory Pseudotumor  in the context of Renal IgG4-Related Disease

case_report: A 63-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital after a focal liver mass was incidentally found on ultrasonography. The patient experienced upper abdominal discomfort but had no other symptoms and no significant medical history. Physical examination revealed no abnormalities, including no splenomegaly or superficial lymph node enlargement. Laboratory tests, including blood routine examination, hepatic and renal function tests, alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9), were all within normal limits. Tests for hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) were negative, and no abnormal rheumatic or immunity indices were detected. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed no Helicobacter pylori (HP) infection or tumors. Abdominal ultrasonography identified a hypoechoic liver mass in segment VI (S6). Enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a 1.6- × 1.7-cm solitary mass with T1 hypointensity and T2 hyperintensity. The mass exhibited enhancement in the arterial phase and washout in the portal phase, with low signal intensity in the hepatocyte-specific phase. No extrahepatic masses were detected by MRI. Contrast-enhanced ultrasonography (CEUS) showed mild heterogeneous hyperenhancement of the nodular lesion in the arterial phase, followed by washout in the portal phase. Based on imaging results, the patient agreed to undergo needle biopsy and radiofrequency ablation (RFA).
test_results: Histological analysis revealed diffuse and uniform infiltration of typical centrocyte-like lymphoid cells, and lymphoepithelial lesions could be observed in some bile ducts infiltrated with these small-to medium-sized lymphocytes. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for CD20, B-cell lymphoma-2 (BCL-2), and CD21 (irregular expansion of the follicular dendritic cell (FDC) network). Histological evidence of bile duct injury and ductal proliferation was highlighted by cytokeratin AE1/AE3 immunostaining. Moreover, CD3, CD5, CD10, CD23, CD43, BCL-6, and cyclin D1 activity were negative, and the Ki-67 index was approximately 5%.
diagnosis: primary hepatic extranodal marginal zone B-cell mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue  lymphoma

case_report: A 5-year-old boy from South India, born to parents who are not related by blood, was brought to the emergency room for management of high blood pressure. He had been experiencing continuous urine dribbling for the past three years, occurring throughout the day with a weak urine stream, but without urgency, fever, burning sensation during urination, or reduced urine output. There were no symptoms indicating a hypertensive emergency. His birth and developmental history were normal. He had a history of Grade I rectal prolapse, which was treated conservatively, and a urinary tract infection treated with antibiotics two years ago. The boy was underweight (12 kg) and short for his age (95 cm), with a body mass index of 13.3. His blood pressure readings were consistently high (160/90 mmHg), above the 95th + 12 centiles for his age and height. He exhibited facial dysmorphism, including a peculiar grimace when attempting to smile, mild conjunctival pallor, and bilateral periorbital edema. The child was developmentally normal for his age with an average IQ. External examination of the spine was normal, and no sensory or motor neurological deficits were observed. His renal function tests were abnormal (urea = 80 mg/dL, serum creatinine = 2 mg/dL) with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 19 mL/minute/m2.
