Arterial blood gas analysis showed metabolic acidosis (pH = 7.26, HCO3− = 15.5 mmol/L, pCO2 = 33 mmHg). An abdominal ultrasound revealed bilateral hydroureteronephrosis and a thickened bladder wall. The patient was found to have Stage IV chronic kidney disease secondary to obstructive uropathy, with associated short stature, metabolic acidosis, and normocytic normochromic anemia. Urine routine and culture tests ruled out urinary tract infections.
test_results: Video urodynamic study showed an initial bladder residual volume of 150 mL, detrusor pressure of 55 cmH2O, and leak patient pressure of 59 cmH2O, suggested detrusor–sphincter dyssynergia. Although the expected bladder capacity is 210 mL, the bladder started leaking at 60 mL. Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) showed bilateral vesicourethral reflux (VUR) with trabeculated bladder with Christmas tree pattern with multiple outpouchings and dilated posterior urethra, suggestive of neurogenic bladder. Cystoscopy ruled out posterior urethral valve. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) spine was normal, ruling out any spinal cord lesions as cause for his neurogenic bladder. Dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) scan showed bilateral renal scarring with diminished functioning of the right kidney (21%) compared with the left kidney (79%).

case_report: A 50-year-old woman (gravida 1, para 1) presented with abdominal distension, anorexia, and exertional dyspnoea. She had been in good health and postmenopausal for 1 year. Physical examination revealed a significantly distended abdomen. Abdominal ultrasound identified a pelvic mass and extensive ascites. She was referred for further evaluation and surgery. Transvaginal ultrasound confirmed marked ascites and a large solid and cystic mass, 8 cm in diameter, in the left ovary. Chest X-ray showed a right-sided pleural effusion without lung metastases. CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed extensive ascites extending under the diaphragm and a heterogeneous mass in the left adnexa. Precontrast scans showed a part of the solid component with higher attenuation and strong enhancement, along with calcifications along the cystic wall. No lymphadenopathy or peritoneal dissemination was observed. Pelvic MRI showed an unremarkable uterus and right adnexa. The left pelvic mass exhibited homogeneous low intensity on T1-weighted MRI and heterogeneous low and high intensities on T2-weighted MRI, indicating cystic and solid lesions. The cystic lesions had varying intensities on T2-weighted MRI and were separated by thickened septa. Solid parts, including the thick septa, were uniformly low intensity on T2-weighted MRI and well enhanced on contrast-enhanced MRI. No fatty components were present. The patient's serum CA 125 level was 1237 U/ml (normal value < 35 U/ml), while serum CEA, CA 19–9, and SCC levels were within normal ranges. Whole-body FDG PET/CT did not show any lesions with strong FDG uptake. Abdominal paracentesis was performed multiple times to alleviate discomfort from the ascites and to examine the ascitic fluid, which revealed benign mesothelial cells without malignant cells. Compared to typical imaging appearances, the solid component of the pelvic mass had a higher attenuation lesion and calcifications on CT, and a relatively smoother margin on MRI. The cystic component exhibited various intensities on T2-weighted images.
test_results: 131I scintigraphy showed strong uptake in the normal thyroid and the pelvic mass.

case_report: A 65-year-old male farmer with a normal birth and developmental history reported experiencing nonprogressive postural and action tremors of the fingers for 30 years. These tremors did not affect his daily activities, and there was no limb or stance ataxia. Over the past 5 years, he began experiencing myoclonic jerks in both his limbs and axial muscles, which were more pronounced in the early morning and absent during sleep. In the last year, these jerks became more frequent, occurring throughout the day and even during sleep. The jerks were sensitive to stimuli such as bright light and loud sounds, with increased intensity upon exposure to sunlight and television light. He also experienced recurrent tonic-clonic seizures, particularly in the early morning upon waking. He was treated with sodium valproate (1 g/day in divided doses), which effectively controlled his seizures. Over the past year, he experienced cognitive decline, including executive dysfunction and recent memory loss. General physical examination was normal, with no organomegaly. Nervous system examination showed a mini-mental state examination (MMSE) score of 10/30, with deficits in registration and recall. Detailed lobar function tests indicated involvement of the frontal and temporal lobes, evidenced by executive dysfunction and memory impairment. Cranial nerve examination and optic fundus were normal. Muscle strength was 4/5 at all joints, and sensory examination was normal. Action and postural tremors were observed in both upper limbs, more distally, without intention tremors. Myoclonus in the upper limbs and axial muscles was triggered by exposure to torch light and loud claps.
test_results: Electroencephalogram (EEG) showed paroxysm of generalized sharp and slow wave complexes. Intermittent photic stimulation (IPS) at frequencies between 10-25 Hz triggered generalized spike and wave complexes. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain was normal.
diagnosis: Autosomal Dominant Cortical Tremor, Myoclonus, and Epilepsy

case_report: The patient is a 16-year-old boy who was referred to the Center for Comprehensive Genetic Services in Tehran, Iran, in 2015. He is the first child of healthy first-cousin Iranian parents. Their second child had congenital microcephaly and hypotonia and passed away at 12 months old. The patient was born at 40 weeks of gestation via normal vaginal delivery following an uneventful pregnancy. His birth occipito-frontal head circumference (OFC) was 30 cm, which was 3 standard deviations below the population average for his age, sex, and ethnicity. Postnatally, he exhibited hypotonia, delayed developmental milestones, seizures, and mental retardation. He also had a history of bilateral cryptorchidism, inguinal hernia, and Hirschsprung disease, all of which were surgically corrected. At 16 years old, his OFC was 52.5 cm, within the normal range. Physical examination revealed gait disturbance, facial dysmorphism, speech defect, excessive drooling, spasticity, and dry eyes. Cytogenetic analysis showed a numerically normal male karyotype. Brain MRI indicated brain atrophy and corpus callosum hypoplasia. Informed consent was obtained from the parents in accordance with the protocol approved by the local institutional Ethics Committee. Blood samples were collected from the patient and his parents in EDTA tubes, and DNA was isolated using the standard salting out method.
test_results: A novel nonsense (stop gain) homozygous mutation was detected in KIAA1279 gene (KIAA1279: NM_015634:exon6:c.C976T:p.Q326X). This variant has not been reported in generalist polymorphism databases (ExaC or exome variant server (EVS)), dbSNP and 1000 genome project. Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion (CADD) tool indicated that this variant would be deleterious with a score of 17.21. Targeted sequencing on the parents showed the expected segregation pattern.

case_report: A 40-year-old Filipino male presented with a three-month history of reduced vision in his right eye. The patient had a known allergic hypersensitivity to fluorescein, with no other significant medical or ocular history. He did not have systemic conditions such as hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or hypercholesterolemia. There was no history of retinal detachment, radiation exposure, intraocular inflammation, tapetoretinal degeneration, or vascular occlusion. His family history was unremarkable, and he was not taking any medications or using illicit drugs. Best-corrected visual acuity was 0.1 in the right eye and 1.0 in the left eye. The patient was orthophoric with normal intraocular pressure in both eyes. Anterior segment examination showed clear corneas, deep anterior chambers, and clear crystalline lenses in both eyes, with no rubeosis iridis. Dilated fundoscopy of the right eye revealed a clear vitreous, temporal retinal telangiectasia, and extensive exudation reaching the macula. The left eye showed normal vasculature with no signs of retinal degeneration or detachment.
test_results: Dilated optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrated intraretinal and subretinal macular fluid with a central retinal thickness of 716 µm.

case_report: A 47-year-old female from Jiangxi Province exhibited an unsteady gait and slurred speech for the past 3 years. She occasionally experienced choking while drinking water. Her condition progressively worsened, and a year ago, cervical MRI at a local hospital showed cervical disc herniation. She underwent micro-invasive cervical vertebral surgery without improvement. Her symptoms were continuous, with no episodic occurrences. She did not report memory loss or psychiatric symptoms such as anxiety, depression, hallucinations, or delusions. There was no history of frequent diarrhea, drug or food allergies, or alcohol use. She denied exposure to toxic agents and had not been on long-term medication. Her family history revealed ataxia in 8 members across 3 generations. Her mother had similar symptoms at age 55, diagnosed as cerebellar atrophy, and passed away at 59. Her younger brother showed ataxia and depression at 35 and died by suicide 4 years later. Affected family members typically died between ages 35 and 59, 4-6 years after symptom onset. Physical examination showed dysarthria, horizontal and vertical nystagmus, wide-based and unsteady gait, and difficulty with finger-to-nose and heel-knee-shin tests. Rapid alternating hand movements were clumsy. Romberg’s sign was abnormal with eyes open and closed. Babinski’s sign was positive bilaterally, with no other pathological reflexes. Muscle tone was mildly decreased, muscle strength was normal, and there was no muscular atrophy. Sensation was intact, and there were no signs of autonomic dysfunction or insight impairment. The Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) was normal for her education level, with normal calculation, language, and execution abilities, and mildly impaired short-term memory. Routine blood tests, including blood cell counts, electrolytes, and routine urine and stool tests, were normal. Blood vitamin levels (A, B1, B2, B6, B9, B12, E) and serum copper concentration were within normal ranges. Thyroid function was normal, tumor markers were negative, and antibodies for common autoimmune diseases were negative. Electroencephalogram (EEG) and cerebrospinal fluid tests were normal. Brain MRI showed cavum vergae and mild diffuse brain atrophy. Cervical spinal cord MRI revealed intervertebral herniation at C5/6 and C6/7, causing mild spinal cord degeneration. The brain MRI findings were limited in contributing to the clinical picture. Cervical intervertebral herniations were noted but did not account for dysarthria and nystagmus. The patient exhibited cerebellar ataxia with a significant family history.
test_results: We identified a heterozygous mutation: prion protein gene (PRNP) Exon2 c.305C>T p.(Pro102Leu).

case_report: A 29-year-old male sought a second opinion at our clinic. His family history was unremarkable, and there was no consanguinity. He was born with severe hypotonia and experienced multiple episodes of apnea and respiratory failure in early childhood, necessitating intensive care. Previous medical records noted ophthalmoparesis and fatigable bilateral ptosis without diplopia. Extensive evaluations were conducted at other medical centers. A muscle biopsy at age 3 showed no significant morphological changes, but an analysis of respiratory chain activity in muscle tissue indicated complex IV deficiency. A second biopsy at age 12 revealed normal histology and respiratory chain activity. During his first visit to our clinic, the patient reported severe muscular fatigue with daily fluctuations and exacerbations due to stress or prolonged physical activity. He did not report muscle pain, myoglobinuria, dysphagia, or other neurological or systemic symptoms. Neurological examination revealed bilateral asymmetrical ptosis with a positive Cogan sign, ophthalmoparesis with restricted vertical movements and adduction bilaterally, and fatigable symmetrical weakness in the cervical and upper limbs (MRC grade 4/5 before and 3/5 after fatigability maneuvers in proximal muscles of the upper limbs). He was unable to jump, run, or rise from the floor or a chair without assistance.
test_results: A neurophysiological study revealed a pathological low-frequency (3 Hz) RNS with a decrement of 17% in the trapezius muscle after spinal accessory nerve stimulation. Additionally, a 13% decremental response was observed in ADM after stimulating the ulnar nerve. A genetic analysis identified two pathogenic variants in the RAPSN gene: a frameshift c.1185del, p.(Thr396ProfsTer12) variant of maternal origin; and a predicted missense c.264C>A, p.(Asn88Lys) variant of paternal lineage.

case_report: A 46-year-old male patient presented with diarrhea for one month and shortness of breath accompanied by fever for one week. The patient had a history of chronic renal failure and underwent a living donor kidney transplant in July 2019, receiving a left kidney from his father. The donor-recipient blood type was A, with a human leukocyte antigen mismatch of 2. Preoperative tests showed a negative penal reactive antibody and a complement-dependent cytotoxicity test of 3%. The donor underwent laparoscopic kidney resection, and the recipient had a conventional kidney transplantation at the right iliac fossa. Rabbit anti-human thymocyte immunoglobulin was administered intra- and post-operatively. The patient was discharged 14 days post-surgery without complications and was maintained on a triple immunosuppressive regimen of tacrolimus, morte-tacrolimus, and glucocorticoids, with tacrolimus trough levels kept between 5 and 10 ng/mL. One month prior to admission, the patient experienced 5-6 watery stools per day without mucus, pus, or blood. Outpatient treatment with anti-diarrhea medication and intestinal flora regulation was ineffective. Adjustments to the immunosuppressive regimen reduced diarrhea frequency to 2-3 times daily. One week before admission, the patient developed shortness of breath and fever with a maximum temperature of 38.5 °C. On admission, the patient had loose stools twice and urinated 1200 mL. He reported a weight loss of approximately 2.5 kg over the past month. The patient denied any recent unclean diet, contact with febrile patients, or history of hypertension, diabetes, coronary heart disease, tuberculosis, hepatitis B, trauma, blood transfusion, allergies, or exposure to infectious or toxic agents. He had no history of smoking or drinking and no significant travel history. Family members were reported to be healthy. Initial examination showed a temperature of 37.8 °C, pulse 106/min, respiration 28/min, blood pressure 123/85 mmHg, and finger pulse oxygen 91%. Physical examination revealed shortness of breath, medium body shape, and general nutrition. Pupils were equal, round, and reactive to light. No jaundice or petechiae were observed. No enlargement of superficial lymph nodes was detected. Breath sounds were coarse with a few wet rales in the middle and lower lungs. Heart rhythm was uniform without murmurs. Abdominal and neurological examinations were unremarkable, and no abnormalities were found in external genitalia or limb joint movements. Laboratory results showed leukocytes at 8.94 × 10^9/L, lymphocytes at 4.3%, absolute lymphocyte count at 0.38 × 10^9/L, neutrophils at 90.5%, absolute neutrophil count at 8.09 × 10^9/L, calcitoninogen at 0.45 μg/L, creatinine at 131.0 μmol/L, blood sodium at 132.1 mmol/L, blood chloride at 79.9 mmol/L, blood glucose at 8.43 mmol/L, albumin at 32.5 g/L, and ultrasensitive C-reactive protein at 24.94 mg/L. Routine stool tests and cultures for Vibrio cholera, Salmonella, and Shigella were negative. Tacrolimus blood concentration was 4.76 ng/mL.
test_results: Chest computed tomography (CT) showed multiple exudates in both lungs.

case_report: An 11-year-old girl with Fitzpatrick skin phototype 3 presented with a lesion on the right sole. The patient reported occasional pain during walking and dancing. There was no relevant family history of skin or nail disorders. The lesion first appeared at age 4 and had gradually increased in size. It was previously treated with cryotherapy as a wart, but there was no improvement. On examination, the lesion exhibited cylindrical-conical keratotic horns. The surrounding skin was smooth, without any swelling or inflammation.
test_results: Dermoscopic analysis revealed a surface made irregular by transverse grooves at the periungual sulcus base.

case_report: A 14-year-old female patient was admitted with symptoms of fever, body ache, and vomiting for 15 days. Upon admission, she was administered ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously every 12 hours, mannitol 50 ml intravenously, dexamethasone 4 mg intravenously every 8 hours, ranitidine 50 mg intravenously every 12 hours, ondansetron 8 mg intravenously every 8 hours, normal saline 500 ml intravenously every 8 hours, and Ringer’s lactate solution 500 ml intravenously every 8 hours. Routine investigations included a complete blood count, renal function test, Widal test, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination, sputum examination, urine examination, culture and sensitivity test of blood and urine, stool examination, ultrasonography, HIV testing, and viral marker testing with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Relevant results of these investigations are listed in Table. The patient was prescribed antituberculosis therapy following brain MRI findings. On day 2, the same treatment was continued, and an injection of 200 ml of O positive red cell concentrates was added to address low hemoglobin levels. Based on MRI and CSF reports, a category 2 regimen (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, and streptomycin, as per weight band) was initiated. The patient had a history of antituberculosis therapy started by a private physician, which was discontinued after 3 months due to adverse reactions, including skin lesions on the head and limbs. The same treatment was continued on days 3 and 4. On day 5, the patient reported fever, common cold, muscle weakness, joint pain, convulsions, multiple skin lesions, and multiple oral ulcers. Sodium valproate 200 mg orally every 8 hours was prescribed for the convulsions.
test_results: A positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) profile report was obtained.

case_report: A 41-year-old Caucasian male visited the endocrinology clinic with a prolonged history of weakness, constipation, and low mood. He also reported experiencing pain in the right lower ribs for several months. He denied any history of fractures, tooth loss, cavities, muscle pain, intellectual disability, or vitamin supplementation. His family history included several members with premenopausal osteoporosis, poor response to bisphosphonates, and fractures. One sister had long-term low plasma ALP levels during adulthood, fractures, and poor dental health. Physical examination showed a slight lack of enamel on his teeth. Laboratory tests indicated normal levels of plasma calcium, phosphate, magnesium, thyroid and parathyroid hormones, kidney function, albumin, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D). Historical test results showed decreased ALP levels for at least 2 years, ranging from 18-20 U/L (normal range 45-115 U/L). Bone-specific ALP was 4.8 μg/L (normal range in males 6.5-20.1 μg/L). Vitamin B6 was elevated at 328.7 nmol/L (normal range 20-125 nmol/L). Levels of vitamins A, B1, B2, B3, B5, and B12 were normal. A radiograph of the ribs showed no abnormalities, and a kidney ultrasound revealed normal kidneys.
test_results: This showed that the patient was heterozygous for a pathogenic variant, c.1474del, which is predicted to result in a frameshift and premature protein termination (p.Ala492Profs*29).

case_report: The patient, an 11-year-old female, was seen at the pediatric dental clinic of Prince Sultan Military Medical City in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, for recurrent traumatic injuries to the lower lip and oral cavity. Her medical history includes multiple episodes of unexplained fever since infancy. Clinical findings revealed a lack of pain sensation, absence of sweating, and intellectual disability. She has had recurrent fevers and wounds that progressed to cellulitis, requiring hospitalization. An IQ assessment showed a score of 61, and she attends a special education school.
test_results: A comprehensive genetic work-up at eight months of age revealed a homozygous variant in the NTRK1 gene.
diagnosis: Congenital Insensitivity to Pain with Anhidrosis
Orpha_name: Congenital Insensitivity to Pain with Anhidrosis

case_report: An 8-year-old male child, born to parents who are related by blood, has a history of recurrent focal seizures on the right side that have generalized since early childhood. The child also exhibits delayed developmental milestones and cognitive impairment. He has been hospitalized multiple times for seizure management since infancy. Physical examination revealed a distinctive skin lesion on the forehead that extends vertically into the scalp along the midline. Additionally, the child has right-sided hemiplegia.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed left hemimegalencephaly (HME).

case_report: The patient is a one-month-old girl, the third child of healthy Albanian parents with no history of consanguinity. During pregnancy, the mother experienced oligohydramnios. The baby had a birth weight of 2500g and was born at term but was small for gestational age. Her APGAR score was 8/10. She was discharged on the third day but was readmitted to neonatology at 20 days old due to jaundice, weight loss, feeding difficulties, failure to thrive, and lower limb contractures. At one month old, she was transferred to the gastrohepatology service for cholestasis. At this time, her weight was 2350g. Nasogastric tube feeding was initiated. Initial blood tests indicated cholestasis with direct bilirubin at 5.2 U/L, total bilirubin at 8.9 U/L, ALT at 85 U/L, AST at 66 U/L, and GGT at 30 U/L. Abdominal ultrasound revealed significant ascites. A blood transfusion was performed due to severe anemia. Lower limb contractures were identified as talipes calcaneovalgus in consultation with a neurologist and geneticist. Recent urine analysis showed glucosuria, basic urinary pH, and aminoaciduria. Additionally, hyperchloremia and low bicarbonate levels were noted. Cranial computed tomography was unremarkable. A liver biopsy was not performed due to abnormal prothrombin time.
test_results: Three weeks later we had a response of molecular biology that was sent abroad which confirms VPS33B mutation

case_report: A 27-year-old Han Chinese woman was admitted on July 13, 2017, due to a menstrual disorder persisting for 4 years. She experienced reduced menstrual frequency, with cycles extending up to 4 months and decreased menstrual flow. Concurrently, she developed black, coarse hair on her mandible, medioventral line, and areola, with thicker pubic hair and breast shrinkage. She also reported increased hunger. No hoarse voice or facial acne was noted. Progesterone treatment at a local hospital induced withdrawal bleeding, but symptoms recurred after discontinuation. Her menarche occurred at age 15, with cycles ranging from 28 to 120 days and a duration of 4-5 days. Her last menstruation was on June 1, 2017, following progesterone administration. There was no family history of similar conditions. An outpatient test showed a testosterone level of 4.07 nmol/L (reference range: 0.43–2.06 nmol/L). Gynecological color Doppler ultrasound revealed bilateral ovaries measuring approximately 44 mm × 23 mm on the left and 50 mm × 26 mm on the right, with more than 10 small follicle echoes in both ovaries, indicating multiple cystic changes. Adrenal computed tomography showed enlargement of the medial limb of the left adrenal gland, suggesting proliferation. Physical examination on admission recorded a body temperature of 36.8 °C, pulse of 100 beats/minute, respiration of 20 breaths/minute, and blood pressure of 119/79 mmHg. The patient's BMI was 16.89 kg/m2. She had a normal appearance without facial acne, full moon face, buffalo hump, or acanthosis nigricans. Heart, lung, and abdominal examinations were normal. Black, coarse hair was present on the upper lip, lower jaw, chest, bilateral areolas, and medioventral line of the lower abdomen. The bilateral breasts were symmetrical with slightly invaginated nipples. Pubic hair was thick, and the clitoris was hypertrophied. The Tanner stage was B3P5. Laboratory tests for six gonadal hormones showed: LH 4.96 IU/L (1.8–11.78 IU/L), FSH 2.04 IU/L (3.03–8.08 IU/L), estradiol 129.0 pmol/L (77.1–921.2 pmol/L), progesterone 1.03 nmol/L (< 0.318–0.954 nmol/L), prolactin 494.0 mIU/L (108.8–557.1 mIU/L), and testosterone 3.40 nmol/L. Cortisol levels were normal with a present secretion rhythm, and inhibition was observed with an overnight 1-mg dexamethasone suppression test. The OGTT met the criteria for diabetes, with significantly elevated synchronized insulin levels (0 minutes: 701.70 pmol/L; 120 minutes: > 6945 pmol/L). Dehydroepiandrosterone concentration was 7.44 ng/ml (0.80–10.50 ng/ml), dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate was 27.20 nmol/L (18.00–144.00 nmol/L), 17-OHP was 1.44 ng/ml (0.05–1.02 ng/ml), and human anti-Müllerian hormone was 16.40 ng/ml (2.80–6.30 ng/ml). Karyotype analysis showed 46,XX. Liver and kidney function, blood lipids, and thyroid function were normal. A recheck of gynecological color Doppler ultrasound confirmed a polycystic state of both ovaries and small cysts in the cervix. Urinary system and abdominal color ultrasound showed no abnormalities. The patient was treated with pulsatile gonadotropin-releasing hormone via a pump to restore hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis function and promote menstrual cycle recovery with ovulation, along with metformin to improve insulin sensitivity. After 1 year of monthly follow-ups, testosterone levels remained above normal, fluctuating between 2.37 and 2.63 nmol/L, with no improvement in menstrual disorder, hirsutism, or other symptoms. Reexamination on July 19, 2018, showed testosterone at 2.74 nmol/L and fasting insulin at 464.50 pmol/L. The patient was hospitalized again on July 31, 2018. A supplementary medical history revealed that her parents were not close relatives, her father had type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, and her mother and three brothers had no history of diabetes. OGTT was performed on the patient and her mother, and a steamed bread meal test was conducted on the father. A human insulin receptor (INSR) antibody test showed negative results for serum INSR antibodies.
test_results: The patient and her father had a heterozygous missense mutation, c.3601C>T, p.Arg1201Trp, in the INSR gene (NM_000208). The gene sequence of the mother was normal at the same locus. Two of the patient's three brothers also had the mutation at the same site.

case_report: An 11-month-old Iranian girl from a consanguineous family was evaluated in October 2020. The patient exhibited multiple traumas without any signs of discomfort. She had various lesions and injuries, including those on the oral cavity and tongue. Eye issues such as nystagmus were noted as the initial indication of visual abnormalities. Additionally, the patient had dry skin without sweating and experienced recurrent unexplained fevers. A general examination revealed multiple scars and non-tender ulcers on the limbs and face. Neurologic examination showed a loss of reflexes and a general absence of pain and temperature perception. The parents provided informed consent for the study.
test_results: The variant filtration strategy was initiated by excluding variants with an allelic frequency higher than 0.01 in extensive normal population databases, including gnomAD, ExAC, and an in-house variant frequency dataset derived from an extensive cohort of over 12 000 samples representative of the Iranian population. Subsequently, the integration of homozygous variants based on familial pedigree data further refined the candidate variants. To prioritize variants associated with neuropathy disorders, a meticulously curated gene list was curated by the Genomics England PanelApp (Hereditary neuropathy ID: 85), leading to the identification of a potential causative variant within the PRDM12 gene. Following the stringent guidelines set by the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG), the allelic frequency of the c.826_840dupTGCAACCGCCGCTTC (p.Cys276_Phe280dup) variant in exon 5 of the PRDM12 gene was observed to be notably low in the normal population (PM2). Computational analysis utilizing the PaPI tool predicted a deleterious impact for this variant, assigning it a high score of 0.904 (PP3). Notably, missense and in-frame shift variants within this specific region of PRDM12, known as the zinc finger domain ‘C2H2-type 2,’ have been documented as likely pathogenic and uncertain of significance, respectively, with a conspicuous absence of benign variants. (PM1). Protein coding length changes as a result of in-frame variant in gene PRDM12, and this variant is not located in a repeat region (PM4). Collectively, this variant has been identified as likely pathogenic according to the ACMG guideline. Crucially, the identified in-frame variant does not locate with any repeat regions, enhancing its significance. Finally, the detected mutation was confirmed using Sanger sequencing. Both parents were heterozygote for PRDM12 mutation.
diagnosis: Hereditary Sensory and Autonomic Neuropathy Type VIII
Orpha_name: Hereditary Sensory and Autonomic Neuropathy Type VIII

case_report: The third patient (#3), a 44-year-old man, presented with progressively worsening weakness and atrophies of the upper and lower extremities. At the age of 17 years, he consulted a neurologist due to muscle atrophy of the lower extremities. Since then, he has experienced progressively worsening weakness of the lower extremities, and since the age of 30 years, additional weakness of the upper extremities. His past medical history was unremarkable except for an episode of hematuria of unknown cause in childhood. On physical examination, there were marked atrophy of the calves and feet, and pes cavus bilaterally. On the hands, moderate atrophy of the thenar eminence and of the dorsal interosseous muscles and finger clubbing bilaterally were noted. Muscle strength, graded according to the MRC scale, was 3+/5 centrally in all four extremities, 3+/5 in wrist extensors, 3/5 in the plantar flexors of the foot, and 2/5 in the dorsiflexors of the foot bilaterally. The patient had gait impairment showing steppage type gait and complete inability to walk on his heels. Tendon reflexes were absent in all four extremities and plantar responses were flexor bilaterally. Abdominal reflexes were abolished. Romberg sign was positive, with a tendency for the patient to fall to the left; this could not be accounted for by the absence of significant sensory disturbances but could be attributed to subclinical involvement of the sensory tracts. Also, there was no dysmetria when performing the finger–nose and heel–shin tests. Higher cognitive function and cranial nerve testing showed no significant abnormalities. Electrophysiological testing many years earlier, at the age of 18 years, showed moderately decreased median and ulnar nerve motor conduction velocities (in the range of 33–38 m/s), with increased sensory and motor latencies in both nerves. In the lower extremities, it was not possible to elicit CMAPs of the peroneal nerves, whereas there was mild reduction in the motor conduction velocity of both tibial nerves (in the range of 33–36 m/s). EMG testing showed evidence of acute denervation (positive sharp waves and fibrillation potentials). There was also a distinct pattern of chronic reinnervation with decreased recruitment of large motor units with increased duration along with polyphasia in most of the tested muscles. Laboratory testing, including CBC, serum biochemistry, thyroid function testing, virology screening, and screening for autoimmune disorders, failed to reveal abnormal findings. Brain MRI scan showed a few small foci of abnormal (high on T2 sequences) signal intensity of uncertain clinical significance in the subcortical white matter, given that the patient had no signs or symptoms suggestive of CNS involvement. Incidentally, a venous angioma at the lower left basal ganglia was also found. The patient had been tested for PMP22 deletion/duplication about 10 years earlier, and the results were negative.
test_results: WES identified the hemizygous c.491G>A (p.Arg164Gln) pathogenic variant in gap junction protein β-1 gene (GJB1; OMIM 304040).

case_report: A 3-year-old Iranian girl presented with progressive weakness, lassitude, and pallor over the past 6 months. She was born at 38 weeks’ gestation to second-degree consanguineous parents, with a birth weight of 2900 grams (10th-25th percentile) and a head circumference of 35 cm (50th percentile). Chronic anemia was noted at 1 year of age, unresponsive to oral iron and other hematinics. There was no history of bleeding or bone pain. Her intellectual and motor development were normal, and she was fully immunized according to the national vaccination schedule without complications. Physical examination revealed pale skin and mucosa, a weight of 12.5 kg (10th-25th percentile), and a height of 83 cm (<3rd percentile). There was no icterus, lymphadenopathy, or purpuric spots. The spleen was palpable 6-7 cm below the costal margin, but the liver span was normal. No deformities of the radial bones or thumbs were observed. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable. Initial blood work showed a hemoglobin concentration of 5.7 g/dL, hematocrit of 16.5%, platelet count of 48,000/µL, and leukocyte count of 4,900 cells/µL (with a differential of 47% neutrophils, 1% bands, 45% lymphocytes, and 6% monocytes). The reticulocyte count was 2%, and the MCV was 76.8 fl. Liver function tests, uric acid, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and electrolytes were within normal limits. Peripheral blood smear indicated normochromic, normocytic anemia with moderate thrombocytopenia. Iron studies and hemoglobin electrophoresis were normal. Direct Coombs test, G6PD, and osmotic fragility tests showed no abnormalities. Serology tests for CMV, EBV, and leishmaniasis were negative. Bone marrow needle aspiration performed twice revealed normocellularity with normoblastic erythropoiesis and no atypical cells. Bone marrow biopsy showed unremarkable bone trabeculae with severely hypocellular marrow.
test_results: Radiographic examination showed widening of diaphysis with symmetrical endosteal thickening of the long bones of extremities. Erlenmeyer deformity of distal femoral metadiaphysis was seen.

case_report: The patient is a 13-year-old Japanese boy who was born at a normal weight of 2954 g. He presented with ectrodactyly in the right hand and left foot, along with syndactyly in both feet. Surgical correction was performed on the left foot at 1 year of age and on the right foot at 11 years of age, with no complications reported. Post-surgery, he is able to walk comfortably, and no further interventions are planned. Additionally, the patient exhibited dry skin and café au lait spots, as well as dental anomalies characterized by notched and narrower edges of the incisors, resulting in a peg-shaped appearance. There were no observations of cleft lip and palate, mammary gland hypoplasia, lachrymal duct atresia, or ankyloblepharon. The patient also has attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). There is no history of carcinomas in the patient or his parents.
test_results: The results showed no de novo, homozygous, and compound heterozygous mutations. Deleterious mutations (nonsynonymous, frameshift, or splice site mutations) with a frequency <0.5% in the general population of p63 that were transmitted from one of the parents were analyzed, and a maternally transmitted missense mutation (c.956G>A, p.(R319H), ENST00000264731) was found.

case_report: A 32-year-old male presented with a mildly itchy, red rash on the left side of the chest, arm, and forearm, persisting for the past 3–4 months. Physical examination revealed multiple red, slightly scaly patches, round to oval in shape, ranging from 0.5 to 5 cm in size, with a coppery hue. These patches were located on the anterior part of the left chest (not crossing the midline), the flexor aspect of the left upper limb, and the left palm. Other skin and systemic examinations were normal. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits.
test_results: Dermoscopy revealed coppery-red background, linear white and red lines, red globules, red and brown dots, and scaling. On histopathological examination, the epidermis appeared mildly atrophic with loss of dermal papillae and the basal layer showed focal vacuolization. Dermis revealed edema, dense perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, and extravasation of red blood cells (RBC).

case_report: A 9-year-old boy was referred to a neuromuscular clinic from the orthopedic service for evaluation of generalized muscle and joint contractures. His pregnancy, labor, and delivery were uncomplicated. His mother noticed contractures of his limbs starting from the 6th month after birth, which gradually progressed over the years. He exhibited no cognitive impairment, and there was no family history of similar conditions. Previous evaluations ruled out Morquio's syndrome due to the absence of other mucopolysaccharidosis signs such as corneal clouding, glaucoma, and organomegaly, along with normal laboratory tests including a negative urine test for glycosaminoglycans and negative enzyme analysis for sulfatases. Physical examination revealed a short neck, blepharophimosis, a flattened face, hypertrichosis of the eyelids, prominent eyebrows, a high arched palate, low set ears, and micrognathia. He also had short stature for his age and several skeletal deformities, including kyphosis, coxa valga, and significant limitations in the range of motion of his joints, including fixed contractures of the hips, knees, and elbows. Neurological examination showed proximal muscle hypertrophy, distal muscle wasting, and generalized hyporeflexia. Bone X-ray revealed a pseudofracture of the humerus.
test_results: Electromyography revealed continuous myotonic discharges at rest with no waxing and waning in all tested muscles of upper and lower limbs.

case_report: A 16-year-old African American female presented with a new-onset petechial rash and palpable purpura. Skin biopsy revealed superficial dermal perivascular lymphocytes, neutrophils, eosinophils, and extravasation of red blood cells. Staining of vessels in the dermal papillary tips was positive for C3 and fibrinogen. Laboratory tests showed a positive ANCA with cytoplasmic staining (c-ANCA), elevated proteinase 3 ANCA (PR3-ANCA), positive rheumatoid factor, and antinuclear antibody (ANA, titer 1:160) with speckled and cytoplasmic patterns. Tests for anti-double stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) and extractable nuclear antigen antibodies were negative. C3 and C4 complement levels were near the lower limit of normal. Coagulation studies did not indicate a thrombotic disorder. High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest showed central predominant bronchiectasis and scattered ground glass opacities. The patient had no other systemic vasculitis manifestations, and the skin condition resolved without intervention after 6 months despite persistently elevated PR3-ANCA. Her medical history included developmental delay, seizures, recurrent infections, and lymphadenopathy. Between ages 2–10, she had recurrent sinusitis and otitis media, necessitating tonsillectomy, adenoidectomy with two revisions, and tympanostomy tube placement with yearly revisions between ages 7–10. Otitis media episodes persisted despite these surgeries. She was hospitalized at age 2 for cervical lymphadenitis due to Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and at age 3 for a vesicular rash from varicella zoster virus (VZV). Chronic lymphadenopathy began at age 4, leading to an excisional biopsy of a deep right cervical lymph node, which showed follicular hyperplasia with poorly formed germinal centers, mantle zone attenuation, and an irregularly expanded marginal zone. Flow cytometric analysis did not reveal aberrant B-cell or T-cell populations; the CD4:CD8 ratio was 1.8:1. At age 14, she developed recurrent axillary lymphadenopathy and/or infectious adenitis responsive to antimicrobials. Immune evaluation showed elevated IgM and IgG levels, normal IgA levels, and low CD3+ T-cells, CD4+ T-cells, and CD4 + CD45RA+ and CD8 + CD45RA+ naïve T-cells. Absolute values of CD8+ T-cells, CD19+ B-cells, and CD16/56+ NK-cells were normal. B-cell phenotyping indicated an increased percentage of transitional B-cells (CD19 + CD38 + IgM+) and a decreased percentage of CD21+ mature B-cells, with normal percentages of class-switched memory B-cells (CD19 + CD27 + IgD−IgM−). Antibody titers to T-dependent (tetanus and diphtheria) and T-independent antigens (pneumococcus) were appropriate. Lymphocyte proliferative responses to phytohemagglutinin and pokeweed mitogens were normal.
test_results: Genetic sequencing revealed a heterozygous mutation in the PIK3CD gene at c.3061G > A encoding the known pathogenic E1021K variant.

case_report: A two-year-old boy presented to the pedodontics and preventive dentistry unit with a primary concern of missing teeth. The child, of Indian origin, was born prematurely via cesarean delivery in the seventh month and is the only child of his parents. Both parents, a businessman and a homemaker, are non-smokers and non-alcoholics with no significant medical history. Family history was non-contributory. During the initial visit, an intraoral examination showed the absence of 17 primary teeth. In the maxillary arch, all primary teeth were missing, while in the mandibular arch, only teeth 83, 84, and 73 were present. The child's pre-cooperative behavior made imaging challenging. Developmental milestones were on track. The child was breastfed for one year and had never been bottle-fed. His height was 30 inches (76 cm) and weight was 10.7 kg, consistent with normal growth parameters. The child exhibited mouth breathing. Extraoral examination revealed a depressed nasal bridge, straight profile, and brachycephalic head. Ectodermal features such as skin, hair, and nails appeared normal.
test_results: The OPG revealed the presence of tooth buds 83, 84, 85, 46, 73, 75, 36, 16, 53, 55, 63, 65, and 26 and the absence of other tooth buds. The complete blood count was within the normal limits, except the serum alkaline phosphatase level, which was high. The chromosomal karyotyping examination was normal for a male (46XY).

case_report: A 4-year-old boy, firstborn to third-degree consanguineous parents of north Indian origin, exhibited progressive spasticity in the lower limbs and regression of motor milestones starting at 1 year of age. The antenatal and perinatal periods were uncomplicated, and there were no affected family members. He achieved motor, adaptive, social, and language milestones appropriately until 1 year of age. Prior to the onset of symptoms, he could walk with one handheld, had a mature pincer grasp, waved bye-bye, and spoke two meaningful words. Initially, he experienced gait instability, toe walking, and frequent falls without diurnal fluctuation. By 2 years of age, he ceased walking and had significant difficulty standing independently, with a crouch at the knee. He also developed tightness in the bilateral lower limbs at the knee and ankle. Despite slower progress compared to peers, he continued to gain social and language milestones. At 4 years old, he had a vocabulary of 10–20 words and could indicate bowel and bladder needs but required assistance. He had difficulty with fine motor tasks in the upper limbs and slurred speech. Examination revealed Ashworth grade III spasticity, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign, and dynamic flexion contractures at the ankles in the lower limbs. In the upper limbs, there was grade I spasticity, exaggerated deep tendon reflexes, and spastic dysarthria. Anthropometry and physical examination were otherwise normal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and spine showed no abnormalities. A clinical trial of levodopa/carbidopa combination over 4 weeks, with doses ranging from 1–5 mg/kg/day, showed no favorable clinical response. Nerve conduction studies were normal.
test_results: Next-generation sequencing detected a novel homozygous two base pair deletion in exon 2 of the CYP2U1 gene (c.1080_8081delTT [p.Leu361AlafsTer19]) that results in a frameshift and premature truncation of the protein 19 amino-acid downstream to codon 361.

case_report: Case 1, male, 6 years old, onset age of 2 years and 9 months with episodes of sudden weakness in the left leg while walking or standing, leading to falls. The patient could quickly stand up again after falling. These episodes occurred approximately 7 to 8 times a day, sometimes up to 20 times a day, and walking was unsteady. Two months after onset, episodes characterized by nodding and tilting of the body, sometimes accompanied by decreased consciousness, were observed. Five months after onset, episodes involving flexion and shaking of one limb, with partial consciousness and inability to speak, lasting about 1–2 minutes, occurred approximately half an hour after falling asleep, three times in one week.
test_results: These seizures were found as continuous ENM in V-EEG, the left lower extremity flexion corresponds to the high amplitude spike slow wave in the right rolandic area of EEG, especially in Pz, and with the short rest of EMG in the left lower extremity. Interictal EEG: electrical status epilepticus in sleep (ESES), spike-slow-wave index (SWI) in non-rapid eye movement sleep was 65% to 85%. During the same period, EEG showed high-amplitude spike slow waves in the bilateral rolandic area, which could spread widely. At the same time, EMG of the upper extremity showed intermittent rest.
diagnosis: atypical benign epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes

case_report: A 30-year-old female patient presented with a history of a growth in the upper right molar region for the past 2 months. The mass gradually increased in size and was occasionally associated with pain and bleeding. No swelling or trismus was observed externally. On clinical examination, a 5 cm × 5 cm × 3 cm well-circumscribed, nodular, non-tender, non-fluctuant mass was noted in the distal aspect of the upper right third molar region, extending backward to the pharynx. The right submaxillary lymph nodes were palpable and tender. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 3.7 cm × 1.4 cm × 2.2 cm well-defined dumbbell-shaped lesion in the area posterior to the right upper third molar tooth. The lesion appeared hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with widening of the pterygomaxillary fissure and lateral extension. During surgery, the lesion exhibited a tendency to bleed. Macroscopic examination showed a firmly circumscribed mass with a gray-white cut section.
test_results: Histopathology showed tumor cells arranged around dilated vascular spaces in a storiform pattern. Alternating zones of hypercellular and hypocellular area were also seen. Individual tumor cells were round to ovoid and spindle shaped with a moderate amount of eosinophilic cytoplasm and elongated vesicular nucleus with bland chromatin. Immunohistochemical studies were done and tumor was diffusely positive for CD34 and was negative for CD99, Bcl-2, vimentin, desmin, S-100 and CD68.

case_report: An 18-year-old male, working as a farmer, visited the out-patient department (OPD) with complaints of intermittent generalized maculopapular pruritic rash and vague pain in the left iliac fossa for the past 4-6 months. During this period, he had been seen by multiple physicians and dermatologists and received treatments including albendazole, ivermectin, cetirizine, and a short course of oral corticosteroid (prednisolone 1 mg/kg for 10 days). Upon admission, his temperature was 98°F, pulse rate was 90/min, blood pressure was 130/90 mm Hg, and respiratory rate was 18/min. Examination of the chest and heart showed no specific abnormalities. Abdominal examination did not reveal any significant findings. The patient was conscious and had no focal neurological deficits. Initial laboratory investigations showed hemoglobin at 10.6 g/dl, total leukocyte count at 8.8 × 10^3/cmm, differential count with P68%, L26%, E4%, and absolute eosinophil count at 380/cmm. Total platelet count was 220 × 10^3/cmm, erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 46 mm in the first hour. Random plasma glucose was 118 mg/dl, blood urea nitrogen was 18 mg/dl, serum creatinine was 0.8 mg/dl, serum sodium was 146 mmol/l, and serum potassium was 4.6 mmol/l. Urine examinations did not reveal any abnormalities.
test_results: Stool examination revealed numerous bile stained spherical eggs, 70-80 μm in diameter, which lacked polar filaments and presented a thick shelled outer membrane and a thin inner membrane containing six hooklets.

case_report: A 3-year-old boy was brought in for clinical evaluation. His growth is below the third percentile. The facial skeleton is small, with deep-sunken eyes, wide-set eyes, an increased philtrum length, a small nose and nostrils, and a small mouth that is difficult to open. The lips are positioned as if whistling. He has a highly arched palate, a small tongue, and a skin dimple on the chin shaped like an inverted V. There is a significant orofacial malformation that requires specialized orthodontic care. The limbs are thin with poor musculature and limited mobility, particularly in the shoulder joint and forearm rotation. The fingers are flexed, mainly at the metacarpophalangeal joints, with ulnar deviation. Examination of the foot showed severe forefoot adduction, lateral subluxation at the talonavicular joint, and heel valgus. The deformity is very rigid. Vision, hearing, and neurological examinations were normal, but language skills are limited, and there are issues with social behavior. The child has normal genitalia. Other tests, including an abdominal ultrasound, karyotyping, and metabolic tests for calcium, phosphorus, and vitamin D metabolism, were normal. Family history includes healthy first-degree cousins and a mother with a history of multiple spontaneous abortions of unknown cause.
test_results: Radiographic findings, lateral skull radiograph showed significant hyperostosis of the skull base associated with total sclerosis of the lambdoid sutures and partial sclerosis of the coronal sutures respectively. The anteroposterior length of both base and cranium are relatively shorter than that of the facial height. Lateral view showed an increased talocalcaneal angle indicative of valgus of the hindfoot. Coronal reformatted CT scan showed a line drawn to the head of the talus and through the body of the talus, makes a Z shape.

case_report: A 10-month-old girl was brought to the endocrine unit due to significant and rapid weight gain. She was delivered at full term via normal vaginal delivery, weighing 3.0 kg at birth. She is the second child of healthy parents who are not obese, with third-degree consanguinity. There was no history of gestational diabetes, hypertension, hypothyroidism, or excessive maternal weight gain during pregnancy. Increased appetite was observed at around two months of age, with feeding demands every half to one hour. Her weight increased to 9.5 kg at four months and 15 kg at six months. There were no reports of lethargy, dry skin, constipation, excessive hair growth, seizures, or visual or sleep disturbances. A paternal uncle and a male cousin had a history of early onset obesity. Physical examination showed generalized body fat distribution, a rounded face, and deep skinfolds, with acanthosis nigricans in the axillae and neck folds. Vital signs were normal. Her weight was 19 kg, length 71.0 cm, and body mass index 37.7 kg/m2. Anthropometric measurements were calculated using WHO Anthroplus software. Ophthalmological evaluation was normal. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed normal routine hematological and biochemical parameters, except for elevated serum liver aminotransferases. Abdominal ultrasound revealed normal kidney morphology, a liver span of 12 cm, and signs of hepatic steatosis. Brain MRI, including detailed imaging of the pituitary and hypothalamus, showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Sequencing identified a homozygous missense mutation in exon 3 of the LEP gene (chr7:127894610;c.298G>A) resulting in the amino acid substitution of asparagine for aspartic acid at codon 100 (p.Asp100Asn). Validation of the identified mutation was done by Sanger sequencing to exclude false positivity. The Asp100Asn variant lies in the functional domain of the leptin protein and has not been reported in the 1000 Genomes database. It has a minor allele frequency of 0.0008% in the Exome Aggregation Consortium (ExAC) database. The reference codon is conserved across species. Sequencing also revealed a homozygous missense variation in exon 11 of Bardet-Biedl syndrome-1 (BBS1) gene (chr11:66291279; G>A; Depth 168x) resulting in amino acid substitution of isoleucine for valine at codon 346 (p.Val346Ile). This variant has a minor allele frequency of 0.16% and 0.1% in the 1000 Genomes and ExAC databases respectively. The reference codon is conserved across mammals. Sanger sequencing of exon 3 of the LEP gene and exon 11 of BBS1 gene of the unaffected parents identified the same variations as in the index patient but with heterozygous inheritance.
diagnosis: Severe Early Onset Obesity due to a Novel Missense Mutation in the LEP Gene
Orpha_name: Obesity due to congenital leptin deficiency

case_report: A 48-year-old Thai woman with congenital mutism presented with a 3-month history of intermittent swelling of both lower limbs. She was otherwise well and did not report joint pain, headache, photophobia, rash, dyspnea, orthopnea, palpitations, hair loss, or bowel symptoms. Her appetite was normal. She had no history of clinically significant underlying diseases; she was not receiving any drug treatments; and she did not drink alcohol or smoke. Her physical examination revealed that she was well; her weight was 41 kg, and her body temperature was 37.2 °C, pulse rate was 103 beats/minute, blood pressure was 116/70 mmHg, and respiratory rate was 20 breaths/minute. She had no abnormal findings of her head, ears, eyes, nose, throat, heart, lungs, and abdomen. The only abnormal sign was bilateral pitting edema 3+ below the knee without erythema and increased warmth. Routine laboratory tests showed that she had a mild microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 9.4 mg/dl, mean corpuscular volume 73 fl). Her serum total protein and albumin concentrations were low, but she had hyperglobulinemia and raised liver enzymes (aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, and alkaline phosphatase). Her serum creatinine was 0.82 mg/dl, for an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 85.49 ml/min/1.73 m2, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) 21.20 mg/dl, sodium 137 mEq/L, potassium 4.0 mEq/L, and chloride 103 mEq/L. Her hepatitis (anti-hepatitis C virus antibodies, hepatitis B surface antigen) and human immunodeficiency virus serology results were negative. Her urine was yellow and turbid, and dipstick urinalysis demonstrated a specific gravity of 1.021, pH 6.0, protein 3+, blood 3+, red blood cells 20–30 cells/high-power field (HPF), white blood cells 5–10 cells/HPF. Microscopy of the urine sediment showed few fine granular casts 0–1/low-power field (LPF) and coarse granular casts 5–10/LPF. By spot urine, her total protein and creatinine were 1.339.4 mg/dl and 143.79 mg/dl, respectively. Additional investigations revealed a positive antinuclear antibody with a titer of 1280, showing homogeneous and fine speckled patterns, while nucleolar, peripheral, and cytoplasm patterns were observed in a titer of less than 80. The patient’s C3 complement concentration was 50.0 mg/dl (normal 81–157 mg/dl), and her C4 complement concentration was < 8.0 mg/dl (normal 13–39 mg/dl). Her urinary protein excretion over 24 hours was 9.3 g. The result of a second urine analysis was similar to that of the first analysis. The patient was prescribed prednisolone 1 mg/kg.
test_results: Several rapidly moving, large, ovoid-shaped ciliated parasites were seen by light microscopy; these findings were confirmed by two additional microscopic analyses of her urine sediment.

case_report: A nine-month-old male, born via cesarean section due to macrosomia with a head circumference at the 50th percentile, and with normal motor development, was brought to the emergency room after experiencing three days of fever at 38 °C and irritability. On the third day, he had a left clonic focal seizure lasting 30 seconds with a rectal temperature of 38.5 °C. Seven hours later, he experienced two more left clonic focal seizures, each lasting one minute. Upon admission to the emergency room, his rectal temperature was 39.5 °C, head circumference remained at the 50th percentile, and he exhibited no skin lesions. He showed episodes of irritability and drowsiness, global hypotonia, hyperreflexia, and no meningeal signs. The photomotor reflex was present, and no cranial nerve abnormalities were noted. Laboratory results indicated leukocytosis with neutrophilia and positive qualitative and quantitative IgG for COVID-19. On the fourth day, he presented with stupor, a fever of 40 °C, and a left focal febrile seizure lasting more than five minutes, leading to febrile focal status epilepticus. Management of the epileptic state was initiated and controlled with a midazolam infusion at 7 mcg/kg/minute, intubation, and ventilatory support. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed mild leukocytosis, with normal protein and glucose levels, and a negative PCR panel for 14 pathogens in CSF. By the sixth day, his seizures were controlled, and mechanical ventilation was discontinued. During follow-up, he exhibited signs of autonomic dysfunction and continued to have compromised sensorium, necessitating treatment with immunoglobulins at 4 grams per day for five days. After 72 hours of treatment, a slight improvement in the neurological exam was observed, and the patient became hemodynamically stable. Additional tests showed increased D-dimer and lactic dehydrogenase levels, with normal ferritin and vitamin D levels. Quantitative IgG for COVID-19 showed a cut-off index (COI) of 62.5 using a time-resolved immunofluorometric assay (TR-IFMA). RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 in a nasopharyngeal swab was negative, as was PCR for influenza detection.
test_results: A brain MRI was performed on the 15th day of the disease onset, which showed areas of necrosis at the thalami and at the cortico-subcortical junction in the parietal and occipital lobes with no contrast enhancement. Areas of restricted diffusion were seen on the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the posterior body of the corpus callosum and corona radiata, as well as at the cortico-subcortical junction of occipital lobes. A follow-up brain MRI two weeks later showed loss of parenchyma on previously affected areas as well as a blooming artifact on susceptibility-weighted images, suggestive of hemorrhagic changes.

case_report: A 14-month-old boy was transferred to our hospital on October 27, 2011, due to an enlarged and thickened left ventricle (LV), low neutrophil count, and developmental delay. He was born at full term with a birth weight of 3.2 kg. At 16 days old, he was hospitalized for persistent irritability. A chest X-ray indicated an enlarged heart, and an echocardiogram showed reduced LV contractility with an ejection fraction of 24%. He had been managed for one year before coming to our hospital. The patient also had feeding difficulties and developmental delays from birth. Prior to referral, he had been hospitalized seven times for infections. His medications included furosemide, spironolactone, enalapril, and carvedilol. At 14 months old, his body weight was 6 kg and his height was 71 cm, both below the 3rd percentile. He had delayed motor development and could not sit independently but could say 'mama' and 'papa.' His blood pressure was 94/30 mmHg, and his heart rate was 132 beats per minute. Physical examination revealed no heart murmur, and the liver was not palpable. Persistent neutropenia was noted, with a white blood cell count of 8,800/µL and neutrophil count of 2% (176/µL). The B-natriuretic peptide level was 1,045 pg/mL. A chest X-ray showed mild cardiomegaly with a cardiothoracic ratio of 62.8%, and an electrocardiogram showed low QRS voltage in the limb leads. An echocardiogram revealed a dilated and hypertrophied LV with hypertrophied papillary muscle and hyper-trabeculation. The LV internal diameter at diastole was 37.7 mm (Z = 10.2), ejection fraction was 36.6%, and LV mass index was 75.6 g (Z = 6.3). Thoraco-abdominal CT angiography with contrast dye showed no abnormalities in the kidneys, other organs, or vessels. Following the CT angiography, the patient developed a high-grade fever and secretory diarrhea (800 cc per day) with metabolic acidosis. His white blood cell count dropped to 3,290/µL and neutrophil count to 1% (33/µL). The B-natriuretic peptide level exceeded 4,901 pg/mL. He had no respiratory symptoms, and tests for respiratory and gastrointestinal viruses were negative. Blood and stool cultures were also negative. The C-reactive protein level was 7.08 mg/dL. Despite supportive care, including intravenous fluids and empirical antibiotics, his condition worsened, leading to severe metabolic acidosis and respiratory difficulty, necessitating transfer to the ICU. Just before ICU transfer, his serum pH was 6.881, bicarbonate level was 7.8 mmol/L, and total CO2 was 41.4 mm Hg. Despite intensive ventilator care, multiple inotropic agents, and other supportive measures, the patient succumbed to aggravated metabolic acidosis and acute heart failure seven days after ICU admission.
test_results: The gene sequence analysis revealed that his TAZ gene harbored a novel hemizygous frameshift mutation, c.227delC (p.Pro76LeufsX7).

case_report: A 58-year-old woman presented with persistent symptomatic low magnesium levels that did not improve with oral magnesium supplements. Her medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, class II obesity, hypothyroidism, fibromyalgia, and degenerative disk disease, for which she was taking levothyroxine, dulaglutide, and pioglitazone. Over the past few years, she experienced generalized weakness, malaise, diffuse muscle pain, nausea, chronic fatigue, lack of concentration, intermittent headaches affecting the whole head, and occasional dizziness, significantly limiting her daily activities. She reported no alcohol consumption, smoking, or illicit drug use, and did not experience diarrhea or weight loss. She also denied using over-the-counter medications or proton-pump inhibitors but noted temporary symptom relief with magnesium supplementation. Despite ongoing oral magnesium supplementation and occasional intravenous infusions, her low magnesium levels persisted, although other laboratory results were generally normal. Physical examination revealed symmetrically decreased sensation to fine touch, position sense, and vibration in her lower extremities.
test_results: Laboratory investigations revealed serum magnesium of 1.2 mg/dL (1.6-2.5 mg/dL). The fractional excretion of magnesium was 8.9%. Glycated haemoglobin was 7.9%. Serum calcium, creatinine, potassium, parathyroid hormone, and thyroid-stimulating hormone were in the normal range.
Orpha_name: Autosomal dominant primary hypomagnesemia with hypocalciuria

case_report: A 63-year-old right-handed Chinese male of Han nationality, with a history of well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus for 1 year, hypertension for 15 years, and ascending aorta aneurysm for 6 years, presented with progressive and untreated gait disturbance since his 50s. His regular medication includes metformin, candesartan, aspirin, and atorvastatin. He was admitted to the hospital with an acute neurological episode, complaining of dizziness, vomiting, urinary incontinence, fever, and subsequent consciousness disturbance in the previous 6 hours. He had experienced a similar attack one year ago, lasting for several days before full recovery. Upon admission, he was in a light coma with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 8/15. The physical examination revealed a temperature of 38.5 °C, a pulse of 95 beats/min, a breath rate of 16 times/min, and a blood pressure of 136/81 mmHg. Neurological examination revealed no abnormalities in cranial nerve function except miosis, with bilateral pupil diameter of 1.5 mm. The bilateral knee reflex, Achilles tendon reflex, biceps reflexes, and triceps reflexes were diminished. The bilateral plantar responses were flexor. His limbs showed a flexion response to pinprick stimulation. He had no meningeal irritation signs. Laboratory tests revealed normal random blood glucose (9.8 mmol/L) and normal blood lactate (2.09 mmol/L), excluding possibilities of hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis. Routine blood tests revealed the patient’s leukocyte count was 9.65 × 10^9/L (the normal range is 3.50–9.50 × 10^9/L), and his neutrophil percentage was 82.2% (the normal range is 40.0–75.0%). His C-reactive protein level was 50.2 mg/L (the normal range is 0.0–3.0 mg/L), and he had normal procalcitonin (0.48 ng/mL). Cardiac marker tests revealed a slightly elevated level of seral NT-proBNP (644 pg/mL) but normal high-sensitive cardiac troponin T (0.017 ng/mL). Electrocardiography and blood tests including electrolytes, blood ammonia, hepatorenal function, thyroid hormones, ceruloplasmin, and autoantibodies showed no abnormalities. He had a normal titer of antibodies against viruses such as HIV, herpes simplex virus, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus, as well as Treponema pallidum. Computed tomography (CT) revealed leukoaraiosis in the brain, chronic inflammation in both lungs, aneurysmal dilatation of the ascending aorta, coronary atherosclerosis, and cardiomegaly. Aortic dissection was excluded by computed tomography angiography (CTA). However, lumbar puncture was not conducted because of the unwillingness of the patient’s guardian. On the 3rd day after admission, his consciousness gradually recovered, allowing further examinations. He showed limb ataxia but not tremor. His gait was wide-based and ataxic. Muscle weakness was not observed. Cognitive scales were assessed, with a Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score of 22/30. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed abnormal signals in the white matter region of the brain, especially in the middle cerebellar peduncle (MCP sign) and cerebral deep white matter, in addition to brain atrophy and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) hyperintensities along the corticomedullary junction (subcortical lace sign). T2 and DWI hyperintensities in the midbrain were also noted. Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) demonstrated decreased flow but no intracranial aortic stenosis or occlusion. On the 7th day after admission, he received a bedside video electroencephalogram (EEG) for 15 hours. EEG revealed generalized slow waves, with medium-to-high amplitude (1.7–7.0 Hz, 30–100 µV) and scattered or paroxysmal distribution, in the awakening periods, whereas no epileptic waves were detected. Holter electrocardiography showed no abnormalities. To identify the etiology of this case, a skin biopsy was performed on the right leg. Hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed eosinophilic spherical inclusion bodies in the nuclei of some fibroblasts and adipocytes. Immunofluorescence staining showed these intranuclear inclusions were p62-positive. Observed by electron microscope, intranuclear inclusions were membraneless and composed of disorderly-oriented and electron-dense fibrils. He denied a family history of neurological disease, but his 32-year-old daughter suffers from amenorrhea since her 20s and was diagnosed with premature ovarian failure.
test_results: Genetic tests using repeat-primed PCR and GC-rich PCR revealed an expansion of 111 CGG repeats in FMR1 gene.

case_report: A 41-year-old female with a history of NF1 presented with a 3-year history of recurrent epigastric soreness, heartburn, and diarrhea. Endoscopic examinations repeatedly showed recurrent duodenal ulcers. Symptoms were alleviated with proton-pump inhibitors but returned upon cessation of the medication. The patient had a family history of NF1, with her brother, sister, and second son also exhibiting fully developed features of the condition. She exhibited normal intellectual development without cognitive dysfunction or learning disabilities. Physical examination identified several café-au-lait spots, multiple small nodules on the anterior chest and areolar area, and multiple axillary freckles. A biopsy of a skin nodule confirmed neurofibromas. During admission, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed multiple shallow ulcers in the descending duodenum. Tests for Helicobacter pylori, including the rapid urease test and urea breath test, were negative.
test_results: The serum fasting gastrin level was >1,000 pg/mL and 837 pg/mL in two consecutive measurements. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans showed a 3 × 2-cm, clearly defined, well-enhanced mass adjacent to the duodenal loop in the subhepatic space. No metastatic lesions were observed in the liver or regional lymph nodes.

case_report: Case 2 involves a 38-year-old female of Portuguese descent, born to nonconsanguineous parents. Her developmental milestones were within the normal range, though she exhibited more clumsiness and slower movements compared to peers. She achieved average academic performance and completed a college degree by age 24. Subsequently, she developed paranoid thoughts, such as believing her husband was unfaithful and that colleagues were tampering with her notes and gossiping about her. She was diagnosed with bulimia nervosa and required hospitalization due to severe hypoalbuminemia. At age 27, she experienced psychosis with complex persecutory delusions and visual hallucinations. Treatment with antidepressants and neuroleptics led to significant drowsiness, slowness, and clumsiness, even at low doses. Her psychiatric symptoms fluctuated as medications were adjusted. Eventually, aripiprazole treatment stabilized her condition, but she remained unable to work and continued to exhibit a clumsy gait and fine motor skill difficulties. At age 32, she had an uneventful pregnancy and delivered a healthy baby. At her first evaluation, she was taking aripiprazole 2.5 mg daily. Examination showed facial hypomimia with overactivity of the frontalis muscle. Eye movement assessment revealed upgaze restriction and a tendency to blink and use head thrusts to initiate saccades. She had scanning dysarthria. The palmomental reflex was present on the left side. There was global slowness, mild bradykinesia more pronounced on the left, and a mild irregular postural tremor. Pyramidal signs included hyperreflexia with brisk jaw jerk and deep tendon reflexes, unsustained ankle clonus, and moderate leg spasticity. She exhibited a wide-based spastic gait without arm swing and was unable to perform tandem gait. Neuropsychological assessment indicated multidomain cognitive impairment with significant deficits in attention, moderate deficits in executive function and verbal memory, and mild deficits in visual memory.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed atrophy affecting mainly the cerebellar vermis and hemispheres and to a lesser extent both parietal lobes and the corpus callosum. Mild hyperintensity of the forceps minor of the corpus callosum was present, with a subtle 'ear of the lynx' sign on the left. A DaTscan revealed an asymmetric reduction (worse on left) of dopamine uptake. A next-generation sequencing panel for recessive ataxias in the patient and subsequent testing of the unaffected parents disclosed 2 pathogenic variants in the ATP13A2 gene in compound heterozygosity NM_022089.4:c.[1472_1473del];[c.2567_2568del], giving rise to 2 copies of a truncated protein (NM_022089.4:p.Gln491ArgfsTer29 and NM_022089.4:p.Pro856ArgfsTer26).

case_report: A 27-year-old male, employed as an electrical mechanic with extensive travel history to Germany, China, Russia, and South Korea, initially sought medical attention for worsening back pain. He was admitted to an orthopedic department due to back pain and a developing neurological deficit in the lower extremities. MRI of the spine identified an atypical mass in the left upper lung lobe encasing the Th3-Th4 vertebrae. CT of the thorax revealed a 3.9 cm x 2.9 cm mass in the left upper lung lobe. Histological analysis of a biopsy from the mass showed the presence of histiocytes, lymphocytes, and plasma cells. Following neurosurgical intervention, the neurological deficit improved, and the patient was discharged. The lung mass was surgically removed in a subsequent operation, and histological examination confirmed similar findings. Infectious agents including mycobacteria, legionella, Borrelia burgdorferi, pneumocystis, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), herpes simplex virus, human immunodeficiency virus-1/2, parvovirus, respiratory viruses, cytomegalovirus (CMV), other bacteria, stool pathogens, and urinary histoplasma antigen were excluded. Over the next two years, the patient received intermittent corticosteroid treatment and low-dose radiation therapy to manage local tumor growth. Two-and-a-half years later, the internal fixator was removed without complications. Shortly after, the patient experienced dizziness and mild fever, but the operation wound appeared normal and laboratory tests showed no infection. Symptoms worsened over the next two weeks, leading to hospital admission. CT and MRI ruled out postoperative spondylodiscitis, but CT revealed enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes and hepatomegaly. The patient developed systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) and was transferred to the intensive care unit. Blood cultures, initial bone marrow aspiration, biopsy, and transesophageal echocardiography were negative or normal. Histologic examination of mediastinoscopy and bronchial lavage samples showed no malignant cells, with a normal CD4/CD8 ratio and no granulomas. Both elbows became swollen and hot; a biopsy ruled out fasciitis but showed histiocytic inflammation with CD68-positive foamy histiocytes and no CD1a immunoreactivity. Liver biopsy indicated a mild non-specific inflammatory response with no signs of sarcoidosis. Subclonal tests using semi-nested PCRs on lung biopsy material showed no evidence of malignant B- or T-cell lymphoma. PET CT scan revealed no hypermetabolic regions.
test_results: Histological evaluation of a second bone marrow biopsy showed haemophagocytic histiocytes. Flow cytometric analysis revealed the absence of NKT cells and an increased expression of CD163 on all bone marrow cells. In the peripheral blood, we also found a slight increase of the relative amount of B-lymphocytes as well as an increased expression of CD63 and CD11b on bone marrow cells.

case_report: A 35-year-old male presented with sudden onset of speech difficulties, swallowing issues, and mild weakness in the right limb. Two years prior, the patient experienced speech difficulties and was found to have a pontine infarct at a local hospital. One year ago, the patient presented with speech difficulties and limb weakness. MRI revealed acute infarcts in the bilateral frontal lobes and corona radiata, multiple small cavities in the cerebral hemispheres and brain stem, and white matter changes. The patient had a full-term vaginal birth, normal development, and completed middle school. The patient's maternal grandfather died in his 30s, and his maternal grandmother died of cerebral infarction in her 80s. No cerebrovascular disease history was reported among the patient's mother's five siblings. Mild cognitive impairment was noted, with Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MOCA) and mini-mental state examination (MMSE) scores of 21 and 25, respectively. No significant cerebrovascular risk factors were identified. Laboratory tests showed normal blood lipids, blood glucose, and blood homocysteine levels. Additional tests for thyroid function, rheumatoid factor, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, complement C3 and C4, immunoglobulin, anticardiolipin antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, and antinuclear antibody spectrum revealed no abnormalities. Renal and cardiac ultrasounds were normal. Ophthalmic examination showed normal retinal vasculature. Brain MRI indicated acute cerebral infarcts in the pons and left corona radiata, multiple small cavities in the pons, subcortical white matter, and periventricular white matter, multiple small bleeds in the pons, bilateral thalamus, and basal ganglia, and white matter changes. Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) showed no significant abnormalities in the cerebral arteries.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing was performed using Illumina HiSeq platform and a heterozygous missense mutation in exon 40 of COL4A1 (chr13:110826321, c.3431C>G, p. Thr1144Arg) was found. No mutations were found in ABCC6, APP, COL3A1, COL4A2, COLGALT1, CST3, FOXC1, GLA, HTRA1, NOTCH3 and TREX1. To further confirm the genotype of the patient’s parent, COL4A1 gene was tested using Sanger sequencing. The heterozygous mutation c.3431C>G in the exon 40 of COL4A1 was identified in the patient’s mother.
diagnosis: Pontine Autosomal Dominant Microangiopathy with Leukoencephalopathy
Orpha_name: Pontine Autosomal Dominant Microangiopathy with Leukoencephalopathy

case_report: A 49-year-old Chinese female presented with occasional abdominal distension and acid reflux for 1 month. She reported no weight loss, anemia, fever, or family history of cancer. Her medical history was unremarkable. Ultrasonography (US) and computed tomography (CT) showed an enlarged spleen. A bone marrow biopsy indicated normal granulocyte proportions with no obvious atypical cells. The patient declined a repeated biopsy and was referred to our hospital. Upon admission, physical examination revealed a soft abdomen with a palpable spleen under the left costal arch. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 3 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin level of 125 g/L, and platelet count of 151 × 10^9/L. Liver function and coagulation function were normal. US indicated a spleen thickness of 5.7 cm with a smooth contour and uniform, meticulous echo of the spleen parenchyma. Enhanced CT showed splenomegaly with a maximum diameter of 23 cm and no swollen lymph nodes in the abdomen.
test_results: The spleen is obviously enlarged, and the specimen of the resected spleen was roughly dark reddish.
