Both number and size of the splenic white pulp were increased, and small lymphocytes proliferate in the nodules. The involvement of the splenic hilar lymph nodes was also noted. Immunohistochemistry was positive for Ki67, Bcl-2, CD43, CD79a, and CD20.

case_report: An 87-year-old male presented with an egg-sized mass in the right axillary fossa. Two months later, the patient experienced severe pain and numbness in the upper arm, radiating to the forearm, persisting even at rest. The patient had a history of diabetes and hypertension. Laboratory tests were normal except for an elevated C-reactive protein level (15.8 mg/L). Physical examination showed a clear, hard mass measuring 5 × 4 cm in the right axillary fossa, with poor mobility and no obvious adhesion to the skin. Computed tomography revealed a lesion with rim enhancement, clear borders, and a maximum cross-sectional area of approximately 6.8 × 6.3 cm. The right brachial artery and its small branches were visible at the inner edge of the mass, with local blood vessels appearing thinner. Due to claustrophobia, MRI was not feasible. Conventional ultrasound and CEUS were performed using ultra-high frequency (15 MHz), high-frequency (9 MHz), and low-frequency (4 MHz) linear transducers. CEUS assessed the perfusion pattern of the tumor. Conventional ultrasound showed a heterogeneous mass measuring 123.3 × 66.2 × 50.2 mm adjacent to the humerus, with an irregular shape, clear boundaries, and uneven internal echo, with minimal blood flow signals in and around the tumor. Numerous smaller homogeneous hypoechoic masses with indistinct boundaries were observed near the tumor, involving the brachial artery and axillary artery adventitia, measuring 4 × 3 mm. The axillary artery and the unclear demarcation between the adventitia of the axillary artery and the mass were observed within the deep tumor. The axillary vein showed interruption at the level of the deep tumor, with an unclear boundary and absent blood flow. Additionally, a hypoechoic mass surrounding the median nerve with detectable dotted blood flow and an elliptical hypoechoic mass adjacent to the ulnar nerve (measuring 8.9 × 8.7 × 6.9 mm) were visualized. The tumor severely impeded the radial nerve and medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm, making them unrecognizable by ultrasound. In CEUS, an MI setting of 0.08 was used. A total of 4.8 mL of contrast agent (SonoVue®; Bracco, Dalian, Liaoning, China) was administered intravenously in 2 bolus doses of 2.4 mL, with the second dose given 15 minutes after the first. A saline flush of 5ml followed each dose, and the perfusion of the tumor was recorded in a continuous 3-minute movie loop. The contrast enhancement mode of the tumor showed centripetal high-enhancement, uneven internal enhancement, a visible enhanced bridge, and a non-enhancing central area. The enhancing tumor displayed wash-in after 13 seconds and wash-out after 3 minutes and 26 seconds.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed a tumor composed of spindle cells with localized interstitial myxoid degeneration accompanied by curvilinear small capillaries. Some areas showed a high density of tumor cells with hyperchromatic and irregularly shaped nuclei. Other areas exhibited abundant myxoid matrix with necrotic regions present. The immunohistochemical results demonstrated focal positivity for Desmin, negative staining for NF and S-100, positive staining for SMA and CD56, negative staining for CD34 and MUC4, and a high Ki-67 proliferation index of 50%.

case_report: A 14-year-old female, born after an uneventful pregnancy, presented with a history of a diaphyseal clavicle fracture in early childhood, treated conservatively. At age 10, bilateral hand osteopenia was incidentally found following a low energy injury to the right ring finger. At age 12, a skeletal survey showed osteopenia in the forearm, distal humerus, and worsening osteopenia in the hands. Following a high energy injury, she sustained an uncomplicated wedge fracture of the T12 and L1 vertebrae. The patient reported left hip pain months before the injury, with musculoskeletal assessment revealing painful restriction of hip rotation. No coarsening of facial features, gum hypertrophy, subcutaneous nodules, or skin hyperpigmentation were observed. Intelligence, ophthalmic examination, and cardiac evaluation, including echocardiogram, were normal. Laboratory tests for antinuclear antibody (ANA) and rheumatoid factor (RF) were negative. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), c-reactive protein (CRP), and complete blood count (CBC) were unremarkable. An anterior-posterior radiograph of the pelvis showed joint space narrowing and bone irregularity of the left hip. Bone scintigraphy with (99m)Tc-MDP indicated significantly increased uptake in the left acetabulum, with abnormal uptake also noted in the ipsilateral knee and foot. MRI arthrography of the left hip revealed epiphyseal edema, abnormal signal of the epiphysis, synovial thickening, and an abnormal amount of joint fluid. Whole-body bone densitometry (DEXA) was within the lower normal limits (z-score = -1.4), but the lumbar spine assessment indicated osteopenia (z-score = -2.4), leading to the recommendation of calcium and Vitamin D3 supplements. A 24-hour urine collection showed hypercalciuria.
test_results: Genomic analysis showed compound heterogenicity for MMP2. The patient carries the exon 3 point mutation c.529G>A, causing the amino acid substitution p.(Glu177Lys) and affecting RNA splicing. Another mutation was detected in exon 9 (c.1462_1464del), resulting in the amino acid deletion p.(Phe488del). DNA sequencing confirmed that each parent had one of the pathogenic variants.

case_report: A 3-year-old Palestinian girl presented with persistent chronic diarrhea and low albumin levels since the age of one. She exhibited significant photosensitivity and a severe scaly skin rash affecting her face, neck, and extremities. Additional symptoms included recurring painful oral ulcers and very low energy levels. She was admitted for severe chronic malnutrition. Physical examination revealed abnormally low growth parameters (weight 10 kg and height 83 cm, both two standard deviations below normal), generalized pitting edema, and mild abdominal distension without organomegaly. Initial laboratory evaluations showed anemia (Hgb 10.1 g/dl), coagulation abnormalities (Prothrombin Time 17.4, INR 1.6), alkaline phosphatase 171 U/L, ALT 26 U/L, AST 34 U/L, total protein 6.2 g/dl, and albumin 1.9 g/dl. Rheumatoid factor, anti-nuclear antibody, HIV status, vitamin B12, folate, ferritin level, and urine organic acids were all normal. Celiac screening was abnormal with tissue transglutaminase IgA antibodies >200 U/ml and total IgA 150 mg/dl. Upper endoscopy revealed significant duodenal blunting and scalloping, with biopsies consistent with Marsh scale 3b. The patient was started on nasogastric tube feeding with a high-protein, gluten-free diet, supplemented with Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN), intravenous zinc sulfate, microelements (Pediatrace), and multivitamins (Infuvite Pediatric). Zinc levels returned normal. After two weeks of aggressive treatment, only mild clinical and laboratory improvement was observed. Multiple albumin infusions provided only transient improvements. A short course of parenteral steroids (Methylprednisolone 2 mg/kg for 10 days) did not improve her clinical status. Due to the combination of non-improving clinical course and persistent symptoms, she was started on oral niacin (50 mg three times daily), which led to a dramatic improvement and subsequent complete resolution of her symptoms within four weeks. Dietary history indicated adequate protein intake from fish, meat, and dairy products.
test_results: Her urine aminoacids chromatography showed increased levels of excreted neutral amino acids (glutamine, valine, phenylalanine, leucine, asparagine, citrulline, isoleucine, threonine, alanine, serine, histidine, tyrosine, tryptophan). Her urine excretion of proline, hydroxyproline and arginine was normal.

case_report: A 19-year-old male presented with mild breathlessness on exertion for two months, with no history of fever, hemoptysis, or cough. Vital signs included a pulse of 82 beats per minute, blood pressure of 120/70 mmHg, and a respiratory rate of 16 per minute. The trachea was observed to be shifted to the left side. Chest examination showed a bulge in the right posterior axillary area, resulting in noticeable chest asymmetry. Percussion over the bulged area was hyper-resonant compared to the opposite side. Tactile vocal fremitus and breath sounds were reduced in intensity over the affected area. Cardiac and abdominal examinations were normal, except for the cardiac apex being 2 cm lateral to the midclavicular line.
test_results: X-ray of chest showed tracheal shift to left, hyperlucent right lung, crowded vascular markings toward right paracardiac area, attenuated but maintained vascularity in the hyperlucent lung and notably no pleural demarcation of pneumothorax. CT of chest featured as hyperexpansion of the posterior segment of right upper lobe with attenuated vascular markings and compression of right middle lobe and right lower lobe. The mediastinum was seen shifted toward left side but no air in pleural cavity was noted. The posterior segment of right upper lobe bronchus was seen traversing the hyperlucent lung parenchyma with no pleural demarcation of pneumothorax. No bronchocele or intraluminal foreign body was seen and lung parenchyma was normal. Left lung was free of any abnormality. In addition, no intrinsic or extrinsic mass lesion of the airways was identified. Pulmonary function tests were FEV1-86.66% of predicted, FVC-90.60% of predicted, FEF 25-75 -77.96% of predicted, VC -2.48L, FEV1/VC-88.3% and MVV -73.6L. Bronchoscopic examination revealed no abnormality. Echocardiography was normal.

case_report: A 35-year-old female presented with multiple nodules on her face, which began appearing at the age of 5 and have gradually increased in size and number. Additional nodules appeared on her scalp 5 years ago and have also grown in size. Her family history includes similar lesions in her son, younger and elder sister, father, father's sister, and grandmother. Physical examination revealed multiple, asymptomatic, skin-colored, firm papulonodular lesions ranging from 2 to 8 mm with a smooth surface on the central part of her face. The scalp exhibited pinkish, firm, dome-shaped nodules with a smooth surface, measuring approximately 1 to 3 cm. Systemic examination showed no abnormalities. Routine blood and urine tests were normal.
test_results: Histopathological examination of punch biopsy sample from lesion over face showed basaloid inclusions with multiple immature hair follicles and abundant stroma. The lesions over scalp showed well-circumscribed epithelial neoplasm in mid and deep dermis comprising of basaloid cells arranged in closely crowded reticulated pattern giving a jigsaw puzzle appearance. Within these nodules, several scattered ductal structures lined by eosinophilic cuticle and pink colloidal intracytoplasmic bodies were present.

case_report: A 6-year-old girl was admitted for evaluation due to shortening of the second and third fingers on both hands. Her height and development were consistent with general Korean standards. Her prenatal and birth history were unremarkable, and there was no family history of shortened fingers. Upon examination, the first, second, and third fingers were observed to be short. The fourth finger was the longest and appeared normal. The distal phalanx of the left second finger was deviated towards the ulnar side, while the distal phalanx of the left third finger was deviated towards the radial side. Mild clinodactyly was noted in the fifth finger of both hands. The range of motion in individual joints was normal, and her feet showed no abnormalities. No other skeletal or non-skeletal abnormalities were detected.
test_results: Radiographs showed shortening of the thumb metacarpals and middle phalanges of the second, third, and fifth digits. Sequence analysis of GDF5 revealed a missense mutation at c.1312C>T that resulted in a change in the protein level of p.Arg438Cys.

case_report: A 29-year-old white woman presented with a growth on the right thigh that had been present for two years. Physical examination revealed a firm nodule approximately five centimeters in diameter without any signs of inflammation. Ultrasound imaging showed a heterogeneous mass measuring 5.0 × 6.5 × 4.5 cm with coarse calcifications within the mass. Additionally, hemangiomas were noted in the upper extremities.
test_results: Histopathological analysis of excisional biopsy specimen showed fusiform and vasoformative tissue. Immunohistochemical analysis suggested a well-differentiated myxoid liposarcoma.

case_report: A 3-year-old boy was evaluated for severe bilateral ocular-surface disease, more pronounced in the right eye. His medical history included neonatal cholestatic jaundice, which led to a comprehensive systemic evaluation. At 9 months old, he was noted to have a prominent posterior embryotoxon in both eyes. The patient exhibited distinct facial features such as a prominent forehead, bulbous nose, and pointed chin. During infancy, he experienced failure to thrive, necessitating the insertion of a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube for additional caloric supplementation along with fat-soluble vitamins. He also had significant developmental delays, beginning to walk at 2.5 years old, and severe growth retardation despite full caloric and pancreatic-enzyme supplementation (weighing 7.2 kg at 3.5 years old, below the 3rd percentile). He received chronic daily treatment with ursodeoxycholic acid and fat-soluble vitamins (AquADEKs, 1 ml until 1 year old, then 2 ml; 1 ml contains vitamin A as 87% β-carotene and 13% palmitate, 5,751 IU). Several months before his examination at our clinic, he began experiencing severe bilateral ocular irritation. Due to constant eye-rubbing, he was initially treated with topical antihistamines for presumed vernal keratoconjunctivitis, but showed no improvement and was referred for further evaluation. At the initial assessment, a central corneal ulcer with marked opacity and central thinning was observed in the right eye. The left eye showed mild opacities and diffuse superficial punctate keratitis. The fundus was not visible in the right eye, but the left eye exhibited mild tilting, optic-disc pallor, and a few retinal pigmentary changes. A culture from the corneal ulcer in the right eye tested positive for Staphylococcus mitis. The patient was treated with intensive topical cefamezine, garamycin, and lubrication, resulting in gradual improvement. Three weeks after the initial presentation, the corneal infiltrate resolved, but significant thinning remained. He underwent amniotic membrane transplantation with lower punctual occlusion.
test_results: Liver biopsy revealed paucity of the intrahepatic bile ducts. Cardiac echography revealed a left-to-right shunt through an atrial septal defect and mild stenosis of the pulmonary arteries. Serum analysis of vitamin A measured 2 μg/dl; this is significantly lower than the normal range of 30–120 μg/dl.

case_report: A three and a half month old female child was referred from another hospital where she had been treated. The child had a history of cough, coryza, fever, and respiratory distress starting from the tenth day of life. Initially, she was admitted and treated for pneumonia. A chest X-ray at that time showed collapse consolidation of the apical segment and lower lobe of the right lung. She received intravenous antibiotics and was subsequently discharged. The child required four additional hospital readmissions with similar symptoms. Throughout this period, her blood tests remained within normal limits, and a two-dimensional echocardiogram was also normal. Screening for cystic fibrosis returned normal results. Upon referral to Lok Nayak Hospital, New Delhi, the child was found to be alert and active with stable vital signs. Blood tests were again normal. Venous blood gas analysis showed a pH of 7.2, PCO2 of 54, and a base excess of 5.4. A chest X-ray revealed hyperlucency in the right upper and middle zones with a slight mediastinal shift to the left. Additionally, an inhomogeneous opacity was observed in the right middle zone along with a thin linear opacity in the left hemithorax.
test_results: CT scan showed collapse of apical and posterior segments of the right upper zone along with hyperinflation of the right middle lobe. Consolidation with subsegmental collapse was seen in the apical segment of both lower lungs.

case_report: A 65-year-old male presented with hypertension and low potassium levels. He reported no discomfort in recent months but mentioned experiencing muscle weakness with cramping, increased urination, and nighttime urination. Six months prior, during an annual health check-up, he was found to have hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. On physical examination, his blood pressure was recorded at 148/72 mmHg. There were no signs of purple striae, central obesity, buffalo hump, proximal muscle weakness, or skin hyperpigmentation. His serum potassium level was measured at 2.2 mmol/l.
test_results: Hormonal studies demonstrated excess of serum cortisol with loss of diurnal pattern, elevated urine free cortisol and a non-suppressible dexamethasone test. The aldosterone level and plasma renin activity were in normal limits. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) showed a 7.8 × 4.8 cm heterogenous lobulated enhancing mass lesion at the right adrenal gland with suspicious local invasion to the posterior segment of the liver. Microscopic examination revealed a sheet architectural pattern and focal necrosis. The neoplastic cells had acidophilic cytoplasm with pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, and high nuclear grade. There was sinusoidal and capsular invasion. The immunohistochemical stains revealed that the tumor cells were immunoreactive for melan A and alpha-inhibin diffusely and for calretinin focally.

case_report: A 7-year-old Caucasian girl, born to non-consanguineous parents, was admitted to the Rheumatology Department of 'Bambino Gesú' Children Hospital with a 5-day history of febrile cough and chronic polyarthritis reported to have been present for years. Physical examination revealed reduced left basal breath sounds and disseminated crackles, along with swelling and flexion deformities in both knees and wrists. Laboratory results at admission showed neutrophilic leukocytosis and thrombocytosis (white blood cells 40,000/µL, neutrophils 34,000/µL, lymphocytes 3,720/µL, platelets 700,000/µL, hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL) and elevated C-reactive protein (180 mg/L). Blood chemistry indicated increased levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT 109 U/L) and γ-glutamyl transferase (GGT 203 U/L). Chest X-ray revealed a retrocardiac left basal consolidation with bronchiectasis. A chest CT scan showed significant pulmonary impairment, including left basal lobe consolidation, bilateral bronchiectasis, and interstitial lung disease. The patient was treated with intravenous ceftriaxone, which promptly resolved the respiratory symptoms. Her medical history included at least six episodes of pneumonia since age 4, requiring hospitalization and intravenous antibiotics. At age 3, she developed synovitis in both wrists, ankles, and knees, treated with oral and intraarticular glucocorticoids with partial benefit. She exhibited stunted growth (-3 SD for height and weight) and a wobbly gait, consistent with chronic arthritis and joint deformities. She began walking at 19 months and showed little improvement in her gait, with walking difficulties and occasional falls reported by age 3. Pediatric sarcoidosis was previously considered due to inflammatory granuloma in a liver biopsy, performed because of persistently elevated transaminase levels and mild periportal hyper echogenicity on ultrasound. Sarcoidosis was ruled out after normal angiotensin converting enzyme and chitotriosidase blood levels were detected. Immunological examinations were conducted due to recurrent pneumonia with bronchiectasis, revealing complete IgA and IgE deficiency, undetectable antibody levels in response to Pneumococcal, Tetanus Toxin, and Hemophilus Influenzae B vaccines, low numbers of B cells, CD4+/CD8+ T cell ratio, and recent thymic emigrants (1.4%). Serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) levels were elevated (276 ng/mL, normal value < 7 ng/mL). Neurological examination showed normal cranial nerve function, normal tendon reflexes, and muscle strength, with a subtle telekinetic tremor and mild dysmetria noted.
test_results: Whole Exome Sequencing showed a pathogenic homozygous nonsense variant c.8831_8832del in the ATM gene (p.Leu2945ValfsTer10).

case_report: A 77-year-old woman of West Indian origin experienced malaise during the 2014 epidemic in Jamaica and improved after one week of Paracetamol. Upon returning to the UK, she had occasional headaches, polyarthralgia, and fatigue. In June 2015, she experienced her first episode of generalized tonic–clonic seizures, requiring admission to the Intensive Treatment Unit where Phenytoin was administered to stop the seizures. During her hospital stay, laboratory investigations were unremarkable. She regained consciousness after 5 days and subsequently had multiple seizure episodes with inter-ictal confusion. She was treated with Levetiracetam, which was discontinued after several weeks of being seizure-free.
test_results: In hospital, she had unremarkable lab investigations including lumbar puncture done, N-methyl d-Aspartate receptor (NMDA) and voltage gated potassium channel (VGKC) antibody titres. November 2015, she had another seizure episode and MRI brain at that time was suspicious for a right mesial temporal lobe low-grade glioma. December 2015, she had a normal electroencephalogram (EEG). Subsequent MRI done January and March 2016 showed T2 Weighted Imaging Fluid Attenuated Inversion Recovery (T2WI/FLAIR) changes in the right medial temporal lobe. Right hippocampal signal change was suspicious of low-grade glioma with a differential diagnosis of post viral limbic encephalitis. There was no enhancement with intravenous gadolinium administration and no other suggestion of a focal malignant disease. She remained clinically well and repeat MRI done October 2016 showed areas of signal abnormalities focused around the posterior horns of the lateral ventricles and but no sign of right temporal lobe low-grade glioma or encephalitis. All of these signal changes resolved completely with repeated MRI and she had no further seizures.
diagnosis: Delayed central nervous system manifestation of Chikungunya virus

case_report: A 16-year-old male with a history of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and previous splenectomy presented with a 2-day history of fever and upper respiratory symptoms. He had recently been hospitalized for left basal pneumonia and treated with crystalline penicillin. On physical examination, he exhibited regular clinical status, hypotension, poor perfusion, tachycardia, and signs of moderate dehydration. He was admitted and received fluid management and antibiotic treatment with ceftriaxone.
test_results: Initial laboratory exams showed metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate levels, mild thrombocytopenia (115.000/mm3), and presence of schistocytes on peripheral blood smear. Blood cultures showed a sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae. ADAMTS-13 levels were measured without adjacent deficit (>5%).
diagnosis: Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome  associated with Streptococcus pneumoniae

case_report: A 38-year-old Syrian man presented with multiple nonscarring alopecia on the beard and diffuse brown reticulate hyperpigmentation. He was born to Syrian second-degree relatives with no family history of similar conditions, although a cousin had the same symptoms. The patient exhibited normal physical, social, and mental development with no significant medical, surgical, or drug history. Examination revealed reticulate hyperpigmentation on the neck, trunk, extremities, and more prominently on the axilla and palms, which began at birth and intensified into adulthood, slightly decreasing in intensity at age 30 but remaining present. The oral mucosa was unaffected, with no oral leukoplakia or pallor, and no dental abnormalities were noted. Scalp and body hair were thin since childhood, with no loss of eyebrow, axillary, or pubic hair. Nine months prior, he developed multiple nonscarring alopecia on the beard. The hair pull test was negative, and the hair shaft morphology was normal on clinical and microscopic examination. Onychodystrophy was observed in many fingernails and toenails, starting at age 13, with fingernails improving over the last 10 years while toenail dystrophy worsened. Nail clipping for fungus and fungal culture were negative. The patient had a history of hyperhidrosis and hypoplastic dermatoglyphics on fingers and toes, with no palmoplantar hyperkeratosis or acral dorsal nonscarring blisters. Neurological, cardiovascular, respiratory, auditory, and visual examinations were normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed no abnormalities. Blood chemistry analysis, thyroid function tests, cortisol, total testosterone levels, tumor markers, hematology profile, blood film morphology, urinalysis, and 24-hour porphyrins urine test were all normal. Genetic phenotyping could not be conducted due to unavailability.
test_results: Histopathological examination of skin biopsy revealed unremarkable epidermis. Scattered variable numbers of melanophages in the papillary dermis and pigment incontinence with marked tendency of melanophages to be situated around blood vessels. Melanophages showed both spindle and epithelioid morphology with some particularly; large forms contain prominent coarse melanin granules, adnexal structures were absent.

case_report: A 20-year-old woman presented with scaly skin primarily affecting her face, arms, and hands. A skin punch biopsy showed lamellar ichthyosis. She had elevated aminotransferase levels without symptoms. The patient had scaly and erythematous skin since birth, and her parents noted frequent diaper rash, treated with local ointments. There was no history of feeding difficulties, jaundice, dark urine, or pale stools. She had a unilateral congenital cataract and strabismus, but her vision was normal. Her skin remained diffusely hyperkeratotic and scaly as she grew. Over the past two years, she experienced muscle cramps and pain, which were not addressed. Her skin condition worsened in winter, leading to a dermatology visit where elevated transaminases were first noted. Dermatologic examination showed fine white translucent scaly lesions on the face, abdomen, and arms. Palms, soles, teeth, and nails were normal. There was generalized abdominal distension with firm, non-tender hepatomegaly, and the liver was palpable 1 cm below the costal margin in the midclavicular line. The spleen was not palpable. Growth and development were normal, but her parents reported mild mental retardation, though her IQ was never measured. Neurological examination showed no deficits, with normal muscle tone, power, and deep tendon reflexes. Gait was normal. Ophthalmological examination revealed corticonuclear cataract, strabismus, and mild ectropion. Audiological examination was normal. Other systemic examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed elevated aspartate aminotransferase (AST: 61 U/L), alanine aminotransferase (ALT: 59 U/L), creatinine kinase (CK: 765 U/L), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH: 893 U/L). Complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, fasting blood sugar, renal and thyroid function tests, alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase, bilirubin, albumin, ceruloplasmin levels, and coagulation parameters were normal. Protein electrophoresis, immunoglobulin levels, and blood lipid profile were normal. Viral hepatitis markers were negative. Bile acid levels were not measured. Anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA), antinuclear antibody (ANA), and anti-liver-kidney microsomes (LKM-1) were negative, while anti-smooth muscle antibody (ASMA) was positive at 1/40 dilution. Hematological parameters, including serum iron, total iron-binding capacity, and ferritin, were normal. Due to increased muscle enzyme levels (CK and LDH) and mild muscle pains, electromyography (EMG) was performed and showed normal findings. Abdominal ultrasound revealed mild hepatomegaly with increased echotexture, suggesting grade 2 hepatosteatosis.
test_results: Needle liver biopsy showed degeneration in the liver parenchymal cells with inflammatory infiltrate and moderate macrovesicular steatosis and large lipid vacuoles in the cytoplasms of the hepatocytes. Lipid droplets were seen on Giemsa-stained peripheral blood smear as vacuoles in granulocytes and monocytes. Dermatologic examination revealed fine white translucent scaly skin lesions in face, abdomen, and arms.
Orpha_name: Neutral lipid storage disease with ichthyosis

case_report: A six-year-old male presented with a history of normal birth but exhibited delayed developmental milestones from birth. Over the past three years, there has been cognitive regression, and for the last four years, the patient has experienced epileptic spasms. Physical examination noted microcephaly and facial dysmorphism. Neurological assessment showed bilateral spastic quadriparesis, brisk deep tendon reflexes, extensor plantar responses, and ataxia. Imaging studies included a CT brain scan revealing intraparenchymal calcification, with corresponding gradient MR images showing blooming. MRI brain scans indicated cerebellar atrophy and hyperintense T2 signal changes in the subcortical white matter of the frontal and temporal lobes. An electroencephalogram showed diffuse slowing and multifocal epilepsy. Laboratory tests, including arterial blood gas, serum lactate, serum ammonia, and tandem mass spectrometry, returned normal results.
test_results: Targeted next-generation sequencing revealed homozygous variant (c.493 + 2_493 + 6delTGAGG) in intron 4 of the FOLR1 gene and it is confirmed by multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification.
Orpha_name: Neurodegenerative syndrome due to cerebral folate transport deficiency

case_report: A 75-year-old male presented with multiple neck swellings persisting for 4 years and recent onset of breathing difficulties accompanied by a productive cough with yellowish sputum for 2 weeks. The patient has a history of receiving pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) treatment more than three times. He also mentioned that his brother had similar issues and possibly died from respiratory complications related to numerous neck swellings. On physical examination, the patient was alert and exhibited finger clubbing. Several mobile, firm, unmated lymph nodes were found in the submandibular, cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, and inguinal regions. Additional findings included hepatomegaly, bilateral basal crepitation, a respiratory rate of 24 breaths per minute, and an oxygen saturation of 93% on 4 liters of oxygen. Examination of other systems was essentially unremarkable. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest and abdomen showed bilateral axillary, mediastinal, hilar, and cervical lymphadenopathy, left lower lobe consolidation, right apical and basal consolidation, a moderate pleural effusion on the left, and paraaortic, mesenteric, iliac, and inguinal lymph node enlargement with central calcification. Gene Xpert for TB and HIV testing results were negative, and routine blood parameters were within normal limits.
test_results: Histopathology of excisional biopsy from one of the neck mass revealed mantle zones thickening with lymphocytes arranged in layers giving the appearance of skin onion skin. The cell did not express human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8) immunoreactivity. The concentric rings of follicular cells were positive for CD21 while the germinal centers cells demonstrated CD10 immunopositivity.

case_report: This is a 25-year-old woman, the first child of healthy and unrelated parents. Her younger brother was described as unaffected. She was born at term following an uneventful pregnancy and uncomplicated vaginal delivery. Birth parameters were normal. Psychomotor development and education were within normal limits. She recalled congenital contortionism (i.e., positive five-point questionnaire). At 3 years of age, the mother noted trigger fingers of multiple digits in both hands, which were treated surgically at 16 years of age with complete resolution. She also underwent orthodontic therapy for dental crowding and a high-arched palate. No visual or auditory issues were reported. The patient experienced constipation since infancy. At 14 years of age, she was diagnosed with rectal prolapse. She consistently experienced easy bruising and a tendency to arterial hypotension. More recently, the patient sought rheumatological consultation due to a tendency for soft-tissue injuries and easy fatigability, although she never reported dislocations or fractures.
test_results: At examination, she displayed normal upper limb span/height ratio, bilaterally positive wrist sign, bilaterally negative thumb sign, Beighton score (7/9) with genua recurvata, marked hypermobility of the fingers and toes, flatfeet, brachydactyly (due to shortened metatarsals—brachydactyly type E), of the 2nd and 3rd toes bilaterally, brachydactyly type D of the hands (i.e. shortened and broad distal phalanx of the thumbs), soft, doughy and significantly hyperextensible skin, absence of distrophic scars, palmoplantar hyperlinearity, mild palpebral ptosis and bilateral euryblepharon.

case_report: Patient 5 is a 6-month-old male, the first child of parents who are not related by blood. He was delivered at 32 weeks of gestation via cesarean section due to the mother's comatose state caused by pregnancy-induced hypertension syndrome. His birth weight was 1800 grams. There was a reported history of asphyxia at birth. The patient exhibits developmental delay and increased muscle tone. At 6 months of age, he is unable to sit independently or suck his thumb.
test_results: GC-MS results showed increased pyrimidine and metabolite levels in urine.

case_report: A 63-year-old female presented in October 2011 with weight loss and fever. Laboratory results showed the following hematological parameters: White blood cell count was 5.43×10^9 cells/l, with a differential count of 32.4% neutrophils, 24.4% lymphocytes, 38.5% monocytes, 0.61% eosinophils, and 4.1% basophils. The platelet count was 1.32×10^9 cells/l, and hemoglobin levels were 9.61 g/dl. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels were elevated at 1,121 U/l (normal range: ≤480 U/l). No treatment had been administered prior to these tests.
test_results: Karyotyping was performed prior to chemotherapy and the result was 47,XX,+8,t(3;12)[18]/47,XX,+8[2]. Dual-color-FISH using a CEP probe specific for chromosomes 3 and 12 was mixed with the TEL/AML1 translocation probe. Thus, the following final karyotype was obtained: 47,XX,+8,t(3;12)(q26;p13)[18]/47,XX,+8[2]. The t(3;12) translocation was further studied by RT-PCR and the analysis revealed a typical fusion transcript of 144 bp in length, which confirmed the presence of an ETV6/MDS1/EVI1 fusion transcript. Immunophenotyping analysis of the peripheral blood showed that the abnormal cell population was CD45 (96%), CD33 (78%), CD13 (78%), CD18 (91%) and CD11c (55%), and that CD34 (32%), HLA-DR (58%), CD117 (32%), CD32 (26%), CD16 (54%), CD15 (20%) and CD235a (29%) were expressed heterogeneously.

case_report: The neonatal patient was born at 34 weeks and 4 days via normal spontaneous vaginal delivery to a 19-year-old first-time mother at an outside institution. The pregnancy was uncomplicated, and prenatal labs were normal. There was no known maternal exposure to drugs, alcohol, or other teratogens. Apgar scores were 9 and 10 at one and five minutes, respectively, and the initial birthweight was 3105 grams. On physical examination, the patient exhibited bilateral polydactyly, microphallus, and mild respiratory distress. On the third day of life, the patient experienced bilious emesis. An abdominal X-ray suggested a small bowel obstruction. A follow-up contrast enema showed no visualization of the colon past the hepatic flexure, and an upper gastrointestinal study indicated that contrast did not pass beyond the jejunum. The patient subsequently underwent exploratory laparotomy, rectal and intestinal biopsies, and a diverting jejunostomy with a mucus fistula, without bowel resection. Pathology results indicated long-segment Hirschsprung’s disease. The patient was transferred to our institution for further evaluation and long-term management. Additional testing revealed a karyotype of 46XY, with low levels of growth hormone and testosterone.
test_results: The MRI demonstrated a large non-enhancing prepontine mass measuring 26 x 19 mm causing superior displacement of the optic chiasm and mildly deforming the ventral pons. The signal characteristics of the mass closely followed that of gray matter on T2 and diffusion-weighted images. Single-voxel proton MR spectroscopy (TE=144 msec) was performed which demonstrated no significant discrepancy in spectroscopic characteristics of the mass compared to control-voxel imaging of the adjacent left frontal white matter. Laryngoscopy demonstrated a bifid epiglottis and tracheomalacia.

case_report: A 20-year-old woman presented with persistent ulcerated skin lesions of varying severity for five years, recurrent abdominal pain with episodes of diarrhea, and joint pain in both knees accompanied by swelling and local redness since childhood. She also reported chronic anemia that did not respond to multiple treatments. Physical examination revealed short stature (below the 3rd percentile), skin ulcerations with violaceous edges, interspersed with scar tissue and pustules with friable, bleeding, and granular central areas, along with purulent exudate and blood crusts, affecting both lower eyelids, breast, and legs. Additionally, there was pronounced enlargement of the liver and spleen. Histopathological examination of the skin lesions was nonspecific but showed features compatible with pyoderma gangrenosum. Initial laboratory investigations showed pancytopenia, an inverted albumin/globulin ratio (0.55; normal: 1.9–1.63), elevated C-reactive protein (CRP = 35; normal < 10 mg/L), and hepatosplenomegaly on ultrasonography, which also revealed preserved parenchyma with extramedullary hematopoiesis in the liver biopsy histopathologic analysis. The patient also had portal hypertension with esophageal varices and pronounced osteoporosis, including a pathological T12 vertebra. Serum levels of zinc and calprotectin were measured at 869 μg/L (normal 70–120 μg/L) and 642 μg/L (normal < 1.6 μg/L), respectively. Treatment with Cyclosporin A (3.5 mg/kg/day) and prednisolone (1.5 mg/kg/day) was initiated, resulting in wound healing, weight gain, and partial improvement of anemia. However, the therapeutic response worsened after an attempt to reduce the medication, leading to aggravation of preexisting lesions and the development of an ulcerated lesion at the site of a transcutaneous hepatic biopsy, consistent with pathergy. Immunosuppressive therapy was restored, including biweekly infusions of adalimumab 40 mg, which led to significant but partial improvement in the skin lesions.
test_results: In the genetic assessment of the patient, the c.748G>A variant (Glu250Lys) was found in heterozygosis in the exon 1 of the PSTPIP1 gene. This variant is constituted by a substitution of glutamic acid for lysine at the codon 250 of the translated protein.

case_report: A 20-year-old female patient with a history of epilepsy and mild intellectual disability reported recent blood in her urine and abdominal discomfort persisting for one year. The discomfort started gradually, was localized to the left lumbar region, and was exacerbated by physical activity and decreased fluid intake. Additionally, she observed dark urine two days ago, which was consistent throughout urination. She also experienced intermittent burning during urination and occasional pain in the lower abdominal area.
test_results: Both kidneys were enlarged. There were multiple varying sizes of mixed-density lesions in both kidneys, showing areas of fat attenuation, soft tissue component, and enlarged vessels, the largest one in the left kidney measured approximately 8.3 × 7.6 × 14.3 cm in APxTRxCC dimensions. Additionally, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was performed, revealing subependymal calcification, and cortical tubers.

case_report: A 10-year-old male presented with a four-month history of increasing left-sided nasal blockage and occasional nosebleeds. He experienced a fever five days prior to the visit. The patient had no other medical issues. Coagulation tests were within normal limits. Anterior rhinoscopy showed a delicate, lobulated, red-gray, smooth, and polyp-like mass originating anteroinferiorly to the left inferior turbinate and occupying the vestibule. Posterior rhinoscopy appeared normal.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) scan of the nose and paranasal sinuses demonstrated a soft tissue opacity that filled the vestibule of the left nasal cavity, without any sinus invasion and bony destruction. On postcontrast study, the soft tissue is showing intense enhancement. Histopathological examination of the excised masses (hematoxylin-eosin stain) showed a metaplastic squamous epithelium with the respiratory epithelium remnants on the tumor surface. Under the epithelium, we found many irregular blood vessels ranging from capillaries and sinusoids to large vessels, lined with one layer of flat endothelial cells lying in a fibrous stroma. Several fields of proliferative fibrosis at the sites of repetitive haemorrhages were seen.

case_report: A 62-year-old female experienced increasing difficulty in breathing during physical activity over a period of 6 months. Upon admission, she exhibited a normal body temperature, rapid breathing, a heart rate of 120 beats per minute, blood pressure of 110/60 mm Hg, and elevated mean jugular venous pressure. Auscultation revealed a mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed an echogenic mass measuring 48 mm × 14 mm originating from the left atrial roof and extending into the left atrial cavity. A transesophageal echocardiogram identified a 65 mm × 28 mm large, wide-based, multilobed, irregular-shaped, heterogeneous mass with multiple hypoechoic areas arising from the posterosuperior aspect of the interatrial septum. This mass infiltrated the septum and surrounding myocardium, extending into the left atrial and left ventricular cavities, causing moderate functional mitral stenosis. Further imaging with cardiac magnetic resonance and positron emission tomography (PET) scan was recommended for additional characterization of the mass, but the patient declined and was discharged. Three weeks later, she returned to the emergency department with worsening symptoms and pulmonary edema, and was found to be in atrial fibrillation. After initial medical stabilization, she underwent successful surgical removal of the left atrial mass. The excised mass was firm, cherry red, somewhat elongated, and multilobed.
test_results: Histopathology revealed both hypocellular and hypercellular areas. The hypocellular areas showed myxoid degeneration with thin-walled staghorn blood vessel proliferation, whereas the hypercellular areas revealed sheets of neoplastic cells with moderate nuclear atypia, pleomorphism, and atypical mitosis.

case_report: The patient is a five-year-old Brazilian girl, the second child of non-consanguineous parents. Her perinatal period was normal, but she was delivered at 35 weeks of pregnancy. At birth, she weighed 2.575 kg, measured 45 cm in length, and had an occipital frontal circumference of 34 cm. Her skin was diffusely red and scaly, and she lacked hair, eyelashes, and eyebrows. She was followed by a dermatologist from early life, who prescribed an emollient topical cream. At 2 years old, liver function tests showed mildly elevated aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels, with normal gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT), serum albumin, and bilirubin levels. Massive hepatomegaly was also detected. At 2 years and 5 months, a liver biopsy revealed diffuse micro and macro-vesicular steatosis without fibrosis. At 3 years old, multiple laboratory tests showed mildly elevated AST (85 IU/L) and ALT (77 IU/L), elevated GGT (28 IU/L), normal total bilirubin (0.2 mg/dL) and serum albumin (4.4 g/dL), alkaline phosphatase (AP) activity at 93%, and an international normalized ratio (INR) of 1.03. At 4 years and 3 months, Jordans’ bodies were observed in granulocytes, with normal AST (46 IU/L) and serum albumin (3.8 g/dL), slightly elevated ALT (64 IU/L), increased GGT (35 IU/L), AP activity at 72.5%, and INR at 1.2. Lipid analysis showed normal total cholesterol (112 mg/dL) and triglycerides (73 mg/dL). There was no clinical evidence of myopathy, but a mild elevation of creatine kinase was noted. At 4 years and 9 months, her liver was palpable 10 cm below the right costal margin, and a low-fat diet with medium-chain triglycerides (MCT) was initiated, along with the usual dermatological treatment. At 5 years and 5 months, she weighed 19.1 kg, measured 109.5 cm in length, had diffusely fine skin, and her liver was palpable 7.5 cm below the right costal margin. Since the age of 2 years, she experienced recurrent acute otitis media, and at 4 years old, mild conductive hearing loss was detected by audiometry and impedanciometry.
test_results: ABHD5 gene analysis detected a 3955 bp homozygous novel deletion associated with a 26 bp insertion (NG_007090.3: g.43728907_43732862del3955ins26). The rearrangement affected a region located 3.5 kb upstream of the ATG start codon and also the exon 1. This mutation was submitted to GenBank (accession number KF169942). The large deletion completely removed the first putative promoter region. In the cDNA from patient, no ABHD5 mRNA could be detected. In parents, only a partial decrease of ABHD5 mRNA level was observed in comparison with control cDNA sample.
Orpha_name: Neutral lipid storage disease with ichthyosis

case_report: Case 2 involves a 45-year-old architect with a history of childhood asthma. Throughout most of his adult life, his asthma has been well managed with minimal exacerbations and no hospital admissions. Recently, he has experienced a reduction in exercise tolerance and an increase in cough, producing purulent sputum with occasional thick or solid components. He has had several significant respiratory exacerbations that did not respond well to standard steroid and antibiotic treatments. During one severe episode, he required emergency hospital admission due to respiratory distress, which improved after expectorating very thick sputum. Chest radiographs during these episodes showed variable pulmonary infiltrates. Initial blood tests at a general respiratory clinic revealed marked eosinophilia.
test_results: A CT scan showed significant central bronchiectasis. His total IgE was >2000 IU·mL−1, his Aspergillus IgE was 750 IU·mL−1 and Aspergillus IgG was 45 IU·mL−1.

case_report: A 42-year-old woman was referred to Hokkaido University Hospital, Sapporo, Japan, for evaluation of presyncope and worsening shortness of breath during physical activity (World Health Organization [WHO] functional class III). She had no family history or personal medical history related to pulmonary hypertension. Heart auscultation revealed a continuous murmur at the left third intercostal space and a pronounced pulmonary component of the second heart sound. Extensive blood tests did not show any risk factors for pulmonary hypertension, including autoimmune disorders.
test_results: Right heart catheterization (RHC) exhibited elevated mean PA pressure (mPAP) and pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) values of 45 mmHg and 21.3 Wood units (WU), respectively, and a reduced cardiac index (CI) of 1.36 L/min/m2. Pulmonary arterial wedge pressure (PAWP) was 5 mmHg. Echocardiography revealed right atrial and RV dilatation, severe tricuspid regurgitation, pericardial effusion, and dilatation of the inferior vena cava. The tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE) was decreased to 9.7 mm. Electrocardiography showed right axis deviation and RV hypertrophy. Chest radiography indicated enlargement of the right atrium and ventricle. A ventilation/perfusion scan showed no mismatched perfusion defects.

case_report: A 47-year-old Caucasian man with a long history of a specific chronic intestinal condition presented with painless jaundice, weight loss, and general discomfort, without fever. He had a 33-year history of a penetrating form of this intestinal condition affecting the colon and was on thiopurine monotherapy at the time of presentation. Initial treatment included budesonide and mesalamine, followed by azathioprine (150-200 mg per day) for 14 years. He later received infliximab at ages 33 and 36 for remission induction and maintenance therapy, respectively, but discontinued due to neurologic side effects. His medical history includes right and left hemicolectomy at ages 18 and 30, and a permanent ileostomy at age 41 due to active perianal fistulating disease in the preceding three years. The condition had been in remission for five years before his current presentation. Physical examination showed an enlarged liver and spleen without swollen lymph nodes, confirmed by computed tomography and positron emission tomography. Laboratory tests revealed anemia, low platelet count, and abnormal liver tests. Imaging did not show dilated bile ducts or other obstructive abnormalities. Viral causes of hepatitis, including Epstein-Barr virus, were ruled out by serology.
test_results: Liver biopsy showed sinusoidal and portal infiltration of atypical lymphocytes. Immunophenotyping of both biopsies confirmed a T-cell population with the surface proteins listed in Table B.

case_report: An 11-year-old boy visited the Department of Pediatric Dentistry at Government Dental College and Hospital, Rajiv Gandhi Institute of Medical Sciences, Kadapa, India, due to irregular teeth alignment. The patient exhibited noticeable cranial and facial abnormalities. Examination revealed an enlarged cranial vault with frontal bossing, underdeveloped maxilla, and relatively prominent mandible. Eye-related findings included shallow orbits, wide-set eyes, bilateral protrusion of the eyes, and strabismus. Additional facial characteristics included a short and incompetent upper lip, a depressed nasal bridge, and low-set ears without hearing impairment. His hands and feet appeared normal. According to the parents, these features began developing gradually after birth, and the patient had undergone cranial surgery at 9 months old to address closed skull sutures. Prenatal, delivery, and postnatal histories were unremarkable. There was no family history of similar conditions. He is the first child of healthy parents from a nonconsanguineous marriage. His developmental milestones were normal, and he exhibited normal intelligence with minor speech difficulties. At birth, his father was 36 years old, and his mother was 22 years old. Intraoral examination showed a V-shaped maxillary arch with a high-arched palate and bilateral palatal swellings resembling a pseudocleft, a retruded maxilla with a relatively large mandible. Oral hygiene was poor, with crowded upper and lower teeth, reverse over-jet, posterior crossbite, anterior open bite, tongue tie, and decayed teeth.
test_results: The skull radiographs revealed the ‘scaphocephalic’ skull shape, hypoplastic maxilla and zygoma with shallow orbits. Prominent cranial markings of the inner surface of the cranial vault seen as multiple radiolucencies appearing as depressions resulting in the ‘hammered silver’ (beaten metal/copper beaten) appearance. Three-dimensional computed tomographic (CT) scans of the skull showed fused sagittal and lambdoid sutures and surgically opened coronal sutures, moderate degree of hydrocephalus with diffuse indentation of inner table of skull.

case_report: A 75-year-old African-American female with a medical history of chronic kidney disease, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia was referred for evaluation of chronic microcytic anemia. The patient had been receiving iron supplementation due to concurrent iron deficiency, but her hemoglobin levels did not improve despite prolonged treatment. Physical examination revealed 'half and half' nails. The patient was asymptomatic and had no history of vaso-occlusive crises. Family history was negative for similar conditions in relatives.
test_results: A low Hemoglobin A (18.2 %), a slightly elevated Hemoglobin F (5.9%), and Hemoglobin A2 (5.7%) with a predominant presence of Hemoglobin S (70.2%) was seen. Hemoglobin count of 7.8 g/dl, a mean corpuscular volume (MCV) of 73.5, a reticulocyte count of 2.85%, and hematocrit was 24.9.

case_report: The patient is a 24-month-old Korean girl, born at 40 weeks gestation via vaginal delivery at a regional general hospital. Her birth weight was 2,900 grams. She is the second child in the family, with one female sibling. At the time of her birth, her mother was 29 years old and her father was 31 years old. Clinically, the patient exhibited mild midfacial hypoplasia, hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, strabismus, a beak-shaped nose, and plagio-brachycephaly. Additionally, she had mild neurodevelopmental delay. Her hearing was intact, and there were no extracranial bony abnormalities. The mother's family history included cephalo-facial anomalies. The mother, two of the mother's unmarried sisters, and the maternal grandfather displayed similar physical characteristics, including strabismus and short stature. The severity of brachycephaly varied among these family members.
test_results: Three-dimensional reconstruction computed tomography (3D-CT) and magnetic resonance imaging studies of the cranium revealed bilateral coronal craniosynostosis, palgio-brachycephaly, bilateral lateral ventricle dilatation, proptosis, and a small cerebellum. The Pro250Arg mutation of exon 7 (IgII-IGIII linker domain) in FGFR3 was detected in the patient. The same mutation was found in the patient's mother, two maternal aunts and the maternal grandfather.

case_report: A 33-year-old right-handed female reported experiencing limb clumsiness and an unsteady gait that began gradually at the age of 24. Her parents were non-consanguineous, and there was no family history of similar symptoms or epilepsy. She was on a medication regimen that included escitalopram 10 mg/day, baclofen 20 mg/day, and memantine 10 mg/day. Clinical examination revealed a pancerebellar syndrome. Observations included gaze-evoked nystagmus, hypermetric saccades, scanning speech, dysmetria in all four limbs, a steady postural tremor in the upper limbs bilaterally, kinetic tremor in all four limbs, and ataxia affecting both stance and gait. Tendon reflexes were hyperactive in all four limbs. Hoffman's reflex was negative, and plantar reflexes were flexor. Sensory examination, including pinprick, light touch, two-point discrimination, position sense, and stereognosia, was normal. There was no evidence of myoclonus or dystonia.
test_results: Genetic study showed a homozygous splice site c.1219-1G>T ANO10 mutation (chromosome 3p22). Brain MRI demonstrated a diffuse cerebellar cortical atrophy sparing cerebellar nuclei.

case_report: A 60-year-old monolingual woman, single, an accountant with 11 years of education, visited the cognitive and behavioral neurology outpatient clinic at Universidade de Pernambuco on July 7th, 2015. Eight years prior, she experienced three episodes of syncope over the course of a year, each followed by transient stuttering without further clinical investigation. According to her sister, after one year, the patient began confusing the names of family members of the same sex, had difficulty finding words during conversations, was unable to form sentences, read, write, or manage household finances, and struggled to express her thoughts verbally. Her verbal fluency progressively decreased, and she occasionally stuttered at the beginning of sentences. She had a family history of dementia and Down syndrome. The patient had controlled glaucoma but no language impairment or other clinical illnesses, such as seizures. Neurological examination was normal except for the presence of Myerson’s sign. The Edinburgh handedness inventory confirmed her left-handedness, and both the patient and her sisters reported that she had been strongly left-handed since childhood, with three left-handers in the family history. Upon admission, she demonstrated insight and independence in self-care and housekeeping, with mild impairment (9/30) as confirmed by Pfeffer’s scale, but also showed moderate emotional detachment and apathy. Detailed language examination revealed spontaneous muteness, but she could repeat syllables and speak simple compound words and sentences. Agrammatism was evident in her speech. Despite progressive speech disturbances, her semantic domain was mildly impaired, and comprehension was preserved, though her repetition was limited to isolated words. She was unable to read or write. General neuropsychological evaluation showed deficits in attention, visuospatial and executive functions, visual memory, and praxis. Difficulties in expressing language caused her some distress and hastiness, but no behavioral disturbances were reported. Her cognitive performance included a score of 03/30 on the MMSE in the Pierre Marie subtest. Routine blood tests, including thyroid function testing, vitamin B12, and syphilis screening, showed no abnormalities.
test_results: MRI showed signs of cortico-subcortical involution characterized by enlargement and grooves, Sylvian fissures and basal cistern, beyond what was expected for the age range, with mild to moderate predominance in the frontal and left temporal lobes. There is prominence of the choroidal fissures and temporal horns of the lateral ventricles, including the hippocampus, but due to wasting of the neocortex. Compensatory dilation of the lateral ventricles. Fazekas’s scale = 2. SPECT scan showed moderate to severe hypoperfusion in the left cerebral hemisphere, including the hippocampus.
diagnosis: Crossed non-fluent variant of primary progressive aphasia

case_report: A 5-month-old male infant was admitted to the Pediatrics Department of The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University on March 14, 2022, due to a fever lasting four days, with a peak temperature of 40°C. The infant did not exhibit symptoms of cough, wheezing, breathing difficulties, vomiting, consciousness disorder, or convulsions. He was a first-born, delivered full-term, with a birth weight of 3.25 kg, and had an unremarkable perinatal period. He was fed a combination of breast milk and formula but experienced feeding difficulties. At 4 months, he had unstable head control, and by 5 months, he could roll over. Upon admission, physical examination revealed a temperature of 38.4°C, heart rate of 168 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 40 per minute, blood pressure of 112/69 mmHg, height of 61 cm, weight of 6.4 kg, head circumference of 41 cm, chest circumference of 40.5 cm, and abdominal circumference of 38 cm. The infant showed growth and developmental delays, coarse breathing sounds in both lungs with audible wet rales, fast heart rate, muffled heart sounds, regular rhythm, no audible murmurs at valve auscultation areas, an enlarged liver palpable 5 cm below the right costal margin and 3 cm below the xiphoid process, spleen not palpable, and reduced muscle tone. Laboratory tests showed: pH 7.46, carbon dioxide pressure 39.0 mmHg, oxygen pressure 69.0 mmHg, residual base 3.90 mmol/L, glucose 6.0 mmol/L, white blood cell count 19.15 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 80.0 g/L, platelet count 437 × 10^9/L, neutrophil percentage 45.4%, lymphocyte percentage 47.0%, procalcitonin 0.954 ng/ml, C-reactive protein 111.41 mg/L, interleukin-6 9.56 pg/ml, calcium 2.40 mmol/L, phosphorus 0.89 mmol/L, alanine aminotransferase 189 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 206 U/L, creatine kinase 972 U/L, creatine kinase isoenzyme 52.9 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase 1,317 U/L, hypersensitive troponin T 0.124 ng/ml, N-terminal pro b-type natriuretic peptide 10,066.50 pg/ml, and troponin I 0.131 μg/L. Other lab results were not significantly abnormal. Cardiac echocardiography showed diffuse thickening of the left ventricular wall, with the anterior wall approximately 9.5 mm thick, the interventricular septum around 8 mm, the lateral wall about 9 mm, and the inferoposterior wall approximately 9 mm. The thickened myocardial wall had increased echogenicity and stiffness, with generally reduced movement amplitude. The endocardium of the left ventricle was thickened, up to about 5 mm. The ejection fraction (EF) was 62%, and the shortening fraction of the left ventricular short axis (FS) was 31%. Color Doppler Flow Imaging (CDFI) showed no shunt at the ventricular level. A small left-to-right shunt was observed at the middle of the interatrial septum (foramen ovale), approximately 2 mm wide. A small amount of regurgitation was noted at the mitral valve, and a trace regurgitation signal was seen at the tricuspid valve with a regurgitation speed of 1.8 m/s, estimating pulmonary artery pressure at 18 mmHg (right atrial pressure assumed to be 5 mmHg). Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly and edematous gallbladder walls. Chest CT scan revealed normal translucency in both lungs with disordered patterns, patchy areas of increased density, localized consolidation with visible air bronchograms, normal hilar shadows, and clear airways. The cardiac silhouette was enlarged, with thickening of the left ventricular myocardial wall. The electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia, enlargement of the left atrium and left ventricle, accompanied by ST-T changes. The patient was treated with cefoperazone and acyclovir for infection control, nebulized medication to reduce airway inflammation, and hepatoprotective drugs. Fluid management included low-dose diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide and spironolactone) to improve heart failure and hepatomegaly caused by excessive circulatory load. Propranolol was administered to slow down the heart rate, reduce left ventricular contractility and wall stress, and improve diastolic function. Benazepril was also given to mitigate myocardial remodeling. After one week of regular anti-infection treatment, liver protection, and heart function improvement, the infant's body temperature normalized, and a recheck showed a significant decrease in N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide (1,730.94 pg/ml). CT scans indicated reduced lung inflammation.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed a homozygous mutation c.2662G>T(p.E888) in the GAA gene in the infant. Further testing for GAA enzyme activity in the patient showed reduced activity.
Orpha_name: Glycogen storage disease due to acid maltase deficiency, infantile onset

case_report: A 48-year-old male reported experiencing intermittent diarrhea and vague abdominal pain over the past 2 years. He also noted a persistent issue with significant heartburn and reflux, which had intensified in frequency and severity in the recent months. The patient mentioned a weight loss of about 10 kilograms during this period. Physical examination showed no abnormalities. Colonoscopy, barium enema, and small bowel follow-through tests all returned negative results.
test_results: An upper GI endoscopy demonstrated significant gastritis and multiple duodenal ulcers. His fasting serum gastrin (FSG) level after stopping all anti-secretory medications was moderately elevated at 288 pg/mL (normal < 100 pg/mL) and Chromogranin A level was also elevated at 340 ng/mL (normal < 34 ng/mL). Both enhanced computerized tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans demonstrated a solitary 7.0 × 5.7 cm lesion within the right lobe of the liver. An image-guided core biopsy was consistent with a neuroendocrine tumour. Whole body octreotide scan and SPECT showed a solitary liver mass with no evidence of disease outside the liver.
diagnosis: Primary Hepatic Gastrinoma causing Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome

case_report: A 35-year-old Asian male, born to parents who are not related by blood, reported a gradual decrease in vision in both eyes over the past year. He also mentioned experiencing night blindness for the past three years. His visual acuity was measured at 6/36 in the right eye and 1/60 in the left eye. Examination of the anterior segment revealed no abnormalities. The fundus examination showed degenerative changes with noticeable yellow crystalline deposits at the posterior pole, and the choroidal blood vessels were prominently visible in these regions.
test_results: FFA on Spectralis showed an area of central hypofluorescence with surrounding hyperfluorescence. A peripapillary ring and small central area were seen to be preserved. Ultra-widefield Optos FAF showed central hypoautofluorescence with surrounding mottled autofluorescence indicating retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) involvement in these areas along with peripheral involvement. Topcon FAF also showed few hyper-autofluorescence (AF) areas around the margin. The Optos ultra-widefield green reflectance showed central macular changes with few dispersed hyper-reflective spots, whereas the red reflectance showed prominent choroidal vasculature with no hyper-reflective spots. The deposits were seen more prominently on the RF imaging on Topcon and NIR on Spectralis. The Enhanced depth imaging – OCT showed disorganisation of the RPE, photoreceptors and choriocapillaris at macula with exception of a small central island. Retinal and choroidal thinning was prominent, with intra-retinal hyper-reflective dots corresponding to deposits. Outer retinal tubulation (ORT) suggestive of degenerating RPE cells was also seen in both eyes.

case_report: A 37-year-old Caucasian male presented with a firm, mobile nodule on the left index finger, which had been present for several months. The nodule appeared suddenly and remained unchanged in size. The patient reported no pain, itching, or trauma to the area, and no changes in the lesion. His medical history included one year of joint pain in the right hand and both knees, which he attributed to his work as a factory employee. He also experienced bilateral plantar fasciitis and tendonitis in both wrists, for which he was taking ibuprofen. Additionally, he had a history of eczema managed with topical steroids as needed. Family history was notable for a father with long-standing arthritis. Physical examination revealed a single 0.8 x 0.6 cm indurated, flesh-colored to pink nodule on the dorsal surface of the left hand, just distal to the second metacarpophalangeal joint. The rest of the physical examination and review of systems were unremarkable.
test_results: Histopathologic evaluation of the patient’s cutaneous nodule revealed diffuse dermal fibrosis with prominent fibroblastic proliferation. The spindled fibroblasts demonstrated positive immunoreactivity for CD34, variable reactivity for Factor XIIIa, and Verhoeff-Van Gieson stain revealed the loss of dermal elastin fibrils. Staining for S100 and SOX10 was negative, and colloidal iron staining revealed no evidence of dermal mucin deposition. Serologic testing was negative for antinuclear antibodies and rheumatoid factor.

case_report: A 17-day-old female infant was admitted due to episodes of respiratory distress observed since the second day of life. The infant was born at term via normal delivery to a primigravida mother, with no complications during pregnancy, and cried immediately after birth. The birth weight was 2000 g. No maternal history of exposure to teratogenic drugs or radiation was reported, and no antenatal ultrasonography was performed. Congenital malformations were noted at birth in a rural hospital. The family history did not indicate any congenital anomalies or mental retardation. Upon admission, the infant's weight was 1750 g (small for gestational age), length was 42 cm (<5th percentile), and occipitofrontal circumference (OFC) was 32 cm (<5th percentile). The respiratory rate was 42 breaths per minute with episodes of rapid breathing up to 100 breaths per minute lasting 1-3 minutes, followed by apnea for 12-15 seconds without bradycardia or cyanosis. Physical examination revealed posteriorly rotated low-set ears, a prominent upper forehead, sublingual nodules, bimanual heptadactyly, bilateral hallucal polysyndactyly, an accessory right postaxial toe, coarse crepitations in the right chest, generalized hypotonia, and diminished deep tendon reflexes. Neonatal reflexes were depressed. Other findings were unremarkable, and fundoscopic examination was normal. Routine blood and urine tests, serum CRP, blood sugar, blood urea, SGPT, serum calcium, abdominal ultrasonography, and echocardiography were all normal. Chest radiography showed pneumonitic changes in the right mid- and upper zones. Hand X-rays revealed Y-shaped right third, left fourth, and left fifth metacarpals with bimanual central polydactyly, a right postminimus, and a left postaxial extra digit, along with short middle phalanges of all fingers. Foot X-rays showed duplication of the first metatarsal and hallucal phalanges, an extra epiphysis in the soft-tissue hallux between the normal and accessory bony hallux, and syndactyly of the first three toes bilaterally.
test_results: MRI of brain demonstrated a hypoplastic cerebellar vermis with a molar tooth sign on axial image at the level of the isthmus.

case_report: A 29-year-old male presented with abnormal findings on a urine dipstick test, showing the presence of blood and protein. Additionally, there was a noted increase in serum creatinine levels from 70 to 91 µmol/L. The patient had been on a regimen of 720 mg fumaric acid esters (FAEs) for one year, after experiencing adverse effects from a lower dose, which included exacerbations of psoriasis and liver toxicity from previous methotrexate treatment.
test_results: Elevated urinary RBP of 13 100 µg/L, with a low-normal serum phosphate of 0.89 mmol/L.

case_report: A 72-year-old female was brought by her son with a 2-year history of excessive use of chewable tobacco, consuming around 12–15 packets per day. This behavior was initially unnoticed by the family until it escalated to five to six packets per day, accompanied by repeated demands for money to purchase tobacco. Upon discovering this, the family restricted her access to money. Within a year, she began stealing money and selling small household items, including her grandson's mobile phone, to buy tobacco. When questioned about her actions, she became irritable and abusive, which was uncharacteristic of her usual behavior. Additionally, she started consuming large quantities of sugar, mixing half a glass of sugar in water to drink, and adding sugar to all her food. She also drank around 3–4 liters of milk per day and ate 8–10 raw eggs. The family observed disinhibited behaviors such as changing clothes in inappropriate places and being abusive toward others. Over time, she became forgetful about minor issues, repeatedly asked for food even after meals, and accused family members of taking her belongings, which she had misplaced. Physical examination showed no significant findings, with stable vitals and a normal systemic examination. During the mental status examination, the patient was uncooperative, exhibited disinhibited behavior, occasional irrelevant speech, irritable affect, paranoid delusions, and deficits in immediate and recent memory. Routine blood tests indicated elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone (10.8 mU/l) and triglyceride (250 mg/dl) levels.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of brain showed significant atrophic changes in bilateral frontal and medial basal temporal lobes (right > left side) and perisylvian cortex. Mini Mental Status Examination score was 13 out of 31, which is suggestive of moderate cognitive impairment. Bender Gestalt Test (BGT) revealed difficulties in visual–motor integration, in discriminating visual stimuli, and in shifting attention from the original design to what is being drawn, features suggestive of significant visuoconstructive deficits. The test also showed memory disturbances and difficulties in concentration and comprehension.

case_report: Mrs. Kim, age 57, presented with a recently enlarging neck mass and hoarseness that began 5 days prior to hospital admission. She reported a very hard, fixed lump on the right side of her neck that had been present for months. She had a history of intermittent treatment for hyperthyroidism over the last three decades and had previously taken antithyroid agents prescribed by a private hospital. On admission, she showed no symptoms associated with thyrotoxicosis. She had no other symptoms or medical problems. The patient was conscious and in no acute distress, with stable vital signs: blood pressure of 130/90 mm Hg, pulse of 76 beats per minute, respiration rate of 20 breaths per minute, and a temperature of 36.5℃. Physical examination revealed no globe protrusion, scleral icterus, or conjunctival anemia. There were no enlarged cervical lymph nodes or jugular vein engorgement. A hard and fixed thyroid nodule measuring approximately 5×4 cm was palpated without neck tenderness. Normal heart and breath sounds were observed on auscultation, and no pitting edema was noted in her extremities. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 6,460/mm3 (neutrophil 57.4%, lymphocyte 36.6%, monocyte 7.7%, eosinophil 0.6%), hemoglobin of 11.6 g/dL, hematocrit of 35.2%, and platelet count of 295×103/mm3. Urine test results were normal. Serum biochemical examination revealed blood urea nitrogen/creatinine of 25/0.6 mg/dL, total protein/albumin of 7.4/4.3 g/dL, aspartate aminotransferase/alanine aminotransferase of 22/20 IU/L, Na/K/Cl of 142/5.1/105 mEq/L, Ca of 4.6 mEq/L (normal range, 4.5 to 5.2), erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 19 mm/hr, and C-reactive protein <0.2 mg/day. Thyroid function tests showed thyroid stimulation hormone of 0.07 µIU/mL (normal range, 0.4 to 4.5), free T4 of 3.86 ng/dL (normal range, 0.7 to 2), TBII of 51% (normal range, 0 to 15), thyroglobulin of 493 ng/dL (normal range, 2 to 60), antithyroid microsomal antibody of 3.1 U/mL (normal range, 0 to 8), and negative thyroglobulin antibody of 22 U/mL (normal range, 0 to 55). Imaging revealed normal sinus rhythm, signs of emphysema, and a right to left shift of the trachea due to the thyroid nodule. A well-defined irregular and hypoechoic nodule measuring 4 cm in diameter with large scattered dense calcifications was observed in the right thyroid lobe. No enlarged cervical lymph nodes or invasion into the parathyroid glands were noted. An aspiration technique yielded a very small amount of cytologic specimen, which showed no malignant cells. A 4.3×4.0 cm nodular lesion occupied most of the right lobe of the thyroid, with peripheral calcified lesions and severe marginal calcification in the inferior portion of the nodule. Unilateral fixed vocal cords were observed in a paramedian position, suggesting vocal cord paralysis on the right side. A total thyroidectomy was performed, revealing a 4.5-cm solid mass in the right thyroid lobe closely adhered to the surrounding airway and recurrent laryngeal nerve. The resected mass was covered by a thin capsule, with a cut surface showing mixed strips of white, yellowish-brown, and pink colors, along with peripheral dense calcification.
test_results: Thyroid follicles were replaced by extensive inflammatory and fibrous tissue. Inflammation was also noticed in the vein, which was encased in fibrous tissue, but no malignant cells were found.

case_report: A 59-year-old male presented to the emergency department with a 5-6 day history of fever, cough, and shortness of breath. Initial vital signs included a temperature of 37.8°C, blood pressure of 120/70 mmHg, oxygen saturation of 93% on room air, and a pulse rate of 92 beats per minute. Physical examination revealed slightly yellowish sclera and coarse crackles in the middle and lower lobes of both lungs. Heart sounds were normal, and the abdomen was unremarkable with no palpable organ enlargement. No peripheral lymph node enlargement was noted. The patient was not on any medications and had no recent alcohol or toxin exposure. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 3.11x10^3/uL, hemoglobin of 14 g/dL, platelet count of 84x10^3/uL, C-Reactive Protein of 16 mg/L (normal range 0–5), procalcitonin of 0.06 ng/mL, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) of 78 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) of 48 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT) of 124 U/L, alkaline phosphatase (ALP) of 164 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase of 349 U/L, total bilirubin of 4 mg/dL (normal <1.2), direct bilirubin of 3.1 mg/dL (normal <0.3), INR of 1, and albumin of 36 g/L. Other biochemical parameters, including urea, creatinine, electrolytes, amylase, and lipase, were within normal limits. A SARS-CoV-2 PCR test from a throat swab was positive. Chest computed tomography showed slight atypical viral pneumonia in both lungs. Treatment included favipiravir, enoxaparin, nasal oxygen, and supportive care. The patient's symptoms improved, respiration normalized, and oxygen saturation returned to normal. However, direct bilirubin levels continued to rise weekly from an initial level of 3.1 mg/dL.
test_results: In magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography, liver parenchyma was normal, and intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts were normal.

case_report: A 32-year-old adequately nourished male was admitted with complaints of shortness of breath for 1 month, which had worsened over the past 2 days. He had no other accompanying symptoms. The patient, who worked as a tailor and consumed a mixed diet, was found to be well-built and nourished with a body mass index of 25.3 kg/m2. On examination, he was tachypneic, had tachycardia, and a mild fever. Oral thrush was observed, and scrapings were sent for fungal culture. There were no apparent risk factors for immunosuppressive states. A chest X-ray showed scattered inspiratory crackles, and his SpO2 was 87%. High flow oxygen was initiated, and he was transferred to the Intensive Care Unit for further management. Blood gas analysis revealed a PO2 of 47 mmHg and a PCO2 of 24 mmHg. A chest roentgenogram showed bilateral perihilar infiltrates. Empirical antibiotics, fluconazole, and oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) were started along with steroids. Lactate dehydrogenase was elevated at 916 U/L, and high-resolution computed tomography of the thorax showed ground glass opacities in both lung fields, predominantly perihilar. Other routine blood work was normal. The patient remained tachypneic on high flow oxygen and intermittently required noninvasive ventilation. Bronchoalveolar lavage revealed pneumocystis organisms. Acid-fast bacteria and routine bacterial and fungal cultures were negative. The fungal scrapings grew Candida albicans, which was sensitive to fluconazole.
