HIV ELISA tests were negative on two separate occasions. Western blot and HIV-RNA polymerase chain reaction tests were also negative.
test_results: The CD4 turned out to be 110/mm3 and the CD4% was 14.3. The CD8 counts were 312/mm3 with a CD4:CD8 ratio, inverted (0.35; normal: 1.4–1.7). This test was repeated after 6 weeks and the results were the same.

case_report: A 31-year-old male with end-stage renal disease due to chronic glomerulonephritis (IgA nephropathy) underwent a kidney transplant in December 2010 from a 25-year-old male donor who had experienced cardiac death following craniocerebral trauma. The patient had been on hemodialysis for one year before the transplant and had a history of tuberculosis contact and digestive tract hemorrhage. Preoperative chest X-rays, electrocardiograms, and echocardiography showed no abnormalities. Both the donor and recipient were seronegative for cytomegalovirus and hepatitis B and C viruses. The surgical follow-up was uneventful. The immunosuppressive regimen included 0.5 g intravenous methylprednisolone during surgery and 0.5 g/day for the first three days post-transplant. Tacrolimus was administered based on the patient's body weight of 65 kg at a dose of 6.5 mg/day for the initial three days, then adjusted according to the trough concentration to maintain levels of 6–8 ng/ml for the first six months and 5–6 ng/ml for months 6–12. Mycophenolate mofetil was given orally at 0.75 g every 12 hours, later reduced to 0.5 g every 12 hours for maintenance. Prednisolone was initially given at 80 mg/day and tapered over six months to 10 mg/day for long-term maintenance. The allograft functioned excellently immediately post-surgery. On day 11 post-transplant, the patient experienced chest pain, dyspnea, and a reduction in urinary output from over 2,000 ml/day to 1,000 ml/day. Physical examination revealed tachycardia, decreased systolic pressure, and jugular venous distention.
test_results: Echocardiography and chest computed tomography scans revealed an abundant compressive circumferential pericardial effusion (echo-free space, 62.3 mm) and pleural effusion with 49% of the left ventricular ejection fraction. Pericardiocentesis was performed and a lemon-colored exudative fluid (3,000 ml; protein level, 51.4 g/l; fluid/serum ratio, >0.5) with abundant polymorphonuclear cells was removed. Further investigations revealed that the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 6 mm/h, the serum creatinine level was 200 μmol/l, the serum lactate dehydrogenase level was 339.3 U/l (serum/fluid ratio, >0.6) and the adenosine deaminase level in the pericardial fluid was 3.5 U/l. Negative results were observed for serum anti-nuclear antibodies and tumor markers, including carcinoembryonic antigen, carbohydrate antigen (CA) 125, CA 15-3 and CA 19-9. Serological tests for cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, mycoplasma, chlamydia, coxsackie virus, herpes simplex virus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis and toxoplasma were negative. In addition, direct examination of the pericardial fluid for mycobacteria, Aspergillus and yeast, as well as a pericardial fluid culture for bacteria, were negative. The drainage was maintained for 12 days. A repeated echocardiogram scan did not detect any pericardial effusion. The patient was readmitted after 20 days with pericardial tamponade, which required pericardiocentesis to be performed. A lemon-colored exudative fluid (600 ml) was removed and a catheter was maintained. The aforementioned etiological examinations were performed again, with all tests negative, with the exception of the enzyme-linked immunospot test (ELISPOT) for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. At day 48 following transplantation, a two-month period of empirical antituberculous therapy (rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide and moxifloxacin) was proposed, which was prolonged to three months. During this time period, the volume of pericardial drainage fluid remained at 200–600 ml per day. At day 77 following transplantation, a pericardial window with thoracic close drainage was performed due to the frequent obstruction of the catheter. Postoperative pericardial histopathological assessment revealed chronic inflammatory changes without any evidence of malignancy or tuberculosis. The culture of pericardial fluid tested negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis after 60 days. At day 127 following transplantation, a pericardiocentesis was performed again to replace the blocked thoracic close drainage with a catheter. The ELISPOT was repeated and negative results were achieved.

case_report: A 19-year-old female presented with multiple hyperpigmented pits on the face, trunk, and groin for the past 5 years. The lesions were gradually progressive and asymptomatic. There was a history of acne that had healed with hyperpigmentation. A family history revealed similar pitted lesions in three other family members: her father (aged 55 years), her paternal aunt (aged 45 years), and her paternal aunt's son (aged 25 years). Dermatological examination showed multiple comedo-like lesions measuring 1–3 mm and a few papules on the face, back, buttocks, and trunk. Post-acne hyperpigmentation was noted on the back. The palms and soles were unaffected. Examination of mucosa, hair, and nails was normal. Systemic examination was also within normal limits.
test_results: A skin biopsy taken from the comedo-like lesions revealed focal slender outgrowths of rete ridges with hyperpigmentation in basal layer showing accentuation in tip of rete ridges along with few attempted horn cysts.

case_report: MR, a 1-month-old male infant, was seen at the Pediatric Neurology Clinic, Soetomo Hospital, Surabaya, Indonesia in 2014 due to frequent tonic spasm seizures since birth, which increased in frequency recently, often occurring after waking up. There was no recorded family history of seizures. He was born via caesarean section due to cephalo-pelvic disproportion at 38 weeks of gestation, weighing 3400 grams at birth. Written informed consent was obtained from the parents. On physical examination, the infant was alert and weighed 4300 grams. Notable findings included an asymmetric dysmorphic face, hypertrophy of the right skull and right ear, a subcutaneous mass measuring 5x6x7 cm on the right cheek and neck, and the presence of linear nevi. Additional observations included nystagmus, a high-arched palate, an elongated face, and a low nasal bridge. A biopsy of the right cheek mass showed no signs of malignancy and was identified as a lipoma.
test_results: Craniocervical MRI with contrast revealed hemimegalencephaly right cerebral hemisphere with the features of pachygyria and lipoma of the right facial; multiple congenital deformity with the feature of left cerebral hemisphere hemiatrophy, hypoplasia of the posterior corpus callosum and closed lip schizencephalic; non-enhancing septated cystic lesion of right infra-auricular led to hygromacolli. EEG described PLEDs in the right frontal region; asymmetry decreased background rhythm in the right frontotemporal, burst suppression in the right frontotemporal.

case_report: A 6-year-old boy, born to healthy parents who are related by blood, was delivered at full term with an average birth weight and no complications during the perinatal period. His growth and neuromotor development were within normal ranges. There was no enlargement of the liver. An eye examination showed hypermetropia, but no other abnormalities were noted. Examinations of other systems were unremarkable. Liver function tests and urine glucose analyses returned normal results. Bilirubin levels were within normal limits, and an abdominal ultrasound did not show any abnormalities.
test_results: GALM gene analysis showed that he was homozygous for p.(c.829G>A)/p.Gly277Arg mutation.

case_report: An 8-year-old Chinese boy presented with fever, dizziness, and recurrent vomiting for 3 days. He had been treated for bacterial meningitis at another tertiary hospital with cefatriaxone, vancomycin, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), and mannitol for 2 days. His medical history includes an episode of acute bacterial meningitis at 4 years old and an episode of pneumonia and sepsis with Staphylococcus epidermidis at 5 years old. There was no history of recurrent infections or blood transfusions. He was born at term by Caesarean section with a birth weight of 2.8 kg. His parents and a 15-year-old female sibling are healthy, and there is no family history of recurrent severe infections or immunodeficiency disorders. On physical examination, the patient was febrile, tachycardic, and tachypneic. Neck rigidity, Kernig’s, and Brudzinski’s signs were positive, but there was no focal neurological deficit. Other systemic examinations were normal. His weight was 24.1 kg and height was 119.3 cm, with height at the fifth percentile for age and weight within the normal range. Immunoglobulin levels before IVIG treatment were IgG: 1.9 g/L, IgA: 0.27 g/L, and IgM: 0 g/L. Routine blood examination showed WBC: 40.9 × 10^9/L, neutrophils: 90%, lymphocytes: 2%, platelets: 322 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin: 102 g/L, and C-reactive protein (CRP): 243.80 mg/L. Urine and stool analysis were normal. Liver, cardiac, and renal function tests were within normal limits. Serum lactate and electrolytes were normal. HIV and syphilis serology were negative. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed WBC: 548 cells/μL, neutrophils: 57%, protein: 1.83 g/L, and glucose: 0.96 mmol/L. Gram staining and India ink staining were negative. CSF and blood cultures were negative. PCR tests for DNA of herpes simplex virus, cytomegalovirus, enterovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, mycoplasma pneumonia, and chlamydia pneumonia were negative. Immune parameters before treatment in our hospital were shown in Table. Chest X-ray, echocardiography, and ultrasound of the abdominal and pelvic cavity were normal. MRI of the brain suggested meningoencephalitis and nasosinusitis. EEG was normal, and brainstem auditory evoked potential (BAEP) showed prolonged latency of bilateral waves I and III. Bone age was normal. The patient was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics, vancomycin, and meropenem. By the following day, the fever resolved, and dizziness and vomiting disappeared. During the first episode of bacterial meningitis at 4 years old, CSF and blood culture showed growth of pneumococci. MRI of the brain revealed meningitis, subdural effusion, nasosinusitis, and mastoiditis. Immune parameters before treatment were shown in Table. The patient received intravenous vancomycin and meropenem and responded well to the treatment.
test_results: Sequencing of the BTK coding regions revealed a point mutation, hemizygous c.1349 + 5G > A, which is an intron mutation.

case_report: A 41-year-old Japanese woman came to the clinic with a 4-month history of pain in both groins and the right buttock, with the right hip being more painful than the left. She had no history of trauma, alcohol abuse, or steroid use. Her medical history included iron-deficiency anemia diagnosed 2 years prior, for which she had been taking iron supplements. She had no previous fractures, including fragility fractures. Her height was 155 cm, her weight was 42 kg, and her body mass index was 18.7 kg/m2. She could walk for about 10 minutes without assistance, though at a slow pace. Limitations in passive motion of both hip joints were noted: flexion was 100°, internal rotation was 5°, external rotation was 15°, and abduction was 20° on both sides. She could perform a straight-leg raise of the right limb with significant pain. The neurovascular status of both lower extremities was normal. According to the Japanese Orthopaedic Association scoring system for hip-joint function, her right hip scored 46 points and her left hip scored 56 points out of a possible 100 points, with the score comprising 40 points for pain, 20 for range of motion, 20 for the ability to walk, and 20 for activities of daily living.
test_results: MRI of both hips presented a low signal line in the subchondral region of the femoral head in the T1 weighted image and high signal region in almost all of the femoral head in the short tau inversion recovery (STIR). The oblique axial views of the proton density-weighted image showed a low-signal sinuous line in the anteromedial region of the femoral head. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) values were low in both femoral necks. Bone mineral density was 0.909 g/cm2 in the lumbar spine, 0.594 g/cm2 in the right femoral neck, and 0.529 g/cm2 in the left femoral neck. Laboratory findings were as follows: C-reactive protein (CRP) 0.03 mg/dl; alkaline phosphatase 608 IU/l; calcium 9.0 mg/dl; albumin 4.4 g/d; and hemoglobin 9.7 g/dl. Bone turnover markers were as follows: tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase 5b (TRACP-5b) 463 mU/dl and total procollagen type 1 N-terminal propeptide (Total P1NP) 72.7 ng/ml.
diagnosis: bilateral stress fracture of the femoral neck secondary to osteonecrosis of the femoral head

case_report: A 45-year-old Tunisian man presented with a three-year history of memory issues, speech difficulties, confusion, and hallucinations. The family also noted a loss of independence in daily activities, disrupted sleep, and mood instability. The patient was initially treated with fluoxetine (20 mg/day) and olanzapine (10–20 mg/day), but there was no improvement. Physical examination revealed a livedo racemosa pattern primarily on the trunk and upper limbs. The patient also reported experiencing Raynaud's phenomenon in his fingers. Neurological and psychiatric evaluations identified delusions of persecution with auditory and visual hallucinations, mild dysarthria, and pyramidal syndrome. The patient scored 19 out of 30 on the Mini-Mental Status Examination, showing signs of dysexecutive syndrome and hippocampal amnesic syndrome. The family history included stroke and hypertension.
test_results: The immunological workup revealed positive antiphospholipid antibodies. Brain MRI showed multiple ischemic lesions on T2-weighted imaging, some gadolinium-enhanced cortical–subcortical regions, and diffuse atrophy of the left occipital lobe and left and right parietal lobes. Cerebral angiography revealed decreased vessel diameter and parietal irregularities in the distal cerebral arteries.

case_report: A 21-year-old male presented with itching and indigestion. He was in military service at the time. He had a fever and sore throat for 4 days and was treated with amoxicillin. Two weeks later, he developed jaundice, dark urine, and icteric conjunctiva, along with a recent weight loss of 5 kg. He was referred to a tertiary center. His past medical history included orthopedic leg corrective surgery, with no other significant medical or family history. He denied smoking and was a social alcohol drinker for 3 years. On physical examination, his temperature, pulse, and blood pressure were within normal ranges. Laboratory results showed a total bilirubin level of 25.52 mg/dL (normal range: 0.2–1.2 mg/dL), alanine aminotransferase level of 62 IU/L (normal range: 0–40 IU/L), aspartate aminotransferase level of 48 IU/L (normal range: 0–40 IU/L), and alkaline phosphatase level of 445 IU/L (normal range: 30–115 IU/L). His GGT level was 22 IU/L (normal range 8–35 IU/L), which was normal. Ultrasound imaging indicated a normal liver parenchyma. Extensive diagnostic work-up showed negative results for viral, autoimmune, and hepatitis markers. Abdominal computed tomography and magnetic resonance cholangiography scans revealed normal bile duct and liver structure. Liver biopsy showed marked canalicular and hepatocellular cholestasis, mild lobular and portal inflammation, mild lobular disarray, and giant cell change in some hepatocytes, with no fibrosis. Specific histologic features suggestive of autoimmune hepatitis or other etiologies were not observed. ATP8B1 sequencing test showed a wild type, and bile salt export protein immunohistochemical staining indicated normal canalicular expression.
test_results: Genomic DNA was extracted from EDTA blood specimen. Exome capture was performed using SureSelect V6-Post (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). Sequencing was performed using NovaSeq 6000 (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA). Sequence reads were aligned to the reference genome, UCSC assembly hg19, using BWA (v.0.7.12, MEM algorithm). Mean depth of coverage was 100× (>20×=98%). Variants calling, annotation, and prioritization were performed as previously described. However, no specific variants were reported at the time of testing. During follow-up, we were notified of the genomic results for whole genome sequencing, which had previously been reported as negative with an updated database. Potential compound heterozygous variants in splicing site of USP53 were detected (NM_001371395.1:c.972+3_972+6del, and c.973-1G>A). Both variants were located in the canonical splice site of USP53. They were predicted to alter splicing and result in a loss or disruption of protein function.

case_report: A 54-year-old male presented to the emergency department due to episodes of presyncope. The patient was undergoing treatment for idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy. He had no history of arrhythmic episodes, and his family history was unremarkable. Four years prior, the patient experienced a minor stroke with complete neurological recovery. His medical history included hypercholesterolemia managed with statins and non-insulin-dependent diabetes. Current medications included angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs), diuretics, and beta-blockers. During his hospital stay, the patient maintained a predominant sinus rhythm (SR). Laboratory results showed Brain Natriuretic Peptide (BNP) levels at 2800 pg/mL and N-terminal pro-b-type natriuretic peptide (NT pro-BNP) levels at 980 pg/mL. Hypokalemia was identified (2.8 meq/L) and treated with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRA). Highly sensitive troponin I levels were within normal range. Two-dimensional transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) revealed a hypokinetic left ventricle with a dual chamber-like appearance. The following day, the patient experienced another presyncope episode, and an ECG showed re-entrant ventricular tachycardia (VT), which was managed with external electrical cardioversion (EVC) due to hypotension and clinical instability.
test_results: Cardiac Magnetic Resonance (CMRI) showed the presence of an apical accessory cavity connected to the ventricle, which contracted in synchrony with the heart chambers. No thrombus or communication evidence with the right ventricle (RV) was demonstrated.

case_report: A 60-year-old male patient presented to the gastroenterology clinic in June 2004 with a three-year history of fatigue, itching, and palpitations, previously identified as monoclonal gammopathy. The patient was referred for consultation regarding the itching. It was noted that the rash had appeared years prior, initially localized to the face, periorbital region, and forehead, and had progressively worsened over the last two years. Family history was negative for hyperlipidemia and xanthoma. Physical examination revealed flat, slightly infiltrated yellow-orange and yellow-brown plaques on the forehead, eyelids, preauricular area, neck, proximal arms, upper trunk, buttocks, and lower extremities, with a more linear configuration on the extremities. Bruises were present over the plaques due to severe and persistent itching. Histological examination of a skin biopsy showed an infiltrate of foamy macrophages in the papillary dermis and perivascular region, with the foamy cells negative for S-100 and CD1a antibodies. The overlying epidermis was normal. Direct immunofluorescence investigations for IgA, IgG, IgM, C3, and C4 were negative. Laboratory investigations revealed: Hemoglobin, 11.2 g/dL; WBC, 8900/mm3; ESR, 64 mm/h; total protein, 7.6 g/dL (4.5-7.6); serum albumin, 2.4 g/dL (2.5-4.5); platelet count, 75000/mm3; liver enzymes SGOT, 74 U/L (0-40); SGPT, 56 U/L (0-45); GGT, 64 U/L (0-60); Apo A, 180 mg/dL (73-169); and Apo B, 143 mg/dL (58-138). Renal and thyroid function tests, autoantibodies, serum electrolytes, cryoglobulins, and alkaline phosphatase were within normal ranges or negative. No Bence Jones proteinuria was detected. A bone marrow biopsy and aspirate showed marked plasma cell proliferation. Liver biopsy showed no abnormalities. Fasting serum cholesterol and triglycerides were: Triglycerides, 277 mg/dL (50-150); cholesterol, 344 mg/dL (0-200); high-density lipoprotein (HDL), 58 mg/dL (45-65); and low-density lipoprotein (LDL), 228 mg/dL (0-130). Serum levels of IgA, IgM, IgE, and IgG were normal. Urine tests showed λ light chain at 57.5 mg/dL (0-18.5) and 50.0 mg/dL (0-50), respectively, while serum tests showed 2320 mg/dL (629-1350) and 723 mg/dL (313-723), respectively. Serum immunofixation electrophoresis identified IgG λ light chain, and urine immunofixation electrophoresis detected λ light chain. Serum immunoelectrophoresis revealed a monoclonal IgG Κ protein, interpreted as monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance. The patient was readmitted in 2005 due to upper gastrointestinal tract bleeding. An endoscopy of the upper gastrointestinal tract revealed varices in the esophagus and fundus.
test_results: Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) angiogram detected a thrombus at the level of diaphragm in inferior vena cava inferior and thrombi were observed in hepatic veins in hepatic venography.

case_report: A one-day-old male from Bangladesh presented with a congenital red plaque with blisters on the right calf. He was born at term via cesarean section to parents who are not related. The pregnancy was complicated by gestational diabetes and an excess of amniotic fluid. The lesion measured 13 x 6 cm and nearly encircled the calf. Since birth, the lesion has shown changes in appearance, including swelling, blistering, ulceration, and healing. A specific skin reaction was observed. There was no enlargement of the liver or spleen, and no swollen lymph nodes. Routine blood and biochemical tests were normal, and bacterial and viral cultures were negative.
test_results: Histopathology revealed full-thickness dermal infiltration with a dense monomorphic infiltrate of epithelioid and spindle cells without significant pleomorphism. Immunohistochemistry with anti-c-KIT was strongly positive. Staining with Ki-67 demonstrated low mitotic activity. Toluidine blue staining demonstrated metachromasia allowing the identification of mast cells.

case_report: A 16-year-old female presented with low back pain persisting for 4 weeks. Initial management by a primary care physician included NSAIDs, activity restriction, and physical therapy. Subsequent evaluation by an orthopaedic surgeon included plain X-rays of the pelvis and continuation of the treatment regimen, but symptoms persisted. Physical examination showed point tenderness below the right posterior superior iliac spine, with normal hip joint and lumbar spine motion, including a normal FABER's test. Laboratory tests (WBC, ESR, CRP) were within normal limits. Anteroposterior radiographs of the pelvis were initially interpreted as normal, prompting further imaging. CT scans revealed significant erosions involving the right sacroiliac joint. MRI showed a heterogeneous, lobulated lytic lesion in the right ilium affecting the sacroiliac joint. Fine-needle aspiration and cultures were nondiagnostic. A triple phase bone scan indicated increased uptake in the right ilium. An open biopsy of the right sacroiliac joint identified multiple lesions in the area.
test_results: Histology revealed multiple foci of cartilage surrounded by a rim of lamellar bone, consistent with multiple enchondromas.

case_report: A 3-year-old girl was evaluated in the rehabilitation medicine department due to developmental delay. She is the first child of non-related parents. Her mother was 23 years old and her father was 30 years old at the time of her birth. She was delivered at 40 weeks of gestation following an uncomplicated pregnancy, with a birth weight of 3,500 g (50th–75th percentile). At 2 years old, an ophthalmologic evaluation identified bilateral blepharophimosis and strabismus. She achieved sitting at 10 months and walking at 18 months. Speech development was delayed; she began saying a few simple words at 2 years and could form 2–3 word phrases by 3 years. Her social and emotional development regressed, and she exhibited shyness and minimal interaction with others. At 3 years old, her physical examination showed a height of 90 cm (25th–50th percentile), weight of 12 kg (below 25th percentile), and occipitalfrontal circumference of 46 cm (below 3rd percentile). She presented with an immobile face, blepharophimosis, ptosis, a broad and flat nasal bridge, and low-set, large protruding ears. Routine laboratory tests, including thyroid function tests, brain MRI, EEG, and joint X-rays, were normal. During the examination, her father was noted to have a similar facial appearance and a contracture deformity in his metacarpophalangeal joints, preventing him from making a tight fist. He had completed college and was employed in a manufacturing job. His intellectual quotient was 66 according to the Korean–Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-IV. The family history revealed that the patient's uncle had moderate intellectual disability, and her deceased grandmother had severe intellectual disability.
test_results: Sanger sequencing identified KAT6B missense mutation in c.2292C>T p.(His767Tyr) in the patient and her father.

case_report: A 44-year-old female presented with a subcutaneous swelling in the epigastric region for 2 years, which had progressively enlarged over the past 3 months and had become mildly painful. There were no changes in bowel habits or weight loss. Physical examination revealed a 5 cm epigastric mass, identified as an epigastric hernia with a 15 mm neck. The mass protruded with the Valsalva maneuver but did not reduce when the patient was lying supine. The hernia contents appeared fatty and were incarcerated but painless. Ultrasound confirmed the presence of an epigastric hernia. Blood tests showed no abnormalities. The patient was admitted for laparoscopic hernia repair. During the procedure, a moderate amount of mucoid, bright yellow peritoneal fluid was observed upon port introduction. Inspection revealed abundant mucinous ascites and gelatinous deposits covering most intra-abdominal organs, the omentum, and part of the abdominal wall, especially in the pelvic recesses. The hernia sac contained gelatinous implants. The appendix had an engorged tip filled with mucinous material, and the right ovary appeared to be involved by the same mucinous material as the appendix. A peritoneal cancer index of 24 was estimated. The hernia repair was postponed. Samples of peritoneal fluid and omentum were collected.
test_results: Histology reported peritoneum extensively covered by mucus and bundles of cylindrical and caliciform epithelial cells. The tumor cells stained positively for CK20, CDX2 and negatively for CK7.

case_report: A 15-year-old male, born to parents who are second-degree relatives, presented with non-painful, scaly skin lesions on his extremities that have been present for 5 years. The lesions initially appeared on the tops of his feet and gradually spread to his knees and hands. These skin changes have been persistent and have not moved to other areas. There is no family history of similar skin conditions. The patient has had steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome since infancy. Physical examination revealed well-defined, darkened, thickened, scaly plaques symmetrically located on the tops of his hands and feet, elbows, knees, and Achilles tendons. His palms and soles appeared normal. There were no abnormalities in his hair, nails, or mucous membranes. Additionally, there were no issues with his musculoskeletal or ocular systems. The patient exhibited facial puffiness with features consistent with Cushing's syndrome and had swelling in his feet.
test_results: Skin biopsy revealed hyperkeratosis, focal parakeratoses, acanthosis, normal granular layer, and a moderate mononuclear infiltration in upper dermis.

case_report: A 29-year-old male presented with a serum creatinine level of 1.40 mg/dL and an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 70 mL/min/1.73 m2. He had a history of mild hypertension managed with 8 mg of candesartan. Urinalysis indicated microalbuminuria with an albumin/creatinine ratio of 36 mg/g. Renal ultrasound revealed medullary nephrocalcinosis. The patient also exhibited mild nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, characterized by isosthenuria and a daily urine output of 3 to 4 liters. Historical medical records indicated that the patient experienced failure to thrive at three months old, with a total serum calcium level of 4.2 mmol/L, hypercalciuria, and nephrocalcinosis. At that time, he was receiving 800 IU of vitamin D3 daily, which was discontinued after his serum 25(OH)D3 level was found to be 123 ng/mL. Treatment included prednisolone and a calcium-free formula, leading to normalization of serum calcium levels. Subsequent development on a low calcium diet was normal. Total serum calcium levels remained in the upper normal range or slightly elevated (2.4–2.6 mmol/L), while hypercalciuria persisted (0.35–0.45 g calcium/g creatinine). Intact PTH levels were consistently suppressed. During the first four years of life, 25(OH)D3 levels were elevated (110–609 ng/mL) but later normalized. At 13 years of age, 1,25(OH)D3 levels were in the upper normal range (65 pg/mL). Current assessments of calcium and vitamin D metabolism are provided. Bone density measured by DEXA was normal, with lumbar spine density at 1.247 g/cm2 (T score 0.2) and femoral neck density at 1.175 g/cm2 (T score 0.7).
test_results: Sequencing analysis revealed that the patient was homozygous for three common DNA polymorphisms (rs2296241, rs2762934 and rs6022987) and additionally for a yet undescribed nonsynonymous mutation in exon 4 (c.628T>C), causing tryptophan to be replaced with arginine in codon 210 (W210R).
diagnosis: Idiopathic Infantile Hypercalcaemia with a novel CYP24A1 mutation

case_report: A 4-year-old girl was admitted to Instituto de Pediatria e Puericultura Martagão Gesteira, Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in March 2010, presenting with recurrent infections and severe neutropenia. Over a 12-year follow-up period, key clinical events and laboratory tests were documented. Initial peripheral blood analysis revealed hemoglobin levels at 9.8 g/L, platelet count at 234 × 10^9/L, and a white blood cell count of 6.9 × 10^9/L, with a neutrophil count of 0.56 × 10^9/L.
test_results: The bone marrow (BM) presented: hypocellularity with a granulocytic maturation arrest and micromegakaryocytes without fibrosis. BM immunophenotyping using the EuroFlow panel and settings showed granulocytic maturation blocked with the absence of CD10 expression in mature neutrophils, together with CD13 and CD64 overexpression in promyelocytes and in the whole granulocytic maturation, respectively. Further, both monocytes and neutrophils abnormally expressed CD56. The cytogenetic analysis by G-banding and fluorescence in situ hybridization showed: 46,XX,t(3;8)(p26;q21)c [25].
diagnosis: Chronic Myelodysplastic Syndrome with Increased Blasts
Orpha_name: Refractory anemia with excess blasts type 2

case_report: A 69-year-old female experienced difficulty walking for 6 months prior to admission, accompanied by a gradual increase in weakness in her limbs. Upon admission, a neurological examination revealed weakness in the muscles closest to the trunk and decreased deep tendon reflexes. Routine laboratory tests showed no abnormalities. Tests for antinuclear antibodies, anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies, and anti-voltage-gated calcium channel antibodies were negative. Imaging studies of the chest and abdomen via CT scans showed no abnormalities. A nerve conduction study indicated slightly low compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitudes, with normal nerve conduction velocities in the median and ulnar nerves. Needle electromyography (EMG) demonstrated early recruitment and polyphasic motor unit potentials (MUPs) with short durations and low amplitudes, indicative of myopathic changes. Notably, these EMG findings improved after a sustained strong muscle contraction for 10 seconds; the MUP sizes normalized, and the early recruitment of MUPs during weak contraction was clearly normalized in the biceps brachii muscle.
test_results: The RNS test showed an obvious incremental response of the CMAP amplitude of the abductor digiti minimi muscle after high-rate stimulation of the ulnar nerve.

case_report: A four-month-old previously healthy Sri Lankan male infant from an urban area presented with a high-grade fever of 102-103 °F lasting for 2 days. Clinical examination revealed conjunctival redness, bilateral pedal edema, a scaly rash on the cheeks, and a sandpaper-like papular erythematous rash on the trunk and bilateral upper and lower limbs. Both the liver and spleen were palpable 2 cm below the costal margin. The tongue was not red, and there was no cervical lymphadenopathy. Other system examinations were normal, except for high blood pressure measured by both manual and electronic methods, which was above the 99th percentile. Initial laboratory results showed a total white cell count (WBC) of 18,000/uL with neutrophil leukocytosis of 53%, a platelet count of 552,000/uL, and a hemoglobin level of 12 g/dL. C-reactive protein (CRP) was 130 mg/dL, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 10 mm in the 1st hour. Serum sodium was 134 mmol/L and potassium 5.4 mmol/L. Renal and liver function tests were normal. Covid-19 rapid antigen and PCR tests were negative. The patient was empirically started on intravenous cefotaxime and flucloxacillin based on local sensitivity patterns, suspecting either streptococcal or staphylococcal septicemia. However, blood culture was sterile, and high fever spikes continued despite ongoing antibiotic treatment. An ultrasound scan of the abdomen on day four was normal, and no coronary artery dilatations were observed.
test_results: 2D echocardiogram showed dilated coronary arteries (left main coronary artery 5.3 mm, left anterior descending artery 6.5 mm, right coronary artery 5 mm) and a thin pericardial effusion.

case_report: A 75-year-old male with a history of psoriatic arthritis, previously managed with methotrexate and etanercept, reported experiencing nausea, vomiting, and an unintentional weight loss of 30 pounds over several months. Physical examination identified an enlarged spleen. Initial laboratory results are available in Table . A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed signs of portal venous hypertension, an enlarged liver and spleen, and thickening of the gallbladder wall (Figure ).
test_results: His liver biopsy showed lymphocytes infiltrating the parenchyma in a sinusoidal pattern. Immunohistochemistry was positive for CD3, CD8, and CD57. The polymerase chain reaction was positive for alpha/beta TCR. Bone marrow biopsy revealed a hypercellular marrow with atypical interstitial and intrasinusoidal lymphocytic infiltrates. Flow cytometry revealed aberrant CD8+, CD57+, and TCR alpha/beta T-cell population.

case_report: JA, a 6-month-old female, was the second child of consanguineous parents. Her older sibling, a 5-year-old girl, is healthy. JA was born at full term via normal spontaneous vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 3 kg. The mother had gestational diabetes managed with a diabetic diet. There was no history of neonatal intensive care unit admission. At 4 months, JA exhibited respiratory distress with desaturation and was admitted with acute bronchiolitis. Clinical assessment showed global developmental delay, hypotonia with head lag, microcephaly, and micrognathia. No hypopigmented skin or hair was noted. Abdominal examination and external genitalia were normal. During hospitalization, JA had weak sucking and swallowing with recurrent choking. Gastroesophageal reflux disease was investigated with no abnormalities found. On the 8th day of hospitalization, JA developed frequent tonic-clonic seizures with up-rolling of the eyes. Electroencephalography showed abnormal focal epileptic discharge, and levetiracetam was initiated. Routine laboratory tests were normal, and immunological workup showed normal immunoglobulin levels. Ophthalmological examination revealed bilateral congenital cataracts. Brain MRI indicated brain atrophy, corpus callosum agenesis, poor grey and white matter differentiation, and scarce myelin sheath. Echocardiography showed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, mitral regurgitation, tricuspid regurgitation, and pulmonary hypertension. Chromosomal studies revealed a normal karyotype (46XX).
test_results: Molecular genetic testing with whole exon sequencing identified the pathogenic homozygous variant c.4751T>A p. (Leu1584∗) on exon 27 of the EPG5 gene.
diagnosis: Vici syndrome with pathogenic homozygous EPG5 gene mutation

case_report: A 68-year-old Japanese man presented with an extensive type 0–IIc lesion in the upper gastric body extending to the hypogastric lesser curvature, identified during an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy in September 2019. Biopsy indicated a poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma, and the patient was referred for surgery. His medical history included hypertension and hyperlipidemia, with no family history of malignancy. In November 2019, he underwent robot-assisted laparoscopic distal gastrectomy, D1+ lymph node dissection, and Roux-en-Y reconstruction. Postoperative recovery was uneventful, and he was discharged 6 days later. The surgical specimen showed a 50 × 35-mm 0–IIc lesion with shallow depression from the upper gastric body to the hypogastric lesser curvature. Histopathological examination confirmed poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with negative resection margins, staged IA (pT1aN0M0) according to the UICC TNM Classification of Malignant Tumors, 8th edition. The patient did not receive adjuvant chemotherapy and was monitored regularly. Two years post-surgery, a 38 × 36 mm soft tissue mass was detected on the greater curvature side of the residual stomach during a CT scan. Retrospective review of a 1-year postoperative CT scan showed partial thickening of the gastric wall, initially deemed within normal limits. No recurrent metastasis was observed at other sites. Blood tests showed carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) at 1.8 ng/mL, carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9) at 8.5 U/mL, and soluble IL-2 receptor at 396 U/mL. FDG-PET/CT revealed moderate FDG accumulation (SUVmax, 5.25) in the soft tissue mass on the left side of the residual stomach, with no other areas showing FDG accumulation. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the abdomen showed the soft tissue mass on the greater curvature side of the residual stomach with a high, heterogeneous signal on T2-weighted images, a low signal on T1-weighted images, and a slow contrast effect. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed no mass lesions in the remnant stomach. Transgastric ultrasonography identified a 43 × 30 mm borderline oligo-hypoechoic mass in the splenic hilum, which was biopsied using endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration (EUS-FNA). The biopsy revealed multiple spindle-shaped cells, but no significant positive findings were obtained from immunostaining for CD34, c-kit, desmin, S-100, and β-catenin. The biopsy specimen did not conclusively indicate the histological type of the tumor.
test_results: Immunostaining was positive for vimentin, desmin, and β-catenin and negative for α-SMA, S-100, CD34, c-kit, STAT6, estrogen receptor (ER), and progesterone receptor (PgR).

case_report: A 23-month-old male Chinese child experienced four episodes of tonic seizures over a 10-day period at 16 months of age. The child exhibited enamel hypoplasia and hypotonia in the trunk and limb muscles. Developmental assessments showed a developmental quotient (DQ) and mental index (MI) both below 70. Brain MRI indicated long T1 and long T2 signal changes in the white matter near the anterior and posterior horns of both lateral ventricles. Video-electroencephalography (EEG) monitoring revealed abnormal brain waves during sleep. Liver function tests showed elevated plasma alanine aminotransferase (ALT) at 117 IU/L (normal range: 9–50 IU/L) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 50 IU/L (normal range: 15–40 IU/L), with normal plasma bilirubin levels. Plasma citrulline was elevated at 220.94 μmol/L (normal range: 7.00–35.00 μmol/L), while plasma arginine was within normal limits. Seven months later, plasma ammonia levels increased to 175 μmol/L (normal range: 11–51 μmol/L), and plasma levels of ALT (335 IU/L), AST (106 IU/L), and citrulline were higher than previous measurements. Follow-up brain MRI showed ventricular dilation and cerebral atrophy of the left hemisphere with malacia. After two weeks of treatment with a restricted protein diet and arginine supplementation, plasma ammonia levels decreased to 70 μmol/L. The patient subsequently died from a severe infection several months after being discharged from the hospital.
test_results: The genetic analysis of the infant was performed.

case_report: A 5-year-old girl was brought to our institute with significant delays in mental and motor development. She is the younger of two children born to a nonconsanguineous Indian Hindu couple. She was delivered at term through normal vaginal delivery, cried at birth, and had an uneventful neonatal period. Severe developmental delays were observed from early infancy. There was no history of exposure to infections, drugs, or radiation during pregnancy. Her elder sibling, a 7-year-old girl, is apparently healthy. There is no family history of brain malformations, developmental delays, facial abnormalities, or chromosomal abnormalities. On physical examination, the child exhibited partial neck control, reached for objects with an immature grasp, recognized only family members, and vocalized meaningless vowel sounds. She weighed 13.5 kg (<3rd percentile) and had a head circumference of 48 cm (5–15th percentile). Dysmorphic facial features included metopic prominence, bushy eyebrows with synophrys, broad nasal root, flat nasal bridge, telecanthus, and a shallow philtrum. Neurological examination showed normal cranial nerves, bilaterally symmetrical muscle bulk with increased tone in all limbs, and generalized hyperreflexia. The rest of the systemic examination was normal.
test_results: On magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), deficient interhemispheric fissure was observed in posterior frontal and parietal regions with failure of separation of posterior frontal and parietal lobes. The anterior and posterior parts of the interhemispheric fissure were normally formed. Sylvian fissures showed abnormal vertical orientation and were fused across midline over the vertex of brain. Genu and splenium of corpus callosum were normally formed, and the body was absent in the region of interhemispheric connection. Septum pellucidum was absent. Basal forebrain structures were normally cleaved. Brainstem and posterior fossa structures were normal.

case_report: A 95-year-old right-handed woman, native Portuguese speaker, with no prior history of neurological or psychiatric conditions and 5 years of formal education, was brought by her daughter with her eyes shut and unresponsive to verbal and gestural attempts to elicit any response. At the age of eighty-nine, the patient developed a fear of being robbed and assaulted, particularly at night. Her daughter and son-in-law, with whom she lived, initially attributed this to concerns about their neighborhood. Despite reassurances, the patient's fears intensified, leading her to seek comfort in their bed at dawn. A psychiatrist prescribed 50 mg of sertraline at bedtime for major depression, which initially improved her condition. However, she later became less active and socially withdrawn, responding emotionally only to her great-grandson. Her sertraline dose was increased to 100 mg without benefit and later reduced back to 50 mg due to concerns about SSRI-related apathy. Three years later, her behavior changed significantly; she used inappropriate language, insulted caregivers, and displayed unusual kindness towards her grandsons and granddaughters' boyfriends. She confided in a friend about an affair and exhibited inappropriate behavior towards cab drivers. She engaged in compulsive genital self-stimulation and experienced significant weight loss due to refusal to eat. A year before her first appointment, she began speaking unintelligibly, her gait deteriorated, and she became unable to walk and doubly incontinent. In the weeks before her first appointment, she became mute, rarely opened her eyes, and spent most of her time lying on her left side, embracing her flexed legs. She refused food, water, and grooming, contracting her lips and slapping anyone who offered assistance. On examination, she kept her eyes shut, resisted attempts to open them, and sustained passively imposed body positions for several minutes. She occasionally opened her eyes and responded with unintelligible words or echoed the examiner's speech. Oral prehension and right manual grasp reflexes were easily elicited. She met 12 of 14 screening items and scored 41 of 69 points on the Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale. On the Northoff Catatonia Scale, she scored a total of 34 points (Motor subscale = 10; Affective subscale = 6, Behavioral subscale = 18). A 10 mg diazepam IV challenge produced no effect. Olanzapine, 10 mg at bedtime, was prescribed for 6 weeks without benefit and was discontinued. Six sessions of electroconvulsive therapy, administered three times per week, also produced no benefit and were discontinued.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed asymmetric cerebrocerebellar and brainstem atrophy, which was more marked in the right frontal and parietal lobes, right ventral midbrain and pons as well as in the anterior temporal lobes. An abnormally high caudate index (= 0.19; normal ≤ 0.09) and a normal bifrontal index (0.37; normal ≥ 0.30) indicated caudate atrophy greater than expected from hemispheric atrophy alone.

case_report: The patient is a 15-year-old boy who was born full-term by cesarean section with a birth weight of 4,200 g after an uneventful pregnancy. He is the fifth child of a healthy non-consanguineous couple of Chinese Han ethnicity. His three older sisters are healthy, but his brother experienced intractable diarrhea, recurrent fever, and severe malnutrition, and died at the age of 2 years. The patient had noticeable eczema during his first year of life and a history of food allergies in childhood. At the age of 3 years, he presented with recurrent vomiting and was treated with conventional antibiotics and symptomatic therapies in a local hospital for suspected acute gastroenteritis, but the symptoms did not improve. An esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) showed multiple gastric ulcers, and a gastric biopsy revealed a marked infiltration of eosinophils and HP positivity. The colonoscopy was unremarkable. He received anti-HP treatment, antacid medication, and nutritious formula feeding, but the vomiting did not improve over the next 2 years. At the age of 5 years, he experienced frequent vomiting, and an EGD showed multiple gastric ulcers with eosinophil infiltration. No presence of duodenal villous blunting was observed. Vomiting and gastric ulcers improved after 5 months of oral methylprednisolone, but he started to present with feeding difficulties and malnutrition. He could not eat meat or rice because it caused vomiting, and the symptom did not improve with symptomatic therapies and nutritional support in the following years. At the age of 7 years, he was admitted to our hospital for further evaluation. Physical examinations revealed severe failure to thrive (height, 107 cm, Z-score, −3.12; weight, 15.2 kg, Z-score, −4.22; BMI, 13.13 kg/m2, Z-score, −2.42). An EGD showed redness, erosion, and edema throughout the stomach. Pyloric stricture and stiffness were observed, and the endoscope could not enter the duodenal bulb. Upper gastrointestinal radiography revealed pyloric stenosis with a slow barium passage. A biopsy of the antrum suggested moderate non-atrophic gastritis, infiltration of eosinophils (10–30 eosinophils/HPF), and HP infection. The colonoscopy was normal, and no presence of villous blunting was observed in the terminal ileum. Laboratory blood tests were unremarkable, including normal eosinophil counts, complement, immunoglobulin G (IgG), IgA, IgM, and IgE levels. Serum tests of antineutrophil cytoplasmic and other autoantibodies, including antinuclear, antidiabetes-related (anti-insulin and anti-islet cell antibodies), and antithyroglobulin autoantibodies, were all negative. Balloon dilation was applied to treat the pyloric stenosis. He received oral methylprednisolone (4 mg per day), proton pump inhibitors (PPI), L-glutamine and sodium gualenate granules, and anti-HP treatment. However, vomiting reoccurred after improvement, and the pyloric stenosis did not improve. In the following years, he was repeatedly admitted to our department and managed with a series of symptomatic and supportive treatments, including multiple balloon dilations, enteral nutrition, and oral methylprednisolone. At the age of 9 years, an EGD showed that the pyloric stenosis was aggravated. Endoscopically assisted duodenal feeding tubes beyond the second portion of the duodenum were placed for enteral nutrition and liquid food. At the age of 10 years, due to the appearance of a perianal abscess and gastric non-necrotizing granulomas with inflammatory cell infiltration, he received infliximab (eight times) and azathioprine treatments in the following year. The level of serum infliximab did not achieve an adequate concentration (1 µg/ml) after three instances of intravenous infusions at a dose of 5 mg/kg. Then, the infliximab dose increased to 8 mg/kg, and the serum infliximab level increased to 3.5 µg/ml. The serum anti-infliximab antibody concentration was below 4 ng/ml. However, the infliximab infusion remained sub-therapeutic despite a dose escalation. The gastric lesions persisted, and the perianal abscess recurred after a partial improvement during the treatment. At the age of 12 years, upper gastrointestinal radiography showed gastric retention and severe pyloric stenosis. The barium did not pass through the pylorus after 6 hours. A laparoscopic jejunostomy feeding tube placement was performed after 1 month of treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone. An EGD was placed through the surgical incision, and an intestinal biopsy showed normal intestinal villi without villous blunting or atrophy. A gastrojejunal anastomosis bypass and jejunal-jejunal end-to-side anastomosis were performed 5 months later. Vomiting improved, and he was able to eat, resulting in significant weight gain after the surgery. At the age of 13 years, he had a height of 125 cm (Z-score, −4.21), weight of 29 kg (Z-score, −2.99), and BMI of 18.56 kg/m2 (Z-score, −0.06). Although he had a steady increase in height with age, his body weight fluctuated along with the recurrent symptoms and changes in nutrient intake. His weight increased to 31.5 kg at the age of 13.5 years but dropped to 28.4 kg over the next 6 months due to the loss of appetite.
test_results: A 3 bp deletion in exon 7 of the FOXP3 gene, c.748–750del (p.Lys250del), was identified and further confirmed by Sanger DNA sequencing. Genotyping of the unaffected family members by Sanger sequencing showed that his mother and third sister carry this mutation, and his father and two other sisters are normal. The c.748–750del (p.Lys250del) mutation is located in the leucine zipper domain of the FOXP3 protein.

case_report: A 32-year-old woman presented with a painful swelling in the maxillary gingiva. She had a history of an inflammatory lesion at the same site and had used antibiotics 10 months prior. The lesion did not reduce in size. Following the extraction of the upper left second premolar, the lesion continued to grow. She was referred to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon. Extraoral examination showed facial asymmetry and the disappearance of the left nasolabial fold. Intraoral examination revealed a firm, sessile, pink exophytic ulcerative mass with a lobulated surface on the maxillary left buccal gingiva, extending from the canine to the distal of the first molar. The lesion was tender and bled easily upon palpation. The first premolar was mobile. Periapical radiography showed PDL widening in teeth numbers 10, 11, and 12.
test_results: The microscopic examination of the hematoxylin and eosin-stained sections revealed a neoplastic proliferation of spindle-shaped tumor cells in the adjacent connective tissue. Normal structures were destroyed by the invasion of tumor cells. The highly cellular neoplastic tissue was composed of predominant spindle cells in which some foci exhibited a fascicular pattern. In addition, marked cellular pleomorphism and nuclear hyperchromasia with prominent nucleoli, scattered atypical mitotic figures, and bizarre giant cells were identifiable among tumoral cells. Using immunohistochemical (IHC) staining, the tumor cells were positively reacted with specific markers for myogenic differentiation such as anti-Desmin, anti-Myogenin, and anti-MyoD1 antibodies. In addition, a highly positive staining (more than 10%) for Ki-67 was observed.

case_report: A 20-year-old female patient with a 6-year history of progressive bilateral vision loss was referred to our clinic. The patient had no known systemic disease, previous trauma, family history, history of drug or cigarette use, or consanguineous marriage in her family. Her visual acuity was 3-4/10 in both eyes; intraocular pressure was 11 mmHg in the right eye and 13 mmHg in the left eye. No pathologies were detected during anterior segment examination. Fundus examination revealed no pathologies other than mild retinal vessel tortuosity. Both eyes appeared normal on FAF imaging. Mild central hyporeflectance was observed in both eyes on fundus IR imaging. FFA was normal. Foveal thickness was determined by OCT thickness profile analysis as 155 µm and 188 µm in the right and left eyes, respectively. Disruption of the photoreceptor IS/OS junction was observed. The extension of the IS/OS band disruption on the horizontal axis was measured as 696 µm in the right and 348 µm in the left eye. On MP analysis both eyes exhibited relatively unstable fixation which was more pronounced in the right eye, and areas of absolute scotoma consistent with OCT were observed. Retinal sensitivity in the central 20° field of the macula was measured as 13.9 dB in the right and 13.5 dB in the left eye. Full-field ERG was normal.
test_results: mfERG revealed a bilateral reduction in central response which was more pronounced in the right eye.

case_report: A five-year-old female, recently migrated from Africa, presented with a persistent scalp infection and otitis media. She exhibited symptomatic hyperglycemia, with a history potentially extending back to the age of two. Physical examination revealed distinct cutaneous and facial features. Laboratory tests confirmed biochemical insulin resistance, with a fasting plasma insulin level of 1836 pmol/L (normal range: 9–80 pmol/L). At the age of six, she was found to have diabetes mellitus characterized by daytime postprandial hyperglycemia and paradoxical nocturnal fasting hypoglycemia.
test_results: Genetic testing demonstrated a homozygote mutation at position 119 of the mature alpha subunit of the insulin receptor, but a normal beta subunit.

case_report: An 8-year-old girl from a Syrian family, residing in a refugee camp in Sulaymaniyah, northern Iraq since 2014, is the second child among four daughters. She was born in August 2010 and received the BCG vaccine on the 7th day of life. Two months later, she developed ipsilateral axillary lymphadenitis followed by generalized lymphadenopathy. She exhibited symptoms of disseminated BCG infection, including fever, weight loss, disseminated maculopapular rash, and hepatosplenomegaly, which were managed with a prolonged course of anti-TB medications including isoniazid and rifampin. According to her mother, the patient experienced repeated episodes of non-specific illnesses, such as relapsing/remitting maculopapular skin rash, oral thrush, respiratory infections, gastroenteritis, and urinary tract infections treated in an outpatient setting, and one episode of meningitis treated in Syria. At 4 years old, after fleeing the war in Syria to a camp in northern Iraq, her condition severely deteriorated, presenting with fever, night sweats, diarrhea, and poor appetite. She was admitted to the intensive care unit at Hiwa Hospital in Sulaymaniyah. Upon admission, she appeared toxic, cachexic, and feverish, with generalized lymphadenopathy including cervical, axillary, inguinal, and epitrochlear lymph nodes. The lymph nodes were multiple, asymmetrical, visibly enlarged (largest being 3.5 × 3 cm in the left axilla), firm, non-tender, and discrete. The abdomen was distended with hepatosplenomegaly and ascites, and there was right lung crepitation. Her growth parameters were below the third centile. Laboratory investigations revealed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 110 mm/h (normal range 3–13 mm/h), hypochromic microcytic anemia, leukocytosis, and elevated immunoglobulin-G levels. Ascitic fluid analysis showed lymphocytic predominance with a serum-to-ascites albumin gradient of < 1.1 gm/dl, and normal liver and renal function tests. HIV and hepatitis screenings were negative. Imaging studies, including chest X-ray and CT of the chest and abdomen, showed pulmonary consolidation in the right lower lung and mesenteric lymphadenitis. Despite the absence of microbiological and histopathological evaluations, she was treated empirically with a 12-month course of four anti-TB medications: isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and streptomycin (later changed to ethambutol). She showed significant clinical and laboratory improvement. However, several months after stopping anti-TB therapy, she relapsed with generalized lymphadenopathy and maculopapular skin rash. She also experienced episodes of abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, disturbed sleep, and weight loss. The patient underwent several excisional biopsies from axillary, cervical, and groin lymph nodes in Syria and Iraq, but the results were inconclusive. During periods of suspected infection with leukocytosis and lymph node neutrophilic infiltration, cultures were not regularly performed due to limited laboratory facilities and outpatient treatment. There was no family history of BCG disease or TB.
test_results: The patient had an ESR of ≥ 100 mm/h, hypochromic microcytic anemia, leukocytosis, neutrophilia, lymphopenia with hypercellular marrow examination, and low CD3 and CD4 by flowcytometry.
Orpha_name: Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial diseases due to complete IL12RB1 deficiency

case_report: A 17-year-old female with a 2-year history of erosive nodular seropositive rheumatoid arthritis followed Chinese herbal treatment for repeated joint pain in 2011. One year later, she developed jaundice, an enlarged liver and spleen, and swollen lymph nodes. Physical examination showed deformities in the proximal interphalangeal joints, metacarpophalangeal joints, wrists, and ankles. Lymph nodes in the posterior neck, axillary fossa, and inguinal area were enlarged, measuring 0.5–1 cm in diameter. In August 2012, she presented with a fever exceeding 39°C. Blood tests indicated a white blood cell count of 4.12×10^9/l with an absolute neutrophil count of 3.15×10^9/l, hemoglobin levels at 80 g/l, and a platelet count of 159×10^9/l. Glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase levels were 352 U/l, and glutamate pyruvate transaminase levels were 136 U/l. Bilirubin levels were 112.8 μmol/l, and lactate dehydrogenase levels were 548 U/l. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 35 mm/h, and C-reactive protein levels were 60.2 mg/l. Cultures of blood and secretions showed no microbial infection. Tests for human immunodeficiency virus, syphilis, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and autoimmune hepatitis-associated antibodies, as well as a purified protein derivative skin test, were negative. The antinuclear antibody titer was 1:320, while tests for anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, and anti-Rnp antibodies were negative. Complement C3 and C4 levels were normal. Rheumatoid factor, antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptides, anti-keratin antibodies, and anti-perinuclear factor autoantibodies were negative. X-rays of the joints, including the wrists and hands, showed soft-tissue swelling, bone erosion, and narrowing of the joint cavity.
test_results: A bone marrow biopsy showed normocellular and maturing trilineage hematopoiesis. Splenomegaly (54×124 mm) with uniform density and multiple enlarged lymph nodes distributed along the retroperitoneal space, omental bursa, mesentery root and surrounding hepatic hilar was shown by abdominal computed tomography (CT). A lymph node biopsy from the right cervical node revealed chronic inflammation, with positive results for cluster of differentiation (CD)79α and CD20 in interfollicular regions, and for CD5 in the paracortical area. Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-positron emission tomography revealed lymphadenectasis of the bilateral submandibular and superficial anterior cervical lymph node, axillary fossa, retroperitoneal space, pelvic wall and inguinal area without FDG uptake. The proliferation of hypermetabolic lesions was observed in the shoulder, hip, knee, ankle and interphalangeal joints, as well as knee joint-effusion. FDG uptake in the liver and spleen occurred with a maximal standardized uptake value of 1.4 and 2.0, respectively.

case_report: A 37-year-old woman, with a history of gallbladder removal due to recurrent biliary colic, presented to the emergency room with abdominal pain and nausea for the past two days. The pain was located in the epigastric region, rated 10/10 in intensity, cramping in nature, and radiating to the back. Upon admission, the patient was hemodynamically stable, with notable epigastric tenderness on deep palpation. Her blood pressure was 118/85 mmHg, heart rate was 88 beats per minute, and temperature was 97.6°F. Laboratory results showed a total bilirubin level of 4.1 mg/dL with a direct fraction of 3.1 mg/dL. Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels were 850 IU/L and 1025 IU/L, respectively. Serum amylase and lipase levels were elevated at 581 IU/L and 1328 IU/L, respectively. The patient was admitted with a Bedside Index of Severity in Acute Pancreatitis (BISAP) score of zero and a Ranson’s Score on admission of one. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast revealed a common bile duct measuring 1.6 cm with dilation of the intrahepatic biliary system and mild peripancreatic fat stranding. On the second day, the patient developed a temperature of 99.6°F. A hepatitis immunity panel was negative for acute hepatitis. The patient was started on intravenous antibiotics (ciprofloxacin and metronidazole).
test_results: ERCP showed mild dilated intrahepatic ducts, CBD dilation of 1.6 cm, and a choledochal cyst at CBD. Sphincterotomy was done and good bile drainage was reported. Post-procedure MRCP showed mild intra- and extra-hepatic biliary dilation. No focal filling defect was seen in the biliary tree.

case_report: Patient 2 is a 3-year-old boy, born to second-degree consanguineous parents at term via cesarean section due to prolonged labor. His birth weight was 2.5 kg (−2 SD), and he cried immediately after birth. He is the only child of his parents. A maternal antenatal scan at 6 months of gestation indicated fetal limb deformity, which was confirmed postnatally. He was referred for evaluation of deformities in both feet, elbows, and the right knee, noted since birth. Additionally, he was found to have a cleft palate at birth, which was surgically corrected at 1 year of age. At 6 weeks, his height was 52 cm (−2 SD), head circumference was 37 cm (−2 SD), and weight was 3.3 kg (−2 SD). Physical examination revealed a prominent forehead, depressed nasal bridge, long philtrum, telecanthus, and a high arched palate. His hair was curly, and his teeth and nails were normal. Hypermobility of both hip joints was observed, along with dislocated knees, elbows, and bilateral clubfeet. He had spatulate thumbs, cylindrical fingers with short and broad fingertips, and joint laxity. Hearing was normal, and there was no evidence of compressive myelopathy. All other examinations were unremarkable. Echocardiography showed a normal heart. Developmentally, he achieved head control at 5 months, rolled over at 7 months, sat with support at 10 months, sat without support at 15 months, and crawled at 20 months. He began babbling at 6 months, spoke bisyllables at 15 months, and used a few meaningful words at 20 months. Imaging of the skull was unremarkable. Ultrasound of the knees at 6 weeks of age indicated an absent right patella.
test_results: Radiographs showed bilateral dislocated elbows, absent right patella, coronal clefts in vertebrae, cervical vertebral kyphosis with subluxation at C4-C5, and double calcaneum ossification with club feet. Radiographs at 3 months and 1 year suggested delayed carpal ossification. Radiographs at 3 months and 1 year showed thoracolumbar scoliosis and small capital femoral epiphysis.

case_report: A 22-year-old woman was admitted to our department following a loss of consciousness after a caesarean section. This patient, who was at term pregnancy (Gravid 1, Para 1), initially presented at another hospital. She had no prior discomfort during this pregnancy. Upon presentation, her blood pressure was recorded at 150/100 mmHg. Laboratory results were within normal limits except for urinalysis, which showed protein at 3+. An emergency operation was performed due to severe preeclampsia and fetal distress. Post-operation, she was administered intravenous magnesium sulfate and antihypertensive medication. Her blood pressure remained at 150/100 mmHg. Three hours post-operation, she reported nausea, vomiting, and upper quadrant abdominal pain. Four hours after the operation, she experienced convulsions and loss of consciousness.
test_results: The laboratory studies gave the following results: serum aspartate aminotransaminase (AST), 263 IU/L; serum alanine aminotransaminase (ALT), 203 IU/L. The laboratory studies gave the following results: serum aspartate aminotransaminase (AST), 306 IU/L; serum alanine aminotransaminase (ALT), 224 IU/L; serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), 2260 IU/L; serum urea and creatine were normal; hemoglobin, 18.6 mg/dL; platelet count, 34 × 103 μ/mL.

case_report: A 17-month-old female presented with fever, poor growth, and recurrent respiratory tract infections over several months. Her height was 71 cm (<3rd percentile), weight was 7.5 kg (<3rd percentile), and occipitofrontal head circumference was 43 cm (<3rd percentile). Physical examination noted a broad forehead, mild hypertelorism, a short upturned nose, a prominent philtrum, mild retrognathism, pallor, petechiae, hepatomegaly (3 cm below the costal margin), and splenomegaly (8 cm below the costal margin). Laboratory results showed leukocytosis (53.7x10^9/L), monocytosis (11.1x10^9/L), anemia (Hb: 8.9 g/dL), and thrombocytopenia (platelets: 46x10^9/L). Peripheral blood smear revealed a leukoerythroblastic picture, dysplastic monocytes, and monocytosis (23%).
test_results: Bone marrow examination revealed cellular smears with myeloid hyperplasia, features of dysmyelopoiesis, and presence of 3% blasts. Cytogenetic studies of the patient revealed a normal karyotype with absence of the BCR/ABL fusion gene, monosomy 7, or any other chromosomal abnormality. Genetic analysis of the peripheral blood samples revealed heterozygous germline mutation in c-CBL exon 8 p371 Y>H. The same genetic mutation was detected in DNA isolated from the hair follicles, indicating the germline origin of the mutation.
diagnosis: Juvenile Myelomonocytic Leukemia  with CBL syndrome

case_report: The patient is an 11-month-old female, born at 33 weeks gestation via in vitro fertilization. Clinical observations include delayed motor skills, persistent drooling, short stature, and slow growth. Physical examination revealed low muscle tone, delayed tooth eruption, a high palatal arch, thumb adduction, increased joint mobility, and ligament laxity. Imaging identified hypoplasia of the corpus callosum.
test_results: A de novo frameshift deletion of ASXL1, c.3762delT (p. N1254fs), was identified. We did not detect chromosomal aneuploidy or genome copy number variants of 100 kb or more that are known to cause disease. The first-generation sequencing results showed that the proband had c.3762delT heterozygosity in the ASXL1 gene, and neither the father nor the mother was a carrier. The 0.32 Mb region at q11.2 on chromosome 14 was missing. Querying of the DGV, DECIPHER, OMIM, UCSC, and PubMed public database resources revealed that this fragment does not contain any known genes.
diagnosis: Bohring-Opitz syndrome  caused by a novel ASXL1 mutation

case_report: A 3-year-and-3-month-old boy presented with abnormal renal function, frontal bossing, low-set ears, dolichocephaly, sparse hair, and short limbs. He was the seventh child of his unrelated parents and was delivered naturally at full term with a birth weight of 3.8 kg. He could walk at the age of 1 year and 3 months and has language retardation. On admission, a physical examination showed that the patient was developmentally delayed, with longer skull diameter, macrocephaly, sparse and delicate hair, narrow eye cleft, hypertelorism, low bridge of the nose, sparse teeth with dysplasia, short and curved fingers/toes, and the testes were not touched in the bilateral scrotum. Computed tomography (CT) examination of the head revealed that the bilateral frontocephalic space had widened, the anteroposterior diameter of the skull had increased, and the sagittal suture was partially closed. Frontal chest radiographs showed increased heart volume, decreased bone density, and enlarged trabeculae. Electrocardiogram and color echocardiography were normal. The abdominal color ultrasound examination revealed that the liver volume was increased, the parenchymal echo was dense and enhanced, the intrahepatic hypoechoic mass was enlarged, and the intrahepatic bile duct was widened. Dysplasia of both kidneys enhanced parenchymal echo, unclear demarcation of the cortex and medulla, hydronephrosis of the right kidney and ureter, and dilatation of the left calyces. The spleen is enlarged with open sinuses. In particular, the child had an abnormal testicle position, with the right testicle located in the iliac fossa and the left testicle situated in the groin, and a hydrocele existed on both sides. The biochemical indicators of the patient showed that the urea value was 28.3 mmol/L (reference range: 1.7–7.1 mmol/L), the creatinine value was 432.1 umol/L (reference range: 18–80 umol/L), and the uric acid value was 393.8 umol/L (reference range: 134–415 umol/L). The 24-hour urine volume was only 350 ml (reference range: 300-1500 ml), and the 24-hour urine protein quantity was 0.416 g (reference range: 0.03–0.15 g/24 h). Urine-specific gravity is 1.010 (reference range: 1.015–1.025), and pH is 7.0 (reference range: 5.5–6.5). The urinary protein and creatinine ratio was 4.32 mg/mmol (reference range: ≤0.2 mg/mmol), urinary microalbumin was 595.0 mg/L (reference range: 0–20 mg/L), α1-microglobulin was 39.56 mg/L (reference range: 0–12 mg/L), urinary transferrin was 2.52 mg/L (reference range: <1 mg/L), and urinary β2-microglobulin was 422.70 ug/L (reference range: 0-300 ug/L). His parathyroid hormone level was 739.400 pg/mL (reference range: 15–65 pg/mL). These data indicate that the child’s renal function is significantly abnormal. Moreover, routine blood tests showed that the value of erythrocytes was 2.28 × 10^12/L (reference range: 3.5–5.5 × 10^12/L) and the hemoglobin value was 65 g/L (reference range: 120–170 g/L), suggesting moderate anemia. The patient had no family history and no genetic disease or nephropathy among his family members. He has three healthy sisters, and his mother has experienced three miscarriages. The child has a unique appearance and multi-system and multi-organ abnormalities of the body.
test_results: The patient carried a c.2590 C > T (p.Gln864*) nonsense variant and a c.2408_2416del (p.Asn803_Ala805del) in-frame variant of the WDR35 gene (NM_001006657), which were derived from his father and mother, respectively.

case_report: A 30-year-old male presented with persistent proteinuria. His medical history included hypertension and dyslipidemia. He was treated with angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, statins, and a trial of oral steroids, but there was no change in proteinuria levels. Family history revealed familial dyslipidemia among several first-degree relatives. His sister had end-stage renal disease (ESRD) and was on hemodialysis, with the cause of ESRD undetermined. The patient reported no symptoms except for lower-limb edema at initial presentation. On examination, his blood pressure was 159/95 mmHg, pulse 82/min, and he was afebrile. He denied urinary symptoms, loin pain, or analgesic use. Physical examination showed a healthy-looking young male of average build with a body mass index of 24.8 kg/m2. Cardiovascular, chest, neurological, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Notably, bilateral corneal ring opacities were observed. Laboratory results showed serum creatinine at 1.31 mg/dl, normal serum electrolytes, hemoglobin at 13 g/dl, and platelets at 200 × 109/L. Serology for hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, and HIV 1 and 2 antibodies were negative. Serum total cholesterol was 309 mg/dl, triglycerides 545 mg/dl, LDL 177 mg/dl, and HDL 23 mg/dl. Liver enzymes and coagulation profile were within normal limits. Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) was negative, and complement C3 and C4 levels were normal. Urinalysis indicated protein 3+ and red blood cells 20-30 per high power field. The 24-hour proteinuria was 3.55 grams. Renal ultrasound showed bilateral echogenic kidneys with the right kidney measuring 10.1 cm and the left kidney 10.4 cm.
test_results: Light microscopy with periodic acid-Schiff stain revealed glomerular mesangial matrix expansion and irregular thickening of the glomerular basement membranes. When stained with Jones Methenamine Silver, it further illustrated the glomerular basement membranes with an irregular vacuolated appearance. Immunofluorescence microscopy was negative for immunoglobulins and complement components. Electron microscopy revealed lipid deposits appearing as abundant lacunae. The lacunae contains electron-lucent deposits with an electron-dense core involving the mesangial matrix as well as the glomerular basement membranes.

case_report: A 30-month-old boy experienced cardiac arrest during anesthesia induction with sevoflurane and nitric oxide before undergoing plastic surgery for bilateral cutaneous syndactyly of the fingers (third, fourth, and fifth digits) on June 7, 2004. Sinus rhythm was restored after 10 minutes of resuscitation. Prior to the operation, the patient had not undergone any electrocardiographic evaluation. An echocardiogram showed no intracardiac anomalies and normal ventricular function. Preoperative biochemical analysis and electrolyte levels were normal. The patient presented with a round face, small upper jaw and teeth, and nearly bald head. He had fused fingers but normal toes, no history of seizures or syncope, and normal neurodevelopment. He was born via vaginal delivery without complications. The patient's family, including his older sister, had no history of syncope, seizure, or sudden death. Electrocardiographic evaluation of the father, mother, and sister showed no significant QT interval prolongation. An epinephrine stress test on his sister revealed a paradoxical QT interval prolongation (QTc baseline 0.4 → peak 0.53 sec), though she remained asymptomatic. Genetic tests were not conducted on the patient's parents and sister.
test_results: An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed a prolonged QT interval (QTc, 0.58-0.60 sec). During the Holter study, T-wave alternans and functional 2:1 AV block due to QT prolongation was also observed. The result of the gene study performed during this time was negative for KCNQ1 and KCNH2 mutations. At the age of 10 yr (2011), mutations were absent in the KCNE1, KCNE2, and SCN5A genes, but point mutation c.1216G > A in exon 9 in CACNA1C was confirmed.

case_report: The patient is a 28-year-old female, the only child of consanguineous parents from São Miguel, Portugal, born after a full-term pregnancy without complications. Starting from the second day after birth, she experienced hemorrhagic blistering of the skin and oral mucosa, along with a hoarse cry. At around 5–6 years old, she had recurrent upper respiratory infections, extensive nail dystrophy, and weak hair. Her hair was thin, dull, and shed extensively, although no specific tests on hair morphology were conducted. Developmental milestones were normal except for weight, which was below the 5th percentile. Skin blistering decreased with age, but hair loss from the scalp and eyebrows increased without preceding blistering in those areas. Muscle weakness began in adolescence and progressively worsened, leading to difficulty in performing daily activities. No similar cases were reported in the family. Physical examination revealed sparse, tense hemorrhagic blisters and crusts on the body, diffuse non-scarring alopecia on the scalp, and thinning of the eyebrows. Laboratory tests showed normal thyroid hormone function, and there was no family history of alopecia. All 20 nails exhibited onychodystrophy (pachyonychia). Dental issues included caries and enamel hypoplasia. The patient also had dysphonia and severe muscle atrophy in the extremities. Neurological examination showed profoundly diminished reflexes.
test_results: This strategy revealed the patient to be homozygous for the novel nonsense mutation PLEC (NM_000445):c.7159G > T (NP_000336:p.Glu2387*) in exon 31. Bioinformatic analysis revealed a score of 9 at this mutated position, indicating a very high sequence evolutionary conservation. Both results showed a probable deleterious effect with a PROVEAN score of − 3.158 (cut-off value of − 2.5), and a prediction value of 1 for Mutation Taster. The PLEC:c.7159G > T (p.Glu2387*) mutation results in a premature stop codon, which predicts truncated polypeptides and may also cause down regulation of the corresponding mRNA through nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. Putative splice site variants were also analyzed by two in silico tools, both suggesting that this mutation has no impact on splicing.
diagnosis: epidermolysis bullosa simplex with muscular dystrophy and diffuse alopecia
Orpha_name: Epidermolysis bullosa simplex with muscular dystrophy

case_report: A 3-month-old male was admitted to Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hospital presenting with recurrent cough, prolonged fever, and an axillary mass. He is the second child of healthy, unrelated parents, born at full term with a birth weight of 3.7 kg and a 5-minute Apgar score of 10.
