Upon admission, the patient exhibited a widespread erythematous rash on his torso. Physical examination revealed tachycardia and rough pulmonary breath sounds. There was moderate enlargement of the liver and spleen, as well as tender, enlarged bilateral axillary lymph nodes. A chest X-ray indicated pneumonia on the right side. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin levels at 100 g/l and platelet levels at 185 × 10^9/l. C-Reactive protein was elevated at 82.5 mg/dl (normal < 5 mg/dl), procalcitonin was 0.2 ng/ml (normal < 0.1 ng/ml), and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 45 mm/h (normal < 15 mm/h). Tests for 1-3-β-D glucan and galactomannan for fungal infections were negative, as were tests for rubella, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasma, herpes, and HIV. Syphilis tests, including the tolulized red unheated serum test and treponema pallidum particle agglutination assay, were also negative. The purified protein derivative skin test was negative, and liver and renal function tests were within normal limits. Analysis of T cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) in the patient and his parents showed that the patient had 5 TREC copies, significantly lower than the age-matched healthy control group, which had 178 copies (range, 102–319; P < 0.001).
test_results: Whole exome sequencing revealed a paternally inherited frameshift mutation (c.2491_2497del, p. K830fsX4) and a missense mutation (c.2923 C > T, p.R975W) in exon 2 of RAG1.

case_report: The patient is an 11-year-old boy, the first child of a non-consanguineous couple, born at full term following a monitored pregnancy. Initial otoacoustic emissions in the neonatal period were normal. At age 4, he was referred for a pediatric consultation due to a delay in expressive language development. A global developmental delay was identified, with the language area being the most affected. Subsequently, behavioral issues were noted. He began speech and occupational therapy, showing some progress and improvements. At age 8, a cognitive assessment using the Weschler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC III) indicated a full-scale intelligence quotient (IQ) of 55, a verbal IQ of 51, and a performance IQ of 65. His attendance at medical appointments and follow-up tests has been irregular and incomplete.
test_results: Sensorineural hearing loss (70 dB bilaterally) was diagnosed at 9 years.

case_report: A 2.5-month-old girl was admitted to the hospital due to episodes of rapid breathing and pauses in breathing, along with low muscle tone. She is the first child of healthy parents who are related by blood. The baby was born at full term through vaginal delivery after an uneventful pregnancy and did not cry immediately after birth. Upon admission, she exhibited episodes of breathlessness with a respiratory rate reaching up to 100 breaths per minute, alternating with pauses in breathing lasting 15-20 seconds accompanied by cyanosis. Physical examination revealed a weight of 2500 grams (<3rd percentile), a length of 47 cm (<3rd percentile), and a head circumference of 36.5 cm (3rd percentile). Facial features included a broad forehead, arched eyebrows, a left-sided squint, epicanthic folds, and widely spaced eyes. Examination of the oral cavity showed a midline upper lip cleft, bilateral fleshy nodules on the underside of the tongue, bumps on the lower alveolar ridge, and a high-arched palate. Skeletal examination identified post-axial and mesaxial polydactyly of both hands and pre-axial polydactyly of both feet. Other physical examination findings were normal. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, hepatic enzymes, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, electrolytes, blood sugar, and urine analysis, were normal. Echocardiography, abdominal ultrasonography focusing on the kidney, ureter, and bladder region, and ophthalmological examination were normal, except for the left-sided squint. X-ray of both hands confirmed mesaxial polydactyly with a Y-shaped metacarpal.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging showed hypoplasia of the cerebellar hemispheres and vermis and a narrowed isthmus of the mid brain with a characteristic 'molar tooth appearance'.

case_report: A 1-month-old female child was referred from a private hospital for further evaluation. The patient had a history of umbilical discharge on the 27th day after birth. Laboratory results showed a total serum cholesterol level of 7000 mg/dl and serum triglycerides (TGs) of 8530 mg/dl. The child was born to parents who are second-degree relatives.
test_results: Anterior segment of both eyes was within normal limits. Posterior segment revealed small yellowish optic discs, salmon pink retina, and dilated tortuous milky white retinal blood vessels.

case_report: The patient's best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 6/60 in both the right eye (OD) and the left eye (OS). Clinical examination revealed foveal and temporal peripheral schisis in both eyes. Additionally, rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD) was present in both eyes, limited to the temporal schisis areas. A c.583A>G transition resulting in the substitution of isoleucine with valine at position 195 was identified, which has not been previously documented and is not highly conserved across species.
test_results: A c.583A>G variation was identified in an 11-year-old male.

case_report: A 77-year-old female with a medical history of dyslipidemia, hypertension, and hypothyroidism was transferred to our intensive care unit from a community hospital due to a significant skin eruption. She had been hospitalized for approximately one month for cholangitis complicated by sepsis, iatrogenic pancreatitis, and portal vein thrombosis. During her previous hospitalization, she received Piperacillin Tazobactam for 20 days and Ibuprofen as needed. She also underwent two contrast radiologic exams 5 and 21 days before the skin eruption. Upon initial evaluation, the patient was intubated due to severe vasoplegic shock with acute kidney failure. She exhibited erythema covering 80% of her total body surface and skin detachment on 35%, including the external genital area, but no ophthalmic lesions. Multiple bullae with purulent liquid were observed. A positive Nikolsky sign was noted on her arms, abdomen, and neck region. Her body temperature increased to 38.2 Celsius within 24 hours of admission, and her leukocyte level reached 16.8 × 10^9/L. She was treated with intravenous immunoglobulins at a dosage of 1 g/kg/day for three days.
test_results: These biopsies showed sub-corneal pustules with edema of the papillary dermis and an inflammatory infiltrate containing eosinophils. Scattered necrotic keratinocytes were described, but there was no confluent epidermal necrosis. Necrotic keratinocytes were also noted in the intraepidermal portion of a sweat gland. Direct immunofluorescence was negative.

case_report: A 43-year-old female office worker presented in 2020 with a 3-year history of headaches and over a year of cognitive issues. She had been experiencing migraines without aura since 2017, initially lasting a few minutes to half an hour, but progressively worsening in frequency and duration. After more than a year of headaches, she developed memory decline and slow cognitive responses, initially struggling with recall and later showing emotional indifference, abnormal communication, and reticence. She had no prior infectious illnesses. In her thirties, she experienced two ischemic strokes, resulting in slow movements and limb weakness. She also had lumbar spondylosis and lumbago for 5 years, with urinary retention occurring 6 months ago. Her low back pain varied in duration and intensity, sometimes requiring painkillers. She had thinning hair since childhood. There was no history of chronic diseases like hypertension, diabetes, or cardiovascular disorders. Her mother had moderate cerebral infarction and lumbar disc herniation, while her father, who was otherwise healthy, died suddenly in an accident. She has two healthy daughters. Upon admission, physical examination showed normal blood pressure and thinning hair, especially on the crown. There was a decline in response, calculation, and memory retention abilities. Her Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score was 16, and her Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score was 19. She exhibited slow movements, a staggering walk with a spastic gait, and weakened strength in her right arm and both legs. Babinski signs were positive on both sides. Sensory examination and tendon reflex assessment were mostly normal. Blood tests, including immunological indicators, blood routine, blood sugar, blood lipids, antiphospholipid antibodies, and platelet function, showed no abnormalities. Cerebral fluid examination results were normal, with no oligoclonal bands detected.
test_results: Diffuse white matter lesions, infarctions, and microbleeds were observed in the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of her brain. Lumbar spine MRI revealed the presence of lumbar disc herniation and degenerative lesions. A heterozygous missense mutation c.905G>A (p.Arg302Gln) was detected. No Notch 3 mutation was observed. Her mother carried the same mutation but her two daughters did not.
diagnosis: Cerebral Autosomal Recessive Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy

case_report: The patient is a five-year-old girl from Bahrain, born via cesarean section at term to consanguineous parents who are first cousins. Her birth weight was 2.9 kg, and her APGAR scores were 9 and 10 at one and five minutes, respectively. She had a down-slanted palpebral fissure and a cleft palate, which was surgically corrected. She was current with all vaccinations and had no family history of liver or metabolic disorders. At six months old, she presented in Iran with lethargy and loss of appetite but was lost to follow-up. At five years old, she presented again with similar symptoms. Liver function tests showed elevated AST (86 U/L) and ALT (119 U/L). Biochemical tests revealed high ANA (1.83). An abdominal ultrasound indicated a fatty liver of normal size. A liver biopsy was requested, and she was referred to Bahrain for further testing. No other interventions were implemented at that time. Later that year, she visited a pediatric gastroenterologist in Bahrain with continued lethargy, poor appetite, a protruded abdomen, and right upper quadrant pain. She weighed 17.1 kg, was 103 cm tall, and had a BMI of 16.1 kg/m2, placing her in the 33rd percentile for weight and 9th percentile for height. Physical examination showed she was pink, active, and anicteric, with a slightly distended abdomen but no hepatosplenomegaly or ascites. Eye examination was normal. Further investigations ruled out viral hepatitis and other liver disorders. LFTs showed a high ALT (110 U/L). Biochemical tests indicated lipemia, and blood tests showed a normal vitamin D level (53 nmol/L). Tests for hepatitis A, B, and C were negative. Serology tests were positive for EBV IgG and high CMV IgG, with negative IgM for both viruses. Total immunoglobulin levels were normal. Tests for anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, celiac screen, and auto-liver serologies were negative. Serum copper, urinary copper, and ceruloplasmin levels were normal. A repeat upper abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable. The patient was admitted and underwent a liver biopsy. She was started on intravenous methylprednisolone and later discharged on oral prednisolone. After three weeks, she returned with no improvement in LFTs and developed a cushingoid appearance. A liver biopsy with reticulin and Masson trichrome stains showed dense fibrosis of the portal triads without significant inflammatory infiltrates. No giant cell formation was noted in the hepatocytes. Repeat ANA testing was negative, and prednisolone was halted.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing (WES) revealed a homozygous variant of uncertain significance mutation in the AMACR gene (c.553-3A>G).
Orpha_name: Congenital bile acid synthesis defect type 4

case_report: A 70-year-old male presented with fatigue, reduced urinary output, and progressively worsening peripheral edema over the past month. He denied experiencing orthopnea, palpitations, chest pain, cough, sputum production, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. His medical history included arterial hypertension, dyslipidemia, and Parkinson's disease. His medications included losartan, amlodipine, simvastatin plus ezetimibe, rasagiline, levodopa, carbidopa, entacapone, rivastigmine, amantadine, ropinirole, omeprazole, acetylsalicylic acid, mirtazapine, sertraline, diazepam, clonazepam, and quetiapine. Physical examination revealed diminished basal respiratory sounds, pitting edema of the lower limbs, periorbital edema, and anasarca. Laboratory tests indicated mild anemia, mild lymphomonocytosis, acute kidney injury, and urinalysis showed proteins, leukocytes, erythrocytes, and pathological cylinders. Chest radiography indicated pleural effusion. Follow-up studies revealed new onset of mild thrombocytopenia and neutropenia, with a progressive increase in lymphocytosis and no improvement in renal function. Additionally, palpable inguinal adenopathies and splenomegaly were noted. A computed tomography scan on day 7 of admission showed a homogeneous 18 cm spleen, whereas an abdominal ultrasound on the day of admission reported a spleen size of 12.8 cm, which was considered within normal limits.
test_results: The immunophenotypic study revealed the presence of 9.68x103/µL leukocytes, of which 7.30x103/µL were lymphocytes. Of these, 95.88% were T lymphocytes, of which 94.33% were CD4, 5.53% were CD8, 0.08% were doubly positive, and 0.16% were doubly negative for CD4 and CD8. Of the CD4 cells, 95% were detected to have clonality to the Vbeta2 region of the T-cell receptor (TCR) and to have overexpression of the oncogene TCL1. Lymph node biopsy showed diffuse interfollicular proliferation of small lymphocytes with slight atypia and patent mitotic activity, which in the immunohistochemical study were positive for CD3, with a marked predominance of CD4 (90% of cells) over CD8 (only 10% cells).

case_report: A 22-year-old male reported a 10-year history of progressive brownish-black discoloration on the backs of his hands and feet. The pigmentation gradually extended to the front and back surfaces of his limbs, neck, and chest. His medical history was otherwise unremarkable, with no photosensitivity, chemical exposure, or significant drug use. There was no family history of similar symptoms or consanguinity among his parents. Physical examination showed punctate, irregular, slightly atrophic brown macules in a reticulate pattern on the backs of his hands and feet, as well as on the extensor and flexor surfaces of his forearms, and the flexor aspects of his neck and chest. Brownish pigmentation was also noted on his palms, with absent dermatoglyphics beyond the distal crease, and his fingernails were dystrophic. Plantar pitting was observed. His facial skin and teeth appeared normal. Systemic examination did not reveal any abnormalities. Routine laboratory tests, including complete blood counts, urinalysis, liver function tests, renal function tests, and serum electrolytes, were all within normal limits. Tests for Venereal Disease Research Laboratory and ELISA for HIV were nonreactive.
test_results: Skin biopsy showed digitate and filiform elongation of rete ridges, with clumps of heavy melanin pigmentation at their tips. There was melanin incontinence in the papillary dermis.

case_report: A 7-month-old male infant with Fitzpatrick type 5 skin presented with a history of multiple dark-colored skin lesions on the trunk for five months. There were no associated symptoms such as wheezing, flushing, vomiting, or diarrhea. The patient had no history of hospitalization for drug allergy or anaphylaxis, and there was no relevant family history. Physical examination revealed multiple hyperpigmented macules on the back and chest. Gentle rubbing of the lesions produced wheals. Dermoscopic examination using a hand-held dermatoscope (Dermlite DL3, 3Gen Inc, USA) and images captured with a Sony DSC W-800 20.1 MP digital camera (Sony Corp., Tokyo, Japan) showed a dark brown pigment network, which is an exaggeration of the reticular pigment network seen in normal skin. This pigment network corresponds to melanin accumulation in the basal layer of the epidermis.
test_results: Histopathology of lesion over the back showed increased melanization of the basal layer with nests of oval mast cells infiltrating the upper and lower dermis with metachromatic granules visualized using toluidine blue stain.

case_report: A 22-year-old male visited the University of Florida College of Dentistry, Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery clinic with concerns about his jaw. He reported lifelong poor dentition and described his teeth as deteriorating. His medical history was otherwise unremarkable, with no significant family history. He denied experiencing pain, numbness, facial asymmetry, or drainage. An intraoral examination identified condyloma acuminatum on the lower lip.
test_results: A pantomograph revealed mixed radiopaque lesions in the maxilla and mandible with multiple impacted and malformed teeth. The CBCT depicts a generalized multilocular mixed radiopaque appearance in the tooth-bearing regions of both jaws with the trabecular pattern having a mixed lytic and sclerotic appearance. There is absence of enamel in multiple maxillary and mandibular teeth. There is elongated pulp chamber, apically positioned furcation, shortened roots in tooth #19 and molars of right side. The morphology of many of these teeth is consistent with taurodontism. There are multiple large radiolucent spaces within the bone. There is enlargement in several regions of the mandible and maxilla, especially in the left side of the mandible. There is thinning of the buccal cortical plate on the left side of the mandible and disruption of the lingual cortical plate.

case_report: A 50-year-old woman with no notable medical history was referred for a retroperitoneal mass. An abdominal pelvic CT scan identified a homogeneous adipocytic mass measuring 30 cm in the right retroperitoneal area, encasing the right kidney and displacing the right colon to the left. A core needle biopsy (CNB) was performed, and pathology indicated a well-differentiated liposarcoma (WDLPS) with MDM2 amplification confirmed by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). The patient was enrolled in a protocol comparing preoperative radiotherapy to surgery alone and was assigned to the surgery alone group. The surgical procedure involved a compartmental resection of the tumor along with the kidney, the colon, and the aponeurosis of the psoas. Pathological analysis of the resected specimen confirmed a 30 x 26 cm WDLPS grade 1 with negative resection margins. Ten months later, an abdominal CT scan showed a 5-6 cm undifferentiated mass on the mesentery near the staple line of the ileocolic anastomosis. Due to the inaccessibility of the location for a CNB, the multidisciplinary tumor board (MTB) considered it a local recurrence. Given the short interval since the initial surgery, the patient received neoadjuvant chemotherapy with four cycles of doxorubicin. Post-chemotherapy surgery revealed the tumor attached to the ileocolic anastomosis. The previous anastomosis and the mesentery were resected, and a new anastomosis was performed. Pathological examination of the specimen showed a 6 x 5 cm fibroblastic proliferation without microscopic features of malignancy. Fluorescence in situ hybridization showed no MDM2 amplification.
test_results: Genetic analysis showed a mutation in the exon 3 of the CTNNB1 gene (T41A) coding for beta-catenin.

case_report: A 30-year-old male patient visited the dermatology outpatient department with multiple dark, raised skin lesions on the trunk, face, and upper limbs, persisting for the past 3 years. The patient reported that the lesions, which were occasionally itchy, initially appeared on the face and subsequently spread to the chest, back, and upper limbs. Over time, the lesions increased in both size and number. There was no reported sensitivity to sunlight, and no similar skin conditions were observed in other family members. Physical examination of the skin revealed the presence of hyperkeratotic plaques and annular plaques with raised margins on both exposed and non-exposed areas of the body.
test_results: Skin biopsy revealed marked hyperkeratosis, irregular acanthosis, and papillomatosis. Multiple foci of vertical layered parakeratosis and few foci of hypergranulosis were seen. Base of the parakeratotic columns contained vacuolated keratinocytes with few apoptotic keratinocytes and dyskeratotic cells. Lymphohistiocytic infiltrates and melanophages were noted in the upper dermis.

case_report: The patient is a 35-year-old male who reported experiencing temperature fluctuations since November 2020. These episodes, occurring two to three times daily, alternated between intense sweating and low body temperature with chills, each lasting a few hours before subsiding. Upon initial presentation, the patient's oral temperature was recorded at 92°F (33.3°C). Physical examination noted features including a child-like facial appearance, a wide and flat nasal bridge, closely set eyes, a tongue with irregular patches, and widespread sweating.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain demonstrated dysgenesis of the corpus callosum and Viking's helmet appearance of the lateral ventricles. The patient was subsequently transferred to an outside hospital where an MRI pituitary was obtained, demonstrating no pituitary pathologies on imaging but re-demonstrating severe corpus callosum dysgenesis as well as absent septum pellucidum with hypoplastic cingulate gyrus, possibly fused anteriorly, and azygos configuration of the anterior cerebral artery, possibly representing mild holoprosencephaly or lobar holoprosencephaly.

case_report: On 16 December 2014, a 4-year-old Chinese boy was admitted to the hospital with a 2-year history of persistent microscopic hematuria and recurrent pneumonia. Since the age of 2, he had been hospitalized four times for pneumonia. Physical examination revealed wheezing on pulmonary auscultation, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, otitis media, and sinusitis. Multiple enlarged lymph nodes were found in the neck, axilla, and inguinal region. Laboratory tests showed perinuclear ANCA positivity and immunoglobulin levels of IgG 20.8 g/L (reference range 9–13), IgM 2.49 g/L (0.5–1.8), IgA 1.98 g/L (0.6–1.5), IgG1 24.80 g/L (4.9–11.4), and IgG2 1.87 g/L (1.5–6.4). Urinary microscopic examination revealed 50 red cells per high-power field, with 70% of the urinary erythrocytes being heteromorphic. A CT scan showed pneumonia and bronchiectasis, hepatosplenomegaly, multiple lymph node enlargement, bilateral maxillary sinusitis, ethmoid sinusitis, and bilateral mastoiditis. A bone marrow biopsy indicated granulocyte proliferation without significant dysplasia or blast expansion. An excisional biopsy of a left inguinal lymph node showed reactive lymph node hyperplasia, with no antibodies to Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) found in the lymph node. Bronchoscopy revealed cobblestone-like changes in the airway mucosa, and alveolar lavage fluid contained a large number of red blood cells with a high number of EBV DNA copies (2.8 × 105 copies/mL). Renal biopsy showed mild mesangial cell proliferation with no immune deposits. The patient began treatment with oral prednisone (initial dose of 20 mg/day). From March to July 2015, he received intravenous cyclophosphamide (CTX) once every 2 weeks for a total of seven treatments (cumulative dose of 2.8 g). Subsequently, he was treated with oral mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) (0.25 g twice per day). Immunotherapy improved his hematuria and reduced his lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. He was also started on oral trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis (0.24 g twice per day, later reduced to once per day) to prevent infections. Although he continued to have intermittent respiratory tract infections, the frequency decreased. Ganciclovir was administered to treat his EBV infection. In April 2015, a right lung biopsy showed peribronchiolar infiltration of lymphocytes, proliferation of fibrous tissue and collagen fibers, and alveolar dilatation, with no necrosis or vasculitis. In March 2016, the patient again had enlarged left cervical lymph nodes and microscopic hematuria. An excisional biopsy of a left cervical lymph node showed similar results to previous findings, and flow cytometry identified no significant malignant clonality. Peripheral blood tests showed persistently low levels of lymphocytes, low percentages of CD19- and CD20-positive cells, decreased or reversed CD4/CD8 ratios, and persistent positivity for EBV early antigen-IgM and cytomegalovirus IgM. These findings indicated immunodeficiency. He received one session of intravenous Ig (IVIG) replacement therapy (30 g) on demand during severe infection. Beginning in April 2017, the frequency of pneumonia increased. CT scans showed worsening pulmonary lesions and bronchiectasis, along with enlarged lymph nodes in the mediastinum and other regions. Increasing the glucocorticoid dose did not result in improvement.
test_results: Whole-exome sequencing revealed a c.1574A>G mutation in PIK3CD.

case_report: A 27-year-old woman reported experiencing severe lower back pain radiating to the thoracic region for one month, along with a low-grade fever. An outpatient MRI of the thoracolumbar spine was conducted. Her medical history includes a congenital right foot deformity that has been surgically treated since she was 13 years old. At age 17, initial investigations of the lower extremities revealed scoliosis, but a detailed examination at that time did not identify multiple congenital abnormalities, which are now evident upon closer inspection. The patient also has a longstanding pilonidal cyst with recent symptoms of low-grade fever and persistent discharge, requiring further investigation. Her mother had an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, with no history of gestational diabetes, folate deficiency, maternal obesity, or exposure to teratogenic medications. Neurological examination showed intact cranial innervation. Weakness in dorsiflexion of the right foot (1–2 points) was noted, related to bone lengthening surgery performed at age 13, while muscle strength in other muscle groups was graded at 5 points. Romberg’s test demonstrated stability, and coordination tests were performed accurately. The patient exhibited an antalgic posture, and her gait was cautious. A right-sided scoliotic curvature was observed, with bilateral equal tendon reflexes (+), and tenderness was noted paravertebrally in the lumbar spine upon palpation. Meningeal symptoms were absent, and functions of the pelvic region remained unaffected.
test_results: The MRI examination of the thoracolumbar spine unveiled several intricate anatomical abnormalities. Scoliosis was evident within the thoracolumbar region, coupled with vertebral rotation. A butterfly deformity of the T11 vertebra was observed, with fusion of its right side to the T12 vertebral body. Multiple sacral vertebrae defects were identified, classified as type IVB hemisacrum according to Pang’s classification. Notably, a complete absence of the S5 and coccyx (Co1–5) vertebrae was confirmed, indicating full coccygeal agenesis. Further examination revealed sacralization of the L5 vertebra on the right side, classified as Castellvi IIIA. Posterior arch defects (spina bifida) were uniformly present across all sacral vertebrae. Moreover, intricate spinal cord anomalies were noted, including conus medullaris positioned below the L2 level and diastematomyelia type II—characterized by a split spinal cord with a single thecal sac initiating from the L1 level. Remarkably, the dural sac extended seamlessly into the sacral region without any discernible inelastic structures. Additionally, a cystic collection indicative of syringomyelia was detected at the Th12-L1 level across T1, T2, and STIR sequences. Further pathology included multiple instances of disc protrusions and foraminal stenosis predominantly concentrated at the L4–L5 level. Lastly, a sinus tract extending from the end of the spinal canal to the skin was identified.

case_report: A 3-year-old Japanese girl presented with short, tightly curled scalp hair since birth, and sparse scalp hair was noted. Her facial and body hair appeared normal but were lighter in color compared to her mother's hair. No hormonal abnormalities were observed, and routine laboratory results were within normal limits. The patient had a history of atopic dermatitis diagnosed two years prior to the clinic visit. Her father and brother also had atopic dermatitis, and her brother had asthma. There was no family history of hair disorders. The patient had no history of systemic diseases, trauma, or exposure to radiation or medications. Trichoscopy revealed that her hair was undulated, lighter brown than her mother's hair, thinner, and of uniform thickness.
test_results: The direct sequencing of the coding exons in LIPH (NM_139248.3) revealed a homozygous pathogenic variant (rs201249971;c.736 T > A; p.Cys246Ser) in exon 6. The scanning electron microscopic (SEM) examination revealed that her affected hair had an irregular and rough cuticle compared to her mother’s hair. Many irregular small projections and longitudinal grooves were seen on the surface of the patient’s hair shaft, and some free margins of the hair cortex were raised or serrated.

case_report: A 3-year-old male presented with developmental delay and extra digits. The child was born to parents who are not related by blood. The pregnancy was uneventful, and there was no history of birth asphyxia. There were no reports of abnormal breathing patterns, apnea, or unusual movements. Upon examination, the child was conscious, alert, and had stable vital signs. There were no skin abnormalities or facial irregularities. Developmental assessment showed delays in gross motor, fine motor, speech, and social skills, with a developmental age of approximately 9-12 months. There was no evidence of cranial nerve issues, and motor examination revealed generalized hypotonia with normal deep tendon reflexes. Soft-tissue masses were observed on the dorsum of the tongue, and the child had polydactyly with six digits on both hands and the left foot. The child also exhibited signs of protein energy malnutrition Grade II and rickets; other clinical examinations were normal. Laboratory investigations, including complete blood count, thyroid function test, arterial blood gas, renal function test, electrolytes, and liver function test, were all within normal limits.
test_results: MRI revealed vermis hypoplasia with deep interpeduncular fossa with thick and elongated superior cerebellar peduncle and midbrain giving 'molar tooth' appearance. In addition, there was heterotrophic gray matter in the right centrum semiovale and periventricular white matter.
diagnosis: Joubert Syndrome with orofacial digital features

case_report: A 35-year-old male patient visited the outpatient clinic with complaints of reduced vision in his left eye for two months. He reported no pain, sensitivity to light, redness, history of trauma, previous episodes of eye inflammation, or prior laser treatments. The patient had no history of systemic conditions such as diabetes, hypertension, or high cholesterol. On examination, his best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/20 in the right eye and limited to counting fingers at 50 cm in the left eye. The anterior segments of both eyes appeared normal. Fundus examination of the right eye was unremarkable, while the left eye showed extensive lipid exudates in the macular area involving the fovea, forming a plaque-like exudate measuring approximately two-disc diameters vertically and two and a half-disc diameters horizontally, with areas of microaneurysms and telangiectatic vessels. Additionally, there was a peripheral inferotemporal vascular malformation with adjacent retinal hemorrhage. No signs of inflammation, vasculitis, drusen, retinal pigment epithelial changes, or evidence of healed choroiditis were observed in either eye.
test_results: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) (OS) showed significant macular edema, while (OD) was unremarkable. Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) (OS) showed a hypofluorescent area in the macula due to blockage of the background fluorescence by macular lipid exudates and leakage from telangiectatic vessels. There was also a well-defined inferotemporal hyperfluorescent area corresponding to abnormal vasculature with leakage, and FFA (OD) was normal.

case_report: An 18-year-old female presented with skin discoloration on the left side of the face, present since childhood. Physical examination revealed a bluish patch covering the forehead, area around the eyes, temple, cheek, and jaw region. Examination of the left eye showed dark pigmentation of the conjunctiva, bulging of the cornea, corneal opacity, and an appearance of the eye being pushed forward. The right eye appeared normal. Visual acuity was no light perception in the left eye and 20/20 in the right eye. Ultrasound of the left eye showed no intraocular mass and indicated optic nerve head cupping; the axial length was measured at 31 mm. A previously conducted MRI of the brain was reported as normal.
test_results: Histopathological examination of enucleated eye revealed melanocytic proliferation in the conjunctiva, iris, cilary body, choroid and sclera.

case_report: A 39-year-old female presented with several months of right knee pain, swelling, and instability, especially when descending stairs. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medications provided only mild relief. She reported no night pain, systemic symptoms, or recent trauma. Her medical history included congenital hip dysplasia, and there was no family history of inflammatory diseases, bone disorders, or dysplasia. Physical examination revealed a mild antalgic gait, right knee effusion, and tenderness along the lateral joint line. A firm, palpable mass was noted on the anterolateral proximal tibia without erythema or skin ulceration. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable.
test_results: Radiographs of the right knee revealed an unusual calcific density measuring 2.0 cm × 1.0 cm above the anterolateral tibial plateau. Computed tomography (CT) of the right knee revealed an exophytic, lobulated, sclerotic mass measuring 2.4 cm × 0.9 cm × 0.8 cm involving the anterolateral margin of the anterior lip of the lateral tibial plateau. An MRI showed a 1.2 cm well-marginated lesion abutting the anterolateral cortical surface of the lateral tibial plateau following bone marrow on all sequences. Whole body bone scan also revealed mild to moderate uptake at the site of the lesion.

case_report: A 4-year-old female patient was admitted to Children’s Hospital Affiliated to Zhengzhou University with recurrent upper respiratory infections lasting for 2 months. Despite antibiotic treatment, there was no improvement. The patient and her parents, all Han Chinese from Henan province of China, had no recorded family history of similar conditions. The study received approval from the ethics committee of Children’s Hospital Affiliated to Zhengzhou University, and written informed consent for publishing data and images was obtained from the parents. The patient presented with a low fever and cough, with a recorded temperature of 38.5 °C during regular examination. Physical examination revealed hypopigmentation of the skin on the neck and knee, and slight hepatomegaly was detected via supersonic inspection. Blood analysis indicated a reduction in platelets (PLT, 88*10^9/L) and white blood cells (WBC, 2.7*10^9/L), while red blood cell count was normal (RBC, 4.9*10^12/L). Peripheral smear showed leukocytes with giant intracytoplasmic inclusions, which was confirmed by bone marrow aspirate. Neurological examination results were normal.
test_results: Genetic test for the patient and her parents was recommended.

case_report: A 65-year-old Chinese woman with a medical history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, systemic hypertension, and hypothyroidism underwent cemented total knee arthroplasty (TKA) in October 2017 for osteoarthritis. Postoperatively, she was administered intravenous cefuroxime. On the second day after surgery, she developed a fever of 39.3°C and erythema at the wound site. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 25.5 × 10^9 cells/L, C-reactive protein levels of 201 mg/L (normal: 0–10), and procalcitonin levels of 0.16 ng/mL (normal: 0–0.05). Systemic antibiotics were administered. Despite 8 days of antibiotic treatment, the wounds did not improve and became painful. On the ninth postoperative day (hospital day 12), she underwent surgical irrigation and debridement with retention of the prosthesis. Negative pressure wound therapy was initiated due to superficial necrosis around the wound. The patient exhibited a suboptimal response to insulin therapy. Blood cultures, Gram staining of direct smears from the discharge, and wound cultures from debridement were all negative. Histology showed neutrophil infiltration into the soft tissue of the knee. The fever persisted, and the lesion rapidly worsened and increased in size, with the wound showing yellow-white pus, black crusts, and a clear red border. A pus blister appeared on the ipsilateral lower leg 2 days after debridement. Emergent debridement and resection of the prosthesis were performed on hospital day 17. Postoperatively, the patient was transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) due to 2 quickSOFA points (30–35 breaths per minute, somnolence). The wound showed minimal purulence and persistent superficial necrosis. All wound cultures remained negative, but a pus swab culture obtained in the ICU revealed extensively drug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii. Despite two rounds of debridement and broad-spectrum antibiotics, the lesion continued to worsen. The wound's infectious status was unclear to both physicians and surgeons. An unbiased metagenomic approach detected A. baumannii from superficial tissue swabs of the pus blister on the ipsilateral lower leg, while deep samples remained negative. Tests for ANCA, ANA, and anti-CCP were negative.
test_results: Abundant neutrophilic inflammation in the dermis and subcutaneous cellular tissue.

case_report: A 68-year-old male was admitted to the Emergency County Hospital in Arad, Romania, presenting with superior digestive tract hemorrhage. His medical history includes type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and previous surgeries (cholecystectomy and dental extraction without prolonged postoperative bleeding). The patient experienced an initial bleeding episode at home and was brought to the Emergency Room (ER) an hour later. Endoscopic hemostasis using clips was performed, temporarily stopping the bleeding. During the procedure, the patient lost consciousness, necessitating orotracheal intubation and subsequent admission to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU). Upon ICU admission, the patient had an altered mental status (Glasgow Coma Scale – 12) and required ventilator support (synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation). Hemodynamic status was stable with a blood pressure of 100/60 mmHg. Laboratory results on admission were: hemoglobin 6.3 g/dL, hematocrit 22%, blood urea 94 mg/dL, blood creatinine 0.7 mg/dL, lactic acid 4.5 mmol/l, glycemia 350 mg/dL, activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) 38 seconds, international normalized ratio (INR) 0.8, transaminases 9.9 U/L, direct bilirubin 0.13 mg/dL, total bilirubin 0.3 mg/dL, serum total protein 5 g/dL, serum albumin 28 g/L. The patient received transfusions of whole blood and fresh frozen plasma, along with continuous saline and colloid infusion. Hemostatic and prokinetic agents, as well as a continuous infusion of proton pump inhibitor (Pantoprazole), were administered. Osmotic diuretic therapy was used to manage pulmonary congestion and potential cerebral edema. The patient's condition improved, and he was weaned off the ventilator two days after ICU admission. Radiographs indicated changes in pulmonary congestion. Despite initial treatment, the patient experienced four additional bleeding episodes, prompting further endoscopic hemostasis attempts. Chest CT angiography was performed to investigate potential complications. Due to prolonged prothrombin time unresponsive to transfusions, additional clinical investigations were conducted. Blood samples were sent to an external laboratory, with results available after 3–4 days.
test_results: The low plasma value of FVIII was established through coagulometer test (12% of the normal value).

case_report: A 12-year-old girl was admitted with fainting episodes, including one after climbing stairs. She was born to non-consanguineous parents and had no history of systemic disease, medication use, or toxin exposure. She had two previous fainting episodes during exercise four months earlier. On physical examination, her heart rate was 95 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 25 per minute, and blood pressure was 90/55 mmHg. Her body temperature was 37 °C. While awake, her respiratory sounds were diminished. Laboratory tests revealed leukocytosis (13,500 mm3) and elevated acute phase reactants (erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 83 mm/h; C-reactive protein: 8.2 mg/dL). Chest X-ray showed bilateral diffuse pneumonic consolidation and mild cardiomegaly. Electrocardiography (ECG) showed stable ST depression but was otherwise normal. Echocardiography revealed thickening of the mitral and aortic valves, mild mitral valve insufficiency, and a mildly dilated left ventricle with normal systolic function (ejection fraction: 68%). Troponin-1 level was elevated (66 mcg/dL, upper limit: 0.04 mcg/dL). Influenza A virus DNA was detected by respiratory viral panel screening. Toxicologic screening was negative, and throat, blood, and urine cultures were negative. Antistreptolysin O titer was within normal limits. Cranial computed tomography and electroencephalography were normal. No arrhythmia was detected by 24-hour ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring. Intravenous immunoglobulin was administered for myocarditis treatment. Combined wide-spectrum antibiotics and antiviral oseltamivir treatments were initiated. By the third day, she had no complaints, and acute phase reactants and cardiac markers were negative. Chest X-ray showed normal cardiac size and clear lung fields. Antibiotics were discontinued after ruling out bacterial infection. However, stable ST depression persisted in the inferior leads on ECG. Computed tomography coronary angiography displayed a suspected atheroma plaque in the left anterior descending (LAD) aorta. She experienced another fainting episode, with ECG showing ST depression in the inferior leads, but cardiac markers were negative. A cardiovascular stress test showed significant ST depression in the inferior leads.
test_results: Conventional coronary angiography revealed a significant occlusion of the LAD artery and circumflex artery. High serum levels of total cholesterol (756 mg/dL) and LD-cholesterol (LDL-C) (556 mg/dL) were noticed. Carotid artery Doppler imaging showed moderate occlusion in both carotid arteries.

case_report: A 10-day-old male neonate arrived at the emergency department exhibiting cyanosis, which had progressively worsened since birth. Pulse oximetry indicated severe hypoxia, with an oxygen saturation level of 62%. An infusion of prostaglandin E1 was administered, resulting in an improvement of oxygen saturation to 80%. Clinical evaluation noted persistent cyanosis without signs of heart failure. Auscultation revealed a normal first heart sound and a single second heart sound, accompanied by a grade 3/6 systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border. The patient showed no signs of respiratory distress, cardiomegaly, or hepatomegaly. A chest radiograph displayed a left-sided heart of normal size with pulmonary oligemia. The electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm, right axis deviation, and right ventricular hypertrophy.
test_results: The echocardiogram showed usual arrangement of the abdominal vessels and atrial appendages. The systemic and pulmonary venoatrial connections were normal. The atrioventricular connections were concordant. The aortic root was seen to be overriding the crest of a deficient ventricular septum, with half supported by each ventricle in the presence of discontinuity between the leaflets of the aortic and mitral valves. There was continuity between the leaflets of the tricuspid and mitral valves posteroinferiorly, making the septal defect perimembranous, and the right ventricular outflow was atretic. The great arterial trunks spiraled as they extended into the mediastinum, with the pulmonary trunk lying to the left and anterior of the aorta. The pulmonary arteries themselves were confluent and good-sized, with the right and left arteries measuring 5 mm and 4.5 mm in diameter, respectively. A vascular channel arising from the ascending aorta could be traced to a termination at the confluence of the pulmonary arteries. The channel was constricted at its pulmonary end, resulting in a gradient of 30 mmHg on Doppler interrogation. Computed tomography was performed for better demonstration of the anatomy, confirming the origin of the vascular channel from the posteromedial aspect of the ascending aorta proximal to the origin of the brachiocephalic artery, and demonstrating its tortuous course to its termination at the confluence of the pulmonary arteries.
diagnosis: Persistence of the artery of the fifth pharyngeal arch

case_report: A 69-year-old Caucasian female was admitted to the University Hospital, Roskilde, in August 2014, presenting with high fever and septicaemia. Two weeks prior, she had visited her general practitioner due to fever and was prescribed penicillin for suspected pneumonia. A few days later, she was admitted to the surgical department with abdominal and lower back pain, and diarrhea. Her medical history included hypertension managed with two-drug therapy and a smoking history of over 50 years. She was transferred to other hospitals twice for further evaluation of potential aorta aneurism and cholecystitis. Initial laboratory results showed normal hemoglobin and leukocyte levels, but thrombocytes were 53 × 10^9/L (normal range: 145–390 × 10^9/L). C-reactive protein (CRP) was significantly elevated at 210 mg/L (normal value <8 mg/L) and Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was 1770 U/L (normal range: 105–205 U/L). The leukocyte differential count indicated an abnormal state.
test_results: Flow cytometry confirmed a serious leukemic condition.

case_report: An 11-year-old male patient presented with a history of generalized weakness persisting for over six years. He had been treated at multiple hospitals with various empirical treatments, including multivitamins and antibiotics, but showed minimal to no clinical improvement. The parent reported poor academic performance, frequent falls, inability to keep up with peers during sports due to excessive fatigue, progressive muscle weakness, and difficulty climbing stairs. There was no history of muscle pain, preceding trauma, or signs of infection. Family history indicated that his maternal uncle, now in his late teens, had similar symptoms and is currently bedridden. On physical examination, the patient exhibited slight muscle wasting, was fully conscious with a Montreal cognitive assessment score of 20, indicating significant cognitive impairment. He was afebrile (36.7°C) and displayed a waddling gait, lumbar hyperlordosis, toe walking, reduced power in the proximal muscles of the lower limbs, calf hypertrophy, flat feet (pes planus), and a positive Gowers’ sign. Cranial nerve examination was normal, and there were no signs of upper or lower motor neuron lesions. Laboratory investigations revealed a normal complete blood count, but biochemistry analysis showed significantly elevated levels of creatine kinase (20,232.3 U/L), alanine aminotransferase (206 U/L), aspartate aminotransferase (192.4 U/L), and lactate dehydrogenase (645 µg/dl).
test_results: Muscle biopsy results revealed an extensive loss of skeletal muscle fibers that are replaced by fat tissue, and extensive fibrosis noted.

case_report: A 24-year-old male presented with lower urinary tract symptoms related to voiding for the past year and a history of two episodes of urinary tract infection (UTI). There were no gastrointestinal or systemic symptoms reported. Clinical examination revealed a palpable bladder and tenderness in the right epididymis, with the rest of the examination being unremarkable. Imaging showed the right kidney was replaced by a 3 × 2 cm cyst located in the right iliac fossa, while the left kidney appeared normal. Routine blood tests were within normal limits. An attempt at per urethral catheterization was unsuccessful, leading to the performance of a suprapubic cystostomy.
test_results: The patient was found to have short midbulbar urethral stricture with right vesicoureteral reflux. Also, opacification of the right vas deferens along the entire course till testis was seen on MCUG.
diagnosis: Ectopic Vas Deferens with Dysplastic Kidney and Urethral Stricture

case_report: A 23-year-old male reported experiencing an absence of sweating, which caused discomfort during the summer months, and a progressively darkening skin tone over the past 17 years. He also noted thickening of the skin on his palms and soles, as well as thinning hair. His medical history was otherwise unremarkable, and there were no similar complaints in his family. Physical examination showed widespread reticulate pigmentation, most noticeable on the trunk and the upper parts of the arms, along with miliaria-like lesions. There was also palmoplantar keratoderma with a yellowish hue. Additional findings included nail dystrophy, nonscarring alopecia in the frontal area, madarosis, and loss of eyelashes. The skin was generally dry. A systemic review did not reveal any additional issues. Routine blood tests were within normal limits. A 10% KOH mount from a fingernail scraping tested positive for fungal elements.
test_results: Biopsy and subsequent histopathological examination revealed the presence of hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, follicular plugging, and basal cell melanization.

case_report: A 28-year-old woman presented with painless swelling in both lower extremities since birth. The swelling, which began in her feet, gradually progressed to include her calves, shins, and lower thighs. By the age of 10, the swelling was prominent in her calves and shins, and during adolescence and early adulthood, it extended to her lower thighs. The swelling was symmetric and equal in both legs. She reported no other symptoms such as weight loss or other systemic issues. Her medical history was unremarkable, and she did not use tobacco or alcohol. She had no known medication allergies. Previous evaluations by multiple providers had not resulted in a definitive diagnosis. On physical examination, she appeared normal and was afebrile with a heart rate of 70/min, blood pressure of 116/76 mm Hg, and a respiratory rate of 14/min. The general examination showed bilateral nonpitting pedal edema up to the mid-calves. There were no signs of ascites, abdominal organ enlargement, or lymph node enlargement. Cardiac and chest examinations were normal, with no murmurs or decreased air entry. Laboratory investigations, including a complete blood cell count with differential, basic metabolic profile, renal function, liver function tests, serum albumin, and inflammatory markers (sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein), were all normal. An ultrasound of the lower extremities with Doppler showed no venous obstruction. Chest X-ray and abdominal and pelvic ultrasounds were also normal.
test_results: There was evidence of decreased uptake of radioactive tracer in proximal lymph nodes (inguinal nodes), suggesting impaired lymphatic drainage in the lower extremities.

case_report: The patient is a 19-year-old Persian male with a history of sinusitis and allergic rhinitis for four years, and episodes of wheezing and shortness of breath for two years. He was admitted due to fever, productive cough, and worsening dyspnea over the past two months. Two weeks before admission, he experienced increased shortness of breath, blood streaks in his sputum, and gradual paresthesia in his right lower leg. On physical examination, he was in respiratory distress with coarse crackles, generalized ronchi, and wheezing at the lung bases. His SPO2 level was 74% upon admission and increased to 91% with 6 liters of 40% oxygen via a venturi mask. Hemodynamics were stable except for tachypnea, and he was not febrile. A complete blood count revealed a white cell count of 18,000 with 23% eosinophils, no anemia, and a platelet count of 215,000 per cubic millimeter. Liver and renal function tests, blood coagulation studies, and electrolytes were within normal limits. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 3mm/h 15 days prior to admission and 14mm/h at the hospital. Blood cultures were negative one week after admission. Urinalysis was normal. Tests for rheumatoid factor (RF), anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA), circulating anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (cANCA), perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (pANCA), as well as C3, C4, and CH50 were negative. The skin tuberculin test (PPD) was negative at 72 hours. Cardiac echography was normal. On the second hospital day, the patient developed hyperesthesia and severe pain in his right lower leg, which led to a foot drop on the same side the following day.
test_results: EMG (electromyography) and NCV (nerve conduction study) studies showed neuritis and axonopathy along the common peroneal nerve located below the right knee level. Lung pathology showed infiltration with eosinophilic and limited number of multinucleated giant cells. Bronchi and lung parenchyma were free of signs of vasculitis but accumulation of eosinophils in the alveoli was seen. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) revealed neither mycobacteria nor cancerous cells.

case_report: Patient 6 is a white male who reported experiencing reduced night and peripheral vision starting at approximately 25 years old. He has no family history of similar symptoms. His medical history includes hearing loss in adulthood, which necessitated the use of hearing aids, and peripheral neuropathy, leading to decreased sensitivity in distal regions and ataxia. Although he did not personally notice any issues with his sense of smell, his wife observed that he often fails to detect odors in their home. At the age of 79, his best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was measured at logMAR 0.9 in the right eye (OD) and 0.5 in the left eye (OS). A retinal examination revealed extensive retinopathy affecting the macula.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed PHYH:c.823C>T. Phytanic acid testing was undertaken and was found to be within normal limits (undetectable levels). Analysis of the patient's BAM file revealed the second variant, c.678+5G>T.

case_report: A 42-year-old male patient presented with swelling on the left side of the mandible for 1 month. Intraoral examination revealed a solitary, oval swelling measuring 4 × 2 cm on the left side of the mandible, extending from teeth 33 to 36. The swelling was hard with a smooth surface, diffuse margins, and was nontender upon palpation. The buccal and lingual cortices were thinned out. The associated pain was insidious, dull, nonradiating, and intermittent. Panoramic radiograph showed a large osteodestructive lesion with well-defined multilocular radiolucency and thin corticated borders on the left side of the mandible, extending from teeth 36 to 45. Fine needle aspiration yielded a serosanguinous fluid containing acute inflammatory cells (mainly polymorphonuclear neutrophils) and cystic macrophages in an eosinophilic background.
test_results: Histopathological examination demonstrated cystic lumen lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium showing prominent basal cells with hyperchromatic nuclei which is polarized. The suprabasal layer resembles stellate reticulm like cells which are proliferating intraluminally with few vacuolated cells. The cystic lining shows squamous metaplasia of varying thickness at many places. The underlying connective tissue capsule shows inductive hyalinized eosinophilic band just beneath the epithelium.

case_report: A 56-year-old Caucasian female, with no prior medical conditions, initially visited her primary care physician due to severe generalized fatigue and muscle pain, particularly in her calves and thighs. She was treated supportively without symptom improvement. A year later, she developed pain in both hips and knees along with prolonged morning stiffness. She also experienced intermittent fevers reaching up to 38.9 °C, which initially occurred at night but later showed no time pattern. A non-itchy intermittent rash began on her chest and later spread more diffusely. Additional symptoms included intermittent bluish discoloration of the fingernails and diarrhea. Tests for Raynaud’s phenomenon and celiac disease were negative. She was referred to rheumatology and dermatology for further evaluation. Due to worsening pain and weakness in her lower extremities, an MRI of the lumbar spine was performed. Autoimmune tests including antinuclear antibody (ANA), rheumatoid factor, perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (p-ANCA), cytoplasmic anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (c-ANCA), SSA/SSB, SM-Ab IgG, and RNP IgG were negative. However, inflammatory markers were elevated with a CRP of 30 mg/L and an ESR of 37 mm/h. Tests for Lyme disease were negative. Additional tests revealed a monoclonal gammopathy of 0.3 g/dL. A skin punch biopsy showed changes consistent with chronic urticaria. The rash persisted despite antihistamine treatment. Due to the combination of symptoms and elevated inflammatory markers, she was started on steroids. Initial response to steroids was followed by a quick recurrence of symptoms upon dose reduction. A 6-month course of Celebrex and Plaquenil was ineffective and discontinued. She underwent right hip arthroplasty due to worsening hip pain, with pathologic examination showing acute and chronic synovitis in the synovial soft tissue. This was followed by left hip arthroplasty, with pathology showing osteocartilaginous tissue with reactive changes, reactive synovium with chronic synovitis, and focal lymphoid aggregates. Neither pathology showed changes indicative of steroid-induced osteonecrosis. Repeated autoimmune tests again showed elevated ESR, CRP, and monoclonal gammopathy. She was started on high-dose steroids and referred to hematology for further evaluation of her monoclonal gammopathy.
test_results: Molecular testing was positive for MYD88, c.794T>C (p.L265P) mutation and negative for C-KIT mutation. Bone marrow biopsy showed a normocellular marrow with maturing myeloid and erythroid series without any immature forms or mast cells. A plasma cell population of 5-10% was seen without light chain restriction. Congo red stain was negative.

case_report: The patient is a 58-year-old woman from Jiangsu Province, China, who presented with symptoms of restless legs and insomnia. Over two years ago, she began experiencing severe discomfort and stiffness in her left lower extremity without any apparent cause, which was temporarily alleviated by movement. A few months later, these symptoms persisted even at rest and during sleep, leading to insomnia. She also reported patchy pain and numbness in the left sole, which worsened upon contact with the floor, making walking difficult. Approximately a year ago, she started acupuncture treatment, which did not alleviate her symptoms. Recently, her symptoms have worsened, with increased discomfort in the left lower limb and mild discomfort in the right lower limb. The prolonged discomfort and insomnia have led to low mood and irritability. She is a non-smoker with no history of hypertension, diabetes, cerebral infarction, or myocardial infarction, and she denied any bladder dysfunction. During the examination, her cooperation was limited. She was alert and oriented but appeared anxious. Her orientation was mostly intact, with no significant memory or calculation impairments. Speech was clear, bilateral nasolabial folds were symmetrical, and the tongue was midline. Both pupils were equal and reactive to light, measuring 3.0 mm in diameter. Examination revealed significant enhancement (++) in bilateral biceps and triceps reflexes, slight elevation in muscle tone in the left lower limb, markedly increased bilateral patellar reflexes (+++), and mild enhancement in bilateral ankle reflexes (+). Muscle strength in both limbs was Grade 5, bilateral Babinski sign was negative, and sensory perception was symmetrical. The neck was relaxed with no signs of Brudzinski’s or Kernig’s signs. Eye assessment showed no abnormalities, hearing was normal, and intelligence was within the normal range. Cerebellar signs were normal.
test_results: The brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the proband showed mild brain atrophy. The spinal cord MRI scans were normal. The findings indicated a reduction in the amplitude of the action potential of the left common peroneal nerve in the proband. The electromyography results revealed the absence of spontaneous muscle activity in the examined muscles of the proband’s left lower limb. The electroencephalogram (EEG) showed mild abnormalities. After analysis, a heterozygous splice variant (chr8:126088744T>C/NM_014846.4: c.712–2A>G) in WASHC5 was identified in the proband. Co-segregation analysis showed that the c.712–2A>G variant was not present in the healthy members (II-1, III-1, III-2, and IV-1) in this family. The c.712–2A>G variant resulted in a 337 nucleotide aberrant PCR product in the proband. The Sanger sequencing of the mutant transcript confirmed that 30 nucleotides of intron 6 of the WASHC5 are preserved in the open-reading frame. The retention of 30 nucleotides leads to the insertion of 10 aberrant amino acids (LSRGVVLTLR) at position 237 of the WASHC5 protein, thus resulting in an abnormally prolonged protein (1,169 aa).

case_report: A 34-year-old female with a history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis, managed with synthetic thyroid hormone (50 μg/day) for five years, presented with high-grade intermittent fever, chills, rigors, headache, and breathlessness. She had no significant family history of thyroid disease and was not on any other medication. On examination, the patient was disoriented, appeared pale with anemic conjunctiva, and had icteric sclera. Her blood pressure was 110/90 mm Hg, body temperature was 101°F, and pulse rate was 120 per minute. Physical examination revealed minimal, firm thyromegaly, tenderness in the right hypochondrium, and mild splenomegaly on an abdominal ultrasound scan. There were no enlarged peripheral lymph nodes or any enlargement on the abdominal ultrasound scan. There were no signs or symptoms of overt hypothyroidism. Laboratory investigations were negative for malaria, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C virus antibody, Dengue, HIV, Syphilis, and Leptospirosis. Antinuclear antigen and Anti-ds DNA tests were negative. Hematological findings included low hemoglobin, hematocrit, red blood cells, and platelet count, with a high mean corpuscular volume. Peripheral blood smear examination showed marked anisocytosis with macrocytes, polychromatic cells, and microspherocytes, along with a high percentage of nucleated red blood cells and thrombocytopenia. No hemoparasites or abnormal cells were observed. Bone marrow aspiration revealed hypercellular marrow with erythroid hyperplasia and increased megakaryopoiesis. Hematological examination indicated hemolytic anemia with thrombocytopenia and reactive marrow hyperplasia.
test_results: The patient had a positive direct antiglobulin test, evidence of hemolysis in the form of reticulocytosis, elevated indirect bilirubin, and serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). She also had increased anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody levels.

case_report: A 7-year-old female, second-born child from a third-degree consanguineous marriage, delivered full-term via lower segment caesarean section due to breech presentation. The antenatal period was uneventful, and her birth weight and length were within normal ranges. At birth, she exhibited megalocornea with a horizontal corneal diameter of 13 mm and vertical corneal diameter of 12.5 mm, along with blue sclerae. Despite these findings, the neonatal period was uneventful, and she showed no visual impairment during follow-up. At 9 months, routine developmental surveillance revealed hypotonia and gross motor delay (DQ—55), with normal deep tendon reflexes and no postural abnormalities. Neurological examination was otherwise normal. MRI brain at 10 months showed abnormal T2 and FLAIR hyperintense signals in the bilateral peritrigonal and frontal white matter and bilateral centrum semi-ovale, without diffusion restriction or foci of blooming. Occupational and physiotherapy were initiated for hypotonia, leading to gradual improvement in motor milestones. After a 3-year gap in follow-up, she presented at 7 years with gait abnormality, hypermobile joints, and short stature. Motor delay noted in infancy was no longer evident, and her development was normal on assessment scales. Physical examination revealed proportionate short stature (height 105 cm, −2 to −3 SD), mid-parental height of 156.5 cm (between 0 and −2 SD), and weight of 15.02 kg (−2 to −3 SD). Mild hypotonia causing a waddling gait was observed, with the rest of the neurological examination being normal. Additional findings included hypermobile joints (Beighton score—8), hyperextensible skin (2.8 cm on volar forearm, 1.5 cm on volar palm), finely wrinkled palms, and pes planus. No scars or ecchymosis were noted. Megalocornea dimensions remained unchanged and non-progressive, with no visual impairment. Family history was negative for similar phenotypes. Systemic screening and thyroid function tests for short stature were normal. Bone age was 6 years, and height age was 4 years at the age of 7. Comprehensive systemic screening, including complete blood count, basic metabolic profile, liver and renal function tests, urine analysis, stool analysis, and celiac screening, were normal. Karyotype was 46XX. Neuroimaging at 7 years showed similar findings to the MRI at 10 months, with no progression of white matter changes.
test_results: A homozygous missense variation c.682G > A in exon 6 of the SLC39A13 gene (chr11:g.47413633G > A) that results in the amino acid substitution of Asparagine for Aspartic acid at codon 228(p.Asp228Asn) was found. Another homozygous variant of uncertain significance was found in CEP57 gene in exon 2(c.154C > T), which is known to cause mosaic variegated aneuploidy syndrome 2, not correlating with our phenotype.

case_report: A 15-day-old female neonate was brought in with breathing difficulty and cyanosis for nine days, following a referral from a district hospital. Examination revealed a respiratory rate of 74 breaths per minute, significant chest in-drawing, a right-sided thoracic bulge with reduced air entry, and stony dull percussion. The mother reported that this was her second child, born in a hospital via normal vaginal delivery. She mentioned a history of oligohydramnios detected during a routine ultrasound at the end of the second trimester. The delivery was otherwise uneventful, except for a delayed cry and an APGAR score of 6/10 at birth, with the umbilical cord around the neck. The infant first experienced breathing difficulty on the sixth and twelfth days of life, leading to her referral and admission to our tertiary hospital. Upon admission, oxygen saturation was maintained, and intravenous fluids were initiated. Due to the patient's worsening condition, a laboratory workup for sepsis was conducted, and intravenous antibiotics were administered, including Ampicillin (200 mg/kg/day in two divided doses), Amikacin (15 mg/kg/day in two divided doses), Ceftazidime (150 mg/kg/day in two divided doses), and Vancomycin (45 mg/kg/day in three divided doses). The complete blood picture results from the first, second, and third days of admission are detailed in the accompanying table, along with other baseline laboratory parameters.
test_results: Chest X-ray revealed right hemithorax with a mediastinal shift to the left side. No cystic lesion was noted on X-ray. The pleural fluid analysis showed protein 2.6 g/dl, total cell count 680/mm, red blood cell 10-15/HPF, neutrophil 40%, lymphocyte 60%, no gram staining, and acid-fast bacilli (AFB) was noted. The second pleural tab revealed greenish fluid. Chest intubation drained around 250 ml fluid. Computed tomography (CT) showed bilateral pleural effusion, pneumothorax, and subcutaneous emphysema on the right side while moderate pleural effusion was noted on the left side.

case_report: A 13-year-old Hispanic, Puerto Rican female patient presented with severe developmental delay, microcephaly, and strabismus. She had thick scales on her legs for the past 3 years. Since birth, she exhibited diffuse xerosis and subtle erythema on her extremities, both managed with emollients. At the age of 10, she developed fine scales on her extremities and progressive thickening of her toenails and soles. Physical examination showed marked dysmorphic facial features, clubbing of the feet, and contractures on distal joints. There was fine ichthyosiform erythema and follicular prominence on her arms and legs, along with dystrophic toenails. Her mucosae and hair were normal. There was also prominent diffuse plantar hyperkeratosis.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging were consistent with dysgenesis of cerebral hemispheres and microcephaly. A genetic sequencing panel for PPK and ichthyotic disorders confirmed a homozygous pathogenic variant in the SNAP29 gene, exon 2, c.354dup (p.Leu119Alafs∗15).

case_report: A 32-year-old male reported experiencing gait ataxia for the past two months. Upon examination, the patient exhibited right-sided hemiparesis with a muscle strength of 4/5 according to the Medical Research Council (MRC) grading system, left-sided facial nerve weakness graded as House-Brackmann (H and B) grade III, and signs indicative of right cerebellar dysfunction. The remainder of the neurological examination showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Head CT revealed a heterogeneous solid cystic mass arising from the brainstem and extending to right cerebello-pontine angle. MRI revealed a right middle cerebellar peduncle lesion (33 × 30 × 28 mm) extending to right cerebello-pontine angle with necrotic and hemorrhagic areas. The lesion was isointense on T1W, hyper intense on T2W with inhomogeneous postcontrast enhancement. There was mild mass effect over fourth ventricle, but no upstream hydrocephalus. Microscopic examination showed a malignant tumor arranged in sheets comprising of round to oval to spindle cells with scant amount of cytoplasm and vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli. Mitoses were frequent. Some of the cells had more eosinophilic cytoplasm. The tumor cells showed diffuse immunopositivity for synaptophysin, chromogranin and focal immunopositivity for desmin and myogenin. MIB-1 labeling index was 6%. The tumor cells were immunonegative for p53, GFAP, epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), pancytokeratin (CK) and TTF-1.

case_report: A 25-year-old white female presented in 2006 at age 19 with nephrotic syndrome. Her serum creatinine (SCr) was 0.9 mg/dL (79.6 μmol/L) with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 74 mL/min/1.73 m2. Serum albumin (SAlb) was 2.9 g/dL (29 g/L). Urinalysis showed 4+ protein and large blood by dipstick. A 24-hour urine protein measurement was 6.4 g/day. She had no history of gross hematuria, hearing difficulty, or visual changes. Family history was negative for proteinuria, renal failure, but positive for microscopic hematuria in her maternal grandmother and aunt.
test_results: Light microscopy (LM) contained six glomeruli, one of which was globally sclerotic. The remaining glomeruli had preserved architecture with delicate basement membranes, patent glomerular capillaries and normal mesangial matrix and cellularity. Tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis involved 5% of the cortex, and interstitial foams cells affected 10–15% of the cortex. IF demonstrated weak mesangial staining for IgM (trace–1+) and C3 (trace). The tissue was stained with antibodies to the alpha 1, 3 and 5 chains of type IV collagen. This revealed 1–2+ segmental/mosaic staining of the GBM with the alpha 3 chain of type IV collagen. Staining for the alpha 5 chain of type IV collagen also showed 1+ segmental/mosaic staining of the GBM. There was no staining of the dTBM for either the alpha 3 or the alpha 5 chains of type IV collagen. Electron microscopy (EM) demonstrated diffusely thinned GBMs, measuring 124 nm in average thickness. Segmental foot process effacement involved 50% of the total glomerular capillary surface area.

case_report: A 28-year-old male presented with frothy urine and swelling of the feet for 2 months. He experienced blurring of vision, which was corrected with glasses. There were no signs of systemic disease, hypertension, or diabetes mellitus. He was born to non-consanguineous parents and was the youngest of three children, with no other family members affected. Physical examination revealed pedal edema, cloudy cornea, and arcus juvenilis. Respiratory, cardiovascular, and nervous system examinations were normal. Laboratory results showed urine specific gravity of 1.015, protein 3+, and blood 3+. Microscopy revealed 1–2 pus cells per high power field, a few epithelial cells, and 30–35 red blood cells per high power field. Twenty-four-hour urine protein was 5732 mg. Fasting blood sugar was 104 mg/dl, postprandial sugar 117 mg/dl, serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dl, sodium 143 mmol/l, potassium 3.8 mmol/l, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol 59 mg/dl, triglycerides 253 mg/dl, total cholesterol 122 mg/dl, very-low-density lipoprotein 51 mg/dl, and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) 12 mg/dl. Ultrasound examination showed the right kidney measuring 12.1 × 4.7 cm and the left kidney measuring 12.2 × 5.5 cm. Eye examination confirmed cloudy cornea and arcus juvenilis.
test_results: Renal biopsy showed enlarged glomeruli, with nodular deposits in the mesangium with irregularly thickened basement membrane, foam cell infiltrate of macrophages containing lipid material in capillaries and mesangial areas. Tubulo interstitial compartment and blood vessels were normal. Stain for amyloid was negative. Immunofluorescence revealed insignificant mesangial deposits of IgM and C3c. Electron microscopy showed diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes, capillary loop and mesangial regions were distended by electron lucent lipid material containing electron dense proteinaceous matrix.

case_report: The 29-year-old male patient is the first child of healthy unrelated Lithuanian parents. He was born at full term. His psychomotor development was delayed. He attended a regular school until the age of 16 years and then continued his education in a professional school. An IQ evaluation at the age of 20 showed a score of 69. At his latest evaluation at the age of 29 years, his height was 164 cm, his weight was 85 kg, his BMI was 31 kg/m2, and the circumference of his head was 60 cm (90th percentile). Other anthropometric measurements were as follows: total upper limb length of 66 cm, upper arm length of 35 cm, forearm length of 25 cm, hand length of 15 cm, palm length of 8.5 cm, middle finger length of 6.5 cm, total lower limb length of 87 cm on the left and 86 cm on the right, thigh length of 42 cm on both sides, calf length of 45 cm on the left and 44 cm on the right, and feet length of 23 cm. The patient has minor facial anomalies, including a flat face, sloping forehead with prominent supraorbital ridges, sparse and broad brows, depressed nasal ridge, short nose, long philtrum, and malar hypoplasia. Additionally, dental malocclusion, parodontosis, red and sparse scalp hair, male pattern baldness, and short neck are apparent. The patient is overweight and has limited elbow extension, brachydactyly of both hands, short rectangular nails, a single palmar crease, valgus deformation of the knees, brachydactyly of toes II–V of both feet, short rectangular toenails, and relative hyperplasia of the halluces. The patient complained of premature tiredness, excessive perspiration, and poor fine motor function. He has primary arterial hypertension, and a cardiac ultrasound showed a mitral valve prolapse. An ophthalmological examination revealed hypermetropia. Hormonal screening showed elevated levels of serum PTH (13.9 pmol/l, normal range 1.6–7.3 pmol/l) and somatotropin (12.2 mIU/l, normal range < 9.0 mIU/l). TSH, T3, T4, FSH, LH, testosterone, cortisol, and ACTH were within normal limits. 25-OH vitamin D was 51.4 nmol/l (normal range 75–100 nmol/l), serum calcium was 2.58 mmol/l (normal range 2.10–2.55 mmol/l), serum phosphorus 0.82 mmol/l (normal range 0.74–1.52 mmol/l), and serum glucose was 6.09 mmol/l (normal range 4.2–6.1 mmol/l). The glucose tolerance test was normal. The ultrasound of the thyroid gland and MRI scan of the hypophyseal gland showed no abnormalities. The X-ray of the hands showed very short and broad tubular bones. Metacarpals II–V are proximally pointed. Coning of phalanges is present in the middle and proximal phalanges of the second to fifth fingers. There is relative sparing of the thumb. The metatarsal bones and phalanges are markedly shortened, and there is disproportionate plumpness of the tubular bones of the hallux.
test_results: Heterozygous missense variant NM_001104631.2:c.581G > C (NP_001098101.1:p.(Arg194Pro)) located in exon 2 of the gene PDE4D was detected in the proband’s DNA sample by Sanger sequencing. Family segregation analysis of the identified variant revealed it’s de novo occurrence.

case_report: A 32-year-old female presented with a 5-month history of swelling in the right parieto-occipital region, which had progressively enlarged to approximately 8 × 8 cm. The skin over the swelling appeared normal, and the scalp was mobile over the area. There was no history of head injury, and her family history was unremarkable. Blood tests, including biochemistry and hematology, were within normal limits. Neurological examination revealed exaggerated deep tendon reflexes on the left side and a positive Babinski sign on the left side. No regional lymphadenopathy was noted. A thorough examination of the entire body was conducted to check for any cutaneous or subcutaneous lesions.
test_results: Findings were suggestive of a calvarial soft tissue lesion in the right parieto-occipital region with destruction of the adjacent parieto-occipital bone with intracranial extra-axial extension. The lesion appeared hyperintense on spin-spin relaxation time (T2)/fluid attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) images. It also showed peripheral hyperintense rim on spin-lattice relaxation time (T1) images with postcontrast enhancement, not suppressed on fat suppression or fat saturation (FAT SAT) images.
