Dimensions of the lesion were 5.4 × 4.3 × 5.4 cm. There was indentation of the sulco-gyral spaces but no midline shift was seen. There was indentation of the posterior aspect of the superior sagittal sinus at places. Additional studies like contrast enhanced computed tomography (CECT) thorax, abdomen, and pelvis and bone scan were negative for any metastatic lesions. Microscopic sections of the tumor showed dilated irregular vascular spaces filled with blood and fibrin. These spaces were lined by pleomorphic atypical endothelial cells. Many giant and bizarre tumor cells were also seen. Large areas of hemorrhage were seen. On immunohistochemistry, the atypical endothelial cells were highlighted by CD34, CD31, and factor VIII-related antigen.

case_report: A 20-month-old girl was referred to our center with symptoms of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS). She exhibited eyelid swelling and abdominal distension. Corticosteroid therapy had been initiated for nephrotic syndrome at a local hospital. Upon admission, physical examination revealed a low nasal bridge, broad nasal tip, very short stature with a short trunk, hyperpigmented skin macules, and corneal opacities. Hip radiograph indicated laterally displaced femoral capital epiphyses. Kidney function tests were normal, urinalysis showed nephrotic-range proteinuria, and blood count indicated leukopenia (3.5 × 10^9/L). Due to the rapid progression of nephropathy, peritoneal dialysis (PD) was started at the age of 2.5 years. The patient experienced episodic hypertension, which was attributed to insufficient compliance with fluid restriction. At the age of 6 years, she began to experience severe neurological complications, including headaches, ischemic strokes, and transient ischemic attacks, which manifested as right upper limb palsy and expressive aphasia.
test_results: Immunologic examination revealed significant T-cell deficiency with decreased CD4 and CD8 cells. Repeated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed non-specific gliotic scars and progressive occlusive disease filling both internal carotid arteries and both middle cerebral arteries.

case_report: A 30-month-old boy was admitted to the Pediatric Clinic, University of Sassari, Italy, with a 7-day history of fever. Two weeks prior to hospitalization, the patient experienced a brief episode of diarrhea. Laboratory tests conducted just before admission showed a white blood cell (WBC) count of 49,920/mm3 with an eosinophil count of 26,310/mm3, mild microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL), and elevated serum total IgE levels (968 UI/mL). The child resided in a rural area of Sardinia, had close contact with animals, and had no prior medical issues. He was not atopic, had received regular vaccinations, and had not taken any medications before hospital admission. There was no history of recent travel. Upon admission, the patient appeared well and afebrile, with no other clinical symptoms. Physical examination revealed no hepato-splenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Subsequent laboratory tests indicated an increased WBC count (58,020/mm3) and eosinophil count (33,400/mm3; 57.5%), along with a moderate rise in CRP levels (2.85 mg/dL). Serum electrolytes, hepatic, and renal markers were within normal ranges.
test_results: IgG anti-nematode antibodies were detected in serum samples from the patient and his father by ELISA test.

case_report: In November 2019, a 7-year-old boy was referred to our ophthalmology department due to poor vision in his right eye following a pre-school physical assessment. The best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/160 in the right eye with an objective refraction of +1.00 diopter and 20/20 in the left eye. There was no evident strabismus in either eye. The anterior segment, intraocular pressures (IOPs), and ocular adnexa of both eyes were normal. A widefield color fundus image of the right eye revealed a large optic disc covered with glial tissue in the center, bordered by chorioretinal pigmentary disturbance, and straight retinal vessels extending radially from the disc margin in increased numbers. The left eye's fundus appeared normal. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) showed a conical excavation of the optic disc with a central tuft of glial tissue on top. His parents reported no histories of familial disease, abnormalities in pregnancy, prematurity, or low birth weight. Other systemic examinations were normal.
test_results: The CT scan of the orbit demonstrated a hyperdense choroidal plaque with the same density as bone at the level of the optic disc in the right eye. The b-scan ultrasonography revealed a highly reflected mass covering the optic disc detected at even a very low gain, whereas the vector scan showed a high echo spike originating from the surface of the lesion. The enhanced depth imaging (EDI-OCT) image depicted a well-defined peripapillary choroidal lesion with hyperreflective lamellar lines in the inner part and spongiform pattern in the outer part, which replaced the normal choriocapillaris. The fluorescein angiography (FA) showed early patchy hyperfluorescence and diffuse late staining around the optic disc. On indocyanine green angiography (ICGA), there was an area of early hypofluorescence and diffuse late staining corresponding to the elevated lesion. During the early stages of ICGA, supranasal to the optic disc, the vascular patterns were obtained, and the 6 × 6 mm OCT angiography (OCTA) centered at these locations delineated clusters of linear vessels on en face visualization. A cross-sectional OCTA b-scan indicated blood flow signals in these lamellar choroidal lesions.
diagnosis: Morning Glory Disc anomaly with choroidal ossification

case_report: An 18-year-old female presented with a painless, firm swelling in the left maxillary buccal alveolus region, persisting for the past 3 years. Initially, the swelling progressively increased in size but has remained stable for the past 2 years. Physical examination revealed a poorly localized swelling extending from the left first molar region to the midline, measuring approximately 4 cm by 2 cm, and raised 1 cm above the surface. The adjacent teeth were displaced inferiorly. The swelling was bony hard, non-tender, and had an irregular surface upon palpation. A panoramic radiograph showed an ill-defined radiolucency with a sparse trabecular pattern in the left maxillary alveolus region. CT imaging demonstrated an expansile lesion with coarse, sparse trabeculae, extending from the left first molar region to the midline.
test_results: A contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) scan of the area revealed an ill-defined enhancing soft tissue mass lesion with involvement of the left maxillary alveolar arch with its expansion and rarefaction. In the arterial phase of CECT scan, enhancing vascular channels were seen with feeder vessels from the left facial artery, without any dilatation of the supplying vessel. In the delayed phase, homogeneous enhancement of the lesion was seen.

case_report: A 48-year-old female presented with a 3-month history of left ankle pain. She had no history of trauma, and her medical and family histories were unremarkable. Physical examination showed mild swelling and edema over the lower leg and ankle, particularly on the lateral side, with tenderness over the distal fibula. There were no neurovascular deficits, and the ankle had a full range of motion, though painful at the terminal range. No inguinal or popliteal adenopathy was observed. General and other system examinations were normal. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, calcium, phosphorus, and alkaline phosphatase levels, were within normal limits. Radiographs of the left ankle revealed a coarse, perpendicular periosteal reaction with a 'hair on end' pattern and thickening of the distal fibula shaft cortex, without scalloping or erosion. The lesion's intensity decreased from the cortical base toward the surface, with the fibula cortex remaining intact. Computed tomography showed a lesion occupying about half the fibula's circumference without obvious medullary involvement, along with mineralization foci continuous with the periosteal reaction. Magnetic resonance imaging indicated periosteal elevation on the posterior, lateral, and medial aspects of the distal fibular shaft over a length of 7 cm. A 2.1 × 1.7 cm lytic focus within the periosteal reaction was noted on the posteromedial aspect, appearing heterogeneously T2 hyperintense, T1 hypointense with mild diffusion restriction. Mild diffuse edema was observed in the surrounding posterior leg muscles, and minimal edema was noted in the adjacent fibular marrow, which was not significant relative to the periosteal changes. Other visualized bones, joints, medial and lateral ligaments, and tendons around the ankle were normal. Further imaging studies, including ultrasonography of the abdomen and thyroid, and a mammogram, were unremarkable.
test_results: USG-guided tru-cut biopsy showed spindle-shaped cells arranged in sheets. The cells had moderate cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei with occasional mitotic figures. Areas of osteoid formation were noted within the spindle cell proliferation.

case_report: The patient is a female infant born to a 27-year-old Japanese woman who had a history of epilepsy since infancy. The mother, who had been seizure-free for several years, resumed antiepileptic medication at age 17 after experiencing a seizure. At the time of pregnancy, she was taking 1400 mg/day of VPA, 140 mg/day of phenobarbital, and 1200 mg/day of carbamazepine. Blood concentrations were 80 μg/ml for VPA, 26.1 μg/ml for phenobarbital, and 10.5 μg/ml for carbamazepine, all within their respective therapeutic ranges. Despite this medication regimen, the mother experienced convulsions approximately three times per week. She was informed about the potential effects of her medication but chose to continue her pregnancy while taking 5 mg/day of folic acid. At 13 weeks of gestation, she was referred to our hospital. The mother had a body mass index of 30 kg/m2. A second-trimester ultrasound at 20 weeks did not reveal any fetal malformations, although the image quality was compromised due to maternal obesity.
test_results: At 25 weeks of gestation, contracture of the fetal right wrist joint suggestive of a radial ray defect was detected by ultrasonography. The fetus demonstrated growth retardation starting from 32 weeks of gestation. At 34 weeks of gestation, the estimated fetal weight was 1660 g (−2.5 SD: standard deviation), the biparietal diameter was 74.9 mm (−2.8 SD), mother’s abdominal circumference was 261.7 mm (−1.5 SD), and the femur length was 58 mm (−1.3 SD). The right ulna was shorter than the left ulna; the right was 35 mm (−8.4 SD), and the left was 53 mm (−1.1 SD). The right radial ray was not detected. At 37 weeks of gestation, saddle nose as a facial anomaly was observed on a three-dimensional ultrasound.

case_report: The patient is a 52-year-old male with a history of chronic productive cough lasting 7 years, which began after relocating to a new office. The cough was more severe at night and aggravated by exposure to cigarette smoke. The sputum was white, sticky, and difficult to expectorate. Initial blood tests showed an eosinophil count of 2220/uL (36.2%). Pulmonary function tests revealed an FEV1 at 98.3% of the predicted value and an FEV1/FVC ratio of 70.04%. A methacholine challenge test was positive (PD20 = 2.504 mg). Induced sputum analysis showed an eosinophil count of 64%. The patient was initially treated with inhaled budesonide formoterol without symptom improvement, followed by oral montelukast sodium and prednisone 10 mg daily, which led to slight symptom improvement but no reduction in eosinophil count. The patient was admitted to the hematology department, where a bone marrow biopsy indicated eosinophilia. Prednisone 40 mg daily was administered, resulting in slight cough improvement. The patient continued intermittent prednisone treatment for 4 years, but the eosinophil count remained elevated at 4020/μL. The patient was later admitted to the respiratory department due to persistent cough and elevated eosinophil levels. Physical examination revealed dry rales on exhalation. Blood tests showed an eosinophil count of 1550/uL (27.0%). A CT scan of the paranasal sinuses was normal, while a chest CT scan revealed multiple scattered nodules in both lungs. Total IgE was 157 kU/L, and BNP and troponin levels were normal. Induced sputum analysis showed an eosinophil count of 18.5%. Fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) was 96 ppb. Pulmonary function tests showed an FEV1 at 110% of the predicted value and an FEV1/FVC ratio of 70.84%. A methacholine bronchial challenge test was positive (PD20 = 1.877 mg). Biopsies of the bronchial and gastric mucosa showed eosinophilic infiltration. Ultrasound examination indicated splenomegaly (126 mm long). Parasite antibody tests were negative. Given the patient's history of consuming raw river fish, albendazole 0.4 daily for 1 week and inhaled beclomethasone/formoterol were prescribed, but there was no significant improvement in cough or reduction in eosinophil count.
test_results: The bone marrow biopsy showed eosinophilia. Examination for PDGFRa, PDGFRb, FGFR, JAK2 or FLT3 fusion genes proved negative.
diagnosis: PDGFRA negative hypereosinophilic syndrome  associated myeloid neoplasm

case_report: An 18-year-old female presented with a one-year history of progressive muscle atrophy and weakness, initially affecting the upper limbs and later involving the lower limbs, leading to difficulty in walking independently. The patient had no significant past medical history and reported the onset of bilateral hearing loss concurrent with the motor symptoms. There was no history of trauma, ototoxic drug usage, loud noise exposure, or similar complaints in her family. Physical examination revealed normal higher mental functions, weakness, and muscle atrophy in both upper and lower limbs. Neurological examination showed decreased muscle tone and bulk, generalized weakness more pronounced in distal muscles, muscle power of 3/5 in both upper and lower limbs, normal superficial reflexes, bilaterally exaggerated deep tendon reflexes, and extensor plantar responses bilaterally. Fasciculations were observed in the tongue and legs.
test_results: Nerve conduction studies (NCS) were performed. Suggestive motor axonal polyneuropathy and Electromyography (EMG) were performed and suggestive of anterior horn cell disease affecting three segments (bulbar, cervical, lumbosacral). Audiometry confirmed bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, predominantly affecting high-frequency sounds, with no evidence of conductive hearing impairment. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and spinal cord was undertaken to rule out alternative diagnoses and assess for structural abnormalities which came out to be normal.

case_report: A 26-year-old woman visited her primary care physician due to a two-month history of recurring sore throat, fever, and gum bleeding/persistent hematoma. Physical examination revealed cervical lymphadenopathy. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 1,800/L with 21% circulating blasts, platelet count of 8,000/L, and hemoglobin level of 5.4 g/dL. A computerized tomography (CT) scan confirmed the presence of cervical lymphadenopathy.
test_results: Bone marrow biopsy and aspiration revealed 37% myeloblasts with immunohistochemistry studies showing KMT2A-MLLT3 rearrangement; cytogenetics were positive for t(9; 11) translocation. Immunophenotyping showed CD13+ CD33+ CD34− blasts with two populations (one CD117− and one CD11b−). Molecular studies were negative for other abnormalities.

case_report: A 65-year-old male reported a recent decline in vision in both eyes. He had a history of retinitis pigmentosa with non-recordable electroretinograms from approximately 15 years ago and had been attending hospital visits sporadically. His best-corrected visual acuity, measured in decimal, was 0.4 in the right eye and 0.6 in the left eye. Visual field tests indicated a concentric narrowing of the visual fields in both eyes. Ophthalmoscopic examination revealed that the large choroidal vessels were visible from the posterior pole to the periphery in both eyes.
test_results: OCT showed a loss of the ellipsoid zone and tubulations around the fovea. FAF showed that the entire posterior pole was hypoautofluorescent except for an isolated area of hyperautofluorescence which included the fovea. Some of the larger choroidal vessels were hyperreflective. The choroid capillary slab of the OCTA images showed the medium and large choroidal vessels clearly in the 8×8 mm size macular images. The small vessels were observed in a relatively wider area than the hyperautofluorescent area in the FAF images. These smaller vessels, probably the choriocapillaris, were seen, especially in the 3×3 mm OCTA images.

case_report: An 18-month-old Caucasian boy was referred with a history of spontaneous mucocutaneous bleeds starting at nine months old. Initial complete blood count revealed a low platelet count, and he was previously diagnosed with ITP. There were no abnormalities in child development or physical examination, and there was no family history of bleeding. He was the only child of nonconsanguineous parents. During follow-up, he experienced spontaneous, non-sustained increases in platelet counts. During one thrombocytopenic episode, a short course of prednisone was prescribed, but there was no response. Upon evaluation at our center, laboratory results showed a low platelet count (32 × 10^9/L) and mild microcytic anemia, with no other abnormalities. Persistently low mean platelet volume (MPV) was noted, ranging from 5.6 to 6.5 fL (normal range: 7.2–11.1 fL). Peripheral blood smear revealed two distinct platelet populations: one normal and another with markedly reduced size. Weekly platelet counts over the following months confirmed an intermittent pattern of thrombocytopenia, with counts ranging from 12 to 208 × 10^9/L.
test_results: We identified a lower expression of the protein in the patient’s peripheral blood leukocytes. A missense mutation on exon 2 of the WASP gene, resulting in a p.Thr45Met amino acid change, was detected.

case_report: A 26-year-old male presented with generalized weakness, atrophy of the peroneal muscles, and deformities in the extremities. His family history revealed that his parents and two elder sisters were healthy and did not have any neurological conditions. He was born at term via normal spontaneous vaginal delivery at home, assisted by a midwife. Birth metrics such as weight, height, and head circumference were not recorded. At birth, he exhibited weakness in both thumbs and feet. He began walking at the age of 6, although his gait was unstable and he had fallen arches in his feet, which developed gradually. At age 16, he underwent bilateral foot straightening surgery at a local hospital, which improved his right foot more than his left. Despite multiple hospital visits, the cause of his condition remained unidentified. His medical history included chronic gastritis for 10 years starting in junior high school, but no other significant illnesses or substance abuse. During an examination in August 2019, his vital signs were normal (body temperature: 36.5°C; pulse rate: 104 beats/minute; respiratory rate: 20 breaths/minute; blood pressure: 123/85 mm Hg). He exhibited a myopathic gait due to lower extremity weakness. Physical examination revealed scoliosis, deformities of both thumbs and feet (pes cavus), and symmetric atrophy of the bilateral thenar, hypothenar, and lower leg muscles. Muscle strength was graded as IV in the bilateral upper distal limbs, IV+ in the bilateral upper proximal limbs, IV in the bilateral lower distal limbs, and IV− in the bilateral lower proximal limbs. Tendon reflexes were absent in the extremities, and there was deep sensory dysfunction in the right leg along with a positive Romberg sign.
test_results: Genetic analysis of the patient's blood sample revealed a heterozygous mutation in PMP22 (NM_153322, c.54_55insGTGCTG, p.(L19delinsVLL)). EMG results revealed that nerve conduction was not elicited in the motor and sensory bilateral median nerves, bilateral ulnar nerves, bilateral tibial nerves, and common peroneal nerves. Spontaneous potential was observed from the right anterior tibial muscle, and EMG results revealed neurogenic damage. Spontaneous potentials were also observed from the right abductor pollicis brevis, but motor unit potentials were not recorded. Above EMG results indicated that the patient has a polyneuropathy.

case_report: The patient is a 5-year-old girl who exhibited muscle weakness shortly after birth. She is the first child of a healthy couple with no consanguinity and was delivered vaginally at full-term with normal weight and Apgar scores. Early observations included bilateral eyelid ptosis, infrequent limb movements, and difficulties in chewing and swallowing. She could not lift her head until 6 months old, crawl until 10 months old, or sit until 1.5 years old. She has never been able to stand. She cannot move her upper arms bilaterally or hold objects steadily in both hands. Language development was delayed; she began babbling at 1.2 years old and currently speaks slowly with poor articulation. Previous genetic testing was negative for spinal muscular atrophy and peroneal muscular atrophy. Physical examination revealed physical retardation (height: 97 cm, weight: 16 kg), bilateral ptosis, hyperextension of ankle and carpal joints, foot drop, amyotrophy in bilateral proximal lower limbs, hypotonia in all four limbs, absent tendon reflexes, and low muscle strength (MRC scale: grade 3 in cervical muscle, grade 2 in bilateral proximal upper limbs, grade 3 in distal upper limbs, grade 1 in bilateral proximal lower limbs, and grade 2 in distal lower limbs). Sensation and cutaneous plantar reflex were normal. Additional findings included a high-arched palate, enamel hypoplasia, and a small jaw, with no nystagmus observed. X-ray imaging showed thoracolumbar scoliosis and right acetabular dysplasia. Serum CK level was normal (118.9 U/L), and tests for anti-AChR and anti-MuSK antibodies were negative. A neostigmine test was negative. Electromyography (EMG) indicated spontaneous potentials (positive sharp waves and fibrillations) and reduced motor unit recruitment in limb muscles. Motor unit potential (MUP) duration was prolonged (14.2 ms in the left extensor digitorum communis and 14.4 ms in the right tibialis anterior) with normal amplitude. Sensory and motor nerve conduction velocities were decreased, with reduced amplitudes of CMAP and SNAP and prolonged peak latencies. H-reflex waveforms were absent. The patient did not cooperate with repeated nerve stimulation examination. Electroencephalography (EEG) showed extensive 3–4.5 Hz θ and δ waves mixed with non-sustained low-amplitude spike/sharp waves during shallow sleep. The Wechsler Intelligence Scale assessment revealed a low verbal IQ of 52, and the performance IQ could not be determined due to the inability to perform bilateral hand movements. Blood-urinary metabolic screening, electrocardiography, visual/auditory evoked potentials, and MRI of the head and spinal cord showed no abnormalities. The patient's parents declined muscle biopsies.
test_results: Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was performed.

case_report: The patient is a 42-year-old married man from Ardakan, Yazd, Iran. He has one healthy daughter and comes from a middle-class background. Since he was 6 months old, he has experienced transgradient palmoplantar keratoderma (PPK). He lost his deciduous teeth and later his permanent teeth, becoming edentulous by age 15. Concurrently, he developed PPK with hyperkeratosis on his elbows and knees. A pathology report from 2009 indicated hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate in the upper and mid dermis. He is the first-born child with two healthy siblings, a sister and a brother. His parents were first-degree cousins. His father passed away due to a brain tumor, and his mother has seizures and is on anticonvulsive and antidepressant medications. Neither his parents nor his siblings have PPK. At age 15, he began treatment with corticosteroids and Neotigason, but due to arthralgia and bone pain, the Neotigason dose was reduced. For the past few years, he has been taking Roaccutane 20 mg two to three times a week, which has stabilized his skin lesions. Dermatologic examination revealed transgradient PPK with involvement of the knees and elbows, flexion contracture of toes, onychogryphosis, and arachnodactyly. In January 2020, he developed fever, malaise, sleepiness, and right-sided weakness, which resolved spontaneously after a week. A similar episode occurred in mid-September 2020, also resolving spontaneously. He reported tiredness after walking over the past 2-3 months. Following the September 2020 episode, he was admitted to the neurology ward of Rasul-e-Akram hospital in Tehran, Iran. Neurologic examination showed a spastic gait with a wide base, increased deep tendon reflexes (DTR), upward plantar reflexes, and bilateral dysmetric finger-to-nose tests. Ophthalmologic examination was normal. Laboratory tests, including acute phase reactants and viral markers, were unremarkable. Serum NMO and MoG antibodies were negative. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis was normal.
test_results: A positive oligoclonal band test was performed. Brain MRI showed multiple bilateral non-enhancing hypersignal lesions mostly in periventricular, subcortical, juxtacortical, infratentorial (pons and cerebellar peduncles) regions in T2 and FLAIR sequences. In cervical MRI, C1-C2 and C2-C4 levels had multiple T2 and STIR hyperintense patchy foci without enhancement.

case_report: A 56-year-old Caucasian female with a medical history including type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, intravenous drug use, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obstructive sleep apnea, adrenal insufficiency, and hepatitis C presented with chest pain, shortness of breath, and recurrent falls. Seven years ago, she experienced an episode of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, confirmed via cardiac catheterization, and was temporarily treated with beta-blockers. Since then, she has had multiple admissions with both typical and atypical angina symptoms. Her most recent echocardiogram showed normal to impaired left ventricular function with an ejection fraction of 60%-65%, and a Holter monitor test was negative. The patient was re-admitted with chest pain rated 5/10 in severity, radiating to the left arm. Her home medications included clonazepam, trazodone, Spiriva, albuterol, hydrocortisone, and gabapentin. Initial vital signs were normal. Electrocardiogram (EKG) displayed deep inverted T-waves in leads I, II, aVL, and V2-V6. Laboratory tests indicated troponin levels within normal limits and a pro-brain natriuretic peptide (proBNP) level of 2035 pg/ml. A chest X-ray was unremarkable, while a chest CT scan showed an “ace-of-spades” appearance in the cardiac transverse section.
test_results: A transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) demonstrated localized apical hypertrophy with end-systolic cavity obliteration and with an EF of 65%-70%, with a normal-sized left ventricle, normal wall thickness.

case_report: A 7-year-old Japanese boy visited a clinic due to a growing mass and pain in his left ankle over the past 6 months. He had previously sprained his left ankle several months before these symptoms began. The increasing pain made it difficult for him to walk long distances and participate in physical activities. Physical examination at our hospital showed a palpable hard mass on the anterior and posteromedial sides of his left ankle. His ankle had a range of motion of 15° in dorsiflexion and 40° in plantar flexion with his knee bent. An anterior drawer test on his left ankle indicated instability and apprehension.
test_results: Left ankle plain radiography revealed multiple oval free bodies 10–15 mm in size at the anterior and posterior ankle joint spaces. Computed tomography images showed intra-articular multiple ossified oval mass lesions and some protrusions arising from the talus. Magnetic resonance imaging showed an intra-articular oval mass with low intensity on T1-weighted images and partially high intensity on T2-weighted and short T1 inversion recovery (STIR) images. Diffuse STIR high-intensity lesions were confirmed on the protuberance from the talus and talar body underneath it, suggesting a bone marrow lesion of the protuberance and talus.

case_report: An 8-year-old Indian girl, born to parents who are not related by blood, visited the outpatient department with primary concerns of light-colored hair on her scalp and body, along with light-colored spots across her skin. Upon examination, she exhibited silvery grey hair on her scalp, especially in the frontal and temporal regions, as well as on her eyebrows and eyelashes. Numerous distinct hypopigmented macules were observed on a background of diffuse hyperpigmentation, covering her body and fine grey hair. These hypopigmented macules were notably more prominent on her face, trunk, and lower limbs. The remainder of her physical and systemic examination was normal, and no other family members showed similar characteristics. There was no history of recurrent infections or growth issues.
test_results: A trichogram revealed coarse unevenly distributed clumps of melanin pigment in the medulla of the hair shaft. Skin biopsy from the hypopigmented macule revealed enlarged hyperpigmented melanocytes with sparsely pigmented adjacent keratinocytes in the basal layer of the epidermis. Immunohistochemistry with HMB-45 showed an enlarged and increased number of pigment laden melanocytes. Masson Fontana stain from the hyperpigmented lesion showed uniform prominence of enlarged hyperpigmented melanocytes and from the hypopigmented lesion showed patchy prominence of enlarged hyperpigmented melanocytes.

case_report: A 29-year-old pregnant woman, gravida 2, para 1, was referred to the Department of Medical Genetics and Prenatal Diagnosis Center of West China Second University Hospital. She and her spouse were non-consanguineous, with no notable medical conditions, and denied a family history of genetic diseases or a known history of neurological disorders. She was in her second pregnancy at 12 weeks with no complications and had no notable history in her first pregnancy. The firstborn, a 2-year-old girl, was born naturally at full term with a normal occipitofrontal circumference (33.5 cm) and weight (3.2 kg) at birth. During her first year of life, macrocephaly was observed, with a head circumference of 46 cm (> +3 SD) at 6 months and 48.5 cm (> +3 SD) at 8 months. At 1 year and 3 months, her head circumference increased to 53.5 cm (> +3 SD), while her height (75 cm) and weight (10 kg) were normal. The child exhibited severe motor developmental delay and low muscle tone, unable to roll over at 6 months, stand until 1 year and 6 months, or crawl and independently sit and walk until 2 years old. She often walked unsteadily and had poor motor coordination. There were no early-onset seizures, epilepsy, or spasticity before 2 years of age, and her vision and hearing functions were normal. Cognitive functions were delayed; she could say a few enunciated words but often spoke to herself unconsciously and could not understand the meaning of words, follow instructions, express her intentions, or otherwise verbally communicate. At 19 months of age, she had a motor developmental index of less than 50 and a cognitive developmental index of 52 on the Bayley Scales of Infant Development (BSID-II), corresponding to the levels of 10- and 12-month-old infants, respectively. These results indicated substantial deficits in her motor, cognitive, and language development levels outside the normal range.
test_results: Brain MRI at 13 months revealed swelling in the bilateral cerebral cortex and diffuse signal abnormalities in the cerebral white matter, showing a low signal on T1-weighted images and a high signal on T2-weighted images, as well as fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images; however, subcortical cysts were not seen in all sections.

case_report: The patient, an eight-year-old boy with mildly delayed developmental milestones, was referred for evaluation of gradually progressive left spastic hemiparesis over three months. At 18 months old, his eyes showed retinal telangiectasia and exudates. He underwent laser photocoagulation in the right eye, multiple sessions of Avastin (Bevacizumab) injections, and vitreous lavage. On physical examination, his vitals were stable. Neurological examination revealed mild left facial weakness and spasticity in the left upper and lower limbs. Deep tendon reflexes were brisk bilaterally, more pronounced on the right. Additional findings included a convergent squint of the right eye, premature graying of hair, two café-au-lait spots on the forearm (1×2 cm), and bilateral contracture of the Achilles tendon (left more than right). Radiological surveys, including X-ray, echocardiogram, and ultrasound of the chest, indicated dextrocardia with situs inversus. Skeletal survey X-rays showed osteopenia with flaring of the metaphyseal region.
test_results: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) of the brain revealed mixed intensity solid cystic lesion in the bilateral thalami (T1W image), T2 and flair hyperintensities involving bilateral frontal and parieto-occipital deep white matter, brainstem and bilateral middle cerebral peduncle. Several tiny cystic spaces were seen in the bilateral parieto-occipital regions. The right ocular globe showed evidence of retinal detachment (T2W). SWI phase image showed hypointense signal intensity in the areas of blooming consisted with the calcification changes. CT scan of the brain showed calcifications in bilateral thalamus, right parieto-occipital and left parietal regions. Ophthalmologic examination showed absent perception of light on the right side with just perception of hand movements in the left eye along with corneal opacity; leukocoria in the right eye were also noted.

case_report: The 16-year-old male patient has experienced poor vision and sensitivity to light since the age of 4. Best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was measured at 0.4 LogMAR in the right eye (RE) and 0.52 LogMAR in the left eye (LE). Refractive error was noted as −5.75 sph −3.00 cyl/15° D in RE and −6.00 sph −3.50 cyl/170° D in LE. Fundus examination revealed a normal optic disk, absence of the foveal reflex, and mottling of the peripheral retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Fundus autofluorescence imaging showed central hypofluorescence with a mild perifoveal hyperfluorescent area in both eyes. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging indicated disruption of the foveal photoreceptors, normal central macular thickness, and relative preservation of the paracentral retina. Flash full-field electroretinography (ERG) recordings demonstrated reduced responses, predominantly affecting the photopic component. Visual field testing identified a central scotoma.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed that the proband carried the known nonsense variant p.(Arg137*) and the novel p.(Thr26Asn) missense variant in compound heterozygous state.

case_report: A 23-year-old male presented with a sudden decrease in vision in both eyes and bilateral hearing loss for the past 15 days. He had a history of a penetrating injury to the right eye with an iron rod. Three months prior, he underwent scleral tear repair followed by vitreo-retinal surgery, which included the removal of a metallic intraocular foreign body and silicone oil injection. Post-surgery, his vision improved to 3/60 and 6/24 reduced Snellen's visual acuity (RS) with a well-attached retina and silicone oil in situ in the right eye. Upon systemic evaluation, the patient was not following verbal commands, appeared restless and anxious, and was disoriented to time, place, and person. The best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) in the right eye was counting fingers close to the face, and in the left eye, it was perception of light. Slit lamp examination of the right eye revealed moderate anterior uveitis with anterior chamber cells 2+ and flare 2+, aphakia, and inferior peripheral iridectomy. Fundus examination of the right eye showed a hyperemic optic disc with a large retinal break surrounded by laser chorio-retinal atrophy in the supertemporal quadrant and silicone oil in situ. The left eye exhibited pigmented keratic precipitates, anterior chamber cells 3+, flare 3+, and retrolental cells in the anterior vitreous. The left eye also showed dense media haze due to grade 4 vitritis with retinal detachment that was barely discernible. Intraocular pressure in both eyes was 9 mm Hg (Goldmann Applanation tonometer).
test_results: Ultrasound B-scan showed shifting fluid confirming the presence of an exudative retinal detachment with increased choroidal thickness measuring 2.3 mm in the left eye. Pure tone audiometry showed a sensorineural deafness for both lower and higher frequencies with a hearing threshold of 60 dB.

case_report: A 15-year-old Asian male presented with a gradual onset of blurred vision in the right eye over the past month. There were no additional vision-related complaints. The patient had no prior history of systemic or ocular diseases. He had a previous diagnosis of posterior uveitis in the right eye. His best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 6/6 (0 logMAR) in both eyes, with a prescription of minus cylindrical lens 1.25 diopters at an axis of 5° for the right eye and minus cylindrical lens 0.25 diopters at an axis of 5° for the left eye. Intraocular pressure (IOP) and eye movement were within normal limits. The anterior segment of both eyes showed no signs of inflammation or cataract. Examination of the posterior segment of the right eye revealed extensive lipid exudates, predominantly in the inferior retina, while the foveal area remained unaffected (Fig. a).
test_results: Fluorescein angiography (FA) was performed, showing hyperfluorescence indicating telangiectatic vessels, leakages corresponding to areas of lipid exudation, and hypofluorescence indicating capillary nonperfusion (CNP), predominantly within the inferior retina. Despite the normal macula upon fundus photo and FA, optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the right eye revealed a small amount of subfoveal fluid.

case_report: A 20-day-old male neonate presented with jaundice and TAPVC since birth. There was no history of other ailments or past illnesses, and no family history of genetic diseases. The father exhibited distinct facial features: a prominent forehead, deep-set eyes with mild hypertelorism, a pointed chin, and a saddle-shaped nose with a bulbous tip. Physical examination of the infant revealed a weight of 3.2 kg, jaundiced skin and sclera, and a triangular facial appearance similar to his father's. The infant also had abnormalities in both eyes (posterior embryotoxon). Lung examination showed no positive signs, but heart auscultation revealed abnormal sounds and murmurs. The liver was palpable with a soft edge 4.0 cm below the right costal margin. Biochemical analysis indicated increased levels of serum gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase, total bilirubin (TBil), direct bilirubin (DBil), and total bile acids (TBAs), consistent with cholestasis. X-ray imaging did not reveal obvious skeletal deformities, while chest computed tomography (CT) angiography identified a butterfly vertebra at the seventh thoracic vertebra. CT angiography also showed that four pulmonary veins (PVs) converged and drained into the vertical vein (VV), which then flowed into the dilated left innominate vein (LIV), subsequently into the superior vena cava (SVC), and finally into the right atrium (RA).
test_results: A heterozygous variant (c.3197dupC) in the JAG1 gene was identified. This is a frame shift mutation. It is expected that the protein products encoded by this gene will be cut off prematurely, which is considered pathogenic.

case_report: A 31-year-old Irish woman living in the midwestern USA experienced a gradual decline in left hand dexterity and the onset of a rest tremor. Eight months later, she had episodes of pre-syncope triggered by activities such as climbing stairs or exposure to hot environments. Initial neurological examination showed rigidity, bradykinesia, reduced left arm swing, and rest/action tremor in the left hand, with no signs of pyramidal or cerebellar involvement, and no objective orthostatic hypotension. Her Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale motor subsection part III (UPDRS III) score was 18. Routine blood tests, ceruloplasmin levels, and a cerebral MRI scan were normal. She initially declined medication until symptoms spread to her left lower extremity and right hand a year later. She began treatment with pramipexole 0.75 mg three times daily, which was effective. Six months later, she and her husband planned to have a child. Due to limited safety data on pramipexole during pregnancy, her medication was switched to levodopa/carbidopa. She responded well to levodopa/carbidopa, experiencing mild dyskinesias at an optimal dose of 900 mg levodopa/day. Five months after starting levodopa, her UPDRS III score improved from 20.5 to 11 points, and she became pregnant. In her second month of pregnancy, she experienced syncope upon rising from a supine position and noted reduced responsiveness to levodopa. Her ON state total UPDRS score was 48 points, with a UPDRS III subscore of 30 points. She had significant orthostatic hypotension, with a supine blood pressure of 116/70 mmHg and standing blood pressure of 70/50 mmHg. Her motor function deteriorated, and by week 30 of pregnancy, her total UPDRS score was 56.5 points, with a UPDRS III subscore of 38.5 points. The levodopa dose was not increased during pregnancy to avoid worsening orthostatic hypotension. At age 35, she delivered a full-term 2.9 kg girl via caesarean section due to breech presentation, with Apgar scores of eight at one minute and nine at five minutes. The baby's general and neurological examinations were normal, and routine neonatal blood tests were normal. The mother did not breastfeed. At age five, the child developed normally except for recurrent strabismus and a dermoid cyst in the anterior neck. One week postpartum, the mother's total UPDRS score decreased to 37 points, with a UPDRS III subscore of 22 points, on the same levodopa dose. Her blood pressure was 110/60 mmHg lying down and 100/62 mmHg standing. Despite initial symptom improvement postpartum, her condition worsened, with a UPDRS score of 60.5, necessitating an increase in levodopa. Entacapone was added after midodrine improved her orthostatic hypotension. She initially responded well but developed significant motor fluctuations, increased OFF time, peak-dose/diphasic dyskinesias, and orthostatic hypotension despite multiple medication adjustments. At age 37, she underwent bilateral subthalamic nuclei deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery after an inpatient motor evaluation showed a response to levodopa (OFF and ON states with UPDRS III subscores of 62 and 20.5, respectively). A pre-surgical brain MRI scan showed no atrophy or abnormal signals in the putamen or pons. However, she had limited and transient benefit from DBS therapy despite multiple programming attempts. She developed urinary incontinence, progressive dysarthria, dysphagia, and inhalatory/exhalatory stridor within a few months. Her dysarthria and dysphagia worsened after medication, but she could still eat orally. Within a year, she required a wheelchair, assistance with all daily activities, an indwelling urinary catheter for urinary retention, and an augmentative communication device for dysarthria. Her body mass index (BMI) was 20.5 two months before her death, compared to 23 at the time of her initial diagnosis.
test_results: Post-mortem macroscopic examination revealed markedly depigmented substantia nigra and locus coeruleus, and mildly atrophic brainstem and cerebellum. The two stimulation electrodes terminated in the subthalamic nuclei. Microscopic examination showed severe loss of neurons, gliosis, and extracellular pigment in the substantia nigra and locus coeruleus; there was also gliosis and neuronal loss in the basis pontis, medulla oblongata, and cerebellum. There were numerous α-synuclein-immunoreactive glial cytoplasmic inclusions (GCIs) in the substantia nigra, red nucleus, crus cerebri, striatum, pallidum, medulla oblongata, and white matter of the frontal lobe and cerebellum. Fewer GCIs were seen in the white matter of the temporal and parietal lobes, hippocampus, thalamus and subthalamic nucleus. There were numerous GCIs, few glial intra-nuclear inclusions (GIIs), dystrophic neurites (DNs), and scattered neuronal intra-nuclear inclusions (NIIs) and few neuronal cytoplasmic inclusions (NCIs) throughout the pontine nuclei. Although there was no macroscopic atrophy noticed in the putamen, minimal neuronal loss, mild gliosis and numerous α-synuclein-immunoreactive GCIs were observed. No tau-positive pre-tangles or α-synuclein immunoreactive Lewy bodies were seen.

case_report: A 29-year-old male presented with erythematous scaly lesions that had been present since he was 2 years old. He had previously undergone two biopsies and received long-term oral acitretin treatment without improvement. His parents were not related, and no other family members had similar conditions. A recent dermatological examination revealed extensive erythematous patches and plaques with fine scaling, particularly on the lower limbs. The scaling was prominent at the borders of the erythematous plaques, with unaffected areas between the plaques on the back and limbs. The face and scalp showed mild erythema and fine scales resembling seborrheic dermatitis. There was no ectropion, nail dystrophy, or palmoplantar involvement. Histopathologic examination of a punch biopsy showed orthohyperkeratosis, focal parakeratosis, flattening and merging of rete ridges, and mild perivascular lymphocytic infiltration. Dilated follicular infundibulum with hyperkeratotic plug was not observed. Lipid vacuoles were noted in the cytoplasm of basal keratinocytes. Muscle strength was normal, and electromyographic (EMG) examination showed no signs of myopathy. The patient reported no hearing or visual problems, and his mental status and neurological examination were normal. Laboratory results indicated elevated liver transaminases, creatine kinase (CK), and serum triglyceride (TG) levels (alanine transaminase: 132 U/L, normal 5–35 U/L; aspartate transaminase: 83 U/L, normal 5–17 U/L; CK: 580 U/L, normal 22–200 U/L; TG: 381 mg/dl, normal 35–130 mg/dl). Abdominal ultrasonography showed hepatomegaly associated with hepatosteatosis. The patient had a history of hyperlipidemia associated with hepatomegaly, and his skin lesions worsened when serum triglyceride levels increased.
test_results: Prominent intracytoplasmic vacuoles (JBs) were detected in neutrophils when stained with MGG.
Orpha_name: Neutral lipid storage disease with ichthyosis

case_report: A 10-year-old female presented with difficulty seeing in low light conditions. She had no significant personal or family medical history, except for farsightedness of +9 diopters. During an eye examination, her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye. Both biomicroscopy and intraocular pressure were within normal limits. Fundus examination revealed yellowish, rounded subretinal lesions in both eyes, distributed along the temporal vascular arches, sparing the macula. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed no macular abnormalities. Autofluorescence imaging displayed hyperfluorescent lesions corresponding to the subretinal findings, with no other pathological features. Neurophysiological tests, including visual evoked potentials (VEP) and electroretinogram (ERG), along with a 30-2 visual field test, were conducted. VEP results indicated normal wave latency peaks and amplitudes. The ERG showed irregular morphology potentials, with normal latencies for a-waves and increased b-waves in both photopic and scotopic conditions. The 30-2 visual field test revealed peripheral arciform defects and a general reduction in sensitivity in both eyes, with a mean deviation of -5.93 dB in the right eye and -7.46 dB in the left eye, and a standard deviation above the average of 1.91 dB in the right eye and 1.82 dB in the left eye.
test_results: The genetic test was positive for the mutation in the gene that codes for retinaldehyde-binding protein 1 (RLBP1).

case_report: A 27-year-old male experienced headaches and seizures for 4 months. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a space-occupying lesion in the right frontal lobe. The tumor was surgically removed via craniotomy, and histopathological examination identified it as a low-grade astrocytoma. Subsequently, he received a total dose of 65 Gy of external beam radiotherapy. Post-irradiation, he developed radiation dermatitis and postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, which partially subsided over 6 months. Three months later, he observed a linear depressed lesion at the surgical site on his forehead and scalp. Shortly after, firm erythematous plaques appeared on his thighs, forearms, and trunk, which evolved into hyperpigmented, atrophic, indurated plaques. Within a year, generalized skin hardening over the abdomen, chest, and forearms led to restricted arm mobility, preventing full elbow extension. Examination revealed two linear hyperpigmented depressed scars on the forehead with a “en coup de sabre” appearance. The skin on both arms and forearms was tight and difficult to pinch. There was no sclerodactyly, Raynaud's phenomenon, or other systemic symptoms. Laboratory tests showed positive ANA, but anti-Scl-70, anti-ds-DNA, anticentromere, anti-Ro-La, and anti-topoisomerase antibodies were negative. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 54 mm/h, and differential leukocyte count indicated eosinophilia (13%). Chest X-ray, computed tomography thorax, and electrocardiogram were normal.
test_results: A biopsy from the lesion on his lower back showed markedly thickened, hyalinized, closely packed collagen bundles in reticular and papillary dermis. Sparse perivascular and periappendageal lymphohistiocytic infiltrate, atrophy of pilosebaceous units was seen. There was no mucin deposition.

case_report: The patient is a 9-year-old male, firstborn in a nonconsanguineous family, who exhibited normal development until the age of 8. At that time, he began experiencing frequent falls, an unsteady gait, and slowed movements. Subsequently, he had generalized tonic-clonic seizures that did not respond to anticonvulsant medications. Over several months, the parents observed a regression in developmental milestones, with the child's current developmental age being approximately 1.5 to 2 years. Language skills also regressed to monosyllabic speech. Despite multiple anticonvulsant treatments, seizures persisted. There was no history of abnormal movements or psychiatric symptoms, and no other family members were affected. Physical examination revealed an unsteady gait, slowed movements, difficulty with eye movements, rigidity, and signs indicative of cerebellar involvement. Fundus examination was normal. There were no signs of chorea, small head size, facial abnormalities, or enlargement of the liver and spleen. Electroencephalography (EEG) results were normal.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain showed hyperintensity involving caudate nucleus and putamen on both sides with atrophy and volume loss. Positron emission tomography (PET) scan showed severe hypometabolism in bilateral striatum. DNA polymerase chain reaction showed 83 expanded trinucleotide CAG repeat sequences.

case_report: A 22-year-old male presented with a painless swelling over the left eye and mechanical ptosis of the upper lid. Proptosis of 2 mm was observed. The patient noted a gradual increase in size over 2 years. No diplopia or pain was reported. Examination revealed a mass located anterior to the orbital rim in the superolateral part of the orbit, with the posterior edge not palpable as it was within the orbit. The mass was firm to hard in consistency, smooth-surfaced, and nontender. There was no globe displacement, motility restriction, or diplopia. The patient reported no history of fluctuating size. Anterior segment evaluation, intraocular pressure, and fundus examination of both eyes were normal. Computed tomography showed an iso-to-hypodense mass lesion in the superotemporal aspect of the left orbit, possibly arising from the lacrimal gland, which could not be clearly delineated from the mass. No obvious changes to the bony orbit were noted on the scans. Fine needle aspiration cytology smears showed no malignant cells, but a conclusive diagnosis could not be made. An excision biopsy was performed. Intraoperatively, the mass was pink, vascular, and well-circumscribed but not encapsulated. The lacrimal gland was seen in close relation to the mass, compressed between the mass and the superolateral orbital bony rim. The mass was excised completely and measured 20 mm × 20 mm × 7 mm. The cut surface was homogeneous without distended vascular channels, lacrimal tissue, or cystic dilatations.
test_results: On microscopic examination, spindle cells in compact sheaves closely opposed to thin walled vessels were seen in a fibrocollagenous background. The nuclei were open, oval, and contained small, uniform nucleoli. No necrosis was noted, and a few engorged vessels were seen in the outlying area. No lymphoid aggregates or germinal centers were identifiable. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the tumor cells stained positive for CD 34 and CD 31. Furthermore, the tumor stained positive for smooth muscle actin and negative for CD68. HMB-45 immunostaining was negative, and the Ki-67 proliferation index was low with <5% of the cells staining positive.
diagnosis: Solid variant of angioleiomyoma of the orbit

case_report: A 20-year-old male presented with a palpable mass located at the back of his knee, persisting for 3 years. The mass was painless, gradually increasing in size to 10x9 cm. The patient experienced difficulty squatting for the past 3 months. On examination, the mass was non-tender, had a soft-to-firm consistency, well-defined edges, smooth surface, and was non-movable without any visible or palpable pulsations. It was non-reducible and not attached to the overlying skin, which showed no signs of local inflammation. Knee flexion was slightly reduced due to the mass, causing discomfort. Distal pulsations were symmetric, and there was no neural deficit. Lateral plain radiography of the right knee revealed a diffuse, non-specific soft-tissue density without calcifications or bone involvement. Ultrasonography showed a heterogeneously hypoechoic lesion measuring 9.6x8.6 cm in the right popliteal fossa, with increased internal vascularity and signs of inflammation, but no knee effusion. Due to financial constraints, MRI was not performed. The patient was informed about the importance of MRI and consented to an excisional biopsy. The biopsy was performed using a posterior approach, revealing the mass between the two heads of the gastrocnemius muscle, under the superficial fascia. The mass was encapsulated, with no major adhesions, and was easily separated from surrounding soft tissue using blunt dissection. A solid, brownish-red mass was excised and sent for further examination. The mass was well-circumscribed, with a gray-white myxoid change and a yellowish fatty center with interspersed vascularity on the cut surface.
test_results: Spindle-shaped fibroblasts arranged in fascicular pattern. Cells were slender, and elongated with oval nuclei and prominent nucleoli. Intervening collagenous stroma shows myxoid changes with a few blood vessels and focal inflammation.

case_report: The patient is a 17-year-old Caucasian female who began experiencing upper extremity symptoms at 10.5 years old. Initially, she had mild difficulty extending the left index finger, which progressed to include the right middle finger after one year. By age 12, she developed more noticeable hand weakness, predominantly on the left side. The weakness worsened in cold weather, and her hands were often cold and sweaty. No sensory deficits were observed. There was no history of cervical trauma, but she experienced a growth spurt in the year before symptom onset, growing approximately 8 cm (between the 75th and 90th percentile for growth velocity). There was no family history of neuromuscular disorders. A neurological examination at age 13 revealed significant weakness (MRC 2 to 3−) in the extension of the index and middle fingers bilaterally and in the abduction of the left thumb. There was also weakness (MRC 3+ to 4) in the extension of the ring and little fingers bilaterally, abduction of the right thumb, and abduction and adduction of the left fingers II-V, as well as flexion of the left fingers II-V. Postural tremor and poly-mini-myoclonus of the fingers on extension were observed. There was marked wasting of the right thenar and mild wasting of other intrinsic hand muscles. Muscle strength in wrist flexion and extension, pronation, and supination of the forearms, flexion and extension of the elbow, and shoulder abduction was normal. Sensory deficits were absent, and deep tendon reflexes were intact. Neurological examination of the lower extremities was normal. Cervical spine motility and forward flexion of the whole spine were normal. A motor deficit affecting roots C7 to T1, more pronounced on the left side, was noted. At age 13, her height was 175 cm (5 cm above the 97th percentile), and her weight was 58 kg (75th–90th percentile). By age 14, the pattern of weakness and wasting remained unchanged, though the severity of weakness had slightly increased, stabilizing over the last six months. Follow-up examinations in subsequent years showed no further changes in the pattern or extent of weakness or wasting.
test_results: Nerve conduction studies of the median and ulnar nerves showed reduced compound motor unit action potentials (MUAPs) and a slightly reduced motor conduction velocity on the left side. No conduction blocks were found and sensory nerve conduction studies of the median, ulnar, and radial nerves were normal. Nerve conduction studies of the right peroneal nerve were normal. Needle electromyography of the first, left interosseus muscle showed high-amplitude, long-duration MUAPs indicating chronic denervation. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the cervical spine in an orthotopic head position and under head anteflexion showed flattening and a slight intramedullary signal alteration of the myelon between segments C5 and C7.

case_report: An eight-year-old girl was brought to our hospital by her parents due to a progressive change in the shape of her right fifth finger. Her mother observed an increasing forward curvature of the tip of the right fifth finger over a period of 3 to 4 months. There was no history of injury, cuts, or any form of trauma. The patient did not experience any fevers or redness around the finger. Physical examination showed a lag in the extension of the DIP joint and a forward curvature of the distal phalanx.
test_results: Initial radiographs revealed abnormal volar and radial curvature of the distal phalanx of the right fifth finger with widening of the epiphyseal plate. MR images demonstrated the abnormal curvatures of the distal phalanx without evidence for underlying osteomyelitis. No abnormal soft tissue enhancement was seen. There was normal insertion of the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon.

case_report: The patient is an 11-year-old male from Saudi Arabia who was referred to the endocrine clinic at the age of four due to short stature. At that time, his height was 86.3 cm (-3.84 SD) and his weight was 14 kg (-1.32 SD). He exhibited facial dysmorphism. He was born full-term from a consanguineous marriage with a birth weight of 3 kg. His perinatal, natal, and postnatal history were unremarkable. The patient had a history of delayed speech and language development, with his first word spoken at three and a half years old. He also had recurrent otitis media, recurrent dental caries, and a history of cleft palate surgery. His systematic review and developmental milestones were normal except for mild intellectual disability, delayed speech, and dysarthria. Physical examination revealed multiple dysmorphic features. Other systemic examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, electrolytes, celiac serology, thyroid function test, luteinizing hormone, and follicular stimulating hormone, were all within normal ranges.
test_results: Chromosomal analysis result was obtained. A growth hormone stimulation test confirmed a deficiency of growth hormone.

case_report: A 25-year-old male presented with facial swelling that had been present for one day. He reported experiencing similar episodes over the past two years, with the swelling gradually subsiding without any treatment. Each episode was preceded by minor trauma. There was no history of wheals, systemic complaints, drug intake, food allergies, or similar issues in the family. Physical examination revealed edema of the eyelids, left cheek, and lips. The patient was treated in the emergency department with injections of hydrocortisone, epinephrine, and chlorpheniramine, but there was no significant improvement. The swelling gradually subsided over three days. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, urine examination, antinuclear antibody test, chest X-ray, and X-ray of the paranasal sinuses, were all within normal limits.
test_results: Complement C4 levels were 1.44 mg/dl (N 10 -40 mg/dl) and C1 esterase inhibitor levels were 38 mg/L (N 275 – 400 mg/L).

case_report: A 59-year-old male with a history of verruca vulgaris on his hands presented with pain in the left fifth toe. Physical examination revealed a wide fifth toenail with a longitudinal split in the nail plate. This condition was observed on both feet but was more pronounced and symptomatic on the left side, with the split located approximately one-third of the distance from the lateral edge of the nail plate. The patient reported that this condition had remained unchanged for decades. He denied any significant trauma or surgery to the left fifth toenail but experienced discomfort when wearing shoes. There was no known family history of similar findings.
test_results: Our patient underwent radiographs of his feet which did not show any bone abnormalities.

case_report: A 53-year-old woman presented with multiple papules on the lower gums, which developed one year earlier and spread over the gingiva. Her medical history includes a hysterectomy for uterine myoma 10 years ago, a diagnosis of multinodular goiter 5 years ago, and invasive apocrine-type ductal carcinoma of intermediate grade (score 7) in the left breast 4 years ago. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed asymptomatic hamartomatous hyperplasia in the right cerebellum. She had not taken medications known to induce gum hypertrophy, such as cyclosporine, phenytoin, or calcium channel blockers. There was no family history of malignancy or genetic disorders. Physical examination showed multiple 2 to 7 mm skin-colored papules on the lower gums and adjacent gingiva, giving a cobblestone-like appearance. Histological examination of a papule on the lower gums revealed fibroepithelial hyperplasia with prominent inflammatory cell infiltration. No other remarkable dermatological findings were observed on the face or body. The patient was referred to the Department of Gastroenterology for further evaluation. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and colonoscopy revealed multiple polyps in the gastric mucosa, rectum, and around the ileocecal valve.
test_results: Sequence analysis revealed a heterozygous mutation, c.987_990delTAAA, in exon 8. This four-nucleotide deletion (p.N329fs*14) in the C2 domain of PTEN protein leads to a frame shift at amino acid position 329, resulting in premature translation termination at the 14th position from the altered site.

case_report: A 14-year-old right-handed female presented with involuntary jerking movements of her left arm, particularly noticeable during arm movements or writing. These symptoms began at age 7 and have persisted without progression. The jerking worsens when she attempts to write with her left hand. She was referred to our clinic by a neurologist from her hometown, who did not start any treatment. Her medical history is unremarkable. Family history includes consanguineous marriage with a third-degree relative. Neurological examination revealed only involuntary movements, with no other abnormal findings. The involuntary movements are brief, focal, and dysrhythmic, exacerbated by certain postures and movements, and are more pronounced in the distal part of the left arm. Biochemical analysis did not reveal any significant abnormalities.
test_results: Her electroencephalographic (EEG) examination did not demonstrate cortical discharges associated with myoclonic jerks. On her electromyograms (EMGs) myoclonic activities correlated with clinically observed involuntary movements with varying monophasic or polyphasic amplitudes recurring at irregular intervals were noted. During examination of her somatosensory evoked potentials (SEPs) tibial SEP was evaluated as within normal limits. On examination of median SEP, SEPs with relatively longer latency, and higher amplitude were detected. C reflex was absent.

case_report: A 12-year-old girl visited the dermatology clinic for an evaluation of a non-painful, hyperpigmented, and hairy patch on the right side of her face. This patch was present since birth, originating around her right eye and gradually extending to cover the right side of her face. The patient had no developmental delays or physical issues, and there was no relevant family history. Physical examination revealed a well-defined, light brown patch with increased hair growth on the right side of her face, along with slight facial asymmetry. Dental examination showed unilateral gingival and lip enlargement on the right side, with irregularly spaced teeth on the same side. Ophthalmologic examination indicated that the opening of her right eye was larger than that of her left eye, leading to a finding of hyperopia.
test_results: A biopsy of the hyperpigmented patch on her right cheek showed basal hypomelanosis with elongation of rete ridges. Dental panoramic radiography showed hyperplasia of the right maxillary alveolus and basal bone with missing teeth, consisting of the upper right first and second premolars and the lower right first premolar.

case_report: Patient 2 was a boy aged 2 years and 7 months. He had a normal birth history and typical physical and mental development. He experienced a febrile illness induced by influenza A virus infection, which led to convulsions and a deep coma. He was admitted to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU). During the course of the illness, the coma progressively worsened, and he exhibited limb paroxysmal tremors, shaking, and increased muscle tone with passive extension. Immunoglobulin and methylprednisolone were administered. Vitamin treatment was not provided during hospitalization.
test_results: Brain MRI revealed multiple signal abnormalities in the bilateral basal ganglia, thalamus margin, and brainstem. Blood was collected for genetic testing.

case_report: A 27-year-old Emirati male presented to the emergency department at Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi in September 2015 with severe abdominal pain. The pain had been episodic over the past 4 years, significantly impacting his work and family life. He had been admitted to multiple hospitals in Abu Dhabi and had seen various specialists. He underwent numerous investigations, including blood tests (CBC and differential count, liver and renal profiles, and CRP), gastroscopies, colonoscopies, CT scans, and a laparoscopy. All clinical assessments and investigations showed no significant findings. During one acute admission, an immunologist reviewed the patient. A detailed examination of his medical history revealed that he experienced two swelling episodes per week affecting his face, hands, feet, or scrotum, along with severe abdominal pain twice a week. These episodes appeared suddenly without any obvious triggers, developed over 36 hours, and resolved spontaneously within 5-7 days without medication, including analgesics. He reported no laryngeal swellings or respiratory issues and denied fevers, night sweats, weight loss, changes in bowel habits, or blood in his stools. Occasionally, the swelling episodes were associated with a non-pruritic red skin rash, which was previously treated as chronic urticaria with Omalizumab (300mg every 4 weeks) for 9 months without benefit. His response to various analgesics, high-dose antihistamines, antibiotics, and corticosteroids was unsatisfactory. He is a thalassemia carrier but otherwise healthy with no significant past medical history. There is no family history of immunodeficiency, inflammatory bowel disease, autoimmunity, or FMF. On examination, he was in pain with a soft, tender abdomen, guarding, and decreased bowel sounds. There was no rebound tenderness, rigidity, distension, or ascites, and no peripheral swellings were noted.
test_results: Blood tests showed reduced C4 and absent C1 inhibitor function. Detailed immunological investigations revealed markedly reduced C4 level and absent C1 inhibitor function with normal C3 and C1q levels and raised C1 inhibitor serum levels.

case_report: This 1-year-old boy is the first child of non-consanguineous parents. He was born at term following an unremarkable pregnancy and delivered by cesarean section. Apgar score at 5 minutes was 9. Birth weight was 2900 grams, and head circumference was 34 centimeters. At birth, he exhibited axial hypotonia and hypertonicity in his limbs. At 2 months, binocular nystagmus was observed, which stabilized by 6 months of age. At 8 months, he showed head nodding and had markedly increased tone in both lower extremities at times. Currently, he has global developmental delay, progressive limb spasticity, abnormal eye movements, and axial hypotonia.
test_results: Visual and brainstem evoked potentials are abnormal. MR study reveals poor myelination and dysmyelination of periventricular and sub cortical white matter in T1W and T2W images comparing normal myelination process for the patient's age. Similar finding in infra-tentorial white matter is also seen. DNA sequencing revealed duplication in the PLP1.

case_report: A 27-year-old African American woman, gravida 4, para 2-1-0-3, at 18-week gestation with a history of chronic hypertension and no prenatal care presented with conjunctivitis and a blood pressure of 183/108 mmHg. She had been diagnosed with chronic hypertension at age 13 and had multiple partial evaluations and hospital admissions for severely elevated blood pressures. Her medical records indicated hypokalemia dating back to at least age 17. She had uncomplicated vaginal deliveries in 2008 and 2010, and in 2013, she had an induction of labor and vaginal delivery at 28 weeks due to severely elevated blood pressure readings up to 250/120 mmHg. She reported a family history of hypertension in her two brothers, two sisters, mother, and 4-year-old child, with one sibling unaffected. Most family members had hypertension onset between ages 15 and 30. On admission, her serum potassium was 2.6 mMol/L, sodium 140 mMol/L, and creatinine 0.47 mg/dL. Urine potassium was 15 mMol/L, urine sodium 112 mMol/L, and urine chloride 110 mMol/L. Renin activity was 0.8 ng/mL/hr, aldosterone was <3.0 ng/dL, and Aldosterone/Renin Activity (A/RA) was <3.8. The A/RA ratio was challenging to interpret due to the renin level being near the lower limit and the aldosterone level being below the reported range. Serum adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), urine metanephrines, and urine vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) were within normal ranges. Baseline 24-hour urine showed 357 mg of protein. A renal ultrasound showed normal echotexture with no evidence of hydronephrosis or nephrolithiasis, and no size discrepancy between the kidneys. A previous computed tomography scan of the abdomen showed normal-appearing kidneys, renal vasculature, and adrenal glands.
test_results: Genetic testing confirmed a heterozygous frameshift mutation in the SCNN1B gene.

case_report: A 10-year-old male African child presented at the emergency department with cellulitis related to necrosis of the maxillary first right permanent incisor. After 1 year, he returned for a general consultation. He had no history of medical conditions, and no hair, skin, or nail defects were noted by clinicians or reported by parents. Oral examination revealed a healthy mucosa without bone abnormalities. However, the teeth showed significant structural and eruption abnormalities. The enamel was dark yellow, streaked, and severely worn, appearing translucent in the areas of wear. The enamel radio-opacity was similar to that of dentin. On orthopantomography, taurodontism was observed on the first permanent molars. The tooth eruption was severely disturbed, with the first permanent molars and mandibulary first left deciduous molar impacted. Roots appeared shorter than normal. After several dental infections, dental extractions and complete denture removal were performed. The proband's mother had a reported condition associated with painless mandibular bone exostosis from a previous visit. Clinically, the enamel was orange-brown and appeared severely worn out. Panoramic radiography confirmed multifocal areas of high density in the mandibular bone. Dental examination revealed teeth with thin or absent enamel, numerous endodontic treatments and restorations, and missing teeth. Whole-body scintigraphy revealed only one point of hyperossification on the right ankle. Radiographic examination of the left hand after a single painful episode revealed only a faint modification of the fifth phalanx. There were no hair, skin, or nail defects noted. Residual teeth (except for two mandibular molars, left and right) were extracted, and rehabilitation was performed using a complete maxillary and partial mandibulary removable denture. These oral conditions were not reported for the patient's brothers, aged 2 and 5 years, or father. A clinical condition was established for the proband according to specific criteria.
test_results: A pathogenic variant in DLX3, exon 2, c.398G > C, p. Arg133Pro, was identified in both patients I.1 and II.1, but not in I.2 (DNAs for II.2 and II.3 were not available).

case_report: A 62-year-old male patient was admitted to our hospital in December 2018 presenting with dizziness, nausea, and vomiting. Initial laboratory tests included blood routine examination, liver and kidney function tests, electrolyte levels, myocardial enzyme profile, thyroid function tests, lymphocyte subsets, cytokine levels, pre-transfusion examination, tumor markers, and inflammatory indicators. Physical examination revealed no significant abnormalities.
test_results: Positron emission tomography (PET) and computed tomography (CT) indicated that the patient had soft-tissue density lesions with calcification in the left lower lobes of the thymus and multiple nodules of different sizes in bilateral lungs. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed the status of the mediastinum and lungs: (1) A mass (45 mm × 30 mm × 38 mm) was found in the superior mediastinum of the left lobe of thymus and fat space between the lesion and the surrounding mediastinum vascular, trachea, esophagus, and upper thymus gland; trachea shifted to the right, and the tumor showed equal T1 and long T2 mixed signals with obvious heterogeneous enhancement; (2) Multiple nodules with smooth margin were found in bilateral lungs. The largest one (19 mm × 18 mm) was located in the left lower lobe of lung, and displayed marked enhancement. Immunohistochemical results (lung puncture biopsy under the guidance of CT in the left lung) showed that the expression of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PCK) and P40 in tumor cells revealed positive and the expression of CD5, CD20, CD117, terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT), and Ki-67 revealed negative. The above immunohistochemical indexes were not detected in the tissue specimens of the ectopic thymoma of left lower lung. Similarly, for the immunohistochemical indexes thyroid transcription factor 1 (TTF-1), synapsin (Syn), CD34, signal transducer and activator of transcription 6 (STAT6), smooth muscle actin (SMA), S100, Desmin, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) were detected in ectopic thymoma of the left lower lung but not detected in the tissue specimens of the anterior mediastinal thymoma.
diagnosis: Type A Thymoma with Ectopic Thymoma in the Lung

case_report: The patient was delivered via Cesarean section at 38 weeks of gestation after an uncomplicated pregnancy. The mother was 21 years old and the father was 26 years old at the time of birth. Birth weight was 3.02 kg (25-50th percentile), head circumference was 34.9 cm (50-75th percentile), and birth length was 44.4 cm (below the 5th percentile). At birth, dysmorphic features and microphthalmia of the right eye were observed. An ocular prosthetic was placed at approximately 3 months of age. Developmental delays were noted starting at 4 months, including failure to roll over. Vocalization was normal, but object tracking was mildly impaired. The patient exhibited a weak grip, significant central hypotonia, decreased muscle bulk, and head lagging. At 1 year of age, the patient uses one non-specific word ('dada'), cannot sit up independently or crawl, but can 'scoot'. Current measurements are weight 6.24 kg (<3rd percentile), length 67 cm (<3rd percentile), and head circumference 44.1 cm (5th percentile). The anterior fontanelle is not fused (1.5 cm × 1.5 cm). Physical examination reveals microphthalmia, micrognathia, a wide nasal bridge, thick hair, a low anterior hairline, two posterior hair whorls, long and prominent eyelashes, sacral hypertrichosis, small and down-slanted palpebral fissures with telecanthus, tapered fingers, partial 3-4 syndactyly on the left hand, mild pectus excavatum, and small feet and hands. Genetic testing showed a normal karyotype (46, XY) and SNP-CMA. A spinal canal ultrasound at 4 months ruled out neural tube defects, and an abdominal ultrasound ruled out gross malformations of the liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, and kidneys. No brain MRI has been performed. Family history is unremarkable except for a paternal half-brother with a unilateral dysplastic kidney. Two other paternal half-siblings and one full sibling are healthy, as are the parents. There is no consanguinity. The patient receives weekly physical and occupational therapies, which started at 5 months, and has made substantial gains in motor functioning and expressive language.
test_results: Exome Sequencing was performed in the UCLA Molecular Diagnostics Laboratories using clinically validated protocols. The proband and both parents were sequenced in each case (trio analysis).
