All genes harboring de novo, homozygous or compound heterozygous variants with allele frequencies <1% in the general population were evaluated by a Genomics Data Board. Variant Annotator X (VAX) was used for rich annotation of DNA variants. Criteria for high confidence for de novo variants was: quality score >=Q500 in each individual; variant observed in <2 reads in any individual parent; variant not observed in the general population. Clinically significant variants were confirmed using PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing of the proband and both parents.

case_report: A 16-year-old girl was referred for genetic counselling due to congenital hearing loss and subtle physical features. She is the second child of non-consanguineous parents and has two healthy sisters. She was born at term with a birth weight of 3200 g and a length of 53 cm. Her Apgar score was 10. At birth, synophrys and low set ears were observed. Her early psychomotor development was normal, with no notable delays. Speech impairment due to hearing problems was noted at the age of 2, and she attended a school for children with hearing impairment. At the age of 16, she was hospitalised at the Endocrinology Unit for hirsutism and hypercholesterolemia. Physical examination revealed seborrheic dermatitis, astigmatism, and profound sensorineural hearing loss. Hirsutism was scored at 6 on the Ferriman-Gallwey scale. Sex hormone levels were normal. Examination at the genetic counselling centre showed wide set eyes with brilliant blue irides, dystopia canthorum, shortened upslanting palpebral fissures, hypoplastic alae nasi, and hirsutism. Synophrys was not visible as she plucks her eyebrows. She did not present a white forelock, though it cannot be excluded that she dyes her hair. Intellectual development was normal. Both parents were phenotypically normal and did not present any notable features.
test_results: Chromosomal analysis was performed according to standard procedures on GTG-banded metaphase spreads, obtained from peripheral blood lymphocytes. An oligo array-CGH was performed using the Human Genome CGH Microarray Kit and SurePrint G3 4x180K Human Kit (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA), according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood lymphocytes. Fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) was performed on metaphase spreads by using PAX3 Breakapart Probe (Cytocell, Cambridge, UK) according to manufacturer’s protocol. Metaphases were analysed with Nikon Eclipse fluorescent microscope. Images were analysed and archived with Applied Spectral Imaging software (Applied Spectral Imaging, Edingen, Neckerhausen, Germany).

case_report: A 2-year-old boy presented with a slowly enlarging mass under the tongue for 6 months. He was born without any anomalies and had average developmental milestones, except for delayed speech due to the mass at the floor of the mouth. Physical examination revealed a left sublingual cystic lesion measuring 1.0 × 1.0 cm. Ankyloglossia was noted. Cervical lymph nodes were not palpable. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a multi-lobulated cystic mass approximately 3.15 × 2.1 × 2.9 cm in size, with hypersignal intensity on T2-weighted images and hyposignal intensity on T1-weighted images, including T1 fat suppression and T1 fat suppression with gadolinium. The mass involved the left sublingual, submandibular, pharyngeal, and parapharyngeal spaces. Surgery was performed under general anesthesia, including a frenotomy and complete removal of the cystic mass with minimal leakage. A sclerosing agent was injected at the surgical site to prevent any residual undetected cystic formations. Macroscopic examination of the specimen revealed a multi-lobulated cystic cavity with fluid leakage.
test_results: Pathological examination demonstrated a unicystic lesion lined by ciliated pseudostratified columnar and cuboidal cells. Subepithelial stroma revealed fibrovascular tissue. There was no other mesenchymal component such as smooth muscle bundles and cartilages.

case_report: A 22-year-old female from Attock, Pakistan, married for two months and without children, was admitted to the gynecology unit of a tertiary care hospital due to heavy menstrual periods. Comprehensive examination by gynecology department physicians revealed no gynecological abnormalities. The patient reported a history of easy bruising and purpura following minor trauma since childhood. Physical examination showed pallor, multiple petechiae, and purpura across the body. Further management steps were planned.
test_results: She had a deranged clotting profile, i.e., prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) but normal bleeding time. Her platelets count was also normal. Her clotting factors VIII and IX were normal. Ristocetin assay test for functional platelet disorder also came back normal. Factor I was normally given in the disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) profile. The patient's test results for hepatitis B and hepatitis C virus were negative. DIC was also ruled out as her D-dimers, fibrinogen, and platelet count were normal.

case_report: A 48-year-old female from Katwe suburb, south of Kampala City, visited the Oral Surgery and Jaw Injuries Unit at Mulago National Referral and Teaching Hospital on July 25, 2011. She reported a three-week history of tongue discoloration and swelling, along with difficulty in chewing and speaking. She had been taking antibiotics and pain relievers. There was no history of trauma, dental procedures, bleeding, swelling in other body parts, or treatment for chronic diseases. No social history was recorded, her HIV status was unknown, and her extremities were not examined. Physical examination revealed a female in good general condition with swelling of the lower face and bilateral non-tender submandibular lymph nodes. The anterior part of the tongue was swollen and red, with a firm, tender lump measuring 2 × 4 millimeters. The mucosa, gingiva, palates, jaw, and neck movements were normal. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 14.5 × 103/μL and a neutrophil count of 10.2 × 103/μL, both elevated above the reference ranges of 4–11 and 2–7 respectively. Bleeding indices were normal. The lump was removed and the patient was prescribed a cetrimide-lidocaine hydrochloride mouthwash and gargle. A week later, the facial swelling and submandibular lymphadenopathy had resolved. There were no records of follow-up visits.
test_results: Microscopy of formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded Haematoxylin and Eosin-stained tongue sections had shown a space-occupying lesion within skeletal muscle. This was surrounded by numerous neutrophils, macrophages and giant cells, some lymphocytes and occasional eosinophils. Several oval-shaped structures, some intact some cracked, aggregated in compartments that occupied most of the space. Discontinuous spiral-bound elongations at the periphery of the lesion represented the flea’s chitinous exoskeleton.

case_report: A 59-year-old male arrived at the emergency department (ED) with complaints of crampy, diffuse abdominal pain, nausea, and watery diarrhea that had persisted for four days. He had visited the ED two days earlier with similar symptoms, and a computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast had shown diverticulosis. He was discharged in stable condition with prescriptions for oral dicyclomine 10 milligrams (mg) and ibuprofen 600 mg. The following day, his primary care physician prescribed hydrocodone/acetaminophen 5/325 mg for pain management. Due to worsening abdominal pain unrelieved by these medications, he returned to the ED for further evaluation. His medical history included Barrett’s esophagus, chronic kidney disease, diverticulosis, gastroesophageal reflux disease, gout, hyperlipidemia, and hypertension. He had previously undergone esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) for gastrointestinal issues. He was compliant with his medications, which included amlodipine, atorvastatin, lisinopril, and omeprazole. His social history included a 45-pack per year smoking history and moderate alcohol consumption on a weekly basis. Upon arrival at the ED, his vital signs were: temperature 97.9 degrees Fahrenheit, pulse 71 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, blood pressure 150/89 millimeters of mercury (mmHg), and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical examination showed a nontoxic, mildly uncomfortable patient with mild, diffuse abdominal tenderness to palpation, but no distention, rebound, or abdominal bruit. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable. Initial diagnostic workup, including complete blood count, complete metabolic panel, lipase, urinalysis, urine drug screen, lactate, electrocardiogram, troponin I, and chest radiograph, was unremarkable. Upon reevaluation, the patient's symptoms had somewhat improved, but he reported some tenderness to palpation in the midline of his back.
test_results: A CT angiogram of the chest and abdomen with three-dimensional reconstructions revealed stenosis at the origin of the celiac artery with characteristic 'hooked' appearance.

case_report: A 34-year-old Palestinian female with a history of gestational diabetes two years ago and a COVID-19 infection 30 days prior presented to the emergency department with a three-week history of severe pain on the left side of her face, loss of vision, and impaired movement on the left side. Her symptoms began immediately after a 10-day recovery period from COVID-19. One week before presentation, she was treated with ceftriaxone 2 g once daily and dexamethasone 4 mg three times daily for presumed facial nerve palsy without improvement. She had received multiple steroid injections for COVID-19 treatment from an outpatient clinic and had no history of follow-up or diabetes treatment. Upon admission, she was alert, oriented, and hemodynamically stable. Examination revealed periorbital edema, complete left eye proptosis, a dilated non-reactive pupil, left eye ophthalmoplegia, vision loss, trigeminal nerve involvement (v1, v2, v3), decreased hearing on the left side, and a vesicular rash on the left cheek. Laboratory results were as follows: hemoglobin 13.2 g/dl, white blood cell count 14.5 K/uL (90% neutrophils), platelet count 269 K/uL, creatinine 0.54 mg/dl, serum potassium 4.9 mmol/l, random blood sugar 277 mg/dl, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 101 mm/hr, and C-reactive protein 174 mg/dl. The patient was empirically treated with vancomycin (1 g twice daily), piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g four times daily), enoxaparin (80 mg twice daily), and methylprednisolone (1 g once daily).
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with orbital view showed multifocal infarction, a paranasal sinus extensive mucosal disease, and cavernous sinus thrombosis.

case_report: The patient is a 2-year-old Japanese girl born to healthy, unrelated parents. She exhibits significant underdevelopment of the lower jaw and a rounded facial structure with prominent cheeks. There is an external ear malformation characterized by question-mark shaped ears. Oral abnormalities include a small mouth, a lobular underdeveloped tongue with soft-tissue projections, a cleft palate with an underdeveloped soft palate, and fusion of the temporomandibular joints. She experiences difficulties with feeding and speech articulation. Additional findings include narrowing of the ear canal, internal ear malformations affecting the semicircular and cochlear ducts, and moderate sensorineural hearing loss. A tracheostomy was performed due to upper airway obstruction. Three-dimensional computed tomography (3D-CT) revealed absence of the mandibular condyle, very short rami, and a receding lower jaw. The mandibular rami were fused with the medial and lateral pterygoid plates, and both mandibular angles were indistinct. The intracranial structure, nasal cavity, orbital cavity, and maxilla appeared normal. No other general malformations, growth retardation, or developmental delays were noted.
test_results: By trio-based filtering, we identified a novel de novo non-synonymous variant in exon 7 of GNAI3 (NM_006496.4:c.807C>A:p.(Asn269Lys)). The variant was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. It was not found in the ExAC, gnomAD, 1000 genome or the inhouse database of WES from over 4000 Japanese individuals. Asn269 within the G4 box domain of the Gαi3 forms a hydrogen bond with the N7 atom of the guanine moiety. In silico structural analysis reveals that the substitution of Asn269 to Lys is expected to disrupt the hydrogen bond, which may interfere downstream of Gαi3 signal.

case_report: A 35-year-old man with a history of polysubstance use was brought to the Emergency Department after an unwitnessed cardiopulmonary arrest. Initial rhythm was pulseless electrical activity, and spontaneous circulation returned after 25 minutes of chest compressions. Electrocardiogram was unremarkable, blood glucose was undetectable, and the Full Outline of UnResponsiveness (FOUR) score was 1 (E0M0B0R1). Urine toxicology tested positive for cocaine and fentanyl. Neurological examination showed generalized myoclonus, increased muscle tone in the lower extremities, and sustained clonus at both ankles. Initial computed tomography (CT) of the head showed preserved gray-white differentiation and hypodensity in the left cerebellar hemisphere. The patient was resuscitated in the intensive care unit (ICU) and cooled to 33°C for 24 hours as per institutional protocol. Neuron specific enolase was elevated at 28.7 ng/ml. Continuous electroencephalogram (cEEG) showed a background suppression ratio of 85%, which improved to 10% overnight. On hospital day 3, the FOUR score improved to 9 (E4M0B4R1), and cEEG revealed continuous reactive background with theta-delta slowing. The patient's eyes opened spontaneously but did not react to noxious stimuli. Somatosensory evoked potential (SSEP) showed bilaterally absent cortical potentials.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of brain and cervical spine revealed symmetrical diffusion restriction with surrounding edema in the juxtacortical white matter, hippocampi, superior cerebellar peduncles, dorsal pons, dorsolateral medulla within the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS), and cerebellum. Punctate hyperintensities were apparent in the left ventral spinal cord at C3-C4 on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences indicating subacute infarct. There were no vascular abnormalities identified on magnetic resonance angiogram (MRA) of head and neck vessels.

case_report: A 77-year-old woman, under medical treatment for hypertension, was referred to our hospital due to elevated serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (γ-GTP) levels. She was asymptomatic and had no history of biliary tract disease, abdominal surgery, autoimmune disease, allergies, or abdominal trauma. She also had no history of heavy alcohol consumption or smoking. Her brother had a history of pancreatic cancer. Physical examination revealed no skin yellowing or abdominal tumor. The patient’s general condition was good, with a body mass index of 22.7 kg/m2. Laboratory tests showed slightly elevated serum aspartate aminotransferase (52 IU/L; reference: 13–30 IU/L), alanine aminotransferase (54 IU/L; reference: 17–23 IU/L), ALP (414 IU/L; reference: 106–322 IU/L), and γ-GTP (449 IU/L; reference: 9–32 IU/L) levels. Serum total bilirubin and direct bilirubin levels were normal. The patient tested positive for serum hepatitis C virus antibody, while serum tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9) and IgG4 levels were within normal limits. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and total colonoscopy showed no lesions. Axial view of contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CE-CT) revealed dilation from the intrahepatic to the upper common bile duct and an irregular mass lesion in the distal bile duct. Coronal view showed the lesion as multiple overlapping leaf-like folds. T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) indicated an irregular signal defect in the middle bile duct. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) also showed a signal defect and mild dilation of the proximal bile duct. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (18F-FDG-PET/CT) revealed no uptake in the lesion. Biliary cytology and brushing cytology were performed twice, with no malignant disease detected in any specimens. Surgical treatment was performed with full patient consent.
test_results: The bile duct lesion showed dense fibrosis under the mucosal layer and severe inflammation of the peribiliary glands. Marked lymphoplasmacytic cells invasion under the dense fibrosis was observed. These cells formed numerous lymphoid follicles containing germinal centers. IHC showed positive for CD3, CD20 and CD79a in infiltrated lymphoplasmacytic cells under the thickening fibrosis. Many CD138-positive plasma cells were scattered around the lymphoid follicles, but IgG4-positive plasma cells were few.

case_report: A 25-year-old black female patient was referred from a nearby town and presented to the neurology clinic of Tikur Anbessa Specialized Hospital in Addis Ababa. Her primary complaint was a gradual, painless swelling of her left upper lip, which extended to her left cheek. She experienced difficulty closing her left eyelid for the past 5 days. Her medical history included two episodes of peripheral facial weakness on the same side. The first episode in 2016 resolved on its own without treatment. During the second episode, two years later, she visited a nearby clinic and received corticosteroid treatment, which led to complete resolution of her symptoms. She did not recall any specific cause or trigger for her symptoms. She reported no recent infections of the ear, nose, throat, sinus, or dental structures, and no recent trauma to the head or neck. She also denied any skin rash, sensory symptoms, or history of sarcoidosis, Crohn’s disease, autoimmune conditions, or other chronic illnesses. Her family history was negative for similar conditions, and she had no history of food allergies or other allergic reactions. On examination, she had diffuse, non-pitting swelling of the left cheek with peri-orbital fullness, mild flattening of the left naso-labial fold, and a fissured tongue (lingua plicata). Her vital signs were normal, and no sensory changes in the face were detected. The rest of her examination was unremarkable. Clinical and laboratory evaluations for potential causes of recurrent peripheral facial palsy, including diabetes mellitus, syphilis, Guillain–Barre syndrome, hypothyroidism, leukemia, or other tumors, were non-revealing.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head showed a normal brain parenchyma and clear course of the seventh nerve.

case_report: The patient, a 32-year-old female, was born after an uneventful pregnancy as the first child of non-consanguineous German parents. Her cognitive and motor development were normal. At 6 years old, she exhibited an unsteady gait and by 8 years old, she developed pointed feet. Her symptoms gradually worsened, and by 17, she required significant assistance to walk and began using a wheelchair. At this age, she also developed tremor and ataxia in the upper extremities, which progressively affected her head, trunk, and legs, severely impacting daily activities such as eating and drinking independently. She developed a prominent no-no head tremor and dystonic laterocollis. Repeated cranial MRIs between the ages of 23 and 30 showed non-progressive severe supra- and infratentorial leukoencephalopathy. The pallidum appeared FLAIR- and T2-hypointense without clear abnormalities on iron-sensitive sequences. Clinical examination revealed severe dysarthria with scanning and voice tremor, making her speech nearly incomprehensible. She had impaired smooth pursuit, macro-saccadic intrusions, and nystagmus on upward and downward gaze. Severe spastic paraplegia was noted with increased reflexes, bilateral positive Babinski sign, and sustained foot clonus. There was mild rest tremor but severe slow and coarse postural and intention tremor, particularly when holding out the arms and during finger-nose testing, with an amplitude exceeding 30 cm, resembling Holmes-like tremor. Alcohol temporarily alleviated her symptoms, especially the tremor, but symptoms worsened significantly after the effect wore off. At 27, treatment with levodopa (up to 1400 mg daily) led to mild symptom improvement. Three years later, she underwent bilateral DBS in the ventralis intermedius (VIM) nucleus of the thalamus, which significantly improved her tremor, allowing her to eat and drink independently. The Fahn tremor scale improved from 87/144 to 70/144 immediately post-operation. However, over two years, the tremor moderately progressed, though the amplitude remained below preoperative levels. The family history showed no neurological disorders. The patient has a healthy younger sister. Extensive metabolic workup did not reveal any abnormalities. Tests for HSP-SPAST (SPG4), HSP/ATX-SPG7 (SPG7), ATX-ATXN1 (SCA1), ATX-ATXN2 (SCA2), ATX-ATXN3 (SCA3), ATX-CACNA1A (SCA6), ATX/HSP-SACS (ARSACS), and Alexander’s disease (GFAP) were negative.
test_results: Re-evaluating exome data in 2020 within the GPAP platform of the SolveRD project, identified two potentially pathogenic, intronic variants in the VPS13D gene (NM_018156.4: c.941 + 3A > G and c.2237−1G > A), which had been linked to spastic ataxia and spastic paraplegia.
Orpha_name: Infantile hypotonia-oculomotor anomalies-hyperkinetic movements-developmental delay syndrome

case_report: A 21-year-old woman experienced numbness and weakness in her limbs. Initial blood tests and physical examination showed no abnormalities. She was treated with alprazolam (1.2 mg) for psychological stress. Subsequently, she developed numbness of the tongue, headache, difficulty opening her eyes, unfocused vision, and noticed circular eye motions (nystagmus). The next day, she felt exhausted and unable to walk unaided, presenting at the Department of Psychiatry. She was observed sitting slumped in a wheelchair, responding to questions with slight nods, and raising her voice when asked about workplace conflicts. She was admitted for further evaluation. Upon admission, she initially responded only by nodding until her elder sister visited, after which she became excited, cried, and talked loudly. She later became unresponsive, groaned as if in pain, cried out loudly, and made backward jerking motions. Her vital signs included a temperature of 37.2°C, pulse of 72 beats/min, and blood pressure of 106/67 mmHg. Pupillary diameter was 5 mm with normal light reflex bilaterally. Deep tendon reflexes and Babinski sign were normal. Blood tests showed no abnormalities in liver or kidney function, electrolytes, or thyroid function indices, but serum anti-thyroglobulin antibody (630.0 IU/mL) and anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody (15.4 IU/mL) were positive. MRI of the head showed no abnormalities in the brain parenchyma, cerebral blood vessels, or intracranial structures. EEG revealed widespread low-voltage slow waves between 5 and 7 Hz, with 4- and 15-Hz spindle waves in the frontal, parietal, and occipital regions, unchanged by photic stimulation. Five days post-admission, she was unresponsive to stimulation. She also developed pyrexia and nuchal rigidity. CSF analysis showed a slight increase in monocytes (7 cells/µL), normal glucose (0 mg/dl) and protein (41 mg/dl) levels, and negative TPOAb and TgAb. CSF did not show albuminocytologic dissociation, and oligoclonal bands were not evaluated. Nerve conduction velocity examination showed normal compound motor action potentials and sensory conditions of the median and ulnar nerves. Ultrasonography revealed distinct thyroid enlargement. Steroid pulse therapy (methylprednisolone at 1 g for 3 days) was initiated. Her consciousness improved soon after completing the therapy, and by day 4 post-treatment (day 10 after admission), she was able to converse and eat. Further neurological examinations revealed double vision, numbness of the left arm, abductive movement disorder of the right eye, reduced grip strength (9.6/8.2 kg), and cerebellar ataxia.
test_results: Serum anti-GQ1b and anti-GT1a antibodies were positive.

case_report: A 12-year-old boy was bitten by a southern Pacific rattlesnake (Crotalus oreganus helleri) near the lateral malleolus while walking past a tarp in his uncle's garage in southern California. He described the pain in his foot as intense, comparing it to being 'lit on fire and run over by a truck.' The snake was found and identified by a local herpetologist. Initial treatment in the emergency department included intravenous opioids for pain management, CroFab® antivenom [Crotalidae polyvalent immune Fab (ovine)], and fluid hydration. Vital signs were stable, and coagulation studies showed mildly elevated D-dimer and fibrinogen levels and mild thrombocytopenia, which resolved the next day. Progressive envenoming signs were controlled with two additional doses of antivenom, totaling 14 vials. Two months later, the patient visited a chronic pain specialist with symptoms progressing up the ipsilateral leg to just below the patella, in the distribution of the sural nerve. Physical examination revealed lower extremity edema up to the knee, erythema, hyperalgesia, hot and cold dysesthesia, and motor and sudomotor changes in the area around the original bite site. These symptoms extended up his leg to the subpatellar region.
test_results: Budapest Criteria were met for the presence of edema up to the knee, erythema, hyperalgesia, hot and cold dysesthesia, and sudomotor changes.

case_report: A 56-year-old Filipino male with hypertension, diabetes, PTSD, and bipolar disorder (type 1) was brought to the emergency room due to altered mental status. The patient was fully functional until three weeks prior when he began experiencing episodes of agitation and nighttime awakenings, reliving war experiences. During this period, he also increased his fluid intake and was observed wandering at night with his luggage, believing he was traveling to America. He was admitted to a psychiatric facility where his medications—risperidone, clonazepam, biperiden, and lithium carbonate—were continued. Despite this, his agitation persisted, and his lithium dosage was increased from 600 mg to 900 mg per day. Two days before admission, he had prolonged sleep and no oral intake. Upon arrival at the emergency room, he presented with generalized seizures and progressed to status epilepticus. His vital signs were: BP 120/60 mmHg, heart rate 137/min, respiratory rate 24/min, and temperature 36.7°C, with no other abnormal systemic physical exam findings. Interictally, he was obtunded with a Glasgow coma score of 8 (E2V1M4). There were no cranial nerve abnormalities, focal weakness, or nuchal rigidity. Initial work-up revealed hypoglycemia (57 mg/dL), elevated lithium (2.8 mEq/L), elevated creatinine (10.54 mg/dL), elevated potassium (5.4 mEq/L), low sodium (130 mEq/L), and combined metabolic and respiratory acidosis on ABGs. A plain cranial CT scan was unremarkable. The patient received intravenous valproic acid and a midazolam drip for seizure control. He underwent intermittent hemodialysis to clear the lithium, and all psychiatric medications, including lithium, were discontinued.
test_results: An electroencephalogram (EEG) was done the following day which showed a generalized slowing of the background activity with occasional spike waves in the frontal region. Lithium levels were monitored with a decreasing level down to 0.14 mEq/L after 5 days. Despite clearance of benzodiazepine and lithium (now at 0.01 mEq/L), the patient did not regain full consciousness. Subsequent EEGs still showed a generalized theta slowing and with no more epileptiform discharges seen.

case_report: A 21-year-old woman visited our outpatient clinic with a 2-year history of recurring episodes of non-itchy hives and skin swelling, swelling at the proximal interphalangeal joints and wrists, widespread joint pain, and fever reaching up to 39 °C, occurring without a clear pattern or identifiable trigger, particularly in the evening. She had previously been evaluated by infectious disease, dermatology, and allergy specialists and had been treated with corticosteroids, antihistamines, cyclosporine (100 mg/day), and omalizumab without improvement. There was no family history of fever, rheumatic, dermatologic, or autoimmune conditions. At the time of her visit, she was in partial remission while taking 37.5 mg of prednisone daily. Upon admission to our ward, extensive laboratory tests showed elevated CRP (59 mg/L, normal range 0–5 mg/L) and ESR (74 mm/h, normal range 0–20 mm/h), microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 9.5 g/L, mean cellular volume 82.0 fL), and neutrophilic leukocytosis (white blood cells 22.9 x 10^9/L, neutrophils 21.2 x 10^9/L). IgM levels were slightly elevated (2.75 g/L, normal range 0.4–2.3 g/L), while IgA, IgE, and IgG levels were within normal limits. Antinuclear antibodies were positive at a titer of 1:80 with a homogenous pattern. Other autoimmunity, oncologic, hematologic screenings, infectious disease assessments, and bone turnover evaluations did not show any abnormalities. Chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasound were performed, showing no pathological findings, including no evidence of an enlarged spleen or bone lesions.
test_results: Serum protein electrophoresis revealed an inflammatory pattern, without any monoclonal gammopathy. PET-CT showed diffuse homogenous bone marrow uptake and slight splenic uptake. A cutaneous biopsy revealed leukocytoclastic neutrophilic infiltration with minimal vasculitic aspects and a minimum amount of dermal edema.

case_report: A 74-year-old female presented with post-menopausal bleeding lasting for a month, occurring intermittently and requiring approximately 1–2 pads each day. The patient also reported intermittent pelvic tenderness, more pronounced on the right side. She has two living children delivered via spontaneous vaginal delivery and no history of abortions. Menopause occurred 22 years ago. Her past personal and familial medical history were unremarkable. Physical and gynecological examinations revealed normal findings. Initial ultrasonography on July 31st, 2018, indicated that the uterine cavity was filled with fluid due to a blockage at the endocervix, though the cause was undetermined. The patient was referred to a tertiary hospital for further evaluation. During a hysteroscopic examination by a gynecology oncology consultant with over 10 years of experience, several glomerular masses with atypical vessels were observed, resembling malignant endometrial lesions. The biopsy appearance suggested a serous lesion, with no normal endometrial tissue or hyperplastic zones identified.
test_results: Histopathologic specimen showing cancerous cells with no normal tissue. Glomerular growing mass with atypical vessels. MRI examination (September 1st, 2018) found two masses: at the tube and endometrium. Endometrial mass was prominent to anterior junctional zone with 13 mm thickness, did not invade the myometrium, and covered <50% of the endometrial surface in accordance to T1A-N0-M0 staging. There were right tubal mass sized 29/30/31 mm and right hydrosalpinx with T2A-N0-M0 staging. There were no signs of metastasis.

case_report: A 10-month-old Sri Lankan Sinhalese male infant exhibited widespread darkening of the skin and accelerated growth since birth. He was delivered at full term following an uneventful pregnancy and had a normal perinatal period without any episodes of low blood sugar or circulatory issues. He is the only child of consanguineous parents. At birth, his growth measurements were within normal ranges: weight 3.3 kg, length 50 cm, and head circumference 35 cm. His growth chart showed rapid increases in weight, length, and head circumference from birth. His parents noted skin darkening at birth, which progressively worsened. Developmentally, he showed slight delays in gross motor skills; at 10 months, he could sit without support but could not move to a seated position independently, stand with support, or crawl. His vision, fine motor skills, speech, and social development were appropriate for his age. He had no history of hospital admissions, recurrent infections, seizures, shock episodes, or documented low blood sugar. On physical examination, his length was 84 cm, weight was 12.6 kg, and head circumference was 48 cm. He had generalized darkening of the skin, including the oral mucosa, palms, and soles. The rest of the physical examination, including cardiovascular system, blood pressure, abdomen, and genitalia, was normal. Basic hematological and biochemical tests, including full blood count, C-reactive protein, renal and liver function tests, and serum electrolytes, were normal. His random blood glucose was 76 mg/dl.
test_results: Subsequent investigations revealed very low serum cortisol (< 22 nmol/l; normal 55–304 nmol/l) and very high ACTH (> 1734 pg/ml; normal 10–50 pg/ml). His serum aldosterone level was normal. An ACTH stimulation test demonstrated markedly reduced basal cortisol levels (< 4.39 nmol/L) with no cortisol response following administration of synthetic ACTH (cortisol remained < 4.39 nmol/L, 30 and 60 minutes after ACTH stimulation). MRI of his brain showed normal pituitary gland with marginal dilatation of the trigone and the body of the lateral ventricles; however, there was no hydrocephalus or structural brain abnormalities.

case_report: A 66-year-old woman was seen by an endocrinologist due to a calcitonin level of 45.6 pg/mL following a total thyroidectomy with central node dissection. The surgical specimen contained two tumors measuring 1.2 cm and 0.7 cm. A total of 27 lymph nodes were excised from levels II to VI on both sides, with metastasis identified in two lymph nodes, one at right level IV and another at level VI. Her preoperative calcitonin level was recorded at 1,750 pg/mL. The patient has a 15-year history of high blood pressure and a 2-year history of diabetes. Abdominal CT revealed adrenal tumors measuring 1.0 cm on the right and 0.6 cm on the left. Twenty-four-hour urine tests showed MN and VMA levels slightly above the upper normal limits.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed the D631Y mutation in the patient and his eldest son. A cervical ultrasound examination of the son revealed two hypoechoic nodules of 0.3 cm, and blood calcitonin was slightly elevated at 13 pg/mL.

case_report: A 14-year-old female presented with a one-year history of seizures. The episodes included focal dyscognitive seizures with secondary generalization, characterized by transient dizziness, a vacant stare, loss of awareness, eye deviation to the left, and tonic-clonic movements in the left upper and lower limbs, followed by a 3-4 minute loss of consciousness and subsequent amnesia. She experienced four such episodes before seeking medical consultation. She was born from a non-consanguineous marriage via normal vaginal delivery, with no perinatal complications and normal developmental milestones. Since birth, she had multiple hyperpigmented lesions on her neck, abdomen, and back, which progressively became more pigmented and hyperkeratotic over the past 3-4 years without preceding blistering or inflammatory changes. There was no family history of endocrinal, dermatological, or systemic disorders. Physical examination revealed normal skeletal and mental development for her age, with no abnormalities in respiratory, cardiac, gastrointestinal, or central nervous system examinations. Multiple hyperpigmented, hyperkeratotic verrucous plaques were observed on her face, arms, legs, chest, back, and abdomen in a blaschkoid pattern, along with acanthosis nigricans on the nape of her neck. She did not exhibit hirsutism or obesity and had no hair or nail abnormalities. Posterior subcapsular cataracts were noted in both eyes. Echocardiography and abdominal ultrasonography results were normal. Electroencephalography showed focal right temporal sharp and slow wave discharges, while brain magnetic resonance imaging with contrast revealed no abnormalities. Routine investigations, including fasting glucose and insulin levels, were normal.
test_results: Skin biopsy showed epidermal acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, orthokeratosis, papillomatosis, and finger-like papillary projections without any signs of epidermolysis, with variable pigmentation of basal layer of epidermis.

case_report: A 26-year-old male patient without hypertension was admitted on August 11, 2016, with an 8-year history of elevated serum creatinine (SCr) and a 7-year history of maintenance hemodialysis (HD). The following day, due to preoperative SCr of 893 umol/L and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) of 27.32 mmol/L, he underwent a kidney transplant from a deceased donor. Post-transplant, the patient was administered standard triple immunosuppression and underwent regular follow-up assessments. Despite substituting Cyclosporine A (CsA) with Tacrolimus (Tac), the renal graft showed signs of delayed graft function (DGF) with SCr of 534 umol/L and BUN of 30.06 mmol/L. An ultrasound-guided renal biopsy was performed on postoperative day 38.
test_results: Molecular genetic testing identified two mutations in the AGXT gene: first, exon 1: c.33dupC (p. Lys12fs), frameshift PV; second, an A to T transversion (c.215A > T) in exon 2 resulting in p. Asn72Ile, missense VUS. One mutation in the MUT gene (Exon11: c.1897G > C (p. Val633Leu), missense VUS) was detected in the patient. Deposition of diffuse CaOx crystals as well as acute TCMR (2015 Banff 2A) was detected in renal graft biopsy. Bone marrow biopsy showed intertrabecular spaces occupied by abundant CaOx crystals.

case_report: A 2-year-old Javanese boy presented with recurrent fever and urinary symptoms, including painful urination and difficulty urinating. He was delivered via cesarean section at 34 weeks of gestation, weighing 2250 grams, which is classified as low birth weight. His medical history includes multiple organ abnormalities, such as atresia ani and a unilateral undescended testicle. In his first year, he underwent several surgeries, including colostomy, anoplasty, and orchidopexy. Currently, he is experiencing recurrent fever and urinary symptoms. A CT scan of the abdomen revealed an abnormality in the urinary tract.
test_results: There was a duplication in the left ureter and the absence of a collecting system on the left side.

case_report: A 5-year-old boy, second in birth order from a nonconsanguineous marriage, presented with a high-grade intermittent fever and a rash on the lower limbs for 3 months. His elder brother had passed away 6 months earlier at the age of 7 due to an undiagnosed medical condition. On examination, the patient, of average build and nutrition, was febrile with a heart rate of 142/min, respiratory rate of 22/min, blood pressure of 102/64 mmHg, severe pallor, hepatosplenomegaly (liver 2 cm below the right costal margin and spleen 3.5 cm below the left costal margin), and a soft ejection systolic murmur. He exhibited generalized hypopigmented skin with golden-brown hair. Both lower limbs had multiple, well-defined, tender, erythematous to hyperpigmented nodular lesions extending from mid-thighs to feet, some with scab formation. The parents mentioned that their deceased elder son had similar hypopigmented skin, though no other family member was affected. Initial investigations showed hemoglobin at 4.1 g/dL, total leukocyte count at 2,500/mm3, lymphocytes at 73.7%, neutrophils at 18.6%, platelets at 33,000/mm3, erythrocyte sedimentation rate at 11 mm (1st hour), and C-reactive protein at 21 mg/L. The peripheral blood smear revealed normocytic, normochromic red blood cells with mild anisocytosis and a corrected reticulocyte count of 3.2%. Bone marrow aspiration smears indicated erythroid hyperplasia, predominantly normoblastic, with normal maturation of the myeloid series, no megakaryocytes, and no abnormal cells or parasites. Neither the peripheral blood smear nor the bone marrow aspiration smears showed large granules in neutrophils. Kidney and liver function tests, serum electrolytes, uric acid, chest skiagram, and Mantoux test results were within normal limits. Blood and urine cultures were sterile. Tests for common infections, including Widal test, rapid malaria antigen test, rK 39 antigen, Dengue serology, and Weil Felix test, were negative. Hepatitis B surface antigen and human immunodeficiency virus serology were negative, and immunoglobulin levels were within normal range. Serum ferritin was 1,334 ng/mL. Antinuclear antibody (ANA) showed speckled positivity (1+), anti-dsDNA was borderline positive at 50 IU/mL, and RA factor was negative. An ultrasound of the abdomen showed an enlarged spleen (13.5 cm) and liver (15 cm). A skin biopsy from the lower limb lesions suggested erythema nodosum (EN). The patient was treated with antipyretics, blood product transfusions, and intravenous ceftriaxone. However, the patient's condition worsened with increasing pancytopenia, enlargement of the liver and spleen, and aggravation of the rash. Given the weakly positive ANA and presence of EN, an empirical trial of oral prednisolone at 2 mg/kg/day was initiated.
test_results: A hair shaft examination of the younger sibling revealed large sized melanin granules, distributed irregularly along the length of the hair shaft mainly near the medulla. Under polarized light microscopy, the hair appeared monotonously white. Genetic analysis revealed a novel homozygous mutation in RAB27A gene on chromosome 15 (exon 3) showing a single-base substitution (c.136T>A p.F46I), leading to an amino acid change from phenylalanine (TTC) to isoleucine (ATC). Parents were found to be heterozygous for the same mutation.

case_report: A 36-year-old male presented with subacute onset of excessive fatigue, increased thirst, frequent urination including nighttime urination, and sensitivity to cold. Initial urinalysis showed no signs of infection. Laboratory results revealed elevated white blood cell count (40,600/μL with 32% neutrophils and 17% blasts), low hemoglobin (8.9 g/dl), and normal platelet count. He was admitted and treated with hydroxyurea 500 mg daily and allopurinol 100 mg daily. A bone marrow aspirate and biopsy were performed, and he was discharged the same day. He returned the next day due to increased bleeding from the biopsy site. The bone marrow results indicated chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML-2)/acute myeloid leukemia (AML) with normal karyotype and mutations in DNMT3A, CBFB, and PTPN11. Following hydroxyurea treatment, he was started on decitabine and received continuous intravenous hydration with isotonic fluids. His urine output was noted to be 12–16 liters per day. Laboratory findings included a serum osmolality of 297 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality of 99 mOsm/kg, and urine sodium less than 20 mEq/L.
test_results: The patient underwent a water deprivation test along with administration of one dose of desmopressin acetate (0.05 mg) following which his urine osmolality was found to be 260 mOsm/kg. Further workup with an MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) of the brain showed focal nodular enhancement at the proximal pituitary infundibulum with a measured value of 0.4 cm with slight effacement of the infundibular recess. The pituitary gland also demonstrated heterogeneous enhancement. Additionally, there was a loss of the normal posterior pituitary high-intensity signal on a pre-enhanced T1WI.

case_report: A 45-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital due to ongoing speech and movement issues, which have led to multiple hospitalizations in the past. These symptoms began around 7 years ago, 2 years after her second childbirth. Initially, she experienced slurred speech, followed by a tremor in her right upper limb and periodic tremors in her left upper limb. The symptoms have progressively worsened. She mentioned experiencing stressful situations at work a few years ago, which prompted her first neurological consultation. There is no family history of neurological disorders (both parents, sister, and brother are healthy, as well as her two children aged 13 and 10). Her perinatal and early childhood history was uncomplicated, although she was noted to be clumsy. Unspecified extrapyramidal symptoms first appeared at age 7, leading to hospitalization, but no further diagnostic steps were taken. She also had learning difficulties as a child but completed higher education. At age 31, she underwent a left ankle stabilization procedure due to generalized ligamentous laxity, diagnosed in early childhood. She reported no other movement-related disorders. Neurological examination revealed slightly dysarthric speech, cervical dystonia, dystonia of the lower face, positional and terminal tremor of the upper extremities (more pronounced on the right), ataxia of both upper and lower extremities, and a dystonic-cerebellar gait disorder. Physical examination showed normal muscle tone and strength in all extremities, with exaggerated deep tendon reflexes. Her pupils were properly reactive, with slight exophthalmos observed, and no signs of Kayser–Fleischer rings. No oculomotor disturbances were noted; oculography showed no latency extension, no decrease in amplitude, and normal velocity of saccadic movements in the horizontal direction. A speech therapist consultation revealed mild dysarthria with a predominance of the cerebellar component. According to the patient, speech disorders were persistent but fluctuated in intensity, worsening in stressful situations. She also reported excessive saliva and loud swallowing. Her handwriting showed a tendency to micrography. Although the patient did not notice any cognitive difficulties, neuropsychological consultation revealed selectively diminished cognitive function. Verbal material learning was slowed, with susceptibility to interference and a tendency to perseverate. Short-term memory was decreased, but long-term memory retrieval was preserved. Difficulty in planning complex actions was noted. Working memory efficiency, attention switching, and abstract verbal reasoning skills were also decreased. Praxis, visual-spatial, and verbal functions were without relevant deficits. Compared to a previous examination, there was a slight exacerbation of deficits noted during a second neuropsychological consultation. The patient no longer reported a depressed mood but showed a trend toward an anxious response. Despite slightly diminished cognitive function, the patient remains professionally active and raises two children by herself.
test_results: WES results detected the presence of two variants in the MRE11 gene: c.77 T > C (p.Met26Thr) and c.1090C > T (p.Arg364Ter). Both gene variants are known and described in databases (HGMD, ClinVar) as pathogenic or potentially pathogenic.

case_report: A 23-year-old Caucasian male was referred to the nephrology outpatient clinic due to proteinuria (2 g/day) and elevated plasma creatinine (109 µmol/L). At the time of referral, he was asymptomatic. His medical history included attention-deficit/hyperactive disorder, for which he was being treated with methylphenidate. A renal biopsy was conducted, and light microscopic examination of medullary tissue revealed medullary interstitial fibrosis, tubular atrophy, and calcinosis in medullary tubules. Immunofluorescence and electron microscopy of glomeruli did not show any specific changes, and there were no signs of segmental sclerosis. Fibrosis was noted in the interstitium. Physical examination was unremarkable, and the patient had a blood pressure of 125/79 mmHg. Laboratory findings included elevated plasma creatinine (123 µmol/L), normal plasma glucose (5.7 mmol/L), elevated hemoglobin (11.3 mmol/L), slightly elevated ionized calcium (1.35 mmol/L), and low parathyroid hormone (1.2 pmol/L). Urine dipstick testing indicated ++protein, ++blood, and ++glucose. A 24-hour urine collection showed proteinuria of 1.74 g/day, hypercalciuria of 10.5 mmol/day, and a low amount of citrate in the urine (0.34 mmol/day). Two months later, his blood pressure had increased to 155/85 mmHg, and plasma creatinine had risen to 154 µmol/L, leading to the initiation of ramipril (2.5 mg daily). Three months later, he was hospitalized due to abdominal pain with fluctuating intensity. A computed tomography scan revealed calcinosis and small kidney stones, 4 mm in diameter. Sonographic images showed slightly small kidneys, with the right kidney measuring 10.3 cm and the left kidney 9.9 cm, without signs of urinary tract obstruction. The patient was prescribed thiazide with potassium chloride (2.5 mg daily) to reduce hypercalciuria. Prior to this treatment, his plasma electrolytes were normal: potassium 3.8 mmol/L, phosphate 0.67 mmol/L, ionized calcium 1.29 mmol/L, and plasma creatinine 157 µmol/L. After 2 months, his general practitioner reported severe hypokalaemia (2.5 mmol/L) despite potassium supplementation (1500 mg daily) for a few days. It was recommended to discontinue thiazide with potassium chloride and to prescribe potassium while increasing the dose of ramipril to 10 mg/day. Laboratory tests showed proteinuria, hypercalciuria, glycosuria, nephrocalcinosis, and severe hypokalaemia following thiazide administration, along with elevated plasma creatinine. Urine protein electrophoresis indicated elevated β2-microglobulin (80× normal range), urine albumin (10× normal range), and glycosuria.
test_results: Sanger sequencing of the CLCN5 and OCRL genes identified the variant CLCN5 (c.473G>A, p.Gly158Asp). No variant form of the OCRL gene was identified.

case_report: A 10-year and eight-month-old boy was admitted to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit for severe vomiting, convulsions, and coma. He was born full term via normal delivery and is the third child of healthy parents. The first child was premature and passed away at two months due to asphyxia, while the second child is 24 years old and healthy. The boy experienced his first symptoms 24 hours after birth, characterized by very poor oral intake. At one year old, he was treated for frequent convulsions with antiepileptic therapy, which was discontinued at age three when the severity of the attacks decreased. Despite this, convulsions continued to occur frequently up to age 10. Recently, he developed strabismus and vision loss in the right eye. He also exhibited significant intellectual development delay. Initial laboratory tests showed hypoglycemia (glucose: 0.6 mmol/L), hyperlactacidemia (12.6 mmol/L), metabolic acidosis (pH: 6.91, base excess: −22.1 mmol/L), and hyperuricemia (uric acid: 892 μmol/L). During hypoglycemia, blood samples indicated insulin levels of 14 μIU/mL, ACTH levels of 19.6 pg/mL, and cortisol levels of 38.5 μg/dL.
test_results: The cranial MRI results showed that several parts of the brain harbored symmetrical, patchy, abnormal signals, including the cerebellum, frontoparietal area, basal ganglia, and thalamus. Cranial magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) identified a significantly increased lactate peak with a reduced N-acetyl aspartate (NAA) peak, indicating hypoxic lesions of the brain. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly and pyoperitoneum.

case_report: A 50-year-old woman with a history of SLE and Sjogren’s disease presented to the emergency room with fever and malaise for 2 weeks. She had been on oral antibiotics for suspected pneumonia as an outpatient but did not improve, leading to her hospital visit. She appeared very ill, was able to follow commands but easily fatigued, and had a temperature of 104.7 F. Examination revealed palpable cervical lymph nodes. A chest x-ray showed infiltrates, and she was admitted for sepsis likely secondary to community-acquired pneumonia and started on Ceftriaxone and Azithromycin. The next day, the patient became lethargic, developed severe shortness of breath with a respiratory rate of 40, heart rate of 169, and continued to have high-grade fevers. With suspicion of aspiration pneumonia, she was moved to the ICU, and antibiotics were broadened to include vancomycin, meropenem, and metronidazole. Blood work showed a white blood cell count of 7000, red blood cell count of 3000, hemoglobin of 9 mg/dl, hematocrit of 28 mg/dl, and platelet count of 249. The chemistry panel indicated metabolic acidosis, elevated liver enzymes, and normal renal function. After failing to improve, a CT scan of her chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed extensive lymphadenopathy in the cervical, axillary, retroperitoneal, and inguinal areas, along with an enlarged liver and spleen. Further blood work showed Ferritin of 5098, Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) of 138, C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 44, Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) 1116, lactic acid of 11, and normal Complement levels (C3 and C4). A right axillary lymph node biopsy showed extensive degeneration and necrosis with positive Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) cells without any evidence of malignant cells. A Viral Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) test indicated a positive viral load for both EBV (more than 20,00000 copies/ml) and Cytomegalovirus (more than 300,000 copies/ml). The patient tested negative for Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV-1), Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), Influenza A and B, Streptococcal Pneumonia Antigen, and Legionella Antigen. She was started on antiviral treatment with Ganciclovir. One week after the initial presentation, the patient continued to have high-grade fevers, remained hypoxic with increasing lactic acid levels. Her white blood cells dropped to 3000, platelets dropped to 100,000, hemoglobin to 6.9, with negative blood and urine cultures. Antibiotics were further broadened with three antibacterial drugs, micafungin for possible fungal infection, and an antiviral agent. Other than viremia from EBV and CMV, no other source of infection was found.
test_results: Immunological workup revealed positive Antinuclear Antigen (ANA, titer 1:1280), positive Sjogren’s Antibodies (SSA and SSB), positive Sm/RNP antibodies and highly positive Interleukin-2 Receptor Alpha Chain (IL-2Ra/CD25) of 24885 pg/mL (reference range: 532–1891 pg/ml).

case_report: A 14-year-old male presented with a hairless patch on the scalp, noted since birth, initially the size of a peanut and gradually enlarging to its current dimensions. The patch was not linked to any other congenital anomalies, and there was no family history of similar lesions. Physical examination revealed a 6 cm × 3 cm alopecic patch on the right temporal region of the scalp, characterized by multiple discrete pits filled with keratinous material and comedo-like lesions. A dilated cribriform pit was observed at the center of the lesion, with the surrounding skin appearing normal. No other physical, mental, or cutaneous abnormalities were detected. Routine blood tests were normal, and the Mantoux test was negative.
test_results: Epidermis showed hair follicles invagination filled with keratin resembling dilated hair follicles. Dermis showed rudimentary hair follicles and sebaceous gland lobules. High-power field of same histopathological slide showed large hair follicles containing lamellated keratin but absent hair shaft.

case_report: A 5-year-old boy presented with recurrent high fever lasting 18 days, accompanied by mild cough, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and hematochezia. Despite treatment with intravenous antibiotics and immunoglobulin, the fever persisted. He was the first child in his family and had a history of mild pneumonia at 4 months old, treated with intravenous antibiotics. There was no history of recurrent respiratory infections, eczema, or prolonged umbilical stump. He had not contracted chickenpox and was not vaccinated against it. Physical examination revealed moderate malnutrition, multiple ulcers in the oral cavity and on the tongue, with no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory tests showed elevated inflammatory markers: white blood cell count of 19.44 × 10^9/L with 66.4% neutrophils, C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 17.34 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 73 mm/h, and serum procalcitonin level of 0.412 ng/ml. The patient also had moderate anemia with a hemoglobin level of 84 g/L and decreased serum albumin level at 27.4 g/L. Serum antibodies against cytomegalovirus (CMV) and Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) were negative, as was a T-SPOT TB test. The number of CD19+ B lymphocytes was reduced to 16.45% (reference range: 18.5–28.0%) of lymphocytes; CD3+ T lymphocytes were 54.1% (reference range: 56.0–68.0%), CD4+ T lymphocytes were 31.45% (reference range: 29.0–40.0%), and CD8+ T lymphocytes were 18.35% (reference range: 19.0–25.0%). The CD4+/CD8+ T cell ratio was normal at 1.71 (reference range: 1.1–2.0/1). Abdominal computed tomography scan showed irregular wall thickness and enhancement of the ascending colon and terminal ileum wall, along with enlargement of the abdominal lymph nodes. Intestinal ultrasound indicated thickened walls of the terminal ileum and colon, with inflammation affecting the vermiform appendix.
test_results: Colonoscopy was performed, and multiple ulcers in the terminal ileum and colon were detected. The area of the largest ulcer was approximately 3 cm × 4 cm. The ulcers had sharp margins, and most had no exudate or edema; these lesions were mainly located in the ascending colon and cecum. There were also scattered ulcers located in the rectum. Histological study of a mucosal biopsy indicated segmental chronic active inflammation of the colon and terminal ileum, cryptitis and crypt abscess were observed at the colon; additionally, several noncaseating granulomas was observed in the ileum and descending colon. Microbial metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of the intestinal biopsy did not reveal any opportunistic pathogens.
diagnosis: Very Early Onset Inflammatory Bowel Disease  due to a novel variant of the X-linked Moesin gene
Orpha_name: Combined immunodeficiency due to Moesin deficiency

case_report: Patient 2 (#726) is a 12-year-7 month-old boy, first child of nonconsanguineous and healthy parents. He was born at term by caesarian after a pregnancy of normal course. His birth weight was 3,500 g (50th centile). He exhibited speech delay and experienced three episodes of myoclonic seizures. Psychometric evaluation at 11 years recorded an IQ of 50. Physical examination at 11 years and 6 months showed: height 138 cm (25th centile), weight 35 kg (50th centile), OFC 54 cm (75th centile), triangular face, and long ears. His language was simple, and he displayed hyperactivity and abnormal behavior.
test_results: Array-CGH analysis (105 K) was normal.

case_report: A 33-year-old woman from Bogotá, Colombia, presented with recurrent episodes of weakness, dizziness, occasional headaches, symmetric numbness in her face and arms, and sensations of imminent fainting. These episodes resolved spontaneously within a few minutes, typically occurring after main meals, and had increased in frequency over the past 5 years. The patient measured her blood sugar during these episodes, recording levels between 40 and 60 mg/dL. Two years prior, her general practitioner recommended lifestyle changes, including reducing high glycemic index foods and increasing meal frequency to six times a day, every 3 hours. These changes led to only partial symptom relief. The patient did not recall any discomfort after consuming fruits or juices during childhood but noted an increase in postprandial symptoms starting in adolescence, which eventually became very uncomfortable. Her parents were not consanguineous, and she did not exhibit hepatomegaly or altered linear growth. In April 2013, during a routine laboratory work-up that included pre- and post-meal plasma glucose measurements, she experienced asymptomatic hypoglycemia (2 hours post-meal: 29 mg/dL). She consulted our department with these results. Her past medical history included a pulmonary thromboembolism and upper limb deep venous thrombosis in 2011 due to protein C deficiency. She was treated with subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg daily from 2011 until July 2015, when she switched to daily oral aspirin 100 mg. Her surgical history included appendectomy and two herniorrhaphies. She reported a family history of deep venous thrombosis, throat cancer, and diabetes mellitus.
test_results: We identified a single homozygous point mutation consisting of a T˃A substitution in position 1693 of the ALDOB transcript (c.1693T˃A against cDNA reference sequence NM_000035.3), within the 3’UTR of exon 9, 515 nucleotides downstream the stop codon.

case_report: A 22-year-old female with developmental delay and short stature presented with abdominal pain, a palpable lump, and three episodes of seizures occurring two months prior. Physical examination revealed central obesity, hoarseness, hirsutism, and hypertension. Laboratory tests showed normal levels of estradiol, T3, T4, TSH, FSH, and 24-hour urinary metanephrine. Elevated levels of testosterone and serum cortisol were noted. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a large exophytic mass measuring 9×8 cm originating from the upper lobe of the right kidney, with the right adrenal gland not separately identifiable. During surgery, the tumor was found to be adherent to the inferior surface of the liver, kidney, and inferior vena cava. The excised mass was grayish-brown, weighed 356 grams, and measured 12.5×6.5×5.5 cm, with a partly circumscribed and friable texture.
test_results: The tumor was composed of polygonal cells arranged in solid sheets and thick trabecular patterns with delicate sinusoids lined by flattened endothelial cells. Uninucleate, multinucleate tumor giant cells, atypical mitoses, necrosis, vascular and capsular invasion were seen. Mitoses were >20 per HPF. Focal areas showed tumor cells with bizarre nuclei. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) study was positive for vimentin and inhibin and negative for cytokeratin and chromogranin.

case_report: A 5-month-old female infant presented with a round, painless swelling on the second toe of the right foot, noted since birth. The swelling was situated on the dorsum of the toe near the nail and had progressively enlarged, covering the nail bed. The parents sought medical attention due to the increasing size of the mass. On physical examination, a pedunculated, non-tender soft tissue mass measuring 4.5 x 3 cm was observed, with its base on the middle phalanx of the right second toe, extending over the nail bed. Imaging showed a soft tissue mass on the right second toe without affecting the bone. The mass was surgically removed, and the wound was closed primarily. Initial bleeding was managed with a pressure dressing, and the infant was discharged. The wound healed well without complications.
test_results: At the histopathology laboratory, we received a piece of cystic tissue measuring 2x2x1 cm. Sectioning revealed greyish white solid tissue and an empty cystic cavity. Microscopic examination revealed skin tissue with intact epidermis, proliferating fibroblasts arranged in bundles, forming a poorly defined nodule within the dermis on Haematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) stain. Also seen were characteristic perinuclear eosinophilic inclusions on high power. Masson's trichrome (MT) stained the intracytoplasmic inclusions red.

case_report: The patient is a seven-year-old male from Saudi Arabia who has been experiencing progressive difficulties with walking, frequent falls, and facial muscle weakness. He is one of three siblings. Both parents are carriers of a genetic variant and are related by first-degree consanguinity but are otherwise healthy with no known neurological or hereditary conditions in the family. The patient was born at full term through a spontaneous vaginal delivery without complications. He began walking at 18 months but had frequent falls. His walking difficulties have worsened over time, though he remains ambulatory with bilateral foot drop. Nerve conduction studies, including those of the facial nerve, indicated widespread axonal motor and sensory polyneuropathy. Electromyography (EMG) showed chronic denervation without signs of re-innervation. He has no history of seizures and performs excellently in school without learning difficulties. Physical examination revealed no dysmorphic features but noted kinky thick hair, horizontal nystagmus, facial weakness, and greater distal than proximal weakness in both upper and lower limbs, along with reduced deep tendon reflexes. He also exhibited a positive Romberg sign, moderate speech delay, and a high steppage gait. Audiogram and ocular assessments were normal. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count (CBC), metabolic profile, blood glucose, lactate, ammonia, renal function tests, vitamin B12, creatinine kinase, and thyroid hormones, were all within normal ranges. A brain MRI performed when the patient was six years old showed normal results.
test_results: We identified a novel (NM_022041.3: c.1456G>A) mutation in the GAN gene.

case_report: A 3-year-old boy presented to the hospital outpatient department with a heart murmur. An echocardiogram indicated mild left ventricle (LV) hypertrophy, leading to a referral to Seoul National University Children's Hospital for further management. A transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed mild LV hypertrophy with an increased LV mass index (89 g/m2 or 52 g/m2.7). No other cardiac anomalies, including coarctation of the aorta, were observed. Although the patient was asymptomatic, carvedilol 3.125 mg every 12 hours was administered for LV reverse remodeling. Nine months later, a routine follow-up echocardiogram revealed abnormally increased celiac artery velocity with a diastolic tail (peak velocity greater than 4 m/sec), and the patient's right arm systolic BP was 155 mmHg. At 4 years of age, he was hospitalized for evaluation of renovascular hypertension and BP management. Upon admission, the patient remained asymptomatic, with no complaints of headache or chest pain. His body weight was 21.2 kg (>97th percentile) and height was 110.1 cm (>97th percentile). His BP was elevated (206/113 mmHg in the right arm and 194/104 mmHg in the right leg). A grade 2/6 systolic heart murmur was audible at the left sternal border. A chest X-ray showed no significant cardiomegaly, and a 12-lead electrocardiogram revealed LV hypertrophy. Laboratory findings on admission were as follows: serum blood urea nitrogen, 17.0 mg/dL; serum creatinine, 0.53 mg/dL; serum renin activity, 21.0 ng/mL/h (reference value, <6.7 ng/mL/hr); and serum aldosterone, 39.4 ng/dL (reference value, 3–35 ng/dL). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was normal. Renal artery Doppler ultrasonography showed an intermittent tardus parvus spectrogram in both renal arteries with a smaller right kidney.
test_results: The CT angiography revealed severe stenosis at the bilateral renal artery, the ostium of the celiac branch, and the ostium of the superior mesenteric artery with diffuse luminal narrowing of the abdominal aorta into the femoral artery. Abdominal aortogram confirmed diffuse luminal narrowing of the abdominal aorta into the femoral artery and the renal artery.

case_report: A term male infant, larger than average for gestational age, was delivered via spontaneous vaginal birth to a 34-year-old mother. The pregnancy had minimal prenatal care, and maternal serologies were not available. Labor was extended, with membranes ruptured 29 hours before delivery. The infant needed oxygen and brief bag mask ventilation, with Apgar scores of 4 at 1 minute and 9 at 5 minutes. Within the first hours of life, a hematoma was observed on the forehead and left parietal area. A complete blood count at birth showed a normal hematocrit of 37.6%. The next morning, the physician noted an increase of 2 cm in the frontal-occipital circumference. The infant also exhibited increased respiratory effort. A subsequent blood test indicated a significant drop in hemoglobin from 12.5 g/dL to 8.6 g/dL, with a new hematocrit of 25.7%.
test_results: FVIII levels were measured at <0.01 U/mL. The PTT was very elevated. A CT of the head showed a subdural hematoma on the right side and a subgaleal hematoma involving the left and right frontoparietal region. The electroencephalogram confirmed epileptiform activity.

case_report: The patient, at 38 years old, was evaluated for gradually worsening difficulty in walking and climbing stairs, which began at age 35. There was no reported family history of neuromuscular disorders or consanguinity. Neurological examination revealed atrophy in the scapular, anterior, and posterior thigh muscles. Muscle strength assessment using the British Medical Research Council (MRC) scale showed weakness in shoulder girdle muscles (arm flexion and abduction possible against gravity up to 90°), inferior trapezius (2/5), arm extensors (2/5), elbow flexors (3/5), hip flexors (3/5), hip extensors (2/5), knee flexors and extensors (4/5), and dorsal foot extensors (4/5). There was no involvement of cranial nerves, and no joint contractures or skeletal deformities were noted. The patient exhibited a waddling gait with increased lumbar lordosis and was unable to rise from the floor. Upper limb functional ability was rated 3 on the Brooke scale, and lower limb function was rated 3 on the Vignos scale. Creatine kinase (CK) levels were slightly elevated at 253 UI/l. Electromyography (EMG) indicated myopathic findings in all tested muscles, with fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves. A muscle CT scan showed moderate fatty changes in the bilateral quadriceps, hamstrings, and medial gastrocnemius. Respiratory and cardiac functions were normal. Over the following years, symptoms worsened, and the patient lost the ability to climb stairs by age 45. A muscle biopsy from the left quadriceps at age 38 showed fiber size variability, a few central nuclei, scattered degenerative fibers, a few cytochrome oxidase-negative fibers, and rare ragged red fibers (about 1%). Immunostaining for dystrophin, sarcoglycans, caveolin 3, and alpha-dystroglycan was normal, as were dysferlin and calpain 3 immunoblotting. Respiratory chain activity and mitochondrial DNA analysis by Southern blot were normal.
test_results: By next generation sequencing analysis, a heterozygous G > A transition (c.G2453A) in exon 20 of the TNPO3 gene was found. The G > A point mutation changes the arginine in position 818 with a glutamine in a highly conserved residue. This mutation is now listed in dbSNP (rs587777431) and it is present in gnomAD (The Genome Aggregation Database) with a population frequency of 0.00004215. This variant was not found in the two healthy sisters.

case_report: The patient, a male born at full-term via uncomplicated delivery, required advanced cardiopulmonary resuscitation immediately after birth, including chest compressions at a 3:1 rhythm and face mask lung inflation with 21% oxygen and 30 cm of water pressure. He remained hospitalized for the first 20 days of life, receiving supplemental oxygen. Upon discharge, the patient exhibited hypotonia and feeding difficulties. At 6 weeks old, he was hospitalized in a Rural Hospital for neonatal sepsis and presented with generalized muscle weakness, hypotonia, feeding difficulties, macroglossia, cardiomegaly, and hepatomegaly. By 3 months of age, he developed breathing difficulties, heart failure, and neurological deterioration characterized by hypoactivity and hypotonia, necessitating mechanical ventilation and diuretics. An echocardiogram showed concentric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with left-diastolic dysfunction, a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 65%, and a ventricular septal thickness of 10 mm. A thoracic X-ray revealed severe cardiomegaly. Laboratory tests indicated elevated levels of creatine-phosphokinase (453 UI/L; normal range: 24–170 UI/L) and lactate dehydrogenase (951 U/L; normal range: 91–180 U/L). At 5 months old, due to poor response to treatment, he was referred to the Hospital Infantil de México and admitted to the Department of Lysosomal Diseases.
test_results: We performed a dried blood spots test to assess GAA activity finding low levels (0.21 nmoL/ml blood/hr; normal range 1.29–5.7 nmoL/ml). Urine glucose tetrasaccharide (GLc4) level was 342.6 mmol/mg/creat (normal range: 0.14–1.29 mmol/mg/creat), and 50% of PAS-positive vacuolated lymphocytes were found in the peripheral blood smear. Amplification by a polymerase chain reaction and subsequent analysis with standard fluorescent sequencing protocol in both forward and reverse directions of all 19 coding exons of the GAA gene and immediate flanking intron sequences revealed a novel homozygous 4 bp deletion in exon 15 (c.2066_2069delAGCC), leading to frameshifting of the coding sequence and causing a predicted premature stop codon to appear six triplets downstream (p.Glu689Glyfs*6).
Orpha_name: Glycogen storage disease due to acid maltase deficiency, infantile onset

case_report: A 50-year-old Korean male presented with hairless patches and multiple cystic formations on his scalp. These formations had progressively enlarged and increased in number over a span of five years. Physical examination revealed asymptomatic, smooth, skin-colored cystic nodules distributed across the entire scalp, with no similar formations observed on the trunk, extremities, or face. The sizes of these formations varied from 2 mm to 4 cm in diameter. Larger nodules were surrounded by irregularly shaped hairless patches. The patient's medical and family histories were unremarkable, and routine laboratory tests showed normal results. The patient reported no habit of hair-pulling. Upon incision and compression of a nodule, a uniform, creamy, odorless, yellowish substance was expelled.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed an empty cyst within the lower dermis and subcutaneous fat. The folded cystic wall was lined with stratified squamous epithelium and contained flattened sebaceous gland cells. The numbers of catagen and telogen hairs were increased, although there was no sign of fibrosis or inflammatory change. Some pigment casts were present in the hair papillae and perifollicular regions.

case_report: A 14-year-old boy with no prior health issues presented with left periorbital swelling and redness persisting for 1 year, along with muscle weakness and joint pain for 4 months. Physical examination revealed purple discoloration and swelling around the left eye, Gottron's papules over the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints on both hands, and muscle weakness graded at 3/5 in the proximal muscles and 4/5 in the distal muscles. Laboratory results showed a normal complete blood count (CBC), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 33 mm/hr, and C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 0.383 mg/L. Liver function tests indicated abnormalities with aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 281 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) at 95 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) at 24 U/L, alkaline phosphatase (ALP) at 149 U/L, and creatine kinase (CK) at 4585 U/L. Antinuclear antibodies were negative, and extractable nuclear antigen (ENA) panel was also negative. Renal and thyroid function tests were within normal limits.
test_results: MRI muscle revealed diffuse muscle edema involving the muscles of the pelvis, thighs, legs, and upper extremities as well as the muscle of back suggestive of inflammatory myopathy. CT orbital shows soft tissue swelling in the anteromedial and superior aspects of the left orbit which shows minimal enhancement in the postcontrast, there was an appearance of a left-sided preseptal periorbital cellulitis with no evidence of abscess formation. Muscle biopsy was performed and revealed mildly and focally increased endomysial and perimysial connective tissues. There was perivascular chronic inflammatory cells infiltration in the perimysial areas with few mononuclear inflammatory cells that were scattered in-between the muscle fibers. The muscle fibers showed mild to focally moderate variation of size and shapes and the majority had peripheral nuclei. Scattered foci of myofiber necrosis and regeneration were evident. Perifascicular atrophy was not a prominent feature, but it could be focally appreciated. Ultrastructural examination revealed findings that were in keeping with light microscopy, including prominent myofibrillar disarray. In addition, scattered rod-like structures and cytoplasmic bodies were detected. Skin biopsy of the left lower lid showed evidence of mild hyperkeratosis in the epidermis. The dermis showed heavy chronic inflammation cell infiltration that consists mainly of lymphocytes and plasma cells, infiltrating the hair follicles. Adjacent mild dermal fibrosis, focal solar elastosis, and pigment incontinence are noted.

case_report: A 5-year-old girl with no significant family or personal medical history was brought to the emergency department at night following a brief episode of unconsciousness that occurred after experiencing abdominal pain, crying, and urges. Her parents noted pallor, cyanosis, loss of muscle tone, and ocular revulsion during the episode. For several months, she had frequently complained of abdominal pain and had short episodes of absence. Additionally, her parents reported a frequent cough and reduced exercise tolerance. Upon admission, physical examination revealed a systolic regurgitant murmur. Laboratory tests indicated slight metabolic acidosis, elevated ultrasensitive Troponin T (65 ng/l), and increased liver transaminases (ASAT 82U/l and ALAT 48U/l). N-terminal pro-Brain Natriuretic Peptide (NT-Pro-BNP) levels were elevated at 1,024 ng/l (normal range 12–214 ng/l). An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed an incomplete right bundle branch block, consistent with right ventricular hypertrophy. Echocardiography revealed slight enlargement of the right ventricle and right atrium, tricuspid regurgitation with an estimated elevated systolic right ventricular pressure of over 45 mmHg, and pulmonary artery dilation. During the next few hours, the patient experienced three more collapses while being monitored. Each episode began with tachycardia and decreased oxygen saturation, followed by bradycardia and tonic-clonic seizures. The first episode resolved spontaneously, while the subsequent two episodes were successfully managed with intrarectal diazepam. Electroencephalography (EEG) indicated partial epileptic seizures, and cerebral magnetic resonance imaging was normal. Treatment with valproic acid was initiated. Follow-up echocardiography the next day confirmed right cardiac cavity dilation, tricuspid regurgitation III/IV, and an estimated right ventricular pressure of 55 mmHg. Polysomnography ruled out sleep apnea syndrome. Laboratory values normalized by day 2. After showing improvement with anticonvulsant therapy, the patient was discharged. However, she continued to experience increased breathlessness during exercise, particularly in the late afternoon and evening, and persistent abdominal pain. Subsequent echocardiography showed further dilation of the right atrium and right ventricle, with an estimated right ventricular pressure of 75–80 mmHg and signs of left ventricular compression with a flattened interventricular septum.
test_results: Pulmonary artery pressure was 33 mmHg for the systolic, 17 mmHg for the diastolic and 25 mmHg for the mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) and pulmonary vascular resistances index (PVRI) were elevated at 4.5 Wood units *m2, reaching 58% of systemic values.
