There was no fall of pulmonary arterial pressure with 100% of oxygen (O2).

case_report: A 63-year-old male with a 20-year history of diabetes mellitus and ischemic heart disease was admitted after experiencing several health issues. He had been in good health and completed a Hajj pilgrimage, but a few months after returning, he began to suffer from abdominal colic, which was initially suspected to be cholecystitis but remained unconfirmed. The patient reported a poor appetite, abdominal pain, loose stools, a weight loss of approximately 7 kg over one year, fatigue, and headaches. He later developed slowness of gait, falls, subjective weakness on the left side of his body, balance issues, slurred speech, involuntary movements of the eyes, face, and limbs, and difficulty swallowing, characterized by coughing while swallowing. He also exhibited a lack of initiative, forgetfulness for recent events, and visual hallucinations that were non-stereotyped and recurrent. He was treated for Parkinson's disease at a regional hospital without improvement. As his condition worsened, he was brought to our center. Upon admission, his HMSE score was 19. Clinical examination revealed involuntary, disconjugate, arrhythmic eye movements, eyebrow lifting, dyskinetic movements of the upper lips and cheeks, mild shoulder elevation, and occasional trunk twisting. He had skew deviation of the eyes, saccadic initiation defects, broken saccades, slow vertical saccades, and multiple saccadic oscillations. He exhibited a tendency to stoop forward, swayed while walking with two-person support, had anteroposterior trunk movements while sitting, mild finger-nose incoordination, and completely illegible, effortless speech diagnosed as mixed dysarthria with intermittent drooling and choking. He had poor respiratory support while speaking, poor lip seal, and slow tongue movements. General examination revealed itchy, scaly skin lesions with nodularity, pigmentation, and serous ooze over the scalp, cheek, nose, and chin, which were slightly tender. Laboratory investigations showed normal routine blood counts, liver functions, renal functions, and thyroid functions. Vasculitic workup, HIV, Venereal Disease Research Laboratory, and ultrasound abdomen were normal. Vitamin B12 levels were low at 188.11 pg/ml. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed chloride 121, sugar 154, protein 72, and cells 3. India ink preparation and culture were normal. PCR for WD was not performed due to lack of availability. Tests for N-methyl-D-aspartate, voltage-gated potassium channel, and anti-GAD were negative. Cardiac evaluation indicated apical hypokinesia.
test_results: Duodenal biopsy showed lamina propria showing focal lymphoplasmacytic cell collections and few histiocytes.

case_report: A 46-year-old woman with a history of menometrorrhagia for 5–6 years due to a large uterine fibroid was admitted with fever (temperature over 39 °C) and severe pelvic pain. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed diffuse fibromatosis and two distinct uterine masses: one measuring 53 × 57 mm, submucous, located in the fundus-anterior wall; the other measuring 97 × 70 mm, subserous, located in the isthmus-posterior wall. Despite the size of the masses, no alarming features were observed. The patient expressed a desire to avoid total hysterectomy to preserve pelvic stability, so a laparoscopic myomectomy was considered. During hospitalization, the patient exhibited signs of inflammation (elevated fibrinogen and C-reactive protein) with intermittent fever (not exceeding 38 °C). Blood cultures were negative. Serum LDH total activity measurements were normal or slightly elevated, with a peak value of 304 U/l (reference range: 125–243). An abdominal CT with and without contrast showed increased uterine volume with two masses: a smaller one (4 × 3 cm) subserous on the fundus, and a larger one (12 × 10 cm) para-uterine on the left, with intraligamentary growth and areas of colliquative necrosis. An abdomino-pelvic MRI with and without contrast confirmed the presence of both masses (3.2 × 5 cm and 15x10x9 cm), with the larger one appearing capsulated and non-infiltrative. MRI findings showed no enhanced signal intensity in T1 and weak, inhomogeneous signal in T2. Electrophoresis of LDH isoenzymes revealed the following: LDH1 = 15.6% (reference range: 16.1–31.5%), LDH2 = 23.3% (29.2–41.6%), LDH3 = 21.0% (17.0–26.2%), LDH4 = 13.6% (5.9–12.3%), LDH5 = 26.5% (3.2–17.3%), and LDH5/LDH1 ratio = 1.7 (normal value: < 1). There was an elevation of muscle isoforms (4 and 5) and a decrease in heart isoforms (1 and 2), with an increased LDH5 to LDH1 ratio. Based on these findings and the CT report, a total abdominal hysterectomy was performed instead of the initially preferred laparoscopic myomectomy to avoid risks associated with morcellation.
test_results: Histological examination of the surgical sample showed a malignant mesenchymal proliferation constituted by hypercellular areas with epithelioid or pleomorphic cells alternating with hypocellular myxoid areas. Necrosis and high mitotic index were observed. Immunohistochemistry showed positivity for caldesmon, muscle specific actin and CD10 and focal positivity for smooth muscle actin.

case_report: A 6.5-year-old girl was referred to the outpatient clinic due to short stature and brachydactyly. She was born at term to non-consanguineous parents, with a birth weight of 2300 g (<10th percentile) and a birth height of 45 cm (<10th percentile). Neonatal examination identified developmental dysplasia of the hip. Motor development milestones included smiling at 3 months, head control at 9 months, sitting at 24 months, and walking at 3 years. Physical examination showed short stature (height: 109 cm, -1.75 SD), low body mass index (BMI=13.5 kg/m2, -1.59 SD), round face, full cheeks, depressed nasal bridge, short neck, and brachydactyly of all digits (hand length: 9.5 cm, <3rd percentile). Subcutaneous heterotopic ossification was noted at the right iliac crest (3x2 cm). Initial laboratory tests showed normal serum calcium (9.7 mg/dL) and phosphorus (5.3 mg/dL) levels, with elevated serum PTH (138.1 pg/mL). Subsequent PTH levels were 98.5 pg/mL and 111.2 pg/mL. Serum levels of free triiodothyronine (fT3), free thyroxine (fT4), TSH, alkaline phosphatase (ALP), creatinine, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25-OHD) were normal. X-rays indicated marked shortness and thickness of metacarpal and metatarsal bones with cone-shaped epiphyses in all tubular bones of the hand, and coxa valga with acetabular dysplasia. Bone age was consistent with chronological age. Cranial MRI findings were normal. Chromosomal analysis showed a 46,XX karyotype. Audiological and ophthalmological examinations revealed bilateral minimal conductive hearing loss and retinitis pigmentosa. Gsα function was measured at 48.1% of normal, indicating reduced activity.
test_results: A heterozygous novel missense mutation (c.128T>C) was detected in exon 1 in the GNAS gene.

case_report: A 56-year-old Japanese man presented with a 3-month history of asymptomatic brown follicular hyperkeratotic plaque/papules spread across the body, with significant hair loss on the scalp. Some papules exhibited a comedo-like appearance and/or signs of infection. Additionally, there was a slight reduction in pubic and axillary hair growth. The patient had been on dialysis for 3 years due to chronic renal failure. There was no family history of similar conditions, no use of medications related to the symptoms, and no exposure to dioxins. The patient did not have COVID-19 and had not received any COVID-19 vaccines. Blood and imaging tests showed normal blood dioxin and sex hormone levels, and no signs of malignancies or collagen diseases.
test_results: Trichoscopy of the scalp revealed keratotic open follicular pores lacking hair shafts as well as hyperkeratosis and hyperpigmentation of the interfollicular epidermis. Histological examination of a scalp specimen revealed an enlarged follicular infundibulum, filled with keratin plugs, and follicular lichenoid tissue reactions in the infundibulum and isthmus. The interfollicular epidermis showed hyperkeratosis and partial vacuolar alteration along with numerous melanophages in the upper dermis. In the transverse section between the infundibulum and isthmus, a perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrate was seen with lichenoid tissue reactions and mild perifollicular fibrosis. A specimen from the trunk also revealed an enlarged follicular infundibulum with keratin plugs as well as dense lymphocytic infiltration with vacuolar alteration and dyskeratotic cells in the isthmus.

case_report: A 71-year-old male presented with abdominal distension and no other discomfort. Symptoms of bloating began a month prior and worsened in the week before admission. Two years ago, the patient had physical examinations and liver function tests at a local hospital and received liver protection treatment, but liver function did not improve. Occasionally, the patient experienced yellow urine but no significant physical discomfort. Personal and family history were unremarkable. Upon admission, vital signs were: body temperature 36.8 °C, heart rate 68 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, blood pressure 134/74 mmHg, and blood oxygen saturation 99%. Physical examination revealed chronic liver disease, moderately yellowish skin and sclera, but no liver palms or spider angioma. The abdomen was soft, without tenderness or rebound pain. Liver area percussion was negative for pain, and the liver and spleen were not palpable below the ribs. Murphy's sign was negative. Neurological examination showed no abnormalities. Liver function tests showed albumin 23.9 g/L (normal 40-55 g/L), alanine aminotransferase 135 U/L (normal < 50 U/L), aspartate aminotransferase 127 U/L (normal < 40 U/L), γ-glutamine acyltranspeptidase 131 U/L (normal < 60 U/L), total bilirubin 49.3 μmol/L (normal < 24 μmol/L), and direct bilirubin 17.3 μmol/L (normal < 6.8 μmol/L). Blood tests showed hemoglobin 116 g/L (normal 160-175 g/L) and platelet count 75 × 10^9/L (normal 125-350 × 10^9/L). Coagulation tests showed prothrombin time 16.4 s (normal 9.8-13.2 s) and international normalized ratio 1.46 s (normal 0.85-1.20 s). Erythrocyte sedimentation rate, neutrophil count, and hypersensitivity C-reactive protein were normal. Stool and urine routine tests were normal. Hepatobiliary enhanced magnetic resonance imaging revealed an unsmooth liver contour, imbalanced liver proportion, enlarged left lobe, reduced right lobe, non-uniform liver parenchymal signal, and multiple diffuse nodules. T1-weighted imaging showed isointensity, T2-weighted imaging showed low signal, OutPhase signal was not lower than InPhase, and no significant abnormalities were observed in the liver parenchyma after enhancement. The main portal vein's internal diameter was normal, and the intrahepatic bile duct was not significantly dilated. The spleen volume was increased with no significant signal abnormalities. The examination indicated liver cirrhosis, splenomegaly, and ascites. Tests for coxsackie virus antibody, Epstein-Barr virus antibody, hepatitis B surface antigen, and cytomegalovirus-DNA were negative. The patient had no history of alcohol consumption or inappropriate drug use. Antinuclear antibody and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies tests were negative.
test_results: A heterozygous missense mutation (c.710A>G) in the 33998775 position of exon 5 of the AMACR gene was found, which occurred in the protein CoA-transferase family Ⅲ domain. The frequency of this site in the normal East Asian population is 0.0001.
diagnosis: Inborn error of bile acid synthesis type 4
Orpha_name: Congenital bile acid synthesis defect type 4

case_report: A 73-year-old Caucasian woman with a history of hypertension presented to the emergency department with intermittent fever, anorexia, weakness, and fatigue for 2 weeks. She experienced nightly fevers and night sweats, but her weight remained stable. She had a persistent non-productive cough without sore throat or rashes. Her only medication was enalapril. Family history was non-contributory. She had been evaluated by her family doctor for the same symptoms 2 weeks earlier, where routine investigations were unremarkable. At that time, she had left knee pain after a hike, but X-rays of her knee and femur were normal, and the pain resolved within a week without treatment. She had no sick contacts, sexual partners, insect or tick bites, or known exposure to tuberculosis. She traveled to the Channel Islands 3 months prior and had no animal exposures or history of injection drug use. On examination, she appeared non-toxic with a temperature of 38.6 °C, heart rate of 96 beats/minute, blood pressure of 130/65 mmHg, and oxygen saturation of 99% on room air. There were no rashes or lymphadenopathy. Thyroid examination was normal. Jugular venous pulse was 2 cm above the sternal angle. Heart sounds were normal with no extra sounds or murmurs. Lungs were clear with equal breath sounds bilaterally. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender with no hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, or asterixis. Knee examination showed no redness, warmth, effusions, or pain. Neurologic examination was grossly normal with full strength bilaterally and normal reflexes, tone, and coordination. She was admitted for further investigation of her fever. Empiric piperacillin-tazobactam and intravenous saline were started. Laboratory investigations included an unremarkable peripheral smear, normal serum free light chains, no monoclone on serum protein electrophoresis, and bland urine analysis. Five sets of blood cultures, urine culture, and Lyme serology were negative. Chest X-ray and CT scans of the head, neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis were unremarkable. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed a normal heart with no vegetations. She had one further temperature of 39.4 °C in the hospital without a clear infectious source. Piperacillin-tazobactam was stopped once blood cultures were negative. She was discharged after an 8-day hospital stay with plans for outpatient follow-up. One month after discharge, she reported no improvement in symptoms and recurrence of left leg pain. Examination revealed a large, warm, left thigh mass, and her C-reactive protein (CRP) was 207 mg/L.
test_results: An urgent ultrasound revealed a 4.5 × 6.8 × 11.6 cm spindle-shaped, well-defined soft tissue mass with internal vascularity. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) found that the mass met the femur but was not invading. An initial biopsy revealed a poorly differentiated malignant neoplasm.

case_report: A 27-year-old male visited the outpatient department exhibiting reduced sweating and minimal body hair. His medical history included asthma with frequent episodes, managed with regular use of inhaled corticosteroids and bronchodilators. During childhood, he experienced easy overheating due to reduced sweating. His teeth were malformed and cone-shaped, but he received dental replacements 10 years prior. Physical examination revealed frontal bossing, a prominent supraorbital ridge, sunken cheeks, thick lips, sparse hair, scanty eyebrows, and low-set, overfolding ears.
test_results: A physical examination showed hypotrichosis with fine, sparse and brittle scalp hair with excessive fragility. Body hair was also diminished and sweat glands were found only over the axilla region. Sexual hair, beard and pubic hair, was normal. The patient also had generalized dry and hypopigmented skin with reduced hair follicles. Dermatitis resembling atopic skin was mainly noted over his bilateral extremities.

case_report: A 3-month-old female infant was admitted to the hospital presenting with difficulty in breathing, rapid breathing, and labored respiration with retractions, which were observed during a routine pediatric check-up. She is the first child of healthy, unrelated parents with no family history of neuromuscular disorders or sudden infant death syndrome. The infant was delivered via caesarean section at 34 weeks of gestation due to intrauterine growth retardation, decreased fetal movements, and placental abruption. Her birth weight was 1,550 grams (< 10th percentile), and she had an Apgar score of 8/10. She experienced neonatal respiratory distress immediately after birth, necessitating mechanical ventilation and pulmonary surfactants for 3 days. Upon admission at 3 months, a physical examination of the lungs revealed severe bilateral hypoventilation with crackles. A chest X-ray indicated bronchiolitis, and she was treated with corticosteroids and oxygen, but there was no improvement. Her condition worsened to severe respiratory failure, requiring mechanical ventilation. Attempts to wean her off the ventilator were unsuccessful. Limb weakness developed, progressing from distal to proximal, accompanied by significant generalized muscle weakness, absence of reflexes, bilateral foot deformities (equinovarus), and Achilles tendon contractures. There were no tongue fasciculations. Laboratory tests, including serologic and biochemical parameters, creatinine kinase levels, and cerebrospinal fluid analyses, were normal. Additional tests for infectious and metabolic conditions did not yield any significant findings.
test_results: On electrophysiological examination, sensory potentials were abolished in the lower limbs and fingers. The only recordable potential was that of the median nerve (amplitude 2.6 µV, SCV 21 m/s). Concentric needle examination revealed severe partial denervation in all examined muscles of the upper and lower limbs. Complete denervation of the left hemidiaphragm was demonstrated. Genetic analysis for Survival Motor Neuron (SMN1) gene was negative. Muscle and nerve biopsies were performed at 5 and 10 months of age. At 5 months muscle biopsy was nearly normal. However, sural nerve biopsy at that age demonstrated significant decrease in myelinated fiber density with no evidence of inflammation. At electron microscopy examination, no onion bulbs or axonal cluster formation were present. Microtubules and neurofilaments were normal. Giant axons, metachromasia, or lysosomal storage were absent. Electrophysiological examinations at 11 months of age demonstrated complete denervation in the most distal muscles (tibialis anterior, gastrocnemius, and foot muscles) and severely reduced interference pattern in the most proximal ones (vastus lateralis, deltoid, and facial muscles). At that age, marked atrophy of both type I and type II fibers was found in muscle biopsy with fibers showing prominent nuclei and increased oxidative activity, clearly demonstrative of a neurogenic process showing features of immature fetal phenotype.
diagnosis: Spinal Muscular Atrophy with Respiratory Distress type 1
Orpha_name: Spinal Muscular Atrophy with Respiratory Distress type 1

case_report: A 69-year-old Belgian Caucasian man reported experiencing cramps in the right calf and difficulties walking, which had progressively worsened over the past 6 months to the extent that he needed to use the banisters for support when climbing stairs. He did not experience any sensory disturbances. His medical history included arterial hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, complete deafness in the right ear following a mastoidectomy in early childhood, and asymptomatic elevated alkaline phosphatase levels identified 7 years earlier, confirmed by bone diphosphonate technetium-99m scintigraphy. His family history included a sister who died at 62 years with dementia and a mother who died at 67 years with dementia and walking difficulties. Initial neurological examination revealed slight weakness in the dorsal extensors of the left foot, left quadriceps, and right deltoid muscle, atrophy of the left thigh, and diffuse tendon hyperreflexia. Fasciculations were observed in the right deltoid muscle, but not in the tongue, which showed no atrophy. Cranial nerves and sensory functions were intact, and there was no Babinski sign. Electromyography (EMG) showed a diffuse chronic neurogenic pattern in all tested muscles of the left leg and the right deltoid muscle, without signs of subacute denervation such as fibrillations or positive sharp waves. Motor nerve conduction of the right peroneal nerve was markedly slowed, without conduction block. Laboratory tests were largely normal except for slight elevations in alkaline phosphatase (115 mU/mL, normal range 30-90 mU/mL) and lactate dehydrogenase (308 mU/mL, normal range 140-280 mU/mL). MRI of the lumbar spine and CT scans of the cervical spine and pelvis did not show significant abnormalities. Over the next 3 years, the patient found it difficult to walk for more than 20 minutes, experienced falls, and had intermittent paresthesias in the left big toe. He presented with a right Babinski sign and absent ankle reflexes. Further electrophysiological studies indicated diffuse sensorimotor neuropathy with a chronic neurogenic denervation pattern in the bilateral tibialis anterior and rectus femoris muscles, the right vastus lateralis, and soleus. Signs of subacute denervation (fibrillations and/or fasciculations) were noted in the right tibialis anterior muscle, the left vastus lateralis, and the right biceps. Muscle and nerve biopsies were discussed but declined by the patient. Somatosensory evoked potentials (SEP) suggested subcortical, supramedullary slowing of central somatosensory pathways, while motor evoked potentials (MEP) induced by transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of the central motor pathways showed elevated stimulus thresholds and slightly delayed central conduction, restricted to the lower limbs. A lumbar puncture revealed normal protein, glucose, cytology, and IgG index, with identical oligoclonal bands in the serum and cerebrospinal fluid. Tests for syphilis and borrelia were negative. Levels of serum human T-lymphotropic virus 1 antibodies, serum arylsulphatase-A, and urinary catecholamines were normal. Further investigations for polyneuropathy, including vitamin B status, diabetes screening, thyroid function, protein electrophoresis, and tumor markers, did not identify any metabolic, inflammatory, paraneoplastic, or toxic causes. MRI of the brain showed bilateral frontotemporal atrophy. MRI of the dorsal spine revealed focal atrophy spanning approximately 5 cm of the spinal cord at the D4 level, with secondary centromedullary dilatation.
test_results: A sequence analysis of the 17 coding exons of the VCP gene confirmed the existence of a simple base mutation in codon 159 (Arg>His).
diagnosis: Inclusion Body Myopathy with Paget's Disease of Bone and Frontotemporal Dementia
Orpha_name: Inclusion body myopathy with Paget disease of bone and frontotemporal dementia

case_report: A 77-year-old male presented with heartburn and discomfort behind the sternum. He did not report any abdominal pain or weight loss. His medical history included well-managed hypertension with medication. There was no notable personal or family medical history. Physical examination did not reveal any specific findings. Laboratory tests, including tumor marker evaluations, showed no abnormalities.
test_results: During esophagogastroduodenoscopy, a superficial lesion was found in the distal esophagus. White light endoscopy revealed a flat lesion of approximately 2.5 cm × 1.5 cm in size at a distance of 36-38 cm from the incisors, 2 cm away from the esophagogastric junction and slight reflux esophagitis (Los Angeles classification grade A) without Barrett’s esophagus. The central part of the lesion was uneven and slightly elevated. The lesion represented slight reddening of the mucosa with a coarse surface. Most of the lesion was covered by a scattered white membranous substance and mucous that was difficult to remove with water flow, and a normal vascular network could not be seen. Narrow-band imaging (NBI) showed a well-demarcated brownish area with background coloration. Magnifying endoscopy with NBI (ME-NBI) showed that under the membranous substance there were irregularly and dendritically branched abnormal vessels without loop formations, classified as type B2 according to the classification of the Japan Esophagus Society (JES classification). Additionally, intrapapillary capillary loops with morphological irregularities, including dilation, tortuous, and caliber changes, were observed in the peripheral area, classified as type B1. Iodine staining (1%) allowed the visualization of the lesion as an unstained area with a comparatively clear boundary, and pink-color sign could be seen. Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) revealed a hypoechoic mass confined to the mucosa layer, which did not seem to completely disrupt the muscularis mucosa, and the submucosa layer was intact. Computed tomography (CT) scanning was performed to rule out lymph node or distant metastasis.
diagnosis: Superficial Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Esophagus
Orpha_name: Squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus

case_report: A 13-year-old boy was admitted to the Endocrinology Department for evaluation of his short stature. He was born after a full-term pregnancy and normal delivery, as the second child in a non-consanguineous family. His parents reported that his birth weight and length were normal, but he gradually developed short stature after birth. Additionally, he frequently experienced respiratory infections and had his tonsils removed. No intellectual impairment was noted. Upon admission, routine examination revealed that the boy's weight was 81 kg (>97th percentile) and his standing height was 152.2 cm (3rd percentile). Pubertal development was normal. Other notable physical features included markedly thin and sparse scalp hair, protruding ears, a bulbous pear-shaped nose, and a long philtrum with a thin upper lip. Laboratory tests indicated that serum levels of calcium, inorganic phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, free T4, TSH, PTH, corticosteroid, and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) were within normal ranges. The karyotype was 46, XY.
test_results: Extremity and radiological examinations showed brachydactyly of fingers and toes.

case_report: A 78-year-old, right-handed Caucasian woman came to the clinic with speech difficulties. Approximately 4 months prior, she began experiencing increasing difficulty in finding the right words and responding to questions, resulting in disjointed and less clear sentences. In addition to speech issues and mild limb ataxia, her neurological examination was otherwise normal. She exhibited moderate orthostatic hypotension without falls and mild urinary incontinence. Her mental status showed no cognitive impairment, with a Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score of 25. Polysomnography was not conducted as there were no clinical signs of sleep-related disorders. Her medical history included hypothyroidism and episodic supraventricular tachycardia, managed with levothyroxine and beta blockers. Her family history was unremarkable. Initial MRI during the first hospitalization revealed mild brain atrophy and small vascular lesions. Chronic cerebral ischemia was diagnosed based on anamnesis, MRI, ultrasound investigations, and laboratory findings.
test_results: MRI revealed reduction of the anteroposterior diameter of midbrain at the superior collicular level from 15.5 mm on the first examination to 13.5 mm on follow-up images. Mild midbrain atrophy with concave upper surface was seen on sagittal images. Midbrain to pons area ratio on the midline sagittal plane was 0.24, remaining within normal range. Only minor putaminal hypointensity on T2-weighted images was noted. There was also progression of generalized brain atrophy, more prominent in the posterior frontal lobes. FDG-PET revealed diffuse hypometabolism of both cerebral hemispheres, especially pronounced in the middle and posterior part of the left frontal lobe. Small areas of hypometabolism were also present in the left lateral part of the temporal lobe and the left hemisphere of cerebellum. Diffusely decreased metabolism was reported in basal ganglia. Occipital lobes were less hypometabolic in comparison to the other brain areas.

case_report: A two-year-old girl was referred to the Urology Department for the management of vesicoureteral reflux (VUR). She had initially experienced a urinary tract infection (UTI) before presentation at the age of two, when right hydronephrosis and VUR on the same side (Grade IV) were observed. She was born to nonconsanguineous parents as a twin at 29 weeks' gestation, with a birth weight of 2,069 g. Antenatal ultrasound had shown no abnormalities, and she had no limb or anal deformities at birth. There was no significant past medical history, and her mother was not diabetic. On examination, she was active, alert, in satisfactory general health, and had met normal mental milestones. Her lower region and buttocks appeared normal, with no natal cleft or dimples at the hips and knees. A slight equinovarus deformity was present but had not been noted in previous medical checkups. She could walk and move her lower limbs, had sensations in the lower limbs and perineum, and exhibited normal tendon reflexes, including the anocutaneous reflex. There was no anal stenosis or deformity. She did not have constant urine leakage but experienced urine dribble during emptying, which her parents had not recognized as abnormal. Other systems were clinically normal. Urinalysis showed pyuria without bacteria. Ultrasound revealed bilateral hydronephrosis of grade III according to The Society for Fetal Urology guidelines.
test_results: X-ray and CT of the lower region showed the absence of the sacral bone under S2 and distal lumbar vertebrae. The limb bones were not hypoplastic. MRI T1- and T2-weighted sagittal images of the lumbosacral spine showed partial agenesis of the sacrum, a truncated cord and filum terminale. A cystogram showed a trabeculated bladder with fairly poor capacity and with grade IV reflux. Urodynamic study showed sphincter-detrusor dyssynergia (DSD) with maximum bladder pressure of 80 cmH2O. The maximum bladder capacity was 170 mL with no leakage. DMSA showed renal scarring on both kidneys.

case_report: The patient is a 15-year-old boy from São Paulo, Brazil, born to non-consanguineous parents. At age 4, he was referred for evaluation due to persistent eczema, which was initially thought to be associated with milk and egg allergy. He also had rhinitis and asthma, with negative skin prick tests for common inhalant allergens in Brazil, including house dust, fungi, animal epithelium, and cockroach. An oral food challenge with egg and milk was negative. A skin biopsy revealed acanthosis, parakeratosis, and agranulosis in the epidermis with micro abscesses in the stratum corneum. The papillary dermis showed vascular ectasia with a mix of inflammatory cells, predominantly neutrophils, consistent with chronic eczema. Topical corticosteroids and tacrolimus were ineffective, so the patient was treated with oral cyclosporine (2.5–4.2 mg/kg/day) for three years, which was discontinued after improvement. At age 7, routine laboratory work revealed selective IgA deficiency (IgA levels of 0.4 mg/dL). The patient also developed diffuse arthralgia with knee enlargement, leading to a diagnosis of Idiopathic Juvenile Arthritis. Treatment with Anti-TNF (Etanercept—45 mg/2 weeks) and methotrexate (17.5 mg/week) controlled the articular symptoms and prevented skin condition relapse for five years. At age 12, while still on methotrexate and Anti-TNF therapy, he developed new symptoms including alopecia areata, vitiligo, and non-bloody, non-mucoid diarrhea. A colonoscopy showed lymphangiectasis and diffuse colitis, leading to a presumed diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease. Anti-TNF and methotrexate were discontinued, and oral mesalazine was started, partially resolving the diarrhea without worsening arthritis. Screening for autoimmune diseases, including endocrinopathy, anti-GAD, ANA-antibodies, and rheumatoid factor, was negative. No growth alterations were observed over the years. At age 14, while on oral mesalazine and two years free of Anti-TNF and methotrexate, peripheral quantification of FOXP3 was normal.
test_results: A genetic sequencing was requested that came out positive to an already reported mutation in the FOXP3 gene.

case_report: A 59-year-old male, with no significant medical history, reported a 25-year duration of persistent, slowly progressing skin lesions on his hands. His past medical history and system review showed no abnormalities. His parents are not related by blood, and no family members have similar skin conditions. Physical examination of the skin revealed numerous small brownish keratotic pits on both palms. No similar lesions were observed on other parts of his body. Examination of hair, nails, and mucous membranes showed no abnormalities. Laboratory tests including complete blood count with differentials, peripheral blood smear, liver enzymes, urea, creatinine, and electrolytes were within normal limits. Imaging studies, including ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis, chest X-ray, and computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, were also normal.
test_results: Punch skin biopsy from the lesion revealed epidermal depression with an overlying column of compact orthokeratosis.

case_report: A 5-year-old boy with no previous medical history began experiencing involuntary movements in his left hand in August 2014, which later affected his right hand and eventually both upper limbs. His family noticed a decline in his handwriting abilities. He was seen by a pediatric neurologist who noted these movements and started him on valproate 2.5mL (125 mg) twice daily. Upon further examination, the boy exhibited twisting of his hands and frequent jerking movements. His heart examination was normal, and there were no nodules or erythema on his skin.
test_results: Electroencephalography was normal. Laboratory tests demonstrated antistreptolysin O (ASLO) titre of 80 IU/mL (normal range: < 250 IU/mL), negative oropharynx culture, C-reactive protein of 0.03mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 4mm/1st hour, normal levels of acid alpha1-glycoprotein and normal serum electrophoresis. Positive antinuclear antibodies with a titre of 1:640, dense fine speckled pattern. Anti-dsDNA, anti-ribosomal P, anti-Ro/SS-A, anti-La/SS-B, anti-U1RNP, anti-Sm, ANCA, anti-CCP, anti-thyroglobulin, anti-thyroperoxidase, rheumatoid factor, IgG and IgM anticardiolipin and lupus anticoagulant were all negative. Complement levels were normal. Vitamin B12 was 813 pg/mL,25-OH-vitamin D of 42 ng/mL, increased TSH of 6.2 mU/mL (nr: 0.3–4.0 mU/L), and normal free T4 0.99 ng/dL (nr: 0.9–1.8 ng/dL). Serology for syphilis, HIV 1 and 2, and HTLV I and II were negative. A magnetic resonance imaging of the brain was normal. A transthoracic echocardiography was interpreted as normal. A cerebrospinal fluid study was completely normal.
diagnosis: Sydenham’s Chorea as the first manifestation of Rheumatic Fever

case_report: A 4-day-old full-term male infant, born to a 19-year-old mother, was admitted to the neonatal ICU due to bilious vomiting and delayed passage of meconium. Physical examination revealed discoloration of the forehead hair, eyes, and right forearm. An erect abdominal X-ray showed an air-fluid level indicative of intestinal obstruction. Blood tests indicated elevated coagulation parameters, urea, and creatinine levels. Initial management included nasogastric (NG) tube decompression and nil per os (NPO) status. Following correction of laboratory abnormalities, surgical intervention was performed. A right supra-umbilical transverse incision was made, and the entire intestine was examined. No atresia was found; however, a normal caliber intestine was observed up to the terminal ileum, where a reduction in caliber was noted. The lumen was confirmed to be patent. The large bowel appeared normal, and the abdomen was closed. Over the next 8 days, spontaneous stool passage did not occur, and bilious drainage continued via the NG tube.
test_results: Contrast clongraphy revealed a narrowed colon to the terminal ileum.

case_report: A 3.5-month-old female was referred to our bone center. She was delivered after a 38-week pregnancy without complications, weighing 2.8 kg (33rd percentile, Z-score −0.43) and measuring 48 cm in length (67th percentile, Z-score 0.43). Initially, she was exclusively breastfed. The patient exhibited left facial palsy, which later progressed to affect both sides, with a more pronounced effect on the right side. Jaundice was observed to persist until the seventh week of life. Laboratory tests at one month of age showed elevated serum alkaline phosphatase levels, low serum phosphorus (3.0 mg/dL; normal range 3.8–6.5), and low to normal serum calcium (8.8 mg/dL; normal range 9.0–11).
test_results: Computed tomography confirmed hyperostosis of the mandible, maxilla and skull base, with narrowing of the internal auditory canals and under-pneumatization of the mastoid, maxillary and ethmoid sinuses. No intracranial lesions were seen on magnetic resonance images. A subsequent skeletal survey at 3 months of age revealed mild sclerosis of the facial bones and skull base. Furthermore, multiple rachitic changes were evident, including metaphyseal widening and flaring of the distal femur, as well as cupping of the distal tibia, fibula, radius, ulna and ribs.

case_report: A 66-year-old multiparous female patient presented with recurrent vaginal bleeding and dull lower abdominal pain for 2 months. She had recently undergone vaginal sonography at a private gynecologic clinic. On admission, physical examination results were unremarkable, and her vital signs were normal. Laboratory testing indicated a CA-125 level of >1,000 U/mL (reference value, 0 to 35). A Pap smear test showed atrophy and inflammation but no evidence of malignancy.
test_results: EUS-guided FNB identified papillary tumor cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and frequent mitosis. Both abdominopelvic CT and pelvic dynamic MRI revealed an 8×5×5 cm heterogeneous irregular enhancing mass, at the cul-de-sac extending to both adnexa, that had directly invaded the rectal wall. EUS revealed a sausage-shaped hypoechoic mass, 8 cm in size, with irregular margins and heterogeneous internal echoes extending to both adnexa. The solid echogenic adnexal mass had nearly obliterated the lumen of both fallopian tubes and had invaded the fundus of the uterus. Dual imaging with the conventional gray-scale B-mode EUS image and elastographic image demonstrated that the mass had a blue color pattern, representing hard stiffness, and heterogeneous green/red coloration outside the tumor, representing intermediate stiffness. The B/A strain ratio of the adnexal mass was 15.61.

case_report: A 49-year-old Spanish Caucasian woman experienced hip pain following a traffic accident. She measured 165 cm in height and weighed 59 kg, resulting in a body mass index of 21.6 kg/m2. Radiographs did not reveal any fractures. Her medical and family history were unremarkable, with no records of recurrent inflammation, infection, or known skeletal disorders. Her father passed away suddenly in his 80s, and her mother died from an unspecified cancer. She has one healthy brother and one teenage son. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count, creatinine, calcium, phosphate, transaminases, lactic dehydrogenase, and C-reactive protein, as well as fluoride and tryptase levels, were within normal limits. Serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) was 47 U/L (reference range 46–118); bone-specific ALP was 18 U/L (reference 14–43). Serum procollagen type I N-propeptide (PINP) was 48 ng/mL (reference 19–102), collagen C-terminal telopeptide (CTX) was 0.23 ng/mL (reference 0.13–1.04); Intact PTH was 19 pg/mL (reference 18–88), and 25-hydroxyvitamin D was 22 ng/mL (reference 20–50). DXA results showed Z-scores of +1.3 at the lumbar spine, +0.7 at the femoral neck, +1.3 at the total hip, and +0.3 at the forearm. An extensive search for a primary tumor was conducted, yielding negative results.
test_results: A 99mTc-DPD scintigraphy showed multiple foci of increased uptake at the thoracic and lumbar spine, pelvis, proximal left femur, and right humerus. An 18F-NaF PET/CT revealed intense uptake in those areas. MRI and CT showed patchy osteosclerotic lesions within the trabecular areas of those bones. Percutaneous bone biopsies at the iliac crest and lumbar vertebral bodies revealed increased trabecular thickness without neoplastic cells or any retained cartilage.

case_report: The patient is a 50-year-old woman with no relevant family history of muscle weakness and no consanguinity. At 5 years old, she experienced difficulty blowing up balloons, whistling, and puffing her cheeks. Her mental development was normal, and the progression of her condition slowed over time. By 30 years old, she exhibited asymmetrical proximal muscle weakness in the lower limbs and milder asymmetrical proximal muscle weakness in the upper limbs, along with mild waist weakness. The muscle weakness progressed slowly. She was unable to climb stairs, jump, run, or rise from the floor, but had no breathing difficulties. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were normal. A positive bilateral eyelash sign and a shallower right nasolabial fold compared to the left were noted. She could not grimace or puff her cheeks. Mental function and other cranial nerve function tests were normal. Limb muscle weakness was asymmetrical (Medical Research Council (MRC) Grades 4/5 proximally and 5/5 distally, with bilateral hip extensors at 2/5) without muscle atrophy. Beevor's sign was positive. Sensations were normal, and muscle stretch reflexes were absent. Laboratory studies showed a slightly elevated serum creatine kinase (CK) level of 291.5 IU/L (normal range: 26–174 IU/L). Respiratory parameters and cardiac evaluations, including echocardiogram (echo) and electrocardiogram (ECG), were unremarkable.
test_results: Electromyography (EMG) showed myopathic changes, and nerve conduction was normal. The lower limb muscle MRI showed that the bilateral posterior thigh groups were markedly fattened, especially of the lateral femoral muscle edges and central preservation. A significant enlargement of the medial head of the gastrocnemius and anterior tibial muscles was observed in both lower legs. Muscular pathological findings showed that the right tibial premuscle muscle fibers were clearly unequal in size, some of the muscle fibers were more clearly atrophied, some of the muscle fibers were mildly hypertrophied, a few muscle fiber nuclei were internally displaced, individual muscle clefts and nuclei aggregation were seen, muscle fiber degeneration and necrosis were not visible, and collagen VI immunostaining revealed a normal staining pattern. Molecular studies, using the whole-genome sequencing technology, identified the heterozygous mutation c.6817-2(IVS27)A>G in the COL6A3 gene. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the mutation was not detected in her mother or her son.

case_report: A 4-year-old boy was brought to the hospital due to parental concerns about a decline in motor abilities. Over the past month, he experienced difficulties with sitting, standing, and walking. His mother reported that he had achieved the ability to stand and walk, though unsteadily, by 29 months. His language skills also regressed; he was using simple one and two-syllable words appropriately by 19 months, but his speech became slurred and dysarthric by 29 months. Upon examination at 48 months, he was alert and responsive, with normal vision and hearing, but exhibited a bilateral convergent squint. Reflexes were normal, but he had low muscle tone and bilateral weakness across all muscle groups. No abnormal or involuntary movements were observed. His occipitofrontal circumference (OFC) was 46 cm. Laboratory results showed a random blood sugar level of 4.7 mmol/L, serum ammonia level of 45 µmol/L, and a lactic acid level of 8.9 mmol/L, indicating lactic acidosis. He is the second child in a nonconsanguineous marriage, and his older brother is healthy.
test_results: CT Scan of his brain identified bilateral cerebral and cerebellum leukodystrophy/ischemic change. A compound heterozygous variant in SURF1 gene was identified (c.229 G > C[p.Gly77Arg] and c.792_793delAG[p.Arg264Serfs*27]).

case_report: A 49-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital with the primary concern of 'pulmonary nodules identified for over 2 months.' She reported visiting a local hospital 2 months prior due to 'cough and sputum lasting 2 weeks,' where a chest CT revealed 'a ground glass nodule in the middle lobe of the right lung, approximately 0.7 cm in size' (Fig. A). Despite receiving anti-infective treatment, her symptoms did not significantly improve, and a follow-up chest CT was conducted (Fig. B). The patient had been in good health previously, with no pulmonary nodules detected on a chest CT from the previous year. Upon admission to our hospital, no positive signs were observed during the examination. Laboratory tests showed negative results for hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibody, HIV, and syphilis-specific antibodies. Routine blood, urine, and stool tests, as well as liver function, coagulation, and blood biochemistry, were normal. PCT, CRP, and ESR levels were within normal ranges, and tumor marker tests were normal. Electrocardiogram, cardiac ultrasound, and cranial CT revealed no significant abnormalities. Lung function tests were normal. A 3D imaging CT examination of both lungs indicated a ground glass nodule in the middle lobe of the right lung, measuring approximately 1.5 cm × 1.1 cm (Fig. C).
test_results: The pathology showed diffuse lymphocytic infiltration with varying numbers of small lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages and histiocytes infiltrating the alveolar septa, widened and enlarged alveolar septa, and scattered lymphoid follicles. Immunohistochemically, CD20 positive in follicular area, CD3 positive in interfollicular area, Ki-67 showed high proliferation index in the germinal center, Bcl-6 and CD10 positive in the germinal center, CD38, IgG, IgG4, kappa, lambda scattered positive, CD21 positive in dendritic cells.

case_report: A 49-year-old female from Nagasaki, Japan, presented in early February 2017 with skin papules on both forearms. By late February, she developed a painful mouth ulcer and multiple neck swellings. She consulted her dentist, who referred her to the internal medicine department for hospitalization. Initial examination at the internal medicine department revealed a painful small ulcer in the middle of the soft palate with a pain score of 5/18 and cervical lymph node swellings. The complete blood count was normal, and a biopsy showed no malignancy. The condition was identified as candidiasis, and anti-fungal treatment was prescribed, resulting in an improvement of the pain score to 1/18, but the ulcer did not heal despite adherence to therapy. By late March 2017, the palatal ulcer had progressed, and the cervical lymphadenopathy had not improved, leading to the patient's re-admission for further clinical assessment and laboratory investigations.
test_results: Flow cytometry showed CD4: 77.9%, CD8: 12.3%, CD25: 72.1%, CCR4: 68.1% and TSLC1: 68.7%. High level of HTLV-1 monoclonal bands was recognised by Southern blot method (>45, normal: <1 cutoff-index), also serum level of soluble interleukin-2 receptor (sIL-2R) was very high (3420 U/mL) which then raised to 5960 U/mL one month later (in asymptomatic HTLV-1 carrier it should not exceed 800 U/mL). Histopathologic examination of pharyngeal biopsy revealed infiltration by malignant lymphoid cells with hyperchromatic enlarged nuclei and scanty cytoplasm while immune-histochemical staining showed CD3 (+), CD4 (+) and CD8 (–) cells.

case_report: A 60-year-old female patient was admitted to the hospital on May 21, 2019, due to 'unstable walking and stiff legs for more than 10 days.' The patient experienced instability while walking for over 10 days prior to admission. During walking, she exhibited muscle tension in the lower limbs, which affected her ability to walk and led to falls in severe cases. These symptoms gradually eased after about 1 minute, and she fell 5 times during the course of the condition. She also reported itching in the right lower extremity, mainly around the hip. The symptoms worsened with tension, emotional excitement, and touch. The patient denied any history of trauma, infection, poisoning, drug use, psychiatric disease, or family genetic history. Upon admission, she was alert and well-oriented. Neurological examination revealed small horizontal nystagmus in both eyes, increased muscle tension in both lower extremities, marked rigidity in the lower limbs, active tendon reflexes, hyperreflexia in the extremities, and ankle cramps in both legs. There were no sensory disturbances. Laboratory tests showed normal results for blood routine, urine routine, liver and kidney function, blood lipids, ions, surgical comprehensive, and tumor markers. Thyroid function tests indicated normal T3 and T4 levels, TSH at 6.67 uIU/ml, antithyroid peroxidase antibody at 96.51 uIU/mL (<35), antithyroglobulin antibody at 272.5 uIU/mL (<115), IG antibody at 18 U/L (0–12), anti-SSA-60 positive, granular type 1 at 100, anti-SSA-52/Ro52 positive, anti-mitochondrial M2 antibody positive, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein at 6.03 mg/L (0–3.5 mg/L). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Electromyographic examination: continuous motor unit activity (CMUA) was seen. After the injection of 10 mg of diazepam, the CMUA gradually weakened and disappeared. The serum anti-GAD antibody IgG was positive and anti-GAD antibody in cerebrospinal fluid was not detected. Anti-islet cell antibody also was positive. CT of the thorax revealed an anterior superior mediastinal mass, suggestive of a thymoma.
diagnosis: Progressive Encephalomyelitis with Rigidity and Myoclonus
Orpha_name: Progressive Encephalomyelitis with Rigidity and Myoclonus

case_report: A 1-week-old male newborn, born at 35 weeks of gestation via in vitro fertilization, was admitted with undetectable TREC on NBS (normal range >20 copies/microliter). There was no family history of immunodeficiency. Initial lab results showed a T−/B+/NK+ immune phenotype. Pharmacologic prophylaxis against infections was started with acyclovir, fluconazole, and pentamidine, along with intravenous immune globulins (IVIG). The mother was cytomegalovirus (CMV) seronegative, and the patient had no detectable CMV viral load by PCR, allowing breastfeeding. Further tests confirmed undetectable serum viral loads of HIV, EBV, and adenovirus by PCR. At 1 and 3 months of age, profound T cell lymphopenia (TCL) persisted (<300 cells/μl), and the proportion of naïve CD45RA+CD4+ T-cells was below normal (60%, normal >90%). Maternal engraftment was ruled out by short tandem repeats (STR) analysis, and a microarray was normal. The patient continued to exhibit significant CD4+ and CD8+ lymphopenia, while B and NK cell counts remained normal. After the initial IVIG dose, the patient was switched to subcutaneous immunoglobulin replacement therapy (IgRT), maintaining IgG levels within the normal range. IgA levels were consistently low (<7 mg/dL), and IgM levels remained normal. Lymphocyte proliferation to phytohemagglutinin (PHA) and pokeweed mitogen (PWM) at 1 month of age, measured by chemically labeled EdU incorporation, were normal. At 3 months of age, lymphocyte proliferation to PHA, concanavalin A (ConA), and PWM, measured by radioactive thymidine incorporation, were also normal. TCR Vβ spectratyping showed abnormalities: one probe had no peak, 8/28 (29%) demonstrated oligoclonality (<5 peaks), and 15/28 (53%) showed a polyclonal, non-Gaussian distribution.
test_results: Next generation sequencing identified two heterozygous missense variants in trans in RAG1 (RAG1 c.983G>A p.Cys328Tyr [C328Y] and RAG1 c.1856C>T p.Pro619Leu [P619L]). The first variant had been previously published as a homozygous trait in a patient with OS and was also present in the patient's father, who was a heterozygous carrier. The second variant was a novel variant of uncertain significance (VUS); the patient's mother was a heterozygous carrier for this variant. These findings confirmed the compound heterozygous status of the patient.
diagnosis: Atypical Severe Combined Immunodeficiency  due to compound heterozygous RAG1 variants
Orpha_name: Combined immunodeficiency due to partial RAG1 deficiency

case_report: A 12-year-old girl was referred to the sleep unit of the Pediatric Department at Ponderas Academic Hospital Bucharest for a respiratory evaluation and sleep study using PSG. She exhibited symptoms including morning headaches, irritability, and aggressive behavior. She was born at term following a normal pregnancy to a non-consanguineous healthy family. She experienced motor developmental delays, achieving independent walking at 18 months with normal cognitive development. From the age of two, she demonstrated a chronic, progressive motor deficit affecting all four limbs, manifesting as difficulties with running and walking. Her current clinical examination revealed a weight of 43.5 kg (50th percentile), height of 159 cm (90th percentile) (arm span used as a surrogate measurement for height), and BMI of 17.2 kg/m2. She had thoracic dextroscoliosis with an asymmetric posture, an elevated right hip, and bilateral high foot arches with hammertoes. Her mental status was normal, though she appeared hesitant and somewhat anxious; no psychiatric diagnosis was made. Cardiovascular assessment was normal. Neurological examination showed muscle atrophy in the upper limbs and the lower third of her thighs, with chronic, progressive muscle weakness. The lower limbs were more affected (grade 3 on the Medical Research Council Scale for Muscle Strength) than the upper limbs (grade 4 on the Medical Research Council Scale for Muscle Strength). She had a positive Gowers maneuver and joint retraction in both ankles (more pronounced on the right side) and shoulders. Cervical muscle weakness was noted, particularly in the neck flexors. Additionally, she exhibited a distinctive gait with a tendency towards asymmetric digitigrade walking, especially on the right limb, poor exercise tolerance, and could walk no more than 200 meters, reporting muscle fatigue and diffuse pain.
test_results: A heterozygous variant in the COL6A2 gene c.784 G > T, p.(Gly262Cys) was detected. It is classified as a likely pathogenic variant (class 2).
diagnosis: Bethlem myopathy 1  or Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy 1

case_report: A 59-year-old Caucasian woman presented with progressive visual impairment in both eyes, which began in her thirties. She reported no family history of eye disorders. Her best corrected visual acuity was measured at 0.6 LogMAR in the right eye and 0.4 LogMAR in the left eye using ETDRS charts. Examination of the anterior segment revealed normal findings in both eyes, with no crystal deposits observed at the corneal limbus. Intraocular pressure was recorded at 16 mmHg in both eyes. Fundus biomicroscopy showed extensive chorioretinal atrophy in both eyes, accompanied by multiple crystalline deposits primarily located at the edges of the atrophic areas. Scotopic and photopic full-field electroretinograms were significantly reduced, while the electrooculogram remained within normal limits.
test_results: Next Generation Sequencing unveiled two pathogenic variants in CYP4V2 (c.424_427 del (p.(Lys142Glyfs*8)) and c.173C>A (p.(Pro58Gln)).

case_report: A 76-year-old, right-handed, Caucasian female presented with significant gait impairment. She has a history of SS, evidenced by a decade of sicca symptoms, reduced tear production as shown by Schirmer's test, and the presence of anti-Ro/SS-A antibodies. Over the past 6 months, her gait rapidly worsened, leading to frequent falls and necessitating the use of a wheelchair for mobility outside her home.
test_results: There was urogenital dysfunction leading to multiple urinary tract infections, absence of tremor with bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity, a festinating gait with inability to take more than 10 steps without support, and upper-motor findings (ie, hyperreflexia and Babinski findings) without structural disease of the brain or spinal cord on MRI neuroimaging studies.

case_report: An 8-year-old female patient was brought to the Department of Oral Medicine and Radiology, Bapuji Dental College and Hospital, Davangere, with a complaint of non-eruption of the upper front tooth for the past 6 to 7 months. The father reported that the upper front milk teeth had fallen out approximately 6 to 7 months ago due to mobility. There was no history of trauma. The patient had previously consulted a dentist about a year ago for concerns regarding esthetic appearance but received no treatment. The family history included consanguineous marriage between the parents and three siblings: two elder sisters aged 15 and 12 years, and a younger brother aged 5 years, all of whom were short in height. The patient brushed her teeth once daily in the morning, had a mixed diet, and had attained developmental milestones appropriately. General physical examination revealed short stature with shortened limbs, absent transverse flexural palmar creases, clinodactyly of the second and fifth fingers, broad toes, and nail dysplasia. Extraoral examination showed macrocephaly, frontal bossing, hypertelorism, prominent eyes, down-slanting palpebral fissures, broad nasal bridge, upturned nose, long philtrum, deficient malar prominence, and mandibular retrognathism. Oral features included a triangular-shaped mouth with downturned angles exposing the maxillary incisors and gums, and a midline indentation of the upper and lower lips. Intraoral examination revealed a high arched palate, narrowed and V-shaped mandibular arches, maxillary and mandibular alveolar ridge hypertrophy, and a short lingual frenulum indicating partial ankyloglossia. The teeth present were 11, 52, 53, 54, 55, 16, 21, 62, 63, 64, 26, 31, 32, 72, 73, 74, 75, 41, 82, 83, 84, 85. There was palatal eruption of 12, over-retained 52, 62, 72, 82, lingual eruption of 32, 42, and mesiolingual rotation of 31, 41. Orthopantomography showed erupting 11, 22, 36, 46. Lateral cephalograph indicated midfacial hypoplasia and mandibular micrognathism. Hand wrist graphs showed normal skeletal maturity with clinodactyly of the fifth finger.
test_results: Full skeletal survey revealed vertebral deformities.

case_report: A 6-month-old girl was referred for management of renal dysfunction, detected during evaluation for acute gastroenteritis, pallor, and generalized swelling. She was born at full term to parents from Farukhabad, Uttar Pradesh, India. Her perinatal period was uneventful, but she exhibited failure to thrive and developmental delay. Acute peritoneal dialysis was started due to abnormal renal function tests (blood urea: 161 mg/dl; creatinine: 5.7 mg/dl), acidosis (pH: 7.28, bicarbonate: 17.5 mEq/l), and electrolyte imbalances (sodium: 125 mEq/l; potassium: 5.4 mEq/l). Laboratory results showed hemoglobin at 7 g/dl, calcium at 7.4 mg/dl, phosphate at 7 mg/dl, alkaline phosphatase at 129 IU/l, and parathyroid hormone (PTH) at 563 pg/ml. Urinalysis was normal. Ultrasound imaging indicated increased echogenicity of the medullary papillae.
test_results: Renal biopsy revealed that proximal and distal tubules were filled with hexagonal crystals; additional findings included tubular dilatation and atrophy, interstitial fibrosis, and periglomerular fibrosis.

case_report: A 38-year-old Afro-Brazilian male with no prior medical history presented to the emergency department with sudden abdominal pain, jaundice, fever, nausea, weakness, and malaise. His vital signs included an arterial blood pressure of 90/50 mmHg, heart rate of 90 bpm, axillary temperature of 35°C, and signs of dehydration. Laboratory results showed serum creatinine at 0.8 mg/dl, platelet count at 142 x 10^3/mm3, serum fibrinogen at 221 mg/dl, an increased international normalized ratio (INR) of 1.9, total bilirubin at 3.9 mg/dl, direct bilirubin at 2.3 mg/dl, ALT at 751 U/l, AST at 540 U/l, ceruloplasmin at 17 mg/dl, ferritin at 3200 ng/dl, iron at 276 mcg/dl, total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) at 267 mcg/dl, transferrin saturation at 103%, hemoglobin (Hb) at 14 g/dl, and hematocrit (Ht) at 41.3% without signs of acute bleeding. Ultrasound imaging indicated inflammation, liver fibrosis, and iron overload.
test_results: First ROTEM test showed in EXTEM CT 80s, CFT 105s, alfa-angle 70°, MCF 52 mm, and ML 37%; FIBTEM MCF 13 mm and APTEM MCF 53 mm and ML 20%. Second ROTEM test presented improvement in the hyperfibrinolysis but not completely, with EXTEM CT 64s, CFT 105s, alfa-angle 69°, MCF 51 mm, and ML 24%; FIBTEM MCF 11 mm, APTEM MCF 51 mm, and ML 20%. The third ROTEM test showed persistence of maximum lysis above 15% with EXTEM CT 83s, CFT 133s, alfa-angle 66°, MCF 50 mm, and ML 21%; FIBTEM MCF 10 mm and APTEM MCF 51 mm and ML 19%. Fourth ROTEM test was normal with EXTEM CT 64s, CFT 122s, alfa-angle 68°, MCF 50 mm, and ML 15%; FIBTEM MCF 12 mm and APTEM MCF 51 mm and ML 15%. Thromboelastometry was normal despite CCT were still altered. Liver biopsy was performed which succeeded with no signs of bleeding and without need of further transfusion.
diagnosis: Decompensated Liver Disease with Factor XIII Deficiency

case_report: A 65-year-old woman with no family history of endocrine tumors was referred to the General Surgery Unit. Over the past 18 months, she experienced increasing weakness, weight loss of up to 15 kg, angular cheilitis, and glossitis. She had a traumatic fracture of her left humeral head and underwent dual energy x-ray absorptiometry and laboratory investigations as an outpatient, which indicated severe osteoporosis (t-score −4 at the lumbar spine and −2.4 at the femoral neck), primary hyperparathyroidism (pHPT), Hashimoto’s thyroiditis with hypothyroidism, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Recently, she developed widespread itching and painful rashes on the perioral skin, perineum, and groin folds. She was admitted to an Internal Medicine Unit for further assessment. Her father had died at age 84 due to myocardial infarction and her mother at age 69 after colorectal cancer surgery. A 60-year-old brother had arterial hypertension, and a 32-year-old daughter had severe obesity. Menarche occurred at 12 years of age and menopause at 39 years following hystero-adnexectomy for post-partum uterine rupture. There were no other significant medical history details, and she was not taking any medications. Biochemical studies showed iron-deficiency anemia and confirmed Hashimoto’s thyroiditis with mild hypothyroidism, diabetes mellitus, and mild pHPT (Calcium: 10.4 mg/dl [normal range 8.8-10.6], 24-hour urinary calcium excretion: 358 mg/dl [normal range 130–300], iPTH: 147 pg/ml [normal range 8–87], Creatinine: 0.74 mg/dl [normal range 0.84-1.25]). A 99mTc-sestamibi scan and ultrasound of the neck identified an inferior right hyperfunctioning parathyroid. A 9 mm nodule was detected by ultrasound in the left thyroid lobe. Endoscopic studies revealed mild antral gastritis and diverticulosis of the colon, while abdominal ultrasound showed no pathological findings. Skin culture indicated candidiasis secondary to Candida albicans with bacterial superinfection. The patient was discharged with prescriptions for oral antidiabetics, iron therapy, proton pump inhibitors, bisphosphonates, levothyroxine, and antifungal/antibiotic agents. After one month, with no improvement in the rash, she was referred to the Dermatology Unit, where a generic deficiency dermatitis was diagnosed based on histological examination of a skin biopsy. Oral zinc and vitamin supplements were added to her diet, but no improvement was observed over the following two months.
test_results: Abdominal enhanced multidetector-row computed tomography (MDCT) revealed a low-density 2x3 cm mass between the body and tail of the pancreas, with intense contrast enhancement. Somatostatin receptor scintigraphy (OctreoScan) with SPECT acquisition showed an area of increased uptake between the body and tail of the pancreas corresponding to the tumor revealed by previous MDCT.

case_report: A 10-year-old female patient first visited a neurologist at age 5 due to progressive difficulty in walking and loss of strength. By age 6, she was referred to a geneticist because of challenges in ambulation linked to hypotonia in both lower and upper limbs. Physical examination identified genu valgus and joint hypermobility. Karyotype, muscle enzyme levels, and radiologic studies were within normal ranges. At age 7, the patient exhibited pubic hair growth and a possible menstrual episode, with normal levels of LH, FSH, estrogen, and progesterone. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed pituitary cysts and widespread hypomyelination of the central nervous system. By age 10, she required a wheelchair for mobility. Orthopedic surgery was performed to address Achilles tendon shortening. A dermatological assessment noted curly hair distinct from her parents' hair, including involvement of the eyelashes.
test_results: Sequence analysis of GAN gene demonstrated the mutation c.1456G>A (p.GLU486LYS). Scanning electron microscopy revealed longitudinal grooves on the surface of the hair at low magnification and a polygonal shape at higher magnification, typical findings of pili canaliculi.

case_report: The patient is an 11-year-old girl born to healthy, unrelated parents after a normal pregnancy at 40 weeks of gestation, with a birth weight of 3.455 kg and a height of 54 cm. At 13 months old, during an evaluation for a febrile illness, she was found to have thrombocytopenia with large platelets (61 × 10^9/L, MPV 17 fl) and no leukocyte inclusion bodies. There is no family history of bleeding. Platelet morphology indicated inherited thrombocytopenia.
test_results: A diagnostic workup for febrile illness at the age of 13 months revealed thrombocytopenia with large platelets (61 × 109/L, MPV 17 fl) but no leukocyte inclusion bodies.

case_report: A 28-year-old male from the East Mediterranean region presented to the hematology department with symptoms of abdominal pain, diarrhea, and a weight loss of 25 kg over the past six months. Clinical examination revealed a blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg and a pulse rate of 90 beats per minute (regular). The patient appeared pale and cachectic, with clubbing of the fingers, edema, and signs of dehydration. No palpable lymph nodes or splenomegaly were detected. Laboratory results showed a hemoglobin level of 11.6 g/dl, hematocrit level of 35.7%, red blood cell count of 4.44×10^6/mm3, platelet count of 361×10^3/mm3, mean corpuscular volume of 80.4 fl, and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration of 32.4%. The total white blood cell count was 22.5×10^3/mm3, with a lymphocyte count of 12.4×10^3/mm3 and a neutrophil count of 9.5×10^3/mm3. Peripheral blood smear showed lymphocytosis. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 90 mm/h. Plasma biochemical abnormalities included albumin at 2.0 g/dl, total protein at 5.2 g/dl, low plasma potassium at 2.9 mmol/L, serum iron at 42 μg/dl, iron binding capacity at 464 μg/dl, and iron saturation at 9%. Serum folic acid level was low, while cobalamin and zinc levels were normal. Stool studies for bacteriological, virological, and parasitological agents were negative. Chest x-ray was normal, and abdominal x-ray showed air levels in a non-dilated large bowel. Barium x-ray studies indicated segmentation, bowel loop dilatation, mucosal fold thickening, and delayed intestinal transit. Endoscopic examination revealed mild duodenitis, with no abnormalities found in colonoscopic examination. CT scans of the abdominal region showed multiple mesenteric lymphadenopathy and thickening of the small bowel, with the largest lymph nodes measuring up to 3 centimeters. Duodenal biopsy samples showed moderate infiltration by normal-appearing plasma cells, with no evidence of Helicobacter pylori on microscopic evaluation. Serum IgG, IgA gliadin antibodies, and IgA endomysial antibodies were negative. Stool and duodenal aspiration fluid examinations for parasites were normal. The immunological profile was normal except for elevated IgA, which was polyclonal. Immunoelectropheresis revealed an abnormal precipitin line of IgA with no response to light chains.
test_results: Histological examination of the excised jejunal biopsy showed subtotal villous atrophy and dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltration limited to mucosa and submucosa. The extensive plasmacytic infiltration was established in mesenteric lymph nodes. CD 20 were found positive in the mesenteric lymph node. In the immunohistochemical analysis of the intestinal and lymph node biopsy material, LCA, CD-79, CD-20 and IgA were found positive while kappa and lambda heavy chain, IgD and IgM were found negative. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy revealed diffuse lymphoplasmacytic infiltration. Malabsorption was confirmed by abnormal D-xylose absorption (urine excretion of D-xylose was 1.20 g/5 h; normal value >4.5 g/5 h).

case_report: A 9-year-old boy presented to the dermatology department with a history of light skin and hair since infancy. There was no history of fever, jaundice, abdominal pain, convulsions, or photosensitivity. He was born to parents who are not related by blood, and his prenatal and birth periods were uneventful. His physical development was within normal limits. His younger sibling did not have similar issues. On skin examination, he had silvery gray hair, eyebrows, and eyelashes. Bronze tan hyperpigmentation was observed on his face and other exposed areas of his fair skin. His teeth and nails appeared normal. Systemic examination showed no abnormalities. There was no enlargement of the liver or spleen, and examinations of the central nervous, respiratory, and cardiac systems were normal. Ophthalmological examination did not reveal any abnormalities. Laboratory investigations showed a normal hematological profile and normal immunoglobulin levels.
test_results: On light microscopic examination of hair, uneven clusters of aggregated melanin pigment, accumulated mainly in the medullary area of the shaft was seen instead of the homogeneous distribution of small pigment granules as seen in normal hair. Skin biopsy showed increased deposition of melanosomes in melanocytes in the dermal layer with poorly pigmented adjacent keratinocytes.

case_report: An 11-month-old male was admitted for assessment of developmental delays. He was delivered at full term following an uncomplicated pregnancy, with a birth weight of 2,600 grams and normal Apgar scores. The family history included a maternal uncle with developmental delay, but no other relevant conditions. The patient exhibited nystagmus, spasticity, strabismus, and head nodding. At 1 month old, his parents observed jerky eye movements and head nodding. Subsequently, he continued to show frequent head nodding and mild hypertonia in the lower limbs. At 7 months, he underwent a hearing evaluation at another facility due to concerns about hearing loss. Brainstem auditory evoked potentials were normal, and imaging revealed a choroidal cyst in the right medial temporal lobe. By 11 months, he had not yet achieved independent sitting. Laboratory tests, including serum amino acid and urine organic acid levels, were within normal limits.
test_results: Brain MR imaging revealed the absence of myelination of the white matter; there had been no progression of myelination compared to brain MR images obtained at 7 months of age. MR spectroscopy showed increased NAA and creatine peaks in the white matter and basal ganglia. Genetic analysis by multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) showed duplication of the PLP1 gene.

case_report: Case 1 involves a 2-year-old boy with a novel identified de novo missense heterozygous variant c.814T>C [p.Phe272Leu]. At 6 months old, he was unable to hold his head up steadily. Seizures began at 10 months, characterized by leftward eye gaze, perioral cyanosis, occasional jaw tremor, right lower limb raising, and hand tremor. These seizures occurred in clusters, up to eight times per day, for 2–3 days each month. He has been seizure-free since 12 months of age with levetiracetam monotherapy. Developmental milestones included sitting and crawling independently at 1 year old, walking without support at 1 year and 3 months, though he still walks unsteadily. He started vocalizing at 1 year old but has not yet produced the sounds “babamama.” No apparent malformations were observed. Brain MRI results were normal. Initial serum magnesium level was 0.56 mmol/L.
test_results: EEG showed focal frontal epileptic discharge. The electrical-clinical features indicate that his seizures were focal seizures. He was diagnosed with causative gene.
Orpha_name: Infantile hypotonia-oculomotor anomalies-hyperkinetic movements-developmental delay syndrome

case_report: A 2-year-old girl was admitted for evaluation due to recurrent episodes of elevated aminotransferase levels. At 6 months old, she was initially diagnosed with hepatitis at another hospital after presenting with fever, vomiting, and diarrhea. Physical examination revealed hepatomegaly, palpable four finger breadths below the costal margin. Laboratory tests showed elevated aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 2,017 IU/L and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) at 1,242 IU/L, along with prolonged prothrombin time. Liver enzymes normalized following supportive care. Similar episodes of elevated aminotransferase levels occurred at 15 months and 23 months of age, coinciding with symptoms of upper respiratory infections. Laboratory results at these times showed AST levels of 240 IU/L and 457 IU/L, and ALT levels of 260 IU/L and 530 IU/L, respectively. Upon admission to our hospital at 2 years old, her height was 115.7 cm (25th to 50th percentile) and her weight was 12.9 kg (25th to 50th percentile). Vital signs included a blood pressure of 116/77 mm Hg, heart rate of 136/min, respiratory rate of 32/min, and body temperature of 36℃. Physical examination was unremarkable. She had no siblings and no family history of liver or genetic diseases. Laboratory findings included hemoglobin at 11.8 g/dL, white blood cell count at 6,200/mm3 (neutrophils 28%, lymphocytes 54%, monocytes 14%, eosinophils 2%), platelet count at 397,000/mm3, total protein at 7.0 g/dL, albumin at 4.0 g/dL, AST at 88 IU/L, ALT at 68 IU/L, total bilirubin at 0.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin at 0.1 mg/dL, gamma-glutamyltranspeptidase at 23 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase at 187 IU/L, glucose at 91 mg/dL, prothrombin time at 141% (0.87 INR), and activated partial thrombin time at 27.2 seconds. Serologic markers for hepatitis A, B, and C viruses, Epstein-Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus were negative. Ceruloplasmin, creatine kinase, and lactate dehydrogenase levels were normal. Liver sonogram indicated hepatomegaly with diffuse increased liver parenchymal echogenicity. Histologic examination of a liver biopsy revealed moderate macrovesicular fatty changes with periportal and perivenular fibrosis. Dietary history indicated a self-avoidance of sweetened foods and fruits.
test_results: The patient is a homozygote for a novel frame-shifting mutation c.[758_759insT]+[758_759insT] (p.[val253fsX24]+[val253fsX24]).

case_report: A two-week-old male infant was admitted to the Neonatology department presenting with swelling around the eyes and lower limbs, abdominal swelling, elevated body temperature, and poor weight gain. He was born at 34 weeks of gestation with a birth weight of 2300 g, a height of 43 cm, and a head circumference of 30 cm. His Apgar scores were 7 at the first minute and 8 at the fifth minute. The prenatal period was uneventful, and there was no notable family history. The weight of the placenta was not recorded. Upon admission, his weight remained 2300 g, and a right inguinal hernia was observed. Urinalysis indicated significant proteinuria (4+). Urinary sediment analysis showed 15-20 red blood cells and 10-12 white blood cells per high power field. Laboratory results revealed a red blood cell count of 4.4 x 10^12/mm3, a white blood cell count of 20900/mm3, hemoglobin level of 11.5 g/dL, platelet count of 155000/mm3, total serum proteins at 34 g/L, albumin at 17 g/L, creatinine at 101.4 µmol/L, urea at 11.4 mmol/L, cholesterol at 7.29 mmol/L, C-reactive protein at 120 mg/L, and procalcitonin at 1.03 ng/ml. The TORCH test was negative. A lumbar puncture revealed a high number of leukocytes, and the cerebrospinal fluid culture was positive for Klebsiella pneumoniae, which was treated for 21 days according to antibiogram results. An abdominal ultrasound showed enlarged, hyperechogenic kidneys with abnormal cortico-medullary differentiation. A cranial ultrasound did not reveal any pathological changes.
test_results: Genetic examination demonstrated two heterozygous pathogenic variants of NPHS1 gene: I. c.248 dupA (protein. Tyr 83*) in exon 2 and II. c.1048 T.C (protein: Ser 350Pro) in exon 9. Not any pathogenic variant were detected in other gene of the panel by sequencing (ACTN4, CD2AP, INF2, NPHS2, TRPC6, WT1).

case_report: A 20-year-old male with a history of neonatal bleeding tendency visited the otorhinolaryngology department for a preoperative evaluation for chronic maxillary sinusitis surgery. He reported a family history of easy bruising in his father and conductive hearing issues following childhood meningitis. Previous laboratory tests since birth showed no coagulation abnormalities. During the preoperative evaluation, his blood counts and serum chemistry were normal. Initial coagulation screening revealed prolonged prothrombin time (PT, 24.5 sec; normal 10.4-12.5 sec) and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT, 47.3 sec; normal 26.0-41.0 sec). Bleeding time was within normal limits (2 min and 30 sec; normal 1-5 min). PT and aPTT mixing test results suggested factor deficiency. Fibrinogen degradation product (FDP) and d-Dimer levels were normal. Other coagulation tests were also normal. Plasma fibrinogen activity measured by the Clauss method was below the detection limit (<25 mg/dL; normal 140-460 mg/dL), while the antigen level measured by fibrinogen ELISA was normal (437 mg/dL). A familial genetic study was initiated after obtaining written informed consent.
test_results: PCR and direct sequencing revealed that only the patient in his family was heterozygous for a point mutation in the FGG gene. The mutation was a mutation substituting the 310th codon ATG (Met) to ACG (Thr), (c.1007T>C).

case_report: A 10-year-old girl presented with patchy hair loss on the scalp for nearly a year. The initial lesion appeared a year ago, with rapid progression over the past six months. Her mother reported continuous development of new lesions and enlargement of older ones. There was no history of papules, pustules, or plaques before the hair loss. The patient had no other skin or systemic illnesses and no family history of alopecia. Cutaneous examination revealed an irregular but well-defined confluent patch of hair loss on the vertex, resembling a footprint in snow. The patch showed minimal atrophy and wrinkling, with shiny skin lacking follicular ostia and a few normal hair follicles within the lesion. The lesions were asymptomatic, with no inflammation, scaling, crusting, or follicular papulopustules.
