The hair pull test was positive, but there were no exclamation mark hairs or leukotrichia in the surrounding area. The rest of the facial and body hair were unaffected, and there were no other skin, mucosal, or nail abnormalities. Potassium hydroxide examination of adjacent hair was negative for tinea capitis. Trichoscopy revealed loss of follicular ostia, ivory white macules, and pigmentation in some areas.
test_results: The section showed atrophy of epidermis with the absence of viable pilosebaceous follicles, replaced by fibrosis. Fibrosis extended up to subcutaneous fat.

case_report: A 63-year-old female with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and type 2 diabetes was initially treated for breast cancer characterized by estrogen receptor (ER) positive, progesterone receptor (PR) negative, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER-2) negative, grade 3, T2N0M0. Treatment included lumpectomy and chemotherapy with doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, and paclitaxel. She experienced chemotherapy toxicity and was diagnosed with cirrhosis and portal hypertension, leading to discontinuation of chemotherapy. Due to a history of venous thromboembolism (VTE) and osteoporosis, she was not on adjuvant anti-endocrine therapy. Two years later, she had recurrent disease and metastasis, prompting a change in chemotherapy to fulvestrant and palbociclib. After five months, she developed cytopenia, resulting in the discontinuation of palbociclib. A positron emission tomography (PET) scan showed no new metastatic lesions and resolution of previous metabolically active lesions. Eighteen days later, she presented to the ER with generalized weakness. She reported a two-week history of severe diarrheal illness, nausea, and vomiting, which had resolved by the time of ER presentation. Physical examination revealed bilateral muscle weakness and hyporeflexia in both upper and lower extremities, with the weakness being symmetric and more pronounced in the distal regions, particularly the ankles and hands.
test_results: MRI lumbar spine showed abnormal enhancement involving multiple cauda equina nerve roots. Antibody testing for autoimmune and paraneoplastic causes was negative.
diagnosis: Guillain-Barré syndrome  / acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy

case_report: C.P. is a 61-year-old right-handed man who was evaluated in August 2015 after experiencing a 3-year history of increasing difficulties with perceiving objects and judging distances, particularly while driving and cycling. He also reported challenges with dressing, reading, calculating, and finding words. Additionally, his wife noted that he had been tripping over his words for over a year, although his comprehension remained unaffected. Neuropsychological assessment at that time showed a Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score of 24 out of 30. There were some impairments in recognition memory for visual material, with scores in the 25th percentile for words and below the 5th percentile for faces. Visuospatial and visuoperceptual functions were also affected, with scores below the 5th percentile in the Visual and Object Space Perception Battery for fragmented letters and position discrimination. The medical examination did not reveal any neurological or other significant findings.
test_results: An MRI scan showed marked biparietal atrophy. CSF evidence consistent with AD pathology: total tau = 296; A beta1–42 = 311; ratio = 0.95, p-tau = 33.

case_report: A 43-year-old Caucasian male presented to the emergency department with a headache and weakness in the left limbs. The patient reported no prior medical history and denied any recent neck trauma. The only noted cardiovascular risk factor was a history of tobacco smoking for a decade. Neurological examination showed verbal aphasia and left-sided hemiparesis.
test_results: During CT angiography of the neck and head, segmental dissections of the right internal carotid artery (ICA) at the level of the cranial basis were discovered. The lumen of the ICA was decreased to 4 × 2.5 mm (60 % of normal flow). Cerebral CT showed a recent infarction involving the medial part of the right temporal lobe and deep structures of the right hemisphere including the thalamus, the genu and the posterior limb of the internal capsule. CT angiography of the neck and head also showed a duplication of the left vertebral artery (LVA) with two origins, both from the left subclavian artery. The duplicated segments were fused at level of the C5–6 vertebrae into a single vertebral artery, which then entered the transverse foramen of C5. The first LVA originated from the left subclavian artery at a distance of 7 mm from the aortic arch. It measured 2.9 and 2.8 mm in diameter at the points of origin and just before fusion, respectively. The course of the artery was 101 mm. The second LVA arose from the left subclavian artery 37 mm distal to the first (44 mm from the aortic arch). It measured 2.4 and 2.2 mm in diameter at the points of origin and just before fusion, respectively, and its course was 89 mm. Both vertebral arteries possessed a regular lumen. The diameter of the LVA after fusion was 3.3 mm (at level C5–6). The right VA arose as the first branch from the left subclavian artery, 43 mm from the aortic arch. Its course was normal. The diameters of the right VA were 4 mm at the points of origin and 3.8 mm at the C5–C6 vertebrae. Both thyrocervical trunks were seen to originate separately from the subclavian arteries. Additionally, complementary but independent to CT angiography Doppler Sonography B-flow mode of the vertebral arteries also revealed a duplicated LVA.

case_report: A 35-year-old female with a long-standing history of chronic proteinuria since early childhood was evaluated due to end-stage kidney disease. She had no family history of chronic renal disease. At 5 years old, she exhibited proteinuria of 2.9 g/day and was treated with meprednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 12 weeks, followed by a tapering regimen, without improvement. At 9 years old, with proteinuria of 3.9 g/day and normal kidney function without nephrotic syndrome, she underwent her first kidney biopsy. She was placed on a low-protein and low-sodium diet and given enalapril 5 mg twice daily. The biopsy showed focal and segmental glomerulosclerosis with minimal interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy. Various immunosuppressive treatments, including steroids, cyclophosphamide, cyclosporine, and tacrolimus, were administered over the years, but none succeeded in reducing proteinuria, which progressively worsened into adulthood. At 29 years old, with a glomerular filtration rate of 55 mL/min and proteinuria of 6 g/day, a second biopsy was performed. This biopsy revealed 8 obliterated glomeruli, focal and segmental glomerulosclerosis with segmental hyalinosis of the glomerular tuft in the remaining 9 glomeruli, and 40% interstitial fibrosis. At 34 years old, she was referred to our clinic for a second opinion regarding a kidney transplant, which had been recommended at another hospital, where plasmapheresis was planned as part of the induction therapy, with her father as the potential donor.
test_results: The genetic study informed that the patient was heterozygous for LMX1B c.737G > A, p. (Arg246Gln), which was classified as pathogenic.

case_report: A 44-year-old Japanese woman underwent a routine health check at her local hospital. An ultrasound scan identified a lesion resembling a uterine myoma, measuring 5.9 cm in diameter. Upon a follow-up examination 12 months later, the lesion had approximately doubled in size. The patient was then referred to our clinic for further evaluation. Initial internal examination revealed an enlarged uterus comparable to the size of a newborn's head, with unremarkable cervical and vaginal discharge. The adnexa were not palpable on either side. Blood test results were within normal limits. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed an isoechoic solid mass with an indistinct boundary between the lesion and the uterus. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right pelvic cavity revealed a tumor measuring 110 × 90 × 80 mm, displaying a slightly lobular pattern with smooth margins. The internal mass had a density similar to that of myometrium on T1-weighted MRI and a low density on T2-weighted MRI in the horizontal plane. Several flow void regions were observed between the lesion and the uterus. The right ovary was not identifiable, while the left ovary appeared normal. A laparoscopic myomectomy was planned based on a preliminary clinical assessment. Laparoscopic findings showed a 10-cm right ovarian mass without intra-abdominal adhesion or tumor rupture. The uterus and left appendages were of normal size. A laparoscopic right adnexectomy was performed. The ascitic fluid was serous, and cytological evaluation was negative. Macroscopically, the tumor's cut surface was homogeneous and solid with a yellowish-white pigment, and there was no necrosis or hemorrhage within the tumor.
test_results: The tumor cells consisted of dense cellular proliferations of spindle fibroblast-like cells, arranged in a fascicular structure, without significant cytological atypia. In addition, a portion of the tumor cells proliferated in a trabecular pattern and a collagen band was distributed around the stroma. The tumor was composed of cells with ovoid to spindle-shaped nuclei and a scant cytoplasm. Some of the nuclei had a nuclear groove. No severe cytological atypia was detected. The mitotic activity index was estimated at >15 mitotic figures per 10 high-power fields. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for vimentin, muscle-specific actin, alpha-smooth muscle actin, alpha-inhibin and progesterone receptor, and negative for calretinin, epithelial membrane antigen, desmin, estrogen receptor, CD10, CD99, chromogranin A, synaptophysin and tumor protein p53. The Ki-67/MIB-1 labeling index was 9.5 %. Reticulin staining showed reticular fibers surrounding each cell. We further analyzed genomic DNA (isolated from formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tumor tissue sections) for a FOXL2 c.402C > G (p.C134W) point mutation. The FOXL2 mutation was absent from our case and the negative control.
diagnosis: Mitotically Active Cellular Fibroma  of the ovary

case_report: Patient V is a 6-year-old girl from Sardinia. Her birth was without complications, but she later experienced difficulties with feeding. Her motor development was somewhat delayed, though she was able to walk by 18 months. She also exhibited a mild delay in speech. By the age of 3, she was noted to be very clumsy and exhibited low muscle tone. A neurological examination at 5 years old showed a characteristic facial appearance with a triangular mouth and divergent strabismus in the right eye. She had both proximal and distal muscle weakness, along with joint hyperlaxity in her hands. Her tendon reflexes were diminished. She could rise from the floor using the Gowers maneuver and was unable to run or jump. Additional findings included flat feet and mild scoliosis. Nerve conduction studies were normal, and electromyography indicated myopathic damage. Her creatine kinase levels were slightly elevated at 200 U/L.
test_results: Her muscle biopsy showed a great variability in fiber diameter, an increase of connective-adipose tissue, the presence of several central nuclei and rare necklace fibers. An asymmetric pattern was observed in the MRI with the tibialis anterior and soleus affected on the left side. The de novo missense variant identified in patient V results in a reduction of the protein expression.

case_report: A 41-year-old male presented with warty lesions. The lesions appeared 3 months prior and measured between 1–2.5 cm, located on both sides of the groin. The patient reported no discharge, burning, or itching, and no pustules or ulcers before the lesions appeared. Multiple sessions of cryotherapy were administered without success. Human papillomavirus (HPV) polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing showed no evidence of HPV DNA. Upon referral to a dermatologist, a body examination revealed hyperpigmented, purple macules and papules in the axillary area, which were asymptomatic. Additionally, an oral examination identified a few small mucosal erosions that developed after the inguinal lesions.
test_results: Pathology evaluation showed focal areas of suprabasal clefts containing a few acantholytic cells along with eosinophils. In addition, hyperkeratosis with focal parakeratosis along with marked acanthosis and spongiosis associated with some eosinophilic microabscess in the epidermis and hair follicles were observed. Direct immunofluorescence evaluation confirmed the intercellular deposition of IgG within the lower epidermis.

case_report: A 54-year-old female patient was born to non-related healthy parents. The perinatal clinical history was not available. The patient has a first-degree maternal male cousin with intellectual disability and cleft lip palate. Other family history is unremarkable. Since childhood, the patient has had several conditions: an umbilical hernia (surgically corrected), several periodontal infections, proneness to tooth loss, scoliosis (treated only with physical therapy), anemia, dysmenorrhea, learning difficulty (as reported by herself), and left eye refractive error. At 50 years of age, the patient underwent a hysterectomy for endometriosis. Before this procedure, she was never pregnant by her own decision and has no children. At 51 years old, visual acuity evaluation showed that the left (before and after the cover test: 20/200, 20/80, respectively) and right eye (before and after the cover test: 20/25, 20/20, respectively) had refractive defects, with the latter more affected. Ophthalmology evaluation revealed hypertelorism, rotational nystagmus, and strabismus (endotrophic left eye). At 53 years old, the patient attended a physical examination by clinical genetics for the first time, revealing brachycephaly, flat occiput, midface hypoplasia, wide nasal bridge, bifid nasal tip (surgically corrected), hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, high-arched palate, dental crowding, severe pectus excavatum, unilateral breast hypoplasia, brachydactyly, a low-set fifth finger of the right hand with hypoplastic metacarpal, and a single left transverse palmar crease. The patient did not have longitudinal ridging and splitting of nails. A three-dimensional computed tomography scan (3D-CT) of the skull showed coronal craniosynostosis, sinusoidal nasal septum with a large right bone spur, mucosal thickening of the maxillary and ethmoidal sinuses, lack of pneumatization and poor development of frontal sinuses, and left parietal bone prominence. Thorax CT confirmed the presence of pectus excavatum. Cranial tomography showed no nervous system alterations, an echocardiogram test was within normal range and renal echography did not show renal involvement. Uterine defects were not possible to study given the hysterectomy procedure performed on the patient, and other alterations such as bifid uvula were not noticed during the physical examination. Karyotype results showed a karyotype 46, XX and no chromosomal abnormalities. Despite her learning difficulty (as reported by herself), she went to college and has a bachelor’s degree in education. Furthermore, during the interview normal intelligence was noticed, however, a formal IQ evaluation was not done. Her height was 162 cm (42nd percentile) and her weight was 54 kg (30th percentile). The patient reported that about 5 years before the evaluation by clinical genetics, chronic pain in the left hemibody started and is treated to date with physical therapy.
test_results: The test revealed the heterozygous variant c.374A>C (p.Glu125Ala) in the EFNB1 gene (OMIM: 300035) classified as probably pathogenic according to the College of Medical Genetics and Genomics ACMG criteria. This variant has been reported neither in the literature nor in the Clinvar, gnomAD, 1,000 genomes, or HGMD databases. This variant is predicted to be deleterious by SIFT (0), and probably damaging by Polyphen2 (0.99). Its DANN and CADD scores are 0.99 and 27.1, respectively.

case_report: A 47-year-old woman visited our clinic with a 6-year history of non-painful red papules on her trunk and limbs. Initially, the lesions appeared on her right leg and healed on their own, leaving behind atrophic scars. Over the next 5 years, similar lesions gradually spread across her body. At 46, she experienced a 2-hour episode of reduced visual field in her right eye. Two months later, she reported numbness in her right calf and a painless decrease in vision along with permanent visual field constriction in her right eye, prompting her to seek medical advice. Physical examination of the skin revealed multiple, round and linear, atrophic white papules measuring 5-10mm in diameter on the trunk and limbs, some with a red telangiectatic border. Neurologic examination showed reduced sensation and muscle weakness in the right calf. Examination of the cranial nerves indicated impairment of the abducent and optic nerves, leading to weakened movement on the right side, visual deterioration, and visual field constriction in the right eye. Tendon reflexes were normal, and Babinski signs were negative.
test_results: Histopathology revealed central epidermal atrophy, papillary dermal sclerosis, and perivascular lymphocytic inflammatory cell infiltrates, in addition to vascular thrombosis. Visual evoked potential showed the optic nerve was damaged. Electromyologram (EMG) showed right quadriceps femoris neurogenic damage.

case_report: A 28-year-old male patient presented with distinct facial features including a long and narrow nose, small teeth with enamel hypoplasia, and a high arched palate. He is the only child of his parents. At birth, he had bilateral syndactyly of the fourth and fifth fingers, which was surgically corrected. His toes were normal. The corneal diameters measured 9.51 mm in the right eye (OD) and 9.56 mm in the left eye (OS), indicating microcornea in both eyes. His best-corrected visual acuity was 1.0 in both eyes. The refractive error was −6.0 + 3.0 × 90 in the right eye and −5.0 + 2.5 × 70 in the left eye. Axial lengths were 22.63 mm (OD) and 22.49 mm (OS). Corneal thickness was 542 μm (OD) and 544 μm (OS). Intraocular pressure was 14 mmHg in both eyes. The optic nerve head appeared healthy in both eyes. The anterior chamber depth was 2.34 mm (OD) and 2.26 mm (OS), with an anterior chamber angle of 23.8–26.7 degrees (OD) and 22.9–25.4 degrees (OS), indicating a shallow anterior chamber with a narrow angle. Gonioscopy confirmed a narrow angle, reaching up to Schaffer Grade III. The ocular fundus was normal in both eyes. The patient's parents did not exhibit any similar symptoms. The father had no refractive errors, while the mother had moderate myopia (spherical equivalent [SE] −6.0 D in OD/−4.5 D in OS). The maternal grandfather had high myopia (SE −18.0 D in OD and −20.0 D in OS).
test_results: Sequence analysis detected a pathogenic heterozygous missense mutation, c.413G>A, p. Gly138Asp in the cytoplasmic loop of connexin 43 protein.

case_report: Patient 4, an 8-month-old girl born at full term via natural delivery, was referred to the hospital due to developmental delay. Clinical examination revealed a slow pupillary light reflex, reduced reflexes, and decreased muscle tone in all limbs. Cerebral MRI showed widened ventricles, cisterns, and sulci. EEG results were normal.
test_results: Urinary organic acid analysis showed an increased excretion of GHB. A compound heterozygous mutation of c.1344-2delA/c.1529C > T was identified in exons 9 and 10 in this girl. The mutation c.1344-2delA located in the intron splice site, and p.S510F (c.1529C > T) belongs to the NAD-binding domain.

case_report: A 37-year-old male, living with HIV since 2012 and on stable combination antiretroviral therapy (lamivudine + tenofovir + efavirenz), with an undetectable HIV-1 RNA plasma viral load since the beginning of treatment, presented with symptoms that began 3 days prior. These symptoms included a night fever of 38.5 °C, chills, and generalized muscle pain. His last CD4-positive cell count was 604 (41%) in December 2021. He also reported a burning sensation in the urethra during urination. The following morning, he noticed small papules/vesicles on an erythematous base located on the glans and scrotal sac. Additionally, five other small lesions were observed on his forehead, nose, thorax, and left leg. These lesions were mildly painful and non-pruritic. Initially, he was seen by a urologist who ordered tests for sexually transmitted infections and prescribed doxycycline (100 mg bid for 10 days) and ceftriaxone (1 g IM, single dose). He began this treatment and scheduled a follow-up visit with an infectious disease specialist. The patient has been in a stable relationship with the same partner for over 15 years. He recently returned from a business trip to Europe (Italy) 22 days before the onset of symptoms. He denied close contact with others during the trip but mentioned receiving oral sex from an occasional partner 14 days before symptom onset. He had no information on the health status of this partner, who is known to travel frequently. The patient does not use psychoactive substances, consumes alcohol moderately, and has never smoked. During the medical evaluation, he was in good clinical condition with a normal temperature. The described lesions were present, some of which were ulcerated but showed no signs of bacterial infection or crusts. Physical examination revealed lymphadenopathy, with enlarged and tender inguinal lymph nodes, the largest measuring 1.2 × 0.5 cm.
test_results: The PCR was carried out at the Laboratório de Pesquisa em Infectologia (LAPI), at Hospital Universitário Professor Edgard Santos, Federal University of Bahia.

case_report: A 26-day-old female infant was brought to the department due to ongoing vomiting, which initially was non-bilious but turned bilious over the past 2 days. She was born via caesarean section at 33 weeks of gestation to unrelated parents, with a birth weight of 2.25 kg. Her parents had previously sought medical attention 2 weeks earlier for the persistent non-bilious vomiting, and she received supportive care, which did not alleviate the symptoms. Upon examination, the infant exhibited signs of dehydration and failure to thrive, with a current weight of 1.6 kg. Her abdomen was distended but non-tender.
test_results: A hugely dilated stomach with secondary reflux up to the level of the cervical oesophagus and malrotation, where the duodenojejunal flexure was positioned in the right midabdomen.

case_report: A 79-year-old male was admitted to the hospital in June 2018 due to an elevated white blood cell count (38 x 10^3/µL; lymphocytes 84%, neutrophils 16%). The patient had a history of ischemic heart disease and exhibited small superficial lymph nodes (<1–2 cm) in the bilateral neck, axillary, and inguinal regions. Bone marrow aspirate revealed extensive lymphoid infiltration, primarily consisting of small 'mature' lymphocytes with very rare nucleoli, accounting for approximately half of the total cells. A CT scan identified multiple abdominal lymph nodes.
test_results: FCM immunophenotyping of both PB and BM aspirates showed the presence (50% and 60%, respectively, on all nucleated cells) of sCD3-, cyCD3+, CD8-, CD2+, CD7+, CD5+, CD4+, CD56-, CD57-, CD16-, HLA-DR-, CD34-, CD1a-, TdT-, CD10-, TCRαβ- and TCRγδ- pathological T cells; the 75% of these cells expressed CD45 on their membrane. These T-cells were mixed with a small population of clonal B lymphocytes (3,1% of leukocytes in PB, 2.2% of all nucleated cells in BM), that expressed CD19, CD5, CD20 (dim), CD23, CD43, CD200, sIgkappa (dim). Trephine BM biopsy showed two nodular aggregates of small and sometimes medium-sized lymphoid elements with predominantly T phenotype (CD57-, CD8-, CD5+, CD3+, CD4+, CD56-), mixed with rare CD20+, CD79α+ small B lymphocytes. FISH analysis, performed on unpurified nuclei, documented ATM and 13q14.3 deletions in 50% of cells, while 36% only displayed ATM deletion. A second FISH performed on purified CD19+ cells showed only the deletion of chromosome 13q14.3. IGHV sequences showed an unmutated status. Molecular analysis highlighted no mutations for both the exon 16 of the STAT5b gene and the exon 21 of the STAT3 gene.
diagnosis: T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia , small cell variant

case_report: A 9-year-old girl was admitted to the Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital with recurrent epileptic seizures. The symptoms first appeared 3 years ago, including vigorous limb spasms, foaming at the mouth, locked jaw, rolled eyes, and loss of consciousness. Each episode lasted about 20 minutes and resolved on its own without incontinence or prodromal symptoms. Similar episodes recurred a total of 5 times. Physical examination revealed short stature (height 119 cm, −2SD to −3SD), round face, brachydactyly with short metacarpals, positive metacarpal sign, and mild mental retardation. Her weight was 26.5 kg (−1SD to median), not meeting the criteria for obesity. Family history indicated that her parents and younger brother were normal, except her mother had short stature. Laboratory tests showed hypocalcemia (1.45 mmol/L [2.20–2.70]), hyperphosphatemia (2.74 mmol/L [0.8–1.6]), elevated serum PTH (671.9 ng/L [15.0–65.0]), and decreased 24-hour urinary calcium and phosphorus (0.141 mmol and 0.846 mmol respectively, [2.5–7.5] and [2.10–8.19], respectively). Additionally, there was a slight elevation in plasma TSH (6.24 mIU/L [0.35–4.94]) with normal thyroid hormone levels (TT3 1.04 ng/mL [0.57–1.59]; TT4 5.36 μg/dL [4.87–11.72]; FT3 2.95 pg/mL [1.71–3.71]; FT4 1.06 ng/dL [0.70–1.48]), and a moderately elevated thyroperoxidase antibody level of 251.35 IU/mL ([0.00–5.61]). Levels of follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, growth hormone, and IGF-1 were normal. X-ray of the hands showed short 4th and 5th metacarpals on the left hand and short 3rd, 4th, and 5th metacarpals on the right hand. Cranial computed tomography scan revealed bilateral calcifications in various regions of the cerebrum and cerebellum, particularly in the basal ganglia.
test_results: A novel heterozygous 1-base pair (bp) deletion in exon 4 (c.313delG) was found in the proband and her mother. The deletion of this nucleotide sequence is predicted to cause a frameshift mutation and might lead to a premature stop codon in the new frame, thus producing truncated gene products (p.Glu105Lysfs∗7). The mutation was absent in the unaffected family members, including the patient's father and her brother, thereby indicating that the mutation is on the maternal allele.

case_report: In July 2010, a 53-year-old woman with no significant neurologic history experienced a single convulsion. Four months later, she experienced two similar convulsions, quickly progressing to status epilepticus. She was treated at an outside institution and recovered full function and returned to work. Initial MR imaging at that time was reported as normal. Despite AED treatment, she continued to have focal seizures, characterized by clonic jerks of the right face. Over the next year, her seizures increased in both frequency and semiology, involving the right arm as well as language. Admission to an outside epilepsy monitoring unit (EMU) revealed both electroclinical (semiology of right face/arm movements) and purely electrographic seizures arising from the left frontal region in the context of minimal responsiveness, consistent with focal status epilepticus. She was again treated for status epilepticus and discharged on AED polytherapy: phenytoin, valproic acid, levetiracetam, and oxcarbazepine. As her epilepsy became more refractory, a very extensive etiologic work-up was performed at an outside institution, approximately 2 years from epilepsy onset.
test_results: MRI demonstrated a left parietal FLAIR hyperintensity with mild associated volume loss. Admission to an outside epilepsy monitoring unit (EMU) revealed both electroclinical (semiology of right face/arm movements) and purely electrographic seizures arising from the left frontal region in the context of minimal responsiveness, consistent with focal status epilepticus. Brain PET imaging performed showed overall left hemisphere hypometabolism, with areas of increased metabolism in the left frontal, parietal, and occipital regions. Extensive serum and CSF studies, notably paraneoplastic and autoimmune encephalitis antibody testing as well as genetic testing for CADASIL and MELAS were also negative. The biopsy showed only mild gliosis and rare T lymphocytes, without evidence of vasculitis, microglial nodules, or viral cytopathic changes.

case_report: A 46-year-old Caucasian woman visited the Haematology Outpatient Department with an itchy rash covering her body. She had previously been seen by an infectious diseases specialist who considered a scabies-related rash. The patient described itchy, red, blister-like lesions that had developed over the past 14 days. Due to scratching, the blisters had turned into crusts. She reported no signs of infection, no fevers, chills, or other systemic symptoms, and denied insect bites or close contact with domestic animals. She was not on any medication except for ibrutinib, which she had been taking for 18 months. She recalled receiving a thimerosal-containing influenza vaccination 10 days before the skin lesions appeared. She had no history of similar rashes. The patient had a history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and had undergone allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) in 2017. She was taking ibrutinib for a persistent CLL clone with bone marrow infiltration of 5%. More than three years post-allo-HSCT, she presented for an additional outpatient visit due to the itchy rash. There was no personal or family history of similar conditions. On examination, she was afebrile. She had papulonodular, crusted skin eruptions (2-3 mm in diameter) on her neck, back, arms, and legs. A painful, enlarged lymph node (3 cm in diameter) was palpable under her left armpit, the same side where she received the influenza vaccination. Her white blood cell count and absolute eosinophil count were within normal ranges (7.94 × 10^9/L and 0.27 × 10^9/L, respectively). Serological and PCR-based tests ruled out reactivation of herpes simplex virus 1 and 2, varicella zoster virus, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus.
test_results: The skin biopsy from the right thigh revealed irregular acanthosis of the epidermis, associated with diffuse superficial and deep perivascular and interstitial inflammatory cell infiltrates composed predominantly of eosinophilic granulocytes admixed with lymphocytes and histiocytes. The inflammatory cell infiltration extended into the septa and lobuli of the subcutaneous fatty tissue.

case_report: A 52-year-old woman with a history of multiple myeloma (IgA/k, ISS stage III), arterial hypertension, and depressive syndrome was admitted to the hospital. Bone marrow biopsy showed 70% monotypic plasma cell infiltration with CD138+, CD38+, CD20+, and PAX5+ markers. FISH analysis was positive for t(11;14) in 95% of nuclei and negative for del17p, gain1q, t(4;14), t(14;16), and t(14;20). Molecular analysis revealed a TP53 mutation (exon 5). At the start of induction therapy with Daratumumab, Bortezomib, Thalidomide, and Dexamethasone, blood counts indicated ≥5% circulating plasma cells and pancytopenia. Prophylactic low-dose aspirin (100 mg/dL) was administered. The patient was hospitalized the next day for severe epistaxis, leading to the discontinuation of aspirin and Thalidomide. Admission lab results showed Hb 6.4 g/dL, WBC 2.04/mm3 with ANC 1080/mm3, circulating plasma cells 6%, platelets 46,000/mm3, creatinine 0.92 mg/dL, calcium 8.7 mg/dL, AST 24 U/L, ALT 12 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL (direct 0.4 mg/dL), γGT 43 U/L, ALP 174 U/L, LDH 76 U/L, total serum protein 11.4 g/dL, serum M-protein 3.6 g/dL, IgG 397 mg/dL, IgA 7196 mg/dL, IgM 26 mg/dL, serum free light chains (sFLC) k/λ 930.65/6.53, ratio 142.159, NT-proBNP 8522 pg/mL (nv 0–125 pg/mL), PT ratio 1.5, PTT 34.9 s, AT 65%, and fibrinogen 119 mg/dL. No prior coagulation profile data were available. A total body CT scan showed multiple osteolytic lesions and hepatosplenomegaly (spleen diameter 15.5 cm; liver right lobe diameter 25 cm) without significant lymphadenopathies. Attempts to cauterize a bleeding varix in the left nostril were unsuccessful, necessitating repeated nasal tamponade over 5 days. Fresh frozen plasma (15–20 mL/kg daily), platelet transfusions (2 to 3 units per week), and tranexamic acid (1000 mg IV TID) were administered to manage coagulopathy, but bleeding persisted. Daily packed red cell transfusions were required due to severe anemia. Despite extensive FFP infusion, PT ratio remained prolonged (1.5–1.7) with corrected fibrinogen levels. A 3-day course of IV vitamin K did not correct the PT.
test_results: A PT mixing test indicated a corrected result. FVII level turned out to be low at 22%.

case_report: A 60-year-old male presented with worsening difficulty in breathing and swallowing solids over one week. He also reported a six-month history of hoarseness, occasional blood-stained sputum, weight loss, and reduced appetite. He had a 20-year history of smoking but did not consume alcohol. He had no known medical conditions or family history of cancer. Physical examination showed a cachectic appearance and inspiratory stridor. Flexible nasoendoscopy revealed an exophytic growth on the laryngeal surface of the epiglottis, which prolapsed into the laryngeal inlet during inspiration, causing a ball-valve type obstruction and obstructing the view of the vocal cords. No palpable cervical lymph nodes were detected, and the rest of the ear, nose, and throat examinations were normal. A CT scan of the neck and thorax showed a soft tissue mass in the anterior epiglottis measuring 2.7 x 2.2 x 2.5 cm, extending to the base of the epiglottis, with bilateral cervical lymph nodes at levels Ib and II, the largest being 1.2 x 0.8 cm. The patient underwent a tracheostomy under local anesthesia due to the risk of airway obstruction. Tumor debulking was performed, followed by direct laryngoscopy, which confirmed that the mass was confined to the epiglottis without affecting the vocal cords, arytenoid cartilages, or pyriform fossa.
test_results: Microscopy demonstrated islands and clusters of malignant basaloid looking cells with coarse chromatin pattern, numerous mitotic figures, and apoptotic bodies. Some cells showed presence of intercellular bridging denoting squamous differentiation. Immunohistochemically, the cells were positive for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), neuron-specific enolase (NSE); and negative for chromogranin and synaptophysin.
Orpha_name: Squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus

case_report: A 62-year-old woman presented to the dermatology out-patient department with a single painful, red, elevated lesion covered with pustules on the left breast, persisting for 6 months. There was no history of systemic involvement, fever, drug intake, eye or mucosal complaints, similar past or family illness, or topical application. Examination revealed a single well-defined polycyclic erythematous plaque, 6 × 7 cm in size, with pustules mainly at the periphery on the left breast. KOH mount for fungus was negative. She was treated with oral Fluconazole 150 mg once a week and terbinafine cream applied locally twice daily for 2 weeks. At the 2-week follow-up, there was no improvement; the lesion had progressed to involve the entire left breast, forming a single well-defined moist, verrucous vegetating plaque, 8 × 10 cm in size, with multiple pustules, yellow to brown crusts, and some raw oozy areas, surrounded by a broad rim of erythema. A similar verrucous lesion developed in the left groin at the subsequent 2-week follow-up. The rest of the mucocutaneous examination was normal. Nikolsky's sign was negative. Tzanck smear showed eosinophils but no acantholytic cells. Gram stain for bacteria revealed a mixed inflammatory infiltrate with eosinophil predominance, and acid-fast bacteria staining was negative. Pus culture from the pustule was sterile. Routine laboratory studies, including complete blood count, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, liver and renal function tests, and chest X-ray, were all within normal limits. Human immunodeficiency virus serology was negative. There was no evidence of inflammatory bowel disease.
test_results: Histopathological examination showed suprabasal cleft with acantholytic cells, numerous eosinophils, intraepidermal eosinophilic abscesses, and dense inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) revealed intercellular Immunoglobulin G (IgG) deposits in the epidermis.

case_report: A 6-year-old boy presented to the pediatric outpatient clinic with episodes of unilateral hemifacial flushing and sweating that occurred within minutes during or after physical exercise or exposure to heat. These episodes had been happening for the past 2 years without any change in severity. His birth history was normal, and he had no history of trauma or surgery. He was not on any medications, and there was no family history of similar symptoms. Neurological examination revealed normal findings, including normal pupil responses, cranial nerve functions, and muscle stretch reflexes. The rest of the systemic examination was unremarkable. Blood pressure and heart rate were normal, and no asymmetric flushing or sweating was observed at rest. Electrocardiographic findings were normal. Laboratory tests showed normal white blood count, hemoglobin levels, glucose levels, electrolyte levels, and renal, liver, and thyroid function.
test_results: After exercise-induced sweating, there was pale and nearly complete anhidrosis on the right side of the face with compensatory hyperhidrosis and flushing on the opposite side with sharp demarcation. The oil-paper firmly stuck to the left side of the patient's face owing to sweating, but immediately slipped off the right side of his face. He had mild anisocoria. The right pupil was 1.5 mm in size, while the left pupil was 2.5 mm in size; no ptosis, miosis, or enophthalmos was noted, and both pupils responded normally to light and accommodation. No evidence of Horner's syndrome. No abnormalities were noted in the cerebrum and cervicothoracic spinal cord.

case_report: A 13-year-old Caucasian girl was referred for a comprehensive clinical examination. The evaluation included visual acuity testing, ophthalmoscopic assessment, structural OCT, and both photopic and scotopic ERG. Autofluorescence imaging of both eyes revealed a hyperautofluorescent halo around the fovea, extending 360°. Her best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was measured at 75 letters on the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) chart in the right eye and 60 letters in the left eye. OCT imaging showed deformation of the retinal profile and the presence of cystic spaces in both eyes. This condition was described as 'schisis at an early stage.'
test_results: ERG showed non-recordable rod response, and reduced maximal and cone responses with a decreased b-wave to a-wave ratio. Responses to 30 Hz flicker were reduced and delayed. S-cone-mediated ERGs were recorded in response to a blue (420 nm) stimulus of 30 degrees flickered at 4 Hz and presented on a steady yellow background. ML-cone-mediated ERGs were obtained in response to a red (580 nm) stimulus of 30 degrees flickering at 4 Hz and presented on a steady blue (420 nm) background. Blue and red stimuli were photopically matched. In this particular patient, S-cone ERG was of larger amplitude (1.2 times) compared to ML cone. The peak times of both responses were comparable. Genetic analysis showed two variants in NR2E3 (NM_014249.3): a missense variation c.1118T>C, which leads to substitution of leucine with proline in amino acid position 373, and c.349+5G>C, which involves a gene sequence near a splicing site.

case_report: A 46-month-old male patient with a history of recurrent bronchiolitis, inability to walk, inability to speak, and seizures presented to the clinic with respiratory distress. Physical examination showed delayed neuromotor development, fever, and rales and rhonchi on lung auscultation. The parents were second cousins. Laboratory results were: WBC: 3320 /mm3, ANC: 2870/mm3, ALC: 130/mm3, Hb: 11.4 g/dL, PLT: 284000/mm3, UA: 0.6 mg/dL, IgG: 741 mg/dL, IgA: 28 mg/dL, IgM: 38 mg/dL, LP: CD3 4.2%, CD19 0.46%, CD4 2.2%, CD8 2.7%, CD3-CD16/56 90%, CD3 HLA DR 2.4%. CMV viral load (DNA quantitative) was 3311 IU/mL. Respiratory virus panel indicated influenza, and stool examination showed rotavirus. During ICU hospitalization, tracheal aspirate culture and skin lesion tissue fungal examination revealed Candida albicans. HRCT indicated bronchiolitis obliterans. Anemia developed during follow-up, and a direct Coombs test was (+++). Resistant convulsions occurred during follow-up. Cranial computed tomography showed cerebral and cerebellar atrophy and deepening of cerebral sulci. A fully suitable HSCT from the father was planned, but the patient was lost before it could be performed due to resistant fever, septic shock, and multiorgan failure despite multiple antibiotherapy, antifungal, and antiviral treatments.
test_results: A homozygous p.R58X stop codon mutation was found in the patient, and the parents were found to have heterozygous c.172 C>T (p.Arg58Ter) mutations.

case_report: The patient, a 27-year-old pregnant woman, was referred to the Maternal Fetal Medicine (MFM) clinic due to a history of obesity and chronic renal disease following a kidney transplant. At 16 weeks and 1 day of gestation, an ultrasound revealed severe oligohydramnios. Due to low amniotic fluid, maternal body habitus, and early gestational age, the bladder and fetal kidneys were not clearly visible. The patient reported no symptoms of vaginal fluid loss and had no known exposure to teratogens or relevant medications. Her medical history included being induced near term due to early prenatal anhydramnios, which later normalized, and a diagnosis of a solitary dysplastic left kidney. She also had a right ureteropelvic junction obstruction and progressive segmental sclerosis, leading to end-stage renal disease at 20 years old, necessitating a kidney transplant the previous year. A three-generation pedigree was reviewed. The patient was the second child of a non-consanguineous couple of Irish and French-Canadian descent. Her older sibling had three healthy children and terminated a pregnancy with an isolated hypoplastic left heart. Her partner is one of three healthy siblings of English and Dutch background. A follow-up ultrasound at 18 weeks and 5 days gestation again showed severe oligohydramnios with a maximum vertical pocket of 1.1 cm. The bladder was visualized, but the kidneys and renal arteries were not clearly seen. No anomalies were identified, and growth was adequate for the gestational age. The couple was informed about the likely poor perinatal prognosis due to severe oligohydramnios and its association with pulmonary hypoplasia. Prenatal investigation options and pregnancy termination with early induction, postnatal autopsy, and testing were discussed. The couple chose to continue with the pregnancy, understanding the high likelihood of poor perinatal outcomes and the need for close follow-up. At 21 weeks gestation, a repeat ultrasound showed the fetal kidney and renal artery, which appeared grossly normal but smaller in size. Subsequent biweekly ultrasounds showed gradual improvement in fluid levels.
test_results: The CAKUT next-generation sequencing panel revealed a pathogenic variant involving the PAX2 gene described as c.76dup: p. Val26Glyfs*28: NM_003990.4.

case_report: A 43-year-old male reported a gradual decline in visual function over the past seven years. He did not experience other ocular symptoms such as nystagmus or photophobia. His medical history indicated stable vision of 20/40 following an eye injury at age 14. No systemic abnormalities or malformations were noted. At the initial visit, his best-corrected vision was 20/400 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye, with intraocular pressures of 25 mmHg in the right eye and 23 mmHg in the left eye. Slit lamp examination revealed a diffuse haze with a flaky stromal pattern across the entire cornea. The right eye showed decreased vision and denser homogenous opacities compared to the left eye. Family history indicated that corneal changes were observed only in the patient's mother at age 69, with no other family members reporting similar issues. The patient's father had no reported ophthalmic abnormalities before his death, and his mother had diffuse corneal opacities of unknown cause in both eyes, experiencing decreased vision since childhood without significant impact on daily life. The patient's siblings had no symptoms or ophthalmic/systemic abnormalities. No other relatives were known to have eye problems. Slit lamp examination of the right eye showed normal endothelium and Descemet's membrane, with no gross abnormalities like Haab's striae or features of posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy. Previous medical records indicated normal endothelial cell shape and count in both eyes six years prior, but current specular microscopy showed indeterminate endothelial cell forms due to stromal opacity. The left eye's endothelial cell count was 2564 cells/m2 using a Konan Noncon Robo-8400 noncontact specular microscope. It was assumed that the right eye had a similar endothelial cell count and morphology. Ultrasound corneal pachymetry measured central corneal thickness at 658 µm in the right eye and 632 µm in the left eye. The patient was scheduled for penetrating keratoplasty of the right eye, and a corneal button was sent for light and electron microscopic analysis.
test_results: DNA sequencing analysis of the decorin gene in chromosome 12q22 was positive in both the patient and his mother. The novel mutation of a heterozygous, nucleoside substitution (c.1036T>G) point mutation in the decorin gene was detected in both patients. The c.1036T>G mutation resulted in a change of amino acid sequence (p.Cys346Gly).

case_report: A 2-month-old male infant was admitted to a local hospital due to widespread swelling. During prenatal examination, an elevated α-fetoprotein (AFP) level (20.85 MoM) was detected in the maternal serum at the 18th week of pregnancy. The infant was born at 36 weeks of gestation with a birth weight of 2.57 kg. The placenta's weight was reported as normal. Apgar scores were 9 and 10 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. Shortly after birth, the infant exhibited breathing difficulties and abdominal swelling. He has normal male external genitalia. Laboratory tests showed significantly low serum albumin (1.2 g/dL), high urinary protein excretion (7,959 mg/m2/day), and hypothyroidism. There was no evidence of congenital infection. The parents and his older brother are healthy, except the mother is a hepatitis B virus antigen carrier. The infant was started on captopril (0.1 mg/kg/day), synthyroid (2.7 µg/kg/day), and intermittent albumin infusions. Despite these treatments, the generalized swelling worsened, necessitating frequent albumin infusions. At 2 months old, he was transferred to Seoul National University Children's Hospital due to persistent generalized swelling and respiratory difficulty. On admission, his body weight was 4.49 kg (3-10 percentile), and height was 52 cm (<3 percentile). He exhibited mild chest retraction, and coarse breathing sounds with crackles were noted in both lung fields. Laboratory results showed serum albumin at 1.6 g/dL, serum creatinine at 0.3 mg/dL, a random urine protein/creatinine ratio of 110 mg/mg, a platelet count of 888×103/µL, and a serum immunoglobulin G level of 64 mg/dL (normal range, 176-201 mg/dL). The nasopharyngeal aspirate tested positive for human respiratory syncytial virus A. Supportive lung care was provided, and intravenous immune globulin (0.5 g/kg) was administered. The infant was treated with indomethacin (4 mg/kg/day), captopril (4.7 mg/kg/day), dipyridamole (3 mg/kg/day), warfarin, and synthyroid, along with a high protein (up to 4 mg/kg/day) and high-calorie diet (120 Cal/kg/day). Frequent albumin infusions (2 g/kg/day) continued to be necessary to manage respiratory issues and generalized swelling. A Chemoport® was implanted into the right atrium via the right external jugular vein to maintain a central venous line.
test_results: Genetic analysis of the NPHS1 gene revealed compound heterozygous frame-shifting mutations, 8-bp deletion in exon 16 (c.2156_2163 delTGCACTGC causing p.L719DfsX4), and 1-bp insertion in exon 24 (c.3250_3251insG causing p.V1084-GfsX12). The former mutation was inherited from mother, and the latter from father.
diagnosis: Congenital Nephrotic Syndrome of Finnish Type

case_report: A 12-year-old Bahraini girl was born at Salmaniya Medical Complex at full term through vaginal delivery, with Apgar scores of 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. A prenatal sonography performed in the last trimester showed a congenital abnormality affecting the nose. The mother’s age during pregnancy was 38 years. The patient was the fifth child of consanguineous parents who had four other healthy daughters and had one abortion. After delivery with a birth weight of 2,640 g, the patient’s physical examination revealed dysmorphic features in the form of hypoplastic alae nasi, microcephaly, mild hypotelorism, and cutis aplasia on the scalp. Eye examination was normal. Other systemic examinations were unremarkable. The patient underwent extensive evaluation by multiple medical teams, including specialists in neonatology, otorhinolaryngology, plastic surgery, endocrinology, and radiology. Laboratory results showed a hemoglobin level of 9.2 g/dL with low indices. Subclinical hypothyroidism was initially noted, but the thyroid-stimulating hormone level improved spontaneously from 10.6 to 6.7 mIU/L (normal level <6 mIU/L). Serum electrolytes, calcium, phosphorus, urea, creatinine, liver function tests, and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase levels were all within the normal range. A stool fat globules test was positive, but fecal tryptic activity was normal with a dilution of 1:3200. Abdominal ultrasound (US), echocardiogram, and brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were all reported to be normal. Hearing assessment was done using an auditory brainstem response test, which showed no response up to 100 dB normal hearing level (nHL) in both ears (average hearing threshold for healthy newborns: 20-40 dB nHL).
test_results: The microarray study showed a novel sequence change mutation of the UBR1 gene (1 bp duplication causing a frameshift). Both parents were heterozygous carriers of this mutation.

case_report: A 24-year-old female with no significant past medical history presented to the emergency department with severe, diffuse abdominal pain, primarily in the lower quadrants. The pain was sharp, non-radiating, and sudden at rest. She also experienced fever, chills, and nausea for three days prior to admission. Her last menstrual cycle was 20 days before presentation. She was sexually active with one male partner and used protection intermittently. She had never been tested for sexually transmitted infections (STI). She had no personal or family history of gallstones, was not pregnant, and was not overweight. On arrival, she was afebrile with a blood pressure of 85/54 mmHg and a heart rate of 100 beats per minute. On physical examination, she was in severe acute distress, lying very still due to pain. She had no scleral icterus or conjunctival pallor. Her abdomen was firm with severe tenderness on minimal palpation, associated with rebounding and guarding. Bowel sounds were normoactive, and no organomegaly was noted. Murphy's sign was positive. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete metabolic panel and complete blood count. Elevated troponin levels (68 pg/mL; reference range 3-17 pg/mL) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH; 291 units/L; reference range 140-271 units/L) were noted. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and free T4 were within normal limits. Urinalysis and an STI screen, including HIV, were negative. A computerized tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast revealed a small right-sided basilar pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, a small amount of perihepatic fluid, and a thickened gallbladder wall. There was also a complex hemorrhagic and cystic lesion of the right adnexa with free pelvic fluid, suggesting an ovarian cyst rupture. A transvaginal pelvic ultrasound confirmed a right ovarian hemorrhagic cyst measuring approximately 3.4 cm. A right upper quadrant abdominal ultrasound indicated gallbladder wall thickening with pericholecystic fluid without gallstones. Sonographic evidence of Murphy’s sign was present. Due to hemodynamic instability and peritoneal signs, a surgical evaluation was conducted. A repeat CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast showed an increase in pleural effusions, pericardial effusions, and intra-abdominal and pelvic fluid collections. The patient was taken to the operating room, where complex bilateral ovarian cysts and a moderate amount of clear ascitic fluid were found in the peritoneal cavity. Pathology of the peritoneal fluid showed mostly bland-appearing mesothelial cells with a few scattered acute and chronic inflammatory cells, and no malignant cells. The remaining fluid was suctioned intra-operatively. The cysts were not hemorrhagic at that time. The gallbladder was edematous but showed no evidence of cholecystitis and was not removed. During the first 72 hours of admission, the patient had multiple random blood glucose readings in the 50s and 60s (mg/dL), leading to an adrenal workup. Both adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) (72 pg/mL) and morning cortisol (1.1 mcg/dL) levels confirmed primary adrenal insufficiency.
test_results: The autoimmune panel was significant for a positive antinuclear (ANA) immunofluorescence with a speckled pattern titer of 1:320 detecting the RNP antigen.

case_report: A 32-year-old female presented with a red, swollen plaque on the inner side of her left forearm, which had been present for 10 days. She experienced general discomfort before the appearance of the lesion, followed by itching and a burning sensation at the site. Initially small, the lesion grew to approximately 5 cm by 4 cm. The plaque started as pink-red and changed to a violet color over 10 days, eventually fading within 3 weeks and leaving slight darkening of the skin. She reported having had 15 similar episodes over the past 18 months, with the lesion recurring at the same location and accompanied by mild general symptoms. The severity of these episodes varied, sometimes necessitating the use of antihistamines and oral steroids for relief. Laboratory tests showed normal hemoglobin and total white blood cell counts. The absolute eosinophil count was 440 cells/mm3 (normal range: 40–440 cells/mm3). Other tests, including random blood sugar, liver and kidney function tests, urinalysis, chest X-ray, and antinuclear antibodies, were all normal.
test_results: Histopathologic examination from a biopsy taken from the plaque showed moderately dense superficial and deep perivascular and periappendageal infiltrate of eosinophils and lymphocytes. Several eosinophils were scattered in the interstitium of reticular dermis and around the deep vascular plexus. The papillary dermis showed moderate edema.

case_report: A 2-month-old girl was brought to our hospital in April 2016 due to difficulties with feeding and respiratory failure. She was delivered at full term (40 weeks) via planned repeat caesarean section, weighing 2 kg at birth. Despite the lack of records for height and head circumference at birth, she experienced intrauterine growth retardation. Initially, she gained weight appropriately with exclusive breastfeeding, but her sucking ability gradually weakened, and weight gain ceased by the end of the first month. The patient has healthy consanguineous parents from Syria. Her family history includes four siblings who died suddenly within 10 weeks of life following feeding difficulties and cyanosis, and two siblings who were aborted due to suspected fetal hydrops. Multiple consanguineous marriages were noted in the family, but no other children were affected. Upon examination, her height was 49 cm, weight was 3.2 kg, and head circumference was 39 cm, all below the 3rd percentile. No dysmorphic features were observed. Neurological examination revealed hypotonia, grade-V muscle power in all extremities, positive palmar and plantar grasp reflexes, and normal deep tendon reflexes. She had weak sucking power but normal swallowing coordination, necessitating nasogastric tube feeding. Mechanical ventilation was required due to shallow respiration, decreased breath sounds on pulmonary auscultation, and respiratory acidosis. Laboratory tests showed mildly elevated liver enzymes: aspartate aminotransferase at 137 IU/L (reference range [RR], 22–63), alanine aminotransferase at 110 IU/L (RR, 12–45), and gamma-glutamyl transferase at 101 IU/L (RR, 8–90); other values were within normal limits. Imaging studies, including chest radiographs, abdominal ultrasound, and brain MRI, revealed no abnormalities. Given the family history and mildly elevated liver enzymes with feeding intolerance, further investigations were conducted. Tests for inborn errors of metabolism, including tandem mass spectrometry, serum amino acid, and urine organic acid analysis, showed no significant abnormalities. Enzyme assays for lysosomal storage disorders, such as Gaucher disease, Niemann-Pick disease types A and B, and lipoprotein lipase deficiency, were normal.
test_results: Homozygotic mutations of c.1273C>T (p.Arg425Cys) in IGHMBP2 (NM_002280.2) were identified and confirmed by Sanger sequencing.
diagnosis: Spinal Muscular Atrophy with Respiratory Distress Type 1
Orpha_name: Spinal Muscular Atrophy with Respiratory Distress Type 1

case_report: An 18-year-old male with no prior health issues presented with a three-week history of high-grade fever, dry cough, throat pain, and joint pain affecting the knees, ankles, and elbows. The fever was intermittent, occurring once daily, reaching up to 39 °C, and was alleviated by acetaminophen. He experienced unintentional weight loss and fatigue. Prior to hospital admission, he was treated with a seven-day course of empiric antibiotics for suspected bacterial pharyngitis without improvement. He reported no cough, hemoptysis, night sweats, rash, or gastrointestinal or urinary symptoms. He also denied any contact with sick individuals, exposure to tuberculosis, or recent travel. There was no family history of recurrent fever or joint pain. On examination, he was conscious, oriented, and hemodynamically stable with a temperature of 39.2 °C. Mild pallor was noted, but there was no jaundice. Small, painless, soft, and mobile cervical lymph nodes were palpable. The rest of the physical examination, including the ankle and knee joints, was unremarkable with no signs of inflammation. Laboratory findings showed microcytic anemia, marked neutrophilic predominant leukocytosis, elevated C-reactive protein (CRP), mild transaminitis, and normal lactate levels. Blood and urine cultures taken during fever spikes were sterile. Tests for malaria, brucellosis, and mycoplasma were negative. Viral hepatitis serology, respiratory viral panel, cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), and adenoviral polymerase chain reaction (PCR) were all negative. Sputum acid-fast bacillus (AFB) stain and sputum TB PCR were negative on two occasions. The autoimmune workup was normal. Electrocardiogram (ECG) and chest X-ray were unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound showed no hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, or fluid collection in the abdomen and pelvis. Echocardiography did not reveal any signs of infective endocarditis. CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast showed no enlarged lymph nodes or collections. Peripheral blood film did not show any blast cells, and bone marrow aspiration and biopsy indicated healthy cellular bone marrow with trilineage hematopoiesis and no hemophagocytosis. Despite receiving broad-spectrum antibiotics for an appropriate duration, the patient continued to experience daily fever spikes. His ferritin level at presentation was unremarkable.
test_results: The patient exhibited marked hyperferritinemia.

case_report: A 4-year-old male presented to the ENT outpatient department with complaints of nosebleeds and nasal blockage in the left nasal cavity for 10 days. The child experienced a sudden left nasal hemorrhage during sleep 10 days prior, which was significant and required emergency treatment at a local hospital. Bleeding was controlled by filling the left nasal cavity with an inflated sponge. The child removed the sponge the following day without significant bleeding. Persistent left nasal obstruction followed, accompanied by white purulent nasal discharge that was difficult to expel. Occasional blood was noted in the nasal discharge. The child also exhibited sleep snoring, open mouth breathing, and episodes of suffocation during sleep. The patient was admitted for further evaluation. Physical examination revealed a pinkish lesion in the nasal passages of both nasal cavities. The child had no prior health issues.
test_results: A Computed Tomography Scan of the paranasal sinuses showed bilateral posterior nasal passage obstruction, a 2.5 cm × 2.7 cm size soft tissue density shadow in the nasopharyngeal, and there was no bony erosion. Enhanced Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) of paranasal sinus presented abnormal signal of nasopharynx with obvious enhancement.

case_report: In August 2015, a 20-year-old man presented with an intermediate cytogenetic risk stratification. His bone marrow showed complete remission after two courses of induction therapy. Following three courses of consolidation therapy, granulocyte-colony stimulating factor (G-CSF)-mobilized peripheral blood stem cells (PBSC) from his human leukocyte antigen (HLA) 4/6 matched father were infused on April 20–21, 2016. The conditioning regimen included decitabine (20 mg/m2/day, days -11 to -7), cytarabine (3 g/m2/day, days -9 to -7), busulfan (3.2 mg/kg/day, days -5 and -4), and cyclophosphamide (1.8 g/m2/day, days -3 and -2). For graft vs. host disease (GVHD) prophylaxis, a regimen of tacrolimus, short-term methotrexate (MTX), and mycophenolate mofetil was administered. Neutrophil and platelet engraftment occurred on day +10 and +13, respectively. On day +30, his bone marrow showed complete remission and complete donor chimerism, with normal results maintained until November 16, 2017. Due to repeated mild liver chronic GVHD, tacrolimus was continued until day +350.
test_results: His left posterior iliac bone marrow aspirate smear revealed a blast percentage of 52%. The blasts expressed CD34 dim, CD117, CD33 strong, HLA-DR, CD13, and did not express CD7, CD19, CD56, CD11b. The immunophenotype was the same as the first diagnosis.

case_report: A 72-year-old Caucasian male with a history of prostate hypertrophy presented with a nodule on his right forearm. The growth of this nodule coincided with an increase in his blood prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level. The nodule became palpable approximately 3 years prior, at which time his blood PSA level had risen above 4 ng/ml during a routine blood test. The patient reported no pain or abnormal sensations in the right hand and forearm, even when pressure was applied to the nodule. Ultrasound examination revealed that the nodule was associated with the median nerve. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) identified the nodule as approximately 3 cm in size. Despite being painless, the nodule was large enough to warrant medical intervention and was surgically removed without significant neural damage.
test_results: Histological examination of the surgical specimen established the diagnosis of schwannoma. The excised tumor consisted in spindle-shaped cells with poorly defined eosinophilic cytoplasm, without atypia, and with nuclear palisading. The nodule comprised compact areas (Antoni A), foci of palisaded nuclei (Verocay bodies), and a less frequent loose-textured component with round nuclei and loose-knit processes (Antoni B). Focal thick-walled, hyalinized blood vessels, lymphocytic infiltrate, foamy histiocytes, and degenerative tumoral spaces were also present. In addition, strong and uniform immunoreaction for S100 protein was seen in all tumor cells. Immunohistochemistry with human PSA antibodies was completely negative.

case_report: A 57-year-old woman reported experiencing multiple skin lesions over the past 10 years, which were occasionally painful, particularly when exposed to cold or pressure. Upon physical examination, numerous erythematous-to-brownish papules and nodules with a smooth surface were observed, clustered on the upper back. Her medical history included a hysterectomy performed 11 years ago due to uterine leiomyomas. Family history revealed that her sister also had both skin and uterine leiomyomas.
test_results: The histological examination revealed a leiomyoma. Immunohistochemistry showed positivity for smooth muscle actin. The result was a heterozygous deletion of FH exon.
Orpha_name: Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer

case_report: A 2-year-old male child with Fitzpatrick type 5 skin presented with multiple brownish skin lesions predominantly over the trunk for six months. There was no family history of similar conditions, and the child's development was normal. There was no history of urticarial flushing or bullae. On examination, multiple hyperpigmented macules were observed over the trunk and extremities. No wheal formation or erythema was noted upon stroking. There was no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Dermoscopy revealed brownish reticular thick lines forming a pigment network, which were relatively lighter.
test_results: Histopathological examination of lesional skin showed infiltration of numerous mast cells in perivascular and periappendageal location in the upper dermis.

case_report: A five-year-old girl presented with bronchitis. During the physical examination, in addition to signs of a respiratory infection, the girl exhibited generalized short, curly hair covering the entire scalp. The family history revealed that 23 family members also had this hair characteristic, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with incomplete penetrance. Some family members displayed hair with features intermediate between normal and the observed anomaly.
test_results: The hair appeared to be thinner than normal for age and to be twisted on the longitudinal axis.

case_report: A 73-year-old Japanese woman with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia presented with bilateral hand tremor. The tremor was present in both hands from the beginning. She had no family history of neurological conditions. Initial treatment with arotinolol hydrochloride at 20 mg/day was ineffective. After 2 years, she returned with worsening hand tremor and difficulty walking. Neurological examination revealed resting, positional, and intentional tremor in both upper limbs. The resting tremor increased with cognitive activity and walking. She did not exhibit bradykinesia or rigidity, and her gait was slightly unsteady but not ataxic. No other neurological abnormalities were observed. Surface electromyography of the right common digital extensor muscle and ulnar flexor muscle showed muscle activity discharges at frequencies of 6 and 3 Hz, respectively. Brain MRI showed dilation of the lateral ventricle, moderate cerebral atrophy, and high-intensity areas in the cerebral white matter on T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images. MRI diffusion-weighted imaging revealed a high-intensity signal in the corticomedullary junction. 99mTc-L,L-ethyl cysteinate dimer (ECD) SPECT indicated normal uptake in the thalamus and basal ganglia. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal, and blood tests showed normal thyroid function. Cardiac uptake of 123I-metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) during myocardial scintigraphy was normal (H/M ratio early: 2.55, delayed: 2.49).
test_results: Immunofluorescence analysis with anti-ubiquitin antibody revealed intranuclear inclusions in the adipocytes, sweat gland cells, and fibroblasts.

case_report: A 19-month-old girl presented with haemolytic anaemia and developmental delay. She was the first child of third-cousin parents, born at 38 weeks following an uncomplicated pregnancy. She was hospitalized in the neonatal intensive care unit for 38 days due to neonatal jaundice and early sepsis, requiring five blood transfusions immediately after birth and an exchange transfusion on the second day of life due to maternal-foetal ABO incompatibility. Another blood transfusion was required at 30 days old for non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia. At 9 months, she experienced multiple haemolytic crises triggered by infections and exhibited mild psychomotor developmental delay, unable to sit independently. At 11 months, she was diagnosed with hereditary spherocytosis through a pathologic osmotic fragility test. At 19 months, she was referred with symptoms of an inability to walk and sit without support. Physical examination revealed a weight of 7.3 kg (<3 percentile; z-score −3), height of 78 cm (9th percentile; z-score −1.3), and head circumference of 44.5 cm (5th percentile; z-score −1.6). She exhibited severe malnutrition, paleness, axial hypotonia with muscle bulk loss, and muscle weakness. Decreased deep tendon reflexes, muscle atrophy, and hyperelasticity of the joints were noted in the extremities. Laboratory findings showed severe macrocytic anaemia with haemoglobin 6.5 g/dL, haematocrit 13.1%, mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration 31 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 104 fL, normal white blood cell count 8.868 × 10^9/L, platelet count 95,000/mm3, elevated total bilirubin 24.63 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin 18.58 mg/dL. Plasma amino acids, very long-chain fatty acids, serum transferrin isoelectric focusing, and urine organic acids with GCMS were unremarkable. The acylcarnitine profile by MSMS showed normal C0 (62.8 µmol/L, normal range: 10–90 µmol/L) and elevated C3 (7.1 µmol/L, normal range: 0–4.9 µmol/L), with negative methylmalonic acid in the urine by GCMS. Plasma vitamin B12, folic acid, and homocysteine levels were normal. Bone marrow aspiration was normocellular. Ophthalmologic fundus examination, brain stem electric response audiometry (BERA), electromyography, and brain magnetic resonance imaging were all normal. No epileptic activity was observed in the electroencephalography. Muscle biopsy indicated myopathy. During follow-up, the patient required multiple hospitalizations due to haemolytic crises, recurrent lower respiratory tract infections, and gastroenteritis. At 3 years old, she was admitted to the intensive care unit for pneumonia, required a tracheostomy, and lost most of her acquired developmental milestones.
test_results: Molecular analysis using next-generation sequencing disclosed a p.E105D (c.315G>C) homozygous mutation in the TPI1 gene.

case_report: A 52-year-old African American man presented with a history of subcutaneous nodules appearing across various parts of his body and a noticeable reduction in subcutaneous fat. These symptoms emerged twelve years after an initial episode at the age of 34, during which similar nodules were observed but resolved without intervention.
test_results: Skin punch biopsies were taken from the right chest and right forearm, showing lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate primarily involving the subcutis with some extension into the deep dermis and periadnexal fat with abundant mucin deposition. Lymphocytes were CD3+ and CD5+ with a subpopulation of CD8+ and CD4+ T-cells. Staining was positive for beta F1 and most of the CD8+ cells were expressing TIA-1. Stainings for CD30, CD25, and TCR gamma were negative. Laboratory studies showed bi-lineage cytopenias, as well as abnormal liver function tests, hyperferritinemia, hypertriglyceridemia, hypofibrinogenemia, hypoalbuminemia, and an elevated D-dimer. Serum inflammatory markers were elevated. Positron emission tomography and computerized tomography scans showed nonspecific metabolically active enlarged axillary and inguinal nodes and a normal sized spleen (12.7 cm). Bilateral bone marrow biopsies revealed a hypercellular bone marrow (∼90%) with an atypical polymorphous lymphohistiocytic infiltrate admixed with eosinophils and plasma cells, scattered hemophagocytosis, and no evidence of lymphoma involvement.
diagnosis: Acquired Generalized Lipodystrophy associated with Subcutaneous Panniculitis-Like T-cell Lymphoma and Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis

case_report: A 5-year-old boy presented with firm, non-tender bilateral submandibular masses. The swellings had been present for approximately six months, initially small and painless but later increasing significantly in size. The child has a history of allergic rhinitis, with no other significant medical history. Initial treatment with antibiotics and anti-inflammatory medications was ineffective. Prior to the swelling, the child experienced an acute episode of upper respiratory tract infection. Family history revealed no chronic diseases. On examination, the child was in good general condition, afebrile, with normal weight, balanced cardiorespiratory and digestive systems, supple abdomen, normal diuresis and stool, and no meningeal signs. Clinical examination revealed two firm, 2.5×2 cm bilateral submandibular masses, with no latero-cervical lymphadenopathy, pain on palpation, or skin lesions. General and oral examinations were normal. The child had no history of dry eyes or mouth. Infectious disease consultation ruled out viral and bacterial etiologies. Laboratory investigations, including complete blood count, inflammatory tests, liver transaminases, urea, creatinine, blood glucose, amylase, lipase, sideremia, calcium, lactate dehydrogenase, creatine kinase, fibrinemia, and coagulation, were within normal limits.
test_results: Ultrasonography showed diffuse enlargement with homogenous echotexture in both submandibular glands. No sialolithiasis was identified. No other cervical nodules or lymph node enlargements were present.

case_report: The patient is an 11-year-old boy who presented to our clinic with global developmental delay and verbal apraxia at the age of four. He is the third of four children born to non-consanguineous parents of Chinese descent. The mother and paternal grandmother have a history of recurrent spontaneous pregnancy losses of unknown cause. The parents and three siblings are reportedly healthy. The patient was born at 39 weeks via caesarean section due to fetal distress, with Apgar scores of 8 and 9 at one and five minutes, respectively. His birth weight was 2175 grams (<3rd percentile), length was 47 cm (10th percentile), and occipito-frontal circumference (OFC) was 34 cm (25th percentile). Clinical features included feeding difficulty, low muscle tone, bilateral ptosis, club foot, bilateral undescended testes, and flexion contracture of the hand and wrist. Laboratory tests, including routine karyotype, subtelomeric FISH, fragile X testing, biochemical assessments, cranial MRI, and CT scan, were normal. A 709.2 kb duplication of 16p11.2 (29,425,199–30,134,432) was identified via Affymetrix Genome-Wide Human SNP Array 6.0 and confirmed by FISH, with maternal inheritance. The siblings were not tested for this duplication at the family's request. The mother, a carrier of the 16p11.2 duplication, was examined and showed no signs of intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, psychiatric disorders (anxiety, depression, obsessive-compulsive disorders), underweight, or microcephaly. She also had no history of epilepsy, speech and motor delay, or congenital anomalies.
test_results: Two novel splicing mutations of VPS13B (8q22.2) with compound heterozygous inheritance were identified in the proband and subsequently confirmed by Sanger sequencing. A sequence variant of c.1426-1G > A located in the acceptor splice site of intron 10 was identified in Proband A and his mother. The second variant, a nucleotide change of G > T at c.4157 + 1 situated in the donor site of intron 27, was inherited from his father. PCR on cDNA samples of proband and a control using two separate sets of primers covering exons 9–12 and 26–29 of VPS13B, followed by Sanger sequencing of the PCR products confirmed that both variants abolish the canonical splice sites and create aberrant RNA sequences. Real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) for VPS13B demonstrated reduced expression in the proband compared to two controls. The mother also showed reduced RNA expression compared to one control.

case_report: A 21-year-old female patient presented with a growth on the anterior maxillary gingiva, which was excised and sent for routine histopathological examination. The initial assessment suggested a fibroma. Histopathological analysis of Hematoxylin and eosin-stained sections revealed stratified squamous parakeratinizing epithelium over a fibrocellular stroma. The stroma contained loosely arranged collagen fibers, bundles of differentiated smooth muscle fibers, nerve fascicles, thick-walled blood vessels, and ectopic cartilaginous tissue. Masson Trichrome staining was used to differentiate the connective tissue components. Clinical examination showed a normal-statured, well-oriented female in apparent good health. Extra-oral findings included micrognathia, pseudo-clefting of the lower lip, two midline pits in the labial philtrum, and low set ears. The patient's skin was dry with thin, scanty hair, and crops of milia were observed on the nose, nasolabial folds, and chin. Intra-oral examination revealed mesio-labial rotation of the right maxillary central incisor, a midline diastema associated with a median alveolar cleft, high labial frenal attachment, and a small soft tissue gingival swelling (approximately 1x1.5 cm) near the left maxillary central incisor. There were no abnormalities in the hands and feet, and her medical history was unremarkable. The patient's mother reported a non-consanguineous marriage, premature birth with low birth weight (exact weight unknown), and learning difficulties. The patient has a completely normal younger male sibling.
test_results: The CBCT and the OPG confirmed the presence of a median alveolar cleft of the maxilla. The karyotyping test revealed an apparently normal karyotype as assessed by conventional cytogenetic analysis (CCA).

case_report: A 22-year-old male from Nepal experienced intermittent nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, and breathlessness over the past two months. These symptoms worsened in the last 10 days, accompanied by facial puffiness, pedal edema, decreased urine output, and continued breathlessness. He reported no orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, seizures, hematuria, pyuria, or lithuria. There was no family history of similar conditions. Ten years ago, he sustained a spinal fracture from a fall, which was treated with open reduction and internal fixation.
