Physical examination showed a pulse rate of 86 beats per minute and blood pressure of 140/80 mm Hg. He appeared pale with an elevated jugular venous pressure of approximately 7 cm. Bilateral pitting pedal edema was noted. Nail deformities were observed in all fingers and toes, particularly in the thumbs. He also had deformed knee joints and fixed flexion deformity of both hip joints. Chest examination revealed fine crepitations in the basal regions. Cardiovascular examination indicated normal heart sounds with a functional systolic murmur in the pulmonary area, without pericardial rub. Abdominal and central nervous system examinations were normal. Fundus examination showed grade II hypertensive retinopathy. Laboratory results indicated renal impairment with urea at 20 mg% and creatinine at 28%. Initial arterial blood gas analysis revealed metabolic acidosis. A 24-hour urine protein test showed nephrotic range proteinuria (3 g/day) without active sediments in the routine urine examination. Ultrasound of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder revealed a right kidney measuring 9.9 cm with an ill-defined corticomedullary junction and a non-visualized left kidney, suggesting it might be ectopic or absent.
test_results: X-Ray of B/L knee joint showed dysplastic patellae. X-Ray of the pelvis showed B/L iliac horn. A computerised tomogram of B/L kidneys revealed the presence of both shrunken left and right kidneys (7 cm each).

case_report: A four-year-old girl from a consanguineous family was seen at the pediatric clinical immunology outpatient clinic due to recurrent infections and recurrent neutropenia over the past year. Her medical history revealed delays in motor milestones and feeding difficulties during her early months. She is currently unable to consume solid food. There is no history of seizures. Her parents are healthy, and there is no family history of similar symptoms. She has no siblings, but her mother experienced a stillbirth in her first pregnancy. On examination, the patient presented with microcephaly, hypotonia, hypermobile joints, motor developmental delay, slender fingers, and a cheerful disposition. She also exhibited speech delay and had recently begun to speak a few words. Facial features included a low hairline, short philtrum, prominent upper central incisors, wave-shaped eyelids, thick and long eyelashes, and a prominent nasal root. Eye examination was normal. Laboratory results over the past six months showed an absolute neutrophil count ranging from 0.5 to 2.32 (103/μL) and a neutrophil percentage ranging from 7.8% to 30%, with other complete blood count components within normal limits. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), serum IgG, IgM, IgA, and IgE levels, serum T3 and T4, TSH, urea, creatinine, and fasting blood sugar were all normal. Serum alkaline phosphatase was below normal at 135 U/L.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing for the patient was performed at the Dr. von Hauner Children’s hospital NGS facility using Agilent V6 + UTR library preparation and an Illumina NextSeq 500 sequencing platform. The bioinformatics analysis pipeline uses Burrows-Wheeler Alingner (BWA 0.7.15). Genome Analysis Tool Kit (GATK 3.6), Variant Effect Predictor (VEP 89) and frequency filters with public and in house databases (e.g. ExAC [], GenomAD [] and GME []). We found a novel homozygous frameshift variant in the VPS13B gene: VPS13B (LRG_351t1: c.7095del; p.Ser2366AlafsTer49). Based on the classical 5-tiered system introduced by the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics, this variant is classified as a pathogenic variant and there is very strong evidence for its pathogenicity. This mutation confirmed our early diagnosis.

case_report: A 57-year-old male with a history of diabetes and hypertension, and previous cerebrovascular strokes in 2013 and 2016 (modified Rankin score (mRS) 1), arrived at the emergency room in August 2018. He reported an 11-hour duration of gait instability to the left, vertigo, nausea, vomiting, followed by difficulty swallowing fluids with nasal regurgitation, hoarseness, and partial ptosis of the left eye due to partial involvement of the descending sympathetic tract (National Institute of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) 5). MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) showed left lateral medullary infarction. A few hours post-admission, he experienced rapid breathing with oxygen saturation dropping to 60%, followed by a heart rate decrease to 17 beats per minute and gasping. He was transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) and intubated for assisted ventilation using bi-level positive airway pressure (BiPAP) mode for 24 hours, after which he stabilized and was extubated. Twelve hours later, he had a cardiopulmonary arrest, underwent cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and was placed back on BiPAP mode. Two days later, he was switched to continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) but experienced recurrent nighttime apnea episodes and was returned to BiPAP mode. Electrocardiogram (ECG), cardiac enzymes, coagulation profile, and D-dimer were within normal limits. Carotid duplex showed diffuse atherosclerosis, echocardiogram (ECHO) indicated grade I diastolic dysfunction and mild concentric left ventricular hypertrophy. Glycated hemoglobin was 8.5, and lipid profile was normal. Follow-up MRI showed no changes, and chest X-ray was clear. A week later, he was extubated and remained stable on room air.
test_results: Polysomnography showed an increased percentage of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. After 90 min from sleep initiation, he developed prolonged central apnea (102 s) with a drop of oxygen to 49% and bradycardia with average heart rate of 39.3 beats per minute, all of which were corrected by re-administration of assisted ventilation.

case_report: A 1 year 3 month old Chinese male child presented to the pediatric department with pain and swelling on the left side of his face for the past 2 weeks. The swelling had progressively worsened over this period. Two days prior to hospital admission, the pain and tenderness intensified. There was no history of trauma to the head or neck. Physical examination revealed mild soft tissue edema on the left upper face with severe pain upon pressure. The patient did not exhibit fever, weight loss, palpable lymphadenopathy, or organomegaly. Laboratory results, including blood count, differential, liver, and renal function tests, were within normal limits. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the head showed multifocal osteolytic lesions in the facial bones: left zygomatic bone (1.5 × 1.0 × 1.0 cm), left orbital bone (0.5 cm in diameter), and right maxillary bone (1.0 cm in diameter). The left zygoma was largely destroyed, and an associated soft tissue mass was noted. The lesions displayed moderate enhancement following meglumine diatrizoate injection. No enlarged lymph nodes were detected in the head and neck. A CT scan of the neck and abdomen revealed no pathological findings, including no lymphadenopathy. A CT-guided needle biopsy of the left zygomatic bone initially showed fibrosis with inflammatory cell infiltration. The patient underwent extensive curettage of the zygomatic and maxillary lesions due to ill-defined margins. The postoperative period was uneventful, and no further treatments were administered. The pain resolved postoperatively, and the patient was monitored regularly for 24 months after discharge. A follow-up CT scan at 6 months post-surgery showed an unchanged lesion in the left orbital bone with no signs of recurrence or lymph node enlargement.
test_results: Under microscopic examination, both zygomatic and maxillary lesion showed an ill-defined neoplasm within the osseous fragments. The lesions were composed of multiple delicate interconnecting vascular channels with papillae formation which projected into the lumen lined by atypical plumped endothelial cells. Some of those papillae contained hyalinized core. The vascular channels were also lined by plump cuboidal endothelial cells with focal hobnailed or 'match-head' appearance. In some areas, endothelial cells formed solid-appearing aggregates with vessel lumens. A variable number of lymphocytes are seen within and around the vascular channels. Mitotic figures were rare and necrosis was not observed in the lesions. Immunohistochemistry stains done on these lesions were positivity for CD34 and CD31. Staining for CD31 was stronger than that for CD34. Endothelial cells of lumens expressed CD31, CD34 and D2-40, but the intraluminal tumor cells were negative for D2-40. These lesions did not express CD1a, S-100 protein, cytokeratin (AE1/AE3), EMA, langerin, CD68 and SMA. The Ki-67 labeling index of the lesions was low, accounting for 2% of the tumor.

case_report: A 35-year-old female from a rural area presented with a history of chronic diarrhea lasting over 3 years, rickets, elevated serum immunoglobulin A levels, and anemia. Previous treatments at other hospitals included a gluten-free diet for over 6 months and antibiotics such as tetracycline, metronidazole, and ampicillin for over 1 month, without improvement. Physical examination revealed pallor, nervousness, and a body mass index (BMI) of approximately 15.6 kg/m2. Initial laboratory tests indicated severe electrolyte imbalance and anemia, with normal liver and renal functions. There were no allergic food ingredients, pathogenic bacteria in stool cultures, or parasites in stool examinations. Tests for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and autoimmune antibodies were negative, and serum and urine light chains, including kappa and lambda levels, were normal. The Helicobacter pylori (HP) hydrogen breath test was negative. Serum immunoglobulin A titer was approximately 22,900 mg/L (normal value below 3820 mg/L). Bone marrow aspiration showed no evidence of lymphoma, plasmacytoma, or multiple myeloma. The smear of bone marrow revealed about 3% mature and 2.5% immature plasma cells (normal ratio) and numerous megakaryocytes with small round nuclei, indicating sideropenic and megaloblastic anemia. Protein electrophoresis and immunofixation electrophoresis did not show definitive monoclonal immunoglobulin protein bands in her serum.
test_results: Duodenal and ileac biopsies revealed atrophy and blunting villi. The bowel lamina propria was infiltrated with slightly increased intraepithelial lymphocytes and mainly with diffuse plasma cells. The following enzyme labeling immunohistochemistry results were strongly positive to alpha-heavy-chain, but negative to lambda and kappa light chain. Computed tomography (CT) manifested she had no hepatosplenomegaly and no lymphadenopathy but had diffuse thickening of small intestine wall.

case_report: A 10-year-old male patient presented with irregularly positioned front teeth. The patient had a history of bilateral congenital cataracts, which were surgically treated at 6 months of age, and he wore corrective spectacles. His medical history was otherwise unremarkable, and there was no significant family history. Extraoral examination showed mild facial dysmorphism, including a long narrow face, mandibular prognathism, a large narrow nose with a high narrow nasal bridge, and large protruding anteverted ears. The patient exhibited no signs of intellectual impairment, performed well in school, and responded appropriately to instructions. Intraoral examination revealed multiple dental anomalies: incisors with conical or screwdriver shapes and notched incised edges, prominent Talon's cusps on the upper lateral incisors, and molars with central supernumerary cusps and a globular appearance. Generalized spacing was observed, with a predominantly permanent dentition except for unerupted permanent canines. Numerous carious lesions were present in the permanent molars. A blood serological investigation was conducted.
test_results: Radiological examination revealed the presence of impacted supernumerary teeth in relation to 46 and 36. Multiple pulp stones in relation to 16 and 26 and enlarged pulp chambers suggestive of taurodontism in relation to 13 were also evident.

case_report: A 64-year-old male of Asian descent reported experiencing gradually worsening vision in the left eye (OS) over the past five years. There was no history of inflammation, trauma, night blindness, or family history of retinal disorders. The patient had a known history of hypertension and was on regular medication. His best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/20 in the right eye (OD) and 20/32 in the left eye (OS). The anterior segment examination was unremarkable in both eyes (OU). Central visual fields were normal. Fundus examination revealed pigment clumps along the retinal veins with varying degrees of chorioretinal atrophy extending from the optic disc to the equator in both eyes (OU). Additionally, there was intraretinal and subretinal exudation with telangiectasia along the superotemporal vein in both eyes, more prominently in the left eye (OS).
test_results: Fluorescein angiography showed areas of hyperfluorescence in atrophic areas in the peripapillary area and hypofluorescence corresponding to the pigment clumps along the retinal veins along with its branches with telangiectasia and exudation along superotemporal vein OU and multiple macro aneurysms with capillary nonperfusion areas OS.
diagnosis: Pigmented Paravenous Chorioretinal Atrophy  with Coat's Like Response

case_report: A 52-year-old male with no prior medical conditions reported an asymptomatic ring-shaped atrophic patch on the distal part of his fourth toe, persisting for 2 years. Initially, the lesion appeared as a small keratotic bump that progressively expanded outward. Various treatments were administered, including cryotherapy, topical corticosteroids, antifungals, and antibiotics, but none led to improvement. Dermoscopic evaluation showed a scaly, atrophic, and erythematous central region with a clearly defined peripheral hyperkeratotic structure.
test_results: A skin biopsy of the edge of the lesion revealed a cornoid lamella with a column of parakeratotic cells extending from an invagination of the epidermis with absence of granular layer.

case_report: A 50-year-old woman reported a 10-year history of gradual hemifacial atrophy accompanied by facial pain. Her medical history included high blood pressure. Physical examination revealed facial asymmetry with significant underdevelopment on the right side of the face and right enophthalmos. The patient experienced a continuous, dull, aching pain on the right side of her face, primarily in the supra- and periorbital regions, temple, ear, and zygomatic area. The pain was mild and did not vary significantly throughout the day. Other clinical and neurological examinations, including a detailed sensory examination, were normal. Soft brush and pinprick stimulation of the skin did not cause pain. Large myelinated fibers were assessed using masticatory muscle electromyography and trigeminal reflexes, while small myelinated and unmyelinated fibers were tested with laser-evoked potentials. Cutaneous innervation was evaluated by measuring intraepidermal nerve fiber density after a skin biopsy of the supraorbital regions. The methods followed European Guidelines and published recommendations. The blink reflex was triggered by electrical stimulation of the supraorbital nerve, with EMG signals recorded from the orbicularis oculi. The masseter inhibitory reflex was evoked by electrical stimulation of the infraorbital and mental nerves, with EMG signals recorded from the masseter muscle. Laser-evoked potentials were studied using a previously reported technique, recording the main Aδ- and C-LEP complex, N2–P2, from the vertex. Peak latency and amplitude of the N2–P2 vertex complex were measured. Skin biopsies were taken above the eyebrow after local anesthesia, processed for bright-field immunohistochemistry using antibodies against protein gene product (PGP) 9.5. Neurophysiological and intraepidermal nerve fiber data were compared with normative ranges. Laboratory tests showed no abnormalities, and investigations for rheumatic disease, including rheumatoid factor, anti-dsDNA antibody, and extractable nuclear antigen screening, were normal.
test_results: Computerised tomographic (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans showed severe hemiatrophy involving facial subcutaneous tissues and facial bones, but no brain lesions.

case_report: A 60-year-old male arrived at the emergency department with recent confusion, nausea, and vomiting. Ten days prior, he had received the second dose of the nucleoside modified mRNA SARS-Cov2 vaccine BNT162b2 (Comirnaty®, Pfizer-BioNTech). He reported experiencing progressive chest discomfort and shortness of breath over the past week. His family doctor had identified H. pylori and a urinary tract infection. His medical history included long-standing hypertension, hyperlipidemia, benign prostate hyperplasia, and depression. One week after the first dose of BNT162b2, he had a cerebrovascular ischemic stroke. He was transferred from a smaller hospital and was on the following medications: clopidogrel, irbesartan, atorvastatin, escitalopram, esomeprazole, ciprofloxacin, cobalamin, and quercetin. Upon arrival, his general condition was fair (GCS 15; blood pressure 150/80 mmHg; heart rate 70 beats per minute; temperature 34.6°C). During the physical examination, he had a brief episode of altered mental state with transient aphasia but no new focal neurological deficits. The rest of the examination was unremarkable. A cerebral computed tomography showed residual signs of the previous ischemic stroke but no new findings. Laboratory results indicated microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (hemoglobin 89 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase 885 U/L, total bilirubin 98 μmol/L, haptoglobin <0.1 g/L, 35% schistocytes on the peripheral blood smear), severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count 25 × 10^9/L), a normal coagulation profile except for elevated D-dimer levels (1,728 μg/L), and normal creatinine. High-sensitivity troponin T was transiently elevated while creatine kinase was normal. The ECG showed new flattened anterolateral T waves, but a transthoracic echocardiogram revealed no wall motion abnormalities. Antibodies against platelet factor (PF) 4/heparin complex were negative.
test_results: ADAMTS13 activity <5% in the presence of a positive anti-ADAMTS13 IgG ELISA result (16.7 AU/mL; normal range <12 AU/mL), the functional ADAMTS13 inhibitor was negative.

case_report: A 54-year-old male presented with multiple subcutaneous nodular masses of varying sizes located on the scalp, groin, and back. The patient reported the presence of these nodules since age 18, with gradual growth over the years. The largest nodules from each region were surgically excised. The excised nodules included a scalp lesion measuring 7.4 × 5.6 × 3.8 cm, a right groin lesion measuring 4.7 × 2.7 × 1.9 cm, and an upper back lesion measuring 4.4 × 3.5 × 3.2 cm. Post-excision, all three nodules exhibited a similar gross appearance, described as gray-tan, firm, and nodular masses. Scalp and back lesions were subjected to frozen sectioning during the procedure, but the results were inconclusive regarding specific pathology.
test_results: Permanent sectioning revealed an irregular globular jigsaw of basaloid cell morphology of the dermis in all specimens. Hyaline droplets and focal ductal differentiation were also present in all specimens. No nuclear pleomorphism or mitotic elements were present. The tumor cells were positive for cytokeratin 7 (CK7), periodic acid-Schiff (PAS), and epithelial membrane antigen (EMA).

case_report: A 6-year-old Pakistani boy, born to non-consanguineous parents, presented with early-onset global developmental delay, spastic quadriplegia, seizures, acquired microcephaly, and failure to thrive. Metabolic workup and chromosomal analyses (karyotype and chromosomal microarray analysis) showed no abnormalities. He was born at term with a birth weight of 3 kg and had an unremarkable perinatal history. Developmental milestones included smiling at 3 months, rolling over at 10 months, and sitting at 11 months. However, he lost the ability to sit after experiencing his first febrile seizure at 16 months, which was managed with levetiracetam. By 18 months, he regained some abilities such as rolling over and sitting with a curved back but could not crawl, pull to stand, or cruise. He could reach for objects, hold them, and transfer them between hands but lacked a pincer grasp. His speech was delayed, and he communicated through screaming and sounds. He maintained good eye contact but was socially anxious around strangers, could clap, and wave bye. His development was globally affected. Muscle spasticity, more severe in the lower limbs, was managed with baclofen and routine botulinum toxin injections, which improved muscle tone but required continuous administration. The spasticity progressed to the upper limbs, and his condition remained severely progressive, necessitating wheelchair use. He was seizure-free on levetiracetam until age 5 when new seizure types emerged, including myoclonic seizures and episodes resembling tonic spasms, occurring up to 8 to 10 times during sleep. He experienced failure to thrive and recurrent aspiration pneumonia due to feeding difficulties, confirmed by swallowing studies, and is currently fed via a nasogastric (NG) tube. Additional medical history includes a ventricular septal defect (VSD) and recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs). He was hospitalized for acute gastroenteritis with prerenal azotemia, managed with intravenous fluids and supportive care.
test_results: Compound heterozygous variants (deletion and missense) in SLC1A4 were detected.
diagnosis: Spastic tetraplegia, thin corpus callosum, and progressive microcephaly due to compound heterozygous variants in SLC1A4
Orpha_name: Spastic tetraplegia-thin corpus callosum-progressive postnatal microcephaly syndrome

case_report: A 13-year-old girl was admitted to our hospital with a history of persistent jaundice and skin itching for one month. She is the first child of a nonconsanguineous couple with no notable family history and was born healthy via normal delivery, weighing 3200 g at birth. No significant abnormalities were observed during the perinatal period. During infancy, she exhibited skin hyperkeratosis and mild limb bone abnormalities, which progressed to ichthyosis and pronounced claw-like hands and feet by the age of 6 years. Additionally, she experienced progressive itching and recurrent desquamation of the hands and feet since the age of 6. One month prior to admission, she sought medical attention at a local hospital due to worsening jaundice and severe skin itching. At the local hospital, she was found to have acute liver failure, cholestasis, hypoalbuminemia, and abnormal blood coagulation. She received various treatments, including hepatoprotective therapy, plasma exchange, albumin infusion, and methylprednisolone pulse therapy. Following these treatments, her liver function, hypoalbuminemia, and blood coagulation improved, but jaundice and skin itching persisted. The patient was then discharged after blood samples were taken for further genetic analysis.
test_results: WGS results revealed novel compound heterozygous mutations of VPS33B, c.1081 C > T (p.Q361X,257)/c.244 T > C (p. C82R), which was inherited from her father and mother as the parents are heterozygote carriers. Liver biopsy revealed the absence of the bile duct, and the gross bile ducts were severely dilated and filled with fine particles of bile. Electron microscopy showed hepatocytes of unequal size and disorganized arrangement with dilated hepatic sinuses. The mitochondria were swollen, the rough endoplasmic reticulum was hyperplastic and vesicular, the lysosomes were increased, and no viral particles were seen.

case_report: A 28-year-old male patient presented with multiple, asymptomatic, skin-colored nodules on the forehead and scalp, persisting for 10 years. Initially appearing on the face, the lesions gradually extended to the scalp. The patient reported the emergence of new lesions and the enlargement of existing ones, both in size and number. Physical examination revealed multiple, nonpruritic, nontender, flesh-colored papules and nodules measuring between 0.3 to 1 cm in diameter. These lesions had a smooth surface and soft consistency, with some expressing yellowish, oily-to-cheesy material through a punctum, depending on the lesion's duration. There was no family history of similar lesions.
test_results: Histopathology revealed a cyst in the mid-dermis, characterized by 2- to 3-layered stratified squamous epithelium with absence of a granular layer, an eosinophilic, crenulated cuticle showing sharp invaginations into the lumen, and amorphous keratinous, eosinophilic material in the cyst cavity. Dermatoscopy was performed, both polarized and nonpolarized. The latter showed a yellowish structureless area with diffuse margins. However, on polarized dermoscopy, lesions showed a distinctive yellowish glow, surrounded by a darker rim, over a backdrop of a pseudoreticular pigmentary pattern. The yellow structureless area correlated with sebum contained in the cyst cavity. Vellus hairs, wherever entrapped in the cystic cavity, imparted a greenish tinge to the yellow area.

case_report: A 64-year-old woman presented with reduced vision. Her best-corrected visual acuity was counting fingers at three meters in the right eye and 6/18 (Snellen) in the left eye. The left eye appeared normal upon clinical examination. Central corneal thickness was measured at 668 micrometers in the right eye and 559 micrometers in the left eye.
test_results: Confocal microscopy findings in the right eye showed needle-shaped lesions suggestive of scarring in the stroma. Large vesicles were noted in the endothelium. The borders of the endothelial cells appeared indistinct. The left eye showed plenty of hyperreflective dot-like lesions in the endothelium and polymegathism. The endothelial cells could not be counted in the right eye due to indistinct cell margins while the endothelial cell density in the left eye was 1541 ± 45 cells/mm 3 (normal: 1250 to 2010 cells/mm 2).

case_report: A 57-year-old female patient, accompanied by her spouse, visited the Clinic for Cognitive Neurology at the University Hospital Leipzig, Germany, due to a gradual onset of visual impairment over the past 3 years. The patient, who worked as a secretary, reported difficulties with typing on a computer keyboard, using computer programs, and organizing schedules. Additionally, she and her husband noted challenges in daily activities, such as telling time on watches, maintaining lines while reading and writing, using a key to open doors, plugging in electrical devices, operating kitchen appliances, organizing cutlery, loading the dishwasher, storing shoes and clothing, dressing, and finding words. The patient described her visuospatial and visuoperceptual issues as “things don’t fit together” and “I cannot find any order.” Despite three ophthalmologic evaluations, no specific pathology was identified, though glasses were recommended. One year prior to admission, she was diagnosed with burn-out syndrome and prescribed the antidepressant venlafaxine. Structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) conducted 2 and 1 year before admission, along with visual evoked potentials (VEP), showed no abnormal findings.
test_results: A lumbar puncture revealed reduced amyloid-beta 1–42 levels and normal values for total and phospho tau as well as negative protein 14-3-3 in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). A structural MRI revealed brain atrophy especially in parietooccipital regions and, accordingly, enlargement of posterior ventricles. Single small white matter lesions did not reach pathologically relevant extent. Positron emission tomography (PET) with F18-fluorodesoxyglucose (FDG-PET) revealed glucose hypometabolism bilaterally in parietooccipital cortex, more pronounced on the right side, and in the right frontotemporal cortex. PET with F18-florbetaben showed amyloid accumulation in the gray matter of the neocortex (posterior cingulate, parietooccipital, and frontal cortex).
diagnosis: Posterior Cortical Atrophy  with underlying Alzheimer's disease

case_report: A 62-year-old female patient was transferred due to sudden onset of gait disturbance and radiating pain (VAS 7) in all extremities during admission at a gynecological clinic. She presented with a short neck and low posterior hairline. She had a 10-year history of posterior neck pain, occipital hypoesthesia, radiating pain and numbness in all extremities, and subjective gait disturbance. She had not sought medical attention previously as the symptoms were mild and did not interfere with daily activities. Neurological examination showed normal motor power in the arms, but there were positive Hoffmann's sign and mild spasticity bilaterally. She exhibited mild paraparesis (grade IV) with spasticity in the legs and an unstable gait. Pain and temperature sensation were normal, but proprioception was decreased in the legs bilaterally.
test_results: The forms of deformity, stenosis, and cord lesion were similar to those of case 1 on cervical spine radiograph, CT, and MRI. The ADI was 2.5mm on both flexion and extension lateral views without any definitive craniocervical instability. There were stenosis and spinal cord compression by anteriorly displaced C1 arch on preoperative CT and MRI.

case_report: The patient is a 14-day-old male infant. At 32 weeks of gestation, foetal ventriculomegaly was identified, leading to a referral to the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology at Takatsuki General Hospital in early March 2014. Foetal MRI revealed lissencephaly, hydrocephalus, an encephalocele, and cerebellar hypoplasia. The infant was delivered via caesarean section at 38 weeks and 4 days of gestation, with a birth weight of 2,543 grams and Apgar scores of 5 at 1 minute and 7 at 5 minutes. Muscle hypotonia was observed at birth, and serum creatine kinase levels were elevated at 12,530 IU/l. At 2 days old, the encephalocele was surgically repaired, and a ventriculoperitoneal shunt was placed to manage hydrocephalus. Respiratory status stabilized, and the infant was referred for an ophthalmological evaluation at 14 days old. Intraocular pressure was within normal limits: right eye 10.6 mm Hg and left eye 16.8 mm Hg. Both corneas were transparent, and no cataracts were detected, but a persistent hyaloid artery was noted posterior to the lens. Fundus examination revealed widespread loss of fundus pigmentation, visible choroidal vessels, and absence of a distinct macular reflex. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed no foveal pit, some laminar structure of the outer retinal layer, and an indistinct laminar structure of the inner retinal layer.
test_results: Genetic testing after birth showed a mutation in POMT1, a gene encoding glycosyltransferase.

case_report: A 74-year-old female arrived at the emergency department with hoarseness and difficulty swallowing following an incident of choking on chicken and subsequent vomiting. Gastroenterology performed an esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) which revealed Barrett’s esophagus but no foreign body. Post-EGD, the patient exhibited right facial droop, prompting a code stroke and a computed tomography arteriogram (CTA) of the head and neck. The CTA showed no acute bleeding but did reveal an area of enhancement along the medial aspect of the right temporal lobe. Neurology assessed the patient and suggested further imaging, which showed no signs of acute stroke. Otolaryngology (ENT) was consulted for the swallowing difficulty. Initial evaluation revealed right-sided facial nerve paralysis (House Brackmann 6/6) of unknown duration. The patient had a raspy voice but no airway compromise. Further physical examination identified vesicles over the medial aspect of the right antihelix and mild swelling with cellulitic changes to the right auricle, which was not tender to palpation.
test_results: MRI of the brain demonstrated a right-sided meningioma medial to the temporal lobe as well as subacute infarction of the corpus callosum. Flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy demonstrated a widely patent airway with a right-sided paralyzed true vocal cord with near complete glottic closure from compensation of the left true vocal cord.

case_report: A 19-year-old Asian male presented for an ophthalmologic examination due to sudden blurred vision in his left eye, which began 2 days after receiving the second dose of the Moderna SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccine. The day following the vaccination, he experienced a fever of 39.7°C and a headache. Three days post-vaccination, a physician noted macular discoloration and disruption of the macular ellipsoid zone, prompting a referral to our hospital. He visited our hospital 9 days after the vaccination. He had not received any treatment from the previous physician and had no history of systemic or ocular disease. Laboratory tests indicated that his complete blood count and levels of serum alanine transaminase, aspartate transaminase, alkaline phosphatase, creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, and C-reactive protein were within normal ranges. Initial ophthalmological examination revealed a best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 20/16 in both eyes. Intraocular pressure was measured at 12 mmHg in the right eye and 10 mmHg in the left eye. His pupillary light reflex was normal, with no relative afferent pupillary defect in either eye. Slit-lamp examination of the anterior segments and lenses of both eyes showed normal results. Bilateral fundoscopy revealed a clear vitreous and a small yellowish-white patchy discoloration of the fovea in the left eye.
test_results: OCT revealed a discontinuity in the fovea and temporal ellipsoid zone of the left eye. The choroidal thickness of the eye was within normal limits. Near-infrared reflectance (NIR) imaging of the left eye revealed multiple patchy hyporeflective lesions that involved the fovea and extended temporally. Fundus autofluorescence (FAF) showed hyperfluorescence in the area corresponding to the hyporeflective lesions on NIR. Visual field analysis performed using the Humphrey field analyzer (HFA) 10-2 program showed loss of sensitivity in the center of the left eye.

case_report: A 38-year-old male was admitted to the hospital due to a 3 cm right renal mass identified during a routine health check-up via abdominal ultrasonography and confirmed by computed tomography. He underwent a right radical nephrectomy, and the pathology report indicated clear cell type renal cell carcinoma with capsular invasion, but no distant metastasis. Preoperative serum calcium level was 10.9 mg/dL (normal range: 8.8-10.8 mg/dL). One year post-surgery, during a follow-up visit, he was referred to the Endocrinology and Metabolism department for persistent hypercalcemia. The serum calcium level was 11.1 mg/dL, inorganic phosphorus was 3.5 mg/dL (normal range: 2.5-4.5 mg/dL), serum alkaline phosphatase was 67 U/L (normal range: 30-120 U/L), intact PTH was 32 pg/mL (normal range: 10-65 pg/mL), and urine calcium was 20 mg/day (normal range: 100-300 mg/day). The ratio of urine calcium to creatinine clearance was 0.0019. Thyroid and adrenal hormone levels were within normal limits. There was no evidence of local recurrence or metastasis of carcinoma. Bone mineral density of the femoral neck and lumbar spine, assessed by dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry, was normal (femoral neck T-score: 1.0; lumbar spine T-score: -0.6).
test_results: The proband had a heterozygous mutation of E297K (GAG→AAG, Glu→Lys, nucleotide 889 G A, exon 4) of CaSR gene. The proband had a heterozygous loss of an Mnl I site.

case_report: An 8-year-old girl presented with cyanosis on the lips and loss of consciousness following physical activity. Upon examination, rales were heard on auscultation. She was initially treated for pneumonia with antibiotics and started on non-invasive ventilation for elevated carbon dioxide levels, which later required intubation and mechanical ventilation. Laboratory tests indicated low sodium levels and liver dysfunction. After 4 days, she was transferred to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit for further evaluation. She was born at term with normal birth weight and length, with no consanguinity between her parents and three healthy siblings. She experienced rapid weight gain and uncontrollable eating starting at age 5. Over the past month, her mother observed breath-holding during sleep and excessive sweating. During her hospital stay, she did not exhibit pain or distress during needle phlebotomy. Her weight was 50 kg (+3.52 SDS), height was 135 cm (+1.43 SDS), and her body mass index (BMI) was 27.4 kg/m2 (+3.44 SDS). Laboratory results showed sodium at 155 mmol/L (normal range: 135–145 mmol/L), aspartate transaminase at 315 U/L (normal range: 8–45 U/L), alanine aminotransferase at 798 U/L (normal range: 7–55 U/L), and urine density at 1,021. Other blood biochemical studies were normal. The hypernatremia was corrected to 141 mmol/L with intravenous fluid replacement therapy. Hormonal tests were normal, and pituitary imaging showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Pulmonary hypertension was detected in her echocardiography. Diffusion restriction in white matter was detected in cranial MRI. Widespread atelectasis on thorax CT.
Orpha_name: Rapid-onset childhood obesity-hypothalamic dysfunction-hypoventilation-autonomic dysregulation syndrome

case_report: A 28-year-old unmarried woman with regular menstruation experienced vaginal bleeding one week after her last menstrual cycle. Initial serum hCG level was 44,681 mIU/mL during the first examination at another hospital. Color Doppler ultrasound identified a teratoma approximately 3.8 × 3.4 cm in size in the right adnexa area. A hypoechoic mass, 3.1 × 2.1 cm in size, was noted in the left adnexal area, along with a strong adjacent echo, 1.5 × 1.3 cm in size. The patient had no abdominal pain or other discomfort and was advised to be hospitalized for surgical intervention. She declined the diagnosis of ectopic pregnancy and sought further evaluation at our hospital's Reproductive Department. Ultrasound examination revealed a teratoma sized 3.7 × 3.5 × 3.8 cm in the right ovary. A slightly strong echo, approximately 1.5 × 1.6 × 1.5 cm in size, was observed in the left ovary, with a distinct boundary and no blood flow signal detected. Another heterogeneous echogenic mass was detected in the left adnexal area, approximately 3.9 × 4.2 × 5.2 cm in size, with an unclear boundary between the mass and ovary and abundant blood flow signals. The patient exhibited elevated levels of serum hCG (137,822.2 mIU/mL) and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9) (102.6 U/mL; normal reference value < 30.9 U/mL), while other tumor markers such as cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), alpha-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and neuron-specific enolase were within normal ranges. Experts in gynecological oncology, gynecological radiochemotherapy, and medical imaging reviewed the case, supplemented with unenhanced and enhanced multidetector computed tomography images of the head, chest, abdomen, and pelvis, which showed no other lesions. The patient consented to laparoscopic surgery. No ascites were detected during surgery, and no abnormalities were found in the uterus, omentum, intestine, diaphragm, liver, or peritoneum. A mass approximately 6 cm in diameter was observed in the left ovary, presenting as a nodular, uneven, and kermesinus protrusion with dilated blood vessels on the surface. The tumor had a soft and fragile texture, with sections showing kermesinus and spongy characteristics, along with evident bleeding and necrosis. Additionally, the right ovary had a cyst approximately 4 cm in diameter, smooth in appearance and containing hair and fat. The ovarian tumors were resected, placed in specimen bags, and extracted via the trocar port in the abdomen.
test_results: Rapid freezing pathological examination revealed the following: <left ovarian tumor> a large number of dysplastic trophoblasts with hemorrhage and necrosis and no precise placental villi were observed; <right ovarian cyst> mature cystic teratoma.
diagnosis: stage IA mixed germ cell tumor of the left ovary
Orpha_name: Malignant non-dysgerminomatous germ cell tumor of ovary

case_report: A 1-month-old boy, the second child of a non-consanguineous marriage, was referred to the pediatric endocrine service. He was born full term via elective lower segment caesarean section, with a birth weight of 2.93 kg. Initial laboratory results showed serum phosphate at 1.43 mmol/L (reference range 1.64-2.47), serum calcium at 2.49 mmol/L (reference range 2.05-2.85), serum creatinine at 46 µmol/L (reference range 23-46), serum alkaline phosphatase at 332 U/L (reference range 70-350), and serum 25-hydroxy vitamin D at 46.3 µg/L (>30: normal). Urine phosphate was 4.2 mmol/L and urine creatinine was 0.7 mmol/L, with a normal urine phosphate to creatinine ratio of 6.0 (reference range 1.2-19). The calculated fractional excretion of phosphate was 19%, and the renal threshold for phosphate concentration was 1.18 mmol/100 mL glomerular filtration rate (GFR), which was higher than the normal range for infancy (reference range 0.15-0.34 mmol/100 mL GFR). He was monitored with serial growth and serum phosphate levels. At 3 months, he had very mild genu varus. Serum phosphate decreased to 1.13 mmol/L (reference range 1.64-2.47), and serum alkaline phosphatase increased to 434 U/L (reference range 70-350). The urine phosphate to creatinine ratio was 8.5 (reference range 1.2-19), and the renal threshold phosphate concentration was 0.92 mmol/100 mL GFR, still higher than the normal range for infancy. At 5 months, serum phosphate was 1.00 mmol/L, with a normal urine phosphate to creatinine ratio of 7.6 (reference range 1.2-19). The renal threshold for phosphate concentration was 0.98 mmol/100 mL GFR, which remained higher than the normal range of 0.12 to 0.26 mmol/100 mL GFR. At 7 months, his recumbent length was 69.0 cm (50th to 75th percentile), weight was 7.52 kg (25th to 50th percentile), and head circumference was 45.2 cm (90th to 97th percentile). The anterior fontanelle was small, and there was persistent mild genu varus with no flaring of the wrists or ankles. Serum phosphate was 1.05 mmol/L (reference range 1.64-2.47), serum alkaline phosphatase was 459 U/L (reference range 70-350), and the urine phosphate to creatinine ratio was 11.7 (reference range 1.2-19). The renal threshold for phosphate concentration was 0.84 mmol/100 mL GFR, which was above the normal range for infants. A plain radiograph of the lower limbs showed evidence of rickets with cupping and splaying of the metaphyses and bilateral genu varus.
test_results: Genetic testing of the PHEX gene demonstrated a novel splice-site mutation c.1080-2A>C.

case_report: A thirty-year-old man presented with a gradual onset of sensory neural hearing loss, ataxia, and spastic paraparesis over a period of seven years. His condition progressively worsened, and he also experienced severe headaches. He was admitted to the neurosurgery department with hydrocephalus and underwent shunting. The patient reported mild sphincter dysfunction but no issues with erectile function. He denied any problems with smell, vision, memory, seizures, or consciousness. There was no history of trauma, surgery, CNS tumors, or intracranial hemorrhage. He also had no history of intracranial or spinal surgery and no family history of similar conditions. General physical examination was unremarkable. Neurological examination showed bilateral hearing loss (air conduction greater than bone conduction), bilateral Babinski sign, dysarthria, spastic quadriparesis, and limb ataxia, with no sensory deficits. His mental state was normal, and he had no cognitive impairment, with an MMSE score of 28. Laboratory tests, including blood, urine, liver function, renal function, blood electrolytes, coagulation, thyroid function, folic acid, B12, and ferritin, were all within normal limits.
test_results: Brain MRI indicated low signal intensity coating the surface of the brain and spinal cord and atrophy of cerebellar vermis.
diagnosis: Idiopathic superficial siderosis of the central nervous system

case_report: A 6-month-old female child, born to parents who are second-degree relatives, exhibited developmental delay and multiple bluish-black spots on her body. According to the mother, these hyperpigmented macules were present on the buttocks and lower limbs since birth, with additional lesions developing on the anterior abdominal wall and back as the child grew. The lesions increased in size proportionally with the child's growth. On physical examination, the lesions were macular, blue-black, and varied in shape and size from a few millimeters to centimeters. The child had generalized hypotonia, hepatosplenomegaly, and facial features including a flat nasal bridge and a long philtrum. Ophthalmological examination revealed bilateral cherry red spots. Laboratory tests showed mild transaminitis with aspartate transaminase at 172 IU/L and alanine transaminase at 80 IU/L, while bilirubin levels were normal. Radiographic imaging indicated anterior beaking of the vertebrae and bullet-shaped phalanges. MRI of the brain showed subtle hyperintensity of the thalamus and a mixed pattern of myelination.
test_results: Low level of β-galactosidase activity (1.2% of mean normal) in leukocytes.

case_report: A four-month-old male patient, born to non-consanguineous parents from the countryside of São Paulo, was brought to our clinic with chronic diarrhea, protein-energy malnutrition, and skin lesions. Upon admission, the patient exhibited exulcerations with honey-colored hematic crusts on the anterior chest, upper limbs, dorsal area, face, and notably on the scalp. Additional findings included a cleft palate, ear deformities, sparse eyelashes and eyebrows, erythematous papules on the lower limbs, micropenis, nail dystrophy, and a history of surgery for ankyloblepharon.
test_results: Skin biopsy result suggested epidermolysis bullosa.

case_report: A 4-year-old girl, the first child of a healthy Portuguese couple, exhibited normal growth and neurodevelopment. At 2 years old, she experienced cardiorespiratory arrest following a respiratory viral infection. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) was detected in respiratory secretions, and Human herpesvirus 6 (HVV6) was found in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). During recovery, her lactate levels remained elevated (up to 5 mmol/L, normal range [NR] <2.0 mmol/L). Electrocardiogram, echocardiogram, and brain MRI results were normal. She was discharged with pending metabolic results but was lost to follow-up. At 3 years old, she was readmitted after another cardiac arrest due to acute respiratory insufficiency. Her parents reported nasal discharge, cough, fever, reduced appetite, and decreased activity over the previous 4 days. On the day of admission, she was lethargic and had difficulty breathing before the cardiorespiratory arrest. Post-resuscitation, her physical examination was normal except for rhonchi on pulmonary auscultation. Investigations showed persistently high lactate levels (2.3-4.1 mmol/L, NR <2.0 mmol/L), normal blood and CSF counts (CSF lactate not tested), negative C-reactive protein, and sterile blood culture. She did not have hypoglycemia, and her initially elevated liver enzymes and creatine kinase (CK) levels (3-4 times the upper normal limit) quickly normalized. Chest X-ray showed no pneumonia, and RSV was again isolated in respiratory secretions. Cardiac evaluations (electrocardiogram, echocardiogram, and continuous electrocardiographic recording) were normal. Immunodeficiency was ruled out with normal immunoglobulins, flow cytometry, and adequate vaccine responses. Plasma amino acids were normal, but acylcarnitines revealed low free carnitine (6.5 μM, NR 19-48 μM) with normal acetylcarnitine. Urinary organic acids on admission showed ketonuria and moderate excretion of 3-methylglutaconic acid (3-MGA) at 154 μmol/mmol creatinine (NR <19 μmol/mmol creatinine), mild excretion of 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid (3-OH-IVA) at 85 μmol/mmol creatinine (NR 10.4-67.0 μmol/mmol creatinine), and 3-hydroxymethylglutaric acid (3-HMG) at 93 μmol/mmol creatinine (NR 6.2-49.7 μmol/mmol creatinine).
test_results: At this point, she enrolled in a research study for the diagnosis of mitochondrial disorders by an NGS approach.

case_report: A 46-year-old woman reported a gradually enlarging, painless swelling inside her mouth over a period of 3 years, specifically located at the tip of her tongue. The patient had no prior health issues and no history of genetic or familial diseases. On physical examination, a well-defined, elastic, firm, non-tender mass was observed.
test_results: A spiral computed tomography (CT) study showed a round very well-delineated soft tissue mass centered in the muscle of the tip of the tongue with homogeneous hypodensity compared with that of muscle. Immunohistochemically, these neoplastic cells stained positively for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), but the tumor cells failed to stain for S100 protein, CD34 or smooth muscle actin (SMA).
diagnosis: Soft tissue perineurioma of the tongue

case_report: A 42-year-old male experienced abdominal discomfort for one month. Physical examination identified a hard mass in the left upper quadrant and tenderness in the left flank area. His medical history was clear, and laboratory tests showed no abnormalities. An abdominal CT scan revealed a large tumor with a hypodense lesion and a well-defined margin in the left perirenal space. A left partial nephrectomy was performed. Post-surgery, the patient recovered well, and imaging 24 months later showed no signs of local recurrence or distant metastasis. The tumor, measuring 10 cm at its largest point, was well-defined with a clear boundary from the surrounding thin renal tissue. It appeared white to yellowish in color and had a soft to firm consistency.
test_results: Histologically, at lower magnification, the tumor was clearly demarcated from the surrounding renal parenchyma, which seemed to originate from the renal capsule. In general, the tumor was hypocellular and showed alternating zones of collagenous and mucinous stroma. It was composed of spindle cells with tapering nuclei and elongated bipolar cytoplasmic processes arranged in a storiform and whorled architecture surrounding thin-walled small blood vessels. No atypia, mitosis or tumor necrosis was noted. IHC analyses revealed that the tumor cells were positive for EMA and CD34 and negative for claudin-1, GLUT1, S100 protein, MUC4, STAT6, SMA, HMB45 and P16. FISH studies demonstrated that the tumor was negative for amplification of MDM2 and rearrangements of EWSR1, FUS, and KMT2A. Genetic testing using targeted NGS for 425 cancer-relevant genes revealed a low level of TMB (0 mutations per megabase) and a likely pathogenic mutation of FLT1 at chromosome 13:28,964,050 with exon 13 c.1852 A > T(p.T618S, missense variant), which has a VAF of 1.5 %. No genomic alterations in NF1 or NF2 were present.
diagnosis: Soft tissue perineurioma involving the kidney

case_report: A 28-year-old woman with a history of mild hypothyroidism experienced sudden, painless left-sided foot drop at 16 weeks of her first pregnancy. MRI ruled out lumbar nerve root compression. Six weeks after symptom onset, electroneurographic and electromyographic tests showed an isolated axonal lesion of the sciatic nerve, mainly affecting the peroneal portion. There was no trauma history, and her family history was negative for neurofibromatosis type 1, hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy, or other neuromuscular diseases. She was advised to undergo physiotherapy focusing on strengthening exercises for the left tibialis anterior muscle. The paresis persisted throughout her pregnancy without additional neurological symptoms or sensory deficits. She had an uneventful Caesarean delivery at 40 weeks and gave birth to a healthy girl. A thorough neurological examination three weeks postpartum and a follow-up MRI of the lumbar spine were normal. Routine laboratory tests were unremarkable, and cerebrospinal fluid examination showed normal immunologic and infectiologic parameters, except for a slightly elevated protein level (730.4 mg/l). Intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIG) were administered for 3 days without improvement. The patient received a brace for her left leg and continued physiotherapy. One year later, follow-up examination revealed persistent weakness in the left foot (grade 2/5), toe extension (grade 3/5), and ankle eversion (grade 2/5). Electroneurography showed stable findings with prolonged distal motor latency in the tibialis and peroneus nerves and significantly reduced amplitudes in the peroneus nerve. Three years after the initial presentation, during her second pregnancy, she reported gradual worsening of the residual paresis in her left leg starting at 8 weeks of gestation and slight weakness in foot extension in the right leg. At 28 weeks of gestation, neurological examination showed complete palsy of left foot and toe extension, ankle eversion, and slight weakness in ankle inversion and plantar flexion (grade 4/5). The right leg exhibited paresis in foot and toe extension (grade 4+/5). Sensation remained normal, and the patient reported no pain. Motor nerve conduction studies indicated deterioration with absent conduction in the left peroneal nerve. A detailed history revealed a pattern of intermediate worsening of the paresis related to the menstrual cycle, occurring 2-3 days before menstruation.
test_results: MRI of the pelvis revealed bilateral fusiform irregular expansion of the sciatic nerves with separation of single nerve fascicles and hyperintensity on T2-weighted images. Compression of the nerves by other anatomical structures could be excluded.

case_report: The patient is a 9-year-old boy who presented with an abnormal gait persisting for 2 years. Around 2 years ago, he began experiencing an unstable gait accompanied by a left foot drop, leading to frequent falls during running and jumping, without any associated pain or numbness over the dorsum of the left foot. There was no history of trauma or preceding illness. Initially, these symptoms were not noticed by the family, and the condition gradually worsened. The patient was unable to stand on his left foot alone, and his left leg showed noticeable thinning compared to the right leg. One year ago, he underwent left peroneal tendon transfers, which did not result in any improvement in his gait. His developmental milestones were normal, and there were no complications during pregnancy or the perinatal period. The family denied consanguinity, and his parents and other family members were in good health. On examination, muscle strength in both upper extremities and the right lower extremity was grade V; proximal muscle strength in the left lower extremity was grade V, while distal muscle strength in the left lower extremity was grade IV. Muscle atrophy was observed in the distal left lower extremity. The patient exhibited reduced left ankle dorsiflexion and foot eversion, with normal plantar flexion and knee jerks. Sensation to light touch and pinprick was decreased over the dorsum of the left foot. There was no discrepancy in foot size or limb length between the lower limbs. Serum creatine kinase levels were within normal limits.
test_results: In electromyography (EMG) studies, an absent sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) was observed in the left sural nerve. The compound muscle action potential (CMAP) and F-wave latency in the left tibial nerve were mildly longer than those in the right tibial nerve, with normal conduction velocity. The CMAP latency in the left common peroneal nerve was significantly longer than that in the right common peroneal nerve, with prominently decreased conduction velocity and CMAP amplitude. MRI of both lower extremities demonstrated abnormal hyperintense signals on the T2-weighted images in the lateral portion of the left sciatic nerve. The involved portion of the nerve was moderately enlarged and enhanced on the postgadolinium images. The involvement of the left sciatic nerve extended from the level of the piriformis to the distal tibial nerve at the ankle level. Left sural nerve biopsy was performed at the ankle level. Histology of the biopsy specimen showed concentric whorls of perineural cells around the nerve fibers (onion-bulb like), and the lamellae of the onion bulbs were highlighted by the stain for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), while the centers were positive for S100 protein.

case_report: A 68-year-old female patient was admitted to the neurosurgical department with a chronic headache and a rapidly enlarging painful mass on her head. Physical examination identified a tender, 11×9 cm mass on the right frontal region of the skull. Her cranial nerve examination was normal. Imaging of the skull revealed significant lytic changes in the frontal bone. MRI of the head showed an extra-axial mass. MRI angiography indicated a bilateral shift of the anterior cerebral arteries due to the mass. A frontal craniotomy was performed, and the mass was partially removed. The mass was soft, highly vascular, and had a poorly defined border on the bone. It was attached to the dura without spreading into the brain tissue. The dura remained intact during the operation. Post-removal, the tumor tissue was fixed in 10% formalin solution, dehydrated with graded alcohols, and embedded in paraffin.
test_results: Hematoxylin-eosin stained sections of tumor revealed a monomorphous appearance of plasma cells with characteristic round-oval cells, eccentric nuclei, and abundant cytoplasm. The tumor cells were positive for κ-chain, CD138 and CD38. However, they were negative for cytokeratin, CD45, CD20, λ-chain, and CD3.
diagnosis: Solitary Plasmacytoma of the Frontal Bone

case_report: A 79-year-old female presented with abdominal pain persisting for two months. The pain was described as increasing in intensity, non-radiating, generalized, and diffuse. She also experienced generalized weakness. The patient did not report fever, chills, weight loss, night sweats, headache, chest pain, dysuria, melena, diarrhea, or constipation. Her medical history includes multiple myeloma in remission, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, and a past episode of complicated sigmoid diverticulitis. Surgical history includes subtotal colectomy with ileorectal anastomotic reconstruction, ventral hernia repair, and left nephrectomy. Physical examination revealed a firm abdominal wall mass without overlying skin changes or drainage. Blood tests showed leukocytosis with 15,800 leukocytes per microliter and a hemoglobin level of 8.8 g/dL. Liver function tests were within normal limits, with an alkaline phosphatase of 128 U/L, alanine transferase of 15 U/L, aspartate transferase of 23 U/L, total protein of 6.7 g/dL, and albumin of 3.4 g/dL. Computed Tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis without IV contrast identified a large mass-like structure in the anterior abdominal wall, extending into the abdomen and through the mesentery, partially involving the left hepatic lobe and distal stomach. The mass measured 17.9 x 15.9 x 8.5 cm, had soft tissue density with circumscribed margins, and measured 38 Hounsfield units without adjacent inflammatory changes. Additional masses were observed abutting the posterior right hepatic lobe and spleen, with a prominent mass in the mid-mesentery.
test_results: A core needle biopsy confirmed the presence of monoclonal CD138+ plasmacytoid cells consistent with a plasma cell neoplasm.

case_report: A 20-year-old woman presented to Gazi University Department of Prosthodontics with concerns about tooth discoloration, gaps between teeth, unsatisfactory appearance, and slight tooth sensitivity. Her medical and dental history indicated no family history of similar dental issues. A renal ultrasound scan was normal, showing no signs of nephrocalcinosis. Laboratory tests revealed normal levels of serum electrolytes, calcium, phosphate, urea, creatinine, alkaline phosphatase, and parathormone. Clinical examination revealed insufficient enamel thickness and discoloration of both anterior and posterior teeth. Panoramic radiography indicated that the thin enamel layer was indistinguishable from the underlying dentin. There were no anterior open bites or missing teeth, but additional findings included short crowns, multiple gaps between teeth, occlusal wear with exposed dentin in the posterior areas, poor contact points, and dental caries. The roots were of normal length and form, and the pulp chambers were regular in size. The patient's oral hygiene was acceptable with no signs of gingivitis. The maxillary and mandibular left third molar teeth were extracted. These teeth were completely covered by mucosa.
test_results: SEM analysis showed that there was an insufficient enamel layer. Histological findings revealed that dentin structure was intact and there was no irregularity in tubular structure.

case_report: A 20-year-old female patient presented with missing teeth. She reported a history of discolored primary teeth that exfoliated 8–10 years prior. Her medical history was non-contributory, with no major illnesses, prolonged hospitalizations, or medications. She had previously undergone root canal treatment on the mandibular right first molar and restoration of the maxillary left first molar. Family history indicated that her younger brother exhibited similar dental abnormalities. There was no history of consanguineous marriage between the parents. Intraoral examination showed erupted teeth at positions 17 (partially erupted), 16, 12, 11, 21, 26, 27 (partially erupted), 36, 31, 41, and 46. Generalized gingival hyperplasia was noted. The teeth exhibited generalized attrition of the cusp tips and incisal edges, resulting in shortened cervico-occlusal length and a yellowish-white smooth occlusal surface.
test_results: Intraoral periapical radiograph of the maxillary first molar region revealed the loss of enamel cap. Panoramic radiograph showed multiple impacted teeth with respect to 18, 15, 14, 13, 23, 24, 25, 28, 37, 35, 34, 33, 32, 42, 43, 44, 45 and 47. Panoramic radiograph also showed generalized loss of enamel cap, multiple pulp calcifications, and multiple dilacerations in the apical third of impacted and erupted teeth.

case_report: A 17-year-old male presented with concerns about missing teeth. His medical history was unremarkable. He had previously visited a dentist for restoration of the maxillary right first molar and extraction of a retained deciduous tooth in the maxillary anterior region. Extraoral examination showed no significant findings. Intraoral examination revealed the presence of erupted teeth at positions 16, 12, 11, 21, 22, 24, 26, 36, 35, 34, 32, 31, 41, 42, 44, 45, and 46. Retained deciduous teeth were observed at positions 54, 55, 63, 65, and 83. There was generalized attrition of the crowns with a yellowish-white smooth surface on the teeth.
test_results: Panoramic radiograph revealed generalized loss of enamel cap, multiple unerupted teeth, and pulp calcification with 17 and 26.

case_report: A 14-year-old male patient presented with yellow discoloration of teeth persisting for 5-6 years. Previous dental records indicated discolored primary teeth. Both anterior and posterior teeth across all segments exhibited brownish discoloration. The crowns of the upper and lower posterior teeth were reduced in height. The enamel and dentin were noted to be hard in consistency. There was no evidence of enamel chipping in any tooth.
test_results: Panoramic radiograph showed presence of a thin layer of enamel with radiodensity of enamel more than dentin.

case_report: Case 1, female, 35 years old, presented with no noticeable symptoms. In 2006, during a routine physical examination, an abnormality was incidentally discovered. Laboratory tests showed all parameters within normal ranges, including routine blood tests, serum electrolytes, liver function tests, and serum levels of twelve tumor markers. Tests for HAV, HBV, and HCV were all negative.
test_results: Computer Tomography (CT) showed multiple small hemangiomas of the patient's right hepatic lobe and one low-density lesion under the right hepatic lobe capsule. B-ultrasound showed the hypoechoic lesion with inhomogeneous internal echo. Gross examination: there was a 4 cm × 3 cm × 3 cm sized gray nodule into the part liver with the size of 5 cm × 5 cm × 3 cm, which boundary was clear with around congestive hemorrhage zone. The other send two pieces of tissue with purple-brown cut surface which size was 1.2 cm × 0.8 cm and 0.5 cm × 0.5 cm, respectively, were both diagnosed hemangiomas. Light microscope: the central part of nodule was eosinophilic coagulation necrosis lesion which could be seen a small amount of cell ghosts of remaining liver cells and multinucleated giant cells. In the meanwhile, the stove gathered inflammatory cells could also be seen, which included lymph cells, histocytes, neutrophils, and plasma cells. Fibrous tissue wrapped around the necrotic area, in which fibrous tissue produced hyperplasia with hyaline degeneration, accompanying infiltration of inflammatory cells including small-to-moderate amount of lymphocytes, and some eosinophils, plasma cells, monocytes, and multinucleated giant cells. The liver tissue surrounding the nodule were mild edema, cholestasis, and steatosis. Liver sinus filled the blood. Fibrous tissue of portal area was mild hyperplasia with a few of lymphocyte infiltration. Sublobular and interlobular veins were expansion. Immunohistochemistry and histochemistry staining: periodic acid-Schiff reaction (PAS) was negative, negative for acid-fast staining and iron staining, and Ag + Van gieson (Ag + VG) staining showed that the outline of reticular fibers and collagen was intact. Vimtin (Vim) was positive for necrotic tissue and surrounding fibrous tissue. CD34 was positive for a great number of blood vessels ghosts, CD68 was diffuse positive. Cytokeratin (CK) was positive for a few residual cells.
diagnosis: Solitary Necrotic Nodule  of the liver
Orpha_name: Solitary necrotic nodule of the liver

case_report: A 30-year-old Caucasian male with no prior medical history presented at the Emergency Department with acute pain in the right upper quadrant, a high-grade fever of 38.5°C, and vomiting. Laboratory tests showed significant leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 19,810/ml and abnormal liver function tests, including AST at 218 IU/L, ALT at 280 IU/L, ALP at 123 IU/L, γ-GT at 147 IU/L, and total bilirubin at 0.84 mg/dl. Serology tests for hepatitis B and C were negative. There was no documented history of alcohol abuse.
test_results: Abdominal US revealed a 7 cm hyperechoic lesion at the right liver lobe. Computed tomography demonstrated a single lesion, located in segments V and VI, with hemorrhagic features. After contrast administration the lesion appeared to be encapsulated with peripheral enhancement, a necrotic core and contrast wash out at the venous phase. A CT-guided core-needle biopsy was performed and revealed numerous lymphocytes and necrotic material but not atypia.
diagnosis: Solitary necrotic nodule of the liver due to sinusoidal portal vein thrombosis
Orpha_name: Solitary necrotic nodule of the liver

case_report: A 76-year-old Japanese female, with no prior medical history and no symptoms, visited our hospital after an abdominal ultrasonography (US) incidentally revealed a heterogeneous hypoechoic lesion in liver segment VI. Routine laboratory tests, including liver function tests, serology for hepatitis B and C, and tumor markers such as CA 19-9, alpha-Fetoprotein, and CEA, showed no abnormalities. There was no documented history of alcohol abuse. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) showed a 1.1 cm low-density lesion with mild ring enhancement on the rim during the arterial phase, located in liver segment VI. Further evaluation was conducted.
test_results: The specimen showed necrotic tissue with trabecular pattern alignment of reticulin fibers in silver stain. The immunohistochemistry examination showed no positive staining with CK7, CK19, CK20, and hepatocyte in the tissue. Histologically, the liver nodule was necrotic tissue without viable cells and signs of inflammation, which had fibrous capsule and central cystic change. In silver stain, the nodule showed trabecular pattern alignment of ghost cells and reticulin fibers orthogonal to the capsule.
diagnosis: Solitary necrotic nodule of the liver
Orpha_name: Solitary necrotic nodule of the liver

case_report: A 50-year-old male with a history of lumbar herniated disc surgery at age 37 and hypertension managed with medication since age 42 presented with epigastric pain and difficulty swallowing that began 3 months prior. He was referred to our hospital following findings of external compression observed during a gastroscopic examination at a local clinic. Initial physical examination showed normal heart and lung sounds, a flat and soft abdomen without tenderness, and no palpable superficial lymph nodes. Hematological and biochemical tests were within normal limits.
test_results: Gastroscopy revealed a submucosal tumor with a smooth surface at the 9 o'clock position in the lower esophagus. Barium esophagogram showed extrinsic compression from the lower esophagus to the gastroesophageal junction. Good expansion and smooth mucosa were noted. Endoscopic ultrasonography showed a cystic mass in the esophageal wall extending from the lower esophagus to the cardiac region of the stomach, with the suspected presence of viscous fluid inside the cyst. Computed tomography (CT) showed an iso-enhanced dumbbell-shaped mass (3.5 × 3 cm) with a smooth surface and homogeneous content, which extended from the lower thoracic esophagus to the cardiac region of the stomach. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a mass that was hyperintense and moderately hyperintense on T1- and T2-weighted imaging, respectively, with and without fat suppression.

case_report: A 52-year-old woman was referred to our hospital following an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy conducted during a routine health check-up at a local community hospital. The endoscopy revealed a submucosal tumor without ulceration in the distal esophagus. The patient reported no history of gastrointestinal symptoms such as difficulty swallowing or upper abdominal pain. Both physical examination and standard laboratory tests showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Barium esophagography showed a well defined filling defect arising from the anterior left side of the distal esophagus. The chest computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a unilocular cystic mass, measuring 4×3 cm, and it was not enhanced by contrast dye. Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) demonstrated a heterogenous hypoechoic mass within the muscularis propria of the esophagus.

case_report: A 2-month-old male infant presented with a history of fever and increased respiratory rate for 3 days. The infant was born full term, weighing 2600 g, via caesarean section to a first-time mother. Both antenatal and perinatal periods were uneventful. Physical examination revealed tachycardia, tachypnea with subcostal retractions, and an oxygen saturation of 88% on room air. There were no facial abnormalities or other obvious congenital malformations. Bilateral rhonchi were noted upon chest auscultation, while other systemic examinations were normal. Hemogram and other biochemical tests were within normal limits. A chest radiograph showed bilateral hyperinflation. The infant was given supportive treatment. Despite these measures, wheezing persisted after 7 days.
test_results: The bronchoscopy revealed external airway compression. MRI scan of the neck revealed a well-defined lobulated smoothly marginated lesion of altered signal intensity in pre-/left para-esophageal region at subcarinal level. Lesion was abutting the esophagus medially, trachea anteriorly and aortic arch laterally.

case_report: A 29-year-old male patient presented with a 7-day history of high-grade fever accompanied by chills and vomiting. For the past 2 days, he also had a skin rash primarily located on the abdomen and trunk. Upon admission, he developed a hemorrhagic rash. There were no notable findings in his family or past medical history. Physical examination revealed an unstable general condition with cyanosis. The patient was febrile, had a pulse rate of 90 beats per minute, and a systolic blood pressure of 70 mm Hg. Neurological examination indicated positive Kerning and Brudzinski signs. The rash was observed over the entire body, with a concentration on the abdomen and trunk.
test_results: CT scan confirmed adrenal hemorrhage.

case_report: A 62-year-old female with a history of diabetes mellitus, asthma, HIV/AIDS with a CD4 count of 494, and substance use disorder experienced dizziness at a methadone clinic. Emergency Medical Services found her hypotensive with a MAP <65, leading to her admission to the Emergency Department. Despite fluid resuscitation of 30 cc/kg, she remained hypotensive and exhibited tachycardia and tachypnea. She also reported nausea, vomiting, and chronic neck and back pain, typically managed with methadone. Clinical examination showed worsening mentation, necessitating endotracheal intubation for airway protection. On cardiac monitoring, she had wide complex tachycardia, which persisted after electrical cardioversion attempts but resolved following administration of 2 g of magnesium sulfate and 150 mg of intravenous amiodarone bolus. She was then started on an amiodarone drip of 1 mg/kg for six hours followed by 0.5 mg/kg and maintained on norepinephrine for hemodynamic support. Laboratory results revealed a lactic acid level of 10.10 mmol/L and a white blood cell count of 26.3 x10^3/uL with a left shift. She was admitted to the medical intensive care unit for presumed septic shock, suspected secondary to acute cholecystitis. Ultrasonography showed minor pericholecystic fluid, gallbladder wall thickening, and a gallstone. Surgical intervention was ruled out based on imaging findings showing cholelithiasis without biliary dilatation. Norepinephrine was discontinued due to its chronotropic effects, while vasopressin and phenylephrine were continued. Blood cultures were sent, and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, including cefepime, vancomycin, and metronidazole, were administered. Blood cultures later showed Gram-negative coccobacilli. The patient was transferred to the medical intensive care unit (MICU) for further management. An initial lumbar puncture was attempted but failed; a repeat lumbar puncture was performed days later using fluoroscopic guidance by interventional neurology, revealing significant cerebrospinal fluid findings.
test_results: The CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis disclosed a minor bilateral adrenal hemorrhage with Hounsfield units of 46.47.

case_report: Patient 4 is a 75-year-old man with 5 years of education, working as a dealer. In 1999, he experienced a car accident while driving on an overpass with his 5-year-old grandchild. The car was suspended over a canyon for one hour before being secured and rescued by the breakdown service. The patient experienced recurring dreams of the accident for 3 months and developed anxiety, leading to an inability to drive. He was treated with antidepressants, benzodiazepines, and psychotherapy, which alleviated his symptoms within a year. He resumed normal activities and driving. Three years later, the patient exhibited reduced language abilities with occasional difficulty in naming objects. The following year, he developed difficulties with arithmetic and exhibited challenges in planning tasks, such as ordering foodstuffs for his grocery store. The patient was referred to our memory clinic.
test_results: An MRI scan showed the presence of initial regional left-sided atrophy in the temporal and frontal lobe. EEG recording at rest showed a dominant frequency stable at 8.0 Hz in posterior derivations and delta-theta activity at 3–6 Hz in temporal derivations. He underwent lumbar puncture which showed increased level of tau and phospho-tau proteins (total tau 401 pg/ml, phosporylated-tau protein 98 pg/ml, Aβ 1-42 level 856 pg/mL).

case_report: Patient 3 is a 69-year-old man with 17 years of education and a background as a retired middle school teacher. In 1999, while teaching a chemistry class, an individual entered the classroom, brandishing a firearm and making threats. The intruder forced the patient and students to listen to him for several hours until law enforcement intervened and apprehended the individual. Following this incident, the patient experienced significant distress, including anxiety, agitation, insomnia, and frequent crying. He was treated with benzodiazepines and sertraline 100 mg daily. The patient returned to work and reported improvement for three years. Subsequently, he began experiencing episodes of word-finding difficulties during teaching and forgetfulness in daily activities, such as misplacing keys and forgetting the location of his parked car. He also reported challenges in performing sequential tasks, including meal preparation and driving.
test_results: MRI showed frontal atrophy more prominent in the left hemisphere. EEG showed posterior dominant frequency stable at 10 Hz, with inscription of theta sequences and sharp waves in temporal derivations. Lumbar puncture showed increased level of tau and phospho-tau proteins (total tau 385 pg/ml, phosphorylated-tau protein 77 pg/ml, Aβ 1-42 level 878 pg/mL).

case_report: A 61-year-old, right-handed male experienced a sudden alteration in mental status following a notable decline in functionality over the past 2 years. Previously, he was highly functional and held an executive position at a Fortune 500 company. The change in mental status included several behavioral alterations such as cruelty toward family members and pets, promiscuity, adultery, drug abuse, excessive spending, and a lack of empathy. His family also observed changes in his speech patterns, specifically in phonation and pronunciation of words. Initially, he was treated for bipolar disorder but did not respond to mood-stabilizing medications. After losing his job, he was admitted to the psychiatric ward due to suicidal tendencies.
test_results: The MRI demonstrated diffuse parenchymal atrophy, which was slightly more extensive in the temporal lobes. There was a lacunar infarct in the right thalamus. The resultant PET/MR images demonstrated a pattern of decreased FDG uptake that was predominantly confined to the temporal lobes and was particularly severe in the amygdalae and hippocampi. The decrease in activity was greater on the left side and extended superoposteriorly toward the parietal lobe and Wernicke's area. The other atrophic areas and white matter changes seen on the MRI had intact glucose metabolism. The lacunar infarct also had decreased FDG uptake.

case_report: A 62-year-old woman was found to have a positive fecal occult blood test during a medical examination. An endoscopy performed by her previous physician revealed a tumor in the ascending colon, and a biopsy indicated poorly differentiated cancer. She was referred to our institution for surgical intervention.
