Blood tests showed carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels at 76.1 ng/mL (normal range < 5.0 ng/mL) and carbohydrate antigen (CA) 19-9 levels at 192 U/mL (normal range < 37 U/mL). Colonoscopy identified a semicircular type 3 tumor opposite the Bauhin valve in the ascending colon. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) revealed wall thickening with contrast enhancement in the ascending colon, enlarged peripheral lymph nodes, and a uterine leiomyoma. An 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron-emission tomography (FDG-PET) scan showed FDG uptake at the lesion in the wall of the ascending colon (SUVmax 22.9), peripheral lymph nodes (SUVmax 23.8), peritoneum of the left upper abdomen (SUVmax 13.4), and pelvic floor on the left dorsal side (SUVmax 5.2). Based on these findings, the tumor was considered a malignant neoplasm of the ascending colon with peritoneal dissemination. Ileocecal resection was performed, and numerous intra-abdominal nodules were observed during the operation, indicating peritoneal dissemination.
test_results: keratin-positive, chromogranin-negative, synaptophysin-positive, CD56-positive, alcian blue/periodic acid Schiff-negative, and MIB-1 index of 57%.
diagnosis: Large Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma  in the ascending colon with inguinal lymph node metastasis

case_report: A 55-year-old Turkish woman reported experiencing hoarseness for two years. She had no history of tobacco or alcohol use and had been managing diabetes mellitus for three years. Her medical history was otherwise unremarkable, and her family history did not contribute any relevant information. An endoscopic laryngeal examination revealed a mass in the supraglottic region, affecting the laryngeal surface of the epiglottis and the medial aspect of the pyriform sinus. Vocal cord mobility was observed to be normal. Neck examination showed no palpable lymphadenopathy. The rest of the otorhinolaryngological, general physical, and pulmonary examinations did not reveal any abnormalities. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, Westergren erythrocyte sedimentation rate, glucose level, and electrolytes, were within normal ranges. Cervical computed tomography (CT) identified a supraglottic mass extending from the right medial glossoepiglottic fold to the right aryepiglottic fold and pyriform sinus, with involvement of the parapharyngeal fat tissue. No lymphadenopathy was detected on cervical CT. Thoracic and abdominal CT scans showed no evidence of metastases or additional lesions. Under general anesthesia, direct suspension laryngoscopy was performed, revealing a laryngeal mass with a smooth surface. Multiple punch biopsies were taken from the mass.
test_results: Pathological examination of the biopsy showed tumor infiltration, with trabeculae and small nests of round eosinophilic cells with uniform hyperchromatic nuclei, displaying a 'salt and pepper' chromatin pattern. There was no marked pleomorphism or necrosis. The cells were strongly immunopositive for neuron-specific enolase, chromogranin, synaptophysin and pancytokeratin.
diagnosis: Typical carcinoid tumor of the larynx

case_report: In January 2006, a 32-year-old male visited our otolaryngology department for a second opinion regarding a seven-year history of fullness in the right ear and mild hearing loss. Five years earlier, he had been evaluated by an otorhinolaryngologist for right-sided ear pain and facial paralysis on the same side. He was treated with oral amoxicillin and steroids for a suspected middle ear infection with facial paralysis. A few months later, an antero-inferior myringotomy was performed due to a presumed middle ear effusion, but no fluid or mass was found. The patient reported no ear discharge, vertigo, tinnitus, visual symptoms, headaches, or any other significant past or present illnesses. Otoscopy revealed a posterosuperior retrotympanic mass with a normal tympanic membrane. Audiometry indicated a mixed hearing loss in the right ear. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the temporal bone showed opacity in the superior part of the middle ear extending into the mastoid cavity, with no bone erosion or ossicular destruction, consistent with chronic otomastoiditis.
test_results: Histologic examination of the excised tumor showed an epithelial neoplasm with a predominantly glandular architecture embedded in fibrous tissue. The tumor was composed of cuboidal cells with uniform nuclei and no identifiable mitotic activity or necrosis. Focally, the tumor cells had a well-developed plasmacytoid morphology. Single cells were also seen infiltrating into the fibrous stroma. An immunohistochemical evaluation showed strong positivity for neuron specific enolase (NSE) and synaptophysin and weak positivity for chromogranin.

case_report: A 64-year-old female with a history of hypertension and headaches presented with a 2-year history of progressively worsening pulsatile tinnitus and a sensation of ear fullness that did not improve with medical treatment. She recently developed left-sided ear pain but reported no ear discharge, sudden changes in hearing, or any past injuries or surgeries to her ears. Physical examination revealed an intact left tympanic membrane with a red mass located deep in the posteroinferior quadrant. The external auditory canal appeared normal. Audiologic testing indicated mild to moderate mixed hearing loss in the left ear, with a mild sensorineural component and a type A tympanogram.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) of the temporal bones demonstrated an enhancing soft tissue mass arising from the hypotympanum, adjacent to the inferior tympanic canaliculus. CT angiogram identified a tumor blush in left tympanic region supplied by left ascending pharyngeal artery.

case_report: A 65-year-old female patient of South American descent presented to the surgical outpatient department with a one-year history of intermittent post-meal epigastric pain, nausea, bloating, and occasional diarrhea. She did not smoke or consume alcohol. Her medical history included a cesarean section and a total abdominal hysterectomy. There was no family history of cancer. On physical examination, her abdomen was soft and non-tender. Laboratory tests showed mildly abnormal liver function with a bilirubin level of 16 umol/L (reference range <20), alkaline phosphatase (ALP) at 87 U/L (reference range 30-110), gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) at 17 U/L (reference range <38), alanine transaminase (ALT) at 48 U/L (reference range <34), and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 38 U/L (reference range <31).
test_results: An ultrasound performed by her general practitioner revealed an unusual gallbladder appearance and irregular thickening of her gallbladder wall up to 8 mm. The MRCP revealed a 10 x 15 x 23 mm focal gallbladder wall thickening in the medial aspect of the fundus which was isointense on T1 with restricted diffusion. There were no internal T2 hyperintensities within this region. The MRCP also demonstrated an anomalous pancreatobiliary junction with a 23 mm long common channel. There was a focal narrowing of the distal common bile duct (CBD) at the site where it joined the dilated common channel and there was no evidence of cholelithiasis or choledocholithiasis. A positron emission tomography (PET) demonstrated moderate to intense fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) avidity in the area of abnormal enhancement and wall thickening in the gallbladder body. There was no evidence of FDG avid nodal metastases in the abdomen or peritoneal metastases. There was a single moderate to intensely FDG avid upper mediastinal lymph node, immediately anterior to the trachea (2R). There was also focal moderate FDG uptake in the distal thoracic esophagus. The patient underwent a gastroscopy and biopsy of the lower esophagus which revealed Los Angeles (LA) classification grade B esophagitis. There was no dysplasia or malignancy present. Endoscopic bronchial ultrasound-guided biopsy of the PET avid pre-tracheal node was consistent with a reactive lymph node with no malignant cells identified.
diagnosis: Large Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma of the Gallbladder with Mixed Adenocarcinoma Component

case_report: A 75-year-old woman presented to our cardio-oncology clinic with worsening shortness of breath, fatigue, swelling in the legs, and occasional palpitations. Her medical history included a diagnosis of gastrointestinal neuroendocrine neoplasia with liver metastasis identified through ultrasound imaging and endoscopy four years prior. Due to the inoperability of her condition, she was treated primarily with alkalizing agents. She was also managed for heart failure with medications such as aspirin, atorvastatin, losartan, MetoHEXAL, and furosemide, but did not have regular follow-ups. Additionally, she had a history of long-term hypertension. During the physical examination, her heart rate was approximately 80 beats per minute, and her blood pressure was around 140/75 mm Hg. Breath sounds were reduced over the right lower lung field, and jugular venous pressure was normal. Cardiac examination revealed normal first and second heart sounds and a grade II/VI systolic ejection murmur along the left sternal border. There was noticeable lower limb edema without cyanosis. The patient had previously undergone 2D transthoracic echocardiography, but the results were unavailable; therefore, a comprehensive 2D TTE examination was performed at our clinic.
test_results: The findings were normal left ventricular size with mild systolic dysfunction and diastolic dysfunction; severe right atrial (RA) and right ventricular (RV) enlargement with RV dysfunction; a thickened, retracted, and semi-mobile tricuspid valve; severe free tricuspid regurgitation caused by the absence of leaflet cooptation; and no valvular stenosis. The assessment of the pulmonary valve also showed thickened, malcoapted valves with severe insufficiency, but without stenosis. Moreover, the left heart valves were mildly thickened.

case_report: A 22-year-old male from Turkey reported experiencing intermittent daily headaches over the past five years, localized to the left retro-orbital and orbital regions. The pain was unilateral, occasionally shifting sides within the same episode. He experienced between four and twenty episodes per week, leading to significant social distress. The headaches began suddenly, reaching peak intensity within five minutes, and lasted between 30 and 120 minutes without any preceding aura or identifiable triggers. During these episodes, he experienced rhinorrhea, lacrimation, and ptosis, but did not report nausea, vomiting, or photophobia. Previous treatments included verapamil 160 mg three times daily, naproxen 500 mg three times daily, ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily, dexketoprofen trometamol 25 mg twice daily, indomethacin 25 mg three times daily, loratadine 5 mg daily, and prednisolone 60 mg daily, all without success. Both general and neurological examinations conducted between episodes, as well as hematological and biochemical screenings, were normal. There was no significant past medical history or family history of headaches.
test_results: An ophthalmological examination revealed lacrimation, conjunctival injection and ptosis without miosis. Pupils measured 3.5 mm, with normal pupillary reactions to both light and near stimulation. The magnetic resonance (MR) images of his brain and orbit and MR angiography of his brain and carotid artery were within normal limits.

case_report: A 21-year-old female, two months postpartum, presented with a three-day history of fainting episodes. The first episode happened when her son triggered her cell phone alarm, and the second occurred while her son was playing a loud video game. She was monitored in the emergency department and experienced another fainting episode, during which she was found to be in polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (PVT).
test_results: EKG revealed a QTc of 530 msec. The patient was also found to be hypokalemic. Her QT interval remained prolonged following repletion.

case_report: A 4-year-old boy of Arab origin was first evaluated for elevated calcium levels at the age of 9 months following an episode of febrile convulsion. Routine laboratory tests at that time revealed increased calcium levels. His parents are nonconsanguineous. He was born late preterm at 35 weeks gestation via normal vaginal delivery, with no significant postnatal complications and was discharged home after birth. His surgical history includes the repair of bilateral inguinal hernia. Family history includes congenital heart disease in the mother, specifically pulmonary stenosis treated with balloon dilatation, and a sister with PDA (patent ductus arteriosus) closed by catheterization. The mother has alpha-thalassemia trait, and the father had bilateral congenital cataract. Upon admission and further evaluation for elevated calcium levels, the patient exhibited persistent low urinary calcium to creatinine ratio adjusted for age, slightly elevated magnesium levels, normal PTH, phosphate, and vitamin D levels, and high alkaline phosphatase. The mother was also found to have elevated calcium levels, low urinary calcium, normal magnesium, phosphate, and alkaline phosphatase, and low vitamin D levels. Physical examination of the boy revealed subtle facial dysmorphic features including upslanting palpebral fissures, wide mouth, and high-arched palate, with normal growth parameters. Comprehensive evaluations including karyotype analysis, FISH for Williams syndrome, renal ultrasound, brain CT, and echocardiography were all normal.
test_results: WES confirmed a heterozygous mutation in the AP2S1 gene, on chr19_47349359 C>T, c.44G>A, p.Arg15His in both the proband and his mother.

case_report: A 63-year-old male patient, 164 cm tall and weighing 68 kg, with an American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status score of III, was scheduled for left hip arthroplasty under general anesthesia due to hip osteoarthritis. He had been experiencing bilateral hip pain and was referred for management. His medical history included chronic rheumatoid arthritis since age 56 and a ten-year history of diabetes mellitus managed with dietary therapy and oral medications. He had been diagnosed with pneumonia four times since age 60. He reported no relevant family history. Preoperative complete blood count showed a hemoglobin concentration of 10.5 g·dL-1, while other laboratory studies, including electrolytes, renal function, blood glucose, liver function, hemostasis evaluation, and urinalysis, were normal. Pulmonary function tests indicated reductions in forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) and forced vital capacity (FVC) to 57.6% and 55.1% of predicted values, respectively, with a preserved FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.79. Electrocardiography revealed atrial fibrillation, and echocardiography showed first-degree mitral regurgitation with mild left atrial and left ventricular enlargements. Anesthesia was induced with 100 µg of fentanyl, 0.4 µg·kg-1·min-1 of remifentanil, and a target-controlled infusion (TCI) of 3.0 µg·mL-1 of propofol. Rocuronium (50 mg [0.73 mg·kg-1]) was administered for tracheal intubation. Anesthesia was maintained with 0.12-0.4 µg·kg-1·min-1 of remifentanil and a propofol TCI of 1.7 µg·mL-1. Neuromuscular blockade was monitored using an acceleration-sensing muscle relaxation monitor (TOF-Watch™). The accelerometer sensor was attached to the left thumb, and electrical stimulation was performed at the ulnar nerve proximal to the wrist. The train-of-four (TOF) was measured at a 2-Hz stimulation frequency with a current amplitude of 50 mA and a pulse width of 0.2 msec. Monitoring began after rocuronium administration, with an initial TOF count of 0. No additional rocuronium was given during the 273-minute surgery. The TOF count of the left arm remained at 0 throughout the surgery, prompting a temporary move of the accelerometer to the right arm, which also showed a TOF count of 0. At the end of surgery, 300 mg of sugammadex was administered. After five minutes, the TOF count and posttetanic contraction count (PTC) were 0 and 2, respectively. Additional doses of sugammadex (200 mg, 200 mg, 300 mg within 20 minutes, and 200 mg at 60 minutes post-surgery) were administered. The patient communicated by blinking ten minutes after cessation of intravenous anesthesia but could not breathe. Despite a total sugammadex dose of 1,200 mg, the TOF ratio of the left adductor pollicis muscle was 0, and the PTC was 6. The patient remained intubated and was mechanically ventilated under continuous midazolam sedation at 3 mg·hr-1, maintaining the Richmond Agitation Sedation Scale at -1 to -2. No adverse events such as hypotension, bradycardia, bronchospasm, or hypersensitivity reactions were observed during sugammadex administration. Eighteen hours after rocuronium administration, the patient could breathe spontaneously. The TOF ratio of the right adductor pollicis muscle recovered to > 0.9, but the left adductor pollicis muscle remained at 0. He was able to grip with his hands, and his trachea was extubated. Arterial blood gases ten minutes after extubation, on oxygen via face mask, were: pH 7.40; partial pressure of carbon dioxide 45 mm Hg; partial pressure of oxygen 178 mm Hg; and base excess 2.1. Postoperative physical examination revealed superficial sensory loss predominantly in the distal parts of both feet, pes cavus, and weakness in both the tibial and upper limb muscles. In a postoperative interview, he reported muscle loss over the past five years, recent difficulty opening plastic bottle lids, and stumbling while walking.
test_results: Conduction delay in the nerve transmission velocity of 20 m·sec-1 and mutated duplication of the PMP22 gene.

case_report: A 10-month-old male presented with recurrent fever, cough, tachypnea, and cyanosis for 8 days, following a history of antibiotic therapy. He was admitted to the emergency department with respiratory distress requiring ventilatory support. Initial blood gas analysis revealed: pH 7.35; PCO2 32 mmHg; PO2 71.3 mmHg; BE -7.0; HCO3 18.9 mmol/L; and Lac 1.5. Routine blood tests showed white blood cell count of 11,000/mm³ with 9.1% segmented cells, 81.6% lymphocytes, 5.2% eosinophils, platelet count of 288,000/mm³, and hemoglobin of 10.7 g/dL. C-reactive protein was 8 mg/L. Chest computed tomography indicated diffuse nonsegmental ground glass opacity in both lungs and left axillary lymph node calcification. Noninvasive ventilation was used to maintain oxygen supply. Pulse oximetry showed SpO2 of 80% in room air, increasing to 98% with 5 L/min oxygen. On day 2, extended pathogen screening, immunological evaluation, and metabolic markers were initiated. Immunologic assessment revealed low IgG (<1.39 g/L), low IgA (<0.0647 g/L), and elevated IgM (1.89 g/L). Complement proteins C3 and C4 were 0.912 g/L and 0.167 g/L, respectively. Blood and urine genetic metabolism screening were normal. Serologic tests for common viruses were normal, and the PPD test for tuberculosis was negative. ELISA tests for IgG and IgM against mycoplasma were negative. Sputum and blood cultures were normal. EBV and CMV-DNA analyses were negative. A multiplex PCR test for respiratory viruses from a nasopharyngeal swab showed positive CMV-LRB-2.60E+8 copies. The G-test was positive (152.4 pg/mL), while the GM-test was normal. Next-generation sequencing for nasopharyngeal swabs was performed, with results detailed in Table. The patient was treated for pneumonia from PCP combined with CMV and fungal infection.
test_results: Genetic analysis performed through whole-exome sequencing (WES) and Sanger sequencing of CD40LG revealed amino acid changes in exon 1 of CD40LG (C.86_87del).

case_report: A 5-year-old boy presented with recurrent fever for 1.5 months and intermittent pain in the right hypochondrium along with vomiting for 1 month. On examination, he had tender hepatomegaly and pallor. Imaging revealed multiple small hypodense lesions in the liver indicative of microabscesses. Laboratory results showed hemoglobin at 8.8 gm/dL, WBC count at 17,400/mm3, platelet count at 438,000/mm3, bilirubin at 0.8 mg/dL, SGOT at 102 IU/L, SGPT at 68 IU/L, total proteins at 5.5 gm/dL, and albumin at 2.4 gm/dL. Stool examination revealed cysts of E. histolytica, and blood culture did not grow any organism. HIV ELISA was negative. He was initially treated with IV piperacillin/metronidazole and oral chloroquine for 10 days without response. Subsequently, he experienced a drop in hemoglobin level, leukocytosis (34,500/mm3), and thrombocytopenia, necessitating 5 units of blood transfusion. Antibiotics were changed to vancomycin and ceftazidime. He also developed ascites, and ascitic fluid analysis showed 1920 cells/mm3 (80% polymorphs, 20% lymphocytes). Urine examination revealed the presence of fungal hyphae, and the child was treated with amphotericin B.
test_results: Serum immunoglobulins showed low serum IgG (530 mg/dL (normal = 971-1746 mg/dL)), normal IgA (104 mg/dL (normal = 75-178 mg/dL)), and high serum IgM (183 mg/dL (normal = 66-153 mg/dL)).

case_report: In June 2016, a 19-year-old Syrian man with a 6-month history of throat irritation was admitted to a Danish hospital. He arrived in Denmark as a refugee in 2015. He had no history of severe illness or frequent infections, although a scar on his arm indicated previous cutaneous leishmaniasis. His family history included a healthy mother and sister, and a deceased father who had also been healthy. Several days before hospital admission, his symptoms worsened to severe throat pain and fever. Laryngoscopy showed significant swelling of the mucosa in both the pharynx and larynx. The epiglottis and uvula were swollen and red with papilloma-like lesions. A biopsy of the uvula showed histiocytic inflammation and Donovan bodies, confirming leishmaniasis.
test_results: The species L. tropica was identified by polymerase chain reaction.

case_report: A two-and-a-half-year-old first female child, born to parents who are not related by blood, was referred with a history of frequent infections since birth. The child experienced recurrent diarrhea and skin boils, with cultures showing growth of Staphylococcus aureus. Laboratory tests indicated an increased leukocyte count and eosinophilia. Blood samples were collected in EDTA after obtaining informed consent. The laboratory evaluation showed a white blood cell (WBC) count of 11400/mm3, an absolute lymphocyte count of 9690/mm3, and an absolute neutrophil count of 1026/mm3. Hemoglobin was measured at 11.7 gm/dl, and the platelet count was 624 × 103/μl. Lymphocyte subset analysis using a six-color TBNK BD antibody revealed normal counts of NK-cells and elevated counts of T-cells (CD4, CD8) and B-cells. Nitroblue-tetrazolium and Dihydrorhodamine tests were normal. Serum immunoglobulin levels showed low IgG, IgA, and IgE, with an elevated IgM level. CD154 analysis was normal, but CD40 expression was absent on the B-cells.
test_results: This showed a novel deletion of 3bp (AAG) [g.4407_4409delAAG p.Glu107GlyfsX84] in a homozygous state in exon 4, leading to a frame-shift mutation and generation of a stop codon at p.192 in exon 7. This mutation was also found in a heterozygous condition in both the parents.
diagnosis: Hyperimmunoglobulin syndrome due to CD40 deficiency

case_report: A 77-year-old male presented with a complaint of a droopy left eyelid. His medical history includes hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and hyperlipidemia, managed at a local clinic. Three days after receiving the first dose of ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 (AstraZeneca, AZ) vaccine, he noticed gradual ptosis of the left eyelid. Eleven days post-vaccination, he experienced weakness in the left facial muscles. Physical examination showed impaired blink reflex on the left side, ptosis, and weakness in the left facial muscles, including the orbicularis oris. Extraocular movements and light reflexes were normal in both eyes. No vesicles or blisters were observed on his face. Laboratory tests, including thyroid function, vitamin B12, folate, glucose, cell count, electrolytes, renal function, and liver function, were within normal limits. He was treated with prednisolone (40 mg QD) for 14 days, but the ptosis showed minimal improvement. He then sought further evaluation for the persistent droopy eyelid. His corrected visual acuity was 6/7.5 in the right eye and 6/6 in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was 18 mmHg in both eyes. Slit-lamp examination was notable for puffy eyelids on the left side with intermittent myokymic motion of the left upper and lower lids. Marginal reflex distance 1 (MRD1) was 1 mm on the left eye compared to 3 mm on the right. The left eye closed tightly when he was asked to open his mouth or smile, although his smile was symmetric during the examination.
test_results: Fundus imaging and optical coherence tomography of his macula and disc were unremarkable, and no obvious inflammatory lesions, including on the oculomotor and facial nerve region, were observed on the brain MRI.

case_report: A 33-year-old woman, who returned from a trip to South Africa 3 days prior, presents to the emergency department with an eschar on her ankle. She reports that this eschar has been present for 2 weeks. She also complains of a 1-week persistent fever. Ceftriaxone is started for suspected cellulitis. The patient returned 2 days later to the emergency for persistent fever and new maculopapular rash despite antibiotic treatment. The blood tests are unremarkable except for an increased C-reactive protein (48, normal <5). A dermatology consultation is requested. A rickettsia serology follows and proves to be in the gray zone (1/128).
test_results: The polymerase chain reaction of the Rickettsia genus is positive. Histology demonstrates lymphomatoid vascular reaction.

case_report: A 60-year-old woman visits the emergency department due to a wound on her foot. She had returned from a trip to South Africa 5 days earlier. The ulcer has been present for 10 days, progressively enlarging, and is accompanied by fever, headache, and muscle pain. Physical examination reveals a necrotic ulcer approximately one centimeter in size, surrounded by redness, swelling, and warmth on her foot. Additionally, the patient has several red papules and small red or purple spots on her limbs and back. Routine blood tests show no abnormalities. A dermatology consultation is conducted, and biopsies of the papules on her leg show lymphocytic vasculitis.
test_results: Rickettsia serology is positive (1/64).

case_report: A 27-year-old male patient was consulted postoperatively for chronic ITP after undergoing a splenectomy for further follow-up. His medical history revealed that he had been managed at another center for ITP since the age of three, receiving treatments such as steroids, intravenous immune globulin, and platelet suspension as needed. During an investigation for proteinuria, he was found to have chronic kidney failure four years ago and has since been prepared for renal replacement therapy. Despite having no hearing complaints, mild hearing loss in one ear was detected. His eye examination was normal. It was noted that there were family members with thrombocytopenia, although they had not been examined for this condition. One month after the splenectomy, initial hematologic examination showed thrombocytopenia (4,000/mm3) and mild anemia (hemoglobin 9.52 g/dL). Peripheral blood smear (PBS) revealed giant platelets almost as large as erythrocytes, with a platelet count in PBS calculated at 40,000/mm3. No Döhle bodies were observed in the granulocytes.
test_results: The patient was found to have a c.287C>T; p.(Ser96Leu) mutation in polymerase chain reaction amplification of the targeted genomic region which was sequenced on a next-generation sequencing platform. This mutation in the MYH9 gene is associated with MYH9-RD.

case_report: A 64-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital due to progressive shortness of breath. Preoperative trans-esophageal echocardiography showed severe mitral regurgitation and mitral leaflet prolapse. The aortic and tricuspid regurgitation were minimal. Measurements included an end-diastolic diameter of 69 mm, an end-systolic diameter of 48 mm, and an estimated ejection fraction of 56%. The estimated systolic pulmonary artery pressure from tricuspid regurgitation was 47 mmHg. No intra-cardiac mass, thrombi, or pericardial effusion were observed. Coronary catheterization indicated normal coronary arteries. The patient's medical history included hypercholesterolemia and hypertension. Atrial fibrillation was newly detected on the day of admission, although no arrhythmia had been documented five years prior. Laboratory results were as follows: hemoglobin, 14.2 g/dL; glucose, 100 mg/dL; urea, 17 mg/dL; creatinine, 0.9 mg/dL; serum cholesterol, 117 mg/dL; triglycerides, 171 mg/dL; Pro-BNP, 2381 pg/mL, and thyroid function was within normal range. The patient underwent mitral valve repair with annuloplasty and maze operation. Intraoperative trans-esophageal echocardiography at the end of the procedure showed moderate mitral regurgitation. The surgical team decided to convert the mitral valve repair to mitral valve replacement with a 29-mm bileaflet mechanical prosthesis. During the replacement, the anterior and posterior leaflet chordae were preserved and reattached to the mitral ring near both commissures. The central portion of the anterior mitral valve leaflet was excised, and the remaining anterior leaflet was divided into anterior and posterior segments. These segments were shifted and reattached to the mitral ring at the respective commissural areas, and the prosthetic valve was implanted with the ventricular side of the remnant leaflet in contact with the prosthetic sewing ring. Post-procedure, the patient's hemodynamic condition was stable.
test_results: Routine trans-thoracic echocardiography (TTE) performed on the 2nd postoperative day showed a normal functioning mitral prosthesis and slightly decreased ventricular function. TTE showed an abnormal aortic valve mass (size: 0.3 × 0.6 cm by TTE). Reevaluation on the 7th and the 14th postoperative day with TTE showed a normal functioning mitral prosthesis and no significant change in mass size around the aortic valve. The mobile mass was hanging at the continuous margin of the mechanical valve and it had high echogenicity. That area revealed very high pressure below the aortic valve and moved along in the cardiac cycle.
Orpha_name: Anomaly of the mitral subvalvular apparatus

case_report: A 38-year-old woman was referred to our hospital in July 2004 with fever, a heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules, polyarthralgia, and proximal muscle weakness. Laboratory tests showed elevated serum creatine kinase (CK) levels, and chest X-rays revealed reticular and granular shadows in the lower lung fields. She was hospitalized and started on 50 mg of prednisolone (PSL) daily. As her muscle symptoms and serum CK levels improved, the PSL dose was gradually reduced. In June 2006, when the PSL dose was reduced to 10 mg daily, her muscle weakness returned. She also experienced a sensation of abdominal fullness and severe abdominal pain, leading to rehospitalization. Physical examination showed abdominal distension, tympanitic sounds on percussion, and absence of bowel sounds on auscultation.
test_results: Abdominal X-ray, CT, and endoscopy with a lower gastrointestinal tract fiberscope revealed an intestinal obstructive ileus with no discernible mechanical cause.

case_report: An 82-year-old female arrived at the emergency department with abdominal pain. She had been experiencing generalized abdominal pain and soreness, which she thought was due to constipation. The patient had not had a bowel movement for three days before her visit, despite using multiple bisacodyl suppositories. Her medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), congestive heart failure (CHF), paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), peripheral artery disease (PAD), hypothyroidism, chronic constipation, and a history of uterine cancer treated with hysterectomy. Two weeks prior, she had been hospitalized for three days for a COPD exacerbation and was discharged with a prednisone taper. During the interview, she reported abdominal discomfort at rest, bloating, dry mouth, generalized weakness, and a headache. She denied other systemic symptoms. Physical examination showed a flat, soft abdomen with mild tenderness to palpation. She reported right upper quadrant pain and some distension. Bowel sounds were hypoactive. There was no rebound tenderness, muscle guarding, hepatosplenomegaly, or pulsating abdominal mass. Upon admission, her white blood cell count was elevated at 16.6 x 103/uL (reference range: 4.5-11), and her thyroid stimulating hormone was low at 0.115 uIU/mL (reference range: 0.300-4.500). A chest X-ray showed mild chronic interstitial disease with emphysematous changes consistent with her COPD and mild bibasilar infiltrates.
test_results: A CT scan showed colonic thickening and induration involving the rectum and sigmoid colon, marked dilatation of the cecum, and severe bilateral centrilobular emphysematous changes in the lungs.
diagnosis: Acute Colonic Pseudo-Obstruction  or Ogilvie's syndrome

case_report: A 16-day-old female newborn from Saudi Arabia was brought to the clinic with a skin defect on the scalp present since birth. The infant had no other health issues, and her medical history was clear. Her 32-year-old mother reported no illnesses, infections, or medication use, including NSAIDs or methimazole, during pregnancy. The mother completed 38 weeks of gestation and had a normal vaginal delivery. The newborn experienced no birth injuries, other abnormalities, or feeding difficulties. She did not require intensive care and was discharged home with her mother. On local examination, the defect was solitary, irregularly shaped, and measured approximately 6×6 cm. The lesion affected only the epidermis and the upper dermis.
test_results: No deep tissue involvement was noted.

case_report: A woman in her early twenties with a lifelong history of alopecia presented with 2–3 months of intermittent, dull, throbbing, and localized tenderness in one of the alopecic patches. The affected area, located on the right parietal-occipital scalp, had been stable in size and appearance since birth. Additionally, three other round patches of alopecia, also present since birth, remained asymptomatic. Clinical examination of the scalp revealed an atrophic white patch of alopecia. Surrounding the lesion, there was ill-defined bogginess extending to the central and posterior occipital scalp.
test_results: On dermoscopic examination, the alopecic patch showed a translucent epidermis with multiple branched blood vessels and hair bulbs at the edge of the patch. A non-contrast head CT showed no evidence of osseous, vascular, neural, or soft tissue defects.

case_report: A 31-year-old Taiwanese woman, gravida 1, para 0, who conceived naturally, received prenatal care from the first trimester. At 21 weeks and two days of gestation, an isolated umbilical hernia was detected, with no other structural abnormalities observed. The estimated fetal weight was 460 g, placing it in the 79th percentile. Cytogenetic analyses and chromosome microarray analysis (CMA) were conducted to identify any chromosomal or genomic variants associated with the fetal anomaly. Both tests indicated a normal female karyotype without pathogenic copy number variations (CNVs), 46,XX.arr(X,1−22)×2. The pregnancy continued without complications until birth. A female infant was delivered at 38 weeks of gestation via cesarean section, with a birth weight of 3850 g (96th percentile) and Apgar scores of 8 and 9 at the first and fifth minutes, respectively. The infant presented with macrosomia and an umbilical hernia featuring a 3 cm abdominal wall defect with small bowel protrusion. No neonatal hypoglycemia or asymmetric extremities were observed. Neonatal abdominal ultrasonography showed normal kidney and liver sizes without intraabdominal tumors. Umbilical hernia repair surgery with small bowel reduction was performed on the first day after birth, and the infant was discharged without complications a few days later.
test_results: The result showed ICR2 hypomethylation (8.3%) on chromosome 11p15. The methylation status in ICR1 was within the normal range (48.9%). No copy number change was detected in ICR1 and ICR2.

case_report: A 17-year-old girl was referred to our department due to rapidly enlarging masses in her left breast. Her medical history includes a condition identified at birth. There is no family history of hereditary diseases. Physical examination revealed asymmetry with the left side of her body being larger than the right. The left breast was significantly larger than the right, with two palpable masses, each approximately 10 cm in size. Laboratory tests, including tumor markers, were within normal limits.
test_results: High-resolution chromosome banding indicated no structural abnormalities of chromosome 11.

case_report: A 19-year-old female presented with recurrent episodes of hemoptysis and oral ulceration. Her initial episode of hemoptysis occurred 2 years prior, leading to hospitalization. At that time, diffuse alveolar hemorrhage was observed. Medical treatment with prednisolone and azathioprine was initiated. Two years later, she experienced another episode of hemoptysis. Examination revealed a hyperemic nodular lesion within the anterior basal segmental bronchus of the right lower lobe (RLL), but biopsy was unsuccessful due to minor bleeding upon contact with the nodule. The patient was discharged with the same medication after conservative management. She experienced another episode of hemoptysis and was referred to Seoul Asan Medical Center emergency room. Consultations with a rheumatologist and an ophthalmologist were conducted. A gynecologist also examined the patient. Physical examination revealed oral ulcers but no genital ulcers, uveitis, or skin lesions. Her past history indicated no skin lesions for the past 2 years, and hemoptysis occurred independently of her menstrual cycle.
test_results: Bronchofiberscopy revealed diffuse alveolar hemorrhage; however, there were no specific findings for the cause of hemoptysis. The exam revealed a hyperemic nodular lesion within the anterior basal segmental bronchus of the right lower lobe (RLL). Biopsy failed because of the little bleeding that occurred when the nodule was touched. Chest computed tomography showed residual ground-glass opacity in RLL due to aspirated blood, but no definite endobronchial lesion or vascular abnormality were observed as the cause of hemoptysis. Chest X-ray showed no specific findings. The patient's blood test was normal except for a mild elevation of the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (29 mm/hr). For the differential diagnosis, anti-nuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, serum complement levels (C3 and C4), and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (c-ANCA and p-ANCA) were tested; all of them showed negative results. During the exam, a small polyp was observed at the anterior basal segmental bronchus of the RLL and excisional biopsy was proceeded. After the excisional biopsy using laser, active bleeding occurred; therefore, emergent surgical resection was decided upon. Basal segmentectomy of the RLL was performed using video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery. After transection of the basal segmental bronchus, intraoperative bronchoscopy showed no bleeding focus in the endobronchial area. Pathological examination revealed abnormally dilated vascular structures in the bronchial submucosa with rupture.

case_report: A 50-year-old male presented to the emergency room with sudden onset severe shortness of breath classified as New York Heart Association class IV, lasting for one day. His medical history includes essential hypertension for a decade and minimal coronary artery disease identified via coronary angiography six months prior, which was performed due to nonspecific chest pain. At that time, an electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed a 1st degree AV block, and transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) indicated mild left ventricular hypertrophy (LV mass = 98 g/m2) without any valvular dysfunctions. A 24-hour Holter monitor showed no significant findings, leading to his discharge without treatment. Five months later, he returned to the outpatient clinic after experiencing two episodes of syncope while playing golf. An ECG at that visit showed complete AV block, and following an electrophysiologic study of the AV node, a DDD type permanent pacemaker was implanted. During the second admission, TTE still showed mild LV hypertrophy with no interval change, but a mild degree of aortic regurgitation was observed. At this time, his blood pressure was 110/70 mm Hg, and his pulse rate was 88 beats per minute. Physical examination revealed a grade IV/VI diastolic murmur at the left middle sternal border and rales in both lung fields. A chest X-ray indicated pulmonary congestion in both lower lung fields. The ECG showed right ventricle pacing beats of P wave tracing by the permanent pacemaker.
test_results: On the TTE examination, newly developed severe AR was noted and transesophageal echocardiography revealed non-coronary cusp of aortic valve billowing and prolapsing with aortic root dilatation (4.0 cm). Pathergy test was negative.

case_report: A 26-year-old Chinese female presented with dull right chest pain for 30 days and intermittent cough and expectoration for 5 days. She was admitted on August 24, 2018. A CT scan at the outpatient Daping Hospital revealed abnormal, lamellar, high-density shadows in the middle and lower lobes of the right lung. Two months prior to hospitalization, she experienced recurrent oral ulcers and constitutional rashes. Lung auscultation revealed no adventitious sounds. Physical examination showed red papules and nodular lesions on the skin of her upper limbs and legs, along with a rash trace on her lower limbs. Laboratory results were as follows: WBC, 9.68 × 10^9/L; Neu%, 69.6%; IL-6, 48.23 pg/L; CRP, 119.6 mg/L; ALP, 152.5 U/L; LDH, 709.7 U/L. Tests for AKA, CCP, ACA, pANCA, cANCA, RNP, dsDNA, (1,3)-β-d-glucan detection, and galactomannan were unremarkable. T. SPOT and HIV tests were negative. The patient was treated with moxifloxacin hydrochloride (400 mg q.d.) for 1 week, which alleviated her cough and expectoration but worsened her right chest pain. A follow-up CT scan on August 31, 2018, showed reduced lamellar high-density shadows in the right lung but new lesions in the left lower lung. She continued antibacterial therapy for 2 weeks. A subsequent CT scan on September 13, 2018, showed an increase in the size of the lesion in the left lower lung, while the right lung lesions were alleviated. IPA was detected in her BALF. The patient also reported black cerumen from her left external auditory canal. Otolaryngological examination revealed a congested left external auditory canal and tympanic membrane, with Aspergillus auriculatus detected in the excretions. Aspergillus niger was found in cultured secretions from the left external auditory canal. The patient had been exposed to moldy herbal medicine 3 months prior. She was treated with itraconazole oral solution (200 mg q.d.). Two weeks after starting antifungal treatment, a CT scan on September 26, 2018, showed resolution of lesions in both lungs. The patient continued antifungal therapy after discharge.
test_results: A biopsy from genital ulcers revealed superficial necrosis and ulcer formation as well as neutrophil and lymphocyte infiltration in the dermis. Thrombi were found in several peripheral vessels.

case_report: A 2-day-old full-term male infant, weighing 2100 grams, exhibited excessive salivation and vomiting following attempts to feed. An IFT was inserted and passed approximately 20 cm, creating the false impression that the tip had reached the stomach, while it actually remained coiled in the long, dilated upper esophageal pouch. Due to the ongoing symptoms, a pediatric surgical consultation was requested.
test_results: Radiographs confirmed the presence of obstruction at T8/T9 vertebral level. Esophagogram revealed upper pouch at a T5 vertebral level.

case_report: A 1-day-old male neonate weighing 2.1kg was born to a 21-year-old first-time mother at full term. The baby was delivered normally and was the result of a non-consanguineous marriage. The pregnancy was largely uneventful except for polyhydramnios identified 3 days before delivery. The neonate's abdomen appeared scaphoid. No obvious associated anomalies were observed. A nasogastric tube could not be passed into the stomach. A plain abdominal x-ray showed no gas, indicating isolated EA without a distal TEF. The neonate had 13 pairs of ribs and no vertebral anomalies. Echocardiography results were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography showed moderate left hydronephrosis. A staged repair of EA was planned. During laparotomy for abdominal esophagostomy, the stomach was found to be distended. A right thoracotomy was then performed, revealing a long-gap EA with the proximal esophageal pouch barely reaching the thoracic inlet and a right-sided aortic arch. An 8 mm long, blindly-ending, distensible tracheal diverticulum was identified and excised. The right upper lobe bronchus was observed to arise from the carina. The thorax was then closed, and cervical and abdominal esophagostomies were created.
test_results: Post-operatively, a MRI chest was done that confirmed the diagnosis of right TB.
diagnosis: Tracheal Trifurcation Associated With Esophageal Atresia

case_report: A 2-day-old preterm (30 weeks) male infant was admitted urgently due to breathing difficulties, fever, and refusal to feed. The mother had three antenatal visits without ultrasound scans, no illnesses during pregnancy, and no fever during labor. The delivery was marked by prolonged labor with excess amniotic fluid (meconium-stained), resulting in the birth of a male preterm infant weighing 1.9 kg with APGAR scores of 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. On examination, the infant exhibited respiratory distress (respiratory rate = 65 cycles/min), was febrile (temperature = 38°C), had yellowish stains on nails (likely from meconium), pale bluish extremities, and no jaundice. Chest examination revealed thoraco-abdominal asynchrony, tachycardia (heart rate = 160 beats/min), no murmur, and crackles in both lungs. The abdomen appeared normal, and the anal canal was patent. Laboratory results showed leukocytosis on a Full Blood Count, and a Chest X-Ray indicated hyperinflation of the lungs with patchy infiltrates in the lower lung fields. Arterial blood gases were not performed. The infant underwent oropharyngeal suctioning, was placed on oxygen, kept warm, and received intravenous hydration and antibiotic therapy. After 2 days of treatment, the general condition improved. On the 4th day of admission, the infant experienced choking and regurgitation upon starting feeds but had no fever. A repeat Full Blood Count was normal. The mother was reassured, and treatment continued. On the 5th day, regurgitation persisted, along with difficulty breathing during feeds, peripheral cyanosis, and frothy salivation, which the mother reported had been present since birth. There was no abdominal distension, and the infant passed stool.
test_results: A repeat Chest and Abdominal X-ray with tube in place showed mild pulmonary infiltrates with no air in the stomach and duodenum respectively.

case_report: A 3-month-old male infant presented with a 20-day history of bilious and projectile vomiting after each feed, accompanied by significant weight loss and lethargy. He was born full-term with a birth weight of 3 kg (50th percentile weight for age) to healthy consanguineous parents, had an uneventful prenatal history with a normal antenatal ultrasound, and is developmentally age-appropriate. The patient had been admitted twice to different hospitals for fluid therapy. During his last admission, almost 5 days prior to the current presentation, an abdominal ultrasound was performed. On examination, the infant appeared cachectic, lethargic, and severely dehydrated, with multiple cautery marks on his abdomen from a traditional healer. His weight upon admission was 2.9 kg (below the 3rd percentile weight for age). He had a scaphoid abdomen and visible peristalsis transversely across the epigastrium from left to right. Test feeding demonstrated a palpable firm, nontender mass in the right upper quadrant, measuring 1 to 2 cm in diameter. Bilateral reducible inguinal hernias were also noted. The rest of the examination was normal. Laboratory investigations showed normal complete blood count (CBC) and serum chemistry values, including potassium (K+ 4.3 mmol) and chloride (Cl− 96 mmol/L). Venous blood gas (VBG) analysis revealed uncompensated metabolic alkalosis with a pH of 7.54, pCO2 of 35.7 mmHg, cHCO3 of 31.1 mmol/L, and cBase of 7.4 mmol/L. An abdominal ultrasound showed a markedly distended stomach and the first part of the duodenum with no signs of pyloric stenosis.
test_results: Barium meal revealed an abnormally distended stomach, paucity of distal gas, and triple bubble sign.

case_report: A 41-year-old African American male arrived at the emergency room of a large academic urban hospital with complaints of abdominal pain and worsening nausea and vomiting, which he had been experiencing intermittently over the past two years. He had been managing these symptoms with hot showers. He reported no abdominal distention, fever, or constipation. The patient had a history of smoking cannabis two to three times daily for the past 20 years. His vital signs were stable, and the physical examination revealed no abnormalities, with a normal body mass index. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT scan) revealed a large hiatal hernia and significant thickening of the distal esophagus and gastroesophageal junction.
test_results: Upper endoscopy showed diffuse salmon-colored mucosa and nodularity from 20cm to the esophagogastric junction at 30cm. Histology showed columnar mucosa with intestinal cell metaplasia and glandular atypia indefinite for dysplasia.

case_report: A 13-year-old Caucasian male with mild intellectual disability, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, and constipation was transferred to our tertiary care facility due to a two-month history of difficulty swallowing and recurrent vomiting episodes. Initially, vomiting occurred only after ingesting solids, but it progressed to include liquids. Obtaining further history was challenging due to the child's intellectual disability and speech delay. Information from family members and caregivers at the psychiatric institution indicated that the boy also experienced self-induced vomiting, heartburn, and a seven-pound weight loss in one week. His medications included polyethylene glycol and ranitidine. Physical examination upon admission was unremarkable. Laboratory values, including complete blood count and differential, serum electrolytes, glucose, amylase, lipase, liver and kidney function tests, and thyroid-stimulating hormone level, were within normal limits. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen, initially performed to rule out obstructive causes for his symptoms, revealed stool retention. Despite treatment with polyethylene glycol, which resolved the stool retention, he continued to have immediate postprandial vomiting. Additional testing with a barium esophagram revealed focal persistent narrowing of the proximal and mid-esophagus. A CT angiogram of the chest ruled out external compression of the esophagus and showed circumferential thickening of the esophagus.
test_results: The biopsy results indicated the presence of erosive esophagitis.

case_report: A 28-year-old female patient, with a light skin tone, working in rural areas, and originating from Itabaianinha-SE, visited the dermatology service due to multiple papular, erythematous, and itchy lesions on her abdomen for the past 2 months. She reported no additional symptoms and mentioned frequent bathing in rivers. Physical examination revealed round papules approximately 3mm in diameter, erythematous, and confluent, with some forming plaques, giving a zosteriform appearance to the lesions, located in the abdominal region (epigastrium, mesogastrium, and left upper quadrant). No enlargement of internal organs was noted. Laboratory tests showed 12% eosinophilia, with no other abnormalities detected.
test_results: Stool examination detected the presence of S. mansoni eggs. The anatomopathological examination showed granuloma of epithelioid macrophages involving egg with viable miracidium associated with an inflammatory infiltrate composed of lymphocytes and eosinophils, eggs in the process of degeneration with internal calcification and totally degenerated with deposition of fibrinoid material, revealing granuloma fibrosis.

case_report: A 76-year-old Korean man presented with a 2-cm dark-brown and erythematous scaly plaque on the left lower leg, which had been present for 2 years. The patient reported no history of trauma or previous treatments at the site. There were no symptoms of itching or burning. The lesion had shown gradual growth over the 2-year period. Physical examination revealed no additional skin lesions in the axilla, groin, genitalia, perianal area, and umbilicus. No palpable lymph nodes were detected in the cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions. The patient's medical history included diabetes mellitus, for which he was on medication.
test_results: Punch biopsy specimen showed tumor cells in the epidermis with acanthosis. The tumor cells had abundant pale cytoplasm and large pleomorphic nuclei. Immunohistochemical staining was focally positive for cytokeratin 7 (CK7). The excised specimen was negative for CK7, CK20, carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), and S-100. It shows positivity for p63, CK5/6, and epithelial membrane antigen (EMA).

case_report: A 48-year-old female with a medical history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and hypothyroidism was brought to the emergency department following two episodes of syncope accompanied by involuntary jerking movements. There were no preceding symptoms such as dizziness, palpitations, or sweating. While awaiting discharge, she experienced a third collapse, which was followed by a cardiac arrest with a shockable rhythm. Her regular medications included aspirin and levothyroxine. The initial two episodes resolved on their own without any subsequent confusion. Upon arrival at the emergency department, she was hemodynamically stable. It was noted that the patient had a son who passed away at the age of 19 years.
test_results: This ECG shows normal sinus rhythm with a widened QRS complex (140 ms) at 66 beats per minute with a left axis deviation. On careful inspection, ST-segments in V1 and V2 show a <1 mm elevation and flattening of T waves in V1. When the cardiac arrest occurred, the initial rhythm was found to be ventricular fibrillation. The ECG, obtained two days after these events, shows a right bundle branch block (RBBB) with an ST-segment elevation of ≥2 mm followed by a negative T wave with no isoelectric separation and a QTc 440 ms as well as nonspecific T wave changes. Cardiac MRI demonstrated neither structural heart disease nor abnormal myocardium.

case_report: A 24-year-old male visited the clinic with a history of painless, gradually increasing radial abduction of his right thumb, which was affecting his grip and pretension. He reported growing discomfort while working at the computer. There was no history of specific trauma or other symptoms. Seven years prior, two sclerotic skin lesions over the radial aspect of the distal third of the first metacarpal bone were excised. On physical examination, the patient appeared healthy with no dysmorphic features. No skin lesions were observed. The right thumb was radially deviated 60° at the metacarpophalangeal (MP) joint and 25° at the interphalangeal (IP) joint. A scar from a previous operation was present over the radial aspect of the base of the thumb. The patient demonstrated a full active range of motion, and the thumb joints were stable.
test_results: Radiological examination of the hand showed a spotted pattern with multiple circular or ovoid sclerotic lesions, consistent with osteopoikilosis. The skin biopsy showed macroscopically a white nodule in the dermis. Microscopically, the nodule was hypocellular and consisted of interlacing thick collagen fibres and rare elastic fibres. A segmental biopsy of the metacarpal bone of the right thumb showed a nodular thickening of the cortical bone. Histology revealed in the nodular thickening of the cortical bone a remodelling with formation of network of thick bone trabecules and formation of numerous enlarged Havers’s channels with fibrotic tissue. The histological findings of the bone were consistent with osteopoikilosis and the skin showed the variant of a collagenous fibrotic nodule instead of a nodule with high concentration of elastic fibres. This revealed the heterozygous mutation c.1832T>A, which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing and is predicted to result in a premature stop codon (p.Leu611*).

case_report: A 72-year-old Caucasian woman with no prior health issues reported experiencing progressive skin tightening and discoloration over a period of six months. These changes affected her arms, shoulders, chest, and lower legs. She also developed painful erythematous patches on her back, breasts, and belt line. There was no family history of scleroderma or autoimmune diseases. Physical examination revealed firmly indurated and hyperpigmented lesions on the arms, shoulders, chest, belt line, and lower legs. Additionally, scaly erythematous and partially bullous patches were observed over both breasts. There were no signs of sclerodactyly, nailfold microvascular abnormalities, or other systemic sclerosis manifestations. Serologic tests for antinuclear, anti-Scl-70, and anti-centromere antibodies were negative.
test_results: Radiographs of the hands, feet, and knees revealed numerous well-demarcated bone densities (osteopoikilosis) bilaterally.

case_report: A 73-year-old woman visited the cornea clinic with complaints of a dense white spot, sensitivity to light, and slightly worsened vision in her left eye for the past month. She had been receiving treatment with topical and systemic antifungal medications without any improvement. Ophthalmological examination showed a visual acuity of 20/30 in the left eye and 20/80 in the right eye. Intraocular pressure was measured at 6 mmHg in the right eye and 17 mmHg in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination of the left eye revealed conjunctival and limbal hyperemia, dense stromal edema extending over two clock hours in the inferior cornea, and active deep and superficial neovascularization. The overlying epithelium was intact, with mild anterior chamber inflammation and a few keratic precipitates on the endothelium near the edema. There was also a grade 2 nuclear sclerosis cataract. Corneal sensation was moderately reduced in the left eye but normal in the right eye. The right eye exhibited pseudophakia, advanced glaucomatous cupping, and a functional trabeculectomy bleb. The patient reported a past history of a corneal ulcer with a small white spot in her left eye several years ago. She also mentioned having had a moderate COVID-19 infection in May 2021, during the second wave of the epidemic in India, one month before the onset of symptoms in her left eye. She was treated for COVID-19 with systemic steroids and noninvasive ventilation.
test_results: Confirmed by positive reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) testing from AC tap fluid.

case_report: A 48-year-old female, who had undergone bilateral radial keratotomy (RK) with 8 corneal incisions per eye 27 years ago, presented with pain and visual loss in her right eye. She worked at a nursing facility, assisting the elderly with various tasks, which involved direct contact with them. She had not had any long-term follow-up examinations post-RK due to a stable and satisfactory postoperative course for 27 years. Five days prior to admission, she experienced sudden pain in her right eye, followed by redness and a foreign body sensation the next day, and blurred vision two days later. She was initially diagnosed with bacterial keratitis by her primary care physician but was not prescribed any eye-drop medication. She was referred to the emergency room of Kyoto Prefectural University of Medicine Hospital, Kyoto, Japan, after an initial examination at a secondary medical care facility. The patient had no significant systemic medical history, ocular trauma, or contact lens use. Initial examination of her right eye showed a best-corrected visual acuity (VA) of 20/40. A small-sized focus area with inflammatory infiltrate (1.8 × 1.3 mm) and endothelial plaque was observed in the deep site in the radial incision at the 6-o'clock meridian, along with conjunctival injection and inflammatory cells in the anterior chamber with hypopyon. No epithelial defects or aqueous humor leakage were noted. Both eyelids showed no signs of blepharitis or meibomian gland dysfunction. Treatment was initiated with hourly topical administration of 1.5% levofloxacin and 0.5% cefmenoxime eye drops. Despite this treatment, the following day's ocular findings indicated worsening conjunctival injection, focus, and hypopyon. Anterior segment-optical coherence tomography (AS-OCT) revealed a corneal plaque at the endothelial side of the cornea, increased corneal thickness, and steepening of the inferior cornea around the focus area. Due to the lack of improvement with the initial treatment, natamycin ointment drops were added.
test_results: Laboratory examination of the obtained RK-incision specimens and anterior chamber specimen showed numerous gram-positive cocci and only white blood cells, respectively.

case_report: A 60-year-old male patient had cataract surgery on his left eye, which included a 3 mm clear corneal incision on the superior nasal side at another medical facility. To address left eye astigmatism, a limbal relaxing incision was performed opposite the corneal incision. This incision measured 0.5 mm in depth with a 70° arc width along the keratometric steep axis (135°). The patient has a history of severe conjunctivitis in both eyes during childhood and experienced right facial nerve palsy 20 years ago. At the time of the surgery, he presented with lower lid ectropion and lagophthalmos in both eyes. On the 11th day after surgery, the patient experienced sudden onset of ocular pain in his left eye.
test_results: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy revealed a punch-out epithelial defect (1.5 × 1.5 mm) with a border of hazy epithelium along with stromal edema on the pre-existing corneal opacity near the limbal relaxing incision. A corneal sensitivity test using a Cochet-Bonnet esthesiometer revealed decreased sensation in the inferior and infero-temporal areas of the left cornea compared to other locations in the left cornea and to all locations in the right (non-operated) cornea (p < 0.05).

case_report: A 57-year-old female presented to the ophthalmology department with complaints of decreased visual acuity. Her medical history includes a long-standing condition of trigeminal neuralgia. She had previously undergone a central nervous system examination, which revealed an incidental epidermoid cyst affecting the trigeminal nerve. She had brain surgery for partial removal of this cyst. Post-surgery, her trigeminal neuralgia symptoms subsided for several years but later recurred, leading her to seek treatment at the anesthesiology clinic for pain management. She received a right trigeminal nerve block, including percutaneous blocks of the maxillary and mandibular nerves with alcohol, as well as an infraorbital nerve block. Under fluoroscopic guidance, the needle tip for the maxillary nerve block was positioned right lateral to the foramen rotundum and pterygopalatine fossa, while for the mandibular nerve block, the needle tip was placed at the midportion of the foramen ovale. Post-procedure, her pain decreased, accompanied by right-side facial numbness. Three days after the trigeminal block, she developed vesicles over the right lower lid and cheek. She was clinically diagnosed with a herpes zoster infection of the maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve and was started on oral famciclovir 250 mg every 8 hours. Approximately 10 days after the trigeminal block and during her treatment with famciclovir, she experienced progressively decreasing visual acuity. She was then referred to the ophthalmology department at St. Vincent's Hospital. This was her first visit to an ophthalmologist.
test_results: On initial examination, her visual acuity was 0.06 (0.25 with pin-hole correction) in the right eye and 0.16 (0.8 × −3.25 Dsph; −0.50 Dcyl A × 94) in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was 13 mm Hg (right eye)/10 mm Hg (left eye). At slit lamp examination, her cornea showed an irregular epithelial defect with Descemet's membrane folding. There was no cell reaction in the anterior chamber.

case_report: A 27-year-old woman presented with long-standing bilateral blurred vision and discomfort. She experienced similar symptoms 13 years prior, which were partially alleviated with topical treatment but never fully resolved. Her medical history includes APS-1, Addison disease, Hashimoto thyroiditis, hypoparathyroidism, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. She does not have diabetes mellitus. The patient has a height of 147 cm and a weight of 37 kg, and hair loss was observed. She wore soft contact lenses for about 5 years but discontinued their use 3 years ago. Ocular examination showed corrected distance visual acuity of 20/40 in the right eye and 20/50 in the left eye, with normal intraocular pressure. Slit-lamp examination identified 2 patches of corneal erosions in the right eye and diffuse superficial punctate erosions with filaments on the lower corneal surface of the left eye. Bilateral meibomian gland dysfunction was also observed. Schirmer testing under anesthesia indicated dry eye.
test_results: IVCM using Confoscan 3.4.1 revealed significant abnormality of the sub-basal nerve plexus and stromal nerve bundles in both eyes. The squamous epithelial cells in the most superficial layer of the cornea were found to be elongated with a tendency to slough off easily, highlighting the poor differentiation of the corneal epithelial layer. The sub-basal nerve plexus was torturous and beading; it lost its parallel pattern in the right eye and became short and segmented in the left eye. In both eyes, the stromal nerve bundles became very thin and torturous, which is quite different from the thick stromal nerve bundles in normal corneas. There was no significant change in the corneal endothelial layer.

case_report: A 27-year-old male patient presented for refractive surgery with no reported medical or ocular history. His manifest refraction was −3.00 −1.50 × 90 in the right eye and −4.75 DS in the left eye, with a corrected distance visual acuity (CDVA) of 20/15 in both eyes. Examination revealed a 2.5 mm × 3 mm paracentral nummular scar in the corneal stroma at the 2 o'clock position in the right eye. After obtaining informed consent, an uneventful LASIK procedure was performed using the AMO IntraLase femtosecond laser. Flap diameters were 8.4 mm in the right eye and 8.3 mm in the left eye, with a thickness of 100 μm. The optical zone was 6.5 mm with a transitional zone of 1.25 mm in both eyes, using the WaveLight EX500 Excimer Laser. Postoperative treatment included ofloxacin 0.3% four times daily for one week, ketorolac 0.5% drops twice daily for 3 days, prednisolone acetate 1% drops four times daily for 1 month followed by a slow taper of fluorometholone 0.1% drops, and artificial tears. The first 3 months post-surgery were unremarkable, with manifest refraction of +0.25 −0.25 × 101 in the right eye and +0.50 −0.50 × 41 in the left eye, and uncorrected distance visual acuity (UDVA) of 20/20 in both eyes. Ten months post-surgery, the patient reported blurry vision in the right eye for several days, with UDVA declining to 20/50 in the right eye.
test_results: Slit-lamp examination revealed fine KPs and diffuse corneal edema. Specular microscopy imaging of the right eye endothelium was unsuccessful and failed to show good endothelial integrity compared to the left eye.

case_report: A 14-year-old Hispanic male with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) due to congenital cystic renal dysplasia presented with a 10-month history of right knee pain and a two-month history of worsening brawny hyperpigmentation of the skin on the distal extremities, along with painful contractures of the fingers and wrists. The patient has been on chronic hemodialysis for nearly 10 years, following a failed cadaveric kidney transplant received between the ages of two and three. Prior to the age of two, he was on peritoneal dialysis. He continues to undergo hemodialysis three times a week. His medical history includes renal osteodystrophy, seizure disorder, and reactive airway disease. Medications include Procardia XL, calcitriol, aspirin, erythropoietin, a Fentanyl patch, folic acid, iron, vitamins, flovent, and albuterol. Physical examination revealed a debilitated, wheelchair-bound adolescent with a heart rate of 130 beats/min, respiration rate of 30/min, and blood pressure of 140/84 mmHg. He was afebrile and hemodynamically stable but exhibited mild respiratory distress. Chest auscultation revealed an S3 gallop, diminished air entry at the right base, and bibasilar crepitations. Moderate hepatomegaly and ascites were also noted. The patient had diffuse areas of thickened skin with hyperpigmentation, associated with painful contractures of the hands, knees, and feet. Laboratory data showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 98 mm/h, C-reactive protein (CRP) of 5.89 U, and negative serologic antibody testing for ANA, anti-smith, anti-SSA/SSB, lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, and anti-SCL-70. Serum intact parathyroid hormone levels and serum calcium levels over the previous 2-4 years ranged from 580-1160 and 9-11 mg/dl, respectively. Chest x-ray indicated mild cardiomegaly, increased pulmonary vascular markings, and a right pleural effusion. A two-dimensional echo Doppler study showed moderate concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, mild mitral regurgitation, small discrete areas of calcification in the interventricular septum, and mild tricuspid regurgitation with a gradient of 64 mmHg and an estimated pulmonary artery pressure of 70 mmHg (concomitant blood pressure, 130/80 mmHg). Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed a moderate right pleural effusion, large discrete areas of pulmonary calcification, and cardiac calcification involving the aortic root, proximal coronary arteries, left atrium, and mitral valve ring.
test_results: A 4-mm punch biopsy from the dorsum of the right foot revealed prominent dermal collagen bundles and an increased number of banal CD34/procollagen dual positive spindles.

case_report: A 19-year-old male presented with a concern about the outward deviation of his right eye, which had been progressively worsening over the past three years. He had no history of diurnal variation, trauma, ocular surgery, or previous use of glasses. He had a history of recurrent vernal keratoconjunctivitis starting at age 5, treated with topical steroids, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and mast cell stabilizers. At the time of presentation, he was using mast cell stabilizers and did not report itching. There was no family history of atopy or eye deviation. His 24-year-old brother had no signs of ocular allergy or corneal ectatic disorders upon examination. On examination, the uncorrected visual acuity was 1/60 in the right eye and 6/36 in the left eye. Retinoscopy showed no scissor reflex, and refraction revealed high against-the-rule astigmatism in both eyes. Vision did not improve with a refractive correction of +2DS/-12DC at 90° in the right eye, while the left eye improved to 6/12 with +0.0DS/-4.5DC at 90°. The patient had a normal head posture, and the Hirschberg test showed 15º exotropia in the right eye with a full range of version and duction movements. The prism base cover test indicated a 40 prism diopter base in exotropia for near vision. The right eye was suppressed on the Worth four dot test. Mild papillary reaction in the upper tarsal conjunctiva suggested allergic conjunctivitis. Slit lamp examination revealed a band of thinning in the inferior cornea from 4 to 8 clock hours in both eyes, located 2 mm above the inferior limbus. The cornea above the thinning was steep and bulging, visible when light was shone from the opposite side. No cone-shaped bulge was observed in the light reflex. Central corneal thickness appeared normal in both eyes, with no striae, scarring, or vascularization. Munson’s sign was absent in both eyes. Dilated fundus examination was normal. These findings indicated corneal ectasia in both eyes, more pronounced in the right eye. A trial of rigid gas permeable contact lenses was unsuccessful due to poor corneal fit, but vision improved to 6/9 in both eyes with miniscleral contact lenses.
test_results: Corneal scans showed against the rule astigmatism. A crab claw pattern with central flattening of the vertical meridian was seen in the Atlas. In the right eye, the pentacam showed that the steepest part of the cornea was just below the thinnest part of the cornea. In the Belin Ambrosio Display (BAD) map relatively lower BAD D values were observed, especially in the left eye. The thinnest part of the cornea was not coinciding with the thinnest part of the epithelium in the optovue, especially in the right eye.

case_report: A 41-year-old Japanese woman (gravida 2, para 0) experienced two previous first-trimester miscarriages. She achieved pregnancy through in vitro fertilization. Ultrasound examinations during the second and third trimesters did not show signs of placenta accreta. At 36 weeks of gestation, she developed preeclampsia and underwent a caesarean section. She delivered a healthy male infant weighing 2178 grams, with Apgar scores of 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. The placenta did not separate spontaneously, necessitating manual removal by the operator. The placenta was tightly adhered, and during the procedure, no uterine inversion or perforation was noted, nor were there any uterine cavity adhesions. The manual removal was completed successfully. Continuous bleeding followed the removal of the placenta, leading to uterine gauze packing, which effectively stopped the bleeding. On the first postoperative day, minimal bleeding was observed, prompting the obstetrician to remove the gauze. However, severe bleeding recurred, and a Bakri® Balloon was inserted into the uterine cavity, successfully stopping the bleeding again. The balloon was removed on the third postoperative day, with no further active bleeding observed. One month after the operation, the patient reported no abnormal complaints. Her menstrual cycle resumed two months postoperatively.
test_results: We detected an adhesion at the fundus of her uterus, in the location of the placenta accreta.

case_report: A 50-year-old Korean male presented with a tumefactive nodule on the frontal scalp, which had enlarged over a period of 2 months. The patient reported a history of playing soccer and frequently heading the ball with the affected area of the scalp. He also mentioned a recent incident where he forcefully bumped his frontal scalp against a ball shortly before the nodule appeared. His medical history was otherwise unremarkable, and a review of systems revealed no additional symptoms. On physical examination, a 5×5 cm, well-defined, dome-shaped, salmon-colored, waxy nodule with overlying purpuric plaques was observed on the frontal scalp. The lesion exhibited mild tenderness.
test_results: There were follicular plugging, thinning and flattening of stratum malpighii in the epidermis and deposition of acellular amorphous eosinophilic materials throughout the entire dermis. There were a mild to moderate perivascular and interstitial lymphocytic infiltrate admixed with plasma cells, mast cells, and a few eosinophils and a little interstitial mucin deposition in the upper and deep dermis. Congo red staining with polarizing microscopic examination revealed apple-green birefringence throughout the whole dermis. An electron microscopic examination revealed uniform, long, and straight filaments.

case_report: A 23-year-old female reported experiencing itchy and darkened patches on the upper back in the scapular regions bilaterally and on the extensor surfaces of both arms. The patient has a history of dry skin, resides in a hot and humid climate, and applies non-medicated moisturizer to her skin. The condition was not accompanied by nodules, inflammation, pus, or fever. There was no history of using loofahs, scrubs, other skin irritants, or any topical medications. Laboratory tests were conducted and returned normal results.
test_results: A lesion biopsy showed lymphocytic infiltration and amorphous deposits in the dermis.

case_report: A 40-year-old female patient reported experiencing recurring pain. Her medical history was unremarkable except for a cesarean delivery performed several years prior. She observed that the pain was more pronounced in the left rectus muscle, distant from the cesarean scar. Initially, she sought advice from her obstetrician, who recommended treatment with pain relievers and hormonal therapy, including oral contraceptives and a gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist. These treatments did not alleviate her pain.
test_results: Ultrasound and CT scan showed a mid-rectus lesion.

case_report: A two-day-old preterm male infant (29 weeks gestational age), weighing 1.240 kg, with an Apgar score of 5/6, was transferred from the maternity ward to the intensive care unit due to respiratory difficulties and low birth weight. Antenatal ultrasonography at 27 weeks gestational age showed several hypoechoic areas indicating dilated stomach and small bowel. The amniotic fluid volume was normal, with minor hyperechoic changes possibly related to the presence of blood. Cytogenetic analysis of the amniotic fluid confirmed a normal male chromosome set. Upon admission, the infant exhibited rapid and irregular breathing, cyanosis with bluish discoloration of the extremities, reduced spontaneous activity, decreased reactivity to stimuli, weak crying, discomfort, and occasional groaning. The abdomen was below the level of the thorax, soft, and moved with respiration. The external genitalia were typical for a male, and the anal opening was normally positioned. There were no limb deformities. Muscle tone was reduced, activity was slowed, and reflexes were present. Due to respiratory instability, the infant was intubated and placed on ventilator support. A nasogastric tube was inserted, which drained bilious aspirate.
test_results: Plain radiograph of the abdomen showed the classic dilatation of the proximal duodenum and stomach with total absence of distal bowel gas.
diagnosis: Duodenal atresia with apple-peel configuration of the ileum and absent superior mesenteric artery
