case_report: An 8-year-old boy with no prior medical or surgical history presented to a tertiary academic center due to worsening difficulty in breathing. His parents reported episodes of cyanosis after breastfeeding during infancy and also after crying. Between infancy and school age, he experienced shortness of breath during physical activities, which was accompanied by rapid heartbeats and shallow breathing. Upon reaching school age, his breathing difficulties became more pronounced, with audible stridor. Over the past three months, both his dyspnea and stridor had intensified. He did not report fever, chest pain, weight loss, or coughing. On examination, he measured 125 cm in height and weighed 27 kg. Physical examination showed a heart rate of 120 beats per minute, a respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute, mild hypotension with a blood pressure of 90/70 mmHg, and an oxygen saturation of 85%. Laboratory tests were within normal limits, showing no signs of anemia or leukocytosis. The patient underwent a rigid bronchoscopy, which revealed normal tracheal mucosa and a compressible soft tissue mass. A subsequent neck CT scan identified a vascular mass located behind the larynx and cervical trachea.
test_results: At MRI, a multiloculated nodular lesion in the intraluminal part of the trachea and also partly in the infra-glottic area, measuring 12×8 mm and taking up half of the tracheal lumen, was found. The lesion was hypo-signal in the T1 sequence, hyper-signal in the T2 sequence, and heterogeneous after the contrast injection.

case_report: A 35-year-old male presented with a history of progressive weakness in both lower limbs over the past two years, which worsened in the last six months. Initially, he experienced a shaking sensation while walking, which gradually intensified. Recently, he reported stiffness and weakness in both lower extremities, increased difficulty in walking and defecating, frequent falls, occasional urinary difficulties, and numbness and pain in the limbs, along with muscle atrophy. There was no significant weight change since the onset. Since junior high school, he had hyperpigmentation over his body, including the lips, oral mucosa, gums, and areola. He had no history of alcohol or tobacco use and no exposure to toxic substances. His parents were healthy, not consanguineous, and his mother had six siblings without similar conditions. Physical examination revealed normal consciousness, dark skin, pigmentation of the lips, intraoral mucosa, gums, and bilateral areola. Higher cortical functions were normal, speech was fluent, and cranial nerve examination was unremarkable. Muscle strength was grade 5 in the upper extremities and grade 4 in the lower extremities, with normal muscle tone in the upper extremities and increased tone in the lower extremities. Reflexes in the upper extremities were brisk, and knee reflexes were also brisk. Pain sensation was intact, ataxic examination was normal, but kinesthesia and vibration sensation in the lower extremities were slightly decreased. The patient exhibited a scissor gait, positive double Bartholomew sign, and negative Romberg sign. Laboratory tests, including blood routine, liver and kidney function, cardiac enzymes, lipids, blood glucose, electrolytes, antinuclear antibody profile, tumor markers, ASO, RF, CRP, and routine urine and stool tests, showed no significant abnormalities. Tests for hepatitis B, syphilis, and HIV were negative. MRI of the spinal cord indicated mild atrophy of the thoracic medulla and mild posterior protrusion of the cervical 5 to 6 disc. MRI of the pituitary gland was normal, and cranial MRI showed no significant abnormalities. Nerve conduction studies revealed multiple peripheral nerve damage in both lower extremities, affecting motor and sensory fibers, with myelin and axonal involvement. Thyroid function was normal. Hormone levels were as follows: plasma cortisol (8 AM): 2.83 μg/dL, serum adrenocorticotropic hormone: >440.400 pmol/L, prolactin: 19.28 ng/mL, luteinizing hormone: 10.16 Miu/mL, follicle-stimulating hormone: 30.83 Miu/mL. Progesterone, testosterone, estradiol, and 24-hour urinary free cortisol were within normal ranges.
test_results: Complete serum very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs) and genetic testing indicated increased serum concentrations (c24:0-LPC): 0.764 μmol/L, reference range: 0.015–0.172 μmol/L; c26:0-LPC: 0.797 μmol/L, reference range: 0.008–0.085 μmol/L; C24:0 LPC/c20:0-LPC ratio of 3.322, reference range: 0.124–1.087; C26: 0-LPC/C20:0-LPC ratio of 3.465, reference range: 0.066–0.716; C24: 0-LPC/c22:0-LPC ratio of 7.14, reference range: 0.481–3.172.; C26: 0-LPC/C22: 0-LPC ratio of 7.449, reference range: 0.183–2.316. Molecular genetic test report: chromosomal location: chrX: 152991482; nucleotide change: c.761C>T; amino acid change: p. Thr254Met; exon/intron: Exon1; variant type: hemizygous; variant classification: missense mutation; father: no variant found; mother: no variant found.

case_report: This 22-year-old male, born from a non-consanguineous marriage with a normal birth and developmental history, began experiencing generalized hyperpigmentation of the body at age 4. The hyperpigmentation started at the knuckles and spread to the entire body over 4-5 months. He had recurrent episodes of dizziness with brief loss of consciousness, without tonic-clonic movements, tongue bite, or urinary incontinence. Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)-stimulated serum cortisol was measured at 1 pg/dl. Treatment with glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids led to a reversal of hyperpigmentation and a reduction in syncopal episodes. One year later, he developed gradually worsening weakness in all four limbs, starting distally in the lower limbs and spreading to the upper limbs over 3-4 months. The weakness was predominantly distal and accompanied by muscle wasting. He required support to walk. Subsequently, he experienced difficulty swallowing liquids, occasional nasal regurgitation, slurred speech with nasal intonation, and cognitive decline, including learning difficulties and poor academic performance. There were no sensory symptoms, sphincter incontinence, headaches, vomiting, or muscle twitching. Neurological examination showed a mini-mental status examination (MMSE) score of 26/30, spastic dysarthria with nasal intonation, left lateral pterygoid weakness, normal jaw jerk, bilateral 7th, 9th, and 10th cranial nerve palsy with decreased gag reflex, spastic paraparesis, and a fissured tongue. There was distal predominant muscle wasting in all extremities, marked hypertonia in the lower limbs, generalized hyperreflexia, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Sensory and cerebellar examinations were normal. Laboratory evaluations, including complete hemogram, blood sugar, liver and renal function tests, and electrolytes, were within normal ranges. Brain and cervical magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans were normal. Nerve conduction studies indicated symmetric motor and sensory predominantly axonal polyneuropathy. Electromyography (EMG) showed a denervation pattern. Visual-evoked potential and brainstem auditory-evoked response studies were normal.
test_results: Serum analysis showed elevated very long chain fatty acids (VLCFA).

case_report: A 64-year-old male patient presented with a high fever and dehydration lasting three days. He reported leg spasticity beginning in his teenage years. By his mid-30s, he experienced difficulty running, frequent urination, and urinary incontinence. He worked in healthcare until the age of 55. At 58, he required a wheelchair and developed recurrent red macules on the bony prominences of his sacral region. At 63, following the death of his primary caretaker, he became mostly bedridden, receiving weekly home care services, and suffered from poor nutrition and hygiene, leading to severe edema in his legs and feet. Two months prior to admission, 5 cm bullae appeared on both heels. Physical examination showed a temperature of 39.2°C, pulse of 120 beats/minute, respiratory rate of 20 breaths/minute, and blood pressure of 120/90 mmHg. He had deep pressure ulcers with black necrotic tissue on the sacral region, bilateral lateral malleus, and left lateral heel. The bullae on his heels had ruptured, revealing dark red erosions. Small dark pigmentations were noted on his lips. Neurological examination indicated normal cognition and speech, intact cranial nerves, and an inability to stand, walk, or sit without assistance. Hypertonus was observed in the lower extremities with slight contractures limiting hip, knee, and ankle extension. Muscle strength was graded 5/5 in the upper extremities and 1/5 in the lower extremities. The finger-nose-finger test showed no ataxia. Sensation was severely decreased in the bilateral lower extremities. Muscle stretch reflexes were hyperactive at the knees and absent at the ankles, with extensor plantar responses. The patient also experienced urinary and fecal incontinence.
test_results: Laboratory testing showed an inflammatory response and hypoalbuminemia. ACTH and cortisol were within normal limits, while the C26/C22 ratio of VLCFA was elevated. A spinal MRI showed the atrophy of the thoracic and lumbar spinal cord. A brain MRI showed normal findings with no contrast-enhancing lesions. A nerve conduction study revealed an absence of the compound motor action potential and sensory nerve action potential of the lower extremities. He had the p.Gly298Ser variant in the ABCD1 gene but did not have the p.Leu272Ser variant in exon 5 of the SPAST gene.

case_report: A 49-year-old Sri Lankan female reported experiencing severe aches and pains along with spasms in her hands and feet for the past 2 years. Initially, she noticed vague aches and pains accompanied by shoulder stiffness, followed by episodic cramps and spasms in her hands and feet. She did not experience memory issues, behavioral changes, or seizures. Her appetite, weight, and bowel habits remained stable, and she did not report lethargy or cold intolerance. Thirteen years ago, she had a history of toxic multinodular goiter and underwent subtotal thyroidectomy. Histology revealed papillary carcinoma of the thyroid, leading to a completion thyroidectomy and subsequent I-131 treatment. She has been on a long-term thyroxine replacement therapy of 200 μg daily with regular follow-ups and remained well until 2 years ago. There were no records of low calcium levels post-surgery, and she had not been on calcium or calcitriol treatment until her current presentation. On physical examination, she appeared well and of average build, with no signs of alopecia, fungal infections, or vitiligo. A thyroidectomy scar was noted, but there were no neck lumps or cervical lymphadenopathy. She did not have papilloedema or cataracts, and her upper and lower limb examinations were normal. Positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs were observed. Her abdominal, respiratory, and cardiovascular examinations were normal, with a pulse rate of 80 bpm.
test_results: Her serum calcium was low with marginally high serum phosphate. The PTH level was low at 9 pg/ml.
Orpha_name: Secondary hypoparathyroidism due to impaired parathormon secretion

case_report: A 12-year-old female was referred to the Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery Department by an orthodontist due to an ectopic upper left canine and buccal alveolar expansion between the 22 and 24 teeth. Examination revealed firm, bony expansion in this area with associated root displacement. The 22 and 24 teeth were not mobile, and the overlying mucosa appeared normal. The patient did not report any symptoms. Radiographic imaging showed an ectopic 23 tooth, which seemed to be within the maxillary sinus or surrounded by a large cystic radiolucency, along with an indistinct area of bony expansion between the 22 and 24 teeth. There was no evidence of root resorption in the 22 and 24 teeth. Cone beam computed tomography (CT) indicated expanded bone in the 23 region with a normal trabecular pattern and intact buccal and palatal cortices, but some buccal cortical expansion. The 23 tooth was located in the left zygomatic bone, with the crown facing buccally and causing dehiscence of the zygomatic bone. The roots were oriented toward the left maxillary sinus, with the dilacerated apex projecting into the sinus. The cause of the buccal alveolar expansion and migration of the 23 tooth was not clear. The patient underwent exploration of the 23 region under general anesthesia, including a bone biopsy of the lesion and a left middle meatal antroscopy. The 23 tooth was not visible during the examination of the left maxillary sinus. The expanded buccal bone appeared firm but abnormal with slight bleeding.
test_results: Histopathology results showed vital lamellar bone with uniform osteoblast layer with minimal evidence of resorption. The soft tissue component was a mixture of adipose and highly vascular fibrous tissue. Numerous blood vessels ranged widely in size, some having muscle wall and appeared to be displacing adipose tissue.

case_report: A 10-month-old female presented with recurrent infections in the maxillofacial region, characterized by swelling or abscess formation in the left cheek and purulent discharge from a preauricular pit over a period of 4 months. Physical examination revealed a swollen, erythematous lesion on the left cheek. Additionally, a pit with white purulent secretions was noted in the intertragic notch, along with a small cutaneous dimple in the left parotid gland area. Examination of the external auditory canal showed no fistula track, and other head and neck examinations were normal. Ultrasound of the maxillofacial area indicated inflammatory changes. Other auxiliary examinations, including otoscopy, pure tone audiometry, and renal ultrasound, showed no abnormalities. There was no history of prior incision or drainage procedures, and no significant family history was reported.
test_results: The results revealed two conjunctive tracts: one tract arose from the skin surface anteroinferior to the EAC, beneath the facial nerve, and passed into the deep lobe of the parotid gland and projected to the masseter; the other tract extended from the superficial lobe of the left parotid to the intertragic notch.

case_report: A 19-year-old male presented in June 2019 with a mass located behind the right earlobe, accompanied by recurrent swelling and pain in the postauricular region since childhood. The patient had undergone abscess incision drainage three times at a local hospital. Additionally, the patient experienced severe hearing loss in the right ear since birth. Physical examination revealed a 2 cm × 3 cm fluctuant and tender mass in the postauricular area, along with bony atresia of the external auditory canal. The patient had no other significant medical history.
test_results: A computed tomography (CT) scan of the temporal bone showed a hypointense cystic mass protruding into the area of the atretic EAC. Color Doppler ultrasound showed a mucocele-like lesion with inhomogenous internal echoes. Pure-tone audiometry showed severe conductive hearing loss with an air-bone conduction gap of 56 decibels (dB).

case_report: A 4-year-old girl from Jamaica presented with recurrent abscesses on the left side of her neck, which had been managed with multiple courses of antibiotics. On physical examination, a 4-cm firm and tender mass was observed in the left thyroid region, accompanied by overlying redness and hardening of the skin.
test_results: Neck computed tomography scan demonstrated a 3.9-cm poorly defined, partially cystic left thyroid mass. Barium esophagram revealed a fistulous tract arising from the left pyriform sinus to the left neck with accumulation of contrast in the left thyroid cyst.
diagnosis: Branchial Cleft Cyst with Mycobacterium Infection

case_report: A 13-year-old female presented with a non-tender mass on the right side of the upper neck and a mild sore throat. The swelling was first noticed by her mother about a month prior and had been increasing in size. The patient reported no fever, cough, fatigue, weight loss, palpitations, or breathlessness. Her medical history included two syncopal episodes in the past year and idiopathic adolescent scoliosis diagnosed a year ago, for which she was undergoing regular physiotherapy. She was eight months post-menarche and had no allergies. The patient had recently traveled to Sri Lanka and was active in swimming twice weekly. The syncopal episodes were unprovoked and occurred seven months apart. The first episode happened during a physiotherapy session, where she felt dizzy, lost consciousness for 10 seconds, had a blood pressure of 87/48, and was tired upon regaining consciousness. The second episode occurred in the morning while she was preparing to eat breakfast, resulting in a two-minute loss of consciousness. She had no syncopal episodes during exercise or stress. Vital signs were normal. Examination of the neck swelling revealed it was unilateral, located in the submandibular and upper cervical regions, approximately 4 cm in diameter, with no overlying skin changes, non-tender, well-defined borders, slightly vague margins, soft, fluctuant, and not transluminant. The pharynx was mildly erythematous, and the chest was clear to auscultation. The abdomen was soft, non-tender, with no distension, hepatosplenomegaly, or groin swelling. No palpable lymph nodes were found in the axillae bilaterally. Blood tests including CMV IgM antibody, anti-VCA IgM, anti-EA IgG, anti-EBNA-1 IgG, full blood count, CRP, ESR, and peripheral smear were conducted. All tests returned negative results, showing no evidence of infectious or malignant etiology.
test_results: Ultrasound imaging of the right side of the neck showed a large hypoechoic oval lesion in the right infra-auricular region. The parotid gland and submandibular glands on either side appeared normal. There was left-sided level II lymph node prominence. The region of interest in the right upper third neck showed a fairly well-defined hypodense lesion with a uniform density, which was insinuated deep in the SCM muscle and the lower end of the parotid gland. This measured around 31x22x20 mm in size. It abutted the carotid sheath without any infiltration. No calcifications were seen in or surrounding the lesion. There were multiple lymph nodes in the left posterior triangle of the neck as well as the jugulodigastric trunk, which were reactive in nature. The findings in this CT scan confirmed the presence of a cystic non-enhancing soft tissue mass in the right upper neck.

case_report: An 11-month-old girl presented with a swelling on the left side of her face, which had been present since birth. The parents reported no associated pain, difficulty in chewing, opening the mouth, hearing issues, or neurological deficits. Physical examination revealed a swelling measuring approximately 10 cm × 7 cm, located on the lateral part of the face. The swelling extended superiorly to the left temporo-parietal region, medially to the mid-cheek and lateral part of the upper eyelid, and posteriorly, it displaced the ear backwards and downwards. The overlying skin appeared normal, and no neurological deficits were observed. Routine blood tests were within normal limits, and serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) was measured at 7.3 ng/ml (reference range: 0–10 ng/ml).
test_results: Ultrasound showed a solid-cystic mass with septations in the left temporoparietal region. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and face showed a large extracranial well-defined rounded mixed intensity mass lesion measuring approximately 8 cm × cm 6 × 9 cm along the left side of skull vault. Internally lesion was multicystic with areas of fat intensity. There was scalp defect with curvilinear communication of the mass lesion with extradural space. On computed tomography (CT) correlation, there were no areas of calcification seen within the lesion.

case_report: A 7-month-old male infant was brought to the surgical outpatient department with a history of a mass on the left side of the neck. This swelling had been present since birth and measured approximately 5.6 × 7 × 7.6 cm. The infant was feeding well, and his sensory and motor milestones were appropriate for his age. There were no signs of respiratory distress.
test_results: A complex heterogeneous solid cystic and calcification enhancing mass lesion in the left cervical region with extensions into the left parotid space, left buccal space, left submandibular space, left carotid space, left parapharyngeal space and left retropharyngeal space. The tumor was found in a gray-white to brown with globular measuring as 6 × 5 × 4.5 cm. The cut section portrayed a variegated appearance with focal areas of cystic degeneration. Microscopic examination revealed a sebaceous glans, cartilage adipose, thyroid tissue, calcification area, choroid tissue, melanocyte pigment and trabeculation of bone. There was no euroephitelial component found.

case_report: A 3-year-old male with a medical history of DiGeorge syndrome, single cardiac ventricle anatomy post-aortic reconstruction, Glenn, and Damus-Kaye-Stansel procedures, heart block with pacemaker, T-cell lymphopenia, gastrostomy tube dependence, developmental delay, and intellectual disability presented with fever and 24 hours of increasing swelling and redness of the right eye, along with mild protrusion of the eye. Pupils were equal in size and reactive to light, with no apparent visual field deficits. Parents noted a skin dimple over the right pterion present since birth, intermittently releasing hair and purulent material. On presentation, the patient had a fever of 38.3°C and leukocytosis at 14.65 thousand. Laboratory results showed a C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 5.0 mg/dL (normal 0.0 - 0.7 mg/dL), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 18 mm/h (normal 1-15 mm/h), and a neutrophil count of 10.66 thousand (normal 1.80-7.40 thousand). Blood cultures taken in the emergency department showed no growth, although antibiotics were administered before the cultures were obtained. The patient was treated with intravenous steroids, vancomycin, and ceftriaxone for broad-spectrum antibiotic coverage.
test_results: The obtained images demonstrated an intraorbital, extraconal rim-enhancing fluid collection along the superolateral wall of the right orbit measuring approximately 1.4 x 1.4 x 0.5cm immediately adjacent to a lytic bone lesion within the right sphenoid wing/posterolateral orbital wall with intracranial epidural extension anterior to the right temporal pole. This was associated with a circuitous cutaneous tract extending through the right temporal soft tissue.

case_report: A four-year-old girl came to our clinic with a swelling in her left preauricular region that had been present for 2 years. She had no history of disease, surgery, or trauma in that area. The girl was otherwise in good health, with no fever, lymphadenopathy, or weight loss reported. Physical examination revealed a painless, firm, and nonfluctuant mass in the left parotid gland area. Facial nerve function was normal bilaterally.
test_results: Ultrasonography showed a well-defined, homogenic, round, and hypodense mass with a measured diameter of 2.5 cm. The mass was embedded in the superficial lobe of the parotid gland and seemed to be capsulated. An MRI allowed a better preoperative evaluation referring to anatomy and dignity. While the mass was not infiltrating into the surrounding tissue, it was, however, in close neighborhood to the external auditory canal. It showed a signal enrichment in T2 weighting and an intermediate signal in T1. It did not show any enhancement of the contrast medium. Pathological lymph nodes were also not detected. Pathological examination showed a benign cyst with lining of squamous cell epithelium and associated skin appendages. The lumen of the cyst contained several coreless squamous cells and keratin debris. The wall of the cyst contained fibrocartilaginous tissue with mild lymphocyte infiltration. An infiltration of lymphocytes, neutrophil granulocytes, and older adiponecrosis was found in parts of the underlying stroma.
diagnosis: Dermoid cyst of the parotid gland

case_report: A 7-month-old male infant presented with difficulties in feeding and swelling of the tongue. Physical examination revealed a cystic lesion near the left side of the tongue base, causing the tongue to protrude to the opposite side. No other abnormalities were noted on physical examination, and the child's medical history was unremarkable. The patient was admitted for surgical intervention. During the procedure, a 3-cm diameter opaque, thick-walled cyst was found closely adherent to the tongue base. The cyst was completely excised using bipolar diathermy under general anesthesia. Preparations for an emergent tracheostomy were made in case orotracheal intubation was not feasible, but no respiratory issues occurred during intubation or extubation. Postoperatively, the patient was able to feed early and experienced no complications other than increased salivation.
test_results: The cystic lesion was lined with intestinal mucosa accompanied by goblet cells. Stratified squamous epithelium was also present in some areas.
diagnosis: Enteric duplication cyst located at the posterior tongue
Orpha_name: Digestive duplication cyst of the tongue

case_report: A 5-day-old female infant from a rural area was presented to the maxillofacial surgery department due to an oral mass that was interfering with feeding. The mother, a 16-year-old who had not attended regular prenatal visits, was previously healthy. Laboratory tests for Toxoplasma (IgM-IgG), Hepatitis B virus, HIV, and other routine tests showed no signs of prenatal infection, and thyroid stimulating hormone levels were normal. The infant was born at 38 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery, with an APGAR score of 91/105, a birth weight of 2550 g, a length of 44 cm, and a head circumference of 32 cm. Physical examination revealed a 2.0 cm cystic, nonpulsatile, renitent, translucent lesion at the tip of the tongue, with a base of equal size, which was obstructing mouth closure, suction, and breastfeeding. The mass was surgically removed without complications, enabling normal breastfeeding. The patient was discharged without further interventions and has shown good progress in weight gain and neurodevelopment during follow-up evaluations.
test_results: Upon macroscopic examination, the 2.0 cm cystic lesion was translucent, unilocular, filled with a clear, watery fluid, possessed no papilla on the external or internal surfaces and had an average wall thickness of 0.2 cm. The microscopic analysis shows a benign cystic lesion, whose internal surface was covered by epithelial cells, most of them squamous admixed with respiratory and antral type epithelia. The wall of the cyst was composed of dense connective tissue with thin strands of striated and smooth muscle, and congestive small vessels. No teratoma elements were identified.
diagnosis: Enteric duplication cyst  of the tongue
Orpha_name: Digestive duplication cyst of the tongue

case_report: A two-year-old boy was brought to the clinic by his parents due to a growing mass on the upper right side of his nose, present since birth. The child had no history of medical complications or surgeries, and the mass had been gradually increasing in size. Prenatal, natal, and postnatal histories were normal. There was no family history of similar conditions, and the parents were not related by blood. On physical examination, a 1 × 1 cm dome-shaped, subcutaneous nodule was observed on the upper right side of the nasal bridge. The nodule was erythematous, firm, noncompressible, and nontender. The transillumination test was negative. No other skin lesions were detected on the body. Examination of the hair, nails, and mucous membranes showed normal findings.
test_results: MRI of the facial region with contrast showed a nasal dorsum lesion measuring 10 × 16 × 10 mm with a draining sinus tract anterior to the nasofrontal junction with no intracranial extension. The histopathology report showed a polypoidal tissue covered by unremarkable keratinized stratified squamous epithelium and underlying skin adnexal, including hair follicles and sebaceous glands. Lobules of mature adipose tissue and skeletal muscle bundles separated by a thin, fibrous capsule were also noted.

case_report: A 15-year-old girl reported experiencing intermittent headaches in the occipital region for the past 7 months. These headaches intensified with walking and standing but were alleviated by rest, with no changes related to posture. She mentioned a history of a road traffic accident 6 months ago, from which she recovered without complications and did not sustain any injury to the occipital area. Physical examination revealed a small sinus at the occipital protuberance, without any active discharge or underlying swelling. Neurological examination showed normal results, and no cerebellar signs were observed.
test_results: MRI brain showed a well defined lesion in the region of the vermis-hypointense on T1W, hyperintense on T2W with a patchy contrast enhancement and causing compression on the vermis. Fourth ventricle was normal in shape. There was no obstructive hydrocephalus. A thin tract was seen to extend from the skin surface, coursing downwards and entering the bone just to the left of midline at the level of the torqula.
diagnosis: Dermoid cyst with a sinus tract

case_report: A 4-year-old female presented with a swelling on the nose that had been present for 1 year and had increased in size over the past 2 months. There was no history of facial trauma, infection, surgery, or familial inheritance. Clinical examination showed a swelling on the nasal dorsum and a well-defined groove between the two alar domes, leading to an increased columellar width. The anterior edge of the nasal septum was thick and separated in a 'Y' shape, resulting in a bifid appearance of the nose. Additionally, a midline punctum was observed over the swelling.
test_results: CT scan axial view showed a soft tissue swelling overlying glabella and in between nasal septum with no evidence of intracranial extension.
diagnosis: Midline nasal dermoid cyst with Tessier's 0 cleft

case_report: A 25-day-old male infant was brought to the hospital with a midline swelling located over the nose and upper lip. This swelling had been present since birth and did not result in nasal obstruction or nosebleeds. The infant also had a cleft palate. He was delivered at full-term through a normal vaginal delivery. Physical examination revealed a facial anomaly characterized by a 5 cm × 4 cm swelling extending from the dorsum of the nose to the vermilion border of the upper lip. The swelling exhibited a purplish color with multiple small, dilated blood vessels on its surface. It was non-tender and non-pulsatile. No mass was observed inside the nasal cavity. Additionally, the infant had a type II cleft palate extending to the incisive foramen.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) of the brain showed a superficial midline nasal mass with no direct connection to the brain.

case_report: A two-month-old male infant was born with a full Apgar score. He experienced neonatal jaundice that was managed with low-intensity phototherapy and was later discharged home. His mother observed noisy breathing starting from the second week of life, which intensified with activity. Additionally, the infant began having feeding difficulties. Upon admission and referral to the otorhinolaryngology team, physical examination revealed soft intermittent inspiratory stridor accompanied by subcostal and intercostal recession. Oxygen saturation was maintained at 100% with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP).
test_results: Bedside flexible laryngoscopy showed features of laryngomalacia, tubular epiglottis, tight aryepiglottic fold, and floppy arytenoids. There was a pooling of secretions at the pyriform fossae. The child underwent direct laryngoscopy under general anesthesia, which revealed a cystic mass over the valleculae. Similarly, a Hopkins telescope (zero degrees) was introduced transorally to facilitate visualization of the vallecular cyst endoscopically.

case_report: A 10-year-old female patient arrived at the Emergency Room with significant bleeding from the left side of the mouth after a tooth extraction due to caries. The bleeding was managed by packing the mandible and administering a blood transfusion. The patient had no prior history of medications, blood transfusions, bleeding disorders, or hospitalizations. A systemic examination revealed no abnormalities, and there was no noticeable facial asymmetry.
test_results: The orthopantomogram (OPG) was suggestive of a large expansile radiolucent lesion with soap bubble appearance in left ramus and angle of mandible extending up to molar area. The NCCT showed a large expansile lytic lesion with cortical thinning and destruction involving the left ramus of mandible. Contrast study showed an enhancing lesion with abnormal tuft of tortuous, dilated feeding vessels at the site of lesion. The lesion was seen extending into left masticator space. On CT angiography, multiple arterial feeders to the lesion were seen originating from left external carotid artery with venous drainage into left external jugular vein.

case_report: A 59-year-old male with a 20-year history of liver cirrhosis and recurrent hepatic encephalopathy (HE) presented with a cough and sputum production lasting for 2 months. He had no history of trauma, surgery, or other significant medical history. Physical examination revealed a very thin appearance without other notable findings. Laboratory tests showed severe microcytic hypochromic anemia with a hemoglobin level of 78 g/L and an albumin level of 24 g/L. Blood ammonia was measured at 171 μmol/L. Tumor markers (CEA, CA-125, CA-199, and AFP), connective tissue disease markers, and hepatitis markers were all negative. Chest computed tomography (CT) indicated significant mediastinal enlargement with a liquid-like density without enhancement, peribronchovascular infiltrations, ground-glass opacities, and a small amount of effusion in the left pleural cavity (Fig. A and B). Bronchoscopy revealed a smooth and edematous mucosal surface with diffuse thin-walled translucent vesicles in the mucosa of both bronchi (Fig. C and D). Following bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), the patient's cough symptoms worsened suddenly, accompanied by excessive chyloptysis. Emergency surgical intervention was performed, including surgical ligation of the thoracic duct.
test_results: Histologically, dilated, irregular, and anastomozing vascular structures positive for D2–40, which are markers of the vascular endothelium, were found.

case_report: A 31-year-old woman underwent a barium enema examination during a routine medical checkup. She had no specific complaints and no notable past medical or family history. The patient measured 161 cm in height and weighed 44 kg. She appeared well, and the physical examination revealed no abnormalities. Laboratory tests, including complete blood cell count, biochemical analysis for hepatic and renal function, urine analysis, and fecal occult blood test, were all within normal limits. Tumor markers for CEA and CA 19-9 were also normal. No abnormalities were detected on upper endoscopy and abdominal ultrasound.
test_results: On the air contrast barium enema, multiple thumbprint-like lesions ranging from 7 to 20 mm in diameter were observed from the cecum to the hepatic flexure, mainly in the ascending colon. The colonoscopy revealed clusters of round submucosal tumors with a gentle slope and smooth surface from the cecum to the hepatic flexure. The color and surface characteristics of the lesions did not differ from those of the surrounding normal mucosa; however, they were noted to be pale to transparent. The lesions had a positive cushion (pillow) sign, and there were no ulcerations or erosions. The EUS was performed with a radial scanning catheter probe (12 MHz, Fujinon Inc., Saitama, Japan) that showed each of the submucosal lesions as an echo-free cyst, with a clear border, in the submucosal layer. The inner structure was uniform and some of the cysts had septal walls. Some of the lesions were punctured and aspirated, and a transparent yellowish, serous liquid resembling lymphatic fluid was collected. The submucosal lesions easily caved in during aspiration. The endoscopic biopsy revealed a submucosal cyst with occasional multinucleated cells; however, there were no fat or blood cell components. The D2-40 immunostaining, which is a specific lymphatic endothelial marker, showed positive reactivity for lining endothelial cells of the lymphatic spaces.

case_report: A 9-year-old female child from Palestinian parents (first cousins) of Muslim origin had an unremarkable pregnancy and delivery, with a birth weight of 3 kg. Development was reported as normal until 18 months of age, when unsteady gait and frequent falling were observed. These symptoms persisted until 7 years of age, at which point learning difficulties became apparent, including attention and memory deficits, difficulties manipulating objects, and dysgraphia. Behavioral changes were also noted, such as an abnormal sleep pattern with night terrors and purposeless movements. At the initial evaluation at 7 years old, the child weighed 18 kg (5th percentile), had a height of 116 cm (25th percentile), and a normal head circumference of 51.5 cm. Physical examination showed no facial dysmorphisms or organomegaly. Neurological examination revealed normal eye movements, cogwheel rigidity in the upper limbs with normal tone in the legs, and an unsteady wide-based gait. Deep tendon reflexes were normal. Laboratory tests, including blood and urine work for lactate, ammonia, CPK, hepatic assessment, urine organic acids, and plasma amino acid chromatography, showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Brain MRI showed mild cerebellar vermis atrophy and symmetrical bilateral hyperintensity of lentiform nucleus in T2 and diffusion weighted images, with cavitated aspects in FLAIR sequence.
diagnosis: Isolated Complex III Deficiency due to TTC19 Mutation

case_report: A 24-year-old African woman was admitted to the hospital for a femoral neck fracture following a fall on the stairs. Surgical fixation was planned. Preoperative evaluation did not determine the genetic type of her condition. She exhibited minor skin changes on her face and hands, with no history of tumor surgery. Neurological examination revealed a minor decline in intelligence quotient (IQ), an end tremor of the extremities, and an ataxic gait. She was calm, cooperative, and oriented in time and space, with normal muscle strength and deep tendon reflexes. Cardiovascular and pulmonary evaluations, as well as biological test results, were normal.
test_results: A preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan did not show any sign of brain abnormalities. The images did not show any lesions that could explain these symptoms.

case_report: A 5-day-old female infant presented with bilious vomiting and abdominal distention since birth. The infant was delivered at term via caesarean section to a 30-year-old first-time mother, with a birth weight of 2.79 kg. Antenatal ultrasonography at 32 weeks gestation showed multiple, dilated, fluid-filled bowel loops. Upon admission, the infant exhibited signs of dehydration and had a distended abdomen. Other systemic examinations were normal. Blood tests were within normal limits.
test_results: X-ray abdomen revealed few dilated bowel loops, paucity of distal gas shadows and nasogastric tube in the right upper quadrant of abdomen. Ultrasound abdomen revealed liver predominantly on the left side of abdomen, multiple spleen like structures on the right side with distended bowel loops. Echocardiography revealed ostium secundum atrial septal defect of 5 mm with levocardia.
diagnosis: Situs inversus abdominalis with polysplenia and complex jejunal atresia

case_report: A 31-year-old male with no notable medical history presented with continuous seizures. He experienced a headache, a fever of 39°C, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures without regaining consciousness. His vital signs were stable except for the fever. Neurological examination revealed no abnormalities other than a stuporous mental state during frequent generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Initial blood tests indicated no leukocytosis and normal levels of inflammatory markers, including C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed 108 leukocytes/mm3 (83% polymorphonuclear leukocytes and 17% lymphocytes) with normal glucose (78 mg/dL) and protein (42 mg/dL) levels. Serologic tests of both blood and cerebrospinal fluid were normal.
test_results: Initial brain MRI showed T2 hyperintensity and swelling of isolated bilateral hippocampus, especially CA1 region without any abnormal lesion in other areas. Electroencephalography (EEG) showed frequent spike and waves on bilateral fronto-temporal areas dominantly on temporal areas.

case_report: A 67-year-old female presented with gross hematuria. Cystoscopy revealed a mass lesion approximately 1 cm in size on the left side of the bladder neck. The patient, a non-smoker with no additional systemic diseases and not on any medications, had a subtotal hysterectomy over 10 years ago due to uterine myoma. Physical examination showed no further positive findings. Following preoperative preparations, a complete transurethral resection (TUR) of the bladder tumor was performed at the primary hospital. Hematoxylin-eosin (HE) staining was used for pathological evaluation. To prevent recurrence, bladder perfusion with gemcitabine was administered. Hematuria reappeared after four cycles of bladder perfusion. Routine laboratory tests showed hemoglobin at 13.7 g/dL, creatinine at 49 umol/L, urine analysis with leukocytes at 30/HPF, and erythrocytes at 9/HPF. After completing necessary preoperative preparations, another TUR of the bladder tumor was performed at our hospital. The tumor was then examined using the HE staining method.
test_results: Mart-1, HMB-45, and S-100 were positive, while cytokeratin was negative.

case_report: Patient 2 is a 38-year-old woman who was identified incidentally following the observation of low dried blood spot acylcarnitine levels in her first-born child during newborn screening. The baby's plasma acylcarnitine concentrations were found to be within normal limits. Patient 2 has no notable medical history and does not exhibit any muscle-related symptoms.
test_results: Plasma acylcarnitine analysis demonstrated low total (5 μmol/L; RR 21-70), free (5 μmol/L; RR 13-56), and acetylcarnitine (0 μmol/L; RR 3-23) concentrations. Carnitine transport activity in the patient’s skin fibroblasts was markedly reduced (3% of controls). DNA sequencing of SLC22A5 identified two variants; c.424G>T and c.1463G>A. The genomic data was re-interrogated for the c.-149G>A promoter variant, which was successfully identified.

case_report: A 62-year-old man presented with a gradually evolving widespread papulonodular eruption on the face, flexors, and trunk over the past 30 years. Physical examination revealed multiple, well-defined, yellowish-brown papules and nodules, as well as tumor-like lesions symmetrically located on the upper and lower eyelids. Similar papules were noted on the cheeks and perioral region. On the anterior neck, the lesions were confluent, forming a diffuse plaque. Hundreds of red to brown papules were symmetrically distributed on the axilla, genitalia, popliteal regions, and trunk, with some confluent areas forming plaques or tumor-like lesions. Additional papules and nodules were observed on the nasal mucosa. The patient had no history of polyuria or any previous medical history. Urine osmolality analysis showed no abnormalities. Laboratory findings included a white blood cell count of 10,300 cells/mL with 74% neutrophils, a C-reactive protein level of 7 mg/dL (normal up to 0.5 mg/dL), fasting cholesterol of 148 mg/dL (normal up to 200 mg/dL), and triglycerides of 141 mg/dL (normal up to 150 mg/dL). Chest X-ray results were normal, and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and pituitary showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Histopathologic examination of skin biopsies showed a dense dermal diffuse histiocytic infiltration interspersed with mixed inflammatory cells and giant cells. Abundant foam cells were also seen. Immunohistochemistry was positive for CD68 (KP1) and negative for S-100 protein.

case_report: A 47-year-old male patient reported a 5-year history of multiple skin lesions located on the oral mucosa, head, neck, trunk, and upper limbs. His personal and family medical history showed no notable issues. He did not report any systemic symptoms. Dermatological examination revealed numerous symmetrical yellow to brown papules and nodules, which had grown into plaques and tumoral lesions, particularly in the intertriginous areas. Laboratory tests indicated normal results with the exception of moderate leukocytosis and a slightly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Electrocardiography and chest X-ray results were normal.
test_results: Histopathologic examination revealed diffuse dermal infiltration by histiocytic cells, foamy cells, and Touton-type giant cells. Immunohistochemical studies showed positive staining for CD68, factor XIIIa, and fascin, and negative staining for S100.

case_report: The patient is a 56-year-old Caucasian man with no significant past medical history. He presented with a 12-year history of swollen eyelid lesions that occasionally flare up with itching. The patient reported some improvement over the past 4 months using hydrocortisone valerate 0.2% cream applied twice daily. No other treatments have been tried. He also mentioned experiencing a burning sensation in the eyes occasionally but denied any other eye-related symptoms. There are no other skin or mucous membrane lesions reported. A review of systems was unremarkable. Physical examination revealed confluent, yellow-brown plaques on both the upper and lower eyelids. Additionally, non-palpable purpura was observed on the left upper eyelid. There was no evidence of macroglossia, and the ophthalmic examination was normal.
test_results: Histopathology shows a diffuse xanthomatized histiocytic infiltrate focally admixed with lymphocytes throughout the dermis into the subcutis. There are frequent Touton type giant cells noted.

case_report: A 65-year-old female presented with a 3-year history of gradually enlarging, periorbital, asymptomatic lesions. One of the lesions had been surgically removed 2 years ago at another hospital, but it recurred within a few months, accompanied by new, larger nodules. There was no history of ulceration or involvement of other sites, nor any eye complaints or significant systemic symptoms. The patient's medical history was unremarkable. On examination, multiple yellowish-brown, firm nodules were observed symmetrically in the periorbital area, ranging from 3 to 7 cm in their widest dimensions. The surface of the nodules exhibited a few telangiectasias and mild atrophy. Mild right-sided ectropion was also noted.
test_results: Histopathological examination of a surgical wedge biopsy showed ill-defined large foci of dense granulomatous infiltrate of large histiocytes and histiocytic foamy cells with lymphocytes and few plasma cells. Several histiocytic giant cells resembling Touton giant cells were present. Immunohistochemistry was positive for CD 68 and negative for CD 1a and S100.
diagnosis: Isolated Cutaneous Necrobiotic Xanthogranuloma  without Paraproteinemia

case_report: A 90-year-old male presented with a three-month history of asymptomatic skin lesions on his scalp. Physical examination revealed multiple violaceous confluent papules, nodules, and plaques with a central hemorrhagic crust on the scalp. Additionally, an enlarged preauricular lymph node measuring 1.5×1.5 cm was observed. The patient was in good general health, and routine laboratory tests returned results that were either negative or within normal limits.
test_results: The pathological evaluation revealed hyperkeratosis of the epidermis, with multiple tumor nodules with central necrosis infiltrated in the dermis. The medium-sized tumor cells had abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Reniform nuclei and nuclear grooves were occasionally observed. Multinucleate giant cells and eosinophils were absent. Immunohistochemical analyses showed that the tumor cells were positive for CD1a, S100, CD31, partially positive for CD68 (PGM1), and negative for Langerin, CD34, FXIIIa, Fli-1, HMB45, A103, EMA and PCK. The Ki-67 proliferation index was 35%.

case_report: A 55-year-old woman, generally in good health, reported experiencing burning sensations and clusters of red papules on her face and arms over the past six months. Previous treatments for rosacea had not been effective. A biopsy was conducted, revealing cells with specific characteristics on H&E staining. Further biopsies were taken from the chin and the arm.
test_results: Histopathologic examination demonstrated a dense nodular infiltrate of mononuclear cells. Immunoperoxidase staining of this infiltrate was strongly positive for CD1a and S100, as well as less densely positive for CD68. Staining for Langerin was performed and was negative. No appreciable neutrophils or eosinophils were present, and there was no significant epidermotropism.

case_report: A 23-year-old male presented with breathing difficulties and weight loss persisting for 8 months. Dermatology consultation was requested for skin lesions. Physical examination revealed pallor and enlarged submandibular and occipital lymph nodes. Skin examination identified multiple erythematous papules and nodules on the trunk, face, and scalp, with ulceration and scarring in both axillae. Some lesions had central umbilication and others were covered with adherent scales. Bronchial breath sounds were noted over the lower chest bilaterally with occasional crepitations. Peripheral blood smear showed normocytic normochromic red blood cells, neutrophilic leucocytosis, and relative lymphopenia, with no atypical cells or blasts. Hemoglobin was 8.5 gm/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 37 mm/hour, C-reactive protein was 10.2 mg/L, and total serum protein was 4.8 gms/dL. High-resolution computed tomography of the thorax revealed multiple bullae with panlobular emphysematous right residual lung and left-sided mild pleural effusion. Ultrasonography of the abdomen showed multiple complex cystic and solid lesions in the liver, mildly coarsened hepatic echotexture, and minimal ascites. Non-contrast computed tomography of the brain and skull showed an intact bony calvarium with no other abnormalities. Fine needle aspiration cytology from the lymph node revealed reactive lymphoid cells.
test_results: Biopsies from the trunk papules as well as from the right axillary ulcerative lesion revealed intermediate-sized cells arranged in nodules in the dermis and in perivascular locations. These cells had bland chromatin with nuclear indentation and grooves with abundant cytoplasm. Epidermotropism was present with occasional mitosis. No eosinophils were seen. On immunohistochemistry (IHC), the atypical cells were strongly positive for CD1a. S100 and CD4 were strongly positive in a few of these cells and, CD68 was positive in few superficial cells only. Langerin and myeloperoxidase (MPO) were negative in these cells.

case_report: A 60-year-old male presented with asymptomatic reddish raised skin lesions and significant weight loss over the past two years. The lesions gradually increased in size and number. He was started on multidrug therapy for leprosy, but the condition continued to worsen. Physical examination revealed multiple erythematous, non-tender infiltrated papules and nodules of varying sizes on the abdomen, back, neck, extremities, face, axillary, and inguinal regions. Some nodules on the posterior axillary fold and trunk exhibited ulceration and verrucous margins. Involvement of the right eyelid caused disfigurement and closure of the palpebral fissure. Indirect laryngoscopy showed swelling, congestion, and cobblestoning of the laryngeal mucosa, while the oropharyngeal, nasal, and conjunctival mucosa were unaffected. A large lesion over the right knee and ankle resulted in functional deformity of the right leg. Additionally, a few ichthyotic patches were observed on the extremities. There was no evidence of peripheral cutaneous nerve thickening or sensory impairment. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Routine hematological and radiological investigations were normal.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the nodule revealed ulcerated epidermis with dermal aggregates of proliferating spindle cells admixed with foamy macrophages. Biopsy from ichthyotic patch demonstrated epidermal spongiosis and superficial perivascular infiltrates. There was no evidence of acid fast bacilli (on slit skin smear and on biopsy), abnormal lymphocytes, or intracellular amastigote forms (on Giemsa stain). A strong positivity for CD68 and negative reaction for CD1a and S100 protein on immunohistochemistry.

case_report: A 37-year-old Caucasian male presented with multiple persistent lesions on his forehead and right temple. His past medical history included premature atrial contractions managed with propafenone and escitalopram. Laboratory results showed normal triglycerides and borderline elevated cholesterol (total 5.41 mmol/L; LDL 3.38 mmol/L). Initially, the patient reported 2-3 lesions, which increased in number over the following months. The lesions were described as moderately painful pink violaceous papules and nodules with irregular borders. An initial biopsy showed a prominent xanthogranulomatous infiltrate in the dermis and was diagnosed as a xanthoma. Treatment with intralesional triamcinolone was unsuccessful, and the number of lesions continued to increase.
test_results: Histologic evaluation of the recurrent/persistent lesions revealed an intense dermal infiltrate of foamy tissue macrophages with a minor admixture of plasma cells, lymphocytes, and scattered multinucleated giant cells. Other areas showed a predominance of spindled cells and associated extracellular collagen fibers. The nuclei of lesional cells did not exhibit hyperchromasia or pleomorphism, and no mitotic figures were seen. Adjacent skin adnexa were spared. The lesional cells were positive for CD163 and CD68 and negative for CD1a, thus confirming them to be of mononuclear-macrophage lineage.

case_report: A 32-year-old woman experienced a sudden onset of hearing loss in her right ear and severe rotational vertigo immediately after blowing her nose. She received corticosteroid treatment and was advised to rest in bed for one week. Initially, her vertigo symptoms subsided. However, on the seventh day, the severe rotational vertigo returned, and the hearing loss in her right ear remained. She was subsequently referred to our hospital.
test_results: An otoscopic examination showed bilateral intact tympanic membranes. Pure tone audiometry showed a severe right-sided mixed hearing loss. A high-resolution temporal bone CT scan on the 10th day showed pneumolabyrinth in the right vestibule.

case_report: A 9-year-old male presented to the outpatient clinic in April 2009 with a primary concern of a large, painless mass in the left thigh. The mass was initially noticed as a small lump by the patient and his parents, which progressively increased in size over the course of a year. Upon physical examination, a firm, immobile mass approximately 10 cm in diameter was observed on the anteromedial aspect of the left thigh, located about 15 cm above the knee joint. The mass was non-tender, not warm to the touch, and there were no alterations in the skin overlying the mass.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the left thigh revealed a well-defined soft tissue mass, heterogeneously enhanced, measured 6.5 × 4 × 10 cm, displaced and invaded the lower vastus medialis muscle. There was no involvement or invasion of underlying bones and no evidence of a periosteal reaction. The superficial femoral vein and artery were displaced laterally. An open incisional biopsy revealed multiple fragments of white soft tissue. Microscopic study showed sheets of malignant cells arranged in a nested pattern. They were large, polygonal with distinct cell borders and eosinophilic cytoplasm; they were separated by thin-walled vascular channels. The tumor cells contained intracellular crystals that were PAS-positive and diastase-resistant. Immunostaining was negative for pan-cytokeratin, actin, desmin, myogenin, chromogranin, HMB45, melan A, vimentin, inhibin and S100.

case_report: A 66-year-old female presented in June 2014 with underdeveloped and dystrophic fingernails leading to roughened nails on all fingers. She also exhibited widespread redness of the proximal and lateral nail folds and experienced severe pain. Her medical history included rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, and anorexia nervosa. Her medications included misoprostol, naproxen, and multivitamins. She had a family history of unspecified arthritis. The patient had been seen once before in December 2009 for fragile fingernails and fingertip fissures and was prescribed hydrocortisone cream and fluocinonide ointment. She had also used petrolatum and moisturizing cream. Between June 2014 and October 2018, the patient had numerous rheumatology and dermatology consultations regarding her fingernail dystrophy. Various differential diagnoses over her treatment course included infections, chronic dermatitis involving the fingertips and nails, lichen planus, Raynaud’s disease, and Bazex syndrome. A negative workup for aerodigestive malignancy indicated that it was unlikely Bazex disease. She had negative testing on two occasions for connective tissue disease. She also presented to many clinic visits with secondary infection with bacterial and candidal colonization which complicated her course. Initial treatments between 2014 and 2017 included topical agents (calcipotriol-betamethasone, tazarotene, clobetasol propionate, and mupirocin), as well as systemic agents acitretin, methotrexate, and phototherapy, all with little benefit. Acitretin seemed to worsen her condition. Her course was complicated by several small ulcerations on the fingers, which were treated unsuccessfully with fusidic acid 2% ointment.
test_results: A biopsy demonstrated candidiasis.

case_report: An 8-year-old Saudi boy presented to the dermatology clinic with pustular eruptions on his fingers and toes, accompanied by a burning sensation, dryness, and scaling for 8 months. During this period, nail changes occurred, resulting in the detachment of all fingernails and several toenails, except for the left fourth and right second, third, and fourth toenails. There was no reported history of joint pain, lower limb edema, or jaundice. The patient also had no family history of psoriasis. Physical examination showed scaly erythematous plaques with pus and crust formation on all distal digits and multiple areas on the palms and soles. The nails exhibited severe onychodystrophy with confluent pustules covering the nail bed, sparing the left fourth and right second, third, and fourth toenails.
test_results: A skin punch biopsy revealed psoriasiform hyperplasia, parakeratosis containing numerous neutrophils (Munro-like microabscesses), and focal spongiosis with absent granular layer. The dermis showed increased vascularity within the dermal papillae. This was accompanied by the presence of chronic inflammatory cells infiltrating the upper dermis. These features were consistent with subacute psoriasiform dermatitis/pustular psoriasis. On radiological examination, there was focal soft tissue swelling at the tips of fingers of both hands with irregular outline and fissure-like indentation. Underlying terminal tufts showed focal areas of bone resorption, particularly over the fourth and fifth left digits. X-ray of the feet did not show any remarkable joint or osseous abnormalities.

case_report: A 25-year-old male presented with a 2-year history of red and peeling inflammation of the lips with pustules. The lesions did not improve with multiple treatment cycles using corticosteroids and emollients. Clinical examination revealed that the upper lip was red, cracked, and covered with thick white-yellowish scales along with small, non-merging pustules. The rest of the skin examination was normal, and there were no lesions on the oral mucosa, tongue, or nails. The patient was otherwise in good health. He reported no personal or family history of psoriasis or other skin conditions and no history of smoking. He denied any history of lip licking or contact with lipstick, topical antibiotics and steroids, or other cosmetics. Routine hematology and biochemistry tests, total IgE serum level, and IgE microarray ImmunoCap assay results were within normal ranges. Bacteriological tests of the pustules were negative. Patch testing with the standard series and dental materials series recommended by the Italian Society of Occupational and Environmental Allergological Dermatology (SIDAPA) did not show contact allergic sensitization.
test_results: The analysis showed a stratified squamous epithelium with confluent parakeratosis and focal loss of the granular cell layer. Acanthosis and irregular elongation of the rete ridges were also noted, with ectatic vessels and a lymphocytic inflammatory cell infiltrate. There were collections of neutrophils, with the aspect of both Munro microabscesses and spongiform pustules of Kogoj. No fungi or spirochetes were found with specific stainings.

case_report: A 10-year-old girl was referred to our cardiovascular department for evaluation of a cardiac mass identified during a routine transthoracic echocardiography. The patient initially opted out of further observation. Upon returning to our institution 5 years later, the mass had significantly increased in size, and the patient agreed to have the abnormal cardiac mass removed. Chest radiography revealed a small opacity in the left lower lobe.
test_results: Cardiac magnetic resonance was obtained with four-chamber and coronal view depicting a hypointense tumorous mass (48 mm × 57 mm) extending from the internal wall of pericardium towards the adjacent wall of the left ventricle with the left ventricle being squashed severely. T1-weighted sequence demonstrated a clear adipose line between the mass and the left ventricle. Cardiac cine magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a clear boundary of the mass and the ventricular ejection fraction was 49%.

case_report: The patient, a male in his early 70s, had no significant medical history. He experienced rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (RBD) starting around 1993 and visual hallucinations (VH) beginning in 2017. He resided with his daughter's family following the death of his wife approximately 10 years prior. He and his daughter sought medical attention at a memory hospital, where donepezil treatment was initiated. Following the start of donepezil, his visual hallucinations became less severe. In 2018, he and his daughter consulted the author's department.
test_results: His MMSE score was 28 and his Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA-J) score was 24.

case_report: A 62-year-old man with a history of insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus for eight years, which has not been well-controlled, reported experiencing itching primarily on his lower limbs, soles, palms, and upper arms for two years. This itching has worsened over the past eight months, accompanied by the appearance of nodular, red skin lesions in areas of intense itching. Six months ago, he underwent endoscopic band ligation for an acute variceal bleed and has since been managed with beta-blocker therapy. At that time, he was noted to have cirrhosis of the liver due to non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and skin changes consistent with diabetic dermopathy. He was advised to maintain strict glycemic control, use emollients, and take anti-histamines. Initially, there was some improvement, but the itching gradually worsened, and new lesions appeared on his lower back and thighs. Over the past two months, he also developed new-onset fatigue. Upon visiting our outpatient department, physical examination revealed mild bilateral pedal pitting edema. Multiple erythematous nodular lesions of varying sizes with central scaling, bleeding spots, or hyperpigmentation, along with several excoriations, were observed on the thighs, legs, upper arms, and lower back, with some lesions showing confluence.
test_results: Immunoglobulin A antibody to tissue transglutaminase was strongly positive at 202 U/mL.

case_report: A 60-year-old Caucasian man visited the dermatology clinic with a 40-year history of chronic plaque psoriasis, which had worsened over the past 5 years, and a 3-month history of intensely itchy bullous eruptions on the back, hips, and hands. His medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, ischemic heart disease with previous double coronary artery bypass grafting, and an L4–L5 lumbar spinal fusion. His medications were amlodipine, ramipril, atorvastatin, aspirin, and metformin. There was no personal or family history of bullous or other skin diseases. He had previously been treated with various topical and systemic therapies for psoriasis, including betamethasone dipropionate, prednisolone, and methotrexate, without success. Physical examination revealed multiple large, fixed, well-demarcated erythematous plaques on his back and typical nail psoriasis features such as onycholysis, pitting, and splinter hemorrhages. Additionally, there were multiple vesicles along the edges of the psoriatic plaques on his back and hips, as well as vesiculobullous eruptions on his fingers. Histopathological examination of a vesicle from the plaque edge on the mid-back showed subepidermal vesicle formation with dermal neutrophils and fewer eosinophils. No fungal organisms were detected with period acid-Schiff staining.
test_results: Direct immunofluorescence of the perilesional skin on the back showed fine granular IgA deposits in the papillary dermis, without evidence of a linear pattern of IgA deposition within the basement membrane zone. CD serology showed anti-gliadin IgA titres of 69 U/mL (>20 = positive), anti-gliadin IgG titres of 54 U/mL (>20 = positive) and anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA titres of 31 U/mL (>4 = positive).

case_report: A 37-year-old male patient, who has been bedbound for 30 years, experienced dyspnea and chest pain on the evening of 21 October 2011 while at his nursing home. His blood pressure was recorded at 60/30 mmHg, and he exhibited drowsiness. He was transferred to the emergency room of a university hospital, where emergency treatment, including intubation, was administered. After 8 days in the emergency room, he was moved to the intensive care unit at Busan St. Mary's Medical Center at the request of a guardian. The patient presented with hematochezia, fever, and chills. Laboratory results showed a WBC count of 5,200/mm3, hemoglobin concentration of 12.5 g/dl, and a C-reactive protein level of 159.45 mg/L. Chest CT scans indicated bronchiectasis in the left lung field, while abdominal CT scans showed no specific findings. Several hours after ICU transfer, 38 maggots were removed during oral cavity suction, followed by the removal of 5 additional maggots two hours later. A fecal occult blood test returned positive, and hemoglobin measured the next day was 11.6 g/dl, which is below the normal range.
test_results: Laryngoscopic examination revealed no additional maggots or wounds in the nasal cavity or laryngopharyngeal space.
diagnosis: Oral Myiasis caused by Lucilia sericata

case_report: A 51-year-old woman presented with pain and mobility in the upper front teeth, and reported observing insects emerging from her gums. She has a history of leprosy and filariasis, for which she received treatment. Extraoral examination showed no active infection in her hands or legs. Intraoral examination revealed poor oral hygiene and grade III mobile teeth. The patient exhibited an anterior open bite and was a habitual mouth breather. Examination of the labial gingiva showed a deepened gingival sulcus and a deep periodontal pocket near the upper left lateral incisor and canine teeth. The surrounding mucosa was inflamed and tender with pus discharge. Hematological results were normal. A medical opinion confirmed no active infections in her hands or legs, and no contraindications for dental procedures were noted.
test_results: Orthopantamography revealed mild bone destruction in relation to the mobile anterior maxillary teeth. Microscopic examination revealed five fingers like process in the anterior spiracle, incomplete peritreme in the posterior spiracle, and straight spiracular slits which belong to the family Calliphoridae.
diagnosis: Oral myiasis caused by larvae of Chrysomya bezziana

case_report: A 38-year-old Korean woman presented in June 1998 with intermittent palpitations persisting for 2 years. She had previously been treated for hyperthyroidism starting in June 1996, but discontinued medication after six months. Upon initial evaluation, her weight was 53 kg, height 158 cm, blood pressure 130/80 mmHg, and pulse rate 90 beats/min. There was no family history of thyroid diseases. Physical examination revealed a diffusely symmetrically enlarged thyroid gland without thrill, bruit, or exophthalmos. Thyroid function tests showed free T4 at 2.60 ng/dL (range, 0.7-1.8), T3 at 150 ng/dL (range, 80-200), TSH at 3.0 µIU/mL (range, 0.1-4.2), anti-thyroglobulin antibody at 20.34 U/mL (<0.3), and anti-microsomal antibody at 11.30 U/mL (<0.3). The patient was lost to follow-up after three visits. In December 2004, thyroid function tests at a primary care clinic showed free T4 at 2.51 ng/dL, T3 at 163 ng/dL, and TSH at 14.24 µIU/mL. In February 2005, she was prescribed methimazole 10 mg for diffuse goiter. She was referred again in July 2005 for further evaluation and treatment. Thyroid function tests in March 2005 showed free T4 at 1.89 ng/dL, T3 at 224 ng/dL, and TSH at 33.59 µIU/mL. Methimazole was discontinued, and follow-up thyroid function tests one month later revealed free T4 at 3.53 ng/dL, T3 at 300 ng/dL, TSH at 3.0 µIU/mL, and thyroxine-binding globulin at 23.08 µg/mL (range, 11.3-28.9). Tests for thyroid autoantibodies showed TG antibody at 68.04 U/mL, anti-microsomal antibody >100 U/mL, thyroid stimulating immunoglobulin at 0% (<15), and negative T3 and T4 autoantibodies. The patient was treated with atenolol 100 mg for 4 weeks, after which palpitations ceased and medication was discontinued. Thyroid scans indicated a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland without abnormal focal lesions. Basal serum TSH levels were abnormally high and increased significantly after stimulation with 200 µg of TRH. The TSH subunit level was 0.41 mIU/mL (range, 0-0.9), TSH α-subunit/TSH ratio was 1, and sex hormone-binding globulin was 39.23 nmol/L (range, 30-100). MR imaging of the sellar region showed no abnormal findings.
test_results: The result revealed a missense mutation in exon 11 and an amino acid alteration, namely, a substitution of valine for methonine at codon 349.

case_report: A 26-year-old female presented for follow-up regarding her thyroid status. She had been on carbimazole for hyperthyroidism for the past 5 years. She reported being the shortest in her class during school years and had a history of subnormal intelligence, poor academic performance, hearing loss, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). There was a family history of short stature on the maternal side, with relatives being treated for hyperthyroidism. She developed a goiter 10 years ago but did not exhibit symptoms typically associated with hyperthyroidism such as palpitations, tremors, or moist skin, nor did she have any ocular signs or symptoms. During the evaluation for goiter, her thyroid hormone levels were found to be elevated (T4, T3, free T4, and free T3) with a normal thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), leading to the initiation of antithyroid drugs. On clinical examination, she was conscious and alert, with a height of 142 cm and weight of 47 kg. She had a pulse rate of 102/min, was normotensive, and afebrile. Examination of the thyroid gland revealed diffuse enlargement, classified as World Health Organization Grade 2, without palpable nodules. There was no bruit on auscultation, and her eye examination was normal. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory investigations showed elevated T3 (3.15 nmol/L), free T3 (5.12 pg/mL), T4 (233 nmol/L), and free T4 (3.1 ng/L), with a normal TSH (4.39 µIU/L). Ultrasonography of the thyroid revealed multiple hyperechoic well-defined subcentimetric nodules with peripheral halo and no internal vascularity in both lobes, suggestive of multinodular goiter. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pituitary was normal. Sex hormone binding globulin levels were within normal range (48.3 ng/L). Pure tone audiometry indicated moderate hearing loss with a mixed component at mid frequency.
test_results: Thyroxin suppression testing showed poor suppression of TSH (3.29 µIU/L).

case_report: A 13-year-old girl was evaluated in 2007 for hypertension, which had been managed since 2005 with Acebutolol 400 mg/day and Captopril 50 mg/day. She was born at full term and had normal neonatal development. At the initial visit, her weight was 67 kg (>97th percentile), height was 174 cm (+3 SD), blood pressure was 150/10 mmHg, and pulse rate was 90 beats/min. The thyroid gland appeared normal, but she exhibited symptoms such as finger tremor and moist skin, without any ocular signs. There was no family history of thyroid diseases. Thyroid function tests showed free T4 at 17.9 pmol/L (normal range 10.3–24.4) and TSH at 7.84 μUI/mL (normal range 0.4–4.0). Subsequent tests revealed free T4 at 15.2 pmol/L (normal range 11–25), free T3 at 9.5 pmol/L (normal range 3.9–6.8), and TSH at 18.5 μUI/mL (normal range 0.17–4.0). Other potential causes of secondary hypertension, such as renal causes, Cushing's syndrome, acromegaly, pheochromocytoma, and hypermineralocorticism, were ruled out. Anti-TPO antibodies were positive at 238 UI/mL, indicating mild chronic thyroiditis. Ultrasonography showed a heterogeneous thyroid without goiter. Family members had normal FT4 and TSH levels. The TSH α-subunit level was 0.33 μIU/mL (range 0.05–0.9) with a TSH α-subunit/TSH ratio of 1. Magnetic resonance imaging of the sellar region showed no abnormalities.
test_results: The result revealed a novel mutation I54V in exon4 of the TRβ gene with a substitution of isoleucine for valine.

case_report: The patient is a 12-year-old Korean boy with a history of partial seizure disorder treated for 2 years. He presented to the pediatric orthopedic clinic due to intermittent knee pain over the past few months. His height is 144.6 cm (20th percentile) and his body weight is 41 kg (60th percentile). His father and mother have heights of 170 cm and 160 cm, respectively. The father also experiences intermittent mild knee joint pain. Both the patient and his father do not exhibit muscle weakness or pain. Physical examination shows no Gower sign or Trendelenberg sign. Laboratory tests indicate normal levels of creatine kinase and lactate. Informed consent was obtained from the parents. Clinically, the patient exhibits mild genu valgum deformity in the lower extremities. The knee joints have a full range of motion. Imaging reveals that the distal femoral and proximal tibial epiphyses are primarily affected, with less severe involvement of the distal tibia and distal radius epiphyses. The femoral head epiphysis appears normal. The distal femoral and proximal tibial epiphyses show loss of height, joint surface irregularities, and fragmentation. The distal tibia epiphysis shows lateral shortening and fragmentation. There are no abnormalities in the distal fibular epiphysis or the talar dome. The tarsal navicular and cuneiform bones exhibit irregular ossification. The distal radius epiphysis is wedge-shaped, and the distal ulnae epiphyses are relatively small. The carpal bones show dysplasia and flattening. The spine and proximal femoral epiphyses appear normal. X-rays of the patient's father show osteoarthritis of Kellgren-Lawrence grade I, particularly on the medial side, with the proximal femoral epiphyses spared. Other family members are not affected.
test_results: A novel missense mutation c.104G>A in exon2 of COL9A3, which resulted in p.Gly35Asp, was identified. RefSeq ID: NM_001853.3 reference sequence was used for cDNA nucleotide numbering. Also, comparative evolutionary analysis showed that the glycine residue at codon 35 is a highly conserved amino acid during evolution. And the same mutation was observed in the proband’s symptomatic father. We performed Sanger sequencing of 100 healthy controls and none harbored a c.104G>A mutation in exon 2 of COL9A3.
diagnosis: Multiple Epiphyseal Dysplasia  due to a novel COL9A3 mutation
Orpha_name: Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia due to collagen 9 anomaly

case_report: A 36-year-old male presented with episodes of loss of consciousness and falling immediately after ejaculation, followed by tonic-clonic movements in all four limbs, as observed by his wife. Each episode lasted a few minutes, and upon regaining consciousness, he experienced a heaviness in his head and a dazed feeling. These episodes began approximately 5 years ago, after 10 years of normal sexual interactions. The frequency of sexual intercourse gradually decreased due to these episodes. Three years later, he reported additional episodes where he dropped objects, became unresponsive, and slumped to the ground, each lasting a few seconds. These incidents occurred at various times of the day and were not linked to sexual activity. Neurological examination showed no significant findings. There was no history of head trauma, and he had no history of alcohol or substance abuse. He was only on antiepileptic medication.
test_results: Interictal electroencephalograms were normal. Computed tomography scan and magnetic resonance imaging (T-3) testing of the brain revealed no structural abnormality. His blood examination findings were normal.

case_report: A 62-year-old female with a medical history of anxiety, fibromyalgia, coronary artery disease, major depressive disorder, essential hypertension, and tobacco use arrived at the emergency department with shortness of breath that began several hours earlier. She had no significant family history and smoked half a pack of cigarettes daily. She had no known genetic history. Her medications included fluoxetine, lorazepam, tizanidine, amlodipine, aspirin, and atorvastatin. Upon admission, her vital signs were: blood pressure 136/76 mmHg, heart rate 116 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 per minute, temperature 98.5° Fahrenheit, oxygen saturation 92% on room air, and a BMI of 21.46. Arterial blood gas results showed a pH of 7.50, bicarbonate 33 mEq/L, and pCO2 70 mmHg. Her D-Dimer level was elevated at 900 ng/ml.
