She was given oxygen via nasal cannula at 3.0 L/min due to increased oxygen demand, although she typically required only room air. She had a 13-pack year smoking history but had quit 3 years prior. She had been hospitalized for a respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection one month earlier. Physical examination revealed clear lung sounds bilaterally, no wheezing or rhonchi, and no cough. Initial chest radiograph showed mild cardiomegaly and mild thickening of the interstitial lung markings but was otherwise unremarkable.
test_results: A subsequent CTA of the chest revealed an intraluminal filling defect in the right bronchus intermedius. No embolism was seen on imaging. However, there was a large dilation of the main pulmonary artery measuring 5.0 × 6.4 cm in transverse and anteroposterior dimensions.

case_report: A 5-year-old Iranian boy presented with speech difficulties, lack of concentration, walking disability at age 4 leading to quadriplegia, spontaneous laughing and crying, clumsiness, psychomotor delay, and vision deterioration at age 5. Brain MRI and EEG revealed bilateral white matter signal changes with preservation of white matter. No histopathological studies or skin biopsy were available. Urine organic acids were analyzed using GC-MS, showing a normal pattern with no evidence of metabolic disorders. There was no indication of tyrosinemia, glutaric aciduria, methylmalonic aciduria, Canavan disease, propionic aciduria, isovaleric aciduria, or other known organic acidurias in Iran. Neonatal screening, clinical chemistry, and metabolism assays were normal. The patient's parents are first cousins and have had three pregnancies: the first ended in spontaneous abortion before 4 weeks, the second is the male patient described, and the third is a 2-year-old girl who currently shows no signs or symptoms and appears normal.
test_results: We ended up with only two novel variants in MFSD8 and AFF2 genes. The c.325_339del (p.Val109_Ile113del) variant in the MFSD8 gene was a previously unreported variant and found to be homozygous in our patient whereas his parents were heterozygote carriers. It is a deletion of 15 base pairs (bp), which causes the loss of five residues. The c.259A>G (p.Asn87Asp) variant found in AFF2 was a hemizygous change in our patient; his mother was also heterozygous whereas his father was negative for this variant.

case_report: A 34-year-old first-time pregnant woman was referred to the obstetric anesthesia outpatient clinic at 26 weeks of pregnancy. She had a history of significant bruising during early childhood and experienced difficulty in stopping bleeding after a tooth extraction. At the age of 15, she required a blood transfusion during a laparotomy for ovarian hemorrhage. Due to recurrent ovarian hemorrhage, her menstrual cycles were managed with estrogen and progesterone preparations. Additionally, she had a family history of low platelet counts and intracranial hemorrhage. Her platelet count was consistently around 100,000/μL and was initially monitored as idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura. At the age of 25, during a conization procedure, she received a prophylactic transfusion of 400 mL of platelet concentrate, and her postoperative recovery was free of hemorrhagic complications.
test_results: Normal ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation, suppressed adenosine diphosphate (ADP) aggregation to 39% when ADP 3.00 μM was added (normal range 70–90%), and collagen aggregation to 20% when collagen 2.00 μg/ml added (normal range 70–90%), but normal CD41 (glycoprotein IIb/IIIa) antigen.

case_report: A 37-year-old woman with a 16-year history of well-controlled ulcerative colitis presented to Peking Union Medical College Hospital with a 4-week history of continuous fever, reaching a maximum body temperature of 39 °C. She experienced epistaxis, sweating, and gradually developed disseminated 2–5 mm papules and nodules over the abdomen, back, and four limbs, along with a 7-kg weight loss. No other symptoms were reported. Her family history included gastrointestinal tumors in three out of four of her mother’s uncles and her grandmother. Upon admission, her body temperature was 38.5 °C. Physical examination revealed disseminated reddish to brown itchy papules and nodules over the whole body, sternum tenderness, a liver palpable 3 cm below the costal margin, and a spleen palpable 1 cm below the costal margin. Laboratory findings included a white blood cell (WBC) count of 42.4 × 10^9/L, a platelet count of 24 × 10^9/L, and hemoglobin level of 70 g/L. The peripheral blood smear showed 53% eosinophils and 28% basophils.
test_results: The bone marrow smear revealed markedly hypercellular bone marrow with 7% myeloblasts as well as significantly increased eosinophil and eosinophil precursors at different stages (39.5%) and increased basophil and basophil precursors (21.5%). Targeted amplicon sequencing on the Illumina MiSeq sequencing platform using the patient’s peripheral blood found mutations in DNMT3A, NPM1, and GATA2; no abnormalities in the rest 31 genes of the panel, including PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, and JAK2 were noticed. Paired-end, 101-bp RNA sequencing of over 900 fusion genes using the Illumina NextSeq 500 instrument identified an out-of-frame fusion of exon 1 of ETV6 to exon 2 of ACSL6 with a fusion transcript abundance of 17.83%; the rearrangement of other fusion genes, including FIP1L1-PDGFRA, IGH-FGFR3, TEL-FGFR3, and BCR-ABL, was not detected. Oral mucosal epithelial cells obtained from the patient and her mother for germline testing showed that the GATA2 mutation was not detected by Sanger sequencing using an ABI 3500 DX Genetic Analyzer.

case_report: A 44-year-old male was admitted to the Department of Head and Neck at Shanxi Tumor Hospital (Shanxi, China) in November 2017 with a 10-day history of a left cervical mass. Physical examination revealed an enlarged left cervical lymph node measuring 4 cm by 1 cm. Laboratory findings included a hemoglobin level of 129 g/L, a white blood cell count of 3.45 × 10^9/L, and a platelet count of 118 × 10^9/L. The levels of lactate dehydrogenase (216 U/L) and beta2-microglobulin (8.03 mg/L) were within normal ranges. Liver and kidney function tests, as well as coagulation tests, were normal. Imaging via positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) showed lymphadenopathy in bilateral cervical, axillary, inguinal, mediastinal, and para-iliac regions, along with retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy and mild splenomegaly.
test_results: A biopsy of the enlarged left cervical lymph node was performed. Histopathology showed diffuse infiltration of two different populations of lymphoid cells. Immunohistochemistry confirmed the co-existence of two malignancies, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) results showed the expression of clonal T-cell receptor gamma (TCR-G) and beta (TCR-β). The first population of large lymphoid cells was characterized by vacuolar nuclei, eosinophilic nucleoli and a rich cytoplasm. The cells were immunopositive for CD15, CD30, PAX-5, MUM-1 and Ki-67 60%+, and they were characterized as Reed–Sternberg (R–S) cells. The second population of small lymphoid cells was characterized by heterotypic nuclei and condensed chromatin. The cells were immunopositive for PD1, CD2, CD3, CD5, CD7, CD8, CD4 (weakly positive), CD8 > CD4, TIA1 and Ki-67 40%+, and immunonegative for GrB, CD10, CD20, CD56 and CXCL-13.

case_report: A 36-year-old male presented with hypogammaglobulinemia and recurrent sinopulmonary infections since the age of 15. He was referred to a specialized immunodeficiency institute and received regular immunoglobulin infusions for 20 years. Despite treatment, he experienced recurrent sinopulmonary infections complicated by mastoiditis, pleural effusion, and bronchiectasis, requiring hospitalization from the age of 14. Physical examination revealed atrophic endobronchial mucosa, exercise tachypnea, finger clubbing, and obstructive sleep apnea. Sputum cultures frequently identified Hemophilus influenzae or Pseudomonas aeruginosa despite prophylactic antibiotics including amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, azithromycin, and cefuroxime. A combination of isoniazid, rifampin, and pyrazinamide was administered for one year for a suspected pulmonary mycobacterial infection. The patient did not require hospitalization for pneumonia despite winter exacerbations. At 27 years old, he developed preseptal Staphylococcus aureus cellulitis and E. coli epididymo-orchitis. Imaging revealed an engorged portal vein, splenomegaly, splenic artery dilation, and a coarse liver surface. Liver function tests showed normal levels of AST, ALT, albumin, γGT, bilirubin, and αFP, with a mild elevation of ALP (125 U/L, normal: 28–94 U/L). RT-PCR tests for hepatitis viruses A-E, CMV, and Epstein–Barr virus were negative. These findings were consistent with nodular regenerative hyperplasia. The patient opted for conservative therapy and declined liver transplantation and biopsy. Steroid treatment (1 mg/kg/day) for two months was attempted to alleviate portal vein hypertension but was unsuccessful. Exacerbation of bronchiectasis increased pulmonary artery pressure, reopened a closed atrial septal defect, and progressed to cor pulmonale. The patient did not experience opportunistic infections or common autoimmune disorders such as thyroid dysfunction, hemolytic anemia, or IBD-like diarrhea. Auto-antibodies against pancreatic, thyroid, and liver antigens, as well as anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome, were negative, along with a negative Coombs test (direct and indirect). Lymphocyte proliferation was consistent with wild-type candidate genes, not supporting a T-B-NK+ SCID presentation.
test_results: A 1 base pair deletion was identified at position 71 in the coding sequence (c.213 del A), which led to a frameshift at position 71 and a premature stop codon at position 110.
diagnosis: Common Variable Immunodeficiency  due to a novel CD3G mutation
Orpha_name: Combined immunodeficiency due to CD3gamma deficiency

case_report: A 16-year-old male presented to a children's hospital in Tabriz, Iran on May 30, 2009, with recurrent bleeding episodes in the left knee. The patient had a history of severe bleeding following circumcision at six months of age. Laboratory analysis involved extracting genomic DNA from 2.5 mL of EDTA-anticoagulated peripheral blood using SDS-proteinase K. Amplification of genomic DNA was performed for all 26 exons with exon-intron boundary regions in 37 segments using specific primers. The amplified DNA fragments were visualized on a 1.5% agarose gel stained with ethidium bromide. Fragments larger than 400bp underwent further analysis, and fragments shorter than 400bp were analyzed using different techniques. Abnormal electrophoretic mobility in the PCR products was further examined by sequencing and analyzed using specialized software. The sequences were then compared with a reference sequence.
test_results: Only PCR product of exon 14F with 686bp long displayed unmatched shift in CSGE. A novel point mutation was detected from sequence analysis of exon 14F PCR product.
diagnosis: Moderate Haemophilia A due to a novel missense mutation, E1623G, in the human Factor VIII gene

case_report: An 80-year-old male was admitted due to left-sided weakness and altered consciousness at his workplace early in the morning. His medical history was negative for head injuries, drug use, malignancies, blood disorders, or autoimmune conditions. He had no prior bleeding episodes and his family history was unremarkable. Upon admission, his vital signs were: blood pressure, 150/78 mmHg; heart rate, 105 bpm; respiration rate, 17 breaths/min; temperature, 36.7°C; and oxygen saturation, 97% on room air. Laboratory results showed a prolonged APTT of 39.8 seconds (normal range, 25–35 seconds) and a normal prothrombin time of 92.9% (normal range, 75–125%). Other laboratory values were within normal ranges: platelet count of 186 × 10^3/μL (normal range, 152–382 × 10^3/μL); hemoglobin, 14.9 g/dL (normal range, 14.0–17.0 g/dL); and hematocrit, 44.6% (normal range, 43.0–51.0%). No vital abnormalities were noted at presentation, but neurological examination revealed left hemiparesis, including facial involvement. CT imaging showed a right-sided thick acute subdural hematoma (ASDH) with midline shift. CTA excluded vascular abnormalities such as cerebral aneurysms and vascular malformations. Surgical resection of the hematoma with external decompression was performed due to the altered consciousness and left hemiparesis. Postoperative CT indicated a small residual hematoma and improved midline shift. However, a CT scan the next day revealed a large subcutaneous hemorrhage resembling an acute epidural hematoma (AEDH). The APTT was 41.3 seconds immediately before a repeat surgery to achieve hemostasis. Hemorrhagic sources were identified in the subcutaneous and muscle tissues, and hemostasis was achieved using standard surgical techniques. CT on postoperative day 1 showed a small persistent hematoma and improved midline shift. The APTT was 42.4 seconds after the second surgery, and the patient's clinical course was favorable with rehabilitation therapy. He was self-sustaining in daily activities in the hospital, with APTT values ranging between 35 and 40 seconds. Cranioplasty was performed 40 days after hospitalization when his general condition stabilized, although the APTT remained slightly prolonged at 35.2 seconds. Post-cranioplasty CT imaging showed a small amount of hematoma and air immediately after the procedure and a slightly thickened AEDH the following day, similar to the initial surgery. The APTT immediately after cranioplasty was 58.6 seconds. Neurological findings post-surgery were normal, and the AEDH on CT images gradually decreased. No further reoperation for hemostasis was required, although postoperative bleeding recurred.
test_results: The patient had a plasma factor VIII value of 25% (normal, 62–145%) and was negative for factor VIII inhibitor and had a normal value for von Willebrand factor.

case_report: An 8.10-year-old boy presented to the Pediatric Dentistry Postgraduate Clinic with his parents, who reported no significant bleeding events or medical disorders. The primary concern was the lack of eruption of both permanent upper central incisors. Oral examination revealed that both incisors were palpable but covered with fibrous gingival tissue, with no associated bleeding. Informed consent was obtained from the parents before treatment. A vestibular squared incision over the gingiva with flap apical reposition was performed to expose the incisal third of both incisor crowns. The procedure was conducted under local anesthesia using a water-irrigated laser hand-piece system and sutures on both sides of the flap. The patient was discharged with postoperative hygiene and diet instructions, showing no immediate complications. Three days later, the patient returned with profuse gingival bleeding that was difficult to control with external pressure using wet gauze. Routine laboratory blood tests for blood clotting times were performed, revealing normal results except for a slightly lower aPTT. The wound was resutured and covered with Gelfoam and a surgical splint. The patient was monitored closely on an outpatient basis. After 2 days, the bleeding persisted, and the child appeared pale and weak.
test_results: The clot factor VIII manifested a deficit of 6% regarding the normal plasmatic level.

case_report: A 43-year-old woman experienced progressively worsening proximal muscle weakness over a decade, leading to difficulties with fast walking, climbing stairs, and rising from a chair. She had normal growth and development. She also reported lumbar back pain. The proximal lower limb weakness extended to her arms, making tasks like washing clothes challenging. Her family history included similar symptoms in her father, sister, brother, three paternal aunts, one paternal uncle, and the uncle’s son, though their symptoms were less severe. Muscle weakness was observed in the biceps and triceps (MRC 4+/5), wrist flexor extensor muscles (MRC 4/5), iliopsoas muscles (MRC 3/5), and quadriceps muscles (MRC 4−/5). Distal arm strength was rated at 4. She exhibited a waddling gait and muscle atrophy in the quadriceps and distal lower legs. She was unable to walk on her toes. Deep tendon reflexes were absent, and Gower’s sign was present. No cranial nerve dysfunction or sensory disturbance was noted. Her serum creatine kinase level was twice the upper normal limit. An electromyogram showed mild myogenic changes. Echocardiography and electrocardiogram evaluations revealed no cardiac abnormalities. MRI of the lower limbs showed fatty degeneration in the vastus intermedius, vastus lateralis, semimembranosus, adductor magnus, and the long head of the biceps femoris muscles, with slight involvement of the rectus femoris. No abnormalities were found in the gracilis, sartorius, or semitendinosus muscles. At the distal leg level, the soleus, gastrocnemius medialis, and gastrocnemius lateralis showed degeneration with fatty infiltration. A skeletal muscle biopsy from the tibial anterior muscle, precooled with isopentane and frozen in liquid nitrogen, revealed increased fiber size variability with atrophic and hypertrophic fibers, muscle fiber necrosis, and phagocytosis. There was a mild increase in connective tissue, and non-rimmed vacuoles were commonly present. Some fibers showed structural changes with abnormal material deposits after staining with hematoxylin-eosin (HE) and modified Gomori’s trichrome (MGT). Oxidative enzyme activities were focally reduced in some fibers, occasionally resulting in core-like lesions after staining with succinate dehydrogenase (SDH), NADH-tetrazolium reductase (NADH-TR), and cytochrome c oxidase (COX). Electron microscopy showed myofibrillar deposits of thin filaments interspersed with dense granular material between myofibrils, often in spheroid shapes, surrounded by radially arranged thin filaments.
test_results: Next generation sequencing identified a 15-nucleotide deletion (c.2791_2805del, p.931_935del) in the immunoglobulin (Ig)-like domain 7 of the FLNC gene. Genetic testing revealed that this deletion had been passed to the patient from her father and carried by her other symptomatic relatives.

case_report: The patient is a 37-year-old male from a non-consanguineous Chinese family. At age 35, he began to experience progressive weakness in his hands, with a notable reduction in grip strength, particularly in the right hand. Six months later, muscle atrophy and fibrillation were observed in his hands, leading to an inability to hold objects or write. One year later, he developed weakness in his lower extremities without sensory disturbances. He currently has difficulty climbing stairs, standing up from a squatting position, lifting his foot upward, and frequently trips. Physical examination showed normal cranial nerves and no orolingual fasciculations or atrophy. Neck flexion strength was rated 5 on the MRC muscle scale (grades 0–5). Muscle strength on both sides was as follows: triceps and biceps 3/3, forearm flexors 2/2, intrinsic hand muscles 1/1, iliopsoas muscles 4/4, quadriceps muscles 3/3, tibialis anterior and gastrocnemius muscles 2/2. Deep tendon reflexes were absent. There were no sensory abnormalities or coordination difficulties in any limbs. Muscle atrophy was prominent, especially in the interosseous muscles of the hands, bilateral gastrocnemius, and anterior tibial muscles. Muscle fibrillation was noted in the biceps and quadriceps muscles. Serum creatine kinase level was 668 U/L (normal range: 50–310 U/L). Tests for extractable nuclear antigens were negative, and serum sex hormone levels were normal. Peripheral neuropathy antibodies, including GM1-antibody and GQ1b-antibody, were negative, and cerebrospinal fluid showed no albuminocytological dissociation. Nerve conduction studies revealed severe reductions in compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitudes and motor conduction velocities in the bilateral median, ulnar, and radial nerves, with normal sensory conduction. Right ulnar nerve F-waves were absent. Electromyogram (EMG) showed chronic denervation/reinnervation (e.g., motor unit action potentials of increased amplitude and duration, with reduced interference patterns) in three regions, including the bilateral extremities and sternocleidomastoid muscles, along with spontaneous activity (positive sharp waves). Echocardiography and electrocardiogram evaluations showed no cardiac abnormalities. Lower limb muscle MRI indicated significant involvement of the gastrocnemius muscle at the calf level, with a strongly increased signal intensity in turbo inversion recovery magnitude (TIRM) sequences, suggesting muscular edema. Mild signal intensity increases in the soleus and tibialis anterior muscles were observed in the T2 sequence, indicating fat replacement. Slight fatty degeneration was detected in the posterior compartment of the proximal leg, including the semimembranosus and semitendinosus muscles.
test_results: Next-generation sequencing identified a heterozygous missense mutation (c.7123G > A, p.V2375I) in the Ig-like domain 21 of FLNC. Confirmation of the variant was undertaken by Sanger sequencing using an ABI 3730XL DNA Sequencer. The mutation was absent in the DNA of 100 healthy unrelated controls, and the allele frequency in the Asian population is zero according to the Exome Aggregation Consortium. The p.V2375I missense mutation affects valine at position 2375, which is highly conserved from mice to humans.
diagnosis: Myofibrillar myopathy with lower motor neuron syndrome due to FLNC gene mutation

case_report: A 40-year-old female presented to the outpatient clinic with symptoms of blurry vision, foreign body sensation, tearing, and sensitivity to light, persisting for several years. Her medical history includes primary adrenocortical insufficiency for 11 years, for which she has been on hormone replacement therapy with fludrocortisone acetate. On examination, her best corrected visual acuity was measured at 5/10 in the right eye and 6/10 in the left eye. Laboratory tests showed a serum cortisone level of 31.62 nmol/L, which is below the normal range (64–536 nmol/L). Other blood tests indicated that serum parathormone, thyroid hormone, thyroid stimulating hormone, sodium, calcium, potassium, and phosphorus levels were within normal limits.
test_results: Slit-lamp examination revealed a dull and irregular reflex from the corneal surface. There was corneal epithelial haze and classic “waterfall” or “whorled” epithelium extending to the central cornea. Superficial peripheral corneal neovascularization was also observed in both eyes.

case_report: An 18-year-old male presented with a history of light sensitivity and excessive tearing of the eyes, more pronounced in the mornings, for 2 years. He had a history of alopecia areata and dry, scaly patches in the perioral region, hands, and feet since the age of 3. Born from a second-degree consanguineous marriage, his elder sibling had similar symptoms and passed away as an infant. The patient was started on zinc and riboflavin supplements. Prior to this, he had no ocular symptoms. Currently, in addition to the ocular symptoms, he reported a worsening of skin lesions. There was no history of recurrent fever, impaired wound healing, diarrhea, or weight loss. He had no history of decreased vision, ocular pain, discharge, or redness of the eyes. There was no history of ocular trauma or surgery.
test_results: Slit-lamp examination showed the presence of bilateral, symmetrical, subepithelial corneal opacities adjacent to the superior limbus, extending to the visual axis in radiating lines. Fluorescein staining of the cornea demonstrated a whorling pattern superiorly (OS >OD), extending from the limbus to the center of the cornea.

case_report: A 6-year-old girl, with no parental consanguinity, presented with chronic white lesions on the oral mucosa that began at the age of 2 years, as reported by her mother. She received treatment for mucosal candidiasis for over 3 years without improvement. No other family members exhibited similar lesions. The lesions were asymptomatic, except for occasional burning sensations when consuming acidic or spicy foods. Physical examination revealed white, irregular plaques with well-defined borders and symmetric distribution on the buccal mucosa. There was no associated erythema, and the plaques did not scrape off when using a tongue blade. No similar lesions were observed on other mucosal surfaces.
test_results: Histopathological examination showed superficial parakeratosis, acanthosis, and spongiosis with perinuclear eosinophilic condensation of epithelial cells. A minimal lymphocytic infiltration was present in the stroma. PAS coloration was negative.

case_report: A 21-year-old male from Iran presented with a white, itchy spot on the buccal mucosa. The primary concern was a white bilateral lesion in the oral mucosa, which the patient reported had been present since birth. The patient was in good general health and reported no similar conditions in immediate family members or elsewhere on his body. Clinical examination revealed bilateral, symmetrical white plaques and patches on the buccal and labial mucosa that could not be removed. These plaques were smooth with a velvety texture and had irregular, well-defined borders. There was no elevation or erythema, and the margins were clear with no noticeable lymph nodes. The patient's oral hygiene was good, and other oral structures appeared normal.
test_results: Oral mucosa covered by stratified squamous epithelium revealed prominent hyperparakeratosis and marked acanthosis with clearing of the cytoplasm of cells in the spinous layer. Eosinophilic condensation was noted in the perinuclear region of the cells in superficial layers. Underlying connective tissue was normal in appearance with rare chronic inflammatory cell infiltration.

case_report: A 13-year-old female presented with pain in the mandibular right posterior region. Intraoral examination showed a severely decayed tooth #46, which was tender on percussion and exhibited periapical radiolucency. Additionally, diffuse, soft, thickened white plaques with a corrugated surface were observed on the buccal mucosa bilaterally, extending from the retro-commissural area to the retromolar region and involving the soft palate. Similar lesions were found on the dorsal surface of the tongue, lower labial mucosa, and the mucosa of the hard palate. These plaques could not be removed by scraping and were asymptomatic. The patient was referred to Ophthalmology and Obstetrics/Gynecology to check for any conjunctival and genital lesions, respectively. No other sites were identified. Cytologic preparation from the lesion did not reveal any fungal hyphae with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) staining. There were no contributing factors such as tobacco use or chemical burn. The lesions had been present since early childhood, though it was unclear if they were present since birth. Family history indicated similar lesions in the father (aged 56 years) and the eldest brother (aged 31 years). The father had bilateral lesions on the buccal mucosa, while the brother had scattered bilateral lesions on the buccal mucosa.
test_results: Histopathologic examination of the lesional tissue revealed hyperplastic keratinized squamous epithelium, with prominent hyperparakeratosis, marked acanthosis and spongiosis. Cells showing clearing of the cytoplasm with perinuclear eosinophilic condensation were noticed.

case_report: A six-month-old female infant from Germany was brought to the emergency room in January 2023 with a three-week history of vomiting and decreased fluid intake. Her medical history included a respiratory infection at five months old and a COVID-19 infection at four months old. She also exhibited failure to thrive, weighing 5,380 grams (91st percentile) at seven weeks and 6,300 grams (12th percentile) at admission. The family history noted benign paroxysmal postural vertigo in the mother but was otherwise unremarkable. On admission, the infant showed signs of mild dehydration, including sunken eyes, a mildly prolonged capillary refill time (3 seconds centrally, 2-3 seconds peripherally), mild tachycardia (151 beats per minute), and a blood pressure of 105/52 mmHg. Laboratory results revealed severe hyponatremia (106 mmol/L), hyperkalemia (7.0 mmol/L), hypochloremia (81 mmol/L), and compensated metabolic acidosis (pH 7.41, HCO3− 19.9 mmol/L, pCO2 27.8 mmHg, base excess −5.2 mmol/L). Additionally, there was an elevated C-reactive protein level (59.1 mg/L), along with leukocyturia, erythrocyturia, proteinuria, and nitrituria. Urine cultures identified Klebsiella oxytoca, and urine sodium was measured at 23 mmol/L.
test_results: Abdominal ultrasound showed II°–III° hydronephrosis and enlargement of the right kidney.

case_report: A 20-day-old female infant was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit due to poor oral intake. She exhibited lethargy and had been consuming only 10 to 20 mL of formula per feeding over the past two days, though her urine output remained high, with 10 to 14 diaper changes per day. There were no signs of vomiting or diarrhea. She was delivered at 38+2 weeks of gestation via cesarean section, weighing 3380 g (50th–75th percentile). Her prenatal and immediate postnatal periods were unremarkable. She is the first child of healthy, nonconsanguineous Korean parents with no notable family history. Upon admission, her weight was 3100 g (25th–50th percentile), length was 53 cm (50th–75th percentile), and head circumference was 36 cm (50th–75th percentile). Vital signs were within normal limits for her age: heart rate 150 beats/min, blood pressure 78/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 48 breaths/min, and body temperature 36.5 °C. Physical examination revealed dry lips, prolonged capillary refill time (5–6 seconds), both thumbs in palms, frontal bossing, prominent upper lip, high arched palate, sparse frontal scalp hair, and bilateral 5th finger clinodactyly. Initial capillary blood gas analysis indicated severe metabolic acidosis with a pH of 7.16, pCO2 of 28.3 mmHg, pO2 of 42 mmHg, HCO3− of 17.3 mmol/L, and base excess of -17.3 mmol/L. She received 20 mL/kg of normal saline intravenously over 1 hour. Admission laboratory results were: serum sodium 113.3 mEq/L, serum potassium 8.79 mEq/L, serum chloride 90.8 mEq/L, total CO2 8.1 mEq/L, serum lactic acid 1.0 mmol/L, serum ketone body 24 µmol/L, blood glucose 83 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 55.1 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 0.65 mg/dL. Urinalysis showed a specific gravity of 1.014 and pH of 5.0, with no white or red blood cells. Spot urine sodium and potassium levels were 74 and 27.7 mEq/L, respectively. Serum and urine osmolality were 232 and 229 mOsm/kg, respectively. Neonatal screening tests, including TSH (1.2 mIU/L), 17-hydroxyprogesterone (1.6 ng/mL), total galactose (1.0 mg/dL), and mass spectrometry for various metabolic disorders, were normal. Plasma ammonia was 97 µg/dL. Plasma renin activity was 142.0 ng/mL/h, and serum aldosterone was 4560 ng/dL. Renal ultrasonography showed mild hydronephrosis in the right kidney. Cardiac echocardiography and brain MRI were normal. To address severe hyponatremia, 60 mL of 3% sodium chloride was administered intravenously over 8 hours. On the first day, urine output was 8.45 mL/kg/h. Hyponatremia and hyperkalemia improved with intravenous fluids and oral sodium chloride supplementation (8 mEq/kg/day). The patient subsequently consumed an adequate amount of milk (170–200 mL/kg/day) and gained weight appropriately (40–80 g/day) after oral sodium chloride supplementation.
test_results: CMA revealed a 203 kb heterozygous deletion at 4q31.23: arr[GRCh37] 4q31.23(148865586_149069090)x1. This deletion spans exons 7–9 of NR3C2 and exons 15–23 of the ARHGAP10 gene.

case_report: In September 2022, a five-month-old German female infant, previously in good health, arrived at the pediatric emergency room with a four-day history of increased stool frequency and vomiting. Physical examination showed a pale child in a generally reduced condition, with signs of moderate dehydration including a sunken fontanelle, mild tachycardia at 129 beats per minute, a peripheral capillary refill time of 2–3 seconds, dry lips, moist eyes without tears, dry nappies, and cold extremities. The blood pressure recorded at admission was 78/55 mmHg. The family history was unremarkable. The patient was admitted for further evaluation and management.
test_results: Blood gas analysis revealed severe hyponatremia (109 mmol/L), hypochloremia (81 mmol/L), hyperkalemia (8.5 mmol/L, venous serum 9.6 mmol/L) and compensated metabolic acidosis (pH 7.36; HCO3− 15.5 mmol/L, pCO2 22.2 mmHg, base excess −12.2 mmol/L). Repeated blood gas analyses as well as serum measurements confirmed these findings. Urine sodium was <20 mmol/L. Urine cultures were conducted which grew Enterobacter cloacae. Abdominal ultrasound showed a dilated right ureter, pyelectasis and a blurry differentiation between the renal medulla and cortex.

case_report: On January 2, 2023, a 30-year-old male patient presented with intermittent epigastric distension and pain that had persisted for over a month and worsened over the past week. One month prior, the patient experienced epigastric tenderness without associated referred pain, nausea, vomiting, acid belching, or hiccups. On January 26, 2023, an abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan from another hospital indicated a soft tissue mass in the left middle abdomen with a connection to the transverse colon, gas accumulation within the mass, a blind end, peripheral exudation, and multiple enlarged lymph nodes. The patient received rehydration and pain relief treatments, but there was no significant improvement, leading to a transfer to our hospital for further evaluation of abdominal pain. Upon admission, the patient reported significant swelling pain and occasional colic with cold sweats, but no cough or eating obstruction. The patient also reported poor sleep, normal urination, and 2-3 bowel movements per day without black or bloody stool. There was no family history of congenital intestinal diseases or previous abdominal surgery. Physical examination revealed a flat abdomen with no visible gastrointestinal type or peristaltic waves, mid-upper abdominal tenderness, rebound tenderness, and no palpable mass.
test_results: The left middle abdominal soft tissue mass is occupied, there is pipeline communication between the lesion and the transverse colon, and the gas accumulation is seen in it, the other end is the blind end, and the periphery of the lesion exudes, and multiple enlarged lymph nodes can be seen. The patient was diagnosed with a soft tissue mass in the left middle abdominal tube with a size of approximately 6.4*4.7 cm. The mass showed a long T1 and long T2 signal, and multiple gas signals were seen inside the lesion. The sac-like long T1 long T2 signal shadow was seen behind the left peritoneum, the size was approximately 2.1*1.3 cm, and the enhanced scan did not show strengthening. The results suggest the presence of left mid-quadrant lesions. Moreover, there was a left retroperitoneal cystic mass. In the case of barium enema colitis, the upper right edge of the transverse colon is seen to the right to left, with a walking curved thin bowel tube-like shadow. The base is approximately 42 mm wider, and in the supine position, it is inflated, the prone position is full, the liquid level is visible in the distal section of the vertical position, the total length is approximately 190 mm, the blind end is seen, and a titanium clip can be seen in the proximal section. The results suggest an abnormal open bowel lesion in the transverse colon. A painless colonoscopy revealed a dilated lumen and an open-like structure in the reverse scope. Pathological diagnosis showed chronic inflammation of mucosal tissue covered with squamous epithelium and gastric columnar epithelium. Intraoperative exploration revealed a palpable mass near the splenic flexure at the back of the transverse colon, measuring approximately 8.0 cm by 9.0 cm, with an intact capsule, inflammatory edema of surrounding tissues, and adhesions. The mass did not invade adjacent organs, and the root was connected to the middle section of the transverse colon. The root of the mass was exposed, revealing nourishing blood vessels emanating from the ligament of Treitz, and a dissected specimen showed the presence of intestinal mucosal tissue in the mass.

case_report: A 44-year-old woman visited the Ear, Nose, and Throat Department of our hospital due to a left submandibular mass and sore throat that had persisted for one week. Physical examination revealed that the mass was fixed and soft, without any tenderness. The patient also exhibited a stiff neck but did not experience any difficulty breathing, swallowing, or other neurological symptoms.
test_results: Axial and sagittal fat-suppressed T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a 3.5- × 3.1- × 4.1-cm hyperintense mass that was abutted against the left C3 nerve root and extended into the left retropharyngeal space through the left neural foramen of C2/3. Minimal focal invasion of the left lateral body of C2 and widening of the left neural foramen of C2/3 by the mass were observed. Axial and sagittal gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted fat-suppressed MRI showed heterogeneous enhancement. Transfemoral cerebral angiography revealed that the feeding artery branched from the left proximal external carotid artery. In the permanent section, the lobules were separated by thin fibrous septa with inflammatory cells. Tumor cells showing eosinophilic cytoplasm and intracytoplasmic vacuoles were arranged in a retiform pattern. The nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio differed across cells, and nuclear atypia was frequently observed. A few multinucleated tumor cells were found. Immunohistochemical staining showed diffuse positivity for pan-cytokeratin and brachyury, patchy positivity for epithelial membrane antigen, focal positivity for S100, and negativity for progesterone receptor and synaptophysin. The Ki-67 labeling index was 2%.

case_report: A 72-year-old woman came to the hospital with discomfort in the right cheek area. She had a medical history of hypertension and dyslipidemia, for which she was taking medication. Twelve years prior, an MRI incidentally revealed a mass in the prepontine cistern. This mass was monitored over time with MRI, which showed a gradual increase in size. Upon examination at our hospital, there was abnormal sensation in the second branch region of the right trigeminal nerve. Other physical examinations and laboratory tests were normal. A noncontrast-enhanced head CT scan revealed a 40-mm, well-defined, homogeneous, low-density mass in the prepontine cistern, without obvious fat or calcification. The mass compressed the midbrain, pons, and basilar artery dorsally, but there was no significant bone destruction of the clivus. MRI findings included low signal intensity on T1-weighted images (T1WI) and markedly high signal intensity on T2-weighted images (T2WI), similar to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), with mildly high signal intensity on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) images. Diffusion-weighted images (DWI) with a b-value of 1000 s/mm2 showed high signal intensity, and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps showed higher signal intensity than brain parenchyma and lower signal intensity than CSF (ADC value: 1.13×10-3 mm2/s). Contrast-enhanced T1WI showed very faint honeycombed enhancement within the mass. Constructive interference in steady state (CISS) imaging indicated that the mass extended into the right Meckel’s cave and compressed the right trigeminal nerve laterally. Faint contrast enhancement within the mass was not observed at this point. The patient underwent tumor resection due to the mass's tendency to increase in size and cause symptoms. Intraoperative findings revealed that the tumor was entirely located in the intradural space, compressing the brainstem, the right oculomotor nerve, the right facial nerve, and the right vestibulocochlear nerve laterally.
test_results: Hematoxylin-eosin staining showed that tumor cells with vacuolated or pallid cytoplasm were proliferating in irregularly shaped cord-like or foci-like fashion, accompanied by myxoid or cartilage-like stroma. Mild nuclear size discrepancy was observed. Immunohistological findings were positive for cytokeratin AE1/AE3, epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), S100, and brachyury.

case_report: A 70-year-old female with a history of chronic back pain experienced a significant worsening of symptoms over several months. Approximately six months prior to hospital admission, the patient began experiencing severe lower back pain that radiated to the bilateral anterior thigh regions, which was exacerbated by movement and had no relieving factors. The patient had previously sought pain management at various emergency rooms and urgent care clinics. She reported no recent trauma, fever, upper respiratory illness, urinary urgency, frequency, dysuria, changes in bowel habits, or unintentional weight loss. Her medical history includes chronic back pain, coronary artery disease, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, gastroesophageal reflux, and hyperlipidemia. She has no known drug allergies and her surgical history is noncontributory. Her home medications include hydrocodone-acetaminophen, clopidogrel, aspirin, metoprolol, losartan, metformin, insulin, pantoprazole, and atorvastatin. Social history reveals a 38 pack-year smoking history, with cessation 20 years ago, and no use of alcohol or recreational drugs. Family history includes diabetes mellitus and cardiovascular disease. On physical examination, her temperature was 97.5°F, heart rate 99 beats per minute, blood pressure 167/79 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. The patient appeared chronically ill and obese but was alert and oriented. Pupils were round and reactive to light, and mucosal membranes were moist. She had a full range of neck motion, clear lung sounds bilaterally, and normal heart sounds without gallops, murmurs, or pericardial rub. The abdomen was soft, non-distended, with normal bowel sounds and no tenderness. The lower back showed normal inspection, painful range of motion, and midline tenderness. Neurological examination revealed intact cranial nerves 2-12, normal speech, bilateral lower extremity weakness, and positive Hoffman sign bilaterally. Laboratory results showed leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 13.3 uL and a neutrophil shift of 85.4%, hemoglobin of 14.4 g/dL, hematocrit of 43.5%, and platelet count of 186 uL. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 36 mm/hr, C-reactive protein was 1 mg/dL, and carcinoembryonic antigen was 2.4 ng/mL. The comprehensive metabolic panel was unremarkable except for elevated blood glucose at 250 mg/dL. Urinalysis indicated 1+ proteinuria without hematuria. Initial lumbar radiograph imaging revealed a lytic lesion in the pedicle of the second lumbar vertebral body (L2). Computed tomography (CT) of the lumbar vertebra confirmed an isolated heterogeneous lytic osseous lesion at the posterior left L2 vertebral body extending into the posterior element.
test_results: The resected fragments of bone were composed of large epithelioid cells arranged in nests and cords with an extensive extracellular myxoid matrix, small hyperchromatic nuclei, and abundant vacuolated cytoplasm. Immunohistochemical stains demonstrate the tumor cells were positive for brachyury, calcium-binding cytosolic protein (S100), cytokeratin 19 (CK19), and cytokeratin cam 5.2 protein.

case_report: A 49-year-old female with a history of asthma, Dupuytren's contracture, and migraines reported swelling and pain in the left shoulder for the past 1.5 years. Her medications included vitamin D supplements, omeprazole, desloratadine, and occasional use of Ventolin. She had a minimal smoking history, having quit after three years of therapy. Her family history included type 1 diabetes mellitus in first- and second-degree relatives. The patient had previously received two corticosteroid injections for presumed bursitis, but the pain persisted with a severity score of 8, significantly affecting her daily activities and sleep despite the use of diclofenac. Physical examination showed a painful swelling in the left sternoclavicular area, with visible redness and warmth. Laboratory tests revealed a slightly elevated C-reactive protein level of 5.4 mg/L (reference < 5 mg/L) and an alkaline phosphatase level of 114 U/L (reference 20–140 U/L). Additionally, gamma-glutamyl transferase levels were elevated, ranging from 49 to 63 U/L (reference < 25 U/L), suggesting a hepatic origin. Creatinine clearance remained within the normal range throughout the treatment, ranging from 65 to 74 µmol/L (reference 49–90 µmol/L).
test_results: A CT scan of the chest-wall displayed a non-specific bilateral linear calcification of costa 1 and unilateral sclerosis of the left proximal clavicula. Preliminary calcification of the left costoclavicular ligament was also detected. Skeletal scintigraphy showed increased uptake of left proximal clavicula at the level of the sclerotic area, but not at the sternal side in sternoclavicular transition.

case_report: A 16-year-old female with a history of Hodgkin's lymphoma presented to the emergency department with sudden difficulty breathing and decreased oxygen levels two hours after starting a leukocyte-poor packed red cell transfusion for severe anemia. Her vital signs included a temperature of 38°C, a pulse rate of 140 beats per minute, a respiratory rate of 40 breaths per minute, blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg, and an oxygen saturation of 80% on room air. She weighed 67 kilograms and was 162 centimeters tall. Physical examination revealed pale conjunctiva without yellowing of the eyes. Bilateral crackles were heard in the lower lungs without signs of jugular venous distention or abnormal heart sounds. There was no enlargement of the liver or spleen. A maculopapular rash was noted on both extremities. Neurological examination was normal. The blood transfusion was stopped. She was given oxygen via a mask with a reservoir bag at an FiO2 of 1.0, which increased her oxygen saturation to 98-99%. Intramuscular adrenaline, intravenous chlorpheniramine, and hydrocortisone were administered due to the possibility of anaphylaxis. Arterial blood gas analysis showed severe hypoxemia with a PaO2 of 37 mmHg, a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 37, and an oxygen saturation of 70%, with normal PaCO2 and bicarbonate levels. Complete blood count revealed hemoglobin at 6 g/dL, hematocrit at 18.2%, white blood cell count at 2.7 × 10^9/L (with 72% neutrophils and an absolute neutrophil count of 1.9 × 10^9/L), 12% lymphocytes, 14% monocytes (absolute monocyte count of 0.38 × 10^9/L), 2% band forms, and a platelet count of 17 × 10^9/L. There were no indications of hemolysis. Serum electrolytes and glucose levels were normal. Serum tryptase was measured due to initial concerns of anaphylaxis and was found to be normal.
test_results: Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral pulmonary infiltration.

case_report: A 38-year-old Hispanic male with a history of anxiety arrived at the emergency room with complaints of fever, shortness of breath, productive cough with green phlegm, and body aches for the past two days. He reported no contact with sick individuals or recent travel. He mentioned using CBD/THC products, which he recently bought from a dispensary in Los Angeles County. Upon arrival, his vital signs were as follows: temperature 102.5 °F, heart rate 113 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/82 mm Hg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87% on room air. Physical examination revealed respiratory distress and bilateral coarse breath sounds upon auscultation. Laboratory results showed elevated ESR and procalcitonin levels, and the urine drug screen was positive for cannabinoids/THC.
test_results: Initial CXR showed bilateral infiltrates. CT chest without contrast showed bilateral patchy glass opacities with subpleural sparing and small right pleural effusion.

case_report: A 49-year-old male with a history of asthma managed without medication presented with chest pain. Two months prior, a health check showed no abnormalities. The patient has no significant family history, does not consume alcohol or tobacco, and has no known allergies. Laboratory tests showed no notable findings. Imaging of the chest revealed a mass located at the proximal end of the right clavicle.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) showed an approximately 36-mm tumoral lesion suspicious of infiltration into the right first rib and intercostal muscles, with changes in the density of the lung parenchyma around the mass, making it difficult to distinguish whether the mass was intrapulmonary or extrapulmonary. Hematoxylin and eosin staining revealed a partially hyalinized collagenous fibrous tissue containing abundant inflammatory cells, including neutrophils and lymphocytes. In areas with abundant fibroblast-like spindle-shaped cells, storiform fibrosis, and no cellular atypia were observed. Immunostaining was positive for vimentin and α-smooth muscle actin and negative for anti-cytokeratin (AE)1/AE3, cytokeratin 7, cluster of differentiation (CD) 34, desmin, soluble 100 protein (S-100), and B-cell lymphoma protein 2. CD3 and CD20 showed positive staining in background small lymphocytes, and the number of CD3-positive lymphocytes was higher than that of CD20-positive lymphocytes. CD138-positive plasma cells remained in nonspecific clusters. Ki67 positivity was approximately 5%. 18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/CT (18 F-FDG PET/CT) performed 4 days after CT-guided biopsy showed a tumoral lesion with a maximum standardized uptake value of 16.73 in the same area as the CT image, with no abnormal accumulation in other organs. Histopathological examination revealed that the tumor was predominantly fibroblastic, and there were no obvious malignant findings. Additional immunostaining for anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) with a D5F3 antibody revealed a very faint positive image in half of the spindle-shaped cells.

case_report: An 11-year-old girl with no prior health issues, medications, or allergies experienced complications with the eruption of her left maxillary canine tooth (23) and first premolar (24). Panoramic tomography revealed significant resorption on the mesial side of the root of tooth 24. There was no history of trauma in the affected area. Clinical examination showed marginal gingivitis around teeth 22-24, both labially and buccally, along with external resorption of tooth 24. Gingival pockets measuring 6-8 millimeters in depth were found adjacent to teeth 23 and 24. The patient reported soreness in the area. An orthodontic specialist noted a lack of space, leading to the extraction of tooth 24 and enucleation of granulation tissue. No tissue was collected for further analysis at that time. Twelve weeks later, a significant bone defect was noted, and tooth 23 remained in infraocclusion. The patient was referred to the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at Turku University Hospital (TUH) in Turku, Finland. At TUH, the bone defect was confirmed. Clinical examination showed no swelling, deep gingival pockets, or mobility of the teeth in the affected region. Adjacent teeth were vital, though there was a slight decrease in vitality in the second premolar and first molar. The gingiva in the region exhibited a bluish discoloration. Panoramic and intraoral X-rays indicated external resorption in the roots of the left maxillary lateral incisor and canine teeth. An osteolytic area in the same region (teeth 22-23) was consistently observed with an image taken three months earlier. Cone beam tomography revealed a cystic, osteolytic area on the left palatal side of the roots from the lateral incisor to the first premolar. The palatal cortex was perforated. The clinical and radiographic findings were nonspecific. Resorption of multiple teeth and perforation of the palatal cortex suggested locally aggressive lesions.
test_results: Histopathological investigation revealed a compact cellular spindle cell proliferation with collagenous stroma with storiform architecture. The proliferation started directly under the oral mucosal epithelium continuing throughout the tissue samples. The uniform spindle cells contained ovoid nuclei with rather pale eosinophilic cytoplasm. Only mild nuclear pleomorphism was seen. Mitotic activity was low as detected with Ki-67 level. Inflammatory component was minor with single or small groups of lymphocytes scattered around the spindle cell proliferation. The tumor tissue was positive for smooth muscle actin (SMA), vimentin, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). Calponin, myoglobin, and HHF35 antibodies showed moderate staining in myofibroblasts. Immunostaining of CD34 showed intense vascularisation of the whole tumor. There was no immunoreactivity for S-100, pancytokeratin, desmin, or Myf4. No HSV-8 or EBV was detected.

case_report: A 73-year-old woman with significant myopia presented with bilateral vision deterioration. She did not experience photopsias or scotomas. Her best-corrected visual acuity measured 20/70 in the right eye and 20/80 in the left eye, with a refraction of −15.5 + 3.00 × 113 in the right eye and −18.5 + 2.25 × 72 in the left eye. Examination of the anterior segment showed mild nuclear sclerotic cataracts in both eyes. Fundus examination identified bilateral staphylomas, optic nerve crescents, and changes consistent with degenerative myopia.
test_results: Fluorescein angiography revealed a normal choroidal pattern, window defects in the macular regions and staining of the optic nerve crescents in both eyes.
diagnosis: Macular Foveoschisis associated with Degenerative Myopia

case_report: A 68-year-old woman with a history of Hashimoto thyroiditis presented with chest pain lasting for 3 days. Initial laboratory tests at a local hospital revealed severe neutropenia, with a white blood cell count (WBC) of 1.9 × 10^9/L and a neutrophil count (NE) of 0.1 × 10^9/L. She was subsequently transferred to our hospital. Upon arrival, a complete blood cell count showed a WBC of 2.1 × 10^9/L, NE of 0.0 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin level of 94 g/L, and platelet count of 328 × 10^9/L.
test_results: Chest computed tomography scan revealed a 7.6 × 6.3 cm anterior mediastinum with uneven density, smooth borders, and a significantly enhanced mass in the arterial phase after enhancement. Bone marrow analysis and biopsy showed that the proportion of granulocytes at each stage decreased or was absent. Flow cytometric analysis of the bone marrow demonstrated a significant reduction in the number of granulocytes.
diagnosis: Thymoma  associated with pure white cell aplasia

case_report: A 64-year-old male visited the outpatient clinic with red patches and small raised bumps on the inner part of his left thigh, which had been present for two years. A skin examination revealed that these red patches and bumps were merging in the specified area. No abnormalities were observed on other parts of the body.
test_results: Histological examination of multiple punch biopsies showed diffuse infiltration of small-medium-sized atypical lymphocytes throughout the dermis. Immunohistochemical studies found the atypical lymphocytes were positive for CD2, CD3, CD4 in 95%, CD8 in 5%, and CD20 in 2% but negative for CD7 and CD30. BCL-6 and PD-1 expression was positive in 10% and 1–2% of the atypical lymphocytic infiltration respectively.
diagnosis: Primary Cutaneous CD4+ Small/Medium Pleomorphic T-Cell Lymphoproliferative Disorder
Orpha_name: Primary cutaneous CD4+ small/medium-sized pleomorphic T-cell lymphoma

case_report: In January 2011, an 18-year-old male with a history of progressive dilated cardiomyopathy underwent orthotopic heart transplantation. Post-surgery, he was placed on a standard triple-agent immunosuppressive regimen consisting of cyclosporine, prednisolone, and azathioprine. In May 2012, the patient noticed a painless mass in the left inguinal region that had been increasing in size over the past four months. Physical examination revealed a reddish, ulcerative mass approximately 3 cm in diameter located in the left inguinal area. There was no lymphadenopathy in the inguinal, axillary, or neck regions. The patient had a wide-local excision of the mass. The excised specimen showed a dense proliferation of pleomorphic small to medium-sized lymphoid cells with irregular nuclear borders and scant cytoplasm, with the infiltration extending into the deep dermis.
test_results: Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining showed that the neoplastic cells were CD4 and CD3 positive with aberrant loss of CD5 and negative B-cell markers (CD20, CD79 α, and PUX5).
diagnosis: Primary Cutaneous CD4-Positive Small/Medium-Sized Pleomorphic T-Cell Lymphoma
Orpha_name: Primary cutaneous CD4+ small/medium-sized pleomorphic T-cell lymphoma

case_report: A 63-year-old female patient presented with multiple well-defined erythematous nodules, some with central ulceration, ranging from 1 to 3 cm in size, located on the face, abdomen, and all four extremities. The lesions initially appeared as erythematous macules four months before consultation. They were not associated with itching or systemic symptoms. Laboratory tests revealed elevated levels of alkaline phosphatase, lactic dehydrogenase, and tumor markers CA 15-3, CA 19-9, and CA 125.
test_results: Biopsy revealed a focal epidermotropic and band-like dermal lymphocytic infiltrate, composed of medium-sized atypical lymphocytes, extending to subcutaneous tissue. There was no evidence of angioinvasion or adnexal damage. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated a positive CD3, CD4, CD8, TIA1, and granzyme B (cytotoxic granules) immunophenotype, with loss of CD20, CD30, BCL-6, and CD45RO. Approximately 60% of cells were Ki67+.
diagnosis: Primary Cutaneous CD8+ Aggressive Epidermotropic Cytotoxic T-cell Lymphoma
Orpha_name: Primary cutaneous aggressive epidermotropic CD8+ T-cell lymphoma

case_report: A 28-year-old male with no significant past medical history presented with persistent skin nodules on the trunk and extremities. Symptoms began 4 years ago, accompanied by spiking fever, nausea, and vomiting. These initial symptoms resolved after 6 months but recurred with generalized weakness, joint pain, chest pain, and multiple firm, subcutaneous nodules. The nodules were non-tender, prone to ulceration, and self-resolving. Initial histopathology from an outside institution suggested a different condition, leading to azathioprine therapy despite negative lupus serology. Imaging studies at that time did not show any ongoing systemic issues. Although the fever improved, the nodules persisted and progressed after one year of treatment, prompting the initiation of methotrexate and oral prednisone. Clinical examination revealed erythematous and indurated subcutaneous nodules scattered on the arms and legs, as well as an erythematous and indurated plaque with central necrotic crust on the back.
test_results: Histopathology of two different nodules demonstrated similar findings, revealing an epidermotropic, dermal and subcutaneous infiltrate comprised of medium-to-large, atypical lymphocytes and numerous histiocytes forming granulomas. There was notable angiodestruction, necrosis and syringotropism. Immunohistochemical stains showed the atypical lymphocytes to be positive for CD3, CD8, CD56 and TCR δ with loss of CD7 and diminished expression of CD5. These cells were negative for CD4, CD20, CD30, EBV in situ hybridization, CD34, CD117, MPO and TdT. Beta F1 was negative in the malignant cells while highlighted in the benign CD4 T-lymphocytes. The histiocytes appeared to be of non-Langerhans type and expressed CD63 (PGM1) and CD163. CD68/163 cells represented around 70% of the malignant infiltrate. The presence of granzyme and TIA confirmed the cytotoxic nature of the infiltrate. A T-cell gene rearrangement study was additionally performed and confirmed a clonal T-cell population.

case_report: A 69-year-old male presented with recurrent cutaneous nodules over a period of 2 years, which showed a pattern of self-regression. There were no notable symptoms or findings outside of the skin. Initial skin samples indicated a CD30+ lymphoproliferative condition, and the skin lesions were managed with topical steroids. After 2 years of fluctuating lesions, the patient developed persistent subcutaneous nodules on the legs and trunk.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed a dense predominant dermal and subcutaneous infiltrate of small to medium-size lymphocytes expressing a CD3+ CD4− CD8− CD56− granzyme B+ TIA-1+ TCRβ− TCRγ+ phenotype. GeneScan analysis identified a dominant T-cell population in skin lesions. PET did not display any hypermetabolism suspect of extracutaneous involvement.

case_report: A 66-year-old female presented with a 6-month history of a progressively enlarging lump located behind her right knee. The lesion was clinically asymptomatic and initially thought to be a cyst. Physical examination showed a firm, erythematous, non-tender subcutaneous nodule. MRI imaging revealed a 2.6 by 2.4 cm area with ill-defined enhancement within the subcutaneous fat and adjacent skin thickening.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the lesion revealed a predominantly subcutaneous infiltrate comprised of a variable mixture of small-to-medium sized, atypical-looking lymphocytes and abundant histiocytes forming small granulomas. Occasional mitotic figures were noted. Immunohistochemical (IHC) markers revealed the atypical lymphocytes were exclusively T-cells that expressed CD3, CD8, CD56, granzyme B, TIA-1 and TCR γ while being negative for CD4, CD5, BF1 and CD30. CD68 highlighted abundant histiocytes. CD68-positive cells represented 70–80% of the malignant infiltrate. EBV ISH showed strong nuclear staining in approximately 50% of the lymphocytic population. Flow cytometry demonstrated that the atypical lymphocytes lacked CD7, while DNA from the specimen revealed the presence of a clonal rearrangement of the T-cell receptor gamma gene.

case_report: A 42-year-old male exhibited several skin lesions located on the neck, trunk, and upper arms. These lesions were characterized by infiltrated deep red to violaceous nodules, each measuring between 1 and 1.5 cm. The lesions had been present for 8 months. The patient is a carrier of hepatitis C, but shows no biochemical evidence of chronic active hepatitis.
test_results: Histopathological examination showed a diffuse infiltrate sparing the epidermis. The central area infiltrate contains mainly small CD20+ and CD45RA+ B cells. Molecular analysis for detecting if there existed clonal proliferation of lymphoid cells and it had showed to be negative. Staining for Bcl-6, CD10, CD21 and CD45RA were positive. A small number of follicular and extrafollicular B cells showed expression of Bcl-2 protein. The t(14; 18) translocation with RTQ-PCR (Taqman) method was not found. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for Borrelia burgdorfer flagellin gene was negative in formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue of skin biopsy. Investigation for other nodal and extranodal MALT lymphoma was negative. Laboratory tests, including Borrelia burgdorferi serology and Helicobacter pylori, were all normal, apart from confirming the previously diagnosed hepatitis C. Other investigations including CT scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, showed no abnormalities. The bone marrow exam was negative.
diagnosis: Primary Marginal Zone Cutaneous B-cell Lymphoma
Orpha_name: Primary cutaneous marginal zone B-cell lymphoma

case_report: A 36-year-old male patient reported an 8-month history of a growing, painless lesion on his lower back. On physical examination, a well-defined, firm, reddish plaque measuring 1 x 2 cm was observed. Dermoscopy showed a salmon-colored background, serpiginous vessels, and multiple rosettes. No lymph node enlargement or additional lesions were detected on the rest of the skin.
test_results: The histopathological examination presented preserved epidermis and a dense dermal lymphoid infiltration, which was arranged in a nodular pattern. The immunohistochemistry was characterized by the expansion of the marginal zone cellular population BCL 2 + and CD 20 +. Nodal lymphocytes were CD3 - and peripheral lymphoid population was CD3+.
Orpha_name: Primary cutaneous marginal zone B-cell lymphoma

case_report: A 53-year-old male presented with multiple, dusky reddish nodules on the trunk, persisting for 7 years. These lesions were bilaterally distributed along the lateral sides of the trunk and had shown slight progression. The patient has a medical history of arterial hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. There were no systemic symptoms indicating involvement of other organs. The patient did not report any specific triggers causing induction or exacerbation of symptoms. Stroking the lesions resulted in swelling, itching, and redness of the skin.
test_results: Histological findings of the biopsy specimen showed nodular to diffuse dermal infiltration of lymphocytes with irregular nuclei, eosinophils, plasma cells, and mast cells. Kappa light chain restriction was suggested in the immunostaining results of the immunoglobulin (Ig) light chain. CD20 staining, a B-cell marker, revealed reactive lymphoid follicles with patch positivity. Periphery of lymphoid follicles showed BCL-2 positivity and BCL-6 positivity focally at the center. Toluidine blue and CD117 staining showed positivity, and several mast cells were confirmed. MUM1 and CD138 showed diffuse positivity and confirmed positive reaction in plasma cells. The Ig heavy chain gene rearrangement result showed B-cell monoclonality. Of the Igs measured in serum, only the IgG level was elevated to 1905.80 mg/dL. Peripheral blood smear and immunofixation electrophoresis results in serum and urine showed no abnormality. The patient did not show any evidence of hypermetabolic metastasis on whole body positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT).
diagnosis: Primary cutaneous marginal zone B-cell lymphoma , plasmacytoid type with mastocytosis
Orpha_name: Primary cutaneous marginal zone B-cell lymphoma

case_report: A 45-year-old Caucasian male with no prior health issues presented with infiltrated plaques and coalescent nodules on the left parietal region, which appeared one year ago. He mentioned experiencing local trauma six months before the lesion appeared. He reported no local or systemic symptoms such as fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Dermatological examination revealed hard, erythematous plaques and nodules measuring approximately 8x4 cm. No palpable lymphadenopathy was detected.
test_results: The histopathological exam demonstrated a large diffuse dermal infiltrate that spared the epidermis, with a partial follicular component. The infiltrate was composed of a population of central follicle cells, predominantly with multilobed nuclei, associated with large centroblasts and mixed centrocytes and surrounded by a great quantity of small reactive T lymphocytes. Immunohistochemistry was positive for CD5 and CD20 and negative for CD30.

case_report: A 16-year-old girl from Saudi Arabia visited the outpatient dermatology clinic at King Fahad Hospital of the University. She had a single, painless, red nodule on her left forearm that had been gradually enlarging over the past two years. Previous treatments at various hospitals included antibiotics, oral antihistamines, and topical steroid creams, none of which were effective. She reported no fever, night sweats, weight loss, or widespread itching. Additionally, she had no history of insect bites, trauma, or recent travel. Physical examination revealed a solitary nodule on the left forearm, measuring 1.5 cm × 1 cm, with a smooth surface that was red to darkened in color and firm to the touch. Initial considerations included dermatofibroma and benign adnexal neoplasms. A skin biopsy was suggested, which the patient initially declined but later consented to.
test_results: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained sections of skin show a dense dermal nodular, periadnexal and perivascular lymphoid infiltrate. The infiltrate involved the superficial and deep dermis, focally extending to the subcutis, and sparing the epidermis in a follicular growth pattern. It was composed predominantly of small, elongated CD20 positive B cells with irregular nuclei and inconspicuous nucleoli. A small proportion of the neoplastic B cell (less than 10%) showed larger, more rounded nuclei with multiple peripheral nucleoli. CD3 positive reactive T lymphocytes were admixed with the infiltrate. Apoptosis was focally identified; however, mitoses were not prominent. The B-cell population was positive for BCL2 and showed variable BCL6 positivity in more than 30% of the neoplastic cells. Only a few scattered cells were positive for CD10. Additionally, CD30, CD43 and TDT were negative. CD21 highlighted expanded follicular dendritic meshworks. BCL6 positive cells were seen extending beyond the meshwork in some areas. BCL2 gene rearrangement was not detected by interphase fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) performed on paraffin embedded tissue but Immunoglobulin heavy chain gene rearrangement was detected, confirming the monoclonal nature of the B-cell population.

case_report: A 56-year-old brown male patient, trader, observed the development of nodular formations on the abdomen 2 months prior. He noted a gradual increase in size and the appearance of additional similar lesions, accompanied by mild local pain. He reported no itching or secretion drainage and had not received any prior treatment. Physical examination revealed nodules of different sizes with a smooth and glossy surface, some of which were ulcerated and erythematous, located on the face, abdomen, and upper limbs.
test_results: A biopsy of one of the nodules revealed on histopathological examination atrophic epidermis and nodular neoplastic infiltration of the dermis under the Grenz zone at all levels. The subcutaneous tissue revealed dense aggregates of epithelioid cells with scant eosinophilic cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, more than two nucleoli, nuclear-cellular pleomorphism, and frequent atypical mitosis figures. Immunohistochemical examination showed positivity for CD20, PAX-5, CD10, BCL-2, and BCL-6.

case_report: A 32-year-old woman presented with multiple tender, red papules on her right forearm, which had been present for 1 month. These lesions were located over an arteriovenous (AV) fistula created for renal dialysis. The patient had a history of renal failure since her early twenties and had been undergoing renal dialysis since then. She noted that the lesions on her forearm were increasing in number and size and becoming more painful. Physical examination revealed multiple red papules and nodules on the forearm, which were firm and tender to touch. One of the nodules exhibited superficial ulceration. The presence of the nodule over an AV fistula prompted consideration of a broad range of vascular tumors.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed grenz zone and diffuse infiltration of large pleomorphic cells occupying the whole dermis. Some mitotic figures were noted. CD20 was found to be diffusely positive for all these atypical cells and CD4 was negative. Further immunohistochemical analysis showed diffuse Bcl-2 positive staining and few scattered Bcl-6 positive staining. CD10 and MUM1 were negative.
diagnosis: Primary Cutaneous B-Cell Lymphoma, Leg Type
Orpha_name: Primary cutaneous diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, leg type

case_report: A 28-year-old male visited the clinic on July 22, 2019, presenting with multiple asymptomatic, merging scarlet plaques on the lateral side of his right thigh. He reported a single, painless, warty lesion with a slight tingling sensation that had grown over a period of 5 years. The patient did not have a history of joint pain or muscle pain. He was afebrile, and no lymph node enlargement was detected. A thorough skin examination revealed that he was otherwise in good health, except for a cluster of 12 cm by 12 cm erythematous, infiltrated, consolidated papulonodules on the extensor surface of his proximal right lower extremity.
test_results: Excisional skin biopsy demonstrated a condensed disseminated infiltration of lymphocytes in the entire dermis with a granz zone between the epidermis and dermis. Clustered atypical cells and abundant neoplastic immunoblasts and centroblasts can be seen in the dermis. Immunohistochemical staining showed that the tumour cells expressed diffuse positivity for B-cell markers, including CD20 and CD79a. CD3, Bcl-2, Bcl-6, CD5, CD10, CD30, MYC, and Ki-67 also showed positive expression. MUM-1 was negative. PET-CT showed increased metabolic rate in the lower part of the right thigh.
diagnosis: Primary Cutaneous Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma, Leg Type
Orpha_name: Primary Cutaneous Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma, Leg Type

case_report: Patient information: A 15-year-old unmarried girl presented with a history of severe lower abdominal pain during menstruation for two days, accompanied by two episodes of vomiting. Upon admission, the patient was stable, afebrile, acyanotic, and anicteric, with normal vital signs and physical examination. Her menstrual cycles began at the age of 12 and were irregular, occurring every 30-40 days and lasting four to five days. She reported no medical or surgical history and no drug allergies. Clinical findings: The USG of the pelvis revealed an isoechoic structure with echogenic content located behind the urinary bladder and to the right of a normal uterine body and fundus, which appeared continuous with one cervix. Both ovaries were identified separately and appeared normal. Both kidneys were also normal. No HSG or transvaginal USG study was performed as the patient was unmarried. The patient was advised further evaluation.
test_results: MRI of the pelvis revealed a globular structure measuring approximately 2.3 x 3.1 x 4.5 cm seen lying on the right side of the uterus. The MR morphology of this globular structure was indicative of uterine in origin with a maintained zonal architecture. It had internal components that were hyperintense on T1-weighted images (WI) and T2WI. It did not demonstrate any obvious connection with the normal uterine lumen. Both ovaries were normal with multiple developing follicles within.
diagnosis: Unicornuate uterus with a non-communicating rudimentary horn and hematometra

case_report: A 27-year-old woman, who is pregnant for the first time and at 15 weeks and 6 days of amenorrhea, experienced severe abdominal pain 2 days prior to admission. Upon arrival, she exhibited signs of hypovolemic shock, including pallor, low blood pressure (88/47 mmHg), and a rapid heart rate. Her abdomen was tense, and the symphysis-fundal height measured 18 weeks. There was no vaginal bleeding observed. She had reported abdominal pain 7 days earlier, and was informed at another hospital that her pregnancy was normal. No other significant medical history was noted.
test_results: Transabdominal ultrasound showed a viable fetus with the 16-week size beside the normal uterus. Much abdominal effusion was described. 3 mL of nonclotting blood was pumped by abdominal paracentesis.

case_report: A 13-year-old girl came to the outpatient department with severe, progressively worsening menstrual pain since her first period at age 11. Her menstrual cycles have been regular. One year ago, she experienced a sudden severe abdominal pain and was treated at a local hospital where an emergency laparotomy was performed. The appendix appeared normal during the surgery. Despite the procedure, her symptoms persisted, leading to her dropping out of school due to the increasing severity of her menstrual pain. On physical examination, her abdomen was soft, with no tenderness or enlargement of organs.
test_results: Transabdominal 2D USG revealed a 4.5 cm × 3.3 cm lesion in the right uterine myometrium indenting the endometrial cavity. Bilateral ovaries were normal. MRI showed a heterogeneous lesion of size 5.4 cm × 4.5 cm in the right lateral wall of the uterus abutting the adjacent junctional zone medially, not communicating with the endometrial cavity. On laparoscopy, a bulge was noted on the right side of the uterus with the right round ligament, the fallopian tube and the ovary attached to the lesion. Hysteroscopy revealed a tubular cavity with a single ostium seen on the left side.

case_report: A 24-year-old woman visited the Reproductive Endocrinology Department due to a gradually enlarging right ovarian cyst, measuring 3 cm in diameter. This cyst and a uterine developmental abnormality were identified a year earlier at a local hospital. Despite these findings, she wished to pursue pregnancy, as her tumor biomarker levels were normal and she had not undergone further examinations or treatments. She began menstruating at age 13 and experienced regular menstrual cycles every 30 days, lasting 7 days, with mild dysmenorrhea that sometimes required medication. A gynecological examination revealed a normal vulva, vagina, and cervix. The uterus was of normal size, with the right corpus slightly larger than the left.
test_results: Three-dimensional ultrasound showed that the uterus was divided by a septum. The right uterine hemicavity did not communicate with the single cervix, but was accompanied by hematometra. Two cysts were located in the right and left adnexa (7 cm and 1.8 cm, respectively), and these were provisionally diagnosed as ovarian endometrioma.

case_report: An 83-year-old male, who has been smoking for 180 packs per year and has a history of hypertension and coronary heart disease for over a decade, noticed a mass in his right axilla one year ago. The mass was not accompanied by redness, swelling, or pain. The mass gradually increased to approximately 3 cm in size, prompting the patient to visit a nearby hospital where he underwent local tumor resection on October 26, 2020. Subsequent imaging examinations, including CT, MRI, and PET/CT, revealed no abnormal enhancement or mass in the breast, no enlarged lymph nodes in the right axilla, and no signs of distant metastasis.
test_results: A 3-cm-diameter nodule with skin was found on postoperative pathology. Histologically, poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma was found in subcutaneous fibrous tissue. Positive immunohistochemical staining for anti-gross cystic disease fluid protein-15 (GCDFP-15), GATA-3, cytokeratin (CK), CK7, and EMA and negative for estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), prostate-specific antigen (PSA), CK20, CDX2, p504S, p63, P40, TTF-1, NapsinA, PLAP, Syn, and CgA. The expression of HER2 was 2+ by immunohistochemistry, and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) showed no amplification, and Ki67 was 20% positive.

case_report: In December 2015, a 24-year-old male patient experienced recurrent vomiting, pain in the right side of the abdomen, and weight loss. An abdominal CT scan showed a 6 cm mass located in the right upper retroperitoneal and abdominal area.
