Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EDG) identified a fungating ulcerating mass in the second part of the duodenum. A tru-cut biopsy from the abdominal mass and a biopsy from the duodenal mass were performed, leading to a planned Whipple procedure. In February 2016, the patient arrived at our center.
test_results: Review of his original pathological slides revealed a germ cell tumor with large areas of necrosis, as well as focal granulomatous reaction. The tumor cells were diffusely strongly positive for SALL4, OCT 3/4, and CD30, with focal positivity for pan CK AE1/E3. Scattered groups of tumor cells were positive for Glypican3. The tumor cells were negative for alpha-fetoprotein.

case_report: A 25-year-old Bulgarian man was referred to our center by his regular medical doctor due to severe fatigue lasting for the past three weeks and sharp epigastric pain with dorsal radiation causing nocturnal awakening, worsening over the past month. The patient had not experienced recent weight loss or anorexia. He had a moderate smoking habit but no significant surgical or medical history. Clinical examination revealed a body mass index of 19 and epigastric tenderness without any detectable abdominal mass. Bowel movements were regular, but dark stools were noted over the last week. A digital rectal exam showed no mass or blood. The patient was afebrile and exhibited marked skin pallor. Laboratory results indicated hemoglobin at 6.8 g/dL, consistent with iron deficiency anemia (serum iron: 2 μmol/L, mean corpuscular volume: 76.5 fL, and ferritin: 4 μmol/L). He received a transfusion of 4 units of packed red blood cells upon admission. There was no evidence of an inflammatory syndrome (leukocytes: 8.88 Giga/L, C-reactive protein: 22.3 mg/L). Liver function tests indicated cytolysis (glutamic pyruvic transaminase: 218 U/L, glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase: 76 U/L) and anicteric cholestasis (gamma-glutamyl transferase: 644 U/L, alkaline phosphatase: 507 U/L, total bilirubin: 2.7 μmol/L). Lipase levels were 2591 U/L and decreased rapidly. Tumor markers were measured: carcinoembryonic antigen: < 1 μg/L, carbohydrate antigen 19-9: 17.2 kU/L, alpha-fetoprotein: 2.1 μg/L, β human chorionic gonadotropin < 3 UI/L, lactate dehydrogenase: 117 U/L. Rectoscopy up to 40 cm from the anal margin did not reveal any specific findings.
test_results: Gastroscopy has revealed a circumferential vegetating lesion with a villous appearance on the second portion of the duodenum. This lesion became indurated and ulcerated at the third portion of the duodenum and was responsible for a tight stenosis. Biopsy findings were evocative of a slightly differentiated adenocarcinoma of biliopancreatic origin (cytokeratin 7+ and cytokeratin 20-). A computerized tomography (CT) of the chest, abdomen and pelvis showed a circumferential lesion thickening of up to 2 cm at the level of the second and third portions of the duodenum with a bi-ductal dilatation (of the common bile duct and main pancreatic duct). An 8 mm adenomegaly could be noted in a retropancreatic position. No secondary lesion was observed. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pancreas and magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) confirmed this duodenal tissue thickening spreading from the proximal part of the second portion of the duodenum up to the duodenojejunal flexure, which was accountable for pancreatic duct and bile duct upstream swelling without any secondary hepatic lesion. Some very short contact adenomegalies were also observed there.

case_report: A 12-year-old male presented with a week-long history of cough, sputum production, and fever. The patient's family history was negative for genetic diseases, tumors, infectious diseases, and surgeries. Physical examination indicated diminished breath sounds in the left lung, solid percussion sounds in the middle and lower lung regions, and an elevated body temperature of 38.3°C. Laboratory tests revealed increased white blood cell count and hemoglobin levels, with decreased platelet count, albumin, serum calcium, and phosphorus levels. Other laboratory values were within normal limits. Tumor marker analysis showed elevated levels of neuron-specific enolase, carbohydrate antigen 199 (CA-199), carbohydrate antigen 125 (CA-125), and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). A chest X-ray showed a large, dense shadow in the left lung field, with the heart displaced to the right. Computed tomography (CT) imaging revealed a large, unevenly dense mass in the mediastinum extending into the left thoracic cavity. The radiologist initially considered the mass to be a fibroma or neurogenic tumor.
test_results: The tumor cells of different sizes are round or ovoid, arranged in loose meshes, and the endodermal sinus bodies can be seen between the cells. AFP, glypican-3, SALL4, CK, and vimentin were positive, CK5/6 squamous epithelium was positive, and OCT4 and CD117 were weakly positive. CD34 was positive in tumor blood vessels, and Ki-67 was about 50% positive, while CD30, calretinin, MC, S100, and other tumor cells were not expressed.

case_report: A 33-year-old male patient presented with vague abdominal discomfort in the left lower quadrant and a history of infertility. He had a background of a neglected undescended left testicle. Imaging revealed a 2-centimeter mass in the pelvic area. The mass was subsequently removed by a general surgeon via a lower midline incision. He was referred to our urology clinic. On physical examination, he appeared as a phenotypically normal male. The chest and abdominal exams were unremarkable, aside from the lower midline incision scar. He had a normal-appearing penis and a right-side testicle.
test_results: An ultrasound (US) was performed which revealed a 2-centimeter mass in the pelvic area. Lab evaluation, two weeks after surgery, revealed elevated β-HCG and LDH levels (β-HCG: 4645 IU/L, LDH: 527 U/L) with normal AFP level (2.34 ng/mL). In computed tomography (CT) imaging, a 40 mm retrovesical mass was detected. Chest CT imaging was negative for metastasis. A tumor marker recheck two weeks later did not indicate any dramatic change. Upon completion, the size of the retrovesical mass did not change; however, the tumor marker levels dropped while only LDH remained elevated (β-HCG: <0/1 IU/L, LDH: 636 U/L, and AFP: 2/99 ng/mL). In fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) evaluation, the mass did not show any metabolic activity.

case_report: A 19-year-old nulliparous British-Caucasian woman presented with a one-day history of worsening pain in the right iliac fossa, accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Her medical and gynecological history was unremarkable, and her menstrual cycles were regular, lasting four days with a 28-day cycle. On abdominal examination, there was percussion tenderness over the right iliac fossa and a positive Rovsing's sign. Laboratory tests showed mildly elevated white cell count and C-reactive protein levels. The patient was taken to the operating theater for an open appendectomy. During surgery, free fluid was observed in the pelvis, and the appendix appeared normal. The right adnexa was twisted three times and necrotic, with the ovary measuring 8 cm and the fallopian tube distended and necrotic. A right salpingo-oophorectomy was performed, and the left ovary was found to be normal.
test_results: The histological analysis showed congestion, hemorrhage and coagulative necrosis of the fallopian tube. The broad-based papillary lesion showed a fibrotic stroma forming broad leaf like projections lined by a low cuboidal ciliated epithelium. The ovary also showed severe hemorrhage and congestion with coagulative necrosis.
diagnosis: Benign cystadenofibroma of the fallopian tube

case_report: A 32-year-old woman, who has been pregnant three times and has two children, initially experienced abdominal pain that resolved on its own. Four months later, she reported worsening pain in the right lower abdomen that had persisted for four days. The patient is a smoker and has no history of medical conditions, including hypertension. During the initial examination, she was afebrile with stable vital signs. Her blood pressure readings were 134/73 mm Hg. Laboratory tests revealed normal values except for a slight increase in C-reactive protein (0.18 mg/dL), white blood cell count (9,100/L), and hemoglobin (15 g/dL). Serum tumor markers, including carcinoembryonic antigen, CA125, CA19-9, alpha-fetoprotein, and squamous cell carcinoma antigen, were within normal limits. Imaging studies, including non-contrast-enhanced CT and ultrasonography, identified a mass lesion in the right lower abdomen.
test_results: On MRI, a heterogeneous mass measuring 48 mm in longitudinal diameter connected with a tortuous structure that appeared to be a fallopian tube was identified in the right-lower abdomen. The right ovary, which appeared normal, was identified at a slightly distant location. On contrast-enhanced CT, loss of enhancement in this solid mass supported the diagnosis of IFTT with heterogeneous mass. Histological examination exhibited massive ischemic necrosis of excised tumor tissue and fallopian tube for the most part. In the viable peripheral tissue, closely packed nests, showing a 'zellballen' appearance, were identified. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for neural cell adhesion molecule (CD56), neuron-specific enolase, and S-100 protein in viable tumor cells, while staining for the cytokeratin marker (AE1/AE3) and estrogen receptor was negative. The percentage of Ki-67 positive cells was <1%.

case_report: Patient information: In 2018, a 39-year-old Eastern Slavic woman was diagnosed with uterine leiomyoma and was regularly monitored by a gynecologist. During a routine examination, rapid growth of the uterine tumor was noted. The patient's health was satisfactory, and her menstrual cycle remained regular. Her medical history included one birth via cesarean section with blood transfusion and one medical abortion. There were no infectious or general somatic symptoms, and her family history was not significant for otopathology. Clinical findings: Pelvic sonography showed a postoperative scar on the anterior wall of the lower uterine segment. A 27 mm node with reduced echogenicity was observed on the posterior uterine wall, which was avascular in the ROWER mode and on CDL Doppler. No structural changes were noted in the cervix or cervical canal. The endometrium was in the late proliferative phase with medium echogenicity. Both ovaries were of normal size, structure, and folliculogenesis for her age. A rounded neoplasm up to 30 mm in diameter with a well-defined contour was seen in the right parametrium. Anechoic areas of 2-3 mm in diameter were present in the peripheral region, giving a “ground-glass” appearance. Neoplasmic vascularization in the ROWER mode and on CDL Doppler was minimal. The neoplasm was not connected to the ovary or uterine body. Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and small pelvis with intravenous contrast agent tomohexol 350 showed a subserous leiomyomatous node on the posterior uterine wall measuring 23x28 mm and an oval-shaped neoplasm of unclear origin in the right corner of the uterus measuring 34x30 mm, with diffuse contrast accumulation. No pathological deviations were observed in other examined organs. Clinical laboratory tests were within normal limits [Ca-125, 38 U/mL; HE4, 42.10 pmol/L; ROMA-1 (calculation before menopause), 5.4]. Surgical intervention: Due to the presence of a neoplasm of unclear origin in the small pelvis, diagnostic laparoscopy was performed. Laparoscopy revealed a subserous leiomyomatous node up to 28 mm in diameter on the posterior surface of the lower uterine segment. No abnormalities were found in the ovaries or left fallopian tube. The right fallopian tube was pinkish-colored, deformed, and thickened up to 30 mm at the point of connection with the uterus. The right fallopian tube was removed, and a conservative myomectomy was performed.
test_results: The presence of strong and monotonous immunoreactivity for CD31 and CD34 in endothelial cells lining the interior surface of the spaces confirmed the diagnosis of a benign vascular tumor. Low mitotic activity of the tumor cells (Ki-67 proliferation) and absence of estrogen receptor expression were revealed.
diagnosis: Capillary Hemangioma of the Right Fallopian Tube

case_report: A 62-year-old postmenopausal para0+2 female presented with a two-month history of dysuria, postmenopausal bleeding, and associated cramping. She had a history of using estrogen cream for vaginal atrophy. General physical examinations, including vital signs and abdominal exams, were unremarkable with no abdominal tenderness or mass. A gynecologic exam showed normal genitalia and anal region. Examination of the introitus revealed a fleshy, friable but firm mass around the urethral meatus. A speculum exam identified a 3 cm sessile, firm mass in the right upper quadrant of the vagina just inside the introitus. The cervix appeared normal. A bimanual exam indicated a slightly enlarged uterus. An attempt to pass an endometrial biopsy catheter was unsuccessful, and an endometrial biopsy was not obtained. A transvaginal ultrasound showed a symmetrical uterus with a uniform endometrial thickness of 0.50 cm and no other abnormalities. An MRI of the pelvis revealed uterine intramural and subserosal fibroids, the largest measuring 3 cm, and a 2.3 cm mass in the lower one-third of the vagina affecting the distal urethra. The mass was bilobed with another component measuring 1.8 cm in the middle third of the vagina. No rectal invasion or pelvic lymphadenopathy was observed, and there were no suspicious osseous lesions. Examination under anesthesia followed by cystourethroscopy was performed. The urethral opening was nearly obliterated by a fungating mass at the anterior portion of the vagina. A flexible cystoscope identified the urethral orifice at about 11 o'clock in relation to the vaginal mass. The urethra and external sphincter were not involved, but there was a significant mass effect pushing the urethra anterolaterally. The cystoscopy showed a normal-appearing bladder. A vaginal exam revealed two fungating masses, one near the urethra in the anterior vagina and one in the posterior vagina. The cervix showed no abnormalities. A liquid-based pap smear was taken, and both masses were separately biopsied for pathological examination.
test_results: The biopsies from posterior and anterior vaginal periurethral masses showed similar features on the histological examination. The tissue revealed moderately formed glands with a complex structure including a cribriform growth pattern that invaded the stroma. The glands were lined by atypical pseudostratified cuboidal to columnar cells with pleomorphic, hyperchromatic nuclei. There were scattered cells with intracytoplasmic mucin, but abundant extracellular mucin was not present. The tumor cells were mitotically active with frequent intraluminal necrosis. The tumor cells from both biopsy sites were positive for cytokeratin 20 (CK20), caudal-type homeobox 2 (CDX2), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), and epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) (focal) and negative for cytokeratin 7 (CK7) and estrogen receptor (ER). Additionally, progesterone receptor (PR), paired box gene 8 (Pax8), and vimentin were negative.
diagnosis: vaginal invasive moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of intestinal-type

case_report: An 82-year-old Caucasian female presented on December 12, 2021, for evaluation of a right breast mass. She reported a rash over the mass, which she had been treating with Neosporin. Her last clinical breast examination in 2014 revealed a mass in the upper outer and lower outer quadrant of the right breast with an overlying petechial rash. The mass was painless, mobile, and measured approximately 10 cm. Clinical examination of the axilla showed no lymphadenopathy. Diagnostic imaging at that time included a mammogram showing a macrolobulated mass measuring 14×12×12 cm in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. Limited ultrasound revealed a hypoechoic mass greater than 12×10 cm with internal vascularity and one lymph node with uniform cortical thickening up to 5 mm. Her previous mammogram in June 2014 showed a mass measuring 9.5×8×6.8 cm. The patient had no prior history of breast, ovarian, colon, or pancreatic cancer and denied any family history of breast cancer. Her medical history included a right breast mass in the same location since 2004. Review of prior imaging showed the mass measured 5.8 cm in 2004, 6.3 cm in 2007, and 7.4 cm in 2009. During this period, clinical examination remained stable with a 5 cm mass. The patient had an ultrasound-guided core biopsy on September 30, 2009, which showed a benign fibroepithelial lesion consistent with fibroadenoma. A second ultrasound-guided core biopsy on June 12, 2021, revealed a spindle cell neoplasm. A CT of the chest was performed to check for pulmonary metastasis.
test_results: Histologic findings revealed a fibroepithelial neoplasm demonstrating spindle-shaped stromal cells with markedly increased stromal cellularity, stromal overgrowth, mild-to-moderate nuclear atypia, and increased mitotic activity.

case_report: A 26-year-old woman was admitted to the West China Hospital, Sichuan University, China, with a complaint of spontaneous nipple discharge from her left breast for one month. Her medical history included a previous lumpectomy on her left breast due to a palpable mass. The postoperative pathological report indicated a complex fibroadenoma with stromal cell proliferation and local lobulated structures. She reported no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Physical examination revealed a firm mass with a clear margin in the lower inner quadrant near the nipple of the left breast, measuring approximately 2.5 cm in diameter. A single duct non-bloody discharge from the left nipple was observed upon squeezing. There was no evidence of nipple retraction or skin dimpling. Ultrasonography identified mammary duct ectasia and a solid-cystic mass measuring 28 × 20 × 20 mm near the nipple-areola complex (NAC) of the left breast. Galactography of the left breast showed mammary duct ectasia and multiple irregular filling defects in the dilated duct. The mass and the associated mammary duct were removed through a circumareolar incision. Two intraductal neoplastic lesions measuring 20 × 20 × 20 mm and 28 × 20 × 20 mm respectively were found in the dilated duct system. Cytology of the nipple discharge showed no tumor cells.
test_results: The histological examination showed a biphasic tumor, with mesenchymal and epithelial components. The mesenchymal cells highlighted moderate stromal hypercellularity, marked nuclear atypia and occasional mitoses. Ki67 immunohistochemistry to assess the index of proliferation showed 20% to 30% positive.
diagnosis: Borderline Phyllodes Tumor of the Breast

case_report: A 26-year-old female visited the surgical outpatient department due to a right-sided breast lump that had been present for one year. The lump was painful. The patient was neither pregnant nor lactating. On physical examination, a substantial right breast lump measuring approximately 25 × 15 cm was observed, encompassing the entire breast. The overlying skin appeared mostly normal, except for some redness at the 9 o'clock position. There was no nipple retraction or skin puckering. No axillary lymphadenopathy was detected.
test_results: True-cut biopsy showed predominantly fibrocollagenous tissue along with few benign ductal elements. No increase in stromal cellularity, atypia, mitosis, or malignancy was noted. Histopathological examination showed epithelial and stromal proliferation with some cystic dilatation of ducts and focal apocrine changes. Some sections also showed areas of sclerosing adenosis, foci of microcalcification, and stromal hyalinization. Focal squamous metaplasia was also seen. No atypia or dysplasia was noted in multiple levels.

case_report: On July 25, 2022, a 14-year-old female was admitted to the Department of Thyroid and Breast Surgery at the First Affiliated Hospital of Dali University in China for assessment of a large mass in the left breast, which had been growing over approximately six months. Initially the size of a mung bean, the mass had increased to the size of a hen’s egg. The patient reported regular menstrual cycles and no family history of breast masses. She had no history of other illnesses, chest disease, radiation exposure, or estrogen use. There was no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Physical examination identified a 100.0 mm × 40.0 mm mass in the left breast with an indistinct border, firm texture, limited mobility, and tenderness. There were no signs of skin redness, surgical scars, or nipple retraction on the affected breast. The right breast and both axillae appeared normal. Laboratory tests, including routine blood tests, blood biochemistry, blood coagulation function, and routine stool and urine tests, showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Breast ultrasonography (BUSG) of the patient’s left breast showed a large hypoechoic solid lesion (110.4 mm × 41.6 mm in size), which had an oval shape, clear boundaries, horizontal growth, and even distribution. A few irregular liquid dark areas were noted in the breast mass without obvious calcifications and no enlarged lymph nodes in the bilateral axillae. A color Doppler examination revealed few punctate flow signals at the edge of the breast mass. The lesion was classified as Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) category 3.

case_report: A 45-year-old woman attended the Takahashi Breast and Gastroenterology Clinic for a routine breast cancer screening. During the physical examination, a mass measuring 1.5 cm was palpated in the E region of her left breast. Mammography (MMG) revealed a tumor shadow in the left S region, with a high-density area inside the tumor indicative of bone or cartilage formation. The MMG was categorized as category 3. Ultrasound (US) imaging showed a poorly defined tumor measuring 14.3 × 14.8 × 10.7 mm with relatively smooth margins and inhomogeneous high-echo content. Color Doppler US indicated a hypovascular pattern. A linear shadow was observed passing transversely and slightly obliquely downwards, anterior to the tumor, corresponding to the needle used in the biopsy. The needle traversed the solid tumor steadily and accurately.
test_results: The tumor showed proliferation of small cells forming glandular duct-like structures or anastomosed funicular structures, and the cells in the basilar portion were spindle-shaped and transitioned to the stroma. Cartilaginous metaplasia, calcification, and ossification were observed in some areas. Intraductal papilloma was also observed in some areas.

case_report: A 7-year-old boy presented with difficulty in chewing and concerns about appearance. Examination revealed sparse, thin, light blond hair on the scalp, scanty eyebrows and eyelashes, a depressed nasal bridge, frontal bossing, and prominent supraorbital ridges. His lips were dry, everted, and prominent, and his skin was dry and wrinkled. There was hyperpigmentation around the eyes and plantar dyskeratosis. Oral examination showed partial absence of teeth, underdeveloped conical teeth, and delayed eruption of permanent teeth. His nails were normal, and his intelligence was within the normal range. According to his mother, the child experienced recurrent episodes of high fever and thirst, was unable to sweat, and required precautions to prevent overheating during physical activity or in warm weather. The child was born to parents who are not related by blood, and no other family members exhibited similar characteristics.
test_results: Panoramic radiograph showed four cone-shaped crowns suggestive of primary canines. Maxillary primary molars and incisors were also present. There was some evidence of tooth formation in both jaws and eight tooth buds probably related to the permanent canines, and first molars and maxillary incisors were present. However, hypodontia in the right and left side was asymmetric, and mandible had more missing teeth than maxilla.

case_report: A three-month-old, caucasian male infant was brought in due to reduced sweating, dry skin, and lack of hair on the scalp. There was no notable family history of inherited diseases. The mother exhibited normal facial features, hair, teeth, skin, and nails. The infant was the second child of healthy, unrelated parents, with the first child being a healthy female. He was delivered spontaneously following a normal pregnancy, with no complications during birth or the perinatal period. Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. Birth measurements included a weight of 2390 g (4th centile), length of 47 cm (12th centile), and head circumference of 33 cm (19th centile). Physical examination revealed scaphocephaly, a prominent forehead, forehead bumps, dark rings under the eyes, wide-set eyes, an epicanthic fold, an upturned nose, a depressed nasal bridge, and prominent lips. Both upper and lower eyelids had sparse eyelashes. The scalp and eyebrows were devoid of hair. The skin was thin, pale, dry, and peeling, with widespread eczematous dermatitis, particularly on the scalp. The skin around the eyes and mouth was wrinkled and hyperpigmented. The parents noted dryness of the eyes. Neuromotor and mental development scores on the Bayley II scale were within normal limits. Abdominal and cerebral ultrasound screenings showed no anomalies, and routine ECG and echocardiogram evaluations were normal.
test_results: The analysis revealed the hemizygous variant, NM_001399.4: c.1142G > C (p.Gly381Ala) in EDA gene located on the X chromosome. The variant was tested for familial segregation showing heterozygous maternal state. The same variant was not found in the father of the proband and the sibling. Pedigree analysis showed an X-linked pattern of inheritance.

case_report: A 52-year-old woman with no known chronic medical conditions presented to the emergency department with left lower extremity weakness, left facial droop, and slurred speech for 3 days. The patient also reported diffuse body itching, yellow skin, and dark urine for 7 days. She denied any history of stroke or other cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, liver disease, exposure to hepatitis, alcohol abuse, or intravenous drug use. She had a family history of lupus in her maternal grandmother and two aunts. Body mass index was 26.63 kg/m2. Physical examination was notable for yellowing of the sclera and xanthelasma of bilateral medial lower eyelids. Neurological examination demonstrated left facial weakness, decreased strength (4 of 5) of left upper and lower extremities, and decreased rapid repetitive movement with ataxic finger-to-nose testing on the left side. Laboratory tests showed elevated aspartate aminotransferase (AST) (93 IU/L), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) (115 IU/L), total bilirubin (10.4 mg/dL), direct bilirubin (5.0 mg/dL), and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) (838 IU/L). Computed tomography (CT) of the head and subsequent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain both revealed acute thalamic infarction of the right side with no evidence of hemorrhagic stroke. Ultrasonography of the abdomen showed mild splenomegaly with no evidence of gallstones or biliary dilatation. CT of the abdomen showed no evidence of biliary obstruction or active hepatocellular disease except incidentally found hepatic hemangioma. The patient was admitted to the hospital and started on aspirin 81 mg and rosuvastatin 20 mg for acute thalamic stroke management. Bilateral carotid duplex test showed 1%-19% stenosis of left proximal internal carotid artery (ICA) and right bulb, but no stenosis in right ICA or left bulb. Echocardiogram showed no evidence of intracardiac shunts. The patient's neurological symptoms subsequently resolved with minimal residual deficits. Further workup was performed for hepatic manifestations. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography showed patent intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts including common bile duct with no evidence of focal stricture or filling defect.
test_results: Antimitochondrial antibody titer was high at >1:320.

case_report: A 46-year-old Japanese man was admitted to our hospital for evaluation as a candidate for LDLT. On admission, the model for end-stage liver disease (MELD) score was 20, and the updated Mayo risk score was 11.3. The patient’s younger sister, aged 43 years, was the only living donor candidate. Her height and body weight were 153 cm and 57 kg, respectively.
test_results: Multidetector row CT was employed for preoperative dynamic CT. The predicted left liver graft volume with the middle hepatic vein (MHV) was 403 mL. 3D CT angiography was performed twice but could not reveal the anatomical structure of the left and middle hepatic arteries (LHA and MHA) in either case. The degree of contrast enhancement was quantified by measuring HU values by positioning the region of interest at the aorta, right hepatic artery (RHA), umbilical portion of the portal vein, and anatomical structures, such as the LHA or MHA, which were 363.9 ± 21.1, 304.1 ± 20.4, 123.8 ± 24.0, and 148.8 ± 26.8 HU, respectively. Because CT numbers of anatomical structures, such as the LHA or MHA, were much lower than those of the aorta or the RHA and were comparable to those of the surrounding umbilical portion of the portal vein, the LHA and MHA were deleted in the process of constructing the image of 3D CT angiography. Conventional angiography was performed, which demonstrated that A2, A3, and A4 individually originated from the PHA. Each branch was approximately 1 mm in diameter.

case_report: At the initial consultation, the patient was a 25-year-old first-time pregnant woman at 22 weeks and 4 days of gestation. The pregnancy had been mostly uneventful except for findings on antenatal anatomy scans. Ultrasounds showed a fetus with both kidneys enlarged and echogenic, multiple cysts within the kidney tissue, absence of amniotic fluid, and a non-visible bladder. Prenatal screening for Trisomy 21 and Trisomy 18 was negative. A three-generation family history was taken, revealing German and Scottish ancestry for the patient and Irish and English ancestry for her partner, with no known consanguinity or congenital anomalies. Due to the poor prognosis for the fetus, labor was induced for therapeutic termination of pregnancy. A male stillborn fetus was delivered at 22 weeks and 5 days of gestation. External examination and autopsy were conducted. The fetus exhibited facial features consistent with Potter sequence, a high-arched palate, and maxillary hypoplasia, with no orofacial clefting. Severe elbow contractures and bilateral elbow pterygia were noted. The left hand had post-axial polydactyly (six digits) and full cutaneous syndactyly between the second and third, and fourth and fifth digits. The right hand had partial syndactyly between the third and fourth digits. No polydactyly or syndactyly was observed in the toes. Bilateral clubfeet could not be excluded, considering positional changes. The skin examination was consistent with the gestational age and otherwise unremarkable. Autopsy confirmed pulmonary hypoplasia and bilaterally enlarged kidneys with multicystic renal cortical dysplasia. The right kidney weighed 8 g, and the left weighed 5 g, with a combined weight of 13 g (age-related norm: 4.77 ± 1.39 g). The cysts were disorganized, varied in shape and size, and up to 0.5 cm in diameter, lined by simple cuboidal epithelium with collars of smooth muscle. The ureters and bladder were identified without obvious abnormalities. The testes were intra-abdominal and consistent with the gestational age. A skeletal survey showed no obvious skeletal congenital anomalies beyond the post-axial polydactyly of the left hand.
test_results: This identified a de novo heterozygous pathogenic variant in exon 5 of the TP63 gene: p.His247Arg: c.740A>G (NM_003722.4).

case_report: A 25-year-old female with no known co-morbidities or history of previous illness or trauma presented to the neurosurgery outpatient department. She reported that three months ago, she began experiencing severe left frontal headaches that lasted for hours to days. These headaches were throbbing in nature and not accompanied by nausea, vomiting, dizziness, or seizures. She also experienced episodes of double vision during severe headaches. Over the same period, she noticed her left eye bulging outward with pulsation, which gradually became more pronounced and noticeable over the past month. General physical examination was unremarkable. She was conscious and well-oriented to time, place, and person. Her higher mental functions, gross motor, fine motor, and sensory functions were intact. Local examination of the left eye revealed non-axial pulsatile proptosis with outward displacement of the left eyeball. Visual acuity assessment showed emmetropia with diplopia in the left eye. Ocular movements in both eyes were normal. There was no tenderness on palpation, but pulsations were felt in the left eye. No bruit was heard on auscultation.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain with contrast study showed deficient bone on left orbital roof and floor with left frontal gliotic brain compressing the eyeball causing it to move out and down. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain and orbit with contrast study showed an asymmetrical deformity of the skull and left cerebral hemisphere which was bulging towards the left orbit, causing extrinsic pressure resulting in proptosis of the eyeball. It also showed widened cortical sulci due to decreased volume. There was indirect evidence of widening of left lateral ventricle and Sylvian fissure due to hemi-atrophic changes. Right orbit, right hemisphere, brainstem, and cerebellum appeared normal. There was no evidence of demyelination or any intracranial mass. The affected orbit was larger and downwards than normal. There was an absence of floor and roof of the left orbit.

case_report: A 60-year-old female with a history of multiple head traumas in her youth, due to falls while horseback riding, but without documented skull fractures. Her medical history includes type two diabetes managed through lifestyle changes and breast cancer treated with surgery in 2002 and chemoradiation in 2003. She initially presented with a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Physical examination revealed a palpable hard protuberance on the right frontal area of the skull. An EEG indicated intermittent low-amplitude polymorphic delta slowing in the right anterior head region, without clear epileptiform discharges. She was administered levetiracetam for seizure prevention. Her neurological examination remained normal, and she did not experience further seizures.
test_results: The computed tomography (CT) of her head demonstrated a 3.7 cm × 3.4 cm × 1.5 cm lytic lesion of the right frontal calvarial bone with the erosion of the inner table. The magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of her brain suggested herniation of the right frontal lobe parenchyma into the bony defect.

case_report: A 59-year-old male was referred to our hospital due to elevated serum creatinine levels found during medical examinations. Renal dysfunction was identified at the age of 59 years, concurrent with the presence of cataract and sensorineural deafness. His family history includes a father who experienced sensorineural deafness starting at the age of 20 years and passed away from cerebral infarction at the age of 84 years. His mother had hypertension beginning at the age of 50 years. Blood and urinary analysis results are documented. A peripheral blood smear revealed thrombocytopenia, giant platelets, and neutrophil inclusion bodies (Döhle-like bodies) using May-Giemsa staining. Immunofluorescence micrographs of neutrophils displayed granular accumulation of NMMHC-IIA in the neutrophils.
test_results: Genetic mutation analysis revealed p.E1084del mutation (c.3250_3252delGAG) in MYH9 exon 24.

case_report: A 56-year-old male was referred to our hospital for the management of chronic kidney disease. At the age of 17 years, he exhibited hematuria and proteinuria. At the age of 30 years, he presented with thrombocytopenia, sensorineural deafness, and cataract. At the age of 56 years, he was referred to our hospital for the management of hypertension and elevated serum creatinine level. His son had thrombocytopenia. His mother passed away from subarachnoid hemorrhage at the age of 61 years, and his younger brother had thrombocytopenia and renal dysfunction.
test_results: In the peripheral blood smear, thrombocytopenia, giant platelets, and neutrophil inclusion bodies (Döhle-like bodies) were observed with May-Giemsa staining. We found a few large NMMHC-IIA aggregates in the neutrophils. Mutational analysis of the MYH9 gene revealed a heterozygous duplication of 21 nucleotides in exon 24 (p.E1066_A1072dup, c.3195_3215dup).

case_report: A 57-year-old man presented with a two-week history of recurrent nausea, lack of appetite, fatigue, and inability to sleep, along with left lower quadrant pain and a feeling of fullness in his mid-abdomen. A colonoscopy revealed a 10 mm polyp in the terminal ileum with slight central umbilication and a 2 mm polyp in the descending colon. The rest of the examination was otherwise normal. Biopsy results were inconclusive, and a CT abdomen-pelvis with contrast was performed for further characterization. Imaging revealed an 8.0 cm partially exophytic left posterior renal mass with central necrosis. The tumor extended centrally into the renal sinus, abutting Gerota's fascia posteriorly and crossing the axial renal midline. A 2.0 cm exophytic right upper pole renal mass located above the upper polar line was also found. There was a concern for metastasis into the adrenals bilaterally due to the presence of adrenal nodules, with the left being 1.4 cm and the right being 2.8 cm. The patient was referred to a regional comprehensive cancer care center, where he was scheduled for a robotically assisted right partial nephrectomy and possible right adrenalectomy. In the interim, the patient was worked up by urology and found to have an elevated plasma norepinephrine of 1266 pg/ml. As a result, the adrenal biopsy was canceled, and the patient progressed to the planned resection of the adrenal mass. The patient was started on doxazosin 6 mg PO QD for the alpha blockade, and the surgery timeline was pushed forward. An evaluation of Von Hippel Lindau was negative, including an MRI and genetic testing. The operation was successfully completed. A 2.3 x 1.7 x 1.7 cm mass was removed from the right kidney, whose histologic analysis confirmed the diagnosis of renal clear cell carcinoma. Staging of the cancer was initially designated as pT1a pNX pM1 with suspected metastasis into the ipsilateral adrenal gland. The tumor was staged as pT1a because it appeared to be confined to the kidney with no contiguous direct extension into the ipsilateral adrenal gland, despite apparent metastatic involvement. The right adrenal gland was not entirely removed, targeting only the mass. However, by that point, it had made up a sizable portion of the adrenal gland, and following mass resection and hemostasis, not much viable gland was left. Immunostaining of the right adrenal mass was inconclusive but seemed to be more indicative of a RCC metastasis rather than a pheochromocytoma. The final staging of the right tumor was pT4 pNX pM0. The operation had no complications, and the patient was discharged home after a couple of days of inpatient observation following surgery. Based on the staging and prognosis of his bilateral RCC with suspected metastases, this patient was enrolled in a pembrolizumab study receiving treatment every three weeks. His course was complicated by cytokine release syndrome. A month and a half later, outpatient follow-up lab work revealed a further elevated plasma norepinephrine level of 1710 pg/mL. A month after this, his planned left nephrectomy was canceled in lieu of a recent syncopal episode with anosmia, acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 3 with creatinine, and vision loss. Nephrology consultation attributed recent symptoms to possible adrenal insufficiency with renal hypoperfusion complicated by iatrogenic alpha blockade and catecholamine-induced volume contraction. Despite this, a meta-iodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scan and metanephrine analysis were negative for pheochromocytoma. The patient markedly improved following excess antihypertensive removal and rehydration. Two weeks later, the patient underwent a laparoscopic left radical nephrectomy and adrenalectomy. Final histopathology showed clear cell renal carcinoma without adrenal extension and no significant abnormalities in the ipsilateral adrenal gland, staged at pT1b pNX pM0 pR0. Due to final pathology reports not indicating pheochromocytoma in either adrenal gland, the prior elevations of plasma norepinephrine were attributed to the patient's use of venlafaxine for depression. Due to the functional BA, the patient now had adrenal insufficiency. During his hospitalization, the patient received IV hydrocortisone 50 mg three times per day and oral fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily. He was hospitalized for seven days. The patient recovered well with intermittent nausea, pain, and an increase in creatinine which did return to baseline. At discharge, the patient continued 137 mcg of levothyroxine for his hypothyroidism and started on oral hydrocortisone 25 mg daily and fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily. Given decreased renal mass, the patient was counseled on the importance of nephrology follow-up. The patient was also referred to endocrinology for continued management of his adrenal insufficiency. A few days after discharge, the patient followed up with endocrinology. The endocrinologist determined that the patient was taking adequate doses of hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. The patient was educated on the possible side effects of steroid overdose and on increasing his hydrocortisone to 2-3 daily doses for 3-5 days in case of illness. The patient was also given injectable steroids if unable to tolerate oral medication. The patient was scheduled to return in one month. Shortly after the appointment, the patient fell ill, complaining of diarrhea. He was advised to increase his dose of hydrocortisone for 3-5 days, hold and subsequently decrease the dose of levothyroxine from 137 mcg to 112 mcg daily. At the follow-up one month later, the patient reported he had been feeling unwell for one week. He was experiencing back pain, generalized weakness, orthostatic hypotension, and decreased urinary output. He continued to take his medicines correctly, not missing any doses, and kept his pills down with no nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. The increased hydrocortisone dose was reported to be helpful. Two months later, the patient presented with weight gain and fluid retention. His hydrocortisone dose was decreased to 20 mg daily, and the patient was advised to decrease the fludrocortisone dose to half of a 0.1 mg tablet daily should swelling reoccur. On subsequent visits, the patient's hydrocortisone replacement was considered adequate, and the patient's adrenal insufficiency remained stable. Two years later, the patient's labs were notable for elevated ACTH at 796 pg/mL. Eight months after the initial finding of elevated ACTH levels, the patient presented with hyperpigmentation on both hands, darkening on the knuckles and palmar creases, and elevated ACTH at 696 pg/mL. Due to the patient's low BP and no weight loss, the patient's adrenal replacement regimen was left unchanged. In that interim, the patient had been compliant with his adrenal replacement, and his condition was well controlled.
test_results: The results of the imaging were unremarkable for any pituitary tumor.

case_report: A 58-year-old Asian female visited an outpatient endocrinology clinic with pronounced hyperpigmentation on her face and neck. She had a history of an ACTH-secreting pituitary macroadenoma, which was surgically removed via transsphenoidal resection eight years prior. Post-surgery, residual tumor tissue was noted to extend into the right cavernous sinus, and she underwent two radiation therapy sessions to address this. Microscopic examination of the specimens, including immunostaining, showed positive ACTH and focally positive prolactin. About a year after surgery, she began to notice hyperpigmentation on her face and neck, which progressively worsened over the following eight years. Despite consulting multiple dermatologists and using various prescribed topical steroid creams, there was no improvement in her hyperpigmentation. Apart from the visible hyperpigmentation, she did not exhibit other symptoms commonly associated with adrenal insufficiency, such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, muscle pain, joint pain, or weight loss. Her physical examination was otherwise normal, and her electrolytes were within the normal range. Most of her laboratory results were normal, but she had elevated ACTH levels and low-normal AM cortisol levels.
test_results: The MRI results showed stable post-surgical changes with stable residual enhancing soft tissue along the right aspect of the sella extending into the cavernous sinus.

case_report: A 44-year-old man with no significant medical history reported an 8-year history of a painless nodule on the sole of his right foot. Over the past 6 months, he experienced discomfort while walking. Physical examination revealed subcutaneous nodules on the medial side of the plantar surface of the right foot. There was no family history of similar conditions. The patient was not on any medication and was otherwise in good health. Vital signs and laboratory tests were within normal limits.
test_results: An ultrasound of the plantar arch showed a hypoechoic and homogeneous nodule of the plantar fascia with increased color Doppler flow. MRI of the foot confirmed the ultrasound data, showing a hyperintense nodule on proton density images which was hypointense on T1-weighted images, at the distal part of the superficial medial plantar fascia. The lesion was intensely enhanced after injection of Gadolinium. Histological examination of the nodule demonstrated increased fibroblastic activity and a reduction of the collagen network.

case_report: A 77-year-old woman was transferred to our hospital for the management of congestive heart failure. She had experienced prolonged general malaise, loss of appetite, loss of concentration, and insomnia over the previous 4 months, leading to an inability to walk and subsequent admission to a psychiatric hospital. She was given clomipramine for 2 days without effect. Her plasma sodium level was 125 mEq/dL, and her brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) level was elevated. She was diagnosed with congestive heart failure at the psychiatric hospital and referred to our institution. She had no history of traumatic brain injury, cerebrovascular diseases, steroid use, or diuretic use. Upon admission, her vital signs were: blood pressure, 123/73 mmHg; heart rate, 101 beats/min; body temperature, 36.2°C; respiratory rate, 18 breaths/min; and SpO2, 99% on room air. She was disoriented, had a feeble voice, was thin, had joint contractures, and was unable to ambulate. She exhibited pitting edema in both legs. Peripheral blood tests revealed mild to low levels of red blood cells (480 × 10^4/μL). Biochemical analysis showed low levels of albumin (2.5 g/dL), sodium (119 mEq/L), and chloride (88 mEq/L), with high levels of C-reactive protein (2.21 mg/dL) and BNP (610 pg/mL). Hyperkalemia, eosinophilia, and hypoglycemia were absent. Plasma osmolality was 243 mosm/kg. TSH level was slightly high (5.6 mIU/L), but F-T4 was normal. Urine tests showed high osmolality (330 mosm/kg) and sodium level (114 mEq/L). Serum vitamin B1 level was normal. Chest radiograph indicated cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio of 60%) and pleural effusion. Electrocardiogram showed inverted T waves in leads II, III, aVF, and V4-6. Echocardiography revealed diffuse hypokinesis of the left ventricular wall and slight pericardial effusion, with no valvular abnormalities. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) showed bilateral pleural effusion and chronic cholecystitis, with no other significant findings. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain, particularly the pituitary gland, showed no abnormalities. Initial treatment included compensation for hyponatremia with 3% saline and enteral feeding. Due to the absence of congestion and dyspnea, diuretics and oxygen were not administered. Three days post-admission, the patient developed a fever of unknown origin. Despite a week-long course of antibiotics (CTRX 2 g/day), the fever persisted without an identifiable cause.
test_results: ACTH and cortisol levels were low (<2.0 pg/mL and 2.9 μg/dL, respectively). Her urinary free cortisol level was low. Neither ACTH nor cortisol levels adequately increased in response to administration of corticotropin-releasing hormone. However, the cortisol level increased in response to administration of ACTH.
diagnosis: Secondary adrenal insufficiency caused by isolated ACTH deficiency

case_report: A 15-year-old female presented with progressive pulsatile exophthalmus and dystopia in the right eye, which began at an early age. At age 4, she underwent trabeculectomy on the right eye for congenital glaucoma. She had no history of chronic disease or trauma. No congenital or acquired patches or rashes were observed on her skin. Her family history was negative for genetic diseases.
test_results: A large hypoplasic bone defect of 20.6×30.7 mm (35.8 cm2) was observed in the superior orbital fissure of the greater wing of the right sphenoid bone. The anterior-posterior diameter of the right bulbus oculi, which measured 27.9 mm, was relatively larger than the anterior-posterior diameter of the left bulbus oculi, which measured 22 mm; the distance between the two medial canthi, which measured 33.1 mm, was increased, and the right bulbus oculi was seen to have been displaced to the inferior by 5.9 mm. The right orbita was markedly exophthalmic. The T1- and T2-weighted images obtained on MRI showed the left temporal lobe, with the subarachnoid membrane extending into the orbita through the defect.

case_report: A 10-year-old Chinese girl was admitted to our hospital for severe pain along with shortening and deformity of the right leg. Five years prior, at the age of 5, the patient visited our hospital due to limping and mild pain in her right thigh, which intensified with stretching or touch.
test_results: Radiographs revealed multiple lytic lesions in the proximal part of the right humerus, distal part of the right clavicle, proximal and distal parts of the right femur, and proximal parts of the right tibia and fibula. Histopathological examination showed spindle-shaped fibroblastic and collagenous stromal tissue, characteristic of the NOF.

case_report: A 20-year-old female patient presented with primary complaints of low-grade fever and whitish cloudy urine. She did not report loin pain, painful urination, increased frequency of urination, swelling of feet, facial puffiness, or any bleeding issues. The patient was of average build and nourishment. Physical examination showed no lymph node enlargement or swelling of the feet. Laboratory tests indicated hemoglobin at 13.6 gm%, total white blood cell count at 7400/mm3, with neutrophils at 31%, lymphocytes at 22%, and a significant eosinophil count at 43%. Urine analysis revealed no casts, dysmorphic red blood cells, white blood cells, or malignant cells. Urine triglyceride level was 200 mg/dL, consistent with chyluria. The 24-hour urinary protein level was within normal limits, and urine culture results were sterile.
test_results: Ultrasonography of abdomen showed complex multiloculated cystic lesions in bilateral adenexal mass along with an incidental finding of a left-sided dermoid cyst. The cystic lesions showed the characteristic 'dancing larvae sign'. Contrast-enhanced computerized tomography (CT) showed rind of nonenhancing, cystic lesions around the aorta, inferior vena cava, renal artery, and proximal iliac vessels likely representing dilated lymphatic channels. A large, nonenhancing, complex cystic pelvic mass was seen involving bilateral adenexal mass and a dermoid cyst on the left side. The mass was encasing the ureters. However, there was no hydronephrosis. The aorta and the inferior vena-cava were encased without luminal compromise.
diagnosis: bilateral tubo-ovarian filariasis with retroperitoneal extension

case_report: A 60-year-old Moroccan male with a history of well-controlled hypertension visited our cardiology department for a routine evaluation. The patient reported no chest pain, fatigue, or difficulty breathing. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 130/60 mmHg, a heart rate of 80 bpm, a respiratory rate of 16 cpm, an oxygen saturation of 97%, and no detectable heart murmur.
test_results: Echocardiography revealed modest connectivity between the ascending aorta and the right side of the pulmonary trunk of about 4 mm in width, with a left-to-right shunt on color Doppler. The left atrium, right, and left ventricles, as well as the pulmonary trunk, were all mildly dilated. Mild regurgitation of the mitral and tricuspid valves was also detected. There was a little reduction in left chamber function. There was echocardiographic evidence of an intermediate probability of pulmonary hypertension (PH) and preserved right ventricular function.

case_report: The patient is a 16-year-old female (height: 1.58 m, weight: 41.7 kg) who recently received her first infusion of infliximab two days ago. She was admitted to the gastroenterology service due to severe abdominal pain that started that morning. The patient also experienced severe nausea, making it difficult for her to tolerate oral intake.
test_results: The grayscale US demonstrated a narrowing of the terminal ileum, with a thickened submucosal layer and decreased peristalsis. Contrast US showed avid contrast enhancement of the narrowed terminal ileum. Quantitative evaluation of the terminal ileum, compared to the jejunum as an internal control, demonstrated more prompt wash-in, higher peak intensity, and higher area under the curve. Average elastography value of the terminal ileum was 0.64 m/s. MRE demonstrated wall thickening and inflammation in the terminal ileum, resulting in narrowing and proximal dilation in the distal ileal segments. Adjacent to the terminal ileum, there was mesenteric inflammation as evidenced by contrast enhancement.

case_report: A 28-year-old African American male with no history of smoking presented with severe HS. Initial treatment included topical and systemic antibiotics, but the condition progressed to affect the axillary, groin, and back of the neck, necessitating surgical excision and skin grafting. During hospitalization, laboratory tests revealed iron deficiency anemia with a hemoglobin level of 9 g/dL. The patient also reported experiencing episodes of diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and blood in his stools. Following discharge, the patient was referred to gastroenterology.
test_results: A colonoscopy revealed mucosal edema and inflammation with skip ulcerations throughout the colon. Pathology reports showed focal ulceration with evidence of chronic inflammation.

case_report: In August 2019, a 22-year-old Chinese woman, born to consanguineous parents, experienced generalized tonic-clonic seizures (GTCS). Her early physical and intellectual development was typical, and there was no relevant family medical history. Initial treatment for GTCS was administered at a local hospital. The patient later discontinued several anti-seizure medications, including valproate, clonazepam, and oxcarbazepine. Her family observed reduced responsiveness to external stimuli and decreased speech production and fluidity. The patient exhibited childlike behavior without clear cause and developed action- or posture-induced myoclonus affecting the trunk and extremities, especially the legs. She also reported difficulty walking and intolerance to physical exercise. By January 2020, she experienced multiple GTCS episodes, which decreased in frequency after starting levetiracetam and lamotrigine. She was referred to our hospital in October 2021 for further evaluation. Upon admission, physical examination revealed horizontal nystagmus, mild dysarthria, gait ataxia, hypotonia, hyperreflexia in all limbs, bilateral pyramidal signs, and pes cavus. The finger-to-nose and rapid alternating movement tests were abnormal. Involuntary shaking-like movements were noted in her head and limbs while walking or standing. Her orientation in space and time was normal, but attention, calculation, and comprehension were impaired. She did not cooperate during sensory testing. Laboratory tests and cerebrospinal fluid evaluation were normal, including screening for autoimmune encephalitis and paraneoplastic syndromes-related antibodies. Ultrasound examination showed no visceromegaly or evident masses. Optical coherence tomography fundus images were normal. Nerve conduction studies indicated reduced motor nerve conduction velocity, decreased compound muscle action potential amplitude of median nerves, and reduced sensory conduction velocity of peroneal and sural nerves, suggesting demyelinating peripheral neuropathy. The interictal electroencephalogram (EEG) showed severe generalized slowing waves. Brain MRI revealed a right occipital cortical ribbon sign on T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences, along with global brain atrophy and ventricular enlargement. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) sequences showed no additional abnormalities.
test_results: The whole-exome sequencing (WES) analysis identified pathogenic homozygous missense mutations of the GALC gene, c.1901T>C (p.Leu634Ser). The Sanger sequencing confirmed that these mutations were inherited from her parents. Serum GALC enzyme activity was found to be ~3.3 nmol/17 h/mg protein (normal range > 12.7 nmol/17 h/mg protein).

case_report: A 25-year-old male from China, born to unrelated parents, was presented to the First People’s Hospital of Huizhou city, China. The patient exhibited spastic gait disturbance and vision loss. By the age of 5 years, he experienced mild gait difficulties, characterized by unstable ambulation and frequent falls. Vision loss was noted at the age of 8 years, while cognitive development remained normal. He was born at full term following an uncomplicated delivery. Neurological examination revealed ocular motility disorders, horizontal nystagmus, absence of the left pupillary light reflex, pes cavus, spastic paraparesis in the lower limbs, exaggerated bilateral patellar tendon reflexes, ankle clonus, and a positive Babinski sign. No abnormalities were detected in the finger-to-nose test or sensory function. Laboratory biochemical studies, including full blood count, liver function, plasma electrolytes, thyroid function, vitamin B-12 and folate levels, sex hormone levels, autoantibody profile, and syphilis serology, showed typical results.
test_results: Cerebrospinal fluid tests revealed increased protein (1186 mg/L); the normal value was 140–450 mg/L. The GALC enzymatic activity detected by Bio-Tek FLx 800 fluorescent analyzer in leukocytes was decreased (3.9 nmol/mg/17 h); the normal value was 18–75 nmol/mg/17 h protein. The direct sequencing of the GALC gene (Reference mRNA sequence: NM_000153) in this patient identified a novel missense mutation (c.865G > C: p. G289R) in exon 8 along with a known missense mutation (c.136G > T: p. D46Y) in exon 1. The former mutation was heterozygous in the mother, while the latter was heterozygous in the father. Brain MRI revealed a high-intensity signal in the left central gyrus cortex by fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) as well as T2-weighted images, while a decreased signal in the T1-weighted images and high-intensity lesions in the bilateral corticospinal tracts were detected. Cervical spine and thoracic spine MRI showed mild atrophy of the spinal cord. Electromyography indicated peripheral nerve demyelination, and both visual evoked potentials (VEP) and brainstem auditory evoked potential (BAEP) were normal.

case_report: A 39-year-old Chinese male presented with a 9-year history of progressive weakness in all four limbs. At the age of 30, he initially experienced difficulty holding objects with his right hand. Over time, he developed increasing weakness in his limbs, an unsteady gait, numbness, and mild speech difficulties. He underwent treatments including glucocorticoid pulse therapy, intravenous immunoglobulin, and plasma exchange, but his condition continued to deteriorate. Physical examination revealed muscle strength of 4/5 in the proximal upper and lower extremities and 3/5 in the distal extremities. There was noticeable atrophy in the bilateral interphalangeal muscles, thenar and hypothenar muscles, and the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles. Additional findings included muscle fasciculations, absent deep tendon reflexes, and bilateral positive Babinski signs. The patient's Barthel index score was 85.
test_results: Analysis of CSF showed elevated protein levels of 0.69 g/l but normal cell counts and glucose levels. Oligoclonal bands were negative. The value of arylsulfatase A was 133.97 nmol/17 h/mg (normal range: >58 nmol/17 h/mg). Nerve conduction studies revealed severe motor and sensory demyelinating polyneuropathy associated with axonal damage. The needle EMG showed fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves in the right biceps and tibialis anterior. Wide duration, high amplitude, and polyphasic form were observed in the right biceps during mild voluntary activity, which indicated neuropathy. MRI of the brain showed asymmetric consecutive hyperintensity along bilateral corticospinal tracts (from the precentral gyrus down to the pons on the left and in the level of the centrum semiovale on the right) and in the optic radiation and corpus callosum on T2W and T2W FLAIR images. MRI of the spinal cord revealed inconsecutive lesions with high signal intensity in the cervical cord at C1–C5 on T2W images. WES detected two missense GALC mutations in this patient: c.461C>A (p.P154H) and c.1065G>C (p.W355C).

case_report: A 15-year-old phenotypic female visited the gynecology clinic due to the absence of menstruation. Her medical history included short stature and delayed puberty, with no history of migraines, motor or learning impairments, or surgeries. There was no family history of cancer. Her 9-year-old brother had normal height and cognitive development for his age, while her father was 180 cm tall, and her mother was 145 cm tall. Physical examination revealed a generally normal appearance, with a height of 141 cm and slight breast development (B3). There were no signs such as a short webbed neck, disproportionate body segments, or multiple nevi.
test_results: A chromosomal analysis indicated 45XO/46XY.

case_report: Mr. B, a 68-year-old male with a history of primary B-cell lymphoma diagnosed 15 years ago and two previous relapses, had been in complete remission for 5 months. He presented with a 15-day history of right foot drop, along with paresthesias and numbness along the lateral aspect of the right leg, dorsum, and sole of the right foot. A general examination revealed a single palpable lymph node in the left supraclavicular region. He had been diagnosed with L5-S1 radiculopathy at another center based on MRI findings and was referred to our center for surgery. On examination, he exhibited severe weakness in ankle dorsiflexion (MRC grade 1/5), ankle plantar flexion (2/5), ankle inversion, ankle eversion (2/5), and knee flexion (3/5). The right ankle jerk was absent. All sensory modalities were impaired below the right knee, sparing the medial aspect of the leg. Routine blood investigations were normal except for thrombocytopenia. An electrophysiological work-up indicated sciatic neuropathy.
test_results: Gadolinium-enhanced MRI revealed localized longitudinal thickening of the right sciatic nerve with contrast enhancement in the mid-thigh region. FDG-PET showed intense FDG uptake in the right sciatic nerve in the same region with involvement of bone marrow. A lymph-node biopsy in the left supraclavicular region confirmed high-grade diffuse large-B-cell lymphoma.

case_report: A 48-year-old male patient with a history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia confirmed by flow cytometry was scheduled for six cycles of rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone. Initial imaging showed multiple FDG-avid hypermetabolic lymph nodes in both supra- and infra-diaphragmatic regions. After three cycles of chemotherapy, follow-up imaging on October 5, 2015, indicated a significant reduction in size and metabolic activity of the lymph nodes, categorized as a Category III Deauville score. Following the fifth cycle of chemotherapy, the patient experienced fever, dyspnea on exertion, and prolonged postchemotherapy febrile neutropenia, necessitating hospital admission for treatment. Upon symptom improvement and rising cell counts, the patient was discharged. Ten days later, in March 2016, the patient reported left foot drop.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of spine and pelvis revealed diffuse nodular and thickened nerve roots at L4, L5, S1, and S2 more marked on the left side extending up to greater sciatic foramen. No evident disc herniation, epidural soft tissue, or intrinsic cord abnormality was noted. Similar characteristic findings were seen along left C4 and bilateral C5–C8 nerve roots. Subsequent PET-CT scan revealed moderate-grade FDG avid lymph nodes involving bilateral external iliac regions and low-grade FDG avid lymph nodes in retroperitoneum. Non-FDG avid cervical and mediastinal lymph nodes were noted. There was high-grade FDG avid uptake (maximum standardized uptake value – 12) along the lumbosacral plexus more marked on the left side and along brachial plexus on either side.

case_report: A 61-year-old male presented with severe difficulty swallowing for 3 days. He had a history of hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cervical stenosis with anterior discectomy and fusion from C3 to C6 five months prior, and right-sided facial paralysis four weeks earlier that resolved with oral prednisone. He had a forty-pack-year smoking history and quit four years ago. Clinical examination revealed an inability to swallow and a hoarse voice, with the rest of the cranial nerve exam being normal. Limb strength, sensation, deep tendon reflexes, and coordination were also normal. Mild difficulty with tandem walking was noted. Computed tomography of the neck with contrast showed no structural lesion in the pharynx. A video-fluoroscopic swallow study showed complete paralysis of the right true vocal fold and partial paralysis of the left. Rheumatologic and inflammatory lab workup was normal. CSF analysis showed elevated protein at 86 mg/dL (normal = 15–45 mg/dL) and 1 white blood cell. Infectious screening was negative for cytomegalovirus, enterovirus, herpes simplex virus, West Nile virus, syphilis, and Borrelia burgdorferi DNA. MRI of the brain with gadolinium contrast was unremarkable. Nerve conduction studies, including bilateral nasalis studies and blink reflexes, were normal; electromyography was attempted but not completed due to patient intolerance. The patient received 2 gm/kg IVIG over 5 days. Antibodies to GQ1b, GD1a, GD1b, and GM-1 gangliosides were absent; paraneoplastic antibodies to Hu, Ri, and Yo antigens were negative. No improvement in dysphagia was noted during treatment. A PEG tube was placed, and the patient was discharged to a skilled nursing facility. One month later, his dysphagia had modestly improved, but he reported new hearing loss, vertigo, and left-sided facial weakness. Oral prednisone was administered, and facial weakness resolved. Symptoms gradually improved over six months, allowing the patient to resume a normal diet without the PEG tube. At the next follow-up, the patient reported recurrence of dysphagia, hoarseness, and significantly worsened hearing loss. Repeat MRI of the brain with gadolinium contrast showed a uniformly enhancing 2 cm by 2 cm mass in the left posterior temporal lobe with surrounding vasogenic edema and focal leptomeningeal enhancement. The mass appeared contiguous with the dura and was reported as a meningioma. Additionally, there was enhancement of the bilateral eighth cranial nerves.
test_results: Pathologic evaluation revealed large monomorphous lymphocytes which stained positively for CD10, CD20, and BCL-6 with a proliferation index of >95%. Fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis for cMYC gene rearrangement was within normal limits.

case_report: A 14-year-old male presented with a 4-day history of fever, which began suddenly and remained consistently high at 102°F. The fever was accompanied by chills and rigors and was alleviated by antipyretics. On the third day of fever, the patient experienced acute onset pain in both thigh and calf muscles, which was non-radiating and severe enough to restrict activity. There was no history of abdominal pain, vomiting, or bleeding from mucosal sites. The patient had no prior history of trauma or similar muscle pain. Vital signs were stable with maintained blood pressure and good pulse volume. The patient exhibited mild stunting but had a normal weight for age. General physical examination revealed facial flushing without petechial spots. The chest examination showed clear lungs with equal breath sounds on both sides. The abdomen was soft and non-tender, with the liver just palpable and the spleen not palpable. Neuromuscular examination was notable for slight swelling and tenderness in the calf muscles. Leg movements were painful but preserved throughout the range of motion.
test_results: Serum CPK levels improved from 3908 IU/L to 127 IU/L over 7 days.

case_report: A four-year-old female with no prior medical or surgical history presented to the emergency department with bilateral lower limb pain and difficulty walking without assistance for one day, accompanied by one episode of vomiting. She also had a subjective fever, runny nose, sore throat, and mild cough. Four days before the ED visit, she developed a subjective fever and cold-like symptoms. At a private hospital, her temperature was recorded at 38.5 °C, and she received two doses of intravenous antibiotics and nebulizations of salbutamol and budesonide. The lower limb pain was not associated with joint pain, swelling, or skin rashes. She had decreased oral intake and activity. There was no recent trauma, vigorous exercise, ingestion of contaminated food or medications, or gastrointestinal symptoms. Her family denied any neurological issues or changes in urine frequency, color, or smell. There were no bleeding tendencies or easy bruising. She had traveled one week prior to the ED visit and had a family history of a recent upper respiratory tract infection. There was no known contact with COVID-19 patients. She was vaccinated up to the age of two, had no known allergies, and followed a regular diet. Her parents are second-degree relatives with no chronic diseases in the family. She has five healthy siblings and appropriate developmental milestones for her age, attending kindergarten. Upon arrival at the ED, her vital signs were stable: blood pressure 111/67 mmHg, heart rate 136 beats per minute, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, temperature 38.4 °C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. She was fully conscious with no respiratory distress or marked discoloration. Mild dehydration was noted, and her chest examination revealed clear lungs. She was well and alert, with no cyanosis, pallor, or jaundice. Intravenous fluids were administered due to mild dehydration. The HEENT assessment showed normal ears without tympanic membrane redness, throat congestion without exudate or pus, and no lymphadenopathy. Neuromuscular examination showed normal activity and full range of motion in all limbs, normal muscle tone and power, intact deep tendon reflexes, and no sensory or motor deficits. Meningeal signs were negative, and all cranial nerves were intact. During gait assessment, she refused to walk independently but could bear weight and took a few steps with assistance. The Gower sign was negative. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds (S1+S2), intact peripheral pulses, and a capillary refill time of less than two seconds. Chest examination showed equal bilateral air entry without adventitious sounds. Gastrointestinal assessment revealed a soft, non-distended abdomen with no splenomegaly or organomegaly.
test_results: The respiratory virus panel confirmed a positive result for influenza A virus and negative results for COVID-19, influenza B virus, and respiratory syncytial virus.
diagnosis: Viral Myositis Secondary to Influenza A

case_report: A 26-year-old male began experiencing excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) and occasional partial episodes of muscle weakness at the age of 13. At 15 years old, he visited our Sleep Medicine Center (Clinical Neurology Unit, Udine University Hospital, Italy) with an uncontrollable urge to sleep, reflected by an Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) score of 14. He also reported infrequent partial episodes of muscle weakness, characterized by facial muscle sagging and head drooping triggered by emotions, each lasting a few seconds.
test_results: The patient showed a sleep latency of 6.0 minutes with a Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep latency of 1.0 minute. The MSLT revealed a mean sleep latency of 3.2 minutes and Sleep Onset Rapid Eye Movement Periods (SOREMPs) in five tests out of five. He tested positive for HLA-DQB1*0602.

case_report: The patient is a 17-year-old male who presented to the Neurology outpatient service with complaints of recurrent falls and brief alterations in consciousness. These symptoms began two years prior, following an episode witnessed by his university roommate where he experienced a brief loss of consciousness lasting less than a minute. The episodes were characterized by head drops, occasional squat drops, and drop attacks, but the patient denied losing consciousness, describing a sensation of weakness instead. He reported a feeling of heaviness or tingling in his head before the falls. There were no associated symptoms of vision loss, tonic-clonic movements, or bladder/bowel incontinence. There was no personal or family history of epilepsy or cardiac conditions. He had been previously treated for juvenile absence epilepsy with anti-seizure medications, but his symptoms persisted. Further details revealed that the episodes were related to emotional situations such as laughter, excitement, and pleasant surprises. The patient also reported excessive daytime sleepiness despite adequate night-time sleep, often dozing off during monotonous activities but staying awake when engaged in enjoyable activities. He experienced sleep paralysis and weight gain starting three years prior but had no other sleep-related symptoms such as snoring, intermittent awakenings, hallucinations, or behaviors suggestive of REM sleep behavioral disorder. There were no symptoms of sustained weakness, double vision, imbalance, facial sensory deficits, dysphagia, voice changes, skin lesions, cough, fever, breathlessness, or nausea. There was no history of depression, hypothyroidism, or substance use disorder, and no family history of sleep disorders. The patient had a history of degenerative myopia, anisometropia, and left exotropia managed with corrective lenses since age five, as well as a mild speech impediment and limb length discrepancy. Physical examination and mental status examination were unremarkable, though the patient expressed some distress due to his symptoms. Routine investigations, including complete blood count, random blood glucose, malaria parasite screen, and serum electrolytes, were normal. An electroencephalogram (EEG) showed no abnormalities, and a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan also revealed no abnormalities. The patient was admitted for an adapted multiple sleep latency test and/or event monitoring. He was instructed to ensure at least six hours of sleep per night for three days prior to the test. Using a routine EEG machine in a controlled environment, sleep latency was defined as the time from lights out to sleep onset, with sleep onset marked by specific EEG changes. After four sleep trials, a mean sleep latency of 6 minutes 39 seconds was recorded, with individual latencies of 2 minutes 2 seconds, 1 minute 45 seconds, 20 minutes, and 2 minutes 49 seconds.
test_results: The result came out weeks later as <30 pg/mL.

case_report: A previously healthy, three-year-old Kuwaiti girl with no familial history of autoimmune bullous diseases presented with itchy, ring-shaped vesicular lesions that began appearing four months prior. Physical examination revealed ring-shaped, red plaques and vesicles on both forearms and legs. Nikolsky's sign was negative. There was no involvement of the nails or mucous membranes. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable.
test_results: Histopathological analysis of a forearm skin biopsy revealed epidermal acanthosis, marked spongiosis, and numerous intra-epidermal blisters. The blister cavity contained eosinophils and neutrophils. A superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, accompanied by eosinophils and neutrophils, was also observed in the dermis. Through direct immunofluorescence, intercellular IgG deposits were observed within the epidermis of the lesional skin. The substrate for indirect immunofluorescence, the monkey oesophagus, demonstrated intercellular binding of IgG antibodies. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays for desmoglein 1 and desmoglein 3 were negative.

case_report: A 35-year-old male presented with widespread small itchy blisters that started 7 months ago. Initial outpatient evaluation labeled the lesions as eczema, but the treatment provided did not yield improvement. Ten months before the onset of these symptoms, the patient had surgery for a thymic tumor, which was identified during a routine annual check-up. Pre-surgery blood counts showed normal lymphocyte counts and proportions. The tumor was classified as a type AB thymoma according to the WHO classification. Physical examination showed a negative Nikolsky's sign, and serum tests did not detect antibodies to Dsg or bullous pemphigoid.
test_results: Pathology results described the formation of blisters in the epidermis as well as a large number of neutrophils in the blisters. Lymphocytes, neutrophils, and eosinophils had also infiltrated the superficial dermis. Immunofluorescent revealed the intercellular staining of IgG (++), IgA (+), and C3 (±) among epidermal spinous cells.

case_report: A 58-year-old male with a history of hepatitis C presented with an arterial enhancing mass in the right lobe of the liver, identified on CT imaging. The mass measured approximately 6 × 8 cm in the longest cross-sectional diameter and was located in liver segments 7/8. There was also evidence of branch portal vein thrombosis.
