Laboratory results showed elevated alpha fetoprotein levels. The patient was considered for Y-90 SIRT using SIR-Spheres®. Biochemical tests indicated underlying liver dysfunction with the following values: albumin at 29 G/L, bilirubin at 26 umol/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 164 U/L, alanine transaminase (ALT) at 57 U/L, and prothrombin time (PT) at 12.1 seconds. These values were within acceptable limits for Y-90 SIRT.
test_results: A 58-year-old gentleman with a history of hepatitis C was detected to have an asymptomatic arterial enhancing right liver lobe mass on CT imaging, measuring approximately 6 × 8 cm in the longest cross-sectional diameter in liver segments 7/8, with evidence of branch portal vein thrombosis. His alpha fetoprotein levels were elevated as well. The CT angiogram demonstrated good vascular blush in liver segments 7/8, corresponding to the tumor seen on prior CT imaging. However, subsequent portal venous enhancement was noted, indicating hepatic arterial-portal venous shunting. SPECT/CT imaging revealed minimal accumulation of MAA in the tumor in liver segment 7/8, with conversely more intense tracer localization in the surrounding liver parenchyma, resulting in an ‘inverse’-type localization of microspheres within the liver. Based on the findings of the Tc99m-MAA SPECT/CT, the calculated TNR by partition dosimetry model was 0.18 with a liver lung shunting value of 19%. With a calculated dose limit to the normal liver parenchyma of 70 Gy, the radiation dose to the tumor was 36 Gy and to the lung was 15Gy.
diagnosis: Hepatocellular Carcinoma with Hepatic Arterial-Portal Venous Shunting

case_report: In February 2019, a 56-year-old male presented with a 2-month history of dull upper abdominal pain, without abdominal distention, nausea, vomiting, or any preceding event. Initial computed tomography (CT) at a local hospital indicated an infectious hepatic lesion in the hepatic V segment. The pain persisted despite antibiotic therapy, leading to further evaluation at our hospital. The patient was admitted with a space-occupying lesion of the liver. His medical history includes Hepatitis B for 1 year, managed with Lamivudine, 1 tablet daily. There is no family history of liver-related conditions. Physical examination revealed abdominal tenderness without rebound tenderness, muscular tension, nausea, vomiting, or fever. There were no signs of weight loss, cough, jaundice, pruritus, or cholangitis. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell (WBC) count of 10.1∗10^3/μl with 74% neutrophils, ALT 61 U/L, AST 63 U/L, ALP 176 U/L, and serum total bilirubin 18.2 μmol/L. Tumor markers were within normal limits except for an SCCA level of 1.8 ng/mL. Urinary routine and microscopy were normal, and blood cultures were sterile. HBsAg and HBeAb were positive. Ultrasound (US) revealed a hypoechoic lesion measuring 5.1 by 4.0 cm in the hepatic V segment with a thick, irregular, and shaggy margin. There was no intrahepatic biliary radical dilatation, and the common bile duct appeared normal. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) showed an irregular, thick circular hyper-enhancement with no enhancement in the inner lesion during the arterial phase, and washout of the surrounding tissue in the early portal phase with hypo-enhancement in the venous phase. Enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated significant enhancement of the irregular margin with no enhancement of the central cystic necrosis. The portal venous phase showed decreased enhancement.
test_results: US-guided biopsy was performed (2019.2.22) and revealed hepatic coagulative necrosis and pseudolobuli formation with lobular fibrous tissue hyperplasia and ductular proliferation. Lab values were as follows: WBC 12.3∗103/μl with 79% neutrophils and a total serum bilirubin 23.2 μmol/L. The second diagnostic biopsy was performed alongside a liver abscess drainage (2019.2.26). CEUS-guided biopsy from the enhanced wall of the lesion and drainage from the abscess cavity revealed a thick, purulent material. A culture of the abscess was sterile and cytology revealed abundant pus only. Pathology studies showed fibrous tissue proliferation with focal acute, and chronic inflammatory invasion with small ductular proliferation and a section of atypical tissue. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) expressed Vimentin with a population of fibroblasts. A third US-guided diagnostic biopsy was suggested (2019.3.28) and the following pathological diagnosis showed a poorly differentiated carcinoma with an IHC positive for cytokeratin (AE1/AE3) and vimentin (2019.4.17).

case_report: A 38-year-old male patient presented with a long-standing history of multiple non-tender scalp swellings ranging from 2.5 to 3.5 cm in diameter, which have progressively grown over the past year. The skin over the swellings appeared normal. Clinical examination showed multiple nodular lesions coalesced on the anterior region of the scalp, which were solid and movable from the underlying surface. Routine blood investigations were within normal limits. Excisional removal was planned under general anesthesia followed by primary closure.
test_results: The excised specimen showed lobules of epithelial cells arranged in a jigsaw or mosaic pattern. Prominent red basement membrane-like structure encircles the tumor lobules. Each lobule shows a peripheral lining by dark basaloid cells and an inner larger and paler zone of cells.

case_report: A 32-year-old woman presented with multiple asymptomatic swellings on the scalp, face, neck, legs, and chest, progressively increasing in size and number over the past 12 years. Similar lesions were reported in her family, including her mother, aunt, cousins, grandfather, and elder child. Physical examination revealed multiple, rounded, smooth-surfaced, firm, non-tender, skin-colored to reddish papules and nodules of varying sizes on the scalp and face, extending to the nose, arms, and legs. Examination of mucosa, nails, and hair showed no abnormalities. Laboratory investigations were within normal limits. Computed tomography of the brain showed multiple lobulated masses on the scalp and face, which could represent neoplastic or inflammatory pathology.
test_results: The susceptibility locus has been mapped to chromosome 16q12-q13. The most distinctive feature in the aspirated material was the homogenous hyaline globules stained purple with MGG. These globules were surrounded by cohesive benign epithelial cells with dark uniform nuclei. The background was clean and no mitosis was noticed. On gross examination, the lesion was nodular with irregular surface. Cut surface was solid and homogenously grey white. Histopathologically, the lesion consisted of well-circumscribed islands of epithelial cells surrounded by a dense membrane material, and focally containing hyaline globules. Islands of epithelial cells fit together like pieces of “jig-saw” puzzle. Two distinct cell populations were seen; smaller peripheral basaloid cells in palisade arrangement and larger central cells with vesicular chromatin.

case_report: A 78-year-old male presented with a pinkish multi-nodular mass on his frontal scalp, which had been present for several decades. The lesion recurred twice following incomplete surgical excision. There was no family history of similar conditions, no history of trauma, and no current medical history. The patient initially declined further treatment due to economic reasons. After one year, the mass had grown to 5.0 cm × 2.5 cm, and the patient expressed willingness to undergo surgery.
test_results: Skin biopsy demonstrated a homogeneous basaloid cell nest arranged in a jigsaw pattern, composed of central cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and peripheral cells with basophilic nuclei and scant cytoplasm. Histopathologically, the upper dermis of the main tumor mass was similar to that seen in the initial biopsy. However, the lower dermis and periosteal layer had some stromal infiltration of cell nests with a loss of the jigsaw pattern. In high magnification images, atypical cells with mitosis, apoptosis, and hyperchromatic nucleoli were identified. The Ki-67 index increased to 10%~30%. These stains were positive for p63 and Bcl-2, focally positive for C-kit and epithelial membrane antigen, and negative for carcinoembryonic antigen.

case_report: A 7-year-old boy began experiencing seizures at 4 months old. These episodes occurred approximately 30 times per week and were not addressed with treatment until he was 2 years old. The seizures, characterized by sudden, uncontrollable laughter, typically lasted between 10 to 30 seconds. Initial treatment included Topamax 100mg/day and Depakine 500 mg/day at a provincial General Hospital, but there was no noticeable improvement. Despite being evaluated and treated at various hospitals, the episodes persisted. The boy developed normally without any sexual or behavioral issues. In 2015, during his first visit to the Department of Neurosurgery at Viet Duc Hospital, the episodes were re-evaluated and recorded on camera. The laughter was observed to be accompanied by a generalized seizure and brief unconsciousness lasting less than 1 minute.
test_results: The 17-channel scalp-EEG (multiple recordings) revealed paroxysmal sharp waves spreading over both hemispheres. Brain MRI 1.5 Tesla (coronal and sagittal sequences) revealed a small lesion measuring 12*14*8 mm located on the right of the third ventricle, attached to mammillary nuclear and between tuber cinereum and optic chiasma. It was isointense with grey matter, hypointense on T1, and non-enhancing on sagittal T1W after Gadolinium and lightly hyperintense on T2W.

case_report: A 30-year-old female presented with a large, firm lump in the upper quadrant of the right breast, which had been present for 4 years and gradually increasing in size, accompanied by pain. The mass measured 10×10 cm and was fixed to the underlying structures. The overlying skin appeared normal, and the nipple was not retracted. No axillary lymph nodes were palpable.
test_results: Smears showed abundant pink mucoid material. There were numerous moderately pleomorphic epithelial cells lying either discretely forming loose clusters or entrapped within stromal material. At places, the cells were forming tubular structures. Mitotic figures were also seen.

case_report: A 71-year-old Caucasian female visited the breast clinic due to a painless growth on her right nipple that had been present for six weeks. She reported no itchiness, discharge, or bleeding from the growth and had no other breast-related symptoms. Her medical history included severe osteoarthritis affecting her joints, including her shoulders. She had no previous breast issues and no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. She was nulliparous and did not consume alcohol. On examination, a polypoid hemispherical growth measuring 40 by 25 mm was observed on her right nipple, characterized by a highly vascular appearance and a necrotic slough-covered surface. Additionally, a firm lump measuring 25 by 25 mm was detected in the lower outer quadrant of her right breast at the 8 o'clock position, 5 cm from the nipple. No palpable masses were found in her left breast, and no palpable lymph nodes were detected in her right axilla. However, an enlarged firm lymph node measuring 20 by 20 mm was noted in her left axilla. Bilateral mammography and ultrasound scans of the lower outer quadrant of her right breast and both axillae were performed. Mammography of the right breast revealed a 30 mm lesion in the lower outer quadrant. The left breast mammography showed no suspicious features. The ultrasound scan of the right axilla was normal, while the ultrasound scan of the left axilla revealed an enlarged lymph node with poor corticomedullary differentiation.
test_results: Trucut biopsy of the lump in the right breast lower outer quadrant showed ductal carcinoma in situ. Trucut biopsy of the radiologically indeterminate lymph node in her left axilla showed reactive changes only.

case_report: A 56-year-old woman experienced slight gingival bleeding for 3 months, lasting for 5 days, which resolved on its own. A dentist identified a gingival lesion during an evaluation. The patient does not smoke or consume alcohol and uses eye drops for glaucoma. Upon admission, she was in good general condition. Examination revealed a smooth-surfaced nodular lesion approximately 8x3mm in size near the second upper left molar (tooth 27), with no signs of lymph node enlargement.
test_results: The histopathological examination revealed low-grade epithelial neoplasia that was suggestive of low-grade acinar cell carcinoma of the minor salivary gland. Computed tomography revealed a 25x22x16mm lesion near tooth 27, extending to the floor of the left maxillary sinus, with extension to the palate mucosa.
Orpha_name: Salivary gland type cancer of the breast

case_report: A 79-year-old woman experienced a fall while ascending stairs, leading to a chest injury. A chest computed tomography scan identified a mass in the left breast. Further breast-specific imaging was conducted, and multiple core samples from the left breast were obtained. Two areas showed fibroadenoid changes and were consistent with each other. The patient has a family history of breast cancer in her daughter. Her medical history includes hypertension and morbid obesity. Her overall performance status was good.
test_results: A 1.5-cm, upper inner left breast mass was interpreted to be an invasive ductal carcinoma with basaloid features on core biopsy. This was estrogen receptor low positive (1%), progesterone receptor negative, and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 negative.
Orpha_name: Salivary gland type cancer of the breast

case_report: A 59-year-old postmenopausal woman, gravida 2, para 2, experienced vaginal bleeding and sought medical attention at a local clinic. Cytological tests of the uterine cervix and endometrium returned negative results. A uterine tumor was identified, prompting a referral to our hospital. Vaginal examination indicated an enlarged uterus, and ultrasound scans showed a large heterogeneous mass filling the entire uterine cavity. A repeat cytological test of the endometrium was negative. Fractional endometrial curettage revealed fibrous tissue with epithelial-like cells. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) identified a heterogeneous solid tumor measuring 77 × 76 mm. Serum CA125 levels were slightly elevated at 41.4 U/mL, while CA19-9 and CEA levels were normal. The patient was admitted and underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and pelvic lymphadenectomy. During laparotomy, the uterus was found to be fist-sized with no serosal invasion, and both ovaries were intact. The tumor originated from the uterine body and occupied the entire uterine cavity.
test_results: Glandular epithelium with little atypia and proliferation of atypical mesenchymal cells were seen. Mitosis exceeded 2 per 10 high power fields. No myometrial invasion or lymph node metastasis was seen. The lesion was confined to the uterus. Peritoneal cytology revealed no malignant cells.

case_report: A 38-year-old woman with multiple childbirths presented with lower abdominal pain, irregular vaginal bleeding, and foul-smelling vaginal discharge persisting for at least six months. She had a history of breast cancer and had undergone a modified radical left mastectomy with left axillary dissection four years prior. Pathological findings from that surgery indicated a grade 3, progesterone receptor-positive, c-erb-B2 score 3, estrogen receptor-negative invasive ductal carcinoma. Post-operative treatment included four chemotherapy courses with cyclophosphamide (600 mg/m2), adriamycin (60 mg/m2), and 5-FU (600 mg/m2), followed by nine weeks of herceptin (6 mg/kg) and docetaxel (75 mg/m2). Subsequently, she was treated with tamoxifen (20 mg/day) for 30 months. Upon admission, pelvic examination revealed a large, foul-smelling polypoid mass protruding through the cervix and an enlarged uterus.
test_results: Magnetic resonance images showed that a 192x100 mm uterus and a 75x65 mm solid heterogeneous mass filled the endometrial cavity without signs of invasion to surrounding tissues. A biopsy from the protruding polypoid mass was reported as a large area of necrosis with neoplastic mesenchymal cells. Fresh frozen sections taken during the operation revealed an endometrial stromal sarcoma. Histopathologically, the tumor was a biphasic lesion with benign epithelial elements and a sarcomatous stroma. Tubular glands, cysts, and cleft-like spaces were distributed throughout the tumor. These glands were lined by a benign proliferative endometrioid type epithelia. The mesenchymal component consisted of low-grade sarcoma, which was typically more cellular around the glands resulting in periglandular cuffs. In these cellular areas, there was a maximum of 9 mitotic figures/10 HPF; the sarcomatous cells appeared to contain focal atypia and pleomorphic endometrial stromal cells or fibroblasts. Immunohistochemically, the benign-appearing epithelial cells and sarcomatous tumor cells showed nuclear reaction with progesterone receptor and estrogen receptor, and stromal cells showed cytoplasmic reaction with CD10.

case_report: A 72-year-old woman with valvular heart disease was admitted to our hospital for investigation of hematochezia. Laboratory tests showed low hemoglobin concentration (7.4 g/dL; normal range, 13 to 17 g/dL), mean cellular volume (74.4 fL; normal range, 80 to 97 fL), and mean corpuscular hemoglobin (23.3 pg; normal range, 26 to 34 pg). The serum levels of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), carbohydrate antigen 19-9, and alpha fetoprotein were within normal limits. On colonoscopic examination, a 3-cm sized Yamada type IV polypoid mass with surface ulceration was noted at the cecum. Colonoscopic polypectomy was performed. The cut surface of the polyp was gray to white and friable. The resection margin was grossly involved by the tumor.
test_results: Microscopically, the overlying mucosa was effaced by the tumor. There was no mucosal dysplasia or transition area between the normal mucosa and tumor. The tumor cells were spindling or polygonal. The spindle cells had round to ovoid nuclei with coarse chromatin pattern, distinct nucleoli, and formed fascicular pattern. The polygonal cells had large bizarre nuclei and abundant eosinophilic glassy cytoplasm and lacked cohesiveness. Histologically, the tumor showed anaplastic feature and did not make any organoid pattern. The mucin stains such as PAS, mucicarmine, and alcian blue failed to reveal mucin-producing cell. Most tumor cells showed diffuse strong immunoreactivity to vimentin, but there was a distinct area showing immunoreactivity to epithelial markers such as cytokeratins, EMA. This area was also positive for CEA. The tumor did not express other specific markers, such as SMA, desmin, S-100 protein, C-kit, CD34, and HMB45. A small number of tumor cells were weakly immunoreactive to p53.

case_report: A 69-year-old Caucasian male presented with a progressively enlarging, asymptomatic mass in the left submandibular region over a period of 3 months. His medical, family, and psychosocial history were unremarkable, and he had no history of previous surgical treatments. On physical examination, the mass measured 8 × 5 cm, originating from level Ib (submandibular region) and extending into levels III and IV. The mass was adherent to underlying structures and had a soft texture. There was no pain or other symptoms. Examination of the right cervical region, oropharynx, thyroid, and upper respiratory airways showed no abnormalities. Ultrasound evaluation revealed the mass had mixed tissue consistency with cystic and solid areas separated by high flow vascular fibrous septa in level Ib. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the head and neck showed a 5 × 4 × 3 cm multilobed mass originating from the left submandibular gland, containing both fluid and solid components. No distant metastases were detected. Subsequent head and neck CT indicated areas of colliquation surrounded by thick pathological peripheral tissue within the mass. Fine-needle aspiration cytology showed malignant cells without distinctive features, and a subsequent US-FNAC also failed to identify the primary type of lesion.
test_results: Histological examination showed a neoplastic proliferation characterized by two cellular components, substantially distinct from each other. No fusion of the different cell types could be seen. The first cellular component consisted of medium size elements with multilobed nucleus and slightly eosinophilic cytoplasm. Such elements appeared arranged in solid cell nests with central necrosis and cribriform areas. Cytokeratin and PAS positivity were evident. The second cellular component consisted of mesenchymal elements of medium or large size with elongated hyperchromatic and pleomorphic nuclei. Such cellular elements appeared to be arranged around an eosinophilic material attributable to an osteoid matrix. Immunohistochemical study showed vimentin positivity. Tumor showed several cellular atypia, mitoses, areas of necrosis, or bleeding as well as angioinvasion.

case_report: A 46-year-old Caucasian female premenopausal patient, gravity 2 parity 2 (G2P2), presented in the ED with fever (up to 38.9°C), abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) for one month, fatigue, and dizziness. Apart from the fever, her vital signs were within normal range, although she appeared pale. Speculum examination showed active uterine bleeding with a foul smell. Cervical inspection was technically difficult due to menorrhagia but showed no pathology. There was no tenderness on cervical motion or fornix palpation bilaterally. Bimanual pelvic examination revealed a large uterus. A transvaginal ultrasound scan showed a large anteverted leiomyomatous uterus, and the ovaries could not be imaged due to the uterine size. No free liquid was observed in the recto-uterine pouch. A chest X-ray and a PCR test for COVID-19 were performed to investigate the fever, both of which showed no pathology. A urine culture indicated a urinary tract infection caused by Escherichia coli (>10^5 CFU/mL). Blood tests revealed hemoglobin at 4.4 g/dL, hematocrit at 16.5%, and elevated platelets (522000/μL). The patient was admitted for severe anemia and received transfusions. She was treated with micronized progesterone (200 mg x 3), ferric proteinsuccinylate (800 mg x 3), ampicillin/sulbactam (1 g/2 g x 3), and azithromycin (500 mg x1). An upper and lower abdominal CT scan with oral sodium amidotrizoate showed a large (approximately 7.5 cm diameter) hypodense lesion with clear boundaries in the uterine cervix and body. No enlarged lymph nodes were observed. A thoracic CT scan revealed multiple small round nodules bilaterally, with the largest nodule (1 cm diameter) in the right upper lobe. A pulmonologist reviewed the chest CT findings, considering the patient's past medical history of mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. The patient became afebrile after 3 days of IV antibiotics. During hospitalization, she received seven units of red blood cells (RBC) and three units of fresh frozen plasma (FFP). After one week, she was discharged with hemoglobin at 9.1 g/dL and hematocrit at 30.3%. She was advised to undergo total hysterectomy in an oncology center. Six days post-discharge, she returned to the ED with fatigue, dizziness, tachycardia, and worsened AUB. Blood tests again showed severe anemia with hemoglobin at 4.8 g/dL and hematocrit at 16.3%. She was re-admitted for hemodynamic stabilization and transfusion. After five days, despite receiving five units of RBC and two units of FFP, she experienced loss of consciousness while trying to stand. Her hemoglobin was 6.3 g/dL and hematocrit was 19.3%. After receiving three more units of RBC and one unit of FFP, she remained hemodynamically unstable and tachycardic (120 beats per minute). Due to nonresponding hemodynamic instability, she was taken to the operating theatre urgently to control menorrhagia. Dilatation and curettage were performed, removing endometrial tissues and solid material. Due to persistent uterine bleeding, an emergency hysterectomy was performed under general anesthesia. The uterus was removed en bloc with both fallopian tubes and ovaries via Pfannenstiel incision. The uterine cervix was dilated, the myometrial thickness was 3.5 cm, the endometrial cavity was dilated, and an 8 cm x 4 cm x 6 cm polypoid mass was observed intracavitary, attached to the endometrium of the uterine fundus. The patient received three units of RBC and two units of FFP during the hysterectomy. She was discharged on the third postoperation day, hemodynamically stable, and in good general condition with hemoglobin at 7.7 g/dL and hematocrit at 23.9%.
test_results: The polypoid mass consisted of spindle cells with severe atypia and eosinophilic cytoplasm, which were arranged in bundles. Coagulative necrosis and cellularity were observed. Mitotic index was greater than 20 mitotic figures per 10 high-power-fields. The tumor’s stalk showed signs of local invasion of the myometrium.

case_report: A 40-year-old nulliparous woman of South Indian origin presented with a mass in the lower abdomen for one year and lower abdominal pain for three months. Initially asymptomatic, she noticed a gradually enlarging mass in the lower abdomen over the past year, with a rapid increase in size over the last three months. The associated lower abdominal pain was dull, aching, dragging in nature, continuous, and without any aggravating or relieving factors. Her menstrual cycles were regular and normal, with no history of genital bleeding. On examination, pallor was noted, but vital signs were normal. She was thinly built. Abdominal examination revealed an irregular midline mass arising from the pelvis, with discernible upper and lateral borders but an unascertainable lower margin. The mass was firm to hard, had restricted mobility, was nontender, and there was no free fluid. There was no hepatosplenomegaly. Vaginal examination showed an enlarged uterus to 20 weeks' gestational size, nodular, occupying the whole pelvis, with no separate mass from the uterus. A CT scan indicated a large, multiloculated, multiseptate growth with both solid and cystic elements arising from the pelvis and extending into the abdomen, measuring 25 × 17 cm, adherent to both the uterus and bladder. CA125 was 94.80 ng/mL (0-35 ng/mL). Other results were normal, and the patient was scheduled for exploratory laparotomy. Intraoperatively, omental adhesions to the mass were observed. A mass of 20 weeks' size was arising from the fundus of the uterus, lobulated with solid, cystic, and hemorrhagic components. Both ovaries were normal, and the fallopian tubes were edematous. A total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy was performed. The uterus measured 8 cm × 5 cm × 3 cm with a subserosal bosselated growth from the fundus measuring 18 cm × 15 cm × 11 cm with variable consistency. Omental biopsy and external iliac lymph node biopsy were taken and sent for further examination.
test_results: Histopathologic examination showed a cellular tumor arranged in interlacing bundles of spindle cells with elongated hyperchromatic nuclei. The tumor cells were exhibiting moderate pleomorphism and bizarre nuclei with multinucleate tumor giant cells. There were scattered areas and normal and abnormal mitotic figures (> 4/high-power field) with marked nuclear atypia.

case_report: A 49-year-old woman presented with a 15-day history of mild, intermittent abdominal pain, black-colored stool, nausea, loss of appetite, and generalized weakness. Upon admission, she was pale, afebrile, with a pulse rate of 110/min, blood pressure of 150/90 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 26/min, and random plasma glucose of 230 mg/dL. She experienced dyspnea on exertion. Her skin was warm without any rash or discoloration. The abdomen was soft with audible bowel sounds and generalized tenderness, along with an irregular lump near the epigastrium. The patient was conscious, well-oriented, and exhibited no neurological deficits. She had undergone percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty (PTCA) to the right coronary artery 8 years prior. There was no history of alcohol abuse or use of drugs known to cause hepatitis idiosyncratically. Laboratory results were as follows (reference ranges in parentheses): hemoglobin 9.1 g% (12–15), PCV 28.2% (36–46), total count 7000/cumm (4000–10,000), RBC 3.27 million/cumm (4.5–5.5), platelet 1.59 lakhs/cumm (1.5–4), total bilirubin 1.8 mg/dL (up to 1), direct bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL (up to 0.3), glycosylated hemoglobin 10.7% (6–8), total protein 5.7 g/dL (6.5–8.1), albumin 2.4 g/dL (3.5–5), alanine transaminase 257 U/L (0–31), aspartate transaminase 224 U/L (0–32), alkaline phosphatase 793 U/L (30–279), gamma glutamyl transferase 477 U/L (1–94), lipase 96 U/L (up to 160), amylase 48 U/L (25–125), lactic dehydrogenase 1203 U/L (266–500), and prothrombin time 18 seconds (control 11.5) INR 1.58. Urea, creatinine, alpha-1 antitrypsin, serum copper, and electrolytes were within reference ranges. Viral serologies for antibodies to hepatitis B surface antigen, antihepatitis B surface antigen, antihepatitis B core antigen, antihepatitis C virus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, herpes simplex virus, and human immunodeficiency virus were all negative. Immunoglobulin G was 1987 mg/dL (700–1600 mg/dL). Antinuclear antibody (ANA) by IFA (1:320 titer) on Hep-2 cells revealed anticentromere antibodies showing 40–60 discrete speckles distributed over the nucleus, either dispersed or gathered closely together on the chromosomes of cells undergoing division. Four positive ANA controls (homogeneous, speckled, centromere, and nucleolar) included in the kit were also run for comparison. ANA repeated by enzyme immunoassay was 195.6 units (<20). Immunochromatography showed centromere B and soluble liver antigen/liver-pancreas antigen (SLA/LP) antibodies to be positive. Antithyroid antibodies (antiperoxidase and antithyroglobulin) and antigastric parietal cell antibodies were not detected by line immunoassay.
test_results: Liver biopsy showed a portal mononuclear cell infiltration, interface hepatitis in the liver tissue, and bridging fibrosis.

case_report: A 31-year-old man, previously healthy and a regular blood donor until March 2015, began working at a glove factory in July 2015. During his first 15 days at work, he intermittently placed his bare hands in a diluted solution of DMF without wearing gloves, despite receiving occupational safety education. He did not use any drugs or consume excessive alcohol. In late August 2015, he experienced nausea, fatigue, and intermittent hand cramping, leading to hospital admission. Laboratory results showed serum total bilirubin at 3.1 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 292 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) at 273 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase at 72 IU/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase at 89 IU/L, positive antinuclear antibodies (ANA) with a titer of 1:160, and an elevated IgG level at 3,275 mg/dL.
test_results: The pathology report showed chronic hepatitis, probably toxic, and the liver copper content was sufficiently normal (28 ug/g) to exclude Wilson's disease.

case_report: A 42-year-old Caucasian woman, employed as a nurse, presented with an elevated alanine transaminase concentration of 469 U/L (normal range: 10-35) during an evaluation for sub-fertility. Other liver function tests, including albumin levels and coagulation screen, were within normal limits. She exhibited no symptoms or signs indicative of liver disease. Her medical history included recurrent urinary tract infections and previous miscarriages. She was taking folic acid and nitrofurantoin 50 mg daily for the past two years. There was no reported history of excessive alcohol consumption or use of herbal remedies or supplements. Physical examination did not reveal any abnormalities. Additional tests showed a significantly abnormal autoimmune profile, with positive anti-nuclear antibodies at a titre of 1:640, smooth muscle antibodies at a titre of 1:320, and anti-mitochondrial antibodies at a titre of 1:320. Anti-Rho, extractable nuclear antibody, and rheumatoid factor were also positive. Immunoglobulin G levels were elevated at 22.8 g/L, while IgA and IgM levels were within normal ranges. Tests for chronic hepatitis viruses were negative, and serum ferritin was measured at 300 μg/L.
test_results: Liver biopsy showed marked chronic inflammation within the portal tracts and extensive fibrosis and some features of cirrhosis.

case_report: A 39-year-old female presented with intermittent irregular vaginal bleeding over the past 2 months and urinary retention for the last 2 days. On examination, the patient appeared pale and unwell. Per speculum examination showed a large, shaggy mass measuring 8 cm in diameter protruding from the cervical os, with the cervical rim palpable around it and a high pedicle. The uterus was approximately 8 weeks in size, soft, anteverted, and both fornices were clear. Pelvic ultrasound revealed a well-defined cervical mass lesion measuring 9 × 8 × 8 cm with heterogeneous echogenicity. The uterus appeared bulky with the endometrial cavity displaced anteriorly, and both adnexae were normal. A polypectomy was performed.
test_results: Gross examination of the polyp showed a globular mass measuring 6 × 5.5 × 4 cm. Cut surface was fleshy, grayish pink in color. Microscopic examination of the polyp showed a cellular tumor with a close morphological resemblance to nonneoplastic proliferative-phase endometrial stromal cells. The tumor cells were small uniform looking with dark staining round to oval nuclei, granular chromatin, and inconspicuous nucleoli. Areas of sex cord-like differentiation were also seen. Mitosis was minimal and less than three mitotic figures per high power field were seen. Stromal myometrial interface was not provided hence myometrial invasion could not be commented upon. Microscopic examination of the polyp showed a similar histological picture as described. These tumor cells were arranged concentrically around spiral arteriole like vessels with cord-like projections into the myometrium. Lymphovascular invasion was not seen. Both ovaries showed luteal cysts and the tumor was restricted to the uterine wall. Immunohistochemical analysis showed neoplastic endometrial stromal cells, which were immunoreactive for CD10 monoclonal antibody, while staining for Desmin was negative. There were areas of sex cord-like differentiation that showed reactivity for Inhibin, which was not detected in the other stromal areas.

case_report: A 58-year-old woman (gravida 13, para 10) who became menopausal 10 years ago was referred to our hospital due to increasing heaviness in the vagina. Her medical history includes hypothyroidism, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia, all managed with medication. Gynecological examination identified a firm mass measuring 3 cm in maximum diameter protruding from the left side of the vagina. Additionally, a small endocervical polyp approximately 1 cm in maximum diameter was noted. Ultrasound examination did not reveal any other abnormalities. An excisional biopsy of the cervical polyp indicated it was benign and inflamed. Resection of the vaginal mass suggested a low-grade spindle cell neoplasm.
test_results: The tumor cells are strongly positive for vimentin, CD10, estrogen and progesterone with focal areas of positive staining for CD99. The proliferation marker Ki67 (MIB1) was positive in 10% of the tumor cells. The lesional cells were negative for h-Caldesmon, calponin, desmin, smooth muscle actin, CD68, CD34, Bcl-2, NSE, S100 protein, cyclin-D1, GFAP, HMB45, inhibin, EMA and synaptophysin.

case_report: A 68-year-old male undergoing a routine colonoscopy was found to have multiple tubular adenomas (TAs) measuring 5-8 mm, including one in the ascending colon with surrounding ulcerated, irregular, and slightly raised mucosa, which was also biopsied. Under microscopic examination, an infiltrating poorly-differentiated malignant tumor was identified in the ulcerated lesion in close vicinity to an overlying TA. The tumor demonstrated pathological findings such as increased mitotic figures and apoptosis.
test_results: Immunohistochemical studies performed on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue sections revealed positive staining for keratin Cam5.2, neuroendocrine markers synaptophysin and chromogranin but negative for lymphoma (LCA/CD45), colorectal adenocarcinoma (CDX2, CK20, CK7), lung adenocarcinoma (TTF-1) and prostatic adenocarcinoma (PSA) markers.
Orpha_name: High-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma of the corpus uteri

case_report: In February 2018, a 48-year-old Chinese male presented at the Department of Ophthalmology, West China Hospital of Sichuan University, with a 2-month history of progressive right eye proptosis. There was no history of ocular discharge or thyroid eye disease. Best-corrected visual acuity, measured using the logarithm of the minimum angle of resolution (LogMAR), was 2.47 cm in the right eye and 0.1 in the left eye. Clinical examinations showed proptosis with Hertel’s exophthalmometry readings of 19 mm for the right eye and 14 mm for the left eye, conjunctival oedema with protrusion beyond the eyelid fissure, sluggish pupillary reactions, and mild optic disc pallor observed through indirect ophthalmoscopy. Computed tomography (CT) imaging revealed a well-defined, heterogeneous density retrobulbar nodule measuring 3.3 × 3.0 × 2.8 cm in the posterior part of the right orbit, surrounding the optic nerve and compressing extraocular muscles. Eye surgery was performed via a lateral orbitotomy approach, during which a brittle red neoplasm was found in the intraconal space and lateral rectus muscle.
test_results: Histological examination of the tumour showed positive staining for pan cytokeratin, thyroid transcription factor-1, neural cell adhesion molecule 1 (also known as CD56), epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), chromogranin A, and a MIB-1 rate of 80%.
Orpha_name: High-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma of the corpus uteri

case_report: A 65-year-old female, gravida 2 para 2, presented with abnormal vaginal bleeding persisting for 2 months. Pelvic ultrasound revealed a 7.0×4.5 cm oval-shaped mass occupying the uterine cavity with vascularization. Extensive imaging, including chest X-ray and thoracic CT, showed no abnormalities. Biochemical tests indicated normal levels of tumor markers CA-125, CA-199, and CEA, but serum alpha fetoprotein (AFP) was elevated at 359 ng/ml. Cervical cytology was negative for intraepithelial lesions or malignancy. The patient had a one-year history of diabetes managed with metformin. Curettage of the endometrium was performed, revealing only a small amount of endometrial atrophy due to limited tissue samples. Subsequently, total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy were carried out. The excised uterus measured 12.0×8.0×5.5 cm and weighed 185 g. Sectioning showed a 10 cm deep uterine cavity containing a 7 cm diameter brown polypoid tumor originating from the endometrium and extending 0.2 cm into the myometrium, which had a total thickness of 2.0 cm. The tumor was well-circumscribed, non-encapsulated, with a brown soft cut surface and large areas of hemorrhage and necrosis. No hair or teeth were observed. The remaining endometrium was 0.1 cm thick. The cervix appeared normal, measuring 2 cm in length and 2.5 cm in diameter. The uterine serosa, bilateral ovaries and fallopian tubes, abdominal and pelvic walls, and omentum showed no unusual features.
test_results: Various morphological patterns were revealed by microscopic examination. A yolk sac tumor was the predominant component of the specimen and accounted for 40% of the entire tumor. The tumor cells were arranged in reticular and microcystic architecture. The stroma was loose and myxoid. The second most predominant component (accounting for approximately 30%) was embryonal carcinoma, in which the tumor cells grew in solid, sheet, or nest patterns with gland differentiation. The solid pattern showed smaller polygonal cells with scant cytoplasm. The polygonal cells had vesicular nuclei with coarse, basophilic chromatin and one or two prominent nucleoli. Embryonal glands were visible, and the glands were lined with columnar cells. Based on histological features, it was concluded that immature teratoma (Grade 1) comprised only a small portion of the specimen (approximately 5%). The immature teratoma included primitive neuroectodermal tubules lined by overlapping, hyperchromatic cells with numerous mitoses. Moreover, mature teratoma, which appeared in the form of benign mucinous glands and mature bone tissue, composed the rest of the tumor (approximately 25%). Large areas of necrosis and hemorrhage were observed. The tumor also showed local infiltration of the myometrium. However, no tumor was found in the cervix, bilateral ovaries, or fallopian tubes. Immunohistochemical studies revealed that AFPs were diffusively distributed in both yolk sac tumor components, that the embryonal carcinoma component, OCT3/4 was positive in embryonal carcinoma component, and that AE1/AE3 was positive in glandular areas. GFAPs were positive in the neuroectodermal tubule component. Ki-67 was positive in 90% cells, whereas CD117 and PLAP were negative in all tumor cells.
diagnosis: Mixed Germ Cell Tumor of the Endometrium
Orpha_name: Malignant germ cell tumor of the corpus uteri

case_report: A 45-year-old woman with a history of three pregnancies and one childbirth (G3P1) reported experiencing significant vaginal discharge for the past five years. A ThinPrep cytology test indicated moderate inflammation. Multiple transvaginal ultrasonography scans showed an edematous cervix with numerous cysts exhibiting a honeycomb pattern. The inner cervical wall appeared irregular, and tumor marker levels were within normal limits. After undergoing cervical conization for the cervical cysts, biopsies indicated chronic cervical inflammation, retention cysts, and squamous metaplasia in the fundic portion of the cervix. The patient subsequently had a laparoscopic cystectomy and biopsy, hysteroscopy, fractional curettage, and cervical biopsy. Histopathological examination confirmed chronic inflammation of the cervical mucosa. Despite these interventions, the vaginal discharge persisted. A pelvic MRI revealed multiple cervical cysts and fluid accumulation in the pelvic cavity. The patient was otherwise in good health, with a medical history notable only for an appendectomy in 1983. Upon admission to our department, a gynecologic examination confirmed large amounts of vaginal discharge and cervical hypertrophy, with no other abnormalities detected.
test_results: The microscopic examination revealed cervical mucilaginous glands that were irregular in size and shape with increased apophysis, part of the glands were surrounded by a loose edematous or desmoplastic stromal response, the glands typically exhibited deep invasion of the cervical wall and were adjacent to the cervical adventitia. The glandular epithelial cells exhibited foci of heteromorphism.
diagnosis: Minimal Deviation Adenocarcinoma of the Uterine Cervix

case_report: A 38-year-old multiparous female with no past medical history presented to the emergency department with six days of intermittent achy, cramping mid-back pain. Her symptoms began three months earlier as bilateral shoulder pain, which resolved on its own. Several weeks later, she experienced episodes of upper back pain, which was diagnosed during multiple emergency department visits as muscle spasms and arthritis. One week prior to hospital admission, her mid-back pain returned, accompanied by bilateral leg weakness, causing her to fall several times. She denied trauma to her back or legs, numbness or tingling, or urinary or bowel incontinence. She reported a one-month history of vaginal bleeding varying from blood clots to light spotting without postcoital bleeding, which she attributed to her period. The patient had six pregnancies, with the last delivery over 14 years ago, shortly after which she had a copper intrauterine device placed, which was never removed. She had not seen a primary care doctor or a gynecologist in the last several years but was told she had fibroids. Her periods were regular, and her last menstrual period was about 1.5 weeks prior to presentation. She did not recall her last pap smear or any other sexually transmitted diseases but was treated for an episode of chlamydia in the past. She smoked marijuana frequently but denied using other forms of illicit drugs. Since her initial emergency department visit, she occasionally took ibuprofen and cyclobenzaprine as needed for her pain. The patient had a family history of ovarian cancer in her maternal aunt. In the emergency department, her vitals were stable, and her cardiovascular and respiratory exams were normal. Her strength on the right hip, knee, and foot plantar flexion was 4/5 and was 5/5 on the right knee extension and foot dorsiflexion. Her strength in all other extremities was 5/5. She was moving all extremities spontaneously without any apparent focal deficits. The straight leg raise test was not done. Her neurological exam showed decreased sensation to light touch at the umbilicus and below to the perineal area. No pronator drift was noted, and her rectal tone was preserved. A manual pelvic exam was also done but due to body habitus, pain, and positioning, it was able to visualize only the lower half of the cervix, which appeared normal without signs of a mass, bleeding, or discharge. Pap smear was negative for human papillomavirus (HPV) genotypes 16, 18, 31, and 33. The patient’s labs were significant for a white blood cell count of 16 (normal: 4-11) x10^3/uL, hemoglobin of 11.2 (normal: 12-16) g/dL, and platelet count of 241 (normal: 150-450) x10^3/uL. Sedimentation rate was elevated at 30 (normal: 0-20) mm/hour and C-reactive protein was elevated at 28 (normal: 0-5) mg/L. Prothrombin time (PT), partial thromboplastin time (PTT), and international normalized ratio (INR) were normal. Her chemistry panel and procalcitonin were normal. The serum pregnancy test was negative. The pelvic ultrasound showed a large uterus with multiple calcified fibroids but preserved blood flow. CT scans of her chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed an osteolytic process of the T6 vertebrae with burst fracture, multiple enlarged pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes, and an enlarged fibroid uterus with calcifications. A follow-up MRI showed cervical spondylosis with posterior ridging at the C3-C7 vertebrae abutting the cervical cord, loss of height at the T6 vertebrae with cord compression, and demineralization at the T12 vertebrae. She was given steroids and taken to the operating room for emergent T5-T7 laminectomy, T4-T8 posterior thoracic fusion, and biopsy of the T6 vertebral lesion. She also underwent a pelvic exam under anesthesia that was significant for a 20+ week-sized globular mobile uterus with an irregular 3-4 cm mass on palpation of the posterior cervix. Brain MRI showed both cerebral and cerebellar metastases.
test_results: Biopsy of the T6 vertebrae stained strongly positive for synaptophysin, neuron-specific enolase (NSE), chromogranin, and CD56. Biopsy of the cervix was positive for NSE, p16, and vimentin.
diagnosis: Small Cell Neuroendocrine Cancer of the Cervix
Orpha_name: High-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix uteri

case_report: A 53-year-old Portuguese female came to the hospital with a history of chronic constipation and abdominal discomfort lasting six months. She reported no changes in appetite or weight. Her medical history included a total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy performed eight years ago due to uterine fibroids and endometriosis. She did not report any postmenopausal or gastrointestinal bleeding. On physical examination, she appeared to be an average-sized female in no acute distress, and her systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin at 13.1 g/dL (normal range: 12.5–16.0 g/dL), white blood cell count at 9.75 × 10^3/uL (normal range: 4.5–11.0 × 10^3/uL), and platelet count at 254 × 10^3/uL (normal range: 150–450 × 10^3/uL). Blood urea nitrogen, serum creatinine, and electrolytes were within normal limits. A CT scan of the abdomen revealed an abnormal soft tissue density in the sigmoid colon, measuring approximately 4.7 cm in anterior-posterior dimension and 2.2 cm in maximum transverse dimension. An enlarged lymph node adjacent to the sigmoid colon measured approximately 1.6 × 1.6 cm. Additional enlarged lymph nodes were observed superiorly, just below the bifurcation of the abdominal aorta into the common iliac arteries, with the largest measuring 1.2 × 1.1 cm anterior to the sacrum. The visualized portions of the urinary bladder were normal, and the kidneys showed no hydronephrosis. CA-125 and CEA levels were 6.4 U/mL (normal range: 0–30 U/mL) and 0.8 ug/L (normal range: 0.0–3.0 ug/L), respectively. A surgical consultation was obtained, and a rectal biopsy was performed.
test_results: The histopathology revealed an epithelioid malignancy with variable differentiation patterns including solid areas with basaloid and squamoid features and pseudoglandular areas. However, the typical dirty necrosis seen in conventional colonic adenocarcinomas was absent. Immunohistochemical stains (IHC) were positive for CK7, negative for CK20, and only very focally and weakly positive for both CDX2 and p63. IHC for chromogranin, synaptophysin, and TTF-1 were negative.

case_report: A 27-year-old woman presents with complaints of dyspepsia and abdominal distension persisting for several months. Her medical history is unremarkable. Laboratory tests reveal an elevated CA 125 level of 1,309 UI/ml. Physical examination indicates significant abdominal distension and dullness in the lower abdominal quadrants, consistent with the presence of ascites.
test_results: A transabdominal ultrasound confirms the ascites in all peritoneal recesses and reveals a bulky mass, which occupies almost entirely the abdominal cavity and the pelvis. It appears predominantly solid, with few cystic components and heterogeneous echotexture. Internal blood flow is demonstrated on ultrasound color Doppler. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis confirms the findings highlighted on the ultrasound: diffused ascites and a multiloculated, voluminous solid mass with definite margins measuring 20 × 10 cm on the axial view, with cranio-caudal extension of 23 cm. The mass occupies partially the abdomen and entirely the pelvis, and presents contextual cystic components, the largest of which was 6 × 4 cm, and calcifications, the largest of which measured 14 mm. It shows heterogeneous vascularity during the arterial phase and presents few septa and pseudosepta, which have a lively enhancement on postcontrast images, especially during the portal/venous phase. The mass dislocates the intestinal loops but does not show signs of local invasion. There are no enlarged lymphnodes. The uterus is normal; the ovaries are not viewable.

case_report: A 36-year-old female visited the Gynecology Out Patient Department (OPD) with primary complaints of painful intercourse and bleeding after sexual activity. During the gynecological examination, a large polyp was observed originating from the endocervix, which bled upon contact. The patient had no other significant medical conditions and was prepared for the surgical removal of the polyp. During the surgery, there was excessive bleeding following the removal of the polyp. The polyp measured 5x3 cm and had a blood-stained external surface. It was fully processed.
test_results: The histological examination revealed a stromal tumor composed of marked cytological atypia with nuclear pleomorphism, high N:C ratio, and markedly pleomorphic cells with scant cytoplasm and bizarre nuclei, with the presence of binucleation and undifferentiated atypical blastemal cells with conspicuous nucleoli. Brisk mitosis was noted with 1-2 atypical mitotic figures per high-power field (1-2/HPF). A few strap cells were also present scattered within the tumor cells. The tumor cells encroached upon the blood vessels, but no frank vascular invasion was noted. Areas of hemorrhage and necrosis were also present. Atrophic endometrial glands were also found within the tumor. Immunohistochemical (IHC) evaluation revealed tumor cell reactivity to Vimentin, Desmin, Myo D1, and Myogenin but was non-reactive for SMA and CK7. The Ki 67 proliferative index was 50-60% in the most proliferative focus.
diagnosis: Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma of the uterine cervix, an anaplastic variant

case_report: A 45-year-old female presented with a painful swelling in the left buccal mucosal region, first noticed 3 months prior, which had progressively increased in size. The pain was mild and continuous. Intraoral examination revealed an ill-defined swelling in the left posterior buccal mucosa near the molar region. Palpation identified a tender, well-defined, freely movable swelling measuring 1 × 1 cm, with a soft to firm consistency. The overlying mucosa appeared normal. Panoramic radiography showed no bone changes in the maxilla or mandible. Ultrasonography indicated a hypoechoic mass with a uniform internal structure and well-defined borders, without calcification, and unattached to neighboring structures. The lesion was surgically excised.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed loss of cellular architecture and cribriform pattern of tumor cells with many microcytes. Perineural invasion was present.
Orpha_name: Adenoid cystic carcinoma of the cervix uteri

case_report: A 46-year-old male presented with pain in the upper left back tooth region of the jaw for one month, accompanied by swelling. Extraoral examination showed no abnormalities or lymphadenopathy. The patient's medical history was unremarkable, though he had a smoking habit for several years. Intraoral examination revealed deep mesio-occlusal caries in tooth 26, associated with a solitary erythematous swelling with clear borders in the left posterior hard palate. The swelling, initially small, had gradually increased in size, extending from the mesial aspect of the canine to 2 cm anterior to the tuberosity on the left side, involving the palatal area but not crossing the midline. The mucosa over the swelling was smooth and continuous with adjacent mucosa, with a small punctum and no surface discharge. Palpation confirmed these findings, showing no mobility of the involved teeth but tenderness on palpation. The swelling was nontender, nonfluctuant, firm, and immobile. Additionally, a grayish patch with a wrinkled surface was observed on the anterior part of the soft palate, which was nontender and non-scrappable on palpation. Routine blood tests were normal. Cone-beam computerized tomography showed a well-circumscribed soft-tissue density lesion measuring approximately 20.5 mm × 17.1 mm in the left palatal region adjacent to the premolars and molars.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed fibrovascular connective tissue stroma with mild chronic inflammatory cell infiltrate consisting predominantly of lymphocytes. There was the presence of numerous islands of small cuboidal to polygonal-shaped cells with little cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei resembling basaloid epithelial cells along with multiple cylindrical cyst-like spaces filled with eosinophilic material.
Orpha_name: Adenoid cystic carcinoma of the cervix uteri

case_report: A 50-year-old female patient visited the Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology Department for an evaluation of an ulceration on her upper lip, including the philtrum, which had been present for 2 years. The patient reported a history of chewing tobacco multiple times daily for approximately 10 years. Clinical examination showed a large, destructive ulceration with induration, measuring approximately 7 cm × 3 cm × 5 cm. This ulceration extended beyond the middle third of the upper lip area, involving the outer skin and exposing the upper anterior mucosa. No regional lymphadenopathy was observed.
test_results: Computed tomography scan revealed an ulcero-infiltrative soft-tissue lesion which measures approximately 4.1 cm × 1.8 cm × 1.3 cm involving the upper lip extending across the midline, causing erosion of the outer cortex of the superior alveolar arch in the region of the incisor and canine teeth. Microscopic examination of the hematoxylin- and eosin-stained tissue revealed cribriform islands with cystic spaces lined by basaloid epithelial cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and scanty eosinophilic cytoplasm. The cells showed mild-to-moderate atypia. The cystic spaces are separated by hyalinized stroma and contained scanty mucoid material. Areas of ductal, tubular, and pseudo-glandular structures lined by epithelial cells and islands of basaloid hyperchromatic cells are evident. The connective tissue was also observed to be hyalinized and interspersed with adipose tissue and extravasated blood elements. Overlined epithelium was seen to be parakeratotic with blunt rete ridges without any dysplastic features.
Orpha_name: Adenoid cystic carcinoma of the cervix uteri

case_report: A 20-year-old African American female presented with a history of a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) on Pap smear. A colposcopy was performed, resulting in three cervical biopsies and an endocervical curettage. All samples showed no significant pathologic alteration except for one cervical biopsy that exhibited HPV-effect. During a subsequent procedure, multiple erosions of inflammation were observed overlying the cervix.
test_results: The gross LEEP specimen measured 1.3 cm in diameter and 0.4 cm in depth. The cervical mucosa was purple-tan, smooth and glistening. No demonstrable lesions were present. Microscopically, hematoxylin- and eosin-stained sections showed cervical stroma involved by scattered cellular proliferations arranged in nests with a striking peripheral palisading arrangement and microcyst formation. A stromal reaction to these nests was not present. The cells were uniform, round to oval, and had scant cytoplasm. Nuclei were hyperchromatic, showing inconspicuous nucleoli and minimal nuclear atypia. Mitotic figures were not identified. The squamous epithelium showed occasional, sporadic foci of lymphocytic infiltration not necessarily coincident to the underlying tumor nests. Definitive squamous intraepithelial lesions were not present. A stain for EMA showed strong, diffuse cellular membrane staining of the tumor cells, whereas stains for PSA and collagen IV did not highlight cells from the lesion.
diagnosis: Adenoid Basal Carcinoma of the Cervix
Orpha_name: Adenoid basal carcinoma of the cervix uteri

case_report: A 30-year-old patient, who has never been pregnant, was admitted in March 2005 to the Gynecologic Oncology Unit of the Catholic University of Campobasso due to irregular vaginal bleeding following sexual intercourse. The patient's medical history showed no significant issues. Gynecological history indicated menarche at age 12 and regular menstrual cycles until six months prior to the onset of symptoms. Upon gynecological examination, the uterus was found to be of normal size, and no masses were detected in the adnexal regions. An ulcerated lesion with a maximum diameter of 2 cm was observed in the posterior esocervix. The parametria and vagina appeared unaffected.
test_results: Colposcopy-guided biopsy and curettage of endocervical canal were performed revealing an invasive squamous cell cervical carcinoma with areas of poor differentiation.
diagnosis: Glassy cell carcinoma of the cervix
Orpha_name: Glassy cell carcinoma of the cervix uteri

case_report: A 7-month-old female was admitted with respiratory distress, rapid breathing, low oxygen levels, and severe growth failure not explained by confirmed gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). She is related to another patient from the paternal side. Born at term via spontaneous vaginal delivery after an uneventful pregnancy, her birth weight was 3.2 kg. At 5 hours old, she developed respiratory distress with rapid breathing and cyanosis, requiring oxygen therapy through a nasal cannula. At 10 days old, she was hospitalized for 50 days and diagnosed with severe GERD through an upper gastrointestinal contrast study. Anti-reflux therapy was initiated but did not lead to significant improvement. Extensive investigations, including bronchoscopy and bronchoalveolar lavage, were conducted. Her condition worsened, complicated by respiratory syncytial virus-positive bronchiolitis, necessitating mechanical ventilation for 10 days. A CT scan of the chest revealed ground-glass opacities in both lungs and airspace disease features in the bilateral lower lobes, with no pleural effusion or significant interstitial abnormalities.
test_results: The genetic result was homozygous nonsense mutation in exon 29 of the ABCA3 gene. This mutation is defined as C.4545delC.
Orpha_name: Chronic respiratory distress with surfactant metabolism deficiency

case_report: A 38-year-old woman, who smokes 2 cigarettes daily, was referred to the oral medicine service at Andres Bello University due to 'white spots' in her mouth. Her medical history includes insulin resistance managed with metformin, with no other significant medical issues. Intraoral examination revealed multiple non-removable, painless white plaques of varying sizes and thickness on the attached gingiva, with no involvement of the free marginal gingivae and alveolar mucosa. A similar white plaque was observed across the hard palate, sparing the free marginal gingival. The dorsal side of the tongue showed elongated, thickened, and whiter-than-normal filiform papillae, giving the appearance of a white coating. No other abnormalities were noted. The patient reported not noticing anything unusual in her mouth but mentioned having thick yellowish focal plaques on both soles. No similar lesions were found on other parts of her body, including the palms of her hands. The patient also mentioned that her father and grandmother have similar lesions on their palms and soles.
test_results: Histopathologically, both specimens revealed a hyperplastic and hyperorthokeratinized stratified squamous epithelium with basal hyperplasia containing multiple normal mitosis. The spinous, granular and corneum stratum showed dispersed basophilic keratohyalin granules. At higher magnification, the keratinocytes contained paranuclear bodies, seen as round eosinophilic condensation that indented the nuclei, giving it a coma or 'Pac-man' shape. The connective tissue underneath was of normal appearance, demonstrating a dense collagenized chorion, containing multiple fibroblasts, hyperemic capillaries and the presence of chronic inflammatory cells.
diagnosis: Focal palmoplantar and gingival keratosis disorder

case_report: A 60-year-old woman with hypertension and no significant past medical or surgical history presented with joint stiffness, a burning sensation, and generalized weakness. She received symptomatic treatment with ibuprofen and omeprazole. Basic investigations were conducted, including an electrocardiogram (ECG), chest X-ray, and ultrasound sonography (USG) of the abdomen and pelvis, all of which returned normal results. Laboratory findings were as follows: Hemoglobin: 11.5 g/dL; RBC count: 3.83 million/mm3; WBC count: 7900/mm3; platelet count: 2.48/mcL. Serum creatinine: 0.61 mg/dL; serum potassium: 3.13 mEq/L; serum sodium: 144 mmol/L; serum urea: 18.45 mg/dL. Albumin: 3.45 g/dL; alkaline phosphatase: 70.56 U/L; alanine transaminase (ALT): 15.64 U/L; aspartate aminotransferase (AST): 28.07 U/L; bilirubin (total): 0.42 mg/dL; HDL cholesterol: 34.34 mg/dL; total cholesterol: 157.46 mg/dL; LDL cholesterol: 98 mg/dL; triglycerides: 122.94 mg/dL; C-reactive protein (CRP): 0.3 mg/dL; erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 18 mm/hr.
test_results: Antinuclear antibody: positive; rheumatoid factor: positive; anti-U1-riboprotein (RNP): positive; anti-centromere antibody: negative.

case_report: A 66-year-old male presented with bright red blood per rectum for two months. His medical history includes benign prostatic hypertrophy and obstructive sleep apnea, with a past surgical history of vasectomy. He is a social drinker and a former smoker, having quit over 30 years ago. The patient was adopted but knows his biological mother died from an unspecified gynecological cancer, and multiple maternal uncles died from cancer of unknown types between the ages of 30 and 40. Physical examination was unremarkable. Colonoscopy revealed a 3 cm friable mass in the transverse colon at approximately 70 cm, a 4 mm polyp in the cecum, polyps in the ascending colon measuring 1.5 cm and 4 mm, and an 8 mm polyp in the sigmoid colon. Histological analysis showed invasive adenocarcinoma arising from a tubular adenoma in the transverse colon, tubular adenomas with high-grade dysplasia in the descending colon, and tubular adenomas in the sigmoid and ascending colon. Carcinoembryonic antigen level was normal. CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis indicated circumferential wall thickening in the transverse colon. The patient underwent a subtotal abdominal colectomy, which removed all lesions. Pathological evaluation confirmed moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the transverse colon with twenty-three benign lymph nodes.
test_results: DNA sequencing of the patient's germline identified a cytosine (C) to thymine (T) transition at codon 414, exon 9, and c.1240 C > T, heterozygous in one allele of the APC gene. DNA sequence analysis identified a guanine (G) to adenine (A) transition at codon 2502 (c.7504 G > A, heterozygous). The final interpretation of the germline genetic analysis identified two variants: APC gene unclassified variant p.R414C; c.1240 C > T and APC polymorphism: p.G2502S (c.7504 G > A). The patient tested negative for MYH gene coding regions and for Lynch syndrome.

case_report: A 23-year-old man with no prior medical history was referred to Gangnam Severance Hospital after multiple gastric polyps were incidentally discovered. The patient had a gastric tubular adenoma with dysplasia located in the antrum of the stomach. An endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) was performed for the gastric adenoma in the antrum, and multiple biopsies were taken from polyps of varying sizes in the upper body and fundus. The final pathology report indicated tubular adenoma with low-grade dysplasia for the antral lesion, while the polyps in the upper body and fundus were identified as fundic gland polyps. During a subsequent colonoscopy, fewer than 100 colorectal polyps, each measuring 3 to 5 mm, were observed from the hepatic flexure to the rectum. Pathology confirmed these colorectal polyps as tubular adenoma with low-grade dysplasia. Colonic polyps close to or equal to 5 mm in size were endoscopically removed using a polypectomy snare.
test_results: Genetic analysis using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) denaturing high performance liquid chromatography and direct sequencing revealed a novel frameshift mutation in the exon 15 of the APC gene. Deletion of adenine-guanine (AG) and insertion of thymine (T) in codon 3833-3834 resulted in the formation of stop codon 1287 (c.3833-3834delAGinsT).

case_report: A 64-year-old Polish-speaking female, scheduled for her regular dialysis session, was found to have a hemoglobin level of 6.1 g/dl in outpatient labs. She was sent to the emergency department where she reported increased fatigue and mild abdominal pain for three months. She mentioned a recent diagnosis of Clostridium difficile (C. diff) three months ago at another facility, treated with vancomycin 125 mg PO, which resolved her symptoms. She also noted a small amount of bright red blood with bowel movements, attributing it to external hemorrhoids. She denied fevers, chills, nausea, headache, light-headedness, syncope, or other constitutional symptoms. Her medical history included atrial fibrillation on Eliquis, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, gout, glaucoma, coronary artery disease status post stent placement, recurrent C. diff colitis infection, and external hemorrhoids. She was undergoing dialysis for end-stage renal disease. Family history included colon cancer in her mother. The patient had never undergone cancer screening before and was reluctant to provide further medical and family history due to her status as an undocumented immigrant. On examination, the patient was hemodynamically stable with negative orthostatic blood pressure. Physical examination revealed pallor conjunctiva and non-bleeding external hemorrhoids. Rectal examination showed maroon-colored guaiac positive stool. Given her low hemoglobin of 6.1 mg/dl, high reticulocyte count, and ferritin levels, she was administered two units of packed red blood cells (pRBC). Due to the chronicity of symptoms, multiple comorbidities, and dialysis requirement, she was admitted for further care. She continued all previous home medications except for aspirin and Eliquis. Dialysis sessions proceeded as scheduled.
test_results: The patient was found to have multiple polyps in the entire colon with significant 30 mm polypoid lesions in the cecum and the proximal ascending colon and 40 mm lesion in the sigmoid colon. Pathology was significant for moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma with intact MMRP immune-histochemical staining. Genetic testing turned out to be negative for APC gene mutation.

case_report: A 73-year-old woman was referred to the radiology department for a brain MRI. In 2019, she had an invasive moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the sigmoid colon, followed by a sigmoid colon resection and end-to-end colorectal anastomosis. She received chemotherapy and was doing well, but had not yet undergone radiotherapy. She has no history of hypertension, diabetes, or amyloidosis. She is the only child of her deceased parents; her father passed away due to a cerebrovascular accident. She has one child. As part of her metastatic workup, a brain CT scan was performed at another hospital. The CT scan images showed diffuse hyperdense lesions in the infratentorial (pons), basal ganglia, and other supratentorial regions of the brain, which lacked features such as perilesional edema and ring enhancement.
test_results: The MRI of the brain performed with T1- and T2-weighted imaging (T1WI and T2WI), Fluid Attenuation Inversion Recovery (FLAIR), GRE/T2∗, and Susceptibility-Weighted Imaging (SWI) sequences revealed multiple diffuse bilateral cerebral, basal ganglia, midbrain, pons, and cerebellar lesions of varying sizes ranging from 2 mm to 20 mm. No enhancement was noted postgadolinium contrast administration. No other associated abnormalities like arteriovenous malformations, aneurysms, or capillary telangiectasia were visualized.

case_report: A 51-year-old male was admitted to the hospital with sudden drowsiness. Neurological examination showed mildly confused orientation, restricted gaze to the left in both eyes, mild weakness on the left side of the face, and weakness on the right side of the body. The patient had a history of hypertension, which was being treated with medication. Brain CT scan revealed a hematoma in the posterior part of the lower pons with minimal mass effect. After 2 months of conservative treatment, the patient's mental status and gaze limitation fully recovered, while the facial weakness and right-sided weakness improved but persisted.
test_results: Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) revealed a fusiform aneurysm in the right VA. Angiography showed the fusiform aneurysm was located distal to the origin of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery. A hemodynamic difference between the pre- and post-ligation MRAs was identified. The left VA, which was compressing the facial nerve REZ, did not change architecturally but enlarged in diameter. The facial nerve REZ was found to be compressed by an elongated VA.

case_report: A 49-year-old right-handed man, working as a magazine editor with 16 years of education, presented to the emergency room with a sudden onset of headache, vomiting, and mild weakness in his right upper extremity. Initial imaging showed an acute intracerebral hemorrhage in the left parieto-occipital lobe. He was admitted to the neurosurgery department and received conservative treatment. One day later, his weakness in the right upper and lower extremities worsened, and he developed new symptoms of aphasia. Emergency stereotactic hematoma aspiration with catheterization was performed, and he was subsequently transferred to the department of cardiac surgery for management of his underlying cardiac sarcoma. After treatment and several rehabilitation sessions over four months, he was discharged home with improved motor and language functions. Nine months after the intracerebral hemorrhage, he visited the Rehabilitation Medicine outpatient clinic with ongoing cognitive and speech impairments. He also reported difficulties in writing, calculation, and recognizing fingers.
test_results: Brain computed tomography revealed acute intracerebral hemorrhage in the left parieto-occipital lobe. MMSE score was 18 out of 30 and cognitive function test showed impairment in auditory and visual attention, linguistic visual learning ability and long-term memory, and executive functions. Raven’s coloured progressive matrices revealed 13 out of 36 points suggesting low nonverbal intelligence for patient’s age and level of education. Written calculation test revealed acalculia, especially in subtraction, multiplication, and division. Right-Left orientation and Benton Right-Left Discrimination Test showed impairment in orientation, especially in his own body. Although all 3 questions were correct in the finger agnosia test, the patient frequently showed obvious symptoms of finger agnosia in the detailed clinical examination. The language assessment using Paradise Korean version of Western Aphasia Battery-Revised revealed mild anomic aphasia with aphasia quotient of 89.9 out of 100 points. In the expansion tests for reading and writing, the scores were 83 and 54 out of 100 points, respectively, and language quotient score was 81.4 points with typical agraphia symptoms. The patient had spelling errors and showed severe difficulties in describing pictures with sentences and dictating sentences and words. In the diffusion tensor tractography (DTT), fibers of left SLF, MdLF, U-fibers and CC (especially most posterior segment, C5) were disrupted around the left parietal lobe lesion, but fibers of ILF and AF was preserved. The DTT of the MdLF also showed disruption of distal part to the left parietal lobe lesion. The FA values of left SLF, CC and its C5 segment were decreased by more than 3 standard deviations from the FA values of the control group.

case_report: A 43-year-old right-handed male patient, with a history of anabolic steroid use, mitral valve replacement (biological) two years ago, and atrial fibrillation without regular follow-up, arrived at the emergency room reporting sudden onset of language difficulties and right-sided sensorimotor weakness, predominantly affecting the face and arm. Upon admission, his vital signs were stable, and blood glucose levels were within normal range. The general clinical examination showed an irregular heartbeat and a systolic murmur in the mitral region (3+/6+) radiating to the left midaxillary line, with no other abnormalities detected. Neurological examination conducted approximately six hours after symptom onset revealed the patient was alert, cooperative, and oriented in time and space. The strength examination indicated a deviation of the labial commissure to the left and weakness in the proximal right upper limb (strength grade IV+). Coordination and sensory tests were normal. Neuropsychological assessment identified aphasia with low speech fluency (less than 10 words per minute), inability to repeat words, difficulty naming simple objects, and reduced spontaneous naming (fewer than 12 animals per minute). There was no ideomotor apraxia for transitive and intransitive gestures. The patient exhibited agraphia, struggling to write letters and words spontaneously, from dictation, or by copying. He also had acalculia for simple addition and subtraction, finger agnosia (difficulty following commands to move specific fingers and recognizing his own fingers), and right-left disorientation (e.g., difficulty pointing to the right foot with the left hand). Initial cranial computed tomography (CT) was normal, and the electrocardiogram showed an irregular rhythm and absence of p waves, without ischemic changes. No echocardiographer was available for an emergency assessment. The patient was not eligible for endovenous thrombolysis due to the time interval exceeding four and a half hours from symptom onset to hospital arrival. After receiving clinical support, the patient stabilized without complications.
test_results: Cranial CT revealed a hypodense area in the left inferior frontal lobe. Brain MRI disclosed hypersignal and restricted diffusion in the left anterior and posterior insular cortex, with sparing of the topography corresponding to the angular and supramarginal gyri.
diagnosis: Transient Gerstmann syndrome as a manifestation of stroke

case_report: A 10-year-old boy visited the Department of Pediatric Dentistry with a primary concern of loose teeth in the upper and lower back regions and requested their removal. His medical history was unremarkable, and no abnormalities were found during the external examination. The intraoral examination showed that all present primary teeth exhibited mobility before shedding, specifically the upper second molar in the right quadrant, lower second molar in the left quadrant, and both the first and second lower molars in the right quadrant. All other teeth in the mouth appeared normal. Additionally, the upper second premolars were not observed in the oral cavity, and a radiograph was taken to verify these findings.
test_results: The OPG revealed the maxillary second premolars were missing along with the absence of right mandibular second molar. The right primary mandibular first molar was single rooted.

case_report: A 47-year-old woman, measuring 145 cm in height, has had type 2 diabetes mellitus for the past 20 years. She has experienced severe sensorineural hearing loss for 12 years and ischemic heart disease for 5 years. Her mother and maternal aunt developed diabetes and hearing loss before turning 40. Her siblings and son have no systemic issues. The best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/20p in both eyes (right eye -4.75 DS, left eye -5.00 DS). The anterior segment and intraocular pressure were normal in both eyes. The fundus examination revealed well-defined, round to oval areas of atrophy surrounding the fovea in a circumferential pattern in both eyes. Autofluorescence imaging highlighted these features, showing sharply defined discontinuous areas of perifoveal hypoautofluorescence surrounded by speckled hyperautofluorescence, which were not clinically apparent.
