test_results: The OCT showed depression of inner retinal surface, inner retinal hyporeflective spaces [pseudocysts], disorganization/thinning of outer retina, outer retinal tubulation (ORT), loss of external limiting membrane, ellipsoid and interdigitation zone, and thinning of the RPE and choriocapillaris. OCT angiogram showed some reduced flow at the area temporal to the fovea in the superficial retinal slab and artifacts showing superficial vessels due to retinal thinning in the deep retinal slab. Outer retinal slab appeared to have 2 unmasking artifacts in the area of atrophy, and the choriocapillaris slab showed signal void areas at the uninvolved area along with unmasking of underlying choroidal vessels at the involved area. The multifocal electroretinogram (mfERG) revealed reduced foveal and perifoveal amplitudes which were more depressed in the right eye compared to the left eye.

case_report: An 18-year-old woman of African origin came to the emergency room due to progressively worsening stress-related shortness of breath and expiratory wheezing over the past year, with significant deterioration in the last six months. She also experienced chest tightness and a productive cough, but no coughing up blood or fever. Her birth history was normal, and there were no similar symptoms reported among her siblings. She was not on any medication and did not smoke. Physical examination showed reduced breath sounds at the right lung base, dullness on percussion, and decreased vocal fremitus on the right side. Her oxygen saturation was 100%, and her heart rate and breathing rate were normal.
test_results: Contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography (CT) demonstrated complete atelectasis of the right lung with short-blind right main bronchus and compensatory hyperinflation of the left lung. Lung function tests confirmed restrictive lung disease, with FEV reaching 40% of the predicted value and FVC 43%. Bronchoscopy revealed a fibrotic scar area on the right side of the trachea with dimple at the place of opening of right main bronchus.

case_report: A 28-year-old man was admitted to the internal medicine department presenting with fatigue, thirst, frequent urination, a five-kilogram weight loss, diarrhea, and palpitations. He has a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) diagnosed at age 19, managed with intensive basal-bolus insulin therapy (70 units per day). He has a smoking history of approximately twenty cigarettes per day for ten years. There is no family history of autoimmune thyroid disease or other immunological disorders. On physical examination, his height was 157 cm, weight 59 kg, body mass index (BMI) 23.9 kg/m2, blood pressure 100/70 mm Hg, and pulse 130 beats per minute. Neurological examination indicated distal symmetric polyneuropathy. The thyroid gland was palpable without signs of ophthalmopathy. Laboratory findings showed high blood glucose (350 mg/dL), acetone in urine, and metabolic acidosis, leading to a diagnosis of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).
test_results: Low TSH, high free T4 (FT4), high free T3 (FT3), positive thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibody (TRAb), and a diffuse homogenous thyroid gland enlargement with increased blood flow by thyroid ultrasound. Elevated levels of aminotransferases (AST = 277 IU/L, ALT = 313 IU/L) and total bilirubin (1.6 mg/dL). Positive ANA, ASMA, and liver biopsy, and negative viral markers.

case_report: A 16-year-old male with a 10-year history of hair loss, initially presenting as patchy and progressing to complete hair loss, is described. His grandfather also experienced total hair loss. Five years ago, the patient began treatment with levothyroxine 150 μg daily after testing positive for thyroid peroxidase autoantibodies (314.7 UI/mL; normal range [NR] 0–34) and exhibiting elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone levels (80.57 μUI/mL; NR: 0.51–4.30) with normal free thyroxine. One year ago, he experienced increased urination and thirst, and blood tests showed elevated blood sugar levels (314.4 mg/dL; NR 50–80), a glycosylated hemoglobin value of 10.4% (NR 4.8–5.9), borderline normal C-peptide values (1.10 ng/mL; NR: 1.1–4.4), and negative anti-insulin antibodies. He began insulin treatment. Physical examination revealed a complete absence of scalp and body hair, along with nail changes such as trachyonychia and longitudinal ridges on three fingers.
test_results: Typical features of AA were found: multiple yellow dots, few vellus hairs, and areas devoid of any follicular units.
diagnosis: Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type III C

case_report: A 36-year-old male presented with a perianal mass and recurrent pus discharge persisting for over a decade. During this period, the perianal masses occasionally enlarged and were accompanied by additional painful masses and ruptured pus. Despite receiving anti-inflammatory treatment, the condition showed minimal improvement. On physical examination, with the patient in a lithotomy position, seven masses were observed at the 12, 1 to 3, and 5 o'clock positions, located approximately 2 to 7 cm from the anus. These masses exhibited light pressure pain, ulceration, and pus discharge, with a cord-like mass extending towards the anus. No other masses were detected upon rectal palpation. Laboratory tests and colonoscopy results were within normal limits. The patient reported no history of tuberculosis, and secretion cultures were negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
test_results: Enhanced MRI of the anal canal showed that 2 canal-like structures were seen on the left side of the anal canal, with low T1 and high T2 signal, with restricted diffusion and significant enhancement, and the internal opening was about 2 o’clock and 7 o’clock sites, one of which traveled posteriorly along the sphincter gap, and the other traveled forward through the external anal sphincter.

case_report: A 55-year-old female patient reported a painful, palpable mass on the anterolateral right thigh that had been present for one year. Her medical history included open reduction and internal fixation with a plate and screws for a mid-1/3 diaphyseal fracture of the femur following a car accident in 1984, with the implant removed one year post-surgery. Physical examination identified a 20 cm scar on the lateral thigh and a painful mass on palpation in the middle third of the right anterolateral thigh. Radiographs indicated cortical irregularities and thickening of the femur consistent with the patient's surgical history.
test_results: MRI showed an unencapsulated mass adjacent to the middle third of the femur with relatively well-defined margins. On T1 and T2 images, the tissue was seen to have fatty and fibrous components like tiger stripes. On gadolinium contrast T1 images, there was a heterogeneous low level of enhancement. The lesion was 75 x 32 x 29 mm in dimension. The histopathological analysis revealed that the majority of the biopsy sample consisted of striated muscle tissue. There were also abundant abnormal eosinophilic elastin fibers admixed with collagen and mature adipose tissue. Wavy, fragmented, coarse, elastic fibers with serrated edges were observed with Verhoeff elastin stain (EVG).

case_report: A 46-year-old female reported experiencing a diffuse soft-tissue swelling in her back for the past 2 years, which had been gradually increasing in size. The swelling was nontender. Upon physical examination, a mass was identified in the right inferior subscapular region, measuring 8 cm × 6 cm, with a smooth surface. Routine blood and biochemical tests were normal. MRI findings indicated a focal ill-defined altered signal intensity lesion in the right posterolateral chest wall, deep to the serratus anterior muscle. The patient underwent fine needle aspiration (FNA) cytology, which was reported as lipoma. Subsequently, she had an excisional biopsy. The lesion was irregular, not encapsulated, and measured 7 cm × 5 cm. The cut section was firm with grayish-white areas.
test_results: The lesion was poorly circumscribed and showed an admixture of collagenous tissue with mature adipocytes. The presence of numerous elastic fibers was noted. The elastic fibers were large, coarse, and deeply eosinophilic in nature. Additionally, there were many fragmented ones, which gave the appearance of beads on a string. There was no area of necrosis or increased mitotic activity. The Verhoeff's elastic stain confirmed the elastic nature of the fibers.

case_report: A 59-year-old woman was referred by her dentist for evaluation and management of an ulcerated lesion on the tongue. The patient reported that the lesion was first noticed approximately 6 months prior and experienced periods of worsening and improvement. She initially managed it with local application of baking soda. Her medical history included rheumatoid arthritis treated with prednisolone 7.5 mg/day and leflunomide 20 mg/day for the past 6 years, as well as hypertension and hypercholesterolemia managed with olmesartan and atorvastatin, respectively. She did not smoke or consume alcohol. Clinical examination revealed an irregularly shaped ulcer covered by a fibrinopurulent membrane and partly surrounded by a firmly attached white plaque on the ventral surface of the right side of the tongue. The ulcer measured approximately 1x0.5 cm and was soft and slightly painful on palpation. Small, white epithelial fragments around the lesion were easily removed with gauze, while the rest of the oral mucosa appeared normal. The lesion was in contact with broken amalgam fillings and decayed tooth roots. Complete dental restoration was recommended, and the patient was prescribed oral rinses with a dexamethasone oral drops solution (2 mg/ml x 10 ml) and local applications of chlorhexidine gel for 2 weeks. Upon re-examination six weeks later, the amalgam fillings had been replaced with composite resin fillings, and the roots were extracted approximately 2 weeks prior. Despite ongoing use of the dexamethasone solution, the lesions persisted. The patient declined a partial biopsy. Following her rheumatologist's advice, leflunomide was discontinued, and a re-examination a month later showed less than 50% healing of the ulcer. Another month later, the ulcer had not fully healed, and due to a relapse of rheumatoid arthritis, leflunomide was reintroduced at a reduced dose (10 mg/day). The patient then consented to the biopsy.
test_results: Microscopic examination of formalin-fixed and paraffin-embedded tissue sections showed an ulceration covered by a fibrinopurulent membrane and based by granulation tissue. It was surrounded by hyperparakeratotic and acanthotic stratified squamous epithelium, showing drop-shaped rete ridges, irregular stratification, loss of polarity of basal cells, increased nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio, cellular pleomorphism, increased nuclear size, increased number and size of nucleoli, dyskeratosis, as well as increased number of mitotic figures. The underlying connective tissue showed dense inflammatory infiltrates of lymphocytes, plasma cells and polymorphonuclears, mostly in a band-like subepithelial distribution. Atypical cell were not found in the connective tissue. A periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain did not reveal candidal hyphae.
Orpha_name: High-grade dysplasia in patients with Barrett esophagus

case_report: A 4-year-old Indian boy from a low-income farming family was admitted to the hospital for a routine blood transfusion. His weight and height were between the 10th and 50th percentile, with Z-scores of -1.71 and -1.54, respectively. He has O positive blood type and requires 10-12 blood transfusions annually. Medical records indicate his adult hemoglobin (HbA) is greater than 3%, with a mean corpuscular volume (MCV) of 74.89 fl and a mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) of 30.4 pg. Physical examination revealed knee pain and an enlarged spleen extending more than 3 cm below the costal margin. Family history shows that one of his two deceased male siblings had a similar condition, while his sisters are healthy.
test_results: The genomic DNA was isolated using the gDNA Blood Mini Kit (Chromous Biotech, Bengaluru, India). The BLAST method in the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) database was used to confirm the identification of the collected sequences. By comparing mutations to reference sequences, direct counting was used to determine their presence (NG 000007.3 Homo sapiens chromosome 11). The dbSNP, Clinvar, Ithanet, and HbVar databases were used to look for mutations that had been identified in other populations.

case_report: A 20-year-old female with a history of fever and thrombocytopenia tested positive for dengue via ELISA. She received symptomatic treatment and recovered within a few days. One week after the fever subsided, she experienced sudden difficulty swallowing, more pronounced with liquids than solids, and nasal regurgitation. She also had bilateral facial weakness, making it hard to close her eyes, expose her teeth while brushing, and causing food to accumulate between her cheek and gums during eating. Additionally, she had trouble manipulating and propelling the food bolus inside her mouth and oropharynx. Examination revealed bilateral involvement of cranial nerves 7 and 9–12, and areflexia in the upper limbs, while reflexes in the lower limbs were normal. Brain and cervical spine MRI were normal. Blood counts, liver function tests, renal function tests, thyroid hormone levels, serum Vitamin B12, and folic acid were all within normal ranges. Serum antinuclear antibody and anti-Ds DNA antibody levels were also normal.
test_results: CSF examination showed a protein level of 105 mg/dl, sugar 80 mg/dl, and no cells suggesting albuminocytological dissociation. Nerve conduction study showed reduced compound muscle action potential amplitude in bilateral upper limb nerves with normal conduction in the lower limb. Repetitive nerve stimulation test was done in the trapezius and abductor digiti minimi muscle showed no decremental response.

case_report: A 14-year-old Asian male arrived at the hospital with a two-week history of weakness in both upper limbs, nasal-sounding voice, difficulty swallowing, and trouble walking. Initially healthy, he began experiencing upper limb weakness that started gradually and progressed over the first week before stabilizing. This was accompanied by tingling and numbness. He had trouble holding objects and performing overhead movements. Seven days before admission, he developed difficulty swallowing, and his voice became nasal. Subsequently, he experienced difficulty walking and clumsiness in his lower limbs. There were no episodes of altered consciousness, loss of consciousness, or seizures. Bowel and bladder functions were unaffected at the onset. He did not report any preceding symptoms of respiratory infections or diarrhea. His medical history was unremarkable, and he had not received any immunizations in the month prior. There was no history of drug or heavy metal exposure, nor any similar conditions in family members. General physical examination was normal. The patient exhibited dysarthria, nasal intonation of voice, and a weak gag reflex. The uvula was central with reduced movement. Neck muscle strength was preserved, and there was no facial deviation. All other cranial nerves were intact. Muscle strength was graded 4/5 in the upper limbs and 5/5 in the lower limbs according to the Medical Research Council (MRC) grading. Deep tendon reflexes were absent in both upper and lower limbs, and plantar reflexes were downgoing bilaterally. Sensations were intact in both upper and lower limbs. His single breath counting was normal. Other system examinations were unremarkable. Routine blood and urine tests were within normal limits.
test_results: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination revealed total leukocyte count, 5 cells/mm3; protein, 60 mg/dL; glucose, 3.5 mmol/L. Nerve conduction study (NCS) showed increased latencies of the right and left common peroneal nerves (CPN) (8.44 milliseconds and 13.5 milliseconds, respectively, normal: less than 6.5 milliseconds); features suggestive of acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy of motor nerves.

case_report: A 55-year-old male arrived at the neurological emergency department with a three-day history of worsening speech difficulties and trouble swallowing solids, along with numbness in the tongue. Following this, the patient experienced tingling sensations and weakness in the upper limbs. There was no prior history of illnesses or infectious diseases. Vital signs were normal. Neurological examination showed normal mental status. Cranial nerve assessment indicated bilateral facial weakness (inability to keep eyelids closed against resistance), a symmetric uvula with limited elevation of the soft palate, an absent gag reflex, and restricted tongue movement against resistance. No issues with eye movement or coordination were noted. Muscle strength evaluation revealed weakness in the neck flexor and extensor muscles, and bilateral, symmetric upper limb weakness with a 2/5 Daniels score in the deltoids, biceps, and hand extensor muscles. Lower limb muscle strength was normal with a 5/5 Daniels score in the iliopsoas, quadriceps femoris, and tibialis anterior muscles. Reflex examination showed reduced reflexes in the upper limbs and increased reflexes in the lower limbs. Plantar reflexes elicited a flexor response. Proprioception, exteroception, gait, and cerebellar functions were intact.
test_results: Protein levels of 35 mg/dL (normal range: 15-45 mg/dL), glucose levels of 53 mg/dL (normal range: 50-80 mg/dL), and no cells in the cerebrospinal fluid (WBC: 0-5/mm3; RBC: 0/mm3). Nerve conduction studies reported acute motor and sensory axonal neuropathy (AMSAN).

case_report: A 31-year-old previously healthy female experienced 4 days of bilateral numbness starting distally in her feet and hands, which then spread to all four extremities and the front and back of her trunk. During the same period, she lost her balance, initially becoming unable to walk and then unable to sit without falling to either side. She also had difficulty reaching for objects. She did not report double vision, slurred speech, facial numbness or droop, tremors, limb weakness, abdominal distention, sphincteric issues, or dryness of the mouth or eyes. There was no weight loss, joint stiffness, swelling, or pain. Family history was unremarkable. She had a generalized skin rash 10 days before the onset of neurological symptoms, diagnosed as primary Chickenpox infection by a dermatologist who prescribed oral acyclovir. Neurological examination showed normal higher mental functions and intact cranial nerves, with no nystagmus, ptosis, or limitation of eye movements. Muscle strength was 5/5 throughout. Sensory examination revealed severe impairment in joint position and vibration sensation in both upper limbs to the elbows and lower limbs to the knees. Pain and temperature sensation were symmetrically impaired over both upper and lower limbs and the trunk, with more pronounced impairment over the anterior trunk. There was no sensory level. Reflexes were absent throughout. Babinski’s sign was negative bilaterally. Coordination tests showed impaired finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin movements, significantly worsened by eye closure. She could not maintain a sitting position due to severe truncal ataxia and exhibited pseudo-athetoid movements in the hands. There were no dysautonomic signs such as blood pressure and pulse fluctuations, and no ileus. Initial basic laboratory tests were normal.
test_results: Lumbar puncture revealed CSF protein 61.1 mg/dl (reference range 15–45 mg/dl), with normal CSF white cell count (3 cells). CSF cultures and viral PCRs were negative. Brain MRI with and without contrast was normal. Whole spine MRI with contrast demonstrated enhancement in multiple thoracic and lumbar nerve roots. NCS performed on the fifth day of admission showed absent sensory responses in her four extremities, with normal motor responses and F-waves. Initial electromyography “EMG” using concentric needle was normal. Serum VZV IgM was elevated (18.9).

case_report: A 43-year-old female presented with numbness in the distal lower limbs, which spread to all limbs over a period of four days. She was admitted to the First Affiliated Hospital of Dalian Medical University on April 26, 2011. Two weeks prior to admission, she experienced nonspecific flu-like symptoms and a mild sore throat. Initially, she noticed numbness on the soles of her feet, which progressed to her knees within two days, leading to difficulty walking and poor balance. Over the following days, she developed a markedly unsteady gait and increased tingling sensations in the distal lower limbs, which spread further. She also experienced occasional clumsiness in the upper limbs and pseudoathetosis. The symptoms reached their peak within three weeks.
test_results: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) routing revealed 1,194 mg/l of protein and a cell count of 2×106/l. Routine NCSs revealed absent sensory potentials, while the motor NCS was normal. Sagittal T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans of the cervical spine revealed a normal appearance of the posterior column, despite a number of disc osteophyte complexes with mild central canal stenosis at the cervical level. Light microscopy showed moderate subperineurial edema, mild loss of myelinated fibers and a few thinly myelinated fibers without inflammatory changes. The form of regenerated nerve fibers have complete structure of myelinated nerve fascicles, and these myelinated nerve fibers are thicker than other parts of the biopsy. Electron microscopy revealed normal myelinated and unmyelinated axons, however, the Schwann cell nucleui were broken down and the cytoplasm of the Schwann cells were pale watery moderately. Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated that the majority of the cells within the nerve fascicles were strongly positive for S-100, moderately positive for neuron-specific enolase (NSE) and mildly positive for neurofilament (NF), while the perineurium was mildly positive for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA). No anatomical abnormalities were observed and the density of the fibers moderately decreased.

case_report: A 13-month-old girl was admitted due to inadequate weight gain. She is the second child of healthy, unrelated parents with heights of 190 cm (father) and 175 cm (mother). The patient was born at 37 weeks gestation. During the 4th to 8th weeks of pregnancy, the mother experienced vaginal bleeding. Intrauterine growth retardation was noted at the 8th week due to placental insufficiency. The mother smoked throughout the pregnancy. The newborn was asymmetrical and small for gestational age, with a birth weight of 2420 g (<3rd percentile, z-score: -1.93) and a length of 44 cm (<3rd percentile, z-score: -2.76). Head circumference was 34.5 cm (70th percentile, z-score: 0.52). She was partially breast-fed for the first 30 days. Due to difficulty in accepting formula milk, she was transferred to the pediatric gastroenterology department at nine months, where a 24-hour nasogastric tube was placed and hypercaloric oral supplements were given, but there was no significant weight gain. At 13 months, physical examination revealed that the infant was small and thin. Her length was 60 cm (<3rd percentile, z-score: -6.03) and her weight was 5470 g (<3rd percentile, z-score: -4.35). Head circumference was 45 cm (40th percentile, z-score: -0.27) with a triangular head shape and open fontanelles. Hair was sparse, ears were low set, and the nasal bridge was underdeveloped. Dental development was delayed with only one tooth present. Motor milestones were delayed; she could sit but not stand. Systematic clinical examination of the heart, lungs, and abdomen showed no abnormalities. Complete blood count, hemoglobin levels, glucose concentrations, and renal function were normal for her age. Karyotype analysis indicated a normal female genotype of 46 XX. Thyroid and adrenal hormone levels were within normal ranges. Tests for celiac disease and food allergies were negative.
test_results: Serum GH response to clonidine, glucagon and arginine stimulation tests revealed very poor response, with a peak GH value of 4.77 ng/mL.
diagnosis: Isolated Growth Hormone Deficiency Type Ib
Orpha_name: Isolated Growth Hormone Deficiency Type Ib

case_report: A 38-year-old female presented to the emergency room with a one-week history of high-grade intermittent fever. She subsequently developed progressive jaundice, dark urine, itching, and left upper abdominal discomfort. Over the past five days, she experienced gradually worsening shortness of breath without orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Additionally, she had an altered sleep-wake cycle for two days without melena or hematemesis. Her medical history included recurrent red blood cell transfusions (one to two packed red blood cells per month) since childhood, but no hematological disease had been diagnosed. On examination, she exhibited pallor, jaundice, yellow skin discoloration, and tachypnea with an oxygen saturation of 88% on room air. Hepatomegaly was noted with a liver span of 20 cm, and the spleen was palpable 10 cm below the left costal margin. Respiratory, cardiovascular, and neurological examinations were normal. Laboratory findings showed bicytopenia with microcytic hypochromic red blood cells, nucleated red blood cells, hemoglobin of 4.6 g/dL, a reticulocyte index of 3.48, a total white cell count of 62 ×10^9/L, and a platelet count of 60 ×10^9/L. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was elevated at 2510 IU/L. Liver function tests indicated direct hyperbilirubinemia with a total bilirubin of 47.8 mg/dL and direct bilirubin of 41 mg/dL. Kidney function tests showed urea at 103 mg/dL and creatinine at 2.21 mg/dL. Prothrombin time and international normalized ratio (PT/INR) were 28 seconds and 2.15, respectively. C-reactive protein (CRP) was 192 mg/L, and serum procalcitonin was greater than 75 ng/mL. Initial management included treatment for sepsis with multiple organ dysfunction. Due to high leukocyte count and procalcitonin levels, empirical antibiotics were started to cover community-acquired pneumonia and tropical infections. An ultrasound of the abdomen showed no biliary obstruction or cholangitis. A chest X-ray revealed left-sided pleural effusion. Arterial blood gases indicated moderate acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), which improved with supplemental oxygen. Acute kidney injury improved with intravenous hydration. The patient had acute liver failure with grade 2 hepatic encephalopathy and abnormal coagulation, managed with oral lactulose and rifaximin. No gastrointestinal bleeding was observed. Blood cultures for bacteria and fungi were negative, as were bacterial cultures of pleural fluid and urine. Tests for dengue, malaria, scrub typhus, leptospirosis, hepatitis B and C, HIV, and autoimmune hepatitis were negative. Despite multiple packed RBC transfusions, the patient had worsening anemia and a high reticulocyte index. Serum LDH was elevated. Coombs' test was non-reactive. Ultrasound of the abdomen suggested splenic sequestration. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) of the thorax and abdomen revealed left-sided mild to moderate pleural effusion and splenomegaly with large hypo/non-enhancing areas, indicative of splenic sequestration.
test_results: High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) was done, and reports revealed hemoglobin S (Hb S) of 26.1%.
diagnosis: Sickle Cell Anemia with Acute Chest Syndrome

case_report: A 50-year-old female presented to the emergency department with a three-day history of widespread abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea. She reported recent cocaine use. Blood tests indicated a serum total bilirubin level of 2.5 mg/dL (normal range: 0.3–1.9 mg/dL). Physical examination showed a distended and generally tender abdomen. Her vital signs included a blood pressure of 124/77, pulse rate of 93, temperature of 37.3°C, and an oxygen saturation of 95% on room air.
test_results: A computed tomography (CT) scan showed a splenic infarct, mildly dilated small bowel loops, and moderate ascites.

case_report: A six-year-old girl was seen at the Strabismus and Pediatric Ophthalmology Service at the Shahid Mottahhari Clinic in southern Iran due to outward deviation and reduced visual acuity in her left eye. She is the first child in her family and was delivered via cesarean section due to her mother's uncontrolled gestational diabetes mellitus. Her birth weight was 3.2 kg. At two years old, she had a lensectomy and posterior intraocular lens implantation for a congenital cataract in her left eye. There is no family history of congenital cataract or ocular deviations, and she has no neurodevelopmental delays. Ophthalmologic examination showed best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 20/25 in the right eye and 20/300 in the left eye. Cycloplegic refraction was +0.25–0.25*125 in the right eye and +1.5–2.00*170 in the left eye. Intraocular pressure, measured by air puff tonometry, was 17 mmHg in the right eye and 13 mmHg in the left eye. She exhibited a left exotropia of 8 prism diopters in the primary position.
test_results: Ocular motility examination showed limitation in adduction and abduction with narrowing of the palpebral fissure and downshoot and upshoot upon attempted adduction in the left eye.

case_report: A seven-month-old male presented with an eye turn since birth. Examination revealed esotropia at near measuring 60 prism-diopters, alternate fixation with a preference for the right eye, and -4 abduction in both eyes. Cycloplegic refraction was +1.50 diopters in both eyes, and the rest of the ophthalmic examination was unremarkable. Surgical intervention included a 6mm medial rectus muscle recession in both eyes and a 6mm lateral rectus resection in the left eye. One week after surgery, the patient exhibited orthotropia with a palpebral fissure in the left eye that was 1 mm narrower than that of the right eye.
test_results: Forced duction test revealed no resistance to abduction and slight resistance to adduction in either eye.

case_report: A 23-year-old male army officer visited the clinic with complaints of decreased visual acuity in his left eye over the past 5 months. He had no prior history of eye diseases or surgeries and reported no symptoms such as itching, redness, photophobia, or tearing. Clinical evaluation showed his best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/20 with −4.50 sph −0.75 cyl 40° in the right eye. The BCVA in the left eye was 20/300 and could not be improved with a refractive correction of −19.00 sph −4.25 cyl 45°. Intraocular pressures measured by a noncontact tonometer were 6 mm Hg in both eyes. Examination of the anterior ocular segment using a slit lamp was unremarkable, with clear cornea and lens, and no signs of inflammation in the anterior chamber. Pupils were equal in diameter and reactive to light, with no relative afferent pupillary defects observed. Dilated fundus examination showed no edema, exudation, or abnormalities in the retina or optic papilla. B-ultrasound scanning revealed no obvious morphological changes in either eye. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed no detachment, schisis, or holes in the macular retina, with foveal thickness measured at 259 μm in the right eye and 252 μm in the left eye. The thickness of the peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer was within normal limits in both eyes. Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) showed no leakage of fluorescence in any phase in either eye, and indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) revealed no abnormalities. Electroretinography (ERG) performed with a Ganzfeld stimulator showed no significant changes in amplitude and peak time in both dark-adapted and light-adapted responses, with comparable data between both eyes. Pattern visual evoked potentials (PVEP) recorded a slightly reduced amplitude and delayed peak time in the P100-wave of both the 1° and 0.25° PVEP in both eyes, with the delayed peak time more pronounced in the right eye and the reduced amplitude more pronounced in the left eye. Flash visual evoked potentials (FVEP) showed reproducible and reliable waveforms in both eyes, with the amplitude and peak time of the P2-wave within normative ranges and comparable between both eyes.
test_results: An asymmetrical bowtie pattern of the cornea was found in both eyes, which was more obvious in the OS.

case_report: A 45-year-old female, housewife, presented in May 2002 with a 40-day history of voice changes and snoring. She had no history of smoking, pulmonary disorders, or previous laryngeal issues. Physical examination revealed a mass in the right side of her neck. Laryngoscopic examination showed a bulging near the ventricular fold and the right aryepiglottic fold.
test_results: CT scan and MRI revealed a large cystic lesion filled with air.

case_report: A 56-year-old male with a history of B-related chronic hepatitis under antiretroviral treatment was referred to the surgical department by the Infectious Diseases Unit, where he was being monitored. The patient did not report any gastrointestinal symptoms. An abdominal ultrasonography revealed a hypoechoic, round-shaped mass measuring 4.7 cm with regular margins, situated between the left lobe of the liver and the anterior surface of the pancreatic body. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a cystic mass with complex content located anterior to the gastroesophageal junction. Further imaging showed a hypoechoic mass with slightly heterogeneous internal echoes and regular margins, located just below the gastroesophageal junction. The lesion measured approximately 4.5 cm and appeared contiguous to the fourth layer of the gastric wall (muscularis propria).
test_results: The puncture was practiced using a 22 G needle, which, unexpectedly, penetrated very easily into the mass as it was cystic. We were able to aspirate only a few milliliters of a clear mucus-like fluid, and then a cytological sampling was made from the cystic wall. The collected material was judged adequate by an onsite cytopathologist. The cytological smear showed cylindrical cells isolated or aggregated in small groups with a palisade organization. These cells showed long cilia and brush borders similar to the ciliated cells of the respiratory tract. These basal cells had oval nuclei with finely dispersed chromatin and small nucleoli, if any. The background consisted of proteinaceous material containing debris, crystal formations and engulfed hystiocytes.
diagnosis: Foregut duplication cyst of the stomach

case_report: An 11-year-old boy with global developmental delay and autistic features, without congenital defects or facial dysmorphic features, and a negative family history for neurodevelopmental disorders was referred for whole exome sequencing (WES). The gestation and delivery period were uneventful. The first epileptic seizures appeared at the age of 2 years. At that time, there was also profound hypotonia with preserved tendon reflexes. The boy was not able to walk independently or communicate verbally.
test_results: The EEG showed generalized paroxysmal changes with slow spike-and-wave complexes (<3 Hz). Brain MRI and neurometabolic workup were normal.

case_report: A 19-year-old male experienced his first generalized seizure at the age of 8 without any identifiable cause. He occasionally reported seeing bright or colorful flashing lights, blurry vision, and changes in distance perception in both visual fields before seizures, predominantly on the right side. These visual disturbances typically lasted several minutes and sometimes occurred independently of seizures. At age 17, he began having transient nodding episodes, often without any preceding visual disturbances. By age 18, he frequently experienced sudden dropping episodes, characterized by clenched hands and slight forearm flexion. Post-episode, he could stand up on his own without any preceding visual disturbances or memory of the event. These nodding and dropping episodes occurred 2–10 times over 4–5 days, often in clusters. He was previously diagnosed with refractory epilepsy and underwent presurgical evaluation at another facility. MRI scans showed no abnormalities, and he was monitored using stereotactic electroencephalography (SEEG) targeting the temporal, parietal, and occipital regions, particularly on the left side, but without clear lateralization or localization. Despite receiving vagal nerve stimulation (VNS) and five different antiepileptic medications, there was no significant improvement. Consequently, he was admitted to our hospital for further treatment. His family, perinatal, and growth history, as well as physical examination results, were unremarkable.
test_results: Wakeful background on video electroencephalography showed 9–10 Hz alpha rhythm in bilateral occipital regions. Interictal EEG showed generalized 2–2.5 Hz slow spike waves (SSWs) during wakefulness and generalized paroxysmal fast activities (GPFAs) during sleep. There were also multifocal independent spikes, especially in the bilateral occipital and posterior temporal regions where the left side was more predominant than the right. Compared with SSWs and occipital discharges, GPFA was more prominent, followed by occipital discharges. Epileptic spasms, tonic seizures, and atypical absence were recorded, which showed EEG onsets with a little localization value. MRI showed a suspiciously unclear gray-white matter boundary around the left calcarine sulcus, which also showed low metabolism on positron emission tomography. Neuropsychological tests showed moderate cognitive impairment. No abnormalities were found on genetic testing and perimetry.

case_report: A 68-year-old Japanese male reported experiencing increased urination and excessive thirst for a duration of 3 months. His medical history was unremarkable, with no prior illnesses or treatments, including immunotherapy or radiotherapy. Family and social histories were also unremarkable. Physical examination indicated mildly dehydrated skin. The patient did not report any headaches or issues with visual fields. Laboratory tests showed normal sodium levels (140 mEq/L), undetectable serum AVP concentration, and low urine osmolarity (199 mOsm/kg).
test_results: T1-weighted MRI showed the absence of hyperintensity in the posterior lobe of the pituitary. Contrast-enhanced imaging revealed thickening of the infundibulum (4.88 mm) and delayed enhancement of the whole pituitary. Serum anti-Rabphilin 3A antibody was positive. An AVH test revealed an increase in urine osmolarity after administration (470 mOsm/kg), whereas a low maximal AVP (1.6 pmol/L) with raised plasma osmolarity (311 mOsm/kg) was observed on 5% hypertonic saline infusion.

case_report: A 72-year-old male, previously a high school mathematics state champion with an IQ of 164, presented with difficulties in word-finding and performing calculations. There was no family history of dementia, except for his mother, who experienced cognitive decline in her 90s. Genetic analysis revealed an ApoE genotype of 3/3. Neuropsychological testing indicated features consistent with subcortical dementia.
test_results: His CSF showed reduced Aβ42 and increased p-tau. He underwent HLA-DR/DQ testing, which revealed that he carried the uncommon, multiple biotoxin sensitivity haplotype 4-3-53. Urine testing was positive for mycotoxins.

case_report: A 70-year-old male received a [18F]Florbetaben PET/CT scan one day after his first dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine administered in the right arm. The patient had no related symptoms at the time. Additionally, he had a history of hypertensive disease and early signs of heart failure, with potential cardiac amyloidosis. Consequently, the thorax was included in the imaging field.
test_results: A moderate amyloid burden on the bilateral frontal and parietal brain cortex in the absence of cardiac beta-amyloid deposition was identified. Subcutaneous uptake on the vaccination site in the right arm’s deltoid region and focal uptake next to an ipsilateral axillary lymph node were noted. Tracer injection was via the left antecubital fossa. [18F]Florbetaben MIP (A), PET (axial-B, coronal-G), CT (axial-C, coronal-E), PET/CT (axial-D, coronal-F) images demonstrated ill-defined uptake in the right arm’s subcutaneous tissues (SUVmax 5.6; white-arrows) and next to a possible right-axillar lymph node (SUVmax 4.75; yellow-arrows) evident on low-dose CT scan without breathing control (red arrows).

case_report: A 59-year-old, right-handed female with 12 years of education presented with a 2-year history of difficulty understanding spoken language. She had a background of well-controlled hypertension for 5 years. The patient reported that spoken conversation sounded like noise or buzzing, especially in crowded areas. She could not understand spoken questions during the interview but could comprehend and respond correctly through lip reading or gestural cues. She struggled to understand television dialogue but could follow foreign movies with Korean subtitles without issue. Environmental noises like doorbells and ringing phones were perceived and responded to appropriately. Her family noted no issues with her ability to express thoughts, recall events, navigate directions, or use public transportation. She managed household tasks, financial matters, and social activities without difficulty. A hearing aid prescribed by an otolaryngology clinic did not improve her comprehension. One year after symptom onset, she began making errors in simple mathematics and her spoken language comprehension declined significantly, though she could still read and write. Her writing style became rough with frequent spelling errors. She occasionally forgot things but it did not impact daily life. She had trouble recalling names of familiar neighbors but recognized them visually. Her demeanor and personal relationships remained unaffected. On examination, she scored 17 out of 30 on the Mini-Mental State Examination, with specific deficits in calculation, recall, and language. Neurological examination was unremarkable except for mild rigidity in the right upper extremity. The Korean version of the Western Aphasia Battery showed fluent spontaneous speech with phonemic paraphasia and mild neurogenic stuttering. Severe impairments were noted in comprehension and repetition, with mild impairments in visual confrontational naming and word generation. She could read aloud and understand written words and sentences, and communicate in writing with some literal errors. Audiological examination revealed mild bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with pure-tone thresholds of 30 dB in the left ear and 35 dB in the right ear within the 500-2,000 Hz range. Speech audiometry thresholds were 50 dB in the left ear and 60 dB in the right ear, with speech discrimination abilities of 32% at 80 dB in the left ear and 20% at 85 dB in the right ear. Brainstem auditory evoked potential responses were normal. She recognized six out of eight nonverbal animal sounds and correctly matched four out of six songs to their written titles. Neuropsychological test instructions were given in written form. She performed below normal on the Korean version of the Boston Naming Test, ideomotor praxis, Rey figure-copying test, calculation, finger naming, and the semantic subtest of the controlled oral association word recall test. In a Navon figure task, she recognized only small letters, indicating simultanagnosia. She had difficulty naming famous people but could describe the occupations of some she could not name. Routine laboratory tests showed no evidence of comorbid disease.
test_results: [11C] PIB-PET revealed elevated PIB binding in diffuse cortical areas, especially in the temporoparieto-occipital cortices. 18FDG-PET scan revealed hypometabolism in bilateral temporoparietal areas, with greater effects on the left. Brain MRI demonstrated mild atrophy in both temporal lobes, with the left side more affected.

case_report: A 12-year-old boy visited the Paediatric Department with complaints of severe headache. His medical history included congenital hypothyroidism and idiopathic growth hormone insufficiency. His body mass index (BMI) was 13, and he was receiving thyroxine treatment. Additionally, he was in the 8th week of recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) treatment at a dose of 1.5 mg daily (or 4.5 IU daily). On the same day, he was referred to the Eye Department for further evaluation. Initial examination showed his best corrected visual acuity was 6/9 in both eyes. Intraocular pressures (IOPs) were measured at 12 mmHg in the right eye and 15 mmHg in the left eye. Color vision tested via Ishihara plates showed no defects in either eye. The anterior chamber and papillary reflexes were normal, and no relative afferent papillary defect (RAPD) was detected in either eye. Fundoscopy revealed bilateral hyperaemic optic nerve edema, absence of spontaneous venous pulsations, and increased retinal vessel tortuosity. There was elevation of the nasal and temporal circumference of the optic nerve, obscuring some segments of the major retinal vessels, and a halo surrounding the disc was noted in both eyes (Stage 3, staging scheme of swelling of the optic nerve head by Frisen). Initial visual field testing was inconclusive due to patient non-cooperation. A subsequent visual field test showed an enlargement of the blind spot in both eyes without other abnormalities. Further investigations, including blood pressure measurements and blood tests, were within normal limits. The patient was also assessed by a neurologist.
test_results: The CT scan showed normal ventricular size, swelling of optic nerve heads, and a partially empty sella without any evidence of mass, haemorrhage, edema, or midline shift. Lumbar puncture revealed an elevated opening pressure of 36 cm water and a normal spinal fluid composition.

case_report: A 31-year-old woman of mixed Jamaican and English heritage presented to the emergency department with a 4-week history of menorrhagia and a 3-week history of lethargy, palpitations, exertional dyspnea, postural dizziness, syncopal episodes, headache, and vomiting. Initially, she denied visual symptoms and was admitted to the gynecology unit for treatment and monitoring. She had a normal body mass index of 24, and her medical, drug, and family history were unremarkable, except for a congenital left esotropia corrected with bilateral medial rectus recession during childhood. The following day, she reported developing pulsatile tinnitus, intermittent blurred vision, and transient visual obscurations over the past 2 weeks. Three days prior to admission, she experienced neck pain and photophobia, and 2 days prior to admission, she noticed mild clumsiness of the right arm and hand and numbness on the right scalp and right fingertips. An urgent ophthalmic and orthoptic examination revealed severe papilledema (grade 5 on Frisén scale) and partial right lateral rectus palsy. She was afebrile and mildly hypotensive (blood pressure 87/62 mmHg). Best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 6/9 in the right eye and 6/6 in the left eye. Standard color vision test with Ishihara plates was 16/17 in the right eye and 15/17 in the left eye. No relative afferent pupillary defect was observed. Intraocular pressure and anterior segment were unremarkable. The peripheral retina, vessels, and other cranial nerves were normal. An urgent inpatient neurological review and peripheral neurological examination were normal. Goldmann visual field testing showed an enlarged left blind spot and constriction of peripheral fields in both eyes. Ultra-widefield imaging (Optos®) confirmed severe papilledema, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrated subretinal fluid in the peripapillary and macular area. Blood tests revealed a hemoglobin level of 74 gm/L and mean cell volume of 63.0 fL consistent with microcytic anemia, as well as a platelet count of 584 × 10^9/L consistent with thrombocytosis. Peripheral smear showed microcytic hypochromic red blood cells with anisopoikilocytosis. Iron studies indicated iron deficiency: serum iron 2.2 μmol/L, serum total iron binding capacity 94.7 μmol/L, transferrin saturation 2.3%, and ferritin 2 μg/L. The remainder of the full blood count, serum chemistry, liver function, renal function, thyroid function, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, clotting screen, C-reactive protein, vitamin B12, and folate were normal. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed no uterine abnormalities. Comprehensive infection and autoimmune screens were negative. Apart from menorrhagia, no other etiology for iron deficiency anemia was found. An urgent CT head and CT venogram showed no intracerebral lesions but revealed bilateral focal narrowing at the transverse and sigmoid junctions, more conspicuous on the left. There were filling defects at the proximal right sigmoid sinus consistent with arachnoid granulations, and no evidence of venous sinus thrombosis. There was prominence of the perioptic cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) spaces with minimal flattening of the sclera, especially on the left. CSF opening pressure on lumbar puncture was 63 cm H2O and closing pressure 27 cm H2O. Cytological and biochemical analyses of CSF were normal. Bacterial culture, viral polymerase chain reaction, and malignant cytology were negative. No other hormonal or metabolic cause of raised intracranial pressure was found.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with venography revealed findings of bilateral transverse sigmoid sinus narrowing, prominence of the perioptic nerve spaces and an empty sella.

case_report: A 35-year-old male presented with a swelling in the right lower abdomen, which had been present for three months. Initially, he experienced pain in the right lower abdomen that radiated to the right lower limb. The pain worsened with exertion and was partially alleviated by rest and analgesics. Over time, he noticed a progressively enlarging swelling in the right iliac region. There was no history of trauma. Physical examination revealed a smooth, immobile, and firm swelling in the right iliac fossa. The patient exhibited a right hip fixed flexion deformity of 30 degrees, with further flexion possible up to 110 degrees. Routine blood tests were normal. A plain radiograph showed a lytic lesion in the right iliac wing, measuring 5 × 6 cm, with minimal periosteal reaction. Ultrasound imaging revealed a 12.5 × 12.8 cm solid mass in the right iliac fossa with destruction of the underlying iliac bone. A bone scan indicated a primary lesion in the right iliac bone. MRI findings included a large lytic lesion involving the right iliac bone with a significant soft tissue component, heterogeneous signal intensity, lobulated margins, and a hypointense capsule, without encasement of the neurovascular bundle. The gluteal and iliopsoas muscles were also involved. A trucut biopsy was performed, but the sample was inadequate, necessitating a repeat biopsy under ultrasound guidance. The ultrasound-guided biopsy of the right iliac fossa soft tissue mass was conducted under local anesthesia and revealed friable and necrotic tissue.
test_results: Microscopically, it consisted mostly of organized hematoma, with central signs of recent haemorrhage. No signs of malignant degeneration were seen. The tumor consisted mainly of organized hematoma with a fibrous capsule.

case_report: In August 2021, a 22-year-old woman from Cameroon, who had been residing in Italy for 4 months, visited the Emergency Ophthalmology Department at Policlinico di Bari with symptoms of photophobia, tearing, and itching in her left eye. Her medical history included a year-long period of abdominal discomfort, dysmenorrhea with a history of polycystic ovaries, a spontaneous abortion in January 2021, and a fracture of the orbital floor that required hospitalization in July 2021. She reported a migration journey that began in 2017, passing through Nigeria, Niger, Algeria, and Libya, where she lived for 18 months. During the clinical examination at the Emergency Ophthalmology Department, a moving parasite was observed in the subconjunctiva of the temporal region, accompanied by conjunctival hyperemia and eyelid edema, but without ulceration. No subcutaneous serpiginous cord was noted, but a recent 0.7-cm papular lesion on the dorsal surface of the right wrist and a 0.5 × 1.5 cm nodular lesion in the scapular region were detected. An orbital and head computed tomographic scan showed no abnormalities, while a total body computed tomographic scan revealed bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy. She was admitted to the Ophthalmology Unit for surgical removal of the parasite, but the following day, the parasite was no longer visible in the eye. The patient was then transferred to the infectious disease ward, where she reported cutaneous itching and lower abdominal pain during a physical examination. Throughout her hospitalization, the eye parasite was not visible, although she continued to experience a foreign-body sensation in the eye and conjunctival hyperemia.
test_results: On microscopic examination of blood collected during daylight hours, microfilariae were observed. The parasitological test confirmed the presence of microfilariae (MF) in two blood samples collected in the morning of two different days (at 8:00 am and 11 am, respectively) showing a different parasitic load of 144 MF/mL and 460 MF/mL, respectively.

case_report: A 20-year-old male visited the outpatient dermatology clinic with multiple widespread areas of increased and decreased pigmentation on his body, which began when he was eight years old. These areas initially appeared on the trunk and upper parts of the limbs and gradually became more numerous. The pigmentation changes were observed on the trunk, limbs, and neck, but not on the face, palms, or soles. Hair, nails, and mucous membranes were unaffected. There were no signs of skin scarring or visible small blood vessels. The patient had no notable medical history, including issues like light sensitivity, seizures, diabetes, or the use of any topical or systemic medications. He was born to parents who are not related by blood, and no other family members had similar symptoms, indicating a sporadic occurrence.
test_results: The pathology sections showed skin tissue with mild hyperkeratosis, basal layer hyperpigmentation, obvious melanin incontinence, and scattered lymphocytic infiltration in the upper dermis.

case_report: A 31-year-old unmarried male presented with progressively increasing, generalized mottled pigmentation since the age of 3 years. The lesions began on the neck and trunk and spread centrifugally to the extremities over a period of 10 years. There was no history of photosensitivity, direct handling of chemicals, or significant drug intake. Similar lesions were noted in his younger brother, while his younger sister was unaffected. There was no history of consanguinity among the parents, who were also unaffected. Dermatological examination revealed multiple hyper- and hypo-pigmented macules of varying sizes (2 to 30 mm) in a reticulate pattern without atrophy on the forehead, trunk, and upper and lower extremities. Reticulate pigmentation was also present on the palms with absent dermatoglyphics distal to the distal creases. Dystrophic changes in the fingernails, including longitudinal striations, ragged cuticles, and pterygium in one fingernail, were observed. Mucous membranes and soles were normal. Systemic examination did not reveal any abnormalities. Routine investigations, including complete blood counts, urinalysis, liver function tests, renal function tests, and serum electrolytes, were within normal limits. Venereal Disease Research Laboratory test and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for human immunodeficiency virus were both nonreactive.
test_results: Histopathological examination from hyperpigmented lesions showed mild hyperkeratosis. The basal layer showed pigmentation with some coarse melanocyte granules, predominantly in the lower 2–3 layers of the epidermis. There was prominent melanin incontinence with melanophages in the dermis. Sparse lymphohistiocytic infiltrates were seen in the perivascular areas.

case_report: A 38-year-old married male presented with generalized, asymptomatic, symmetrical, and spotty hyper- and hypopigmented macules over the body. The lesions appeared in infancy and progressed with age, starting over the extremities and gradually spreading to the trunk over six years. The face was spared. There was no history of photosensitivity, photophobia, preceding dermatosis, or associated systemic involvement. He was born to healthy non-consanguineous parents following an uneventful pregnancy. Similar lesions were reported in his brother, sister, and paternal grandmother's sister. The patient did not have any children. Cutaneous examination revealed multiple discrete circular and irregular-shaped mottled hyperpigmented and hypopigmented macules measuring 2-3 mm in size, distributed symmetrically over the trunk and upper limbs. There was symmetric, diffuse hypopigmentation with spotty hyperpigmented macules on the lower limb, sparing the knees and dorsum of the foot. Symmetric hypopigmented patches with spotty hyperpigmented macules were observed on the palms. The soles were not affected. There was no atrophy or telangiectasia of the affected skin. The face was spared. Mucous membrane, hair, and nails were uninvolved. Systemic examination did not reveal any abnormality. Laboratory examination, including complete hemogram, renal and liver function tests, blood HIV, and HbsAg, were nonreactive or within normal limits. Ultrasonogram of the abdomen showed no detectable abnormality.
test_results: The section studied showed keratinized thinned out epidermis. The dermis showed a few pilosebaceous units surrounded by sparse lymphocytic infiltrate. There was no evidence of increased epidermal pigmentation or pigment incontinence.

case_report: A 28-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1 at 36 weeks' gestation, presented to a maternal-fetal outpatient clinic with a fever and headache. She had no significant past medical history and consumed alcohol occasionally. Her pre-pregnancy body mass index (BMI) was 27. She was prescribed analgesics and scheduled for follow-up. Two days later, she was brought back by her husband due to a subacute onset of impaired consciousness. Blood tests revealed a significant elevation in liver enzymes and C-reactive protein (CRP), prompting her transfer to a tertiary hospital. Upon arrival, her Glasgow coma scale (GCS) was E4V4M5, body temperature was 40.6℃, pulse rate was 147/min, respiratory rate was 24/min, oxygen saturation was 99% in room air, and blood pressure was 116/91 mmHg. The abdomen was nontender. Abdominal ultrasound indicated increased liver brightness. Cardiotocogram showed no signs of non-reassuring fetal status (NRFS). Blood tests revealed a white blood cell count of 8,830/μL, platelet count of 133,000/μL, hemoglobin concentration of 10.7 g/dL, serum urea nitrogen of 8 mg/dL, creatinine of 0.51 mg/dL, uric acid of 8.0 mg/dL, ammonia of 17 μg/dL, amylase of 60 U/L, aspartate transaminase (AST) of 566 U/L, alanine transaminase (ALT) of 345 U/L, total bilirubin of 1.4 mg/dL, gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (γ-GTP) of 83 U/L, CRP of 26.27 mg/dL, procalcitonin of 4.65 ng/mL, and glucose of 110 mg/dL. Coagulogram results included a prothrombin time of 11.9 seconds with an international normalized ratio (INR) of 0.99, activated partial thromboplastin time of 39.6 seconds, fibrinogen of 904 mg/dL, and fibrin degradation products (FDP) of 93.9 μg/mL. Antigen tests for COVID-19 and influenza were negative. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the head showed no evidence of intracranial hemorrhage.
test_results: Liver biopsy results showed large and small droplet fatty deposits.

case_report: A 43-year-old woman presented to Mie University Hospital with complaints of fatigue and vomiting. Initially, she experienced sudden malaise, thirst, and vomiting in April 2019 and consulted a medical practitioner. Laboratory results revealed elevated blood glucose levels (428 mg/dL), a slight increase in hemoglobin A1c (6.6%), and the presence of ketone bodies in urine. She was administered insulin therapy for four days. Subsequently, her treatment was changed to oral medications including metformin 500 mg/d, empagliflozin 10 mg/d, and vildagliptin 100 mg/d. Her condition improved, and she was discharged two days after switching to oral treatment with a blood glucose level of 203 mg/dL. Two days post-discharge, she visited Mie University Hospital's outpatient department with ongoing fatigue and vomiting. Clinical examination findings included: height 159.3 cm, weight 58.6 kg, body mass index 23.0 kg/m2, blood pressure 128/83 mmHg, heart rate 107 beats/min, body temperature 37.4 ˚C, and peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) at 98% on room air. The physical examination also noted significant dryness of the oral cavity. She had no prior medical history.
test_results: Arterial blood gases demonstrated metabolic acidosis (pH, 7.18; pCO2, 18 mmHg; HCO3, 6.6 mEq/L; base excess, -19.3 mmol/L; A-gap, 27.6 mmol/L), with normal level of lactic acid (1.0 mmol/L). Fasting blood glucose (184 mg/dL) was mildly elevated with increased glycated hemoglobin/hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) (7.3%). Urinalysis showed high levels of glucose (2000 mg/dL) and ketone bodies (3+). The plasma levels of 3-hydroxybutyric acid (6585 μmol/L) were markedly high. The renal function markers (blood urea nitrogen 9.1 mg/dL; serum creatinine 0.40 mg/dL) were within the normal range. Additional laboratory analysis showed reduced urinary C-peptide level (8.6 μg/d) and decreased fasting serum C-peptide level (0.3 ng/mL). Islet-related autoantibodies, including anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase antibody, insulin autoantibody, islet cell antibody, insulinoma-associated protein-2 antibody, and zinc transporter-8 autoantibody, were undetectable. An abdominal computed tomography showed a normal pancreas, and the blood level of pancreas exocrine enzymes, including amylase and lipase, were within the normal range.

case_report: In November 2019, a 59-year-old non-smoker man with a body mass index of 27.5 kg/m2, no personal or family history of diabetes, was admitted to the hospital due to coughing for half a month and bloody sputum for 1 week. A chest CT scan revealed a 6.4x5.3 cm mass with irregular margins in the right lower lung. A biopsy via fiberoptic bronchoscopy identified small cell lung cancer. He was treated with sintilimab 200 mg combined with etoposide (100 mg/m2) and cisplatin (75 mg/m2) every 3 weeks. In March 2020, before the sixth sintilimab infusion, the patient reported experiencing polyuria and polydipsia, with self-monitored blood glucose levels at 23.0 mmol/L (414 mg/dL). He was urgently admitted to the pneumology department. Upon admission, his physical examination showed a temperature of 36.2°C, heart rate of 113 bpm, blood pressure of 118/84 mm Hg, and O2 saturation of 97% without oxygen therapy. Initial laboratory results included glycemia at 25.0 mmol/L (450 mg/dL), urinalysis showing 4+ glucose and ketones, arterial blood pH at 7.271, bicarbonate at 12.3 mmol/L, base excess at −15 mmol/L, and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) at 7.4% (normal range 4.0%–6.5%). The patient was treated with intravenous fluids and insulin therapy, along with oral rehydration and potassium. His polyuria and polydipsia symptoms significantly improved, and arterial blood pH normalized the next day. Intravenous insulin therapy was followed by multiple injections of insulin aspart and insulin glargine with gradually increasing doses, which normalized glycemia and clinical features. The patient then received the sixth infusion of sintilimab and continued using insulin aspart and insulin glargine combined with acarbose to manage glycemia.
test_results: β-cell related autoantibodies were negative, C-peptide was undetectable (<0.003 nmol/L), abdominal CT showed no signs of pancreatitis, and no other endocrine dysfunctions were found.

case_report: A 41-year-old woman with a history of peripartum cardiomyopathy, mitral regurgitation, and hypertension was brought to the emergency department due to significantly high blood pressure. The patient reported experiencing shortness of breath for one week and mild chest pressure during physical activity. She mentioned having similar symptoms over a decade ago when she had a pulmonary embolism. Three days before her symptoms began, she discontinued her hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) medication due to increased urinary frequency but continued taking losartan. Upon arrival, her vital signs were: temperature 37.2 °C, blood pressure 218/150, heart rate 121, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Physical examination revealed a well-appearing patient with no apparent distress. Lung auscultation was clear, and there were no signs of S3, jugular vein distention, or lower extremity edema. The rest of the physical examination was normal.
test_results: Two initial troponin levels were mildly elevated at 0.08 µg/L, but down-trended thereafter to 0.05 µg/L. There was mild cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vasculature on chest x-ray, and a new left bundle branch block (LBBB) on EKG. At the time of the initial BSE, BP was 252/163 [mean arterial pressure (MAP) = 170)] and PLS was − 3.5%. The EF was not calculated, but estimated to be mildly reduced. Six hours later, the BP was 171/94 (MAP = 123) and a repeat BSE was performed and PLS was recalculated. The MAP had been reduced by 27% and the PLS improved to − 14%. Repeat EKG after the IV medications continued to show a persistent LBBB.

case_report: A 28-year-old Caucasian male from London visited a walk-in GP clinic reporting four instances of hematospermia over a span of 10 days. During the first three instances, the semen appeared brown, while the fourth instance showed distinct red blood streaks in the semen. The patient is heterosexual with a single sexual partner who has no history of sexually transmitted infections. They use barrier contraception for family planning. The patient has no significant past medical history except for mild childhood asthma. He reported no headaches, vision changes, cardiac or respiratory symptoms, recent trauma, or changes in urinary or bowel habits. He also had no pain, fever, sweats, weight loss, or fatigue, and had not traveled abroad recently. The patient has never smoked or used illicit substances. His diet is reasonably healthy, and he walks about 5 km daily. He consumes approximately 32 units of alcohol per week, which he acknowledges exceeds medical guidelines. There is no family history of inheritable diseases. On physical examination, the patient was comfortable at rest and clinically euvolemic. His abdomen was soft and non-tender, with non-palpable kidneys and no renal bruits. The scrotum showed no enlargement or masses. A digital rectal examination revealed a normal prostate with no enlargement or nodularity. Respiratory examination showed normal breath sounds. The central and peripheral nervous system examinations were normal. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds, no peripheral edema, normal jugular venous pressure, no radio-femoral delay, and normal fundoscopy.
test_results: His blood pressure was noted to be 228/135 mmHg, and his heart rate was 90 beats per minute and regular.

case_report: The patient is a 14-year-old male, the third child of a 21-year-old mother and a 30-year-old father, both of whom are healthy and non-consanguineous. He has two healthy brothers aged 20 and 18 years old. He was born after an uneventful pregnancy; his birth weight was 2300 g (<3rd percentile), and his height was 49 cm (>15th percentile). At 7 years old, the patient was referred to our hospital due to genital anomalies. Upon admission, a global developmental delay was detected, which was most profound in the area of language. He also presented with short stature, microcephaly, facial asymmetry, midface hypoplasia, a broad and prominent forehead, mild hypertelorism, strabismus, a broad nasal bridge, a long and smooth philtrum, a thin upper lip, a high palate, and low-set ears with a prominent antihelix. Additionally, subglandular hypospadias and cryptorchidism were observed, along with hands featuring fifth finger clinodactyly, abnormal palmar creases, and severe bilateral hallux valgus. The patient’s brain MRI was normal, while auditory evoked potentials revealed normal left hearing and right conductive superficial hearing loss (secondary to serous otitis media). An X-ray of the hands showed a three-year delayed bone age, feet with an absence of mid-foot bone structures, such as cuneiform bones, only cuboid and navicular bones were observed, as well as bilateral hallux valgus, which was surgically repaired at 13 years old.
test_results: Karyotype and Array CGH Agilent 60 K reported a 12.7 Mb deletion at 7p14.2p15.3, which was confirmed by FISH with a specific 54.95Kb probe targeted to 7p15.2 inside the deleted region. The specific nomenclature is as follows: 46,XY.ish del(7)(p15.2)(D7Z1+,HOXA6−,HOXA13−).arr[GRCh37/hg19] 7p15.3p14.3(22574164_35288260)x1dn.

case_report: The patient is a 20-year-old unmarried male with non-consanguineous parents and a healthy sister. He has experienced a productive cough and shortness of breath for the past 6 years. He began having recurrent coughs around the age of 1 and has a history of chronic otitis media and sinusitis. Despite undergoing multiple courses of anti-infection treatments with macrolides and treatments aimed at tuberculosis, his respiratory symptoms have persisted.
test_results: Lung high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) showed diffuse nodules among small airway and bronchiectasis in right middle lung and both lower lungs. Sinus HRCT showed sinusitis and bilateral inferior turbinate hypertrophy. Pulmonary function test showed predicted forced expiratory volume during the first second (FEV1) was 64.2%. Fiberoptic bronchoscope examination demonstrated suppurative inflammation of bronchus. The nasal nitric oxide level was 9.0 nL/min.

case_report: A 22-year-old unmarried female patient was admitted due to a history of recurrent cough and expectoration for over 20 years. The patient, a young non-smoking Chinese female, experienced recurrent cough and expectoration since birth, along with occasional dyspnea, persisting into adulthood. Despite repeated use of antibiotics, antivirals, and small doses of hormone anti-inflammatory medications, the symptoms persisted. The patient had no prior medical history. Her uncle also had a history of recurrent cough and expectoration since birth but did not seek medical assistance or formal treatment. Upon admission, the patient's vital signs were stable. Bilateral lung percussion was clear, and auscultation revealed reduced respiratory sounds in both lungs. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 13.4 × 10^9/L and a neutrophil ratio of 78.4%. Inflammatory markers were within normal ranges, and fungal and bacterial cultures were negative. Acid-fast staining and T-SPOT tests were negative. Tests for Hepatitis B, syphilis, and HIV were all negative. Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed marked bronchiectasis with infection, a typical 'tree bud sign', and miliary nodules in the lower left lung. Sinus CT scans indicated bilateral maxillary and ethmoid sinusitis. Abdominal ultrasound and cardiac ultrasound did not show any signs of visceral transposition.
test_results: Some epithelial cells had few cilia, with missing and short cilia. There was no ciliated power arm after 1000 magnification.
diagnosis: Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia  due to CCNO mutation

case_report: A 42-year-old male patient, with a body mass index of 28.75, was transferred to our University Surgery Clinic due to right hypochondria pain. The patient reported experiencing this pain for one month, without any other significant symptoms. His medical history includes chronic cholecystitis and mild hepatic steatosis. He identified himself as a social drinker. No other significant diseases or information were noted. Physical examination revealed a large abdominal mass in the right hypochondria and the inferior edge of the liver, located 2.5 cm below the rib cage. Laboratory results showed a serum lymphocyte level of 16.4% and a neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) of 4.42. Serum levels of tumor-specific markers such as α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and human choriogonadotropin were not evaluated, but immunohistochemistry staining denied their positivity. Ultrasonography described a non-homogeneous round mass measuring 119.2 mm × 108.3 mm, with increased echogenicity, located in the 8th segment of the right liver. The patient's history suggested a hepatic cyst, hepatosplenomegaly, and hepatic steatosis. Additionally, a right renal malrotation was suspected, with the right kidney located in the epigastrium and no visible ureteral jet from the right side of the bladder.
test_results: The scan confirmed the hepatomegaly and presence of a well-defined 126 mm × 121 mm × 146 mm macronodular encapsulated cystic lesion. The wall thickness was estimated to be approximately 6 mm. The fluid content was estimated to be clear, with a density of 10 HU. The cystic mass was thought to involve the convex side of the right kidney, with the upper limit at the visceral face of the liver, the lateral limit at the abdominal wall and the inferior limit at the bifurcation of the abdominal aorta. It displaced the right kidney in the anterior and medial direction. Hydronephrosis or signs of disorders of secretion or excretion of the right kidney were not described, neither were modified lymph nodes. Free abdominal fluid was observed.

case_report: A 41-year-old male, heavy smoker, with a history of recurrent urinary stones, presented with left flank pain and one episode of gross hematuria. Upon presentation, he was afebrile and did not report chills. Physical examination showed a soft, non-tender abdomen with left costovertebral angle tenderness and no palpable lymph nodes. Blood tests, including complete blood count, electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and hepatic enzymes, were normal. Urinalysis revealed 23 white blood cells (WBC) and 38 red blood cells (RBC) per high-power microscopic field in urinary sediment. Urinary cytology findings led to further investigations. A computed tomography (CT) urography scan identified a 5 cm mass in the left renal pelvis and multiple infracentimetric perihilar lymph nodes. A few days later, a laparoscopic left nephroureterectomy with perihilar lymph node dissection was performed. Gross examination showed a 3 × 2.5 cm vegetative tumor in the renal pelvis infiltrating the adjacent renal parenchyma and perihilar fat. Microscopic examination revealed a high-grade transitional papillary carcinoma of the renal pelvic lumen infiltrating the muscular layer of the renal pelvis, adjacent renal parenchyma, and perihilar fat, with multiple tumoral emboli in adjacent venous structures. Urothelial carcinoma in situ (CIS) was also present in the mucosa. Four out of six dissected lymph nodes showed disease metastasis. The patient received adjuvant chemotherapy with cisplatin-gemcitabine and was monitored with CT and urinary cytology for two years without signs of relapse. After a year without follow-up, the patient returned with periumbilical abdominal pain and recent weight loss. Physical examination and laboratory tests were unremarkable. A CT scan revealed a left paraaortic mass infiltrating the left psoas muscle over a length of 12 cm. Biopsy of this mass showed carcinomatous proliferation with polygonal cells, eosinophilic and dense cytoplasm, irregular hyperchromatic nuclei with multiple nucleoli, and occasional clear cells.
test_results: Immunohistochemical profiling showed diffuse and strong positivity of tumoral cells for anti-CK7 and anti-HMWCK while having negative results with CD10 and CD117 stains.

case_report: A 27-year-old female with a history of hypertension and hyperthyroidism presented with bilateral lower extremity weakness, chest pain, and palpitations for 1 day. The chest pain was left-sided, non-radiating, and non-exertional. She had previous episodes of elevated heart rate and was evaluated at other medical centers but did not recall the diagnosis. She had been noncompliant with metoprolol for 2 months. Her family history was negative. She was not on any medications like amiodarone, and there were no signs of thyroiditis on physical examination. The patient denied any exogenous uptake of iodine or thyroid hormone. Initial vital signs showed hypertension with a blood pressure of 165/95 mmHg and tachycardia with a heart rate of 130 bpm. Physical examination revealed a tachycardic heart rate with a regular rhythm and a nontender chest wall. Her BMI was 15.8, and the rest of the physical examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory tests showed elevated troponin, low thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), normal free thyroxine (T4), hypercalcemia, and hypomagnesemia. An electrocardiogram (EKG) showed sinus tachycardia with a ventricular rate of 113 bpm. The patient was diagnosed with a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction, and a cardiologist was consulted. A left heart catheterization revealed an 80% stenosis of the LAD artery, and a drug-eluting stent (DES) was placed. She was started on dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin, clopidogrel, and high-intensity statin therapy. A thyroid ultrasound showed bilateral thyroid nodules up to 1.7 cm. Further evaluation for hypercalcemia revealed significantly elevated PTH and normal vitamin D levels, indicating primary hyperparathyroidism. The hypercalcemia and hypomagnesemia were complications of her primary hyperparathyroidism.
test_results: Serum calcitonin levels were found to be significantly elevated at 779 pg/mL. Serum and urine metanephrines and norepinephrines were very elevated. Computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a large heterogeneous right adrenal mass measuring 7.9 cm × 6.8 cm × 8 cm. A nuclear medicine parathyroid scan revealed a 1.6 cm soft tissue density in the left cervical neck, consistent with attributes of a parathyroid adenoma.

case_report: A 40-year-old morbidly obese white female presented with a history of easy bruising, menorrhagia complicated by iron-deficiency anemia treated with IV iron transfusions, and tracheal stenosis requiring dilatation every two years without bleeding complications. She had a prior episode of epistaxis lasting forty minutes, controlled with a nasal tampon. There was no history of recurrent epistaxis, blood in stools, dark stools, hematemesis, petechiae, or bleeding gums. Her menstrual cycle, irregular due to peri-menopause, involved heavy bleeding one to two times a year lasting several weeks, necessitating pad changes five to six times a day. Before peri-menopause, her cycles also required daily pad changes five to six times. Obstetric history included one vaginal delivery without bleeding complications. She had a tonsillectomy in the past with no bleeding complications and no other surgeries. The calculated BS was 6. Additional medical history included obstructive sleep apnea, hypertension, and hypothyroidism. Social history was unremarkable. Physical examination was unremarkable.
