A ventriculoperitoneal shunt was placed to relieve the hydrocephalus. Laboratory tests, including coagulation studies, were within normal limits. Tumor markers in serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), including beta subunit of human chorionic gonadotropin and alpha-fetoprotein, were normal. CSF cytology showed no malignant cells. The patient was discharged and scheduled for a stereotactic biopsy of the pineal lesion 2 weeks later. Her upward conjugate gaze paresis resolved completely by the second admission. She experienced a recurrence of the upward conjugate gaze paresis, likely due to a post-biopsy intra-tumoral hemorrhage, a day after the biopsy. She then underwent craniotomy for lesion excision via the infratentorial supracerebellar approach, achieving complete macroscopic excision. Post-operative CT scan confirmed complete tumor resection and resolution of hydrocephalus. No post-operative complications were observed. The patient was discharged 3 weeks later with no neurological deficits.
test_results: The histological studies revealed a moderate cellular tumor composed of small cells with round and generally uniform nuclei, fine chromatin, and small nucleoli. A few foci of cells with mild nuclear atypia were also found. Mitotic figures were rare (fewer than one per ten high-power field). Small pineocytomatous rosettes were focally found. Extensive hemorrhaging occurred in the adjacent granulation tissue, gliosis, and hemosiderin-laiden macrophages. The immunohistochemistry was positive for neurofilament, enolase, synaptophysin, and CD 56, but negative for NeuN. The Ki-67 proliferation index was 20% to 30%.
diagnosis: Grade II Pineal Parenchymal Tumor of Intermediate Differentiation
Orpha_name: Pineal parenchymal tumor of intermediate differentiation

case_report: A 39-year-old male presented to the emergency department with a 1-month history of difficulty walking, instability while standing, speech issues, and episodes of incontinence. His medical history includes communicating hydrocephalus, which was surgically managed at 14 months old with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt, and a subsequent distal shunt revision at 16 years old. Upon admission, the neurological examination showed temporospatial disorientation, no focal motor deficits, no sensory changes, normal and symmetrical deep tendon reflexes, a shuffling gait with a wide base, and multiple body oscillations during the Romberg test.
test_results: Brain computed tomography (CT) scan showed the presence of 5 cm mixed-density pseudonodular lesion. Contrast-enhanced brain CT study confirmed the presence of an enhancing 57 mm left frontotemporal non-homogeneous neoformation, with several calcifications, hypodense colliquated areas, and perilesional edema. Preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with gadolinium contrast medium showed a lesion with lobulated margins, non-homogeneous post contrast enhancement and heterogeneous signal intensity in relation to the presence of solid component mixed with necrotic-colliquative areas and calcifications. In particular, in the peripheral frontal portion, a small oval-shaped component was visible, surrounded by strongly hypointense peripheral border in FFE sequences, arguably due to hemosiderin deposition. The tumor presented a maximum diameter of 6.2 × 4.1 cm on the axial plane, 6.3 × 3.5 cm on the sagittal plane, and 3.6 × 3.3 cm on the coronal plane, and it extended cranially to the knee of the corpus callosum, displacing the large falx to the right and causing a compressive effect on the frontal horn of the right lateral ventricle. Pathological examination revealed a population of neuronal lineage (Sinaptophysin+, neuron specific enolase+, glial fibrillary acid protein−) consisting of roundish monomorphic cells mixed with a proliferation of capillary vessels and the presence of widespread calcifications; the Ki-67 index was <5%, there was no evidence of mitosis or areas of necrosis.

case_report: A 3-month-old male was referred to our hospital for the management of a congenital intracranial mass and infective endocarditis in the bicuspid aortic valve. At birth, the child exhibited lower limb weakness, left seventh nerve palsy, and left neck swelling, along with difficulty in head turning. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a left pontine-bulbar lesion extending upward into the cerebellum. The fourth ventricle and the cerebellar vermis were displaced. A few days later, the patient developed a fever associated with Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia. An echocardiogram identified vegetative endocarditis in the bicuspid aortic valve with an ejection fraction of 45%. The patient was treated with antibiotic therapy for the infection. After being transferred to our center, he underwent aortic valve replacement via the Ross Procedure without complications. Subsequently, he experienced neurological deterioration, presenting with left-sided hemiparesis, dysphagia, and recurrent episodes of apnea. One month post-cardiac surgery, he underwent suboccipital craniotomy in the prone position with intraoperative neuronavigation and neurophysiologic monitoring. The surgery was interrupted during resection of the infiltrating bulbar component due to sustained bradycardia and arterial hypertension, resulting in a sub-total resection (STR). Post-surgery, the patient maintained a stable neurological status but required a tracheostomy for mild pulmonary insufficiency.
test_results: Histology showed proliferation of small/medium-size round cells with a central round nucleus, finely speckled chromatin, and small nucleolus. Ganglioid cells, intermediates between neurocytes and ganglion cells, were evenly distributed and differentiation toward fully mature ganglion cells was observed. Neoplastic cells were strongly positive for synaptophysin and neurofilaments, mildly positive for Neu-N, and negative for GFAP and CD34, indicating a neuronal nature of the tumor. Additional immunohistochemistry revealed weak positivity for p53 (<5%), mTor, phospho-mTor and EGFR. Ki67 was low (1% with some areas up to 3–4%). Mitoses were 3–4/10 HPF. BRAFv600E mutation was assessed by DNA sequencing and resulted positive.

case_report: A 39-year-old Italian male presented with a history of headache and nausea over several months. The patient had no other medical conditions, had not undergone any surgeries, and was not on any medication. He had no history of alcohol consumption, tobacco use, or drug use. He is married with two children and works as a cook in a family-owned restaurant. There was no family history of similar cases or tumors. Neurological examination upon admission revealed no sensorimotor deficits, no cranial nerve deficits, normal reflex responses, and stable standing and walking abilities. Vital signs, including blood pressure, pulse, and temperature, were within normal limits. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, liver function, renal function, and C-reactive protein, were also within normal ranges.
test_results: CT and MRI revealed an ill-defined, 39 × 37 × 29 mm (anterior-posterior×transverse×cranial-caudal) tumor. On CT, the lesion presented as slightly hypointense with poor contrast enhancement. On MRI, a hyperintensity on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequence and on T2-weighted imaging was detected. On T1-weighted imaging, the lesion showed a hypointensity. The lesion showed poor contrast enhancement of the right cerebellar hemisphere without an obstructive hydrocephalus on T1-weighted images with contrast enhancement. On histopathological examination, hematoxylin and eosin-stained paraffin sections showed predominantly small to moderately cellular tumor growing compactly, sometimes diffuse, infiltrating the surrounding cerebellar tissue. Tumor cells contained mainly light eosinophilic, sometimes clear, cytoplasm and round to oval nuclei and smaller nucleoli. Some tumor cells showed an astrocytic differentiation. Furthermore, around 10% of the tumor area comprised focal lipidized cells. No significant mitotic activity, < 1 mitosis/20 high-power field (HPF), and no necrosis were observed. In immunohistochemical analysis NeuN was detected in 80% and synaptophysin was detected in 30% of the non-lipomatous cells. Tumor cells were negative for neurofilament and chromogranin A. Glial fibrillary acid protein (GFAP) was observed in 20% of the tumor cells. Ki-67/MIB-1 proliferation index, as determined by nuclear MIB1 monoclonal antibody staining, was around 2%.

case_report: A 5-year-old right-handed boy was admitted to the neurosurgery department with a 5-month history of headache, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and dysphoria, along with visual blurring during the peak of the headache. Over the course of nearly a month, these symptoms progressively worsened. The boy reported difficulty maintaining balance while walking or standing. There was no similar clinical history reported in his family. Neurological examination revealed bilateral grade II papilledema, gait ataxia, and positive results for both the finger-nose and Romberg tests.
test_results: A computerized tomography (CT) scan showed a heterogeneous dense large mass in the 4th ventricle of the brain, combined with unclear edges and significant dilation of bilateral and 3rd ventricles. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a large, irregular, heterogeneous mass of approximately 4.9×5.4×6.2 cm, which herniated to the orientation of the foramen magnum, extending to the C2 level. In addition, the bilateral cerebellar hemisphere, cerebellar tonsils, medulla oblongata, and cervical cord were particularly compressed. Iso- and hypointensity signals were seen on T1-weighted imaging (T1WI) and T2-weighted fluid attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR). Mixing isointensity and hyperintensity signals were seen on T2-weighted imaging (T2WI). On enhancement, the tumor showed moderate heterogeneous enhancement with an ill-defined boundary. In addition, there was significant presence of hydrocephalus and periventricular edema. Upon histopathological examination, hematoxylin and eosin-stained paraffin sections showed predominantly small to moderately, round or ovoid tumor cells, with low mitotic activity. These tumor cells grew in a sheet shape with clusters of fat cells were observed in the center or formed chrysanthemum-liking clusters. Immunohistochemical analysis indicated that the Ki-67 index was ± 5% mostly, and only 10-20% focally. In addition, the neoplasm was positive for synaptophysin, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), neuron-specific enolase (NSE), microtubule associated protein-2 (MAP-2), vimentin, and negative for isocitrate dehydrogenase-1 (IDH1)-R132H, neurofilament, oligo-2, S-100, and epithelial membrane antigen (EMA).

case_report: A 6-year-old female presented with a four-week history of headache and vomiting. The headache was gradual in onset, dull in nature, primarily on the left side, and more severe in the morning, with vomiting providing relief. Additionally, she experienced difficulty with walking. Neurological examination revealed a fully conscious child with normal higher cerebral functions. She exhibited truncal ataxia, but other cerebellar functions were intact. Examination of other systems showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Cranial computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging revealed left cerebellar tumor with obstructive hydrocephalus.

case_report: A previously healthy 22-year-old woman initially presented with right-sided muscle weakness and episodes of right-sided sensory changes, both of which had begun one year earlier. She also had a one-year history of intermittent loss of consciousness unrelated to these symptoms. General physical examination and neurological findings were unremarkable. Routine electroencephalography (EEG) demonstrated diffuse cerebral dysfunction over the left hemisphere, but no epileptic or epileptiform discharge was noted.
test_results: MR studies of the brain using a 1.5-T system revealed a well demarcated broad-based mass, 2 cm in size, on the falx cerebri and prominent peritumoral edema. Relative to gray matter, the mass was hypointense on T1-weighted MR images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images. Gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted images demonstrated strong homogeneous enhancement. Along its lateral margin, the tumor's cystic structure was isointense relative to cerebrospinal fluid. Microscopic examination showed that it was composed of relatively mature ganglion cells and abundant collagen-rich stroma in which spindle stromal cells and lymphocytes were observed. Both the cytoplasm of the ganglion cells and stromal cytoplasmic processes stained positively with antibody for synaptophysin, though glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) staining failed to reveal a glial component.

case_report: A 66-year-old female with a medical history of hypertension and depression reported experiencing progressive generalized weakness, fatigability, mild nonspecific headaches, and confusion over the past 10 months. Her condition notably deteriorated in the week prior to her visit, leading to multiple falls. In the emergency department, she denied experiencing visual changes, seizures or seizure-like activity, any specific pattern to her headaches, nausea, vomiting, or other constitutional symptoms. Her neurological examination revealed no apparent focal neurological deficits and was within normal limits.
test_results: Computed tomography scan of the head showed an intraventricular mass lesion with associated obstructive hydrocephalus. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with gadolinium, time-of-flight angiogram, and magnetic resonance spectroscopy sequences was obtained for further delineation of the lesion and operative planning. The lesion was approximately 2.8 × 4.1 × 3.9 cm in maximal transverse by anterior posterior by craniocaudal dimensions. It was localized to the inferior aspect of the right lateral ventricle, contacting the septum pellucidum, and extending through the right foramen of Monro into the third ventricle. It expanded the ventricle without evidence of parenchymal invasion. It also appeared to come into contact with the inner surface of the body of corpus callosum. The lesion appeared to have a diffuse pattern of enhancement on T1 + Gd sequences. It seemed of intermediate intensity on T2-weighted sequences. It had uniformly low-grade restricted diffusion. There was no calcification or evidence of hemorrhage. MR angiogram showed small branching vessels within and along the margin of the mass. MR spectroscopy showed markedly elevated choline peak and diminished but preserved N-acetyl aspartate (NAA) peak.

case_report: A 9-month-old male infant presented to the emergency department with a noticeable bulging in the right parietal region of the head. The patient had no documented history of head trauma. Clinical observations included an increased head circumference measuring 47 cm, placing it in the 90th percentile. Additionally, there was a noted motor delay over the past 1.5 months and a rapid onset of epileptic seizures occurring 2 weeks prior to presentation. Cranial computerized tomography (CT) scans revealed a defect in the cranial bone located in the right parietal area.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed that the tumor was characterized by a cystic mass with a central homogeneous solid component enhancing with gadolinium attached to the dura, leading to a large effect on the ventricles in the temporoparietal region. The histological examination revealed a mixed glial-neuronal tumor presenting with a nodular pattern involving the cerebral cortex and subcortex. Astrocyte-like cells had large, round and vesicular nuclei with surrounding large amphiphilic cytoplasm. Neuronal cells had vesicular chromatin and polygonal nuclei with large perikarya. A few multinucleate cells were observed. The cells were surrounded by diffuse reticulin and collagen fibers. There was only atypia, with no mitotic figures, necrosis or vesicular euchromatic nuclei (VEP). Vasogenic edema was present around the neural tissue, with non-gemistocytic gliosis. Tumor cells were immunohistochemically stained for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), synaptophysin, chromogranin, S-100 and epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), and they were negative for CD34, NFP and progesterone. Nearly 2% of tumor cells were labeled with Ki-67/MIB-1, and approximately 1/3-2/3 of cells showed moderate nuclear staining for p53.

case_report: A 1-year-old male child of Pakistani origin with Down’s syndrome presented with a progressively enlarging head and developmental regression over the past few months. He was born at 38 weeks via vaginal delivery after an uncomplicated pregnancy to non-consanguineous parents (mother 33 years old, and father 38 years old). His birth weight was 2.95 kg, length was 52 cm, and head circumference was 35 cm. His APGAR scores were 7 at 1 minute and 10 at 5 minutes. Down’s syndrome was diagnosed shortly after birth based on typical facial features and the presence of a palmar crease, later confirmed by karyotyping for Trisomy 21. His two siblings, aged 6 and 4 years, are alive and healthy. Further social and family history was unremarkable. At birth, he was in the 10th percentile for weight and 25th percentile for length. At both 6 months and 1 year, he was in the 25th percentile for weight and 50th percentile for length. His head circumference was in the 50th percentile at birth, 97th percentile at 6 months, and 20 standard deviations above the 99th percentile at 1 year. At 9 months, he met several growth milestones, including smiling, laughing at “peek-a-boo,” lifting his arms to be picked up, crawling, and sitting up without support. However, by 12 months, he exhibited increased crying, stopped responding to his name, preferred to lay flat rather than crawl or sit, and showed decreased vocalization and interest in toys. Physical examination revealed macrocephaly and signs of Down’s syndrome, such as a flat nasal bridge, upward slanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, and a simian crease. He appeared mildly irritable. Cardiac, respiratory, abdominal, genitourinary, and integumentary examinations were unremarkable. Neurological examination showed intact cranial nerves and sensation to noxious touch, but generalized muscular hypotonia with muscle wasting, −2 bilateral knee and ankle reflexes, and bilateral upgoing plantars. Initial blood tests were normal, with hemoglobin at 11.5 g/dL and white blood count at 13 × 10^9/L with a normal differential. Liver and renal functions were within normal limits, as were prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time. Hepatitis B and C serology were negative. Urinalysis and chest X-ray did not show any abnormalities.
test_results: A computed tomography (CT) scan was performed, which showed a large cystic tumor in the right parieto temporo occipital regions. Subsequent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with contrast showed a 10.9 × 11.4 × 8.9 cm, heterogeneously enhancing, mixed solid and cystic supratentorial mass, with surrounding vasogenic edema in the right parieto temporo occipital lobe. The solid component was dural based, measuring 6.4 × 6.0 cm, showing heterogeneous intensity on T2W imaging with marked enhancement on post-contrast images. There was a midline shift towards the left, with compression on the ipsilateral right lateral ventricle. Moderate obstructive hydrocephalus was also noted. The tumor specimen was sent for histopathological examination, which revealed low cellularity with intervening bands of fibrous tissue and collagen fibers. Neoplastic cells had a high nuclear/cytoplasmic (N/C) ratio with hyperchromatic nuclei. Some areas showed hypercellular pleomorphism, necrosis, and microvascular proliferation. Some cells with rhabdoid morphology were also present with abnormal mitosis. Staining was performed for integrase interactor 1 (INI-1), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), desmin, creatine kinase (CK), synaptophysin, and Ki-67. INI-1 came out strongly positive, ruling out atypical teratoid and rhabdoid tumors. A large proportion of tumor cells were positive for GFAP and negative for synaptophysin, desmin, and CK. Ki-67 index was low in the majority of the tumor. However, areas with increased cellularity had raised Ki-67 to 50%.

case_report: A 66-year-old right-handed Cambodian male with a medical history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and benign prostatic hyperplasia reported experiencing seizures since the age of 14, following a head injury from a bicycle accident. Initially, he had two to three seizures until the age of 20, after which the frequency increased. He was first prescribed phenytoin approximately 10 years after the onset of seizures, but it was ineffective, with the patient experiencing one seizure per week. Later, after moving to the United States, he was prescribed carbamazepine and topiramate. Genetic testing revealed he was HLA-B*15:02 positive, indicating a hypersensitivity to carbamazepine, which was then replaced by levetiracetam. The patient reported mood changes with levetiracetam, leading to a switch to valproate. Despite adherence to medication and achieving therapeutic levels, he continued to have seizures approximately every 6-12 months, with occasional longer intervals. Recently, he began taking cenobamate at a low dose, which resulted in a noticeable reduction in seizure frequency. He identified stress, anxiety, intense focus, and consuming greasy pork as seizure triggers, with pork consumption accounting for 50-70% of his seizures. He did not identify any other food triggers. His seizures were often preceded by an aura characterized by electric-like shocks in his back and a sensation of being pulled into the seizure. He sometimes experienced isolated auras without progressing to a seizure. His typical seizures lasted two to five minutes, involving sudden loss of consciousness, body rigidity, and twisting. His left hand flexed upward toward his face, while his right hand and lower extremities extended. His eyes fluttered upward, and his head turned to the left. Post-seizure, he experienced brief confusion and extreme fatigue.
test_results: He had an EEG 10 months prior to the EMU study, which reported generalized paroxysmal rhythmic high-amplitude slowing. He had an MRI one year prior, which demonstrated a posterior right frontal lobe 1.8x1.4x2.6 cm cystic non-enhancing lesion adjacent to the precentral sulcus with peripheral edema. A follow-up MRI demonstrated a non-enhancing T2-hyperintense, bubbly-appearing intraparenchymal cortical or subcortical lesion in the posterior aspect of the right superior frontal gyrus, unchanged in size or appearance from the prior MRI.

case_report: A 26-year-old right-handed male financial analyst presented with recurrent episodes of rotatory vertigo accompanied by nausea and palpitations. These episodes occurred three to four times daily without any specific time pattern. The initial episode lasted approximately 10 minutes, while subsequent episodes were shorter, lasting 10 to 15 seconds. The onset of these episodes was not associated with changes in head position. The symptoms had persisted for six months and did not respond to physical therapy or Lorazepam. An orthopedist ruled out a cervical origin by noting an almost natural curve of the cervical spine. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed an irregularly shaped lesion in the right temporal lobe, measuring 2.0 × 2.4 cm. Electroencephalogram (EEG) results were negative. In our clinic, a consistent, spontaneous downbeat nystagmus (DBN) was observed, which intensified with head shaking and diminished in the supine position. Caloric test and audiometry results were unremarkable. During a follow-up visit, the patient experienced a brief episode with a déjà vu sensation. A 24-hour EEG monitoring recorded ictal sharp and slow waves originating from the temporal lobe, coinciding with the onset of vertigo and palpitations. Rhythmic changes lasting 15 to 20 seconds were also detected by synchronous EEG.
test_results: Histopathologic analysis of the tumor demonstrated classical grade I findings: circumscribed neuroglial tissue composed of mature ganglion cells existing in a background of low-grade astrocyte-like cells with coarse processes. Ganglion cells contained Nissl substance and vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli and were randomly distributed in a haphazard fashion without polarization of cell processes. Molecular-genetic diagnosis included BRAF-V600E mutation.

case_report: An 8-month-old boy presented with persistent crying and vomiting. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain at a local hospital showed a posterior fossa tumor and obstructive hydrocephalus. Due to elevated intracranial pressure (ICP), a ventriculoperitoneal shunt was placed, and the child was referred to our hospital for further care. Upon admission, the child was alert and exhibited no signs of increased ICP. Neurological examination was normal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a heterogeneously enhancing large solid-cystic tumor in the fourth ventricle, compressing the cervicomedullary junction dorsally. A clear separation from the floor of the fourth ventricle or inferior cerebellar vermis was not visible. The child underwent a midline suboccipital craniectomy. The tumor was moderately vascular, grey in color, and varied in consistency from soft to firm, extending dorsally from the medulla into the fourth ventricle. An attempt was made to excise most of the tumor while sparing the medullary tissues, which lacked a distinct boundary from the tumor.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed a combination of neoplastic ganglion cells mixed with neoplastic astrocytic cells. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated that the pleomorphic glial cells were positive for glial fibrillary acid protein, and the neoplastic ganglion cells and the intervening stroma were intensely positive for neurofilament protein and synaptophysin.

case_report: A 13-year-old African American female with a history of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and mild scoliosis presented with a new onset contracture of the right elbow. Three years earlier, she experienced a sudden inability to straighten her right elbow, accompanied by stiffness and pain in the right shoulder. Recently, she reported recurring episodes of enuresis. There is no significant family history related to her symptoms. Physical examination showed hyperreflexia in the right upper extremity (3+) and lower extremity (4+ with clonus and positive Babinski reflex). She exhibited weakness in the right upper and lower extremities (4/5 strength), decreased muscle bulk, and increased muscle tone. There were no signs of dysmetria, ataxia, or gait abnormalities.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the cervical spine revealed a 4.1 × 1.2 × 1.5 cm mixed cystic and solid intramedullary mass spanning C3-C6 with cord edema extending superiorly and inferiorly to these levels.

case_report: A 38-year-old, otherwise healthy, right-handed man reported a two-year history of gradually worsening motor speech difficulties and a three-month history of increasing weakness in his right hand. Additionally, he experienced a brief episode of numbness and weakness in his right leg. Neurological examination revealed asymmetrical reflexes (more pronounced on the right side), reduced sensation on one side of the body, partial weakness on one side (4/5 strength), and a positive Babinski sign on the right.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed a 54 x 54 x 52 mm cystic lesion of the left frontal lobe in front of the precentral gyrus with a septum attached to the posterior wall of the cyst. The cyst was hypointense on T1-weighted images (T1WI) and hyperintense on T2-fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) scans. MRI scans with gadolinium showed a slight contrast accumulation in the cystic walls and homogeneous accumulation in the septum without perifocal edema. The medial part of the tumour was in close proximity with the left lateral ventricle and subarachnoid spaces were shallow on the left with a 7-mm midline shift present.

case_report: A 37-year-old Japanese man underwent imaging, which revealed a 10 mm cystic lesion with a mural nodule near the anterior horn of the right lateral ventricle. Despite the absence of neurological symptoms, the patient was monitored over a period of 10 years. During this time, the lesion increased in size from 10 mm to 18 mm, and the patient experienced worsening headaches.
test_results: MRI showed a 10 mm cystic lesion with a mural nodule near the anterior horn of the right lateral ventricle. After a follow-up period of 10 years, the lesion started to increase in size from 10 to 18 mm, accompanied by worsening of headaches. MRI revealed that the increased size of the lesion was attributable to an enlargement of the cystic component and the mural nodule. A cystic mass with a gadolinium (Gd)-enhancing cyst wall and mural nodule were present. Signal intensity of the cystic component was high on T2-weighted imaging and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) imaging. The cyst wall and nodule showed low signal intensity on T2*-weighted imaging.

case_report: A 32-year-old man presented with severe vertigo, dizziness, vomiting, and headache persisting for several weeks. Physical examination identified left sixth nerve palsy with diplopia, nystagmus, and ataxia. Initial computerised tomography (CT) scan showed a mass in the fourth ventricle with intralesional bleeding and calcification areas. The solid component exhibited patchy enhancement. Obstructive hydrocephalus was also noted. An emergent endoscopic third ventriculostomy and external ventricular drainage were performed to improve the patient's neurological status. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed a lesion in the fourth ventricle extending to the supravermian cistern and the posteroinferior third ventricle, containing a haematoma and lacking significant peritumoral oedema. Postcontrast images showed minimal enhancement.
test_results: The tumour was composed of low-density cellular proliferation with both astrocytic and neurocytic components. The neurocytic cells formed neurocytic rosettes with eosinophilic centres and perivascular pseudorosettes. The cores of these neurocytic rosettes showed positive immunostaining for synaptophysin and negative for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA). The astrocytic component showed glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) positivity. There were no necrosis areas or vascular proliferation. Ki67 proliferative index was very low (less than 1%) in both glial and neuronal components.

case_report: A 22-year-old woman experienced episodes of transient dizziness, nausea, and vomiting. Physical examination showed no neurological deficits. Initial computed tomography (CT) scan identified multiple cystic hypo-dense mass lesions in the bilateral cerebellar hemispheres, brain stem, and left thalamus with indistinct boundaries. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed these lesions as hyper-intense on axial T2-weighted images and hypo-intense on axial T1-weighted images. Some lesions displayed solid components on axial T2-weighted images. Axial T2 FLAIR images showed iso-hyperintense signals. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) indicated no restricted diffusion. Post-contrast imaging revealed mild peripheral enhancement in one tumor, while others showed no enhancement, and small nodule-like higher signals were observed in T2-weighted images. Perfusion-weighted imaging indicated hypo-perfusion of the lesions. The patient was admitted to the infectious diseases department for empirical anti-infective therapy and scheduled for a follow-up MRI examination after 2 weeks. During this period, additional laboratory tests, including enzyme-linked immunotransfer blots (EITBs), were conducted, all yielding negative results. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed no eosinophilic cells or lymphocytes, and no parasite antibodies were detected. After 15 days, MRI findings remained unchanged.
test_results: The tumors showed that small round nuclear tumor cells were distributed in a network and arranged into a chrysanthemum-shaped cluster surrounding the nerve with single permutation. Synaptophysin immunopositivity in the pericapillary area of a perivascular pseudorosette was shown, along with scattered neurons in the focal areas were also visible. Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) in the astrocytic component of the tumor was diffuse distribution.
diagnosis: WHO grade I Rosette-forming Glioneuronal Tumor

case_report: A 45-year-old female patient presented with a left renal mass identified incidentally. The patient did not exhibit any symptoms. Biochemical test results were as follows: glucose 95 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, urea 28 mg/dL; AST, ALT, ALP, and GGT levels were within normal ranges; WBC count was 5.41 × 10^3/µL and hemoglobin was 13.7 g/dL.
test_results: USG and CT showed a 100 × 71 × 66 mm heterogeneous solid mass located in the upper pole of the left kidney and lymphadenopathy in the renal hilus. Macroscopic examination of the radical nephrectomy material measuring 18 × 7 × 5 cm showed a solid, gray-white colored tumor measuring 10 × 7 × 3 cm, located in the upper pole of the kidney but without any direct relation to the kidney. Focal adrenal tissue was observed in the cross-section of the tumor. The kidney and surgical margins were tumor-free. Three lymph nodes measuring 1 cm in diameter were detected in the renal hilus. The microscopic examination revealed mature ganglion cells in Schwannian stroma. The immunohistochemical examination showed strong positive staining for S100, neuron-specific enolase, synaptophysin and chromogranin.

case_report: A 45-year-old female patient was admitted to the Second Hospital of Shandong University (Jinan, China) on October 31, 2012. The patient exhibited excessive thirst and urination for 19 years, cessation of menstrual periods for two years, headache for nine days, difficulty walking, and a decline in mental state. There were no signs of visual field defects or swelling of the optic disc.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated the presence of a mass in the anterior third ventricle with dimensions of 3.2×2.4×2.3 cm, appearing with low intensity on T1-weighted images, and hyperintensity on T2-weighted images. Strong gadolinium enhancement was present with the exception of at the hemorrhagic center. The tumor had spread to the left section of the lateral ventricles, and the third and lateral ventricles were dilated. Immunohistochemical staining of α-fetoprotein (AFP) showed strong cytoplasmic staining.
Orpha_name: Yolk sac tumor of central nervous system

case_report: A 10-year-old girl was brought to the hospital due to issues with her visual field. She had been experiencing worsening headaches, nausea, and weight loss over the past six months. Her medical history and family history were unremarkable. Upon admission, she was initially thought to have gastroenteritis. However, she later developed abducens nerve palsy in her left eye along with visual field disturbances.
test_results: Non-contrast computed tomography (CT) of the head found a solitary mass with heterogeneous high density in the suprasellar region. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a lobulated mass with a well-defined margin with mixed high-intensity and isointense signal on T1-weighted imaging and mixed low-intensity and high-intensity signal on T2-weighted imaging. These imaging findings suggested the presence of large hemorrhage, necrosis, and small cyst in the tumor. The tumor showed a heterogeneous high-intensity area on diffusion-weighted images, low-intensity area on ADC map. On contrast-enhanced MRI, the tumor exhibited a ring-like enhancement. Microscopic examination revealed that the resected tumor tissue was composed of mononucleated cytotrophoblastic cells and large multinucleated syncytiotrophoblastic cells. Hemorrhage and necrosis were also confirmed. Immunohistochemical staining for hCG was strongly positive.
Orpha_name: Choriocarcinoma of the central nervous system

case_report: In November 2005, a three-month-old boy was admitted with a three-week history of increased irritability and reduced oral intake. He was born via vaginal delivery in August 2005 without complications. At birth, a mild scalp bulge was noted, which was considered to be a cephalhematoma. A head CT scan revealed a widened foramen rotundum and an abnormal density in the right cavernous sinus. The boy was discharged as he showed no abnormal neurological signs. Two months later, he returned with continued poor oral intake, increased irritability, and nighttime insomnia.
test_results: An MRI scan of the head showed a large cystic lesion filling the entire middle cranial fossa, compressing the right temporal lobe. There was also evidence of a relatively small solid portion of varying signal intensity; this area enhanced heterogeneously after the administration of intravenous contrast medium. The lesion was also in the pterygopalatine fossa, and the two areas communicated through a more widened foramen rotundum as compared to the previous study. The right cavernous sinus was occupied entirely by the lesion, with medial displacement of the internal carotid artery.
Orpha_name: Teratoma of the central nervous system

case_report: A 62-year-old male, with a 2-month history of pain between the shoulder blades, presented with sudden onset of paraplegia at the T2 level. MRI revealed a well-defined mass within the intradural extramedullary space at the C7-T1 level, positioned in front of the spinal cord. The T2-weighted images showed an isointense lesion with a broad attachment to the dura, and the enhanced study indicated heterogeneous enhancement along with compression and backward displacement of the spinal cord. An urgent decompressive C7-T1 laminectomy was performed, resulting in partial removal of the mass. During surgery, the cervicodorsal dura appeared blackened, and the lesion was noted to be firm.
test_results: The histopathologic examination revealed large cells, oval to polygonal in shape with prominent nucleoli, and eosinophilic cytoplasm filled with melanin pigment. There was no significant increase in mitosis (1/10 HPF and low proliferation index Ki 67: 2%). On immunohistochemistry tumor cells showed positivity with S100, Vimentin and HBM45 and negativity for EMA.

case_report: A 27-year-old woman presented with a headache persisting for 10 days. The headache began without any clear cause and did not improve with rest. She did not report nausea, vomiting, dizziness, or other symptoms. During a visit to the outpatient department of a local hospital, a physical examination showed that her general condition was good, and she was alert. Both pupils measured approximately 3 mm and responded normally to light. Muscle tone in her limbs was normal, and tests for pathological signs, as well as the finger-to-nose and heel-knee-shin tests, were negative. There was no history of melanoma affecting her skin, mucosa, or eyes. Laboratory test results were noted to be potentially abnormal.
test_results: A computerized tomography (CT) scan demonstrated a high-density mass in the left cerebellum with patchy calcification at the posterior edge, and heterogeneous enhancement was observed on a contrast-enhanced scan. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a high signal intensity on T1WI and low signal intensity on T2WI. The tumor showed noticeable homogeneous enhancement on contrast-enhanced T1WI. The signal characteristics of FLAIR were similar to those of T2WI, and the diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) sequence showed limited diffusion of the tumor. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy revealed increased choline (Cho) levels. It decreased the creatine (Cr) and N-acetyl aspartate (Naa) levels in the tumor. Intraoperatively, the dural tension was high, and a dark hard mass was observed on the left side of the cerebellar vermis. The dura mater and foramen magnum near the tumor are dyed black. The tumor, dark meninges, and dark bone tissues were completely resected and sent for pathological examination. Macroscopic observation showed a solid, black, and slightly hard tumor with a clear boundary, about 3.0 × 2.5 × 2.3 cm3 in size. The adjacent dura and skull were black stained. Microscopic examination revealed that the tumor area was composed of spindle and oval epithelioid cells arranged in sheets and bundles. These cells were moderately heterotypic, with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli. Chromatin was found to be distributed at the cell edge. The cytoplasm was abundant and a wide range of cells contained many black pigment granules. A large amount of pigmentation was observed between the cells. Hemorrhage and necrosis were observed in some areas. The dura and skull were invaded by tumor cells. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) showed diffuse positivity for HMB-45, Melan-A, S-100, and Vimentin, but negative for pCK, EMA, and GFAP. Ki-67 hotspots were approximately 15%. Genetic tests showed GNAQ gene variation, whereas BRAF, BRCA2, CDK4, CDKN2A, CTNNB1, GNA11, KIT, MAP2K1, NF1, NRAS, PTEN, and TP53 gene variations were not detected.
Orpha_name: Primary melanoma of the central nervous system

case_report: A 50-year-old right-handed woman experienced a gradual decline in vision in her left eye over a period of two years. She also reported feeling fatigued, having dry skin, brittle nails, and thinning hair. Her visual acuity was measured at 20/50 in the right eye and 20/70 in the left eye. Visual field testing showed no deficits. Pupillary response, eye movement, and fundus examinations were all within normal limits. No abnormalities were found in the rest of her neurological and general physical examinations.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a left-sided 1 centimeter by 1 centimeter enhancing lesion arising from the posterior orbital canal with extension into the paraclinoid region. The mass appeared to compress the left optic nerve.

case_report: A 36-year-old male was admitted due to progressively worsening vision in the left eye. Ophthalmologic evaluation of the retina showed no significant findings. Visual acuity was measured at 8/10 in the right eye and 1/10 in the left eye. Formal visual field testing using the standard Goldman perimetry study revealed a deficit in the left upper temporal quadrant. Neurological examination was otherwise normal. No endocrine dysfunction was identified preoperatively. A brain computed tomography (CT) scan showed a sellar mass with sellar enlargement and erosion of the dorsum sella. Further imaging with brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a 3 cm sellar mass that intensely and homogeneously enhanced after intravenous (IV) administration of gadolinium. The mass exhibited suprasellar extension, inferior displacement of the infundibulum, and upward displacement of the optic chiasm and anterior communicating artery complex.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the tumor showed a cellular proliferation of stromal cells, interlaced by numerous thin-walled vessels, foam, and vacuolated histiocytes. No mitoses were identified. In histochemical and immunohistochemical stains, stromal cells were positive to vimentin and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and in limited locations, also positive in EMA and neuron-specific enolase (NSE) while negative in CK7, CK20, CK 5/6, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), pancytokeratin, CK34βΕ12, S-100, and α-inhibin. The cellular proliferation index ki67 was less than 1%.

case_report: An 80-year-old Caucasian woman was admitted with a 12-year history of a stable sellar mass lesion measuring 13 mm in diameter. She had been asymptomatic with no deficiencies in pituitary hormones or visual impairments. Her medical history included hypertension and osteoporosis. Recently, she experienced two severe headache episodes, with the last one accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and blurred vision. Laboratory tests revealed hyponatremia (120 mEq/L) with low serum osmolality (247 mOsm/L) and highly elevated urine osmolality (695 mOsm/L). Endocrinological evaluation showed hypocortisolism without other hormone disturbances. Fundoscopy was normal, but Goldman perimetry confirmed bitemporal hemianopsia, more pronounced on the right side. Neurological examination was otherwise normal. After hydrocortisone substitution therapy, her condition improved rapidly, and the headaches subsided. MRI findings suggested an acute hemorrhage in the sellar region. Apart from age-related vascular leukoencephalopathy, no other pathological findings were noted on imaging. Surgical removal of the tumor was performed using a transnasal, transsphenoidal approach. Intraoperatively, the tumor appeared yellowish-brown, relatively firm, and was located within a sellar hematoma cavity, which was evacuated. Postoperatively, her visual field deficits improved significantly, and Goldman perimetry confirmed partial recovery. Endocrinological studies indicated panhypopituitarism with partial and transient diabetes insipidus. She received hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, and transient desmopressin therapy. Overall, she remained in good health with satisfactory performance. A follow-up MRI 16 months post-surgery showed good chiasmatic decompression with no residual tumor mass.
test_results: The resected tumor was examined with light microscopy, which revealed a small, well circumscribed, non-adenomatous tumor surrounded by slightly compressed remnants of adenohypophyseal parenchyma. The tumor was richly vascularized with an observable reticular mesh of thin-walled capillaries interspersed with large epithelioid-looking cells. Pale eosinophilic cytoplasm showed xanthomatous or vacuolar change. Immunohistochemistry confirmed the expression of the endothelial-associated markers CD31 and CD34 in the intratumoral capillaries, although not in the stromal cells themselves. Conversely, the stromal cells were diffusely immunoreactive for vimentin, with a minority of cells also coexpressing S100 protein and epithelial membrane antigen. No inflammatory infiltrate was detected except for the occasional mast cell. Staining for cytokeratins tested negative, as did the Langerhans-cell-associated marker CD1a. Less than 1% of lesional cell nuclei were labeled with the cell proliferation-associated antigen Ki-67.

case_report: A 48-year-old male patient was admitted due to a 3-year history of worsening hearing loss on the left side. Clinical examination revealed left-sided hearing loss. Additionally, the patient exhibited an abnormal finger-nose pointing test, abnormal rapid alternating movements, and heel-knee-shin ataxia on the left side. There was no evidence of facial palsy, and muscle tone in the extremities was normal.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed a round mass with a size of 5.42 × 4.27 × 5.35 cm in the left CPA region. The lesion was hypointense in the T1-weighted imaging (T1WI) and unevenly hyperintense in the T2-weighted imaging (T2WI). Heterogeneous enhancement in the tumor was observed in the contrast-enhanced MRI. The left cerebellum, the fourth ventricle, and the brain stem were compressed. Computerized tomography angiography (CTA) of the head revealed a high-density, patchy calcification shadow on the left CPA region. The lesion had a clear boundary with the intracranial vessels, and no intracranial artery malformation was observed. The tumor was not stained on the CTA image.

case_report: An 18-year-old female presented with pain and swelling on the left side of the face for six months. She had no prior surgical history or known diseases. Physical examination revealed a 3 cm × 4 cm swelling on the left side of the maxilla, located posterior to the second premolar tooth. The swelling was diffused, tender upon palpation, non-bleeding, non-compressible, and non-fluctuant. There was no associated paresthesia. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) indicated a mass in the left maxillary alveolar area displacing the teeth and extending into the maxillary sinus, causing bone destruction. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed an ill-defined T2 hyperintense heterogeneous lesion involving the posterior aspect of the tooth-bearing alveolar process of the maxilla.
test_results: The histopathology yielded spindle cells with wavy hyperchromatic, elongated nuclei and scant cytoplasm, along with fibrocollagenous tissue. Few masts cells were also seen. No dysplastic tissue or mitotic figures were seen. Staining of the sample was found positive for S-100 protein.

case_report: A 39-year-old female presented with a lesion on the palate. The patient was edentulous and exhibited a single, asymptomatic, sessile, and fibrous pink nodule with a smooth surface, measuring 30 × 30 × 05 mm, located on the right side of the posterior region of the hard palate near the alveolar border. The lesion had been present for three years. Her medical history was unremarkable. X-ray images did not reveal any abnormalities. An incisional biopsy was performed, and the specimen was sent for analysis.
test_results: Histological exam showed fusiform cell proliferation with undulated nuclei distributed in a disorganized fashion on the fibrous connective tissue. All the neoplastic cells were immunopositive for protein S-100.

case_report: A 51-year-old Caucasian male visited the gastroenterology clinic for a routine check-up. He reported no symptoms and was in good health. He had no history of gastrointestinal issues, fever, chills, or unexplained weight loss. His medical and surgical history was unremarkable, and he was not on any medication. His father had hypertension, but there was no family history of cancer. Vital signs were as follows: temperature 37 °C, heart rate 75 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, blood pressure 129/72 mmHg, and body mass index 23.4 kg/m2. Physical examination revealed no abnormalities; the abdomen was soft without tenderness or palpable masses, and there were no skin lesions or unusual pigmentation. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, and coagulation profile, were all normal. Hepatic serology results were negative.
test_results: He underwent a screening colonoscopy and was found to have a 3-cm submucosal pedunculated polyp about 15 cm from anal verge adjacent to the second rectal fold. Mucosal biopsies were obtained during the procedure. The specimen included fragments of colonic mucosa and a spindle cell tumor. As the mucosal specimens were unrevealing, the patient underwent magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis which showed a 2.3 cm × 1.4 cm lesion in the submucosa with no adenopathy. A subsequent endoscopic ultrasound revealed an ill-defined avascular lesion of mixed echogenicity measuring 2.8 cm × 15.2 cm in the submucosa with no communication with muscularis mucosa or propria. Fine needle biopsy, with 19G SharkCore™ needle (Covidien), was obtained for pathology assessment. The tumor showed bland spindle cell proliferation in a uniform fascicular pattern with edematous stroma. The cells were elongated, with oval/wavy nuclei. No mitotic figures, necrosis, or tumoral hemorrhage were seen. The tumor showed strong and diffuse S100 staining, with rare penetrating axons deep within the tumor. Tumor cells were negative for c-kit, desmin and had low Ki-67 index.

case_report: A 21-year-old male, previously treated for a brain condition 16 years ago with surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation, was admitted to our hospital in 2008 under pediatric oncology care due to abdominal pain lasting three months. He was found to have stage 3B Burkitt lymphoma, with no residual or recurrent brain condition. He achieved a complete metabolic response following chemotherapy according to UKCCSG B-NHL Group B guidelines (cyclophosphamide, vincristine, prednisone, doxorubicin alternating with cytarabine, high-dose methotrexate, and cyclophosphamide). After five years of active surveillance, he was discharged. In 2017, he presented with a left thigh mass diagnosed as an osteochondroma and was referred to an orthopedic surgeon for excision. In 2019, he returned to the adult oncology clinic with abdominal pain for one month. Examination showed no hyper or hypopigmentation on the skin of the trunk or extremities. Further evaluation revealed multiple polyps in the descending colon and rectum. Histopathology indicated tubulovillous adenomata with low-grade dysplasia and moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon. He underwent a right hemicolectomy (pT3N1a: AJCC 8th edition) and received five cycles of chemotherapy (capecitabine/oxaliplatin), followed by a completion colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis. Multiple tubulovillous adenomata were found throughout the colon, none showing high-grade dysplasia or invasive adenocarcinoma. The patient remained under active surveillance with regular endoscopies and imaging. Follow-up imaging in December 2021 revealed hepatic hypo-dense lesions involving adjacent right-sided hepatic ducts. He underwent an open total right hepatic lobectomy with cholecystectomy; histopathology confirmed metastatic adenocarcinoma of the colon.
test_results: Exome-based next-generation sequencing performed on the histopathology specimen revealed a high tumor mutation burden (74.91 mutations/megabase), MSI-high with a germline, bi-allelic, pathogenic loss of function mutation of MSH6, and a loss of function mutation (p.R2763*(c.8287C>T) in ataxia-telangiectasia mutated (ATM) kinase.

case_report: An 11-year-old girl was admitted to the hospital due to a polyp mass protruding from the anus. Physical examination identified multiple café-au-lait macules (CALMs) primarily on the anterior abdominal wall and lower back. These lesions exhibited areas of skin hypopigmentation with irregular borders and dense freckles. Additionally, a pigmented cutaneous nevus with hair was observed on her right forearm. Colonoscopy identified two large polyps in the rectum and anus. Pathological examination of the endoscopically-resected specimens revealed tubular adenomas with low-grade dysplasia. At the age of 16, she experienced a severe headache, and brain MRI revealed a right temporal-occipital ring-enhancing lesion measuring approximately 3.5 × 4.5 cm. She subsequently underwent gross total resection of the tumor, and pathological analysis indicated glioblastoma multiforme (WHO grade II) and partial anaplastic astrocytomas (WHO grade III).
test_results: The sequencing on genomic DNA demonstrated a homozygous deletion NM_00535.5:c.1577delA (p.Asp526fs) in exon 11 of the PMS2 gene. All other exons and their flanking regions showed a normal sequence. The result showed high-frequency microsatellite instability (MSI-H). Immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining detected expression loss of PMS2 protein in both CRC and non-neoplastic tissue, while MHL1, MSH2 and MSH6 were all expressed.

case_report: A 78-year-old Chinese woman presented with an isolated mass in her right breast discovered during a health checkup. A pulmonary CT scan identified multiple lesions in both lungs. She reported a history of cough and expectoration for two months, without fever, chest pain, dyspnea, or other symptoms. Physical examination revealed a firm, non-tender nodule measuring approximately 2.0×2.0 cm in the lateral superior quadrant of the right breast. Routine blood tests and tumor marker screening showed no significant abnormalities, but anti-SS-A and anti-SS-B antibodies were positive. Elevated levels of polyclonal serum immunoglobulins were noted: IgA at 485.00 mg/dL (reference range: 70 to 400 mg/dL), IgG at 2030.00 mg/dL (reference range: 700 to 1600 mg/dL), Ig light-chain kappa at 432.00 mg/dL (reference range: 170 to 370 mg/dL), and Ig light-chain lambda at 249.00 mg/dL (reference range: 90 to 210 mg/dL). A whole-body PET/CT scan was performed for staging purposes, using a Siemens Biograph TruePoint™ 64 system, 60 minutes after intravenous injection of 6.5 mCi (240 MBq) of 18F-FDG. The scan covered the area from the bottom of the skull to the mid-thigh. The PET maximum intensity projection image showed a hypermetabolic nodule in the right breast and slightly increased FDG uptake in the lymph nodes at the hilus of the lungs and posterior cervical region bilaterally. Transverse PET/CT images revealed a 2.3×1.9 cm, round, well-circumscribed homogenous isodense nodule in the right breast with a maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) of 7.30. Multiple irregular nodules with slight to mild FDG uptake were observed in the lungs, with the largest lesion being a 2.7×2.5 cm, round, well-defined solid nodule in the right lower lobe, having an SUVmax of 2.96. The bilateral posterior cervical lymph nodes were normal in size with an SUVmax of 4.48. Surgery on the mammary lesion was performed three days later.
test_results: The mammary lesion showed abundant plasma cells and sinus histiocytes, including large pale pathognomonic histiocytes that exhibited emperipolesis. Lymphoid follicle formation, patchy fibrosis, and obliterative phlebitis, accompanied by atrophy and loss of mammary lobules, were observed. Large histiocytes were positive for S-100 protein and CD-68 protein but negative for CD1a. The average number of IgG4+ cells was 118 per high-powered field, and the ratio of IgG4+ to IgG+ cells was 65%. Deposition of strongly Congo red-positive materials with few histiocytes and fibrotic cell infiltration in the lung tissue. Reactive lymphoproliferation and deposition of Congo red-positive materials within the adjacent connective tissue were observed in the cervical LN.
diagnosis: Rosai-Dorfman disease with IgG4-positive plasma cell infiltration
Orpha_name: Familial sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy

case_report: A 41-year-old woman with a history of presumed spinocerebellar ataxia presented with right heart failure due to an invasive mediastinal mass causing near complete occlusion of her pulmonary arteries. Initially, she experienced bilateral lower extremity edema and progressive dyspnea on exertion, leading to her first emergency department visit in February 2017. Imaging revealed an amorphous, invasive superior left mediastinal mass affecting the main and left pulmonary arteries, resulting in occlusion of the left pulmonary arterial tree and severe narrowing of the right pulmonary artery. Additional findings included moderate cardiomegaly with right heart enlargement, elevated right heart pressures, and several scattered, small nonspecific pulmonary nodules. A PET scan showed marked FDG avidity of the anterior mediastinal mass. An arteriogram indicated a severely stenosed but patent right main pulmonary artery with no filling of the left main pulmonary artery. Initial pathology from an intravascular biopsy revealed only thrombus material and a minute fragment of unremarkable intima. The patient was unable to complete a scheduled cardiac MRI and was lost to follow-up until May 2017, when she presented to the thoracic surgery clinic after a progressive decline. On admission, echocardiogram showed a severely dilated right atrium and right ventricle with the interatrial septum bowing to the left, indicating right heart failure. A second biopsy via bronchoscopy was nondiagnostic, showing only fragments of fibrous tissue with a mixed inflammatory infiltrate. A third biopsy via repeat intravascular approach was also nondiagnostic, revealing vessel wall fragments with myxoid degeneration and few small crushed cells, favoring an inflammatory infiltrate. Due to the significant risk of hemodynamic instability from the mass, she underwent pulmonary artery stenting. The interventional radiology team successfully stented the right pulmonary artery, but could not intervene on the totally occluded left pulmonary artery. Her gradients improved immediately after stenting, and she tolerated the procedure without complication.
test_results: A fourth biopsy taken at the time of stenting ultimately revealed fibrous tissue with lymphohistiocytic and plasma cell infiltrate with positive staining for S100, CD68, and CD163, negative staining for CD1a and Factor XIIIa, and emperipolesis. Pathologic analysis revealed no significant increase in IgG4+ plasma cells and no evidence of bacteria, acid fast, or fungal organisms on Gram, Fite, AFB, Grocott, and PAS stains.
Orpha_name: Familial sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy

case_report: An eight-year-old male child presented to the Pediatric Outpatient Department with facial asymmetry and polydactyly, along with bilateral microtia since birth. The child was delivered vaginally at a government hospital, with a birth weight of 2.5 kg. He is the second born in his family, with no family history of malformations. No mental retardation was observed during examination. The child was undernourished, weighing 15 kg and measuring 110 cm in height, both below the fiftieth percentile. Physical examination revealed facial asymmetry, right-sided infranuclear facial palsy, bilateral microtia with bilateral ear tags, a short neck, a high arched palate, and skin tags on the nape of the neck. Dental caries were present, but dental development was normal. There was lower motor neuron weakness of the facial nerve on the right side, indicated by an inability to close the right eye and loss of the nasolabial fold on the same side. Asymmetric crying facies were noted, with the right lower lip being pulled down during crying or chewing. The left eye closure and nasolabial fold were normal. Left preaxial polydactyly was present, while the other hand was normal, and the length of both hands was equal. The parents were normal on clinical examination, and the first and third children, both boys, were normal. Ophthalmological examination revealed a right-sided iris coloboma. Cardiac auscultation showed normal S1 and S2 sounds, with a soft systolic murmur in the pulmonary area. No other abnormalities were detected on systemic examination. Audiometry indicated moderate-to-severe bilateral conductive hearing loss. Abdominal sonography was normal. Renal function tests, liver function tests, and thyroid function tests were normal. Echocardiography and Color Doppler did not reveal any cardiac lesions. X-ray examination of the skull and vertebral column did not show any vertebral abnormalities.
test_results: A computed tomography (CT) scan of the temporal bone revealed bony atresia of the external auditory canal, with absence of mastoid pneumatization of the right ear and left ear, showing auricular tags with bony atresia of the external auditory canal, with a deformed ossicular chain.

case_report: A 23-year-old white male with a 4-year history of Crohn's disease presented with a sudden onset of malaise, fever, abdominal pain, vomiting, and stomal diarrhea over two days. He reported joint pains in the shoulders, elbows, wrists, metacarpophalangeal joints, knees, and ankles. Additionally, he had a rash on the elbows, ankles, and feet, which started as red macules and progressed to vesico-pustular lesions followed by crusting. There was no history of sexual exposure or recent infections. He was not on any regular medication but had stopped taking Pentasa four months prior. One month earlier, he had a laparotomy to remove a complex ileo-cutaneous fistula with blind tracts, and two weeks earlier, a defunctioning ileostomy was performed due to ongoing abdominal pain. The cutaneous fistula had been present for a year and was associated with a terminal ileal stricture and ileo-rectal fistula for at least two years. His bowel disease had not responded to immunosuppressive drugs, including azathioprine, corticosteroids, and three infusions of Infliximab a year earlier. There had been no extra-intestinal symptoms. Upon hospital admission, he was thin, afebrile, with a resting heart rate of 125 beats per minute. The rest of the cardio-respiratory examination was normal. The abdomen was minimally tender around the ileostomy without guarding or rebound tenderness. Skin examination revealed pustules and crusts around the elbows, ankles, and feet, sparing the buttocks. Clinical signs of synovitis were observed in the wrists, proximal interphalangeal, and metacarpophalangeal joints, as well as both ankles. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 13.1 gm/dl, white blood cell count of 15.8 × 10^9/L, platelet count of 585 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein level of 37.7 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 69 mm/hr. Urea and electrolytes, complement levels, urine analysis, and microscopy were normal. Tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, cryoglobulins, and Hepatitis B and C serology were negative. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed no signs of endocarditis, and multiple blood cultures were sterile.
test_results: A skin biopsy from the ankle revealed a perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with prominent neutrophils and associated fibrinoid necrosis of vessels consistent with 'leukocytoclastic' vasculitis.

case_report: A 39-year-old male with a history of ulcerative colitis presented to the emergency department with a 4-day history of severe bilateral pain and swelling at the Achilles' tendon insertion sites, along with bilateral knee swelling and tenderness. The patient reported a persistent fever (>38.7°C) that did not respond well to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Two weeks prior to admission, the patient noticed a new skin rash on the upper and lower limbs. The ulcerative colitis was diagnosed nearly 3 years ago, based on clinical history of bloody diarrhea, weight loss, and histopathological findings of distorted and inflamed crypts with inflammatory cells in the lamina propria from a colonoscopy biopsy. Initial treatment included methylprednisolone, followed by a maintenance regimen of prednisone with a tapering plan, mesalamine (5-aminosalicylic acid), and azathioprine. Despite this, the patient never achieved complete remission but continued on maintenance therapy until the current presentation. The patient denied any history of unprotected sexual intercourse, recreational drug use, recent travel, or newly initiated medications. On initial assessment, the patient was febrile (38.5°C) with a heart rate of 117 beats per minute. Skin examination revealed erythematous papular, maculopapular, and urticaria-like rash with some vesiculopustular lesions, some of which were crusted. The lesions, averaging 3–7 mm in diameter, were not well demarcated and were predominantly on the limbs rather than the trunk, with no exudates. Joint examination showed severe tenderness, significant swelling, redness, and restricted movement at the Achilles' tendon insertion sites bilaterally, as well as swelling, erythema, and tenderness in both knees. The rest of the clinical examination was unremarkable.
test_results: Colour Doppler ultrasound confirmed enthesitis and enthesopathy at the insertion sites of Achilles' tendons. Bedside skin biopsy from the left upper arm skin rash demonstrated neutrophilic, perivascular lymphohistiocytosis infiltrates with edema in the dermis.

case_report: A 57-year-old male with an 8-year history of poorly controlled Type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, two previous episodes of transient ischemic attacks, and underlying cirrhosis of the liver secondary to hepatitis C and alcohol abuse presented with a two-day history of inability to walk. The patient reported that his symptoms began approximately two months prior, with a sudden onset of right calf pain, erythema, and swelling. Initial treatment with various courses of antibiotics by a family physician was unsuccessful. The pain progressively worsened until the day before admission, when the patient could no longer bear weight on the affected leg. He denied any history of fever, trauma, animal bites, or infection. Initial laboratory results showed moderate leukocytosis (white blood count of 14.7 × 10^9 cells/L), normal electrolytes, and unremarkable liver function tests. At presentation, the patient had a blood glucose level of 28.5 mmol/L and a glycated hemoglobin of 13.9%. The spot urine albumin/creatinine ratio indicated significant microalbuminuria. Additional diabetic workup did not reveal any signs of retinopathy or neuropathy. Blood cultures were obtained, and the patient was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics. A doppler ultrasound study of both legs ruled out deep vein thrombosis. Antibiotic therapy did not alleviate his symptoms, and subsequent cultures showed no bacterial growth, leading to the discontinuation of antibiotics. Initial computed tomography imaging of both legs did not show any signs of infection or abscess.
test_results: MRI revealed significant edema, inflammation, necrosis of gastrocnemious and soleus muscles and identified a number of associated communicating fluid collections.

case_report: A 52-year-old Hispanic male with recently identified diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and ischemic cardiomyopathy presented with a one-month history of nonradiating right thigh erythema, pain, and swelling. He worked as a warehouse clerk but was on disability due to severe, debilitating pain in his right thigh. The patient required maximal assistance for ambulation and occasionally used a wheelchair. He denied fever, physical trauma, or intravenous drug use. The patient had multiple emergency department and urgent care visits before our evaluation, with no significant improvement on oral antibiotics. Vital signs on presentation were blood pressure 108/69 mm Hg, heart rate 77 beats per minute, temperature 37.5°C, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Physical examination revealed a hard, tender, erythematous 7 × 4 inch mass on the right anterior thigh with accompanying right upper thigh edema. Distal pulses were 2+ on palpation. The right lower extremity had 3+ pitting edema, while the left lower extremity had 2+ pitting edema. Severe tenderness was noted in the right groin region with associated painful groin lymphadenopathy. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 10.7 × 10^3 cells/mcl, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 49 mm, elevated C-reactive protein of 7.98 mg/dL, aldose value of 3.8 units/L, elevated creatinine of 1.31 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen of 25 mg/dL, urine albumin/creatinine ratio of 1,342.8 mcg/mg Cr, creatinine kinase of 844 unit/L, and hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) of 10.3%. Blood cultures were negative. Laboratory values for polymyositis and dermatomyositis were negative. A venous Doppler ultrasound of the right leg was negative for deep vein thrombosis.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) without contrast of the femur demonstrated bilateral inflammatory changes with disproportionate enlargement and diffuse heterogeneity of the right vastus medialis muscle with patchy areas of intramuscular hemorrhage, extensive subcutaneous edema, interfascial free fluid, and severe myositis.

case_report: A 58-year-old male reported experiencing severe pain in the bilateral groin for six weeks. He did not have fever, urinary symptoms, incontinence, trauma, weight loss, or saddle anesthesia. His medical history included diabetes mellitus and hypertension. On physical examination, there was tenderness in the suprapubic region, normal testicles, no inguinal hernias, and hyperpigmentation from the groin to the left mid-thigh. Laboratory results showed elevated creatinine at 1.56 mg/dL (normal 0.60 to 1.30 mg/dL), creatine kinase (CK) at 177 U/L (normal 24 – 223 U/L), C-reactive protein (CRP) at 180 mg/L (normal <10.01 mg/L), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) at 106 mm/hr (normal 2 – 37 mm/hr). Hemoglobin A1c was 11.4% (normal 4.0 – 6.4%). Ultrasound of the scrotum and computed tomography of the abdomen/pelvis did not provide conclusive information.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the bilateral lower extremities revealed acute myoedema involving the left obturator internus, externus and proximal adductor muscles of the left thigh.

case_report: An 11-year-old girl from eastern Algeria, the younger of two children from a first-degree consanguineous marriage, presented with erythematous patches on her face and back starting 20 days after birth, along with recurrent fever primarily occurring in cold weather. These symptoms typically resolved after 3 weeks but reappeared with cold exposure. At one year old, she experienced nodular erythema on her neck, swollen and painful fingers with acrocyanosis, multiple papules on the soles of her feet, and arthralgia, which may have affected her ability to walk (she began walking at age 3). She also exhibited mental retardation noticeable when she started school at age 6. Physical examination showed she was small for her age, weighing 25 kg (−4.9 SD) and measuring 114 cm in height (−2.23 SD), with a BMI of 19.23 kg/m2. She had a fever (38.7°C) at admission. Multiple erythematous patches and nodular annular erythema were observed, especially on her extremities, along with lipodystrophy mainly in the upper extremities. The patches were purple to pink, and she had clubbed, swollen fingers. She reported acrocyanosis, arthralgia, and difficulty walking when exposed to cold weather. Laboratory results showed a WBC count of 14.7 × 103/mm3, hypochromic microcytic anaemia with a haemoglobin level of 8.1 g/dl, mean corpuscular volume of 73 fl, and a platelet count of 68 × 103/mm3. Additional tests revealed an ESR of 56 mm/h, C-reactive protein level of 20 mg/l, and elevated alpha- and gamma-globulin levels. Autoimmunity parameters including cryoglobulin, transglutaminase antibodies, rheumatoid factors, antinuclear antibodies, and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide were within normal limits.
test_results: Histopathological examination of a skin lesion under a light microscope was indicative of mastocytosis. Ultrasound examination revealed homogeneous hepatomegaly and splenomegaly.

case_report: A 4-year-old Chinese boy presented with progressive erythematous plaques on his nose for 6 months, which gradually spread to his hands and feet, accompanied by intermittent fever. He did not report symptoms such as stomachache or diarrhea. His parents denied any history of trauma or allergies, and there was no parental consanguinity or notable family history. Physical examination revealed moderately enlarged lymph nodes in the bilateral axillary regions, with no obvious abnormalities in internal organs. Multiple erythematous plaques were observed on his face and extremities. The patient exhibited clubbed fingers and toes, along with mild joint contracture in his fingers. Laboratory analysis indicated slight anemia with hemoglobin at 107 g/L (normal range: 120-140 g/L). Elevated levels of serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 44 IU/L (normal range: 15-40 IU/L), lactic dehydrogenase (LDH) at 347 IU/L (normal range: 120-250 IU/L), and hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (HBDH) at 286 IU/L (normal range: 26-195 IU/L) were noted, while erythrocyte sedimentation rate, ANA series tests, and other routine tests were negative. Chest X-ray showed increased lung markings. Serial cranial CT scans revealed no basal ganglia calcification, and an abdominal CT scan did not show hepatosplenomegaly. A skin biopsy from a hand lesion showed hyperkeratosis, irregular epidermal hyperplasia, mild spongy edema, and single necrotic keratinocytes in the epidermis, along with mild vacuolar degeneration. Medium monocytes with neutrophilic cells were observed infiltrating around dermal vessels, with nuclear dust and mitotic figures present. Immunohistochemical examination indicated that most infiltrating cells were positive for CD3, CD68, and MPO.
test_results: The results showed compound heterozygous mutations c.373C > T (p.R125C) and c.355G > A (p.D119N) in the exon3 of the PSMB8 (NM_004159.5; MIM 177046) gene in proband. His parents were both heterozygous carriers with no clinical symptom.

case_report: A 32-year-old woman reported experiencing painless unilateral blurring of vision in her left eye for the past three months. Her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/250 in the left eye. Examination of the right eye was normal with a cup disc ratio (CDR) of 0.5. The left eye showed engorged episcleral vessels, a relative afferent pupillary defect, grade III nuclear sclerosis with cortical cataract, and a CDR of 0.9 on fundus examination. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 16 mmHg in the right eye and 42 mmHg in the left eye, as measured by Goldman applanation tonometry. Gonioscopy indicated open angles in both eyes. There was no proptosis or audible bruit, and extraocular movements were full. Color vision and Humphrey visual field analysis 24-2 were normal in the right eye, while the left eye exhibited severely depressed fields with central 10° around fixation preserved. Treatment for the left eye included topical timolol maleate 0.5%, dorzolamide 2%, and travoprost 0.004%, along with systemic acetazolamide 250 mg twice daily.
test_results: Neuro-imaging showed no evidence of tumor, thrombosis, or arterio-venous malformations.
Orpha_name: Okihiro syndrome due to a point mutation

case_report: The patient is a 39-year-old male, the eldest of two siblings. His mother experienced progressive proximal muscle weakness, had a pacemaker implanted at 40 years old due to a slow heart rate, and passed away from sudden cardiac arrest at 50. His younger brother also had proximal lower limb weakness and died by suicide at 31. The patient began toe-walking and experiencing frequent falls around age 5. During adolescence, he developed proximal leg weakness and exhibited Gowers' sign. At 30, he was diagnosed with atrial fibrillation and prescribed aspirin and an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. Mild ankle contractures were also observed. Electromyographic studies showed myopathic changes in the biceps brachii and rectus femoris, with small amplitude muscle potentials and short-duration polyphasic waves. His baseline creatine kinase level was approximately 200 IU/L (reference range for males: <190 IU/L). At 36, he reported chest tightness, and electrocardiography revealed atrial fibrillation with a slow ventricular rate, right bundle branch block, and transient ventricular tachycardia, leading to the implantation of a VVI pacemaker. He later experienced acute right limb weakness and speech disturbance, prompting immediate hospitalization. Neurological examination indicated global aphasia, right hemianopia, left gaze deviation, and right hemiplegia, with an NIHSS score of 22. Initial head CT showed no intracranial hemorrhage. Intravenous thrombolytic therapy with recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (73 mg, 0.9 mg/kg) was administered within 3 hours of stroke onset. Subsequent CT angiography revealed near-total occlusion of the left distal internal carotid artery and proximal middle cerebral artery, while CT perfusion imaging showed reduced cerebral perfusion in the left hemisphere. Follow-up head CT the next day showed a hypodensity lesion in the left MCA territory, smaller than the previous perfusion defect. Transcranial color-coded sonography indicated partial recanalization with a visible MCA flow signal and mildly reduced flow velocity.
