Two-dimensional echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 47% and enlargement of both ventricles and the left atrium. Twenty-four hours post-thrombolytic therapy, his NIHSS score improved to 16, and one week later, it further improved to 5. He was prescribed oral anticoagulation for secondary stroke prevention. Post-rehabilitation, his right hemiplegia and aphasia gradually improved. Six months after the stroke, he could walk unaided and speak fluently, with only mild naming difficulty.
test_results: The confirmatory sequencing demonstrated a heterozygous mutation of “G” to “A” transition at the splicing donor site at intron 2 (c.513+1 G>A / wild type). The nucleoside change was not identified in screening 50 Taiwanese controls.
Orpha_name: Autosomal dominant limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 1B

case_report: A premature female infant was born to a 28-year-old woman (G3, P2) at 28 weeks of gestation. The mother had been admitted at 26 weeks due to respiratory difficulty. Imaging revealed polyhydramnios, necessitating therapeutic amniocentesis with approximately 2000 ml of amniotic fluid drained. Imaging also identified a solid mass in the right kidney. Two weeks later, the mother experienced early labor and delivered vaginally. The infant was born with apnea, cyanosis, and bradycardia but was successfully resuscitated. Upon admission to the NICU, her vital signs were stable. She required mechanical ventilation and surfactant therapy. Physical examination on the first day revealed a palpable mass in the right flank, occupying most of the right side of the abdomen. By the end of the first week, the infant developed hypertension, which was managed with hydralazine. Serum creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, and serum electrolytes were within normal ranges. Serum renin and aldosterone levels were not assessed.
test_results: Abdominal ultrasonography showed a 55mm × 40mm heterogeneous solid mass involving the right kidney area. CT scan confirmed a large hypodense mass with heterogeneous enhancement arising from the right kidney with cortical enhancement. Gross pathological examination showed a solid renal tumor weighing 50 grams and measuring 4 × 5 × 4.5 cm. No necrosis or hemorrhage was identified. Microscopy revealed a moderately cellular spindle cell neoplasm infiltrating adjoining renal parenchyma, perirenal fat and renal sinus. The renal pelvis and calyces and the suprarenal gland were not infiltrated, no vascular invasion was seen. There was a moderate nuclear pleomorphism and mild to moderate mitotic activity. The neoplastic cells showed positive immunoreactivity for vimentin. There was no reactivity for desmin, actin, keratin or S-100 protein.

case_report: A 17-day-old full-term male infant was brought to our Department due to a noticeable mass on the left side of the abdomen, difficulties with feeding, and insufficient weight gain. The pregnancy and birth history were normal. Upon admission, the physical examination revealed significant overall growth restriction, with a weight of 2,480 grams (<0.4th percentile, -2.9 SD), a length of 47 cm (<0.4th percentile, -2.9 SD), and a head circumference of 33 cm (<0.4th percentile, -2.6 SD). The abdomen appeared enlarged with visible veins and a palpable mass on the left side. No other abnormalities were detected.
test_results: Abdominal US documented a solid mass in the left kidney measuring 7.5 × 6.5 cm, with hypoechoic areas of necrosis without infiltration of the vascular pedicle. Abdominal CT better defined the neoformation, which was located in the left renal lodge and characterized by inhomogeneous enhancement and absence of lymph node enlargement or infiltration. Subsequent histological examination disclosed a neoformation characterized by oval and spindle-shaped cells arranged in bundles, with necrosis and mitotic activity of 10/10 per high-power field; molecular analysis revealed the ETV6-NTRK3 fusion.

case_report: This case report has received approval from the Medical Ethics Committee of First Hospital of Jilin University (2020-371), and written informed consent was obtained from the patient and caregiver. A 29-year-old pregnant woman (G2P0) with a natural pregnancy participated in this study. She reported no unhealthy lifestyle habits and denied any previous exposure to radioactive materials, chemical raw materials, or pesticides. Results from Down's screening and an oral glucose tolerance test were normal. Her spouse was healthy and did not have any harmful habits. In 2019, the woman underwent two systematic ultrasound examinations at 24 and 31 weeks of gestation. No abnormalities were detected in the right kidney of the fetus, and there was an increase in the amniotic fluid index (AFI) from 19.3 cm to 20.8 cm.
test_results: Prenatal routine ultrasonography identified a fetal right renal mass at 35 weeks of gestation. The tumor was about 3.3 × 3.0 × 2.7 cm, solid, well-defined, and hyperechoic with uniform internal echo. Color Doppler ultrasound presented a large nutrient vessel entering the inside of the tumor, and circular blood flow signal could be seen around the tumor with an AFI of 25.3 cm. MRI showed that the posterolateral contour of the right kidney of the fetus was plump, locally convex, about 3.0 × 1.9 × 2.6 cm in size. The signals of TIWI, T2-haste and T2-trufi were similar to those of the renal parenchyma, while the signals of diffusion weighted imaging were slightly higher than those of the renal parenchyma, and the boundary between the lesion and the adjacent structures were clear. Postnatal ultrasonography showed a solid, well-defined, heterogeneous mass of 3.9 × 3.0 × 3.8 cm in the posterior upper part of the right kidney of the neonate.

case_report: A 45-year-old Caucasian male presented with reduced visual acuity in both eyes since childhood. His medical and family history were unremarkable. Best-corrected visual acuities were 20/60 in each eye with corrections of −8.00–2.00×135 OD and −8.00–1.25×020 OS. External examination was normal. Intraocular pressures (IOPs) were 17 mmHg in the right eye and 18 mmHg in the left eye. Dilated fundus examination with binocular indirect ophthalmoscopy and scleral depression showed an intact retina without holes, tears, or pigmented cells in the vitreous. Optic disc hypoplasia was noted in both eyes. Over a period of 3 years, IOPs ranged from 15 to 19 mmHg in both eyes. During this time, retinal nerve fiber layer thinning and corresponding visual field defects were observed. Glaucoma therapy was initiated using Travatan Z ophthalmic solution once daily in both eyes. IOPs stabilized at 13 mmHg in each eye, and the patient continues to be monitored for any changes.
test_results: Slit lamp examination revealed midperipheral iris transillumination defects, pigment on the corneal endothelium and dense, and symmetrical pigment on the posterior lens capsules. Gonioscopy revealed angles open to ciliary body with grade 2+ pigment in all quadrants and no evidence of angle recession. The optic nerves were small: ~1 mm ×1 mm as measured with Spectral Domain Optical Coherence Tomography (SD-OCT). The pattern of pigment was dense, oblique, and curvilinear and located along the posterior lens capsules. The pigment on the posterior capsule created shadows on the retina, which were best documented with Optos Daytona ultra-widefield imaging. Over time, it appeared that there was an increase in pigment deposition along the posterior lens capsule. Comparing photos 1 year apart, one can observe the apparent increase in the size of pigment deposition. Photos taken 2 years later showed a marked decrease in pigment deposition on the posterior lens capsules.

case_report: A 23-year-old female patient sought consultation for refractive surgery. Her manifest refraction was −11.50 −2.50 × 5° in the right eye (OD) and −11.15 −2.00 × 175° in the left eye (OS). Corrected distance visual acuity (CDVA) was 20/30 in both eyes. OD endothelial cell count was 3250 cells/mm², anterior chamber depth (ACD) was 3.00 mm, and crystalline lens rise (CRL) was 380 μm. OS results showed an endothelial cell count of 3299 cells/mm², ACD of 2.97 mm, and CRL of 260 μm. No signs of pigment dispersion were observed in either eye. Given her ACD deeper than 2.9 mm and healthy corneal endothelium, she was considered suitable for iris-claw phakic pIOL, the type used at our institution. It was explained that residual astigmatism might persist post-surgery. The patient underwent iris-claw pIOL (Artisan®) implantation in both eyes in November 2015, with superior iridectomies performed in both eyes. On the first postoperative day, uncorrected distance visual acuity (UCDVA) and CDVA were 20/30 in OD, with a refraction of −0.25 −0.50 × 40°. OS had a UCDVA of 20/40, a refraction of +0.25 −2.25 × 160°, and a CDVA of 20/30. The pIOLs were well positioned in both eyes. One week post-surgery, UCDVA was 20/25 in OD and 20/40 in OS. OS improved to 20/25 with a correction of Plano −2.00 × 155°. The corneas were clear, there were no signs of intraocular inflammation, the pIOLs were stable and well-positioned, and intraocular pressure (IOP) measurements were normal. The patient then returned to her hometown in a neighboring country. Three months later, she reported a change in the color of her OD, along with redness and pain a few days prior. She had been seen by an ophthalmologist in her country who prescribed timolol 0.5%. At the time of examination at our institution, she was asymptomatic. UCDVA was 20/20 in OD and 20/30 in OS. Slit-lamp examination of OD revealed noticeable depigmentation of the peripheral iris. The pIOL was correctly positioned and well fixated to the iris. Examination of OS showed the iris-claw pIOL with minimal pigment deposits in the optic. IOP was 15 mmHg in OD and 16 mmHg in OS.
test_results: Gonioscopy showed discontinuous peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) in all quadrants (>180°) in OD and open angle without PAS in 360° in OS. Endothelial count was 3 309 cells/mm2 in OD and 3 056 cells/mm2 in OS.

case_report: A 61-year-old female was referred for evaluation. Her medical history includes diabetes mellitus and hypertension. Initial symptoms began at age 21 with shoulder girdle weakness and subsequent difficulty walking. Physical examination revealed winged scapulae, weakness in the shoulder girdle, facial muscles, and trunk, along with a steppage gait. Cardiac function was normal with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 75%. Vital capacity decreased from 74% in the sitting position to 46% in the supine position, indicating diaphragm muscle impairment. Additionally, sniff nasal inspiratory pressure was significantly reduced at 17 cmH2O, and maximal inspiratory pressure was 12 cmH2O, indicating reduced diaphragm muscle strength.
test_results: The imaging exam disclosed an opposite side to side hemi diaphragm displacement, either during sniff maneuver or deep inspiration maneuver, with a cranial abnormal reduced motion of the right hemi diaphragm whereas the left hemi diaphragm moved caudally during inspiration or sniff maneuver.

case_report: A 40-year-old male presented with asymmetric weakness in both upper and lower extremities. He reported bilateral shoulder weakness starting at age 10 and a right winged scapula at age 13. Additionally, he experienced bilateral leg weakness since age 24. Physical examination showed a transverse smile, winged scapula, 'Popeye' arm appearance, facial weakness, and asymmetric, proximal dominant arm and leg weakness, with the right side being more affected than the left. Serum creatinine kinase levels were mildly elevated at 319 unit/L. His father and elder brother exhibited similar symptoms. The elder brother, who had been receiving care at another hospital since age 10, had muscle pathology indicating severe chronic myopathic changes, including marked size variability, hypertrophic fibers, degenerating and atrophic fibers, endomysial fibrosis, mild fatty infiltration, disruption of the intermyofibrillar network, and lobulated fibers, with normal dystrophin immunoreactivity. The elder brother was diagnosed based on clinical phenotype but declined genetic testing.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing revealed a novel frameshift mutation (c.3801delG, p.Glu1267Aspfs*5) in SMCHD1. Methylation-sensitive Southern blot analysis with FseI showed mildly reduced D4Z4 repeat size on 4q (41kb/39kb) and reduced D4Z4 methylation ratio (14.6%).

case_report: A 57-year-old Caucasian male presented with acute pneumonia and progressive difficulty swallowing. He reported painless swallowing difficulties, dry mouth, hoarseness, and a sensation of a mass in the upper esophagus. His medical history includes type II diabetes, chronic bronchitis, chronic gastritis, urate nephropathy with a history of kidney stones, and coronary artery disease. The patient has a history of daily alcohol and nicotine use for 40 years. Physical examination revealed bilateral eyelid drooping and mild facial weakness. Observations included a wet voice and insufficient cough reflex after consuming solids and liquids, leading to aspiration. Laryngoscopy indicated incomplete glottic closure and impaired vocal cord mobility. A video-radiological barium examination showed aspiration during and after swallowing. Contrast-enhanced CT scans identified a homogeneous mass (1.5 × 2 cm) in the preepiglottic space, behind the hyoid bone. Panendoscopy and esophagus-gastroscopy were performed under general anesthesia. Endoscopic findings did not reveal any obvious cause for the progressive swallowing difficulty. A deep incision biopsy of the preepiglottic space was performed, showing only fatty tissue without any suspect structures. Histopathological evaluation confirmed the presence of fatty tissue without malignant pathology. Family history revealed that four of his eight siblings developed similar symptoms around the age of 50, with one brother experiencing only mild swallowing difficulty. Additionally, the patient's father, one paternal uncle, one paternal aunt, and her son have swallowing difficulties and eyelid drooping. The patient's family is of native German origin without French-Canadian or Jewish ancestry. The patient underwent bilateral eyelid surgery to correct drooping one year ago. Genetic counseling was initiated considering the family history of swallowing disorders.
test_results: DNA testing revealed a heterozygous (GCG)10 expansion of the (GCG)-mini-repeat, located in exon 1 of the poly(A) binding protein, nuclear 1gene (PABPN1).

case_report: An 80-year-old male patient presented with progressive difficulty swallowing over a period of 5 years. The swallowing difficulty primarily concerned solid foods, but also liquids to a lesser extent. He reported difficulties with swallowing his saliva, nasal regurgitation, and frequent coughing. Additionally, he noticed a change in his voice that became poorly articulate. His weight remained relatively stable over the years. The general medical history was unremarkable. Physical examination showed phlegm in the oral cavity, hoarseness, and unilateral drooping of the eyelid. Laboratory evaluation revealed elevated levels of C-reactive protein, creatinine kinase, and lactate dehydrogenase. Intubation of the esophagus during esophagogastroduodenoscopy was difficult due to an asymmetry of the pharyngeal recess, especially on the right side. Histology revealed moderate esophagitis. Barium swallow showed severe hypotension of the hypopharynx with aspiration of contrast dye into the airways. Esophageal manometry showed a non-specific motility disorder with more than 10% simultaneous contractions and dropouts, whereas complete relaxation of the upper esophageal sphincter was noticed. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head and neck ruled out a malignant or central ischemic process.
test_results: A DNA analysis revealed a rare homozygous elongation of the GCN repeat area ((GCN)6(GCN)4(GCN)) of the poly-(A) binding protein nuclear 1 (PABPN1) gene.

case_report: Patient 4 is a 27-year-old male with a history of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and previously treated pediatric asthma. He is the older sibling of patient 3. His father and sister have a known medical condition. He was admitted to the hospital for evaluation. He reported numbness and pain in both lower limbs and a decrease in grip strength. Neurological examination did not reveal noticeable abnormalities such as myotonia or muscle atrophy. Laboratory examination results were within normal limits. The WAIS-III assessment showed IQ levels of FIQ 93, VIQ 92, and PIQ 97, with a significantly lower processing speed index score compared to other indexes. Developmental assessments confirmed ASD, with noted deficiencies in communication and social skills, and difficulty maintaining prolonged work. His mother observed excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS). He was indifferent to his sleep issues and scored six on the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS). Polysomnography (PSG) indicated severe obstructive sleep apnea, with an apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) of 30.5 events per hour and a 3% oxygen desaturation index (ODI) of 18 events per hour. Multiple Sleep Latency Tests (MSLTs) showed he fell asleep during all naps with sleep latencies of 14, 21, 14, 6, and 19.5 minutes, resulting in a mean sleep latency of 14.9 minutes. Sleep onset rapid eye movement periods (SOREMP) were recorded once. His daytime cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) orexin level was 228 pg/ml.
test_results: The results of a TP PCR revealed an expanded CTG repeat allele. Southern blot analysis revealed a CTG expansion of 250 repeats.

case_report: Patient 1 (P1) is an 11-year-old girl from a non-consanguineous Japanese family, born at 41 weeks and 6 days with intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR). Her birth weight was 2352 g (−2.8 SD) and her birth height was 48.0 cm (−1.3 SD). She experienced severe newborn jaundice. Laboratory results showed NK cell cytopaenia (73 /µL, 1.4% of PBMCs) and low NK cell cytotoxic activity (6%). By the age of 2 years, she had been hospitalized seven times due to severe viral and bacterial infections. At birth, she had skin pigmentation and elevated adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) levels. Her cortisol levels did not increase in response to an ACTH loading test, indicating adrenal insufficiency due to ACTH resistance, for which cortisol replacement therapy was initiated. Motor development milestones included holding her neck up at 5 months, sitting without support at 7 months, hands-and-knees crawling at 14 months, and standing with assistance at 18 months. She exhibited delayed mental development, with an IQ of 33 at 9 years of age according to the Tanaka-Binet intelligence scale, indicating severe intellectual disability. At 2 years of age, she developed growing right cervical lymphadenopathy.
test_results: Excisional biopsy revealed Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL).

case_report: A 49-year-old woman came to our neurology department with acute, persistent neck pain on the left side, which did not respond to ibuprofen. The pain, located over the left common carotid artery, began 3 weeks ago and worsened over the past 8 days. There were no associated focal neurological deficits. An ultrasonographic evaluation at an outpatient facility revealed wall thickening of the left common carotid artery, prompting an urgent referral to our clinic. Her medical history includes hypertension, dyslipidemia with hypercholesterinemia, and a second mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccination with elasomeran (mRNA-1273, Spikevax®) in the left upper arm 7 days before the onset of symptoms.
test_results: CT angiography performed upon admission showed a semilunar hypodense thickening of the left CCA with a slight accompanying luminal narrowing. An additional MRI revealed a periarterial rather than ventrally situated STIR-signal enhancement in the middle third part of the left CCA on the postcontrast T1-weighted Dixon sequence. Furthermore, a membranous structure within the CCA and a distinct ventrally accentuated circumjacent contrast enhancement were found. An ultrasonographic examination performed in our department revealed a focal eccentric 30 mm long medially located hypoechoic to moderately echogenic wall thickening of the middle third of the left CCA, which exhibited a multilayered appearance. A local, hemodynamically irrelevant stenosis of the left CCA was additionally seen. No intraluminal thrombus or dissection membrane could be demonstrated in the high-resolution sonographic exploration (18 MHz probe).

case_report: A 27-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department following her first episode of seizures. During the initial evaluation, she reported experiencing tension headaches and sensitivity to sound for the past three days, with no other symptoms. She mentioned being treated for both colon and uterine cancer with chemotherapy and radiotherapy, and stated there were no known cerebral metastases. Her follow-up was managed by another health center, and no electronic medical records were available. She denied any other known medical conditions. Upon examination, the patient had a fever (38.0ºC) and high blood pressure (200/170 mm Hg). The clinical exam was otherwise normal, including a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15, normal pupil reactions, no neck stiffness, and no focal neurological deficits. She had a body mass index of 31.2 kg/m2. During the examination, she experienced two generalized tonic-clonic seizures. After the second seizure, she did not fully regain consciousness and was intubated to secure her airway. A urinary catheter was placed due to a distended bladder. Laboratory tests showed metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate levels (pH 7.25, PaCO2 22 mm Hg, PaO2 110 mm Hg, HCO3- 9.3 mmol/l, SaO2 98%, lactate 10.3 mmol/l, glucose 101 mg/dl). Blood tests indicated leukocytosis with neutrophilia, but no renal, hepatic, thyroid dysfunction, or electrolyte imbalances. Toxicology screens and preliminary infectious disease assessments were negative. A cranial computed tomography scan was normal. A lumbar puncture revealed turbid cerebrospinal fluid with high protein, low glucose content, and polymorphonuclear cell predominance despite a low cell count. The patient was treated with vancomycin, ceftriaxone, acyclovir, dexamethasone, levetiracetam, and sodium valproate, and transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU). She developed hypoxemia within the first hours of ICU admission, and a computed tomography pulmonary angiogram ruled out pulmonary emboli but showed bilateral basal lung consolidations suggestive of an infectious cause, likely community-acquired pneumonia. Additional tests were inconclusive. After 24 hours in the ICU, the patient had not regained consciousness despite reduced sedation. An electroencephalogram showed no paroxysmal activity, and the remaining neurological evaluation was normal. She remained hypertensive despite multiple antihypertensive medications (labetalol, amlodipine, and captopril). Due to a lack of detailed medical history, her boyfriend and family were consulted. They confirmed her cancer treatment but had no further details as she attended medical appointments alone. The health center she mentioned was contacted, but no records were found under her name, and it did not have an oncology department.
test_results: The immunology pregnancy test was positive. The serum beta-human chorionic gonadotropin dosing (8739 mIU/ml) and obstetric echography confirmed the pregnancy. The suprapubic ultrasound disclosed a 25-26 week gestation and oligohydramnios. The urinalysis showed proteinuria.

case_report: A 35-year-old female with a BMI of 43.2 kg/m2 and a past medical history of bradycardia, anxiety, depression, and Herpes simplex virus-2 presented to the ER one week after giving birth, reporting shortness of breath and a sensation of a bubble in the middle of her chest. She also had bilateral lower extremity swelling. Her pregnancy and vaginal delivery were without complications, and there was no family history of cardiac disease. Upon admission, her vital signs included a heart rate of 48, blood pressure of 170/90 mmHg, respiration rate of 38 breaths/minute, temperature of 98.9 degrees Fahrenheit, and an oxygen saturation of 97%. The patient appeared breathless and anxious. Heart and lung auscultation revealed normal S1 and S2 sounds with clear lung fields. Cranial nerves II-XII were intact. Bilateral lower extremity swelling was noted without pitting. An initial electrocardiogram showed bradycardia with a regular rhythm and no ST changes. A chest X-ray indicated mild pulmonary edema with small bilateral pleural effusions. An echocardiogram revealed normal ventricular function with an estimated ejection fraction of 60-65% and moderate mitral regurgitation. Ventricular and atrial chamber sizes were within normal limits.
test_results: Her complete blood count (CBC) revealed normocytic anemia and her complete metabolic panel revealed an elevated N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), alkaline phosphatase, alanine transaminase, and aspartate transaminase. Urinalysis (UA) demonstrated turbidity with the presence of elevated protein, red blood cells, and white blood cells without the presence of bacteria.

case_report: A 30-year-old woman (gravida five, para five) with a history of migraine with aura delivered a healthy girl at 38 weeks of pregnancy via caesarean section. During her pregnancy, she developed leg edema and gestational diabetes. She maintained normal blood pressure and had no proteinuria throughout her pregnancy and postpartum period. On postpartum day 53, she reported a sudden severe headache and temporary visual loss in her left visual field. She was admitted to a local hospital where her neurological examination was normal except for left-sided hemianopsia. Her blood pressure was recorded at 180/90 mmHg. A CT scan of the head showed hypodensities in the cerebellum. An MRI scan of the brain revealed hyperintense signals on T2-weighted images predominantly in the right cerebellar hemisphere. Both a lumbar puncture and a transesophageal echocardiogram were normal. Three days after admission, she experienced two generalized tonic-clonic seizures. A subsequent CT scan indicated an intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) in the right frontal lobe. She was then transferred to our neurological intensive care unit for further management of the ICH. Upon admission, her neurological examination showed a somnolent state, bilaterally reduced vision, and moderate left-sided hemiparesis.
test_results: Brain MRI and magnetic resonance arteriography/venography (MRA/MRV) showed an ICH of the right frontal lobe, hyperintensities on FLAIR sequences of the right frontal lobe rostral of the ICH and in the right occipital lobe, whereas DWI revealed no abnormalities, thus suggesting a vasogenic edema in these areas. There was no evidence for an intracranial sinus thrombosis on MRV. Urinanalysis indicated a proteinuria.

case_report: A 65-year-old Caucasian male presented to the Department of Otolaryngology with a neck mass persisting for six months. The patient had undergone a left-side total parotidectomy over ten years ago, with no available records of the procedure. He reported no additional therapy and was not under any follow-up care. Physical examination identified a non-tender, soft, and irregular mass in the left posterior triangle of the neck. Additionally, a small subcutaneous lesion was noted in the parotid masseteric region on the same side. Facial neurological examinations were normal.
test_results: Post-contrast neck computed tomography (CT) scan demonstrated a very large cystic cervical mass (46 × 23 mm) with papillary projections in the antero-lateral aspect of the left neck zone Vb. Moreover, there was a small heterogeneously enhancing nodule with small central cystic components in the left pre-auricular region (at the site of the prior surgical bed). Ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration of the neck mass was done, and microscopic examinations revealed a hyper-cellular smear with a bloody background, composed of large polygonal oncocytic cells with abundant cytoplasm, round to oval large nuclei and distinct nucleoli, without mitotic activity, arranged in sheets, cohesive clusters, and isolated cells. Histopathology sections revealed a multi-nodular proliferation of neoplastic cells infiltrating adipose-muscular tissue, with variable architectural patterns including papillary, cribriform, closely packed micro-cysts and tubules lined by bland-looking cells with abundant colloid-like Periodic acid Schiff (PAS) positive and diastase resistant bubbly secretions. The neoplasm was associated by hemorrhagic foci, hemosiderin depositions, and cholesterol clefts with no evidence of lymph node residue. Tumor cells had eosinophilic and vacuolated cytoplasm with a high nuclear to cytoplasm (N/C) ratio, relatively monomorphic round vesicular nuclei, and small distinct nucleoli. Foci of HGT, including of desmoplastic stromal reaction, comedo-type necrosis, nuclear pleomorphism, and loss of secretory activity with perineural invasion were noted. Evaluation of the pre-auricular mass revealed a low-grade conventional SC without HGT or even neural invasion. By immune-staining tumoral cells were strongly positive for Ck7 and S100, patchy positive for Mammaglobin and GATA3, while negative for GCDFP-15, DOG1, ER, AR, Synaptophysin and P63.
Orpha_name: Malignant epithelial tumor of salivary glands

case_report: A 67-year-old male visited an otolaryngology clinic with a five-month history of an ulcer on the right floor of the mouth (FOM). The patient had previously undergone an initial evaluation at another facility, where an excisional biopsy identified a poorly differentiated and high-grade adenocarcinoma. A detailed examination at the clinic revealed a 2.0 cm shallow lesion affecting the right FOM and the ventral surface of the tongue.
test_results: An excisional biopsy showed a poorly differentiated and high-grade adenocarcinoma. A PET/CT scan following injection of 11.9 mCi of 18-fluoro-2-deoxyglucose (FDG) identified a hypermetabolic focus within the right tongue but no evidence of hypermetabolic activity within the neck or elsewhere. Further pathological examination of the surgical specimen contained a 2.6 cm infiltrative submucosal neoplasm centered under focally ulcerated squamous mucosa. Histologically negative margins were achieved. Examination of ipsilateral neck dissection revealed one involved lymph node. Microscopically, the tumor showed a biphasic differentiation. The epithelial component was predominantly composed of poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma comprising nests, ductules, and sheets of round basaloid cells with cytoplasm that varied from sparse to abundant cytoplasmic clearing. Intermixed within the carcinoma were scattered chondrosarcomatous foci characterized by a chondroid matrix and atypical nuclei. Immunostaining demonstrated that the carcinomatous component diffusely expressed cytokeratin AE1/AE3 and CK7. Notably, a few cytokeratin-positive cells were identified in the sarcomatous stroma. Vimentin was exclusive to chondroid areas while S100 and p63 positivity was scattered within the carcinoma but negative in the sarcomatous area. Focal expression of androgen receptor (AR) was present, along with weak and patchy expression of SOX10. The tumor was negative for HER2(neu) by immunohistochemistry and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). There was no evidence of coexisting or preexisting pleomorphic adenoma. RUNX1c.1183C>G is reported as a variant of unknown significance with an allelic variation of 48.0%. RNA sequencing revealed overexpression of the following genes: ERBB3, FGFR2, FGFR1, ERBB2 (HER2), CDKN2A, AR, and NY-ESO-1.
diagnosis: de novo carcinosarcoma of salivary gland origin
Orpha_name: Malignant epithelial tumor of salivary glands

case_report: A 61-year-old male had been aware of a right parotid mass for about 10 years but did not seek treatment as the mass was painless. Upon experiencing significant right parotid pain, he visited our affiliated hospital. Physical examination revealed a painful mass in his right parotid gland approximately 30 mm in diameter and ipsilateral facial nerve palsy of House–Brackmann (HB) grade III. Laboratory findings showed a leukocyte count of 12,190/μL and C-reactive protein (CRP) of 0.18 mg/dL. Computed tomography (CT) revealed an enhanced irregularly shaped mass in the right parotid gland. T1-weighted SE MR imaging of the mass showed lower intensity compared to the native parotid tissue. T2-weighted SE MR imaging showed intermediate signal intensity with partial hyperintensity. Nine days after the appearance of symptoms, he was referred to our hospital. On physical examination, the mass was still present but the pain had eased. Additionally, the facial nerve palsy had improved to HB grade II. Ultrasound examination revealed an inhomogeneous, lobulated mass (approximately 30 × 25 mm) in the right parotid gland. CT showed that the tumor had become smaller than at the time of the previous scan in our affiliated hospital. Ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) was attempted twice, initially finding necrotic material and subsequently a large number of histiocytes and acinar cells, along with a small number of eosinophilic cells, with no atypical findings observed. A total parotidectomy including exeresis and reconstruction of the facial nerve was planned, with preparations to preserve the facial nerve if a benign tumor was suggested during surgery. The patient underwent surgery 31 days after the appearance of symptoms. A modified Blair incision was made, revealing a dumbbell-shaped parotid tumor extending from the superficial to the deep lobe of the parotid gland. The buccal and marginal mandibular branches of the facial nerve were pinched by the tumor. The nerve branches were in contact with the tumor but not involved. The temporal and zygomatic branches were present on the tumor capsule. A portion of the tumor was cut off and used for frozen section diagnosis (FSD). It was found to consist of solid and cystic components. The solid component was surrounded by a fibrous capsule, and the wall of the cyst component was lined by stratified squamous epithelium, which did not show any atypical changes. Based on these results, the tumor was considered benign. The facial nerve was preserved using microscissors, and the tumor was removed between the zygomatic and buccal branches.
test_results: Histopathological examination showed the tumor contained clear cells, which formed a clear boundary between the normal parotid gland tissues. The Ki-67 labelling index was exceedingly low and the mitotic count was negative.
Orpha_name: Benign epithelial tumor of salivary glands

case_report: A 48-year-old woman presented to the Department of Otolaryngology at the Medical University of Gdańsk, Poland, with palpable masses in the parotid region that had been gradually enlarging on both sides over the past six months. She reported no additional symptoms and had no significant medical, family, or psychosocial history. Examination of the facial nerves showed normal function. Physical examination identified firm, movable tumors in both parotid glands, measuring 2 × 1.5 cm on the right and 3 × 3.5 cm on the left, with no discharge from the salivary ducts. Additionally, no lymphadenopathy was detected. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy results were reported as non-diagnostic on two occasions.
test_results: The examination confirmed the presence of tumors within the superficial lobe of the left parotid (3.6 × 3.2 × 3.7 cm) and the inferior part of the superficial lobe of the contralateral parotid (2.9 × 2.6 × 3 cm). It revealed the second lesion in the deep lobe of the right parotid gland (4.8 × 3.6 × 4 cm) extending into the parapharyngeal space. All three lesions had smooth, well-defined margins. They presented as heterogeneous structures, with central cystic areas, partially with higher protein content and signs of bleeding, and enhancing, more peripherally placed solid components. Tumours did not show signs of diffusion restriction with apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) values of approximately 1.48 × 10−3 mm2/s.
diagnosis: Basal cell adenomas of the parotid gland
Orpha_name: Benign epithelial tumor of salivary glands

case_report: A 64-year-old female patient presented with a primary concern of a painless swelling in the mouth persisting for 1 year. Intraoral examination identified a moderately firm, well-defined, ovoid, solitary swelling in the left sublingual region, measuring approximately 3 cm × 2 cm. The swelling was mobile upon bimanual palpation. An occlusal view showed no signs of erosion or bony destruction of adjacent structures. The swelling was surgically removed, and the excised specimen was sent for further examination.
test_results: The H&E-stained sections at ×4 showed a well-circumscribed tumor mass. Tumor cells were arranged in small clusters, cords and trabeculae and at places forming microglandular patterns. Cells with uniform round to oval nuclei with scanty cytoplasm, bland nuclear chromatin with inconspicuous nucleoli were seen. Intervening stroma showed inflammatory cells, blood capillaries and few areas of hemorrhage.
diagnosis: Basal Cell Adenoma of the sublingual salivary gland
Orpha_name: Benign epithelial tumor of salivary glands

case_report: A 3-year-old male child, born to parents who are not related by blood, presented with three slow-growing, painless, hard masses on the outer aspect of the right leg, first noticed at 2 months of age. The child was delivered at full term without any congenital abnormalities. Over time, he developed multiple asymptomatic, solid, elevated, skin-colored lesions that eventually merged into larger hard masses. The child had a history of low birth weight and delayed gross motor development milestones, but exhibited no mental retardation or gait abnormalities. There was no history of trauma, prior inflammation, or similar lesions in family members. Physical examination revealed a single large, non-tender, subcutaneous hard mass measuring 4 cm × 5 cm on the anterolateral aspect of the right thigh, with the skin over the lesion being pinchable. Additionally, there were two smaller lesions measuring 2 cm × 3 cm and 2 cm × 2 cm on the outer aspect of the right lower leg, with the surface showing atrophy and scaling. No other skeletal deformities were observed.
test_results: Plain radiograph of lower limbs in anteroposterior and lateral views showed calcified areas in subcutaneous plane corresponding to the areas of the skin lesions. Histopathological examination showed irregular woven bone spicules in the deep dermis.

case_report: On April 02, 2021, a 5-year-old Chinese boy visited our hospital with a progressively growing mass under the skin of his right foot for 1 year. The boy was born at full-term after an uncomplicated pregnancy with a birth weight of 2.8 kg. At 4 years of age, his parents noticed a hard mass under his right foot, with no signs of redness or swelling over the skin. The family visited a local hospital, where radiographs revealed ossification of the right foot. Further investigations were recommended, however, the patient’s parents refused and requested only observation at the time. Over the following year, the mass grew, however, it was manageable during mechanical loading. The boy was healthy prior to this. Physical examination at our hospital revealed that the boy was 102.5 cm tall (-2 SD) and weighed 14.5 kg (-2 SD). He was a slim, right-handed boy with Tanner I pubertal development and no signs of mental retardation or developmental delay. A comprehensive subcutaneous mass was palpable in the sole of the right foot, which extended to the Achilles tendon and caused minimal limitations in ankle movement. The mass could not be precisely localized. The remainder of the physical examination results were normal. The serum levels of calcium, phosphorus, and alkaline phosphates were found to be normal. An anteroposterior radiograph of the right foot showed long sheets of opacification across the plantar aspect of the foot and heel, some opacified sheets were continuous with metatarsals and tarsal bones. Axial computed tomography (CT) images revealed ossification in the right foot between the second and third metatarsals, which was continuous with the foot bones. Three-dimensional CT revealed progression of the ectopic ossification. X-ray screening was performed to identify other sites of heterotopic ossification, small areas of intramuscular ossification were observed at the superior margin of bilateral proximal humerus. Additionally, a limited radio-dense lesion was noted in the right popliteal fossa. Soft-tissue ossification-causing rheumatic diseases, such as juvenile dermatomyositis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and systemic sclerosis, were ruled out as the patient showed no systemic clinical features and tests for autoantibodies were negative.
test_results: A de novo heterozygous inactivating mutation (c.175C > T, p. Q59X) was identified in exon 2 of the GNAS gene.

case_report: A 48-year-old male presented to the Oral and Maxillofacial Radiology Clinic with pain and tenderness in the preauricular regions of the temporomandibular joints, along with restricted mandibular movement persisting for 24 years. The patient reported no systemic illnesses but had a history of trauma from a fall off a roof 24 years ago, which resulted in a jaw fracture treated with intermaxillary fixation. Post-treatment, the patient experienced a lasting restriction in mandibular movement. Physical examination showed joint crepitus and limited mandibular movement. An earlier panoramic radiograph indicated degenerative changes in the bone structure.
test_results: An irregular-type radiopaque lesion was detected on the superior aspect of the right condyle as well as degenerative osseous changes on both TMJs.
diagnosis: Osteochondritis Dissecans of the Temporomandibular Joint

case_report: An 18-year-old male presented with a 6-month history of pain and swelling in the right fourth PIP joint, which occurred during and after playing the Japanese drum. He reported no history of acute trauma. He had been practicing the instrument for more than 2 hours daily since the age of 12. Physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness on the radial side of the right fourth PIP joint. Disability scoring of the arm, shoulder, and hand (DASH) showed 0.9 points in the disability/symptom section and 81.3 points in the sports/music section.
test_results: Plain X-ray and computed tomography (CT) images showed a bone defect with a tiny adjacent fragment at the radial side of the head of the fourth right proximal phalanx. T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the hand showed low signal in the fourth proximal phalangeal head without an associated radial collateral ligament tear.

case_report: A 13-year-old ethnic Macedonian girl visited the Zan Mitrev Clinic with her parents for a pediatric examination and genetic counseling. She exhibited an abnormal gait attributed to reduced joint mobility. Examination revealed destruction of carpal bones in both hands, olecranon bursitis, marfanoid habitus, cachexia, cutis laxa, and mild facial abnormalities including a triangular face, eye bulging, and micrognathia. There were no signs of intellectual disability, and her parents did not display any morphological abnormalities. The symptoms initially appeared in her wrists and ankles during her toddler years.
test_results: At 13 years of age, her radiological examination showed osteolysis of carpal bones, destruction of the elbow joints with pathological dislocation of both elbows, osteolysis of the tarsal bones and first metatarsal with pathological dislocation of the first metatarsophalangeal joints, and cyst-like structures on the right femoral epiphysis. Previous nephrology evaluation via ultrasound scanning revealed asymmetry in the size of the kidneys at 2 years of age. At that time, Tc99mDMSA scan showed 33% decreased uptake of the right kidney, however her blood work including renal function parameters were within reference limits. A recent ultrasound examination confirmed significant kidney hypoplasia of the right kidney (59 × 25 mm), in contrast, the left kidney was compensatorily hypertrophic with dimensions 107 × 45 mm. Computed tomography (CT) scan confirmed the ultrasound findings. Upon taking written and signed informed consent from the proband's legal guardians, she underwent clinical exome sequencing (CES) (TruSight One panel) from Illumina. In brief, DNA was extracted from 400 μl of whole blood on a SaMag-12 automatic nucleic acid extraction system (Sacace Biotechnologies, Como, Italy). Libraries were pooled together and underwent two rounds of hybridization and capture, and additional quantification and size assessment. Between 19 and 26 million reads were obtained with a NextSeq machine (Illumina, San Diego, USA), with a coverage of at least 50x for 80–90% of all sequences. Sequence quality control was done with FastQC, and sequences were mapped to Hg19 with BWA. SNP and INDEL calling, together with advanced variant annotation were done with proprietary technologies such as PEPPER™ and MOKA™, respectively, both integrated within the Sophia DDM platform (Sophia Genetics, Saint-Sulpice, Switzerland). Later on, mapping, SNP and INDEL calling, annotation, and in-depth analyses were carried out with the Genoox platform. The analysis focused on virtual gene panels composed of genes causing skeletal dysplasia, and connective tissue disorders using the Sophia DDM platform (Sophia Genetics). The analysis failed to identify known Clinvar mutations. We detected several (>10) heterozygous candidate variants based on ACMG computational criteria. In order to accurately pin down the causal variant, we performed additional CES of her parents. Upon analysis of high confidence de novo mutations (present in the proband, but absent in the parents), using an in-built tool in the Genoox platform we identified the c.188C>T (p.Pro63Leu) variant in the MAFB gene. This finding was confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

case_report: In 2008, a 75-year-old woman was found to have a bilateral condition affecting her eyes. She has a medical history of hypertension, hyperthyroidism, and rheumatoid arthritis, for which she is taking ramipril, methimazole, and lorazepam. At the age of 62, she underwent surgery for breast cancer and had cataract surgery on both eyes in 2006. There is no family history of eye conditions, diabetes, hypertension, or autoimmune diseases. She has not used chloroquine or similar compounds in the past but reported smoking 10 cigarettes per day from the age of 30 to 50. No detailed information is available regarding her diet or antioxidant intake. Starting in 1948, at the age of 15, she worked as a farmer for about 8 years and then for 2 years as a 'mondina,' a role involving the transplanting of young rice plants into water-flooded fields and manual weed removal. This job exposed her to high levels of sunlight due to long working hours, including during the central hours of the day, in late spring and early summer, with minimal protective equipment. After this period, she worked for 3 years in a chemical plant producing synthetic textiles (rayon fibers) with no detectable exposure to occupational risk factors for eye conditions. She then dedicated herself to home life and family care.
test_results: Several drusenoid detachments of the retinal pigment epithelium (PED) were observed in the right eye along with the confluence of drusen in the left eye.

case_report: A 34-year-old woman, the only child of a nonconsanguineous couple, was referred for evaluation of reproductive risk. She was born following a spontaneous, normal pregnancy with no reported gestational diabetes, uterine malformations, or exposure to toxic environments. Delivery occurred at full term with normal growth parameters. At birth, she exhibited congenital downward displacement of the shoulders. Her psychomotor development during infancy was normal. At 34 years of age, physical examination showed a long face with a high and narrow nasal bridge, a beaked nose, a high arched palate, a narrow mandible, prominent ears with large and flat conchae, and a long neck with asymmetrically downward sloped shoulders and clavicles. She demonstrated an inability to elevate, abduct, and flex her shoulders forward. Her stature and cognitive development were assessed as normal using adaptive behavioral and descriptive clinical criteria.
test_results: Chest radiograph demonstrated small, low, and laterally set scapulae, with the glenohumeral joints 10 cm lower than normal and down-turned clavicles. Tonal audiometry showed mild bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.

case_report: A 47-year-old male presented to the emergency department with complaints of blurred vision and pain in his left eye for the past four weeks. Initially, the patient attributed these symptoms to a headache or a previous condition related to his medical history of multiple sclerosis. Over time, his vision worsened, accompanied by the appearance of floaters and increased pain two weeks before seeking medical attention. Physical examination revealed a visual acuity of 20/60 in the left eye and a superior temporal field cut. The right eye, previously affected by vision loss, could only perceive light. Intraocular pressure was measured at 14 mm Hg in the left eye and 11 mm Hg in the right eye. The neurologic examination showed no other abnormalities. Ophthalmologic examination indicated left conjunctival injection and ciliary flush. A dilated ophthalmic examination identified peripheral retinal whitening in the superonasal area of the left eye, along with high-grade inflammation in the anterior chamber (3+ cell) and vitreous cavity (2+ cell).
test_results: Laboratory testing revealed a rapid plasma reagin titer of 1:256, with the patient testing negative for HIV. Ultrasonography of the eye revealed echogenic particles within the vitreous, with a possible undulating membrane that moved freely and swirled on dynamic exam. The patient’s retina was attached, and the diameter of the optic nerve was within normal limits.

case_report: A 40-year-old female with a history of hypertension, alcohol use, anxiety, and a previous spontaneous miscarriage presented with bilateral lower extremity wounds. These wounds began as erythematous patches resembling sunburns three weeks prior and progressed to blisters, bullae, and necrotic eschars. Initially located on the anterior thighs, the lesions spread laterally and to the lower back. The patient had no family or personal history of autoimmune disease. Her medications included melatonin, clonazepam, fluoxetine, metoprolol, omeprazole, amlodipine, and lisinopril. She reported no prior use of warfarin. Approximately 1.5 months before presentation, she had a prolonged hospitalization for acute cardiac arrest secondary to acute hypoxic respiratory failure following a COVID-19 infection and superimposed pneumonia. During that admission, she required increased oxygen due to acute bacterial pneumonia secondary to COVID-19, experienced cardiac arrest with 4 minutes of chest compressions before return of circulation, and was intubated and mechanically ventilated for five days. She had no significant renal dysfunction requiring dialysis. After 14 days, she was stabilized and discharged to a skilled nursing facility. The wounds were not present before or during her COVID-19 hospitalization. Upon admission to our hospital, she was vitally stable. Laboratory results showed hyponatremia, mild leukocytosis, and elevated C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, with normal kidney function, serum calcium, and parathyroid hormone levels. Her HgbA1C was mildly elevated at 5.9% (reference: <5.7%). She had no significant history of tobacco use and no known corticosteroid use except during her previous hospitalization for respiratory failure. Physical examination revealed multiple large indurated retiform purpuras on the bilateral medial and lateral thighs, with large thick eschars centrally located within the retiform purpura on the medial thighs and similar thick eschars on the bilateral lower lateral hips.
test_results: Pathology revealed intravascular calcification within subcutaneous adipose tissue and surrounding necrosis.

case_report: A 71-year-old female patient presented for a plastic surgery consultation due to a single painful necrotic skin lesion on the right leg. Her medical history included obesity and well-controlled type II diabetes mellitus for the past 20 years. She was on daily metformin 1000 mg and vitamin D3 20000 IU for the past six months. On physical examination, a 2 x 2 cm painful necrotic skin ulcer with stellate borders and a black eschar was observed on the right leg, surrounded by purpuric skin. The leg was warm, edematous, and exhibited poorly demarcated erythema. There were no signs of sepsis. The patient was admitted for analgesic and antibiotic therapy, as well as wound care. Laboratory tests showed normal kidney function. Levels of parathyroid hormone, 25-hydroxy-vitamin D, calcium, and phosphate were within normal ranges. Screening for vasculitis, thrombophilia, and malignancies returned negative results.
test_results: Skin biopsy was consistent with NUC.
diagnosis: Calciphylaxis secondary to vitamin D supplementation

case_report: A 21-year-old male patient was referred from the neurology department to the internal medicine department at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) Hospital, Islamabad, Pakistan, due to complaints of progressive backache and proximal muscle weakness over the past eight weeks. The patient reported a history of hearing difficulties since childhood and generalized backache for the past eight months. His symptoms had worsened, making daily activities challenging. The back pain affected both the upper and lower back, with associated shooting pains in the legs and arms. He maintained normal bowel and bladder control but had developed a stooped posture. There was no history of trauma, fever, weight loss, night sweats, or corticosteroid use. Additionally, there was no history of joint pains, myalgia, difficulty swallowing, or joint deformities. Physical examination revealed prominent frontal bossing, knocked knees, and bony prominence at the elbows. Generalized bony tenderness was noted, along with lower extremity weakness, with proximal muscle power rated at 3/5 and distal power at 4/5. Bilateral lower extremity hyperreflexia with clonus was also observed. Extensive workup was conducted to rule out various conditions. A muscle biopsy indicated mild degenerative and regenerative activity without fibrosis and inflammation.
test_results: CT spine without contrast indicated diffuse osteopenia with cortical thinning and prominent trabecular pattern of all visualized bones with multilevel endplate erosive changes. There were multilevel lytic expansile lesions in the vertebral bodies and extending in the posterior element at the C3 and C4 levels causing canal stenosis at this level. Bone mineral density test indicated spine and distal forearm osteoporosis with hip joint osteopenia. A Z score of -2.9 in the lumber spine and forearm and a Z score of -1.9 in the hip joint were obtained. The technetium-99m whole body bone scan showed an increased overall tracer uptake in the bones, such as the parietal region of the skull, maxillae, mandible, multiple cervical, thoracic and lumber vertebrae, bilateral ribs, bilateral femora and tibiae, humeri, radii, and pelvic bones.

case_report: A 63-year-old woman underwent total thyroidectomy with tracheal resection and primary anastomosis followed by local external radiation therapy at a total dose of 6000 cGy in 1998 due to papillary thyroid carcinoma with tracheal invasion. She did not receive radioactive iodine therapy. In April 2000, she experienced severe localized bone pain, primarily in the shoulders and chest wall, and was admitted to a local hospital. A bone scan revealed multiple areas of increased uptake in the skull and ribs. She was referred to our hospital for further management. She reported no history of bone deformities, fractures, hearing impairment, or chronic headache. Physical examination showed bony tenderness over the lower ribs bilaterally. Laboratory results were mostly normal except for a mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase level of 165 U/L (normal range, 50-120 U/L). Serum calcium was 2.31 mmol/L (normal range, 2.1-2.60 mmol/L), albumin was 31 g/L (normal range, 28-46 g/L), and phosphate was 1.11 mmol/L (normal range, 0.8-1.45 mmol/L). Parathyroid hormone was 52 ng/dL (normal range, 15-65 ng/dL), and 25-OH vitamin D was 45 nmol/L (normal range, 22-116 nmol/L). Serum thyroglobulin was less than 0.1 ng/dL; anti-thyroglobulin antibodies were 13 U/L (normal, <115 U/L); TSH (thyroid stimulating hormone) was 2.92 mU/L (normal range, 0.4-4.27 mU/L); and FT4 (free thyroxine) was 14.6 pmol/L (normal range, 12-22 pmol/L). A radioiodine whole-body scan 1 year earlier was negative with undetectable thyroglobulin while off thyroid hormone therapy, with a TSH of 30 U/L and FT4 of 0.4 pmol/L, indicating complete remission of papillary thyroid cancer. Plain x-ray of the thoracic spine showed compression fractures of thoracic vertebrae. A bone scan indicated areas of increased uptake in the parietal bone, ribs, and thoracic vertebra. CT of the skull revealed multiple lytic and sclerotic lesions.
test_results: This was done under CT guidance and showed a distorted bone structure with multinucleated osteoclasts.

case_report: A 64-year-old male presented with acute pancreatitis. His medical history, recent social history, right upper quadrant ultrasonography, and hepatitis panel did not indicate a cause for the acute pancreatitis. The patient had a remote history of smoking and heavy drinking during his teenage years but denied illicit drug use. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography revealed dilated intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, a distal common bile duct stricture, and a moderately enlarged head of the pancreas. Laboratory tests during hospital admission were negative for anti-mitochondrial antibody, anti-smooth muscle antibody, immunoglobulin G (IgG) subclasses, antinuclear antibody (ANA), and the hepatitis panel was also negative. The patient's symptoms gradually improved, and he was discharged home. A few days after discharge, the patient experienced new onset of persistent diarrhea. Initial fixed sigmoidoscopy showed a circumferential lesion, and a subsequent colonoscopy revealed skipped lesions. The ileum was not involved, but the rectum was affected. The findings from the colonoscopy and histological evaluation indicated features of both ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease, leading to a determination of indeterminate colitis.
test_results: Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) showed a pancreatic head mass. Core biopsy of the pancreatic mass revealed benign glandular cells, rare mildly atypical ductal cells, few plasma cells, few inflammatory cells, and stains for immunoglobulin G4 (IgG4) and CD138 demonstrated nonspecific staining. Background debris with no malignant cells was also identified.

case_report: A 15-year-old male, with no chronic medical conditions and a nonobese physique, presented with abdominal pain that started 10 days prior. The pain was localized to the epigastric region, constant, cramp-like, and nonradiating. Postprandial pain intensified to a stabbing quality, severe enough to disrupt sleep if the patient went to bed shortly after eating. The patient reported no diarrhea, hematochezia, or tenesmus, and had no history of recurrent abdominal pain, chronic weight loss, or growth stunting. Physical examination showed an afebrile, uncomfortable adolescent without jaundice or scleral icterus. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the epigastric region without peritoneal signs. Laboratory results showed a lipase level of 5,419 U/L and a γ-glutamyl transferase level of 373 U/L. Aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase, and both total and direct bilirubin levels were within normal limits. The patient did not have an elevated white blood cell count and was not anemic. Imaging via abdominal ultrasound indicated common bile duct thickening and enlargement, with no evidence of cholelithiasis or choledocholithiasis; the pancreas was not visualized.
test_results: Subsequent magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) revealed delayed contrast enhancement of the pancreas, diffuse parenchymal enlargement, and lack of normal lobulation. The MRCP image also displayed biliary duct wall enhancement and dilation of the intrahepatic, extrahepatic, and common bile ducts; there was no noted stricture or narrowing. The patient's serum IgG4 level was found to be 66 mg/dL.

case_report: A 53-year-old African-American female with a history of gastric ulcer was admitted with a 2-week history of abdominal pain accompanied by nausea and a 2-month history of an unexplained 20-pound weight loss. Physical examination revealed tenderness in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen, radiating to the back. Vital signs were stable, with no signs of tachycardia or fever. Laboratory results showed elevated levels of total bilirubin, direct bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, alanine aminotransferase, and aspartate aminotransferase. Serum lipase was within normal limits at 48 U/L. Other laboratory values were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT imaging indicated a slight diffuse enlargement of the pancreas with heterogeneous attenuation and multifocal heterogeneous hypoattenuating hypoenhancing masses, along with mild segmental pancreatic ductal narrowing and minimal ductal dilatation. These findings were confirmed by contrast-enhanced MR imaging on a 1.5-T scanner and magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP), which also showed areas of mild main pancreatic ductal narrowing.
test_results: Pathology from the fine needle aspiration demonstrated areas of fibrosis and periductal lymphoplasmocytic infiltrate as well as neutrophils in close approximation to the ductal epithelium. No evidence of malignancy or IgG4-positive plasma cells was identified. Subsequent serum total immunoglobulin (IgG) was within normal limits, and serum IgG4 was only marginally elevated measuring 90 mg/dL (normal range: 4–86 mg/dL).

case_report: A 5-year-old male exhibited unsteady walking for 7 months, accompanied by headaches and nasal regurgitation for the past 2 months. The child was lethargic but responsive to commands. Visual acuity was limited to counting fingers close to the face. Physical examination revealed swelling of the optic disc and a reduced gag reflex on both sides.
test_results: A noncontrast CT head showed a hyperdense midline posterior fossa mass lesion involving the fourth ventricle extending into the left foramen of Lushka with obstructive hydrocephalus. On MRI, the lesion was isointense on T1 and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2 sequences, showed intense enhancement and measured 4.8 cm × 3.5 cm × 5.2 cm.

case_report: A 35-year-old man, who does not smoke, was admitted with a history of recurrent hemoptysis and cough with expectoration for four years. He had previously undergone antitubercular treatments without any improvement in clinical or radiological findings. On admission, his vital signs were as follows: pulse rate of 102 beats per minute, blood pressure of 112/74 mmHg, and respiratory rate of 26 breaths per minute. General examination showed no significant abnormalities. Respiratory system examination revealed coarse crepitations over the basal part of the left hemithorax. A chest X-ray showed a double-contour of the left cardiac border and inhomogeneous infiltrates in the left lower zone. Blood tests indicated a normal hemogram. The tuberculin skin test was negative, and sputum samples tested negative for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) on three consecutive days. During his hospital stay, the patient showed clinical improvement after receiving an appropriate course of antibiotics, although the opacity in the left lower zone remained.
test_results: It revealed a cavity with fluid level localized to left lower anterobasal and posteromediobasal segments. His aortography revealed that the anterobasal and posteromediobasal segments of left lower lobe were perfused via a single feeding vessel originating from descending thoracic aorta. His selective angiography revealed an arterial supply from descending thoracic aorta, and venous drainage occurred via pulmonary veins.

case_report: A 10-year-old boy presented with a 2-day history of severe left-sided chest pain and vomiting, without fever or sputum. Physical examination, medical history, and family history were unremarkable. The patient had no prior antenatal ultrasound screening or pre-incident imaging. Radiographs from a local hospital showed a high-density mass in the left thoracic cavity with a small amount of pleural effusion. The patient was transferred to our center immediately. Upon admission, the patient continued to experience chest pain but had stable vital signs and no guarding during the abdominal examination. Laboratory tests revealed a white blood cell count of 12.74 × 10^9/L with 81.1% neutrophils, and a myoglobin level of 38.12 ng/mL. Other laboratory values were within normal ranges. Abdominal ultrasonography was not performed due to the availability of radiographs from the local hospital and the emergency situation.
test_results: Contrast medium-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the chest and abdomen revealed a well-defined, nonenhanced mass with soft-tissue density (3.8 × 4 × 4.7 cm) in the left thoracic cavity above the diaphragm. The surrounding structures did not show any abnormalities except slight uplifting of the diaphragm and a small amount of pleural effusion on the left side. On the CT scan, a suspected feeding artery arising from the aorta could be identified.
diagnosis: Extralobar Pulmonary Sequestration  with infarction due to torsion

case_report: AL is a 14-year-old male with cerebral palsy who presented with a 3-day history of cough and haematemesis, with an estimated volume of ~125 mL. He had previously received treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis based on prolonged coughing and radiological changes, though microbiological confirmation was not obtained. The chest radiograph from the initial treatment facility was not available. Clinically, he was apyrexial and haemodynamically stable, with no pallor or clubbing. Chest examination was normal except for epigastric tenderness. He was administered omeprazole for acute gastritis, and a non-urgent gastroscopy was planned. A chest radiograph showed an irregular right-sided hilar opacity. Upon discharge, he experienced another significant episode of haemoptysis with vomiting, with approximately 500 mL of blood noted. Despite this, he remained haemodynamically stable, though his haemoglobin level decreased from 9.1 g/dL to 8 g/dL. Coagulation parameters, including platelets, were normal. A repeat chest radiograph showed no changes from the initial one. Repeated sputum analyses for Gene Xpert and TB culture were negative. Gastroscopy revealed a dilated and abnormal oesophagus with an ulcer, and biopsy results indicated mild oesophagitis. Bronchoscopy showed normal airway anatomy with no visible fistula opening, pulmonary haemorrhage, or endobronchial lesions, but purulent secretions were observed from the right lower lobe segments.
test_results: A computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest showed an irregular contrast-enhancing inflammatory mass, with cavities located in the superior segment of the right lower lobe. Two large arteries originating from the right lateral aspect of the descending aorta were noted to supply this mass, with another arterial supply by the bronchial artery. The upper (more cranial) artery divided: one branch supplied the mass and the second ran superior and posterior. An upper gastrointestinal contrast study confirmed the presence of a fistulous tract between the oesophagus and the cavities within the mass and the right lower main bronchial segments. There was also severe gastro-oesophageal reflux.
diagnosis: Complex hybrid congenital pulmonary airway malformation with broncho-oesophageal fistula

case_report: A 48-year-old female presented to the emergency department with a two-month history of worsening epigastric discomfort. She had no associated symptoms. Clinical examination revealed a firm, tender mass in the left upper quadrant. It was nonpulsatile, dull to percussion, and moved inferiorly with respiration. It was not possible to palpate a superior edge while the lower margin was palpable. She had previously undergone a right ovarian cystectomy for a benign dermoid cyst. Initial haematological and biochemical indices were all within normal parameters. Ultrasound revealed a large (9 cm × 10 cm × 11 cm), poorly vascularised mass, separate from the spleen, containing mixed solid and cystic elements. Internal septations were also apparent. CT imaging demonstrated a multiseptated cystic mass with multiple foci of calcification within its walls. There were associated elevation of the left hemidiaphragm and displacement of the pancreatic tail and stomach anteriorly and the spleen laterally. MR imaging showed high signal on T2-weighted views and confirmed its separation from spleen, stomach, pancreas, and adrenal glands. There was no vascular invasion or associated lymphadenopathy. Since the mass was causing significant discomfort and of uncertain malignant potential, a decision was made to excise this mass. The patient was placed in a supine position. An upper midline incision facilitated adequate access to the left upper quadrant. The cystic mass was adherent to the membranous portion of the left hemidiaphragm. This was excised en bloc following aspiration of 700 millilitres of viscid fluid. An intercostal drainage tube was placed in the left hemithorax attached to an underwater seal and the diaphragmatic defect was closed with 2/0 polydioxanone. She made a favourable postoperative recovery and was discharged home on the 6th postoperative day. She remained well at outpatient follow-up.
test_results: The multiloculated structure was lined by ciliated respiratory-type epithelium with a florid granulomatous reaction. Deposits of calcium and amorphous degenerative material were seen within the cystic spaces. Islands of cartilage and adipose were also noted between the cystic spaces.

case_report: A 67-year-old woman was hospitalized for 5 days due to hemoptysis and a long-standing history of recurrent cough. She had a history of consuming approximately 100 g of alcohol daily for 15 years, with no other significant personal or family medical history. Physical examination revealed moist rales in the lower lobe of the right lung. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 11.1*10^9/L, a neutrophil count of 7.1*10^9/L, a D-dimer level of 1.97 mg/L, and a normal procalcitonin level. Tuberculin test and tumor-related markers were negative. Chest CT imaging identified a nodular shadow with relatively regular morphology and uneven enhancement in the right lung. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy revealed significant local mucosal congestion in the right lower lobe and a suspected blockage in the lumen of the posterior segment of the right lower lobe. A brush biopsy was performed, resulting in approximately 100 mL of bleeding, which was managed with local hemostasis. Pathological examination of the biopsy indicated inflammation. The patient experienced two episodes of massive hemoptysis during treatment. In the first episode, she expectorated approximately 300 mL of material, including clots, which was sent for pathological examination. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining showed degenerated alveolar tissue structure. Despite temporary cessation of bleeding after hemostasis treatment, the patient had another episode of massive hemoptysis about 8 hours later, expectorating approximately 700 mL. This was followed by confusion, respiratory failure, and hemorrhagic shock. Emergency measures included a blood transfusion, mechanical ventilation, and vascular intervention.
test_results: Body arterial angiography revealed a twisted and deformed artery originating from the thoracic aorta that was supplying blood to the lesion in the right lower lobe of the lung. Upper gastrointestinal (UGI) radiography revealed an abnormal connection between the bronchus and esophagus.

case_report: A 45-year-old male, employed in defense, with a history of smoking and significant alcohol consumption, presented with fever accompanied by chills, cough with sputum production, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain for one month, along with a notable weight loss of 5 kg. He had been started on antitubercular treatment (ATT) based on radiological findings by a local physician, but experienced no symptomatic improvement and was subsequently admitted to our center for further management. The patient reported having completed ATT for similar symptoms and right-sided effusion 10 years ago and again 2 years ago. On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs and a room air oxygen saturation of 96%. General and systemic examinations were unremarkable except for diminished breath sounds on the right side of the chest posteriorly. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin at 11.3 gm%, total leukocyte count at 7100/cu mm with a normal differential count (polymorphs 67% and lymphocytes 29%), platelets at 3.70 L/cu mm, and normal liver and kidney function tests. Chest radiographs revealed an air-fluid level on the right side within a large solitary lesion, suggestive of encysted hydropneumothorax or an infected giant bulla. Sputum tests for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear were negative, and pyogenic culture showed no growth. Hydatid serology and serum galactomannan tests were negative. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) of the thorax showed a large smooth-walled cystic lesion with an air-fluid level below the oblique fissure, with the upper margin of the cyst abutting the fissure and infiltrating the right lower lobe (RLL). Aortography indicated no independent arterial supply to the cyst. These findings suggested the presence of an encysted hydropneumothorax in the oblique fissure. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy revealed thick purulent secretions in the RLL, and bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for AFB smear, fungal smear, and pyogenic culture. A CECT of the thorax performed 2 years prior showed similar findings but with a smaller lesion size.
test_results: Histopathology of specimen revealed intact cystic lesion with cyst wall lined with ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium (bronchiolar type) without cartilage and surrounding lung showing alveoli filled with proteinaceous periodic acid-Schiff-negative exudate and hemorrhage.
diagnosis: Congenital Pulmonary Cystic Adenomatoid Malformation with Infection and Hemorrhage

case_report: A 66-year-old Chinese woman, originally from Beijing, presented with a 3-month history of cough and expectoration. She reported no fever, night sweats, weight loss, chest pain, or hemoptysis. Her medical history was notable for the absence of tuberculosis and smoking. Physical examination findings were within normal limits. Electrocardiography and routine laboratory tests also showed normal results.
test_results: Contrast-enhanced computerized tomography of the chest showed 35 × 22 mm irregular cystic lesion in right lower lobe, wall thickness of 0.5 mm to 3.5 mm, smooth inner margin, septum was seen within the cyst. The lesion also showed mild distortion of surrounding lung tissue with no evidence of abnormal arterial blood supply. Histopathology showed cystic tumor of 4.5 × 2.0 × 1.5 cm, composed of multiple varying sized cysts lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with few areas of necrosis.

case_report: A 25-year-old female presented with recurrent right-sided pneumothorax, previously managed twice with a chest tube, resulting in full lung expansion. Her medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Imaging via chest CT identified a 5-cm diameter, thin-walled pulmonary cyst in the right lower lobe. Due to the recurrent pneumothorax, she underwent right-sided video-assisted thoracoscopy with wedge resection of the apical right upper lobe, radical parietal pleurectomy, and resection of the right lower lobe cyst. Examination of a frozen section from the right lower lobe cyst indicated a benign pulmonary cystic process.
test_results: Histology showed a 1.8-cm thin-walled cystic lesion with a smooth inner surface wall and cystic structures lined by bronchiolar ciliated epithelium, without any atypia. The cyst wall comprised smooth muscle and elastic fibres.

case_report: A 5-month-old female child, previously healthy and growing well (weight: 5.3 kg, length: 60 cm, weight/height: -1 SD to -2 SD as per WHO growth chart, head circumference: 40.5 cm), presented with a 6-day history of fever followed by 2 days of rapid breathing. Chest X-ray revealed a large pneumothorax on the left side with mediastinal shift to the right, prompting referral for further management. Upon admission, the patient was euthermic and irritable with a heart rate of 168/min, respiratory rate of 68 bpm, blood pressure of 98/60 mmHg, and peripheral capillary oxygen saturation (SpO2) of 88% on room air. Physical examination showed reduced chest expansion on the left side, decreased breath sounds, and a hyperresonant note on the left. High-flow oxygen was administered, and the patient was transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU). In the PICU, a left-sided intercostal drainage tube was inserted, releasing a gush of air followed by thick, white-colored pleural fluid that was exudative. Laboratory results indicated hemoglobin level of 10 gm%, total leukocyte count (TLC) of 37,400/mm3 (P 80% and L 15%), and a positive C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 18.3 mg/dL. The HIV ELISA test was negative. The patient was treated with Ceftriaxone, Ampiclox, and Clindamycin, along with other supportive measures. Her respiratory distress improved over the next 24 hours, but a follow-up chest X-ray after 5 days showed incomplete expansion of the left lung with multiple cavitations. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest revealed collapse consolidation of the left lung with multiple cavitations and a cavity in the lower lobe communicating with the pleural cavity. A left thoracotomy with decortication and lower lobe lobectomy was performed. The gross surgical specimen measured 10 cm × 8 cm × 5 cm, with a congested pleural surface and a firm cut surface with minimal normal lung parenchyma.
test_results: Microscopic examination of the patient showed signs of pleuritis with underlying suppurative inflammation of the lung indicative of abscess. Adjacent lung tissue showed vague lobulated architecture with interlobular fibrosis, definite increase in the number of bronchiolar structures, and small alveolar spaces lined by plump cuboidal epithelium.
diagnosis: Stocker type III congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation

case_report: A 48-year-old woman reported experiencing floaters, flashes of light, blurred vision, and eye pain in both eyes for several days before her visit.
