She had a 10-year history of diabetes mellitus and was on glibenclamide and metformin. Examination showed visual acuity of 20/160 in the right eye and 20/50 in the left eye, with no significant refractive error. Both pupils reacted normally, and there was no afferent pupillary defect. Slit lamp examination revealed 1+ cell presence in the anterior chamber, pigmentation on the anterior lens capsule, 2+ nuclear sclerosis, and 1+ to 2+ vitreous cells in both eyes. Intraocular pressure was measured at 16 mmHg in both eyes. Fundus examination identified multiple well-defined creamy-yellow subretinal lesions primarily located in the equatorial and peripapillary regions, along with dot and blot retinal hemorrhages, macular edema, and extensive neovascularization of the optic discs.
test_results: Fluorescein angiography (FA) demonstrated early hypo- and late hyperfluorescence of the lesions. Apart from diffuse optic disc leakage, macular leakage was also notable. On indocyanine green (ICG) angiography, the lesions remained hypofluorescent through all phases of the angiogram.

case_report: A 27-year-old Iranian female dentist, who was not pregnant and had no prior health issues, received the first dose of the Sputnik V (Gam-COVID-Vac) COVID-19 vaccine. Initially, she experienced pain at the injection site for two days, followed by fatigue, weakness, and a low-grade fever. On the third day post-vaccination, she reported numbness on the left side of her tongue, though her taste sensation remained unaffected. Five days after vaccination, she was unable to fully close her left eye and observed that the left side of her upper lip deviated to the right during activities such as chewing, laughing, or speaking. The following day, similar symptoms appeared in her lower lip, and she had difficulty drinking with a straw. Three hours later, she experienced severe sharp pain along the sternocleidomastoid muscle, radiating to the ear, mastoid, and retromaxillary region on the same side. Twelve hours later, a neurologist conducted a physical and neurological examination, revealing hemiparalysis of the facial nerve. Her cerebellar function was normal, and there were no cutaneous signs of herpes zoster infection. Her vital signs were stable, and she was afebrile. She had no history of COVID-19 infection and was not on any medications.
test_results: Brain MRI was normal.

case_report: A 16-year-old male presented with an eight-month history of tremors in the left hand, which were present only at rest and did not change in frequency. Three months later, he began experiencing difficulty walking. Over the past two years, he reported increased restlessness, sweating, and nervousness, particularly in social situations. He was born to parents who are related by blood and has no notable past medical or family history. Treatment with propranolol and cognitive-behavioral therapy did not yield any improvement. On examination, his Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) was 15/15 (E4, V5, M5). Vital signs included a blood pressure of 120/70 mmHg, heart rate of 80 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute, and he was afebrile. He exhibited an expressionless face and reduced eye blink frequency. Resting tremors were observed in his left hand. Cranial nerve examination revealed slow vertical saccadic eye movements, but vision and funduscopic examination were normal. Slit-lamp examination showed no Kayser-Fleischer ring. Limb examination indicated Grade 2 rigidity in the left upper and lower limbs with 5/5 muscle strength and +2 deep tendon reflexes. Slowness was noted in hand movements, finger tapping, and toe-tapping. During ambulation, he had difficulty maintaining balance and swayed to the left. Writing was also impaired, with progressively smaller letters. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood profile, comprehensive metabolic panel, serum iron, copper, ceruloplasmin, and 24-hour urine copper levels, were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and spinal cord, as well as visual evoked potentials, were also normal.
test_results: Sequence analysis revealed a homozygous deletion on exon 22 that resulted in the replacement of serine with threonine, followed by a stop codon.

case_report: In 2019, a 56-year-old man with a history of metastatic melanoma, treated with nivolumab and complicated by pneumonitis requiring high-dose prednisone and infliximab, developed an itchy pustular rash on the scalp, face, chest, and back. He also experienced a gritty sensation in his eyes and sensitivity to light. He began nivolumab treatment in the fall of 2018, and prednisone 140 mg daily (2 mg/kg/day) was initiated three months later for immune-mediated pneumonitis. One month before the rash appeared, he received a single dose of infliximab 10 mg/kg, which he had also received in 2016 for colitis related to adjuvant immunotherapy with ipilimumab. Additionally, he recently completed a two-week course of fluconazole and several doses of itraconazole for prednisone-induced thrush. He visited the emergency department and was given antihistamines and topical steroids. Two days later, he visited the dermatology clinic with a worsening itchy rash. Examination revealed diffuse, red papules and pustules on his face, neck, chest, and back. He had redness along the eyelid margins and conjunctival injection. He was started on oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, clobetasol 0.05% scalp solution, triamcinolone 0.1% cream for the trunk, and hydrocortisone 2.5% topical cream for the face. Bacterial culture of pustules was negative. A punch biopsy of the left chest showed suppurative folliculitis. Ophthalmology urgently evaluated him due to photophobia and diagnosed him with meibomian gland dysfunction. He was prescribed neomycin/polymyxin B/dexamethasone ophthalmic ointment and artificial tears. One week later, he returned without improvement, and topical steroids were discontinued.
test_results: Microscopic examination of several eyelashes and the contents of pustules did not show mites.

case_report: A 46-year-old woman reported experiencing itching, a burning sensation, and a rash on her face for 4 weeks. She had no underlying health conditions and was not on any regular medication. Symptoms began gradually with a warm, slightly burning, and periodically itching sensation on both cheeks after wearing a face mask for more than 8 hours a day over a 3-week period during October in Thailand. She had no prior history of this condition and had not used any new cosmetics or topical products in recent months. Initially, she wore a surgical face mask but switched to a cloth mask, suspecting irritation or allergy. Despite the change, symptoms worsened, with increased itching, burning, and a noticeable rash under the masked area. During this period, she was prescribed 2% hydrocortisone cream and aloe vera gel for the affected facial area. These treatments provided only partial relief, and symptoms returned after stopping the treatment. Physical examination showed mild swelling, dry erythematous and purpuric patches with fine follicular scales on both cheeks and chin in the mask-covered area.
test_results: Microscopic examination of 1 cm2 surface area sample from the skin lesion revealed 6 adult mites from the left cheek, 4 adult mites from the right cheek.

case_report: A 74-year-old man with a history of obstructive sleep apnea, depression, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis on nintedanib 150 mg twice daily, asbestos exposure, hypertension, and gout, visited his primary care clinic for joint pain. He had recently received two doses of the Pfizer-BioNTech SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccine in January and February 2021. Ten days after the first dose, he experienced bilateral hip and shoulder pain, morning stiffness lasting 15 minutes, and left thumb pain. He also developed a migratory, pruritic, papular rash over the left ankle, right knee, and right wrist. Dermatology was consulted in February before the second dose, and he was treated with antihistamines and steroid creams for the rash. An infectious disease specialist recommended the second dose as he did not have a severe reaction to the first dose. After the second dose, he reported the same joint pain and visited the rheumatology outpatient clinic in late February. Physical examination revealed tenderness in the first carpometacarpal (CMC) joint with a positive grind test and tenderness in the right acromioclavicular (AC) joint with mildly limited range of motion. No rash was present at that time. A full rheumatologic workup was performed. In early March, his pruritic rash returned, and he developed weakness in his thigh and shoulder muscles. He started using a cane, fell multiple times, had difficulty bending over, rising from a seated position, and raising his hands above his head. Pain and stiffness were worse in the morning and at night but improved during the day and with ibuprofen. He visited the emergency department and received an intramuscular ketorolac injection, which relieved most symptoms. On the same day, he contacted his rheumatology provider with a few lab results available: CRP was 15 mg/L, and RF was 24 IU/ml (low positive). He was initially prescribed prednisone 20 mg orally daily with a slow taper. In late March, two weeks after starting steroids, physical exam showed motor power of 5/5 in all limbs. He reported improvement on 20 mg prednisone, but symptoms recurred when the dose was tapered to 15 mg, with more pain and stiffness lasting two hours in the morning and motor weakness. His prednisone dose was increased to 30 mg. On the same day, he visited the emergency department again with a five-day cough that had not improved with azithromycin. He was discharged on levofloxacin for mild pneumonitis. He gradually tapered his steroids as symptoms improved and CRP levels decreased. However, symptoms returned when prednisone was tapered below 10 mg, so he resumed the 10-mg daily dose. In June, his symptoms resolved, and inflammatory markers normalized (CRP 5 mg/L, ESR 4 mm/h). Over the next two months, symptoms recurred when prednisone was tapered below 10 mg. In early September, he developed arthritis in the right wrist and multiple MCPs, with morning stiffness and pain that improved during the day and with NSAIDs. As the primary caretaker of his household, he had significant difficulty with daily living activities.
test_results: Repeat laboratory testing showed a highly positive RF of 74.

case_report: A 16-year-old female was referred to the Pediatric and Adolescent Endocrinology Department for thyroid function evaluation due to a large goiter. Her perinatal history was normal, with an APGAR score of 10 and a birth weight of 3400 g. Developmental milestones were achieved on time, and her general health was good with no significant diseases reported. Laboratory results were normal. During the consultation, her voice was notably deep. Her medical history showed normal sexual maturation, with menarche at 13.5 years. Over the past 2.5 years, she exhibited androgenic symptoms including decreased breast volume, balding, enlarged clitoris, progressive voice deepening, acne on the face, back, and neckline, a hirsutism score of 18 points (Polish norm < 8 points), and menstrual irregularities leading to secondary amenorrhea in the last 12 months. She also reported consistent genital spotting for the past two months but had not seen a gynecologist. She had consulted an otorhinolaryngologist twice in the past 1.5 years for her deepening voice, and testosterone levels were found to be elevated on two occasions (6.1 ng/mL and 4.17 ng/mL, norm < 0.48 ng/mL). Due to the gradual enlargement of her thyroid, her family doctor referred her to a pediatric endocrinologist. The evaluation revealed she was euthyroid with TSH at 1.9 uIU/mL (N 0.3–4.0) and fT4 at 16.6 pmol/L (N 10–25). TPOAb, TgAb, and TRAbs tests were negative. Further hormonal testing showed increased testosterone at 3.52 ng/mL (N < 1), estradiol at 71.3 pg/mL (normal for her age), suppressed FSH at <0.3 mIU/mL, LH at 3.94 mIU/mL (normal for her age), and 17 OHP at 5.04 ng/mL (normal for her age). The patient had a tall stature and macrocephaly, with a final height of 172 cm (+1.0 SDS) and a head circumference of 58 cm (+2.24 SDS). Point-of-care ultrasonography identified a multinodular 68 mL goiter with 15 isoechogenic cystic–solid lesions containing macrocalcifications, with no increased vascularization in the solid parts. An abdominal ultrasound identified a 5.7 × 6.9 cm solid mass in the right adnexal region, displacing the uterus to the left. Magnetic Resonance Imaging findings suggested a solid mass. A right ovariectomy was performed, and histopathology confirmed a moderately differentiated Sertoli–Leydig cell tumor. Hormonal tests 11 days post-surgery showed an increase in estradiol to 104.1 pg/mL, disinhibition of FSH at 4.1 mIU/mL, and LH at 8.94 mIU/mL, with normalization of testosterone to 0.30 ng/mL. Menses resumed 34 days post-surgery and are currently regular. The patient was referred to a speech therapist, and after six years of consistent voice exercises, her voice tone improved. She also underwent a total thyroidectomy due to dyspnea and dysphagia caused by the large neck tumor. Histopathology revealed benign follicular cell-derived neoplasms indicating thyroid follicular nodular disease bilaterally. The patient is currently euthyroid on levothyroxine and continues annual health evaluations. Six years post-surgery, she reported recurrent cysts of the left ovary, treated effectively with oral contraceptives. Multinodular goiters were also detected in her mother, maternal grandmother, maternal sister, and a daughter of her maternal brother, all of whom underwent total thyroidectomies due to hoarseness. Pathological evaluations reported benign follicular cell-derived neoplasms indicating thyroid follicular nodular disease bilaterally in all cases.
test_results: Molecular analysis using NGS, confirmed with the Sanger method, revealed a pathogenic heterozygotic variant c.2953C>T [p.Gln985*] in exon 18 of the DICER1 gene.

case_report: A 16-year-old male, who has been on long-term therapy with beta-blockers and an ARB inhibitor since the age of 3 due to aortic root dilatation (36 mm on echocardiography), experienced a significant decline in left ventricular function over the past year. The left ventricular ejection fraction decreased from 60% to 20%, and the left ventricular end-systolic diameter increased from 40 mm to 60 mm. An ECG revealed a normal sinus rhythm with a Wolf Parkinson White (WPW) pattern, although no arrhythmia was detected during 24-hour Holter monitoring. The patient was classified as New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class II.
test_results: CMR confirmed the dilation of the aortic root (36 mm, z-score of 3.65) and the presence of mitral valve prolapse with only mild end-systolic regurgitation (regurgitant fraction < 5%). There was significant MAD (approximately 11 mm) and signs of increased mechanical tethering of the sub-valvular apparatus (hypokinesia of the posteromedial papillary muscle). The LV was globular and mildly dilated with a severely reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 32%). Diffuse hypokinesia was noted, more prominent on the septum, which appeared to be thinned and almost akinetic. There was no valvular disease (no aortic regurgitation, only mild mitral valve regurgitation) to justify the severity of the LV dilatation and systolic function impairment. Late gadolinium study (LGE) revealed prominent fibrosis of a non-ischaemic pattern involving both the thinned septum (linear mid-wall LGE) and the basal inferior and lateral walls (sub-epicardial/mid-wall LGE). The fibrosis extent was calculated using the five standard deviation (SD) method, at approximately 11% of the total LV mass.

case_report: A 40-year-old Caucasian woman with a history of long-standing joint pain and chronic fatigue syndrome visited the primary care setting for a health maintenance check-up, presenting with new-onset right shoulder pain. The pain started one month ago, characterized by a grinding sensation and a feeling of joint 'displacement' when leaning on her right side. During the review of systems, it was noted that she experiences chronic headaches, joint pain, 'sensitive skin,' and general itchiness. Her past medical history is extensive. Musculoskeletal symptoms include TMJ disorder, chronic joint and muscle pain, low back pain, and repetitive motion injuries. She reported that her pain began around the age of 12. She described lifelong joint injuries, including frequent sprained ankles occurring without any apparent cause. She also reported easy bruising and had an unconfirmed previous diagnosis of arthritis in her right thumb. Her cardiovascular history includes a diagnosis of orthostatic hypotension in her youth, which has never been treated with medication; she continues to experience dizziness and lightheadedness upon standing. Her gastrointestinal history includes irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and frequent nausea. She is currently being treated for vitamin D deficiency with supplements and B12 deficiency with subcutaneous injections. She has recently developed various chemical sensitivities but reported no medication allergies. Other unrelated previous diagnoses include diabetes mellitus type 2, hyperlipidemia, and depression. The patient's family history was noncontributory except for her daughter, who is currently being tested for POTS.
test_results: The musculoskeletal examination revealed normal strength in all extremities, with pain to palpation over the rotator cuff. Joints were examined for hypermobility using the Beighton scale criteria. The patient scored a 5/9: bilateral fifth digit passively extended to 90°, the left thumb was opposable to the forearm (examination of the right thumb was deferred secondary to prior arthritis pain), and bilateral elbow extension past 10°. She was unable to palm the floor. Integumentary examination revealed soft, velvety skin with normal extensibility. Upon drawing a tongue depressor across her forearm, an erythematous wheal appeared in under 30 seconds.

case_report: A 22-year-old male presented with a painless, gradual decrease in vision in both eyes, more pronounced in the right eye, over the past year. He has worn high-power glasses (-12.0 DS) for distance vision since early childhood. On examination, best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was hand movements close to face (HMCF) with inaccurate projection of rays in three quadrants in the right eye and 6/24 (0.6 logMAR) with accurate projection of rays in the left eye. Ocular examination showed a port-wine stain on the right upper lid, bluish-black scleral pigmentation, and dilated prominent episcleral vessels in both eyes. The cornea was clear, the anterior chamber was deep, the iris pigmentation was homogeneously dense, and the lens was clear. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 50 mm Hg in the right eye and 44 mm Hg in the left eye, requiring systemic hyper-osmotic agents for control. Visual field testing was not possible in the right eye due to poor vision, while the left eye showed advanced field loss with incomplete double arcuate scotoma involving fixation. Facial and ocular pigmentation had been present since early childhood. There was no history of seizures, hemiparesis, or mental retardation. Bilateral varicose veins had been noted over the last ten years, requiring surgical intervention one year prior. There was no family history of similar conditions, indicating sporadic inheritance.
test_results: Gonioscopy revealed wide angle recess with an anterior or high insertion of iris reaching up to the anterior trabecular meshwork at places, along with homogeneously dense trabecular pigmentation and concavity of iris configuration. Posterior segment examination revealed both optic nerves to be average in size; OD showed a 0.9 cupping with up to 270o neuro-retinal rim loss; OS showed 0.8 cupping with a bipolar notch. There was pigmentation within the inferotemporal optic disc margin bilaterally, without any associated choroidal or retinal pigmentation. On systemic examination, bilateral port-wine stain could be noted on the face, over the cheek, upper jaw and chin, more on the left side along with brownish-black pigmentation over temples and forehead extending onto cheek and medial aspect of lower lid bilaterally and also upper jaw on the left side. Similar pigmentation was seen on the hard palate centrally along with palatal vascular malformation on the left side. Neuroimaging by MRI could not document cerebral calcification or atrophy.

case_report: A 45-year-old male presented for a routine health check-up and was found to have a low HbA1c level of 3.9%. Fasting blood glucose and glycated albumin levels were within normal ranges. Chromatogram analysis showed no abnormalities. Blood tests revealed a reduction in red blood cell count and hemoglobin concentration, along with an elevated reticulocyte count. Biochemical tests showed a slight increase in direct bilirubin levels. Mild hemolysis was observed in the serum. Blood smear analysis indicated an increase in oval-shaped red blood cells of varying sizes, along with the presence of teardrop-shaped, fragmented, and rod-shaped red blood cells. The Coombs test returned negative. The patient reported a family history of anemia in his father and uncle.
test_results: A heterozygous missense mutation c.G2303A (p.G768D) was detected in the SPTB gene. The results were consistent with high-throughput sequencing.

case_report: A 2.5-year-old male presented with a 2-year history of bone deformities in both upper and lower extremities and short stature. Hair loss began at 4 months of age, progressing to complete hairlessness by 7 months (alopecia totalis). Prominent wrist joints were observed bilaterally at around 8 months, and bowing of both lower limbs was noted by 1 year. Antenatal and birth events were normal. There was no family history of short stature, skeletal disorders, or consanguinity. The patient exhibited delayed gross motor development. At the time of presentation at age 2, symptoms included bone pain, stunted growth, teeth deformities, and wrist swelling. The patient had total alopecia. Anthropometric measurements were below the 3rd percentile, while head circumference was at the 97th percentile.
test_results: X-ray of right and left leg before treatment at the time of presentation there was the lack of provisional zone of calcification, widening of physis with metaphyseal cupping and fraying with generalized osteopenia. Biochemical parameters showed low levels of serum calcium, elevated levels of alkaline phosphatase, PTH and 1,25(OH)2D before initiating the treatment.
diagnosis: Hereditary Vitamin-D Dependent Rickets Type II

case_report: A 22-month-old male presented with poor growth, inability to walk, and delayed verbal expression, being able to say only one word other than 'mom' and 'dad.' He was born at full term (40 weeks) without perinatal complications to healthy, non-consanguineous parents. At birth, his weight was 3.3 kg (-0.1 SDS) and his height was 50 cm (0.06 SDS). He is the second child in the family. The father's height is 170 cm (-0.81 SDS) and the mother's height is 161 cm (-0.01 SDS). His 40-month-old elder sister has normal growth and development. There is no family history of rickets. He was breastfed for 1 month before transitioning to formula feeding. Weaning foods were introduced at 5–6 months. At 15 months, he experienced frequent loose stools after milk feeding, leading to a reduction in milk intake and worsening dietary calcium deficiency. At 19 months, his mother started giving him 400 IU of vitamin D daily. Developmental delays were not noticed by his parents until he was 12 months old. By 12 months, he could not stand without support or walk independently. His parents were not concerned about his delayed gross motor development, as his elder sister had started walking at 14 months. After 12 months, his parents observed longer sleep durations, decreased food intake, reduced physical activity, and no weight gain. At 18 months, he had a fever followed by a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting a few minutes, considered a febrile seizure, with no medical evaluation performed. By 22 months, he still could not stand or walk independently and was referred for evaluation of growth retardation and delayed development. Physical examination revealed features such as frontal bossing, delayed closure of the anterior fontanel, Harrison's groove, rachitic rosary, and palpable widening of the wrists and ankles. His height was 76.5 cm (<3rd percentile), weight was 9.5 kg (<3rd percentile), and head circumference was 46.3 cm (10th–25th percentile).
test_results: CYP27B1 was analyzed by Sanger sequencing of the entire coding region, and 2 novel pathogenic variants (NM_000785.3: c.57_69del and c.171dupG) in exon 1 were found. The c.57_69del variant was predicted to substitute a glutamic acid with a proline at amino acid position 20 and a stop codon at amino acid position 22 (p.Glu20Profs*2). The c.171dupG variant was predicted to substitute a leucine with an alanine at amino acid position 58 and create a new reading frame (p.Leu58Alafs*275). Family study revealed that c.57_69del was inherited from his mother, while c.171dupG was inherited from his father. The elder sister was a heterozygous carrier of c.171dupG.

case_report: A 4-year-7-month-old girl (currently 18-month-old girl) presented with hypotonia, weakness, impaired mobility, and poor growth. Laboratory findings indicated hypocalcemia. The patient had no recent complaints of constipation and loss of appetite. Her weight and height were 8.800 g and 73.5 cm, respectively, both below the third percentile. Linear growth showed a slow trend in height growth and inappropriate weight gain. Developmental assessment indicated the patient could walk with assistance. Vision, cognition, perception, motor skills, and expressive language comprehension were normal. The patient could crawl and stand up, with no abnormal head circumference or poor tooth development observed. Head examination was normal. No signs of alopecia were observed, and hair distribution was normal. Examination revealed muscle weakness, reduced subcutaneous fat, and global hypotonia. The wrists were wide, and the left ankle was slightly deviated. The patient could lift her limbs in both supine and upright positions. Radiographs of the wrists and ankles were consistent with rickets before therapeutic intervention. Other findings included a small chest wall with normal expansion and rachitic rosary. There was no history of seizures. The patient had a history of severe shortness of breath caused by pneumonia. She was the second child in her family, delivered by cesarean section with a birth weight of 3.3 kg. Nutritional and perinatal care were normal. Her parents were consanguineous and asymptomatic, with no report of miscarriage in the family history. A metabolic disorder was identified in her family history, and the first child died of hypophosphatemic rickets. Baseline laboratory profile included hemoglobin (Hb): 11.2 mg/dL, mean corpuscular volume (MCV): 75.7 fL, calcium (Ca): 8.9 mg/dL, and phosphorus: 3.4 mg/dL. Initial treatment included Rocaltrol capsule 0.25 microgram (six capsules) every 12 hours, Calmerz syrup 5 cc every 4 hours, Phosphate Sandoz tablet 500 mg (3/4 tablet) every 6 hours, ferrous sulfate tablet 50 mg, and folic acid 1 mg. After 2 months, she was referred to our clinic. She had no trouble walking or running. Her appetite was normal, and she had no history of constipation. Her mental condition was normal. Examination of the extremities showed no evidence of Coxa vara or Coxa valga. Her weight and height were 9.5 kg and 75 cm, respectively, both below the third percentile. Laboratory tests included PTH: 95.4 pg/mL, ferritin: 64 micg/L, ALP: 780 U/L, Hb: 11.7 mg/dL, MCV: 77.1 fL, thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH): 1.76 m IU/L, Free T4: 1.20 m IU/L, Ca: 10.2 mg/dL, phosphorus: 4.3 mg/dL, and vitamin D: 25.7 ng/mL. Only Calmerz syrup was changed to 5 cc every 6 hours. Follow-up for the next 2 months indicated no signs of rachitic rosary and movement problems. She had a normal appetite and did not complain of constipation. She also had flat feet and suffered from orthopnea. The patient's weight and height were 9 kg and 77.5 cm, respectively, both below the third percentile. Lab tests included PTH: 7.66 pg/mL, creatinine (Cr): 0.4 mg/dL, ALP: 343 U/L, Ca: 11.1 mg/dL, phosphorus: 5 mg/dL, and vitamin D: 20.6 ng/mL. Her regimen was changed to Phosphate Sandoz 500 mg tablets every 6 hours, Calmerz syrup 5 cc every 8 hours, and Rocaltrol capsule (5 capsules) every 12 hours. Follow-up for the next 1 month showed complaints of anorexia and polydipsia. Her movement was acceptable. Grade 3 hydronephrosis of the left kidney was detected in the kidney and urinary tract ultrasound report. Laboratory profile included PTH: 22.1 pg/mL, ferritin: 79.6 micg/L, fasting blood sugar (FBS): 88 mg/dL, 2-hpp glucose: 106 mg/dL, Bun: 44 mg/dL, Cr: 0.6 mg/dL, ALP: 337 U/L, Hb: 10.5 mg/dL, MCV: 71.5 fL, Ca: 10.3 mg/dL, phosphorus: 4 mg/dL, vitamin D: 36.1 ng/mL, growth hormone (GH): 4.3 IU/L, and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1): 51 IU/L. The possibility of renal tubular acidosis (RTA) was ruled out due to the absence of polyuria and normal blood potential of hydrogen (pH).
test_results: A known homozygous mutation (c.195 + 2T > G) in the CYP27B1 gene with autosomal recessive inheritance has been reported. This mutation is located in exon 1 of chromosome 12q13 and is a splice-site pathogenic variant.

case_report: A 37-year-old woman reported experiencing dry mouth and dry eyes starting in June 2017. By July 2018, she developed progressive muscle weakness, which eventually led to an episode of paralysis. She was admitted to the hospital in November 2018. Her serum creatinine level was normal in June 2018. Two months prior to admission, her blood potassium level was 1.7 mmol/L, sodium was 144 mmol/L, and chloride was 109.5 mmol/L. Blood gas analysis showed a pH of 7.36 and a bicarbonate concentration of 20.7 mmol/L, with an anion gap of 13.8 mmol/L. Her serum creatinine was 1.17 mg/dL, and the antinuclear antibody was positive at a titer of 1:320. Anti-SSA and anti-SSB antibodies were negative. Urine analysis revealed a pH of 7.50, with no glucose, protein, or hematuria detected. The 24-hour urine protein was 0.69 g. Elevated levels of urine β2 microglobulin (0.64 mg/L), α1 microglobulin (12.1 mg/L), and 24-hour urine potassium (98.7 mmol) were noted. Postural stimulation to exclude primary aldosteronemia was negative. The Schirmer test and fluorescein staining were normal. The unstimulated salivary flow rate was less than 0.1 mL/minute. Focal lymphocytic sialadenitis was confirmed by labial gland biopsy. The patient was treated with 30 mg of prednisone daily and 750 mg of mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) twice a day. Potassium supplementation ranged from 2 to 6 g daily. Following this treatment, the patient's paralysis was alleviated. Routine tests showed potassium levels between 2.8 and 3.4 mmol/L, with serum creatinine levels ranging from 1.12 to 1.32 mg/dL.
test_results: Renal pathology was remarkable for the diffuse and mild fibrosis and evident infiltration of inflammatory cells in the renal interstitium on light microscopy. Glomeruli were intact. Focal and segmental IgG deposits (+) were observed in the glomerular mesangial area and capillary loops. Electron microscopy revealed diffusely thin glomerular basement membrane and infiltration of lymphocytes and monocytes in the interstitium.
diagnosis: Primary Sjögren syndrome-associated acute interstitial nephritis and type 3 renal tubular acidosis

case_report: A 32-year-old individual presented for a rheumatologic evaluation due to several months of fatigue, dry eyes, dry mouth, weight loss, hair loss, joint pain, and shortness of breath during physical activity. Medical records indicated an unusual visit to a local emergency room 4 years prior, where the patient experienced severe weakness and was found to have significantly low potassium levels, with serum potassium at 1.4 milliequivalents per liter. At that time, the patient also had a non-anion gap metabolic acidosis, with serum bicarbonate levels between 12–14 milliequivalents per liter and a urine pH of 7–8. Magnesium levels were normal. This episode was not fully explained but was thought to be related to a possible undetected diarrheal illness, despite the patient denying any such illness. The low potassium levels were corrected with potassium chloride supplementation, and the patient continued on potassium supplements for some time afterward. About a year after this incident, the patient began experiencing flank pain and recurrent kidney stones. A CT scan revealed nephrocalcinosis.
test_results: After her Rheumatology visit further work up included a positive ANA and positive double-stranded DNA (ds DNA) titer of 1:320. She also had a positive SSA and SSB. Rheumatoid factor was elevated at 28. C-ANCA was positive at 1:160 but specific PR 3 and MPO antibodies were negative. Serum protein electrophoresis revealed a polyclonal gammopathy. At that time her sedimentation rate was elevated at 50 mm/hr with a CRP that was mildly elevated at 2.2 mg/dL. She was found to have hypocomplementemia with a C3 level of 32 mg/dL and a C4 of 2.1 mg/dL. Microalbumin to creatinine ratio was within normal limits at 27 mg/g. Urinalysis revealed no proteinuria, but microscopic hematuria was present with 3–5 nondysmorphic red blood cells/high power field but no white blood cells or casts. A complete blood count showed a white blood cell count at that time was 4.7 k/mcL with a hemoglobin of 10.7 g/dL and a platelet count of 251 k/mcL. Serum creatinine at that time was 0.9 mg/dL with a potassium of 4.3 meq/L and a serum bicarbonate level of 18 meq/L.
diagnosis: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus  and Sjogren's syndrome

case_report: A 55-year-old man presented to the thrombosis clinic with a history of unprovoked right leg deep venous thrombosis (DVT) diagnosed three months earlier based on Doppler ultrasound findings. He was on a therapeutic dose of rivaroxaban (20 mg daily) and tested negative for thrombophilia. During the current visit, he reported a one-month history of progressive unilateral lower limb pain and swelling. He had no chronic medical conditions. He mentioned a weight loss of approximately 8 kg over three months, without fever or night sweats. Physical examination revealed a large, warm, and extremely tender mass in the middle of the right thigh, measuring 19 × 18 × 35 cm, with erythematous skin and dilated superficial veins. There was lower limb pitting edema, but peripheral pulses were palpable. Routine blood tests showed a white blood cell count of 26.09 × 10^9/L, neutrophils at 88.10%, hemoglobin at 10.00 g/dL, platelets at 352 × 10^9/L, plasma lactate dehydrogenase at 1,709 U/L, alkaline phosphatase at 255, erythrocyte sedimentation rate at 118 mm/hour, and C-reactive protein at 288 mg/dL. Vascular ultrasound of bilateral lower limb veins showed no evidence of acute DVT but identified a large isoechoic heterogeneous lesion extending from the right thigh to below the knee, with internal vascularity. Radiographs and a CT scan of the thigh revealed a large heterogeneous soft-tissue mass measuring approximately 19.8 × 18.5 × 35 cm in transverse, anteroposterior, and cranial-caudal diameters, respectively. The mass occupied all compartments of the thigh (quadriceps, hamstring, and adductors) and extended intra-articularly to the knee joint, with bone destruction involving the distal femoral condyles. Multiple subcutaneous lesions/nodules were noted in the leg. An ultrasound-guided fine needle biopsy showed pleomorphic large cells with prominent nucleoli and intact membranes.
test_results: The neoplastic cells showed focal CD45 and CD79a positivity, diffuse CD138, EBV-ISH, CD45RO, CD30, BCL2, and MUM-1. Cells were negative for CD19, CD21, CD23, CD56, MPO CD20, PAX5, CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, CD7, CD8, CD10, TDT, Synaptophysin, ALK-1, GRANZ-B, CK, EMA, S100, and BCL-6. The cells also showed surface Kappa light chain restriction.

case_report: A 29-year-old male, with a history of heavy smoking and HIV positive status diagnosed 10 years ago, presented to the Department of Medicine and Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at Hospital El Carmen de Maipú. The patient was referred from periodontics due to a 2.5 cm mass located in the vestibular gingiva between teeth 1.2 and 1.3, which had developed over the past two weeks. The patient reported minimal friction without pain and no sensation of paresthesia. Intraoral examination revealed a violaceous, ulcerated mass with a partially pedicled base, asymptomatic, and exhibiting active bleeding. No other lesions were found in the oral cavity. Orthopantomography showed no osteolytic or radiopaque lesions. Palpation did not reveal any peripheral cervical adenopathies. Laboratory tests indicated a significant deficiency in CD4 cells (164 cells/mm3) and a high viral load (36,000 copies/ml). Hemogram and coagulation tests were normal, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was within normal limits (27 mm/hr).
test_results: The histopathological examination revealed an oral mucosa with a lymphoplasmacytic proliferation with diffuse disposition. The examination showed plasma cells with medium size and abundant mitosis. Immunohistochemistry showed expression of CD3, CD138 and KI-67 in all cells, CD30 and CD79A in almost all cells and CD45 in a group of cells. The sample was positive for EBV. CD20 was not expressed. The sample was positive to MUM-1 and EMA, and negative to CD56.

case_report: A 49-year-old male garment factory worker with no history of smoking was admitted to the hospital on 30 December 2018 due to experiencing “intermittent blood in his phlegm for more than 4 months”. The patient reported intermittent bright red blood streaks in his phlegm after extended work hours before April, without having received any formal diagnosis or treatment. A chest computed tomography (CT) scan conducted one week prior to admission identified two masses in the left lower lobe of the lung: one in the dorsal segment near the hilum measuring 31.3 × 35.6 mm, and another in the posterior basal segment measuring 18.4 × 20.2 mm. Both masses exhibited superficial foliation, peripheral burr, and a halo sign. Additionally, the CT scan indicated slight infection in the middle lobe of the right lung and the lower lobe of the left lung. Upon physical examination, the patient's vital signs were stable, with slightly moist rale sounds in the lungs, and no swelling or clubbed fingers were observed. Tumor marker tests returned negative results.
test_results: Under bronchoscopy, the opening of the left dorsal segment was narrowed, and the lens body (Olympus BF-P260F) could not reach the distal end, but no new organisms were found. Lavage, brushing and transbronchial lung biopsy were performed. The pathology of the dorsal segment showed poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. The immunohistochemistry results were as follows: leukocyte common antigen (+) lymphocytes, synaptophysin (−), chromogranin A (−), Ki-67 (+, 30%), pan-cytokeratin (+++), CD56 (−), thyroid transcription factor 1 (−), p40 (+++), cytokeratin 5/6 (++) and napsin A (−). In situ hybridization of Epstein–Barr virus (EBV)-encoded small RNA 1 (EBER-1) was diffusely positive.

case_report: A 72-year-old Chinese female with a history of blood hypertension for over 30 years, chronic bronchitis for over 20 years, and diabetes for 6 years, was admitted to the hospital after experiencing a productive cough for three weeks, which worsened significantly over the following week. Physical examination revealed diminished and coarser respiratory sounds in the right lung field.
test_results: Laboratory examination revealed a high percentage of monocytes, a low level of hemoglobinn and a low mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration. A hypermetabolic mass in the upper lobe of the right lung as well as the enlargement of right hilar and subcarinal lymph nodes were determined by F-FDG PET-CTA. The tumor was measured as 2.8 × 2.2 × 3 cm and ulcerated. Routine histologic sections stained with hematoxylin-eosin showed that tumor cells grew infiltrative in fibrous interstitium and arranged in sheets and syncytial pattern with marked pleomorphism. Neoplastic cells presented vacuolar nucleus with prominent nucleoli and a marked lymphocytes infiltration. The tumor cells were strongly positive for CK5/6 and P40. The tumor cells showed negative immunostaining of Napsin A, TTF1, CD56, CgA, and Syn. Latent membrane protein (LMP1) expression of the Epstein-Barr virus was positive in tumor cells. Chemiluminescence analysis of EB virus antibodies showed that EBV-EA IgA and EBV-VCA IgG were both positive. The patient was formerly infected by cytomegalovirus (CMV), so the CMV-Ab IgG was positive as well. Microscopic examination further excluded the vessel invasion, nerve invasion, and pleural invasion. No metastasis was found at the resection margin of the bronchus or in group 7 lymph nodes, but in the bronchial lymph nodes.

case_report: A 40-year-old Caucasian female from Prince Edward Island, Canada, presented with a left preauricular mass that had been present for two years. Recently, the mass had become firmer and more noticeable. The patient reported no pain, tenderness, or facial weakness. Her medical history included a sleeve gastrectomy, ankle injury repair, and cholecystectomy. She was not taking any medications, did not smoke or consume alcohol, and had no known allergies. There was no family history of head and neck malignancies. Physical examination revealed a rubbery, fixed, 5-centimeter nontender mass in the left parotid region. No cervical lymph nodes were palpable, and facial nerve function was normal. Flexible nasopharyngoscopy showed no abnormalities.
test_results: An initial fine needle aspiration (FNA) was done on the parotid mass at a satellite head and neck clinic on Prince Edward Island, revealing atypical cells. Imaging was also requested, and a computed tomography (CT) scan demonstrated a heterogeneously enhancing solid mass in the left parotid, measuring 3.5 cm × 3.2 cm × 4.6 cm with a component of deep lobe extension and ill-defined margins. Multiple pathological lymph nodes were also seen along the vicinity of the mass and in the neck. A second FNA was performed in Halifax, Nova Scotia with the hope of a better diagnostic yield. The results indicated the presence of malignant cells, consistent with a poorly differentiated carcinoma.
diagnosis: Primary lymphoepithelial carcinoma of the parotid

case_report: A 75-year-old Japanese man presented with sudden, asymptomatic gross hematuria. Imaging studies, including ultrasonography and abdominal X-ray, indicated the presence of a bladder calculus. Further evaluation with computed tomography (CT) revealed a 1.8 cm intramural calculus in the right ureter and a well-defined, hypervascular mass approximately 2.1 cm in size at the right trigone of the urinary bladder. Both kidneys showed no signs of hydronephrosis. Cystoscopy was performed, revealing a non-papillary nodular mass at the right trigone, covered by normal urothelium and suggesting a submucosal location. The mucosa was elevated behind the mass, but the right ureteral orifice and calculus were not visible preoperatively. CT indicated that the mass was adjacent to the calculus, potentially obstructing its passage. Magnetic resonance imaging showed no invasive growth. Urine cytology results were negative for malignant cells. The patient underwent transurethral resection (TUR) of the mass, which allowed visualization of the right ureteral orifice and the intra-ureteral calculus. Subsequently, transurethral lithotripsy was performed. The patient recovered without perioperative complications and has remained free of recurrence for 5 months.
test_results: On histologic examination, the urothelium was largely denuded; however, residual urothelium showed no atypia. In the submucosal lesion, we observed spindle-shaped to oval-shaped cells that had mildly hyperchromatic nuclei and eosinophilic elongated or tapering cytoplasm arranged in loose fascicles or perivascular whorls around often-hyalinized blood vessels or in a vague storiform-growth fashion, embedded in variably fibromyxoid or edematous stroma associated with dilated thin-walled blood vessels. Mitotic figures are rare. On immunohistochemical examination, the tumor cells were positive for alpha-smooth muscle actin (SMA), desmin, CD34, and h-caldesmon, and CD99 was weakly and focally expressed. The cells were negative for S-100, CAM5.2, AE1/AE3, epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), STAT6, MUC4, and claudin-1.

case_report: A 75-year-old woman reported experiencing postprandial cramps and heartburn for three months. Imaging of the abdomen and pelvis identified a 6.7 × 5.8 × 5.3 cm enhancing mass in the pelvic region, appearing to originate from the right ovary. This was accompanied by severe hydronephrosis on the right side and a dilated, tortuous right ureter. No local lymphadenopathy or metastasis was observed. The patient did not report dysuria or gross hematuria. Her surgical history includes a transabdominal hysterectomy with left salpingo-oophorectomy.
test_results: A computed tomography scan of her abdomen and pelvis revealed an incidental, 6.7 × 5.8 × 5.3 cm, enhancing pelvic mass thought to be originating from the right ovary, with associated right-sided severe hydronephrosis and a dilated tortuous right ureter. There was no evidence of local lymphadenopathy or metastasis.

case_report: The patient is a 14-year-old male born in Peru via natural delivery to consanguineous parents. Birth weight was 3060 g and length was 52 cm. He achieved his first words on time and began walking independently at 12 months. Psychomotor development and growth were normal until the age of 3 years, when a slowdown in growth and a progressive decrease in motor abilities were noted. At the age of nine, the patient was evaluated and found to have skeletal abnormalities, aortic stenosis, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Since 2012, he experienced multiple syncopal episodes. In 2015, severe diplegia of the lower limbs was observed. Metabolic analyses were normal. At the age of 14, the patient presented with short stature, a short trunk, scoliosis with accentuated lordosis, facial dysmorphisms, pterygium colli, varus knees, lower limbs diplegia, and platyspondyly. Dental evaluations indicated hypodontia and enamel defects.
test_results: Radiographic examinations of upper limbs and pelvis disclosed slightly widened appearance of the proximal epiphyseal region of the tibiae and of the distal epiphyseal region of the femurs.

case_report: A 73-year-old woman experienced intense pain in the right scapular region, rated 8.9 out of 10 on the numerical rating scale. This severe pain persisted for one week before gradually decreasing in intensity. Three weeks after the initial onset of symptoms, she encountered difficulty raising her right arm and was unable to comb her hair or wash her face. Physical examination revealed 2/5 strength in the right shoulder abductor and flexor muscles, and 4/5 strength in the right elbow flexor muscle. Sensation to pin prick was equal in both upper extremities. Deep tendon reflexes were absent in the right biceps brachii and right triceps brachii.
test_results: Electrophysiologic study performed at seven weeks from the onset was compatible with right brachial plexopathy, mainly involving upper trunk. An HSI lesion extended from the postganglionic right C5 and C6 root to the level of cord in the T2 STIR images and in DW MR neurographic images. This lesion showed mild enhancement in Gd-enhanced T1-weighted image.

case_report: A 55-year-old woman presented with a history of neck pain persisting for many years following a motor vehicle accident twenty-one years ago. She also reported paresthesia and pain in the right arm, accompanied by a burning sensation near the shoulder girdle. Intermittent numbness was noted in the toes and both hands. Physical examination revealed a restricted range of motion in the neck when turning the body to the left. Long tract signs were positive for Babinski and Hoffman signs, with hyperreflexia observed in the lower extremities and the right arm. Weakness was noted in the right wrist extensor and the right hip flexor. Imaging showed deformity of the cervical spine with kyphotic angulation and spinal cord compression. At C5-C6, there was grade 1 retrolisthesis, and at C3-4, there was grade 1 anterolisthesis. Severe canal stenosis with cord compression and severe bilateral foraminal stenosis were observed, along with abnormal signal in the spinal cord at C5-C6 and C4-C5, suggesting myelomalacia. At C6-C7, there was right-sided disc herniation causing cord compression on the right side. Surgical intervention included cervical laminectomy from C3 to C7 with lateral mass fusion from C3 to C7. Neurophysiological monitoring (SSEP and EMG) remained stable throughout the procedure, with satisfactory signal responses obtained from all four extremities before and during surgery. No complications occurred during surgery, and the patient was conscious and neurologically unchanged in the recovery room compared to the preoperative exam. Twenty-four hours post-surgery, the patient experienced significant pain in the left para-cervical and shoulder area extending into the arm, along with numbness in the entire arm without a specific dermatome pattern. The following day, she reported increased pain in the left arm and newly developed weakness in the deltoid, biceps, triceps, wrist extensor, grip, and intrinsic muscles, resulting in difficulty using the arm both proximally and distally. Post-operative imaging showed a well-decompressed cervical spine. An MRI scan of the brain showed negative findings.
test_results: Post-operative MRI scan of the brachial plexus revealed edema within the three trunks of the brachial plexus.

case_report: A 46-year-old female patient with no significant past medical history presented with fatigue and shortness of breath for the previous three months. Physical examination was unremarkable. ENT endoscopy identified a mass in the nose, and histopathology of the biopsy indicated nasopharyngeal cancer. The patient received Intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) with a dose of 42Gy/21fx and chemotherapy with a Cisplatin regimen at a local hospital. After six days of radiation therapy, the patient experienced frequent nosebleeds and severe back pain. Complete blood count showed hemoglobin at 8.6 g/dl, platelet count at 19 x 10^9/L, white blood cell count at 0.7 x 10^9/L, and a differential count of neutrophils at 66%, lymphocytes at 23%, and monocytes at 5%. Peripheral blood smear revealed a leuco-erythroblastic picture with thrombocytopenia, rouleaux formation, and large atypical cells. Bone marrow smears showed 72% large atypical cells with marked nuclear convolutions that were negative for all cytochemical staining markers. Biochemical markers indicated high levels of LDH at 1842 IU/ml, total serum protein at 6.6 g/dl, serum albumin at 3.39 g/dl with an albumin to globulin ratio of 1.06:1. Serum calcium was 9.12 mg/dl, and renal and liver function tests were normal. Quantification of heavy chain immunoglobulins was normal, with a kappa/lambda ratio of 12.9:24.7 (0.52:1). HIV, HBV, and HCV viral serology were all negative. Ultrasound examination showed no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed multiple lytic bone lesions on the lumbar spine L1 - L5 and bilateral sacrum and pelvis.
test_results: Bone marrow smears showed 72% large atypical cells with marked nuclear convolutions that were negative for all cytochemical staining markers. The initial panel of flowcytometric immunophenotyping on bone marrow was negative for CD45, CD34, TdT, HLA-DR, CD19, CyCD3, CD79a, MPO, CD71, CD235, CD41, CD61, and CD38 markers. An extended panel consisting of CD138, CD56, CD117 was applied and came out positive along with a kappa light chain. Hypercellular bone marrow biopsy sections revealed near-total replacement of undifferentiated large atypical cells that were strongly positive for CD138, CD56, Ki67 but negative for CD38. Cytogenetic analysis revealed a complex karyotype comprising gain of chromosome segments 1q and loss of chromosome 4q. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) studies demonstrated a t(4;14) (q31;q32) - immunoglobulin heavy chain (IgH) translocation in 70% of the cells.
diagnosis: Anaplastic Plasma Cell Myeloma with CD38 Negativity

case_report: The patient is a 66-year-old female with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus with neuropathy, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. She presented with a five-month history of progressive lower extremity weakness, difficulty walking, and frequent falls. Her A1C was normal, and she was on basal insulin, short-acting insulin, and metformin. Eight months prior, she received the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine series, experiencing mild fever and malaise after the second dose, followed by residual fatigue for several weeks. Three months later, she woke up with no sensation in both legs and right arm weakness, leading to a hospital admission for stroke evaluation. Brain imaging was unremarkable, and the stroke workup was negative. She was discharged on aspirin and atorvastatin with a neurology follow-up. A urinary tract infection was identified and treated with antibiotics. Her leg weakness continued to worsen over the next two months, accompanied by electric, shooting pain from toes to hips and bilateral arm weakness. Over the next three months, her symptoms progressed more rapidly, necessitating the use of a wheelchair due to inability to rise from a seated position. She experienced one to two falls daily, numbness and tingling in the upper extremities, poor oral intake, and unintentional weight loss of 40 pounds over eight months. Bilateral leg weakness showed a waxing and waning pattern with an overall decline in strength. She used ibuprofen as needed for extremity pain. Neurology evaluation revealed hyporeflexia. Cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine MRIs were unremarkable, showing no abnormal spinal cord signal, intrathecal enhancement, or thecal sac stenosis. A screening colonoscopy was also unremarkable. Physical examination showed decreased motor strength in all extremities, more pronounced in the legs, decreased light touch sensation in all extremities, and absent deep tendon reflexes in the lower extremities. Muscle tone and bulk were normal. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, creatine kinase, and thyroid-stimulating hormone, were unremarkable. Serum protein electrophoresis indicated a questionable protein band in the gamma globulin region. Serum immunofixation revealed IgG kappa monoclonal protein and a slightly abnormal IgG lambda monoclonal protein. Urine protein electrophoresis showed predominantly glomerular proteinuria with an additional protein band. Urine immunofixation revealed IgG kappa monoclonal protein. Vitamin B1, folate, vitamin D, copper, and vitamin B12 levels were normal. Lumbar puncture revealed clear cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with albuminocytological dissociation: CSF protein was 237 mg/dL, glucose was 56 mg/dL, and total nucleated cell count was 2. CSF angiotensin-converting enzyme was normal. Serology tests, including antinuclear antibody, anti-double-stranded DNA, HIV, and West Nile virus, were negative. CSF PCR testing for West Nile virus and SARS-CoV-2 was negative. Brain MRI was unremarkable.
test_results: Nerve conduction studies demonstrated an absent sural sensory nerve response. The peroneal motor nerve response distal latencies were prolonged with significantly reduced amplitudes and significantly slowed proximal conduction velocities. The tibial motor nerve response distal latencies were significantly prolonged with reduced amplitudes. The F response was absent on the right and prolonged on the left. The nerve conduction results were consistent with prolonged distal latencies and decreased amplitudes in the bilateral peroneal and tibial motor nerve conductions, absent right sural sensory potential, and widespread active and chronic denervation in all muscles tested in both lower extremities. Concentric needle electromyography of the lower extremities demonstrated diffusely abnormal insertional activity with both fibrillations and positive sharp waves in all the tested muscles. The activated motor units of the lower extremities demonstrated increased motor unit complexities, increased amplitudes, and reduced recruitment patterns.

case_report: A 23-year-old man presented with frequent ventricular ectopic beats. He was hemodynamically stable and reported no other significant symptoms. He had no history of syncope and was unaware of any family history of cardiomyopathy or sudden cardiac death. His medical history included an episode of acute myocarditis one year prior, during which he experienced chest pain, elevated troponin levels, and T wave inversion in the inferolateral leads on ECG. A coronary angiogram at that time showed normal coronary arteries. Imaging revealed a non-dilated left ventricle with low-normal ejection fraction and normal right ventricle dimensions and function. T2-weighted images indicated mid-wall myocardial edema in the interventricular septum, with mid-wall late gadolinium enhancement observed on post-contrast images. The patient was discharged with a recommendation for close clinical follow-up.
test_results: Genetic testing identified a heterozygous variant in DSP (c.5428C>T, p.Gln1810Ter). A new CMR study confirmed the mildly reduced LV EF with no evidence of myocardial edema. Post-contrast images revealed a diffuse circumferential subepicardial LGE involvement of the LV myocardium. Echocardiography showed an initial reduction of LV EF, with an area of hypo-akinesia involving the lateral wall, and preserved RV dimensions and function.
Orpha_name: Inherited isolated arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, dominant-left variant

case_report: A 47-year-old female arrived at the emergency department experiencing multiple episodes of sudden dizziness and near-fainting. The initial episode happened one week before her visit while she was driving; she managed to stop the car safely, and the dizziness subsided after one minute. She continued to have episodes of near-fainting, which increased in severity and duration, prompting her visit to the emergency department. She reported no palpitations, shortness of breath, chest pain, or complete loss of consciousness. Physical examination showed no abnormalities. Her medical history was clear, and she was not taking any medications. She was an active smoker with a 10-pack-year history and consumed minimal alcohol. A detailed family history did not indicate any instances of sudden cardiac death or heart disease.
test_results: The initial electrocardiograph (ECG) revealed multiple ventricular ectopics, right bundle branch block (RBBB), and ST changes inferolaterally with T-wave inversion inferiorly. Complete blood count, urea and electrolytes, and troponin were all within normal limits. Telemetry showed a high burden of premature ventricular contractions (25%), with frequent runs of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia. Two-dimensional echocardiography revealed a severely reduced left ventricular (LV) systolic function (20-25%) with severe global hypokinesia and mild to moderate LV dilatation (60 mm), LV wall thickness being normal. Cardiac magnetic radiography (MRI) cine imaging revealed global LV hypokinesia along with moderately reduced right ventricular function. Disproportionate hypokinesis in the entire septum and LV inferior wall was noted. Post-contrast cardiac MRI demonstrated extensive fibrosis from the base of the left ventricle to the right ventricular septum. It also noted prominent epicardial fibrosis throughout the inferior wall of the LV. She was screened for sarcoidosis through cardiac positron emission tomography (PET) scan, and sarcoidosis was ruled out. Genetic screening for desmoplakin gene mutation and other genes of inherited cardiac disease was negative. Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme and calcium level were normal. Investigations to rule out other potential causes for cardiac fibrosis - Lyme and Fabry’s disease - were unremarkable. A coronary angiogram was performed which demonstrated minimal non-obstructive coronary artery disease.
Orpha_name: Inherited isolated arrhythmogenic ventricular dysplasia, biventricular variant

case_report: A 68-year-old male presented with chest discomfort, palpitations, and light-headedness, followed by a syncopal episode with urinary incontinence, and was admitted to the emergency room. His medical history included progressive difficulty in performing daily activities, heart failure, and unspecified ventricular tachycardia treated with electric cardioversion one year prior. On examination, continuous cardiac monitoring was initiated. Vital signs included a heart rate of 66 bpm, blood pressure of 103/64 mmHg, oxygen saturation of 98%, and a respiratory rate of 12 breaths per minute. His medications were bisoprolol 2.5 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, acetylsalicylic acid 100 mg, and amiodarone 100 mg. He reported no family history of cardiovascular symptoms or diseases in first-degree relatives. Initial laboratory tests were normal except for mild hyponatremia (134 mEq/L). Continuous monitoring revealed sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse on the 12-lead ECG, which was treated with pharmacological cardioversion, successfully restoring sinus rhythm. Post-cardioversion ECG showed low QRS voltages in limb leads and T-wave inversion in the left precordial leads (V4-V6). A transthoracic echocardiogram showed reduced left ventricular systolic function with a 2D ejection fraction of 30%, right ventricular systolic dysfunction (TAPSE of 17 mm, S’ of 5.2 cm/s, and RV fractional area change of 27%), enlargement of both atria (left atrial indexed volume of 56.41 mL/m2, right atrial indexed volume of 34.14 mL/m2), and biventricular global hypokinesia. Cardiovascular computed tomography showed no atherosclerotic plaques (CAD-RADS 0).
test_results: The long-axis view demonstrated noteworthy enlargement of the left ventricle (end-systolic volume of 95 ml, end-diastolic volume of 144 mL and stroke volume of 49 mL) and the right ventricle (end-systolic volume of 126 mL, end-diastolic volume of 173 mL and stroke volume of 47 mL), moderate LV systolic dysfunction (LVEF 34%) and severe RV systolic dysfunction (RVEF 27%). The RV outflow tract did not show any abnormalities with an infundibular portion of 29.5 mm. Pulmonary arteries were confluent with a functional diameter of the pulmonary trunk of 25.5 mm, right pulmonary artery of 19 mm, and left pulmonary artery of 17 mm. The tricuspid valve area was normal (5.6 cm2). The LV outflow tract was reported within normal range with an aortic valve area of 3.69 cm2. Aortic segments were also within normal range with an aortic annulus of 24 mm, aortic sinuses of 30 mm, sinotubular junction of 27.3 mm, and ascending aorta of 27 mm. A mild mitral insufficiency was reported with distal thickening of the anterior leaflet. The balanced steady-state free precession (bSSFP) cine imaging revealed biventricular enlargement with LV predominance with global hypokinesia and septal dyssynchrony. T2 weighted imaging short-axis view showed a linear hypointensity in the basal third of the septal wall. Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) in a short-axis view demonstrated extensive LV subepicardial enhancement with septal predominance in a ring pattern and an irregular morphology of the RV free wall. In addition, a four-chamber view showed diffuse LGE involving the subepicardial layer of the LV free wall and septum, and a vertical long-axis view demonstrated LGE in the anterior LV wall.
Orpha_name: Inherited isolated arrhythmogenic ventricular dysplasia, biventricular variant

case_report: A female infant was born at 35 weeks and 5 days gestation to a 26-year-old mother with a history of two pregnancies and two births. The infant's birth weight was 1.984 kg, placing her in the ninth percentile for preterm girls according to the Fenton growth chart. The pregnancy was complicated by maternal tobacco use. The mother tested positive for group B streptococcus and received clindamycin for intrapartum prophylaxis due to a penicillin allergy. Prenatal care began at 20 weeks gestation. Other prenatal tests were unremarkable, and no abnormalities were detected on prenatal imaging. The mother experienced spontaneous preterm labor and delivered with vacuum assistance. The infant was vigorous at birth and did not require resuscitation. After birth, multiple congenital anomalies were observed, prompting transfer to a level 4 neonatal intensive care unit (NICU). Upon arrival, the infant exhibited several congenital anomalies: brachydactyly and hypoplasia of the nail beds of the fifth digits on both hands, absence of the distal phalanx of the second digit on the left hand, oligodactyly of the fifth digits on both feet, right 2-3 syndactyly, left 2-3-4 syndactyly, abnormal medial malleolus at the tibial insertion with circumferential narrowing of the lower leg, and a caudal appendage measuring 3 cm × 0.5 cm located 2.5 cm to the right of the midline in the lumbosacral region without apparent bony involvement. Imaging studies conducted in the NICU, including head ultrasound, renal ultrasound, and echocardiogram, were normal.
test_results: A skeletal survey confirmed the limb abnormalities noted at the physical exam. A spine ultrasound showed that the conus medullaris terminated at L2-3 (lower limit of normal) and had a thickened filum with decreased oscillation. Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine revealed a small syrinx at the distal thoracic cord. There was an elongated soft tissue appendage (caudal appendage) emanating from the level of the right iliac crest and extending inferiorly along the right gluteal region. It did not appear to involve or extend from the ileum or iliac crest. There was evidence of a central fibrous structure. Chromosomal microarray results showed a small deletion that included EPHA3.

case_report: A female newborn was delivered by a 35-year-old first-time mother at term (39 weeks) via cesarean section. The mother reported a consanguineous marriage and no history of teratogenic medication, diabetes, hypertension, recent infection, or drug exposure during pregnancy. An antenatal ultrasound at 28 weeks revealed a frontal encephalocele. On physical examination, the newborn weighed 3500g and had difficulty breathing. There was a partial absence of the skull bones, specifically the left parietal, left temporal, and frontal bones. Due to this defect, abnormal brain tissue protruded and was covered only by a membrane similar to the dura mater. Malformations along the facial midline included bilateral cleft lip and palate and nasal deformity. Bilateral proptosis was also observed. Changes in the extremities included hypoplastic second and third fingers on the right hand conjoined by fibrous tissue (syndactyly), and constriction rings around the third and fifth fingers on the left hand, with amputation of the distal phalanx of the fourth finger. Congenital clubfoot was also noted.
test_results: Cranial computed tomography (CT) evidenced a great amount of protruding malformed brain tissue through the skull bone defect caused by the partial absence of the frontal, left temporal, and left parietal bones.
diagnosis: Amniotic Band Syndrome  associated with exencephaly

case_report: A 2-year-old boy exhibited abdominal swelling, constipation, and greenish vomiting for three days. A week prior, he had been irritable and had a fever. Upon examination, the child had a temperature of 100°F, a pulse rate of 140 beats per minute, and signs of dehydration. The abdomen was swollen with visible bowel loops. A mass was felt in the right iliac fossa, accompanied by tenderness and guarding in the lower abdomen. A digital rectal examination revealed an empty rectum.
test_results: X-ray abdomen erect showed a complete cut-off sign indicating intestinal obstruction. Ultrasound abdomen depicted excessive gaseous shadows in the lower abdomen. Laboratory test showed Hb 10g/dl and WBC count of 22000 with 80% of neutrophils.

case_report: A 10-day-old newborn, delivered via elective C-section with APGAR scores of 8 and 9, was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) due to severe respiratory distress that appeared a few hours post-birth. The pregnancy was without complications, with normal fetal ultrasounds and negative noninvasive prenatal testing (NIPT) for chromosomal aneuploidies and major microdeletions. Blood tests showed a slight increase in C-reactive protein (CRP). Both chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasound were normal. Echocardiography identified a patent foramen ovale (PFO) with a mild shunt. After approximately 48 hours of supportive therapy, including mechanical ventilation and antibiotics, the respiratory distress resolved. Upon transfer to the nursery, the newborn displayed inconsolable crying and reduced mobility in the left lower limb. An X-ray revealed a mid-diaphyseal tibial fracture. The mother reported no history of trauma. The limb was casted, and the patient was returned to the NICU.
test_results: A CT scan of the lower limb reveals a morphostructural alteration of the left tibia, with curvature in the distal diaphyseal segment. In the mid-diaphyseal regions of the tibia, there are evident discontinuities in the bone cortex, which also appears thickened. Simultaneously, multiple irregularly distributed hypodense areas are present along the tibia, extending to the bone cortex. The fibula, also curved, exhibits a small area of hypodensity in the proximal diaphyseal region, altering the cortical profile. No CT scan alterations are observed in the surrounding soft tissues.

case_report: A 12-year-old female child was referred from a secondary center with a history of enlargement of the first and second toes of the right foot since birth. The child has not been on follow-up since the initial observation. The parents brought the child due to the progressive increase in size of the toes over the years, which caused difficulty in finding proper footwear and led to troubled ambulation. The child did not report any pain during walking, even for long distances or when climbing stairs. This child is the third of four siblings from a non-consanguineous marriage. She was born via spontaneous vaginal delivery, with no significant prenatal or perinatal history. There is no family history of similar presentations or congenital anomalies in other siblings. On examination, the first and second toes of the right foot are noticeably enlarged, with the first toe being larger than the second. The other toes appear normal in size, similar to those on the left foot. Both enlarged toes grew in a divergent manner with significant soft tissue overgrowth on the plantar aspect. Neurovascular status was intact, and there were no skin color changes, ulceration, palpable thrill, or pigmentation over both toes. The rest of the right foot appeared normal upon physical examination. No cutaneous manifestations of neurofibromatosis were observed.
test_results: Radiographical imaging showed large first and second metatarsals, along with large all phalanges of the first and second toes. There was a marked increase in the soft tissue surrounding both toes, with a lateral view of the imaging showing gross soft tissue overgrowth over the plantar aspect. The MRI of the right foot showed bone and soft tissue enlargement of the first and second toes. There is an accumulation of fat tissue with no discernible capsule around the first and second toes, medial and lateral aspects of the first metatarsal with extension up to the medial plantar arch of the foot. A soft tissue lesion was noted deep to the flexor hallucis longus, involving the lateral digital nerve of the first toe. There was no evidence of infiltration to adjacent bone and joint seen, and no features of vascular malformation were seen. The flexor and extensor tendons of the foot appear intact.

case_report: A 28-day-old female infant, the first child of non-consanguineous parents, was admitted to our hospital due to muscle weakness, neonatal seizures, and elevated serum very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs) levels on March 19, 2018. She was delivered vaginally at 38 weeks and 2 days of gestation, with a birth weight of 2.21 kg. At birth, she presented with generalized muscle weakness and feeding difficulties, and experienced a seizure with low oxygen saturation one day post-birth. Despite normal results from her newborn screening, including tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS), further metabolic evaluation for neonatal seizures showed elevated VLCFA levels: C26:0 was 11.47 μmol/L (normal range < 1.31 μmol/L); C24:0/C22:0 ratio was 2.21 (normal range < 1.39), and C26:0/C22:0 ratio was 0.5 (normal range < 0.023). Phytanic and pristanic acid levels were undetectable at 15 days of age. Physical examination revealed a high forehead, large anterior fontanel, midfacial underdevelopment, high-arched palate, low-set ears, and clubfoot.
test_results: The compound heterozygous mutations c.350A>T (p.Asp117Val) and c.836T>C (p.Phe279Ser), located in representative of 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency in HSD17B4 (NM_000414.3), were identified and inherited from the mother and father, respectively. The allele frequency of c.350A>T was 0.000109 in East Asian and c.836T>C have not reported yet.

case_report: A 1-day-old male infant was admitted to the Department of Neonatology at Yuying Children's Hospital Affiliated to Wenzhou Medical University in August 2020 due to shortness of breath and hypotonia for 1 day, along with convulsions for 8 hours. The infant was born at 39 weeks of gestation via cesarean section due to decreased fetal movement. There were no abnormalities in the placenta, umbilical cord, or amniotic fluid, and the Apgar scores were 8 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes (with deductions for respiration and muscle tone). The birth weight was 2,900 grams (25th percentile), and the length was 50 cm (25th-50th percentile). The infant's parents are non-consanguineous, and he has a healthy 11-year-old sister with no family history of genetic diseases. On the first day of life, the infant exhibited convulsions and hypotonia. The convulsions involved fist clenching, eye gazing, and cyanosis of the lips, lasting for 10 seconds and resolving spontaneously. During the interictal period, the infant was conscious but showed poor responses, including no spontaneous activity, no eye pursuit, and abnormal sucking and swallowing. Physical examination revealed craniofacial deformities, including a long head (158 mm), high forehead, wide eye distance, high arch of the palate, varus of both feet, and left cryptorchidism. Basic reflexes such as swallowing, sucking, and coughing were depressed. The patient received oxygen inhalation with a hood, nasogastric feeding with formula, phenobarbital injection for convulsions, intravenous fluid support, and other treatments. On the first day after admission, the patient had another convulsion with similar manifestations. The frequency of convulsions increased, and the infant's responsiveness did not improve. On the 9th day after birth, the patient experienced apnea due to sputum blockage and required tracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. On the 11th day, the patient developed a fever with elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and received anti-infection treatment. At 14 days old, the infant had frequent convulsions, and levetiracetam oral solution was administered and gradually increased, but the convulsions persisted. At 21 days old, midazolam injection was maintained for 1 week with a gradual increase in dose, but convulsions continued. At 22 days old, the levetiracetam dose was increased to 60 mg/kg/day. On day 28, the endotracheal tube was removed, and the patient was switched to hood oxygen support. At 35 days old, sodium valproate oral solution was introduced. Oxygen support was withdrawn at 40 days old. Antiepileptic therapy was adjusted during hospitalization with the assistance of a pediatric neurologist. At 42 days old, the infant continued to have more than 10 convulsions per day despite treatment with levetiracetam, topiramate tablets, and sodium valproate oral solution. The patient was discharged with medications after the family was trained in nasogastric feeding. At 5 months old, the child died at home due to food refusal and respiratory failure.
test_results: Two heterozygous mutations were monitored in the subject on gene HSD17B4 in 5q23.1. They are c.972+1G>T heterozygous mutation and c.727T>A heterozygous mutation. The splicing mutation c.972+1G>T is located in intron 12 and may lead to functional defects in hydratase unit; the non-synonymous single-nucleotide variant (SNV) mutation c.727T>A (p.W243R) is located in exon 10, resulting in changes in the short-chain dehydrogenase unit. Peripheral venous blood was collected from the proband's parents and sister for validation and source analysis by whole-exome sequencing. The results suggested that his father was a carrier of the c.972+1G>T mutation and his mother was a carrier of the c.727T>A (p.W243R) mutation. Thus, the patient contained a mixed heterozygous mutation in HSD17B4, including c.972+1G>T in the paternal allele and c.727T>A (p.W243R) in the maternal allele.

case_report: An 82-year-old Caucasian male presented to the hospital following a near-syncopal episode. He reported experiencing shortness of breath during physical activity over the past few weeks. His medical history includes hypertension, hypothyroidism, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and coronary artery disease with a history of coronary artery bypass grafting. Four weeks prior, he was treated for COVID-19 with remdesivir and low dose dexamethasone and was discharged after a three-day hospital stay. The night before his current presentation, he experienced a nosebleed and had noticed widespread bruising on his arms several days earlier. He denied any history of blood disorders. Upon admission, his vital signs were as follows: temperature 98.7°F, pulse rate 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 17 breaths per minute, blood pressure 141/63 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 89% on room air. Physical examination revealed extensive bruising on the upper extremities, scattered bruising on the lower extremities, some dried blood in the nostrils, and rales and rhonchi in the left lower lung lobe.
test_results: White blood cell count 7,430/mm3, hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL, platelet count 1,000/mm3, prothrombin time 10.0 seconds, international normalized ratio 1.01, activated partial thromboplastin time 29 seconds, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 99 mmol/L, carbon dioxide of 25 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 45 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.4 mg/dL.

case_report: A 66-year-old woman with no significant medical history reported a persistent fever that began two months prior to her initial presentation.
