She experienced weakness in her left limbs and was admitted to a city hospital for evaluation of fever and left-sided weakness. She was transferred to our hospital three weeks later for further assessment. Upon examination, her general condition was stable, except for an elevated body temperature of 38.0° Celsius. No lymph nodes were palpable. She did not report symptoms such as dry mouth, night sweats, or weight loss. The patient was alert with normal cognitive function. Physical examination revealed left-sided weakness (grade 4 on the Manual Muscle Strength Testing scale) with brisk deep tendon reflexes on both sides and extensor plantar responses. Sensory extinction was noted in her left limbs. Blood tests showed a slightly elevated C-reactive protein level (0.68 mg/dl) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (17 mm/h), along with a high titer of antinuclear antibodies (x1280, speckled pattern). Anti-SS-A and anti-Ro52 antibodies were positive, while the anti-SS-B antibody was negative. A lip biopsy showed no inflammation. Immunoblotting indicated IgG-k monoclonal gammopathy, but bone marrow histology revealed 10% proliferation of clonal plasma cells without light chain restriction, and no Bence-Jones protein was detected. Tumor markers were negative, and soluble interleukin-2 receptor (sIL-2R) levels were within the normal range. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed slight pleocytosis (11/μl; mature lymphocytes 94%, no atypical cells) with normal glucose and protein levels (73 mg/dl and 26 mg/dl, respectively). There were increases in both the IgG index (1.26) and interleukin 6 (29.4 pg/ml), but no increase in sIL-2R. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed hyperintense signals in the splenium of the corpus callosum and right-hemisphere dominant deep subcortical white matter without contrast enhancement. MR spectroscopy showed normal concentrations of choline, creatine, and N-acetyl aspartate. 123I-IMP single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) demonstrated increased blood flow in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem, while 201Tl-scintigraphy showed no abnormal accumulation in the brain. 67Ga-scintigraphy did not indicate systemic malignancy. The patient was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone (mPSL) pulse therapy (1 g over three days), which temporarily resolved her fever. Three months after the fever onset, she developed generalized tonic-clonic seizures (GTCS) that were unresponsive to antiepileptic medications. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) (0.4 g/kg over five days) was also ineffective. A follow-up brain MRI showed extensive lesions in the bilateral frontotemporal lobes.
test_results: The histopathological examination showed atypical lymphoid cells with enlarged round nuclei diffusely infiltrating the cortical gray and subcortical white matters. No necrosis was present, and mitotic figures were scant in number. Atypical cells were strongly labeled by antibodies for CD20, a B-cell marker. Additional immnunohistochemical studies revealed that tissue was positive for BCL-2, BCL-6 and MUM-1 but negative for CD5 and CD10.
diagnosis: Lymphomatosis cerebri  variant of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Orpha_name: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the central nervous system

case_report: A 28-year-old man presented with symptoms of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and a weight loss of 10 kg over a period of 4 months. His past medical history was unremarkable. On physical examination, there was mild tenderness in the epigastric region. Laboratory tests revealed mild iron-deficient anemia with a hemoglobin level of 11.6 g/dl, iron level of 19 µg/dl, and an iron binding capacity of 272 µg/dl. Gastroscopic examination identified an ulceroinfiltrating mass lesion with a fragile surface and deep exudations located in the third part of the duodenum.
test_results: Histopathologic examination of the biopsies showed small lymphocytes and histiocytes in the lamina propria with atypical morphology, together with large malignant cells having pleomorphic vesicular nuclei and prominent nucleoli. Immunohistochemical examination of neoplastic cells is as follow: CD20 (+), CD30 (+), CD3 (−), cytokeratin (−), PLAP (−), CD15 (−), EBV (−), LCA (+), LSP1 (+), and fascin (−).
Orpha_name: T-cell/histiocyte rich large B cell lymphoma

case_report: An 80-year-old female patient presented with weakness. Laboratory results showed white blood cell count of 24 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin level of 11.9 g/dL, and platelet count of 204 × 10^9/L. Peripheral smear indicated absolute lymphocytosis with mature morphology: neutrophils 22%, lymphocytes 64%, eosinophils 7%, basophils 0%, and monocytes 7%. Bone marrow aspiration revealed small mature lymphocytes accounting for 30% of nucleated cells. Immunohistochemical staining showed lymphoid cells positive for CD20 and CD23, and negative for CD10, cyclin D1, TDT, CD3, and CD5. The patient had been monitored for two years without medication. Two years later, she presented with malaise, fatigue, loss of appetite, 10 kg weight loss over three months, cough, sputum production, fever, and altered consciousness over the past month. Initial physical examination revealed confusion, tachypnea, and tachycardia. Lung examination showed decreased breath sounds in the basal parts. Abdominal examination revealed splenomegaly, with no peripheral lymphadenopathy. Laboratory results showed white blood cell count of 13 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin level of 8.9 g/dL, and platelet count of 58 × 10^9/L. Biochemical analysis indicated hyperglycemia (glucose: 242 mg/dL) and elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) at 412 U/L (normal range 0–248 U/L). Chest X-ray revealed homogenous density increases in the lower zones and consolidation areas in the right lower zone. Cranial CT was normal, while thorax CT showed a cavitary lesion measuring 2.9 × 3.5 × 3.1 cm in the superior segment of the right lower lobe, diffuse multiple nodular lesions in the lungs, and multiple mediastinal and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathies, the largest measuring 1.5 cm in diameter. Bronchoscopy was performed, and samples were taken for cultures and PCR for tuberculosis, candida, and other infections, all of which were negative. PET/CT revealed bilateral cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, mediastinal, and abdominal lymph nodes with SUVmax involvement between 4.5 and 10.5, a cavitary lesion in the superior segment of the right lower lobe with SUVmax 10.3, and a consolidated mass in the lower lobe of the left lung with SUVmax 19.1.
test_results: In the pathological examination of the transbronchial biopsy from cavitary lesion wall, infiltration composed of large, atypical lymphoid cells, which formed scattered, small groups among the small lymphoid cells were observed. Atypical lymphoid cells made up less than 10% of T cells in the ground. In the immunohistochemical staining, CD20, MUM-1, CD30, and PAX5 were positive in the atypical lymphoid cells. Staining with CD3 and CD5 in small, mature T lymphocytes was observed.
diagnosis: T cell rich, large B-cell lymphoma
Orpha_name: T-cell/histiocyte rich large B cell lymphoma

case_report: A 45-year-old male presented with abdominal swelling and generalized weakness. His medical history included diabetes mellitus and alcoholic chronic liver disease. An abdominal ultrasonogram revealed significant enlargement of the spleen and mild enlargement of the liver, with no notable intra-abdominal lymph node enlargement. Routine blood tests showed a total leukocyte count of 300×10^9/L. A peripheral blood smear examination identified atypical lymphocytes with numerous finger-like projections. A bone marrow aspirate showed 79% atypical lymphoid cells with inconspicuous nucleoli and circumferential hairy-like projections. The TRAP (tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase) stain was negative. Flow cytometric analysis indicated negativity for CD103, CD123, and Annexin-A1.
test_results: The BM trephine biopsy confirmed an intrasinusoidal and interstitial infiltrate of atypical lymphoid cells highlighted by CD20 and DBA-44, and non-reactive for CD5, CD23 and Annexin-A1 immunostaining. Histological examination showed a tumor growing diffusely in the red pulp sinuses and cords with extensive obliteration of the splenic white pulp. Tumor cells were monotonous, small and round with smooth nuclear contours, inconspicuous nucleoli, and scant cytoplasm. Mitotic activity was also inconspicuous. IHC showed diffuse positivity for CD20, PAX-5, CD79a and DBA-44 with a low MIB-1 proliferation index of 2% to 4%. The tumor cells were negative for CD3, CD25, Cyclin-D1, CD123 and Annexin-A1. Cytogenetic analysis also did not reveal any of the known mutations associated with SMZL, HCL and HCL-V.
diagnosis: splenic diffuse red pulp small B-cell lymphoma
Orpha_name: splenic diffuse red pulp small B-cell lymphoma

case_report: A 29-year-old female with a seven-year history of an enlarged spleen, no signs of portal hypertension, and chronic non-replicating hepatitis B virus infection (AntiHbC total positive, AntiHbe positive, AgHbe negative, AgHbs positive, AntiHbs negative) with a quantitative PCR for HBV showing less than 20 IU/ml (normal range: 20-170,000,000 IU/ml) presented with worsening spleen enlargement and symptoms including fever, night sweats, and weight loss over the past two months. Laboratory results revealed hemoglobin at 8.1 g/dl, platelets at 80 × 10^9/l, and white blood cells at 12 × 10^9/l, with 85% atypical lymphoid cells.
test_results: Immunophenotyping demonstrated strong expression of CD45, positivity for the B-cell antigens CD20 and CD19, weak expression of CD25, partial expression of CD23 and CD200 and negativity for CD11c and CD103. Monoclonality for kappa light chain Ig was demonstrated in both the peripheral blood and bone marrow. The karyotype was complex, with structural abnormalities in the 14q32 region, deletions on chromosomes 6 and 7, isochromosomes 8 and 17 and trisomy 18. Fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis revealed an extra copy of the MYC gene and a p53 deletion. FDG-PET-CT showed splenomegaly (standard uptake value [SUV]: 6.1), hepatomegaly (SUV: 3.2), abdominal lymph node enlargement (SUV: 6.3) and cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. The spleen dimensions were 33.0 x 20.6 x 7.5 cm. The spleen showed infiltration by small to intermediate-sized mature lymphoid cells, with large cells among them, primarily in the red pulp and sinusoidal space of the spleen and secondarily in the white pulp of the spleen. Immunohistochemical analysis showed expression of CD20 and DBA44, with Ki67 of 40%. The cells were negative for CD5, CD10, CD23, CD3 and cyclin D1. A hepatic biopsy demonstrated nodular lymphoid infiltrate involvement. A hilum splenic lymph node (measuring 2.6 x 1.1 x 1.0 cm) showed lymphoid neoplasia of mature cells with predominance of intermediate to large cells with a nodular pattern.
diagnosis: splenic diffuse red-pulp small B-cell lymphoma
Orpha_name: Splenic diffuse red pulp small B-cell lymphoma

case_report: An 88-year-old man was admitted with several days of gross hematuria. He had a history of invasive bladder cancer and had undergone radical cystectomy and ileal neobladder reconstruction 17 years prior. The patient did not report any other symptoms such as fever, night sweats, weight loss, or fatigue. He had no history of inflammatory bowel disease and was not on immunosuppressant medication. Initial imaging with computed tomography (CT) scan revealed an enhancing lesion on the dome and posterior wall of the neobladder with mucosal thickening, along with multiple enlarged retroperitoneal lymph nodes, including paraaortic, aortocaval, retrocaval, right common iliac, and ileocolic mesenteric lymph nodes, measuring up to 4 cm. Multiple metallic clips from the previous neobladder surgery were noted in the pelvic cavity but were distant from the mass lesion. Cystoscopy showed a diffuse, sessile mucosal lesion on the dome and posterior wall, consistent with the CT findings. Colonoscopy revealed normal colonic mucosa without any definite mass formation or abnormal vasculature. Positron emission tomography (PET)–CT scan showed a hypermetabolic irregular mass measuring about 6.7 cm in length at the dome and posterior wall of the neobladder, with enlarged hypermetabolic retrocrural, retrocaval, paraaortic, aortocaval, right common iliac, and ileocolic lymph nodes measuring up to 4 cm in diameter. No specific radiologic abnormalities were noted in other organs. The patient underwent transurethral resection under general anesthesia for the mucosal lesion on the ileal neobladder. The mass lesion was too hard to be obtained by biopsy forceps, so it was resected using a bipolar resectoscope at multiple sites. The surgery was uneventful without neobladder perforation. The biopsied samples of the ileal neobladder consisted of several fragments of soft tissue measuring 2×1×1 cm in aggregates.
test_results: Microscopic examination revealed different histology in each fragment. The severity of infiltration with CD20-positive atypical B lymphocytes was variable from diffuse infiltrates to focal aggregates. The neoplastic cells had large nuclei, prominent nucleoli, irregular nuclear membranes, and scant cytoplasm. Angioinvasion by atypical lymphocytes with intravascular thrombosis was noted with high EBV-encoded small RNA 1 and 2 (EBER) positivity. The EBER positivity was prominent near ulcerated mucosa and perivascular area. The CD20-positive atypical lymphocytes showed the non-germinal center immunophenotype with negative reaction to CD10, BCL6, but positive reaction to multiple myeloma oncogen-1 with Ki-67 index over 40%. Patchy CD30 positivity of 10% and scattered p53 positivity of 40% were also noted. The chronic inflammation area was noted in a patchy manner within ileal tissue with focal epithelioid histiocytic reaction resembling granuloma and CD3-positive T cells. Blood tests for EBV antibodies showed that IgG for EBV viral capsid antigen (EBV-VCA) and IgG for Epstein-Barr nuclear antigen were positive, but IgM for EBV-VCA and IgM/IgG for EBV early antigen diffuse and restricted were not detected. EBV DNA was not found in the blood by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay. Bone marrow study showed no lymphomatous lesion.
diagnosis: Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma associated with chronic inflammation
Orpha_name: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with chronic inflammation

case_report: A 75-year-old female experienced hypogammaglobulinemia due to prolonged steroid treatment for Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD). Twenty-seven years prior, she underwent a left-sided mastectomy with adjuvant hormonal therapy for an invasive breast carcinoma of no special type (NST), followed by bilateral prosthetic reconstruction using textured implants. Nineteen years later, she had a bilateral capsulectomy and prosthesis replacement due to bilateral Baker grade IV capsular contracture and leakage. The capsulectomy specimen was evaluated radiologically and histologically, confirming implant rupture. Eight years after this procedure, she presented with a rapidly enlarging palpable mass in the right breast and reported a 5 kg weight loss, but no other B-symptoms.
test_results: Clinical examination and imaging studies confirmed a tumoral mass at the upper-external quadrant of the right breast, in close contact with the implant with a layer of fluid surrounding the implant. There were no lymphadenopathies nor other suspicious PET-positive lesions. LDH level was highly elevated (587 U/L) and there was mild inflammation (CRP 25.8 mg/L). An EBV viral load of 14,747 IU/ml was detected in the peripheral blood. Cytological examination of the peri-prosthetic fluid identified the presence of an atypical lymphoid cell population, that could not be observed in a cytological specimen of the right axillary lymph node. A core needle biopsy (CNB) of the mass was performed under ultrasound-guidance, which was partially necrotic and showed a diffuse infiltrate of large, atypical cells. Apoptotic cells and mitotic figures were frequently observed but no diagnostic hallmark cells were identified. The large atypical cells strongly expressed CD30, CD20 and were positive on EBER in situ hybridization (EBER ish), and CD3 was only expressed in small reactive T-cells.
diagnosis: Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma  associated with chronic inflammation
Orpha_name: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with chronic inflammation

case_report: The patient is a male infant, aged 31 weeks and 1 day, presenting with jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools that began 2 weeks prior. He was born at 40 weeks of gestational age, weighing 3600 g, with no history of neonatal jaundice or other comorbid conditions. The mother had gestational diabetes managed exclusively with diet. Baseline biochemical tests indicated cholestatic syndrome. Serology for cytomegalovirus was negative. An abdominal ultrasound at hospital admission revealed an enlarged liver with slightly heterogeneous parenchyma, a distended gallbladder, and dilatation of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic systems. At 37 weeks and 1 day old, the infant underwent exploratory laparotomy, which revealed a gallbladder with a thin and distended wall, adherence of the intestinal loops to the hilum of the liver, and an indurated, fibrotic, extrahepatic bile duct system.
test_results: Transoperative cholangiography showed that there was failure to fill at the junction of the hepatic ducts and a lack of drainage to the small intestine.

case_report: Patient_22, a male child, was admitted at 1 year and 8 months old due to difficulty standing. The mother had two pregnancies and two births, with the boy having a healthy 4-year-old sister. During early pregnancy, there was a need for fetus preservation due to bleeding. He was born at 32 weeks via normal vaginal delivery, weighing 3.3 kg. The child could sit and turn over at 8 months and began speaking at 1 year and 6 months but was unable to stand independently. He exhibited a preference for shaking his head while talking. No similar features were reported in other family members. Physical examination revealed skull asymmetry and a head circumference of 48 cm. There were delays in intelligence, motor, and language development, hemifacial hypertrophy on the right side, facial asymmetry, a high forehead, hypertelorism, downturned corners of the mouth, strabismus, drooling, and protruding ears. Facial ultrasound indicated thickening of the subcutaneous fat layer and abnormalities in subcutaneous and muscular tissue. Multiple bulging masses were observed on the back, with ultrasound confirming subcutaneous fat layer thickening. Slight pectus excavatum and lower limb asymmetry were noted, with the right leg being approximately 0.5 cm larger than the left leg. The child had pes planus, and the second toe crossed over the third toe on the right foot. A head MRI revealed multiple punctiform and patchy high signals on FLAIR sequences, demyelination in bilateral frontal and parietal white matter, and a thick corpus callosum.
test_results: Trio-WES demonstrated a hemizygous variant of c.256G>A,p.Glu86Lys (NM_153252) in BRWD3. The variant was inherited from his mother and was validated by Sanger sequencing.

case_report: The patient is a 23-year-old man with severe intellectual disability, born to consanguineous parents who are second cousins. His mother experienced five miscarriages before his birth and has one healthy son. The pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. During the first two years, the patient had normal development in speech, motor function, and social interactions, despite recurrent upper airway infections. However, he later experienced a global decline, losing previously acquired skills, particularly in language, and developed severe aggressive behavioral issues, making normal contact difficult. At age 3, he was evaluated at a specialized outpatient department for child and adolescent psychiatry. One year later, he was referred to a child neurology clinic for developmental regression. Physical and neurological examinations revealed no abnormalities or dysmorphisms. Laboratory tests, including MRI brain scans, were normal. Over the years, further genetic, neurological, metabolic, ophthalmological, and dermatological examinations, as well as a second MRI under general anesthesia, were conducted, all showing no abnormalities. Due to aggressive behavior and temper tantrums, he attended an activity center for people with intellectual disabilities, where various short-term pharmacological treatments were attempted but discontinued due to increased disinhibited and aggressive behaviors or motor side effects. Persistent sleep disturbances, intermittent urine incontinence, and diarrhea were noted. At age 12, he was referred for specialized neuropsychiatric evaluation. Behavioral observation indicated ritualistic, stereotyped, and autistic traits with mood instability, requiring structured individual guidance. He could not read, write, calculate, or tell time. Physical and neurological examinations showed no abnormalities, and relevant haematological and biochemical parameters were normal. He communicated using simple sentences, body language, and pictorial signs. Developmental age scores on the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scale (VABS) were 19 months for communication, 42 months for motor skills, 11 months for socialization, and 24 months for daily activities, indicating severe intellectual disability. At that time, he was treated with homeopathic compounds, including a very low dose of promethazine, and 0.4 mg haloperidol twice daily for behavioral control. Single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) array analysis showed no abnormalities. At age 14, he developed severe headache, vomiting, neck flexion, urine incontinence, and unstable gait, leading to the discontinuation of haloperidol. Multiple brain imaging revealed a brain tumor in the posterior fossa. He underwent a fossa posterior craniotomy, and a benign right-sided cerebellar hemangioblastoma was successfully removed. Genetic testing excluded Neurofibromatosis type I and Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. Post-surgery, he returned to his premorbid level of functioning without neurological symptoms and continued his structured activity program. Severe sleep problems, intermittent urine incontinence, and diarrhea persisted. To improve sleep, 2 mg zuclopenthixol was prescribed. No significant changes in behavior were expected, so neuropsychiatric consultation was not requested.
test_results: Trio-based exome sequencing demonstrated a homozygous pathogenic nonsense variant in the first exon of the HNMT gene (g.138722149C>T:NM_006895.2:c.88C>T(p.Gln30*)) leading to a premature stop codon, which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Both parents were shown to be heterozygous carrier of this variant.

case_report: A 60-year-old female patient reported experiencing pain in the gluteal area. She had no history of trauma and no other systemic illnesses were noted. Imaging of the thigh in the anterior-posterior view revealed a linear calcification in the left thigh. Laboratory tests showed that serum calcium, phosphorus, parathormone, and alkaline phosphatase levels were all within normal ranges.
test_results: Tc-99m MDP whole body bone scintigraphy revealed an increased uptake with a heterogenic character, in the bilateral gluteal and thigh regions. SPECT/CT of thigh showing increased uptake localized to the linear soft tissue calcification in the thigh.
Orpha_name: Familial hyperphosphatemic tumoral calcinosis/Hyperphosphatemic hyperostosis syndrome

case_report: A 60-year-old woman presented with back pain without neurological deficits and no history of trauma. Her medical history included hypertension, dyslipidemia, and dependence on benzodiazepines and alcohol. She had no familial history. She was admitted for further evaluation due to elevated white blood cell count (10,400/mm3) and C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration (10.7 mg/dL). Chest and abdominal computed tomography (CT) scans did not show any inflammatory lesions. Thoracic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed low intensity in the T10 vertebral body on both T2- and T1-weighted images, and a small epidural mass at the T9 dorsal side of the central canal, which was hyperintense on T2-weighted images and isointense to hyperintense on T1-weighted images. Conservative therapy was initiated, and her laboratory results improved without antibiotic therapy. She was discharged 15 days later. Two months post-discharge, her back pain worsened after a fall, and she developed leg paralysis. She visited another hospital and was subsequently transferred back for surgical treatment. Physical examination showed a body temperature of 36.7°C, blood pressure of 172/102 mmHg, and a heart rate of 119 in sinus rhythm. Neurological examination revealed complete paraplegia and numbness in both lower limbs, graded as B on the American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) Impairment Scale. Her white blood cell count was 17,200/mm3 and CRP concentration was 18.6 mg/dL. The calcium × phosphate product concentration was within the normal range. Thoracic MRI showed high intensity in the T10 vertebral body on T2-weighted images and low intensity on T1-weighted images, with an enlarged epidural mass at the T9 dorsal side of the central canal, which was low intensity on both T2- and T1-weighted images. The mass compressed the spinal cord at this level. CT demonstrated a T10 burst fracture and a cavity in the vertebral body, with increased density of the epidural mass near the T9/T10 facet joint. Bone mineral density measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry at the lumbar spine and proximal femur was 93% and 85% of young adult means, respectively. Laboratory data indicated signs of infection. Decompression surgery without fixation was performed, including T9–T11 laminectomy. The yellow ligament was present, but epidural fat was unclear, indicating inflammation. No obvious pus was found, and soft tissue culture results were negative. The epidural mass was attached to the dura mater, detached, and removed.
test_results: Histopathological examination of this mass revealed a multifocal massive deposition of calcified amorphous material.
Orpha_name: Familial hyperphosphatemic tumoral calcinosis/Hyperphosphatemic hyperostosis syndrome

case_report: A 56-year-old female with a history of primary biliary cirrhosis presented with pruritus, fatigue, jaundice, and refractory ascites. She experienced cognitive decline over one month, leading to a leave of absence from her job as a business executive. Her medical history included arterial hypertension, gastroesophageal reflux, and cervicogenic headaches. She was on diuretics, lactulose 10 ml TID, sodium benzoate 3g OD, metronidazole 250 mg BID, calcium carbonate 500 mg BID, and ursodiol 500 mg BID. Risperidone 1 mg OD and quetiapine 50 mg HS were added after the onset of neuropsychiatric symptoms. A review found no correlation between her behavioral changes and the medications. Laboratory results at admission showed albumin 34 g/L (N= 37-48 g/L), ammonia 20 mcg/dl (N= 15-45 mcg/dl), GGT 331 UI/L (N= 7-55 UI/L), ALT 74 U/L (N=9-30 U/L), AST 74 U/L (N=13-39 U/L), alkaline phosphatase 565 UI/L (N=36-110 UI/L), and INR 1.1. She exhibited personality changes, psychomotor agitation, elevated mood, incongruous affect, ideoaffective discordance, tangential and logorrheic speech, and slightly decreased judgment, while maintaining intact orientation and insight. Her MOCA score was 17/30, indicating global cortical impairment. Neuroleptics improved her disorganization, perseveration, and hallucinations. Neurological examination was unremarkable, with no ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus, areflexia, gait instability, or primitive reflexes. Despite PRN doses of olanzapine and haloperidol managing her agitation, she remained significantly disorganized. Lithium and regular doses of olanzapine were introduced without success. A biopsy confirmed Child-Pugh class C liver cirrhosis.
test_results: A brain MRI featured bilateral basal ganglia hyperintensities.

case_report: A 40-year-old male with no known comorbid conditions arrived at the emergency department reporting slurred speech and left facial weakness lasting eight days. He also experienced heaviness of the tongue and difficulty swallowing, leading to drooling from the left side of his mouth. The symptoms were stable, with no additional neurological or systemic issues noted. His medical and surgical history was unremarkable. He mentioned working as a steel welder for seven years without consistently using personal protective equipment or a filtering face mask. On physical examination, he appeared slightly anxious but was vitally stable and not in apparent distress. Findings included left-sided upper motor neuron facial weakness and spastic dysarthria, while higher mental functions were normal. Other cranial nerves were intact, and there were no significant abnormalities in strength, coordination, sensation, gait, or the autonomic system. Laboratory tests conducted before admission were normal. An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm without notable abnormalities. A computed tomography scan of the brain revealed ill-defined hypodensities in the basal ganglia, with no signs of hemorrhage or ischemic infarction. The patient was admitted to the stroke unit with a National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score of 4 for further evaluation. He was administered a prophylactic dose of aspirin 75 mg, intravenous fluids, and a mashed diet.
test_results: A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was done on the following day, which showed bilateral signal alteration in the form of T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensities involving the globus pallidus and corticospinal tract, extending superoinferiorly from the corona radiata to the cerebral peduncles of the midbrain, more extensive on the right side. The basal ganglia and cortical gray matter were relatively spared, and no restricted diffusion was noted.

case_report: The patient is a 49-year-old Caucasian male with a primary school education. He has a long history of working as a metalworker and welder. His medical history includes mild hypertension, managed with 25 mg of hydrochlorothiazide daily. He was referred due to experiencing paranoid ideation, thoughts of reference, sleep disturbances, and unusual behaviors. He was initially treated with 2 mg of risperidone daily, which led to a gradual reduction in these symptoms over two weeks, allowing the dose to be decreased to 1 mg daily. Physical and neurological examinations showed no abnormalities. Routine blood tests, including hemoglobin, lipoprotein profile, and fasting glucose, were all within normal limits. Tests for Borrelia and lues were negative. A systematic evaluation ruled out the use of medications, over-the-counter preparations, and illicit drugs. There was no personal or family history of psychiatric conditions.
test_results: MRI scanning of the brain demonstrated high T1 signal intensity of the globus pallidus bilaterally. The serum concentration of Mn was increased (52 to 97 nmol/L, reference values: 7 to 20 nmol/L).
diagnosis: Apathy syndrome caused by chronic overexposure to manganese

case_report: The patient is a 40-year-old male who presented with memory loss. On April 9, 2019, he visited a local hospital with symptoms including tremor, involuntary urination, and incoherent speech. On April 1, 2019, he experienced disorientation while driving on a familiar road to work, resulting in a minor car accident, and he could not recall the details of the incident. These symptoms appeared 2–3 days following the accident. He reported intermittent headaches and memory loss over the past 5 years. His medical history includes being an ex-smoker with a 10 pack-year history and heavy alcohol consumption, averaging 8–10 bottles of soju per week for approximately 15 years. There is no relevant family history of brain disorders. Both the patient and his wife confirmed that there were no external circumstances outside of his workplace that could lead to poisoning from toxic substances. A review of his medical records and the history from the Korean National Health Insurance Service over the past 10 years showed no evidence of acute poisoning from toxic substances, except for exposure to CO2 arc welding at his workplace. The patient also reported experiencing difficulty breathing during welding operations due to several enclosed spaces in the workplace.
test_results: The T2 weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) images showed lesions with high signal intensity in the bilateral globus pallidus. Subtle high signal intensity lesions were also seen in the bilateral cerebral white matter. An approximately 3-mm vascular outpouching lesion was suspected in the anterior communicating artery from the images, with mild stenosis in the mid portion of the basilar artery. Multifocal acute infarction in the centrum semiovales, parietal lobes, and occipital lobes bilaterally. Both the size and shape of the ventricle were normal. No brain atrophy or abnormalities in the brain parenchyma were noted. A mild cerebral dysfunction was observed.
Orpha_name: Delayed encephalopathy due to carbon monoxide poisoning

case_report: A 60-year-old woman with a history of major depression attempted suicide by burning charcoal in a closed room 3 weeks prior to admission. She was found unconscious and transported to a nearby hospital, where she regained full consciousness within 1 day under high-flow oxygen therapy. She was discharged without any medications. One week before admission, she began experiencing cognitive impairment, behavioral changes, unsteady gait, and urinary incontinence. Her family also noted restlessness and involuntary limb movements. Upon admission to our hospital, she was alert but unable to obey or understand commands. Her vital signs were as follows: blood pressure 128/84 mmHg, heart rate 79 bpm, respiration rate 18 breaths/min, and body temperature 36.5˚C. Pupil light reflexes and eye movements were normal. She exhibited akinetic mutism, limb rigidity, and a short-stepped gait. Deep tendon reflexes were normal, muscle strength in the limbs was Medical Research Council Grade 4, and Babinski's sign was absent. She had persistent, rapid, irregular, involuntary choreic movements of the whole body, which were not present during sleep. Blood studies, including biochemistry, endocrine, and autoimmune tests, were normal.
test_results: Electroencephalography showed a poorly sustained alpha background and generalized slow waves, predominantly at the bilateral fronto-temporal lobes. T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed bilateral, symmetric, confluent areas of high signal intensity in the periventricular, subcortical white matter, corona radiata, centrum semiovale and globus pallidus. Diffusion-weighted MRI and the corresponding apparent diffusion coefficient map showed restricted water diffusion at the periventricular white matter, corona radiata, and centrum semiovale. Brain single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) with technetium-99 ethylene cysteine dimer showed inhomogeneous perfusion in the cerebral cortex, with decreased uptake in bilateral frontal regions. Uptake in bilateral basal ganglia and the thalamus was normal.
diagnosis: Delayed encephalopathy after acute carbon monoxide intoxication
Orpha_name: Delayed encephalopathy due to carbon monoxide poisoning

case_report: A 39-year-old man with a history of opium and amphetamine use for several years presented with loss of consciousness and fever. He had been admitted to the intensive care unit in another hospital a month prior due to methadone overdose, rhabdomyolysis, and acute renal failure, and was discharged with a normal level of consciousness. A week after discharge, he exhibited symptoms including delusion and loss of consciousness. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis and other tests showed results within normal ranges. Upon admission to our hospital, he was febrile, aphasic, unconscious, and unresponsive to painful stimuli. Laboratory studies revealed white blood cells: 9800/mm3, hemoglobin: 10.4 g/dl, platelets: 239000/mm3, creatinine: 1.1 mg/dl, sodium: 142 mEq/L, potassium: 4.3 mEq/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 16 mm/hr, and C-reactive protein: 1. Thyroid and liver function tests, vasculitis tests, antibodies for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis C virus, and hepatitis B surface antigen were all within normal limits. CSF smear, culture, herpes simplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and autoimmune encephalitis panel were negative with normal analysis. Serum HIV RNA PCR was negative. Serum vitamin B12 and folate levels were normal.
test_results: The EEG result revealed a generalized slowing pattern.
Orpha_name: Delayed encephalopathy due to carbon monoxide poisoning

case_report: An 8-month-old boy, born to consanguineous parents, presented with persistent seizures and significant developmental delays. Physical examination revealed a small head size with overlapping sutures, a small jaw, a large right ear, and a narrow forehead. Eye examination showed dislocated lenses. Brain ultrasound indicated widespread brain tissue loss, mild softening of brain tissue, and enlarged brain ventricles.
test_results: Uric acid results demonstrated a hypouricaemic hypouricosuric pattern. Sulfocysteine, xanthine and hypoxanthine were elevated in urine.
Orpha_name: Sulfite oxidase deficiency due to molybdenum cofactor deficiency type C

case_report: A 17-year-old female presented with a 7-month history of intermittent swelling in the lower extremities, protein in the urine, and blood in the urine. A renal biopsy conducted at another hospital 4 months prior suggested possible IgA nephropathy, and she was treated with the angiotensin receptor blocker valsartan, but her symptoms persisted. She had no history of drug use, infections, malignancy, or family history of hepatitis B or C, HIV, rheumatic disease, or tumors. She was normotensive, and both general physical and funduscopic examinations were normal. Her lung fields were clear without rales or fremitus. A 24-hour urine protein test showed a total protein level of 2.75 g. Urinalysis revealed 24 erythrocytes per high-power field. Serum levels of urea, creatinine, and albumin were within normal ranges. Autoantibody tests were unremarkable, and serum antiphospholipase A2 receptor antibodies were negative. Renal ultrasound findings were normal. A review of the previous renal biopsy showed 22 glomeruli, with 1 (4.5%) showing global sclerosis and 1 (4.5%) showing focal segmental sclerosis. There was mild mesangial expansion, thickening of the glomerular basement membrane, endothelial swelling, focally swollen podocytes, and hypercellularity. Swelling of the tubular epithelium and patchy infiltration of lymphocytes and monocytes in the interstitial area were noted, without interstitial fibrosis. The capillary walls in the interstitial area showed no lesions. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed granular deposits along the capillary walls for IgM, C3, C1q, and kappa and lambda light chains, with mild staining for IgG and IgA. IgG subclass staining showed segmental positivity for IgG1 but negativity for IgG2, IgG3, IgG4, and antiphospholipase A2 receptor. Granular deposits along the capillary walls, especially for lambda and C1q, indicated immune complexes. Silver staining showed spike-like projections at the 3-o'clock position, indicating a spiked glomerular basement membrane around the immune complexes. Masson staining showed scattered fuchsinophilic deposits, indicating immune complexes. The lesions of mesangial cells, endothelial cells, and podocytes were noted. Lupus nephritis was excluded due to the absence of systemic lupus manifestations and negative immunoserological markers except for an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:100. No solid tumors or hematological malignancies were detected by computed tomography or hematological examinations, and all tumor biomarkers were negative.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed compound heterozygous mutations of MMACHC (NM_015506). The proband was a compound heterozygote for two transitions: one in exon 1 (chr1:45966084, c.80A>G) and the other in exon 4 (chr1:45974520, c.482G>A) of MMACHC. These predicted p.Gln27Arg and p.Arg161Gln missense changes at the amino acid level.
diagnosis: Secondary Membranous Nephropathy due to Cobalamin C Disease
Orpha_name: Vitamin B12-responsive methylmalonic acidemia, type cblDv2

case_report: A 14-year-old male presented to the neurogenetics outpatient clinic in a wheelchair, with a history of progressive disabilities over eight years. He was born at full term via vaginal delivery without complications. At six years old, he developed tremors in his right hand during activities such as writing or eating. By age seven, the tremors worsened, and he exhibited a staggering gait and slow reactions. Concurrently, he experienced speech difficulties, including slurred pronunciation and slow speech. At nine years old, he developed difficulty swallowing and occasionally coughed while drinking water. His speech and coordination issues continued to deteriorate, requiring assistance for walking. At age 12, he began experiencing painful walking spasms, increased ataxia, and more severe speech difficulties, with occasional falls. He also became irritable, cried frequently, sweated excessively at the extremities, and developed urinary incontinence. An MRI scan performed at a local hospital revealed cerebellar atrophy. He was treated with vitamins and neuroprotective drugs without symptom improvement. His parents are non-consanguineous and in good health.
test_results: The whole exome sequencing (WES) data showed that this boy had a known point variation (c.1509-26G > A, rs201580118) and a novel copy number variation (CNV) variant (chr5: g.74012742_74052694del) in HEXB. The results were further confirmed by Sanger sequencing and CNV analysis, indicating he inherited the rs201580118 variant from his mother and the CNV variant from his father. The point variation in HEXB c.1509-26G > A was considered as pathogenic/likely pathogenic according to ClinVar database. Another CNV variant chr5: g.74012742_74052694del contained a part of two coding genes HEXB and GFM2. It covered from the 9th intron of HXEB gene to the 5th intron of GFM2 gene, which was not reported in the Decipher syndrome, ClinVar and gnomAD databases. The patient had a fragment deletion in HEXB inherited from his father and a maternal c. 1509-26G > A variation of HEXB, which fell within the paternal fragment deletion region of HEXB. demonstrating a homozygous form in Sanger sequencing, although it should be attributed to a compound heterozygous variation of HEXB in this patient. Results showed that leukocytic HEXA&B and HEXA actives of this patient were decreased by 92.4% and 21.7% compared to the low limit of normal ranges, which were 75.4-158.6nmol/mg/h and 54.5-140.3nmol/mg/min.

case_report: Case 1 involves a 19-year-old woman. She was born at 37 weeks gestation with a birth weight of 2890 g, length of 47 cm, and a head circumference of 32 cm. Both pre- and neonatal periods were normal. At 5 months of age, she experienced her first seizure, which was prolonged and febrile. Subsequently, she developed afebrile focal seizures and intractable generalized seizures, including myotonic, tonic, and tonic-clonic types. She has had multiple episodes of convulsive status epilepticus. Her early development was initially typical; she developed normal hand function, including a pincer grip, and used up to 15 words. She began walking independently at 17 months. However, from around 15 months, her developmental progress slowed, and she gradually lost previously acquired skills. She ceased using her hands, lost her spoken words, and her gait became broad-based and ataxic. She developed midline rubbing hand movements, bruxism, breath-holding spells, and occasional hyperventilation. Her sleep was disrupted with nighttime screaming and occasional laughing spells. Between one and two years of age, she exhibited autistic traits and experienced a deceleration in head growth from the 50th to the 10th percentile. At 19 years old, clinical examination showed intense eye contact, ongoing stereotypic hand movements with hand dyspraxia, a broad-based gait with notable ataxia, breath-holding, and teeth grinding. She was 141 cm tall with normal weight for her height. Her musculature was generally hypotonic, and she had a slight scoliosis. Despite intensive anti-epileptic treatment, she continued to have daily seizures (focal, tonic, and tonic-clonic). CT and MRI scans of the brain were unremarkable.
test_results: SCN1A was Sanger sequenced and this disclosed the novel splice variant NG_011906.1:g.76169G > C, (NM_001165963.2): c.4284 + 1G > C. This variant was scored as pathogenic. Parental testing indicated that the mutation was de novo.
diagnosis: Rett syndrome  associated with a de novo mutation in SCN1A

case_report: D. S., a 4-year-old female, was admitted with symptoms including repeated vomiting and lethargy, accompanied by two episodes of fever reaching 39°C within the 36 hours prior to admission. Her medical history noted a recent episode of chickenpox in the past month. Physical examination identified painful hepatomegaly, with the liver margin extending 4.5 cm below the costal arch, and a tendency towards drowsiness.
test_results: Laboratory tests revealed hypertransaminasemia (AST/ALT = 12500/9500 U/L), increased serum LDH (28000 U/L), hyperammonemia (150 μg/L), leukopenia (White Blood Cells = 1500/mm3), mild thrombocytopenia (Platelets = 120000/mm3) and severe deficiency of coagulation factors (Prothrombin Activity <15%). The CSF analysis, the culture tests and the serologies for hepatitis A, B and C, CMV and EBV were negative. The EEG record found mild diffuse alterations (theta waves and rare medium voltage delta waves) and liver ultrasound showed a probable steatosis (liver of increased size and inhomogeneous structure, brighter than normal).

case_report: A 7-year-old boy from the countryside of Maranhão, northeastern Brazil, was admitted to the PICU with a 6-day history of fever, headache, vomiting, maculopapular rash, severe abdominal pain, conjunctival hyperemia, photophobia, raspberry tongue, hyperemia with lip desquamation, right cervical lymphadenomegaly, and edema. He also exhibited mild tachypnea without respiratory symptoms in normal room air. Upon admission, a fluorescence immunoassay for SARS-CoV-2 showed reagent immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies with titers >30.0 AU/mL (normal, <1.4 AU/mL) and nonreactive immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibodies with a titer of 0.1 AU (normal, <1.1 AU). The mother reported flu-like symptoms in the child one month prior. Laboratory tests indicated inflammatory responses: C-reactive protein at 96 mg/dL, lymphopenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, hypoalbuminemia (2.3 g/dL), hypertriglyceridemia (262 mg/dL), and elevated levels of transaminases, ferritin (1,812 ng/mL), d-dimer (8,500 ng/mL), and troponin (0.26 ng/mL). The patient's blood type was O positive. Serology tests for dengue IgG and IgM and anti-HIV were nonreactive. Serology tests for toxoplasmosis, cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, herpes simplex 1 and 2, and rubella were negative. Blood and urine cultures showed no bacterial growth. Real-time PCR of nasopharyngeal swabs for influenza A, influenza B, and respiratory syncytial virus were undetectable, as were PCR tests of nasopharyngeal and rectal samples for SARS-CoV-2. The patient had normal C3, C4, and CH50 serum complement levels. Other test results included negative direct Coombs, normal reticulocytes, and a normal simple urine test. Chest CT scan revealed moderate bilateral pleural effusion with fissure thickening on the right, interlobular septa thickening, mild infectious/inflammatory opacity, and mild pericardial effusion. Abdominal CT scan showed diffuse subcutaneous tissue edema and large amounts of free fluids in the abdominal and pelvic cavities. Transthoracic echocardiogram indicated aneurysmal dilation of the right coronary and left main coronary arteries. The patient received intensive support, including antimicrobials (ceftriaxone, oxacillin, and azithromycin) and intravenous human albumin. Treatment also included a single IVIG dose of 2 g/kg by continuous infusion over 10 hours and ASA, initially at an oral anti-inflammatory dose of 80 mg/kg per day (every 6 hours) until the child was afebrile for 48 hours, then reduced to a maintenance dose of 5 mg/kg per day as an antiplatelet agent due to coronary dilations. Two weeks after IVIG and ASA administration, while still hospitalized, the patient experienced a seizure crisis, a lowered level of consciousness, and eventually coma. He was intubated and managed with neuroprotective and anticonvulsant measures. The patient also had increased liver enzymes.
test_results: Laboratory tests showed significant liver function damage and an ammonia level of 150 μmol/L. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was collected with a cell count of 6/mm3, normal protein (33.9 mg/dL), and normal glucose (66.32 mg/dL). Other results included negative CSF Gram stain bacterioscopy and liquor culture without growth. Latex agglutination reactions were performed with specific antibodies for groups A, B, C, Y, and W-135 Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and type B Haemophilus influenzae, and these were all undetectable. Electroencephalogram showed no epileptiform activity. Skull CT demonstrated no abnormal changes.

case_report: A 56-year-old woman arrived at the emergency department with impaired consciousness and respiratory failure. She had experienced symptoms resembling influenza, such as cough and fatigue, without fever, two days before admission. She had no prior medical history but had taken an over-the-counter medication containing ibuprofen for a headache. The patient measured 139 cm in height and weighed 29.0 kg. Her vital signs were as follows: blood pressure was 131/78 mm Hg, heart rate was 78 beats per minute and regular, axillary temperature was 35.1°C, respiratory rate was 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation (SpO2) was 85% with oxygen administered via a face mask at 3 liters per minute. On admission, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was E3V3M5.
test_results: Rapid viral testing was positive for influenza A virus. Significant laboratory results included hypoglycemia (serum glucose, 48 mg/dL), transaminitis (aspartate aminotransferase [AST] 12,548 IU/L and alanine aminotransferase [ALT] 5,725 IU/L), hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 3.5 mg/dL and direct bilirubin 1.6 mg/dL), elevated international normalized ratio (INR; 3.16), hyperammonemia (ammonia 102 μg/dL), lactic acidosis (7.0 mmol/L), azotemia (blood urea nitrogen 55 mg/dL), hypercreatinemia (serum creatinine 2.32 mg/dL), hyponatremia (134 mmol/L), hyperkalemia (6.7 mmol/L), hypolipidemia (total cholesterol 114 mg/dL and triglyceride 29 mg/dL). Carnitine was normal (223 μmol/L). The head magnetic resonance imaging showed hyperintense signals at the bilateral globus pallidus in diffusion-weighted images and fluid attenuation inversion recovery (FLAIR)-weighted images and a hyperintense signal at the left front parietal lobe in FLAIR-weighted images. Abdominal CT revealed fatty and enlarged liver. Chest CT showed diffuse alveolar type infiltrates in the patient's right middle lobe with air bronchograms and respiratory muscle loss.
diagnosis: Reye's syndrome induced by influenza A virus

case_report: A 19-year-old female presented with pain in the mandibular anterior region for the past 2 days. She is one of two siblings from non-consanguineous parents, with no family history of orofacial or acral malformations. Her antenatal, neonatal, and infancy periods were uneventful. At the age of 7, she underwent surgical management for an atrial septal defect. She reported menstrual irregularities, with menarche occurring at age 16. She is moderately built, well-nourished, and appears to have normal intelligence. Her height is 167 cm (75th percentile), while her weight (42 kg) and head circumference (20 inches) are both below the 3rd percentile. General physical examination showed broad halluces bilaterally with valgus deformity and dysmorphic nails. There is duplication of the 5th toe on the right foot with syndactyly of the supernumerary digit with the 5th toe. Flexion contraction of the 4th and 5th toes on the left foot and the 4th toe on the right foot was noted. The upper limbs are normal except for a broadened right thumb and nail, and bilateral clinodactyly. No functional deficits in the hands or feet were observed. Extra-oral examination revealed an acrocephalic skull, flattened frontal and occipital regions, and a low hairline. The patient has a leptoprosopic flat face with mild maxillary hypoplasia, relative mandibular prognathism, and a prominent chin. An increased gonial angle was noted on profile view. The nose is long, thin, and pointed with a flattened nasofrontal angle, presenting as a wide root of the nose. Thick eyebrows, prominent eyelashes, mild convergent strabismus, and marginal hypertelorism were observed. Intra-oral examination showed a high arched palate and generalized enamel hypoplasia. The patient is currently undergoing orthodontic treatment for arch crowding and has an anterior deep bite with 100% overlap of mandibular teeth. She has a history of endodontic treatment and apicoectomy of teeth 31 and 41, and currently reports pain in the same region along with vestibular obliteration and tenderness.
test_results: Orthopantomogram confirmed a cystic lesion in mandibular anterior region, increased gonial angles bilaterally and occlusal plane irregularities. Further radiographic examination of craniofacial skeleton (P-A skull and Lateral skull radiographs) revealed evidence of coronal sutural synostosis with prominent copper beaten appearance, flattened occiput and frontal bones, shallow orbits, gross prognathism with obtuse mandibular plane angle, maxillary sinus hyperpneumatization and falx calcification. Hand and wrist radiograph showed short and broad distal phalynx of right thumb, however all bones were otherwise normal. Radiograph of feet revealed duplication of distal phalynx of halluces and valgus deformity at distal interphalyngeal joint bilaterally. There was also evidence of partial duplication of 5th toe; Y-shaped proximal phalynx with one supernumerary phalynx in postaxial position exhibiting soft tissue syndactyly with 5th toe. Fourth and fifth digits of left foot were bent in clinically fixed flexion.

case_report: An 8-year-4-month-old girl presented with breast enlargement that began six months prior. She was the first child, born at 32 weeks via cesarean section, with a birth weight of 1.3 kg (-1.5 SD) and a birth length of 42 cm (0.0 SD). The mother had a healthy pregnancy. Developmental milestones included raising her head at 4 months, sitting at 7 months, speaking at 12 months, and walking at 14 months. She exhibited no cognitive impairment and had no family history of consanguinity. Physical examination showed Tanner stage 2 breast development and Tanner stage 1 pubic hair. Her height was 128.7 cm (-0.31 SDS) and weight was 26.5 kg (+0.42 SDS), with a BMI of 16.0 kg/m2. External genitalia were normal, and no pelvic examination was performed due to virginity. Laboratory results included basal LH at 0.19 IU/L, basal FSH at 2.77 IU/L, peak LH level of 11.5 IU/L, peak FSH at 13.8 IU/L following GnRH stimulation, E2 at 5 pg/mL, and DHEA at 122 ug/dl. Routine hematological and biochemical analyses were normal. Bone age was assessed at 9.7 years using the TW3 method, with a predicted height of 152 ± 5 cm. Karyotype analysis showed 46, XX, and results from whole exome sequencing (WES) and copy number variation (CNV) sequencing were negative. Spine X-ray was normal.
test_results: Abdominal-pelvic ultrasound and MRI revealed ovary of pubertal volume (right ovary: 2.0 × 1.0 × 0.9 cm; left ovary: 1.9 × 1.1 × 1.0 cm) and dysplasia of the uterus. Brain MRI revealed a pineal cyst.
diagnosis: Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome  with central precocious puberty

case_report: A 28-year-old married woman with primary amenorrhea was referred to our medical imaging department for further evaluation of a shapeless pelvic mass and to assess the functionality of her ovaries and uterus. Initial assessments included measurements of height, weight, body mass index, and secondary sexual characteristics. The patient exhibited pubic and axillary hair (Tanner Stage III), breast development at Tanner Stage IV, and a blind vagina upon examination. The uterus was not detectable through physical examination. The onset of secondary sexual characteristics, such as larche and pubarche, occurred around the age of 13 years, with no family history of amenorrhea. Laboratory tests revealed normal levels of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) at 2.5 mIU/ml, luteinizing hormone (LH) at 3.5 mIU/ml, serum creatinine at 0.6 mg/dl, and prolactin at 9.45 ng/ml. The anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) level was below the normal range at 1.5 ng/ml. Additionally, a buccal smear test for gender determination was normal.
test_results: A bilateral renal agenesis with a 95 mm × 72 mm ectopic pancake-shaped kidney on the left side of the pelvic cavity was seen in the ultrasound examination. In addition, the complete absence of the uterus, the cervix, and the upper part of the vagina was also identified during the ultrasound procedure. The size of the ovaries was normal with the echo pattern of follicles between 10 and 14 mm in diameter. MR images confirmed ultrasound findings, including the uterovaginal atresia with normal ovaries in shape and size. The coronal section revealed an ectopic pancake-shaped kidney with no evidence of hydronephrosis. An MR angiogram (time of flight technique) showed that the middle sacral artery was the principal artery that supplied the ectopic pelvic kidney.

case_report: A 27-year-old Pakistani male presented with a painless lump in his right breast, first noticed approximately 1.5 years ago. Initially, he observed a thickened patch of skin that gradually increased in size and developed areas of bluish discoloration. In the past few months, this patch evolved into a lumpy swelling. There was no family history of breast, prostate, or testicular cancer, and the patient did not exhibit systemic signs or weight loss. Physical examination revealed a 4 × 3 cm lump in the lower outer quadrant of the right breast, extending upward to the nipple. The lump was attached to the overlying skin but was freely mobile over the underlying muscle. The skin over the lump showed telangiectatic patches. No palpable axillary lymph nodes were detected bilaterally. Imaging studies, including mammography and ultrasonography, identified a well-defined 35 × 27 mm hypoechoic lesion at the 7 to 8 o'clock position in the right breast, corresponding to the palpable nodule and showing increased vascularity on ultrasound. MRI of the breast revealed a lobulated 4.9 × 3.5 × 2.5 cm lesion with more intense signals on T1- and T2-weighted images compared to muscle tissue, and a plateau on the time-intensity curve. The lesion was classified as a BI-RADS IV lesion. The left breast and bilateral axillary lymph nodes appeared normal.
test_results: Histopathological examination showed marked cellular proliferation comprising monomorphic spindle cells arranged into a tight storiform pattern. Immunohistochemically, the cells were positive for CD34, bc12, CD99, β-catenin, and vimentin.

case_report: A 42-year-old female presented with a palpable lesion in the right breast. There was no history of pain, nipple discharge, or axillary lumps. Mammography showed scattered fibro-glandular densities in the breasts, with adipose tissue replacing normal parenchyma in the area of the palpable lesion. No discrete mass, spiculation, or malignant microcalcification was observed. Targeted ultrasound of the right breast identified a hyperechoic nodule measuring 0.8 x 1.0 cm at the 6 o’clock position, 9 cm from the nipple. The patient chose to proceed with a biopsy, which showed hypercellular fibrous tissue infiltrating adipose tissue. Excision was recommended for further evaluation. The patient underwent a right breast excisional biopsy, revealing a 0.3 x 0.2 cm tan-white indurated mass near the superior margin.
test_results: Histologically, there was a bland spindle cell lesion, identical to the previous biopsy. The uniform spindle cells infiltrating the surrounding stroma and fibro-adipose tissue were identified. No areas of cytological atypia, necrosis, or mitosis were seen. The tumor was present at the inked superior excision margin. Immunohistochemical analysis showed the spindle cells were positive for CD34, and smooth muscle actin (SMA) immunostains. Pan keratin, Cytokeratin-7, Cytokeratin 34BE12, Cytokeratin-8/18, p63, and Desmin were all negative. Beta-catenin showed a cytoplasmic staining pattern.

case_report: A 54-year-old female with no prior health issues presented with a slowly enlarging mass in the right thigh over the course of one year. An enhanced computed tomography scan revealed a 2.2 cm, well-defined subcutaneous nodule in the right thigh with moderately heterogeneous enhancement. The mass was surgically excised with narrow margins. Follow-up at 12 months post-operation showed no signs of recurrence or metastasis. Gross examination of the excised mass showed a 2 cm, well-circumscribed nodular mass with a firm, gray-white cut surface. Under low power magnification, the tumor appeared well-defined and partially encapsulated, located in the subcutaneous tissue without dermal involvement. The tumor consisted of cellular, fairly uniform, slightly rounded spindle cells with scant cytoplasm and ovoid, mildly atypical nuclei, exhibiting brisk mitotic activity (up to 10 mitotic figures per 10 high power fields). The cells were primarily arranged in elongated fascicles and herringbone patterns. The stroma was minimal, featuring scattered small round vessels and focal thick, band-like collagen bundles. No necrosis was observed in the tumor. At the periphery, there were minor areas with vague storiform growth of less cellular and more bland-appearing tumor cells within a more collagenized stroma, occasionally containing entrapped mature adipose tissue. Immunohistochemical staining showed the tumor cells were moderately and diffusely positive for CD34 and focally positive for SMA, while negative for Cam5.2, epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), desmin, calponin, TLE-1, CD99, Stat6, anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK, 1A4), SOX10, and S100 protein. The Ki67 proliferation index was approximately 20%. Fluorescence in-situ hybridization (FISH) analysis was negative for fusion of the COL1A1 and PDGFB genes using the dual spanning probe set. Assessment for rearrangements of the NTRK1/2/3 locus using the corresponding break-apart probe sets was also negative.
test_results: A fusion product between TNC exon 15 and PDGFD exon 6 with the variant allele frequency (VAF) of 85.37% was identified. The fusion result was confirmed through manually reviewing on the Integrative Genomics Viewer. This fusion was further confirmed by nested reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) amplification followed by Sanger sequencing.
diagnosis: fibrosarcomatous dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans with TNC-PDGFD fusion

case_report: A 12-year-old boy presented with a primary complaint of an ulcer on the dorsum of his tongue, which has been causing a burning sensation when consuming spicy foods for the past year. The patient has no notable medical history. Extraoral examination revealed no abnormalities. Intraoral examination identified a single irregular red and white ulcerative lesion, approximately 2.5 × 1.0 cm in size, with granulation tissue at the center and an inflammatory red border on the dorsum of the tongue. There was depapillation of filiform papillae in and around the lesion. The patient's oral hygiene was good, with no dental restorations. There was no history of drug intake or habits that could potentially cause oral mucosal ulcerations.
test_results: Histopathological examination showed hyperparakeratosis of stratified squamous epithelium and basal cell degeneration with dense band-linked lymphocytic infiltration at the epithelial-connective tissue interface.

case_report: A 34-year-old male patient visited a dental clinic with a primary concern of a grayish white patch on the right buccal mucosa, without experiencing any burning sensation or other local discomfort. The patient reported a habit of snuff inhalation, consuming four to five packets daily for the past 7 years. The patient did not provide any drug history and had not undergone any dental procedures to date. Intraoral examination revealed a unilateral, grayish white non-scrapable patch extending from teeth 44 to 48, measuring approximately 3 × 4 cm. No cutaneous lesions were observed during the general examination.
test_results: Histopathologically, a parakeratinized epithelium with liquefaction degeneration of basal cell layer and subepithelial band of chronic inflammatory cells which is chiefly composed of lymphocytes were seen. Immunohistochemical staining showed a strong positive expression of CD8 + T cells subepithelially.

case_report: An 18-year-old male visited the orthopedics clinic due to lower back pain persisting for the past 6 months. The pain began spontaneously after a minor fall, worsened with physical activity, and was alleviated by rest and pain relievers. There was no variation in pain based on time of day or posture. Physical examination revealed muscle spasm in the paravertebral muscles and a reduced range of motion in the lumbar spine. No neurological deficits were observed. There was no visible spinal deformity or noticeable swelling.
test_results: Digital X-ray of lumbosacral spine showed irregularity in superior end plate of L3 vertebrae with decreased lordosis in lumbar region. MRI of lumbosacral spine showed anterior wedging in L3 vertebral body, erosion of superior end plate of L3 vertebra, narrow disk space of L3–L4, and schomrl nodes in L3 vertebrae. Blood parameters CBC, ESR, and CRP were within normal limits.

case_report: A 19-year-old male presented with lower back pain, numbness in the lower limbs, and radiating pain to the legs for one week. The pain is progressive and worsens with movement. Tingling sensations accompany the pain in both lower limbs. The patient reported back pain after prolonged sitting and strenuous exercise. There was no recent history of trauma, heavy weightlifting accidents, falls from height, or congenital anomalies. During the general examination, the patient was supine with both anterior superior iliac spines at the same level, conscious, and well-oriented. Inspection showed a normal lumbosacral spinal curvature with no scars or sinuses. Active toe movement and distal circulation were normal. Vital signs included a pulse of 88/min, respiratory rate of 15, and blood pressure of 120/80 mm Hg. There was no history of loss of consciousness, vomiting, or internal bleeding. Physical examination revealed paraspinal muscle spasms over the lumbar region without hypoesthesia. The straight leg raise test showed the patient could lift his left leg to 50° and his right leg to 60°. No distal neurovascular deficits were observed. Laboratory results indicated an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 12 mm/hr (normal range: 0 to 22 mm/hr), calcium level of 8.2 mg/dl (normal range: 8.6 to 10.3 mg/dl), creatinine level of 0.7 mg/dl (normal range: 0.74 to 1.35 mg/dl), sodium level of 139 milliequivalents/liter (normal range: 139 to 145 milliequivalents/liter), and potassium level of 3.7 millimoles/liter (normal range: 3.6 to 5.2 millimoles/liter).
test_results: X-rays and MRIs were done, which presented the following results: MRI of the whole spine was performed using a T2W sequence in the sagittal plane. Several observations were made, which highlighted that there was a straightening of the cervical spine with loss of normal lordosis. Degeneration was seen in intervertebral discs in the form of T2 hypointensity at multiple levels. Osteophyte (bone spur) disc complexes were seen at C3-C4, C4-C5, and C5-C6 levels. Reduced vertebral body height with end plate irregularities was seen at C3, C4, and C5 levels. The intervertebral disc spaces show normal height, and no evidence was seen of any cord abnormality. Intervertebral discs show degeneration in the form of T2 hypointensity at multiple levels.

case_report: A 23-year-old Saudi male visited the neurology clinic due to involuntary movements in his left upper limb that had been occurring for 6 months. These movements, described as supination and pronation, lasted for a few seconds and ceased when the arm was held by the other hand. They were triggered by stressful situations or lack of sleep and were confined to the left arm. There was no alteration in consciousness during or before these episodes, and no other symptoms were reported. His medical history included tonic-clonic seizures between the ages of 9 and 14, with approximately 6–8 episodes occurring during sleep over those years. He had been treated with carbamazepine 200 mg per day, which was discontinued when the seizures stopped. He had no other significant medical history. Birth history indicated a term delivery by cesarean section and a 17-day stay in an incubator for unspecified reasons. His surgical history included open reduction and internal fixation of a pathological fracture of the tibia and fibula following a minor sports injury, attributed to a nonossifying fibroma. Family history was noncontributory. General and systemic physical examinations were normal. Neurological assessment revealed hyperreflexia in the left upper limb (+3 for brachioradialis, biceps, and triceps reflexes). Motor, sensory, and cerebellar examinations were normal, and the Babinski sign was negative. Hematological and biochemistry blood tests showed no abnormalities. EEG recording demonstrated a well-regulated alpha rhythm at 9 Hz with a maximum amplitude of 70 µV (referential). Photic stimulation elicited a good driving response, and hyperventilation did not provide additional information. Interictal EEG was normal, consistent with a normal EEG.
test_results: Brain MRI with contrast showed corticosubcortical cystic encephalomalacic changes, centered on the right superior frontal gyrus and contacting the right lateral ventricle frontal horn. These changes included a dominant large unilocular cystic component, measuring around 4 × 3 × 2.3 cm, which followed the CSF signal on all sequences and lacked overt hemosiderin staining. Thinning of the overlying cortical mantle was present, with mild scalloping of the adjacent calvarial inner table. The dominant cyst was surrounded by smaller cystic changes.

case_report: A six-year-old boy was brought to the emergency department following an episode of convulsion. The episode involved jerky repetitive movements of all extremities lasting approximately two minutes, with spontaneous resolution. During the episode, the child was unresponsive, and his skin color turned blue. The episode was accompanied by urinary incontinence and frothy secretions from the mouth. There were no preceding warning signs or complaints of unpleasant sensations. The event occurred suddenly while the child was playing. He had not been sleep-deprived prior to the event. Post-episode, the child appeared tired and fell asleep. There was no history of febrile illness or similar previous episodes. The child had a medical history of well-controlled asthma and eczema, with no previous surgeries. His perinatal history was uneventful; he was born full-term with a birth weight of 3.8 kg and was up-to-date with vaccinations. There was no consanguinity in the family, and no family history of epilepsy. Social history was non-contributory. On examination, the child was alert and conscious with no dysmorphic features. He was not pale, jaundiced, or cyanosed. Vital signs were: temperature 36.5℃, heart rate 90 bpm, blood pressure 80/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 23 bpm, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. His speech and comprehension were age-appropriate, and his social and behavioral skills were normal. Examination of the upper and lower limbs showed normal tone and power, and his gait was normal. Cardiorespiratory examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory investigations showed hemoglobin of 14.2 g/dL, leukocyte count of 7,000 cells/µL, and platelet count of 390,000/µL. Random blood sugar and other biochemical findings, including electrolytes, hepatic, and renal profiles, were within normal limits.
test_results: The scan demonstrated a large well-defined extra-axial cystic lesion occupying most of the left hemisphere that is connected to the ventricular system. The lesion had no grey-matter lining and it strictly followed the cerebrospinal fluid in all sequences.

case_report: A 70-year-old Asian-Japanese woman presented with frequent urination and dysuria in October 2018. Ultrasound revealed left hydronephrosis. Intravenous urography indicated left lower ureteral stenosis. Blood and urinary analysis were unremarkable, and urinary cytology was class II. Contrast-enhanced CT showed thickening of the lower ureteral wall with contrast effect, and retrograde pyelography demonstrated that a guidewire could not pass through the left ureter due to stenosis. A left ureteroscopic biopsy was performed in November 2018, revealing a papillary tumor in the left lower ureter. Four biopsies were taken, and pathological examination showed regenerative atypia with inflammatory cells but no malignant findings. Intraoperative urine cytology showed class III in the left renal pelvis urine and class I in the left ureteral urine. Due to the ureteroscopic findings and insufficient sample volume, a total resection of the left renal pelvis and ureter was performed in January 2019.
test_results: DFS staining and polarized light microscopy were positive.

case_report: A 46-year-old woman presented with a recent onset of neck swelling. She reported a fourteen-year history of amenorrhea, along with weight gain, frequent headaches, nasal enlargement, increased shoe size, and the need to resize her rings over the past several years. She did not experience galactorrhea or visual disturbances. Her medical history included hypertension for four years and dyslipidemia for one year. Physical examination revealed a grade II palpable thyroid gland, acral enlargement, and central obesity. Laboratory tests were conducted.
test_results: Her initial laboratory findings demonstrated hyperglycemia, hyperlipidemia, normal thyroid functions, low gonadotropin levels, and severe prolactin elevation with macroprolactin absence (serum prolactin > 40000 mIU/L, normal ranges: 33.36–580.80). The diagnosis of acromegaly was confirmed with elevated IGF-1 level (serum IGF-1: 550 ng/mL, normal ranges: 94–210) and failure to suppress GH levels with a 100 g oral glucose load. Accompanying Cushing's disease was excluded with a low-dose dexamethasone suppression test. Her thyroid ultrasonography revealed multinodular goiter with the largest nodule exhibiting 15 mm diameter. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the sella showed a pituitary macroadenoma which has maximum diameters of 6 × 5 × 5.5 cm extending to the sphenoid sinus via clival destruction, suprasellar cistern, and prepontine cistern. Left cavernous sinus, left middle cranial fossa, and left orbital apex were invaded, wherein optic chiasm and circle of the Willis were elevated. The macroadenoma was encasing the cavernous portion of the left internal carotid artery. A minimal central scotoma in the right eye was found when her visual field was evaluated.

case_report: A 64-year-old male with diabetes was brought to the emergency department by his wife following a fall the previous day. The patient had bruises on the head and chest from the fall. He had a history of recurrent falls over the past three months, but no investigations had been conducted during previous visits to the emergency department; he was only reassured and discharged. During the current visit, the triage doctor assigned him to a monitored bed due to head trauma and his advanced age. The patient's wife reported that he had been experiencing an unsteady gait for the past three months. There were no reports of syncope, nausea, vomiting, body weakness, seizure, headache, dysarthria, or altered level of consciousness. The patient had a diabetic foot and a three-month history of proliferative diabetic retinopathy in both eyes. He had been receiving physical therapy for his walking issues, which he and his wife attributed to his diabetic foot, but his condition continued to worsen. The patient's wife also reported three instances of fecal incontinence and noted that he had been forgetful over the last two months, frequently misplacing his mobile phone and keys and repeatedly asking about their plans. The rest of his medical history was noncontributory. Upon examination, the patient was vitally stable with a heart rate of 99 beats per minute, blood pressure of 133/77 mmHg, respiratory rate of 19 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 99% on room air. His gait was shuffling and bradykinetic, with a mild drift to the right. Pupils were equally reactive to light, and all cranial nerves were intact. Full sensation and strength were observed, and all reflexes were normal. Blood tests, including a complete blood count with differentials, liver function, renal function, electrolytes, venous blood gas, and random blood sugar tests, were unremarkable.
test_results: A non-enhanced axial computed tomography scan of the brain revealed brain tissue volume loss with disproportionate dilation of the lateral and third ventricles, with no obvious obstructive lesions. Subtle periventricular hypodensity was also seen. There was no evidence of acute territorial infarction or acute hemorrhage. No mass effect or midline shift was observed. The posterior fossa structures were unremarkable. The visualized orbital structures and paranasal sinuses were within the normal limits, but a redundant optic nerve sheath complex was seen bilaterally. A lumbar puncture with 40 ml of CSF tapping produced normal opening pressure (18 mmHg) (normal range: 5-18 mmHg or 70-245 cmH2O).

case_report: A 45-year-old male presented with an 8-month history of imbalance and progressive gait disorder, accompanied by memory issues. His medical history includes bipolar disorder and type II diabetes mellitus. He had a COVID-19 infection 2 months prior to the onset of neurological symptoms, characterized by fever, anosmia, dysgeusia, and anorexia. The infection was confirmed by a real-time reverse-transcriptase-polymerase-chain-reaction assay (Allplex™ SARS-CoV-2 Assay—N/RdRP/S genes). He was hospitalized for seven days and required oxygen via nasal cannula. Upon discharge, he could walk unassisted. Two months post-COVID-19 infection, he developed a progressive gait disorder, describing a sensation of his feet being glued to the ground.
