Subsequently, he experienced memory lapses, excessive daytime sleepiness, and a blunted affect, as reported by his family. He also developed executive dysfunction, impacting his work performance. There was no history of head trauma, subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis, or family history of neurological diseases. Neurological examination showed short-term memory loss, slow processing speed, inattention, planning difficulties, and executive dysfunction. Mild tetraparesis with brisk deep tendon reflexes in all four limbs was noted, without clonus and with flexor plantar responses. Mild rigidity in the upper limbs was observed, without cogwheeling. His gait was slow and magnetic, characterized by short steps, feet close to the ground, and postural instability. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, renal function, liver enzymes, thyroid hormones, and vitamin B12 levels, were normal. Serology for Syphilis and HIV was negative.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) disclosed moderately dilated supratentorial ventricular system with callosal angle reduction and aqueduct flow-void. A high-volume (40 ml) lumbar tap test was performed and revealed an opening pressure of 100mmH2O (normal range < 200 mmH2O). There was marked improvement of gait and balance after the procedure—10 m timed up and go (TUG) before the procedure of 18.4 s (32 steps) and after the procedure of 16.7 s (27 steps).

case_report: A 34-year-old woman presented with loss of appetite, frequent episodes of cough, foul-smelling breath, recurrent pneumonia, pain in the left lower back, and occasional coughing up of blood over a period of two months. These symptoms did not improve with antibiotics or other medical treatments. The frequency of coughing up blood increased in the last week, including one episode of significant bleeding. She had completed a full course of treatment for sputum acid-fast bacilli (AFB)-positive pulmonary tuberculosis five years prior to this presentation. On physical examination, her vital signs were within normal limits. Chest auscultation indicated reduced air entry in the left lower chest. A chest X-ray showed an opacity in the left lower lobe.
test_results: A computed tomography (CT) chest showed left lower lobe collapse-consolidation changes with an ill-defined heterogeneous area with nonenhancing hypodensities and cystic and necrotic changes in the absence of air bronchogram within. A large artery arising directly from the posterolateral aspect of the thoracic aorta was supplying the left lower lobe mass.

case_report: A 59-year-old male with a history of laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma and lung adenocarcinoma was referred for evaluation. Physical examination revealed asymmetry in shoulder size, with the left shoulder appearing smaller than the right. The left upper limb exhibited weakness and an abnormal position. The patient reported that these skeletal abnormalities were present since birth and that he did not frequently use his left upper limb. Additionally, the patient has been limping since a previous motor accident.
test_results: Significant asymmetric size of scapulae but the normal-appearing shape and slightly higher position of the left scapula are detected. Other findings were mild cervicothoracic scoliosis as well as slightly asymmetric upper limbs. Focal uptake at midshaft of the right tibia was compatible with a recent trauma.

case_report: A 7-year-old girl was presented with an abnormality of the right shoulder. On physical examination, the right scapula appeared smaller and positioned higher than usual, but shoulder movement was not restricted. The scapula showed an increased horizontal to vertical length, and plain radiographs did not reveal any bony connection between the scapula and the vertebrae.
test_results: MRI showed a thin hypointense band extending from the superomedial angle of the scapula to the 7th cervical vertebra's spinous process.

case_report: A 12-year 7-month-old Caucasian female with no significant medical or family history presented with progressively worsening acne, hirsutism, and a deep voice. She reported excessive hair growth on the face, chest, abdomen, and back. She denied salt craving, increased thirst, prolonged illnesses, dizziness, headaches, or vision changes. She had experienced breast development for approximately 2.5 years and had not yet begun menstruating. Her growth chart indicated an acceleration in linear growth around ages 9 to 10, with stable height over the past year and a body mass index at the 29th percentile. Physical examination revealed a normotensive, normocardic female with a deep voice. She exhibited mild acne on the face and upper chest, significant hirsutism with a Ferriman-Gallwey Score of 22 (upper lip: 4, chin: 4, chest: 3, upper abdomen: 2, lower abdomen: 3, thighs: 3, lower back: 2, and upper back: 1), and grade 1 acanthosis nigricans on the neck. Pubertal examination showed mild clitoromegaly (5 cm long by 0.5 cm wide) with slightly enlarged labia minora larger than the labia majora, Tanner stage V pubic and axillary hair, and Tanner stage III breast development. Initial laboratory values drawn at 2 pm indicated a 46 XX karyotype, with estrogen, prolactin, follicle stimulating hormone (FSH), and luteinizing hormone (LH) in the pubertal range, and an LH–FSH ratio greater than 2:1. Electrolytes and thyroid function were normal. The patient had elevated androstenedione and testosterone levels, and a borderline elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone. Bone age was assessed as 14 years, nearly 2 standard deviations advanced.
test_results: Nine am laboratory values prior to the stimulation test demonstrated multiple elevated steroids and androgens including 17-hydroxypregnenolone, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, 11-deoxycortisol, dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), androstenedione, and testosterone. Additionally, she had a normal progesterone, estrone, and estradiol. There was minimal response of any axis to ACTH. Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging showed normal adrenal glands and no focal lesion. Pelvic ultrasound was notable for normal size ovaries (2.1 × 3.6 × 3.1 cm on the right and 2.5 × 2.7 × 2.7 cm on the left) with small peripheral cysts and normal blood flow and an anteverted uterus measuring 4.5 × 1.7 × 3.7 cm with a suboptimally visualized endometrial stripe. Adrenal androgens (progesterone, deoxycorticosterone, 11-deoxycortisol, and cortisol) suppressed whereas the ovarian androgens (11-hydroxypregnenalone, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, DHEA, androstenedione, and testosterone) did not suppress, indicating an ovarian source of androgen production.

case_report: A 47-year-old male with no known comorbidities was started on a course of oral prednisone (60 mg once daily) following a routine diagnosis of bilateral anterior uveitis, with a consequential improvement in his visual acuity. In the ensuing two weeks, he developed generalized weakness and fatigue, which hindered his ability to walk without assistance. This prompted his visit to our emergency department. In a detailed interview, he did not complain of any chest pain, dyspnea, altered bowel habits, previous syncopal episodes, headaches, dizziness, or prior substance abuse. Initial assessment disclosed a patient with bilateral periorbital puffiness, who was visibly lethargic but alert and well-oriented, with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 15/15. His heart rate was 80 beats per minute with a blood pressure of 70/50 mm Hg, a respiratory rate of 20 per minute and a temperature of 98.6°F. An extensive neurological exam revealed 4/5 power in all muscle groups, intact perception to pain, touch, and proprioception, an absence of cerebellar signs or impaired plantar reflexes. An ophthalmological examination revealed normal visual acuity, pupillary reflexes, extraocular movements and fundoscopic examination. In lieu of the severe hypotension, the patient was admitted to the medical floor and started on a combination of intravenous fluids, norepinephrine, hydrocortisone (100 mg every eight hours) as well as tazobactam/piperacillin (4.5 g every eight hours) to treat for any underlying sepsis. His initial laboratory investigations are shown in Table , and Table shows the trend of laboratory investigations over a period of a next few days. The patient underwent an extensive workup to determine the etiology of his generalized weakness and hypotension. An initial diagnosis of septic shock was ruled out following normal blood and urine cultures. A secondary explanation for the elevated total leukocyte count (TLC) with neutrophilia was attributed to the patient’s previous oral prednisone prescription which was supplemented with hydrocortisone injections in the hospital. Due to the previous history of uveitis, and a mild elevation of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) in the blood, sarcoidosis was considered as a possible cause of his condition, which was further supplemented by the findings on chest x-ray (CXR), which revealed bilateral hilar and perihilar interstitial prominences with bilateral nodular opacities in the middle and lower lung zones (Figure ). This possibility was ruled out owing to the patient’s hasty deterioration and lack of response to the corticosteroid therapy. The patient’s antinuclear antibody (ANA) was negative, and an antineuronal profile ruled out Lambert-Eaton syndrome, myasthenia gravis, and other autoimmune polyneuropathies. Echocardiography revealed an ejection fraction of 60%, which ruled out cardiogenic shock. Further evaluation showed an evening serum cortisol of 59 µg/dL, which was still inappropriately low (considering the patient’s clinical predicament). The adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) level was found to be low (4.17 pg/mL) as well.
test_results: A contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed an enlarged right adrenal gland with a heterogeneous hyperdense area. A smaller heterogeneous lesion was present in the lateral limb of the left adrenal gland.

case_report: In late June 2015, a 22-year-old male with no prior health issues arrived at a community hospital in Montreal, Quebec, experiencing vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea for two days. He had recently completed four weeks of military training in Alberta from April to May 2015. Upon examination, he had a fever of 39.3°C and an elevated heart rate, but no other significant findings were noted. Broad spectrum antibiotics were administered. The next day, his condition worsened rapidly, necessitating intubation due to hypoxic respiratory failure. A chest radiograph showed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates with effusions. Due to persistent low oxygen levels and poor blood flow, he was moved to a tertiary care center ICU for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Cultures of blood, urine, and stool were negative, as was a respiratory virus PCR from a nasopharyngeal swab. The patient was gradually weaned off intubation and discharged from the hospital without any lasting effects.
test_results: Hantavirus serology was positive for both Hantavirus Sin Nombre IgG and IgM. PCR targeting the conserved region of Hantavirus M segment detected the presence of Hantavirus from a nasopharyngeal swab sample. Further Hantavirus typing demonstrated similarity to Sin Nombre reference strains from Montana and Alberta.

case_report: A 55-year-old woman, who does not smoke and has no known cancer risk factors other than age, underwent an MCED test as part of her healthcare benefits. The test results indicated a CSD with predictions pointing towards the kidney as the primary site and the pancreas/gallbladder as the secondary site.
test_results: An abdominal MRI showed a 4.4 cm exophytic right lower pole renal mass with no evidence of retroperitoneal adenopathy or intra-abdominal metastasis or other lesions.
diagnosis: Stage I clear-cell renal cell carcinoma

case_report: A two and a half year old male child from Darfur province, west of Sudan was brought by his parents due to abdominal distension for 8 months prior to admission. The distension was associated with mild pain and no symptoms related to the urinary or gastrointestinal systems. His past medical history was unremarkable apart from poor socioeconomic status and contact with livestock and sheepdogs. Physical examination revealed a slightly pale child with no jaundice and no lymphadenopathy. The abdomen was grossly distended with bulging of the right flank, and there was an umbilical hernia. There were cautery marks, striae, and superficial veins. The abdomen was tense with a palpable right-sided abdominal mass extending from the right renal angle to the umbilicus, measuring approximately 15 × 25 cm. There was no hepatosplenomegaly and negative shifting dullness. His vital signs, including blood pressure, were normal. Investigations included a full blood count which showed nutritional anaemia, ESR 57 mm/h. His renal and liver function tests were entirely normal. Urine analysis was also normal. Chest X-ray was normal. The first abdominal ultrasound revealed a large right cystic renal mass containing small daughter cysts arranged eccentrically as well as few septations, with a normal left kidney. A repeat ultrasound in a different setup showed the same findings. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest was normal, and CT abdomen showed a large cystic mass arising from the right kidney. A dynamic renal scan showed a nonfunctioning right kidney with features of parenchymal effacement. The child was commenced on Albendazole (antihelminthic drug) and a radical right-sided nephrectomy was performed 4 weeks later, during which the cyst ruptured. The dimensions of the mass were 7×13 cm.
test_results: Histopathological examination showed multiple cysts separated from renal tissue by fibrous tissue, the cysts were lined by flattened to columnar epithelium, some showing hobnail pattern. The renal tissue was composed of hyalinized glomeruli, atrophied tubules and mixed inflammatory cellular infiltration.
Orpha_name: Multilocular cystic renal neoplasm of low malignant potential

case_report: A 66-year-old male presented to the Urology Department with complaints of painful urination, frequent urination, and a recent urinary tract infection. His medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and an appendectomy performed 50 years ago. The patient reported a recent urinary tract infection caused by Escherichia coli, which did not respond to a two-week course of ciprofloxacin. Physical examination revealed mild tenderness in the left kidney area. Laboratory tests were generally normal, except for the presence of microscopic blood in the urine. Urine cytology showed no signs of malignancy.
test_results: The results of US demonstrated a well-demarcated cystic mass of the left kidney (about 4 cm in max. diameter) with thickened walls and hyperechoic appearance as large calcifications which occupied the middle part of the kidney. Computed tomography (CT) showed a 4.2×2.6 cm, unilocular, well-circumscribed cyst containing numerous calcifications on the walls and with unremarkable thin or relatively thicker septa from the border with the renal parenchyma, but no solid components. An enhanced CT scan showed a poorly enhancing cystic lesion protruding into sinus. Non-enhanced, cortical phase, and nephrographic phase CT attenuation measurements were 13.0, 15.1, and 24.4 HU, respectively. The mass was compressing the calycle system and vascular structures at hilum, but no peripheral invasion or distant metastases were detected.
Orpha_name: Multilocular cystic renal neoplasm of low malignant potential

case_report: A 20-year-old Caucasian woman visited the outpatient department due to a mass on her left kidney. This mass was discovered incidentally during an abdominal imaging study conducted as part of an evaluation for ongoing flank pain. She has no history of urologic conditions. Her medical history includes heterozygous beta Mediterranean anemia. The patient has a body mass index of 33.4 kg/m2, indicating obesity. A subsequent thoracic imaging study showed no abnormalities.
test_results: According to the CT finding, the mass was located on the lower pole of the left kidney (83 × 111 × 111mm) and there was no other pathologic finding. The immunohistochemical examination showed that the epithelial cells were positive for the cytokeratins AE1/AE3 and PAX-8. The stromal cells were positive for the progesterone receptors, estrogen receptors and CD10.
Orpha_name: Multilocular cystic renal neoplasm of low malignant potential

case_report: A 50-year-old male was referred to our institution after an incidental finding of a 2.5 cm enhancing mass located at the lower pole of the left kidney. This mass was initially detected via ultrasound imaging during investigations for symptoms of bloating and constipation. A subsequent computed tomography (CT) scan with intravenous contrast was performed, revealing a low-density but mildly enhancing lesion. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was conducted to further evaluate the mass, showing a 26 × 21 mm exophytic mass at the lower pole of the left kidney with a low T2 signal. The patient underwent an ultrasound-guided biopsy of the mass. The lesion was accessed using a 17-gauge needle with a coaxial sheath, and two fine needle aspiration (FNA) biopsies were performed. Core biopsies were then taken using an 18-gauge core biopsy needle with the coaxial sheath in place, resulting in two passes to obtain six cores. The core sizes were 6 mm, 5 mm, 4 mm, 4 mm, 4 mm, and 3 mm in length, all embedded in two blocks.
test_results: Pathological assessment of the FNA and core biopsy specimens confirmed the presence of a low-grade neoplasm consisting of closely packed cells with small rounded nuclei forming clusters and some mucin filled tubules.

case_report: A 34-year-old male, seven years and three months post-kidney transplantation, presented in February 2016 with symptoms including reduced appetite, weight loss, visible blood in urine, fatigue, and significantly reduced urine output (less than 200 mL). The patient had received a living kidney transplant from his 41-year-old mother on November 27, 2008, after two months of hemodialysis for end-stage renal disease (ESRD). The transplanted kidney was placed in the right iliac fossa. Initial biopsy of the graft showed no significant abnormalities. Induction therapy included a total of 2.5 g of methylprednisolone, and maintenance immunosuppression consisted of tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), and prednisone, with a target tacrolimus trough level of 8-10 ng/mL for the first year post-operation. Pre-transplant creatinine level was 6.93 mg/dL, which decreased to 0.98 mg/dL two weeks post-operation. The patient was regularly followed up at another hospital. Three and a half years post-transplant (May 2012), creatinine level increased to 1.92 mg/dL, and urine test showed proteinuria (3+). The patient had no other complaints but declined a biopsy of the kidney graft. Panel reactive antibody (PRA) testing was negative, kidney graft ultrasonography was normal, and tacrolimus trough level was 6.2 ng/mL. Methylprednisolone was administered at a total dose of 1.5 g (500 mg/day for three days), but creatinine levels continued to rise. Six years post-transplant (November 2014), creatinine level further increased to 5.31 mg/dL, and a biopsy of the kidney graft revealed T-cell mediated acute rejection (Banff 1A) and sclerosing glomerulonephritis. Ultrasound showed a mass in the upper pole of the graft, measuring 2 cm × 3 cm × 3 cm. The patient declined further examination and treatment. On admission in February 2016, the patient weighed 37 kg, having lost approximately 20 kg over two years. Physical examination revealed pale palpebral conjunctiva and hyponychium, and a large, partially mobile mass with clear boundaries was palpable in the right abdominal region. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin at 53 g/L, white blood cell count at 5.03 × 10^9/L, platelet count at 212 × 10^9/L, and creatinine level at 11.23 mg/dL.
test_results: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a giant heterogeneous cystic-solid mass, measuring 10 cm × 10 cm × 15 cm, involving the upper pole of the kidney allograft. The solid lesion of the tumor was enhanced by the contrast medium, whereas the cystic part of the mass was not enhanced. No lesion was found in the liver and both native kidneys. No abdominal and pelvic lymphadenopathy was revealed. Head CT showed no abnormalities. The R.E.N.A.L nephrometry score was 11x. Based on the TNM classification, the lesion was scored as stage II, T2bN0M0.

case_report: A 56-year-old woman presented with an incidental left renal mass discovered during an evaluation for hypertension. She measured 167 cm in height and weighed 52 kg. Her blood pressure was 166/102 mmHg, and her heart rate was 116 bpm. She had a history of uncontrolled hypertension and was taking amlodipine 10 mg once daily. She reported a slight headache. Physical examination revealed significant ascites. General blood chemistry tests and blood counts were normal. Serum catecholamine levels were elevated: adrenaline at 148 pg/mL (normal 0–100 pg/mL), noradrenaline at 902 pg/mL (normal 100–450 pg/mL), and dopamine at 28 pg/mL (normal 0–20 pg/mL). A 24-hour urine collection showed adrenaline at 13.6 μg/day (normal 3.4–26.9 μg/day), noradrenaline at 250.6 μg/day (normal 48.6–168.4 μg/day), and dopamine at 1146 μg/day (normal 365–961.5 μg/day). CT imaging revealed an 11.5 × 8.6 cm tumor in the upper to middle pole of the left kidney with a central liquid component. 123I-MIBG scintigraphy indicated increased 123I-MIBG uptake in the tumor. MRI showed a capsule around the kidney tumor with hypo- to iso-intensity on T2-weighted images and reduced diffusion activity. Additionally, a 16.1 × 13.8 cm ovarian tumor was observed. For the ovarian tumor, MRI images initially suggested a fibroma or fibrothecoma, but metastasis from the left renal mass could not be ruled out. An alpha-blocker, doxazosin mesilate, was initiated at 4 mg/day and increased to 16 mg/day over two weeks. Hypertension was not controlled with the alpha-blocker alone, so the patient was given doxazosin mesilate 24 mg, amlodipine 10 mg, and bisoprolol fumarate 2.5 mg. During the clinical course, serum renin activity was 0.5 ng/mL/h, aldosterone concentration was 243 pg/mL, and the renin/aldosterone ratio was 486. A captopril test was positive. No nodules were detected in either adrenal gland. Due to the elevated catecholamine levels, an angiographic contrast agent could not be used. Surgery for the left kidney tumor was planned before further localization.
test_results: Microscopic findings showed that the tumor consisted of a tubular or sheet-like growth pattern of cuboidal to low columnar cells with deeply eosinophilic cytoplasm. Centrally located nuclei were uniformly round with prominent nucleoli. Arrangement of tumor cells in well-defined solid nests separated by a loose hypocellular fibrous stroma, which is characteristic of renal oncocytoma was not observed. Involvement of perirenal fat was identified. The tumor showed positivity along the luminal sides for colloidal iron stain. Immunohistochemically, tumor cells showed diffuse positivity for CK7, c-kit, and E-cadherin, focally positive for vimentin, EMA, CD10, c-kit, and RCC, but were negative for AMACR, Chromogranin A and synaptophysin. Ultrastructure study showed numerous mitochondria with tubulocystic cristae in the cytoplasm of tumor cells.
diagnosis: Chromophobe Renal Cell Carcinoma Oncocytic Variant

case_report: A 12-year-old male patient, with no prior medical history, came to the emergency department after experiencing pain in the left iliac fossa for 20 days, which had progressively worsened. The patient did not report any fever, weight loss, blood in urine, or other urinary symptoms. During the physical examination, pain was noted upon palpation of the left flank, and fist percussion on the same side was also positive.
test_results: Abdominal ultrasound and contrast abdominal MRI showed a left renal mass, retroperitoneal lymphadenopathies in renal hilum and paraaortic location, with no evidence of metastasis. CT of the chest ruled out pulmonary metastasis. Frozen section biopsy of the renal mass and lymph nodes suggested malignant neoplasia, with an absence of INI1 expression, and positive for EMA, AE1/AE1, and vimentin. Hb electrophoresis confirmed a Hb SC disease.

case_report: A 29-year-old female with no prior medical history arrived at the emergency department experiencing a chronic cough and fever for 6 weeks. A chest X-ray revealed mediastinal widening. A subsequent computed tomography (CT) scan identified multiple masses in the mediastinum, lung, liver, and retroperitoneum, with the largest measuring up to 3 cm. Additionally, a large infiltrative mass was observed in the lower pole of the left kidney, extending into the renal pelvis, measuring 5.7 × 5.6 × 6 cm. Initial laboratory tests showed normocytic anemia, a mildly elevated white cell count, and an elevated platelet count (Hg of 8.9 g/dL, MCV 87 fL, WBC 12,000/µL, platelets 573,000/µL). Chemistry labs indicated elevated LDH levels (584 U/L) while kidney and liver function remained normal. An HIV workup returned negative results.
test_results: Pathology results showed atypical large cells with high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio, the chromatin was coarse, and nucleoli were noted with expression of CDX2 and CK7, and loss of expression of INI1.

case_report: A 13-year-old male presented with a right flank mass and occasional dull, localized pain for a duration of 3 months. The patient also experienced intermittent episodes of painless hematuria. There was no history of fever, urinary tract infection, anorexia, or weight loss. Physical examination revealed an 8 × 6 cm, firm, and mobile mass in the right lumbar, right hypochondrium, and umbilical regions, extending across the midline. Laboratory investigations were within normal limits.
test_results: The ultrasonography was suggestive of a large (10.2 × 9.4 × 10.3 cm) nodular heteroechoic mass in the right kidney with calcifications and was invading the renal vessels. The abdomen’s contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) revealed a 9.6 × 7.8 cm heterogeneously enhancing soft tissue density in the mid and lower body of the right kidney with foci of patchy calcifications. The mass was encasing the inferior mesenteric artery and vein. The left kidney had multiple hypodense lesions on the lower pole. There was a large left para-aortic lymph node. There were multiple cortical cysts bilaterally. There was no thrombus in the inferior vena cava. CECT chest was normal with no metastasis. An ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy was performed that demonstrated tumor cells composed of tubules with a mucoid matrix, which on immunohistochemistry was positive for vimentin and epithelial membrane antigen. However, no high-grade mitotic activity, malignant features, or sarcomatoid histology could be appreciated in the sections studied.
diagnosis: Mucinous Tubular and Spindle Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma
Orpha_name: Mucinous tubular and spindle cell renal carcinoma

case_report: A 67-year-old man presented with abdominal pain. Imaging revealed a 4.5 cm mass in the ascending colon with associated pericolonic lymphadenopathy, as well as liver and lung metastases. Additionally, a 3.5 cm mass was identified in the left kidney, described as a hypoenhancing solid mass. A biopsy of a 2.2 cm lesion in the right lower lobe of the lung showed metastatic adenocarcinoma of colon origin. The patient received chemotherapy for metastatic colonic adenocarcinoma, and no biopsy was performed on the kidney lesion.
test_results: A computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a 4.5 cm mass consistent with an ascending colon carcinoma with pericolonic lymphadenopathy, liver, and lung metastases. Also seen was a 3.5 cm left kidney mass. A CT-guided biopsy of a 2.2 cm lesion in the right lower lobe of the lung revealed metastatic adenocarcinoma of colon origin. The kidney lesion was described as a hypoenhancing solid mass. About 7 months later, the renal lesion remained unchanged with chemotherapy whereas other metastatic sites decreased in size. CT-guided FNA and concurrent core biopsies were performed at this time. FNA smears were stained with Diff Quik and Papanicolaou stains. Smears were cellular and showed crowded small and large clusters and branching sheets of bland epithelial cells with uniform round to ovoid nuclei and small but visible nucleoli. Pseudopapillary aggregates lacking vessels in the center were present. Cells ranged in appearance from round/oval epithelial to spindled. Background contained metachromatic mucoid material staining magenta color with Diff Quik and pale blue on Papanicolaou stains. Cell block contained epithelial cells arranged in loose sheets/aggregates and tubular/acinar pattern. No significant atypia, mitosis, or necrosis was present. Core biopsy revealed several small fragments of tumor cells with uniform low grade nuclei that formed a tubular/acinar architecture intermixed with mucinous material. Immunohistochemistry studies showed that the tumor cells were positive for PAX8, CK7, and AMACR and negative for CD10.
diagnosis: Mucinous Tubular and Spindle Cell Carcinoma
Orpha_name: Mucinous tubular and spindle cell renal carcinoma

case_report: A 65-year-old African American male had a right nephrectomy 25 years ago. Five years later, he started hemodialysis due to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) caused by hypertension and insulin-dependent diabetes. In 2010, during an evaluation for a potential renal transplant, a contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen showed multiple small low-attenuation cysts and a 3.1 cm × 2.6 cm nonenhancing lesion in the upper pole of the left kidney, identified as a Bosniak class II renal cyst. No further follow-up was recommended based on these findings. In 2012, he received a living-related kidney transplant and was placed on an immunosuppression regimen that included rabbit antithymocyte globulin (thymoglobulin; Genzyme Corp., Cambridge, MA) for induction (day 0 to day 3 at 1.5 mg/kg) and maintenance therapy with tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and a tapering dose of prednisone. Five months post-transplant, the patient reported hematuria and left leg swelling. An abdominal CT scan showed an enlarging, minimally enhancing hypodense 3.3 × 3.8 cm cystic mass, Bosniak class IV, in the upper pole of the native left kidney. A venous duplex of the left leg revealed deep venous thrombosis extending from the popliteal to the left common femoral vein. The patient underwent thrombolysis, placement of an inferior vena cava filter, and systemic anticoagulation, followed by a laparoscopic left radical nephrectomy without complications.
test_results: Immunohistochemical analysis of the neoplastic cyst-lining cells was positive for racemase, CD10, vimentin, and focal positive staining with CK7, as well as negative staining with EMA.

case_report: A 21-year-old male presented with a progressively enlarging right flank mass since childhood, accompanied by dull aching pain for the past 2 years. The patient also reported constipation and burning sensation during urination. Physical examination revealed a large, nontender lump measuring approximately 18 × 12 cm, firm to hard in consistency, with well-defined borders and side-to-side mobility, located in the right hypochondrium, lumbar, and iliac fossa regions, extending to the epigastric, hypogastric, and umbilical regions. The patient had no significant weight loss or loss of appetite. Renal function tests were within normal limits. Urine bacteriologic examination showed no microorganism growth. Urine samples collected over 3 consecutive days for cytology were deemed unsatisfactory due to insufficient urothelial cells. Abdominal ultrasound revealed an enlarged right kidney with multiple cysts of varying sizes, some containing hypoechoic heterogeneous contents, and a few cysts with multiple septations and small solid components. The left kidney was of normal size with a few small cystic lesions. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging indicated that the right kidney was replaced by numerous cysts, many showing T1 hyperintense signals and fluid-fluid levels suggestive of hemorrhage or high mucinous content. Some cysts had peripheral enhancing solid components and multiple enhancing internal septations. Four to five cystic lesions were classified as Bosniak category IV cystic renal masses. The renal capsule remained intact with no invasion into adjacent structures. The inferior vena cava was compressed at the level of the right kidney, with multiple right perirenal collaterals forming. Imaging established multifocal cystic renal malignancy in the right kidney. The patient underwent a right radical nephrectomy, and a multiloculated solid cystic mass replacing the entire right kidney was sent for further evaluation.
test_results: The microscopic examination revealed a tumor composed of variable-sized tubules, anastomosing papillae, and variable-sized cysts. These cysts were separated by fibrous septa. The tubules and cysts were lined by a single layer of low cuboidal to columnar cells and many hobnail cells. These cells were mild to moderately pleomorphic, having round nuclei, conspicuous nucleoli (International Society of Urological Pathology grade 3), and clear to abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm. Areas of calcification and a focal area of ossification were also seen. The solid areas had papillae with fibrovascular cores lined by cuboidal to low columnar cells with moderate to abundant dense, eosinophilic cytoplasm. Focal areas of necrosis were seen. Mitoses were infrequent. The ureter and renal sinus were free of tumor invasion. No lymphovascular or perineural invasions were seen. Eight lymph nodes were resected, and all were free from tumor invasion. No sarcomatoid or rhabdoid features were identified. The capsule and perinephric fat were free from tumor invasion. The tumor cells demonstrated immunoreactivity for PAX8, vimentin, and AMACR. The tumor cells were not immunoreactive for CK7 and CD117. No immunoreactivity for estrogen receptors and progesterone receptors was noted in the stroma.

case_report: A 35-year-old Japanese woman presented with left-sided back pain. Imaging via computed tomography showed a hemorrhagic cyst measuring 7×8 cm located in the upper pole of her left kidney. Despite her relatively young age, she declined further examination or surgical treatment. Follow-up was conducted every 6 months using magnetic resonance imaging. During this period, she remained asymptomatic, including the absence of back pain. Approximately 3 years later, she reported left-sided back pain again. Subsequent magnetic resonance imaging indicated an increase in the size of the left renal cyst to 10×12 cm, with a slightly enhanced cystic wall. The cyst was classified as Bosniak type III based on radiological findings. A left nephrectomy was performed.
test_results: The tumor showed circumscribed proliferation with cystically dilated tubules. The tubules and cysts were lined by a single layer of flat, hobnail, and cuboidal cells. Papillary structures were observed within the cysts. The tumor cells were strongly positive for E-cadherin and P504S. The tumor cells did not stain positive for WT1, cytokeratin (CK) 34β12, transcription factor E3 (TFE3), and CD10.

case_report: A 42-year-old male with no history of exposure to industrial toxins or radioactive substances was admitted in November 2018. He presented with ecchymosis on the left lower limb persisting for over a month, gingival bleeding, and fatigue for 10 days, which had worsened over the past 2 days. Physical examination revealed anemia, scattered mucosal and skin bleeding spots, normal heart rhythm, clear lung sounds, a soft abdomen, no palpable liver or spleen below the ribs, and no lower limb edema. Initial blood chemistry results showed a white blood cell count of 8.1 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin concentration of 69 g/L, platelet count of 16 × 10^9/L, prothrombin time of 14.6 seconds, activated partial thromboplastin time of 21.4 seconds, thrombin time of 21.5 seconds, potassium level of 3.71 mmol/L, sodium level of 141 mmol/L, calcium level of 1.89 mmol/L, γ-glutamine acylase level of 144 U/L, total protein level of 57.2 g/L, and albumin level of 33.2 g/L.
test_results: Bone marrow (BM) analysis revealed abnormal promyelocytes (89.2%) of different sizes with quasi-round shapes and tumor-like processes on the edge of the cytoplasm, medium amounts of cytoplasm, blue staining, purplish red granules in the cytoplasm, round nuclei, visible depressions, loose and fine chromatin, and visible nucleoli. In addition, erythroid differentiation was inhibited, megakaryocytes were absent, and platelets were rare. Fluorescence in situ hybridization of the BM showed that 68% of the 400 cells analyzed within the detection range revealed the presence of the PML/RARa fusion gene. Further genetic screening revealed mutations to NRAS (NM_002524,cxon2:c.G35A:p.G120rs121913237) and TET (NM_001127208,cxon11:c.A5284G:p.11762Y). Flow cytometry analysis of the BM revealed the presence of abnormal cells that were positive for CD117, CD13, CD33, CD38, CD64, CD123, CD58, and cMPO, with partial expression of CD71, but negative for CD19, CD3, and CD34. BM morphological analysis revealed that 31.0% of the monocytes were primitive and immature with varied cell sizes, medium to rich cytoplasm, large nuclei, fine chromatin that was twisted and folded, visible nucleoli, granulocyte content of 6.5%, some vacuoles throughout the cytoplasm, active red proliferation, visible plasma, reticular cells with normal morphologies, 237 megakaryocytes in one smear, and visible platelets. Flow cytometry revealed that 44.75% of the primitive immature cells were nucleated and positive for CD34, CD38, CD13, CD15, CD117, CD33, CD7, and HLA-DR, but negative for CD3 and CD19. Myeloid expression was abnormal, which conformed to the AML phenotype. The PML-RARα gene was negative by fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis. Qualitative detection of 38 fusion genes specific to leukemia was also negative. Gene mutation analysis by next generation sequencing identified an insertion mutation to the CEBPA gene (c.912_913insTTG (p.Lys304_Gln305insLeu; heterozygous mutation frequency, 28.5%) and a code shift mutation (c.326del (p.Pro109ArgfsTer51; heterozygous). BM cytogenetic studies revealed a normal karyotype of 46, xy (20).
diagnosis: Acute Myeloid Leukemia with CEBPA double mutation
Orpha_name: Acute myeloid leukemia with CEBPA somatic mutations

case_report: A 76-year-old male with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus visited the ophthalmology clinic due to excessive tearing for approximately 6 months. He had previously undergone a nasolacrimal recanalization procedure, which did not alleviate his symptoms. The patient reported no fever, chills, night sweats, or significant weight loss. He also denied experiencing new vision loss, ocular pain, redness, or photophobia. His other medical and surgical history was unremarkable. During the examination, a mass was observed on the nasal conjunctiva near the medial canthus of the right eye, which was subsequently removed.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed effacement of the normal architecture and replacement by closely packed variable sized and shaped non-polarized follicles that are evenly distributed throughout the specimen. The mantle zone is generally attenuated. Most of the follicles revealed monomorphic appearance and are predominantly composed of small lymphoid cells with both cleaved and noncleaved centrocytes. Most of the nuclei are characteristically twisted, indented, elongated, and angulated with inconspicuous nucleoli. Centroblasts constitute <16 cells per 400× field on average within the nodules. Immunoperoxidase studies were performed and revealed that the atypical lymphocytes mark as CD20-positive B-lymphocytes that coexpress CD10, BCL6, and LMO2, and aberrantly coexpress BCL2. The nodules are centered on CD21-positive follicular dendritic cell meshworks. CD3 highlights reactive background T-lymphocytes.

case_report: A 15-year-old boy, in good general health, visited the emergency department at Dhahran Eye Specialist Hospital due to a two-month history of increasing swelling near the medial canthus of his left eye. Examination revealed a pink mass on the conjunctiva of the left eye's medial aspect. The mass was firm, well encapsulated, mobile, and had a broad base with negative transillumination. The right eye also exhibited a small, firm, and mobile conjunctival mass on its medial aspect. Other ocular structures appeared normal. No lymph nodes were palpable during the examination. Anterior segment optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed no signs of retinal extension.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed lymphoid tissue with expanded and irregular serpiginous follicles, minimal mantle cell zone, and reduced interfollicular space. The germinal centers were predominantly composed of blastoid cells with numerous mitotic figures and multiple tingible body macrophages, giving the germinal centers a 'starry sky' appearance. The blastoid cells were intermediate in size and had nuclear pleomorphism and multiple nucleoli. A few centrocytes and plasma cells were also present within the germinal centers. Reactive follicles were present at the periphery of the specimen. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) examination was positive for CD20, CD79a, BCL6, and CD10, and negative for BCL2 and MUM1. The interfollicular spaces contained T-cells (CD3+). The CD21 and CD23 positivity highlighted the presence of an expanded follicular dendritic cell meshwork. The Ki-67 proliferation index within the germinal centers was approximately 95%.

case_report: A 71-year-old male with type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypothyroidism, managed at home with icosapent ethyl, insulin (aspart and glargine), levothyroxine, and rosuvastatin, was admitted to the hospital due to worsening cognitive difficulties, slow speech, and severe fatigue over the past week. He also experienced slow body movements and a sluggish gait for several months. Upon admission, his medication was adjusted to include omega-3 (non-formulary replacement), enoxaparin for prophylaxis, and acetaminophen as needed for headache or pain. During the examination, the patient exhibited long pauses and difficulty maintaining conversations. His daughter provided his history due to his confusion. He was normally independent in his daily activities. He denied symptoms such as cough, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia, polyuria, oliguria, or rashes. The rest of the review of systems was unremarkable. Physical examination revealed that he appeared tired and exhausted but not in distress or pain. Heart and lung sounds were normal, and the cranial nerve examination was unremarkable. The neurological exam was limited due to poor interaction, and the remaining physical examination was normal. Vital signs included a blood pressure of 132/65 mmHg, heart rate of 65 bpm, temperature of 36.1°C, respiratory rate of 18/min, and oxygen saturation of 99% on room air. Initial laboratory workup indicated hypo-osmolar hyponatremia with a sodium level of 122 meq/L (normal range: 135-145 meq/L), serum osmolarity of 275 mOsm, serum uric acid of 2.3 mg/dL (normal range: 3.6-8 mg/dL), TSH of 3.5 mcIU/mL (normal range: 0.45-4.5 mcIU/mL), and AM cortisol of 24 mcg/dL (normal range: 4.3-22.4 mcg/dL). Free thyroxine (FT4) was not measured at admission but was 1.3 ng/dL (normal range: 0.82-1.77 ng/dL) four months later, with a TSH of 1.02 mcIU/mL while on the same dose of levothyroxine. Urine studies showed a urine sodium level of 92 meq/L and osmolarity of 672 mOsm. Brain MRI did not reveal any structural abnormalities. A chest CT showed mild bronchial wall thickening and peripheral ground-glass density in the left lower lobe. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered empirically for possible community-acquired pneumonia. SIADH was managed with fluid restriction of 1.5 L/day and urea 15 mg BID. Sodium levels gradually improved to 133 meq/L by discharge. Follow-up in the clinic with nephrology, neurology, and pulmonology showed normal serum sodium (133 mEq/L) and elevated urine osmolality (774 mOsm/L), leading to the continuation of the urea solution.
test_results: The patient was found to have mild arm rigidity, bradykinesia, resting tremors, and a stiff abnormal gait.

case_report: A 75-year-old female with a history of hypertension for over 20 years, atrial fibrillation, and dyspnea with signs of progressive heart failure of unknown cause during the past 10 years. Heart surgery was performed due to higher levels of mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, including mitral and tricuspid valve annuloplasty. She experienced acroparesthesia since childhood. Earlier medical documentation indicated a creatinine level of 125 µmol/L and proteinuria slightly above reference values. The patient was not interested in further examinations. An echocardiographic examination performed earlier showed moderate left ventricular hypertrophy with hyperechogenic and hypokinetic left ventricular walls and a reduced ejection fraction of the left ventricle at 30% according to two-dimensional transthoracic imaging.
test_results: Alpha-galactosidase level was 1.7 µmol/L/h, lyso-GL-3 was 7.5 ng/mL, and a heterozygous mutation was detected (c.[902G>T]).

case_report: A 6-year-old boy presented shortly after birth with a red rash and hemorrhagic blisters on the palms, which later spread across the entire body. This was accompanied by solitary subcutaneous nodules and purple swelling around the eyes. The rash worsened during fever episodes. He was hospitalized multiple times due to severe inflammation. No vaccinations were given after 3 months of age. Three skin biopsies from active lesions showed inflammation with lymphocytes, neutrophils, macrophages, and mast cells (CD117+), with some areas showing leukocytoclasis. At 1 year and 5 months, he was started on methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/day, which had a reasonable effect on the rash and fevers, but symptoms relapsed when the dose was reduced. Hydroxychloroquine and methotrexate were tried as alternatives but were discontinued due to lack of effect. At 2 years and 10 months, he presented with daily high fevers up to 39.9°C, persistent skin eruptions with nodules, red and purple papules and macules on the head, body, limbs, palms, and soles, and purple swelling around the eyes. Hypertrichosis was noted all over the body, and there was significant lipodystrophy in the subcutaneous adipose tissue. The arms, shoulders, and face had a well-defined muscle outline, giving a false impression of increased muscularity. The parents reported episodes of joint pain and swelling in the knees and fingers, but there was no objective evidence of contractures or joint space narrowing. The face showed atrophic facial muscles and absence of buccal fat pads, giving an aged appearance, along with hypertelorism and epicanthus. Other symptoms included cough, rapid breathing, and enlarged liver. The patient was significantly stunted for his age, with a height of -4.1 SDS and weight of -2.3 SDS. Bone age was 1 year and 3 months according to Greulich and Pyle’s atlas (<-2.0 SDS). Blood tests showed elevated CRP (114.09 mg/L), neutrophilia, and anemia with serum iron < 2 mcmol/L. No cardiac, pulmonary, or neurological involvement was found at the time.
test_results: The patient was found to have compound heterozygous mutations in the PSMB8 gene (p.A92V/p.K105Q).

case_report: A 20-year-old male presented with severe lower abdominal pain persisting for four days. He reported a dull aching pain in the left iliac region for the past month, which had intensified over the last four days. The pain was not accompanied by fever, burning sensation during urination, or vomiting. The pain subsided with the use of antispasmodics and rest. The patient had no notable past medical history. There was no consanguinity between his parents, and his elder brother was healthy with two children. On physical examination, the patient appeared phenotypically male with well-developed external male genitalia and normal male hair distribution. The external phallus was of normal size, and the urethral orifice was in the typical position without hypospadias. The right testis was located in the right scrotal sac and was of normal size, while the left scrotum was empty. There was no lymphadenopathy. The patient reported experiencing erections but had no history of sexual activity. Tenderness was noted in the left iliac region, but no mass was palpable. Laboratory investigations showed normal levels of total Testosterone (482.82 ng/dl) and Estradiol (16 pg/ml) for a male. Luteinizing hormone (16.32 mIU/ml) and follicle-stimulating hormone (28.74 mIU/L) levels were elevated. Serum Prolactin and Dehydroepiandrosterone levels, as well as thyroid function tests, were within normal ranges.
test_results: The cytogenetic analysis of the karyotype showed genotype 46XY. Abdominopelvic ultrasonography showed a well-circumscribed, ovoid, heterogeneously hypoechoic lesion of 2.2×2.6×1.3 cm size in the left iliac region. It also showed the presence of a small uterus adjacent to the bladder wall. MRI showed multinodular, sharply defined, 2.1×2.6×1.2cm homogeneous tumour of low signal intensity on T2-weighted images and areas of signal intensity heterogeneity related to haemorrhage or necrosis.

case_report: A 16-year-old individual, raised as female, visited the outpatient department with concerns of primary amenorrhea and absence of secondary sexual characteristics. The patient's medical and surgical history was unremarkable, and there was no family history of pubertal delay. The patient was born from a nonconsanguineous marriage. Physical examination revealed average build and nourishment, with a height of 170.18 cm, weight of 61.5 kg, and a body mass index of 21.2. Blood pressure was within the normal range for the age group. Breast development was at Tanner Stage II, and axillary and pubic hair were sparse, also at Tanner Stage II. Abdominal examination showed a soft abdomen with no organomegaly or masses in the inguinal region. The vulvar region was well developed, including normal labia majora, labia minora, clitoris, and external openings of the urethra and vagina. The vaginal introitus measured 1.5 cm, and the vaginal length was 3 cm. No Turner stigmata were observed. Routine biochemical investigations and hormone levels were conducted, revealing a follicle-stimulating hormone level of 128.53 mIU/ml, luteinizing hormone level of 37.43 IU/L, and an anti-Mullerian hormone level of 0.46 ng/ml.
test_results: Karyotype report shows pattern 46 XY normal male chromosome. Phenotype female. Ultrasonography suggestive of small uterus with a thin endometrium. Bilateral ovaries are small in size. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pelvis suggestive of perineal vaginal atresia/hypoplasia with poorly visualized fallopian tubes and ovaries, uterine remnant visualized, endometrium atrophic.

case_report: A 28-day-old phenotypic female infant was brought to the pediatric endocrinology clinic at Al-Zahra Hospital, affiliated with Isfahan University of Medical Sciences, due to poor weight gain and lethargy. She was born full-term with a birth weight of 3250 grams (50th percentile), a length of 51 cm (50th percentile), and a head circumference of 34 cm (50th percentile). The infant had no perinatal complications and was the first child of nonconsanguineous parents. Upon admission, she exhibited lethargy without a history of vomiting or diarrhea. There was no family history of similar presentations or endocrine disorders. The infant had not taken any medications except for vitamin A+D. Physical examination revealed lethargy, a depressed fontanelle, mild dehydration, and decreased skin turgor. Skin examination showed mild hyperpigmentation, including in the oral cavity. The external genitalia appeared to be of normal female type without ambiguity. No abdominal or inguinal masses were detected during the abdominal examination. Her body weight was 2900 grams, length was 51 cm, and head circumference was 33.5 cm, all below the 5th percentiles. Vital signs included a blood pressure of 60/40 mmHg, a respiratory rate of 39/min, a pulse rate of 112/min, and a body temperature of 37.1°C. Initial biochemical tests showed serum sodium at 129 meq/l (normal range: 135-145), serum potassium at 6.1 meq/l (normal range: 3.5-5.5), blood sugar at 45 mg/dl, blood urea nitrogen at 73 mg/dl, serum creatinine at 0.5 mg/dl, negative C-reactive protein, and negative blood culture. Venous blood gas results were pH: 7.3, HCO3: 11.9 mmol/L, and PCO2: 35 mmHg, indicating metabolic acidosis.
test_results: Cortisol: 0.2 μg/dl, ACTH: >1000 pg/ml, 17 OHP: 0.3 ng/ml. Ultrasonographic examination revealed small hypoplastic uterus (6*7*3 ml) or atretic ovaries and adrenal glands had normal sizes.
Orpha_name: Classic congenital lipoid adrenal hyperplasia due to STAR deficency

case_report: The patient is a 9-year-old female with no significant medical history but a family history of cardiac events. She experienced a witnessed sudden cardiac arrest while running and was transferred to the emergency hospital. QT prolongation was observed under mild hypothermia the next day, and propranolol was initiated. Upon presentation at our hospital 18 days after the event, she exhibited both QT prolongation and bigeminy of ventricular premature contractions on Holter electrocardiography (ECG). Propranolol treatment was continued. Conventional genetic testing results showed no pathogenic mutations in genes related to long QT syndrome.
test_results: Genetic testing using next-generation sequencing (NGS) revealed a RYR2 mutation.

case_report: A 16-year-old male experienced recurrent episodes of syncope triggered by physical exertion and was referred to our hospital following defibrillation at a local emergency department (ED). He lost consciousness during a volleyball test at school, which was also emotionally stressful. Paramedics found him pulseless and initiated cardiopulmonary resuscitation. An initial ECG at the local ED showed ventricular fibrillation. His arrhythmia was converted to sinus rhythm after defibrillation, but he remained stuporous and had repeated episodes of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia (VT). Upon referral to our hospital, ECG monitoring in the ED and intensive care unit revealed intermittent nonsustained VT and bidirectional VT. When the patient became agitated, his heart rate increased, and the ECG showed nonsustained polymorphic VT despite intravenous administration of a β-blocker. He was sedated and placed on mechanical ventilation. Two days later, his heart rate was regular, and no additional episodes of VT were observed. Sedation was stopped, and the patient was weaned from the ventilator. His ECG showed a sinus rhythm with a corrected QT interval of 423 msec. Routine laboratory findings, including electrolytes and two-dimensional echocardiography, were unremarkable. The patient's detailed history included several episodes of syncope since the age of 8 years associated with physical activities such as sprinting, playing football, and fighting with a sibling. His father also experienced an episode of syncope associated with sprinting at the age of 9 years. No other family members had histories of syncope or sudden cardiac death.
test_results: The patient and his family underwent a genetic analysis, and his father and mother each had one different de novo missense mutation in RyR2 (exon 97 c.14009T>A p.L4670H in the father and exon 37 c.5428G>C p.V1810L in the mother). The symptomatic proband inherited both mutations. An exercise ECG test and epinephrine infusion test (intravenous bolus of 0.1 µg/kg followed by continuous infusion at rates of 0.1 µg/kg per minute) were performed. However, only premature ventricular complex (PVC) bigeminy was induced with no episodes of syncope during the exercise ECG test and epinephrine only increased his heart rate without an arrhythmia.

case_report: A 13-year-old female presented with a one-year history of Raynaud's phenomenon and thickened, indurated skin on her fingers, followed by a one-month history of digital pitting scars on her right index finger. She had no past or family history of rheumatic or autoimmune diseases. Examination revealed normal vital signs, a mask-like face, and moderate thickening and induration of the skin on her fingers, hands, forearms, feet, and lower legs. Her modified Rodnan skin score was 23. Digital pitting scars were noted on the right index finger. Erythema was observed on the extensor surfaces of her knees and elbows, resembling dermatomyositis, but without significant heliotrope rash, muscle weakness, or muscle pain. Laboratory tests showed mild elevation of serum creatine kinase (CK) at 648 U/L and aldolase at 16.8 U/L. There was no increase in C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), or other inflammation markers. Serum levels of N-terminal pro b-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) and KL-6 were within normal limits. Autoantibody levels were normal or negative. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lower legs did not reveal significant skeletal muscle inflammation.
test_results: Needle electromyography revealed myopathic changes. Muscle biopsy of the triceps brachii revealed mild perivascular inflammatory cells infiltration, muscle fiber necrosis, and regeneration.
diagnosis: Juvenile Systemic Sclerosis Overlapped with Dermatomyositis

case_report: A 76-year-old Japanese woman presented with elevated neutrophil levels, mild kidney dysfunction, and protein in her urine and was referred to our Department in year X. Her elevated neutrophil levels were first identified during a medical check-up at age 74 (year X-2), and her neutrophil count continued to rise. Her serum G-CSF was 161 pg/mL, significantly higher than the normal range (< 39.0 pg/mL). An 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (18F-FDG-PET/CT) scan showed high uptake in the bone marrow but no signs of a malignant solid tumor or bacterial infection. Fluorescence in situ hybridization on peripheral blood smears showed no clonality in her neutrophils. She had tested positive for urinary occult blood since age 50 and developed proteinuria after her neutrophil count exceeded 20.0 × 10^3/μL in year X-1. Her blood pressure was 118/59 mmHg, and other vital signs were normal. Physical examinations were unremarkable. Upon admission in year X, laboratory tests showed: white blood cell (WBC) count of 35.9 × 10^3/μL (neutrophil count of 31.3 × 10^3/μL, 87.2% of WBC count); hemoglobin level of 11.5 g/dL; platelet count of 27.3 × 10^4/μL; serum creatinine of 0.85 mg/dL; estimated glomerular filtration rate of 49.4 mL/min/1.73 m^2; blood urea nitrogen of 16 mg/dL; lactate dehydrogenase of 170 U/L; total protein/albumin of 8.0/3.6 g/dL; and immunoglobulin G (IgG) of 2901 mg/dL. Serum immunoelectrophoresis showed a monoclonal IgG λ peak, with normal levels of other immunoglobulins, and bone marrow aspiration revealed less than 10% clonal plasma cells, indicating monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS). Tumor markers including carcinoembryonic antigen, squamous cell carcinoma antigen, and cytokeratin fragment were within normal ranges. C-reactive protein and complement levels were normal, and tests for antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor were negative. Tests for hepatitis B and C viruses were negative. Urinary protein excretion was 2.55 g per gram urinary creatinine, with a proteinuria selectivity index of 0.17. Urinary sediment analysis showed hematuria (20–29 red blood cells/high-power field) and granular casts.
test_results: A renal biopsy was performed, and sections evaluated by light microscopy showed many lobulated glomeruli. Mesangial proliferation and focal double contouring of the glomerular capillary walls were also present. Additionally, endocapillary proliferation was observed in the glomeruli. Immunoperoxidase staining for neutrophil elastase revealed some neutrophils infiltrating the glomeruli. Double immunofluorescence staining for neutrophils and macrophages showed that the infiltration of macrophages was mainly around the glomeruli, and the glomeruli contained more neutrophils than macrophages. We identified intratubular cellular casts and interstitial expansion in the tubulointerstitial area. Expansion of the subendothelial space suggesting injury of glomerular endothelial cells and effacement of the podocyte foot processes were seen in sections evaluated by electron microscopy. There were no electron dense deposits.

case_report: A 49-year-old Japanese male was admitted to the hospital due to worsening renal function and swelling. He was diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes at 42 years old. At 46, he had surgery for diabetic foot gangrene and laser treatment for diabetic retinopathy. Through strict diet control, his weight decreased from 115 kg to 90 kg, and his hemoglobin A1c levels improved from around 10% to 5.4% without the use of hypoglycemic agents. During that period, his serum creatinine ranged from 0.9 to 1.2 mg/dL, and his urine protein excretion was 1.77 g/day. He had not sought medical care since then. One month prior to admission, he experienced a fever and consulted his previous doctor. Urinalysis revealed pyuria, and he was treated with ceftriaxone for a urinary tract infection, which resolved the fever. Despite this, his serum creatinine rose to 4.3 mg/dL within a few days, and he developed leg edema, leading to his referral to our hospital. Upon admission, he was 169 cm tall and weighed 85.8 kg. His blood pressure was 178/84 mm Hg, and his temperature was 36.7 °C. Significant pitting edema was noted in both legs. Neurological examination indicated decreased vibration sensation (6 s/6 s) and numbness in the soles of both feet. Laboratory results showed hypoalbuminemia (albumin, 1.9 g/dL) and acute kidney injury (urea nitrogen, 42 mg/dL; creatinine, 3.35 mg/dL). Elevated serum C-reactive protein (CRP) was observed (6.3 mg/dL). Serum complement levels were low (CH50, 37 U/mL; C3, 35.0 mg/dL; and C4, 34.0 mg/dL).
test_results: The anti-streptolysin O (ASO) concentration was 1424 IU/mL. Twenty-four-hour urinary protein excretion was 7.33 g, and the urine sediment contained 11 to 30 red cells and less than 1 white cell per high-power field.

case_report: A 62-year-old male reported experiencing a gradual decrease in vision in both eyes over the past six months. He had no other systemic health issues. His best-corrected visual acuity was measured at 6/12 in both eyes. Examination of the anterior segment revealed pseudophakia in both eyes. Fundus examination of both eyes showed a dull gray area at the fovea with abnormal blood vessels. Additionally, the right eye exhibited asteroid hyalosis. Fundus autofluorescence imaging of the right eye displayed a pinpoint area of increased autofluorescence at the fovea, while the left eye showed a moderate increase in foveal autofluorescence.
test_results: Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) of BE revealed inner retinal cavitation with preservation of the internal limiting membrane and mild foveal thinning. SD-OCT revealed a subfoveal dome-shaped elevation suggestive of SFD along with hyporeflective cystoid spaces in the inner and outer retinal layers suggestive of IRF. An OCT angiography (OCTA) was done which showed a minimal increase in space between vessels in the superficial and the deep vascular network in BE.

case_report: A 56-year-old female patient presented in 2019 with visual acuity (VA) of 20/40 in both eyes at University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust. The patient received panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) treatment in the left eye. Laboratory results showed an HbA1c level of 6.9% (51.9 mmol/mol), indicating the need for good diabetic control. In 2020, the VA in the right eye declined to 20/120. In 2021, additional laser treatment was recommended for the left eye due to neovascularization elsewhere (NVE).
test_results: Fluorescein angiography revealed areas of non-perfusion, focal hyperfluorescence in the area of NVE and bilateral temporal diffuse macular leakage.

case_report: A 70-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital with dizziness lasting for 1 day without chest pain. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 148/62 mmHg, heart rate of 74 beats/minute, and respiratory rate of 20 breaths/minute. General physical and systemic examinations were normal, with no abnormal heart sounds or murmurs detected. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (diffusion-weighted imaging sequence) indicated a fresh lacunar infarction in the left parietal lobe and the right frontotemporal lobe. On the second day, routine electrocardiography showed ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Laboratory tests revealed a significantly elevated troponin I level. Aspirin, clopidogrel, and unfractionated heparin treatment were initiated immediately. Coronary angiography demonstrated subtotal occlusion and a thrombus-like filling defect in the right coronary artery, while the left coronary arteries appeared normal. Coronary angioplasty and stenting (3.0 × 29 mm) were successfully performed, achieving a Thrombolysis In Myocardial Infarction grade 3 flow. Initially, the patient had a slightly elevated platelet count (466 × 103/mm3), which doubled to 978 × 103/mm3 over 3 days.
test_results: Bone marrow biopsy showed a markedly high number of megakaryocytes, which were clustered and increased in size. Genetic testing showed 30% mutation of the JAK2 V617F gene, while the BCR-ABL gene was negative.

case_report: Patient 2 is a 38-year-old female with a history of SARS-CoV-2 infection in October 2020. Prior to the infection, her typical sleep duration was approximately 9 hours per day. Around 4 to 6 weeks post-infection, she began experiencing significant daytime sleepiness and an increased need for sleep, leading to frequent absences from work. Eight months following the infection, she continues to face substantial challenges with concentration and has an overwhelming need for naps in the afternoon.
test_results: An actigraphy documented a mean nocturnal sleep time of over 11 h per night on weekdays and about 14 h per night on weekends. A 48 h sleep laboratory workup was performed about 1 month later, i.e., 9 months after infection. The borderline MSLT results (mean sleep latency 8.1 min).

case_report: A 27-year-old female presented with a decade-long history of difficulty initiating sleep, excessive daytime sleepiness, and sleep drunkenness. These symptoms began mildly and progressively worsened. The excessive daytime sleepiness was accompanied by tiredness, exhaustion, and unrefreshing naps. Recently, these symptoms have significantly impacted her daily activities, including watching television, talking on the phone, conversing, and waiting at a stop while driving. She reported no loud snoring, gasping for air, or wheezing during sleep. She also did not experience sudden weakness in her limbs or neck, nor did she feel different while falling asleep or waking up. Her Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) score was 19 at the initial visit. She had previously used cannabidiol (CBD) gummies and melatonin to improve sleep quality, but these were not effective; melatonin caused a sensation of paralysis at night. Her medical history includes well-controlled hypothyroidism managed with levothyroxine (37.5 micrograms), with recent thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels within normal limits. She also has psoriasis and migraine headaches, both well-managed with medications. Additionally, she has irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and lactose intolerance, managed with a gluten- and lactose-free diet and probiotics. She occasionally consumes alcohol but not to aid sleep. Physical examination was unremarkable, with no sinus tenderness, increased neck circumference, elevated body mass index (BMI), or other notable findings. A home sleep study showed an Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI) of 3.5 and a Respiratory Disturbance Index (RDI) of 3.5, which did not indicate obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) as the cause of her symptoms. The patient was advised to follow proper sleep hygiene measures and was prescribed 100 mg of modafinil for daytime symptoms. She was scheduled for further evaluation and instructed to return in six weeks if there was no improvement.
test_results: Individual latencies for the naps were as follows: nap #1, 3.5 minutes; nap #2, 1.5 minutes, and nap #3, 0.1 minutes. MSLT revealed a mean sleep latency of 1.70 minutes with no REM onsets observed. The patient remained awake in between naps well during the study.

case_report: A 25-year-old female with no history of trauma, significant medical conditions, or family medical history presented with a white patch on her nose that had been present for 3 years. Initially, it appeared as erythema, gradually expanded, and eventually became a white patch without any symptoms. Physical examination showed a well-defined, mildly atrophic porcelain-white patch with a violaceous border on the left side of her nose. Detailed inspection of the affected area revealed comedo-like openings on the surface of the lesion. No other areas were affected, and the systemic examination was normal.
test_results: Histopathologic examination of the lesion showed atrophy of the epidermis, follicular plugging, focal basal cell vacuolization, and homogenization of dermal collagen along with a moderate lymphomononuclear cell infiltrate.

case_report: A 33-year-old male industry worker reported experiencing painful and itchy skin lesions on his right foot, leg, and thigh for the past six months. The lesions first appeared on the right foot and gradually spread upwards to the leg and thigh. There was no notable past or family medical history. Physical examination revealed a linear, hypopigmented, atrophic plaque with follicular plugging on the right foot and leg, extending to the anterolateral aspect of the right thigh. Laboratory tests, including hemogram, liver, renal, and thyroid function tests, were within normal limits.
test_results: Histopathology showed thinning of the epidermis with hyperkeratosis and follicular plugging, with the basal layer showing hydropic degeneration. The upper dermis showed homogenization of the collagen and edema with mild inflammatory infiltrate.

case_report: A 29-year-old Sinhalese Sri Lankan female, previously in good health, presented with unexpectedly high blood pressure. She is a mother of two children and reported no history of hypertension during her pregnancies. She also noted a decrease in appetite and perceived weight loss over the past few months. On physical examination, her blood pressure was recorded at 180/120 mmHg on two separate occasions, consistent in both arms. Her pulse rate was 88 beats per minute, with no delays between radial or femoral pulses. There were no detectable renal masses, and no bruits were heard over the carotid, renal, or femoral arteries. Cardiovascular and central nervous system examinations were normal, and fundoscopy showed no signs of retinopathy. There were no peripheral signs of atherosclerosis or endocrine disorders. Laboratory tests, including renal function tests, serum electrolytes, urine analysis, complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and liver function tests, were all within normal limits. Both the electrocardiogram and transthoracic echocardiogram showed no abnormalities. An ultrasound scan of the abdomen revealed that the left kidney was not visualized.
test_results: DTPA renogram showed a small left kidney with normal perfusion and function of the right kidney. CTA revealed significant stenosis of the left main renal artery and an accessory renal artery supplying the lower pole of the left kidney.

case_report: A 12-year-old Chinese boy presented with swelling and pain in the right 1st metatarsophalangeal joint, along with tophi, starting at age 10. Subsequently, arthritis affected both ankles. Physical examination revealed tenderness, redness, and swelling in the right 1st metatarsophalangeal joint and both ankles, with tophi present. Laboratory results showed serum creatinine at 61.7 μmol/L (reference range 50-80 μmol/L) and blood urea nitrogen at 5.65 mmol/L (reference range 2.9–7.14 mmol/L). Hyperuricaemia was noted with serum uric acid at 461.4 μmol/L (reference range 155–357 μmol/L) and decreased uric acid excretion (24-hour urine uric acid at 0.51 mmol, urinary uric acid excretion at 0.109 mg·kg−1·h−1, urinary uric acid clearance at 1.22 ml/min per 1.73m2, and fractional excretion of uric acid at 1.1%). Blood pressure, routine urinalysis, serum complements, ANA, anti-dsDNA, ANCA, rheumatoid factor, electrolytes, and kidney ultrasound were normal or negative. CT of the feet showed multiple bone destruction and bony defects in the ankles and feet, along with soft tissue swelling. Renal biopsy under light microscopy revealed one-in-six glomeruli with global sclerosis and extensive tubular atrophy. Electron microscopy showed vacuolar and granular degeneration of renal tubules, segmental basement membrane thickening (500–1000 nm), interstitial fibrosis, inflammatory cell infiltration, and foot process fusion. Direct immunofluorescence staining was negative for immunoglobulin and complement. Family history included an older brother diagnosed with gout at age 17, a mother diagnosed with gout and stage 4 CKD at age 38, a cousin diagnosed with gout at age 28, an uncle who died of gout and CKD at age 33, and a maternal grandfather and two of his brothers who died of similar conditions in their mid-forties. None had other chronic diseases. Informed consent was obtained from all participants, and clinical data, blood, and urine samples were collected from 3 affected and 8 unaffected family members.
test_results: Genetic testing revealed that the 3 affected members carried a novel heterozygous missense variant (c.674C > G, p.T225R) in the UMOD gene. This likely pathogenic variant was not found in 8 unaffected members.

case_report: A 28-year-old male, the first child of healthy parents with a consanguineous marriage, was admitted to Hasheminejad hospital presenting with high blood pressure, swelling in the lower extremities, and elevated serum creatinine levels. His medical history included elevated uric acid levels and gout. Upon admission, his blood pressure was recorded at 160/90, and pitting edema was observed in both lower limbs, with no abnormalities noted in other organs. Sonographic examination revealed the right kidney measured 114 mm and contained a thick-walled cyst measuring 23 × 24 mm, while the left kidney measured 90 mm and showed increased cortical echogenicity in both kidneys. Doppler sonography indicated RI values of 0.65 in the right kidney and 0.7 in the left kidney. Family history included consanguinity between his parents, an elder brother diagnosed with gout and renal failure at age 33, and two cousins with elevated uric acid levels and kidney stones. Laboratory tests showed renal failure with normal kidney size. A renal biopsy indicated advanced glomerulosclerosis in a focal and segmental pattern, severe tubular atrophy, and proportional fibrosis, mostly secondary, along with mild to moderate arterionephrosclerosis.
test_results: Sequencing analysis showed that the patient is homozygous for a novel nonsense mutation, c.589G>T; p.E197X, in exon 3 of the UMOD gene.

case_report: A 17-year-old male reported experiencing pain and swelling in the small joints of his hands, feet, knees, ankles, elbows, and wrists for the past 2 years, along with nodules on the right little finger and the left ear lobe. Physical examination revealed swellings on the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints and the third proximal interphalangeal joints. Tophi measuring 2–3 cm with whitish discharge were observed on the right little finger, and a 0.5 cm tophus was noted on the left ear lobule. His blood pressure was within normal limits. Laboratory tests showed a serum uric acid level of 13.9 mg/dl and a serum creatinine level of 1.4 mg/dl. The fractional excretion of uric acid was 2.93%. Ultrasonography indicated normal-sized kidneys with normal echogenicity. Multiple family members were affected by a similar condition; some exhibited only joint issues, while others had both joint and kidney problems. His father passed away at the age of 42 due to chronic kidney disease and had joint issues. Additionally, one of his elder brothers and a paternal cousin have both joint and kidney issues, while another brother has only joint issues.
test_results: The 10 coding exons of UMOD gene were amplified by polymerase chain reaction and cycle sequenced by capillary electrophoresis using an ABI 310 sequencer (Applied Biosystems Foster City, CA, USA). A heterozygous missense variant (c. 949 T >G) in exon 5 was identified in the proband and two affected brothers causing substitution of cysteine by glycine at codon position 317 (p.C317G). This particular amino acid change was not present in the unaffected sister. It is a novel variant, not reported in 1000 genomes, Clinvar, Human Genome Mutation Database, and Human Genome Variation. The affected residue locates within the cysteine-rich 2 domain and is immediately preceded by a highly conserved cysteine residue. Various bioinformatics tools predicted it to be pathogenic. This amino acid residue is conserved across other animal species.

case_report: A 6-year-old male of Turkish origin has been receiving treatment since birth for adenohypophysis aplasia and ectopic neurohypophysis, resulting in panhypopituitarism with secondary adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, and growth hormone deficiency. Persistent hypoglycemia, muscular hypotonia, hyperbilirubinemia, and unclear respiratory and hemodynamic conditions led to a cranial MRI (cMRI), which revealed adenohypophysis aplasia and a punctiform enhancement in the pituitary stalk for the neurohypophysis. Laboratory results showed blood plasma cortisol levels of <0.5 μg/dl and free cortisol <10 μg/24 h in urinalysis. ACTH levels were <5 pg/ml. Thyroid-stimulating hormone levels were <0.1 μIU/ml (reference range: 0.35–4.5 μIU/ml), fT4 was 0.1 ng/dl (reference range: 1.5–2.6 ng/dl), growth hormone (GH) was <0.05 ng/ml (random sample, reference range: 0.43–2.40 ng/ml), Insulin-like growth factor binding protein 3 (IGFBP-3) was 0.88 mg/l (reference range: 0.80–3.60 mg/l), and Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) was <25 ng/ml (reference range: 41–313 ng/ml). Replacement therapy was initiated with hydrocortisone, L-thyroxine, and growth hormone. From the age of 2 years, the patient experienced recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, vomiting, and elevated temperature. No infectious causes were identified, and these episodes were managed with adjustments in treatment. During a hospitalization for treatment optimization, the patient presented with recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, vomiting, headache, and fever (38–40 °C).
