The parents reported similar episodes occurring twice a month, lasting for one day, over the past four years. Despite increasing the hydrocortisone dosage, no clinical improvement was observed. Clinical examination during these episodes showed a pale boy in pain with diffuse moderate abdominal pain, normal bowel sounds, and normal cardiopulmonary findings. Blood tests during these episodes were normal, including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, and levels of ferritin and alpha-1-acid glycoprotein (AGP). Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 70 mm/h (normal value: <10 mm/h). Infectious causes were excluded as urine tests, stool microbiology and virology, and stool calprotectin were normal. There was no indication of chronic inflammatory bowel disease. The parents reported a female cousin with similar symptoms of relapsing abdominal pain, joint pain, and fever since the age of 6 years. The parents are consanguineous. Laboratory diagnostics showed serum amyloid A (SAA) elevated at 1180 mg/l (normal value: <10 mg/l).
test_results: Molecular genetic testing revealed a homozygous M694V mutation of the MEFV gene (p.Met694Val, c.2080A>G).

case_report: A 32-year-old male presented to the infection clinic in April 2011 with fever, abdominal pain, and vomiting. He had no significant past medical history, family history, or history of tobacco, alcohol, illegal drug use, or travel. The patient reported experiencing recurrent episodes of fever, abdominal pain, and vomiting every three months for the past three years. During the latest episode, he experienced abdominal discomfort for two days and fever for three days, accompanied by generalized abdominal pain and vomiting, which resolved spontaneously. Between episodes, he maintained a normal daily life. Previous evaluations, including blood tests, abdominal CT, gastroscopy, and colonoscopy conducted at two other hospitals a year prior, did not identify the cause of his symptoms. On admission, his vital signs were: blood pressure 120/68 mmHg, pulse 97/min, respiratory rate 22/min, and body temperature 40.0℃. Physical examination revealed mild tenderness and hypoactive bowel sounds throughout the abdomen. Initial laboratory results showed leukocyte count of 9,980/µL (neutrophil count 8,830/µL), hemoglobin 16.8 g/dL, platelet count 171,000/µL, C-reactive protein 85.71 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 6 mm/hr. Various tests, including antibody screenings for infections and autoimmune diseases, blood complement levels, blood cultures, peripheral blood smear, tumor markers, and hormone tests, were all negative. Abdominal CT with contrast enhancement revealed edematous wall thickening and dilatation of the proximal jejunum, lymphadenopathy, and a small amount of ascites. Capsule endoscopy showed mild lymphangiectasia throughout the small intestine. Biopsies taken via double balloon enteroscopy indicated only mild mucosal inflammation. The patient's symptoms subsided spontaneously after approximately three days. Abdominal ultrasonography on the fourth day of admission showed near-complete resolution of jejunal dilatation and lymphadenopathy.
test_results: Two missense mutations were detected in the exon 2 of the MEFV gene, c.329T > C (p.Leu110Pro) in heterozygous and c.442G > C (p.Glu148Gln) in homozygous.

case_report: A 62-year-old female with a history of hypertension treated with amlodipine reported the appearance of a rash on her face, neck, chest, and arms within 24 hours following the administration of the Pfizer-BioNTech SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. She did not experience pain or itching. After receiving the second dose of the vaccine, she observed an expansion of the rash. There was no reported personal or family history of autoimmune conditions.
test_results: A physical exam revealed a depigmented rash on her head and neck, and further examination of the skin demonstrated similar findings on her chest and arms. There was no evidence of erythema, purulence, maculopapular changes, or excoriation.

case_report: A 7-year-old girl from Italy presented with a notable strong body odor, as reported by her mother. She is the third child in a family with two older brothers, aged 16 and 10, who are both in good health. The parents are healthy and not related. Laboratory tests showed that her hematological parameters, as well as biochemical indices for renal, thyroid, and liver function, were all within normal limits. The study received approval from the local ethics committee, and written informed consent was provided by the parents.
test_results: The proband was found heterozygous for the previously reported polymorphism c.472 G>A p. E158K (rs 2266782) in exon 4, and a G-to-A transition at codon 158 (GAG to AAG) resulting in a glutamic acid to lysine substitution (Glu158 to Lys158). The proband was heterozygous also for two polymorphisms in intronic regions: c.627+10 C>G (IVS5+10G>C) (rs 2066534) and c.485-21 G>A (IVS4-22G>A) (rs 1920149). Analysis of the urine samples collected for 24 hours from both parents and two brothers under normal dietary conditions showed the presence of relatively small amounts of TMA excreted. The N-oxidation metabolic ratio (TMA/TMAO ratio) for the four subjects ranged from 0.02 to 0.04. For the proband the TMA excretion accounted for only 29.0% of total TMA excretion. The N-oxidation metabolic ratio for the proband was 2.4, two orders of magnitude greater than those observed for the parents and two brothers. After oral TMA challenge, the amount of urinary TMA excreted as TMAO, in the parents and two brothers remained high and it was very similar to the values under normal dietary conditions. N-oxidation metabolic ratio ranged from 0.02 to 0.04. After oral TMA challenge, in the proband, TMAO excretion accounted for 19.4% of total TMA excreted.

case_report: A 3-year-old girl presented with a persistent strong bodily odor following the consumption of fish. Her birth weight was 2.52 kg, she experienced no perinatal complications, and had no notable medical history. Approximately one to two years ago, after consuming fish, the odor intensified, and she developed a fever a week prior to the visit. Her parents did not exhibit similar symptoms. Physical examination showed a height of 94.8 cm (−0.57 standard deviation score [SDS]) and a weight of 14 kg (−0.44 SDS). Her growth and development were within normal ranges. Laboratory tests, including complete blood cell count, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, uric acid, and urinalysis, returned normal results. A provocation test using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry was not performed due to the complexity of the test methods.
test_results: Compound heterozygous variants of c.172G>A (p.Val158Ile) and c.1091C>A (p.Ser364X) were detected in the patient. A genomic DNA sequence analysis revealed a compound heterozygous mutation; one was a missense mutation for p.Val158Ile in exon 3 and the other was a nonsense mutation for p.Ser364X in exon 7 of the FMO3 gene. A familial genetic analysis showed that the p.Val158Ile was derived from father and that p.Ser364X was derived from the mother. The p.Ser364X is a novel mutation.

case_report: The patient is a 14-month-old male admitted for chronic diarrhea, abdominal distention, and failure to thrive. He is the second child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents. Both his father and brother experienced frequent episodes of diarrhea during their youth. The patient was born at 39 weeks with a height of 50 cm and a weight of approximately 3 kg (15–25th percentile). He was breastfed initially and showed normal growth until 3 months old (weight: 6 kg, 15–25th percentile), when food diversification began with goat milk, rice paste, etc. Following this dietary change, he began experiencing seven to eight episodes per day of non-bloody watery stools and poor weight gain. Various formula changes, including deep hydrolysis and amino acid formulas, were tried without improvement. He was admitted to multiple hospitals at 6 months, 9 months, and 12 months, but treatments for cow's milk protein allergy were ineffective. Physical examination revealed an alert infant with severe reduction in subcutaneous fat, weighing 5.6 kg (below the 3rd percentile) and no weight gain for 11 months. He was unable to sit, crawl, or walk independently. Laboratory tests showed normal blood count levels, C-reactive protein levels, liver function, renal function, and other blood or stool tests. Abdominal radiographs indicated changes in intestinal motility without signs of obstruction. Although his parents did not consent to an invasive biopsy of small bowel tissue, they agreed to further genetic testing.
test_results: Two novel heterozygous mutations, c.2626C > T (p.Q876*) (inherited from his father) and c.2872C > T (p.R958C) (inherited from his mother), in the SI gene were identified and confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

case_report: The patient is a 52-year-old woman with a history of laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) performed 9 years ago for a refractive error of −5.50−3.00×180 in both eyes. She has no systemic disorders and is not on any systemic medications. Her ocular examination from two years ago showed the following: Best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 6/10 in the right eye and 3/10 in the left eye with corrective lenses of −4.00−1.00×30 and −13.00−5.50×180, respectively, while wearing rigid gas permeable (RGP) contact lenses. Slitlamp examination identified a LASIK flap and signs of corneal ectasia in the left eye, along with mild nuclear sclerosis changes in both eyes. Other slitlamp findings were unremarkable. Orbscan images (Orbscan II, Bausch & Lomb, Salt Lake City, USA) are available. Examination of the anterior chamber angles showed they were widely open with no synechiae.
test_results: Intraocular pressure (IOP) by Goldmann applanation tonometry (GAT) was 10 and 12 mmHg in the right and left eyes respectively. Central corneal thickness (CCT) measured 431 and 322 microns in her right and left eyes respectively. Fundus examination revealed average-sized discs with vertical cup to disc ratios of 0.9 and 0.8 in the right and left eyes respectively, together with inferior rim loss; the macula, vessels and periphery were unremarkable. At this time, IOP was measured by the ocular response analyzer (ORA) which reported cornea-compensated IOP (IOPcc) of 22 and 21 mmHg in the right and left eyes, respectively.

case_report: A 33-year-old male patient presented in February 2015 with decreased visual acuity in the left eye. His medical history includes a traumatic brain injury from a war explosion in January 2012, resulting in severe craniocerebral trauma with a temporal bone fracture and an epidural hematoma, which was drained three days post-admission. Upon discharge two months later, the documented conditions were traumatic brain injury due to explosion, mixed hypoacusis in the left ear (both conductive and sensorineural), posttraumatic left peripheral facial palsy, and lagophthalmos. Between 2012 and 2015, he underwent various surgeries: neurosurgical drainage of the hematoma, eight ENT surgeries from 2012 to 2014 for ear drum reconstruction, myringotomy, and removal of bone fragments narrowing the ear meatus, and ophthalmological procedures including total blepharorrhaphy, partial opening of the blepharorrhaphy in March 2013, and total opening of the blepharorrhaphy in December 2014.
test_results: Ophthalmologic examination revealed: OD: - visual acuity: 1 without correction - refraction: +0.25/- 0.5* 11˚ - intraocular pressure: 13 mmHg NCT - slit lamp examination: normal anterior segment - fundus examination: well defined contour and normal color of the optic disc, C/ D ratio of 0.4, neuroretinal rim respecting the ISNT rule, normal macula and retinal vessels. OS: - visual acuity: 0.8 without correction - refraction: +0.00/ -0.25*17˚ - intraocular pressure: 12 mmHg NCT - slit lamp examination: discrete inferior, superficial corneal opacities - fundus examination: well defined contour and pale color of the optic disc, C/ D ratio of 0.9, superior and temporal narrowing of the neuroretinal rim and absent inferiorly, normal macula and retinal vessels. Investigations: - pachymetry: OD: 540 microns, OS: 541 microns - visual field examination (Humphrey Field Analyzer, Zeiss): OD: small peripheral defects in all four quadrants; MD: -5.27 dB; OS: severe decrease in retinal sensitivity, MD: -21.7 dB; glaucoma hemifield test: outside normal limits; subtle inferior arcuate defect, deep superior arcuate defect, no altitudinal defect. - retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) analysis: OD: decreased thickness in three quadrants, OS: decreased thickness in all four quadrants. - retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) analysis at the level of Bruch membrane opening: OD: mild temporal, superior and inferior thinning of the RNFL (borderline changes), OS: important thinning of the RNFL (outside normal limits).

case_report: Mr. AA, a 48-year-old shop attendant, visited the eye unit of a teaching hospital due to a history of gradual, painless vision loss. His unaided visual acuity was counting fingers at 1 meter in the right eye and 6/60 in the left eye. Both corneas were clear, and the pupils exhibited a slow reaction to light. A right relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) was noted. The right eye had a nuclear sclerotic cataract, which obstructed a clear view of the optic nerve head. The vertical cup-to-disc ratio (VCDR) in the right eye was approximately 0.9, barely visible through the dilated pupil with the binocular indirect ophthalmoscope. The VCDR in the left eye was 0.8.
test_results: Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 32 mmHg (right eye) and 30 mmHg (left eye) by applanation tonometry. Gonioscopy showed open angles in both eyes.

case_report: A 33-year-old male presented with reduced vision in his right eye for a duration of 6 days. He was referred from another center with concerns about serous retinal detachment. His medical history includes a diagnosis of MS 7 years prior, for which he received intramuscular interferon beta 1a therapy [Avonex®, 30 µg (6 million IU) once a week] for 2 years, but the treatment was discontinued due to side effects, and he has since been monitored without medication. His best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was recorded as 0.1 in the right eye and 1.0 in the left eye using a Snellen chart. Slit-lamp examination showed a normal anterior segment in both eyes. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 14 mmHg in both eyes, measured with a pneumotonometer. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed a raised pink mass and significant exudation in the inferior retina, while the left eye showed sporadic atrophic chorioretinal areas.
test_results: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed serous detachment, brush border pattern, and an epiretinal membrane over the fovea. Fundus fluorescein angiography showed a hyperfluorescent area in the inferotemporal periphery consistent with the raised lesion base, ponding associated with exudative detachment extending to the macula, leakage of the peripheral vessels, and hyperfluorescence of the optic disc in the right eye, while the left eye appeared normal.

case_report: A 25-year-old woman reported experiencing visual distortion and a blind spot near the central vision of her left eye for one month. One week before these visual symptoms began, she experienced night sweats, headaches, and a sudden loss of smell. The night sweats and headaches lasted for 3 days, while the loss of smell persisted for 2 weeks. She had multiple confirmed COVID-19 contacts at her workplace prior to the onset of her symptoms. Best corrected visual acuity was measured at 20/20 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye. Intraocular pressures, previously recorded as normal, were 20 mmHg in the right eye and 24 mmHg in the left eye after one month of topical difluprednate therapy. The anterior chambers of both eyes were quiet with no cell or flare observed. Examination of the vitreous showed rare cell presence and no haze in both eyes. Dilated fundus examination revealed placoid lesions in the macula and midperiphery of both eyes, along with peripheral punched-out scars and Schlaegel lines.
test_results: Fundus imaging demonstrated hypoautofluorescent lesions in the macula and midperiphery of both eyes with irregular hyperautofluorescent borders. Hypofluorescent lesions were observed on indocyanine green angiography in a distribution more widespread in the left eye than appreciated on fundus examination. Fluorescein angiography (FA) demonstrated early progressive staining and leakage from the placoid lesions without significant early blockage. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated bilateral outer retinal disruption.

case_report: A 20-year-old male presented with general weakness, pain in the right hypochondrium, lip pain, difficulty with food intake, and speech. A thorough general physical, extraoral, and intraoral examination was performed. The patient had a normosthenic build. On external body examination, the skin appeared yellowish. No enlarged lymph nodes were detected. Auscultation of the heart and lungs revealed a regular heart rate with clear tones and bilateral vesicular breathing sounds. Blood pressure was 110/70 mm Hg, and pulse was 77 beats per minute. On palpation and percussion, the abdomen was painless and slightly inflated, the Pasternatsky sign was negative bilaterally, and urination was voluntary. Extraoral examination showed swollen upper and lower lips. Intraoral examination revealed several carious teeth and numerous painful aphthae in the mucous membrane of the lips. Complete blood count revealed no deviations, and urine test showed leukocytes. Biochemical blood test values were within normal limits, except for direct bilirubin levels at 10.6 μmol/L, 8.8 in dynamics, and indirect bilirubin levels at 58.6 μmol/L, 40.1 in dynamics. Abdominal ultrasound showed an enlarged spleen at 15.8 cm, a left kidney measuring 11.2 cm, and an enlarged liver palpable under the hypochondrium. There was moderate periportal infiltration and no portal hypertension. The gallbladder and pancreas showed no abnormal changes; all aforementioned organs were of homogenous structure. Chest radiography did not reveal any abnormalities; echocardiography detected 0-1 mitral valve regurgitation. Antibodies to hepatitis and infections were negative. Consultations with specialists in hematology and infectious diseases were conducted.
test_results: Homozygous UGT1A1∗28 alleles were identified.

case_report: A 4-year-old girl presented with blue sclera and wrinkled skin. She was the only child of parents who were third-degree relatives (father aged 30 years, mother aged 24 years). She was delivered at term via LSCS with a birth weight of 2.25 kg. The perinatal period was uneventful. She exhibited motor developmental delay and mild learning difficulty. Physical examination revealed a weight of 12 kg (<3rd percentile), height of 97 cm (3rd-10th percentile), and head circumference of 44 cm (<3rd percentile). Notable features included palpebral down slant, bilateral epicanthal folds, blue sclera, flat nasal bridge, sagging cheeks, and prominent ears. She had generalized loose, wrinkled skin folds, especially on the face, neck, abdomen, and extremities. Systemic examinations were normal. Skeletal evaluation indicated bilateral hip dislocation. Ophthalmologic examination confirmed blue sclera and shallow anterior chambers. Echocardiography and abdominal ultrasonography results were normal. Isoelectric focusing for transferrin showed mildly elevated levels of A-, mono-, and di-sialotransferrin, with slightly reduced levels of tetra-sialotransferrin.
test_results: Mutation analysis showed mutations c. 826-2A > G in intron 9 and c. 1973_1976del (p.Val660LeufsX682) in exon 16 of the ATP6V0A2 gene in a compound heterozygous state.
Orpha_name: Autosomal recessive cutis laxa type 2, classic type

case_report: A 69-year-old male arrived at the emergency room after experiencing recurrent syncopal events over the past 3 days. His medical history included a pacemaker (Medtronic Sensia SR/single chamber) implantation one year earlier due to a complete atrioventricular block. The patient had not attended follow-up appointments for approximately 8 months. Upon admission, he was haemodynamically stable. An initial electrocardiogram showed a pacemaker rhythm (VVI) with a heart rate of 60 bpm, and there were no signs of pacemaker malfunction. The patient was moved to the general ward for further evaluation of the syncope. During the early observation period, no significant events occurred. Blood tests returned normal results with no detected abnormalities. However, the patient experienced another syncopal episode followed by cardiac arrest. Resuscitation was performed, and the ECG indicated ventricular asystole without pacemaker spikes. The patient was then taken to the catheterization laboratory for transvenous temporary pacemaker insertion. During the procedure, it was observed that the permanent pacemaker lead was correctly positioned at the right ventricular apex, but there was a noticeable breakage in the lead continuity.
test_results: The pacemaker interrogation revealed high impedance (1.780 ohms) suggesting a lead fracture, with a high pacing threshold.

case_report: A 34-year-old male, who regularly trained at a gym and worked as a nurse, presented with swelling, heaviness, and skin discoloration in the left upper limb for 1 day. Symptoms appeared 6−8 hours after a moderate-intensity workout, with no significant history of trauma. The patient was a nonsmoker and did not consume alcohol, with no notable medical history. He had an athletic build, weighing 78 kg and standing 178 cm tall (BMI of 24.7 kg/m2). Vital signs were as follows: temperature 37.6°C, pulse rate 100 beats/min, blood pressure 107/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Examination of the left upper limb showed noticeable swelling and a dusky skin appearance, with no neurological deficits. Other systemic examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, and coagulation profile, were all within normal limits. Screening for thrombophilia, including protein C, protein S, antithrombin-III, activated protein resistance, factor V Leiden, and antiphospholipid antibodies, yielded results within acceptable limits.
test_results: Ultrasonography with Doppler study of the left upper limb was suggestive of DVT in the left axillary and subclavian vein. Computed tomography (CT) venography showed the extension of thrombus from the left subclavian vein into an innominate vein.

case_report: A 21-year-old male with a recent history of gym membership and weightlifting presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of pain and swelling in the right upper limb. His past medical history includes COVID-19 infection 12 months ago, with no family history of thromboembolic conditions. Physical examination showed a swollen and erythematous right upper limb, with palpable peripheral pulses comparable to the left side. The range of motion in the right upper limb was intact. The left upper limb and both lower limbs appeared normal. There were no signs or symptoms indicative of pulmonary embolism.
test_results: Right upper limb POCUS was concerning for subclavian vein thrombus with a distended right subclavian vein. Blood work up revealed a non-negative D-dimer at 0.93 mg/l (reference range <0.50mg/l). His chest x-ray showed no obvious abnormalities, and no evidence of an accessory rib. An urgent formal ultrasound confirmed an acute 6 cm thrombus within the right subclavian vein. Furthermore, it showed normal compressibility and colour flow within the right basilic vein, brachial vein, cephalic vein and axillary vein without any evidence of thrombosis. The IR venogram showed an acute thrombotic occlusion of the right subclavian vein with a high-grade stenosis at the junction of the first rib and clavicle.

case_report: A 42-year-old male reported experiencing pain and swelling in his left arm following a series of intense, repetitive weightlifting exercises. He mentioned a long-term engagement with weightlifting and noted that he had been experiencing these symptoms for some time. His medical history did not reveal any significant issues. Laboratory tests indicated the presence of antithrombin 3 and factor V Leiden, both of which are associated with coagulation.
test_results: Contrast-enhanced MRA revealed near-complete occlusion of the proximal left subclavian vein and distal collateral formations. CDUS showed a heterogeneous thrombotic mass that filled almost the entire proximal segment of the left subclavian vein. Thrombosis extended into the proximal segment of the left internal jugular vein (IJV). Extensive venous collateral formations were presented in the left proximal cervical localization.

case_report: A 28-year-old male of mixed race has experienced scalp skin redundancy for two years. The condition is characterized by deep cerebriform folds and wrinkles, specifically in the parietal and occipital regions. The patient reports no comorbidities, no similar family history, no consanguinity, and no use of anabolic steroid drugs. Additionally, there is no history of skin or scalp inflammatory diseases. Neurological and ophthalmological examinations revealed no abnormalities.
test_results: The anatomopathological exam revealed epidermis and dermis within histological standards of normality. Skull X-ray, computed tomography of skull and sella turcica, nuclear magnetic resonance of the sella turcica and serum growth hormone dosage showed no alterations. TSH serum dosage, free T4, complete blood count, fasting blood glucose, total cholesterol and fractions, and Venereal Disease Research Laboratory test - VDRL were within normal limits.

case_report: A 46-year-old Caucasian female reported experiencing generalized hair loss over the past nine months, which had progressively worsened. She had no neurological or ophthalmological issues. Her medical history included Graves' disease and atrial fibrillation, with no record of inflammatory skin conditions. Surgical history included pacemaker placement, salivary gland excision, and Achilles tendon repair. Family history was non-contributory. She was a former smoker and consumed less than one alcoholic drink daily, with no illicit drug use. She had allergies to shellfish-derived foods but no known drug allergies. Current medications were venlafaxine, buprenorphine/naloxone, levothyroxine, metoprolol succinate, trazodone, and alprazolam. The review of systems was negative for weight loss, night sweats, and fatigue. On physical examination, the patient appeared healthy and was not in acute distress; vital signs were normal. Notable findings included prominent skin folds on the right and left superior parietal scalp, and right and left superior occipital scalp. There was also diffuse non-scarring hair loss on the posterior mid-parietal scalp and right superior occipital scalp.
test_results: One 6.0 mm punch biopsy of the right superior occipital scalp was obtained for hematoxylin and eosin stain, which showed subtle, non-scarring, non-inflammatory alopecia, representative of telogen effluvium. No features of a deposition disorder were identified; however, there is background intradermal melanocytic nevus with congenital features.
diagnosis: Cutis Verticis Gyrata with Underlying Cerebriform Intradermal Nevus

case_report: A 22-year-old primigravida patient presented with progressive blackening of fingers on both hands and feet bilaterally, following claudication pain for three years, with non-healing ulcers and flaking skin over the lesions at the 17th week of gestation. The patient had no history of tobacco use, smoking, or exposure to passive smoking. There was no personal or family history of cardiac events, diabetes, or hypertension. On general examination, the patient was normotensive with mild pallor. Systemic examination revealed no abnormalities. Bilateral examination of the fingers of the upper limbs showed dry, shriveled skin that was brown to black, with a clear line of demarcation at 2-3 cm from the terminal end of nine digits, sparing the thumb of the left hand. The extremities of the limbs were colder. Brachial artery pulsations were normal, and radial artery pulsations were regular and collapsing in nature. Bilateral examination of the toes of the lower limbs showed dry, shriveled skin that was brown to black, with a clear line of demarcation at 4-5 cm from the terminal ends of all ten digits. Dorsalis pedis arterial pulsations were not palpable. Hematological investigations revealed a platelet count of 4.29 lacs/cumm and a hematocrit of 29.8%. Other blood indices were within normal ranges. Blood glucose levels and lipid profile were normal. Tests for Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) B5 (51/52), antinuclear antibody (ANA) profile, tuberculosis (TB) antigen enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), beta-2 glycoprotein (IgG and IgM), anti-cardiolipin antibody, anti-phospholipid antibody, and lupus anticoagulant were negative. Two-dimensional echocardiography showed no positive findings except for reduced left ventricular compliance.
test_results: Bilateral upper limb arterial doppler showed monophasic flow with reduced volume in both radial and ulnar arteries, whereas normal triphasic flow was noted in the axillary and brachial arteries. Bilateral lower limb arterial doppler showed biphasic flow with normal volume in the proximal right popliteal artery and anterior tibial artery and distally there were corkscrew collaterals.

case_report: A 51-year-old Korean man was admitted to the hospital with severe left flank pain, hematuria, and oliguria for 3 days. He also reported epigastric discomfort and generalized weakness but denied having fever or vomiting. His medical history included hypertension for 1 year and a 10-year history of a condition associated with intermittent claudication. He had both great toes amputated 10 years ago due to gangrenous changes. At that time, imaging showed significantly reduced blood flow in the right distal portion of the popliteal artery and the proximal portion of the tibiofibular artery due to occlusion. The left superficial femoral artery was also occluded from its origin, with collateral arteries having developed. He was taking beraprost but continued to smoke approximately 1 pack per day for 30 years. Four years later, imaging revealed progression of occlusion in the left superficial femoral artery, bilateral tibial, and peroneal arteries. He had no history of diabetes mellitus, collagen disease, or cardiac disease. On presentation, his blood pressure was 180/100mmHg, and his body temperature was 36.4°C. He exhibited severe tenderness in the left costovertebral angle area. There were no signs of Raynaud’s toe, skin nodules, or phlebitis. Laboratory results were as follows: white blood cell count (WBC) 9700/uL, hemoglobin (Hb) 12.7g/dL, platelets 201×10^3/uL, serum creatinine 14.02mg/dL, creatinine clearance 3.6ml/minute/1.73m2 (CKD-EPI formula), β2 microglobulin 19.80mg/L, phosphorus 5.48mg/dL, intact parathyroid hormone (PTH) 329.5pg/mL, creatine phosphokinase (CPK) 74U/L, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 1687IU/L. Urine sediment contained 0 to 2 WBC and 3 to 5 red blood cells (RBC) per field. Urine protein electrophoresis showed no paraprotein bands. Blood lipid profile, coagulation tests, protein C, protein S activity, complement fractions, antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, anti-Scl-70, anticardiolipin, antiphospholipid, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were all negative or within normal limits. Electrocardiography and echocardiography results were normal.
test_results: Contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography (CT) demonstrated left kidney enlargement (9.3cm) with a multifocal infarcted area and a shrunken right kidney (7.6cm). Neither renal artery was visualized. Abdominal and lower extremity angiography showed that the vascular status in both lower limbs and the viscera had worsened. His superior mesenteric artery, inferior mesenteric artery, both renal arteries, left common iliac artery, and left superficial femoral artery were not visualized, and the arteries below both his knees were occluded. Collateral vessels were well developed in his lower extremities.
diagnosis: End stage renal disease caused by thromboangiitis obliterans

case_report: A 30-year-old male with a history of anxiety and disordered eating presented to the Emergency Department. Upon arrival, the patient collapsed and nearly lost consciousness, leading to admission for further evaluation. He was not on any medications and reported no use of alcohol, substances, or tobacco. Family history included treated breast cancer in his mother, with no other physical or psychiatric conditions noted. Initial recovery and vital sign examination showed a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15/15. The patient was bradycardic with a heart rate of 33 beats per minute and hypotensive with a blood pressure of 87/49 mmHg. Respiratory rate was normal at 14 breaths per minute, and temperature was 35.9°C. Capillary blood glucose level was 71 mg/dL. The patient appeared icteric, pale, and extremely weak, with a mild tremor. His weight was 49.2 kg, height was 184 cm, and BMI was 14.5 kg/m2. Clinical examination revealed cachexia and total body paleness. The torso was hairless, while the extremities had lanugo hair. The skin and tongue were extremely dry and scaly. The rest of the clinical examination was unremarkable.
test_results: Blood was drawn for a complete blood count and full biochemical profile. An electrocardiogram showed sinus bradycardia at 35 beats per minute without further abnormalities, and a chest X-ray was unremarkable. An echocardiogram showed a normal heart size without any notable changes except for the remains of a Eustachian tube. Evaluation for other potential sources of liver damage (hepatitis A, B, C viruses, hepatotropic viruses, human immunodeficiency virus, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, and autoimmune hepatitis antibodies) was performed, with negative results. During the first 48 hours, biochemical parameters further worsened, and an upper abdominal ultrasound revealed no apparent disorders.
diagnosis: Elevated liver enzymes due to anorexia nervosa

case_report: An 18-year-old male with a history of excision of a benign melanocytic nevus from the left lower eyelid presented to the emergency department with bilateral scrotal pain lasting one day. There was no history of trauma or infection. Physical examination revealed nontender, mobile testicles with multiple hard masses. The patient also had skin pigmentations and freckling on his back. Laboratory tests, including serum tumour markers LDH, AFP, and BhCG, were within normal limits. Testicular ultrasound showed extensive calcifications in both testes with multiple lobulated heterogeneous lesions. MRI revealed six masses on the right testis and three on the left testis, with calcifications and cystic changes, but no signs of extra-testicular invasion. PET-CT and staging CT scans showed no evidence of metastatic disease. Following sperm cryopreservation, the patient underwent right inguinal excisional testicular biopsy, during which four well-circumscribed lesions, each less than one cm and surrounded by healthy testicular tissue, were excised.
test_results: Histopathology, sections show a well-circumscribed testicular tumour composed of lobules of cells arranged in solid sheets and cords. The tumour cells are epithelioid and have a round nucleus, prominent nucleoli with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. There are multiple large, laminated calcifications, there is no evidence of marked pleomorphism, necrosis, or atypical mitosis. By immunohistochemistry, the tumour cells are strongly and diffusely positive for calretinin, inhibin and S100, with focal positivity for Melan-A and cytokeratin AE1/AE3. However, the tumour cells are negative for EMA. The proliferative index Ki-67 is very low (less than 2 %). Genetic testing is positive for a pathogenic mutation c.491_492del in the PRKAR1A gene-confirming Carney Complex.
diagnosis: Large cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumour

case_report: A 21-year-old female presented with mild abdominal pain, hirsutism, and oligomenorrhea. She had her first menstrual period at age 13. One year prior to admission, she experienced hirsutism and menstrual cycles occurring more than 60 days apart. She visited a gynecologic clinic and was prescribed oral contraceptives, which led to a mild improvement in symptoms. No further examinations were documented, and details from the previous visit were unavailable. Her mother had a hysterectomy due to multiple leiomyomas. Other family and medical history were unremarkable. On physical examination, there was abdominal tenderness, a palpable pelvic mass, and mild hirsutism on the thigh. Her body mass index (BMI) was 19.1 kg/m² (height: 150 cm, weight: 43 kg). Ultrasonography showed a large left ovarian mass measuring 154 × 104 mm, compressing the uterus. No enlarged pelvic lymph nodes or effusion in the Douglas pouch were observed. A computed tomography (CT) scan showed no additional lesions.
test_results: Microscopic examination demonstrated diffuse and nodular proliferation of medium-sized to large polygonal neoplastic cells with pale to granular eosinophilic cytoplasm, small round nuclei, and mild atypia. The cells were separated by a vascular stroma, with no evidence of capsular invasion. Few scattered foci of necrosis and hemorrhage were observed, whereas the mitotic rate was less than 2 per 10 high-power fields, and crystals of Reinke were not observed. Immunohistochemistry revealed positivity for Inhibin-a, Calretinin, and ER, whereas CD99, PR, and AR showed negative expression, and expression of Ki-67 was estimated to be less than 20%.

case_report: A 40-year-old male presented with a painless scrotal swelling that had gradually increased in size over two years. He exhibited no hormonal symptoms. Physical examination revealed an enlarged, firm left testis and a hydrocele with a positive translucency test. Ultrasonography showed a significantly enlarged left testis measuring 7.6×4.5 cm with a diffusely heterogeneous echo-texture. Multiple well-defined nodular and heterogeneously echoic lesions were observed within the left scrotum, adherent to the wall. A large amount of free fluid was present in the left scrotal sac. The right testis and epididymis appeared normal. The patient had previously undergone testicular FNAC one year prior, which indicated a mesenchymal tumor. A review of the slides showed a cellular smear with 3-dimensional clusters and groups composed of bland-looking spindle cells. The patient subsequently underwent a left high inguinal orchidectomy, and the specimen was sent for further examination. The excised testis was firm, measuring 7.5×7×6.5 cm, with a partially attached tunical sac containing multiple well-defined nodules on its inner surface. The cut surface of the testis was gray-white and mostly solid, with a few cystic areas. A thin rim of normal-appearing testicular tissue was present.
test_results: Microscopically, sections from the testis and the tunical sac nodules showed nests of spindle cells arranged in bundles separated by variable amounts of collagen. The nuclei were fairly uniform with evenly dispersed chromatin and mitotic figures of up to 2 MF/10 high power fields were present. Occasional foci showed tubules which were lined by cuboidal cells and contained central hyaline materials. On immunohistochemical examination, the tumor cells showed strong immunoreactivity for vimentin and were immunonegative for calretinin, WT-1, inhibin, pancytokeratin, cytokeratin 5/6, smooth muscle actin, CD 34 and S 100 protein. The ki 67 proliferative index was 2%. Lining cells of the tubule were immunoreactive for inhibin.
diagnosis: Testicular Fibroma of Gonadal Stromal Origin with Minor Sex Cord Elements

case_report: A 62-year-old woman was admitted to the Emergency Department due to a painful and rapidly enlarging mass on the left back area. She had a medical history of surgery and skin grafting for a large hematoma on the right back area 30 years prior. Initial physical examination in the ED showed vital signs with a blood pressure of 160/90 mmHg, heart rate of 120 beats/min, respiratory rate of 20 breaths/min, and an axillary temperature of 36.5℃. A soft mass measuring 10×5×3 cm with tenderness on palpation was noted on the left back area. The mass was scarlet-colored, non-pulsating, and had a well-demarcated border. Multiple areas of hyperpigmentation (café-au-lait spots) were observed on her torso and extremities, along with axillary freckling. Routine blood samples taken on admission showed a white blood cell count of 11,400/µL, hemoglobin concentration of 12.4 g/dL, hematocrit of 37.2%, platelet count of 244,000/µL, an international normalized ratio of 1.01 (reference range, 0.85-1.30), and a partial thromboplastin time of 29.9 sec (reference range, 29.0-44.0). Over the next 3 hours, the mass expanded, and the hemoglobin level dropped to 8.1 g/dL. The patient became hemodynamically unstable with a blood pressure of 73/50 mmHg and a heart rate of 100 beats/min. She was resuscitated with 2.5 L of crystalloid fluid and 1 unit of packed red blood cells, stabilizing her blood pressure to 106/60 mmHg.
test_results: Abdomen and pelvis computed tomography (CT) revealed a huge, subcutaneous, 13×7.6 cm-sized hematoma, along with fluid collection in the posterior and left lateral subcutaneous layer of the thoracolumbar and left lower back area.
diagnosis: Neurofibromatosis Type 1  with recurrent massive subcutaneous hemorrhage
Orpha_name: Neurofibromatosis type 1 due to NF1 mutation or intragenic deletion

case_report: A 44-year-old woman reported experiencing dull aching pain in the right eye for 5 days. Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. She had no history of night blindness and no known systemic illnesses. Examination of the anterior segment in both eyes was normal. Fundus examination of both eyes showed multiple yellow-white fleck-like lesions arranged in a concentric pattern, sparing the macular region. The centrally located flecks were small and dot-like, particularly near the optic disc and papillomacular region, and appeared linear temporal to the macula. The peripheral flecks were either pisiform or oblong in shape. Additionally, there was disc edema in the right eye.
test_results: Fundus autofluorescence (FAF) revealed hyperautofluorescence of the fleck lesions. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) of BE revealed a normal foveal contour. In addition, there was presence of intraretinal cystoid spaces nasal to the fovea at the papillomacular region along with disc edema in the RE. SD-OCT line scan through the affected outer retina revealed multiple small-rounded as well as conical hyperreflective lesions seen at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and impinging on the photoreceptor layer in BE corresponding to the flecks. The enhanced depth imaging OCT in BE revealed normal subfoveal choroidal thickness. SD-OCT angiography (SD-OCTA) imaging of BE revealed hyperreflective interspersed linear pisiform lesions at the outer retina just above the RPE in BE, with a normal underlying choriocapillaris. RE B-scan showed disc elevation and the presence of T-sign. Electroretinogram (ERG) showed normal rod and cone responses in BE.

case_report: A 6-year-old girl arrived at our pediatric department with a history of recurrent skin lesions over the past 3 years, fever for 3 months, and a cough lasting 8 days. Initially, the skin lesions appeared on her scalp, trunk, lower limbs, and face without any clear cause. These lesions progressed slowly, transitioning from papules to vesicles, necrosis, and eventually healing with atrophic scars. She did not exhibit sensitivity to sun exposure or mosquito bites. Despite receiving multiple antibiotics and various antihistamines at local hospitals, the lesions persisted with periods of improvement and worsening. Three months ago, she began experiencing intermittent fever (38–39 °C). Eight days prior to admission, she developed a non-productive cough and persistent fever (38–40.5 °C). At a local hospital, she was found to have hepatosplenomegaly and anemia, leading to her referral to our facility. Upon admission, her temperature was 38 °C, and she had facial swelling. The skin lesions were polymorphic, including papules, vesicles, bullae, necrosis, and atrophic scars, affecting her face, scalp, abdominal wall, and lower limbs. The liver and spleen were palpable 6 cm and 4 cm below the costal margin, respectively. No lymphadenopathy was observed. Hemoglobin concentration was 84 g/L, and C-reactive protein was 62 mg/L (normal <8 mg/L). Blood biochemical analysis was largely normal except for an elevated lactate dehydrogenase level (538 U/L). Blood culture, autoimmune antibody tests, and bone marrow aspiration examination results were negative.
test_results: Histopathologic findings revealed epidermal blister formation, dense lymphoid cell infiltration throughout the dermis and surrounding perivascular area, focal necrosis, and presence of lymphocyte with atypia. Immunohistochemically, the infiltrate was composed of lymphocytic cells expressing CD3ε, CD4, TIA-1, but not CD3, CD8, CD20, CD79a, CD30, CD56, and GrB. Approximately, 50% cells expressed Ki-67. Positive signals of EBV-encoded RNA (EBER) were detected in skin biopsy specimens by in situ hybridization. TCR-γ gene monoclonal rearrangement was present. Serologic assays of EBV-VCA IgG and EBV- NA IgG were positive in the absence of EBV IgM, EBV-VCA IgM, and EBV-EA IgM. The amount of EBV DNA in peripheral blood was increased to 7.4 × 107 IU/mL.

case_report: A 14-year-old boy with no significant family, pregnancy, or perinatal history. At 3 months old, he was found to have cytomegalovirus (CMV) and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infections with severe hepatitis, confirmed by PCR. He did not meet criteria for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). Immunity parameters were normal at that time. At age 5, he experienced diarrhea followed by pneumonia with pleural empyema, necessitating decortication of the left lung. He exhibited high sensitivity to insect bites. Immunology tests at age 5 showed agammaglobulinemia (IgG 0.5 g/l; IgA <0.06 g/l; IgM 0.12 g/l), normal CD19+ cell counts, and an inverted CD3+CD4+/CD3+CD8+ ratio. A decreased percentage of memory switched B cells was also noted. Genetic tests at age 13 revealed a mutation in the TNFRSF13B gene, affecting TACI protein production, and a heterozygous variant in the STX11 gene. Substitution therapy with intravenous human immunoglobulin began at age 5, transitioning to subcutaneous infusions after one year, continuing for 7 years without complications. At age 13, he developed an erythematous papular rash on his lower limbs, followed by papulopustular skin lesions that left deep scars, and periodic periorbital edema. New skin lesions were accompanied by high fever. Laboratory tests showed thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, and elevated transaminases. After three months, serous-filled vesicles appeared around the erythematous papules. Skin lesions fluctuated between exacerbation and remission. Tests excluded HHV6, Adenovirus, Parvovirus B19, VZV, HSV 1, HSV 2, HIV, Aspergillus spp, influenza A, influenza B, RSV, SARS-CoV-2, tuberculosis, and other mycobacteriosis. Staphylococcus epidermidis was cultured from scalp vesicle swabs. Targeted treatment was ineffective. A rapid increase in EBV viremia (>5X106 IU/ml) was observed. Four doses of rituximab were administered, resulting in a temporary reduction in EBV viremia but no clinical improvement, followed by complete B cell depletion. An increased percentage and absolute number of CD3+CD8+ cells (cytotoxic T cells) were also observed.
test_results: Histopathological examination showed features of vasculitis. The consulting pathologist recognized EBER+ CD8. The child was assessed for T-cell receptor (TCR) clonality in peripheral blood T lymphocytes. The result was normal. PET-CT scanning showed features of scalp involvement, with no changes in the lymph nodes, liver and spleen.

case_report: A four-year-old male child, born to non-consanguineous Indian parents, presented at two years of age with gait imbalance. The child had achieved independent walking by 12 months but later developed progressively worsening abnormal gait characterized by abnormal posturing and dragging of the right foot, along with frequent falls. His fine motor, social, cognitive, and language milestones were age-appropriate, though his speech was unclear. Antenatal, natal, and postnatal history were non-contributory. On examination, anthropometry was normal. The child exhibited asymmetrical generalized dystonia, predominantly affecting the lower limbs, along with oromotor dystonia, dysarthric speech, drooling, and central hypotonia. External ocular movements were complete, and there was no apraxia, nystagmus, or telangiectasia. Basic biochemistry, metabolic work-up, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain were normal. An empiric trial of low dose levodopa was initiated at an initial dose of 2 mg/kg/day and increased to 4 mg/kg/day, with the best results observed at 2.5 mg/kg/day. On three-month follow-up, parents reported immediate relief in drooling and oromotor dystonia, with significant gradual improvement in generalized dystonia, gait, and balance.
test_results: WES detected homozygous, two base-pair deletions in exon-61 of ATM (NM_000051.3:c.8833_8834del; depth: 67x) that resulted in frame-shift variant and premature protein truncation, (p.Leu2945ValfsTer10). Serum alfa-fetoprotein (AFP) was high (106 ng/ml, normal range 0–8); immunoglobulin profile returned normal. Targeted parental Sanger sequencing revealed a heterozygous state in the mother while the father carried wild-type ATM allele.

case_report: A 31-year-old female patient presented with intermittent pain in the left flank and a noticeable abdominal mass. There were no urinary symptoms, including hematuria or dysuria. Her medical history and family history of malignancy were unremarkable. Routine blood and urine tests, along with tumor markers such as AFP, AFP-L3, CEA, CA199, CA125, and SCC, were all within normal limits.
test_results: Enhanced computed tomography (CT) demonstrated a hypoechoic mass (18 cm × 14.5 cm × 14 cm) from the left renal with central necrosis, no invasion to renal veins or inferior vena cava (IVC) was reported. Microscopic examination revealed a small round cell tumor with focal necrosis, endovascular tumor thrombi and adrenal involvement were detected. The tumor cells were arranged in sheet with fiber segmentation. Immunohistochemistry results indicated positive stained for AE1/AE3, CD99, CD56, synaptophysin (Syn), Ki-67(50%), and negatively stained for S-100, EMA, CgA, WT1, Desmin, SMA and MyoD1. The diagnosis was further confirmed by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) by detecting the rearrangements of t (22q12): EWS-FLI1 type 1 translocation.
diagnosis: Primary Ewing sarcoma of the kidney

case_report: A 45-year-old female presented with a two-week history of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and bloating. She had no significant medical or menstrual history. There were no signs or symptoms of hypercalcemia. On general physical examination, the patient appeared anemic and thinly built. Abdominal palpation revealed a soft and tender abdomen with a palpable mass in the left lower quadrant. Pelvic examination indicated a uterus of 2-to-4-week size and a palpable mass in the left adnexa. Imaging studies, including ultrasound and computed tomography (CT) scan, identified a mass measuring 27x17x12 cm originating from the left adnexa. The patient subsequently underwent an exploratory laparotomy, total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, and omentectomy.
test_results: On gross examination, uterus and cervix measured 10x6x3 cm. On cutting, endometrial cavity was patent and endometrial thickness measured 0.4 cm. Myometrium showed three intramural and one subserosal fibroids varying in diameter from 1.5 to 5 cm. Right fallopian tube and ovary were unremarkable. Left ovary was enlarged and measured 27x17x12 cm. The ovarian capsule was intact and external surface was bosselated. Cut section of tumor revealed solid and cystic areas filled with yellowish, watery, and hemorrhagic fluid. Cysts varied in diameter from 0.5 to 18 cm with wall thickness varying from 0.2 to 0.8 cm. Intervening solid grey-white areas had variegated appearance with yellowish friable necrotic areas; at places, there were dark brown hemorrhagic areas along with foci of shiny mucoid areas. Microscopically, the tumor cells were arranged in solid nests and focally forming rosettes along with large central areas of necrosis within the nests. The tumor cells were small with high nucleocytoplasmic ratio, mildly pleomorphic nuclei, granular chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, and scant cytoplasm. Mitotic count was high (>5/10hpf). Present case showed positivity for Pan CK, synaptophysin, NSE, and EMA, and focal positivity for chromogranin. Tumor cells were negative for inhibin, TTF-1, and CD99.
Orpha_name: Small cell carcinoma of the ovary

case_report: Patient IV-1: A 14-year-old female was first evaluated at the age of three years for global developmental delay, short stature, and failure to thrive. She was born at 39 weeks of gestation, weighing 3.8 kg, with no complications at birth. Developmental concerns were observed after six months, including developmental issues associated with poor feeding and failure to thrive. No facial dysmorphic features were noted. Seizures and retinal degeneration were identified during the first two years of life.
test_results: An Electroencephalogram (EEG) showed bilateral and symmetric spike/wave complexes and polyspikes.

case_report: Patient IV-2: A 12-year-old female with severe atopic dermatitis, developmental delay, and failure to thrive. She was born at full-term with a weight of 3.6 kg. At the age of three years, she exhibited quadriplegic cerebral palsy, moderate axial hypotonia, frequent purposeless movements, and mild spasticity of the distal lower extremities. She could not talk but vocalized without forming words. She was unable to follow any commands. Brain MRI results were normal, and qualitative diffusion tensor imaging was noted. By the age of six, she was unable to sit and had a severe movement disorder. Her developmental quotient was seven. She was able to feed by mouth and was dependent on others for all activities of daily living. Her growth parameters were in the 1st percentile for weight, 2nd percentile for height, and 5th percentile for head circumference, similar to her elder sister.
test_results: An EEG showed multifocal sharps but no seizures.

case_report: Patient IV-3: A 9-year-old male born at 39 weeks of gestation. Developmental milestones were delayed; at nine months, he could not sit, roll, or crawl. Vision and hearing impairments were assessed around twelve months of age. A brain MRI performed at six years old showed normal results. By two years old, he began pulling to a stand, cruising on furniture, and babbling. He had no speech but communicated through babbles and gestures. His skin was clear. He was able to self-feed. On physical examination, his growth, weight, and height were all below the 1st percentile. Neurologically, he was more alert than his sisters but remained nonverbal and did not follow commands. He had no eye contact, exhibited some spasticity in his legs, but could cruise with assistance.
test_results: An EEG showed multifocal bilateral sharps with seizures.

case_report: An 18-year-old female with no prior health issues arrived at the emergency department (ED) experiencing sudden, sharp, burning pain in the lower abdomen and groin for two weeks. The pain, described as feeling like 'glass shards,' worsened with urination and movement but was somewhat relieved by high water intake. She also reported bright red blood in her urine, frequent urination, and painful urination during this period. There was no history of similar symptoms, and her family history was negative for renal, bladder conditions, or autoimmune diseases. She was not sexually active and had never been sexually active. She denied any vaginal pain. Her only medication was a combined oral contraceptive pill (TriNessa: norgestimate and ethinyl estradiol), which she began two weeks before the onset of symptoms. The ED staff conducted laboratory studies and a physical examination, including a pelvic examination. Urinalysis revealed microscopic hematuria, but other routine laboratory results were within normal ranges. She was discharged with a diagnosis of acute urinary tract infection (UTI) and prescribed a 10-day course of ciprofloxacin, with instructions to follow up with her primary care clinician. The patient reported no improvement in symptoms following antibiotic treatment. Since discharge, she experienced urination over 60 times per day, pelvic pain, and a sensation of incomplete voiding. Her intermittent pelvic pain became constant over the next few months. She consulted multiple physicians in family medicine, internal medicine, and urology for further evaluation. Various treatments were attempted, including nitrofurantoin for UTI, phenazopyridine for nephrolithiasis pain management, and nystatin cream for fungal vaginitis, but none provided symptom relief.
test_results: Outpatient cystoscopy was attempted but immediately terminated due to extreme pain.

case_report: A 25-year-old male presented with a primary concern of teeth misalignment since childhood. The patient also reported experiencing hearing difficulties in the left ear from a young age. Extra-oral examination revealed a transverse cleft at the right angle of the mouth, preauricular tissue tags, and incompetent lips. There was noticeable bilateral facial asymmetry and macrostomia, with an inter-incisal distance of 43 mm. Intraoral examination showed missing teeth 16 and 47, spacing between teeth 11, 12, 13, 14, 42, 43, and 44, proclined teeth 11, 12, 13, and 43, a crossbite involving teeth 24 and 34, increased overjet, and a high arched palate.
test_results: OPG revealed reduction in size of body of mandible, condyles, coronoid process and ramus on the right side. The border of the mandible was well defined and intact. The trabecular pattern and the course of mandibular canal were normal with normal surrounding structures. PA view of skull revealed reduction in size of body of mandible, condyles, coronoid process and ramus on the right side of mandible with normal surrounding structures. Lateral cephalogram revealed proclined maxillary incisors with increased overjet. Impedance Audiometry revealed hearing sensitivity of right ear to be in normal range whereas severe loss of hearing was noted in left ear. Ultrasonography of abdomen revealed no abnormality.

case_report: A 5-year-old girl from Saudi Arabia was referred in March 2016 to the radiology department at Ibn Al-Nafees Hospital in Manama, Bahrain, by a maxillofacial surgeon. The patient is the only surviving child of a young couple who had a history of a first-trimester miscarriage and an ectopic pregnancy. The mother, aged 28, had polycystic ovary syndrome and a complex medical history, leading to an intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) procedure where three embryos were transferred. The patient was one of a set of dizygotic twins, with the other twin miscarried at 11 weeks of gestation. The mother had a history of hypochromic microcytic anemia with hemoglobin levels ranging from 7-9 gm/dl and was suspected to be a carrier of alpha thalassemia. During the 12th week of gestation, the mother's hemoglobin dropped to 6 gm/dl, requiring a blood transfusion. At 26 weeks, signs of preterm labor were managed with medication, and the pregnancy concluded with a Cesarean section. The mother, who had multiple drug allergies, received hormonal therapy for ovulation regulation, medications before and after ICSI, folic acid (5 mg/day), and calcium from the 4th month of pregnancy. Post-delivery, the mother, with a 5-year history of migraines and limb tingling, experienced an epileptic attack and was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis. There was no gestational diabetes, smoking history, or family history of craniofacial malformations. Written informed consent was obtained from the parents for publication of this case report and accompanying images. The full-term baby, diagnosed antenatally with cleft lip and palate, exhibited dysmorphic features and intrauterine growth restriction at birth. Due to upper airway obstruction from craniofacial malformations, mechanical ventilation and a tracheostomy tube were temporarily required. After stabilization, the patient was referred to an ENT specialist for cleft lip repair at 6 months and cleft palate and preauricular ear tag repair at 18 months. Subsequent referrals were made to ophthalmologists, pediatric and plastic surgeons, and a maxillofacial specialist for further interventions.
test_results: The patient had features of craniofacial anomalies including microcephaly, asymmetrical face, right microphthalmia, but normal left eye with preserved vision. She had mandibular and maxillary hypoplasia, in addition to cleft lip and palate in the right side, macrostomia to right side, micrognathia, malocclusion, crowded teeth with caries, difficulties of mastication, and abnormal tongue shape. Right grade I microtia, bilateral preauricular rudimentary ear tags and bilateral membranous ear canals. The three dimensional-CT scan of the skull revealed asymmetrical facial bones, and a small right orbit. Bilateral parietal osseous defects, represented asymmetrically enlarged parietal foramina were found, being larger on the right side, in addition, a persistent midline occipital foramen, was seen. A right rudimentary eye with a dislocated lens or dermoid cyst, and an oval soft tissue lesion interpreted as a pseudotumor. Abnormal bone arising from the inner table of the right occipital bone and extending along the tentorium cerebelli was detected, and a small lipoma at the right tentorium cerebelli was seen. Bilateral atresia of external auditory canals were detectable, and right abnormal middle ear with small size ossicles mainly the malleus, whereas inner ear was normal on both sides. Through the big right parietal foramen, a slight herniation of the underlying meninges was evident, to conform to the defect, connected to the superior cerebellar cistern.

case_report: A 38-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital with a 6-month history of joint pain and dry mouth, which caused her to wake up from thirst at night. She did not report any history of dry eyes, blurred vision, abdominal pain, fever, or bruising of the lower extremities. She had no history of head and neck radiotherapy and no relevant medical history. Laboratory tests revealed negative results for rheumatoid factor, anticyclic citrullinated polypeptide antibody, ANA, and ANAs, along with elevated C-reactive protein levels and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Additional findings included a high immunoglobulin G (IgG) level of 20.4 g/L, normal blood glucose levels, normal submandibular gland and bilateral parotid gland function but impaired excretion function, and a positive Schirmer test (4.8 mm/5 minutes for the bilateral lacrimal glands). An upper abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan with enhancement showed no abnormalities.
test_results: The labial gland biopsy revealed multiple foci of lymphocyte infiltration, structural destruction of the parotid lobules, and partial atrophy of the acini. Pathological examination of the tissue showed chronic inflammatory changes and Chisholm grade 4 lymphocyte infiltration.

case_report: A 51-year-old Hispanic woman presented with progressive loss of pigmentation on her chest, abdomen, and bilateral flanks. She first noticed the hypopigmented patches two years earlier after experiencing a severe sunburn at the beach. Her medical history includes hypothyroidism, diagnosed 26 years ago, and managed with levothyroxine 75 mcg daily. Physical examination showed hypopigmentation on her chest, extending from the anterior shoulders to the breasts bilaterally. The absence of pigment was also observed on her lower abdomen, from the umbilicus to the suprapubic region, extending bilaterally to involve the flanks and lower back. There was no hypopigmentation around the eyes, mouth, vulvar, perianal areas, or distal extremities.
test_results: Laboratory results were notable for a positive ANA titer (1:80; normal, <1:80) with a homogenous pattern and an elevated SS-B/La antigen (4.3 AI; normal, < 0.9 AI).

case_report: A 25-year-old male, born to parents who are not related by blood, visited the outpatient department with skin pigmentation, painful cracks on the hands and feet, and reduced sweating since birth. He experienced skin tightening on the distal extremities for the past 15 years. His family members did not exhibit similar symptoms. There was no history of Raynaud's phenomenon, photosensitivity, growth or mental retardation, or exposure to chemicals or drugs that could cause sclerotic skin. Physical examination revealed diffuse scleroatrophy with fissuring and hyperpigmentation on both palms and soles. The skin on the distal extremities showed reduced pinchability, generalized atrophy, dyschromia, telangiectasia, and dryness. There was an ulnar deviation at the left wrist due to contracture along the ulnar border of the palm. A raised, tender nodular lesion measuring approximately 1 cm × 1.5 cm was observed on the left thenar eminence, without ulceration or bleeding. Nail changes included minimal growth of the third and fifth toenails on both feet and absence of the nail on the second right toe. All finger and toenails exhibited longitudinal ridging and discoloration. Routine blood tests were within normal limits.
test_results: Excisional biopsy of the thenar nodule revealed mild hyperkeratosis with dysplasia of the basal keratinocytes and formation of small buds extending into the papillary dermis. Biopsy of palms and soles revealed massive hyperkeratosis and acanthosis and that of the sclerosed skin on the left forearm showed acanthosis with an accentuated granular layer, orthohyperkeratosis with sparse mononuclear cell infiltrate. Immunohistochemistry analysis showed a marked reduction in CD1a, Lag+ and S-100 epidermal Langerhans cells.

case_report: A 27-year-old male postman from southwestern China visited the hospital for treatment. He exhibited brownish-black plaques symmetrically located on the dorsum of his hands and feet, which had been present for the past three years. These lesions turned white and macerated after being immersed in water. The patient reported that he did not have these plaques three years prior to his hospital visit. The condition worsened during warm, humid summers and improved in winter. Sweating or water exposure triggered the plaques, which disappeared after the affected areas dried. The patient did not experience itching, pain, or any other discomfort. He was in good health, with no history of systemic disease, medication, hand and foot hyperhidrosis, or family history of hereditary diseases or conditions related to his current symptoms. The most notable clinical feature was dark brown to brownish-black pigmented keratotic lesions with a rough surface, sharply demarcated, and symmetrically distributed around the wrists, dorsal hands, elbows, ankles, and dorsal feet. The patient did not show symptoms of classical palmoplantar keratoderma. The lesions became white and macerated after approximately five minutes of water immersion or sweating, but returned to their original appearance after drying. Physical examination revealed no abnormalities in other skin and mucous membranes.
test_results: Histopathological findings showed hyperkeratosis of the skin, thickening of the stratum spinosum and mild perivascular lymphocytic infiltration in the papillary layer of the dermis.

case_report: A 62-year-old female was admitted to the hospital for evaluation of an incidentally detected hepatic lesion. During a routine health examination at a local hospital, a hepatic mass was identified. The patient did not report any specific symptoms such as abdominal pain or loss of appetite. Physical examination showed no notable findings, including the absence of hepatomegaly. Laboratory results were within normal ranges. Hematologic studies revealed a red blood cell (RBC) count of 4.7×10^6/mm3, hemoglobin level of 14.3 g/dL, and hematocrit of 42.1%. The white blood cell (WBC) count was 5,100/mm3, and the platelet count was 228,000/mm3. Biochemical tests indicated serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) at 22 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 15 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) at 85 IU/L. Serum protein was measured at 7.6 g/dL, and albumin at 4.8 g/dL. Total bilirubin was 0.9 mg/dL. Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) was 1.6 ng/mL, and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) was 2.5 ng/mL. The hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) test was negative, while the anti-HBs test was positive.
test_results: US showed about a 4-cm sized cystic liver mass in right lobe. It showed irregular margin with internally homogenous fluid-like echo with several peripheral echogenic septa-like structures. Precontrast computed tomography (CT) scan showed a lobulating contoured homogenous low attenuated mass in right lobe posterior superior segment. The attenuation was measured as about 10 Hounsfield number that indicated clear fluid. After contrast media injection, arterial phase and portal phase images were taken, and there was no contrast enhancement in the mass.

case_report: Patient information: a 48-year-old man, non-smoker, non-alcoholic, with no medical or surgical history, who presented with abdominal pain. Clinical findings: clinical examination revealed tenderness in the right hypochondriac region, with no palpable mass. Timeline of current episode: an ultrasonography of the abdomen was performed revealing a liver nodule. A biopsy along with initial histological and immunohistochemical study were conducted, showing a diffuse expression of cytokeratin 7 (CK7), without expression of cytokeratin 20 (CK20), transcription termination factor 1 (TTF1) and prostate-specific antigen (PSA). The Paraffin embedded tissue blocks were addressed to our laboratory for proofreading.
test_results: The histological examination of the tissue blocks revealed a well delimited lesion, composed of multiple duct-like structures, disposed in a fibrous stroma. The duct structures are of small to medium size, irregularly shaped or rounded, lined by a single layer of bland-looking cuboidal epithelium. Mitotic figures were absent.

case_report: Patient information: a 94-year-old woman, non-smoker, non-alcoholic, with no medical or surgical history, who presented with abdominal pain. Clinical findings: clinical examination revealed tenderness in the right hypochondriac region, with no palpable mass. Ultrasonography of the abdomen revealed a cephalic mass of the pancreas. In July 2020, the patient underwent a placement of a biliodigestive bypass with cholecystectomy, along with a biopsy of a hepatic nodule, which was found incidentally during the surgical procedure.
test_results: The histological examination of the hepatic nodule revealed a collection of numerous dilated and cystic ductal structures embedded in a dense fibrous stroma, lined by a single layer of cuboidal epithelium. The cells were not atypical, showing round nuclei with homogeneous chromatin and eosinophilic cytoplasm. Mitotic figures are absent. Focal inspissated bile was noticed within the lumina of the ductal structures.

case_report: A 36-year-old male visited the outpatient clinic with a 21-year history of recurring nodules on his face, body, and limbs, along with abscesses on his buttocks. His family history included similar symptoms in his mother, younger brother, maternal grandmother, and an uncle. There was no presence of diabetes mellitus, hirsutism, inflammatory bowel diseases, or obesity in the family. Only his grandmother was noted to be a smoker. Upon initial examination, multiple nodules and pustules of varying sizes were observed on his body and limbs. The patient had undergone several surgeries and had been treated with various antibiotics, which provided only palliative relief. Six years after his first visit, a tumor appeared on his right buttock. Despite undergoing chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and surgical excision, the tumor recurred and spread to the sacral bone and inguinal lymph nodes. The patient passed away from SCC eight years after his initial visit. In his family, 5 out of 12 members exhibited similar symptoms, while 7 did not. Five family members participated in a study, with the proband and his younger brother presenting similar symptoms and the brother receiving antibiotic treatment. The proband’s maternal grandmother and mother had milder symptoms, but their treatments were not documented. Written informed consent was obtained from participants or their legal guardians, adhering to the Declaration of Helsinki. The study received approval from the Medical Ethics Committee of Nihon University (permission number: 194-0).
test_results: A tumour developed on his right buttock, and a diagnosis of SCC was made based on histopathological findings. A heterozygous single-nucleotide mutation c.1285C>T (p. R429X) in the exon 11 of NCSTN gene (reference sequence GenBank accession number NM_015331.2) was detected in the proband (III-2), his younger brother (III-3), and his mother (II-2).

case_report: An 18-year-old Indonesian woman presented to the general surgery department with a primary complaint of chronic constipation since childhood. She reported having bowel movements only once or twice a month and had only used over-the-counter cathartic drugs for relief. She did not recall any details about her early bowel habits. There were no reported issues with growth or development. Physical examination revealed a slightly distended abdomen and a collapsed rectal ampulla upon digital rectal examination.
test_results: Plain abdominal radiograph revealed that the air distribution in the colon and small intestine was increased with coiled spring appearance. There was neither stepladder appearance nor subdiaphragmatic free air. A contrast enema study was performed and showed that the sigmoid colon was dilated and the rectum was narrowed with rectosigmoid index less than 1 and irregular rectosigmoid mucosa. The study also showed neither rat tail appearance nor filling defects.

case_report: In January 2020, a 29-year-old male presented to the gastroenterology department with diarrhea occurring five or six times per day, characterized by watery or bloody stools, along with abdominal pain, bloating, nausea, and vomiting for the past month. He had a history of severe diarrhea with watery or bloody stools, abdominal pain, and an anal fistula at 21 years old. Initial treatment included prednisone 40 mg/day orally to induce remission and mesalamine 2 g/day for maintenance. Despite treatment, symptoms recurred. Laboratory tests showed an elevated white blood cell count (10.1 × 10^9/L) and procalcitonin level (2.69 ng/mL). Stool examination revealed 15–20 white blood cells and 15–20 red blood cells per high-power field, with no pathogens detected. Inflammatory markers were significantly elevated: C-reactive protein at 47.3 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate at 65 mm/h, tumor necrosis factor-α at 10.6 pg/mL, interleukin-6 at 41.1 pg/mL, and D-dimer at 2.31 mg/L. Epstein-Barr virus DNA level was 526.1 IU/mL (whole-blood specimens), and the T-SPOT.TB test was positive (spot numbers for ESAT-6 and CFP-10 wells both >50). Tests for Cytomegalovirus DNA, hepatitis B virus surface antigen, hepatitis C virus antibody, and Clostridium difficile (glutamate dehydrogenase and tcdA/B) were negative. Colonoscopy revealed longitudinal ulcers, a cobblestone pattern in the mucosa, and a sigmoid colon stricture. Computed tomography enterography (CTE) showed uneven segmented colonic wall thickening from the transverse colon to the rectum and a suspicious jejunal–sigmoid fistula. The patient was treated with antibiotics (levofloxacin 0.5 g/day and metronidazole 1 g/day) and enteral nutrition via tube feeding. Anti-tuberculosis treatment (isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol) was administered for 3 months. In April 2020, the patient was admitted for emergency care due to nausea, retching, vomiting, and cessation of defecation and passing gas after eating an apple one week prior. Physical examination showed full abdominal wall resistance, abdominal tenderness, and rebound tenderness. Plain abdominal radiograph and CTE indicated an intestinal obstruction proximal to the sigmoid colon with acute peritonitis.
test_results: Post-operative pathological examination showed a deficiency of myenteric and submucosal neurons in the rectum and sigmoid colon.

case_report: A 20-month-old male child presented to the pediatric emergency department with a 15-day history of fever, poor urinary stream, and constipation. On examination, the child was febrile, lethargic, severely malnourished, and had bilateral percutaneous nephrostomies (PCN) in place. His weight was below the 3rd percentile and his height was below the 10th percentile according to the Indian Academy of Pediatrics growth standards. The child was born via normal vaginal delivery with uneventful antenatal and postnatal periods. At 2 months old, the mother noted a poor urinary stream and constipation (one bowel movement every 2-3 days). At 3 months old, he was admitted for fever, poor urinary stream, and failure to gain weight. An abdominal ultrasonography (USG) revealed bilateral hydronephrosis with a thickened bladder wall. A micturating cystourethrogram (MCU) showed a small capacity trabeculated bladder with a high riding bladder neck and dilated posterior urethra. These findings were confirmed by cystoscopy, and fulguration of the valves was performed. The patient was discharged in stable condition. After a few months, his symptoms recurred, and he was admitted to a tertiary care center with fever, urinary dribbling, and failure to thrive. A subsequent USG showed bilateral hydronephrosis and an irregular thickened urinary bladder (wall thickening of 6.5 mm). Bilateral PCN were placed, and he was referred to our center with PCN in situ. Current hematological evaluation showed: Hb 7.8 g/dl, total leukocyte count 21,000/mm3, differential leukocyte count (polymorphs 81% and lymphocytes 23%), and platelet count 230,000/mm3. Urinalysis revealed protein 2+, pus cells 120–130/Hpf, and red blood cells 8–10/Hpf. Blood urea nitrogen was 11.68 mg/dl, and serum creatinine was 0.2 mg/dl. Urine culture grew Enterobacter cloacae, which was treated with appropriate parenteral antibiotics. Thyroid function tests were normal with a thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level of 2.86 mIU/L. A repeat MCU showed an elongated urinary bladder with a trabeculated outline without vesicoureteric reflux.
