The child also had gradually progressive abdominal distension, likely due to chronic constipation, which was managed with laxatives and enemas. A barium enema revealed a dilated rectum and proximal sigmoid colon with a short-segment persistent narrowing in the distal sigmoid colon.
test_results: Rectal biopsy confirmed the absence of ganglion cells in the affected segment of the sigmoid colon.

case_report: A 20-year-old male patient was admitted to the Evandro Chagas National Institute of Infectious Diseases (INI/Fiocruz) with a high fever of 39 °C in the first week of February 2021. He had been under the care of a pulmonologist due to a persistent dry cough following a mild case of COVID-19, confirmed by a positive real-time reverse-transcription PCR (RT-PCR) of a nasopharyngeal swab, 4 months prior. The patient reported significant dust exposure while playing soccer on a ground field with bird excreta 5 weeks before the onset of fever. Initial imaging included a chest tomography, which showed small nodular opacities without calcifications, measuring up to 0.8 cm, located on the periphery of the anterior segment of the upper left lobe, associated with some confluent vessels, as well as enlargement of the left pulmonary hilum and small mediastinal lymph nodes. Laboratory analyses, including hematological and biochemical tests, were within normal ranges except for an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 34 mm (normal range <15 mm). Anti-HIV serology was negative. Following the onset of fever, levofloxacin was administered, but there was no improvement after 48 hours of regular antibiotic use. A subsequent RT-PCR of the nasopharyngeal swab was negative.
test_results: The M band in double immunodiffusion test was present.

case_report: A 27-year-old female, an active smoker with no significant past medical history, came to the emergency department due to a worsening productive cough, night sweats, and a 20-pound weight loss over six months. She reported no recent travel, sick contacts, or illicit drug use, and had no personal or family history of malignancies. Upon arrival, her temperature was 100.1F and her heart rate was 100 beats per minute. Physical examination revealed decreased breath sounds in the right upper lung field, with no palpable lymph nodes or organomegaly. Laboratory tests indicated leukocytosis (15,600 mm/L) with a granulocytic predominance, while her comprehensive metabolic panel and lactate dehydrogenase levels were normal. A chest X-ray showed multiloculated cavitary lesions in the right upper and middle lobes. A subsequent chest CT scan revealed a 13.1 x 10.9 x 10.7 cm heterogeneous mass with internal cavitation in the right middle and upper lobes, along with prominent prevascular/mediastinal lymph nodes measuring up to 1.9 x 1.2 cm. The mass was observed to be encasing the pulmonary artery. The patient was treated with ceftriaxone and azithromycin for presumed community-acquired pneumonia, but her symptoms persisted. An infectious workup, including bacterial cultures, acid-fast and Gram staining, serum quantiferon, cryptococcal antigen, and HIV serology, returned negative results. Bronchoscopy with ultrasound-guided biopsy and bronchoalveolar lavage did not yield diagnostic results.
test_results: Pathology revealed extensive necrosis with rare atypical cells suspicious for malignancy. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) was positive for cluster of differentiation (CD) 30, melanoma ubiquitous mutated protein (MUM), organic anion transporter (OCT) 2, negative for CD20, and indeterminate for B-cell Oct-binding protein (BOB) 1. Paired Box (PAX) 5 was dim. CD15 and CD45 could not be determined since they were obscured by numerous strongly staining background cells, which consisted of a mixture of both B-cells (CD20+, PAX5+) and T-cells (CD 3+).

case_report: A 61-year-old man with a history of smoking 30 packs a year presented with a chronic productive cough, intermittent fever, and joint pain for 2 years and was admitted to our hospital in May 2019. An initial chest CT scan at a local hospital revealed multiple nodules and areas of consolidation. His symptoms and lung infiltrates typically improved with antibiotics or low-dose corticosteroids. Over the 2 years, he experienced multiple episodes with migratory lung consolidations. He denied drug abuse, occupational, and environmental exposures. On admission, crackles were heard at the left lung base during auscultation. Tenderness was observed at the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints, and the wrist and knee joints were swollen and warm. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (44 mm/h). Blood hemoglobin level, leukocyte count, platelet count, rheumatologic screening including anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, tumor markers, and infection tests were all negative. Arterial blood gas analysis showed a pH of 7.41, PaCO2 of 38.8 mm Hg, and PaO2 of 75.4 mm Hg on room air. Pulmonary function tests indicated a restrictive pattern with a total lung capacity of 74.9% predicted and a diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) of 70% predicted. Chest CT scan showed multiple consolidations and nodules along the bronchial vascular bundle. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) from the right middle lobe retrieved 56% lymphocytes and 43% macrophages. Flow cytometry of BAL lymphocytes detected abnormal phenotypic lymphocytes (CD3−/CD4+) at 27%. No pathogens were found in the smear or culture of the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF). Transbronchial cryobiopsy revealed OP on pathologic examination. Ultrasound examination detected polysynovitis. As the joint pain worsened, intramuscular diprospan (betamethasone 2 mg/betamethasone dipropionate 5 mg, every 2 weeks) was administered following a rheumatologist's consultation. The nodules and consolidation resolved significantly, leading to the cancellation of a planned biopsy. The patient was discharged with a regimen of prednisone (30 mg daily) and leflunomide (20 mg daily) and was followed up regularly. Four months later, a routine follow-up CT scan showed new consolidation and nodules. Further PET-CT demonstrated increased F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake in lung lesions, with a peak standard uptake value (SUV) of 6.5 in the superior right lower lobe, without lymphadenopathy or other abnormal uptake.
test_results: Pathologic examination showed organizing nodules, and large atypical lymphoid cells of mono-, bi-, or multi-nuclei with prominent nucleoli, scattered in an abundance of lymphoid cells, neutrophils, histiocytes, and eosinophils background. Immunohistochemical staining revealed CD20−, CD3−, CD30+, PAX5+, OCT-2+, BOB.1-. Epstein-Barr virus encoded RNA was negative in in situ hybridization.

case_report: The patient, a 2-year-old boy with no prior health issues and negative for HIV, presented with persistent red, raised skin lesions over the right deltoid muscle at the site of BCG vaccination and on the right side of his chest wall, along with swelling in both fingers. Following BCG vaccination at birth, a nodule appeared at the vaccination site, surrounded by a cluster of raised papules that eventually merged into a red, non-healing plaque-like lesion without fistulation. At 18 months old, a similar cluster of papules developed on the right anterior chest wall, below and to the side of the right nipple. Concurrently, he experienced swelling in his fingers. Imaging of the hands and chest showed multiple areas of bone lucency in the phalanges of both hands, the right distal humerus, both clavicles, and the left scapula, indicative of multifocal osteomyelitis.
test_results: Skin biopsies of the BCG site and chest wall lesions cultured Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, which on molecular testing was confirmed to be BCG, susceptible to both rifampicin and isoniazid. Immunological evaluation revealed raised IgG, IgM, and IgA concentrations, normal CD3, CD4, CD8, CD19 and CD16/56 cell counts, and a normal oxidative burst test (dihydrorhodamine 123 (DHR) as oxidative probe).
Orpha_name: Susceptibility to viral and mycobacterial infections due to STAT1 deficiency

case_report: A 48-year-old right-handed Thai male presented with a large, painful lump in the left axillary region. The patient first noticed the mass one year ago, and it significantly increased in size over the past six months. The pain intensified over time despite the use of painkillers, with no cold hypersensitivity or neurological deficits in the area. The patient had no prior medical conditions and no personal or family history of tumors. Physical examination revealed a large, solid, soft tissue mass in the left axillary region, which was mildly tender upon palpation but showed no pulsatile sensation. Tinel’s sign was negative, and no neurological deficits were noted. However, the patient experienced limited range of motion in the left shoulder due to pain. Laboratory results indicated a white blood cell count of 7280/μL with 62% neutrophils, hemoglobin level of 14.1 g/dL, platelet count of 247300/mm3, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 15 mm/h, lactic dehydrogenase level of 150 U/L, and normal electrolyte profile. The human immunodeficiency virus antibody test was negative.
test_results: Histologically, the tumor was composed of sheets and cords of relatively uniform tumor cells with moderate amounts of foamy, lightly eosinophilic cytoplasm and round to oval mildly hyperchromatic nuclei without atypia. Immunohistochemical studies revealed the tumor cells to be positive for smooth muscle actin, vimentin and collagen type IV, and negative for S100, AE1/AE3, CD34, GCDFP-15, chromogranin, and synaptophysin. Plain radiography revealed soft tissue shadow around his left axillar. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a 9.6 cm × 11.2 cm × 9.8 cm heterogeneous contrast-enhancing mass bulging from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus and encasing the axillary artery and vein associated with vascular invasion. Furthermore, the pre-operative chest computerized tomography displayed a 3-mm nodule at the posterior basal segment of the right lower lung.
diagnosis: Glomus tumor of uncertain malignant potential

case_report: A 25-year-old woman reported experiencing persistent shoulder pain since her teenage years. Over the years, she had tried various treatments including different non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), local steroid injections, and physiotherapy. The pain was described as diffuse, vague, and chronic, without significantly limiting her range of motion. It was more intense at night, leading to multiple episodes of sleep disruption. Physical examination revealed notable tenderness on the clavicle. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count (CBC), C-reactive protein (CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and other biochemical tests, showed no abnormalities. Despite receiving NSAIDs based on clinical findings, there was no significant reduction in pain intensity. Physiotherapy sessions were initiated, but the first session exacerbated the shoulder pain. Subsequently, an intra-articular steroid injection was administered, but it did not provide lasting relief.
test_results: MRI by GAD shows a large heterogeneous enhancing mass in supraclavicular area with extension to clivus. Bony parts were unremarkable. Histologic sections of the tumor showed small and round uniform cells with indistinct cytoplasmic borders, no mitosis, and no atypia. No necrosis has been identified. IHC staining showed positive CD31, factor 8 antigen, vimentin and smooth muscle actin (SMA). The cells were negative with cytokeratin, CD99, and leukocyte common antigen (LCA). Ki-67 was very low and less than 1%.

case_report: A female infant, aged 21 minutes and weighing 830 grams at 28+6 weeks of gestational age, was admitted to our hospital on May 9, 2020, due to premature birth and shallow breathing. She received endotracheal intubation in the delivery room after resuscitation, and a pulmonary surfactant was administered through the endotracheal tube. Once stable, she was transferred to the NICU with T-piece ventilation. Upon admission, her breathing condition improved, leading to the removal of the endotracheal tube and initiation of nasal continuous positive airway pressure. She was also treated with vitamin K1, cefoperazone sodium/sulbactam sodium combined with ampicillin, caffeine citrate, minimal enteral feeding, intravenous fluid infusion, and warming. With parental consent, a 3.5 Fr umbilical arterial catheter (UAC) and umbilical venous catheter (UVC) were inserted on the day of admission. The UAC was used for continuous invasive arterial blood pressure monitoring, and the UVC was used for intravenous medication and parenteral nutrition administration. UAC patency was maintained by flushing with 0.5 IU/mL heparin solution every 6 hours, along with continuous infusion of the same solution. On May 18, the UAC and UVC were removed, and a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC; 1.9 Fr) was inserted via an upper limb. On May 19, the patient exhibited significant abdominal distension, a visible bowel pattern, and weakened bowel sounds, leading to a pause in feeding. The infant was delivered by cesarean section at 28+6 weeks of gestational age to a gravida 3 para 1 mother. The pregnancy was complicated by severe preeclampsia, diamniotic-dichorionic twins (one survived and one died), abnormal liver function, fatty liver, bilateral hydronephrosis with dilatation of the upper ureter, and thrombocytopenia. The infant’s Apgar scores at 1, 5, and 10 minutes were 6, 9, and 9, respectively. Physical examination revealed prematurity, poor responsiveness, a temperature of 36.1 °C, a pulse of 158/min, a respiratory rate of 65/min, irregular spontaneous breathing, and retraction. No abnormalities were observed in the heart and abdomen, and bowel sounds were normal.
test_results: Abdominal X-ray showed inflation of the small intestine but no obvious dilatation of the intestinal lumen or effusion. Color Doppler ultrasound showed partial thrombosis of the abdominal aorta (2 cm × 0.3 cm) and abdominal effusion. On May 21, abdominal X-ray showed that the range of intestinal inflation increased over previous measurements.

case_report: A two-day-old female, born at 39 weeks gestation, was transferred from a community hospital to a tertiary level neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) due to the presence of bloody stools. The pregnancy was largely uneventful, and the infant was delivered via spontaneous vaginal delivery after induction for pre-eclampsia. The mother, a 28-year-old G1P0, had no significant medical history, and her serologies for rubella, herpes, HIV, and syphilis were protective. Group B Streptococcus testing was negative, and there was no known maternal cytomegalovirus status. The only medication taken by the mother was prenatal vitamins. There were no infections, diabetes, or familial gastrointestinal issues reported. The infant was born with APGAR scores of 8 and 9 at one and five minutes, respectively. The umbilical cord gas showed a pH of 7.17 and a base excess of -7.7 mmol/L. Standard newborn care was provided, including a subcutaneous injection of vitamin K. During the first 24 hours, the infant experienced latch issues while breastfeeding and underwent an ankyloglossia release. The infant continued breastfeeding and was also given formula three times. The family noted approximately ten dark green to black, loose, foul-smelling bowel movements, and the infant became less interested in feeding. On the second day of life, initial vitals at the mother's bedside showed a heart rate of 180 beats per minute and a temperature of 38.3 °C. Upon reassessment in the nursery, the heart rate was 130 beats per minute, and the temperature was 37.3 °C, with other vitals within normal limits. The physical exam revealed the infant was less active but responsive and appropriate with handling. Bowel sounds were present, the abdomen was soft, and no hemangiomas were observed on the skin. There was a questionable anal fissure at the 12 o'clock position. Initial complete blood counts showed a white cell count of 8 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin of 19.2 g/dL, platelets of 258 × 10^9/L, and no eosinophils. Capillary sample gas and electrolytes were within normal limits; C-reactive protein was 21.5 mg/L, and plasma lactate was 4.2 mmol/L. Over the next ten hours, the infant had approximately four moderately bloody stools. A coagulation profile was within normal limits, and blood cultures were negative. Antibiotics were initiated. An abdominal X-ray showed a nonspecific bowel gas pattern without pneumatosis or dilated bowel loops. The infant was transferred uneventfully to the tertiary NICU. Upon arrival at approximately 55 hours of life, while hemodynamically stable on room air, the infant began producing copious bilious emesis without signs of discomfort.
test_results: Abdominal x-ray showed pneumoperitoneum.

case_report: A 63-year-old female presented with discomfort in the right lower quadrant, ongoing since January 2011. Physical examination showed no tenderness but identified a palpable, fist-sized mass in the right lower quadrant. Imaging revealed a 60-mm cystic mass at the appendix with calcification in its wall. The mass showed no thickening or contrast enhancement in its entire wall. Surgical removal was recommended, but the patient opted for outpatient follow-up. Three months later, imaging showed no changes. The patient was advised to return in 3 months but did not. The patient later reported persistent pain in the right lower quadrant since August 2012. Examination revealed a similar mass with tenderness. The patient was admitted for further evaluation. The patient had no history of alcohol or smoking, and prior medical history included surgery for internal hemorrhoids at age 59. No significant family history or current oral medication use was reported. On admission, the patient was alert with a blood pressure of 123/73 mmHg, pulse rate of 60 beats/min (non-arrhythmic), and body temperature of 37.5°C. The palpebral conjunctiva was not anemic, and no yellow discoloration of the bulbar conjunctiva was noted. Heart and breath sounds were clear. The abdomen was flat and soft with a palpable, slightly hard, minimally movable, fist-sized mass in the right lower quadrant with tenderness but no rebound tenderness or muscular rigidity. The liver and spleen were not palpable. Hematological examination showed mild anemia (hemoglobin, 11.4 g/dl) and increased inflammatory reaction (C-reactive protein, 6.5 mg/dl). Tumor marker levels were not elevated.
test_results: Abdominal CT on day 2 revealed no change in the size of the existing cystic mass from the previous CT scan performed in January 2011; however, it revealed thickening of the mass wall on the appendicular ostium and contrast enhancement at the corresponding site. No projection was observed in the mass cavity. On abdominal US on day 2, the mass was anechoic overall and demonstrated a partly layered echo pattern. The mass wall on the appendicular ostium was thickened with a 13-mm projection protruding toward the cavity from part of the wall. Another 9-mm projection was also observed in the appendicular tip. CEUS was then performed to assess blood flow using a Toshiba SSA-790A US system (Aplio XG; Toshiba Medical Systems, Otawara, Japan) with a 3.75-MHz convex probe (PVT-375BT). Imaging was performed with a mechanical index of 0.21 and the focus was adjusted to the depth of the mass. After imaging conditions were set, Sonazoid (perfluorobutane; GE Healthcare, Oslo, Norway) was infused at the recommended dose of 0.015 ml/kg via the cubital vein. Contrast enhancement was observed in the thickened wall of the mass on the appendicular ostium and in the projection on the same side; however, not in the projection on the appendicular tip.

case_report: A 45-year-old male presented with penile growths that had been present for 8 months without causing any symptoms. The patient first noticed a small elevated keratotic growth following circumcision, which was performed 10 months ago for preexisting phimosis. The growths had gradually increased in size and number over time. There was no history of trauma or systemic disease, and no history of exposure to sexually transmitted diseases. Previous treatment with topical antibiotic cream did not result in any improvement. Clinical examination revealed multiple hard, yellowish, bark-like horny masses on the glans penis, sparing the urethral meatus. The lesions were confined to the glans penis, with the penile shaft and scrotum appearing normal. Inguinal lymph nodes were not palpable. Serological tests for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B and C viruses were negative. Routine laboratory investigations, including basic blood counts, blood glucose levels, and renal and liver function tests, were within normal limits.
test_results: Histopathology of the lesion revealed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with extensive hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, acanthosis, individual cell keratinization, and atypical cells. Dermis showed dense lymphoplasmacytic inflammatory infiltrate.
diagnosis: pseudoepitheliomatous keratotic and micaceous balanitis evolving to squamous cell carcinoma of the glans penis
Orpha_name: Squamous cell carcinoma of the penis

case_report: A 60-year-old male presented with a growth over the glans penis for two months, accompanied by pain. There was no history of contact bleeding. The patient was not circumcised. He had noticed a swelling on the scrotum for the past six months. On examination, there was a 2 x 3 cm ulceroproliferative growth over the glans extending over the corona onto the shaft of the penis. The ulcer was fixed to the ventral aspect of the glans penis with induration proximally extending up to the mid-shaft of the penis. Bilateral inguinal lymph nodes were palpable, 3-4 on each side, 0.5 cm in size, firm and mobile in nature. The patient also had a right-sided primary vaginal hydrocele.
test_results: Histopathological analysis revealed an ulcerated stratified squamous epithelial lining with underlying lesion composed of fascicles of spindle cells with moderate pleomorphism. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) was done from bilateral inguinal nodes which revealed reactive hyperplasia.
Orpha_name: Squamous cell carcinoma of the penis

case_report: A 49-year-old woman, who does not smoke and works as a farmer, was admitted for clinical evaluation. She had no significant history of lung disease. One month prior to admission, she experienced mild shortness of breath and a dull pain in the right side of her chest. She did not have a fever, cough, sputum production, or coughing up blood. Spirometry results indicated a moderate obstructive syndrome. A chest X-ray revealed a well-defined homogenous opacity with a partially calcified wall in the right side of the chest.
test_results: CT scan of the chest showed a bilocular cystic mass, 15 × 9.5 cm at its maximum diameter, in the inferior and middle lobes of the right lung, close to the right atrium and vena cava. Bronchoscopy did not show any endobronchial lesion and the cytological examination of the bronchoaspirate was negative for malignant cells. Immunohistochemical analysis showed positive immunostaining for CK7 and CEA and negative immunostaining for CK20, HBME, calretinin and TTF-1. P53 and Ki67 (MIB-1) positive immunostaining was found respectively in about 50% and 30% of the neoplastic nuclei.

case_report: A 67-year-old woman, who showed no symptoms and was not on any medications, underwent testing during a routine physical examination. She had no notable medical history, but her mother had a history of multiple myeloma. The MCED test indicated a CSD result with CSO predictions pointing to the uterus as the first prediction and the ovary as the second prediction.
test_results: Pelvic ultrasound showing an 8.5 cm × 8.7 cm heterogeneous pelvic mass followed by a CT scan confirming a vascular pelvic mass arising from the left ovary.
Orpha_name: Clear cell adenocarcinoma of the ovary

case_report: A 71-year-old female, gravida 2, para 2, presented with worsening abdominal distention over the past year. Her medical history includes appendicitis treated with an appendectomy in her thirties. Family medical history is unremarkable. Physical examination revealed a very large, minimally movable mass in both hypochondria. Pelvic and abdominal ultrasonography identified a large cystic mass with a solid component. Serum tumor marker levels were as follows: carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) at 2.0 ng/mL (normal < 37.0), CA19-9 at 459.2 U/mL (normal < 37.0), SCC at 18.9 ng/mL (normal < 1.5), and CA125 at 329.9 U/mL (normal < 35.0). Other blood tests were within normal limits. Pelvic MRI showed a large cystic mass with an enhanced nodular component and diffusion restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging. Computed tomography (CT) revealed a 3 cm mass in the liver. Fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) demonstrated FDG uptake in the pelvic tumor (SUVmax = 22.9) and the hepatic nodule (SUVmax = 13.7), indicating potential metastases.
test_results: The pathology showed metastatic cells in normal hepatocytes. Immunohistochemical staining showed that p40, p63, and hepatocytes were all negative.
diagnosis: Ovarian clear cell carcinoma arising from ovarian mature cystic teratoma
Orpha_name: Clear cell adenocarcinoma of the ovary

case_report: A 65-year-old Caucasian female with a medical history including hypertension, gastroesophageal reflux disease, iron deficiency anemia, and rheumatoid arthritis presented with exposed left mandibular bone and a persistent neck fistula 3 weeks following the extraction of tooth #20. She had undergone an extraoral incision and drainage for a submandibular abscess by an external practitioner. The patient had a history of bisphosphonate use for osteoporosis, specifically Risedronate (Actonel) for 4 years, followed by yearly Zoledronic Acid (Reclast) injections for 2 years, with the last dose administered approximately 1 year before the tooth extraction. Additionally, she began receiving Denosumab (Prolia) subcutaneously about 1 week prior to the extraction. Physical examination revealed a 1 cm cutaneous fistula in the left submandibular region. Intraoral examination showed an area of exposed bone approximately 1 cm in size on the buccal aspect of the mandible near tooth #20, along with a separate area of exposed bone on the lingual aspect. There was a minimal amount of thin purulent drainage observed both intraorally and on the neck bandage. The patient was scheduled for follow-up to discuss treatment options.
test_results: CT scan showed sclerotic changes involving the mandible diffusely.

case_report: A 58-year-old woman visited a dental clinic in December 2008, reporting severe spontaneous pain on the right side of her lower jaw following a prosthesis replacement in an area where a dental implant had been placed sixteen years earlier. Her medical history indicated that she began taking Fosamax® (alendronate sodium) 70 mg weekly for rheumatoid arthritis in 2004. She had no history of smoking, radiotherapy, infections, or trauma in the maxillofacial region, and the dental implant had been functioning normally until the onset of symptoms. Clinical examination revealed mild erythema in the mucosa around the right dental implant, with no signs of purulent discharge, gingival recession, or bone exposure. Probing indicated increased depth values and detachment of the mucosa from the peri-implant bone, along with a loss of the biological seal.
test_results: A computed tomography (CT) showed a substantial radiolucency around the involved dental implant, featuring loss of the crestal bone. The results of histological analysis revealed necrotic lamellar bone fragments with chronic and acute inflammatory cells, as well bacterial colonies. The serum C-terminal cross-linking telopeptide of collagen (CTX) test revealed normal values (250 pg/mL).

case_report: A 50-year-old housewife reported experiencing severe pain, early-morning stiffness, and swelling in the joints of her left ring and little fingers. These symptoms began 3 months ago and have progressively worsened. The pain was most intense in the morning and did not improve with rest. Pain levels, measured using the IASP Pain Scale, ranged from 6 to 8, with temporary relief after taking analgesics such as paracetamol and diclofenac. She observed painless joint deformities in these fingers a year ago and sought medical attention. There was no history of trauma, fever, hair loss, or oral ulcers. She had no known prior medical conditions and no family history of hand osteoarthritis or other skin or joint diseases. Additionally, there was no personal or family history of atopic eczema, asthma, allergic rhinitis, or allergic conjunctivitis. The patient also noticed multiple itchy skin rashes on both ankles and knees over the past year, which were minimally scaly. Physical examination showed deformity of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints of the left ring and little fingers, with fixed flexion of both joints. The little finger’s distal phalanx was curved inward. The joints were swollen, erythematous, and tender upon palpation, with limited range of motion due to pain. A radiograph of the left hand revealed abnormalities at the DIP joints of the ring and little fingers, showing irregularities, sclerotic joint margins, narrowed joint spaces, and marginal osteophytes. Blood tests indicated normal white cell counts (7.42 × 10^9/L), a slightly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 22 mm/hour (normal range: 1–20 mm/hour), and negative results for antinuclear antibody (ANA), rheumatoid factor (RF), and anticyclic citrullinated protein antibody (ACCPA). Other blood cell counts, as well as renal and liver profiles, were normal. Skin examination revealed multiple red-violaceous, flat-topped papules and plaques with minimal scales on the ankles (left more than right) and superficial excoriation. There were also hyperpigmented scaly plaques on both knees and vertical ridges on her fingernails. Oral examination showed normal dentition with no mucosal streaks, erosion, or ulcers. The rest of the skin, scalp, and other system examinations were unremarkable. Dermoscopic examination using DermLite DL4 revealed a dermoscopic Auspitz sign over a light red background, minimal white scales, and regularly distributed dotted blood vessels.
test_results: Punch biopsy of the skin lesion on the left ankle showed parakeratosis at the surface of the epidermis with elongation of the rete ridges; spongiosis of the epidermal layer and small capillaries proliferation seen in the papillary dermis with surrounding mixture of inflammatory cells, predominantly lymphocytes.

case_report: A 33-year-old male of European descent visited the dermatological outpatient clinic due to recurrent paronychia unresponsive to multiple courses of terbinafine. The patient has a history of atopy, including hay fever and atopic dermatitis (AD) from early childhood. In his early 20s, his AD was managed with a one-year course of cyclosporine, and since then, it has been controlled with topical steroids. There is no personal or family history of psoriasis. Over the past year, he experienced painful joint swelling in his hands along with nail changes. Despite these symptoms, the severity of his eczema remained relatively stable, with minor flare-ups likely related to stress. Upon examination, oil drop signs were observed on nearly all fingernails and the nails of both big toes, along with mild distal onycholysis. Additionally, there was noticeable swelling and redness in the distal interphalangeal joints of the right index finger and left little finger.
test_results: An X-ray of the patient's hands showed entheseal expansion of the DIP of the right ring finger and left little finger.

case_report: A 66-year-old Japanese woman visited a local hospital with a primary complaint of two days of malaise. She exhibited subcutaneous hemorrhage in both forearms and was subsequently referred to the hematology department. Her medical history included pneumonia but was otherwise unremarkable. Physical examination showed a body temperature of 37.1°C, blood pressure of 136/86 mmHg, pulse rate of 85 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation of 99% in ambient air. No palpable lymphadenopathy was noted, and chest auscultation revealed no rales or murmur. The abdomen was soft with no palpable hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory tests indicated hyperleukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 97,800 cells/µL. The differential count was as follows: blasts 51.0%, neutrophils 31.5%, monocytes 2.5%, metamyelocytes 5.5%, lymphocytes 5.0%, and basophils 4.5%. Anemia was present with a hemoglobin level of 7.6 g/dL, and thrombocytopenia was noted with a platelet count of 6.5 × 10^4/μL. Additionally, hyperfibrinolysis was observed with an elevated d-dimer level of 12.4 µg/mL, fibrin/fibrinogen degradation products at 26.9 µg/mL, and an elevated lactate dehydrogenase level of 1,398 IU/L.
test_results: According to the bone marrow examination, blasts accounted for 30.4% of cells and presented with delicate nuclear folds and a high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio. The size of the blasts ranged from medium to large, and some presented with cytoplasmic nucleoli and granules. Most blasts were myeloperoxidase negative, although some were positive. Flow cytometry CD45 gating revealed that the blasts expressed CD34, CD13, CD33, and CD117. G-banding of tumor cells and T cells in peripheral blood samples revealed the t(7;7)(p15;p22) translocation [20/20] and 46, XX [20/20], respectively.
diagnosis: Acute Myelogenous Leukemia  with t translocation

case_report: A 1-month-old female infant was admitted to our hospital with significant abdominal swelling. She was delivered at 39 weeks’ gestation to a healthy mother, and her initial postnatal period was uneventful. Upon admission, she had no fever but showed signs of hepatomegaly and substantial ascites, leading to respiratory distress. Laboratory findings included: white blood cells at 42.5 × 10^9/L with 1.5% atypical blast cells, 66% neutrophils, and 16.5% lymphocytes; hemoglobin at 10.9 g/dL; platelets at 18 × 10^9/L; aspartate aminotransferase at 944 U/L; alanine aminotransferase at 390 U/L; total bilirubin at 3.5 mg/dL; direct bilirubin at 2.1 mg/dL; lactate dehydrogenase at 2783 U/L; undetectable fibrinogen; fibrinogen degradation product at 69.1 g/mL; and ferritin at 12,610 g/L. Enhanced CT imaging revealed marked hepatomegaly with patchy fibrotic regions and narrowing of the intrahepatic portal vein and the inferior vena cava at the hepatic portal area. Bone marrow analysis showed hypercellularity with dysplastic erythroid hyperplasia (60% of bone marrow cells) with megaloblastic changes, some of which were PAS-positive. Prominent hemophagocytosis was also noted. Flow cytometric analysis indicated that less than 5% of total cells were in the CD45low-int/side scatter (SSC) blast gate, with no monoclonal increases in specific populations. Evaluations for potential causes of acute liver failure, including infections and metabolic disorders, were unremarkable based on blood and urine analyses and culture tests. A liver biopsy was not performed due to the patient's severe condition. Cytological examination of the ascites sample was negative for malignancy, and peripheral blasts were no longer present by day 4 post-admission. The patient received pulsed steroids and plasma exchange for hepatic failure of unknown origin, but her liver function and ascites continued to deteriorate. By day 14 of hospitalization, her white blood cell count had normalized to 10.1 × 10^9/L, but blast cells reappeared in the blood, accounting for 4% of the white blood cell count.
test_results: The results of G-banded karyotyping of the initial bone marrow sample revealed t(1;22)(p13;q13).
Orpha_name: Megakaryoblastic acute myeloid leukemia with t(1;22)(p13;q13)

case_report: A 65-year-old White female homemaker from Juazeiro, Bahia, Brazil, has experienced pain and swelling in her left metatarsophalangeal and right metacarpophalangeal joints for approximately two years. These symptoms have progressively affected her right foot, left hand, ankles, and wrists. She has been treated by several orthopedists with prednisone and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and was later referred to a rheumatologist who continued the same medications. Despite continuous use of prednisone (20mg/day), she developed erythematous nodules on her face, upper and lower limbs, paresthesia in her feet and hands, and worsening joint pain and swelling. She was subsequently treated with prednisone and clonazepam. A few days later, she experienced fever, worsening skin lesions, and increased joint pain, leading to hospitalization. Complementary exams brought by the patient showed normal liver and kidney function tests, C-reactive protein, protein electrophoresis, VDRL, ANF, urinalysis, and glycemia. The sedimentation rate was elevated at 19mm in the first hour, and the leukogram showed 14,900 with 46 lymphocytes (normal up to 39). Clinical examination revealed erythematous-purplish plaques, erythematous papules, and nodules on the face, trunk, upper and lower limbs, facial infiltration, a moving claw deformity of the fifth finger on the right hand, and edema in the hands and feet.
test_results: AARB search in lymph smear was positive - bacterial index 3.5

case_report: A 17-year-old male was referred to the urology department following a routine imaging study that revealed a 2.3 cm enhancing mass in the mid-pole of the right kidney. His medical history includes treatment for a right-sided inguinal lymph nodal malignant fibrous histiocytoma and a right-sided pelvic high-grade pleomorphic and spindle cell sarcoma, treated 6 and 3 years ago, respectively, through surgical excision and radiation therapy (60 Gy/30 fractions to the pelvis). He has no history of hypertension or diabetes. Follow-up care has included biannual pelvic MRI and chest imaging, as well as annual PET-CT scans. No evidence of recurrence or metastasis was observed until the detection of the current renal mass.
test_results: A routine computed tomography (CT) scan detected a right-sided enhancing mid-pole renal mass measuring 2.3 cm.
diagnosis: clear cell papillary renal cell carcinoma
Orpha_name: clear cell papillary renal cell carcinoma

case_report: A 26-year-old male, with no consanguinity, presented with multiple painless swellings on his body for the past 12 years, with no notable family history. The initial swelling appeared in the sacral region and gradually increased to a size of 20 cm × 15 cm × 10 cm. Over time, additional swellings emerged in various locations, including the buttocks, extensor aspects of the elbows and knees, and on the hands and feet. These swellings ranged in size from 2 cm × 2 cm on the dorsum of the hands to 15 cm × 10 cm on the buttocks. Upon examination, the swellings were firm, non-tender, mobile, and showed no skin changes. Routine investigations, including hemogram and X-rays, were unremarkable. Fine needle aspiration cytology indicated a spindle cell tumor. The sacral swelling was surgically removed along with the overlying skin, and primary closure was performed. The excised specimen was a firm, homogenous grey-white mass. Histopathological examination revealed collections of foam cells and lipid-laden macrophages with areas of fibrosis and cholesterol clefts, consistent with tuberous xanthomas.
test_results: Lipid profile revealed raised levels of low-density lipoproteins (LDL) and total Cholesterol. Triglycerides and other lipoprotein fractions were normal.

case_report: A 9-year-old boy was referred to the pediatric respiratory clinic with a persistent dry cough since birth, tachypnea at rest, and failure to gain weight. He was born at 37 weeks and 1 day, weighing 1.6 kg, and experienced respiratory distress at birth, requiring 21 days of hospitalization and 10 days of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). There was no history of aspiration, oily stools, ear or nasal symptoms, or exposure to allergens. Family history indicated that the paternal grandfather had died from an undiagnosed lung condition at 35 years. A chest CT at 1 year old during an exacerbation showed patchy bilateral consolidation but otherwise normal lung parenchyma. Extensive evaluations during infancy, including an Immunoglobulin profile, sweat chloride analysis, and clinical exome sequencing, were normal. The child was treated with pulse steroids with minimal improvement. Over the years, he continued to have a persistent dry cough, exercise intolerance, and failure to gain weight, leading to multiple hospitalizations and treatments with antibiotics, nebulized bronchodilators, and steroids. Upon presentation, the child was significantly malnourished (height 115 cm and weight 18 kg, both below the 3rd percentile), had grade 3 clubbing, tachypnea (rate 35/min) with suprasternal and subcostal retractions, hypoxemia (saturations 91% in room air), and hypercarbia (Pc02 46 mmHg) at rest. Systemic examination revealed diffuse bilateral coarse crackles predominantly in the bases, with other systems being normal. A chest X-ray showed significant bilateral hyperinflation. Pulmonary function tests indicated a combined restrictive and obstructive pattern (FVC 46%, FEV1/FVC 63% with 21% improvement post-bronchodilator). A second opinion on the chest CT from age 1 suggested early bronchiectasis.
test_results: A high-resolution CT of the chest with both inspiratory and expiratory hold showed central and peripheral bronchiectasis involving the right middle lobe, lingula, and bilateral lower lobes. There was significant ballooning of 3rd generation bronchi with an inspiratory hold (Inspiratory diameter–6.2 mm) with subsequent collapsibility of the bronchiectactic segments on expiratory hold (Expiratory diameter–3 mm). Bronchoscopy showed, normal upper airways with significant collapsibility of 3rd and 4th generation bronchioles on gentle negative pressure suctioning with suction pressure of 20–30 mm Hg.

case_report: A 43-year-old man experienced a sudden, painless decrease in vision in his left eye three days after receiving the first dose of the Covishield COVID-19 vaccine (Batch No. 4121MC028; Expiry October 31, 2021). He had no history of smoking, ocular surgery, systemic illness, trauma, excessive physical exercise, or dehydration. Two months later, he visited our ophthalmology outpatient department and tested negative on reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction for COVID-19. His blood pressure was 130/90 mmHg. Laboratory results were within reference ranges except for a slightly elevated glycated hemoglobin level. Electrocardiogram and echocardiography showed no ischemia or other significant findings. Ocular examination revealed best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of LogMAR +0.2 (20/32, 6/9) in the right eye and LogMAR +1.5 (20/630, 6/190) in the left eye. The left eye's pupils reacted sluggishly to light. Intraocular pressure was 16 mmHg in both eyes. The anterior chamber had normal depth and open angles, with no neovascularization of the iris or angle. Fundus examination of the left eye showed optic disc edema, dilated tortuous veins, dot-blot and flame-shaped hemorrhages across the fundus, and a blunted foveal reflex. The right eye's findings were unremarkable.
test_results: The optical coherence tomography (OCT) in the LE showed disorganization of the inner retinal layers, disruption of the inner segment-outer segment junction, and distorted foveal contour with large cystic spaces. The central foveal thickness (CFT) measured 854 microns. The foveal contour was normal in the RE, and the CFT measured 242 microns. The OCT angiography showed an enlarged distorted foveal avascular zone (FAZ) and capillary non-perfusion in a 12-mm x 12-mm scan in the LE and normal-sized circular FAZ in the RE. The fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) revealed that the LE had delayed venous filling, blocked fluorescence from retinal hemorrhages, and capillary non-perfusion areas extending through 360 degrees in the peripheral fundus but no neovascularization of disc or elsewhere. The FFA of the RE was normal. The flash electroretinogram showed the scotopic and photopic amplitudes of the b-wave at 230 and 110 microvolts in RE and 80 and 50 microvolts in LE, respectively.
diagnosis: Ischemic Central Retinal Vein Occlusion  and Cystoid Macular Edema

case_report: A 10-year-old boy with a history of ocular hypertension, megalocornea, and hypermetropia came to the emergency department after experiencing transient blurred vision and perceived visual field impairment in his left eye, along with headache and eye ache the previous day. At the onset of symptoms, intraocular pressure (IOP) was recorded at 28 mmHg in the left eye by his general ophthalmologist. The patient's father mentioned that the boy became upset and agitated during a dispute at home the evening before the symptoms appeared, during which his face turned red and he held his breath for 10 seconds. There was no history of breath-holding spells, but similar episodes had occurred before according to the father. Upon examination in the clinic 24 hours later, the symptoms had regressed. At the time of admission, best corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye. IOP measured by Goldmann applanation tonometry was 16 mmHg in the right eye and 12 mmHg in the left eye. There was no relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). Slit lamp examination revealed clear megalocorneae with white-to-white corneal diameters of 15.7 mm in the right eye and 15.9 mm in the left eye, and a normal anterior segment.
test_results: Dilated fundus exam revealed tilted and hyperemic, minimally swollen optic disc with a flame shaped hemorrhage at 7 o’clock, markedly engorged and tortuous veins and one cotton-wool-like spot at the superior arcade. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the optic disc showed a slight increase of retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) particularly left, compared to prior examinations. Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) showed slightly enlarged optic nerve sheds on both sides and an acute sinusitis on the right side. Duplex sonography of the carotid arteries was normal.

case_report: An 81-year-old woman presented to the Retina Clinic with a history of decreased visual acuity in the left eye for the past 3 months. She has a medical history of uncontrolled hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes mellitus. On examination, her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/30 in the left eye. Funduscopic examination of the left eye revealed venous tortuosity and intraretinal hemorrhage in all four quadrants of the fundus.
test_results: Fluorescein angiography (FA) and OCTA showed loss of small capillaries but nonperfusion areas were not observed. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed retinal thickening in the fovea with associated inner retinal cysts.

case_report: The patient, a 13-year-old female, with no familial history of hearing loss, was found to have profound bilateral deafness at 1.6 years of age. Otoacoustic emissions testing showed no response in both ears. Brainstem-evoked potentials revealed no V-wave at 90 dB nHL, and pure-tone audiometry did not elicit a response at high intensity across all frequencies tested. Due to the lack of hearing response with the most powerful hearing aids available, a cochlear implant was selected. Radiological evaluation for cochlear implant placement using cranial computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed no abnormalities in the central nervous system, cochlea, nerve, or auditory pathways. A cochlear implant (CI 513, cochlear) was placed in the right ear when the patient was 3 years old.
test_results: A c.2051C>T nucleotide change was observed in the g.6303573 position of chromosome 4 (GRCh37), causing an alanine exchange for valine (p.Ala684Val) in WFS1 gene (NM_006005.3). Sanger sequencing confirmed the presence of a heterozygous c.2051C>T variant in the patient’s WFS1 gene but not in either of her parents. Additionally, NGS analysis showed a heterozygous deletion c.932delC in the g.121768924 position of chromosome 6 (GRCh37), resulting in p.Ala311Valfs37* in the GJA1 gene (NM_00165.3). After Sanger sequencing validation, an exhaustive analysis with BLAST® (NCBI) showed that the sequence corresponded instead to the FER tyrosine kinase (FER) pseudogene in chromosome 5 (NG_011445.2). We ruled out the presence of the p.Arg445His missense pathogenic variant in the OPA1 gene in all family members by Sanger sequencing. The patient’s initial eye examination performed at the age of 8.2 years included visual acuity (VA), color vision test, biomicroscopy, funduscopy, visual field, optical coherence tomography (OCT), and visual-evoked potentials. The ophthalmologic manifestation in the patient included reducing acuity, dyschromatopsia, and visual field deficit. Despite showing correct VA at log MAR 0.0 in each eye and no alterations in the color test, fundoscopy and retinography showed bilateral papillary pallor and marked thinning of the peripapillary RNFL retinal nerve fiber layer on OCT. No signs of vascular narrowing and/or diabetic retinopathy were detected, all suggestive of optic atrophy.

case_report: A 43-year-old man visited the outpatient endocrine clinic at Tabriz University of Medical Sciences, Tabriz, Iran, accompanied by his sister, for an assessment of skin lesions. The patient exhibited multiple lesions on his shoulders, back, the lateral and medial parts of the dorsal surface of his feet, the medial and lateral malleus of both feet, and the dorsal and palmar surfaces of both hands. His siblings have been monitored in the same clinic for similar skin conditions. These conditions were characterized by palmar, eruptive, tuberous, and trauma site xanthomas, along with elevated levels of both total cholesterol and triglycerides in the plasma. Both parents had normal serum lipid levels. There was no history of coronary artery or other atherosclerotic disorders in the patient or his siblings. The patient reported no other complaints and maintained an active lifestyle as a greengrocer. A pathology report from a skin lesion biopsy performed by a dermatologist a few months prior indicated the presence of lipid-laden macrophages.
test_results: Fasting serum lipid levels reported as: Total cholesterol = 507 mg/dl, Triglycerides = 470 mg/dl and High Density Lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol = 41 mg/dl.

case_report: A 33-year-old female patient visited the prosthodontic department requesting a denture due to missing posterior teeth. She reported that none of her posterior teeth had ever been extracted. Imaging revealed the presence of all her missing teeth, and she was referred to the orthodontic department for further evaluation. Her medical history was unremarkable, with no history of radiation or unusual drug therapy. Her family history was also normal, with no relatives having unerupted teeth. Laboratory tests, including thyroid function tests, parathormone levels, hormone assays, serum calcium, and phosphorus levels, were all within normal limits. Intra-oral examination showed 2 retained deciduous teeth (54 and 55). The only permanent teeth present were 11, 12, 21, and all 4 lower incisors. The erupted teeth had normal anatomy. There was grade 1 mobility of the lower incisors in a buccolingual direction. A torus palatinus was observed, along with bulging related to the unerupted teeth, without signs of pain or crackling. A class III incisor relationship with a deep bite and bilateral posterior open-bite were noted. Examination of mandibular movements showed no displacements, excluding pseudo class III malocclusion.
test_results: Panoramic radiograph revealed two retained deciduous teeth, 13 unerupted permanent teeth in the maxilla and 12 unerupted permanent teeth in the mandible. A total of 25 unerupted teeth: 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38, 43, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48. The upper left lateral incisor was located above the root apex of the upper left central incisor. The upper left canine and the first premolar were in transposition. The lower canines were horizontally impacted below the apices of the lower incisors and have transmigrated across the midline, with the right canine lying above the left canine. Root development was complete for all unerupted permanent teeth except 44 and 38. The mesial root of 46 appeared to be dilacerated. The 34, 35, and 45 were labially inclined. The lower molars on both sides were near to the inferior border of the mandible. Cephalometric radiograph revealed normal skeletal features, increased proclination of lower incisors.

case_report: A 17-year-old male patient was referred to the department by a private practitioner due to difficulty chewing on one side. The practitioner aimed to correct the patient's bite through orthodontic treatment and requested an evaluation before proceeding. Clinical examination showed a posterior open bite on the right side, an anterior deep bite, and multiple submerged teeth, along with retained teeth 53, 54, 55, and 84.
test_results: The orthopantomogram showed submerged permanent molars and premolars on the right side in both maxillary and mandibular arches without any evidence of ankylosis. Mechanical obstruction due to retained deciduous teeth was seen in relation to 53, 54, 55, and 84 region.

case_report: A 27-year-old female patient with a history of recurrent coughing and hemoptysis for over 10 years visited our hospital in January 2019. Previously, she had been diagnosed with pneumonia and received symptomatic treatment at a local clinic, which temporarily alleviated her symptoms, though they frequently recurred. The patient has no family history of lung malignancy or genetic diseases. She is 155 cm tall, weighs 42 kg, and has a lean body shape. Her thorax is symmetrical without deformity. The trachea is slightly deviated to the right. No obvious rhonchi, moist rales, or wheezing rales were detected. The heart rhythm is regular, with the auscultation area of heart sounds noticeably shifted to the right thorax. No significant abnormalities were found during the abdominal physical examination.
test_results: A chest radiograph and computed tomography were performed for the patient showed a giant abnormal space-occupying lesion in the hilum of right lung. The tumor was closely related to the right pulmonary artery and bronchus. The right lung was atelectasis and some of the left lung as well as heart were obviously deviated to the right thoracic cavity. A Chest MRI showed a mass abnormal signal tumor in the region of right hilum about 10.0 × 4.5 cm in size. The T1WI was isointense, while T2WI and DWI were both hyperintense. A 3D reconstruction of the hilar structures have shown a complete anatomical disorganization of right pulmonary artery and vein. A neoplasm with smooth surface was observed in the right main bronchus by bronchoscopy examination. Pulmonary function showed a severe obstructive mixed ventilation dysfunction. The forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) was 1.36 L, accounting for 45% of the predicted value, Maximal voluntary ventilation (MVV) was 27.63L, accounting for 43% of the predicted value. The renal function, electrolyte, coagulation function, arterial blood gas analysis were all normal. The patient’s blood routine examination showed moderate anemia with hemoglobin 69 g/L. Biochemical examination showed moderate malnutrition, with prealbumin only 85 g/L, albumin 31 g/L. The patient’s tumor markers showed CA125 434.77 µ/ml, CEA 12.43 ng/ml, CA724 233.3 μ/ml, while CA242, CA199, AFP, SCCA, NSE were all normal. No sign of abnormality or metastasis was found in enhanced MRI of brain and bone scan. No abnormal or enlarged lymph nodes were observed in neck and supraclavicular region by ultrasound examination.

case_report: A 45-year-old female reported significant vision loss in the left eye (LE) upon waking 20 days ago. She had previously experienced a sudden, painless vision loss in the right eye (RE) two months earlier. Her medical history includes diabetes, hypertension, anemia, and chronic kidney disease, for which she has been undergoing bi-weekly hemodialysis for the past three years. She noted that both episodes of acute visual loss occurred the day after dialysis. She denied experiencing headache, pain with eye movement, limb weakness, transient ischemic attacks, fever, muscle pain, jaw pain, seizures, or any focal neurological deficits. On examination, her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 6/60 in the RE and hand movements close to face (HMCF) with accurate light projection in the LE. Intraocular pressure was measured at 14 mm Hg in the RE and 15 mm Hg in the LE. The LE exhibited a grade 1 relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). Anterior segment examination of both eyes (BE) was normal. Fundus examination of the RE revealed optic disc pallor with obliteration of the cup, vessel sheathing around the disc indicating secondary optic atrophy, arteriolar attenuation, and arterio-venous (A-V) crossing changes. Fundus examination of the LE showed pallid disc edema with flame-shaped retinal hemorrhages in the peri-papillary region, attenuation of the retinal arterioles, and arterio-venous crossing changes, without any signs of background diabetic retinopathy. Humphrey visual field testing in the RE indicated a severely depressed field, while field examination in the LE was not possible due to significant visual loss.
test_results: Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) of LE showed delayed filling of the disc especially superior part in the early phase and staining of disc in the late phase.

case_report: A 2-year 11-month-old male with a history of chronic hemodialysis due to polycystic kidney disease (PCKD) and bilateral nephrectomy presented with various clinical findings. He had a compound heterozygous phosphomannomutase 2 promoter and missense mutation, associated with PCKD and congenital hyperinsulinism. His left kidney was removed in February 2017 due to respiratory insufficiency from mass effect. Seven months later, he underwent a right nephrectomy due to respiratory compromise and hypertension. Post-second nephrectomy, he started intermittent hemodialysis five days a week, later reduced to four days a week after six months. Prior to the second nephrectomy, he was on an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, beta-blocker, and furosemide for hypertension. Post-nephrectomy, his intradialytic systolic blood pressure was around 68 mmHg, leading to the administration of 2.5 mg midodrine during hemodialysis for systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg. Ultrafiltration was minimized to prevent further hypotensive episodes, but his systolic blood pressure remained around 60 mmHg. Other medications included diazoxide, omeprazole, levothyroxine, and darbepoetin. He was G-tube fed without salt restriction. Blood work five days prior to presentation showed normocytic, mild anemia (hemoglobin 95 g/L) with a reticulocyte count of 20 × 10^9/L. Electrolytes were within normal ranges (sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 3.8 mmol/L, chloride 91 mmol/L, and calcium 2.77 mmol/L), but albumin was low at 30 g/L. Creatinine was elevated at 421 μmol/L. Echocardiogram indicated normal biventricular function. In June 2018, nine months after starting hemodialysis, he presented to the emergency department with an unsteady gait and difficulty focusing and following objects, starting approximately two hours post-hemodialysis. Parents observed a change in pupil size from small to large bilaterally, documented at 8 mm. Initial neurological examination revealed dilated but responsive pupils, poor visual acuity, and an unsteady gait. He was alert, oriented, and comfortable. Vital signs included a blood pressure of 59/33 mmHg, heart rate of 92 bpm, and he was afebrile. Admission laboratory findings showed normocytic, mild anemia with a hemoglobin level of 101 g/L and an MCV of 92.7 fL. Sodium was low at 127 mmol/L, potassium was 4.4 mmol/L, and chloride was 98 mmol/L. Repeat blood work showed a sodium level of 134 mmol/L, negating the need for hypertonic saline. Creatinine was elevated at 166 μmol/L. Tox screen was negative, and AST, ALT, and INR were normal. There was no history of trauma, toxin ingestion, sick contact exposure, or seizure activity. Head CT revealed nonspecific bifrontal subcortical white matter hypodensities.
test_results: MRI displayed multiple foci of increased fluid-attenuated inversion recovery signal, mainly on bilateral subcortical white matter of the frontal lobes and corona radiata. Optic nerve size and signal intensity were normal. Ophthalmology noted decreased visual acuity to hand motion and optic disk pallor, and diagnosed optic nerve atrophy.

case_report: A 44-year-old male was admitted to the hospital in September 2015 with the primary complaint of vomiting blood. His medical history included long-term use of diazepam and sodium valproate tablets for epilepsy. Laboratory tests showed mild anemia with a hemoglobin level of 103 g/L. Serum levels of carcinoembryonic antigen, carbohydrate antigen 199, carbohydrate antigen 125, and alpha-fetoprotein were within normal limits. Gastroduodenoscopy revealed a protruding lesion with an ulcerated surface in the cardia. A biopsy specimen indicated chronic superficial gastritis.
test_results: Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) revealed a solid submucosal mass 2.2 × 3.0 cm in size located 40 cm from the incisors. The mass had a mixed echo pattern with an intact muscularis layer. Microscopic examination showed that the tumor had invaded the submucosal layer. Histologically, the tumor was predominantly composed of ductal epithelial and myoepithelial cells, and the tumor cells were arranged mostly in a tubular pattern and partly in a cribriform pattern. Immunohistochemically, the tumor cells expressed cytokeratin, cluster of differentiation 117, p63, and calponin.
diagnosis: Adenoid cystic carcinoma  at the gastroesophageal junction
Orpha_name: Carcinoma of esophagus, salivary gland type

case_report: An 82-year-old Japanese woman visited our hospital for evaluation of an esophageal tumor. Her medications included clopidogrel for right internal carotid artery stenosis, and she had a history of a prior cerebral ischemic event. She was undergoing an upper gastrointestinal examination as part of her annual health check-up. She reported no symptoms, including difficulty swallowing. Laboratory tests showed no signs of anemia or abnormalities in liver or kidney function. There was no family history of esophageal disease, and tumor marker levels for adenocarcinoma and SCC were within normal limits. She was referred to our hospital for further evaluation of a protruding submucosal lesion in the middle esophagus, which was observed during an upper gastrointestinal examination conducted a month before her visit.
test_results: Endoscopic examination with normal white light revealed a brownish submucosal tumor, located 25 cm from the incisor of the middle esophagus. The tumor surface showed mild reddening with a central planar depression, and was elastic, mobile and hard when compressed with the forceps. Image enhancement with narrow band imaging (NBI) magnification revealed a central brownish area with slightly dilated, non-uniform diameter intrapapillary capillary loops. The central planar depression stained slightly with the application of Lugol’s solution. EUS revealed a solid 8 mm × 4.2 mm mass, primarily involving the second and third layers of the esophagus; the tumor was hypoechoic and homogeneous with a thickened hyperechoic submucosa, and slight irregularity of the third layer was recognized. The biopsy showed esophagitis and no distinct tumor; enlarged lymph nodes or other lesions suspicious for metastases were not observed with contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT). Hematoxylin and eosin staining findings showed proliferative heterotypic cells with cribriform nuclei distributed in an alveolar pattern and having numerous glandular cavities and small cyst-like structures in the alveoli. The upper border of the tumor partially extended to the luminal surface. With higher magnification, the nuclei of the heterotypic cells showed a dark chromatin core and a narrow eosinophilic border. Cells with an eosinophilic cytoplasm lined the wall of the glandular cystic cavity and formed a two-layer structure with small cells and having a high nuclear/cytoplasm ratio forming the outer layer. Immunostaining showed slight staining with cytokeratin CAM 5.2, which stains duct epithelium but not squamous epithelium. The glandular cavities and small cystic structures stained positively with epithelial membrane antigen, which stains glandular epithelium. Carcinoembryonic antigen staining, which stains ductal epithelium, was positive in the intraluminal epithelium and in those areas with differentiation into ductal components. p63 staining, which stains basal cells, was not observed in the intraluminal epithelium, and tumorization of the basal cells was not observed. Alpha-smooth muscle actin staining, which stains smooth muscle cells, was weakly positive in the cells of the outer layers of the cysts. Staining with calponin, which stains smooth muscle cells, was slightly positive in the outer cyst wall cells.
Orpha_name: Carcinoma of esophagus, salivary gland type

case_report: A 53-year-old male, with no symptoms, visited Lishui Municipal Central Hospital in Lishui, China, where a mass was found during a routine medical examination. The patient has a history of smoking 40 cigarettes daily for 30 years. He has no history of diabetes mellitus, hepatitis, hypertensive disease, or tuberculosis. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for the publication of this study.
test_results: Gastroscopy revealed a mass in the lower esophagus with rigid tissue. Pathological examination indicated heterotrophic hyperplasia of epithelial cells and possible malignancy. Esophageal CT showed thickening of the wall of the lower esophagus with a thickness of about 0.7 cm, and an enhanced scan showed uneven enhancement of the thickened esophageal wall.
Orpha_name: Carcinoma of esophagus, salivary gland type

case_report: A 21-year-old male reported experiencing continuous flickering tiny dots across his entire visual field since the age of 15. He also noted a gradual onset of persistent sensitivity to light and described seeing 'whitish smoke' on a dark background when his eyes were closed. He denied experiencing palinopsia or night blindness. At age 10, he had been diagnosed with migraine with aura, characterized by a small scintillating scotoma that expanded over approximately 20 minutes with varying sides during different episodes, followed by headache, nausea, sensitivity to light, and sensitivity to sound. He had not had any migraine attacks in the past 2 years. He reported no history of illicit recreational drug use. Neurological examination showed no abnormalities. Ophthalmological evaluation indicated a slight increase in intraocular pressure (R: 23 mm Hg, L: 24 mm Hg). His visual field and fundoscopic examinations were normal. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) were also normal.
test_results: Decreased perfusion on bilateral sides of the occipital cortex and fusiform gyri with a preponderance on the right. This right-sided hypoperfusion was found to encompass an area extending from the occipital cortex to the inferior temporal gyrus.

case_report: A seven-day-old Caucasian baby girl with Down syndrome was referred to our department due to elevated white blood cell count. The baby was born vaginally at 39 weeks and two days of gestation. Her Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at one and five minutes, respectively. Her birth weight was 3420 g and her body length was 49 cm. The patient exhibited typical features of trisomy 21, confirmed by karyotype analysis (47, XX, +21). On the second day after birth, she presented with reduced feeding intake. Peripheral blood test results showed a white blood cell (WBC) count of 70.8 × 10^9 cells/mm3 with 70% blasts. Due to the elevated white blood cell count, the patient was referred to the Hematology Oncology Unit of the Second Pediatric Department of Aristotle University of Thessaloniki. Upon admission, the patient had hepatosplenomegaly, abdominal distension, hypotonia, and dyspnea, likely due to increased blood viscosity. Echocardiography identified a ventricular septal defect (VSD), pericardial effusion, and persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN). An abdominal ultrasound confirmed hepatosplenomegaly with increased liver echo signaling. Biochemical data showed elevated levels of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) (2027 IU/L), serum inorganic phosphorus (P) (6.0 mg/dL), and uric acid (UA) (4.2 mg/dL). Blood gas analysis results were within normal ranges. The laboratory hematological, biochemistry, and coagulation test results on admission are shown in the table.
test_results: Bone marrow aspiration revealed hypercellular marrow with an excess of blasts. The blasts were negative for myeloperoxidase, positive for CD33, CD34 and CD61, and showed weak coexpression of CD7. The lymphoid and erythroid populations exhibited no antigenic aberrations or atypicality.

case_report: A 31-year-old male presented with a history of progressive weight gain and fatigue over a decade. Over the past two years, he also experienced swelling in his hands and face, along with back pain. Physical examination showed a plethoric moon face, truncal and centripetal obesity, and abdominal cutaneous striae. His blood pressure was recorded at 160/90 mmHg upon admission. Laboratory tests indicated leukocytosis with normal serum electrolytes and normal fasting and post-prandial glucose levels. Further endocrinological tests revealed no diurnal variation in plasma cortisol levels. The plasma cortisol level was not suppressed by 1 mg overnight or by 8 mg of standard dexamethasone. Plasma adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) levels were significantly low (less than 10 pg/ml). Levels of plasma free T3, free T4, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), and urinary catecholamines were within normal ranges. There were no increases in plasma concentrations of parathormone, calcitonin, testosterone, dehydroepiandrosterone sulphate, androstenedione, or 24-hour urinary calcium excretion. A chest X-ray showed normal results. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scanning indicated osteopenia at the femur head with a T score of -2.46. T scores for the trochanter, Ward's triangle, L3, and L4 were -2.54, -4.07, -4.42, and -3.36, respectively, consistent with osteoporosis.
test_results: Computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a 7 cm × 5 cm mass in the right adrenal gland.

case_report: A 55-year-old Chinese female presented with exertional dyspnea persisting for over 10 years. Over the past 2 years, she developed truncal obesity and facial rounding, without acne, hirsutism, or wide purple striae. She had a family history of hypertension and was diagnosed with hypertension 10 years ago, for which she had been taking irbesartan, metoprolol, and nifedipine XR. Additionally, she was diagnosed with hyperlipidemia 5 years ago and was on statins. She reported no history of alcohol or drug abuse, including steroid use. On admission, her physical examination revealed elevated blood pressure (164/104 mmHg) and a normal heart rate (74 beats per minute). Her height was 156 cm, weight 51 kg, and waist circumference 88 cm, resulting in a body mass index (BMI) of 20.96 kg/m2. She exhibited a plethoric moon-shaped face, centripetal obesity, buffalo hump, ecchymosis, and slight edema in both lower limbs. Neurological examination was normal except for slight muscle weakness in the lower extremities. Routine laboratory tests showed normal complete blood cell count and hepatorenal function, with a slightly elevated serum triglyceride level. Fasting plasma glucose was 7.33 mmol/L, and glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c) was 6.6%.
test_results: Twenty-four-hour urine free cortisol (24 h UFC) elevated to 634.8μg/24 h (reference range: 20.26-127.55μg/24 h). The next morning (8 a.m.) serum cortisol level after an overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test (DMST) was 787.5 nmol/L. Three adrenal nodules were found with adrenal contrast-enhanced CT. One on the right side was 2.5 cm in diameter, and the other two on the left side with diameters of 2.3 cm and 0.6 cm, respectively. Adrenal venous catheterization was successful. The adrenal vein to inferior vena cava cortisol (AV: IVC) gradient was 13.57 on the right side and 13.88 on the left side. The left and right AV to IVC gradient of aldosterone were 5.58 and 6.79 respectively. The cortisol/aldosterone ratio (CAR) in adrenal veins was 292.52 on the right and 359.29 on the left, along with a left-to-right odds ratio of 1.23.
diagnosis: ACTH-independent Cushing’s syndrome due to bilateral cortisol-secreting adrenal adenomas

case_report: A 55-year-old man was admitted to our hospital following the discovery of a pancreatic mass on a contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan, which was initially performed due to acute alcoholic pancreatitis. Laboratory tests showed a mildly elevated serum cancer antigen 19-9 level at 54 U/mL (normal range, 0–37 U/mL). Abdominal CT imaging identified a 40-mm heterogeneous mass with a clear boundary located in the tail of the pancreas.
test_results: Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) showed a heterogenous hypoechoic mass with partial necrosis. Histological examination of an EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration (EUS-FNA) specimen revealed the presence of tumor cells with round nuclei and eosinophilic vesicles. Immunohistological staining was positive for BCL-10.

case_report: A 33-year-old male visited our hospital for evaluation of an adrenal mass, initially identified via abdominal ultrasonography during a routine check-up. An abdominal CT scan revealed a mass located in the tail of the pancreas rather than the adrenal gland. Physical examination showed no abnormalities. Laboratory results indicated slightly elevated AST and ALT levels: WBC count was 6.49 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin was 14.3 g/dL, platelets were 269 × 10^3/µL, AST/ALT levels were 66/101 U/L, amylase/lipase levels were 78.9/45 U/L, and CA 19-9 was 28.7 U/mL. The CT scan identified a 4-cm heterogeneous low-attenuation mass with a smooth margin in the tail of the pancreas, showing iso-enhancement compared to the surrounding pancreatic tissue during the adrenal enhancement phase. MRI revealed a 4.2-cm well-demarcated cystic mass in the tail of the pancreas, with a relatively low enhancement pattern in the MR arterial phase. EUS indicated that the 5-cm cystic mass was composed of numerous tiny cysts.
test_results: Smear and cell block sections showed hypercellularity and sheets and clusters of monotonous small cells with round nuclei. Immunostaining was positive for β-catenin and CD10, whereas staining was negative for neuroendocrine markers, such as synaptophysin and chromogranin.
diagnosis: Solid Pseudopapillary Tumor of the Pancreas

case_report: An 11-year-old girl visited the outpatient department in August 2016 due to abdominal pain. She had a history of left partial nephrectomy in 2012 for a nonfunctioning lower segment of the left kidney with significant ureterohydronephrosis in a duplex system. Follow-up ultrasound of the entire abdomen revealed a large cyst in the left kidney. In 2015, she underwent endoscopy and excision of a transverse vaginal septum for hematocolpos. In August 2016, she reported abdominal pain again. Computed tomography urography showed an enlarged left kidney with a large 70 mm cystic area affecting the upper and middle calyces. Additionally, a heterogeneously enhancing soft tissue density lesion was observed near the tail of the pancreas, adjacent to the spleen and the left kidney with the cyst.
test_results: The pancreatic FNAC showed smears composed of a monotonous population of neoplastic cells. The cells were arranged in loose groups, singly dispersed, and around fibrovascular hyalinized stalks. The cells showed minimal anisonucleosis, with delicate cytoplasm, round to oval, regular nuclei with finely granular chromatin. Pinkish myxoid material was seen between the cell clusters and in the background. No mitotic figures or necrosis was identified.
diagnosis: Solid Pseudopapillary Neoplasm of the pancreas
Orpha_name: Solid Pseudopapillary Neoplasm of the pancreas

case_report: A 25-year-old unmarried woman with no significant past or family history of neoplasms was admitted to our hospital due to a tumor located at the pancreatic neck, which was incidentally discovered during an abdominal ultrasound performed as part of a medical check-up. Physical examination showed no abnormalities. Clinical laboratory tests, including serum amylase level and tumor markers such as AFP, CA199, CEA, CA125, and CA724, were within normal limits. Precontrast abdominal CT revealed a round hypo-attenuation mass approximately 4.5 cm in diameter with a clear margin. Post-contrast imaging showed peripheral enhancement of the tumor, corresponding to its solid part, while the central zone exhibited hypo-attenuation without enhancement, indicating cystic degeneration. The pancreatic duct upstream was not dilated, and there was no evidence of parenchymal atrophy or vessel invasion. Additionally, the left kidney was not visualized within the coverage of the abdominal CT scan.
test_results: The pancreatic tumor showed inhomogeneous FDG uptake with a maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) of 7.5 in the peripheral zone of solid component. The left kidney was still not found. PET image showed two foci of slight FDG-accumulation at the uterine cavity, and uterus didelphys were suspected.
diagnosis: Solid pseudopapillary tumor of the pancreas

case_report: A 71-year-old Caucasian female presented with chest pain. Imaging included a chest CT scan that identified a 6.3 cm mass in the right aspect of the left lateral liver, spanning segments 2, 3, and 4a. The mass was most clearly seen in the precontrast and arterial phases, showing heterogeneous contrast enhancement with multiple low attenuation areas. A PET scan revealed a 1.9 cm hypermetabolic focus within a 4.3 cm tumor. The patient experienced bilateral upper abdominal pain but did not report nausea, vomiting, or changes in weight. There were no signs of jaundice, altered bowel habits, or gastrointestinal bleeding. The patient had no significant history of alcohol or intravenous drug use, no history of transfusions, and no personal or family history of liver or biliary disease. Laboratory tests showed normal liver function, serum alpha fetoprotein, CEA, and CA19-9 levels.
test_results: Biopsy showed biliary epithelium arranged in cysts and tubules with a fibrotic/spindled stroma.
Orpha_name: Adenocarcinoma of the liver and intrahepatic biliary tract

case_report: A 64-year-old Japanese woman underwent a health examination where an abdominal ultrasound revealed a mass in segment 1 of the liver. The patient was asymptomatic and had no significant family history or history of smoking or alcohol consumption.
