Her medical history included an appendectomy for acute appendicitis, a hysterectomy for uterine myoma, a right ovariectomy for ovarian thecoma, a right adrenalectomy for Cushing syndrome, and a laparoscopic cholecystectomy for a gallbladder polyp. Nine years prior, a contrast-enhanced CT scan at another hospital did not show any lesions in segment 1 of the liver. The patient also had a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and osteoporosis. Physical examination revealed no abnormalities, including the absence of lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory tests showed normal liver enzyme levels and tumor markers, including alpha-fetoprotein, carbohydrate antigen 19-9, carcinoembryonic antigen, and protein induced by vitamin K absence or antagonist II. Tests for hepatitis B and C viruses were negative.
test_results: Abdominal ultrasound revealed that the tumor comprised two distinct components on the ventral and dorsal sides in S1 of liver. The ventral portion showed low echogenicity, and the dorsal portion showed high echogenicity. While the latter component touched widely with the inferior vena cava, their boundary was clear. Abdominal contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a tumor of 50 mm diameter in S1 of the liver. The ventral portion had an irregular margin and showed early enhancement predominantly in peripheral area and gradual enhancement in central area. In the superior aspect of the lesion, the middle and left hepatic veins were obstructed and narrowed, respectively, suggesting venous invasion of the tumor. The dorsal portion was a well-defined and low-attenuated mass. It showed heterogeneous early enhancement and partial wash-out. On MR imaging, the ventral portion exhibited slightly low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, slightly high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, markedly low signal intensity on heavily T2-weighted images, diffusion restriction (apparent diffusion coefficient [ADC] = 1.1 × 10−3 mm2/s), and no uptake of gadoxetic acid in the hepatobiliary phase. The dorsal portion showed low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, high signal intensity on T2-weighted and heavily T2-weighted images, no diffusion restriction (ADC = 1.5–2.5 × 10−3 mm2/s), and no uptake of gadoxetic acid in the hepatobiliary phase. On FDG-PET/CT, FDG accumulation was high in the ventral portion (standardized uptake value [SUV]max = 8.3), and accumulation was mild in the dorsal portion, except the border region, and comparable to background liver accumulation (SUVmax = 2.8). No extrahepatic tumor was detected.
diagnosis: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma arising from biliary adenofibroma
Orpha_name: Adenocarcinoma of the liver and intrahepatic biliary tract

case_report: A 65-year-old male Caucasian patient presented with painless jaundice. The patient had a history of colon cancer (American Joint Committee on Cancer stage II, pT4, pN0, G2, M0, R0) 8 years prior, which was treated with left hemicolectomy followed by adjuvant therapy with capecitabine. Subsequent regular follow-up examinations showed no tumor recurrence. Four years ago, elevated transaminases were noted, leading to the identification of non-alcoholic steatohepatitis. No other chronic liver diseases were identified.
test_results: MRI-scan showed a malignant tumor mass in Klatskin-position, type IIIb according to Bismuth-Corlette classification. No distant organ manifestations of the tumor were visible in MRI and CT-scans. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiography (ERC) showed an unaffected major duodenal papilla. Further examination of the biliary tree revealed a stenosis of the common hepatic duct and left hepatic duct with possible affection of the right hepatic duct, consistent with Bismuth-Corlette type IIIb/IV Klatskin-tumor. The tissue obtained from the bile duct during ERC showed formations of a partially necrotic solid and invasively growing malignant tumor with strong tumor-associated inflammation composed of a quite homogenous large-sized tumor cells. Immunohistochemistry showed positivity of the tumor cells for broad spectrum Cytokeratin (AE1/3) as well as partially for Cytokeratins (CK) 18, 19 (∼60% of tumor cells), and 20. All other markers aiming at a further lineage differentiation were negative.
Orpha_name: Undifferentiated carcinoma of liver and intrahepatic biliary tract

case_report: A 63-year-old man was readmitted to our hospital for further evaluation of a hepatic cystic lesion. One year prior, he experienced pain in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen and fever, leading to a visit to a local hospital. An abdominal sonogram revealed a cystic lesion approximately 10 cm in size in the right lobe of the liver, and pus-like material was aspirated. He was then referred to our hospital for further management. Upon admission, his temperature was 38.0°C, pulse 80 per minute, respiration 20 per minute, and blood pressure 110/70 mmHg. Laboratory tests showed: leukocyte count 12,900/mm3; hemoglobin 12.9 g/dl; total bilirubin 4.6 mg/dl; AST 39 IU/L; ALT 74 IU/L; alkaline phosphatase 590 IU/L; GGT 90 IU/L. HBsAg and anti-HCV were negative. Antiamebic antibody (IHA) was positive at a 1:512 titer. Urinalysis and stool examination were within normal limits. The patient declined further studies and was treated as a liver abscess. He did not follow up for about a year without specific problems. Upon readmission, he reported anorexia and weight loss of over 1 kg in the past month. His temperature was 37.0°C, pulse 80 per minute, respiration 20 per minute, and blood pressure 120/80 mmHg. Physical examination showed no abnormalities in the eyes, ears, nasal or oral mucosa. Chest auscultation revealed normal breath sounds and a regular heart sound without murmur. The liver was palpable three finger breadths below the costal margin. Routine examination results were: hemoglobin 13.3 g/dl, hematocrit 39%, leukocyte count 11,600/mm3 (neutrophil 67%, lymphocyte 27%, monocyte 6%), and platelet count 273,000/mm3. Liver function tests showed: total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 0.6 mg/dl, AST 29 IU/L, ALT 13 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 70 IU/L, GGT 38 IU/L. Antiamebic antibody (IHA) was negative below a 1:64 titer. Urinalysis and stool examination were within normal limits. Tumor markers were within normal limits: AFP 3.1 ng/ml, CEA 0.4 ng/ml, CA 19-9 8.96 U/ml, and CA 125 40.1 U/ml. Chest and abdominal X-rays showed no abnormalities. Abdominal CT revealed a large cystic lesion measuring 10×10 cm in the right liver with focal irregular wall thickening and internal papillary projections. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiography (ERCP) showed a mildly dilated common bile duct and some filling defects in the right intrahepatic duct. The cystic lesion was connected to the right intrahepatic duct, and some filling defects were observed within the cystic lesion. Mucin-like material was drained using a balloon catheter after sphincterotomy. Celiac angiography indicated a large cavitary lesion supplied by the hepatic artery.
test_results: Histologic examination showed papillary proliferation of atypical cuboidal epithelium with mucin production in the cystic area.

case_report: A 41-year-old woman arrived at the emergency department with complaints of urinary frequency and urgency over the past 3 days. She described an abrupt, compelling need to urinate that she could not delay, often resulting in loss of urinary control. Urination was accompanied by a burning sensation. She needed to urinate every 3 hours and woke up multiple times at night to urinate. There was no change in urine color. She did not report any flank pain or fever. Her medical history included recurrent urinary tract infections, with episodes of cystitis approximately every 5 months for the past 15 years. She also had asthma and beta-thalassemia minor. Her surgical history included a transsphenoidal hypophysectomy performed 10 years ago for a pituitary adenoma. The patient was a heavy smoker with a 30 pack-year history but did not consume alcohol. She worked as a taxi driver. Her family history was non-contributory. On examination, she appeared comfortable. Vital signs were a heart rate of 90 bpm, respiratory rate of 14 bpm, temperature of 37.0℃, and blood pressure of 110/78 mmHg. Oxygen saturation was normal on room air. Abdominal examination revealed no tenderness or rigidity, and bowel sounds were normal in intensity and frequency. Examination of other systems was non-contributory. Initial laboratory results showed a hemoglobin level of 14.2 g/dL, leukocyte count of 5200/μL, and platelet count of 380,000/μL. Inflammatory markers, including erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein, were within normal limits. Urinalysis revealed numerous leukocytes with positive leukocyte esterase and nitrite. Despite her history of recurrent urinary tract infections, she had not previously undergone any imaging studies. The urology team recommended an abdominal computed tomography scan to investigate potential structural abnormalities.
test_results: The patient underwent a contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan, which demonstrated the presence of a fluid-filled structure arising from the dome of the bladder and extending superiorly toward the umbilicus.

case_report: A 16-month-old male patient presented with perianal openings and stool discharge from these openings for approximately two weeks. The child was born to a 28-year-old primigravida mother via normal vaginal delivery without post-natal complications or the need for neonatal intensive care. The perianal openings were acute and progressive in number and size, accompanied by weight loss and failure to thrive. The patient had a history of chronic diarrhea since nine months of age, for which medical attention was sought but no definitive cause was identified. Stool analyses were performed multiple times, yielding no pathogens. On physical examination, the patient appeared pale and cachectic. Multiple perianal openings of varying sizes and depths were noted, surrounded by erythema and tenderness on palpation. Laboratory results on admission included a C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 255 mg/L. The vasculitis profile showed cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic autoantibody at <3 U/mL, perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody at <3 U/mL, and glioblastoma multiforme at <3 U/mL, all of which were negative. The indirect Coombs test was negative. Clinical chemistry results were as follows: blood urea nitrogen (BUN) = 3 mg/dL, creatinine = 0.34 mg/dL, serum glutamic-pyruvic transaminase = 40 U/L, serum glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase = 74 U/L, all within normal ranges. Albumin was 2.7 g/dL (normal range = 3.5-5.5 g/dL). Serum electrolytes showed Na = 136 mEq/L, Cl = 101 mEq/L, and K = 3.3 mEq/L.
test_results: A colonoscopy showed severe disease at the ileocecal valve, ascending colon, and sigmoid colon, and pseudopolyps in the ilium with a fistula at the distal sigma.
diagnosis: Very Early Onset of Fistulizing Inflammatory Bowel Disease with RIPK1 Mutation

case_report: A 57-year-old male was admitted to an outside hospital with S-T elevation myocardial infarction (MI). During his stay, he experienced acute hypotension and required emergent central venous access through the right subclavian vein for vasopressors. He was stabilized at the outside facility. Two days later, he exhibited acute left hemiplegia and right gaze deviation. Transfer to our facility was arranged. During transport, he had a focal seizure and was intubated for airway protection. In the emergency department, his Glasgow coma scale score was 10 (E: 4, V: 1, M: 5). He was opening his eyes spontaneously. He had a right gaze deviation. He was localizing with the right lower and upper extremities but was plegic on the left side of his body. He experienced a cluster of seizures and was started on levetiracetam and propofol infusion.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) of the head showed loss of gray-white matter differentiation in the right frontal lobe and a right frontal hypodensity. CT angiography (CTA) of the head was negative for large vessel occlusion. His CTA of the neck showed a catheter extending from the right side of neck into the right common carotid artery with tip located in the arch of the aorta with the presence of a thrombosis.
diagnosis: Ischemic Stroke due to Inadvertent Central Arterial Catheterization

case_report: A 9-year-old girl presented with right-sided weakness and was admitted to our department around 8 hours after the onset of symptoms. She had no prior medical history, no history of surgeries, and was not on any prescribed medications. She did not report any headaches or transient ischemic symptoms. Upon arrival, her vital signs were within normal limits.
test_results: Initial diffusion-weighted (DWI) magnetic resonance imaging showed acute infarction in the basal ganglia in the lenticulostriate artery territory. MRA showed mild stenosis from the distal ICA to the middle cerebral artery (MCA) and anterior cerebral artery (ACA), and 3D-SPACE showed mild shrinkage of the outer diameter with the same internal caliber as that found on MRA. At 7 days after admission, DSA of the left ICA indicated mild irregular stenosis with a banding pattern from the distal ICA to MCA and occlusion of the ACA.

case_report: A fourteen-year-old girl presented with a history of fever, painful subcutaneous nodules with ulcerations on both lower limbs for two months, and digital gangrene of the right index finger for one month. There was no history of purpura, Raynaud's phenomenon, recurrent oral ulcers, hair loss, or malar rash. The patient also had no history of throat pain, jaundice, or past tuberculosis. General physical examination revealed normal vital signs, multiple subcutaneous ulcers predominantly on both lower limbs, and bluish-black discoloration of the distal phalanx of the index finger. Laboratory tests indicated normal renal and liver function. The peripheral smear showed an elevated total count, and the Anti-streptolysin O (ASLO) titer was elevated. Throat and urine cultures showed no bacterial growth. Ultrasonography of the abdomen and echocardiography of the heart were normal.
test_results: The deep incisional skin biopsy taken from the subcutaneous nodule revealed leukocytoclastic vasculitis of the dermal vessels.

case_report: An 8-year-old male presented with a 1-month history of pain and swelling in his right knee following a minor sprain. The patient, a first-born child of non-consanguineous parents, had a birth weight of 3800 grams and current weight of 30 kg. He had a history of normal neurodevelopment and was a native of Afghanistan with no known history of specific diseases. There were no positive points in the family history regarding rheumatologic disorders, and there were no smoker parents. Knee arthrotomy and joint fluid cultures revealed no bacterial growth. The patient's symptoms progressed to migratory arthritis involving both knees, wrists, and metacarpophalangeal joints over the course of 2 weeks. In addition to the presenting symptoms, he also noticed a blue discoloration of the pulp of his second and fifth fingers on his right hand. Due to worsening symptoms, persistent fever, continuation and worsening of arthritis and joint contracture with severe pain, blue discoloration and concern about progression to necrosis and ischemia, a rheumatology consultation was sought, and the patient was transferred to Mofid Children's Hospital Rheumatology Center in Tehran, Iran. Upon admission, the patient exhibited a constellation of symptoms including severe illness, pallor, fever, generalized arthralgia with severe pain. On physical examination, the patient exhibited a temperature of 39.5°C, heart rate of 112 bpm, and blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg. He had no Raynaud's phenomenon, livedo, skin ulcers, or ocular lesions. Musculoskeletal examination revealed flexion contractures of both knees, with active arthritis in the metacarpophalangeal and wrist joints. Concerning findings included a blue discoloration and ischemic changes of the pulp of his second and fifth fingers on the right hand, as well as painful subcutaneous nodules on his forearm. The timing of the digital ischemia and color changes did not seem to correlate with cold exposure or winter months, suggesting the vascular involvement was not directly triggered by cold stimuli in this case. Laboratory investigations revealed elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP, WBC) and abnormal Ferritin level. Bone marrow aspiration and thoracoabdomenopelvic CT scan ruled out malignancy. Despite initial broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment, the patient continued to experience persistent fever and elevated inflammatory markers. Interestingly, laboratory tests showed elevated IL-6 and ASO titer.
test_results: A skin biopsy revealed active leukocytoclastic vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis of medium-sized deep dermal and hypodermal vessels.

case_report: A 7-year and 6-month-old boy was admitted to the hospital with fever and pain in the extremities. He had been diagnosed with stomatitis a week earlier but did not respond to outpatient treatment. Initially, he developed mild fever, which escalated to above 38°C, accompanied by increased pain in the left lower extremity and upper extremities. His past medical history included occasional upper respiratory tract infections and a toothache three weeks prior that resolved without dental intervention. He had received a second dose of the hepatitis B vaccine five months earlier. His parents reported no recent lack of appetite, weight loss, excessive sweating, abdominal pain, headache, or testicular pain. Upon admission, the boy was in a moderately severe condition, febrile, and in pain. Pain in the extremities hindered normal movement, with both active and passive movements causing severe pain in the knee, ankle, wrist, and left hip joints. Physical examination revealed severe pain in the form of whole-body hyperesthesia, palpable soft, tender subcutaneous nodules about 2 cm in diameter in the sternal area, subcutaneous edema around the knee, ankle, and wrist joints, and ecchymosis near the left anterior iliac spine. Muscle strength was reduced, especially on the left side, with decreased left hip abduction. The tongue was tender with a whitish coating, the tonsils were enlarged, and erosions were observed in the mucosa and tonsils. Arterial pressure was normal, below the 90th percentile, and other vital signs such as pulse and breathing were normal for his age. Laboratory tests showed high inflammatory marker activity with normal procalcitonin levels, anemia, thrombocythemia, leukocytosis with a predominance of neutrophils on peripheral blood smear, and a high tetrazolium reduction test result (82%, normal up to 12%). Aminotransferases, lactic dehydrogenase, creatine kinase, aldolase, kidney function tests, and complement components C3c and C4 levels were normal. Anti-CMV IgM and anti-parvovirus B19 IgM antibodies were detected, while HbsAg and antibodies against Epstein-Barr virus, hepatitis C virus, Borrelia, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae were not detected. The γ-interferon release assay was negative. Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide autoantibodies (ACPA), rheumatoid factor (RF), anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA), myeloperoxidase anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (MPO-ANCA), proteinase-3 anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (PR3-ANCA), anticardiolipin antibodies (ACA), the Venereal Diseases Research Laboratory (VDRL) test, and anti-vascular endothelial cell antibodies (AECA) levels were all negative. Bone marrow features excluded neoplasm. Multiple blood and urine cultures were sterile, and swabs and cultures of the upper respiratory tract and stool material were normal. Ultrasound imaging revealed splenic enlargement and an effusion in the left hip joint. Electromyography (EMG) indicated chronic nerve conduction impairment consistent with multifocal mononeuropathy. Imaging and function tests, including chest radiographs, echocardiography, electrocardiography, ultrasound imaging of the remaining peripheral joints, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head and the thoracic and lumbosacral spine, and capillaroscopy, showed no pathological changes. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed no abnormalities. A neurologist noted increased muscle tone and muscle weakness in the upper extremities, enhanced left patellar reflex, and left ankle clonus. Dental assessment revealed several gangrenous teeth, while an ophthalmological examination showed no abnormalities. The boy's condition remained moderately severe, with persistent fever and pain. In the following days, cyanotic, tender, soft subcutaneous nodules emerged and quickly expanded (up to 3 cm) within the chest and thorax, the auricles, above the left knee joint, and on the fingers of the right hand. Ultrasound imaging revealed these were dilated subcutaneous vessels with thickened walls and impaired flow, along with a subcutaneous perivascular inflammatory infiltrate.
test_results: Increase in small vessels, surrounding infiltration made up primarily of CD4+ lymphocytes; aggregates of CD3+ and CD4+ lymphocytes, neutrophils (CD15+) and histiocytes (CD68+) between adipose tissue lobules in the subcutaneous tissue, increase in vessels in the adipose tissue between muscle fibers, surrounded by aggregates of B lymphocytes (CD20+) and T lymphocytes (CD3+, CD4+, CD8+), granulocytes (CD15+), individual plasma cells (CD138+) and histiocytes (CD68+).

case_report: A 31-year-old single woman of Mediterranean descent from Lebanon presented with deep, painful genital ulcers and multiple oral aphthae for two weeks. She experienced joint pain in the knees and elbows, light flashes, and blurry vision in both eyes. Her medical history included recurrent genital lesions and photosensitivity. She had no history of sexual activity or recent travel. Physical examination revealed well-defined punched-out erosions over the buccal and gingival mucosa, and multiple deep ulcers with yellow exudate and black eschar covering two-thirds of both labia majora and minora, sparing the clitoris, with non-violaceous borders and bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. The pathergy test was negative. Ophthalmological examination showed reduced visual acuity in both eyes; 20/60 in the right eye and 20/30 in the left eye with quiet anterior segments. Dilated fundus examination revealed a few cotton wool spots and intraretinal hemorrhage. There was no evidence of vitritis, retinitis, or vasculitis. Fundus fluorescein angiography indicated multiple arteriolar infarctions involving the macula in both eyes, more pronounced in the right eye. The retinal venous system appeared unaffected. Optical coherence tomography of both eyes showed hyper-reflectivity in the inner nuclear and outer plexiform layers, indicating ischemia. Immunological tests were negative for antinuclear antibody (ANA), double-stranded DNA, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), and complement C3 & C4. Tests for herpes simplex virus (HSV) IgM 1 and 2, hepatitis B and C viruses, cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgM, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), QuantiFERON-TB, and syphilis were negative. The HLA B-51 was positive.
test_results: Microscopic examination of hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained tissue sections from the vulvar biopsy revealed epidermal hyperplasia and dense dermal and subcutaneous inflammatory infiltrate with large numbers of neutrophils. A medium-sized subcutaneous artery was involved and showed neutrophilic infiltration of its wall. No granuloma was observed. Stain for elastic lamina showed medium-sized subcutaneous artery involvement.
diagnosis: Coexistence of Polyarteritis Nodosa in a Behçet's Disease Patient

case_report: A 54-year-old woman presented with a two-week history of persistent pain in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen, along with nausea, fatigue, fever, and unintentional weight loss. The patient has a history of smoking and a family history of systemic lupus erythematosus in a cousin. She has no significant medical history, surgeries, or drug use. On physical examination, her temperature and vital signs were within normal limits. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. The abdominal examination showed minimal tenderness in the epigastrium and right hypochondrium, with no signs of peritoneal irritation.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis revealed circumferential thickening of the wall of the common hepatic artery with a narrowed but filiform lumen and dilatation of the distal celiac trunk before the origin of the common hepatic artery. Abdominal arteriography revealed a fusiform aneurysm of the celiac trunk before bifurcation. The proximal two-thirds of the common hepatic artery displayed dilation, while it was completely obstructed in the distal segment, preventing passage of the guidewire or contrast medium. The splenic, left gastric, and superior mesenteric arteries were all normal. The results of the 18-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) scan revealed hypermetabolism with a maximum standardized uptake value (SUV) of 3.89 in the hepatic artery and hypermetabolism with a maximum SUV of 6.02 in the ascending colon, accompanied by thickening of the colonic wall. FDG concentration was found to be within normal limits in all other vascular structures.
diagnosis: Single-Organ Vasculitis  of the Hepatic Artery

case_report: An 84-year-old woman was referred to our general medicine department for evaluation due to a history of persisting fever for more than 2 weeks. There were no accompanying symptoms, such as headache, chest pain, dyspnea, abdominal pain, back pain, diarrhea, constipation, arthralgia, rash, or numbness. Her general condition was good, with vital signs within normal range, except for a body temperature of 38.2°C. The physical examination was unremarkable, with no evidence of joint inflammation or temporal arteritis. Laboratory results showed leukocytosis (9300 /μl), elevated serum C-reactive protein (181.2 mg/L), and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 66 mm/hour. Liver and kidney function tests were normal, as were electrolyte levels. Tests for antinuclear antibodies and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic autoantibodies were negative. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) imaging of the chest and abdomen and echocardiography were unremarkable. Additionally, 2 sets of blood cultures were negative.
test_results: The FDG PET/CT revealed positive uptakes of FDG in the left breast, with a standardized uptake value (SUV) of 2.9. The biopsy specimen revealed rupture of the elastic plate and evidence of fibrinoid necrosis of arteries.
diagnosis: Polyarteritis Nodosa  with Single Organ Vasculitis  of the left breast

case_report: A 43-year-old male experienced six weeks of intermittent fever, joint pain, muscle pain, abdominal pain in the left lower quadrant, and a rash. He was initially treated with antibiotics for presumed diverticulitis, which partially alleviated his abdominal pain. Following the start of antibiotics, he developed a rash and was given a short course of steroids, which temporarily resolved the rash and other symptoms. However, within a week of stopping steroids, he had recurrent fever and systemic symptoms, leading to hospital admission. Upon admission, normal laboratory results included serum creatinine, serum blood urea nitrogen, liver function panel, hematocrit, and platelets. His white blood cell count was elevated to 15,000/mL with 86% neutrophils, C-reactive protein (CRP) was elevated to 256 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was elevated to 32 mm/hr. Urinalysis showed 3+ blood with more than 50 red blood cells (RBCs) on microscopic analysis but was negative for protein, nitrite, or leukocyte esterase. Blood cultures showed no growth. Physical examination revealed a rash with scattered pink papules on the arms, legs, and forehead, and a few purpuric macules on the palmoplantar surfaces. A biopsy of a papule on the right arm showed a sparse dermal lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltrate. He was treated with prednisone 1 mg/kg for three days, which led to minimal improvement. While the body rash improved, his fevers, systemic symptoms, and the purpuric macules on his palmoplantar surfaces persisted and became more tender. Additionally, new splinter hemorrhages were observed on three fingernails. Subsequently, he developed chest pain and was diagnosed with an ST elevation myocardial infarction, requiring intervention for an occluded circumflex artery.
test_results: This demonstrated a medium caliber artery with intravascular thrombi and focal vasculitis without involvement of small caliber vessels or capillaries. Stains for organisms, including Brown and Brenn, acid-fast bacilli (AFB), and Grocott methenamine silver (GMS), were negative. Tissue cultures obtained from a purpuric macule demonstrated no growth on aerobic, AFB, and fungal media. Subsequently, he underwent diagnostic cerebral angiography, which showed an aneurysm of the right posterior communicating artery, as well as signs of CNS vasculitis elsewhere, including dilation, irregularity, and branch blocks within branches of the right internal carotid artery.

case_report: A 4-year-old girl experienced acute tonsillitis and was treated with benzathine penicillin. She also had chronic polyarthritis with swelling, tenderness, and pain during movement for 2 months. The joints involved included elbows, right wrist, all proximal interphalangeal joints, knees, ankles, and the first metatarsophalangeal joint. She experienced morning stiffness lasting 30 to 60 minutes, which was associated with limited motion in the elbows, right wrist, and knees. After 45 days, she developed painful subcutaneous nodules and erythematous-violaceous lesions on the extensor regions of her upper and lower limbs. She was admitted to the teaching hospital with high fever, malaise, muscle pain, loss of appetite, a weight loss of 1.0 kg, severely painful skin lesions, and severe functional disability. She was bedridden due to chronic polyarthritis with restricted movement. Her systolic and diastolic blood pressures were above the 95th percentile for her height. She was treated with naproxen 20mg/kg/day, paracetamol, and tramadol. Laboratory tests revealed hemoglobin at 10.9g/dL, white blood cell count at 25,380/mm3 (67% neutrophils, 19% lymphocytes, 13% monocytes, and 1% eosinophils), platelets at 683,000/mm3, erythrocyte sedimentation rate at 53mm/first hour, and C-reactive protein at 246.4mg/dL (normal range: 0 to 0.3mg/dL). Aspartate aminotransferase was 15U/L (normal range: 15 to 40U/L), alanine aminotransferase was 9U/L (normal range: 10 to 35U/L), urea was 24mg/dL (normal range: 15 to 45mg/dL), and creatinine was 0.35mg/dL (normal range: 0.6 to 0.9mg/dL). C3 was 174mg/dL (normal range: 90 to 180mg/dL) and C4 was 21.2mg/dL (normal range: 10 to 40mg/dL). Anti-streptolysin O was 1,687UI/mL. Urinalysis was normal and the urine protein/creatinine ratio was 0.39g/day. Immunological tests, including antinuclear antibodies (ANA), anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA), anti-Sm, anti-RNP, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), anti-topoisomerase, anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB, and IgG and IgM anticardiolipin antibodies, were negative. Serologies for hepatitis (A, B, and C) virus, HIV, VDRL, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and toxoplasmosis were also negative. Echocardiogram and Doppler ultrasonography of the renal artery were normal. Thoracic and abdominal magnetic resonance angiographies were also normal.
test_results: Skin biopsy revealed necrotizing vasculitis in medium- and small-sized vessels.

case_report: A 10-day-old, full-term Caucasian male infant was admitted to a local hospital with symptoms of viral gastroenteritis. During the hospital stay, pediatric surgical services were consulted due to left scrotal swelling, and a left hydrocele was identified. The patient was subsequently discharged. Seventeen days later, at four weeks of age, the infant returned with a 24-hour history of left scrotal swelling, redness, fever, and a pus-like discharge from an ulcerated area in the left hemi-scrotum. An abdominal examination showed normal results, while a scrotal examination revealed a left scrotal abscess and a hard, swollen left testis. No hernia was detected. Immediate surgical exploration was planned. Intravenous antibiotics (amoxicillin with clavulanic acid and flucloxacillin) and fluids were administered due to the local scrotal infection. A midline raphe scrotal incision was performed, and a small amount of pus was drained. Necrotic scrotal wall tissue was excised back to healthy tissue margins. The tunica vaginalis was noted to be thickened, and the testis was found to be edematous with a normal blood supply. No evidence of testicular torsion was observed. The wound was thoroughly washed with antiseptic solution, and the dartos muscle and skin were closed using absorbable sutures. The fever subsided shortly after surgery, and the swelling, redness, and pain decreased over the next 48 hours.
test_results: Wound cultures revealed Enterococcus sp. (ampicillin-sensitive) and Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-sensitive). Histology confirmed the intra-operative diagnosis.

case_report: An 18-year-old male from rural Washington, residing in a mobile home with his family, experienced mild throat and left ear pain 5 days before hospital admission. His symptoms progressively worsened, becoming severe 3 days before admission, with minimal relief from ibuprofen 600 mg and chloraseptic spray. Two days prior to admission, he developed a fever of 38.4 degrees Celsius, malaise, poor oral intake, nonproductive cough, difficulty swallowing, painful swallowing, and 3-4 episodes of nonbilious, nonbloody vomiting. His medical history includes a repaired tethered spinal cord from infancy and a smoking habit of 1–1.5 packs per day, with no alcohol or illicit drug use. Upon arrival at the local rural hospital, he was febrile and tachycardic but managing his secretions adequately and appeared nontoxic. Laboratory results showed a leukocyte count of 26,000.
test_results: A CT scan of his neck with IV contrast revealed extensive air in the parapharyngeal and retropharyngeal space extending to the supraclavicular region and mediastinum.

case_report: A 46-day-old male infant presented with recurrent episodes of shortness of breath and cough. He was born at full term (41 weeks of gestation) with a birth weight of 3,660 grams. On the first day after birth, he experienced shortness of breath without an identifiable organic cause. One week later, he developed a single cough that progressed into a continuous, paroxysmal cough, accompanied by shortness of breath and sputum production. Despite multiple treatments at local hospitals, his symptoms did not improve. The patient was admitted to our hospital due to worsening cough and shortness of breath. A chest X-ray revealed multiple patchy shadows in both lung fields, and high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest showed large scattered ground-glass opacities in both lung fields. He is the second child of non-consanguineous parents. His older brother had a history of recurrent pneumonia after birth and passed away from severe pneumonia at 7 months old.
test_results: On day 70 of life, whole exome sequencing revealed compound heterozygous variants in the ABCA3 gene (NM_001,089); paternally inherited c.4035+5G > A in intron 26 and c.668T > C (p.M223T) in exon 8, and maternally inherited c.1285+4A > C in intron 11. Sanger sequencing was performed to verify the three variants in the patient and his parents. The three variants of the ABCA3 gene were all absent from the gnomAD and ExAC databases. The intron variants c.4035+5G > A and c.1285+4A > C were predicted to affect RNA splicing by several different splice site algorithms. The predicted tertiary structure of the ABCA3 transporter showed the location of the missense variant p.M223T, and the variant was predicted to be deleterious by different algorithms.
diagnosis: Interstitial Lung Disease  caused by bi-allelic mutations in the ABCA3 gene
Orpha_name: Interstitial lung disease due to ABCA3 deficiency

case_report: A 34-month-old boy experienced recurrent coughing episodes starting at 9 months old. He was born at full term (39 weeks) with a birth weight of 3,000 grams. Initially, the cough was triggered by cold temperatures, physical activity, and crying, and was accompanied by cyanosis and wheezing. Despite multiple outpatient and inpatient treatments, the cough persisted but showed improvement with azithromycin. Physical examination revealed clubbing of the fingers. A chest X-ray showed bilateral diffuse plaque-like shadows. Chest HRCT scan indicated multiple striped fuzzy shadows and ground-glass opacity in both lung fields. Both parents were asymptomatic, and there was no reported family history of genetic diseases.
test_results: The genetic analysis showed compound heterozygous ABCA3 variants; paternally inherited c.704T > C (p.F235S) in exon 8, and maternally inherited c.4037_4040del (p.T1346Nfs*15) in exon 27. The two variants in the ABCA3 gene were both absent from the gnomAD and ExAC databases, and have not been reported in the literature.
diagnosis: Interstitial Lung Disease  caused by ABCA3 gene mutations
Orpha_name: Interstitial lung disease due to ABCA3 deficiency

case_report: A 6-month-old male infant was referred to a tertiary pulmonary service due to ongoing respiratory distress and failure to thrive since birth. He was born at 36 weeks gestation with symmetrical intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR) and spent 5 days in the neonatal intensive care unit for unexplained tachypnea and respiratory distress, which improved but did not fully resolve. The patient, the first child of a non-consanguineous couple from the same tribe, presented with shortness of breath, persistent cough, and intermittent fever. He had been treated at various district hospitals for bronchiolitis, pneumonia, recurrent wheezing, and possible asthma, receiving multiple courses of antibiotics, nebulized bronchodilators, and inhaled steroids without improvement. A barium meal indicated gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), but anti-reflux management and nasogastric feeding did not lead to improvement. Despite optimal nutritional management with a high protein and calorie formula, he continued to fail to thrive. Upon arrival at the center, he exhibited persistent respiratory distress characterized by tachypnea, intercostal and subcostal recession, and an oxygen saturation of 78% in room air. Breath sounds were decreased bilaterally without additional sounds. He had no dysmorphic features, and his head circumference, weight, and height were all below the third centile. Clinical examination revealed an enlarged liver with a span of 10 cm and axial hypotonia with preserved reflexes. Metabolic work-up showed recurrent hypoglycemia attributed to nutritional status, while endocrine work-up revealed primary hypothyroidism with elevated thyroid stimulating hormone and low thyroxine, which normalized with thyroxine replacement therapy. Hematology work-up indicated nutritional anemia and unexplained thrombocytopenia. Immunology investigations showed normal immunoglobulin and lymphocyte function. Low albumin levels were noted, attributed to nutritional status, with normal liver function tests and no albuminuria in urine examination. Pulmonary investigations included an initially normal arterial blood gas that later showed respiratory acidosis, chest x-ray indicating diffuse alveolar disease, and chest CT scan showing bilateral basal infiltration and atelectasis. Bronchoscopy revealed a tracheal bronchus with otherwise normal structures, and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was milky with a high cell count (8442 C/L) and neutrophilic predominance. Cultures were negative, and cytology was negative for periodic acid-Schiff stain but positive for lipid-laden macrophages. Despite intensive care support with conventional and high-frequency ventilation, the patient's condition deteriorated, leading to death due to respiratory failure. He was not stable for interventional therapeutic lavage.
test_results: Whole exome sequencing revealed a novel homozygous variant of the MARS gene, c.854T>C p.(Ile285Thr). The allele frequency was 0.000037 in ExAc and 0.00020 in 1000G. This variant segregated with the family as both parents were found to be heterozygous.
diagnosis: Pulmonary Alveolar Proteinosis  caused by a novel mutation in the MARS gene
Orpha_name: Severe early-onset pulmonary alveolar proteinosis due to MARS deficiency

case_report: A 24-year-old female presented with a 2-year history of continuous right-sided headache with superimposed exacerbations. The continuous pain was dull, mild to moderate in severity, and most intense in the retro-orbital and supraorbital areas. The exacerbations, described as excruciating pulsatile pain, occurred every alternate day to up to 4 times a day and lasted for 30 minutes to 4 hours. Exacerbations were rated as 9-10 on the visual analogue scale (VAS). During exacerbations, the patient exhibited marked restlessness or agitation, including hitting her head against the wall, pacing, and crying. Cranial autonomic features were reported during exacerbations, occurring contralateral to the pain side, including conjunctival injection, tearing, and eyelid edema. These features were never on the side of the pain. Nausea and phonophobia were occasionally noted during exacerbations. Nocturnal attacks were also reported. There were no identified precipitating or aggravating factors for the exacerbations. Family history of headache was negative. Past treatments included amitriptyline, propranolol, topiramate, flunarizine, sodium valproate, naproxen, diclofenac, paracetamol, and ibuprofen, none of which provided significant improvement. Physical examinations and investigations, including MRI of the brain, were normal. The patient experienced two exacerbations in the next 36 hours.
test_results: Conjunctival injection, tearing and eyelid edema were observed during exacerbations.

case_report: A 66-year-old retired male patient visited the pain clinic in mid-2014 with complaints of episodic headaches over the past 10 years. These headaches occurred up to 8 times daily, beginning as a sharp pain near the right eye and spreading to the right side of the face, vertex, and upper back of the head. Each episode lasted between 45 and 75 minutes, with pain-free intervals in between. The pain was described as intense and unbearable, accompanied by rhinorrhea in the right nostril and conjunctival injection in the right eye without swelling. The patient experienced significant restlessness during these episodes. Treatment with a greater occipital nerve block using 40 mg methylprednisolone and 20 mg bupivacaine provided complete pain relief within minutes, lasting for 12 months. This treatment was repeated twice, each time offering 6 months of relief. By mid-2016, the headaches had subsided, and the patient remained headache-free for 2.5 years. His medical history included an abdominal aortic aneurysm surgery, and his family history was unremarkable. In July 2019, the patient returned to the clinic with a new, constant stabbing pain radiating from the back of the right side of his head to the right side of the vertex, forehead, right ear, and jaw, accompanied by numbness and paresthesias. He did not report neck pain. The right eye exhibited continuous tearing, conjunctival injection, and eyelid edema, along with excessive rhinorrhea. The patient felt particularly restless at night. His baseline pain score was 6 out of 10, with exacerbations reaching 9 out of 10, occurring 2-3 times daily and lasting 20-30 minutes, sometimes triggered by neck movements. Physical examination revealed mild tearing, conjunctival injection, and slight eyelid edema in the right eye, along with hyperesthesia over the right vertex and forehead. Neurological examination was otherwise normal. Passive neck extension was extremely limited and reproduced severe pain exacerbations. Palpation of the right SCM muscle elicited tenderness and exacerbated the referred pain. An injection of 30 mg of 1% lidocaine into the right SCM muscle resulted in a reduction of pain from a score of 7 out of 10 to 0 within 4 minutes. The numbness in the forehead and vertex disappeared, neck range of motion improved, and right-sided tearing and conjunctival injection began to subside, followed by resolving eyelid edema. Symptom relief lasted for 4 weeks before partially relapsing. In September 2019, the patient returned and received another injection, this time with 20 mg lidocaine and 10 mg bupivacaine, resulting in complete pain resolution for an additional 2 months.
test_results: The pain was relieved within 24 h of the indomethacin trial.

case_report: A 44-year-old Polynesian male experienced a sudden loss of vision in his left eye (OS) following blunt trauma from a heavy plastic object one day prior. His ophthalmic history includes a right eye (OD) rhegmatogenous retinal detachment 20 years ago due to blunt trauma, treated with a scleral buckling procedure. Six years ago, he had an episode in the right eye that resolved spontaneously after 2 months, with vision returning to pre-episode levels. At discharge, his vision was 6/19 OD and 6/5 OS. His past medical history is unremarkable, with no medications taken and no systemic symptoms reported, including stress. There were no ocular issues since his previous discharge. Upon presentation, his visual acuity was 6/19 OD and hand movements OS. Examination of the left eye revealed mild non-granulomatous anterior uveitis (1+ cells) without hyphaema. There was no relative afferent pupillary defect. Intraocular pressures were 18 mmHg OD and 20 mmHg OS. Both optic discs appeared normal with no pits. Fundal examination of the left eye showed macular neurosensory retinal detachment without retinal breaks, commotio retinae, or choroidal rupture. There was no evidence of vitritis, chorioretinal lesions, or vascular changes indicative of active or previous posterior uveitis in either eye.
test_results: Optical coherence tomography examination confirmed sensory retina elevation with significant sub-retinal fluid and several macular small pigment epithelial detachments (PEDs) in the left eye. The right OCT was normal. There were no signs of posterior scleritis on ultrasound examination of the left eye. FFA showed dye pooling within a PED and areas of hyperfluoresence superior to the fovea with no leakage.

case_report: A 45-year-old male reported a decrease in vision in both eyes over the past 2 years. He works night shifts, does not smoke or consume alcohol, and has no history of steroid use or systemic issues. The best-corrected visual acuity was measured at 20/200 in the right eye and 20/600 in the left eye. Examination of the anterior segment in both eyes showed no abnormalities. Upon dilated fundus examination, the right eye exhibited pigmentary changes at the fovea and a large serous retinal pigment epithelium detachment along the superotemporal arcade. Additionally, vascular proliferation was observed at the inferotemporal margin of the right eye's optic disc. The left eye displayed pigmentary changes at the macula and a linear area of subretinal fibrosis extending inferonasally from the foveal center. Both eyes showed bony spicules in the inferior retina.
test_results: Enhanced depth imaging on spectral domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) noted chronic SMD and large serous RPED in the RE. The LE OCT revealed hyper-reflective fusiform thickening corresponding to subretinal fibrosis above RPE along with few intraretinal cystoid spaces. Pachychoroid was evident in BE. Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) showed window defects at the macula and intense hyperfluorescence from retinal neovascularization in RE. In addition, inferior retina of RE showed large area of capillary nonperfusion and adjoining retinal neovascularization. Indocyanine green (ICG) angiography showed late choroidal hyperpermeability along with dilated choroidal vessels and an area of hypofluorescence corresponding to RPED in the RE. Choroidal hyperpermeability was evident in LE as well. Optical coherence tomography angiography confirmed neovascularization at the edge of the optic disc in RE.

case_report: A 28-year-old male presented for evaluation of a recurrent, central right-upper lid chalazion previously treated with incision and curettage (I&C). Conservative management with erythromycin ointment and warm compresses was unsuccessful, leading to a repeat I&C. Due to the persistent nature of the chalazion, a 0.5-mL injection of triamcinolone acetonide (10 mg/mL) was administered within the chalazion excision margins in an intrapalpebral manner. One month after the procedure, the patient reported noticing a 'purple spot' in the central vision of his right eye (OD). Examination of the right eye (OD) revealed unchanged visual acuity (VA) of 20/20, normal intraocular pressure, and intact visual fields.
test_results: Fundus examination revealed subretinal fluid that was confirmed on optical coherence tomography (OCT), which also revealed a small pigment epithelial detachment (PED) in OD; intravenous fluorescein angiography revealed pooling into the PED in the early phases along with an expansile dot pattern of leakage in later phases.

case_report: A 79-year-old female with a medical history of hypertension, chronic sinusitis, asthma, and seropositive deforming rheumatoid arthritis with loss of cervical lordosis (antinuclear antibody (ANA) titer 1:1280) came to the clinic reporting five months of voice changes, difficulty breathing during physical activity, excessive throat mucus, and throat pain. The patient did not report fevers, chills, night sweats, neck masses, or unintentional weight loss. Physical examination revealed no cervical lymphadenopathy and no change in neck mobility from baseline. There was no enlargement of the liver or spleen. The patient exhibited a harsh and rough voice quality with a moderately restricted pitch range.
test_results: Flexible laryngoscopy showed a left-sided supraglottic submucosal mass without extension to the true vocal folds obstructing 50% of the laryngeal inlet. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the neck with contrast showed a 1.4 x 1.7 x 4 cm supraglottic soft tissue mass to the left of the pre-epiglottic space and left aryepiglottic fold thickening, resulting in moderate airway narrowing. Immunohistochemical staining of the excised mass revealed sheets of small lymphoid cells with large confluent aggregates of plasma cells with Dutcher bodies that expressed CD138 and IgM. Flow cytometry results were consistent with a monotypic, kappa-restricted B-cell population negative for CD5, CD10, and CD23.

case_report: A 34-year-old physically active, previously healthy, Caucasian male, classified as ASA I, presented to the emergency room with a two-month history of persistent headache that began while surfing. The day before the onset of symptoms, he had been practicing gymnastics on a trampoline, an activity he regularly engaged in. The headache was described as constrictive, non-pulsatile, with a severity of 10 out of 10 on a numerical scale. It was located in the occipital region and radiated to both parietal regions, subsiding when in a supine position. Additional symptoms included nausea, vomiting, and sensitivity to light and sound. The patient reported that the pain significantly impaired his daily activities. Blood tests and a computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain showed no abnormalities, and he was discharged with pain medication. Despite medical treatment, the symptoms persisted for two months.
test_results: The MRI showed multiple cervical-dorsal collections of epidural CFS and a possible dural continuity solution at T2-T3 level. A myelo-CT scan, with injection of radiographically opaque dye in the subarachnoid space, showed five cervical CSF fistulas: C1-C2 bilaterally, C2-C3 right, C3-C4 left and C4-C5 right.

case_report: A 25-year-old woman reported experiencing shortening of her fingers, nail deformities, and yellowish papules on her hands and forearms for 21 years. These issues began in childhood with the gradual shortening of the terminal phalanges in a few fingers, eventually affecting all fingers on both hands, while the toes remained unaffected. Concurrently, she developed asymptomatic papules on her hands. Upon examination, she had non-follicular yellowish papules on her fingers, hands, and elbow extensors, which were mostly discrete but some had coalesced. The terminal phalanges were notably short with a relatively broadened appearance, and her nails had a racket-like appearance. There was no history of Raynaud's phenomena, bleeding disorders, exposure to vinyl chloride gas, playing musical instruments, or recurrent trauma. Her menstrual history was normal. A thorough cutaneous and systemic examination did not reveal palmoplantar keratoderma, hirsutism, dental abnormalities, or other musculoskeletal abnormalities. Routine investigations, including blood counts, liver and kidney function tests, calcium levels, parathyroid hormone status, and abdominal ultrasonography, were all normal. Antinuclear Antibodies (ANA) were negative.
test_results: Roentgenogram of the hands showed destructive osteolytic changes in the terminal phalanges of all 10 fingers. A biopsy for histopathology was taken from the yellowish papule revealing hyperkeratosis, focal parakeratosis and acanthosis of epidermis. The dermis was thickened, with abundant collagen bundles surrounding the eccrine coils. The hypodermis was characterized by loss of adipocytes and septal thickening associated thickened eosinophilic collagen bundles.

case_report: A 5-year-old male child presented with severe gingival attachment loss. The child, accompanied by parents, had no notable medical history. Over the past 2 months, the child experienced gingival bleeding and pain while chewing. Clinical oral examination showed full primary dentition, minimal plaque, moderate gingival inflammation, severe attachment loss around teeth 52, 53, 62, 63, 54, 55, 64, and 65, and a supernumerary tooth in the 51 and 61 region. Bleeding on probing was observed, and periodontal pockets around the first primary molars measured 5 mm with furcal involvement. Panoramic radiograph indicated severe generalized vertical and horizontal bone loss. A complete medical evaluation was conducted, revealing normal levels for complete blood count, creatinine, alkaline phosphatase, coagulation factors, and T4 lymphocyte counts. Slight elevations were noted in absolute monocyte and neutrophil counts and erythrocyte sedimentation rates. Microbiological evaluation of unstimulated saliva identified both aerobic and anaerobic microorganisms.
test_results: This revealed the presence of A. actinomycetemcomitans and Porphyromonas gingivalis from tissue biopsy.

case_report: A 71-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital with jaundice and dark urine persisting for the past 2 years. She had a previous diagnosis of cholangiocarcinoma without biopsy and underwent biliary drainage, which alleviated her symptoms after one year. Subsequent abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed no evidence of pancreatic or bile duct tumors. Laboratory results indicated a total bilirubin level of 39 μmol/L, gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase at 311 UI/L, alanine aminotransferase at 34 UI/L, and alkaline phosphatase at 32 UI/L. Renal function tests were normal. Tests for anti-nuclear antibodies, anti-liver kidney microsomal antibodies, anti-Smith antibodies, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative.
test_results: The serum IgG4 level was very high, up to 7,596 mg/L (normal range: 39–864 mg/L). MRI of the abdomen with contrast showed dilated bile ducts with stricture, and the wall of bile ducts appeared to be thickened, showing a smooth inner wall with no evidence of any masses or stones in the bile duct or the head of the pancreas. Both kidneys showed multiple, hypointense, wedge-shaped lesions on T2-weighted images. The diffusivity of the lesions revealed restricted diffusion, and the kidneys were enhanced inhomogeneously. A computed tomography scan performed in 2020 after drainage showed a decrease in dilation, and the lesions in both kidneys were late-enhancing, with the density levels of the pre-contrast, arterial, and venous phases recorded as 37, 66, and 90 Hounsfield, respectively.

case_report: A 57-year-old male with a history of hypertension and diabetes was admitted to an outside hospital in February 2021 due to rigors and fatigue. His medical history included a prolonged hospitalization for COVID-19 in November 2020, during which he experienced severe pneumonia, respiratory failure, and required a tracheostomy. Complications included a right atrial and right ventricular thrombus with pulmonary embolisms. He was managed with a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube and discharged from a skilled nursing facility three months later. He had no known history of complicated biliary disease, cholangitis, pancreatitis, or obstructive jaundice, and prior imaging did not show liver disease. One month post-discharge, he presented with a fever of 38.3 °C, tachycardia, and hypotension. Initial blood work revealed leukocytosis with a WBC count of 19 x 10^9/L, alkaline phosphatase of 870 U/L (normal range: 30-135 U/L), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) of 77 U/L (normal range: 10-55 U/L), and bilirubin of 1.3 mg/dL. Ultrasound indicated cholelithiasis and a dilated common bile duct (CBD) measuring 9 mm, with an echogenic focus in the distal CBD. Repeat COVID-19 PCR tests were negative. He received 5 L of crystalloids and broad-spectrum antibiotics. He developed septic shock and was stabilized on norepinephrine with improved serum lactate levels. Transferred to our institution for higher care, a CT scan showed a moderately distended gallbladder, mild gallbladder wall thickening, and pericholecystic fluid, consistent with acute cholecystitis. Several tiny stones were also noted in the distal CBD.
test_results: ERCP confirmed a distal linear filling defect within the lower CBD. There was CBD dilation without intrahepatic duct dilation. A sphincterotomy and balloon sphincteroplasty were performed. The linear bile duct stone in the shape of a bile duct cast was extracted using balloon sweep. There was mild oozing from his sphincterotomy, and hence his bile duct was stented. A bile duct aspirate grew Staphylococcus epidermidis. After the procedure, his condition was found to be good with improvement in his liver enzymes. His antibiotics were deescalated to oral medications and his diet was advanced. His acute cholecystitis was managed with antibiotics. General surgery reviewed his case and offered an outpatient cholecystectomy. A repeat outpatient ERCP was performed for stent removal. During this exam, his stents and further bile duct casts were removed. However, the second ERCP was indicative of significant intrahepatic ductal disease.
diagnosis: Secondary Sclerosing Cholangitis in Critically Ill Patients

case_report: A 47-year-old male patient experiencing homelessness was admitted with respiratory distress and septic shock. The patient had a history of intravenous drug use and heavy smoking (30 pack-years). Apart from chronic hepatitis C, there was no history of liver or gastrointestinal disease, and no significant alcohol consumption was noted. On admission, vital signs indicated hypotension (mean arterial pressure <65 mm Hg), tachycardia (heart rate = 130/min), and oxygen saturation of 80%. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (18,000/µL), elevated CRP (250 mg/dL; reference <5) and procalcitonin (2.2 ng/mL; reference <0.5), and significantly elevated liver enzymes (ALT 50 times the normal value, AST 100 times the normal value). Bilirubin, gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and albumin levels were normal. The HCV-antibody test was positive with a viral load exceeding 7 million IE/mL, while the HIV test was negative. Computed tomography revealed bilateral pneumonia, and abdominal ultrasonography showed normal findings. Mechanical ventilation was initiated for respiratory failure, and high-dose catecholamine was administered for hemodynamic instability. The disease course included complications such as kidney infarction and paralytic ileus of the colon, which resolved after endoscopic decompression. After one week, liver enzyme levels returned to normal. Following 10 days in the ICU, the patient was transferred to a tertiary hospital for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation therapy due to further respiratory deterioration. After 30 days of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation therapy, the patient was transferred back to our hospital. On the second admission, liver tests were normal except for a slight increase in GGT. During the stay in the normal ward, there was a gradual increase in cholestatic parameters (GGT increased 30 times, ALP increased 10 times, and bilirubin remained normal).
test_results: We removed multiple biliary casts from the bile ducts via ERCP. The cholangiography showed rarefication with multiple segmental stenoses of the intrahepatic bile ducts.
diagnosis: Secondary Sclerosing Cholangitis in Critically Ill Patients

case_report: A 62-year-old male presented with a painless swelling in the right lower half of the face and reduced mouth opening for two weeks. This was the third occurrence of such swelling in the buccal region over the past 8 years. The first episode, 5 years ago, involved pus discharge and was treated by incision and drainage. The swelling resolved spontaneously during the second occurrence 2 years ago. The patient has been managing diabetes with regular medication for the past year. A comprehensive medical examination was conducted, screening for anomalies in the skin, eyes, skeletal system, endocrine system, nervous system, and other developmental disorders, with no syndromic associations found. Examination revealed significant asymmetry on the right side of the face. A large ovoid submucosal swelling (6 × 6 cm) was noted, extending from the right lateral canthus of the eye to 1 cm below the corner of the mouth and from the corner of the mouth to the mandibular ramus. The lesion's borders were ill-defined on palpation, and its consistency ranged from soft to firm. The overlying skin appeared normal. There was no history of pain or fever associated with the swelling. No submandibular or cervical lymphadenopathy was detected. There was no paresthesia, facial palsy, or swelling of the right parotid gland. Intraorally, the ovoid swelling caused a slight elevation of the buccal mucosa without obliterating the buccal vestibule, extending from 1 cm from the lip commissure to 1 cm short of the pterygomandibular raphae. The buccal mucous membrane was stretched and glistening without signs of inflammation. Mouth opening was restricted due to the lesion's size.
test_results: Computed tomography revealed a well-defined lesional mass with cystic areas involving the buccal space. Intracystic loculation was visible with a pus-like dense cystic content. Erosion of the posterior buccal cortex was evident with no perforation of the maxillary bone. The maxillary antral wall was compressed. Microscopically, the tissue sections showed a cystic lumen lined by parakeratinized epithelium of uniform thickness. The basal cells were cuboidal to columnar in shape exhibiting nuclear palisading. The spinous layer was thin and the parakeratin layer showed surface corrugations. Some areas were lined by flattened, stretched epithelium whereas other areas exhibited numerous infoldings of the epithelium into the connective tissue wall. The epithelium connective tissue interface was smooth and flat with no rete ridges. Underlying fibrous connective tissue was thin and mature with fibrocytes and fibroblasts with few odontogenic rests. Areas of haemorrhage and blood vessels were evident in the stroma. No daughter cysts, epithelial islands, skeletal muscle tissue, or any appendages were present in the connective tissue wall.

case_report: A 63-year-old male patient presented with a painful swelling on the inside of the right cheek, which had been increasing in size over the past month. He reported no history of jaw cysts. Clinical examination identified a firm, mobile nodule on the right buccal mucosa, just anterior to the ramus mandibulae, measuring 2.5 cm in diameter. The overlying mucosa was intact. A panoramic radiograph showed no bony lesions. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head and neck revealed an oval cystic structure in the retromolar trigone with a maximum diameter of 1.8 cm. An excision biopsy was performed.
test_results: Microscopy showed a cyst wall, with a parakeratinized stratified squamous epithelium of 5–6 cell layers in thickness, a corrugated surface and basal palisading.

case_report: A 35-year-old woman with a history of genital herpes on valacyclovir presented to the emergency department due to sharp 10/10 left upper quadrant pain, fever, and loss of appetite. On presentation, she had a temperature of 101 °F and a heart rate of 108. The physical exam revealed an ill-appearing woman with severe discomfort due to abdominal pain and tenderness in the left upper quadrant on palpation. Initial laboratory results showed severe anemia with hemoglobin at 5.6 g/dL, necessitating a transfusion of 2 units of packed red blood cells, a white blood cell count of 11.2 × 103/µL, sodium at 130 mmol/L, and elevated alanine transaminase at 101 IU/L and aspartate transaminase at 115 U/L. After stabilizing her hemoglobin, the patient continued to experience persistent left upper quadrant pain with no change in intensity.
test_results: CT abdomen and pelvis (A/P) without contrast revealed a left upper quadrant nonspecific 5.5 cm × 4.2 cm mass containing a small amount of fluid and air, multiple unquantified hepatic lesions, the largest measuring 3.3 cm × 4.8 cm, splenomegaly with splenic infarcts, and possible masses of the pancreas or porta hepatis. Preliminary results demonstrated rare Gram-positive cocci which speciated to Streptococcus intermedius. Her anaerobic blood cultures also contained Streptococcus intermedius. A repeat CT A/P performed seven days later, showed no marked improvement in the sizes of her lesions despite antibiotics, with the largest lesion approximating 5.8 cm × 4.6 cm. Esophagoduodenoscopy (EGD) revealed a nodular mass in the third portion of the duodenum, from which a biopsy was obtained. An MRI of the abdomen was subsequently performed for better characterization and revealed a partially cystic soft tissue mass in the left mid abdomen measuring 3.6 cm × 4.4 cm × 4.8 cm, along with at least 24 variably sized lesions in the liver. Genetic mutational analysis of her biopsied mass revealed very low levels of the c-KIT mutation on exon 9 [c.1504_1509dup (p.A502_Y503dup)] and negative mutations of D816V on exon 17 and PDGFRα. Immunohistochemical staining was notable for the presence of CD117, patchy staining for CD34, and negative staining for actin and desmin.

case_report: A 74-year-old male arrived at our rural district general hospital with severe upper abdominal pain that began one day prior. His medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, polycystic kidney disease, gout, vitamin B12 deficiency, and a hiatus hernia. He has undergone previous surgeries for an open inguinal hernia repair and an open repair of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm. Laboratory results showed a normal white cell count and a mildly elevated C-reactive protein level of 22 mg/dL. Liver function tests and serum amylase levels were within normal ranges. An abdominal CT scan with contrast was performed, which did not identify the cause of his symptoms but revealed a dilated fusiform appendix measuring 2.2 cm × 2.2 cm. There were no signs of appendicitis, appendiceal faecoliths, or metastases, and no focal lymphadenopathy was observed. A follow-up CT scan of the thorax confirmed the absence of pulmonary metastasis.
test_results: Pathological examination confirmed complete resection of a mitotically inactive spindle cell tumour measuring 1.5 cm in maximum dimension. CD34, CD117, and DOG1 testing were positive. Ki-67 was <1%.
diagnosis: Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumor  of the Appendix

case_report: A 22-month-old boy was admitted to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit in June 2010 with recurrent partial seizures affecting the right side of his body. The patient had been experiencing cough and intermittent fever for a month, which did not improve with oral antibiotics. His medical history included developmental delay, poor weight gain, and recurrent oral candidiasis since he was 4 months old. Investigations for metabolic, immunologic, and endocrine disorders were inconclusive. Two weeks prior to admission, the infant developed right hemiparesis due to a stroke, resulting in an inability to sit independently. He was the first child of consanguineous parents, born at 32 weeks of gestation with a birth weight of 2300 grams. Upon admission, physical examination revealed severe hypertension (160/100 mmHg), significant hepatomegaly, and right hemiparesis. Laboratory findings included a WBC count of 9400/mm3 with 82% segmented cells, hemoglobin of 9.7 g/dl, MCV of 69 fl, and normal platelet count. Serum biochemistry was normal except for mildly elevated liver enzymes. LDH level was 1056 IU/L, prothrombotic factors were normal, and Alfa-Feto Protein (AFP) was 446.3 IU/ml (normal: up to 5.5 IU/ml). Vanilmandelic Acid (VMA) and Homovanillic Acid (HVA) in 24-hour urine were normal in two separate measurements. Cortisol, metanephrine, normetanephrine, epinephrine, and norepinephrine in 24-hour urine were also normal. Abdominal sonography revealed multiple solid and isoechoic masses in both liver lobes, confirmed by abdominal CT scan. Chest CT scan showed pneumonia. Brain MRI indicated gliosis in the medial portions of the biparietal lobes and left occipital lobe due to a previous vascular event. Echocardiography ruled out coarctation and other heart diseases. Renal function tests were normal, and Doppler sonography did not show renal artery stenosis. Plasma renin activity was markedly increased (200 miclu/ml, normal level up to 46.1), while plasma aldosterone levels were normal. Bone marrow aspiration was normal. Hypertension and seizures were subsequently controlled, but pneumonia progressed despite various antibiotic and antifungal therapies. The patient required assisted ventilation due to respiratory distress and decreased consciousness. His overall condition deteriorated despite supportive therapy.
test_results: Histological examination of the tumor showed sheets of small, round, uniform cells with moderate amount of eosinophilic or clear cytoplasm, and distinct cytoplasmic membranes. The cells arranged into these trabeculae, usually two or three cells thick, with alternating light and dark areas.

case_report: A 47-year-old female with a history of uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency department with complaints of shortness of breath, subjective fever, night sweats for 7 days, and a productive cough with yellowish sputum. She also reported left-sided chest swelling that had been increasing in size over the past week, without redness or discharge. There was no history of anorexia or weight loss. On examination, she was vitally stable and afebrile. The patient had a history of contact with a TB patient. Initial imaging studies showed obliteration of the left costophrenic angle and left lower lobe opacification. Laboratory results revealed leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 17 (10∗9/L) and a C-reactive protein level of 257 mg/dL. Kidney function tests showed creatinine at 50 μmol/L, platelets at 445 (10∗9/L), alanine transaminase at 10.3 U/L, aspartate transaminase at 19.5 U/L, and HbA1c at 14.8%. Physical examination revealed a bronchial breathing pattern in the left lower lobe and normal breath sounds in the right lung with no additional sounds. A palpable, fluctuant collection was noted on the left side of the chest wall, overlaying the 6th to 8th ribs along the axillary line. The collection was soft, exhibited crepitations upon palpation, and showed retractability after reduction. The skin over the swelling was intact with no erythema or pus discharge. Treatment for community-acquired pneumonia was initiated, including intravenous ceftriaxone, intravenous azithromycin, and intravenous acetaminophen for pain control. Eight acid-fast bacillus sputum samples and three TB polymerase chain reaction (TB-PCR) samples were collected and returned negative after three days. The patient showed significant improvement with intravenous antibiotics.
test_results: The CT scan showed patency of trachea and major airways with bilateral ground-glass opacities and consolidation with atelectasis involving the left lower lobe. In addition, a loculated left-sided heterogeneous pleural effusion with internal air foci extends throughout the chest wall with clear area of communication. Drained fluids were sent for TB-PCR, acid-fast bacillus culture, culture, and sensitivity and pleural fluid analysis for microscopic examination; and the results were negative for Mycobacterium with culture being positive for Klebsiella pneumoniae sensitive to fluoroquinolones.

case_report: A 31-year-old male reported experiencing repeated episodes of rotational vertigo lasting several hours over the past four years (since September 2017). These episodes were accompanied by nausea and vomiting, but there was no tinnitus or hearing loss during these attacks. Starting in June 2018, the patient began to experience fluctuating tinnitus and sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear, along with vertigo and a sensation of fullness in the ear. These episodes occurred two to three times a week and lasted between 15 minutes and 2 hours. His medical history was otherwise unremarkable, with no family history of dizziness or autoimmune disease.
test_results: The caloric test showed left horizontal semicircular canal paresis (CP = 79%). No obvious abnormality was found in the electrocochleogram. No frequency of the left ear was elicited by distortion product otoacoustic emissions (DPOAE). Ocular vestibular evoked myogenic potential (oVEMP) showed prolonged latency and low amplitude on the left-sided ear. A lower amplitude on the left side was observed by cervical vestibular evoked myogenic potential (cVEMP).

case_report: A 74-year-old woman with left eye amblyopia and no other significant medical history reported experiencing two or more spontaneous episodes of vertigo, each lasting between 20 minutes to 12 hours. She had low to medium frequency sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear on at least one occasion, along with fluctuating aural symptoms such as hearing changes, tinnitus, and fullness in the right ear. Over the past 5 years, she experienced fluctuating low and mid-frequency hearing loss with mild sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear (PTA 40 dB-HL), while her left ear maintained normal hearing (PTA 20 dB-HL). The fluctuating hearing loss in the right ear was accompanied by recurrent vertigo attacks lasting 30 to 60 minutes, along with tinnitus and fullness in the right ear, occurring monthly before treatment. Vertigo attacks were well-controlled with Betahistine (16 mg every 8 hours) and four doses of intratympanic Dexamethasone (1.5 ml with a dilution of 15 mg/ml) administered to the right ear on two occasions (2017 and 2019). At the most recent consultation, she reported occasional vertigo attacks with mild instability that did not interfere with daily activities. Cerebral and posterior fossa magnetic resonance imaging showed no abnormalities, and no other general or neurological symptoms were noted during the 5-year period. Physical examination revealed normal bilateral otoscopy and normal smooth pursuit during bedside testing. Horizontal head impulse testing showed corrective saccades when her head was turned to the right side, but no corrective saccades for leftward head impulses.
test_results: During rightwards head impulses the patient had enhanced slow phase eye velocity (i.e., with eye velocity greater than head velocity, so VOR gains for the right were >1). The measured VOR gain for rightward impulses was 1.17, and for leftward impulses was 0.89. This patient also showed backup saccades during rightward head movements in low frequency visual vestibular (VVOR) testing at a frequency of 1.84 Hz. The measured VOR gain on the right side was 1.07 and 0.91 on the left.

case_report: A male patient aged between 55 and 60 years reported experiencing episodes of vertigo and tinnitus over a period of 3 years. The patient was on a daily dose of 4 mg silodosin for benign prostate hyperplasia. Each vertigo episode lasted approximately 30 minutes and was associated with nausea, vomiting, and tinnitus in the right ear. These episodes frequently occurred during sexual intercourse and physical activities such as jogging and swimming. Physical examination revealed no spontaneous, gaze-evoked, or positional nystagmus. However, left-beating nystagmus was observed following horizontal head-shaking and during vibratory stimuli applied to either mastoid or brow.
test_results: PTA documented fluctuating right sensorineural hearing loss especially involving the low-frequency with a pure tone average of 55 dB. The results of bithermal caloric tests, cervical and ocular VEMPs were normal. Brain MRIs taken elsewhere were normal.

case_report: A 49-year-old Asian man with no significant medical history presented to our hospital with a chief complaint of dyspnea on exertion that had appeared approximately 10 days before presentation. Vital signs were normal, except for tachycardia; further, S3 heart sounds were heard upon auscultation, and his lower legs were warm with mild edema. Blood test results indicated mild anemia, elevated creatinine level, and elevated brain natriuretic peptide level (195.5 pg/mL; normal range 0.0–18.4 pg/mL), and radiography showed mild cardiomegaly and bilateral pleural effusions. An electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia with a heart rate of 100 b.p.m., and echocardiography revealed left ventricular hyperkinesis (ejection fraction 73%) and enlargement of the inferior vena cava (IVC), but without evidence of diastolic dysfunction or structural abnormalities. Diuretics were started. On the 19th day after symptom onset, he was admitted to our hospital because of worsening heart failure despite increased urine output. Right heart catheterization performed on the day of admission showed a marked increase in cardiac output (cardiac index: 9.7 L/min/min) and a marked decrease in systemic vascular resistance (6.4 WU). Oxygen saturation test showed no evidence of intracardiac shunting. However, blood oxygen saturation in both the superior vena cava and IVC was high (85.8% and 84.8%, respectively). No findings of hyperthyroidism, severe anemia, sepsis, vitamin B1 deficiency, or obesity were observed on investigating the cause of the high-output state.
