Although diuretics were administered, heart failure and organ damage continued to progress, and systemic vascular resistance measured by Swan–Ganz catheter continued to decrease despite the administration of noradrenaline and vasopressin. Arteriography and blood gas tests of the iliac region were performed to investigate the presence of extracardiac shunts. Immediately after applying the contrast agent (iopamidol) from the iliac artery onwards, the ilium, sacrum, pubis, femoral neck, and femur on the same side absorbed it, and the iliac vein and IVC were immediately perfused with iopamidol. In addition, there was a significant O2 step-up between the common femoral vein and common iliac vein on both sides.
test_results: Atypical lymphocytes were detected in the peripheral blood for the first time on the day after admission (Day 20), and their count continued to increase thereafter. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pelvic lesion showed extensive bone involvement of tumour cells.

case_report: A 50-year-old man, with no prior medical history, was admitted to the hospital presenting with shortness of breath and upper abdominal pain. His heart rate was recorded at 130 beats per minute and blood pressure at 110/60 mmHg. Physical examination revealed significantly distended jugular veins and a gallop rhythm. A chest X-ray identified pleural effusion, which was confirmed to be exudative through laboratory analysis and showed no abnormal cells. An electrocardiogram indicated sinus tachycardia without changes in the QRS complex, ST segment, or T waves. Spiral CT scan ruled out pulmonary embolism. Echocardiography demonstrated a high cardiac index of 12 L/min/m2, with no signs of pericardial or ventricular dysfunction (left ventricular ejection fraction of 75%) and no evidence suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis. Cardiac catheterization also indicated a high output cardiac state (12 L/min/m2). Laboratory results showed hemoglobin at 9.8 g/dL, white blood cell count at 18,000/mm3, platelet count at 68,000/mm3, creatinine at 136 µmol/L, calcium serum level at 2.62 mmol/L, and elevated LDH levels.
test_results: Peripheral blood contained 35% of plasma cells. A monoclonal immunoglobulin G (IgG) kappa gammopathy (7.4 g/L) was detected. The percentage of plasma cells in bone marrow analysis was 19%. Chromosome 13 deletion was found on cytogenetic analysis. Immunophenotypic study revealed a CD38, CD138 positive staining, and CD19, CD20 and CD56 negative staining.

case_report: A 55-year-old postmenopausal female presented with an abdominal mass persisting for 2 years and recent onset of pain for 2 days. There was no history of vaginal bleeding and no clinical signs of virilization. Physical examination revealed a tender mass in the left hypogastric and iliac fossa. Ultrasonography identified a multicystic lesion measuring 12 cm × 11 cm in the left ovary. During surgery, the left ovarian cyst was found to be twisted with a ruptured cyst wall. A total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy was performed. Gross examination of the ovary showed it weighed 550 g and measured 13 cm × 11 cm × 7 cm, with both solid and cystic areas on the cut section. Microscopic examination revealed round to solid tubules lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium with elongated nuclei, along with conventional endometrioid tumor patterns. The utero-cervix and the rest of the adnexa appeared normal.
test_results: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) showed tumor cells strongly immunoreactive for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), cytokeratin (CK) but negative for inhibin.
diagnosis: Sertoliform Endometrioid Tumor  of the ovary

case_report: A 65-year-old woman with no family history of cancer experienced sudden abdominal pain and visited the emergency department. Ultrasound examination revealed a high echoic right ovarian multilocular mass measuring 83 × 57 × 78 mm, containing ground glass content and a few endoluminal papillae, with moderate vascularization observed on color Doppler. Laboratory results showed elevated CA 125 levels at 127 U/mL. During surgery, intraoperative frozen sections identified a carcinoma with a solid growth pattern. The patient underwent a hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, omentectomy, and peritoneal biopsies via laparoscopy, and the ovarian mass was removed using in-bag morcellation.
test_results: Histological examination revealed a solid carcinoma characterized by high-grade basaloid cells with areas of necrosis and diffuse ghost cell keratinization, which extended beyond the ovary and infiltrated the fallopian tube. The carcinoma showed a minor low-grade endometrioid component and appeared to arise in a borderline seromucinous tumors. Several keratin granulomas were observed in the surrounding tissues. Immunohistochemically, the tumor showed diffuse nuclear expression of β-catenin and CDX2. Neuroendocrine markers chromogranin and synaptophysin were focally expressed, while Müllerian markers PAX8, estrogen receptor, and progesterone receptor were completely negative. The tumor was positive for cytokeratin 7, while p63 was focally expressed. Mismatch repair proteins expression were preserved, and p53 expression was wild-type. Molecular analysis showed mutations in CCDN1, CTNNB1, ARID1A, and PIK3CA.
diagnosis: Pilomatrix-like High-Grade Endometrioid Carcinoma  of the ovary

case_report: A 50-year-old male presented with difficulty swallowing and a progressively enlarging, painless swelling in the left submandibular region over a period of 4 months. The mass had previously been drained and treated with a week-long course of narrow-spectrum antibiotics at an Ear Nose Throat clinic. Intraoral examination revealed a firm bulging of the left soft palate and left lateral pharyngeal wall, crossing the midline and displacing the uvula to the right, with smooth overlying mucosa. Digital palpation indicated that the left tonsil was firm. Despite the non-tender lesion causing significant difficulty swallowing, the patient reported no major complaints. He had no fever and did not experience throat soreness. The mass extended from the left side of the nasopharynx to the oropharynx, pushing the left tonsil towards the midline of the oropharynx. Externally, there was noticeable swelling in the left submandibular region. Clinical examination showed no involvement of cranial nerves.
test_results: CT and MRI scan showed homogenously enhancing tumour measuring 5 × 4 cm in the left parapharyngeal space. Fine needle aspiration cytology of the mass in the neck was consistent with benign mixed tumour.
diagnosis: Pleomorphic Adenoma of the Parapharyngeal Space

case_report: A 47-year-old male experienced hematochezia following a gastrointestinal infection. A colonoscopy revealed 23 polyps, with three located in the caecum and the remainder in the left colon. Polypectomy was conducted, and pathology of eight polyps indicated six tubular adenomas with low to moderate dysplasia and two tubulovillous adenomas, one of which exhibited severe dysplasia. The largest adenoma measured 20 mm × 8 mm × 15 mm. The patient had no family history of colonic adenomas or cancer, and no genetic testing was performed. The patient was placed under routine screening, and over a 10-year period (2007–2017), annual colonoscopic polypectomies removed approximately 40 polyps, with around eighty percent being adenomas. In June 2018, at age 58, a colonoscopy identified and removed 55 new polyps that had developed over the previous 6 months. Pathology described four of the five polyps as adenomas, with the remaining polyp identified as a sessile serrated polyp. The most recent colonoscopy in December 2018 revealed 20 polyps, all of which were tubular adenomas with low dysplasia. To date, the patient has developed 133 polyps and has declined a recommended colectomy.
test_results: A homozygous nonsense variant (NM_002528):c.268C>T, p. Gln90Ter in the NTHL1 gene was identified. No alterations were found in the other examined genes.

case_report: A 55-year-old woman from northeast China, born to non-consanguineous parents, presented with a gradually enlarging erythematous plaque on her face over the past 30 years. At 23 years old, she noticed several red papules on her forehead, which expanded over time with occasional itching but no pain. She was treated with itraconazole 400 mg/day for approximately 1.5 years following a diagnosis at a local hospital. Despite treatment, the skin lesions enlarged and spread to her forehead, cheek, and eyelid. Dermatological examination showed a protuberant dark red mass on her face with erosion, crust, and pus, covering the forehead and cheek with a clear boundary.
test_results: A skin biopsy from the lesion showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia of the epidermis and intense dermal inflammatory infiltrations with the presence of multiple sclerotic cells within the dermis. A smear of the lesion scrapings showed brown sclerotic cells with cross septa. Cultures of the biopsied tissue specimens showed filamentous fungus, whose colony was dense, brown to black after 21 days on potato dextrose agar at 28 °C. Further microscopic examination of the cultured organisms revealed vase-shaped sporogenous cells with collar-like structures and flower-like arrangements of small conidia, which implied it belongs to Phialophora spp. We sequenced the ITS and BT2 rRNA genes using PCR. We constructed the phylogenetic tree based on ITS and BT2 and found this species belonged to the P. expanda clade.
diagnosis: chromoblastomycosis caused by Phialophora expanda with CARD9 deficiency
Orpha_name: Predisposition to invasive fungal disease due to CARD9 deficiency

case_report: A 62-year-old man with a 45-day history of generalized itching since February 2017 presented to the medical department. He had previously been treated with antihistamines and emollient cream for 20 days without complete relief. He did not smoke or consume alcohol and had a history of hypertension. Physical examination revealed slight scratch marks but no other notable findings. Blood tests showed normal erythrocyte, leukocyte, and platelet counts. Urinalysis and chest radiography were unremarkable. There was no evidence of renal or thyroid dysfunction, and liver chemistry was normal. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 35 mm/h. A color duplex sonography of the abdomen revealed a large hypervascular, low-level echo, heterogeneous mass in the right kidney. An intravenous pyelogram showed irregularity of the margin of the right renal calices. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a heterogeneous mass originating from the upper pole of the right kidney and infiltrating the renal calices. Helical CT angiography (CTA) demonstrated a right renal tumor with a tumor thrombus in the right renal vein that did not extend into the inferior vena cava (IVC). Further evaluation, including a bone scan, did not show any evidence of metastases.
test_results: Microscopy revealed that the mass consisted of nests and cords of cells separated by fine, arborizing fibrovascular septa. The collagenous material intermingled among tumor cells, which were cuboidal or polygonal in shape. The nuclei were optically clear with fine chromatin and round to oval in shape, lacked prominent nucleoli, and exhibited infrequent mitosis. There was necrosis in the tumor. Microtumor thrombi were present in small vessels of the tumor. The histopathologic characteristics of the tumor thrombus in the renal vein were the same as those of the tumor in the kidney. Silver staining demonstrated reticular fibers often outlining individual tumor cells. With immunostaining, tumor cells were positive for expressed vimentin, neural cell adhesion molecule (NCAM, CD56), and Ki-67 and focally positive for p53, Bcl-2 and CD10. Immunostaining for alpha B-crystallin, alpha-smooth muscle actin, CAM5.2, CD34, chromogranin (Chr), Cytokeratin7, M2A oncofetal antigen (D2–40), Desmin, epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), hemopoietic cell kinase (HCK), neuron specific enolase (NSE), P63, renal cell carcinoma marker (RCC-Ma), S100, Wilms’ tumor 1 (WT1), CD57 and CD15 were negative. A prominent vascular network with positive reactivity for CD34 was found in the tumor. RCC-Ma was positive in the luminal surface of Bowman’s capsule adjoining the tumor. EMA and CAM5.2 were expressed in renal tubules adjoining the tumor.
diagnosis: Clear cell sarcoma of the kidney

case_report: A forty-three-year-old female patient presented with an ulcerated lesion on the left lateral edge of the tongue, extending to the floor of the mouth, with a duration of seven months. Chest CT scans showed no abnormal findings. The patient has a history of smoking (7 cigarettes per day) but no history of long-term alcohol abuse. Clinical examination revealed an endophytic tumor on the left lateral edge of the tongue, spreading to the tongue, retromolar base, and trigone. The lesion was categorized as T4a N1 M0.
test_results: The neck CT confirmed the existence of a nodule on the floor of the mouth; also some submental and left jugular lymphs were observed. An incisional biopsy whose histopathological study showed an infiltrating, nonkeratinized moderately differentiated OSCC was carried out. A second biopsy was taken from the tumor and microscopical exam revealed a carcinoma with two neoplastic cellular components, on one hand a proliferation of atypical spindle cells and on the other hand nests of squamous epithelial cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and atypical mitosis. The studies with IHC revealed that vimentin was strongly positive in the component of spindle cell as in epithelial cells. Cytokeratin AE1/AE3 was strongly positive in epithelial cells and focally positive in spindle cells. EMA antigen was positive for epithelial neoplastic cells and a weak expression in the spindle component was observed. Both neoplasia components were negative for desmin, S-100, and smooth muscle actin alpha.
Orpha_name: Squamous cell carcinoma of the oral tongue

case_report: A 62-year-old man, who chews tobacco, presented with a polypoidal growth at the tip of the tongue for four months. He has a history of a growth on the right lateral border of the tongue four years ago, which was treated with wide local excision and primary closure of the defect, along with right supra-omohyoid neck dissection. The final evaluation at that time showed well-differentiated features with clear margins, and no additional therapy was given. On current examination, a 5 cm × 5 cm polypoidal growth with a 1 cm stalk was observed at the tip of the tongue, located more than 2 cm away from the previous surgery scar. No cervical lymph nodes were palpable.
test_results: The punch biopsy was suggestive of a poorly differentiated malignant tumor. Histopathological examination revealed a 6.5 cm × 4.0 cm × 3.0 cm polypoidal growth with a stalk. The external surface was lobulated with cleft-like spaces. The cut section showed a solid grayish-white surface with a variegated appearance with focal areas of haemorrhage with no necrosis. The distance between the tumour and the stalk margin was 8 mm, and the stalk margin was free of tumor. Microscopic examination showed extensive areas of surface ulceration with granulation tissue along with sub epithelium showing oval to elongated moderately pleomorphic cells arranged in a herringbone pattern and short and long fascicles. Cells showed scanty cytoplasm, coarsely clumped chromatin, and one to two prominent nucleoli. The tumour cells were immunopositive for CK (membranous) and focally positive for p40 (nuclear) and negative for EMA, CD34, BCL2, CK, and SMA. Fifteen nodes were identified in the neck dissection specimen, all free of tumor.
diagnosis: Spindle cell variant of squamous cell carcinoma  of the tongue
Orpha_name: Squamous cell carcinoma of the oral tongue

case_report: A 43-year-old woman was referred to our hospital due to an enlarged heart observed on a chest X-ray. Physical examinations showed a generally healthy appearance, though heart sounds were faint. Laboratory tests returned results within normal limits. The patient had no history of trauma, congenital heart disease, thoracic surgery, or tuberculosis. Transthoracic echocardiography identified a significant accumulation of fluid in the pericardial cavity without affecting blood flow dynamics.
test_results: Diagnostic pericardiocentesis was performed with 500 mL of a milky-colored pericardial fluid aspirated. Routine examination of the pericardial fluid revealed pH 6.8, protein 5.0 g/dL, and LDH 234 IU/L. WBCs and RBCs were uncountable due to cell clumping. Routine bacterial and tuberculous cultures were subsequently reported as negative, as was the cytological examination, and the adenosine deaminase level was 15.5 U/L. Repeated pericardiocentesis was performed, and an immediate gushing out of 700 mL of a milky-yellowish fluid ensued. An examination of the pericardial fluid showed pH 6.8, protein 7.0 g/dL, glucose 98 mg/dL, LDH 560 IU/L, cholesterol 97 mg/dL, and triglyceride 1078 mg/dL. RBCs and WBCs were uncountable due to cell clumping. The adenosine deaminase level was 17.0 U/L and the CEA level 1.15 ng/mL. Routine cultures for bacteria and tuberculosis were subsequently reported as negative and a cytologic examination showed no tumor cells.
diagnosis: Primary Idiopathic Chylopericardium Associated with Cervicomediastinal Cystic Hygroma

case_report: A 61-year-old male presented with painless gross hematuria persisting for two weeks. The patient has a history of hypertension for over a decade without systematic treatment. There is no notable personal or family medical history. Vital signs recorded were: temperature at 35.6 °C, heart rate at 80 bpm, respiratory rate at 20 breaths per minute, and blood pressure at 121/74 mmHg. Clinical urological examination revealed no abnormalities. Laboratory tests including routine blood examination, C-reactive protein test, routine stool examination, and liver and kidney function tests were within normal limits. Routine urine examination indicated a positive urine occult blood test (+++). Neoplastic markers (CA153, CA199, CEA, AFP, NSE, and CA125) were negative. Initial urinary ultrasonography identified a ureteral calculus at the distal end of the right ureter. Additionally, multiple masses originating from the retroperitoneum and pelvis were incidentally discovered.
test_results: The contrast-enhanced abdominal-pelvic CT revealed multiple well-defined hypodense cystic lesions arising from retroperitoneum and pelvic space without enhancement. The lesions grew along the peritoneal interstitial space, the pelvic wall, and external iliac vascular deformation area, some of which showed shaping and suture-like changes. The largest one was 3.3 cm × 2.5 cm. No uptake by the masses was observed on fused PET/CT images.

case_report: A one-and-a-half-year-old boy presented with widespread scaling across the entire body and redness on both cheeks. The child was born to parents who are related by blood, following a prolonged labor and a normal vaginal delivery. At birth, the baby weighed 2.3 kg and measured 36 cm in length. There was no history of a collodion membrane. Scaling began at 3 weeks of age, worsening in winter and improving in summer. Immunizations were up-to-date according to the schedule. There was no family history of similar conditions, no prior drug intake before the onset of scaling, and no history of atopic diathesis. Physical examination revealed fine white to brown scaling over the entire body, including the palms and soles, with a glistening surface and involvement of flexures. The scalp showed fine whitish-grey and grayish-brown scaling, with some areas of thick crusting that, when removed, revealed a moistened surface. Large grayish-brown scales were noted on the frontal scalp margin. Both cheeks were erythematous with scaling, and scales were also present on the upper eyelid, upper lips, and nose. Mild ectropion was observed, but there were no other eye abnormalities or signs of seborrheic blepharitis. The patient had left-sided cryptorchidism and was referred to pediatric surgery, with a recommendation to wait another 6 months before considering surgical intervention. Ophthalmological examination showed no abnormalities. Blood tests, chest X-ray, and urine examination were all normal.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed mild hyperkeratosis.

case_report: A 5-year-old boy (43 inches, 50th percentile, and 42 lbs, 50th percentile) visited Parkside Medical Group (Upland, CA) for a neurological evaluation. His mother recalled previous blood tests and an amniocentesis suggesting intellectual disability, but these results were unavailable. Pregnancy and delivery were normal. At birth, he weighed 6 lbs 10 oz (20th percentile). He began walking at 14 months and said “mama” and “papa” at 8-9 months. In early childhood, he avoided other children and adhered to routines, becoming very angry when his favorite TV channel was changed. He spoke Spanish and some English, attended special education at a preschool level, and could count up to 100 but had difficulty focusing in school. He was diagnosed with ADHD and mild autism by a child psychologist six months prior and started on amphetamine-dextroamphetamine ER 10 mg daily, which improved his behavior at home and school, leading to increased participation in group activities. On examination, he had a high anterior hairline, triangular face, short chin, widely spaced eyes, prominent nasal bridge, and conical teeth. There were no corneal opacities or preauricular scales. He could answer questions about his name, age, and preferences but showed a lack of reciprocity and eye contact. He had no tics but was fidgety, could not wait his turn, wandered about, talked excessively in Spanish, and interrupted his parents. His Adderall XR was increased to 20 mg daily, but he became weepy and emotional, so the dose was lowered back to 10 mg daily. Seven months later, the dose was increased to 15 mg daily due to persistent ADHD symptoms. He was also treated for insomnia with guanfacine 0.5 mg at night. He had a history of asthma and was treated with budesonide 0.5 mg/2 mL suspension and montelukast 4 mg daily. Family history was unremarkable, with a healthy 11-year-old sister and no history of consanguinity. His EKG was normal. There was no history of seizures, and EEG was not performed due to lack of cooperation. Lab results were normal (cholesterol, TG, HDL, LDL, FSH, LH, TSH, ACTH, vitamin A, free retinol, and plac Lp PLA2) except for elevated human growth hormone (1.6 ng/ml; normal range 0.01–0.97 ng/ml). He tested negative for fragile X syndrome with 29 CGG repeats.
test_results: Chromosomal microarray (CMA), performed at the Mayo Clinic (Rochester, MN), demonstrated a 1.7 Mb deletion at Xp22.31, which included 6 genes; STS, pseudouridine 5′-phosphatase (PUDP), microRNA 4767 (MIR4767), variable charge, X-linked (VCX), patatin-like phospholipase domain containing 4 (PNPLA4), and microRNA 651 (MIR651).

case_report: A forty-six-year-old female arrived at the emergency department with a two-month history of headache and increasing numbness in her right leg. She also reported experiencing nausea and dizziness two weeks prior to admission. Her medical and family history were unremarkable. Upon admission, she appeared excitable and had a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 14 (E:4; V:4; M:6). Other vital signs were within normal limits. A general examination showed no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Neurological examination indicated numbness in the right lower limb without motor dysfunction, cranial neuropathy, or signs of increased intracranial pressure.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of her brain showed multifocal lesions scattered across the left occipital and parietal lobes; the largest one measured 16 mm in its transverse dimension. These lesions demonstrated a hypointense signal on the T1W sequence, a hyperintense signal on FLAIR, and no abnormal diffusion restriction on DWI images. They also revealed rim enhancement following gadolinium contrast injection. Microscopically, the lesions were composed of small lymphocytes and neoplasm cells with plasma cell morphological features. The immunohistochemical (IMH) test showed tumor cells are positive for CD79a, CD138, CD38, and MUM-1, but negative for CD3 and CD20.

case_report: A 35-year-old female with a history of diabetes mellitus was found to have a tumor incidentally discovered on imaging during a workup for a complicated urinary tract infection at a referral hospital 9 years ago. The patient did not seek any medical intervention following the discovery and remained asymptomatic until 5 months ago when she experienced an exacerbation of right flank pain, prompting further evaluation. The patient reported no history of anorexia or weight loss. Upon arrival at our hospital, she appeared well-nourished, in moderate pain, and exhibited no pallor or jaundice. Physical examination of the abdomen showed moderate tenderness in the right flank area without any palpable masses. Laboratory results were as follows: haemoglobin: 9.2 g/dl, leucocyte count: 6.24 × 10^9/L, haematocrit: 31.2%, and platelet count: 249 × 10^9/L. Liver function tests, renal function tests, and coagulation profiles were all within normal ranges. Hormonal profiles, including serum cortisol, aldosterone, metanephrine, normetanephrine, 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, adrenocorticotropic hormone, and renin, were also within normal ranges.
test_results: CT scan of abdomen and pelvis showed an interval increase in the size of the right adrenal mass (from 3 × 4.3 cm to 6 × 5 cm). CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed right adrenal mass measuring approximately 6 × 5 cm oval-shaped soft tissue mass lesion in the right adrenal gland. It showed fatty contents with thin internal septations. No definite invasion of adjacent organs was detected. No other masses were found.

case_report: A 5-month-old female with Fitzpatrick I skin presented with four vascular growths on the back of the neck, first observed within the initial weeks of life. These growths showed rapid enlargement over a 4-week span and limited the patient's neck mobility. She did not exhibit any neurological symptoms, such as seizures or abnormal muscle tone. The patient experienced a 10-second apnea episode during her first week of life and had wheezing until she reached a weight of 3.6 kg. She was born weighing 2.5 kg via emergency Caesarean section at 38 weeks due to stalled labor and being small for gestational age. She is otherwise healthy and has achieved normal developmental milestones. Examination of the back of the neck revealed a series of four 4–5 cm growths with a red-violaceous hue. The right lateral growth had multiple white papules measuring 1–3 mm. Above the umbilicus, there was a 0.4 cm round, protruding red-violaceous papule. None of the lesions showed ulceration. No sternal or umbilical raphe was observed.
test_results: MRI of the head, spine and thorax showed four superficial and deep lesions involving the posterior neck, bilateral carotid spaces and extending to the prevertebral/retropharyngeal space. No evidence of posterior fossa abnormalities and no anomalies of the aortic arch. Foetal origin of bilateral cerebral arteries with some tortuosity, but no evidence of aneurysm.

case_report: A 68-year-old man was referred to our hospital in January 2011. During a regular medical checkup in December 2010, a protruding mass was found at the gastric angle by simple upper gastrointestinal endoscopic examination. Endoscopic biopsy of the mass revealed chronic gastritis. Initially, the patient's vital signs were stable with blood pressure and body temperature within normal limits. The patient was a nonsmoker and on medication for benign prostatic hyperplasia. He reported persistent mild dyspepsia for a considerable period. Laboratory examination showed a hemoglobin level of 12.15 g/dl, a platelet count of 195,000/mm3, an albumin level of 4.1 g/dl, a blood urea nitrogen level of 18.4 mg/dl, a creatinine level of 0.99 mg/dl, an aspartate transaminase level of 18 IU/L, an alanine transaminase level of 16 IU/L, a glucose level of 119 mg/dl, a CEA level of 8.54 ng/ml, a cancer antigen 19-9 level of 24.07 U/ml, and a partial thromboplastin time/activated partial thromboplastin time of 10.7/33.8 seconds. There were no specific abnormal findings except for negligible anemia and an increased CEA level. Normal active bowel sounds were heard, and there was no palpable mass or tenderness on physical examination.
test_results: A Borrmann type II AGC-like protruding mass had been found at the gastric angle by simple upper gastrointestinal endoscopic examination in December 2010. Endoscopic biopsy of the mass revealed only chronic gastritis. A second upper gastrointestinal endoscopy examination was performed to confirm the lesion in January 2011. A large protruding ulcerative mass originating from the submucosa at the anterior wall of the lower body of the stomach and a small raised erosion at the cardia were observed. Histopathological diagnosis of a specimen from each lesion was of chronic active gastritis with intestinal metaplasia. Radiological findings via CT revealed a 4.8×1.7 cm sized submucosal gastric tumor with central ulceration involving the lesser curvature of the lower body of the stomach. There was no evidence of metastasis in any other organs.

case_report: A 38-year-old female, at the 21st week of her first pregnancy, was admitted to the hospital with symptoms of abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and weight loss. She had no prior history of liver disease or gastrointestinal issues. Laboratory tests indicated anemia and elevated C-reactive protein levels. Abdominal ultrasonography identified ascites, grade II hydronephrosis, and fluid in the pleural cavities. Magnetic resonance imaging showed thickening of the gastric wall, enlarged perigastric lymph nodes, and ascites.
test_results: Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed an infiltrative ulcerated tumor in the lesser curvature of the stomach ~ 4 cm in size. Serum AFP level was elevated to 79,6 kU/l (normal range 0,5–5,5kU/l). Biopsy revealed an ulcerated tumor infiltrating lamina propria and the submucosal tissue. The tumor stained positively for cytokeratins (PanCK 100%/CK7 80%/CK20 30%), CDX2 (50%), HepPar-1 (15%) and AFP (10%). Positivity for E-cadherin, SMAD4, PMS2/MSH6 was retained, scattered Synaptophysin positive cells were seen. WT1, S100, HER2 reactions, H. pylori test were negative. Tumor DNA was sequenced using AmpliSeq for Illumina Cancer Hotspot NGS panel. The data analysis revealed two somatic mutations in the PIK3CA gene: c.1023_1024insTACT (p.Thr342TyrfsTer12) and c.1025_1026insTA (p.Tyr343ThrfsTer3). Both mutations were located in exon 20 of PIK3CA gene and resulted in an early stop codon.

case_report: An 84-year-old man visited the Neurology clinic due to worsening symptoms of restless legs syndrome (RLS) that did not improve with a total daily dose of 4 mg ropinirole. He had been initially prescribed 0.5 mg ropinirole nightly by his primary care provider (PCP) about 4 years earlier, which had initially improved his symptoms significantly. However, over the past year, his symptoms worsened and began occurring earlier in the day. His ropinirole dosage was increased to 2 mg during the day and 2 mg at night, but this provided only minimal relief. His medical history included major depressive disorder managed with sertraline and a history of prostate cancer diagnosed at age 65. He was a former smoker with a 40 pack-year history. Three months before his Neurology clinic visit, he was hospitalized for COVID-19 pneumonia, and his lab results at that time showed normocytic anemia with a hemoglobin (Hb) level of 8.0 g/dL (normal range for men: 12.5–17 g/dL). His electronic health record indicated that his Hb was 12.1 g/dL the previous year and within normal range in the past 5 years. Serum iron studies had not been conducted previously. During the Neurology clinic visit, he described his legs as having a mind of their own, making it difficult to sleep. He was cognitively alert and fully oriented, with intact attention and concentration but impaired delayed recall. His cranial nerves were intact. He frequently walked around the room during the interview, but his neurological examination was otherwise normal. An MRI brain scan from a year prior showed scattered foci of T2 prolongation in the hemispheric white matter, consistent with chronic microvascular disease. Following the visit, iron studies were conducted, revealing a serum iron level of 15 μg/dL (normal range: 49–181 μg/dL), ferritin level of 8 ng/mL (normal range: 18–464 ng/mL), and normal transferrin levels. He was started on oral ferrous sulfate 324 mg daily, and his PCP was informed for further evaluation of iron deficiency anemia. One week later, during a follow-up with his PCP, he denied any gastrointestinal or other bleeding, weight change, poor appetite, nausea, vomiting, constipation, or diarrhea. He continued to experience severe RLS symptoms. His repeat Hb level improved to 11.1 g/dL from 8 g/dL after iron supplementation. He mentioned he had never undergone a colonoscopy for cancer screening and was strongly encouraged to do so.
test_results: His colonoscopy revealed a cecal polyp with high grade dysplasia. CT abdomen and pelvis showed no metastatic spread.

case_report: A 77-year-old right-handed male presented with a rash over the ulnar half of his left hand and forearm, extending to the posterior aspect of his left upper arm and behind the left shoulder. He experienced stabbing and burning pain in this area, with the rash blistering and then drying up over two weeks. One week after the rash appeared, he noticed weakness in his left hand, particularly affecting his grip and ability to pinch. This weakness was confined to the left hand and worsened over two weeks. Pain management required a high dose of gabapentin, and he was treated with famciclovir. His medical history includes hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and chronic obstructive airway disease. His medications are lisinopril, atorvastatin, and gabapentin. He has a history of smoking one pack per day, quitting in 1974. On examination, his blood pressure was 120/84, pulse 76 beats per minute, height six feet, weight 202 pounds, and BMI 27.4. Heart and carotid examinations were normal. His gait was stable, and he could stand on his heels and toes. Speech and cranial nerve examinations were normal. There was no evidence of Horner's syndrome. Muscle strength in the right upper and both lower extremities was 5/5. In the left upper extremity, deltoids, biceps, coracobrachialis, brachialis, triceps, and wrist extensors and flexors were 5/5, pronator teres was 5/5, flexor pollicis longus was 2/5, finger flexion at the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints was 3/5, abductor pollicis brevis was 3/5, and finger spreaders (interossei) were 2/5. Mild atrophy was observed in the left first dorsal interosseus, abductor pollicis brevis, and ulnar half of the left forearm. Sensory examination showed hyperesthesia to touch over the left C8 distribution. Weakness in the left flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum superficialis resulted in an inability to form the letter 'O' with the thumb and index finger. Atrophy was noted in the ulnar half of the left forearm and left hypothenars.
test_results: This demonstrated a reduced left median motor amplitude, markedly reduced left ulnar motor amplitude, normal left median sensory, and diminished left ulnar sensory amplitude. The left lateral antebrachial cutaneous sensory was preserved with an absent left medial antebrachial cutaneous sensory amplitude. Left radial motor and sensory amplitudes were normal. This combination of findings of abnormal left median and ulnar nerves, with absent left medial antebrachial cutaneous sensory amplitude and preserved median sensory amplitude, is highly suggestive of a left medial cord plexopathy. The lack of radial nerve involvement precludes the lower trunk of the brachial plexus; note normal left radial motor and sensory amplitudes, also noting that the median sensory nerve emerges from the lateral and not from the medial cord of the brachial plexus. It should be noted that the sensory and motor velocities and distal motor latencies of the left median and ulnar nerves were normal or slightly reduced and are not listed in the table. There was also no evidence of ulnar nerve entrapment at the left elbow. The reduced ulnar sensory amplitude with absent left medial antebrachial cutaneous sensory amplitude with preserved left lateral cutaneous antebrachial cutaneous and median sensory amplitudes are demonstrated graphically below. The electromyography (EMG) study reveals acute and florid denervation of the left median and ulnar innervated muscles of the hand and forearm, with the preservation of radial, axillary, and musculocutaneous nerves. Selected EMG of the involved muscles of the left hand and forearm reflecting the clinical pattern of weakness on examination; noting acute and florid denervation with fibrillation potentials and positive waves of involved muscles. One should also emphasize the absence of left lower paraspinal muscle denervation precluding cervical C8 motor nerve root involvement. However, cervical C8 sensory nerve root involvement is not excluded, as the rash extends beyond the territory of the ulnar sensory and medial antebrachial cutaneous sensory nerves, to behind the left upper arm and left shoulder.

case_report: A 34-year-old female presented with a primary complaint of rapid vision loss in the right eye over three months. Her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was counting fingers near face in the right eye and 6/9 in the left eye. She reported bilateral eye protrusion, more pronounced in the left eye, persisting for 11 years. The patient had a history of primary hyperthyroidism diagnosed at age 22 and was prescribed carbimazole 20 mg twice daily but was non-compliant. Three years later, she noticed neck swelling and increased eye protrusion, more on the left side, which gradually worsened over 12 years. She received intravenous methylprednisolone thrice for increasing proptosis but did not adhere to the treatment regimen. Upon presentation, her BCVA in the right eye had deteriorated from 6/9 to counting fingers near face over three months. Detailed examination revealed that color vision and contrast sensitivity could not be assessed in the right eye due to poor vision, while the left eye had normal color vision and 6% contrast sensitivity. Intraocular pressure (IOP) measured with a Perkins applanation tonometer was 12 mmHg in the right eye and 11 mmHg in the left eye in straight gaze, increasing to 27 mmHg in the right eye and 19 mmHg in the left eye in up gaze. Hertel’s exophthalmometer readings showed 25 mm in the right eye and 27 mm in the left eye, up from previous values of 25 mm and 21 mm, respectively, over the past three months. The palpebral fissure height was 16 mm in the right eye and 18 mm in the left eye. Extra-ocular movements were restricted in all gazes, more so in the right eye. Examination also revealed Mobius sign, Von Graefe’s sign, Dalrymple’s sign, and Enroth sign. The right eye pupil had a sluggish and ill-sustained reaction to light, while the left eye pupil responded briskly. The rest of the anterior segment was unremarkable. The clinical activity score (CAS) was more than four, with eyelid swelling, conjunctival redness, increased proptosis of more than 2 mm, and a decrease in visual acuity of more than 1 Snellen line. Humphrey visual field analysis in the left eye showed peripheral visual field constriction; it was not performed in the right eye due to poor vision.
test_results: The CT scan of the orbit revealed significant changes in muscle thickness of both eyes. The superior rectus muscle of the right eye exhibited a substantial 25% increase from the normal reference range, which was followed by growth in other muscles as follows: the inferior rectus by 19%, the lateral rectus by 15%, and the medial rectus by 11%. Similarly, the left eye displayed a significant 23% enlargement in the inferior rectus, leading to subsequent growth in other muscles as follows: the superior rectus by 18%, the medial rectus by 15%, and the lateral rectus by 12%. Apart from this, both eyes showed hypertrophy of the levator palpebrae superioris and oblique muscles. All the muscles had thickening of the belly with sparing of their tendinous insertions. Also seen was retro-orbital fat stranding.

case_report: A 68-year-old male presented in May 2006 with a visible protrusion under the lateral part of his mildly swollen right upper eyelid and occasional double vision. The protrusion had a yellowish purple color and was soft and non-tender to touch. Examination showed retraction of the upper eyelid and limited upward movement in the right eye. Laboratory tests indicated normal thyroid function with a borderline increase in anti-TSH receptor antibodies: 8.8 (normal <9, sensitivity 0.8).
test_results: An orbit MRI outlined anterior herniation of intraorbital fat with slight displacement of the lacrimal gland temporally in the involved right orbit as opposed to normal appearance of the lacrimal gland on the left side.

case_report: A 28-year-old female patient was admitted to N. N. Blokhin National Medical Research Center of Oncology in June 2016 after being referred from another hospital for further evaluation and treatment of multiple renal cell tumors. The patient provided informed consent for diagnostic procedures, treatment, and participation in the study, including the presentation of clinical and molecular data. This case report received approval from the local Ethics Committee at Sechenov University. According to medical records, the patient had a pituitary adenoma with endo-, supra-, infra-, and latero-sellar growth and partial descending optic atrophy on the left side in 2012. Clinical manifestations at that time included broadening of the feet and fingers, increased sweating, cysts and diffuse changes in the thyroid gland, and elevated growth hormone levels. The pituitary adenoma was partially removed via endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery in 2012, followed by treatment with somatostatin analogs. During a follow-up examination in 2016, no recurrence of the pituitary adenoma was detected, and the patient was advised to continue treatment with somatostatin analog (octreotide depot) 20 mg intramuscularly every 28 days, along with bromocriptine 2.5 mg per day. Concurrently, multiple neoplasms were identified in both kidneys. The patient's family history was negative for oncological diseases at a young age or other signs of known cancer syndromes. At the time of hospitalization, neither the patient's parents nor her child exhibited cancer symptoms.
test_results: Computed tomography with intravenous contrast detected three 1–2 cm tumor lesions with the active accumulation of the contrast agent in the right kidney. In the left kidney, there were four tumor lesions: a 3.5 × 3.0-cm mostly cystic tumor with a soft-tissue component, with parietal accumulation of the contrast dye in the middle one-third portion; a tumor with a diameter of 1.3 cm at the upper pole; a tumor with a diameter of 1 cm in a subcapsular location in the middle one-third; and a tumor of 1.3 cm in diameter at the lower pole; these tumors similarly accumulated the contrast dye.
diagnosis: Hereditary Papillary Renal Cell Carcinoma Type I

case_report: A 51-year-old male patient, with no family history of renal cell carcinoma, underwent computed tomography for hypertension evaluation, which identified multiple tumors in both kidneys. Initially, eight partial renal tumorectomies were performed on the left kidney. Post-surgery, biannual magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was conducted for the right kidney as part of an active surveillance strategy. Two years later, MRI showed growth in the right kidney tumors, leading to a second surgery with five renal tumorectomies. During follow-up, the patient had a left adrenalectomy due to metastasis. Since then, the kidney nodules have remained stable, allowing for annual radiological assessments without additional therapy. The tumors in the left kidney ranged from 0.1 cm to 4 cm in diameter, while those in the right kidney ranged from 0.1 cm to 2.5 cm.
test_results: Absence of germline FLCN mutation. A germline MET mutation c.3712G > A, p.(Val1238Ile) was found, but no VHL germline mutation.
diagnosis: Hereditary Papillary Renal Cell Carcinoma  Syndrome

case_report: A one-year-old caucasian female presented with severe normocytic anemia, without hemodynamic instability. Since three months of age, she experienced hematochezia while exclusively breastfed. This was initially managed with a maternal diet free of milk and derivatives, but symptoms persisted despite a dairy-free diet during weaning. Upon admission, anemia was suspected to be due to gastrointestinal bleeding. Colonoscopy revealed colonic lymphoid nodular hyperplasia with ulcerated and bleeding mucosa. Histological examination showed active colitis without chronic features. Intravenous steroid therapy (methylprednisolone 2 mg/kg daily) was initiated during hospitalization, followed by oral steroid therapy (betamethasone 0.2 mg/kg daily) upon discharge. Oral iron supplementation was also started due to low hemoglobin levels, and a gastroenterological follow-up was scheduled. Two weeks later, during steroid withdrawal, she presented to the Emergency Room with acute panniculitis of the limbs, normal vital signs, and no significant abnormalities on cardiovascular, thoracic, and abdominal examination. Anti-inflammatory therapy was prescribed. Within 48 hours, her skin condition worsened, and she developed fever and painful edema of the limbs with ulcerative and necrotic lesions. She was hospitalized again, and intravenous steroid therapy was resumed. Blood tests indicated elevated inflammation markers (WBC 35,000/µl with neutrophil predominance, CRP 28 mg/dl, serum amyloid 100 mg/L), while tests for infectious and neoplastic conditions were negative. First-level autoimmune tests (VES, complement system, immunoglobulins, TNF, lymphocyte subpopulations, ASCA, and ANCA antibodies) were normal. Skin biopsy showed leukocyte exocytosis in the epidermis and histiocytic and lymphocytic inflammation in the dermis. Eye examination was negative for uveitis. Fecal occult blood tests were positive in three samples, and fecal calprotectin was elevated (>1,000 µg/g). IFN signature was normal, and ADA-2 deficiency was excluded. Considering the laboratory results and early-onset gastrointestinal symptoms, blood tests were performed, but genetic studies were negative. The patient had a family history of autoimmune conditions on the paternal side, including her father with recurrent oral aphthosis, vitiligo, and thyroiditis; her father's brother with recurrent oral aphthosis and vitiligo; a paternal grandfather with early-onset liver disease; a paternal great-uncle who died at 16 from an unknown disease; and another paternal great-uncle with Crohn's disease.
test_results: We identified a heterozygous variant in TNFAIP3, namely NM_006290.4:c.460G > T, resulting in a premature stop codon p.(Glu154Ter). Additionally, a heterozygous known risk allele in TNFRSF13B, NM_012452.3:c.204dupA, p.(Leu69ThrfsTer12), was identified.

case_report: The patient is a 2-year and 3-month-old girl admitted with a history of recurrent fever, diarrhea, and vomiting persisting for over two years. Her mother experienced no complications during pregnancy and delivery. At three months old, the child began experiencing recurrent episodes of fever, diarrhea, and vomiting, each lasting 1 to 2 weeks with intervals of 1 to 5 months, totaling 11 episodes to date. During these episodes, elevated levels of procalcitonin (PCT), C-reactive protein (CRP), and white blood cell (WBC) count were observed, along with numerous WBCs in the stool. She received cephalosporin treatment for about a week during each episode, which led to improvement. The child also frequently developed oral ulcers and had been previously diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia, with hemoglobin levels fluctuating between 80 to 90 g/L despite oral iron dextran treatment. She has allergies to milk, eggs, mango, seafood, and other foods, which can cause severe vomiting and diarrhea. Prior to admission, she experienced vomiting, fever, and diarrhea after consuming half a quail egg, with a maximum temperature of 39.2°C, and had been limping for nearly a week. Her parents reported no history of photophobia, tears, blurred vision, joint pain, or vulvar ulcers. Physical examination revealed a body temperature of 38.4°C, heart rate of 134 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 26 breaths per minute, weight of 12 kg, and height of 88 cm. She exhibited facial pallor, no skin rash, no conjunctival congestion, and an oral ulcer measuring approximately 0.5 × 0.3 cm. Cardiac and pulmonary examinations were normal. Abdominal examination showed distention, with the liver palpable 2 cm below the costal margin and the spleen palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. Shifting dullness was negative, and there was no tenderness or muscle tension. No abnormalities were found in the vulva and perianal areas, and the neurological examination was unremarkable. Laboratory results included WBC 12.22 × 10^9/L, NE 8.52 × 10^9/L, HB 87 g/L, PCT 0.24 ng/mL, CRP 65.5 mg/L, IL-6 65.5 mg/L, VitB12 1118 pmol/L, APTT 69 s, DRJT 942 ng/mL, ESR 58 mm/h, VitB12 118.2 pmol/L, IgE 96.81 IU/ml, natural killer cells 25.2%, total B cells 27.8%, CD4/CD8 ratio 1.0, ANA 1:100, and anticardiolipin antibody 18 RU/mL. Gastrointestinal ultrasound revealed uneven thickening of the ascending colon and surrounding mesentery, approximately 0.4 cm, indicating inflammatory changes. Ultrasound of the right knee joint showed effusion and thickened synovium. Colonoscopy indicated colonic mucosal congestion. Lung CT revealed multiple granulomas.
test_results: There was a heterozygous mutation (c.436_437deTC) in the TNFAIP3 gene, resulting in a frameshift mutation of an amino acid (p.L147Qfs∗7). The family verification analysis showed no mutation in the parents, indicating a spontaneous mutation. This variation in the normal population database was a low-frequency variation, preliminarily determined as pathogenic variation according to the ACMG guidelines.

case_report: A 13-year-old female with no significant past medical history, except for recent COVID-19 exposure and a positive PCR test without symptoms, presented with a week-long history of headache, abdominal pain, vomiting, vision changes, right-sided arm and leg weakness, and difficulty walking. In the emergency department, she received IV fluids, acetaminophen, and MiraLAX. She reported some improvement and was discharged. A few days later, she experienced worsening right-sided weakness, occasional blurry vision when looking to the left, and increased difficulty walking. On the day of admission, she visited her primary care physician, where she fell and was subsequently sent back to the emergency department, where a stroke alert was initially called.
test_results: An urgent brain MRI was done and showed Innumerable foci of increased T2 signal in the white matter of the brain, including the cerebellum and cervicomedullary junction. There was some enhancement of these lesions, some with ring enhancement and some with restricted diffusion suggesting lesions of different ages. Spinal MRI was then obtained and showed numerous small foci of T2 hyperintensity and enhancement involving the white matter of the spinal cord, mostly in the cervical spine on the right with one focus seen in the lower cord at the level of T11-12. The rest of the diagnostic workup showed positive CSF oligoclonal bands, high CSF IgG index, elevated CSF protein, negative viral PCR panel, negative NMO antibodies, and negative MOG antibodies titers.

case_report: A 7-year-old girl experienced upper abdominal pain after lunch, leading to early dismissal from school on three occasions over the past 10 days. She also had a low-grade fever and indigestion in the days leading up to her visit. Physical examination revealed slight tenderness in the right upper quadrant upon deep palpation, consistent with Murphy's sign. Laboratory tests showed a slight increase in serum alkaline phosphatase, with other liver function test parameters remaining normal.
test_results: Sonographic evaluation of the abdomen suggested the presence of a distended GB with a long, dilated, and tortuous cystic duct (13 mm). The CBD was also dilated, mildly though in its entirety. The IHBRs were not dilated. The findings upon ultrasonography were confirmed with MRCP. In addition to the cystic duct and the CBD, the CHD was also dilated distal to the confluence. The pancreatic duct was entering the CBD outside the sphincter of Oddi. Tiny calculi were present in the dependent portion of the distal, mildly dilated CBD.
diagnosis: Choledochal Cyst of the Cystic Duct

case_report: A 26-year-old female presented with pain and jaundice. Laboratory findings showed a mild increase in total and direct serum bilirubin, along with elevated levels of alkaline phosphatase. Previous ultrasound imaging revealed a mass in the gall bladder, with prominent hepatic ducts and the common bile duct (CBD). A tortuous cystic lesion was observed along the course of the cystic duct. The patient was referred for further radiological evaluation.
test_results: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of abdomen showed an enhancing mass lesion involving the gall bladder with regional lymphadenopathy. Cystic duct was dilated and tortuous and showed wide communication with CBD. A calculus was seen in distal CBD. MRI and MRCP showed grossly dilated and tortuous cystic duct with a wide opening into a prominent common hepatic duct, in addition to gall bladder mass. The CBD was normal in caliber.
diagnosis: Choledochal cyst of the cystic duct

case_report: A 50-year-old Caucasian male was referred to our clinic in late 2010 for elevated liver enzymes. Approximately two years before his initial visit, he experienced jaundice after taking terbinafine, which resolved on its own after three months. He reported no recent use of prescription medication, herbal medication, alcohol, or illicit drugs. There was no family history of recurrent cholestatic disorder or liver disease. Physical examination revealed marked jaundice and scleral icterus, with no signs of chronic liver disease. Laboratory tests showed a white blood count of 3300/μL, hemoglobin at 13 g/dL, platelets at 186,000/μL, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) at 91 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 96 U/L, alkaline phosphatase (ALP) at 712 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT) at 643 U/L, total bilirubin at 2.4 mg/dL, albumin at 4.3 g/dL, total protein at 7.7 g/dL, international normalized ratio at 1, and creatinine at 1.1. Hepatitis A, B, and C serology were negative. Iron studies, ceruloplasmin, alpha 1-antitrypsin, serum immunoglobulins, and protein electrophoresis were normal. Anti-nuclear (ANA), anti-smooth muscle, anti-mitochondrial (AMA), and anti-liver-kidney microsome antibodies were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed no evidence of intra- or extrahepatic biliary dilation or cholelithiasis. Magnetic resonance imaging/magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRI/MRCP) revealed a normal pancreatic duct, common hepatic duct, and common bile duct without ductal dilation, and a normal liver. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy did not show evidence of inflammatory bowel disease. Further evaluation with endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) revealed a normal pancreatic and biliary system, without evidence of any large- or small-duct disease.
test_results: Chronic biliary disease with duct injury, duct loss in at least 4 out of 15 portal tracts, prominent cholestasis and mild periportal fibrosis.

case_report: A 19-year-old male presented with abnormal liver function tests (LFTs) and was referred to the outpatient clinic. Abnormal LFTs had been detected repeatedly over the past four years and one month, although the patient remained asymptomatic. He had no history of liver disease during infancy or childhood, no previous drug treatments, and no symptoms such as jaundice, itching, or abdominal pain. There was no history of smoking, alcohol consumption, or medication use. His mother had chronic type B hepatitis. Physical examination revealed no abnormalities. Laboratory results were as follows: hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL, white blood count 7090/mm3, platelets 376,000/mm3, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 147 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 123 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase (ALP) 1345 IU/L, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT) 576 IU/L, total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, and albumin 4.0 g/dL. Serum iron, transferrin saturation, ferritin, alpha 1-antitrypsin, and ceruloplasmin levels were within normal ranges. Serological tests for anti-smooth muscle, anti-neutrophil-cytoplasm, anti-nuclear, anti-mitochondrial, anti-liver-kidney microsome antibodies, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C virus were negative. An abdominal CT scan showed normal liver echogenicity with no evidence of cholelithiasis or biliary dilation. Over a six-month follow-up period, LFTs continued to show elevated transaminases and alkaline phosphatase levels without any clinical symptoms. The patient was admitted for further evaluation. An endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) revealed normal extrahepatic bile ducts and minimal irregularities in the intrahepatic bile ducts of the left lobe. A colonoscopy was normal.
test_results: Percutaneous liver biopsy showed a lack of interlobular bile ducts. In 19 portal tracts, only eight bile ducts were found. Mild chronic inflammatory infiltrates consisting primarily of lymphocytes and liver parenchymal spotty necrosis were also found.

case_report: A 31-year-old female patient, who was asymptomatic, had a liver mass detected incidentally during a screening sonography. Her medical history and family history were unremarkable, and her physical examination showed no abnormalities. She reported no drug or alcohol abuse and did not use steroids or oral contraceptives. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits: hemoglobin was 13.9 g/dL, leukocyte count was 8,000/mm3, platelet count was 274,000/mm3, total protein was 6.6 g/dL, albumin was 4.2 g/dL, total bilirubin was 0.5 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase was 17 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase was 13 IU/L, and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase was 17 IU/L. Serologic tests for hepatitis A, B, and C were negative. Tumor markers including AFP, CEA, and CA 19-9 were within normal ranges. Abdominal sonography revealed an approximately 3 cm, oval-shaped mass-like lesion with heterogeneous echogenicity in the right hepatic lobe, while the rest of the liver's echogenicity and echotexture were unremarkable. Doppler study showed no hypervascularity of the lesion and no significant perilesional hemodynamic abnormality. CT scans were performed for further evaluation. On noncontrast CT, the lesion appeared mildly low in density compared to the surrounding parenchyma. The liver density was normal, with no signs of hepatic steatosis or iron overload. During the hepatic arterial phase of the contrast-enhanced CT, the lesion showed no enhancement and had an irregular, infiltrative margin. Most of the lesion exhibited isoattenuating enhancement with the adjacent liver on the venous phase, except for a small branching tubule-like low attenuation area in the center. There was no evidence of portal thrombophlebitis or bile duct dilatation around the lesion.
test_results: Histopathologic examination revealed localized marked dilatation of sinusoids forming blood-filled spaces and thinning of hepatic cell cords and reticulin fiber network was lost in the affected area. The dilated sinusoidal cells were negative for CD 34, but were positive for factor VIII.

case_report: A 68-year-old Japanese woman presented in September 2013 with abnormal uterine bleeding. She was 10 years postmenopausal and had a history of corneal transplantation in her right eye in 2002. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed an abnormally thickened endometrium. Hysteroscopy showed an enlarged uterus with an irregular endometrial lining and several easily bleeding uterine polyps. Endometrial biopsy indicated endometrial adenocarcinoma, histologic grade 1, nuclear grade 2, with neoplastic myometrium infiltration. Pelvic MRI showed uterine myomas and a thick, heterogeneous endometrium measuring 1.2 cm. Chest CT scan revealed multiple bilateral nodules in both lungs. CT-guided biopsy of a pulmonary nodule confirmed metastatic endometrial adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemistry results were β-catenin negative, thyroid transcription factor 1 negative, progesterone receptor and estrogen receptor positive, vimentin negative, CK7 positive, and carcinoembryonic antigen negative. Megestrol acetate 160 mg daily was prescribed in December 2013 to control uterine bleeding, but the bleeding persisted, leading to a total hysterectomy in February 2014. Pathologic analysis of the uterus confirmed moderately differentiated endometrial adenocarcinoma, histologic grade 1, with infiltration of more than two-thirds the depth of the myometrium and vascular invasion. Final pathologic staging was pT1bNxM1. In February 2014, abdominal and pelvic MRI indicated highly vascularized liver nodules, primarily in the right lobe, measuring approximately 0.8 cm, with lack of perfusion in the adjacent parenchyma. Physical examination and routine laboratory investigations, including liver enzymes, were unremarkable. A conservative approach with regular follow-up visits was adopted. The patient continued megestrol acetate 160 mg daily and remained asymptomatic. Abdominal MRI was repeated every 3 months, showing no change in the number or size of liver nodules until March 2015, when MRI indicated growth of the nodules from 0.8 cm to 1.4 cm.
test_results: The histologic result showed a cystic lesion filled with erythrocytes throughout the lobule, with moderated sinusoidal dilatation and atrophy of the adjacent hepatocytes. The portal space had a few lymphocyte infiltrations, and there was no fibrosis or any malignancy in this sample.

case_report: A 64-year-old woman presented with a weight loss of six kg over the past year. Her medical history included idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) treated with long-term corticosteroid therapy three years ago. She reported nonspecific epigastric pain and a sensation of abdominal distension. Vital signs were as follows: blood pressure 147/76 mm Hg, heart rate 78 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and temperature 37℃. Physical examination revealed a firm, non-tender liver edge palpable two cm below the right costal margin, with no other findings such as jaundice, cutaneous stigmata of chronic liver disease, ascites, or splenomegaly. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 5.6 × 10^9/L (normal 4 × 10^9-10 × 10^9), hemoglobin of 11.2 mg/dL (normal 13.1-17.5 g/L), hematocrit of 29% (normal 39-52%), platelet count of 34 × 10^9/L (normal 140 × 10^9-400 × 10^9 /L), alkaline phosphatase of 163 IU/L (normal <220 IU/L), alanine aminotransferase of 32 IU/L (normal <43 IU/L), aspartate aminotransferase of 44 IU/L (normal <38 IU/L), and prothrombin time of 13.5 seconds (normal 11-15 seconds). Serologic markers and acid-fast bacilli (AFB) levels were within normal limits. Axial contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) images in the late arterial and portal venous phases showed heterogeneous enhancing lesions infiltrating the hepatic parenchyma with a mosaic pattern of perfusion. Liver magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed marked liver enlargement, diffuse infiltrative lesions, and collapse of the inferior vena cava and hepatic vein. There was no sign of a mass effect or vascular thrombosis despite extensive lesions dominating the liver parenchyma. Lesions exhibited high signal density on T2-weighted images and persistent enhancement on delayed-phase CT and MRI.
test_results: Histological examination of the biopsy specimen showed marked sinusoidal dilation and focal sinusoidal occlusion with loose fibrous tissue. Histologically, the disease process resembled focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH) of the telangiectatic type. However, the lesion's diffuse infiltrative features on imaging made the diagnosis of FNH unlikely. There was no evidence of veno-occlusive disease or hepatocellular adenoma.

case_report: An 8-year-old female child presented with pain in the right upper abdomen. Laboratory tests showed elevated levels of serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase (SGPT), serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase (SGOT), and alkaline phosphatase. Ultrasound imaging revealed atrophy of the right lobe of the liver and multiple heteroechoic focal lesions within the liver.
test_results: Multidetector computed tomography (MDCT) images showed multiple lobulated and well-defined isodense and hypodense lesions scattered throughout the liver, predominantly in the right lobe. Arterial phase showed mild and homogenous enhancement of all focal lesions except one lesion which showed a heterogeneous enhancing pattern. Unenhanced CT images showed multiple small hyperdense foci within the segment VI/VII indicating hemorrhagic foci. The hepatic artery was hypertrophied and tortuous. Portal phase of the multiphase CT showed a hypoplastic left portal vein. Right intrahepatic portal vein was seen to drain directly into the hepatic segment of inferior venacava (IVC). Biopsy of a liver focal lesion and its histopathological analysis showed benign hepatocellular hyperplasia.

case_report: A 63-year-old Caucasian female with a history of diabetes mellitus reported a progressively enlarging cutaneous nodule in the lower mid-back region. She did not experience trauma, skin discharge, weight loss, fever, or night chills but did report mild fatigue. Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine revealed a diffuse abnormal signal over an area measuring approximately 11 cm × 8 cm. Ultrasound examination of the region demonstrated asymmetric abnormal echogenicity to the right of the midline.
test_results: Computed tomography–guided skin biopsy demonstrated a diffuse infiltration of malignant cells of moderate size with ovoid to irregular nuclear contours and many nucleoli with significant mitotic activity. Flow cytometric analysis identified an abnormal population of cells accounting for the majority of events analyzed, showing surface lambda light chain restriction; coexpression of CD19, CD20, FMC-7, and HLA-DR; and aberrant coexpression of both CD10 and CD5. Immunohistochemical stains for CD20, CD10, BCL2, MUM1, and c-MYC were strongly positive, BCL6 was moderately positive, and the malignant cells had a proliferation index (Ki-67) of greater than 90%. CD3 and Cyclin D1 were negative. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis was performed using DNA probes for aggressive B-cell lymphoma. Two hundred interphase nuclei were examined for each probe and revealed a rearrangement of the MYC gene in 93.5%, a rearrangement of the BCL6 gene in 97.5%, and a gain of BCL2/18q21 in 69.5% of nuclei. There was no evidence of a BCL2 gene rearrangement.
Orpha_name: High grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and/ or BCL2 and/or BCL6 rearrangement

case_report: A fifty-year-old male received a liver transplant from a deceased donor in September 2003 due to liver cirrhosis caused by chronic hepatitis C infection. The donor, a 27-year-old male, had died from head trauma. Both the donor and recipient tested positive for cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus antibodies in their serum. The cold ischemia time was 5 hours and 43 minutes. For induction therapy, the patient was administered Daclizumab (anti-CD25 monoclonal antibody) at a dose of 1 mg/kg. Maintenance immunosuppressants included Tacrolimus and steroids, with the steroids being tapered off three months post-transplant. There were no episodes of acute rejection or signs of recurrent hepatitis C until the patient developed PTLD. Seven years post-transplant, the patient was admitted to the hospital with acute abdominal pain. A simple abdominal X-ray revealed multiple dilated small bowel loops with air-fluid levels, which were resolved within 24 hours through nasogastric tube decompression. The patient was discharged without further study or specific treatment. However, the patient was re-admitted 7 days later with symptoms and signs of complete intestinal obstruction. A simple abdominal X-ray showed similar findings to the previous admission. Due to the recurrence within a short period, an emergency laparotomy was performed without additional radiologic imaging. During the operation, intussusception of the jejunum was found approximately 300 cm distal from the ligament of Treitz, with no abnormal lymphadenopathy in the mesentery of the small intestine. A simple resection of the small bowel was carried out as no other pathology was identified in the abdominal cavity. The post-operative recovery was uneventful, and the patient was discharged 4 days after surgery. The surgical specimen revealed a tan, firm, well-circumscribed mass measuring 4 × 3.9 cm that occluded the lumen of the jejunum. Microscopically, the tumor extended from the mucosal surface through the muscularis layers and approached the serosal surface. The tumor cells were large, with a high nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio, delicate chromatin, and prominent centroblastic features.
test_results: The tumor cells were positive for CD20, CD79a, CD10, and BCL-6 by immunohistochemistry. They were negative for CD3, CD5, BCL-2, S-100 and keratin. Ki-67 index was high (greater than 90%). Fluorescent in situ hybridization analysis was positive for translocation between chromosomes 8 and 14 (IGH/MYC) in 10% of interphase nuclei, and negative for translocation between chromosomes 14 and 18. In situ hybridization demonstrated that the tumor was negative for EBV.
diagnosis: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma  of germinal center phenotype with MYC translocation
Orpha_name: High grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and/ or BCL2 and/or BCL6 rearrangement

case_report: A 10-year-old male patient presented with a mass in the right temporomandibular region that had been noticeable for one month. The swelling was firm and sensitive to touch. The patient exhibited full range of motion in the mandible, with no restrictions in any direction. The mass resulted in facial asymmetry. There was no loss of sensation in the areas served by the right mandibular nerve or the right facial nerve. The patient reported no history of trauma to the affected area.
test_results: A posterior-anterior radiography of the skull was obtained revealing a radiolucent region in the condyle of the right mandible. A three-dimensional CT reconstruction showed the presence of a radiolucent and multilocular lesion in the condyle region. It was possible to appreciate that the lesion had totally replaced the mandibular right condyle and part of the mandibular ascending ramus. The lesion substituted the bone marrow of these anatomical structures and the cortical bone was substantially expanded and perforated. The condyle was so ballooned that it was evident through extra oral examination. Part of the coronoid process was affected by the infiltrative osteolytic process. The magnetic resonant imaging (MRI) demonstrated a high-signal intensity within the lesion itself and a low-signal at the periphery.

case_report: An 18-year-old male reported experiencing severe pain in the right eye and excessive tearing for one week. Additional symptoms included double vision on the right side, headache on the right side, sensitivity to light, nausea, and vomiting. The patient had a history of chronic sinusitis and did not report any recent head or facial injuries. The initial physical examination revealed double vision on the right side without any cranial nerve palsies. Laboratory tests returned normal results.
test_results: MRI revealed a cystic mass with superior displacement of the planum sphenoidale, pituitary gland, and infundibulum. There was expansion into the sella turcica and suprasellar cistern with enhancing sidewalls, lateral encroachment on the cavernous sinus, and destruction of the anterior clivus. CT of the paranasal sinuses with contrast demonstrated a cystic, expansile lesion centered in the sphenoid body and sella turcica with peripheral enhancement. There was a breakdown of the posterior and right lateral walls of the sphenoid sinus and osseous remodeling of the clivus, dorsum sellae, and walls of the sphenoid sinus. There was leftward nasal septal deviation. CT angiogram revealed a large hypodense lesion filled with a predominately homogenous fluid of nine Hounsfield units, compatible with water density. Further, there was surrounding bony erosion and expansion anteriorly into the sphenoethmoid junction and inferiorly into the clivus. Nasal endoscopy demonstrated chronic pansinusitis, a deviated nasal septum with a hypertrophied nasal turbinate, and a sphenoid mass. Histologic sections demonstrated a mixed cystic and solid tumor. Cystic blood-filled spaces were present with septa containing giant cells and spindled fibrous stroma without endothelial lining. The central solid areas contained frequent osteoclast-like giant cells, which were diffusely spread throughout the tumor. The giant cells uniformly contained less than 10 nuclei and were separated by mononuclear ovoid and spindled stromal cells along with numerous hemosiderin-laden macrophages and scattered lymphocytes. Lace-like immature osteoid was located throughout the lesion with accentuation at the periphery of the tumor. The osteoid at the periphery of the tumor varied from areas with long linear deposits of immature osteoid with a buckled, crinkled appearance to areas with a rigid, trabecular arrangement, which was often calcified. No malignant appearing osteoblasts, atypical stromal cells, or chondroid components were present. Additionally, there was no high mitotic activity nor atypical mitotic figures.

case_report: A 31-year-old male patient experienced a decrease in platelet count to approximately 5 × 10^10/L without any clear cause at a local hospital 5 years ago. The patient did not report abdominal pain, distension, nausea, vomiting, chest tightness, shortness of breath, or fever, and showed no apparent signs of liver cirrhosis. From July 10 to July, 2021, the patient was hospitalized due to fever without an obvious trigger, with a platelet count of 3.1 × 10^10/L. Tests for autoantibodies, hepatitis B antibodies, and hepatitis C antibodies were negative. Abdominal enhanced CT indicated liver cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension, esophageal and gastric varices, and splenic hilum varices. Symptomatic treatment led to a slight increase in platelet count. For further treatment, the patient was admitted to our hospital in July, 2021. Upon admission, the patient was conscious, with no jaundice in the skin or sclera, no liver palms, or spider nevi. Cardiovascular examination revealed a regular heart rhythm, and clear breath sounds were heard in both lungs. The abdomen was soft with no tenderness or rebound tenderness. The liver was not palpable below the ribs, and there was no percussion tenderness in the liver area. The spleen was palpable 5 cm below the ribs, with a soft texture and no tenderness. Murphy sign was negative, and there was no shifting dullness. No edema was present in the lower extremities. The pulse was 103 beats/min, the respiratory rate was 17 breaths/min, the blood pressure was 139/83 mm Hg, and the body temperature was 36.9°C. The patient's father was healthy, the mother had hypertension, one elder brother had deceased due to an enlarged liver and spleen of unknown cause, and two elder sisters were healthy. There was no known history of hereditary, familial, infectious diseases, or tumors. Laboratory examinations showed a white blood cell count of 2.9 × 10^9/L, platelet count of 4.6 × 10^10/L, blood ammonia level of 39 μmol/L, total bilirubin of 20.65 μmol/L, direct bilirubin of 8.97 μmol/L, and prothrombin time of 14.4 seconds. Fecal occult blood test was positive. Levels of albumin, globulin, cholinesterase, alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, and tumor markers were normal. Tests for hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibodies, series of autoantibodies, and autoimmune hepatitis antibodies were negative. Initial ultrasound revealed liver cirrhosis with portal hypertension, splenomegaly, portal vein enlargement, and a patent umbilical vein. Gastric filling ultrasonography indicated esophageal gastric varices in the lower part, with a width of approximately 1.1 cm, recommending endoscopic examination. Endoscopic examination revealed reflux esophagitis, chronic superficial atrophic gastritis with erosion, and no apparent gastric varices. Upper abdominal enhanced MRI showed liver cirrhosis, splenomegaly, abnormal collateral circulation, and slight dilation of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. Computed tomography portal venography (CTV) showed multiple collateral circulations involving the abdominal wall veins, umbilical vein, esophagus, and gastric fundus. The patient had no history of liver-damaging drug intake, blood transfusion, unclean injections, liver diseases, or heavy alcohol consumption.
test_results: Pathological findings indicated cirrhosis complicated with ductal plate malformation. The results of Immunohistochemistry and special staining were CD10 (+), CK7 (+), CK8/18 (+), HBcAg (−), HBsAg (−), PAS (+).

case_report: A 10-year-old Caucasian girl was seen at the Pediatric Hematology-Oncology Outpatient Clinic for low platelet count (68 × 103/mm3) and an enlarged spleen. Her family history was notable only for her mother having microhematuria and asymptomatic proteinuria. The girl's medical history included asymptomatic microhematuria since age 4. Three weeks prior to the clinic visit, she developed a headache and an itching rash resembling rubella. Physical examination was normal except for a spleen enlargement of 4.5 cm. Blood tests showed thrombocytopenia (68 × 103/mm3) with other values within normal ranges: hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 75.8 fL, leukocytes 4.2 × 103/mm3, neutrophils 2.5 × 103/mm3, reticulocytes 41 × 103/mm3. Kidney and liver function tests were normal: aspartate aminotransferase 34 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 24 U/L, bilirubin 21.7 umol/L, γGT 12 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 177 IU/L, creatinine 39 umol/L. Coagulation tests (PT 58%, IRN 1.42, PTT 33 sec) and haptoglobin were normal, and the Coombs Test was negative. Serological tests for various infections including hepatitis B and C, HIV, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and others were negative. Peripheral blood smear and bone marrow aspirate were normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed an enlarged spleen (17 cm) with normal-sized liver and kidneys. Doppler ultrasound indicated normal portal blood flow. Thorax x-ray was normal.
