Two months later, due to ongoing low platelet count (57 × 103/mm3), tests for antiplatelet antibodies, antinuclear antibodies, antiDNA, anti-extractable nuclear antigen, antimitochondrial and anti-parietal cell antibodies, and anti-muscle antibody were all negative. Three months after the initial evaluation, physical examination, thrombocytopenia, and abdominal ultrasound findings remained unchanged, and the child was in good general condition. Six months later, due to persistent low platelet count (50 × 103/mm3) and spleen enlargement, an abdominal CT scan confirmed the spleen enlargement and revealed portal vein ectasia, liver enlargement with the left lobe extending to the left posterior axillary region, and dilatation of intrahepatic bile ducts, mainly in the right liver lobe. The girl was then admitted to the Pediatric Gastroenterology and Hepatology Unit for further evaluation. Tests showed ceruloplasmin 0.29 g/l, cupremia 9.9 umol/l, cupruria 0.543 umol/24 h, α-fetoprotein 1.3 ug/l, and α1-antitrypsin 135 mg/dl, all within normal ranges. An abdomen MRI showed a reduced volume of the right liver lobe, hypertrophy of the lateral segment of the left liver lobe, and spleen enlargement. Cholangio-MRI indicated slight dilatation of the biliary tract in the right lobe, with normal hepatic duct and choledoch. Hepatobiliary scintigraphy revealed left lobe liver enlargement with normal radionuclide uptake; after 45 minutes, there was faint visualization of some biliary tract parts and the bowel, with elevated parenchymal activity persisting after one hour. Two hours post-fat meal, there was elevated bowel activity; the left lobe outflow was complete, while activity persisted in the lateral portion of the right lobe. Gastroscopy showed esophagogastric varices.
test_results: The liver biopsy, performed on both the right and the left lobe, demonstrated the persistence of bile ducts remnants, abnormal branching of the intrahepatic portal veins and fibrosis of the portal tracts on both lobes.

case_report: An 11-year-old female presented with a lumbar spine fracture following a fall during exercise, leading to persistent back pain. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the spine identified a fracture at the L-2 level. She was admitted to Seoul St. Mary's Hospital for further evaluation. A chest X-ray showed a left lower lobe infiltrate with pleural effusion, and a chest CT scan revealed bilateral pleural effusions with multiple, diffuse nodules in both lungs. Positron emission tomography (PET)-CT indicated whole-body tumor involvement. Biopsies of the bone marrow and the sole of the right foot confirmed stage IV rhabdomyosarcoma. After 5 months of chemotherapy, PET-CT showed a complete metabolic response, and after 11 months of treatment, the lung lesions and pleural effusions had largely resolved. However, two nodules remained in the left lung, one in the upper lobe and the other in the superior segment of the lower lobe. Wedge resection of these two nodules was performed via mini-thoracotomy for further evaluation and treatment. The patient's recovery was uneventful, and she was discharged on postoperative day 6. The resected nodules were firm and ovoid, each measuring 3 mm in diameter.
test_results: Tumor proliferation was lepidic, marked by cuboidal to columnar cells with scanty cytoplasm following alveolar contours.

case_report: A 34-year-old male experienced upper arm pain for a duration of 3 months without any prior history of trauma to the arm. Initial imaging indicated an abnormality in the humeral shaft, leading to his referral to our hospital. Upon examination, tenderness was noted in the distal part of the upper arm, while no swelling or limitation in the range of motion of the elbow joint was observed.
test_results: Plain X-ray images showed an osteolytic lesion with slight marginal sclerosis in the anterior cortical bone of the distal part of the humeral shaft. A computed tomography (CT) scan revealed calcifications as well as marginal sclerosis in the lesion. Although the lesion protruded to the anterior side, it did not break the anterior cortical wall of the humerus and there was no invasion of the soft tissues. The lesion had an intermediate signal intensity on T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, and was enhanced by an injection of gadolinium. The histological appearance showed a fibro-osseous lesion without malignancy, which could exclude NOF.

case_report: A 14-year-old post-pubertal girl reported experiencing pain and swelling in her left collar bone, which began gradually and worsened over the course of a year. She had intermittent fever and a history of serous discharge from a wound over the swelling for the past six months. Examination revealed the patient was febrile with diffuse swelling of the left clavicle, extending from the sternal end to the left shoulder. The skin over the swelling had a healed scar and a discharging sinus nearby. Palpation indicated a local rise in temperature, tenderness, and a bony hard consistency of the swelling. Four discrete, non-tender lymph nodes were palpable, two in the axillary group and two in the cervical group, with the largest measuring 0.5 cm × 0.5 cm. The left shoulder's range of motion was painful and globally restricted. Laboratory tests showed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (40 mm/h) and leukocytosis with a neutrophilic predominance. The Mantoux test was equivocal. Bacterial and acid-fast bacilli staining and culture of the wound discharge were sterile. Radiographs indicated diffuse periosteal thickening around the clavicle from the sternal end to the lateral third, with a normal shoulder joint. Computed tomography revealed irregularity and sclerosis of the left clavicle with heterogeneous ossification. Magnetic resonance imaging showed altered heterogeneous T2 signal within the clavicle marrow and ill-defined cortical delineation with significant periosteal thickening. A Tc99m labeled methylene diphosphonate bone scan indicated active bony inflammation in the left clavicle.
test_results: A repeat biopsy showed immature woven bone with characteristic osteoblastic rimming in a background of fibrovascular stroma. Isolated cells in the fibrous stroma were cytokeratin (AE1/AE3 + CK-1) positive.

case_report: The patient is the first male child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents; the mother is a 28-year-old preschool teacher, and the father is a 33-year-old businessman. There was no history of medication use or radiation exposure during pregnancy. The mother was a smoker prior to the pregnancy. A history of decreased fetal movement was noted, and the intrauterine presentation was breech. The child was delivered at a private hospital by Cesarean section at 35+4 weeks due to the breech presentation and premature membrane rupture (9 hours). The Apgar score was 7 and 8 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. The birth weight was 1,970 g (within ± 2 SD), the head circumference was 31 cm (within ± 2 SD), and the length was 47 cm (within ± 2 SD). He was transferred from the hospital immediately after birth because of abnormal leg features. His heart rate was 148 per minute, and the respiratory rate was 52 breaths per minute at the time of admission. His activity was moderate to poor, but he was not floppy. His inhalation power was poor. A physical examination upon admission demonstrated the following cylindrical contractures involving the lower extremities: (1) knees were fixed symmetrically in the hyperextended position with a range of motion (ROM) of 0°; (2) hips were fixed in the flexed position by nearly 90° and limited in abduction with a ROM of 0-45°; and (3) thin subcutaneous tissues and absence of skin creases of the lower extremities. The sensation of the lower extremities was intact, although the deep tendon reflexes could not be evaluated due to the fixed extension of both knees. The feet, upper extremities, and shoulders showed no deformities. His hands lacked Simian lines. Otherwise, he had no remarkable physical findings, except for an undescended right testicle.
test_results: Simple knee X-rays showed increased soft tissue densities in the joint cavities.

case_report: A 51-year-old male presented with a 2-year history of snoring and changes in voice. He reported loud snoring and had been observed to experience obstructive sleep apnea along with excessive daytime sleepiness. His Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) score was 13. He did not report any episodes of shortness of breath. His medical history included mild hypertension and diabetes. The patient’s height was 160 cm, weight was 62 kg, and body mass index (BMI) was 24.2 kg/m2. Physical examination revealed a Friedman tongue position of grade III, where only the soft palate was visible, and the tonsils were not visible as they were hidden in the tonsillar fossa.
test_results: On flexible laryngoscopy, about a 20×20 mm sized round cystic mass at the base of tongue was identified. The cyst bended the epiglottis posteriorly, which made the airway narrow. The vocal cords could not be observed because of the lesion. The computed tomograms showed a 33×31×27 mm sized well-defined cystic lesion located at the midline of the tongue base, compressing the oropharyngeal airway. The epiglottis was displaced posteriorly by the cystic lesion. SVF showed that the pharyngeal airway was completely obstructed during both inspiratory and expiratory phase when the mass pulled the epiglottis down and backward. The tip of epiglottis was in contact with the posterior pharyngeal wall irrespective of respiratory cycle. The histopathology showed that the cyst was lined by stratified squamous epithelium, and that the deeper tissue showed fibrosis, skeletal muscle fragments and laryngeal gland cysts.

case_report: A 15-month-old female presented with a painful mass in the abdomen. She had previously undergone surgery for a ventricular septal defect at 8 months old, with a good recovery. Her vital signs were within normal limits, except for a temperature of 38.0 °C. Physical examination revealed an elastic hard mass on the right side of the abdomen, with a normal-appearing umbilicus. Blood tests showed a white blood cell count of 14,500/μL, a C-reactive protein level of 2.4 mg/dL, a hemoglobin level of 9.6 g/dL, and an amylase level of 98 U/L (44−132 U/L). Abdominal radiography did not show any signs of intestinal obstruction.
test_results: Abdominal ultrasonography (US) revealed a large intraabdominal cyst. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) showed that a cystic lesion that was 4 cm in diameter was located in the abdominal wall, beneath the umbilicus. The cystic lesion contained a 1 cm enhanced lesion. On the immediate right side of this cyst, a 7 cm hematoma was found within the abdominal wall. Aspiration revealed bloody fluid with an amylase level of 38,250 U/L, and no bacterial infection was observed.
diagnosis: Omphalomesenteric cyst with aberrant pancreas and associated hematoma of the abdominal wall

case_report: A 6-month-old female infant had presented five times to medical services since birth with a history of discharge from the umbilicus. On days 2 and 4, she presented with bleeding from the umbilical stump, which was managed with a pressure dressing. At 2 weeks of age, she attended a general practitioner surgery with discharge of watery liquid from the umbilicus, and it was treated with silver nitrate application. She came to the paediatric assessment unit of the local district general hospital at 3 weeks of age because of ongoing discharge. The periumbilical skin area appeared raw with features of a chemical dermatitis. An umbilical swab was taken and treatment with oral flucloxacillin commenced. The child presented again with ongoing symptoms. This time, it was treated with miconazole and neomycin. The discharge was mainly serous fluid which occasionally turned serosanguinous but did not contain pus. At 6 months of age, she was rereferred by the general practitioner for persistent umbilical discharge with intermittent blood-stained fluid whilst she had been on her third course of antibiotics.
test_results: The ultrasound showed a cystic structure of 5 mm diameter with echogenic walls situated deep to the umbilicus. There was no communication with the bowel. A fistula extended through the anterior abdominal wall to the umbilicus.
diagnosis: Omphalomesenteric duct cyst containing gastric mucosa

case_report: A 4-year-old female patient presented with complaints of discolored teeth, pain in the lower jaw, and significant wear of all teeth. The patient's father reported that the discoloration had been present since the teeth first erupted. Family history indicated that the patient's mother, maternal grandfather, two aunts, and their sons also experienced similar dental issues. The mother and her sisters had not sought dental treatment, resulting in progressive tooth substance loss. There was no reported history of bone abnormalities in the family. Clinical examination showed extensive loss of enamel and dentin, with teeth exhibiting hard brown dentin and worn incisal and occlusal surfaces, in some cases down to the gingival level. The mandibular first molars were exposed, and an abscess was noted in relation to the mandibular right first molar.
test_results: Orthopantomograph revealed obliterated pulp chambers in most of teeth and constricted in some teeth. Full mouth IOPA radiographic survey also showed the same findings.

case_report: A 35-year-old male presented with occasional chipping of teeth during eating and issues with a dislodged fixed partial denture. The patient reported abnormal dentition since childhood and had some primary teeth extracted due to caries. The primary teeth were yellowish in color. He experienced continuous chipping of tooth structure, particularly in the lower dentition, while masticating. Six years ago, his lower left molars were extracted due to fracture and attrition. Last year, he had extractions of teeth 16, 27, 46, and 47, followed by the fabrication of a nickel-chrome fixed partial denture covering teeth 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 33, 34, 35, 43, 44, 45, 46, 47, and 48. These dentures frequently dislodge during eating, and the patient uses cotton for retention while eating and removes the dentures at other times. There is no history of major illness or hospitalization. The patient's grandfather had opalescent brown, worn-out dentition.
test_results: OPG full mouth and IOPA X-rays revealed total obliteration of pulp chambers with 33,34,35,43,44,45,48. Partial obliteration of pulp chambers with rest of the teeth with abnormal pulpal morphology. No evidence of any periapical pathology with any tooth was revealed. Posterior to anterior (PA) chest and PA skull were normal. Maxillary badly destructed second molar was sent to lab for histological examination. It was revealed that there was normal enamel rods, irregular calcified dentinal tubules, and almost completely obliterated pulp chamber.

case_report: An 18-year-old female presented with reduced lower facial height. Her parents noted discoloration of primary teeth and enamel chipping. She was born from a second-degree consanguineous marriage, and no other family members (siblings and parents) reported similar issues. Examination revealed a decrease in lower facial height due to severe attrition reaching the gingiva. Intraoral findings included generalized brownish discoloration of teeth and enamel loss. There were no carious lesions observed.
test_results: Panoramic study showed narrow pulp chamber with severe coronal attrition and multiple periapical radiolucencies. Unstained ground section with photomicrography showed irregular dentinal tubules with increased hypomineralized interglobular dentin and obliterated pulp chamber.

case_report: An 89-year-old woman presented with a protruding horn-shaped mass on her left cheek. The lesion had been present for several years and was gradually increasing in size. There was a history of recurrent swelling over the past 6 months. The swelling was painless and non-tender. The patient did not report any previous trauma or infection. The lesion was a single, hard, erythematous, movable mass measuring 1 cm × 1.5 cm × 1.2 cm over the left malar area, with a cutaneous horn. On examination, there was no neck node lymphadenopathy. The rest of the systemic examination was normal, except that the patient had Parkinson's disease.
test_results: The tumour was composed of lobulated nests of squamous cells, and the encapsulated tumour pushed into the adjacent stroma. The nests showed proliferating squamous epithelium with trichilemmal keratinisation. The squamous cells had mild atypia, as shown by an increased nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio, nuclear polymorphism and the presence of few atypical mitoses.

case_report: A 53-year-old female reported a one-year history of a progressively enlarging lesion on her nose, which had shown noticeable growth over the past three months. She did not report any history of trauma or insect bites in the affected area. Her past medical history was unremarkable. Physical examination revealed a localized, non-tender, skin-colored nodule with a smooth surface and soft consistency, measuring 0.5 x 0.5 cm on the nose. No palpable lymphadenopathy was detected. The lesion was surgically excised with a 0.5 cm margin of normal tissue.
test_results: Hematoxylin-eosin stain revealed a multilobular, noncapsulated tumor occupying all the dermis. Lobules were formed by peripheral palisading of small basaloid cells, differentiating towards large keratinocytes with ample eosinophilic cytoplasm and abrupt keratinization without a granular layer. Areas of calcification with cholesterol crystals were observed within the compact eosinophilic keratin. The tumor cells showed moderate nuclear atypia and scarce mitoses.

case_report: A two-month-old female, born from a twin pregnancy, presented with a mass located in the sacral region. The mass had been present since birth and had slightly increased in size over the past two months, measuring approximately 10 x 8 cm at the time of presentation. The patient exhibited no issues with bowel or bladder function. Upon examination, the mass was well-defined and soft, with irregular margins and mobility. It showed a positive fluctuation test and caused anterior displacement of the anal opening.
test_results: On X-ray, a well-defined soft tissue density lesion was visible at the sacrococcygeal region, also showing tiny calcifications and few lucent areas within indicating fat. No underlying bony erosion or destruction was noted. On ultrasound, a well-defined lesion with solid and cystic components was noted with fatty tissue within the solid component. Few of the cystic components were anechoic and few showed debris within. A small extension of the lesion was seen internally posterior to the urinary bladder, which was multi-cystic in appearance. On histopathology, it had areas of stratified squamous epithelium, ciliated and mucin secretion columnar epithelium, and transitional epithelium. It also had fibro adipose tissue as well as muscle bundles at places along with cartilage and adnexal structures like sebaceous glands and sweat glands.

case_report: A 51-year-old female patient, who has had three pregnancies and two live births, came to the clinic with complaints of vaginal itching, irritation, and a tearing sensation near the top of the vaginal area, persisting for one year. She noted that the discomfort varied in intensity over time but had become more severe in recent months. She did not report any excessive vaginal odor, general pelvic pain, fever, or chills, and had no concerns about sexually transmitted infections. The patient mentioned that physical activity and moisture from daily swimming exacerbated her discomfort. Upon physical examination, a 1.5 cm firm bilateral vulvar lesion with shallow red ulcerations was observed at the lower mons pubis. Initial testing included a 3 mm punch biopsy of the lesion, which was sent for virologic and pathologic analysis. Testing for herpes simplex virus 1 and 2 (HSV1/2) by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) returned negative results.
test_results: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining showed both papillary and reticular dermal nests composed of hyperchromatic keratinocytes with peripheral cell palisading. Keratinocyte nests showed uniform membranous immunohistochemistry (IHC) for epithelial cell adhesion molecule (EPCAM/BER-EP4) and diffuse cytoplasmic staining for B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL2).

case_report: A 64-year-old female patient presented with a vulvar mass. Over the past decade, she observed a gradually enlarging mass in the left labia majora. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed a firm, painless, immobile mass in the labia majora extending to the Mons pubis, measuring 7 × 4 cm. Laboratory tests were normal. Surgical history indicated previous recurrences of vulvar tumors. In 2000, a mass in the Bartholin’s gland was excised in 2007, and examination showed a proliferation of tubules and cystic structures lined by double-layered epithelium, sometimes filled with eosinophilic material, embedded in mucoid and fibrous connective tissue. A recurrence in the labia majora occurred one year later, leading to another excision, which revealed a lobular glandular proliferation of cuboid cells. The patient also had a benign breast lumpectomy and cholecystectomy. Medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a heterogeneous, regular, hypervascular mass located directly under the skin, measuring 4.2 × 8 cm. Abdominal and pelvic multi-slice CT scan revealed a 3.8 × 7.2 cm heterogeneous, well contrast-enhancing, high-density area on the right side of the left labia majora extending to the anterior perineum. A low-density focus in the left hepatic lobe was noted, suspected to be a simple cyst or hemangioma. The mass was excised and measured 7 × 3 × 4 cm, grey-colored.
test_results: Histopathology showed proliferation of uniform small cells having dark, compact nuclei and scant cytoplasm, reveals some mitotic figures. There are epithelial components that made up of elongated branching tubular structures with two cell layers. The stromal components are made up of chondroid to fibrous/hyaline stroma.
diagnosis: Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma  of the Bartholin's gland

case_report: A 16-year-old female patient visited the radiotherapy department in July 2008 with a persistent hoarse voice that had been ongoing for the past year. The condition developed gradually. Initial treatments aimed at addressing common cold symptoms were ineffective. The patient did not experience sore throat, ear pain, localized pain or tenderness over the thyroid cartilage, difficulty swallowing, or signs of airway obstruction. She does not smoke, consume alcohol, or have a history of marijuana use. There was no history of previous neck irradiation. A detailed family history did not reveal any instances of cancer. An indirect laryngoscopy revealed that both vocal cords were mobile with no visible growths.
test_results: Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the neck showed a small irregular lesion over the left vocal cord at the junction of anterior one third and posterior two thirds. Thickening of left true vocal cord with loss of paraglottic fat is seen. Fiber-optic laryngoscopy confirmed the CT scan finding, showing irregular lesions along the medial margin of the left vocal cord. Histopathological examination under low-power and high-power fields showed severe dysplasia and full-thickness replacement of epithelium with dysplastic cells.
diagnosis: Carcinoma in situ of the vocal cord
Orpha_name: Squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx

case_report: A previously healthy four-year-old boy experienced vomiting and headaches for one week. Imaging of the brain showed a large mass in the posterior fossa with associated hydrocephalus. There was spread over the cerebellum's surface and metastases in the distal spinal cord. No family history of cancer was noted. The patient had most of the mass surgically removed, but residual tissue remained in the left cerebello-pontine angle. Histopathology initially identified the tumor as nodular medulloblastoma, later reclassified as classic medulloblastoma, Group 4. Staining revealed small, round, blue cells with compact and nodular structures. The cells were positive for synaptophysin and negative for GFAP, which only stained background astrocytic processes. Reticulin staining was absent, and β-catenin staining was confined to the cytoplasm. The Ki-67 proliferation index was about 30%. Treatment followed the Children’s Oncology Group protocol CCG-99701 Arm B, including radiation and chemotherapy. Radiation included 36 Gy to the craniospinal axis and additional doses to specific areas. Carboplatin and vincristine were used as radiosensitizers. Six cycles of chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, cisplatin, and vincristine were administered. Imaging at the end of therapy nine months later showed no residual or recurrent disease. The patient was monitored regularly with clinical exams and imaging. Long-term effects of therapy included neuro-cognitive impairment, bilateral hearing loss, panhypopituitarism, bilateral cataracts, and scoliosis/kyphosis, which were managed accordingly. At nearly 16 years old, 11 years after initial treatment, the patient reported two weeks of numbness in the left hand and foot. Examination showed new left-sided seventh cranial nerve palsy, mild left upper limb weakness, and reduced sensations in a glove and stocking pattern.
test_results: An MRI showed an enlarging mass within the pons and upper medulla with an expanding lesion showing an area of cavitation and rim enhancement at its posteroinferior margin.

case_report: An 11-year-old girl experienced horizontal double vision when looking at distant objects, which persisted for 2 weeks. She typically engaged in near-work activities for about 3 hours daily. She had no history of head trauma, systemic illness, or psychological stress. Her uncorrected visual acuity was better than 20/20 in both eyes. Refraction measurements were: Right eye (S −0.50D C + 0.50D A 170°) and Left eye (S + 0.00D C + 0.25D A 175°). Intraocular pressure was 19 mm Hg in the right eye and 17 mm Hg in the left eye. Both pupils were round and equal with a complete light reflex, and no nystagmus was observed. Examinations of the anterior segment, ocular media, and fundus were normal in both eyes. The single prism cover test showed basic esotropia of 30 prism diopters (PD) at near fixation and 35 PD at distant fixation. Ocular rotations were full without nystagmus. The Hess red-green test indicated inward displacement of both eyes, but no restriction of eye movement was observed under prism neutralization, confirming comitant esotropia.
test_results: Brain MRI revealed a swollen internal nonuniform high-signal area on T2-weighted image. On gadolinium contrast-enhanced brain MRI, the T1-weighted image had poor contrast. Additional head computed tomography showed a lesion with unclear borders and poor contrast enhancement at the same site.

case_report: A 21-year-old female patient presented with linear verrucous lesions confined to the right palmar area. Parental consanguinity was evaluated and excluded. No dermatological conditions were reported in her immediate family, including her father, mother, and sister. The patient reported that the lesions had been present since childhood. Clinical examination revealed multiple, well-demarcated, hyperkeratotic, and yellowish streaks on the right palm, following Blaschko lines, with no similar findings on the left palm. No other cutaneous regions exhibited similar lesions. A thorough skin examination, including flexures, did not reveal any hyperkeratosis or ichthyotic lesions. The lesions displayed a nevoid distribution intersecting the palmar creases, consisting of three main stripes: one across the radial longitudinal crease below the thenar eminence, another along the middle and thenar creases, and a third extending from the hypothenar eminence to the distal transverse crease.
test_results: The molecular analysis showed the presence of a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) identified by rs14024.

case_report: A 3-year-old boy, the only child of non-consanguineous parents, exhibited widespread warty eruptions covering the body, including the genital area, but excluding the scalp, face, palms, and soles. The skin changes began at 3 weeks of age, initially appearing symmetrically on the anterior thighs, then spreading to the axillae, and over approximately 6 months, progressed to the current widespread distribution. There was no history of blisters or generalized redness at or after birth. The condition showed improvement during summer and worsened in winter. The child was otherwise in good health with no developmental delays or visual or hearing difficulties. There was no significant family history. Physical examination revealed multiple, bilaterally symmetrical, verrucous plaques following the lines of Blaschko, extensively involving the trunk and extremities. The plaques were oriented transversely on the trunk and longitudinally on the limbs. Hair, nails, and oral cavity appeared normal. Systemic examination showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Histopathological examination of lesional biopsy showed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and papillomatosis. Focal epidermolytic hyperkeratosis was evident in the form of perinuclear vacuolization of keratinocytes of the upper epidermis with coarse keratohyaline granules.
diagnosis: bilateral, systematized epidermolytic verrucous epidermal nevus

case_report: A 64-year-old Chinese male presented with multiple dark-brown papules on the scalp for 1 year. The lesions were asymptomatic and gradually increased in number over time. He had a history of androgenetic alopecia (AGA) for a decade and used topical 5% minoxidil for only 1 month, 5 years ago. The patient was otherwise healthy with no relevant family history. Physical examination showed discrete, 1- to 3-mm, flat-topped, brownish papules over the crown and vertex area of the scalp. Dermoscopic examination revealed a whitish scar-like center surrounded by brownish dots or brown fine streaks radiating from the center, located in a background of hair and scalp alteration typical of AGA.
test_results: Deposition of pink amorphous material was identified in the papillary dermis with scattered melanophages in the expanded dermal papillae. The deposits were highlighted by Congo red staining.

case_report: A 55-year-old male presented with a 10-year history of persistent itchy lesions distributed across the body. Physical examination identified multiple, discrete waxy papules on an erythematous base located on the lower back, thighs, legs, and a few on the arms. Additionally, irregular, reddish-brown, lace-like macules were observed on the outer surface of the arms, back of the neck, and around the knees. Erosions and vesicles with hyperkeratosis were interspersed among the lesions on the extremities. No oral lesions were noted. The patient had no significant medical history. There was no clinical evidence of systemic involvement such as organomegaly or macroglossia. Laboratory results showed a complete blood count with hemoglobin at 12.6 g%, white blood cell count at 5200 cells/cumm, and platelets at 1.8 lakhs. Liver function tests revealed serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase at 30 U/L, serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase at 35 U/L, total bilirubin at 0.6 mg/dl, and total protein at 5.4 g/dl. Serum creatinine was 0.7 mg/dl, urine Bence Jones proteins were absent, and protein electrophoresis showed no abnormalities. The electrocardiogram was normal, indicating no systemic involvement. A strong family history was noted, with both parents, one sister, two brothers, and two paternal uncles having similar lesions. In total, eight family members were affected.
test_results: Histopathologic examination of skin biopsy specimens showed a subepidermal blister with irregular acanthosis and hyperkeratosis of the overlying epidermis. A few eosinophils were found in the blister. Deposits of eosinophilic, homogenous amyloid were visible in the dermal papillae, which were confirmed on Congo red staining. The deposits were not seen around blood vessels or adnexal structures.
diagnosis: Bullous Variant of Familial Biphasic Lichen Amyloidosis

case_report: A 35-year-old Caucasian woman with skin phototype I/II presented with multiple severely itchy papules on her limbs, persisting for 8 years. She had a medical history of a prediabetic state. Physical examination revealed multiple pinpoint skin-colored papules on both the upper and lower extremities. Videodermoscopy showed central white hubs arranged linearly, with grayish dots and globules both centrally and peripherally. Numerous dotted, globular, and linear vessels were observed between the white hubs.
test_results: Histopathology showed hyperkeratosis, vessels with thickened walls in the dermis, pigment incontinence, and eosinophilic deposits, which stained positive with Congo red.

case_report: A 26-year-old male reported experiencing painful urination and blood in the urine for approximately one month. During a digital rectal examination, a large, hard mass with an uneven surface was detected. The serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level was measured at 0.44 ng/mL, which is within the normal range. Additional tumor markers were also found to be within normal limits.
test_results: MRI revealed an uneven multinodular mass located mainly within the central zone of the prostate and extending to the right peripheral gland at the bottom level of the central gland mass. The mass showed homogeneous low signal intensity on T1-weighted imaging and heterogeneous high signal intensity with pseudocapsule on T2-weighted EPI. In DCE-MRI, the central gland portion of the mass showed a weak gradual enhancement containing cystic areas, whereas the right peripheral gland showed a moderate gradual enhancement. DWI showed the prostatic mass as an area of marked high signal intensity. Coronal T2-weighted imaging demonstrated enlarged internal iliac lymph nodes. The resected specimen predominantly comprised elongated ducts and cellular stroma that contained areas of necrosis with calcification. Hypercellular stroma without glands was specifically detected. Although epithelial components did not show malignant changes, stromal cells showed ovoid, spindle-shaped and hyperchromatic nuclei in cellular areas, and spindle-shaped nuclei in myxomatous areas. An average of two mitoses per high-powered field was counted. Epithelial cells showed positive immunostaining for pan-cytokeratin (AE1/AE3, CAM5.2). In stromal cells, positive immunostaining was detected for vimentin, CD34, and progesterone receptor; whereas, negative results were obtained for pan-cytokeratin, CD31, S-100, HHF-35, desmin, α smooth muscle actin, MyoD1, c-kit, and estrogen receptors. The MIB-1 labeling index was elevated to > 50%.

case_report: A 52-year-old Caucasian woman with a history of severe hypertension and non-insulin dependent diabetes mellitus presented with bilateral subacute visual loss over eight to 10 days, resulting in light perception only in the left eye and hand movements only in the right eye. This visual loss was preceded by dull ocular pain, which continued after the onset of visual loss. The patient experienced pain with eye movements but did not have double vision. There was no tenderness over the temporal arteries, and temporal pulses were palpable on both sides. Fundoscopic examination revealed swollen optic discs in both eyes without any retinopathic changes associated with diabetes or hypertension, and no venous engorgement was observed. Color vision was reduced in both eyes, and a left relative afferent pupillary defect was noted. Visual field mapping indicated a left central scotoma and a normal right visual field. The patient's blood pressure was 152/80 on admission and decreased during her hospital stay. The rest of the neurological examination was unremarkable. There were no indications of connective tissue disease or sarcoidosis based on her history and physical examination. Initial blood tests showed normal full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, C-reactive protein (< 1), and plasma viscosity, with a raised glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) of 7.3% (normal 4 to 6.1). Chest X-ray was normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis from a lumbar puncture showed normal white and red blood cells, normal angiotensin converting enzyme level, no oligoclonal bands, and a marginally elevated protein level of 467.7 mg/L (normal 150 to 450 mg/L). MRI of the brain and spinal cord was normal. The patient was initially treated with aspirin and omeprazole. Upon review by the neurology team, she received a three-day course of intravenous methyl prednisolone. Vision improved to 6/6 in both eyes within two days, with full restoration of color vision and visual fields. However, ten days later, vision in the right eye deteriorated to 6/36 with temporal peripheral field loss, and the relative afferent pupillary defect switched to the right eye. The patient was then treated with 500 mg oral methyl prednisolone for five days, resulting in the return of normal visual acuity and visual fields within two days. A subsequent auto-immunity screen, including aquaporin-4 antibodies, was negative.
test_results: Visual evoked potentials performed twelve days after the onset of the second episode of visual loss were delayed bilaterally indicating bilateral optic nerve dysfunction.

case_report: A 17-year-old male patient experienced a significant decrease in vision in his right eye 7 hours following MR vaccination. Upon examination, visual acuity was measured at 20/400 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. A relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) of +2 was noted in the right eye. External ocular examination, slit-lamp examination, and fundus examination revealed no abnormalities in either eye.
test_results: Automated perimetry revealed extensive visual field loss sparing only the superior nasal quadrant.

case_report: A 26-year-old man with a history of CVID presented with vision loss in both eyes. His initial CVID symptom was hemolytic anemia at age 14. He later had episodes of autoimmune thrombocytopenia and neutropenia. Since his diagnosis, he experienced a significant infection, salmonella sepsis, at age 23. His current treatment regimen included intravenous immunoglobulin (0.4 g/kg every three weeks) and prednisone (10 mg daily). Upon presentation, he reported a progressive vision loss that started five days prior, accompanied by mild pain with eye movement. His visual acuity was 0.1 with diminished color perception, and both pupils had a poor response to light. A confrontational visual field test indicated a broadly decreased visual field in both eyes. Slit-lamp examination results were negative for uveitis, and the optic disk appeared normal on funduscopic examination. He was afebrile, and general physical and neurological examinations were unremarkable. There was no family history of eye disorders.
test_results: An MRI of the brain, orbit and spine revealed a mild enhancement of both optic nerves without other abnormalities. Pattern-shift visual evoked potentials showed marked delay of the P100 component from both eyes and attenuation of P100 wave amplitude.

case_report: A 26-year-old female reported a gradual decline in vision in the right eye over a period of three weeks. She had no history of trauma or contact with animals such as cats. There were no accompanying symptoms like fever. Upon examination, her best-corrected visual acuity was measured at 6/12 for the right eye and 6/6 for the left eye. The optic disc in the right eye appeared hyperemic with indistinct margins. The veins were noted to be dilated and tortuous. A slit-lamp examination using a 90-D lens revealed mild macular edema, while the retinal periphery appeared normal.
test_results: VEP showed a lower amplitude on the right side with a latency of 107 ms. ERG was normal. Fluorescein angiography showed diffuse leakage from the disc but not from the macula or retina. Central fields of this patient revealed a centrocaecal scotoma in the right eye and normal left eye fields. Ultrasonography of the right eye showed an elevation of 2 mm of the optic nerve head. Radiological examination of the skull and paranasal sinuses was normal. MRI of the brain and MR venogram were within normal limits. The results of all blood tests, including serological tests for syphilis, Lyme disease, toxoplasmosis and toxocariasis and the remaining serology were negative.

case_report: A 37-year-old woman reported experiencing painful vision loss in her left eye for a duration of two weeks. Prior to the onset of visual symptoms, she had a fever and ocular pain. No other neurological conditions were noted. The best-corrected visual acuity was measured at 20/20 in the right eye and 20/200 in the left eye. A relative afferent pupillary defect was observed in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination showed a clear anterior segment with occasional cells present in the vitreous cavity of the left eye.
test_results: A fundus picture taken by a fundus camera showed sRD and hard exudates arranged in a star figure around the fovea in the left eye. Swept-source optical coherence tomography showed subretinal fluid between the optic disc and the macula. Both inner and outer retinas were swollen and hyperreflective foci were detected from the inner nuclear layer through the outer nuclear layer. Moreover, the choroid was thickened, accompanied by blurry visible choroidal lumina, and the corresponding retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) line was elevated. Fluorescein angiograms showed hyperfluorescence at the disc and hypofluorescence corresponding to the area of sRD. Wide-field indocyanine green angiograms showed multiple hypofluorescent spots in both the posterior pole and the mid-periphery of the left eye. Visual field examination of the left eye demonstrated a dense centrocecal scotoma.

case_report: A 27-year-old Japanese man presented with blurred vision in the upper field of his left eye and ocular pain/headache associated with eye movement that had persisted for two months. His visual acuity was 20/300 in his left eye. Examination revealed swelling and erythema of his left optic disc. Goldmann perimetry indicated an enlargement of Mariotte's blind spot and a paracentral scotoma in his left eye. Laboratory tests showed a CRP level of 0.5 mg/dl, with ESR, ACE, FTA, and ANCA all within normal limits. Hematology tests, renal and liver function tests, urine analysis, chest radiography, and computed tomography results were all normal. MR images showed no abnormalities in the brain.
test_results: The area around his left optic nerve showed a high intensity.

case_report: A previously healthy 27-year-old Malay male experienced sudden, severe blurring of vision in the right eye for one week, accompanied by frontal headache and vomiting. There was no pain during eye movement and no history indicating infection or connective tissue disease. The visual acuity of the right eye was counting fingers at 2 feet, while the left eye had a visual acuity of 6/18, improving to 6/12 with pinhole. A relative afferent pupillary defect was observed in the right eye. Red saturation and light brightness were diminished in the right eye, with an absence of color vision. A confrontation test revealed a central scotoma in the right eye, extending superiorly to the paracentral area. Initially, the left eye showed normal optic nerve function and visual field, but color vision declined two days after the initial presentation. The anterior segment of both eyes appeared normal. Examination of the posterior segment showed bilateral generalized optic disc swelling, tortuous vessels, and splinter hemorrhages, more pronounced in the right eye. The macula in both eyes was normal. Apart from the optic nerve findings, the rest of the neurological examination was unremarkable.
test_results: An urgent computed tomography scan showed bilateral enhancement of the optic nerves with normal brain parenchyma. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated abnormal enhancement surrounding the intraorbital optic nerves, seen as 'doughnut sign' on coronal views and 'tram track' sign on axial views. Slight tortuosity of the optic nerve was seen on the right side.

case_report: A 26-year-old woman reported experiencing cold-like symptoms for 2 weeks before her initial visit. She mentioned having 5 days of eye pain associated with movement and 3 days of reduced vision in the left peripheral visual field. Additionally, she had a headache. There was no prior history of eye disorders. She was on antibiotics (phenoxymethylpenicillin and chloramphenicol eye drops) for her symptoms. Initial examination showed no relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). Best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 1.3 in the right eye and less than 1.0 in the left eye. Fundus examination revealed a normal retina, papilla, and macula in both eyes. The SST color vision test showed no abnormalities (0p). A confrontation visual field test suggested a possible inferior temporal defect in the left eye. Due to the overall lack of significant findings, no medical treatment was initiated. Two weeks later, during a trip abroad, her vision worsened, with the right eye only able to perceive hand waving and the left eye able to count fingers.
test_results: An MRI scan of the spinal cord, brain, and orbita revealed increased signal intensity in the optical nerve sheaths of both eyes. There was no evidence of any other abnormalities in the brain or spinal cord.

case_report: A 65-year-old female presented with mid-facial swelling persisting for 4 months. Extraoral examination revealed diffuse swelling on the left side of the face, causing elevation of the orbital floor and deviation of the nasal septum. The lesion was tender and soft upon palpation. Intraorally, the swelling was observed to be obliterating the buccal vestibule in the upper left molar region, with the overlying mucosa remaining intact.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a destructive hypodense solid mass, occupying the whole of maxillary sinus destroying the lateral wall of nose, floor of orbit and alveolar process. Immunohistochemical analysis showed strong cytokeratin (CK) positivity with negative vimentin, confirming the epithelial origin of tumor cells. Negative mucicarmine staining ruled out the glandular origin of the lesion.
diagnosis: Papillary squamous cell carcinoma of maxillary antrum-clear cell variant
Orpha_name: Squamous cell carcinoma of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses

case_report: A 70-year-old female patient presented with a primary complaint of swelling in the submandibular region persisting for one and a half months. A similar swelling had occurred two years prior and had subsided with medication. The current swelling had been progressively enlarging, was not associated with systemic symptoms, and was unrelated to food intake. Physical examination revealed a solitary, spherical swelling measuring 3 × 3 cm, which was tender, non-mobile, and firm. No additional swellings were detected in the neck. The oropharyngeal cavity appeared normal, and general examination showed no abnormalities. Routine blood tests were within normal limits, and fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of the swelling was inconclusive. A wide surgical excision was performed, and a biopsy was sent to the oral pathology department for further analysis. A salivary gland along with three lymph nodes and skin were submitted for examination. Gross examination revealed thinning and color change in the specimen, suggesting skin involvement. Cross-section of lymph nodes indicated possible involvement. Four bits of soft tissue were processed: one larger bit measuring 11.5 × 7.5 × 2.8 cm and three smaller bits measuring 0.8 × 0.6 cm, 1.1 × 1.3 cm, and 2 × 1.6 cm. The tissue was soft to firm in consistency, grayish-brown in color, and irregular in shape and surface.
test_results: The histopathology report reveals skin with subcutis and salivary gland tissue. An infiltrating tumor was seen, composed of cells arranged in nests, solid sheets and focally in a glandular pattern. The cells were round to polygonal with pleomorphic vesicular nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm. Foci of keratinization was seen. Few mitotic figures and many giant cells were also seen. A few questionable lymphovascular emboli were seen. No peri-neural invasion was seen in these sections. The overlying skin was not involved by tumor. A dense mixed inflammatory cell infiltrate and focal necrosis was noted. No mucous cells were seen in these sections. The special stains like periodic acid-Schiff (PAS), mucicaramine, alcian blue revealed absence of any type of mucin. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) was done and it showed positivity for cytokeratin (CK, 90%) and p63 (80%). Epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) and S-100 were negative. Neck nodes were free of metastasis.
diagnosis: Moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the submandibular salivary gland
Orpha_name: Squamous cell carcinoma of salivary glands

case_report: A 54-year-old female presented with pain and swelling in the right lower back region of the jaw for three months. Initially, pain was noted in the teeth of the fourth quadrant, followed by localized swelling. Within a month, the teeth became mobile and were extracted, but the swelling persisted and grew. The patient had no significant medical history but had a habit of quid chewing two to three times daily for 20 years. Physical examination revealed signs of anemia with pale conjunctiva and nail beds. There was noticeable facial asymmetry with diffuse swelling on the middle and lower third of the right side of the face, extending from the ala-tragus line to about four centimeters beyond the inferior border of the mandible. The swelling extended anteriorly to the angle of the mouth and posteriorly to the posterior border of the ramus of the mandible. On palpation, two swellings were noted: one fixed swelling extending from the ala-tragus line to the inferior border of the mandible, and another ovoid swelling below the inferior cortex, approximately four centimeters in diameter. Both swellings were tender and firm. The condyle of the mandible on the same side was not palpable, and the jaw deviated to the right on opening and closing. Bilateral submandibular lymph nodes were palpable, tender, firm, and not fixed. Intraorally, vestibular obliteration was observed from the canine to the anterior border of the ramus. The extraction socket distal to the second premolar showed an erythematous granular mass partly covered with necrotic slough. There was no obvious relation between the mandibular mass and the overlying mucosa. On palpation, the swelling was tender and indurated with no cortical expansion. The first and second premolars were vertically compressible into their sockets. Panoramic radiograph showed significant destruction of the right body and ramus of the mandible, extending from the right lower canine to the mandibular notch, with bay and promontory appearance of the margins. The right lower premolars had a floating tooth appearance with radiopaque flecks of bone within the lesion. Posterior-anterior radiograph of the mandible showed involvement of both medial and lateral cortical plates. A chest radiograph was normal. CT scan revealed a destructive lesion in the right half of the mandible, extending from the subcondylar to the right parasymphyseal region, with a unicentric lesion and permeative type of destruction. The margins were indistinct with a wide zone of transition. The masseter and part of the pterygoid muscle appeared bulky, suggesting infiltration. CT scan also showed a large oval well-defined submandibular mass with central necrosis. High-resolution ultrasonography revealed a well-defined nodular mass inseparable from the right submandibular salivary gland with central cavitation and papillary projections. Aspiration of the submandibular mass yielded clear straw-colored fluid. Cytological smear showed squamous cells with mild pleomorphism and numerous inflammatory cells on a background of eosinophilic acellular material.
test_results: Histopathological report revealed islands of tumor epithelial cells with abundant keratin formation scattered over a densely fibrous stroma with dense chronic inflammatory infiltrate.
diagnosis: Well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the mandible
Orpha_name: Squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity

case_report: A 40-year-old male presented with pain and a burning sensation in the right posterior region of the lower jaw for one month, following toothbrush trauma 1½ months prior. The pain was severe, continuous, and worsened with food intake, leading to cessation of brushing on the affected side and resulting in poor oral hygiene. He had previously consulted a dentist 15 days earlier and was prescribed painkillers and amoxicillin 500 mg t.i.d. for 5 days, with only mild pain reduction observed. The patient's medical history was non-contributory, but he had a history of chronic smoking (4–5 cigarettes daily) for nearly 20 years. Extraoral examination revealed a solitary, palpable, firm, nodular, non-tender, and mobile submandibular lymph node on the right side. Intraoral examination showed moderate gingival inflammation with approximately 4 mm clinical attachment loss buccally in relation to teeth 45, 46, 47, and 48. An irregular ulcerative lesion with raised edges was noted on the buccal gingiva near the mucogingival line in relation to teeth 46 and 47. The lesion had a central yellowish core with a reddish periphery, white necrotic areas, and was covered with yellowish-white slough indicating food debris. The lesion measured 8 mm mesiodistally and 4 mm buccolingually. The entire buccal gingiva in the 4th quadrant appeared bright red. Palpation confirmed the site, shape, size, and extent of the lesion, with raised and firm borders, a firm, fixed, and broad base, and no bleeding or exudation. The surrounding gingiva in the 4th quadrant and alveolar mucosa were inflamed and tender on percussion. Gingiva in relation to teeth 47 and 48 showed grade II recession, insufficient attached gingiva, and an obliterated vestibule. Other mucous membranes were within normal limits, with grade I recession of marginal gingiva in relation to teeth 12, 13, and 42. Initial intraoral periapical radiograph and orthopantomogram showed no bony involvement. The patient underwent supragingival debridement and was prescribed etoricoxib + serratiopeptidase 10 mg b.i.d. for 5 days, chlorhexidine mouthwash twice daily for 1 week, and Hexi-M gel 3–4 times daily for 1 week. However, healing was unsatisfactory at the 1-week recall. All biochemical investigations (complete blood picture, random blood sugar, human immunodeficiency virus I and II – tridot method) were normal except for reactive HbsAg. An excisional biopsy of the lesion was performed, and the patient was prescribed amoxicillin 250 mg + clavulanic acid 125 mg t.i.d. for 5 days post-biopsy.
test_results: The sample presented with islands of epithelial cells, altered nuclear–cytoplasm ratio, cellular and nuclear pleomorphism, hyperchromatism, abnormal mitotic figures within the subepithelial connective tissue which showed epithelial cells arranged in chords and strands, infiltrating muscle, and blood vessels. The surface epithelium showed normal stratification with absence of rete ridges.
diagnosis: Moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma  of the gingiva
Orpha_name: Squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity

case_report: A 63-year-old female presented with swelling in the left lower jaw, which she first noticed six months ago. The swelling was accompanied by pain radiating to the left temporal region. The patient has a history of chewing betel quid 5-6 times daily for the past 30 years. On extra-oral examination, facial asymmetry was observed. Intra-orally, there was an ulcerated, erythematous rough mass extending from the region of tooth #34 to #38, measuring approximately 3.5 x 2.5 cm and covering the buccal vestibule. Panoramic radiography showed a poorly defined radiolucency with ragged borders in relation to tooth #35, involving the edentulous alveolar bone up to the molar ramus areas and extending inferiorly to the mandibular canal. A soft tissue shadow was noted above the affected area. A solitary left submandibular lymph node was palpable, non-tender, and fixed to the underlying bone.
test_results: The hematoxylin and eosin stained sections exhibited proliferation of dysplastic epithelium into connective tissue showing nuclear hyperchromatism, altered nuclear cytoplasmic ratio, individual cell keratinization, numerous normal, and abnormal mitotic figures. Dysplastic epithelium infiltrating into the connective tissue were arranged in the form of islands and ductal pattern. These ductal patterns showed peripheral cells, which are of columnar to cuboidal with central regions showing squamous cells, keratin pearls and occasional individual cell keratinization. The surrounding connective tissue is made up of both mature and immature collagen fibers with moderate infiltration of chronic inflammatory cells. Periodic acid Schiff and Alcian blue staining showed no intracellular or extracellular mucinous material in the tumor, including acantholytic and pseudoglandular areas. These tumor cells were negative for mucicarmine.
diagnosis: Adenoid Squamous Cell Carcinoma  of the oral cavity
Orpha_name: Squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity

case_report: An 81-year-old female with a history of hypertension managed with lisinopril for many years presented with progressive lip swelling and a rash over a period of 3 days. The rash appeared suddenly, initially consisting of small, rounded, vesicular lesions on her extremities, particularly on her palms and soles, which later developed into target-like lesions. She also reported lip swelling and skin peeling. She denied experiencing fever, flu-like symptoms, urinary symptoms, joint pain, muscle aches, changes in bowel habits, or recent changes in diet, body products, or living environment. She had no history of similar episodes. She was allergic to sulfonamides, lisinopril, and iodinated contrast media. She had been experiencing back pain for a week and had been taking naproxen. Upon presentation, her vital signs included an afebrile state, a heart rate of 80 beats per minute, and a blood pressure of 143/80 mm Hg. Physical examination revealed a bilateral and symmetrical rash composed of well-defined, rounded, target-like lesions on the distal segments of her extremities, mainly the palms and soles. Some lesions had superficial ulceration and crusting in the center, surrounded by three zones of erythematous halos. Additionally, she had superficial ulcerations and desquamation of her lips. No bullae were observed.
test_results: A skin biopsy from one of the lesions in the extremities showed necrotic keratinocytes.

case_report: A 24-year-old male presented with multiple red, itchy papules and plaques on various body sites. He has been employed in a lithium battery factory and experienced a chemical burn from lithium two weeks prior. One week after the burn, a single red papule appeared on his right wrist, the site of the chemical burn, and this lesion spread to both arms and thighs within a day. Physical examination showed multiple red to purple-red papules and plaques with a central dark area on the wrists, arms, and thighs. The oral and genital mucosal areas were unaffected. There was no history of herpes simplex infection, and laboratory findings were normal except for a white blood cell count of 11,750/µl.
test_results: A punch biopsy showed a scattered lymphocytic infiltration, vacuolar degeneration, and necrotic keratinocyte.

case_report: A 42-year-old female experienced nonspecific upper abdominal pain for 4 years, without fever or weight loss. The symptoms worsened over the past year. Initially, she was treated for chronic gastritis with stomach-protective drugs for 6 months, which did not provide significant relief. Annual abdominal MRI from 2015 to 2017 showed diffuse pancreatic enlargement, expansion of the main pancreatic duct, parenchymal enhancement, no obvious mass, and clear peripancreatic fat space. No abnormalities were noted in the liver, gallbladder, spleen, or kidneys. She was then treated for chronic pancreatitis with pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy, which improved her symptoms. Her symptoms recurred and were managed with oral enzyme supplementation. One year ago, her abdominal pain worsened, and she developed jaundice. She was treated with methylprednisolone tablets and ursodeoxycholic acid, which slightly improved her condition. She continued methylprednisolone 16 mg/d for 1 year until her symptoms worsened again. The patient had no history of diabetes, hypertension, or other underlying diseases, and no family history. Physical examination revealed slight abdominal tenderness without rebound tenderness or tension. Laboratory tests showed slightly elevated serum alanine aminotransferase (100 IU/L) and aspartate transaminase (89 IU/L), with normal amylase and lipase levels. Serum immunoglobulin G4 (IgG4) was normal at 0.217 g/L, and the antinuclear antibody spectrum was negative. Serum tumor markers, including carcinoembryonic antigen (4.21 ng/mL) and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9) (153.2 U/mL), were elevated. Retrospective analysis from 2016 to 2018 showed fluctuating alanine aminotransferase (100-150 IU/L) and aspartate transaminase (70-100 IU/L) levels, with increasing CA19-9 levels (from 38.20 to 153.2 U/mL). IgG4 was negative during this period. Fasting blood sugar levels were normal. MRI at this admission showed a lesion at the head of the pancreas with sausage-like diffuse enlargement, gallbladder and common bile duct enlargement (common bile duct diameter: 2.0 cm), and no suspicious lymph nodes or liver metastasis. Pancreatic enlargement had progressed compared to previous images. The gallbladder was enlarged without lithiasis or thick wall, and the main pancreatic duct was dilated due to an oval mass in the head of the pancreas. Abdominal multi-detector computed tomography (MDCT) revealed similar findings to MRI, with no substantial space-occupying lesion. The pancreas showed diffuse enlargement, predominantly at the head, with heterogeneous characteristics. The patient had dull upper abdominal pain with jaundice only once and never experienced acute pancreatitis. After 1 year of steroid therapy, pancreatic enlargement remained unchanged, and CA19-9 levels increased annually.
test_results: EUS-guided fine needle aspiration biopsy (EUS-FNA/FNB) was performed from the pancreas head.

case_report: A 69-year-old Japanese man was admitted to our hospital for further evaluation of weight loss and worsening diabetes mellitus. He was a smoker and social drinker with no signs of obesity and no history of pancreatic disorders. His latest serum HbA1c level had risen to 9.8%. His vital signs were as follows: body temperature of 37.6°C, blood pressure of 146/80 mmHg, pulse rate of 80 beats/min, respiratory rate of 18/min, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. Physical examination revealed mild left-upper quadrant tenderness without rebound tenderness. Laboratory tests showed that a complete blood count and coagulation function were unremarkable. Serum biochemistry analysis revealed increased lactic dehydrogenase levels (LDH; 1118 U/L), C-reactive protein (CRP; 5.16 mg/dL), and decreased total protein and albumin levels. Tumor markers showed a mild elevation in carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA; 7.5 ng/mL), carbohydrate 19–9 (CA19–9; 109 U/mL), and a marked elevation in neuron-specific enolase (NSE; 270 ng/mL; normal value: <16.2 ng/mL). The level of duke pancreatic monoclonal antigen type 2 (DUPAN-2) was within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a well-defined, irregular-shaped, heterogeneous mass at the pancreatic tail. The MPD was dilated with hyperechoic structures. Abdominal precontrast computed tomography (CT) showed a 97 × 77-mm irregular hypodense mass in the pancreatic tail. Ascites was noted around the liver and pelvis. Dynamic contrast-enhanced CT revealed that the mass in the pancreatic tail had solid and cystic components. The solid components of the lesion showed hypo-enhancement, whereas the cystic components of the lesion showed non-enhancement during all phases. The MPD was diffusely dilated up to 27 mm (predominantly in the tail) without both obstruction and wall thickness, accompanied by marked atrophy of the pancreatic parenchyma. Multiple, well-defined, predominantly solid nodules were observed in the peritoneum and omentum. Following magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), T2-weighted images showed a heterogeneous and hyperintense mass in the pancreatic tail. The area corresponding to the solid component seen on CT showed hyperintensity on diffusion-weighted images with b factor of 800 s/mm2 and hypointensity on the apparent diffusion coefficient map, indicating diffusion restriction. The signal intensity of the MPD in the tail was high on the T1-weighted image and low on the T2-weighted image, suggesting the presence of a highly viscous substance like mucin within the MPD. The correlation between the cystic components of the lesion and MPD was suggested but not confirmed following CT and MRI. The MRI signal pattern of peritoneal and omental nodules was similar to the solid component of the pancreatic mass. Contrast-enhanced harmonic EUS (CH-EUS), the solid component of the pancreatic tail tumor, showed mixed hypo- and non-enhancement patterns. Additionally, the hyperechoic lesions in the MPD showed non-enhancement, suggesting mucus clots. EUS-TA for the pancreatic mass was not performed owing to the intervening cystic components of the tumor and the avascular areas suggesting tumor necrosis. The features of the pancreatic tumor with cystic components that were communicated with the MPD favored the possible diagnosis of IPMC. Since the MPD was diffusely dilated, POPS-guided direct tumor biopsy under endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) guidance was planned. The ampullary orifice was dilated to the so-called fish-mouth appearance. After ERCP catheter insertion into the MPD, extrusion of highly viscous mucus from the pancreatic orifice of the ampulla was observed. Contrast injection during ERCP confirmed the correlation between the MPD and the mass at the pancreatic tail. Pancreatography revealed that the MPD was filled with contrast defects, suggesting large amounts of mucus. A pancreatoscope (SpyGlass DS, Boston Scientific Corporation, Marlborough, MA, USA) was inserted into the pancreatic tail along with the guidewire kept in the MPD. The wall of the MPD was smooth and no papillary lesions were observed. POPS revealed an irregular-shaped solid mass in the pancreatic tail after the removal of the abundant and highly viscous mucin. Visually directed biopsies were performed from the reddish and raised part of the mass in the pancreatic tail.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the biopsied material with hematoxylin and eosin staining showed a marked proliferation of small round atypical cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and scanty cytoplasm. Immunohistochemical analysis showed that the constituent cells were positive for synaptophysin, chromogranin A, and CD56 and negative for leukocyte common antigen, MUC1, MUC2, and MUC5AC. They had a Ki-67 labeling index of 90%.

case_report: A 77-year-old male presented with headache and difficulty in performing skilled motor activities. His medical history includes hypertension, diabetes, and chronic idiopathic pericardial effusion. On physical examination, his Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score was 14 (E4V4M6), and he exhibited finger agnosia and left-right disorientation, similar to Gerstmann syndrome. Blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analyses were normal. Tumor marker levels, including CEA, CA19-9, NSE, AFP, and IL-2R, were within normal ranges. Head computed tomography (CT) revealed a large neoplastic lesion measuring 6.6 cm in diameter in the left temporal and parietal lobes, causing significant edema. The lesion had a high-density area dorsally, indicating hemorrhage, and showed ring enhancement on enhanced CT. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head displayed a subcortical lesion with cystic and hemorrhagic components. The central portion appeared low on T1-weighted imaging (T1WI) and high on T2-weighted imaging (T2WI). The cyst within the tumor did not enhance, but other areas showed inhomogeneous enhancement. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) indicated a low-intensity area. Whole-body CT scanning did not reveal any additional neoplastic lesions. Angiographic examination demonstrated tumor staining via the left middle cerebral artery, with no arteriovenous shunts observed.
test_results: The tumor was filled with necrosis, and a large number of cells with nuclear atypia were recognized around the vessels. The atypical cells were characterized by their oval shaped nuclei, high N/C ratio, and markedly increased chromatin. There was a portion where the disposition appeared to be flowing and enlarged nuclear bodies were not seen. Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) was negative, and cytokeratin-pan AE1/AE3 was positive. Cytokeratin 7 was positive, cytokeratin 20 was negative, and epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) was positive. Lymphocytic markers were negative. Chromogranin A, CD56, and synaptophysin were slightly positive. Thyroid transcription factor 1 (TTF-1) was positive on most tumor cells, and surfactant apoprotein was negative. Thyroglobulin and calcitonin were negative. CD99 was negative. Both 34βE12 and E-cadherin were negative.

case_report: A 2-year-old African American girl with a history of extreme prematurity at 25 weeks gestational age and a seizure disorder was transferred to our hospital with a 1-day history of a rash, conjunctival injection, and crusting around the eye. The mother noted that the child was reluctant to have her skin touched, possibly due to pain, and reported fever, decreased appetite, and reduced energy levels. There was no previous occurrence of a similar rash. The patient did not exhibit rhinorrhea, cough, or congestion. Her medication history included a recent switch from levetiracetam to zonisamide for seizure management approximately two and a half weeks before presentation, as recommended by neurology for better seizure control and adherence due to once-daily dosing. No new medications, including antibiotics, were introduced in the past month. On physical examination, the patient was afebrile and difficult to console. She presented with erythematous targetoid macules, papules, and plaques with dusky centers on her face, neck, chest, abdomen, back, bilateral upper extremities, and bilateral lower extremities, covering 75% of her body surface area (BSA). Nikolsky sign was positive in 9% BSA at presentation, progressing to approximately 20% BSA within 24 hours. Tense bullae were observed on her face, arms, and legs, with sloughing noted on the left upper arm at the site of a prior bandage. Mucosal involvement included erosions and crusting of the lips, conjunctival injection, and erythema and erosions of the labia minora.
test_results: Biopsies revealed full-thickness epidermal necrosis with a pauci-inflammatory infiltrate.
Orpha_name: Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis overlap syndrome

case_report: A 17-year-old female from Kathmandu, Nepal, arrived at the emergency department with a widespread painful skin rash and extensive blistering involving mucosal areas, which had developed over one day. She had experienced cough, sore throat, and fever a few days before the rash appeared and had been taking oral azithromycin. On the third day of medication, she developed a non-itchy, painless rash that began on the trunk and spread across her body. Her eyelids and lips became swollen, followed by blistering and crusting. Approximately 20% of her body surface area showed skin detachment. Azithromycin was discontinued to investigate the cause of the skin condition. Two days after stopping the medication, her symptoms did not improve, and new lesions appeared. A bedside cold agglutination test was performed, showing macroscopic hemagglutination after cooling the blood at 4°C, which disappeared when warmed to 35.8°C and reappeared at 4°C. Blood tests were conducted for mycoplasma IgM and IgG antibodies. Serial dilutions of the patient's serum mixed with 0.2% washed human O group erythrocytes showed clumping up to a titer of 1:128 after overnight incubation at 4°C, which dissociated at 37°C. The complete blood count revealed a total leukocyte count of 8000/μl with 60% lymphocytes and an elevated ESR of 70 mm/hour. Liver enzymes and serum creatinine levels were normal. Tests for syphilis (RPR and TPHA), HIV, hepatitis B and C viruses, herpes simplex virus, Epstein–Barr virus, influenza A/B, and Chlamydia pneumoniae were negative.
test_results: Mycoplasma IgM antibody report was positive (2550 U/ml).
diagnosis: Mycoplasma pneumoniae-associated Stevens–Johnson syndrome-toxic epidermal necrolysis  overlap
Orpha_name: Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis overlap syndrome

case_report: A 19-year-old male first presented at the age of 3 with short stature, hypothyroidism (Hashimoto’s disease), and Evans syndrome, characterized by autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA), thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia. He had been dependent on glucocorticoids since his initial presentation. Although his AIHA initially responded to prednisone, multiple vertebral compression fractures were later identified, leading to the cessation of glucocorticoids due to concerns about bone metabolism. Various immunosuppressive therapies, including immunoglobulins (IVIG), rituximab, sirolimus, bortezomib, and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), were attempted but either failed to improve his cytopenias or caused severe side effects such as transaminitis (sirolimus) and anaphylaxis (bortezomib), necessitating their discontinuation. After a brief period of stability on MMF, the patient's AIHA recurred, requiring prolonged courses of oral steroids and prompting a referral to immunology for further evaluation.
test_results: Trio whole-exome-sequencing (WES) revealed biallelic compound heterozygous pathogenic variants in the ACP5 gene (c.325G>A, p.Gly109Arg/c.526C>T, p.Arg176*). Both parents were identified as heterozygous asymptomatic carriers of one of the variants.

case_report: A six-year-old boy with a history of spastic diplegic cerebral palsy and celiac disease presented to the emergency department with gross hematuria for two days following a viral infection. Laboratory investigations revealed hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia, leading to his admission. He had a fever of 39℃ that responded to antipyretics, dark urine without dysuria or changes in smell or volume, and a petechial rash on his lower limbs. He also experienced lower leg pain without arthritis, fatigue, pallor, and decreased activity. At one year old, he had a similar episode with a three-week fever suspected to be due to an upper respiratory tract infection, treated with antibiotics, packed red blood cells, and platelet transfusion. He recovered but had difficulty standing and walking, which improved over months with assistance. Diagnosed with spastic diplegia and celiac disease at three years old, confirmed by biopsy, he was advised a gluten-free diet but was not fully compliant. He had short stature due to growth hormone deficiency and was on growth hormone therapy. Family history included a sibling with celiac disease. On presentation, he was active, alert, and vitally stable except for tachycardia (129 bpm). Physical examination showed a purpuric rash on his lower limbs and buttocks. He could stand and walk a few steps with support, tiptoeing with ankle-foot orthoses, and had normal cognition and speech. Laboratory results showed low hemoglobin and platelet levels, elevated ESR, normal white blood cells, liver, and renal function, and significantly elevated lactate hydrogenase. ASO titers were negative, and C3 and C4 serum levels were normal. Urine dipstick showed +++ hemoglobin. NPA was positive for adenovirus and coronavirus. Other biochemical and microbiological studies were unremarkable. The direct Coombs test was positive. He received one pint of packed red blood cells, improving hemoglobin levels. Initial treatment included IVIG (human) 10% (Privigen) infusion of 1 g/kg for 2-3 days, followed by methylprednisolone sodium succinate (Solu-Medrol) 2 mg/kg for three days, then oral prednisone, and follow-up with red blood cell morphology. After the first IVIG dose, he experienced tachypnea and tachycardia, which resolved. Due to fever spikes, he received antibiotics after repeated blood and urine tests. Blood tests improved but did not normalize, and urine culture was negative. IVIG was extended to five days, methylprednisolone continued for another three days, and rituximab was planned but not added. He was maintained on good hydration to prevent pigment-induced acute kidney injury. Chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable except for echogenic kidneys with mild bilateral collecting system distension. He later developed mild abdominal pain, with an abdominal X-ray showing no abnormalities. He also developed a headache with photophobia and hypertension, maintaining normal consciousness and reactive pupils despite O2 desaturation and poor limb perfusion. Hydralazine and IV paracetamol normalized his blood pressure but only slightly improved the headache. A brain CT scan showed no signs of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, brain edema, bleeding, or hemorrhage, with multiple calcifications in the basal ganglia. Within an hour, he experienced sudden vision loss, respiratory distress, and oxygen desaturation requiring a non-rebreathing mask. A chest X-ray was unremarkable. Peripheral blood smear showed no signs of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. He received fresh frozen plasma, and urgent MRI and MRA were ordered. He was transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit, where his condition deteriorated, leading to cardiac arrest. Despite CPR, he did not revive, with the rapid deterioration possibly due to cerebral venous thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, potentially resulting from a hypercoagulable state.
test_results: A homozygous likely pathologic variant was identified in the APC5 gene. ACP5, c.549del p.(Gln184Serfs*28) creates a shift in the reading frame starting at codon 184. The new reading frame ends in a stop codon 27 position downstream. It is classified as likely pathogenic (Class 2).

case_report: A 45-year-old woman was referred to the orthopedic surgery department for treatment of symptoms in her left hand. The patient, who had no significant medical history, worked as a cleaner and was regularly exposed to strenuous and repetitive hand activities. Ten years prior, she experienced similar symptoms in her right hand and underwent a procedure that alleviated the issue.
