Over the past year, she developed persistent pain and paresthesia in her left thumb, index, and middle fingers. These symptoms were constant and did not fluctuate. Physical examination revealed positive Tinel’s and Phalen’s tests. However, two electrophysiological examinations did not show any abnormalities. An ultrasound examination of the anatomy revealed a median artery in close proximity to the radial side of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel.
test_results: Doppler US showed the pulsatile character of the median artery that led to direct mechanical impact on the radial side of the median nerve.
diagnosis: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome caused by vascular nerve impairment

case_report: A 21-year-old unmarried female presented with a history of irregular menstrual cycles since menarche. Ultrasound imaging showed polycystic ovaries bilaterally. Laboratory tests indicated an increased luteinizing hormone to follicle-stimulating hormone ratio and elevated serum testosterone levels. She was prescribed a low-dose oral contraceptive pill containing ethinylestradiol 0.03 mg and levonorgestrel 0.15 mg, to be taken once daily for 21 days. After two months, she reported experiencing tingling and pain in the right wrist and the lateral four fingers of the right hand. There was no history of diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, or osteoarthritis. Physical examination revealed dry skin on the thumb, index, and middle fingers. No sensory deficits or muscle atrophy in the thenar eminence were observed.
test_results: Phalen's test was positive.

case_report: A 14-year-old girl from a rural area, the first child among two siblings, with a younger brother who has no significant health issues, and parents who are second-degree relatives, was born from a full-term pregnancy without significant incidents. The mother had no exposure to radiation or drugs, except for vitamins and iron. The vaginal delivery at a birth center was uneventful, and the placental examination was normal, though the presence of a single umbilical artery was not documented. At 14 years old, she presented with primary amenorrhea and cyclical lower abdominal pain persisting for six months. Physical examination showed a normal body type, appropriate height, and well-developed secondary sexual characteristics, with breast and pubic hair development corresponding to Tanner stage 5 and Marshall stage 3. A mobile, non-tender mass extending from the pelvis to the umbilicus was palpated in the abdomen. Inspection of the vulvo-perineal area revealed clitoral hypertrophy, labia hypoplasia, and the absence of an external vaginal opening. Rectal examination identified a tense cystic mass anteriorly. ENT evaluation showed normal external ear morphology and auditory canals, but severe conductive hearing loss of 70 dB in the right ear.
test_results: Abdominal-pelvic ultrasound showed hematocolpos proximal to the perineum and hematometra with an otherwise normal-appearing uterus and ovaries. It also revealed the presence of a small dedifferentiated atrophic right kidney associated with compensatory hypertrophy of the contralateral left kidney.

case_report: A 38-year-old male visited the clinic due to recurring pilonidal abscesses. Laboratory tests showed an elevated white blood cell count of 18,700/L, with lymphocytes making up 64% of the total. The patient mentioned experiencing a similar issue two years prior. There is a notable family history of cancers, recurrent abscesses, and ongoing elevated lymphocyte levels.
test_results: Flow cytometric immunophenotyping was done on peripheral blood. A total of 10,000 events were acquired using FACSCanto flow cytometer with FACS Diva software (Becton Dickinson, San Jose, CA). It revealed three distinct cell populations. Of all these, the largest population which appeared to be of lymphocytes was gated with CD 5 Vs CD19. This segregated these cells into three distinct populations. A significantly large population of cells which was negative for both CD19 and CD5 neither belonged to B or T lymphocyte groups. FMC 7 versus CD23 gating ruled out mantle cell lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Monoclonality was precluded as kappa and lambda showed normal distribution of plasma cells. On CD3 Vs CD16/56 gating the population of interest was positive for CD16/56. This population was tagged in red colour which later proved to be negative for CD4 and CD8. This CD16/56 positive population in red confirmed to be CD2 positive and CD7 positive. Taking all this evidence into account, these CD45, CD16/56, CD2, and CD7 positive cells were confirmed to be NK cells. This NK cell population represented 43% of the total analyzed cells.
diagnosis: Chronic Lymphoproliferative Disorder of Natural Killer Cells
Orpha_name: Chronic Lymphoproliferative Disorder of Natural Killer Cells

case_report: On March 17, 2022, a 62-year-old woman was admitted to the neurology unit with a 15-day history of progressive numbness and weakness in all four extremities. Initially, she experienced numbness in both hands and feet, which was followed by pain in both lower limbs three days later. These symptoms gradually worsened, leading to weakness in both lower limbs and unsteady walking at the time of admission. Neurological examinations showed level V- muscular strength in both lower extremities, absent deep tendon reflexes in all extremities, and decreased sensation to a pinprick in the distal portions of the lower extremities. No other symptoms or physical findings were noted except for the neurological signs. Eleven days after admission, she was almost unable to walk and reported severe burning pain in both lower extremities. Neurological examinations at this time revealed level V- muscular strength in both upper extremities and level II in both lower extremities. The patient has a 10-year history of hypertension, managed with nifedipine delayed-release tablets (20 mg per day), and has no relevant family history.
test_results: Flow cytometry analysis, which performed on bone marrow specimens, revealed 84% of the lymphocytes are NK cells that mainly expressed CD56, combined with variable expression of CD16, CD2, CD7, CD94, granzyme B, perforin, and CD158 but negative for CD3. Peripheral blood smear observed large granular lymphocytes (LGLs), with round or reniform nucleus and an abundant cytoplasm that contained azurophilic granules. Nerve conduction study (NCS) demonstrated conduction blocks in left median nerve, left ulnar nerve, right tibial nerve, and right peroneal nerve, and reduced nerve conduction velocity in sensory nerve action potential of bilateral tibial nerves. F wave was unrecordable in left tibial nerve. H reflex was absent in bilateral tibial nerves. A needle electromyography revealed increased amplitude in bilateral tibialis anterior and left vastus medialis with spontaneous potentials in bilateral tibialis anterior. These electrophysiological findings indicated a sensorimotor polyneuropathy with predominant demyelinating. Left sural nerve biopsy was done. Hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed that a plethora of lymphocytes infiltrated into nerve fascicles, which was further being identified as NK cells by immunohistochemical method.
diagnosis: Chronic Lymphoproliferative Disorders of Natural Killer Cells
Orpha_name: Chronic lymphoproliferative disorder of natural killer cells

case_report: A five-year-old white boy, in good general health, attended a routine kindergarten eye exam where a drooping right eyelid was observed. His uncorrected visual acuity measured 20/40 in the right eye and 20/200 in the left eye. Refractive error was recorded as +5.50 + 0.75 × 105 (20/25) in the right eye and +7.25 + 0.50 × 128 (20/80) in the left eye. The boy exhibited normal eye alignment with full range of eye movements and stereoacuity of 80 seconds of arc. According to his mother, since the age of three, he has experienced periodic swelling of the right upper eyelid, occurring every two to three months and lasting between two to seven days, resolving on their own. These episodes were often preceded by fever and flu-like symptoms. During these episodes, the right eyelid would become red, fully swollen, and tender to touch, without any associated swelling of the face or tongue, and no changes in vision or other symptoms. There was no history of trauma, and family history included a maternal aunt with rheumatoid arthritis. Physical examination revealed a 2mm ptosis of the right eyelid with excess, crepe-like skin and visible subcutaneous telangiectatic vessels. Levator function was good at 12 mm. The left eyelid appeared normal. Both conjunctiva and periorbital tissues, including lacrimal glands, were normal without any palpable masses. Valsalva maneuver caused mild redness in the right eye and eyelid. Initial treatment included oral and topical antibiotics for preseptal cellulitis. However, recurrent episodes persisted and began to affect the left eyelid as well.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the orbits revealed soft tissue swelling but no focal mass.

case_report: A 13-year-old girl visited the ophthalmology clinic for a refractive eye examination. Her intraocular pressure (IOP) measured 38 mmHg in the right eye (OD) and 36 mmHg in the left eye (OS). She reported no pain, lacrimation, or blepharospasms. Visual acuity was 20/20 with -12.0 DS/-3.00 DC x140 degrees in OD and 20/20 with -13.0 DS/-2.75 DC x160 degrees in OS. Central corneal thickness was recorded at 560 µm OD and 555 µm OS. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy showed a shallow anterior chamber in both eyes. The lenses were thicker and steeper than usual, bulging forward into the pupil. The lens edges and long, weak zonules were visible on slit-lamp examination after pupillary dilation. Lens thickness after pupillary dilation was 4.93 mm OD and 4.96 mm OS. Anterior chamber depth was 2.00 mm OD and 2.02 mm OS. Axial length was 20.23 mm OD and 20.28 mm OS, indicating lenticular myopia. A detailed family history was not available, but there was a known family history of high myopia and poor vision on the mother's side. The patient's brother also has myopia and a history of elevated intraocular pressure with appositional angle closure in both eyes. No systemic anomalies were detected during a detailed pediatric examination. Mental status was normal for both siblings. Heidelberg retinal tomography results were within normal limits for both eyes. Standard automated perimetry showed minimal visual field loss and Seidel’s scotoma in both eyes.
test_results: Ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) showed anteriorly displaced small and spheric crystalline lenses and almost 360 degree closed angles. Gonioscopic examination revealed completely closed angles and no anterior synechia was observed with indentation.

case_report: A 45-year-old Nepalese woman reported experiencing acute pain and reduced vision in both eyes for the past two months. She had been treated with oral acetazolamide and 4% pilocarpine drops, and had undergone laser iridotomy in the left eye. There was no prior history of similar episodes. Upon examination, both eyes had light perception vision, with intraocular pressure (IOP) measured at 50 mmHg in the right eye and 54 mmHg in the left eye. The left eye exhibited a mid-peripheral patent laser iridotomy. The anterior chambers were nearly flat, with diffuse pigmentation observed on the posterior corneal and anterior lens surfaces. Both eyes displayed signs of acute angle closure, including iris atrophy, glaucomflecken, prominent iris vessels, and closed angles on indentation gonioscopy. Retinoscopy was attempted but was unsuccessful due to poor fundal glow caused by diffuse pigmentation on the posterior corneal surface. The axial length was measured at 21.63 mm in the right eye and 22.52 mm in the left eye.
test_results: Ultrasound Biomicroscopy (UBM) showed an anteriorly displaced crystalline lens with extensive irido-lenticular contact and peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) closing the angles completely in both eyes. B-Scan ultrasonography showed normal posterior segments in both eyes.

case_report: A 65-year-old female presented with progressive worsening of vision in her left eye. Her medical history did not include any previous eye diseases. She had a notable medical record of 50% narrowing of the right internal carotid artery. The best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was measured at 20/32 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left eye. Both eyes had an axial length of 22.1 mm. Examination of the anterior segment of the eye using biomicroscopy showed cataract LOCS 2+ in both eyes.
test_results: Indirect ophthalmoscopy showed no significant changes in the left eye but an enlarged optic disc with wide excavation, circumferentially radiating vessels, and accompanied by surrounding depigmentation in the right eye. Structural optical coherence tomography during the contraction revealed complete closure of the optic disc excavation by the tissues of the excavation walls moving inward and upward. There were no transient changes in the adjacent retina. At the peak of the contraction, optical coherence tomography revealed a hyperreflective ovoid structure with muscular morphology visible at the nasal side of the optic nerve. During the contraction, the walls of the excavation moved centripetally. Closure of the excavation was observed with optical coherence tomography throughout the entire excavation depth. The presumed muscular structure pushed the excavation walls toward the center of the excavation raising the overlying retina toward the vitreous cavity. At the peak of the contraction, this structure occupied the space between the retina and the lamina cribrosa. Computed tomography did not find any visible abnormality in extraocular muscles or the retrobulbar part of the optic nerve in either the left or right orbit.

case_report: A 7-year-old boy presented to the Outpatient Department of Ophthalmology in July 2018 with complaints of photophobia, tearing, and blurred vision in both eyes. This was his third episode. He reported no fatigue and had no systemic diseases. He also denied recent contact with individuals with influenza or a cold. His birth history, growth history, and family history were unremarkable. He had experienced ocular irritation in both eyes twice before. The first episode occurred 4 months prior, lasting for 1 month, with symptoms of ocular pain, tearing, and photophobia. Ocular examination at that time revealed pin-like nebula in both corneas. Symptoms did not significantly improve after 2 weeks of local antiviral treatment but resolved dramatically after discontinuation of the eye drops. No follow-up was conducted as the patient was symptom-free. The second episode occurred 2 months prior, with main complaints of photophobia, tearing, and a foreign body sensation, and the boy was observed repeatedly rubbing his eyes. Ocular examination showed anterior lid margin telangiectasia and scattered punctate nebula in the center of the cornea. He was treated with erythromycin and tobramycin dexamethasone, resulting in significant symptom relief and a transparent cornea after 1 month. Smears and cultures for bacteria and fungi, as well as a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test for herpes simplex virus, were negative during the first visit at the local hospital.
test_results: The ocular examination performed during this visit revealed that the best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of the right eye (OD) and the left eye was 20/20 and 20/25, respectively. The anterior segment, including the lens, anterior chamber and palpebral conjunctivae, appeared normal in the slit lamp examination. Multiple slightly raised lesions were observed in the pupillary area within the epithelium of both corneas. These lesions were whitish-grey, coarse, and oval-shaped, and some lesions were stained with fluorescein. The lesions involved the epithelium and subepithelium without invasion of the stroma or endothelium. The corneal sensitivity was intact and equal in each eye according to a cotton swab test. The tear breakup time (TBUT) in both eyes was reduced to 6 seconds. The IOPs were 17 mmHg (OS) and 18 mmHg (OD). The eye movements were normal in both eyes (OU). Abnormalities were not found in the posterior segment evaluation.

case_report: A 58-year-old Caucasian male presented with unilateral pain, tearing, photophobia, and decreased vision in the right eye (OD). Symptoms began 4 months prior following ocular trauma involving a vegetal corneal foreign body. After removal of the foreign body at another Ophthalmology Service, the patient was treated with topical broad-spectrum antibiotics and lubricants in the affected eye, but symptoms persisted. One month before presentation, the treatment was changed to include topical antivirals and lubricants. Past ocular history includes partial optic nerve atrophy in both eyes (right eye - following an episode of non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy 7 years ago, left eye - due to contusive ocular trauma 5 years ago). Family medical history was unremarkable. Clinical ocular examination revealed best corrected visual acuity of 0.1 in the right eye and 0.2 in the left eye, with intraocular noncontact pressure of 20 mmHg in both eyes.
test_results: The slit lamp exam of the right eye revealed conjunctival injection, a peripheral, crescent-shaped corneal ulcer situated 2 mm from the limbus, extended on approximately 180° inferiorly and nasally (between 7:00 and 1:00 o’clock). The defect involving the epithelium and the superficial stroma is better illustrated after fluorescein staining. Conjunctival blood vessels invading the peripheral margin of the ulcer were documented. The corneal sensitivity was normal. At the examination of the left eye’s anterior pole, no pathological findings were noted. Fundus examination of both eyes revealed a pale neuroretinal rim (superior two thirds in the right eye, entirely in the left eye), an absent foveal reflex, numerous macular, small, round, white-yellow subretinal deposits, located around the fovea. The RNFL exam showed decreased thickness in the superior, temporal and nasal quadrants in the right eye, while in the left eye RNFL thickness was decreased in the superior, nasal and inferior quadrants, with borderline values for the temporal quadrant. The visual field examination revealed a dense inferior altitudinal defect in the right eye and severe visual field constriction in the left eye. An extensive laboratory evaluation was initiated. The blood investigations including complete blood count, biochemistry, coagulation tests, liver and kidney function, glycemia, electrolytes and inflammatory markers were within normal limits. Hepatitis C markers (anti-HCV antibodies, viral ARN) and syphilis screening test (RPR) were negative. Further immunological tests were also performed: rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP antibodies, antinuclear antibodies, pANCA, cANCA, anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies were within normal range. Urinary sediment analysis revealed no modifications. A superficial corneal swab was collected for several microbiological cultures and the results proved to be negative.

case_report: An 82-year-old woman was referred to a tertiary hospital for evaluation of persistent symptoms following a Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) infection. Her medical history includes autoimmune thyroiditis, hypertension, osteoporosis, and a history of curative surgery for malignant melanoma five years ago. She had discontinued losartan six months prior and was not on any other medications associated with her condition. Four weeks before admission, she experienced sudden-onset watery diarrhea and tested positive for C. difficile. She was treated with a two-week course of vancomycin (125 mg every other day). Despite treatment, her diarrhea continued, leading to her admission with 20-25 watery bowel movements per day, abdominal pain exacerbated by eating, and dehydration with a 5% weight loss. Upon admission, repeat stool PCR tests were negative for C. difficile and 19 other common intestinal pathogens. A CT scan revealed normal organs with fluid content in the colon and no bowel dilations. Blood tests showed low albumin (3.2 g/dL), hypopotassaemia (3.0 mM), and acute renal insufficiency (creatinine 210 mM or 2.38 mg/dL), consistent with dehydration. Combined ileocolonoscopy and esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed normal findings in the colon but notable flattening of villi in the duodenum and terminal ileum. Celiac antibodies were within normal limits (<1 kU/L tissue transglutaminase IgA, <1 kU/L deamidated gliadin peptide IgG, normal levels of IgA, IgG, and IgM). The patient was managed with total parenteral nutrition while awaiting further results. Despite no oral intake, she continued to have 10-15 bowel movements per day and watery diarrhea.
test_results: Histological examination of duodenal biopsies showed blunting of the villi, crypt lymphocytosis, and intraepithelial lymphocytosis in the surface epithelium (>40 lymphocytes/100 enterocytes). In addition, there was severe chronic inflammation in the lamina propia. The same changes were seen in biopsies from the terminal ileum, and colonic biopsies showed marked apoptosis, intraepithelial lymphocytosis, and diffuse inflammation.

case_report: A 28-year-old female presented with bilateral lower limb swelling and non-bloody diarrhea accompanied by steatorrhea persisting for a month. She experienced an unintentional 10 kg weight loss, accounting for 15% of her body weight. Physical examination revealed pitting edema up to both thighs and nail clubbing, with no other abnormalities. Her medical history includes a complicated pregnancy with repeated urinary tract infections, leading to early delivery at eight months. Family history is unremarkable. Laboratory tests indicated iron deficiency anemia, hypokalemia, and folate deficiency. Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibody levels were slightly elevated. Serology tests for HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C virus antibody, and stool cultures were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed mild ascites and hepatosplenomegaly. A computed tomography scan revealed increased enhancement of the gastric, jejunal, and colonic mucosa, indicating an inflammatory process, particularly in the jejunum and to a lesser extent in the terminal ileum.
test_results: The esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed duodenal villous atrophy with focal erythema. Villous blunting was observed in the histopathological evaluation of duodenal biopsies, with scattered intraepithelial lymphocytes (37/100 enterocytes), crypt hyperplasia in the lamina propria, and significant lymphoplasmacytic infiltration admixed with neutrophils, as well as eosinophils (Marsh 3b).

case_report: A 53-year-old woman with no prior health issues presented with a fever lasting 3 days, along with a four-month history of worsening shortness of breath and generalized body swelling. She also experienced increased sweating. On physical examination, she was febrile with a heart rate of 101 beats per minute and an oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. Bilateral ankle edema and extensive abdominal wall edema were noted. Jugular venous pressure was elevated, and a pansystolic murmur was heard over the left sternal border. The respiratory system examination was clinically normal. Basic blood investigations, including full blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein levels, renal function tests, and liver function tests, were within normal limits. Cholesterol levels were found to be low, with a total cholesterol of 61 mg/dl (normal range: 140–239), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDLC) of 26 mg/dl (normal range: 75–159), and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDLC) of 20 mg/dl (normal range: 35–85).
test_results: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level was 0.004 µIU/ml (normal range: 0.4–4.0) with free thyroxin (FT4) 5.48 ng/dl (normal range: 0.89–1.76) and free triiodothyronine (FT3) 11.48 pg/dl (normal range: 1.5–4.1). TSH receptor antibodies were positive with 4.39 IU/L (normal < 2 IU/L). Ultrasound of the thyroid showed diffusely enlarged glands with increased vascularity.

case_report: A woman in her 40s was referred for an enlarging thyroid nodule known for 2 years. She has no other medical history and was not taking any medications. She denied a family history of thyroid cancer or disease. Ultrasonographic thyroid examination revealed a left solid, hypoechoic nodule measuring 1.3 cm in maximum diameter. Fine needle aspiration biopsy indicated papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC). Given a low-risk profile for disease recurrence, a hemithyroidectomy was performed. The surgery was uncomplicated, and the patient was discharged home on the same day. Pathology described a classic PTC measuring 1 cm in maximum diameter with no aggressive or invasive features. It also showed evidence of mild chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis. One month after her surgery, during a regular follow-up visit, the patient reported experiencing palpitations.
test_results: The thyrotropin (TSH) was 0.01 (0.35–5.0 mU/L), free thyroxine (fT4) 24.6 (12–22 pmol/L), free tri-iodothyronine (fT3) 10.2 (3.4–5.9 pmol/L), thyroglobulin 136 (10–65 µg/L) with negative antithyroglobulin antibodies.

case_report: The patient is a 56-year-old male who had an appendectomy at 15 years old due to severe abdominal pain. Post-surgery, he experienced acute abdominal pain intermittently, approximately once a week, leading to repeated hospital admissions for several days. Between the ages of 33 and 34, he underwent five different surgical procedures and was hospitalized for a total of 9 months due to persistent abdominal pain. At 35 years old, he had a jejunectomy for intestinal obstruction, followed by adhesiotomies at 36 and 48 years old, and a jejunum-colic bypass at 50 years old. From the age of 46, opioids were administered to manage severe abdominal pain, and he regularly visited the hospital for treatment. Additionally, he experienced upper respiratory tract edema four times at the ages of 48, 49, and 53, and priapism twice, once in his 30s and again at 53 years old. Over the past decade, he required hospitalization on average 19 times a year due to severe abdominal pain.
test_results: Low levels of serum C4 (3–16 mg/dl) and CH50 (29 U/ml) with normal serum C3 levels (79–102 mg/dl). Characteristic computed tomography (CT) scan findings of submucosal edema of the intestinal tracts and colectasia during an acute attack. Extremely low function level of C1-INH (25.2%).
diagnosis: Hereditary Angioedema due to C1-inhibitor deficiency

case_report: A 65-year-old male presented in May 2008 with a 1-year history of decreased vision in both eyes. He had primary open angle glaucoma and dense cataract. There was no specific material observed in either eye. The patient underwent manual small incision surgery with trabeculectomy in both eyes the same year. The posterior capsules were intact, and rigid PMMA intraocular lenses were placed in the sulcus. He returned in May 2011 for decreased vision in both eyes. Following dilatation, material was observed on the intraocular lens in the left eye. This material was distributed in a concentric ring as radial striations and on the posterior surface of the intraocular lens where it appeared as multiple granular spots.
test_results: Gonioscopy of LE showed open angles with patchy PAS in the inferior angle and darkly pigmented trabecular meshwork.

case_report: A 63-year-old Japanese woman, employed as a farmer, experienced a gradual worsening of her ability to walk and issues with urination over a period of about six months. One month before seeking medical attention, she reported feeling generally fatigued. She was found to have chronic post renal failure due to urinary retention and was on medication for mild hypertension. She had no history of lumbar puncture, myelography, spinal surgery, or spinal injury. Upon admission, she was barely able to walk without support from a wall or table. Neurological examination indicated bilateral muscle weakness (manual muscle testing levels one to two) and numbness in the lower extremities. Sensory testing with a pin-prick revealed disturbances in both lower legs. Deep tendon reflexes were reduced in the Achilles tendons, with no pathological reflexes observed. Due to urinary retention, a urinary catheter was placed. She also had difficulty with bowel movements. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count and biochemical analysis, showed no significant abnormalities except for elevated creatinine and blood urea nitrogen levels.
test_results: A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan revealed a space-occupying lesion at the level of L1 to L3. An MRI scan revealed an intramedullary mass lesion extending from vertebral level L1 to L3, with mixed iso- and high-intensity change in T1-weighted images, and with isointensity change in the T2-weighted image. Upon gadolinium enhancement, the mass lesion was heterogeneously enhanced. A myelography and computed tomography (CT) myelography showed a filling defect at the L1 to L3 vertebral levels.
Orpha_name: Dermoid or epidermoid cyst of the central nervous system

case_report: An 8-week-old female infant arrived at the emergency department with a 5-day history of intermittent nonbilious vomiting. Initially, the vomiting resembled gastroesophageal reflux but later became more forceful. The infant, who was exclusively breastfed, showed hunger and eagerness to feed between vomiting episodes. There was no history of fever, upper respiratory symptoms, diarrhea, rash, or contact with sick individuals. On the day of presentation, the parents noted decreased interest in feeding and the need for frequent stimulation to keep the infant awake. Despite this, she was still voiding well but was generally less active than usual. The infant was born to a healthy 38-year-old mother at 38 weeks gestation, with a birth weight of 3.7 kg (50th–75th percentile). The pregnancy was mostly uneventful except for mild polyhydramnios observed on antenatal ultrasound. There was no significant past medical history or family history, and no developmental concerns. On initial examination in the emergency department, the infant was moderately dehydrated. After receiving fluid resuscitation with 20 mL/kg normal saline, she became more alert. Her blood pressure was 80/65 mmHg, and her heart rate was 140 beats per minute. At this time, her weight was 3.85 kg (fifth percentile), and she appeared nondysmorphic. Examinations of the head, neck, respiratory, and cardiovascular systems were unremarkable. Her abdomen was soft and mildly distended, with no palpable masses or hepatosplenomegaly. No other abnormal findings were noted in the remainder of the examination.
test_results: Initial serum biochemistry revealed the following: potassium 2 mmol/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, chloride 57 mmol/L, bicarbonate 51 mmol/L, and glucose 7.1 mmol/L. Blood urea nitrogen was 1.4 mmol/L, and her creatinine was 26.5 μmol/L. Calcium and magnesium levels were normal. Complete blood count was normal, apart from a mild thrombocytosis of 470×10/L. The patient’s venous blood gas values were pH 7.59, pCO2 of 52 mmHg, pO2 50 mmHg, and HCO3 50 mmol/L, with a base excess of +15 mEq/L. An ultrasound of the abdomen was normal; specifically, there was no evidence of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.

case_report: A 15-month-old girl was brought to our department in 2011 for issues related to growth and feeding difficulties. She was born at 32 weeks of gestation with a birth weight of 2050 g and a body length of 42 cm. Post-birth, she was admitted due to abdominal distention, absence of meconium, and dilated bowel loops observed in abdominal X-rays and sonography. She received conservative treatment and was discharged after 7 weeks with normal feeding and defecation. At discharge, her serum sodium was 139 mEq/L, potassium was 3.7 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) was 19 mg/dL, and creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL. Abdominal ultrasonography showed normal kidneys, liver, and spleen, but dilated intestinal loops. Two months later, she was hospitalized for moderate dehydration with serum sodium at 110 mEq/L, potassium at 2.7 mEq/L, BUN at 40 mg/dL, and creatinine at 0.5 mg/dL. Urine analysis was normal with a pH of 6. She was discharged in stable condition after 5 days. Ten days later, she was admitted again for poor feeding and anuria. On admission, she exhibited severe dehydration, severe failure to thrive, mild diarrhea, and low-grade fever. Laboratory results showed white blood cell count of 5800/mm3, hemoglobin of 10.6 g/dL, platelets at 880 × 103/mm3, serum sodium at 133 mEq/L, potassium at 2.6 mEq/L, BUN at 130 mg/dL, and creatinine at 5.1 mg/dL. Blood gas analysis indicated normal anion gap acidosis with a pH of 6.9, pCO2 of 10 mmHg, and HCO3− of 4 mEq/L. Liver enzymes were normal. She underwent peritoneal dialysis, and after 4 days, her creatinine level decreased to 1.1. She was prescribed Shohl's solution and discharged in stable condition. During a 6-month follow-up while on Shohl's solution, thiazide, and zinc sulfate, she did not gain weight and returned with severe dehydration. Resuscitation with 40 cc/kg normal saline was performed. New lab results showed serum sodium at 134 mEq/L, potassium at 2.1 mEq/L, and chloride at 82 mEq/L. Metabolic alkalosis (pH = 7.57, pCO2 = 32 mmHg, HCO3- = 34 mEq/L), hyperreninemia (129 μIU/ml), and hyperaldosteronemia (317 pg/ml) were noted. She responded well to intravenous therapy, and hypokalemia resolved quickly. Urine electrolytes on admission were sodium at 67 mEq/L, potassium at 28.3 mEq/L, and chloride at 2 mEq/L. All treatments were stopped, and a new diagnostic workup was initiated. A detailed history from the mother revealed that the patient had loose stools since infancy, which were mistaken for urine.
test_results: Stool electrolytes showed Na+ of 64 mEq/L (normal: 20-30 mEq/L), K+ of 50 mEq/L (normal: 55-65 mEq/L) and Cl− of 120 mEq/L (normal: 5-20 mEq/L). Stool pH was 5.

case_report: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 4, para 3, was referred to our hospital at gestational age 33 + 1 due to prenatal ultrasound findings of small bowel dilatation and polyhydramnios, suggesting fetal intestinal obstruction. At 36 + 4 weeks of gestation, an emergency caesarean section was performed due to worsening polyhydramnios causing maternal discomfort and pain. The newborn boy had a birthweight of 2915 g, length of 49 cm, and head circumference of 34 cm. Apgar scores were 10/1 and 10/5. Arterial umbilical cord blood analysis immediately after birth showed pH 7.30 and base excess −0.9 mmol/L. The boy exhibited abdominal distension and secreted thin yellow fluid per rectum but was otherwise stable. Abdominal X-rays at 4, 16, and 18 hours, a contrast enema, and an upper gastrointestinal contrast study indicated intestinal malrotation. A routine presurgical echocardiography revealed patent foramen ovale, patent ductus arteriosus, and normal cardiac structures. Subsequent capillary blood sample results included hemoglobin 9.4 mmol/L, lactate 1.6 mmol/L, normal C-reactive protein, pH 7.36, base excess −0.7, sodium 140 mmol/L, and plasma glucose 5.2 mmol/L. The boy was withheld from enteral nutrition and received intravenous glucose 10% with sodium (20 mmol/L) infusion. He continued to produce yellow fluid per rectum and did not pass meconium. On day 5, a laparotomy confirmed intestinal malrotation. Blood analyses revealed hyponatremia, which was corrected with intravenous sodium chloride infusion. Despite surgical correction, the boy did not gain weight and continued to have abdominal distension, aspirates, and frequent thin stools. He was breastfed and received intravenous fluids. On day 10, breastfeeding was sufficient, and intravenous fluids containing glucose and sodium chloride were discontinued. Over the following days, he lost weight and appeared pale and chronically ill. Blood analyses showed hyponatremia, normal potassium levels, metabolic alkalosis with pH 7.47, and base excess +5.7. Nutritional changes were attempted without effect. Clinical improvement was only achieved by correcting hyponatremia. A stool sample analyzed in the hospital laboratory showed a high fecal chloride concentration of 98 mmol/L.
test_results: DNA analysis displaying a homozygous mutation in the SLC26A3 gene. This mutation is the well-known Polish founder mutation: c.2024-2026dup, an in-frame duplication.

case_report: A 52-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital in November 2010 with chronic cough, exertional dyspnea, and lower extremity edema. Approximately six years prior, she exhibited Gottron's sign, heliotrope rash, mechanic's hand episodes, and nail fold capillary changes without muscle weakness. Serologic tests at that time, including ANA and anti-dsDNA, were negative, and C3, C4, and CH50 levels were normal. Biopsy of ischemic ulcers on her hand knuckles showed lymphoplasma cell infiltration without overt vasculitis. In April 2004, she experienced fever, cough, diarrhea, and vomiting while on prednisolone and azathioprine. Following antibiotic therapy and due to cytopenia, her medication was switched from azathioprine to cyclosporine. Over the next six years, she had multiple hospital admissions for dry cough, exertional dyspnea, and fever. Initial chest CT and echocardiography were normal, but later pulmonary function tests indicated a restrictive pattern, and high-resolution CT showed fibrosis in the anterior segment of the right upper lobe. She developed diabetes mellitus and hypertension three years ago. Her medications included prednisolone, cyclosporine, hydroxychloroquine, amlodipine, triamterene, hydrochlorothiazide, aspirin, and glybenclamide. On her last admission, her body temperature was 37°C and blood pressure was 160/85 mmHg. Physical examination revealed a heliotrope rash on the upper eyelids, coarse crackles at the base of the right lung, and pitting edema of the lower extremities. Laboratory results showed mild anemia with hemoglobin at 11.1 g/dL, white blood cell count of 7900 cells/mm3, blood urea nitrogen at 28 mg/dL, creatinine at 1 mg/dL, 24-hour creatinine clearance at 83 cc/min, triglycerides at 325 mg/dL, total cholesterol at 340 mg/dL, high-density lipoprotein at 68 mg/dL, low-density lipoprotein at 207 mg/dL, and abnormal urinalysis with 2+ proteinuria and urinary protein excretion of 2.2 g/day. Serum creatine kinase was 34 IU/L, lactate dehydrogenase was 579 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase was 23 IU/L, and aspartate aminotransferase was 16 IU/L. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 75 mm/hour and C-reactive protein was 2+ positive. Anti-dsDNA, p-ANCA, and c-ANCA were negative, and complement levels (C3, C4, and CH50) were normal. Serologic tests for hepatitis B and C were negative. Later assays showed a positive fluorescent ANA result with a homogeneous pattern, but the anti-Jo1 test was not available.
test_results: Microscopic examination revealed diffuse enlargement of glomeruli with thickening of the capillary walls, thickened mesangial matrix, mesangial cells proliferation causing lobulation of the tufts, and scattered infiltration of neutrophils. The capillary wall had tram-track appearance in silver staining. The interstitium had no significant pathological changes. Immunofluorescence showed granular pattern of C3 and IgG deposition along the capillary walls and mesangial matrix.

case_report: A 54-year-old white male presented with a 1-week history of swelling in both feet, increased blood pressure, and a rise in serum creatinine from 111 μmol/L to 213 μmol/L over a 2-week period. Laboratory tests showed microscopic hematuria and proteinuria at 24 grams/day. Serum albumin decreased from 35 g/L to 24 g/L over the same period. Additional tests revealed negative results for hepatitis B and C, a weakly positive speckled antinuclear antibody (ANA) titer of 160 (normal <40), double-stranded DNA at 0 IU/mL (normal <7), normal serum free light chains ratio, negative cryoglobulin screen, negative serum protein electrophoresis, and normal C3 (1.77 g/L) and C4 (0.38 g/L) levels. The patient's medical history included hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea, and colorectal carcinoma with liver metastasis. Initial treatment for cancer involved neoadjuvant chemotherapy with capecitabine and bevacizumab, 26 fractions of radiotherapy, followed by right hemicolectomy and partial right hemihepatectomy, and 6 months of capecitabine and bevacizumab. One year later, a 74 mm metastatic lesion appeared in the remaining right liver lobe, and a 16 mm mucin-secreting adenocarcinoma was found at the left vesicoureteric junction, managed by distal ureterectomy. The patient resumed treatment with capecitabine, bevacizumab, and cetuximab, continuing until the onset of nephrotic syndrome.
test_results: Functioning glomeruli showed mesangial hypercellularity, endocapillary proliferation, and double contours in capillary loops. No hyaline deposits were noted in the capillary loops and no segmental sclerosis was seen. There was interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy together with lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils in the scarred interstitium. Immunofluorescence showed moderate granular deposition of IgG and C3 in the mesangial areas and around the capillary loops. Electron microscopy showed deposits in the mesangial, paramesangial, and subendothelial regions. Focal duplication of the glomerular basement membrane was seen and there was mild expansion of mesangial matrix.

case_report: A 53-year-old male presented with a slowly enlarging, firm, non-painful mass in the right parotid gland region. The patient reported no additional symptoms and had no history of autoimmune disorders or cancer. Laboratory evaluations were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) revealed a 3.3×2.0 cm homogenous mass with several enhanced nodules nearby. Surgical resection was planned, and a superficial parotidectomy was performed via a preauricular incision, preserving the left facial nerve and parotid duct. The excised mass measured approximately 5.7×3.0 cm and had a dumbbell shape. Hematoxylin and eosin staining of the specimen showed small atypical lymphoid cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and minimal cytoplasm.
test_results: Malignant lymphoid cells were positive for CD20 and Bcl-2 proteins and negative for CD3, showing a low Ki-67 proliferative index.
diagnosis: grade 1–2 follicular lymphoma originating from B lymphocytes

case_report: A 59-year-old male with a history of end-stage chronic renal failure was admitted to the hospital and underwent a double kidney transplant on 7 September. Post-surgery, he was transferred to the intensive post-transplant care unit (ICU). The following day, 8 September, he was moved to the nephrology dialysis and transplant ward in another building of the same hospital. Fourteen days post-surgery, on 21 September, he was transferred back to the ICU, where he remained until his death on 1 October. Seven days after the surgery, on 14 September, the patient experienced severe hypogastric pain, increased inflammation indices, and clots in the bladder catheter. Rectal swabs were taken, and the patient tested positive for KPC-producing Kp. He was isolated and started on an antibiotic regimen of co-trimoxazole (MIC = 40 mg/L) and amikacin (MIC = 8 mg/L). Initial rectal swabs taken at admission were negative. On 21 September, chest radiography was performed due to flu-like symptoms and breathing difficulty, revealing a bilateral pulmonary infection. Physical examination of the chest showed reduced vesicular murmur, SatO2 of 93%, and a C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 26. The patient was moved back to the ICU, and an antibiotic therapy combining linezolid with piperacillin/tazobactam (600 mg twice daily) was initiated, along with ongoing treatment with thyroglobulin (60 mg/daily) and glucocorticoids (methylprednisolone sodium succinate 40 mg twice daily).
test_results: The UAT and real-time PCR were positive. Increased antibody titer was observed (IgG = 354 U/ml; IgM= 1,153 U/ml).

case_report: A 46-year-old male presented with chest discomfort, experiencing exertional chest tightness for 2 years, worsening over the past 6 months. He was on medications including aspirin, clopidogrel, atorvastatin, metoprolol, metformin, and insulin. Recently, his chest tightness has intensified, causing breathlessness after walking 20 meters. He has been treated for type 2 diabetes for 15 years and has no history of hypertension, smoking, or alcohol use. He is married with two daughters and has no family history of cardiac disease, surgery, or trauma. Physical examination showed a blood pressure of 102/66 mmHg and a pulse rate of 77 bpm, with no abnormalities, jugular-venous distention, murmurs, extra heartbeats, or leg edema. Lung sounds were clear. Cardiac troponin I levels were elevated twice (0.086 ng/mL; reference range, <0.03 ng/mL) during episodes of chest pain. Red blood cell count and hemoglobin levels were normal (RBC 4.55 × 10^12/L; reference range, 4.30–5.80 × 10^12/L; HGB 134 g/L; reference range, 130–175 g/L). Electrolyte, renal, and liver functions were normal. Glucose, HBA1C, and glycated albumin levels were normal. N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (115 pg/mL; reference range, 0–100 pg/mL) and troponin-T (0.082 pg/mL; reference range, 0–0.03 pg/mL) levels were elevated. D-dimer level was 0.18 mg/L (reference range, 0–0.8 pg/mL). Transthoracic echocardiography showed a left ventricular wall thickness of 16 mm and normal left ventricular diameter, with an estimated left ventricular ejection fraction of 57%. Coronary angiography revealed no significant stenosis in coronary arteries. Cardiac MRI indicated an abnormal signal in the front wall of the left ventricle, unrelated to the heart’s blood supply. 99mTc-PYP imaging suggested a low likelihood of myocardial ATTR amyloidosis with a myocardial uptake ratio of 0.88 in the left ventricle. Serum immunoglobulin levels were normal, and serum immunofixation tests showed no monoclonal gammopathy (κ: 21.3 mg/L, normal range 6.7–22.4 mg/L; λ: 24.4 mg/L, normal range 8.3–27.0 mg/L). The patient had no history of stroke-like episodes but exhibited abnormal serum lactic acid levels (pre-exercise: 3.5 mmol/L, immediate post-exercise: 9.25 mmol/L, and 10 min post-exercise: 6.97 mmol/L; reference range, 0.7–2.1 mmol/L).
test_results: The WES analysis has confirmed the presence of a m.3243A>G mutation in the MT-TL1 gene, with a mutation abundance of 14.2% detected in the blood sample. Transmission electron microscopy disclosed local myofibril fragmentation, disorderly arrangement, sarcomere disappearance, apoptotic bodies, and a significant amount of collagen. While mitochondrial swelling was mild, lipid droplet accumulation was notable. Modified Gomori trichrome staining of the skeletal muscle biopsy revealed broken red fibre infiltration. Cranial MRI exhibited punctate high signals on T2WI and T2-FLAIR, signifying lacunar infarction.

case_report: The patient is a 56-year-old Caucasian female, with a height of 168 cm and weight of 57 kg, who was referred for replacing carbamazepine (CBZ) with another antiepileptic drug (AED) that does not cause hyponatremia or thrombocytopenia. Her medical history includes a fracture of the petrosal bone after a collapse at age 16, a right bimalleolar fracture at age 23, chronic alcoholism until age 38 with a relapse between ages 45 and 46, and icterus and hepatopathy at age 39. At age 43, she received bilateral breast implants. At age 46, she developed epilepsy with partial complex and generalized seizures, initially attributed to chronic alcoholism, but these occurred during abstinence. She also experienced a psychotic episode with optic hallucinations and developed hemianopia to the left. Imaging revealed a right occipital lesion hyperintense on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC), and T2-weighted images with bleeding in the center of the lesion, in the absence of arterial hypertension or coagulopathy, and a small lesion on the left precentral gyrus. Five months later, a left occipital lesion (hyperintense on DWI, ADC, and T2-weighted images) not confined to a vascular territory developed. Various investigations, including imaging, functional studies, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) investigations, blood tests, electroencephalography (EEG), and brain biopsy via a left occipital drill-hole, were negative for several conditions. The occipital lesions evolved into gliosis, cysts, and siderosis over the years. Cortical blindness, psychosis, and epilepsy persisted. At age 47, transient arterial hypertension without long-term medication and hyponatremia, first recognized after adding oxcarbazepine (OXC), became apparent. OXC was replaced with CBZ. An AV-block-1 was recorded. At age 49, a pacemaker was implanted due to recurrent syncopes from sinus arrest. Bilateral glaucoma was also diagnosed. At age 53, an ischemic stroke in the left posterior cerebral artery territory occurred. She reported muscle cramps of the small foot muscles (carpopedal spasms) and hypoacusis for years. The patient had various AEDs since the onset of epilepsy, including levetiracetam (LEV), OXC, LTG, lacosamide (LAC), and CBZ, but adherence to these drugs was poor. The family history includes breast cancer in her mother. Since age 53, the patient has been supported by a legal representative.
test_results: EEG showed occasional spikes in the right temporal projection. Cerebral computed tomography (CT) showed generalized atrophy and the known left temporal and bilateral occipito-temporal defects.
diagnosis: Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, and Stroke-like episodes

case_report: A 51-year-old woman was referred to a heart failure clinic due to increasing heart size. She had a dual-chamber pacemaker implanted 24 years ago for a high-degree atrioventricular block and has been under electrophysiology follow-up. She has been managing Type 2 diabetes mellitus for 23 years with subcutaneous insulin glargine 8 units once daily, metformin 1000 mg once daily, alogliptin 25 mg once daily, and glimepiride 4 mg once daily, maintaining a haemoglobin A1c level of 7.1%. She underwent a right total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid cancer and has been using hearing aids for 12 years due to sensorineural hearing loss. For the past 2 years, she has been treated with antibiotics, including azithromycin and ethambutol, for non-tuberculous mycobacterial lung disease. There is no family history of cardiac disease or genetic syndrome. Chest radiography over the past 2 years showed progressive heart enlargement. At the heart failure clinic, she reported dyspnoea on exertion for 1 month and paraesthesia in her extremities. Her blood pressure was 139/75 mmHg, and her pulse rate was 89 bpm. Physical examination revealed a regular heartbeat without murmurs, clear lung sounds, and a generally ill appearance. Transthoracic echocardiography showed severe global hypokinesia of the left ventricle with enlarged cardiac chambers (LV end-diastolic dimension of 56 mm) and an LV ejection fraction of 26%. The myocardium had a sparkling texture with fine bright particles, and the thickness of the interventricular septum and LV posterior wall increased to 11 mm from 7 mm in 2012. A small pericardial effusion was noted, with no significant valvular dysfunction except for Grade 1 mitral regurgitation. Mitral inflow indicated elevated LV filling pressure (E/e′ 20.2). Pacemaker interrogation showed 100% ventricular pacing with complete AVB rhythm, indicating pacemaker dependency. Laboratory tests showed normal thyroid function, slightly low serum sodium (126 mmol/L), elevated N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (1961 pg/mL; reference range, 0–249 pg/mL), and increased troponin-T (39 pg/mL; reference range, 0–14 pg/mL). Urinary tests revealed heavy proteinuria (spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio, 7.22 g/gCr; albumin-to-creatinine ratio, 5811 mg/gCr) and non-selective proteinuria on 24-hour urine electrophoresis. A nerve conduction velocity study confirmed bilateral sensorimotor polyneuropathy.
test_results: The m.3243A > G heterozygote mutation of the MT-TL1 gene was confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

case_report: A 17-year-old female with a BMI of 24.3 kg/m² was admitted for evaluation due to recurrent syncopes. Blood glucose measurements revealed mild hyperglycemia with values ranging from 6.7 to 10 mmoL/L. Hemoglobin A1c was found to be 6.5% (48 mmoL/moL). An oral glucose tolerance test using 75 g of glucose showed a fasting glucose level of 6.5 mmoL/L and a 2-hour glucose level of 14.6 mmoL/L. Fasting insulin concentration was measured at 3.6 μU/mL, increasing to 66.1 μU/mL after two hours. The patient has a significant family history of diabetes, with her brother, father, and paternal grandparents all diagnosed with the condition. Her grandmother is on oral antidiabetic medication (glimepiride). The patient also mentioned a previous diagnosis of mild hyperglycemia ten years ago, which did not lead to any treatment or follow-up analyses.
test_results: Sequencing of the PCR products identified a novel phenylalanine330 (TTC) → serine (TCC)-/p.Phe330Ser-/F330S substitution encoded by exon 8.

case_report: A 23-year-old female presented with severe diarrhea, lower abdominal pain, vomiting, fever, fatigue, and rashes on her hands and feet. She had been in good health until seven years ago when she began experiencing intense diarrhea, significant abdominal pain, vomiting, fever, and generalized fatigue. The diarrhea was triggered each time she consumed wheat bread, while milk consumption did not produce a similar effect. The fecal matter was pale, devoid of blood or any foul odor. The abdominal pain was persistent, localized to the lower abdomen, and alleviated only with medication. She experienced frequent vomiting, up to four to five times a day, characterized by a yellowish hue without any associated foul smell or chest discomfort. The fever, fluctuating between 100 and 101°F, was more pronounced in the mornings and evenings and was exacerbated by regular meals, which also triggered diarrhea. Distinct rashes appeared on her hands and feet, which were neither painful nor discharging. Despite attempting home remedies, her condition deteriorated. She became severely anemic, necessitating a blood transfusion. She eliminated wheat bread from her diet and observed an initial improvement, but her symptoms resurfaced within weeks. Six years ago, she was treated for jaundice. As her health continued to decline, she was referred to a tertiary care hospital for a comprehensive evaluation.
test_results: Diagnostic tests revealed positive tTG-IgA antibodies. Further investigations, including endoscopy and histopathological examination of the gut, indicated reduced fold height in the second part of the duodenum and an increased presence of intraepithelial T-cell lymphocytes.

case_report: A 22-year-old male patient visited the Department of Oral Medicine and Radiology for a routine dental checkup. His medical and dental histories were unremarkable. Family history indicated recurrent ophthalmic and cardiac issues in his father. General examination showed vital signs within normal limits. The patient exhibited long, slender upper and lower extremities, flat feet, and a thin body habitus with the lower segment of the body being longer than the upper segment. The fingers were long and slender. His height was 164 cm, arm span was 159 cm, and body weight was 47 kg, with an upper to lower segment ratio of 0.75. The chest was flat with prominent ribs, and scoliosis was noted. Wrist and thumb signs were positive. Extraorally, the patient had a long, narrow face with a convex profile. Intraoral examination showed a high arch palate with crowding of the anterior teeth and poor overall periodontal status. Routine blood and urine tests were within normal ranges. Chest X-ray did not reveal significant changes.
test_results: Ophthalmic examination showed ectopia lentis on the right eye with iridodonesis. On the left eye, aphakia was noticed due to complete dislocation of lens floating free within the vitreous cavity.

case_report: A 28-year-old female patient was referred for an eye examination due to a mitral valve prolapse. Physical examination revealed pectus excavatum, long limbs, dolichostenomelia, positive wrist and ulnar signs, arachnodactyly, camptodactyly of both hands, malar hypoplasia, blue sclera, and a gothic palate. During a detailed ophthalmic evaluation, the best corrected visual acuity was 20/20-1 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye. Refraction measurements were -2.50DS +1.00DC x 105˚ for the right eye and -3.00DS +1.25DC x 75˚ for the left eye. Slit lamp examination showed a smooth velvety iris without iridodonesis. There was minimal upward lens dislocation in the left eye. Indirect ophthalmoscopy revealed asymmetric cupped optic nerves, with intact vessels, maculae, and peripheries. Optical coherence tomography indicated retinal fiber layer thickness of 95 mm in the right eye and 94 mm in the left eye, with an average cup-to-disk ratio of 0.60 in the right eye and 0.58 in the left eye. Visual field testing showed a mean deviation of -1.92 dB (p<10%) in the right eye and -1.80 dB (p<10%) in the left eye. The patient is not currently on any systemic medications and is not being prescribed any ophthalmic medications despite being a glaucoma suspect.
test_results: It showed a heterozygous mutation in the FBN1 with a novel presumed pathogenic variant c.4001G>A (p.Gly1334Asp) on exon 32.

case_report: A previously healthy two-year-old African American female presented with a two-month history of nosebleeds and easy bruising. She was admitted to the University of South Alabama Children’s and Women’s hospital in May 2015. Examination revealed a few healing bruises without enlargement of the liver or spleen. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin of 8.4 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume of 75 fL, white blood cell count of 14800/μL, platelet count of 61000/μL, and reticulocyte count of 8%. Her aspartate aminotransferase (AST) was 387 IU/L and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) was 449 IU/L. Coagulation studies were normal, and viral panels including anti-HAV-IgM, HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HCV, CMV-IgM, EBV-VCA-IgG, EBV-VCA-IgM, EB early Ag, EBnA, Parvovirus, and HSV-IgM were negative. Further laboratory evaluations showed a negative anti-nuclear antibody, positive antiplatelet antibody, and a positive direct Coomb’s test for both IgG and anti-complement factor 3 antibody. She was treated with a single 1 g/kg dose of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) followed by oral prednisone at 2 mg/kg per day, resulting in an improvement in hemoglobin from 8.4 to 10.9 g/dL. Corticosteroids were discontinued, but she was lost to follow-up over time. She was hospitalized a few times for intravenous antibiotics due to bacterial pneumonia and acute bacterial sinusitis. Her condition remained stable during this time. Immune workup showed normal immunoglobulin levels (Immunoglobulin G 1.090 mg/dL, Immunoglobulin A 114 mg/dL, Immunoglobulin M 86 mg/dL, and Immunoglobulin E 148 kU/L), normal absolute lymphocyte counts, and sub-set population (including CD3, CD4, CD8, CD56, no double negative T cells) via flow cytometry without evidence of autoimmune lymphoproliferative disorder. One year later, she developed jaundice and itching, with an enlarged liver measuring 13 cm and increased echogenicity without gallstones on abdominal ultrasound. Laboratory findings included AST 547 IU/L, ALT 600 IU/L, albumin 2.6 g/dL, total protein 7.9 g/dL, total bilirubin 10.2 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 8.8 mg/dL, prothrombin time (PT) 13.5 s, partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) 31 s, International Normalized Ratio (INR) 1.02, positive anti-nuclear antibody (1:40), positive smooth muscle antibody (1:40), positive F actin antibody (39 units), and elevated total serum IgG (1090 mg/dL). The anti-liver-kidney-microsome antibody, anti-HAV-IgM, HBsAg, anti-HBc, and anti-HCV were all negative. Serum alpha-1-antitrypsin and ceruloplasmin concentrations were normal. Prior to a procedure, she received packed red blood cells (for associated AIHA flare with hemoglobin 4.9 g/dL and reticulocyte count 44%) and fresh frozen plasma. Her pre-procedure hemoglobin was 11.5 g/dL with a platelet count of 101000 /mcL, PT 10.9 s, INR 1.0, and aPTT 31 s.
test_results: Liver biopsy revealed interface hepatitis with a mixed inflammatory infiltrate including lymphoid cells, eosinophils, neutrophils, histiocytic cells and plasma cells in addition to periportal fibrosis with rare portal-portal septa (stage 2 fibrosis) along with canalicular and hepatocytic cholestasis.

case_report: A 37-year-old female presented with generalized body swelling for 2 months and epigastric pain for 10 days. The swelling began in the abdomen and later spread to the entire body, worsening with prolonged standing. The epigastric pain was non-radiating, unrelated to meals, and showed no postural variation. She had a history of jaundice 2 months prior. There were no reports of fever, vomiting, hematemesis, melena, weight loss, or loss of appetite. Bowel and bladder habits were normal. She had no history of blood transfusion, drug abuse, tattoos, sexual promiscuity, or recent travel. She had been managing diabetes mellitus type II with insulin therapy for 1 year. She did not smoke or consume alcohol. On initial examination, she was well-oriented to time, place, and person, with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 14/15. General physical examination revealed icterus and bilateral pitting edema, with no cyanosis, clubbing, or pallor. Vital signs included an axillary temperature of 36.1°C, blood pressure of 120/84 mm Hg, heart rate of 86 beats per minute, and respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute. Abdominal examination showed distension, hepatomegaly, and splenomegaly. Other systemic examinations were normal. Laboratory results showed hemoglobin at 9.4 gm%, total leukocyte count at 4620 cells/mm³, neutrophils at 72%, lymphocytes at 21%, and platelet count at 157,000 cells/mm³. Prothrombin time was 22 seconds with an INR of 1.58. Alanine transferase (ALT) was 310 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) was 936 U/L, serum albumin was 2.4 g/dL, total bilirubin was 16.10 mg/dL, direct bilirubin was 5.20 mg/dL, and total protein was 6 g/dL. Random blood sugar level was 111 mg/dL, and serum levels of sodium, potassium, creatinine, and urea were normal. C-reactive protein (CRP) was 11 mg/L. Serum immunoglobulin (IgG) level was 1095 mg/dL (700-1600 mg/dL). Tests for anti-hepatitis A virus IgM, anti-hepatitis E virus IgM, HbsAg, and antinuclear antibody (ANA) were negative. Serum antigens anti-Liver/Kidney microsomal (LKM) and anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA) were negative. Serum markers anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (c-ANCA), perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (p-ANCA), and anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM) were negative, while anti-smooth muscle antibody (ASMA) was positive. Ultrasonography (USG) of the abdomen and pelvis showed absent flow in the right branch of the portal vein with a few dilated collateral veins in the peripancreatic region, thickened gallbladder wall with sludge, and a bulky uterus (9 x 5.6 x 5 cm). Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) revealed a few collaterals in the peripancreatic and left lumbar regions draining into the superior mesenteric veins, and splenomegaly.
test_results: The biopsy of the liver showed multiple cores of liver parenchyma with prominent bridging fibrosis with nodule formation highlighted by Masson's trichrome. There was marked interface hepatitis and lobular inflammation that was composed predominantly of lymphocytes, plasma cells and few neutrophils. The hepatocytes show marked feathery degeneration with rosette formation.

case_report: SM, a 3-year-old girl with no prior health issues, presented with worsening jaundice, fatigue, and loss of appetite. Upon admission to a local hospital, she was found to have jaundice and an enlarged liver and spleen, but no fluid accumulation in the abdomen. There was no family history of early deaths, liver disease, or autoimmune conditions. Laboratory tests showed cholestatic hepatitis without liver function impairment. Her condition worsened within 24 hours, showing signs of acute liver failure, including an International normalized prothrombin ratio (INR) of 2, increasing blood ammonia levels from 55 to 105 and up to 196 mMol/L, and neurological decline. Five days later, she was transferred to the Pediatric Liver Transplant Centre (Ospedali Riuniti, Bergamo) with stage I hepatic encephalopathy.
test_results: Ultrasound examination demonstrated a hyper-echogenic left hepatic segment with structural alteration, suggestive of chronic parenchymal damage. AMA and LKM were strongly positive (> 1:640), and total serum IgG and IgM levels were elevated. Histological examination showed a normal liver architecture with mild mixed inflammatory infiltrate and minimal portal fibrosis. Immunohistochemical staining for CK-7 demonstrated marked proliferation of medium and small sized bile ducts in portal and periportal areas. Focal hepatocytes demonstrated biliary metaplasia. Mixed steatosis was observed in about 20% of liver cells. Portal tracts were expanded, fibrotic and oedematous, with a moderate inflammatory infiltrate, mainly represented by lymphocytes with spill-over features and isolated granulocytes. Interlobular bile ducts were affected by destructive lesions with focal destruction of basal membrane by inflammatory cells, occasionally migrating within the biliary epithelium.

case_report: In 2003, a routine health checkup revealed an 8 cm pancreatic cyst in a 51-year-old woman. The cyst was monitored with follow-up care on an outpatient basis. By 2010, the cyst had grown to 12 cm and further increased to 19 cm within approximately six months. The patient was then referred to our hospital for treatment. During the initial visit, she reported experiencing abdominal bloating. Her medical history showed no significant issues, including no history of pancreatitis, abdominal trauma, or alcohol consumption. Physical examination indicated no anemia in the palpebral conjunctiva or jaundice in the bulbar conjunctiva; the abdomen was soft, flat, and nontender, with no palpable tumor mass. Blood tests showed normal pancreatic enzyme levels and no elevation in tumor markers.
test_results: The lining membrane had a papillary structure composed of cuboidal cells with round nuclei. The cells stained PAS-positive and diastase PAS-negative, indicating the presence of glycogen.
diagnosis: Serous Cystic Neoplasm  of the Pancreas

case_report: A 20-year-old Asian male patient, with no family history of tumors or genetic diseases, presented with a painful anterior mediastinal mass in March 2010. Laboratory tests showed elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) at 327.6 ng/mL (normal range, 0–10.0 ng/mL) and human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) at 116.1 mIU/mL (normal range, 0–5.0 mIU/mL). He underwent complete surgical removal of the tumor, and histopathology revealed a malignant mixed germ cell tumor with seminoma and immature teratoma components. Post-surgery, AFP levels decreased to 85.4 ng/mL and β-HCG normalized to 1.2 mIU/mL. The patient then received 4 cycles of cisplatin-based chemotherapy along with three-dimensional conformal radiotherapy, with a total absorbed dose of 3060 centigrays (cGy) in 17 fractions of 180Gy each, targeting the primary mediastinal lesion, middle and superior mediastinum, and double supraclavicular area. At the end of 2014, a metastatic lesion was found in the posterior basal segment of the lower lobe of the left lung. He underwent pneumoresection, and pathology confirmed a single immature teratoma. He then received 6 cycles of chemotherapy with vindesine, ifosfamide, and cisplatin. The patient remained in stable remission. In early 2020, he was admitted to the hospital with persistent chest pain and severe fatigue lasting one day. Clinical examination revealed low-grade fever, flushed skin, and splenomegaly. Blood tests showed anemia (hemoglobin: 8.2 g/dL), leukocytosis (15.66*10^9/L), and thrombocytopenia (38*10^9/L). Coagulation tests indicated an elevated D-dimer value (2340 µg/L) and a slightly prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (37.4 s). Chemical analysis showed high lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels (878 U/L) in the peripheral blood. Imaging studies, including computed tomography scan and transabdominal ultrasound, revealed hepatosplenomegaly and seroperitoneum. Positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) showed a diffuse increase in systemic bone metabolism and hepatosplenomegaly with slightly increased FDG metabolism, consistent with blood system diseases. There was no evidence of a second recurrence of the germ cell tumor.
test_results: BM aspiration showed substantial infiltration (67% of all nucleated cells) from morphologically heterogeneous atypical circles to oblong cells containing abundant cytoplasm with metachromatic coarse granules. Chemical staining results showed that atypical cells were negative for nonspecific esterase (NSE), peroxidase (POX), and naphthol AS-D chloroacetate esterase staining (NAS-DCE), except for toluidine blue staining. An analysis of the BM aspirate via multiparameter flow cytometry revealed that abnormal cells were positive for CD45, CD117, CD13, CD33, and CD9 but weakly positive for CD2 and CD22, and negative for CD16, CD7, κ, λ, CD19, CD38, HLA-DR, CD35, CD65, CD15, CD11b, CD123, CD79a, CD10, CD25, CD34, and MPO. The chromosomal G banding analysis showed a normal karyotype (46, XY). 16 myeloid leukemia-associated fusion genes, including MLL-AF6, CBFB-MYH11, AML1-ETO, PML-RARα, and BCR-ABL, were negative through reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). In addition, fluorescence in situ hybridization detected that RARα rearrangement was negative. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) of the BM aspirate identified stable mutations in TP53 P301Qfs*44, FLT3 R973X, SETBP1 N272D, and JAK3 I688F, whereas KIT mutations were not detected. The bone marrow biopsy revealed atypical cells that were mainly oval and short spindle cells distributed in clusters and eosinophilic by hematoxylin-eosin (HE) staining, accounting for 80% of the nucleated cells. Immunohistochemical staining confirmed positivity for CD117 and negativity for MPO, CD25, and CD34.

case_report: A 5-year-old boy, the second child of his unrelated parents, was admitted to the Affiliated Hospital of Qingdao University due to focal seizures and somnolence lasting for half a day. The seizure involved double-eye gaze, cyanosis of the lips, and shaking upper limbs, lasting approximately 1 minute. His body temperature was 38°C. Laboratory tests, including blood routine, blood electrolytes, ammonia, glucose, and calcium, were all within normal ranges. Brain CT showed no significant abnormalities. Neurological examination revealed a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 8. Muscle strength and tone in the extremities were normal. Babinski's sign was positive bilaterally, while other pathological signs and meningeal stimulation signs were negative. The patient had a normal birth and developmental history, with regular intellectual and motor development. He experienced febrile seizures starting at 1 year old, occurring three times by the age of 2. He had a history of viral encephalitis 3 years prior. Two years ago, he experienced headache, nausea, and vomiting following mild head trauma, with normal brain CT results, and symptoms resolved with rest. His mother had a history of seizures, and his sister, diagnosed with epilepsy and treated with valproic acid, also had a history of seizures and coma after mild head trauma. Upon admission, further tests including blood biochemistry, blood homocysteine, blood culture, and herpes simplex virus test were normal. A brain MRI was not performed initially due to the patient's lack of cooperation. The patient received treatment with mannitol (2 g/kg/d), methylprednisolone (2 mg/kg/d), meropenem (60 mg/kg/d), acyclovir (27 mg/kg/d), and vitamin B6 (6 mg/kg/d). On the second day, he had another seizure lasting about 4 minutes, with a body temperature of 38.2°C. He was treated with midazolam and underwent a lumbar puncture. CSF analysis showed normal glucose, chloride, protein levels, cell count, and classification, with negative results for bacteria, viruses, and fungi. The patient continued to receive temperature-lowering measures and combination therapy. By the fourth day, his temperature normalized, and no further seizures occurred. His consciousness gradually improved with ongoing treatment. A brain MRI performed on the 13th day was normal. By the 14th day, the patient had recovered to his pre-onset condition.
test_results: The result showed a missense mutation c.2143G>A (p. Gly715Arg) in exon 16 of the ATP1A2 gene previously reported as a pathogenic mutation. The same mutations were confirmed in the patient's mother and sister.

case_report: A 33-year-old female arrived at the emergency department with a headache, weakness on the right side of her body, and vomiting. Three days prior, she experienced severe throbbing pain on the right side of her head, which was acute and continuous, accompanied by nausea. She took paracetamol 500 mg, but the pain persisted. She had a history of similar headaches with nausea. The following day, during breakfast, she felt a sensation like an 'electric current' from the right side of her head to her right upper extremities, along with heaviness and numbness on the right side of her body and a headache. There was no history of loss of consciousness, speech, vision, fever, trauma, or seizures. She also reported a sensation of objects crawling over her right lower limbs. Two days after symptom onset, the headache continued with nausea and vomiting. She had one episode of vomiting, filling a 3L bucket with food contents, after which she lost consciousness and was taken to the hospital. Her medical history included hypertension diagnosed six months ago, for which she was taking amlodipine 5 mg/day but had stopped two months prior. There was no history of cardiac disease, coagulation disorder, connective tissue disease, diabetes mellitus, smoking, alcohol, or recreational drug use. No family history of similar complaints was reported. On admission, her vitals were within normal ranges: arterial blood pressure 126/92 mmHg, temperature 98.4°F, SpO2 98%, heart rate 78/minute, and respiratory rate 20 breaths/minute. An intravenous cannula and Foley catheter were introduced, and she was monitored. General examination and examination of the chest, cardiovascular system, and abdomen were unremarkable. On central nervous system examination, she was drowsy and disoriented to time, place, and person. She exhibited right hemiparesis with muscle power scale 2/5 in her right upper and lower extremities and a hemiplegic gait.
test_results: No bleeding was detected on the non-contrast CT head. No thrombus was detected in the MRI.

case_report: A 55-year-old Pakistani male was admitted to the neurology department with symptoms of slowed movements, resting tremors in the right hand, and weakness in all four limbs. He first noticed a decrease in movement speed twelve months ago, followed by resting tremors in his right hand two months later. Six months prior to admission, he experienced upper-limb weakness, which later affected his lower limbs, making walking difficult. He also reported severe leg stiffness. Initially, he could walk and climb stairs without help, but his condition worsened over five months, requiring assistance to walk on flat surfaces and making stair climbing impossible. His family noted his voice had become muffled recently. There was no history of cognitive issues, abnormal behaviors, mood changes, aggression, or hallucinations. He did not report neck or back pain, or changes in touch, pain, or temperature sensations. There were no episodes of vertigo, syncope, lightheadedness, palpitations, sweating changes, urinary or fecal issues, or sexual dysfunction. He had no drooling, facial weakness, double vision, eyelid drooping, or other visual problems. He also had no difficulty with chewing, swallowing, breathing, or smelling. The patient had normal blood pressure, was not diabetic, and had no significant past medical history. He had a two-pack-year smoking history but no alcohol or substance abuse. His diet included poultry, vegetables, and red meat regularly. There was no family history of similar symptoms. On physical examination, his vital signs were normal with no orthostatic hypotension. Neurological evaluation revealed signs of Parkinsonism, including a muffled voice, expressionless face, resting tremors in the right hand, and cogwheel rigidity in the right wrist, which worsened with distraction. Bradykinesia was noted during hand and heel tapping. Motor system examination showed significant atrophy of the small muscles in both hands and tongue muscle atrophy with fasciculations. The Modified Ashworth scale showed grade 4 spasticity in the lower limbs, and muscle strength was graded 4 out of 5 in all limbs. Deep tendon reflexes were reduced in the upper limbs, except for the right triceps reflex, which was increased, while lower limb reflexes were exaggerated with flexor plantar responses bilaterally. The patient had difficulty initiating walking, took slow, short, shuffling steps with limited arm swing, and had trouble turning; the retropulsive pull test was positive. Primitive reflexes such as palmomental, snout, and glabellar reflexes were present, along with an exaggerated jaw jerk. Eye movements and cerebellar function were normal, and the sensory system examination was unremarkable. Cognitive assessment scored 28/30 on both MMSE and MoCA, indicating normal cognitive function. The rest of the systemic examination was unremarkable. Routine blood tests, including muscle enzymes and inflammatory markers, were normal. HbA1c and thyroid function tests were also normal. Serum electrophoresis, CT scans of the chest, abdomen, pelvis, and bone scans were unremarkable. Radiological investigations, including X-rays of the cervical spine, CT brain, and MRI of the brain, craniocervical junction, and cervical spine with contrast, showed no significant pathology except for a non-compressive central disc bulge at the CC5–6 level on the MRI.
test_results: Electromyography revealed early neurogenic changes suggestive of anterior horn cell disease.

case_report: An 11-year-old male presented with chest pain and breathlessness lasting for two weeks. He had difficulty swallowing liquids, which later included solid foods. Initially treated for bronchopneumonia at a local hospital, he was transferred to our institute with endotracheal intubation and inotropic support. Two years prior, he experienced difficulty swallowing both liquids and solids, nasal regurgitation of liquids, and a nasal twang. He had residual bulbar weakness from a previous neurological illness. The child was ambulant and appeared normal until three months ago when he developed respiratory distress and was treated locally before referral. He had a dog bite three months ago and received five doses of ARV. Born from a non-consanguineous marriage, his antenatal, natal, and postnatal histories were insignificant.
