His elder sibling was healthy, and he was appropriately immunized for his age. There was no family history of neurological illness or sibling death. The child was afebrile with stable vital signs. Cardiovascular examination revealed a short systolic murmur in the left parasternal region. Neurological examination showed normal sensorium, bilateral facial weakness, and palatal paralysis. Extra-ocular movements were full, and pupils were normal. He had continuous drooling of saliva, leading to intermittent dehydration, and wasting of small muscles in both hands with polyminimyoclonus. Muscle tone was normal, reflexes were brisk, and limb power was 3/5. There was no gynecomastia, and testicular volume was normal. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, urea, creatinine, liver enzymes, thyroid profile, serum calcium, pyruvate, lactate, ammonia, and CPK, were normal. Chest X-ray and CT chest indicated pneumonitis. Echocardiography showed a patent foramen ovale. Blood gases were within normal limits, and a corneal smear was negative for rabies antigen. Barium swallow was normal. Multiple weaning attempts were unsuccessful, leading to a tracheostomy for continued ventilatory support due to respiratory muscle weakness. He was on antibiotics for a respiratory infection. Examination of the tongue during reintubation showed atrophy with fasciculations. Hearing evaluation was normal. Pulmonary function tests indicated a restrictive pattern. MRI brain with entire spine screening was normal, PCR for Survival motor neuron gene (SMN gene exon 728) was negative, and nerve conduction study (NCS) was normal.
test_results: Electromyography (EMG) showed spontaneous fibrillation potentials with high amplitude polyphasic potentials and incomplete pattern of interference. His muscle biopsy revealed neurogenic atrophy.

case_report: A 48-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 5-year history of declining concentration and behavioral disinhibition. Recently, she experienced alternating right- or left-sided facial pain of varying intensity, which improved with carbamazepine. She also reported significant vertigo, difficulty following conversations in noisy environments, hyperacusis, tinnitus, and hoarseness. Her sleep was disrupted by vivid nightmares and frequent leg movements. Her medical history included migraine, hypertension, sinusitis, asthma, and depression. Her father died at age 60 years after a stroke, and several paternal relatives reportedly had early-onset cognitive decline, though details were unavailable. Her Folstein Mini-Mental State Examination score was 27/30, with points lost for orientation and sentence generation. There was evidence of executive dysfunction and cognitive slowing, despite preserved memory and perceptual functions, confirmed by neuropsychometry. The general neurologic examination was unremarkable. Brain MRI showed diffuse, confluent T2-weighted hyperintensity in the supratentorial white matter, basal ganglia, and thalamus, with extensive involvement of the midbrain, pons, and medulla, including auditory pathways. Pure tone audiometry indicated sensorineural hearing loss with a 'cookie-bite' profile, most pronounced at midfrequencies, and transient otoacoustic emissions, consistent with mild cochlear dysfunction. Auditory evoked brainstem responses at 6 kHz showed delayed wave V, not attributable to cochlear dysfunction (given the normal wave I latency and 6–8 kHz tone detection). A test of spatial noise perception showed abnormal binaural interaction, indicating superior olivary nuclei involvement. Peripheral vestibular assessment with electronystagmography and caloric tests revealed subtle smooth pursuit deficits, consistent with brainstem localization. Polysomnography showed moderate periodic limb movements during sleep and loss of REM atonia, suggestive of REM sleep behavior disorder. Extensive investigations for metabolic and genetic causes of leukodystrophy were inconclusive.
test_results: The patient was shown to have a pathogenic c.973C>T, p.R325C missense mutation in the CTSA gene.
diagnosis: Cathepsin A–related arteriopathy with strokes and leukoencephalopathy

case_report: A 50-year-old man presented for a cardiological examination due to several months of exertional dyspnea. He had no prior medical evaluations, never smoked, and did not use any drugs. He was asymptomatic at rest. Vital signs included a heart rate of 75 beats per minute, blood pressure of 135/80 mmHg, and oxygen saturation of 94% on room air. Physical examination revealed mildly reduced breath sounds in both lungs, a soft systolic murmur on cardiac auscultation, and mild peripheral edema. Electrocardiogram (ECG) showed sinus rhythm with a heart rate of 75 bpm, right bundle branch block, and left anterior fascicular block. Transthoracic echocardiography indicated normal left ventricular chamber size and wall thickness (end-diastolic diameter 48 mm, interventricular septum 10 mm, and posterior wall 9 mm) with normal systolic function (Simpson rule ejection fraction 60%). The right ventricle was dilated (basal diameter 46 mm) with preserved longitudinal systolic function (TAPSE 24 mm, S’: 12 cm/s). There was paradoxical movement of the interventricular septum due to volume overload in the right ventricle. Estimated systolic pulmonary pressure was elevated (55 mmHg). No pericardial effusion was noted, and the inferior vena cava was mildly dilated (21 mm) with reduced respiratory excursions. Color-Doppler imaging revealed a significant left-to-right shunt at both the interatrial and interventricular septum, along with moderate mitral valve regurgitation, likely due to a cleft in the anterior leaflet.
test_results: A 25 mm ostium primum defect with hemodynamically significant left-to-right shunting, a 'cleft' in the anterior leaflet leading to moderate regurgitation of AV valve, a restrictive small ventricular septal defect.

case_report: A 41-year-old woman who does not smoke presented with a facial rash and joint concerns. She experiences recurrent episodes of low-grade fever, fatigue, facial rash, and right knee joint effusion lasting 3 to 6 days, predominantly in the winter. She reported no eye or abdominal symptoms during these episodes. The symptoms began at age 5 to 6 with fever and muscle pain, occurring mainly in winter and often linked to outdoor activities like sledding. These episodes have occurred 3 to 4 times annually, increasing in frequency and severity over the past 5 years to 7 to 8 times per year, especially in winter. The facial rash has been present for the past 4 years, worsening during episodes. Recent episodes have included severe joint swelling, hindering mobility, and accompanied by joint pain, muscle pain, and low blood pressure. The episodes have also evolved to include chest pain, leading to multiple hospital visits. Electrocardiogram and laboratory tests during these visits were normal, and the chest pain was considered musculoskeletal. Steroid treatment provided minimal relief and did not reduce the frequency of episodes. Her medical history includes Rosacea, Ménière’s disease, bilateral chronic sensorineural hearing loss unrelated to Ménière’s disease, and chronic oral ulcers that worsen during episodes. Laboratory studies before referral showed an ANA titer of 1:40 with a homogenous pattern.
test_results: The genetic testing revealed a variant mutation in the NLRC4 gene. This variant was a 93-base-pair in-frame deletion of the genomic region of Exon 5 of the leucine rich repeat (LRR) domain that preserved the integrity of the reading frame (Exon 5 starting at c.2258 [5′ end] and ending at c.2350 [3′ end]). This same in-frame deletion was observed in her father who shares a similar clinical phenotype.
diagnosis: Familial Cold Inflammatory-like Syndrome secondary to NLRC4 gene deletion

case_report: A 70-year-old French/Algerian man was admitted to the hospital after a fall at work. He was previously independent in daily activities, including driving and working. Initial physical examination showed fasciculations in all muscles of the lower limbs, leading to further investigation and admission. The patient had stable non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus. Neurological assessment revealed normal cognition, speech, and swallowing. Examination of the central and peripheral nervous systems showed no abnormalities except for fasciculations in the lower limbs and mild asymmetrical leg weakness. His mini mental state examination score was 25, and his clock drawing test score was four out of five, which were within normal limits for his age and background. Addenbrooke’s cognitive assessment and total functional capacity were normal. There were no upper motor neuron signs, and he could walk without assistance. An initial MRI scan showed no abnormalities in the brain or cervical spine. Nerve conduction studies were normal, and an EMG on day 9 showed widespread active and chronic partial denervation in all sampled skeletal muscles, with fibrillation and fasciculation potentials present in all examined muscles and limbs. A week after presentation, the patient had increased difficulty walking and worsening leg weakness. Fasciculations had spread to the lumbar and thoracic paraspinal muscles and upper limbs. EEG revealed nonspecific slow wave changes without epileptiform activity. By day 10, the patient experienced worsening lower and upper limb weakness and some cognitive decline. On day 16, he reported short-term memory loss, had a supranuclear palsy of upgaze, and worsening limb weakness. Fasciculations had spread to his neck and facial muscles, but his tongue remained normal without fasciculations. There was marked cognitive deterioration. By day 30, his limb strength had further deteriorated, and he became progressively bed-bound and confused.
test_results: The 14-3-3 protein was detected in his cerebrospinal fluid, which was otherwise normal and without malignant cells. A repeat MRI scan revealed multiple areas of diffusion-weighted imaging positivity in the basal ganglia, right cingulate gyrus and the anterior border of the right caudate head. A second EEG revealed increases in slow wave activity. Six days later, the EEG demonstrated isolated epileptogenic activity in the left temporal and parietal regions with diffuse periodic discharges. A postmortem examination revealed patchy neuronal loss, mild reactive astrogliosis and numerous diffuse neuritic plaques within the brain, with several leptomeningeal and cortical blood vessels positive for beta-amyloid. Spongiform change was widespread in the neocortex. Immunohistological staining for the 12F10 prion antibody revealed patchy synaptic-like positivity in the cerebral cortex, thalamus, cerebellar cortex and brainstem motor neurons. The brain and spinal cord were macroscopically normal.

case_report: A five-year-old girl exhibited an inability to use her hands, with symptoms starting at the age of three. All fingers on both hands were locked in an extended position, and she was unable to actively flex the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints. Passive flexion did not release the locked positions. Palpable nodules were present over the proximal phalanges of all fingers. Thumb movements were normal, but there was noticeable thenar muscle wasting. Urine analysis for glycosaminoglycans excretion was negative.
test_results: Serum enzyme analysis revealed beta-glucoronidase 14.1564 mU/ml (norm: 0.281-1.991 mU/ ml); alpha-mannosidase 15.9537 mU/ml (norm: 0.10-0.262 mU/ml); beta–mannosidase 48.1079 mU/ml (norm: 3.918-11.65 mU/ml); total hexamin 229.6 mU/ml (norm: 8,916-27.07 mU/ml).

case_report: A 12-year-old female patient presented to the Department of Oncology, Tbilisi State Medical University (Tbilisi, Georgia) in July 2013 with complaints of swelling and pain on the right side of the lower jaw. Clinical examination identified a firm, palpable mass primarily located within the body of the right mandible. Radiological imaging showed the lesion had regular contours and a marginal amount of calcification. The patient underwent a partial resection of the right lower jaw, and the lesion was completely removed surgically. Reconstruction of the jaw defect was performed using titanium implants and an autologous VI rib graft. Macroscopic examination of the excised mass revealed an oval shape, measuring 3.5 cm at its greatest diameter, with a brown, nodular outer surface and a predominantly red cut surface. The mass had a rough consistency, with both soft and firm areas of bone tissue.
test_results: Histopathological analysis revealed vascularized fibrous connective tissue with bony trabeculae, which was lined by numerous osteoblasts and scattered osteoclasts.

case_report: A 63-year-old woman experienced abdominal pain and diarrhea for two weeks. An initial transabdominal ultrasonography at a local hospital revealed a dilated main pancreatic duct in the pancreatic tail, prompting a referral to our hospital. The patient had no personal or family history of pancreatic disease. Physical examination showed no abnormalities. Laboratory tests indicated normal levels of serum amylase, lipase, and tumor markers such as carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9). Contrast-enhanced pancreas computed tomography (CT) demonstrated moderate dilatation of the main pancreatic duct in the pancreatic tail without any obstructive mass. There was no evidence of peripancreatic fatty infiltration or lymph node enlargement.
test_results: The unenhanced and gadolinium-enhanced pancreas MR images showed an enhancing mass in the dilated main pancreatic duct of the pancreatic body, which resulted in obstruction and dilatation of the upstream main pancreatic duct. MRCP showed a filling defect due to an intraductal mass with dilatation of the upstream main pancreatic duct with no dilatation of the downstream main pancreatic duct. An endoscopic retrograde pancreatogram showed a filling defect of the contrast media due to a mass in the dilated, yet patent main pancreatic duct.
diagnosis: Intraductal Tubular Carcinoma  of the Pancreas

case_report: A 22-year-old breastfeeding woman presented with a two-day history of metamorphopsia in her right eye. She had myopia (-5.5 D) in both eyes. On initial examination, her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/50 (6/15 in Snellen visual acuity of 6 meters) in the right eye and 20/20 (6/6 in Snellen visual acuity of 6 meters) in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination of the ocular anterior segment showed no significant abnormalities in either eye. Fundus photography revealed a distributed yellow-white lesion in the macular region of the right eye. The patient was advised to follow up without any treatment. Two weeks later, she returned with a complaint of decreased visual acuity in the right eye, which had worsened to 20/200 (6/60 in Snellen visual acuity of 6 meters). A small yellow-white lesion was observed in the inferior nasal area of the fovea.
test_results: SD-OCT imaging revealed disruption of the EZ zone with minimal sub-retinal fluid and a slight elevation of RPE, while no choroidal hyper-or hypo-transmission below the level of RPE was observed. SD-OCT imaging showed a moderate reflective material under RPE with disruption of BM (Bruch’s membrane), and hyper-transmission in the choroid. The 3×3 mm SD-OCTA en face image showed an abnormal vascular network. SD-OCT images began to show an area of choroidal hypo-transmission adjacent to the areas of a choroidal hyper-transmission.
diagnosis: Choroidal Neovascularization secondary to Punctate Inner Choroidopathy

case_report: A 26-year-old Caucasian woman reported experiencing blurred vision in both eyes for the past year. She had no notable systemic illnesses or family medical history. The best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was measured at 20/30 in the right eye (RE) and 20/20 in the left eye (LE). No clinically significant refractive error was detected.
test_results: Fundoscopy evidenced multiple, small, round, yellow-white lesions limited to the posterior pole of both eyes, with greater macular involvement in the RE. Fluorescein angiography (FA) revealed the presence of multiple hyper fluorescent lesions more evident in the later stages of the angiogram in both eyes. On indocyanine green angiography (ICG), these lesions appeared hypofluorescent in both early and late phases. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) showed the presence of focal elevations of the RPE with underlying hyporeflective space, bilaterally.

case_report: A 26-year-old female reported experiencing vision loss and metamorphopsia in her left eye over the past five days. Her refractive error was measured at -7.25 D in both eyes. The best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/20 (6/6 in Snellen visual acuity of 6 meters) in the right eye and 20/40 (6/12 in Snellen visual acuity of 6 meters) in the left eye. Examination of the anterior chamber and vitreous cavity showed no signs of inflammation. Fundoscopy of the left eye revealed sporadic, small, round, yellow-white spots confined to the posterior pole, with no evidence of hemorrhage.
test_results: SD-OCT showed the presence of focal elevation of the EZ band with underlying hyper-reflective material. RPE and BM were integral and neither choroidal hyper-transmission nor hypo-transmission was observed below the lesion. No sign of CNV was found using OCTA.

case_report: A seven-year-old male presented with short stature and skeletal abnormalities. He was born to parents who are not related by blood, and there is no known family history of similar conditions. Physical examination revealed a pigeon-chest deformity and noticeable bowing of the lower limbs. The patient demonstrated normal cognitive function. Measurements showed his height in the 50th percentile, with a disproportionate shortness of the trunk and a distended abdomen, but no enlargement of the liver or spleen was detected.
test_results: X-ray showed genu valgum in the lower extremities, with the bowing of lower legs. Further laboratory reports confirmed the presence of rickets and inclusion bodies in the lymphocytes of the patient.

case_report: An 83-year-old male with a history of hypertension, stage three chronic kidney disease, hypothyroidism, transient ischemic attack, and sleep apnea presented with three weeks of pleuritic chest pain, fatigue, subjective fevers, and progressive shortness of breath. Initial ECG showed supraventricular tachycardia interpreted as new-onset atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response. Laboratory results indicated no electrolyte abnormalities, with creatinine at 1.5 mg/dL (baseline 1.5-1.9 mg/dL) and troponin-I within normal limits at 0.01 ng/mL. Tests for Influenza A, B, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) via nasal PCR were negative, as was the COVID-19 nasal rapid PCR. Thyroid-stimulating hormone was within normal limits at 1.902 lU/ml. Elevated levels were noted for C-reactive protein (8.3 mg/dL), fibrinogen (583 mg/dL), and brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) (182 pg/mL). A trans-thoracic echocardiogram showed a preserved ejection fraction of 55-60% with moderate concentric hypertrophy and no pericardial effusion. The patient initially received intravenous diltiazem boluses, followed by a brief continuous diltiazem infusion, which was discontinued due to hypotension. Intravenous amiodarone was administered for rhythm control, and renally dosed apixaban was given for a CHA₂DS₂-VASc score of five. Short-acting intravenous diltiazem was restarted and up-titrated for adequate rate control with hemodynamic stability. Adenosine administration revealed atrial flutter with variable AV block. Persistent elevated rates despite initial rate and rhythm control strategies led to consideration of cardioversion for rhythm control. Intracardiac thrombi were excluded via transesophageal echocardiography, and the patient underwent successful electrical cardioversion.
test_results: A post-cardioversion 12 lead ECG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm with ST elevations present in the precordial leads with concomitant T-wave abnormalities in V2 through V6, limb leads I, II, and aVL. PR-segment depression was seen in leads I, II, V2, V3, and ST depression in lead aVR.

case_report: A 62-year-old woman with a history of adenocarcinoma of the rectum and genital cancer underwent abdominoperineal resection with a permanent left ostomy and total hysterectomy at the age of 37. Nine years later, she was found to have colonic polyps with malignant transformation and was treated by surgical resection (colotomy and polypectomy). In 1993 and 1997, she had benign colonic polyps which were excised endoscopically. In March and June 2003, she was referred to our surgical outpatient department with subcutaneous lesions, first on the left side of the abdominal wall and then on the right buttock.
test_results: The lesions were excised under local anesthesia and were reported to be sebaceous adenomas.

case_report: A 30-year-old female experienced episodes of transient loss of consciousness, blurred vision, hearing loss in both ears, tinnitus, and slurred speech. Prior to her visit to our department, she had been consulting the gastroenterology department for over three years due to recurrent epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Despite undergoing peroral and transanal enteroscopy, no significant abnormalities were detected. At the age of 23, she had a left ovarian teratoma removed, and at 26, she was identified with a teratoma in the right ovary but did not receive treatment for it.
test_results: Her cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) demonstrated 1 leukocyte/μL, moderately elevated protein (72 mg/dL), and negativity for oligoclonal immunoglobulin G (IgG) bands (OCBs), and no neoplastic cells were found. She tested for CSF and serum AQP4-IgG, MOG-IgG, glial fibrillary acidic protein antibody (GFAP-IgG), and the autoimmune encephalitis antibody panel, which were all negative. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintense and contrast-enhancing lesions in the thalamus, hypothalamus, and area postrema. MRI was also done on the spinal cord, but no lesions were remarkable.
Orpha_name: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder without anti-MOG and without anti-AQP4 antibodies

case_report: A 30-year-old Asian man presented with a sudden onset of high fever reaching 40°C, chills, and severe headache in June 2015. Upon admission to a local hospital, initial treatment with anti-infection therapy was ineffective. One month later, he was admitted to our neurology ward with a fever of 39°C and neck stiffness, while remaining conscious. Laboratory tests showed a peripheral blood white blood cell (WBC) count of 12 × 10^9/L with 89.7% neutrophils. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed an opening pressure of 180 mmH2O, a WBC count of 205 × 10^6/L (61% neutrophils and 32% lymphocytes), and a protein level of 0.67 g/L, with normal glucose and chloride levels. Brain contrast-enhanced MRI showed no abnormalities. Empiric therapy with ceftriaxone and ganciclovir for 5 days did not improve his condition. Tests for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and CSF smear were negative. Vancomycin was added for 1 week without positive results. Elevated C-reactive protein (CRP, 30 μg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR, 49 mm/h) were noted, but extensive serological and microbiological examinations of the CSF, including bacterial culture, brucella, syphilis, human immunodeficiency virus, and virus nucleic acid and antibodies for herpes simplex virus I/II, cytomegalovirus, rubella virus, and toxoplasma, were unremarkable. Repeated lumbar punctures showed minimal changes, except for a decreased CSF glucose level (1.9 mmol/L). Empiric antituberculosis treatment and dexamethasone (10 mg/day for 1 week) were initiated, leading to symptom improvement. The patient was discharged and continued antituberculosis medication. One month post-discharge, he experienced dizziness, left-sided numbness, and bilateral lower limb weakness. Lumbar puncture at this time showed no evidence of disease, but he was readmitted in August 2015. Neurological examination revealed pain disorder below the chest and muscle strength of grade four out of five in both lower limbs. He also experienced frequent hiccups during hospitalization.
test_results: MRI revealed abnormal T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery signals in the dorsal pons adjacent to the fourth ventricle, left medial thalamus, dorsal medulla (area postrema), and gray matter of the spinal cord (C3–T6). Autoimmune antibodies tests both with a tissue-based assay and a cell-based assay in CSF and serum, including tests for anti-AQP4 and anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) antibodies, were all negative. The Oligoclonal bands and myelin basic protein in CSF were also negative. Rheumatic-associated antibodies including anti-nuclear antibodies and anti-SSA/SSB antibodies, as well as the thyroid-related antibodies were all negative. Visual evoked potential was normal.
diagnosis: Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder , anti-AQP4/anti-MOG negative
Orpha_name: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder without anti-MOG and without anti-AQP4 antibodies

case_report: A 35-year-old African American female presented with vision loss in the right eye. Nine days prior, she experienced sudden painful vision loss in the right eye, transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus, headache, and nausea. An MRI of the brain was normal. She received three days of daily one-gram IVMP without improvement. Over the next nine days, her vision worsened, and she required assistance to navigate. She denied numbness, balance issues, diplopia, fatigue, urogenital dysfunction, dizziness, slurred speech, cough, shortness of breath, rashes, and arthralgias. Her medical history included a second-trimester pregnancy loss but was otherwise non-significant. She had no history of tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drug use, and her family history was unremarkable. Physical examination showed she was 5 feet 4 inches tall, weighed 212 pounds, with a BMI of 36.4. She ambulated without difficulty, had a normal gait and posture, and a negative Romberg sign. Facial strength was full and symmetrical, and gross hearing was intact. Her right eye could barely perceive light, and she could not count fingers. The left eye had some light perception and vague image perception described as shadows. Both eyes exhibited a Marcus-Gunn pupil. Accommodation could not be tested due to poor visual acuity. Extra-ocular motion was full in all directions. The rest of the cranial nerves were normal. Muscle strength was 5/5 in all extremities, and deep tendon reflexes were 2+ bilaterally. Sensory examination was normal in the fingers and toes. Lumbar puncture revealed a normal CSF pressure of 15 cm of water. CSF analysis and plasma serology showed negative MOG and AQP-4 autoantibodies, with non-inflammatory CSF and normal immunoglobulin indices. Chest CT scan showed no hilar adenopathy, and carotid duplex ultrasound showed no stenosis. An additional five-day course of daily one-gram IVMP did not improve her vision.
test_results: A repeat MRI of the brain and orbits with and without contrast revealed enhancement of the right optic nerve and its sheath in its intracanalicular and prechiasmatic portion. There was also evidence of enhancement in the left optic nerve.
Orpha_name: Isolated optic neuritis without anti-MOG antibodies

case_report: A 15-month-old boy with normal developmental milestones presented to the hospital with a 3-day history of fever, followed by a seizure episode in the afternoon. Post-seizure, the patient became comatose. Upon evaluation, his Glasgow Coma Score (GCS) was 3/15 (E1V1M1). Physical examination revealed small pupils and absence of pharyngeal, pupillary, corneal, and orbital reflexes. No meningeal signs were observed. Prior to hospitalization, he received intravenous ceftriaxone at a clinic.
test_results: The MRI images showed inhomogeneous areas of increased signal in T2-weighted images in the dorsal part of pons, midbrain, medulla, bilateral thalamus, and right frontal cortex and left cerebellar hemispheres. An electroencephalogram revealed generalized cerebral dysfunction with no definitive irritable foci. Lumbar puncture revealed that the cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) cell count was 3 × 106/L cells (67 % lymphocytes, 33 % neutrophils), protein was 604 mg/L, and glucose was 3.4 mmol/L (capillary blood glucose was 4.1 mmol/L), and chloride was 114 mmol/L.
diagnosis: acute disseminated encephalomyelitis  with bilateral abducens nerve palsy
Orpha_name: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis without anti-MOG antibodies

case_report: A 30-year-old Korean man presented with a growing palpable mass in the abdominal region, which he had noticed enlarging over a period of 6 months. There was no family or personal history of tuberous sclerosis. On physical examination, a non-tender, palpable mass was found in the periumbilical area. A chest radiogram was normal. Colonoscopic examination revealed non-specific abnormal findings. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen showed an intraabdominal mass approximately 7.5 cm in size, appearing to originate from the falciform ligament. The mass was well enhanced and exhibited wall calcification. Laboratory data showed no abnormalities. Surgical excision was performed. The resected specimen weighed 199.1 grams and measured 8.0×7.0×5.5 cm. It was a uniloculated cystic mass with a solid portion. The solid portion was yellow-brown in color and showed areas of hemorrhage and necrotic changes.
test_results: Histological examination showed sheets of spindle-to-epithelioid cells with clear-to-eosinophilic cytoplasm. Tumor cells were positive for HMB-45 and smooth muscle actin (SMA). They were also positive for the S-100 and were negative for the CD117 (c-kit). The tumor cells were also negative for Factor VIII, CD34, CD31, CK, and desmin. The tumor showed high cellularity and necrotic foci. The Ki-67 proliferative index was approximatively 15 percent of cells.

case_report: An 18-year-old female presented with a palpable mass in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. She had no relevant past medical or family history. Imaging revealed that the mass had increased in size from 1.5 × 1.3 cm to 3.4 × 2.7 cm within a seven-month period. The patient visited Samsung Medical Center in Seoul, Korea, following a procedure in another hospital.
test_results: Ultrasonographic examination revealed that the mass had increased in size from 1.5 × 1.3 cm to 3.4 × 2.7 cm within a seven-month period. The gross examination showed a well-encapsulated, 4 × 3.2-cm–sized mass, and the cut surface was homogeneously solid and brown. Microscopic findings revealed a thick fibrous capsule wherein epithelioid cells were arranged in a nested architecture surrounded by branching thin-walled vessels. The individual epithelioid cells had clear to granular cytoplasm. Spindle cells were not observed. The nuclei of the tumor cells were uniform and round, and showed mild atypia. Occasional melanin pigments were noted in the cytoplasm of the tumor cells. Necrosis was not identified, and mitoses were counted at up to 3 per 10 high-power fields (HPFs). The tumor showed diffuse strong positivity to HMB45 and TFE3. TSC2 was also positive. Melan A, smooth muscle actin, S100 protein, and cytokeratin were not expressed. Moreover, progesterone receptor (PR) was positive, while estrogen receptor (ER) was negative.
diagnosis: Perivascular Epithelioid Cell Tumor  with TFE3 expression

case_report: A 62-year-old woman attended a routine check-up following a minor foot injury. Elevated liver enzyme levels were observed. Abdominal ultrasonography identified a submucosal mass in the stomach. The patient had no signs of tuberous sclerosis complex or a family history of it. Abdominal computed tomography showed a 4.2-cm subepithelial mass with a broad base in the prepyloric antrum. Endoscopic ultrasound revealed a hypoechoic mass involving the proper muscle layer. A laparoscopic wedge resection of the stomach was performed. No lymph node enlargement or peritoneal metastasis was detected. The patient was discharged post-surgery without complications. Gross examination of the subepithelial mass showed it measured 4.2×3.2×2.0 cm with a fleshy cut surface and a well-defined border.
test_results: Microscopically, the tumor displayed a nested pattern of epithelioid tumor cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and round to oval nuclei. The nests were surrounded by thin walled capillaries and a radial arrangement of tumor cells was found around the vascular lumens. The tumor cells showed mild pleomorphism, but coagulation necrosis was not observed. The mitotic count was 1 in 50 high power fields (HPF). Lymphovascular or perineural invasion was not found. The tumor was focally positive for human melanoma black 45 (HMB-45), smooth muscle actin (SMA), and desmin, and negative for Melan A, vimentin, CD117, CD34, S100, pancytokeratin, and transcription factor E3 (TFE3). The Ki-67 labeling index was 1%.

case_report: A 53-year-old male with a history of hypercholesterolemia and colon polyps reported experiencing penile pain and burning during urination for the past 10 years. The pain, described as burning, was localized at the distal end of the penis and did not extend along the shaft, with an intensity of 6-8/10 on the numerical rating scale (NRS). There was no history of trauma, and no lesions or erythema were observed on the penis. The pain intensified during defecation and was partially alleviated by taking amitriptyline 50mg once daily. Pelvic physical therapy over several months provided minor, temporary relief. The patient had been in a monogamous relationship for 25 years and tested negative for sexually transmitted infections. Previous evaluations revealed a mildly elevated prostate-specific antigen, leading to prostate biopsies that were negative, and subsequent bladder biopsies were also negative. Pelvic and genital examinations showed no abnormalities. A rectal exam was not performed.
test_results: The patient underwent bilateral pudendal nerve blocks with 4 ml of 1% lidocaine and 10 mg of dexamethasone being administered on each side. The nerve block was performed using the anatomical, landmark and nerve stimulator-guided approach. This resulted in a 60% reduction in burning micturition pain and a 75% reduction in distal penile pain for a duration of 1 week.

case_report: A 60-year-old male reported experiencing a tingling sensation and burning pain in the right buttock and perineal area. The pain intensified while sitting, rated as 8 on the Numerical Rating Scale (range, 0–10), and was alleviated when lying down or standing. One month prior, he visited a local pain clinic for pain management in the right buttock and inguinal area. He had been diagnosed with isthmic spondylolisthesis of L4 on L5 and L5 on S1 and received multiple spinal epidural steroid injections. Despite this treatment, his pain persisted, leading him to seek care at our outpatient rehabilitation center. He had no prior history of illness or trauma. He reported the aforementioned symptoms and did not experience any pelvic organ dysfunction, such as issues with urination or defecation. Physical examination revealed preserved muscle strength and deep tendon reflexes, with no definite sensory loss in the right lower extremity.
test_results: Pelvis magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed multiple cysts through the right ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament at the entrance of Alcock's canal.
diagnosis: Pudendal Nerve Entrapment Syndrome due to a Ganglion Cyst

case_report: A 40-year-old Thai man experienced a gradual increase in weakness in his left leg and left arm over a period of 7 years. He was unable to flex his left foot upward and had difficulty using his left hand. Over the past 4 years, he also noticed weakness in his right leg and right hand. Physical examination showed muscle atrophy in both arms and legs. The muscle volume and strength of distal muscles on both sides of the extremities were significantly reduced, particularly in the forearms, hands, and feet. Motor power on both sides of the body, assessed using the Medical Research Council Scale, was as follows: tibialis anterior 2/5, quadriceps 4/5, gastrocnemius and soleus 5/5, forearm flexors and intrinsic hand muscles 3/5, and triceps and biceps 5/5. Muscle strength of the deltoid and supraspinatus on the left side was 4/5, while on the right side it was 5/5. Deep tendon reflexes at the ankle were diminished. No other neurological abnormalities were noted. There was no clinical or laboratory evidence of systemic or connective tissue diseases. Serum creatine kinase (CK) levels were mildly elevated at 293 IU/l. Initial treatment with corticosteroids did not result in significant clinical improvement.
test_results: A nerve conduction study and electromyogram were consistent with chronic myopathy predominantly involving the intrinsic hand muscles and tibialis anterior muscles.

case_report: A 42-year-old male presented with bilateral lower limb weakness and difficulty walking for eight to nine years. He also reported easy fatiguability for the same duration, difficulty rising from a squatting position for seven to eight years, a nasal tone for seven to eight years, and breathlessness when climbing three to four flights of stairs and performing daily household activities for four to five years. Nine years ago, relatives and friends noticed a defect in his walking, which he was initially unaware of. Six to seven months later, he sought medical attention for bilateral lower limb weakness, difficulty walking, and a high-stepping gait. The weakness had an insidious onset and was gradually progressive, eventually impairing his ability to perform daily activities. He also experienced blurred vision and was diagnosed with cataracts upon ophthalmological examination, along with deranged blood sugar levels. The patient reported a similar history in his mother and maternal uncle. He confirmed having good intellect and was studying law. He had difficulty holding his neck in a lying down position and swallowing. As his condition progressed, he was referred to a tertiary center for further management. On general examination, he was thinly built with a body mass index of 17 kg/m2, afebrile, with a pulse rate of 90 beats per minute, blood pressure of 100/60 mmHg, respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute, and SpO2 of 97% on room air. He was cooperative, conscious, and well-oriented to time, place, and person. Severe wasting of bilateral lower limbs with temporal hollowing and frontal baldness was observed. Central nervous examination revealed normal deep tendon reflexes with no other focal neurological deficits. Cardiovascular and respiratory system examinations were normal. Routine investigation reports are highlighted in Table. Two-dimensional echocardiography (2D ECHO) showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60% with normal valves. MRI brain with spinal screening revealed no significant abnormalities. Genetic tests for both dystrophia myotonica 1 (DM1) and dystrophia myotonica 2 (DM2) were normal. Pulmonary function tests indicated severe obstruction and severe restriction with poor resolution post-bronchodilator. Ultrasonography showed normal testicles: right (length 20mm and breadth 22mm) and left (length 20mm and breadth 18mm).
test_results: The needle examination showed increased insertion activity with myotonic discharges waning and waxing spontaneously. Short-duration polyphasic motor unit action potentials (MUAPs) were predominant and an early recruitment pattern was seen in bilateral abductor pollicis brevis, deltoid, first dorsal interosseous, and mentalis muscles. On nerve conduction study, his distal latency compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitude was normal. He had normal conduction velocity in the median, ulnar nerve, peroneal nerve, and tibial nerve on both sides. Sensory nerve conduction showed normal sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) amplitude from the median nerve, ulnar nerve, and sural nerve on both sides. Electromyography (EMG) showed normal F wave latency from both lower limbs.

case_report: A 56-year-old Caucasian male visited the cardiology clinic reporting several months of fatigue, decreased exercise capacity, palpitations, atypical chest pain, and swelling in the lower limbs. His medical history included hypertension, well-managed type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, obesity, and a history of smoking (15 pack-years). He also experienced progressive muscle weakness and had a family history of a genetic condition confirmed in his brother and daughter. An electromyogram indicated a specific muscle disorder, but genetic testing was not performed due to cost considerations. He had no significant history of alcohol or illicit drug use, cancer, HIV, family history of heart muscle disease or early coronary disease, or personal history of cardiovascular conditions such as heart attack or myocarditis. His medications included lisinopril (10 mg daily), ezetimibe (due to statin intolerance), insulin, and metformin. Physical examination revealed normal vital signs, no jugular venous distention, clear lung sounds, a regular heart rate and rhythm without murmurs, peripheral edema, and mild proximal muscle weakness. Laboratory tests showed elevated creatine kinase at 495 U/L (reference range 30–300 U/L) and elevated N-terminal prohormone of brain natriuretic peptide at 384 pg/mL (reference range 0–125 pg/mL), with normal Troponin I levels. Other laboratory results, including electrolytes, renal and liver function, and complete blood count, were within normal limits. An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed normal sinus rhythm with inverted T waves in V4 and flat T waves in V5–6. A 72-hour ambulatory cardiac monitor recorded sinus rhythm with short episodes of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia but no atrioventricular conduction abnormalities.
test_results: Cardiac magnetic resonance revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 28%, global hypokinesis, and a severely enlarged (6.9 cm) LV cavity. Regadenoson stress perfusion imaging showed no ischaemia. Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) imaging showed mid-myocardial enhancement in the basal and mid-septal and lateral segments with a total scar burden of 12%.
diagnosis: Cardiomyopathy associated with Myotonic Dystrophy Type 2

case_report: A 46-year-old male initially visited the rheumatology clinic ten years ago with joint pain and swelling in both small and large joints of his upper and lower limbs. These symptoms were accompanied by prolonged early morning stiffness and swelling in his extremities. He experienced severe pain and stiffness, making movement difficult. Laboratory tests at that time showed normal results, including a complete blood count (CBC), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 14, negative rheumatoid factor (RF), and C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 4.930. He received treatment with intravenous methyl prednisolone 60 mg for three days, followed by oral methotrexate 15 mg weekly and folic acid 10 mg weekly. Significant improvement was noted. He continued methotrexate for two years, achieving remission, and then discontinued the medication on his own. He remained well until two years later when he developed reddish-brown soft nodules on the lateral sides of his nose, leading to a referral to a plastic surgeon.
test_results: The deep dermis showed dermal fibrosis and mixed dense inflammatory infiltrate consisting of lymphocytes, neutrophils, eosinophils, plasma cells, histiocytes, and mast cells. Blood vessels were dilated and red cell extravasation was noted.

case_report: An 83-year-old male presented with a lesion on the central forehead persisting for 5 years. The lesion appeared without any prior trauma and was primarily a cosmetic concern. Despite undergoing two excisions by plastic surgery, the lesion recurred and developed a spontaneous, very tender ulcer. The patient reported no other health issues and was not on any medication. On examination, he appeared well and had Fitzpatrick type III skin. In the glabellar region, there was a single 7 cm × 5 cm brown-purple, shiny, bossellated, annular, firm plaque with prominent telangiectasias. A 1-cm deep ulcer was present at the center of the plaque, and there was no cervical lymphadenopathy.
test_results: Skin biopsy showed inflammation involving the entire dermis composed of lymphocytes, plasma cells, histiocytes, neutrophils, and eosinophils. There was a grenz zone, and the epidermis showed mild spongiosis. The vessels showed marked swelling of endothelial cells. Tissue culture for bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial infection was negative.

case_report: A 63-year-old male with a history of lymphoma presented with a 2-year history of a reddish/brown plaque in the right preauricular region, accompanied by swelling and tenderness. The plaque's size had varied over the past months, and there was associated right-sided facial paraesthesia. There was no itching, history of local skin trauma, or discharge from the site. Additionally, the patient reported a 2-month history of a similar plaque on the left posterior axilla. The patient was otherwise in good systemic health, with no fevers, night sweats, fatigue, weight loss, or infection symptoms. His medical history included indolent lymphoma with monoclonal gammopathy, Sjögren syndrome, and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. His regular medication was esomeprazole, and he had no known drug allergies. He was an ex-smoker and rarely consumed alcohol. Physical examination showed a well-demarcated violaceous plaque in the right preauricular region with central ulceration. Follicular plugging was not prominent. The mass was firm, rubbery, and mobile on palpation. There was a flattened, erythematous, atrophic plaque with induration in the left posterior axilla. There was no palpable lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly, and the general examination was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including a full blood count, urea/electrolyte values, and renal and liver function, were normal. Imaging studies, including an ultrasound of the right preauricular region and a CT scan of the head and neck, were also unremarkable.
test_results: The histology of the two specimens showed similar findings. The epidermis was unremarkable, and there was a thin grenz zone of unremarkable dermis superficially. Deep to this, throughout the full thickness of the dermis, there was a moderately dense, inflammatory infiltrate including neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils. These were arranged in tight perivascular cuffs. Some of the vessels showed swelling of endothelial cells with infiltration of vessel walls by neutrophils. There was no true fibrinoid necrosis or leukocytoclasis. Small aggregates of foamy histiocytes were noted within the superficial dermis.

case_report: A 13-year-7-month-old Chinese girl, adopted shortly after birth, exhibited normal growth and development. At 3 years and 5 months old, she experienced a febrile convulsion. Brain imaging and electroencephalogram results were normal. At 8 years and 9 months old, she developed a febrile respiratory infection and was treated with amoxicillin granules, which proved ineffective. Two days later, with a persistent fever of 39.3°C, she exhibited acute neurological symptoms including drowsiness, agitation, and ataxia. Upon admission, various laboratory tests were conducted. Blood glucose, electrolytes, ammonia, blood cell count, toxic and drug screen, liver and kidney function tests were all normal. A semi-quantitative urine ketone body test was positive (2+). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed normal cell count and glucose levels, with no elevated protein concentration or oligoclonal bands. Extensive viral and bacterial testing ruled out infectious meningoencephalitis.
test_results: Brain MRI showed bilateral, symmetric signal abnormalities in the white matter (WM) of the centrum semiovale and the periventricular regions, signal abnormalities in the splenium of the corpus callosum, and the head of the caudate nucleus. The WM showed hyperintense in the T2-weighted axial and FLAIR axial views, and restricted diffusion in the diffusion-weighted imaging. Brain magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) was performed, the result of which showed normal lactate and NAA peaks. No other urine test abnormalities were observed, except for an increased urinary excretion of α-ketoglutaric acid.
diagnosis: Compound Heterozygous Variants of SLC13A3 Associated with Acute Reversible Leukoencephalopathy and α-Ketoglutarate Accumulation
Orpha_name: Acute reversible leukoencephalopathy with increased urinary alpha-ketoglutarate

case_report: A 26-year-old patient, gravida 3 para 2 (G3P2+0), with two previous normal deliveries, was referred to the emergency labor room at an estimated 37 weeks of pregnancy due to vaginal leakage and decreased fetal movement accompanied by fetal bradycardia. The patient conceived during lactational amenorrhea and was uncertain about the gestational period. She had attended only one antenatal check-up at a local health center, where she reported excessive nausea and was estimated to be between 14 and 16 weeks pregnant. During that visit, she received a tetanus toxoid injection and was prescribed iron, calcium, and folic acid supplements, along with antiemetic medication. Her previous obstetric history was uneventful, with all deliveries occurring in medical institutions. Her last child was one year old at the time of her emergency visit. On general examination, the patient appeared dehydrated, dyspneic, and pale, with bipedal edema. Her blood pressure was recorded at 116/74 mmHg, and her pulse rate was 112 beats per minute. Obstetrical examination revealed an unduly enlarged uterus, indicative of polyhydramnios, and the fetal heart sound was muffled.
test_results: Doppler ultrasound measured the fetal heart rate at 102 beats per minute.

case_report: A 31-year-old G2P1 woman with a history of pregnancy and cesarean section for her first child due to early placental abruption experienced a spontaneous and well-progressed pregnancy. At 38 weeks and 2 days of gestation, an emergency cesarean section was performed following membrane rupture. The procedure proceeded without issues until uterine suturing began, at which point an intramuscular hematoma formed on the anterior wall of the uterine body. Subsequently, a hematoma developed from the right uterine horn to the ovarian adnexa, accompanied by bleeding. Repeated ligation attempts failed to control the bleeding, leading to the patient experiencing shock. An intravenous route was established, blood was drawn for testing, and fluid loading along with continuous noradrenaline administration was initiated. Hematoma formation extended from the right basilar ligament to the ovarian adnexa, nearly causing rupture. Intraoperative blood tests showed hemoglobin (Hb) at 5.3 g/dl, platelets at 113,000/μl, and fibrinogen at 184 mg/dl. Emergency transfusion included 6 units of Type O red blood cells (RBC) and 4 units of AB fresh frozen plasma (FFP). The hematoma was incised, and the right adnexa was removed. Although significant bleeding was controlled, complete hemostasis was not achieved. The operation was concluded without full hemostasis due to the need for improved coagulation function through blood transfusion. Total blood loss was 1869 ml, including amniotic fluid. Post-transfusion blood tests showed Hb at 5.5 g/dl, platelets at 85,000/μl, and fibrinogen at 92.8 mg/dl, prompting the administration of an additional 8 units of RBC and 10 units of FFP. Subsequent blood tests indicated improvement with Hb at 9.0 g/dl, platelets at 67,000/μl, and fibrinogen at 232 mg/dl. The patient's condition improved, and she was discharged on the 8th postoperative day.
test_results: zinc coproporphyrin-1 (Zn-CP1), < 1/6 p mol/l; sialyl Tn antigen (STN), 23.0 U/ml < 45.0 U/ml; decreased C3 levels, 76.0 mg/dl < 80 mg/dl; C4, 14.0 mg/dl > 11.0 mg/dl; and C1 esterase inhibitors, 61.0 % > 42.0 %.

case_report: A 42-year-old woman, gravida 4, para 2, was admitted to the hospital due to premature rupture of membranes at 39 weeks of pregnancy, occurring 32 hours before the onset of dyspnea with hypotension. She had gestational hypertension with a blood pressure of 143/87 mmHg and was not on any anti-hypertensive medication. She had no known allergies or family history of note. Upon admission, her blood cell counts and coagulation screening were within normal ranges: hemoglobin (Hb) at 112 g/L, platelet count (Plt) at 221 × 10^9/L, fibrinogen (Fib) at 4.56 g/L, prothrombin time-international normalized ratio (PT-INR) at 0.88, activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) at 29.0 seconds, and D-dimer at 2.3 µg/mL. No abnormal blood cell morphology was reported, and the serum sample was not hemolyzed. Chemistry laboratory results were also normal: aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 12 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) at 6 IU/L, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) at 165 IU/L, gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (γ-GTP) at 9 IU/L, total bilirubin at 0.4 mg/dL, urea nitrogen at 8 mg/mL, creatinine at 0.45 mg/dL, and uric acid at 4.1 mg/dL. Labor was induced the next morning with an oxytocin drip infusion, 4.5 hours before the onset of dyspnea with hypotension. Fetal heart rate (FHR) monitoring showed mild variable deceleration two hours later, which progressed to recurrent severe late deceleration with tachysystole after 40 minutes. Physical examination revealed no vaginal bleeding. Ultrasonography indicated the placenta was located in the anterior uterine wall without retroplacental hematoma. The oxytocin infusion rate was reduced by half, but FHR tracing showed persistent bradycardia 90 minutes before the onset of dyspnea with hypotension. Concurrently, her blood pressure rose to 216/55 mmHg and was unresponsive to apresoline infusion. Following a blood draw for preoperative screening, she underwent an operation under spinal anesthesia for pregnancy termination and fetal delivery. The uterine lower segment incision revealed bloody amniotic fluid, and she delivered a baby boy weighing 3,068 g with Apgar scores of 3 at one minute and 7 at five minutes. The umbilical artery blood pH was 7.14. The placenta was removed with gentle traction, showing no macroscopic evidence of abruption or accreta. The uterine serosa exhibited diffuse petechial hemorrhage over the entire uterine wall. Preoperative blood screening results at this point were: Hb at 129 g/L, Plt at 195 × 10^9/L, Fib at 1.79 g/L, PT-INR at 1.08, APTT at 35.4 seconds, and D-dimer > 60.0 µg/mL, indicating activation of blood coagulation with a decreased Fib level.
test_results: Serum zinc coproporphyrin-1 and sialyl Tn were markedly increased.
diagnosis: Consumptive Coagulopathy due to Amniotic Fluid Embolism

case_report: A 77-year-old white male presented with abnormal sensations in the left heel, pain in the left great toe, and continuous involuntary movements of the left great toe, which intensified at night. He had previously tried multiple medications including Carbidopa/Levodopa, Ropinirole, and Tramadol without success. His medical history included left ankle surgery and hemochromatosis requiring regular blood removal. There was no history of diabetes mellitus. Neurological examination showed normal mental status, cranial nerves, and coordination. The motor exam revealed normal strength but involuntary, non-suppressible flexion and extension movements of the left great toe. Vibratory sensation was reduced at the toes. Reflexes were decreased at the knees and absent at the ankles. His gait was steady and slow with a mild limp due to chronic left hip pain. He also had 2+ leg edema.
test_results: Electromyogram/nerve conduction study (EMG/NCS) showed a mixed pattern polyneuropathy.
diagnosis: Painful Legs and Moving Toes Syndrome
Orpha_name: Painful Legs and Moving Toes Syndrome

case_report: A 16-year-old female presented with tingling pain in her left leg and continuous involuntary movements of her left great toe one month following a second untethering surgery. The movements, characterized by extension and flexion of the great toe, occurred during wakefulness and early sleep stages and could not be voluntarily controlled. The pain was not aggravated by walking, sitting, or straining. At birth, she had a sacral dimple at the S2–3 vertebral level. Four years prior, she experienced voiding difficulty and underwent untethering surgery to address a lipomeningomyelocele at the S2 level of the conus medullaris. A nerve conduction velocity study indicated polyradiculopathy at the left L5 level and below with axonal involvement. A needle electromyogram revealed abnormal spontaneous activities in the left gastrocnemius medial head, abductor hallucis, and tibialis anterior/posterior. She did not report any movement-related symptoms. Additionally, she had a plantar fasciotomy due to equinovarus deformity of both feet. Five months later, voiding difficulty reappeared, necessitating a second untethering surgery. Postoperatively, she developed a fever and signs of meningeal irritation. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed a red blood cell count of 60,000/mm3, a white blood cell count of 150/mm3 (polymorphonucleocytes 69%, lymphocytes 18%), a protein level of 274 mg/dL, and a glucose level of 39 mg/dL. No specific organisms were cultured from blood, urine, or cerebrospinal fluid samples. Her fever and meningeal irritation signs resolved after intravenous administration of teicoplanin. Due to neutropenia (absolute neutrophil count=600/mm3) observed in the complete blood count, teicoplanin was discontinued.
test_results: A nerve conduction velocity study (NCVS) showed polyradiculopathy at the left L5 level and below with axonal involvement. A needle electromyogram (EMG) showed abnormal spontaneous activities of the left gastrocnemius medial head, abductor hallucis, and tibialis anterior/posterior. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed a red blood cell count of 60,000/mm3, a white blood cell count of 150/mm3 (polymorphonucleocytes 69%, lymphocytes 18%), a protein level of 274 mg/dL, and a glucose level of 39 mg/dL. Brain computed tomography and electroencephalography (EEG) showed no pathologic findings. Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine showed reactive inflammatory changes in the operative scar and a decreased extent and degree of reactive meningeal enhancement compared to the previous study. NCVS showed no significant interval change compared to the previous study. Needle EMG showed abnormal spontaneous activities of the left gastrocnemius medial head, abductor hallucis, and tibialis anterior/posterior with no significant interval change since the previous study.
diagnosis: Painful legs and moving toes syndrome
Orpha_name: Painful legs and moving toes syndrome

case_report: An 11-month-old Palestinian male infant presented with an enlarged abdomen, liver, and spleen. His body weight was 8.2 kg (third percentile), height 76 cm (75th percentile), and head circumference 45.8 cm (75th percentile). The patient’s parents are first-degree cousins, and he has three healthy female siblings. They are of Arab Muslim descent from Seer village, Qalqilya district, Palestine. Comprehensive metabolic screening, blood count, differential tests, immunology screen, infectious disease screen, urine and biochemical tests, and amino acid screening were conducted. Genomic DNA was extracted from the patient and his mother’s blood. The father's blood sample was not analyzed. The entire SMPD1 gene was amplified and sequenced. The PCR product was visualized, cleaned, quantified, and used to prepare a next-generation sequencing library. The DNA sequences were assembled and aligned to the human reference gene, and multiple sequence alignment was performed. Due to fever and cough, chest X-ray imaging was performed and was normal. Ultrasound imaging showed liver size of 12.1 cm (upper limit for normal 10 cm) and spleen size of 8.3 cm (upper limit for normal 8.0 cm). No lymphadenopathy was observed. Ophthalmic examination revealed a cherry-red spot in the macula of both eyes. Complete blood count, differential test, and coagulation test were normal. Microbiology blood culture was negative. Tests for Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), hepatitis (A–C), rubella, Toxoplasma, visceral leishmaniasis, pediatric respiratory panel, and anti-tissue glutamines were negative. Urine analysis was normal. Molecular microbiology showed negative results for EBV and CMV by quantitative PCR. Hyperlipidemia was noted with high total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), and triglycerides, while high-density lipoprotein (HDL; 0.16 mmol/L) was lower than normal. The cholesterol/HDL ratio (30.25) was significantly elevated compared to the normal ratio (≤ 4.5). Amino acid screening showed elevated levels of methionine (63 Umol/L) and threonine (216 Umol/L). Serum alkaline phosphatase (ALK), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), and C-reactive protein (CRP) were above normal limits. Several metabolic enzymes were tested and found to be normal. Alpha-galactosidase was slightly low but not within the disease range. Urine oligosaccharide levels did not indicate oligosaccharidosis. A sialic acid assay showed no increase in free N-acetylneuraminic acid (NANA) storage or excretion. Free and total plasma carnitine levels were slightly decreased.
test_results: Sphingomyelinase activity showed remarkable reduction of 0.1 nmol/ml per hour (reference, > 2.5 nmol/ml per hour). The amplified product of the two DNA samples (from our patient and his mother) showed bands of approximately 4276 bp using the two primers SMPD1-P1F and SMPD1-P4R. A DNA sequence of 4225 and 4229 bp was obtained from mother and patient samples, respectively. SMPD1 sequence analysis of the samples of our patient and his mother revealed the same two heterozygous mutations: a deletion of one base, thymidine, in exon 2 at position 573 of the coding sequence and a substitution mutation at position 107 (T>C) in exon 1. The NGS identified four sequence variants: single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) 579C/T was detected in variant 1. Variant 2 was shown to be normal and a frameshift c.573delT (NM_000543.4(SMPD1):c.573delT (p.Ser192Alafs) was detected in variant 3. The fourth variant was c.107 leading to conversion of valine to alanine at position 36 (NM_000543.4(SMPD1):c.107T>C (p.Val36Ala)). DNA sequence analyses revealed no pathogenic variants in these regions.

case_report: A 14-year-old female presented with concerns regarding the absence of pubertal onset. She was in good health and performed well academically. Family history included a maternal aunt with autoimmune hypothyroidism, but no other significant medical history. The patient's parents were first cousins, and she had two brothers who experienced normal pubertal development. Her mother had menarche at age 12, had no issues with conception, and was not menopausal at age 50. Physical examination showed no breast development (B1), sparse pubic hair (P2), and no axillary hair (A1). Her height and weight were at the 50th percentile, with a mid-parental height at the 75th percentile. The rest of the examination was unremarkable.
test_results: Investigations revealed positive thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies, markedly raised gonadotropins (LH 42 IU/L; FSH 96 IU/L), and an undetectable serum estradiol concentration. Further testing at a reproductive medicine unit two months later demonstrated similar gonadotropin concentrations, a 46,XX karyotype, weakly positive TPO antibodies, negative adrenal (adrenal cortex 21-hydroxylase) antibodies, normal thyroid function, and a negative fragile X screen.

case_report: A 17-year-old Taiwanese female visited the gynecology clinic with concerns about not having started menstruation and lacking secondary sexual characteristics. Her height was 158.8 cm (40th percentile), weight was 45 kg (10th percentile), and body mass index was 17.8 (within the normal range of 17.7–22.7). She exhibited normal intelligence. Her parents' heights were 149 cm (mother) and 175 cm (father), with a mid-parental height estimate of 156 cm ± 7 cm. She was born to parents who are related by blood and had normal developmental milestones. She has no siblings. Physical examination revealed no significant findings in the cardiovascular, respiratory, and central nervous systems. She had pubic and axillary hair but no breast development (Tanner stage B1PH3). The external genitalia were under-developed. Her bone age was estimated to be 13 years using the Greulich and Pyle method.
test_results: Pelvic ultrasonography and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) both revealed the absence of the uterus and vaguely visible bilateral ovaries. Laboratory investigation reported high random follicular-stimulating hormone/luteinizing hormone (FSH 58.89 mIU/mL, LH 20.46 mIU/mL) and estrogen (13 pg/mL) levels. Prolactin levels and both renal and thyroid functions were normal. A Gonadotropin-receptor hormone stimulation test reported highly elevated FSH/LH (FSH peak 86.99 mIU/mL, LH peak 72.77 mIU/mL) levels and low estrogen level (<10 pg/mL). Karyotype report a normal female 46, XX genotype. A bone marrow density with dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) skeletal survey assessment reported a Z-score of − 2.7.

case_report: A 30-year-old woman visited our infertility clinic due to primary infertility lasting 7 years. She reported the onset of breast development at age 11 and her first menstrual period at age 12, with regular cycles lasting 3 to 5 days. Her medical history included occasional migraine headaches without neurological symptoms and a maternal uncle with mental retardation. Physical examination showed a healthy woman with a BMI of 26, Tanner stage V development, and a normal pelvic exam, including a well-estrogenized vaginal epithelium. At age 25, routine infertility evaluations, including hormonal levels on the 3rd day of the cycle (FSH: 6 IU/L, LH: 5.5 IU/L, E2: 27 pg/mL), semen analysis, hysterosalpingography, and transvaginal ultrasound, showed no abnormalities. Controlled ovarian hyperstimulation (COH) and intrauterine insemination (IUI) were recommended. She conceived during the second cycle of COH and IUI but had an ectopic pregnancy in the right fallopian tube, treated with laparoscopic salpingectomy at 7 weeks gestation. The laparoscopic examination showed a normal uterus and left adnexa, and the right salpingectomy was performed using electrocautery without complications. The patient experienced vaginal bleeding 4-5 weeks post-operation. Following severe emotional stress due to a family death, her menstrual periods ceased. Eight months later, she reported hot flushes, dyspareunia, and loss of libido. At this time, she was 26 years old. Physical examination was unremarkable except for secondary amenorrhea lasting 8 months and a hypoestrogenized vaginal epithelium. Vaginal smears showed intermediate cells.
test_results: Transvaginal ultrsonography demonstrated normal size uterus with thin endometrum and small ovaries (right ovary 2.1cm3, left ovary 2.3cm3) with 3-4 primordial follicles in each ovary. Progesterone–withdrawal test was negative. Serum FSH and LH levels were high (FSH=62 IU/ L, LH =34.8IU/ L). Progesterone level was (0.3ng/m L), and estrdiol level was less than (10pg/ m L). The 3rd day hormonal assay was repeated 4 months later (basal FSH level=135 IU/ L, LH level=88 IU/ L, E2 level= 10 pg/m L). Karyotype was 46 XX, fragile X mutation testing revealed normal size alleles with normal ranges of CGG repeats.

case_report: A 1-week-old male, born full-term and small for gestational age (weight: 2,610 g—5th percentile) to non-consanguineous parents, had a birth history notable for maternal pre-eclampsia. Initial newborn hearing screen results were unavailable. The immediate newborn period was otherwise unremarkable. At 6 days old, he was found to be febrile (101.6°F) with scalp cellulitis at the site of a previous scalp electrode used during delivery. He was hospitalized and started on broad-spectrum antimicrobials, including ampicillin, gentamicin, acyclovir, and vancomycin. Blood cultures and scalp wound cultures were positive for Escherichia coli, and he was transitioned to cefepime based on antibiotic sensitivity results. Urine culture and serum HIV 1/2 RNA were negative. Additional scalp wound cultures, including fungal cultures and HSV-PCR surface cultures, were negative. Lumbar puncture results for cell counts, protein, and glucose were unremarkable. A BioFire® meningitis/encephalitis panel was negative. Brain MRI indicated possible osteomyelitis, leading to an increased cefepime dose for meningitis coverage. Repeat imaging 10 days later showed soft tissue inflammatory changes without osteomyelitis. Initial and repeat newborn screen results were unsatisfactory/inconclusive. His white blood cell (WBC) count was 500 cells/ml, with no neutrophils, an absolute lymphocyte count (ALC) of 400 cells/ml (80%), and an absolute monocyte count of 100 cells/ml (20%). Granulocyte colony-stimulation factor (G-CSF) was initially given at 10 μg/kg/day without improvement in neutrophil counts and was discontinued after 10 days. Immunoglobulin G level was normal at 413 mg/dl, with undetectable IgA and IgM. He developed thrombocytopenia (nadir 39,000 platelets/ml) without anemia and later showed improvement in platelet counts. Initial lymphocyte flow cytometry at day 16 showed a T-cell (CD3+) count of 320 cells/μl (78%), B-cell (CD19+) count of 13 cells/μl (3%), and NK-cell count of 68 cells/μl (17%). The naïve T-cell (CD3/CD45RA+) count was 26 cells/μl (15%), with a CD3/CD45RO+ percentage of 83%. A primary immunodeficiency next-generation sequencing panel could not be processed due to insufficient DNA. The patient was transferred to our institution and started on Pneumocystis and fungal prophylaxis with pentamidine and fluconazole, respectively. Mitogen proliferation to phytohemagglutinin (PHA) was normal. Maternal engraftment was not detected, and the red blood cell adenosine deaminase 1 (ADA) level was normal. Subsequent lymphocyte flow cytometry showed improvement in T- and NK-cell counts, with low B-cell counts. Multiple repeat newborn hearing screens were abnormal, likely due to anatomical obstruction from the scalp lesion. G-CSF was restarted and increased to 30 μg/kg/day without notable improvement in neutrophil counts, and it was discontinued after 20 days.
test_results: Bone marrow aspirate showed no increased blasts, increased hematogones (29%), absence of maturing granulocytic elements (including neutrophil production), and active erythropoiesis without dysplasia.
Orpha_name: Immune deficiency due to impaired neutrophil phagocytosis and migration

case_report: A 58-year-old male rural farmer has experienced superficial mycosis affecting his hands, nails, and right ankle for 20 years. Recently, a 20 × 15 cm desquamative pruritic lichenified fungal plaque with regular and thin erythematous borders has extended to the inguinal and abdominal areas. Additionally, a similar 10 × 10 cm fungal lesion appeared on his upper right paravertebral dorsum. The patient has undergone prolonged treatment with griseofulvin (1990–2000; 2016–2018), terbinafine (1985–1990; 2001–2015), and itraconazole (since 2018) without success. His brother exhibited similar symptoms but responded to standard antifungal therapy. There is no additional relevant family history or consanguinity. Mycological scraping identified Trichophyton rubrum. An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy confirmed the absence of invasive fungal infection.
test_results: Immunological screening showed deficient T cell proliferative response to specific stimuli and impaired neutrophil burst oxidative after specific stimulation with Candida albicans.
diagnosis: Functional defect of neutrophils causing dermatophytosis
Orpha_name: Immune deficiency due to impaired neutrophil phagocytosis and migration

case_report: A 48-year-old man of Middle-Eastern descent was diagnosed with ulcerative pancolitis at the age of 23. At 39, he underwent a two-stage proctocolectomy with J-pouch due to corticosteroid-refractory UC and rectal adenocarcinoma. Before the ileostomy reversal, he received adjuvant chemotherapy, and the malignancy has remained in remission. Eight years post-ileostomy reversal, he experienced fecal urgency and frequency with up to 15 bowel movements per day, partially alleviated by fiber supplements and diphenoxylate/atropine. Annual pouch endoscopies since the ileostomy reversal were normal. For four years prior to presentation, he had nearly constant, tender oral cavity ulcers. Additionally, he developed an intermittent, erythematous, papular rash on the face, trunk, and extremities. A punch biopsy of the rash showed acanthosis and hypergranulosis of the epidermis, with a perivascular and interstitial lymphocytic infiltrate in the dermis. The patient also reported severe joint pain in the lower extremities, with a migratory pattern, joint swelling, and morning stiffness. Laboratory tests showed normal thyroid stimulating hormone and immunoglobulin G and E levels. Serology was negative for anti-transglutaminase antibody, anti-nuclear antibody, microsomal antibody, rheumatoid factor, and human leukocyte antigen B27.
test_results: Genetic testing of NOD2/CARD15 revealed the IVS8+158 variant.
diagnosis: Auto-inflammatory disease associated with NOD2/CARD15 mutations

case_report: The patient is a 21-month-old male born prematurely at 33+4 weeks of gestation via elective caesarean section, with a birth weight of 1,780 g. The pregnancy was marked by severe polyhydramnios, necessitating multiple amniocenteses. Post-birth, he was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit for 21 days. A chromosome study showed a karyotype of 47, XYY. At 1 month old, he began experiencing frequent vomiting. At 7 months, attempts to introduce solid foods were unsuccessful due to swallowing difficulties, although his growth remained normal. At 13 months, he had a urinary tract infection. His height was 78.6 cm, weight 10.5 kg, and head circumference 46.5 cm, all within the 50-75th percentiles. Developmentally, he was at the level of an 8-month-old. Renal ultrasonography indicated possible bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis. At 17 months, he was assessed for persistent vomiting. His height was 83.5 cm, weight 11.5 kg, and head circumference 47.5 cm, with development at a 9-month-old level. Brain MRI showed a slight increase in subarachnoid space, and esophagography was normal. Hypokalemia was noted, and kidney ultrasonography confirmed bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis. Subsequently, his growth was inadequate, and he began losing weight. At 21 months, he was referred for further evaluation. He no longer had frequent vomiting but continued to struggle with solid foods, consuming 2-2.5 L of liquids daily and producing 1.5-2 liters of urine. His weight was 10.8 kg (third-fifth percentile), height 89.9 cm (50-75th percentile), and head circumference 48 cm (10-25th percentile). He could walk but with an unstable gait and was unable to climb stairs. His speech was limited to simple words. Blood pressure was 100/54 mmHg. Dental examination showed delayed tooth eruption without decay or periodontal disease. Esophagography indicated slight passage delay and minimal gastroesophageal reflux. Brain CT was normal. Plasma renin activity was 40.8 ng/mL/hr, and serum aldosterone was 888 pg/mL. Serum sodium was 140 mmol/L, potassium 3 mmol/L, and total CO2 25-31 mmol/L. Serum calcium was 10.5 mg/dL, phosphorus 5.2 mg/dL, magnesium 2.4 mEq/L, and creatinine 0.5 mg/dL. Urine specific gravity was 1.003, with no proteinuria or hematuria. Spot urine showed sodium 7 mmol/L, potassium 38.5 mmol/L, chloride 9 mmol/L, and a calcium to creatinine ratio of 1.52. Tubular reabsorption of phosphate was 82%, and trans-tubular potassium gradient was 13.78. After a 12-hour water deprivation test, urine specific gravity was 1.008 and urine osmolality was 276 mOsm/kg.
test_results: Compound heterozygous mutations in the SLC12A1 gene were detected; c.G1277A causing p.Cys(TGT)436Tyr(TAT) in exon 10 and c.T1679C causing p.Leu(CTT)560Pro(CCT) in exon 12. L560P mutation was not detected in 50 control Korean and 50 control Japanese. There was no pathogenic mutation in other genes tested.

case_report: An 8-year-old male presented to the nephrology clinic with bilateral nephrocalcinosis, discovered during the evaluation of recurrent urinary tract infections. The patient exhibited significant thirst and frequent nighttime bedwetting despite being continent during the day. His height and weight were below the 0.4th percentile. Dental examination revealed carious, irregular, and hypomineralized teeth, while other ectodermal structures appeared normal. There was no family history of renal, skeletal, or dental conditions. Laboratory tests showed mild hypokalaemia (3.4 mmol/L) with normal serum bicarbonate (25 mmol/L), creatinine, calcium, phosphate, magnesium, alkaline phosphatase, and parathyroid hormone (PTH). Elevated serum 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol levels were noted (229 pmol/L, normal range 20–120 pmol/L). Urinary biochemistry indicated hypercalciuria (urinary calcium creatinine ratio 1.64 mmol/mmol, normal 0.04–0.08 mmol/mmol) and mild proteinuria (urine protein creatinine ratio 86 mg/mmol creatinine, normal <20). Radiological assessment showed a bone age of 4.85 years at a chronological age of 8.37 years. Hormonal evaluations, including growth hormone levels, were normal. Dental findings were consistent with amelogenesis imperfecta (AI), leading to several dental extractions. A low-salt diet was recommended to reduce urinary calcium excretion. However, the patient experienced worsening enuresis, including new daytime wetting. Uroflow assessment suggested poor bladder emptying, and cystoscopy revealed a lobulated, irregular bladder and urethral mini-valves, which were not considered to be contributing to his symptoms. Spinal imaging was normal. Management strategies included optimizing stooling, double voiding, and excision of the mini-valves. Persistent hypercalciuria (urinary calcium creatinine ratio between 1.5 and 2.3 mmol/mmol) led to the use of chlorothiazide, which was poorly tolerated and discontinued. Renal function declined, with ongoing hypokalaemia, hypochloraemia, and alkalosis. The patient remained normotensive with static proteinuria.
test_results: This confirmed heterozygous variants in KCNJ1, a previously reported frameshift variant c.965del p.(Gly322Alafs*7), and a novel missense variant c.233G>C p.(Arg78Thr).

case_report: A 43-year-old German woman was evaluated following incidental findings of bilateral nephrocalcinosis during her second pregnancy. Her recent medical history was unremarkable, but she reported experiencing strong thirst and frequent urination during childhood. She did not have a strong appetite for salty food, although she noticed beneficial effects after consuming salt-rich foods. She did not use laxatives or diuretics and did not consume alcohol or other drugs. The patient reported no symptoms of nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, weakness, fever, night sweats, weight loss, or heat intolerance. She is the mother of two healthy daughters.
