Physical examination revealed normal findings. Blood pressure was 136/80 mmHg, and no edema was present. ECG results were normal.
test_results: Ultrasound image demonstrating renal medullary nephrocalcinosis in her left kidney.

case_report: A 34-year-old male presented with nausea, vomiting, and decreased appetite for 10 days. He reported a history of excessive thirst, frequent urination, nighttime urination, and recurrent carpopedal spasms during childhood. He was born at full term via normal vaginal delivery with no complications during the antenatal or neonatal periods. The patient denied any history of limb paralysis or weakness, recurrent urinary tract infections, fractures, hearing issues, or vision loss. There was no family history of renal diseases. Four years ago, his creatinine level was 2 mg%, and he was under the care of a nephrologist. Physical examination showed a moderately built and well-nourished individual with short stature (height: 140 cm) and no obvious deformities or skeletal dysmorphic features. Blood pressure was 120/80 mm Hg, and both ECG and 2D Echo were normal. Laboratory tests indicated severe azotemia (urea: 139 mg%, creatinine: 10 mg%), hypokalemia (3.28 meq/L), hypocalcemia (5.0 mg%), and hyperphosphatemia (7.0 mg%) with normal sodium (140 meq/L) and chloride (96 meq/L) levels. Vitamin D levels were low (20 ng/ml) with normal PTH levels (90 pg/ml). Arterial blood gas analysis showed normal pH and low bicarbonate with respiratory compensation (pH = 7.41, serum bicarbonate = 18 mmol/l). A 24-hour urinary examination was limited due to decreased residual renal function with a urine output of approximately 100 ml/day. Immunological profile (ANA, dsDNA, Anti Sm, and Anti Ro/La) and viral markers (HIV, HbsAg, and HCV) were negative. X-ray of the lumbosacral spine and hands showed mild changes of renal osteodystrophy but were otherwise unremarkable. Ultrasound of the abdomen suggested medullary nephrocalcinosis with normal-sized kidneys, confirmed by a computed tomography scan. A percutaneous kidney biopsy from the lower pole of the left kidney revealed 1/6 glomeruli with segmental sclerosis, a large area of interstitial fibrosis, and diffuse dense infiltration of lymphocytes and plasma cells in the interstitium. Tubules showed intraluminal calcification and destruction, with unremarkable vessels. The patient was started on hemodialysis via a temporary right internal jugular venous catheter, and transplant evaluation was initiated.
test_results: The analysis revealed a homozygous missense variation in exon 2 of KCNJ1 gene in the chromosome 11 that results in the amino-acid substitution of glutamic acid for glycine at codon 167.

case_report: A 23-year-old male, previously healthy and active in the army, arrived at the emergency department with a one-month history of intermittent vomiting after meals and leg cramps, which had intensified over the past two days, leading to vomiting up to ten times a day. He reported no loin pain or blood in urine. On examination, he was alert, with normal skin color, no jaundice, and no signs of cachexia. His vital signs included a blood pressure of 130/73 mmHg, a pulse rate of 92 beats per minute, and an oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. Initial blood tests revealed severe metabolic alkalosis, hypokalaemia, hypocalcaemia, and renal impairment. Specific values included blood urea at 9.1 mmol/L, serum creatinine at 218.3 μmol/L (eGFR 35.5 ml/min/1.73 m2), potassium at 1.6 mmol/L, and sodium at 126 mmol/L. Venous blood gas analysis showed a pH of 7.56, bicarbonate at 62 mmol/L, pCO2 at 73.3 mm Hg, pO2 at 29.1, and SO2 at 52.2%. Corrected serum calcium was 2.04 mmol/L, and serum phosphate was 1.0 mmol/L. Full blood count results included haemoglobin at 12.2 g/L, total white blood cell count at 10.2 × 10^9/L, and platelets at 302 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein was measured at 0.28 mg/dL. There were no previous baseline investigations or arterial blood gas results available for comparison. Shortly after the initial assessment, the patient experienced a generalized tonic seizure followed by cardiac arrest with pulseless electrical activity. Blood pressure was unrecordable, necessitating cardiopulmonary resuscitation for 70 minutes, during which 14 direct current shocks were administered for ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation, eventually restoring circulation. The patient was intubated and required inotropic support due to persistent hypotension despite adequate fluid resuscitation. Post-resuscitation, 300 ml of urine was collected via urinary bladder catheterization, likely representing residual urine before the collapse, but the patient subsequently became anuric and started on renal replacement therapy. A nasogastric tube placed post-intubation drained nearly 2 liters of gastric content, and the patient was unable to tolerate feeding through the tube. Multiple corrections for hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia were administered using intravenous potassium chloride and calcium gluconate infusions.
test_results: CT thorax, abdomen, and pelvis showed distended elongated stomach with air contrast level. There was no enhancing lesion or compression at the pylorus and antrum of the stomach. The D3 segment of the duodenum was significantly smaller in calibre at the precaval and preaortic region with lack of mesenteric fat. There was a reduced aortomesenteric angle measuring 21 degrees (normal: 25–60 degree) with reduced distance measuring 8 mm (normal: 10–28 mm). The contrast was seen opacifying the duodenum, jejunum and ileal loops.

case_report: A 35-year-old Caucasian man presented to the Gastroenterology Department at Aleppo University Hospital with postprandial non-projectile vomiting that began 2 months prior, without accompanying abdominal pain. The patient had a history of significant weight loss due to hunger and malnutrition related to the Syrian war, dropping from 135 kg (BMI: 42.61 kg/m²) to 100 kg (BMI: 31.56 kg/m²) over 5 months before the onset of vomiting. Following the onset of vomiting, he lost an additional 40 kg, reaching a weight of 60 kg (BMI: 18.94 kg/m²) over 4 months. He had no other comorbidities. Physical examination revealed a soft, non-distended abdomen, with normal vital signs and other system reviews. Laboratory tests showed a mild decrease in serum albumin and a mild increase in aspartate transaminase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT). Abdominal echography did not reveal any issues. Endoscopy showed no gastric outlet obstruction or other abnormalities. Upon reaching the second part of the duodenum and inflating air to visualize the third part, a narrowing was observed in the third part of the duodenum. The mucosa of the stomach and duodenum appeared normal, with no inflammatory changes noted.
test_results: Multi-slice computerized tomography (MSCT) showed compression of the third part of the duodenum between the aorta and the SMA due to decreased distance (3.9 mm) and narrowed angle (14.6°) between these two arteries.

case_report: A 67-year-old Caucasian female was admitted to the Emergency Department of Pescara General Hospital on March 17th, 2021, presenting with seizures, vertigo, vomiting, nausea, postural instability, and recurrent falls for approximately 10 days. She had a history of Crohn’s Disease (CD) since 1991 and underwent hemicolectomy with gastric resection and ileostomy in 2007. The patient had consistently declined biological therapies, opting for steroids to manage disease activity phases. During hospitalization for refractory diarrhea, a gastroenterologist recommended reintroducing steroids, attributing her symptoms to relapsing CD. Neurological examination revealed vertiginous syndrome with postural instability, difficulty controlling eye movements with vertical nystagmus, and retropulsion. A brain CT scan showed no ischemic or hemorrhagic lesions. At admission, she was on a treatment regimen of 500 mg/daily of mesalazine. The patient lost consciousness during her stay in the Emergency Department and was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU), where she received Propofol, Fentanyl, and Rocuronium, along with intubation and mechanical ventilation. Her condition improved the next day; she was extubated and transferred to the Neurology unit for further evaluation. An X-ray of the shoulders revealed a compound fracture of the humerus head, likely from a previous fall. A chest X-ray indicated bilateral pleural effusion. A brain MRI scan showed altered signal intensity in the peritrigonal region, corona radiata, and centrum semiovale, consistent with leukoencephalopathy. Cerebral Spinal Fluid (CSF) analysis showed no cells, negative Pandy’s reaction, glucose at 60 mg/dL, and total CSF proteins at 26 mg/dL. All viral and microbiological tests on CSF and serum were negative. Immunological CSF examinations reported normal levels of IgA (1.48 mg/L, reference: 0.0-2.0 mg/L), IgG (10.3 mg/L, reference: 4.8-58.6 mg/L), and IgM (0.417 mg/L, reference: 0.0-2.0 mg/L). CSF and serum electro-isofocusing analysis showed oligoclonal bands with a mirror pattern (type 4), indicating no intrathecal synthesis.
test_results: Western blot analysis on serum revealed a high titre of onconeural anti-SOX1, whereas Amphiphysin-Ab, CV2-Ab, Ma2/Ta-Ab, Ri-Ab, Yo-Ab, Hu-Ab, Recoverin-Ab, Titin-Ab, zic4-Ab, GAD 65-Ab, Tr-Ab showed all negative results.

case_report: A 59-year-old female with no significant past medical history arrived at the emergency room presenting with fever, headache, drowsiness, and body pains for one week. Acyclovir was administered. Post-admission, the patient experienced a generalized tonic-clonic seizure (GTCS). Brain MRI excluded cerebrovascular accident. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis did not indicate meningoencephalitis. Serum sodium was measured at 122 meq/mol, and the patient was treated with 3% normal saline. The patient initially recovered, achieving a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Six hours later, she became drowsy and developed respiratory failure with a partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2) of 55, necessitating non-invasive ventilatory support. The patient experienced another GTCS. Subsequent examination revealed altered sensorium, disorientation, confusion, and faciobrachial dystonic seizures (FBDS).
test_results: A serum autoimmune panel was ordered, which came back negative.
diagnosis: Seronegative Autoimmune Encephalitis with Super-Refractory Status Epilepticus
Orpha_name: Non-specific autoimmune supratentorial encephalitis without characteristic antibodies

case_report: A 63-year-old male with a medical history including asthma, hypertension, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (on Apixaban), hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis (on methotrexate), morbid obesity, and obstructive sleep apnea was brought to the emergency room due to confusion two days before hospital admission. He had been seen at another hospital five days earlier for low-grade fever, chills, fatigue, and nonproductive cough, and tested positive for COVID-19 via PCR. Managed conservatively, he was discharged after one day. Post-discharge, he continued to experience fevers and chills, and his family noted confusion, prompting a return to the emergency room. Initial evaluation showed hypoxia and a fever of 101.3 F. Due to confusion, a complete review of systems was not possible. Mental status examination revealed orientation only to self, with pupils equal and reactive and no cranial nerve deformity. He could follow some commands and move all extremities without focal weakness. Sensory system assessment was limited by his mental status. Lung auscultation revealed scattered crackles in all fields. The abdominal exam was benign with no tenderness or fluid signs. Initial labs showed elevated inflammatory markers: C-reactive protein at 7.7 mg/dl (normal 0-0.8 mg/dl), fibrinogen at 623 mg/dl (normal 90-480 mg/dl), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) at 343 U/l (reference 98-192 U/l). Electrolyte panel, renal, and hepatic function tests were normal. Chest X-ray was unremarkable, while a contrast-enhanced CT scan showed subpleural ground-glass infiltrates in the right lower lobe and left upper lobe, consistent with COVID-19 pneumonia. A head CT scan was performed to evaluate mental status changes and showed no gross acute intracranial abnormality. He was admitted and treated with systemic steroids, intravenous remdesivir, bronchodilators, and anti-pyretics. The infection triggered atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, managed by adjusting flecainide and metoprolol doses. His fever and respiratory status improved over three days, but mental status did not. He developed oral dyskinesias and a comprehensive neurological exam revealed truncal ataxia and a broad-based gait, with no other focal neurological defects. Further history review showed no psychiatric history or antipsychotic use.
test_results: MRI of the brain without contrast enhancement showed bilateral cerebellar white matter signal abnormalities extending to bilateral cerebellar peduncles. MRI of the brain with and without contrast revealed bilateral brachium pontis lesions implying persistent inflammation in the bilateral anterior inferior cerebellar artery territories.

case_report: A 10-year-old boy was admitted with severe headache, vomiting, and irritability for 4 days. The headache was diffuse, severe, throbbing, persistent throughout the day, interfered with sleep and daily activities, and was not relieved by oral analgesics. The headache was accompanied by multiple episodes of projectile vomiting and irritability. There was no recent history of vaccination or head trauma, and no history of seizures or loss of consciousness, although the patient remained irritable. Approximately 2 weeks prior to these symptoms, he experienced fever, cough, and cold for 3–4 days. On examination, the child was afebrile (98.2°F) with a pulse rate of 86/min, respiratory rate of 30/min, and blood pressure of 100/62 mm Hg. His anthropometric measurements were within normal limits. General physical examination showed no pallor, icterus, or other significant findings. At admission, he was conscious and irritable but able to follow verbal commands. There was no evidence of cranial nerve palsies, and fundoscopy revealed marginal blurring of disc margins. Motor system examination showed no focal neurological deficits. There were no signs of meningeal irritation. Measures including mannitol, dexamethasone, and broad-spectrum antibiotics (ceftriaxone and vancomycin) were initiated. Preliminary laboratory tests indicated mild leukocytosis with neutrophilia (total white cell count 13,000/mm3; neutrophils 83%), normal serum sodium (137 mEq/L), serum alanine aminotransferase levels (36 IU/L), serum bilirubin (0.9 mg/dL), and serum creatinine (0.7 mg/dL).
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of his brain revealed mild obstructive hydrocephalus with periventricular ooze, ill-defined altered signal intensity area with contrast enhancement in the bilateral cerebellum, and mild tonsillar herniation. Cerebrospinal fluid examination showed pleocytosis (60–70 white blood cells/mm3, predominantly lymphocytes), proteins 31mg/dL, glucose 84mg/dL (94mg/dL blood sugars), and culture being sterile. The blood culture was sterile. Serum was tested for Immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibodies against M. pneumoniae using enzyme immunoassay and the test result was found to be positive. Serologic tests for EBV were negative.

case_report: A 70-year-old male arrived at the emergency department with dizziness lasting for 2 days. He reported no issues with double vision, blurred vision, headaches, numbness, or weakness. Neurological examination showed no specific abnormalities. Laboratory tests indicated elevated blood sugar (415 mg/dL), glycated hemoglobin (19%), osmolality (301 mOsm/kg H2O), and blood ketone bodies (5.9 mmol/L). Renal and hepatic functions, as well as blood gas levels, were normal. Brain computed tomography conducted in the emergency department showed no abnormalities. The patient was admitted and treated with oral hypoglycemic agents, including Metformin (1000 mg/day) and Glimepiride (2 mg/day), with intermittent subcutaneous insulin administered if blood sugar levels exceeded 200 mg/dL. After 2 days, the patient developed acute involuntary movements in his left limbs, with a blood sugar level of 168 mg/dL. Blood sugar levels remained stable during these 2 days. The patient stayed conscious, and no other neurological deficits were observed. Additional laboratory tests, including blood cell count, renal function, liver function, thyroid function, vitamin B12 level, autoimmune profile, human immunodeficiency virus antibody titer, and rapid plasma reagin, were all within normal limits.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed no infarction or hyperintensity lesion in the right basal ganglion and subthalamus.

case_report: A 17.8-year-old girl, measuring 168 cm (1.37 SDS) in height and weighing 58 kg (1.08 SDS), was referred to our hospital due to an unusual physical appearance and lack of menstruation. She was born at full term weighing 3.25 kg, with her mother experiencing sparse hair, acne, an enlarged nose, and a deepened voice during pregnancy, which partially resolved after delivery. The patient had multiple congenital anomalies and had sought medical treatment on several occasions. She exhibited bilateral facial paralysis, mild cerebellar atrophy, mandibular deformity, an infantile uterus, labial fusion, and disordered toes (with the 4th toes being short and hidden among the other toes). She had undergone vulvar plastic surgery and excision of the 4th toes prior to her visit to our center. Since birth, she had recurrent otitis media, mild hearing impairment, and experienced spontaneous fractures of the humerus or phalanx five times. Physical examination revealed a depressed nasal bridge, underdeveloped nasal alae, pear-shaped nose, short and deep philtrum, a prominent median nodule on the upper lip, high palate, misaligned teeth, micrognathia, low-set and cupped ears without antihelix, a single earlobe crease, arachnodactyly, short 4th metacarpals, and thenar muscle atrophy. She also had disordered metatarsals, short 3rd toes, absence of the 4th toes (postoperative), and bilaterally limited movement of the elbows and metacarpophalangeal joints. Her breast development and pubic hair were consistent with Tanner stages IV and II, respectively.
test_results: She exhibited bilateral facial paralysis with mild cerebellar atrophy on MRI, ultrasound-confirmed infantile uterus.
diagnosis: Antley-Bixler syndrome caused by cytochrome P450 oxidoreductase deficiency
Orpha_name: Antley-Bixler syndrome with genital anomaly and disorder of steroidogenesis

case_report: A 4-month-old girl from the Ibibio tribe was referred in August 2019 to the Radiology Department at UUTH, Uyo, Nigeria from the Orthopedic Unit for imaging of her lower limbs due to a short left lower limb observed since birth. Her parents reported that the left lower limb was progressively shortening, but no other abnormalities were noted. Antenatal history, past medical history, and family history were unremarkable. There was no history of maternal trauma during pregnancy or perinatal radiation exposure. Developmental milestones were normal. Physical examination revealed a well-nourished infant with active mobility in both lower limbs. The left lower limb was shortened and externally rotated. Measurements showed the right lower limb at 27 cm and the left lower limb at 23 cm, both measured from the anterior superior iliac spine to the tip of the medial malleolus. Both knee and hip joints had a normal range of motion, and hip abduction was complete. The back examination was normal. The upper limbs had no anomalies and exhibited a full range of movement. An abdominopelvic ultrasound revealed an umbilical hernia but no other congenital abnormalities.
test_results: Plain radiographs of her thigh and lower limbs showed shortened and hypoplastic left femur with preserved left femoral capital epiphysis. Her left femur had normal configuration but had a shorter shaft than the contralateral femur. The shaft of her left femur measured 9.41 cm whereas the shaft of her right femur measured 11.88 cm.

case_report: A 26-year-old female presented to the Dental Department with concerns about facial appearance persisting for eight years. She had a history of neck surgery for a cyst eight years ago, followed by the onset of facial swelling one to two days post-surgery. The swelling remained unchanged in size and was not painful. There were no issues with breathing or eating. Examination revealed facial asymmetry with a growth on the right side. The skin on the right side of the face was thickened, hyperpigmented, and exhibited a soft, loose overgrowth. Numerous small and large nodular growths, both sessile and pedunculated, were observed on the right side of the neck, with dark-colored underlying skin. The right cheek and chin areas had coffee-colored pigmentation (café-au-lait spots). A soft, compressible, nontender growth was noted on the lower lip. The right ear showed disfigurement and hypertrophy, with thickened cartilage and hyperpigmented skin. Intraoral examination revealed multiple soft tissue growths with a sessile base on the right buccal mucosa and tongue, which were soft, compressible, and nontender. Laboratory findings indicated an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 70 mm in the first hour, a hemoglobin level of 7.5 gm%, and a nonreactive enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). A panoramic radiograph showed asymmetric enlargement of the right side of the mandible, loss of cortication of the lower border in the midline, expansion of the mandibular body causing tooth displacement on the right side, expansion of the right inferior alveolar nerve canal, an enlarged mental foramen, resorption of the roots of the mandibular right teeth, and loss of the right antegonial notch. The right side of the maxilla exhibited a deficiency with posterior teeth crowding. A right lateral oblique radiograph revealed a deep sigmoid notch, loss of the antegonial notch, an enlarged and rounded coronoid process, and resorption of the mandibular right teeth.
test_results: The histopathological slide revealed a non-encapsulated tumor of the dermis with a normal overlying epidermis. The tumor consisted of loosely spaced spindle cells and wavy collagenous strands in a clear matrix.

case_report: A full-term 30-day-old girl born via normal vaginal delivery with no significant perinatal history developed increasing difficulty breathing, hoarseness, bluish discoloration with feeding, and lethargy. She was treated for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) pneumonia and required supplemental oxygen and parenteral feeding. The feeding with bluish discoloration persisted after five days, prompting a visit to our hospital for a second opinion. Upon arrival, the patient had an oxygen saturation of 89% on room air and was admitted to the ward for further management. The oxygen saturation improved to 100% with supplemental oxygen. She was alert with no audible stridor at rest but had mild subcostal retractions. The heart and breath sounds were normal. Otolaryngology was consulted and bedside nasoendoscopy reviewed a left vocal fold paralysis. The right vocal fold was mobile and the glottic gap was three millimeters. The remainder of the scope findings was normal. There were no palpable neck masses, and thorough examination of the ears and oral cavity was normal as well. Chest X-ray showed mild air space consolidation at the right perihilar region and possibly the left retrocardiac region, likely related to underlying pneumonia. The patient was treated presumably for aspiration pneumonia and was weaned off supplemental oxygen after a few days.
test_results: This revealed a nonenhancing left carotid space mass measuring 2.4 × 1.5 × 1.3 cm, with compression on the left internal jugular vein and displacement of the internal and external carotid arteries anteriorly. Ultrasound scan of the lesion showed multiple intralesional calcifications.

case_report: The patient is a 15-year-old boy with a painless mass on the left side of his neck for over 10 years. His parents noticed soybean-sized masses on the left side of his neck at birth, which were painless and without numbness. He also has a deformity in his right leg. Two years ago, he was admitted to a hospital but did not receive any specific treatment. The patient has no personal medical history. His mother has a history of a similar condition. The patient visited our hospital on July 24, 2020. Physical examination revealed that his right shoulder is approximately 5 cm lower than his left shoulder, and there is a deformity on the left side of his face. The skin under the left jaw is relaxed, soft, and incompressible with noticeable folding and drooping. Multiple superficial brown masses of varying sizes are present in the submandibular region, neck, and behind the mastoid process. These masses are incompressible and have a texture similar to rosary nodules. The skin temperature is normal. The left earlobe is adhered to the sternocleidomastoid muscle at 2 cm, and there is visible skin pigmentation on the shoulder and 1 cm behind the armpit. The skin between the left shoulder and chest is visibly relaxed, folded, and drooping. Café au lait spots of different sizes are observed on the back and lower limbs. A soft, incompressible bump with a clear boundary, no adhesion, and poor motility is present between the index finger and middle finger on the back of the left hand.
test_results: Histological examination showed subepidermal pale blue mucoid degeneration. The fibrous fusiform cells in the dermis had a fascicular and woven arrangement. The focus was the palisaded obvious boundary, wavy nucleus, and focal pigmentation.

case_report: A 79-year-old female arrived at the Emergency Department with blurred vision in her right eye. She also experienced flashes of light, sensitivity to light, pain during right-sided eye movement, nausea, and one episode of vomiting. These symptoms began suddenly while she was at church, and she had no prior history of similar issues. Her ophthalmic history included cataract surgery. Upon arrival, her vital signs were stable: heart rate was 64 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 18 breaths per minute, and blood pressure was 175/77 mmHg. Physical examination revealed bilaterally dilated and sluggish pupils, painful right-sided eye movements, an injected right conjunctiva, and elevated intraocular pressure in both eyes. There was no tenderness in the temporal region. No other significant findings were noted on examination. The medical workup included an electrocardiogram, basic metabolic panel, and complete blood count, all of which showed no significant abnormalities. The ophthalmology team was consulted.
test_results: The right eye IOP was 88 mmHg, and the left eye IOP was 75 mmHg. The ophthalmology team confirmed that the patient did have an elevated IOP in the right eye, but upon examination found that the patient did not have an elevated IOP in the left eye. They also found that the patient had an open angle in the right eye.

case_report: A sixty-two-year-old Caucasian female arrived at the emergency room with sudden changes in vision in her right eye over the past 12 hours. She described experiencing image distortion, blurriness, and central vision loss accompanied by 'flashing lights.' Additionally, she had mild redness in her right conjunctiva and reported episodic blurry vision with headaches over the past several months. Her medical history includes CVID and ulcerative colitis. Initial immunologic tests showed a low IgG level of 223 mg/dL, with normal IgA and IgM levels. She was on daily sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim prophylaxis due to recurrent upper respiratory infections, including sinusitis and bronchitis. Despite this, she continued to have persistent sinusitis and was later started on immunoglobulin therapy, which reduced her infections. She also reported intermittent blurry vision in her right eye for several years. During the acute episode, her right eye vision distortion worsened, prompting an emergency room visit. The physical examination revealed a mildly injected right conjunctiva, visual acuity of 20/70 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye, and intraocular pressures of 34 mmHg in the right eye and 12 mmHg in the left eye. Color vision was normal in both eyes, and pupils were reactive and equal. There were no signs of trauma, photophobia, eye drainage, or hyphema. Extraocular movements were intact, and no other focal neurological deficits were observed.
test_results: The ophthalmology slit lamp examination showed 4-5 trace cells in anterior chamber of right eye confirming anterior chamber uveitis. There were no keratic precipitates, and the iris appeared normal on direct illumination bilaterally. The left eye exam did not show any cells in the anterior chamber or evidence of corneal edema. Gonioscopy and dilated fundus examination were unremarkable. Cup to disc ratio was within normal limits, and no afferent pupillary defects were noted.

case_report: An 18-month-old boy, born full-term to non-consanguineous parents with an uncomplicated delivery and normal neonatal period, presented with bilateral ptosis (margin reflex distance = 1 mm), congenital right esotropia, and hypertropia. Family history revealed no ocular abnormalities. The patient exhibited no light perception in the right eye, while the left eye responded normally to light. Cycloplegic refraction measured −13.00 sphere in the right eye and +1.5–0.75 × 70 in the left eye. Slit lamp examination identified a microcornea (9.0 mm × 7.5 mm) and a persistent pupillary membrane. Intraocular pressures were within normal limits in both eyes. No pathological findings were observed in the fellow eye, and there was no associated systemic disease.
test_results: Fundus examination revealed absence of the right optic nerve head and central retinal vessels, and a large chorioretinal coloboma with rudimentary retinal vessels originating from the choroid at the margin of the coloboma with localized hemorrhage in the retina. Orbital and brain MRI was normal, and a narrow optic nerve was observed on the right side. Fluorescein angiography (FA) showed bilateral choroidal flush, and hypofluorescent presumed optic disc and macula. Electroretinogram (ERG) was flat in the same eye.

case_report: A 13-year-old girl was admitted with sudden onset of difficulty breathing. She reported experiencing intermittent chest discomfort over several months, with no history of fever. Her oxygen saturation was 93% on pulse oximetry, and her other vital signs were stable. The patient had no known underlying diseases, medication history, or significant family history. Routine laboratory tests were normal. A chest X-ray showed loss of retrocardiac lucency and reduced volume of the left hemithorax, suggesting left lower lobar atelectasis. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest revealed an infiltrative lesion with soft tissue attenuation in the middle mediastinum, encasing and narrowing the left lower lobar bronchus. Bronchoscopy revealed obstruction of the left main bronchus due to external compression. A biopsy of the mediastinal lesion primarily contained blood and some squeezed lymphocytes, with no evidence of malignancy. The pathology department recommended a re-biopsy for further evaluation.
test_results: The intraoperative findings revealed fibrotic tissue between the aorta and pulmonary artery, encasing the left main bronchus. The pathological findings revealed diffuse fibrosis with dense collagen deposition and squeezed lymphocytic infiltration. Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) staining results for fungal studies were negative. Granulomatous inflammation was not observed within the specimen.

case_report: An 80-year-old male, who has never smoked, presented with worsening shortness of breath. He first experienced respiratory issues as a teenager after significant exposure to sanding materials without a mask, describing symptoms such as wheezing and cough. In his twenties, he worked in a bakery and reported prolonged inhalation of dust from baking products like sugars and flour, which further aggravated his respiratory symptoms. After college, he became a dentist and experienced significant exposure to inhaled irritants from dental drilling without a mask. In his late thirties, he developed significant shortness of breath and was found to have a pleural effusion. He underwent thoracotomy and mediastinoscopy, which revealed granulomas. There is no record confirming whether the granulomas were caseating or non-caseating, and no confirmatory testing for tuberculosis was performed. Approximately 10 years later, he developed Legionnaires' disease, which worsened his respiratory complaints. In his early seventies, his respiratory symptoms worsened, and he was seen by a pulmonologist.
test_results: The CT revealed diffusely calcified infiltrating soft tissue changes around the right hilum which were encasing the airways and obstructing the right bronchus intermedius. The infiltrating tissue was also found to obstruct the right pulmonary artery but not the main pulmonary trunk or left pulmonary artery tree. Imaging also noted multiple calcified granulomas in the right lung consistent with the findings from prior thoracotomy.

case_report: A 23-year-old male presented with weakness in the left arm following a period of deep sleep. The initial neurological examination revealed proximal left arm weakness with an MRC grade of 3. The patient also reported a previous episode of wrist drop on the right side after engaging in a strenuous drill during military service, which resolved after 6 months. He denied any family history of similar symptoms. Brain CT and MRI results were normal. Following consultation with the Department of Neurology, further evaluations were conducted.
test_results: These studies revealed multifocal peripheral neuropathy with demyelination, superimposed by suprascapular neuropathy in the left side. The nerve conduction study showed significantly reduced compound muscle action potential in left suprascapular nerve with active denervations observed in the left supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles only.
diagnosis: Hereditary Neuropathy with Liability to Pressure Palsy
Orpha_name: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies

case_report: A 60-year-old female with a history of metastatic renal clear carcinoma to the lungs and left adrenal gland, status post right radical nephrectomy, was on combined Nivolumab 240 mg and Ipilimumab 85 mg IV. She presented to the hospital following a fall at home. Her medical history included persistent atrial fibrillation on warfarin, chronic systolic heart failure, and essential hypertension. After her first cycle of Nivolumab and Ipilimumab, she reported fatigue and muscle pain. During the pre-procedure evaluation for the second dose, her serum sodium level was 132 mEq/L, and conservative management with rehydration was initiated. Post-second cycle, she experienced nausea, vomiting, and hot flashes, for which Ondansetron 8 mg IV every six hours as needed was administered, providing symptomatic relief. Eight days later, she had another fall at home, accompanied by progressive weakness and vertiginous symptoms. Her serum sodium was 119 mEq/L, leading to her admission for acute symptomatic hyponatremia. Vital signs included a blood pressure of 88/59 mmHg and a heart rate of 113 beats per minute with atrial fibrillation with RVR. Metoprolol tartrate 2.5 mg IV was administered, resulting in a controlled ventricular rate of 73 beats per minute. Other vitals were stable. Endocrinology recommended methylprednisolone 80 mg IV push. Further tests showed a morning cortisol level of 1.8 mcg/dL (2.5-19.5 mcg/dL), ACTH level of <5.0 pg/mL (0-46 pg/mL), FSH of 7.4 mlU/mL (25.8-134.8 mIU/mL), LH of 1.00 mlU/mL (7.7-58.5 mIU/mL), prolactin of 0.1 ng/mL (4.8-23.3 ng/mL), TSH of 0.06 ulU/mL (0.27-4.2 uIU/mL), and free T3 of 1.6 pg/mL (2.5-4.3 pg/mL). Urine sodium was <20 mmol/L, and urine osmolality was 386 mOsm/kg. Nephrology recommended fluid restriction and tolvaptan 15 mg per os. Fludrocortisone 50 mcg per os daily, hydrocortisone 15 mg IV in the morning daily, and 10 mg IV in the evening daily were administered.
test_results: MRI of the brain with IV contrast showed abnormal enhancement and thickening of the pituitary stalk.

case_report: A 64-year-old Caucasian man with a history of metastatic colorectal cancer recurrence, currently receiving ipilimumab and nivolumab, presented with a persistent central throbbing headache lasting five days. He had completed his first cycle of immunotherapy one month before the onset of symptoms. The headache was described as central, non-radiating, sharp, and throbbing. Initially, the pain intensity was rated at 4-5, but it progressively worsened to 9/10 by the time of admission. The headache was accompanied by nausea and fatigue. The patient did not report fever, chills, vision changes, double vision, weakness, numbness in the extremities, hearing loss, tinnitus, or changes in gait. Physical examination revealed no focal neurological deficits. A CT scan of the head showed no acute intracranial abnormalities or masses.
test_results: MRI brain showed mild prominence of the pituitary gland measuring about 11 mm in the craniocaudal dimension.

case_report: A 4-year-old girl, born to consanguineous parents, presented with atopic eczema and multiple flat warts on the trunk, along with numerous molluscum contagiosum on the face and perivulval area. She had a history of multiple episodes of pyoderma on the scalp, which were sometimes generalized, starting from the age of 1 year. She experienced recurrent episodes of upper and lower respiratory tract infections and recurrent diarrhea, leading to two hospitalizations. Her elder sister had a similar medical history and passed away at the age of 10 years due to a severe gastrointestinal infection. Dermatological examination showed eczema over flexures, macerated intertrigo in the groin with perivulval molluscum, and multiple periorbital molluscum with blepharitis. Numerous flat warts were observed on the trunk and hands. There was no lymphadenopathy. Other cutaneous examinations, including nails, mucosae, and hair, were normal. Systemic examinations were within normal limits. Initial assessment ruled out HIV infection.
test_results: Elevated serum IgE level, hypereosinophilia, and a low CD4 and CD8 counts.
Orpha_name: Autosomal recessive hyper-IgE syndrome due to ZNF341 deficiency

case_report: A 33-year-old African American male presented with multiple nodular skin lesions, primarily located in the axilla and inguinal areas. He reported an increase in the number and size of draining pustules. The patient also experienced generalized joint pains, including swelling and redness in the left knee and right elbow. These symptoms typically occur 1 to 2 times yearly and subside with antibiotic treatment. On skin examination, generalized suppurate nodules and chronic scars were observed, along with sinus tracts in the intertriginous areas. Joint examination revealed effusions in the ankles, knees, elbows, wrists, and digits, with a notable swelling in the right second phalanx.
test_results: Synovial fluid analysis from the left knee revealed yellow cloudy fluid, 190 white blood cells/mm3, and 4180 red blood cells/mm3, with no crystals seen. Radiographic studies of left hand revealed erosions at the head of second, fourth, and fifth proximal phalanges as well as base of the second middle and proximal phalanges. Erosive arthritis was also noted in radiographs of wrist and ankle.

case_report: A 14-year-old boy, educated up to class 6, from a middle socioeconomic status family in an urban area, presented with a 3-year history of academic decline and a 2-year history of hearing voices. The child was born from a nonconsanguineous marriage, following an unplanned but uneventful pregnancy. Developmental milestones were achieved on time. Early childhood exposure to aggressive behavior from his father, who was abusive at times, was noted. Parental marital problems and domestic violence led to their divorce when the child was 10 years old. The following year, the child and his mother moved to his maternal grandparents' home, and his school was changed. Within a year, there was a noted decline in academic performance, handwriting deterioration, and irritable and sad behavior. The school reported frequent fist fights and undesirable behavior. The child preferred solitary activities and avoided eating with the family. There was also a decline in daily routine activities. A private psychiatrist treated him with sodium valproate up to 400 mg/day for nearly 2 months, which reduced irritability and aggression. However, the medications were gradually tapered and stopped. Over the next year, he began hearing voices of a commanding nature and suspected family members, including his mother, of colluding with unknown persons to tease him. He eventually dropped out of school, stayed awake late at night, muttered to himself, and shouted at unseen persons, with further deterioration in socialization and self-care. Another psychiatrist treated him inpatient for 2 weeks with risperidone 3 mg, olanzapine 2.5 mg, and oxcarbazepine 300 mg/day, resulting in some symptom improvement. Significant weight gain led to poor medication compliance and relapse within 3 months of discharge. Frequent aggressive episodes over the next year resulted in multiple hospital admissions. He was brought with acute exacerbation of symptoms and was receiving divalproex sodium 1500 mg/day, aripiprazole 30 mg/day, trifluperazine 15 mg/day, olanzapine 20 mg/day, and lorazepam injection as needed. He was admitted for medication rationalization. Physical examination revealed an elongated face with large ears. He was non-cooperative for mental state examination and exhibited aggressive and violent behavior. He was observed muttering and laughing to himself. His mood was irritable, speech was laconic, and he lacked insight into his condition.
test_results: Rubella antibodies (serum IgG = 64.12 U/mL, IgM = 2.44 U/mL) and polymerase chain reaction for Fragile X syndrome (repeat size = 24) were normal.

case_report: A 38-year-old Caucasian woman presented in November 2017 for evaluation of secondary amenorrhea. The absence of her menstrual cycle followed the discontinuation of oral contraception, in the context of a spontaneous deep venous thrombosis (DVT) in 2015. She experienced menarche at age 13, and her menstrual cycles were regular before starting oral contraceptives. The patient had no history of infertility, having had two pregnancies and two deliveries, and reported a weight gain of approximately 4 kilograms over the past 2 years. She denied symptoms such as acne, hirsutism, or voice deepening. She had a history of high blood pressure for the past 5 years but no history of diabetes. At the initial evaluation, her medications included nebivolol/hydrochlorothiazide 5/25 mg once daily, rivaroxaban 20 mg once daily, and aceclofenac 100 mg twice daily. The patient reported progressive and persistent right hip pain that began around 4 months after her second pregnancy and persisted for 3 years, limiting her mobility. Hip magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed avascular necrosis of the right femoral head, leading to right hip arthroplasty 1 year before the endocrinology evaluation. Although her mobility improved post-surgery, she continued to experience proximal muscle weakness. She denied any significant family medical history. Physical examination revealed a body mass index (BMI) of 25.96 kg/m2, facial redness, truncal obesity, and supraclavicular fat pads. Muscular atrophy and easy bruising were noted. No skin striae, hirsutism, or acne were observed.
test_results: Serum cortisol of 21.5 µg/dL after overnight dexamethasone suppression test (DST) (normal < 1.8 µg/dL). Elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC) (728.9 µg/day; normal 36.0–137.0 µg/day). Suppressed morning plasma ACTH (< 1.0 pg/mL; normal < 63.3 pg/mL). Adrenal computed tomography (CT) scan showed a 25 mm lesion in the left adrenal gland, with density non-suggestive of adenoma.
diagnosis: Cushing syndrome due to adrenal cortex adenoma
Orpha_name: Cushing syndrome due to cortisol-producing adrenocortical adenoma

case_report: A 34-year-old G2P1 female patient visited the West China Hospital of Sichuan University, reporting abnormal blood glucose levels for the past 4 years. She had experienced a weight gain of 10 kg in the last year, along with muscle weakness and elevated blood pressure over the past 4 weeks. Four years prior, she had been diagnosed with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) during her first pregnancy at a local hospital. Postpartum, she maintained near-normoglycemia through dietary changes, exercise, and other lifestyle interventions. One year ago, the patient developed centripetal obesity, and her attempts at weight control through diet and exercise proved ineffective. An oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) revealed a 1-hour blood glucose concentration of 5.37 mmol/L and a 2-hour blood glucose concentration of 10.76 mmol/L after a 75g glucose load. Subsequently, she was found to be pregnant again and received treatment for GDM. During pregnancy, the patient gradually suffered from facial and back acne, abdominal purple lines, increased body hair, and decreased hairline. Laboratory findings and HPA on admission were shown. Due to safety concerns, the pregnant woman declined further MRI examination. The patient underwent a cesarean section at 33 weeks of gestation, delivering two male infants who required intensive care for 10 days and at-home feeding after 1 month. During a subsequent visit, a 1mg dexamethasone suppression test (DST) was conducted.
test_results: A 1mg dexamethasone suppression test (DST) revealed non-inhibition of cortisol. Enhanced abdominal computed tomography (CT) displayed a 22 mm occupation of the left adrenal branch. An MRI of the sellar region revealed no abnormalities in the pituitary glands. The 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC) levels were 585.9 ug/24h and 738.6 ug/24h, respectively. Adrenal contrast-enhanced CT revealed a 2.7x2.5 cm soft tissue density nodule of the left adrenal gland.
diagnosis: Cushing's syndrome due to left adrenal cortical adenoma
Orpha_name: Cushing syndrome due to cortisol-producing adrenocortical adenoma

case_report: The patient is a 20-year-old woman born at term to non-consanguineous parents after a pregnancy complicated by a threatened abortion. There was no reported exposure to teratogens during pregnancy. At birth, her weight was 2,500 g (4th centile, −1.76 SD), length was 48 cm (26th centile, −0.65 SD), and head circumference was 33 cm (9th centile, −1.22 SD). APGAR scores were 7 at 1 minute and 9 at 5 minutes. Developmental milestones were delayed: she walked alone at 20 months, spoke her first words at 24 months, and had limited language development by 36 months. Physical examination revealed dysmorphic features including mild synophrys, long and arched eyebrows that were low-set relative to the upper eyelid, long eyelashes, generalized hypertrichosis, a bulbous nasal tip, a wide mouth, brachycephaly, bilaterally supernumerary nipples, and short hands and feet. A brain MRI showed slightly enlarged lateral ventricles with a dysmorphic aspect on the left. From late childhood, she exhibited behaviors such as stubbornness, compulsivity, anxious demeanor, repeated panic attacks, emotional outbursts, poorly controlled fits of rage, and a short attention span, necessitating psychotherapy with limited benefit. She experienced recurrent bronchitis and pneumonia shortly after birth, with confirmed P. aeruginosa colonization. Mucus was noted to be thick, and a pulmonary CT scan at 10 years showed multiple bronchiectasis, requiring periodic mechanical mucus aspiration. Gastroesophageal reflux was noted at birth. She had dysphagia for solid food starting at 6 months and was on a semiliquid diet until 8 years. She also suffered from severe chronic constipation from 6 months of age, with multiple fecalomas requiring periodic manual evacuations. A rectal mucosal biopsy was negative for Hirschsprung disease and intestinal neuronal dysplasia. She experienced biliary sludge and cholelithiasis, which were treated pharmacologically. At 10 years, she was found to have left convex lumbar scoliosis, managed with a corrective corset until 14 years. Additionally, she had hypermetropia.
test_results: CGH-array analysis and NIPBL, SMC1, SCM3 and RAD21 genes testing provided negative results.

case_report: A 12-month-old girl presented to the emergency room with a high fever and worsening paraparesis. She had normal developmental milestones and began walking at around 10 months of age. Fifteen days prior to the visit, she developed a fever reaching 39.5℃ and was treated for pharyngitis with antibiotics and antipyretics at a local clinic. Her fever initially subsided, but she began experiencing repetitive vomiting 10 days before the visit. Five days ago, her high fever returned, and she intermittently showed lethargy and reluctance to walk. She received further examinations and supportive treatment for infectious disease at the local clinic. When her condition worsened, showing overt paraparesis, she was transferred to our hospital. Upon arrival, she appeared acutely ill and lethargic. Her vital signs were: heart rate 137 beats/min, blood pressure 123/56 mm Hg, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, and body temperature 38.6℃. She was alert but exhibited quadriparesis with motor grades of I/I for the upper extremities and 0/0 for the lower extremities. She had profound hypesthesia below the C4 dermatome. Bilateral biceps jerks were weak, and bilateral knee and ankle jerks were absent. No signs of meningeal irritation were observed. A palpable mass, identified as a distended bladder, was found in her abdomen. A small dimple was noted in the midline of the upper sacral area, located above the gluteal folds and approximately 6 cm from the anus. Manual pressure on the dimple produced a small amount of whitish thick discharge. Laboratory tests showed blood leukocytosis (15500/µL), decreased hemoglobin (10.9 g/dL), decreased hematocrit (31.6%), and elevated C-reactive protein (5.83 mg/dL). Her parents reported noticing the skin dimple during her neonatal period but did not seek further evaluation, believing it to be harmless.
test_results: The MRI revealed diffuse high signal intensity along the spinal cord up to the medulla oblongata. There was a low-lying conus down to the S3 level. An enlarged central canal and thick gadolinium-enhancement of the lining up to the T1 level was observed. There were multiple cystic dilatations with rim enhancement in the lumbosacral cord. A dermal sinus tract ran obliquely upward from the conus at the S3 level to the skin.
diagnosis: Infected Congenital Dermal Sinus with Massive Holocord Pyomyelia

case_report: A 61-year-old Caucasian male presented with colicky pain in the lower abdomen, nausea, and increased bowel movements for the past 2 days. Initial examination revealed mild hypertension. The patient had a history of smoking (10 packs/year) but no other known medical conditions. Symptoms worsened after admission, including vomiting and fever, despite treatment with painkillers, scopolamine, and metoclopramide, along with an increase in blood pressure. The patient later experienced decreased consciousness, cold extremities, tachycardia, and severe hypotension (blood pressure of 50/30 mmHg). Cardiac and pulmonary examinations were normal, but the abdomen was generally tender, and a reducible crural hernia was noted. Rectal examination was normal, and the patient's condition improved with saline volume resuscitation. Laboratory results indicated normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin: 7.8 g/dL; reference value [RV]: 13-15 g/dL), normal blood cell count, hyperglycemia (glucose: 276 mg/dL; RV: < 100 mg/dL), prolonged prothrombin time (INR = 1.69; RV: 1.0), and metabolic acidosis (pH = 7.26 with HCO3 = 12 mEq/L; RV: 14 mEq/L). Electrolytes, renal function tests, amylase, lipase, liver enzymes, and myocardium necrosis markers were within normal limits. The electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia.
test_results: The multidetector abdominal computed tomography showed, in the arterial phase, the presence of a hyperattenuating fluid in the epiplon retrocavity and peripancreatic regions, and within the free abdominal cavity, consistent with intra-abdominal hemorrhage. The angiographic study showed signs of small- and medium-sized vessels arteriopathy. Several branches of the celiac trunk, and the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries, showed diffuse caliber reduction, contour irregularity associated with narrowing and dilation, as well as segmental thrombosis. Saccular aneurysms were also found in the branches of both renal arteries close to the hilum and in the medium colic artery that emerged from the celiac trunk. Active bleeding signs were not identified during the tomographic examination.

case_report: A 58-year-old female with a history of protein C and S deficiency, deep vein thrombosis (on Warfarin), systemic lupus erythematosus, and hypothyroidism presented to urgent care with right flank and upper quadrant abdominal pain for 3 days. Urinalysis showed blood and leukocyte esterase, and she was discharged on Cephalexin. Her abdominal pain persisted, and she developed nausea, leading her to visit the emergency department. A CT scan of her abdomen indicated findings consistent with a recently passed calculus, and she was discharged with a plan for outpatient follow-up. She returned 12 hours later due to worsening abdominal pain. Her vital signs were blood pressure 154/80 mm Hg, heart rate 85 beats per minute, respiratory rate 17 per minute, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Physical examination revealed diffuse abdominal tenderness and right costovertebral angle tenderness. Initial laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 9.1 bil/L, hemoglobin 13 g/dL, platelets 257 bil/L, and INR 4.4. The basic metabolic panel was unremarkable. Liver function tests revealed aspartate aminotransferase 658 U/L (previously 104 U/L 12 hours prior), alanine aminotransferase 772 U/L (previously 82 U/L 12 hours prior), bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 70 U/L, and albumin 4.6 g/dL. Extensive workup, including infectious and rheumatologic testing, was grossly unremarkable.
test_results: An axial CT angiography abdomen/pelvis with contrast showed new right hepatic lobe infarct measuring 6.5 × 6.5 cm with hypervascular lesion suspicious for pseudoaneurysm of right hepatic artery and occlusion of the anterior right portal vein at the site of aneurysm resulting in anterior right hepatic lobe infarction. An MRI of her abdomen showed a wedge-shaped hepatic ischemia to portions of segment 5/8 likely secondary to a 3 cm intrahepatic pseudoaneurysm with compression of anterior branch of right portal vein.

case_report: A 53-year-old Japanese man was brought to our hospital due to a sudden severe headache and altered consciousness. Upon arrival, his Glasgow Coma Scale score was E4V5M6, and he exhibited no neurological deficits. The patient underwent a right frontotemporal craniotomy. During the surgery, the right A1 segment of the anterior cerebral artery (ACA) was found to be dilated and fusiform, resembling a blood blister-like aneurysm. The right A1 segment of the ACA was trapped with cisternal drainage and external decompression to protect the perforators. Post-surgery, the patient had no neurological deficits, and routine maintenance infusion and pain medication were continued. His systolic blood pressure remained below 180 mmHg without the need for blood pressure medication. On the seventh day following the subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), the patient developed right hemiparesis and aphasia. An urgent carotid artery stenting (CAS) was performed for a symptomatic left internal carotid artery (ICA) dissection. Prior to the procedure, 200 mg of aspirin and 300 mg of clopidogrel were administered to prevent thrombotic complications. An 8 mm × 60 mm stent (Protégé RX; Covidien, Irvine, CA) was used to fully cover the dissected segment of the left ICA, resulting in improved blood flow. The patient’s symptoms resolved after the procedure. Postoperative magnetic resonance imaging revealed a left cerebral infarction in the anterior watershed area, but there were no signs of symptomatic cerebral vasospasm or secondary hydrocephalus. Laboratory tests indicated normal C-reactive protein levels, and immunological tests for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody and antinuclear antibody were negative.
test_results: Head computed tomography (CT) revealed a thick SAH with Sylvian hematoma (Fisher Group 4), and CT angiography (CTA) revealed a fusiform aneurysm of the right A1 segment of the ACA and a saccular aneurysm of the left vertebral artery (VA). The right A1 segment of the ACA was identified as the site of rupture based on the distribution of the hematoma. The left intracranial ICA was not clearly visible on CTA. Digital subtraction angiography showed ICA dissection at the cervical portion with delayed distal flow. Abdominal CTA showed dissecting aneurysms of the celiac and superior mesenteric arteries.

case_report: A 2-year-old Japanese girl presented with erythema and papules on her fingers and knees. After one month, she developed facial erythema following sun exposure. She was treated with a topical corticosteroid, but the skin condition persisted. Four months later, she was referred for further evaluation due to the worsening skin rash. Physical examination showed a characteristic rash on the face, hands, fingers, and knees. There was no clinical evidence of muscle pain. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 8,570/µl, elevated serum creatinine kinase levels at 467 U/l (normal range: 43–290), and aldolase levels at 13.5 U/l (normal range: 2.7–7.5). Indirect fluorescent antinuclear antibody testing revealed circulating autoantibodies against the nucleus at a titre of 1:320 with a speckled pattern. No signs of active lung involvement were found on auscultation or chest X-ray imaging.
test_results: Inflammation of the bilateral quadriceps muscles was detected by magnetic resonance imaging. A biopsy specimen from an erythema on the knee showed dermal perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates and marked oedema of the superficial dermis with mucin deposits. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs) for MSAs were positive for Tif1γ and Mi-2 at titres of 60 (cut-off < 32) and 54 (cut-off < 53), respectively. The patient’s sera reacted with Tif1γ and Mi-2 in immunoprecipitation-Western blotting analysis.

case_report: A 22-year-old male presented with a rash and joint pain persisting for four months, along with breathlessness for one month. Five months prior to admission, he had a butterfly tattoo on his right chest using blue and red ink. Four months before admission, erythema appeared on various skin areas, including the face, the extensor surface of both elbows, the metacarpophalangeal joints (MCP2–4), the neck, the chest, and the right side of the back. There was no muscle weakness reported. Over time, he experienced increasing shortness of breath following physical activity.
test_results: A computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest indicated ILD.

case_report: The patient is a 43-year-old Korean male who works as a welder and has no significant medical history. In February 2015, he experienced fever and headache and was admitted to a local hospital. During his stay, he developed right supraorbital swelling and cramping pain in both legs. Laboratory results were: D-dimer 395 ng/mL, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 412 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 217 IU/L, and creatine phosphokinase (CPK) 1,610 IU/L. Immunofluorescence assay results were negative for antinuclear antibodies (ANAS), serum anti-Sm/RNP, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, anti-SSa and anti-SSb antibodies, anti-cardiolipin antibodies, anti-dsDNA antibodies, and anti-Jo-1 antibodies. Chest radiography revealed haziness in both lower lobes. Computed tomography (CT) showed multifocal peribronchial consolidation and ground-glass opacity in both lower lobes, particularly in the right subpleural area, along with effusion. A filling defect (1.5 cm in diameter) was observed in the distal right lower pulmonary vein. The patient was treated with oral moxifloxacin 400 mg and intravenous methylprednisolone 125 mg for 4 days, which led to slight symptom improvement. He was referred to our hospital in March 2015, presenting with persistent fever and headache. Upon admission, his height was 173 cm, weight was 54.2 kg, body temperature was 37.3 °C, and other vital signs were normal. Physical examination revealed skin rashes, heliotrope rash, and swelling on both eyelids, as well as eruptions on the knuckles of both hands, prepatellar areas, both shoulders, and the back. Laboratory findings included: white blood cell count 6,310/µL, hemoglobin 13.9 g/dL, platelets 177,000/µL, CPK 293 IU/L, AST 90 IU/L, ALT 70 IU/L, and aldolase 14.0 U/L. A paranasal sinus (PNS) film indicated fluid level in the right maxillary antrum, suggestive of acute sinusitis or blood accumulation. Neurological examination showed no motor weakness. An electromyogram did not reveal definitive evidence of myopathy or polyneuropathy.
test_results: Skin punch biopsies of rashes on his left hand, left knee, and right back revealed superficial and deep perivascular dermatitis.

case_report: A 53-year-old African-American female with a medical history including morbid obesity, hypertension, bipolar disorder, anxiety, and asthma, presented with weakness, numbness, and foot drop in the right lower extremity. She reported multiple falls in the preceding weeks and had been experiencing right leg numbness and urinary incontinence for six months. Cervical MRI showed compressive cervical myelopathy due to disc protrusions. She underwent a corpectomy of C6 and an anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) of C4-C7, followed by transfer to a rehabilitation facility. Two months later, she was readmitted with complete loss of strength in her right lower extremity, which had progressed to involve the left lower extremity. Physical examination revealed complete loss of strength and sensation in the right lower extremity. Strength examination of the left lower extremity showed: hip flexion 0/5, hip abduction and adduction 2/5, quadriceps 4/5, hamstring 3/5, tibialis anterior 4/5, and gastrocnemius 4/5. Deep tendon reflexes were diminished in both lower extremities, and no rash was observed.
test_results: Pathology findings showed mixed myopathic and neuropathic features, myocyte hypertrophy with a dominance of type I fibers, CD20 B-cell and CD4 T-cell predominant chronic inflammatory infiltrate involving the perimysial connective tissue, and presence of nuclear bag fibers and atrophic angular fibers without fiber type grouping. Electromyography (EMG) of LE musculature revealed signs of extensive axonal denervation. Initial nerve conduction studies (NCS) of LE showed profoundly diminished tibial nerve compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitude and no peroneal responses distally or proximally with absent sural and superficial peroneal sensory responses. A lumbosacral MRI showed no nerve root compression. However, it revealed symmetric areas of edema within the paraspinal and pelvic musculature.
diagnosis: Dermatomyositis Sine Dermatitis complicated by Neuromyositis

case_report: A 20-year-old Caucasian male presented to the Emergency Clinic 3 days prior with nonspecific abdominal pain and was discharged with symptomatic treatment. He was later admitted to the General Surgery Clinic exhibiting signs of acute abdomen. The patient had no comorbidities or notable medical history. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 120/70 mmHg, pulse rate of 86 beats per minute, respiration rate of 16 breaths per minute, and a temperature of 36.8°C. Examination of the abdomen showed tenderness, guarding, and rebound tenderness in the right lower quadrant. Digital rectal examination was unremarkable. Laboratory results indicated a white blood cell count of 11,200, hemoglobin level of 12.8 g/dL, and a platelet count of 133,000.
test_results: Abdominal X-ray revealed a few air-liquid levels in the left upper quadrant. In abdominal ultrasonography, intestinal ansae were found to be dilated at the lower quadrants, and a noncompressible appendix in 6 mm thickness was observed at the right lower quadrant.

case_report: A 39-year-old female arrived at the emergency department with a 9-day history of pain in the right lower quadrant. She had previously started oral antibiotic treatment at another hospital. Laboratory results indicated an inflammatory condition, with a white blood cell count of 16,500/μL and a C-reactive protein level of 22.01 mg/dL.
test_results: CT showed a 5 cm abscess of the pericecal area.

case_report: A 4-year-old girl undergoing chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia was in the remission induction phase. Her treatment regimen included prednisolone (60 mg/m2/day for 28 days, tapered over 9 days starting from day 29), vincristine (1.5 mg/m2/day on days 8, 15, 22, and 29), L-asparaginase (5,000 U/m2/day on days 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30, and 33), daunorubicin (30 mg/m2/day on days 8 and 15), and intrathecal methotrexate (age-adjusted dosage). She experienced deep neutropenia upon hospital admission. On day 27 of chemotherapy, she developed a fever. Laboratory results showed a leukocyte count of 0.5 × 109/L, an absolute neutrophil count of 0.0 × 109/L, and a C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 2.6 mg/dL. Renal and liver function tests, as well as urinalysis, were normal. Blood cultures were taken from both the port catheter and peripheral vein, and broad-spectrum antibiotics were started empirically, leading to a postponement of chemotherapy. Physical examination revealed no focal source of fever, normal oral mucous membranes, no oral mucositis, and no palpable liver or spleen. The patient had no abdominal tenderness, distension, or other signs of abdominal distress, maintained good oral intake, and had normal stool and no vomiting. A thorax radiograph was normal. The fever persisted for two days but resolved by the third day of antibiotic treatment. On the fourth day, while still afebrile, the patient developed abdominal pain. Physical examination then showed abdominal distension and tenderness. Abdominal ultrasonography was performed, but the presence of free intense air superposition hindered optimal evaluation of the bowels.
test_results: Plain abdominal radiograph demonstrated subdiaphragmatic free intra-abdominal air and the one obtained in lateral decubitus revealed free air movement within the abdominal cavity.
diagnosis: Neutropenic Enterocolitis with Spontaneous Intestinal Perforation

case_report: A 23-year-old female presented with a 6-month history of chest pain, dry cough, hoarseness of voice, and recent onset of stridor. The chest pain was retrosternal, severe, continuous, radiated to the back, and was associated with shortness of breath on mild exertion. The cough was dry, intermittent, and progressively worsened over time, accompanied by hoarseness of voice, recent stridor, and dysphagia mainly for fluids. There was no history of fever, hemoptysis, night sweating, or weight loss. The patient had no history of smoking, recent travel, or contact with tuberculosis patients. Physical examination revealed no abnormalities. Blood investigations were within normal limits, and sputum analysis for Gram-stain and culture showed no growth of organisms. Chest X-ray revealed a left mediastinal mass. Enhanced chest computed tomography (CT) scan identified a left upper mediastinal mass, cystic in nature, located along the arch of the aorta, with thick, enhanced, and irregular walls, measuring 5 cm in diameter. Additionally, multiple enlarged bilateral superior mediastinal lymph nodes were observed. Fiber-optic bronchoscopy confirmed bilateral vocal cord paralysis; however, the cords were not in the median position as the laryngeal entrance was open. Broncho-alveolar lavage for cytology was negative for malignant cells.
test_results: CT-guided transthoracic tru-cut biopsy revealed granulomatous inflammation and caseous necrosis with chronic inflammatory cells, epithelioid cells infiltration, and multinucleated giant cells.

case_report: A 35-year-old male visited the outpatient department with pain in the right buttock. He reported a dull, aching pain in the right buttock for the past 6 months, which had intensified over the last 2 months. The pain worsened when sitting, particularly on hard surfaces, and was not accompanied by swelling. He had been using oral pain relievers for 6 months, which provided partial relief. He also experienced intermittent low-grade fever, insignificant weight loss, normal appetite, and disturbed sleep. There was no history of contact with tuberculosis. Physical examination showed non-inflamed skin over the right buttock, tenderness on deep palpation, and no sinus formation. Pain was noted during hip flexion beyond 70° and terminal internal rotation. No inguinal lymphadenopathy was observed. The sacroiliac joints, lumbosacral spine, and knees appeared normal. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin at 9.2 g/dl, total leucocyte count at 10,800/mm3 with a predominance of lymphocytes, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) at 62 mm/hour, and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels at 2.6 mg/dl, both elevated. The Mantoux test showed an induration of 24 mm, and the chest radiograph was clear. A plain radiograph of the pelvis revealed an osteolytic lesion on the right ischial tuberosity, distinct from the opposite side. Computed tomography (CT) imaging indicated irregularity and destruction of the right ischial tuberosity with associated soft-tissue thickening and fat stranding. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed involvement of the right ischial tuberosity with changes in signal intensity but no collection.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the tissue obtained by CT-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology from the lesion showed epithelioid granuloma. Mycobacteria could not be cultured.

case_report: A seven-year-old female presented with a tender swelling around the right eye and cheek for two months. There was no decrease in vision, discharge, photophobia, or fever. Examination revealed swelling in the right upper and lower eyelid and upper cheek, which was firm, tender, warm, and erythematous, with negative fluctuation tests and no pus points or discharging sinuses. Visual acuity was 6/6 in both eyes. Anterior and posterior segment examinations of the eye were normal. Despite the swelling, extraocular movements were full and free. Direct and consensual light reflexes were normal. Enlarged submandibular lymph nodes were noted, measuring 2x2 cm, non-tender, non-conglomerated, firm, and not fixed to the skin. The overlying skin was not red and non-tender. The child was afebrile with no other systemic complaints. The patient had been treated with oral antibiotics at a peripheral center for one month, with the swelling increasing in size. Noncompliance with the prescribed treatment was reported. The child was admitted for intravenous antibiotics. A contrast-enhanced CT of the orbit and paranasal sinuses showed a peripherally enhancing collection in the anterolateral aspect of the right maxillary sinus and zygomatic arch, extending superiorly along the lateral aspect of the right orbit, with lytic erosive changes, periosteal thickening, and bony sequestration in the zygoma. The child had no history of fever, night sweats, previous TB, or contact with TB. The swelling did not resemble a typical tubercular cold abscess, and the lymph nodes were not matted or fixed to the skin. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was raised, but the complete blood count and liver function tests were unremarkable. The tuberculin sensitivity test (TST) showed 20 mm after 48 hours. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) from the swollen submandibular lymph nodes showed necrotic changes but no granuloma or acid-fast bacilli (AFB). Sputum and gastric aspirate microscopy for AFB showed no evidence of AFB. Antigravity aspirate of the swelling was performed with a 26-gauge needle under local anesthesia, yielding around 1 ml of watery yellowish fluid, which was sent for gram stain, bacterial and fungal cultures, and further testing.
test_results: CBNAAT turned out to be positive. The bacterial and gram stain reports were negative.
diagnosis: Primary Tubercular Osteomyelitis of the Right Maxilla

case_report: A 27-year-old previously healthy African male medical intern experienced a needle-stick injury to his little finger from a wide bore needle (gauge 18) while performing a lumbar puncture on a patient. The injury resulted in a small lesion that bled slightly, which he immediately washed with water and soap. He was promptly started on postexposure prophylaxis Anti-Retroviral drugs (ARVs): Zidovudine, Lamivudine, and Kaletra for 28 days according to the Kenya National AIDS Control Program protocol. Initial rapid HIV test (Determine) and a PCR test done after completing the ARVs were both negative. He had no significant past medical history. The patient source, an African Female, was in WHO clinical stage 4, not on ARVs, and was being investigated for meningitis. She passed away shortly after the lumbar puncture, and her results were not followed up until several months later. Two weeks post-injury, the intern developed swelling of the little finger with a persistent dull ache, leading to surgical intervention. Pus was aspirated from the finger, and incision and drainage were performed under local anesthesia. Culture of the pus grew Staphylococcus aureus sensitive to flucloxacillin, which was administered. Despite debridement and various antibiotic regimens including levofloxacin, clindamycin, ceftriaxone, and vancomycin, the open wound on his little finger persisted for several months. The intern continued daily cleaning and dressing of the wound. Six weeks post-injury, he developed painless axillary lymphadenopathy. Over the next 6 months, the swelling of the little finger persisted and appeared to spread to the hand, accompanied by low-grade fever, night sweats, and subjective weight loss. He underwent surgical debridement 6 months post-injury and was started on levofloxacin. Intraoperatively, necrotic debris was found. Radiographic examinations during the illness showed no bone involvement. Serial blood counts revealed persistently elevated lymphocytes and a raised ESR. Liver function tests and renal tests were normal.
test_results: Histological examination of the tissue taken revealed a chronic inflammatory process, granulomatous tubercles with epithelioid cells, giant cells of Langerhans, and a mononuclear infiltrate but no acid-fast bacilli (AFB) were demonstrated on Ziehl–Nelson stain.

case_report: A 24-year-old male presented with a 15-day history of persistent swelling of the upper lip that ulcerated 2 days prior. He reported no history of trauma, fever, cough, weight loss, or drug or tobacco usage, and his past medical and dental history was non-contributory. The patient was thin built with normal vital signs and no lymphadenopathy. Examination revealed a diffuse, non-tender swelling of the lower lip with mild eversion. A reddish-pink granular lesion was observed involving the vermillion border, labial mucosa, floor of the mouth, and mandibular anterior gingiva. The lesion exhibited patchy areas of brown crustation, bleeding, and purulent discharge. A plain chest radiograph and complete hemogram were within normal range. Serologies for syphilis and Leishmania, Mantoux test, and Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for HIV were negative.
test_results: An incisional biopsy from the lesion revealed numerous necrotizing epitheloid granulomas with Langhans type giant cells. Ziehl-Neelsen staining showed multiple rods like acid fast bacilli.

case_report: A 66-year-old female with a history of peripheral arterial disease, previously treated with left common iliac stenting, and neurogenic claudication due to L3-L4 spinal stenosis, presented with generalized weakness, fatigue, and headache for 3 weeks. She also reported intermittent back pain, fever, chills, and night sweats. Over the past month, she experienced a new onset of migraine-like headaches with photophobia. She denied coughing, shortness of breath, history of headaches, or any other new symptoms. Four months ago, she underwent minimally invasive L3–L5 lumbar fusion surgery with allograft bone graft placement. Her family history was unremarkable. She had a social history of 20 pack years of prior tobacco use, having quit smoking 2 years ago, and denied alcohol or recreational drug use. Upon admission, her vital signs, including temperature, were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed that she was oriented to person and place but not to time. She understood the reason for her admission but was unable to answer all questions appropriately. Healed incisions without erythema, pus, or drainage were observed at the L3–L5 level. Cranial nerves II–XII were grossly intact. Bilateral lower extremity strength was 4/5, consistent with previous assessments, and no other focal deficits were noted. Laboratory results showed a sodium level of 117 mmol/L, down from 129 mmol/L two months prior, chloride at 77 mmol/L, and an elevated platelet count of 425,000/μL. ESR and CRP were elevated at >130 mm/h and 61.8 mg/L, respectively. TSH was normal at 2.4 mIU/mL. The random cortisol level was elevated at 29.5 μg/dL. Serum osmolality was 256 mOsm/Kg, urine osmolality was 487 mOsm/kg, and urine sodium and potassium were 32 mmol/L and 47 mmol/L, respectively. Urine toxicology and HIV tests were negative.
test_results: A chest X-ray showed diffuse miliary nodular pattern of both the lungs, which was confirmed by the presence of innumerable micronodules on CT chest. MRI of the brain with contrast did not show any evidence of hydrocephalus, space-occupying lesions, or basilar meningitis. MRI of the lumbar spine showed L4-L5 osteomyelitis and postsurgical changes. MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine was negative for any structural lesions.
diagnosis: Disseminated Tuberculosis  from contaminated bone graft

case_report: A 30-year-old Moroccan male with no significant medical history presented with left back pain, urinary frequency, and visible blood in the urine for six months. Physical examination showed the patient was exhausted, had anorexia, and had lost 10kg over six months. Urogenital examination revealed left epididymitis and a normal-sized prostate with a slightly firmer consistency than typical for a young patient, but no nodules were detected. Laboratory tests indicated normal kidney function with a creatinine level of 66.2μmol/L, an inflammatory response with an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 120mm/hour, and a C-reactive protein level of 200mg/L. Other laboratory results were unremarkable. Renal and pelvic ultrasound identified left hydronephrosis and hydroureter.
