Further imaging with CT urography showed left ureterohydronephrosis in the left lumbar ureter due to focal wall thickening.
test_results: The results proved strongly positive.

case_report: A 2.5-year-old female, born to healthy, non-consanguineous Caucasian parents, was delivered at 35 weeks gestation due to fetal bradycardia and intrauterine growth retardation, necessitating an emergency C-section. Family history is notable for a maternal uncle and a paternal first-cousin with suspected autism spectrum disorder. At birth, the patient required positive-pressure ventilation for 3 minutes. Apgar scores were 1 at 1 minute and 7 at 5 minutes. Birth weight was 1698 grams (<1st percentile). She was hospitalized for 3 weeks in the neonatal intensive care unit due to prematurity and intrauterine growth restriction, weighing less than 2000 grams. Feeding difficulties necessitated nasogastric tube feeding, but she was discharged after 20 days on full oral feeds. At 8 months, she had plagiocephaly with torticollis, which was resolved with molding helmet therapy. Developmental milestones were not met at 1 year. At 13 months, gross motor skills were at the 10-month level, fine motor and receptive language skills at the 9-month level, and expressive language skills at the 5-month level, indicating delays of 3 to 8 months. At 15 months, her developmental quotient was between 50 and 55, indicating mild to moderate psychomotor delay. She had strabismus, corrected surgically at 16 months, and bilateral tympanostomy tubes were implanted at the same age. Intensive therapies led to improvements, and she began walking independently at 18 months. She exhibits hypotonia, a wide-based gait, and poor balance, falling more frequently than expected. Her expressive language skills are limited, with a spoken vocabulary of about 12 words and some use of sign language. She is social, curious, interactive, highly active, and has a short attention span compared to peers.
test_results: An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed sinus bradycardia with heart rate of ∼50 at the age of 18 months. A 24-h Holter monitor showed evidence of sinus node dysfunction, with over 3,000 sudden rate drops and pauses that exceeded 3 s.
diagnosis: Intellectual Developmental Disorder with Cardiac Arrhythmia
Orpha_name: CDK13-related congenital heart defects-intellectual disability-facial dysmorphism syndrome

case_report: A 48-year-old female with a history of steroid-responsive right-sided facial nerve palsy at ages 43 and 47 presented with sudden onset of double vision and right-sided pain behind the eye for 3 days. Neurological examination revealed right-sided horizontal double vision due to right abducens nerve palsy. Non-contrast-enhanced brain MRI showed no abnormalities. Vital signs and laboratory tests, including random blood sugar, were within normal limits. Oral prednisolone 60 mg daily was prescribed, but her symptoms worsened with involvement of the oculomotor nerve after 1 week. Comprehensive screening for infectious, autoimmune, metabolic, and endocrine conditions identified newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus (HbA1C: 7.8%).
test_results: Contrast-enhanced brain MRI showed enhancement in the right cavernous sinus. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination revealed mildly elevated CSF protein (47.2 mg/dL) and glucose (101 mg/dL) with a normal cell count.

case_report: A 31-year-old male presented with a three-week history of progressively worsening headaches, requiring frequent use of analgesics. Initially, the headache was holocephalic but later intensified and localized to the right temple and the right peri- and retro-orbital areas. By the end of the third week, he developed double vision and drooping of the right eyelid, which worsened over the next five days. He reported mild light sensitivity and a subjective feeling of imbalance but did not experience sound sensitivity or significant nausea. He denied any prior history of recurrent headaches, fever, rash, nasal symptoms, or other systemic symptoms. His past medical history included a prescription for oral doxycycline and acyclovir seven days before the onset of the headache, for asymptomatic chlamydia and herpes simplex 2 (HSV2) infections detected via PCR testing of his urine during a routine sexually transmitted infection check. There was a family history of migraine in his mother. On physical examination, he was afebrile and had no rash. Neurological examination showed complete right oculomotor nerve palsy with spared pupils. Other ocular motor nerves were normal, as were his optic discs and facial sensation. Visual acuity and color vision were normal, and there were no signs of meningeal irritation. No bruit was heard over his globes.
test_results: A contrast-enhanced MRI of the head did not show any intracranial abnormalities or abnormal enhancement patterns. There were no visible inflammatory lesions nor enhancement patterns within the cisternal portion of the oculomotor nerves. A dedicated contrast-enhanced MRI of the orbit did not show any orbital lesions. Intracranial MRA, digital subtraction angiography (DSA), and magnetic resonance venography (MRV) did not show any aneurysms, fistulae, or venous sinus thrombosis. A blood draw revealed mild lymphopenia with normal inflammatory markers. Basic cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies, as well as CSF oligoclonal bands, syphilis and Lyme serology, and angiotensin-converting enzyme assay, were similarly unremarkable. Electroencephalography (EEG) showed intermittent generalized slowing in the theta-delta frequency range.

case_report: A 58-year-old woman experienced left periorbital pain, ptosis, and painful ophthalmoplegia over a period of three weeks. Initially, she had left nasal pain that intensified with Valsalva maneuvers and did not improve with oral Amoxicillin. One week later, she developed increasing pain around the left eye and behind the eye. This was followed by cranial nerve III palsy, resulting in painful left eye ophthalmoplegia, double vision, and ptosis. Fourteen days before the onset of these symptoms, she had received her third COVID-19 vaccination (Comirnaty, Pfizer-BioNTech), with no adverse effects from her previous two vaccinations 4 and 5 months earlier. Six years ago, she had a single episode of biopsy-confirmed bilateral idiopathic dacryoadenitis that resolved completely with corticosteroids. She was not on any regular medications and had not received any other recent vaccinations. On examination, her visual acuity was 6/4.5 in both eyes, and intraocular pressures were normal. External examination showed partial ptosis of the left upper eyelid without periocular erythema, edema, or proptosis. Ocular motility examination revealed cranial nerve III palsy with 15 prism diopters of left exotropia and hypotropia. Optic nerve function was normal, and both anterior and posterior segment examinations were unremarkable. During a follow-up, she reported new altered sensation in the cranial nerve V1 distribution. Initial laboratory tests showed normal inflammatory markers: white cell count (WCC) 8.57 × 103/μL, C-reactive protein (CRP) 1.7 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 9 mm/hr. Autoimmune serology (ACE, ANA, ANCA, and ENA) and IgG4 levels were normal, with no atypical expression of cell lymphoid markers.
test_results: MRI orbital scans revealed enhancement and enlargement of the left cavernous sinus and clinoid, with dural enhancement and extension through the superior orbital fissure to the orbital apex with mild apical nerve sheath enhancement. The lobulated appearance, lack of hyperostosis of the anterior clinoid and the enhancing clinoid were less consistent with meningioma.

case_report: A 31-year-old woman reported experiencing intermittent pain and redness in her right breast for over a year. She did not have a history of fever, rash, joint inflammation, muscle pain, swollen lymph nodes, or other systemic symptoms. Her medical, surgical, family, and social histories were unremarkable. Initial clinical findings and ultrasound suggested an inflammatory condition of the right breast, but pus cultures did not show bacterial growth. She received treatment involving incision and drainage along with antibiotics, but there was no improvement. She underwent multiple incision and drainage procedures at various centers without significant relief. Symptoms persisted for 3 months despite these repeated interventions and antibiotic courses.
test_results: An incisional biopsy revealed granuloma without any fungal components or atypical cells. A tissue sample for mycobacterium tuberculosis was negative. Evaluation for autoimmune or infectious granulomatous disease was negative, including inflammatory markers, differential cell count, and chest imaging.

case_report: A 46-year-old Saudi woman presented to the emergency room with complaints of pain and a mass in her right breast. She noticed the mass about a month ago, and it had been growing rapidly and becoming more tender. A previous mammogram indicated findings of concern (BI-RADS 5). She exhibited nipple retraction but did not have fever, redness, or discharge. She was a nonsmoker, did not consume alcohol, was breastfeeding, and was on oral contraceptives. She had a history of mastitis due to milk stasis, which was treated with antibiotics. Her obstetric history included 7 full-term pregnancies and 2 miscarriages, and she had a cesarean section three years ago without complications. There was no family history of breast, colon, ovarian, or prostate cancer. At the breast surgery clinic, her vital signs and laboratory results were normal. Physical examination showed slight peau d’orange changes, skin thickening, a retracted nipple, and a 5 × 4 cm retro-areolar mass with no palpable axillary lymph node. A mammogram was performed, showing an incomplete evaluation of the right breast (BI-RADS 0) and a normal left breast (BI-RADS 1). Breast ultrasound indicated changes in the right breast with a predominantly inflammatory pattern (BI-RADS 4B), and further evaluation of the right axillary lymph node and right breast was suggested.
test_results: A right axillary lymph node biopsy revealed reactive lymphoid tissue, and a core needle biopsy of the right breast showed non-necrotizing granulomatous inflammation, centered on the lobules, with lymphocytes, plasma cells, epithelioid histiocytes, scattered multinucleated giant cells, and neutrophils. A polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test for tuberculosis (TB) was negative.

case_report: A 44-year-old female with a history of hypothyroidism and diabetes mellitus presented with abdominal pain and vomiting for the past 3 days. The pain was described as aching and crampy, diffuse, located in the epigastric region, and radiating to the back between the shoulders, not relieved by antacids or food. She also experienced nausea and multiple episodes of watery, non-bilious projectile vomiting over the same period. She had been taking levofloxacin for a urinary tract infection diagnosed on urine analysis for the last 3 days. Her medications included amlodipine for hypertension and insulin for diabetes, with which she was compliant. She reported no alcohol consumption, drug abuse, or use of medications other than those for diabetes and hypertension. There was no history of trauma or similar symptoms. On examination, she appeared uncomfortable and was clutching her abdomen. Vital signs were stable with blood pressure at 100/70 mmHg, respiratory rate at 21/min, and heart rate at 99/min. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the epigastric region without rigidity or guarding. Bowel sounds were present, and no visceromegaly was noted. The remainder of the systemic examination was unremarkable.
test_results: Her initial laboratory evaluations revealed elevated serum lipase and amylase levels. Abdomen CT showed diffuse and generalized enhancement of the pancreas with ill-defined borders and fat stranding, and localized edema. No gallstone, biliary sludge, pseudocyst, or biliary tract abnormality was appreciated.

case_report: A 20-year-old male from Brazil presented with low back pain persisting for 8 months, without any associated trauma. Initial spinal radiographs taken in March 2019 revealed significant changes, prompting a referral to the Orthopedics Service at the Hospital of Federal University of Juiz de Fora. The patient was prescribed orthopedic braces, advised to undergo physical therapy, and referred to the Osteometabolic Diseases outpatient clinic of the Endocrinology and Rheumatology Services in October 2019. Radiographs indicated a notable decrease in bone density, a scoliotic curve with left convexity, and reduced height of the lumbar vertebrae, with partial collapses at T12, L1, L2, L3, and L5, and recent collapses at T12 and L1, indicative of bone fragility fractures. Subsequent magnetic resonance imaging confirmed these findings. Bone scintigraphy performed in August 2019 showed no hyper flow or abnormal hyperemia in the thoracolumbar spine, but later images revealed increased tracer uptake in the lumbar spine (vertebrae T10–T12, L2–L4), which was nonspecific and raised questions about osteoarticular processes or ankylosing spondylitis. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) in October 2019 demonstrated low bone mineral density in the lumbar spine, femoral neck, and total femur, based on Z Score evaluation. Consequently, treatment with vitamin D 7000 IU per week and bisphosphonate alendronate 70 mg weekly was initiated due to vitamin D3 insufficiency. The patient's medical history included fully treated syphilis in 2018 and surgical resection of perianal condyloma in September 2017 and February 2018. Family history noted a maternal uncle who died of systemic sclerosis. The patient denied alcohol consumption and smoking. Physical examination revealed no lentiginous skin areas or blue nevi, but wide violet streaks on the upper limbs and abdomen, facial plethora, increased fat in the temporal facial region and hump, limb ecchymosis, hypotrophy of the arms and thighs, central obesity, and kyphoscoliosis. Blood pressure was 150 × 90 mmHg, BMI was 26.09 kg/m2, and waist circumference was 99 cm, with height maintained at 1.55 m. Laboratory tests were conducted to investigate secondary causes for osteoporosis.
test_results: The microscopic analysis described the expansion of the zona fasciculate, with the formation of multiple nonencapsulated nodules composed of polygonal cells with ample and eosinophilic cytoplasm and frequent depletion of intracytoplasmic lipid content. No areas of necrosis or mitotic activity were observed.
diagnosis: Cortical Pigmented Micronodular Hyperplasia of the Adrenal Gland
Orpha_name: Isolated primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease

case_report: A 44-month-old girl presented with complaints of excessive weight gain, growth failure, and mood changes. Her blood pressure was recorded at 150/80 mmHg. She measured 96 cm in height, placing her in the 25th percentile, and weighed 19.7 kg, which is above the 97th percentile. Her body mass index was calculated to be 21.4 kg/m2, also above the 97th percentile. Physical examination revealed a plethoric moon face, hypertrichosis, and spotty pigmentation on the conjunctivae, lips, and oral mucosa. There was no notable family medical history, including any history of tumors or adrenal diseases.
test_results: Her urinary cortisol level was 966.2 µg/m2/24 hr (reference range [RR], <70 µg/m2/24 hr), and her serum cortisol level after a high dose dexamethasone suppression test was basal 34.6 µg/dL (RR, 5–23 µg/dL), peak 32.9 µg/dL (RR, <5 µg/dL). The 24-hour urine cortisol levels of six-day Liddle's dexamethasone suppression test revealed following values; 1,380.0; 1,357.2; 1,064.4; 897.0; 944.0; 755.6 µg/24 hr from day 1 to 6, respectively. Her computed tomography of the adrenal gland revealed 5-mm nodular thickening of the left adrenal gland and a nearly normal right adrenal gland.

case_report: A 12-year-old female presented with seizure disorder, nystagmus, severe receptive and expressive language delays, severe intellectual disability, and stereotypic behavior. Anemia was initially considered but later ruled out through examination and lab workup. Physical examination revealed settled dysmorphic features including a low-set ear, small jaw, synophrys, microcephaly, and a high-arched palate. Additional findings included hirsutism on the back with a low hairline, skin laxity, hypotonia, and lower limb eczema. The patient was born full-term via cesarean section with a history of hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, requiring a week-long stay in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit. She had a low birth weight of 1.5 kilograms due to fetal distress and oligohydramnios, and presented with 5th finger clinodactyly and cyanosis at birth. Pulmonary stenosis was identified and surgically corrected at five months of age, with a history of chest tube insertion noted. Nystagmus was present since birth, and seizures began at six years old. Initial treatment with Levitericitam was discontinued by the mother after one month. The patient had undergone approximately six blood transfusions, each associated with transfusion pyrexia. Vaccinations were up to date. The patient was the first child of a consanguineous marriage (1st-degree cousins) and had three healthy younger siblings. No family history of neurological or genetic issues was reported. The patient experienced frequent mixed seizures, with the most recent occurring a day before presentation. No family history of neonatal death, abortion, genetic or metabolic diseases, hematological diseases, autism, intellectual disability, or similar conditions was reported. Her weight, height, and head circumference were all in the third percentile. Physical examination revealed three well-circumscribed hyperpigmented lesions on the abdomen and left thigh, with no hypopigmented lesions. The patient did not make eye contact, was non-interactive, and did not respond to her name. She exhibited lateral gazes, finger mannerism, flapping hand movements, unusual facial grimacing, high pain tolerance, extreme distress to sounds, and excessive mouthing. A high-risk M-CHAT score of 16 was recorded. Motor milestones were delayed; she sat without support at one year and walked alone at two years. At presentation, she could run and use stairs with rails but could not jump, ride a bike, or walk backward, indicating severely delayed fine motor skills. Only the palmar grasp reflex was present. She could not draw or copy shapes, feed herself, or dress/undress, and was fully dependent on her mother for daily activities. She spoke her first word at eight years old and had not spoken since, with severely delayed expressive and receptive language and adaptive skills. Repetitive vocalization was occasionally observed. Audiological evaluation indicated normal hearing bilaterally with no risk factors for progressive or late-onset sensorineural hearing loss. Cardiac examination excluded atrial septal defect and pulmonary stenosis, with an echocardiogram showing no cardiac disease, atrial septal defect, or residual pulmonary stenosis. The electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm, and there was no pericardial effusion. Chest examination revealed good bilateral air entry. Last recorded vitals were blood pressure of 95/53 mmHg, pulse of 93 bpm, axillary temperature of 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), and respiration rate of 18 bpm.
test_results: The whole exome sequence (WES) revealed a heterozygous VUS in the DHX30 gene. DHX30 (NM_138615.2:c.2387C>T):c.2387C>T p.(Pro796Leu) was classified as a variant of uncertain significance (class 3). MRI findings of the head revealed a smaller size of the head, implying microcephaly, and a thickened calvarium with a hyperplastic marrow signal diffusion restriction, diffuse moderate enhancement, and a FLAIR hyperintense marrow signal, signifying marrow hyperplasia. On MRI, there was diffuse, mild cortical volume loss, mildly dilated ventricles, and no midline shift or mass effect. There was also a diffuse FLAIR signal in the cingulate gyrus, extending superiorly into the precuneus bilaterally. Volume loss and abnormally shaped atrophic gyri were seen in the precuneus, especially along the medial cortex, and were best appreciated in axial T2 sequences. Additionally, there were areas of subcortical and juxtacortical white matter. A FLAIR hyperintense signal abnormality was seen in the frontal lobes bilaterally (axial FLAIR series 400/120). There was a focal blurring of gray-white differentiation in the left medial frontal gyrus. There were normal hippocampal formations and fornices, the basal ganglia, the pituitary gland, the corpus callosum, the brainstem, and the cerebellum. Myelination was complete, and there was no sign of acute infarcts, hemorrhagic lesions, or masses. The post-contrast sequences showed no enhancing lesions. Moreover, there was no significantly increased leptomeningeal or dural enhancement. However, there was a mild mucosal thickening in the paranasal sinuses, with predominantly mucosal thickening seen in the right frontal, sphenoid, and maxillary sinuses and ethmoid air cells, implying right ostiomeatal pattern inflammatory sinusitis. MR spectroscopy revealed no abnormal metabolites in the basal ganglia or the white matter. The area of abnormality in the medial frontal cortices also showed no abnormal metabolites.
diagnosis: Neurodevelopmental Disorder, Severe Motor Impairment, and Absent Language  due to a novel de novo mutation in the DHX30 gene

case_report: Patient 5 is a 4-year-old male born prematurely at 24 weeks of gestation. He was discharged from the neonatal intensive care unit at 84 days of life. Microcephaly developed in early childhood. He experienced feeding difficulties, reflux, silent aspiration, and constipation. He underwent tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy for sleep apnea. He exhibited global developmental delay and was diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. Self-injurious behaviors were observed. Physical examination revealed truncal hypotonia with hypertonicity in the distal extremities, choreiform movements, and intention tremor. An MRI of the brain was unremarkable. Ophthalmologic findings included retinopathy of prematurity, cortical visual impairment, and strabismus. Chromosomal microarray analysis and methylation studies for Angelman and Prader-Willi syndromes were negative.
test_results: Trio whole-exome sequencing detected a de novo frameshift variant in CTNNB1 (c.1665dupG, p.T556fs).

case_report: A 42-year-old woman with multiple previous pregnancies presented to the emergency room with back pain. One month prior, she underwent a cesarean section and a left ovarian cystectomy without any complications. She breast-fed her baby post-delivery. Her height was 159 cm and her weight was 56 kg. She had no other bone abnormalities and did not engage in regular exercise. She had no history of past surgeries, family medical issues, or trauma. Physical examination revealed diffuse back pain, which was severe enough to cause difficulty in getting up for 7 days.
test_results: The lumbar spine anteroposterior (AP) and lateral revealed recent compression fractures of T12, L1, and L3. A bone scan also revealed increased bone uptake, perfusion, and multiple recent compression fractures of T12-S1. Bone marrow density determined using dual energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) revealed that the T-scores for the lumbar vertebrae L1-L4, femoral neck, and femoral total were significantly low in the patient.

case_report: A 35-year-old woman presented with severe back pain (visual analogue scale; VAS = 10/10) following her third pregnancy. Her family history was negative for osteoporotic fractures. She had no history of using heparin or other medications associated with osteoporosis risk. The patient did not smoke or consume alcohol. During her adolescence, she led a sedentary lifestyle. There was no history of oral contraceptive use. She breastfed for 9 months during her first pregnancy and 12 months during her second pregnancy, with no back pain reported during those periods. Laboratory tests, including biochemical examinations and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, were within normal limits. Her Vitamin D level was 31 ng/ml. No secondary causes of osteoporosis were identified.
test_results: Acute bone marrow edema was observed at the level of T11 vertebra and loss of height was observed at T5–7, 9 and L1 vertebrae in the thoracolumbar MRI. Lumbar total Z score −3.7, lumbar BMD = 0.687 g/cm2, femur total Z score −1.5, femur total BMD = 0.815 g/cm2 were detected.

case_report: A 36-year-old woman, who has a 6-year-old son, was pregnant again. At 37 weeks of gestation, she experienced a fall from a standing height, resulting in minor trauma to her right wrist. She presented to the emergency department with right wrist pain. During her first pregnancy and 12 months of breastfeeding, she did not experience any discomfort or pain in her hips or lower back. The patient had no history of anorexia nervosa, diabetes mellitus, thyroid or parathyroid diseases, rheumatoid arthritis, kidney diseases, or other chronic conditions. She did not consume alcohol, smoke, or use drugs. There was no family history of osteoporosis or pathological fractures. She had stopped taking calcium and vitamin supplements during her pregnancy. Her height was 163 cm, and she weighed 62 kg (body mass index 23.3 kg/m2). Examination revealed swelling and deformity of the right wrist with restricted range of motion. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable, except for lumbar tenderness. An emergency MRI was performed, revealing a Barton fracture in the right wrist. Although surgical intervention was indicated, a temporary closed reduction and plaster external fixation were applied due to the patient's imminent delivery. At 38 weeks of gestation, she delivered a healthy boy and began breastfeeding. Three days postpartum, she was admitted to the orthopedic ward for surgery.
test_results: Bone mineral density (BMD) was measured with dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA, HOLOGIC®Discovery-A), which showed the BMD of the lumbar (L1–L4) as 0.714g/cm2 (Z-score = −2.9) and total hip as 0.717 g/cm2 (Z-score = −1.7).

case_report: A 47-year-old male presented with swelling in the left eye for 2 months, which has been gradually increasing and is associated with pain and redness. There is a swelling near the limbus on the temporal side for the past 1.5 months, also gradually increasing in size, with redness and intermittent mild pain. The patient reported no history of trauma or systemic illness such as fever, joint pains, or recent weight loss. He has been using topical antibiotics and lubricating eye drops for 2 months. Imaging performed elsewhere revealed a 10 × 7.5 mm well-defined mass lesion in the temporal aspect of the left eye, involving both intra- and extraocular components. The patient had been previously diagnosed with an ocular tumor and was advised to undergo plaque brachytherapy, and was referred to our clinic for further evaluation.
test_results: MRI showed a 10 × 7.5 mm well-defined mass lesion in the temporal aspect of the left eye with both intra- and extraocular components. Slit lamp examination of the left eye revealed a nodular, elevated mass arising from the sclera measuring 10 × 8 mm associated with congestion and mild tenderness.

case_report: A 52-year-old female of West African origin was referred to the Department of Ophthalmology, Zealand University Hospital. The patient had been using Dexamethasone (1 mg/ml) eye drops (Maxidex, Alcon) intermittently over the past 5 years due to a red right eye (RE). The local therapy was ineffective, and the patient had stopped the treatment weeks before her admission. Upon admission, she reported a persistent feeling of ocular congestion and pain in the RE. The left eye (LE) was asymptomatic. Visual acuity was measured at 20/40 in the RE and 20/15 in the LE. Slit-lamp examination revealed violaceous ocular injection around a subconjunctival nodular thickening located 4 mm from the limbus, along with vessel dilation in both the superficial and deep vascular plexuses. Anterior segment OCT (spectral-domain OCT, 3D OCT-2000; Topcon Corp, Tokyo, Japan) at the center of the hyperemic lesion showed hyporeflective spaces and hyperreflective nodules on the episcleral tissue band. Hyporeflective spaces bisecting the scleral lamellae were also observed. Ultrasound B-scan and dilated fundus biomicroscopy showed no signs of posterior involvement. Swabs from the conjunctiva for M. tuberculosis PCR analysis were negative. A comprehensive serologic evaluation was conducted, including tests for venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL), rapid plasma reagin (RPR), antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), and angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE).
test_results: The patient tested positive on Quantiferon assay.

case_report: A 50-year-old female presented with redness, watering, and severe ocular pain in her right eye (RE) for 1 day. Visual acuity was measured at 6/18 in the right eye (RE) and 6/6 in the left eye (LE). The left eye (LE) exhibited a deep anterior chamber (AC) and a normal fundus. Slit lamp examination of the right eye (RE) showed conjunctival chemosis, circumcorneal congestion, a shallow anterior chamber (AC), and no AC cells. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was recorded at 38 mmHg in the right eye (RE) and 12 mmHg in the left eye (LE) using applanation. Additional observations in the right eye (RE) included swelling of the upper eyelid, scleral tenderness, a clear cornea, a reactive round pupil, fine choroidal folds, shallow peripheral annular choroidal detachment, and restricted ocular movement accompanied by pain. The patient reported a similar episode three years prior.
test_results: An ultrasonogram (USG) B-scan of RE showed fluid accumulation in the subtenon space with thickening of the ocular coats. Ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) revealed thickening of the sclera and supraciliary effusion along with some anterior rotation of the ciliary body. Fundus fluorescein angiography made the choroidal folds obvious.

case_report: A 12-year-old male presented to the Ophthalmology Emergency Clinic with a 1-week history of decreased vision in the right eye. There was no history of redness, pain, trauma, ocular surgery, or major systemic disease. Examination revealed best corrected visual acuity in the right eye of −6/9 with (0.25/−0.50 cyl × 90 [no improvement with pin hole]), and in the left eye, it was 6/5 with 0.50/−0.25 cyl 90. Both eyes had normal anterior segment, direct and consensual pupillary reaction, intraocular pressure (12 mmHg), and extraocular muscle movements. Color vision (Ishihara PseudoIsochromatic Chart) was normal in both eyes. Amsler chart testing showed metamorphopsia in the right eye but was normal in the left eye. Visual field charting (Humphreys Visual Field Analyzer C-120) was normal in both eyes. Fundus evaluation revealed a cup-disc ratio of 0.1 in the right eye and 0.3 in the left eye. The optic disc in the right eye was hyperemic with blurred margins. Horizontal striae were observed in the posterior pole between the optic disc and the fovea, as well as in the parafoveal and perifoveal regions deeper to the retinal blood vessels. The retinal blood vessels and the fovea appeared normal in the left eye.
test_results: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of macula OD showed folding of the inner retinal layers in the posterior pole, with a central thickness of 254 μ and a parafoveal thickness between 400 and 420 μ. Macular region OS was normal. B-scan ultrasonography (USG) OD showed diffuse thickening of the choroid and sclera and was normal OS. Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) showed early leakage of the dye from the disc OD and normal dye transit OS. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was normal, but right orbit showed diffuse isointense swelling that became hyperintense with contrast on T1-weighted and hypointense on T2-weighted images. The left eye was normal.

case_report: A 79-year-old woman had primary pterygium excision and conjunctival autograft transportation with mitomycin C (MMC) in her left eye in June 2016. Eighteen months after the surgery, she reported minor congestion at the excision site. She was prescribed topical fluoroquinolone and fluorometholone to be used four times daily. Three months later, she experienced redness and pain in her left eye. Examination revealed diffuse anterior scleritis with multiple peripheral corneal infiltrates, but no scleral necrosis was observed. The anterior chamber showed no flare or cells. Fundus examination was not possible due to a cataract and posterior synechia. B-mode echography indicated an intravitreal shadow and retinal detachment.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium showed hyperintensity around the left ocular globe including the posterior sclera, indicating an inflammatory reaction. Vitreous samples were histologically negative for malignant cells, and culture revealed no growth of bacteria or fungi. The IL10:IL6 ratio in the vitreous was low at 0.36, essentially ruling out malignant lymphoma. The samples from the vitreous and anterior chamber were negative for bacteria, fungi, herpes simplex virus, and varicella-zoster virus DNA using real-time PCR. Microscopic examination revealed that the deposits were inflammatory granulomas, but not bacterial masses or malignant tissue. Serological examination indicated that antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) with p-type was positive.
diagnosis: Surgical-Induced Necrotizing Scleritis  with intraocular inflammation

case_report: A 22-year-old woman arrived at the emergency room with sudden visual loss the day after undergoing rhinoplasty surgery for aesthetic purposes at Khatam Hospital, affiliated with Mashhad University of Medical Sciences, Mashhad, Iran. The surgery was performed under general anesthesia by an ENT surgeon, who reported no complications during the procedure. Vasoconstrictors (epinephrine) were applied topically and locally to minimize bleeding and maintain a clear surgical field, which is standard practice in nasal surgeries. The patient's medical history included intermittent episodes of reduced vision over the past two years, with cardiologic and neurologic evaluations yielding negative results. These transient visual disturbances were attributed to migraine aura due to vasospasm. Upon examination, the visual acuity of the left eye was 20/20, while the right eye had no light perception. A relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) of 4+ was noted in the right eye. The anterior segment examination using a slit lamp was normal for both eyes.
test_results: The posterior segment examination showed nerve fiber layer swelling, cherry-red spot in the macula, vessel attenuation, and ischemic retina in the right eye.

case_report: A 76-year-old male with a history of hypertension managed with anti-hypertensive medication experienced a sudden, painless decrease in vision in the left eye (OS) for one day. The best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 6/9 in the right eye (OD) and counting fingers close to face (CFCF) in the OS. A relative afferent pupillary defect was observed in the OS. Intraocular pressure was within normal limits in both eyes (OU) (OD 14 mmHg, OS 16 mmHg). The anterior segment examination was unremarkable in both eyes. Fundus examination of the OD was normal. The OS fundus examination revealed a normal-appearing optic disc with a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.3:1, arteriolar narrowing with segmental blood flow (box-carring), and diffuse background pallor with a small area of normal-appearing retina temporal to the optic disc, corresponding to patent cilioretinal arteries.
test_results: Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) showed diffuse retinal thickening and inner retinal hyperreflectivity except in the small area corresponding to the patent cilioretinal arteries. Optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) showed an absence of flow signals in superficial, deep, and outer retinal plexuses except in a well-demarcated area nasal to the fovea. OCTA of the disc and macula OS showed the presence of three cilioretinal arteries and flow void in the rest of the vasculature.
diagnosis: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion  with triple cilioretinal artery sparing

case_report: A 76-year-old female arrived at the emergency department due to sudden, painless vision loss in her left eye. She experienced severe blurring and reduced peripheral vision in the affected eye upon waking. Her medical history includes significant thromboembolic events such as pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, and middle cerebral artery territory infarction with subsequent recurrent ischemia. Visual acuity was measured at 20/30 in the right eye and only hand motion was detectable in the left eye. Intraocular pressures were recorded at 13mm in both eyes. Neurologic and standard external eye examinations showed no other abnormalities.
test_results: POCUS immediately recognized the classic 'Spot sign'. CT Angiogram followed by an MRI of the brain did not show any acute neurologic infarction.

case_report: A 24-year-old man presented with stupor, mutism, and food refusal. He had no personal or family history of mental illness until four years prior to admission. At the age of 20, he was first hospitalized after being found wandering dazed in the streets. He received haloperidol initially but was switched to olanzapine and lorazepam. He recovered and returned home, but about twelve months later, he was again admitted to a local hospital for two months with profound stupor, immobility, and inanition. He recovered on a combination of haloperidol and lorazepam. As an outpatient, haloperidol was switched to olanzapine, but both olanzapine and lorazepam were subsequently discontinued due to side effects of weight gain and sedation, resulting in a recurrence of symptoms and re-hospitalization about ten months after his last discharge. During a complicated admission lasting four months, he underwent sequential trials of olanzapine, risperidone, and lorazepam without any improvement in symptoms. A trial of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) was initiated, but despite receiving ten bilateral brief-pulse treatments over one month with an average stimulus energy dosage of 386.2 millicoulombs resulting in ten seizures lasting an average of 37.9 seconds, he showed no change or improvement in his symptoms and remained stuporous. He finally recovered on a combination of parenteral haloperidol and lorazepam, and was discharged on oral lorazepam and risperidone with monthly paliperidone injections due to suspected medication non-adherence. After discharge, he showed no signs of residual psychosis or mood disorder for over eight months and was able to return to employment. During remission, his speech was spontaneous, he showed greater emotional expressiveness, and he had no psychomotor retardation. However, his affect was mildly blunted and he had limited insight. Due to his complaint of lethargy and the possibility that some of his residual symptoms represented drug-related extrapyramidal side effects, oral risperidone and lorazepam were discontinued over the next six months, at which time an acute episode recurred and he was admitted to our hospital.
test_results: He showed negativistic behavior and was rated 21 on the Bush-Francis catatonia rating scale (BFCRS). Extensive laboratory investigations, including serum chemistries, hematology, serology, toxicology, cerebrospinal fluid examination, neuroimaging and electroencephalography, revealed no significant abnormality.

case_report: A 27-year-old female with a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, systemic lupus erythematosus, and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis was admitted for acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Upper and lower endoscopies were planned. Preoperative peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) was 98% in room air. The patient underwent rapid sequence intubation with video laryngoscopy, and the endotracheal tube (ETT) was secured at 20 cm at the lip. During the procedure, the patient experienced brief episodes of hypoxia (SpO2 85-90%), which temporarily improved with alveolar recruitment maneuvers. After the reversal of neuromuscular blockade and emergence from inhalational anesthesia, the patient was breathing spontaneously at a rate of more than 25 breaths per minute with low tidal volumes, leading to continued intubation. Shortly after, SpO2 rapidly decreased to 70%. Manual ventilation and additional recruitment maneuvers were performed with minimal improvement. Copious clear secretions were observed in the ETT that were not initially present.
test_results: The ETT was noted to be in the right main stem bronchus and withdrawn 2 cm. The right upper bronchus was seen to arise above the carina. All branches of the right main bronchus were visualized for verification and the ETT was re-secured at 18 cm at the lip, above the tracheal bronchus opening.

case_report: A 32-year-old Korean male was admitted to Inha University Hospital in Incheon, Korea, presenting with dyspnea and right chest pain for one day. Physical examination revealed decreased breath sounds in the right lung fields without displacement of the maximal cardiac impulse point. The patient had a history of right pneumothorax treated with tube thoracostomy one and a half years prior. He had no history of pulmonary or bronchial tuberculosis. The patient was a smoker. A posteroanterior chest radiograph showed increased radiolucency, overinflated lung parenchyma, and sparse vasculature in the upper half of the right lung. Additionally, a v-shaped branching opacity was observed in the right parahilar area, and pneumothorax was noted in the right lower pleural cavity. A 32 Fr chest tube was inserted into the right pleural cavity.
test_results: The chest CT taken in the state of full expansion of the right lung after tube thoracostomy showed a branching soft tissue density in the region of the posterior segment of the right upper lobe. The orifice of the posterior segmental bronchus was visualized but the orifice of the subsegmental branch of the posterior segmental bronchus could not be visualized separate from the origin. Perfusion lung scan showed a perfusion defect in the right upper lobe. The pathological findings of the resected right upper lobe showed overinflation of the posterior segment. There were no obstructed lesions of the orifices of the three segmental bronchi of the right upper lobe. However, one of the subsegmental branch of the posterior segmental bronchus was obstructed and there was a 2.5×1.5×1.5 cm sized cystic mass containing brownish mucus material at the distal portion of the obstructed subsegmental bronchus.

case_report: A 62-year-old male from India visited the orthopedics department due to a progressively worsening low back ache. He reported no other symptoms, and his bowel and bladder functions were normal. There was no history of trauma, and the patient appeared healthy and well-nourished. Physical examination revealed no tenderness in the pelvic bones, and neurological examination showed no motor deficits. A whole body bone scan was conducted to investigate potential skeletal issues. The scan involved an intravenous injection of 555 megabecqueral of 99mTc methylene diphosphonate (MDP), followed by initial dynamic imaging of the pelvis and high-resolution anterior and posterior whole body images taken three hours later using a dual head variable angle E Cam Gamma camera. The scan revealed an abnormal focal site of MDP uptake at the sacrum S2 level, indicating sacral osteoblastic activity of uncertain origin.
test_results: A cystic lesion was reported in right neural foramen of S2 of 25 × 15 × 25 mm size whose intensity was the same as cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). No contrast-enhanced findings were observed. Similar lesions were also noted in S1, right T3-T4, right T7-T8, and left T6-T7 neural foramina but with no corresponding hot spots in MDP bone scan. Initial and a 6-h delayed CT myelography showed no free communication between cyst and subarachnoid space. There was surrounding sacral bony erosion around this cyst.

case_report: A 10-year-old boy presented with facial puffiness, swelling in both lower limbs, and reduced urine output. The patient also experienced fever and hematuria for two days. Clinical examination showed anemia, facial puffiness, and bilateral pedal edema. Blood pressure was recorded at 130/100 mm Hg. Abdominal examination identified a mass in the suprapubic and umbilical regions, along with an undescended left testis. Further examination of the abdominal mass indicated a hydronephrotic pelvic kidney.
test_results: Ultrasonogram showed a gross hydronephrosis of a low-lying left pelvic kidney with renal pelvis crossing the midline. The contents were turbid. The right kidney collecting system was normal but showed a rotational anomaly. The Color Doppler study showed the possibility of a horseshoe kidney with abnormal vasculature. Micturating cystourethrogram (MCU) was normal. An intravenous pyelogram (IVP) was performed which revealed that the left side of the horseshoe kidney showed no function, whereas the right half functioned well with collecting system showing rotational anomaly. Cranially, the intravenous urogram (IVU) revealed a normal appearing collecting system.

case_report: A 52-year-old female patient was admitted to our hospital on October 5, 2022, presenting with recurrent diarrhea for the past year. Symptoms included unexplained diarrhea, weight loss, fever, night sweats, and abdominal pain, persisting for over a year. Her medical history includes diabetes and cervical spondylosis. There is no available personal or family medical history. Physical examination revealed no palpable lymph nodes, organomegaly, or skin lesions. Laboratory tests showed normal peripheral blood counts and biochemical parameters, including liver and renal function and serum lactate dehydrogenase levels. Bone marrow smear and biopsy did not indicate any abnormal cell involvement.
test_results: Colonoscopy revealed a large ulcer in the blind. Immunohistochemistry showed the following: CD3+, CD5-, CD4-, CD8+, CD56+, TIA+, BcL-2+, Ki-67+ (approximately 40%), CD20-, PAX5-, CD10-, Bcl-6-, CD21-, CD23-, CyclinD1-, PD-1-, CD79α-, CD30-, C-Myc-, and EBER-. Pathological gene detection of JAK3 deletion mutations revealed a mutation frequency of 24.6%. Positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) showed that the ileocecal intestinal wall was slightly thickened, the thickest part was approximately 2.6 cm, and the uptake was increased, with a maximum standardized uptake value (SUV) value of 6.3. Several enlarged lymph nodes could be seen around, the short diameter of the large one was approximately 1.5 cm, the uptake was increased, and the maximum SUV was 6.1. Rectal and colorectal wall uptake was increased, and the maximum SUV was approximately 7.0.

case_report: A 77-year-old female experienced abdominal discomfort starting in early September 2019, accompanied by night sweats and fever, with minimal symptom relief. On September 30, she developed acute severe abdominal pain and was taken to the emergency room. Examination revealed a fever of 38 degrees Celsius, rebound pain in the lower abdomen, and muscular defenses. CT scans indicated thickening of the jejunum and ileum walls, fatty deposits around the small intestinal tract, and thickening of the nearby intestinal wall. Gastrointestinal perforation could not be excluded. Additionally, CT scans showed adhesions due to inflammation of the sigmoid colon and part of the ileum. She was referred to our hospital for further evaluation. Laboratory tests showed a C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 6.80 mg/dL (normal range: 0–0.14 mg/dL) and an interleukin 2 receptor (IL2R) level of 3,652 U/mL (normal range: 121–613 U/mL). Transanal small bowel balloon endoscopy revealed mild edema with petechial erythema around 100 cm from the Bauhin valve, which was considered to be lymphatic follicular hyperplasia. The colon showed no abnormal findings. Transoral small bowel balloon endoscopy identified shallow erosions and edematous mucosa around 200 cm from the anal side near the Trites ligament, with ulcers and disrupted villous structures in the same area. Specimens were obtained from both the erosion and ulcer sites.
test_results: All specimen showed atypical lymphocytes infiltrating the small intestinal mucosa demonstrating intraepithelial lymphocytosis. Immunohistochemical staining showed that infiltrated lymphocytes were positive for CD3, CD7, and CD56, but negative for CD4, CD5, and CD8. EBER-ISH was negative. PET-CT showed abnormal uptake in the irregular wall thickening of the small intestine and the mesenteric lymph nodes. Diffuse hyperaccumulation of the ribs, spine and pelvic bone (SUVmax: 8.30) was also observed, but there were no findings in bone marrow aspiration.

case_report: A 33-year-old Chinese male presented to the Urology Department due to the incidental discovery of a retroperitoneal mass on a computerized tomography (CT) scan during a routine health examination. The patient reported no symptoms, including abdominal or back pain, episodic hypertension, palpitations, or lower limb edema. Both his medical history and physical examination were unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, and D-Dimer levels, were within normal ranges. Additionally, tests for paraganglioma, such as 24-hour urinary catecholamine levels and somatostatin receptor imaging, returned negative results.
test_results: Contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed a stenosis of IVC in the suprarenal segment, a 34 mm × 30 mm × 33 mm retroperitoneal mass on the right side of the infrarenal IVC and a small mass about 10 mm in diameter in the retroperitoneal area that was considered an enlarged lymph node. No thrombosis was found in the IVC.

case_report: A two-and-a-half-year-old Saudi girl with no significant past medical history arrived at the emergency room with a 3-day history of frequent falls, unsteady gait, tremors, slurred speech, and difficulty swallowing accompanied by excessive drooling. On the second day of admission, she developed a dystonic posture in her lower limbs, severely limiting her ability to walk and stand. There was no history of decreased consciousness, seizures, or ophthalmoplegia. Initially, the mother reported no history of drug ingestion, trauma, recent infection, behavioral changes, or neurodevelopmental regression. However, after receiving the toxicity test results, the mother disclosed that her daughter had ingested approximately 20 mL of ethyl alcohol used in perfumes one day before the symptoms began. The parents reported that the child's developmental milestones were achieved at the appropriate ages. She was born to consanguineous parents and has an older brother with a similar presentation. Physical examination showed the patient to be alert, conscious (Glasgow coma scale 15/15), and vitally stable, with no meningeal signs. She spoke in full sentences but with dysarthria. Her pupils were equal, round, and reactive to light, and her extraocular muscles were intact. Her face was symmetric. Neurological assessment revealed normal muscle power and deep tendon reflexes, with a bilateral plantar flexor response. Daily assessments showed increased muscle tone in the legs, which maintained an extended posture with ankle inversion and plantar flexion. She could support herself on her legs but was unable to walk unassisted due to ataxia. Tremors were observed in both upper extremities. The patient was admitted to a high-dependency unit for monitoring. Initial laboratory tests showed normal complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, and basic metabolic workup. A toxicity test later revealed an ethyl alcohol level of 10 mg/dL.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed bilateral symmetrical areas of abnormal signal intensity, which was high on the fluid-attenuated inversion recovery, T2 weighted image and restricted diffusion on the diffusion-weighted images and apparent diffusion coefficient noted in the basal ganglia in both putamen and caudate nuclei. The cerebral cortex, subcortical white matter, cerebellum, and brainstem were relatively spared.

case_report: A 29-year-old, single Saudi female with an 18-year history of well-controlled, insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, presented with a recent, painless enlargement of the left breast. Physical examination identified a 4×1 cm, well-circumscribed, retro-areolar hard mass in the left breast, which was not fixed and non-tender, with no changes to the overlying skin. The right breast and both axillae showed no abnormalities. The patient has a significant family history of breast cancer, with her sister diagnosed at age 27, and her mother and aunt also affected. The affected family members were not tested for BRCA1 and 2 gene mutations. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, renal, and liver function tests, showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Ultrasound (US) imaging revealed a highly suspicious, ill-defined hypoechoic lesion in the left lower outer quadrant consistent with a Breast Imaging, Reporting & Data System (BI-RADS) 4 category. Mammographic examination revealed both breasts were of normal shape with bilateral dense glandular parenchyma (breast composition category C). Microscopic examination revealed acellular fibrous-sclerotic tissues with normal-looking lobules and ducts, surrounded by dense lymphocytic infiltrate. No evidence of any malignancy was detected.

case_report: A 33-year-old woman with a long-standing history of insulin-dependent diabetes complicated by diabetic retinopathy presented to the Breast Clinic for evaluation of a new, painless breast lump. She discovered a lump in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast 3 months prior, which had gradually increased in size. She reported no breast pain, nipple discharge, or skin changes. Regarding breast cancer risk factors, she was nulliparous, menopausal due to a hysterectomy for dysfunctional uterine bleeding with intact ovaries, had no previous breast biopsies, and was a nonsmoker. She had no personal or family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Her only medication was a NovoLog insulin pump. Physical examination revealed a dominant 3 × 1 centimeter hard, irregular, movable, painless mass in the left upper outer quadrant and a smaller, less defined lesion in the left lower quadrant of the breast. Imaging evaluations included a diagnostic mammogram showing extremely dense breasts. An ultrasound of the palpable area was negative for abnormality. A bilateral MRI of the breast showed multiple regions of enhancement and a small incidental fibroadenoma in the left breast; no abnormality was detected in the area of palpable concern. A second look ultrasound and left diagnostic mammogram with magnification were performed, and while the fibroadenoma seen by MRI was detected by ultrasound, the area of palpable abnormality showed normal tissue with no mass.
test_results: Pathology demonstrated benign breast parenchyma, dense stromal fibrosis, and periductal lymphocyte infiltrate.

case_report: A 43-year-old man, the only child of non-consanguineous parents, visited the allergy clinic with a history of peach allergy (oral allergy syndrome) since childhood. A few years earlier, the patient had been identified with low IgG, low IgM, and recurrent upper respiratory tract infections. During follow-up at our hospital, he was found to have a nonspecific lipid transfer protein (nsLTP)-mediated peach allergy. Low IgG levels and absent IgM were confirmed. Detailed history-taking revealed other infectious episodes prior to the identification of low immunoglobulin levels, including a severe varicella zoster virus (VZV) infection at the age of 4 that required hospitalization. During adolescence, he had mild warts on the hands that resolved without treatment in 3 to 4 years. The patient also reported bilateral pneumonia due to type A influenza infection that required ICU admission for 6 days at age 38 years. There was no family history of severe infections.
test_results: CT sinus scanning showed chronic rhinosinusitis that required 2 to 3 antibiotic courses per year during the following two years, without hospital admission. The chest CT study was normal.
Orpha_name: X-linked combined immunodeficiency due to SASH3 deficiency

case_report: A 15 year 8-month old female patient was born at 36 weeks gestation with a weight of 2880 g (P21), length of 47 cm (P12), and head circumference of 33 cm (P23). Pregnancy was uncomplicated, and birth was by cesarean section due to prolonged labor, but otherwise unremarkable, with normal Apgar scores. Metabolic screening and otoacoustic emissions were normal. Parents (mother aged 30 and father aged 33) were non-consanguineous and healthy, and the patient has a healthy younger sibling. Developmental milestones included a social smile at 2 months, sitting unsupported at 9 months, walking autonomously at 17 months, speaking the first intelligible words at 4 years, and building sentences at 5 years of age. The Griffiths III Mental Development Scale assessment showed a general quotient of 52 at 9 years of age. Pubertal development is adequate for the current age. The patient exhibited impaired social interaction, restricted interests, and repetitive behavior at 18 months of age. Throughout development, the patient has also shown symptoms consistent with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and oppositional defiant disorder. The patient has an IQ of 52 as measured by the WISC-III. Additionally, the patient has a mixed language disorder and developmental coordination disorder. No other specific neurological symptoms were observed, such as dystonia, sensorineural hearing loss, visual symptoms, or epilepsy. Two brain MRIs (one at 3 years and another at 15 years of age) and an electroencephalogram at 18 months of age showed no structural abnormalities or changes. No dysmorphic features were observed. At the current age of 15, the most impacting symptoms are related to behavior, with repeated bouts of auto and hetero-aggressive behavior, attention deficit, and frequently obsessive conduct. Multiple treatment regimens have been tried, including several drug types such as antipsychotics, antidepressants, mood stabilizers, and stimulants, with mixed results in managing the psychiatric disorder. Multiple episodes of extrapyramidal adverse effects of antipsychotics have also been observed in the patient.
test_results: The GNB1 variant is predicted to be deleterious by several in silico tools (Condel, 0.558; SIFT, 0.000; Polyphen-2, 0.976; Massessor, 1.000). The GNB1 variant was confirmed by Sanger sequencing in the patient and shown to occur de novo, since it was not detected in either parent.
diagnosis: GNB1 mutation causing global developmental delay with intellectual disability and behavioral disorders

case_report: A 48-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 2-month history of recurrent abdominal pain, which had worsened over the past 2 weeks. He had previously undergone an exploratory laparotomy for acute diffuse peritonitis 50 days prior at a local hospital. During the surgery, numerous 0.2–0.4 cm yellow-white tubercles were observed on the surface of the congestive small intestine, colon, appendix, greater omentum, and mesenterium, particularly in the distal ileum, without any apparent perforation. Rapid pathology of the appendix and omentum indicated acute nonspecific inflammation, and intestinal tuberculosis was initially suspected. Saline and metronidazole were used for irrigation, and abdominal drainage was placed. The patient was discharged with intermittent slight abdominal pain on the 15th day post-operation. Twenty days later, he experienced sudden severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and fever (39°C). He was readmitted to the local hospital and subsequently transferred to our ICU due to worsening condition. Physical examination revealed significant abdominal tenderness, rebound tenderness, and weakened bowel sounds. Additionally, generalized skin eruptions with an atrophic porcelain-white center surrounded by an erythematous rim were noted on the trunk and extremities, measuring 0.2–1.2 cm. The patient had no history of chronic diseases, alcohol use, family history, herbal agents, or suspected drug use. Laboratory tests and radiographic results were as follows: WBC 8.65*10^9/L (3.5–9.5*10^9/L), NEUT% 0.938 (0.40–0.75), procalcitonin 171.45 ng/ml (0–0.05 ng/ml), HBV-DNA 9.15E+08 IU/ml (<5.0E+02 IU/ml). Tuberculin test, Widder test, anti SS-A, and SS-B antibodies were negative. ANA was 1:100 weakly positive, and Anti Ro-52 antibodies were positive. Computed tomography revealed a small amount of free air bubble, edema, thickening of the small bowel wall, and massive seroperitoneum. An exploratory laparotomy was performed due to the primary diagnosis of Crohn's disease with intestinal perforations. During the operation, more than 100 whitish-yellow plaques, dozens of intestinal perforations, and purulent materials were found. Two meters of the perforated small bowel were resected, and the seromuscular layer was sutured in the wafery areas, followed by enterostomy and abdominal drainage tube placement. On the 5th day post-operation, intestinal contents drained again, indicating recurrence of perforation. Attention was then directed towards the correlation between the perforation and skin lesions.
test_results: Biopsy of skin eruption showed atrophy of epidermis, hyperplasia and collagen of dermal fibrous tissue, degeneration of elastic fibers, significantly reduction and partial necrosis of skin appendages, fibrinoid necrosis in small vessels of the deep dermis and thrombosis in local lumen. Histopathology of the resected intestine showed edema and hyperaemia, thrombus organization of both tiny artery and veins lumen with acute and chronic inflammatory cell infiltration.

case_report: A 35-year-old Hindu woman visited the dermatology outpatient department with complaints of painful depigmented lesions lasting for 1½ years. On physical examination, the lesions appeared as porcelain white atrophic papules with surrounding erythema, located on the trunk, upper limbs, thighs, and chest. The lesions were mildly tender. The patient reported a history of joint pain for the past 7–8 years and experienced headaches, dizziness, and ocular pain over the last 3 months. She did not report any proximal muscle weakness or skin tightening. Her menstrual cycles were regular. She had a history of irregular bowel habits, specifically constipation. There was no history of hypertension, diabetes, or any other medication use. Laboratory tests for antinuclear antibody, lupus anticoagulant, cardiolipin antibody, and β2-glycoprotein were all negative. An ultrasonography of the abdomen showed no abnormalities. An ophthalmological examination revealed myopic astigmatism in both eyes. Stool occult blood testing was negative.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the sections showed atrophic epidermis with mild hyperkeratosis and flattened rete ridges focally. The underlying papillary was showing a band-like mucin deposit along with focal sclerosis. The middle and deep dermis had patchy mucin along with focal fibrosis. Cuffing of mild to moderate lymphomononuclear infiltrate was observed around perivascular areas in the dermis. Few of the blood vessels were showing endothelial cell proliferation. Scant subcutaneous tissue was available in the biopsy. The result of Alcian blue staining for dermal mucin was positive.

case_report: A 46-year-old female visited the dermatology clinic with a seven-month history of asymptomatic pink-to-violaceous macules and papules mainly on the legs, with a few on the abdomen and left ventral forearm. The lesions measured 1-2 mm in diameter and exhibited various morphologies. Newer papules appeared bright pink to red, while older lesions were violaceous. Dermoscopy showed visible capillaries and small vascular dots in some lesions, along with lesions featuring a central white sclerotic area. The patient's medical history included uncontrolled diabetes mellitus with diabetic ketoacidosis, infiltrating ductal carcinoma of the right breast, prior sepsis, atrial fibrillation, osteoporosis, cervical spine degeneration due to spinal stenosis, myofascial pain dysfunction syndrome, chronic abdominal pain with cramping, and chronic headaches.
test_results: The histologic findings showed epidermal atrophy with basement membrane thickening and vacuolar change at the dermal-epidermal junction and papillary dermal hemorrhage. There was markedly increased dermal mucin shown by an Alcian blue stain, as well as rare vessels containing luminal organizing thrombi. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) revealed strong granular staining with immunoglobulin M (IgM) along the dermal-epidermal junction, but was negative for IgA, IgG, C3, and fibrinogen.

case_report: A 17-month-old boy was admitted to the Department of Neurosurgery, Children’s University Hospital in Cracow due to worsening balance issues. A week prior, his parents observed that he had a tendency to tilt his head to the right and experienced choking while drinking. Neurologic examination revealed cerebellar disturbances of balance, evidenced by staggering and an inability to walk, compulsory head tilting to the right, slight right pyramidal hemiparesis, left VI and VII cranial nerve palsies, bulbar signs such as choking, weak pharyngeal and palatal reflexes, and a suspected visual field lesion which could not be confirmed due to the child's lack of cooperation.
test_results: Computer tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed an enormous tumor (44 × 35 × 45 mm in CT and 35 × 36 × 32 mm in MRI) in the brainstem, mostly in the left pons and medulla oblongata. The tumor was hyperintense in T2 and showed heterogenous contrast enhancement in T1 with narrowing of the fourth ventricle. There were no features of supratentorial hydrocephalus in spite of evidence of elevated pressure in the posterior fossa.
diagnosis: Embryonal tumor with abundant neuropil and true rosettes

case_report: The patient is a 55-year-old woman with a history of muscle tightening episodes for over 10 years, primarily occurring at night. She also experiences a squeezing sensation in her feet, which is worsened by wearing shoes. These symptoms have progressively worsened, leading to medical evaluation. Neurological examination showed no abnormalities in mental status, cranial nerves, muscle strength, cerebellar function, or reflexes. Sensory examination for light touch, vibration, proprioception, pin prick, and temperature was normal. Her gait, tested with shoes, was tentative, indicating foot discomfort. No trophic changes were observed in her hands or feet. Neurophysiological testing indicated normal motor and sensory nerve conduction parameters. Needle electromyogram of selected leg muscles showed no abnormalities, and the study did not indicate any large fiber neuropathy.
test_results: Quantitative sudomotor axon reflex test showed significantly decreased sweat production in both proximal and distal segments of the right leg. Skin biopsy showed significant reduction in the epidermal nerve fiber density 0.93 (nl>8.3) in the distal thigh and 0.88 (nl>4.3) in the distal leg.

case_report: A 26-year-old African American female with a history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), end-stage renal disease (ESRD) due to lupus nephritis (LN), a past episode of Steven–Johnson Syndrome from a sulfa allergy, and resistant hypertension presented to the emergency department with a painful, peeling, blistering rash and fever. The rash had developed over three months with intermittent response to prednisone therapy and worsened three weeks prior to presentation. Fever began one week before presentation. The rash initially appeared on her arms and spread progressively. She also experienced shortness of breath with a productive cough containing green, bloody sputum, as well as nausea and vomiting. The patient reported adherence to her home dose of prednisone but inconsistent use of mycophenolate mofetil. She missed two consecutive hemodialysis sessions due to pain from the blistering rash on her feet. On physical examination, she had a fever of 100.6°F and a heart rate of 130 beats per minute. Skin examination revealed brown plaques on the forehead and bilateral cheeks, sparing the nasolabial folds, with erosions and hemorrhagic crusts on the philtrum, ears, forehead, nose, chin, and lips. Dark brown plaques with erosions and atrophic scars were noted on the forearms and lower legs, along with deep red to violaceous painful targetoid lesions on the palms and soles. The trunk had pink eroded macules, and the back had pink patches within a background of dusky necrotic plaques. There were multiple full-thickness epidermal necroses with large areas of bleeding and denuded skin on the arms and chest in sun-exposed areas. The oral mucosae were free of lesions. Laboratory results showed pancytopenia with a white blood cell count of 2.03 × 10^3/UL, absolute neutrophil count of 1.25 × 10^3/UL, hemoglobin of 8.8 g/dL, hematocrit of 28.9%, and platelet count of 69 × 10^3/UL. Electrolytes were within normal limits except for elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN) at 41 mg/dL and creatinine at 5.49 mg/dL. Calcium was low at 7.2 mg/dL, and albumin was 3.2 g/dL. Phosphorous was elevated at 5.0 mg/dL. Liver enzymes showed AST at 286 IU/L and ALT at 31 IU/L. Total bilirubin was 0.5 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase was 136 IU/L, CK was 91 U/L, serum lactate was 0.80 mmol/L, and ferritin was 5885 ng/mL. Electrocardiogram indicated sinus tachycardia. Chest X-ray showed no lung infiltrates or effusions. Abdominal ultrasound revealed no acute process, with normal liver echogenicity, echotexture, and size, and no splenomegaly. Sputum gram stain and cultures were unremarkable, and blood cultures were negative for bacteria and yeast. The patient was anuric due to chronic dialysis. Evaluation of lupus activity showed double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) antibody at 42 IU/mL, complement 3 (C3) at 43 mg/dL, and complement 4 (C4) at 9 mg/dL. Rheumatoid factor was negative. Sjogren's anti-SSA was >8.0 AI, and Sjogren's anti-SSB was <0.2 AI. HIV screen and viral hepatitis panels for hepatitis A, B, and C were negative.
test_results: Skin biopsies showed focal interface changes. Periodic acid Schiff (PAS) stain was negative for fungal microorganisms. Gram stain highlighted surface cocci bacteria. VZV and herpes I/II immunostains were negative. Direct immunofluorescence revealed finely granular deposition of C3, IgM, and fibrinogen consistent with lupus.

case_report: A 55-year-old African man visited the ophthalmologist due to a growth on his right upper eyelid that had been present for 8 months. The swelling began at the orbital ridge and extended to the entire upper lid. The patient reported spontaneous bleeding from the lesion, eye discharge, and rashes before the visit. He was unable to fully open the affected eye. There was no history of trauma, photophobia, weight loss, or tearing. The patient had undergone surgery and chemotherapy for rectal carcinoma 6 years ago, with the last chemotherapy session 5 years prior to this visit. He has a known history of asthma and no family history of similar conditions. On examination, the right eye showed a projecting fleshy mass on the upper eyelid, measuring 3.3 × 2.0 cm. The mass was firm, lobulated, and nontender with irregular rough surfaces. Additionally, there was a mildly tender, mobile, nonmatted right preauricular lymph node.
test_results: Histology of the mass showed an effaced architecture due to proliferating malignant epithelial cells disposed as trabecules, solid nests, and tongues. The individual malignant cells were basaloid, with marked nuclei pleomorphism, irregular nuclei outline, and open vesicular chromatin with prominent nucleoli. Mitoses were up to 11 per high power field with few atypical forms. In some areas, these cells appeared multivacuolated. Areas of squamous differentiation were also present. Microscopic examination of the lymph node showed variably sized and shaped lymphoid follicles with few prominent germinal centers. The lymph node was not infiltrated by malignant cells.

case_report: A 35-year-old woman with no history of smoking experienced left back pain following a 2-hour flight and began coughing the next day. She has a medical history of acute myeloid leukemia (French-American-British classification type M1) diagnosed at 1 year and 8 months old. She underwent an allogenic bone marrow transplant from her older sister at 2 years and 3 months old. Methotrexate was used as a preventive measure. At 3 years old, she developed a rash and symptoms including dry mouth and reduced tear production. Three years prior to the current presentation, at age 32, she had pneumonia in the right lung, which was treated with ceftriaxone sodium hydrate, though no specific bacteria were identified.
test_results: Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed centrilobular granular shadows, bronchiectasis, and pleural thickening of the apex of both lungs. Pulmonary function test results indicated the following: forced vital capacity (FVC), 1.66 L (56%); forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1), 1.04 L (40%); absent bronchodilator response; and FEV1/FVC, 63%.
diagnosis: chronic graft-versus-host disease  presenting with bronchiolitis obliterans  and pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis

case_report: A 43-year-old South Asian male, with no known past medical history, presented with an eight-month history of asymptomatic, hyperpigmented patches, characterized by discrete central atrophy. The lesions were violaceous in color and ovoid in shape, appearing gradually over the dorsal aspect of hands bilaterally, and over the medial aspect of both thighs. Small multiple unilateral lesions were also noted over the lateral aspect of the right lower limb. There was no history of any recent or distant trauma, tick bites, new medication use, or any recent fungal infections reported by the patient. The patient reported that these lesions had shown the same form, texture, and color since their initial appearance, with slow and nominal growth in size noted over the course of the past eight months. Both his prior medical and familial history was deemed unremarkable. With the exception of these dermal lesions, the patient’s general health and overall physical condition were exceptional. On dermatological examination, there were two large hyperpigmented violaceous patches with atrophic changes noted on the bilateral dorsum of hands, measuring 3 x 4 cm and 4 x 6 cm in size. Small, multiple, brownish, and hyperpigmented patches with a depressed shiny center were noted over the lateral aspect of the right lower limb as well as on the medial aspect of both thighs. All patches were observed to be ovoid in shape, with a central atrophic, “cigarette paper”-like appearance, conserved pathognomonic “cliff-drop” borders, and minimal surrounding peripheral desquamation. The patient reported a lightly diminished sensation within the patches, and hence a pinprick examination was performed in and around the lesions. The sensation was deemed to be intact in all areas.
test_results: Histopathologic findings of this specimen revealed focal basal hyperpigmentation. The dermis displayed marked dermal atrophy, with mildly thickened collagen fibers and minor perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate. There was no obvious dermal sclerosis appreciated nor any absence of the dermal appendages. There were no signs of epidermotropism or any evidence of epidermal infiltration. The rest of the skin adnexa was unremarkable. Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stains were negative for fungal elements.
diagnosis: Idiopathic Atrophoderma of Pasini and Pierini

case_report: A 2-year-old girl exhibited an erythematous atrophic lesion on her right shoulder, present since birth. The lesion had gradually increased in size over time, but its shape, color, and texture remained unchanged since it was first noticed. Her family and medical history were unremarkable. Physical examination revealed slightly depressed erythematous plaques on the right shoulder, with no induration observed.
test_results: Histopathological examination of a specimen from the involved skin showed markedly reduced dermal thickness when compared with adjacent normal skin. The collagen bundles in the dermis were slightly homogenized in appearance. The elastic tissue stain showed no abnormality.
diagnosis: Congenital Atrophoderma of Pasini and Pierini

case_report: A 49-year-old male presented with right upper quadrant abdominal pain and jaundice for a duration of 2 days and was admitted to the Fifth Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University. The patient's pulse rate was regular, and both temperature and blood pressure were within normal ranges. The patient reported a dietary history that included consumption of raw freshwater fish. Stool specimen analysis using the direct smear method (with each specimen smeared onto 3 labeled slides) did not reveal the presence of parasite eggs.
test_results: Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) revealed obstruction of the common bile duct by a stone with obviously diffuse dilation of intrahepatic ducts. A flat, leaf-like worm was found under the choledochoscope at the extremitas inferior common bile duct during the operation.

case_report: A 16-year-old female reported a gradual, painless decrease in vision in both eyes over six months. She had a history of slow growth, dental issues including decay, loss, and misalignment, hearing problems, developmental delays in childhood, and poor academic performance. She experienced seizures over the past four years. Her menstrual history was normal, with menarche at age 14. She was born from a nonconsanguineous union and delivered at home without significant neonatal issues. Ocular examination showed visual acuity of 1/60 in both eyes. The anterior segment revealed bilateral total white cataracts with normal pupillary reactions. B-scan ultrasound of the posterior segment showed bilateral optic disc edema without optic disc drusen. General physical examination noted short stature (138 cm, 80% of expected), a rounded chubby face, short stubby hands and feet (brachydactyly), particularly affecting the fourth and fifth metacarpals, and obesity (BMI of 25.26). Chvostek's sign and Trousseau sign were present. Oral cavity examination showed hypodontia and misaligned teeth. Her sexual maturity rating was Tanner's stage III.
test_results: A computerized tomographic scan of the brain showed extensive intracranial calcifications bilaterally. An electrocardiogram showed prolongation of QT interval. The biochemical profile revealed hypocalcemia (Ca2+ 7.3 mg/dl; normal range, 8.5-10.2 mg/dl), hyperphosphatemia (S. PO43- 6.7 mg/dl; normal range, 2.5-4.1 mg/dl), normal alkaline phosphatase (15 KAU; normal range, 2-17 KAU), normal serum creatinine (0.8 mg/dl), and markedly elevated serum PTH level (526 pg/ml; normal range, 10-60 pg/ml).
