case_report: A 55-year-old woman with a history of short stature and neurocognitive impairment, living with her brother and entirely dependent, presented to the emergency department with dyspnea and increased abdominal perimeter for one week. On admission, she exhibited tachypnea with peripheral oxygen saturation between 87-89% on room air, bilateral crackles on pulmonary auscultation, abdominal tenderness in the left quadrants, and bilateral peripheral edema. Laboratory findings on admission included global respiratory insufficiency with slight acidemia (pH: 7.330, pCO2: 68.6 mmHg, pO2: 53.4 mmHg, saturation of 85.8%, normal lactate and bicarbonate). Computed tomography showed no significant changes. The patient was treated with non-invasive mechanical ventilation and admitted to the internal medicine department. During hospitalization, her respiratory insufficiency resolved, and initial ionic imbalances were corrected. However, she developed subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH 6.30 µUI/mL and serum-free thyroxine (T4) 0.8 ng/mL). She was discharged a week and a half after admission, fully compensated, and referred to internal medicine consultation with ion oral supplementation.
test_results: The genetic test revealed the variant c.989A>G p.(Glu330Gly) in heterozygosity in the GNAS gene, with a normal PTH (48.2 ng/L) value.

case_report: A 16-year-old Afghan girl was referred to the French Medical Institute for Mothers and Children (FMIC) in Kabul, Afghanistan, by a provincial hospital. She had a history of abnormal limb and eye movements since early childhood, which were poorly controlled. Her family history was unremarkable, and there was no consanguinity between her parents. On general physical examination, she exhibited short stature, a round face, and a short, depressed neck. Additional features included sparse scalp hair, a depressed nasal bridge, coarse facial and skin texture, dental caries, and poor periodontal status. She had brachydactyly of the fourth and fifth digits of both hands and feet. The patient was obese with a body mass index (BMI) of 35.3, a height of 133 cm, and a weight of 62 kg. Laboratory investigations showed low serum calcium at 4.6 mg/dL, high serum phosphate at 7.6 mg/dL, and a parathyroid hormone (PTH) level of 85 pg/mL. She also had a vitamin D deficiency with a level of 5 ng/mL, while her thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level was normal.
test_results: Calcification involving basal ganglia, periventricular region, and cerebellar hemispheres.

case_report: A 45-year-old elite female runner experienced sudden anterolateral left knee pain and a popping sensation at mile 17 during a marathon. The patient noted a painful pop in her knee during extension. Pain intensity was reported as high as 10 out of 10 during walking and running but was alleviated with rest. Past medical history, surgical history, and review of systems were unremarkable. On physical examination, the patient exhibited an antalgic gait. A visible pop was observed on the anterolateral aspect of the patellar tendon with acute knee extension, accompanied by focal tenderness upon manual palpation of the anterolateral fat pad and minimal knee joint effusion. A firm, tender nodule was palpable when the knee was in full extension. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.
test_results: An magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was obtained and showed a well-defined intermediate to low signal intensity soft tissue nodule in the deep proximal lateral border of the infrapatellar fat pad measuring 1.3 cm by 0.9 cm. This nodule was adjacent to the inferior lateral margin of the patella, in close proximity to the anterior margin of the lateral femoral trochlea. Pathology report described a well-circumscribed tan nodule with rusty-orange pigmentation measuring approximately 1.5 cm in the greatest dimension. The nodule was composed of mononuclear cells with discreet eosinophilic cytoplasm and round nucleus with interspersed multi-nucleated giant cells, small collections of foamy macrophages and hemosiderin deposits.

case_report: A 39-year-old female presented with a palpable lump in the right breast that had been present for 3 months. She had previously undergone bilateral breast augmentation a year prior. Physical examination identified a rubbery, well-defined, solitary mass located at the 6 o’clock position of the right breast. Ultrasonography showed a regular hypoechoic mass measuring 3.0 cm × 2.4 cm × 2.8 cm, situated 4 cm from the nipple. No palpable axillary lymph nodes were detected. Due to the risk of prosthesis rupture from biopsy and the well-defined boundary of the mass, a wide excision was performed for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. The excised mass was well-circumscribed, measuring 3 cm in diameter, with a grayish-yellow cut surface and was solitary.
test_results: Histologically, there was a regular collagenous capsule around the mass. Most areas of the mass had a flat surface covered with finger-like projections or villi. These sheets of cells were composed of many rounded macrophage-like synovial cells and fibroblasts synovial cells and represented as synovial metaplasia. Hemosiderin granules were distributed in the lesion. The tumor was composed of round and polygonal synovium-like monocytes with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and rounded and reniform nuclei. The main part of tumor was blended with nested and scattered xanthomatous cells and osteoclast-like giant cells. The osteoclast-like giant cells contained an abundant cytoplasm and many evenly distributed and usually centrally located oval nuclei, some of which contained small nucleoli. Only a few lymphocytes were scattered in the monocytes. Neither seepage of material from prosthesis nor from foreign refractile material was identified in this nodule. Epithelial cells in spindle cell elements were not observed. Cleft-like spaces, rare mitotic figures, and hyalinized stroma could be seen. The immunohistochemical analysis revealed that the synovium-like monocytes and xanthomatous cells were positive for Bcl-2, SMA, CD68, and CD10. P63 was focally positive in mononuclear cells. Ki67 was positive in about 10%. The tumor cells were negative for desmin, CD34, S-100, EMA, PCK, TLE-1, CK5/6, HMB45, ALK, and CD30. In terms of fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) detection for the translocation of CSF1 gene and USP6 gene, the results were negative.
diagnosis: Giant Cell Tumor of Tendon Sheath

case_report: In December 2012, a 41-year-old male with a 15-year history of a slow-growing, painless mass in the left knee and no history of trauma was referred to Shinshu Ueda Medical Center (Ueda, Japan) by the patient’s doctor. Physical examination revealed a mass, 8 cm in diameter, in the anterior aspect of the left knee. No localized warmth, redness, or tenderness was observed in the left knee; however, there was minimal effusion. The range of motion was 0–125° in the left knee compared with 0–140° in the right knee. The patient displayed normal gait and no neurovascular deficit was observed. Plain lateral radiographs identified bone erosion in the proximal tibia, but no bone lesions were observed in the distal femur and patella. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) identified a well-localized mass that extended from the subcutaneous tissue in the anterior aspect of the knee to the infrapatellar fat pad, and deep into the patellar tendon and tibia, exhibiting a homogenous low signal intensity on T1-weighted (repetition time (TR)/echo time (TE), 540/12 msec) and T2-weighted (TR/TE, 4000/84 msec) images and diffuse enhancement. An axial image revealed that the tumor was wrapped around the patellar tendon.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the biopsy specimen revealed prominent histiocytes, as well as a variable number of foamy cells, hemosiderin-laden macrophages and multinucleated giant cells. No mitotic activity or malignant features were observed.
diagnosis: Giant Cell Tumor of the Tendon Sheath

case_report: A 59-year-old woman presented with upper abdominal discomfort, weight loss, and vomiting for 2 months, along with hot flushes over the past 3 months. Her past medical history, family history, and physical examination were unremarkable. Laboratory results showed mild to moderate anemia (Hb = 10.8 g/dL, HCT = 35.4%, MCV = 81.5 fL, MCH = 24.9 pg) and elevated lactate dehydrogenase levels (378 IU/L, normal <280 IU/L). Abdominal ultrasonography did not reveal significant findings, prompting the use of magnetic resonance enterography (MRE). MRE indicated circumferential thickening in the wall of the proximal jejunum, bowel loop distention, shouldering appearance of the lumen’s margins, and mucosal destruction. An enlarged lymph node was also noted on the posterior aspect of the greater curvature of the stomach. Due to symptoms indicative of small bowel obstruction, the patient underwent jejunal resection and anastomosis with margins of 6.5 cm from the duodenal site and 15 cm from the jejunal site. Intraoperative assessment confirmed anastomotic integrity, and a feeding jejunostomy was placed 36 hours post-operation. The patient began a diet six days after admission and was discharged in good condition.
test_results: Histologic investigation of the resected tumor demonstrated discohesive sheets of medium-sized immature cells with round to oval, lobulated, or indented nuclei. These cells mostly had clear to eosinophilic cytoplasm. Giemsa staining showed a metachromatic tone in the tumor cells’ cytoplasm. On immunohistochemistry assay, LCA, and C-kit (CD117) were positive in tumor cells while CD1a, CD20, CD3, MPO, Cytokeratin (AE1/AE3, CK7, CK19, and CK20), and Vimentin tests showed negative results. The Ki-67 marker of proliferation was measured, and the results showed levels as high as 30%. No bone marrow cytogenetic abnormality or involvement was found. KIT mutation analysis showed gain-of-function mutations in the KIT receptor tyrosine kinase, an aspartic acid to valine substitution (D816V).

case_report: A 61-year-old man visited the hospital for a medical checkup. He did not report any digestive or other specific symptoms. Blood tests, physical examination, plain radiography of the chest and abdomen, peripheral blood smear, and serum tryptase measurement were performed. The physical examination did not reveal any unusual findings, such as skin lesions, hepatomegaly, or splenomegaly. Results from blood tests, peripheral blood smear, and imaging tests were unremarkable. Serum tryptase levels were within the normal range at 5.3 μg/L. The patient's medical history included hypertension and diabetes, with no other significant findings.
test_results: Colonoscopy revealed a 1-cm mass with a white gyral pattern and a slightly swollen transverse colon. The biopsy findings showed mature and normally differentiated mast cells only.

case_report: A 45-year-old male patient was admitted with increasing episodes of recurrent muscular paralysis. His medical history includes diabetes, coronary heart disease, and a previous myocardial infarction. Current medications include 250 mg of metformin taken three times daily and 100 mg of aspirin taken once daily. The episodes of periodic weakness lasted for 13 days. The first instance of limb flaccid paralysis occurred at age 4, lasting between 5 to 13 days. During these episodes, his muscle strength was significantly reduced, with the ability to lift limbs from the bed rated at 3/5, and proximal limb strength rated at 2/5. Symptoms were most severe in the mornings and were often triggered by cold and humid weather. Oral potassium chloride intake exacerbated the symptoms. The patient also experienced recurrent respiratory muscle paralysis, characterized by shortness of breath, slight decreases in intraarterial PaCO2 and PaO2, and symptom relief with inhaled budesonide. Routine laboratory tests revealed elevated fasting glucose levels (17.98 mmol/L, normal <6.10 mmol/L), elevated glycosylated hemoglobin (11.40%, normal <6.00%), and elevated creatine kinase (CK) levels (843.84 U/L, normal <170 U/L). Blood potassium levels fluctuated between 4.3 and 5.1 mmol/L (normal range 3.5-5.5 mmol/L) during hospitalization. Multiple family members were affected, although respiratory muscle paralysis was unique to the proband. Symptoms were alleviated with large doses of normal saline during attacks, and the patient was administered 250 mg of acetazolamide twice daily during intermittent periods. The patient declined neurophysiological testing.
test_results: Gene sequencing showed a heterozygous mutation of c.4774A > G in the nucleotide sequence of SCN4A. The mutation resulted in a change from methionine to valine (p.M1592V). His children had the same heterozygous mutation point in the exon region of the SCN4A gene.

case_report: A 42-year-old female presented with sudden, widespread hair loss from the scalp occurring over a 1-day period. The patient has a history of vitiligo vulgaris and has been receiving treatment with topical tacrolimus 0.1% ointment, fluticasone ointment, and spot Narrow-band UVB (NB-UVB) phototherapy for the past 8 months. She underwent an appendicectomy 1 month ago and subsequently developed cellulitis of the left hand.
test_results: Dermoscopy showed the presence of black dots, yellow dots, and short vellus hair.

case_report: A 64-year-old male with a history of vascular graft surgery, congestive heart failure, hyperlipidemia, and hypertension presented with an itchy and painful blistering rash for 14 days. He had vascular graft surgery 3 months earlier and was prescribed doxycycline as a preventive measure against infection. He then returned to Mexico, where he resides and works as a surfing instructor. Without using sun protection, he spent long hours in the sun wearing only swim trunks and developed a widespread red, itchy rash in sun-exposed areas 1 month after starting doxycycline, which was considered to be due to sun exposure. His medication was changed from doxycycline to amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, and he reduced his sun exposure. He later experienced diarrhea and stopped taking amoxicillin-clavulanic acid after 3 weeks. Despite stopping the antibiotics, the widespread redness continued. Two weeks before hospitalization, the rash became painful and blistered. A dermatologic examination revealed numerous tense vesicles and bullae on large red plaques, along with a few weeping crusted erosions on the scalp, neck, upper torso, arms, hands including palms, and thighs down to mid-calf. No mucosal involvement was observed. His other medications included metoprolol, aspirin, clopidogrel, and simvastatin, which had been stable for 2 years. Cilostazol was started one and a half months before the rash appeared.
test_results: H&E staining demonstrated a clean, subepidermal split and a mixed inflammatory cell infiltrate containing lymphocytes, histiocytes, and eosinophils in the superficial dermis. Direct immunofluorescence demonstrated linear deposition of C3 and IgG along the basement membrane zone (BMZ), with a salt-split study showing linear deposition of IgG along the roof of the blister and linear deposition of C3 on the roof and floor of the induced blister. Indirect immunofluorescence was notable for positive IgG on monkey esophagus (1:640) and positive IgG on human split skin substrate (1:1280). An enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay study demonstrated a positive IgG BP antigen 180 antibody level (106 U/mL; normal/negative: <9 U/mL) and negative IgG BP antigen 230 antibody level (6 U/mL).

case_report: A 46-year-old woman presented to the rheumatology department in May 2001 with polyarthralgia and myalgia. Examination revealed soft tissue swelling and tenderness in the proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints bilaterally, along with morning stiffness lasting at least one hour. Over three months, she developed proximal motor weakness in her upper arms and legs. Magnetic resonance imaging of both thighs indicated myositis. Laboratory tests showed elevated muscle enzymes, including creatine kinase (CK), aldolase, alanine aminotransferase (AST and ALT), and lactate dehydrogenase. Antinuclear antibody was positive at 1:80 with a speckled pattern and 1:2,560 with a cytoplasmic pattern. Auto-antibodies such as anti-Jo-1, anti-RNP, anti-double stranded DNA, anti-Sm, and anti-SS-A/SS-B were absent. Rheumatoid factor was elevated at 3,420 IU/mL, while C3 and C4 levels were within normal ranges at 97.9 mg/dL and 30.8 mg/dL, respectively. A chest radiograph showed a pattern consistent with interstitial lung disease, and pulmonary function tests revealed significantly decreased DLCO. She was treated with prednisolone, azathioprine, and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Over time, myositis symptoms subsided, but she continued to experience synovitis and joint pain in her right knee and small joints of both hands. Her treatment regimen was adjusted to include cyclosporine and bucillamine. Twenty months later, she developed erythematous flaccid blisters on her chest, axillae, and back. These blisters consisted of erythematous patches and superficial erosions with turbid bullae. Nikolsky's sign was positive. Laboratory tests showed a C-reactive protein level of 0.831 mg/dL (normal range <0.8 mg/dL) and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 66 mm/hr. Liver function, renal function, CK, and electrolytes were normal.
test_results: A skin biopsy revealed intraepidermal vesicle formation with acantholysis and the vesicle formation is suprabasal. Indirect immunofluorescence demonstrated no IgG, IgA and C3 staining along epidermis and papillary dermis.

case_report: A 38-year-old male, who is HIV positive and works as a goldsmith, experienced a sudden weight loss over the past 3 months. Laboratory tests showed a CD4 T-cell count of 53/μL, and HAART was initiated. Three weeks after starting HAART, bullous lesions appeared on the trunk and face. Physical examination revealed multiple erosions and crusted lesions covering almost the entire body, including the soft palate and inner side of the lips. Nikolsky sign was positive. Subsequent tests showed an increase in CD4 T-cell count to 274/μL. Nevirapine was discontinued immediately, but the lesions persisted.
test_results: Tzanck smear from fresh lesion showed acantholytic cell under light microscope. Histopathology from a fresh lesion showed intra-epidermal bullae. DIF from perilesional skin showed IgG deposition within the epidermis in lacy pattern.

case_report: A 27-year-old male patient presented with fluid-filled blisters on the skin that progressed to ulceration over widespread areas of the body for the past 3 months. The patient reported a history of painful oral ulcers for one and a half years, which caused difficulty swallowing and resulted in an 8 kg weight loss due to limited food intake. The patient has a 2-year history of diabetes mellitus managed with insulin. Past dental and personal history were non-contributory. Previous treatments with antiseptic gel and oral analgesics for oral ulcers did not yield improvement. On general examination, the patient appeared moderately built, with all vital signs within normal limits. Oral examination revealed multiple intraoral ulcers on the soft and hard palate, with no fluid-filled vesicles observed in the mouth. There were widespread ulcers covered with crusts on the scalp, back, and genitalia. Nikolsky's sign was positive.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed suprabasal split and acantholysis with few inflammatory cells.

case_report: A 12-year-old Japanese boy presented with a mass lesion at the limbus of the left eye. He had been previously treated with topical pemirolast and corticosteroids (fluorometholone or betamethasone) for 2 months for allergic conjunctivitis. The initial complaint of itching had resolved with betamethasone, but a limbal mass lesion appeared and persisted during treatment. The patient had no history of atopic diseases, previous eye conditions, or family history of allergies. On examination, a milky-white mass with partial redness was observed at the inferior-temporal limbus of the left eye. No corneal changes, including superficial punctate keratitis, were noted in either eye. Horner-Trantas’s dots were present at the superior limbus of the left eye. Mild papillae formation was noted on the upper tarsal conjunctiva of both eyes, but not as large as cobblestones. The bulbar conjunctiva and limbus of the right eye appeared normal. A pseudomembranous structure covering the limbal mass was easily dissected.
test_results: Hematoxylin-eosin staining detected rich infiltration of eosinophils and lymphocytes in the subepithelial lesion and the substantia propria of the mass lesion. Fibroblasts were also observed in both areas. Immunohistochemical staining detected that CD3-positive T lymphocytes had predominantly and diffusely infiltrated in the subepithelial lesion and the substantia propria of the mass lesion. Relatively small numbers of CD20-positive B lymphocytes and CD138-positive plasma cells were locally detected and tended to aggregate.

case_report: A 25-year-old gravida 3 para 2 Hispanic female with pregnancy-related anemia was admitted to the labor and delivery unit at 38 weeks gestation while in labor. She had regular prenatal visits, and her pregnancy was uncomplicated. She had no history of complicated pregnancies, surgeries, smoking, alcohol use, or illegal drug use. Her medications included ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily and prenatal vitamins. Upon admission, her vital signs were: pulse 89 bpm, blood pressure 130/85 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, temperature 98.6°F, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Physical examination, including respiratory and cardiovascular assessments, was normal. Pelvic examination was appropriate for gestational age, and fetal heart rate showed moderate variability with no decelerations. She reported no recent fever or respiratory/cardiovascular symptoms. Laboratory results indicated a white blood cell count of 15.9/mcL with 90% neutrophils and hemoglobin of 8.8 mg/dL, with low mean corpuscular volume and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration, consistent with microcytic and hypochromic anemia. A healthy male infant was delivered vaginally within one hour of admission without the need for instrumentation or surgery. The placenta was completely removed, and a second-degree laceration was repaired successfully. There were no postdelivery complications or bleeding. Six hours post-delivery, the patient experienced dyspnea, tachycardia, and tachypnea. She did not report chest pain, loss of consciousness, nausea, or vomiting, and had not received any new medications, food, or blood transfusions. Her vital signs at that time were: pulse 142 bpm, blood pressure 140/78 mmHg, and temperature 97°F.
test_results: CT pulmonary angiography (CTA) was negative for PE but showed dense bilateral opacities. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast only showed an enlarged uterus, and no other abnormalities were observed. Bedside transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) showed left ventricular ejection fraction (EF) > 75%, without diastolic dysfunction or hemodynamically significant valvular abnormalities, and there were no vegetations. Arterial blood gases (ABGs) showed hypoxic respiratory failure, and the initial PaO2/FiO2 ratio was 95 (PaO2 38 mmHg while on Venturi mask with 40% oxygen saturation).
diagnosis: Severe Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome secondary to Atypical Amniotic Fluid Embolism

case_report: A 33-year-old female with a history of autoimmune hepatitis post orthotopic liver transplantation in 1999, Crohn's disease post colectomy in 2019, and asthma presented to the hospital with worsening shortness of breath over the past day, not relieved by nebulized albuterol. Five days before hospital admission, she experienced a sore throat, dry cough, and nausea. She was treated with amoxicillin for otitis media at an urgent care facility four days before hospital admission, but her symptoms persisted. She reported fevers, chills, and rhinorrhea starting two days before hospital admission. She denied any contact with sick individuals. On the way to the hospital, she received 15 liters of supplemental oxygen via a non-rebreather mask due to increased breathing effort and suspected low oxygen levels. Her home medications included oral tacrolimus 2mg twice daily and oral budesonide 3mg twice daily. Initial vital signs were blood pressure 152/88 mmHg, pulse rate 121, respiratory rate 49, temperature 99.1 °F, and oxygen saturation 98% on high flow nasal cannula with settings of 60L flow rate and 100% fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2). Physical examination revealed an ill-appearing female in acute distress, with rapid heart rate, rapid breathing, use of accessory muscles, and increased work of breathing. A chest radiograph showed bilateral opacifications in the lower lung fields. Initial laboratory tests showed bandemia without an increase in white blood cells, normocytic anemia, high anion gap metabolic acidosis with concurrent respiratory alkalosis on the given oxygen settings, elevated lactate, elevated serum creatinine, and a normal urinalysis.
test_results: A nasopharyngeal swab sample demonstrated a positive result for human rhinovirus. A computed tomography (CT) angiogram of the chest demonstrated bilateral lower lobe consolidations with air bronchograms and no evidence of pulmonary embolism.
diagnosis: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome  secondary to rhinovirus infection

case_report: A 25-year-old male, referred by the military, reported occasional wheezing and shortness of breath following mild exercise. He mentioned being prescribed inhalers during childhood. The patient had no other medical conditions, did not use illicit drugs, and was a non-smoker. There was no family history of lung conditions. A review of his medical records revealed an abnormal chest CT scan from 10 years prior.
test_results: An abnormal chest CT scan from 10 years ago was discovered. Multiple lung cysts were seen on chest CT at the time, and this was confirmed by a follow-up scan that revealed no progression of the findings. Bilateral cystic changes were noted on chest X-ray at three months of age. He then underwent spirometry and a methacholine challenge test, which was positive at PC 20 of 7.91 mg/ml.

case_report: Patient 2 is a 17-year-old Qatari boy with significant weight gain. His birth weight was 4 Kg, and he was born to consanguineous parents. He began gaining weight at the age of 2 years; his current weight is 277 Kg with a BMI of 88.4 Kg/m2 (Z-score of +3.8) and a BMI percentile >99.99th centile. He exhibits marked hyperphagia, experiences difficulty breathing, and has elevated liver enzymes (ALT: 85 U/L (5–30 U/L), AST: 128 U/L (0–39 U/L), ALP: 191 U/L (52–171 U/L)).
test_results: His mother does not carry the variant, and the phenotype and DNA of the father were not available for assessment.
diagnosis: MC4R mutation leading to morbid obesity
Orpha_name: Obesity due to melanocortin 4 receptor deficiency

case_report: A 68-year-old man in China experienced sudden pain in the left lower extremity for 14 hours. He had a history of thrombectomy of the left femoral artery 17 years ago and had been on an irregular course of cilostazol and beraprost sodium since then. He had no history of other vascular diseases, such as aortic aneurysm. Additionally, he had a history of hypertension for 7 years and was taking irbesartan 150 mg and amlodipine besylate tablets 5 mg once a day. His blood pressure control status was unknown. He had no history of diabetes mellitus or coronary heart disease. The patient reported smoking and drinking for 40 years but had no drug allergies or history of blood transfusions. His family had no records of vascular diseases. Upon emergency admission, his vital signs showed a normal temperature, heart rate, and breathing rate, but his blood pressure was 173/93 mmHg. The patient appeared acutely ill. The numerical rating scale (NRS) score was one. Physical examination revealed accessible bilateral femoral artery pulsation and unavailable pulsation of the dorsal artery of the left foot and left posterior tibial artery. The skin temperature of the left lower extremity was cold. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 187 g/L, an erythrocyte count of 5.63 × 10^12/L, a platelet count of 223 × 10^9/L, and a hematocrit value of 0.560.
test_results: Emergency double lower extremity vascular ultrasound revealed acute occlusion of the left superficial femoral artery and left posterior tibial artery.

case_report: A 63-year-old female patient was treated for partial tonic–clonic status epilepticus affecting the right side of her body in the emergency room and subsequently in the intensive care unit. She reported a worsening headache and numbness on the right side over the past few days. Her medical history included occasional, nonspecific headaches but no chronic diseases, medications, or smoking history. On physical examination, she was alert and conscious, with no signs of nuchal rigidity or meningeal irritation. She exhibited hypoesthesia and reduced motor muscle strength (3–4/5) on the right side. Laboratory results showed leukocytosis and thrombocytosis with a hematocrit of 54.7%, hemoglobin of 18 g/dl, platelet count of 447 × 10^9/l, and leukocyte count of 20.85 × 10^9/l. Ultrasound of the abdomen revealed splenomegaly. Emergency diffusion-weighted MRI indicated restriction in the left temporo-occipital region extending to the vertex level. Follow-up brain MRI and MRI venography identified a large lesion in the left temporo-occipital region extending to the vertex level, which appeared iso-hypo dense in T1A series and hyperintense in T2A fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images. Superior sagittal sinus calibration was decreased and not clearly visible after the posterior and inferior sagittal sinus levels. The right transverse sinus showed slowed flow, while no flow was observed in the left transverse sinus. Electroencephalography revealed asymmetry in ground activity, frequency, and amplitude between the two hemispheres.
test_results: The patient was positive for Janus Kinase 2 (JAK-2) V617F mutation. The patient had hemoglobin >16 g/dl, hematocrit >48%, and myeloproliferation in bone marrow.

case_report: A 27-year-old Asian male presented with shortness of breath during physical activity, which had progressively worsened over the past 5-6 years and had become more severe in the last 3 months. Physical examination showed a normal body build without features of Marfan's syndrome. Vital signs were: blood pressure 126/78 mm Hg, pulse rate 95 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and body temperature 36.7℃. Slight engorgement of both jugular veins was noted. A high-pitched, blowing, holodiastolic murmur (grade V/VI) was heard at the right sternal border of the third intercostal space. No abnormal lung sounds were detected, and the abdominal examination was unremarkable. Electrocardiogram indicated left ventricular hypertrophy and bi-atrial enlargement with normal sinus rhythm. Chest X-ray showed mild enlargement of the heart without signs of pulmonary congestion. Blood tests were within normal ranges: fasting glucose 92 mg/dL, total cholesterol 214 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 g/dL, blood urea nitrogen 21 mg/dL, uric acid 5.7 mg/dL. Echocardiogram revealed left ventricular enlargement (end-diastolic dimension 73 mm), left ventricular hypertrophy (septal wall thickness on diastole 15 mm), and moderate left ventricular systolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 36%. The sinus of Valsalva measured 56 mm, and the aortic valve opening was 34 mm. The aortic valve leaflets appeared normal on a 2D echocardiogram, but severe aortic valve regurgitation due to aortic root dilation was observed on Doppler echocardiogram. Chest CT confirmed significant aortic root dilation and ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm.
test_results: Multiple variable-sized cystic lesions in the liver and both kidneys were observed in an abdominal-pelvic CT scan.

case_report: An 11-year-old boy reported experiencing abdominal pain and bloody urine after a minor abdominal injury. Physical examination revealed normal findings except for tenderness in the left costovertebral angle. Anthropometric measurements and blood pressure were within normal limits. Urinalysis indicated 3+ blood and 1+ protein, with numerous isomorphic erythrocytes observed in the microscopic evaluation of the sediment. Serum biochemistry results, including renal and liver functions, electrolytes, calcium, phosphorus, and alkaline phosphatase levels, were all normal.
test_results: Both kidneys were larger than normal and had numerous millimetric cysts. There were bigger cysts at the upper pole of the right kidney and upper and lower poles of the left kidney reaching 10 mm, 12 mm, and 13 mm in diameter, respectively. There were numerous millimetric calculi in both kidneys with 3 large calculi in the right (8, 5, and 5 mm) and one in the left (9 mm) kidneys.

case_report: A 2-year-old boy was brought to our unit due to recurrent vomiting and a persistent cough. His medical history includes a prenatal diagnosis of left congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). He was delivered via elective cesarean section at 37 weeks of gestation and required immediate intubation and high-frequency ventilation. At 2 days old, he underwent surgical repair of the CDH, which was completed without complications. He spent the first two months of life in the neonatal intensive care unit. At 1 month old, he was noted to have failure to thrive, vomiting, and feeding difficulties. Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) was identified, and he was started on omeprazole (10 mg daily), which initially improved his symptoms. At 2 years old, despite prolonged antireflux therapy, his esophageal symptoms persisted.
test_results: Endoscopy revealed only mucosal erythema in the lower half of the esophagus. Esophageal biopsy specimens taken from different parts of the esophagus showed a mean eosinophil count of 40 eosinophils per high-power field [HPF].

case_report: A 5-year-old girl was evaluated for breast enlargement observed over the past 4 months. She had no history of headaches, visual disturbances, behavioral changes, or neurological issues. There was no history of head trauma, surgery, gelastic seizures, encephalitis, or radiation exposure. Family history was unremarkable, and the perinatal period was normal. On physical examination, her weight was 21 kg (medium), height was 128 cm (+2 standard deviations), and mid-parental height was 157 cm. Psychomotor development was normal. The patient exhibited an elevated areola above the contour of the breast, forming a 'double scoop' appearance (Tanner stage 4). There was downy pubic hair (Tanner stage 1) and no axillary hair. Abdominal examination showed no masses. Hand bone age, assessed using the Greulich and Pyle atlas, was advanced by approximately 3 years compared to her chronological age.
test_results: Decapeptyl test showed a predominant FSH response (FSH increased from 3.8 mUI/mL to 5 mUI/mL), while the LH presented a modest response (LH increased from 0.9 mUI/mL to 7 mUI/mL), LH/FSH > 1. Pelvic ultrasound revealed an uterine long axis of 55 mm (normal 35 mm), anteroposterior diameter of 9.7 mm, transverse diameter of 6.6 mm, and a large a central vacuity line. A uterine body/cervix ratio > 1, there were 3 increased follicles in the ovary, and the maximum diameter of follicle was 9 mm without ovarian cysts or pelvic mass. Endocrine analysis showed high estrogen value: 18.29 pg/mL.

case_report: A 14-month-old girl presented with loose motion and bloody stool since 8 months of age, passing 4 to 8 stools per day. Blood was mixed with stool and mucus, and defecation was associated with tenesmus. The child exhibited poor growth over the same duration. There was no history of fever, contact with tuberculosis, convulsions, respiratory distress, cough, oral or perianal ulcers, or other major illnesses. Various antibiotics and drugs were administered for diarrhea without improvement. Physical examination revealed the child was ill-looking, moderately pale, mildly dehydrated, moderately wasted, and stunted, with nontender hepatomegaly. Other physical findings were normal. Laboratory results showed hemoglobin at 8 g/dL with microcytic hypochromic anemia, a total white blood cell count of 8,500/cumm, and a platelet count of 237,000/cumm. Gastrointestinal infections were ruled out by culture and sensitivity tests. Liver and renal function tests were normal. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 53 mm in the first hour, and C-reactive protein was 24 mg/L. Meckel's scan was negative. Tests for IgM cytomegalovirus and Herpes simplex I and II were negative. Serum immunoglobulin levels were normal. A barium study of the gastrointestinal tract was normal.
test_results: Colonoscopy showed diffuse ulcers and pseudopolyps formation in colon. Biopsy showed diffuse inflammation of mucosa and submucosa, crypt abscess, and depletion of goblet cells.

case_report: A 39-year-old female presented with pain, swelling, and heaviness in the left lower limb, accompanied by recurrent skin ulceration that began 4 years prior. Over time, similar symptoms developed in the right lower limb, including heaviness, pain, and swelling. The patient had a history of left lower extremity deep venous thrombosis 10 years earlier, treated with a 6-month course of anticoagulation therapy. She experienced a gradual onset of progressive left lower limb swelling, pain, and heaviness, which worsened with walking and led to skin ulceration. Despite multiple healthcare visits, effective management was not achieved. Physical examination revealed a body mass index of 27.2, significant swelling in the left leg with coldness on palpation, minimal pitting edema, and circumferential erythematous skin changes. Multiple skin ulcerations were present, primarily on the anterior and medial sides of the leg, with the largest ulcer located on the distal anterior third of the leg, measuring approximately 10 × 6 cm. The ulcer bases were granulating, with the largest ulcer extending deeply into subcutaneous fat and exhibiting minimal discharge. Circumferential measurements of the affected limb below the knee at 5-cm increments were 47, 47, 42.5, and 38 cm, with a calculated volume of 1.857 L. In comparison, the contralateral limb measurements were 41.5, 41.5, 37.5, and 34 cm, with a calculated volume of 1.452 L.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) assessment showed diffuse circumferential fatty hypertrophy and thickened hyperintense dermis with extensive reticular edema in the left lower limb. Lymphoscintigraphic evaluation of both lower extremities showed intact lymphatic system which ruled out lymphedema as a potential diagnosis. Perfusion assessment of the involved limb was done through indocyanine green (ICG) imaging and showed impaired foot tissue perfusion with low fluorescence signal intensity.

case_report: A 22-year-old Chinese female was brought to the emergency room due to unconsciousness. Initial monitoring revealed a blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg, heart rate of 122 bpm, pulse SpO2 of 90%, and respiratory rate of 41 bpm. An emergency head contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan identified a left frontal hematoma with rupture into the ventricular system and cerebral arteriovenous malformations (CAVMs) in the left-middle cerebral artery. She underwent immediate surgery for intracranial hematoma removal, arteriovenous malformation repair, and bone plate decompression. The patient exhibited hypoxemia, with blood gas analysis showing pH: 7.48, PaCO2: 28 mmHg, PaO2: 54 mmHg, and SaO2: 90%.
test_results: TTCE showed that the contrast agent entered the left heart from the pulmonary veins at the beginning of the third cardiac cycle and that the left heart was completely filled with the dense microbubbles.

case_report: Patient III-1 is a 14-year-old male who experienced difficulty seeing in low light conditions starting at age 6. At age 11, his best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was measured at 1.2 in the right eye with a prescription of +6.50 diopters, cylindrical correction of −2.00 diopters, and an axis of 180°. In the left eye, BCVA was 1.0 with a prescription of +7.00 diopters, cylindrical correction of −1.50 diopters, and an axis of 10°.
test_results: A dark-adapted single flash ERG performed at another hospital showed that there were reduced responses in both eyes. Fundus examination revealed retinal degeneration of the inferotemporal areas in his right and left eyes. The OCT images showed that there was marked thinning of the ONL and disruption of the IS/OS line, except for the foveal region of his right and left eyes. GP showed constriction of visual fields with small scotomas in his right and left eyes. A fundus autofluorescence image revealed a perifoveal hyperautofluorescent ring in his right and left eyes.

case_report: A 49-year-old male reported visual impairment in his left eye for over 20 years, which he had previously ignored. He visited the hospital on March 3, 2020, with a primary complaint of visual disturbance in his right eye that began the previous year. Family history revealed no notable abnormalities. At the initial visit, corrected visual acuity was 20/12.5 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye. Intraocular pressures were measured at 16 mmHg in the right eye and 14 mmHg in the left eye. Examination showed clear cornea, anterior chamber, and lens. Chorioretinal atrophy with pigmentation along the retinal veins was noted in the right fundus. Autofluorescence imaging showed loss of autofluorescence corresponding to the pigmented area. Extensive changes were observed in the left eye on both the fundus photograph and the autofluorescence fundus photograph. Dynamic quantitative visual field testing identified a scotoma in the right eye corresponding to the area of retinochoroidal atrophy. Visual field constriction was noted in the left eye.
test_results: An electroretinogram test was performed on August 18, 2021, and the waveforms of right and left eye showed an attenuated and negative pattern, respectively.

case_report: A 22-year-old male visited the outpatient department with dark-colored skin lesions that have been present since he was 10 years old. Initially, the lesions appeared on both arms and spread to the trunk and lower limbs over the next 2 years. The lesions darkened over time, and no new lesions appeared for the next 9 years. However, in the past year, he noticed multiple white-colored, pinpoint lesions developing over the darkened areas without any preceding itching or redness. There was no history of warty lesions or blisters before the appearance of these skin changes. The patient reported no recurrent lower respiratory infections or issues with the cardiovascular and central nervous systems. His mother also had similar dark-colored skin lesions on the trunk, arms, and legs, but without any light-colored patches. There was no family history of consanguinity, recurrent fetal deaths, vitiligo, or other autoimmune disorders. Systemic examination showed no abnormalities. Skin examination revealed multiple, whorled, dark macules arranged bilaterally and symmetrically along the lines of Blaschko on the abdomen, chest, and back. Similar lesions were arranged linearly on the extensor and flexor aspects of the arms and legs. Multiple pinpoint white macules were observed in the areas of streaky pigmentation. The skin texture was normal over the streaks, the intervening skin, and the depigmented areas. No signs of Koebner phenomenon or leukotrichia were noted. Hematological and routine biochemical tests were normal.
test_results: Histopathological evaluation of the depigmented lesion showed complete absence of melanocytes. The pigmented macules revealed increased pigmentation of the basal cell layer with melanocytes present up to the mid-epidermis. No focal areas of pigmentary incontinence were noticed in the dermis.
diagnosis: Linear and Whorled Nevoid Hypermelanosis with punctate hypopigmentation

case_report: A 21-year-old female presented with asymptomatic dark skin lesions present since birth. According to her mother, the lesions initially appeared on the trunk and spread to the upper limbs, lower limbs, neck, face, and back within two years. The lesions darkened over time and stabilized after the age of 10, with no new lesions appearing. There was no history of erythema, vesiculobullous, or warty lesions before the onset of the pigmented lesions. The patient had no history of recurrent lower respiratory infections, cardiovascular issues, central nervous system involvement, developmental delays, or ocular abnormalities. Medical history included skeletal deformities since birth, right ear deafness since age 9, and primary amenorrhea. Chromosome analysis of peripheral blood lymphocytes performed in 2019 was normal. There was no family history of consanguinity, recurrent fetal deaths, or similar skin lesions. Systemic examination was normal except for musculoskeletal findings, which included scoliosis, short stature, syndactyly, brachydactyly of toes, sandal gap deformity of the left foot, and swan neck deformity of fingers. There were no dental anomalies, and secondary sexual characteristics were well developed. Dermatological examination showed multiple bilaterally symmetrical whorls of hyperpigmented macules along the lines of Blaschko on the chest, abdomen, and back, with similar linear lesions on the face, neck, and limbs. Ocular examination revealed left eye macular degeneration, and audiometry indicated unilateral (right) sensorineural hearing loss. Routine blood tests, ECG, and 2D ECHO were normal. Ultrasound of the abdomen showed bilateral small ovaries and uterine hypoplasia.
test_results: Histopathological evaluation of the skin lesion revealed increased melanin in the basal layer. There was no pigmentary incontinence.

case_report: A 22-year-old man, the youngest of three siblings, had a family history of consanguinity, with his maternal grandparents being married cousins and his maternal and paternal great-great-grandfathers being siblings. Both parents had type II diabetes mellitus. There was no recorded perinatal history or early developmental milestones. At 8 years old, he experienced learning difficulties. His vision began to deteriorate, leading to blindness by the age of 12, and retinal pigmentary degeneration was noted at 14 years old. He did not exhibit epilepsy or ataxia. At 18 years old, he was diagnosed with diabetes mellitus and started on oral antidiabetic medication. At 22 years old, during a hospital visit, neurological examination revealed a sluggish light reflex, normal eye movement, normal deep tendon reflexes (DTR), and no ataxia.
test_results: Blood examination revealed lymphocyte vacuolization. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed mild brain atrophy, enlargement of the lateral ventricle, and periventricular white matter lesion. An ocular fundus examination revealed pigmentary retinal degeneration. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed marked retinal thinning.

case_report: A 45-year-old male patient was admitted to the Endocrinology Department in November 2013 due to recurrent abdominal pain over the past 10 years. Initially, he experienced lower abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and constipation, leading to surgery for intestinal obstruction, though the cause was unclear. Over the next decade, he had multiple similar episodes, often triggered by consuming indigestible food or alcohol, and was treated for intestinal obstruction with supportive care each time. In February 2012, he had recurrent urinary retention, irritability, hallucinations, delirium, lower limb muscle pain, weakness, and hyponatremia. Hallucinations and delirium resolved after sodium supplementation. In September 2013, he presented with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, normal serum potassium, sodium at 119.7 mmol/L, and chloride at 87.3 mmol/L. He developed dark-colored urine without stones, lower limb muscle pain, fatigue, sleepiness, and illusions. Urinary sodium excretion was 257.09 mmol/24 h during hyponatremia. A chest CT scan was normal, and electromyography indicated decreased nerve conduction velocity in the right peroneal nerve. Treatment included water intake restriction and oral sodium supplementation, normalizing serum sodium levels. The patient had a 20-year history of smoking and drinking, with no family history. Physical examination showed normal vital signs, and no abdominal pain or neurological symptoms were present upon admission. Serum and urine electrolyte analysis, as well as plasma hormone levels of thyroxine and cortisol, were within normal ranges.
test_results: Random urine PBG was positive. Sequencing of the HMBS gene was positive for a missense mutation G>A in exon 9 of HMBS, R173Q (CM900131).

case_report: A 6-year-old girl, born to parents who are not related by blood, presented with an unusual patch of hair observed for the past 4 years. Her parents noted a distinct area on the vertex of her scalp where the hair exhibited curling and coiling, along with a change in texture. Her birth and developmental milestones were normal. There was no family history of similar conditions. On physical examination, a single, well-defined patch measuring 5 cm by 6 cm was found on the vertex of the scalp. The hair in this patch was different in texture, lighter in color, thinner, and tightly coiled. The rest of the scalp hair appeared normal. The skin over the affected patch was unremarkable. Additionally, a linear epidermal nevus was observed extending from the chin to the neck. There were no signs of palmoplantar keratoderma or early onset of puberty.
test_results: Light microscopy of hair revealed irregularities of the cuticle and twisting of hair. Dermoscopy revealed snake crawl appearance and knotting of hair.

case_report: A 23-year-old male from Turkey with a history of visual problems reported recurrent nosebleeds following a septoplasty. His medical history included prolonged bleeding after circumcision and an appendectomy. He had no recurrent infections. His parents were not related, and he had one brother and one sister, both unaffected. Physical examination showed distinct skin and hair color and bruising under the eyes. No other bruising or small red or purple spots were observed on his body. Eye examination revealed involuntary eye movement, outward deviation of the eyes, and underdeveloped central retina. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 10 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin level of 14 g/dL, and a platelet count of 252 × 10^9/L. Fibrinogen, prothrombin time (PT), partial thromboplastin time (PTT), and platelet counts were within normal ranges, but the bleeding time was extended. A peripheral smear showed many platelet clusters with normal white blood cell distribution and red blood cell morphology.
test_results: Absent dense bodies on the whole-mount of the platelets.

case_report: An eight-year-old girl presented with a complaint of poor vision in both eyes since birth. Clinical examination revealed very light-colored hair, fair skin, and light blue-colored irises. Best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 0.4 in the right eye (OD) and 0.5 in the left eye (OS). Cycloplegic refraction was +6.50 DS + 0.50 DC X 90 in the OD and +6.50 DS + 0.50 X 110 in the OS. The eyeglasses prescription was +5.75 DS OU. A latent pendular nystagmus with horizontal and torsional oscillations was observed in both eyes. Slit lamp examination showed mild peripheral iris transillumination, more prominent in the right eye. The patient reported mild photophobia. Anterior chambers were normal in both eyes. Testing with Ishihara pseudoisochromatic plates showed no color vision defect. Previous ophthalmic history indicated an accommodative esotropia of 45 prism diopters in the OD, first noted at six months of age, with incomplete follow-up data. There was no history of major illnesses or prematurity, and family history was insignificant. Dilated fundus examination revealed a reduced circumfoveal light reflex in both eyes, confirmed by fundus photography. No changes in foveal pigmentation or abnormalities of the optic discs or vessels were detected. OCT imaging showed a lack of foveal depression and persistence of the inner retinal layers in both eyes, with normal structural characteristics of individual retinal layers. RNFL analysis indicated no pathological changes in peripapillary thickness.
test_results: Genetic testing confirmed a mutation in the OCA2 gene.

case_report: A 6-year-old girl presented with multiple asymptomatic, 1–2 mm whitish papules located on her hands, feet, and face. The papules on her hands and feet had been present for three years, while those on her face appeared last year and have been increasing in number. There was no history of trauma or wounds at the sites of the lesions. The patient has trisomy 21 (Down syndrome), hypothyroidism, grade III vesicoureteral reflux, and atrial and ventricular septal defects. She is currently on levothyroxine (Levotiron®) for her hypothyroidism. Dermoscopic examination did not reveal any typical changes.
test_results: Skin biopsies of the lesions revealed an accumulation of well-defined, dense, basophilic material surrounded by fibrous tissue in the dermis.

case_report: A 14-year-old Japanese girl presented with persistent, unilateral, itchy plaques that did not respond to previous treatments. She had been using topical steroid and calcipotriol hydrate without significant improvement. Upon examination, there were brown to skin-colored, infiltrated, scaly erythema and papules observed on her left trunk, upper limbs, and lower extremities, following the Blashko line. Laboratory tests, including a full blood count and biochemical profile, showed results within normal limits.
test_results: A biopsy specimen showed elongated rete ridges, parakeratosis, and dilated tortuous vessels in the dermal papillae, and neutrophils were rarely detected in the specimen.

case_report: A 6-year-old boy presented with a linear, mildly itchy lesion on the left side of the nose. The lesion had been previously treated with various topical and systemic antibiotics over the past year without improvement. Upon examination, a linear dyskeratotic erythematous plaque with a slightly pigmented halo and fine superficial desquamation was observed on the nose.
test_results: Minimal hyperkeratosis, spongiosis with a pattern closer to the honeycombed one with thickened, highly refractive intercellular space between keratinocytes. Non-rimed connective tissue papillae were observed at the level of the epithelial-connective tissue junction. Below the basal layer, connective tissue papillae appeared disrupted and confluent in large dark areas, signs of interface dermatitis.

case_report: A 24-year-old male reported experiencing an itchy, softened plaque primarily located in the left perineal area, which has been present since he was 5 years old and has shown periods of worsening and improvement. The affected area extends from the perineal region to the scrotum and the inner part of the left thigh. A comprehensive examination did not reveal any other abnormalities in the body. There was no notable family history.
test_results: Histopathology revealed hyperkeratosis with a characteristic alternating orthokeratosis, hypergranulosis with parakeratosis and agranulosis along with upperdermal lymphocytic infiltrate.

case_report: A three-year-old black female from Rio de Janeiro exhibited widespread darkened macules that were present since birth and progressively became darker and more keratotic. She was delivered vaginally at term and showed psychomotor development appropriate for her age. Dermatological examination identified velvety dark papules on the face, neck, trunk, and limbs. The lesions on the posterior trunk followed the Blaschko lines. No additional abnormalities were noted during the physical examination.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the cervical region showed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and papillomatosis. Genetic analysis of peripheral blood and of the skin lesion detected a mutation in the Aa542-545 region of the PIK3CA gene.

case_report: A 24-year-old male (height: 169 cm, weight: 44 kg, blood pressure: 168/75 mmHg) presented with sudden episodes of consciousness disturbance and muscle spasms. He had a history of cerebral haemorrhage, with two previous incidents occurring between the ages of 23 and 24 years. He was an only child, and his parents had no history of haemorrhage or abnormal skin conditions. The patient was referred to the endocrinology department with multiple intracranial calcifications, acute intracerebral haemorrhage, and several other notable features. test_results: The results showed a missense mutation within exon 5 of LMNA (c.898G>C) that caused a substitution of aspartate 300 by histidine (p.Asp300His). There were no WRN mutations.
diagnosis: Atypical Werner Syndrome  due to LMNA mutation

case_report: A 51-year-old Latino male, in good overall health, reported a two-month duration of itchy, scaly plaques on his face, scalp, and trunk, along with sensitivity to sunlight. The patient also exhibited redness on the cheeks and nose. Initial treatment for seborrheic dermatitis, prescribed by a non-dermatologist, was ineffective despite multiple courses of oral antibiotics, and the condition worsened. The patient also experienced joint pain and Raynaud’s phenomenon. A punch biopsy from a lesion on the right inframammary crease showed features consistent with transient acantholytic dermatosis (Grover’s disease). The patient was treated with topical triamcinolone (0.1%) and calcipotriene (0.005%). After one month, the condition continued to worsen, with the development of superficial blisters and scaling plaques. A subsequent biopsy from the posterior scalp area revealed subcorneal acantholysis with areas of missing stratum corneum and separation of the granular layer. Direct immunofluorescence was not conducted due to insurance limitations.
test_results: Indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) revealed IgG (1:160) and IgG4 (1:40) intercellular antibodies on monkey esophagus. The serum enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) was positive for desmoglein 1 autoantibodies (151.4 ELISA units) and negative for desmoglein 3 autoantibodies (3.2 ELISA units). The patient was also positive for antinuclear antibodies (ANA 1:640), anti-dsDNA, and Sjögren’s anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies.

case_report: A 2-month-old male infant, born to nonconsanguineous parents, presented with increased head size, high-grade fever, and dark yellow discoloration of the sclera and urine for the past week. There was no significant neonatal history. The mother had a history of fever with a blistering rash during the 2nd month of pregnancy, which resolved spontaneously, leaving hyperpigmentation for 2 months. The infant's weight was 2.7 kg (<3rd centile). Physical examination revealed a large head with open sutures of the anterior fontanelle, a coarse face with a depressed nasal bridge, icteric skin, and a distended abdomen. There were no petechiae or other signs of bleeding. The liver and spleen were moderately enlarged and palpable. A large bluish-gray macule covered the back, buttocks, and anterolateral abdominal wall. Additionally, an extensive reddish birthmark was present on the face, neck, upper chest, and left arm. An accessory preauricular tragus was noted on the left side. In the presternal and epigastric area, a thick, cord-like varicosity with multiple thinner varicosities radiating from it was observed. The legs exhibited a marbled appearance. Laboratory results showed hemoglobin at 6.4 g, total leukocyte count at 15,400/mm3, and platelet count at 161,000. Liver profile was abnormal with bilirubin at 16.6 mg/dl, serum glutamate oxaloacetate transaminase at 1072, serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase at 234, alkaline phosphatase at 481, and gamma-glutamyl transferase at 102. Protein levels were normal. The 25-hydroxy Vitamin D level was 3 ng/ml. Tests for venereal disease research laboratory, rapid plasma reagin, and TORCH were negative. Urine showed precipitation. Brain ultrasonography did not reveal any calcification or hydrocephalus. No intra-abdominal abnormalities were detected except for an undescended testis in the right iliac fossa. Echocardiography identified four tiny muscular ventricular septal defects with a left-to-right shunt. X-rays of the limbs and thorax showed normal bone mineralization, joint spaces, and alignment. Bone length was normal, with no lytic or sclerotic lesions. The heart and aorta appeared normal on X-rays. The left brachiocephalic vein and major deep veins of the left arm were obliterated.
test_results: Histopathological examination of biopsies obtained from the two skin lesions showed findings compatible with segmental dermal melanocytosis and nevus flammeus. Fundus examination revealed absent macular foveal reflex, and the periphery of retina was tessellated. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan showed multiple anomalies involving the left subclavian, left brachiocephalic, and right inferior jugular veins.
diagnosis: Phacomatosis Cesioflammea overlapping with Phacomatosis Cesiomarmorata

case_report: A 5-year-old male patient was observed with asymptomatic, pink-red, irregularly shaped patches on the right lower limb and linear brown verrucous plaques on the right side of the chest. These skin findings have been present since birth. The rest of the physical examination showed no additional abnormalities, including neurological and ocular assessments. Magnetic resonance angiography of the right lower limb revealed no abnormalities.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the verrucous plaque showed acanthosis with epidermal papillomatosis and hyperkeratosis.

case_report: Early history: An 8-year-old girl has been monitored at our tertiary eye care center since she was 17 months old. She has a history of buphthalmos in both eyes and mild photophobia, first noticed at 3 months of age. The child was born to non-consanguineous parents with no family history of similar conditions. At birth, she exhibited abnormal pigmentation in the sclera of both eyes and red-colored patches of skin with widened vessels on both sides of the face, upper body, and trunk. These skin lesions have remained unchanged since birth. She was treated for eczema with prolonged steroid ointment application for 16 months. Late-onset bilateral glaucoma: At 17 months, she was evaluated under anesthesia. Her intraocular pressure (IOP) was 27 mmHg in both eyes, with corneal diameters of 13 mm in the right eye and 12.5 mm in the left eye. Pachymetry readings were 520 micrometers in the right eye and 517 micrometers in the left eye. Refraction was -0.50 D in the right eye and +1.00 D in the left eye. The optic nerve cupping was 0.60 in the right eye and 0.65 in the left eye. She was treated with dorzolamide 2%/timolol 0.5% ophthalmic solution in both eyes twice a day, and steroid ointments were discontinued. After a few months, her IOP was controlled, and antiglaucoma treatment was stopped. She remained medication-free with normal IOP for the next four years, with follow-ups every six months. At six years old, her IOP increased again, and antiglaucoma treatment was restarted using brinzolamide 1%/brimonidine tartrate 0.2% fixed combination once a day. Her IOP has been stable, below 20 mmHg, without adverse effects. Bilaterally symmetric skin lesions: Systemic examination showed erythematous marble-like macules with a reticulated vascular pattern on the face, aligned with the three divisions of the trigeminal nerve. Similar hyperpigmented marble-like skin was observed on the upper limbs and trunk. There was no asymmetry in the extremities. The patches persisted after warming and were surrounded by normal, atrophic, or erythematous skin.
test_results: The visual acuity was 20/25 in both eyes. The refractive error was −1.5 D in both eyes. The sclera featured hyperpigmentation with melanocytic changes 360° around the cornea in each eye. The corneas were clear without pigmentation and free of Haab’s striae. The horizontal corneal diameter was 13 mm OD and 12.5 mm OS, but central corneal thickness was in the normal range (518 mm OD and 511 mm OS). The anterior chamber was present and deep. The iris showed no signs of alterations, but, as ultrabiomicroscopy revealed, a thickness of 0.83 mm in OD and 0.80 mm in OS. Gonioscopy performed with the Koeppe lens showed four angle elements without pigmentation of the trabecular meshwork, presence of blood in the Schlemm’s canal, and flat iris insertion in both eyes. The lens was clear. IOP, measured with a hand-held tonometer, was significantly greater than expected (IOP 25 mmHg OD and 24 mmHg OS). The optic nerve head was pathologically cupped in both eyes (0.75 OD and 0.7 OS), with a notching of an inferior rim in OS and baring of the inferior blood vessel in OD. The dilated fundus examination yielded no other finding.
diagnosis: Phakomatosis cesiomarmorata with ocular melanocytosis and secondary glaucoma

case_report: An 18-year-old male presented with a painless swelling in the lower third of the face, present since birth and previously operated on at the age of one. The swelling has progressively increased in size, extending across the midline to the right side of the face post-surgery. The patient reported pus discharge followed by blood discharge over the past month, with no other associated symptoms. Extraoral examination revealed a solitary swelling in the lower jaw crossing the midline, measuring approximately 12 × 8 cm, with multiple sinus openings and blood discharge. The margins were ill-defined, and crustations were present on the lesion's surface. On palpation, the surface was lobular, soft to firm in consistency, and freely movable. A tender lymph node was palpable in the right submandibular region. Intraorally, a solitary swelling was observed in the left buccal mucosa, extending from the left angle of the mouth to the distal of tooth 37, obliterating the vestibule from teeth 41 to 36, and extending 1 cm above the occlusal plane. Multiple papular elevations were noted on the buccal mucosa over the fluctuant swelling, which was non-tender. The blood picture was normal except for an increased ESR (60/mm in the 1st hour). Orthopantomograph and lateral cephalogram showed a soft tissue shadow with no bony involvement. Computed tomography revealed a non-homogenous mass of soft tissue density in the buccal aspect, with no evidence of bone destruction, indicating a benign non-enhancing soft tissue mass.
test_results: The incisional and excisional biopsy of the swelling intraorally revealed many dilated cavernous lymphatic channels filled with coagulum close to overlying hyperplastic oral epithelium. Extraorally, enumerable dilated vascular lymphatic vessels of varying configuration containing RBC's and pale eosinophilic coagulam were observed. Thin flattened vessels lined by endothelium, scattered inflammatory cells, small lymphoid aggregates and adipose tissue were also evident. Longitudinal and transverse sections of muscle tissue and extravasated RBC's in fibrous stroma were seen throughout the sections. The lesion was not encapsulated.

case_report: A 32-year-old male patient presented with pain and swelling over the right lower third region of the face extending into the neck up to the midline for the past 8 months. The swelling was accompanied by mild, dull aching, continuous, and nonradiating pain. There was no history of fever, trauma, toothache, or pus discharge, but the patient experienced restricted mouth opening for the past month. Extraoral examination and palpation revealed a single diffuse swelling over the right submandibular and submental region extending into the neck up to the midline, which was soft, tender, and fluctuant. Intraoral examination showed no abnormal findings, and occlusion was normal. Aspiration from the affected area yielded light brown, stringy fluid.
test_results: The computed tomography axial contrast showed a well-defined lobulated, hypodense cystic lesion of size (27.2 mm × 45.9 mm) present on right side in the neck of the midline just below the submandibular gland and compressing the same. Postcontrast axial computed tomography shows no enhancement.

case_report: A 14-year-old female presented with a four-year history of lower lip enlargement following trauma to the same area. The patient reported no pain, bleeding, or discharge. Examination revealed diffuse enlargement of the lower lip with multiple sessile polypoid growths on the lower labial mucosa, extending from 1 cm medial of the right lip commissure to the left commissure. The mucosa over the growths had small pinpoint spiky projections and was normal in color without visible pulsation. The growth was slightly tender and firm upon palpation, with no pus discharge. The diascopy test was negative.
test_results: Ultrasound revealed increased soft tissue swelling with multiple hypoechoic centers showing minimal vascularity. Histopathologically, it showed stratified squamous epithelium. Connective tissue demonstrated numerous dilated lymphatics containing lymph.

case_report: A 4-year-old previously healthy male presented to an outside hospital with 2 days of nausea and bilious vomiting. An abdominal plain film showed small bowel obstruction, and an abdominal ultrasound was inconclusive. Upon transfer to our institution, he continued to experience bilious vomiting and periumbilical abdominal pain. His medical and surgical history was unremarkable, with no history of prior trauma. His mother reported an increase in abdominal girth over the past several months but had not sought medical attention. On physical examination, the child's abdomen was soft, mildly distended, and tender around the umbilical area. There was no rebound tenderness, guarding, or hernias. Review of the ultrasound showed extensive intra-abdominal fluid. An abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a large intraperitoneal cystic mass measuring 13 × 21 × 9 cm in the left abdomen. A small bowel obstruction was also present with signs of volvulus due to mesenteric swirl seen on axial imaging. There was no evidence of compromised intestine on CT. The patient was taken to the operating room for laparoscopy. The cyst, originating from the mesentery of the small intestine, caused a segmental volvulus with congestion of the involved segment. A short vertical midline incision was made to deliver the giant cyst and reduce the volvulus. After reduction, the congested small bowel returned to a normal appearance. The cyst was excised by removing the 8 cm segment of small bowel from whose mesentery it arose. The abdomen was closed, and the patient was discharged in excellent condition. Pathologic inspection of the mass revealed a thin-walled cyst containing milky fluid.
test_results: The cyst lining expressed D2–40 (a marker of lymphatic endothelium), but was negative for keratin, WT-1 and calretinin.

case_report: A 60-year-old woman presented to the obstetrics and gynecology outpatient department with multiple wart-like lesions on the vulva and mons pubis. The patient reported that these asymptomatic lesions had been present for 4-5 years. There was no history of burning, itching, or pain associated with the lesions. Additionally, the patient had no history of pelvic surgery, chemotherapy, gastrointestinal disease, or tuberculosis. Physical examination revealed multiple warty lesions ranging from 3-10 mm in size on the vulva and mons pubis. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography (USG) results were normal. Routine blood tests were normal except for mild leukocytosis.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed acanthosis and hyperkeratosis of epidermis with numerous dilated lymphatic channels containing eosinophilic proteinous material in the epidermis and papillary dermis.

case_report: A 33-year-old male presented with a persistent itchy sensation on his back, ongoing for over a decade. Upon physical examination, a large area with short, irregular hairs was observed covering the entire back. The patient noted that these hairs had never grown longer. Hair in other regions of the body appeared normal. Dermoscopic evaluation revealed that hair follicles contained multiple short hair shafts of varying lengths.
test_results: Histological examination revealed that the follicular structures consisted of different hair shafts, which were enclosed in a common outer root sheath.

case_report: A 57-year-old male exhibited a blue, pigmented area on the left upper back. Dermoscopic examination revealed short, dark, tufted hairs distributed across the entire back. Each follicular opening had multiple hairs measuring less than 1 mm. This presentation was confined to the back, with no prior history of hair removal noted.
test_results: Skin punch biopsy confirmed the clinical diagnosis.

case_report: A 2-day-old female infant was transferred to our hospital due to frequent myoclonic movements and apnea. She was born at 41 weeks of gestation with a birth weight of 4.1 kg (90th–97th percentile). The mother is Chinese and the father is Korean. The father reported no perinatal issues such as gestational diabetes mellitus, prolonged rupture of membranes, polyhydramnios, or oligohydramnios. The infant was delivered vaginally with Apgar scores of 9 at 1 minute and 10 at 5 minutes. Upon transfer at 2 days old, she exhibited frequent myoclonic movements of the limbs and oxygen desaturation around 70%. Initial vital signs included a blood pressure of 69/41 mmHg, heart rate of 158 beats per minute, respiration rate of 50 breaths per minute, and body temperature of 36.7℃. Her weight was 3.8 kg (75th–90th percentile), length was 53.5 cm (90-95 percentile), head circumference was 34 cm (25th–50th percentile), chest circumference was 34.5 cm, and abdominal circumference was 35 cm. She had a symmetric appearance without congenital malformations, was lethargic, and exhibited hypotonic posture. Physical examination revealed clear breathing sounds, a regular heartbeat without murmurs, a soft abdomen with active bowel sounds, and no hepatosplenomegaly. After admission, she continued to have repetitive myoclonic movements, apnea, and oxygen desaturation. A blood sugar test (BST) showed 18 mg/dL. She received an 8 mL bolus of 10% dextrose solution followed by a continuous infusion with a glucose infusion rate (GIR) of 4.07 mg/kg/min. Phenobarbital was also administered. BST was monitored every 30 minutes post-dextrose bolus. The GIR was gradually increased to 20.8 mg/kg/min, raising blood sugar to 95 mg/dL. Once blood sugar normalized, myoclonic seizures and apnea ceased. Initial blood work revealed hemoglobin of 18.4 g/dL, hematocrit of 55%, white blood cell count of 24,830/mm3, and platelet count of 283,000/mm3. Initial serum blood glucose was 2 mg/dL, and BST showed 18 mg/dL. Serum sodium was 141.3 mmol/L, potassium 5.1 mmol/L, chloride 104.4 mmol/L, calcium 8.8 mg/dL, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L, and ammonia 69 µg/dL (reference range, 19–87 µg/dL). C-reactive protein was 4.6 mg/dL (reference range, 0–5 mg/dL), and blood culture showed no bacterial growth. Laboratory results indicated no ketone bodies in serum and urine, insulin at 9.1 mIU/L (reference range, 2.0–25.0 mIU/L), and C-peptide at 5.96 ng/mL (reference range, 1.1–4.4 ng/mL) with serum glucose at 13 mg/dL. Free fatty acids were 124 µEq/L (reference range, 172–586 µEq/L). Chest X-ray showed no ground glass opacity. On the second hospital day, brain MRI with diffusion revealed high signal intensity lesions in the left parietal lobe, both occipital cortices, and subcortical white matter. On the fourth day, abdominal ultrasonography showed no pancreatic lesions. Electroencephalogram indicated some background attenuation, and echocardiogram revealed a hypertrophied interventricular septum (5.9 mm, >97th percentile) and a left ventricular posterior wall (4–5 mm, upper normal limit) without left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. Computed tomography and positron emission tomography of the pancreas were not performed due to radiation risk. The infant was fed via Levin tube due to poor sucking and swallowing on the first admission day. When feeding volume reached 150 mL/kg, blood glucose levels fluctuated between 31 to 162 mg/dL despite a high intravenous GIR of 11.06–16.57 mg/kg/min. Corticosteroid treatment was initiated but did not stabilize blood glucose. Diazoxide was prescribed on day 10, but blood glucose remained unstable with 20 mg/kg/day of diazoxide, leading to the addition of subcutaneous octreotide 21 days post-admission.
test_results: Genetic analysis revealed a new heterozygotic variation of c.4608G>A on exon 38 of ABCC8.
diagnosis: Congenital Hyperinsulinism  due to a novel mutation in the ABCC8 gene
Orpha_name: Autosomal recessive hyperinsulinism due to SUR1 deficiency

case_report: A 50-year-old Caucasian male was referred to the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at East Carolina University School of Dental Medicine for evaluation of multiple radiopaque areas observed on a panoramic radiograph. His medical history includes stage 4 rectal and liver cancer, for which he underwent ostomy bag placement surgery and completed chemotherapy approximately one year prior to his visit. He also had multiple epidermal cysts surgically removed. A thorough head and neck examination showed facial asymmetry on the left side of the mandible, which felt hard upon palpation. The patient reported no symptoms and mentioned that the facial swelling had been present for over ten years. An extraoral examination identified multiple smooth, non-ulcerated epidermal cysts with yellow-white discoloration in the right malar-temporal area, which were soft to the touch. Intraorally, the patient exhibited multiple missing and mobile teeth, along with poor oral hygiene marked by calculus and debris accumulation. The left mandibular second premolar was partially erupted, and several deciduous teeth, including the right maxillary second primary molar and right mandibular first and second primary molars, were retained and mobile. The panoramic radiograph showed multiple ill-defined radiopaque regions throughout the maxilla and mandible. Large lobulated radiopaque lesions were noted near the inferior border of the left mandibular angle and the anterior surface of the left ascending ramus. Additionally, the right maxillary permanent canine, first and second premolars, left maxillary permanent second premolar, left mandibular permanent first premolar, and right mandibular permanent first and second premolars were found to be impacted.
test_results: Multiple osteomas, including 1 attached at the left mandibular angle and 1 abutting the anterior border of the left ascending ramus, were noted. Multiple impacted teeth and widespread idiopathic osteosclerosis causing alveolar expansion were also observed in the maxilla and mandible on reconstructed orthogonal and panoramic projections.

case_report: A 21-year-old white male with a history of childhood excision of paravertebral neurofibroma, nuchal fibroma, and epidermoid cysts, and no relevant family history, was admitted to the Internal Medicine Department with a two-month history of general symptoms.
