The patient also reported a single episode of hematochezia, previously attributed to hemorrhoids, with no other associated symptoms. On admission, he appeared noticeably pale. Physical examination revealed mild hepatomegaly, with no other significant findings. Laboratory tests showed microcytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin: 8.5 g/dL) with iron deficiency (serum iron < 10 µg/dL and ferritin of 12.3 ng/mL), leukocytosis (14,720/µL), thrombocytosis (6.44 × 104/µL), elevated lactate dehydrogenase (2802 IU/L), mild C-reactive protein elevation (16.7 mg/L), mild hypoalbuminemia (36.6 g/dL), and mild erythrocyte sedimentation rate elevation (34 mm/1 h). Serologic markers for HIV and hepatitis B and C were negative. A computed tomography angiography revealed multiple hepatic nodules and a right adrenal gland nodule. Upper endoscopy showed numerous polyps carpeting the stomach and duodenum, with the duodenum displaying bulbous mucosa and a micronodular aspect in the second portion. Lower endoscopy documented nodularity of the terminal ileum, extensive colic polyposis (>100), and a vegetative lesion in the descending colon. Biopsies from these exams revealed fundic gland polyps (gastric polyps) and duodenal mucosa with focal low-grade dysplasia. The vegetative colon lesion biopsy showed adenoma with low-grade dysplasia and a necrosing area in one fragment. A liver biopsy indicated adenocarcinoma of probable gastrointestinal origin. The adrenal nodule's functional study was compatible with a benign adenoma. The patient underwent a thyroid ultrasound, which showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Sequencing of the APC gene revealed a pathologic heterozygotic c.4612_4613delGA p.(Glu1538Ilefs∗5) variant.

case_report: A 41-year-old male with no prior history of systemic illness visited the dental clinic at the Federal Medical Centre, Ebute-Metta, Lagos, Nigeria, due to a painful swelling at the left angle of the mandible that had persisted for 8 months. The pain intensified when lying down. The patient had undergone herniorrhaphy for an inguinoscrotal hernia a year before this visit. There was no reported family history of abdominal diseases. Initial examinations identified a middle-aged man with a single, solitary, bony hard, and slightly tender swelling measuring 3 cm by 2 cm at the left angle of the mandible, which was not attached to the overlying skin. A similar swelling, approximately 0.6 cm at its widest diameter, was found at the right angle of the mandible. Additionally, multiple bony swellings were observed on the forehead, along with soft, mobile subcutaneous swellings in the midline of the posterior neck, upper limbs, and gluteal area, all appearing at different times. The submandibular lymph nodes were clinically normal. Physical examination findings are shown in Figure. Intraoral examination revealed a mesiodens, a retained upper left deciduous canine, missing upper right first incisor, upper left second incisor, and canine. The lower left third molar was covered by an inflamed and tender pericoronal flap. A panoramic radiograph was ordered, which showed multiple radiopaque elements indicative of multiple impacted teeth, multiple odontoma, and osteomas.
test_results: Endoscopy revealed multiple sessile and pedunculated polyps in the second part of the duodenum, caecum, transverse colon, sigmoid colon, and multiple polyps in the rectum, all estimated to be more than one hundred in number. Histological evaluation of the multiple intestinal polyps showed varying degrees of dysplasia as follows: There is a polypoid fragment of tissue comprising of crypts and mucosal glands lined by dysplastic epithelium having hyperchromatic nuclei with nuclear spindling and focal nuclear stratification extending up to the luminal surface in areas. In addition, there is focal loss of basal polarity, consistent with tubular adenoma with high-grade dysplasia. The histological sections of the caecal polyp exhibiting low-grade dysplasia of the surface epithelium. The histological section of the transverse colonic polyp exhibiting features consistent with tubular adenoma with low-grade dysplasia. The histological sections of the sigmoid polyp reveal focal areas of dysplastic colonic epithelium having hyperchromatic nuclei with nuclear spindling, focal nuclear stratification limited to the lower third and loss of polarity. Some of the apical glands show slight reduction of mucin content and the lamina propria appear moderately infiltrated by chronic inflammatory cells in keeping with tubular adenoma with low-grade dysplasia. Histological sections of the rectal polyp showing features that are consistent with tubular adenoma with low-grade dysplasia.

case_report: A 72-year-old female was admitted due to worsening bilateral leg swelling and shortness of breath. Her medical history includes well-managed type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension, and she has never smoked. Physical examination showed pitting edema in both legs and the left arm, along with reduced breath sounds in the lower lung fields on both sides. Chest X-ray indicated pleural effusions. Fifteen months earlier, she had presented with similar symptoms at another hospital, where bilateral chylothorax was identified. Laboratory tests, chest and abdominal CT scans did not reveal any abnormalities. Liver sonography with transient elastography excluded cirrhosis and portal hypertension. Lower limb lymphoscintigraphy using 99mTc-nanocolloid showed significantly delayed lymphatic transport, confirming lymphedema without pinpointing any obstruction or leakage of lymphatic fluid. A thoracoscopic pleural biopsy showed chronic nonspecific inflammation without evidence of malignancy or infection. Treatment included subcutaneous octreotide (100μL three times daily), a low-fat diet with medium-chain triglycerides (MCT) supplementation, and bilateral chest tube drainage. Despite ongoing drainage, chest tubes were eventually removed, and she was discharged for outpatient follow-up. Over the next 15 months, her lymphedema progressively worsened, affecting her arms, and thoracentesis was occasionally needed despite adherence to dietary recommendations. Upon hospitalization in our department, dietary modifications were reinstated, and octreotide therapy was resumed. The left-sided effusion was tapped, revealing milky fluid with a high lymphocyte count (85%), marginally exudative characteristics (pleural fluid and serum protein 2.7 g/L and 5.4 g/L, ratio 0.5; pleural fluid and serum lactate dehydrogenase 78 IU/L and 160 IU/L, ratio 0.49), and elevated triglyceride levels of 164 mg/dL, consistent with chylothorax. Microbiological tests were negative for infection, and cytology showed no malignant cells.
test_results: Noncaseating granulomas were demonstrated on lung biopsy specimens.

case_report: A 49-year-old woman from Bangladesh presented with a three-month history of progressive difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids, dry cough, malaise, and an unintentional weight loss of 30 pounds. She had been admitted to multiple hospitals for similar symptoms, but no formal diagnosis was made. She denied any fevers or coughing up blood. An endoscopic gastroduodenoscopy (EGD) performed two weeks prior to admission showed a peptic ulcer but was otherwise unremarkable. She had been diagnosed with right-sided facial nerve palsy a month prior and treated with a two-week course of corticosteroids, but her symptoms returned after stopping the medication. During her admission, her vital signs remained stable. Physical examination revealed significant weight loss and new left facial weakness consistent with facial nerve palsy. She was alert with no cognitive impairment and unable to completely close her right eye. There was no conjunctival chemosis, proptosis, or periorbital edema. An ophthalmologic exam ruled out uveitis. She had decreased sensation in the right V1–V3 distribution, reduced hearing on the right compared to the left, decreased sensation in the right oropharynx, symmetric rise of the palate, and her tongue appeared midline on protrusion. Other cranial nerves were intact. She had decreased muscle bulk throughout, 5/5 strength in the arms, 4/5 proximal strength, and 5/5 distal strength in the legs. Reflexes were normal in both upper and lower extremities. Laboratory investigations showed BUN 3.97 mg/dl and Na 132 mmol/L. She was initially placed on airborne precautions due to constitutional symptoms and positive Quantiferon tuberculin testing, which were discontinued after sputum samples were negative for acid-fast bacilli. Chest radiograph showed hilar prominence without focal airspace opacities. CT of the chest revealed extensive bilateral paratracheal, subcarinal, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Fiber-optic endoscopy for dysphagia showed immobility of the right vocal fold, significant pooling of secretions, hooding of arytenoids with erythema and edema, and oropharyngeal dysphagia. Videofluoroscopic study showed indentation of the hypopharynx at the cricopharyngeal muscle, but the study was aborted due to inability to clear moderate puree residue and significant coughing, gagging, and hocking without aspiration. She was placed on aspiration precautions and started on enteral feeding via nasogastric tube. Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 15 mmHg, white cell count of 18 [0–10/UL] with 93% lymphocytes [40–80%], red blood cell count of 3, protein 66 [20–100 mg/dl], and glucose 62 [40–170 mg/dl]. Oligoclonal banding was absent. Various serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies for neoplastic, paraneoplastic, infectious, and inflammatory causes were unremarkable. Tests for HIV 1/2 EIA, serum and CSF VDRL, serum HSV 1/2 PCR, serum EBV panel, and serum and CSF Lyme disease total Antibody IgG/IgM were negative. Angiotensin Converting Enzyme levels in serum and CSF were 65 [14–82 U/L] and 2.1 [0.0–2.5 U/L], respectively. MRI of the brain with and without contrast showed enhancement of the seventh and eighth cranial nerves. MRI of the l-spine showed no acute fractures, no compression of the conus or cauda equina, and no high-grade central canal or neural foraminal stenosis.
test_results: Endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) guided fine needle aspiration (FNA) with multiple lymph node biopsies revealed non-caseating granulomas without malignant cells. Further testing showed the absence of acid-fast bacilli by AFB stain, absence of fungi by GMS stain, and absence of immunophenotypic evidence of a lymphoproliferative disorder by flow cytometry.

case_report: A 39-year-old Japanese woman with a history of one miscarriage at 6 weeks' gestation became pregnant while on anticoagulation treatment with 2500 U danaparoid sodium and 100 mg aspirin per day from 4 weeks' gestation at Nagoya City University Hospital. She has a 22-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), which had been in remission for more than 4 years under a treatment of 5 mg prednisolone daily. Anticoagulant treatment was administered during pregnancy due to strongly positive lupus anticoagulant (LA) results by diluted activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) methods and diluted Russel's viper venom time (RVVT) before pregnancy. Prednisolone therapy was interrupted before this pregnancy because the patient believed it affected fertility. Edema and proteinuria appeared at 17 weeks' gestation. Her blood pressure was 121/78 mmHg, and laboratory studies showed anti-β2-glycoprotein I (β2GPI) 9.4 U/mL (normal range < 1.9), aPTT 30%, LA by aPTT 30 seconds, LA by RVVT 1.47, and urinary protein 2.0 g/day at 17 weeks of gestation. At 21 weeks of gestation, she had body edema and proteinuria (8.1 g/24 h). She was hospitalized at 21 weeks of gestation due to severe edema and acute renal dysfunction, and treatment with 40 mg prednisolone daily started at 22 weeks of gestation. She developed epigastric pain and vomiting. Thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, liver and renal dysfunction, and an elevated level of C-reactive protein were observed.
test_results: Her renal biopsy showed lupus nephritis INS/RPS class IV with mesangial interposition, massive subendothelial, subepithelial and mesangial deposit, fibrinoid necrosis, karyorrhexis, swelling of endothelial cells, and foam cells.

case_report: A 15-year-old Iranian girl was referred to an endocrinology clinic in southern Iran with severe fatigue and weakness. She exhibited irritability, abdominal pain, vomiting, salt craving, and right thigh pain. These symptoms had begun three months prior and progressively worsened. Three months later, she was hospitalized due to dyspnea, cough, and fever, and was diagnosed with pneumonia and a lung hydatid cyst. A chest CT scan revealed mild to moderate bilateral pleural effusion and a subpleural cystic structure measuring approximately 32 × 22 mm in the left lower lobe. ELISA confirmed the presence of a hydatid cyst. Surgery was indicated due to a ruptured infected hydatid cyst. Preoperative workup showed prolonged PT (15.1 s), INR (1.12), PTT (108.2 s), and pancytopenia (WBC 2.1, Hb 6.1, plt 61 × 10^9), leading to the cancellation of the surgery. Mebendazole treatment was initiated and was successful, resulting in discharge after 24 days with hematologist follow-up. The patient remained ill with severe fatigue. Physical examination revealed hypotension (blood pressure 80/50 mmHg), tachycardia (heart rate 120/min), fever (temperature 38°C), and generalized abdominal pain without guarding or tenderness. Significant hyperpigmentation was noted, particularly in the buccal mucosa, mouth, and extremities. She had a limp, and edema and swelling were observed in the right lower extremity. Her weight was 53 kg (a loss of 5 kg over three months), and her height was 159 cm. She was admitted for further evaluation and treatment. Color Doppler sonography of the lower extremity veins indicated thrombosis of the right common femoral vein. The patient was critically ill, with hypotension and hyponatremia. Due to the emergent condition, the stimulatory test was not performed.
test_results: Laboratory data showed high ACTH 8 am and low cortisol level.
diagnosis: Adrenal Insufficiency due to Secondary Antiphospholipid Syndrome

case_report: A 56-year-old female store seller experienced her first episode of altered tactile sensation in her legs 16 years ago. She received treatment at the Mexican Institute of Social Security and the INR. The case was examined in the CAPD laboratory in 2011 and 2014. During an interview in 2011, she reported stable tinnitus and poor auditory discrimination since 2010, although audiograms were normal for both ears. She exhibited a phonemic discrimination deficit, poor sound localization, mixed dysarthria, walking instability with a tendency to fall, and memory disorder. The initial CAPD study showed no significant alterations, with only a slightly higher percentage of correct answers for the DDR test in the right ear. The study was repeated in 2014 with the same symptoms and persistent tinnitus. Three out of four monaural tests indicated a dominance of left ear processing, with a higher percentage of successes for the left ear, and a similar profile in the frequency pattern discrimination test. The DDR test in 2014 showed a higher percentage of correct answers for the right ear compared to 2011.
test_results: In brainstem auditory evoked potentials (BAEPs) from the right ear, we observed a mild retardation in interwave interval I–III, and the left ear response presented bad morphology definition and retarded latencies. We also found a retardation of the left N2 wave in LLAEP.

case_report: A 42-year-old Malay woman was referred for surgical management of an intramedullary spinal cord lesion in July 2002. Her symptoms began in April 2002 with a subacute onset of progressive quadriparesis, and by the time of admission, she had developed urinary incontinence and was bedridden. Imaging of the spine indicated an intramedullary lesion at the C1-C5 level. Decompressive laminectomy and biopsy of the lesion were performed in July 2002. Histological examination showed features consistent with demyelination. Her medical history included two previous episodes of acute neurological deficits with partial recovery in October 1998 and March 2002, presenting as mild paraparesis with bladder involvement over a period of 2 weeks, followed by a complete return to baseline. Physical examination revealed bilateral pale optic discs with normal visual acuity, quadriparesis with brisk reflexes, upgoing plantar responses, and sensory loss at the T12-L1 level. Routine blood tests, serology for syphilis, hepatitis, and HIV, and screening for autoimmune antibodies were all negative. Visual evoked potential (VEP) was slightly prolonged in the right eye, while brainstem auditory evoked potential (BAEP) was within normal limits.
test_results: An MRI scan of her brain revealed demyelinating plaques in the centrum semiovale.

case_report: A 3-year-old girl of Greek descent was referred to our hospital due to gait disturbance and undiagnosed skin lesions. The patient exhibited bilateral spasticity of the legs. Motor skill acquisition was delayed, with standing without support achieved at 13 months and walking at 16 months. At 16 months, she spoke 8–10 words. There was no history of epileptic seizures. Examination revealed extensive hyperkeratosis and scaling of the skin, particularly on the palms and soles, and hyperpigmented skin flexures. Her hair and fingernails were normal. There was a history of recurrent chalazia. She was born at full-term (39 weeks) following an uneventful pregnancy. She is the fourth living child of a consanguineous couple who are third cousins, with no significant medical history in her siblings. Height (104 cm), weight (16.5 kg), and head circumference (53.5 cm) were within normal age limits at presentation. Neurological evaluation showed spastic diplegia of the lower extremities, mild generalized increase in muscle tone, deep tendon reflexes of the lower extremities, and positive Babinski reflexes bilaterally. Intelligence was normal (IQ 95). Electroencephalopathy, otoacoustic emission test (OAE), abdominal and renal ultrasound, and X-ray of the chest and hips were normal. Conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed diffuse symmetrical high-intensity lesions in the deep white matter of the centrum semiovale and the frontal lobes, with milder-intensity diffuse lesions in the posterior parietal lobes and the corpus callosum. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) showed a moderate increase in lipid and myoinositol levels, while other metabolites like N-acetyl aspartate (NAA), choline (Cho), and creatine (Cr) were within normal limits. Fundoscopy showed no abnormal features in either eye, confirmed by optical coherence tomography of the macula, which showed no retinal deposits or other pathology. Cycloplegic retinoscopy revealed high refractive error (right eye C −4.50 D × 20°, left eye C −4.00 D × 170°). Visual acuity, measured with the ETDRS chart at 4 meters, was LogMAR 0.5 in the right eye and LogMAR 0.3 in the left eye with glasses, presumed to be due to refractive amblyopia. Histopathology of a skin biopsy from the right axillary region and right thigh showed orthokeratotic hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and papillomatosis of the stratum spinosum.
test_results: Sequencing of the polymerase chain reaction product using the exon-specific primers revealed a c.551C>T mutation of the ALDH3A2 gene on chromosome 17p11.2 in homozygous state.

case_report: The patient is a 12-year-old boy admitted for generalized skin dryness and developmental delay. He has moderate mental retardation and is unable to walk. He is the second child of healthy consanguineous parents and was born pre-term at 32 weeks of gestation via normal vaginal delivery. There was no history of maternal diabetes or exposure to teratogenic agents during pregnancy. Birth weight, length, and head circumference measurements are unknown. At 2.5 years of age, he was first evaluated for delayed walking, and imaging detected symmetrical white matter lesions. He has global developmental delay and has experienced generalized seizures since the age of 7, which have been controlled with valproic acid. Physical examination revealed generalized skin dryness, most prominent around the umbilicus and on the bilateral lower limbs. The face, palms, and soles were also affected, but nails and teeth appeared normal. No skeletal abnormalities such as short stature or kyphoscoliosis were observed. Neurological examination showed moderate mental retardation and spasticity. Deep tendon reflexes were brisk in the lower limbs, and muscle strength was graded at 3/5 in both lower limbs, resulting in an inability to walk. Ophthalmologic examination was normal. Laboratory metabolic investigations, including serum lactate, pyruvate, tandem mass spectrometry, urine organic acids, and phytanic acid, were normal. Electroencephalogram (EEG) showed symmetrical slow background activity without other abnormalities.
test_results: Cerebral magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) had detected symmetrical white matter lesions. MRI of the brain showed diffuse and symmetrical high-signal intensity in bilateral deep periventricular white matter in the corona radiata.

case_report: An 11-year-old girl visited the emergency department after spraining her left ankle while ice skating. Examination and plain radiographs showed no obvious injury, and she was sent home. She returned three days later, unable to bear weight on her left leg, and was seen in the fracture clinic. She was found to have a soft-tissue injury and was given a functional walking boot, with a follow-up scheduled for two weeks later. At the follow-up, she exhibited tenderness on both the lateral and medial malleolus, ankle swelling, and a decreased range of movement, but her neurovascular status was intact. Repeat plain films showed a periosteal reaction at the left distal tibia. She continued using the walking boot and was referred for physiotherapy. A month later, she developed swelling and blue discoloration in the right leg; a lower limb duplex confirmed a right-sided deep vein thrombosis (DVT).
test_results: Hematological review and subsequent thrombophilia screen were deemed normal.
Orpha_name: Hereditary thrombophilia due to congenital antithrombin deficiency

case_report: A 46-year-old male presented with general fatigue and dizziness upon exertion. He reported experiencing chronic lower back pain for the past 10 years but had not sought orthopedic consultation. An electrocardiogram revealed a severe conduction disturbance with a heart rhythm of 20-30 beats per minute, advanced and complete atrioventricular block, and severe bradycardia. Serum creatinine and electrolyte levels were within normal limits, and the plasma level of brain natriuretic peptide was 160 pg/mL at the time of admission. Continuous isoproterenol injection therapy was initiated for heart rate control on the day of admission. By the following day, his heart rhythm improved to Mobitz II second-degree atrioventricular block, and his symptoms generally resolved. Transient advanced and complete atrioventricular blocks were observed only during sleep. A coronary artery angiogram ruled out ischemic heart disease, although mild coronary arteriosclerosis was noted. Ultrasonography indicated mild arteriosclerotic changes in the carotid artery. Echocardiography showed normal cardiac function with no signs of valvular diseases, including aortic regurgitation and basal septum degenerative changes. The patient had a family history of a specific condition affecting his father, younger paternal half-brother, and female cousin on the paternal side.
test_results: X-ray and magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated bilateral sacroiliitis. Laboratory test results for HLA-B27 were positive.

case_report: A 39-year-old male, working as a businessman, presented to the neurological rehabilitation outpatient department with complaints of worsening walking ability and generalized stiffness for the past year. He had a history of a minor fall in the washroom in March 2021, which resulted in weakness in all four limbs. An MRI of the spine at the time of injury revealed C4-5 subluxation with cord edema extending from C4 to C5. He underwent surgical fixation at another facility. Over the next six months, he experienced gradual sensorimotor recovery in all four limbs and began walking short distances with the assistance of one person. Despite taking multiple anti-spasticity medications (Tablet Baclofen 60 mg, Tizanidine 12 mg, and Tolperisone 900 mg in divided doses daily), he experienced severe stiffness throughout his body. He sought further evaluation and management. Upon admission to the neurological rehabilitation ward, he was classified as ASIA D SCI with a neurological level at C5. Examination revealed predominantly axial stiffness and MAS 1+ spasticity in the bilateral wrist flexors, triceps, hamstrings, and gastrocnemius muscles. The Schober test was positive, and the FABER test was negative. A detailed history revealed that he had experienced early morning stiffness in the lower back for the past 10 years, for which he took over-the-counter medication. He was able to perform daily activities without difficulty before the spinal cord injury. He denied any history of red eye, burning during urination, altered bowel habits, or skin and nail lesions. He had previously been diagnosed with a condition but had discontinued long-term medication on his own.
test_results: Radiographic evaluation suggesting bridging syndesmophytes with bilateral sacroiliitis. MRI of cervical spine showed myelomalacic changes at C4 spinal level. The pulmonary function test revealed severe restrictive lung disease. The urodynamic study revealed good cystometric capacity and terminal detrusor overactivity with detrusor-sphincter-dyssynergia.

case_report: A 61-year-old male agriculturist from Oaxaca, Mexico, presented for a dermatological consultation with a warty nodular plaque measuring 5 cm in diameter, featuring well-defined edges, situated on the anterior medial part of the right forearm. The lesion had been present for one year. The patient had no comorbidities and had undergone several empirical treatments before the consultation.
test_results: A direct examination of the plaque was performed using 40% KOH, followed by a biopsy and culturing in Sabouraud medium at 28 °C for 8 days. The first culture was negative. The histopathology revealed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and suppurative granuloma; no parasitic elements were observed after Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) and Gomori-Grocott staining. A colony with the typical macroscopic and microscopic morphology of the S. schenckii complex was isolated in the culture. The identity of the pathogen was confirmed by the amplification of a 331 bp fragment of the CAL gene (calmodulin) using multiplex PCR.

case_report: A 37-year-old male reported a 3-year history of worsening vision in the right eye, with no prior visual issues except for a congenital color vision deficiency identified early in life. He had no history of antimalarial or retinotoxic drug use, no night vision problems, and maintained a normal diet. He experienced head trauma during a soccer game, leading to the discovery of a 6 mm colloid cyst in the third ventricle. There was no family history of consanguinity, inherited retinal disease, poor vision, or color vision disturbances. His father, recently diagnosed with chronic central serous retinopathy, showed significant improvement with systemic spironolactone treatment. Examination findings included a visual acuity of 6/24 in the right eye and 6/6 in the left eye, normal pupil reactions, 1/15 Ishihara color vision test plates read correctly with each eye, full ocular motility, and an otherwise normal cranial nerve examination. Anterior segment examination was unremarkable. Fundus examination revealed scattered atrophy and pisciform fundal flecks at both maculae, more pronounced in the right eye.
test_results: Fluorescein angiography demonstrated a silent choroid and partial bull's eye maculopathy which was worse in the right eye. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed loss of photoreceptors at both maculae with partial central sparing in the left eye. Photopic and scotopic flash electroretinograms (ERGs) showed reduced amplitudes of responses in the major ERG components in the right eye and amplitudes within the lower range of normal in the left eye. Implicit times in both eyes were within normal limits. The pattern ERG and multifocal ERG demonstrated central retinal dysfunction with the retention of peripheral function. Next-generation sequencing analysis with the Oxford Genetics Testing Laboratory Macular Gene Panel revealed 2 mutations in the ABCA4 genes: c.5882G>A p.(Gly1961Glu), a common ABCA4 mutation, and c.2486C>T p.(Thr829Met).

case_report: A 6-year-old female exhibited a decline in reading abilities. Visual acuity measurements were RE 1.3 and LE 1.0 (LogMAR), with no notable refractive errors detected. Colour vision assessment showed no abnormalities on Ishihara plates. Examination of the fundus revealed bilateral atrophic changes in the macular region at the level of the photoreceptors/RPE.
test_results: Electrodiagnostic tests identified that she had cone responses to flash stimulation within the noise level, while her 30 Hz flicker responses were still evident, but reduced in amplitude. She had normal rod system ERG responses in either eye. She was not able to cooperate for a PERG recording, while her pattern-reversal VEP was very abnormal, indicating loss of macular function. Genetic testing confirmed a mutation in the ABCA4 gene.

case_report: A 69-year-old female patient reported experiencing a gradual decline in vision. Her parents were first cousins. She had a history of smoking for 15 years and had previously been diagnosed with retinitis pigmentosa 27 years ago. Her medical history included hyperlipidemia and hypothyroidism. During a thorough eye examination, her best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was measured as counting fingers at 5 feet in the right eye and 3 feet in the left eye. Retinoscopy revealed a refraction of –1.00 + 0.50×70 in the right eye and –2.00 + 1.00×5 in the left eye. The examination also noted pale optic discs, significant deep atrophy of the central macula, epithelial pigment hyperplasia, and multifocal atrophy in the right eye. The left eye exhibited macular atrophy.
test_results: In the patient’s fundus autofluorescence (FAF) imaging, there was evidence of central hypoautofluorescence of the macula, with diffuse outward centrifugal extension from its center to its periphery. Macular optical coherence tomography (OCT) determined that the average macular thickness was 191 µM and 193 µM in the right and left eyes, respectively. Macular volume was 6.9 mm3 and 7.0 mm3 in the right and left eyes, respectively. No macular edema, cysts, or subretinal fluid was found in either eye. A visual field test revealed that the patient had mean deviations of –23.75 dB and –24.56 dB in the right and left eyes, respectively. Pattern standard deviations were +3.69 dB and +4.69 dB in the right and left eyes, respectively. The results of a full-field electroretinogram (ERG) showed a normal rod response and decreased cone response, bilaterally. A single pathogenic homozygous intronic variant c.5714+5G>A of the ABCA4 gene was found upon sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis using next-generation sequencing.

case_report: A 9-year-old boy presented with decreased vision in the left eye for eight months. He denied any headaches, nausea, or vomiting. His past medical history was unremarkable. On physical examination, his vital signs were stable; height and BMI were at the 90th percentile and weight was at the 94th percentile. He was alert, conscious, and oriented to time, place, and person. Visual exam through Snellen’s chart indicated a loss of vision and impaired visual field in the left eye. He had normal sensory, motor, and reflexes exam of the upper and lower extremities. Pubic and axillary hairs were at the Tanner I stage, testicles were 3 cm bilaterally (Tanner II), and penile length was 7.5 cm. Laboratory tests revealed hyponatremia 132 mMol/L, low serum osmolality 275 mOsm/kg, an inappropriately elevated urine osmolality 886 mOsm/kg, pubertal testosterone 109 ng/dL, a pubertal luteinizing hormone level (LH) 2.0 mIU/mL and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) 5 mIU/mL, an advanced bone age (12 years); normal insulin-like growth factor binding protein 3 (IGFBP3) 3.5 mcg/mL, normal thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) 0.89 uIU/mL, and free thyroxine (FT4) 0.92 ng/dL.
test_results: The initial brain MRI with contrast demonstrated a 5.6x4.1x3.2 cm third ventricle AC, severe obstructive hydrocephalus, enlarged sella with a mass effect on the pituitary gland, and deviation of the pituitary stalk along with papilledema.
diagnosis: Third Ventricle Arachnoid Cyst causing Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion

case_report: A 78-year-old male patient was admitted to the hospital due to severe skin pain lasting for 3 weeks. Upon admission, scattered rashes were observed on the right side of the forehead, upper eyelid, and periorbital skin. The patient reported drooping eyelid, restricted eye movement, and double vision for 2 weeks. Right oculomotor paralysis was noted. A lumbar puncture was performed after excluding contraindications and obtaining informed consent. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed an elevated white blood cell count (0.041, normal: 0–0.005) and increased protein levels (0.60, normal: 0.15–0.45). Routine blood tests, liver function, renal function, electrolyte concentration, thyroid function, cortical hormone levels, tumor biomarkers, and autoimmune antibodies were all within normal limits. The patient's medical history included hypertension and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), for which he was taking amlodipine tablets and tiotropium bromide powder for inhalation. Intravenous acyclovir and dexamethasone were administered. Gabapentin was gradually increased to 300 mg three times per day to manage skin pain. An ophthalmologic consultation revealed keratitis, and ganciclovir eye gel was prescribed. Nearly 2 weeks after starting this treatment, a repeat lumbar puncture showed that CSF parameters had returned to normal. The patient reported improved eye movement, but skin pain around the lesion persisted. Duloxetine at a daily dose of 60 mg was added to his regimen. The other medications remained unchanged. After 2 doses of duloxetine, the patient experienced fatigue, disorientation, and lethargy. While asleep, he exhibited arm movements and random groping. Upon waking, he described these actions as catching chickens or carrying a bucket.
test_results: Blood electrolyte indicated hyponatremia (125, normal: 132–145 mmol/L) and hypochloridemia (89, normal: 90–108 mmol/L). Serum osmolality was 254 mOsm/L and urine osmolality was 430 mOsm/L.
diagnosis: Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion

case_report: A 44-year-old male veteran was seen for follow-up due to long-standing daytime sleepiness, which included sudden sleep episodes even while standing, with periods of lost time up to 30 minutes. He reported no occurrences of cataplexy, hypnogogic hallucinations, or sleep paralysis. An initial evaluation in another state in 1993 included sleep studies that documented 32 awakenings, 2 apnea/hypopnea events, a mean sleep onset of 5.9 minutes across 5 naps (with no sleep during one nap), and REM sleep observed in at least two naps, possibly four out of five naps. After relocating, he presented to our sleep disorders center in 2004 with ongoing excessive daytime sleepiness and no specific treatment. He also described continued episodes of sleepwalking, including instances of walking on the roof of a chemical plant where he worked or smoking a cigarette on his front porch.
test_results: During the MSLT, sleep occurred on all four nap opportunities, the mean sleep latency was 10 minutes and there were no sleep onset REM periods. During the subsequent MSLT, sleep occurred on all five nap opportunities, the mean sleep latency was 2.6 minutes, and REM sleep occurred on naps two and three.

case_report: Patient 3 is a 54-year-old male with a history of hypertension and sleep apnea syndrome, managed for several years, who was referred to our clinic. In May 2021, he was diagnosed with SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia, which did not necessitate hospitalization. Two months post-infection, he experienced dyspnea and frequent episodes of uncontrollable sleepiness resulting in daytime naps. His nocturnal sleep duration increased from 6-7 hours per day before the SARS-CoV-2 infection to 9-10 hours per day afterward, along with one or two daytime naps. These naps were initially restorative but were followed by a quick return of sleepiness. He also reported dizziness, memory and attention issues, and irritability. He did not experience sleep hallucinations, sleep paralysis, or cataplexy. There was no prior indication of narcolepsy before the COVID-19 infection. His adherence to continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy was good, averaging 6 hours and 45 minutes per night before the infection, and it was effective, with no residual fatigue and an apnea-hypopnea index of 3.4 per hour as per the built-in software. A cardiopulmonary exercise test revealed dysfunctional breathing with hyperventilation. A specialized respiratory rehabilitation program alleviated his dyspnea, but episodes of daytime sleepiness continued, leading to a 48-hour sleep laboratory evaluation 17 months post-infection.
test_results: The MLST found a mean sleep latency of 7 min 42 s with three sleep onset rapid eye movement periods.

case_report: A 43-year-old perimenopausal female, recently diagnosed with hypertension for the past 6 months, presented for evaluation. She was taking amlodipine 5 mg/day and atenolol 25 mg/day. There was no history of edema. Physical examination revealed high blood pressure (190/110 mmHg) with no asymmetry or postural drop. Fundus examination was normal. Laboratory tests showed a normal hemogram with hemoglobin at 13.3 g/dl, total leukocyte count at 10,200/cumm, and normal platelet count and peripheral smear. Urine examination indicated proteinuria with microscopic hematuria and bland sediment, with proteinuria quantified at 5.83 g per day. Fasting blood sugar was elevated at 132 mg/dl, while serum creatinine was normal at 0.84 mg/dl. Lipid profile was within normal limits. Ultrasonography showed kidneys of normal size with no other abnormalities. Coagulation profile was normal, and screening for HIV, HBsAg, and anti-HCV was negative. Protein electrophoresis and immunofixation revealed a normal pattern with no abnormal protein bands.
test_results: A renal biopsy performed showed 14 glomeruli which were enlarged, a prominent mesangial widening with an eosinophilic fibrillary appearance and a peripheral interposition along with basement membrane giving it a thickened appearance. These deposits were negative for periodic acid Schiff (PAS), silver methanamine, and Congo red stains. There was associated PAS positive peripheral hyalinosis in some glomeruli. The glomeruli showed no increase in cellularity, segmental lesions, or crescents. Few tubules had eosinophilic casts within and the interstitium showed a patchy mild lymphomononuclear infiltrates. The larger arteries showed intimal sclerosis. Direct immunofluorescence study showed focal and segmental deposits of C3c corresponding to peripheral hyalinosis. Electron microscopic study was performed to identify conclusively the type of deposits. The biopsy cores fixed with gluteraldehyde revealed abundant subendothelial deposits of large fibers (97 nm in width) with long spacing striations (25–30 nm), which were characteristic of collagen fibers.

case_report: A 28-year-old Caucasian male with no significant personal or family medical history experienced odynophagia and a dry cough in November 2022, subsequently testing positive for SARS-CoV-2. The following week, he developed severe fatigue and malaise, leading to the cessation of his daily 4-5 hour triathlon training. He also experienced a loss of appetite, occasional epigastric pain, vomiting, and a craving for salty foods, resulting in a weight loss of approximately 6 kg (from 76 to 70 kg) about one month after the COVID-19 diagnosis. Concurrently, his family and friends observed a darkening of his skin. During this period, he had multiple consultations with his family physician and emergency room visits, often receiving general blood tests, fluids, and antiemetic treatments, but without medium to long-term improvement. His condition progressively deteriorated, leading to another emergency room visit in April 2023, approximately six months after the initial COVID-19 diagnosis. Physical examination revealed dehydration and hypotension (blood pressure: 90/50 mmHg). Generalized hyperpigmentation of the skin and mucosal surfaces was observed. Laboratory tests indicated normocytic normochromic anemia, acute kidney injury, hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, and compensated metabolic acidosis. A CT scan of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis showed small adrenal glands.
test_results: Serum cortisol collected at 8 AM was low (25.07 nmol/L). Serum ACTH was increased (2000.0 pg/mL). Anti-adrenal antibodies were negative. Autoantibodies against the steroidogenic enzyme 21-hydroxylase antibodies (21OH-Abs) were positive.

case_report: A 37-year-old Caucasian female from São Paulo, Brazil, delivered a healthy male infant in February 2009 via vaginal delivery at 40 weeks gestation. The newborn weighed 3510g and had Apgar scores of 9 and 10, with no obstetric complications. Within the first 24 hours, the infant developed petechiae and severe thrombocytopenia (14,000/mm3), while hemoglobin and white blood cell counts remained normal and there was no sign of infection. The newborn was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) for further evaluation. The platelet count dropped to its lowest level of 9,000/mm3 on day 4, despite receiving daily platelet transfusions and intravenous immunoglobulin at a dose of 1g/kg. By day 8, the platelet count increased to 51,000/mm3, and the infant was discharged on day 9 with a platelet count of 81,000/mm3, without experiencing any bleeding complications.
test_results: Human platelet antigen (HPA) genotyping showed that the mother was HPA-1b1b, the father HPA-1a1a and the child HPA-1a1b. Maternal antibodies against HPA-1a were detected by monoclonal-specific antibody immobilization of platelet antigens (MAIPA).

case_report: Patient 1 is a two-year-old girl, the first child in her family, born to a healthy 26-year-old mother and a 28-year-old father of Turkish origin. Antenatal research data were not available. She was born at term through spontaneous vaginal delivery without complications. Her birth weight was 3100 grams (25–50 percentile) and her birth length was 50 cm (50–75 percentile). The occipitofrontal circumference (OFC) at birth is not known. Upon examination, her weight is 11 kg (25–50 percentile), her length is 87 cm (50–75 percentile), and her OFC is 48.5 cm (50–75 percentile). Biochemical tests for thyroid, kidney, and liver function were normal. Ophthalmological examination and echocardiogram results were normal. Ultrasound imaging revealed hepatomegaly and renal hypoplasia. Blood count and peripheral smear were normal. Minor dysmorphic features such as brachycephaly, upslanting palpebral fissures, broad nasal base, and epicanthus were observed. No single transverse palmar crease was noted.
test_results: Karyotype from the peripheral lymphocytes using G-banding is ‘mos 45,X[41] / 47, XX,+21[59]’.

case_report: A 9-year-old girl has experienced left groin pain during activity for the past 5 months. She did not report any tenderness in the sacroiliac joint, inflammatory pain in the lower back, eye inflammation, or systemic symptoms. Physical examination revealed a slight limp and limited range of motion in the left hip. There was no inflammation at tendon or ligament attachment sites. Laboratory results showed HLA-B27 positivity, ANA titers at 1:160, and a negative rheumatoid factor. An x-ray of the left hip appeared normal.
test_results: MRI of the pelvis showed left hip synovitis, trace amount of fluid and subchondral changes within the femoral head. The SI joints were normal.

case_report: A 9-year-old girl experienced a left supracondylar fracture one year before visiting our clinic. Four weeks after the cast removal, she reported persistent elbow pain and reduced elbow movement. Despite undergoing intensive physiotherapy, her pain persisted, and elbow movement further decreased. Upon examination, the left elbow showed signs of effusion, tenderness, warmth, and significant flexure contracture. Laboratory results indicated ANA positivity at 1:160, while RF and anti-CCP antibodies were negative. PPD testing was also negative.
test_results: X-ray of the left elbow showed joint space narrowing and atrophy of the elbow’s articulation. CT of the left elbow demonstrated subchondral bone erosions, bone overgrowth and accelerated trochlear ossification. The MRI revealed a small elbow effusion, marked synovial thickening, post-gadolinium enhancement of the radial head, trochlea, olecranon and coronoid bones, ballooning of the humeral epiphysis and multiple articular erosions.

case_report: A 72-year-old Japanese woman with a history of chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis and goiter presented with elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels (6.56 μIU/ml), high TPOAb levels (> 600 IU/ml), and high anti-Tg levels (> 4000 IU/ml), while maintaining normal levels of free triiodothyronine (T3; 3.08 pg/ml) and thyroxine (T4; 1.18 ng/ml). Her medical history was notable for hypertension, and she had no recent fever, neck pain, or medication use that could affect thyroid function. Her social, family, and environmental histories were unremarkable. For the past 6 months, she had been consuming a health drink containing soybean and kale powder extract at a dose of 9 g/day. Over time, she developed general malaise, edema, and hoarseness. Upon presentation to the hospital, her TSH level was markedly elevated (373.3 μIU/ml), and her T3 (< 0.26 pg/ml) and T4 (0.10 ng/ml) levels were very low. Additional laboratory findings included increased levels of total cholesterol, triglyceride, lactate dehydrogenase, aspartate transaminase, creatine phosphokinase, and immunoglobulin G. Physical examination revealed a swollen goiter with mild hardness, a blood pressure of 123/77 mmHg, a body temperature of 36.0 °C, and a pulse rate of 55 beats per minute.
test_results: Computed tomography and thyroid ultrasound revealed bilateral thyroid enlargement. Her uptake rate of 99mTc-pertechnetate was reduced. After she discontinued consuming the health drink, two components quickly disappeared, and the other three components gradually decreased. The five ingredients that disappeared or decreased were highly suspected to be soy isoflavones.
diagnosis: Hypothyroidism induced by soy isoflavones in a patient with chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis

case_report: This report details the clinical observations of an adolescent girl who first presented in June 2012 at the age of 9. The patient experienced a significant increase in motor tics concurrent with elevated anti-streptolysin O (ASO) antibody levels (472 IU/mL; positive threshold >200 IU/mL). Historical records from the children’s neuropsychiatric public department of Azienda Sanitaria Locale Cuneo 1 (ASL CN1) indicated the onset of tic disorders at age 7. The patient also exhibited learning disabilities, borderline intellectual functioning, and phobic anxiety disorder. Routine laboratory tests were within normal ranges, and there was no documented history of previous GAS infection. Parental consent was obtained for the child’s participation in a clinical and laboratory survey. The study involved physical examinations, interviews, questionnaires, and periodic blood draws to measure ASO, anti-streptococcal deoxyribonuclease B (DNase B), and anti-staphylolysin antibody (ASTA) titers, as well as white blood cell (WBC) counts and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Duplicate throat and nasal swabs were collected for microbiological analysis, which were processed by two different laboratories: Centro Diagnostico Cernaia (Cuneo, Italy) and the Microbiology Department of ASL CN1 (Mondovì, Cuneo, Italy). Additionally, an analysis for autoimmunity against brain antigens was conducted three times during the final 18 months of the study by Wieslab AB Medical Laboratory (Malmo, Sweden), measuring antibody titers against dopamine D1 and D2 receptors, lysoganglioside-GM1, and beta-tubulin, as well as antibodies that activate calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase type II (CaM kinase II).
test_results: During her first visit in June 2012, the patient’s tic severity score was 25, indicating the presence of motor tics alone, and her ASO titer was elevated (472 IU/mL; positive = >200 IU/mL). Her ASO titers remained high (between 350 and 400 IU/mL) for almost 3 years. Additionally, her anti-DNase B titers were always in the upper range (between 360 and 340 IU/mL; positive = >200 IU/mL). Four autoimmunity tests out of a panel of five were significantly positive based on the reference values of the test panel manufacturer.

case_report: The patient is a 68-year-old right-handed woman who first observed tremors in both hands during activities at age 30. Her father also experienced similar hand tremors. She has been on sertraline for the past decade for depression. One year ago, she developed tremors in both hands while at rest and noticed tremors affecting her handwriting. Bupropion was administered five months before her office visit but was discontinued after four months due to increased tremor amplitude in her hands and trunk. She also tried a combination of sertraline and an experimental selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, LY2216684, for two weeks before her visit. During the examination while on sertraline, she exhibited a bilateral 1+ amplitude thumb flexion/extension tremor at rest with a frequency of 7 Hz. Additionally, there was a no-latency 1+ amplitude postural tremor in both upper extremities, involving thumb flexion/extension and metacarpophalangeal joint abduction/adduction. Mild bradykinesia was noted bilaterally in the upper extremities during finger taps, hand grips, hand pronation/supination, as well as in the lower extremities during foot taps and heel taps. There was a decreased right arm swing, but no worsening of the rest tremor during walking. Significant instability was observed during tandem stance.
test_results: 123I-FP-CIT SPECT scan was physiologic. EMG evaluation of the left flexor and extensor pollicis brevis muscles revealed a 7 Hz synchronous postural tremor and a 7 Hz synchronous rest tremor.

case_report: A 46-year-old male presented to the emergency department with a two-week history of cough, fever, generalized muscle aches, sore throat, progressively worsening shortness of breath, and night sweats. He had been treated with amoxicillin-clavulanate for seven days for pneumonia as prescribed by his primary care physician. On the eighth day, he developed tremors without fever, which made walking difficult. He reported no nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, chest pain, or abdominal pain. He had no significant medical history, was not on any other medications, and did not consume alcohol. He mentioned that some co-workers had flu-like symptoms before he went into self-quarantine, but he did not know if they had been tested for COVID-19. In the emergency department, his vital signs were: blood pressure 130/87 mmHg, temperature 36.6°C (97.9°F), pulse rate 108 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Respiratory examination revealed clear and equal breath sounds bilaterally. Neurologic examination showed that he was mentally alert and oriented to person, date, and place, with no speech difficulties or neglect. Cranial nerve examination was notable for saccadic intrusions during smooth pursuit. A generalized tremor was observed while lying down, which worsened with movement, and there was a postural tremor in all extremities. Heel-to-shin testing was tremulous but not dystaxic, and there was a bilateral intention tremor. Motor examination showed normal muscle tone and full strength (5/5) in all muscle groups of the upper and lower extremities. He exhibited a wide-based, unsteady gait but no dysmetria, pronator drift, or truncal ataxia. Sensation to light touch was intact. No other abnormalities were found on physical examination. Neurology was consulted due to the persistent tremors. Computed tomography (CT) of the head and CT angiogram showed no significant findings. Toxicology screening was negative, and levels of thyroid-stimulating hormone, thiamine, and folate were normal. Chest radiograph indicated clear lungs with no focal consolidation.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) done during his hospital stay showed hyperintense foci in the bifrontal subcortical and deep white matter on scattered T2-weighted, fluid-attenuated inversion recovery.

case_report: A 5-year-old girl presented with a congenital absence of most scalp hair and hair loss. At birth, she had a small amount of black scalp hair in patches. Between 6 and 12 months of age, she lost most of her hair with no subsequent regrowth. A physical examination revealed one terminal hair on the vertex scalp, but otherwise, there was a complete absence of scalp hair. Numerous skin-colored to white 1-2 mm papules were observed on the scalp. The eyebrows and eyelashes were sparse with minimal hair growth. The patient had a history of global developmental delay without a known specific causative genetic mutation.
test_results: Genetic testing confirmed a biallelic mutation in the HR gene with likely pathogenic variants, including c.3515G>A and p.W1172X.

case_report: An eleven-year-old male, born to parents who are related by blood, exhibited complete hair loss on the scalp starting at six months old. Initially, he had sparse hair on the scalp at birth, which gradually disappeared. He also had sparse hair on his eyebrows and eyelashes. For the past three years, he reported multiple raised lesions on his face and upper trunk. There was no history of delayed developmental milestones, reduced sweating, bone pain, hearing loss, seizures, or similar conditions in the family. Physical examination revealed hair loss on the scalp, underarms, and pubic area, with sparse hair on the eyebrows and eyelashes. Multiple discrete, skin-colored, firm papulo-nodular lesions, ranging from 0.5 to 1.0 cm in size, were observed on the face, neck, upper limbs, and trunk. His physical growth was appropriate for his age, and his teeth, nails, and mucous membranes appeared normal. There were no bony abnormalities or systemic issues. Blood tests showed normal counts and liver and renal profiles, except for elevated alkaline phosphatase at 1343.9 U/l (normal range: 0-258 U/l). Vitamin D3 levels (1,25 dihydroxy cholecalciferol) were 30.2 ng/ml (normal: 30-74 ng/ml), and parathormone levels were 16 pg/ml (normal: 12-72 pg/ml), as measured by radioimmunoassay. Wrist joint radiographs were normal.
test_results: Biopsy from a papule over the trunk revealed multiple mid-dermal keratin cysts. Biopsy from the scalp showed a few vellus follicles in the mid-dermis with sparse peri-follicular lymphocytic infiltrate and number of follicles were reduced. There were no terminal hairs and sebaceous glands.

case_report: A 72-year-old man presented with a one-week history of persistent fever, fatigue, and lower back pain in December 2019. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 162 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin level of 8.5 g/dL, and platelet count of 220 × 10^9/L. The differential count revealed 66% segmented cells, 15% stab cells, 5% metamyelocytes, 7% myelocytes, 4% promyelocytes, 1% blasts, and 2% monocytes. No dysgranulopoiesis was observed. Elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels were noted, at 936 IU/L and 5.3 mg/dL, respectively. Physical examination indicated significant splenomegaly, with the spleen palpable 5 cm below the costal margin. Bone marrow examination showed a markedly hypercellular marrow with increased granulopoiesis and 0.5% blasts, without dysplastic features. Cytogenetic analysis showed a normal karyotype. Fluorescence in situ hybridization for BCR/ABL, PDGFRA, PDGFRB, and FGFR1 was negative. Mutation screening for JAK2, CALR, and MPL was also negative. Clinical sequencing was performed to identify driver mutations. The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board (No. 2020-1-0422) in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, and written informed consent was obtained from the patient.
test_results: Mutations in CSF3R (T618I), ASXL1, TET2, and SRSF2 identified.

case_report: A 6-year-old girl presented with a 10-month history of recurring skin plaques and abscesses. Initially, the abscesses were thought to be furuncles and improved after rupturing. These skin issues reappeared every 1–2 months and resolved within a week. Four weeks ago, plaques and abscesses reappeared on her limbs. The abscesses ruptured and disappeared three weeks ago, but she began experiencing joint pain in her limbs two weeks ago. Physical examination revealed multiple dull red plaques on the lower limbs and an enlarged spleen extending 3 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 105.32 × 10^9/L, with neutrophils at 87.3%, lymphocytes at 9.1%, monocytes at 0.9%, eosinophils at 0.3%, and basophils at 2.4%. Red blood cell count was 3.01 × 10^12/L, hemoglobin was 99 g/L, and platelet count was 190 × 10^9/L. A peripheral smear indicated a predominance of mature neutrophils with rare blasts (1%).
test_results: Bone marrow studies revealed hypercellular marrow with granulocytic hyperplasia, negativity for BCR/ABL and a + 8 karyotype. Genomic analysis revealed a CSF3R T618I somatic mutation and a CBL c.1096-1_1097delGGA frameshift somatic mutation. Skin biopsy revealed a few blasts infiltrated in the dermis without dermal edema. The blasts expressed CD33, CD68, CD117, Ki67 (5%+), and MPO but not CD2, CD3, CD30, CD56, or TdT.
diagnosis: Chronic Neutrophilic Leukemia  with Leukemia Cutis

case_report: A 41-year-old male has experienced erythrocytosis and elevated hematocrit levels for the past 5 years. Initial laboratory tests reveal high hemoglobin (17.8 g/dL) and hematocrit (54%), with normal white blood cell count (6.7 × 10^9/L) and platelet count (203 × 10^9/L). Erythropoietin levels are below the local laboratory reference range (3.9 mU/mL [4.3–29]). A JAK2 mutation with a 2.8% variant allele frequency is identified in peripheral blood granulocytes. Data on exon 12 and/or additional exon 14 mutations are not available.
test_results: A BM biopsy features cellularity within age-related limits, preserved maturation of erythroid and myeloid lineages, and only a minor increase in megakaryocytes. The latter are sparse in distribution, with predominant mature-type morphology and only rare, scattered large forms.

case_report: A 62-year-old male with a history of being overweight, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia presented with a hemoglobin level of 20.4 g/dL and a hematocrit of 0.59. The white cell and platelet counts were within normal ranges, and there was a mild increase in eosinophils. Physical examination showed no signs of PV, a normal spleen size, and normal oxygen saturation levels. Laboratory tests indicated no endogenous erythrocyte colony formation, no abnormal hemoglobin, and no family history of hematological abnormalities. The patient was managed with intermittent venesection for nine years. Genetic testing showed no evidence of JAK2 p.V617F mutations or JAK2 exon 12 mutations. At 149 months after initial presentation, the patient developed thrombocytopenia with a platelet count of 75 × 10^9/L and an increased eosinophil count of 1.9 × 10^9/L, along with a low serum erythropoietin (EPO) level of 0.6 IU/L (normal range 2.6–18.5 IU/L). At 154 months after initial presentation, the patient experienced a temporoparietal stroke.
test_results: Bone marrow biopsy demonstrated 4% myeloblasts. Subsequent bone marrow investigations showed progressively increasing myeloblast cell numbers by both morphological and immunophenotypic evaluation with reduced dysplastic megakaryocytes, dyserythropoiesis with basophilic stippling, and binuclear red cell forms.
diagnosis: Myelodysplastic Syndrome  progressing to Acute Myeloid Leukemia
Orpha_name: Acute myeloid leukaemia with myelodysplasia-related features

case_report: A 57-year-old female patient was identified with a condition in 2015. At that time, Interphase-FISH analyses did not show abnormalities in PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, ATM, ETV6, or TP53 in 200 analyzed interphase nuclei. Three months earlier, a JAK2 V617F-mutation had been found, and the presence of BCR::ABL1 fusion transcripts was not detected in peripheral blood cells. Starting in 2015, the patient was treated with cytoreductive and anti-thrombotic agents, specifically hydroxyurea and acetylsalicylic acid. Seven years later, at the age of 64, the patient exhibited symptoms including fatigue, progressive shortness of breath, chest pain, and rapid heart rate. Blood tests revealed severe anemia with hemoglobin levels of 4.2 g/dL and low platelet count (50/nL), but a normal white blood cell count (5.1/nL) without circulating immature cells.
test_results: Cytomorphology after bone marrow biopsy revealed a hypercellular bone marrow with a blast infiltration of 60–70% and minimal differentiation. CBA showed a complex karyotype with a derivate chromosome 11, which was interpreted as a translocation t(1;11)(q21;p15), as well as several other chromosomal rearrangements.
diagnosis: Acute Myeloid Leukemia with myelodysplasia-related changes
Orpha_name: Acute myeloid leukaemia with myelodysplasia-related features

case_report: A 49-year-old Japanese man with no history of regular health check-ups or hospital visits presented with a 2-month history of general fatigue and constipation. He experienced discomfort in the left side of his abdomen while sleeping 16 days prior, which gradually developed into pain. Abdominal CT at another hospital showed adipose tissue turbidity around the left adrenal gland, but the cause of the pain was not identified, and the pain resolved spontaneously after a few days. On the day of admission to our hospital, he felt similar discomfort in the right side of his back after lunch, which worsened into intense pain rated as 9 to 10 on a 10-point scale. Analgesics were ineffective, leading to his referral and admission for further examination. His systolic blood pressure had decreased by approximately 20 mmHg over the past 2 months, ranging from 80 to 90 mmHg for the past 2 weeks. He had a smoking history with a Brinkman index of 580 and consumed more than 50 g/day of alcohol. His family history included colorectal cancer in his father. On admission, he was alert with a body temperature of 38.5°C, heart rate of 101 beats/min, blood pressure of 148/84 mmHg, respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. Physical examination revealed pallor of the eyelid conjunctiva, a soft and flat abdomen, and tenderness throughout the whole abdomen, strongest in the epigastrium, with no signs of peritoneal irritation. His back pain was spontaneous with no significant findings on physical examination. Blood tests showed leukopenia, anemia, and thrombocytosis, with mild abnormalities in the coagulation system but normal blood glucose and electrolyte levels. Thyroid-stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, growth hormone, luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, soluble interleukin 2 receptor, somatomedin C, and prolactin were within the reference range. The antinuclear antibody level was normal, and the anticardiolipin antibody level was 2 U/mL. On the third day of admission, the adrenocorticotropic hormone level was 0.30 pmol/L, and the cortisol level was 775 nmol/L. An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm, and a chest radiograph revealed no abnormalities. Thoracoabdominal CT with contrast enhancement showed diffusely enlarged bilateral adrenal glands with increased CT value in the surrounding adipose tissue. There were no high-attenuation areas suggesting hemorrhage within the adrenal glands, but low-attenuation areas suggesting adrenal infarction were observed. CT showed no splenomegaly or other causes of abdominal tenderness besides the enlarged adrenal glands. Considering the patient's history of hypotension and fatigue, hydrocortisone at 200 mg daily was administered. Pain was controlled with fentanyl, and aspirin was started for platelet hyperplasia. Three days after admission, the platelet count normalized to 289 × 10^9/L, and aspirin was stopped. Abdominal tenderness resolved in 4 days. Abdominal MRI with contrast enhancement on the third day of hospitalization showed that the adrenal glands were enlarged but smaller than on admission. Post-contrast T1-weighted images revealed an area of partial low density suggesting ischemia in the left adrenal gland, with most blood flow preserved. The adrenocorticotropic hormone and cortisol levels before hydrocortisone administration on admission could not be measured as the patient visited outside regular hours. A rapid adrenocorticotropic hormone test showed a low cortisol response of 140 nmol/L before loading and 286 nmol/L after 60 minutes. A peripheral blood panel on admission showed an erythroblast level of 24.5%, megakaryocytes, promyelocytes, and myelocytes.
test_results: Histopathological examination of the bone marrow revealed an atypical myeloblast level of 22.4% with positive myeloperoxidase staining. Background cells exhibited dysplastic features such as megakaryocytes with multiple nuclei, multinucleated erythroblasts, and multinucleated megakaryocytes. Pathological examination of the bone marrow revealed the notable presence of immature cells among granulocytes, a relative reduction in erythroblasts, and an increase in megakaryocytes. A pathological increase in iron granulocytes was not observed, and findings suggestive of erythroleukemia were absent. Flow cytometry showed 5.9% blasts, negativity for CD56, and positivity for myeloperoxidase and CD177. WT1mRNA was positive.
diagnosis: Acute Myeloid Leukemia with Myelodysplasia-related Changes
Orpha_name: Acute myeloid leukaemia with myelodysplasia-related features

case_report: In November 2012, a 65-year-old male was admitted to the First Affiliated Hospital of Chongqing Medical University (Chongqing, China) with a one-month history of dizziness and a two-week history of melena. Physical examination revealed pallor and rashes, including erythematous and maculopapular skin lesions on the legs and hands. The patient declined a skin biopsy. Maculopapular rashes appeared around the injection site shortly after intravenous injection. Blood tests showed a hemoglobin level of 6.4 g/dl, hematocrit of 19.10%, platelet count of 58×10^9/l, and total leukocyte count of 4.55×10^9/l, with 8% blast cells and 6% mature basophils. The fecal occult blood test was positive, ferritin level was 1,138 ng/ml, and levels of vitamin B12 and folic acid were within normal ranges. Serum autoantibodies, including anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), myeloperoxidase (MPO)-ANCA, and proteinase 3-ANCA, were negative. Gastroscopy revealed a gastric antral ulcer (stage A1) according to Sakita’s endoscopic staging system, and endoscopy biopsy indicated mild mucosal inflammation without specific features.
test_results: The results of a bone marrow aspirate (stain, Wright-Giemsa) were as follows: Blast cells, 13%; atypical immature basophils, 14%; mature basophils, 8%; normal mature neutrophils, 11%; and erythroid cells, 13%. The blast cells contained basophilic granules, and the vacuoles in the cytoplasm and nuclei were oval and bilobed and contained nucleoli. The blast cells were positive for peroxidase and periodic acid-Schiff staining (PAS) and negative for α-naphthyl acetate esterase. The blast cells exhibited metachromasia as a result of staining with toluidine blue. Six days later, the bone marrow aspirate with Wright-Giemsa stain was conducted again, and showed 13% blast cells, 16% atypical immature basophils and 8% mature basophils, with 9% normal mature neutrophils. Cytogenetic studies using GTG banding revealed an abnormal karyotype, 44 XY,add()(p26),-5,-11,add()(q32),+mar1, +mar2,inc[18]/46,XY[2]. Flow cytometric analysis of the blast cells was positive for cluster of differentiation (CD)11b, CD13, CD22, CD25, CD33 and CD123.

case_report: An 81-year-old male was admitted in October 2015 due to bilateral pitting edema in his legs, persisting for about a month. He had a history of prostate cancer surgery twelve years prior and Vater papilla cancer surgery five years prior, with no further treatments post-surgery. Physical examination revealed bilateral pitting edema in the legs, with no abnormalities detected in the thorax and abdomen. In November 2015, a renal biopsy indicated minimal change nephrotic syndrome (MCNS). He began immunosuppressive treatment with cyclosporine (CsA) and prednisolone (PSL), achieving complete remission for MCNS within a month, leading to the cessation of CsA and gradual tapering of PSL. During this treatment, he experienced occasional fevers exceeding 38°C and general malaise, which laboratory tests attributed to normocytic anemia. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell (WBC) count of 4.2 × 10^9/L with no abnormal cells, hemoglobin (Hb) level of 9.2 g/dL, and platelet (Plt) count of 53.6 × 10^10/L. A bone marrow smear revealed 6.4% blasts and significant dysplasia in neutrophils and erythroid precursor cells. Flow cytometric analysis indicated that the blasts were positive for CD13, CD33, CD34, CD56, and HLA-DR. Chromosomal analysis by G banding identified an additional add(7)(q22) in 2 out of 20 metaphase cells. At that time, basophils constituted 2.0% of all nucleated cells in the bone marrow. He received one pack of red blood cell (RBC) transfusion as palliative therapy and reported feeling better during oral PSL therapy.
test_results: The bone marrow smear showed 30.4% myeloblasts and 16.8% mature basophils. Flow cytometric analysis showed that the myeloblasts were positive for CD13, CD33, CD34, CD56, CD117, and HLA-DR. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis showed neither fusion signals of the BCR and ABL genes nor those of the DEK and NUP214 genes. Chromosomal analysis by G banding showed monosomy 7 in 14 out of 20 metaphase cells and additional add(1)(q21) in 4 out of 20 metaphase cells analyzed. Monosomy 7 was confirmed by FISH analysis. The loss of chromosome 7 was found in myeloblasts and basophils of the bone marrow.
diagnosis: Acute Myeloid Leukemia with Basophilic Differentiation

case_report: A 71-year-old male was referred to hematology by his primary care provider due to a complete blood count (CBC) showing a platelet count of 64,000/µL, a white blood cell (WBC) count of 48,700/µL, and an absolute monocyte count of 36,000/µL. Previous laboratory investigations 3 months prior indicated a CBC within normal limits. The patient reported a weight loss of 25 pounds over the past 2 months. He denied experiencing fevers, chills, night sweats, swollen glands, or changes in appetite. An abdominal computed tomography (CT) revealed a significantly enlarged spleen measuring 19 cm. The patient’s coagulation profile, liver and renal function tests, viral testing for hepatitis and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and autoimmune profile were all unremarkable.
test_results: The bone marrow biopsy from the right iliac crest showed extensive involvement by atypical lymphocytes with round nuclear contours, prominent nucleoli, and moderate to abundant cytoplasm. Immunohistochemical stain for PAX5 demonstrated that the atypical lymphocytes accounted for 60% of the total cellularity. Additional immunohistochemical stains demonstrated that the atypical lymphocytes were positive for BCL2 and negative for BCL6, LMO2, and cyclin D1. The proliferation index by Ki67 was 5-10%. The peripheral blood for flow cytometry showed a prominent monoclonal B-cell population with a high-side light scatter. The B cells were positive for CD19, CD20, CD22, human leukocyte antigen-DR (HLA-DR), and bright kappa light chains. They were negative for CD10, CD5, CD23, CD25, CD11C, CD103, and CD123. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) showed both the loss of 17p13.1 (p53) and 13q14.

case_report: A 75-year-old woman presented with sudden onset of painless right ptosis, double vision, and vertigo. Physical examination showed inferomedial displacement of the globe and an S-shaped ptosis. CT imaging identified an enlarged right lacrimal gland with central hypodensity areas. Her medical history included Sjogren's syndrome, an abdominal aortic aneurysm, and a surgically treated colonic adenocarcinoma from two years prior. A biopsy of the lacrimal gland through a superior lid crease approach revealed necrotic and inflamed tissue with granulomatous inflammation, but further biopsy was declined by the patient. She later experienced fever, malaise, and cough. Chest CT showed a necrotic mass in the left upper lobe involving hilar vessels and a suspicious lesion in the right lung, along with hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Abdominal CT revealed multiple hepatic lesions. Bronchial biopsy histopathology showed florid necrotizing inflammation with palisading granulomas. Blood tests indicated elevated CRP levels (150 mg/l) and anemia (Hb-10 g/dl), with negative ANCA and normal CEA levels (2 μg/L). The patient was treated with Prednisolone 25 mg/day and Cyclophosphamide 100 mg/day. She was readmitted one month later with worsening systemic condition. Follow-up CT of the orbits showed normal findings and complete resolution of the lacrimal gland enlargement. However, chest CT revealed new left lower lobe parenchymal infiltrates and resolution of liver lesions compared to the previous study.
test_results: The histopathology showed a polymorphous atypical lymphoid infiltrate of CD20 positive B cells with positive labelling for EBV admixed with CD3 positive T cells. The lesion displayed focal necrosis and focal angiocentricity.

case_report: A 30-year-old female presented with a 2-month history of cough, hemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss, fever, and chest pain. She had no history of lung disease, smoking, or medication use. Previous investigations at another center ruled out tuberculosis 3 weeks prior. Physical examination revealed no palpable peripheral lymph nodes, and diminished breath sounds were noted over the right lung. Laboratory tests showed normal hemogram and biochemical parameters, including kidney and liver functions. No symptoms of immunodeficiency were observed, and serum immunoglobulin levels were normal. Chest X-ray indicated a right-sided pleural effusion, leading to a diagnostic thoracentesis and pleural biopsy. The pleural effusion was exudative, but cytological analysis of the pleural fluid was inconclusive. The pleural biopsy indicated chronic pleuritis. Computed tomography (CT) imaging showed a 4.5 × 5 cm irregular, thick-walled, pleural-based cavitary mass lesion in the right upper lung fields, near the hilar bronchoalveolar structures, with no mediastinal or hilar lymph node enlargement. F-18 fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (PET) detected a hypermetabolic pleural-based cavity mass (SUVmax: 5.27). The thoracic surgery department performed an upper lobe wedge resection with right mini-thoracotomy, and samples of the lesion and nearby lymph nodes were examined by the pathology department.
test_results: The immunohistochemical study showed granulomatous cells stained positive by anti-CD20, anti-CD30, anti-CD3 and negative with anti-CD15. In situ hybridization (ISH) showed numerous Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-encoded small nuclear RNA (EBER) positive cells.

case_report: A 54-year-old male presented with a non-tender swelling on the left side of the scrotum. Scrotal ultrasound revealed a hypoechoic, hypervascular mass with microcalcifications in the left intratesticular region, measuring 3.2 × 2.4 × 3.2 cm. The patient underwent a left radical inguinal orchiectomy. Gross examination of the testicular mass showed a tan-red, hemorrhagic, well-circumscribed circular mass measuring 5.0 × 4.0 × 3.4 cm, with focal areas of tan-white friable necrosis. The mass did not involve the epididymis (2 × 1.2 × 3 cm) and was adjacent to the tunica albuginea. The remaining testis parenchyma was tan-yellow and unremarkable. Histological examination revealed diffuse, solid sheets of densely packed neoplastic cells infiltrating the testicular parenchyma, hilar soft tissue, epididymis, and spermatic cord, sparing the seminiferous tubules. The tumor consisted of medium-sized neoplastic cells with blastoid morphology, scant agranular cytoplasm, irregular nuclei with fine to vesicular chromatin, and small nucleoli. There was increased mitotic activity with atypical mitotic figures, areas of necrosis, and abundant apoptotic debris. An initial immunohistochemistry (IHC) panel including CD3, CD20, AE1/AE3, and SALL4 was performed, and the neoplastic cells were negative for all four markers. A second IHC panel including CKIT, CD45, CD68, S100, Ki-67, and CD138 was performed. The neoplastic cells were weakly positive for CD45 and positive for CD68 with a granular dot-like pattern. Ki-67 was expressed in 80% of cells. CKIT, S100, and CD138 were negative. The patient's medical history included previous chemotherapy and a bone marrow transplant less than three months prior, following an initial presentation of scalp nodules.
test_results: The neoplastic cells were diffusely positive for CD4 and CD56, and CD123 was positive in only rare cells.

case_report: In May 2017, a 35-year-old Asian man presented with an infiltrative erythematous plaque and a nodule on his left upper shoulder. He had no fever, chills, or any other symptoms. Initially, he was treated with two courses of azithromycin and clarithromycin (500 mg orally on day 1 followed by 250 mg orally daily on days 2–5 for both antibiotics) to address a possible infection. Over the next 6 months, there was no response to the treatment, and a palpable cervical mass appeared that persisted despite antimicrobial therapy. Two months later, he was referred to an oncologist for further evaluation. His past medical and family history were insignificant. Physical examination revealed cervical and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. A cervical lymph node biopsy showed diffuse malignant lymphoma, and immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining identified the tumor subtype as follicular center cell lymphoma. On IHC, malignant cells were positive for CD10, CD20, BCL2, TdT, LCA, and ki67, and negative for CD3, CD4, CD5, CD16, CD30, CD56, CD79a, BCL6, and PAX-5. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy showed no infiltrative lesion or malignancy.
