Thoracic and abdominopelvic computed tomography (CT) scans revealed enlargement in the left side of the neck and supraclavicular lymph nodes (up to 24 mm in diameter), nasopharyngeal soft tissue thickening, and a hypodense lesion in the right liver lobe.
test_results: Skin biopsy showed that medium-sized monomorphic blast-like cells focally infiltrated the dermis without any significant signs of mitotic activity or necrosis. IHC staining of the lesion revealed diffuse positive immunostaining of atypical cells with CD43 and CD4. The tumor also showed scattered ki67 staining (5–10%) and focal dot-like cytoplasmic forms in CD68 immunostaining with weakly positive CD33, CD56, CD123, and LCA. These CD markers were absent: CD20, CD3, CD30, CD5, CD34, PAX5, CD79a, MPO, Pan CK, Melan A, TdT, C-kit, and CD138. Negative LCA and B-cell markers including PAX5, CD20, and CD79a in the IHC study panel made any kind of B-cell lymphoma unlikely.

case_report: A 38-year-old male presented with erythematous-violaceous plaques and nodules accompanied by itching, located on the trunk, upper limbs, and forehead. The patient reported no weight loss, fever, or lymph node enlargement and had no significant past medical history. A biopsy was conducted with considerations including drug reaction, sarcoidosis, urticarial vasculitis, and mycosis fungoides.
test_results: Histopathological examination disclosed a dense, superficial and deep dermal infiltrate, with diffuse and periadnexal involvement. The infiltrate was characterized by cells with blast morphology, displaying irregular nuclei, granular chromatin, one or more nucleoli, and scarce agranular cytoplasm. There were frequent mitoses (more than five mitoses per 1 mm2), including atypical forms. Necrosis and angioinvasion were not observed. The epidermis was preserved and separated from the neoplasm by a Grenz zone. Immunohistochemistry showed positivity for CD45, CD4, CD43, CD56, TDT, CD123, a high cell proliferation index (Ki-67 estimated at 50%) and negativity for the other tested markers (CD3, CD20, CD30, CD34, CD138, and myeloperoxidase).

case_report: A 30-year-old Caucasian female with a history of arthritis presented with a two-month history of a painless, non-healing mass on the left breast. The patient reported no fevers, chills, night sweats, weight loss, nipple discharge, or family history of cancer. Physical examination revealed an erythematous, thickened, well-circumscribed lesion on the lateral aspect of the left breast, measuring approximately 4 x 4 cm, with no active drainage. There was no palpable hepatosplenomegaly, and no supraclavicular, axillary, or inguinal lymphadenopathy was detected. Informed consent was obtained from the patient.
test_results: Excisional biopsy of the left breast mass was done and the pathological exam, including microscopic evaluation, and flow cytometry, showed medium-sized mononuclear cells with vesicular nuclei. There were brisk mitotic activity and small zones of necrosis. The mononuclear infiltrate showed diffuse positivity for CD45, CD3, and CD56. TIA-1 was strongly positive within tumor cells, indicative of a cytotoxic phenotype. EBV in situ hybridization was also strongly positive within the tumor cells.

case_report: A 73-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with sudden severe abdominal pain and fever. Physical examination revealed a high fever (39℃), chills, abdominal tenderness, and muscular defense. The patient did not exhibit diarrhea, body-weight loss, history of malnutrition, or food intolerance. No palpable cervical lymph nodes were detected. Laboratory tests showed mild leukocytosis (white blood cell count of 13,050/mm2) and azotemia (serum blood urea nitrogen/creatinine of 18/1.2 mg/dL). Peripheral blood morphology indicated normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin of 9.9 g/dL) with anisopoikilocytosis, and serum electrophoresis patterns were nonspecific. Chest radiography showed no definite free air under the diaphragm. Abdominal computed tomography revealed an 8.5 cm length of wall thickening in the distal small bowel, with central necrosis and pseudoaneurysmal dilatation. Multiple homogeneous enhancing lymphadenopathies were observed in the pelvic area on the mesentery near the mass. Laparoscopic exploration was planned. Laparoscopic findings indicated localized peritonitis due to perforation of the terminal ileum, with the lesion adherent to the bladder and sigmoid colon. A segmental resection of the perforated ileum and side-to-side anastomosis were performed through a minilaparotomy after meticulous dissection. The resected ileum showed diffuse thickening of the central wall with a relatively well-defined encircling mural mass measuring 10.0 cm in length, gray-white to tan in color, with indications of hemorrhage and necrosis.
test_results: Immunohistochemical staining was positive for CD5, CD3, CD56, CD8, and Ki-67, and negative for CD20, CD15, and the Epstein-Barr virus. The T-cell nature of the tumor was reflected in its reactivity for CD3 and CD8, and its negativity for the B-cell marker CD20. The patient expressed the HLA-DQ6 and HLA-DQ9 alleles.

case_report: A 25-year-old female with 5 months of amenorrhea presented with multiple painful nodules over a duration of 3 months on the face, trunk, both arms, and left leg, accompanied by a low-grade fever for the past 2 days. The nodules were multiple, discrete, and skin-colored, ranging from soft to firm on the face and scalp, with the largest measuring 7cm × 6cm × 3cm. Some nodules exhibited central necrosis. Similar skin-colored nodules were observed on the back and both arms, varying in size from 1cm to 3cm in diameter. No lesions were found on the oral and genital mucosa. Sensations were intact, and there was no nerve enlargement.
test_results: Cerebrospinal fluid examination revealed malignant cells. Computed tomography scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed multiple enlarged lymph nodes and multiple lytic lesions in the vertebrae.
diagnosis: Primary Cutaneous Peripheral T-cell Lymphoma-Not Otherwise Specified
Orpha_name: Primary cutaneous peripheral T-cell lymphoma not otherwise specified

case_report: A 78-year-old female with no significant past medical history presented with a two-week history of a rapidly enlarging nodule on her right shoulder. The nodule occasionally bled when caught on clothing but was otherwise asymptomatic. The patient applied Polysporin topically without any signs of healing or reduction in size. No other lesions were noted. She reported feeling generally unwell but denied experiencing weight loss, night sweats, fevers, or loss of appetite. Her family history did not include any malignancies. Physical examination revealed a solitary 5 cm, ill-defined, red-violaceous, immobile, irregular nodule on the right posterior shoulder. The lesion was not indurated, fluctuant, or tender to palpation, and there was a small area of excoriation with crusting.
test_results: Biopsy revealed a dense pan-dermal infiltrate of medium- to large-sized atypical lymphocytes with irregular nuclei and perinuclear halos (>25% large cells). The lymphocytes exhibited epidermotropism, blurring the dermal-epidermal junction and epidermis. The infiltrate formed large groups within the epidermis and extensively infiltrated the subcutaneous adipose tissue. Scattered mitotic figures were also identified. Immunohistochemical staining showed CD4-positive T-cell population that coexpressed CD5, CD45, and CD7. EBV, CD30, and CD56 were negative.
diagnosis: Primary Cutaneous Peripheral T-Cell Lymphoma, NOS
Orpha_name: Primary cutaneous peripheral T-cell lymphoma not otherwise specified

case_report: In February 2018, a 3-year-old Omani male, previously healthy, sought medical advice due to unstable gait and recurrent upper respiratory infections. A novel homozygous mutation in the ATM gene was identified. Family history was unremarkable, and parents were first-degree relatives. Other siblings were healthy, except for his younger sister who was diagnosed with the same condition in 2022. He began monthly and lifelong intravenous immunoglobulin treatment at a prophylactic dose of 0.4 milligrams per kilogram. In May 2018, he presented with a 1-week history of fever and cough. Upon presentation, he was febrile with an average temperature of 38.7 ℃, heart rate of 110 beats per minute, and blood pressure within normal limits for his age and sex. Physical examination revealed enlarged submandibular, cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes, with the largest being 3 × 3 cm in the right axilla, and no detectable hepatosplenomegaly. Neurological examination showed nystagmus and an unbalanced gait. Romberg sign was negative, and deep reflexes were normal. An abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable for any intraabdominal lesions or organomegaly. Blood tests showed severe neutropenia (neutrophil count 0.2 × 10^9/L) with total white blood cells of 3.9 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin of 9 g/L, and platelet count of 214 × 10^9/L. Lactate dehydrogenase was 275 U/L, and Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) was undetectable by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Other blood tests, including liver function and renal function tests, were within normal ranges for his age. The patient received general supportive care with intravenous hydration, antipyretics (paracetamol 15 milligrams per kilogram intravenously), and intravenous ceftriaxone at a dose of 50 milligrams per kilogram twice a day for 5 days.
test_results: Microscopic analysis demonstrated infiltration with atypical lymphoid cells having small, medium to large nuclei and clear cytoplasm localized around high endothelial venules. Immunohistochemical stains showed positivity of the atypical lymphoid cells for CD3, CD4, CD10, BCL6, and PD1. The diagnosis was confirmed by molecular studies, which revealed detection of clonal T cell receptor gamma chain gene rearrangement as well as clonal B cell IgH/Kappa chain gene rearrangement.

case_report: A 71-year-old Japanese man presented with severe thrombocytopenia. His medical history included postoperative lung and bladder cancer, coronary stenting for myocardial infarction, pacemaker implantation for sick sinus syndrome, and Helicobacter pylori eradication. A year prior, a right retroperitoneal mass was incidentally detected on a whole-body CT during a follow-up visit after lung cancer surgery. CT-guided biopsy of the mass indicated reactive lymphoid hyperplasia. At presentation, the only clinical finding was petechial hemorrhage in the lower leg. Complete blood counts showed anemia (10.7 g/dL; normal range, 14.0–17.5 g/dL) and severe thrombocytopenia (10 × 10^3/μL; normal range, 158–348 × 10^3/μL). Biochemical tests revealed mild hypoalbuminemia (2.7 g/dL; normal range, 4.1–5.1 g/dL) and elevated lactate dehydrogenase (275 IU/L; normal range, 124–222 IU/L). Serological tests showed elevated C-reactive protein (2.90 mg/dL; normal range, 0.00–0.30 mg/dL), ferritin (376.7 ng/mL; normal range, 21.8–274.6 ng/mL), and soluble interleukin-2 receptor (sIL2-R) (2900 IU/mL; normal range, 122–496 IU/mL). The patient had polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia and strongly positive antinuclear antibody, but no physical findings suggestive of collagen disease. Platelet-associated immunoglobulin G was elevated (1570 ng/10^7 cells; normal range, ≤ 46 ng/10^7 cells), and platelet binding-IgG was detected. A whole-body CT revealed small cervical, axillary, and para-aortic lymphadenopathy, but the right retroperitoneal mass had resolved. Due to severe thrombocytopenia, a lymph node biopsy was not performed. The patient declined a bone marrow examination and was treated with PSL (0.5 mg/kg daily), leading to a gradual recovery in platelet count. Thrombocytopenia recurred when the PSL dose was reduced to 7.5 mg daily, necessitating an increase to 10 mg daily. Approximately two and a half years after starting PSL treatment, cervical lymphadenopathy had slightly progressed without other clinical symptoms. Positron emission tomography-CT showed increased fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in systemic enlarged lymph nodes. Blood test results were similar to those at initial presentation, with improvements in thrombocytopenia, hypoalbuminemia, and liver function, but worsened creatinine and sIL2-R levels, and detection of Epstein–Barr virus (EBV)-DNA.
test_results: Histological examination of the biopsy specimen using hematoxylin and eosin (H & E) staining revealed the dense proliferation of medium-sized lymphoid cells between enlarged follicles. These medium-sized lymphoid cells were CD3+, CD4+, CD5+, CD7+, CD8−, CD10−, CD20−, programmed cell death (PD)-1+, and inducible T-cell co-stimulator+ (partially) on immunohistochemistry. These tumor cells proliferated around the residual non-neoplastic germinal centers where follicular dendritic cell meshwork (CD21+ area) was maintained, showing a “T-zone pattern”. Neither high endothelial venule, nor clear cells, were observed. Ki-67 labeling index was high and in situ hybridization for EBV-encoded small RNA revealed scattered positive cells.
diagnosis: Nodal Peripheral T-cell Lymphoma with T Follicular Helper Phenotype

case_report: A 70-year-old male was admitted to our hospital with a 1-month history of recurrent fever, night sweats, weight loss, and rash. These symptoms began after thyroid surgery, which was performed following the incidental discovery of thyroid masses on a CT scan. Postoperative pathology confirmed papillary thyroid microcarcinoma. Upon discharge, the patient experienced chills and fever, which recurred over the next month with body temperatures reaching up to 40°C. A chest CT scan indicated a minor infection in the right upper lobe. The patient was treated with antibiotics (cefoperazone tazobactam, levofloxacin, and metronidazole), but the treatment was ineffective. On the fifth day of antibiotic treatment, a papular rash developed. Antibiotics were discontinued, and loratadine was administered, temporarily controlling the fever and rash, which relapsed two days before admission. The patient's medical history included type 2 diabetes diagnosed two months prior, hepatitis B, and previous varicose vein surgery. Physical examination upon admission revealed generalized lymphadenopathy (supraclavicular, cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes), splenomegaly, and a skin rash. Laboratory results showed decreased counts of lymphocytes, red blood cells, hemoglobin, and platelets, with increased levels of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), β2-microglobulin, hs-CRP, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. HBsAg was positive, but hepatitis B virus DNA was less than 1.0 × 102 IU/mL. The Coombs direct antiglobulin test was positive, and the T-SPOT test was negative. Albumin and globulin levels were within the reference range, and liver and renal functions were normal. Serum viral loads for cytomegalovirus and Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) were negative. Chest CT scan showed infectious lesions in the right upper lobe and generalized lymphadenopathy (bilateral axillary and mediastinal lymph nodes). Neck color Doppler ultrasound revealed bilateral neck lymphadenopathy, with the largest node measuring 25 × 12 mm. Abdominal color Doppler ultrasound indicated splenomegaly with a thickness of 50 mm. Fine needle aspiration cytology of the left cervical lymph node suggested reactive and proliferative lesions. Blood cultures identified Staphylococcus epidermidis and Staphylococcus haemolyticus infections. Given the recent surgical history, the patient was treated with anti-infective agents (linezolid and biapenem). Symptoms were initially controlled after admission, but relapsed on the 13th day, accompanied by recurrent rash. Multiple subsequent blood cultures were negative. The patient continued to have a fever after discontinuation of antibiotics. Bone marrow aspiration cytology, biopsy, immunohistochemistry, and gene rearrangement results were all normal.
test_results: Hematoxylin and eosin staining showed effaced nodal architecture, marked proliferation of HEVs, and diffused infiltration of atypical lymphocytes with clear cytoplasm. Immunohistochemical staining indicated that the neoplastic infiltrate was positive for CD3, CD5, LCA (leukocyte common antigen), B-cell lymphoma/leukemia (BCL)-2, BCL-6, weakly positive for programmed cell death protein 1, and negative for CD10, CD30, CD15, paired box gene 5, CD20, CD79a, octamer-binding transcription factor 2, B-cell-specific octamer binding protein 1, multiple myeloma oncogene 1, anaplastic lymphoma kinase1, CD68, CD163, S-100, CD1a, cyclinD1, sex-determining region Y-related high-mobility-group box transcription factor 11, immunoglobulin D, cellular myelocytomatosis oncogene, and protein 53. Both Ki-67 index and minichromosome maintenance complex component 2 index were approximately 40%. Irregular hyperplasia of FDC highlighted by immunostaining of FDC markers, including CD21, CD23, and CD35, was also discovered in immunohistochemical staining. Detection of EBV by chromogenic in situ hybridization suggested positive expression by a few background cells. T-cell receptor (TCR) gene rearrangements were detected positive.

case_report: A 63-year-old white woman with a history of splenectomy presented to an outside hospital with 2 weeks of right-sided neck swelling. A computed tomography scan of her neck revealed asymmetric soft tissue fullness posteriorly in her tongue on the right side, which suggested a possible infectious or inflammatory process involving her tongue. She was given a single dose of ampicillin-sulbactam intravenously and transferred to our emergency department for further evaluation. After evaluation by an otolaryngologist, she was prescribed a 10-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate for lingual tonsillitis and discharged. She returned 1 week later with fevers, dysphagia, and worsening pain in her neck. She was admitted to our hospital and underwent a positron emission tomography (PET) scan, which demonstrated hypermetabolic soft tissue fullness at her right tongue base with extension into the vallecula and a maximum standardized uptake value (SUV) of 4.5. The PET scan also showed an intensely hypermetabolic and destructive soft tissue mass in her right skull base with a maximum SUV of 31.6. Given the presence of a mass in her right skull base, a lumbar puncture was performed, which revealed rare, large mononuclear cells suggestive of atypical monocytes/macrophages.
test_results: A subsequent bone marrow biopsy contained a neoplastic infiltrate of large pleomorphic cells with frequent folded/irregular nuclei, variably prominent nucleoli, fine chromatin, and abundant amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm. A few multinucleated neoplastic cells were noted. The malignant cells were positive for CD68 (granular), CD163, lysozyme (granular), CD4, CD45 (partial, weak), and S-100 (variable) and negative for CD20, PAX5, CD3, AE1/AE3, SOX10, CD43, ALK, CD30, granzyme, CD2, CD56, MPO, CD1a, CD21, CD35, HMB-45, MELAN-A, EBER, and CD138. The Ki67 proliferation index in the neoplastic infiltrate was at least 90%.

case_report: A 63-year-old male with no prior medical history presented to the Emergency Room with sudden abdominal pain. Physical examination of the abdomen showed rebound tenderness. An abdominal CT scan with contrast revealed the presence of free air in the abdominal cavity and fluid accumulation near the liver. Emergency surgery was conducted, revealing purulent peritonitis and a 7 × 4 cm mass in the small intestine, which was perforated and adhered to the omentum. A 20 cm segment of the small intestine was resected, followed by manual anastomosis. The patient had an uneventful postoperative recovery. Examination of the resected tissue showed an ulcerative and infiltrative mass that had perforated the intestinal wall. The cut section of the mass was gray-white with areas of hemorrhage and necrosis.
test_results: Histologically, it was composed of poorly cohesive large cells arranged in nests and cords separated by a rich vascular network and lymphocytes, plasma cells, benign histiocytes and eosinophils. Tumor cells had pleomorphic nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Mitotic figures were numerous and often abnormal. On immunohistochemical study, tumor cells were diffusely positive for CD68 and CD45, focally positive for S-100 protein but negative for HMB45, Melan A, Dog1 and c-Kit. Immunostaining with epithelial, vascular, lymphoid, neuroendocrine markers was also negative.

case_report: A 45-year-old woman with a history of type II diabetes managed with insulin and primary hyperparathyroidism presented with a gradually enlarging infiltrated nodule and associated ulcers on her right thigh since 2006. She underwent surgery, and subsequent analysis revealed ulcerated epidermotropic dermo-hypodermal tumor proliferation. Immunohistochemical staining showed positivity for anti-PS100, anti-CD1a, and anti-Ki67 (60%), and negativity for anti-CD68. The patient received 25 sessions of radiotherapy and six courses of low-dose oral methotrexate chemotherapy, resulting in stable skin lesions. In 2020, she reported an increase in skin lesions, including new infiltrating nodules, scaling, crusted papules, and ulcerated plaques. She was treated with methotrexate, prednisone, and vinblastine, achieving a stable response with limited lesion regression. After two courses, she was lost to follow-up. One year later, she was referred to hematology for a significant increase in skin lesions, with new lesions on her thigh. Dermatological examination revealed well-defined, purplish, necrotic ulcers of varying sizes on the right thigh, which were not painful or warm. The mucous membranes and integuments were unaffected. The patient was afebrile, obese (BMI 44.8), and had unremarkable abdominal and cardiovascular examinations. No tumoral syndromes or B signs (fever, weight loss, night sweats) were observed. A complete assessment indicated cutaneous involvement without visceral involvement. A CT scan of the chest and abdomen was normal. Extensive investigation showed no systemic involvement, and serum thyroid hormone levels were normal. Endocrine workup, including cortisolemia and parathormone assessment, confirmed primary hyperparathyroidism.
test_results: The microscopic examination revealed a cutaneous tissue with an infiltrate of large cells involving the dermis and realizing an epidermotropism. The infiltrate was composed of atypical cells with abundant, pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, irregular and elongated or lobed nuclei with prominent nuclear grooves and folds, fine chromatin, and indistinct nucleoli. Multinucleated giant tumor cells, high cytonuclear atypia, and marked nuclear pleomorphism were seen. The mitotic figures were increased. The neoplastic cells also showed a mixed inflammatory background with variable numbers of reactive lymphocytes, plasma cells, benign histiocytes, and eosinophils associated. The immunohistochemical stains had shown a diffuse strong and heterogeneous positivity for CD1a and S100 and variable positivity for CD45. All other markers studied were negative, including CD68, cytokeratins (AE1/AE3), and melanocytic marker (MelanA). The Ki-67 proliferation index was high (50%).

case_report: A 34-year-old female presented with upper abdominal pain and was initially investigated for biliary colic. Radiographic investigations included an ultrasound and a computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen, which revealed a large mass on the left sidewall of the pelvis. The patient had no medical history, no significant family history, and was a non-smoker. Further imaging with pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) indicated that the mass was separate from the left ovary and located outside the peritoneal cavity, within the left pelvic sidewall, immediately medial to the external iliac vessels. The mass measured 66x60x76 mm and showed no invasion into the anterior abdominal wall muscles or other pelvic structures. Positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) demonstrated a large, homogenous mass in the left iliac fossa with moderate fludeoxyglucose (FDG) avidity. It was identified as a solitary lesion with no other synchronous or distal lesions. Multiple samples were taken via CT guidance for further characterization of the lesion and surgical planning. These samples were reviewed by multiple pathologists and referred to a hematopathologist for additional evaluation.
test_results: The biopsy showed a sclerosing lesion associated with lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. Histology showed a highly unusual neoplasm comprising loose fascicles and whorls of spindle cells with an infiltrate between lymphoid follicles, associated with a prominent lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. The neoplasm had arisen in a lymph node with normal nodal tissue around the periphery. On immunohistochemistry, the spindle cells were focally positive for S100, SMA, CD31, CD138 and negative for CD21, CD23, CD3, CD20, SOX10, BRAF, ALK.

case_report: Patient BC, a 61-year-old female with a history of diabetes mellitus and hyperlipidemia, presented to the emergency room in June 2015 due to episodes of confusion and memory issues over the preceding weeks. She also reported experiencing intermittent, diffuse headaches over the past week. Initial examination showed she was neurologically intact without noticeable memory deficits. A noncontrast head CT scan revealed a 4 cm hematoma in the right frontal lobe with associated edema, sulcal effacement, and a 3 mm right-to-left midline shift. Further imaging was conducted, and an MRI of the brain with and without contrast on the night of admission showed stable acute hemorrhage in the right frontal lobe with underlying dural-based lesions, including a dominant hemorrhagic lesion measuring up to 2.4 cm. Radiographic characteristics suggested metastatic disease. A screening CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed mild hepatomegaly and calcifications in the right breast but no obvious signs of malignancy. A PET scan indicated no evidence of extracranial disease. The patient was started on dexamethasone and underwent additional imaging to fully evaluate the intracranial hemorrhage. No other sites of disease were found during the evaluation for a primary malignancy source. Surgical resection was decided upon, and the patient underwent a right frontal craniotomy with resection of the dural-based lesion without adverse events. Postoperatively, steroids were tapered, and she was transferred to an acute rehabilitation facility. A postoperative MRI of the brain with and without contrast showed enhancement along the margins of the resection cavity, consistent with a resolving residual hematoma.
test_results: Histologic examination revealed a mitotically active neoplasm with spindled and epithelioid components, conspicuous infiltration by chronic inflammatory elements, including many lymphocytes, and with associated hemorrhagic necrosis. On immunohistochemical staining, there was focal labeling for CD35 and more diffuse expression of clusterin. The tumor cells focally expressed smooth muscle actin, minimally and focally expressed CK7, but not CK20 or CAM5.2, retained INI 1 expression, and did not express ALK, CD20, CD21, CD31, Chromogranin, EMA, ERG, GFAP, HMB45, Melan A, MyoD1, Myogenin, NeuN, SOX10, STAT6, or Synaptophysin.
diagnosis: Hemorrhagic intracranial follicular dendritic cell sarcoma

case_report: A 78-year-old female presented with several months of abdominal discomfort and bloody stool. The patient also reported irregular bowel movements. There was no fever, body weight loss, night sweating, or malaise. Physical examination showed no evidence of lymphadenopathy. Laboratory data showed mild anemia with hemoglobin at 10 g/dL and normal carcinoembryonic antigen level. Barium enema performed one month prior to endoscopy revealed an oval-shaped filling defect in the colon. Colonoscopic examination revealed a 3 cm pedunculated polyp in the transverse colon, 50 cm from the anal verge. An endoscopic biopsy showed granulation tissue with inflammatory exudates. Two weeks later, the patient underwent polypectomy. The resected tumor, measuring 3.9×1.9×1.7 cm, was polypoid with ulceration. The cut surface was solid and tan without necrosis or hemorrhage. Abdominal computerized tomography and chest X-ray were negative. The patient was free of disease five months after the polypectomy without adjuvant chemotherapy. Microscopically, the polypoid tumor showed focal ulceration and a florid lymphocytic infiltration with germinal center formation and a vascular stroma. There were no epithelioid granulomas or hyalinized blood vessels entering the germinal centers. The interfollicular areas were extended by small lymphocytes and numerous plasma cells and included some large ovoid to spindled cells with vesicular nuclei and open chromatin with lightly eosinophilic syncytial cytoplasm. There were essentially no eosinophils visualized in the stroma. Occasionally, multinucleated giant cells and rare mitotic figures were discernible. These atypical cells were dispersed and were more prominent beneath the area of ulceration. They were often accompanied by small sclerotic bands and were mostly scattered individually without forming intersecting spindle cell fascicles.
test_results: Immunohistochemical studies showed that these large cells expressed CD21, CD23, CD35, CD45, p53, D2-40, and epithelial membrane antigen and weakly expressed estrogen receptors, but not CD34, CD68, CD117, DOG-1, S-100 protein, pan-cytokeratin, and progesterone receptors. Staining for smooth muscle actin was strongly positive in the spindle cells, but less intense in the areas where FDC markers such as CD21 were strongly expressed. The spindle cells were also positive for EBV-encoded mRNA (EBER) by in situ hybridization. The background lymphocytes were mixed small T and B cells; and the plasma cells were polytypic for light chain expression. The polymerase chain reaction-based clonality study for B-cell receptor gene rearrangement showed no amplification using IGH/FR3 primers.
diagnosis: Follicular Dendritic Cell Sarcoma, Inflammatory Pseudotumor-like variant

case_report: A 32-year-old male presented with a two-month history of hoarseness and difficulty swallowing. Imaging via computed tomography revealed a 3.1 × 2.0 × 2.0 cm isolated mass in the right tonsil, with no evidence of lymphadenopathy or other lesions. An excisional biopsy showed the tonsil extensively replaced by epithelioid cells arranged in nested and alveolar patterns, with scattered small lymphocytes. The tumor cells were large to pleomorphic, featuring slightly irregular vesicular nuclei, small nucleoli, and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Multinucleated giant cells were also present. Immunohistochemical staining indicated that the tumor cells were positive for CD4 and CD30, and negative for ALK, CD2, CD3, CD20, CD68, CD163, lysozyme, cytokeratin, S100, and desmin. The patient underwent multiple lines of chemotherapy, including EPOCH (etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and doxorubicin hydrochloride), ESHAP (etoposide, methylprednisone, cytarabine, and cisplatin), and GDP (gemcitabine, dexamethasone, and cisplatin), as well as radiotherapy.
test_results: Histologic examination of the excised mass revealed a tumor exhibiting multiple morphologic components with numerous pleomorphic spindle cells growing in fascicles or a storiform pattern being the major component. Nuclear pseudoinclusions were easily seen in these cells. Relative monotonous plump spindle or ovoid cells arranged in meningioma-like whorls and epithelioid tumor cells seen in the initial biopsy were also presented focally. Clusters of foamy cells and cholesterol-like crystal deposit with foreign body-giant cell reaction were seen peripherally. The tumor cells were positive for CD4, CD21, CD23, and CD35, and negative for ALK, CD3, CD20, CD30, CD45, cytokeratin, S-100, HMB45, desmin, and EBER. Immunostains for CD21, CD23, and CD35 performed retrospectively on the initial specimen were positive in the tumor cells. TCR rearrangement analyses were performed at an outside consultation institution, and no monoclonal TCR gamma or TCR beta rearrangement was detected.

case_report: A 77-year-old female was referred to the urology department for evaluation of a left renal mass and multiple nodules in both lungs. The patient had no family history of renal cancer. The bilateral lung nodules were first observed one month ago on a chest X-ray taken during a preoperative examination for a pituitary adenoma, which was identified at another hospital following the patient's complaint of restricted visual field. The patient had been diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis 14 years ago and had been on low-dose methotrexate (2–12 mg/week) for 13 years.
test_results: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed a slightly enhanced, 3-cm left renal mass and multiple pulmonary nodules with a maximal diameter of 2.5 cm.

case_report: A 72-year-old female with type II diabetes and hypertension initially presented in January 2020 with a year-long history of chronic, progressively indurated erythematous plaques on both legs, accompanied by ulceration on the right leg. Despite undergoing 10 sessions of radiotherapy in March 2020, the lesions advanced (GMF stage IIB). Treatment with MTX, starting at 5 mg/week, and acitretin 10 mg/day was initiated. Interferon-α at 3 million units three times a week was stopped after two months due to adverse effects. MTX dosage was increased to 25 mg/week without improvement. Twenty-seven months after starting MTX, at a dosage of 15 mg/week, the patient reported a new round erythematous plaque on her right leg and a nodule on the left leg, each measuring 2–3 cm in diameter with ulceration and a central necrotic crust. These were in addition to preexisting large brownish ulcerative plaques on her lower legs. She did not report systemic symptoms or fever. Oral administration of a retinoid derivative and systemic psoralen and ultraviolet A (RePUVA) was added but proved ineffective.
test_results: Skin biopsy showed dermal atypical lymphoid infiltrate with granulomatous reaction, positive on immunohistochemistry for CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, and CD7 and negative for CD8, CD20, CD30, CD34, and CD56. In-situ hybridization showed the absence of Epstein–Barr virus-encoded small RNA (EBER) in atypical lymphoid cells. T-cell receptor gene rearrangement defined monoclonal proliferation. Complete staging work-up including computed tomography scan, biopsy of enlarged inguinal nodes, and bone marrow biopsy demonstrated no overt evidence of systemic lymphoma. Biopsy from the new nodule on her left lower leg showed dense, diffuse atypical monomorphous large lymphoid infiltrate involving the entire dermis. The atypical cells were strongly positive for CD20 and EBER in-situ hybridization. Additional immunohistochemistry identified expression of CD30, MUM1, and Ki-67 (>90%), but not CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, CD7, CD8, CD10, CD56, LANA1, and BCL6 stains. Computed tomography imaging of the chest and abdomen revealed no evidence of systemic involvement.
diagnosis: cutaneous methotrexate-related Epstein–Barr virus-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

case_report: A 57-year-old Japanese woman presented with right-sided chest pain and underwent computed tomography (CT) at a familial orthopedic hospital for rheumatoid arthritis. The CT scan incidentally revealed a 44 mm nodule in the left lung and a 14 mm nodule in the right lung. Additionally, multiple nodules, the largest measuring up to 55 mm with pale ring enhancement, were observed in the liver. The patient had a history of left nephrectomy for renal cell carcinoma (RCC) five years prior and had been receiving annual postoperative follow-ups, with no evidence of recurrence observed in thoracoabdominal CT scans a year before her current visit. She was referred to our department for further evaluation. The patient's previous pathological diagnosis of the primary tumor indicated unclassified-type RCC (pT1a) without vascular and lymphatic permeation, and a Fuhrman nuclear grade of 2. At the time of her visit, she was on a regimen of methotrexate (8 mg/day) and prednisolone (2 mg/day) for the past 8 years. Blood tests showed mildly elevated levels of aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 42 IU/L and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) at 39 IU/L, while tumor markers for lung cancer (CEA and SCC) were within normal limits. No new mass lesions were observed on thoracoabdominal CT, and the sizes of the lung and liver masses remained unchanged.
test_results: Pathological findings revealed diffuse proliferation of lymphoid cells. Necrosis and perivascular growth were also observed. The majority of lymphoid cells were positive for CD20 and CD79a but negative for AE1/AE3. A small amount of CD3 positive was observed. Almost all lymphoid cells were positive for EBER by in situ hybridization.

case_report: A 5-month-old girl, born full-term via vaginal delivery, presented with a history of fever followed by seizure and subsequent unilateral body weakness. There was no prior history of seizures, and her motor and language development were appropriate for her age. According to her parents, she was in her usual state of health and behaving normally before developing a fever. A few hours after the onset of fever, she experienced a seizure. She was brought to Gandhi Memorial Hospital (GMH), Rewa, while actively seizing and was administered intravenous midazolam, phenytoin, valproate, and levetiracetam. Following the seizure, she exhibited weakness on the left side of her body. The seizure lasted approximately 10–15 hours in total. By the third day of hospitalization, her mental status had improved, but she still showed left-sided hemiparesis and was not speaking spontaneously. Over the next four days, her condition began to improve with continued antiepileptic treatment.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans showed diffuse right hemicerebral diffusion restriction, whereas the left cerebral cortex was normal. MR angiography was carried out, which was normal.

case_report: A 3-year-old male was discovered in bed experiencing a tonic–clonic seizure with left eye deviation. The duration of the seizure was unknown as his mother had last seen him 3–4 hours prior. The patient had a fever of 102.5°F before the seizure, and upon EMS arrival, his temperature was 100.5°F. He was transported to a local hospital where seizures were managed with lorazepam and levetiracetam, and he was transitioned to his home zonisamide regimen. Initially, there was an assumption of Todd’s paralysis, but he did not return to baseline. The patient's medical history includes hypotonia, global developmental delays, febrile seizures, breath holding spells, small stature, and patent foramen ovale. He was born at 41 weeks to non-consanguineous parents after an uncomplicated delivery and was noted to have intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), a two-vessel cord, ear indentations, branchial cleft cyst, small phallus, and thrombocytopenia. During the first week of life, he developed apnea and staring spells. An MRI on postnatal day 8 showed no structural abnormalities or infarcts. Subsequent magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) revealed an asymmetrically small but patent right transverse sinus. Karyotype and chromosome microarray analysis identified an unbalanced 1;3 translocation resulting in a 6.9-Mb deletion on the distal long arm of chromosome 1 containing 22 genes and an 8.6-Mb duplication on the distal short arm of chromosome 3 containing 15 genes [46,XY,t(1;3)(q43;p26.1). arr[hg18] 1q43q44(240,287,612-247,190,999)x1,3p26.3p26.1(35,332-8,625,632)x3].
test_results: MRI showed thinned and truncated corpus collosum, diffusely increased T2/FLAIR signal intensity throughout the cortices of the left hemispheric gray matter with associated restriction diffusion, left hemispheric edema, 6.8 mm midline shift, effacement of the left ventricle, and dilation of the right ventricle.

case_report: A one and a half year-old girl, born preterm with a very low birth weight of 1.2 kg via vaginal delivery to a mother with eclampsia, presented with fever, seizure, and loss of consciousness. There was no prior history of seizures, and her development was appropriate for her age. According to her parents, she experienced a high-grade fever followed by abnormal movements in all four limbs and loss of consciousness. She was admitted to a local hospital with ongoing seizures for 6 days, where she was treated for cerebral malaria, but the seizures persisted. She was then referred to GMH, Rewa, where she received intravenous midazolam, phenytoin, and valproate. After the seizure episode, she developed weakness on the left side of her body. The total duration of the seizure activity was approximately 6 days. On the 9th day of her hospital stay, she regained consciousness but exhibited left-sided hemiparesis.
test_results: MRI scans were similar to other cases.

case_report: A 49-year-old Chinese female from Shantou, China, presented to the outpatient department of the Mental Health Center, Shantou University Medical College, in March 2016, accompanied by her elder brother. She exhibited excessive talking, nosiness, rash spending, decreased need for sleep, and an irritable mood for 3 weeks. The patient measured 138 cm in height. Physical examination revealed a short neck, multiple pigmented nevi on the face, moderate hearing impairment in both ears, small breasts, flat nipples, thin flat vulva, and sparse armpit and pubic hair. Her weight was 40 kg, and her blood pressure was 97/70 mmHg. Electrocardiogram showed inverted T waves in leads V3–V6. Electroencephalogram and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain appeared normal. Ultrasonography indicated small ovaries and uterus, a smaller right kidney, and diffuse hyperplasia in the thyroid glands without abnormal blood flow signals. During the examination, the patient was conscious and made good eye contact but talked about irrelevant issues and showed inattention by looking elsewhere. The full-scale Wechsler IQ (Chinese version) score was 66, with a performance IQ of 73 and a verbal IQ of 75. Laboratory results showed decreased levels of estradiol (19 ng/L), progesterone (0.3 μg/L), and serum testosterone (0.07 μg/L), with normal levels of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH; 69.8 IU/L), luteinizing hormone (LH; 14.1 IU/L), and cortisol (10.4 μg/dL). Fasting blood sugar was 8.5 mM/L, and glycosylated hemoglobin was 7.5%, while serum insulin was 12.8 IU/mL. Total thyroxine (TT4) was 66.6 μg/L, total triiodothyronine (TT3) was 0.9 ng/mL, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) was 7.9 IU/mL, and autoantibody to thyroid peroxidase (TPO) was 180 U/mL. The patient was born full-term via vaginal delivery. Her mother had taken medication to attempt to abort the pregnancy. She was the youngest of eight children in a lower-class family. Two of her brothers had a history of mood disorders that were successfully treated. She experienced slow development during childhood and was shorter than her peers. She had significant academic difficulties, did not complete primary education, and never held a job. She did not experience menstruation after puberty. She married at 32 but did not have children. Due to amenorrhea and short stature, she became depressed, self-blaming, and lacked self-confidence, isolating herself and hesitating to meet others. She had poor appetite and sleep and attempted suicide. She was admitted to the mental health center in 1991, diagnosed with depression and secondary hypopituitarism, and treated with doxepin, which improved her symptoms. In November 1992, she was readmitted for depressive mood and suspicion of others, suspecting her home had been stolen by her sister-in-law, and exhibited lack of impulse control and temper loss. She was treated with perphenazine (16 mg/day) and doxepin (100 mg/day), which improved her symptoms, and she was discharged. She continued her medication at home. In 1995, after discontinuing medication, she was readmitted for excessive talking, hyperactivity, buying things for others without reason, and excessive praying. She had difficulty controlling herself at home, with outbursts of shouting, crying, and disruptive behavior. She was treated for pulmonary tuberculosis, shown in a chest X-ray, and hypopituitarism, with antituberculosis drugs and clozapine, which improved her symptoms, and she was discharged. She was hospitalized in 2001 and 2004 for similar manic episodes, including excessive talking, hyperactivity, rash spending, and difficulty controlling herself. In 2005, she became depressed, slow in movements, lazy, and maintained erratic hours.
test_results: The karyotype of 45, X/46, X, i(Xq) was identified.

case_report: A 3-month-old male infant was found to have a noticeable abdominal mass. Abdominal radiographs identified a large lesion in the left upper quadrant, which caused the bowel loops to shift inferomedially. Ultrasound imaging revealed a substantial mass with both solid and cystic components in the same region. Unenhanced abdominal CT scans showed a well-defined heterogeneous mass featuring intratumoral nodular calcifications and an area with fat density. Enhanced abdominal CT scans demonstrated a large, solid and cystic mass extending from the greater curvature of the stomach, with a connection between this curvature and the mass's intraluminal extension. The solid part of the mass exhibited significant enhancement.
test_results: The tumor contained mature components such as chondroid tissue, squamous epithelium, and keratin, and multifocal aggregates of immature neural tissues of neuroblasts.

case_report: A 31-year-old male reported experiencing abdominal pain that had intensified over the past 3 months. He had been dealing with intermittent epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting for the past year. The recent increase in abdominal pain prompted him to seek medical attention. Additionally, he experienced a weight loss of 2 kg over the past month. He was found to have partial gut obstruction. During an exploratory laparotomy, a 10-cm mass was discovered in the duodenal region, situated in the retroperitoneal area near the aorta. A gastrojejunostomy was performed, but the mass was not removed due to the high risk of aortic injury. A lymph node biopsy was conducted, and histopathology showed reactive lymphoid hyperplasia. The patient was subsequently referred to our hospital. He had no history of underlying diseases or medication use. Physical examination at our facility revealed a well-healed midabdominal surgical scar and a palpable, ill-defined mass on the left side of the abdomen with mild tenderness. Other organs were found to be within normal limits. All blood tests returned normal results.
test_results: The computed tomography scan revealed a multiseptated cystic tumor at the retroperitoneal area, adhering to the duodenum and close to the abdominal aorta and left renal vein, compressing the left ureter. No bony structure was detected.

case_report: A 15-year-old girl initially presented at the age of 13 with episodes of visible blood in the urine and significant protein loss in the urine. Laboratory tests showed normal levels of serum electrolytes, albumin (3.2 g/dL), urea (24 mg/dL), and creatinine (0.6 mg/dL), with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 106.7 mL/min/1.73. Hemoglobin was within normal range (12.8 mg/dL), as were white blood cell count (9.3 × 103/µL) and platelet count (240 × 109/L). A peripheral blood film revealed irregularly shaped red blood cells and burr cells, but no abnormal white blood cell inclusions. The patient had no reported hearing or vision issues. Her mother, aged 43, had a history of hearing difficulties, microscopic blood in the urine, and episodes of visible blood in the urine, with an eGFR of 80.0 mL/min/1.73. The patient's grandfather experienced kidney failure and was on dialysis at the age of 70. Upon examination after referral, the patient showed no signs of swelling, had normal blood pressure (93/63 mmHg, at the 50th percentile for age and height), and a normal heart rate. Urine analysis indicated mild protein loss, an albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) ranging from 140 to 286 mg/g, and blood in the urine. Serum electrolyte, urea, and creatinine levels remained normal, with an eGFR of 96.2 mL/min/1.73.
test_results: Ultrasonography revealed normal-sized kidneys with normal parenchymal echogenicity but some loss of corticomedullary differentiation. Slit-lamp examination and audiometry were normal.

case_report: Patient 28. A 10-year-old male presenting with mild bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Family history indicates that both his father and grandfather experienced mild hearing loss, with the condition being progressive in his father. He has one brother who is healthy. No records of an audiological examination at birth were found, but a screening conducted at the age of 5 years showed abnormal results.
test_results: WES revealed a heterozygous, likely pathogenic mutation in COL4A3 inherited from his father (c.4826G > A, p.(Arg1609Gln)).

case_report: The patient is a 28-year-old pregnant woman, gravida 2 para 0, with a height of 163 cm and a weight of 53 kg. Two years prior to pregnancy, she exhibited abnormal proteinuria (++) and urine occult blood (+). During her pregnancy, from 8 to 27 weeks of gestation, her 24-hour proteinuria ranged between 2.10 to 3.94 g, and her albumin levels were between 25 to 29 g/L. A 4-dimensional ultrasound indicated that fetal development was consistent with the gestational age. There was no edema in the lower extremities. Starting from 9 weeks of gestation, she received 4000 IU LMWH every other day for anticoagulation therapy, along with intermittent albumin infusions (10 g), and oral supplements of compound amino acids, calcium, and vitamin D to prevent preeclampsia. At 29 weeks of gestation, her 24-hour proteinuria increased to 6.84 g, and fetal development lagged by one week. By 36 weeks of gestation, her 24-hour proteinuria further increased to 9.32 g, and fetal development lagged by three weeks, with a biparietal diameter of 8.8 cm, an abdominal circumference of 28.3 cm, an amniotic fluid index of 13.1 cm, and an umbilical artery blood flow S/D value of 1.99. The pregnancy was terminated by cesarean section at 37 weeks of gestation, resulting in the delivery of a live girl weighing 2370 g with Apgar scores of 9’-10’-10’. One month postpartum, her 24-hour proteinuria was 7.26 g. During a one-year postpartum follow-up, she continued to exhibit high levels of proteinuria, with 24-hour proteinuria fluctuating between 3.26 to 6.84 g. The patient did not show any ocular or inner ear involvement. She denied consanguineous marriage and had no family history of hematuria, proteinuria, hearing impairment, or vision loss.
test_results: Sanger sequencing revealed that patient had novel compound heterozygous mutations [c.1315 G>T (p.G439C) and c.4847 G>A (p.C1616Y)] in COL4A3 gene. Light microscopic examination of kidney biopsy indicated that the glomerular basement membrane was extremely irregular, and the dense layer was torn and delaminated, forming a basket-like structure.

case_report: The patient is a 21-year-old pregnant woman, gravida 1 para 0, with a height of 160 cm and weight of 45 kg. At 13 weeks of gestation, she exhibited abnormal proteinuria (+++) and abnormal urine occult blood (++). Hematological tests revealed mild anemia with a hemoglobin level of 107 g/L, and biochemical tests indicated hypoproteinemia with total protein at 53.8 g/L and albumin at 29.2 g/L. Between 13 and 26 weeks of gestation, her 24-hour proteinuria ranged from 2.03 to 3.45 g, and albumin levels fluctuated between 24 and 29 g/L. At 27 weeks of gestation, her 24-hour proteinuria increased to 5.05 g, and a 4-dimensional ultrasound showed that fetal development was smaller than expected by one week. She also presented with positive lower extremity edema (+). The patient was hospitalized and received conventional treatment, including intravenous albumin (10 g) every two weeks, oral compound amino acids, calcium, vitamin D, and subcutaneous injections of 4000 IU low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) every other day for anticoagulation. At 35 weeks of gestation, her 24-hour proteinuria was 11.72 g, and fetal development lagged by two weeks. The pregnancy was terminated by cesarean section at 36 weeks, resulting in the birth of a live male infant weighing 2400 g with Apgar scores of 9’-10’-10’. Three months postpartum, her 24-hour proteinuria was 13.03 g. One year after delivery, she continued to exhibit high proteinuria, with 24-hour proteinuria ranging from 2.67 to 5.31 g, and developed high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss.
test_results: The novel compound heterozygous mutations [c.1315 G>T (p.G439C) and c.4847 G>A (p.C1616Y)] of COL4A3 gene were found in the patient. Pathological examination of renal puncture showed mild hyperplasia of mesangial cells and stroma, uneven thickness of basement membrane with diffuse stratified changes in the dense layer, extensive fusion of epithelial foot processes, and vacuolar degeneration of renal tubular.

case_report: A 51-year-old male was admitted to the local hospital after being bitten on the hand by a hump-nosed viper while gardening. The snake was identified as Merrem's hump-nosed viper (Hypnale hypnale). The patient experienced severe pain and swelling in the hand. The following day, his urine output decreased, and he was transferred to a tertiary care institute for hemodialysis. Upon admission, the patient was conscious, rational, febrile, and in pain. He appeared pale and mildly icteric. There was significant swelling and redness in his right hand with blistering at the bite site. His pulse rate was 92 beats per minute, and his blood pressure was 118/78 mmHg. Heart auscultation revealed normal S1 and S2 sounds with no murmurs. Respiratory examination was normal except for a few fine basal crepitations. Abdominal examination showed no organ enlargement or free fluid. Neurological examination was normal with no signs of ophthalmoplegia or cranial nerve paralysis. Laboratory results were as follows: white cell count, 12,700 (80% neutrophils); platelet count, 40,000/μl; hemoglobin, 9.9 g/dl; International normalized ratio, 1.46; activated partial thromboplastin time, 43 s; serum creatinine, 1,040 μmol/l; Na+, 130 mmol/l; K+, 5.4 mmol/l; erythrocyte sedimentation rate, 10 mm/Hr; C-reactive protein, 1 mg/L; aspartate transaminase, 54 u/l; alanine transaminase, 42 u/l; serum bilirubin, 22.7 μmol/l; total protein, 52 g/l (albumin 33 g/l). Peripheral blood smear showed marked red cell fragmentation, polychromasia, and reduced platelet count. Serum calcium was 7.7 mg/dl; serum phosphate, 3.1 mg/dl; creatine phosphokinase, 122 u/l; urine microscopy revealed 10-12 pus cells and 1-2 red cells per high power field with no casts. Trace amounts of protein were present in the urine. An abdominal ultrasound scan showed enlarged and globular kidneys. The patient was started on hemodialysis. After 12 sessions, he remained dialysis-dependent, and a renal biopsy was performed 8 weeks post-bite. The biopsy showed patchy areas of tubular atrophy with interstitial edema and chronic inflammation, indicating subacute interstitial nephritis. There was no evidence of acute tubular necrosis. Glomeruli appeared normal. Ten weeks after the bite, the patient's renal function and urine output improved. He was discharged with a serum creatinine of 1.9 mg/dl and serum potassium of 3.9 mmol/l, to be followed up as an outpatient.
test_results: Arterial pH was 7.31 and PCO2 18 mmHg, PO2 121 mmHg, and HCO3 − 10.3 mmol/l. His serum potassium level was 7.0 mmol/l with sodium 130 mmol/l and chloride 114 mmol/l. Serum creatinine was 114 μmol/l with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 76 ml/min. Blood anion gap was normal at 5.7 mmol/l. Urine pH was 5.0. Urinary electrolytes were as follows: Na+ 77 mmol/l, K+ 16 mmol/l, Cl− 84 mmol/l, pH 5.0, serum osmolality 300 mosm/kg, urine osmolality 380 mosm/kg, and urinary anion gap was 9 mmol/l. Transtubular potassium gradient (TTKG) was 1.80.

case_report: A 42-year-old male presented with low-grade fever, diffuse headache, and joint pains for 8 weeks. There was no history of head injury. The patient reported pain and swelling in the knees, ankles, wrists, and elbows, without morning stiffness. He also experienced decreased appetite and a 6 kg weight loss. Physical examination by a general practitioner showed blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg and a temperature of 38°C. Systemic examination was normal. Laboratory results included hemoglobin of 14 g/dL, total leukocyte count of 13,200/cmm, and platelet count of 4,53,000/cmm. Urine albumin was negative, and urine microscopic examination was normal. Renal, liver, and thyroid function tests were within normal limits. Peripheral smear for malarial parasite and HIV serology were negative. Blood and urine cultures were sterile. Chest radiography and abdominal ultrasound were normal. Brain MRI showed a subdural hematoma (subacute stage) in the left fronto-parietal region. The neurosurgeon recommended surgical evacuation of the hematoma, but the patient did not consent. He was treated with empirical antibiotics and cerebral decongestants. A non-contrast CT scan of the head confirmed the subacute subdural hematoma in the left fronto-parietal region. On the 50th day of illness, the patient developed right hemiparesis, and a repeat CT scan of the head showed an infarct in the left basal ganglia extending to the parietal region. The patient presented to the emergency room with right-sided body weakness for 7 days, along with a history of fever, headache, and joint pains for 3 months. There was no history of chronic upper respiratory symptoms, except for 4-5 episodes of epistaxis 6 months prior, which resolved without treatment. The patient was conscious and oriented, with right upper and lower limb power graded at 3-4/5 and hyper-reflexia. Urinalysis and renal function tests were normal. Detailed investigations for fever were conducted. Urine and blood cultures were sterile, and tests for malarial parasite were negative. X-ray chest, liver biopsy, and bone marrow biopsy were normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed mild hepatomegaly with fatty liver and multiple hypoechoic lesions in the spleen. Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen revealed irregular wedge-shaped hypodense lesions in the spleen with attenuation values of 6 × 35 HU. The patient was started on empirical anti-tubercular treatment but did not respond. Five weeks later, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest showed thin-walled cavitary lesions in both upper lobes with a parenchymal mass. The patient also developed episcleritis.
test_results: Cytoplasmic anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (cANCA) levels were found to be raised. Renal biopsy showed evidence of pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis.

case_report: A 63-year-old male was admitted to the hospital on October 5, 2022, presenting with 'lung occupancy for 1 year, headache for 1 month, hearing loss for 2 weeks.' The patient had previously undergone particle implantation for a 'lung mass,' and postoperative pathology revealed infiltration and aggregation of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils in the lung tissue interstitium. One month prior to admission, the patient experienced persistent left temporal pain with a visual analog scale (VAS) score of 10 and a sensation of tightness at the back of the neck. There were no reports of fever, blurred vision, facial numbness, limb sensation, or movement disorders. Cranial MRI, magnetic resonance angiography, and magnetic resonance venogram scans showed no apparent abnormalities. Color ultrasound examinations of the bilateral carotid arteries, bilateral vertebral arteries, and the heart also revealed no apparent abnormalities. Laboratory tests indicated elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), white blood cells, and platelet counts. Cerebrospinal fluid routine, biochemistry, and culture showed no abnormalities. The patient's symptoms were alleviated by oral prednisone acetate (60 mg/qd), but the headache worsened when the dosage was reduced to 30 mg/qd. Two weeks before admission, the patient experienced severe pain in the right temporal region and hearing loss in both ears, with a VAS score of 10, and no nasal congestion or bloody or purulent discharge. Physical examination upon admission revealed a soft neck, negative meningeal irritation, and no sinus area tenderness. Elevated levels of CRP, ESR, and anti-protease 3 (PR3) antibody were noted. Antinuclear extract antibody, complement, immunoglobulin anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, immunoglobulin G4 (IGg4), and ferritin levels were within normal ranges. Infection indices, including giant cell, herpes virus, procalcitonin, T-SPOT.tuberculosis (T-SPOT.TB) test, and tumor markers, showed no abnormalities. Chest CT revealed flaky and dense areas in the upper lobe of the right lung with multiple granular high-density radial artifacts. Dynamic enhancement of cranial MR and diffusion-weighted imaging inner ear MR plain scan showed soft tissue around the nasopharynx and bone destruction adjacent to the soft tissue. Bulbotoiditis was observed in the middle ear of both ears. Contrast-enhanced CT of the nasopharynx indicated the presence of soft tissue surrounding the nasopharynx.
test_results: Nasopharyngeal pathological biopsy revealed necrotic tissue and bacterial flora on the surface. It indicated the presence of chronic inflammation of mucosal tissue in nasopharyngeal tissue.

case_report: A 45-year-old woman reported experiencing pain and ulceration on the index and ring fingers of her left hand for one month, followed by blackening of the index, ring, and little fingers of the same hand over the course of a week. Similar lesions were observed on the second and fourth toes of her right foot. She had no history of diabetes, hypertension, Raynaud’s phenomenon, joint pain, difficulty swallowing, oral ulcers, or fever. Upon examination, she was conscious and alert. Her pulse was regular, all peripheral pulses were present, and her blood pressure was 100/60 mmHg. Mild pallor was noted, but the rest of the general physical examination was normal. There was dry gangrene on the fingers of her left hand (excluding the thumb) distal to the metacarpophalangeal joints, with absent sensations. Similar but less severe findings were present on the second and fourth toes of her right foot. Systemic examination revealed no abnormalities. Laboratory results showed thrombocytosis with a platelet count of 640,000/mm3. Infections, sepsis, endocarditis, and coagulation abnormalities were ruled out. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no evidence of infective endocarditis. Blood and urine cultures were sterile, and serum procalcitonin levels were normal. Urine analysis showed no active sediments or proteinuria. Coagulation tests, including prothrombin time, fibrin degradation products, D-dimer, and peripheral smear, were normal. The patient had no history of diabetes mellitus or hypertension, and her serum lipid profile and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels were normal. Funduscopy and Schirmer’s test results were normal. No fever was recorded during her hospital stay. Imaging studies, including CT chest with angiography of the upper limb arteries, showed no evidence of arterial thoracic outlet syndrome. Additionally, CT angiography of the abdominal vessels did not reveal any microaneurysms in the celiac axis or renal vessels, ruling out medium vessel vasculitis.
test_results: ANA by indirect immunofluorescence returned positive +++, coarse speckled with cytoplasmic reticular staining pattern. Antibodies to extractable nuclear antigens by line immunoassay was positive for anti-Ro and U1RNP. Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) by indirect immunofluorescence was positive (++) with a peri-nuclear staining pattern (pANCA).

case_report: A 51-year-old Chinese female experienced progressive left leg weakness for 14 days before being admitted to our department. Initially, the patient presented with dizziness and left lower limb weakness, and the symptoms continued to progress despite treatment. Upon transfer to our department, physical examinations were normal. Neurologic examination revealed that proximal and distal muscle strength of the left lower limb was 3/5 by manual muscle testing (MMT). Sensory examinations using a cotton swab, tuning fork, and pinprick showed normal results for all sensory modalities, and tendon reflexes were normal with no pathologic reflexes observed. Cranial nerve function and mental examination were also normal. There was no documented family history of neurological disease or metabolic-related disorders in her medical records.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a lesion on right parietal lobe that was hypointensity on T1-weighted, hyperintensity on T2-weighted images, and high signal on FLAIR. There was slim contrast enhancement along the surface of swollen gyrus lesion after Gd-DTPA injection (10 mL/kg of body weight). MRS showed slightly decreased NAA and increased Cr and Cho peak on the right parietal lobe lesion compared to same region on normal left side. Blood analysis showed erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 40 mm/h and C-reactive protein of 55.1 mg/L. In the tests for autoantibody, the antinuclear antibody (ANA) was positive, and the titer was greatly elevated to 1:10,000. Lumbar puncture was performed and showed a normal intracranial pressure; the biochemical and hematologic tests of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) revealed a normal glucose, chloride and protein level; the white cell count was elevated 27 × 106/L with increasing percentage of lymphocyte 77.8%; and the CSF cultures for bacteria, viruses, and fungi were all negative.

case_report: Case 4 involves a 67-year-old woman with a complex medical history. She experienced one miscarriage during the second trimester of pregnancy and an antenatal death due to a preterm fetus. At the age of 42, she had a 9-month episode characterized by unexplained fever and joint pain. She had two episodes of transient ischemic attack at ages 51 and 54, with the second episode including new onset headache and a 3-month period of sensitivity loss. Last year, she was identified with recurrent periorbital rash and hypothyroidism by the Allergy Department. She reported recurrent rash flares, eye dryness, and Raynaud phenomena. Physical examination revealed residual periorbital erythema, a round bright hyperkeratotic pink plaque on the ankle, and livedo reticularis.
test_results: Immunology tests showed ANA 1/1280 and anti-TPO 507. The only echocardiographic hallmark was a 48 mm left auricle and diastolic dysfunction.

case_report: A 43-year-old male with a history of chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) since 2015, treated with Imatinib, experienced dull aching pain in the back (right side at the level of the 10th rib) starting in December 2019. The pain worsened in a supine position and with movement, accompanied by a feverish sensation and chills, but without night sweats, headache, or neurological symptoms. A CT scan on December 30, 2019, revealed a right postero-lateral heterogenous enhancing lesion with bone destruction of the 10th rib (14 × 8 cm), encasement of the right paraspinal muscle, and the transverse process of the right 10th rib. Additional findings included fine calcifications, mild right-sided pleural effusion with thickening of the right lower pleura, and a calcified cystic structure in the fourth segment of the liver (4 cm). A tru-cut biopsy indicated a poorly differentiated malignant neoplasm of hematolymphoid origin, consistent with a myeloid sarcoma. Pathological review showed large undifferentiated blasts, eosinophils, and reactive B and T lymphocytes (CD20 and CD3 positive). The neoplasm was positive for CD45, CD34, CD43, C-MYC, and focally positive for C-Kit. In January 2020, a bone marrow biopsy showed slightly hypercellular trilineage bone marrow with 75% cellularity, increased immature megakaryocytes, and +1 fibrosis. Cytogenetic testing revealed an abnormal karyotype with t(9;22) (Philadelphia translocation). Real-time PCR for AML1-ETO, CBFB-MYH1, and PML-RARa fusion transcripts were negative, as were tests for NPM1 and FLT3 mutations. Major BCR-ABL fusion gene was detected, but the minor gene was not. Molecular analysis showed no specific TKI resistance mutations. Immunophenotyping showed 3.4% blasts, 4.3% monocytes, 80% granulocytes, and 6.2% lymphocytes, with no excess blast percentage. Lumbar puncture and CSF analysis were normal. CBC results included low albumin (3.21 g/dL), low calcium (8.17 mg/dL), high LDL (364 u/L), low total protein (5.58 g/dL), low RBCs (3.83 × 10^6/μL), low hemoglobin (11.1 g/dL), and high fibrinogen (618.38 mg/dL). A PET-CT scan in February 2020 showed FDG metabolic activity in the cervical glandular tissue, right lower chest wall hypermetabolic soft tissue with rib destruction (SUV max 4.3), marked pleural effusion, collapsed right lower lobe lung, and a right liver lobe calcified hydatid cyst. There was also a moderate hypermetabolic bony lytic lesion in the left mandible (SUV max 6.3). The patient was started on Ponatinib (45 mg daily) and considered for a bone marrow transplant, but declined chemotherapy. A bone marrow biopsy in June showed no changes from the previous one, and real-time PCR for major BCR-ABL fusion transcript was negative. A PET-CT scan in August showed no changes in the head, neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis, and the hypermetabolic lesion in the left mandible was no longer visible. In September, the patient reported shortness of breath, fatigue, and low back pain radiating to the left lower limb with numbness. An X-ray showed right-sided pleural effusion, and paracentesis revealed inflammatory cells with many neutrophils, but no malignancy. WBCs were 178/μL (30% lymphocytes, 70% granulocytes), RBCs were 53000/μL, LDH was 200 u/L, and fluid pH was 8. Cytology and PCR for BCR-ABL were negative. A whole spine CT scan showed normal vertebral bodies height and alignment, no spinal cord compression, but a large L5/S1 disc bulge. The patient underwent laminectomy for the disc bulge. One month later, the patient experienced worsening back pain, numbness, loss of sphincter tone, and decreased power in both lower limbs. A whole spine CT scan showed L5 left side laminectomy with soft tissue edema and thickening, canal stenosis, and diffuse disc bulges at L3-4 and L4-5.
test_results: MRI showed that there was a region of abnormal signal intensity within the thoracic cord extending from the mid T6 vertebral body level (superiorly) to the T11-T12 disc level inferiorly associated with a patchy abnormal enhancement within the mid aspect of this lesion. There was a region of abnormal bone marrow signal intensity and apparent osteolysis involving the posterior medial aspect of the right 10th rib and small posterior disc herniations at multiple levels throughout the spine.

case_report: A 42-year-old woman underwent screening mammography, which revealed an abnormal finding in her left breast. A stereotactic biopsy was conducted, and the pathology results showed DCIS. Given her strong family history of breast cancer, a bilateral mastectomy was performed. Eight months post-surgery, a Tc-99m MDP bone scan indicated asymmetric radiotracer activity in the right orbital region. Previous imaging from several years ago at another hospital showed stable right intraocular calcifications over time. The patient has a history of chronic vision loss in the right eye and was born prematurely.
test_results: Irregular calcifications were noted along the posterior right globe, within the posterior natural lens and the posterior chamber of the eye. The right globe volume was also decreased. The left globe demonstrated a senile calcific scleral plaque at the insertion of the lateral rectus muscle.

case_report: A 14-day-old male infant was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit from the emergency room with febrile convulsions. Two days prior to admission, the parents reported seizure-like symptoms including mouth twitching, roving eye movements, and eyelid blinking. They initially consulted a local pediatrician. On the day of admission, the infant had a fever of 38.2 °C and similar seizure-like symptoms, prompting the parents to bring him to the emergency room. He was born at 40+5 weeks of gestation, weighing 3270 g (44th percentile, z-score: −0.16) via vaginal delivery, with no prenatal or postnatal complications. He is the first child of a healthy Korean family. At admission, his weight was 3420 g (17th percentile, z-score: −0.94), height was 51 cm (25th percentile, z-score: −0.68), and head circumference was 36.5 cm (70th percentile, z-score: 0.52). Vital signs included a heart rate of 144 beats/min, blood pressure of 67/42 mmHg, respiratory rate of 48 breaths/min, and body temperature of 38.5 °C. The infant was alert with normal pupil size and light reflex, and no signs of irritability, lethargy, or vomiting. There were no external injuries, and the parents denied any history of trauma. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin at 12.4 g/dL, white blood cells (WBC) at 19,980/µL (neutrophil 62%), platelets at 582,000/µL, C-reactive protein at 0.21 mg/dL, procalcitonin at 0.20 ng/mL, and electrolytes (sodium/potassium/chloride) at 136.7/5.04/100.1 mEq/L. Liver enzymes were aspartate aminotransferase at 33 IU/L and alanine transaminase at 13 IU/L, with amylase at 10 U/L and lipase at 8 U/L. Coagulation profiles were normal. Urinalysis was positive for leukocyte esterase with WBC ≥ 16~20/high power field. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed bloody fluid with 1,260,000/mm3 red blood cells and 2350/mm3 WBCs. Empirical antibiotics were administered for a urinary tract infection, and the fever subsided. No further seizure-like movements were observed during hospitalization. Electroencephalography showed a normal stage one sleep record. Brain ultrasonography on the fourth day revealed increased echogenicity in the right caudothalamic groove, increased echogenicity in the cortex of both hemispheres, and brain swelling.
test_results: His brain MRI showed subacute SDH along the posterior aspect of the falx cerebri and occipital convexity, subarachnoid hemorrhage in the sylvian fissure and along the sulci of both cerebral vertices, multiple cortical hemorrhages with edema, microhemorrhages in the left frontal lobe, and diffuse axonal injury in the periventricular white matter, corpus callosum, right thalamus, and both internal and external capsules.
Orpha_name: Moderate and severe traumatic brain injury

case_report: A 42-year-old female presented for neurosurgical evaluation with ongoing neck pain and numbness in her left fingers, two years following a traumatic fall on stairs where she struck her head but did not lose consciousness. Initially, at an outside hospital, she exhibited left-sided neck and upper extremity pain, paresthesias, and reduced upper extremity strength bilaterally, along with pain-limited lower extremity strength bilaterally. Facial lacerations, bruising, headache, and dizziness were noted. Brain and cervical computed tomography (CT) scans showed no acute intracranial processes or cervical fractures, dislocations, or spondylotic changes. She declined an MRI due to claustrophobia. The outside hospital physician discharged her with a rigid cervical collar and recommended outpatient follow-up with neurosurgery. By approximately six months post-injury, she had regained most motor function and discontinued the rigid cervical collar on her own without any acute neurological deterioration. Her chronic neck and left shoulder pain and weakness did not improve with acetaminophen or occupational therapy. She did not inform her primary care provider about her fall and was referred for neurosurgical evaluation. This occurred during a state of emergency in the northeastern USA due to COVID-19. The patient resided in rural New England, over an hour away from the hospital, and faced difficulties attending appointments due to public health measures. During a telemedicine evaluation, she discussed her fall and reported persistent issues with memory, concentration, and decision-making.
test_results: A non-contrast T2-weighted cervical MRI from 1 month before neurosurgical evaluation revealed a 4 mm area of hyperintensity within the spinal cord at the C4–C5 level.

case_report: An 11-year-old right-handed girl, born full-term with a history of non-epileptic staring spells, presented with rapidly worsening back pain and paraplegia. She experienced sudden lumbar back discomfort while lifting heavy wooden planks, which quickly spread to both legs, accompanied by patchy areas of abnormal sensations. She reported no trauma, popping sensation, or prior infectious symptoms. Approximately 20-30 minutes after the back pain began, she developed weakness in both legs, leading her family to seek medical attention. She did not report any weakness or sensory changes in her arms, nor did she have headaches, vision changes, or difficulties with swallowing, talking, or breathing. She had trouble urinating. Physical examination revealed flaccid paraplegia, absence of reflexes in the lower extremities, and no response to plantar stimulation bilaterally. Her mental status, cranial nerves, and motor/sensory/coordination functions in the upper extremities were normal. There was a lower thoracic sensory level to temperature, light touch, and pinprick. Joint position and vibratory sense were normal in the upper extremities but reduced in the toes and ankles bilaterally. An MRI of the lumbar spine without contrast, performed about 6 hours after symptom onset, showed no cord signal changes, vertebral or disc abnormalities, or masses. A lumbar puncture performed at an outside emergency department revealed CSF glucose of 62 mg/dL (serum glucose 111 mg/dL), protein of 17 mg/dL, total nucleated cell count of 0, RBC count of 1, and negative xanthochromia. She was admitted to our hospital for further management.
test_results: MRI thoracic/lumbar spine with contrast obtained 1 day after symptom onset showed new development of T2 hyperintensity within the anterior portion (anterior horns) of the distal thoracic cord (T10) to the conus medullaris. There were no signal abnormalities in the vertebrae or discs, and the brain MRI exam was normal.

case_report: A previously healthy 42-year-old woman experienced fever, headache, and sore throat for three days, followed by sudden bilateral visual loss, dysarthria, confusion, and severe irritability requiring sedation. Examination revealed a heart rate of 142 beats per minute, body temperature of 39.6°C, neck stiffness, and tender maculopapular rashes on both hands and feet. Fundus examination showed multiple scattered retinal hemorrhages with a white center in both eyes. Hematologic assays indicated leukocytosis of 12,700/μL (neutrophil 94%), hemoglobin of 9.6 g/dL (hematocrit 29.9%), and platelet counts of 135,000/μL. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed pleocytosis (1,020/mm3, neutrophil 80%), RBC of 200/mm3, protein at 166.0 mg/dL, and glucose of 55 mg/dL (serum glucose 122 mg/dL). The patient was administered 2.6 g of vancomycin and 4 g of ceftriaxone per day. Blood culture later identified methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
