Transthoracic echocardiography showed a hypermobile vegetation (1.7 cm × 1.1 cm) attached to the mitral valve, leading to a valve replacement operation 20 days after symptom onset. Upon regaining consciousness 1 day post-operation, she reported dizziness, hearing loss, and tinnitus in the right ear. Examination revealed no spontaneous nystagmus with or without visual fixation, but horizontal head-shaking induced left beating nystagmus. Horizontal saccades and smooth pursuit were normal. She exhibited a tendency to fall to the right when attempting to stand or walk. Other neurologic examinations showed no weakness, sensory changes, or cerebellar dysfunction.
test_results: Video HITs were abnormal for the right horizontal and posterior canals. Bithermal caloric tests showed right canal paresis of 81%. Pure-tone audiometry documented right hearing loss. Cervical and ocular VEMPs showed no responses during right ear stimulation. Brain MRIs disclosed gadolinium enhancements of the vestibule, cochlea, and semicircular canals on the right side as well as multiple scattered infarctions in the frontal and occipital lobes.
diagnosis: Acute Unilateral Audiovestibulopathy due to Embolic Labyrinthine Infarction

case_report: A 23-year-old woman with a body mass index of 32.3 and a history of polycystic ovarian syndrome presented with significant liver issues requiring orthotopic liver transplantation. Originally from India, she had been taking homeopathic medications for several years without known toxicity. She had no history of alcohol, tobacco, or other drug use. While living in the United States, she was unable to refill her homeopathic product containing eggshells from India and had been off all medications and supplements except Berberis vulgaris for about a month. She then obtained a similar homeopathic product with eggshells as the primary ingredient, initially taking 4 pills per day for 10 days, then increasing to 10 pills per day for another 10 days due to uncertainty about the appropriate dose. She developed orange urine discoloration and nausea without any muscle-related symptoms and subsequently stopped all medications and supplements. About two weeks later, she visited the emergency department for nausea and malaise. Laboratory results showed negative mononucleosis screen and hepatitis panel, and no evidence of hepatic encephalopathy. An abdominal ultrasound revealed hypoechoic liver parenchyma. She was discharged with a recommendation for gastroenterology telehealth follow-up. One week later, she reported worsening nausea, vomiting, anorexia, jaundice, and fatigue. She visited a local emergency department, received intravenous vitamin K, and underwent further laboratory evaluation. She was then transferred to another hospital for higher-level care and admitted with acute liver injury. Treatment included intravenous N-acetylcysteine, ursodiol, albumin, vitamin K, and fresh frozen plasma transfusions for coagulopathy.
test_results: Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrated no evidence of biliary obstruction or chronic liver disease (no ascites, contour nodularity, mass, or lymphadenopathy), though liver size noted to be small (11.5 cm in span).

case_report: A 59-year-old male patient (163 cm, 70 kg) experienced severe pain in both legs immediately following intraocular foreign body removal under general anesthesia. The patient had been hospitalized for surgery after a 3 mm iron particle entered his left eye during a construction site accident. Upon admission, physical examination revealed no abnormalities except for the left eye injury, and the patient did not report any leg discomfort. Preoperative electrocardiogram (ECG), chest radiography, and laboratory findings were normal. In the operating room, standard monitoring was conducted, including ECG, pulse oximetry, noninvasive blood pressure, end-tidal CO2 (EtCO2), and esophageal stethoscope temperature measurement. Initial (pre-induction) vital signs were: heart rate (HR) 60 beats/min, oxygen saturation (SpO2) 100%, systolic blood pressure (SBP) 179 mmHg, diastolic blood pressure (DBP) 78 mmHg, EtCO2 30 mmHg, and respiratory rate (RR) 20 breaths/min. The surgery, which lasted 4 hours and 45 minutes, involved phacoemulsification, vitrectomy, intraocular foreign body removal, endolaser photocoagulation, and fluid-air exchange. The patient was in a supine position without restraints, and graduated compression stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression devices were not used. Immediately after emergence from general anesthesia, the patient reported extreme pain in both legs. The patient had a history of hypertension for over 10 years (baseline SBP/DBP, 160-180/100-78 mmHg) but had not taken antihypertensive medication for years. He also had varicose veins in both legs and was a heavy-drinking smoker, consuming more than 50 g of alcohol and smoking 18 cigarettes per day. There was no family history of hypercoagulable disorders. After the surgical drape was removed, cyanosis was observed in both feet, and the pulse was not palpable in the bilateral dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries. The patient was referred to the vascular surgery department for further evaluation and treatment.
test_results: Doppler signals of the bilateral dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries were absent. Filling defects in the bilateral popliteal arteries, bilateral proximal anterior tibial artery, and bilateral tibioperoneal trunk were visible.

case_report: A 47-year-old woman presented with visual impairment in both eyes. She experienced muscle weakness and atrophy in the distal lower extremities starting at around 7 years old, eventually leading to wheelchair use due to progressive symptoms. Muscle weakness and atrophy in both hands began around 20 years old, with symptoms gradually worsening and spreading to the entire upper extremities. Four months prior to her visit, her visual acuity in both eyes began to decline. Recently, she had difficulty recognizing people's faces from a 5-meter distance, but did not experience color vision deficiency or ocular pain. She had normal cognitive development and excelled academically, completing graduate school and currently working as a teacher. Physical examination showed normal cognitive function, with pupils measuring 3 mm/3 mm, symmetric and reactive to light.
test_results: There were no electric potentials in sensory and motor nerve conduction studies and needle electromyographic examinations revealed giant motor unit action potentials and reduced interference patterns. Pattern reversal visual evoked potentials were significantly prolonged in both eyes. MRI scanning of the cerebral hemispheres, orbits and optic nerves was normal, but high signal intensities were found in bilateral middle cerebellar peduncles on diffusion-weighted and fluid attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) imaging. Corrected visual acuity was 20/130 in the right eye and 20/200 in the left eye, and uncorrected visual acuity was 20/500 in the right eye and 20/1,000 in the left eye. Bilateral optic disc pallor was detected on the temporal sides in fundus photogram. Central scotoma in both eyes was found on Goldmann perimetry. Heterozygous transversion of cytosine to thymine (c.617C>T) in the seventh coding exon of MFN2 was identified.
diagnosis: Hereditary Motor and Sensory Neuropathy Type VI
Orpha_name: Hereditary Motor and Sensory Neuropathy Type VI

case_report: A 9-year-old girl presented to the Emergency Department 4 days after experiencing blunt trauma to her left leg. Upon admission, she was afebrile. Physical examination revealed an area of edema, warmth, erythema, and tenderness with indistinct margins on the anteromedial aspect of the left leg. The remainder of the physical examination was normal, except for obesity, and her medical history was unremarkable. An X-ray of the leg showed no abnormalities. She was initially treated with oral amoxicillin/clavulanic acid for a clinical diagnosis of cellulitis. Despite this, the symptoms persisted for 2 more days, leading to her readmission to the Pediatrics Department. The oral antibiotic was replaced with intravenous amoxicillin/clavulanic acid (75 mg/kg/day). Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 13.6 × 10^3/μL (neutrophils 74.4%, lymphocytes 17.8%, monocytes 6.8%, eosinophils 0.8%), hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL, platelets 292 × 10^3/μL, C-reactive protein 94.1 mg/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 67 mm at 1 hour, and normal blood chemistry. Due to unsatisfactory improvement, the antibiotic therapy was changed 4 days later to cloxacillin (100 mg/kg/day) and ampicillin (100 mg/kg/day). Gradual improvement was noted over the next two days; edema, warmth, and erythema became mild, and tenderness resolved. The patient was discharged 6 days after admission with oral cephalexin (35 mg/kg/day). At a scheduled outpatient visit three days post-discharge, physical examination showed erythema and induration of the skin on the left leg without tenderness or edema, and laboratory findings were within normal range. Ultrasound of the left shin revealed swelling of the soft tissue in the anteromedial aspect with several hypoechoic collections, the largest measuring 0.9 × 2.13 × 2 cm, with indistinct margins and unclear fluid, no increased blood supply, and intact bones, excluding osteomyelitis. Antibiotic therapy was continued based on the impression of deep tissue infection. On a follow-up visit after three weeks on cephalexin, erythema, stiffness, and induration of the skin were still present but reduced compared to the previous examination. A repeated ultrasound showed swelling of the subcutaneous tissue without localized collection or abscess.
test_results: MRI demonstrated edema of the subcutaneous fat medially to the tibial bone with thickening of the subcutaneous septations and unclear boundaries. There was no involvement of bone cortex or marrow and no enhancement was evident.

case_report: A 57-year-old woman with a history of diabetes mellitus presented with swelling in her right leg for the past 2 years. She reported erythema and swelling in the right leg, accompanied by pain. Dermatological examination showed an erythematous, violaceous, indurated sclerotic plaque on the posterolateral aspect of the right tibia. Multiple varicose veins were observed in the posterior tibial area. There was no history of trauma or discharge. The patient had a history of thrombophlebitis in the same leg, occurring twice, four years ago and six years ago. Doppler ultrasound indicated no evidence of deep vein thrombosis. Bilateral dilated varicose veins were detected, with more prominence in the right leg.
test_results: The subcutaneous fat had microcystic changes within the fat lobules. The membrane caused small pseudopapillae with periodic acid-Schiff stain. Macrophage accumulation was found in the subcutaneous tissue. Fibrosis was present in the reticular dermis.

case_report: A 45-year-old male presented with a new erythematous plaque on the left upper chest. Previously, erythematous patches and plaques were noted on the scalp. The new lesion on the left upper chest exhibited raised dusky, violaceous, and erythematous borders with central clearing and overlying scaly crusts. Erythematous plaques were also observed behind both ears bilaterally. No sensory loss was detected over the lesions, and they were non-painful and non-pruritic. The patient did not exhibit any systemic symptoms. He reported a history of improvement with oral steroids. There was no family history of autoimmune diseases. No palpable cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy was found. Other cutaneous examinations of hair and nails were unremarkable.
test_results: A 4-millimeter punch biopsy from lesional skin showed an orthokeratotic and mildly atrophic epidermis with extensive vacuolar degeneration of the basal layer. There was a dense superficial dermal lichenoid-type of lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate with scattered melanophages and presence of colloid bodies. Marked perieccrine chronic inflammation was noted, extending into the deep dermis. Minimal interstitial chronic inflammation, along with dermal mucin, was present. Antinuclear antibody and anti-Ro were positive with speckled titer pattern.

case_report: A 22-year-old African American male presented with reddish-purple atrophic plaques and erythematous patches on the scalp, accompanied by hair loss in the affected areas. The lesions were also observed on the head, primarily on the cheeks, and on the trunk. The patient reported no systemic symptoms such as joint pain, muscle pain, fatigue, Raynaud's phenomenon, or gastrointestinal issues. Laboratory tests showed a normal complete blood count and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Serum electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, liver function tests, urinalysis, and chest radiograms were all within normal limits. Tests for antiphospholipid, anti-Smith, anti-double stranded DNA, anti-histone, anti-ribonuclease-sensitive antigen, extractable nuclear antigen, small nuclear antigen, ribonucleoproteins, U1, U2, anti-SS-A, and anti-SS-B antibodies were negative. Complement levels were normal.
test_results: Examination of the H&E tissue sections demonstrated mild epidermal hyperkeratosis with focal follicular plugging. A mild interface infiltrate of lymphocytes, histiocytes and plasma cells was noted. Rouleaux of erythrocytes were noted in multiple superficial dermal blood vessels. Within the dermis, a superficial and deep, perivascular and periadnexal infiltrate of lymphocytes, histiocytes and plasma cells were observed. Neutrophils and eosinophils were rare, and dermal mucin was not appreciated. DIF displayed positive (+++) deposits of FITC conjugated IgG, present as pericytoplasmic and perinuclear staining within the stratum spinosum of the keratinocytes, and in a linear pattern along the basement membrane zone (BMZ). Additional antibody staining: IgA (+, pericytoplasmic and perinuclear staining of stratum spinosum keratinocytes); IgM (-); IgE (-); complement/C1q (+, linear at the BMZ); complement/C3 (++, mild staining on dermal vascular walls); albumin (+++, pericytoplasmic and perinuclear staining of stratum spinosum keratinocytes, and mild linear staining along the BMZ) and fibrinogen (+++, linear pattern along the BMZ). The IHC staining revealed strong positivities to HLA-DPDQDR and ZAP-70 in most of the dermal inflammatory infiltrate, primarily around dermal blood vessels and within the extracellular matrix. The antibody to COX-2 was also overexpressed around the dermal vessels, and within the dermal extracellular matrix in focal areas surrounding inflammatory cells.

case_report: A 39-year-old Japanese man noticed erythema on his right eyelid and right cheek in 2010. He was treated with topical hydrocortisone butyrate propionate at a local dermatological clinic, but his symptoms did not improve. Laboratory tests at the neighborhood clinic showed no abnormal findings. In 2012, he visited our hospital for further examination of his skin condition. Clinical examination from the frontal view showed eruptions on his bilateral inner and upper eyelids. The main signs included well-demarcated, mildly elevated, dark-red erythemas with pityriasis scales, keratotic papules, and pustules. Swelling around the eyelids was also visible. Additional findings included linearly distributed erythemas with lamellar scales, 1-cm dark-red erythemas with pityriasis scales, and very mild cutaneous atrophy on the right side of his face. These eruptions had coalesced into one large annular, mildly elevated eruption with central pigmentation, although no scales and erythemas were noticeable. Central healing and peripheral elevation were observed. Hyphae were not detected after potassium hydroxide extraction, and his neck and cervical lymph nodes were not palpable. Laboratory testing revealed a slightly decreased white blood cell count of 2,180/ml (normal 3,000–7,800) and slightly elevated antinuclear antibody titers of 40 U (normal <40). Other laboratory results were normal: hemoglobin 10.5 g/dl (normal 10.4–14.4), total protein 7.2 g/dl (normal 6.5–8.0), and albumin 4.7 g/dl (normal 4.0–5.2). Liver and renal function tests were normal. C-reactive protein level was 0.08 mg/dl (normal <0.5), and tests for anti-double-strand DNA antigen, anti-SSA antigen, anti-SSB antigen, and human immunodeficiency viral antibodies were negative.
test_results: Cutaneous histopathological analysis with hematoxylin and eosin staining revealed parakeratosis and hyperkeratosis of the horny layer. Hydropic degeneration and vacuolar changes to the basal layer were also observed. In the dermis, typical dense lymphoid cells were observed around the follicles and eccrine glands. Mucin depositions were observed in the dermal stroma, and periodic acid-Schiff stain revealed that the basement membranes were thicker than those in normal skin. A direct immunofluorescence histopathology test revealed IgG deposition on the basement membrane zone and perifollicular areas.

case_report: A 75-year-old Caucasian woman experienced sudden, painless vision loss in her left eye upon waking. She reported no headaches, jaw pain, or other symptoms. Her past eye history included a brief episode of vision loss with zigzag lines in the left eye three months prior, accompanied by a short-duration headache that resolved on its own. She had a history of essential hypertension and had suffered from Raynaud's phenomenon for 20 years, which had worsened recently. Examination revealed visual acuity of 20/20 in the right eye and the ability to count fingers at 0.5 meters in the left eye, with a left relative afferent pupillary defect. The anterior segment examination was normal, and intraocular pressures were within normal limits. A dilated fundal examination showed a cherry-red spot in the left foveal area, with no visible arteriolar embolus. The right eye had two cotton wool spots, but was otherwise unremarkable. Superficial temporal arteries were palpable, non-tender, and not thickened or nodular, with good flow. Cardiac and carotid artery examinations were unremarkable. Blood tests, including ESR, CRP, platelet counts, and liver function tests, were normal. Fundus fluorescein angiography on the third day showed no choroidal ischemia. She was initially treated with 80 mg of oral prednisolone daily, but this was stopped after three days based on blood test results and angiogram features. She was then started on 150 mg of aspirin. Further examination of her hands revealed tethered skin and spindly fingers. She was referred to rheumatology for further evaluation of her hand condition, Raynaud's phenomenon, and eye symptoms.
test_results: Positive ANA's at 8.1 U (0–1.0 reference range) with a positive anti-centromere antibody and a negative anti-Scl-70 and anti-ds DNA antibody.

case_report: A 67-year-old Caucasian female presented to the emergency department with complaints of difficulty swallowing, itching, and musculoskeletal pain in the arms. The patient also reported chronic musculoskeletal pain and episodes of blue discoloration of the extremities, which had not been previously evaluated. Her medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder (COPD) due to long-term smoking and treatment for arterial hypertension. Initial clinical examination showed normal blood pressure (115/72 mmHg), normal heart rate (77 bpm), and no abnormal findings during abdominal auscultation and palpation. Heart and lung auscultation were unremarkable. Skin redness was observed at the site of itching. Blood tests did not reveal significant abnormalities, but biochemical tests indicated disrupted liver function. Tests for HBV and HBC were negative. A cancer index test showed no signs of neoplasia. Thyroid function tests (Free T4, TSH) and thyroid ultrasound were normal. Quantitative immunoglobulins test showed increased levels of IgA, IgM, and IgE. A CT scan without intravenous contrast, due to a reported allergy, did not show any liver pathology except for dilation of intrahepatic bile ducts, which was later confirmed by ultrasound. Elevated levels of ALP, AST, and γGT were noted. Further specialized tests (ANA and AMA tests) were positive.
test_results: Anti-centromere antibodies (ACAs) test proved positive.

case_report: In 2011, a 48-year-old woman presented with multiple new calcifications in the skin of her back, hips, and shoulders. These calcifications remained stable over the next 5 years. In 2015, she developed symptoms consistent with Raynaud syndrome, and firm plaques were observed on her skin. By March 2016, her condition had worsened, showing edema of the fingers ('puffy fingers'). Radiography confirmed the presence of skin calcifications. Treatment was initiated with systemic prostaglandins, bisphosphonates, and D-penicillamine. After 2 years of treatment, the calcifications reduced in size, but the symptoms of Raynaud syndrome persisted, leading to the prescription of bosentan.
test_results: In the main test, in 100% of swallows, no esophageal contractions were detected. The integrated relaxation pressure was normal. CCv3.0 classified such results as major disorders of peristalsis, in particular, absent contractility. During a multiple rapid swallow test, esophageal contractions were not detected. In both cases, the EGJ-CI was null, indicating significant hypotension of the EGJ, decreased barrier function, and increased risk of pathological reflux. Atrophic changes with diffuse sclerosis were revealed in the longitudinal and circular muscular layers of the esophagus, as well as perivascular and perineural sclerosis. In the myenteric plexus, inflammatory infiltration composed predominantly of lymphocytes was observed. Microcirculatory vessels were also implicated in the disease, appearing with thickening of the vessel wall, and proliferative endarteritis with obliteration of the lumen of the blood vessels.
diagnosis: CREST syndrome with esophageal motility disorder

case_report: A 30-year-old female patient presented with difficulty in chewing due to reduced mouth opening over the past few months. Examination outside the mouth showed multiple poorly defined white patches on the forehead and cheeks. The facial skin appeared smooth, tight, and mask-like, and it was firm and could not be lifted. The temporomandibular joint was stiff upon palpation. Around the mouth, there was fibrosis leading to a small mouth opening with characteristic furrows radiating from the mouth, giving a 'purse string appearance.' The lips were thin, and the nasal alae were atrophied, giving a pinched appearance to the nose, known as 'mouse facies.' Inside the mouth, examination was challenging due to the small mouth opening (28 mm). The tongue was rigid with reduced mobility upon palpation. Periodontal examination showed generalized mild chronic periodontal disease with probing depths ranging from 3-5 mm. Periapical intraoral radiographs indicated normal lamina dura with widening of the periodontal space, most noticeable in the posterior teeth. Stiffening of the phalangeal joints in both fingers and toes was noted, along with flexure contractures resulting in shortened, 'claw-like' fingers.
test_results: Roentgenographic examination of hands showed resorption of terminal phalanges (acro-osteolysis).

case_report: A 47-year-old man with no prior history of autoimmune diseases and previously in good health experienced mild flu-like symptoms including tiredness, fever, cough, and sore throat starting on November 12th. An oropharyngeal swab for SARS-CoV-2 returned positive on November 17th. The patient isolated at home and did not require hospitalization. After three weeks, his fever, cough, and sore throat resolved, but he reported extreme fatigue, abdominal discomfort, and skin redness. On January 1st, he sought emergency care for abdominal pain, vomiting, a generalized skin rash with diffuse erythema, and a burning skin sensation. He also had eyelid swelling and conjunctivitis. Lung and heart auscultation were normal, and no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly were observed. The patient had no history of drug abuse, was not on any medication, and did not smoke. Laboratory tests showed normal ESR, CRP, complete blood count, and serum creatinine. Chest radiography, oxygen saturation, EKG, blood pressure, and heart rate were all normal. The patient was not hospitalized and was treated at home with a proton pump inhibitor for acid reflux and antibiotic ointment for conjunctivitis and blepharitis. The patient showed only marginal improvement and sought care again two weeks later. The generalized skin rash had resolved but was replaced by a heliotrope rash. He still had periorbital edema, conjunctivitis, and a burning sensation in the skin, particularly in the fingertips and around the mouth. The patient reported Raynaud’s phenomenon, swollen fingers, and fingertip pain in the middle finger. He also experienced muscular discomfort and weakness in the chest. Vomiting and abdominal pain had resolved, but he reported dysphagia. Physical examination revealed puffy fingers and a depressed area without clear ulceration at the fingertip of the middle finger.
test_results: Immunofluorescent antinuclear antibody test using HEp-2 cells (ANA) showed strongly positive nucleolar pattern. Anti-PM/Scl 75 and PM/Scl 100 tested positive. Anti-Scl-70, anti-Jo 1, anti-RNA-polymerase III, and other autoantibodies tested negative.

case_report: A 37-year-old female patient arrived at the emergency department with central chest pain persisting for 7 days, radiating to her left shoulder. She reported hemoptysis for the past 8 days, occurring 10–15 times daily, and had one episode of vomiting with blood streaks 2 days before presentation. There were no reports of sweating, palpitations, difficulty breathing, fainting, black stools, or fever. She had a history of severe pulmonary valvular stenosis treated with balloon valvular dilatation in childhood. She was previously identified with a deficiency in a specific blood factor after developing a hematoma post-surgery. She had not been on regular follow-up or treatment for extended periods and had no significant bleeding episodes requiring medical attention. Her last menstrual period was 16 days ago. On examination, her heart rate was 71 beats per minute, all peripheral pulses were palpable, blood pressure was 200/130 mmHg, respiratory rate was 18 breaths per minute, and blood oxygen saturation was 99% on room air. She appeared pale on general examination. Heart auscultation revealed an ejection murmur in the left 2nd parasternal area. Respiratory, abdominal, and neurological examinations were normal. An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed ST-segment depression in leads I, aVL, II, III, aVF, and V4–V6. Her troponin I level was 0.09 ng/ml.
test_results: Echocardiography revealed severe pulmonary stenosis and right ventricular hypertrophy with no regional wall motion abnormality and good left ventricular systolic function.

case_report: A 47-year-old male patient visited the vascular surgery clinic due to recurrent bleeding from large varicose veins on the right thigh. He had previously received sclerotherapy for varicose veins in the same limb and had undergone saphenofemoral ligation and stripping at a young age. Physical examination revealed extensive varicosities on the right thigh and leg with an unusual distribution pattern. The right thigh's circumference was notably larger than the left thigh, but there was no difference in limb length. An ulcer was present on the right thigh at a recent bleeding site. The left limb showed no varicose veins. Palpation indicated that the dilated veins were pulsatile and did not empty when the limb was elevated. Pulse examination showed no abnormalities, and no murmurs were detected during the pre-cordial examination.
test_results: A duplex scan of the right lower limb showed an arterial type of flow pattern in the superficial varices and the femoral vein. A CT angiogram of the lower limbs demonstrated a large AVM involving the right thigh and the leg. The main feeding vessels were from the superficial femoral artery and the popliteal artery.

case_report: A 19-year-old female patient presented with irregular, diffuse swelling for the past year involving the right upper limb and axilla. The swelling was soft in consistency and compressible. Additionally, there was elongation of the right upper limb. Patchy areas of skin discoloration with a reddish-pink hue were observed on the palmar aspect of the right hand and the right extensor forearm, indicating capillary malformations.
test_results: A plain radiograph of the right upper limb showed soft tissue thickening involving upper arm and hand, as well as a few radiodense foci in soft tissue indicating phleboliths. MRI of the right upper limb revealed multiple dilated vascular channels in the subcutaneous and muscular planes in the right upper limb and right axilla, with soft tissue showing venous phase enhancement on post-contrast images. A nidus was identified in the lateral aspect of the right arm on MR angiography (TWIST) images, supplied by the brachial artery. The axillary and subclavian veins were seen dilated and draining the malformation. The rest of the dilated vascular channels in the right forearm and hand did not show early arteriovenous shunting. MRI findings showed diagnostic arterio-venous malformations in the right arm and slow flow vascular malformations in the right forearm and hand.

case_report: A 12-year-old girl visited the maxillofacial department of Shar hospital with a history of painless, bilateral, slow-growing posterior jaw swelling for 3 years. She had undergone multiple consultations and treatments without resolution. Clinical examination revealed symmetrically swollen parotid glands that were firm, non-movable, non-pulsatile, and non-tender to palpation, with normal-colored, intact overlying facial skin. The other two major salivary glands showed no palpable changes. Intraoral examination indicated signs of reduced salivary flow rate, including multiple cervical caries, large restorations on the permanent molars, and remnants of food debris due to decreased saliva washing action. Her parents reported that she drinks plenty of water during meals to aid swallowing. Systemically, her parents denied any symptoms such as fever, malaise, cough, shortness of breath, loss of appetite, or weight loss. The child reported dryness in her eyes, for which she was prescribed eye drops by an ophthalmologist. Her past medical history included an episode of bilateral painful knee joint swelling at age 8, which was treated with aspiration and painkillers.
test_results: The result was 0.2 mL/15 min.

case_report: A 76-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 3-year history of a recurrent itchy rash on the hips, thighs, and under the breasts, accompanied by intermittent lesions resembling vesicles and bullae. Previous treatments with topical and intralesional corticosteroids provided minimal relief. The patient also experienced swelling in the lower extremities. She had a history of long-standing severe lichen sclerosis et atrophicus. Several months before the onset of the rash, she underwent radical vulvectomy and bilateral inguino-femoral lymph node dissection for stage 2/grade 2 invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the vulva. Physical examination revealed multiple erosions with hemorrhagic crusts and multiple clustered translucent papules on the inframammary breasts, abdomen, hips, and proximal thighs. Both legs exhibited 4+ pitting and nonpitting edema along with scattered small vesicular lesions.
test_results: Biopsies from representative lesions showed superficial dermal thin-walled dilated vascular channels surrounded by hyalinized collagen and scant perivascular lymphohistiocytic inflammation. The ectatic vessels showed endothelial cell staining with D2-40. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin was negative.

case_report: A 59-year-old male presented with erythematous skin lesions on the trunk and upper limbs that appeared 20 years ago and regressed after a few months, leaving behind hyperchromic lesions. The patient reported no itching associated with these lesions. Physical examination revealed erythematous-brownish macules, ranging from 0.5 to 5.0 cm in diameter, confluent, and distributed across the abdomen, chest, back, and upper limbs, along with residual hyperchromic macules. Darier sign was negative. Dermoscopy of the erythematous-brownish lesions showed thin and tortuous linear vessels, mild erythema, and a fine pigment network, consistent with the patient's skin type. There was no lymphadenomegaly or bone changes, and laboratory tests, including blood count and chemistry, were normal.
test_results: Histopathological examination showed dilated vessels with moderate inflammatory reaction around, mainly composed of mast cells, best visualized with Giemsa stain.

case_report: A 7-year-old girl presented with intermittently itchy papules and nodules on her bilateral legs, lower back, and dorsal left hand that appeared over 16 months. Her review of systems was negative, and her medical history was unremarkable. Family history included hypothyroidism in her mother, a large congenital nevus and café au lait macule in her father, and cancer in both grandparents (paraganglioma with positive SDHA mutation in paternal grandmother and chronic lymphocytic leukemia in her paternal grandfather) and was negative for similar skin papules. Laboratory results showed antinuclear antibody 1:160, speckled, LDH 329 U/L, and thyroid stimulating hormone 6.67 mcunit/mL. Paraprotein and celiac disease screenings were normal. She was seen by a pediatric endocrinologist, and repeat thyroid testing was normal. Physical examination revealed skin-colored papules and nodules (2–10 mm) clustered around the left anterior knee, as well as sparsely distributed skin-colored papules and nodules on the right lower leg, left lower back, and left dorsal hand.
test_results: Medial thigh shave biopsy revealed superficial and mid-dermal spindle cell proliferation with increased dermal mucin deposition. An Alcian blue stain demonstrated a prominent increase in dermal mucin.

case_report: A 13-year-old male presented with non-painful skin lesions on the abdomen, arms, and legs that developed over a period of five months. The patient also experienced chronic intermittent abdominal pain and diarrhea, but no other symptoms were reported, and he did not have joint pain. His medical history included infantile eczema and irritable bowel syndrome, with no family history of similar skin conditions. Laboratory results showed alkaline phosphatase at 287 U/L, white blood cells at 12,300 cells/uL, and hemoglobin at 12.6 g/dL. Paraprotein screening and celiac disease antibody tests were within normal limits. A pediatric gastroenterologist conducted an evaluation, which was unremarkable. Physical examination identified approximately 30 pink-yellow nodulopapular lesions, ranging from 8 to 15 mm, primarily on the arms and legs, with fewer lesions on the torso. The lesions on the lower legs were flatter and had a pink-brown color.
test_results: Forearm shave biopsy revealed dermal mucin deposition separating the collagen bundles with an increased number of fibroblasts and a histiocytic infiltrate. PAS stain was negative for fungal forms.

case_report: A 5-year-old Caucasian boy presented with acute swelling and pain in the left knee and left elbow. He reported no trauma or other symptoms, but had an upper respiratory tract infection without fever two weeks prior. Laboratory tests, including complete blood cell count, hepatorenal function, serum electrolytes, C-reactive protein (CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), autoantibodies ANA, ENA, anti-dsDNA, and mycoplasma serology, were all within normal limits. Ultrasound examination of the affected joints showed mild joint effusion. The child was treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSDAIs) for 10 days, resulting in clinical resolution. One year later, he experienced swelling of the left knee for two months, which persisted despite NSDAIs treatment. Ultrasound examination revealed a Baker’s cyst and joint effusion in the suprapatellar recess. An intra-articular steroid injection was administered to the knee. Three months later, the child was admitted to the hospital due to persistent knee swelling. Ultrasound and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) confirmed a large Baker’s cyst and showed resolution of the joint effusion in the suprapatellar recess. Laboratory tests, including autoimmunity, were negative. Physical examination identified non-tender, mobile, skin-colored papules in the gluteal and umbilical regions, plaques in the right lumbar region, and nodular lesions in the left lumbar, left scapular, and left anterior and medial femoral regions. The child’s parents noted that the first skin lesions had appeared two years earlier, at which time connective tissue nevus had been diagnosed.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed the presence of a perivascular chronic inflammatory infiltrate in the superficial dermis and interstitial mucine deposition in the reticular dermis.

case_report: A 70-year-old male presented with a single pinkish nodule located on the back of his right hand. The patient reported no symptoms such as itching or pain. His medical history includes long-term psoriasis, which has been treated with topical medications. He reported no family history of skin or hormonal disorders. Despite the lack of symptoms, the patient sought further information about his condition.
test_results: Blood tests showed no endocrine abnormalities including thyroid function. Histopathological examination of a biopsy specimen obtained from the nodule on the dorsum of his hand revealed orthokeratotic hyperkeratosis with patchy parakeratosis, prominent hypergranulosis, and diffuse dissecting mucinous deposition between collagen bundles, along with some bland-looking spindle cells throughout the dermis.

case_report: A 24-month-old Japanese boy was brought to our hospital for assessment of his short stature. He was born at 38 weeks and 4 days gestation with a submucous cleft palate and micrognathia. His birth weight was 3225 g (+0.53 SD for average Japanese male infants), and his birth length was 45 cm (−1.80 SD). The submucous cleft palate was surgically repaired at 18 months, and tympanostomy tubes were inserted for secretory otitis media. Auditory brainstem response testing was normal. At 22 months, bilateral leukocoria was observed, and phacoemulsification with anterior vitrectomy for bilateral lens opacities was performed at another hospital. He was noted to have Pierre Robin sequence, but the connection to his eye symptoms was not explored. He received speech therapy for speech delay. Upon presentation, his weight was 11.6 kg (−0.33 SD) and his height was 79.1 cm (−2.52 SD). His arm span measured 79 cm, and his sitting height was 48.5 cm (sitting height/height ratio 0.61). Physical examination revealed ocular hypertelorism, prominent eyes due to shallow orbits, a flat midface with a depressed nasal bridge, anteverted nares, micrognathia, low-set ears, and limited bilateral elbow flexion. There was no hypotonia, hyperextensible joints, or joint pain. His family, including his parents and two brothers, were healthy. His parents are not consanguineous. His father's height was 182 cm (+1.93 SD for average Japanese adult men), and his mother's height was 147 cm (−2.09 SD for average Japanese adult women). Radiographs indicated thickening of the calvaria, widening of the distal humeral metaphysis, absence of femoral head ossification, deformity of the femoral neck, and distal femoral and proximal tibial epiphyseal ossification centers, consistent with mild spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia. Serum insulin-like growth factor-1 was 20.17 nmol/L (154 ng/ml) (normal range 2.36–20.17 nmol/L [18–154 ng/ml]). An L-arginine stimulation test for growth hormone (0.5 g/kg arginine) showed a peak growth hormone level of 16.4 ng/ml. A luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone/thyrotropin-releasing hormone stimulation test (3 μg/kg luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone; 10 μg/kg thyrotropin-releasing hormone) showed prepubertal and normal thyroid-stimulating hormone responses. His karyotype was 46,XY. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed no abnormalities. Echocardiography revealed no mitral valve prolapse. No mutation was found in exons or exon/intron boundaries of the COL11A1 gene.
test_results: Sequence analysis showed a novel heterozygous mutation in exon 19 of COL2A1, c.1142G > A (p.Gly381Asp). The glycine at amino acid 381 was located in the Gly-X-Y triplet repeats region of the type II collagen triple helix, and it is phylogenetically conserved throughout species. This variant has not been described in the Single Nucleotide Polymorphism database, the 1000 Genomes Project, Leiden Open Variation Database 3.0, or the Human Genetic Variation Database in Japanese.

case_report: A two and a half year old male presented with significant myopia and facial features including maxillary hypoplasia and a flattened nasal bridge. There was no evidence of sensorineural hearing loss, although the patient had a recent history of glue ear. Physical examination showed a beaded vitreous appearance and a high-arched palate, with no midline clefting observed.
test_results: Deletions of exons 41 and 42 [c.3025-3168, p.Gly1009-Val1056] were detected by MLPA.

case_report: A 7-week-old female infant was referred to dermatology for evaluation of multiple superficial hemangiomas located on her head and trunk. She was delivered at full term with a birth weight of 2.8 kg following an uncomplicated pregnancy. The infant had a history of neonatal hypotonia and hypoglycemia, which resolved within 2 days. Her newborn screening test results were normal. There were no reported issues with breathing or feeding. Her parents noted that she had infrequent bowel movements, occurring every 2-3 days. Physical examination revealed a large superficial hemangioma measuring 5 × 4 cm with slight central graying on the midline of her neck. Additionally, there was a small 1-mm superficial hemangioma lateral to this area, suggesting a possible evolving segmental pattern. Three more superficial hemangiomas, each measuring between 1 and 2 cm, were observed on the scalp and upper trunk. No sternal or midline defects were identified, and there were no signs of airway obstruction. Due to the size and distribution of the neck hemangioma, further evaluation was conducted.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging of the head and neck detected an ectopic pituitary gland. The pituitary stalk was not visualized. No vascular anomalies were present. Endocrinology assessment revealed extreme cortisol deficiency (<3 nmol/L [normal range 68-327]) and unrecordable adrenocorticotropic hormone levels (<0.7pmol/L [ref 2.2-13.3]). Gonadotrophins were undetectable (luteinizing hormone <1.0 U/L [ref 2.4-12.6], follicle-stimulating hormone <1.0 U/L [3.5-12.5]). She had a central pattern of hypothyroidism (thyroid stimulating hormone 1.81mU/L [ref 0.4-4.2], free T4 9 pmol/L [ref 10.5-22.8]). Serum prolactin level was elevated (882 mU/L [ref 102-496]). Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) and IGF-binding protein 3 were normal. Screening for diabetes insipidus was negative.

case_report: A 74-year-old male arrived at the emergency department experiencing chest pain, palpitations, and worsening shortness of breath over the past 24 hours. His medical history included high blood pressure and dyslipidemia, for which he was taking lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide and simvastatin. He also had an acquired atrioventricular block managed with DDDR pacing. Over the past year, he reported symptoms such as fatigue, weakness, lack of energy, intolerance to cold, reduced muscle strength, loss of appetite, decreased libido, and changes in hair distribution. His blood pressure had decreased, leading to the discontinuation of lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 102/84 mmHg, heart rate of 65 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 28 breaths per minute, normal oxygen saturation on ambient air, and a temperature of 36.6°C. Signs of heart failure were present, including jugular venous distention, peripheral edema, and pulmonary congestion. Cardiac auscultation noted a protodiastolic gallop. An electrocardiogram showed an atrioventricular sequential paced rhythm with left bundle branch block morphology, no ST-segment deviation, deeply inverted T waves in leads DI, aVL, and precordial leads, and a prolonged QTc interval of 560 ms. Laboratory tests revealed normal complete blood count, serum electrolytes, renal function parameters, and blood glucose levels. Troponin I was mildly elevated at 0.79 ng/mL. Echocardiography indicated a nondilated left ventricle with apical dyskinesia, hyperdynamic basal contraction, a systolic ballooning pattern, and a moderately depressed ejection fraction of 37%. Coronarography showed no significant coronary artery disease, and a left ventriculogram revealed typical apical ballooning. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was not performed due to the presence of a noncompatible pacemaker. During hospitalization, the patient was treated with diuretics, a beta-blocker, and an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. Laboratory data showed a peak troponin I level of 1.38 ng/mL. Urinary meta- and normetanephrines measurements excluded pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma. The patient was referred for endocrine consultation.
test_results: A formal pituitary dynamic test was performed after an overnight fast: growth hormone-releasing hormone 100 μg, corticotropin-releasing hormone 100 μg, thyrotropin-releasing hormone 200 μg, and gonadotropin-releasing hormone 100 μg bolus (intravenous) at time 0; baseline/peak hormone levels were as follows: growth hormone (<2 ng/mL): 0.15/0.18; prolactin (2–18 ng/mL): 21/35; cortisol (4–23 μg/dL): 1.5/4.1; follicle-stimulating hormone (1–18 U/L): 2.2/2.8; luteinizing hormone (3–35 U/L): 0.3/1.1; other baseline values were insulin-like growth factor 1 (48–188 ng/mL): 33; adrenocorticotropin (0–46 pg/mL): 31; triiodothyronine (60–181 ng/dL): 81; thyroxine (4.5–10.9 μg/dL): 2.2; free thyroxine (0.89–1.80 ng/dL): 0.42; total testosterone (188–772 ng/dL): <10. Thyroid autoantibodies were negative. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed a normal sized and positioned pituitary gland with no morphological abnormalities and a centered pituitary stalk.

case_report: A 56-year-old male was admitted on August 30, 2011, presenting with a 6-month history of increasing chest discomfort. Previously, he had experienced brief episodes of chest discomfort once or twice annually over several years. Approximately six months prior to admission, the frequency of these episodes increased, and he reported repetitive chest discomfort and a sensation of rapid heartbeat starting the day before admission. A chest radiograph showed dextrocardia, which he mentioned was first identified incidentally in 2008 at another facility, with no further evaluation conducted at that time. No other significant medical history was noted.
test_results: A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed a heart rate of 190 bpm and wide QRS complex tachycardia. A follow-up electrocardiogram revealed a shortened PR interval (112 ms), a slurring and slow rise of the initial upstroke of the QRS complex (delta wave), and secondary ST segment and T wave changes. A 24-hour Holter revealed baseline sinus rhythm with rare premature ventricular complexes and short-runs of paroxysmal atrial tachycardia. A computed tomography (CT) angiography was performed. There was no significant intracoronary abnormality except myocardial bridging in a diagonal branch. Persistent left SVC draining into the right atrium via the coronary sinus was observed. The PA sling, in which the left PA arose from the right PA, was constricting the distal trachea. A right tracheal bronchus was also detected.
diagnosis: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia

case_report: A 72-year-old male Caucasian patient with a history of ischaemic cardiomyopathy, equipped with a two-chamber ICD for secondary prevention, presented to the emergency department due to ongoing tachycardia. He had experienced an increased heart rate for several days. He did not report any chest pain or fainting episodes. Physical examination revealed a consistent tachycardia but was otherwise unremarkable. Since 2017, he has been on long-term medication with amiodarone (200 mg once daily) and bisoprolol (5 mg twice daily).
test_results: The electrocardiogram (ECG) performed upon arrival revealed a regular broad complex tachycardia with a ventricular frequency of 117/min, superior axis, positive concordance in precordial leads (V1–V6) and a deflection time >100 ms in lead V1 compatible with VT or antidromic AVRT involving a left-posterior accessory pathway (AP). Monophasic positive P-waves in leads V1–V6 with an atrial rate of ∼235/min were registered, suggestive of atypical atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction. Interrogation of the ICD showed atrial flutter (cycle length, 260 ms) with 2:1 atrioventricular (AV) conduction. The electrophysiological study revealed a bidirectionally conducting, left-posterior AP. Right ventricular (RV) pacing induced a C-shaped activation sequence of the 10-pole coronary sinus (CS) catheter and atrial pacing with decreasing cycle length led to increasing preexcitation of the QRS complex; 12-lead ECG-morphology of the pre-excited QRS complex was identical to the broad complex tachycardia upon admission.

case_report: A 32-year-old male presented with a history of infertility for three years following four years of marriage. Over the past three years, he experienced reduced sexual desire, decreased frequency of intercourse, reduced ejaculation volume, shorter erection duration (less than 2 minutes), and penile weakness before ejaculation. He did not report any symptoms such as headache, dizziness, or visual disturbances. Physical examination revealed thin beard and pubic hair, while his Adam’s apple, bilateral testis, and breasts appeared normal. Seminal analysis conducted twice before surgery indicated oligoasthenozoospermia. Preoperative gonadal hormone levels are detailed in table 2. Levels of FSH, LH, prolactin (PRL), cortisol, thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), and growth hormone (GH) were within normal ranges. Testosterone (T) and estradiol (E2) levels were significantly below the minimum reference values but showed marked improvement following hCG administration. The GnRH stimulation test indicated a low response of serum LH and FSH levels after administering 0.1 mg GnRH. The patient's karyotype was 46 XY.
test_results: The sella turcica was clearly enlarged, which contained an elliptic lump (2.5 ×2.0 ×1.8 cm) and appeared as slightly longer T1 and T2 signals. In front of the lump, several cycloid cysts appeared as long T1 and T2 signals. The basilar part of the sella turcica clearly sagged and the pituitary stalk was not clearly visible because of space occupation in the sphenoid sinus and sellar area. The optic chiasma was obviously oppressed and its location was moved upward. The bilateral carotid arteries were encased due to oppression of the surrounding tissues.

case_report: A 75-year-old male reported experiencing double vision and a drooping left eyelid for a duration of two weeks. He did not report any headaches or episodes of vomiting. Physical examination showed mild ptosis along with restricted upward, inward, and downward movements of the left eye. There were no differences in pupil size or abnormalities in the pupillary light reflexes. The findings indicated an isolated impairment of the left oculomotor nerve.
test_results: MRI revealed an 18 mm homogeneously enhanced pituitary tumor that extended latero-posteriorly on the left side. There was no evidence of intratumoral hemorrhage. CT revealed an erosion of the left posterior clinoid process. CISS MRI revealed compression of the left oculomotor nerve by the tumor at the oculomotor triangle.

case_report: A 78-year-old Caucasian woman with a history of essential hypertension, left total hip arthroplasty, depression, and hyperlipidemia arrived at the emergency department experiencing generalized weakness, tongue twitching, and involuntary jerking movements of her lower limbs for one month. She also mentioned intermittent diffuse headaches, loss of appetite, and an unintentional weight gain of approximately 10-15 pounds over the past six months. She did not report any sudden severe headaches, numbness, tingling, vision changes, or recent memory loss, nor did she experience any speech or gait abnormalities. Upon admission, her vital signs were as follows: temperature 96.9 °F, blood pressure 115/83 mmHg, pulse 55 beats/min, and respiratory rate 18. Her BMI was 28. The neurological examination showed tongue fasciculation and bilateral lower extremity myoclonus, while her visual field testing was normal. Basic laboratory tests, including a complete blood count and metabolic panel, were unremarkable. A chest X-ray did not reveal any acute abnormalities. A CT scan of the head identified an apparent seller mass but no acute pathology. The seller mass alone did not account for the neurological symptoms. Additional neurologic, infectious, and rheumatologic evaluations were negative for antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, Lyme disease, and West Nile serology. An MRI of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine showed no mass effect.
test_results: Pituitary MRI with and without contrast showed a 2.0 x 1.5 x 2.3 cm sellar/suprasellar mass. The mass was mildly deforming the optic chiasm, invading the left cavernous sinus, and deviating the infundibular stalk to the right side.
diagnosis: Panhypopituitarism due to non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma

case_report: A 4-year-old male child, born to parents who are not related by blood, visited the pediatric outpatient department with symptoms of abdominal distension, poor weight gain, and short stature. There was no history of excessive urination or excessive thirst. The child had no prior history of trauma or surgery. He was delivered at term through normal vaginal delivery and received vaccinations according to the national immunization program of India. There was no past history of tuberculosis or chronic illness. On examination, the child weighed 8 kg and measured 82 cm in height, both below the 5th percentile, and was identified as having failure to thrive. He was admitted for further evaluation. Examinations of the central nervous system, cardio-respiratory system, and abdomen were normal. Visual acuity was 6/6 in both eyes, and funduscopy results were normal. Vital signs were within normal limits for his age. Complete blood count and urine tests were normal. Urine specific gravity and urine osmolality (670 mOsm/kg) were within normal ranges. Tests for Mantoux and HIV ELISA were negative. Ultrasonography of the abdomen and chest X-ray were normal.
test_results: Contrast enhanced MRI revealed normal size sella turcica, thinned out enhancing pituitary gland (2 mm height) in the bottom of sella, midline infundibulum, and nonvisualization of T1-weighted bright spot of posterior pituitary gland. Rest of sella turcica was filled with CSF signal. No intra sellar herniation of optic chiasma or no hydrocephalus was seen. Visualized brain parenchyma was normal.
Orpha_name: Pituitary deficiency due to empty sella turcica syndrome

case_report: A 54-year-old male was referred to the Rheumatology Division of Fornaroli Hospital from the Infective Department. In February 2014, he was admitted to the hospital due to interstitial lung disease of uncertain origin, presenting with fever accompanied by shivering, dry cough, and chest pain. A chest X-ray revealed a right subclavicle interstitial consolidation. Laboratory tests indicated an ESR of 28 mm/h (cut-off value ≤10 mm/h) and a C-reactive protein level of 6.66 mg/dL (normal range: 0–5). Tests for antinuclear antibodies (ANA), cryoglobulin, extractable nuclear antibodies (ENAs), anti-DNA native antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) were negative. Complement levels (C3, C4) were within the normal range. Rheumatoid factor (RF) was 24 UI/mL (normal range <12) and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies were 17 UA/mL (normal range <5). Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) levels were normal. Quantiferon-TB Gold test was negative. Serology for microbial agents including Legionella, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Chlamydia was negative. A restrictive defect on functional lung exams was excluded, and the diffusion capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO) was normal. The patient had no history of smoking.
test_results: A lung/abdominal CT with contrast enhancement showed an interstitial consolidation with centrilobular branching linear structures with bronchial dilatation and multifocal areas of ground-glass attenuation at the right superior and medium lobe of lung in the posterior segment. There were pleura's thickening at the lingula and fibrotic lines with consolidation at the left superior lobe of lung in the anterior segment, also. Moreover, there were some mediastinic bilateral lymphadenopathies. A lung bronchoscopy with a bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was made. Bacterial BAL fluid cultures were negative. Culture and genome for Koch's bacillus were negative. BAL cytology excluded monoclonality disorders and showed increased numbers of neutrophils and eosinophils. A positron emission tomography-computed tomography (18F-FDG PET/CT) showed an elevated glucometabolic activity at bilaterally axillary lymphadenopathies and at level of pulmonary consolidation seen at HR-CT. US of right lung, at the fifth posterior intercostal space, showed the presence of Ultrasound Lung Comets (ULCs).
diagnosis: Nonspecific Interstitial Pneumonia  in Rheumatoid Arthritis

case_report: A 45-year-old woman was referred to our hospital for further evaluation of an abnormality found on a chest X-ray during a routine medical check-up. She has a history of smoking (2 pack-year) but no history of occupational dust exposure. She reported no symptoms such as fever, shortness of breath, or cough, and did not experience arthralgia, muscle ache, or weakness. She has dysmenorrhea and has been on hormone therapy for over a year. Physical examination revealed mechanic’s hands on both fingers, Gottron’s papules on the knuckles, and keratotic erythema on her elbows and knees. No crackles were heard on auscultation. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 6700/μL, C-reactive protein at 0.00 mg/dL, creatine kinase (CK) at 107 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase at 233 U/L, KL-6 at 2990 U/mL, and SP-D at 507 ng/mL. Screening for anti-aminoacyl tRNA synthetase (ARS) antibodies was positive, while other autoimmune antibodies, including anti-Jo-1 and anti-MDA-5, were negative. Spirometry and diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide were within normal limits. Chest X-ray revealed bilateral consolidation, mainly in the lower lung fields, along with volume loss in the lower lobes. Chest CT showed bilateral patchy ground-glass opacifications with interlobular septal thickening and intralobular lines, described as a 'crazy paving' pattern, predominantly in the lower lobes. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was clear, and transbronchial lung biopsy specimens were non-diagnostic.
test_results: Histological findings showed interstitial inflammation and interlobular septal thickening associated with inflammatory cell infiltration, mainly involving lymphocytes and plasma cells scantily associated with the intra-luminal organization. A skin biopsy showed oedematous changes and inflammatory cell infiltration, partly around the capillaries in the epidermis.
diagnosis: Non-specific interstitial pneumonia  associated with clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis

case_report: The patient is a 41-year-old male diabetic stone carver who has not smoked for the past 20 years. He reports experiencing increasing shortness of breath over the last 2 months. He was admitted for further evaluation based on findings from a high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) scan. The patient also reported having periodic fevers and chills. Upon admission, his medications included metformin, verapamil, and propranolol. Physical examinations of the heart and lungs were normal. A thorax CT scan revealed bilateral opacities predominantly in the lower lobes and peripheral regions of the lungs, along with interstitial septal thickening. Complete blood count (CBC) results were within normal limits. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 42 mm/hr. Tests for rheumatoid factor (RF) and antinuclear antibodies (ANA) were negative. An echocardiogram indicated a pulmonary arterial pressure (PAP) of 35-40 mmHg.
test_results: Pathology of lingula and LLL (left lower lobe) biopsy showed mildly distorted alveolar architecture due to diffuse interstitial chronic inflammatory cell infiltration associated with mild fibrosis and scattered Masson bodies, foci of follicular lymphoid aggregates, DIP (desquamative interstitial pneumonia) reaction, peribronchiolar foamy macrophage aggregation, prominent pneumocyte type II hyperplasia and a few subpleural honeycomb changes. There was no evidence of unquestionable fibroblastic foci or heterogeneous involvement of the lung tissue. Trichrome staining revealed no prominent collagenized fibrosis in interstitium.

case_report: A seven-year-old boy presented with mild ptosis and a gradual decrease in vision in the left eye. Physical examination revealed facial asymmetry, left hemifacial hypertrophy, and moderate ptosis and proptosis of the left eye. There was no history of medical or surgical intervention, and family history was unremarkable. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/30 in the left eye. Cycloplegic refraction showed +1.75 diopters in the right eye and +3.5 diopters in the left eye. A relative afferent pupillary defect of +1 was noted in the left eye. The left eye exhibited 2 mm ptosis with normal levator palpebrae function. Hertel exophthalmometry measurements were 14 mm for the right eye and 21 mm for the left eye, with a bar reading of 107 mm. Axial length measurements were 22.21 mm for the right eye and 24.51 mm for the left eye. Extraocular muscle movement was normal. Slit lamp examination revealed a clear cornea and normal anterior chamber depth. The iris was cryptless with a band of hyperpigmentation at the pupil margin. A comprehensive physical examination, including skin and dental assessments, showed no abnormalities. Height and weight were within normal limits for age, and mental and intellectual abilities were age-appropriate. Intraocular pressure was measured at 13 mmHg in the right eye and 28 mmHg in the left eye without medication.
test_results: Gonioscopy showed anterior iris insertion and angle dysgenesis. Peripapillary nerve fiber layer optical coherence tomography (OCT) and perimetry were normal in the right eye, but in the left eye there was severe nerve fiber layer loss in all quadrants in peripapillary OCT and a double arcuate scotoma in perimetry. Axial and coronal orbital computerized tomography (CT) scan showed left proptosis and axial elongation of the left globe.

case_report: An 11-month-old male infant was brought to the hospital due to persistent vomiting, reduced oral intake, and decreased urine output. His medical history included being born prematurely at 30 weeks (twin pregnancy) and a condition identified at four weeks of age. For the past two months, he had experienced intermittent spit-ups, leading to changes in his formula. Despite these changes, the spit-ups increased in frequency and severity, becoming persistent after each feeding two days before hospital admission. The infant also showed reduced oral intake and urine output. Upon arrival, he had a heart rate of 189 beats per minute, a respiratory rate of 24 breaths per minute, and an oxygen saturation of 92% on room air. His growth measurements were below the fifth percentile for weight and length. Physical examination revealed fatigue, dry mucous membranes, and delayed capillary refill. Characteristic facial features were noted. Laboratory tests showed normal sodium (146 mg/dL), potassium (4.4 mg/dL), and chloride (102 mg/dL) levels. Blood urea nitrogen was 55 mg/dL, and creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL, indicating acute kidney injury (AKI). Calcium was elevated at 14 mg/dL. After receiving a weight-based normal saline bolus, the AKI resolved, but calcium remained high at 12.9 mg/dL. The patient was admitted for further management due to hypercalcemia. Parathyroid hormone (PTH) was low at 5.7 pg/mol (reference range: 12-88 pg/mol). Thyroid-stimulating hormone, free T4, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels were normal. Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) was low at 73 U/L. Further tests ruled out a rare inherited disorder based on normal vitamin B6, ALP isoenzymes, and minimally elevated phosphoethanolamine. Parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP) was elevated at 15.3 pmol/L (reference range: <2.5 pmol/L). Additional evaluations, including lactate dehydrogenase, uric acid, human chorionic gonadotropin, homovanillic acid, and vanillylmandelic acid, were normal. Imaging studies, including a neck ultrasound and CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, did not reveal any suspicious masses. A skeletal survey showed normal bone mineralization. The elevated PTHrP was associated with the AKI rather than an underlying malignancy.
test_results: Urine studies demonstrated an elevated urinary excretion of calcium and a follow-up renal US showed bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis.

case_report: A 40-year-old female visited the outpatient department with complaints of dark discoloration of fingers upon exposure to cold for the past 2 years, and tightening and darkening of skin for the past year. The discoloration and pain in her fingers would reverse with re-warming over 15 to 20 minutes, accompanied by redness. A year ago, she noticed skin tightening on her face, which progressively made it difficult to open her mouth completely. This was followed by similar tightening of the skin on her hands, forearms, arms, and feet over the course of a year, with the affected skin becoming progressively darker. She reported difficulty swallowing solid food and experiencing epigastric pain for the past 6 months, and breathlessness while climbing stairs for the past 3 months. She also observed asymptomatic darkening and thickening of the skin over the knuckles of both hands and feet over the past 6 months, which worsened over time. She had no personal or family history of diabetes mellitus, had two children, and regular menstrual cycles. Physical examination revealed diffuse hyperpigmentation on the face, upper and lower limbs, and skin tightening on the face, upper limbs up to the mid-arm, and lower limbs up to the mid-thighs. Laboratory investigations showed normal complete blood count, chest X-ray, ECG, and urine microscopy. Pulmonary function tests indicated a severe restrictive ventilatory defect, and a barium swallow test showed delayed esophageal emptying. Serum ANA levels were elevated with titers of 1:80, and anti-Scl 70 antibodies were present. Further examination showed rugose velvety hyperpigmentation, mainly over the knuckles and toes, with milder changes observed on the neck and axillae. Blood sugar levels were normal, and fasting serum insulin was 9.2 micro units/ml. Serum vitamin B12 level was 304 pg/ml, within the normal range.
test_results: It showed epidermal hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and papillomatosis giving it a church spire appearance. The papillary dermis showed melanin incontinence with melanophages.

case_report: A 51-year-old male presented with intermittent fever reaching up to 40°C, worsening shortness of breath, fatigue, and weight loss. His medical history included arterial hypertension managed with olmesartan and hydrochlorothiazide, with no other reported medical conditions or medications. Upon admission, physical examination revealed bilateral crackles in the lungs and a palpable, hyperpigmented skin lesion with surface desquamation and a velvety texture on the left areola. Oropharyngeal candidiasis was also noted. No additional abnormalities were observed during the physical examination. Laboratory tests showed normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 9 g/dL) and lymphopenia (total lymphocytes 380/μL). Arterial blood gas analysis indicated moderate hypoxemia (pO2 71 mmHg) and hypocapnia (pCO2 30 mmHg). Chest X-ray identified multiple parenchymal infiltrates, and bronchoalveolar lavage samples revealed cysts of Pneumocystis jirovecii. The patient was treated with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (160/800 mg, 2 tablets orally every 8 hours) and fluconazole (200 mg orally every 24 hours). Serological tests were positive for HIV-1 antibodies, with a high plasma HIV-1 RNA viral load (325,000 copies/mL) and a CD4+ T cell count of 37 cells/μL. HIV-1 genotypic drug resistance testing showed a wild-type virus (CRF12_BF), and HLA-B*5701 was negative. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) viremia was detected at 1412 copies/mL. The patient was started on antiretroviral therapy (ART) with raltegravir 400 mg orally every 12 hours and a fixed-dose combination of tenofovir/emtricitabine orally every 24 hours.
test_results: Excisional skin biopsy of the left areola lesion revealed focal hyperkeratosis, mild papillomatosis, and hyperpigmentation of the basal layer. Dermal papillae projected upwards as finger-like projections with prominent verticalisation of subepithelial vessels and scattered deposition of melanophages. The valleys between papillae showed mild acanthosis and seemed occasionally filled with keratotic material.

case_report: A 1-year-old female child with normal growth and developmental milestones presented with progressive darkening and thickening of the skin. The darkening was first noticed around the axillae and groin at about 2 months of age and gradually spread to other body parts, including the palms and soles. The skin became more hyperpigmented and thickened over the flexors. There was no family history of similar conditions, and no history of drug intake, polyuria, polydipsia, or weight loss. Cutaneous examination showed generalized hyperpigmentation and thickening, excluding the face. The skin was more hyperpigmented, thickened, velvety, and rugosed over the neck, axillae, cubital fossae, wrists, groin, buttocks, knees, and ankles. The patient also had tripe palms and plantar keratoderma. The mucosae, nails, hair, and scalp were free of any lesions. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory tests, including serum biochemistry panel, urinalysis, thyroid profile, growth hormone, insulin level, and oral glucose tolerance test, were within normal limits. Chest X-ray and ultrasonography of the abdomen showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Histopathology of the skin revealed hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis and mild acanthosis. The dermal papillae showed upward finger-like projections and the valleys between the papillae were filled with keratotic material. The dermis and the subcutis were absolutely normal.

case_report: An 18-year-old female visited the outpatient clinic with dry, scaly skin covering her body, a condition that began at six months old. There was no history of convulsions or issues with vision, hearing, teeth, or bones. She had not experienced menarche and had a low IQ, leading to her dropping out of school. She was born full-term via normal vaginal delivery to non-consanguineous parents, and no family members had similar conditions. Clinical examination showed ichthyotic skin, especially on the upper and lower limbs. Palmoplantar keratoderma with hyperlinearity of the palms was noted. She was shorter than average for her age (4’5” height, 31 kg weight), with underdeveloped breasts, areola, and nipples, and infantile external genitalia. Hair was absent in the axilla and pubic regions but normal on the scalp. Routine hematologic and biochemical tests were normal, except for mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase (212 IU/L) and low serum calcium (6.8 mg/dl). Hormonal analysis revealed elevated follicular stimulating hormone (FSH - 126.66 IU/L) and luteinizing hormone (LH - 32.47 U/L). Ultrasonography of the abdomen and pelvis showed a hypoplastic, infantile uterus (1.6 × 0.4 cm) and ovaries (right ovary - 18 × 7 mm, left ovary - 14 × 7 mm), a small right kidney, and a bulky left kidney with a dilated pelvicalyceal system. Renal function tests were normal, and there was no clinical evidence of renal impairment.
test_results: Karyotyping showed female character and her buccal mucosa was positive for X-chromatin. A 4 mm punch biopsy obtained from the skin over her right leg revealed features of hyperkeratosis, thinning of suprapapillary epidermal plates, slight elongation of club shaped rete ridges with non-specific mononuclear inflammatory cell infiltrate in the dermis.

case_report: The patient was born to a 26-year-old mother with a history of four pregnancies and three births. The pregnancy was marked by deep vein thrombosis and limited prenatal care. The patient was delivered full-term via vaginal delivery with APGAR scores of 9 at both 1 and 5 minutes. Birth measurements included a weight of 3.43 kg (53rd percentile), length of 49 cm (50th percentile), and head circumference of 36 cm (90th percentile). The patient was admitted to the NICU for 3 days due to respiratory distress and required supplemental oxygen, but was discharged home on room air. At 5 months old, the patient presented with torticollis, hypotonia, developmental delay, failure to thrive, and a small chest. A skeletal survey revealed bilateral metaphyseal flaring of the long bones in both upper and lower extremities, as well as flaring at the costochondral rib junctions. An abdominal ultrasound indicated a small splenule with normal liver and kidney. A G-tube was placed at 1 year of age due to persistent failure to thrive. The patient developed a need for daytime oxygen and nocturnal BiPAP support. At 2 years old, the patient was hospitalized for respiratory failure associated with pneumonia and was transferred to CHOP for evaluation for VEPTR placement.
test_results: Chest x-rays and CT showed a bell-shaped chest and shortened, widened and bulbous ribs. MRI of the chest and spine demonstrated severe chest wall hypoplasia with hypoplastic lungs, dysmorphic vertebrae with loss of vertebral body height at C7–T3, posterior vertebral body hypoplasia at T10–L3, hypoplastic vertebral body at L5, and a horizontal sacrum.

case_report: A 29-year-old woman presented with complaints of headache, nasal congestion, and reduced sense of smell for several weeks. She reported no issues with vision, skin, sensation, or hearing. Her medical history included seasonal rhinosinusitis, with flare-ups in spring and autumn, but was otherwise unremarkable. Over the past week, she had been using a nasal steroid spray and antihistamines, which provided incomplete relief. Physical examination showed asymmetry of the left eye and painful swelling in the upper left orbit. An antibiotic and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory were prescribed.
test_results: The X-ray revealed an opacity of the left frontal sinus and a right shift of the nasal septum. The CT scan revealed expansion of the anterior portion of the left frontal bone, with involvement of the orbital surface and the ethmoid bone. Magnetic resonance imaging and scintigraphy confirmed the presence of lesions in the orbital surface of both the frontal and ethmoid bones. Blood analysis excluded any endocrine abnormality.

case_report: A 25-year-old male presented to the emergency room with quadriparesis following a bicycle accident. He had a history of facial deformities since early childhood, which included nasal blockage, mouth breathing, mild snoring, and progressive bowing of the shins. There was no family history of similar conditions. The patient was employed and had been commuting by bicycle when he fell, landing on his face and sustaining facial bruising. He experienced immediate neck pain and weakness in all four limbs, with limited ability to lift his arms and move his legs. He was transferred to the hospital three days post-injury. Physical examination revealed symmetrical frontal and maxillary bossing, a symmetric soft tissue bulge of the hard palate, broad forearms, sausage-like fingers, and bowing of both legs with saber shins. The nasal bridge was flat and elevated due to soft tissue thickening. No café au lait spots were noted. Neurological examination showed grade 3 muscle power in the arms with significant distal hand muscle weakness and grade 2 muscle power in the legs. All deep tendon reflexes were absent, plantar reflexes were extensor, and there was a sensory level to all modalities at the groin.
test_results: MRI of the spine showed diffuse enlargement of the laminae, transverse processes and spinous processes of the entire spine (mainly involving the posterior elements) with cervical canal stenosis and a cervical cord contusion at C 4–5 level. On T1 weighted images the posterior elements were hyperintense. The facet joints of the cervical vertebrae were also enlarged. Skull X-rays and CT scans with bone windows showed diffuse thickening of the inner and outer tables of all the skull bones with a widened diploe. The brain parenchyma, subarachnoid cisterns and paranasal sinuses were normal.

case_report: A 26-year-old female presented with a painless swelling over the left mandibular region, with no specific duration of onset. The swelling was initially noticed by a photographer, prompting her to seek consultation. She reported no issues with mouth opening, chewing food, facial trauma, or other local symptoms. Her medical history included two episodes of painful bluish discoloration of the fingers when exposed to extreme cold, which were treated symptomatically as chilblains. She was not on any regular medication and reported no lasting disability from these episodes. Physical examination showed normal vital signs, facial asymmetry, and expansion of the left mandible body. Mild discoloration of the fingers was observed upon exposure to cold water. The rest of the systemic and skin examination was unremarkable. Hormonal profile tests indicated normal thyroid, adrenal, and gonadal function.
test_results: A skeletal survey revealed an expansible osteolytic lesion involving the body and candle of the left side of the mandible.

case_report: A 40-year-old female presented with a swelling in the lower right and left posterior teeth region persisting for 6 years. The swelling was asymptomatic. Medical history was noncontributory. Extraoral examination showed a swelling in the right posterior mandible, extending anteroposteriorly from 1.0 cm from the commissure to 4.0 cm in front of the angle of the mandible, and superoinferiorly from 1.0 cm above the lower border of the mandible to 0.5 cm from the commissural line, measuring 4.0 × 3.0 cm. The swelling was ill-defined, hard, and nontender with normal overlying skin.
