Intraorally, the swelling extended from the mesial aspect of tooth 44 to the distal aspect of tooth 47, causing slight obliteration of the buccal vestibule. The lingual cortex showed slight expansion, and the overlying mucosa was stretched but intact. Another extraoral examination revealed a diffuse swelling on the left lower border of the mandible, extending 2.0 cm behind the angle of the mouth to 5.0 cm from the angle of the mandible, measuring 3.0 × 2.0 cm, hard and nontender with normal overlying skin. Intraorally, this swelling extended from the mesial aspect of tooth 34 to the distal aspect of tooth 37 without obliteration of the buccal vestibule, and the overlying mucosa was normal. Submandibular lymph nodes were palpable on both sides, solitary, mobile, and nontender. An orthopantomograph showed a well-defined multilocular radiolucency with specks of radiopacity in the right and left posterior mandible. The radiolucency extended from the region of tooth 43 to the ramus of the mandible on the right side and from the region of tooth 34 to tooth 37 on the left side of the mandible, with tooth 36 missing. The lower border of the mandible was intact. An occlusal radiograph showed expansion of the buccal and lingual cortices on both sides of the mandible, with a ground glass appearance. A computed tomography (CT) scan revealed well-defined lytic lesions with radiopacities involving the right and left posterior mandible regions, with buccal and lingual cortical expansion. Routine blood and urine investigations, along with serum examination for alkaline phosphatase activity and calcium profile, were performed, and the values were within normal limits.
test_results: Specimens were submitted for histopathological examination.

case_report: A nine-year-old male patient presented with a swelling in the right upper back tooth region, which had been growing over the past three months. The patient reported no pain, pus discharge, or other discomfort aside from facial asymmetry. Family and dental history were noncontributory. Physical examination revealed a diffuse, well-defined unilateral swelling measuring approximately 4 × 3.5 cm on the right middle third of the face. The swelling extended from 1 cm below the infraorbital margin to the inferior border of the mandible, from the ala of the nose to the anterior border of the ramus. The skin over the swelling appeared normal. Palpation confirmed the swelling was hard with well-defined borders, non-tender, and without local temperature rise or paresthesia. Intraoral examination showed a solitary, well-defined unilateral ovoid swelling in the upper right buccal vestibule, extending from the upper right front tooth region to the upper right back tooth region, measuring about 4 cm × 3 cm, without crossing the midline. The swelling was normal in color with no surface changes, causing obliteration of the buccal vestibule, buccal cortical expansion, and slight palatal expansion. Palpation confirmed the swelling was hard and non-tender. Intraoral periapical radiographic (IOPA) examination showed radiolucency involving enamel, dentin, and pulp in the upper right posterior deciduous teeth and erupting premolars periapically, with a ground-glass trabecular pattern. The maxillary true occlusal radiograph indicated increased radiopacity and buccal cortical expansion with a ground-glass appearance, without palatal involvement. Cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) axial section revealed expansion of the buccal and palatal cortical plates with a well-defined margin and typical ground-glass trabecular pattern, involving more than half of the right maxillary sinus.
test_results: Microscopically revealed irregularly shaped trabeculae of immature woven bone in a cellular, loosely arranged fibrous stroma. The bone trabeculae were not connected to each other and did not display any functional orientation.

case_report: A 22-year-old female has been monitored annually for a cystic mass located at the tail of the pancreas, initially identified when she was 15 years old during a screening for acute abdominal conditions. Upon transferring to our hospital, routine follow-ups continued to observe the lesion. Six years after the initial identification, she began experiencing intermittent epigastric pain and back pain, typically occurring at night and lasting for 2 to 3 hours. Over the course of six years, the mass increased in size from 3.3 cm to 5.1 cm in diameter, averaging a growth rate of 0.3 cm per year. Notably, in the last three months, the mass expanded rapidly to 6.3 cm, coinciding with the onset of epigastric pain.
test_results: A CT scan detected a solitary, irregularly formed, multilocular cystic tumor with thin septum and calcification. Its septum and capsule are not enhanced, and both splenic artery and vein are not invaded by the tumor. In findings of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), the tumor showed low intensity in T1 and high intensity in a T2 weighted image. Endoscopic ultrasound sonography (EUS) identified a multilocular cystic lesion with calcification, but no nodules on the septal walls were detected. There were no communications between the cystic tumor and the main pancreatic duct (MPD). The distal portion of the MPD was clearly displaced by the tumor. Furthermore, small branches of the pancreatic duct around the tumor were detected.
diagnosis: Acinar Cell Cystadenoma  of the Pancreas

case_report: The patient is a 6-year-old boy from a non-consanguineous marriage, referred to a hand surgery clinic due to short upper limbs. The patient is an Afghan refugee living in Iran. Complete birth information is unavailable. According to the patient's mother, there is no family history of similar issues. Both parents are healthy. The patient has a history of cleft lip surgery in infancy and has undergone surgery for gastroesophageal reflux disease. Examination revealed short arms, with regular shoulder and hand movements. There is a 30-degree flexion contracture in the left elbow, while the right elbow shows no issues. Forearm supination and pronation movements are normal on both sides (87 degrees supination and pronation). Genital examination showed micropenis and cryptorchidism, necessitating referral to a pediatric surgeon. The patient has a height of 147 cm (approximately 50th percentile based on WHO height-for-age chart) and normal intelligence. Dysmorphic facial features include a prominent forehead, round face, hypertelorism, a depressed nasal bridge with a short nose, a long philtrum, bilateral cleft lip, and anteverted nares.
test_results: Both humeruses were short. The condyles, especially the left condyle, were hypoplastic and had a distally tapered view. There was a bilateral dislocation of the upper radioulnar joint. The first metacarpal was short bilaterally. The lower limb radiograph was normal.

case_report: A 48-year-old Caucasian male with no significant past medical history presented with a 3-month history of foot swelling. Physical examination revealed oedema extending to the knees, with no other notable findings. Urine dipstick results showed blood +++ and protein +++. Laboratory tests indicated impaired renal function with a creatinine level of 186 micromol/L and an eGFR of 34 mL/min/1.73m2. CRP was 4 mg/L, albumin 27 g/L, and Hb 113 g/L. The urine protein:creatinine ratio was 228.4 mg/mmol. An immunology screen revealed an anti-GBM level of 32 units/mL, while ANCA and ANA were negative. Serum protein electrophoresis detected a gamma paraprotein too small to quantify and an elevated kappa band at 182 mg/L with a normal lambda band of 16.80 mg/L (ratio: 10.83). C3 and C4 levels were normal, and a virology screen was negative for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C. Computed tomography showed no evidence of pulmonary haemorrhage or lymphadenopathy in the neck, chest, abdomen, or pelvis. Treatment included steroids, cyclophosphamide, and plasma exchange. A biopsy was performed, and light microscopy revealed ten glomeruli with mixed nodular sclerosis, focal mesangial and endocapillary hypercellularity, and focal basement membrane duplication on silver stain. There was no necrosis or crescents, and mild chronic damage with 10% interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy was noted. Immunoperoxidase staining on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue showed linear glomerular and tubular basement membrane positivity for IgG, while IgA and IgM were negative. C3 and C1q showed mesangial positivity in the sclerosing lesions, and kappa and lambda staining was negative in the glomeruli.
test_results: Electron microscopy demonstrated powdery electron dense deposits along the lamina rara interna of glomerular basement membranes and also along tubular basement membranes.

case_report: A 40-year-old male presented with progressively loose skin, particularly affecting his face, neck, and trunk over the past two years. He reported experiencing generalized swelling, difficulty breathing, anemia, and fatigue one year ago. Upon examination, he exhibited bilateral swelling in the feet, pallor, and an appearance that seemed older than his age. There was no family history of similar skin conditions. He was diagnosed with high blood pressure two months prior and had a history of heavy alcohol consumption and smoking for the past 20 years, which he ceased two months ago. Skin examination showed loose ear lobes, drooping eyelids, laxity in the nasolabial folds, and increased skin folds on the neck, armpits, and trunk.
test_results: Renal biopsy showed nodular glomerulosclerosis with positive staining on immunohistochemistry for monoclonal kappa and IgG. Skin biopsy showed markedly reduced elastic fibers. Serum electrophoresis revealed 'M-band' - 0.3 g% in gamma region. Immunofixation electrophoresis showed IgG-κ, with elevation of free kappa, normal lambda chain levels (κ = 100 mg/L, λ = 24 mg/L), and raised κ/λ ratio of 4.2. Bone marrow examination revealed 9% plasma cells with occasional immature forms.
diagnosis: Acquired Cutis Laxa associated with Light and Heavy Chain Deposition Disease
Orpha_name: Light and heavy chain deposition disease

case_report: A 13-year-old girl arrived at the hospital with a five-day history of increasing generalized body swelling and severe difficulty swallowing. The swelling began on the face and gradually extended to the upper and lower extremities. It was pitting in nature, without associated redness or tenderness. Drooling of saliva was observed, necessitating the use of a nasogastric tube. Her parents reported that she had been experiencing difficulty walking and climbing stairs for three months, along with intermittent low-grade fever at night. The patient denied any recent falls, shortness of breath, changes in urine color, recent infections, rashes, previous similar episodes, or recent travel. There was no significant family history of muscular dystrophy or systemic lupus erythematosus. On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs. Neurological examination revealed normal mental function. Symmetric bilateral proximal muscle weakness of the lower limbs was noted. She was unable to stand up from a lying position and could not walk without assistance. Muscle strength was graded 2 in the proximal lower limb muscles and 3 in the distal lower limb muscles according to the Medical Research Council (MRC) scale. Deep tendon reflexes were present, and sensation was intact. Laboratory tests indicated microcytic and mildly hypochromic anemia, a positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) test, and significantly elevated creatinine kinase levels.
test_results: A biopsy of the muscle revealed mild endomysial lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrates with muscle fiber size variation and foci of regenerative changes.

case_report: A 67-year-old woman with a history of primary hyperparathyroidism and fatty liver was admitted in February 2017 for a parathyroidectomy to remove a 15 mm parathyroid adenoma in the left lobe. There was no family history of hypercalcemia. She had a recent influenza A infection and an upper respiratory tract infection (URTI) a few days prior. On admission, her vital signs and physical examination were unremarkable. Initial blood tests showed hyperparathyroidism, elevated C-reactive protein (CRP), anemia, and liver function abnormalities with the following values: WBC count 6.3×10^9/L, hemoglobin 94 g/L, platelets 374×10^9/L, albumin 31 g/L, CRP 68.5 mg/L, aspartate aminotransferase 29 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 69 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 1015 U/L, ɤ-glutamyl transferase 197 U/L, creatine kinase 15 U/L, amylase 53 U/L, creatinine 47.7 µmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 4.7 mmol/L, sodium 143 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, chlorine 108 mmol/L, calcium 3.02 mmol/L, phosphorus 0.94 mmol/L, intact parathyroid hormone 16.2 pmol/L, parathyroid hormone-related protein <1.1 pmol/L, and 1,25-(OH)2 vitamin D 242.4 pmol/L. The surgery involved a 4 cm lateral incision with a total blood loss of 3 mL and was completed without complications, leading to remission of hypercalcemia. Two days post-surgery, the patient developed a moderate fever without other symptoms such as fatigue, pain, redness at the surgical site, joint swelling, or skin eruptions. The fever did not exceed 38°C and fluctuated within 1°C. Preoperative CT scans showed no significant findings. The fever was managed with acetaminophen, which reduced the temperature, but it rose again to 38°C on postoperative day 6. Blood tests showed a persistently elevated CRP (79.8 mg/L) without an increase in WBC. Daily acetaminophen was administered to control the fever. Further screening for collagen diseases, including vasculitis, was conducted. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 10 and scheduled for outpatient follow-up. Three days after discharge, she experienced sudden onset of severe pain in both shoulders and morning stiffness lasting more than an hour, which was severe enough to prevent her from sitting up. Upon readmission, no signs of skin eruptions, peripheral pitting edema, or temporal artery tumors were found.
test_results: A screening blood test for collagen disease performed before discharge was negative, except for ESR (113 mm/h), though an elevated concentration of CRP (112.4 mg/L) and high level of ESR (101 mm/h) were noted. A CT scan did not reveal any inflammatory findings including vasculitis.

case_report: A 75-year-old female with no prior history of autoimmune or rheumatic conditions reported receiving the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine. Four months post-vaccination, she experienced oropharyngeal pain, severe fatigue, and fever. A real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test confirmed COVID-19. Two weeks later, she developed severe joint and muscle pain in the neck, shoulders, and forearms, along with persistent morning stiffness and a 4 kg weight loss. Physical examination showed no fever or arthritis but revealed limited arm mobility. Other physical examination findings were unremarkable. Laboratory results indicated an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 46 mm/hr, normal white blood cell count, normal C-reactive protein (CRP) levels, and a negative rheumatoid factor (RF) test.
test_results: Ultrasound findings with bilateral subacromial–subdeltoid bursitis were observed.

case_report: A 65-year-old male presented with significantly low serum uric acid levels observed over a period of at least 4 years during routine analysis. His physical measurements included a height of 167 cm, a body weight of 73.5 kg, and a body mass index of 26.4 kg/m2. Vital signs recorded were a blood pressure of 138/90 mmHg and a pulse rate of 90 beats per minute. Physical examination revealed no abnormalities. His medical history included revascularization for chronic ischemic heart disease and bilateral inguinal herniography. There was no consanguinity in his parents and no family history of urinary calculi. His regular medications included bisoprolol, atorvastatin/ezetimibe, and pantoprazole, with no history of using antihyperuricemic agents. Laboratory data showed serum uric acid levels below the detection limit of the technique used (<5.95 μmol/L) and normal renal function with a creatinine clearance greater than 90 mL/min/1.73 m2.
test_results: The urine analysis confirmed a low excretion of purines, including uric acid (53.6 μmol/24 h). A renal echography revealed both kidneys with normal size, morphology, and echostructure. In the right kidney, two hypoechoic images (7 and 9 mm) were identified as suggestive of renal lithiasis without repercussion over the excretory system.

case_report: In November 2013, a 3-year-old boy was brought to the Children's Hospital in Vientiane, Laos from Xienquang Province. His height was 88 cm and his weight was 9.3 kg, both below the 3rd percentile for his age. Laboratory tests showed serum sodium at 144 mmol/L, bicarbonate at 18.1 mmol/L, potassium at 2.0 mmol/L, and chloride at 117 mmol/L. The anion gap was normal at 9 mmol/L. Hemoglobin level was 6.2 g/dL, but no peripheral blood smear was conducted. Renal ultrasound indicated medullary nephrocalcinosis in both kidneys, and skeletal X-rays revealed rachitic changes with diffuse osteopenia in both distal radius and ulna. He did not exhibit any hearing impairment. Treatment with sodium bicarbonate and Urocitra® was initiated. Laboratory values improved within 5 days of treatment, with serum potassium at 5.0 mmol/L, bicarbonate at 24 mmol/L, and chloride at 108 mmol/L. After 6 months, the boy was able to run and ride a bike. He grew 8 cm in a year, and by the age of 4.8 years, his height was 96 cm and his weight was 15 kg, corresponding to the 5–10th percentiles and 5th percentile for his age, respectively.
test_results: Mutational analyses revealed the patient was triply homozygous for the loss-of-function mutation, c.2102G>A (p.Gly701Asp) as well as for two benign variations, c.92T>C (p.Met31Thr) and c.166A>C (p.Lys56Glu), in SLC4A1. Both parents were heterozygous for all these three variations.
diagnosis: Primary Autosomal Recessive Distal Renal Tubular Acidosis  caused by a homozygous SLC4A1 mutation
Orpha_name: Autosomal recessive distal renal tubular acidosis without deafness

case_report: A 7-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of nephrocalcinosis. A renal ultrasound was performed after he failed a newborn hearing screen of the right ear. A paternal second cousin developed renal failure of unknown cause in childhood. The paternal grandfather and great-grandfather had multiple renal calculi. Both parents were healthy. Height was 63.6 cm (10th percentile), weight 6.3 kg (<5th percentile), and blood pressure 107/67 mmHg. There were no dysmorphic features. He had normal eyes, ears, and neck, normal cardiac, abdominal, and genital examination, no birthmarks, and normal reflexes. Initial serum concentrations were as follows: sodium 140 mmol/L (normal 133–140 mmol/L), potassium 3.0 mmol/L (normal 4.1–5.8 mmol/L), chloride 110 mmol/L (normal 96–106 mmol/L), carbon dioxide 19 mmol/L (normal 20–26 mmol/L), creatinine 0.3 mg/dL (normal 0.1–0.4 mg/dL), and calcium 10.4 mg/dL (normal 9.2–10.4 mg/dL). Further studies showed: urine pH 8.5, urine calcium/creatinine ratio <0.06, serum phosphorus 5.2 mg/dL (normal 3.8–6.5 mg/dL), serum magnesium 2.1 mg/dL (normal 1.5–2.5 mg/dL), and urine beta2-microglobulin 218,431 μg/g Cr (normal <300 μg/g Cr). The renal ultrasound showed normal-sized kidneys for age and height. The right measured 5.45 cm, and the left measured 5.26 cm. There was no hydronephrosis. No calculi were visualized. There was bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis. Auditory brainstem response at 3 months of age revealed normal low-frequency (500–1000 Hz) hearing sensitivity and a mild-to-moderate high-frequency (2000–4000 Hz) hearing loss on the right with normal hearing sensitivity on the left. At 16 months, otoacoustic emission testing of the left ear was normal. The acidosis was corrected with 3–4 mEq/kg of Bicitra. The first urine oxalate:creatinine ratio was 808 mg/g (normal <280 mg/g). A confirmatory oxalate:creatinine level was also elevated at 397 mg/g. A urine hyperoxaluria panel revealed an elevated glycolate:creatinine of 76 mg/g (normal <61 mg/g) and a normal glycerate:creatinine of 52 mg/g (normal <57 mg/g). Pyridoxine was initiated and titrated up to 65 mg per day (8 mg/kg). Genetic analysis did not reveal any mutations in the alanine:glyoxylate aminotransferase and glycolate reductase/-glycerate dehydrogenase genes. After 1 month of pyridoxine therapy, the oxalate:creatinine ratio remained elevated at 629 mg/g. A liver biopsy showed normal hepatic alanine:glyoxylate aminotransferase activity: 44 μmol/h/mg protein (normal 19.1–47.9), normal glycolate reductase/d-glycerate dehydrogenase activity 100 nmol/min/mg protein (normal 23–207), and normal alanine:glyoxylate aminotransferase and glycolate reductase/d-glycerate dehydrogenase immunoreactivity staining. At 13 months of age, the urine oxalate:creatinine ratio normalized to 146 mg/g; however, the beta2-microglobulinuria (28,396 μg/g Cr) persisted. The initial hypocalciuria (urine calcium/creatinine ratio <0.06) occurred at a time of mild systemic acidosis (carbon dioxide 19 mmol/L). Surprisingly, hypercalciuria (calcium/creatinine ratio 0.65) developed 1 month later after the acidosis was corrected.
test_results: Genetic analysis of the ATP6V1B1 gene showed two different mutations, one of which was novel.
diagnosis: Autosomal recessive distal renal tubular acidosis  with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss
Orpha_name: Autosomal recessive distal renal tubular acidosis with deafness

case_report: A 13-year-old male was admitted due to progressive difficulty in walking and clumsiness, first noticed by his mother around the age of 5. His birth history and early neurodevelopment until 1 year of age were normal. He achieved head control at 3 months, rolled over at 5 months, and sat independently at 10 months. Subsequent developmental milestones were delayed: standing with support at 16 months and walking independently at 21 months. He spoke his first meaningful words at 2 years, formed phrases at 4 years, and constructed simple sentences by 5 years. At 5 years old, his mother observed a slow, broad-based gait and generalized weakness in his movements, but no medical consultation was sought at that time. His walking difficulties gradually worsened, and he recently experienced challenges in academic performance. The patient has one sister. His father died in a car accident at age 40. There is no family history of neurological disorders or renal stones. On admission, physical examination revealed minor dysmorphic features, including a long face, macrognathia, high arched palate, and large ears. Neurological examination showed mild higher cortical dysfunction, dysarthria, upper limb and gait ataxia, hyperreflexia with bilateral extensor toe signs. Motor power and muscle tone were normal. Sensory examination was normal except for impaired vibration and position sense in the lower extremities. Cranial nerve functions were intact, and optic fundi appeared normal. There were no tremors or involuntary movements. Neuropsychological evaluation indicated mild mental retardation with a full-scale intelligence quotient of 62, a verbal scale intelligence quotient of 79, and a performance scale intelligence quotient of 47. Somatosensory evoked potential testing of the posterior tibial nerve showed no cortical waves (P1), indicating central conduction dysfunction through the posterior column of the spinal cord. However, spine MRI did not reveal any structural lesions in the spinal cord. Electromyography, nerve conduction study, and brain MRI were normal. Chromosome analysis and Fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene studies were normal. Routine urinalysis and abdominal ultrasonography showed no evidence of urolithiasis. Cerebrospinal fluid examination, serum and cerebrospinal fluid lactate/pyruvate levels, urine organic acid analysis, and plasma amino acid analysis were normal.
test_results: Quantitative amino acid analysis of the urine disclosed increased excretion of cystine (1,345 µM/g Cr) and an excess of the dibasic amino acids; ornithine, lysine, and arginine. The oral cystine loading test resulted in elevation of plasma cystine levels. Direct sequencing of entire coding region of SLC3A1 and SLC7A9 genes of the patient revealed both a G (normal) and A (mutant) at nucleotide 535 in exon 5, resulting in the presence of a Gly (codon GGA) at amino acid position 173 and a Arg (codon AGA) in heterozygote state.

case_report: A 26-year-old female presented with spontaneous, painful constrictive movements on the right side of her face and a sensation of constriction in her neck, leading to breathing difficulties. Two years prior, she began experiencing spontaneous, intermittent, unilateral, severely painful involuntary spasmodic contractions on the right side of her face, lasting 3-5 minutes and recurring throughout the day. These episodes were relieved by consciously opening her mouth but reappeared upon occlusal contact. Symptoms affected the right forehead, jaw, and neck, with internal throat spasms causing breathing difficulties. During these episodes, her jaws involuntarily closed, her tongue deviated to the opposite side, and she experienced slurred speech. Triggers included brushing, eating, touching the right side of her face, excessive talking, and breathing. Associated findings included grimacing, reddening, and breathlessness. Her past dental history included an uneventful extraction of tooth 48 six months prior. She had no consanguineous marriage or first-degree relatives with neurological disorders. Previous treatments by various specialists, including ENT and Psychiatry, involved tricyclic antidepressants and gabapentin without relief. Stressful events exacerbated her symptoms, leading to feelings of rejection, sadness, frustration, depression, and anxiety. Extraoral examination revealed spontaneous fasciculations on the right side of her face, with diffuse swelling and redness. Intraoral examination showed episodes beginning with fine involuntary fasciculations in the right masseter and temporalis, progressing to severe contractions of the face and neck within seconds, causing grimacing and breathing difficulties. The patient would assume a posture holding the right side of her face and neck, gasping for breath, and attempting to open her mouth to alleviate the spasms, which reduced within 2-3 seconds. TMJ examination showed anterior disc displacement without reduction, with fine fasciculations in the right masseter and temporalis. Marked reddening and a bulge were observed on the right forehead and jaw region.
test_results: Brain MRI did not show any definite abnormal brain findings or brainstem lesion. Blood investigations revealed parameters in normal range. TMJ tomographic views revealed an excessive anterior movement of the condyle on open mouth position.

case_report: An 84-year-old man visited the neurology clinic in December 2018 due to episodes of jerking movements involving his face, neck, and mouth, which impacted his speech and eating. These symptoms worsened during meals. His primary care physician had previously prescribed chlorpromazine, which initially provided some relief, but the symptoms later intensified. The patient experienced intermittent shaking spells throughout the day. During clinic visits, he did not exhibit symptoms, which were reported based on his history. In January 2019, he returned to the clinic with more frequent jerking episodes and increased speech difficulties. The symptoms included muscle spasms and tremors, along with dysarthria and dysphagia. He reported no chills, fever, chest pain, palpitations, cough, shortness of breath, muscle pain, or muscle weakness. His family history included dementia and hypertension in his mother, and heart disease and nephrolithiasis in his father.
test_results: Electroencephalogram (EEG) was normal. MRI was unremarkable except for limited small vessel disease.

case_report: A 20-year-old female was admitted to our gynecology department from another hospital with a complaint of gradual abdominal distension over the past year. Pelvic ultrasound at the referring hospital indicated a cystic mass in the ovary, occupying nearly the entire pelvis and displacing the uterus. The patient was referred to our hospital for surgical intervention. She has a history of Marfan syndrome, which includes kyphoscoliosis, mitral valve prolapse, and severe mitral valve regurgitation. A pelvic examination revealed a mass extending up to the umbilical region. There were no focal neurological deficits observed. Routine blood biochemical tests were within normal limits.
test_results: Preoperative contrast-enhanced pelvic MRI demonstrated large, well-defined multiloculated intrasacral and presacral cysts communicating via two separate broad necks and extending through defects in anterior aspect of sacral vertebrae. A connection between the pelvic multicystic lesion and dural sac was clearly observed on sagittal MRI images. The cystic fluid was similar to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) signal intensity. There were neither nerve roots nor solid components within the mass. No contrast enhancement was detected. Uterus and adnexa were inferiorly displaced by the mass.

case_report: A 3.5-year-old Iranian girl was referred from a pediatric surgery clinic due to a gluteal mass. Her parents reported that the swelling on her right buttock had been present since birth and had gradually increased in size. They did not observe any bowel or bladder issues. The cyst had been aspirated twice by a local physician, 8 and 4 months prior, yielding clear fluid each time, but the mass reappeared after several weeks. The chemical analysis results of the fluid were unavailable. Physical examination revealed a soft, 3 × 4-cm fluctuant, non-pulsatile mass in the gluteal region, covered with normal skin and lacking vascular or hairy stigmata. The mass size remained unchanged with crying or coughing. Transillumination test results were positive. The midline was normal, with no sinus tract or swelling. Sensory, rectal tone, and lower limb motor exams were normal. No abnormal skin lesions or skeletal deformities were noted, and the spinal column curvature appeared normal. Routine laboratory investigations were normal. An anteroposterior X-ray of the lumbosacral region showed spina bifida of the L5 and S1 vertebrae. Ultrasound revealed a well-defined, purely cystic, oblong lesion measuring 3.7 × 4.5 × 2.2 cm in the right upper gluteal region beneath the gluteal muscles, with no internal echoes, solid components, or septae. Myelography was planned but could not be performed due to the patient's allergic sensitivity to the contrast agent (omnipaque).
test_results: A lumbosacral magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a well-defined cystic mass measuring 36 × 21 × 45 mm in her right buttock. The cystic mass appeared as a low signal intensity area on T1-weighted images and a high signal intensity area on T2-weighted images, which was similar to her cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) signal. No obvious communication between the cyst and the spinal canal was perceivable. The position and shape of the cord, roots and lying of the conus were unremarkable.

case_report: A 19-month-old female child presented with constipation since 6 months of age and difficulty in passing urine for the last 6 months. Parents noticed lower abdominal fullness for the past year. The child was born at full term via uncomplicated vaginal delivery to non-consanguineous parents. No antenatal ultrasound screening was performed. There was no history of birth asphyxia or trauma. Despite being advised laxatives and enemas, the constipation persisted. The child passed small amounts of urine frequently. The child weighed 7.2 kg, and other anthropometric parameters, including head circumference, were appropriate for age. Chest examination revealed multiple rib defects on both sides, but air entry was normal without any added sounds. Abdominal examination revealed a cystic mass in the suprapubic region extending from the pelvis to the umbilicus. Digital rectal examination showed normal tone of the normally placed anus, but a large cystic mass was felt posteriorly, preventing further examination. Examination of the spine showed no bony defects, and there was no neurological deficit. Hematological investigations showed hemoglobin of 11.2 g/dL, TLC of 12,000 per cc, and platelets of 117×10^3 per mm^3. Kidney function tests were normal. X-ray chest showed multiple segmentation anomalies of cervicodorsal vertebrae and fusion anomalies of ribs on both sides. Echocardiogram did not reveal any cardiac anomalies. Ultrasound of the abdomen demonstrated a cystic lesion posterior to the urinary bladder measuring 9×4 cm with a well-defined dome-shaped upper margin and tapering inferiorly. No internal echoes were seen within the lesion. The urinary bladder was pushed anteriorly. There was no evidence of hydroureteronephrosis. Barium enema demonstrated Scimitar sign along with increased presacral space, displacement of the rectum anteriorly, and sigmoid colon to the right.
test_results: Computed tomography showed an anterior sacral dysraphic defect with large cystic mass in presacral region displacing the urinary bladder anteriorly and to the right side. Posteriorly, mass was seen entering the spinal canal through large sacral bone defect. There was no hydrocephalus. Both the kidneys were displaced and rotated through their axis but there was no evidence of hydronephrosis.

case_report: A 35-year-old male drywall installer reported experiencing progressive weakness, numbness, and clumsiness in the left upper extremity over the past 2 years. Physical examination revealed 4-/5 strength in the intrinsic muscles of the left hand, reduced sensation to light touch in the left hand, and increased reflexes in the left upper extremity. Electromyography and nerve conduction studies showed mild incidental bilateral ulnar neuropathy at the elbow.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the cervical spine demonstrated cervical spinal cord expansion with T2 hyperintensity at C4-C5. There was an associated defect of the bony posterior elements with projection of the neural elements into the dorsal subcutaneous soft tissue.
Orpha_name: Open spinal dysraphism with a myelomeningocele

case_report: A 75-year-old Indian woman with a history of osteoarthritis and bilateral chronic otitis media was being monitored in the ophthalmology clinic for bilateral pseudophakia and normal tension glaucoma, managed with two topical anti-glaucoma medications (timolol 0.5% twice daily and Xalatan once nightly). Her baseline best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 6/9 in both eyes. She experienced a sudden, painless loss of vision in her right eye, which was generalized and noticed upon waking. She reported no eye redness, discharges, flashes of light, floaters, or recent ocular trauma before the vision loss. There was no history of transient vision loss. She also did not have symptoms such as fever, jaw claudication, scalp pain, or headache. She sought medical attention one week after the onset due to persistent vision loss. At presentation, her visual acuity (VA) was hand motion (HM) in the right eye and 6/12 in the left eye, with a right eye relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). The anterior segment examination of both eyes was unremarkable. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 14 mmHg in both eyes. Fundus examination of the right eye showed retinal whitening at the macula sparing the papillomacular bundle and generalized retinal arteriolar attenuation. The optic disc was pink with a cup-to-disc ratio (CDR) of 0.7, and no new vessels were observed. The left eye fundus showed hypertensive retinopathy changes and glaucomatous optic disc changes similar to the right eye, with a CDR of 0.8. Systemic examination revealed a blood pressure of 175/75 mmHg and a normal, regular pulse rate. There was no scalp tenderness, carotid bruit, or audible murmur on cardiovascular examination. No intervention was performed to restore retinal blood flow due to the delayed presentation. Blood tests showed normal full blood count, fasting serum lipids, and blood sugar, with a hemoglobin A1C (HbA1C) of 5.8%. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 26 mm/hr, which is normal for her age.
test_results: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the right eye macula showed inner retinal thickening, which was confined to the temporal macula. Her ultrasound carotid Doppler showed less than 50% stenosis over the right distal common carotid artery (CCA) and proximal internal carotid artery (ICA), with similar findings over the left side. Echocardiography (ECHO) showed an ejection fraction of 68%, with no valve abnormalities and no regional wall motion abnormality. Subsequently, a computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the brain, circle of Willis, and carotid arteries was performed and showed atherosclerotic diseases of bilateral extracranial ICA and significant stenosis affecting the right proximal ICA with approximately 75% stenosis. The carotid angiogram also showed progressive narrowing of the right ICA, with diameters at the proximal, mid, and distal regions measuring 9.6mm, 5.8mm, and 5.5 mm, respectively.
diagnosis: Neovascular Glaucoma complicating Central Retinal Artery Occlusion

case_report: A 61-year-old woman was referred to our department with complaints of left ocular pain and blurred vision lasting for 5 days. Her medical history includes treatment for diabetes mellitus with hypoglycemic agents 4 years ago and asthma managed with bronchodilators 10 years ago. Upon initial examination, the best-corrected visual acuity was 20/40 in the right eye and 20/60 in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was measured at 13 mm Hg in the right eye and 37 mm Hg in the left eye. The right eye exhibited no signs of inflammation in both the anterior and posterior segments. In contrast, the left eye presented with ciliary hyperemia, infiltrating cells, hyphemia, rubeosis iridis, and cataract in the anterior segment, while the posterior segment showed no vitreous opacity or retinal vasculitis.
test_results: Gonioscopy examination detected nodules and rubeosis on the trabecular meshwork in the left eye. Fluorescence angiography did not detect any retinal vasculitis or retinal ischemia caused by diabetes mellitus. Serum examination detected slight increases in blood glucose (201 mg/dL), HbA1c (6.8%), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (17 mm/h). C-reactive protein, angiotensin-converting enzyme, and interleukin-2 receptor were within normal ranges. Bilateral hilar-mediastinal lymphadenopathy was not detected on chest X-ray. Serum herpes simplex virus (HSV) IgM, HSV IgG, cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgM, CMV IgG, and CMV antigen were negative, and a multiple broad-range polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test using anterior humor did not detect human herpes virus (HHV) 1–8, 16S rRNA, 28S rRNA, tuberculosis, or toxoplasmosis.
diagnosis: Neovascular Glaucoma  caused by Noninfectious Granulomatous Uveitis

case_report: A 63-year-old Caucasian male presented with symptoms of cough, intermittent palpitations, and shortness of breath. The patient had a history of smoking. Blood pressure readings were within normal limits, and clinical laboratory tests returned normal results. A respiratory functional study indicated a moderate, nonreversible obstructive syndrome with a forced expiratory volume in the first second (FEV1) at 58%. Arterial blood gas analysis showed normal oxygen saturation levels. A chest X-ray identified a lesion in the right lung field. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest revealed a rounded, high-density lesion with irregular borders, measuring 24mm in diameter, located in the middle lobe. An abdominal ultrasound and cervical CT scan showed no abnormalities. Positron emission tomography (PET)/CT imaging demonstrated 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) uptake in the pulmonary lesion, with standardized uptake values (SUV) of 2.8. Bronchofibroscopy did not reveal any external pressure or visible alterations. Conventional and brush biopsies did not detect cancer cells.
test_results: The results of the cytological tests were positive for not otherwise specified (NOS) neuroendocrine carcinoma. The immunohistochemistry test results were positive for cytokeratin (CK) AE1\AE3 and natural killer cell-associated antigen CD56, negative for thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1), P63, and leukocyte common antigen (LCA).
diagnosis: paraganglioma of the middle lobe pT1b pN0 cM0

case_report: A 46-year-old male, scheduled for aortic valve replacement, was referred after an invasive coronary angiogram revealed a large cardiac mass surrounding the left coronary artery, with no evidence of coronary artery stenosis. The patient has a family history of atherosclerotic coronary artery disease, hypertension managed with lecardipine and lobizide, type 2 insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, and obesity (BSA = 2.10 m2). The patient provided written informed consent for the study. A third-generation dual source CT scanner (DSCT; Somatom Force, Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany) was used for CCT. Initially, a non-contrast CT with prospectively ECG-triggered high-pitch spiral acquisition was performed to evaluate the calcium score. This was followed by an angiographic CT scan with retrospective ECG gating and automated attenuation-based anatomical tube current modulation (CARE Dose 4D, Siemens). The tube voltage was adjusted using the automated attenuation-based tube voltage selection functionality (CAREkV, Siemens). For the angiographic scan, 70 mL of iodinated contrast agent (Iomeprol 400 mgI/mL, Iomeron 400, Bracco, Italy) was injected at a rate of 5.5 mL/s, followed by 50 mL of saline at the same flow rate. Data reconstruction was done using a third-generation Advanced Modeled Iterative Reconstruction device (ADMIRE, Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany) with medium-sharp convolution kernels (Bv36 and Bv40), a strength level of 3, a section thickness of 0.75 mm with an increment of 0.4 mm, and a pixel matrix of 512 × 512. Postprocessing was carried out on a dedicated workstation (Syngo.Via VB10B, Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany), generating MIP, c-MPR, 3D volume rendering, and cinematic rendering images.
test_results: CCT showed a solid mass above the basal anterior wall of the left ventricle, characterized by intense, progressive, and inhomogeneous contrast enhancement, and a capsule; the core of the lesion was hypovascular/necrotic; in addition, the lesion showed complete encasing of the left main coronary artery, the proximal-middle segment of the left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery, and the proximal segment of the left circumflex coronary artery. CMR findings were as follows: well-circumscribed ovoid/spherical lesions and typical hyperintensity on T2 imaging sequences, with the other features similar to CCT. The location and evidence on the morphological, functional, and metabolic features of the mass all pointed to a solid, hypervascular, capsulated, non-infiltrative, neuro-endocrine type of tumor.

case_report: A 35-year-old woman arrived at the hospital experiencing unusual chest pain and shortness of breath during physical activity for the past six months. On physical examination, her pulse rate was recorded at 90 beats per minute, and her respiratory rate was 24 breaths per minute; other physical examination findings were within normal limits. Electrocardiography showed a normal sinus rhythm with T-wave inversion in leads III and aVF. The chest X-ray did not reveal any abnormalities.
test_results: Transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a 1.9 × 2.4 cm well-circumscribed, sessile, echo-dense mass in the right atrium, attached to the interatrial septum. Transesophageal echocardiography showed a larger mass (2.4 × 3.7 cm) than seen with transthoracic echocardiography. The mass was attached near the coronary sinus ostium without causing obstruction to coronary sinus flow. Multiple views of the mass showed hyperechoic tissue density, except for a small area of central echolucency. Histopathology of the excised mass using conventional hematoxylin and eosin staining revealed homogeneous polygonal cells with moderately pleomorphic nucleoli and moderate eosinophilic cytoplasm. There was scant mitosis with no necrosis. The cell nests were separated by hyalinised fibrous stroma which was rich in vasculature. The tumor tissue was diffusely positive for chromogranin and synaptophysin with patchy focal positivity for CD56.

case_report: A 27-year-old woman pregnant with monochorionic diamniotic twins, conceived spontaneously, attended regular maternal check-ups every two weeks starting at 9 weeks of gestation. At 263/7 weeks of gestation, she was referred to a tertiary center for a traditional perinatal support system. Her pregnancy was uneventful until 312/7 weeks, when the twins, positioned vertex-vertex, showed amniotic fluid pockets measuring 7.9 cm and 2.4 cm, respectively, indicating a slight difference. The estimated fetal body weights were 1683 g and 1531 g, respectively, with no significant weight discordance. Both twins had reassuring fetal statuses and water-filled bladders. Due to the sudden appearance of amniotic fluid imbalance, a plan was made to admit her 7 days later for closer monitoring. She was educated on the importance of daily fetal movement perception as a sign of fetal well-being. She was able to distinguish the movements of each twin due to their consistent locations. Five days before the scheduled admission, she noticed decreased fetal movement in the right twin, while the left twin continued to move as usual. Additionally, she experienced frequent uterine contractions, prompting her to seek urgent consultation.
test_results: Cardiotocogram indicated absent variability in the right twin (I), while reassuring pattern in the left twin (II), with uterine contraction every one to three minutes.

case_report: An 8-year-old male patient weighing 15 kg with congenital heart disease presented with a history of two seizure episodes and fever over the past 20 days. Physical examination showed cyanosis, clubbing, and signs of developmental delay. Auscultation of the chest revealed a Grade IV pansystolic murmur over the precordium. Neurological examination did not show any abnormalities. Laboratory results indicated hemoglobin level of 17.3 g%, normal total leukocyte count, normal platelet count, and sterile blood culture.
test_results: A transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated situs solitus, levocardia, atrioventricular concordance, ventriculoarterial discordance, a large VSD (size 27 mm) with severe pulmonary stenosis (peak gradient of 80 mmHg), and a large (18 mm × 14 mm) mobile mass attached to the pulmonary valve. Computerized tomography pulmonary angiogram showed normal-sized pulmonary vessels with no evidence of pulmonary thromboembolism. A transesophageal echocardiography examination after induction of anesthesia in midesophageal five-chamber view confirmed the presence of a large VSD and a mass attached to the undersurface of the pulmonary valve. In addition, a thick cord-like structure originating from the endocardial surface of the left ventricle was found attached to the mass. Color Doppler examination showed turbulent flow across the pulmonary valve. Continuous-wave Doppler confirmed the gradient across the obstruction. In midesophageal four-chamber view, chordae from the tricuspid valve were seen attached to the tip of interventricular septum (IVS). Midesophageal aortic long-axis view showed a mobile mass attached to the undersurface of the pulmonary valve, a large VSD, and normal-appearing pulmonary and aortic valves. A careful look showed the mass moving with the movement of the pulmonary valve and a chord-like structure attached to the mass after originating from both right and left ventricles.

case_report: A 51-year-old man with no significant medical history experienced nausea, malaise, and joint pain three days after receiving his first dose of the Moderna Covid-19 vaccine. He used over-the-counter non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs with minimal relief. He received his second dose of the Moderna vaccine 28 days later. Two days after the second dose, he developed worsening nausea, vomiting, and mid-epigastric abdominal pain, leading him to visit the emergency department. Upon arrival, his pulse was 68 beats per minute, blood pressure was 114/78 mm Hg, and weight was 77.1 kg. He appeared tired, but the physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed a serum sodium level of 116 mmol/L (reference range, 135-145 mmol/L). Complete blood count and kidney and liver function tests were normal. Thyroid function tests and random cortisol were checked as part of the evaluation for hyponatremia. The thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level was 0.13 µIU/mL (reference range, 0.40-4.50 µIU/mL) and free thyroxine (free T4) level was 0.4 ng/dL (reference range, 0.8-1.8 ng/dL). Both random and morning cortisol levels were below detectable limits (<1.0 µg/dL). He was treated with intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg and underwent a high-dose cosyntropin (250 µg) stimulation test. The baseline cortisol level of <1.0 µg/dL increased to 2.4 µg/dL at 30 minutes and to 3.0 µg/dL at 60 minutes (normal response is > 18 µg/dL at either time point). Baseline adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) was 1.9 pg/mL (reference range, 7.2-63.3 pg/mL). The patient also reported low libido and erectile dysfunction for the past month. Additional hormonal tests showed a prolactin level of 12.9 ng/mL (reference range, 4.0-15.2 ng/mL), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) of 3.3 mIU/mL (reference range, 1.5-12.4 mIU/mL), luteinizing hormone (LH) of 1.9 mIU/mL (reference range, 1.7-8.6 mIU/mL), and 8 a.m. testosterone level of 108 ng/dL (reference range, 193-740 ng/dL). The patient did not report polyuria, nocturia, or polydipsia, and there were no laboratory findings such as elevated serum sodium and osmolality to suggest diabetes insipidus. Hormonal workup indicated secondary adrenal insufficiency, central hypothyroidism, and central hypogonadism.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed asymmetric enlargement of the pituitary gland with a larger more globular component on the right. The total gland measured 1.2 cm AP by 1.8 cm transverse by 0.8 cm craniocaudal, and there was thickening of the pituitary stalk. Computed tomography (CT) of the brain showed eccentric 10 × 15 × 9 mm enlargement of the pituitary gland which was new compared with previous images from 2011.

case_report: A 60-year-old male with a history of NSCLC with liver and brain metastases, initially identified in September 2020, completed whole-brain radiation therapy in October 2020. The patient then received chemotherapy in combination with pembrolizumab (PD-L1 0%). By July 2021, due to the treatment response, the patient continued on pembrolizumab as maintenance monotherapy. During an outpatient clinic visit, 39 weeks after starting immunotherapy, the patient reported muscle weakness in both lower limbs and headache. An electromyogram and brain MRI were performed, with the brain MRI showing a complete response to the previously identified brain metastasis. Laboratory tests revealed low cortisol levels, along with reduced adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH).
test_results: The pituitary MRI revealed the pituitary gland’s enlargement and a progressively enhancing bilateral ring-shaped enhancement.

case_report: A 20-year-old woman with a three-year history of migraine and secondary amenorrhea experienced a sudden onset of severe retroorbital headache and neck pain. Physical examination and visual acuity were normal. Visual fields assessment was not possible due to the severity of the headache, which made ophthalmic perimetry intolerable despite adequate analgesic treatment.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a 22 × 20 × 16 mm pituitary mass with slight suprasellar extension. The pituitary mass was iso- to hyperintense on T2- and hyperintense on T1-weighted images. The typical posterior pituitary bright spot was absent. After i.v. contrast (gadolinium), only slight to moderate and inhomogeneous enhancement occurred, most pronounced in the periphery of the mass. The pituitary stalk and infundibulum were slightly thickened and showed avid enhancement. Pathological evaluation of the excised tissue revealed no adenoma. The key feature was instead an abundance of necrotic tissue with only small areas of anterior and posterior pituitary remaining. These areas were heavily infiltrated by mononuclear cells, with abundant CD8-positive cytotoxic T cells in both anterior and posterior pituitary. The remaining anterior pituitary showed acini of secretory cells surrounded by a reticulin-rich network. Single cells were positive when stained for the different hormones (ACTH, GH, TSH, FSH, LH, PRL). Small areas of the posterior pituitary showed regular pituicytes with partial expression of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP).

case_report: A 68-year-old female patient arrived at the emergency department experiencing chest discomfort and palpitations. She has a history of untreated schizophrenia and anxiety. Endocrinology was consulted regarding adrenal nodules and hirsutism. The patient provided limited historical information and has been living alone for many years. Reports from nursing staff and adult services indicated that her brother mentioned she was previously labeled with a specific term and was kept away from the community by her mother. The patient reported having menstrual periods between the ages of 14 and 16, with no periods since then. She denied any recent changes in hair growth, skin, weight, or voice, although she had a long beard that was shaved by the nursing staff upon presentation. She was not sexually active and denied any history of surgeries, smoking, alcohol, or drug use. Her family history is unknown. Upon admission, her vital signs were as follows: temperature 98.6°F, pulse 105 beats per minute, blood pressure 145/111 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Physical examination revealed that she was awake, alert, and oriented to self. She had a masculine appearance with scanty hair on the scalp, bald spots anteriorly, shaved facial hair, excessive hair on the extremities and back, poor dentition, and well-developed breasts. Genitourinary examination showed pubic hair extending to the umbilicus, excess labial folds, no clitoromegaly, a small vaginal opening, and no palpable testicular tissue.
test_results: A computed tomography (CT) of the chest showed bilateral adrenal masses and enlargement of the right thyroid. CT of the abdomen with contrast showed bilateral adrenal nodules. The left nodule was 6.6×9.7×10.5 cm, and the right nodule was 3×7.6×6.8 cm with variable attenuation, 45 Hounsfield units (HU) in the areas of fat. Heterogenous attenuation noted in the nodules is suggestive of myelolipoma. Pelvic ultrasound showed the uterus with a small simple cystic area. There was no evidence of adnexal or pelvic mass.
Orpha_name: Non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency

case_report: An 82-year-old male with a history of prostate adenocarcinoma (T1cNxMx, Gleason score 4 + 3 = 7) diagnosed 5 years prior. Initially, he was under active surveillance. During this period, his PSA level increased to 14.2 ng/mL, and his testosterone level was 239 ng/dL. He received stereotactic body radiation therapy to the prostate along with leuprolide as androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) due to the absence of radiographic evidence of metastatic disease. Despite this treatment, his testosterone level remained elevated at 87 ng/dL. Consequently, bicalutamide (50 mg daily) was added to his ongoing ADT. He underwent 7 months of leuprolide treatment and 4 months of combined treatment with leuprolide and bicalutamide. His PSA nadir was 0.29 ng/mL, but his testosterone level remained relatively unchanged at 88.4 ng/dL. After completing the combined treatment, his PSA increased to 10.86 ng/dL and testosterone to 218 ng/dL.
test_results: Further laboratory workup revealed elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone at 4910 ng/dL (reference range, < 200 ng/dL) and DHEA-S at 312 mcg/dL (reference, < 16.2 mcg/dL). A positron emission tomography/CT scan (PET/CT) showed bilateral posterior iliac, right sacral, thoracic, and lumbar spine metastases as well as incidental bilateral nodular adrenal enlargement.
Orpha_name: Non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency

case_report: A 32-year-old female presented with obesity. She had a history of hypothyroidism and was on L-thyroxin replacement therapy. Her obstetric history included three pregnancies: one resulting in a healthy boy, one ectopic pregnancy with twins and intrauterine exitus, and a recent miscarriage 4 months prior. She expressed a desire to conceive again. Physical examination showed a body mass index (BMI) of 26 kg/m2, with no purple striae, buffalo hump, or hirsutism; her Ferriman-Gallwey score was 5. Laboratory tests showed normal thyroid function, an insulin resistance HOMA-index of 1.8, and an initial random serum cortisol level of 17.8 μg/dL. Following a 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test (DMST), her cortisol level was reduced to 0.6 μg/dL. Hormonal evaluation during the follicular phase revealed elevated 17-OHP (12.8 ng/mL) and ACTH (56 pg/mL) levels, while other hormone levels, including follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), estradiol (E2), progesterone, prolactin (PRL), dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEA-SO4), and testosterone, were within normal ranges. Pelvic ultrasonography showed no abnormalities.
test_results: 17-OHP levels at basal, 30 and 60 minutes of 14, 21, and 26 ng/mL, respectively.
Orpha_name: Non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency

case_report: The patient, a 10-year-old girl, is the first child of healthy, unrelated parents, born after an uneventful pregnancy. Clinical findings include intellectual disability, attention deficit, behavioral and speech delay, hypotonia, facial dysmorphisms, and eye anomalies. Congenital malformations observed include a cerebral anomaly and a forward anus. At birth, her weight was 3,450 g (50th percentile), length was 50.7 cm (50th percentile), and head circumference was 34 cm (25th-50th percentile). The Apgar score was 9/9. Postnatal medical tests revealed a slightly wider left ventricle on brain ultrasound. The forward anus was noted to be positioned relative to the sphincter floor, leading to electrostimulation therapy and surgical removal of skin vegetation. At a 30-day visit, a cranial ultrasound confirmed a slightly dilated left ventricle, with no cardiologic or skeletal anomalies detected.
test_results: A brain MRI confirm the presence of a wider left ventricle. Standard karyotype was normal. X-Fragile test was normal.

case_report: A 20-year-old female, accompanied by her mother, presented to the Emergency Department (ED) with lower abdominal and back pain. Obstetrics/Gynecology was consulted due to the nature of her pain. The patient reported similar pains in the past, but this episode was more severe and unbearable. She described the pain as a dull sensation radiating to her hips and lower legs. In the ED, she rated her pain as 8/10, which was managed with ketorolac (Toradol) and morphine. She also experienced constipation, having taken multiple doses of MiraLAX with one small bowel movement that day. Additionally, she complained of nausea and multiple episodes of vomiting, which were later controlled with Ondansetron (Zofran). She denied recent fever or voiding difficulties, and all other systems were negative. Further questioning revealed that she had never had a menstrual period and had not had routine visits with a pediatrician or established care with a gynecologist. Her medical history was negative for cancer, cardiovascular, endocrine, genitourinary, gastrointestinal, psychiatric, or blood disorders. According to her mother, she was up to date on all childhood immunizations. Social history included occasional alcohol use and daily vaping, with no recreational drug use. Her family history was unremarkable, and she has two healthy younger siblings. Physical examination in the ED revealed a firm uterus and reproducible bilateral lower quadrant abdominal tenderness with guarding. There was no spinal tenderness, and she had a painless range of motion. The patient displayed age-appropriate secondary sexual characteristics with no notable deviations. The ED workup included urinalysis, qualitative Human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG), Complete Blood Count (CBC) with differential, Complete Metabolic Panel (CMP), urine drug screen, and lipase levels.
test_results: The CT scan demonstrated massive dilatation of the cervix and uterus, consistent with hematometrocolpos with a possible imperforate hymen. Additionally, the CT showed mild left hydroureteronephrosis, likely secondary to the mass effect upon the distal ureter and a 3.84 cm complex cyst in the left adnexa. Ultrasound of the pelvis demonstrated findings consistent with hematometrocolpos as well as a physiologic left ovarian cyst.

case_report: An 11-year-old girl, measuring 158 cm in height and weighing 40 kg, presented to the emergency department with left abdominal pain that had been ongoing for 2 days. She had experienced similar symptoms about a month prior, which resolved on their own within a few days. The patient had no notable medical or surgical history. Breast development had begun at least a year earlier, and her peak growth rate had concluded, but she had not yet experienced her first menstrual period. Upon examination, she was febrile but had normal heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, and blood pressure. Physical examination revealed normal heart and breath sounds, and no palpable lymph nodes in the neck, axilla, or groin. The abdomen was soft with slight distension and tenderness in the left lower quadrant, but no enlargement of the liver or spleen was detected. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 9,100/μL and a C-reactive protein level of 2.1 mg/dL, with no other abnormalities noted.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) showed high absorptive value liquid filling the upper vaginal to uterine cavity, a pale highly absorptive fluid component suggestive of hemorrhagic ascites in the abdominal cavity on both sides of the uterus, and normal bilateral ovaries. MRI revealed a considerable amount of fluid retention from the cervix to the upper vaginal area; however, the retention cavity did not extend to the perineum, and no obvious vaginal structures were observed between the urethra and rectum.
diagnosis: Hematocolpos due to lower vaginal agenesis

case_report: In October 2009, a four-year-old girl was referred to the Rare Disease Unit of Bambino Gesù Children Hospital, presenting with atrophy of the ocular bulb of the left eye. She was the second child of Caucasian, non-consanguineous parents. Since the age of two, she experienced recurrent episodes of conjunctivitis with pseudomembranes on the eyelids. Medical treatments, including topical antibiotics and steroids, were unsuccessful. The lesions were surgically excised but recurred within a few weeks, and conjunctivitis persisted. The surgical procedure was repeated twice. After the third recurrence, she was referred to our unit. At the initial examination, the left eye exhibited a red, woody-like pseudomembrane (9 mm thick) involving the edge of the upper lid and the upper tarsal conjunctiva, causing ectropion of the lid. Slit lamp examination revealed a yellow-white membrane affecting the bulbar conjunctiva, fornix, and cornea, obstructing the evaluation of both anterior and posterior segments. Brain MRI with Optic Nerves study showed severe involvement of the left eye. The right eye examination revealed a small area of corneal de-epithelialization with a paracentral stromal opacity and a whitish-yellow soft pseudomembrane involving the upper tarsal conjunctiva. The bulbar conjunctiva was not involved, and the rest of the ocular examination was normal.
test_results: The DNA sequence analysis showed the variants c.112A > G (p.Lys38Glu) and c.217 T > C (p.Cys73Arg) in compound heterozygosity of PLG gene.
diagnosis: Ligneous Conjunctivitis due to PLG gene mutation

case_report: A 67-year-old man visited the Department of Ophthalmology for treatment advice regarding recurrent conjunctival 'granuloma' in his left eye. The initial occurrence of the conjunctival granuloma was within six weeks post-cataract surgery. The patient had previously undergone one excision in the right eye and five excisions in the left eye, with the most recent surgery on the left eye performed four weeks prior. The patient reported decreased visual acuity, a sensation of a foreign body, and a drooping left eyelid. Apart from these surgeries, the patient had no other eye-related issues. The patient had a medical history of arterial hypertension and hypothyroidism. At the initial presentation, the best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/40 in the left eye. The left eye exhibited a drooping eyelid covering half of the pupil and a wood-like granulation tissue on the bulbar conjunctiva extending from 10 to 1 o'clock from the limbus to the midperipheral cornea. The pseudophakia was regular. The right eye had a BCVA of 20/20 with no recurrence of the granuloma. Intraocular pressure was 14 mmHg in the right eye and 15 mmHg in the left eye. Funduscopic examination showed no abnormalities in either eye. A tumor excision with a free conjunctival autograft was performed on the left eye. On the first postoperative day, the autograft was well localized, and the granuloma was completely removed. Post-surgery, the patient was treated with topical prednisolone acetate, fluoroquinolone, and lubricant, each administered three times a day. The patient was discharged after two nights with a well-adapted conjunctival graft. Histology revealed an intact epithelium with subepithelial chronic inflammation and deposits of mucin and eosinophilic hyaline material. Alcian blue staining showed these deposits, while Congo-red staining showed negative results for apple green birefringence under polarized light and only red-stained erythrocytes. Two weeks later, the patient returned with worsened conditions in the operated left eye. Clinical examination identified two lesions: one at the original excision site and another new lesion at the site of the conjunctival graft at 5 o'clock.
test_results: This showed a plasminogen concentration of 1.5 g/l (normal value: 6-25 g/l) and a plasminogen activity of 21.98% (normal value: 75–150%).

case_report: A 43-year-old male fitness trainer visited the hepatology clinic after being referred by his general practitioner due to elevated serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels, which were 2–3 times the upper limit of normal over a period of 7 months. Bilirubin, gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT), and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels were within normal range. The patient reported a history of a muscle condition diagnosed at the age of 9. He had not been followed up since then. There was no other significant medical history, including no history of alcohol abuse, illicit drug use, hepatitis, or regular medication use. A detailed family history and review of previous investigations revealed that his father and elder brother had elevated serum creatine kinase (CK) concentrations.
test_results: Genetic linkage analysis pointed to caveolin-3 mutations.

case_report: A 64-year-old woman experienced a weight loss of 12 kg over 8 years and generalized hyperhidrosis without night sweats. She did not report symptoms indicative of thyrotoxicosis, compressive symptoms, or other B symptoms. Her medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus with good glycemic control, dyslipidemia, and bilateral carpal tunnel release surgery. Her medications included metformin 1000 mg twice daily, sitagliptin 100 mg daily, and simvastatin 20 mg daily. She was a non-smoker and had no history of cervical irradiation. Her sister had a history of an unspecified thyroid disease. Laboratory results showed a thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) level of <0.005 µIU/mL (normal range: 0.38–5.33 µIU/mL) and a previous TSH level of <0.005 µIU/mL five years ago. Free T4 was 18.3 pmol/L (12–30 pmol/L), and free T3 was 2.78 pg/mL (2.5–4.4 pg/mL). Anti-thyroperoxidase (TPOAb) and anti-thyroglobulin (TgAb) antibodies were negative. Thyroid ultrasound showed an enlarged gland with multiple bilateral thyroid nodules: two dominant nodules in the left lobe measuring 37 × 36 mm and 41 × 26 mm, and one 18 × 10 mm nodule in the right lobe, all with microcalcifications classified as EUTIRADS 5. No suspicious lymph nodes were detected. Previous fine-needle aspiration cytology of a 45-mm nodule in the left thyroid lobe was benign (Bethesda II). Thyroid Tc-99m scintigraphy indicated increased thyroid uptake [9.8% (normal range 0.4–4.0%)] with heterogeneous uptake in the left thyroid lobe and diminished uptake in the right lobe. Methimazole treatment was initiated, and the patient underwent an uneventful total thyroidectomy.
test_results: The histological analysis of the surgical specimen showed multiple thyroid nodules in both lobes with benign thyroid hyperplasia. In the right lobe, a nodule measuring 1.7 × 1.1 × 2.0 cm was seen, well-defined, brownish, and partially encapsulated, microscopically with a large cell lymphoid proliferation that infiltrates part of the hyperplasic nodule. The immunohistochemistry profile displayed positivity for CD20, CD45, Bcl2, Bcl6, and MUM 1 and CD10, CD5, cyclin D1, thyroglobulin, and CAM5.2 negativity.
diagnosis: Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma  localized to the thyroid gland

case_report: A 74-year-old female had a round pulmonary ground-glass nodule (p-GGN) measuring 12 mm in diameter in the right middle lobe of the lung, identified on chest imaging in May 2008 during a preoperative evaluation for right breast cancer. The patient underwent right mastectomy and sentinel lymph node dissection, with pathology showing papillotubular carcinoma without lymph node involvement. She was referred to our department in December 2009 and had another chest imaging in March 2010, which showed no significant change in the nodule size, measuring 11 mm at its largest dimension. Surgical resection was performed to obtain tissue for pathological examination and provide treatment. FDG-PET was not conducted due to anticipated low diagnostic yield for p-GGN. The patient underwent video-assisted thoracoscopic middle lobectomy in April 2009. Intraoperative frozen pathology indicated the tumor was an adenocarcinoma, leading to additional mediastinal lymphadenectomy.
test_results: The tumor located just beneath the visceral pleura exhibited the proliferation of small round to spindle-shaped cells arranged in a spindle cell pattern with finely granular chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, and a scant to moderate amount of eosinophilic cytoplasm. Necrosis and mitoses were rarely detected. The tumor cells were positive for chromogranin A and synaptophysin.
diagnosis: Typical carcinoid tumor of the lung

case_report: A 38-year-old woman with a history of recurrent pneumonia, leading to annual hospitalizations since 1988, was admitted. She had undergone treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis 9 years prior to this admission. The patient is a nonsmoker and has no other known diseases or family history of diseases. Chest radiography revealed a calcified wall in the left lower lung field along with multifocal nodular calcification in the surrounding lung tissue.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) angiography showed a multiseptated cystic mass in the left lower lobe, systemic arterial supply from the descending thoracic aorta, and venous drainage to the left inferior pulmonary vein. A subsequent immunohistochemical study revealed tumor cell reactivity for synaptophysin and chromogranin, which indicated neuroendocrine differentiation.
diagnosis: Bronchial Carcinoid Tumor Arising from an Intralobar Bronchopulmonary Sequestration

case_report: A 38-year-old female presented with a persistent cough. Imaging revealed an enlargement in the anterior mediastinum. Further evaluations identified an oval-shaped extracardiac mass located immediately anterior to the initial segment of the pulmonary artery and in front of the left atrium, without any compression effects. Additional imaging confirmed an encapsulated, heterogeneous mass in the anterior mediastinum, measuring 5.0 × 7.5 cm, with areas of calcification.
test_results: Chest X-ray found an enlargement of the anterior mediastinum. ECG, transthoracic echocardiography, and transoesophageal echocardiography revealed an ovalar extracardiac mass immediately anterior to the first tract of the pulmonary artery and anterior to the left atrium without compression effect. Thoracic medium contrast computerized axial tomography confirmed the encapsulated dishomogeneous expansive anterior mediastinal lesion of diameter 5.0 × 7.5 cm, with some calcification.
diagnosis: Typical carcinoid tumor within a mature cystic teratoma of the thymus

case_report: An 82-year-old man with no significant medical history was admitted with acute left thoracic empyema. Computed tomography identified a solitary mass measuring 7 × 5 × 3 cm in the anterior mediastinum, with no apparent connection to the empyema. The empyema resolved promptly following thoracoscopic surgery. Subsequent imaging of the mediastinal mass, performed with the patient's informed consent, included magnetic resonance imaging, which showed a high-intensity signal in a large portion and a low-intensity signal in the remaining part on diffusion-weighted images, indicating a solid tumor with a liquid component. No additional lesions were found during the metastatic workup. Four months post-empyema surgery, the patient underwent thymectomy via median sternotomy. The tumor was fully resected and was well encapsulated, except for a small area of pericardial adhesion that was removed en bloc. The cut surface of the resected specimen was solid and dark-brownish, indicating extensive pigmentation.
test_results: Histologic examination revealed a well-circumscribed tumor constituted by organoid or nesting proliferation of spindle-shaped cells with necrosis. There were 2–4 mitotic figures per 10 high-power fields. Dark-brownish pigmentation was easily identifiable in the macrophages and dendritic cells but was less obvious in the tumor cells, reflecting the amount of melanin pigment contained in these cells, as confirmed by Fontana–Masson staining. Immunohistochemical study revealed the epithelial nature of the tumor cells based on positive reactivity with cytokeratins AE1/AE3 and CAM5.2, but also revealed their neuroendocrine nature based on positive reactivity with synaptophysin and CD56. In addition, there were numerous sustentacular cells surrounding the tumor cell nests, as confirmed by positivity for S-100. The Ki-67 labeling index was 18.7%. The tumor cells also showed negative reactions with epithelial membrane antigen, p63, p40, CD5, CD68, CD57, CD34, smooth muscle actin, CD99, leukocyte common antigen, glial fibrillary acidic protein, and carcinoembryonic antigen.
diagnosis: Pigmented atypical carcinoid of thymic origin

case_report: A 61-year-old male reported experiencing a painful mass over the lower left scapula for four months. Over the past three weeks, the pain intensified and was associated with restricted movement of the left glenohumeral joint. Physical examination identified a subcutaneous, tender, uniformly firm mass in the lower left scapular area, measuring 4.5 × 4.5 cm. There were no indications of superficial skin inflammation. The patient had no prior history of melanoma or other skin tumors.
test_results: Radiological examination showed an osteolytic lesion in the lower left scapula while bone scanning was positive with increased uptake in the same area. CT scans and MRI images of the thorax and shoulder showed a soft tissue mass 45 × 45 mm localized in the lower scapular region between infraspinatus and teres minor muscles with bone invasion of the lower part of the scapula. There were no lung metastases neither axillary nor mediastinal lymph nodes. The open biopsy specimen consisted of a rubbery, homogenous, white tissue with no attachment to the skin, implying deep location of the tumor. There were compact nests and fascicles with large rounded and spindle-shaped cells separated by connective tissue septa. The large rounded cells had pleomorphic nuclei and large amounts of clear cytoplasm while the spindle-shaped cells had palely staining eosinophilic cytoplasm. Mitoses were moderately numerous. There were areas of necrosis and hemorrhage and tumor spreading into the surrounding muscles and scapula. Immunohistochemical stains were performed with negative staining for CD68, actin and desmin antigens and with positive staining for tumor markers S-100 protein, HMB-45, NSE, EMA, cytokeratins and myosin. Histochemical stains for melanin presence were negative.
diagnosis: Clear cell sarcoma of the scapula

case_report: A 66-year-old Caucasian male was admitted to the hospital for altered mental status. The patient has a history of bipolar disorder and has been residing in a psychiatric facility. Baseline mental state and function were reported as ambulatory, with appropriate interaction and speech, no tremors or movement disturbances, and a steady gait. The patient had been on olanzapine 5 mg nightly, which was discontinued 8 weeks prior due to drowsiness. The patient continued on valproic acid extended release 1,000 mg at bedtime and clonazepam 0.25 mg PO BID for anxiety and irritability. Five days before admission, the patient developed a fever, became bedridden with continuous sleep, a fixed stare, movements similar to oculogyric crisis, and intermittent rigidity. Valproic acid was held, and lorazepam was started q8h for 3 days. The patient's condition worsened, leading to hospital admission. Upon admission, vital signs included blood pressure of 100/70 mmHg, heart rate of 110 bpm, and oxygen saturation of 99%-100% on 2 L nasal cannula. The patient was unresponsive, rigid, and disoriented. Intravenous cefepime, vancomycin, and metronidazole were initiated. A head CT without contrast showed no bleed or acute findings but noted an incidental arachnoid cyst. Physical examination revealed an ill appearance, no obvious lesions, head without tenderness or deformities, pupils equally round and reactive to light and accommodation, fixed stare, poor dentition, no oropharyngeal erythema or injection, audible S1 S2 without murmur, clear chest auscultation, soft non-tender and non-distended abdomen, palpable pulses without edema. The patient was alert, responded to voice with incomprehensible sounds, moved all extremities spontaneously, had a mild resting tremor in distal extremities, intact reflexes, and hypertonia in all four extremities. Lorazepam 2 mg IV every 8 hours was recommended. By day 3, the patient's condition showed minimal improvement in bradykinesia, rigidity, and fixed stare.
