A resting tremor and decreased glabellar reflex were noted. Valproic acid was re-initiated. The neurology team recommended further evaluation. Due to suspicion of dental infection, the oral and maxillofacial team performed excision of carious non-restorable teeth on day 4, with no abscess, fluid collection, or gross infection noted. The patient tolerated anesthesia well, with no notable complications. By days 5-7, the patient's condition remained unchanged, lorazepam was discontinued, and a nasogastric tube was placed for nutritional tube feeds after failing a swallow study.
test_results: An abnormal EEG due to generalized background slowing. No seizures recorded.
diagnosis: Von Economo’s disease and postencephalitic parkinsonism

case_report: A 36-year-old male with a history of HIV presented with behavioral changes, including decreased responsiveness. He had been on a HAART regimen of abacavir-lamivudine, atazanavir, and ritonavir. Initially, he could walk and talk without issues. Four months prior, he experienced neck and back stiffness and reduced verbal communication. His family moved him from a group home to his parents' house, where he stopped his HAART. His symptoms initially improved but later worsened, affecting his speech and gait. His mother restarted his HAART, but his condition continued to decline, leading to multiple falls and almost no verbal communication. He was brought to the emergency room and admitted to internal medicine, showing minimal verbal output, responsiveness, and movement. His HAART was continued, and empiric acyclovir was started. Psychiatry was consulted, and lorazepam was administered without improvement. Neurology was then consulted. The patient was awake and alert but minimally responsive verbally and physically. He mouthed words without audible response, had rigidity in all extremities (more severe in the lower extremities), diffuse hyperreflexia, and sustained bilateral ankle clonus. He required assistance to stand, had difficulty initiating movements, a stooped posture, and a magnetic gait.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain showed extensive leukoencephalopathy with periventricular involvement and subcortical extension in the bilateral frontal and parietal lobes. The patient also had subtle mineralization of bilateral basal ganglia. MRI spine was unremarkable.

case_report: A 45-year-old male was admitted in April 2011 after being found lying naked in the street, talking to himself and cursing passers-by. He was unable to provide his name or home address, so no information was available on his history. On admission, his vital signs were normal (temperature 36.5 °C; pulse, 80 bpm; respiratory rate, 20 times/minute; and blood pressure, 125/80 mmHg) and he had normal muscle strength and reflexes. There were no abnormalities in electrolytes, blood counts, blood glucose, lipid profile, or liver or kidney function tests. Urine and stool tests were normal. EKG, EEG, and ultrasound of the liver, kidneys, pancreas, and spleen found no abnormalities. The sole abnormality on physical examination was that the skin around his eyes and forehead was dark brown to black, and his hands and forearms were covered with flaking skin. Mental status examination on admission found that the patient was conscious but unable to answer questions correctly. He covered his head with a quilt during the examination for no obvious reason. He laughed to himself, manifested inappropriate emotions, and appeared to lack insight into his condition. He had difficulty concentrating, had slowed reactions, and got a score of 20 on the Mini-Mental Status Exam (MMSE)—indicating moderate cognitive impairment. The patient was started on perphenazine 2mg/day. After three days of treatment, he developed severe diarrhea (yellow stool 3 to 4 times a day) and vomiting without an associated fever, with no abnormalities in the stool, and with a normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate. To stop the diarrhea, he was prescribed 5 mg of diphenoxylate, one bag of diosmectite, and 2 capsules of compounded glutamine three times a day. To resolve electrolyte imbalances (K, 2.8mmol/L), he was also given a daily intravenous infusion of 500 ml of 5% glucose and sodium chloride, with 30ml of 10% potassium chloride, 1.0 gram of vitamin C, and 1.0 gram of vitamin B6. Despite these treatments, his diarrhea persisted. By the 15th day of admission, the patient started having fecal incontinence. His level of consciousness deteriorated, he manifested signs of intense fear, stopped answering questions, and was no longer able to feed himself. His temperature was 36.8 °C; pulse, 75 bpm; respiratory rate, 19 times/minute; and blood pressure, 90/60 mmHg. He had marked increased muscle tone. Perphenazine was stopped immediately and (20 days after the initial admission) he was temporarily transferred to the gastroenterology department of another (general) hospital.
test_results: A 24-hour urine test found decreased levels of N-methylnicotinamide (<0.5 mg). A CT of the brain identified abnormalities of the cerebral cortex and diffuse spots around the cerebral ventricles.

case_report: Patient B, a 41-year-old right-handed former professional football player, began experiencing depressive symptoms at age 30, which progressively worsened over time. Over the past three to four years, he exhibited significant mood fluctuations, alternating between sadness, crying, laughter, and anger. He did not seek medical assistance for these mood issues. He gradually lost interest in his hobbies and reduced his daily activities, spending most of his time at home. At around age 39, he began experiencing memory difficulties, which progressively worsened. He had trouble recalling event details and needed to write things down to ensure tasks were completed. He frequently repeated questions throughout the day. His ability to perform daily self-care activities (ADLs) was somewhat compromised; he needed reminders to shower and prompts to dress appropriately for different occasions. His ability to perform tasks necessary for independent living (iADLs) was also affected. While he could shop independently, his wife took over bill payments to ensure they were paid on time, as he often forgot. His driving remained unaffected, with no accidents or instances of getting lost, although he relied on GPS for navigation. He continued to participate in household chores but often required assistance, such as starting the laundry but forgetting to finish it. Patient B began playing football at age 13 and continued for a total of 18 years, including 9 years professionally and 4 years in college. He experienced numerous incidents during games where he saw stars, lights, or felt dazed for a few minutes, though he could not recall the exact number. He specifically remembered being knocked out four times and needing assistance off the field.
test_results: His MOCA score was 23/30 and the CDR was 1. On the neuropsychological testing, patient exhibited significant deficit in multiple domains, including complex attention and executive functioning. MRI was normal. His neuropsychological testing results and clinical history fulfilled the criteria of DSM V for major neurocognitive disorder, for he had deficits, which interfered with daily life in two different domains.

case_report: A 22-year-old male patient with a history of CD presented to the emergency room due to significant hematochezia and hypovolemic shock. He had previously been treated for active CD affecting the ileum and colon with a penetrating phenotype. A CT scan from another facility showed involvement of multiple segments of the small bowel, including the jejunum. He received intravenous infliximab treatment. Upon admission, he was severely malnourished with a BMI of 17.8 kg/m2. Initial laboratory results were: WBC count 22,850/µL; hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL; platelets 157,000/µL; CRP 0.03 mg/dL; protein 3.0 g/dL; albumin 1.8 g/dL; triglycerides 73 mg/dL; cholesterol 119 mg/dL; BUN 6 mg/dL; creatinine 1.09 mg/dL; and prothrombin time/international normalized ratio 20.6 s (1.78). Emergent angiography identified active bleeding from the ileal branch of the superior mesenteric artery, which was treated with embolization using glue and lipiodol. Additionally, abdominal CT indicated a right-sided perianal abscess, which was managed with incision and drainage followed by primary closure. The patient was kept fasting for approximately 3 weeks and received peripheral TPN (Combiflex lipid peri® 1920 mL) without thiamine supplementation during this period. Upon resuming a liquid diet, he reported progressive blurred vision, cognitive dysfunction, intermittent confused speech, and dizziness after 2 days. He also experienced a 10-minute episode of generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Neurologic examination and electroencephalography did not reveal any abnormal neurologic signs except for slight latent nystagmus in the lateral gaze.
test_results: MRI revealed a high signal-intensity lesion at the both right and left sides of the mammillary body and tectum, and the periaqueductal space on a T2-weighted image.

case_report: A 46-year-old woman, previously diagnosed with nasopharyngeal cancer, was admitted for chemotherapy. She had no history of chronic alcohol use, benzodiazepine addiction, malnutrition, surgery, or herbal medication use. Laboratory tests showed no abnormalities. She underwent concurrent chemoradiation therapy with cisplatin (100 mg/m2 at 3-week intervals). One month after completing this therapy, she received chemotherapy with a continuous infusion of 5-FU (1,000 mg/m2/day for 4 days) and cisplatin (75 mg/m2 for 1 hour on the first day of each cycle at 3-week intervals). During the first cycle, she developed grade 2 stomatitis and grade 3 neutropenia, which resolved with supportive care. There was no significant diarrhea or vomiting. On the 20th day of the second chemotherapy cycle, she experienced dizziness and nystagmus, which improved with conservative management. Fifteen days later, she had an acute onset of disorientation, headache, and lethargy. Her mental status was confused, but there were no focal neurological signs or pathological reflexes. Vital signs were: blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, pulse rate 110/min, respiratory rate 14/min, and body temperature 36.4℃. Post-chemotherapy myelosuppression status included a white blood cell count of 1,300/µL (neutrophils 74.4%, lymphocytes 14.3%), hemoglobin concentration of 8.1 g/dL, and platelet count of 62,000/µL. Serum BUN was 10 mg/dL, creatinine 0.6 mg/dL, sodium 133 mM/L, potassium 3.5 mM/L, total protein 5.8 g/dL, serum albumin 3.6 g/dL, triglyceride 67 mg/dL, cholesterol 68 mg/dL, and magnesium 1.9 mg/dL. Her body weight was 52 kg at diagnosis and 54 kg at the time of the event. Serum folic acid concentration was 2 ng/mL, vitamin B12 concentration 1,259 pg/mL, and thiamine concentration 138.1 ng/dL. Ammonia concentration was normal.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed symmetrical high signal intensities in the posterior aspect of the medulla and periaqueductal area of the midbrain. A small amount of subdural hematoma in the right posterior occipital area was noted.

case_report: A 26-year-old otherwise healthy, nulligravida female presented to the emergency department with worsening right lower quadrant pain, diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting for four days. She also reported low back discomfort and abdominal discomfort, which she attributed to forceful vomiting. She had taken a muscle relaxant earlier that morning, but the pain in her right lower quadrant persisted. Her primary care physician advised her to go to the emergency department for evaluation. Over the past two years, she had experienced recurrent and increasing abdominal discomfort, increased heartburn, right and left lower quadrant pain with back pain, and fluctuating periods of diarrhea and constipation. She had been seen in the same emergency department 12 months prior and was treated for a urinary tract infection with antibiotics. Over the past 12 months, she had followed up with her primary care physician and various urgent care clinics approximately four times with similar symptoms; no imaging had been performed at any of those visits. Her history included irregular and heavy periods since she was young. Family history was positive for pancreatic, prostate, breast, and throat cancer spanning three generations. The patient had a noticeably tender abdominal examination, but all vital signs were stable. Laboratory data revealed leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 16.4 with a left shift, pyuria, and bacteriuria. The patient was currently being treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a very large cystic pelvic mass, 35x24 x36cm, extending into the abdomen. The mass displaced bowel loops and the colon and had a thin peripheral rind measuring 5mm. There was also free fluid in the pelvic cavity.
diagnosis: Benign cyst/pseudocyst without identifiable epithelial lining and absence of malignancy

case_report: A 15-month-old Caucasian boy presented with a 6-week history of progressive abdominal distension. He had no renal or gastrointestinal symptoms, and his antenatal scans at 20 weeks gestation were normal. On physical examination, he appeared unwell with a pulse rate of 150 beats/minute and blood pressure of 108/82 mmHg. His abdomen was largely distended and tense, with general discomfort on palpation but no signs of peritonitis. An ill-defined cystic mass was palpable on the right side of his abdomen. Routine blood tests, including haematology, coagulation, biochemistry, C-reactive protein, and liver function tests, showed no abnormalities. Urinary electrolytes, alpha-fetoprotein, and beta human chorionic gonadotropin levels were also within normal limits. An abdominal ultrasound revealed a large, cystic, multiseptated mass with a small solid nodule located in the right flank, extending across the midline and into the pelvis. The origin of the mass was unclear. A chest, abdominal, and pelvic CT scan showed a 14.7 × 13.6 × 15.2 cm complex septated cystic mass arising from the peritoneum, containing enhancing septae and solid nodules. The right kidney was mildly hydronephrotic and displaced supero-laterally but appeared separate from the mass. The left kidney was normal in size and texture. No intrathoracic or abdominal lymphadenopathy was observed. On day 6 of admission, an exploratory laparotomy was performed due to increasing pain and distress. The surgery revealed a large cyst arising from the lower pole of the right kidney, adherent to the duodenum, caecal mesentery, and colonic mesentery. The cyst was completely excised, and a right nephro-ureterectomy was performed.
test_results: The histology of the mass was reported as originating from the kidney with segmental dysplasia and haemorrhagic cyst formation.

case_report: In December 2019, a 6-month-old boy was admitted to the hospital due to edema lasting for one week and fever for one day. The child was born at full term (39 weeks and 2 days) via cesarean section, weighing 3,900 grams, and had no significant medical or personal history. Upon admission, the patient exhibited widespread body edema and pitting edema on the anterior tibial area. Laboratory tests revealed nephrotic-range proteinuria (263 mg/kg/day) and severe hypoalbuminemia (12.2 g/L). Additional laboratory findings included altered coagulation function with decreased antithrombins (AT), slightly elevated D-dimer, and prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), while prothrombin time (PT), fibrinogen degradation products (FDP), and fibrinogen (Fib) were within normal limits. Ultrasound imaging showed enlarged kidneys (left kidney: 8.5 × 4.9 × 4.0 cm; right kidney: 8.6 × 4.9 × 3.7 cm) with hyperechogenicity of the renal parenchyma and indistinct cortical-medullary boundaries. There was also a pelvic and abdominal cavity effusion depth of 3.4 cm. Chest CT revealed multiple bilateral pulmonary foci, partial pulmonary consolidation, bilateral pleural effusion, and poorly inflated adjacent pulmonary alveoli. Cardiac function and the nervous system were normal. Routine urine tests for both parents were normal. The patient was treated with ceftriaxone for infection control and received plasma and albumin infusions to increase colloidal osmotic pressure and manage diuresis. Intravenous enoxaparin sodium (0.06 ml/day, 50 AxaIU/kg/day) was administered for anticoagulation due to severe hypoalbuminemia and fluid management complications. Intravenous immunoglobulin was given intermittently for immune support. Thyroid function tests showed significantly reduced levels of free triiodothyronine (FT3) and free thyroxine (FT4), with a significantly increased thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level, though ultrasound showed no abnormalities. Oral levothyroxine sodium (12.5 μg/day) was administered. The patient developed an intestinal infection caused by norovirus during hospitalization. After excluding tuberculosis, intravenous methylprednisolone (1.6 mg/kg/day) was administered on the fourth day of hospitalization. After 25 days, the patient's condition improved significantly, with subsided edema, reduced 24-hour urine protein (0.43 g/day), and increased plasma albumin (20.5 g/L). Coagulation parameters (AT, D-dimer, APTT, PT, FDP, and Fib) returned to normal ranges. The patient was discharged with instructions to continue oral prednisone (2 mg/kg/day) for 2 weeks, followed by a gradually reducing dosage (2 and 0.5 mg/kg/day alternately in the morning) for 1 month, then 2 mg/kg/day on alternate days for 2 weeks, with a reduction of 2.5 mg every 2 weeks.
test_results: The results indicated a novel hemizygous potentially pathogenic variant, c.2717A>G (p.His906Arg), in exon 17 of the TBC1D8B gene. This potentially pathogenic variant was derived from the mother (who had no history of symptoms and no proteinuria) and the father's gene was normal. The amino acid sequences for this site (His906) showed that it was identical in Homo sapiens, Pan troglodytes, Macaca mulatta, Canis lupus familiaris, Mus musculus, Rattus norvegicus, Gallus gallus, and Danio rerio. The minor allele frequency (MAF) of this site in the gnomAD database was 0.0005 (East Asia).
diagnosis: Steroid-Sensitive Nephrotic Syndrome  associated with a novel TBC1D8B variant
Orpha_name: Steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome without renal biopsy

case_report: A 66-year-old Caucasian female presented to the emergency room with a 4-week history of intermittent abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and poor oral intake. Nephrology consultation was requested due to an elevated creatinine level of 17.54 mg/dl found in the emergency room laboratory results. Approximately 4 months prior, her serum creatinine was within normal range at 1.24 mg/dl. The patient reported generalized weakness. Her medications included amlodipine, benazepril, hydrochlorothiazide, and pantoprazole. Physical examination revealed elevated blood pressure at 160/82 mm Hg, with the rest of the examination being unremarkable. Urinalysis showed 3+ proteinuria and 25–50 red blood cells per high power field. Initial laboratory evaluation indicated elevated blood urea nitrogen at 119 mg/dl and a low hemoglobin level of 8.7 g/dL. A 24-hour urine collection revealed 33 g of protein. Upon admission, all home medications except amlodipine were discontinued. Hemodialysis was initiated for uremia management. Serological tests for hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibody, antinuclear antibody, antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibodies, anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody, cryoglobulins, and human immunodeficiency virus antibody were all negative. Complement levels were normal. Serum immunofixation did not detect any monoclonal immunoglobulin. Renal sonogram showed increased echogenicity in both kidneys.
test_results: On light microscopy, twelve glomeruli were identified in one section. Eight (67%) glomeruli contained large cellular crescents. Of the remaining four glomeruli that did not have crescents, one was globally sclerosed and one showed segmental mild mesangial matrix expansion. There was marked endocapillary hypercellularity seen in several glomeruli. There was no fibrinoid necrosis. Bowman's capsule was focally disrupted by crescents. Eighty percent of the tubules were intact and there was a mild degree of tubular atrophy. There was no evidence of acute tubular necrosis. There was no interstitial fibrosis. However, there was mild to moderate interstitial infiltrates comprising of lymphocytes and occasional eosinophils and neutrophils. Congo red stain was negative in glomeruli. Immunofluorescence microscopy showed 1+ fine granular deposits of IgG along the capillary loops and 1+ deposits of C3 predominately in the mesangium. There was no glomerular staining for IgA, IgM, C1q, kappa, or lambda light chains. Electron microscopy showed severe effacement of epithelial cell foot processes. Structured electron-dense material was seen predominately in the mesangium with some capillary loops having subendothelial deposition. These structures were randomly arranged fibrils measuring from 10 to 35 nm in diameter.

case_report: A 70-year-old woman was admitted to the Juntendo University Shizuoka Hospital. She had previously visited the outpatient clinic 2 years ago due to proteinuria and microscopic hematuria. Despite treatment with an angiotensin II receptor antagonist (losartan, 25 mg/day), her urinary protein excretion increased to the nephrotic range, and pretibial pitting edema was noted. The patient had a 14-year history of NTM, with cultures of gastric lavage samples testing positive for Mycobacterium intracellulare. Antimycobacterial treatment was halted after she developed toxic epidermal necrolysis from isoniazid, rifampicin, and ethambutol. Upon admission, she was alert, well-developed, and slender, appearing her stated age. She reported easy fatigue due to significant pitting edema in the lower extremities. She did not consume alcohol or smoke. Her sitting blood pressure was 138/94 mm Hg, and her pulse rate was 70 beats per minute. Urinalysis indicated a 3+ dipstick test for protein, 2+ for occult blood, and negative for sugar. Urinary sediments showed 20–29 RBCs/HPF, and the urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio was 9.9 g/g Cr. Laboratory tests showed serum urea nitrogen at 24.7 mg/dL (normal: 9–21), creatinine at 1.43 mg/dL (normal: 0.4–0.9), uric acid at 7.3 mg/dL (normal: 3.8–7.5), and an eGFR of 28.6 mL/min/1.73 m2. Hematologic evaluation, liver function, serum cholesterol, and electrolytes were within normal ranges. Serological markers for syphilis and hepatitis B and C were negative. Serum immunoelectrophoresis showed normal IgG, IgA, and IgM precipitin arcs. Tests for antinuclear antibodies, anti-DNA antibodies, PR3-ANCA, MPO-ANCA, and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies were negative. Cryoglobulin tests were negative, and C3 and C4 levels were within normal ranges. Chest radiography revealed small nodular opacities, while computed tomography showed multiple small nodules and multifocal bronchiectasis with small cavities.
test_results: During renal biopsy, 3 cores were obtained by ultrasound-guided needle biopsy. The renal cortex was approximately 70%. LM showed 21 glomeruli that exhibited mesangial widening and thickening of capillary walls. Lobular accentuation was evident in the glomeruli, and the capillary lumens were collapsed. Parts of the lobular centers were sclerosed. The glomerular basement membrane was thickened, resulting in double contour appearance. Subepithelial deposition was evident. Two glomeruli were sclerosed globally, and focal tubular atrophy with interstitial fibrosis and inflammatory cell infiltration were observed in 30% area of the cortex. Congo red staining of the renal tissues was negative for amyloid deposition. In IF, granular deposits of C3 and C1q were observed in the glomerular mesangial areas and capillary walls. Rather scant IgG and IgM deposits were mainly evident in the capillary walls. IgA and fibrinogen showed subtle or negative signals. EM showed marked evidence of massive EDDs in the subendothelial areas and mesangial interposition. EDDs were observed in the glomerular capillary walls and subepithelial areas. The foot processes over the EDDs were effaced. High-magnification views revealed that the EDDs were composed of microtubules with a diameter around 50 nm. These tubules formed parallel arrays. Immunohistochemistry with anti-DnaJ homolog subfamily B member 9 (DNAJB9) antibody, which specifically stains glomerular deposits in the patients with fibrillary glomerulonephritis, revealed background signals in glomeruli, while human exocrine glands in resected pancreas showed strongly positive signals.

case_report: A 49-year-old male presented with widespread swelling, reduced urine output, breathing difficulties, and a weight increase of 12 kg over several months. His medical history includes high blood pressure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hypospadias, dilated cardiomyopathy, and recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes mellitus without diabetic retinopathy. Upon admission, laboratory results indicated a serum creatinine level of 2.9 mg/dL (normal range for men: 0.6–1.2 mg/dL), serum BUN level of 80.1 mg/dL, 24-hour proteinuria of 7 g, HbA1c of 6.5% (normal <5.7%), serum albumin level of 2.5 g/dL (normal range: 3.5–5 g/dL), and total cholesterol level of 348 mg/dL (normal <200 mg/dL). Further tests showed normal levels of serum immunoglobulins and complement components (C3 and C4). Tests for serum-free light chains, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (c-ANCA), anti-dsDNA, and anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) antibodies were negative. Hepatitis B surface antigen was positive.
test_results: Under light microscopy, a total number of 15 glomeruli were observed. Five glomeruli were ischemically collapsed, and all other glomeruli were replaced with amorphous eosinophilic material predominantly with endocapillary localization. The renal tubules were atrophic with protein intratubular casts. Mild interstitial fibrosis with mixed mononuclear cell infiltration was also noted. On immunofluorescence (IF), IgG and C3 were dominant deposits in the glomeruli, with an irregular pattern of distribution. Electron microscopy showed non-branching, hollow-core microtubules in the subendothelial zone.

case_report: A 35-year-old male presented with a low-grade fever and a cough producing mucopurulent sputum for 10 days, with a history of recurrent similar episodes since childhood. General examination revealed pallor and rapid breathing. Chest examination indicated decreased movement of the right hemithorax, a shift of the trachea to the same side, an impaired percussion note, and absent breath sounds on the right side, with scant coarse inspiratory crackles in the mammary area. The left side exhibited a hyper-resonant percussion note, harsh vesicular breath sounds, and coarse crackles. Blood routine examination showed mild anemia with an increased number of neutrophils. The patient was otherwise healthy with no other comorbid illnesses.
test_results: Chest X ray revealed an opaque right hemi thorax with signs of volume loss and compensatory hyperinflation of the left lung. He was investigated with CT thorax, bronchoscopy, bronchogram, pulmonary angiogram. No other congenital anomalies were identified.

case_report: A 19-year-old healthy, Caucasian man presented with a two-year history of nonrestful sleep nearly every night. He was referred by his employer for evaluation. Nine months prior to presentation, he learned for the first time from coworkers that he shook frequently while sleeping. He had one episode of being awoken to find his extremities moving uncontrollably for a few minutes. These events continued nearly every night, presumably as they had before. There were never any nightmares or terrors, other than anxiety from not having control of his body several times upon awakening. He had a normal polysomnography test at that time. This condition prevented him from deploying with his military unit, which greatly saddened him. He discovered that Doxylamine (Unisom), an H1 receptor antagonist, alleviated his symptoms, provided restful sleep, and decreased muscle fatigue in the mornings 100% of the time. Hypothermia, sleep deprivation, extreme exercise, explosions, and stress had never triggered an event. He had no family history of this condition and a completely normal physical exam.
test_results: The patient had a total of four dyskinetic events during slow-wave sleep, two of which were precipitated by external stimuli (knocking on the door and turning on the light with voice). The episodes lasted approximately 40 seconds total and each began with 3–6 seconds of a tonic phase of both upper extremities and truncal flexors, sometimes partially sitting upright. Choreoathetoid movements followed, which involved primarily the upper extremities, most notably in the wrists and fingers. He also had intermittent torticollis to the right. The episodes ended with the patient laying down appearing to try and get comfortable in the bed, fidgeting with the blanket, quickly moving from his left and right sides, with facial grimacing and choreoathetoid movements of his head, neck, and hands as the movements minimized over approximately 15 seconds. Sleep appeared to resume quite suddenly. During one of the episodes, staff carried on a conversation with him in which he was oriented to himself, place, and time. He was aware of what was happening to his body and was able to confirm that the ongoing episode was typical for the episodes he has been aware of in the past. He was not confused at all when the episode ended and remained awake talking with the staff.

case_report: A 3-year-old male presented with a 2-day history of cough, cold, fever, and reduced oral intake. Over the past year, he experienced two episodes characterized by sudden vomiting, cyanosis, and moderate to high-grade fever. These episodes included eye deviation to one side lasting about 30 minutes, followed by a period of unconsciousness lasting from 1 to 12 hours. His birth and developmental milestones were normal, and there was no family history of epilepsy. Upon admission, he was febrile with mild throat congestion. The remainder of the general and systemic examination was unremarkable. Symptomatic treatment was initiated.
test_results: Electroencephalogram (EEG), cerebrospinal fluid studies, and neuroimaging were normal. Neuroimaging and EEG were normal.

case_report: A 4-year-old girl experienced four episodes of prolonged autonomic seizures. There was no history of perinatal complications, head trauma, central nervous system infections, or febrile convulsions. The initial seizure occurred one year prior to the fourth episode. The fourth episode took place half an hour after she had fallen asleep. She woke up abruptly, exhibited a blank stare, appeared pale, and vomited for 10 minutes. During the later stages of vomiting, she was non-responsive to verbal commands. Subsequently, her eyes deviated to the right, followed by clonic movements in her right arm. These hemi-clonic movements persisted for 10 to 15 minutes. Upon arrival at the emergency room, she was unresponsive and flaccid for approximately 30 minutes before gradually regaining normalcy. Post-recovery neurological examination revealed no abnormalities. However, arterial blood gas analysis conducted during her unresponsive state indicated respiratory acidosis with hypoxemia, with the following values: pH 7.14, pCO2 88 mmHg, pO2 50 mmHg, and bicarbonate 29 mmol/L.
test_results: The EEG revealed repetitive bursts of sequential spikes and waves at the left occipital electrode (O1). The brain MRI showed a slightly increased signal change in the left hippocampus on T2 and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery image.

case_report: The patient is a 7.5-year-old male, born at 39 weeks gestation with a birth weight of 3.8 kg. He experienced perinatal asphyxia and required respiratory support in the nursery. He had a motor developmental delay but maintained normal cognitive function. He was later identified with hemiplegic right-sided cerebral palsy, Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) level I. He could perform gross motor activities such as running, jumping, and walking outdoors, albeit with limited balance, speed, and coordination in his right limbs. At 3.5 years old, he experienced a prolonged focal autonomic seizure lasting 30–40 minutes shortly after falling asleep, which began with retching, ictal vomiting, and staring, followed by a focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure with impaired awareness. He remained seizure-free for nearly three years until, at 6.5 years old, he had two seizures within a month while falling asleep. These episodes involved autonomic symptoms such as pallor, pupillary dilation, staring, ictal vomiting, flaccidity, and minor shaking movements of his extremities, each lasting 5–10 minutes. The patient returned to normal after a few hours of sleep. None of the seizures indicated a right-sided onset based on clinical observations. His neurocognitive status remained stable with excellent academic performance and diligent behavior at school. A single sleep-EEG performed at 1.5 years old as part of routine care for his cerebral palsy did not show epileptiform abnormalities.
test_results: His EEG at 3.5 and 6.5 years after the first and second events, respectively, revealed normal background activity during wakefulness and repetitive high voltage tangential dipoles with frontal/central positivity and the main negative peak bi-occipitally maximal in the left occipital area, showing marked drowsiness and sleep activation. His brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, done shortly after the second seizure, displayed asymmetric white matter lesions with mild gliosis and volume loss in periventricular regions, resulting in ex-vacuo dilatation of the left lateral ventricle.

case_report: Case 2 involves an 11-year-old boy with a history of seizures lasting for 9 months. The boy's father began experiencing seizures at the age of 20, and the boy's great-uncle (grandmother's brother) also has a history of twitching. A heterozygous mutation was identified in the LGI1 gene (NM_005097.4:c.215+2T>A:p.Ile187Met), inherited from his father. The family history includes multiple members with seizure activity, specifically the boy's father and great-uncle.
test_results: Patients in this family all possess this mutation (NM_005097.4: c.215+2T>A:p.Ile187Met), which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. This splice-site mutation in LGI1 could cause the length of the protein encoded by it be truncated or degraded. The variant was extremely rare, since it was not included in 1000 Genomes or NHLBI Exome Sequencing Project (ESP), and mutation was clearly predicted to be functionally deleterious based on mutation effect prediction tools. So the variant c.215+2T>A in LGI1 was classified as pathogenic according to the above evidences and ACMG guidelines.

case_report: A 41-year-old male with no significant past medical history experienced abdominal bloating for one month before visiting the Hematology department. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell (WBC) count of 210.74×10^9/L, hemoglobin (Hb) level of 68g/L, and platelet (PLT) count of 17×10^9/L. A manual differential count revealed the following distribution in white blood cells: 95% neutrophils (11% segmented neutrophils, 12% band neutrophils, 27% metamyelocytes, 44% myelocytes, and 1% promyelocytes), 1% monocytes, 2% blast cells, and 2% lymphocytes. Physical examination found hepatosplenomegaly.
test_results: A bone marrow (BM) examination and trephine biopsy were performed and revealed hypercellularity with marked myeloid expansion with primary + promyelocytic granulocytes accounting for 7.5%. These granulocytes mainly predominantly exhibited various developmental stages, including middle, late, and rod-shaped forms, with an unbalanced nuclear morphology and decreased or absent cytoplasmic granules. Flow Cytometry analysis uncovered an abnormal myeloid protocell phenotype characterized by CD34+CD117+CD38dimHLA-DRdimCD13+CD33+CD11B-CD15-CD64-CD56-CD7-, accounting for 1.63% of nucleated cells. Karyotype was normal and an initial molecular analysis targeting BCR/ABL1 rearrangement, as well as mutations of CSF3R, JAK2V617F, CARL, and MPL, did not reveal any genetic abnormalities. Next generation sequencing (NGS) analysis utilizing the Myeloid Proliferative Neoplasm Sequencing Panel (Illumina), covering 77 genes that are known to be frequently mutated in myeloid malignancies, unveiled pathogenic variants in ASXL (p.Y591*, VAF 47.9%), CEBPA(p.L78Wfs*82, VAF 46%), vKRAS(p.A146T, VAF 21.1%), NRAS(p.G12R, VAF 21.4%), and STAG2 (p.L351Tfs*6, VAF 73.9%).

case_report: In April 2010, a 54-year-old male patient reported experiencing fatigue and abdominal pain. Physical examination revealed an enlarged spleen. Blood tests showed an elevated white blood cell count (93.38 x 10^9/L) with a high number of neutrophils and immature cells. Bone marrow analysis indicated increased cellularity with abnormalities in granulocytic and erythroid cells.
test_results: A 46,XY,t(9;22) (p24;q11.2) karyotype was found in 90% of the metaphases examined. The presence of a BCR-ABL rearrangement was ruled out by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) using a BCR-ABL probe. No BCR/PDGFR FIP fusion gene or JAK2 V617F mutation were detected by RT-PCR.

case_report: A 53-year-old female, previously healthy, began experiencing recurrent fever, cough, night sweats, and general weakness in September 2019. Laboratory tests revealed leukocytosis with a WBC count of 37.85 x 10^3/μL (normal range: 4.1–10.8 x 10^3/μL), increased neutrophils at 85.1% (normal range: 54–62%), decreased lymphocytes at 8.5% (normal range: 25–33%), and thrombocytopenia at 127 x 10^3/μL (normal range: 150-350 x 10^3/μL). Blood film analysis showed neutropenia with a left shift, normal RBCs, and platelets. Immunochemistry for ANA-HEP-2 was negative. An abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable. A hematological blood film report on 25th September indicated normocytic, normochromic RBCs with slight rouleaux formation, leukocytosis with segmented neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, and monocytes, and the presence of band neutrophils and myelocytes. A bone marrow biopsy in November 2019 showed no increased plasma cells by CD138 stain. Real-time PCR for major and minor BCR-ABL fusion transcripts t(9;22)(q34;q11) detected no abnormalities. Flow cytometry analysis showed 2% blasts, 89% granulocytes, 2% lymphocytes, and 3.6% monocytes, with no evidence of bone marrow involvement by myeloma cells. On 5th February 2020, CALR Exon 9 mutation analysis and MPL1 W515L/K testing by PCR and Sanger sequencing were both negative. A BCR-ABL major fusion gene (p210) quantification test also showed no detection. Serum protein electrophoresis on 10th February revealed decreased albumin at 48.6% (normal range: 54–66%), slight increase in alpha 1 protein at 2.9% (normal range: 1.4–2.8%), and increased gamma protein at 26.2% (normal range: 10.6–19.2%). Referred to our hospital on 26th February, repeat laboratory studies confirmed leukocytosis and thrombocytopenia (WBC 90.12 x 10^3/μL, normal range: 4-11 x 10^3/μL; neutrophils 74.04 x 10^3/μL, normal range: 2–8.7 x 10^3/μL; decreased lymphocytes percentage, increased neutrophils percentage, and PLTs 90 x 10^3/μL, normal range: 140–440). Basophilia was noted at 0.2% (normal range: 0.0–0.1%) with a basophil count of 0.15 x 10^3/μL (normal range: 0.0–0.1 x 10^3/μL). A BCR-ABL t(9;22) translocation quantitative test by RT-PCR was negative for major and minor criteria, consistent with previous results.
test_results: A bone marrow biopsy was performed that exhibited a hypercellular bone marrow with marked granulocytic hyperplasia with no morphologic evidence of acute leukemia. The reticulin stain, done later on 10th March, was grade 1 fibrosis, the cellularity was 95%, granulocytic precursors were markedly increased, the megakaryocytes were decreased, and the lymphocytes and plasma cells were normal. A day later, a bone marrow biopsy was executed showing that the major BCR-ABL was not detected.

case_report: An 81-year-old man arrived at the hospital with sudden, severe bilateral back pain. His medical history includes bladder and prostate cancer at age 74 and descending colon cancer at age 80, all treated successfully with surgery. Postoperative CT imaging and colonoscopies showed no recurrence of these cancers. Bladder cancer surgery included a urostomy. There were no endocrine or hematologic disorders in his medical or family history. He had a history of smoking 40 cigarettes per day for 45 years, quitting at age 65, and consumed a small amount of alcohol weekly. Vital signs were normal, and physical examination was unremarkable except for severe back pain. There was no skin pigmentation, fatigue, postural hypotension, or recent weight loss. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed bilateral adrenal hypertrophy, non-contrast-enhancing areas, and adjacent fatty inflammatory changes. Laboratory results showed serum ACTH at 34.64 pg/mL, serum cortisol at 24.5 μg/dL, plasma renin activity (PRA) at 0.2 ng/mL/h, and plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC) at 3.34 ng/dL. The patient had been taking Rikkunshito, which contains glycyrrhizin, potentially affecting renin suppression. Blood catecholamine levels were elevated, correlating with severe pain. He was admitted for pain management, and analgesics were administered as needed. By day 3, the back pain had resolved. Abdominal MRI on day 5 showed high signal intensity on diffusion-weighted imaging and no adrenal hemorrhage on T2 star-weighted imaging. Repeat contrast-enhanced CT on day 9 showed improvement in bilateral adrenal hypertrophy, non-contrast-enhancing areas, and adjacent fatty inflammatory changes. Further examinations for thrombophilia or hypercoagulable states revealed no abnormalities. Peripheral blood tests indicated leukopenia, anemia, giant platelets, and blast cells. He was temporarily discharged with plans for further hematological evaluation. On day 62, he returned with stomachache and backache. Repeat contrast-enhanced CT showed similar findings to the initial CT. Laboratory examination on day 63 showed high platelet counts (619,000/μL), persistent leukopenia, and anemia. He was readmitted for further evaluation.
test_results: Bone marrow findings revealed dysplasia in three major hematopoietic cell lineages, the presence of 4.2% blast cells, and megakaryocyte proliferation. No ring sideroblast was found. BCR-ABL1, JAK2, CALR, MPL, and PDGFRA genes were negative for mutations.

case_report: A 54-year-old male patient presented with gum swelling, pain, and fever and was admitted to The First Hospital of Jilin University in November 2013. His medical history was unremarkable. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 4.97 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin concentration of 95 g/L, and platelet count of 26 × 10^9/L. Peripheral blood smear analysis revealed 22% myeloid blasts with visible Auer bodies. Bone marrow biopsy indicated a hypercellular marrow with hyperplasia, and bone marrow smears showed 76.5% myeloid blasts with visible Auer bodies. Cytochemical staining was positive for peroxidase and esterase, and flow cytometry detected CD34, CD117, CD56, CD19, CD33, CD13, human leukocyte antigen-DR isotope (HLA-DR), and CD123 expression on the cell surface of leukemic blasts. An abnormal karyotype with 45, X, -Y, t(8; 21)(q22; q22)[4]/46, XY[7] and mutation in Runt-related transcription factor 1 (RUNX1)/RUNX1 partner transcriptional co-repressor 1 (RUNX1T1) were observed. FMS-like tyrosine kinase 3-internal tandem duplication, nucleophosmin 1, C-KIT, CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein alpha, isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)1/IDH2, and DNA (cytosine-5)-methyltransferase 3A (DNMT3A) mutations were negative. The patient received induction chemotherapy with idarubicin (10 mg/m^2) for 3 days plus cytarabine (100 mg/m^2) for 7 days, achieving complete hematological remission. Deep molecular remission was achieved after two-cycle consolidation chemotherapy, including one cycle with daunorubicin (45 mg/m^2) for 3 days plus cytarabine (100 mg/m^2) for 5 days and another cycle with high-dose cytarabine (2.0 g/m^2 every 12 hours, intravenous injection on days 1, 3, and 5). Three courses of consolidation therapy with high-dose cytarabine were administered, and continued complete remission was maintained until the fourth year of follow-up. In March 2018, the patient was admitted again for fever, with temperature fluctuating between 37.0 and 37.7°C. Prior to admission, the patient had been treated with cefuroxime for 8 days and sulfamethoxazole for 6 days without improvement in body temperature. Hemolysis-related and immune-related examinations were negative. CBC analysis revealed leukocytosis (20.37 × 10^9/L), thrombocytopenia (53 × 10^9/L), and anemia (hemoglobin concentration of 68 g/L). Myeloid blasts were observed in peripheral blood smears, and the differential white blood cell count showed mainly neutrophils accounting for 78% (23% immature precursors, 14% band cells, and 41% segmented cells), eosinophils accounting for 4%, mature lymphocytes accounting for 16%, and monocytes accounting for 2% (monocyte count of 0.6 × 10^9/L).
test_results: Bone marrow biopsy exhibited no evidence of myelofibrosis. Flow cytometry showed 8.34% blasts and positive CD34, CD117, CD13, CD33, CD38, and HLA-DR expression. Cytogenetic analysis revealed a karyotype of 44, XY, -5, -6, -11, -17, -18, +mar×3, with no t(3; 3)(q21; q26), inv(3)(q21q26), or del(5q). TP53 mutation was positive, and there was no evidence of RUNX1/RUNX1T1, BCR/ABL1, platelet-derived growth factor receptor A (PDGFRA), PDGFRB, and fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 (FGFR1) rearrangement or pericentriolar material 1 (PCM1)-Janus kinase 2 (JAK2) gene fusion.

case_report: A 15-month-old boy was identified with a condition involving pro-B cells in June 2001. Laboratory tests showed CD19+ and HLA-DR+ markers. Chromosomal analysis indicated a 46, XY karyotype. The patient reached a state of complete remission following induction chemotherapy and concluded the chemotherapy regimen in January 2005. Thirty-three months post-therapy, the patient exhibited symptoms of fever and swelling of the cervical lymph nodes.
test_results: Bone marrow (BM) analysis revealed 87.0% small-to-medium-sized leukemic blasts with a moderate amount of cytoplasm. Cytochemical and immunocytochemical staining revealed a negative reaction for myeloperoxidase (MPO) and anti-MPO. Flow cytometric analysis showed positivity for CD33, cyCD13, cyCD33, and CD117. Cytogenetic analysis showed 46, XY, t(9;11)(p22;q23). Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis with a MLL-probe showed a signal in 97.5% of blasts.

case_report: A 68-year-old male was admitted to the hospital due to fever, cough, and progressive shortness of breath for 10 days. The patient had been treated with antibiotics (clarithromycin) and antiviral medication (oseltamivir) by his family doctor, with no improvement. Initial clinical evaluation showed acute respiratory failure based on arterial blood gases and multiple diffuse infiltrates on chest X-ray. The patient was immediately admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU). A pharyngeal swab was taken, and real-time Polymerase Chain Reaction (rt-PCR) was positive for SARS-CoV-2, confirming COVID-19. His family history was negative for COVID-19. The patient had a medical history of mild hypertension, treated with candesartan-hydrochlorothiazide, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He was an ex-smoker (80 pack-years) and his lab exams one year ago were within normal limits. Laboratory tests suggested the presence of cytokine release syndrome (CRS). The patient’s clinical course, laboratory findings, and outcome are detailed in a recent publication focused on management with recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rt-PA) and tocilizumab (an antagonist of interleukin-6 receptor). During hospitalization, the patient developed candidemia and bloodstream bacterial infections (by Stenotrophomonas maltophilia and Pseudomonas aeruginosa), which were treated with broad-spectrum antifungal and antibiotic treatments. Three days after the last dose of tocilizumab, serum evaluation revealed the presence of anti-SARS-CoV-2 IgG antibodies and negative PCR for SARS-CoV-2 in blood and stool. Despite this, his clinical condition worsened, and lab tests showed sustained anemia (Hb: 8.2 g/dL) and thrombocytopenia (platelet count: 24 x 10^9/L).
test_results: The presence of myeloblasts in a proportion of 32% was observed. Immunophenotyping revealed that myeloblasts were positive for the expression of CD34, CD38, CD13, CD33, CD117 and HLA-DR molecules.

case_report: An 85-year-old female was referred due to elevated white blood cell count with the presence of blast cells. She exhibited no symptoms. Upon admission, her white blood cell count was 10,900/µL, with 13% blast cells, 0.5% myelocytes, 66.5% neutrophils, 3.5% eosinophils, 13.5% lymphocytes, and 3% monocytes. Her hemoglobin level was 12.2 g/dL, and her platelet count was 378,000/µL. The serum lactate dehydrogenase level was 272 U/L.
test_results: A bone marrow examination revealed a hypercellular bone marrow with a blast cell frequency of 54.8%. Chromosomal analysis of the patient’s bone marrow cells showed the following karyotype: 46,XX,t(5;11)(q35;q13)[]/46,XX[]. Surface marker analysis revealed that the blast cells were positive for CD7 (29.3%), CD56 (63.5%), CD13 (26.5%), CD33 (25.2%), CD34 (81.1%), and human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-DR (97.1%) and negative for CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, CD8, CD10, CD19, CD20, CD16, and CD14.

case_report: A 23-year-old male patient presented to the hospital on October 11, 2020, with a primary complaint of a persistent cough lasting 4 months accompanied by fever. Previous antibiotic treatments had not been effective. The patient's medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Physical examination revealed signs of anemia and palpable lymph nodes in the bilateral submandibular and left axillary regions. The right submandibular lymph node measured 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm, while the left submandibular lymph node measured 4 cm × 4 cm. No enlargement of internal organs was noted. Complete blood count (CBC) results showed a white blood cell count of 3.670 × 10^9/L, a neutrophil count of 1.402 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin level at 44 g/L, platelet count of 437 × 10^9/L, and 7.5% immature cells. Biochemical tests indicated an LDH level of 559 U/L, and coagulation function tests were within normal limits.
test_results: Based on bone marrow aspiration from the left posterior superior iliac spine, proliferation of nucleated cells in the bone marrow was active, with a granulocyte to erythrocyte ratio of 0.50:1. The proportion of blasts was increased, accounting for 16.0% of ANC. FCM analysis of the bone marrow was performed; 50,000 cells were obtained and analyzed. In a CD45/SSC scatter plot, 28.23% of immature cells with an abnormal immunophenotype were detected in the CD45 dim and SS low area. CD34, CD33 and CD38 were positive. CD7 and HLA-DR were partially positive, and CD56 was dim. CD2, CD19, CD20, CD10, CD13, CD117, CD15, CD14, MPO, cCD79a and cCD3 were negative. Bone marrow aspiration from the right posterior superior iliac spine on the 12th day of induction chemotherapy showed that blasts accounted for 24.5% of ANCs. FCM was consistent with the previous immunophenotype of bone marrow blasts. Karyotype results were 90 to 91 < 4n>, XXYY, add(2)(q37) × 2, 6, i(17)(q10) × 2[6]/46,XY[14]. A somatic frameshift mutation, c.1236dup (p. Gln413Thrfster13), in the ETV6 gene was detected in the bone marrow sample. FCM of the left cervical lymph node sample showed 36.4% immature cells with an abnormal immunophenotype in CD45 dim/low SS areas expressing CD34, CD33 and CD7 but not CD2, CD10, CD5, CD4, CD8 and CD117. Immunohistochemistry of immature cells in the left cervical lymph node showed the following: CD7 (+), CD43(+), CD3(−), CD2(−), CD5(−), CD4(−), CD8(−), CD10(+), CD34(+), CD99(+), TdT(−), CD20(−), PAX-5(−), CD15(−), MPO(−), CD21(−), CD117(−), CD123(−), PGM-1(−), KP1(−), CK(−), and Ki-67 90%. The EBER1/2 in situ hybridization result was tumor cells (−).
diagnosis: Acute Undifferentiated Leukemia  with undifferentiated granulocytic sarcoma

case_report: In September 2008, a 68-year-old man presented with left-sided chest pain. Initial hematology tests showed a white blood cell (WBC) count of 133.1 × 10^9/L with 85.5% blasts. Upon referral to our hospital, further laboratory studies indicated a WBC count of 146.5 × 10^9/L with 70.0% blasts, hemoglobin level of 12.4 g/dL, and platelet count of 50 × 10^9/L. Additionally, the serum lysozyme level was found to be elevated.
test_results: Bone marrow examination revealed 68.0% of blasts, which were positive for myeloperoxidase (MPO) and negative for esterase staining. Surface antigen analysis by flow cytometry (FCM) indicated that 82.5, 66.8, 23.4, 43.7, 85.9, and 90.7% of the blasts were positive for CD19, CD79a, CD13, CD33, CD34, and HLA-DR, respectively, while the blasts were negative for CD2, CD3, CD5, CD7, CD8, CD10, CD20, and MPO (using a cutoff of 20%). Monocytic markers such as CD11c, CD14, CD36, and CD64 were not tested by FCM. Screening for leukemia-associated fusion genes resulted in identification of the MLL-AF4 fusion gene. Cytogenetic analysis of bone marrow cells using the G-banding technique demonstrated 47, XY, +X, t(4;11;7)(q21;q23;q22) in five of the 20 analyzed cells, and spectral karyotyping confirmed this alteration. The karyotype of the other 13 analyzed cells was 48, sl, +6 and 2 analyzed cells was 46, XY.

case_report: A 55-year-old Japanese woman presented with increased white blood cell counts, including a significant proportion of blasts. Laboratory results upon admission indicated white blood cell counts of 13.4×10^9/L, with 76% blasts, 1% band cells, 6% segmented cells, 16% lymphocytes, and 1% monocytes. The patient also exhibited anemia with a hemoglobin level of 9.3 g/dL and thrombocytopenia with platelet counts of 110×10^9/L. Coagulation tests were within normal limits. Lactate dehydrogenase levels were slightly elevated at 367 IU/L (normal range 120-245).
test_results: Bone marrow aspiration revealed replacement of normal marrow by blasts (94%). Immunophenotype with double-color flow cytometry showed positivity (>30%) for CD19 (90.8%), CD22 (45.4%), CD79a (92.4%), CD13 (40.9%), CD33 (94.6%), CD34 (95.8%) and HLA-DR (93.8%). MPO was negative (2.0%). Double staining for CD19xCD33 was strongly positive (96.6%). Chromosomal analysis with G-banded karyotype of the bone marrow cells showed 46, XX, t(4;12)(q21;p11), t(15;17)(q22;q12) in all 24 metaphase spreads. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) performed on interphase nuclei using an LSI PML/RARα dual color, dual fusion translocation probe (Vysis, USA) showed two separate PML and RARα signals in 1000 interphase nuclei and all metaphases analyzed. No PML/RARα fusion signal was identified.

case_report: In March 2014, a 28-year-old Korean woman, at 24 weeks of gestation, reported experiencing easy fatigue and had an abnormal blood test. Laboratory results showed a total white blood cell (WBC) count of 2.69×10^9/L with 12% immature cells, a hemoglobin level of 6.8 mg/dL, and a platelet count of 81×10^9/L.
test_results: A bone marrow biopsy showed 78% blasts with various size nucleoli, fine chromatin, and basophilic cytoplasm. Immunophenotyping of the bone marrow revealed that the patient was positive for the following: CD7, CD13, CD19, CD33, CD117, cCD79a, HLA-DR, and terminal deoxynucleotyl transferase (TdT); and negative for the following: CD2, CD3, CD5, CD20, cCD22, CD10, CD14, CD61, and myeloperoxidase. This result showed coexpression of markers for B lymphoid (CD19 and cCD79a) and myeloid lineage (CD117, CD13, and CD33).

case_report: An 84-year-old male with a history of mantle cell lymphoma presented four years ago with weight loss, fatigue, and a 5-cm left axillary mass, which was excised and confirmed as mantle cell lymphoma, stage 4B. Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) identified an IGH/CCND1 fusion rearrangement. The patient received treatment for mantle cell lymphoma, but details of the treatment and remission status are unknown. Recently, he experienced worsening constipation. PET/CT imaging revealed increased radiotracer uptake in the gastrointestinal tract, particularly in the distal colon, without significant nodal or splenic uptake. A colonoscopy identified a 10-cm circumferential, ulcerating, and infiltrative mass in the sigmoid colon without obstruction. Biopsy of the mass showed ulcerated colonic tissue with a diffuse infiltrate of mixed inflammation, predominantly neutrophils, along with scattered eosinophils, lymphocytes, histiocytes, and plasma cells. No glandular dysplasia or carcinoma was observed. Most small lymphocytes were T cells. Large, atypical cells with abundant pale cytoplasm, fine chromatin, and a single prominent nucleolus were present, some of which were bi- or multi-nucleated. Mitotic activity was mainly seen in these large cells. Additionally, there were large atypical cells with condensed cytoplasm and blurred nuclei, referred to as 'mummified cells.'
test_results: These cells were negative for CD45/leukocyte common antigen, CD20, CD3 and other T-cell markers, SOX-11, Bcl-6, cyclin-D1, and ALK. They were weakly positive for Pax-5, CD79a, Bcl-2, OCT-2, and MUM-1. They were positive for CD30 and variably positive for CD15. They did not express kappa and lambda surface or cytoplasmic light chains by chromogenic in situ hybridization (CISH). CISH revealed that these large atypical cells were positive for EBV and negative for cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex virus.
diagnosis: Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma , mixed cellularity variant
Orpha_name: Classic Hodgkin lymphoma, mixed cellularity type

case_report: A 27-year-old Israeli male presented to the emergency department with episodes of dizziness and lightheadedness, accompanied by a month-long history of low-grade fever and night sweats. He had recently been discharged from the army and had come to the United States for his wedding. The patient reported a history of a 'viral infection' and 'pneumonia' a few months prior, which resolved after treatment with Azithromycin. He also experienced a persistent cough, nighttime itching, and a ten-pound weight loss over the past month. Physical examination revealed a palpable spleen 2-3 cm below the costal margin. Laboratory results showed a normal white cell count, hemoglobin at 5.9 gm/dL, hematocrit at 16 gm/dL, and platelets at 234,000 gm/dL. The chemistry profile was within normal limits. Lactate dehydrogenase was elevated at 324 gm/dL, reticulocyte count was 6%, and haptoglobin was less than 7 gm/dL. Total bilirubin was 2.3 mg/dL, predominantly direct, with the rest of the liver function tests being normal. A positive Direct Coomb's test indicated the presence of IgG antibodies. Due to the patient's weakness, an urgent blood transfusion was ordered, but no immediate suitable match was found. The patient declined an abdominal sonogram and was discharged with a prescription of 1 mg per kg of Prednisone daily. At a follow-up appointment a week later, the patient reported improved appetite and reduced night sweats. His hemoglobin levels had also improved, and tests for HIV and ANA were negative. A CT scan of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis showed multiple symmetrically enlarged lymph nodes in the mediastinum and axilla, as well as splenomegaly. Bone marrow biopsy and aspiration revealed erythroid hyperplasia and reticulocytosis, with no evidence of malignancy.
test_results: Lymph node biopsy demonstrated a vague nodular pattern composed of numerous small cells and large atypical Reed-Sternberg cells within the nodules and outside of germinal centers; rare eosinophils and neutrophils were noted. Immunohistochemical stains indicated the RS cells being positive for CD30 and CD20 and negative for CD15 and lymphocyte common antigen.

case_report: A 55-year-old male patient reported experiencing painful swelling at the elbow level of the right arm for nearly a month. During the physical examination, a 2-cm solid, medium-hard mass was found on the medial side of the right forearm. There were no signs of redness, increased temperature, or infection. Ultrasound (US) examination showed a 16 × 12 × 10 mm, ill-defined, oval, and hypoechoic lymph node without a hilar hyperechoic structure. Doppler US examination identified peripheral (capsular) flow signals. Blood count results were within normal limits, with the lymphocyte/neutrophil ratio and leukocyte count also in normal ranges. An excisional biopsy of the epitrochlear lymph node was performed under general anesthesia.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed lymphoid follicles (CD23) with significant germinal centers and significantly widened mantle zones in the lymph node. The neoplastic cells were DC30+, CD15+, CD20−, CD3−, CD5−, CD10−, CD23−, IGD−, and EBV−. Ki67 proliferation indicator was frequently positively stained.

case_report: An 88-year-old Caucasian female presented with worsening pain between her scapula and difficulties in walking. She had experienced upper back pain for several months. Initial plain films did not reveal any abnormalities, and she had been receiving conservative management from pain clinics. Over the past 4 weeks, she developed progressive weakness in her lower extremities, necessitating the use of a walker. She was admitted to the hospital for medical management of her back pain, and within the next 48 hours, she reported worsening weakness in her lower limbs. A review of systems did not reveal any signs of malignancy or B-type symptoms. Physical examination showed no lymphadenopathy. Neurologic examination revealed a positive Rhomberg’s sign and decreased pinprick sensation in both legs extending to the hip (approximately to the L2 distribution). She had a loss of proprioception in all extremities. Rectal tone was normal. Toe responses were described as extensor on the left and equivocal on the right. Blood tests showed normal values except for slight anemia and mildly elevated platelets.
test_results: An MRI of the thoracic and lumbar spine was ordered, showing an epidural lesion from T2 to T4 levels with involvement of the posterior left T4 vertebral body, posterior elements of T2 and T3, as well as extension through the left T2-3 and T3-4 neural foramina. The lesion caused significant cord compression with evidence of mild cord edema. Frozen tissue histology confirmed a malignant infiltrative tumor. The tumor displayed a fibrotic background without frank sclerosis, increased numbers of large atypical cells and a dearth of small lymphoid cells. At high magnification large lymphoid cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm predominated. Most of the large cells exhibited prominent inclusion-like eosinophilic nucleoli with perinucleolar clearing and many of the cells were multinucleated. Large pleomorphic cells, multinucleated cells, and mummified cells were the predominant cell populations in the tumor. There was an abundance of CD30 + RS cells, but neither the B cell lineage marker CD20, nor CD45 were expressed by RS cells. The B-cell transcription factor Bob-1 was positive only in rare large neoplastic cells which were admixed against a scant background of predominantly T lymphocytes, but PAX5 was weakly positive in many of the cells.

case_report: A 92-year-old female initially presented with abnormal vaginal bleeding. During the physical examination, the superficial lymph node was found to be unremarkable. Blood tests showed a white blood cell count of 8,400/μL, a hemoglobin level of 10.8 g/dL, a platelet count of 26,100/μL, a ferritin level of 392 ng/mL, and a soluble interleukin-2 receptor level of 8,080 U/mL.
test_results: Biopsy demonstrated polymorphous infiltration of lymphocytes with scattered Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (H-RS) cells. Magnetic resonance imaging and other imaging methods, including transvaginal ultrasonography, revealed a tumor mass that measured 60 x 46 mm and affected the cervix uteri, corpus uteri, and parametrium. In addition, swollen lymph nodes were observed in the pelvic cavity and retroperitoneum.

case_report: A 40-year-old male truck driver presented with progressive non-cholestatic jaundice without a prodrome, weight loss of 6 kg over 1.5 months, intermittent fever ranging from 39° to 40 °C, and progressive abdominal distension occurring 2 weeks after the onset of jaundice. He had a history of a traumatic fracture of the right hip one year ago, managed with a hip plaster cast. He reported significant alcohol intake (30-40 gm/day, 5-6 times per week) but had been abstinent for a year. He was an occasional smoker and denied any intravenous drug use or other addictions. He had been diagnosed with AIDS and disseminated tuberculosis seven years prior, for which he received HAART and ATT, along with anti-PJP prophylaxis. Upon admission, his vitals were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed pallor, icterus, pedal edema, right cervical non-tender lymphadenopathy, abdominal distension, and a palpable spleen 5 cm below the left costal margin. Blood parameters at admission were recorded. Chest X-ray results were normal. Ultrasonography of the abdomen showed a nodular liver (17 cm) with coarse echotexture and periportal hypodensities. The portal vein measured 18 mm at the porta, and the gallbladder was contracted. Additionally, there was splenomegaly (19 cm), moderate ascites, and bilateral raised renal echogenicity with maintained cortico-medullary differentiation.
test_results: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT - chest and abdomen) revealed right cervical and paraaortic lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, diffuse duodenal and jejunal loops thickening, and bilateral lobulated kidneys.

case_report: A 40-year-old male presented with a 13-year history of generalized hyperpigmented skin lesions that exhibit a wheal-and-flare reaction upon scratching, as well as after exposure to warm and hot baths, and during exercise. The facial area was unaffected by these skin lesions. The patient experienced lightheadedness following exposure to hot baths and exercise but did not require emergency medical attention. He reported no occurrences of angioedema, hives, shortness of breath, wheezing, or anaphylaxis. Additionally, he had no history of adverse reactions to hymenoptera stings.
test_results: Previous workup included an elevated serum tryptase level of 49 (range 2–10 ng/ml) and a bone marrow biopsy with 30% of aggregates of spindle CD117-positive/CD25-positive MCs. Skin biopsy report showed an increase number of MCs around dilated blood vessels within the superficial dermis. Leder stain confirmed an increased quantity of MCs. During his initial evaluation at our clinic, he was found to have generalized hyperpigmented lesions that flared upon scratching with a tongue depressor and hepatomegaly. We requested bone marrow biopsy slides for further review by our Pathology Department, and our pathology review was that immunohistochemical stains demonstrated lymphoid aggregates to contain numerous CD3-positive cells admixed with slightly fewer CD20-positive cells. The atypical spindled MCs were positive for CD117. A bone scan showed no lytic osseous lesions. A c-kit gene analysis reported no known pathogenic mutations in exons 8, 9, 11, 13 or 17 of the kit gene. CT of the chest and abdomen showed no liver, spleen or lymph node enlargement.

case_report: An 18-year-old female was admitted to the cardiology unit due to precordial pain and dyspnea. She arrived using a manual wheelchair, presenting with scoliotic kyphosis, elbow contractures, and reduced activity in the left upper limb. Physical examination revealed muscle hypotrophy in the biceps, triceps, and gastrocnemius muscles, without signs of hemodynamic decompensation. Her family history was negative for sudden death, cardiovascular, and neurological diseases. An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with ventricular repolarization changes, including inverted T waves in V2-V3, poor R wave progression in precordial leads, and high voltages in peripheral leads. An echocardiogram indicated asymmetric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, particularly in the mid-apical anterior wall (24 mm), without left ventricular outflow obstruction, a tricuspid aortic valve, and slight pericardial effusion with epicardial fibrin deposits. Mild deficiencies were noted in the mitral, pulmonary, and tricuspid valves. The patient was born prematurely at 31 weeks via cesarean section and developed respiratory distress and hypoglycemia within an hour, requiring neonatal intensive care with intermittent positive pressure ventilation. During her neonatal hospitalization, she received five blood transfusions for anemia, phototherapy for jaundice, and antibiotic and antifungal treatments for a Candida infection. Perinatal encephalic ultrasound identified a small hemorrhage in the caudate nucleus, bilateral peritrigonal hyperechogenicity, and an inhomogeneous area in the right thalamo-striatal region, likely of hypoxic-ischemic origin. She was discharged after 68 days with diagnoses of prematurity and moderate asphyxiation. At two years old, she developed bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, which worsened by age three, leading to a right cochlear implant and a left retroauricular prosthesis. Brain MRIs before the implant showed stable alterations in bilateral periventricular and peritrigonal white matter. Her clinical history and lower limb spasticity led to a diagnosis of spastic diplegia, initiating physiotherapy, orthosis treatments, and focal therapy with botulinum toxin to reduce hypertonicity. Over the years, her walking ability progressively worsened, necessitating the use of a walker and orthopedic shoes, and was complicated by equinovarus foot deformity and global internal rotation of the lower limbs. At ten years old, she underwent Achilles tendon extension surgery to improve gait. During the cardiology admission, laboratory tests, including serum CK levels (69 U/l, normal range 26-192), were within normal limits. A Holter electrocardiogram recorded rare single supraventricular extrasystoles and some monomorphic ventricular extrasystoles with a superior axis and right bundle branch block morphology, originating from the left ventricle. Spirometry indicated a moderate restrictive ventilatory deficit.
test_results: She and her parents were recruited for a genetic screening by next-generation sequencing (NGS) approach.

case_report: A 40-year-old female, non-smoker, married with two children, was hospitalized in 2005 at another public hospital. She visited our outpatient clinic in 2008 for a routine control visit initiated by her General Practitioner. Her clinical history included recurrent episodes of cold, bronchitis, and rhinorrhea since childhood. During the initial visit, her vital signs were normal, and thoracic auscultation revealed no wheezing or crackles. Spirometry results were within normal limits. No treatment was required.
test_results: In 2008 the nasal brushing was performed, with 100% of the cilia lacking inner dynein arms.

case_report: A 40-year-old man from Taiwan has had mild pallor and jaundice since he was 20 years old. He did not experience any symptoms in his daily life. In August 2019, at the age of 39, he experienced increased epigastric pain and clay-colored stool for several days. Physical examination revealed slight anemia and jaundice, with the spleen barely palpable. Laboratory tests showed Hb at 11.7 gm/dL, WBC at 7500/uL, platelet count at 320,000/uL, MCV at 84.1 fl, MCH at 58.7 pg, MCHC at 34.2%, RDW at 19.1%, and a normal white cell classification. A peripheral blood smear indicated that more than 40% of RBCs were ellipsoid. Biochemical tests revealed total bilirubin at 14 mg/dL, direct bilirubin at 7.7 mg/dL, GOT at 314 IU/L, and GPT at 482 IU/L. Abdominal sonography showed mild splenomegaly, multiple gall bladder stones, and bilateral intrahepatic duct dilatation. Endoscopic retrograde cholangioscopic removal of gall stones was successfully performed. Three weeks later, obstructive jaundice and hepatitis had subsided, with total bilirubin at 3.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin at 1.03 mg/dL, GOT at 29 IU/L, and GPT at 54 IU/L. EMA-labeled RBC by flow cytometry was negative, and the osmotic fragility test was within normal limits.
test_results: Genetic analysis of the SPTA1 gene identified a novel heterozygous exon2, c.86A > C, p.Gln29Prol mutation.
diagnosis: Hereditary Elliptocytosis with a novel SPTA1 mutation

case_report: A 13-year-old boy from Senegal was brought to our hospital due to neonatal jaundice and severe anemia. Blood tests indicated microcytic regenerative anemia with hemoglobin levels at 60 g/L, elevated markers of hemolysis, and a negative direct antiglobulin test. Examination of a peripheral blood smear revealed severe anisopoikilocytosis with fragmented erythrocytes, spherocytes, and ovalocytes. Capillary electrophoresis did not show the presence of HBS or any other variant. Enzymatic assays for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and pyruvate kinase were within normal ranges.
test_results: DNA sequencing revealed compound double heterozygous for mutant α-spectrin SPTA1 (Arg28His) and homozygous αLELY polymorphism (low expression α-spectrin allele).

case_report: The patient is a 12-month-old female with a history of a prior emergency department visit for dehydration due to viral gastroenteritis. According to the father, she has been experiencing fussiness and reduced oral intake for the past two weeks. The father also noted that the patient was reluctant to walk and preferred to sit in one place throughout the day. On the day of the clinic visit, the patient had an episode of non-bilious, non-bloody vomiting after attempting to eat in the morning. She did not have a fever, ear tugging, or cough but had a runny nose for the past week. A week prior, the primary care provider noted a viral upper respiratory tract infection. Since that visit, the patient has lost 700 grams and appeared increasingly pale. Family history includes a sickle cell trait diagnosis in a paternal cousin. Physical examination revealed irritability, mucosal and hand pallor, and a pronounced cardiac flow murmur. Vital signs showed tachycardia, slight hypertension, and an elevated respiratory rate.
test_results: Complete blood count results were notable for a normocytic, profound anemia (hemoglobin/hematocrit: 1.7/5.6 g/dL) with otherwise intact WBC and platelet counts. Flow cytometry data revealed severe anemia with leukoblastosis. Blood smear revealed no RBC abnormalities and was vastly unremarkable for any qualitative defects.

case_report: A 77-year-old male presented to the emergency department on 11 September 2020 due to recurrent episodes of fainting. Upon examination, he was afebrile and exhibited no cardiovascular abnormalities, such as irregular heart sounds. Physical examination revealed pallor without any signs of bleeding, bruising, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or jaundice. Laboratory results showed a hemoglobin level of 37 g/L (normal range: 131–172), red cell count of 0.9 × 10^12/L (normal range: 4.09–5.74), and reticulocyte fraction of 0.34% (normal range: 0.5–1.5). The white cell count was 3.3 × 10^9/L (normal range: 4–10), and the platelet count was 181 × 10^9/L (normal range: 100–300). The patient received an immediate blood transfusion, which alleviated his symptoms. He reported a history of recurrent fatigue, dizziness, fainting, and skin itchiness over the past 6 months. Anemia was first detected a year prior with a hemoglobin level of 99 g/L and a red cell count of 2.58 × 10^12/L, though he did not experience dizziness or fainting at that time and received no treatment. Over the following 3 months, he experienced recurrent fatigue, dizziness, and fainting, with hemoglobin levels dropping as low as 25 g/L. Immediate transfusions were administered, and further investigations were conducted to determine the cause of his anemia. Tests for human parvovirus B19, cytomegalovirus, human immunodeficiency viruses, hepatitis C virus, hepatitis B virus, and Epstein–Barr virus were negative. His vitamin B12, folate, and iron levels were within normal ranges, and he tested negative for autoantibodies, including the anti-erythropoietin antibody.
test_results: The bone marrow aspirate smear showed an absence of erythroblasts with normal distribution and differentiation of other hematopoietic lineages. Flow cytometry revealed the proliferation of γδT cells in the peripheral blood and bone marrow, accounting for 14.075% and 11.162% of all nucleated cells, respectively. The immunophenotype of these γδT cells was CD5−, CD7+, CD16+, CD56+/−, CD94+, CD335−, and CD337−. The CD4/CD8 ratio was 13.075%. Monoclonal TCR gene rearrangement was detected in TCRβ, TCRδ, and TCRγ, while multiclonal patterns were also detected in TCRβ and TCRγ.
diagnosis: Pure Red-Cell Aplasia  caused by proliferation of γδT cells
Orpha_name: Primary acquired pure red cell aplasia

case_report: A 35-year-old pregnant woman, who is HIV-positive, experienced severe anaemia after starting anti-retroviral treatment (ART) with a combination of tenofovir, emtricitabine, and efavirenz (Atroiza). She was diagnosed with HIV at 17 weeks of pregnancy in August 2014 and began ART immediately. Initial laboratory results showed a CD4 cell count of 83 cells/mm3 and a haemoglobin (Hb) level of 8.2 g/dL. After three months, she was admitted with symptomatic, normochromic, normocytic anaemia, with an Hb level of 2.2 g/dL, while her white blood cell and platelet counts remained normal. Tests ruled out haemolysis and autoimmune conditions, and there was no evidence of ongoing blood loss. Electrolytes and liver function tests were within normal ranges. Serology for Epstein-Barr virus, Cytomegalovirus, and hepatitis A, B, and C was negative. She received six units of packed red cells, resulting in a post-transfusion Hb level of 8.9 g/dL. An emergency caesarean section was performed due to foetal distress. Post-surgery, her Hb levels continued to drop, necessitating frequent blood transfusions.
test_results: A bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy revealed adequately represented myeloid series and megakaryocytes, but a marked reduction in erythropoiesis with maturation arrest at the pronormoblast stage.
Orpha_name: Primary acquired pure red cell aplasia

case_report: A 7-year-old male child presented with a history of generalized tonic-clonic seizures for the past 2 years. The child was born via vaginal delivery with a breech presentation. Developmental milestones were delayed, and the child exhibited poor phonation, drooling of saliva, and feeding and swallowing difficulties. Tongue protrusion and movement were moderately impaired. Physical examination revealed muscle atrophy below the knees, exaggerated plantar extensor reflexes bilaterally, and brisk reflexes on both sides. The child also demonstrated bisyllabic speech, typically observed in 12-month-old infants.
