test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed multiple small gyri in bilateral parieto-occipital cortices. There was thickening of the grey matter around the sylvian fissure bilaterally with irregular cortex and widening the fissures. Bilateral sylvain fissures were hypoplastic and extended dorsally up to the perirolandic region. The body of lateral ventricles shows inverted appearances.

case_report: A 4-year-old boy, born to nonconsanguineous parents and with normal developmental milestones, presented with drooping of both eyelids for 1 year. There was minimal fluctuation throughout the day, but symptoms worsened with exertion. Neurological examination revealed bilateral asymmetric ptosis and limited movement of the extraocular muscles, with minimal signs of fatigue upon exertion. Pupillary light reflex was normal. There was significant weakness in the finger extensors. Deep tendon reflexes were reduced. The remainder of the neurological examination was unremarkable. No skeletal deformities were observed, and there was no relevant family history. The neostigmine test was negative, and serum AChR antibodies were absent. Imaging showed no evidence of thymic hyperplasia or thymoma.
test_results: Repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) test done from nasalis muscle at 3 Hz stimulation, showed a decremental response of about 15% in both area and amplitude. Two CMAPs were recorded from the median, ulnar, and the facial nerves after a single stimulus. The decremental response characteristically appeared first in the second CMAP rather than the first. No R-CMAP was recorded in the family members who were also tested.
diagnosis: postsynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome, possibly slow-channel syndrome

case_report: The patient is a 19-year-old woman who was born full-term to a non-consanguineous couple. At birth, she exhibited low muscle tone, and her breathing and crying were weak. During her first month of life, she experienced respiratory failure and required a tracheotomy and mechanical ventilation. Throughout infancy, her muscle weakness persisted; however, she achieved all motor developmental milestones on time. She also experienced intermittent cyanosis due to a patent ductus arteriosus and underwent corrective heart surgery at the age of 2.
test_results: Repetitive stimulation of the left axillary nerve at 2 Hz resulted in a 36% decrement of the compound muscle action potential (CMAP) area. No repetitive CMAPs were observed after single nerve stimulation. Serum antibodies against AChR and MuSK were negative.
diagnosis: Congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by mutations in MUSK

case_report: A 20-year-old male experienced cough, rhinorrhea, wheezing, and dyspnea after exposure to rainy conditions. He had a history of childhood asthma and a family history of asthma, including his mother and three elder sisters. After treatment with inhaled corticosteroids, his symptoms improved over three days. Nine days later, he developed an unsteady gait. By day 3, he experienced blurred vision, dizziness, and nausea. On day 12, he became intermittently drowsy but could be aroused by noxious stimulation. On day 18, he had a tonic-clonic seizure, prompting a neurological evaluation. Neurological examination revealed full consciousness, a wide-based gait, and an inability to stand on one foot. There were limitations in lateral gaze in the left eye and vertical gaze in both eyes, while motor and sensory functions were intact. Brain computed tomography (CT) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination showed no abnormalities. Electroencephalography (EEG) revealed a 4–6 cycle per second slow wave pattern diffusely and a 22–26 cycle per second waveform predominantly over the centroparietal area, bilaterally.
test_results: Nerve conduction study (NCS) revealed peripheral nerve abnormalities characterized by axonal damage. Both motor conduction velocity and sensory conduction velocity were normal in the four limbs. Motor nerve conduction study showed variable decreased amplitude at the median, ulnar, tibial, and peroneal nerves on both sides. The right peroneal nerve showed slightly prolonged latency. Sensory nerve conduction study recorded decreased amplitude at the left tibial nerve, but the right sural nerve, right median nerve and left ulnar nerve were relatively spared. Left median F-wave could not be elicited, but H-wave was evoked normally.
diagnosis: Guillain-Barré syndrome  with predominant axonal damage
Orpha_name: Acute motor and sensory axonal neuropathy

case_report: An 87-year-old male patient was admitted to the rehabilitation ward with postoperative weakness in both lower limbs following a traffic accident that resulted in an incomplete cervical spinal cord injury. The injury was classified as grade D on the American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) impairment scale. Initial symptoms included neck pain, numbness in the bilateral upper limbs over the C5-C7 dermatome, and weakness in all four limbs with a muscle strength grade of 3/5. Preoperative CT and MRI scans showed a fracture in the posterior element of C5-C6, anterior subluxation of C6-C7, and disc herniation compressing the spinal cord. Emergent decompression of C6 and C7, along with anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) of C6-C7 using cervical spine locking plates (CSLP) for fixation, was performed. Postoperatively, the patient experienced partial relief of neck pain, numbness, and limb weakness. Rehabilitation programs were initiated, and one week later, muscle strength in all four limbs improved to grade 4/5, allowing the patient to tolerate a standing position with fair balance. His medication regimen included NSAIDs for postoperative pain, metformin and basal insulin for type 2 diabetes mellitus, an alpha blocker for benign prostate hypertrophy, and a proton pump inhibitor for a gastric ulcer. The patient had a social drinking habit and a family history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus. Two weeks post-surgery, the muscle strength in his bilateral lower limbs suddenly decreased to grade 3/5 and continued to decline. A neurologist was consulted, and various examinations were conducted to investigate potential causes such as electrolyte imbalance, issues related to the cervical spine surgery, lumbar spine problems, or intracranial lesions. The patient had no history of gastrointestinal or respiratory infections before or after the cervical surgery. Laboratory tests and microbiology studies were unremarkable, ruling out ongoing infection. Imaging studies showed no evidence of instrumental backout, new onset of spine stenosis, or intracerebral hemorrhage.
test_results: CSF studies revealed albuminocytologic dissociation, including increased protein levels (167 mg/dL) and an absence of WBC. Motor NCS revealed decreased amplitude over bilateral median, tibial, peroneal, and left ulnar compound action motor potentials (CMAPs); decreased conduction velocities over left ulnar and bilateral peroneal CMAPs. An unresponsive F wave was noted over bilateral median and peroneal nerves. Sensory NCS revealed decreased amplitude over bilateral median, radial, and sural sensory nerve action potentials (SNAPs). Needle EMG showed generalized decreased recruitment over bilateral first dorsal interosseus (FDI), left abductor pollicis brevis (APB), left medial gastrocnemius, left flexor carpi radialis (FCR), and right biceps, and no volitional activity over bilateral tibialis anterior (TA) and right medial gastrocnemius muscles. Few polyphasic waves were noted over bilateral FDI, left APB, and left medial gastrocnemius muscles.
diagnosis: Guillain-Barré Syndrome, acute motor and sensory axonal neuropathy  variant
Orpha_name: Acute motor and sensory axonal neuropathy

case_report: A 21-year-old male fisherman presented with a three-week history of progressive generalized weakness, double vision, decreased appetite, and lethargy, making daily activities difficult. For the past three days, he experienced high-grade fever and shortness of breath. He was managed in the medicine department for aspiration pneumonia with type-1 respiratory failure. Six weeks prior, he was bitten by a yellow-bellied sea snake (Hydrophis platurus) on his left palm during fishing, and no anti-venom was administered. The neurology team was consulted on the second day of admission. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg, a pulse of 85 per minute, and a temperature of 98.2 F. He was on continuous non-invasive ventilation (NIV) support for hypoxia. A well-demarcated, clean healing wound of approximately 2 cm in diameter was observed on his left palm. He was awake, oriented, and had intact higher mental functions. Pupils were 3 mm bilaterally and reactive to light and accommodation. Right lateral rectus palsy was noted. There was no facial muscle weakness, and the tongue was central on protrusion. His speech had a hyper-nasal quality. Movements of the soft palate and uvula were absent on testing, with an absent gag reflex. Motor examination showed normal bulk without fasciculation. Muscle tone was mildly reduced in all limbs. Muscle strength was Medical Research Council (MRC) grade 3/5 in proximal muscle groups and MRC grade 4/5 in distal muscle groups in the upper limbs, while in the lower limbs, it was MRC grade 4/5 in both proximal and distal muscle groups. Deep tendon reflexes were absent in all four limbs. Sensory examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory investigations on day one are shown in Table. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was negative for an acute brainstem stroke or abnormal contrast enhancement (Figure).
test_results: Normal sensory nerve conduction. Motor amplitudes of the bilateral peroneal, right median, and ulnar nerves were reduced without a conduction block.
diagnosis: Guillain-Barre Syndrome , acute motor axonal neuropathy  variant

case_report: A 60-year-old male arrived at the emergency department with a ten-day history of mild generalized weakness. Two weeks prior, he experienced diarrhea for five days. Initial examination showed mild global weakness (MRC grade 4+/5) and hyperreflexia. He was discharged with the understanding that his symptoms were related to the previous gastroenteritis. Ten days later, he returned with worsening weakness in both upper and lower limbs. Neurological examination at this time indicated severe distal weakness (MRC grade 2/5) and mild proximal weakness (MRC grade 4/5) in both upper and lower limbs. Deep tendon reflexes were brisk and symmetrical, with downgoing plantar responses. Sensory examination was normal. MRI scans of the brain and entire spine showed no abnormalities.
test_results: CSF examination revealed increased protein (978 mg/L) with normal white cell count. Serum testing showed high titers of anti-GM1 antibody and antibodies to Campylobacter jejuni. Sensory NCS were normal, while motor NCS demonstrated markedly reduced distal compound-muscle action potentials in upper and lower limbs. EMG revealed diffuse fibrillation potentials.

case_report: An 11-year-old boy presented with visual blurring and headache for one year. No redness was observed in the eyes. The patient reported low vision, particularly during classroom lessons. This was his first visit to an ophthalmic center with no prior consultations. The distance visual acuity of the right eye was 20/60 without correction, improving to 20/20 with a correction of +2 sphere, cylinder of −2.5, and at an angle of 5°. The left eye had a distance visual acuity of 20/40 without correction, improving to 20/20 with a correction of +2.00 (−2.00) 170°. Photomotor reflexes were normal. The lens appeared normal with no defects. Indirect ophthalmoscopy showed no abnormalities in the choroid and retina. Intraocular pressure was recorded at 26 mmHg in the right eye and 24 mmHg in the left eye using both Tonopen and air puff tonometer over three sessions with the patient relaxed. Pachymetry indicated normal corneal thickness in both eyes before starting antiglaucoma drops (Timolol).
test_results: Slit lamp examination revealed a good conjunctiva, transparent cornea and anterior chamber. The pupil in the right eye was pear-shaped with a notch at the inferonasal location. The pupil in the left eye was pear-shaped with a notch toward the left canthus.

case_report: A 33-year-old male patient visited the outpatient clinic with a long-standing history of poor vision in the left eye since childhood. He had undergone left eye strabismus surgery six years prior to address sensory exotropia (XT). His medical history includes type 1 diabetes mellitus, managed with insulin injections. There is no notable family history of ocular or systemic diseases. Ophthalmic examination revealed a best-corrected visual acuity of 20/30 in the right eye (OD) and hand motion in the left eye (OS). Intraocular pressure (IOP) measured 16 mmHg in the right eye and 12 mmHg in the left eye using a non-contact tonometer. The anterior segment examination was normal in both eyes. Eye alignment tests, including the Hirschberg test and cover-uncover test, indicated orthotropic alignment in both eyes. Extraocular muscle movement was full and unrestricted bilaterally. Fundus examination of the right eye (OD) showed a small, circular, well-defined pigmented chorioretinal atrophic lesion with sharp borders, approximately half-disc diameter in size, not involving the foveal center. Fundus examination of the left eye (OS) revealed a large, oval-shaped, well-defined excavated chorioretinal atrophic lesion centered in the fovea, with large choroidal blood vessels visible against a white scleral background. The lesion was pigmented and surrounded by a dark, sharply demarcated rim of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), with some retinal vessels at the margin. It measured approximately two-disc diameters horizontally and one-and-a-half-disc diameters vertically. The optic disc appeared normal, with no signs of diabetic retinopathy in either eye.
test_results: OCT model 2000 was performed for both eyes and showed (OD) neurosensory retina is abnormally atrophied while the RPE showed preservation of the choroid. OCT (OS) showed a crater-like depression and an atrophic neurosensory retina with the absence of retinal pigment epithelium and choroid.

case_report: A 12-year-old boy was referred to our clinic for the evaluation of a macular lesion in the left eye. The past ocular and medical history was non-contributory. The best-corrected visual acuities were 20/20 in the right eye and 20/40 with -0.5 + 0.25 × 180 in the left eye. The anterior segment examination was unremarkable. The fundus examination of the left eye showed a sharply-demarcated, oval-shaped, excavated lesion involving the temporal half of the foveal center with large choroidal vessels and bared sclera at the base. The lesion was approximately four disc diameters (DD) in width and two DD in height, and the retinal vessels were undisturbed at the margin. On red-free retinal nerve fiber layer photography, the papillomacular bundle was not interrupted surrounding the lesion. The color vision test with the Titmus test and the visual evoked potentials were normal. The immunologic tests including toxoplasmosis, rubella, syphilis, cytomegalovirus, herpes virus and human immunodeficiency virus were all negative.
test_results: The OCT showed a crater-like depression accompanying atrophic neurosensory retina, and an absence of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and choroid in the lesion. Increased backscattering due to bare sclera and choroidal vessels were found. Fluorescein angiography showed hypofluorescence corresponding to the size of the lesion in both early and late frames without leakage of dye at any stage.

case_report: A 9-year-old Hispanic female attended a routine ophthalmic follow-up. Her medical history included juvenile idiopathic arthritis, diagnosed at 16 months, and chronic bilateral anterior uveitis, diagnosed at three years. Her medications were methotrexate (0.8 ml) subcutaneously, weekly; prednisolone acetate (1% suspension), every two hours in both eyes; dorzolamide hydrochloride and timolol maleate ophthalmic solution (22.3 mg/6.8 mg per mL), one drop, twice daily in both eyes; and tocilizumab (162 mg/0.9 mL) subcutaneously, every two weeks. Her review of systems, social, and family histories were otherwise unremarkable. During a comprehensive ophthalmic evaluation, her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/30 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye, with a manifest refraction of plano in both eyes. The intraocular pressure was 27 mmHg in the right eye and 12 mmHg in the left eye. The pupils were round and reactive to light, with an afferent pupillary defect in the right eye. Her color vision in both eyes, assessed by the Ishihara color plate test, showed no defects. Extraocular movements were within normal limits.
test_results: A slit-lamp examination (SLE) OD was remarkable for one white, round subepithelial corneal opacity of approximately 0.1 mm in height by 0.1 mm in width, located slightly lateral to the center of the cornea. The rest of the SLE was within normal limits, bilaterally, with no evidence of keratic precipitates, signs of inflammation in the anterior chambers, or vitreous cells in either eye.

case_report: A 22-year-old Asian Indian female reported experiencing a gradual, painless reduction in vision in both eyes. Examination showed best-corrected visual acuity of 20/200 in the right eye and 20/30 in the left eye, with intraocular pressure measured at 16 mmHg in both eyes. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye identified sectoral corneal edema in the nasal quadrant, peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS), corectopia, and minimal iris stromal atrophy in the temporal region. The left eye exhibited sectoral stromal edema with subepithelial calcareous deposits and multiple PAS. Gonioscopy revealed broad-based PAS and a membrane covering the angle structures in both eyes. Central corneal thickness was measured at 565 microns in the right eye and 556 microns in the left eye.
test_results: Ultrasound biomicroscopy of the angle in both the eyes revealed a membrane-like structure extending from corneal endothelium to anterior iris surface. In-vivo confocal microscopy showed an “epithelium-like” transformation of the corneal endothelium with polymegathism and hyper-reflective nuclei and surrounding areas with relatively normal-appearing cells.

case_report: A 26-year-old woman reported a gradual decrease in vision over 5 months in her right eye. Her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/20 in both eyes. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye revealed a mild subepithelial haze on the cornea and a hammered metal appearance of the endothelium. The anterior chamber was shallow, and the iris pattern was disrupted with multiple dark brown nodules and ectropion uveae in the superior and temporal quadrants, leading to pupillary distortion. The fundus examination of the right eye showed advanced optic neuropathy with significant thinning of the neuroretinal rim and a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.9:1. The left eye appeared normal. Intraocular pressure (IOP) measurements were 40 mmHg in the right eye (treated with oral acetazolamide, topical timolol 0.5%, and brimonidine 0.15%) and 12 mmHg in the left eye. Gonioscopy indicated three quadrants of peripheral anterior synechiae in the right eye (covering the entire superior angle and inferonasal angle) and a normal angle in the left eye. Visual field testing showed advanced glaucomatous changes in the right eye with a mean deviation (MD) of -12.76 dB and pattern standard deviation (PSD) of 9.33 dB, with a probability (P) of less than 0.5%, while the left eye had a normal visual field.
test_results: Specular microscopy of the right eye showed pleomorphic endothelial cells with dark-light reversal typical of “ICE cells.”

case_report: A 40-year-old female patient presented with a noticeable change in the shape of the pupil in her left eye, without other eye-related complaints. She wears glasses and has no other systemic conditions. Ophthalmologic examination showed visual acuity of 1.0 in both eyes with correction. External examination was normal for both eyes. Intraocular pressures measured by Goldmann applanation tonometry were 14.0 mm Hg in the right eye and 11.0 mm Hg in the left eye. Biomicroscopic examination revealed a normal right eye. In the left eye, the cornea was epithelialized without edema, and there was iris dystrophy extending from 11:30 to 5:00 o'clock. The lens was in place, and both lenses were clear with a normal vitreous cavity. Fundus examination showed a healthy macula and vessels with an intact retina in both eyes. Gonioscopy of the right eye showed a grade 3 angle with iris processes, while the left eye had broad-based peripheral anterior synechiae from 6 to 6:30 o'clock.
test_results: At the UBM right normal finding, on the left eye from 6–6:30 o’clock, we find iris root glued to the corneal endothelium so that the iris root cannot be separated from the hyperechogenic echo of the corneal endothelium. The structure of the iris is preserved, which is thickened here because it is folded, the echogenicity and homogeneity of the iris stroma are normal, dystrophic stroma is seen in front of the synechia as an irregular iris defect. The structure of the ciliary body is completely orderly. The rest of the circumference is normal. Spectral microscopy of the right eye showed density 3211 cells / mm, on the left we could not get a shot even though the cornea had no changes as well as “Hammered silver”. OCT of the anterior segment showed CCT corneal thickness of 608 Âµm in the right eye and 595 Âµm in the left eye, OCT of the posterior segment showed normal macular region values. The RNFL thickness of the right eye was 103Âµm, and of the left eye 104 Âµm, whereas C / D of the right eye was 0.54 and of the left 0.53.

case_report: A 58-year-old Caucasian female presented with floaters and metamorphopsia in both eyes. Best-corrected visual acuity was 6/6 in both eyes, and intraocular pressure measured 14 mm Hg in the right eye and 15 mm Hg in the left eye. Fundus examination showed white-yellowish flecks in the posterior pole arranged in a nearly symmetrical pattern in both eyes, along with a few hyperpigmented lesions. The patient had no systemic metabolic diseases or significant co-morbidities. Bilateral progression was noted after 6 months.
test_results: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed focal thickening characterized by high reflectance with disruption of the outer limiting membrane, ellipsoid zone, outer photoreceptor segments and interdigitation zone. Autofluorescence revealed lesions characterized by increased autofluorescence with small adjacent areas of decreased autofluorescence within the area of the lesion. Fluorescein angiography depicted a number of hyperfluorescent lesions bilaterally, while there were no signs of “dark choroid” in the mid-periphery. Lastly, pattern ERG was slightly decreased in both eyes (OD 155 μV/40.5 msec and OS 145.5 μV/38.9 msec).
diagnosis: Multifocal Pattern Dystrophy Simulating Fundus Flavimaculatus
Orpha_name: Multifocal Pattern Dystrophy Simulating Fundus Flavimaculatus

case_report: In mid-2008, a 40-year-old Caucasian female presented with recent heart palpitations and chest discomfort during exertion. She had recently delivered her second child a few months earlier. A detailed physical examination was conducted at a regional medical center, and she was referred to our hospital in January 2009 for further evaluation. The patient had a normal body habitus. An electrocardiogram indicated sinus tachycardia with a heart rate of approximately 90 beats per minute. Holter monitoring revealed sinus rhythm with heart rates ranging from 49 to 149 beats per minute, 9 supraventricular ectopic beats, and 13 ventricular ectopic beats. Heart auscultation detected a pansystolic murmur, graded 4/6, audible over the apex. The patient had no coronary artery risk factors and was classified as New York Heart Association functional class I. Laboratory tests, including thyroid hormone levels, were normal, and other findings were within regular limits.
test_results: Her left atrium was enlarged (44mm) and the parasternal long axis showed chordae tendineae that were elongated and formed an unusual net shape, penetrating into her left ventricular cavity. The parasternal short axis of her left ventricle showed a single papillary muscle that was positioned on one side in the posteromedial commissure. The mitral valve orifice was slightly eccentric and all chordae were converting into a single papillary muscle. Transmitral flow showed a normal pattern. Mitral regurgitation was present and was graded as moderate to severe. The dimensions of her left ventricle cavity were normal (end-diastolic dimension, 56mm; end-systolic dimension, 38mm), and revealed normal segmental wall motion with preserved ejection fraction. There was no obstruction of the left ventricular outflow tract. Her aortic valve had three leaflets, with no regurgitation or stenosis. The blood-flow velocity through her aorta was normal. There was no coarctation of her aorta. The right side of her heart was normal. Tricuspidal regurgitation was mild without elevated right heart pressure. Her pericardium was normal.
diagnosis: Exuberant accessory mitral valve tissue with possible true parachute mitral valve

case_report: A 76-year-old woman with a history of an aortic arch aneurysm was admitted due to worsening shortness of breath during physical activity. She did not exhibit hoarseness or signs of airway obstruction. The shortness of breath began two weeks prior to admission and progressively worsened, becoming noticeable even with light exercise. Upon admission, her physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 95/70 mmHg, a heart rate of 100 beats per minute, and an oxygen saturation of 95% as measured by pulse oximetry. After light exercise, her oxygen saturation dropped to 90%. Laboratory tests indicated elevated liver transaminase levels (aspartate aminotransferase at 64 U/L and alanine aminotransferase at 100 U/L) and increased brain natriuretic peptide concentration (1967 pg/mL).
test_results: A computed tomography (CT) scan showed that a large 70-mm diameter saccular aortic arch aneurysm had substantially compressed the periphery of the pulmonary artery and that a large thrombus had protruded into the main trunk of the pulmonary artery. No other CT findings of chronic pulmonary thromboembolism, including abrupt narrowing, obstruction, or calcified thrombi, were found in the pulmonary artery branches. Echocardiography showed preserved left ventricular ejection fraction of 61.5%; decreased left ventricular dimension of 26.6 and 18.2 mm in diastole and systole, respectively; profound pulmonary hypertension characterized by a right ventricular systolic pressure of 95.9 mmHg; moderate to severe tricuspid regurgitation; and pulmonary stenosis indicated by a peak velocity of 3.84 m/s and a peak pressure gradient of 59.2 mmHg. Echocardiography did not show intracardiac or extracardiac left-to-right shunt flow.

case_report: A 56-year-old woman with a history of peptic ulcer disease presented with difficulty swallowing solid foods, a sensation of a lump mostly on the right side of the chest, and occasional chest pain for several years. The chest pain was retrosternal, dull, rated 6/10, with no radiation, and was associated with shortness of breath during moderate exertion, cough, and easy fatigability. On examination, the patient appeared frail. Vital signs were stable. Body mass index (BMI) was 19 kg/m2 (18.5 - 24.9 kg/m2). Other examination findings were unremarkable. Laboratory data showed hemoglobin of 13 mg/dL (12 - 16 mg/dL), white blood cell (WBC) count of 7.5 × 103/µL (4 - 11 × 103/µL), serum creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL (0.4 - 1.0 mg/dL), and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) of 8 mg/dL (5 - 25 mg/dL). Troponins and liver function tests were unremarkable. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. Due to persistent chest pain, a left heart catheterization (LHC) was performed, which was negative for coronary artery disease. Autoimmune antibodies including antinuclear antibody, anti-Jo-1, anticentromere, anti-scl-70, and anti-ribonucleoprotein were all negative. An esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) did not reveal any abnormalities.
test_results: The patient eventually had a barium esophagogram which came back positive for esophageal stricture. A subsequent computed tomography (CT) angiography of the chest revealed an abnormal right subclavian artery around the trachea and esophagus.

case_report: A 9-year-old boy was admitted to a local district hospital for pneumonia. After one week of antibiotic treatment, he showed no symptoms and no signs of respiratory distress. Despite this, his oxygen saturation consistently ranged from 88 to 92%. Initial transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) indicated a structurally normal heart. He was then referred to our hospital for further evaluation. Clinically, he exhibited mild cyanosis. Other clinical examinations, including the cardiovascular system examination, were unremarkable. Further evaluation with TTE confirmed normal heart anatomy. However, contrast echocardiography revealed a right-to-left shunting at the atrial level.
test_results: A transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) showed a membrane across right atrium without causing obstruction to right ventricular inflow. There was also an anterior secundum atrial septal defect (ASD) and the bubble study showed an immediate right-to-left shunting through the ASD.

case_report: A 70-year-old Asian male arrived at the hospital experiencing increased difficulty in breathing during physical activity and extreme tiredness. He mentioned a long-standing heart issue and a murmur that had been present since childhood. The patient did not experience chest pain, difficulty breathing while lying down, or irregular heartbeats. His medical history included essential hypertension and cataracts, with no history of diabetes, high cholesterol, or smoking. There was no family history of cardiovascular diseases. On physical examination, his vital signs were stable. He weighed 45 kg with a body mass index (BMI) of 17.2 kg/m2. The cardiovascular examination revealed a 4/6 systolic murmur with a palpable thrill, most audible at the left lower sternal border, and a right ventricular heave. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 65%, along with moderate to severe mitral and tricuspid regurgitation.
test_results: Transesophageal echocardiography revealed a normal left ventricular size and systolic function with an LVEF of 55-65%. It also showed evidence of a septum within the right atrium. The mitral valve had moderate to severe regurgitation and the tricuspid valve had severe regurgitation. There was an intra-atrial septal aneurysm with a small patent foramen ovale and a right-to-left shunt.

case_report: A 38-year-old woman came to an urgent care facility complaining of chest pain. She has a history of experiencing multiple similar episodes of chest discomfort and had Lyme disease in her early twenties. During the cardiovascular examination, a grade 2/6 early diastolic murmur was noted over the left sternal area. A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed Q-wave changes in V1/V2, indicating an old myocardial infarct in the septal region.
test_results: A mobile membranous structure was visualized within the RA along with mild tricuspid and aortic valve regurgitation. The rest of the echocardiographic indices, including the ejection fraction, were within normal limits. Color flow Doppler did not reveal any obstruction to RA flow.

case_report: A 26-year-old male was admitted to the critical care service from the emergency department for severe anemia with variceal bleeding. The patient presented with active hematemesis and reported a weeklong history of melanotic stool, hematemesis, and lightheadedness. There were no significant past medical or family histories of gastrointestinal or pulmonary diseases. The patient's social history includes consuming 2 glasses of wine per week for the last 4 years. Physical examination revealed an alert, young male with mild epigastric tenderness and no pulmonary or cardiovascular abnormalities. Imaging of the abdomen showed supradiaphragmatic 'downhill' paraesophageal varices without cirrhosis or splenomegaly, as well as pleural thickening with pleural calcifications. Upper endoscopy revealed numerous grade 4 varices from the upper esophagus to the gastroesophageal junction, which were banded.
test_results: CT of the chest showed normal left pulmonary veins with near complete functional arterial and venous systemic isolation of the right lung due to chronic right pulmonary vein obstruction. The left atrium was significant for a vertical septation resulting in complete isolation of the right upper and lower pulmonary veins. A small caliber left to right to shunt was noted between the upper portion of the left atrium and the SVC via a patent sinus venosus. High resolution noncontrast CT revealed right lung findings significant for volume loss, septal thickening of the secondary pulmonary lobules, and a 'cobble stoning' indicative of pathologic interstitial edema. V/Q scan revealed nearly absent right lung perfusion.

case_report: A 15-year-old female with no known past medical history arrived at the emergency department (ED) after collapsing while walking. Family members observed that she was acutely short of breath and she soon lost her pulse. Bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) was initiated, and emergency medical services were called. Upon arrival, paramedics found the patient in pulseless electrical activity (PEA). CPR was continued, bag-valve-mask ventilation was started, intravenous (IV) access was obtained, and IV epinephrine was administered. Two attempts at endotracheal intubation during transport were unsuccessful and were complicated by significant vomiting. Upon arrival at the ED, CPR was continued, and the trachea was successfully intubated. A venous blood gas analysis revealed a pH of 6.89, pCO2 of 43 mmHg, bicarbonate level of 8 mmol/L, and a base excess of -24. After four minutes of CPR, an increase in end-tidal CO2 was observed, and a subsequent pulse check confirmed the return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC).
test_results: Images obtained in the parasternal and apical windows demonstrated a globally hypokinetic left ventricle with significant spontaneous echo contrast in all four chambers of the heart. The apical view demonstrated spontaneous echo contrast passing freely between the left and right ventricles through a large VSD. On the parasternal long axis view, the VSD was confirmed and a septation in the left atrium was noted.

case_report: A 21-year-old male reported experiencing a blurry patch of vision in his right eye for eight days. He had no notable medical history and was not on any regular medication. His best corrected visual acuity was 6/4 unaided in both eyes. Intraocular pressure was normal, and the anterior segments were unremarkable. Dilated fundoscopy revealed a filling defect in a branch of the inferotemporal retinal artery of the right eye, located approximately 1–2 disc diameters from the optic disc, along with pale areas resembling cotton wool spots. These findings were confirmed with optical coherence tomography. After one week, the patient's blurriness had subjectively improved, and the pale areas had reduced in size. Tests for cytomegalovirus, toxoplasma, human immunodeficiency virus, vasculitis, and thrombophilia were all negative. Routine blood tests showed a total cholesterol of 4.6 mmol/L, triglycerides of 1.9 mmol/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 2, and normal renal and liver function. The patient was referred to cardiology for further investigation and was started on aspirin. Cardiological assessments showed a blood pressure of 135/83 mmHg, heart rate of 81 beats per minute, normal heart sounds with no murmurs or added sounds, and no carotid bruits. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head, magnetic resonance angiogram of the head and neck vessels, and carotid doppler scans were all normal. A 72-hour Holter monitoring test indicated sinus rhythm throughout, and conventional transthoracic echocardiography was unremarkable.
test_results: A transthoracic echocardiographic bubble contrast study showed a large right to left shunt at the atrial level within one beat of release of valsalva manoeuvre.

case_report: A 53-year-old female presented with intermittent palpitations and chest tightness for 6 years, which worsened over the past 3 days. Six years ago, she experienced palpitations, chest tightness, and an accelerated pulse without clear causes. Five years ago, she had episodes of irregular uterine bleeding, during which increased bleeding was associated with palpitations and chest tightness. She sought treatment at a local hospital, where coronary angiography showed no abnormalities. Three days before admission, her symptoms of palpitations and chest tightness worsened with activity, and she experienced nocturnal paroxysmal dyspnea and intermittent abdominal pain. An electrocardiogram at the local hospital showed a third-degree atrioventricular block. Despite receiving treatment, her symptoms did not significantly improve. On the fourth day, she visited the outpatient clinic and was admitted to the cardiology department. Physical examination revealed a body temperature of 35.7°C, heart rate of 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute, and blood pressure of 114/80 mm Hg. The patient was alert and cooperative, with no cyanosis on the lips or dilatation of bilateral jugular veins. Moist rales were heard in the left lung, with no dry rales. The heart rate was 78 beats per minute with a regular rhythm, and no murmurs were detected in the valve auscultation areas. The abdomen was soft without tenderness or rebound tenderness, and the liver and spleen were not palpable. Mobile dullness was negative, and there was no lower extremity edema.
test_results: Cardiac color doppler ultrasound showed dilatated left atrium and right heart, a small amount of mitral valve regurgitation, a large amount of tricuspid valve regurgitation, and the increased pulmonary artery pressure with a small amount of pericardial effusion.

case_report: A 46-year-old male with a medical history including atrial fibrillation, an enlarged aortic root, and a bicuspid aortic valve with severe aortic regurgitation (AR) was scheduled for elective aortic valve replacement, aortic root replacement, and a Maze procedure. Preoperative transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) findings indicated normal function of both ventricles, severe AR, and a potential patent foramen ovale (PFO). The TTE report did not provide information regarding the coronary sinus. During the operation, the patient experienced an uneventful induction of general anesthesia.
test_results: Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) was then performed and confirmed the preoperative findings with the exception that there was no PFO identified. During placement of a central venous catheter in the right internal jugular vein, TEE was used to visualize the guidewire. It was noted at this time that the right SVC appeared small. In addition, the coronary sinus was observed to be significantly dilated, measuring 2.1 cm in the deep midesophageal 4-chamber view and 3.3 cm in the midesophageal 2-chamber view. A left-sided intravenous line was in place so a bubble study was attempted. Injection of agitated saline showed bubbles appearing in the coronary sinus prior to entering the right atrium.
Orpha_name: Persistent left superior vena cava connecting to the roof of left-sided atrium

case_report: A 71-year-old male presented to the pulmonary outpatient clinic for interstitial lung disease and was later admitted due to a sudden increase in difficulty breathing and coughing. Lung auscultation revealed inspiratory rales at the bases of both lungs. Arterial blood gas analysis showed a slightly reduced PaO2 level of 80.6 mm Hg. Other laboratory results were within normal limits. A chest X-ray indicated an enlarged heart with a cardiothoracic ratio of 0.59 and reticular opacities in the right costophrenic space. Chest CT scans showed pulmonary fibrosis with a usual interstitial pneumonitis (UIP) pattern, characterized by reticular opacities in the subpleural areas of both lungs, predominantly in the right lower lobe. Additionally, a lobulated hypodense mass approximately 1.7 cm in size was observed at the junction of the right atrium and inferior vena cava. The coronary sinus was significantly dilated, and the coronary sinus ostium was not clearly visible. A left superior vena cava (LSVC) was also identified. There was an indication of coronary sinus ostium occlusion, with coronary venous flow likely draining through the persistent LSVC. Dense calcification was noted on the aortic valve.
test_results: The cardiac CT showed dense calcification in the bicuspid aortic valve with raphe. It also showed a lobulating contoured hypodense mass (18 HU) measuring approximately 1.7 cm and without definite enhancement at the junction of the RA and IVC. Continuity of a contrast-enhanced lumen between the coronary sinus (CS) and RA was not noted on cardiac CT; we therefore reported atresia of the CS ostium. The dilated coronary sinus continued to the persistent LSVC and then drained into the left innominate vein. It finally drained to the right superior vena cava (RSVC) and into the RA. Volume-rendered CT imaging clearly demonstrated the dilated coronary sinus and cardiac veins. On transesophageal echocardiography, a 2 × 1 cm oval echogenic mass attached to the RA wall was visible and the mass contained an internal anechoic cystic lesion. Moderate to severe aortic stenosis was also diagnosed. On histological examination, the cystic mass was confirmed to be a pseudocyst containing blood.

case_report: A 3-year-old girl presented with a history of recurrent hemoptysis starting at the age of 1 year. Bronchoscopy showed open bronchi, with mucosal hyperemia and inflammation in the right bronchi, and no other intrabronchial lesions were observed. The child's hemoglobin level was 12 g%. General physical examination was unremarkable. Chest examination indicated mildly decreased air entry on the right side. A chest radiograph showed a small right hemithorax with consolidation in the right middle and lower zones. A CT scan of the chest revealed a small right hemithorax with a shift of the mediastinum to the same side and multiple areas of consolidation in the lung parenchyma.
test_results: CTA depicted a hypoplastic right main pulmonary artery, with nonvisualization of the pulmonary veins. A prominent bronchial artery supplying the lung was also identified.

case_report: A 71-year-old female patient with a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation was admitted to the cardiology department with symptoms of dyspnea and palpitation. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 130/85 mmHg, pulse rate of 51 bpm, oxygen saturation of 95%, and respiratory rate of 20/min. Cardiovascular examination noted a left-sided apical impulse, with no abnormal findings in other systems upon initial evaluation. Electrocardiography indicated a normal axis, normal sinus rhythm with a heart rate of 47 bpm, and negative T-waves in leads V1–5. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, cardiac biomarkers, and electrolytes, showed typical values. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) displayed an unusual view with the apex positioned posteriorly in the thorax, and the apical window was displaced posteriorly. A posteroanterior chest radiograph revealed a loss of the right heart border, and the lateral view showed a posterior bulging of the heart with the apex.
test_results: CT angiography revealed that the whole heart was shifted in the left hemithorax with the apex pointing posteriorly. Chest CT shows interposition of the lung between the aortic arch and pulmonary trunk.

case_report: A 48-year-old male patient arrived at the emergency department with repeated episodes of shortness of breath and a persistent cough over the past 10 days. Additionally, he experienced two episodes of chest tightness, each lasting one minute, over the last two days, which resolved on their own. His medical history included hypertension for the past eight years, for which he had been on regular medication. Upon examination, his physical findings were unremarkable. Laboratory results and blood work were within normal limits, and cardiac enzymes were negative. An electrocardiogram indicated a normal sinus rhythm. A chest X-ray revealed a large opacity obscuring the right heart border. An echocardiogram showed normal results with no pericardial effusion.
test_results: A CT scan revealed the presence of a 5 × 3 cm cyst at the right cardio phrenic angle.

case_report: A 9-year-old male presented to the emergency department with episodes of palpitations during daily activities. There were no other complications or past medical history noted. Previous episodes were managed with beta blockers (propranolol) over the past year without improvement. The patient was clinically stable upon examination. Initial vital signs included a blood pressure of 100/60 mm Hg and a pulse rate of 130 beats per minute. Auscultation of both lungs was unremarkable, and examinations of the abdomen, spleen, and liver were normal. Electrocardiography (ECG) showed sinus tachycardia with a normal axis. Chest radiography appeared normal.
test_results: An apical four-chamber view echocardiography showed an echolucent space next to the posterior wall of the left ventricle with compression effect. The mass was extrinsic and confined to the pericardium. The right and left ventricular chamber size and function were normal, and there was no valvular heart disease. Then, a chest CT scan with contrast showed a retrosternal mass characterized with a clear serous fluid with compression on the posterior wall of the left ventricle.

case_report: A three-year-old female was transferred from the pediatric clinic due to severe oxygen desaturation in the 20-30% range. The patient presented with fever, normal blood pressure, and a heart rate between 110-120 beats per minute. Physical examination showed central and perioral cyanosis, an increased respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute, and sternal and subcostal retractions. Lung auscultation revealed transmitted upper respiratory sounds. Pulse oximetry readings were in the 60% range. Venous blood gas analysis indicated a pH of 7.42, partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO2) of 23, and bicarbonate (HCO3) of 72 mmol/L. Laboratory results showed a hemoglobin level of 9 g/dL and an elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) of 1284 IU/L. Chest X-ray results were unremarkable, electrocardiography showed normal sinus rhythm, and echocardiogram (ECG) indicated normal cardiac function with no structural abnormalities. The patient received a single dose of Methylene blue at 1 mg/kg before being admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU). Her past medical history includes being born to consanguineous parents, normal growth and development, and a history of cyanosis since infancy. She was hospitalized two years prior for low oxygen saturation (SpO2 in the 50-60% range, Methemoglobin level 12) at another institution. She was discharged with an oxygen saturation in the 60% range and did not follow up after discharge.
test_results: Co-oximetry revealed O2Hb 68%, MetHb 16%, and HHb 14%.
diagnosis: Congenital Methemoglobinemia with Unstable Hemoglobin Variant

case_report: A 28-year-old obese man arrived at the Emergency Room with complaints of epigastric pain radiating to the back for one day. He had a history of three previous admissions for acute pancreatitis associated with hyperlipidemia. His medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus and active pulmonary tuberculosis. His treatment regimen consisted of dietary restrictions, daily NPH insulin injections, and lipid-lowering medications such as fibrate derivatives. His family history revealed that his father had hypertension, a past cerebral infarction, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. His mother had hyperlipidemia (type IV), and his elder brother had recurrent acute pancreatitis and diabetes mellitus. He did not present with xanthoma or xanthelasma. He had no history of alcohol consumption or biliary calculus disease. His height was 176 cm, and his weight was 87 kg, indicating marked obesity. Physical examination showed a slightly distended abdomen with hypoactive bowel sounds and direct tenderness in the epigastrium without rebound tenderness. Laboratory data on admission revealed a white blood cell count of 15,210/mm3. Blood chemistry tests showed a fasting blood sugar level of 228 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase level of 379 IU/L, and aspartate aminotransferase level of 20 IU/L. The serum amylase level was 160 mg/dL, slightly above the normal range (25-125 mg/dL). Serum lipase level was elevated to 1596 U/L (normal range 13-60 U/L). Serum calcium level and blood urea nitrogen level were within normal limits. Lipid profile results included total cholesterol at 272 mg/dL, triglycerides at 605 mg/dL, high-density cholesterol at 28 mg/dL, and low-density cholesterol at 98 mg/dL.
test_results: Serum lipoprotein electrophoresis showed 0% of chylomicron (0-2.0), 62.9% of β-lipoprotein (36.5-59.1), 22.5% of pre-β-lipoprotein (3.8-33.8), and 14.6% of α-lipoprotein (20.4-46.4).

case_report: An eleven-year-old female child, born of non-consanguineous marriage, presented with multiple, asymptomatic, yellow to brownish lesions over various sites including hands, elbows, knees, and eyes. The lesions began at 2 years of age and gradually increased in size and number, initially appearing on the outer aspect of multiple interdigital web spaces of both hands. Over the next 8 years, similar lesions progressively developed over multiple knuckles, palmar creases, both knees, lower aspect of both buttocks, and periocular areas. Family history revealed similar conditions in her elder sister (14 years old) and maternal aunt. There was no history of diabetes, cardiac, liver, or renal diseases in the patient or any family members. The patient had no significant history of drug intake, weight loss, appetite loss, or systemic symptoms. Examination showed multiple, smooth-surfaced, yellow to brownish, well-defined, circular to irregularly shaped solitary papules and coalesced plaques, ranging in size from 0.2 x 0.2 cm to 5 x 10 cm. These were bilaterally and symmetrically distributed over the flexor aspect of the elbows, dorsal aspect of interphalangeal joints and interdigital webs, extensor aspect of knees, upper eyelids, and medial and lateral canthi. The lesions were of soft to firm consistency on palpation, with some showing koebnarization. The child was developmentally appropriate for her age, with no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Systemic examination was normal.
test_results: Investigations revealed Fasting Lipid Profile (FLP) as, Total serum cholesterol (TC). 769mg/dl, High density lipoprotein (HDL)- 31mg/ dl, Serum triglyceride (TGs)- 316mg/dl, Low Density Lipoprotein (LDL) -176mg/dl. Histopathological examination showed infiltration of foamy cells within the reticular dermis with admixture of lymphocytes.
diagnosis: Eruptive xanthomas secondary to familial combined hyperlipidemia

case_report: A 53-year-old white male presented to the emergency room with acute central chest pain lasting 8 hours. The pain occurred mainly at rest, was non-radiating, and was not accompanied by sweating, palpitations, nausea, or vomiting. He experienced three similar episodes in the previous week. He reported no changes in bowel habits or other gastrointestinal symptoms. His medical history included hypertension diagnosed 6 months prior, for which he was prescribed Bendrofluazide, though he admitted to non-compliance. He smoked 20 cigarettes per day and consumed 6–8 units of alcohol daily. His family history included his father and five paternal uncles who died from ischemic heart disease in their early fifties, and his mother who died at 57 from cervical carcinoma. He has one living sister. He was able to walk up to 5 miles a day without chest discomfort before this admission. On examination, he had a heart rate of 103 beats per minute in sinus rhythm, blood pressure of 167/129 mmHg, oxygen saturation of 97% on room air, respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute, and a normal temperature of 36.7°C. His BMI was 27.6. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Fundoscopic examination showed lipaemia retinalis. A 12-lead ECG on admission showed no ischemic changes except for peaked T waves. Chest X-ray was normal. Troponin T levels could not be measured on three occasions due to lipaemia, but CK-MB was normal at 3 μg/l. An exercise tolerance test conducted the next morning was negative for reversible ischemic changes.
test_results: Admission lipid profile revealed a markedly raised TG at 103 mmol/l. Next morning repeats lipid profile; TG and total cholesterol (Tchol) were 57 mmol/l and 32 mmol/l, respectively. HDL cholesterol was unmeasurable with urea 4.5 mmol/l, creatinine 86 μmol/l, total protein 67 g/l, albumin 39 g/l and urine albumin/creatinine ratio 9.7. Fasting glucose and HBA1c were normal at 4.5 mmol/l and 5.8%, respectively. Liver function test revealed a moderately raised ALT and GGT at 60 U/l and 730 U/l, respectively. Serum amylase was normal at 51 U/l.

case_report: A male infant, aged two months, was admitted due to corneal ulceration in the left eye. The pregnancy and delivery were normal, with the child born at term via vaginal delivery, and no maternal systemic diseases were noted. The mother observed a static eyelid anomaly. Initially, the condition was not deemed urgent by the neonatologist, who reassured the parents of a likely spontaneous resolution. At one month old, the child was brought to an ophthalmologist presenting with the absence of eyelashes on the upper left eyelid, excessive tearing, and conjunctival congestion. Examination revealed corneal erosion and spastic entropion in the left eye. Treatment included antibiotic and cycloplegic eye drops, and a therapeutic contact lens was applied. A follow-up was scheduled for 14 days later. However, the mother reported the therapeutic contact lens was expelled spontaneously a few hours post-discharge, with worsening photophobia, increased tearing, and changes in corneal transparency. The patient returned to the clinic after seven days and was referred to the oculoplasty department.
test_results: Examination under general anesthesia allowed for a difficult eversion of the upper eyelid, using the Desmarres retractor, which revealed a horizontal tarsal scar band located at approximately 2–3 mm from the edge of the eyelid, in the middle of the tarsus, accompanied by a shortening of the posterior upper eyelid lamella and the inward twisting of the ciliary margin. It also revealed a central corneal leucoma measuring approximately 6 mm in diameter and a central corneal ulceration measuring approximately 2 mm in diameter.

case_report: A 61-year-old unmarried woman presented with generalized edema. Her height was recorded at 148.1 cm. Echocardiography revealed a bicuspid aortic valve and moderate aortic stenosis. Coronary aortic computed tomography (CT) angiography showed mild luminal narrowing of the aortic isthmus and a persistent left superior vena cava. The patient also exhibited a pectus deformity and scoliosis. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) identified variants in FBN1, TGFBR2, and COL5A1 with uncertain significance. Additionally, the presence of the Y chromosome was noted.
test_results: 45,X[17]/46,X,psu idic(Y)(q11.23) was confirmed.

case_report: A 20-year-old female presented with secondary amenorrhea lasting 8 months. She began menstruating at age 12 and experienced regular cycles for 3 years, which later became irregular. Her menstrual flow was normal for 4-5 days, without excessive bleeding or pain. She had no significant past medical or surgical history and no notable family history. Physical examination revealed short stature, a wide carrying angle, and widely spaced nipples. Abdominal and external genitalia examinations were normal. Blood tests showed elevated follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) at 41.2 mmol/ml, low estradiol at 14.12, low progesterone at <0.10, and low testosterone at 0.07 mmol/ml. Other hormone levels were within normal ranges, with prolactin at 170 and DHEAS at 5.5 mmol/L. An ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis showed normal anatomy with streak ovaries.
test_results: Chromosome analysis revealed a normal X chromosome and an isochromosome of the long arm of the second X chromosome at band Xq10.
diagnosis: Turner Syndrome with Mosaicism of X Chromosome

case_report: A three-month-old male infant, firstborn to a non-consanguineously married Indian couple, was referred for evaluation due to global developmental delay and persistent seizures. The mother provided informed consent. The pregnancy was uneventful, and the baby was delivered at full term via normal vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 3200 g. The neonatal period was initially uneventful, but jaundice was noted on the third day of life with a maximum bilirubin level of 16.3 mg/dL. There was no evidence of ABO or Rh incompatibility, and the infant was discharged home on exclusive breastfeeding. On the eighth day of life, the infant was readmitted due to poor feeding and lethargy. Intravenous fluids and antibiotics were administered after samples were taken for a sepsis screen, which returned negative. The infant showed clinical improvement and was discharged. At the end of the second week, the infant presented to the Pediatric Emergency Ward with frequent episodes of multifocal clonic seizures. Blood glucose on arrival was 77 mg/dL, and seizures were managed with phenobarbitone and phenytoin. There were no skin rashes, abnormal urine odor, rapid breathing, or recurrent hiccups. From the second month of age, the child experienced multiple daily episodes of myoclonus, and seizures remained poorly controlled despite treatment with three antiepileptic medications at adequate doses. No neurocutaneous markers or dysmorphism were observed. Occipito-frontal circumference was 36.5 cm. Ocular examination did not reveal any ectopia lentis. The infant was awake but irritable with an inconsolable cry and exhibited poor quality and quantity of spontaneous limb movements. The infant did not fix or track light, and fundus examination was normal. Pupillary reflexes were normal. Profound axial hypotonia with appendicular hypertonia and brisk deep tendon reflexes were present. There were no involuntary movements. The anterior fontanelle was normal. Complete blood count, blood urea, creatinine, electrolytes, and liver function tests were normal. Serum uric acid was less than 0.5 mg/dL. Blood lactate, ammonia, and serum amino acids were normal. Urinary organic acids were not detected. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal. Electroencephalography performed in the first month of life was normal. Freshly voided urine analysis by calorimetric method revealed increased sulfite excretion (patient value-1425 µmoles/L; normal- 0-96.7 µmoles/L). Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed extensive cystic encephalomalacia involving bilateral parieto-occipital lobes and signal changes in the caudate, putamen, and deep white matter. Basal ganglia exhibited focal T2 hypointensity and corresponding T1 hyperintensity, predominantly involving the head of the caudate and putamen bilaterally, suggestive of early calcification. Diffuse callosal thinning was also noted. Diffusion restriction was observed along the corticospinal tract in diffusion-weighted and apparent diffusion coefficient images. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) showed an elevated lactate peak.
test_results: A homozygous mutation was detected in exon 4 of MOCS2 gene: NM_004531.4: c.218T>C which leads to substitution of Leucine at position 73 to Proline. Leucine at position 73 is a highly conserved residue across different species.
Orpha_name: Sulfite oxidase deficiency due to molybdenum cofactor deficiency

case_report: A 10-year-old male of mixed race was admitted to Hospital Napoleão Laureano with a significant swelling and protrusion of the left side of the face. Additionally, there was a raised and firm area in the maxillary region that had been present for about 25 days. The patient did not have a fever and occasionally experienced pain. Visual acuity, eye structure, and ocular fundus were normal in both eyes.
test_results: The images showed a heterogeneous (DM = 32 UH) mass with soft-tissue density, measuring 1.5 cm × 6.2 cm × 5.0 cm, occupying part of the left half of the face inside the maxillary sinus, and infiltrating and destroying the bone structure of the maxillary sinus, left orbit, ethmoidal cells, nasal cavity, and sphenoid sinus. Inflammatory sinus disease was present in the left maxillary sinus and left exophthalmos due to the compression exerted on the eye. An analysis of the histological sections revealed an undifferentiated malignant neoplasm infiltrating the skeletal muscle tissue. The microscopic examination was positive for the following antigens: MyoD1, myogenin, desmin, and Ki67 (100% positivity in neoplastic cells).

case_report: A 22-year-old woman presented with recurrent seizures that began at the age of six. The seizures initially affected her right hand and then became generalized, lasting for two to three minutes. There were no preceding symptoms such as prodrome, aura, or automatism. Post-seizure, she experienced confusion but no paralysis. Her developmental milestones were normal until the age of six, except for mild mental retardation. She did not attend school. She was able to speak normally before the onset of seizures but experienced progressive speech regression starting at age ten, becoming mute by age twelve. She could follow simple commands. There was no family history of epilepsy. Despite taking multiple anticonvulsants, her seizures were not controlled. Since the age of ten, she has had nearly daily seizures, experiencing 5-10 seizures per day at the time of presentation. She also had occasional rage attacks. Her current medications included sodium valproate 1000 mg/day, carbamazepine 800 mg/day, and levetiracetam 1000 mg/day, which were initiated at ages six, nine, and sixteen, respectively. The patient was apathetic and had expressive aphasia. There was no focal weakness, and both superficial and deep tendon reflexes were normal.
test_results: Her MRI of the brain revealed a complete band of gray matter located deep and parallel to pachygyric overlying cortex. The thickness of the band was more in the posterior part of parietal and occipital cortex. An electroencephalogram (EEG) revealed bi-frontal slow waves which were marked during stage 1 sleep.

case_report: A 48-year-old male with a history of treatment for anaplastic astrocytoma at ages 39 and 46 was referred for evaluation of worsening anemia. Family history included two cases of colon cancer in second-degree relatives. Comprehensive examination identified two advanced carcinoma sites in the descending colon and stomach. Additionally, a 15 mm hypo-vascular mass was found in segment 2 of the liver. Pathological analysis of biopsied and surgically resected specimens revealed poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma in the descending colon, moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma in the stomach, and poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma in the liver, indicating the liver tumor might be a metastasis from the colon. The patient received 5-Fluorouracil-based adjuvant chemotherapy combined with oxaliplatin. During postoperative follow-up, multiple polypectomies were performed for colonic adenomas, including a 10 mm tubular adenoma with severe atypia in the ascending colon.
test_results: This analysis showed a positive result for eight markers (except D5S346), indicating a high frequency of MSI (MSI-high). The IHCs of the descending colon cancer demonstrated abnormal nuclear staining of scanty MSH6, concurrent loss of MLH1 and PMS2, whereas the staining for MSH2 was positive. On the other hand, IHCs of the liver metastasis showed complete loss of MSH6, MLH1, PMS2 and the staining for MSH2 was positive. IHCs of the stomach cancer revealed negative staining of MLH1 and PMS2, whereas the staining for MSH2 and MSH6 were positive. This genetic testing revealed a frame shift mutation in codon 618 (c. 1852-1854delAAG / p.Lys618del) of MLH1.

case_report: A four-year-old male child, born from a non-consanguineous marriage with no significant perinatal history and normal development, arrived at the emergency department with a 15-day history of dry cough that did not improve with symptomatic treatment. The child also experienced shortness of breath for the past three days and abdominal pain for one day. One month prior, the child had a low-grade fever that resolved in one day with paracetamol. A CT scan of the thorax performed externally on the day of admission showed moderate right-sided loculated pleural effusion and complete collapse of the right lower lobe. On examination, the child exhibited moderate dehydration and respiratory distress. Vital signs included a normal temperature, heart rate of 126 bpm, respiratory rate of 50 breaths per minute, and blood pressure of 112/68 mmHg. Oxygen saturation was 86% on room air and 96% on CPAP at 5 liters per minute. The throat was mildly congested, with no lymphadenopathy or clubbing observed. Growth parameters were within normal limits. Chest examination revealed asymmetry in chest expansion, reduced air entry on the right side, and absence of bronchial breathing. Percussion indicated dullness on the right side. Other systemic examinations were unremarkable. An initial chest X-ray showed diffuse opacity predominantly on the right side, obscuring the costophrenic and cardiophrenic angles, with tracheal deviation to the left and no air bronchogram. A right lateral decubitus chest X-ray revealed a significant free fluid level occupying more than half of the ipsilateral hemithorax. Blood tests on the first day of admission showed a normocytic and normochromic blood smear with mild leukocytosis and no blasts. An intercostal drainage tube was inserted due to the significant effusion. The drained pleural fluid was yellowish, thin, and clear, and was sent for routine analysis. The pleural fluid analysis showed a markedly elevated WBC count and the presence of suspicious cells.
test_results: The examination of the pleural fluid smear revealed approximately 65-70% of blasts, measuring 12-14 µm in size, exhibiting a high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio (N:C ratio), indistinct nucleoli, and scant cytoplasm. Immunophenotyping (flow cytometry) unveiled 68.64% blasts with dim to moderate CD45 and low side scatter (SSC) on CD45/SSC gating. The blasts were characterized by the expression of cCD3, sCD3, CD4, CD5, CD7, and CD8, while being negative for HLA-DR, CD34, CD117, cMPO, CD10, CD13, CD19, CD20, CD33, CD64, cCD79a, kappa, and lambda light chains.

case_report: A 21-year-old male experienced gastric discomfort for one week and had an episode of hematemesis. He was admitted to a local hospital four weeks prior, where a chest X-ray (posterior-anterior view) showed right costophrenic angle obliteration with a meniscus sign, indicating a large right-sided pleural effusion. Pleural fluid aspiration was performed, revealing exudative effusion with high adenosine deaminase (ADA). Anti-tubercular therapy (ATT) was initiated. The patient had no prior medical history and was not on any medications before these symptoms. After three weeks, he presented to our hospital with exertional breathlessness, dry cough, and non-radiating chest pain for three days. He also reported loss of appetite and significant weight loss (~12 kgs) over six weeks. There was no history of hoarseness, stridor, dysphagia, fever, chills, night sweats, facial or arm swelling, headaches, hemoptysis, or vomiting. Vitals were: heart rate 113 beats/minute, respiratory rate 33 cycles/minute, blood pressure 100/72 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. The patient was moderately built, conscious, and oriented. Icterus was present, but pallor, cyanosis, clubbing, lymphadenopathy, and edema were absent. Respiratory examination showed dullness on percussion over the right mammary, infra-axillary, and infrascapular regions, with d’espine sign present. Auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds on the right side and normal vesicular breath sounds on the left. Cardiovascular examination showed muffled heart sounds. Abdominal examination was normal. A chest radiograph indicated mediastinal widening with hilum overlay and cardiomegaly. 2D ECHO showed normal chamber dimensions, pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP) of 28 mmHg, moderate pericardial effusion, large right-sided and minimal left-sided pleural effusion, and an ejection fraction of 60%. Routine investigations revealed hemoglobin of 15 g/dl, white blood cells of 8.2 T/mm3, and platelets of 438 T/mm3 with normal peripheral smear and serum electrolytes. Liver function tests were abnormal, leading to the cessation of ATT. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) of the thorax showed a large mediastinal mass lesion abutting the pericardium with loss of fat planes, extending laterally to the left lateral chest wall without rib erosion. Multiple heterogeneously enhancing lymph nodes were noted in the pre-tracheal, cardio-phrenic, prevascular, and aortopulmonary window regions, the largest being ~1.8 x 2.2 cm in the right cardio-phrenic region. Right moderate pleural effusion with collapse or consolidation of the underlying parenchyma was observed. The left lung parenchyma appeared normal with a normal broncho-vascular pattern. A USG-guided biopsy revealed a monotonous population of lymphocytes arranged in sheets and singles. Tumor cells were medium to large with condensed chromatin, round to oval with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and a prominent eosinophilic nucleus. Pleural fluid tested positive for malignancy.
test_results: Immunohistochemistry revealed lymphoblastic cells, which were positive for leukocyte common antigen (LCA), CD 7, TdT, and CD 99, with a Ki67 proliferation index of 90% and negative for CK, CD5, and CD 20.

case_report: A 44-year-old man was admitted to the hospital in April 2020 for evaluation of a hepatic mass. The mass was initially detected during a routine examination at a local hospital five years prior. Ultrasound imaging identified a 4.24 × 2.63 cm hypoechoic nodule in the right lobe of the liver. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) showed a well-defined oval mass with low density in segment 6 of the liver. Enhanced CT scans revealed the mass to be heterogeneous with significant enhancement at the margins. Over the next four years, regular examinations indicated that the mass was growing slowly. By January 2020, enhanced CT scans showed the mass had increased to a maximum diameter of 7.8 cm, located between segment 6 of the liver and the right adrenal gland. The margins of the mass displayed marked enhancement during the arterial phase and hypointensity during the portal and delayed phases compared to the surrounding liver tissue. Throughout the follow-up period, the patient remained asymptomatic. Blood tests showed the patient was negative for serum hepatitis B surface antigen and anti-hepatitis C virus, but positive for hepatitis B surface antibody. Tumor markers, including α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and carbohydrate antigen 199, were within normal ranges. The patient had no history of smoking, drinking, medical conditions, or psycho-social issues. No genetic tests had been conducted previously. Physical examination revealed no significant abnormalities. The mass was situated at the border of segment 6 and segment 7 of the liver, near the inferior right hepatic vein. A partial hepatectomy was performed, and the resected specimen measured 8.5 × 8 × 4.5 cm. On the cut surface, a mass measuring 6 × 5.5 × 4 cm was found just beneath the liver capsule. The mass had a relatively clear margin without an obvious capsule, and its cut surface was solid and yellowish-grey with areas of focal hemorrhage. No necrosis was observed. The surrounding liver tissue appeared normal. Microscopically, the lesion was incompletely encapsulated, with cells arranged in solid sheets and areas of partial hemorrhage. There was minimal stroma and no significant arterialization. Most tumor cells were large, polygonal, with prominent nucleoli and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Pleomorphic nuclei were frequently observed, but the nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio was low. No mitoses, necrosis, or vascular invasion were noted. Smaller cells with small nuclei and granular cytoplasm were found focally. The surrounding liver tissue was near-normal, and the surgical margins were clear.
test_results: The tumor cells were negative for Arg-1, glypican-3 (GPC3), hepatocyte specific antigen (HSA), epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), CK7, CK19, desmin, HMB45, and chromogranin A (CgA). Synaptophysin (Syn), α-inhibin and Melan A were positive. The Ki-67 index was 1 %.

case_report: The patient is a 35-year-old married Chinese female (G3P0) who experienced elevated office blood pressure (approximately 159/96 mmHg) starting from the 16th week of gestation. The blood pressure continued to increase, reaching a maximum of approximately 180/110 mmHg, accompanied by palpebra and ankle edema. The hypertension was not managed with 30 mg nifedipine taken twice daily. At the 20th week of gestation, she was admitted to the Cardiovascular Department of West China Hospital, Sichuan University with hypertension. The patient had no personal or family history of hypertension, chronic kidney disease, diabetes mellitus, or autoimmune disease. Prior to gestation, she was healthy with no evident endocrine disorders. Upon admission at 20 weeks of gestation, her office blood pressure was 168/100 mmHg, weight was 68 kg, height was 162 cm, and body mass index was 25.9 kg/m2. Blood pressure readings were 168/100 mmHg in the left upper extremity, 166/98 mmHg in the right upper extremity, 180/110 mmHg in the left lower extremity, and 184/112 mmHg in the right lower extremity, with a normal upper to lower extremity blood pressure ratio. There were no signs of pulmonary edema, cerebral, or visual symptoms. Baseline serum glucose was 6.0 mmol/L and glycosylated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) was 5.8%. Liver and renal functions were normal. No vascular murmurs were detected in the neck, chest, or abdomen. Hypertensive target organ damage was assessed, revealing a carotid femoral pulse wave velocity (cf-PWV) of 8.9 ± 0.8 m/s and a carotid intima media thickness (IMT) of 0.7 mm bilaterally with no atheromatous plaques. The urinary albumin/creatinine ratio (UACR) was 48.4 mg/g, and proteinuria was 0.43 g in a 24-hour urine collection. Echocardiography showed an interventricular septum (IVS) thickness of 11 mm, a left ventricular ejection fraction (EF) of 66%, mild pericardial effusion, and a left ventricular mass index (LVMI) of 84 g/m2. The plasma level of N terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide was 321 pg/ml. Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) indicated persistently elevated blood pressure with a 24-hour average of 169/102 mmHg, daytime average of 171/103 mmHg, and night average of 158/95 mmHg. Methyldopa was prescribed according to the 2013 American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists guidelines, starting at 250 mg twice daily and increasing to 1 g twice daily, but this did not reduce the blood pressure to a safe level. The hypertension remained uncontrolled with 2 g methyldopa per day. Additionally, the patient developed hypokalemia (baseline serum potassium was 3.14 mmol/L) and preeclampsia in the early second trimester. Further endocrine hormone measurements showed normal levels of catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, and dopamine) in both plasma and urine. Plasma renin, angiotensin II, and aldosterone levels were within normal ranges, with an aldosterone/renin ratio (ARR) of 1.94 ng/dl:ng/ml/h. The 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC) was 1684.3 μg/24 h (normal range: 20.26–127.55 μg/24 h). Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) levels were consistently < 1.00 ng/L in three measurements (normal range: 5–78 ng/L). Plasma cortisol levels lacked circadian rhythm, measuring 866.3 nmol/L at 8:00 am, 794.8 nmol/L at 4:00 pm, and 806.4 nmol/L at midnight.
test_results: Ultrasonography demonstrated a mass (2.9 cm × 2.8 cm) with a weak echo and clear boundary in the right side of the adrenal gland. Color doppler ultrasound showed no blood flow signal in the adrenal gland mass. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) without contrast showed a mass of 3.2 cm in diameter in the right adrenal gland, and T1 weighted (T1W) and T2 weighted (T2W) images both provided mixed signals. The signal of mass in the T1W image in phase was lower than that in the T1W opposed phase, which indicated the tumor was rich in lipid.

case_report: The patient is a 72-year-old male of Swedish ethnicity with a medical history that includes high alcohol intake, sleep apnea, glaucoma, and heart failure. There is no family history of adrenal tumors. In 2012, the patient experienced septicemia after undergoing a core-needle biopsy of the prostate. Physical examination showed high blood pressure, abdominal obesity, and relatively thin limbs.
test_results: An abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan was performed revealing two distinct nodules measuring 27 mm × 22 mm, Hounsfield unit (HU) 9 and 18 mm × 12 mm, HU 1, respectively, in the left adrenal gland. Hormonal analysis demonstrated a pathological overnight dexamethasone suppression test (s-cortisol 361 nmol/L after suppression), which was repeated with similar result (s-cortisol 388 nmol/L after suppression). A 24-h cortisol-ACTH curve (six separate samples) showed a stiff cortisol curve (lowest s-cortisol value 339 nmol/L at 06:00 h, highest s-cortisol value 408 nmol/L at 12:00 h) and s-ACTH suppressed (<1.1 pmol/L) at all times.

case_report: A 57-year-old female presented to Imam Khomeini hospital with exertional shortness of breath. She resides in the southern part of Tehran. Her symptoms began approximately 4 months prior to admission and progressively worsened, accompanied by a non-purulent cough. At the time of admission, she experienced difficulty performing daily activities. Her shortness of breath did not occur at rest, during sleep, or while eating. She did not report orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. There was no history of hemoptysis or exposure to tuberculosis patients. Her medical history included treatment for hyperlipidemia (atorvastatin) and hypothyroidism (levothyroxine). She had no history of other respiratory or cardiovascular diseases, drug or food allergies, or seasonal allergies. Her family history was negative for respiratory and cardiovascular diseases. She did not smoke, consume alcohol, or use drugs. She was a housewife with no specific occupational exposures. Her husband, a farmer, passed away from cardiovascular disease 9 years ago.
