She lives on the first floor of a three-story building in Tehran, not near any industrial plants. On physical examination, she was alert. Vital signs were: pulse rate 78/min, respiratory rate 20/min, temperature 37.1°C, and blood pressure 110/75 mmHg. Her body mass index was 35.5 kg/m2. Lung auscultation revealed inspiratory crackles at the bases of both lungs, more pronounced in the right lung, and to a lesser extent in the mid-zones of both lungs. Arterial blood gas analysis showed an O2 saturation of 78%, with other parameters normal. Complete blood count results were: WBC 10900/mm3, RBC 6.66 × 106 ml/mm3, hemoglobin 18.6 g/dl, HCT 58.9%, MCV 88 fl, MCHC 28 pg, Plt 230000/mm3, MPV 8.5 fl, RDW 15.1%, Poly 63.3%, Lymph 28.3%, Mono 4.6%, Eos 3.3%, Baso 0.5%, with slight anisocytosis. Spirometry indicated a severe restrictive pattern (FVC = 1 L, 47.3% of predicted), confirmed by body plethysmography (TLC = 2.97 L, 76% of predicted). Diffusing capacity (DLCO) was decreased (73.9%). There was a significant response to bronchodilator administration, with a 21% and 17.7% increase in FVC and FEV1, respectively. The purified protein derivative (PPD) test for tuberculosis was negative. An exercise stress test was attempted but not completed due to dyspnea. Transthoracic echocardiography results were: PAPs 40 mmHg, LVEF 55%, normal RV size and systolic function, grade 2 diastolic dysfunction, trivial MR, and mild TR. Chest X-ray showed a reticulo-nodular pattern in both lower lung fields, despite a normal chest X-ray 6 months prior.
test_results: Generalized ground glass opacities in both lung fields and hypo-dense areas due to focal emphysema. Multiple lobular, patchily dispersed areas of air trapping throughout pulmonary fields, on expiratory views, mostly accompanied by mosaic perfusion on the corresponding inspiratory phase views. Interlobular septa were unremarkable. Neither bronchiectasis nor bronchiolectasis was noted, on either side. Interlobular and peribronchchovascular interstitium were ordinary depicted. The main pulmonary artery was dilated. Cardiomegaly was depicted.

case_report: A 60-year-old man was brought to the emergency room at Aichi Medical University Hospital from an outpatient clinic due to difficulty breathing the day after receiving the second dose of the BNT162b2 mRNA COVID-19 vaccine (Pfizer/BioNTech). He had no prior history of respiratory or allergic conditions. He was a current smoker with a 40 pack-year history and had not changed cigarette brands. For the past two years, he had been keeping seven budgerigars (Melopsittacus undulatus) and four cockatiels (Nymphicus hollandicus) indoors. He was admitted to the hospital and started on sulbactam ampicillin for suspected pneumonia. His body temperature was 36.3°C, and his partial pressure of arterial oxygen was 68.7 Torr while receiving 2 L/min of oxygen via nasal cannula. Chest high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) revealed bilateral ground glass opacities without nodules or mosaic attenuation. Laboratory tests indicated normal peripheral white blood cell and eosinophil counts, but elevated levels of serum LDH, C-reactive protein (CRP), Kreb von den Lugen-6, and SP-D. Pulmonary function tests showed restrictive changes with reduced diffusing capacity.
test_results: The results of BALF obtained from the B5 right middle lobe (46% of recovery rate) showed elevation of total cell counts (5.27 × 105/mL), eosinophils (37%), and lymphocytes (34%) with a low CD4/CD8 ratio (0.37). No bacterium or fungus was isolated from cultures of BALF. A TBLB specimen obtained from the B8 right lower lobe showed lymphocytic alveolitis without granuloma and eosinophilic infiltration. The serum immunoglobulin (Ig) E level was low, and IgE specific for feathers and droppings of budgerigars were negative. Moreover, tests for autoimmune antibodies were negative.

case_report: A 15-year-old female presented with pain on the left side of the abdomen and extended menstrual bleeding. She had a history of left nephrectomy at the age of 1 year due to a mass lesion, which was reported to be benign. A first-degree relative had a history of metastatic breast cancer at the age of 30 years. Physical examination revealed hirsutism. Imaging revealed a large mass in the left ovary. Surgical removal of the left ovary and fallopian tube was performed, and the specimen included a left ovarian tumor measuring 18 × 14 × 7 cm with a smooth surface.
test_results: Microscopic examination revealed nodular and diffuse growth of tumor cells with ovoid hyperchromatic nuclei, small nucleoli, amphophilic cytoplasm. Macrofollicle and microfollicle formations containing eosinophilic secretions were identified. The tumor cells were positive for steroidogenic factor 1 (SF-1) and inhibin, focally positive for cytokeratin (CK), and negative for SALL4. Reticulin stain highlighted groups/nests of tumor cells. B-catenin showed a positive membranous staining pattern. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging revealed a pelvic mass measuring approximately 4.5 cm in axial diameter, located to the right of the rectum and probably originating from the right ovary. The tumor cells were positive for SF-1, B-catenin (membranous), alpha-inhibin, and calretinin and negative for SALL4, CK7, and epithelial membrane antigen (EMA).

case_report: A 49-year-old woman, P2G2, BMI 37 kg/m2, presented with chronic pelvic pain and a complex right adnexal mass measuring 8.2 cm, monitored over 4 years. She had a history of left salpingo-oophorectomy due to ovarian torsion. Pelvic examination revealed a soft mass in the posterior cul-de-sac, immobile within the pelvis. CA125 levels were normal. The patient was scheduled for laparoscopic evaluation and potential right salpingo-oophorectomy and hysterectomy. During laparoscopy, a normal-sized uterus was found displaced anteriorly by a retroperitoneal soft mass in the cul-de-sac, closely associated with the sacrum and significant blood vessels. The right ovary and tube appeared normal, and the left adnexa were absent. After consulting with a general surgeon, no surgical intervention or biopsy was performed, and further imaging and biopsy under CT guidance were planned. Endometrial curettage showed disordered proliferative endometrium. A month later, a CT scan identified a 9.0 x 6.9 x 6.9 cm complex cystic mass between the anterior rectal wall and the posterior uterus margin. Six weeks later, MRI measured the mass at 7.4 x 5.2 x 8.4 cm, describing it as relatively well-circumscribed, cystic, with some solid components.
test_results: A US guided biopsy was reported as neoplastic tissue, possible sex cord stromal tumour.
Orpha_name: Malignant granulosa cell tumor of the ovary

case_report: A 54-year-old postmenopausal woman with a history of two pregnancies presented with a 6-month history of increasing facial hair growth and a receding hairline, necessitating daily shaving and causing significant scalp hair loss. She reported no vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain, or distension. Physical examination showed hirsutism with a Ferriman-Gallwey score of 13/36, greasy skin, non-atrophic breasts, and clitoromegaly. There were no signs of striae, acne, bruising, or proximal muscle weakness. Laboratory tests revealed a serum follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) level of 1.1 mIU/mL (postmenopausal reference >30 mIU/mL), serum luteinizing hormone (LH) level of 3.2 mIU/mL (postmenopausal reference >30 mIU/mL), and a serum testosterone level of 7.31 ng/mL (normal range 0.4-0.76 ng/mL). The serum dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEA-S) level was <15 μg/dL (normal range 35-430 μg/dL), and serum testosterone after dexamethasone suppression was 6.32 ng/mL (not suppressed). Other hormone levels, including serum prolactin, cortisol, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and human chorionic gonadotrophin, were within normal limits. Tumor marker CA-125 was 0.55 u/mL (reference range 1.9-16.3). Hematological and biochemical parameters were normal. Imaging studies, including transvaginal ultrasound and computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis, showed no ovarian masses. Ovarian venous sampling under radiological guidance indicated that the right ovary was a source of testosterone, although left ovarian vein cannulation was technically challenging and relatively unsuccessful.
test_results: Microscopic sections of both ovaries revealed infiltrating islands and cords of tumor cells exhibiting round to oval nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. There were no features to suggest malignant behavior such as nuclear atypia, hemorrhage, necrosis or increased mitotic activity. Reinke's crystals were not observed. Immunohistochemically, tumor showed intense reactivity to alpha inhibin. Brown-colored pigment was also noted in the cytoplasm.
diagnosis: Bilateral ovarian steroid cell tumor NOS
Orpha_name: Theca steroid-producing cell malignant tumor of ovary, not further specified

case_report: The patient is a 41-year-old female with a medical history that includes depression, obesity, tobacco use, previously treated cervical cancer, and chronic migraines unresponsive to medication. She underwent a bilateral occipital zone release with neurectomy of the lesser occipital nerve and avulsion neurectomy of the third occipital nerve two weeks before admission. A few days before presenting, she experienced nausea, diarrhea, severe headaches, fever, neck stiffness, and burning and irritation at her posterior scalp incisions. Initially, she presented to a community hospital and was started on vancomycin and cefepime. She rapidly developed respiratory insufficiency and hypotension, necessitating emergent intubation and vasopressor support. The patient was then transferred to our facility for advanced care. Upon admission to the surgical intensive care unit, she was in profound septic shock with acute renal and respiratory failure. Purulent discharge was noted from the left cervical incision site, and she exhibited a diffuse, macular, nonblanchable rash, and petechiae over the anterior neck, chest, abdomen, and lower extremities. Laboratory results showed marked leukocytosis (white blood cell count: 25 × 10^9 cells/L), acute renal failure (serum creatinine 3.08 mg/dL, with a baseline of less than 1 mg/dL), and severe metabolic acidosis (pH: 7.09 and bicarbonate: 11 mEq/L) with a significant base deficit (-19). Mean arterial pressures ranged from 40 to 60 mmHg before vasopressor initiation. The incision was opened at the bedside within two hours and debrided, yielding yellow-brown purulent discharge, but no nonviable tissue, fascial dehiscence, or dishwater fluid was observed.
test_results: During this time, the patient's wound cultures grew Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Strep).

case_report: A 47-year-old Caucasian female arrived at the emergency department with a 2-day history of nausea, vomiting, and increasing epigastric pain. She reported experiencing fever with chills, loose stools, and a feeling of abdominal fullness. Her medical history included chronic alcoholism, consuming 6–8 beers daily, but no history of cirrhosis. Upon arrival, her vital signs were blood pressure: 120/88 mmHg, pulse: 80/minute, respiratory rate: 18/minute, temperature: 98.6 ºF, and oxygen saturation: 97% on room air. She appeared in mild distress with slightly jaundiced sclera. Cardiovascular examination was normal. The abdomen was mildly tender in the epigastric region without guarding or rigidity, and hepatomegaly was noted. Central nervous system examination showed no focal deficits. Skin examination revealed no erythematous lesions. Laboratory results were: haemoglobin 14.2 g/dl, leucocyte count 9 × 103/uL, platelets count 143 × 103/uL, glucose 83 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 48 mg/dL, creatinine 2.52 mg/dL, sodium 129 mM/L, potassium 2.9 mM/L, chloride 94 mM/L, bicarbonate 18 mM/L, anion gap 17 mM/L, albumin 2.5 g/dL, total bilirubin 6.3 mg/dL, AST 71 U/L, ALP 66 U/L, ALT 128 U/L, activated PTT 38.1 sec, PT 12.9 sec, and lactic acid 2.8 mM/L. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed severe, circumferential thickening of the gastric wall, involving the distal esophagus and the first part of the duodenum, along with perigastric stranding, consistent with severe gastritis. Mild mucosal thickening of the transverse and descending colon was also noted. The liver was enlarged with fatty infiltration, and there was a small amount of ascites and a small left-sided pleural effusion. No obstruction, perforation, or intra-abdominal abscess was observed. She was admitted to a medical floor and received a 2-litre bolus of intravenous normal saline, maintenance fluids, intravenous antiemetics, and intravenous pantoprazole. Within 8 hours of admission, she became hemodynamically unstable, requiring intubation and fluid resuscitation, and was transferred to the intensive care unit. Due to bright red blood on nasogastric decompression, she was started on intravenous octreotide. Blood cultures were drawn, and she was started on broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics (vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, and levofloxacin) due to hypotension and systemic inflammatory response syndrome with peritoneal ascites.
test_results: Ascitic fluid analysis showed abundant Gram-positive cocci and 51,500 leucocytes/mm3 with 67% neutrophils. Ascitic fluid was exudative in nature with total protein 3.8 g/dl, albumin 1.6 g/dl, lactate dehydrogenase 5189/UL and glucose 56 mg/dl. Serum-albumin ascitic-albumin gradient was 0.9 g/dl.
diagnosis: Streptococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome  with primary Group A Streptococcus  peritonitis

case_report: An 18-year-old woman with a history of haploidentical hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) presented with a palmoplantar erythematous rash and severe mucositis. Twelve days before the consultation, she underwent allogeneic haploidentical HSCT from her younger sister for acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Three days post-transplant, the patient experienced neutropenic fever and persistent diarrhea; intravenous meropenem, teicoplanin, and metronidazole were administered. Blood and urine cultures showed no bacterial growth. Abdominal computed tomography indicated findings consistent with typhlitis. Twelve days post-transplant, she was referred to our clinic with severe mucocutaneous symptoms. Dermatological examination revealed diffuse hemorrhagic-crusted plaques on her lips and neck, along with dusky-edematous plaques on the volar areas.
test_results: A skin biopsy was taken from the neck which showed mild lymphocytic inflammation and vacuolar change at the epidermal-dermal junction, dyskeratosis in basal layer keratinocytes.

case_report: A 51-year-old male Taiwanese patient had kappa-light chain multiple myeloma, Durie-Salmon stage IIIB, identified in February 2012. He underwent multiple cycles of chemotherapy from 2012 to 2016 and received autologous HSCT in 2012 and 2014, achieving partial response. Due to disease progression, he underwent an allogeneic HSCT in December 2016. On day 53 post-allogeneic HSCT, the patient exhibited extensive hyperkeratotic lichenoid folliculocentric papules with perifollicular erythema on the scalp, neck, trunk, and limbs. Dermoscopic examination revealed a diffuse folliculocentric pattern with significant keratin plug formation. Additionally, mottled hyperpigmentation was observed on the face, along with a white lace-like pattern on the buccal mucosae and lips.
test_results: Histological examination of the follicular papules on the left anterior chest wall showed follicular infundibular dilatation with keratotic plugs, basal layer vacuolization, and few apoptotic keratinocytes in the follicular epidermis. Perivascular and perifollicular mononuclear cell infiltration and pigment incontinence in the upper dermis were also seen. Upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy was performed which showed reflux esophagitis, LA Grade A, and duodenal ulcers. Computerized tomography of the abdomen revealed segmental wall thickening at the terminal ileum and proximal ascending colon that was suggestive of ileocolitis. Routine laboratory studies on day 60 following allogeneic HSCT revealed anemia (hemoglobin: 9.1 g/dl), thrombocytopenia (87 × 103/μl), elevated liver transaminases (aspartate aminotransferase, 194 U/l; alanine aminotransferase, 114 U/l), and serum alkaline phosphatase (106 IU/l). However, the total bilirubin level was in the normal range.
diagnosis: Chronic follicular graft-versus-host disease with overlap syndrome

case_report: A 22-year-old woman with a history of thalassemia was referred to our clinic for decreased vision and ocular discomfort. She had received high-dose chemotherapy followed by allogeneic bone marrow transplantation (BMT) and had been prescribed frequent lubricants as well as topical antibiotics at another center. Upon admission, the patient complained of foreign body sensation and painful sore gritty eyes. Corrected visual acuity was 3/10 and 7/10 in the right and left eyes, respectively. Despite aggressive medical and surgical interventions such as topical cyclosporine and steroids, blepharorrhaphy, and upper and lower punctal occlusion, she experienced worsening of the condition followed by further deterioration of vision in her right eye. A significant decrease in tear meniscus, blepharitis and development of superficial corneal vascularization were noted during follow-up. Corneal vascularization progressed and led to corneal perforation.
test_results: Slit lamp examination revealed a small Seidel-positive corneal perforation approximately 1.5 mm × 1 mm in size in her right eye.
diagnosis: Chronic Graft versus Host Disease  leading to severe dry eye and corneal perforation

case_report: Case 3 involved a 2-year-old boy who exhibited hemoptysis. Various clinical tests were conducted to exclude pulmonary tuberculosis and other infectious causes, all of which returned negative results. Two years later, while residing abroad, he was hospitalized twice for pneumonia, which was likely associated with pulmonary hemorrhage as indicated by the initial occurrence of anemia. Hemoptysis reappeared when he was 3 years old.
test_results: Lung biopsy confirmed pulmonary hemosiderosis. Oral milk provocation led to increased sputum and pulmonary infiltrates on the chest radiograph.

case_report: A 4-month-old girl presented with persistent hematochezia starting 10 days after birth, which worsened 4 days prior to examination. She was born at full term without complications and was fed both mother's milk and cow's milk. On physical examination, her height was 59 cm, weight was 4.25 kg, she had a fever of 38.1°C, and her respiratory rate was 70 breaths per minute with rough breath sounds. Her skin appeared pale without rashes, and her tonsils were neither hypertrophic nor inflamed. Laboratory results showed white blood cells at 16.31 (109 cells/L) (normal range: 8–12), with 31% neutrophils, 51% lymphocytes, 13% monocytes (normal range: 3–8), and 6% eosinophils (normal range: 1–5). C-reactive protein was 16 mg/L (normal range: 0–5), red blood cells were 2.44 (1012 cells/L) (normal range: 4–5.5), and hemoglobin was 70 g/L (normal range: 110–160). Immunoglobulin E (IgE) antibodies to cow's milk were negative, and serum total IgE level was 35.5 IU/mL (normal: < 15). Fecal occult blood test was positive. Serum iron concentration was 4.36 mmol/L (normal range: 7.52–11.82). Peripheral blood PO2 was 59 mmHg (<60), and PCO2 was normal, indicating type I respiratory failure.
test_results: Chest roentgenograms showed bilateral infiltrates and opacities in different lung lobes. The CT scan showed interstitial lung disease. She was subjected to gastrointestinal endoscope, revealing chronic superficial gastritis and hyperplasia in the descending colon. The examination showed granulation tissue infiltrated by acute and chronic inflammatory cells, including some eosinophils (at most three per high-power field).

case_report: A 9-month-old Hispanic female with no significant past medical history presented to the emergency room after a choking episode, followed by a brief episode of hypotonia while playing in the park. Physical examination revealed mild respiratory distress with decreased breath sounds in the left hemithorax. Laboratory results indicated iron deficiency anemia, with hemoglobin of 6.9 g/dL, hematocrit of 22.9%, mean corpuscular volume of 68.3 fL, and iron level of 23 mcg/dL; stool guaiac test was positive. Meckel's scan was negative. A chest radiograph showed a large round lucency in the left lower lobe measuring 4.2 cm × 5.3 cm. A CT angiogram of the chest confirmed a large cystic lesion in the left lower lobe with a single septation and no solid component or abnormal vascular supply. Additionally, several small cysts were observed in the ipsilateral upper lobe. The patient underwent left lower lobe segmentectomy and a wedge resection of the left upper lobe. An abdominal ultrasound was performed due to persistent anemia, revealing a small bowel intussusception with an approximately 2.5 × 1.8 × 1.5 cm soft-tissue lesion acting as a leading point. CT enterography confirmed the ultrasound findings. No other abnormalities were detected in both the abdominal ultrasound and CT. The child did not exhibit any intermittent irritability or abdominal distension.
test_results: The histopathological evaluations of the cystic lung lesions showed cysts separated by thin walled septa lined by ciliated columnar respiratory epithelium with subepithelial condensations of mesenchymal tumor cells giving a sarcoma botryoid-like appearance.

case_report: A 7-month-old female infant with an Italian mother and Kurdish father was brought to our Pediatric Department due to rapidly worsening difficulty in breathing, resulting in severe shortness of breath. Initially, respiratory symptoms appeared intermittently during the first 2 to 3 months of life, particularly during upper respiratory tract infections, but progressively increased in duration and severity. These symptoms were later accompanied by a lack of appetite and poor weight gain. Upon admission, the infant exhibited signs of difficulty in breathing and low oxygen levels, requiring a high level of oxygen supplementation (5L/minute) to maintain an oxygen saturation of 95%. Her vital signs included a blood pressure of 50/90mmHg, a heart rate of 135 beats per minute, and a body temperature of 36.5°C. A chest examination revealed an absence of breath sounds in the right side of the chest. Laboratory results showed white blood cells at 19.23×10^3/mm^3 (with 62.6% neutrophils and 27% lymphocytes), hematocrit at 34.5%, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration at 30.7g/dL, platelet count at 695×10^3/mm^3, and reticulocytes at 182×10^9/L. Lower than normal levels were observed for total proteins (5.3g/dL), albumin (2.8g/dL), iron (17μg/dL), immunoglobulin A (30mg/dL), and immunoglobulin G (625mg/dL). Elevated levels were noted for erythrocyte sedimentation rate (44mm/hour) and C-reactive protein (5.05mg/dL; normal range <0.80mg/dL).
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) scanning showed the presence of an enormous mass resulting in the contralateral displacement of her trachea, with total collapse of right lung parenchyma and compression of her chest wall tissues, causing a structural alteration of her 6th right costal arc along the midaxillary line. Enlarged lymph nodes were detected in both in her mediastinum and her right axillary region. On histological examination, there was a myxoid and fibrous-like stroma showing large areas of necrosis. At higher magnification the tumor was constituted by blastomatous areas (containing epithelioid cells) and sarcomatous areas (containing fusiform cells). The growing pattern was fibrosarcomatous dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans-like, with a high mitotic count (30/10 high-power field) and diffused positivity for vimentin; heterogeneous positivity for S-100 protein and focal positivity for CD56 were noticed.

case_report: This 27-year-old male, son of patient 1, was born with clubfoot and had corrective surgery at age seven. Clinodactyly was observed in his left foot, but there was no evidence of pes cavus. He reported experiencing muscle twitching in his thighs following physical exertion. There was no noticeable muscle weakness, and he did not report any sensory issues or other neurological symptoms.
test_results: In the nerve conduction study, the CMAPs of the right common fibular nerve were not evoked, while the sensory nerves were normal. The EMG examination indicated chronic neurogenic changes, and muscles in his limbs and trapezius muscle were affected with increased duration and large amplitude MUPs.

case_report: The patient is a 58-year-old male born to non-consanguineous parents following an uneventful pregnancy and delivery. He had normal developmental milestones but reported difficulty in playing sports since childhood. At 48 years old, he began experiencing weakness in all four limbs, difficulty holding objects, and trouble walking upstairs. By age 55, he reported numbness in both hands and feet, described as a sensation of wearing gloves and socks. The limb muscle weakness progressively worsened, leading to muscle atrophy. He required external assistance for walking and had significant difficulty holding chopsticks and writing. He has a history of diabetes for over twenty years. Neurologic examination revealed severe scapula muscle atrophy with sloping shoulders, and distinct muscle atrophy in the thenar and lower limbs. Muscle strength was 4/5 in elbow extension, 2/5 in finger extension, 2/5 in hip extension, and 0/5 in ankle dorsiflexion bilaterally. Deep tendon reflexes were absent in both upper and lower extremities, and the Babinski sign was not present. Pinprick and vibration sensations were absent in the feet and moderately reduced in the hands. The pyramidal sign was negative. Hearing was normal, and there were no findings of hoarseness, pes cavus, or scoliosis. Laboratory tests showed a creatine kinase level of 56U/L (within normal range), a glucose level of 7.1 mmol/L (slightly elevated), and a glycated hemoglobin level of 7.1% (normal below 5.7%). Echocardiography indicated a thick interventricular septum with normal contraction function.
test_results: Genetic analysis revealed that this patient had a heterozygous c.946C > T mutation in the TRPV4 gene, resulting in amino acid substitutions of arginine to leucine (p.R316C). Sural nerve biopsy: The semi-thin section showed a severe reduction in the density of myelinated fibers. The scattered pseudo-onion bulbs formed by regenerating clusters were visible. Immunohistochemical staining was negative. Ultrastructural examination represented denervated Schwann cell bands, scattered myelinated axons, and numerous unmyelinated fibers regeneration. There were collections of concentric Schwann cell processes that enclosed unmyelinated axons. More or less Schwann cells sprouted within the fields. Electrophysiology presented that the amplitudes of compound muscle action potentials (CMAPs) were reduced in ulnar nerves and were absent in bilateral peroneal nerves. Sensory nerve action potentials (SNAPs) were not evoked in the right median, ulnar, sural or superficial peroneal nerves. Electromyogram (EMG) showed fibrillation and positive sharp waves in partial muscles. Increased duration and large amplitude of motor unit potentials (MUPs) were found in bilateral calf muscles. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) indicated mild atrophy of bilateral thigh muscles. Both quadriceps and biceps femoris muscles were involved, while the semitendinosus muscle was partially spared. The calf muscle was also atrophic with fat infiltration. The brachial plexus was symmetrically hypertrophy and hyperintense.

case_report: A 14-year-old girl presented with difficulty walking and an unstable gait. Her parents, who are first cousins, are healthy, as is her male sibling. She experienced normal psychomotor development until muscle weakness began at age 11. She reported numbness in her lower limbs but had no issues with hearing or vision. Her mother had a normal term delivery following an unremarkable pregnancy, and the patient had normal motor development with no speech delay or cognitive impairment. At age 14, a neurological examination showed normal mental status, language, and memory. There was weakness in the intrinsic muscles of her hands and severe distal weakness in her lower limbs, leading to bilateral foot drop. Muscle atrophy was observed in both upper and lower extremities, more pronounced in the lower limbs. She exhibited an unstable gait and was unable to walk on her toes or heels. Deep tendon reflexes were reduced, and sensation in the lower limbs was slightly diminished. An electrophysiological study revealed chronic demyelinating sensorimotor polyneuropathy with uniform conduction slowing. Motor conduction velocity in the upper extremities ranged from 21-27 m/s but was unobtainable in the lower extremities. Initial screening of the PMP22 gene duplication using the MLPA method excluded CMT1A.
test_results: Whole-exome sequencing in the proband led to the identification of a homozygous likely pathogenic c.19C > T (p. Arg7*) variant in the HK1 gene (NM_001358263.1), which co-segregates in the family. This variant is absent in public genomic databases, while no homozygous loss of function variants along the whole HK1 gene are seen in population databases. It creates a premature translational stop signal (p. Arg7*) in the first coding region of most HK1 isoforms and is predicted to cause loss of normal protein function either through protein truncation or nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. Regarding the consanguineous background of this patient, 280.02 Mb of her chromosomes were in homozygous regions, in which the c.19C > T (p. Arg7*) variant is located in a long 29.64 Mb ROH interval (chr10:51633027-81270173), supporting the causality of this variant in the patient’s phenotype.

case_report: A 20-year-old Japanese male presented with his first episode of cholestasis at age 17. Laboratory results at that time were: serum total bilirubin, 16.0 mg/dL; alkaline phosphatase (ALP), 682 IU/L; GGT activity, 16 IU/L; serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST), 158 IU/L; and alanine aminotransferase (ALT), 518 IU/L. The patient had no history of drug use, toxin ingestion, alcohol abuse, or metabolic conditions. Tests for autoimmune hepatitis and viral hepatitis, including antinuclear antibodies, antimitochondrial antibody, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C virus antibody, cytomegalovirus antibody, and Epstein-Barr virus, were negative. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography indicated a normal intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary tree and pancreatic ductal system. Liver biopsy revealed significant cholestasis in hepatocytes, Kupffer cells, and bile canaliculi, with no lobular inflammation, hepatic necrosis, or fibrosis. Treatment with ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) at 600 mg/day showed intermittent effectiveness initially. The patient was later referred to our hospital for further evaluation and treatment. Serological markers of liver fibrosis were: serum type IV collagen, 237.0 ng/mL and Mac-2 binding protein glycosylation isomer, 0.23. Liver stiffness measured by transient elastography (FibroScan®) was 7.8 kPa. Further pathological and immunohistochemistry studies showed strong expression of bile salt export pump, multidrug resistance protein 3, multidrug resistance-associated protein 2, and CD10 at the canalicular membrane, with well-preserved intralobular bile duct arrangement.
test_results: Targeted next-generation sequencing detected a heterozygous variant of ATP8B1: c.1429 + 2T > G (NM_005603.4).

case_report: A 44-year-old Caucasian male, 183 cm tall and weighing 85 kg (BMI 24.3 kg/m2), presented to the Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation Unit in May 2017 with severe spontaneous pain in the right ankle, without any prior trauma. The patient, an office worker with a sedentary lifestyle and a history of hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and myocardial ischemia treated with PTCA via the right femoral artery in September 2016, was on ramipril (10 mg daily), atorvastatin (40 mg daily), and clopidogrel (75 mg daily). Symptoms began in February 2017, characterized by severe continuous pain, especially at night, along with swelling, tenderness, and bruising of the right ankle and foot. An ankle X-ray at the emergency room showed no fractures. Initial management included the RICE protocol and oral acetaminophen (1000 mg TID for 5 days). Symptoms worsened after one week, prompting an orthopedic consultation and an MRI, which revealed diffuse subcutaneous and peritendinous edema without significant bone or cartilage findings. The patient was then prescribed oral ibuprofen (600 mg BID for 1 week) and local cryotherapy (20 min, 3 times a day), but symptoms persisted. A vascular surgeon's evaluation, including color Doppler ultrasonography and angiography, ruled out venous thrombosis and peripheral arterial disease. Physical examination revealed swelling, erythema, warmth, and sweating in the right ankle and foot, with pain on touch (mechanical allodynia). Both active and passive range of motion of the ankle were painful and limited (dorsal flexion 5 degrees, plantar flexion 15 degrees). Pain was rated 80/100 mm on the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), with poor scores on the Short-Form McGill Pain Questionnaire (SF-MPQ) and Short Form-36 Health Survey (SF-36). The patient required a crutch for walking. Biochemical assessments showed no abnormalities indicative of rheumatologic or inflammatory disorders. Laboratory results included a normal complete blood count (CBC) and serum levels of erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR, 8 mm/h), C-Reactive Protein (CRP, 0.3 mg/L), glucose (72 mg/dL), creatinine (0.96 mg/dL), uric acid (5.0 mg/dL), alkaline phosphatase (80 U/L), calcium (9.4 mg/dL), phosphate (4.3 mg/dL), creatine kinase (68 U/L), and lactic dehydrogenase (177 U/L).
test_results: 99mTc-MDP TPBS showed an intense flow associated with enhanced distribution in blood pool phases and osteoblastic activity at 3 h at the distal tibial epiphysis.
diagnosis: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome Type I
